units.la: RATIANVS Augustus Ambrosio Religioso Sacerdoti omnipotentis Dei. Cupio valde, vt quem recordor absentem, & cum quo mente sum, cum eodem corpore sim praesenti. Festina igitur ad me, Religiose Dei Sacerdos, vt doceas doctrinam veram credentem, non quo contentioni studeam, aut velim magis Deum verbis quam mente complecti, sed vt magis aperto pectore reuelatio Diuinitatis insideat. Docebit enim me ille, quem non nego, quem fateor Deum ac Dominum esse meum, non ei obiiciens, quam in me video, creaturam, qui Christo nihil me addere posse confiteor: velle tamen, vt etiam Patri me commendem Filium praedicando.
units.tr: Gratian Augustus to Ambrose, religious priest of Almighty God. I greatly desire that the one whom I remember as absent, and with whom I am in mind, I may be in person with the same body present. Hasten therefore to me, religious priest of God, that you may teach the true doctrine to one who believes, not because I am eager for contention, or wish to embrace God more in words than in mind, but so that the revelation of the Divinity may settle more openly in my heart. For he will teach me, whom I do not deny, whom I confess to be God and my Lord, not objecting to him the creature I see in myself, I who confess that I can add nothing to Christ: yet I wish that I may also commend myself to the Father by preaching the Son.

units.la: Non ego in Deo verebor inuidiam; non me talem laudatorem putabo, qui Diuinitatem verbis augeam. Ego infirmus & fragilis, quantum possum, praedico; non quantum est ipsa Diuinitas. Rogo te, vt mihi des ipsum tractatum, quem dederas, augendo illic de Spiritu Sancto fidelem disputationem: scripturis atque argumentis Deum esse cuince. Diuinitas te seruet per multos annos, parens & cultor Dei aeterni, quem colimus, Iesu Christi.
units.tr: I shall not, in regard to God, fear envy; nor shall I think myself such a praiser as would enlarge the Divinity with words. I, weak and frail, proclaim as far as I can; not as far as the Divinity itself is. I ask you to give me that same treatise which you had given, enlarging there upon the Holy Spirit in a faithful disputation: prove by the Scriptures and by arguments that God is. May the Divinity preserve you for many years, parent and worshipper of the eternal God, whom we worship, Jesus Christ.

units.la: Carissimo Augusto Graciano, & Christianissimo Principi Ambrosius Episcopus. Non mihi affectus defuit, Christianissime Principum. Nihil enim habeo, quod hoc verius & gloriosius dicam. Non, inquam, mihi affectus defuit, sed effectum verecundia retardauit, quo minus Clementiae tuae occurrerem. Reuertenti tamen si non occurri vestigio, occurri animo, occurri voto, in quo maiora sunt officia Sacerdotis. Occurri, dico. Quando enim abfui, quem toto sequebar affectu; cui sensu ac mentibus inhaerebam? Et certe maior animorum praesentia est; tuum quotidianum iter legebam, nocte ac die in tuis castris cura & sensu locatus, orationum exuuias praetendebam, etsi inanidus merito, sed affectu sedulus. Et haec quidem cum pro tua salute deferebamus, pro nobis faciebamus. Nihil hic adulationis est, quam tu non requiris, ego alienam nostro ducō officio; sed plurimum gratiae quam dedisti. Scit ipse nostri arbiter, quem fateris, & in quem pie credis, refici viscera mea tua fide, tua salute, tua gloria, neque non solum officio publico debitas pendere praeces, sed etiam amore priuato. Reddidisti enim mihi quietem Ecclesiae, perfidorum ora, atq; (quod vinam) & corda clausisti, & hoc non minore fidei, quam potestatis authoritate fecisti. Nam quid de literis recentibus loquar? Scripsisti tua totam epistolam manu, vt ipsi apices fidem tuam pietatemq; loquentur. Sic Abraham sua manu quondam vitulum occidit, vt hospitibus epulantibus ministraret, nec in ministerio religioso aliorum adiumenta quaesiuit. Sed ille priuatus aut Domino & Angelis aut Domino in Angelis deferebat: tu Imperator dignatione Regali honoras infirmum Sacerdotem. Sed Domino defertur, cum seruulus honoratur. Ipse enim dixit: Quod uni horum minimorum fecistis, mihi fecistis. Ateo humilitatem tantummodo praedico in Imperatore sublimem, ac non amplius fidem, quam vere conscius meriti tui mente dixisti, quam docet te ille, quem non negas. Quis enim nihil alius docere te potuit, vt ei obiicias, quam in te vides, creaturam? Nihil moralius, nihil expressius dici potuit. Creaturam enim Christum dicere, pro obiectu contumeliae est, non pro consessione reuerentiae. Deinde quid tam insolens, quam id eum existimare, quod nos sumus? Docuisti igitur me, à quo te discere velle profiteris: nihil tale adhuc legi, nihil audiui. Quam pium autem illud, quam admirabile, quod in Deo non vereris inuidiam? De Patre remuneratione pro Filii amore praesumis, & laudando filium, non ei te posse aliquid addere confiteris, sed velle vt etiam Patri te Filii praedicatione, commendes. Quod vtique solus te docuit ille, qui dixit: Qui me diligit, diligetur à patre meo. Addidisti ad haec, quia tu infirmus & fragilis non te talem laudatorem putabis, vt diuinitatem verbis augeas, sed quantum possis, praedices, non quantum est ipsa diuinitas. Haec infirmitas in Christo fortior est, sicut & Apostolus dixit: Cum infirmor, tunc potens sum, haec humilitas excludit fragilitatem. Veniam plane, & festinabo, vt iubes, vt haec praesens audiam, cum ex tuo ore procedunt. Misi autem duos libellos, quorum iam quia tuae Clementiae sunt probati, periculum non verebor. De Spiritu vero interim veniam scriptioni peto, quoniam quem iudicem mei sim sermonis habiturus agnoui. Interim tamen sententia & fides tua de Domino & Saluatore deprompta de Dei filio redundat ad assertionem uberrimam, per quam Sancti quoque Spiritus diuinitas sempiterna credatur, vt non ei obiicias, quam in te vides, creaturam, nec Deum Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi Spiritu suo existimes inuidere. Quod enim creaturae caret communione, diuinum est. Si Dominus fauerit, huic etiam Clementiae tuae satisfaciam voluntati, vt cuius accepisti gratiam, eum plane in Dei gloria praeminentem suo nomine existimes honorandum. Beatissimum te & florentissimum Deus omnipotens, Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, tueri aetate prolixa, & Regnum tuum in summa gloria & pace perpetua confirmare dignetur, Domine Imperator Auguste, diuino electe iudicio, Principum gloriosissime.
units.tr: To the most beloved Emperor Gratian, and most Christian Prince, Ambrose the Bishop. Affection was not lacking to me, most Christian of Princes. For I have nothing I could say more truly or more gloriously than this. I say again, affection was not lacking to me; but modesty held back the effect, so that I did not come to meet your Clemency. Yet although I did not meet you on your return with my feet, I met you in spirit, I met you in prayer, in which the duties of a priest are greater. I say, I met you. For when I was absent, whom did I follow with my whole affection? To whom did my mind and feeling cling? And certainly the presence of minds is greater: I read over your daily journey, and night and day, my care and feeling were fixed in your camp; I put forward the spoils of prayers, though deservedly empty, yet zealous in affection. And indeed, while we offered these things for your salvation, we were doing them for ourselves. There is nothing of flattery here, which you do not seek; I count it foreign to our office. But I count as very great the grace which you have given. Our judge, whom you acknowledge and in whom you piously believe, knows that my heart is refreshed by your faith, your salvation, your glory; and that prayers are owed not only by public duty but also by private love. For you have restored to me the peace of the Church, you have closed the mouths of the faithless and (would that it were so) their hearts too, and you have done this by no less authority of faith than of power. For why should I speak of your recent letter? You wrote your whole letter with your own hand, so that the very letters might speak of your faith and piety. Thus Abraham once killed a calf with his own hand, to serve his guests at their feast, and in a religious ministry he did not seek the help of others. But he, a private man, offered it to the Lord and to the Angels, or to the Lord among the Angels; you, an Emperor, honour a weak priest with royal condescension. But when a little servant is honoured, it is offered to the Lord: for he himself said: "What you did to one of these least, you did to me." I do not merely proclaim humility, exalted in the Emperor; nor more faith than you spoke with a mind truly conscious of your merit, which he teaches you, whom you do not deny. For who could teach you to object to him nothing else than what you see in him, a creature? Nothing more foolish, nothing more explicit could be said. For to call Christ a creature is an object of insult, not a confession of reverence. Next, what is so outrageous as to think of him as what we ourselves are? You have therefore taught me, from whom you profess you wish to learn: I have not yet read or heard anything like this. How pious, however, and how admirable is that which you do not fear envy in God! You presume upon the Father's reward for the Son's love, and in praising the Son you confess that you cannot add anything to him, but wish to commend yourself also to the Father through the proclamation of the Son. This surely only he taught you who said: "He who loves me will be loved by my Father." You added besides that, since you are weak and frail, you would not think yourself such a praiser as to increase the divinity with words, but you proclaim what you can, not what the divinity itself is. This weakness is stronger in Christ, just as the Apostle also said: "When I am weak, then I am strong"; this humility excludes frailty. I will indeed come, and I will hasten, as you bid, so that I may hear these things present, when they proceed from your mouth. I have sent two little books, which, since they have already been approved by your Clemency, I will not fear the risk. Concerning the Spirit, however, meanwhile I ask pardon for the writing, since I have recognised whom I am to have as judge of my discourse. Meanwhile, however, your opinion and faith, drawn from the Lord and Saviour concerning the Son of God, flows over into a most abundant assertion, through which the eternal divinity of the Holy Spirit also is believed, so that you do not object to him, as you see in yourself, a creature, nor think that God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ envies him his Spirit. For what lacks fellowship with the creature is divine. If the Lord favours it, I will also satisfy your Clemency's wish in this matter, so that, since you have received grace from him, you may judge that he, eminent in the glory of God, is to be honoured by his own name. May Almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, deign to keep you most blessed and most prosperous through a long age, and to confirm your kingdom in highest glory and perpetual peace, Lord Emperor Augustus, chosen by divine judgment, most glorious of Princes.

units.la: EPISTOLA XXVII.
units.tr: EPISTLE XXVII.

units.la: Diui Ambrosii ad Valentinianum Imperatorem, Legationis suae expositionem insinuantis.
units.tr: The Letter of St Ambrose to the Emperor Valentinian, setting out an account of his embassy.

units.la: VALENTINIANO Imperatori Augustissimo Ambrosius. Etsi superioris Legationis meae fides ita approbata sit tibi, vt ratio eius à me non quaereretur. Satis enim claruit eo ipso, quod aliquot dies retentus sum intra Gallias, me violentiam à Maximo non recepisse, neque iis astipulatum quae ad voluntatem eius magis, quam ad pacem protenderent, denique non commisisses secundam legationem, nisi primam probasses, quia tamen regredienti, mihi decernendi securum imposuit necessitatem, ideo hac epistola expositionem legationis meae insinuandam putaui, ne cuiusquam sermo veris prius vana intexeret, quam reditus meus integra & syncerae veritatis expressa signaculo manifestaret. Cum peruenissem Treuiros, postridie processi ad palatium. Egressus est ad me vir Gallicanus praepositus cubiculi, eunuchus regius. Popoposci adeundi copiam, quasi uit num rescriptum haberem clementiae tuae. Respondi, habere. Retulit, non posse me, nisi in consistorio videri. Dixi non esse hunc morem Sacerdotalem, certe esse aliqua de quibus serio deberem cum suo principe confabulari. Quid plura? Consuluit eum, sed eadem referenda credidit, vt liqueret etiam priora ex illius arbitrio deprompta. Dixi tamen alienum id quidem à nostro munere, sed me recepto officio non defuturum, gratiam mihi esse humilitatem in tuo praesertim, & quod verum est, fraternae pietatis negocio. Vbi sedit in consistorio, ingressus sum, assurrexit vt osculum daret. Ego inter consistorianos steti. Hortari coeperunt alii vt ascenderem, vocare ille. Respondi ego: Quid osculasimilis eum quem non agnoueris? Si enim me agnouisses, non hoc loco videres. Commotus es, inquit, episcope? Non, inquam, iniuria, sed verecundia: quod alieno consisto loco. Et prima, inquit, legatione ingressus es consistorium. Nec illud, inquam, mei erroris fuit: vocantis non ingredientis vitium est. Cur, inquit, ingressus es? Quia, inquam, tunc inferiori pacem petebam, tunc vt aequali. Cuius, inquit, beneficio aequali? Respondi, omnipotentis Dei, qui Valentiniano regnum quod dederat reseruauit. Ad postremum erupit, dicens: Quoniam me lusisti, & ille Bauto qui sibi regnum sub specie pueri vindicare voluit: qui etiam Barbaros mihi immisit, quasi ego non habeam quos possim adducere, cum mihi tot millia Barbarorum militent, & annonas à me accipiant. Quod si ego tunc temporis quando venisti non fuissem retentus, quis mihi obstitisset & virtuti meae? Ad haec ego leniter: Non opus est, inquam, vt commoueris, cum causa nulla sit commotionis, sed patienter audias quae referantur istis. Propterea & ego veni, quia prima legatione dum mihi credis, per me deceptum te esse adsereebas: Gloriosum mihi est hoc pro salute pupilli Imperatoris. Quos enim Episcopi magis, quam pupillos debemus tueri? Scriptum est enim: Iudicate pupillo, & iustificate viduam, & eruite iniuriam accipientem. Et alibi: Iudices viduarum, & patres orphanorum. Tamen non exprobrabo beneficium meum Valentiniano. Vt verum eloquar, vbi ego tuis legionibus obstiti, quo minus influeres in Italiam? Quibus rupibus? qua acie? quibus numeris? An vero corpore meo clausi tibi Alpes? Vtinam hoc meum esset, obiectionem non timerem, non vererer criminationes tuas. Quibus promissis lusi te vt paci acquiescere s? Nonne intra Gallias iuxta vrbem Mogontiacum Comes Victor occurrit mihi quem direxisti vt pacem rogaret? In quo ergo te fefellit Valentinianus, qui prius pacem a te rogatus est, quam postularet? In quo fefellit Bauto qui devotionem Imperatori exhibuit suo? An quia principem suum non prodidit? In quo ego te circumscripsi? Qui vbi primum veni, cum diceres quod Valentinianus ad te quasi filius ad patrem venire deberet, responderim non esse aequum vt aspero hyemis tempore puer cum matre vidua penetraret Alpes: sine matre autem tanto itinere dubiis rebus committeretur. De pace nobis legationem commissam, non de aduentu eius promissionem: spondere nos id non potuisse, certum est, quod mandatum non erat, me certe nihil spospondisse, adeo vt diceres: Expectemus quid Victor responsi referat. Illud autem liquet me retento peruenisse Mediolanum, negatumque ei quod postulabat. De pace tantum conspirare studia, non de aduentu Imperatoris quem moueri non oporteret. Praesens eram vbi Victor rediit. Quomodo ergo reuocaui Valentinianum? Legati iterum missi ad Gallias, qui eis aduentum negarent, apud Valentiam Gallorum me reperierunt: milites vtriusque partis qui custodirent iuga montium, offendi reuertens. Quos ergo tuos reuocaui exercitus? quas de Italia reflexi aquilas? quos immisit Barbaros Bauto Comes? Et quid mirum si hoc Bauto fecisset, Transrhenanus genere, cum tu militeris Imperio Romano Barbarorum auxilia, & turmas translimitaneas, quibus commeatus provincialium tributa soluebant. Vide autem quid interfit inter tuas minitationes, & Valentiniani Augusti pueri mansuetudinem. Tu flagitabas, quod Barbarorum stipatus agminibus Italiae te infunderes, Valentinianus Hunnos atque Alanos appropinquantes Galliae per Alemanniae terras reflexit. Quid habet inuidiae, si Bauto Barbaros cum Barbaris fecit decernere? Quoniam dum tu militem Romanum occupas, dum is aduersum se, vtrinque praetendit, in medio Romanii imperii sinu Iuthungi populabantur Rhetias. Et ideo aduersus Iuthungum Hunnus accitus est. Idem tamen, quia de finitimo proterebat Alemanniam, & iam vicinia mali vrgebat Gallias, coactus est triumphos suos deserere, ne tu timeres. Cofer vtriusque factum. Tu fecisti incursari Rhetias. Valentinianus suo tibi auro pacem redemit. Aspice illum quoque qui tibi ad dextram assistit, quem Valentinianus cum posset suum dolorem vlcisci, honoratum ad te redire fecit. Tenebat eum in suis terris, atque in ipso nuncio necis fraternae transauit impetus: nec tibi vicem etsi non parilis dignitatis, eiusdem tamen necessitudinis retulit. Confer ergo te iudice vtriusque factum. Ille tibi fratrem tuum viuentem remisit, tu illi vel mortuum redde. Quid illi reliquias germani abnegas, qui tibi aduersum se auxilia non negauit? Sed vereris ne exuuiarum reditu renouetur militibus dolor. Hoc enim allegas: Quem viuentem deseruerunt, eum defendent peremptum. Quid eum mortuum times, quem occidisti cum posses seruare? Hostem, inquis, meum peremi. Non ille tuus hostis, sed tu illius. Ille iam non sentit defensionem. Tuam causam consideria. Si quis aduersum te hodie imperium in his partibus vsurpandum putet, quaero vtrum te hostem illius dicas, an illum tibi? Nisi fallor, vsurpator bellum infert: Imperator ius suum tuetur. Ergo quem non debueras occidere, eius reliquias negas? Habeat Valentinianus Imperator vel fratris exuuias, pacis tuae obsides. Et quomodo allegabas quod eum non mandaueris occidi, quem prohibes sepeliri? Poterit igitur credi quod ei non inuideris vitam, cui etiam sepulturam inuides? sed ad me reuertar. Audio te queri quod se ad Theodosium Imperatorem potius contulerint qui sunt cum Valentiniano Imperatore. Quid igitur futurum sperabas, cum te refugientes eos ad poenam posceres, captos necares, Theodosias autem muneribus ditaret, donaret honoribus? Quos, inquit, occidi? Respondi ei, Balionem. At quem virum? qualem bellatorem? Haeccine fuit iusta causa exitii, quod Imperatori suo fidem seruauit? Non ego, inquit, cum iussi occidi. Respondi. Hoc audiuimus quod occidi iussus sit. Sed, inquit, si ipse sibi vim non intulisset, iusseram eum deduci Cabillonem & ibi viuum exuri. Respondi: Ergo propterea & illud creditum est quod eum occideris. Quis autem sibi parcendum putaret, cum occisus sit bellator strenuus, miles fidelis, comes vtilis? Ita dum discessi, vt se tractaturum diceret. Postea cum videret me abstinere ab episcopis qui communicabant ei, vel qui aliquos deuios licet a fide, ad necem petebant, commotus eis iussit me sine mora regredi. Ego vero libenter, etsi me plerique insidias quasurum non crederent, ingressus sum iter, hoc solo dolore percitus, quod Hyginum episcopum senem in exilium duci comperi, cui nihil iam nisi extremus superesset spiritus. Cum de eo conuenirem comites eius, ne sine veste, sine plumario paterentur extrudi senem, extrusus ipse sum. Haec est expositio legationis meae. Vale Imperator, & esto tutior aduersus hominem, pacis inuolucro bellum tegentem.
units.tr: Ambrose to Valentinian, the most august Emperor. My earlier embassy was so well approved by you that no account of it was asked of me. Indeed it was made clear by the very fact that I was detained for some days inside Gaul, that I had not received violence from Maximus, nor had I agreed to those terms which tended more to his wishes than to peace. Finally, you would not have sent a second embassy unless you had approved the first. Yet because, on my return, I was placed under the necessity of not deciding anything on my own authority, I have thought it best to set out an account of my embassy in this letter. This is so that no one's talk may weave empty fictions around the truth before my return reveals the facts, unimpaired and stamped with the seal of pure truth. When I had reached Trier, I went to the palace the next day. The Gallic man, the chamberlain, a royal eunuch, came out to meet me. I asked for an audience, as if to learn whether I had a rescript from your Clemency. I replied that I had one. He reported that I could not be seen except in the consistory. I said that this was not the custom for a bishop, and that there were certainly some matters which I ought to discuss seriously with his prince. What more is there to say? He consulted the Emperor, but he thought the same things had to be reported to him, so that it would be clear that even the earlier points had been drawn from the Emperor's own judgment. I said that this was indeed foreign to my office, but that I would not fail in my duty once I had received it, since I found favour in your humility, especially in a matter of brotherly devotion, as is true. When he sat in the consistory, I went in, and he rose to give me a kiss. I stood among the members of the consistory. Others began to urge me to come up, and he began to call me. I replied: "Why would you kiss a man you have not recognised? For if you had recognised me, you would not see me in this place." "Are you upset, bishop?" he said. "No," I said, "not from offence but from modesty, because I am standing in a place not my own." "But you entered the consistory on your first embassy too," he said. "That was not my error either," I said. "The fault lies with the one who calls, not with the one who enters." "Why did you enter?" he said. "Because," I said, "then I was seeking peace as an inferior, now as an equal." "Equal by whose favour?" he said. I replied: "By the favour of Almighty God, who kept for Valentinian the kingdom that he had given." At last he burst out, saying: "Since you have mocked me, and that Bauto too, who wanted to claim the kingdom under the pretext of a boy; and he has sent Barbarians against me, as if I did not have people I could bring up, when so many thousands of Barbarians serve me as soldiers and receive their rations from me. But if I had not been detained when you came, who would have stood in the way of my valour?" To this I replied gently: "There is no need for you to be disturbed, since there is no cause for disturbance, but listen patiently to what is reported to you. For I too have come for this reason: because you asserted that you had been deceived by me during the first embassy, while you believed me. It is a glorious thing for me to do this for the safety of the boy Emperor. For whom ought we bishops to protect more than orphans? For it is written: Judge the fatherless, and do justice to the widow, and rescue the one who suffers wrong. And elsewhere: Judges of widows, and fathers of orphans. Yet I will not reproach Valentinian with my service. To speak the truth, when did I stand in the way of your legions, so that you could not flow into Italy? By what cliffs? By what battle line? With what numbers? Did I, with my own body, shut the Alps against you? If only this were mine, I would not fear your objection, nor dread your accusations. By what promises did I deceive you into accepting peace? Did not Count Victor, whom you sent to ask for peace, meet me in Gaul near the city of Mainz? In what, then, did Valentinian deceive you, when he was asked for peace by you before he demanded it? In what did Bauto deceive you, who showed devotion to his Emperor? Was it because he did not betray his prince? In what did I circumvent you? When I came first, and you said that Valentinian ought to come to you as a son comes to his father, I replied that it was not fair for a boy with his widowed mother to cross the Alps in the harsh winter season; and without his mother he would be entrusted to so long a journey in uncertain conditions. We were given a commission about peace, not a promise about his coming. It is certain that we could not promise that, since it was not in our instructions, and I certainly promised nothing, so much so that you said: 'Let us wait to see what answer Victor brings back.' But it is clear that I arrived at Milan while still detained, and that what he asked was refused him. Our efforts were united only about peace, not about the Emperor's coming, which ought not to have been pressed. I was present when Victor returned. How, then, did I recall Valentinian? Envoys sent again to Gaul, to refuse his coming, found me at Valence in Gaul. On my return, I met soldiers of both parties guarding the mountain passes. Which armies of yours, then, did I recall? Which eagles did I turn back from Italy? Which Barbarians did Count Bauto send in? And what wonder if Bauto did this, being by birth a Transrhenane, when you use barbarian auxiliaries and squadrons from beyond the frontier in the Roman Empire, whose supplies the taxes of the provinces paid for? But see what difference there is between your threats and the gentleness of the boy Augustus Valentinian. You demanded that you should pour yourself into Italy surrounded by Barbarian troops; Valentinian turned back the Huns and Alans, who were approaching Gaul, through the lands of Alemannia. What odium is there if Bauto made Barbarians fight Barbarians? While you occupy Roman soldiers, while the enemy stretches out on both sides against itself, the Iuthungi were ravaging Raetia in the very bosom of the Roman Empire. And for this reason a Hun was summoned against the Iuthungi. Yet the same man, because he was trampling Alemannia on the neighbouring border, and because the proximity of evil was pressing upon Gaul, was compelled to abandon his triumphs, lest you be afraid. Compare the deeds of each. You caused Raetia to be raided. Valentinian bought peace from you with his own gold. Look also at the man who stands at your right hand, whom Valentinian, though he could have avenged his own grief, sent back to you with honour. He held him in his own lands, and the impulse of the news of his brother's death passed over him; nor did he repay you in kind, though of unequal rank, yet of the same kinship. Compare, then, with yourself as judge, the deeds of each. He sent back your brother to you alive; you, return his to him, even dead. Why do you deny him the remains of his brother, when he did not deny you help against himself? But you fear that the return of the corpse would renew the grief of the soldiers. For you argue this: Those who deserted him alive will defend him dead. Why do you fear him dead, whom you killed when you could have saved him? 'I killed my enemy,' you say. He was not your enemy, but you were his. He no longer feels any defence. Consider your own cause. If anyone today thinks an empire should be seized in these parts, I ask whether you call him your enemy, or whether he calls you his? Unless I am mistaken, the usurper makes war; the Emperor defends his right. Therefore, do you deny the remains of the man you ought not to have killed? Let the Emperor Valentinian have at least his brother's remains, as hostages for your peace. And how did you argue that you had not ordered him killed, when you forbid him to be buried? Can it then be believed that you did not begrudge him life, when you begrudge him burial? But I will return to my own affairs. I hear that you complain that those who are with Emperor Valentinian have betaken themselves to Emperor Theodosius rather than to you. What, then, did you hope would happen, when you demanded that those who fled from you be punished, and that they be seized and killed, while you enriched the Theodosians with gifts and honoured them with offices? 'Whom,' he said, 'did I kill?' I replied: 'Bauto.' 'But what kind of man? What sort of warrior?' Was this a just cause for destruction, that he kept faith with his Emperor? 'I did not,' he said, 'order him killed.' I replied: 'We have heard that he was killed on your orders.' 'But,' he said, 'if he had not laid violence on himself, I would have ordered him taken to Cabillonum and burned alive there.' I replied: 'Then it is also believed that you killed him.' But who would think he should be spared, when a vigorous warrior, a faithful soldier, a useful count has been killed? So, while I departed, he said he would deal with the matter. Afterwards, when he saw me refusing to act against the bishops who were in communion with him, or who sought the death of some who had strayed, though only from the faith, he was moved and ordered me to return without delay. I went, and gladly, though most people did not think I was going to escape a trap; I set out on my journey, moved by this one grief only, that I learned that the aged bishop Hyginus was being led into exile, though nothing but his last breath was left to him. When I spoke with his companions about him, lest the old man be thrust out without clothing or a feather bed, I myself was thrust out. This is the account of my embassy. Farewell, Emperor, and be more wary of a man who covers war with the cloak of peace.

units.la: Vale.
units.tr: Farewell.

units.la: EPISTOLA XXVIII.
units.tr: EPISTLE XXVIII.

units.la: Divi Ambrosii ad Theodosium Imperatorem, seipsum excusantis, &, ut ille facinoris sui poenitentiam agat, rationibus atque exemplis suadentis, rogantis, hortantis, & admonentis.
units.tr: Of St. Ambrose to the Emperor Theodosius, excusing himself, and urging, asking, exhorting, and admonishing him, by reasons and examples, that he should do penance for his crime.

units.la: AVGVSTISSIMO Imperatori Theodosio Ambrosius. Et veteris amicitiae dulcis mihi recordatio est, & beneficiorum quae crebris meis intercessionibus summa gratia in alios contulisti, gratiae memini. Unde colligi potest quod non ingrato aliquo affectu adventum tuum semper mihi ante hac exoptatissimum declinare potuerim. Sed qua causa hoc fecerim, breviter expediam. Sol i mihi in tuo comitatu ius naturae ereptum videbam audiendi, ut & loquendi priuarer munere. Motus enim frequenter es quod ad me pervenissent aliqua quae in consistorio tuo statuta forent. Ego ergo expers communis usum sum, cum dicat dominus Iesus nihil esse occultum, quod non manifestetur? Verecundia igitur quod potui, satisfeci imperiali arbitrio, & prospexi ne aut ipse causam commotionis habeas, cum id egerim, ne quid ad me de imperialibus deferatur statutis: aut ego cum fuero praesens, aut non audiam per metum omnium, & quasi conniuentis famam subibo: aut ita audiam ut mihi aures pateant, vox intercludatur, ut audita non possim eloqui, ne eos qui in suspicionem proditionis venerint, laedam in periculo. Quid igitur facerem? Non audirem? Sed aures non possum cera veterum fabularum claudere. Proderem? Sed quod in tuis iussis timerem, in meis verbis deberem cauere, ne quid cruentum committeretur. Tacerem? Sed quod miserrimum foret omnium, alligaretur conscientia, vox eriperetur. Et vbi illud: Sed si Sacerdos non dixerit erranti, is qui erraverit, in sua culpa moritur, & Sacerdos reus erit poenae, quia non admonuit errantem? Accipe illud Imperator Auguste. Quod habeas fidei studium, non possum negare: quod Dei timorem, non diffiteor. Sed habes naturae impetum, quem si quis lenire velit, cito vertes ad misericordiam: si quis stimulet, in maius exsuscitas, ut eum revocare vix possis. Vtinam si nemo mitigat, nullus accendat, libenter enim committo tibi: ipse te revocas, & pietatis studio vincis impetum naturae. Hunc ego impetum malui cogitationibus tuis secreto committere, quam meis factis publice fortassis movere. Itaque malui officio meo aliquid deesse quam humilitati, & requiri in me ab aliis Sacerdotis authoritatem, quam a te desiderari in me, amantissimi honorificentiam, ut repressio impetu integra esset consilii eligendi facultas. Praetendi aegritudinem corporis reuera grauem, & nisi a viris mitioribus vix leuandam: vel emori tamen maluisem quam adventum tuum biduo aut triduo non expectarem. Sed quid facerem, non erat. Factum est in vrbe Thessalonicensium, quod nulla memoria habet, quod revocare non potui ne fieret. Imo quod ante atrocissimum fore dixi, cum totiens rogarem: & quod ipse sero revocando graue factum putasti, hoc factum extenuare non poteram. Quando primum auditum est, quum propter euentum Gallorum episcoporum synodus convenerat, nemo non ingemuit, nullus mediocriter accepit, non erat facti tui absolutio in Ambrosii communione. In me etiam amplius commissi exaggeratut inuidia, si nemo diceret Dei nostri reconciliationem fore necessariam. An pudet te Imperator hoc facere quod rex Propheta author Christi secundum carnem prosapiae fecit Dauid? Illi dictum est, quia diues qui haberet plurimos greges, vnam pauperis ouem propter aduentum hospitis eripuit & occidit: & cognito quod in hoc ipse argueretur, quia ipse fecisset, ait: Peccaui Domino. Noli ergo impatienter ferre, Imperator, si dicatur tibi: Tu fecisti istud, quod Dauid regi dictum est a propheta. Si enim hoc sedulo audieris, & dixeris: peccaui Domine, si dixeris regale illud propheticum: Venite adoremus, & procidamus ante eum, & ploremus ante Dominum nostrum qui fecit nos: dicetur & tibi, Quoniam paenitet te, dimittit tibi Dominus peccatum tuum; & non morieris. Iterum cum plebem numerari iussisset Dauid, percussus est corde, & dixit ad Dominum: Peccaui vehementer quod fecerim hoc verbum, & nunc Domine aufer iniquitatem serui tui quod deliqui vehementer. Et missus est iterum ad eum Nathan propheta, qui ei trium optionem conditionum offerret, & quam vellet eligeret, famem tribus annis in terra, aut tribus mensibus fugeret a facie inimicorum suorum, aut triduo mortem in terra. Et respondit Dauid: Angustia sunt tria haec vehementer, vetuntamen incidam in manum Domini, quoniam multa misericordia eius nimis, & in manus hominis non incidam. Culpa autem erat, quoniam voluit scire numerum totius plebis quae secum erat: quod scire Deo soli debuit reseruare. Et cum, inquit, mors fieret in plebes, ipso primo die ad horam prandii cum vidisset Dauid percutientem angelum in plebem, ait Dauid: Ego peccaui, & ego pastor malignum feci, & hic grex quid fecit? Fiat manus tua in me, & in domum patris mei. Itaque poenituit Dominum, & iussit angelo vt parceret plebi; sacrificium autem offerret Dauid. Erant enim tunc sacrificia pro delictis; haec nunc sunt sacrificia poenitentiae. Itaque ea humilitate acceptior Deo factus est. Non enim mirandum peccare hominem, sed illud reprehensibile, si non se cognoscat errasse, non humiliter Deo. Iob sanctus & ipse potens in seculo, ait: Peccatum meum non abscondi, sed coram plebe omni annuncian. Ipsi inimani regi Saul dixit Ionathas filius suus: Noli peccare in seruum tuum Dauid. Et, ut quid peccas in sanguinem innocentem, occidere Dauid sine causa? Quia etsi rex erat, peccabat tamen si occideret innocentem. Denique etiam Dauid cum iam regno potiretur, & audisset Abner innocentem occisum a Ioab duce militiae suae, ait; Innocens sum ego & regnum meum usque & usque in aeternum a sanguine Abner filii Ner, & ieiunauit in dolore. Haec ideo scripsi, non ut te confundam, sed ut regum exempla provocerat, ut tollas hoc peccatum de regno tuo. Tolles autem humiliando Deo animam tuam. Homo es, & tibi venit tentatio, vincere eam. Peccatum non tollitur nisi lachrymis & poenitentia. Nec angelus potest, nec archangelus: Dominus ipse, qui solus potest dicere: Ego vobiscum sum, si peccaverimus, nisi poenitentiam deserentibus non relaxat. Suadeo, rogo, hortor, admoneo, quia dolori est mihi, ut tu qui pietatis inauditae exemplum eras, qui apicem clementiae tenebas, qui singulos nocentes non pati debuisti periclitari, tot periisse non doleas innocentes. Etsi in praeliis felicissime egeris, & si in aliis quoque laudabilis, tamen apex tuorum operum pietatis semper fuit. Id tibi innidit diabolus quod habebas praestantissimum. Vince cum dum habes adhuc unde possis vincere. Noli peccato tuo aliud peccatum addere, ut usurpes quod usurpasse multis officit. Ego certe in omnibus aliis licet debitor pietati tuae, cui ingratus esse non possum, quam pietatem multis Imperatoribus praeferebam, uni adaequabam, ego, inquam, causam in te contumaciae nullam habeo, sed habeo timoris. Offerre non audeo sacrificium, si volueris assistere. An quod in unius innocentis sanguine non licet, in multorum licet? Non puto. Postremo scribo manu mea quod solus legas. Ita me Dominus ab omnibus tribulationibus liberet, quia non ab homine, neque per hominem, sed aperte mihi interdictum aduerti. Cum enim essem solicitus, ipsa nocte qua proficisci parabam, venisse quidem visus es ad ecclesiam, sed mihi sacrificium offerre non licuit. Alia praetereo, ut potui cauere. Sed pertuli amore tuo, ut arbitror. Dominus faciat ut omnia cum tranquillitate cedant. Multifarie Deus noster admonet: signis caelestibus, Prophetarum praeceptis, visionibus etiam peccatorum vult nos intelligere, quo rogamus eum ut perturbationes auferat, pacem nobis imperantibus seruet, fides ecclesiae & tranquillitas perseueret, cui prodest Christianos & pios esse Imperatores. Certe vis probari Deo, omnis rei tempus, ut scriptum est, Tempus, inquit, faciendi domine: Et tempus beneplaciti Deus. Tunc offerres, cum sacrificandi acceperis facultatem, quando hostia tua accepta sit Deo. Nonne tu deberes habere gratiam Imperatoris, ut secundum voluntatem tuam agerem, si causa pateretur? Et simplex oratio sacrificium est. Haec veniam refert, illa offensionem: quia haec humilitatem, illa contemptum. Dei enim vox est quod malit ut fiat mandatum eius, quam deferatur sacrificium. Clamat illud Deus, ad populum Moyses annunciat, ad populos Paulus praedicat. Id facito quod intelligis in tempore plus placere. Misericordiam, inquit, malo quam sacrificium. Quare non illi magis sint Christiani qui peccatum condemnant suum, quam qui defendere putant? Iustus enim in exordio sermonis accusator est sui. Qui se accusat cum peccaverit, justus est; non ille qui laudaverit. Utinam Imperator etiam ante mihi potius credidissem, quam consuetudini tuae. Dum puto quod cito ignoscis, cito revocas, ut saepe fecisti: & tu praeuentus es, & ego non declinaui quod cauere non debueram. Sed gratias Domino, qui vult seruulos suos castigare, ne perdat. Istud mihi commune est cum Prophetis, & tibi erit commune cum sanctis. An ego Gratiani patrem non oculis meis praefeeram? Debent veniam sancta alia pignora tua. Dulce mihi nomen antetali, quibus amorem communiter detuli. Amo, diligo, orationibus prosequor. Si credis sequere. Si inquam, credis, ignosce quod dico. Si non credis, ignosce quod facio, in quo Deum praefero. Beatissimus & florentissimus cum sanctis pignoribus fruaris tranquillitate perpetua Imperator Auguste.
units.tr: To the most august Emperor Theodosius, Ambrose. I remember the sweet recollection of our old friendship, and of the many favours you granted to others at my frequent intercession, with the highest kindness. From this it may be inferred that I could not have avoided your coming, which I have always most desired, out of any ungrateful feeling. But I will briefly explain why I did so. I used to see that, in your company, the natural right of hearing was taken from me, and with it the privilege of speaking. For you were often troubled that some decisions made in your council might reach me. Was I then to be without a share in what is common, when the Lord Jesus says that nothing is hidden that shall not be made manifest? So, out of respect, I did what I could: I yielded to your imperial will, and I took care that you should not have cause for offence, since I had arranged that nothing about the imperial decrees should be reported to me. Either I would be present and hear them, and so fear everyone and come to share the reputation of one who connives; or I would hear them in such a way that my ears were open but my voice was shut off, so that, having heard, I could not speak, and so would not harm those who had fallen under suspicion of treachery. What then should I do? Should I not hear? But I cannot stop my ears with the wax of the old tales. Should I speak out? But what I feared in your commands, I would have to guard against in my own words, lest something bloody be done. Should I keep silent? But that would be the most wretched of all: my conscience would be bound and my voice taken away. And where is that saying: But if the priest does not speak to the one who errs, he who has erred dies in his sin, and the priest will be held guilty of punishment because he did not warn the one who erred? Receive that, august Emperor. That you have zeal for the faith I cannot deny; that you have the fear of God I do not deny. But you have a natural impulse, which, if someone wishes to soften it, you quickly turn to mercy; if someone spurs it on, you rouse it to greater heights, so that you can scarcely call it back. Would that, if no one tempered it, no one would inflame it: for I willingly entrust myself to you; you call yourself back, and by your zeal for godliness you overcome the impulse of your nature. I preferred to leave this impulse to your own reflections in private, rather than perhaps to stir it up publicly by my actions. So I preferred that my duty should fall short somewhat, rather than my humility; and that the authority of a priest should be sought in me by others, rather than that you, most beloved, should look for honour from me; so that, with the impulse restrained, the power of choosing a course would remain whole. I pleaded a bodily sickness, truly grave, and scarcely to be relieved except by gentler men. Yet I would rather have died than not waited for your coming for two or three days. But what could I do? It was not possible. There happened in the city of the Thessalonians a thing that no memory records, which I could not prevent from happening. Indeed, what I had said would be most atrocious beforehand, when I had so often asked you, and what you yourself thought a grave deed to recall too late, I could not diminish. When it was first heard of, when a synod of Gallic bishops had met because of the event, no one did not groan; no one received it with moderate feeling; your deed could not be absolved in Ambrose's communion. Even against me, the odium of what was committed was increased, if no one said that the reconciliation of our God would be necessary. Are you ashamed, Emperor, to do what King David, the prophet and the ancestor of Christ according to the flesh, did? To him it was said that a rich man, who had very many flocks, snatched away and killed one poor man's sheep for the arrival of a guest; and when it was recognised that he himself was being accused in this, because he had done it, he said: I have sinned against the Lord. So do not bear it impatiently, Emperor, if it is said to you: You did that, which the prophet said to King David. For if you hear this diligently and say: I have sinned, O Lord, if you say that royal prophetic word: Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us, it will be said to you too: Since you repent, the Lord forgives you your sin; and you will not die. Again, when David had ordered the people to be numbered, he was struck in his heart and said to the Lord: I have sinned greatly in doing this thing; and now, O Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly. And the prophet Nathan was sent to him again, to offer him a choice of three conditions, and let him choose which he would: famine in the land for three years, or to flee three months from the face of his enemies, or death in the land for three days. And David answered: These three are very grievous; but I will rather fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy is very great, and I will not fall into the hand of man. Now the fault was that he wished to know the number of the whole people who were with him, which he ought to have reserved to God alone to know. And when, it says, death came upon the people, on the very first day, at the hour of dinner, when David saw the angel striking the people, David said: I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have done wickedly; but what has this flock done? Let your hand be against me and against my father's house. So the Lord repented, and ordered the angel to spare the people; and David was to offer a sacrifice. For there were then sacrifices for sins; these now are sacrifices of repentance. Thus by that humility he became more acceptable to God. For it is not to be wondered at that a man sins, but it is blameworthy if he does not recognise that he has erred, and does not humble himself before God. Job, holy and himself powerful in the world, says: I have not hidden my sin, but I have declared it before all the people. To King Saul himself, his son Jonathan said: Do not sin against your servant David. And: Why do you sin against innocent blood, to kill David without cause? For even though he was king, he would sin if he killed an innocent man. Finally, David too, when he was already in possession of the kingdom, and had heard that Abner had been killed, an innocent man, by Joab, the commander of his army, said: I am innocent, and my kingdom is innocent for ever and ever before the Lord of the blood of Abner son of Ner; and he fasted in sorrow. I have written these things not to shame you, but to set before you the examples of kings, so that you may remove this sin from your realm. You will remove it by humbling your soul before God. You are a man, and temptation has come to you: conquer it. Sin is not taken away except by tears and repentance. Neither an angel nor an archangel can do it; the Lord himself, who alone can say: I am with you; if we sin, he does not forgive those who do not abandon repentance. I urge, I ask, I exhort, I admonish, because it grieves me that you, who were an example of unheard-of godliness, who held the summit of clemency, who ought not to have allowed the guilty one by one to be put in danger, should not grieve that so many innocent people have perished. Although you have acted most successfully in battles, and though you are praiseworthy in other matters too, yet the summit of your works has always been godliness. The devil has attacked you precisely in what you had most excellent. Conquer while you still have the means by which you can conquer. Do not add another sin to your sin, so that you usurp what usurping has harmed many. I, for my part, though in all other things I am indebted to your godliness, to which I cannot be ungrateful, a godliness I used to set above many emperors and make equal to one alone, I, I say, have no ground of defiance against you, but I have ground of fear. I dare not offer the sacrifice if you wish to be present. Or is what is not allowed in the blood of one innocent man allowed in the blood of many? I do not think so. Finally, I am writing in my own hand, so that you alone may read it. So may the Lord free me from all tribulations, for I perceived that the prohibition came not from a man, nor through a man, but openly to me. For when I was anxious, on the very night on which I was preparing to set out, you did indeed seem to have come to the church, but it was not permitted for me to offer the sacrifice. I pass over other things, as far as I could guard against them. But I bore them, I think, out of love for you. May the Lord bring it about that all things turn out with tranquillity. Our God admonishes us in many ways: by heavenly signs, by the precepts of the prophets, even by visions; he wishes us to understand, and so we ask him to remove the disturbances, to keep peace for us as we rule, and to preserve the faith and tranquillity of the Church, for which it is profitable that the emperors be Christians and godly. Surely you wish to be approved by God. Every matter has its time, as it is written: There is a time, says he, for doing, Lord; and a time, God, of his good pleasure. You would make your offering when you have received the opportunity to sacrifice, when your victim may be accepted by God. Ought you not to have the favour of the emperor, so that I might act according to your will, if the cause allowed it? And a simple prayer is a sacrifice. This brings pardon, that brings offence: this brings humility, that contempt. For it is the voice of God that he prefers his command to be carried out rather than a sacrifice to be offered. God cries this out; Moses announces it to the people; Paul preaches it to the nations. Do that which you understand to be more pleasing in the time. I desire mercy, he says, rather than sacrifice. Why should not those be more truly Christians who condemn their own sin, rather than those who think they must defend it? For the righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech. He who accuses himself when he has sinned is righteous; not he who praises himself. Would that, Emperor, I had believed before rather than your habit. For while I thought that you quickly forgive and quickly recall, as you have often done, you were the one forestalled, and I did not avoid what I ought not to have had to guard against. But thanks be to the Lord, who wishes to chastise his servants so that they may not perish. This is common to me with the prophets, and it will be common to you with the saints. Did I not put Gratian's father before my own eyes? Your other holy pledges ought to receive pardon. Sweet to me is the name of the ancestor, to whom I have shown my love in common. I love, I cherish, I accompany them with prayers. If you believe, follow. If, I say, you believe, forgive what I say. If you do not believe, forgive what I do, in which I put God before you. May you, most blessed and flourishing Emperor, enjoy perpetual tranquillity with your holy pledges.

units.la: EPISTOLA XXIX
units.tr: EPISTLE XXIX

units.la: Divi Ambrosii ad Theodosium Imperatorem vindicari iubentem in Episcopum & Christianos qui Synagogam incenderunt, vehementer eum ob hoc arguentis, atque ut aliam Epistolam dictari iubeat, & quod prius iussum fuerat, emendet, exhortantis.
units.tr: Of the Divine Ambrose to the Emperor Theodosius, who ordered that the bishop and the Christians who burned the synagogue be punished. He sharply rebukes him for this, and urges him to have another letter dictated and to amend what had previously been ordered.

units.la: Clementissimo Principi ac beatissimo Imperatori Theodosio Augusto Ambrosius Episcopus. Exercitus iugibus fere curis sum Imperator beatissime, sed nunquam tanto incestu fui, quanto nunc, cum video cauendum ne quid sit quod adscribatur mihi etiam de sacrilegii periculo. Itaque peto ut patienter sermonem meum audias. Nam si indignus sum, qui a te audiar, indignus sum qui pro te offeram, cui tua vota, cui tuas committas preces. Ipse ergo non audias eum quem pro te audiri vis? Non audies pro se agentem, quem pro aliis audisti? Nec vereris iudicium tuum, ne cum indignum putaris quem audias, indignum feceris qui pro te audiatur? Sed neque imperiale est libertatem dicendi denegare, sacerdotale quod sentiat, non dicere. Nihil enim in vobis Imperatoribus tam populare & tam amabile est, quam libertatem etiam in iis diligere qui obsequio militiae vobis subditi sunt. Siquidem hoc interest inter bonos & malos principes, quod boni libertatem amant, servitutem improbi. Nihil etiam in sacerdote tam periculosum apud Deum, tam turpe apud homines, quam quod sentiat non libere pronunciare. Siquidem scriptum est: Et loquebar de testimoniis tuis in conspectu regum, & non confundebar. Et alibi: Fili hominis, speculatorem te posui domui Israel, in eo, inquit, ut si audiret audientem iustum a iustitia sua, & fecerit delictum, quia non denunciasti ei, hoc est, non dixisti quid sit cavendum, non retinebitur memoria iustitiae eius, & sanguinem eius de manu tua exquiram. Tu autem si distinxeris iusto ut non peccet, & ipse non peccaverit, vita vivet, quia dixisti ei: & tu animam tuam liberabis. Male igitur Imperator bonorum mihi esse tecum, quam malorum consortium, & ideo clementiae tuae displicere debet: Sacerdotis silentium, libertas placere. Nam silentii mei periculo inuoluueris, libertatis bono iuuaris. Non ergo importunus indebitis me intersero, alienis ingero: Sed debitis obtempero mandatis Dei nostri obedio. Quod facio primum tui amore, tui gratia, tuae studio conseruandae salutis. Si id mihi vel non creditur, vel interdicitur, dico sane divinae offensae metu. Nam si meum periculum te exuerat, patienter me pro te offerrem, sed non libenter. Malo enim te sine meo acceptum Deo esse & gloriosum periculo. Sic autem silentii mei dissimulationisque culpa & me in grauat, nec te liberat, malo importuniorem me, quam inutiliorem aut turpiorem iudices. Siquidem scriptum est, dicente sancto Apostolo Paulo, cuius non potes doctrinam refellere: Insta opportune, importune, argue, obsecra, increpa in omni patientia & doctrina. Habemus ergo & nos cui displicere plus periculi sit, praesertim cum etiam Imperatoribus non displiceat, suo quemque fungi munere, & patienter audiatis unumquemque pro suo suggerentem officio, imo corripiatis si non utatur militiae suae ordine. Quod ergo in iis libenter accipitis qui vobis militant, num hoc in sacerdotibus potest molestum videri, cum id loquamur non quod volumus, sed quod iubemur? Scis enim lectum: Cum stabitis ante reges & praesides, nolite cogitare quid loquamini. Non enim vos estis qui loquimini, sed spiritus patris vestri qui loquitur in vobis. Et tamen etsi in causis reipublicae loquar, quamuis etiam illic iustitia seruanda sit, non tanto adstringar metu si non audiar. In causa vero Dei quem audies, si Sacerdotem non audias, cuius maiore peccatur periculo? Quis tibi verum audebit dicere si Sacerdos non audeat? Noui te pium, clementem, mitem atque tranquillum, fidem ac timorem Domini cordi habentem: sed plerunque aliqua nos fallunt. Habent aliqui Zelum Dei, sed non secundum scientiam. Ne igitur hoc etiam fidelibus animis obrepat, cauendum arbitror. Noui pietatem tuam erga Deum, lenitatem in homines, obligatus sum beneficiis tuarum indulgentiarum. Et ideo plus metuo, amplius sollicitor, ne etiam ipse tuo me postea iudicio condemnes, quod mea aut dissimulatione aut adulatione prolapsionem non euitaueris. Si in me peccari viderem, non deberem tacere: Scriptum est enim: Si frater tuus in te peccaverit, corripe illum primo, deinde increpa duobus & tribus testibus. Si te non audieris, dic Ecclesiae. Causam ergo Dei tacebo? Quid igitur sit quod metuam, consideremus. Relatum est a Comite orientis militarium partium incensam esse Synagogam, idque authore factum episcopo. Iussisti vindicari in exteros, Synagogam ab ipso exaedificari Episcopo. Non adstruo expectandam fuisse assertionem Episcopi. Sacerdotes enim turbarum moderatores sunt, studiosi pacis, nisi cum & ipsi mouentur iniuria Dei, aut ecclesiae contumelia. Sit aliquis iste episcopus seruentior in exustione Synagogae, timidior in iudicio, non vereris Imperator ne acquiescat sententiae tuae, ne praevaricetur non times? Non etiam vereris quod futurum est, ne verbis resistat Comiti tuo? Necesse erit igitur ut aut praevaricatorem aut martyrem faciat. Utrumque alienum temporibus tuis, utrumque persecutionis instar: si aut praevaricari cogatur, aut subire martyrium. Vides quo inclinet causae exitus, si fortem episcopum putas, cauto martyrium fortioris: si inconstantem, declina lapsum fragilioris. Plus enim adstringitur, qui labi infirmum coegerit. Hac proposita conditione puto dicturum episcopum quod ipse ignes sparserit, turbas compulerit, populos conduxerit, ne amittat occasionem martyrii, & pro inuaiidis subiiciat validiorem. O beatum mendacium, quo acquiritur sibi aliorum absolutio, sui gratia. Hoc est Imperator quod popposci & ego, ut in me magis vindicares: & hoc si crimen putares, mihi asscriberes. Quid mandas in absentes iudicium? Habes praesentem, habes confitentem reum. Proclamo quod ego Synagogam incenderim, quod ego illis mandauerim, ne esset locus in quo Christus negaretur. Si obiiciatur mihi, cur hic non incenderim? Diuino iam cremari coepit iudicio: meum cessauit opus. Et si verum quaeritur, ideo segnior fui, quia non putabam hoc vindicandum. Quid facerem, quod nullo ultore sine praemio foret? Tangunt haec verecundiam, sed reuocant gratiam, ne fiat opus quo Dei summi contrahatur offensio. Esto tamen, nemo episcopum ad hoc munus conueniat. Rogaui enim clementiam tuam: & licet ipse hoc reuocatum adhuc non legerim, reuocatum tamen constituamus. Quid si alii timidiores dum mortem reformidant, offerant ut de suis facultatibus reparetur Synagoga, aut Comes ubi hoc compererit primo constitutum, ipse de Christianorum censu exaedificari iubeat? Habebis Imperator Comitem praevaricatorem, & huic vexilla committes victricia, huic labarum, hoc est, Christi lactatum nomine signum qui Synagogam instauret, quae Christum nesciat? Iube labarum Synagogae inferri, videamus si non resistunt. Erit igitur locus Iudaeorum perfidiae factus de exuuiis ecclesiae: & patrimonium quod fauore Christi acquisitum est Christianis, hoc transferetur ad donaria perfidorum? Legimus templa idolis antiquitus condita de manubiis Cimbrorum {illegible, ~20 letters} de spoliis reliquorum hostium. Hunc titulí Iudaei in fronte synagogæ suæ scribent. Templum impietatis factum de manubiis Christianorum, sed disciplinæ te ratio Imperator monet. Quid igitur est amplius, disciplinæ species, an causa religionis? cedat oportet censura devotioni. Non audisti Imperator, quia cum iussisset Iulianus reparari templum Hierosolymis, quod diuino qui faciebant repurgari, igne flagrarunt? Non canes ne etiam nunc fiat? Adeo à te nosa fuit iubendum, ut Iulianus hoc iusserit. Quid tamen movet? Utrum quia quodcunque aedificium publicum exustum est, an quia synagogæ locus? Si aedificio incenso moueris vilissimo (quid enim in tam ignobili castro esse potuit) non recordaris Imperator, quantorum Romæ domus praefectorum incensa fuit, & nemo vindicavit? Imo si quis Imperatorum voluit factum severius reprehendere, eius magis, qui tanto est percussus dispendio, causam granauit. Quid igitur dignius ut Calinici castri in parte aliqua aedificiorum incendium, an urbis Romæ vindicandum existimaretur, si oporteret tamen? Constantinopoli dudum domus episcopi incensa est, & filius elementiæ tuæ intercessit apud patrem, ut & suam, hoc est, & filii Imperatoris iniuriam, & domus sacerdotalis incendium non vindicares. Non consideras Imperator ne & hoccum vindicari iusseris, ipse iterum interueniat ne vindicetur? Sed bene illud acquisitum est a patre filio. Dignum erat enim, ut suam iniuriam prius ipse donaret. Bene illud cum gratiæ distinctione diuisum est, ut & filius pro sua, & pater pro filii iniuria rogaretur. Hic nihil est quod filio reservES, & vide ne quid Deo deroges. Non est ergo causa tantæ commotioni idonea, ut propter aedificii exustionem in populum tam seuere vindicetur, multo autem minua, quia synagoga incensa est perfidiæ locus, impietatis domus, amentiæ receptaculum, quod Deus damnauit ipse. Sic enim legimus per os Hieremiæ dicente Domino Deo nostro: Et faciam domui vbi inuocatum est nomen meum super ipsam, in qua confidistis vos, & loco quem dedi vobis & patribus vestris, sicut feci Silo: & proiiciam vos à facie mea, sicut proieci fratres vestros omne semen Ephrem.
units.tr: To the most merciful prince and most blessed emperor Theodosius Augustus, Ambrose, bishop. Most blessed emperor, I am occupied almost constantly with unending cares, but I have never been as troubled as I am now, when I see that I must take care lest something be laid to my charge even on the danger of sacrilege. So I ask that you hear my words patiently. For if I am unworthy to be heard by you, I am unworthy to offer prayers on your behalf, to whom you entrust your vows and your petitions. Will you not hear the one whom you want to be heard on your behalf? Will you not listen to one who speaks for himself, when you have listened to him speaking for others? Do you not fear your own judgment, lest, by thinking him unworthy to be heard by you, you make yourself unworthy of having him speak for you? But it is neither imperial to deny freedom of speech, nor priestly to refrain from saying what one thinks. Indeed, nothing is so popular and so lovable in you emperors as to cherish freedom even in those who are subject to you in the service of your army. For this is the difference between good and bad princes: good princes love freedom, wicked ones love slavery. Nothing is so dangerous for a priest before God, or so shameful before men, as not to speak freely what he thinks. For it is written: "I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed" (Ps. 118[119].46). And elsewhere: "Son of man, I have set you as a watchman to the house of Israel. If, says the Lord, when he hears a word from my mouth, you do not warn him from me, and he, the righteous man, turns from his righteousness and commits sin, I will require his blood at your hand. But if you warn the righteous man that he should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you have warned him, and you will have delivered your own soul" (Ezek. 3.17-19). Therefore, emperor, I prefer to have the company of good men with you rather than of evil men, and so it ought to be displeasing to your clemency that a priest should be silent and that freedom should please you. For by my silence you would be entangled in danger, but by my freedom you would be helped by a good thing. So I am not meddling uninvited, nor forcing myself on matters that are not mine; rather, I obey the commands of our God, which I owe. I do this first out of love for you, for your favour, and from zeal to preserve your salvation. If this is either not believed or forbidden to me, I say it indeed out of fear of offending God. For if my own danger were all that threatened, I would offer myself for you patiently, but not gladly. I would rather that you be acceptable to God and glorious without my peril. Yet my fault of silence and of dissembling weighs on me, and does not free you; I would rather you judged me more troublesome than less useful or more cowardly. For it is written, and the holy Apostle Paul, whose teaching you cannot refute, says: "Be instant in season, out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and doctrine" (2 Tim. 4.2). So we too have one to whom it is more dangerous to displease, especially since it does not displease even emperors that each man perform his own office, and that you patiently hear each man offering counsel suited to his duty, and indeed rebuke him if he does not keep the order of his service. Therefore, if you willingly accept this from those who serve in your army, can it seem troublesome in priests, when we speak not what we wish but what we are commanded? For you know what is read: "When you stand before kings and governors, do not take thought what you shall say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you" (cf. Matt. 10.19-20). And yet, even if I speak in matters of the state, where justice too must be observed, I would not be bound by so great a fear if I were not heard. But in the cause of God, whom you will hear, if you do not hear a priest, by whom is the greater sin committed? Who will dare to tell you the truth if a priest does not dare? I know you to be pious, merciful, gentle and calm, having the fear and worship of the Lord in your heart; but often some things deceive us. Some have "zeal for God, but not according to knowledge" (Rom. 10.2). Therefore I think we must take care that this does not creep even into faithful minds. I know your piety towards God and your mildness towards men, and I am bound by the benefits of your indulgence. Therefore I fear the more, and am the more anxious, lest you afterwards condemn me too in your judgment, because by my dissembling or my flattery I did not avoid the lapse. If I saw a sin committed against me, I ought not to keep silent; for it is written: "If your brother sins against you, reprove him first; then rebuke him before two or three witnesses. If he does not listen to you, tell the Church" (Matt. 18.15-17). Shall I then be silent about God's cause? Let us consider, then, what it is that I fear. It has been reported by the Count of the East, in the military region, that the synagogue was burned, and that this was done at the instigation of the bishop. You have ordered that vengeance be taken on the foreigners, and that the synagogue be rebuilt at the expense of the bishop himself. I do not maintain that the bishop's own statement should not have been awaited. For bishops are moderators of disturbances, lovers of peace, unless they are themselves moved by an injury to God or an insult to the Church. Suppose this bishop was too zealous in the burning of the synagogue and too timid in the judgment; do you not fear, emperor, that he will not agree with your sentence, that he will not prevaricate, and do you not fear that he will resist your count in words? It will then be necessary that he either make himself a prevaricator or a martyr. Both are foreign to your times, and both are like persecution, if he is compelled either to prevaricate or to undergo martyrdom. You see where the outcome of the case tends: if you think the bishop brave, beware of the martyrdom of the stronger man; if you think him inconstant, avoid the fall of the weaker one. For he who forces the weak man to fall is more bound by guilt. Given this condition, I think the bishop will say that he himself scattered the fires, stirred up the crowds, and gathered the people, so that he might not lose the opportunity of martyrdom, and that he might put forward the stronger in place of the weaker. O blessed lie, by which the absolution of others is obtained for oneself! Emperor, this is what I too demand, that you should take vengeance on me rather than on them; and if you consider this a crime, ascribe it to me. Why do you order judgment against the absent? You have the present man, you have the accused who confesses. I declare that I burned the synagogue, that I ordered them to do so, so that there would be no place where Christ is denied. If it is objected to me, why did I not burn it here? It has already begun to burn by divine judgment; my work has ceased. And if the truth be sought, I was the slower for this reason, that I did not think it ought to be avenged. What would I do, when it would be without an avenger and without reward? These matters touch my modesty, but they call back the favour, lest a deed be done by which the offence of the most high God is incurred. Grant, however, that no bishop should be summoned to this office. I have made a request to your clemency; and although I have not yet read that it has been revoked, let us take it that it has been revoked. What if other, more timid men, dreading death, offer that the synagogue be repaired from their own resources; or, when the Count learns of it, what if he himself orders that it be rebuilt from the Christians' property, having first decided on this? You would have, emperor, a prevaricating count, and you would commit to him your victorious standards, to him the labarum, that is, the sign carried in the name of Christ, so that he may restore a synagogue for those who do not know Christ. Order the labarum to be carried into the synagogue, and let us see whether they do not resist. Will there then be a place made for the perfidy of the Jews out of the spoils of the Church? And will the patrimony that was acquired by the favour of Christ for Christians be transferred to the gifts of the faithless? We read that temples were built in antiquity for idols from the spoils of the Cimbrians, {illegible} from the plunder of the other enemies. The Jews will write this inscription on the front of their synagogue: "A temple of impiety made from the spoils of Christians." But the reasoning of discipline, emperor, advises you. What then is more important: the appearance of discipline, or the cause of religion? Surely censure must yield to devotion. Did you not hear, emperor, that when Julian ordered the temple at Jerusalem to be rebuilt, those who were doing it were consumed by fire, because they were trying to cleanse what God had abandoned? Will it not happen even now? It was so much your duty to forbid this that Julian ordered it. But what moves you? Is it that any public building was burned, or that it was the place of a synagogue? If you are moved by the burning of a most worthless building (for what could there be in such an ignoble camp?), do you not remember, emperor, how many houses of prefects were burned at Rome, and no one avenged them? Indeed, if any emperor wished to censure the deed more severely, he made the case weightier by reason of the greater loss suffered by that man. What then would be considered more worthy of vengeance, the burning of some buildings in a part of the camp at Callinicum, or of the city of Rome, if it were necessary to avenge them at all? At Constantinople not long ago the house of the bishop was burned, and your son interceded with his father so that you would not avenge either his own injury, that is, the injury of the emperor's son, or the burning of a bishop's house. Do you not consider, emperor, whether, if you order this also to be avenged, he himself will again intervene so that it is not avenged? But that was well obtained by the son from the father. For it was fitting that he should first pardon his own injury. It was well divided, with a distinction of grace, so that the son should be asked for his own injury and the father for the son's. Here there is nothing that you should reserve for your son; and take care that you do not detract anything from God. Therefore there is no cause sufficient to stir such commotion, that on account of the burning of a building the people should be punished so severely; and much less so, since the synagogue that was burned is a place of perfidy, a house of impiety, a refuge of madness, which God himself has condemned. For thus we read through the mouth of Jeremiah, when the Lord our God says: "And I will do to the house upon which my name is called, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh; and I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your brothers, the whole seed of Ephraim" (Jer. 7.14-15).

units.la: Et tu noli orare pro populo isto, & noli postulare illis misericordiam, & neque accesseris ad me pro illis, quia non exaudiam te. An non vides quid faciunt in ciuitatibus Iudæ? Deus se pro illis prohibet rogari, quos tu vindicandos putas. At certè si iure gentium agerem, dicerem quantas Ecclesiæ Basilicas Iudæi tempore Imperii Iuliani incenderint. Duas Damasci, quarum una vix reparata est, sed Ecclesiæ, non Synagogæ impendiis, altera Basilica informibus horret ruinis. Incensæ sunt Basilicæ Gazis, Ascalonæ, Beryto, & illis fere locis omnibus, & vindicatam nemo quæsivit. Incensa est Basilica & Alexandriæ à Gentibus & Iudæis, quæ sola præstabat cæteris. Ecclesia non vindicata est, vindicabitur Synagoga? Vindicabitur etiam Valentinianorum phanum incensum? Quid est enim nisi phanum, in quo est conuentus Gentilium? Licet gentiles duodecim Deos appellent, isti triginta & duos æonas colant, quos appellant Deos. Nam & de ipsis comperi relatum & præceptum, ut in monachos vindicaretur, qui prohibentibus iter Valentiniani, quo Psalmos canentes ex consuetudine vsuque veteri pergebant ad celebritatem Machabæorum martyrum, moti insolentia incenderunt phanum eorum, in quodam rurali vico tumultuarie conditum. Quot se offerre habent tali opinioni, cum meminerint tempore Iuliani illum quia aram deiecit, & turbanit sacrificium, damnatum à iudice fecisse martyrium? Itaque nunquam alias ille iudex qui audiuit eum, nisi persecutor habitus est, nemo illum congressu, nemo illum vnquam osculo dignum putauit. Qui nisi iam esset defunctus, timeret Imperator ne in eum tu vindicares, quanquam vindictam cœlestem non euaserit suo superstes hæredi. Sed refertur, cognitionem mandatam iudici, scriptumque eo, quod non referre debuerit, sed vindicare. Requirenda quoque sublata donaria, ut omittam alia. Incensæ sunt à Iudæis Ecclesiarum Basilicæ, & nihil redditum est, nihil repertum, nihil quæsitum. Quid autem habere potuit Synagoga in castro vltimo, cum totum quicquid illic est, non multum sit, nihil copiosum? Quid deinde de incendio potuit rapi Iudæis insidiantibus? Artes istæ sunt Iudæorum volentium calumniari, ut dum ista quæruntur, mandetur extra ordinem militaris censura iudicii, mittatur miles fortasse dicturus, quod hic aliquando ante tuum Imperator dixit aduentum. Quomodo poterit nos Christus iuuare, qui pro Iudæis aduersus Christum militamus? Qui mittuntur ad vindictam Iudæorum, suos perdiderunt exercitus, nostros volunt perdere. In quas præterea non prosiliant calumnias, qui etiam Christo falsis testimoniis calumniati sunt? In quas non prosiliant calumnias homines & circa diuina mendaces? Quos non authores seditionis fuisse dicant? Quos non appetant, etiam quos non recognoscant, ut catenatorum ordines, innumeros spectent de Christiano populo, ut captiua videant colla plebis fidelis, ut condantur in tenebras Dei seruuli, ut feriantur securibus, dentur ignibus, mandantur metallis, ne poena cito transeat? Hunc dabiatriumphum Iudæis de Ecclesia Dei? Hoc trophæum de Christi populo? Hæc gaudia Imperator perfidis? Hanc celebritatem Synagogæ? Hos lucus Ecclesiæ? Referet Iudæorum populus hanc solennitatem in dies festos suos, & inter illos profecto numerabit, quibus aut de Amorrhæis, aut de Chananæis triumphanit, aut de Pharaone rege Ægypti, aut de Nabuchodonosor regis Babyloniæ manu liberari potuit. Addet hanc celebritatem significans se de Christi populo triumphum egisse. Et cum ipsi Romanis legibus teneri se negent, ita ut crimina leges putent, nunc velut Romanis legibus se vindicandos putent? Vbi erant istæ leges cum incenderent ipsi sacratarum Basilicarum culmina? Si Iulianus non est vitus Ecclesiam, quia prævaricator erat, tu Imperator vlciscēris Synagogæ in
units.tr: "And do not pray for this people, nor ask mercy for them, nor come before me on their behalf, for I will not hear you." Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah? God forbids himself to be asked on behalf of those whom you think should be avenged. But if I were pleading by the law of nations, I would tell you how many churches the Jews set on fire in the reign of Julian: two at Damascus, one of which has barely been repaired, though with the funds of the Church, not the Synagogue, while the other stands in shapeless ruins. Churches were burned at Gaza, at Ascalon, at Berytus and in almost all those places, and nobody has sought redress. A church at Alexandria, which surpassed all the rest, was burned by the Gentiles and the Jews, and no redress was made for the Church. Will the Synagogue be avenged? Will the burned shrine of the Valentinians be avenged too? For what else is it but a shrine, a meeting place of Gentiles? Although the Gentiles call their gods twelve, these people worship thirty-two aeons and call them gods. I have learned, indeed, that it was reported and ordered that vengeance be taken on the monks who, when the Valentinians forbade their journey, were going, as they customarily did from old usage, to sing psalms at the festival of the Maccabean martyrs; moved by insolence, they set fire to the shrine of those heretics, which had been hastily built in a certain country village. How many people will be ready to hold such an opinion, when they remember that in Julian's time the man who threw down the altar and disturbed the sacrifice made himself a martyr by being condemned by the judge? Accordingly, that judge who heard the case was never regarded otherwise than as a persecutor, no one thought him worthy of association or ever of a kiss. Unless he were already dead, the Emperor would fear that you might take vengeance on him, although he did not escape heavenly vengeance, surviving only to his heir. But it is reported that the inquiry was entrusted to a judge, and it was written that he ought not to report but to avenge. The removed votive offerings must also be sought out, to say nothing of other things. Churches of the Church were burned by the Jews, and nothing has been restored, nothing found, nothing sought. What could the Synagogue have possessed in that remote fortress, since whatever is there is not much, nothing of value? What could have been seized after the fire by Jews who were lying in wait? These are the tricks of Jews wishing to make false accusations, so that while such matters are being pursued, the stern military procedure of a court is ordered outside the ordinary course, and a soldier is sent who will perhaps say what the Emperor once said here before your arrival. How can Christ help us, when we fight for the Jews against Christ? Those who are sent to avenge the Jews have lost their own armies; they wish to destroy ours. Into what further calumnies will they not leap, who slandered Christ himself with false testimony? Into what calumnies will not men leap who are lying even about divine things? Whom will they not call authors of sedition? Whom will they not attack, even those whom they do not recognise? So that they may gaze upon the rows of countless chained Christians, so that they may see the captive necks of the faithful people, so that the servants of God may be shut up in darkness, struck with axes, given to the flames, sent to the mines, lest the punishment pass quickly? Is this the triumph the Jews are to have over the Church of God? This the trophy over the people of Christ? These the joys for the faithless Emperor? This the celebration for the Synagogue? These the glories for the Church? The Jewish people will recall this solemnity on their festival days, and will certainly count it among those by which they could have been delivered from the Amorites, or the Canaanites, or Pharaoh king of Egypt, or the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. They will add this celebration, signifying that they have won a triumph over the people of Christ. And since they themselves deny that they are bound by Roman laws, so that they think crimes are laws, are they now to be avenged as if by Roman laws? Where were those laws when they themselves set fire to the roofs of consecrated churches? If Julian did not spare the Church because it was a transgressor, will you, Emperor, avenge the wrong done to the Synagogue because you are a Christian?

units.la: gæ in ge iniuriam quia Christianus es? Et quid tecum posthac Christus loquetur? Non recordaris quid Dauid ad eundem per Nathan prophetam mandauerit? Ego te de fratribus tuis minorem elegi, & de primato Imperatorem feci. Ego de fructu seminis tui in sede imperiali locaui. Ego tibi subiecti nationes barbaras, ego tibi pacem dedi, ego tibi inimicum tuum in potestatem tuam captiuum deduxi. Frumentum non habebas ad exercitus alimoniam, ipsorum hostium manu patefeci tibi portas, aperui horrea, dederunt tibi hostes tui commeatus suos quos sibi parauerant. Ego perturbaui hostis tui consilia, ut se ipse nudaret. Ego ipsum vsurpatorem imperii ita vinxi, ac mentem eius ligaui, ut cum haberet adhuc fugiendi copiam, tamen cum omnibus suis tanquam metuens ne quis tibi periret, ipse se clauderet. Ego comitem eius atque exercitum ex altera parte naturae, quos ante disperseram, ne ad belli societatem coirent, ad supplementum tibi victoriae congregaui. Et exercitum tuum ex multis indomitis conuenam nationibus, quasi vnius gentis fidem & tranquillitatem & concordiam seruare praecepi. Ego cum periculum summum esset ne Alpes infida Barbarorum penetrarent consilia, intra ipsum Alpium vallum victoriam tibi contuli, ut sine damno vinceres.
