Our adversary is the devil, who, as the Apostle said, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Without doubt he has received, he has received (we are not deceived, but warned) the power of such testing, so that perhaps I might be called back from the purpose of my faith by wounds to my body. You also read that the devil tested the holy Job in many ways, and at last he asked for and received the power to test his body, which he covered with wounds. When it was proposed that we should now hand over the vessels of the Church, I gave this answer: if anything of mine were demanded, whether an estate, a house, gold or silver, which is mine by right, I would gladly offer it; but nothing can be taken from the temple of God, nor can I hand over what I have received to be guarded and not handed over. Then I was asked to consider the Emperor's welfare too, since it would be no advantage to me to hand it over, nor to him to receive it. Let him hear the voice of a free priest, if he wishes his own interests to be considered: let him withdraw from the injury to Christ. These words are full of humility and, I think, full of the goodwill that a priest owes to the Emperor. But since our struggle is not only against flesh and blood, but also (what is more serious) against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places, that tempter the devil, through his ministers, increases the contest and thinks it must be tested by wounds to my body. I know, brothers, that these wounds which we receive for Christ are not wounds by which life is lost, but wounds by which it is extended. Please allow the contest to proceed; it is fitting that you be spectators. Consider that if the city has some athlete, or someone skilled in a noble art, it wishes to bring him to the contest. Why, in the greater matters, do you refuse what you are accustomed to want even in lesser ones? He does not fear arms, he does not fear barbarians; he who does not fear death is not held back by any pleasure of the flesh. Certainly, if the Lord has appointed you to this contest, you are keeping your watch in vain through so many nights and days. The will of Christ will be fulfilled. For our Lord Jesus is almighty. This is our faith, and so what he commands to be done will be done; nor is it fitting for us to resist the divine sentence. You have heard what was read today: the Saviour sent through the Apostles to have a colt of an ass brought to him, and ordered that if anyone resisted, it should be said: "The Lord has need of it." What if now also he orders that colt of the ass to be brought to him, that is, the animal that is accustomed to carry a heavy burden, as is the human condition, to which it is said: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, for it is light." What if, I say, he has now ordered that colt to be brought to him, by sending his Apostles, to those who, already stripped of the body, bear an appearance of angels that our eyes cannot grasp? Will they not say, if anyone resists: "The Lord has need of it"? If the desire for this life resists, if flesh and blood resist, if bodily existence resists, because perhaps we seem agreeable to some people, yet he who loves you here will love you far more if he allows himself to be made a sacrifice for Christ; for "to depart and be with Christ" is far better, and yet to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake. There is nothing, then, for you to be anxious about, beloved brothers. For I know that whatever I suffer, I shall suffer for Christ. And I have read that I ought not to fear those who can kill the flesh. And I have heard it said: "Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it." So if the Lord wills it, it is certain that no one will stand in the way. But if he still delays our contests, why are you afraid? The Lord's servant is not usually guarded by bodily custody, but by the providence of the Lord. You are disturbed because you found the two doors open, which a certain man, blind, is recorded to have opened when he was seeking his own lodging. From this learn that human custody avails nothing. Behold, one who has lost the gift of sight has dissolved all your defences and mocked your guards. But the Lord has not lost the guard of his mercy. Do you not remember that two days ago it was also discovered that someone entered through the left side of the basilica, and you would think it was shut and fortified? Armed men had indeed surrounded the basilica and were watching this entrance and that. They were struck with blindness, so that they could not see what was open. So you do not fail to know that through many nights whatever was open remained open. Therefore cease to be anxious, for this will be what Christ commands, and this is what is expedient. Finally, I will set before you examples from the Law. Elisha was being sought by the king of Syria, and an army had been sent to seize him. He was surrounded on every side. His servant began to fear, because he was a servant, that is, he did not have a free mind and free power. The holy prophet asked that his eyes be opened, and said: "Look, and see how many more are on our side than against them." And he looked, and saw thousands of angels. You notice, therefore, that the servants of Christ are guarded more by those who are not seen than by those who are seen. But if they guard, they guard you, being summoned by your prayers. For you have read that those very men who were seeking Elisha entered Samaria to the very man whom they were eager to seize; not only were they unable to harm him, but they were saved through the intercession of him against whom they had come. The Apostle Peter also gives you an example of both things. For when Herod sought him and seized him, he put him in prison. The servant of God had not withdrawn, but was kept without fear. The Church prayed for him, but the Apostle rested in prison, which is the judgment of one who does not fear. An angel was sent to rouse him as he slept, and through him Peter was led out of prison and escaped death for a time. The same Peter later, when Simon had been defeated, while he was sowing the commandments of God among the people and teaching chastity, stirred up the minds of the Gentiles, who sought him; and the souls of the Christians begged that he withdraw for a little while. And although he was eager for suffering, he was nevertheless swayed by regard for the praying people. For he was asked to preserve himself for the instruction and strengthening of the people. What more? He began to leave the city by the wall at night, and seeing Christ meet him at the gate and enter the city, he said: "Lord, where are you going?" Christ answered: "I am going to Rome to be crucified again." Peter understood that this response concerned his own cross. For Christ could not be crucified again, who had laid aside the flesh of the passion he had undergone; for in that he died, he died to sin once for all; but in that he lives, he lives to God. Peter therefore understood that Christ was to be crucified again in his servant. So he willingly returned, and answered the Christians who asked him, and was immediately seized, and through his own cross he glorified the Lord Jesus. You see, then, that Christ wishes to suffer in his servants. What if he also says to this servant: "I want that one to remain thus, but you follow me," and wishes to eat the fruit of this tree? For if his food was to do the will of the Father, is it not also his food to be nourished by our sufferings? Did he not (to take the example from the Lord himself) suffer when he willed, and when he was sought, was he not found? But when the hour of the passion had not yet come, he passed through the midst of those who sought him, and they could not seize him when they saw him. By this he clearly showed that when the Lord wills, he is found and taken where he wills; but when he delays, even if he meets the hands of those seeking him and is hindered, he is not held. Did I myself not go out every day, either to visit or to go to the martyrs? Did I not pass by the palace's gate going and returning? And yet no one held me, although they had those who drove me out, and they afterwards declared their will, saying: "Leave the city and go where you wish." I expected that something great would happen, like a sword for the name of Christ, or a fire. But they offered me delights instead of sufferings; yet the athlete of Christ does not demand delights, but his sufferings. Let no one therefore disturb you, that they had either prepared a prison, or, as it seemed to them, that harsh threats were uttered by Auxentius himself, who calls himself a bishop. Many have reported that executioners were sent ahead, and that the penalty of death had been decreed. I do not fear those things, and I shall not desert these. For where shall I go where everything is not full of groans and tears, when Catholic priests are ordered to be cast out of the churches, those who resist are struck with the sword, and all the officials are proscribed unless they carry out the order? And these things are written by the bishop's hand and dictated by his mouth; and in order to prove his skill, he did not omit the old example. For we read in the prophet that he saw a flying sickle. Imitating this, Auxentius has sent a flying sword through all the cities. And "Satan transforms himself into an angel of light," and in evil he imitates his power. You, Lord Jesus, redeemed the world in a single moment; Auxentius, in a single moment, was slaughtering as many peoples as lay in his power, some with the sword, some with sacrilege. He seeks my basilica with a bloody mouth and bloodstained hands. The reading of the day answered him well: "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts?" That is, peace and fury do not agree, Christ and Belial do not agree. You also remember what was read today: how Naboth, the holy man, the owner of his vineyard, was asked by royal petition to give his vineyard, where the king, having cut down the vines, would sow a common herb; and Naboth answered: "Far be it from me to surrender the inheritance of my fathers." And the king was saddened that the right that was not his had been justly refused, but Naboth, deceived by a woman's counsel, defended his vines even with his own blood. If he did not surrender his vineyard, shall we surrender the Church of Christ? What, then, was my answer, given stubbornly? For I said when summoned: "Far be it from me to surrender the inheritance of Christ." If he did not surrender the inheritance of his fathers, shall I surrender the inheritance of Christ? But I added this also: "Far be it from me to surrender the inheritance of the fathers," that is, the inheritance of Dionysius, who died in exile for the cause of the faith, the inheritance of Eustorgius the confessor, the inheritance of Myrocles, and of all the faithful bishops before us. I gave the answer that belongs to a priest; what belongs to the Emperor, let the Emperor do. It is worse that he should take away my soul, that is, my faith. But to whom shall I surrender it? The reading of today's Gospel ought to teach us what is sought and from whom it is sought. You heard read that when Christ sat on the colt of the ass, the little boys shouted, and the Jews took it badly. At last they challenged the Lord Jesus, saying that he should make them be silent; he answered: "If these are silent, the stones will cry out." Then, entering the temple, he cast out the money-changers and the seats and the dove-sellers in the temple of God. That reading was not recited by any arrangement of ours, but by chance, and it fits the present times well. Therefore the praises of Christ are always the lashes of the treacherous. And now, when Christ is praised, the heretics say that sedition is being stirred up; the heretics say that death is being prepared for them; and truly they have death in the praises of Christ. For how can they bear to hear his praises, whose weakness they proclaim? And so today also, when Christ is praised, the madness of the Arians is struck. The Gerasenes could not bear the presence of Christ; these men, worse than the Gerasenes, cannot even endure the praise of Christ. They see the boys singing the glory of Christ, because it is written: "From the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise." They mock that little age so full of faith when they say: "Look, what are they shouting?" But Christ answered them: "If these are silent, the stones will cry out," that is, stronger voices will cry out; young men will cry out, mature men will cry out, old men will cry out; those stones, now made solid against him, will cry out, the stone of which it is written: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." Invited, therefore, by these praises, Christ enters his temple, takes up the scourge, and drives the money-changers out of the temple. For he does not permit money-changers in his temple; he does not permit in his temple those who sell seats. What are the seats? Are they not honours? What are the doves, if not simple minds or souls that follow a pure and white faith? Shall I then bring into the temple one whom Christ excludes? For he who sells dignities and honours is ordered to go out. Is he who wishes to sell the simple minds of the faithful ordered to go out? So Auxentius is cast out, and Mercurinus is shut out. He is one monster with two names. For, so that he might not be recognised, he changed his name, so that, since he had been Auxentius, the Arian bishop, he might call himself Mercurinus to deceive the people whom he had held. He changed the name, but he did not change his treachery. He has taken off the wolf and put on the wolf. It does nothing for him to have changed his name; what he is, is recognised. In the regions of Scythia he was called one thing, here he is called another. He has names according to the regions. So he already has two names; and if he goes on from here to another place, he will have a third. For how will he allow his name to remain as a sign of so great a crime? He committed lesser deeds in Scythia, and was so ashamed that he changed his name. Here he has dared more wicked things, and wherever he goes he will want his name to betray him. Will he write the blood of so many peoples with his own hand, and be able to confess it in his mind? The Lord Jesus used to exclude a few from his temple; Auxentius has left no one. Jesus drives out of his temple with a whip; Auxentius with the sword. Jesus, with a whip; Mercurinus, with an axe. The merciful Lord drives out sacrilegious men with a whip; the wicked man persecutes the pious with iron. You said well of him today: "Let him carry his own laws with him. He will carry them, even if he does not want to. He will carry his conscience, and if he does not carry a little paper, he will carry his soul inscribed with blood; even if he does not carry an epistle written in ink." Your guilt, Judas, is written with an iron stylus and an adamantine point, and written on your breast: that is, written there from where it came forth. Does he dare to mention to me the revocation of decisions, full of blood and gore? He who thinks that those whom he could not deceive by speech are to be struck by the sword, dictating bloody laws with his mouth, writing them with his hand, and thinking that a law can impose faith on men. He has not heard what was said today: "Because a man is not justified by the works of the law"? Or: "Through the law I died to the law, that I might live to God"? That is, through the spiritual interpretation of the law he died to the bodily law. And let us also, through the law of our Lord Jesus Christ, die to this law, which decrees the decrees of perfidy. It is not the law that gathered the Church, but the faith of Christ. For "the law is not of faith, but the righteous lives by faith." So faith, not the law, makes a man righteous, because righteousness does not come through the law, but through the faith of Christ. But he who rejects faith and prescribes the rights of the law declares himself unrighteous, since "the righteous lives by faith." Let no one follow that law by which the Council of Ariminum was confirmed, in which Christ was called a creature. But they say: "God sent his Son made of a woman," the letters say, made under the law. So they read "made," that is, "created." Do they not consider this very thing they have proposed: that Christ is said to be made, but of a woman, that is, he was made according to the birth of the virgin, though according to his divine generation he was born of the Father? They have read also today that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. Is Christ a curse according to his divinity? But the Apostle teaches you why he is called a curse, saying: "For it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." That is, he who in his flesh took our flesh, and in his body took our infirmities and our curses, so that he might be crucified. For he was not cursed in himself, but was cursed in you. Finally, you have elsewhere: "He who knew no sin was made sin for us," who took our sins upon himself, so that by the sacrament of his passion he might abolish them. Therefore, brothers, I would discuss these things more fully before you in his presence; but I am certain that you are not ignorant of the faith. He shrinks from your examination, and he has chosen certain Gentiles, about four or five men, as judges for himself, if indeed he chooses any. I would wish them to be present in the assembly of all, not to judge concerning Christ, but to hear the majesty of Christ. Yet they have already pronounced against Auxentius, whom they did not believe when he was daily pleading. What greater condemnation of him is there than that he was defeated without an opponent before his own judges? So we already have their sentence against Auxentius as well; and he who chose the Gentiles rightly deserves condemnation, because he has dismissed the precepts of the Apostle, since the Apostle says: "Does any of you, having a matter against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge this world?" And further on he says: "If there is no wise man among you who can judge between brothers, but brother contends with brother in judgment, and this before unbelievers?" Do you see that what he offered is against the authority of the Apostle? Which should you follow, Auxentius or Paul as your teacher? But why should I speak of the Apostle, when the Lord himself cries out through the prophet: "Hear me, my people, who know judgment, whose heart is my law." God says: "Hear me, my people, who know judgment"; Auxentius says: "You do not know judgment." Do you see that he already despises God among you, who rejects the sentence of the heavenly oracle? "Hear me," he says, "my people, says the Lord." He does not say: hear, nations; he does not say: hear, Jews. For now the people of God who had been has become a people of error. And the people who were a people of error have begun to be the people of God, because they believed in Christ. This people, then, judges, whose heart holds the divine law, not the human: a law not written with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not inscribed on paper, but sealed on the heart; the law of grace, not of blood. Who, then, does you wrong: he who rejects your hearing, or he who chooses to hear? Hemmed in on every side, he flees to the truth of his fathers. He wishes to stir up hatred against the Emperor, saying that a young catechumen ignorant of sacred reading ought to judge, and to judge in the consistory. As though last year, when he was summoned to the palace and the matter was being treated before the consistory in the presence of the leading men, when the Emperor wished to seize the basilica, I was then broken by regard for the court and did not keep the constancy of a priest, nor did I depart with my right unimpaired. Do they not remember that when the people learned that I had gone to the palace, they rushed in with such force that they could not bear its violence, when the military count went out with armed men to scatter the crowd, they all offered themselves to death for the faith of Christ? Was I not then asked to soothe the people with many words, to promise that no one would invade the Church's basilica? And though my office was requested for a benefit, nevertheless, because the people had come to the palace, hatred was stirred up against me. They wish me to return to this hatred. I called back the people, and yet I did not escape hatred; which hatred I think should be moderated, not feared. For why should we fear for the name of Christ? Unless perhaps what they say ought to move me: "Therefore the Emperor should not receive one basilica to go to; and Ambrose wants to have more power than the Emperor, so as to deny the Emperor the freedom to go forward." When they say this, they are eager to seize our words, just as the Jews who tested Christ with a cunning question, saying: "Teacher, is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?" Are the servants of God always to be hated because of Caesar? And does impiety summon this charge for itself, in order to put forward the imperial name? And can those men say that they have no sacrilege, whose teaching they imitate? And yet see how much more the Arians are than the Jews. The Jews asked whether they should think the right of tribute should be paid to Caesar; these men want to give the Emperor the right of the Church. But as the faithless follow their author, so let us also answer as our Lord and author taught us. For Jesus, perceiving the deceit of the Jews, said to them: "Why do you test me? Show me a denarius." And when they had given it, he said: "Whose image and inscription does it have?" They answered: "Caesar's." And Jesus said to them: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." So I too say to those who object to me: "Show me a denarius." Jesus looked at Caesar's denarius and said: "Render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and what is God's to God." Can they offer Caesar's denarius for seizing the basilicas of the Church? But in the Church I know one image, that is, the visible image of God, of which God said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." That image, of which it is written: "Christ is the brightness of glory and the image of his substance." In this image I see the Father, as the Lord Jesus himself said: "He who has seen me has seen the Father also." For this image is not separated from the Father, who taught me the unity of the Trinity, saying: "I and the Father are one." And further: "All things that the Father has are mine." And concerning the Holy Spirit, he says that he is the Spirit of Christ and receives from Christ, as it is written: "He will receive of mine and will declare it to you." What then? Has our answer not been humble? If tribute is demanded, we do not deny it. The fields of the Church pay tribute. If the Emperor desires the fields, he has the power of claiming them; none of us stands in his way. The contributions of the people may flow over to the poor. Let them not stir up hatred over the fields; let him take them if he pleases. I do not give to the Emperor, but I do not deny him. They seek gold; I can say: "I do not seek silver and gold." But they stir up hatred because gold is spent. I do not shrink from this hatred. I have treasurers: my treasurers are the poor of Christ. I know how to gather this treasure. Would that I could always be charged with this crime, that gold is spent on the poor. But if they object that I require protection from them, I do not deny it; I even seek it. I have protection, but it is in the prayers of the poor. The blind and the lame, the weak and the old, are stronger than armed warriors. Finally, the gifts to the poor bind God, because it is written: "He who gives to the poor lends to God." The guards of soldiers often do not deserve divine grace. They also say that the people are deceived by my hymns. Plainly I do not deny this either. That song is great, and nothing is more powerful. For what is more powerful than the confession of the Trinity, which is celebrated every day in the mouths of the whole people? Let all strive eagerly to confess the faith; they know how to proclaim the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit in verses. So all have become teachers, who could scarcely be disciples. What, then, can be more obedient than that we should follow the example of Christ, who, "being found in appearance as a man, humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death"? Finally, he freed all through obedience. "For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many will be made righteous." If, then, he was obedient, let them accept the teaching of obedience, to which we cling, saying to those who stir up hatred against us concerning the Emperor: "We render what is Caesar's to Caesar, and what is God's to God." The tribute is Caesar's; it is not denied. The Church is God's; it certainly ought not to be surrendered to Caesar, because the right of Caesar cannot extend to the temple of God. No one can deny this without dishonouring the Emperor. For what is more honourable than that the Emperor should be called a son of the Church? When this is said, it is said without sin, it is said with grace. For a good emperor is within the Church, not above the Church. For a good emperor seeks the help of the Church, he does not reject it. We say these things humbly, and we set them out with constancy. But some threaten fire, the sword, and exile. We have learned that the servants of Christ do not fear. For those who do not fear, terror is never heavy. Finally, it is written: "The arrows of infants have become their wounds." Therefore enough has seemingly been answered to what has been put forward. Now I ask them what the Saviour asked: "Was the baptism of John from heaven, or from men?" And the Jews could not answer him. If the Jews did not dissolve the baptism of John, does Auxentius dissolve the baptism of Christ? For this baptism is not from men, but from heaven, which the angel of the great counsel brought, so that we might be justified before God. Why, then, does Auxentius think that faithful peoples, baptized in the name of the Trinity, should be baptized again, when the Apostle says: "One faith, one baptism"? And he says that he is an adversary of men, not of Christ, since he despises the counsel of God and condemns the baptism which Christ gave us for the redemption of our sins.

units.la: EPISTOLA XXXIII.
units.tr: Letter XXXIII.

units.la: Diui Ambrosii ad Marcellinam sororem suam, referentis illi quid in causa de Basilicis tradendis actum sit, & in quo statures ipsa nunc consistat.
units.tr: Of the Blessed Ambrose to his sister Marcellina, reporting what was done in the matter of handing over the Basilicas, and in what state the matter now stands.

units.la: QVoniam omnibus epistolis fere sollicite quaeris de Ecclesia, accipe quid agatur. Postridie quam accepi literas tuas, quibus significaueras quod te exagitarent somnia tua, moles inquietudinum grauium coepit moueri. Neciam Portiana, hoc est, extra murana Basilica petebatur, sed Basilica noua, hoc est, intra murana, quae maior est: Conuenerunt me primo, viri comites consistoriani, vt & Basilicam traderem, & prouocarem ne quid populus turbarum moueret. Respondi quod erat ordinis: templum Dei tradi a Sacerdote non posse. Acclamatum est sequenti die in Ecclesia, etiam praefectus eo venit, coepit suadere vt Basilica Portiana cederemus. Populus reclamauit. Ira tunc discessum est, vt intimaturum se Imperatori diceret. Sequenti die, erat autem Dominica, post lectiones atque tractatum dimissis Catechumenis symbolum aliquibus competentibus in baptisterii tradebam Basilicae. Illic nunciatum & mihi comperio, quod ad Portianam Basilicam de palatio decanos misissent, & vela suspenderent, populi partem eo pergere. ego tamen mansi in munere, missam facere coepi. Dum offero, raptum cognoui a populo castulum quendam, quem presbyterum dicerent Arriani. Hunc autem in platea offenderant transeuntes. Amarissime flere, & orare in ipsa oblatione Deum coepi, vt subueniret, ne cuius sanguis in Ecclesia fieret, certe vt meus sanguis pro salute non solum populi, sed etiam pro ipsis impiis effunderetur. Quid multa? Missis presbyteris & diaconibus eripui iniuriae virum. Condemnationes illico grauissimae decernuntur. Primo in corpus omne mercatorum. Itaq; sanctis diebus hebdomadis ultimae, quibus solebant debitorum laxari vincula, strictur catenae, imponuntur collo innocentium, exiguntur ducenta pondo auri intra totum triduum. Respondent aliqui se tantum aut duplum si peterentur daturos, dummodo seruarent fidem. Erat pleni carceres negociatoribus. Palatina omnia officia, hoc est, memoriales, agetes in reb. apparitores diuersorum commitu temperare a processu iubetur, specie qua seditioni interesse prohibebatur: honoratis multa minabantur grauissima nisi Basilicam traderent. Feruebat persecutio: ac si aperuisset portam, proruptui in omne facinus videbantur. Conuenior ipse a comitibus & tribunis, vt Basilicae fieret matura traditraditio, dicentibus Imperatorem iure suo uti, eo quod in potestate eius essent omnia. Respondi, si à me peteret quod meum esset, id est, fundum meum, argentum meum, ius huiusmodi meum, me non refragaturum, quanquam omnia quae mea sunt, vestra sint, pauperum, verum ea quae divina, imperatoriae potestati non esse subiecta. Si patrimonium meum poscit, inuadite: corpus occurram. Vultis in vincula rapere? vultis in mortem? voluptati est mihi. Non ego me vallabo circumfusione populorum, nec altaria tenebo, vitam obsecrans, sed pro altaribus gratius immolabor. Horrebam quippe animo, cum armatos ad Basilicam Ecclesiae occupandam missos cognoscerem, ne dum Basilicam vindicarent, aliquae strages fierent, quae in perniciem totius vergeret civitatis. Orabam ne tantae urbis vel totius Italiae ruina super tanta dolerem. [illegible, ~12 letters] Aderant Gothi tribuni, adorabar eos dicens: [illegible, ~20 letters] Romana suscepi, ut perturbationi publicae vos praebeatis ministros? [illegible, ~10 letters] deleta fuerint, reliquerunt a me ut compesceretur populum. Referebam [illegible, ~8 letters] ne ita iure esse ut non excitarem, sed Dei manu ut mitigaret. Postremo si me incentorem putarent, iam in me vindicari oportere, vel abducerem me in quas vellent terrarum solitudines. His dictis illi abierunt; ego in Basilicam versus noctem exegi diem, inde domum cubiculum me recepi, ut si quis abducere vellet, iam hinc paratum. Ante lucem ubi pedem limina vestibuli, circumfusio militum occupatur Basilica. Idque à militibus Imperatori mandatum dicitur, ut si prodire vellet, haberet copiam, se tamen praesto futuros, si viderent eum cum Catholicis conuenire, alioquin se ad eum coetum quem Ambrosius cogeret transituros. Prodire de Arianis nullus audebat, quia nec quisquam de civibus erat, pauci de familia regia, nonnulli etiam Gothi. Quibus ut olim plastra sedes erat, ita nunc plurimi Ecclesia est. Quocunque foemina illa processerit, secum suos omnes coetus vehit. Circumfusam Basilicam esse gemitu populi intellexi, sed dum legantur lectiones, intimatur mihi plenam populi esse Basilicam etiam nouam, maiorem videri plebem, quam cum esset omnes liberi: lectorem efflagitari. Quid plura? Milites ipsi qui videbantur occupasse Basilicam, cognito quod praecepissem ut abstinerent a communi consortio, ad conuentum huc nostrum venire coeperunt. Quibus visis turbabantur mulierum animi, proripit se vna. Ipsi tamen milites se ad orationem venisse, non ad praelium loquebantur. Clamavit aliqua populus, quam moderate, quam constanter, quam fideliter poscebat ut ad illam Basilicam. In illa quoque Basilica fertur, quod populus praesentiam flagitabat [illegible, ~6 letters].
units.tr: Since you ask in nearly every letter about the Church, hear what is going on. The day after I received your letter, in which you told me that your dreams were troubling you, a heavy storm of troubles began to stir. They demanded the Portian Basilica, that is, the one outside the walls, but it was the New Basilica, that is, the one inside the walls, which is the larger. First the consistorian counts came to me, asking me to hand over the Basilica and to promise that the people would not stir up any disturbance. I replied in keeping with my office: a priest cannot hand over the temple of God. On the following day there was an outcry in the Church. The prefect himself came and began to urge us to give up the Portian Basilica. The people protested loudly. At that point they withdrew in anger, saying they would inform the Emperor. The next day, which was a Sunday, after the readings and the sermon, I dismissed the catechumens and was handing over the Creed to some candidates for baptism in the baptistery of the Basilica. There I was told, and I also learned for myself, that the palace officials had sent deacons to the Portian Basilica and were hanging up curtains, and that a part of the people was going there. Still, I stayed at my post and began to celebrate Mass. While I was offering the sacrifice, I learned that a certain minor cleric, whom the Arians called a presbyter, had been seized by the people. Passers-by had found him in the street. I began to weep bitterly and to pray to God during the very offering, that he would come to help, so that no one's blood would be shed in the Church, and at least that my own blood might be poured out for the salvation not only of the people but of the impious themselves. Why say more? I sent presbyters and deacons and snatched the man from the injustice. The most severe condemnations were decreed at once. First, the whole body of merchants was punished. So, on the holy days of the last week, when the bonds of debtors were usually loosened, chains were tightened and fastened on the necks of innocent men, and two hundred pounds of gold were demanded within three days. Some replied that they would give as much again, or double, if they could keep their faith. The prisons were full of businessmen. All the palace officials, that is, those who draw up petitions and the attendants who handle business for various people, were ordered to refrain from their work, under the pretext that they were forbidden to take part in sedition. The men of rank were threatened with severe penalties unless they handed over the Basilica. The persecution was raging, and it seemed that if I opened the door they would rush into every kind of crime. The counts and tribunes themselves came to me and urged that the Basilica be handed over quickly, saying that the Emperor was using his right, since everything was in his power. I replied that if he asked from me what was mine, that is, my land, my silver, and rights of that kind, I would not resist, although everything that is mine belongs to you and to the poor; but that things belonging to God are not subject to imperial power. If he claims my patrimony, let him seize it; I will go to meet him for my body. Do you want to drag me into chains? Do you want to drag me to death? It is a pleasure to me. I will not protect myself by surrounding myself with crowds of people, nor will I cling to the altars, begging for my life; rather, I will be sacrificed for the altars, which is more welcome. Indeed I shuddered in my heart when I learned that armed men had been sent to seize the Basilica of the Church, lest in defending the Basilica some slaughter should occur, which would threaten the ruin of the whole city. I prayed that I might not grieve over the ruin of so great a city, or of all Italy. [illegible] The Gothic tribunes were present, and I begged them, saying: [illegible] Did I receive the Roman ... that you should become ministers of public disturbance? [illegible] they have been destroyed; they left it to me to restrain the people. I reported [illegible] that it was not right for me to stir them up, but that God's hand should calm them. Finally, if they thought I was the instigator, then I ought to be punished at once, or else I would take myself off into whatever wildernesses of the lands they wished. Having said this, they left. I spent the day and night in the Basilica, and then withdrew to my bedroom at home, so that if anyone wished to take me away, I would already be ready here. Before dawn, when I set foot on the threshold of the vestibule, the Basilica was surrounded by a crowd of soldiers. It was said that the Emperor had ordered the soldiers that if he wished to come out, he would have the opportunity; they themselves, however, would be present if they saw him meeting with the Catholics; otherwise they would go over to the assembly which Ambrose was gathering. No one among the Arians dared to come out, because none of the citizens were among them; there were a few from the royal household, and some Goths too. As once the wagon was their seat, so now the Church is the seat of most of them. Wherever that woman goes, she takes all her followers with her. I understood that the Basilica was surrounded by the groaning of the people, but while the lessons were being read, I was informed that the Basilica was full of people, even the new one, and that the crowd seemed larger than when all of them were free men; they were demanding a reader. What more? The soldiers themselves, who seemed to have occupied the Basilica, when they learned that I had ordered them to abstain from fellowship in common, began to come to our gathering here. When they were seen, the minds of the women were troubled, and one of them rushed forward. The soldiers themselves said that they had come to pray, not to fight. A woman cried out, how calmly, how steadfastly, how faithfully the people demanded that I go to that Basilica. It is also reported that in that Basilica too the people were asking for my presence [illegible].

units.la: Tunc ego hunc adorsus sermonem sum: Audistis fili librum legi Iob; qui solenni munere est decursus, & tempore. Sciunt & vsu hunc librum etiam Diabolus intimandum, quo virtus omnis suae tentationis aperitur & proditur, & ideo se hodie motu maiore concussit, sed gratias Deo nostro, qui nos ita firmauit fide & patientia. Vnum Iob mituratus ascenderam, omnes Iob quos mirarer inueni. In singulis vobis Iob reuixit, in singulis sancti illius patientia & virtus refulsit. Quid enim praelentius dici potuit a Christianis viris, quam id quod hodie in vobis Spiritus sanctus est locutus? Rogamus Augustæ, non pugnamus. Non timemus, sed rogamus. Hoc Christianos decet, ut & tranquillitas pacis optetur, & fidei e veritatis que constantia, nec mortis renouetur periculo. Est enim praesul Dominus, qui fatuos faciet sperantes in se.
units.tr: Then I began to address them: My sons, you have heard the book of Job read, which has been run through in its appointed service and at its proper time. The Devil too knows this book by experience, since in it all his power of temptation is laid open and revealed; and so today he has shaken himself with greater violence. But thanks be to our God, who has strengthened us thus in faith and patience. I had gone up only as far as one Job, but I have found all of you to be Jobs whom I might admire. In each of you Job has come to life again; in each of you the patience and virtue of that holy man have shone forth. For what more fitting thing could be said by Christian men than what the Holy Spirit has spoken today through you? We petition the Empress; we do not fight. We do not fear, but we petition. This is fitting for Christians, that they should desire the tranquillity of peace, and yet the steadfastness of faith and truth, and not renew the danger of death. For the Lord is a judge, who makes foolish those who trust in themselves.

units.la: Sed veniamus ad propositas lectiones. Videtis Diabolo tentandi licentiam dari, ut boni probentur. Inuidet inimicus bonis profectibus, tentat diuersis modis. Tentauit sanctum Iob in patrimonio, tentauit in filiis, tentauit in dolore corporis. Fortior in suo corpore tentatur, infirmior in alieno. Et mihi meas diuitias, quas in vobis habeo, volebat auferre, & hoc tranquillitatis vestrae patrimonium dissipare cupiebat. Vos quoque ipsos mihi bonos filios gestiebat eripere, pro quibus ego quotidie instauro sacrificium, vos ruinis quibusdam publicae perturbationis conabatur inuoluere. Duo igitur iam genera tentationis excepi. Et forte quia infirmiorem me Dominus Deus nouit, adhuc in corpus meum non dedit potestatem. Et si ipse cupiam & si offeram, adhuc me fortasse huic certamini imparem iudicat, & diuersis exercet laboribus. Nec Iob ab isto coepit certamine, sed in hoc consummauit. Tentatus est autem Iob nuncijs coaceruatis malorum, tentatus est etiam per mulierem, quae ait: Dic aliquod verbum in Deum, & morere. Videtis quanta subito moueantur Gothi, Gentiles, multa mercatorum, poena sanctorum. Aduersitis quid iubeatur cum mandatur: Trade Basilicam, hoc est, dic aliquod verbum in Deum. Nec solum dic aduersus Deum, sed etiam fac aduersus Deum. Mandatur, Trade aliud Deo. Vigemur igitur praeceptis regalibus, sed confirmatur Scripturæ sermonibus: quae re- [illegible, ~10 letters] Tanquam ma ex insipientibus locuturus. Non mediocris igitur ista tentatio. Namque aspergationes has esse cognouimus, quae fiunt per mulieres. Denique per Euam etiam Adam supplantatus est: ebque factum, vt à mandatis coelestibus deuiaret. Quo errore cognito, praevaricatricis conscientiæ reus latere cupiebat, sed latere non poterat, & ideo ait ei Deus: Adam ubi es? Hoc est, quid eras ante? vbi nunc esse coepisti? vbi te constitueraм? quo ipse transgressus es? Agnoscis esse te nudum, quia bonæ indumenta fidei perdidisti. Folia sunt ista, quibus nunc vestire optabatis. Repudiasti fructum, sub foliis legis latere cupis, sed proderis. Recedetis a Domino Deo, quod ipsa propter vnam mulierem desiderasti, propterea fugis quem videre quaerebas. Cum vna muliere te abscondere maluisti, relinquere speculum mundi, incolatum Paradisi, gratiam Christi. Quid dicam, quod etiam Heliam Iezabel cruenta persecuta est? Quod Ioannem Baptistam Herodias fecit occidi? Singulae tamen singulos, mihi quo minora longe merita, eo tenta-
units.tr: But let us come to the lessons set before us. You see that the Devil is given license to tempt, so that the good may be proved. The enemy envies good progress and tempts in various ways. He tempted holy Job in his property, he tempted him in his children, he tempted him in the pain of his body. A stronger man is tempted in his own body, a weaker man in another's. He also wanted to take from me my riches, which I have in you, and he desired to squander this patrimony of your tranquillity. He also longed to snatch from me you yourselves, my good sons, for whom I offer sacrifice every day; he tried to entangle you in the ruins of public disturbance. So I have now faced two kinds of temptation. And perhaps because the Lord God knows that I am weaker, he has not yet given the power over my body. Even if I desire it, and even if I offer myself, perhaps he still judges me unequal to this contest, and exercises me with various labours. Nor did Job begin with that conflict, but he was perfected in it. Job was tempted by messengers bringing heaps of evils; he was tempted also through a woman, who said: "Say some word against God and die." You see how suddenly the Goths, the Gentiles, the crowds of merchants, and the punishment of the saints are stirred up. Consider what is commanded when it is ordered: "Hand over the Basilica," that is, "say some word against God." Not only say something against God, but also do something against God. They order: "Hand over something else to God." We are therefore pressed by royal commands, but are strengthened by the words of Scripture, which [illegible] As if I were about to speak as one of the foolish. This temptation is therefore no small one. For we have learned that these are the snares which are laid by women. Indeed, through Eve, Adam too was overthrown, and it came about that he turned aside from the heavenly commands. When he recognised this error, he, guilty of a conscience that had transgressed, wished to hide, but could not hide; and so God said to him: "Adam, where are you?" That is: what were you before? Where have you now begun to be? Where did you place yourself? By what did you yourself transgress? You recognise that you are naked, because you have lost the good garments of faith. Those leaves are what you now wished to clothe yourself with. You have rejected the fruit; you want to hide under the leaves of the law, but you will be exposed. You withdraw from the Lord God, which you yourself desired on account of one woman; therefore you flee from him whom you were seeking to see. You preferred to hide yourself with one woman than to leave the mirror of the world, the dwelling of Paradise, the grace of Christ. What shall I say, that even Elijah was pursued with bloody persecution by Jezebel? That Herodias caused John the Baptist to be killed? Yet each one of these women tempted each man, and the more my merits are far smaller, the more grievous are the temptations [illegible]. The weaker strength, but the greater danger. The turns of women follow one another, hatreds alternate, schemes vary, the elders are gathered together, the injury of the king is put forward as a pretext. What reason then is there for directing heavier temptations against this little worm, except that it is not me, but...

units.la: { } [illegible, ~3 letters] tentamenta grauiora. Virtus infirmior, sed plus periculi. Succedunt sibi mulierum vices, alternantur odia, commenta variantur, seniores conueniuntur, praetextitur regis iniuria. Quae ratio igitur est aduersus hunc vermiculum moliri grauiores tentationes, nisi quia non me, sed Ecclesiam persequuntur? Mundatur denique. Trade Basilicam. Respondeo. Nec mihi fas est tradere, nec tibi accipere Imperator expedit. Dominium priuati nullo potes iure temerare, domum Dei existimas auferendam? Allegatur, Imperatori licere omnia, ipsius esse vniuersa. Respondeo: Noli te grauare, Imperator, vt putes te in ea quae diuina sunt, imperiale aliquod ius habere. Noli te extollere, sed si vis diutius imperare, esto Deo subditus. Scriptum est: Quae Dei Deo, quae Caesaris Caesari. Ad Imperatorem palatia pertinent, ad Sacerdotem Ecclesiae. Publicorum tibi moenium ius commissum est, non sacrorum. Iterum dicitur mandasse: Debeo & ego vnam Basilicam habere. Respondi: Non tibi licet illam habere. Quid tibi cum adultera? Adultera est enim, quae non est legitimo Christi coniugio copulata. Dum haec tracto, suggestum est mihi cortinas regias esse collectas: refertam autem populo Basilicam, praesentiam mei poscere: statimque eo conuerti sermonem meum, dicens: Quam alta & profunda oracula sunt Spiritus sancti. Matutinis horis lectum est, vt meministis fratres, quod summo animi dolore respondemus: Deus venerunt gentes in hereditatem tuam. Et reuera venerunt gentes, & plus etiam quam gentes venerunt. Venerunt enim Gothi, & diuersarum nationum viri, venerunt cum armis, & circumfusi occupauerunt Basilicam. Hoc nos ignari tuae altitudinis dolebamus, sed nostra imprudentia aliud opinabatur. Venerunt gentes, sed vere in hereditatem tuum venerunt. Qui enim gentes venerunt, facti sunt Christiani. Qui ad inuadendam hereditatem venerunt, facti sunt coheredes Dei. Defensores habeo, quos hostes putabam: socios teneo; quos aduersarios existimabam. Completum est illud, quod de Domino Iesu Dauid Propheta cecinit: Quia factus est in pace locus eius, & confregit cornua arcuum, scutum, & gladium, & bellum. Cuius enim hoc munus, cuius opus, nisi tuum Domine Iesu? Videbas ad templum tuum armatos venire, hinc gemere populum, & frequentem adesse, ne Basilica Dei traderetur: inde enim militibus, Imperatori: mortem ante oculos mihi: ne quid inter haec furori liceret, inseruisti te Domine medium, & fecisti vtraque vnum. Compescuisti armatos dicens profecto: Si ad arma concurritur, si in templo meo lis commouetur, quae vtilitas in sanguine meo? Gratias itaque tibi Christe: non legatus, neque nuncius, sed tu Domine saluum fecisti populum tuum, conscidisti saccum meum, & praecinxisti me laetitia. Haec ego dicebam ratus Imperatoris animum studio militum, obsecratione comitum, precatu populi posse mitescere. Interea nunciatur mihi missum notarium, qui mandata deferret. Concessi paululum, mandatumque intimat. Quid tibi visum est, inquit, vt contra placitum faceres? Respondi: Quid placitum sit ignoro, quidue temere factum dicatur, incertum habeo. Ait: cur presbyteros ad Basilicam destinasti? Si tyrannus es, scire volo, vt sciam quemadmodum me aduersum te praeparem. Retuli dicens me nihil in praeiudicium fecisse Ecclesiae: eo tempore quo audieram occupatam esse a militibus Basilicam, gemitum tantummodo liberiorem habuisse: multisque adhortantibus vt eo pergerem, dixisse: Tradere Basilicam non possum, sed pugnare non debeo. Postea vero quam cognoueram cortinas regias inde esse sublatas, cum me populus eo ire deposceret, direxisse presbyteros, me tamen noluisse ire, sed dixisse: Credo in Christo quod ipse nobiscum faciet Imperator. Si haec tyrannis videtur, habeo arma, sed in Christi nomine, habeo offerendi mei corporis potestatem. Quid moraretur ferire, si tyrannum putaret? Veteri iure a sacerdotibus donata imperia, non vsurpata. Et vulgo dici, quod Imperatores sacerdotium magis optauerint, quam Imperium sacerdotes. Christus fugit, ne rex fieret. Habemus tyrannidem nostram. Tyrannis sacerdotis, infirmitas est. Cum infirmor, inquit, tunc potens sum. Cauere tamen ne ipse sibi tyrannum faceret, cui Deus aduersarium non excitauit. Non hoc Maximum dicere, quod tyrannus ego sim Valentiniani, qui si meae legationis obiectu quaeritur ad Italiam non potuisse transire. Addidi, quia nunquam sacerdotes tyranni fuerunt, sed tyrannos saepe sunt passi. Exactus est totus ille dies in moerore nostro, scissae tamen ab illudentibus pueris cortinae regiae. Ego domum redire non potui, quia circumfusi erant milites, qui Basilicam custodiebant. Cum fratribus Psalmos in Ecclesiae Basilica minore diximus. Sequenti die lectus est de more liber Ionae, quo completo hunc sermonem adorsus sum. Liber lectus est fratres quo prophetatur quod peccatores in poenitentiam reuertantur. Acceptum est ita, vt sperararetur in praesenti futurum. Addidi quod vir iustus etiam offensam contrahere voluisset, ne vel spectaret, vel denunciaret excidium ciuitati. Et quod lugubre esset illud dictum, contristatus quoque sit, quod aruisset cucurbita. Deum quoque dixisse ad prophetam: Si tristis es pro cucurbita? Respondisse Ionam: tristis. Dixisse Dominum, si illud doleret quod exusta esset cucurbita, quanto magis sibi cura esse oportere tanta plebis salutem? Et ideo excidium quod paratum toti urbi fuerat, remouisse: Nec mora, nunciatur Imperatorem iussisse vt recederent milites de Basilica, negociatoribus quoque, quod exacti de condemnatione fuerant redderetur. Quae nunc plebis totius laetitia fuit? Qui totius populi plausus? quae gratia? Erat autem dies quo se Dominus pro nobis tradidit, quo in Ecclesia poenitentia relaxatur. Certatim hoc nunciare milites, irruentes in altaria osculis significare pacis insigne. Tunc agnoui quod Deus vermem antelucanum percusserat, vt tota ciuitas seruaretur. Haec gesta sunt, atque vrinam iam finita. Sed grauiores motus futuros, plena commotionis imperialia verba indicant. Ego tyrannus appellor, & plus etiam quam tyrannus. Nam cum Imperatorem comites obsecrarent, vti prodiret ad Ecclesiam, idq; petitum militum facere
units.tr: [illegible] heavier temptations. Their strength is weaker, but the danger is greater. Their roles succeed one another among the women; hatreds alternate, schemes change, elders are gathered together, and the king's wrong is put forward as a pretext. What reason, then, is there for them to launch heavier attacks against this little worm, unless it is because they are pursuing not me but the Church? "Finally, let them be cleansed. Hand over the basilica." I reply: it is not lawful for me to hand it over, and it is not expedient for you, Emperor, to receive it. You cannot violate a private person's property by any right, and do you think the house of God should be taken away? It is alleged that the Emperor may do everything and that all things belong to him. I reply: do not burden yourself, Emperor, by thinking that you have any imperial right over things that belong to God. Do not exalt yourself; but if you want to rule for longer, be subject to God. It is written: "Render to God the things that are God's, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's." Palaces belong to the Emperor, churches to the priest. The right over public walls has been committed to you, not the right over sacred things. Again it is said that he ordered: "I too ought to have one basilica." I answered: "It is not lawful for you to have it. What have you to do with an adulteress? For she is an adulteress who is not joined in the lawful marriage of Christ." While I was dealing with these matters, it was reported to me that the royal hangings had been gathered up, and that the basilica was full of people demanding my presence. Immediately I turned my discourse to that point, saying: "How high and deep are the oracles of the Holy Spirit!" In the morning hours, as you remember, brothers, there was read, and with the deepest grief of mind we responded: "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance." And indeed the nations came, and more than nations came. For the Goths came, and men of various nations; they came with arms and, surrounding it, occupied the basilica. We, ignorant of your depth, grieved over this, but our lack of foresight judged otherwise. The nations came, but truly they came into your inheritance. For those who came as nations became Christians; those who came to seize the inheritance became fellow heirs of God. I have as defenders those whom I thought were enemies; I hold as allies those whom I considered adversaries. That has been fulfilled which the prophet David sang concerning the Lord Jesus: "In peace is his place, and he has broken the bows, the shield, the sword, and the battle." For whose gift is this, whose work, if not yours, Lord Jesus? You saw armed men coming to your temple, the people groaning on this side, and a crowd present lest the basilica of God be handed over; on that side, the soldiers and the Emperor, and death before my eyes. So that nothing might be permitted to fury in the midst of these things, you, Lord, inserted yourself between them and made both one. You restrained the armed men, saying in effect: "If men rush to arms, if strife is stirred in my temple, what profit is there in my blood?" Therefore, thanks be to you, Christ: not an envoy, nor a messenger, but you yourself, Lord, saved your people, you loosed my sackcloth and girded me with gladness. I was saying these things, thinking that the Emperor's mind could be softened by the zeal of the soldiers, the entreaties of the courtiers, and the supplications of the people. Meanwhile I was told that a notary had been sent to deliver orders. I gave way a little, and he announced his commission. "What seemed best to you," he said, "that you should act against the decree?" I replied: "I do not know what the decree is, nor do I have any certain notion of what is said to have been done rashly." He said: "Why did you send elders to the basilica? If you are a tyrant, I want to know, so that I may know how to prepare myself against you." I answered, saying that I had done nothing to the prejudice of the Church. At the time I had heard that the basilica had been occupied by soldiers, I had only allowed myself a freer groaning; and when many urged me to go there, I had said: "I cannot hand over the basilica, but I ought not to fight." Afterwards, when I had learned that the royal hangings had been taken from there, and when the people demanded that I go there, I sent the elders, but I did not want to go myself, saying: "I believe in Christ that he himself will act with us, the Emperor." "If this seems tyranny to you, I have arms, but in the name of Christ; I have the power of offering my body." Why would he delay to strike, if he thought me a tyrant? Empires were granted to the priests by ancient right; they were not usurped. And it is commonly said that emperors have desired the priesthood more than priests have desired empire. Christ fled so that he would not be made king. We have our own tyranny. The tyranny of a priest is weakness. "When I am weak," he says, "then I am strong." Yet let him beware lest he make himself a tyrant, for whom God has not raised up an adversary. I do not say this as Maximus did, that I am a tyrant over Valentinian, who, if the pretext of my embassy is brought forward, could not have crossed into Italy. I added that priests have never been tyrants, but have often suffered at the hands of tyrants. That whole day was spent in our mourning, though the royal hangings were torn by boys mocking us. I could not return home, because soldiers were surrounding us and guarding the basilica. With the brothers we sang psalms in the Church's smaller basilica. On the following day, as is customary, the book of Jonah was read, and when it was finished I took up this sermon. The book was read, brothers, in which it is prophesied that sinners will return to repentance. It was received in such a way that what was to come was hoped for in the present. I added that a righteous man had even been willing to incur offence, lest he either witness or announce the destruction of the city; and that, since the words were mournful, he was also grieved because the gourd had withered. God also said to the prophet: "Are you grieved for the gourd?" Jonah answered: "I am grieved." The Lord said: "If you grieve over the gourd that was scorched, how much more ought I to care for the salvation of so great a people?" And so he removed the destruction that had been prepared for the whole city. Without delay, it was announced that the Emperor had ordered the soldiers to withdraw from the basilica, and that the money-changers, who had been ejected by the condemnation, should be restored. What then was the joy of the whole people? What the applause of the whole populace? What grace? It was the day on which the Lord gave himself up for us, on which repentance is granted in the Church. The soldiers hastened to announce this, rushing into the altars and signifying with kisses the token of peace. Then I recognised that God had struck the worm of the morning, so that the whole city might be saved. These things have been done, and the matter is now concluded. But the imperial words, full of agitation, indicate that heavier disturbances are to come. I am called a tyrant, and more than a tyrant. For when the courtiers begged the Emperor to come out to the Church, and the soldiers asked for this to be done...

units.la: se ludicet ret, respondit: Si vobis iusserit Ambrosius, vinctum me tradetis. Quid post haec vocem suspexit consideram. Quam vocem omnes cohorruerunt. Sed habet à quibus exalperetur. Deinque etiam speciali expressione Calligonus praepositus cubiculi mandare mihi ausus est: Me vivo tu contemnis Valentinianum? Caput tibi tollo. Respondi: Deus permittat tibi vt impleas quod minaris. Ego enim patior quod Episcopi, tu facies spadonis. Atque vtinam Dominus auertat eos ab Ecclesia, & in me omnia sua tela convertant, meo sanguine sitim suam expleant.
units.tr: ...he played the fool and replied: "If Ambrose orders it, you will hand me over bound." After these words I considered what voice had been raised up; all shuddered at that voice. But he has those by whom he is provoked. Then Calligonus, the chamberlain, presumed to threaten me with a special outburst: "While I live, do you despise Valentinian? I will take off your head." I answered: "May God permit you to carry out what you threaten. For I suffer what bishops suffer, and you will do what eunuchs do. And would that the Lord turn them away from the Church, and turn all their weapons against me, and satisfy their thirst with my blood."

units.la: B. HIERONYMI STRIDONENSIS PRESBYTERI EPISTOLA AD EVAGRIVM.
units.tr: The Letter of Saint Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon, to Evagrius.

units.la: Anno Christi 380.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 380.

units.la: Qualiter Presbyter & Diaconus differant: in qua ostenditur, Presbyterum Diacono in honore longe praestare: & in primitiva Ecclesia eundem fuisse Episcopum & Presbyterum, sed in schismatis remedium unum fuisse praepositum, & in hoc orbis potius quam Vrbis sequendam consuetudinem.
units.tr: How a Presbyter and a Deacon differ. This shows that the presbyter far surpasses the deacon in honour, that in the primitive Church the same person was both bishop and presbyter, that one man was set over the others as a remedy for schism, and that in this matter the custom of the whole world, rather than that of the city of Rome, should be followed.

units.la: Egimus in Esaia, sanum fatua loquitur. Audio quendam in tantam erupisse vecordiam, vt Diaconos presbyteris, id est, Episcopis anteferret. Nam cum Apostolus perspicue doceat, eosdem esse presbyteros, quos Episcopos, quid patitur mensarum & viduarum minister, vt super eos tumidus se efferat, ad quorum preces Christi corpus sanguisque conficitur? Quaeris autoritatem, audi testimonium: Paulus & Timotheus servi Christi Iesu omnibus Sanctis in Christo Iesu qui sunt in Philippis, cum Episcopis & Diaconibus. Vis & aliud exemplum? in Actibus Apostolorum ad vnius Ecclesiae Sacerdotes ita Paulus loquitur: Attendite vobis & cuncto gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus posuit Episcopos, vt regeretis Ecclesiam Domini, quam acquisivit sanguine suo. Ac ne quis contentiose in una Ecclesia plures Episcopos fuisse contendat, audi & aliud testimonium, in quo manifestissime comprobatur eundem esse Episcopum atque Presbyterum: Propter hoc reliquite te certe, vt quae deerant corrigeres & constitueres presbyteros per civitates, sicut & ego tibi mandavi. Si quis est sine crimine, vnius vxoris vir, filios habens fideles, non in accusatione luxuriae, aut non subditos; oportet enim Episcopum sine crimine esse quasi Dei dispensatorem. Et ad Timotheum: Noli negligere gratiam, quae tibi data est Prophetia per impositionem manuum presbyterii. Sed & Petrus in prima epistola: Presbyteros, inquit, in vobis precor compresbyter & testis passionum Christi & futurae gloriae, quae revelanda est, participes, regere gregem Christi, & inspicere non ex necessitate, sed voluntarie iuxta Deum. Quod quidem Graece significantius dicitur ἐπισκοποῦντες, id est, Superintendentes, unde & nomen Episcopi tractum est. Parua tibi videntur tantorum virorum testimonia? clangat tuba Evangelica, filius tonitrui, quem Iesus amavit plurimum, qui de pectore Salvatoris doctrinarum fluenta potavit: Presbyter Electae Dominae & filiis eius, quos ego diligo in veritate. Et in alia epistola: Presbyter Caio carissimo, quem ego diligo in veritate. Quod antem postea vnus electus est qui caeteris praeponeretur, in schismatis remedium factum est; ne vnusquisque ad se trahens, Christi Ecclesiam rumperet. Nam & Alexandriae à Marco Evangelista vsque ad Heradam & Dionysium Episcopos, Presbyteri semper vnum de se electum, & in excelsiori gradu collocatum, Episcopum nominabant: quomodo si exercitus Imperatorem faciat; aut Diaconi eligant de se quem industrium noverint, & Archidiaconum vocent. Quid enim facit, excepta ordinatione, Episcopus, quod Pretbyter non facit? Nec altera Romanae urbis Ecclesia, altera totius orbis aestimanda est: & Galliae, & Britaniae, & Africa, & Persis, & Orient, & India, & omnes Barbarae nationes vnum Christum adorant, vnam observant regulam veritatis. Si autoritas quaeritur, orbis maior est urbe. Vbicunque fuerit Episcopus, sive Romae, sive Eugubii, sive Constantinopoli, sive Regii, sive Alexandriae, sive Thanis, eiusdem meriti, eiusdem & Sacerdotii. Potentia divitiarum, & paupertatis humilitas, vel sublimiorem vel inferiorem Episcopum facit: caeterum omnes Apostolorum successores sunt. Sed dicis quomodo ad testimonium Diaconi Presbyter ordinatur? Quid mihi profers vnius urbis consuetudinem? Quid paucitatem, de qua ortum est supercilium, in leges Ecclesiae vindicas? Omne, quod rarum est, plus appetitur. Pulegium apud Indos pipere pretiosius est: Diaconos paucitas honorabiles, Presbyteros turba contemptibiles facit. Caeterum etiam in Ecclesia Romae Presbyteri sedent, & stant Diaconi, (licet paulatim increbrescentibus vitiis inter Presbyteros absente Episcopo sedere Diaconi viderim,) & in domesticis conuiviis benedictiones Presbyteris dare discant. Qui hoc faciunt, non se recte facere sciant, & audiant Apostolos: non est dignum vt relinquentes verbum Dei, ministrare mensis. Sciant quare Diaconi constituti sunt, legant Acta Apostolorum, recordetur conditionis suae. Presbyter & Episcopus aliud ætatis, aliud dignitatis est nomen. Unde quod ad Titum & ad Timotheum de ordinatione Diaconi & Episcopi dicitur, de Presbyteris omnino reticetur: quia in Episcopo & Presbyter continetur, qui prouehitur, de minori ad maius prouehitur. Aut igitur ex Presbytero ordinetur Diaconus, ut Presbyter minor Diacono comprobetur, in quem crescit ex paruo: aut si ex Diacono ordinetur Presbyter, noverit se lucris minorem, Sacerdotio esse maiorem. Et ut sciamus traditiones Apostolicas sumptas de veteri testamento, quod Aaron & filii eius atq; Leuitæ in templo fuerint, hoc sibi Episcopi, & Presbyteri, & Diaconi vendicent in Ecclesia.
units.tr: We have dealt with this in Isaiah: a sane man talks foolishly. I hear that someone has broken out into such madness that he puts deacons above presbyters, that is, above bishops. For since the Apostle plainly teaches that elders and bishops are the same, what right has a server of tables and widows to puff himself up above those at whose prayers the body and blood of Christ are consecrated? You ask for authority? Hear the testimony: Paul and Timothy, the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons. Do you want another example? In the Acts of the Apostles, Paul speaks thus to the priests of one church: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood. And lest anyone contentiously argue that there were several bishops in one church, hear another testimony, in which it is most clearly proved that bishop and presbyter are the same: For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee: if any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly. For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God. And to Timothy: Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. But Peter too, in his first epistle: The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed: feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint but willingly, according to God. In Greek this is said even more expressively as [ἐπισκοποῦντες], that is, superintendents, from which the name of bishop is also derived. Do the testimonies of such great men seem slight to you? Let the Evangelical trumpet sound, the son of thunder, whom Jesus loved most, who drank the streams of doctrine from the Saviour's breast: The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth. And in another epistle: The elder unto the well-beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth. That afterwards one was chosen to be set over the rest was done as a remedy for schism, so that each man, drawing people to himself, would not break the Church of Christ. For at Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist down to Heraclas and Dionysius the bishops, the presbyters always chose one from among themselves, placed him in a higher rank, and called him bishop. It is as if an army should make its own emperor, or as if deacons should choose from among themselves someone whom they judged diligent and call him archdeacon. For what does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do? Nor is the Church of the city of Rome to be esteemed one thing and the Church of the whole world another: Gaul, Britain, Africa, Persia, the East, India, and all the barbarian nations worship one Christ and observe one rule of truth. If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city. Wherever there is a bishop, whether at Rome, or at Eugubium, or at Constantinople, or at Rhegium, or at Alexandria, or at Tanis, he is of the same worth and of the same priesthood. Wealth and power, or the humility of poverty, make a bishop higher or lower, but in all things they are all successors of the Apostles. But you say, how is a presbyter ordained with the testimony of a deacon? Why do you bring forward the custom of one city to me? Why do you claim for the laws of the Church the scarcity from which pride has arisen? Whatever is rare is more sought after: pennyroyal is more valuable than pepper among the Indians. Scarcity makes deacons honourable, and crowds make presbyters contemptible. Moreover, even in the Church at Rome presbyters sit and deacons stand (although, as vices gradually increased, I have seen deacons sitting among the presbyters when the bishop was absent), and they learn to give blessings to presbyters at private dinners. Let those who do this know that they do not act rightly, and let them hear the Apostles: It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables. Let them know why deacons were appointed, let them read the Acts of the Apostles, let them remember their own condition. Presbyter and bishop are names of age, not of dignity. Hence, although what is said to Titus and Timothy about the ordination of deacons and bishops says nothing at all about presbyters, this is because the presbyter is included in the bishop: whoever is promoted is promoted from a lesser to a greater rank. So either a deacon is ordained from among the presbyters, so that the presbyter is shown to be lower than the deacon, into whom he grows from small beginnings; or, if a presbyter is ordained from among the deacons, let him know that in merit he is less, but in priesthood greater. And so that we may know that the Apostolic traditions were taken from the Old Testament, where Aaron and his sons and the Levites were in the temple, let bishops, presbyters and deacons claim these roles for themselves in the Church.

units.la: B. HIERONYMI STRIDONENSIS PRESBYTERI, TRACTATUS
units.tr: Saint Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon, A Treatise

units.la: De correctione, vita & conuersatione Episcopi ac Clericorum: ad Rusticum Episcopum Narbonensem.
units.tr: On the correction, life and conduct of a bishop and clerics: to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne.

units.la: Sufficere quidem fidei tuæ arbitror conuersationem sanctam, quam habes in Christo Iesu ad Sacerdotalis ordinis dignitatem, arctam tibi & angustam intellectus viam in Domino referare: quia præcedentibus meritis ac virtutis insignibus ad hoc officium electus à Deo es. Licet in multis gratia Christi sine operibus comprobetur, & cessante merito conuersationis ac vitæ sola Dei dona fructificent: tamen quia tu præ cæteris electus à Deo comprobaris, qui & legis opera impleuisti, & commoraris in gratia usque ad supereminentem scientiæ caritatem, intellectu Dei tecum loquente festinanter existentibus cogitationibus insignibus hoc vis nosse quod futurus es, totius tibi Ecclesiæ, prout præcipis, Sacramenta reservabo, doctrinæ ordinem & locum custodiens, & quid qualiter obseruare debeas docens: si modo ad iniuriam non reuocet nouellæ exhortationis industriam, ac te non pudeat paulisper minorem esse dum discis; quia sepositio, ut vides, priuilegio dignitatis, habes de nobis amplius quod quæras, & id quod iam pridem in consecratione constitutum te esse cognoscis. Restat quod capias, ne minor inueniaris in Christo, quam in mundo interim nominaris: ac si falsi vocabuli inutilis pastor existas, cum hæc quæ in Domino latent Sacramenta nescires. Nos tamen tenentes in omni disputatione rationem, ac tecum simpliciter fabulantes, verum te Episcopum animarum debere esse monstrabimus, ut factus tibi ipse index, hoc quod loquimur implere festines: & nobis consentiens, verecundia & confusione reiecta, eligas abiectus esse in domo Dei magis, quam habitare in tabernaculis peccatorum. Sic enim Iesus ait: Reges gentium dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent, domini vocantur; vos autem non sic: sed qui maior est vestrum, fiat sicut minor; & qui princeps est, fiat sicut minister, quis enim maior est, qui recumbit, aut qui ministrat? In gentibus quidem qui discumbit; inter vos autem non sic, sed qui ministrat. Ego autem in medio vestrum sum, sicut qui ministrat, & vos qui estis mecum in tentationibus meis: ego dispono vobis, sicut disposuit mihi pater meus regnum, ut edatis & bibatis in mensa mea in regno meo, & sedeatis super sedes duodecim tribus Israel. Et alibi: Rectorem posuerunt te, noli extolli, sed esto tanquam unus ex ipsis. Et alibi: Non ut domineris clero, sed ut forma sis ouibus. Et alibi: Templum Dei estis, & spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Si quis autem templum Dei violauerit, disperdet illum Deus: templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos, quoniam ex ipso, & per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia, ipsi gloria in secula. Unus enim Deus & pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ex quo omnia, & nos in ipso, & unus Dominus Iesus Christus, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Sed non in omnibus est scientia. Cæcitas enim contigit ex parte Israel, donec plenitudo gentium intraret, & sic omnis Israel saluus fieret. Conclusit ergo Deus omnia sub peccato, ut omnium misereatur. Ante omnia humilitatem dilige, quia superbia apostatare facit à Deo, & initium omnis peccati superbia est. Deus enim noster formam serui accipiens humiliauit se usque ad mortem; mortem autem crucis. Omnes scripturas mente percurre, totum canonem lege, atque habens ante oculos exempla sanctorum, imitare quod bonum est, æmulare quod sanctum est, factusque tibi Hierosolyma cœlestis Deo vota reddituc, domum in te & templum Salomonis ædifica, tabernaculum fabrica, & diligentius exornare festina, intra sancta sanctorum indeficiens lumen accende: persectionem in omnibus tene, pone custodiam ori tuo, & ostium circumstantiæ labris tuis. Non des in tentationem animam tuam, & non obdormiet qui custodit. Exalta vocem tuam & dic: omnis caro fœnum, & omnis gloria eius sicut flos fœni, aruit fœnum & flos decidit; verbum autem Domini manet in æternum. Sacerdos enim Domini, qui de ore suo profert iustitiam, & exquirentibus nunciat veritatem, angelus Dei omnipotentis est. In omnibus causis serua iustitiam, peregrinantem, & orphanum, & viduam, & pauperem, vel pupillum vacuo gremio non dimittas: ibique thesaurum tuum, ubi corrum est, conde, cum omnibus fratribus tuis, sicut scriptum est, pacem habe. Consilia fuge, ne, dum iudicas, condemneris, sicut enim scriptum est: beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum, & in via peccatorum non stetit, & in cathedra pestilentiæ non sedit, sed in lege Domini fuit voluntas eius, & in lege eius meditabitur die ac nocte. Potentum personas, diuitum notitias, salutantium obsequia ita accipe ut pauperem non contristes, nec ulli fastidium excusationis inducas. Non recedat liber legis, ut scriptum est, de manu tua; sed meditare in ea die ac nocte. Sic enim scriptum est: sine offensione estote Iudæis & Græcis & Ecclesiæ Dei, sicut & ego omnibus per omnia placeo, non quærens quod mihi utile est, sed quod multis ut salvi fiant. Prius quam audias ne iudices quenquam, atq; ante probationem accusationis illatæ neminem à tua communione suspendas: quia non statim qui accusatur reus est, sed qui convincitur criminosus. Nec præstandum odiis singulorum est, ut innocentum fratrum doneturiniuria: quinimo timorem Domini ante oculos semper habens, ut totum quod agitur Deo & Christo scias esse præsentandum: nam præterit figura huius mundi, & Deo magis obedire convenit, quam hominibus. Qui scit præterita, de futuris æstimat. Uno enim sermone tota lex adimpletur, Omne quod tibi fieri noluveris, alii ne feceris. Domi, si fieri potest, postposita personæ tuæ cura officiique reverentia, servum servis esse te convenit, atque ita Israel in omnibus perdocere, ut, quicunq; audiunt, conversatione tua magis quam sermone proficiant. Sic enim scriptum est; in sapientia ambulate ad eos qui foris sunt. Non te extollat salutatio plurimorum munera divitum & obsequia te non vnicant, quia munera, ut scriptum est, excæcant oculos iudicum, nec plus sit apud te matrona nobilis & dives, quam professa pauper atq; mendica; aut vidua maritali auxilio destituta æqualis ei, quæ habet virum potentem in seculo, videatur. Alienum te à personis omnium reddendum iudica, ac propter iniustitiam in iudicio pauperem non defendas, nec propter gratiam diviti indecenter assistas: aut si hoc non potes facere, cognitionem respue causarum. Sola esto tibi lectione & oratione contentus. Neminem enim, ut scriptum est, diligit Deus, nisi eum qui cum sapientia habitat ac nullum lædit. Ista si feceris, Deo utilis, in omnibus comprobatus, persectum Sacerdotium in te retentabis. Expelle de templo Christi oues, & boues, & columbas vendentes, & numulariorum euerte mensas: quia domus patris nostri domus negotiationis esse non debet, sed orationis. Et quod iudicio Dei proiicitur, desiderari propter damnationis sententiam non optet, ne reprobi inveniamur in Christo: Sicque fiet ut in veritate consistens septiformis Ecclesiæ Sacramentum nosse mereaiis, quod in omnipotentia Dei cum sui veneratione consistit, id est, in Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto; in Archangelis, in Angelis, in sapientia, in hominibus. Quæ omnia si diligenter inspicias, totius in his dispositionibus Ecclesiæ Catholicæ fundamenta cognosces; & per hos gradus si observaveris vniversa quæ scripta sunt, Deus erit in memoria tua, & tu in Dominum tuum reverteris.
units.tr: I think your faith in Christ Jesus is enough to open for you, in the Lord, the narrow and straitened way of understanding, given your holy manner of life, which fits you for the dignity of the priestly office; for you have been chosen by God for this office on account of your previous merits and outstanding virtues. Although in many people grace is approved in Christ without works, and when the merit of conduct and life is absent the gifts of God alone bear fruit, yet because you, above others, are approved as chosen by God, who have both fulfilled the works of the law and remained in grace even to the surpassing love of knowledge, and since with God's understanding speaking within you, remarkable thoughts arise swiftly, you wish to know what you are to become. As you ask, I will reserve for you the sacraments of the whole Church, keeping the order and place of teaching and explaining what and how you ought to observe them; provided that the zeal of a newly-given exhortation does not turn to your harm, and that you are not ashamed to be somewhat lesser while you learn. For, as you see, the setting-apart by the privilege of dignity means you have more from us to seek, and what you know has long since been established in your consecration.
