It remains for you to grasp, lest you be found lesser in Christ than you are called for the time being in the world; and if you were to be a useless minister of a false title, not knowing these sacraments that lie hidden in the Lord. Yet we, holding to reason in every discussion and speaking with you plainly, will show that you ought to be a true bishop of souls, so that, becoming your own judge, you hasten to do what we say; and agreeing with us, casting off shame and confusion, you choose rather to be cast down in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of sinners. For Jesus says: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power are called lords; but you shall not be so: rather, let him who is greatest among you become as the least, and let him who is chief become as the servant. For who is greater, he who sits at table, or he who serves? Among the Gentiles, indeed, it is he who sits at table; but among you it is not so, but he who serves. I am among you as one who serves, and you are those who have continued with me in my trials: I appoint to you, as my Father has appointed to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." And elsewhere: "They have set you as ruler; do not be exalted, but be as one of them." And elsewhere: "Not that you should lord it over the clergy, but that you should be a pattern to the flock." And elsewhere: "You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. If anyone defiles the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, which you are; for of him, and through him, and in him are all things, to him be glory for ever. For there is one God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." But knowledge is not in all. For blindness has come upon part of Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel would be saved. God has therefore shut up all under sin, that he might have mercy on all. Above all, love humility, for pride makes one fall away from God, and pride is the beginning of all sin. For our God, taking the form of a servant, humbled himself even to death, the death of the cross. Run through all the Scriptures in your mind, read the whole canon, and having the examples of the saints before your eyes, imitate what is good and emulate what is holy; and let it be your aim to become a heavenly Jerusalem rendering vows to God; build in yourself a house and a temple of Solomon, construct a tabernacle, and hasten to adorn it more diligently; within the holy of holies kindle an unfailing light. Keep perfection in all things, set a guard on your mouth, and a door of circumspection on your lips. Do not give your soul over to temptation, and he who keeps you will not sleep. Lift up your voice and say: "All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass; the grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains for ever." For the priest of the Lord, who brings forth righteousness from his mouth and declares truth to those who seek it, is the angel of the almighty God. In all causes keep justice; do not dismiss the stranger, the orphan, the widow, the poor, or the fatherless with an empty lap; lay up your treasure there where the moth is, with all your brothers, and, as it is written, have peace. Flee from counsels, lest while you judge you be condemned; for as it is written: blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence, but whose will is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates in his law day and night. Receive the persons of the powerful, the acquaintance of the rich, and the attentions of those who greet you in such a way that you do not sadden the poor, nor bring weariness of excuses on anyone. Let not the book of the law depart from your hand, as it is written, but meditate on it day and night. For thus it is written: be without offence to the Jews, the Greeks, and the Church of God, as I also please all men in all things, not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved. Before you hear, do not judge anyone, and before the proof of an accusation brought, do not suspend anyone from your communion; for he who is accused is not at once guilty, but he who is convicted is criminal. Nor should you yield to the hatreds of individuals, so that the wrong done to innocent brothers is not given over; rather, keeping the fear of the Lord always before your eyes, know that everything that is done must be presented to God and Christ; for the figure of this world passes away, and it is fitting to obey God rather than men. He who knows the past judges the future. For in one saying the whole law is fulfilled: "Whatever you would not have done to you, do not do to another." At home, if it can be done, setting aside care for your person and reverence for your office, it is fitting that you be a servant to servants, and so teach Israel thoroughly in all things, that those who hear may profit more from your conduct than from your speech. For thus it is written: walk in wisdom towards those who are outside. Let not the greeting of many, the gifts of the rich, or their attentions puff you up, for "gifts, as it is written, blind the eyes of judges"; nor let a noble and rich matron be more to you than a professed poor woman and beggar; nor let a widow, destitute of marital help, seem equal to her who has a powerful husband in the world. Judge that you must make yourself a stranger to the persons of all, and do not defend the poor in judgment through unrighteousness, nor unbecomingly attend upon the rich for favour; or if you cannot do this, reject the hearing of causes. Be content with reading and prayer alone. "For God, as it is written, loves no one except him who dwells with wisdom," and who harms no one. If you do these things, you will be useful to God, approved in all things, and you will keep the priesthood perfect in yourself. Drive from the temple of Christ the sheep, the oxen, and the dove-sellers, and overturn the tables of the money-changers; for the house of our Father ought not to be a house of trade, but of prayer. And what is cast away by the judgment of God, let him not wish to be desired on account of the sentence of condemnation, lest we be found reprobate in Christ. And so it will come about that, standing in truth, you will be worthy to know the sacrament of the sevenfold Church, which, in the omnipotence of God, abides with its veneration, that is, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; in the archangels, in the angels, in wisdom, in men. If you look diligently into all these things, you will know the foundations of the whole Catholic Church in these arrangements; and if through these steps you observe all that has been written, "God will be in your memory, and you will return to your Lord."

units.la: B. GREGORII MAGNI, PAPÆ ROMANI EPISTOLÆ DE OBEDIENTIA ERGA IMPERATOREM; ET DE NOMINE VNIVERSALIS PAPÆ IN Ecclesia Catholica non vsurpando.
units.tr: Letters of St Gregory the Great, Pope of Rome, on obedience towards the Emperor, and on not usurping the title of universal Pope in the Catholic Church.

units.la: Regesti Lib. II. Epist. LXII.
units.tr: Register, Book II, Letter LXII.

units.la: Conqueritur de Lege Imperatoris, qua prohibuit, ne Milites in monasterijs susciperentur.
units.tr: He complains of the Emperor's law, by which he forbade soldiers to be received into monasteries.

units.la: AVRITIO AVGVSTO. Omnipotenti Deo retus est, qui serenissimis Dominis in omne quod agat & loquitur, purus non est. Ego autem indignus pietatis vestræ famulus, in hac suggestione neq; ut Episcopus, neq; ut servus iure reipublicæ, sed iure priusto loquor: quia serenissime Domine, & ex illo iam tempore Dominus meus fuisti, quando adhuc Dominus omnium non eras. Longino viro Clarissimo stratore venienti Dominorum legem suscepi, ad quam fatigatus tunc ægritudine corporis, respondere nil valui. In qua Dominorum pietas lanxit, ut quisquis publicis administrationibus fuerit implicatus, ei ad Ecclesiasticum officium venire non liceat. Quod valde laudavi, evidentissime sciens, quia qui secularem habitum deserens, ad Ecclesiastica officia venire festinat, mutare vult seculum, non relinquere. Quod vero in eadem lege dicitur, ut ei in monasterio converti non liceat, omnino miratus sum; dum & rationes eius possint per monasterium fieri, & agi potest, ut ab eo loco in quo suscipitur, eius quoque debita soluantur. Nam etsi quisquam devota mente converti voluisset, prius res male ablatas rederet, & de sua anima tanto verius, quanto expeditior cogitaret. In qua lege subiunctum est, ut nulli, qui interrogatus est, convertilicebat. Quam constitutionem ego, fateor Dominis meis, vehementer expavi, quia per eam cælorum via multis claudituř, & quod nuncusq; licuit, ne liceat prohibetur. Multi enim sunt, qui possunt religiosam vitam etiam cum seculari habitu ducere. Et plerique sunt, qui nisi omnia reliquerint, saluari apud Deum nullatenus possunt. Ego vero hæc Dominis meis loquens, quid sum nisi pulvis & vermis? Sed tamen quia contra auctorem omnium Deum hanc intendere constitutionē sentio, Dominis tacere non possum. Ad hoc enim potestas Dominorum meorum pietatis cælitus data est super omnes homines, ut qui bona appetunt, adiuvetur, ut cælorum via largius pateat, &c. & terrestre regnum cœlesti: regno famuletur. Et ecce aperta voce dicitur, ut ei qui semel in terrena militia signatus fuerit, nisi aut expleta militia, aut pro debilitate corporis repulsus, Domino Iesu Christo militare non liceat. Ad hæc, ecce per me servum vestrum & vestrum respondebit Christus dicens: Ego te de Notario Comitem Excubitorum, de Comite Excubitorum Cæsarem, de Cæsare Imperatorem: nec solum hoc, sed etiam patrem Imperatorum feci; ego Sacerdotes meos tuæ manui commisi, & tu à meo servitio milites tuos subtrahis? Responde rogo, piissime Domine, servo tuo, quid veniens & hæc dicenti responsurus es in iudicio Domino tuo? sed forte creditur, quia nullus eorum puro animo conversatur. Ego indignus famulus vester scio, quanta his diebus meis in monasterio milites conversi miracula fecerunt, signa & virtutes operati sunt. Sed per hanc legem iam ne quisquam talium converti valeat, prohibetur. Requirat rogo Dominus meus piissimus quis prior Imperatorum talem legem dederit, & subtilius æstimet si debuit dari. Et quidem considerandum valdè est: quia eo iam tempore prohibentur quisq; relinquere sæculum, quo appropinquat finis iste sæculorum. Ecce enim mora non erit, & ardente cœlo, ardente terra, corruscantibus elementis, cum Angelis & Archangelis, cum Thronis & Dominationibus, cum Principatibus & Potestatibus tremendus Iudex apparebit. Si omnia peccata dimiserit, & solam hanc legem contra se dixerit esse prolatam, quæ rogo erit excusatio? Unde per eundem tremendum Iudicem deprecor, ne illæ tantæ lachrymæ: tantæ orationes, tantæ ieiunia, tantæq; eleemosynæ Domini mei ex qualibet occasione apud omnipotentis Dei oculos fuscentur, sed aut temperando pietas vestra, aut immutando vigorem eiusdem legis inflectat: quia tunc magis Dominorum exercitus contra hostes crescit, quanto Dei exercitus ad orationem creverit. Ego quidem iussioni subiectus, eandem legem per diversas terrarum partes transmitti feci, & quia lex ipsa omnipotenti Deo minime concordat, ecce per suggestionis meæ paginam serenissimis Dominis nunciani. Utrobique ergo quæ debui exsolui, qui & imperatori obedientiam præbui, & pro Deo quod sensi, minime tacui.
units.tr: To Mauricius Augustus. He is a man who is not pure in everything he does or says before almighty God, and who has to answer to God for his conduct, and I am an unworthy servant of your piety. In this address I speak not as a bishop, nor as a subject bound by the public law of the state, but by a right that is more just: most serene lord, you have been my lord from the time when you were not yet lord of all. When the most distinguished Longinus came as your envoy, I received your lords' law. I was then worn out by bodily sickness and could make no reply to it. In it the piety of my lords has decreed that whoever has been involved in public administration may not come to an ecclesiastical office. I greatly approved of this, knowing very well that whoever, leaving behind secular dress, hurries to ecclesiastical office, wants to change his world, not to abandon it. But I was astonished beyond measure at what the same law says, that it is not lawful for him to be converted in a monastery, since his obligations can be discharged through the monastery, and it can be arranged that, from the place where he is received, his debts are also paid. For even if someone wished to be converted with a devout mind, he would first restore the goods wrongly taken, and he would think about his soul all the more truly for being less encumbered. The law adds that it is permitted to no one who has been questioned to be converted. I confess to my lords that I was greatly alarmed by this enactment, because through it the way of heaven is closed to many, and what has hitherto been permitted to all is now forbidden. For there are many who can lead a religious life even while wearing secular dress, and many who cannot possibly be saved before God unless they have left everything. But when I speak these things to my lords, what am I but dust and a worm? Yet because I perceive that this enactment is aimed against God, the author of all things, I cannot keep silent before my lords. For the power of my lords' piety has been given from heaven over all men for this purpose: that those who seek good things may be helped, that the way of heaven may lie more widely open, and that the earthly kingdom may serve the heavenly kingdom. And now it is plainly stated that he who has once been enrolled in earthly military service may not serve the Lord Jesus Christ as a soldier, unless his military service has been completed or he has been dismissed on account of bodily weakness. To this, Christ will answer through me, your servant and yours, saying: "I made you from a notary a count of the excubitors, from a count of the excubitors Caesar, and from Caesar emperor; and not only this, but I also made the father of emperors. I committed my priests to your hand; and do you withdraw your soldiers from my service?" Answer, I beg, most pious lord, your servant, what you will say to your Lord when you come before him in judgment and speak these words. But perhaps it is believed that none of them is converted with a pure heart. I, your unworthy servant, know how many soldiers, converted in my own days in monasteries, have worked miracles and performed signs and powers. Yet by this law no one of such men may now be converted. I ask my most pious lord to inquire who among the emperors first gave such a law, and to weigh more carefully whether it ought to have been given. Indeed it must be considered most carefully: for now men are forbidden to leave the world, when this end of the ages is drawing near. For there will be no delay, and the dreadful Judge will appear with heaven burning, the earth burning, the elements flashing, with the angels and archangels, with the thrones and dominions, with the principalities and powers. If he forgives all sins and says that only this one law was brought forward against him, what excuse will there be? Therefore I beg, through that same dreadful Judge, that those great tears, great prayers, great fastings and great almsdeeds of my lord may not be darkened before the eyes of almighty God on any pretext; but let your piety either moderate or alter the rigour of that law, since the army of the lords grows stronger against its enemies in proportion as the army of God has grown in prayer. I, indeed, subject to the command, had the same law sent through the various parts of the world; and because the law itself by no means agrees with almighty God, I now announce it to my most serene lords through the page of this address. In both respects, then, I have discharged what I owed: I have shown obedience to the Emperor, and I have not kept silent about what I perceived for God.

units.la: EPISTOLA XLV.
units.tr: LETTER XLV.

units.la: Conqueritur de Lege Imperatoris, ne Milites convertantur in Monasteriis.
units.tr: He complains about the Emperor's law that soldiers may not be converted in monasteries.

units.la: Theodoro Medico, &c. Quanta bona omnipotentis Dei & serenissimi Domini mei Imperatoris habeam, lingua mea non sufficit explere. Pro quibus bonis quid retribuere, nisi eorum vestigia pure amare? Peccatis autem meis facientibus, ex quorum suggestione vel consilio, nescio an vestro, transacto anno talem in republica sua legem protulit, ut quisquis eam pure amat, flere vehementer debeat. Ad quam legem tunc respondere non potui, quia ægrotus fui. Modo autem eidem Domino aliqua suggessi. Præcipit enim, ut nullus qui actionem publicam agit, nullus qui officio, vel munus signatus, vel inter milites fuit habitus, ei in monasterio converti liceat, nisi forte si militia eius fuerit expleta. Quam legem primum, sicut ii dicunt qui leges veteres noverunt, Iulianus protulit, de quo scimus omnes, quantum Deo adversus fuerit. Quod si ideo serenissimus Dominus noster fecit, quia forte multi milites convertebantur, & exercitus decrescebat; nunquid per virtutem militum subiugavit ei omnipotens Deus imperium Persarum? Nunquid non solæ lachrymæ illius auditæ sunt, & eo ordine quem ipse nesciuit, eius Imperio Persarum regnum subdidit? Valde autem mihi durum videtur, ut ab eius servitio milites suos prohibeat, qui ei & omnia tribuit, & dominari eum non solum militibus, sed etiam Sacerdotibus concessit. Nunquid si intentio est servandarum rerum, non poterant ea ipsa monasteria, quæ milites suscepissent, alienas res reddere, atq; ad conversionem homines tantum modo habere? Hæc quia mihi valde dolent, eidem domino suggessi. Sed vestra gloria opportuno tempore secrete suggestionem meam ei offerat. Nolo eam à responsali meo publice dari, quia vos qui ei familiarius servitis, loqui ei liberius & apertius potestis, quæ pro eius sunt anima: quoniam in multis est occupatus, & vix animus eius invenitur à curis maioribus vacuus. Tu quidem gloriose fili pro Christo loquere. Si auditus fueris, lucrum operamur animæ prædicti Domini tui, & aux. Si vero auditus non fueris, lucrum solummodo tuæ fecisti.
units.tr: To Theodore the physician, etc. My tongue is not sufficient to tell of the many blessings I have received from almighty God and from my most serene lord the Emperor. What can I return for such blessings, except to love their footsteps with a pure heart? Because of my sins, however, he issued a law of this kind for his commonwealth last year, at whose suggestion or counsel I do not know, perhaps yours. Anyone who loves that law sincerely ought to weep bitterly. I could not answer this law at the time, because I was ill. Now, however, I have put a few suggestions to the same lord. He orders that no one who is engaged in public business, and no one who has been marked for an office or a duty or has been counted among the soldiers, may be converted in a monastery, unless perhaps his military service has been completed. As those who know the old laws say, Julian first issued such a law, and we all know how hostile he was to God. But if our most serene lord has done this because perhaps many soldiers were being converted and the army was shrinking, did almighty God not subdue to him the empire of the Persians through the courage of the soldiers? Were not his tears alone heard, and did not God, in an order which he himself did not know, place the kingdom of the Persians under his rule? It seems very hard to me, however, that he should forbid his soldiers from serving him, when God has given him everything and has granted that he should rule not only over soldiers but also over priests. If the aim is to preserve property, could not those very monasteries which had received soldiers have given back the goods of others and kept only the men for conversion? Because these things grieve me greatly, I have made these suggestions to the same lord. But let your glory offer my suggestion to him secretly at a suitable time. I do not wish it to be given publicly through my representative, because you, who serve him more closely, can speak to him more freely and openly about what concerns his soul, since he is occupied with many matters and his mind is scarcely free from greater cares. You, glorious son, speak for Christ. If you are heard, we gain the soul of your lord, and help. If you are not heard, you have gained only for yourself.

units.la: Regesti Lib. IV. Epist. XXXI.
units.tr: Register, Book IV, Letter XXXI.

units.la: Conqueritur, sefatum ab Imperatore appellatum: Deinde Sacerdotes honorandos, exemplo Constantini confirmat, &c.
units.tr: He complains that he has been called a fool by the Emperor; then he confirms, by the example of Constantine, that priests are to be honoured, etc.

units.la: Mauritio Augusto. In serenissimis iussionibus suis Dominorum pietas me de quibusdam redarguere studuit, parcendo mihi minime pepercit. Nam in eis vrbane simplicitatis vocabulo factum appellat. In scriptura etenim sacra cum in bona intelligentia ponitur simplicitas, vigilantiae sapientiae atque rectitudini sociatur. Unde etiam de beato Iob scriptum est: Erat vir simplex & rectus. Et beatus Paulus Apostolus admonet dicens: Estote simplices in malo, prudentes in bono. Item Salvator admonet veritas, dicens: Estote prudentes sicut serpentes, & simplices sicut columbæ. Esse valde inutile iudicans, siaut simplicitati prudentia, aut prudentiæ simplicitas deest. Ut ergo servos suos ad cognitionem eruditos efficeret, esse eos & simplices sicut columbas, & prudentes ut serpentes voluit: quatequatenus in eis & serpentis astutia columbæ simplicitatem acueret, & columbæ simplicitas serpentis astutiam temperaret. Ego igitur, qui in serenissimorum Dominorum iussionibus & Arnulphi astutia deceptus non adiuncta prudentia simplex denuncior, constat proculdubio quia fatuus appellor: quod ita esse ego quoque ipse confiteor. Nam si hoc vestra pietas taceat, causæ clamant. Ego enim si fatuus non fuissem, ad ista toleranda, quæ intra Longobardorum gladios hoc in loco patior, minime venissem. In ea autem re, quæ de Arnulpho perhibui, qui toto corde venire ad rempublicam paratus fuit, dum mihi non creditur, etiam mentitus esse reprehendor. Sed etsi Sacerdos non sum: Scio grauem esse hanc iniuriam Sacerdoti, ut veritati seruiens, fallax credatur. Et dudum noui, quoniam Arnulpho plus est creditum quam mihi; Leoni amplius est creditum quam mihi: & nunc eis qui esse ad medium videntur, plus quam meis assertionibus credulitas impenditur. Et quidem si terræ meæ captiuitas per quotidiana momenta non excresceret, de despectione mea atque irrisione lætus tacerem. Sed & hoc me vehementer affligit: quia ego vade crimé falsitatis tolero, inde Italia quotidie ducitur sub Longobardorum iugo captiua. Dumque meis suggestionibus in nullo creditur, vires hostium immaniter excrescunt. Hoc tamen piissimo Domino luggero, ut de me mala omnia quelibet existimet, de utilitate vero reipublicæ & causa ereptionis Italiæ non quibuslibet facile pias aures præbeat, sed plus rebus quam verbis credat. Sacerdotibus autem non extera potestate Dominus noster cuius indignetur, sed excellenti consideratione, propter eum cuius serui sunt, eis ita dominatur, ut etiam debitam reuerentiam impendat. Nam in diuinis eloquiis aliquando Sacerdotes Dii, aliquando Angeli vocantur. Nam & per Moysen de eo qui ad iuramentum deducendus est, dicitur: Applica illum ad Deos, id est, ad Sacerdotes. Et rursum est: Dis non detrahes, scilicet Sacerdotibus. Et Propheta ait: Labia Sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & legem requirent ex ore eius, quia Angelus Domini exercituum est. Quid ergo mirum, si illos vestra pietas dignatur honore, quibus in suo eloquio honorem tribuens, eos aut Angelos, aut Deos ipse etiam appellat Deus? Ecclesiastica quoque testatur Historia, quia cum piæ memoriæ Constantino Principi scripto oblatæ accusationes contra Episcopos fuissent, libellos quidem accusationis accepit, & eosdem qui accusati fuerant Episcopos convocans, in eorum conspectu libellos quos acceperat, incendit, dicens: Vos Dii estis, a vero Deo constituti. Ite & inter vos causas istas discutite, quia dignum non est ut nos iudicemus Deos. In qua tamen sententia, pie Domine, sibi magis ex humilitate, quam illis aliquid præstitit ex reverentia impensa. Ante eum quippe pagani in republica principes fuerunt, qui verum Deum nescientes, Deos lignceos & lapideos colebant, & tamen eorum Sacerdotibus honorem maximum tribuebant. Quid ergo mirum si Christianus Imperator veri Dei Sacerdotes dignetur honorare, dum pagani (ut diximus) principes honorem impendere Sacerdotibus nouerunt: qui Diis ligneis & lapideis seruiebant? Hæc ergo pierati Dominorum non pro me, sed pro cunctis Sacerdotibus suggero. Ego enim homo peccator sum. Et quia omnipotenti Deo incessanter quotidie delinquo, aliquid mihi apud tremendum examen illius esse remedium suspicor, si incessantibus quotidie plagis feror. Et credo quia eundem omnipotentem Dominum tanto vobis amplius placatis, quanto me ei male seruientem districtius afflixitis.
units.tr: To the Emperor Maurice. In your most serene commands, the piety of my lords has sought to rebuke me on certain points, and it has not spared me at all. For in them you call what I did by the name of urbane simplicity. In Holy Scripture, simplicity taken in a good sense is joined with watchfulness, wisdom and uprightness. Hence it is also written of blessed Job: He was a simple and upright man. And the blessed Apostle Paul admonishes, saying: Be simple in evil, wise in good. Likewise the Saviour, who is Truth, admonishes, saying: Be wise as serpents, and simple as doves. Judging it very unprofitable for simplicity to lack wisdom, or wisdom to lack simplicity, he wished his servants, who were to be instructed for knowledge, to be both simple as doves and wise as serpents, so that in them the cunning of the serpent might sharpen the simplicity of the dove, and the simplicity of the dove might temper the cunning of the serpent. I, therefore, who in the commands of your most serene lords am announced as simple without added wisdom, having been deceived by the cunning of Arnulf, am without doubt called a fool. I myself also confess that this is so. For if your piety were silent about it, the circumstances would cry out. Indeed, if I had not been a fool, I would never have come to endure those things which I suffer in this place within the swords of the Lombards. But in the matter I reported about Arnulf, who was ready with his whole heart to come to the commonwealth, I am rebuked, even as one who has lied, because I am not believed. But although I am not a priest, I know that this injury is grave for a priest, that while serving the truth he should be believed to be deceitful. I have long known that Arnulf has been believed more than I have; Leo has been believed more than I have; and now those who seem to stand in the middle receive more belief than my assertions. And indeed, if the captivity of my land did not grow greater every moment, I would quietly bear my contempt and mockery with joy. But this also afflicts me greatly: because I bear the charge of falsehood, Italy is daily led captive under the yoke of the Lombards. And while I am believed in nothing by my representations, the forces of the enemy grow enormously. Yet I beg my most pious Lord to think whatever evil he likes of me, but not to lend his pious ears readily to anyone on the question of the public good and the rescue of Italy; rather, he should trust deeds more than words. Our Lord does not rule over priests by external power, which he disdains, but by excellent consideration, for the sake of him whose servants they are, so that he even bestows due reverence upon them. For in the divine oracles priests are sometimes called gods, and sometimes angels. For through Moses, concerning the one who is to be brought to an oath, it is said: Bring him to the gods, that is, to the priests. And again: You shall not revile the gods, namely the priests. And the Prophet says: The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts. What wonder, then, if your piety deigns to honour those to whom God himself, in his own speech, gives honour, and whom he himself calls either angels or gods? Ecclesiastical history also bears witness that when accusations written against bishops had been offered to the Emperor Constantine of pious memory, he accepted the libels of accusation, and summoning the bishops who had been accused, he burned the libels he had received in their sight, saying: You are gods, constituted by the true God. Go and discuss these causes among yourselves, for it is not fitting that we should judge gods. In that judgment, gracious Lord, he showed himself to them out of humility, rather than bestowing anything upon them out of reverence. For before him there were pagan princes in the commonwealth who, not knowing the true God, worshipped gods of wood and stone, and yet they gave the greatest honour to their priests. What wonder, then, if a Christian Emperor deigns to honour the priests of the true God, since pagan princes (as we have said) knew how to bestow honour on the priests of gods of wood and stone? I offer these things to the piety of my lords not for my own sake, but for all priests. For I am a sinful man. And since I sin daily and without ceasing against almighty God, I suspect that some remedy for me before his dreadful judgment is that I should be struck with daily and unceasing blows. And I believe that you please the same almighty Lord all the more, the more severely you have afflicted me, who serve him so badly.

units.la: Multas enim iam plagas acceperam, & superuenientibus Dominorum iussionibus inueni consolationes, quas non sperabam. Si enim possum, has celeriter plagas enumero. Primum, quod mihi pax subducta est, quam cum Longobardis in Tuscia positis sine vllo reipublicæ dispendio feceram. Deinde corrupta pace, de Romana ciuitate milites ablati sunt, & quidem alii ab hostibus occisi, alii vero Narniis & Perusii positis, & ut Perusium teneretur, Roma relicta est. Post hoc plaga grauior fuit aduentus Agiulphi, ita ut oculis meis cernerem Romanos more canum in collis funibus ligatos, qui ad Franciam ducebantur venales. Et quia nos qui intra ciuitatem fuimus, Deo prætegente manus eius euasimus: quæsitum est unde culpabiles esse viderentur, videlicet cur frumenta defuerint, quæ in hac urbe diu multa seruari nullatenus possunt, sicut in alia suggestione plenius indicaui. Et quidem de me ipso in nullo turbatus sum, quia teste conscientia fateor, aduerla quidem pati paratus sum, dummodo hæc omnia cum salute duntaxat animæ meæ euadã. Sed de gloriosis viris Gregorio Præfecto, & Castorio Magistro militum non mediocriter sum afflictus, qui & omnio quod potuerunt fieri, nullo modo facere neglexerunt, & labores vigiliarum, & custodiæ ciuitatis, in eadem obsessione vehementissimos ptulerant, & posthæc omnia graui dominorum indignatione pcussi sunt. De quibus patenter intelligo: quia eos non sua acta, sed mea persona grauat. Cum qua, quia pariter in tribulatione laborauerant, post labore pariter tribulantur. Quod autem dominorum pietas illud mihi pauendum, & terribile omnipotentis Dei iudicium intentat, rogo per eundem omnipotentem Dominum, ne hoc vlterius quidem faciat. Nam adhuc nescimus, quis ibi qualis sit. Et Paulus egregius prædicator ait: Nolite iudicare ante tempus, donec veniat Dominus qui & illuminabit abscondita tenebrarum, & manifestabit consilia cordium. Hoc tamen breuiter dico, quoniam indignus & peccator plus de venientis Iesu misericordia, quæ de vestræ pietatis iustitia præsumo. Et sunt multa quæ de iudicio illius homines ignorant, quia fortasse quæ vos laudatis, ille reprehendet; & quæ vos reprehenditis, ille laudabit. Inter hæc ergo omnia incerta, ad solas lachrymas redeo, petens ut idem omnipotens Deus piissimum Dominum nostrum, & sua hic manu regat, & in illo terribili iudicio liberum ab omnibus deliciis inueniat. Et me ita placere, si necesse est, hominibus faciat, ut æternam eius gratiam non offendam.
units.tr: For I had already received many blows, and with the arrival of your lords' commands I found consolations which I had not hoped for. If I can, I will count these blows quickly. First, the peace was taken from me, which I had made with the Lombards settled in Tuscany without any loss to the commonwealth. Then, with the peace broken, soldiers were taken away from the city of Rome, some indeed killed by the enemy, others posted at Narni and Perugia, and Rome was left behind so that Perugia might be held. After this came a heavier blow: the arrival of Agiulf, so that I saw with my own eyes the Romans, like dogs, tied with ropes around their necks, being led to Francia to be sold. And since we who were within the city escaped his hands by the protection of God, it was asked why they should seem guilty, namely why the grain was lacking, which cannot be kept for long in this city, as I have indicated more fully in another representation. And indeed I am not at all disturbed on my own account, for, as my conscience bears witness, I am ready to suffer adversity, provided I escape all this with the salvation of my soul alone. But I am not moderately distressed about the glorious men, Gregory the Prefect and Castorius the Master of the soldiers, who neglected nothing that could possibly be done, and who in that siege had endured the labours of watches and the guarding of the city most severely; yet after all this they have been struck with the heavy indignation of my lords. About these men I clearly understand that it is not their own deeds but my person that burdens them. Since they laboured together with me in tribulation, they are now afflicted together after the labour. But as for your piety threatening me with that dread and terrible judgment of almighty God, I beg by the same almighty Lord that you do not do this any further. For we still do not know who is what sort of person there. And the outstanding preacher Paul says: Judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts. Yet I say this briefly: as an unworthy sinner I presume more on the mercy of Jesus who is coming than on the justice of your piety. And there are many things about his judgment which men do not know, for perhaps what you praise he will rebuke, and what you rebuke he will praise. Amid all these uncertainties, then, I return to tears alone, asking that the same almighty God may both rule our most pious Lord here with his hand, and in that terrible judgment find him free from all delights; and that he may make me so to please men, if it is necessary, that I do not offend his eternal grace.

units.la: EPISTOLA XXXII. De Ioanne Episcopo Constantinopolitano, qui sibi VNIVERSALE nomen arripuit.
units.tr: EPISTOLA XXXII. Concerning John, Bishop of Constantinople, who seized for himself the title UNIVERSAL.

units.la: Mauritio Augusto. Piissimus atque à Deo constitutus Dominus noster, intelligenter... ceteras augustorum potius curas conseruandæ quoq; Sacerdotali caritati rectitudine studii spiritalis inuigilat: videlicet pie veraciterq; considerans, neminem posse recte terrena regere, nisi nouerit diuina tractare, pacemq; reipublicæ ex vniuersalis Ecclesiæ pace pendere. Quæ enim serenissime Domine virtus humana, quodq; carnei robur brachii contra vestri Christianissimi culmen imperii irreligiosas præsumeret manus erigere, si studeret concors Sacerdotum mes redemptorem suum lingua pro vobis atq; vt oportebat meritis exorare? Aut quis ferocissimæ gentis gladius in necem fidelium tota crudelitate grassaretur, nisi nostra vita, qui Sacerdotes nominamur, & non sumus, à prauissimis grauaretur oppribus? Sed dum nos per competentia nobis relinquimus, & nobis incompetentia cogitamus, peccata nostra barbaricis viribus sociamns, & culpa nostra hostium gladios exacuit, q reipublicæ vires grauat. Quid autem dicturi sumus qui populum Dei, cui indigne præsumus, peccatorum nostrorum oneribus premimus? qui quod per linguam prædicamus, per exempla destruimus? qui iniqua docemus operibus, & sola voce ea quæ sunt iusta prætendimus? Ossa ieiuniis atterantur & mente turgemus. Corpus despectis vestibus tegitur, & elatione cordis purpuram superamus. Iacemus in cinere, & excelsa non despicimus. Doctores humilium, duces superbiæ, ouina facie Lupinos dentes abscondimus. Sed quis horum finis est, nisi quod hominibus suademus, Deo autem manifesti sumus? Quamobrem prouidentissime piissimus Dominus noster ad compescendos bellicos motus pacem quærit Ecclesiæ, atq; ad huius compagem Sacerdotū dignatur corda reducere. Quod quidem ego opto atq; quantum ad me attinet, serenissimis iussionibus obedientiam præbeo. Quia vero non causa mea, sed Dei est; & quia non solus ego, sed tota turbatur Ecclesia, quia piæ leges, quia venerandæ synodi, quia ipse Domini nostri Iesu Christi mandata superbi atq; pompatici cuiusdam sermonis inuentione turbantur: piissimus Dominus locum secet vulneris, atq; resistentem ægrum augustæ auctoritatis vinculis constringat. Adstringendo enim statum reipublicæ subleuatis: & dum talia reciditis, de regni vestri prolixitate tractatis. Cunctis ergo Euangelium scientibus liquet, quod voce Dominica sancto, & omnium Apostolorum Petro Principi Apostolo, totius Ecclesiæ cura committa est. Ipsi quippe dicitur: Petre amas me? pasce oues meas. Ipsi dicitur: Ecce Sathanas expetiit cribrare vos sicut triticum, & ego pro te rogaui Petre, vt non deficiat fides tua, & tu aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Ipsi dicitur: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram edificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferi non prævalebunt aduersus eam. Et, Tibi do claves regni cœlorum; &, Quodcunque ligaueris super terram, erit ligatum & in cœlis; & quodcunque solueris super terram erit solutum & in cœlis. Ecce claues regni cœlestis accipit, potestas ei ligandi ac soluendi tribuitur, cura ei totius Ecclesiæ & principatus committitur, & tamen vniuersalis Apostolus non vocatur; & vir sanctissimus consacerdos meus Ioannes vocari Vniuersalis Episcopus conatur. Exclamare compellor ac dicere: O tempora, o mores. Ecce cuncta in Europæ partibus Barbarorum iuri sunt tradita, destructæ vrbes, euersa castra, depopulatæ prouinciæ, nullus terram cultor inhabitat: sæuiunt & dominantur quotidie in necem fidelium cultores idolorum, & tamen Sacerdotes, qui in pauimento & in cinere sientes iacere debuerunt, vanitatis sibi nomina expetunt; & nouis ac profanis vocabulis gloriantur. Nunquid ego hac in re piissime Domine propriam causam defendo? nunquid speciale iniuriam vindico? & non magis causam omnipotentis Dei, & causam vniuersalis Ecclesiæ? Quis est iste qui contra statuta Euangelica, contra Canonum decreta, nouum sibi vsurpare nomen præsumit? Vtinam vel sine aliorum imminutione vnus sit, qui vocari appetit vniuersalis. Et certe multos Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ in hæreseos voraginem incidisse nouimus Sacerdotes, & non solum hæreticos, sed etiam hæresiarchas factos. Inde quippe Nestorius, qui mediatorem Dei & hominum Iesum Christum duas esse personas existimans: quia Deum fieri hominem potuisse non credidit, vsque ad Iudaicam perfidiam erupit. Inde Macedonius, qui consubstantialem Patri & Filio Spiritum sanctum Deum esse denegauit. Si igitur illud nomen in Ecclesia sibi quisquam arripuit, quod apud bonorum omnium iudicium fuit: vniuersa ergo Ecclesia, quod absit, à statu suo corruit, quando is qui appellatur vniuersalis cadit. Sed absit à cordibus Christianorum nomen istud blasphemiæ, in quo omnium Sacerdotum honor adimitur, dum ab vno sibi dementer arrogatur. Certe pro beati Petri Apostolorum Principis honore, per venerandam Chalcedonensem synodum Romano Pontifici oblatum est. Sed nullus eorum vnquam hoc singularitatis nomen assumpsit, nec vocabulo vti consensit, nedum priuatum aliquod daretur vni, honore debito Sacerdotes priuarentur vniuersi. Quid est ergo quod nos huius vocabuli gloriam & oblatam non quærimus, & alter sibi hanc arripere etiam non oblatam præsumit? Ille ergo magis est piissimorum diuinorum præceptione flectendus, qui præceptis Canonicis obedientiam præbere contemnit. Ille coercendus est, qui Sanctæ vniuersali Ecclesiæ iniuriam facit, qui corde tumet, qui gaudere de nomine singularitatis appetit, qui honori quoque Imperii vestri se per priuatum vocabulum superponit. Ecce omnes hac de re scandalum patimur. Ad viam ergo rectam reuertatur auctor scandali, & omnia Sacerdotum iurgia cessabunt. Ego enim cunctorum Sacerdotum seruus sum, in quantum ipsi Sacerdotaliter viuunt. Nam qui contra omnipotentem Dominum per inanis gloriæ tumorem atq; contra statuta patrum suam ceruicem erigit, in omnipotenti Domino confido, quia meam sibi nec cui gladius flectit. Quid autem nuper in hac vrbe ex huius auditu vocabuli gestum sit, Sabiniano Diacono ac responsali meo subtilius indicaui. Cogitet ergo Dominorum pietas de me proprio suo, quem specialiter præ cæteris semper fouit atque continuit, qui & vobis obedientiam præbere desiderio, & tamen de mea negligentia reperiri reus in superno tremendoque iudicio perrimesco. Ac secundum petitionem prædicti Sabiniani Diaconi, aut piissimus Dominus ipsum dignetur iudicare negotium, aut saepe nominatum virum, ut ab hac tandem intentione cesset deflectere. Si ergo iudicio pietatis vestræ iustissimo vel clementibus admonitionibus cesserit, omnipotenti Deo gratias referimus, atq; de concessa per vos omni Ecclesiæ pace gaudemus. Sin autem in eadem diutius contentione perstiterit, hanc de re iam veritatis sententiam certam tenemus, quæ ait: Omnis qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Et rursus scriptum est: Ante ruinam exaltatur cor. Ego autem Dominorum iussionibus obedientiam præbens, prædicto Consacerdoti meo & dulciter scripsi, & humiliter, ut ab hac inanis gloriæ appetitione sese emendet admonui. Si igitur me audire voluerit, habet devotum fratrem: si vero in superbia persistit, iam quid assequatur aspicio, quia illum sibi adversarium invenit, de quo scriptum est: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam.
units.tr: To the Emperor Maurice. Our most pious lord, appointed by God, watches with understanding and with a zeal for the spiritual life over the other concerns of the emperors, and he also looks to the preservation of priestly charity. He considers, piously and truthfully, that no one can rightly govern earthly affairs unless he knows how to handle divine ones, and that the peace of the commonwealth depends on the peace of the universal Church. For what human strength, most serene lord, or what strength of a fleshly arm would dare to raise impious hands against the summit of your Christian empire, if the minds of the priests were concordant and strove to entreat their Redeemer with their tongues on your behalf, as they ought and as they deserve? Or what sword of a most fierce people would rage in the slaughter of the faithful with all cruelty, unless our life, we who are called priests and are not, were weighed down by the most wicked burdens? But while we forsake what is fitting to us and think of what is unfitting to us, we join our sins to barbarian strength, and our guilt sharpens the swords of the enemy, which weighs upon the strength of the commonwealth. What shall we say, we who press down the people of God, over whom we unworthily preside, with the burdens of our sins? We who destroy by our examples what we preach with our tongues? We who teach iniquity by our works, and by voice alone put forward what is just? Our bones are worn away by fasts, and our minds are swollen. Our bodies are covered with despised garments, and in the haughtiness of our hearts we surpass the purple. We lie in ashes, yet we do not look down on lofty things. Teachers of the humble, leaders in pride, we hide wolfish teeth beneath a sheep's face. But what is the end of this, except that we persuade men while we are manifest to God? Therefore our most provident and pious lord seeks peace for the Church to quell the movements of war, and deigns to bring back the hearts of the priests to the unity of this body. This indeed I desire, and so far as it concerns me, I show obedience to your most serene commands. But because the cause is not mine but God's, and because not I alone but the whole Church is troubled, because the pious laws, because the venerable synods, because the very commands of our Lord Jesus Christ are thrown into confusion by the invention of a certain proud and pompous phrase, let our most pious lord cut the place of the wound, and bind the resisting sick man with the chains of your august authority. For by tightening, you relieve the state of the commonwealth; and while you cut away such things, you deal with the long-lasting nature of your kingdom. Therefore it is clear to all who know the Gospel that the care of the whole Church was committed by the voice of the Lord to the holy Peter, the chief of all the Apostles. For to him it is said: "Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep." To him it is said: "Behold, Satan has desired to sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren." To him it is said: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." And: "To you I give the keys of the kingdom of heaven"; and: "Whatever you shall bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven." Behold, he receives the keys of the heavenly kingdom, the power of binding and loosing is granted to him, the care of the whole Church and its headship are committed to him, and yet he is not called universal Apostle; and my most holy fellow priest John tries to be called universal bishop. I am compelled to cry out and say: O the times, O the manners! Behold, all the regions of Europe have been handed over to the rule of barbarians, cities are destroyed, camps overthrown, provinces laid waste, and no tiller of the land dwells there. Worshippers of idols rage and rule every day for the slaughter of the faithful; and yet the priests, who ought to lie weeping on the pavement and in ashes, seek for themselves names of vanity and boast in new and profane titles. Am I, most pious lord, in this matter defending my own cause? Am I avenging a private injury, and not rather the cause of almighty God and the cause of the universal Church? Who is this man who presumes to usurp for himself a new name, against the Gospel precepts and against the decrees of the canons? Would that there were only one who desires to be called universal, and that without diminishing the rest! And certainly we know that many priests of the Church of Constantinople have fallen into the whirlpool of heresy, and have become not only heretics but heresiarchs. From there indeed came Nestorius, who, thinking that Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and men, was two persons, because he did not believe that God could become man, broke out into Jewish unbelief. From there came Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Father and the Son, is God. If therefore anyone has seized for himself in the Church that name which was condemned by the judgment of all good men, then the whole Church, which God forbid, falls from its state, when he who is called universal falls. But let this name of blasphemy be far from the hearts of Christians, a name in which the honour of all priests is taken away, while it is madly claimed for himself by one. Certainly, for the honour of blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles, it was offered to the Roman Pontiff through the venerable Synod of Chalcedon. But none of them ever assumed this name of singularity, nor consented to use the title, much less that, if something private were given to one, all priests should be deprived of their due honour. Why then do we not seek the glory of this title, even when it is offered, while another presumes to seize it for himself even when it is not offered? He is rather to be bent by the commands of the most pious ones, who scorns to show obedience to the canonical precepts. He is to be restrained who does injury to the holy universal Church, who swells in heart, who desires to rejoice in the name of singularity, who by a private title sets himself above the honour of your empire. Behold, we all suffer scandal over this matter. Let the author of the scandal therefore return to the right way, and all the quarrels of the priests will cease. For I am the servant of all priests, insofar as they live as priests. For he who, through the swelling of empty glory, raises his neck against the almighty Lord and against the statutes of the Fathers, I trust in the almighty Lord, who will bend his neck, since my neck does not bend to him, nor does any sword. What was done recently in this city on hearing this title, I have pointed out more fully to Sabinianus the deacon, my representative. Let the piety of the lords therefore consider about me, their own servant, whom they have always cherished and kept especially above others, who desire both to show obedience to you and yet, I tremble to be found guilty by my negligence in the heavenly and dreadful judgment. And according to the petition of the aforesaid deacon Sabinianus, either let our most pious lord deign to judge the matter, or let the oft-named man be admonished to cease at last from this intention. If therefore he yields to the most just judgment of your piety or to gentle admonitions, we give thanks to almighty God and rejoice at the peace of the whole Church granted through you. But if he persists longer in this contention, we hold firmly to this sentence of truth on the matter, which says: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. And again it is written: Before ruin the heart is exalted. But I, obeying the commands of my lords, have both written sweetly and humbly to my aforesaid fellow priest, and have admonished him to amend himself from this desire of empty glory. If therefore he is willing to hear me, he has a devoted brother; but if he persists in pride, I already see what he will obtain, because he finds himself an adversary of whom it is written: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

units.la: EPISTOLA XXXIV.
units.tr: EPISTLE XXXIV.

units.la: De superbia Ioannis Episcopi, & de Maximo praevaricatore.
units.tr: Concerning the pride of John the Bishop, and concerning Maximus the transgressor.

units.la: CONSTANTINÆ AVGVSTÆ. Omnipotens Deus, qui pietatis vestræ cor sua dextera maiestatis tenet, & nos ex vobis protegit, & vobis pro temporalibus actibus æterna præmia remunerationis parat. Nam Sabiniano Diacono Responsali meo scribenti cognovi in causis Beati Petri Apostolorum Principis contra quosdam superbos, humiles facientes & blandos, quanta se iustitia vestra serenitas impendat. Et in Redemptoris nostri largitate confido, qui bonum hoc in serenissimo Domino & piissimis filiis in cœlestis quoque patriæ retributione recipietis. Nec dubium est peccatorum vinculis solutis æterna vos bona recipere, qui in causis eius Ecclesiæ ipsum vobis, cui potestas ligandi & solvendi data est, debitorem fecistis. Unde adhuc peto, ut nullius prævalere contra veritatem hypocrisin permittatis: quia sunt quidam, qui iuxta egregii prædicatoris vocem, per dulces sermones & benedictiones seducunt corda innocentium, qui vestte quidem despecti sunt, sed corde rumen, & quasi in hoc mundo cuncta despiciunt, sed tamen ea quæ mundi sunt, simul cuncta adspici quærunt. Qui indignos se omnibus hominibus fatentur, sed privatis vocabulis contenti esse non possunt: quia illud appetunt, unde omnibus digniores esse videantur. Vestra itaq; pietas, quam omnipotens Deus cum serenissimo Domino universo mundo præesse constituit, illi per favorem iustitiæ famulatu suum reddat: a quo ius tantæ potestatis accepit, ut quanto verius in executione veritatis auctori omnium serviat, tanto securius commisso sibi mundo dominetur. Præterea indico, quia Domini piissimi scripta suscepi, ut cum fratre & consacerdote meo Ioanne debeat esse pacificum.
units.tr: To Constantina Augusta. May almighty God, who holds the heart of your piety in his right hand, which is the hand of majesty, protect us through you, and prepare for you eternal rewards in return for your temporal deeds. For when my deputy Sabinianus, the deacon, wrote to me, I learned how greatly your serene highness has exerted itself in justice in the cause of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, against certain proud men who pretend to be humble and flatter. I trust in the generosity of our Redeemer, who will give you this good in the person of our most serene Lord and most pious sons, and will also repay you in the heavenly fatherland. Nor is there any doubt that, once the chains of your sins are loosed, you will receive eternal goods, since in the cause of his Church you have made him, to whom the power of binding and loosing has been given, your debtor. Therefore I still ask that you never allow hypocrisy to prevail against the truth. For there are some who, according to the voice of the distinguished preacher, deceive the hearts of the innocent through smooth speech and blessings: they are despised in their dress, but swollen in heart, and as if in this world they despise everything, yet they seek all the things that are of the world at the same time. They confess that they are unworthy of all men, but they cannot be content with private titles, because they seek that by which they may seem worthier than all. Therefore may your piety, which almighty God has appointed to rule the whole world together with our most serene Lord, render him service through the favour of justice, from whom it has received the right of so great a power: the more truly it serves the Author of all in carrying out the truth, the more securely it will rule the world committed to it. Furthermore, I make known that I have received the writings of our most pious Lords, so that I may be at peace with my brother and fellow-priest John.

units.la: Et quidem sic religiosum Dominum decuit, ut ista præciperet sacerdotibus. Sed cum se nova præsumptione atq; superbia idem frater meus universalem Episcopum appelleret, ita ut sanctæ memoriæ decessoris mei adscribi se in synodo tali hoc superbo vocabulo faceret, quamuis cuncta acta illius synodi, sede contradicente Apostolica, soluta sint: triste mihi aliquid serenissimus Dominus innuit, quod non eum corripuit qui superbit, sed magis ab intentione mea declinare studuit, qui in hac causa Euangelicorum & Canonum statuta, humilitatis atq; rectitudinis virtute defendo. Qua in re prædicto fratre & consacerdote meo contra Euangelicam sententiam, contra Beatum quoq; Petrum Apostolum, & contra omnes Ecclesias, contraq; Canonum statuta agitur. Sed est omnipotens Dominus, in cuius manu sunt omnia, de quo scriptum est: Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum. Et quidem sæpe fatus sanctissimus frater serenissimo Domino multa suadere conatur: sed bene novi, quia tantæ illæ orationes eius & lachrymæ, nil ei a quoquam contra rationem aut animam suam surripi permittunt. Triste tamen valde est, ut patienter feratur, quatenus despectis omnibus, prædictus frater & Coepiscopus meus solus conetur appellari Episcopus.
units.tr: Indeed, it was fitting for such a religious Lord to command these things to the priests. But since my same brother, with new presumption and pride, calls himself universal Bishop, and in such a synod made himself enrolled under this proud title as the successor of my predecessor of holy memory, although all the acts of that synod have been annulled, the Apostolic See opposing, our most serene Lord has hinted to me something sad: that he has not rebuked him who is proud, but has rather tried to turn me aside from my purpose, I who in this cause defend the decrees of the Gospels and the Canons by the virtue of humility and uprightness. In this matter, my aforesaid brother and fellow-priest acts against the sentence of the Gospel, against blessed Peter the Apostle as well, against all the Churches, and against the decrees of the Canons. But the almighty Lord, in whose hand are all things, is the one of whom it is written: There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord. Indeed my oft-mentioned most holy brother tries often to persuade our most serene Lord of many things, but I well know that his many prayers and tears do not permit anything to be taken from him by anyone against his reason or his soul. Yet it is very sad that it should be borne patiently that, with everyone else despised, my aforesaid brother and fellow-bishop alone tries to be called Bishop.

units.la: Sed in hac eius superbia quid aliud nisi propinqua iam Antichristi esse tempora designatur? Quia illum videlicet imitatur, qui spretis in sociali gaudio Angelorum legionibus, adculmen conatus est singularitatis erumpere, dicens: Super astra coeli exaltabo solium meum, sedebo in monte testamenti, in lateribus aquilonis, & ascendam super altitudinem nubium, & ero similis Altissimo. Unde per omnipotentem Dominum rogo, ne pietatis vestræ tempora permittatis unius hominis elatione maculari, neq; tam perverso vocabulo vilum quoquo modo præbeatis assensum, atq; hac in causa nequaquam me plectas vestra despiciat: quia etli peccata Gregorii tanta sunt, ut pati talia debeat; Petri tamen Apostoli peccata nulla sunt, ut vestris temporibus pati ista mereretur. Unde iterum atq; iterum per Omnipotentem Dominum rogo, ut sicut parentes priores vestri Principes, Sancti Petri Apostoli gratiam quæsierunt: ita vos quoq; & hanc vobis quærere, & conservare curetis, & propter peccata nostra, qui ei indigne servimus, eius apud vos honor nullatenus minuatur, qui & modo vobis adiutor esse in omnibus, & postmodum vestra valeat peccata dimittere. Viginti autem iam & septem annosducimus, quod in hac urbe inter Longobardorum gladios vivimus. Quibus quam multa hac ab Ecclesia quotidianis diebus erogantur, ut inter eos viuere possimus, suggerenda non sunt. Sed breviter indico, quia sicut in Ravennæ partibus Dominorum pietas apud primum exercitum Italiæ sacellarium habet qui causis supervenientibus quotidianas expensas facit, ita & in hac urbe in causis tabulis eorum sacellarius ego sum. Et tamen hæc Ecclesia, quæ uno eodemq; tempore clericis, monasteriis, & pauperibus, populo atq; insuper Longobardis tam multa indesinenter expendit, Ecce adhuc ex omnium Ecclesiarum premitur afflictione, quæ de hac vnius hominis superbia multum gemunt, etsi nihil dicere præsumunt. Salonitanæ vero civitatis Episcopus me ac responsali meo ne- sclerate
units.tr: But in this pride of his, what else is indicated than that the times of Antichrist are now near? For he plainly imitates him who, scorning the legions of Angels in their joyful fellowship, tried to break forth to the peak of singularity, saying: I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High. Therefore I ask through almighty God that you not allow the times of your piety to be stained by the exaltation of one man, nor give, in any way, such a perverse title even a sliver of assent. And in this cause let your Highness by no means despise me, for even though the sins of Gregory are so great that he ought to suffer such things, yet the sins of the Apostle Peter are not such that they deserve to suffer such things in your times. Therefore again and again I ask through almighty God that, just as your earlier forebears, the Princes, sought the favour of blessed Peter the Apostle, so you too take care to seek and preserve this for yourselves, and that, on account of our sins, we who serve him unworthily, his honour among you be not diminished in any way, he who both now can be your helper in all things and afterwards can forgive your sins. Now, for twenty-seven years we have been living in this city among the swords of the Lombards. How many things are paid out from this Church every day so that we may live among them, there is no need to recount. But I say briefly that, just as in the parts of Ravenna the piety of our Lords has a treasurer before the first army of Italy, who makes the daily expenses for emergencies that arise, so also in this city I am the treasurer of their accounts in matters of this kind. And yet this Church, which at one and the same time without ceasing spends so much on clergy, monasteries, the poor, the people, and moreover on the Lombards, behold, is still oppressed by the affliction of all the Churches, which groan greatly over the pride of this one man, though they presume to say nothing. Moreover, the bishop of the city of Salona has been ordained without my knowledge and that of my deputy, and a thing has been done which happened under no earlier Princes.

units.la: C sciente ordinatus est, & facta res est, quæ sub nullis antecessoribus Principibus evenit. Quod ego audiens, ad eundem prævaricatorem, qui inordinate ordinatus est, protinus misi, ut omnino missarum solennia celebrare nullo modo præsumeret, nisi prius à Serenissimis Dominis cognosceret, si hoc fieri ipsi iussissent, quod et sub excommunicationis interpositione mandavi. Et contempto me atque despecto, in audaciam quorundam secularium hominum, quibus de multata sua Ecclesia præmia multa præbere dicitur, nunc usque missas facere præsumit, atq; ad me venire secundum iussionem Dominorum noluit. Ego autem præceptioni pietatis eorum obediens, eidem Maximo, qui me nesciente ordinatus est, hoc quod in ordinatione sua mte, vel Responsalem meum, prætermittere præsumsit, ita ex corde laxavi, ac si me auctore fuisset ordinatus. Alia vero perversa illius, mala scilicet corporalia, quæ cognovi, vel quia cum pecunia est electus, vel quia excommunicatus missas facere præsumsit, propter Deum irrequisita præterire non possum. Sed opto, & Dominum deprecor, quatenus nihil in eo de his quæ dicta sunt, valeat inveniri, & sine periculo animæ meæ causa ipsius terminetur. Prius tamen quam hæc cognoscantur, serenissimus Dominus discurrente iussione præcepit, ut eum venientem cum honore suscipiam. Et valde grave est, ut vir de quo tanta & talia nuncientur, cum ante requiri & discuti debeat, honoretur. Et si Episcoporum causæ mihi commissarum apud piissimos Dominos aliorum patroniis disponuntur, infelix ego in Ecclesia ista quid facio? Sed ut Episcopi mei me despiciant, & contra me refugium ad seculares iudices habeant, Omnipotenti Deo gratias ago, peccatis meis deputo. Hoc tamen breviter suggero, quia aliquantulum expecto, & si ad me diu venire distulerit, in eo exercere districtionem canonicam nullo modo cessabo. In omnipotenti autem Domino confido, quia longam piissimis Dominis vitam tribuet, & nobis sub manu vestra non secundum peccata nostra, sed secundum gratiæ suæ dona disponet. Hæc ego tranquillissimæ Dominiæ suggero: quia integerrima serenitas eius conscientia quanto moveatur zelo rectitudinis atq; iustitiæ, non ignoro.
units.tr: When I heard this, I immediately sent to that transgressor, who was ordained in an irregular manner, with the instruction that he should in no way presume to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass unless he first learned from the most serene Lords whether they had commanded this to be done; and I gave this order under the penalty of excommunication. But, scorning and despising me, relying on the boldness of certain secular men, from whom he is said to receive many rewards out of his diminished Church, he presumes to say Masses even up to now, and he has been unwilling to come to me as ordered by the Lords. But I, obeying the command of their piety, have so freely pardoned Maximus, who was ordained without my knowledge, for that which he presumed to omit in his ordination, whether in my presence or in that of my deputy, as if he had been ordained with my authority. But I cannot pass over, for God's sake without inquiry, the other perverse acts of his, the wicked bodily ones I have learned of, either because he was chosen for money, or because, being excommunicated, he presumed to say Masses. But I wish, and pray to the Lord, that nothing of what has been said may be found in him, and that his case may be settled without danger to my soul. Yet before these matters are looked into, our most serene Lord, by a swiftly sent command, has ordered that I receive him with honour when he comes. And it is very grave that a man about whom such great and such serious things are reported should be honoured before he has been called to account and examined. And if the causes of bishops committed to me are being arranged before our most pious Lords by the patronage of others, what do I, unhappy man, do in this Church? But that my bishops despise me and have a refuge against me among the secular judges, I thank almighty God and count it among my sins. I say this briefly, because I am waiting a little while, and if he delays too long in coming to me, I will in no way cease to exercise canonical discipline against him. But I trust in almighty God, who will grant our most pious Lords a long life and will dispose us under your hand not according to our sins but according to the gifts of his grace. I say these things to your most tranquil Ladyship, for I am not unaware how greatly your most upright Highness is moved by zeal for rectitude and justice.

units.la: EPISTOLA XXXVI.
units.tr: EPISTLE XXXVI.

units.la: Ut comminaretur insequantur superbiam Ioannis Episcopi, qui nomen Universalis sibi arrogabat.
units.tr: That he threatens those who pursue the pride of John, the Bishop who claimed the name of Universal for himself.

units.la: Eulogio Episcopo Alexandrino, & Anastasio Episcopo Antiocheno. Dum Prædicator egregius dicat: Quamdiu quidem sum gentium Apostolus, ministerium meum honorificabo; qui rursus alias dicens: Facti sumus ut parvuli in medio vestrum. Exemplum procul dubio nobis sequentibus ostendit, ut & humilitatem teneamus in mente, & tamen ordinis nostri dignitatem serve mus in honore, quatenus nec in nobis humilitas timida, nec erectio sit superba. Ante hos siquidem annos octo sanctæ memoriæ decessoris mei Pelagii tempore, frater & Coepiscopus noster Ioannes in Constantinopolitana urbe ex causa alia occasionem quærens Synodum fecit, in qua se Universalem appellare conatus est. Quod mox idem decessor meus ut agnovit, directis literis ex auctoritate S. Petri Apostoli eiusdem synodi acta cassavit. Quarum videlicet Epistolarum sanctitati vestræ exemplaria studui destinare. Diaconum vero, qui iuxta morem pro Responsis Ecclesiæ faciendis piissimorum Dominorum vestigiis adhærebat, cum præfato consacerdote nostro missarum solennia celebrare prohibuit. Cuius ego quoque sententiam sequens, similia prædicto consacerdoti meo scripta transmisi, quorum exemplaria vestræ beatitudini censui transmittenda: hoc præcipue intendens, ut hac de re, qua ex nova superbia tota universalis Ecclesiæ viscera perturbantur, prius sæpe fati fratris nostri animum modesta intentione pulsemus. Qui si nequaquam à suæ elationis rigore voluerit inclinari, tunc quid fieri debeat, cum omnipotentis Dei solatio subtilius perractetur. Sicut etiam veneranda mihi vestra sanctitas novit, vni per sanctam Chalcedonensem synodum Pontifici ledis Apostolicæ, cui Deo disponente deservio, hoc universitatis nomen oblatum est. Sed nullus unquam decessorum meorum hoc tam profano vocabulo vti consensit: quia videlicet si unus Patriarcha universalis dicitur, Patriarcharum nomen cæteris derogatur. Sed absit hoc, absit à Christiana mente, id sibi velle quempiam arripere, unde fratrum suorum honorem imminuere ex quantulacunque parte videatur. Cum ergo nos hunc honorem nolumus oblatum suscipere; pensate quam ignominiosum sit hunc sibi quempiam violenter voluisse. Propterea sanctitas vestra in suis epistolis neminem unquam Universalem nominet, ne sibi debitum detrahat, cum alteri honorem offert indebitum. Nec hacin re de serenissimis Dominis animum vestrum mordeat siniatra suspicio, quia omnipotentem Dominum metuit, & contra statuta Evangelica, contra sacratissimos canones agere aliquid nullo modo consentit. Ego vero quamuis à vobis per longa terrarum atque maris spatia disiunctus sim, tamen omnino vobis corde coniunctus. Idque de vestra beatitudine erga me modis omnibus confido: quia cum me vicissim diligitis, à me non longe estis. Et magis gratias referimus grano illi sinapis, quia ex modici despicabilisque seminis specie, ita est ramis ex eadem radice surgentibus, atque se distendentibus usque quaque diffusus, ut in eis volatilia cœli cuncta nidificent: Gratiaque sit fermento illi quo tribus farinæ satis totius humani generis massam in unitate conspersit. Atque parvo lapidi, qui abscissus de monte sine manibus, occupavit universam faciem orbis terræ. Qui ad hoc se visquequaque distendit, ut ex omni humano genere in unitatem redacto totius corpus perficeretur Ecclesiæ, atque ita ad totius compaginis pertineret commodum, membrorum parpartialis illa distinctio. Unde nos quoque à vobis non longe sumus. Agamus ergo ei gratias, qui solutis inimicitiis in carne sua fecit, ut in orbe terrarum unus esset grex, & unum ovile sub se uno pastore; memores semper quid nos praedicator veritatis admonet, dicens: Solicite servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis: & Pacem sectamini cum omnibus & sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo videbit Deum. Qui aliis quoque discipulis dicit: si fieri potest, quod ex vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habentes. Vidit enim pacem bonos cum malis habere non posse: & idcirco sicut nostis praemisit, si fieri potest. Sed quia pax nisi in duabus partibus firmari non valet, unum hanc mali fugiunt, boni tenere medullitus debent. Unde & mire dicitur, Quod ex vobis est: ut videlicet in nobis maneat, etiam cum à pravorum hominum mente repellitur. Quam videlicet pacem tunc veraciter tenemus, cum superborum culpas, charitate simul & iustitia insistente prosequimur, cum eos diligimus, & eorum vitia odio habemus. Opus quippe Dei homo est, sed opus hominis vitium. Nos ergo discernamus quid Deus, quid item homo fecerit: & neque propter errorem odio habeamus hominem, neque propter hominem diligamus errorem. Unita ergo mente insequamur in homine malum superbiae, ut ab hoste suo videlicet errore, prius ipse homo liberetur. Praestabit vitas omnipotens Redemptor noster charitatis atque iustitiae; praestabit nobis longe à nobis positis unitatem spiritus sui, ipse cuius artificio quasi in arce modum, quatuor mundi structura lateribus, atque imputribilium lignorum compagine, & bitumine charitatis adstricta, nullius adversitate spiritus, nullius venientis extrinsecus tumore fluctus perturbetur Ecclesia. Sed quemadmodum illius gubernante gratia petendum est, ut nulla nos superveniens exterius unda conturbet; ita ex totis orandum est visceribus fratres charissimi, ut suae providentiae dextera cumulum sententiae in nobis interioris exhauriat. Adversarius quippe Diabolus qui contra humiles saeviens, sicut leo rugiens circuit quaerens quem devoret, non iam, ut cernimus, caulas circuit, sed ita valide in quibusdam Ecclesiae necessariis membris dentes figit, ut nulli sit dubium, quin nisi unanimiter faciente Domino cunctorum providia pastorum turba concarrat, omne, quod absit, citius ovile dilaniet. Perpendite fratres charissimi, quid è vicino subsequitur, cuius & in sacerdotibus erumpunt tam perversa primordia. Quia enim iuxta est ille de quo scriptum est: Ipse est rex super universos filios superbiae, quod non sine graui dolore dicere compellor, frater & Coepiscopus noster Ioannes mandata Dominica, Apostolica praecepta, regulas patrum despiciens, eum per elationem praecurrere conatur in nomine. Vestrae autem beatitudini indicet omnipotens Deus, quam graui considerationis huius gemitu torqueor, quod ille quondam mihi modestissimus, ille omnibus dilectus, ille qui in eleemosynis, orationibus atque ieiuniis videbatur occupatus; ex eo in quo sedebat cinere, ex ea quam praetendebat humilitate; iactantiam sumpsit, ita ut universa sibi tenter adscribere; & omnia quae soli uni capiti cohaerent, videlicet Christo, per elationem pompatici sermonis eiusdem Christi studeat sibi membra subiugare. Nec mirum, quod ille tentator, qui initium omnis peccati scit esse superbiam; & tunc ea in primo homine ante omnia usus est, & nunc eam quibusdam hominibus ponit in fine virtutum, ut qui aliquatenus bonis vitae studiis eius videbatur crudelissimas manus effugere; eis in ipsa meta boni operis; & in ipsa quodammodo opponat perfectionis conclusione tenticulum. Unde magnopere orandum est, & omnipotens Deus assiduis precibus implorandus, ut huncà mente illius averat errorem, hoc ab unitate atque humilitate Ecclesiae malum superbiae, & confusionis amoneat. Et fauente Domino omnibus viribus concurrendum atque providendum, ne in unius veneno sermonis, viuentia in Christi corpore membra moriantur. Si enim hoc dici licenter permittitur, honor Patriarcharum omnium negatur. Et cum fortasse is in errore perit, qui Universalis dicitur, nullus iam Episcopus remansisse in statu veritatis inveniatur. Obtestor ergo ut constanter & sine praeiudicio servetis sicut accepistis Ecclesias; & nihil sibi in vobis haec tentatio Diabolicae usurpationis adscribat: State fortes, state securi, scriptaque cum Universalis nominis salsitate nec dare unquam, nec suscipere praesumatis. Omnes Episcopos curae vestrae subiectos, ab huius elationis inquinatione prohibete, ut universae vos Ecclesiae Patriarchas, non solum in bonis operibus, sed etiam in veritatis auctoritate cognoscant. Si qua autem forsan adversa subsequantur, unanimiter persistentes, etiam moriendo debemus ostendere, quia in damnando generalitatis nomine nostrum specialiter aliquid non amamus. Dicamus cum Paulo: Mihi vivere Christus est, & mori lucrum. Audiamus quid primus omnium pastorum dicit: Si quid patiamini propter iustitiam, beati eritis. Mihi enim credite; quia honorem, quem pro praedicanda veritate suscepimus, si necessitatis causa exigat, securius pro eadem veritate relinquimus; quam tenemus. Promeautem; sicut vestram charissimam beatitudinem decet, orate: ut hoc quod vobis loqui audeo, operibus ostendam.
units.tr: To Eulogius, Bishop of Alexandria, and Anastasius, Bishop of Antioch. Since the outstanding Preacher says, "As long as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will honour my ministry," and elsewhere, speaking again, "We have become as little children in the midst of you," he undoubtedly shows us, who follow him, that we should both keep humility in our minds and yet preserve the dignity of our order with honour, so that there is neither timid humility nor proud elation in us. Some eight years ago, in the time of my predecessor of holy memory, Pelagius, our brother and fellow bishop John, seeking an occasion in a different matter in the city of Constantinople, held a synod in which he tried to call himself Universal. As soon as my predecessor learned of this, he sent letters, issued by the authority of St. Peter the Apostle, and annulled the acts of that synod. I have taken care to send copies of those letters to your holiness. He also forbade the deacon, who, as is the custom, was attached to the feet of the most pious lords to make the Responses of the Church, from celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass with the aforementioned fellow priest of ours. Following his judgment, I too sent writings similar to those to my aforesaid fellow priest, and I have judged that copies of these should be sent to your blessedness. My chief aim in this is that, concerning this matter, by which the whole bowels of the universal Church are disturbed by a new pride, we should first try, by a moderate approach, to move the mind of the aforementioned brother of ours. If he should in no way be willing to be turned from the rigour of his arrogance, then what ought to be done shall be considered more carefully, with the comfort of almighty God. As your venerable holiness also knows, this title of universality was offered to the Pontiff of the Apostolic See of Rome, whom I serve by God's disposition, through the holy Synod of Chalcedon. But none of my predecessors ever consented to use this so profane a title, because, clearly, if one Patriarch is called universal, the name of Patriarch is taken away from the others. But far be it, far be it from a Christian mind, for anyone to want to seize for himself something by which, in whatever small part, the honour of his brothers seems to be diminished. Therefore, since we are unwilling to accept this honour when it is offered to us, consider how shameful it is for anyone to have wished to seize it for himself by force. For this reason, let your holiness never in your letters name anyone Universal, lest you take from another what is due to him when you offer to someone else an honour that is not his due. Nor let any evil suspicion about the most serene lords trouble your mind in this matter, for they fear almighty God and are in no way willing to do anything against the Gospel precepts or the most sacred canons. For my part, although I am separated from you by long stretches of land and sea, I am nevertheless wholly joined to you in heart. I trust this of your blessedness towards me in every way, because, since you love me in return, you are not far from me. And we give thanks even more to that grain of mustard seed, which, from the appearance of a small and despised seed, so spreads its branches, rising from the same root and extending everywhere, that all the birds of the heaven nest in them; and thanks be to that leaven which mixed the mass of the whole human race into unity, in three measures of flour; and to that small stone, which, cut from the mountain without hands, filled the whole face of the earth. It extends itself in every direction so that, from the whole human race brought into unity, the body of the entire Church might be made complete, and so that this particular distinction of members might serve the benefit of the whole structure. Hence we too are not far from you. Let us therefore give thanks to him who, having abolished enmities in his flesh, made it so that there would be one flock on the earth and one fold under one shepherd, always mindful of what the preacher of the truth admonishes us, saying: Be eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; and follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one will see God. He also says to the other disciples: If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, have peace with all men. For he saw that the good cannot have peace with the wicked; and therefore, as you know, he put in the words, if it is possible. But since peace cannot be secured except between two parties, the wicked must flee from it, and the good must hold to it with their whole marrow. Hence it is also wonderfully said, "as far as it depends on you," so that, namely, it may remain in us, even when it is rejected by the mind of wicked men. This peace we truly hold when we pursue the faults of the proud, with charity and justice insisting together, when we love them, and hate their vices. For man is God's work, but the vice is man's work.
