Each of them, with one united and devout purpose, gathered to amend these wrongs. Some were seized, others driven off, and the author of the evils was shut out of the palace and placed in custody, and clothed in a nun's habit. In this way they restored their father to quiet and to some measure of honour. But the sons showed only the slightest forgiveness, and once their good arrangements had been undone by the flatteries of the flesh, by wicked favours and shameless adulation, the woman was again summoned back into the palace as if she were its lawful mistress. She was placed above the counsels and the counsellors, and through her instigations she began to stir up the barbarians with hard horns, to harass the sons and to disturb the peoples. Thus mortals were so afflicted that they did not so much suffer persecutions unjustly as the persecutors carried them out unwillingly and under compulsion; and not only did they carry them out, they also endured them, since they were forced most violently into oaths that contradicted one another. Look and see whether anything of this kind has ever happened. They swore an oath to the younger emperor; then, when he himself acted, some of them swore to the king as well, and at last almost all were compelled to swear to the boy. Nor did even this end it, but as if none of these things had happened, fresh oaths arose. "Shall I not visit for these things, says the Lord, and shall not such a nation be punished for despising God and for defiling his name?" As it is written: "You shall not swear falsely, nor profane the name of the Lord your God" (Jer. 5; Lev. 19). Behold, with the abysses of folly laid open, to what a pass things have come! For when they ought to have been sending an army against foreign nations, and the emperor himself ought to have been fighting against the barbarian peoples, so that they might be brought under the faith and the borders of the faithful kingdom enlarged (for so the universal Church prays in her solemn prayers on the days of the Lord's Passion, for the emperors, that God may make the barbarian nations subject to them), now, on the contrary, the whole kingdom, with its outlying parts, is conspiring together in its own centre, though with differing aims: some are being prepared to spend the kingdom's very vitals, others to appease, if it can be done, a most unjust discord. All of them ought to have weighed with pious mind what is said in those prayers, where the priest admonishes: "Let us also pray for our most Christian emperor, that God and Lord may subject to him all the barbarian nations for our lasting peace." So the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth, prays that the barbarians may be made subject to the most Christian emperor, not that the subjects may be thrown into confusion and made barbarous. For it is not the part of a most Christian emperor to drive out his subjects and to divide those who are united. O Lord God of heaven and earth, why have you allowed your most faithful and most Christian servant, our emperor, to fall into such negligence that he is unwilling to see by what evils he is surrounded? For he loves those who hate him and hates those who love him. And if it is true, as many who seem to understand more closely affirm, that there are some at his side who vainly await the destruction of his sons, and if they see it, they have agreed among themselves to lay hands on the emperor and divide the kingdom between them, whether this is true they themselves know; yet there are many who do not doubt that those of whom it is said lean upon the kingdom like a leaning wall and a pushed-over fence. Hence it is clear that unless God helps, the kingdom will either be given to foreigners, or be divided among many tyrants, or perhaps be handed over to Antichrist, who is to be prepared, and in this he is resembled, since the emperor, who ought to have waged just wars against the kings of the barbarians, is preparing unjust action against his beloved sons. Some also say that the lady of the elder palace, apart from those things which are said about her hidden and open conduct, plays the child, while some of the clergy wait for the outcome; and most of them conclude, following the form which the Apostle writes concerning the choice of bishops: "one who rules his own house well, having his children in subjection with all chastity; for if a man does not know how to rule his own house, how will he take care of the Church of God?" They ought to have preached to the playful lady: if a queen does not know how to rule, how will she take care of the honour of the palace, or how will she diligently wield the helm of the kingdom? They ought also to have brought to her memory what is found above, which can be applied, at least as far as the outward sense goes, namely what Scripture says: "A worthy woman is a crown to her husband; but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones" (Prov. 12). And again: "A continual dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike; whoever restrains her restrains the wind, and grasps oil in his right hand" (Prov. 27). But perhaps someone will say: she is not contentious, but flattering. To this it must be answered that there is no greater contention than to wish to provoke, embitter, dishonour and utterly alienate good sons from a good father; for it is said that beauty alone is loved by a husband without the duty of love. Let it be impressed upon both that the same Scripture says again: "Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain; a woman who fears the Lord shall be praised" (Prov. 31). Now therefore all who fear and love God, the king also and the kingdom, must, in a peaceful fellowship, using the things of the world and enjoying the things of God, labour with all their effort that the wound of iniquity may be drained and the scar of health may be drawn over it, without the shedding of blood, without the slaughter of killing, without the bitterness of quarrels, without the turbulent and foul mingling of unclean spirits; so that it may truly be said of the Church of this kingdom: "This is the house of God and the gate of heaven." Moreover, "the gate of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matt. 16). And again: "The Lord your God in the midst of you is mighty; he will rejoice over you with gladness, he will be silent in his love, and he will exult over you with praise; I will gather those who have fallen away from the law, because they were from you, so that reproach may no longer lie upon you"; and let every apostle say, Amen, Amen, and a hymn to God.

units.la: Sicut verum non est tantum in dictis, sed & in factis, sicenim Apostolus demonstrat dicens: veritatem facientes in charitate crescamus in illo per omnia qui est caput Christus. Et alius Apostolus: Filioli, non diligamus verbo neque lingua, sed opere & veritate. Et iterum: Si dixerimus quoniam societatem habemus cum eo, & in tenebris ambulamus, mentimur & non facimus veritatem. Ita quoque mendacium non est tantum modo verborum, sed & factorum, sicut in Apocalypsi loquitur Dominus dicens: Non intrabit in ea, haud dubium, quin ciuitatem cœlestem aliquid coinquinatum, & facieus abominationem & mendacium. Et paulo post: Omnis qui amat, & facit mendacium. Et Dominus in Euangelio, de inuentore omnium malorum ait: Ille homicida erat ab initio, & in veritate non stetit. Si ergo illa veritas, de qua & in Psalmis cantamus: Prope esto Domine & omnis via tua veritas, omnium hominum mentes possidere, etiam sine rectoribus & principibus res mundi concordi societate pacata manerent: nunc autem quia ille, qui in veritate non stetit, contra veritatem agere numquam desistit; & dominantibus hominibus scandalorum zizania seminare non cessat, aptasibi corda satis inueniens, quæ fouent, & nutriant semina eius; redundat malum commotionis, quod quietem Pacis & unitatis insano furore conturbet. Propter quod sollicite vigilandum est, & sagacitet agendum contra corruptores veritatis, & Pacis, lingua & manu ut aut cohibeantur, aut comprimantur. Commotio itaque huius temporis, & harum Regionum, quæ mira omnipotentis Dei suauitate & dulcedine, sine conflictu armorum sedata est, non segniter memoranda est, sed debet corda fidelium in laudibus Dei & gratiarum actione alacriter succendere, & ad solertiam cautelæ sollicite reddere. Quæ commotio & conturbatio quale habuerit initium, vel originem, non est penitus reticenduum.
units.tr: Just as truth is not only in words but also in deeds, as the Apostle shows when he says: "Speaking the truth in love, let us grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ" (Eph. 4). And another Apostle: "Little children, let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth" (1 John 3). And again: "If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not do the truth" (1 John 1). So too a lie is not only of words but also of deeds, as the Lord speaks in the Apocalypse: "There shall in no way enter into it anything unclean, or one who practises abomination and falsehood" (Rev. 21). And a little later: "Everyone who loves and practises falsehood" (Rev. 22). And the Lord in the Gospel, speaking of the author of all evils, says: "He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth" (John 8). If then that truth, of which we also sing in the Psalms, "Near are you, O Lord, and all your ways are truth," held possession of the minds of all men, the affairs of the world would remain at peace in harmonious fellowship even without rulers and princes. But now, since he who did not stand in the truth never ceases to act against the truth, and does not stop sowing the tares of scandal among men in power, finding hearts fit for him that nourish and foster his seeds, the evil of disturbance overflows, to trouble the peace and unity of quiet with insane fury. Therefore we must watch carefully and act wisely against the corrupters of truth and peace, by tongue and hand, that they may either be restrained or suppressed. The disturbance of this time and of these regions, which has been calmed without armed conflict by the wonderful sweetness and kindness of almighty God, is not to be remembered lightly; it ought rather to kindle the hearts of the faithful eagerly to praise God and give thanks, and to make them diligently alert to careful prudence. Nor is it at all to be passed over in silence what beginning or origin this commotion and disturbance had.

units.la: Igitur cum Christianissimus & piissimus Imperator Dominus Ludouicus, bonæ Coniugis fide & moribus sibi congruentis consortium amisisset, necesse fuit vt aliam sibi acciperet, quæ et posset esse adiutrix in regimine & gubernatione Palatii regni, sed occulto Dei iudicio talis assumpta est; quæ licet in primis annis viri & domini sui virtute & potestate pressa, subdita fuerit, tamen in processu temporis talis inuenta est, quæ magnorum fluctuum commotionis & conturbationis läigus thesaurus esse posset; quæ non solum plebes ac populos, siue Principes, verum etiam elegantissimos Filios Imperatoris etiam coniugatos, & gubernacula regnorum possidentes afflgeret; contristaret, & conturbaret, & pene attereret & exterminaret. Cumq; talibus inter temerarios videret, hi quibus curæ erat de statu & honore Regni, ac tranquillitate pacis, & quiete populi; dehonestari Palatium, obscurati claritatem regni, & ad ignominiam deduci nomen regnantium; coepetunt queri, & murmurare, ac dolere, & deplorare. Inter hæc concitati sunt spiritus virorum honoratorum, & filiorum regis, & crescente conluctio, accedente etiam consilio, conuenerunt singuli de loco suo, & coniunctiad Palatium, effugauerunt ministros sceleris, & Reginam, quæ totius mali causa erat, exclauserunt de domo & honore regni, & constituerunt in retrusionem exilii: Ac deinceps quasi iam liberatum bonum Patrem de laqueo ruinæ, gaudebant se impleße quod inscriptum est: eiice derisorem, & exibit cum eo iurgium, cessabunt causa, & contumelia. Hoc tam irreprehensibile factum & omni laude dignissimum cum complessent, filii redierunt ad sua, restituto Patre honori & gloriæ suæ. His ita transactis inimicus omnis boni, auctorq; omnis mali; qui non reliquerat corda possessa, satagit instaurare & redintegrare malum suum, & Regina, quæ mutato habitu regali putabatur perdurare in habitu sanctimoniali, sicut ordo poscebat, & rectitudo Iudicii docebat, reducta est in Palatium; & assumta in consortium quasi legitima coniunx, quod esse iam nullatenus poterat. Collocata itaq; turpiter & indecenter in fastigio regali, prius malum auxit, & multiplicauit; ad quod bonus filius, quid agere debuit, nunquid dissimulare? nunquid silere? nunquid quiescere? non ita placuit illi indormitabili oculo qui custodit Israel suum, sed suscitauit spiritus filiorum & conuenerunt iterum; ad succidendam reciditam malorum stirpem. Timebant enim ne Patri euenire illud, quod de quodam Rege Scriptura Sancta loquitur, dicens; Igitur non fuit alter talis, vt habet, qui venundatus est vt faceret malum in conspectu Domini: concitauit enim eum Gazabel uxor sua, & abominabilis factus est. Sed forte aliquis diuersæ voluntatis homo, amouere nitatur hæc verba Scripturæ sanctæ; tanquam inconuenientia, eo quod sequatur in rantum, ut sequitur idola Amorrheorum. Nouerit quisquis ille est; non posse euacuari congruentiam eorum in hoc loco, quoniam tempore legis in veteri populo idola & simulacra significabant omnes errores in nouo populo, tempore videlicet Gratiæ: Nam & ipse ordo horum verborum, ita intelligendus est; abominabilis factus est diuersis cupiditatibus & illecebris, ut etiam euidenter ad cultum ruerat idolorum; quisquis autem aliter hic sentire vult; pensat qualiter contradicat Apostolo dicenti: Et auaritiam quæ est simulacrorum seruitus: & videat quam veraciter dictum sit; radix omnium est cupiditas, quam quidam appetentes errauerunt à fide. Si ergo cupiditas etrare facit à fide, & auaritia simulachrorum est seruitus; quod malum remanet, quod non de radice cupiditatis oritur? Propter quod fideliter colligendum est, omnes appetitores diuitiarum gloriæ, & honoris secularis, atque primatus, quam non longe absint ab idolorum cultura: Hæc propterea distinxit. dicimus, vt ostendamus mala & bona, antiquorum malis & bonis congruenter aptari, & hiis qui errant in nouo populo. Et quanquam Ahab concitante se vxore sua errauerit à fide, & ea auctrice perpetrauerit facinus illud de morte Naboth Israelitæ; correptus tamen ab Helia Propheta, non correctus, compulsus est agere pœnitentiam: quia actione pœnitentiæ mala sibi imminentia distulit, non abstulit. Hoc si recte perpendatur, liquido demonstrat, quantum nocent vxores malæ viris suis. Iehu autem, quem Dominus suscitauit in Regem, ad puniendam domum Ahab, & eius decepticem vxorem; licet æternam vitam non promeruerit, eo quod à peccatis Hieroboam non recesserit, quia studiose exercuit visiones Domini de Iezabel, & domum eius, quam illa concitauerat, concessum est ei, vt filii eius vsq; ad quartam generationem regnarent. Post eum beatus quoq; Ioiadas, & sanctus Pontifex, quia Athaliam impiissimam interfici iussit, & Ioas in solio Patris collocauit, & Hierusalem à sordibus & immunditiis purgauit, tali eum laude exornat Scriptura diuina, dicens: Sepelierunt autem Ioiadae Sacerdotem cum regibus, eo quod fecisset bonum cum Israel, & cum domo eius. Ecce iste pius Sacerdos, & temporali & æterna retributione remuneratus est: Iehu autem tantum temporali. Videamus quoq; quid Samson contigerit, quem Apostolus in Catalogo virorum fortium annumerat, amauit itaq; mulierem non amantem se; quæ plus obtemperauit inimicis eius, quam amico amantis se: & quia ille vir iustus credidit mulieri infideli, ideo & lumen oculorum amisit, & ducatum Israelitæ gentis perdidit. Cui licet postea restituta sit virtus pristina, & ignominiosam vitam gloriosa morte finierit; æterna quidem vita non caruit, tamen ducatum pristinum non recuperauit. Sic ergo dignetur Dominus diuum Imperator pie perpendere, vt cœleste & sempiternum regnum non perdat, qui deceptus à muliere, terrenum & temporale amisit: cedat diuinis iudiciis, quia nihil in terra sine causa: Voueat & reddat Domino Deo terribili, & ei qui aufert spiritum Principum. Bonorum enim Regum est dicere, semper, quasi tumentes super me fluctus, timui Deum. Hanc dixit beatus Iob, qui conanti se decipere vxori suæ non consensit, sed rigida indignatione redarguit, dicens, quasi vna de stultis mulieribus locuta es; qui & in alio loco de Deo dicit, apud ipsum est fortitudo & sapientia, ipse novit & decipientem, & eum qui dicitur, & Balthasar regum dissoluit & præcingit lumbos eorum: Et iterum: Qui immutat cor Principum populi terræ, & decipit eos vt frustra incedant per invium. Quod & ipsi beato Iob contingeret, si suasionem vxoris suæ libenter audisset: Ideo ergo terribilis Dominus non tantum populis terræ, sed & ipsis Principibus populi, de quo quidem Rex superbus & humiliatus confitetur coactus dicens, Altissimo benedixi, & viventem in sempiternum laudavi, & glorificavi, quia potestas eius, potestas sempiterna, & Regnum eius in generationem. Et omnes habitatores terræ apud eum in nihilum reputati sunt, iuxta voluntatem enim suam facit, tam in virtutibus cœli, quam in habitatoribus terræ, & non est qui resistat manui eius, & dicat ei, quare fecisti? Et post pauca: Nunc igitur ego Nebuchodonosor laudo, & magnifico, & glorifico regem cœli, quia omnia opera eius vera, & viæ eius iudicia, & gradientes in superbia potest humiliare. Neq; vllo modo, hæc idcirco dicimus, vt Dominum quondam nostrum Imperatorem impiis & in fidelibus Regibus comparemus, sed quia permisit se à Muliere iniqua decipi; contigit illi, quod scriptum est: Qui conturbat domum suam, possidebit ventos. Per quam conturbationem & ventorum possessionem, perpetrata sunt innumerabilia periuria, & depredationes immensæ cum homicidiis, adulteriis, & incestis, pro quibus omnibus pœnitentiis, necessarium est toti loricissimo quondam Imperatori, vt redeat ad cor suum, agatq; pœnitentiam, humiliatus sub potenti manu Dei, cui non est impossibile tribuere illi exaltationem æternæ vitæ: quia exaltatio temporalis vitæ, iam non congruit illi, qui conturbata domo, & mente diuina dispensatione, & iudicio cessit alteri, & locum dedit non cuilibet inimico aut extraneo; sed charissimo filio, propter quod in iucunditate, & exultatione cordis sui, summas gratiarum actiones, summo omnipotenti Deo indesinenter persoluere debet, quia sicut semper optauit, non successit illi in regnum inimicus expugnator, sed filius amator. Nunc ergo audiant omnes in commune tumultuosi & quieti Prophetam dicentem, sileat omnis terra à facie Domini. Et Psalmistam, Timeat Dominum omnis terra, ab eo autem commoueantur omnes inhabitantes orbem, quoniam ipse dixit & facta sunt, &c.
units.tr: Therefore, when the most Christian and most pious Emperor, Lord Louis, had lost a good wife, one whose faith and character suited him, it was necessary for him to take another who might be a helper in the rule and government of the royal palace. By the hidden judgment of God, however, he took a woman who, although in the first years she was held down and subject to the virtue and power of her husband and lord, was in the course of time found to be such that she could become a great treasure of tumult and disorder, and who afflicted, saddened, troubled, and nearly crushed and destroyed not only the common people and the peoples, or the princes, but even the most distinguished sons of the Emperor, who were themselves married and held the reins of kingdoms. When those who cared about the state and honour of the kingdom, and about the peace and quiet of the people, saw that the palace was being dishonoured, the brightness of the kingdom obscured, and the name of its rulers brought to shame by such recklessness, they began to complain, to murmur, to grieve, and to lament. Meanwhile the spirits of honourable men and of the king's sons were stirred up, and as the strife grew, and counsel was added, they gathered each from his own place and came together at the palace. They drove away the agents of the crime and shut out of the house and the honour of the kingdom the queen, who was the cause of all the evil, and they resolved to confine her in exile. Then, as if the good father had at last been freed from the snare of ruin, they rejoiced that they had fulfilled what is written: "Cast out the scoffer, and strife will go out with him; quarrel and reproach will cease." When they had done this blameless and most praiseworthy deed, the sons returned to their own places, and their father was restored to his honour and glory. After these things, the enemy of all good, the author of all evil, who had not left the hearts he possessed, set about to restore and renew his evil. The queen, who had put off her royal dress and was thought to persist in the dress of a religious woman, as order required and the justice of judgment taught, was brought back into the palace, and taken into partnership as if she were a lawful wife, which in no way could be. Once she was shamefully and indecently placed on the royal throne, she increased and multiplied the earlier evil. What ought a good son to have done in response? Should he dissemble? Should he be silent? Should he rest? It did not please Him who keeps Israel, the one who neither slumbers nor sleeps, that it should be so; rather, He stirred up the spirits of the sons, and they gathered again to cut down the evil stock that had been cut back and had sprouted again. For they feared lest what Holy Scripture says of a certain king should befall their father: "There was none like Ahab, who sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord, for Gazabel his wife stirred him up, and he became abominable." But perhaps some man of a different mind will try to set aside these words of Holy Scripture as unsuitable, on the ground that it follows, "he went so far as to follow the idols of the Amorites." Let him know that the fitness of these words in this place cannot be undone, since in the time of the law, among the old people, idols and images signified all errors among the new people, that is, in the time of grace. Indeed the order of these words is to be understood thus: he became abominable through various desires and allurements, so that he even plainly rushed into the worship of idols. But whoever wishes to think otherwise here, let him weigh how he contradicts the Apostle, who says: "And covetousness, which is idolatry"; and let him see how truly it is said: "The love of money is the root of all evils, which some coveting have erred from the faith." If, therefore, greed leads people astray from the faith, and covetousness is the bondage of idols, what evil remains that does not spring from the root of greed? Therefore it must be faithfully gathered that all who seek after riches, worldly glory, honour, and primacy are not far removed from the worship of idols. We have drawn this distinction in order to show that the evils and goods of the ancients are fittingly applied to the evils and goods of those who go astray among the new people. And although Ahab, at the urging of his wife, erred from the faith, and under her guidance committed that crime of the death of Naboth the Israelite, yet, rebuked by the prophet Elijah, though not corrected, he was compelled to do penance, because by the act of repentance he put off the evils hanging over him, and did not take them away. If this is weighed rightly, it clearly shows how greatly evil wives harm their husbands. Jehu, however, whom the Lord raised up as king to punish the house of Ahab and its deceiving wife, though he did not merit eternal life, because he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, yet because he zealously carried out the Lord's visitations upon Jezebel and her house, which she had stirred up, it was granted to him that his sons should reign to the fourth generation. After him, the blessed Jehoiada too, the holy high priest, because he ordered that the most impious Athaliah be put to death, placed Joash on his father's throne, and cleansed Jerusalem from filth and uncleanness, is adorned by divine Scripture with such praise, saying: "They buried Jehoiada the priest with the kings, because he had done good in Israel and toward his house." Behold, this pious priest was rewarded with both temporal and eternal recompense, whereas Jehu received only the temporal. Let us also consider what happened to Samson, whom the Apostle counts among the catalogue of men of strength. He loved a woman who did not love him, who obeyed his enemies more than her lover who loved her; and because that righteous man trusted an unfaithful woman, he therefore lost the light of his eyes and lost the leadership of the Israelite nation. Although his former strength was later restored to him, and he ended his shameful life with a glorious death, he did not lack eternal life, yet he did not recover his former leadership. So may the Lord deign to make the divine Emperor consider piously that he should not lose the heavenly and everlasting kingdom, he who, deceived by a woman, has lost the earthly and temporal one. Let him yield to the divine judgments, because nothing on earth happens without cause. Let him make his vows and pay them to the Lord God, the terrible one, who takes away the spirit of princes. For it is the mark of good kings to say always, as if the waves were swelling over me: "I feared God." This was said by the blessed Job, who did not consent when his wife tried to deceive him, but rebuked her with a stern indignation, saying: "You have spoken like one of the foolish women." Elsewhere too he says of God: "With him is strength and wisdom; he knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived; he loosens the bonds of kings and girds their loins." And again: "He changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth, and makes them wander in a trackless waste to no purpose." This would also have happened to the blessed Job himself, had he gladly listened to the persuasion of his wife. Therefore the Lord is terrible not only to the peoples of the earth, but also to the princes of the people. Concerning this, the proud king, humbled and compelled, confesses, saying: "I blessed the Most High, and I praised and glorified him who lives forever, because his power is an everlasting power, and his kingdom is from generation to generation. All the inhabitants of the earth are reckoned as nothing before him; he does according to his will among the powers of heaven and the inhabitants of the earth, and there is no one who can resist his hand or say to him, 'What have you done?'" And a little after: "Now therefore I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and magnify and glorify the King of heaven, because all his works are true and his ways judgments, and he is able to humble those who walk in pride." Nor do we say these things in order to compare our former Emperor with impious and unfaithful kings, but because he allowed himself to be deceived by a wicked woman, and there happened to him what is written: "He who troubles his own house shall inherit the wind." Through this trouble and possession of the wind, countless perjuries and immense plunderings were committed, along with murders, adulteries, and incests, for all of which repentance is necessary for the once most afflicted Emperor, that he may return to his heart, do penance, and be humbled under the mighty hand of God, to whom it is not impossible to give him exaltation in eternal life. For exaltation in temporal life no longer suits him who, with his house troubled and his mind, through divine disposition and judgment, yielded to another and gave place not to any enemy or stranger, but to his dearest son. Therefore, with joy and exultation of heart, he ought without ceasing to pay the highest thanksgivings to almighty God, because, as he always wished, it was not an enemy conqueror who succeeded him in the kingdom, but a loving son. Now therefore let all, both the restless and the quiet, hear the prophet who says: "Let all the earth keep silence before the Lord." And the psalmist: "Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him, for he spoke and it was done," etc.

units.la: B. PETRI DAMIANI, CARDINALIS ROMANI ET EPISCOPI OSTIENSIS, TRACTATVS DE CORRECTIONE EPISCOPI ET PAPÆ.
units.tr: Blessed Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia, A Treatise on the Correction of a Bishop and of the Pope.

units.la: Llud quod dicitur; Non licet cuilibet Ecclesiæ filium ad maiorem Ecclesiam proprio rectu, Episcopi & quæcunq; sunt corrigenda deferre: nimis absonum, & prorsus Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ probatur aduersum. Nam cui melius dicitur quod delinquit, quam ei, qui magistri officio fungitur; & ideo inter reliquos fratres præminet, vt quod aliis licet, ipse solus per lus per propriæ sedis privilegium errata corrigat sacerdotum? Quis est enim hic arrogantiæ tumor, qui elationis fastus, quæ denique tanta superbia, ut liceat Episcopum per fas & nefas ad propriæ voluntatis arbitrium viuere: & quod insolenter excessum est, à subiectis suis dedignetur audire? Præsertim cum illi non adierint tribunalia præsidum, nec forensium pulsauerint examina cognitorum: Sed Ecclesiam potius adeant, & sacerdotibus iudicabilia sui sacerdotis exponant, ut quod sæcularibus euenire poterat in derisum, graviter & honeste per Sacerdotale corrigatur officium. Vbi profecto dignum est, vt is qui impetitur, vel ex ratione exhibeat innocentem, vel confiteatur humiliter peccatorem. Nec his allegationibus vrendum est, ut dicat, se non debere ab his qui sibi subiecti sunt, accusari, ne videatur excessibus suis velamen obtendere, & iudicium subterfugere, dum conatur in alium montem quæstionis iniuriam retorquere.
units.tr: The claim that it is not lawful for any son of a church to bring the bishop, or any other matter needing correction, directly to a greater church, strikes me as absurd and is plainly contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. For to whom is it more fitting to say what he has done wrong than to the one who holds the office of teacher? Why should he, who therefore stands above the rest of the brothers, be the only one who, by the privilege of his own see, may correct the errors of priests, when others are permitted to do so? What arrogance is this, what swelling pride, what haughtiness, what superbia, that a bishop should be allowed to live by right or wrong at the pleasure of his own will, and should disdain to hear from his subjects what he has insolently done? This is especially so since they have not gone to the courts of governors, nor knocked at the tribunals of lay judges, but rather approach the Church and lay before the priests the matters that their own priest must answer for, so that what might have become an object of mockery before secular judges is corrected gravely and honourably by the priestly office. In such a case it is surely fitting that the man who is challenged should either show his innocence by reasoned argument or humbly confess himself a sinner. Nor should he press the plea that he ought not to be accused by those who are subject to him, lest he seem to cover his excesses with a veil, evade judgement, and try to turn the wrong of the question back upon another ground.

units.la: Quis enim nesciat, quod Princeps Apostolorum Petrus potestatem regni cælestis accepit? Virtutem ligandi siue soluendi quæ vellet in cælis ac terris, obtinuit. Supra mare pedibus ambulauit, sola sui corporis vmbra ægrotantes erexit: mentientes, iaculo nudi sermonis occidit: Oratione mortuos suscitauit. Hic itaque tam sublimis meriti vir, cum ex admonitione Sancti Spiritus ad Cornelium, gentilem videlicet hominem, fuisset ingressus, aduersus eum quæstio facta est, ab his, qui erant ex circumcisione, cur ad alienigenas introiisset, atque cum eis manducare præsumpsisset, insuper & in baptismate recepisset? Hic, inquam, tot donorum cælestium incomparabili virtute suffultus, tot miraculorum ostensione conspicuus, quærela subiectorum non ex potestate restitit, sed rationem reddendo humiliter satisfecit, causamque per ordinem veridicus relator exposuit: quomodo videlicet vas quoddam vel ut linteum, in quo quadrupedia terræ, reptilia atque volatilia inerant, de cælo submitti viderit, vocem audierit: Surge, Petre; macta & manduca. Qualiter etiam tres viri venientes, eum ad Cornelium vocauerunt, qualiter postremo Spiritus Sanctus eum cum illis ire præcepit. Et quemadmodum idem Spiritus Sanctus, qui superuenire iam baptizatis consueuerat, in gentiles ante baptismum venit. Si igitur iste, cum a discipulis culparetur, authoritatem, quam in sancta fuerat sortitus Ecclesia, voluisset obtendere, respondere potuerat, ut pastorem suum oves, qui sibi commissæ fuerant, reprehendere non auderent. Sed si in querela fidelium potestatis suæ titulum obiecisset, dedecorprofecto mansuetudinis non fuisset. Non ergo eos priuilegii sui authoritate repressit, sed humili potius satisfactione placauit: & tanquam solus ipse ad faciendam fidem non sufficeret etiam testes adhibuit: Venerunt, inquit, mecum & sex fratres isti.
units.tr: For who does not know that the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, received the power of the heavenly kingdom? He obtained the power of binding or loosing in heaven and on earth as he willed. He walked on the sea with his feet; the mere shadow of his body raised the sick; he struck down liars with the dart of his bare word; by prayer he raised the dead. So when this man of such exalted merit had, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, gone in to Cornelius, a Gentile, a question was raised against him by those who were of the circumcision: why had he gone in to men of other nations, and why had he presumed to eat with them and, moreover, to receive them in baptism? Here, I say, he, supported by the incomparable power of so many heavenly gifts and conspicuous for the display of so many miracles, did not resist the complaint of his subjects by his authority, but humbly satisfied them by giving an account, and the truthful narrator set out the cause in order: how he had seen a certain vessel, like a sheet, in which were four-footed beasts of the earth, creeping things and birds, let down from heaven, and had heard a voice: Rise, Peter; kill and eat. And how three men, coming, called him to Cornelius, and how finally the Holy Spirit commanded him to go with them; and how the same Holy Spirit, who had been accustomed to come upon those already baptized, came upon the Gentiles before baptism. If, therefore, when he was blamed by the disciples, he had wished to plead the authority which he had received in the holy Church, he could have answered that the sheep committed to him should not dare to reprove their shepherd. But if he had, in answer to the complaint of the faithful, put forward the title of his power, that would certainly not have been an example of meekness. So he did not check them by the authority of his privilege, but rather appeased them by humble satisfaction; and, as if he alone were not enough to make the matter believed, he also called in witnesses: Six brethren, he said, also came with me.

units.la: Discat ergo, cum de suis actibus conuenitur Episcopus, rationem humiliter reddere, non de sui primatus eminentia superbire, nec sibi fieri credat iniuriam, cum a iuniore corripitur, sed consulentem potius, vel medicum sui vulneris arbitretur. Nunquid enim Nathan Propheta, cum Dauid tam austeræ securitatis iniectione corripuit, indignationem Regii motus incutrit? Nunquid ille Regalis excellentiæ culmen oppositum, ac velut illatam a subiecto suo contumeliam iuam propulsauit? Sed mox vt se cognouit ægrotum, suscepit libenter antidotum, detexit vulnus, & sectionis suæ non horruit feramentum. Vide humilem languidum. Peccaui, inquit, Domine. Audi etiam velox medicinæ remedium: Transtulit Dominus peccatum tuum, non morieris. Econtra Rex Achab, qui corripientem se Prophetam audire despexit, vltionis gladium, quem ille minatus est, non euasit. Quia dimisisti, inquit, virum dignum morte de manu tua, erit anima tua pro anima eius, & populus tuus pro populo eius. Dauid ergo culpam suam æquanimiter audiens, sententiam mortis, quam merebatur, euasit: Achab autem correptionis impatiens impiæ pietatis, quam indigno Regi contulerat, veniam non inuenit. Nunquid & mulieres illæ hospitæ videlicet Salvatoris inuicem inter se litigauerunt, dum altera quereretur aduersus alteram, quia solam se ministrare compelleret? poterat enim Maria dicere nostrorum more Pontificum: Accusasti me, & torporis ac negligentiæ condemnasti. Non sane omnis querela protinus accusatio dicenda est. Nam aliud est querela compassionis, aliud accusatio simultatis & odii. Ista nimirum fit, ut offensio corrigatur: illa vero, ut is qui offenderat, condemnetur. Petrum plane in faciem resistens Paulus obiurgat, & coram omnibus reprehensibilem indicat. Quod ille in accusationis non tulit iniuriam, sed benigne & patienter accepit, quod non ex liuore, sed ex charitate procedere perspicue recognouit. Sed ecce dicitur: Ego tum Episcopus, ego sum pastor Ecclesiæ, non debeo a commissis oibus accusationem pati: molestus & nisi in causa fidei, dignus sum etiam in prauis moribus æquanimiter ferri. Sed dic mihi quisquis es: Nunquid non legisti quod in Euangelio scriptum est; Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, corripe eum inter te & ipsum solum: Si te audierit, lucratus es fratrem tuum: si te non audierit, adhibe tecum duos vel tres testes, ut in ore duorum vel trium testium stet omne verbum: si autem eos non audierit, dic Ecclesiæ. Si Ecclesiæ ergo referenda est causa quorumlibet fratrum, quomodo non etiam sacerdotum? Porro si sacerdos qui in Ecclesia peccat, dedignatur in Ecclesia discuti, quis iam ferat Ecclesiæ se legibus coerceri? Porro si Ecclesiæ tuæ filius, vt asseris, aduersum te mutire non liceat, nunquid aliunde producendi sunt testes, qui te & facta tua per absentiam domesticæ cohabitationis ignorant? Beatus Iob dicit: Si tot tempsi subire iudicium cum seruo meo: & tu dicis, absit vt dignet ad examen venire cum clerico meo? Deus Omnipotens per Esaiam clamat: Iudicate pupillo, defendite viduam, & venite & arguite me. Siis qui iudicat omnia, non dedignatur a seruis argui: tu superbis vtique, cum conservo in iudicium venire fastidis? & cum sis terra & cinis, vermis & pulvis, humiliare te despicis, ad imaginem conditoris? Præsertim enim scriptura dicat, Ducem te constituerunt, noli te extollere, sed esto in illis quasi unus ex illis. Quis plane nesciat, quia Samueli Israelitica plebs praeiudicium intulit, eumque de principatu iniuste deiecit? Et cum eos arguere merito potuisset, vltro se arguendum nullius accusationibus obtulit: & vtrum eos in aliquo violenter oppresserit, inquisiuit. Ecce praesto sum, inquit, loquimini de me coram Domino, & coram Christo eius, vtrum bovem cuiusquam tulerim, aut asinum: Si quenquam calumniatus sum, si oppressi aliquem, si de manu cuiusquam munus accepi, & condemnam illud hodie, restituamque vobis. Cum ergo tam incomparabiles, tam eminentes, atque sublimes viri, subiectis suis rationem reddere de propriis actibus non despiciant: quis arrogantiae typus, quis est iste tantae superbiae fastus, quo sacerdos huius temporis intumescens, titulum sui praesulatus opponat, & Ecclesiae suae filiis qui se grauatos asserunt, aequo iudicio non respondeat? Excludatur ergo ab Ecclesiastica disciplina perniciosae consuetudinis regula, tollatur haec subterfugii versuta calliditas, vt is qui tam peruersis audacis superbiae allegationibus vtitur, immunitatem commissi piaculi non lucretur.
units.tr: Let a bishop, therefore, when his actions are called into question, learn to give an account humbly, not to lord it over others on the strength of the eminence of his primacy, nor believe that he is wronged when he is rebuked by a younger man; let him rather regard him as one who counsels him, or as a physician of his wound. For when the prophet Nathan rebuked David with so severe a charge, did he not stir up the anger of the king? Did the king, in the height of his royal dignity, push back against him and repel the insult, as he would have thought it, offered by his subject? No, as soon as he recognised himself as sick, he gladly accepted the remedy, laid bare the wound, and did not shrink from the surgeon's instrument. See the humble invalid: I have sinned, he said, O Lord. Hear also the swift remedy of the medicine: The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die. On the other hand, King Ahab, who despised hearing the prophet who rebuked him, did not escape the sword of vengeance which the prophet threatened: Because you have let go out of your hand a man worthy of death, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people. So David, hearing his fault with equanimity, escaped the sentence of death which he deserved; but Ahab, impatient of correction, found no pardon for that impious piety with which he had indulged an unworthy king. Did not those two women, the hostesses of the Saviour, also quarrel with each other, when one complained against the other because she alone was forced to serve? For Mary could have said, after the manner of our Pontiffs: You have accused me and condemned me of sloth and negligence. Yet not every complaint must straightway be called an accusation. For one thing is a complaint of compassion, another an accusation born of enmity and hatred. The former is made so that the offence may be corrected; the latter so that the one who has given offence may be condemned. Paul surely withstood Peter to his face and rebuked him, and declared him blameworthy before all. Peter did not take that as an injury of accusation, but received it kindly and patiently, clearly recognising that it proceeded not from spite but from charity. But see, someone says: I am the bishop, I am the pastor of the Church; I ought not to suffer accusation for the faults committed by me; I am troublesome if the cause is not of faith, and I deserve to be borne with equanimity even in wicked conduct. But tell me, whoever you are: have you not read what is written in the Gospel? If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother; but if he will not hear you, take with you one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. And if he refuses to hear them, tell it to the Church. If, then, the cause of any brothers whatsoever is to be referred to the Church, why not the cause of priests too? Moreover, if a priest who sins in the Church disdains to be examined in the Church, who will now bear that he is restrained by the laws of the Church? Again, if it is not lawful, as you assert, for a son of your Church to murmur against you, must witnesses be brought in from elsewhere, who, because they do not live in your household, do not know you and your deeds? The blessed Job says: If I have refused to undergo judgement with my servant, what will you say, that God forbid he should deign to come into examination with my clerk? Almighty God cries out through Isaiah: Judge the fatherless, defend the widow, and come and reprove me. If he who judges all things does not disdain to be reproved by his servants, do you, who are proud, disdain to come into judgement with your fellow servant? And since you are earth and ashes, worm and dust, do you scorn to humble yourself, you who are made in the image of your Maker? For Scripture says especially: They have made you a leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them. Who does not know that the people of Israel did Samuel a wrong, and unjustly cast him down from his rule? And although they could justly have been rebuked by him, he of his own accord offered himself to be accused by no one; and he asked whether he had oppressed any of them by violence: Behold, I am here; speak of me before the Lord and before his Anointed: whose ox or whose ass have I taken? If I have defrauded anyone, if I have oppressed anyone, if I have received a bribe from anyone's hand, I will restore it to you this day. Since, then, men so incomparable, so eminent and so exalted do not disdain to give their subjects an account of their own actions, what type of arrogance, what fastidious pride is this, that a priest of this age, swelling with pride, should set up the title of his prelacy and not answer with fair judgement the sons of his Church who say that they are burdened? Let the rule of a pernicious custom, then, be shut out from ecclesiastical discipline, and let this crafty cunning of evasion be removed, so that he who uses such perverse allegations of bold pride does not gain immunity for the crime he has committed.

units.la: B. PETRI DAMIANI EPISCOPI OSTIENSIS, ET CARDINALIS ROMANI, Disceptatio Synodalis: DE ELECTIONE PONTIFICIS ROMANI, INTER REGIS Aduocatum, & Romanae Ecclesiae Defensorem, missa ad Synodum habitam super electione Honorii II. Papae, qui vulgo Cadalous dicebatur.
units.tr: B. Peter Damian, Bishop of Ostia and Cardinal of Rome, Synodal Disputation: ON THE ELECTION OF THE ROMAN PONTIFF, BETWEEN THE KING'S ADVOCATE AND THE DEFENDER OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, sent to the synod held concerning the election of Pope Honorius II, commonly called Cadalous.

units.la: Sed ad haec gloriaris, (alloquitur Cadaloum) & iactas: Rex me & Imperatrix mater elegit ad hunc apicem, me Regia celsitudo prouexit: sed cum hinc aula regia suum tueatur electum, illinc Romana Ecclesia proprium defendat Antistitem, iam in solio constitutum, dignum est, vt sanctorum atque prudentium sacerdotum multitudo conueniat & hanc quaestionem ventilans, sub canonici iuris auctoritate discernat. Quoniam & in proximo, vt speramus, fiet hic Osboriense Concilium, hic iam eiusdem Concilii constituamus velut in quadam tabella picturae praeludium. Iuxta iussionem ergo Danielis, Patrum throni sint positi, iudicium sedeat, libri aperiantur, & solutionis indiga quaestio in medium deducatur. Hic itaque Romanae Defensor Ecclesiae suas allegationes inferat: illic Aduocatus Regius propriae partis argumenta depromat. Taceat Parma cum suo haeresiarcha; aduocatio tantum regia, & Romana inuicem colloquatur Ecclesia: sanctorum vero sacerdotum erecti sint animi, vt & quaeque dicenda sunt, conferant, & peroratae causae iudiciapreviter sententiae calculum ponant. Age igitur, Defensor Apostolicae Sedis incipiat, deinde Regius Aduocatus, quae sibi videbuntur, ostendat.
units.tr: But you boast of this and vaunt yourself (he addresses Cadalous): the King and the Empress Mother chose me for this summit; the royal majesty raised me up. But since, on the one side, the royal court defends its chosen man, and, on the other, the Roman Church defends its own bishop, now seated on the throne, it is fitting that a gathering of holy and prudent priests should meet and, weighing this question, decide it under the authority of canon law. Since, as we hope, the council of Osbory will also be held soon, let us here set out, as it were on a small panel, a prelude to that council's picture. Accordingly, following the command of Daniel: Let the thrones of the Fathers be set, let judgment sit, let the books be opened, and let the question, which needs resolution, be brought into the open. Here, then, let the Defender of the Roman Church bring forward his allegations; there let the Royal Advocate put forward the arguments of his own side. Let Parma keep silent with its heresiarch; let the royal advocacy and the Roman Church talk with each other; and let the minds of the holy priests be kept alert, so that they may weigh whatever must be said, and, once the cases have been pleaded to the end, cast their vote on the judgments. Come, then: let the Defender of the Apostolic See begin, and afterwards the Royal Advocate will set out whatever seems right to him.

units.la: Defensor Romanae Ecclesiae:
units.tr: The Defender of the Roman Church:

units.la: Cum beatitudo vestra, venerabiles Patres, super Apostolicae sedis negotio disputat, ad cunctas Ecclesias pertinere, quod versatur in manibus, non ignorat. Hac enim stante, reliquae stant: sin autem haec, quae omnium fundamentum & basis, obruitur: caeterarum quoque questatus necesse est collabatur. Omnis autem siue Patriarchatus cuiuslibet apicem, siue Metropoleon primatus, aut Episcopatuum cathedras, vel Ecclesiarum culustunque ordinis dignitates, siue Rex, siue Imperator, siue cuiuslibet conditionis homo purus institiut & (prout voluntas, aut facultas tulit) spiritualium prærogatiuarum iura praefixit: Romanam autem Ecclesiam solus ille fundauit, & supra petram Fidei mox nascentis erexit; qui beato vitae aeternae Clauigero terreni similiter & coelestis Imperii iura commisit. Non ergo quaelibet terrena sententia, sed illud verbum, per quod constructum est coelum & terra, per quod denique omnia condita sunt elementa, Romanam fundauit Ecclesiam. Illius certe priuilegio fungitur, illius auctoritate fulcitur. Unde non dubium, quia quisquis cuilibet Ecclesiae ius suum detrahit, iniustitia facit: qui autem Romanae Ecclesiae priuilegium, ab ipso summo omnium Ecclesiarum capite traditum auferre conatur, hic procul dubio in haeresim labitur: & cum ille notatur iniustus, hic est dicendus haereticus. Fidem quippe violat, quia aduersus illam agit, quae mater est Fidei; & illa constantissima inuenitur, qui eam cunctis Ecclesiis praeeluisse cognoscitur. Cum hoc igitur vestra sanctitas indubitanter agnoscat, vos, qui non quilibet, sed nobiliores, & egregii estis filii Romanae Ecclesiae, pietatis viscera circa matrem vestram compatientes ostendite, & vtrum destrui debeat, sibimet eligendo Pontificem, iudicate. Mirum quippe est, si, quod minoribus Ecclesiis canonicus vigor attribuit, illi soli, quæ caput est omnium, non permisit.
units.tr: Venerable Fathers, when your blessedness debates the business of the Apostolic See, you do not fail to recognise that the matter now in your hands pertains to all churches. For if this stands, the rest stand; but if this, which is the foundation and base of all, is overthrown, the rest of the churches must necessarily collapse too. Whether it is the summit of some patriarchate, or the primacy of metropolitans, or the seats of bishoprics, or the dignities of churches of any rank, whether it was instituted by a king, an emperor, or a man of any condition whatever, and whatever spiritual prerogatives it has been granted according to will or ability: the Roman Church was founded by that one alone, and raised up upon the rock of the Faith just beginning to spring up. He entrusted the rights of the eternal life's key-bearer, and likewise of the earthly and heavenly empire, to the blessed one. It is not, therefore, some earthly sentence but that Word through which heaven and earth were made, through which finally all the elements were created, that founded the Roman Church. Certainly it enjoys its privilege and is supported by its authority. Hence there is no doubt that whoever takes away from any church its right does injustice; but whoever tries to remove the privilege of the Roman Church, given by the very highest head of all the churches, undoubtedly falls into heresy: and while the former is called unjust, the latter is to be called a heretic. For he violates the Faith, since he acts against that which is the mother of the Faith; and she is found most steadfast, being known to have gone before all the churches. Since your holiness acknowledges this beyond doubt, you who are not just any sons but noble and distinguished sons of the Roman Church, show compassion for your mother with the tenderness of your devotion, and judge whether she ought to be destroyed by electing a pontiff for herself. Indeed it is a wonder, if the canonical force grants to the lesser churches what it did not permit to that one alone, which is the head of all.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: The Royal Advocate.

units.la: Prolixa declamatio dedit attentionem, benevolentiam, atque docilitatem, & hoc potius iuxta consuetudinem fori iudicialis, quam secundum regulam Concilii Synodalis: vbi scilicet non magnopere curare debemus elucubratæ locutionis vrbanitatem, sed vivæ sententiæ puritatem. Ad quæram ergo coram sanctis sacerdotibus deponendam sufficiat nobis dicere, quoniam intronizatus Papam sine consensu Domini nostri Regis, ad iniuriam scilicet atq; contemptum regiæ maiestatis.
units.tr: A long declamation has won attention, goodwill and receptiveness; and this is more in keeping with the custom of the judicial forum than with the rule of a synodal council, where we ought not to take much care for the polished elegance of an elaborate speech, but for the purity of a living opinion. Therefore, to set out the matter before the holy priests, it will suffice for us to say that he was enthroned as Pope without the consent of our lord the King, namely to the injury and contempt of royal majesty.

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Ordinationem Papæ factam d.ff teri non possumus, nec debemus, Regis autem iniuriam modis omnibus prosequamur. Sed videamus primo si liceat, vtrum Papa sine Rege potuerit fieri, & sic post modum de Regis disputemus iniuria.
units.tr: We neither can nor ought to deny that the ordination of the Pope was made; but we must pursue by every means the king's injury. Yet let us first see whether it was lawful, and whether the Pope could have been made without the King; and afterwards we may discuss the king's injury.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: The Royal Advocate.

units.la: Per te liquido nouimus, quia illi d b.. Pontificem cum ordinatur, eligere, quos sibi, post quam ordinatus fuerit, canonica decretuit auctoritas obedire: Papæ vero, quia vniuersalis est Pontifex, non modo Romanus populus, sed Romanus Imperator, qui caput est populi, obedientiam debet: censendumne ergo est vt Papam sine capite suo populus eligat, & ei, quem non elegit Imperator, obediat? Constat ergo, quod nisi Romani Regis assensus accesserit, Romani Pontificis electio non erit perfecta.
units.tr: From you we clearly know that the clergy, when they ordain a pontiff, choose those whom canonical authority has decreed should be obeyed by him after he has been ordained; but to the Pope, because he is the universal pontiff, not only the Roman people but the Roman Emperor, who is the head of the people, owes obedience. Is it therefore to be judged that the people elect a Pope without their head, and that he should obey one whom the Emperor has not chosen? It is established, then, that unless the assent of the Roman King has been added, the election of the Roman Pontiff will not be complete.

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Perhibendum est itaque; iuxta vestræ disputationis articulum, quod neq; Stephanus, nec Xystus, neq; Cornelius; non denique Clemens, non Syluester, non ipse beatus Petrus Papali nomine digni sunt, qui ab Imperatoribus eodem tempore electi non sunt.
units.tr: It must therefore be said, according to the point of your disputation, that neither Stephen, nor Xystus, nor Cornelius, nor finally Clement, nor Sylvester, nor blessed Peter himself, is worthy of the papal name, if they were not elected at the same time by the emperors.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: Royal Advocate.

units.la: Gentiles Reges non sunt adhibendi ad huius, de qua loquimur, electionis exemplum: qui quoniam ignorabant Fidem Christianam, Christianorum non poterant ordinare Pontificem. Cæterum Christiani Principes semper Romanos elegere Pontifices.
units.tr: Gentile kings are not to be brought forward as examples for the election we are discussing. Since they did not know the Christian faith, they could not ordain a Pope for Christians. But Christian princes have always chosen the Roman popes.

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Qui mentitur in communi colloquio, mendax dicitur; qui autem in præsentia venerabilium sacerdotum falsa protulerit, sacrilegii procul dubio crimen incurrit. Dixisti, Christianos Principes Romanos semper elegisse Pontifices: percurre mecum Eccl. fiastica antiquitatis historias, Romanorum præsulum catalogum studiose disquire, & cum perpatres inueneris in electione suæ regnum accessisse consensum, confitere te perspicuum protulisse mendacium. Quis enim Rex Antonii filium Damasum Hispaniensem? quis Innocentium Innocentii filium Albanensem? quis denique Zosimum Græcum Ebramii filium elegit? Quis præterea Leonem Quintiani filium de Tuscia? Quis Hilarum Crispini filium de Sardinia? quis Cœlestinum Pisci Romani ciuis filium? quis Bonifacium, quis Anastasium æque Romanos? Denique multos attexerem, nisi fastidium generarem.
units.tr: He who lies in ordinary conversation is called a liar; but he who utters falsehoods in the presence of venerable priests undoubtedly incurs the crime of sacrilege. You said that Christian princes have always chosen the Roman popes. Run through the histories of ecclesiastical antiquity with me, search carefully the catalogue of Roman prelates, and when you have found, in the elections of the fathers, the consent of a king present, confess that you have uttered a plain falsehood. For what king chose Damasus, son of Antonius, the Spaniard? Who chose Innocent, son of Innocent, of Albano? Who, finally, chose Zosimus the Greek, son of Ebramius? Who chose Leo, son of Quintianus, from Tuscany? Who chose Hilarus, son of Crispinus, from Sardinia? Who chose Celestine, son of Piscus, a citizen of Rome? Who chose Boniface, who chose Anastasius, both Romans? In short, I could add many more, were I not to cause weariness.

units.la: Sed ne me putes non habentem copiam, ab eorum enumeratione deficere: Quis Imperatorum elegit Simplicium Tiburtinum? Felicem natione Romanum? qui Gelasium Afrum Valerii filium? quis Symmachum Sardiniæ prouinciæ filium Fortunati? quis Hormisdam filium Iusti natione Campanum? Ioannem origine Tuscum, Felicem natione Samnitem, Bonifacium Cibaldi filium, Mercurium Proiecti, Agapitium Gordiani, natura Romanos. Quis enim Regum electioni cuiuslibet isto um suum legitur adhibuisse consensum? cum eorum temporibus Romanæ Reipublicæ Christiani Principis præfuisse legantur, id est, Valentinianus senior, Valens frater eius, qui occisus est in pugna Gothica prope Hadrianopolim, Gratianus, qui a Maximo tyranno peremptus est; Valentinianus iunior, qui necatus est a Comite suo Vienne; Deinde Arcadius, Honorius, Theodosius; Ioannes ille, qui apud Rauennam occisus est; Valentinianus Tertius, qui in campo Martio est peremptus; Martianus, Leo, Maiorianus, Seuerus, Anthemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, Zeno, Nepos ille, qui in villa sua occisus est iuxta Salonas, Augustulus, Anastasius, Iustinus, & cæteri Romani Imperatores; quos cuitandi lacinios styli causa prætereo. Da mihi ergo eorum, quos enumerauimus, aliquem vel Præsulem requirentem vel Principem assensum in electione præbentem, & ego do manum, acte perhibeo laureandum: alioquin si dare non poteris in hoc te comunicatum pet omnia pernecesse est fatearis. Quod autem beato Gregorio legitur adhibuisse Mauritius Imperator assensum, & perpauci alii Principes aliis promouendis, hoc dictauit perturbatio temporum, & tempestas horrenda bellorum.
units.tr: But lest you think I lack the means to go on with their list: which emperor chose Simplicius of Tibur, a Roman by birth? Who chose Gelasius the African, son of Valerius? Who chose Symmachus, son of Fortunatus, of the province of Sardinia? Who chose Hormisdas, son of Justus, a Campanian by birth; John, a Tuscan by origin; Felix, a Samnite by birth; Boniface, son of Cibaldus; Mercurius, son of Proiectus; Agapetus, son of Gordianus, Romans by nature? For is it read that any of these had the consent of a king to his election? In their times, the Roman commonwealth is read to have been governed by Christian princes, namely Valentinian the Elder; his brother Valens, who was killed in the battle with the Goths near Hadrianople; Gratian, who was destroyed by the tyrant Maximus; Valentinian the Younger, who was killed by his count at Vienne; then Arcadius, Honorius, Theodosius; that John who was killed at Ravenna; Valentinian III, who was slain in the Campus Martius; Marcian, Leo, Majorian, Severus, Anthemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, Zeno, that Nepos who was killed in his villa near Salona, Augustulus, Anastasius, Justin, and the other Roman emperors, whom I pass over to avoid tedious detail. Give me, then, one of those we have listed, either a prelate asking or a prince giving his consent to an election, and I will give you my hand and proclaim you worthy of the laurel. Otherwise, if you cannot give one, you must in every respect confess yourself refuted in this. As for what is read of blessed Gregory, that the Emperor Maurice gave his assent, and of a very few other princes who gave assent to the promotion of others, this was dictated by the disturbance of the times and the dreadful storm of wars.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: Royal Advocate.

units.la: Si mentiri est contra mentem loqui, memorarium est me mendacitatem procaciter arguit, qui notvtiq; falsum, sed verum me dixisse putanis tamen assentior, & in hoc superatum me esse nobis abnuo.
units.tr: If to lie is to speak against one's own mind, you boldly charge me with falsehood from your memory; yet although I know that what I said was true, not false, you think otherwise. I do not give way to this, and I deny that I have been beaten in this matter.

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Vt autem id ipsum adhuc manifestius pateat, & te super hac dimicandi materia perdidisse, tibimet ipsi clarius innotescat, lege Constantini Imperatoris edictum, vbi sedis Apostolicæ constituit super omnes in orbe terrarum Ecclesias principatum. Nam postquam supra corpus beati Petri basilicam fundator erexit, postquam Patriarchium Lateranense in beati Saluatoris honore construxit, mox per Imperialis Rescripti seriem Romanæ Ecclesiæ constituit dignitatem. Vbi nimirum beato Siluestro, suisque successoribus obtulit, vt regali more, & aurea corona plectantur in capite, & cateras regii cultus insulas vsurparent. Verum beatus Siluester ornamenta, quæ lacerdotali congruere iudicabat officio, in proprios vsus assumpsit; coronam vero vel cateras, quæ magis ambitiosa, quam mystica videbantur, omisit. Cui etiam Constantinus Lateranense palatium, quod eatenus aula regalis exiterat, perpetuo iure concessit; regnum Italiæ iudicandum tradidit.
units.tr: So that this may appear even more plainly, and so that you may understand more clearly that you have lost the matter of this dispute, read the edict of the Emperor Constantine, in which he established the primacy of the Apostolic See over all the Churches in the world. For after the founder had erected a basilica over the body of the blessed Peter, and after he had built the Lateran palace in honour of the blessed Saviour, he then, through the series of an imperial rescript, conferred the dignity of the Roman Church. There, indeed, he offered it to the blessed Silvester and his successors, that they should be adorned in the royal manner, with a golden crown upon the head, and should use the other insignia of royal dignity. But the blessed Silvester took up for his own use those ornaments which he judged suited the priestly office; the crown and the others, which seemed more ostentatious than mystical, he left aside. To him also Constantine granted in perpetuity the Lateran palace, which until then had been a royal court, and handed over to him the judgement of the kingdom of Italy.

units.la: Nam & ipsius Regis hæc verba sunt: Vnde, inquit, congruum inspeximus, nostrum Imperium & regni potestatem Orientalibus transferri & transmutari regionibus, & in Byzantia prouincia in optimo loco nominis nostro ciuitatem ædificari, & nostrum illic constitui Imperium. Quoniam, vbi principatus sacerdotum & Christiana religionis caput ab Imperatore cœlesti constitutum est, iustum non est, vt illic Imperator terrenus habeat potestatem. Audisti, quia terrenus Imperator non habet in Romana Ecclesia potestatem: quomodo ergo sine illius arbitrio, qui potestatem ibi non habet, non licet eligi sacerdotem? Ipse vero Constantinopolim velut in secunda Roma perpetuo regnaturus abscessit. Longe vero post Theodosius Imperator beati Pauli basilicam cœpit; quo defuncto filius eius Honorius eandem basilicam ad calcem usque perduxit. Hi quoque Romanæ Ecclesiæ priuilegium nihilominus firmarunt. Quomodo ergo prærogatiuam sibi in Romani Pontificis electione relinquerent, qui Romanam Ecclesiam nequaquam sibi studuerunt subdere, sed præferre? non præcipere, sed parere, non præcellere, sed subesse?
units.tr: For these are the very words of the Emperor himself: Hence we have judged it fitting that our Empire and the power of our kingdom be transferred and transformed to eastern regions, and that a city be built in the province of Byzantium, in the best place, bearing our name, and that our Empire be established there. Since, where the principate of the priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the heavenly Emperor, it is not right that an earthly emperor should have power there. You have heard that an earthly emperor does not have power in the Roman Church; how, then, may a priest not be chosen without the consent of one who has no power there? Constantine himself departed for Constantinople, as if to reign perpetually in a second Rome. Long afterwards the Emperor Theodosius began the basilica of the blessed Paul; when he died, his son Honorius carried the same basilica to completion. These also nonetheless confirmed the privilege of the Roman Church. How, then, would they have reserved for themselves a prerogative in the election of the Roman Pontiff, when they did not strive to subject the Roman Church to themselves, but to prefer it; not to command, but to obey; not to excel, but to be subject?

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: The Royal Advocate.

units.la: Assentior plane & ratum duco quod loqueris: sed esto, quod nunc regia celsitudo ex antiquorum consuetudine Principum hoc sibimet allegare non posset; veruntamen tu hoc negare non potes, quod pater Domini mei Regis piæ memoriæ HENRICVS Imperator factus est Patricius Romanorum, a quibus accepit in electione super ordinando Pontifice principatum. Huc accedit, quod præstantius est, quod Nicolaus Papa hoc Domino meo Regi priuilegium, quod ex paterno iam iure fuscepserat, præbuit, & per synodalis insuper decreti paginam confirmauit. Cum ergo priuatus quisque a suo decidere iure non debeat, donec ventilato negotio iudicialis in eum sententia promulgetur: quo pacto maiestas Regia prærogatiuam hanc suæ dignitatis amisit, quam & ex Apostolicæ Sedis liberalitate percepit, & ex paterno Imperialis fastigii iure suscepit? quo, inquam, modo in Romana Ecclesia dignitatis adeptæ locum sine iudicio perdidit, qui Romanam Ecclesiam non offendit?
units.tr: I plainly agree and hold as settled what you say. But grant that the royal majesty could not now claim this for itself from the custom of earlier princes; still, you cannot deny that my lord the King of pious memory, the Emperor Henry, was made Patrician of the Romans, and from them received the leading role in choosing the pope who was to be ordained. Moreover, and what is more weighty, Pope Nicholas granted this privilege to my lord the King, which he had already received by paternal right, and further confirmed it by the page of a synodal decree. Since therefore no private person ought to lose his right to something unless, after the matter has been examined, a judicial sentence has been pronounced against him, by what means has the royal majesty lost this prerogative of its dignity, which it both received from the generosity of the Apostolic See and took up by the paternal right of the imperial rank? In what way, I ask, has it lost, without a judgment, the place of a dignity it had obtained in the Roman Church, when it has not offended the Roman Church?

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Priuilegium inuictissimo Regi nostro ipsi quoq; defendimus, & vt superplenum, illibatumque possideat, optamus. Porro autem Romana Ecclesia multo nobilius atq; sublimius, quam matet carnis, mater est Regis: illa siquidem peperit, vt per eius traducem reuertatur in pulverem; ista genuit, vt Christi sine fine regnantis efficiat coheredem. Et cuncti liquido nouimus, quia Rex licet egregiæ indolis, tamen adhuc puer est. Quid ergo mali fecit Romana Ecclesia, si filio suo, cum adhuc impubis esset, cum adhuc tutela egeret, ipsa tutoris officium subiit, & ius, quod illi competebat, implevit? Quis nescit, quia lacerdotem eligere puer ignorat? Sæpe mater iudicis tribunal irrumpit, testes adscisci, Notarios convocat, siquè per astipulationes & rata, & insuper apicum monumenta omnia bonorum suorum filio iura delegat: interim tamen, vsque dum ille ad iuuenilis ætatis incrementum perueniat, & rationis capax fiat, illa cuncta dispensat, omnia ordinat, siquè quod iam alieni iuris est patrimonium, ad proprias disponit prouisionis arbitrium. Nunquid ob hæc dicenda est mulier illa filio suo concessa subtrahere? immo verius perhibetur, vt pietatis studio deseruire. Quia quæ rudis adhuc filius dilapidare ac prodigere poterat, hæc ibi sibimet apte dispositæ, caute retenta, & rationabiliter ordinata conseruat. Carnalis ergo mater adiuuat filium in rebus terrenis, & mater Ecclesia filio suo Regi præbere non debet auxilium in spiritualibus donis? Obmutescat ergo plecta versutia, quæ scilicet hæc damnat, quod prædicare debuerat; illi crimen imponere nititur, quæ pro beneficiis gloriam promeretur. Huc accedit, quia nonnunquam ob varietatem temporum sæpe mutandus est ordo causarum. Tunc enim, quoniam Pontificem sibi Romana percepit Ecclesia, tantæ simultatis fomes in seditionis ciues accenderat, tantus liuor & odium tumultuantis populi corda turbauerat, vt de tam longinquis terrarum spaciis nequaquam regiæ clementiæ præstolari possemus oraculum. Nisi enim quantocyus ordinaretur Antistes, perniciosus in populo gladius mutuis vulneribus desæuiret, & non parua Romanorum ciuium strages fieret.
units.tr: We also defend the privilege for our most invincible King, and we wish that he may possess it whole and unimpaired. Moreover, the Roman Church is the King's mother in a far nobler and loftier sense than the mother of the flesh: the one bore him so that through her line he would return to dust, while the other begot him so that he might become a co-heir of Christ, who reigns without end. We all clearly know that the King, though of outstanding character, is still a boy. What wrong, then, has the Roman Church done, if, when her son was still under age and still in need of a guardian, she herself took up the office of guardian and exercised the right that belonged to him? Who does not know that a boy does not know how to choose a priest? Often a mother bursts into the judge's tribunal, summons witnesses, calls in notaries, and through stipulations and ratified instruments, and moreover through written records, transfers all the rights over her goods to her son. Yet in the meantime, until he reaches the growth of youthful age and becomes capable of reason, she manages everything and arranges everything, and she disposes the estate, which is now under another's right, according to her own judgment of what is provident. Is that woman, for these things, to be said to withdraw what she had granted to her son? Rather, she is more truly said to serve him out of devoted affection. For what the son, still untrained, could squander and waste, she keeps safe for him, carefully held back and sensibly ordered. So if a fleshly mother helps her son in earthly things, should the mother Church not give her son the King help in spiritual gifts? Let that crafty man then be silent, who condemns these very things which he ought to have proclaimed, and who strives to lay a charge on her who earns glory for her benefits. Add to this that, because of the changing of the times, the order of affairs must often be altered. For then, since the Roman Church had received a Pontiff for herself, so great a spark of enmity had kindled the citizens into sedition, and so great envy and hatred had troubled the hearts of the rioting people, that we could by no means await the oracle of royal clemency from such distant lands. For unless a bishop were ordained with all speed, a deadly sword would rage among the people with mutual wounds, and no small slaughter of Roman citizens would follow.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: Royal Advocate.

units.la: Obtende quod vis, argumentare quod placet, dummodo constet quia nullatenus debuit immutari, quod Papa concessit, quod decreto constituit, quod scriptione firmauit.
units.tr: Put forward whatever you like, argue whatever pleases you, provided it is agreed that what the Pope has granted, what he has settled by decree and confirmed in writing, ought in no way to have been changed.

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Quid mirum, si hominis carnis adhuc fragilitate circumdari statuta mutentur, quoniam omnipotens Deus, qui videlicet omnia quæ futura sunt novit, ea quoque quæ à semetipso constituuntur, immutat? Nam ex eo quod promittit, aliquando aliquid minuit, vel etiam totum subtrahit, aliquando mala minatur, & non infligit.
units.tr: What wonder is it, if statutes are changed while still beset by the frailty of the flesh of man, since almighty God, who of course knows all things that are to come, also changes those things which he himself has established? For from what he promises he sometimes diminishes something, or even withdraws the whole; sometimes he threatens evils and does not inflict them.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: Royal Advocate.

units.la: Ea quæ proposuisti scripta declarentur exemplis. Quid est ergo quod Deus unquam promisit, & minuit?
units.tr: Let what you have put forward be made clear by examples. What, then, is it that God has ever promised and diminished?

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Si non excidit, reminisci potes, quod dixit Dominus ad Noe: Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est, eruntque dies illius centum viginti annorum. Sed cum Scriptura commemorat quingentorum tunc annorum extitisse Noe, quando hæc sibi Dominus loquebatur, sexcentorum tunc iam esse, cum cataclysmus erupit, liquido patet, viginti annos de præscripti numeri spacio fuisse subtractos, vitæque spacium, quod humano generi Deus promisit, imminuit, quia peruersitatis eorum reatus excreuit. Inde quoque per os Patriarchæ Iacob promisit Spiritus sanctus, dicens: Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, & dux de femore eius, donec veniat qui mittendus est. Et tamen nec temporibus Iudicum legimus viros de tribu Iuda semper super Israel tenuisse ducatum, nec Reges ex eadem tribu principatum tenuisse usque ad Christi reperiuntur aduentum. Constat ergo, quia Deus omnipotens sæpe, quod homini promisit, imminuit, quoniam homo, quod Deo debuerat, non impleuit.
units.tr: If it has not slipped your mind, you may recall what the Lord said to Noah: "My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh, and his days shall be a hundred and twenty years." But since Scripture records that Noah was then five hundred years old when the Lord spoke these words to him, and was already six hundred when the flood broke out, it is clear that twenty years were taken from the period of the prescribed number, and that he diminished the span of life which God had promised to the human race, because the guilt of their perversity had grown. Likewise, through the mouth of the patriarch Jacob the Holy Spirit promised, saying: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent." And yet we read that in the times of the Judges men of the tribe of Judah did not always hold leadership over Israel, nor are kings of the same tribe found to have held rule until the coming of Christ. It is established, therefore, that almighty God often diminished what he had promised to man, because man did not fulfil what he owed to God.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: Royal Advocate.

units.la: Doce & ubi Deus promittit bonum aliquod, & efficaciter non impleuit.
units.tr: Show me also where God promises some good and does not effectively fulfil it.

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Recordare quod dixit Dominus ad Iosiam Regem: Pro eo, inquit, quod audisti verba voluminis, & perterritum est cor tuum, & humiliatus es coram Domino, auditis sermonibus contra locum istum, & habitatores eius, & scidisti vestimenta tua, & fleuisti coram me: idcirco colligam te ad patres tuos, & colligeris ad sepulchrum tuum in pace. Et tamen paulò post Scriptura dicit: In diebus eius ascendit Pharao Necho Rex Ægypti contra Regem Assyriorum ad flumen Euphratem, & abiit Iosias in occursum eius, & occisus est in Magedo cum vidisset eum. Ad Sedeciam quoque Regem Iuda per Ieremiam dicitur: Audi verbum Domini, Sedecia Rex Iuda. Hæc dicit Dominus ad te: Non morieris in gladio; sed in pace morieris, & secundum combustionem patrum tuorum, Regum priorum, qui fuerunt ante te, sic comburent te & ve Domine, plangent te, quia verbum hoc ego locutus sum, dicit Dominus. Quod nimirum quomodo potuit fieri, qui seriem scrutatur historiæ, nunquam poterit inuenire. Nam postquam à Rege Babylonis semel est captus, Babyloniamque translatus, nunquam legitur vlterius ab eius vinculis absolutus. Iusto ergo iudicio subtrahit Deus nonnunquam homini bona quæ promisit, cum rebellis homo illius seruare mandata contemnit.
units.tr: Recall what the Lord said to King Josiah: "Because, he says, you have heard the words of the book, and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord, when you heard the words against this place and its inhabitants, and you tore your garments and wept before me: therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your sepulchre in peace." And yet a little later Scripture says: "In his days Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, went up against the king of the Assyrians to the river Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him, and he was killed at Megiddo when he had seen him." Likewise, to Zedekiah, king of Judah, it is said through Jeremiah: "Hear the word of the Lord, Zedekiah, king of Judah. Thus says the Lord to you: You shall not die by the sword, but you shall die in peace, and according to the burning of your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so shall they burn you; and they will lament you, saying, Alas, Lord! for I have spoken this word, says the Lord." How this could have happened, anyone who searches the sequence of history will never be able to discover. For after he had once been taken by the king of Babylon and carried off to Babylon, he is never read of as having been released from his chains afterwards. By just judgment, therefore, God sometimes withdraws from man the good things he has promised, when a rebellious man scorns to keep his commands.

units.la: Regius Aduocatus.
units.tr: Royal Advocate.

units.la: Prosequere etiam, quomodo Deus quod minatus est, non infligit.
units.tr: Go on to show also how God does not inflict what he has threatened.

units.la: Defensor Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Nemo, qui limen Ecclesiæ terit, ignorat, quia Ionas ad Niniuen à Domino missus exclamavit, dicens: Adhuc quadraginta dies, & Niniue subuertetur.
