Ipsius est enim opus, quod coronam gloriae vestrae ita indies ampliatur, & sublimatur mirabiliter, crescens ac proficiens in omni decore & magnificentia apud Deum & homines. Ipsius profecto nuper opus & virtus fuit, quod iter satis laboriosum & meticulosum pro pace regni & Ecclesiae liberatione susceptum, in tanta prosperitate peregistis: Romae siquidem Imperialis culminis plenitudinem gloriosissime assecutus, idque, quod maius fuit, in manu non magna, vt animi fideique magnitudo clarius emineret. Quod si ante tantillum exercitum restra tremuit & quieuit, quantus putamus horror hostium corda inuadere habebat, cum coepit Rex procedere in magnitudine brachii sui? Animabit insuper honestas causae, imo duplex provocabit necessitas. Non est meum hortari ad pugnam; est tamen (securus dico) aduocati Ecclesiae, arcere ab Ecclesiae infestatione schismaticorum rabiem: est Caesaris proprium vindicare coronam ab vsurpatore Siculo. Vt enim constat Iudaicam Sobolem sedem Petri in Christi occupasse iniuriam: sic proculdubio omnis qui in Sicilia Regem se facit, contradicto Caesari. Si autem vtrumque incumbit Caesari, restituere scilicet Caesari quae sunt Caesaris; & quae sunt Dei, Deo: curapud Tullum res Dei minuitur, cum Caesar nihil ibi lucretur? Verendum est ne minimorum neglectus, impedimentum sit maximorum. Hoc est quod dico Ecclesia sancti Gengulfi graviter iniusteque vt dicitur, in illa ciuitate opprimitur: & ajunt vestrae prudentiae, nescio qua fraude, subreptum; vt Domino Papae per iustitiam subuenire paranti, vestrae interventu precis obuiaretis. Obsecro & consulo consultius agi, non xiam reuocari precem, dari locum iustitiae; antequam Ecclesia illa funditus destruatur. Pauper sum ego, fidelis tamen vester: & si videar importunus, fortasse inde est. Dominam Imperatricem in Christi caritate oppido salutamus.
units.tr: To Lothair, by the grace of God Emperor Augustus of the Romans, Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, whatever a sinner's prayer may be worth. Blessed be God, who chose you and raised you up for our salvation, to the praise and glory of his name, to restore the honour of the Empire, to help his Church in an evil time, and finally to work salvation even now in the midst of the earth. For it is his work that the crown of your glory is daily enlarged and wonderfully exalted, growing and advancing in all honour and majesty before God and men. It was indeed lately his work and his power that you carried through, in such great prosperity, a journey rather laborious and fearful, undertaken for the peace of the kingdom and the liberation of the Church. For at Rome you most gloriously attained the fullness of imperial dignity, and, what was greater, with no great army, so that the greatness of your spirit and faith might shine more clearly. But if your enemies trembled and were quiet before your rather small army, what horror do we think had to seize their hearts when the King began to advance in the greatness of his arm? Moreover, the honourable cause will encourage, and a double necessity will spur you on. It is not mine to urge you to battle; yet it is (I say this with confidence) the part of the Church's advocate to ward off the fury of the schismatics from the Church's harassment, and it is the proper task of Caesar to vindicate the crown from the Sicilian usurper. For as is well known, the Jewish offspring has occupied the seat of Peter to Christ's injury; so undoubtedly everyone who makes himself king in Sicily sets himself against Caesar. But if both fall to Caesar's charge, namely to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's, why is God's property diminished at Tulle, when Caesar gains nothing there? We must fear that the neglect of the smallest things may be a hindrance to the greatest. This is what I mean: the church of St Gengulf, as is said, is grievously and unjustly oppressed in that city. And they tell your prudence that it was obtained by some fraud I know not what, so that, while you were preparing to help the Lord Pope through justice, you might by your intervention of prayer oppose it. I beg and advise that the matter be handled more wisely: not that the petition be revoked, but that room be given to justice before that church is utterly destroyed. I am poor, yet faithful to you; and if I seem importunate, perhaps that is the reason. We greet the Lady Empress warmly in the charity of Christ.

units.la: tamus.
units.tr: ...we greet.

units.la: B. BERNHARDI ABBA- TIS CLAREVALLENSIS EPISTOLA AD CONRADVM RE- GEM ROMANORVM.
units.tr: Letter of B. Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, to Conrad, King of the Romans.

units.la: Quod Papa Imperatori debeat esse subiectus in temporalibus; Imperator vero Papae in spiritualibus.
units.tr: That the Pope ought to be subject to the Emperor in temporal matters, and the Emperor to the Pope in spiritual matters.

units.la: Scripta vestra & salutationes tam devotas suscipio, quam modicus sum ad illa: modicus dixerim dignitate, sed non devotione. Quaerimoniae Regis, nostrae sunt; & maxime illa quam dignanter exprimitis, de inuasione Imperii. Regis decus, regni diminutionem nunquam volui: volentes odie anima mea. Legi quippe: omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: &, qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Quam tamen sententiam cupio vos, & omnimodis moneo, custodire, in exhibenda reverentia summae & Apostolicae sedi, & beati Petri Vicario: sicut ipsam vobis vultis ab universo sertari Imperio. Sunt quae non putani scribenda, praesens ea fortassis opportunius intimarem.
units.tr: I receive your letters and your greetings, so devoted, as fully as I am able to answer them; I say "as fully" with respect to my dignity, but not to my devotion. The complaints are ours, and especially that one which you express so graciously, concerning the invasion of the Empire. I never wished for the king's honour to be diminished or for the kingdom to be reduced; God forbid that I should hate my own soul. For I have read: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; and whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God." Yet I desire you, and warn you in every way, to keep this judgment, by showing due reverence to the highest and Apostolic See and to the Vicar of blessed Peter, just as you wish it to be kept whole by the whole Empire. There are some things I did not think should be written; perhaps I shall make them known more conveniently in person.

units.la: B. BERNHARDI ABBATIS CLAREVALLENSIS EPISTOLA AD CONRADVM REGEM ROMANORVM.
units.tr: B. Bernhard, Abbot of Clairvaux: Letter to Conrad, King of the Romans.

units.la: De concordia Imperii & Sacerdotii: & potestate atque iure Romanorum Imperatoris.
units.tr: On the concord of Empire and Priesthood, and on the power and right of the Roman Emperor.

units.la: Nec dulcius & amabilius, sed nec arctius omnino Regnum Sacerdotiumque convenire possent, quam ut in persona Domini ambo haec pariter connetarent, utpote qui factus est nobis ex utraque tribu secundum carnem summus & Sacerdos & Rex. Non solum autem sed & commiscuit ea nihilominus ac confederavit in suo corpore, quod est populus Christianus, ipse caput illius: ita ut hoc genus hominum apostolica voce genus electum, regale Sacerdotium appelletur. In alia quoque scriptura: quotquot sunt praedestinati ad vitam, nonne omnes Reges & Sacerdotes nominantur? Ergo quod Deus coniunxit, homo ne separet. Magis autem quod divina sanxit auctoritas, humana studeat adimplere voluntas, & iungant se animis qui iuncti sunt institutis; invicem se foveant, invicem se defendant, invicem omnia sua portent. Ait sapiens, frater adiuvans fratrem ambo consolabuntur: quia si alterutrum se (quod absit) corroserint & momorderint, nonne ambo desolabuntur? Non veniat anima mea in consilium eorum qui dicunt vel imperio pacem & libertatem Ecclesiarum, vel Ecclesiis prosperitatem & exaltationem imperii nociturum. Non enim utriusque institutor Deus in destructionem ea connexit, sed in aedificationem. Si hoc scitis, quovisque vos communem contumeliam, communem dissimulatis iniuriam? nonne ut Apostolica sedes ita & caput Imperii Roma est? Ut ergo de Ecclesia pacem, num honor Regi est truncum in manibus tenere imperium? Et quidem ignoro quid vobis super hoc consulant sapientes vestri & principes regni: Sed ego insipientia mea loquens, quod sentio non tacebo. Ecclesia Dei ab exordu sui usque ad hanc tempora pluries tribulata est, & pluries liberata est. Denique audite quid ipsa de se loquatur in Psalmo, ipsius enim vox est: Saepe expugnaverunt me a iuventute mea, etenim non potuerunt mihi: supra dorsum meum fabricaverunt peccatores, prolongaverunt iniquitatem suam. Certus esto, o Rex, nec nunc quoque relinquet Deus virgam peccatorum super sortem iustorum. Non est abbreviata manus Domini, nec facta impotens ad salvandum. Liberabit & hoc tempore absque dubio sponsam suam, quia suo sanguine redemit eam, suo spiritu dotavit, donis caelestibus exornavit, ditavit nihilominus & terrenis. Liberabit, inquam, liberabit. Sed si in alterius manus viderint regni Principes, idne honor Regis regnive utilitas sit? non est utique. Quamobrem accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum potentissime, & restituat sibi Caesar quae Caesaris sunt, & quae sunt Dei, Deo. Utrumque interesse Caesaris constat; & propriam tueri coronam, & Ecclesiam defensare: alterum Regi, alterum convenit Ecclesiae advocato. Victoria, sicut in Deo confidimus prae manibus est. Superbia & arrogantia Romanorum plus quam fortitudo eorum. Quid enim? nunquid quispiam magnus vel potens, verbi gratia, Imperator vel Rex sedam rem istam in imperium pariter Sacerdotiumque praesumit? Sed populus hic maledicus & tumultuosus, qui suas nescit metiri vires, cogitare finem, considerare proventum; insipientia sua, furore suo ausus est hoc grande sacrilegium attentare. Absit ut vel ad momentum stare possit ante faciem Regis popularis manus, vulgi temeritas. Factus sum insipiens: qui cum sim vilis ignobilisque persona, tanquam aliquis magnus consiliis, tantae magnitudinis, tantaque sapientiae me ingessi, & de re magna. At quo ignobilior atque abiector, tanto liberior sum ad loquendum quod caritas suggerit. Unde adhuc addo in eadem insipientia mea. Si quis aliud quam locutus sum vobis, quod non credimus, suadere conabitur: is profecto aut non diligit Regem, aut parum intelligit quid Regiam deceat Maiestatem, aut certe quae sua sunt quaerit, & non valde quae vel Dei, vel Regis sunt, curare conuincitur.
units.tr: Nothing could be sweeter or more lovely, yet nothing could join kingship and priesthood more closely, than that both should be united together in the person of the Lord, who was made for us, according to the flesh, both the highest Priest and King, from both tribes. Moreover, he not only joined them but also bound them together and united them in his body, which is the Christian people, of which he himself is the head; so that this kind of man is called, in the apostle's words, "a chosen race, a royal priesthood." In another Scripture also: are not all who are predestined to life called kings and priests? Therefore what God has joined, let not man separate. Rather, let the human will strive to fulfil what the divine authority has decreed; let those who are joined by institution join in spirit; let them cherish one another, defend one another, bear one another's burdens. The wise man says: "A brother helped by a brother is like a strong city," and "both shall be consoled": for if they bite and devour one another (God forbid), will not both be left desolate? Let my soul not enter into the counsel of those who say that the peace and liberty of the Churches will harm the Empire, or that the prosperity and exaltation of the Empire will harm the Churches. For God, the founder of each, did not join them for destruction but for building up. If you know this, how long will you tolerate a common insult and overlook a common injury? Is not Rome the seat of the Apostolic See, and also the head of the Empire? So then, is it an honour for a king to hold an empire with a mutilated hand, while seeking peace from the Church? Indeed I do not know what your wise men and the princes of the realm advise you on this; but speaking in my foolishness, I will not keep silent about what I think. The Church of God, from its beginning until these times, has often been afflicted and often been delivered. Finally, hear what it says of itself in the Psalm, for it is its own voice: "Often have they fought against me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me; sinners have built upon my back, they have lengthened their iniquity." Be assured, O King, that God will not now either leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous. The hand of the Lord is not shortened, nor has it become unable to save. He will deliver his bride at this time too, without doubt, because he redeemed her with his blood, endowed her with his Spirit, adorned her with heavenly gifts, and enriched her also with earthly ones. He will deliver her, I say, he will deliver her. But if the princes of the realm see it placed in the hands of another, will that be the honour of the King or the advantage of the kingdom? It certainly will not. Therefore, most mighty one, gird your sword upon your thigh, and let Caesar restore to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. It is evident that both concern Caesar: to protect his own crown and to defend the Church; the one belongs to the King, the other is fitting for the advocate of the Church. Victory, as we trust in God, is at hand. The pride and arrogance of the Romans are greater than their strength. For what? Does anyone great or powerful, for example an Emperor or King, presume to hold this matter of empire and priesthood together? But this cursing and tumultuous people, which does not know how to measure its own strength, consider the end, or weigh the outcome, has by its folly and its fury dared to attempt this great sacrilege. Far be it that a popular hand, the rashness of the crowd, could stand even for a moment before the face of the King. I have become foolish: though I am a humble and ignoble person, I have thrust myself, as if I were some great counsellor of such magnitude and such wisdom, into a great matter. But the more ignoble and abject I am, the freer I am to speak what charity suggests. Hence I add, still in the same foolishness, that if anyone tries to persuade you of anything other than what I have said to you, which we do not believe, he either does not love the King, or understands too little what befits royal majesty, or certainly is shown to seek his own interests and to care little for what belongs to God or to the King.

units.la: B. BERNARDI ABBATIS CLAREVALLENSIS LIBRI V. DE CONSIDERATIONE AD EUGENIUM III. PAPAM.
units.tr: The Five Books of B. Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, on Consideration, Addressed to Pope Eugenius III

units.la: Prologus.
units.tr: Prologue

units.la: Subit animum dictare aliquid quod te, Papa Beatissime Eugeni, vel aedificet, vel delectet, vel consoletur. Sed nescio quomodo vult & non vult exire laeta quidem, sed lenta oratio: dum certatim illi contraria imperare contendunt, maiestas atque amor; nempe urget ille, inhibet illa. Sed interuenit tua dignatio, qua hoc ipsum non praecipis, sed petis cum praecipere magis te deceat. Maiestate igitur tam dignanter cedente, quidni cedat pudor? quid enim si cathedram ascendisti? nec si ambules super pennas ventorum subduceris affectui. Amor Dominum nescit, agnoscit filium & in infulis, per se satis subiectus est, obsequitur sponte, gratis obtemperat, libere reveretur. Non sic aliqui non sic, sed aut timore ad aliqua impelluntur, aut cupiditate. Hi sunt qui in facie benedicunt, mala autem in cordibus eorum: blandiuntur coram, in necessitate deficiunt. At caritas nunquam excidit. Ego (ut verum fatear) matris sum liberatus officio, sed non depraedatus affectu. Olim mihi inuisceratuses, non tam facile eruueris. Ascende in coelos, descende in abyssos; non recedes a me, sequat te quocunque ieris. Amavi pauperem, & amabo pauperum & divitum patrem. Non enim si bene te novi, quia pater pauperum factus, omnino non pauper spiritu es. In te hanc mutationem factam esse confido, non dere; nec priori statui tuo successisse promotionem, sed ascendisse. Monebo te proinde non ut magister, sed ut mater plane ut amans. Amens magis videar, sed ei qui non amat, ei qui vim non sentit amoris.
units.tr: It occurs to me to dictate something that may build you up, Most Blessed Pope Eugenius, or delight or console you. But I do not know how my speech wants and does not want to come forth, cheerful in its way yet slow, while two opposing forces, majesty and love, struggle to command it in turn: the one urges, the other holds back. Yet your condescension intervenes, by which you do not command this very thing but ask for it, though it would befit you rather to command. Since majesty yields so graciously, why should shame not yield too? For what if you have ascended the chair? Even if you walk upon the wings of the winds, you will not be withdrawn from affection. Love does not know a lord; it recognises a son. Even amid the insignia of office, it is subject enough in itself: it obeys willingly, complies freely, and reveres without constraint. Not so do some others, who are driven to certain actions either by fear or by greed. These are the ones who bless with their faces while their hearts hold evil; they flatter in your presence and fail you in time of need. But love never fails. I, to tell the truth, have been freed from the duty of a mother, yet not robbed of her affection. You once took deep root in me, and you could not be torn out so easily. Ascend into heaven, descend into the depths; you will not leave me, and wherever you go, it will follow you. I have loved the poor, and I shall go on loving them, and the father of both poor and rich. For if I know you well, you have become father of the poor, and you are not altogether poor in spirit. I am confident that this change in you is not a desertion of who you were, nor is your present rank a replacement of your former station but an ascent from it. I shall therefore advise you not as a teacher but as a mother, indeed as one who loves. I may seem more foolish for it, but only to one who does not love and does not feel the force of love.

units.la: LIBER PRIMVS.
units.tr: BOOK I.

units.la: Unde iam ergo incipiam? libet ab occupationibus tuis, quia in his maxime condoleo tibi. Condoleo dixerim, si tamen doleo & tu aliquin doleo magis dixisse debuerat, quia non est condolere, ubi nemo qui doleat. Itaque si doles, condoleo: si non, doleo tamen maxime, sciens longius a salute abstinere membrum quod obstupuit, & aegrum se non sentientem periculosius laborare. Absit autem de te id suspicer: novi quibus deliciis dulcis quietis tuae non longe ante hac fruebare, non potes desuevisse tam cito, ita subito non dolere nuper subtractas: plaga recens dolore non caret. Neque enim iam occaluit vulnus, nec in tam breui versum in insensibile est. Quanquam, si non dissimules, non deest tibi iugis materia iusti doloris a quotidianis iacturis. Invitus (ni fallor) avelleris a tuae Rachelis amplexibus, & quotiens id pati contigerit, totiens dolor tunc renovetur necesse est. At quomodo non contingit? quotiens vis, & in cassum? quotiens moues, nec promoues? quotiens conatus, & non datur ultra eniteris, & non paris; tentas, & abriperis; & vbi incipis, ibi deficis; & dum adhuc ordiris, succidunt te. Venerunt filii usque ad partum (ait Propheta) & vires non habet parturiens. Nosti hoc: nemo te melius. Attrita frontis es, & instar vitulae Ephraim doctae diligenter tritturam: Si (pace tua) sic se habent res tuae. Absit, haec est pars illius qui datus est in reprobum sensum: ab his sane cupio tibi pacem, non cum his. Nihil plus metuo tibi pace ista. Miraris si vnquam possit accidere? etiam dico tibi, si res, vt assolet per consuetudinem in incuriam venerit.
units.tr: Where, then, shall I begin? I should like to start with your occupations, since it is over these that I most grieve for you. I say "grieve," though I ought perhaps to have said it more strongly, since one cannot share a grief when there is no one who grieves. So if you do grieve, I share your grief; if you do not, I grieve all the more, knowing that a limb which has gone numb stays further from health, and that a sick man who does not feel his illness is in more danger. But I hope it is not so with you. I know in what delights of sweet rest you were enjoying yourself not long ago. You cannot have grown unaccustomed to them so quickly, nor can you have stopped grieving so suddenly for what has been taken from you. A fresh wound does not lack pain. The sore has not yet grown hard, nor has it so quickly turned into numbness. Yet, if you will not deceive yourself, there is no lack of a constant cause for just grief in your daily losses. You are torn, I think, unwillingly from the embraces of your Rachel, and each time that happens the grief must surely be renewed. And how could it not happen? How often do you strive, and to no purpose? How often do you stir, and yet advance nothing? How often do you make an effort, and yet you labour on without bringing forth? You attempt, and are dragged away; you begin, and there you fail; and while you are still setting out, you collapse. "The children have come to the birth," says the Prophet, "and there is no strength to bring them forth." You know this; no one knows it better than you. You have a hardened brow, and, like a heifer of Ephraim that is taught, you love to tread out the corn. If (with your leave) your affairs are in this state, then, far from it! This is the lot of those who have been given over to a reprobate mind. I wish you peace from them, certainly, but not peace with them. I fear nothing more for you than that peace. Are you surprised that it could ever happen? I tell you further: it could, if the matter comes to be neglected, as is usual with habit.

units.la: Noli nimis credere affectui tuo, qui nunc est. Nil tam fixum animo, quod neglecto & tempore non obsolescat. Vulneri vetusto & neglecto callus obducitur, & in eo insanabile quo insensibile fit. Deniq; dolor continuus & acerbus, diuturnus esse non patitur: nam si non aliunde extinguitur, necesse est cedat vel sibi. Etiamnunc cito aut de remedio consolationem recipiet, aut de assiduitate stuporem. Quid enim mirertur consuetudo, quod non assiduitate duretur? quid non vsui cedat? quantis quod prae amaritudine prius exhorrebant, vsu ipso male in dulce conuersum est? Audi iustum qui lamentetur super huiusce modi: Quae prius tangere nolebat anima mea, nunc pra angustia cibi mei sunt. Primum tibi importabile videbitur aliquid, processu temporis si assuefactas iudicabis non adeo grave, paulo post & leue senties, paulo post neque senties, paulo post etiam delectabit. Ita paulatim in cordis duritiem itur, & ex illa in auersionem. Sic & grauis & continuus dolor, citum, vt dixi, habiturus est exitum, aut sanitatem profecto, aut insensibilitatem. Hinc prorsus, hinc tibi timui semper, & timeo ne dilato remedio dolorem non sustinens periculo te irreuocabiliter desperatus immergas. Vereor, inquam, ne in mediis occupationibus (quoniam multae sunt) dum diffidis finem, frontem dures, & ita sensum ipsum quodam modo sensu priues, iusti vtilisque doloris. Multo prudentius te illis subtrahas vel ad tempus, quam patiare trahi ab ipsis, & duci certe paulatim quo tu non vis. Quaeris quo? ad cor durum. Nec pergas quaerere quid illud sit, si non expauisti, tuum hoc est. Solum est cor durum quod semetipsum non exhorret, quia nec sentit. Quid me interrogas? interroga Pharaonem. Nemo duri cordis salutem vnquam adeptus est, nisi quem forte miserans Deus abstulit ab eo, iuxta Propheam, cor lapideum, & dedit cor carneum. Quid ergo cor durum? ipsum est quod nec compunctione scinditur, nec pietate mollitur, nec monetur precibus, & minis non cedit, flagellis duratur: ingratum ad beneficia est, ad consilia inuidum, ad iudicia saeuum: inuerecundum ad turpia, impaniedum ad pericula, inhumanum ad humana, temerarium ad diuina, praeteritorum obliuiscens, praesentium negligens, ad futura non prouidens. Ipsum est cui praeteritorum, praeter solas iniurias, nihil omnino non praeterit, praesentium nihil non perit, futurorum nulla, nisi forte ad vlciscendum, prospectio seu praeparatio est. Et vt in breui cuncta horribilis mali mala complectar, ipsum est quod nec Deum timet, nec hominem reuereatur. En quo trahere te habent haec occupationes maledictae: si tamen pergis vt coepisti ita dare te totum illis, nil tui tibi relinquens, perdis tempus; & si licet nunc alterum me tibi exhibere Iethro, tu quoq; in his stulto labore consumeris, quae non sunt nisi afflictio spiritus, euiscer atio mentis, euacuatio gratiae. Nam fructus horum quid nisi arenarum telae? Quaeso te, quaeso te quid est illud de mane vsq; ad vesperam litigare, aut litigantes audire? Et vtinam sufficeret diei malitia sua, non sunt liberae noctes. Vix relinquitur necessitati naturae, quod corpusculi pausationi sufficiat, & rursum ad iurgia surgitur, dies diei eructat lites, & nox noctis indicat malitiam; vsq; adeo non est respirare in bonis, non est alternam capescere requiem, non vel rara interseri ocia. Non ambigo te quoq; ista deplorare, at frustra istud, si non & emendare studueris. Interim tamen sic semper facias hortor, nec te vnquam ad ista duraueris quolibet vsu vel assiduitate. Percussi os & non doluerunt, ait Deus: nihil tibi & illis. Iusti potius tibi aptare curato & affectionem & vocem, qui ait: quae est enim fortitudo mea vt sustineam? aut quis finis meus vt patienter agam? nec fortitudo lapidum fortitudo mea, nec caro mea aenea est. Magna virtus patientiae, sed non hanc tibi ad ista optauerim: interdum impatientem esse probabilius. Tunc approbes illorum patientiam, quibus Paulus dicebat: libenter sufferitis insipientes, cum sitis ipsi sapientes? Ni fallor ironia erat, & non laus sed suggillatio quorundam manuetudinis, quae quasi datis manibus pseudo Apostolis a quibus & seducti erant ad quaeque ipsorum peregrina & prava dogmata trahi se patientissime ferrent: Vnum & subdens, sustinetis enim, inquit, si quis vos in seruitutem redigit. Non bona patientia, cum possis esse liber, seruum te permittere fieri. Nolo dissimules seruitutem in quam certe indies, dum nescis, redigeris: hebetati cordis indicium est, propriam non sentire continuam vexationem. Vexatio dat intellectum auditui, ait quidam, verum est, sed si nimia non fuerit; nam si sit, non plane intellectum dat, sed contemptu. Deniq; impius cum in profundum malorum venerit, contemnit. Expergiscere ergo, & pessimae seruitutis iugum iam iamq; imminens, imo iam non modice premens, non tantum cave, sed horre. An omnino non seruus, quia non vni seruis, sed omnibus? nulla turpior seruitus graviorve quam seruitus Iudaeorum, qua quocunq; ierint post se trahunt, & vbiq; Dominos offendunt suos. Tu quoq; dic quaeso vbi vnquam sis liber, vbi tuus, vbi tuus? vbiq; strepitus, vbiq; tumultus, vbiq; iugum tuae seruitutis te premit. Nec mihi repones nunc Apostoli vocem, quae ait: cum essem liber ex omnibus, omnium seruum me feci. Longe est istud a te. Nunquid hac ille seruitute hominibus inseruiebat, in acquisitione turpis quaestus? nunquid ad eum de toto orbe confluebant ambitiosi, auari, simoniaci, sacrilegi, concubinarii, incestuosi, & quaecunq; istiusmodi monstra hominum, vt ipsius Apostolica auctoritate, vel obtinerent honores Ecclesiasticos, vel retinerent? Ergo seruum se fecit homo, cui viuere Christus erat & mori lucrum, vt plures lucrifaceret Christo, non vt lucra augeret auaritiae. Non est igitur quod de solertissima Pauli industria & charitate tam libera, q; liberali, seruili conuersationi tuae patrocinium sumas. Qua tuo digni tuae apostolatu, quam salubrius tuae conscientiae, quam fructuosius Ecclesiae Dei, audias potius ipsam dicentem: precio empti estis, nolite effici serui hominum. Quid seruilius indigniusq; (praesertim summo Pontifici) quam non dico omni die, sed pene omni hora, insudare talibus rebus & pro talibus? Deniq; quomodo oramus, quomodo docemus populos, quomodo aedificamus Ecclesiam; quomodo meditamur in lege? & quidem quotidie perstrepunt in palatio leges, sed Iustiniani, non Domini. Iustene etiam istud? tu videris. Nam certe lex Domini immaculata convertens animas: haec autem non tam leges, quam lites sunt & cavillationes, subvertentes iudicium. Tu ergo Pastor & Episcopus animarum, qua mente, obsecro, sustines coram te semper sedere illam, garrire istas? Fallor, si non movet tibi scrupulum perversitas haec; puto quod & interdum compellat clamare ad Dominum cum Propheta: narraverunt mihi iniqui fabulationes, sed non ut lex tua. Ergo & te aude liberum profiteri sub tam gravi mole inconvenientiae huius, & cui fas non sit cervicem subducere. Nam si potes & non vis, multo magis servus & huius ipsius tam perversae voluntatis tuae. An non servus, cui dominatur iniquitas? & maxime: nisi tu forte indignius iudices hominem tibi quam vitium dominari. Quid interest volens servias an invitus? nam etsi coacta servitus miserabilior, sed affectata miserior est.
units.tr: Do not put too much trust in your present feeling. Nothing is so fixed in the mind that it does not grow stale when neglected over time. An old and neglected wound grows a callus, and a sore becomes insensible in the very place where it cannot be healed. Finally, continuous and bitter pain does not allow itself to last long; for if it is not extinguished by some other means, it must give way, at least to itself. Even now your sorrow will soon receive either consolation from a remedy or numbness from constant use. For why should habit be surprised that something is not hardened by continual use? What does it not yield to? By how much has what once men shrank from in bitterness been turned, by use alone, into sweetness? Hear the just man who laments over things of this kind: "The things my soul once refused to touch are now, because of my distress, my food." At first something will seem unbearable to you; but if, as time goes on, you judge that you have grown accustomed to it and it is no longer so heavy, a little later you will feel it as light, a little later you will not feel it at all, and a little later it will even give you pleasure. So by degrees men go on to hardness of heart, and from that to aversion. In this way even a heavy and continual grief, as I have said, will come to an end, and it will surely end either in health or in insensibility. It is for this very reason that I have always been afraid for you, and I still fear that, since you cannot bear the pain, you may, by postponing the remedy, plunge yourself irrevocably into a desperate peril. I fear, I say, that in the midst of your occupations (and they are many), while you are worn out seeking an end to them, you will harden your brow and so, in a certain sense, deprive yourself of the very feeling of a just and useful grief. It would be far wiser to withdraw from them, even for a time, than to suffer yourself to be dragged by them and, surely, led little by little to where you do not want to go. You ask where? To a hard heart. Do not go on asking what that is: if you have not been struck with dread, it is your own. The only hard heart is one that does not dread itself, because it does not feel. Why do you ask me? Ask Pharaoh. No one with a hard heart has ever obtained salvation, unless God, perhaps in pity, has taken it away from him, according to the Prophet, and given him a heart of flesh in place of a heart of stone. What, then, is a hard heart? It is that which is not broken by compunction, nor softened by piety, nor moved by prayers, and yields not to threats, and is hardened by blows: it is ungrateful for benefits, envious at counsels, cruel in judgements; shameless in base things, fearless of dangers, inhuman towards men, rash towards divine things; forgetful of the past, careless of the present, heedless of the future. It is that for which, of the past, nothing at all passes by except its injuries; for which nothing of the present is not lost; and for which there is no foresight or preparation for the future, except perhaps for revenge. And, to sum up in a word all the evils of this dreadful wickedness, it is that which neither fears God nor respects man. See where these cursed occupations have a mind to drag you! If you still go on as you have begun, giving yourself wholly to them and leaving nothing of yourself for yourself, you are wasting your time; and even if I may now show you another Jethro, you are being consumed in a foolish labour over things which are nothing but affliction of spirit, weariness of mind, and emptying of grace. For what is the fruit of these things but the web of sand? I beg you, I beg you, what is that business of disputing from morning until evening, or of listening to disputants? And would that the day's wickedness were enough for itself; the nights, too, are not free. Scarcely is there left to the needs of nature enough to refresh the little body, and again one rises to quarrels; day pours forth disputes to day, and night reveals wickedness to night. So far is it from being possible to breathe among good things, to take up rest in turn, or even to admit a few rare intervals of leisure. I do not doubt that you deplore these things too; but that is in vain, unless you also take care to amend them. Meanwhile, I urge you always to act in this way, and never to harden yourself to these things by any habit or constant practice. "I struck them, and they did not feel it," says God: nothing is yours to share with them. Rather, take care to fit to yourself both the feeling and the voice of the just man, who says: "For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should act with patience? Nor is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh of bronze." Patience is a great virtue, but I would not wish you to have it for these things: sometimes it is more fitting to be impatient. You may then approve the patience of those to whom Paul said: "For you gladly bear with fools, since you yourselves are wise." I think this was irony, and not praise, but a rebuke of the meekness of some, who, as if they had given their hands to false apostles by whom they had been led astray, most patiently endured being drawn to all the foreign and wicked doctrines of those men. He adds one thing more: "For you bear it," he says, "if anyone brings you into bondage." It is not good patience, when you could be free, to allow yourself to be made a slave. Do not pretend that you do not see the bondage into which you are surely being driven day by day, while you do not know it. It is a sign of a dulled heart not to feel one's own continual vexation. "Vexation gives understanding to the hearing," says someone; that is true, but only if it is not excessive; for if it is excessive, it does not give understanding at all, but contempt. Finally, the impious man, when he has come into the depths of evils, despises them. Therefore wake up, and do not merely beware of, but dread, the yoke of the worst bondage, which already hangs over you, and indeed is no longer pressing you lightly. Are you not a slave at all, because you serve not one master but all? No servitude is more base or more grievous than the servitude of the Jews, by which they drag their masters after them wherever they go, and offend their own lords everywhere. You too, I ask, tell me where you are ever free, where you are your own, where you are your own? Everywhere there is noise, everywhere tumult, everywhere the yoke of your servitude presses upon you. Nor will you now answer me with the voice of the Apostle, who says: "Though I was free from all men, I made myself a servant to all." That is far from you. Did he serve men in this bondage, in the pursuit of base gain? Did ambitious men, covetous men, simoniacs, sacrilegious men, adulterers, incestuous men, and all such monsters of men, flock to him from the whole world, so that by his apostolic authority they might either obtain ecclesiastical honours or keep them? Therefore a man made himself a slave to others, to whom "to live was Christ, and to die was gain," so that he might win more for Christ, not so that he might increase the gains of greed. There is therefore no reason for you to take, from Paul's most skilful diligence and his charity, so free and yet so generous, a defence for your servile way of life. Worthy of your apostleship, and far more wholesome for your conscience, and far more fruitful for the Church of God, is that you should hear that same Paul saying: "You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men." What is more servile and more unworthy (especially for the Supreme Pontiff) than to toil, not merely every day but almost every hour, at such affairs and for such ends? Finally, how do we pray, how do we teach the peoples, how do we build the Church; how do we meditate on the law? And indeed in the palace the laws are clamouring every day, but they are the laws of Justinian, not of the Lord. Are they just? That is for you to consider. For surely "the law of the Lord is unspotted, converting souls": but these are not so much laws as quarrels and cavillings, subverting judgement. You, therefore, pastor and bishop of souls, with what mind, I beg you, can you bear to sit always in the presence of that business, and to chatter about these matters? I am mistaken if this perversity does not trouble your conscience; I think it sometimes drives you to cry out to the Lord with the Prophet: "The wicked have told me fables, but not as your law does." Therefore dare to declare yourself free even under so heavy a burden of this unfitness, from which it is not right for you to withdraw your neck. For if you can and do not wish to, you are much more a slave even of this very perverse will of yours. Is he not a slave whom iniquity rules? And that most of all: unless perhaps you judge it more unworthy that a man should rule over you than that a vice should. What difference does it make whether you serve willingly or unwillingly? For although forced servitude is more wretched, that which is deliberately chosen is more wretched still.

units.la: Et quid vis me facere, inquis? ut tibi ab his occupationibus parcas, impossibile fortasse respondebis, facilius cathedrae valedicere posse. Recte hoc si rumpere & non magis interrumpere ista hortarer. Audi ergo quid redarguam, quid suadeam. Si quod vis & sapis totum das actioni, consideratione nihil: laudo te, in hoc non laudo. Puto quod & nemo qui a Salomone audierit, qui minoratur actu, percipiet sapientiam: certe necipsi actioni expedit consideratione non praeveniri. Si item totus vis esse omnium, instar illius qui omnibus omnia factus est, laudo humanitatem, sed si plena sit. Quomodo autem plena te excluso? & tu homo es. Ergo ut integra sit & plena humanitas, colligat & te intra sinus, qui omnes recipit: alioquin quid tibi prodest, iuxta verbum Domini, si universos lucraris, te ipsum perdens? Quamobrem cum omnes te habeant, esto etiam tu ex habentibus unus: quid solus fraudaris munere tui? usque quo vadens spiritus & non rediens? usque quo non recipiens te & ipse inter alios vacua? Sapientibus & insipientibus debitor es, & soli negas te tibi? Stultus, & sapiens; servus & liber; dives & pauper; vir & foemina; senex & iuvenis; clericus & laicus; iustus & impius, omnes pariter participant te, omnes de fonte publico bibunt pectore tuo, & tu seorsim sitiens stabis? Si maledictus qui partem suam fecit deteriorem, quid ille qui se penitus reddit expertem? Sane deriuentur aquae tuae in plateas, homines, & iumenta, & pecora bibant ex eis, quando & camelis pueri Abrahae potum tribuas: sed inter caeteros bibe tu de fonte putei tui: alienus, inquit, non bibet ex eo. Nunquid tu alienus? cui non alienus, si tibi es? denique qui sibi neque, cui bonus? Memento proinde non dicosepe; sed vel interdum reddere teipsum tibi. Vtere tu quoq; te inter multos, aut certe post multos. Quid indulgentius? hoc enim dico secundum indulgentiam, non secundum iudicium. Puto & ipso Apostolo indulgentiorem me in hac parte. Ergo plusquam oportet inquis? non insciens: quid si ita oportet? nam tu, ut confido, nostra non eris meticulosa informatione contentus, (sed abundabis magis. Sane sic decet te scilicet abundantiorem quam me audaciorum esse. Ego quoq; mihi totius iudico apud maiestatem timiditate, quam temeritate periclitari: & fortasis non secus monere sapientem oportuit, ut sit quod scriptum est: da occasionem sapienti, & sapientior erit. Audi tamen Apostolum quid de eiusmodi sentiat: sic non est inter vos sapiens, ait ille, qui iudicet inter fratrem & fratrem. Et infert: ad ignominiam vobis dico, contemptibiliores qui sunt in Ecclesia, illos constituite ad iudicandum. Itaq; & secundum Apostolum indigne tibi vsurpas tu apostolicus officium vile; gradum contemptibilium. Vnde & dicebat Episcopus, Episcopum instruens: nemo militans Deo implicat se negotiis saecularibus. Ego autem parco tibi, non enim fortia loquor; sed possibilia. Putasne haec tempora sustinerent, si hominibus litigantibus pro tertena haereditate, & flagitantibus abs te iudicium, voce Domini tui responderes: o homo, quis me constituit iudicem super vos? in quale tu iudicium mox venires? Quid dicit homo rusticanus & imperitus ignorans primatum suum, inhonorans summam & praeexcelsam sedem, derogans apostolicae dignitati? Et tamen non monstrabunt puto qui hoc dicerent, ubi aliquando quispiam Apostolorum iudex sederit hominum, aut divisor terminorum, aut distributor terrarum: isteqe fuisse denique, ergo Apostolos iudicandos, sedisse iudicantes non lego. Erit illud non fuit. Itane immanitatus est dignitatis servus, si non vult esse maior Domino suo, aut discipulus si non vult esse maior eo qui se misit; aut filius si non transgreditur terminos quos posuerunt patres sui? Quis me constituit iudicem, ait illo Dominus magister; & erit iniuria servo discipulo, nisi iudicet vaiuersos? Mihi tamen non videtur bonus aestimator rerum, qui indignum putat Apostolis seu Apostolicis viris non iudicare de talibus, quibus datus est iudicium in maiora. Quidni contemnant iudicare de terrenis possessionculis hominum, qui in caelestibus & angelos iudicabunt? Ergo in criminibus, non in possessionibus potestas vestra, quoniam propter illa, & non propter has, accepistis claves regni caelorum: praevaricatores utique exclusuri non possessores. Vt sciatis, ait, quia filius hominis habet potestatem in terra dimittendi peccata, &c. Quanam tibi maior videtur & dignitas & potestas, dimittendi peccata, an praedia dividendi? Sed non est comparatio. Habent haec infima & terrena iudices suos, Reges & Principes terrae. Quid tandem alienos invaditis? quid falcem vestram in alienam messem extenditis? Non quia indigni vos, sed quia indignum vobis talibus insistere, quippe potioribus occupatis. Deniq; ubi necessitas exigit, audi quid censeat, non ego sed Apostolus: si enim in vobis iudicabitur hic mundus, indigni estis qui de minimis iudicetis. Sed aliud est incidenter excurrere in ista causa quidem urgente, aliud vltro incumbere istis tanquam magnis dignisq; tali & tallium intentione rebus. Itaque haec & innumera talia dicerem, si fortia dicerem, si recta, si sincera. Nunc autem quoniam dies mali sunt, sufficit interim admonitum esse, non totam te necesse semper dare actioni, sed considerationi aliquid tui, & cordis, & temporis sequestrare. Hoc autem dico necessitatem intuens, non aequitatem: quanquam non sit praeter aequum necessitati cedere. Nam si liceret quod deceret absolute per omnia & in omnibus præferendam & vel solam, vel maxime colendam eam quæ ad omnia valet, id est, pietatem, prorsus irrefrigabalis ratio monstrat. Quid sit pietas quæris? Vacare consideratioi. Dicas forsitan in hoc dissentire me ab illo, qui pietatem definiuit cultum Dei: non est ita, si bene consideras, illius sensum meis expressi verbis, etsi tantum ex parte. Quid tam pertinens ad cultum Dei, quam quod ipse hortatur in Psalmo: vacate & videte quoniam ego sum Deus. Quod sane in partibus considerationis potissimum est. Quid denique; tam ad omnia valens, quæq; ipsius quoq; actionis partes benigna quadam præsumtione suas facit; præagendo quodammodo & præordinando quæ agenda sunt? Necessario sane, ne forte quæ & præuisa & præmeditata poterant esse proficuo, præcipitata magis periculo fiant. Quod tibi met, si recordaris, in ipsis actionibus causarum, & in magnis quibusque negotiis, magnarumve consiliis rerum, frequenter accidisse non ambigo. Et primum quidem ipsum fontem suum, id est mentem de qua oritur, purificat consideratio: deniq; regit affectus, dirigit actus, corrigit excessus, componit mores, vitam honestat & ordinat; postremo diuinarum pariter & humanarum rerum scientiam confert. Hæc est quæ confusa disterminat, hiantia cogit, sparsa colligit, secreta rimatur, vera vestigat, verisimilia examinat, ficta & fucata explorat. Hæc est quæ agenda præordinat, acta recogitat, ut nihil in mente resideat aut incorrectum aut correctione egens. Hæc est quæ in prosperis aduersa præsentit, in adversis quasi non sentit, quorum alterum fortitudinis, alterum prudentiæ est. Ibi etiam aduertere tibi est suauissimum quendam concentum complexumq; virtutum, atq; alteram pendere ex altera: sicut hoc loco vides fortitudinis matrem esse prudentiam, nec fortitudinem, sed temeritatem esse quemlibet ausum, quem non parturiit prudentia. Hæc item est quæ inter voluptates & necessitates media quasi quædam arbitra sedens, utrinque certis limitibus disterminat fines, istis assignans & præbens quod sat est; illis quod nimis est demens, & sic ex alterutro tertiam formans virtutem, quam dicunt temperantiam. Nempe intemperantem ipsa consideratio censet, tam eum qui necessariis pertinaciter demit, quam qui indulget superfluis. Non ergo est temperantia in solis resecandis superfluis, est & in admittendis necessariis. Huius sententiæ Apostolus non fautor tantum, sed auctor esse videtur, qui curam carnis nostræ docet non perfici in desiderio, dicens, siquidem, curam carnis non perfici, superflua cohibet, addens, in desiderio necessaria non excludit. Unde mihi videtur non omnino absurde diffinire temperantiam, qui hanc nec præcidere necessitatem, nec excedere dicat: iuxta illud Philosophi, ne quid nimis. Iam de iustitia, quæ una ex qua est, nonne constat consideratione mentem præueniri ut se formet in ea? se enim necesse est prius cogitet, ut ex se normam ducat iustitiæ, nec factura vtiq; alteri, quod sibi fieri nolit; nec quod sibi velit fieri, negatura. In his nempe duobus liquet integrum esse iustitiæ statum. Sed nec ipsa solitaria est: intuere etenim nunc mecum etiam huius pulchram connexionem & cohærentiam cum temperantia, & item ambarum cum duobus superioribus, id est, prudentia & fortitudine. Nam cum iustitiæ dicatur portio, quod sibi non vult fieri quis, alii non facere: porro, perfectio quod, ait Dominus, quacunq; vultis ut faciant vobis homines, & vos facite illis: neutrum horum erit, nisi ipsa voluntas de qua tota ducitur forma, ita ordinata fuerit, ut nec velit aliquid superfluum; nec necessarium quid superstitiose nolit, quod quidem temperantiæ est. Deniq; & ipsi iustitiæ, ut iusta sit, temperantia modum imponit: Noli nimium esse iustus, ait sapiens; ostendens per hoc minime approbandam iustitiam, quæ temperantiæ moderamine non frenetur. Quid quod & ipsa sapientia hoc temperantiæ frenum non respuit, dicente Paulo, secundum sapientiam a Deo sibi datam non plus sapere quam oportet sapere, sed sapere ad sobrietatem? Sed & e conuerso quod temperantiæ necessaria iustitia sit, ostendit Dominus arguens in Euangelio illorum temperantiam, qui abstinebant ut viderentur hominibus ieiunantes. Erat in cibo temperantia, sed non iustitia in animo; quia non Deo placere, sed hominibus intendebant. Quomodo rursum vel ista vel illa sine fortitudine? cum constet fortitudinis esse non mediocris, cohibere, velle & nolle suum inter angustias, parum & nimis, ut sit contenta voluntas modo illo medio, nudo, puro, solo; constante sibi, æquali undique sui, utpote ex omni parte pariter circumciso, quem solum constat esse virtutis. Dicito mihi, quæso, si potes, cuinam potissimum trium harum virtutum meditullium hoc dandum censeas, quod ita cunctis conterminum est, ut videatur esse proprium singularum, an ipsum virtus est & nihil aliud? Sed sic virtus non esset multiplex, sed essent omnes una. An potius quia sine eo virtus non est, omnium quodammodo intima vis una est & medulla virtutum, in qua sic vniuntur, ut perinde una videantur omnes, præsertim quod non illud participando communicant; sed totum a singulis atque integrum possidetur? verbi causa, quid tam iustitiæ, quam modus? alioquin si quid extra modum reliquit, non plane cuique tribuit quod suum est, quod tamen suum ipsius est facere. Quid tam rursum temperantiæ? quæ non aliunde profecto temperantia est, nisi quod nil immoderatum admittit. Sed puto fatebere etiam non minus esse fortitudinis, cum vel maxime ipsa sit quæ ab irruentibus vitiis, & quasi hinc inde suffocare conantibus, purum illud potenter eruit & vendicat in quoddam stabile fundamentum boni, sedemq; virtutis. Ergo modum istum tenere iustitia est, temperantia est, fortitudo est. Sed vide ne in hoc differant, ut iustitiæ quidem affectu res sit, a fortitudine autem efficacia eius. Porro possessio eius atq; usus apud temperantiam. Restat iam ut doceamus ab hac communione prudentiam non excludi. Nonne ipsa est qui modum diu animi neglectu posthabitum, ut vitiorum invidia quasi in abditis reclusum & coopertum quadam vetustatis caligine, prior reperit & aduertit? Propterea dico tibi a paucis aduertitur, quia paucorum prudentia est: itaq; iustitia quærit, prudentia inuenit, vendicat fortitudo, temperantia possidet. Non mihi hoc loco propositum est de virtutibus disputadisputare, sed hoc di terim hortans ad vacandum considerationi, cuius beneficio haec & similia aduertuntur. Cui tamen pio tamque vtili otio nullam in vita operam dare, nonne vitam perdere est? Quid tamen? Si te Philosophiae huic totum repente devoueris, praedecessores tui non ita consueuerunt, eris molestus quam pluribus, quasi qui à patrum vestigiis subito deuiaueris: nempe id videbere sagere in suggillationem illorum, sed & notabere vulgari prouerbio: qui hoc facit quod nullus, miran-tur omnes; veluti qui cupias admirationi fore. Nec potes eorum omnia simul & subito vel errata corrigere, vel excessus redigere in modum: erit cum acceperis tempus, vt secundum sapientiam tibi à Deo datam, paulatim & oportune id studeas; interim sane malo alterius vtere in bonum quod potes. Quamquam si de bonis, & non de nouis sumamus exempla, non defuere Romani Pontifices qui sibi otia inter maxima negotia inuenirent. Obsidio vrbi, & barbaricus ensis ciuium ceruicibus imminebat, nunquid tamen istud terruit beatum Papam Gregorium, quo minus sapientiam scriberet in otio? eo nempe temporis (quod ex eius praefatione liquet) obscurissimam & extremam partem Ezechielis tam diligenter, quam eleganter exposuit. Sed esto, alius inoleuit mos, dies alii sunt, & alii hominum mores, & tempora periculosa non instant iam, sed extant; fraus, & circumuentio, & violentia inualuere super terram, calumniatores multi, defensor rarus. Vbiq; potentiores pauperiores opprimunt, non possumus dicere oppressis, non negare iniuriam patientibus iudicium. Nisi agitentur causae, audiantur partes iudicare quis potest? Agitentur causae, sicut oportet: nam is modus qui frequentatur, execrabilis plane; & qui, non dico Ecclesiam, sed nec forum decerent. Miror namq; quemadmodum religiosae aures tuae, audire sustinent huiusmodi disputationes aduocatorum, & pugnas verborum, quae magis ad subuersionem, quam ad inuentionem proficiunt veritatis. Corrige prauum morem, & praecide linguas vaniloquas, & labia dolosa claude. Hi sunt loqui mendacium, diserti aduersus iustitiam, eruditi pro falsitate. Sapientes sunt vt faciant malum, eloquentes vt impugnet verum. Hi sunt qui instruunt, à quibus fuerant instruendi, astruunt non comperta sed sua; struunt de proprio calumnias innocentiae, destruunt simplicitatem veritatis, obstruunt iudicii vias. Nihil itaq; absque labore manifestam facit veritatem, vt breuis & pura narratio. Ergo illas quas ad te necesse erit intrare causas (neque enim omnes necesse erit) diligenter velim, sed breuiter decidere assuefacas; fructratoriasque & venatorias praecidere dilationes. Causa viduae intret ad te, causa pauperis, & eius qui non habet quod det. Aliis aliás multas poteris committere terminandas, quam plures nec dignas audientia iudicare. Quid enim opus est admittere illos, quorum peccata manifesta sunt praecedentia ad iudicium? Tanta est impudentia nonnullorum, vt cum manifestae ambitionis prurigine fateat tota facies causae eorum, non erubescant audientiam flagitare, publicantes semetipsos ad multorum conscientias, in quo vel sui solius poterant confundi iudicio. Non fuit qui retunderet attritas frontes, & ideo plures facti sunt, & magis induruerunt. Sed & nescio quomodo vitiosus conscientiae vitiosorum non refugit; & vbi omnes sordent, vnius foetor minime sentitur. Quis enim vnquam, verbi causa, aurum aurarus, immundum immundus, luxuriosum luxuriosus erubuit? Plena est ambitiosis Ecclesia, non est iam quod exhorreat in studiis & molitionibus ambitionis; non plus quam spelunca latronum in spoliis viatorum. Si Christi discipulus es, ignescat zelus tuus, exsurgat auctoritas aduersus impudentiam hanc, & generalem pestem. Intuere magistrum sic facientem, & audi dicentem: qui mihi ministrat, me sequatur. Non parat aures vt audiat, sed flagellum quo feriat: verba nec facit, nec recipit; nec enim sedet iudicans, sed insequitur puniens. Causa tamen non tacet, quod videlicet domum orationis negotiationis fecisset. Ergo & tu fac similiter: erubescant vultum tuum istiusmodi negotiatores si fieri poterit; si non timeant. Ete flagellum tenens timeant numularii, nec fidant in nummis, sed diffidant; abscondant aes suum à te, scientes effundere quam accipere paratiorem. Hoc studiose & constanter agendo multos lucrifacies turpium sectatores lucrorum; honestioribus officiis vendicando, multos ne vel audeant huiusmodi attentare, seruabis. Adiice illud quod non parum proficiet & ad ferias quas tibi suadeo: ita nempe non pauca tibi momenta temporum redimes, ad vacandum consideratione, quaedam vt dixi negotia nec audiendo, quaedam aliis committendo: quae tua digna putaberis audientia, fideli quodam & accommodo ipsi causae compendio terminando. De qua consideratione hic addere aliqua cogito, sed sub alterius sane principio libri, atque hic sit finis istius, ne duplo te oneret minus suavis oratio, si & longa fuerit.
units.tr: "And what do you want me to do?" you ask. You will perhaps answer that it is impossible to break free of these occupations, and that it is easier to resign the chair. I would urge you to break free of them, if I were urging you to break them off entirely and not merely to interrupt them. So hear what I would correct and what I would advise. If you give all your energy to action and nothing to contemplation, as you wish and as your wisdom would have you do, I praise you, but in this I do not praise you. I think that no one who has heard Solomon will fail to understand that he who is diminished in action will receive wisdom. Certainly action itself is served best when it is not forestalled by contemplation. Again, if you wish to be wholly everyone's, like one who became all things to all men, I praise your humanity, but only if it is full. But how can it be full if you are left out? You too are a man. So, to make humanity whole and complete, let it gather you too into its embrace, since it receives everyone. Otherwise what good is it to you, in the words of the Lord, if you gain the whole world and lose yourself? Since everyone else has you, be one of those who have you yourself as well. Why should you alone be cheated of your own gift? How long will the spirit go and not return? How long will you not receive yourself, and remain empty while everyone else is filled? You owe yourself to the wise and the foolish, and will you deny yourself to yourself alone? Fool and wise, slave and free, rich and poor, man and woman, old and young, cleric and layman, righteous and wicked: all of them share in you alike, all drink from the common fountain of your breast, and will you stand apart, thirsting? If he is cursed who makes his own portion worse, what of the one who makes himself wholly without a share? Indeed your waters may be channelled into the streets, and men and beasts may drink from them, just as you grant drink to Abraham's servants' camels; but among the others, drink from the well of your own cistern. A stranger, he says, shall not drink from it. Are you not a stranger to yourself? To whom will you not be a stranger, if you are one to yourself? And he who is not good to himself, to whom is he good? Remember, therefore, not always to give, but sometimes to give yourself back to yourself. Make use of yourself too, among many, or at least after many. What could be more indulgent? I say this out of indulgence, not out of judgement. I think I am more indulgent than the Apostle himself in this matter. You will say, then, that I am more than is fitting? I do not say it unknowingly: what if it is fitting in this way? For I trust that you will not be content with our timid instruction, but will abound more. Indeed it becomes you, of course, to be bolder than I am. I too judge that before the Majesty it is better to run the risk of timidity than of rashness; and perhaps it was necessary to advise the wise in this way, so that what is written may hold: give an opportunity to the wise, and he will be wiser. Yet hear what the Apostle thinks of such things: so there is not a wise man among you, he says, who can judge between brother and brother. And he adds: I say this to your shame: appoint to judge those who are of least account in the Church. So, according to the Apostle, you wrongly take up the office of an apostle, a base task fit for the least esteemed. Hence also the bishop, instructing a bishop, said: no one who serves God entangles himself in worldly affairs. But I spare you, for I am not speaking harsh things, only possible ones. Do you think these times could bear it if, when men quarrelling over a third of an inheritance demanded judgement from you, you answered with the voice of your Lord: O man, who made me a judge over you? Into what a judgement would you soon come? What would a rustic and unlearned man say, who was ignorant of his own primacy, dishonouring the highest and most exalted seat and disparaging the dignity of the apostolic office? And yet, I think, those who would say this will not show me where any of the Apostles ever sat as judge of men, or as divider of boundaries or distributor of lands. Let them say this was not done; I do not read that the Apostles sat in judgement, so they must be judged. Is the servate of dignity so unjust that he does not wish to be greater than his lord, or the disciple who does not wish to be greater than the one who sent him, or the son who does not overstep the bounds that his fathers set? Who made me a judge? says the Lord and Master, and will it be an injustice to the servant or disciple unless he judges everyone? Yet it does not seem to me that the man who thinks it unworthy of the Apostles, or of apostolic men, not to judge such matters is a good assessor of things. They have been given judgement in greater things. Why should they scorn to judge the little earthly possessions of men, when they will judge even angels in heavenly matters? Your power, then, lies in crimes, not in possessions, since it was for the former, and not for the latter, that you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven: to exclude transgressors, certainly, and not possessors. That you may know, he says, that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins, and so on. Which seems to you the greater dignity and power: forgiving sins, or dividing estates? But there is no comparison. These lowly and earthly matters have their own judges, the kings and princes of the earth. Why do you then invade what is not yours? Why do you thrust your sickle into another's harvest? Not because you are unworthy, but because it is unworthy of you to engage in such things, since you are occupied with weightier matters. Finally, where necessity demands it, hear what he advises, not I but the Apostle: for if this world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? But it is one thing to run into these matters in passing, when a cause presses, and another to throw yourself headlong into them, as if they were great and worthy of your attention and that of such and such people. So I would say these things and countless others like them, if I were saying bold things, if right things, if sincere things. But now, since the days are evil, it is enough for the present to be reminded that you must not always give yourself wholly to action, but must set aside something of yourself, of your heart and of your time, for reflection. I say this with regard to necessity, not to what is equitable, although it is not beyond what is fair to yield to necessity. For if it were permitted to set before all things, in all matters and in every way, that which is alone or chiefly to be cultivated, and which is of use for everything, namely piety, then reason shows plainly that this is so beyond dispute. You ask what piety is? It is to be at leisure for contemplation. Perhaps you will say that in this I disagree with him who defined piety as the worship of God. It is not so, if you consider well, for I have expressed his meaning in my own words, though only in part. What is so bound up with the worship of God as what he himself urges in the Psalm: be still and see that I am God? Which surely is chiefly a part of contemplation. And finally, what is so serviceable for everything, and which by a kindly presumption makes the parts of action its own, anticipating and in a way pre-ordaining what is to be done? Certainly it does so of necessity, lest what could have been foreseen and premeditated for advantage should instead be rushed into and made more dangerous. I do not doubt that you yourself, if you recall, have often found this to be so in the conduct of cases and in great affairs and the counsels of important matters. And first of all, contemplation purifies the very source from which it springs, namely the mind; then it governs the affections, directs actions, corrects excesses, orders manners, honours and regulates life; and finally it brings knowledge of divine and human things alike. It is this which separates what is confused, gathers what gapes open, collects what is scattered, searches out what is hidden, tracks down what is true, examines what is probable, and detects what is false and painted over. It is this which pre-orders what is to be done and reviews what has been done, so that nothing remains in the mind that is uncorrected or in need of correction. It is this which foresees adversity amid prosperity, and in adversity almost does not feel it; the one belongs to fortitude, the other to prudence. There, too, it is for you to notice a most sweet harmony and interweaving of the virtues, and how each depends on the other: as you see here, prudence is the mother of fortitude, and that daring which prudence has not brought forth is not fortitude but rashness. Likewise it is contemplation which, sitting between pleasures and needs like a kind of arbiter, marks off the bounds of each with fixed limits, assigning and granting to the one what is enough, and to the other what is too much for it to bear. In this way, from the two, it forms a third virtue, which they call temperance. Indeed contemplation judges the intemperate man to be the one who stingily withholds what is necessary and also the one who indulges in superfluities. Temperance therefore lies not only in cutting away superfluities but also in admitting what is necessary. The Apostle seems not merely a supporter but the author of this view, for he teaches that the care of our flesh is not to be carried out in desire; by saying, since the care of the flesh is not to be carried out, he restrains superfluities, and by adding in desire, he does not exclude what is necessary. Hence it seems to me not wholly absurd to define temperance as one who says that it neither cuts off what is necessary nor exceeds it, in accordance with the saying of the Philosopher: nothing in excess. Now concerning justice, which is one of them, does it not stand that the mind must be anticipated by contemplation so that it may form itself in justice? For it must first think within itself, so that from itself it may draw the rule of justice: not to do to another what it would not wish done to itself, nor to refuse to do what it would wish done to itself. In these two things it is clear that the state of justice is whole. But justice is not solitary either: look now with me at its fine connection and coherence with temperance, and likewise of both with the two above it, namely prudence and fortitude. For since justice is said to be a portion of this, that one should not do to others what one does not wish done to oneself; and since the perfection of it is what the Lord said, whatever you wish that men should do to you, do so to them, neither of these will be realised unless the will itself, from which the whole form is drawn, is so ordered that it wishes nothing superfluous, and does not superstitiously refuse what is necessary, which is the business of temperance. Finally, temperance also sets a measure for justice itself, so that it may be just: Do not be overly righteous, says the wise man, showing by this that justice which is not restrained by the moderation of temperance is by no means to be approved. And indeed wisdom itself does not reject this bridle of temperance, since Paul says: according to the wisdom given him by God, not to be wiser than he ought to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety. Conversely, too, the Lord shows that justice is necessary to temperance, when in the Gospel he rebukes the temperance of those who abstained so that they might appear to men as fasting. There was temperance in their food, but no justice in their mind, because they aimed to please men and not God. Again, how can either of these be without fortitude? For it is agreed that it is the mark of no small fortitude to restrain itself, to will and not will its own way amid the straits of too little and too much, so that the will may be content with that middle measure, bare, pure and alone, consistent with itself, equal on every side, as having been pared down equally everywhere; and this alone, it is agreed, is virtue. Tell me, I beg you, if you can, to which of these three virtues you would think this middle point most properly to be given, since it is so bounded on all sides by all of them that it seems to belong peculiarly to each one: or is it virtue itself and nothing else? But in that case virtue would not be manifold, but all would be one. Or is it rather that, since virtue is not without it, there is in some sense one inmost force and marrow of all the virtues, in which they are so united that all seem one, especially because they do not share in it by participation, but each one possesses the whole of it, entire? For example, what is justice more than measure? Otherwise, if it left anything beyond measure, it would not fully give each person what is his own, though it is his own to do. And what again is temperance, but measure? For temperance is surely nothing other than admitting nothing immoderate. But I think you will also confess that it belongs no less to fortitude, since it is above all that which, against the vices that rush upon us and seek to choke us from every side, powerfully rescues that pure middle and claims it for a firm foundation of good and seat of virtue. So to keep this measure is justice, is temperance, is fortitude. But take care that they do not differ in this, that justice is a matter of disposition, while fortitude is its efficacy; and that its possession and use belong to temperance. It remains now for me to teach that prudence is not excluded from this communion. Is it not prudence itself which first discovers and notices the measure of the mind, which has been set aside through neglect of the inner life, shut away and covered like hidden things under a certain mist of age, while the envy of vices hides it? Therefore I tell you that it is noticed by few, because prudence belongs to few; so justice seeks, prudence finds, fortitude claims, and temperance possesses. It is not my purpose here to dispute about the virtues, but to urge you to give time to contemplation, by whose benefit these and similar things are noticed. But to devote no effort at all in life to this holy and useful leisure, is that not to lose life? What then? If you were suddenly to devote yourself wholly to this philosophy, your predecessors have not been accustomed to do so. You will be a nuisance to very many, as one who has suddenly turned aside from the footsteps of the fathers. Indeed you will seem to be doing this in reproach of them, and you will be marked by the common proverb: he who does what no one does, all marvel, as if you were wishing to be an object of wonder. Nor can you correct at once all their errors or bring their excesses into due measure all together. There will come a time, when you have received it, when you may zealously and fittingly pursue this gradually, according to the wisdom given you by God; meanwhile, of course, make use for good of what you can of another's evil. And yet, if we take examples from the good and not from novelties, there have not been lacking Roman Pontiffs who found leisure for themselves amid the greatest affairs. A siege was on the city, and the barbarian sword hung over the necks of the citizens; did that terrify the blessed Pope Gregory, so that he did not write his Morals in leisure? At that very time, as is clear from his preface, he expounded the most obscure and final part of Ezekiel as diligently as elegantly. But grant that another custom has taken hold, that the days are different, that men's manners are different, and that dangerous times no longer threaten but are already present: fraud, circumvention and violence have prevailed over the earth; calumniators are many, defenders rare. Everywhere the powerful oppress the poorer, and we cannot say to the oppressed that we deny judgement to those who suffer injury. Unless causes are heard, who can judge which party is right? Let causes be heard, as is fitting. For the method which is now commonly practised is plainly detestable, and it would not become the Church, let alone the forum. I wonder indeed how your pious ears can bear to hear such disputes of advocates and wrangling over words, which serve the overthrow of truth more than its discovery. Correct the wicked custom, cut off the babbling tongues, and shut the deceitful lips. These are the men who speak lies, skilled against justice, learned in falsehood: they are wise to do evil, eloquent to attack the truth. These are the men who teach, when they ought to be taught by others; they build up not what has been established but their own inventions; they build up slanders against innocence out of their own resources, destroy the simplicity of truth, and block the ways of judgement. Nothing, therefore, makes the truth plain without labour, except a brief and clear account. So I would like you to accustom yourself to deciding briefly those causes which you will have to enter (for not all of them will need to be entered), and to cut off the dilatory and hunting delays that waste time. Let the widow's cause come to you, and the poor man's, and that of one who has nothing to give. You may commit many others to be decided by others, since there are many not worthy of a hearing which you could judge. For why need you admit those whose sins are manifest before the judgement? Some people are so shameless that their whole appearance, marked by the itch of plain ambition, shows their case, yet they do not blush to beg for a hearing, making themselves public to the consciences of many, when they might have been put to shame by the judgement of their own conscience alone. There was no one to blunt their worn foreheads, and so there were more of them, and they grew harder. And somehow the vicious conscience of the vicious does not shrink from itself, and where all are foul, the stench of one is hardly noticed. For who ever, for instance, blushed to be a lover of gold among lovers of gold, or an unclean man among unclean men, or a lecher among lechers? The Church is full of the ambitious; there is nothing now that she shrinks from in the pursuits and machinations of ambition, no more than a cave of robbers shrinks from the spoils of travellers. If you are a disciple of Christ, let your zeal burn, let your authority rise up against this shamelessness and this general pestilence. Look at the Master doing this, and hear him saying: let him who serves me follow me. He does not prepare ears to listen, but a whip with which to strike; he neither makes speeches nor receives them; he does not sit in judgement, but pursues and punishes. Yet the case does not stay silent, namely that they had made the house of prayer a house of trade. So do you likewise: let such traders blush at your face, if that can be done; if not, let them fear. And let the moneychangers, holding the whip, fear, and let them not trust in their coins but distrust them; let them hide their bronze from you, knowing that you are more ready to pour out than to receive. By pursuing this earnestly and steadily, you will gain many who follow shameful gains; by claiming them for more honourable duties, you will keep many from even daring to attempt such things. Add to this that it will greatly help the leisure I recommend to you: in this way you will redeem for yourself not a few moments of time for reflection, by not hearing some matters and by committing others to others, as I said; those which you judge worthy of a hearing you will bring to an end by a faithful and fitting summary suited to the case itself. I am thinking of adding something here about this contemplation, but under the beginning of another book; and here let this be the end of this one, lest a less pleasant discourse burden you doubly, if it were also long.

units.tr: Book Two.

units.la: MEmor promissi mei, quo ecce iam aliquandiu teneor apud te vir optime Papa Eugeni, volo ipso absoluere vel fero. Puderet dilationis, si mihi conscius forem incuriae, aut contemptus. Non ita est, sed incidimus (vt ipse nosti) tempus graue: quod & ipsi pene viuendi visui videbatur indicere cessationem, nedum studiis. Cum Dominus scilicet prouocatus peccatis nostris, ante tempus quodammodo visus sit iudicasse orbe terrae, in aequitate quidem, sed misericordiae suae oblitus. Non pepercit populo suo, non sua nomini. Nonne dicunt in gentibus, vbi est Deus eorum? Nec mirum, Ecclesiae filii & qui Christiano censentur nomine prostrati sunt in deserto, aut interfecti gladio, aut fame consumpti. Effusa est contentio super Principes, & Dominus errare fecit eos in inuio, & non in via. Contritio & infelicitas in viis eorum: pauor, & moeror, & confusio in penetralibus Regum ipsorum. Quare cohibi pedes Euangelisantium pacem, annuntiantium bona? Diximus pax, & non est pax, pmisimus bona, & ecce turbatio. Quasi vero temeritate in opere isto, aut leuitate vsi simus. Cucurrimus plane in eo non quasi in incertum, sed te iubente, imo per te Deo. Quare ergo ieiunauimus, & non aspexit; humiliauimus animas nostras, & nesciuit? Nam in his omnibus non est auersus furor eius, sed adhuc manus eius extenta: quia patienter interim adhuc audit voces sacrilegas, & Ægyptios blasphemantes, quia callide eduxit eos vt occideret in deserto. Et quidem iudicia Dei vera quis nesciat? at iudicium hoc abyssus tanta, vt videar mihi non immerito pronunciare beatum, qui non fuerit scandalizatus in eo. Quomodo tamen humana temeritas audet reprehendere, quod minime comprehendere valet? Recordemur supernorum iudiciorum, quae a seculo sunt, si forte sit consolatio. Nam quidam ita dixit: Memor fui iudiciorum tuorum a seculo Domine, & consolatus sum. Rem dico ignotam nemini, & nemini penitus notam. Nempe sic se habent mortalium corda, quod scimus cum necesse non est, in necessitate nescimus. Moyses educturus populum de terra Ægypti, meliorem illis policitus est terram: nam quando ipsum aliter sequeretur populus solam sapiens terram? eduxit, eductos tamen in terram quam promiserat, non introduxit. Nec est quod ducis temeritati imputari queat tristis & inopinatus eventus. Omnia faciebat Domino imperante, Domino cooperante, & opus confirmante sequentibus signis. Sed populus ille, inquis, durae ceruicis fuit, semper contentiose agens contra Dominum, & Moysem seruum eius. Bene illi increduli & rebelles: hi autem quid? ipsos interroga: quid me dicere opus est, quod fatentur ipsi? Dico ego vnum, quid poterant proficere qui semper reuertebantur cum ambularent? quando & isti per totam viam non redierunt corde in Ægyptum? quia si illi ceciderunt & perierunt propter iniquitatem suam, miramur istos eadem facientes, eadem passos? sed nunquid illorum casus aduersus promissa Dei? ergo nec istorum. Neque enim aliquando promissiones Dei, iustitiae Dei praeiudicant. Et audi aliud: peccauit Beniamin, accinguntur reliquae tribus ad vltionem, necsine nutu Dei: designauit deniq; ipse ducem praeliaturis, itaque praeliantur freti & manu validioti, & causa potiori; & quod his maius est, fauore diuino. At quam terribilis Deus in consiliis super filios hominum! terga dederunt sceleratis vltores sceleris, & paucioribus plures. Sed recurrunt ad Dominum, & Dominus ad eos: ascendite inquit, ascendunt denuo: denuoque fusi & confusi sunt. Ita Deo primum quidem fauente, secundo & iubente, iusti iustum certamen ineunt, & succumbunt: sed quo inferiores certamine, eo fide superiores inuenti sunt. Quid putas de me facerent isti si meo hortatu iterato ascenderent, iterato succumberent? quoniam me audirent monentem tertio repetere iter, repetere opus in quo semel & iam secundo frustrati forent? Et tamen Israelitae vnam & alteram non reputantes frustrationem, tertio parent & superant. Sed dicunt forsitan isti: unde scimus quod a Domino sermo egressus sit? quae signa tu facis vt credamus tibi? non est quod ad ista ipsa respondeam, parcendum verecundiae meae. Responde tu pro me & pro te ipso, secundum ea quae audisti & vidisti, aut certe secundum quod tibi inspirauit Deus. Sed forte miraris me prosequi ista, qui aliud proposueram: facio non oblitus propositi, sed quod a proposito non iudicem aliena; nempe de Consideratione (vt nemini) sermo mihi est ad tuam dignationem. Et sane magna ista res, & egens consideratione non minima. Quia si res magnas a magnis considerari oportet, cui aeque vt tibi id studii competit, qui parem super terram non habes? sed tu secundum sapientiam & potestatem datam tibi desuper, facies de hoc: non est meae humilitatis dictare tibi sic, vel sic fieri quicquam. Sufficit intimasse oportere aliquid fieri, vnde & Ecclesia consoletur, & obstruatur os loquentium iniqua. Haec pauca vice Apologiae dicta sint, vt ipsa qualiacunq; habeat conscientia tua ex me, vnde habeat me excusatum & te pariter: & si non apud eos qui facta ex euentibus aestimant, certe apud teipsum. Perfecta & absoluta cuique excusatio, testimonium conscientiae suae: mihi pro minimo est vt ab illis iudicer, qui dicunt bonum malum, & malum bonum; ponentes lucem tenebras, & tenebras lucem.
