Et si necesse sit vnum fieri e duobus; malo in nos murmur hominum, quam in Deum esse. Bonum mihi si dignetur me vti pro clypeo, libens excipio in me detrahentium linguas maledicas, & venenata spicula blasphemorum, vt non ad ipsum perueniant. Non recuso inglorius fieri, vt non irruatur in Dei gloriam. Quis mihi det gloriari in voce illa, quoniam propter te sustinui opprobrium: operuit confusio faciem meam. Gloria mihi est consortem fieri Christi, cuius illa vox est: opprobria exprobrantium tibi ceciderunt super me. Nunc iam recurrat stilus ad suam materiam, & in ea quae proposueramus suo tramite gradiatur oratio. Et primo quidem ipsam considerationem quid dicam, considera. Non enim id per omnia quod contemplationem intelligi volo: quod haec ad rerum certitudinem, illa ad inquisitionem magis se habeat. Iuxta quem sensum potest contemplatio quidem definiri: verus certusq; intuitus animi de quacunq; re: siue apprehensio veri non dubia. Consideratio autem intensa ad inuestigandum cogitatio: vel intensio animi vestigantis verum: quanquam soleant ambae pro inuicem indifferenter vsurpari. Iam quod ad considerationis attinet fructum, quattuor vt occurrunt tibi consideranda reor: te, quae sub te, quae circa te, quae supra te sunt. At te tua consideratio inchoet, ne frustra extenderis in alia te neglecto. Quid tibi prodest si vniuersum mundum lucreris, te vnum perdens? Et si sapiens sis, deest tibi ad sapientiam, si tibi non fueris. Quantum vero? vt quidem senserim ego, totum. Noueris licet omnia mysteria, noueris lata terrae, alta coeli, profunda maris; si te nescieris, eris similis aedificanti sine fundamento, ruinam non structuram faciens. Quicquid exstruxeris extra te, erit instar congesti pulueris ventis obnoxium. Non ergo sapiens, qui sibi non est: sapiens sibi sapiens erit, & bibet de fonte putei sui primus ipse. A te proinde incipiat tua Consideratio, non solum autem, sed & in te finiatur: quocunque euagetur, ad te retractaris eam cum salutis fructu; tu primus tibi, tu vltimus. Sume exemplum de summo omnium patre, verbum suum & emittente & retinente. Verbum tuum, consideratio tua: quod si procedit, non recedat: sic progrediatur, vt non egrediatur: sic exeat, vt non deferat. In acquisitione salutis, nemo tibi germanior vnico matris tuae: contra salutem propriam cogites nihil. Minus dixi contra, praeter dixisse debueram. Quicquid se considerationi offerat quod non quoquomodo ad tuam ipsius salutem pertineat, respuendum. Et haec tui consideratio in tria quaedam diuiditur: si consideres quid, quis, aut qualis sis: quid in natura, quis in persona, qualis in moribus. Quid? verbi gratia, homo. Quis? Papa, vel summus Pontifex. Qualis? benignus, mansuetus, vel quicquid tale. Quanquam primum illud Propheticum sit magis, quam Apostolicum vestigare: attamen est in definitione hominis, quem dicunt animal rationale mortale: quod diligentius intueri si libet, licet. Non est quod tuae in eo aut professioni obuiet, aut dignitati; est vero quod saluti afferre queat. Nam consideranti duo haec simul, rationale mortaleque, is tibi exinde occurrit fructus, vt & mortale quod in te est rationale humiliet: & rursum rationale mortale confortet; quod neutrum neglectui erit homini circumspecto. Si quaeadhuc praesens consideranda requirit locus, tractabuntur infra, & forte vtilius ex partium collatione: Nunc quis fis, & de quo sis factus aduertendum. Quanquam, quod dixi, de quo id mihi praetereundum putem, tuae potius relinquendum agnitioni illud dico indignum tibi citra perfectum agere de tanta assumto perfectione. Quidni erubescas minimus inueniri in magnis, quite recordaris magnum in minimis extitisse? Non es oblitus primae professionis, non excidit menti quae subducta est manu, sed nec effectui quidem: ipsum ad singula tua imperia, iudicia instituta habere prae oculis, non erit inutile. Haec te consideratio facit honoris contemptorem, in honore etiam ipso. Atq; id magnum. Non recedat a pectore, clypeus est tibi vela sagitta illa, homo cum in honore esset, non intellexit. Loquere ergo tibi: abiectus eram in domo Dei mei. Quale est hoc de paupere & abiecto, leuari super gentes & regna? quis ego, aut quae domus patris mei, vt sedeam excelsis sublimior? Sane qui dixit mihi, amice ascende superius, amicum fore fidit: si minus inueniar, non expedit quidem. Qui eleuauit, & deiicere potest. Sera querela, quoniam eleuans allisisti me. Non est quod blandiatur celsitudo, solicitudo maior: illa discrimen intendit, haec amicum probat. Huic accingamur, si nolumus tandem cum rubore nouissimum locum tenere. Factum superiorum dissimulare nequimus, sed enim ad quid omnibus modis attendendum. Non enim ad dominandum opinor: nam & Propheta cum similiter leuaretur audiuit; vt euellas, & destruas, & disperdas, & dissipes, & aedifices, & plantes. Quid horum faustum sonat? rusticam magis sudoris scemate quodam, labor spiritalis expressus est. Et nos igitur vt multum sentiamus de nobis, impositum seruerimus ministerium; non Dominium datum. Non sum ego maior Propheta, & si forte potestate; sed meritorum non est comparatio. Haec loquere tibi, & doce teipsum qui alios docès: puta te velut vnum aliquem de Prophetis. Annon satis ad te? & nimium: sed gratia Dei es id, quod es. Quid? esto quod Propheta. Numquid plus quam Propheta? Si sapis eris contentus mensura, quam tibi mensus est Deus: nam quod amplius est, a malo est. Disce exemplo Prophetico praesidere, non tam ad imperitandum, quam ad fatigandum quod tempus requirit: disce sarculo tibi opus esse, non sceptro, vt opus facias Prophetae. Et quidem ille non regnaturus ascendit, sed extirpaturus. Putasne & tu inuenias aliquid elaborandum in agro Domini tui? & plurimum. Non plane totum quiuere emundare Prophetae, aliquid filius suis Apostolis quod agerent reliquerunt: aliquid ipsi parentes tui, tibi. Sed nec tu ad omne sufficies, aliquid profecto tuo relicturus es successori; & ille aliis; & alii aliis vsque in finem. Circa vndecimam denique horam operarii ocii arguuntur, & mittuntur in vineam. Antecessores tui Apostoli audierunt, quia messis quidem multa, operarii vero pauci. Paternam tibi vendicato haereditatem: nam si filius, & heres, vt probes haereditatem, euigila ad curam, & non ocio torpeas, ne & tibi dicatur: quid hic stas toto die ociosus? Multo minus inueniri oportet aut delitiis resolutum, aut resupinum pompis. Nil horum tibi tabulae testatoris assignant: sed quid? Si illarum tenore contentus sis, curam potius haereditabis & operam, quam gloriam & diuitias. Blanditur cathedra, speculaest; inde denique superintendis, sonans tibi Episcopi nomine non Dominium, sed officium. Quidni loceris in eminenti unde prospectes omnia, qui speculator super omnia constitueris? Enimuero prospectus iste procinctum parit, non ocium: quoniam libet gloriari, vbi ociari non licet? nec locus est ocio, vbi sedula vrget sollicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum. Nam quid tibi aliud dimisit sanctus Apostolus? quod habeo, inquit, hoc tibi do. Quid illud? vnum scio, non est aurum neque argentum, cum ipse dicat: argentum & aurum non est mihi. Si habere contingat, vtere pro libitu, sed pro tempore: sic eris vtens illis, quasi non vtens. Ipsa quidem (quod ad animae bonum spectat) nec bona sunt, nec mala: vsus tamen horum bonus, abusio mala; sollicitudo peior, quaestus turpior. Esto vt alia quacunque ratione haec tibi vendices, sed non Apostolico iure: nec enim tibi ille dare quod non habuit, potuit: quod habuit hoc dedit; sollicitudinem, vt dixi, super Ecclesias. Nunquid dominationem? audi ipsum: non dominantes, ait, in clero; sed forma facti gregis. Et ne dictum sola humilitate putes, non etiam veritate, vox Domini est in Euangelio: Reges gentium dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur: & infert, Vos autem non sic. Planum est, Apostolis interdicitur dominatus: i ergo tu & tibi vsurpare aude aut dominans Apostolatum, aut Apostolicus dominatum; plane ab alterutro prohiberis: si vtrumq; similisimiliter habere voles, perdes vtrumq;. Alioquin non te exceptum illorum numero putes, de quibus queritur Deus sic: ipsi regnauerunt, & non ex me; Principes extiterunt, & non cognoui eos. Iam si regnare sine Deo iuuat, habes gloriam, sed non apud Deum: at si interdictum tenemus, audiamus edictum. Qui maior est vestrum, ait, fiat sicut minor; & qui praecessor est, sicut qui ministrat. Forma Apostolica haec est: dominatio interdicitur, indicitur ministratio. Quae & commendatur ipsius exemplo legislatoris, qui secutus adiungit: ego autem in medio vestrum sum tanquam qui ministrat. Quis se iam titulo hoc inglorium putet, quo se prior Dominus gloriae praesignuit? Merito Paulus gloriatur in eo dicens: ministri Christi sunt, & ego: & addit, ut minus sapiens dico, plus ego in laboribus plurimis, in carceribus abundantius, in plagis supra modum, in mortibus frequenter. O praeclarum ministerium! quo non id gloriosius principatu? Si gloriari oportet, forma tibi Sanctorum praefigitur, Apostolorum proponitur gloria. Parua ne tibi illa videtur? quis mihi tribuat similem fieri in gloria Sanctorum? clamat Propheta: Mihi autem nimis honorificati sunt amici tui Deus, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum. Clamat Apostolus: mihi autem absit gloriari nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Hoc glorieris opto semper optimo genere gloriae, quod Apostoli, quod Prophetae delegere tibi, reliquere tibi. Agnosce haereditatem tuam in Christi cruce, in laboribus plurimis. Felix qui dicere potuit, plus omnibus laborauit. Gloria est, sed nil in ea inane, nil molle, nil resupinum. Si labor terret, merces invitat: unusquisque enim secundum suum laborem mercedem accipiet. Et si ille plus omnibus laborauit, non tamen totum elaborauit, & adhuc locus est. Exi in agrum Domini tui, & considera diligenter quantis adhuc de veteri maledicto spinis ac tribulis: exi, inquam, in mundum (ager enim est mundus, idque creditus tibi,) exi in illum, non tanquam Dominus, sed tanquam villicus, videre & procurare unde exigendus es rationem. Exi, dixerim, quibusdam tuae passibus intentae sollicitudinis, & sollicitae intentionis: neque enim ipsi qui iussi sunt ire in orbem, circuierunt praesentia corporis, sed mentis prouidentia. Et tu leua oculos quosdam considerationis tuae, & vide regiones si non sunt magis siccae ad ignem, quam albae ad messem. Quia multae quas putaueras fruges, diligenter inspectae vepres potius apparebunt: immo nec vepres quidem, annosae & veternosae arbores sunt; sed non fructiferae, nisi forte glandium aut siliquarum, quas porci manducant. Quousque occupant terram? nonne si exis & cernis ista, pudebit otiosam iacere securim? pudebit sine causa falcem apostolicam accepisse? In hunc quondam agrum Isaac Patriarcha exierat, cum primo Rebecca occurrat ei, & ut Scriptura habet, exierat ad meditandum. Ille ad meditandum, tu ad extirpandum egrediaris necesse est. Tibi iam praecessisse meditatio debet; tempus faciendi prae manibus: si nunc haesitare incipias; id quidem sero. Ante, iuxta consilium Saluatoris, sedisse debueras, ante aestimasse opus, metiri vires, ponderasse sapientiam, merita comparasse, sumtus computasse virtutum. Age ergo, puta tempus putationis adesse, si tamen meditationis praeiuit: si cor mouisti, mouenda iam lingua, mouenda est manus. Accingere gladio tuo, gladio spiritus, quod est verbum Dei: glorifica manum & brachium dextrum in facienda vindicta in nationibus, increpationibus in populis, in alligando Reges eorum in compedibus, & nobiles eorum in manicis ferreis. Si haec facis, honorificas ministerium tuum, & ministrum te. Non mediocris iste principatus, exturbare est hoc malas bestias a terminis tuis, quo greges tui securi in pascua educantur. Domabis lupos, sed ouibus non dominaberis: pascendas utique, non premendas suscepisti. Si bene consideraris quis sis, haec te oportere facere non ignoras: porro scienti & non facienti peccatum est tibi. Non est oblitus vbi legeris: seruus sciens voluntatem Domini, & non faciens digna, plagis vapulabit multis. Sic Prophetae, sic Apostoli fortitudinem tabant: fortes fuere in bello, non molles in sericis. Si filius es Apostolorum & Prophetarum, & tu face similiter. Vendica tibi nobile genus similibus moribus, quod non aliunde nobile, quam morum ingenuitate & fidei fortitudine fuit: per hanc vicerunt regna, operati sunt iustitiam, adepti sunt repromissiones. Hoc chirographum paternae tuae haereditatis quod tibi euoluimus, vbi inspicias portionem substantiae quae te contingit: induere fortitudinem & haereditasti, posside fidem, posside pietatem, posside sapientiam (sed sapientia sanctorum ipsa est timor Domini) & habes quod tuum est. Habes sine defraudatione integrum paternum fundum: preciosissimus fundus virtus est, bonus fundus humilitas, in quo omne aedificium spirituale constructum crescit in templum sanctum in Domino. Per hanc nonnulli possedere etiam portas inimicorum: quae enim virtutum aeque potest daemonum debellare superbiam, tyrannidem hominum? Caeterum cum omni indifferenter personae haec sit quaedam turris fortitudinis a facie inimici, nescio quo pacto tamen vis eius maior in maioribus, & in clarioribus clarior comprobatur. Nulla splendidior gemma in omni praecipue ornatu summi Pontificis, quo enim celsior caeteris, eo humilitate apparet illustrior & se ipso. Arguar forsitan, quod non satis primis explicitis partibus, in secundas stilus nescio quomodo excurrerit, describere inchoans qualem te oporteat esse, cum necdum quis sis plenius expressissem. Credo erubescens in summo positum apice videri hominem nudum, festinauit induere insignibus suis: absque his nempe eo deformior, quo illustrior pares. Nunquid potest abscondi civitatis supra montem positae desolatio? aut latere fumus lucernae extinctae super candelabrum? Simia in tecto? Rex fatuus in solio sedens? Et nunc audi canticum meum, & quidem minus suave, sed salutare. Monstruosa res gradus summus, & animus infimus: sedes prima, & vita ima: lingua magniloqua, & manus otiosa: sermo multus, & fructus nullus: vultus gravis, & actus levis: ingens auctoritas, & nutans stabilitas. Admoui speculum, foedus se in eo vultus agnoscat: tu tuum gaude dissimilem inuenisti. Inspice tamen & tu, ne forte etsi sit unde merito placeas tibi, etiam in quo debeas displicere non sit. Volo gloriari testimonio conscientiae; sed non minus ut eodem ipso humilieris. Rara vox, nihil mihi conscius sum: cautior in bonis ambulas, si & mala non lateant. Quamobrem, ut dixi, noveris te, ut inter angustias quae non desunt fruaris conscientiae bono: magis autem ut scias quid desit tibi. Nam cui non deest, omnia illi desunt, qui nil sibi deesse putat. Quid si summus Pontifex, sis? nunquid quia summus Pontifex, ideo summus? Infimum noris esse, si summum putas. Qui summus? qui addi non possit: graviter erras si te illum existimas, absit. Non tu de illis es, qui dignitates virtutes putant: tibi ante experta virtus quam dignitas fuit. Augustis relinquito illam sententiam, aliisque, qui divis coli honoribus non timuerunt: verbi gratia, Nabuchodonosor, Alexandro, Antiocho, Herodi. Tu vero considera non consummatione summum te dici, sed comparatione: nec me putes comparationem dicere meritorum, sed ministeriorum. Sic te existimet homo ut ministrum Christi, & quod absque praeiudicio cuiuspiam sanctitatis dixerim, summum plane inter ministros. Alias niti te ad summum velim, non putari summum, aut velle putari antequam sis. Nam quomodo proficis, si iam sufficis tibi? non sit proinde tibi aut pigrum vestigare quod desit, aut fateri quod desit verecundum: loquere & tu voce antecessoris tui: non quod iam acceperim, aut iam perfectus sim: & rursum, ego me non arbitror comprehendisse. Haec scientia sanctorum, haec longe ab illa quae inflat: hanc qui apponit, apponit & dolorem; sed dolorem hunc nemo unquam subterfugit. Est quippe medicinalis dolor, per quem stupor ille literalis animi duri & impoenitentis excluditur; & ideo sapiens qui dicere potuit: & dolor meus in conspectu meo semper. Nunc iam repetenda reliquiae, si quae sunt loci illius a quo paulo ante diuertimus: age indagemus adhuc diligentius quis sis, quam geras videlicet pro tempore personam in Ecclesia Dei. Quis es? Sacerdos magnus, summus Pontifex: Tu princeps Episcoporum, tu haeres Apostolorum, tu primatu Abel, gubernatu Noe, Patriarchatu Abraham, ordine Melchisedech, dignitate Aaron, auctoritate Moyses, iudicatu Samuel, poteßate Petrus, unctione Christus. Tu es cui claves traditae, cui oves creditae sunt: sunt quidem & alii caeli ianitores, & gregum pastores; sed tu tanto gloriosius, quanto & differentius utrumque prae caeteris nomen haereditasti. Habent illi sibi assignatos greges, singuli singulos: tibi universi crediti, uni unus. Nec modo ovium, sed & pastorum, tu unus omnium pastor. Unde id probem quaeris? ex verbo Domini. Cui enim non dico Episcoporum, sed etiam Apostolorum, sic absolute & indiscrete totae commissae sunt oves? Simeamus Petre, pasce oves meas. Quas? illius vel illius populos civitatis, aut regionis, aut certe regni? Oves meas, inquit, cui non plane non designasse aliquas, sed assignasse omnes: nihil excipitur, ubi distinguitur nihil. Et forte praesentes caeteri condiscipuli erant, cum committens uni, unitatem omnibus commendaret, in uno grege & uno pastore secundum illud: una est columba mea, formosa mea, perfecta mea. Ubi unitas, ibi perfectio; reliqui numeri perfectionem non habent, sed diuisionem recedentes ab unitate: inde est quod alii singuli singulas sortiti sunt plebes, scientes Sacramentum. Denique Iacobus, qui videbatur columna Ecclesiae, una contentus est Hierosolyma, Petro vniversitatem cedens: pulcre vero ibi positus est suscitare semen defuncti fratris, ubi occisus est ille; nam dictus est frater Domini. Porro cedente Domini fratre, quis se alter ingerat Petri prerogativae? ergo iuxta canones tuos, alii in partem sollicitudinis, tu in plenitudinem potestatis vocatus es. Aliorum potestas certis arctatur limitibus: tua extenditur & in ipsos, qui potestatem super alios acceperunt. Nonne si causa exiterit tu Episcopo coelum claudere, tu ipsum ab Episcopatu deponere, etiam & tradere Sathanae potes? Stat ergo inconcussum privilegium tuum tibi, tam in datis clavibus, quam in ovibus commendaris. Accipe aliud quod nihilo minus praerogativam confirmat tibi. Discipuli navigabant & Dominus apparebat in litore, quodque iucundius erat, in corpore rediviuo: sciens Petras quia Dominus est in mare se misit, & sic venit ad ipsum, aliis navigio pervenientibus. Quid istud? nempe signum singularis Pontificii Petri, per quod non navem unam, ut caeteri quisque suam, sed seculum ipsum suscepérat gubernandum. Mare enim seculum est, naves Ecclesiae. Inde est quod altera vice instar Domini gradiens super aquas, unicum se Christi vicarium designavit, qui non uni populo, sed cunctis praeesse deberet; quidem aquae multae, populi multi. Ita cum quisque caeterorum habeat suam, tibi vna commissa est grandissima navis, facta ex omnibus ipsa universalis Ecclesia toto orbe diffusa. En quis es, sed noli obliuisci etiam quid: nam & ego non sum oblitus id me promisisse repetiturum in opportunitate; quia oportune cum eo quis es, etiam quod ante eras, consideras. Quid dico eras? & nunc es: quid desinas intueri, quod non desisti esse? una sane consideratio quis fueris & quis sis: nam quis sis factus, altera. Non oportet ut ista exstruendat illam in scrutinio tui, es enim, ut dixi, adhuc quod eras: & non minus hoc es, quam quod factus es post, forte & magis. Denique illud natus es, mutatus hoc, non in hoc mutatus: non reiectum illud, sed istud adiectum. Tractemus utrumque simul: nam, ut praefatum me memini, collatae ex invicem ambae utiliores fient. Dixi supra consideranti quid sis, naturam occurrere qua es homo, nam homo natus es: porro, percunctanti quis, personae respondebit nomen, quod est Episcopus, quod quidem factus, non natus es. Quid tibi horum videtur ad putum esse tui, & ad te principalius pertinere, quod factus, an quod natus? nonne quod natus? Hoc ergo consulo consideres maxime, quod maxime es, hominem videlicet. quod natus es. Nec modo quid natus, sed & qualis natus oportet attendas, si non vis tuae considerationis fructu & utilitate fraudari. Tolle proinde nunc hereditaria haec perizomata ab initio maledicta; dirumpe velamen foliorum celantium ignominiam, non plagam curantium; dele fucum fugacis honoris huius, & malae coloratae nitorem gloriae: ut nude nudum consideres, quia nudus egressus es de utero matris tuae. Nunquid infulatus? nunquid micans gemmis, aut floridus sericis, aut coronatus pennis, aut suffarcinatus metallis? Si cuncta haec veluti nubes quosdam matutinales velociter transeuntes, & cito pertransituras dissipes & exsuffles a facie considerationis tuae; occurret tibi homo nudus, & pauper, & miser, & miserabilis, homo dolens quod homo sit, erubescens quod nudus sit, plorans quod natus sit, murmurans quod sit. Homo natus ad laborem, non ad honorem: homo natus de muliere, & ob hoc cum reatu, breui viuens tempore, ideoque cum metu repletus multis miseriis, & propterea cum fletu, & vere multis, quia corporis & animae simul. Quid enim calamitate vacat nascenti in peccato, fragili corpore, & mente sterili? vere ergo repletus, cui infirmitas corporis, & fatuitas cordis cumulatur, traduce sordis, mortis additione. Salubris copula, ut cogitans te summum Pontificem, attendas pariter vilissimum cinerem non fuisse, sed esse. Imitetur cogitatio naturam, imitetur & quod dignius est auctorem naturae, summa imaque conscios. Nonne natura in persona hominis vili limo vitae spiraculum colligavit? nonne auctor naturae in sui persona verbum limumque contemperavit? Ita tibi sume formam, tam de nostrae correctione originis, quam de sacramento redemptionis; ut altus sedens, non alta sapiens sis, sed humilia de te sentiens, humilibusque consentiens. Proinde si consideras quantus es, cogita etiam qualis, & maxime. Haec te sanec consideratio tenet in te, nec a te auolare finit, nec ambulare in magnis, neque in mirabilibus super te. In re consistito, non infra deiici, non attolli supra, non euadere in longius, non extendi in latius: tene medium si non vis perdere modum. Locus medius tutus est, medium sedes modi, & modus virtus. Omnem extra modum habitationem, sapiens exilium reputat. Propterea non est illi habitare in longo quod ultra modum sit, sed nec lato quidem quod extra sit; porro, nec in alto vel imo, quod alterum supra, alterum infra sit: denique & longitudo exterminium habere solet, & dilatatio scissuram, & altitudo ruinam, & profunditas absorptionem. Dico haec planius, ne putes ea loqui, quae Apostolus comprehendere hortatur cum omnibus sanctis, longitudinem, latitudinem, sublimitatem & profunditatem; quod alterius erit & disputationis & temporis. Nunc autem longum dico, cum sibi homo longiorem promittit vitam: latum, cum in superfluas animus distenditur curas: altum, cum de se plus praesumit: profundum, cum se plus deiicit. Qui ergo longa sibi metitur tempora, nonne vere ingreditur iter exterminii, transiens vitae terminos productiori sollicitudine? Inde est quod homines in praesenti a sese exules per oblivionem, in alia per inanem sollicitudinem migrant saecula, non profutura, imo nec futura. Similiter animus distinctus in multa, multis lacerabitur curis necesse est: nempe immoderata extensio extenuationem, & extenuatio nimia scissionem facit. Iam vero alta praesumptio, quid nisi ruinosa praecipitatio est? Legisti namque, ante ruinam exaltatur cor. Quid e regione nimiae pusillanimitatis deiectio, nisi desperata quaedam absorptio est? in hanc fortis non deiicietur; prudens longioris vitae non abducetur incerto; modestus moderabitur curas, temperabit a superfluis, non deerit necessariis. Porro iustus altiora se non praesumet, sed loquitur cum iusto: Si iustus fuero, non leuabo caput. Tu ergo in hac consideratione tui caute ambules, & tota aequitate versaris; ut nec plus vero tibi tribuas, nec plus iusto parcas. Porro plus vero tribuis, non modo arrogando tibi quod non habes bonum, sed & quod habes adscribendo: vigilanter discerne qualis ex te, & qualis sis dono Dei; & non sit in spiritu tuo dolus. Erit autem vbi fideliter partiens tua tibi, & quae sunt Dei, Deo sine fraude resignes. Ex te mala, bona a Domino esse persuasum tibi non ambigo. Sane inter considerandum qualis sis, etiam qualis fueris ad memoriam revocandum; conferenda posteriora prioribus: profecerisne in virtute, in sapientia, in intellectu, in suavitate morum; an ab his forte, quod absit, defeceris; patientior sis an impatientior solito; iracundior leniorve; insolentior an humilior; affabilior an austerior; exorabilior an difficilior; pusillior animo an magnanimior; serius magis an plusculum dissolutus; timoratior an fidentior quam oportet: quia latus tibi patet campus in hoc genere considerandi. Memoror ego pauca, veluti quaedam seminaria proferens, non tamen ipse inserens, sed dans semen serenti. Oporter innotescat tibi zelus tuus, clementia tua, discretio quoque moderatrix earundem virtutum: qualis videlicet in dandis iniuriis, qualis sis in vtroque prouidus: modi, loci, temporis observator. Prorsus consideranda tria haec in via virtutum harum, ne non sint virtutes si praeter haec reperiantur. Nempe eiusmodi virtutes, sed vsus facit: nam ex se indifferentes esse noscuntur. Tuum est aut abutendo & facere vitia: aut bene ordinateque vtendo virtutes. Solent discretionis oculo caligare, interimere loca, terminos occupare. Porro caliginis duae sunt causae; ira, & moles cerebrum enervat, illa praecipitat. Quomodo enim ab altero non perire clementiae, aut zeli rectitudo? Turbatus prae ira oculus, clementer nil intuetur: suffusus muliebri mollitie animi, rectum non videt. Non erit innocens, si aut punias, aut parcendum esset; aut parcas ei qui fuerat puniendus. In tribulationibus quoque qualem te inueneris, non dissimules: si constantem in ruis, condolentem in alienis, gaudentem regione peruersissimi, si in propriis deprehendaris fortasse impatiens, in alieno tamen compatiens sentiaris. Quid in prosperis? nihil est quod consideres? est vtique, si diligenter attendas quam rarus semper exiterit, qui non vel modice in prosperitate animum relaxauerit à sui custodia & disciplina: quoniam hoc incautis non fuit ad disciplinam, quod ignis ad ceram; quod solis radius ad niuem vel glaciem. Sapiens Dauid, sapiens Salomon fuit: sed blandientibus nimis secundis rebus, alter ex parte, alter ex toto defipuit. Magnus qui incidens in aduersa, non excidit vel parum à sapientia: nec minor cui praesens felicitas si arrisit, non irrisit. Quanquam facilius inueneris, qui sapientiam retinuerunt contraria sibi fortuna, quam qui propitia non perdiderunt. Praeferendus ille & magnus est, cui inter prospera saltem risus indecentior, aut sermo insolentior, aut immoderatior cura vestis vel corporis non irrepsit. Et si recte sapiens hortatur, sapientiam scribi in ocio: cauendum & in ocio otium est. Fugienda proinde ociositas, mater nugarum, nouerca virtutum. Inter seculares nugae, nugae sunt: in ore sacerdotis, blasphemiae: interdum tamen si incidant ferendae fortassis, referendae nunquam. Magis interueniendum cauté & prudenter nugacitati, prorumpendum sane in serium quid, quod non modo vtiliter, sed libenter audiant & supersedeant ociosis. Consecrasti os tuum Euangelio, talibus iam aperire illicitum, assuescere sacrilegum est. Labia sacerdotis, ait, custodiunt scientiam, & legem requirunt de ore eius, non nugas profecto vel fabulas. Verbum scurrile, quod faceti urbanive nomine colorant, non sufficit peregrinari ab ore; procul & ab aure relegandum: foede ad cachinnos moueris, foedius moues. Porro detrahere, aut detrahentem audire, quid horum damnabilius sit; non facile dixerim. De auaritia non est quod tuum fatigem intuitum, cum pecuniam tanquam paleam dicaris habere. Non prorsus, non est quod pro illa timeatur à iudiciis tuis: sed est quod non minus saepe, nec noxie minus, insidiari iudicantibus solet: de quo maxime quid in tua lateat conscientia, latere te nolim. Quid illud fit quaeris? acceptio personarum. Non parui te reum peccati existimes, si facies peccatorum sumis, & non potius causas iudicas meritorum. Est item vitium cuius si te immunem sentis, inter omnes quos noui ex his qui cathedras ascendunt; sedebis me iudice solitarius: quia veraciter singulariterque leuasti te supra te, iuxta Prophetam: Facilitas credulitatis haec est, cuius callidissimae vulpeculae, magnorum neminem comperi satis cauisse versutias. Inde eis ipsis pro nihilo irae multae, inde innocentium frequens addictio, inde praeiudicia in absentens. Gratulor autem tibi, nec enim assentationis apud te vereor incurrere notam, gratulor, iniquam, praesidere te vsque adhuc absque horum omnium querela multa, an & sine culpa tu videris. Nunc ad ea quae sub te sunt consideratio intendenda, at alterius principii hoc: siquidem tuis occupationibus sermo breuior, competentior est.
units.tr: Mindful of my promise, which has held me for some time now before you, best of men, Pope Eugene, I wish to release myself from it, or at least try. I would be ashamed of the delay if I were aware of any carelessness or disregard on my part. That is not the case. But, as you yourself know, we have fallen on a grievous time, which seems to have called a halt even to the living of life, let alone to study. The Lord, provoked by our sins, has seemingly judged the world before its time, in justice indeed, but forgetful of his mercy. He has not spared his people, nor his own name. Do not the nations say, "Where is their God?" It is no wonder that the sons of the Church and those who are counted by the Christian name have been cast down in the wilderness, or slain by the sword, or consumed by famine. Contention has been poured out upon the princes, and the Lord has made them wander in a pathless waste, and not on the way. Destruction and misery are in their paths; fear, grief and confusion fill the palaces of their kings. Why then are the feet of those who preach peace and announce good things held back? "We said, Peace, and there is no peace; we promised good things, and behold, turmoil." As if we had undertaken this work rashly or lightly! We have indeed run into it not as into something uncertain, but at your bidding, or rather through you, for God. Why then have we fasted, and he has not looked upon us; have we humbled our souls, and he has not known it? For in all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out: because in the meantime he still patiently hears sacrilegious voices and Egyptians blaspheming, since he cunningly led them out only to destroy them in the wilderness. And indeed, who does not know that the judgments of God are true? Yet this judgment is so deep an abyss that I seem to myself to be right in pronouncing blessed the one who was not offended by it. But how does human rashness dare to find fault with what it is utterly unable to grasp? Let us call to mind the heavenly judgments, which have been from the beginning of the world, if perhaps there may be some comfort. For someone once said: I have remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and I have been comforted. I am saying a thing unknown to no one, and by no one fully known. Indeed, the hearts of mortals are such that we know when it is not necessary, and in necessity we do not know. Moses, about to lead the people out of the land of Egypt, had promised them a better land: for when the people would follow him otherwise, who would have been content with a land merely wise? He led them out, but he did not bring them into the land he had promised. Nor is there any reason why the sad and unexpected outcome should be imputed to the leader's rashness. He did all things at the Lord's command, with the Lord working with him, and the Lord confirming the work with signs that followed. But that people, you will say, was stiff-necked, always contending against the Lord and against Moses his servant. Well, those were unbelieving and rebellious; but these, what of them? Ask them: why should I say what they themselves admit? I say this one thing: what could they accomplish who always turned back when they walked? And these too, throughout the whole way, did not turn back in heart to Egypt. If those fell and perished because of their iniquity, are we to wonder that these, doing the same things, suffered the same? But is the fall of those men against the promises of God? Then neither is the fall of these. For the promises of God never prejudice the justice of God. And hear another example: Benjamin sinned, and the other tribes girded themselves for vengeance, and not without the nod of God. Finally he himself appointed a leader for those about to fight, and so they fought, relying on their hand, which was stronger, and on a better cause; and what is greater than these, on the favour of God. But how terrible is God in his counsels over the sons of men! The avengers of the crime turned their backs to the criminals, and fewer to more. But they returned to the Lord, and the Lord to them: "Go up," he said, and they went up again; and again they were routed and confounded. Thus, with God first favouring them and then commanding, the just men joined a just battle and were defeated; but the less they prevailed in the battle, the more they were found superior in faith. What do you think those men would have done if, at my exhortation, they had gone up a second time and been defeated a second time? When they heard me urging them to repeat the journey a third time, to repeat the work in which they had already been frustrated once and then a second time, what would they have done? And yet the Israelites, not reckoning one or another frustration, prepare themselves a third time and prevail. But perhaps they will say: "How do we know that the word came forth from the Lord? What signs do you show us, that we should believe you?" I need not answer these very questions; my own modesty must be spared. Answer for me and for yourself, according to what you have heard and seen, or at least according to what God has inspired in you. But perhaps you wonder that I pursue these matters, having proposed something else. I do so not forgetting my purpose, but because I do not judge these things foreign to my purpose; indeed, my discourse is about Consideration, as to no one else, addressed to your dignity. And truly this is a great matter, and one needing no small consideration. For if great things ought to be considered by great men, to whom does this study belong as much as to you, who have no equal upon the earth? But you, according to the wisdom and power given you from above, will act in this matter; it is not for my humility to dictate to you that anything be done this way or that. It is enough to have intimated that something ought to be done, by which the Church may also be consoled, and the mouth of those who speak iniquity may be stopped. Let these few words be said by way of apology, so that your conscience may have from me whatever sort of excuse it has, whereby it may have me excused and you likewise; and if not before those who judge deeds by their outcomes, at least before yourself. A complete and perfect excuse for anyone is the testimony of his own conscience. For me it is of little account to be judged by those who call evil good and good evil, who put light for darkness and darkness for light. And if it must happen that one of two things comes about, I prefer that the murmuring of men be against us rather than against God. If he deigns to use me as a shield, I gladly receive into myself the slanderous tongues of detractors and the poisoned darts of blasphemers, so that they may not reach him. I do not refuse to be made inglorious, so that no assault is made upon the glory of God. Who will give me to glory in that voice: "Since for your sake I have borne reproach, confusion has covered my face"? It is glory for me to become a partaker of Christ, whose voice it is: the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me. Now let my pen return to its subject, and let my discourse proceed along its course in the things we have proposed. And first, consider what I mean by consideration itself. For I do not wish the word contemplation to be understood in every respect the same: the former pertains more to the certainty of things, the latter more to inquiry. In that sense contemplation may be defined as a true and certain gaze of the mind upon any matter, or a grasp of truth without doubt. Consideration, however, is a thought intent upon investigating, or an intensity of mind tracking down the truth; although both are commonly used interchangeably. As for the fruit of consideration, I think there are four things that present themselves to you for consideration: you, what is under you, what is around you, and what is above you. Let your consideration begin with yourself, lest you stretch yourself in vain toward other things while neglecting yourself. What does it profit you to gain the whole world, if you lose yourself? And if you are wise, you lack wisdom if you are not wise to yourself. How much so? As I have judged, entirely. You may know all mysteries, you may know the breadth of the earth, the height of heaven, the depths of the sea; if you do not know yourself, you will be like one building without a foundation, making a ruin and not a structure. Whatever you build outside yourself will be like heaped-up dust exposed to the winds. Therefore one who is not wise to himself is not wise; the one wise to himself will be wise, and he will drink from the well of his own cistern first himself. Let your consideration therefore begin from yourself, and not only begin there, but also end in yourself: wherever it wanders, let it be led back to you with the fruit of salvation; you first to yourself, you last. Take the example of the supreme Father of all, who both sends forth and keeps his Word. Let your word, your consideration, be such that if it goes forth it does not depart; let it go forward so that it does not go out; let it go out so that it does not abandon. In the acquiring of salvation, no one is more closely related to you than your mother's only son; and against your own salvation think nothing. I have said "against" less than I ought to have said "beyond." Whatever presents itself to consideration that does not in some way pertain to your own salvation is to be rejected. And this consideration of yourself is divided into three: if you consider what, who, or what sort of person you are: what you are by nature, who you are in your person, what sort you are in your morals. What? For example, a man. Who? The Pope, or the supreme Pontiff. What sort? Kind, gentle, or whatever is of that kind. Although that first inquiry is more prophetic than apostolic, it is nonetheless contained in the definition of man, whom they call a rational mortal animal; if you like, you may look at this more carefully. There is nothing in it that opposes your profession or your dignity; there is indeed something that can bring salvation. For when one considers these two things together, rational and mortal, there comes from this the fruit that the mortal in you humbles the rational, and again the rational strengthens the mortal; neither of which will be neglected by a careful man. If the present place still requires anything further to be considered, it will be treated below, and perhaps more usefully from the comparison of the parts. Now it must be noted who you are and from what you have been made. Although, as I said, I think I should pass over from what I have mentioned, this I say, which is better left to your own recognition: it is unworthy of you to act in a way that is less than perfect, having undertaken so great a perfection. Why should you not blush to be found least among the great, when you remember you once stood great among the least? You have not forgotten your first profession; it has not slipped from your mind, though it has been taken from your hand, nor even from its effect. It will not be useless for you to keep before your eyes, at each of your commands and decisions, what you once were. This consideration makes you a despiser of honour, even of honour itself. And this is a great thing. Let it not depart from your breast; let it be a shield for you, that arrow: man, when he was in honour, did not understand. Speak then to yourself: "I was cast out in the house of my God. What is this, that one so poor and abject should be lifted above nations and kingdoms? Who am I, or what is the house of my father, that I should sit higher and more exalted?" Surely he who said to me, Friend, go up higher, I trust is a friend; if I am found less so, it is not well. He who lifted up can also cast down. Late the complaint: since you lifted me up, you dashed me down. High station should not flatter; greater is its anxiety. It sharpens danger, and it tests the friend. Let us gird ourselves for this, if we do not wish at last to hold the lowest place with shame. We cannot ignore the deeds of superiors, but in every way we must pay attention to what it means. For I do not think it is for dominion: when the Prophet was similarly lifted up, he heard: to pluck up, and to break down, and to destroy, and to scatter, and to build, and to plant. What of these sounds prosperous? Rather, a spiritual labour is expressed in a certain rustic guise of sweat. And so let us also, if we think much of ourselves, reckon that we have been given a ministry, not a dominion. I am not a greater Prophet, even if perhaps in power; but there is no comparison of merits. Say this to yourself, and teach yourself who teach others: consider yourself as one of the Prophets. Is this not enough for you? It is more than enough; but by the grace of God you are what you are. What then? Be a prophet. Is it more than a prophet? If you are wise you will be content with the measure God has measured out to you; for whatever is beyond it is from evil. Learn from the Prophetic example to preside, not so much to command as to labour at what the time requires: learn that you need a hoe, not a sceptre, to do the work of a prophet. And indeed he went up not to reign but to root out. Do you think you too will find something to labour at in the field of your Lord? Very much so. Surely the Prophet could not clean the whole field at once; he left something for his sons the Apostles to do; your parents left something for you. But neither will you be sufficient for everything; you will certainly leave something to your successor, and he to others, and others to others, unto the end. At the eleventh hour, finally, the idle labourers are rebuked and sent into the vineyard. Your predecessors the Apostles heard, because the harvest is indeed great, but the labourers few. Claim for yourself the paternal inheritance, for if you are a son, and an heir, to prove your inheritance, awake to your care and do not grow torpid in idleness, lest it be said to you as well: why do you stand here idle all the day? Much less should you be found either dissolved in delights or lying back in pomp. The tablets of the testator assign you none of these things. But what do they assign? If you are content with their tenor, you will inherit care and labour rather than glory and riches. The chair flatters you; it is a watchtower. From there at last you oversee, and in the name of bishop there sounds to you not dominion but office. Why should you not be placed on high, from which you may survey everything, since you have been appointed a watchman over all things? Indeed, that outlook produces readiness for battle, not idleness; for why should one wish to glory where one may not be idle? And there is no room for idleness where the earnest anxiety of all the Churches presses. For what else did the holy Apostle leave you? What I have, he says, I give to you. What is that? I know only one thing: "It is not silver or gold," since he himself says: silver and gold I do not have. If it happens that you have them, use them as you please, but as the occasion requires; thus you will use them as though not using them. In themselves (as far as the good of the soul is concerned) they are neither good nor evil; yet their good use is good, their abuse is evil; anxiety is worse, gain more shameful. Even if you claim these things by some other reason, you cannot claim them by apostolic right: for he could not give you what he did not have; what he had he gave: anxiety, as I have said, over the Churches. Did he give dominion? Hear him: not lording it, he says, over the clergy, but being examples to the flock. And lest you think this said only in humility and not also in truth, the voice of the Lord in the Gospel is: The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors; and he adds, but you are not so. It is plain that dominion is forbidden to the Apostles; go on then and dare to claim either the Apostolate as dominion or dominion as Apostolic; you are plainly forbidden the one by the other. If you wish to have both in like manner, you will lose both. Otherwise do not think yourself excepted from the number of those of whom God complains thus: They have reigned, but not by me; they have become princes, and I have not known them. Now if it pleases you to reign without God, you have glory, but not before God; but if we hold to what is forbidden, let us hear the edict. Let the greater among you, he says, become as the less; and let the one who is first be as one who serves. This is the Apostolic form: dominion is forbidden, service is enjoined. This is also commended by the example of the lawgiver himself, who, following on, adds: but I am among you as one who serves. Who now would think himself inglorious under this title, by which the Lord of glory first marked himself out? Rightly does Paul glory in it, saying: they are ministers of Christ, and I am one; and he adds, as if I spoke less wisely, I more in labours, more abundantly in prisons, beyond measure in stripes, often in deaths. O splendid ministry! What is more glorious than this principate? If you must glory, the form of the saints is set before you, the glory of the Apostles is proposed. Does that seem to you a small thing? Who will grant me to become like them in the glory of the saints? The Prophet cries out: But to me, O God, your friends are exceedingly honoured; their principate is exceedingly strengthened. The Apostle cries out: But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. This is the glory I wish you always to boast in, the best kind of glory, which the Apostles and the Prophets chose for you and left to you. Acknowledge your inheritance in the cross of Christ, in many labours. Happy is the one who could say, I have laboured more than all of them. It is glory, but nothing in it is empty, nothing soft, nothing lying back. If labour frightens, reward invites: for each one will receive his wage according to his labour. And if he laboured more than all of them, yet he did not labour through the whole, and there is still room. Go out into the field of your Lord, and consider carefully how many thorns and thistles from the old curse remain: go out, I say, into the world (for the world is the field, and it has been entrusted to you), go out into it not as lord but as steward, to see and to take care, for from it you must render an account. Go out, I would say, with some of the steps of an attentive care and an anxious intention; for those who were sent to go into all the world did not travel around in bodily presence, but in the foresight of the mind. And you, lift up some eyes of your consideration, and see whether the regions are not more fit for fire than white for harvest. For many of the crops you had thought you saw, when carefully examined, will appear rather as brambles; indeed not even brambles, but aged and gnarled trees, not fruit-bearing, except perhaps of acorns or pods that pigs eat. How long will they occupy the land? If you go out and see these things, will you not be ashamed to lie idle with the axe? Will you not be ashamed to have taken up the apostolic sickle for no cause? Into this field once went out the Patriarch Isaac, when Rebekah first met him, and, as Scripture has it, he had gone out to meditate. He went out to meditate; you must go out to root out. Meditation ought already to have gone before you; the time for doing is at hand. If you now begin to hesitate, that is indeed too late. Before, according to the counsel of the Saviour, you ought to have sat down, you ought to have weighed the work beforehand, measured your strength, pondered your wisdom, compared your merits, computed the cost of your virtues. Come then, suppose the time for pruning is at hand; yet if you have anticipated meditation: if you have moved your heart, now the tongue must be moved, and the hand must be moved. Gird yourself with your sword, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; glorify your hand and your right arm in executing vengeance upon the nations, rebukes upon the peoples, in binding their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles. If you do these things, you honour your ministry and make yourself a minister. This is no mean principate: to drive these evil beasts from your borders, so that your flocks may be led out securely to pasture. You will tame wolves, but you will not lord it over the sheep: you have undertaken to feed them, not to press them down. If you consider well who you are, you do not fail to know that you ought to do these things: moreover, to one who knows and does not do, it is sin. Do not forget where you have read: the servant who knows the will of his master and does not do what is worthy will be beaten with many stripes. So the Prophets, so the Apostles, cultivated fortitude: they were strong in war, not soft in silks. If you are a son of the Apostles and the Prophets, do likewise. Claim for yourself a noble lineage with similar morals, which was noble for no other reason than the nobility of character and the strength of faith: through this they conquered kingdoms, wrought justice, obtained the promises. This document of your paternal inheritance, which we have unrolled for you, when you look upon the portion of substance that falls to you: put on strength, and you have inherited; possess faith, possess piety, possess wisdom (but the wisdom of the saints is itself the fear of the Lord), and you have what is yours. You have without fraud the whole paternal estate: the most precious estate is virtue, the good estate is humility, in which every spiritual building, constructed, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Through this some have possessed even the gates of their enemies. For what can equally subdue the pride of demons and the tyranny of men as virtue? Moreover, while this is a kind of tower of strength against the face of the enemy for every person indifferently, somehow its power is greater in the greater, and it is shown brighter in the more illustrious. No gem is more splendid in the whole adornment of the supreme Pontiff, for the higher he is above others, the more illustrious he appears by humility, even above himself. I may perhaps be taken to task that, not having sufficiently explained the first parts, my style has somehow run on into the second, beginning to describe what sort of person you ought to be, when I had not yet expressed more fully who you are. I believe that, blushing to be seen as a naked man placed on the summit, he hastened to put on his insignia: without them he is the more deformed, the more he is set in the light. Can the desolation of a city set on a mountain be hidden? Or can the smoke of an extinguished lamp escape notice above the candlestick? A monkey on a roof? A foolish king sitting on a throne? And now hear my song, which is indeed less sweet, but wholesome. A monstrous thing: the highest step and a lowest soul; the first seat and the lowest life; a tongue loud with great words and a hand idle; much talk and no fruit; a grave countenance and light deeds; immense authority and a wavering stability. I have held up a mirror; let your face see its ugliness in it. You have found your own dissimilar, and rejoice in it. Look carefully at yourself too, lest perhaps, although there may be something for which you may rightly please yourself, there may be nothing in which you ought to be displeased. I wish you to glory in the testimony of your conscience, but not less so that you may be humbled by that same testimony. A rare voice is: I am conscious of nothing against myself; you walk more cautiously in good things if evil things are not also hidden. Therefore, as I have said, know yourself, so that among the straits which are not lacking you may enjoy the good of conscience, and still more so that you may know what is lacking in you. For to one who lacks nothing, everything is lacking, who thinks nothing is lacking to himself. What if you are the supreme Pontiff? Is it because you are supreme Pontiff that you are supreme? Know that you are the lowest, if you think yourself highest. Who is the highest? One to whom nothing can be added. You greatly err if you count yourself such: far be it. You are not among those who think dignities are virtues; for in you virtue was tested before dignity. Leave that opinion to the Augusti, and to others who did not fear to be honoured with divine honours: for example, Nebuchadnezzar, Alexander, Antiochus, Herod. But you, consider that you are called highest not by completeness but by comparison; and do not think I am speaking of comparison of merits, but of ministries. Let a man so reckon you as a minister of Christ; and, without prejudice to anyone's holiness, I may say that you are plainly the highest among ministers. Otherwise I would wish you to strive toward the highest, not to be thought highest, or to wish to be thought so before you are. For how do you make progress, if you already suffice for yourself? Let it not be sluggish for you to search out what is lacking, nor shameful to confess what is lacking. Speak also in the voice of your predecessor: not that I have already received, or am already perfect; and again, I do not consider that I have grasped it. This is the knowledge of the saints, this is far from that which puffs up; whoever applies this knowledge applies also sorrow; but no one ever escapes this sorrow. It is a medicinal sorrow, by which that stupor of a hard and unrepentant mind, which is literal, is shut out; and therefore the wise man who could say: and my sorrow is always before my eyes. Now the remainder of that place from which we turned aside a little before must be taken up again, if any remains: come, let us inquire yet more carefully who you are, and what person you bear for the time being in the Church of God. Who are you? The great priest, the supreme Pontiff: you the prince of bishops, you the heir of the Apostles; you in primacy like Abel, in governance like Noah, in patriarchate like Abraham, in order like Melchizedek, in dignity like Aaron, in authority like Moses, in judgment like Samuel, in power like Peter, in anointing like Christ. You are the one to whom the keys have been delivered, to whom the sheep have been entrusted. There are indeed others who are gatekeepers of heaven and shepherds of flocks; but you have inherited a name so much more glorious, and so much more distinct above all others, as you are over both. Those others have flocks assigned to them, each one his own: to you all have been entrusted, to one the one. Not only of sheep but also of shepherds, you alone are shepherd of all. Do you ask how I prove this? From the word of the Lord. For to whom, I do not say of bishops, but even of Apostles, have all the sheep been committed so absolutely and without distinction? Simon, Peter, feed my sheep. Which ones? The peoples of this or that city, or region, or certainly of this or that kingdom? My sheep, he says, to whom he has not plainly designated some, but has assigned all: nothing is excepted where nothing is distinguished. And perhaps the other fellow disciples were present when, committing it to one, he commended unity to all, in one flock and one shepherd, according to that saying: one is my dove, my beautiful one, my perfect one. Where there is unity, there is perfection; the other numbers do not have perfection but division, departing from unity. Hence it is that the others each received their own individual peoples, knowing the sacrament. Finally James, who seemed to be a pillar of the Church, was content with Jerusalem alone, yielding the whole to Peter: and indeed he was fittingly placed there to raise up seed for his dead brother, where he was slain; for he was called the brother of the Lord. But, the brother of the Lord having yielded, who else would thrust himself upon the prerogative of Peter? Therefore, according to your canons, others have been called to a share of the care, but you to the fullness of power. The power of others is confined within fixed limits; yours extends even to those who have received power over others. Is it not so that if there is cause, you may close heaven to a bishop, depose him from the episcopate, and even hand him over to Satan? Your privilege therefore stands unshaken for you, as much in the keys given as in the sheep committed to you. Take another instance which equally confirms your prerogative. The disciples were sailing, and the Lord appeared on the shore, and, what was more joyful, in a risen body: and Peter, knowing that it was the Lord, threw himself into the sea, and so came to him, while the others arrived by boat. What is this? Surely a sign of the singular pontificate of Peter, by which he had undertaken to govern not one ship, as each of the others his own, but the world itself. For the sea is the world, the ships are the Churches. Hence it is that another time, walking like the Lord upon the waters, he marked himself out as the unique vicar of Christ, who ought to preside not over one people but over all: truly the waters are many, the peoples are many. Thus, while each of the others has his own, to you has been committed one very great ship, made of all, the universal Church itself, spread through the whole world. Behold who you are; but take care not to forget also what you were: for I too have not forgotten that I promised to take this up again at the proper time; because, when you consider in season who you are, you also consider what you were before. Why do I say "were"? You are even now: why should you look at what you have not ceased to be? Surely one consideration is who you have been and who you are; another is who you have become. It is not necessary that the one be built up in the scrutiny of the other; for you are, as I have said, still what you were, and this is no less than what you became afterward, perhaps even more. Finally, you were born that, and changed into this, not changed out of that: that was not rejected, but this was added to it. Let us treat both together; for, as I recall I have said before, each will be more useful when compared with the other. I said above that when you consider what you are, the nature in which you are a man presents itself: for you were born a man. Again, when you inquire who you are, the name of your office will answer, which is bishop, which you have indeed become, not been born. Which of these seems to you to pertain more to the true core of yourself, and more essentially to you: that you were made, or that you were born? Is it not that you were born? I therefore advise you to consider above all what you most are, namely a man: what you were born. Nor should you attend merely to what you were born, but also to what sort you were born, if you do not wish to be defrauded of the fruit and usefulness of your consideration. Therefore take away now those hereditary loincloths, cursed from the beginning; break the veil of leaves that hides shame, which does not cure the wound; wipe away the paint of this fleeting honour and the gloss of a bad, coloured glory; so that you may consider the naked as naked, because you came forth naked from the womb of your mother. Are you clothed in mitres? Are you glittering with gems, or flowery with silks, or crowned with feathers, or stuffed with metals? If you quickly dispel and blow away all these things, like morning clouds passing swiftly and soon to pass away, from the face of your consideration: there will meet you a man naked, and poor, and wretched, and pitiable, a man grieving that he is a man, blushing that he is naked, weeping that he was born, complaining that he is. A man born for labour, not for honour; a man born of a woman, and therefore with guilt, living a short time, and therefore filled with fear, full of many miseries, and therefore with weeping, and truly with many, because of body and soul together. For what is free of calamity for one born in sin, with a fragile body and a barren mind? Truly, then, he is filled, to whom bodily weakness and foolishness of heart are heaped up, with the stain of his origin, and the addition of death. Let it be a wholesome union: that, thinking of yourself as supreme Pontiff, you also attend to the fact that most vile ashes were not only once, but still are. Let thought imitate nature, let it imitate also, what is more worthy, the author of nature, aware of the highest and the lowest. Did not nature, in the person of man, bind the breath of life into vile clay? Did not the author of nature, in his own person, mingle Word and clay? So take for yourself the form, both from the correction of our origin and from the sacrament of redemption; so that, seated high, you may be not high in wisdom, but thinking humbly of yourself, and agreeing with the humble. Therefore, if you consider how great you are, think also of what sort you are, and most of all. This consideration holds you within yourself, and does not allow you to fly away from yourself, nor to walk in great things, nor in wonders above you. Stand in the thing; do not be cast down below, do not be lifted up above; do not escape into what is too long, do not be spread out into what is too wide: hold the middle, if you do not wish to lose measure. The middle place is safe; the middle is the seat of measure, and measure is virtue. The wise man counts every dwelling outside measure as exile. Therefore it is not for him to dwell in what is too long beyond measure, nor in what is too broad that lies outside; nor in the high or the low, one above, the other below: finally, length tends to have exile, breadth tends to have rent, height ruin, and depth absorption. I say these things more plainly, lest you think I speak of those things which the Apostle exhorts us to comprehend with all the saints: length, breadth, height and depth; that will belong to another discussion and another time. But now I say long when a man promises himself a longer life; broad, when the mind is stretched out into superfluous cares; high, when one presumes more of himself; deep, when one casts himself down more. He who measures out long times for himself, does he not truly enter upon the road of exile, passing the limits of life with a more prolonged anxiety? Hence it is that men in the present migrate away from themselves into exile through forgetfulness, and in another life through empty anxiety, into ages that will not profit, indeed will not be. Similarly, a mind divided into many things must necessarily be torn by many cares: for immoderate extension makes for thinness, and excessive thinness makes for rending. Now, what is high presumption but a ruinous precipitation? For you have read: before ruin the heart is exalted. And what, on the opposite side of excessive pusillanimity, is the casting down, but a certain desperate absorption? The strong man will not be cast into this; the prudent man will not be drawn away by the uncertainty of a longer life; the modest man will moderate his cares, will restrain himself from superfluities, and will not lack necessities. Moreover, the just man will not presume to be higher, but speaks with the just: If I shall be just, I will not lift up my head. Therefore you, in this consideration of yourself, walk cautiously, and conduct yourself in all fairness; so that you neither attribute to yourself more than is true, nor spare yourself more than is just. But if you attribute more than is true, you do so not only by arrogating to yourself a good you do not have, but also by ascribing to yourself what you do have: diligently discern what is from you, and what is your gift from God; and let there be no deceit in your spirit. There will then be a time when, faithfully dividing what is yours and what is God's, you give back to God, without fraud, what is his. That evils are from you and goods from the Lord, I do not doubt you are persuaded. Indeed, in considering what sort you are, you must also call to mind what sort you once were: compare the later with the earlier; whether you have advanced in virtue, in wisdom, in understanding, in sweetness of manners; or whether perhaps, which God forbid, you have fallen away from these; whether you are more patient or less patient than usual; more angry or gentler; more insolent or humbler; more affable or more austere; more easily entreated or more difficult; smaller in spirit or greater in soul; more serious, or somewhat more loose; more fearful or more confident than is right. For a broad field is open to you in this kind of consideration. I recall a few things, offering them as certain seeds, not inserting them myself, but giving the seed to the sower. Let your zeal be made known to you, your clemency, and likewise the discretion that moderates those same virtues: what sort you are, namely, in giving injuries, what sort you are in each, watchful of measure, place and time. Certainly these three things must be considered on the road of these virtues, lest they cease to be virtues if they are found without them. These virtues are of this kind, but use makes them what they are: for they are known to be indifferent in themselves. It is for you, by abusing them, to make them vices, or by using them well and in order, to make them virtues. They are wont to be dimmed for the eye of discretion, to destroy places, to occupy boundaries. Now there are two causes of this darkness: anger, and a mass that enervates the brain; the former precipitates. For how is it that the rectitude of clemency or of zeal does not perish through the other? An eye troubled by anger sees nothing with clemency; one suffused with the womanly softness of the mind does not see what is right. He will not be blameless if he punishes when he should have spared, or spares one who was to be punished. In tribulations too, do not hide what sort you have found yourself: if you are constant in your own ruins, sympathetic in the misfortunes of others, rejoicing in the ruin of the most perverse; if you are perhaps found impatient in your own affairs, yet perceived to be compassionate in another's. What of prosperity? Is there nothing to consider? There is indeed, if you carefully attend to how rare it has always been that anyone, in prosperity, has not at least slightly relaxed his mind from its guard and discipline; for to the incautious prosperity has been no more a discipline than fire is to wax, or a ray of the sun to snow or ice. The wise David, the wise Solomon, were wise; but when prosperity flattered them too much, the one partly, the other wholly, became foolish. Great is he who, falling into adversity, has not lost even a little of wisdom; and no less great is he whom present happiness, when it smiled on him, did not make mock of wisdom. Yet you will more easily find those who kept their wisdom under adverse fortune than those who did not lose it under favourable fortune. That man is to be preferred and is great, in whose prosperity at least an indecent laughter, or an insolent speech, or an immoderate care for dress or body has not crept in. And if the wise man rightly advises that wisdom is to be written in leisure, then in leisure too one must beware of idleness. Idleness, therefore, is to be fled, the mother of trifles, the stepmother of virtues. Among secular people trifles are trifles; in the mouth of a priest they are blasphemies: yet at times, if they occur, they may perhaps be borne, but never repeated. Trifling is to be met with caution and prudence, and one must indeed break forth into something serious, which they will hear not only usefully but gladly, and which will make idle talkers give way. You have consecrated your mouth to the Gospel; to open it to such things is unlawful, to grow accustomed to them is sacrilegious. The lips of the priest, he says, keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, not, surely, trifles or fables. A scurrilous word, which people colour with the names of wit or urbanity, is not enough to be kept away from the mouth alone; it must be banished far from the ear as well: you are foully moved to laughter, and more foully you move others. Now, to detract, or to listen to one who detracts, which of these is more damnable, I would not easily say. Concerning avarice there is no need for me to weary your gaze, since you are said to hold money as if it were chaff. Certainly, there is no need to fear it in your judgments on its account: but there is something that is no less often, and no less harmfully, wont to lie in wait for judges; and about this, I would not want you to be unaware of what lies hidden in your conscience. Do you ask what this is? The acceptance of persons. Do not think yourself a small offender in sin if you take the faces of sinners, and do not rather judge the causes of merits. There is also another vice, of which if you feel yourself free, among all whom I have known of those who ascend the chairs, you will sit, with me as judge, alone: because truly and singularly you have lifted yourself above yourself, according to the Prophet. This is the facility of credulity, whose most crafty foxes I have found that none of the great have sufficiently guarded against their wiles. Hence many angers arise for them without reason; hence the frequent condemnation of the innocent; hence prejudgments against the absent. I congratulate you, however, for I do not fear to incur the mark of flattery in your regard: I congratulate you that, up to now, you appear to preside, without the many complaints of all these things, and whether also without fault. Now, what lies under you is to be the object of consideration, but that is another beginning; for my discourse should be briefer, and more suited to your occupations.

units.la: LIBER TERTIVS.
units.tr: Book Three.

units.la: FInis superioris libri huic principium ponit: itaque iuxta promissum illius, consideranda quae sub te sunt. Quaenam sint illa, non est quod à me quaerendum putes Sacerdotum Optime Eugeni, rectius fortasse quae non sint, quaeras. Orbe excundum ei, qui forte volet explorare, quae non ad tuam pertinent curam. Parentes tui destinati sunt non aliquas regiones, sed ipsum debellaturi orbem: ite in orbem vniuersum, dictum est illis. Ipsi vero videntes tunicas, emere gladios, ignitum eloquium, & spiritum vehementem, arma potentia Deo. Quo non peruenerunt victores incliti, filii excussorum? quo non sagittae potentium acutae cum carbonibus desolatoriis? Et quidem in omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum, & in fines orbis terrae verba eorum. Penetrabant & incendebant verba illa intensa igni, quem Dominus misit in terram: occumbebant strenuissimi bellatores, sed non succumbebant, triumphabant & mortui. Nimis confortatus est principatus eorum, constituti sunt Principes super omnem terram: eis tu successisti in hereditatem, ita tu heres, & orbis hereditas. At quatenus haec portio te contingit, aut contigerit illos; id sobria consideratione pensandum. Non enim per omnem reor modum, sed sane quodam tenus: vt mihi videtur, dispensatio tibi super illum credita est, non data possessio: si pergis vsurpare & hanc, contradicit tibi quae dicit: meum est orbis terrae & plenitudo eius. Non tu ille de quo Propheta: & erit omnis terra possessio eius. Christus hic est, qui possessionem sibi vendicat & iure creationis, & merito redemptionis, & dono patris. Cui enim alteri dictum est: postula à me, & dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terrae? Possessionem & Dominium cede hinc, tu curam illius habe: pars tua haec, vltra ne extendas manum. Quid inquis? non negas praeesse, & dominari vetas? plane sic: quasi non bene praesit, qui praeest in sollicitudine. Nunquid & villa, villico; & paruus Dominus subiectus est paedagogo? Nec tamen villae illae, nec is Domini Dominus est: ita & tu praesis, vt prouideas, vt consulas, vt procures, vt serues. Praesis vt prosis, praesis vt fidelis seruus & prudens, quem constituit Dominus super familiam suam. Ad quid? vt des illis escam in tempore, hoc est, vt dispenses, non imperes. Hoc fac, & dominari ne affectes hominem homo, vt non dominetur tui omnis iniustitia. At satis superque id intimandum supra, cum quis sis disputaretur: addo tamen & hoc, nam nullum tibi venenum, nullum gladium plus formido, quam libidinem dominandi. Certe vt multum tibi tribuas, si multum deceptus non es; nil te existimas plus accepisse à magnis Apostolis. Recordare nunc vocis illius: sapientibus & insipientibus debitor sum. Et si non indebitam tibi ipsam censes, hoc quoque simul memento; debitoris molestum nomen, seruienti potius, quam dominanti congruere. Seruus in Euangelio audit, quantum debes Domino meo? Ergo si te agnoscis sapientibus & insipientibus non dominatorem, sed debitorem, curandum summopere tibi & tota vigilantia considerandum, quomodo & qui non sapiunt sapiant, & qui sapiunt non desipiant, & qui desi-puere puerè resipiscant. At nullum genus insipientiæ, infidelitate (vt sic loquar) insipientius: ergo & infidelib. debitores, Iudæis, Græcis & Gentibus. Interest proinde tua dare operâ quam possis, vt incredu li conuertantur ad fidem, conuersi non auertantur, auersi reuertantur: porro peruersi ordinétur ad restitudinem, subuersi ad veritatem reuocentur, subuersores inuictis rationibus conuincantur, vt vel emendentur ipsi si fieri potest, vel si non, perdant auctoritate facultatemq; alios subuertendi. Non omnino & ab hoc insipientium genere pessimo, tibi dissimulandum: dico aut hæreticos, schismaticosque; nam hi sunt subuersi & subuersores; canes ad scissionem, vulpes ad fraudem. Erunt, inquam, huiusmodi maxime tuo studio, aut corrigendi ne pereant, aut ne perimant coercendi. Esto de Iudæis excusat te Apostolus: habent terminum suum, qui præueniri non poterit, plenitudinem gentium prius omnium.
units.tr: The end of the previous book provides the starting point for this one. So, as I promised, I must consider what lies under your authority. What those things are, you need not ask me, excellent Eugenius, priest. It would perhaps be better to ask what is not under your authority. Let whoever wants to investigate what does not belong to your care go out into the world. Your forefathers were appointed not to some regions but to conquer the whole world itself: go into all the world, they were told. And they, seeing their tunics, bought swords, a burning word, and a mighty spirit, weapons powerful through God. Where did those famous victors, the sons of those who shook the world, not reach? Where did the sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of desolation, not go? Indeed their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Those fiery words pierced and burned, the fire which the Lord sent upon the earth. The most valiant warriors fell, but were not overcome; they triumphed even in death. Their rule was greatly strengthened; princes were set up over all the earth. You have succeeded them in the inheritance; so you are their heir, and the world is your inheritance. But how far this portion belongs to you, or belonged to them, must be weighed with sober judgment. I do not think it applies in every way, but only to a certain extent. As it seems to me, a stewardship has been entrusted to you over that inheritance, not a possession given to you. If you go on to claim this too, what He says contradicts you: the world is mine, and the fullness thereof. You are not He of whom the Prophet speaks: and all the earth shall be his possession. Christ is the one who claims possession for himself, by right of creation, by the merit of redemption, and by the gift of the Father. For to whom else was it said: ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession? Leave possession and dominion here; take up the care of it. This part is yours; do not stretch out your hand any further. What do you say? You do not deny that you preside, and you forbid lording it over others? Quite so. He presides well who presides in care. Is not the farm entrusted to the farm-steward, and the little lord subject to the tutor? Yet neither those farms nor the lord of the house are his. So you preside in the sense that you foresee, consult, provide, and preserve. You preside to serve, you preside as the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord has set over his household. For what purpose? So that you give them food in due season. That is, you are to dispense, not to command. Do this, and do not aspire to lord it over men as man, so that every injustice does not lord it over you. But this has already been sufficiently pointed out above, when we discussed who you are. Still, I add this as well, for I fear no poison or sword in you more than the lust of domination. Indeed, if you have not been greatly deceived, you attribute much to yourself; you think you have received nothing less than the great Apostles did. Now recall that saying: I am a debtor both to the wise and to the unwise. And if you do not think this debt is undue, remember this too: the name of debtor is burdensome, and better suits one who serves than one who rules. In the Gospel the servant hears: How much do you owe my lord? So if you acknowledge that you are a debtor, not a ruler, to the wise and the unwise, then you must take great care and consider with all vigilance how those who are unwise may become wise, and those who are wise may not become foolish, and those who have played the fool may come back to their senses. But no kind of folly is more foolish than unbelief, so you are also a debtor to the unbelieving: to Jews, Greeks, and Gentiles. It is therefore your concern to do all you can so that the unbelieving may be turned to the faith, the converted not turned away, the turned away brought back; that the perverse may be set right, the subverted called back to the truth; and that subverters may be convicted by unanswerable arguments, so that either they themselves may be corrected, if that is possible, or, if not, they may lose the authority and the means to subvert others. Nor should you altogether overlook that worst kind of fools: I mean heretics and schismatics. For these are both subverted and subverters, dogs for tearing apart, foxes for deceit. Such people, I say, will need your greatest effort: either to correct them lest they perish, or to restrain them lest they destroy others. As for the Jews, the Apostle excuses you: they have their limit, which cannot be anticipated, the fullness of all the Gentiles first.

units.la: Sed de ipsis Gentibus quid respondes? imo quid tua consideratio respondet tibi percunctanti sic? Quid visum est Patribus ponere metam Euangelio? verbum suspendere fidei donec infidelitas durat? qua ratione putamus substitit velociter currens sermo? quis primus inhibuit hūc salutarem cursum? & illis causa forte quam nescimus, aut necessitas potuit obstitisse.
