Nobis quæ dissimulandi ratio est? qua fiducia, qua conscientia Christum non vel offerimus eis, qui non habent? an veritate Dei in iniustitia detinemus? & quidè quandocunq; peruenerit gentium plenitudo necesse est, expectamus vt in eas incidat fides. Cui credere casu contigit? quomodo credent sine prædicatione? Petrus ad Cornelium, Philippus ad Eunuchum missi sunt: & si exemplum recentius quærimus, Augustinus à beato Gregorio destinatus est formam fidei tradere Anglis. Et de his tu ita tecum. Ego addo & de pertinacia Græcorum qui nobiscum sunt, & non sunt; iuncti fide, pace diuisi; (quanquam & in fide ipsa claudicauerint à semitis rectis) & item de hæresi, quæ clam pene vbiq; serpit, apud aliquos sæuit palam. Nam paruulos Ecclesiæ passim & publice deglutire festinant: quæris vbi sit hoc? Vestri qui terrâ Austri tam sæpe visitant, eccè hi sciunt & possunt dicere tibi, eunt & redeunt per medium illorum, aut transeunt secus: sed quid boni adhuc cum illis egeriqt, nondum audiuimus. Et forsitan audiuissemus, nisi præ auro Hispaniæ, salus populi viluisset: tuum est & plagæ huic remedium prouidere. Sed est insipientia, quæ ipsam quoque iam prope modum stultam fecit sapientiam fidei: Quomodo & islam catholicam pene totam hoc virus infecit. Nam dum & ipsa quoque, quæ nostra sunt quærimus, sic vt inuicem inuidentes, inuicem procreantes exerceamur ad odia, animemur ad iniurias, armemur ad lites, cauillemus ad dolos, feriemur ad detractiones, prorumpamus ad maledicta, opprimamur s fortibus, opprimamus inferiores. Quia digne & laudabiliter occupatur meditatio cordis tui aduersus tam pestilens insipientiæ genus, quod corpus ipsum Christi (quæ est multitudo credentium) occupasse confideras. O ambitio ambitientium crux, quomodo omnes torquens omnibus places? Nil acerbius cruciat, nil molestius inquietat, nil tamen apud miseros mortales celebrius negociis eius. An non limina Apostolorum plus iam ambitio, quam deuotio terit? Annon vocibus eius vestrum tota die resultat palatium? Annon quæstibus eius tota legum canonumque disciplina insudat? An- non spoliis eius omnis Italica inhiat inexplebili auiditate rapacitas? Quid ita tua ipsius spiritualia studia non saltem intercidit, sed abscidit? quotiens sancta ac fœcunda tua abortiri ocia fecit inquietum & inquietans malum? Aliud est quod ab oppressis appellatur ad te, aliud autem quod ambitio in Ecclesia per te regnare molitur. Nec deesse illis, nec huic aliquatenus assentire oportet; quia vero inique foueturilla, spernuntur illi: vtrisque debitor es, illis vt eriges, istis vt reprimas.
units.tr: But what do you answer about the Gentiles themselves? Or rather, what does your own reflection answer you when you ask this? What did the Fathers decide to set as a limit for the Gospel? Why suspend the word of faith as long as unbelief lasts? By what reason, we may ask, did the swiftly running word stop? Who first checked this saving course? Perhaps some cause unknown to us, or some necessity, may have hindered them. What reason do we have for concealing it? With what confidence, with what conscience, do we not offer Christ to those who lack him? Or do we hold the truth of God captive in unrighteousness? And indeed, whenever the fullness of the Gentiles comes, we must wait for faith to fall upon them by chance. Who has been granted to believe by chance? How shall they believe without a preacher? Peter was sent to Cornelius, Philip to the eunuch. And if we seek a more recent example, Augustine was sent by the blessed Gregory to hand on the form of the faith to the English. You are thinking this over yourself, and I add something about the obstinacy of the Greeks who are with us and yet are not with us: joined in faith, divided in peace (although they too have limped from the straight paths in the faith itself). Likewise, I add about heresy, which creeps almost everywhere in secret and rages openly among some. For they hasten to swallow up the little ones of the Church everywhere and publicly. You ask where this is? Your men who so often visit the land of the South, behold, they know and can tell you: they go and return through the midst of them, or pass by their side. But what good they have done with them we have not yet heard. And perhaps we would have heard, had not the welfare of the people been cheapened for the sake of Spanish gold. It is yours to provide a remedy for this wound too. But there is a folly which has made even the wisdom of faith almost foolish, just as this poison has infected nearly the whole Catholic Church. For while we seek even those things which are our own, we are exercised in such a way that, envying one another and provoking one another, we are armed for hatred, roused to injuries, armed for quarrels, we engage in tricks, we are struck by slanders, we burst out into curses, the strong oppress us, and we oppress the weaker. It is worthy and praiseworthy that the meditation of your heart is occupied against this pestilent kind of folly, which you see has taken hold of the very body of Christ, that is, the multitude of believers. O ambition, the cross of the ambitious, how do you torment all and please none? Nothing wounds more bitterly, nothing disturbs more painfully, and yet nothing is more famous among wretched mortals than your business. Does ambition not already wear down the thresholds of the Apostles more than devotion does? Does your palace not echo with its voices all day long? Does not the whole discipline of laws and canons labour over its profits? Does not all Italian rapacity gape with insatiable greed for its spoils? Why has it not only cut short your spiritual studies, but cut them off altogether? How often has this restless and disquieting evil made your holy and fruitful leisure miscarry? One thing is appealed to you by the oppressed; another is what ambition strives to reign over in the Church through you. You must not neglect the former, nor in any way assent to the latter. Because the latter is unjustly cherished, the former are spurned. You are a debtor to both: to the former, that you may raise them up; to the latter, that you may restrain them.

units.la: Et quoniam incidit de appellationibus, prosequi aliquatenus non erit ab re. Magno in his & pio opus intuitu est, ne quod magna fuit necessitate prouisum, male vtendo reddatur inutile. Mihi videtur & in multam posse eas deuenire perniciem, si non summo moderamine actitentur. Appellatur de toto mundo ad te, id quidem in testimonium singularis primatus tui: at tu si sapis non primatu gaudebis, sed fructu. Apostolis dictum est: in hoc nolite gaudere, quod spiritus subiiciuntur vobis. Appellatur ad te, vt dixi, & vtinam tam fructuose, quam necessarie: vtinam cum oppressus clamat, sentiat oppressor; & non superbiat impius vnde incenditur pauper. Quid tam decorum vt ad inuocationem tui nominis oppressi effugiant, versuti non refugiant? Quid è regione tam peruersum, tam recti alienum, vt lætetur qui malum fecit, & qui tulit inaniter fatigetur: Inhumanissime non moueris erga hominem, cui illæ iniuriæ cumulauere dolorem; & labor itineris, & damna expensarum. Sed nihilominus ignauissime in illud non moueris; qui huic, tot calamitatum partim auctor, partim extitit causa: euigila, homo Dei, cum contingunt; moueatur miseratio, moueatur & indignatio tua. Alteram læso, alteram lædenti debes; consoleturille damnorum refarcitu suorum, satisfactione iniuriarum, sine calumniarum: cum isto ita agatur vt pœniteat fecisse, quod non timuit facere, & non de pœnis innocentis redeat. Arbitror idem debere pati illum qui sine causa forte appellauit. Formulam hanc iustitiæ præsigit tibi & diuinæ incommutabilis ratio æquitatis, & ni fallor, ipsa appellationum lex: vt illicite vsurpata appellatio, nec prosit appellanti, nec appellato obsit. Vt quid enim frustra fatigatus sit homo? Quia plenum iustitiæ, vt sese potius læserit, qui voluit proximum: appellasse inique, iniquum est; iniques& impune iniquarum appellationum fomes. Iniqua autem omnis appellatio, ad quam iustitiæ inopia non coegit: appellare non vt graues, sed si graueris, licet. Appellandum à sententia, ante sententiam improbe omnino: nisi ob manifestum grauamen præsumitur appellatio. Quid igitur non grauatus appellat, liquet quia aut grauare intendit, aut tempus redimere: non est autem suffugium appellatio, sed refugium. Quantos nouimus appellasse pulsatos, quo interim liceret, quod nunquam licet? Nonnullis etiam, quoad vixerunt, licuisse appellationis suf- fragio. fragio nefaria, scimus: verbi gratia, incestum, adulterium. Quale est hoc turpitudini patrocinari, quod vel maxime formidari a turpibus oportebat? Quousque murmur vniuersæ terræ, aut dissimulas, aut non aduertis? quousque dormitas? quousque non euigilat consideratio tua ad tantam appellationum confusionem atque abusionem? Præter ius & fas, præter morem & ordinem fiunt: non locus, non modus, non tempus, non causa discernitur, aut persona. Præsumuntur leniter passim, plerumque & nequiter. Volentes malignari nonne his potissimum terreri solebant nunc terrori ipsi ex his magis fiunt, atque id bonis. Antidotum versum in venenum, non mutatio dexteræ excelsi hæc. Appellantur boni a malis, ut non faciant bona: & superseddent a voce tonitrui tui formidantes. Denique appellantur Episcopi, ne illicita audeant matrimonia soluere, vel prohibere: appellantur ne rapinas, ne furta, ne sacrilegia, & quæ eiusmodi sunt, punire vllatenus vel cohibere præsumant. Appellantur ne indignas & infames personas a sacris officiis beneficiis que repellere seu amouere queant. Quod tu inuenis remedium morbo huic, ne quod repertum ad remedium fuit, reperiatur ad mortem? Zelatus est Dominus domum orationis factam speluncam latronum. Tu eius minister dissimulas miserorum refugium, datum arma iniquitati. Videas præripi passim partes oppressorum, & protumpere ad appellandum non tam graunatos, quam graurare volentes. Quid hoc mysterii? tuum est considerare, non meum commentari istud. Et cur, inquis male appellati non veniunt ostensuri suam innocentiam, malitiam coniiciuri? Dico quod dicere ad hoc solent: nolumus vexati frustra, in curia esse qui procliuius faueant appellationibus, foneat appellationes; cessuris Romæ, domi cedere satius. Fateor me non omnino decredere his. Quem das mihi in tam crebtis appellationibus quæ hodie fiunt, qui pro expensis itineris vel nummum restituerit illi, quem forte appellarit? Mirum vero si ita omnes, & appellantes iusti, & appellati rei vestro examini inuenti sunt. Diligite, inquit, iustitiam qui iudicatis terram: parum est iustitiam tenere, nisi & diligas. Qui tenent, tenent; qui diligunt zelantur: amator iustitiæ inquirit iustitiam, & prosequitur eam; porro omnem iustitiam persequitur. Nihil tibi & illis qui appellationes venationes putant: pudet elogii, quod apud Ethnicos iam vertitur in parabolam: duos nouimus cæruos pingues; vt mitius loquar, plus facetia, quam iustitiæ hic. Tu si amas iustitiam, appellationes non affectas, sed sustines. Veruntamen quid emolumenti affert Ecclesiis Dei, tua vnius hominis iustitia, vbi sententia prævalet aliter affectorum? at istud loci illius erit, cum cœperint versari quæ circa te sunt. Nunc vero non te existimes otiose vacare considerationi hinc, qua appellationes ad legitimum siferi potest revocces vsum: & si hinc mea quæratur vel potius curetur sententia, dico appellationes vt non contemnendas, sic nec vsurpandas omnino. Porro horum quid insolentius censeam haud facile dixerim, nisi quod vsurpatio quandam videtur inducere contemptus necessitatem, ac per hoc forte acrius insecianda, quam amplius nocet: aut non vere nocentior est mala in se, in partu peior. Nonne ipsæ quæ ipsum ius quoq; naturæ aut extenuat, aut exterminat? Nam sæpe rebus etiam preciosissimis, precii gratia non modo demit, sed adimit. Quid Sacramentis acceptius, vsurpata tamen ab indignis, indigne tractata, minime acceptatur: magis habent damnationem, quia debitam venerationem non habent. Fateor grande & generale mundo bonum esse appellationes, idq; tam necessarium, quam solem mortalibus. Reuera quidem Sol iustitiæ est, prodens ac redarguens opera tenebrarum: prorsus fauendæ & manutenendæ sunt, sed quas extorsit necessitas, non callidas adinuenit. Vsurpatoriæ sunt huiusmodi omnes, non subuenientes in necessitate, sed opitulantes iniquitati, quid ni veniant in conceptum? quanti vt talib. quoq; deferent, eriâ de proprio cessere iure, ne longo & casso itinere fatigarentur? Plures tamen sua amittere non ferentes, appellationes minus oportunas, & celsa nomina importunius contempserunt. Dico aliquid quod ad rem pertinet, exempli causa: quidam sibi publice desponsauerat vxorem, adest dies celebris nuptiarum, parata omnia, inuitati multi: & ecce homo concupiscens vxorem proximi sui, in vocem appellationis inopinate prorumpit, affirmans sibi tradita prius, suam potius esse debere. Stupet sponsus, hærent omnes, sacerdos non audet progredi, frustratur omnis apparatus ille, descendit quisq; in domum suam, sua cœnam manducaturus: sponsa a mensa & thalamo, sponsi suspenditur, quousq; Romæ reditum est. Parisiis contigit hoc, nobili Galliarum ciuitate, sede Regia. Rursum in ciuitate eadem quidam sibi desponsata vxore die constituit nuptiarum; interim emergit calumnia dicentib. quibusdam non deberet coniungi. Ad iudicium Ecclesiæ causa delata est, sed non expectata sententia appellatum est sine causa, sine grauamine, solo frustratoriæ dilationis intuitu. At ille siue perdere qui pararat, siue dilecte tamdiu frustrari consortio nolens, nihilominus quod præposuerat, contempta siue dissimulata appellatione, peregit. Quid illud quod in Antisiodorensi Ecclesia nuper a quodam adolescentulo præsumptum est? nempe defuncto sancto Episcopo, volentib. clericis aliis, vt moris est, eligere sibi: interuenit ille appellans & vetans ne fieret, quousque isset & rediisset ab vrbe; cui tñ appellationi nec ipse detulit. Nam cum videret se contemni, tanq; qui irrationabiliter appellasset, accitis quos potuit sibi, tertia die post facta ab aliis electionem, fecit sua. Cum itaq; ex his & innumeris talib. liqueat, non ex contemptu gigni vsurpationem, sed ex vsurpatione cótemptum, videris tu quid sibi velit, quod zelus vester assidue pene vindicat illa, istam dissimulat. Vis perfectius coercere contemptu? cura in ipso utero pessimæ matris germen nequa, quod ita fiet, si vsurpatio digna animaduersione multetur. Tolle vsurpationem, & contemptus excusationem non habets; porro inexcusabilitas aulum explodet. Non sit proinde vsurpator, & contemptor nullus erit, aut admodum rarus. Bene facis tu quod appellationum negato suffragio, imo suffugio, multa remittis negocia ad cognoscetes, vel qui noscere citius possunt: vbi n, certior ac facilior notio, ibi decisio tutior expeditorq; esse potest, quia plenum gratiæ, q; multorum quoq; per hoc & laborib. parcis & sumptibus: at quibus sic credas, tibi omnimodis attendêdum. Poterâ multa de eodem vtiliter addere his, sed memor propositi mei, contentus interim occasione dedisse, ad alia transeo. Et primum quod occurrit minime transeundũ reor: præes & singulariter; ad quid? eget tibi dico consideratione. Nunquid vt de subditis crescas? nequaquâ: sed vt ipsi de te? Principe te cõstituerunt; sed sibi, nõ tibi, alioquin quo pacto reputas te superiorem his, à quib. beneficium mendicas? audi Dominum: qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur. At istud de his qui foris sunt, quid ad nos? Tu id mendaciter diceris, si non tam beneficus esse, quâ beneficis præesse intendas. Parui deiecti; animi est, de subditis non profectum quærere subditorũ; sed quæstum proprium: in Summo præsertim omniũ nihil turpius. Quâ pulcre magister gentium parentes filiis, non filios debere censuit thesaurizare parentibus. Non mediocris gloria vox illa identidẽ ipsius, non requiro datũ, sed fructum. At iam transeamus & hinc, ne quis morâ in his meam, avaritiæ in te notâ interpretetur: quæ q; longe à te sit in libro secundo testatus sum, sciens quanta & in quanta tua necessitate respueris. Ad te proinde scriplerim ista, non propter te: nêpe q; tibi scribitur, soli prodesse non decet. Hic locus avaritiâ carpit, à quo vitio immunis satis tua opinio est; an & opus, tu videris. Vidimus tũ (vt oblata à pauperib. taceam, quæ tangere nõ acquiescis) germanicos detumuisse saccos: sed precio, non massa. Argentum reputatũ est fœnum, summarii nõ leuati sarcinis, onusti nihilominus repatriant vel inuiti. Noua res; qñ hactenus auiũ Roma refudit? & nunc Romanorum cõsilio id vsurpatum non credimus. Duo venerunt, ambo locupletes; & ambo rei: siquidẽ vnus Moguntinus, Colonien sis alter: alteri gratia gratis reddita est; alter, indignus credo, cui gratia redderetur, audiuit: cũ quali veste errasti, cum tali egrediaris. O vocem magnifica; vocem prorsus Apostolicæ libertatis! Quid minus ab illa hæc habuit; pecunia tua tecũ sit in perditione? nisi q; in illa plus zeli, in ista plus modestiæ sonuit. Quid ille de transmarinis partib. pene à finibus terræ, terra & mari currens Episcopatu, suis & alienis facultatib. rursus emendo? iam n. emerat prius: tulit multa, sed retulit; non omnia tamẽ. Incidit miser in manus alias, accipere q; dare potentiores. Benefecisti tuas in vtroq; seruans innoxias, nec imponere scil. ambitioso, nec supponere iniquo Mammone acquiescens. Non sic, à pauperE Episcopo cõtinuisti, dans quod daret ne immunificus notaretur. Accepit clam q; palam dedit: sic de tuo sacculo consultũ est verecundiæ viri; sic quoq; curiæ morem gerens, tuo beneficio inuidiâ declinauit eorũ qui diligunt munera. Non putes abscondere, & factum nouimus, & personâ. Audire grauat? & ego eo libêtius prædico, quo tu id molestius audis: si tibi sic expedit, & mihi sic. Tâ non oportet Christi gloriâ me silere; quâ nec te quærere tuam: & si pergis murmurare adhuc, respondebitur tibi ex Euangelio: quanto eis præcipiebat, tanto magis plus prædicabant dicentes, bene omnia fecit. Audi aliud, si tñ aliud; ad idem n. fortassis pertinere quis dicat: tua consideratio viderit hoc. Mihi videtur non longe à vero dissentire, qui id forte inter auaritiæ species locandum putauerit: ego vero illius aut speciem esse, aut speciem habere nõ negauerim. Sane interest tuæ perfectionis & malas res, & malas pariter species deuitare: in altero conscientiæ, in altero famæ cõsulis. Puta tibi non licere (etsi alias fortasse liceat) quicquid male fuerat coloratum. Deniq; interroga maiores tuos, & dicent tibi; Ab omni specie mali abstinete vos. Sane minister Domini, Dominum imitetur, quia ipse ait: qui mihi ministrat, me sequatur. Et habes de illo: Dominus regnauit, decorem induit; induit Dominus fortitudinem. Tu quoq; esto fortis in fide, decorus in gloria; & probasti te imitatorẽ Dei. Fortitudo tua fiducia fidelis conscientiæ, decor tuus splendor bonæ opinionis: ita, quæso, induere fortitudinem, etenim gaudium Domini fortitudo tua. Porro speciê tua & pulcritudine tua nihilominus tanquâ propria similitudine delectatur: induere vestimentũ gloriæ tuæ, vestire duplicibus, quib. domesticos suos fortis illa mulier induere consueuit. Non sit in conscientia nutans infirmitas modicæ fidei, non sit in fama nęuus malæ speciei, & vestris duplicibus, & gaudebit sponsus super sponsam animam tuâ, & gaudebit super te Deus vnus. Miraris quorsum hæc, ignarus vsque adhuc quid dicere velim? non te tollo diutius; murmur loquor & querimoniâ Ecclesiarum: truncati se clamitant, ac demembrari. Vel nullæ vel paucæ admodum sunt quæ plagâ istam aut non doleant, aut non timeant. Quæris quâ? subtrahuntur Abbates Episcopis; Episcopi Archiepiscopis; Archiepiscopi Patriarchis siue Primatibus. Bonane species hæc? mirũ si excusari queat vel opus. Si facti- tando probaris vos habere plenitudinê potestatis; sed iustitiæ forte non ita: facitis hoc quia potestis, sed vtrũ & debeatis quæstio est. Honorũ & dignitatum gradus & ordines quibusq; suos seruare positi estis, non inuidere, vt quidã vestrorum ait: Cui honorẽ, honorem. Spiritualis homo, ille qui omnia diiudicat, vt ipse à nemine diiudicetur, omne opus suum trina quadã consideratione præueniet. Primum quidẽ an liceat, deinde an deceat, postremo an expediat. Nam etsi constet in Christiana vtiq; philosophia non decere nisi q; licet, non expedire nisi quod decet & licet: non continuo tamẽ omne quod licet, decet aut expedire cõsequens erit. Age aptemus tria ista, si possumus, operi huic: at quomodo non indecens tibi voluntate pro lege vti, & quia nõ est ad quẽ appelleris, potestatem exercere, negligere rationẽ. Tune maior Domino tuo, qui ait: non veni facere voluntatẽ meam. Quanquâ non minus deiecti, q; elati animi est veluti rationis expertê, non pro ratione, sed p libitu agere: nec iudicio agi, sed appetitu. Quid tâ bestiale? Et si indignũ cuiuis vtenti ratione viuere vt pecus, quis in te rectore omnium tanta cornumeliam naturæ, honoris iniuriâ ferat? sic degenerando, q; absit, generale opprobrium fecisti p- riũ tibi. Homo cum in honore esset nõ intellexit, comparatus est iumentis insipientibus, & similis factus est illis. Quid item tam indignum tibi, q; vt totum tenens non sis contentus toto, nisi minutias quasdam atq; exiguas portiones ipsius tibi creditæ vniuersitatis, tanquã nõ sint tuæ, satagas nescio quomodo adhuc facere tuas? Vbi etiã meminisse te volo parabolæ Nathã de homine q; multas oues habẽs, vnã quæ erat paupe-
units.tr: Since the subject of appeals has come up, it will not be out of place to pursue it a little. Here great care and a godly purpose are needed, so that what was provided out of great necessity does not become useless through misuse. It seems to me that appeals may bring about great harm if they are not handled with the utmost moderation. Appeals are made to you from the whole world. That is indeed a testimony to your singular primacy, but if you are wise you will rejoice not in the primacy but in its fruit. It was said to the apostles: do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you. Appeals are made to you, as I have said, and would that they were as fruitful as they are necessary. Would that when the oppressed cry out, the oppressor might feel it, and that the wicked man would not grow proud at the very thing that inflames the poor man against him. What could be more fitting than that the oppressed should take refuge in invoking your name, while the crafty do not flee from it? And what could be more perverse, more alien to what is right, than that the one who did the wrong should rejoice while the one who brought the appeal is wearied in vain? You are most inhumanly unmoved by a man whom those injuries have loaded with grief, and by the labour of the journey and the losses of expenses. Yet you are most negligently unmoved by that other man, who was partly the author and partly the cause of so many calamities. Awake, man of God, when such things happen; let your pity be stirred, and your indignation too. You owe one thing to the injured party and another to the one who injures. Let the injured man be comforted for the losses he has suffered, by satisfaction for the wrongs done to him, without quibbling. Let the other be dealt with in such a way that he repents of having done what he was not afraid to do, and that he does not get off at the expense of the innocent. I think the one who appealed without cause perhaps ought to suffer the same. The rule of justice and the unchanging reason of divine equity set down this formula for you, and, unless I am mistaken, so does the very law of appeals: that an appeal wrongly taken should neither help the appellant nor harm the one appealed against. For why should a man be wearied in vain? It is wholly just that he who wished to harm his neighbour should rather have harmed himself. To appeal unjustly is itself unjust, and an unjust appeal is an unpunished incitement to injustice. Every appeal is unjust to which a lack of justice has not compelled the appellant. One may appeal not as one who is aggrieved, but if one is aggrieved, one may appeal. One must not appeal from a sentence before the sentence is given; that is wholly wrongful, unless an appeal is presumed on account of a manifest grievance. Why, then, does a man appeal when he is not aggrieved? It is plain that he either intends to aggrieve someone or wishes to buy time. An appeal is not a shelter but a refuge for the guilty. How many have we known to appeal when they were under attack, so that meanwhile they might do what they could never lawfully do? We know that some, for as long as they lived, were permitted by the support of an appeal to commit wicked acts, for example incest and adultery. What is this but defending baseness, which above all ought to be dreaded by the base? How long will you either pretend not to notice or fail to notice the murmur of the whole earth? How long will you sleep? How long will your vigilance not wake to the great confusion and abuse of appeals? They are made beyond law and right, beyond custom and order. Place, measure, time, cause and person are not distinguished. Appeals are admitted lightly everywhere, and very often wickedly. Those who wished to do evil were once accustomed to be terrified by these very things; now they have become a terror to good men, and that is the reverse of what they should be. The antidote has been turned into poison; this is not the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. Good men are appealed against by the wicked so that they may not do good, and they hold back for fear of the voice of your thunder. Finally, bishops are appealed against so that they do not dare to dissolve or forbid unlawful marriages, and so that they do not presume in any way to punish or restrain robberies, thefts, sacrileges and other such things. They are appealed against so that they cannot repel or remove unworthy and infamous persons from sacred offices and benefices. What remedy do you find for this disease, lest the remedy that was discovered for healing be turned to death? The Lord was zealous for his house of prayer, which had been made a den of thieves. You, his minister, overlook the refuge of the wretched, which has been given as a weapon to iniquity. You see the rights of the oppressed snatched away on every side, and men rushing to appeal not so much because they are aggrieved as because they wish to aggrieve. What is the mystery here? It is for you to consider, not for me to speculate about this. And why, you ask, do those who are wrongly appealed against not come to show their innocence and expose the malice of their accusers? I answer with what those who do this are accustomed to say: "We do not wish to be harassed in vain. There are men at court who favour appeals too readily, and they promote appeals. It is better to yield at home than to yield at Rome." I confess I do not entirely believe them. Given so many appeals as are made today, who will give me a single coin to repay the expenses of the journey to the man whom perhaps he has appealed against? It would indeed be strange if all the appellants were found just and all those appealed against guilty by your examination. Love justice, you who judge the earth, it says. It is not enough to hold to justice unless you also love it. Those who hold it, hold it; those who love it are zealous: the lover of justice seeks justice and pursues it, and indeed pursues all justice. Have nothing to do with those who think of appeals as hunting. I am ashamed of the saying, already turned into a proverb among the heathen: we know of two fat stags. To speak more gently, here there is more wit than justice. If you love justice, you do not seek appeals, but you endure them. Yet what benefit does the justice of one man, namely yours, bring to the churches of God, when the sentence is carried by those who think otherwise? But that will have its place when those who are around you begin to be busy. For now, do not think you are idly engaged in considering how appeals may be recalled to their lawful use. If you ask my opinion on this, or rather seek a cure, I say that appeals are not to be despised, and yet they must not be used at all lightly. I would hardly be able to say which of these is the more unseemly, except that the abuse of appeals seems to produce a certain contempt, and so perhaps they should be attacked more fiercely, for they do more harm; or else what is evil in itself is no more harmful than what is worse in its offspring. Do they not themselves weaken or destroy even the very right of nature? For often they take away, and not merely take away but actually remove, the value of things that are most precious. What is more acceptable than the sacraments, yet when they are used by the unworthy and handled unworthily, they are very far from being accepted; they bring condemnation rather, because they lack the reverence that is due to them. I confess that appeals are a great and general good for the world, and as necessary as the sun is to mortals. Indeed the Sun of righteousness is, revealing and rebuking the works of darkness. Appeals must certainly be favoured and maintained, but those that necessity has wrung out, not those that cunning has devised. All the abusive kind, which do not come to help in necessity but support iniquity, why should they not be held in contempt? How many, in order to bring them to bear even on such people, have given up their own right, out of regard for expense, so that they should not be worn out by a long and fruitless journey? Yet many, unable to bear the loss of their own goods, have scorned inopportune appeals and great names more disrespectfully. Let me give an example that bears on the matter. A certain man had publicly betrothed a wife to himself; the day of the celebrated wedding arrived, everything was prepared, many were invited. And behold, a man who coveted his neighbour's wife burst out unexpectedly with a cry of appeal, declaring that she had been given to him earlier and ought rather to be his. The bridegroom was struck dumb, all stood fixed, the priest did not dare to proceed, all that preparation was frustrated, and each man went down to his own house to eat his own supper. The bride was suspended from the table and the bridal chamber of her bridegroom until the matter was referred to Rome. This happened at Paris, a noble city of the Gauls and the royal seat. Again, in the same city, a man who had betrothed a wife fixed a day for the wedding; meanwhile a complaint arose, some saying that she ought not to be joined to him. The case was brought before the judgment of the Church, but before the sentence was awaited an appeal was made without cause, without grievance, from the sole purpose of frustrating delay. But he, whether because he did not want to lose what he had prepared or because he was unwilling to be kept so long from the company of the woman he loved, went ahead with what he had decided, disregarding or ignoring the appeal. And what of that which a certain young man presumed to do recently in the church of Auxerre? When the holy bishop had died, and the other clergy wished, as is customary, to elect a successor, he intervened, appealing and forbidding it to be done until he had gone to the city and returned. Yet even to that appeal he did not himself adhere. For when he saw that he was being disregarded, as one who had appealed irrationally, he gathered together as many as he could, and on the third day after the election had been made by the others, he made his own. Since, then, it is clear from these and countless similar cases that abuse arises not from contempt, but contempt from abuse, see what your zeal means, which almost always avenges the one and tolerates the other. Do you wish to restrain contempt more thoroughly? Then take care to root out the bad seed in the very womb of the worst mother. This will happen if abuse is punished with a fitting penalty. Remove the abuse, and contempt will have no excuse; and without excuse, it will be driven out. Let there be no abuser, and there will be no one who despises, or at least very few. You do well in refusing appeals their support, or rather their refuge, and in referring many matters to those who know them or who can know them more quickly. Where knowledge is more certain and easier, the decision can be safer and quicker, since this saves grace for many people, and by this means you spare labours and expenses. But you must pay full attention to whom you entrust them. I could add much of use on the same subject, but mindful of my purpose I am content for now to have given an occasion, and I pass on to other matters. And first, what occurs to me I think should not be passed over: you are placed over others, and singularly so. For what purpose? I say it needs your consideration. Is it so that you may grow rich from your subjects? By no means; but that they may grow rich from you. They have made you prince, but for their sake, not for yours. Otherwise, in what way do you think you are above those from whom you beg a favour? Hear the Lord: those who have power over them are called benefactors. But what has that to do with us, when it concerns those who are outside? You would be falsely called that if you intended to be not so much a benefactor as one who presides over benefactors. It is the mark of a small and abject spirit to seek the profit of the subjects, not from the subjects, but for oneself; and in the highest of all, nothing is more shameful. How finely the teacher of the Gentiles held that parents ought to lay up treasure for their children, not children for their parents. That famous saying of his is no small glory: I do not seek what is given, but the fruit. But let us now pass on from this as well, so that no one should interpret the delay on these points as a mark of avarice against you. I have testified in the second book that avarice is far from you, knowing how much and in what great need you have refused it. I write these things to you, then, not on your account; for what is written to you should not benefit you alone. This passage touches upon avarice, from which your reputation is sufficiently free; whether your work is also free, you must judge. I have seen you (to say nothing of the gifts offered by the poor, which you are unwilling to touch) cause German sacks to swell, but with money, not with lumps of metal. Silver has been reckoned as hay; the summarists, not relieved of their burdens, return home loaded nonetheless, even against their will. It is a new thing. When has Rome ever cast out such birds until now? And now we do not believe that this has been devised by the counsel of the Romans. Two came, both wealthy, and both defendants: one was the man from Mainz, the other from Cologne. To the one, grace was granted freely; the other, who I believe was unworthy of receiving grace, heard: "In what garment did you go astray, and with what garment do you leave?" O magnificent saying, truly a saying of apostolic liberty! What did this differ from that other, may your money perish with you? Except that the former sounded more zeal, and the latter more modesty. What of that man who, running from the borders of the earth almost to the lands beyond the sea, by land and sea, bought a bishopric again with his own and others' resources? For he had already bought one before. He carried off many things, but he also gave back, though not all of them. The wretch fell into other hands, that were more powerful to receive than to give. You did well in keeping your own hands innocent on both sides, neither offering anything to the ambitious nor yielding to the unjust Mammon. You did not behave in this way towards a poor bishop, giving what he would give so that he should not be marked as ungenerous. He received in secret and gave openly; thus, out of your own purse, the modesty of the man was provided for. Thus too, in obedience to the custom of the court, you ward off the envy of those who love gifts by means of your favour. Do not think you can hide it: we know both the deed and the person. Are you grieved to hear this? I proclaim it all the more freely because you hear it the more painfully; if it is expedient for you, so it is for me. I must not be silent about the glory of Christ, any more than I should seek your own glory. And if you still go on murmuring, you will be answered from the gospel: the more he forbade them, the more they proclaimed it, saying, "He has done all things well." Hear another thing, if indeed it is another; for someone might say that it pertains to the same matter. Your consideration will see to this. It seems to me that he is not far from the truth who has perhaps thought that this should be placed among the kinds of avarice. I would not deny that it is either a kind of avarice, or has the appearance of it. Surely it matters to your perfection to avoid both bad things and bad appearances, the one for the sake of conscience, the other for the sake of your reputation. Suppose that it is not lawful for you (though perhaps it may be lawful in other cases) to do anything that has been wrongly coloured. Finally, ask your elders, and they will tell you: abstain from every appearance of evil. Surely a minister of the Lord should imitate the Lord, since he himself says: whoever ministers to me, let him follow me. And you have this of him: the Lord reigned, he put on beauty; the Lord put on strength. You too should be strong in faith, beautiful in glory; and you will have proved yourself an imitator of God. Let your strength be the confidence of a faithful conscience, and your beauty the splendour of a good reputation. So, I beg you, put on strength, for your strength is the joy of the Lord. Moreover, your appearance and your beauty delight him nonetheless, as if they were his own likeness: put on the garment of your glory, clothe yourself with double garments, with which that strong woman was accustomed to clothe her household. Let there be no wavering weakness of little faith in your conscience, no blemish of a bad appearance in your reputation, and with your double garments the bridegroom will rejoice over the bride, your soul will rejoice, and the one God will rejoice over you. Do you wonder what all this is leading to, not yet knowing what I wish to say? I will not hold you any longer. I speak of the murmur and complaint of the churches: they cry out that they are cut off and dismembered. Hardly any churches, or very few indeed, do not either grieve over this wound or fear it. You ask in what way? Abbots are withdrawn from bishops, bishops from archbishops, archbishops from patriarchs or primates. Is this a good appearance? It would be strange if such a deed could be excused. You prove that you possess the fullness of power by doing these things; but whether you have it rightly, perhaps not. You do this because you can; but whether you ought to, is the question. Each of you has been placed to keep the degrees and orders of honours and dignities, not to envy them, as one of you says: to whom honour, honour. The spiritual man, he who judges all things, so that he himself is judged by no one, will anticipate every work of his by a certain threefold consideration: first whether it is lawful, then whether it is fitting, finally whether it is expedient. For although it is established that in Christian philosophy nothing is fitting unless it is lawful, and nothing expedient unless it is both fitting and lawful, it does not follow at once that everything that is lawful is fitting or expedient. Come, let us apply these three things to this work, if we can. But how is it not unseemly for you to use your will as law, and, because there is no one to whom you can be appealed, to exercise power while neglecting reason? Are you greater than your Lord, who said: I did not come to do my own will? Yet it is no less the mark of a humbled spirit than of an exalted one to act not by reason but by caprice, like one without reason: to be moved not by judgment but by appetite. What is so bestial? And if it is unworthy for anyone who uses reason to live like a beast, who, in you, the ruler of all, could bear such a reproach to nature and such an injury to honour? By degenerating thus, far be it from us, you have made a general disgrace, first for yourself. Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he has been compared with foolish beasts, and has become like them. What also is so unworthy for you, who hold the whole, as not to be content with the whole, but to strive, I know not how, to make your own certain small and meagre portions of the very universe entrusted to you, as though they were not yours already? Here too I want you to remember the parable of Nathan, about the man who had many sheep, and who coveted the one little ewe of the poor man.

units.la: Editor's note: line numbers 5 to 50 in the left margin mark the printed lines; line 50 is the one with "50" beside "sed vtrũ". pauperis concupiuit. Huc quoq; veniat factum, imo facinus Regis Achab, qui rerum summam tenebat, & vnam vineam affectauit. Auertat Deus à te quod ille audiuit: occidisti & possedisti. Nolo autem prætendas mihi fructum emancipationis ipsius, nullus est enim: nisi quod inde Episcopi insolentiores Monachi etiā dissolutiores fiunt: quid quod & pauperiores? Inspice diligentius talium vbiq; libertorum & facultates & vitas, si non pudenda admodum tenuitas in his, & in illis secularitas inuenitur? Matris noxiæ libertatis, genuina soboles hæc. Quidni peccet licentius vagum, & malum liberum vulgus, cum non sit qui arguat? Quidni licentius quoq; spolietur ac depræderetur inermis religio, cum non sit qui defendat? quo n. refugium illis? nunquid ad Episcopos dolentes iniuriā? Ridentib. profecto aspiciunt oculis; siue quæ faciūt mala, siue quæ patiuntur. Quæ demū vtilitas in sanguine isto? Vereor ne illa q; in Propheta cōminatus est Deus: ille, inquiēs, in iniquitate sua morietur, sanguinem autē eius de manu tua requiram. Si n. extollitur qui subtrahitur, & cui subtrahitur vritur, qui subtrahit quomodo innocēs? Parum est, inuoluimus igne audi apertius. Si is qui murmurat secūdum animā mortuus est; qui instigat quomodo viuit? quomodo non reus mortis ambor& & suæ pariter, qui gladium dedit vnde ambo morerentur? Hoc est quod dixerā, occidisti & possedisti. Adde quod qui audiunt scandalizantur, indignantur, detrahunt & blasphemant, hoc est, vulnerantur ad mortem. Non est bona arbor faciens fructus tales, insolentias, dissolutiones, dilapidationes, simulationes, scandala, odia, quodque magis dolendū inter Ecclesias inimicitias graues, perpetuasq; discordias. Vides q verus sit sermo ille, omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia expediunt? Quid si forte non licet? Ignosce mihi non facile adducor licitum consentire, quod tot illicita parturit. Tune deniq; tibi licitum censeas, suis Ecclesias mutilare membris, confundere ordinem, perturbare terminos quos posuerunt patres tui? Si iustitiæ est ius cuiq; seruare suum: auferre cuiquā sua, iusto quomodo poterit cōuenire? Erras si vt summā ita & solam institutam à Deo vestram Apostolicam potestatem existimas. Si hoc sentis, dissentis ab eo qui ait: non est potestas nisi à Deo. Proinde quod sequitur: qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit: & si principaliter pte facit, non tamen singulariter. Deniq; idem ait: omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: nō ait sublimiori, tanquam in vno; sed sublimioribus, tanquam in multis. Non ergo tua sola potestas à Domino; sunt mediocres, sunt & inferiores. Et quomodo quos Deus coniunxit non sunt separandi: sic nos quos subiunxit comparandi. Monstrum facis si manu submouens digitum, facis pendere de capite superiorem manui, brachio collateralem. Tale est si in Christi corpore membra aliter locas, quā dispositurit ipse: nisi tu putas alium esse qui posuit in Ecclesia quosdam quidem Apostolos, quosdam autē Prophetas, alios vero Euangelistas, alios Doctores & Pastores ad consummationem sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in ædificationem corporis Christi. Atq; hoc corpus quod tibi ipse Paulus suo vere Apostolico figurans eloquio, & capiti conuenientissime aptans totum ex eo compactum perhibet & connexum per omnem iacturam subministrationis secundum operationem in mensuram vniuscuiusq; membri, augmentum corporis faciens in ædificationem sui, in caritate. Nec vilem reputes formam hanc quia in terra est, exemplar habet è cœlo, Neq; enim filius potest facere quicquam, nisi quæ viderit patrem facientem, præsertim cum ei sub Moysi nomine dictum sit: vide omnia facias secundum exemplar quod tibi in monte monstratum est. Viderat hoc qui dicebat: vidi ciuitatem sanctam Hierusalem, nouam, descendentem de cœlo, à Deo paratam. Ego enim propter similitudinem dictum reor, quod sicut illic Seraphin & Cherubin ac cæteri quiq; vsq; ad Angelos & Archangelos, ordinantur sub vno capite Deo: ita hic quoq; sub vno summo Pontifice Primates vel Patriarchæ, Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, Presbyteri vel Abbates, & reliqui in hunc modum. Non est parui pendendū quod & Deum habet autorem, & de cœlo ducit originem: quia si dicat Episcopus, nolo esse sub Archiepiscopo; aut Abbas, nolo obedire Episcopo; hoc de cœlo non est. Nisi tu forte Angelorū quempiam dicente audisti, nolo sub Archangelis esse: aut ex alio quolibet inferorum ordinum aliquē non ferentem subesse cuiq; nisi Deo. Quid inquis? prohibes dispensare? non, sed dissipare. Nō sum tā rudis vt ignorē positos vos dispensatores; sed in ædificatione, non in destructione. Deinde quæritur inter dispensatores, vt fidelis quis inueniatur; vbi necessitas vrget, excusabilis dispensatio est. Vbi vtilitas prouocat, dispensatio laudabilis est: vtilitas, dico, cōmunis; non propria. Nam cum nihil horū est, non plane fidelis dispensatio, sed crudelis dissipatio est. Nonnulla tū monasteria sita in diuersis Episcopatibus, q specialius pertinuerint, ab ipsa sui fundatione, ad sedē Apostolicam p voluntate fundatorū, quis nesciat? sed aliud est quod largitur deuotio, aliud q; moliturambitio impatiens subiectionis. Superest vt generaliter sup vniuersum Ecclesiæ statum intendat consideratio tua: si plebes, clericis; si clerici sacerdotibus, si sacerdotes Deo in ea qua oportet humilitate subiecti sint; si in monasteriis & religiosis locis seruetur ordo, vigilet disciplina: si super praua opera & dogmata censura Ecclesiastica vigeat: si floreant venerę honestate & sanctimonia sacerdotum: si flores fructus parturiat obedientia fidelium populorum: si deniq; vestra ipsorum Apostolica mandata & instituta ea qua dignū est sollicitudine obseruentur, ne quid in agro Domini tui aut neglectu incultū; aut fraude surreptum inueniatur: posse inueniri ne dubites. Mihi in proptu est (vt multa & innumera prætermittā quæ passim neglecta iacent) nonnulla etiā ex his quæ plantauit dextra tua, cōuulsa monstrare. Nonne os tuum in Remensi Concilio subiecta capitula promulgauit? Quis ea tenet: falleris, si teneri putas. Si nō putas, ipse peccasti aut statuens quæ non tenerentur; aut quod non tenentur dissimulans. Præcipimus, aisti, vt tam Episcopi quam clerici neq; in superfluitate, seu inhonesta varietate colorum, aut fissura vestium, neq; in tonsura intuentium (quorū forma & exemplū esse debent) offendant aspectum; sed potius ita in suis actib. errata condemnēt & amore innocētiæ conuersatione demōstrent, sicut dignitas exigit ordinis clericorū. Quia si moniti ab Episcopis suis infra quadraginta dies non obtemperauerint, Ecclesiasticis beneficiis eorundem Pontificum auctoritate priuentur. Episcopi vero si præfixam poenam irrogare neglexerint; quia inferiorum culpæ ad nullos magis referenda sunt, quam ad desides negligentesque rectores, tamdiu ab officio Pontificali abstineant, donec poenam à nobis constitutam clericis sibi subiectis imponant. Illud etiam dixiMus annectendum, ut nullus in Archidiaconum, vel Decanum nisi Diaconus & Presbyter ordinetur. Archidiaconi vero Decani & Præpositi qui infra ordines prænominatos sunt, si inobedientes ordinare contempserint, honore suscepto priuentur. Prohibemus autem ne adolescentibus, vel infra sacros ordines constitutis, sed qui prudentia & vita merito clarescunt, prædicti concedantur honores.
units.tr: Editor's note: line numbers 5 to 50 in the left margin mark the printed lines; line 50 is the one with "50" beside "sed vtrũ". He coveted the poor man's one ewe. Consider also the deed, or rather the crime, of King Ahab, who held the highest power and coveted a single vineyard. May God keep from you what he heard: you have killed and taken possession. I do not want you to put forward to me the fruit of its emancipation, for there is none, except that bishops become more insolent and monks even more dissolute. And what of the fact that they become poorer too? Look more carefully at the lives and resources of such freedmen everywhere, and see whether a shameful meagreness is not found in these men and worldliness in those. This is the native offspring of harmful liberty. Why should the wandering, free, bad common people not sin more boldly, when there is no one to rebuke them? Why should defenceless religion not be despoiled and plundered more freely, when there is no one to defend it? For where is their refuge? Surely not to the bishops, who are the ones wronging them? Certainly they look on with laughing eyes, both at the evils they commit and at those they suffer. What, finally, is the use of this bloodshed? I fear the words God threatened through the Prophet: he, it says, will die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand. For if the one who is deprived is exalted, and the one from whom it is taken is burned, how is the one who takes it innocent? Is that too little? Listen more plainly. If he who murmurs is dead in soul, how does he who incites live? How is he not guilty of death, both his own and the other's, who gave the sword by which both would die? This is what I meant when I said, you have killed and taken possession. Add that those who hear are scandalised, indignant, they detract and blaspheme, that is, they are wounded unto death. A good tree does not bear such fruit: insolence, dissolution, squandering, dissimulation, scandals, hatreds, and, what is more lamentable, grave enmities and perpetual discords among the Churches. Do you see how true is that saying, all things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient? But what if perhaps it is not lawful? Forgive me; I am not easily persuaded to think lawful what gives birth to so many unlawful things. Would you then deem it lawful to maim the Churches in their members, to confound the order and disturb the boundaries that your fathers set? If it belongs to justice to keep to each his own, how can it be consistent with justice to take away from anyone what is his? You are mistaken if you think that your apostolic power is the whole and only one instituted by God. If you think this, you dissent from him who says: there is no power but of God. Accordingly, what follows: whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God; and if he acts chiefly as a principal, yet not singly. Finally, the same writer says: let every soul be subject to the higher powers: he does not say to the higher power, as to one alone, but to the higher powers, as to many. So your power is not the only one from the Lord; there are middling powers, and there are lower ones too. And as what God has joined together let no one separate, so let us not set in comparison those whom he has placed under one another. You make a monstrosity if, moving a hand, you make the upper part hang from the head and the arm placed beside it. It is like placing the members of Christ's body otherwise than he himself has arranged them, unless you think there is another who set in the Church some indeed as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as teachers and pastors, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ. And this body, which Paul himself, in his truly apostolic language, portrays for you, and most fittingly fits to the head, says is entirely framed and knit together through every joint of supply, according to the working of each individual member, making the body grow unto the building up of itself in love. Nor should you consider this form cheap because it is on earth: it has its pattern from heaven, for the Son can do nothing except what he sees the Father doing, especially since it was said to Moses: see that you make all things according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain. He had seen this who said: I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven, prepared by God. For I think it was said by way of likeness: just as there the Seraphim and Cherubim and all the rest, even to the Angels and Archangels, are ordered under one head, God, so here also, under one supreme Pontiff, are the Primates or Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, Presbyters or Abbots, and the rest in this manner. It is no small matter that it has God as its author and draws its origin from heaven; for if a Bishop says, I do not want to be under an Archbishop, or an Abbot, I do not want to obey the Bishop, this is not from heaven. Unless perhaps you have heard some angel saying, I do not want to be under the Archangels, or have heard someone from another of the lower orders refusing to be subject to anyone but God. What do you say? Do you forbid dispensing? No, but destroying. I am not so unlearned as not to know that you have been placed as dispensers; but for building up, not for tearing down. Moreover, it is required of dispensers that one be found faithful; where necessity presses, dispensation is excusable. Where usefulness calls for it, dispensation is praiseworthy; I mean common usefulness, not private. For when none of these is present, it is not faithful dispensation but cruel dissipation. Who does not know that some monasteries, situated in various dioceses, which from their very foundation pertained more specially to the Apostolic See by the will of their founders? But one thing is what devotion bestows, another what ambition, impatient of subjection, strives to bring about. It remains that your consideration should range generally over the whole state of the Church: whether the common people are subject to the clergy, whether the clergy are subject to the priests, whether the priests are subject to God in that humility which is fitting; whether order is kept in monasteries and religious houses, and discipline watched over; whether ecclesiastical censure flourishes against wicked deeds and doctrines; whether the honesty and sanctity of the priests flourish in their venerable conduct; whether the obedience of the faithful peoples bears the flower and fruit; and finally, whether your own apostolic mandates and institutions are observed with the care that is due, so that nothing is found in the field of your Lord either left uncultivated through neglect or stolen by fraud. Do not doubt that such things can be found. I have at hand (to pass over many innumerable things that lie neglected everywhere) to show some of those things also which your right hand planted, now torn up. Did not your mouth promulgate the subjoined chapters in the Council of Reims? Who keeps them? You are mistaken if you think they are kept. If you do not think so, you yourself have either sinned by laying down what was not to be kept, or by overlooking that they are not kept. We command, you said, that both bishops and clerics shall not offend the sight, either by superfluity or dishonourable variety of colours, or by the slashing of garments, or by the tonsure of those looking on (whose form and example they ought to be); but rather that they condemn their errors in their acts, and demonstrate by love of innocence and by conduct what the dignity of the clerical order requires. For if, when warned by their bishops, they do not obey within forty days, they shall be deprived of the ecclesiastical benefices by the authority of the same Pontiffs. But if bishops neglect to inflict the penalty set down, since the faults of inferiors are to be ascribed to no one more than to slothful and negligent rulers, let them abstain from the pontifical office for as long as they do not impose on the clerics subject to them the penalty set down by us. We have also said that this should be added: that no one shall be ordained archdeacon or dean unless he is a deacon and presbyter. But archdeacons, deans and provosts who, being below the orders named above, have despised ordaining those who are disobedient, shall be deprived of the honour they have received. Moreover we forbid that the aforesaid honours be granted to young men, or to those placed below the sacred orders, but to those who are distinguished by prudence and merit of life.

units.la: Verba tua hæc, tu lanxisti, quid affectui mancipatum? Adhuc adolescentes, adhuc qui infra sacros ordines sunt, in Ecclesia promouentur. Quod ad primum capitulum pertinet, luxus vestium interdictus; sed non restrictus: poena dictata, sed minime secuta est. Iam quartus annus est, ex quo datum mandatum audiuimus, & neminem adhuc clericorum priuatum beneficio, nemine m Episcoporum suspensum ab officio luximus, ac luctu amarissimo dignum quod secutum est. Quid hoc impunitas incuriæ soboles, insolentiæ mater, radix impudentiæ, transgressionum nutrix. Et beatus si omni satagas cura malorum, omnium primam parentem cauere incuriam: sed adhuc tu operam dabis. Et nunc leua oculos tuos & vide, si non æque ut prius pellicula discolor sacrum ordinem decolorat, si non æque ut prius fissura enormis pene inguina nudat. Solent dicere, num de vestibus cura est Deo, & non magis de moribus? At forma hæc vestium, deformitatis mentium & morum indicium est. Quid sibi vult quod clerici aliud esse, aliud videri volunt? Id quidem minus castum, minusq; sincerum: nempe habitu milites, quæstu clericos, actu neutrum exhibent. Nam neque ut milites pugnant, neque ut clerici Euangelizant. Cuius ordinis sunt? cum utriusque esse cupiunt, utrumque deserunt, utrumque confundunt. Unusquisque inquit, in suo ordine resurget: isti in quo? an qui sine ordine peccauerunt, sine ordine peribunt? aut si summe sapiens Deus, veracicter creditur à summo neque deorsum nihil inordinatum relinquere; vetetor non alibi ordinandos, quam ubi nullus ordo, sed sempiternus horror inhabiter. O miserandam sponsam talibus creditam paranimphis, qui assignata cultui eius, proprio retinere quæstui non verentur: Non amici proferd sponsi, sed æmuli sunt. Et de his satis quæ sub te sunt, & si non ad materiæ copiam quæ est multa nimis, certe ad id quod proposui ego. Visenda iam quæ circa te sunt; sed ad ea ostium nobis quartus liber aperiet.
units.tr: "These are your words. You have weighed it, but what has been given over to passion? Still adolescents, still men below the holy orders, are promoted in the Church. As for the first chapter, luxury in clothing was forbidden, but not restrained. A penalty was prescribed, but it was scarcely followed. It is now the fourth year since we heard the command given, and we have seen no clergyman yet deprived of benefice, no bishop suspending anyone from office, and nothing worthy of the most bitter grief that followed. What is this impunity, the offspring of carelessness, the mother of insolence, the root of shamelessness, the nurse of transgressions? Happy would you be if you bent every care against evils and first guarded against carelessness, the parent of them all. But you will still be at it. And now lift your eyes and see whether the discoloured skin does not still disgrace the holy order as before, whether the enormous slit does not still nearly bare the groin as before. People are wont to say: Does God care about clothing, and not rather about morals? But this fashion of clothing is a sign of the deformity of minds and morals. What does it mean that clergy want to be one thing and seem another? This is surely less chaste and less sincere: they display the soldier in their dress, the tradesman in their gain, and neither in their conduct. For they fight neither as soldiers nor preach the gospel as clergy. To what order do they belong? While they wish to belong to both, they desert both and confuse both. 'Each will rise in his own order,' he says. But these men, in which order? Will those who sinned without order perish without order? Or if God, most wise, is rightly believed to leave nothing out of order, either high or low, it is forbidden that they be ordained anywhere but where there is no order and only everlasting horror dwells. O the pitiable bride entrusted to such go-betweens, who, while they are assigned to her worship, do not scruple to keep the profit for themselves! They are not friends of the bridegroom but his rivals. Enough about those under you, and if not as fully as the matter, which is far too abundant, deserves, at least as far as I intended. Now let us look at what concerns you. But the fourth book will open the door to those matters for us."

units.la: LIBER QVARTVS.
units.tr: Book Four.

units.la: SI mihi plenius innotuisset amantissime Eugeni, priora qualiter acceptaris, secundum hoc vel sidentius in reliquum processissem, vel cautius, aut certe substitissem omnino. Nunc vero quia ob locorum distantiam id minime datur, non mireris si prodit exilior sermo anceps, verecunde fateor ad medium veniens. Primis itaque considerationis partibus libris prioribus pertractatis, in manibus est de his addere, quæ circa te sunt. Et ipsa quidem sub te; sed quo priora, eo importuniora tibi: nempe coram posita incuriam non admittunt, non dissimulationem, non oblivionem: vehementius urgent, turbulentius irruunt, verendum ne obruant. Circa eiusmodi quam sobria & intentata consideratione opus sit, proprio te experimento edoctum satis non ambigo; alioquin si non cauta opportunaque interueniat consideratio, occupatio continuabitur & vexationis non erit modus, & sollicitudinis non erit finis: non tempus vacuum, non liberum cor, plus laboris, & minus utilitatis. Dico autem instantia illa tua quotidiana ab vrbe, à curia, à domestica Ecclesia tua: Hæc inquam circa te sunt, Clerus & populus tuus cui specialiter Episcoparis, ac per hoc specialis Curæ teneris debitor. Hi quoque qui tibi quotidie assistunt seniores populi, orbis iudices & qui item de domo & mensa tua sunt, Capellani, Cubicularii, ministri, quiq; diversis deputati officiis in obsequium tui, hi te familiarius visitant, frequentius pulsant, molestius sollicitant. Hi sunt qui nod verentur suscitare dilectam, & antequam ipsa velit. Et primum quidem clerum illum ordinatissimum esse decet, ex quo præcipue in omnem Ecclesiam cleri forma processit. Deinde omne quod perperam agitur te præsente, id tibi turpius. Interest gloriæ Sanctitatis tuæ vt non quos prae oculis habes ita ordinati, ita sint informati: quatenus totius honestatis & ordinis, ipsi speculum, ipsi sint forma. Inueniantur præcæteris oportet expediti ad officia, idonei ad Sacramenta, ad plebes erudiendas solliciti, circumspecti ad sese custodiendos in omni castitate. Quid de populo loquar? Populus Romanus est: nec breuius potui, nec expressius tamen aperire de tuis parrochianis quod sentio. Quid tam notum seculis, quam proteruia & fastus Romanorum? Gens insueta paci, tumultui assueta: gens immitis & intractabilis, vsque adhuc subdi nescia, nisi cum non valet resistere. Et plaga, tibi incumbit cura hæc, dissimulare non licet. Rides me forsitan, fore incurabilem persuasus; noli diffidere, curam exigeris, non curationem. Deniq; audisti, curam illius habe, & non curare vel sanare illum. Verum dixit quidam:
units.tr: If I had learned more fully, dearest Eugenius, how you received the earlier books, I would have proceeded further in this way, either with more confidence or with more caution, or I would have stopped altogether. As it is, the distance between our places makes such knowledge impossible, so do not be surprised if my discourse comes out thinner and more hesitant, as I confess with some diffidence while I approach the middle. Having treated the first parts of consideration in the earlier books, I now mean to add what concerns you, which is the matter in hand. These things lie beneath you, but the earlier ones are the more troublesome to you. Things set before your eyes allow no carelessness, no pretending, no forgetting; they press harder and rush in more violently, and I fear they may overwhelm you. I do not doubt that you have learned from your own experience how sober and deliberate such consideration must be. Otherwise, if a careful and timely consideration does not intervene, the business will go on without end, the vexation will have no limit and the anxiety no end. There will be no free time, no unburdened heart, more labour and less profit. I mean those constant demands of yours from the city, from the court, and from your own household Church: these, I say, are the things that surround you. There are your clergy and people, over whom you are appointed bishop and to whom you are specially bound by the duty of care. Then there are the senior men of the people who attend you daily, the judges of the world, and those who belong to your household and table: chaplains, chamberlains, attendants, and those assigned to various offices in your service. These visit you more familiarly, knock more often, and importune you more troublesomely. They are the ones who do not hesitate to rouse the beloved before she herself wishes it. First, that clergy ought to be most orderly, since from them the pattern of the clergy has gone out into the whole Church. Next, whatever is done wrongly in your presence reflects more shamefully upon you. It is for the glory of your Holiness that those you have before your eyes should be so ordered and so instructed, so that they may be a mirror and a pattern of all honesty and order. They ought to be found above others ready for their duties, fit for the sacraments, eager to teach the common people, and watchful to guard themselves in all chastity. What shall I say of the people? They are the Roman people. I could neither speak more briefly nor state more plainly what I think of your parishioners. What is so well known through the ages as the arrogance and haughtiness of the Romans? A people unused to peace and accustomed to tumult; a people fierce and intractable, never willing to submit unless it cannot resist. You have this care laid upon you, and you may not shrink from it. You may perhaps laugh at me, persuaded that the disease is incurable. Do not despair: you are required to take care of it, not to cure it. At last you have heard: take care of him, and do not neglect or heal him. Someone has said truly:

units.la: Non est ib Medico semper releuetur vt ager.
units.tr: The physician cannot always relieve the sick man.

units.la: Non ait, plus omnibus profui: aut plus omnibus fructificaui; verbum insolens religiosissime vitans. Alias autem noverat homo quem docuit Deus, quia vnusquisque secundum suum laborem accipiet, non secundum proueniu m. Et ob hoc in laboribus potius, quam in profectibus gloriandum putauit: sicut alibi quoque habes ipsum dicentem; in laboribus pluribus. Ita quæso fac tu, quod tuum est: nam Deus quod suum est latis absque tua sollicitudine & anxietate curabit. Planta, riga, fer cutam, & tuas explicuisti partes: sane incrementum vbi voluerit dabit Deus, non tu. Vbi forte noluerit tibi deperit nihil, dicente Scriptura: reddet Deus mercedem laborum sanctorum suorum. Securus labor queritl quem nullus valet euacuare defectus: & hoc dixerim absque praeiudicio diuinae potentiae & bonitatis. Scio induratum cor populi huius, sed potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae. Quis sit fireuerratur & ignoscat, conuertat & sanet eos? Sed non est propositi mei dicere Deo, quod facere debeat; tibi vtinam possim quod oportet & prout oportet, suadere. At locus dubius, & scrupulosa incidit disputatio: nam vbi adoriar dicere quod lentio, video satis quod imminet. Clamabitur insuetum; nam iustum negari non poterit. Ego vero nec insuetum quidem assentirim, nempe assuetum fuisse scio, ac per hoc in dissuetum potuisse venire, sed non redire in insuetum.
units.tr: He did not say, "I have profited more than all of them," or "I have borne more fruit than all of them": he most religiously avoided that unusual boast. He knew, as the man taught by God, that each one will receive according to his own labour, not according to his success. So he thought he should glory in his labours rather than in his progress, as you will find him saying elsewhere: "in labours more abundant." So I beg you, do what is yours to do, for God will take care of what is his without your anxiety and distress. Plant, water, bear the labour, and you have fulfilled your part. Truly, God will give the increase when he wills, not you. If perhaps he is unwilling, you lose nothing, since Scripture says: God will repay the labours of his saints. Labour is secure which no failure can make void. I say this without prejudice to the divine power and goodness. I know the heart of this people is hardened, but God is able to raise up children of Abraham from these stones. Who will pardon them, convert them and heal them? But it is not my purpose to tell God what he ought to do; I only wish I could persuade you of what is fitting and in the manner fitting. But the place is doubtful, and a delicate question arises. When I begin to say what I think, I see clearly what threatens me. It will be called unusual; for it cannot be denied to be just. Yet I would not even agree that it is unusual, for I know it was once customary, and so it could have passed into disuse, but it cannot return to being unusual.

units.la: An vero assuetum quis neget, quod constat non modo aliquando factum, sed aliquandiu factitatum? Quid illud sit dicam, & non proderit. Cur? quia non placebit satrapis, plus maiestati quam veritati fidentibus. Fuerunt ante te, qui se totos quibus pascendis exponerent, pastoris nomine & opere gloriantes, nil sibi reputantes indignum, nisi quod saluti ouium obuiare putaretur: non quaerentes quae sua sunt, sed impendentes. Impendere curam, impendere substantiam, impendere & seipsos: unde unus illorum; & ego, ait super impendar pro animabus vestris. Et tanquam dicerent, non venimus ministrari, sed ministrare: ponebant quoties oportuisset sine sumptu Euangelium. Vnus erat de subditis quaestus, una pompa, unaq; voluptas: si quomodo eos possent parere Domino plebem perfectam. Id omnimodo satagebant, etiam in multa contritione cordis, & corporis; in labore & erumna, infame & siti, in frigore & nuditate. Vbi nunc quaeso consuetudo haec? Subiit dissimilis valde, longe in aliud mutata sunt studia, & vtinam non in peius. Cura tamen & anxietas, & aemulatio & sollicitudo fateor perseuerant; translata haec, non imminuta. Testimonium vobis perhibeo, quod nec substantiae parcitis, non magis quam ante. Diuersa autem locatio, dissimilitudinem facit: magna abusio, pauci ad os legislatoris, ad manus omnes respiciunt. Nec immerito tamen omne Papale negotium illi agunt.
units.tr: But who would deny that what was customary is what has not only once been done but was long practised? I would say what that custom was, but it will do no good. Why? Because it will not please the satraps, who trust more in majesty than in truth. Before you there were those who gave themselves wholly to feeding those committed to them, glorying in the name and work of shepherd, counting nothing beneath them except what was thought to hinder the salvation of the sheep; not seeking their own things, but spending themselves. They spent care, they spent substance, they spent even themselves. Hence one of them said: and I, he says, shall be spent for your souls. As if they would say, we have not come to be ministered unto, but to minister. They offered the gospel without charge whenever it was needed. There was one gain for the subjects, one display, one delight: if somehow they could prepare for the Lord a perfect people. They laboured for this in every way, even in much affliction of heart and body; in labour and weariness, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness. Where now, I ask, is that custom? It has passed into something very different; their aims have been changed far away into something else, and I wish it were not for the worse. Yet care, anxiety, rivalry and solicitude, I confess, still persist; they have been transferred, not diminished. I bear you witness that you spare your substance no more than before. But the different arrangement makes the difference: great is the abuse, when few look to the mouth of the lawgiver and all look to the hands. Yet they do not undertake all this Papal business without reason.

units.la: Quae dabis mihi de tota maxima urbe, qui te in Papam recepterit, precio seu spe precii non intereunte? Et tunc potissimum voluerit dominari, cum professi fuerint seruitutem: fideles se spondent, ut opportunius fidentibus noceant. Ex hoc non erit consilium tibi a quo se arcendos putent, non secretum quo se non ingerant. Si stante prae foribus quoquam illorum, moram vel modicam fecerit ostiarius; ego tunc pro illo esse nolo. Et nunc experire paucis nouerimine & ego aliquatenus motes gentis: ante omnia sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bonum autem facere nesciunt. Hi inuisi terrae & coelo, utrique iniecere manus: impii in Deum, temerarii in sancta, seditiosi in inuicem, aemuli in vicinos, inhumani in extraneos, quos neminem amantes amat nemo, & cum timeri affectant ab omnibus, omnes timeant necesse est. Hi sunt qui subesse non sustinent, praeesse non norunt; superioribus infidiles, inferioribus importabiles: hi inuerecundi ad petendum, ad negandum frontosi: hi importuni ut accipiant, inquieti donec accipiant, ingrati vbi acceperint. Docuerunt linguam suam grandia loqui, cum operantur exigua: largissimi promissores, & parcissimi exhibitores: blandissimi adulatores, & mordacissimi detractores: simplicissimi dissimulatores & maligni proditores. Excurrimus usque huc, plenius te atque expressius admonendum putantes, horumque circa te sunt in hac parte. Iam ad ordinem recurramus; quale est quod de spoliis Ecclesiarum emuntur, qui dicunt tibi euge, euge? Pauperum vita in plateis diuitum seminatur, argentum micat in luto, accurritur undique, tollit illud non pauperior, sed fortior, aut qui forte citius praecurrit. At te tamen mos iste, vel potius mos ista non coepit, in te utinam desinat: sed reliqua persequamur. Inter haec tu Pastor procedis deauratus, tam multa circumdatus varietate; oues quid capiunt? si auderem dicere daemonum magis quam ouium pascua haec. Scilicet sic factitabat Petrus, sic Paulus ludebat? Vides omne Ecclesiasticum Zelum feruere sola pro dignitate tuenda? honori rerum datur; sanctitati nihil aut parum. Si causa requirente paulo summissius agere ac socialiter te habere tentaueris; absit, inquiunt, non decet, tempori non congruit, maiestati non conuenit, quam geras personam attendito. De placito Dei ultima mentio est, pro lactura salutis nulla cunctatio: nisi quod sublime est, hoc salutare dicamus, & quod gloriam redolet, id iustum. Ita omne humile probro ducitur inter palatinos, ut facilius qui esse, quam qui apparere humilis velit, inuenias. Timor Domini simplicitas reputatur; ne dicam fatuitas: virum circumspectum & amicum propriae conscientiae, calumniantur hypocritam. Porro amatorem quietis, & sibi interdum vacantem, inutilem dicunt. Quid ergo tu? Euigilas ne adhuc ad istos qui circumdederunt te laqueis mortis? quaeso fustine paulisper & supporta me; Imo da veniam non tam temere quam timide haec loquenti: aemulor de aemulatione bona, & vtinam quam vehementi, tam vtili.
units.tr: What will you give me concerning the whole great city, which has received you as Pope for a price, or for the hope of a price that does not perish? And they will wish to rule most especially when they have professed servitude: they pledge themselves faithful, so that they may harm those who trust them more conveniently. From this there will be no counsel for you from which they think they should be kept away, no secret place into which they do not thrust themselves. If, while one of them stands before your doors, the doorkeeper delays him even a little, I for my part would not want to be that doorkeeper. And now learn in a few words, for I too know something of this people's disposition: they are wise to do evil, but to do good they know not. They are hateful to earth and heaven, and they have laid hands on both: impious against God, reckless against holy things, seditious against one another, rivals of their neighbours, inhuman to strangers, whom no one loves because they love no one, and since they seek to be feared by all, all must necessarily fear them. These are they who cannot endure to be subject and do not know how to rule; faithless to superiors, unbearable to inferiors. They are shameless in asking and brazen in refusing; importunate when they are to receive, restless until they receive, ungrateful once they have received. They have taught their tongues to speak big things while they do small ones; they are most lavish in promises and most sparing in performance; most flattering in their adulation and most biting in their detraction; most simple in their dissimulation and malicious in their betrayal. We have run on this far, thinking that you should be warned more fully and more plainly, and so about those who surround you in this part. Now let us return to the order. What is it that is bought from the spoils of the Churches by those who say to you, "Well done, well done"? The lives of the poor are sown in the squares of the rich; silver glitters in the mud; people rush from every side to pick it up, and it is taken not by the poorer but by the stronger, or by whoever perhaps runs faster. But this custom, or rather this habit, did not begin with you; I wish it might end with you. But let us pursue the rest. Meanwhile you go forth as a gilded Pastor, surrounded by so much variety: what do the sheep receive? If I dared to say, these are the pastures of demons rather than of sheep. Did Peter act in this way? Did Paul play such games? Do you see all ecclesiastical zeal boiling only to defend dignity? Things are given to honour; to holiness, nothing or very little. If, when the cause requires it, you try to act a little more humbly and to conduct yourself more sociably, "Far be it," they say, "it is not fitting, it does not suit the time, it does not agree with majesty; consider the person you bear." Of God's good pleasure there is the last mention; there is no hesitation about losing salvation. Unless we say that what is lofty is saving, and what smells of glory is just. So everything humble is counted a disgrace among the courtiers, so that you will more easily find someone who wishes to be, than someone who wishes to appear, humble. The fear of the Lord is reckoned simplicity, not to say foolishness; a man who is circumspect and a friend of his own conscience they call a hypocrite. Further, a lover of quiet, who sometimes keeps time for himself, they call useless. What then will you do? Are you still awake for those who have surrounded you with the snares of death? I beg you, bear with me for a little while and endure me. Nay, pardon one who speaks these things not so much rashly as timidly. I am zealous with a good zeal, and I wish it were as useful as it is vehement.

units.la: Scio vbi habitas, increduli & subuersores sunt tecum: lupi non oues sunt, talium tamen tu pastor. Vtilis consideratio, qua forte inueneris quomodo si fieri possit conuertas eos, ne ipsi subuertantur te. Quid diffidimus posse reuerti in oues, e quibus versi in lupos potuerunt: hic, hic non parco tibi, ut parcat Deus. Pastorem te populo huic certe aut nega, aut exhibe: Non negabis, ne cuius sedem tenes, te neget haeredem.
