Petrus hic est, qui nescitur processisse aliquando vel gemmis ornatus, vel sericis, non rectus auro, non vectus aequo albo, nec stipatus milite, nec circumstrepentibus septus ministris: absq; his tamen credidit satis posse impleri salutare mandatum; si amas me, pasce oues meas. In his successibus non Petro, sed Constantino. Consulo toleranda pro tempore, non affectanda pro debito: ad ea te potius incito, quorum te scio debitorem. Et si purpuratus, & si deauratus incedens; non est tamen quod horreas operam, curamve pastoralem, pastoris heres; non est quod erubescas Euangelium. Quanquam si volens Euangelizes inter Apostolos quidem, etiam gloria tibi est: Euangelizare pascere est. Fac opus Euangelistae, & pastoris opus implesti. Dracones inquis, me mones pascere & Scorpiones, non oues: propter hoc, inquam, magis aggredere eos; sed verbo, non ferro. Quid te denuo vsurpare gladium tenes, quem semel iussus es ponere in vaginam? quem tamen qui tuum negat, non satis mihi videtur attendere verbum Domini dicentis hic, converte gladium tuum in vaginam . Tuus ergo & ipse, tuo forsitan nutu, etsi non tua manu euaginandus: alioquin si nullo modo ad te pertineret & is, dicentibus Apostolis: esse gladii duo hic; non respondisset Dominus, satis est; sed nimis est. Utrumque ergo Ecclesiae, & spiritualis scilicet gladius, & materialis; sed is quidem pro Ecclesia, ille vero & ab Ecclesia exercendus: ille sacerdotis, is militis manu: sed sane ad nutum Sacerdotis, & iussum Imperatoris, & de hoc alias. Nunc vero arripe illum, qui tibi ad feriendum creditus est, & vulnera ad salutem, si non omnes, si non vel multos; certe quos possis. Non sum, inquis, melior quam patres mei; quem illorum domus exasperans, non dico audiuit, sed non irrisit? Ideo tu insiste magis, si forte audiant & quiescant; insiste & resistentibus. Dicendo haec, forte nimius dicar: num nostra illa vox, insta opportune, importune? Hunc, si audes, nimium appellato. Prophetae praecipitur: clama ne cesses. Ad quos nisi ad sceleratos & peccatores? annuncia, inquit, populo meo scelera eorum, & domui Iacob peccata eorum. Prudenter aduerte, & sceleratos perhiberi, & populum Domini. Puta de his idem: & si scelerati & si iniqui, vide ne audias, quod vni ex his meis non feci, nec mihi feci. Fateor populum istum extitisse usque adhuc durafronte, & indomito corde; sed utrum etiam indomabili, nescio unde liquido scire possis. Potest fore, quod nec dum fuit; si diffidis tu: Sed apud Deum non erit impossibile omne verbum. Si dura fronte sunt, durato & tu e contra tuam: nil tam durum, quod duriori non cedat. Dominus ad Prophetam: dedi frontem tuam duriorem frontibus eorum. Unum est quod te absoluit, se egisti, cum populo illo, ut possis dicere: populo meus quid tibi debui facere & non feci? sic, sic fecisti nec profecisti; est denum quod facias & quod dicas: exi de Ur Chaldaeorum, & dicito quia oportet me & aliis ciuitatibus evangelizare, puto nec poenitebit exilii orbe pro urbe commutato. Veniamus ad collaterales & coadiutores tuos; hi seduli tibi, hi intimi sunt, tibi potissimum sunt, si mali aeque plus tibi. Nec te dixeris sanum dolentem latera, hoc est, ne te dixeris bonum malis innitentem: aut si bonus sis, bonitas tui solius quem fructum afferre potest? sicut in superiore libro dixisse me memini. Quid inquam emolumenti affert Ecclesiis Dei, tua vnius hominis iustitia, vbi sententia praevalet aliter affectorum? Sed nec tuta tibi tua bonitas obsessa malis, non magis quam sanitas vicino serpente. Non est quo te subducas malo intestino, & e regione bonum domesticum, eo amplius quo saepius iuvat: sed sine leuent siue graucnt cui rectius imputandum quam tibi, qui tales aut elegisti, aut admisisti? Non de omnibus dico, nam sunt quos non elegisti; sed ipsi te: at potestatem non habent, nisi quam tu eis aut tribueris, aut permiseris. Ad idem ergo reuertimur; tibi imputa quicquid patieris ab eo, qui sine te potest facere nihil. His exceptis, dececetero non inconsiderate vt vides eligendi quoque seu colligendi sunt in opus ministerii huius: tuum est vndecunq; vocare & adscisicere tibi (exemplo Moysi) senes non iuuenes; sed senes non tam aetate quam moribus, quos tu nosti, quia senes populi sunt. Annon eligendi de toto orbe, orbem iudicaturi? Sane huic negotio, non se ingerat rogans: consilio, non prece agendum est. Sunt quae necessario a nobis rogantium aut extorquet importunitas, aut necessitas meretur: at istud in his quae nostra sunt. Vbi autem non licet quod volo facere, quis locus roganti? nisi forte qui me rogat, hic rogat vt quod vult hoc liceat mihi, & non magis vt velim. Alius pro alio; alius forte & pro se rogat: pro quo rogaris sit suspectus; qui ipse rogat pro se iam iudicatus est, nec interest per se an per alium quis roget. Clericum curiam frequentantem qui non sit de curia, ad idem noris pertinere ambientium genus adulantem & ad placitum cuiusque loquentem, vnum de rogantibus puta, etiam si nihil rogauerit. Scorpioni non est in facie quod formides, sed pungit in cauda: si ad talium blanditias cor tuum, vt assolet, molitl senseris, theminemris scriptum: Omnis homo primo bonum vinum ponit, cum autem inebriati fuerit, tunc id quod deterius est. Pari pondere aestimaueris eius humilitatem, qui timet, & eius qui sperat: viri callidi & dolosi proprium esse solet tunc praetendere humilitatem, cum aliquid obtinere voluerit, de qualibus dicit Scriptura: est qui se humiliat nequiter, & interiora eius plena sunt dolo. De vobis ipsis sume sententiam huius euidens ac familiare exemplum: quantos quos supplices admisisti, postmodum sustinuisti gratis insolentes, contumaces, rebelles? quod quidem interius malum tegunt principia, posterioris ... Verbosulum adolescentem & studentem eloquentiae cum sapientiae sit inanis, non aliiiustitiae hostem reputes. Pro huiusmodi falsis fratribus dicit tibi magister: manus cito nemini ... vniverso hoc pestilenti genere hominum; curae tibi maximae sit introducere ... introduxisse poeniteat: turpe est tibi saepius retractare quod feceris, & iudicium tuum ... periclitari non decet. Diligenter proinde omne quod faciendum erit tracta apud te, & cum his qui te diligunt: tracta autem ante factum, quia post factum sera retractatio est. Sapientis consilium est: omnia fac cum consilio, & post factum non paenitebis. Et hoc tibi persuade, qui admittendi sunt difficile in curia posse probari; & ideo si fieri potest viros probatos oportere deligi, non probandos. Nos in monasteriis omnes recipimus; spe meliorandi: at curia bonos facilius lius recipere, magis quam facere consueuit. Quia si plures in ea defecisse bonos, quam malos profecisse probauimus; quærendi sane quibus nec defectus timeatur, nec profectus optetur, utpote iam perfectis. Itaque non volentes, neque currentes assumito; sed cunctantes, sed renuentes: etiam coge illos & compelle intrare. In talibus ut opinor requiescet spiritus tuus, quinon sunt attritæ frontis; sed verecundi, sed timorati, præter Dominum timeant nihil, nihil sperent nisi a Deo: qui aduentantium non manus attendant, sed necessitates; qui stent viriliter pro afflictis, & iudicent in æquitate pro mansuetis terræ; qui sint compositi ad mores, probati ad sanctimoniam, parati ad obedientiam, mansueti ad patientiam, subiecti ad disciplinam, rigidi ad censuram, catholici ad fidem, fideles ad dispensationem, concordes ad pacem; conformes ad unitatem: qui sint in iudicio recti, in consilio prouidi, in iubendo discreti, in disponendo industrii, in agendo strenui, in loquendo modesti, in aduersitate securi, in prosperitate devoti, in zelo sobrii, in misericordia non remissi, in ocio non otiosi, in hospitio non dissoluti, in conuiuio non effusi, in cura rei familiaris non anxii, alienæ non cupidi, suæ non prodigi, ubique & in omnibus circumspecti. Qui legatione pro Christo fungi quotiens opus erit, nec iussi renuant, nec iniussi affectent: qui quod verecunde excusant obstinatius non renuant: qui missi post aurum, non eant; sed Christum sequantur: qui quæstum legationis non existiment, nec requirant datum, sed fructum. Qui Regibus Ioannem exhibeant, Ægyptiis Moysen, fornicantibus Phinees, Heliam idololatris, Heliseum auaris, Petrum mentientibus, Paulû blasphemantibus, negociantibus Christum. Qui vulgus non spernant, sed doceant; diuites non palpent, sed terreant; pauperes non gravent, sed foveant; minas principum non pauent, sed contemnant. Qui non cum turba intrent, nec cum ira exeant: qui Ecclesias non spolient, sed emendent: qui marsupia non exhauriant, sed corda reficiant, & crimina corrigant, famæ prouideant suæ, nec iniuideant alienæ. Qui orandi studiû gerant, & vsum habeant, ac de omni re orationi plus fidant, quam suæ industriæ & labori: quorum ingressus pacificus, non molestus exitus sit: quorum sermo ædificatio, quorum vita iustitia, quorû præsentia grata, quorû memoria in benedictione. Qui se amabiles præbeant, non verbo sed opere; reverendos exhibeant, sed actu, non fastu: qui humiles cû humilibus, & cû innocentibus innocentes; duros dure redarguat, malignantes coerceant, reddant retributionem superbis. Qui non de dote viduæ, & patrimonio crucifixi se vel suos ditare festinent; gratis dantes, quod gratis acceperunt, gratis facientes iudicium iniuriam patientibus, vindictam in nationibus, increpationes in populis. Qui de tuo deniq; spiritu illorum instar septuaginta Moysi accepisse cernantur, per quem siue absentes siue præsentes, contendant placere tibi, placere Deo: qui ad te redeant fatigati quidem, sed non sufficarinati; simul & gloriantes non quod curiosa seu preciosa quæq; terrarum attulerunt, sed quod reliquerint pacem regnis, legem barbaris, quietem monasteriis, Ecclesiis ordinem, clericis disciplinam, Deo populum acceptabilem sectatorem bonorum operum. Dignum nunc ad medium venire factum dulcis memoriæ Martini nostri; nosti hoc, sed an meminceris ignoro; is Cardinalis Presbyter, functus aliquando legatione in Datia, tam pauper remeauit, ut pene expensis & æquis deficientibus vix peruenire Florentiam ibi Episcopus loci donauit ei equum quo Pisas usque, ubi eramus tunc, peruectus est. Postridie credo securus Episcopus (erat enim illi causa cum aduersario, & agendi aderat dies) cœpit requirere suffragia amicorum: cumq; per singulos sollicitaretur, ventum est ad Martinum; fiducia erat maior in illo, qui non posset immemor esse recentis beneficii; tum Martinus: decepisti me, inquit, nesciebam tibi imminere negotium, tolle equum tuum, ecce in stabulo est, & hora eadem resignauit illi. Quid dicis mi Eugeni? nonne alterius seculi res est, redisse legatum de terra auri sine auro, transisse per terram argenti & argentum nescisse, donum insuper quod poterat esse suspectum illico reiecisse? Sed o mihi locum suauem vbi incidit occasio memorandi & nominandi suauissimi odoris virum, Episcopum loquor Gaufridum Carnotensem, qui legationem in partibus Aquitaniæ propriis sumtibus strenue administrauit; idque annos plures. Rem loquar quam vidi ipse, eram cum eo in terra illa, cum à quodam Presbytero præsentatus illi est piscis quem vulgo vocant sturgionem: percunctatus legatus quanti venierit, non accipio, inquit, nisi receperis precium, & resignauit, solidos quinque inuito & verecundo. Item cum essemus in quodam oppido, Domina illius oppidi obtulit ei pro devotione cum manutergio duas vel tres parapsides pulchras, ligneas tamen: quas aliquandiu intuens; homo scrupulosæ conscientiæ, laudauit eas; sed non acquieuit accipere. Quādo argenteas recepisset, qui ligneas refutauit? Nō fuerunt qui possent legato dicere, ditauimus Abraham. Ipse vero cum Samuele libere concionabatur ad omnes: loquimini de me coram Domino & coram Christo eius, utrum bouem cuiusquam talerum aut asinum, si quem pia calumniatus sum, si oppressi aliquem, si de manu cuiusquam munus accepi, & contemnam illud hodie, vobis restituam. O si talium daretur virorum copia, quales perstrinximus nunc? quid te felicius, quid illo iucundius seculo? Nonne lecunda ab æternitate illorum tibi temporum beatitudo videretur, cum te quaqua versum procedens, stipatum videres tam inclito agmine beatorum? Si te nouî hæres; & alium trahens suspirium tecum loqueris; putas fore posse quod dicitur? putas hic simus quousque hæc fiant? quis det viuere, vt videre contingat? O si viderem in vita mea Ecclesiam Dei talibus innixam columnis! O si Domini mei sponsam cernere tantæ commissam fidei, tantæ creditam puritati? quid me beatius, quid me securius? cum eiusmodi circa me vitæ meæ & custodes spectarem, simul & testes? quibus omnia mea secreta secure committerem; communicarem consilia, quibus me totum refunderem tanquam alteri mihi: qui si velle aliquatenus deuiare nō sinerent, frenarent præcipitě, dormientem suscitarent; quorum rae reverentia & libertas oppressa reprimeret, excedentes corrigeret; quorum me constantia & fortitudo nutantē firmaret, erigeret diffidentem: quorum me fides & sanctitas ad quæqʒ sancta, ad quæque honesta, ad quæque pudica, ad quæque amabilia & bonæ famæ provocaret. Et nunc reduc oculos mi Eugeni, ad eum qui nunc est curiæ siue Ecclesiæ statum, & studia prælatorum, eorum præsertim qui sunt in circuitu tuo. Sed de his hactenus ego: palpavi non fodi parietem, tibi licet fodere & videre, vt pote Prophetæ filio, mihi progredi non est fas. Vnum dico quod in facie est; ridicule ministri vestri, vestris se compresbyteris antefferre conantur: non hoc ratio habet, non antiquitas habuit, non consentit auctoritas. Et si de sua consuetudine calumnia struitur, melius profecto illa quam summus ordo contemnitur: friuolum tamen satis, vnde maxime obtinere id volunt. Nos sumus, inquiunt, qui in omni celebritate Domino Papæ coniunctiores assistimus, sedenti propiores assidemus, præcedentem posteriores præcedimus: hoc totum non dignitatis priuilegium, sed sedulitatis debitum est, Diaconi nomen solenni ipsa administratione interpretans. Denique Presbyteris ordinata confessione ambientibus maiestatem, vos ad pedes sedetis, propiores assistitis, vt habeat paratiores. In Euangelijs legimus, quia facta est contentio inter discipulos, quis eorum videretur esse maior: beatus esses si sic circa te cætera tenerentur. Tædet iam curiæ, exeundum palatio, domi expectant nos: hi non modo circa, sed quodam modo intra te sunt. Non est superuacua consideratio, qua intendis disponere domui tuæ, prouidere his qui in sinu tuo & in gremio tuo sunt: ego dico & necessaria. Paulum audi: Si quis domui suæ præesse nescit, quomodo Ecclesiæ Dei diligentiam habebit? Item, Si quis suorum, & maxime domesticorum, curam non habet, fidem negauit, & est infideli deterior. Et hæc dicens, non te moneo summis occupatum intendere infimis, & quasi minutum fieri; in minimis impendere quod maximis debes. Quid te intrices, vnde te eripuit Deus? Hac, inquit, omnia adiicientur vobis. Veruntamen & hoc oportet facere, & illa non omittere: at illa per te agens, per te etiam oportet prouideas, qui pro te de his prouideant. Nam si vnus è seruis per se non sufficit simul & custodiæ, & iumentorum, & curæ mensarum; tu per te quomodo intendere valeas & tuæ domui & Domini pariter de qua scriptum est: O Israel quam magna est domus Domini? vacuum prorsus à sollicitudine rerum minorum & vilium oportet esse animum, tam magnis & tam multis intentum rebus; oportet liberum, quem nulla sibi vendicet violenta occupatio: oportet ingenuum, quem nulla deorsum trahat indigna affectio: oportet rectum, quem nulla seorsum auertat sinistra intentio: oportet cautum, quem nulla subeat furtiua suspicio: oportet vigilem, quem nulla concutiat repentina turbatio; oportet inuictum, quem nulla fatiget vel continua tribulatio: oportet amplum, quem nulla coarctet rei temporalis amissio. His te non dubites & bonis priuandum, & feriendum malis; si animum diuidens & Dei rebus, & tuis pariter reiculis volueris impartiri: procurandus quem implices, qui pro te dico, non tecum. Quædam per temet facies, quædam per te & alios simul, quædam per alios & absque te. Quis sapiens & intelliget hæc? non quod inter ista dormitet consideratio tua: ego vero agenda domus tuæ, sub eo genere, quod nouissimum posui, locanda censuerim; per alium, vt dixi, illa facies. At is si fidelis non fuerit, fraudabit; si non fuerit prudens, fraudabitur. Quærendus proinde fidelis & prudens, quem constituas supra familiam tuam, adhuc inutilis est, si tertium deest: quæris quid hoc? auctoritas. Quid enim prodest ei velle & scire quoque disponere prout necesse est, si quod scit, & vult, non potest? Danda ergo facultas agendi pro libitu: si in præiudicium rationis putas hoc fieri, memento fidelem qui agere nihilominus pro ratione volet, attende prudentem; qui agere nihilominus pro ratione sciet. Sed fidelis solersque voluntas tunc prodit, cum ei affatim suppeter, vnde tota facilitate mancipetur affectui, cunctis sine cunctatione parentibus. Subdendi igitur omnes, nullum patiatur contradictorem; nemo qui dicat, cur feci sic? potestatem habeat excludere, & admittere quos voluerit, mutare ministros, transferre ministeria ad quos & quando voluerit. Ita timori sit omnibus, vt sit & vtilitati: præsit omnibus, vt omnibus prosit, & de omnibus. Clandestinas & subarratas delationes non recipias aduersus eum; magis detractiones censueris. Et hanc velim generalem tibi constituas regulam, vt omnem qui palam veretur dicere quod in aure locutus est, suspectum habeas. Quod si te iudicante dicendum coram ille renuerit, delatorem iudices, non accusatorem: itaque vnus omnibus faciendā iniungat, & vni omnes respondeant. Tu illi habeas fidem, vacans tibi & Ecclesiæ Dei: si quo minus aut fidelis inueniatur, aut prudens; fideli potius committendum; sanè duobus tutius hoc: quanquam si idoneus non reperitur, etsi minus fidelem sustinere potius consulo, quam te immergere labyrintho hunc. Memento Saluatorem Iudam Oeconomum habuisse. Quid Episcopo turpius quam incumbere suppellectili & substantiolæ suæ, scrutari omnia, scicitari de singulis, morderi suspitionibus, moueri ad quæque perdita vel neglecta? Ad verecundiam dico, huiusmodi scrutantium quotidie vnam substantiam suam, numerantium singula, de minutis exigentium rationem. Non ita ille Ægyptius, qui Ioseph omnibus tradidit, quod habebat in domo sua. Erubescat Christianus, Christiano sua non credens: homo ... seruo, super omnia bona sua constituens eum; & hic erat alienigena. Miseri, quibus Episcopi ad manum habent quibus animas credant, & qui suas committant ... non impediunt. Optimi videlicet æstimatores rerum, qui magnam de minimis, ... de maximis curam gerant. Sed vt liquido datur intelligi, pacientius ferimus ... quam nostram: quotidianas expensas, quotidiano reciprocanus scrutinio, & ... Domini gregis detrimenta nescimus. De precio escarum, & numero panum, cum mi-nistris nistris quotidiana discussio est: raro admodum cum Presbyteris celebratur collatio de peccatis populorum. Cadit alina, & est qui subleuet eam: perit anima, & nemo qui reputet. Nec mirum cum nec nostros quidem assiduos sentiamus defectus; nonne ad singulas supputationes ista irascimur, vrimur, anxiamur? quam tolerabilius rerum, quam mentium sustineremus iacturam. Quare, inquit, magis fraudem patimini? Quaeso tu qui alios doces, doce teipsum; si tamen iam non docuisti, pluris te habere, quam tua. Transitoria ista quae fluere tibi nullo pacto queunt; fac vt a te transeant non per te. Riuus qua fluit cauat terram: sic discursus temporalium conscientiam rodit. Si potest torrens in agros excurrere sine laesione satorum, & tu te ista sine laesione satorum, & tu te ista sine vulnere mentis posse tractare confidito. Omnimodis consulo studeas auertere a te concursum horum, multa nescias, plurima dissimules, nonnulla obliuiscaris. Sunt tamen quae ignorare te nolim, mores quorumque & studia: non oportet vt vicia domus tuae vltimus scias, quod quamplurimis nouimus contigisse. Quapropter vt dixi alius alia dispenset, de disciplina tu prouide. Istud nemini credas, si insolentior coram te vel sermo sonuerit, vel habitus apparuerit: manus tua super eiusmodi, tu vlciscere iniuriam tuam. Impunitas ausum parit, ausus excessum. Domum Episcopi decet sanctitudo, decet modestia, decet honestas; horum disciplina custos. Sacerdotes domestici, aut caeteris honestiores, aut fabula omnibus sunt: in vultu, in habitu, in incessu, illorum qui circa te sunt; nihil residere impudicum nil indecens patiaris. Discant a te Coepiscopi tui comatulos pueros & comptos adolescentes secum non habere: certe inter mitratos discurrere calamistratos non decet. & memento quod sapiens admonet: filia tibi sunt, noli facicem tuam hilarem ad ea ostendere. Nec austeritatem tamen suadeo tibi, sed grauitatem: illa infirmiores fugat, haec reprimit leuiores: illa si adsit odibilem, haec si desit contemptibilem reddit; in omnibus tamen modus melior. Ego nec seueritus velim, nec dissolutius. Quid hac mediocritate gratius, vt non de seueritate sis oneri, nec de familiaritate contemptui? In palatio Papam, domi te patremfamilias exhibe: ament te domestici tui, si non, facito vt timeant. Vtilis semper custodia oris, quae tamen affabilitatis gratiam non excludat. Ergo vbique frenanda est lingua praeceps, maxime autem in conuiuio: ille conuenientior habitus si tu actu quidem seuerus sis; vultu serenus, verbo serius. Capellani & qui iugiter diuinis intersunt officiis, non sint sine honore: tuum est tales tibi prouidere, qui digni sunt; seruiatur eis ab omnibus tanquam tibi. Necessaria de manu tua accipiant; his contenti sicut quae tu prouideris illis, tu vide ne egeant. Super hoc quem forte ab aduentantibus petere deprehendes, iudica Giezitam. Id de hostiariis, id de caeteris officialibus discernendum. Verum hoc exabundanti, nam formam istam iam olim a te positam recordamur. Quid tuo dignius apostolatu? quid salubrius ad conscientiam, honestius ad famam, vtilius ad exemplum? Optimus canon qui proiicit auaritiam ex calumnia, hoc est, non a conscientia tantum. Liber iam & hunc claudere librum, sed in calce aliqua velim vel antedicta quasi epilogando repetere, vel addere praetermissa. Consideres ante omnia sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam, cui Deo auctore praees, Ecclesiarum matrem esse non Dominam; te vero non Dominum Episcoporum, sed vnum ex ipsis: porro fratrem diligentium Deum & participem timentium eum. De caetero oportere te esse considera, formam iustitiae, sanctimoniae speculum, pietatis exemplar, assertorem veritatis, fidei defensorem, doctorem gentium, Christianorum ducem, amicum sponsi, sponsae paranimphum, cleri ordinatorem, pastorem plebium, magistrum insipientium, refugium oppressorum, pauperum aduocatum, miserorum spem, tutorem pupillorum, iudicem viduarum, oculum caecorum; linguam mutorum, baculum senum, vltorem scelerum, malorum metum, bonorum gloriam, virgam potentium, malleum tyrannorum, Regum patrem, legum moderatorem, canonum dispensatorem, salterrae, orbis lumen, sacerdotem altissimi, vicarium Christi, Christum Domini, postremo Deum Pharaonis. Intellige quae dico, dabit tibi Dominus intellectum. Vbi malitiae iuncta potentia est, aliquid tibi supra hominem praesumendum: vultus tuus super facientes mala. Timeat spiritum irae tuae, qui hominem non veretur, gladium non formidat: timeat orationem, qui admonitionem contempsit. Cui irascceris tu, Deum sibi iratum non hominem putet: qui te non audierit, auditurum Deum, & contra se paueat. Quod reliquum est, de his quae supra te sunt, incumbit iam disputatio: quam vno libro Deo iuuante soluere speco, & me pariter absoluere promissione mea.
units.tr: I know where you live: the unbelieving and the subverters are with you. They are not sheep, but you are their shepherd. Consider carefully whether you might find a way to convert them, lest they subvert you. Why do we doubt that they can turn back into sheep, when they have already turned from sheep into wolves? Here I will not spare you, so that God may spare you. Either deny that you are a shepherd to this people, or show that you are one. You will not deny it, lest the one whose seat you hold deny you as his heir. Peter is the one who, as far as we know, never went forth adorned with jewels or silks, was not carried on a golden litter or a white horse, was not surrounded by soldiers, and was not hemmed in by noisy attendants. Yet he believed that the saving command could be fulfilled without these things: if you love me, feed my sheep. In these successes you resemble not Peter but Constantine. I advise you to endure what the times require, not to covet what is not owed. I urge you rather toward those things of which I know you are a debtor. And even if you walk about in purple and gold, there is no reason to shrink from the work and the pastoral care that belong to the heir of the shepherd, and no reason to be ashamed of the Gospel. Indeed, if you would willingly preach the Gospel, that is a glory even among the Apostles, for to preach the Gospel is to feed. Do the work of an evangelist, and you have fulfilled the work of a shepherd. You say, "You warn me to feed dragons and scorpions, not sheep." For that very reason, I say, go all the more to them, but with the word, not with the sword. Why do you still hold the sword again, which you were once commanded to put back into its sheath? Yet he who denies that the sword is yours does not seem to me to heed the word of the Lord who says here, turn your sword into its sheath. Therefore it is yours as well, perhaps to be drawn at your nod, though not by your own hand. Otherwise, if it did not pertain to you in any way, the Lord would not have answered the Apostles, who said, here are two swords, with it is enough; he said, it is too much. So both swords belong to the Church: the spiritual sword and the material sword. The one is to be wielded by the Church itself, the other is for the Church to use. The one is in the hand of the priest, the other in the hand of the soldier, yet certainly at the nod of the priest and at the command of the emperor. But of this I will speak elsewhere. Now take up the sword that has been entrusted to you for striking, and wounds for salvation, if not all, if not many, at least those you can reach. "I am no better," you say, "than my fathers. Which of them did their houses, which exasperated them, not only hear but not mock?" Therefore press on all the more, in case they listen and become quiet; press on even against those who resist. In saying this, perhaps I shall be thought too severe. Is not that saying of ours, be urgent in season, out of season? If you dare, call him too severe. To the prophet it is commanded: cry aloud, do not cease. To whom but the wicked and sinners? Declare, he says, to my people their wickedness, and to the house of Jacob their sins. Observe carefully that they are called both wicked and the people of the Lord. Think the same of these men: even if they are wicked and unjust, see that you do not hear, what I have not done to one of these, I have not done to myself. I admit that this people has so far been hard-faced and of an untamed heart. But how you could know clearly whether they are also untamable, I do not know. What has not yet happened may come to pass, if you despair: but with God no word will be impossible. If they are hard-faced, harden yourself in turn against them. Nothing is so hard that it does not yield to what is harder. The Lord said to the prophet, I have made your face harder than their faces. There is one thing that will absolve you: that you have acted with that people so that you can say, "What ought I to have done for my people and did not?" So, so, you have acted, and you have accomplished nothing. There is still one thing you can do and say: go out of Ur of the Chaldeans, and say that I must preach the Gospel to other cities also. I think you will not regret the exile, exchanging city for world. Let us come to your associates and helpers. These are your zealous companions, your intimates, most of all yours, and if they are bad, they are equally more so to you. Do not think yourself healthy while your sides ache; that is, do not think yourself good while you lean on evil men. Or even if you are good, what fruit can your goodness alone bring? As I remember saying in the earlier book. What benefit, I ask, does your righteousness as a single man bring to the churches of God, when the opinion of those disposed otherwise prevails? Your goodness is not safe for you when it is besieged by evils, any more than your health is safe with a serpent nearby. There is no way for you to withdraw from an inner evil, and the good of the household is on the opposite side, all the more so because it helps more often. But whether they relieve or burden you, to whom should this be more rightly imputed than to you, who chose such men or admitted them? I do not speak of all, for there are some you did not choose; but they chose you. Yet they have no power except what you have given them or allowed. So we return to the same point: impute to yourself whatever you suffer from him who can do nothing without you. Apart from these, in the rest, as you see, the men to be gathered and chosen for this work of the ministry must also be considered carefully. It is yours to call and take to yourself, from anywhere, following the example of Moses, elders, not young men; yet elders not so much in age as in character, whom you know, for the elders are the people's. Should men not be chosen from the whole world, since they are to judge the world? Certainly this business should not be pressed by one who asks for himself. It must be done by counsel, not by entreaty. There are things which from us the importunity of those who ask either wrings out, or necessity deserves. But that belongs to things that are ours. When what I want to do is not permitted, what place is there for a petitioner? Unless perhaps the one who asks me asks that what he wants may be allowed me, and not rather that I may want it. One asks for another; another perhaps asks for himself. He for whom you are asked is suspect; he who asks for himself has already been judged, and it makes no difference whether someone asks in his own name or through another. A cleric who frequents the court without belonging to it, you should know, belongs to that kind of ambitious flatterer who speaks according to each man's pleasure. Count him one of the petitioners, even if he has asked for nothing. The scorpion has nothing to fear in its face, but it stings in its tail. If you feel your heart softened, as usual, by the flatteries of such men, remember what is written: every man first sets out good wine, but when he has become drunk, then that which is worse. Weigh equally the humility of the man who fears and that of the man who hopes. It is usually the mark of a crafty and deceitful man to put on humility when he wishes to obtain something, of whom Scripture says: there is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inner parts are full of deceit. Take judgment about yourselves from this clear and familiar example: how many suppliants have you admitted, and afterwards put up with, when they were insolent, contumacious, and rebellious without cause? Their beginnings conceal this inner evil, and what follows... A talkative young man who studies eloquence, since it is empty of wisdom, you should not regard as an enemy of justice. Your teacher speaks to you about such false brethren: lay hands suddenly on no one... to this whole pestilent class of men. Let it be your greatest care to introduce... may you not regret having introduced. It is shameful for you to retract often what you have done, and it does not become you to put your judgment at risk. Therefore deliberate carefully on everything that must be done, both with yourself and with those who love you; deliberate before the deed, because consultation after the deed is too late. It is the counsel of the wise: do everything with counsel, and you will not repent after the deed. And be persuaded of this: those who are to be admitted are hard to prove in the court; therefore, if it can be done, men who have been proved should be chosen, not men who are to be proved. In the monasteries we receive everyone, in hope of improving them. But the court is accustomed to receive good men more easily than to make them. For if we have found that more good men have failed in it than bad men have profited, then surely men should be sought in whom there is no fear of failing and no hope of progress, since they are already perfect. Therefore take those who are not willing and not running, but hesitating and refusing: compel them and urge them to come in. In such men, I think, your spirit will find rest, men who are not brazen-faced, but modest and fearful, who fear nothing but the Lord, and hope for nothing but from God. Men who do not look at the hands of those who approach, but at their needs; who stand boldly for the afflicted and judge with equity for the meek of the earth; who are composed in manners, proved in holiness, ready for obedience, gentle in patience, subject to discipline, strict in censure, catholic in faith, faithful in stewardship, agreeable for peace, conformed to unity; who are upright in judgment, prudent in counsel, discreet in command, diligent in arranging, vigorous in acting, modest in speaking, secure in adversity, devout in prosperity, sober in zeal, not lax in mercy, not idle in leisure, not dissolute in hospitality, not overindulgent at table, not anxious in the care of household affairs, not covetous of another's, not prodigal of their own, circumspect everywhere and in all things. Men who, whenever the work requires an embassy for Christ, do not refuse when ordered, nor seek it when not ordered; who do not stubbornly refuse what they modestly excuse; who, when sent, do not go after gold, but follow Christ; who do not think of an embassy as a source of gain, nor seek the gift, but the fruit. Men who present John to kings, Moses to the Egyptians, Phinehas to fornicators, Elijah to idolaters, Elisha to the greedy, Peter to liars, Paul to blasphemers, and Christ to traders. Men who do not despise the common people but teach them; who do not flatter the rich but frighten them; who do not burden the poor but cherish them; who do not fear the threats of princes but despise them. Men who do not enter with a crowd, nor leave in anger; who do not plunder the churches but mend them; who do not empty purses but refresh hearts, correct crimes, provide for their own good name, and do not envy another's. Men who devote themselves to prayer, and are practiced in it, and in every matter trust more in prayer than in their own industry and labour; whose entrance is peaceful and whose departure is not troublesome; whose speech is edification, whose life is justice, whose presence is pleasing, whose memory is a blessing. Men who show themselves lovable, not in word but in deed; who appear worthy of reverence, but by action, not by pride; humble with the humble, and innocent with the innocent; who sharply rebuke the hard, restrain the malicious, and render retribution to the proud. Men who do not hasten to enrich themselves or their own from the dowry of the widow and the patrimony of the crucified; freely giving what they have freely received, freely doing judgment, suffering injury, vengeance on the nations, rebukes among the peoples. Finally, men who are seen to have received from your spirit something like the seventy elders of Moses, through whom, whether absent or present, they strive to please you and to please God; who return to you tired indeed, but not exhausted; rejoicing not because they brought the rarest and most precious things of the earth, but because they left peace to kingdoms, law to barbarians, quiet to monasteries, order to churches, discipline to clergy, and to God a people acceptable and zealous for good works. Now it is fitting to bring into the midst a deed of our dear Martin, sweet to remember. You know this, but I do not know whether you remember it. He was a cardinal priest who once served as legate in Dacia, and returned so poor that, with his expenses exhausted and his resources failing, he could scarcely reach Florence. There the bishop of the place gave him a horse on which he was carried as far as Pisa, where we were then. The next day, I believe, the bishop, who was secure (for he had a case against an adversary, and the day of pleading was at hand), began to seek the support of friends. As he was pressing each one in turn, he came to Martin. He had greater confidence in him, for Martin could not be unmindful of a recent kindness. Then Martin said: "You have deceived me. I did not know that a matter was hanging over you. Take back your horse; look, it is in the stable," and at that same hour he gave it back to him. What do you say, my Eugene? Is it not a matter of another age, that a legate returned from a land of gold without gold, passed through a land of silver and did not know silver, and besides immediately rejected a gift that could have seemed suspicious? But oh, what a sweet place this is, where the occasion has arisen to recall and name a man of most fragrant savour, I mean the bishop Geoffrey of Chartres, who for many years discharged his legation in the parts of Aquitaine at his own expense and with energy. I will tell a thing that I myself saw. I was with him in that land when a priest presented him with a fish which people call a sturgeon. The legate asked what it would sell for. "I will not take it," he said, "unless you receive the price," and he paid out five shillings, against the seller's will and with embarrassment. Again, when we were in a certain town, the lady of that town offered him, out of devotion, with a towel, two or three fine dishes, though of wood. He gazed at them for some time, and as a man of scrupulous conscience he praised them, but he would not consent to accept them. When would he have accepted silver ones, if he refused wooden ones? There were none who could say to the legate, "We have enriched Abraham." Indeed he himself, with Samuel, spoke freely to all: speak of me before the Lord and before his Christ: whose ox or whose ass have I taken, or whom have I wronged or oppressed, or from whose hand have I received a gift, and I will despise it today and restore it to you. Oh, if there were given a multitude of men such as we have just described! What could be happier than you, what more delightful than that age? Would not the blessedness of those times, from eternity, seem to you a second one, when, as you went forth everywhere, you would see yourself surrounded by so famous a band of the blessed? If I know you as heir, and you, drawing another sigh, speak with me: do you think that what is said can come to be? Do you think we shall be here until these things are done? Who will grant that we may live to see it? Oh, if I might see in my lifetime the Church of God supported by such pillars! Oh, if I might behold the bride of my Lord entrusted to such fidelity, and committed to such purity! What could be happier for me, what more secure, when I looked on men of this kind as the guardians of my life around me, and also as its witnesses? To them I would securely entrust all my secrets; I would share my counsels; I would pour myself out to them as to another self. If they did not allow me to stray in any way, they would curb me when I rushed headlong and rouse me when I slept. Their reverence and freedom would restrain me when I was oppressed, and correct me when I exceeded. Their constancy and fortitude would steady me when I wavered, and raise me when I despaired. Their faith and holiness would call me to all that is holy, all that is honourable, all that is chaste, all that is lovable and of good report. And now, my Eugene, turn your eyes to the present state of the court or Church, and to the pursuits of the prelates, especially those who are around you. But so far I have said enough about these matters. I have touched the wall; I have not dug through it. You may dig and see, as the son of the prophet; I am not permitted to proceed. I say one thing that is plain on its face: your ridiculous ministers try to put themselves before their fellow presbyters. Reason does not support this, antiquity has not held it, authority does not agree. And if a claim is built on their custom, it is certainly better to despise that custom than to despise the highest order. Yet it is a trivial thing, from which they most wish to obtain it. "We," they say, "are the ones who, at every solemn assembly, stand nearer to the Lord Pope, sit nearer to him when he sits, and go before those who precede: all this is not a privilege of dignity, but a debt of diligence, interpreting the name of deacon by the very solemnity of the service." Finally, when the elders are ordered to make confession, and the greatness of the one who asks is being sought, you sit at the feet, stand nearer, so that you may have him more ready. In the Gospels we read that there was a contention among the disciples, as to which of them seemed to be the greatest. Would that you were happy if the rest were held in this way about you! The court is now tiresome; we must leave the palace, for they are waiting for us at home. These men are not merely around you, but in some way within you. The consideration by which you intend to arrange your household, and to provide for those who are in your bosom and in your lap, is not superfluous. I say it is even necessary. Hear Paul: if anyone does not know how to rule his own house, how will he have care of the Church of God? Likewise: if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. In saying this, I do not warn you to be occupied with the highest things and to attend to the lowest, as if you were becoming small, spending on the least what you owe to the greatest. Why do you entangle yourself in the things from which God has rescued you? All these things, he says, will be added to you. Nevertheless it is right to do this too, and not to neglect those other things; but while you act through yourself in those matters, you must also provide, through yourself, for those who provide for them on your behalf. For if one servant alone is not sufficient, at the same time, for guarding, for the beasts of burden, and for the care of the tables, how can you yourself attend both to your house and to the house of the Lord, of which it is written: O Israel, how great is the house of the Lord? The mind must be entirely free from anxiety about lesser and vile things, when it is occupied with such great and numerous affairs. It must be free, so that no violent occupation may claim it. It must be noble, so that no unworthy affection may drag it downward. It must be upright, so that no sinister intention may turn it aside. It must be cautious, so that no stealthy suspicion may creep into it. It must be watchful, so that no sudden disturbance may shake it. It must be unconquered, so that no continual tribulation may weary it. It must be spacious, so that no loss of temporal things may confine it. Do not doubt that you must be stripped of these good things and struck by these evils, if, dividing your mind, you wish to give a share equally to the things of God and to your own trifles. You must have someone to provide for you, whom I say to be your agent, not your companion. Some things you will do yourself, some through yourself and others together, some through others and without you. Who is wise enough to understand these things? Not that your consideration sleeps among them. Indeed, I would judge that the management of your household should be placed under that class which I put last. You will do those things, as I said, through another. But if he is not faithful, he will defraud; if he is not prudent, he will be defrauded. A faithful and prudent man must therefore be sought, whom you may set over your household. Yet he is still useless if the third thing is lacking. Do you ask what this is? Authority. For what does it profit him to wish and also to know how to arrange things as necessary, if he cannot do what he knows and wishes? Therefore he must be given the power to act at his own discretion. If you think this will be to the prejudice of reason, remember that a faithful man, who will nonetheless wish to act according to reason, must be attended to, and a prudent man who will nonetheless know how to act according to reason. But a faithful and diligent will shows itself only when there is abundant means by which it may be wholly devoted to affection, with all submitting without hesitation. Therefore let all be subject, let no one be allowed to contradict him; let no one say, "Why did you do it so?" Let him have power to exclude and to admit whom he will, to change ministers, and to transfer offices to whom and when he will. Thus let him be feared by all, so that he may also be useful; let him preside over all, so that he may benefit all, and be concerned for all. Do not accept secret and sworn accusations against him; you should rather regard them as slander. And I would like you to establish this general rule for yourself: regard as suspect anyone who is afraid to say openly what he has said in your ear. If, when you are judging, he refuses to say it in front of the accused, judge him a informer, not an accuser. Thus let one man impose on all what must be done, and let all answer to one. Have faith in him, being free for yourself and for the Church of God. If no one is found who is either faithful or prudent, what is to be entrusted must go to the faithful man rather. Certainly two are safer for this; yet if no suitable man is found, I advise you to bear with someone less faithful rather than plunge yourself into this labyrinth. Remember that the Saviour had Judas as steward. What is more shameful for a bishop than to bend over his furniture and his little property, to search everything, to inquire into each detail, to be gnawed by suspicions, to be moved by every loss or neglect? I say it with shame: such men of scrutiny daily count over their one substance, reckoning each item, demanding account of small things. Not so did that Egyptian act, who entrusted to Joseph all that he had in his house. Let the Christian blush, who does not trust a Christian with his affairs, a man who set his servant over all his goods, and that servant was a foreigner. Wretched are those men, to whom bishops have at hand men to whom they may entrust souls, and who do not entrust their own... they do not hinder. They are, of course, the best judges of things, who take great care of small things and... of greater things. But as is clearly given to understand, we bear more patiently... than our own. We do not know the losses of the Lord's flock. Our daily expenses, we review with daily scrutiny, and... There is a daily discussion with the ministers about the price of food and the number of loaves; very rarely is a conference held with the elders about the sins of the people. The flock falls, and there is someone to lift it up: the soul perishes, and no one takes account of it. Nor is it surprising, since we do not feel even our own constant defects. Do we not grow angry, burn, and become anxious over every single calculation? How much more tolerable it would be to bear the loss of things than of minds. Why, he says, do you rather suffer fraud? I ask you, who teach others, teach yourself; or, if you have not yet taught yourself, consider yourself worth more than your possessions. These transitory things, which can in no way flow to you, make them pass from you, but not through you. The stream that flows wears away the earth; so the running about of temporal things gnaws at the conscience. If a torrent can run out into the fields without harm to the crops, trust that you too can handle these things without wound to the mind. In every way I advise you to strive to turn away from yourself the crowding of these things. Many things you should not know, most things you should overlook, some you should forget. There are still some things I would not have you ignore: the morals and pursuits of each person. It is not right that you should be the last to know the vices of your household, which we know have happened to very many. Therefore, as I said, let another manage each thing, but you yourself provide for discipline. Do not entrust this to anyone: if a speech sounds too insolent before you, or a dress appears, stretch out your hand against such things and avenge the injury done to you. Impunity gives birth to daring, and daring to excess. Holiness, modesty, and honesty befit a bishop's house; let discipline be their guardian. Household priests, if they are more honourable than others, or if they are a talk to all men, must not be allowed anything shameless or indecent in their face, their dress, their walk, or in those who are about you. Let your fellow bishops learn from you not to keep curly-haired boys and dressed-up youths with them. Certainly it is not fitting for the mitred to run about with curled-up hair. And remember what the wise man warns: you have daughters; do not show your cheerful torch to them. Yet I do not counsel you to austerity, but to gravity. The one drives away the weaker, the other restrains the lighter; the one makes you hated if present, the other makes you despised if absent; yet in all things a better measure is preferable. I would wish you neither too severe nor too lax. What is more pleasing than this moderation, so that you are not a burden through severity, nor an object of contempt through familiarity? In the palace, show yourself as the Pope; at home, show yourself as the father of the family. Let your household love you; if not, see that they fear you. Keep guard over your mouth, which is always useful, but do not exclude the grace of affability. Therefore the rash tongue must be restrained everywhere, but above all at table. Your bearing will be more suitable if you are indeed stern in action, serene in countenance, and sparing in words. Chaplains and those who are constantly present at the divine offices should not be without honour. It is your duty to provide for such as are worthy; let them be served by all as if by you. Let them receive what they need from your hand; be content with what you provide for them, and see that they do not lack. If you find that someone asks for something from visitors, judge him a Gehazi. This must be distinguished in the case of the doorkeepers and of the other officials. But this is superfluous, for we remember that you have already laid down this form long ago. What is more worthy of your apostolate? What is more wholesome for conscience, more honourable for reputation, more useful as an example? It is an excellent rule that drives out avarice, not only from conscience but also from calumny. I am now free to close this book, but at the end I would like either to repeat what has been said, as in a summary, or to add what was omitted. Consider above all the holy Roman Church, over which, by God's authority, you preside: she is the mother of the Churches, not their mistress; and you are not the lord of the bishops, but one of them, and moreover a brother of those who love God and a partner of those who fear him. For the rest, consider that you ought to be a form of righteousness, a mirror of holiness, a pattern of piety, an asserter of truth, a defender of the faith, a teacher of the nations, a leader of Christians, a friend of the bridegroom, the bride's best man, an orderer of the clergy, a shepherd of the peoples, a master of the foolish, a refuge of the oppressed, an advocate of the poor, the hope of the wretched, a guardian of orphans, a judge of widows, an eye of the blind, a tongue of the dumb, a staff of the old, an avenger of crimes, a fear to the wicked, a glory to the good, a rod of the powerful, a hammer of tyrants, a father of kings, a moderator of laws, a dispenser of canons, the salt of the earth, the light of the world, a priest of the Most High, the vicar of Christ, the anointed of the Lord, and finally, the God of Pharaoh. Understand what I say, and the Lord will give you understanding. Where power joined with malice is at work, you must presume something above man: let your face be against those who do evil. Let him fear the spirit of your anger who does not reverence man and does not dread the sword; let him fear your prayer who has despised your admonition. When you are angry with someone, let him think that it is not a man who is angry with him but God, and let him who has not heard you dread that God will hear, and be afraid against himself. As for the rest, which concerns the things that are above you, the discussion now falls to me, which I hope to finish in one book with God's help, and so release myself too from my promise.

units.la: LIBER QVINTVS.
units.tr: BOOK FIVE.

units.la: Libri superiores etsi de consideratione inscribantur, plurimum tamen habent actionis admixtu; dum res aliquas non considerandas tantum, sed agendas docent vel monent: at qui in manibus modo est, sola in consideratione versabitur. Quae enim supra sunt, id quod constat, actu non indigent, sed inspectu: non est quod in eis actites, quae vno modo semper sunt & in aeternum. Poro aliqua & ab aeterno. Et hoc velim solerter aduertas, vir sagacissime Eugeni, quia totiens peregrinatur consideratio tua; quotiens ab illis rebus ad ista deflectitur inferiora & visibilia, siue inuenda ad notitiam, siue appetenda ad vsum, siue pro officio disponenda vel actitanda. Si tamen ita versatur in his vt per haec illa requirat, haud procul exulat: sic considerare, repatriare est. Sublimior iste praesentium ac dignior vsus erit, cum iuxta sapientiam Pauli inuisibilia Dei per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur: sane hac scala ciues non egent, {s}ed exules. Quod vidit ipse huius sententiæ auctor, qui cum diceret inuisibilia per visibilia conspici, signanter posuit creatura mundi. Et vere quid opus scalis tenenti iam solium? creatura cœli illa est, præsto habens per quod potius ista intueatur. Videt Verbum & in Verbo facta per verbum: Nec opus habet ex his quæ facta sunt, factoris notitiam vendicare. Neque enim vt vel ipsa nouerit ad ipsa descendit, quæ ibi illa videt vbi longe melius sunt quam in seipsis: vnde nec medium requirit ad ea corporis sensum, sensus ipsa sibi, seipsa sentiens. Optimum videndi genus, si nullius egueris, ad omne quod nosse libuerit te contentus: alioquin iuuari aliunde, obnoxium fieri est. Minus a perfecto istud, & minus liberum. Quid quod & inferioribus eges? nonne præposterum hoc & indignum? Plane superiorum quædam iniuria est inferiorum operam desiderare, a qua iniuria nemo hominum perfecte vindicabitur; nisi cum quisquam euaserit in libertatem filiorum Dei. Nempe erunt hi omnes docibiles Dei & nulla intereunte creatura sclo beati Deo. Repatriasse erit hoc, exisse de patria corporum in regione Spirituum. Ipsa est Deus noster maximus spiritus, maxima mansio spirituum beatorum; & ne quid hic vsurpet carnis sensus, seu imaginatio: veritas est, sapientia est, virtus, æternitas, summum bonum. Vnde interim absumus, & vbi sumus vallis est, & vallis lacrymarum: in qua sensualitas regnat, & consideratio exulat: in qua libere quidem & potestatiue se exerit sensus corporeus; sed intricatus caligat oculus spiritalis. Quid igitur mirum si ope indigenæ aduena indiget? Et felix secundum tempus viator, qui ciuium beneficium, sine quo transire non potest, in obsequium conuertere potuit: vtens non fruens, vrgens non petens, exactor non supplex. Magnus ille qui vsum sensuum quasdam veluti ciuium opes expendere satagit, dispensando in suam & multorum salutem. Nec ille minor, qui hunc sibi gradum ad illa inuisibilia philosophando constituit: nisi quod hoc dulcius, illud vtilius; hoc felicius, illud fortius esse constat. At omnium maximus, qui spreto iplo vsu rerum & sensuum, quantum quidem humanæ fragilitati fas est: non ascensoriis gradibus, sed inopinatis excessibus auolare interdum contemplando ad illa sublimia consueuit. Ad hoc vltimum genus illos pertinere reor excessus Pauli: excessus, non ascensus. Nam raptum potius suisse, quam ascendisse ipse se perhibet. Inde est quod dicebat: siue mente excedimus Deo. Porro hæc tria ita contingunt, cum consideratio etsi in loco peregrinationis suæ, virtutis studio & adiutorio gratiæ facta superior sensualitatem aut premit ne insolescat, aut cogit ne euagetur, aut fugit ne inquinet: in primo potentior, in secundo liberior, in tertio purior. Puritatis siquidem & alacritatis pariter alis, fit ille volatus. Visne hos consideratiouis species propriis distingui nominibus? Dicamus si placet primam dispensatiuam, secundam æstimatiuam, tertiam speculatiuam. Horum nominum rationes, diffinitiones declarabunt: dispensatiua est consideratio, sensibus sensibilibusque rebus ordinate & socialiter vtens ad promerendum Deum. Æstimatiua est consideratio prudenter ac diligenter quæque scrutans & ponderans ad vestigandum Deum. Speculatiua est consideratio, se in se colligens & quantum diuinitus adiuuatur rebus humanis eximens ad contemplandum Deum. Puto vigilanter aduertis aliarum hanc esse fructum, cæteras si non referantur ad istam, quod dicuntur videri posse, sed non esse. Et prior quidem absque intuitu huius, multa serit, & nihil metit: sequens vero nisi ad istam se dirigat, vadit sed non euadit. Ergo quod prima aptat, secunda adorat, tertia gustat: ad quem tamen gustum perducunt & cæteræ etsi tardius, nisi quod prima laboriosius, secunda quietius peruenitur. Dixisti inquis satis qua ascendatur, & iam quo dicere habes: falleris si id speras, ineffabile est. Tu me existimas loqui quod oculus non vidit, necaurisaudiuit, & in cor hominis non ascendit? nobis, inquit, reuelauit Deus per spiritum suum: ergo quæ supra sunt non verbo docentur, sed spiritu reuelantur. Verum quod sermo non explicat, consideratio quærat, oratio expetat, merceatur vita, puritas assequatur. Sane eorum admonitus quæ supra sunt, non te existimes mitti a me suspicere solem, lunam, stellas, non ipsum firmamentum, non aquas quæ super cœlos sunt: ista siquidem omnia etsi supra loco, preciò infra sunt & dignitate naturæ; sunt enim corpora. Tui portio spiritus est, quo superius quippiam frustra quæris quod non sit spiritus. Porro spiritus est Deus, sunt & Angeli sancti, & hi supra te: sed Deus natura, Angeli gratia superiores sunt. Vnum siquidem tui & Angeli optima, ratio est: Deus vero non sui aliquod optimum habet, vnum optimum totus. Is & qui cum eo sunt beati Spiritus, tribus modus veluti viis totidem, nostra sunt consideratione vestigandi, opinione, fide, intellectu. Quorum intellectus rationi innititur, fides auctoritati; opinio sola veri similitudine se tuetur. Habent illa duo certam veritatem, sed fides clausam & inuolutam, intelligentia nudam & manifestam: cæterum opinio certi nil habens, verum per verisimilia quærit potius quam apprehendit: Omnino in his cauenda confusio, ne aut incertum opinionis fides figat; aut quid firmum fixumque est fidei, opinio reuocet in quæstionem. Et hoc sciendum, quia opinio si habet assertionem, temeraria est; fides si habet hæsitationem infirma est. Item intellectus si signata fidei tentet irrumpere, reputatur effractor, scrutator maiestatis. Multi suam opinionem intellectum putauerunt, & errauerunt: & quidem opinio potest putari intellectus, intellectus non opinio potest. Vnde hoc accidit? profecto quia hæc falli & fallere potest: aut si falli potuit, intellectus non fuit, sed opinio. Verus nempe intellectus certam habet non modo veritatem, sed notitiam veritatis intellectus est rei. Possimus hæc singula hic ita diffinire: fides est voluntaria quædam & certa prælibatio nec dum propalatæ veritatis. Intellectus est rei cuiuscunque inuisibilis certa ac manifesta notitia. Opinio est quasi pro vero habere aliqd, q falsum esse nescias. Ergo vt dixi fides ambiguū non habet, aut si habet fides nō est, sed opinio. Quid igitur distat ab intellectu? nempe q etsi non habet incertum nō magis quam intellectus, habet tamen inuolutū, quod non intellectus. Deniq; quod intellexisti, non est de eo quod vltra quæras: aut si est, nō intellexisti. Nil autē malumus scire, quam quæ fide iam scimus nil supererit ad beatitudinē, cum quæ iam certa sunt nobis, erūt æque & nuda. His ita expeditis, age iam dirigatur consideratio in ea quæ sursum est Hierusalē mater nostra, ac totis tribus memoratis viis caute & vigilater inuestigemus inuestigabilia, quatenus tamē licet, vel magis quatenus nobis donabitur.
units.tr: Although the earlier books are entitled "On Consideration," they contain a good deal of action mixed in, since they teach or advise about things that are not only to be considered but also to be done. The book now in hand, however, will be concerned with contemplation alone. For the things that are above, as is agreed, need not action but only regard; there is no need to be active about them, since they always exist in one way and for eternity. Some things, however, also exist from eternity. And I would have you note carefully, most discerning Eugenius, that your consideration wanders whenever it turns from those higher things to these lower and visible ones, whether to be discovered for knowledge, or sought for use, or arranged and carried out as duty requires. If, however, it is so occupied with these things that through them it seeks those others, it is not far in exile: to consider in this way is to return home. This use will be higher and more worthy of our present state, since, according to the wisdom of Paul, the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made. Citizens certainly have no need of this ladder; exiles do. The author of this saying saw this himself, for when he said that the invisible is seen through the visible, he pointedly spoke of the creation of the world. And indeed, what need has one who already holds the throne for a ladder? That creation belongs to heaven and has ready at hand that through which it may rather look upon these things. It sees the Word, and in the Word, the things made through the Word; nor does it need to claim knowledge of the Maker from the things that were made. For it does not descend to these things in order to know them, since it sees them there, where they are far better than in themselves. Hence it does not require the bodily sense as an intermediary for these things; the sense perceives itself, sensing itself. This is the best kind of seeing: if you need nothing, and are content with whatever you wish to know. Otherwise, to be helped from elsewhere is to be dependent, which is less perfect and less free. What of the fact that you also need lower things? Is this not absurd and unworthy? Plainly it is a wrong done to the higher to desire the work of the lower, a wrong from which no human will be wholly freed, unless someone has come to the liberty of the children of God. Indeed, all these will then be taught by God, and blessed in God, with no creature perishing. To return home will mean this: to have gone out of the homeland of bodies into the region of spirits. Our God is himself the greatest Spirit, the greatest dwelling of blessed spirits; and lest the sense of the flesh or imagination should claim anything here, he is truth, wisdom, virtue, eternity, the supreme good. Meanwhile, we are far from there, and where we are is a valley, a valley of tears, in which sensuality reigns and consideration is in exile; in which the bodily sense indeed exerts itself freely and with power, but the spiritual eye, entangled, grows dim. What wonder, then, if the stranger needs the help of the native? And happy is the wayfarer for a time who has been able to turn to his service the kindness of the citizens, without which he cannot pass through: using, not enjoying; pressing, not begging; demanding, not pleading. Great is he who strives to spend the use of the senses, as it were the wealth of the citizens, in dispensing it for his own and many people's salvation. Nor is he lesser who, by philosophizing, establishes this step for himself toward those invisible things; except that the former is sweeter, the latter more useful; the former is happier, the latter stronger. But greatest of all is he who, having scorned the very use of things and the senses, so far as human frailty allows, is accustomed at times, not by ascending steps but by unexpected ecstasies, to fly away in contemplation to those lofty things. I think the ecstasies of Paul belong to this last kind: ecstasies, not ascents. For he himself says that he was rather snatched up than ascended. Hence he said: whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God. Now these three things happen thus: when consideration, though in the place of its pilgrimage, is made higher by zeal for virtue and by the help of grace, it either restrains sensuality lest it grow proud, or compels it lest it wander, or flees it lest it defile; in the first case it is more powerful, in the second freer, in the third purer. For this flight is made on the wings of purity and eagerness alike. Do you wish these kinds of consideration to be distinguished by their own names? Let us call the first dispensing, the second estimating, the third speculative, if you agree. Definitions will explain the reasons for these names. Dispensing consideration is that which uses the senses and sensible things in an orderly and social way, to deserve God. Estimating consideration is that which prudently and diligently examines and weighs all things, in order to track down God. Speculative consideration is that which gathers itself into itself and, as far as it is divinely aided, withdraws from human things, in order to contemplate God. I think you notice carefully that this is the fruit of the others, which, unless they are referred to it, can seem to be but are not. The first indeed, without looking to this, sows much and reaps nothing; the second, unless it directs itself to this, goes but does not arrive. Therefore what the first prepares, the second worships, and the third tastes; yet the others also lead to that taste, though more slowly: the first is reached with more labour, the second with more rest. You have said, you say, enough about how one ascends, and now you have what to say about where; you are mistaken if you hope for that, it is ineffable. Do you think me to speak of what the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man? God has revealed it to us through his Spirit, says Paul: therefore the things above are not taught by word but revealed by the Spirit. Yet what speech does not explain, consideration should seek, prayer should desire, life should earn, and purity should attain. Indeed, being reminded of those things that are above, do not suppose that I am bidding you look up at the sun, the moon, the stars, nor at the firmament itself, nor at the waters that are above the heavens. For all these things, although they are above in place, are yet beneath in dignity of nature, since they are bodies. The part of you that is spirit is that by which you vainly seek anything higher that is not spirit. Moreover, God is Spirit, and there are holy Angels also, and these are above you: but God is higher by nature, the Angels by grace. For the reason is that you and the Angels have a best, but God does not have some best of his own; he is wholly one best. He and the blessed spirits who are with him are to be sought by our consideration in three ways, as it were three roads: by opinion, by faith, by understanding. Of these, understanding rests on reason, faith on authority; opinion alone finds shelter in probability. The first two have certain truth, but faith has it closed and wrapped up, understanding has it bare and manifest; opinion, however, having nothing certain, seeks truth through likelihoods rather than grasping it. In all this, confusion must be guarded against, lest either the uncertainty of opinion fix faith, or opinion recall to question what is firm and settled in faith. And this must be known: if opinion makes an assertion, it is rash; if faith has hesitation, it is weak. Likewise, if understanding tries to break into what faith has sealed, it is counted a housebreaker, a scrutinizer of majesty. Many have taken their opinion for understanding, and have erred; indeed opinion can be taken for understanding, but understanding cannot be opinion. Whence does this come? Surely because the one can be deceived and can deceive; or if it could be deceived, it was not understanding but opinion. True understanding has not only certain truth but the knowledge of the truth; understanding is the certain and manifest knowledge of any invisible thing. Let us here define these three briefly: faith is a certain voluntary foretaste of a truth not yet revealed. Understanding is the certain and manifest knowledge of any invisible thing whatever. Opinion is, as it were, to hold something as true which you do not know to be false. Therefore, as I said, faith has no uncertainty; if it has, it is not faith but opinion. What, then, distinguishes it from understanding? Namely, that although it has no uncertainty any more than understanding does, it has something wrapped up, which understanding does not. Finally, what you have understood is not something about which you should still ask further; or if you should, you have not understood. We would rather know nothing beyond what we already know by faith, for nothing will remain for blessedness, when what is now certain to us will be equally bare. With these things thus cleared, come, let consideration be directed toward what is above, Jerusalem our mother; and by all three of the said ways let us carefully and watchfully investigate the unsearchable things, as far as it is permitted, or rather as far as it shall be granted to us.

units.la: Et primo quidē ciues spiritus esse illic, potentes, gloriosos, beatos, distinctos in plonas, dispositos in dignitates, ab initio stantes in ordine suo, perfectos in genere suo, corpore æthereos, immortalitate ppetuos, impassibiles non creatos, sed factos, id est gratia non natura, mente puros, affectu benignos, religione pios, castimonia integros, vnanimitate indiuiduos: pace securos, a Deo conditos, Dei laudibus & obsequiis deditos. Hæc omnia legendo cōperimus fide tenemus: quanquā de corporibus horū non modo vnde sint, sed an aliquatenus sint, hæret sententia aliquorū. Vnde si quis inter opinabilia magis id ponendū censuerit, non contendo. Porro intellectu præditos, non fide, nō opinione, sed intel- lect ucapimus, quia non possunt huius expertes, & Dei simul participes esse. Sunt & nomina quædā nota nobis similiter ex auditu, p quæ harum beatitudinū (etiam quæ non liquido mortalū percepit auditus) officia, merita, gradus, ordines, vtcunq; à nobis coniici & discerni queunt. Sed enim quod ex auditu non est, iam nō ex fide: nam fides ex auditu. Itaq; opinando ista dixerimus, ad quod enim cœle- stia nomina innotuerunt, si ne opinari quidā salua fide aliquid licet, de rebus quarum nomina sunt? Angeli, Archangeli, Virtutes, Potestates, Principatus, Dominationes, Throni, Cherubin, Seraphin: hæc nomina; quæ significatio eorū? nulla ne inter illos spiritus simpliciter Angeli, & eos q Archangeli nuncupantur distantia? quid ergo sibi vult gradalis distinctio hæc? Putemus Angelos dici (nisi tu conuenientius aliquid considerasti) q singuli singulis hominibus dati creduntur, missi in ministeriū secundum Pauli doctrinā; propter eos qui hæreditatem capiunt salutis. De quibus Saluator: Angeli eorū semper vident faciem Patris. Putemus his præesse Archangelos, qui conscii mysteriorum diuinorū non nisi ob præcipuas & maximas causas mittuntur: è quibus magnus ille Archangelus Gabriel missus legitur ad Mariam, ob causam vtiq; quæ maior esse non potuit. Putemus super istos virtutes esse, quorū nutu vel opere signa & prodigia in elementis siue ex elementis facta apparent, ad comonitionē mortaliū. Inde est fortassis q cum in Euangeliis legas: erunt signa in Sole & Luna, & stellis; paulò post habes; nam virtutes cœlorū mouebuntur. Hi nimirū spiritus per quos signa fiunt. Putemus potestates superiores istis, quarum virtute potestas tenebrarum comprimitur, & coercetur malignitas aeris huius, nē quantū vult noceat, ne malignari nisi vt prosit possit. Putemus principatus his quoq; præla-tos, quorum moderamine & sapientia omnis in terris principatus constituitur, regitur, limitatur, transfertur, mutilatur, mutatur. Putemus dominationes adeo cunctis supereminere præfatis ordinibus, vt respectu horū cæteri videantur omnes administratorii spiritus, & ad istos tanquā ad Dominos referri regimina principatuū, tutamina potestatum, operationes virtutum, reuelationes Archangelorum, curam & prouidentia Angelorum. Putemus thronos alto etiam ab his euolasse recessu, qui ex eo quod sedent throni dicuntur: & ex eo sedent, q sedet in eis Deus: Neq; enim sedere in eis, qui non sederent possit. Quæris quid illam sententiam sessione? Summam tranquillitatem, placidissimam serenitatē, pacem quæ exuperat omne intellectū. Talis est qui sedet in thronis Dominus Sabaoth, iudicans omnia cum tranquillitate: placidissimus, serenissimus, pacatissimus. Et tales sibi constituit thronos similliimos sibi. Putemus Cherubin ex ipso sapientiæ fonte ora altissimi, haurientes & refundetes fluenta scientię vniuersis ciuib suis. Et vide neis sit quæ Propheta loquebatur, fluminis impetus laetificans ciuitatē Dei. Putemus Seraphin, spiritus totos diuino igne succensos, succedere vniuersa, vt singuli ciues, singulę sint lucernæ ardentes & lucentes: ardentes charitate, lucentes cognitione. O Eugeni quā bonum est hic esse, quā fore melius; si quando tamen toti sequamur quo ex parte præcessimus. Præcedimus animo, & ne ipso quidē toto, sed parte; & parte modica nimis. Affectus iacent mole corporea prægrauati, & luto hærentibus desideriis; spla interim arida & tenuis consideratio prævolat: & tamen ex tantillo q iam datur, libet exclamare: Domine dilexi decorē Domus tua, & locū habitationis gloria tua. Quid si totam se colligat anima, & reductis affectibus e cunctis locis quibus captiui tenentur, timendo quæ nō obsunt, amando quæ non decet, dolendo vane, gaudendo vanius, cū his ineat tota libertate volatū, pulset cū impetu spiritus; & in pinguedine gratiæ illabatur? None cum coeperit circuire lucidas mansiones & sinū illum etiā Abrahæ curiosius perscrutari, & sub altari quodcunq; illud est martyrū reuisere animas, in prima stola secundam patientissime expectantes, multo magis tunc instabit loquens cum propheta: vnā petii à Domino, hanc requirā, vt inhabitem in domo Domini omnibus diebus vitæ meæ. Quidni ibi videatur Dei? quidni ibi, pbetur quæ sit voluntas Dei bona, & beneplacens & perfecta? bona in se, placens in effectibus, bene placens fruentibus, perfecta perfectis & nihil vltra quærētibus. Patent visce- ra misericordiæ patent cogitationes pacis, diuitiæ salutis, mysteria bonæ voluntatis, benignitatis arcana, quę clausa mortalibus etiam ipsis electis suspecta sunt. Id quidem salubriter, de desinant timere dum necdū digne a mare idoneiinueniuntur. Cernere est in his q Seraphin appellatur quomodo amet, q vnde amet, non habet: sed est, & qui nihil horum quæ fecerit odit; quos saluandos fecit, quomodo foueat, quomodo, puehat, quomodo amplexetur, quomodo delicta electæ iuuentutis & palea ignorantiarum eius ignis ille consumens, ipsam sibi purgatissimā & suo amore dignissimam reddat. Cernere est in Cherubin, qui plenitudo scientię dicitur, Deum scientiarum Dominum esse, qui solus sola nesciat ignorantia, qui totus sit lux, & tenebrę in eo nō sint vlla, totus sit oculus, & q minime aliquādo fallitur, quia minime clauditur; q extra se non quaret lumē cui admoueatur vt videat, ipse qui videt, ipse vnde videt. Cernere est in thronis quā non suspectus omni innocentię iudex, sedeat in his q circumuenire nolit circumueniri nō possit, quippe sit amans & videns: nec vacat sessio, tranquillitas insigne est. De vultu tali iudiciū meū ꝑdeat opto; cui insit amor, error absit, absit & perturbatio. Cernere est in Dominationibus, quantæ sit Dominus maiestatis, cuius nutu imperiū constat & imperio vniuersitas atq; æternitas termini sunt. Cernere est in Principatibus, principiū ex quo omnia, & quo modo à cardine ostiū; sic ab ipso regi vniuersitatē. Cernere est in Potestatibus, quam potestatiue idē Princeps quos regit, protegit; contrarias potestates arcens & ꝑpulsans. Cernere est in Virtutibus, vnā vbiq; æqualiter presto esse virtute, p quam omnia, viuificam efficacem, inuisibilē, immobilemq;, omnia tamen mouente vtiliter, tenentem fortiter. Quæ cum in minus visitata effecta apud mortales eruperit, miracula siue prodigia vocant. Cernere postremo & mirari est in Angelis & Archangelis veritatem atq; experientia vocis illius, quoniam ipsi cura est de nobis, qui talium nos & tantorū non definit iocundare visitationibus, instruere reuelationibus, suggestionibus commonere, sedulitate solatiari. Hæc omnia contulit illis spiritibus ipse qui condidit illos, vnus atq; idē summus spiritus, diuidens singulis prout voluit, hæc operatur in illis, hæc dedit operari & illis, sed aliter. Ardent Seraphin, sedigne Dei, vel potius igne Deo: quod præcipuū est in eis, amant; sed non quantum Deus, nec quomodo. Lucent Cherubin & scientia eminent, sed participio veritatis; ac per hoc non vt veritas, nec quantū. Sed throni, sed insidentes beneficio: iudicant & ipsi cum tranquillitate, sed non ad mensurā modum vt pacis pacantis, pacis quæ exsuperat omnem sensum. Dominantur Dominationes, sed sub Domino dominantur, sed seruiunt pariter: quid hoc ad summum, sempiternum, singulareq; Dominiū? Præsunt Principatus & regunt, sed reguntur & ipsi, ita vt regere iam non norint, si regi desierint. Præcellit in Potestatibus fortitudo, sed cui debent ꝙ fortes sunt; & aliter est fortis & plus: nec tā fortis quam ipsa Fortitudo. Virtutes pro suo ministerio & potentatu satagunt excitare corda torpentia hominum, innouatione signorum: virtus vero in eo manens ipsa facit opera; facient & illæ, sed in comparatione eius non faciunt. Deniq; tantū interest, vt quasi singulariter Propheta dicat ad eum: Tu es Deus qui facis mirabilia. Et idem de eo: qui facit mirabilia magna solus. Adsunt Angeli & Archangeli, sed ille germanior nobis, qui non modo adest, sed inest: quia si dicas posse inesse & Angelum, nō inficior; memini scriptum: & Angelus qui loquebatur in me. At qui differentia & in hoc. Inest Angelus suggerens bona, non ingerens: idem hortans ad bonū, non bonū creans. Deus sic inest vt efficiat, vt infundat, vel potius vt infundatur & participetur: ita vt vnum perinde cū nostro spiritum esse dicere quis non timuerit, etsi non vna personam, vnamve substantiā. Habes enim, qui adhæret Deo vnus spiritus est: Angelus ergo cū anima, Deus in anima: ille contubernalis animæ inest, Deus vt vita. Itaq; sicut anima videt in oculis, audit in auribus, odorat in naribus, in faucibus gustat, tangit in toto reliquo corpore: sic Deus diuersa in diuersis spiritibus operatur: verbi gratia, in aliis amantē se exhibens, in aliis agnoscente, in aliis alia facientē; sicut unicuiq; datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatē. Quis est iste tā communis in vocibus, tam longe in rebus? quomodo quē nostris loquimur verbis in sua reconditus maiestate nostros penitus & aspectus effugit, & affectus? Audi ipsum qui loquatur hominibus: sicut exaltatur cœli à terra, sic exaltatæ sunt viæ meæ à viis vestris, & cogitationes meæ à cogitationibus vestris. Dicimur amare, & Deus: dicimur nosse, & Deus: & multa in hunc modum. Sed Deus amat vt charitas, nouit vt veritas, sedet vt æquitas, dominatur vt maiestas, regit vt principium, tuetur vt salus, operatur vt virtus, reuelat vt lux, assistit vt pietas: quæ omnia faciunt & Angeli, faciamus & nos, sed longe inferiori modo, non vtiq; bono quod sumus, sed quod participamus.
