Nunc iam transi spiritus istos, si forte cum sponsa dicere possis & tu: paululū cum peritransissem eos inueni quem diligit anima mea. Quis est? non sane occurrit melius, quam qui est: hoc ipse de se voluit responderi, hoc docuit dicentem Moysē ad populum ipso quidē iniungentē: qui est misit me ad vos. Merito quidem, nil competentius æternitati, quæ Deus est: si bonum, si magnum, si beatum, si sapientem, vel quicquid tale de eo dixeris, in hoc verbo instauratur, quod est, est. Nempe hoc est ei esse, quod hæc omnia esse: si & centum talia reddas, non recessisti ab esse; si ea dixeris, nihil addidisti; si non dixeris, nihil minuisti. Iam si vidisti hoc tam singulare, tam summum esse; nonne in comparatione huius quicquid hoc non est, iudicas potius nō esse, quam esse? Quid item Deus? sine quo nihil. Tam nihil esse sine ipso, quā nec ipsi sine se potest: ipse sibi, ipse omnibus est. Ac per hoc quod amodo solus est ipse, qui suū ipsius est & omniū esse. Quid est Deus? principium. Et hoc ipse de se responsum dedit: multa in rebus dicuntur principia, sed respecta posteriorū; alioquin si ad aliquid præcedens respicias, ipsum potius principiū dabis. Quamobrē si queras verū simplexq; principium, inuenias oportet quod principiū non habuerit; ex quo vniuersum minimo cœpit. Nā si cœpit, aliunde cœperit necesse est; a se enim cœpit nihil se parauerit, quod non erat dare sibi potuisse vt esse inciperet, aut fuisse aliquid, annon ratio non consentit, constat nihil sibimet extitisse principiū: quod primum non fuit; verum ergo principium nequaquā cœpit, sed totum non fuit. Quid est Deus? cui secula nec accesserunt, nec decesserunt, nec coæterna tamē. Quid est Deus? ex quo omnia, per quem omnia, in quo omnia: ex quo omnia creabiliter, non seminabiliter; per quem omnia, non quasi in loco, sed quasi in virtute: ex quo omnia, tanquam vno principio auctore omnium. Per quem omnia, ne alterum inducatur principium, artifex: in quo omnia, ne tertium inducatur, locus: ex quo omnia, nō de quo; quia non est materia Deus; efficiens causa est, nō materialis. Frustra Philosophi materiā quærunt, non eguit materia Deus, non enim officinam quæsiuit, non artificem: ipse per se omnia fecit: unde? de nihilo. Nam si ex aliquo fecit, illud non fecit, ac per hoc nō omnia. Absit ut de sua incorrupta incorruptibiliq; substantia tam multa fecerit, & sibona, corruptibilia tamē. Quæris si in ipso omnia, ubi ipse? nihil non minus invenio: quis capiat locus? quæris ubi non sit? nec hoc quidem dixerim, quis sine Deo locus? Incomprehensibilis est Deus, sed nō parum apprehendisti, si hoc tibi de eo compertum est, q nusquam sit, qui non clauditur loco: & nusquam tamē non sit, q non excluditur loco. Suo autem sublimi atq; incomprehensibili modo, sicut omnia in ipso, sic ipse in omnibus est. Deniq; sicut ait Euangelista, in mundo erat: alias vero ubi erat antequam mundus fieret, ibi est. Non est q quæras ultra ubi erat: propter ipsum nihil erat, ergo in se ipso erat. Quid est Deus? quo nihil melius cogitari potest. Si approbas, non oportet assentiaris esse aliquid quod Deus sit, & q Deus non sit; hoc enim sine dubio melius. Quomodo non melius Deo, si Deus non est, q rē dat Deo ut sit? at melius illam diuinitatē qua dicunt Deum esse, non aliud quam Deū esse fatemur. Non est ergo in Deo, nisi Deus. Quid, inquiunt, negas Deum habere diuinitatē? non, sed quod habet, hoc est. Negas diuinitatē Deum esse? non, sed non alia quam quæ ipse est: aut si tu aliā inveniste, adiuuet me Trinitas Deus, aduersus illam tota me contumacia ergo. Quaternitas orbē disterminat, non signat Deitatē. Deus Trinitas est, Deus triū singula personarum: si quartam diuinitatem adiicere placet, interim ego hanc quæ Deus non est, persuasi mihi minime adorandū; puto quod &tu: nempe Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illi soli seruies. Gloriosa vero diuinitas, quæ sibi honorem non audeat arrogare diuinum: at melius quartū hoc omnino respuimus, quā sine honore recipimus. Multa dicitur esse in Deo, & quidem sane catholicē; sed multa vnū: alioquin ū diuersa putemus nō quaternitatem habueris, sed centenitatem. Verbi causa, dicimus magnū, bonum, iustum, & innumera talia: sed nisi omnia vnū in Deo, & cum Deo, consideres, habebis multiplicem Deum. Mihi vero non deest, quod cogitē melius eiusmodi Deo tuo: quæris quid? mera simplicitas. Vero iudicio, natura simplex multiplici anteferetur; scio quod ad id respondere solent; non multa, inquiunt, sed vnam tantū diuinitatem, quæ omnia illa sunt, Deo ut sit conferre asserimus. Asseritis ergo, etsi non multiplicem, duplicem Deum: & non ad merum simplex peruenistis, neq; ad id, quo melius cogitari non potest. Tam non est simplex, quod vel vni fuerit obnoxium formæ; quā nec virgo, vel vni cognita viro. Securus loquor, ne is quidem qui vel duplex esse erit meus: habeo enim melior. Esto quod hunc numerosō & multiplici anteponam, sed plane præ simplici sperno. Meus Deus ipse catholicē est, tā non habet hoc & illud; quam non hæc & illa: est qui est, non quæ est; purus, simplex, integer, perfectus cōstans sibi, nihil de temporibus, nihil de locis, nihil de rebus trahens in se, nihil ex se deponens in eis, non habens quod ad numerum dividat, non quæ colligat ad vnum; vnum quippe est, sed non vnitum. Non partibus constat ut corpus, non affectibus distat ut anima, non formis subsistat ut omne q factum est. Sed neq; formæ, ut istis visum est; magna laus videlicet Deo, ut se ab informitate vendicet, forma vna esse contentum: hoc est dicere, cætera pluribus, Deum non nisi vni debere quod est: Quid? cuius beneficio sunt quæ sunt, ipse pro suo esse alterius beneficio inclinabit? Laus illa, ut vulgo dicitur, blasphemiam valet. An non pluris est nullo indigere, quam vno? Habe reuerentiam Deo, ut quod pluris est, illi tribuas: si cor tuum vsq; huc ascendere potuit, Deum tuū infra quomodo collocabit? Ipse sibi forma, ipse sibi essentia est. In hoc interim gradu suspicio illum, & si aliter potior appareret, illum potius darem. Nunquid verendum ne cogitatio transfuolet illum? Quantumcunq; in altum proficiat, vltra est: infra quod cogitare possit, altissimū quærere ridiculum est; statuere impium. Vltra non citra quærendus est, ascende si adhuc potes ad cor altius, & exaltabitur Deus: non est formatus Deus, forma est: non est affectus Deus, affectio est: non est compositus Deus, merum simplex est. Et ut liquido noueris quid simplex dicā, idem quod vnum: tam simplex Deus, quam vnus est: est autem vnus & quomodo aliud nihil; si dici possit, vnissimus est. Vnus est Sol, quod non sit alter, vna Luna, quod æque altera non sit: atq; id quidē Deus, sed solus. Quid plus? vnus est etiam sibi. Et hoc vis tibi declarari? idem est semper & vno modo. Non sic vnus Sol, non sic vna Luna; clamat vterque non esse se vnum sibi: ille motibus, illa & defectibus suis. Deus autem non modo vnus sibi, & in se vnus est: nihil in se, nisi se habet; non ex tempore alterationem habet, non in substantia alteritatem. Hinc de eo Boetius, hoc vere vnum in quo nullum est numerus, nullum in eo aliud praeter id quod est: neq; enim subiectū fieri potest, forma enim est. Compara huic vni omne quod vnum dici potest; & vnum non erit: Trinitas est tamen Deus. Quid ergo destruimus quod dictū est de vnitate, quia inducimus Trinitatē? Non, sed statuimus vnitatē: dicimus Patrem, dicimus Filiū, dicimus Spiritum sanctum; non tamen tres Deos, sed vnum. Qui sibi vult iste, ut sic loquar, absq; numero, numerus? Si tria, quomodo non numerus? Si vnum, vbi numerus? Sed habeo, inquis, quid numerē, & quid non numerem: substantia vna est, Personæ tres sunt. Quid mirum, quid vel obscurum in hoc? nihil si personæ seorsum à substantia cogitentur: nunc vero cum tres personæ illa substantia sint, & illa vna substantia tres illæ personæ, quis numerum neget? nam vere tres sunt. Quis numerat tamen? nam vere vnum sunt. Aut si tu facile explicatu id putas dicendo tres: dicito quid numerasti? Naturas? vna est. Essentias? vna est. Substantias? vna est. Deitates? vna est. Non hæc, sed personas numero, inquis, quæ non sint illa vna natura, illa vna essentia, illa vna substantia, illa vna diuinitas? Catholicus es, minime hoc dabis. Personarum proprietas, non aliud quam personas; ipsasq; non aliud quam vnum Deum, vnam diuinam substantiā, vnam diuinam naturam, vnam diuinam & summā maiestatem, catholica confitetur. Numera ergo, si potes, aut sine substantia personas, quæ ipsa sunt; aut sine personis proprietates, quæ ipsæ sunt. Aut si diuidere quis conetur vel personas à substantia, vel proprietates à personis; nescio quomodo Trinitatis se profiteri cultorem possit, quia in tantam rerum numerositatem excesserit. Dica-
units.tr: And first, indeed, that there are citizen spirits there, powerful, glorious, blessed, distinguished into orders, arranged in ranks, standing from the beginning in their place, perfect in their kind, ethereal in body, everlasting in immortality, impassible, not created but made, that is, by grace and not by nature; pure in mind, kindly in feeling, pious in religion, unblemished in chastity, undivided in unanimity, secure in peace, founded by God and devoted to the praises and service of God. We have found all these things by reading, and we hold them by faith, although the opinion of some is in doubt about whether their bodies exist at all, and where they come from. If anyone judges that this should be counted among matters of opinion, I will not contend. Further, we understand that they are endowed with intellect, not by faith or opinion but by understanding, because those who lack this cannot also be sharers in God. There are also certain names known to us in the same way by hearing, through which the duties, merits, grades and orders of these blessed beings (even those which the hearing of mortals has not clearly perceived) can be conjectured and distinguished by us in some measure. But what is not from hearing is not from faith, for faith comes by hearing. So although we speak these things by opinion, since the heavenly names have become known to us, may one not be permitted, without loss of faith, to form some opinion about the things of which they are the names? Angels, Archangels, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Dominions, Thrones, Cherubim, Seraphim: these are the names. What is their meaning? Is there no distinction between those spirits who are simply called Angels and those who are called Archangels? What, then, does this difference of rank intend? Let us suppose that Angels are so called (unless you have considered something more fitting) because they are believed to be given to individual men, one to each, sent to minister, according to the teaching of Paul, for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation. Of them the Saviour said: "Their angels always see the face of the Father." Let us suppose that Archangels preside over them; being privy to the divine mysteries, they are sent only for special and very great causes, of which the great Archangel Gabriel is read to have been sent to Mary, surely for a cause which could not be greater. Let us suppose that above these are the Virtues, by whose nod or work signs and prodigies appear in the elements, or made out of the elements, for the admonition of mortals. Perhaps this is why, when you read in the Gospels, "there shall be signs in the sun and moon and stars," you find shortly after, "for the powers of the heavens shall be shaken." These are indeed the spirits through whom signs are wrought. Let us suppose that there are Powers superior to these, by whose virtue the power of darkness is restrained and the malice of this air is held in check, so that it cannot harm as much as it wishes, and cannot be malicious except to serve good. Let us suppose that Principalities are set over these as well, by whose governance and wisdom every principality on earth is established, ruled, limited, transferred, diminished and changed. Let us suppose that Dominions so far surpass all the aforesaid orders that, in comparison with them, all the other administering spirits seem to be referred to these as to lords; the government of principalities, the protection of powers, the works of virtues, the revelations of archangels, and the care and providence of angels. Let us suppose that Thrones have flown down from a yet higher retreat, and are called thrones because God sits upon them, and God sits upon them because He cannot sit on what cannot sustain Him. Do you ask what that sitting means? It is the highest tranquillity, the most placid serenity, a peace which surpasses all understanding. Such is the Lord of Sabaoth who sits on the thrones, judging all things with tranquillity: most placid, most serene, most peaceful. And such thrones He has made for Himself, most like Himself. Let us suppose that Cherubim, from the very fountain of wisdom, draw up the waters of the Most High and pour forth the streams of knowledge to all their fellow citizens. And see whether this is what the Prophet spoke of: "the rushing of the river makes glad the city of God." Let us suppose that Seraphim, spirits wholly kindled with divine fire, pass on all things, so that each citizen may be a burning and shining lamp: burning with love, shining with knowledge. O Eugenius, how good it is to be here, and how much better it will be, if at some time we follow wholly where we have partly gone before! We go before in mind, and not even in the whole of the mind, but in part, and a very small part. Our affections lie weighed down by the bulk of the body, and our desires cling to the mire; meanwhile a thin and dry contemplation flies ahead, and yet from that little which is now given, we are moved to cry out: "Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells." What if the soul gathers itself wholly, and, having drawn back its affections from all the places where they are held captive, fearing what does not harm, loving what is not fitting, grieving in vain, rejoicing more in vain, it flies with them in complete freedom, strikes with the force of the spirit, and sinks into the fatness of grace? Then, when it begins to go round the bright mansions and to examine more carefully even that bosom of Abraham, and to visit under the altar the souls of the martyrs, patiently awaiting in their first robe the second, then much more will it press on, speaking with the prophet: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life." Why should God not be seen there? Why should there not be proved what is the good, and pleasing, and perfect will of God: good in itself, pleasing in its effects, well-pleasing to those who enjoy it, perfect to the perfect, and seeking nothing further. The bowels of mercy lie open, the thoughts of peace, the riches of salvation, the mysteries of good will, the secrets of kindness, which are closed to mortals and are suspect even to the elect themselves. This indeed is wholesome, so that they may cease to fear while they are not yet found worthy and fit for the sea. In those whom they call Seraphim one can see how He loves, without having a reason from which He loves; and He hates none of the things which He has made; how He cherishes those whom He made to be saved, how He embraces them, how that consuming fire purges the sins of the chosen youth and the chaff of their ignorance, and makes her most clean and most worthy of His love. In the Cherubim, who are called the fullness of knowledge, one can see that God is the Lord of knowledge, who alone knows no ignorance, who is wholly light, in whom there is no darkness at all, who is wholly eye, and who is never deceived, because He is never shut in; who does not seek outside himself a light by which he may be brought to see, but is himself the one who sees and himself the source from which he sees. In the Thrones one sees what a judge free from all suspicion of innocence he is, sitting among those whom he will not deceive and cannot be deceived; for he is loving and seeing, and his sitting is not idle, and tranquillity is his distinguishing mark. From such a face I desire that my judgment should come forth; in which there is love, from which error is absent, and from which disturbance is absent too. In the Dominions one sees how great is the majesty of the Lord, by whose nod dominion stands, by whose dominion the universe is established, and whose eternity is the limit. In the Principalities one sees the beginning from which all things come, and how, as a door turns on its hinge, so the universe is ruled by Him. In the Powers one sees how the same Prince, with power, protects those whom He rules, while He keeps back and drives away opposing powers. In the Virtues one sees that He is everywhere present equally by one virtue, by which all things are quickened, made effective, invisible and immovable, yet He moves all things usefully and holds them firmly. When this virtue breaks forth in effects less often seen among mortals, they call them miracles or prodigies. Finally, in the Angels and Archangels one sees and marvels at the truth and experience of that voice, since He takes care of us and never ceases to gladden us with such and such great visitations, to instruct us with revelations, to admonish us with suggestions, and to comfort us with diligence. All these things the same Spirit who made those spirits bestowed upon them: one and the same supreme Spirit, dividing to each as He wills, He works these things in them, and He gave them to work these things too, but in different ways. The Seraphim burn, and they are worthy of God, or rather they burn with God; what is chief in them is that they love, but not as much as God does, nor in the same way. The Cherubim shine and excel in knowledge, but by participation in truth; and therefore not as truth itself does, nor to the same extent. The Thrones, too, sit by a benefit; they also judge with tranquillity, but not according to the measure of the peace which pacifies, the peace which surpasses all understanding. The Dominions rule, but they rule under the Lord, and they likewise serve; what is this beside the supreme, everlasting and unique Dominion? The Principalities preside and govern, but they too are governed, so that they would no longer know how to rule if they ceased to be ruled. In the Powers strength excels, but they are strong by Him to whom they owe that they are strong; and He is strong in another way, and more so: He is not as strong as Strength itself. The Virtues, by their ministry and power, labour to rouse the sluggish hearts of men by the renewal of signs; but virtue, remaining in itself, does the works itself; they too will do them, but in comparison with Him they do nothing. Finally, the difference is so great that the Prophet speaks to Him as if alone: "You are the God who work wonders." And of Him again: "who alone does great wonders." Angels and Archangels are present, but He is nearer to us, who not only is present but dwells within; for if you say that an Angel can dwell within, I do not deny it, for I remember what is written: "the angel who spoke in me." But here too there is a difference. An Angel dwells suggesting good things, not infusing them; he exhorts to good, but does not create the good. God so dwells that He works, that He pours in, or rather that He is poured in and shared. Thus one would not hesitate to say that He is one spirit with our spirit, even though He is not one person or one substance with it. For "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." The Angel, then, dwells with the soul as a companion; God dwells in the soul as its life. And so, as the soul sees in the eyes, hears in the ears, smells in the nostrils, tastes in the throat, and touches in the rest of the body, so God works diverse things in diverse spirits: for example, showing Himself as loving in some, being acknowledged in others, and doing other things in others, as "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the common good." Who is this, so common in words and so far away in things? How is it that He whom we speak of in our words, hidden in His own majesty, utterly escapes our sight and our affections? Hear Him Himself who speaks to men: "As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts." We are said to love, and God too; we are said to know, and God too; and many things in this manner. But God loves as charity, knows as truth, sits as equity, rules as majesty, governs as the principle, protects as salvation, works as virtue, reveals as light, assists as piety. All these things the Angels also do, and we too may do them, but in a far lower way: not indeed by the good that we are, but by the good in which we share. Now pass beyond those spirits, if perchance you can say with the bride as well: "When I had passed a little beyond them, I found Him whom my soul loves." Who is He? Surely no better name occurs than "He who is." This He Himself wished to be given in reply, and this He taught when Moses asked and He told him to say to the people: "He who is has sent me to you." Rightly, for nothing is more fitting to the eternity which God is. If you call Him good, great, blessed, wise, or whatever such thing you say of Him, all of it is renewed in this word, which is: He is. Indeed to be God is this, that all these things are; and even if you should give a hundred such names, you have not departed from being; if you say them, you have added nothing; if you do not say them, you have taken nothing away. Now if you have seen this so unique, so supreme a being, do you not judge, in comparison with it, that whatever is not this is rather not-being than being? What more, God? Without Him nothing is. As nothing can be without Him, so He cannot be without Himself: He is to Himself, He is to all. Therefore He alone is what He is, who is the being of Himself and of all. What is God? The beginning. And He Himself has given this answer about Himself. Many things in creatures are called beginnings, but with respect to the things that follow; for if you look to something that precedes, you will rather give that as the beginning. Wherefore, if you seek a true and simple beginning, you must find something which had no beginning, from which the universe began at its least point. For if it began, it must have begun from something else; for it could not have begun from itself, since it could not have prepared itself, nor given itself the power to begin to be or to be something. If reason does not agree that something was its own beginning, which did not first exist, it follows that the true beginning never began, but was not at all not-existing. What is God? To whom ages neither came nor departed, and yet He is not co-eternal with them. What is God? He from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are: from whom all things are created, not sown; through whom all things are, not as in a place, but as in power; from whom all things are, as from one beginning, the author of all. Through whom all things are, lest a second beginning be introduced, the craftsman; in whom all things are, lest a third be introduced, a place; from whom all things are, not out of which; for God is not matter, He is the efficient cause, not the material. In vain do the philosophers seek matter: God had no need of matter; for He did not seek a workshop or a craftsman; He made all things by Himself. From what? From nothing. For if He had made them from something, He would not have made that, and so not all things. Far be it that from His own incorrupt and incorruptible substance He should have made so many things, and those good, yet corruptible. If you ask whether all things are in Him, where is He Himself? I find nothing less: what place could contain Him? Do you ask where He is not? I would not even say this: what place is without God? God is incomprehensible, but you have grasped not a little if this has been discovered about Him, that He is nowhere, since He is not shut in by place; and yet He is nowhere not, since He is not excluded by place. In His own sublime and incomprehensible way, as all things are in Him, so He is in all things. Finally, as the Evangelist says, "He was in the world"; but where He was before the world was made, there He is. There is no reason for you to ask further where He was: nothing was before Him, therefore He was in Himself. What is God? Than whom nothing better can be thought. If you approve this, you must not agree that there is something which is God and which God is not; for this would undoubtedly be better. Would it not be better for God, if God were not, that something should give Him the being that He may be? But we confess that the divinity by which they say God is, is nothing other than God Himself. Therefore there is nothing in God except God. "What," they say, "do you deny that God has divinity?" No, but what He has, that He is. Do you deny that divinity is God? No, but it is not other than what He Himself is; or if you find another, may the Triune God help me, and may all my stubbornness be against that one. A quaternity marks off the boundary of the world; it does not signify deity. God is a Trinity, God is the single persons of the three; if you wish to add a fourth divinity, meanwhile I have persuaded myself that this one, which is not God, is in no way to be worshipped; I think you do too: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him alone." But glorious divinity, which would not dare to claim divine honour for itself: yet this fourth I altogether reject, rather than receive it without honour. Many things are said to be in God, and indeed catholically so; but the many are one. Otherwise, if we imagined them to be diverse, we would not have a quaternity but a centenity. For instance, we say great, good, just, and countless such things; but unless you consider all of them as one in God, and with God, you will have a manifold God. For my part, I do not lack the thought of something better than your God of that kind: what do you ask? Pure simplicity. In true judgment, a simple nature is preferred to a manifold one; I know what they are accustomed to answer to this: "not many," they say, "but only one divinity, which is all those things, we assert to be conferred on God so that He may be." So you assert, if not a manifold, then a double God; and you have not arrived at mere simplicity, nor at that than which nothing better can be thought. He is not so simple that He is subject to one form only, any more than a virgin is one who has been known by only one man. I speak securely; even one who would be double would not be mine, for I have a better one. Let it be granted that I put this many-formed one before the simple one; I plainly spurn him in comparison with the simple. My God is catholically itself; He does not have this and that, any more than He is these and those; He is He who is, not what is; pure, simple, whole, perfect, constant to Himself, taking nothing from times, nothing from places, nothing from things into Himself, depositing nothing of Himself in them; not having anything to divide into number, nothing to gather into one; for He is one, but not united. He does not consist of parts as a body does, nor is He distinct by affections as a soul is, nor does He subsist by forms as everything that has been made does. But neither is He of forms, as it has seemed to some; it would be great praise for God, forsooth, to claim himself from formlessness, and to be content with being one form: that is to say, that other things have many forms, and God owes only to one what He is! What? By whose benefit those things exist which exist, will He incline Himself to another's benefit for His own being? That praise, as it is commonly said, is worth blasphemy. Is it not more to need nothing than to need one thing? Show God reverence, by attributing to Him what is greater; if your heart has been able to ascend thus far, how will you place your God below? He is form to Himself, He is essence to Himself. At this level, meanwhile, I would regard Him as the object of my suspicion, and if He appeared otherwise to be the more excellent, I would rather give Him that. Is there reason to fear lest thought fly over Him? However far it advances on high, He is beyond it; to seek the highest below what thought can reach is ridiculous, and to set it up is impious. He must be sought beyond, not below: ascend, if you still can, to a higher heart, and God will be exalted. God is not a form that has been shaped; He is form. God is not an affection; He is the affection itself. God is not compound; He is pure simplicity. And so that you may clearly know what I mean by simple, simple means the same as one: God is as simple as He is one; and He is one and in no way other; if it can be said, He is most one. The sun is one, in that there is not another; one moon, in that there is no equal other moon; and that is indeed God, but He alone. What more? He is one even to Himself. Do you want this declared to you? He is always the same and in one way. The sun is not one in that way, nor the moon; each of them cries out that it is not one to itself: the one by its motions, the other by its eclipses. But God is not only one to Himself, and one in Himself: He has nothing in Himself except Himself; He has no change from time, no otherness in substance. Hence Boethius says of Him: "He is truly one, in whom there is no number, and in whom there is nothing other than what He is"; for He cannot become a subject, since He is form. Compare with this one everything that can be called one, and it will not be one: yet God is a Trinity. Why, then, do we destroy what has been said about unity, because we introduce a Trinity? No, but we establish the unity: we say the Father, we say the Son, we say the Holy Spirit; yet not three Gods, but one. What does that mean, if I may so speak, a number without number? If three, how is it not a number? If one, where is the number? "But," you say, "I have something that I may count and something I may not count: the substance is one, the persons are three." What is strange, or even obscure, in this? Nothing, if the persons are thought of apart from the substance. But now, since the three persons are that substance, and that one substance is the three persons, who would deny number? For truly there are three. Yet who counts them? For truly they are one. Or if you think that this is easy to explain by saying three, tell me what you have counted: natures? There is one. Essences? There is one. Substances? There is one. Deities? There is one. "Not these," you say, "but I count persons, which are not that one nature, that one essence, that one substance, that one divinity?" You are catholic; you will not grant this at all. The Catholic confesses that the property of the persons is nothing other than the persons, and that the persons are nothing other than the one God, one divine substance, one divine nature, one divine and supreme majesty. Number, then, if you can, either the persons without the substance, which they themselves are, or the properties without the persons, which they themselves are. Or if anyone tries to divide the persons from the substance, or the properties from the persons, I do not know how he could profess himself a worshipper of the Trinity, since he has gone so far into such a multitude of things. Let us say...

units.la: Dicamus itaq; tres, sed non ad praeiudicium vnitatis: dicamus vnum, sed non ad confusionem Trinitatis. Neq; enim nomina vacua sunt, nec absq; significantia cassae voces, Sabellianum hoc. Quaeritquis, quomodo hoc q; Catholice esse dicimus, possit esse? sufficiat ei tenere sic esse. Atq; hoc non rationi perspicuum, nec tamen opinioni ambiguum; sed fidei persuasum. Sacramentum hoc magnum est, & quidem venerandum, non scrutandum: quomodo pluralitas in vnitate, aut ipsa in pluralitate? Scrutari hoc teneritatis est, credere pietas est, nosse vita, & vita aeterna est. Vnde si operae precium censes o Eugeni, percurrat ia consideratio multa vna, quo eminentia huius singularis vnius, fiat euidentior. Est vnitas quae collectiua potest dici, cū, verbi causa, multi lapides faciunt acervū vnum: & est vnitas constitutiua, cū multa membra vnum corpus, vel multae partes vnum quodcunq; totū constituunt. Est& coniugatiua, qua fit vt duo iā non duo sint, sed vna caro. Et est natiua, qua anima & caro vnus nascitur homo. Est vnitas potestatiua, qua homo virtutis, non instabilis, non dissimilis, sed vnus sibimet semper nititur inueniri. Est consentanea, cum per charitatē multorum hominū est cor vnum & anima vna. Est & votiua, cū anima votis omnibus adhaerēs Deo vnus spiritus est. Est& dignatiua vnitas, qualimus noster à Dei verbo in vnā assumptus est personam. Verū haec omnia quid ad illum summum, atq; (vt ita dicam) vnice vnum, vbi vnitatem consubstantialitas facit? huic vni quoduis illorū si assimiles, erit quoq; modo vnum: si compares, nullo. Igitur inter omnia quae recte vnum dicuntur, arcem tenet vnita trinitatis, qua tres personae vna substantia sunt. Secundo loco illa praecellit, qua è conuerso tres substantiae vna in Christo persona sunt. Porro haec & quaecunq; alia dici vna possunt, summae illius vnitatis imitatione (non cōparatione) vna appellari vera sobriaq; probat consideratio. Nec abducimur ab hac vnitatis professione assertione trium, cum in hac trinitate non recipiamus multiplicationem, sicut nec solitudinē in vnitate. Quamobrē cum dico vnū, non me trinitatis turbat numerus, qui essentia non multiplicat, nō variat, nec partiatur. Rursum cū dico tria, nō me arguit iniruitus vnitatis, q illa quaecunq; tria, seu illos tres, nec in confusionem cogit, nec in singularitate redigit. Idem me sentire fateor & de illa vnitate, cui secundam ab ista inter cætera vna honorē dedi: dico in Christo verbum, animā, & carnem sine confusione essentiarum vnam esse personam, & item absq; praeiudicio personalis vnitatis in sua numerositate manere. Nec negauerim hanc ad illud quoq; genus vnitatis pertinere, qua anima & caro vnus est homo. Decuit quippe familiarius similiusq; cū hominis conuenire constitutione, quod pro homine constitutum est Sacramentū: decuit & cum summa quae in Deo est, & Deus est, vnitate congruere, vt quomodo ibi tres personae vna essentia; ita hic cōuenientissima quadā contrarietate tres essentiae sint vna persona. Videsne pulcre inter vtramq; vnitatē hanc collocari, in eo vtiq; q constitutus est mediator Dei hominisq;, homo Christus Iesus? Pulcherrima, inquā, conuenientia, vt salutare sacramentum congrua quadam similitudine ambobus respondeant, & saluanti videlicet & saluato. Ita haec vnitas duarū consistens media vnitatū, alteri succumbere, alteri praeminere cognoscitur, quantū superiore inferior, tantū inferiore superior. Tātam deniq; tamq; expressam vnionis vim in se praefert ea persona, in qua Deus & homo vnus est Christus, vt si duo illa de se inuicē praedices; nō erraueris, Deū videlicet hominē, & hominem Deum, vere Catholiceq; pnuncians. Non autē similiter vel carnem de anima vel animam de carne, nisi absurdissimo praedicas: etsi similiter anima & caro sit homo. Nec mirum si non aeque potis anima sit sua illa vitali, etsi non parū valida intentione connectere atq; suis affectibus astringere sibi carnē; vt sibi diuinitas hominē, illum qui praedestinatus est, filius Dei in virtute. Longa cathena & fortis ad stringendum diuina praedestinatio, ab aeterno est enim. Quid longius aeternitate? qd diuinitate potentius? inde est q nec morte incidente vllaten' interdici vnitas haec potuit, etsi carne & anima ab inuicē separatis. Et fortassis hoc sensit ille, qui se indignū professus est soluere corrigiā calceamenti huius. Sed & illa tria sata de Euangelio mixta & fermentata in panem vnum, si quis ad haec tria dixerit pertinere, nō incongrue id mihi facere videbitur. Quā bene illa mulier fermentauit, vt nec diuisione quidē facta carnis & animae, à carne vel anima verbū diuidetur. Mansit & in separatione inseparabilis vnitas: nec enim quae ex parte cōtigit leparatio potuit vnitati praescribere, permanenti in totis tribus. Siue coniunctis siue disiunctis duobus, nihilominus perseuerauit in tribus vnitas personalis; æque vnus Christus, vnaq; persona, verbum, anima, & caro, etiam mortuo homine perdurauit. In vtero virginis (vt sentio ego) commixtio haec fermentatio facta est, & ipsa mulier quae miscuit & fermentauit. Nam fermentum non immerito fortasse dixerim fidem Mariae: plane beata quae credidit, quoniam perfecta sunt in ea, quae dicta sunt ei à Domino. Perfecta autem non essent, si quominus iuxta verbum Domini esset fermentatum totum, & perpetuo fermentatum; seruans nobis in morte, quam in vita pariter vnum atq; integrum mediatorem Dei & hominum cum sua Deitate hominem Iesum Christum. Aduertere est in hoc admirabili sacramento iuxta numerum satorum, mirae & decentissimae distinctionis gradus: nouum, antiquum, aeternum. Nouum, animam quae de nihilo tunc creata creditur, cum infusa: antiquum, carnem quae à primo vsq; hominum, id est ex Adam, traducta cognoscitur: aeternum, Verbum quod ab aeterno Patre, coaeternum illi, genitum indubitata veritate asseritur. Et in his triplex, si diligenter aduertas, diuinae potentiae genus: quod factum sit de nihilo aliquid, de vetusto nouum, aeternum beatumq; de damnato & mortuo. Quid hoc ad nostram salutem? multum per omnem modum. Primum quidem quod peccato redacti in nihil, p hoc quodammodo iterato creati sumus, vt simus initiū aliquod creaturae eius. Deinde q ex vetusta seruitute, in libertatē filiorū Dei translati, in nouitate spiritus ambulamus. Postremo q de potestate tenebrarū vocati, ad regnū claritatis aeternae, in quo iā & sedere nos fecit in Christo. Alieni sunt à nobis, qui Christi à nobis carnē alienate conantur; nouā creatā in virgine, & nō de virgine sumtam impie afferentes. Pulchre Propheticus spiritus lōge ante occurrit huic sententiae, imo blasphemiae impiorū: egredietur, inquiens, virga de radice Iesse, & flos de radice ascendet. Ecce quod nulla humanae conceptionis vsu, sed diuina virtute quasi virga procedat, dum conceptus est ex Spiritu sancto. Ipsa quae virgo fuit, in fructu genuit, vt Christum vnum & pluralem faceret; carnem & animam sine confusione mixtas, à Spiritu sancto; ex virgine nato, perpetuo, sine ullis vitiis, in quo sit vnitas Deitatis & humanitatis in sua distinctione, vt sit vna persona. virga de radice Iesse, & flos de radice eius ascendet. Dixisse poterat, & flos de virga, sed malui de radice ut unde virgam, inde florem duxisse originem demonstraret: inde igitur sumpta caro unde nec noua virgine, quae prodiit ex radice. Forte subsfomachari, si adhuc pergimus quaerere quid est Deus; tum quia totiens iam quaesitus est, tum quia difficilis inuentu iri. Dico tibi Pater Eugeni, sed est Deus qui frustra nunquam quaeri potest, nec cum inueniri nō potest. Doceat te hoc experimentum tuum, aut si non, experto credito, non mihi, sed sancto qui ait: bonus es Domine sperantibus in te, animae quaerenti te. Quid ergo est Deus? Quod ad vniuersum spectat, finis: quod ad electionem, salus: quod ad se, ipse nouit. Quid est Deus? Voluntas omnipotens benevolentissima virtus, lumen aeternum, incommutabilis ratio, summa beatitudo, creans mentes ad se participandum, viuificans ad sentiendum, afficiens ad appetendum, dilatans ad capiendum, iustificans ad promerendum, accendens ad Zelum, fecundans ad fructum, dirigens ad aequitatem, formans ad benevolentiam, moderans ad sapientiam, roborans ad virtutem, visitans ad consolationem, illuminans ad cognitionem, perpetuans ad immortalitatem, implens ad felicitatem, circumdans ad securitatem. Quid est Deus? non minus poena peruersorum, quam humilium gloria. Etenim rationabilis quaedam aequitatis directio incouertibilis atque indeclinabilis, quippe attingens vbiq; cui illisa omnis prauitas, conturbetur necesse est. Quidni in hanc omnem timidum vel distortum impingat & cō quaesetur? Vae vniuerso quod obuiam forte offenderit, cedere nescia rectitudo; nā & fortitudo est. Quid inges voluntatibus tam contrarium & aduersum, quam semper conari, impingere semper, & frustra? Vae oppositis voluntatibus, sola sua profecto auersionis referentibus poenam. Quid tam poenale, quā semper velle & nunquam erit; & semper nolle, & nunquam non erit? Quid tam damnatum quam voluntas addicta huic necessitati volendi nolendiq;, vt ad vtrumlibet ia sicut non nisi perverse, ita non nisi misere moueatur? In aeternum non obtinebit quod vult, & quod noh vult in aeternum nihilominus sustinebit id gne omnino vt qui ad nihil afficitur vnquam decear, ad nihil vnquam quod libeat euadat. Quis hoc facit? rectus Dominus Deus noster, qui & cum puerso peruertitur, nunquam recto prauoq; conueniet. Haec enim sibi inuicem aduersantur, etsi non inuicem laedant: laesio alteritus est, absit vt Dei: durum tibi est, inquit, contra stimulum calcitrare, h.e. non stimulo duitu, sed calcitranti. Est & turpium poena Deus: Lux est enim. Et quid tam inuisum obscoenis flagitiosisq; mentibus? Prosecto omnis qui male agit, odit lucem. Sed dico, nunquid non poterunt declinare? minime omnino: lucet vbiq; etsi non omnibus. Denique; in tenebris lucet, & tenebrae eam non comprehenderunt: videt tenebras lux, cui hoc est videre & lucere; sed non vicissim a tenebris ipsa videtur, quia tenebrae eam non comprehenderunt. Et videntur ergo vt confundantur, & non vident ne consolentur: nec modo a luce, & in luce videntur. A quo, vel a quibus? ab omni vidente, vt p multitudine intuentium sit confusio multa. At nullus de tanta numerositate spectantium molestior oculus, suo cuiusq;: non est aspectus siue in coelo siue in terra, quae tenebrosa conscientia effugere magis velit, minus possit. Non latent tenebrae vel seipsas, sed vident, quae aliud nō vident: opera tenebrarum sequuntur illas, nec est quo se abscondant ab illis ne in tenebris quidē. Hic est vermis qui non moritur, memoria praeteritorum, semel iniectus vel potius innatus & peccatum haesit firmiter nequaquam deinceps auellendus: nec cessat rodere conscientiā, eaq; pastus, esca vtiq; inconsumptibili, perpetuat vitam. Horreo vermem mordacem, & mortem viuacem: horreo incidere in manus mortis viuentis, & vitae morientis. Haec est secunda mors, quae nunquam per occidit, sed semper occidit. Quis dei illis semel mori, & nō moriantur in aeternum? qui dicunt montibus: cadite super nos, & collibus, operite nos: quid nisi morte mortis beneficio aut finire, aut euadere volunt? Denique, invocabunt mortem, ait, & non venient. Intuere id clarius, constat immortale animā esse nec aliquando absq; sua memoria viuere, ne non animā aliquando esse contingat: itaq; durante anima, durat & memoria. Sed qualis? foeda flagitiis, horrida facinoribus, vanitate tumida, contemptu hispida & neglecta. Quae priora, transierunt & non transierunt; transierunt a manu, sed non mente: quod factum est, factū non esse non potest. Proinde etsi facere in tempore fuit, sed fecisse in sempiternum manet: non transibit cum tempore, quod tempore transit. Interno ergo necesse est cruciet, quod perperam te egisse in aeternum meminisse. Experiri erit hoc veritate vocis illius: arguam te, & statuā contra faciem tuā. Dominus locutus est, cui omne aduersum, & sibi aduersari necesse est, vt sit sera querela: O custos quare posuisti me contrarium tibi, & factus sum mihi ipsi grauis! Ita est o Engeni, non potest Deo esse contrarium quid, & sibimet cohaerere: sed qui arguetur a Deo, arguetur & a seipso. Non est sane iam tunc quod aut veritate dissimulet ratio, aut rationis intuitu anima declinet abrupta membris corporis in sese collecta. Quo enim id valeat, sopitis conclusis; in morte sensibus, per quos itaq; curiosus exire, & a se ire solebat in eam quae praeterit mundi istius figuram? Vides turpibus nihil deesse ad confusionem; cum producentur spectaculum fieri, Deo, Angelis, hominibus, sibi ipsis. O quam male mali omnes locati sunt, vtique; oppositi torrenti huic directae aequitatis, & huic lumini palatae veritatis expositi. Nonne hoc est ppetuo tudi, perpetuoq; confundi? Duplici contritione, ait ille, contere eos Domine Deus noster. Quid est Deus? longitudo, latitudo, sublimitas, & profundum. Quid inquis? tenemus te quaternitatis (quā abominatus est), professorem? minime. Abominatus sum, & abominor. Visus sum ptulisse plura, sed vnū est: vnus Deus signatus est, p captu nostro, nō pro suo statu. Diuisus est hic; non ille: voces diuersae, sed semitae multae: sed vnū per eas significatur, vnus quaeritur. Non diuisiones substantiae in quaternario isto expresse sunt, nōn diuersiones quales in corporibus intuemur, nō distinctio personalis qualē in trinitate adoramus, non numerus proprietatū qualem personis ipsis inesse fatemur, etsi nō aliud a personis. Alioquin hoc singulū horum video quod quatuor simul, haec quatuor ipsa quod singulum est. Nobis autem quae non possumus cū Deo simplicitate contendere, dū contendimus apprehendere vnū, occurrit veluti
units.tr: Let us therefore say three, but not to the prejudice of the unity; let us say one, but not to the confusion of the Trinity. For these names are not empty, nor are they words without meaning. This is the Sabellian view. If someone asks how what we call Catholic can be true, it is enough for him to hold that it is so. This is not plain to reason, yet it is not doubtful to opinion; it is a matter persuaded by faith. This is a great mystery, and indeed one to be venerated, not searched out: how is there plurality in unity, or unity in plurality? To search into this is a mark of a tender mind; to believe it is piety; to know it is life, and eternal life. Therefore, Eugenius, if you think it worth the effort, let us run through many kinds of unity, so that the eminence of this one singular unity may become more evident. There is a unity that may be called collective, as when many stones make one heap. There is a constitutive unity, when many members make one body, or many parts constitute one whole. There is also a conjugal unity, by which two are no longer two but one flesh. There is a natural unity, by which soul and flesh together are born one man. There is a unity of power, by which a man, not unstable and not inconsistent, but one, always strives to be found the same with himself. There is a unity of agreement, when through the charity of many men there is one heart and one soul. There is also a unity of will, when a soul clinging to God in all its desires is one spirit with him. There is also a unity of dignity, such as our nature has when it is assumed by the Word of God into one person. But what are all these compared with that supreme and, so to speak, uniquely one unity, where consubstantiality makes the unity? If you set any of these beside that one, it will be one in some way; if you compare them, it will be one in no way. Therefore, among all the things that are rightly called one, the unity of the Trinity holds the citadel, in which three persons are one substance. In the second place stands the unity in which, conversely, three substances are one person in Christ. Moreover, sober and true consideration shows that these and whatever other things may be called one are called one by imitation (not comparison) of that supreme unity. Nor are we drawn away from this profession of unity by the assertion of three, since in this Trinity we admit no multiplication, just as we admit no solitude in the unity. Therefore, when I say one, the number of the Trinity does not disturb me, for it does not multiply, vary or divide the essence. Again, when I say three, the objection of unity does not trouble me, for it neither forces those three, however they are called, into confusion, nor reduces them to singularity. I confess that I think the same also about that unity to which I have given second honour among the others: I say that in Christ the Word, soul and flesh are one person without confusion of the essences, and likewise that, without prejudice to the personal unity, they remain in their own plurality. Nor would I deny that this also belongs to that kind of unity by which soul and flesh are one man. For it was fitting that what was established as the sacrament for man should agree more closely and more similarly with the constitution of man; and it was fitting that it should also agree with the supreme unity that is in God, and is God, so that, as there three persons are one essence, so here, by a most fitting contrariety, three essences are one person. Do you see how beautifully this unity is placed between the two unities, in that man Christ Jesus, who is constituted the Mediator between God and men? It is a most beautiful fitness, I say, that the saving sacrament should correspond to both by a certain suitable likeness, namely to the saviour and to the saved. Thus this unity, standing as a middle unity between two unities, is known to yield to the one and to excel the other: as far as the lower is inferior to the higher, so far the higher is superior to the lower. Finally, the person in whom God and man are one Christ bears in himself so great and so clear a force of union that you will not err if you predicate the two of each other, namely God is man and man is God, speaking truly and catholically. But you will not predicate in the same way the flesh of the soul or the soul of the flesh, unless you do so most absurdly, although the soul and the flesh together are man. Nor is it strange if the soul, by that vital but not weak intention, cannot so fully bind the flesh to itself and tie it to its own affections, as the divinity binds the man whom the Son of God has predestined in power to itself. Divine predestination is a long and strong chain for binding, for it is from eternity. What is longer than eternity? What is more powerful than divinity? Hence this unity could not be dissolved by any death, even though flesh and soul were separated from each other. Perhaps that man felt this, who professed himself unworthy to loose the thong of this sandal. But if anyone should say that those three measures of meal mixed and leavened into one loaf of bread from the Gospel also pertain to these three, it will seem to me that he is not wrong to do so. How well that woman leavened! So that, even when the flesh and soul were divided, the Word would not be divided from flesh or soul. The unity remained inseparable even in separation; for the separation that happened in part could not prescribe terms to the unity, which remains in all three. Whether the two are joined or disjoined, the personal unity nonetheless persisted in three; the one Christ and the one person, Word, soul and flesh, endured equally even when the man was dead. In the womb of the Virgin (as I think) this mixing and leavening was done, and the woman herself who mixed and leavened. For I might rightly, perhaps, call the faith of Mary the leaven: blessed is she who believed, for those things were accomplished in her which were spoken to her by the Lord. But they would not have been accomplished if the whole had not been leavened according to the word of the Lord, and leavened perpetually, preserving for us in death, just as in life, one and whole Mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ with his Deity. In this admirable sacrament one must observe, according to the number of the measures, degrees of a wonderful and most fitting distinction: the new, the old, the eternal. The new is the soul, which is believed to be created out of nothing at the time it is infused; the old is the flesh, which is known to be derived from the first man, that is from Adam; the eternal is the Word, which is asserted with indubitable truth to be begotten from the eternal Father, co-eternal with him. And in these, if you attend carefully, there is a threefold kind of divine power: that something is made out of nothing, that the new is made from the old, and that the eternal and blessed is made from the condemned and dead. What does this mean for our salvation? Much, in every way. First, that we, who were reduced to nothing by sin, have been created again in a sense, so that we might be some beginning of his creature. Then, that we, translated out of old servitude into the liberty of the sons of God, walk in newness of spirit. Finally, that we, called out of the power of darkness, are brought into the kingdom of eternal light, in which he has already made us sit in Christ. Those are alien from us who try to alienate the flesh of Christ from us, impiously asserting that it was newly created in the Virgin and not taken from the Virgin. The prophetic Spirit met this opinion, or rather this blasphemy of the impious, well beforehand: a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root. See, here the rod proceeds not by any use of human conception, but by divine power, since he was conceived of the Holy Spirit. She who was a virgin bore fruit, so that she might make Christ one and yet plural: flesh and soul mixed without confusion by the Holy Spirit, born of a virgin, perpetually, without any vices, in whom there is unity of Deity and humanity in their distinction, so that there is one person. A rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root. He could have said, and a flower from the rod, but I preferred from the root, so that it might show that the flower and the rod drew their origin from the same source. Therefore the flesh was taken from that from which neither the new virgin, who came forth from the root, ... Perhaps you may be annoyed if we go on to ask again what God is, both because he has been asked so many times already and because he will be hard to find. I tell you, Father Eugenius: God is one who can never be sought in vain, nor can he be found when he is not found. Let your own experience teach you this, or if not, let it be believed on experience, not on my word, but on the word of the holy one who says: Good is the Lord to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. What then is God? As regards the universe, he is the end; as regards election, salvation; as regards himself, he alone knows. What is God? An almighty will, most benevolent power, eternal light, unchangeable reason, supreme blessedness, creating minds to share in him, quickening them to feel, stirring them to desire, enlarging them to receive, justifying them to merit, kindling them to zeal, making them fruitful to bear fruit, directing them to equity, forming them to goodwill, moderating them to wisdom, strengthening them to virtue, visiting them for consolation, illuminating them to knowledge, perpetuating them to immortality, filling them to happiness, surrounding them to security. What is God? He is no less the punishment of the perverse than the glory of the humble. For a certain rational direction of equity, unchangeable and unswerving, reaching everywhere, must necessarily strike against whatever is crooked, and be disturbed by all wickedness. Why should it not strike against every timid or distorted thing, and be sought out by it? Woe to whatever chances to stand in its way: righteousness that does not know how to yield is also strength. What is so contrary and hostile to wills as always to strive, always to strike against, and in vain? Woe to opposing wills, which indeed bear their punishment in their very aversion. What is so penal as always to will and never to have, and always to be unwilling and never not to be? What is so condemned as a will bound to this necessity of willing and not-willing, so that it is moved toward either thing only perversely and only wretchedly? It will never obtain for eternity what it wills, and what it does not will it will nevertheless endure for eternity; it is so affected that it never comes to rest in anything, and never escapes into anything it would like. Who does this? The righteous Lord our God, who, though he is perverted by the perverse, will never agree with the right or the wicked. For these are opposed to each other, even though they do not harm each other: harm is of the other, far be it from God. It is hard for you, he says, to kick against the goad, that is, not the goad kicking, but the one who kicks against it. God is also the punishment of the base: for he is light. And what is so hateful to obscene and shameful minds? Certainly everyone who does evil hates the light. But I ask, can they not avoid it? Not at all: it shines everywhere, even if not for everyone. Finally, the light shines in darkness, and the darkness has not comprehended it: the light sees the darkness, for to see and to shine is the same for it; but in turn it is not seen by the darkness, because the darkness has not comprehended it. Therefore they are seen so that they may be confounded, and they do not see so that they may be comforted; and they are seen not only by the light, but in the light. By whom, or by which? By every seeing one, so that through the multitude of onlookers there may be much confusion. Yet no eye is more troublesome to each of them than his own from among so great a number of spectators: there is no look, whether in heaven or on earth, that a guilty conscience would more wish to escape and less be able to. The darknesses do not even hide themselves, but they see what cannot see anything else: the works of darkness follow them, and there is no place to hide from them, not even in darkness. Here is the worm that does not die: the memory of past things, once thrust in, or rather innate, and sin clinging firmly, never to be torn away again. Nor does it cease to gnaw at the conscience, and fed on it, with food that is indeed inconsumable, it perpetuates life. I shudder at the biting worm and at the living death: I shudder to fall into the hands of living death and of dying life. This is the second death, which never kills and yet always kills. Who would not wish to die once for all, and not die forever? They who say to the mountains: fall on us, and to the hills: cover us: what else do they wish, except to end or escape through the benefit of death? Finally, they shall seek death, says the text, and shall not find it. Look at this more clearly: it is certain that the soul is immortal and never lives without its memory, lest it happen that at some time the soul should not be; therefore, while the soul endures, memory endures too. But what kind of memory? Foul with shameful deeds, horrid with crimes, swollen with vanity, bristling and neglected through contempt. The earlier things have passed and yet have not passed: they passed from the hand, but not from the mind; what has been done cannot not have been done. Therefore, even if doing was in time, having done remains forever; what passes with time does not pass with time. It is necessary, then, that you be tormented inwardly by remembering forever that you acted wickedly. This will be experienced in the truth of that word: I will reprove you, and set your sins before your face. The Lord has spoken, to whom everything opposed is opposed, and who must be opposed to himself, so that the complaint is late: O Keeper, why have you set me against you, so that I have become a burden to myself? So it is, O Eugenius: nothing can be contrary to God and yet cohere with itself; but whoever is reproved by God will be reproved also by himself. Certainly there is then no reason either to dissemble the truth, or for the soul, in the sight of reason, to turn aside, its members of the body broken and gathered within itself. For how could that be of use, with the senses shut up and asleep in death, through which it used to go out curiously and wander away from itself into this passing figure of the world? You see that nothing is lacking to the wicked for confusion, when they are brought forth to be made a spectacle to God, to angels, to men, and to themselves. O how badly all the wicked are placed, namely set against this torrent of straight equity and exposed to this light of unveiled truth! Is this not perpetual affliction and perpetual confusion? With a double destruction, he says, destroy them, O Lord our God. What is God? Length, breadth, height and depth. What, you say? Do we hold you to be a professor of the quaternity, which he abhorred? Not at all. I have abhorred and do abhor it. I seem to have brought forth more, but there is only one: one God is signified in our measure, not according to his own state. Here it is divided, there not: the words are different, but the paths are many; yet through them one is signified, one is sought. In this fourfold there are not expressed divisions of the substance, nor diversities such as we see in bodies, nor the personal distinction such as we adore in the Trinity, nor the number of properties such as we confess to be in the persons themselves, though not other than the persons. Otherwise I would see that each one of these is what four together are, and these four are what each one is. But for us, who cannot contend with God in simplicity, while we strive to grasp the one, there presents itself, as it were,

units.la: quadruplicatum. Patet hoc speculum & enigma per quod solum & in ipsam videre datur: cum autem videbimus facie ad faciem, videbimus sicut est. Nec enim iam tunc fragilis acies mentis nostrae quantumlibet vehementer intendens, aliquatenus resiliet, dissiliet ve in suam pluralitatem: colliget se magis, adiuuabit, conformabitq; vnitati illius, vt vna vni facies respondeat faciei: nempe similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Beata visio ad quam merito suspirabit qui ait: exquisiui te faciem meam, faciem tuam Domine requiram. Et quia adhuc in quaerendo res est, interim ascendamus quadrigam istam, vt pote infirmi & imbecilles indigentes tali vehiculo, si forte vel sic apprehendamus in quo apprehensi sumus, id est, huius ipsius vehiculi rationem. Nam hoc monitum habemus ab ipso auriga, & primo currus huius exhibitore, vel studeamus comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis quae sit longitudo, latitudo, sublimitas, & profundum. Comprehendere dixit, non cognoscere; vt non curiositate contenti scientiae, tota cura fructui inhaereamus. Non in cognitione est fructus, sed in comprehensione: alioquin scienti bonum & non facienti (vt ait quidam) peccatum est ei. Et ipse Paulus alio loco: sic currite, inquit, vt comprehendatis. Quid sit comprehendere inferius declarabo. Quid igitur est Deus? longitudo, inquam. Quid ipsa? aeternitas. Haec tam longa vt non habeat terminum, non magis loci, quam temporis. Est & latitudo, & ipsa quid? charitas. Quibus & ista terminis angusteatur in Deo, qui nihil odit horum quae fecerit: Deniq; solem suum oriri facit super bonos & malos, & pluit super iustos & iniustos: ergo & inimicos concludit sinus ille. Ne hoc quoq; contentus, euadit in infinitum: omnem non modo affectionem, sed & cognitionem excedit, adiiciente Apostolo & dicente: scire etiam supereminentem scientiae charitatem Christi. Quid plus dicam? aeterna est, nisi quod hoc plus forsitan est, quia aeternitas est.
units.tr: quadruplicated. This mirror and enigma is open only so far, and only in part does it permit us to see into it; but when we shall see face to face, we shall see as he is. For then the fragile sight of our mind, however earnestly it strains, will no longer slip back or fly apart into its own plurality; it will rather gather itself together, be helped, and be conformed to that unity, so that one face answers to one face. Indeed we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. Blessed vision, for which he rightly longs who said: "I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will seek." And since the matter is still one of seeking, let us in the meantime mount this four-horse chariot, since we are weak and feeble and in need of such a vehicle, so that perhaps even so we may grasp that by which we are grasped, that is, the reasoning of this very vehicle. For we have this warning from the charioteer himself, and the first presenter of this chariot: "that we may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height and depth." He said "comprehend," not "know," so that we, content with idle curiosity about knowledge, should cling with our whole care to its fruit. The fruit lies not in knowledge but in comprehension; otherwise, as someone says, "to him who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin." And Paul himself in another place: "So run," he says, "that you may comprehend." What it is to comprehend I shall explain further on. What, then, is God? Length, I say. What is that? Eternity. This length is so long that it has no end, no more of place than of time. There is also breadth; and what is that? Charity. Even these limits are narrowed in God, who hates nothing of what he has made: finally he makes his sun rise over good and evil, and rains on the just and the unjust; therefore that bosom embraces even enemies. Lest he be content with this either, he passes into the infinite: he exceeds not only all affection but all knowledge, the Apostle adding and saying: "to know also the surpassing charity of Christ." What more shall I say? It is eternal, except that this is perhaps more, because it is eternity.

units.la: Vides tantam esse latitudinem quantam & longitudinem? vtinam sic videas non tantam esse, sed ipsam id esse vnam quod alteram; non minus vnam quam duas, nec plus duas quam vnam. Deus aeternitas, Deus charitas est; longitudo sine protensione, latitudo sine distensione: in vtroq; pariter locales quidem excepit temporalesq; angustias, sed libertate naturae, non enormitate substantiae. Talimodo immensus est qui omnia fecit in mensura, & quamuis immensus, hic tamen modus & ipsius immensitatis. Quid item Deus? Sublimitas; & profundum; in altero supra omnia, in altero intra omnia. Liquet in Deitate husquam claudicare aequalitatem, stare eam undiq; firmiter, constare immobiliter sibi. Sublime, potentiam; profundum sapientiam eius considera. Ex aequo & ista respondent sibi, dum & sublimitas inattingibilis, & profunditas aeque inscrutabilis cognoscatur, Paulo admirante & exclamante: o altitudo divitiarum sapientiae & scientiae Dei, quam inscrutabilia sunt iudicia eius, & inuestigabiles viae illius? Liber & nos exclamare cum Paulo, horum vtrumq; intuentes in Deo & cum Deo simplicissimam vnitatem: o sapientia potens, attingens vtiq; fortiter: o potentia sapiens disponens omnia suaviter. Res vna, effectus multiplex, operatione' quidem diversae: & illa vna res est longitudo propter aeternitatem; latitudo, propter charitatem; sublimitas propter maiestatem; profunditas propter sapientiam. Nouimus haec: num ideo & arbitrantur nos comprehendisse? non ea disputatio comprehendit, sed sanctitas, si quo modo tamen comprehendi potest, quod incomprehensibile est. At nisi posset non dixisset Apostolus: vt comprehendamus cum omnibus sanctis. Sancti igitur comprehenduntur, quaeris quomodo? Si sanctus es comprehendisti & nosti: si non, esto, & tuo experimento scies. Sanctum facit afsectio sancta, & ipsa gemina; timor Domini sanctus, & sanctus amor. His perfecte affecta anima, velut quibusdam duobus brachiis suis comprehendit, amplectitur, stringit, tenet, & ait, Tenui eum nec dimittam, & timor quidem sublimi & profundo, amor lato longoq; respondet. Quid tum timendum quam potestas cui non potes resistere, quam sapientia cui abscondi non potes? Poterat minus timere Deus; alterutro carens: nunc autem perfecte oportet timeas illum, cui nec oculus deest omnia videns, nec manus potens omnia. Quid item tam amabile quam amor ipse quo amas, & quo amaris? Amabiliorem tamen iuncta aeternitas facit, quae dum non excidit foras mittit suspicionem. Ama igitur perseveranter & longanimiter, & habes longitudinem: dilata amorem tuum usq; ad inimicos, & latitudinem tenes: esto etiam in omni sollicitudine timoratus, & sublime profundum q; apprehendisti. Aut si mauis quatuor aeque tuis diuinis quatuor respondere; facis hoc, si stupes, si pavet, si ferutes, si sustines. Stupenda plane sublimitas maiestatis, patenda abyssus iudiciorum: feruorem exigit charitas, aeternitas perseverantiam sustinendi. Quis stupet, nisi qui contemplatur gloriam Dei? quis pavet, nisi qui scrutatur profunditum sapientiae? quis feruet, nisi qui meditatur charitatem Dei? quis sustinet & perseverat in amore, nisi qui aemulatur aeternitatem charitatis? nempe aeternitatis quandam imaginem perseverantia praefert. Deniq; sola est cui aeternitas redditur, vel potius qui aeternitati hominem reddit, dicente Domino: qui perseveraverit usq; in finem, hic salvus erit. Et nunc aduerte in quatuor istis, contemplationis species quatuor: prima & maxima contemplatio est, admiratio maiestatis: haec requirit cor purgatum, vt a vitiis liberum atq; exonerationem peccatis, facile ad superna leuet; interdum quoq; vel per aliquas morulas, stupore & extasi suspensum, teneat admirantem. Secunda autem necessaria est huic, est enim intuens iudicia Dei; quo sane pavido aspecto dum vehementius concutit intuentem, fugat vitia, fundat virtutes, initiat ad sapientiam, humilitatem servat. Virtutum siquidem bonum quoddam ac stabile fundamentum humilitas: nempe si nutat illa, virtutum aggregatio non nisi ruina est. Tertia contemplatio occupatur, vel potius otiatur, circa memoriam beneficiorum, & ne dimittat ingratum, sollicitat memorantem ad amorem benefactoris. De talibus dicit Propheta loquens ad Dominum: memoriam abundantiae suavitatis tuae eructabunt. Enarratio gratiarum actio est. Quarta quae retro sunt obliviscens, in sola requiescit expectatione promissorum: quae cum sit meditatio aeternitatis (siquidem quae promittuntur aeterna sunt) longanimitatem alit, & perseverantiam.
units.tr: Do you see that the breadth is as great as the length? Would that you might see not that they are great, but that the one is the other itself; not less one than two, nor two more than one. God is eternity, God is charity; length without extension, breadth without distension; in both alike he has put aside the narrow limits of place and time, by the freedom of his nature, not by the vastness of his substance. In such a way is he immeasurable who made all things in measure; and although immeasurable, this measure is nonetheless his own immensity. Again, what is God? Height and depth: in the one above all things, in the other within all things. It is clear that in the Deity equality nowhere wavers, that it stands firm on every side and remains immovably consistent with itself. Consider height as his power, depth as his wisdom. These answer to each other equally, since both the unattainable height and the equally unsearchable depth are recognised, Paul marvelling and crying out: "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and his ways past finding out!" Let us also, free, cry out with Paul, looking at both of these in God, and in God the most simple unity: O wisdom mighty, reaching strongly indeed; O power wise, ordering all things sweetly. One thing, many effects, diverse indeed in operation: and that one thing is length on account of eternity, breadth on account of charity, height on account of majesty, depth on account of wisdom. We know these things: do they therefore suppose that we have comprehended them? It is not disputation that comprehends, but holiness, if in any way what is incomprehensible can be comprehended. But unless it could be, the Apostle would not have said: "that we may comprehend with all the saints." The saints, then, comprehend; you ask how? If you are holy you have comprehended and know; if not, be it so, and you will know by your own experience. Holy affection makes a man holy, and this affection is twofold: the fear of the Lord is holy, and holy is love. When the soul is perfectly affected by these, it comprehends, embraces, grasps and holds, as with two arms of its own, and says: "I have held him and will not let him go"; and fear answers to the height and depth, love to the breadth and length. What is to be feared more than power, to which you cannot resist; than wisdom, from which you cannot hide? God could fear less if he lacked either; but now you ought to fear perfectly him whose eye is not lacking, seeing all things, nor whose hand is lacking, powerful over all things. And what is so lovable as love itself, by which you love and by which you are loved? Yet eternity joined to it makes it more lovable, since, while it does not fall away, it casts out suspicion. Love, then, persistently and patiently, and you have the length; extend your love even to enemies, and you hold the breadth; be also fearful in all anxiety, and you have grasped the height and depth. Or, if you prefer to answer these four divine things with four of your own, you do so if you are astonished, if you tremble, if you burn, if you endure. Plainly the height of majesty calls for astonishment, the abyss of judgements for dread; charity demands fervour, eternity the perseverance of enduring. Who is astonished, unless he contemplates the glory of God? Who trembles, unless he searches the depth of wisdom? Who burns, unless he meditates on the charity of God? Who endures and persists in love, unless he emulates the eternity of charity? Indeed perseverance presents a certain image of eternity. Finally, he alone is the one to whom eternity is rendered, or rather, who renders man to eternity, the Lord saying: "he who perseveres to the end, the same shall be saved." And now observe in these four the four kinds of contemplation: the first and greatest contemplation is admiration of majesty; this requires a heart cleansed, free from vices and unburdened of sins, so that it may easily rise to things above, and sometimes also, by some brief delays, suspended in wonder and ecstasy, hold the admirer fast. The second, however, is necessary to this, for it considers the judgements of God; and this fearful gaze, as it shakes the beholder more vehemently, puts vices to flight, pours in virtues, initiates into wisdom, and keeps humility. For humility is the good and stable foundation of the virtues: if it wavers, the gathering of virtues is nothing but ruin. The third contemplation is occupied, or rather at rest, with the memory of benefits, and, lest it let the ungrateful go, it urges the one remembering to love the benefactor. Of such the Prophet speaks, addressing the Lord: "they shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness." Recounting is the act of thanksgiving. The fourth, forgetting what is behind, rests in the expectation of the promises alone; and since it is meditation on eternity (for what is promised is eternal), it nourishes patience and perseverance.

units.la: H rantiæ dat vigorem. Puto namque esse quatuor nostra hæc, quatuor illis Apostoli assignare; dum longitudinem comprehendit meditatio promissorum; latitudinem recordatio beneficiorum; sublimitatem contemplatio maiestatis; profunditum inspectio iudiciorum. Quærendus adhuc fuerat qui nec satis adhuc inventus est, nec quæri nimis potest: at prandô forte quam disputando dignius quæritur, & inuenitur facilius. Proinde is sit finis libri, sed non finis quærendi.
units.tr: It gives vigour to hope. For I think it is possible to assign these four of ours to those four of the Apostle: meditation on promises comprehends length; recollection of benefits, breadth; contemplation of majesty, height; inspection of judgements, depth. The one who is to be sought had still to be sought, and has not yet been sufficiently found, nor can he be sought too much; but perhaps he is sought more worthily at dinner than in disputation, and found more easily. Therefore let this be the end of the book, but not the end of seeking.

units.la: EPISTOLA DECRETALIS INNOCENTII III. SVMMI PONTIFICIS ROMANI, EXSCRIPTA EX ANTIQVIS Collectionibus Decretalium publicatis ab ANTONIO AVGVSTINO Episcopo Ilerdensi editis Ilerdæ in Hispania apud Rob. & Ioannem à Villanoua Anno Christi M. DLXXVI. & Lutetiæ apud Sebastianum Cramoisi M. DCIX.
units.tr: DECRETAL EPISTLE OF INNOCENT III, SUPREME PONTIFF OF ROME, COPIED FROM THE ANCIENT COLLECTIONS OF DECRETALS PUBLISHED BY ANTONIO AUGUSTINO, BISHOP OF LÉRIDA, PRINTED AT LÉRIDA IN SPAIN BY ROBERT AND JOHN OF VILLANOVA IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1576, AND AT PARIS BY SEBASTIAN CRAMOISY, 1609.

units.la: EX Collectione III. lib. 4. t. 11. tit: Qui filii sunt legitimi, quod in Decretalibus Gregorii IX Papæ est 13. eodem titulo.
units.tr: From Collection III, book 4, title 11, "Which children are legitimate," which in the Decretals of Pope Gregory IX is chapter 13 under the same title.

units.la: In hac epistola Innocentius Papa tria dicit maxime notanda pro Rege, & Regno FRANCORVM.
units.tr: In this letter Pope Innocent notes three points especially worth remembering concerning the King and Kingdom of the FRANKS.

units.la: Primo, quod REX FRANCORVM superiorem in temporalibus minime recognoscit, ne ipsum quidem Summum Pontificem.
units.tr: First, that the KING OF THE FRANKS acknowledges no superior in temporal matters, not even the Supreme Pontiff himself.

units.la: Secundo, quod ipse PONTIFEX declarauit per affinitatem quæ allegabatur inter Philippum Regem FRANCORVM, & Reginam quam duxerat in matrimonium, Reginam illam non REGIS ipsius coniugem (affinitate probata) & per consequens aliam sibi videri legitime copulatam (quod quidem erat notorium Pontificia Ecclesiastica Christiana.)
units.tr: Second, that the PONTIFF himself declared, on account of the affinity alleged between Philip, King of the Franks, and the queen he had taken in marriage, that this queen was not the wife of the king (the affinity having been proved), and that consequently he appeared to be lawfully joined to another woman. This was indeed well known in Pontifical, Ecclesiastical and Christian affairs.

units.la: Tertio, quod cum Rex ipse Francorum superiorem in temporalibus minime recognoscat, sine iuris alterius lesione in eo quod ad notionem Pontificiam & Ecclesiasticam pertinebat, submittere se potuerat, in quo forsitan videretur aliquibus quod per se ipsum non tanquam Pater cum filiis, sed tanquam Princeps cum subditis poterat dispensare.
units.tr: Third, that since the King of the Franks himself acknowledges no superior in temporal matters, he could submit himself, without injury to another's right, in what pertained to Pontifical and Ecclesiastical jurisdiction. In this, it might seem to some, he could dispense by himself, not as a father with his sons, but as a prince with his subjects.

units.la: His tribus nihil simile propositum sibi fuisse testatur Innocentius PONTIFEX in supplicatione W. Montispessulani ab Archiepiscopo Arelatensi oblata, qua recitatur in illa Decretali Epist.
units.tr: Pope Innocent testifies that nothing similar was put to him in the supplication of W. of Montpellier, presented by the Archbishop of Arles, which is recited in that Decretal letter.

units.la: Imo valde notandum quod ipse W. terra sua partem ab Ecclesia Magalonensi possidere debatur, quam ipsi per Sedem Apostolicam temporaliter agnoscebat, ut ex Archiepiscopi assertione dicit PONTIFEX: qui quidem Archiepiscopos fassus fuerat illa Magalonensi Ecclesia mediante W. illius Montispessulani terram, aut partem ipsius Pontifici temporaliter subiacere.
units.tr: Indeed, it must be very carefully noted that W. was held to possess a part of his land from the Church of Maguelone, which he acknowledged to hold temporally from the Apostolic See. So the Pontiff says, on the Archbishop's assertion; for the Archbishop had confessed that, through that Church of Maguelone, the land of W. of Montpellier, or a part of it, was temporally subject to the Pontiff.

units.la: Quod utrum verum esset, atq; ita ab Archiepiscopo pro Nobili Viro W. supplicante agnosci debuerit, haud liquet aliunde quam ex iis quæ recitat Pentifex in illa Decretali.
