units.tr: Whether this was true, and whether it ought to have been so acknowledged by the Archbishop for the noble man W., who was petitioning, is not clear from any source other than what the Pontiff recites in that Decretal.

units.la: Verum, quidquid in ea scriptum sit, ex declaratione Pontificis ibi expressa constat aliam longe conditionem fuisse, ut adhuc hodie est Regis ac Regni Francorum, quam illius W. & partis terræ quam à Magalonensi Ecclesia tenere dicebatur, vel id fatente Pontifice, qui maximum agnovit delrimen, dicitque nominatim Regem Francorum in spiritualibus tantum, W. autem M. & in spiritualibus, & in temporalibus Pontificem & Sedem Apostolicam recognoscere, quod nullus unquam REX FRANCORVM fecit in temporalibus, in quibus DEVM solum habet atque agnoscit superiorem, quippe cuius solius gratia REX est.
units.tr: But whatever is written there, it is clear from the Pontiff's declaration expressed in it that the condition of the King and Kingdom of the Franks, as it still is today, was far different from that of W. and of the part of land which was said to be held from the Church of Maguelone. The Pontiff himself admits this, and recognised a great loss; he names expressly that the King of the Franks recognises the Pontiff only in spiritual matters, but that W. recognises the Pontiff and the Apostolic See in both spiritual and temporal matters. No KING OF THE FRANKS has ever done this in temporal matters, in which he has and acknowledges God alone as his superior, since he is king by the grace of God alone.

units.la: Hæc tria in Epistola ista Decretali declarata faciunt pro veritate Regii status, ac suprema & sacra Maiestate Regis Francorum: & ideo Galli omnes pii & veri Franci debent ipsam Epistolam memoriæ commendare.
units.tr: These three points declared in this Decretal letter support the truth of the royal state and the supreme and sacred majesty of the King of the Franks; and therefore all pious Gauls and true Franks ought to commit this letter to memory.

units.la: EX ANTIQVA DECRETALIVM COLLECTIONE III. LIB. 4. TIT. 12. QVI FILII sunt legitimi. Cap. 2. quod in vulgatis editioni- bus est 13. c. tit. 17.
units.tr: FROM THE ANCIENT COLLECTION OF DECRETALS, BOOK 4, TITLE 12, "WHO ARE LEGITIMATE SONS," CHAPTER 2 (in the printed editions it is chapter 13, title 17).

units.la: INNOCENTIVS III. NOBILI VIRO VV. MONTISPESSVLANI.
units.tr: INNOCENT III TO THE NOBLE MAN W. OF MONTPELLIER.

units.la: PER venerabilem fratrem nostrum Arelatensem Archiepiscopum ad sedem Apostolicam accedentem nobis tua humilitas supplicauit, vt filios tuos titulo legitimationis decorare dignaremur, quatenus eis quò minus tibi succederent natalium obiectio non noceret. Quod autem super hoc Apostolica sedes plenam habeat potestatem, ex illo videtur, quod cum diuersis causis inspectis, cum quibusdam minus legitime genitis, non naturalibus tantum, sed adulterinis etiam dispensauit, sic ad actus spirituales illos legitimandos, vt possint in Episcopos promoueri: similius creditur, & probabilius reputatur, vt eos ad actus legitimare valeat seculares: praesertim, si praeter Romanum Pontificem inter homines superiorem alium non cognoscant qui legitimandi habeat potestatem: Quia cum maior in spiritualibus tam prouidentia, quam auctoritas, & idoneitas requiratur, quod in maiori conceditur, licitum esse videtur etiam in minori.
units.tr: Your humility has petitioned us, through our venerable brother the Archbishop of Arles, who came to the Apostolic See, that we would deign to adorn your sons with the title of legitimation, so that the objection of their birth should not stand in the way of their succeeding you. That the Apostolic See has full power in this matter is evident from the fact that, having considered various cases, it has dispensed with some who were born not merely unlawfully but even in adultery, so as to legitimate them for spiritual acts, that they might be promoted to bishoprics. It is therefore more likely to be believed, and more probably judged, that it can also legitimate them for secular acts, especially if the persons concerned recognise no other superior among men besides the Roman Pontiff who has the power of legitimation. For since greater foresight, authority and fitness are required in spiritual matters, what is granted in the greater matter seems lawful also in the lesser.

units.la: Persimile quoque id videtur posse probari cum eo ipso quod aliquis ad apicem Episcopalis dignitatis attollitur, eximitur à paterna potestate.
units.tr: This can be shown to be very much the same from the fact that when someone is raised to the summit of episcopal dignity, he is released from paternal power.

units.la: Praeterea si etiam simplex Episcopus scienter seruum alterius in Episcopum ordinaret, licet ordinatori satisfacere domino iuxta formam canonicam tenereatur, ordinatus tamen iugum eua_ deret seruitutis. Videtur siquidem monstruosum, vt qui legitimus ad spirituales fieret actiones, circa seculares actus illegitimus remaneret. Vnde cum quo in spiritualibus dispensatur, consequenter intelligitur in temporalibus dispensatum.
units.tr: Moreover, if even a simple bishop were knowingly to ordain another's slave as a bishop, then although he would be obliged to make satisfaction to the slave's master according to the canonical form, the one ordained would nonetheless throw off the yoke of servitude. For it seems monstrous that someone who has been made lawful for spiritual actions should remain unlawful for secular acts. Hence, when someone is dispensed in spiritual matters, it is understood to follow that he is dispensed in temporal matters too.

units.la: Id autem in patrimonio Beati Petri liberè potest Apostolica sedes, in quo & summi Principis exequitur potestatem. Cum ergo videtur ex his legitimandi auctoritas non tantum in temporalibus, sed in spiritualibus & penes Romanam Ecclesiam residere, vt super hoc filius tuis gratiam faceremus ob tua, & progenitorum tuorum merita, qui semper in protectione Sedis Apostolicae perstitisti, humiliter ex parte tua idem Archiepiscopus requirebat. Videbatur autem ex eo trahere maiorem audaciam postulandi; quod non longe petere cogebatur exemplum: Sed in fauorem petitionis huiusmodi quod nos in causa simili fecisse dicebat, poterat allegare. Cum enim Carissimus in Christo filius noster Philippus Rex Francorum Illustris Carissimam in Christo filiam nostram I. Francorum Reginam illustrem dimiserit, & ex alia postmodum superducta puerum suscepit, & puellam: & tu similiter exclusa legitima superduxeris aliam, ex qua filios suscepisti, sicut cum filiis Regis, eiusdem, sic cum tuis credebatur de benignitate sedis Apostolicae dispensandum: Praesertim cum maior id necessitas suaderet, & tu nobis specialius sis subiectus: Siquidem Rex Francorum ex inclytae recordationis Regina Francorum olim legitimum suscepit haeredem, qui ei optatur, & creditur in Regni solio successurus: Tu vero ex legitima coniuge masculum non habens haeredem, qui tibi in deuotione nostra, & propria haereditate succedat. Insuper cum Rex ipse in spiritualibus nobis subiaceat, tu nobis & in spiritualibus & temporalibus es subiectus, cum partem terrae tuae ab Ecclesia Magalonensi possideas, quam ipsam per sedem Apostolicam temporaliter recognoscit, quia Magalonensi Ecclesia mediante nobis idem Archiepiscopus asserebat te temporaliter subiacere. Verum, si veritas diligenter inspicitur, non similes res, sed valde dissimilis inuenitur. Nam Rex ipse à praedicta Regina per bonae memoriae Remensem Archiepiscopum Apostolicae sedis Legatum fuit per sententiam separatus: Tu vero vxorem tuam à te, sicut dicitur, temeritate propria separasti: ipse quoque prius quam ad eum prohibitio de non contrahendo cum altera peruenisset, aliam superduxit, ex qua prolem geminam noscitur suscepisse. Sed tu in contemptum Ecclesiae aliam superinducere attentasti: Propter quod ipsa in te gladium exercuit Ecclesiasticae vltionis. Praeterea Rex ipse praedicta Regina contra matrimonium impedimentum affinitatis obiecit, & coram praefato Archiepiscopo testes induxit, cuius sententia, quia cassata fuit solummodo propter iudiciarium ordinem non seruatum, nos ei post restitutionem Regina super hoc Venerabilem Fratrem Episcopum, & dilectum filium I. titulo sanctae Priscae Presbyterum Cardinalem cognitores duximus deputandos. Tu vero vxori tuae nihil, quod diuortium induceret, sicut asseritur, obiecisti: cum etsi fides tua sit vnum de tribus bonis coniugii, non tamen ipsius violatio coniugale vinculum violasset. De filiis ergo Regis eiusdem, vtrum legitimi, vel illegitimi fuerint, quamdiu pendet quaestio affinitatis obiectae, potest non immerito dubitari. Nam si affinitas fuerit comprobata, praedictam Reginam non esse Regis coniugem apparebit; & per consequens alia videtur sibi legitime copulata, & filios ei legitimos perperisse. Detuis vero quod sint legitimi nati, nec tu ipse proponis, nec vlla praesumitur ratione. Insuper cum Rex ipse superiorem in temporalibus minime recognoscat, sine iuris alterius laesione, in eo se iurisdictioni nostrae subiicere potuit & subiecit, in quo forsitan videretur aliquibus quod per se ipsum, non tanquam pater cum filius, sed tanquam Princeps cum subditis potuit dispensare. Tu autem aliis noscetris subiacere, vnde sine ipsorum forsan iniuria, nisi praestarent assensum, nobis in hoc subdere te non posses: nec eius auctoritatis existis, vt dispensandi super his liberam habeas facultatem. Rationibus his inducti Regi gratiam fecimus requisisti, causam tam ex veteri quam ex Nouo Testamento trahentes; quod non solum in Ecclesiae patrimonio
units.tr: The Apostolic See can freely do this in the patrimony of Blessed Peter, where it also exercises the power of the supreme Prince. Since therefore it seems that the authority of legitimation resides not only in temporal matters but also in spiritual ones, and in the Roman Church, the same Archbishop humbly asked on your behalf that we would grant this favour to your sons, on account of your merits and those of your ancestors, who have always remained under the protection of the Apostolic See. He also said that he was compelled, not to seek far afield, to draw greater boldness from the request, since he could cite what we had done in a similar case in support of such a petition. For when our most beloved son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious King of the French, put away our most beloved daughter in Christ, I., the illustrious Queen of the French, and afterwards took another woman in marriage, by whom he had a son and a daughter, it was believed that, just as the King's children were dealt with in this way, yours too should be dealt with by the kindness of the Apostolic See, especially since greater necessity urged it, and you are more especially subject to us. For the King of the French had, by the former Queen of the French of illustrious memory, a legitimate heir, who is desired for him and is believed to succeed him on the throne of the kingdom; but you, not having a male heir by a lawful wife, have none to succeed you in our devotion and in your own inheritance. Moreover, since the King himself is subject to us in spiritual matters, you are subject to us in both spiritual and temporal matters, since you hold a part of your land from the Church of Maguelonne, which the Apostolic See itself recognises as held temporally, for the Archbishop asserted that you were temporally subject to us through the Church of Maguelonne. But if the truth is examined carefully, the cases are found not similar but very dissimilar. For the King was separated from the aforesaid Queen by sentence of the Archbishop of Reims of good memory, who was legate of the Apostolic See; but you, as is said, separated your wife from you by your own rashness. Moreover, before the prohibition against contracting marriage with another reached him, he took another wife, by whom he is known to have had twin offspring. But you attempted to take another wife in contempt of the Church, and for this reason she has brought the sword of ecclesiastical vengeance against you. Furthermore, the King objected to the aforesaid Queen the impediment of affinity against the marriage, and brought witnesses before the aforesaid Archbishop; because that sentence was quashed solely on account of the judicial order not having been observed, we, after the Queen's restoration, appointed as judges in this matter our venerable brother the Bishop, and our beloved son I., Cardinal priest of the title of Santa Prisca. But you objected nothing to your wife that would induce a divorce, as is alleged, since although faith is one of the three goods of marriage, its violation would not have broken the marriage bond. Therefore, concerning the sons of that King, whether they were legitimate or illegitimate, it may not unreasonably be doubted, for as long as the question of the objected affinity is pending. For if the affinity is proved, it will appear that the aforesaid Queen was not the King's wife; and consequently another woman seems to have been lawfully joined to him, and to have borne him legitimate sons. But that your sons were lawfully born, neither you yourself allege nor is any reason presumed. Moreover, since the King himself does not recognise any superior in temporal matters, he could, without injury to the right of another, submit himself to our jurisdiction in that matter, and did so; in which matter it might seem to some that he could dispense by himself, not as a father with his son, but as a prince with his subjects. But you, as we know, are subject to others, so that without perhaps injuring their rights, you could not submit yourself to us in this matter unless they gave their consent; nor are you of such authority that you have free power to dispense in these matters. Moved by these reasons, we granted the King the favour he sought, drawing the case from both the Old and the New Testament; not only in the patrimony of the Church,

units.la: nio, nió, super quo plenam in temporalibus gerimus potestatem, verum etiam in aliis Regionibus certis causis inspectis temporalem iurisdictionem carnaliter exercemus: Non quod alieno iuri praeiudicare velimus, vel potestatem nobis indebitam vsurpare, cum non ignoremus Christum in Evangelio respondisse; Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, & quae sunt Dei Deo: propter quod postulatus, vt haereditatem diuideret inter duos, quis, inquit, constituit me super vos iudicem? Sed quia sic in Deuteronomio continetur; Si difficile & ambiguum apud te iudicium esse prospexeris, inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, lepram & non lepram, & iudicium inter portas tuas videris variari, surge & ascende ad locum quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, venienfq; ad Sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & ad iudicem, qui fuit illo tempore, quarensq; ab eis qui iudicabunt tibi iudicii veritatem: & facies quaecumq; dixerint, qui praesunt loco, quem elegerint, & docuerint te iuxta legem eius, sequerisq; eorum sententiam, nec declinabis ad dexteram vel sinistram. Qui autem superbierit nolens obedire Sacerdotis imperio, qui eo tempore ministrat Domino Deo tuo, & decreto iudicis, morietur, & auferes malum de Israel. Sane cum Deuteronomium lex secunda interpretetur, ex vi vocabuli comprobatur in hoc quod ibi decernitur, vt in Nouo Testamento debeat obseruari. Locus enim quem elegit Dominus, Apostolica sedes esse cognoscitur sic, quod eam Dominus in se ipso lapide angulari fundauit. Cum enim Petrus urbem fugiens exisset, volens eum Dominus ad locum quem elegerat reuocare, interrogatus ab eo, Domine quo vadis? respondit, venio Romam iterum crucifigi quod intelligens pro se dictum, ad locum ipsum protinus est reuersus. Sunt autem Sacerdotes Leuitici generis fratres nostri, qui nobis iure Leuitico in executione Sacerdotalu officii coadiutores existunt. Is vero super eos Sacerdos siue Iudex existit, cui Dominus, inquit, in Petro, quodcumq; ligaueris super terram, erit ligatum & in coelis & quodcumque solueris super terram, erit solutum & in coelis: eius Vicarius, qui est Sacerdos in aeternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech constitutus a Deo Iudex viuorum, & mortuorum. Tria quippe distinguunt iudicia, primum inter sanguinem, & sanguinem, per quod criminale intelligitur, & ciuile. Vltimum inter lepram & lepram, per quod Ecclesiasticum & criminale notatur. Medium inter causam, & causam: quod ad vtrumq;, tam Ecclesiasticum, quam ciuile: in quibus cum aliquid fuerit difficile, vel ambiguum, ad iudicium est Sedis Apostolicae recurrendum, cuius sententiam qui superbiens contempserit obseruare, mori praecipitur, & auferri malum de Israel, per excommunicationis sententiam, velut mortuus a communione fidelium separari. Paulus etiam vt plenitudinem potestatis exponeret, ad Corinthios scribens, ait, Nescitis quoniam Angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis seculuria? Porro secularis officium potestatis interdum, & in qu buldam per se, nonnunquam autem & in nonnullis per alios exequi consueuit. Licet igitur cum filiis saepe dicti Regis Francorum, de quibus an fuerint legitimi, ab initio dubitabatur, duximus dispensandum: quia tamen tam lex Mosaica quam canonica sobolem suscepta ex adulterio detestatur, testante Domino, Mamzer & spurius vsque in decimam generationem in Ecclesiam non intrabunt. Canone vero vetante tales ad sacros ordines promoueri: secularibus quoq; legibus non solum repellentibus eos a successione paterna, sed negantibus ipsis etiam alimenta: supersedendum adhuc duximus petitioni praedictae, nec ad praesens super hoc tuis precibus annuendum. donec si fieri poterit, & culpa leuior, & iurisdictio liberior ostendatur: licet personam tuam specialis dilectionis brachio amplexemur, & in quibus cum Deo & honestate possumus, specialem tibi velimus gratiam exhiberi.
units.tr: over which we exercise full power in temporal matters, but also in other regions, when certain causes have been considered, we actually exercise temporal jurisdiction. This is not because we wish to prejudice another's right, or to usurp for ourselves a power not owed to us, since we are not unaware that Christ in the Gospel answered: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's; and when asked to divide an inheritance between two, he said: Who made me a judge over you? But since it is written in Deuteronomy: If you perceive that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and leprosy, and you see judgments varying within your gates, arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose, and come to the priests of the Levitical race and to the judge who shall be in those days, and ask of them, and they shall tell you the truth of the judgment; and you shall do whatever they who preside in the place which they have chosen shall say, and they shall teach you according to their law, and you shall follow their sentence, and shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left. But he who is proud and refuses to obey the command of the priest who ministers at that time to the Lord your God, and the decree of the judge, shall die, and you shall take away the evil from Israel. Indeed, since Deuteronomy is the second law, it is confirmed by the force of the word that what is decreed there ought to be observed in the New Testament. For the place which the Lord chose is known to be the Apostolic See, in that the Lord founded it upon himself as the corner stone. For when Peter, fleeing the city, had gone out, and the Lord, wishing to recall him to the place he had chosen, was asked by him, Lord, where are you going? he answered, "I am going to Rome to be crucified again"; and Peter, understanding that this was said of himself, at once returned to that place. Now the priests of the Levitical race are our brethren, who by Levitical right are our helpers in the execution of the priestly office. But he who is the priest or judge over them is the one to whom the Lord, in Peter, said: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven; his Vicar, who is a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. For three kinds of judgment are distinguished: the first, between blood and blood, by which is understood criminal and civil matters; the last, between leprosy and leprosy, by which the ecclesiastical and the criminal are signified; the middle, between cause and cause, which applies to both the ecclesiastical and the civil. In these, when anything has been difficult or ambiguous, recourse must be had to the judgment of the Apostolic See; and he who proudly despises its sentence is commanded to die, and the evil to be taken away from Israel, that is, to be separated from the communion of the faithful, like a dead man, by the sentence of excommunication. Paul also, writing to the Corinthians, to set forth the fullness of this power, says: Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more secular matters? Moreover, the office of secular power is accustomed to be exercised sometimes by the power itself in person, and sometimes through others. It is therefore lawful that, with the sons of the aforesaid King of the French, about whom doubt was raised from the beginning as to whether they were legitimate, we have decided to dispense; yet because both the Mosaic and the canon law abhor offspring conceived from adultery, as the Lord testifies, a bastard and a mamzer shall not enter the Church even to the tenth generation; and because the canon forbids such persons to be promoted to holy orders, and secular laws not only exclude them from paternal succession but also deny them maintenance, we have judged that the aforesaid petition must for the present be deferred, and that we should not assent to your prayers in this matter for now, until, if it can be done, both the fault is shown to be lighter and the jurisdiction is shown to be freer; although we embrace your person with the arm of special affection, and wish to show you special favour in whatever matters we can do so with God and with honour.

units.la: RADVLPHI DE COLVMNA, CANONICI CARNOTENSIS, TRACTATVS DE TRANSLATIONE IMPERII.
units.tr: Radulphus de Columna, Canon of Chartres, A Treatise on the Transfer of Empire

units.la: Multæ venerationis & sapientiæ viro, Domino Lamberto de Castello, Legum honorabili Professori, ac suo Patri charissimo; RADVLPHVS de COLVMNA Canonicus Carnotensis, salutem & eius, cui seruire regnare est, iugiter obsequiis inhærere.
units.tr: To the man of great esteem and wisdom, Lord Lambert de Castello, honourable Professor of Laws and his most dear father: Radulphus de Columna, Canon of Chartres, greetings, and constant devotion to Him whom to serve is to reign.

units.la: Vestra nuper dilectio postulauit, vt de statu & mutatione Romani Imperii aliqua sub compendio scriberem, per quæ plena de ipso notitia haberi sub breuitate scripturæ posset. Sed, Charissime, rem difficilem postulasti; cum non possint maria sine mora lustrari, nec facile sit prouinciarum longitudinem in momento transcurrere. Sed magna res quidem succincte à sapiente interdum proponitur: sed rato, vel nunquam perfecte sub angustia sermonis nimia explanatur. Quid autem maius Romano Imperio, ab eo ipso eius exordio? cuius Imperii gesta magnifica vix multorum scriptorum praeclara ingenia disserere ad plenum potuerunt. Sed quia negare nequeo, quicquid iuiungitur, sincera vestra dilectione deuinctus: prout rei natura ferre poterit, & ingenii mei ruditas patitur, faciam quod vestra sincera charitas cohortatur. Statum enim Romani Impe-
units.tr: Your recent affection asked me to write something in brief about the state and transfer of the Roman Empire, so that a full knowledge of it could be had in a short written account. But, dearest friend, you have asked for a difficult thing, since seas cannot be crossed without delay, nor can the length of provinces be traversed in a moment. Yet a great subject is sometimes set out succinctly by a wise man, though it is seldom, if ever, fully explained within the narrow limits of a short discourse. And what is greater than the Roman Empire, from its very beginning? The magnificent deeds of that Empire have hardly been fully treated even by the brilliant minds of many writers. But since I cannot refuse whatever is enjoined on me, bound as I am by your sincere affection, I will do, as far as the nature of the matter allows and my own rough talent permits, what your sincere charity urges. For I shall describe the state of the Roman Empire...

units.la: Anno Christi 1260 Imperii, Deo dante, ea breuitate describam, vt multiloquium fastidium minime pariat: & nimia breuitas quae describitur, intelligentiam non excludat. Grate itaq; suscipite praesens meae dilectionis opusculum: & si quid videritis in ipso corrigendum, prout videbitur vestrae prudentiae, corrigatis. Valete.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1260, by God's grace, I will describe the Empire in such brevity that its wordiness does not breed weariness, and such that the extreme brevity does not hinder understanding. Accept, then, this little work of my affection with goodwill, and if you see anything in it that needs correcting, correct it as your prudence thinks fit. Farewell.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: ROmanum Imperium sub duplici significatione scriptores historiarum assumunt. Vno modo, vt sub appellatione Romani Imperii intelligamus ipsius Romanae urbis initium, ipsiusque primi dominii licet exigui fundamentum. Vnde saepius inuenitur, quod Aeneas post excidium magnae Troiae profugus, per mare Italiam petiit, & in ea Romanum fundauit imperium, in loco vbi nunc est Roma. Qui locus sibi placuit, sementemque Romani generis seminauit. Semenque processu temporis in arborem excellentissimam crescens, per vniuersa mundi climata ramos suae viriditatis extendit. Creuit siquidem id granum sinapis, & super omnia olera exititit mirabiliter exaltatum: sub cuius umbra omnia volatilia coeli, omnes reges humani seculi in pacis pulchritudine quiescebant. Romani enim, qui ab Aenea descenderunt, armorum exercitio, disciplina castrorum, vsu militiae, quiete libertatis, iustitiae cultu, reuerentia legum, finitimarum gentium amicitia, maturitate consiliorum, grauitate verborum & operum obtinuerunt, vt vniuersum orbem suae subiicerent ditioni. Romanus enim populus a rege Romulo in Caesarem Augustum per septingentos annos ita per vniuersum orbem virtuose & potenter arma circuntulit, ita omnia regna mundi propria virtute contriuit, vt qui eius magnifica gesta legunt, non vnius populi, sed totius humani generis facta intelligere arbitrentur. Totque laboribus, tot periculis, fortunaque varia iactatus est, vt constituendo eius Imperium, contendisse simul Romana virtus & fortuna videantur. Alio quidem modo Romanum Imperium pro quodam singulari & vniuersali dominio vrbis & orbis assumitur, quod vniuersale dominium dicitur Monarchia. Quam Monarchiam cum primus Octauianus Augustus, deinde successores eius praeferrent, non vniformiter tenuerunt. Et sub hac appellatione de statu Romani Imperii tractare propono. Imperium Romanum a Iulio Caesare secundum quosdam, sed verius ab Octauiano Augusto primo Romanorum Imperatore inchoatur. Nam secundum historiae veritatem, Iulius Caesar, licet primus fuerit qui arripuit singulare dominium: non tamen fuit Imperator, sed metator Imperii: & idcirco non ponitur in catalogo principum Romanorum. Et vsque ad Constantinum magnum, triginta tres Imperatores & quatuor Caesares numerantur, qui Romani sedem tenuere imperii. Constantinus magnus septimo anno regni sui imperii, sedem mutauit imperii, iplam in Orientem transferens, ad Byzantium ciuitatem, quae nunc Constantinopolis est vocata, & secundum imperialia iura Romae veteris praerogatiua laetatur. Et ibi sedem imperialem constituit, contentus dominio Orientis. Occidentem vero, scilicet Romam & totam Italiam, & omnia occidentalia regna cum omnibus dignitatibus imperialibus, beato Syluestro tunc Romano Pontifici, eiusque successoribus libere disponere concessit: indignum iudicans religiosus Imperator, ibi terrenum Imperatorem dignitatem & potestatem habere, vbi coelestis Imperatoris vicarius morabatur. Hoc plane legitur 1. q. distinct. 7. Constantinus. Clericis vero Romanae Ecclesiae tunc seruientibus, ad instantiam beati Syluestri concessit illam dignitatem praerogatiuam atque honorem, quem tunc amplissimi ordo senatus habebat. Hi quoque qui tunc clerici Romani vocabantur, vocantur hodie Cardinales: sed ante Syluestrum simpliciter clerici seu sacerdotes Romanae Ecclesiae vocabantur, qui quantum ad decorem & dignitatem titulos non habebant: sed quantum ad onus, videlicet quantum ad officium praedicandi, martyres sepeliendi, baptizandi, poenitentias iniungendi, intitulati erant. Haec enim longe ante Syluestrum a temporibus Cleti & Anacleti, Dionysii, Marcelli, fuerant instituta. Sed tempore Syluestri coeperunt habere titulum dignitatis, & illam praerogatiuam atque decorem, quem in Senatus habuit tempore Constantini. Et est aliquantulum aduertendum. Nam Martinus Polonus in suis Chronicis dicit: quod sunt quinquaginta duo, videlicet sex Episcopi, viginti octo Presbyteri, & decem & octo Diaconi. Quorum quidam sunt assidentes summo Pontifici, vt Episcopi, qui episcopi, Papae in solennitatibus assident, & cathedris vtuntur. Quidam sunt assistentes, vt Presbyteri. Quidam vero sunt insistentes, vt Diaconi: insistunt enim ministeriis, ipsi enim Papam induunt, & ei circa altare seruiunt. Sed secundum assignationem titulorum, factam primo per Cletum, postea per Anacletum, & deinde per Marcellum, plures inueniuntur. Sed non est finis faciendi. Nam hoc est & fuit ad initium summi Pontificis. Quod autem beatus Syluester primo instituerit seu nominauerit Cardinales centum, scriptores historiarum dicunt probari per c. presul. 7. q. 3. Ante enim, vt superius dictum, vocabantur Presbyteri vrbis Romanae, vt patet ex Ecclesiastica historia Eusebii. Patet etiam per id quod legitur de Nouatiano haeretico, Presbytero Romanae Ecclesiae qui aspirans ad summum Pontificatum, promotionem Cornelii Papae vilus est impedire.
units.tr: Historians use the term Roman Empire in two senses. In the first sense, by the name of the Roman Empire we understand the beginning of the city of Rome itself and the foundation, however small, of its first dominion. Hence it is often found that Aeneas, a fugitive after the fall of great Troy, sailed to Italy and founded there the Roman Empire, in the place where Rome now stands. That place pleased him, and he sowed the seed of the Roman race. In time this seed grew into a most excellent tree, and it spread the branches of its greenness through all the regions of the world. Indeed, that grain of mustard grew and rose wonderfully above all herbs, and under its shade all the birds of heaven and all the kings of the human age rested in the beauty of peace. For the Romans who descended from Aeneas gained, by the practice of arms, the discipline of the camp, the custom of war, the quiet of liberty, the cultivation of justice, reverence for the laws, friendship with neighbouring peoples, maturity of counsel, and gravity in word and deed, the power to bring the whole world under their rule. From King Romulus down to Caesar Augustus, the Roman people carried their arms through the whole world for seven hundred years, so bravely and so powerfully, and crushed all the kingdoms of the world by their own valour, that those who read of their glorious deeds think they are reading not the deeds of one people but of the whole human race. They were tossed about by so many labours, so many dangers, and such varied fortune, that in establishing their Empire Roman valour and Roman fortune seem to have contended together. In another sense, Roman Empire is taken to mean a certain singular and universal lordship over the city and the world, which universal lordship is called Monarchy. When the first Octavian Augustus, and afterwards his successors, asserted this Monarchy, they did not hold it uniformly. It is under this name that I propose to treat of the condition of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire began, according to some, with Julius Caesar, but more truly with Octavian Augustus, the first Roman Emperor. For according to the truth of history, Julius Caesar, although he was the first to seize singular lordship, was not an Emperor but a measurer out of the Empire, and for that reason he is not counted in the list of Roman princes. Up to Constantine the Great, thirty-three Emperors and four Caesars are counted who held the seat of the Roman Empire. In the seventh year of his reign, Constantine the Great moved the seat of the Empire, transferring it to the East, to the city of Byzantium, which is now called Constantinople, and he rejoices in the prerogative of old Rome according to the imperial laws. There he established the imperial seat, content with the lordship of the East. But the West, namely Rome and all Italy, and all the western kingdoms with all imperial dignities, he granted to be freely disposed of by the blessed Sylvester, then Roman Pontiff, and his successors. The pious Emperor judged it unworthy that the earthly Emperor should hold dignity and power where the vicar of the heavenly Emperor dwelt. This is plainly read in 1. q. distinct. 7. Constantinus. To the clergy of the Roman Church then serving, at the request of the blessed Sylvester, he granted that prerogative of dignity and honour which the most distinguished order of the Senate then had. Those who were then called Roman clergy are today called Cardinals; but before Sylvester they were simply called clergy or priests of the Roman Church, who did not have titles as regards dignity and splendour, but were named with respect to burden, that is, with respect to the office of preaching, burying martyrs, baptizing, and imposing penances. For these had been instituted long before Sylvester, from the times of Cletus and Anacletus, Dionysius and Marcellus. But in the time of Sylvester they began to have the title of dignity and that prerogative and honour which they had in the Senate in the time of Constantine. And something is to be noted a little. For Martin the Pole in his Chronicles says that there are fifty-two of them, namely six bishops, twenty-eight elders, and eighteen deacons. Of these some sit beside the supreme Pontiff, as the bishops, who sit beside the Pope at solemn functions and use chairs. Some stand by, as the elders. Some indeed attend upon him, as the deacons: for they attend to the ministries, they clothe the Pope and serve him at the altar. But according to the assignment of titles, first made by Cletus, afterwards by Anacletus, and then by Marcellus, more are found. But there is no end to the making of them. For this is and was at the beginning of the supreme Pontiff. That the blessed Sylvester first instituted or named one hundred Cardinals, the writers of history say is proved by c. presul. 7. q. 3. For before, as said above, they were called elders of the city of Rome, as is clear from the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius. It is also clear from what is read of the heretic Novatian, an elder of the Roman Church, who, aspiring to the supreme Pontificate, was eager to prevent the promotion of Pope Cornelius.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: TEnuit quoque Constantinus, eiusque successores Imperatores Romani, pacifice dominium Orientis, vsque ad vigesimum annum Imperatoris Heraclii, tunc omnes populi orientales a dominio Latinorum vniuersaliter recesserunt. Sed quae causa, propter quam recesserunt, & modus per
units.tr: Constantine and his successors, the Roman emperors, held lordship over the East peacefully until the twentieth year of the emperor Heraclius. Then all the eastern peoples withdrew universally from the rule of the Latins. But the cause for which they withdrew, and the manner by which they did so, is commonly unknown.

units.la: {y} Note lines not legible in detail. per quem, communiter ignoratur. Idcirco vtile credidi, & delectabile iudicaui, causam & modum describere, quomodo dicti orientales, se à Græcis & Latinis in dominio & cultu omnino diuiserunt. Causa siquidem, quare orientales iam dicti à dominio Imperii recesserunt, fuit tyrannicus principatus huius Heraclii; Nam post magnam victoriam habitam de Persis, Heraclius Persas & alias orientales nationes nimis crudeli dominatu premebat: propter quod occasionem rebellandi concorditer assumpserunt, & sic ab obedientia prædicta recesserunt. Et quod nunquam ad obedientiam traherentur, contentionem Mahumetis, tunc inter Persas dituitis & potentis, occasionem diuersæ credulitatis & fidei (si fides dici debeat) assumentes, vt ad primum dominium de cætero non redirent: forte à Ieroboam sumentes exemplum, qui decem tribubus ipsum sequentibus diuersum cultum tradidit, ne ad pristinum & debitum Dominium in perpetuum rediret. Idem fecerunt Græci. Cupientes enim ab obedientia Romanæ Ecclesiæ separari: cœperunt secundum diuersum ritum, in Ecclesia ministrare: & sic in tres diuersos errores scienter prolapsi sunt. Omnes enim eorum collegæ, qui conseruant & nutriunt schismata, aut sunt Nestoriani, aut Eutycheти, aut Ariani, aut Iacobitæ, aut Hebraici. Sic factum est de illis populis & nationibus illarum regionum, in quibus præcedens inobedientia & rebellio contigerunt. Extirbato enim Romano Imperio, vt rebellio perseueraret, fecerunt schismata: vt non solum recederent ab Imperio, sed etiam à Christianismo, accipientes quædam communia Moysi & Euangelii, vt patet in Alcorano. Et est aduertendum, quod quædam sectæ hæreticorum multum fuerunt familiares Mahumeto Legis Sarracenorum authori, vt sunt Nestoriani, quos Mahumetus commendat & honorat. Vnde Richardus in Chronicis narrat, quod quidam Monachus Græcus Nestorianus, cui nomen Sergius, longo tempore instituxerit Mahumetum. Et hinc est, quod Nestoriani in Dominio Sarracenorum habent magna Monasteria. Causa igitur & modo descriptis, quibus dicti Orientales à dominio Græcorum & Latinorum vhanimiter recesserunt, videamus, qui fuerunt principales populi, qui seditionem huiusmodi occasionibus excitarunt. Quia non solum rebellionis & inobedientiæ audaciam prætenderunt, imo regiones Romani Imperii & Imperatoris vicinias hostiliter invaserunt. Circa hæc, Annonius in gestu Francorum lib. 8 Richardus in suis Chronicis, Martinus, Isidorus concorditer dicunt, quod principaliter ns, quæ in prædictam superbiam elevata, de Arabia, decradice montis Caucasi est progressa. Quæ gens secundum Hieronymum in Chronico, Nabatheavocabatur, à Nabaioth primogenito Ismaelis. Vnde non Sarraceni, sed Agareni, siue Ismaelitæ dici deberent. Hæc natio maledicta, devastans regiones Imp rii, perueniit vsque in Syriam & Iudæam, cui obuiam venit militia Heraclii Imperatoris innumera, quæ tota ab hostibus cæsa est. Nam centum quinquaginta millia de exercitu Imperatoris, Domino permittente, prostrati sunt. Sed hanc humanitatem hostes fecisse dicuntur, quod per Legatos etiam spolia remiserunt. Heraclius autem spoliis huiusmodi, seu manubiis recusatis, in adiutorium ascisceens populos qui dicuntur de montibus Caspiis exiuisse, secundum historias, vbi per Alexandrum inclusi: exercitum reparauit, & infinitam pugnatorum multitudinem congregauit. Sarracenis quoque duo duces præerant, qui ducenta millia pugnatorum in bellum instituxerunt, cum vterque exercitus non procul existeret paratus & instructus ad pugnam: noctequa belli præcedente diem, subito in castris Græcorum, quinquaginta duo millia examinata in castris suis stationisq; repeta sunt. Quo terrore ac metu perculsa reliqua exercitus multitudo, in diuersa loca fugerunt, totum imperium hostibus relinquentes. Heraclius quoque accepto nuncio tantæ cladis diffidens se posse resistere, præ tristitia in morbum incidit: & quasi desperans, in ægritudinem prolabitur animæ. Nam vt historiæ referunt, Eutychetis maculabatur errore: & cum filia sororis suæ Martina nomine, matrimonio se conniunxit. Aliæ quoque historiæ dicunt, quod ante prædictum conflictum, prædicto erat maculatus errore, propter quem Deus eum puniuit. His peractis multiplicatur exercitus Arabum & Nabatheorum, ex diuersis prouinciis ipsis affinibus, & coniunctis, Chaldæis, Ammonitis & Moabitis: quibus Mahumetus adiungitur, qui tenuit in Arabia principatum, vt Richardus in suis Chron cis scribit. Hic Mahumetus attibus magicis instru.ctus, prætextu contemptus Imperii, persuadet eildem de modo viuendi & ad agendum, Dominicum populum multipliciter sua arte deludit & auertit à fide: dicens ipsos non posse tenere principatum, nisi à Christianorum fide diuerterent, & sua documenta seruarent. Simulans quoque aliquid diuini numinis in se habere: & quibusdam præsagiis per ipsum ostensis homines decipiens, tanquam P. Ophetacommuniter in dicto populo habebatur ab omnibus. Quibus magicis artibus quandam nobilem & potentem Dominam, Chadigam nomine, Corazanię prouinciæ, sic delusit, vt eam sibi matrimonialiter copularet, per quam illius regionis obtinuit principatum. Iudæos etiam multos decepit, vt ipsum crederent suum esse Messiam. His ergo versuiis, sua potentia & ampliatione Legis circa venerea, & promissionibus largis circa futura, populos seducebat, & armorum potentia ad suam præfecturam compellebat. Lege enim data per Mahumetum, populi qui arma sumpserunt contra imperium, si quas regiones occupabant, eas legem Moysi suscipere compellebant, nolentes obedire neci tradebant. Vnde de Arabia intrarunt Ægyptum, & sic populum subuertebant. Deinde transierunt in Africam, & ibidem similiter fecerunt. Postmodum venerunt in Hispaniam, & illam ex parte in fidem suam directe coegerunt. Et sic multiplicati per numerum, plus violentia belli, quam prædicatione sermonis.
units.tr: Therefore I thought it useful and judged it worth the trouble to describe both the cause and the manner in which these Easterners wholly separated themselves from the Greeks and the Latins, in both government and worship. The cause, then, why the Easterners withdrew from the rule of the empire was the tyrannical rule of this Heraclius. For after winning a great victory over the Persians, Heraclius pressed the Persians and the other eastern nations with a far too cruel dominion. On account of this they seized the occasion to rebel together and so withdrew from the said obedience. And so that they would never be brought back to obedience, they seized upon the quarrel of Muhammad, then powerful and prominent among the Persians, as an occasion for a different belief and faith (if it ought to be called faith), so that they would never return to their former lordship. Perhaps they took their example from Jeroboam, who gave a different worship to the ten tribes that followed him, so that they would never return in perpetuity to their former and rightful lordship. The Greeks did the same. For, desiring to be separated from obedience to the Roman Church, they began to minister in the Church according to a different rite, and so knowingly fell into three different errors. For all their associates who keep up and nourish the schisms are either Nestorians, or Eutychians, or Arians, or Jacobites, or Hebrews. So it happened with those peoples and nations of those regions in which the earlier disobedience and rebellion had occurred. For when the Roman Empire had been overthrown, in order that the rebellion might persist, they made schisms, so that they would not only withdraw from the Empire but also from Christianity, taking certain things held in common from Moses and the Gospel, as is evident in the Alcoran. It should also be noted that some sects of heretics were very familiar to Muhammad, the author of the Saracen law, such as the Nestorians, whom Muhammad commends and honours. Hence Richard in his Chronicles relates that a certain Greek Nestorian monk, named Sergius, instructed Muhammad for a long time. And hence it is that the Nestorians have large monasteries under Saracen rule. Therefore, with the cause and manner described by which the said Easterners unanimously withdrew from the rule of the Greeks and the Latins, let us see who were the principal peoples who stirred up sedition of this kind on these occasions. For they not only assumed the audacity of rebellion and disobedience, but also invaded hostilely the regions of the Roman Empire and the neighbouring lands of the Emperor. On these matters Annonius in the Deeds of the Franks, book 8, Richard in his Chronicles, Martin and Isidore agree in saying that the people principally raised up in the said pride came out of Arabia, from the root of Mount Caucasus. According to Jerome in the Chronicle, this nation was called Nabathaea, from Nabaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael. Hence they ought to be called not Saracens but Agarenes or Ishmaelites. This accursed nation, laying waste the regions of the Empire, came as far as Syria and Judaea, where the countless army of the emperor Heraclius met them, and the whole of it was cut down by the enemy. For a hundred and fifty thousand of the emperor's army were laid low, the Lord permitting it. But they say the enemy showed this humanity, that through envoys they also returned the spoils. Heraclius, however, refused such spoils or booty, and taking into his aid peoples said, according to the histories, to have come out of the Caspian mountains, where they had been shut in by Alexander, he rebuilt his army and gathered an infinite multitude of fighting men. The Saracens were also led by two commanders, who put two hundred thousand fighters into the battle, while each army stood not far off, prepared and drawn up for battle. But on the night before the day of battle, suddenly in the camp of the Greeks fifty-two thousand men were slain in their camp and at their posts. Struck by this terror and fear, the rest of the multitude of the army fled to various places, leaving the whole empire to the enemy. Heraclius too, when he received news of so great a disaster and despaired of being able to resist, fell into sickness from grief, and, as if in despair, sank into a sickness of the soul. For, as the histories relate, he was stained with the error of Eutyches, and he joined himself in marriage to Martina, the daughter of his sister. Other histories say that before the said conflict he was already stained with that error, on account of which God punished him. After these things the army of the Arabs and Nabathaeans was multiplied, drawn from various provinces, their kinsmen and allies, the Chaldeans, Ammonites and Moabites; to these Muhammad was joined, who held the principality in Arabia, as Richard writes in his Chronicles. This Muhammad, instructed in magic arts, under the pretext of contempt for the Empire, persuaded them concerning their way of life and their conduct, and by his art deceived the Lord's people in many ways and turned them away from the faith, saying that they could not hold the principality unless they turned away from the Christian faith and kept his precepts. Pretending also to have something of the divine power in himself, and deceiving men by certain omens shown through him, he was commonly regarded among the said people by all as a prophet. By these magic arts he so deceived a certain noble and powerful lady, named Chadiga, of the province of Corasan, that he joined himself to her in marriage, and through her he obtained the principality of that region. He also deceived many Jews, so that they believed him to be their Messiah. By these means, with his power and his extension of the Law regarding sensual pleasures, and with lavish promises concerning the future, he seduced the peoples, and by the power of arms compelled them to his rule. For under the Law given by Muhammad, the peoples who took up arms against the empire compelled whatever regions they occupied to accept the law of Moses, and put to death those unwilling to obey. Hence they entered Egypt from Arabia and so overthrew the people. Then they crossed into Africa and did the same there. Afterwards they came into Spain and partly forced it directly into their faith. And so, multiplied in number, they prevailed more by the violence of war than by the preaching of words.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: Chapter III.

units.la: HEraclio igitur mortuo, & imperii sic difformata potentia, quantum ad dominium Orientis, remansit Imperialis sedes in Graecia apud Constantinopolim, vsque ad tempora Constantini sexti, & Leonis filii sui, per triginta tres Imperatores: computato Magno Constantino, per quadringentos quinquaginta vnum annos, & vndecim menses: computatis viginti tribus annis, de imperio Constantini, quos post translatam seu mutatam sedem de Roma in Graeciam superuixit. Tunc Leo Papa tertius, imperium de Graecis in Francos transtulit, in persona magnifici principis Caroli, magni Franciae ac Germaniae regis. Sed quia haec historia propter scriptorum varietatem communiter est ignota, ipsam pro viribus declarabo. Dum itaque vniuscuiusque rei praecipua pars principium sit; quo incognito, raro in cognitionem medii & finis deueniatur, prout mihi videtur, translationem Imperii de Graecis in Francos, & de Francis in Germanos veraciter & sine contradictione describam. Attendendum est igitur diligenter: & principium & causa huius translationis fuit, discordia inter sacram Romanam Ecclesiam & Imperatorem Leonem, propter venerationem sanctarum imaginum. Leo enim tertius Imperator haereticis hoc suadentibus acquiescens, dixit Christi & Sanctorum imagines minime venerandas, quia species idololatriae videbatur. Gregorius vero tertius, qui tunc Romanae Ecclesiae praesidebat, cum catholicis affirmabat, Christi & sanctorum imagines venerandas, & cum veneratione colendas. Imago enim fert intellectum humanum in illum, cuius imago foris dignoscitur, intusque latet. Imploramus enim illius auxilium, cuius est imago, ac debita veneratione recolimus, & imaginem ipsius imaginato reddimus. Necesse eadem ratio de imaginibus & sculptilibus idolorum, quia idolis Spiritus malignus iungebatur, qui in ipsis deceptorie respondebat, & ideo his nulla reverentia debetur. Et ideo veneratio imaginum non idololatria, sed latria, id est, diuinus cultus dici potest proprie. In hoc siquidem errore damnabili sic contumaciter Leo praedictus perseuerauit: & de Constantinopoli Romam veniens, omnes sanctorum imagines quas Romae reperit, violenter abstulit, & secum Constantinopolim asportauit, easque damnabiliter igne cremauit. Propter quod dictus Gregorius Pontifex tertius, ipsum Imperatorem solenniter anathemate condemnauit, Apuliam et Italiam abstulit, tuncque Italiam ab eius dominio & obedientia recedere fecit, eique vectigalia solennia interdixit, Romaeque congregans Synodum, veneratonem sanctarum imaginum confirmauit, & violatores generali sententia anathematis condemnauit. Et demum praedictus Leo, in hoc damnabili errore moritur: Et successit ei in Imperio Constantinus quintus magis impius, non solum in errore praeceptis, sed etiam in omnibus vitiis & peccatis, in maleficis quidem actibus, & luxuria abominabili, in quibus longo tempore superuixit. Vnde de ipso dici potest De radice enim colubri regulus prodit: & de patre nequitiae, filius iniquitatis exiuit. Et quia hic pessimus, Imperator, in nullo iuuabat ecclesiam, imo tanquam haereticus potius offendebat, Papa Stephanus secundus, vltimo anno sui Pontificatus, Imperium transtulit de Graecis in Francos: sicut habetur Extr. de elect. c. venerabilem. Omnia tunc inordinata, vt fieret translatio viuente Pipino in Francos: quorum fauores & beneficia in ecclesiam Romanam multipliciter sentiebat, eidem per Pipinum in multis necessitatibus reuerenter exhibita.
units.tr: After Heraclius died, and the power of the empire had been so reduced that it held only the East, the imperial seat remained in Greece, at Constantinople, until the time of Constantine VI and his son Leo. That was through thirty-three emperors, counting Constantine the Great, over four hundred and fifty-one years and eleven months, counting the twenty-three years of Constantine's reign which he survived after the seat was moved or transferred from Rome to Greece. Then Pope Leo III transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Franks, in the person of the illustrious prince Charles, king of France and Germany. But since this history is generally unknown, because of the variety of the writers, I will set it out as well as I can. Since the chief part of any matter is its beginning, and when that is unknown one rarely reaches knowledge of the middle and the end, I will describe, as truthfully and without dispute as I can, the transfer of the empire from the Greeks to the Franks and from the Franks to the Germans. We must therefore attend carefully: the beginning and cause of this transfer was the quarrel between the holy Roman Church and the emperor Leo, over the veneration of holy images. For the emperor Leo III, yielding to the heretics who urged it, said that the images of Christ and of the saints were by no means to be venerated, because they looked like idolatry. Gregory III, however, who then presided over the Roman Church, maintained with the Catholics that the images of Christ and of the saints were to be venerated and honoured with reverence. For an image carries the human mind to him whose image it outwardly shows and who lies hidden within. We call upon the help of him whose image it is, we honour him with due reverence, and we give to the image the honour of the one it depicts. The same reasoning applies to the images and carved idols, since the evil spirit was joined to idols and answered deceitfully through them, and so no reverence is due to them. Hence the veneration of images is not idolatry but latria, which can properly be called divine worship. The aforesaid Leo persisted obstinately in this damnable error. Coming from Constantinople to Rome, he violently seized all the images of the saints that he found at Rome, carried them off to Constantinople, and wickedly burned them with fire. Because of this, Pope Gregory III solemnly condemned the emperor with anathema, took Apulia and Italy away from him, and caused Italy to withdraw from his dominion and obedience, forbidding him the customary tributes. Then, gathering a synod at Rome, he confirmed the veneration of the holy images and condemned the violators with a general sentence of anathema. At last the aforesaid Leo died in this damnable error, and he was succeeded in the empire by Constantine V, a man more impious, not only in his errors and precepts but also in every vice and sin, in wicked deeds and abominable lust, in which he lived on for a long time. Of him it may rightly be said: For from the root of the serpent comes forth a basilisk, and from the father of wickedness a son of iniquity. And because this most wicked emperor helped the Church in nothing, but rather injured it as a heretic would, Pope Stephen II, in the last year of his pontificate, transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Franks, as is found in Extr. de elect. c. venerabilem. All things were then put in order so that the transfer could take place while Pepin was still living among the Franks, whose favours and benefits toward the Roman Church the Church felt in many ways, since Pepin had shown it reverent service in many of its needs.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: IS siquidem Pipinus Caroli Martelli filius, vir in rebus bellicis strenuus, religione catholicus, & vniuersa morum honestate praeclarus, a Zacharia Papa ad Maioris domus Francorum excellentiam extitit sublimatus. Qui quidem Zacharias regem Francorum Hildericum non tam pro suis iniquitatibus quam pro eo quod tantae potestati erat inutilis, a regno deposuit, & praedictum Pipinum Caroli magni patrem in eius loco substituit: omnesque Francigenas a iuramento fidelitatis quo dicto Hildetico tenebantur, absoluit, vt 15. q. 6. alias. Sed Annonius in gestis Francorum scribit, Pipinum per Francos legitime fuisse electum in Regem & protectorem eleuatum, & per Bonifacium archiepiscopum Remensem vnctum Suessioni, id est, in tali loco, in monasterio sancti Medardi. Hildericus vero, qui tunc sub nomine regio, in deliciis marcebat ocio, in monachum consecratus est. Hic ergo verbum Deposuit, positum in dicto capitulo, aliusglossauit, id est, Deponentibus consensit. Sed qualitercunque dicatur, siue vt praedicta Francorum narrat historia, siue vt alius supra allegatus, salua semper in omnibus veritate: credo authoritatem Papae in talibus omnibus negociis praesupponi, ex eo quod omnis potestas ex eo in hoc dependet, vt Papam Gelasium Imperatori Anastasio legimus rescripsisse, & vt clarius patebit. Qua re, & ex qua causa, & qualiter facta extitit in Francos imperii translatio memoria Pipini praedicti Franciae & Germaniae regis historiam breuiter prosequamur. In Chronicis dicit Annonius, scribens historiam regis Franciae, quod anno natiuitatis Christi septingentesimo decimo quinto, Pipinus filius Ansegisili principabatur in Austria Alemanica, & ex Alpaide pellice siue concubina genuit Carolum Martellum, alias Tutidem, de quo natus est hic Pipinus, de quo postea natus Carolus Magnus, sic cognominatus a magnitudine virtutum & corporis.
units.tr: Pipin, son of Charles Martel, a man vigorous in warfare, Catholic in religion, and outstanding in every kind of moral uprightness, was raised by Pope Zachary to the dignity of Mayor of the Palace of the Franks. Zachary indeed deposed King Childeric from his throne, not so much for his wicked deeds as because he was useless for such great power, and he put in his place the aforementioned Pipin, father of Charlemagne. He also released all the Franks from the oath of fidelity by which they had been bound to the said Childeric. 15. q. 6. alias. But Annonius, in gestis Francorum, writes that Pipin was lawfully chosen king by the Franks and raised up as their protector, and was anointed at Soissons, that is, in that place, in the monastery of St Medard, by Boniface, archbishop of Reims. Childeric, who then languished in idleness and luxury under the royal name, was made a monk. Here, then, another writer has glossed the word Deposuit (he deposed), used in the said chapter, as Deponentibus consensit (he agreed with those who deposed). But however it is put, whether as the aforementioned history of the Franks tells it or as the other writer cited above does, with the truth always preserved in every respect, I believe that the authority of the Pope is presupposed in all such affairs, since all power depends on it in this way, as we read that Pope Gelasius wrote back to the Emperor Anastasius, and as will be made clearer. For this reason, and for what cause and in what manner the transfer of empire to the Franks was made, let us briefly follow the history of the said Pipin, king of France and Germany. In his Chronicles, Annonius, writing the history of the king of France, says that in the year of Christ's birth 715, Pipin, son of Ansegisil, ruled in Austrasia (Alemannic Austria), and by Alpaida, a concubine or mistress, he begot Charles Martel, also called Tudes, from whom was born this Pipin, from whom in turn was born Charlemagne, so named from the greatness of his virtues and of his body.

units.la: H 4. Natu Nam & pectore & fortitudine & virtutibus excedebat omnes. Hic Pipinus factus est rex Franciae, anno Domini 701. consilio & adiutorio Zachariae Papae, Hilderico rege inutili repudiato, & habitu monachali palliato. Demum quia defendit ecclesiam & dictum Papam ab oppressionibus Astulphi, & reduxit Papam in Romam, factusque est Patricius urbis. Filius vero Carolus Magnus successit Pipino in regno, & fit Imperator; causa simili scilicet adiuuando Papam. Et nota hunc Pipinum, in cuius filium conflatum est imperium Germanum, licet regem Francorum etiamsi ex pellice descendisset.
units.tr: H 4. By birth... For he surpassed all men both in stature, in courage and in virtues. This Pipin was made king of France in the year of the Lord 701, by the counsel and help of Pope Zachary, when the useless King Hilderic had been cast off and given a monk's habit. Afterwards, because he defended the Church and the said Pope from the oppressions of Aistulf, and led the Pope back to Rome, he became Patricius urbis (patrician of the city). His son Charlemagne succeeded Pipin in the kingdom and became Imperator (emperor), for the same reason, namely by helping the Pope. And note that this Pipin, into whose son the German empire was transferred, was king of the Franks even though he was ex pellice descendisset (descended from a concubine).

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: MOrtuo igitur Zacharia Papa, qui Pipinum regem sublimauit, vt superius declaratur: Stephanus secundus, natione Romanus, ex Patre Constantino, anno Domini septingentesimo quinquagesimo, ab vrbe condita M. D XXX. in summum Pontificem sublimatur. Hic, vt Annonius scribit in gestis Francorum lib. V. gratiatus a rege Lombardorum Astulpho, venit in Franciam ad Pipinum regem, anno septingentesimo quinquagesimo tertio, pro iustitia sancti Petri recuperanda, qua ipsum spoliauerat Astulphus, cui Pipinus rex catholicus dum ad tertium miliare ciuitatis appropinquaret, occurrit: & de equo descendens, eidem summo Pontifici cum magna reuerentia & deuotione sincera exhibuit seruitoris officium, & usque ad palatium suum regio honore deduxit. Tunc praedictus Pontifex causam sui aduentus diligenter exposuit, & iniurias dicti Astulphi plenius enarrauit. Rex quoque deuotus, volens Ecclesiae Dei & dicti Pontificis satisfacere voluntati, exercitum magnum parat, & cum ipso Pontifice in Italiam vadit pro iustitia sancti Petri recuperanda. Astulphusque totis viribus praedicto Regi obuiat, & iura sancti Petri restituere contradicit. Pugna igitur magna inter ipsos committitur, in qua Astulphus rex superatur, & Pipinus cum Francis victor efficitur. Compulsus sic fuit Astulphus ad restituendum talia. Qui datis quadraginta obsidibus de melioribus regni sui, iura ipsa sub iuramento restituere promisit. Rege Pipino in Franciam redeunte, etiam Stephanus Papa Romam ad suam sedem rediit. Astulphus praedictus, iuramenti sui violator, de his quae Pipino cum iuramento promisit, nihil obseruat. Ob quam causam iterum Pipinus in Italiam contra Astulphum vadit, ipsumque in Papia obsedit, coegitque reddere eum quod promisit. Vadit deinde Pipinus Rauennam, ipsamque cepit, totamque Pentapolim, Romandiolam cum Marchia & Bononia victoriose subegit: quae beato Petro studuit reuerenter offerre. Quae beneficia Papa diligenter attendens, ordinauit translationem Romani imperii fieri de Graecis in Francos. Et sic omnes scripturae, quae dicunt quod hic Papa Stephanus secundus, Imperium de Graecis in Francos transtulit: debent intelligi, vt glossemus: Transtulit, id est, translationem fieri ordinauit. Alius enim Pontifex, scilicet Leo tertius, re ipsa imperium transtulit, sicut euidenter in sequentibus apparebit.
units.tr: Zacharias the Pope, who had raised Pippin to the kingship, as declared above, having died, Stephen the Second, a Roman by birth, son of Constantine, was elevated to the supreme Pontificate in the year of the Lord 750, from the founding of the city 1030. He, as Annonius writes in the Deeds of the Franks, book V., having been favoured by Astulphus, king of the Lombards, came into France to Pippin the king in the year 753, to recover the justice of St. Peter, of which Astulphus had despoiled it. King Pippin, a Catholic, met him as he approached the third milestone from the city; dismounting from his horse, he showed the same Supreme Pontiff the service of a servant with great reverence and sincere devotion, and escorted him to his palace with royal honour. Then the aforesaid Pontiff carefully set out the reason for his coming and related more fully the injuries of the said Astulphus. The king, too, devout and wishing to satisfy the Church of God and the will of the said Pontiff, prepared a great army and went with the Pontiff himself into Italy to recover the justice of St. Peter. Astulphus, with all his might, opposed the aforesaid king and refused to restore the rights of St. Peter. A great battle was therefore joined between them, in which King Astulphus was defeated and Pippin with the Franks became victorious. Astulphus was thus compelled to restore such things. Having given forty hostages from the best of his kingdom, he promised under oath to restore those rights. When King Pippin returned to France, Pope Stephen also returned to Rome, to his see. Astulphus, violator of his oath, observed nothing of what he had promised Pippin under oath. For this reason Pippin again went into Italy against Astulphus, besieged him in Pavia, and forced him to give back what he had promised. Pippin then went to Ravenna, took it, and victoriously subdued all of Pentapolis, Romagna with the March and Bologna, which he took care to offer reverently to St. Peter. The Pope, carefully attending to these benefits, ordained that the transfer of the Roman empire be made from the Greeks to the Franks. And so all the writings which say that this Pope Stephen the Second transferred the Empire from the Greeks to the Franks must be understood, so that we may gloss them: he transferred it, that is, he ordained that the transfer be made. For another Pontiff, namely Leo the Third, actually transferred the empire, as will clearly appear in what follows.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: HOc itaque Pontifice, scilicet Stephano secundo, mortuo sub magno ecclesiae protectore Pipino, atque ipso Pipino post decimum octauum annum regni sui, viam vniuersae carnis ingressso, filioque eius Carolo, qui a virtutum magnitudine dictus est Magnus, magnifice pro patre regnante, tribus Pontificibus intermediis, quorum electionem & vitam causa breuitatis omitto: videlicet Paulo primo, Constantino secundo, Stephano tertio, Adrianus primus, natione Romanus, ex patre Theodoro de regione Viaelatae, Anno Domini septingentesimo, septuagesimo primo, ab vrbe condita M. D LI. in summum Pontificem eligitur, ecclesiamque Romanam annis XXIII. mensibus decem, & diebus XVIII. prudenter & magnifice gubernauit. Hic praeclarus Pontifex Adrianus magnificum principem Carolum Magnum, qui tunc, vt dictum est, Franciae & Germaniae regna tenebat, in auxilium vocauit contra Lombardos, qui ecclesiam tunc vexabant. Mortuo enim Astulpho Lombardorum rege in regno successit Desiderius filius eius, qui patris sequens nequitias, ecclesiam Dei totis viribus opprimebat, villas, ciuitates & castra, & alias possessiones ecclesiae violenter usurpans, & Romanos tyrannico more premens vectigalibus & tributis. Ob quam causam, misit Adrianus Legatum in Franciam, Petrum presbyterum Cardinalem ad Carolum Magnum, petens ab eo auxilium contra Desiderium memoratum. Qui gratiose dictum legatum recipiens, congregansque parlamentum Parium & praelatorum omnium, Pontificis petitioni annuit, dicto legato cum fauore remisso. Parat exercitum copiosum, ipsumque per mare, & iuga montium in Lombardiam, cum non modica difficultate deducit. Veniens igitur in Liguriam & Aemiliam (quae nunc Lombardia plana dicitur) in circuitu Papiae sua tabernacula figit, & castris prudenter circum circa dispositis, in quibus, vt fideliter sequamur historiae, natalem diem celebrauit: relicto exercitu, Romam causa deuotionis accessit, ibique cum summo Pontifice Paschalem diem celebrauit. Facta solennitate Paschali, ad sua castra reuertitur, continuataque obsidione ciuitatem strenue oppugnabat, atque anno septingentesimo septuagesimo quarto domat Desiderium Lombardorum Regem, & eius uxorem Ansam nomine, & filios cepit. Qui Rex amissis filiis suis, Carolo subiicitur, ibique venientes omnes Italici, & de singulis Italiae ciuitatibus Ambasiatores solennes Nuncii, Caroli ditioni se submittunt. Sicque omnibus foeliciter expeditis, Regnum Italiae Pipino filio suo tradidit, & Romam accedens cum curia iura beato Petro restituit, simulque Ducatum Spoletanum & Beneuentanum eidem sua liberalitate donauit. Tunc dictus summus Pontifex Adrianus, mature considerans beneficia tanti principis, ecclesiae Romanae collata, centum quinquaginta trium Episcoporum & Abbatum Romae Concilium congregauit, ibique Adrianus cum vniuersa Synodo, gloriosò Carolo hanc tribuit dignitatem: videlicet, ius & potestatem eligendi Romanum Pontificem, & Apostolicam sedem ordinandi: Dignitatem Patriciatus quoque ecclesiae concessit, qui olim quasi patres Principis videbantur: vt Institution. libr. primo Titulo duodecimo quibus modis ius patr. potest. soluitur. § fil. insuper. Episcopos & Archiepiscopos per singulas prouincias ab eo inuestituras accipere diffinixit: vt nisi à rege laudaretur & inuestiretur Episcopus, à nemine consecraretur, omnesque contra facientes, anathemate condemnauit: vt haec omnia plenius habentur in sexagesim. distinctione cap. Adrianus. Prima siquidem concessione, scilicet potestate eligendi summum Pontificem, & sedem Apostolicam ordinandi, non fuit visus Carolus memoratus: quod ideo fuit, quia pauci summi Pontifices fuerunt tempore sui regiminis à concessione praedicta, quod fuit spacio sexaginta annorum. Solus enim praedictus Adrianus & Leo tertius, praedicti temporis spacio Romani pontifices extiterunt, qui quadraginta & nouem annis Romanae ecclesiae praefuerunt: sed nec ipsum Carolum iure sibi competenti, circa praedicta, expressione memorata, cessisse seu renunciasse reperio. De secunda vero concessione, videlicet de installationibus Episcoporum, bene se aliquando intromisit, vt ex gestis suis, in pluribus locis euidenter apparet. Sed his omnibus iuribus, occasione primae & secundae concessionis competentibus, cessit, & renunciauit Ludouicus Imperator expresse, vt habetur in sexagesim. distinctione cap. Ludouicus, cum pluribus capitulis sequentibus. Sed vt ad propositum facilius & citius venire possimus, multa magna & magnifica de gestis Caroli omittimus, & propositum translationis semper breuiter prosequar.
units.tr: Pope Stephen II having died, and King Pepin, the great protector of the Church, having also died in the eighteenth year of his reign and gone the way of all flesh, his son Charles, called Charles the Great from the greatness of his virtues, reigned magnificently in his father's place. Three intervening popes followed, whose elections and lives I omit for the sake of brevity: namely Paul I, Constantine II and Stephen III. Then Hadrian I, a Roman by birth, son of Theodore of the region of Via Lata, was elected supreme pontiff in the year of the Lord 771, from the founding of the city M. D LI. He governed the Roman Church prudently and magnificently for twenty-three years, ten months and eighteen days. This distinguished pontiff Hadrian called upon the great prince Charles the Great, who at that time, as has been said, held the kingdoms of France and Germany, to help him against the Lombards, who were then harassing the Church. For after Astulf, king of the Lombards, died, his son Desiderius succeeded him in the kingdom. Following his father's wickedness, Desiderius oppressed the Church of God with all his strength, violently seizing estates, cities, fortresses and other possessions of the Church, and tyrannically burdening the Romans with taxes and tributes. For this reason Hadrian sent as legate into France Peter, a cardinal priest, to Charles the Great, asking him for help against the aforementioned Desiderius. Charles received the legate graciously and, having gathered a parliament of the peers and all the prelates, granted the pontiff's request, and sent the legate back with favour. He prepared a large army and led it, not without considerable difficulty, by sea and over the mountain ridges into Lombardy. Coming therefore into Liguria and Aemilia (now called the Lombard plain), he pitched his tents around Pavia, and with his camps prudently arranged round about, he celebrated his birthday there, to follow the history faithfully. Leaving the army, he went to Rome out of devotion and there celebrated Easter with the supreme pontiff. After the Easter solemnities he returned to his camp, and continuing the siege he vigorously attacked the city, and in the year 774 he subdued Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and captured his wife, named Ansa, and his sons. That king, having lost his sons, submitted to Charles, and all the Italians who came there, and solemn envoys from each of the cities of Italy, submitted themselves to Charles's authority. So when everything had been happily settled, he handed the kingdom of Italy over to his son Pepin, and going to Rome with his court he restored the rights to St Peter, and at the same time by his generosity he gave the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento to the same see. Then the said supreme pontiff Hadrian, considering maturely the benefits conferred by so great a prince upon the Roman Church, convened a council at Rome of one hundred and fifty-three bishops and abbots. There Hadrian, with the whole synod, granted this dignity to the glorious Charles: namely the right and power of electing the Roman pontiff and of ordaining the Apostolic See. He also granted to the Church the dignity of patriciate, which formerly seemed to be like that of fathers to the prince, as in Institutes, book 1, title 12, by what means paternal power is dissolved, § fil. insuper. He decreed that bishops and archbishops in each province should receive investiture from him, so that no bishop not praised and invested by the king should be consecrated by anyone, and he condemned all who acted contrary with anathema; all this is more fully set out in Distinction 60, chapter Adrian. Indeed, Charles did not seem to have been much concerned with the first grant, namely the power of electing the supreme pontiff and ordaining the Apostolic See; this was because few supreme pontiffs held office during his reign after that grant, which lasted sixty years. For only the aforementioned Hadrian and Leo III were Roman pontiffs during that span, and they presided over the Roman Church for forty-nine years. But I find that Charles himself never ceded or renounced by express statement, in the matters mentioned, the right that properly belonged to him. Regarding the second grant, namely the installation of bishops, he did indeed sometimes interfere, as is clearly evident in many places from his acts. But all the rights that arose from the first and second grants were ceded and renounced expressly by the emperor Louis, as is found in Distinction 60, chapter Ludovicus, together with several following chapters. But so that we may come more easily and quickly to our purpose, we omit many great and magnificent deeds of Charles, and will pursue briefly the matter of the translation of the empire.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAP. VII.

units.la: Mortuo quoque Adriano Papa, praedicto regnante Carolo Magno Ecclesiae defensore, Leo tertius, natione Romanus ex patre Astulpho, in Romanum Pontificem sublimatur, anno Domini octingentesimo, & ab Vrbe condita M.DLXXII. Hic Pontifex in Lætania maiore Romae captus, exoculatus est, & lingua detruncatur, qui in custodia positus nocte per murum euasit, & ad legatos praedicti regis Caroli, scilicet Vvirundum Abbatem, & Vuinigisum Spoletanum Ducem confugit cum fiducia. Hic gloriosus Pontifex, vt Richardus in suis Chronicis scribit, & aliae historiae veridicae asserunt, restitutis sibi plenarie membris, scilicet oculis & lingua, diuina virtute, ad praedictum Carolum Padenborauum, ad praecipuum eccl. siae protectorem venit in Franciam: qui eum, vt decuit cum omni reuerentia & honore suscepit. Et cum ipso Romam accedens, iniuriam dicti Pontificis & ecclesiae vltus est, iustitia mediante. Annonius quoque in Gestis Francorum, magis copiose scribens, dicit: Quod postquam rex appropinquaret Beneuentum, duodecimo lapide ab vrbe Roma, Leo Papa, qui regem praecesserat, cum magno equitatu occurrit eidem: ipsumque cum esset Vrbis Patricius, cum summa humilitate & honore suscepit, prandensque cum ipso in loco praedicto, vt verbis vtar historiae, dominus Papa ipsum cum sua societate praecessit ad vrbem. In crastinum quoque in gradibus beati Petri stans, amicis obuiam venientibus, conclamarunt laudes, ipse vero cum clero & Episcopis equo descendentem regem, ad gradus ecclesiae ascendentem, dictaque oratione basilica beati Petri, psallentibus cunctis, introduxit. Et post septem dies, cur Romam venisset, omnibus patefecit.
units.tr: When Pope Hadrian had also died, while Charles the Great still reigned as defender of the Church, Leo III, a Roman by birth, son of Astulphus, was raised to the Roman pontificate in the year of the Lord 800, and in the year 1572 from the founding of the City. This pontiff was seized in Rome during the Greater Litany, had his eyes put out and his tongue cut out. Placed in custody, he escaped at night over the wall and with confidence fled to the envoys of the said king Charles, namely Abbot Wirundus and Winigis, Duke of Spoleto. This glorious pontiff, as Richardus in his Chronicles writes, and other trustworthy histories assert, had his members, namely his eyes and tongue, fully restored by divine power, and came into France to Charles at Paderborn, the chief protector of the Church. Charles received him with all reverence and honour, as was fitting. Going back with him to Rome, he avenged the wrong done to the said pontiff and to the Church, by the mediation of justice. Annonius also, writing more fully in the Deeds of the Franks, says: when the king was approaching Benevento, twelve miles from the city of Rome, Pope Leo, who had gone ahead of the king, met him with a great train of horsemen. Since he was Patrician of the City, he received him with the greatest humility and honour, and dined with him in the said place; and, to use the words of the history, the lord Pope went ahead with his company to the city. On the next day, standing on the steps of St Peter's, as friends came to meet them they shouted out praises. The Pope himself, with the clergy and bishops, received the king as he dismounted and came up the steps of the church, and, after a prayer, led him into the basilica of St Peter, with everyone chanting psalms. And after seven days he made known to everyone why he had come to Rome.

units.la: Exinde, ad ea propter quae venerat facienda, quotidie operam dedit. Et quamuis grauia crimina opponerentur summo Pontifici, tamen quia nullus extitit probator legitimus, idem summus Pontifex, coram omni populo, & annuente Rege in basilica beati Petri Apostoli, Euangelicam portans absolutionem conscendit: inuocatoque sanctae Trinitatis nomine, iureiurando obiectis sibi criminibus canonice se purgauit. Aliae historiae addunt, quod tres Cardinales, supra sancta Dei Euangelia ponentes manus, affirmantes ostenderint, esse falsa ipsi opposita, quae quidem purgatio a toto clero & populo fuit solenniter approbata, & à dicto Principe legitime confirmata.
units.tr: Thereafter he gave himself daily to the business for which he had come. And although grave crimes were charged against the supreme Pontiff, yet, since no lawful accuser appeared, the same supreme Pontiff, before all the people, and with the king's assent, climbed into the basilica of the apostle St Peter, carrying the Gospel as his absolution. Invoking the name of the holy Trinity, under oath he canonically cleared himself of the crimes laid against him. Other histories add that three cardinals, laying their hands upon the holy Gospels of God, affirmed and showed that the charges brought against him were false. This purgation was solemnly approved by the whole clergy and people, and lawfully confirmed by the said Prince.
