units.la: Eadem die, vt scribit Annonius in gestis Francorum, quidam Abbas nomine Zacharias, cum duobus monachis, vno de monte Oliueti, alio de sancto Saba in Oriente, Romam venit, quem Patriarcha Hierosolymitanus transmisit. Qui sepulchri Domini claues, Caluariae loci, & ciuitatis Hierusalem cum vexillo detulerunt. Quos benigne suscipiens, per aliquot dies secum cum honore magno detinuit, humaneque valde tractauit. Deinde post aliquot dies, cum muneribus magnis, & donis regiam maiestatem decentibus, eos in Palaestinam remisit. Tradunt eædem historiæ, quod ex illa legatione commotus Rex ad petitionem Constantini sexti, tunc Imperatoris, cum magno exercitu transfretauit, totamque terram Sanctam recuperauit: rege Persarum assentiente, qui tenebat tunc in Palæstina & tota Syria principatum. Iamque per totum Orientem fama celebris nomenque gloriosi Caroli percurrebat. Vnde dictus rex Persarum, qui monarchiam in Oriente tenebat, eius habere gratiam & beneuolentiam affectabat: & per solennes nuncios & legatos preciosa munera ei destinauit. Prædictus rex Carolus, vbique virtuosus, terra Sancta recuperata, per Constantinopolim Romam rediit, ibique natiuitatem Domini solenniter celebrauit cum Leone, ipsa die celeberrima natiuitatis Domini. Cum rex Carolus in missa, ante confessionem Petri surgeret ab oratione deuota, Leo Papa solenniter ordinatis omnibus ad tantam solennitatem necessariis, coronam imperialem capiti eius imposuit, & a cunctis populo Romano acclamatum est: CAROLO AVGVSTO A DEO CORONATO MAGNO ET PACIFICO IMPERATORI, VITA ET VICTORIA DE COELO SIBI MINISTRETVR. Hanc siquidem orationem, per Leonem Papam, & imperalium laudum exclamationem, per plurimum omnes historiæ canunt. Sed post prædicta, more antiquorum principum, fuit ab omnibus vniuersaliter adoratus. Et ablato Patricii nomine IMPERATOR AVGVSTVS est ab omnibus appellatus. Rex autem prædictus Carolus, Romanum imperium XXXIIII. annis tenuit. Post dictam imperialem coronam, ipsum Imperatorem Augustum, omnes annales omnia gesta, omnesque historiæ, quæ de ipso faciunt mentionem, sine aliqua varietate describunt.
units.tr: On the same day, as Annonius writes in the Deeds of the Franks, a certain abbot named Zacharias came to Rome with two monks, one from the Mount of Olives and the other from St Sabas in the East, sent by the Patriarch of Jerusalem. They brought the keys of the Lord's sepulchre and of Calvary, and the standard of the city of Jerusalem. Receiving them kindly, he kept them with him for some days with great honour, and treated them very humanely. Then, after some days, he sent them back to Palestine with great gifts and presents befitting the royal majesty. The same histories relate that, moved by that embassy, the king, at the request of Constantine VI, then Emperor, crossed over with a great army and recovered the whole Holy Land, with the assent of the king of the Persians, who then held the rule over Palestine and all Syria. And already the renown of Charles and his glorious name was spreading through the whole East. Hence the said king of the Persians, who held the monarchy in the East, desired to have his favour and goodwill, and sent him precious gifts by solemn messengers and envoys. The aforesaid king Charles, everywhere virtuous, having recovered the Holy Land, returned to Rome by way of Constantinople, and there celebrated the Lord's Nativity solemnly with Leo, on that most famous day of the Lord's Nativity. When King Charles, during the Mass, rose before the confession of Peter from his devout prayer, Pope Leo, having solemnly arranged everything needful for so great a solemnity, placed the imperial crown on his head, and all the Roman people acclaimed: TO CHARLES AUGUSTUS, CROWNED BY GOD, THE GREAT AND PEACEFUL EMPEROR, LIFE AND VICTORY FROM HEAVEN BE GIVEN. Indeed, this acclamation, pronounced by Pope Leo, and the shout of imperial praises, nearly all histories sing. But after these events, in the manner of the ancient princes, he was worshipped by all universally. And with the title of Patrician set aside, he was called by all EMPEROR AUGUSTUS. Now the aforesaid king Charles held the Roman empire for thirty-four years. After the said imperial coronation, all annals, all deeds, and all histories that mention him describe the Emperor Augustus without any variation.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: QVantum autem roboris habuerit, aut firmitatis, quidve tunc per Romanam ecclesiam factum fuerit de Imperio, patet, & patere potest omnibus euidenter. Prædicta enim Imperii translatio facta per Ecclesiam, de Græcis in Francos, ex causis & rationibus antedictis, adeo valida est, quod per septem generationes, per septem scilicet Imperatores, annis centum tribus duravit, & amplius, nec defecisset in ipsis monarchia Imperii, nisi virtus & devotio erga sanctam Romanam ecclesiam defecisset. Sed virtute ac devotione deficiente, defecit Imperium. Imperator autem Arnulphus, vltimus de dicto genere, effeminatus & vilis fuit, & in defensionem Ecclesiæ non solum remissus & tepidus contra Berengarium tyrannum, qui tunc in Italia ecclesiam Dei impugnabat, & alios qui ipsam in multis partibus molestabant: sed ipsemet erat Ecclesiæ ipsius persecutor, vt Martinus Polonus episcopus Consentinus scribit. In filiis enim Arnulphi prædicti genus Caroli omnino defecit ex imperio. Et cœpit dicit Berengarius in Italia dominari, & Dei Ecclesiam persecutionibus ingentibus lacerare: quia dictus Berengarius ecclesiam molestabat, tum quia ecclesiæ non verus pastor, sed mercenarius præerat, scilicet Iohannes filius Alberti. Tunc, vt tradit Richardus Cremonensis episcopus magnus historiarum scriptor, Cardinales de communi concordia, anno natiuitatis Domini DCCCCL. scripserunt Ottoni Duci Saxoniæ, qui fuit vir magnæ potentiæ. Nam in tota Germania dominabitur. Erat enim vir religiosus fide catholicus, in consilio prouidus, in iudicio iustus, in commisso fidelis, in rebus bellicis strenuus, & vniuersa morum honestate præclarus, erga Romanam Ecclesiam cum omni veneratione devotus, vt Ecclesiam Dei, quæ procellis impellentibus vacillabat, etiam adiuuaret. Qui deuotione promptissimus, signo crucis se muniens, magnum exercitum sedulo studio præparauit: & in Italiam transiens, cum Berengario tyranno pugnauit: eiusdemque Berengarii exercitu victoriose deuicto, ipsum tyrannum occidit: & Romam pergens concilium Cardinalium congregauit, & de ipso Concilio Papam videns incorrigibilem, monuit vt Papatui renunciaret. Quem induratum in castro sancti Angeli violenter inclusit, ipsumque renunciare coegit. Factus tunc est Pastor vniuersalis ecclesiæ Leo octauus, qui mature considerans beneficium collatum ecclesiæ, per prædictum Ottonem ducem Saxoniæ, eadem dignitates Ottoni concessit, quas Catolo contulerat Adrianus, facta Synodo, clero & populo congregatis, vt patet 6t. dist. c. in synodo. Insuper ipsum Imperatorem constituit, nulla precedente electione, quæ postea à XLI. annis instituta fuit. Et sic facta est translatio de Gallicis in Germanos. Patet ergo quod circa ordinationem imperii, habet Papa maximam potestatem, vt habuit. Siquidem hic Otto primus, ex ordinatione ecclesiæ pacifice imperium habuit etiam successiue filius & nepos, qui etiam erga ecclesiam devotissimi extiterunt, vt de Ottone prædicto patet LXIII. dist. c. Tibi Domine. Patet igitur dispositionem & ordinationem summi Pontificis circa prædictos Imperatores fuisse legitimam: quia pro bono pacis, & statu fidei, & vniversalis ecclesiæ, ad quæ summus Pontifex præcipue debet intendere: quia sua interest, non tantum ex collatione imperialium iurium, quantum ex præeminentia status, quæ declaratur manifeste in c. Solita de maio. & obe.
units.tr: How much strength and firmness this had, and what was then done by the Roman Church concerning the Empire, is plain and can be plainly seen by all. For the transfer of the Empire made by the Church from the Greeks to the Franks, for the causes and reasons mentioned above, was so valid that it lasted for seven generations, that is, seven emperors, for one hundred and three years and more, and the monarchy of the Empire would not have failed in them unless virtue and devotion toward the holy Roman Church had failed. But with virtue and devotion failing, the Empire failed. Now the Emperor Arnulph, the last of that line, was effeminate and worthless, and was not only slack and lukewarm in defending the Church against Berengar the tyrant, who was then attacking the Church of God in Italy, and against others who were harassing it in many parts; he was himself a persecutor of that same Church, as Martinus Polonus, bishop of Consenza, writes. In the sons of the aforesaid Arnulph the line of Charles failed entirely from the empire. And Berengar, as they say, began to rule in Italy and to tear the Church of God with huge persecutions; for this Berengar harassed the Church, both because a hireling, namely John son of Albert, presided over the Church rather than a true minister. Then, as Richard, bishop of Cremona, the great writer of histories, relates, the Cardinals, by common agreement, in the year of the Lord's nativity 950, wrote to Otto, Duke of Saxony, who was a man of great power, for he would rule over all Germany. He was a religious man, Catholic in faith, prudent in counsel, just in judgment, faithful in what was entrusted to him, vigorous in warfare, and distinguished by every honesty of conduct, devoted with all reverence toward the Roman Church, so that he would also help the Church of God, which was wavering amid the storms that beat upon it. Most ready in devotion, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, he diligently prepared a great army, and crossing into Italy he fought with the tyrant Berengar; and when Berengar's army had been victoriously defeated, he killed the tyrant himself. Going on to Rome, he gathered a council of Cardinals, and seeing from that council that the Pope was incorrigible, he admonished him to renounce the papacy. He violently shut him up, obstinate, in the castle of Sant'Angelo, and forced him to renounce. Then Leo VIII was made universal Pastor of the Church, who, having carefully considered the benefit conferred on the Church through the aforesaid Duke Otto of Saxony, granted to Otto the same dignities which Adrian had conferred on Charles, a synod having been held with clergy and people gathered together, as appears in Dist. 63, c. In synodo. Moreover, he appointed Otto emperor, with no prior election, which was instituted afterwards, forty-one years later. And so the transfer was made from the Gauls to the Germans. It is plain, then, that in the ordering of the empire the Pope has the greatest power, as he had. For this Otto I, by the ordinance of the Church, held the empire peacefully, and his son and grandson likewise in succession, who also proved most devoted to the Church, as appears concerning the aforesaid Otto in Dist. 63, c. Tibi Domine. It is plain, therefore, that the disposition and ordering of the supreme Pontiff concerning the aforesaid emperors was lawful, because it was for the good of peace, the state of the faith, and the universal Church, to which the supreme Pontiff ought chiefly to attend; for his interest lies not so much in the bestowal of imperial rights as in the pre-eminence of his station, which is declared plainly in c. Solita, De maioritate et obedientia.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: POst hoc mortuo Ottone tertio sine filiis, Gregorius quintus, natione Theutonicus, de parentela Ottonis, in summum pontificem assumitur. Cuius Pontificis tempore, Electores Imperatoris instituuntur septem, scilicet Principes Alemaniæ, tres prælati, & quatuor laici, vt Martinus nus tus scribit. Quia igitur prædicti tres Ottones successive, & quasi hæreditario iure obtinuerunt imperium, per Gregorium Papam quintum est prouisum, & vtiliter ordinatum, vt tantæ sublimitatis ordinatio, quæ non debetur sanguini, sed virtuti, non per viam successionis, sed electionem procederet: vt eligeretur dignus, & non nobilitantum, sed dignissimo donaretur. Fuit igitur per dictum Pontificem institutum, vt septem proceres officiales, imperatorem regem Romanum eligerent, & per summum Pontificem confirmandum, & imperiali diademate coronandum. Quorum sunt tres Prælati, qui sunt Imperii Cancellarii: scilicet Archiepiscopus Coloniensis, qui est Italiæ: Archiepiscopus Treuerensis, qui est Galliæ: & Archiepiscopus Moguntinensis, qui est Germaniæ. Et quatuor Barones, qui imperialib. seruiunt, Marchio Brandenburgensis, qui est camerarius Imperatoris: Comes Palatinus, qui est dapifer: Dux Saxoniæ, qui est pincerna Imperatoris. Quæ ordinatio facta fuit anno Domini M.CCC.IIII. vt gesta Germanorum manifeste declarant.
units.tr: After Otto III died without sons, Gregory V, a German by birth and of Otto's kin, was made supreme pontiff. In his time the electors of the Emperor were instituted as seven: namely the princes of Germany, three prelates and four laymen, as Martin writes. Since the three Ottos had held the empire one after another, and almost by hereditary right, Pope Gregory V provided and usefully ordained that the appointment to so great a dignity, which is owed not to blood but to virtue, should proceed not by succession but by election: so that the worthy would be chosen, and the office given not merely to the noble but to the most worthy. It was therefore established by the said pontiff that seven chief officials should elect the king of the Romans, who was to be confirmed by the supreme pontiff and crowned with the imperial diadem. Of these, three are prelates who serve as the chancellors of the Empire: namely the Archbishop of Cologne, who is chancellor of Italy; the Archbishop of Trier, who is chancellor of Gaul; and the Archbishop of Mainz, who is chancellor of Germany. And four barons who serve the imperial court: the Margrave of Brandenburg, who is the Emperor's chamberlain; the Count Palatine, who is the steward; and the Duke of Saxony, who is the cupbearer of the Emperor. This arrangement was made in the year of the Lord 1304, as the deeds of the Germans clearly show.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: EX prædictis igitur euidenter apparet, per Stephanum Papam secundum, tempore Pipini Regis ordinationem prædictam de translatione de Græcis in Francos, ex causis & probationibus supra declaratis factam, vt notatur de elect. Venerabilem. Et primum Carolum Magnum dispositorem Romanæ ecclesiæ, & Romani Pontificis electorem, & Romanæ urbis Patricium ordinatum, vt LXIII. dist. Adrianus. Sed per Leonem tertium translationem realiter factam, de principibus Græcis in Francos, vt notatur de elect. Venerabilem. Vbi expresse scribitur, quod à Leone tertio Carolus magnus Imperator extitit coronatus: & postmodum processu temporis, per multas reuolutiones annorum, translationem imperii iusta de causa factam esse per Leonem octauum de Gallicis in Germanos, ac postmodum per Gregorium Quintum, electionem Romani Imperii Septem Principibus Alemaniæ prædictis fuisse concessam, qui usque ad moderna tempora Regem Romanorum eligunt, per Romanum Pontificem coronandum. Sic ergo Regnum mundi translatum est ad Germanos vel Theutonicos, qui & regimen hactenus habuerunt, de consecr. dist. 5. c. in die. Nec est Imperium iam modo apud Græcos, licet largo vocabulo Imperator vocetur, de Maior. & solita. Sed nec regimen, nec Imperium habere possunt; nunc præcipue, ex quo extra gremium sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ positi sunt, vt 24. q. sic. illud. Imperator siquidem iste Romanus super omnes Reges est, vt 7. q. 1. in apibus. His Regibus exceptis duntaxat, qui per Priuilegia & consuetudinem sunt exempti. Omnes siquidem nationes subiectæ sunt, vt 11. q. 1. si quis, & 8. dist. c. quoniure. Ipse Dominus mundi est, ff. ad L. Rhod. de iact. l. deprecatio.
units.tr: From what has been said, it is therefore clearly apparent that the aforesaid ordinance concerning the transfer of the empire from the Greeks to the Franks was made by Pope Stephen II in the time of King Pepin, on the causes and proofs declared above, as is noted in de elect. Venerabilem. And first Charles the Great was appointed the disposer of the Roman Church, the elector of the Roman Pontiff, and patrician of the city of Rome, as in LXIII dist. Adrianus. But the actual transfer of the princes from the Greeks to the Franks was made by Leo III, as is noted in de elect. Venerabilem, where it is expressly written that Charles the Great was crowned emperor by Leo III. Afterwards, in the course of time and through many turns of the years, the transfer of the empire from the Gauls to the Germans was made for a just cause by Leo VIII, and later Gregory V granted the election of the Roman Empire to the seven princes of Germany mentioned above, who to this day elect the King of the Romans, to be crowned by the Roman Pontiff. Thus the kingdom of the world was transferred to the Germans or Teutons, who have also held the government up to the present, de consecr. dist. 5, c. in die. Nor is there now an empire among the Greeks, although they are called emperor by a loose term, de Maior. & solita. Indeed they cannot have either government or empire, especially now that they have been placed outside the bosom of our holy mother the Church, as 24 q. sic illud. For this Roman emperor is above all kings, as 7 q. 1 in apibus, with the sole exception of those kings who are exempt by privileges and custom. For all nations are subject to him, as 11 q. 1 si quis, and 8 dist. c. quoniure. He himself is the lord of the world, ff. ad L. Rhod. de iact. l. deprecatio.

units.la: LITTERA, SIVE BULLA BONIFACII PAPÆ. Et ex ea Quæstio disputata in vtramque partem, pro & contra Pont- ificiam Potestatem. Per ÆGIDIVM DE ROMA, ARCHIEPISCOPVM Bituricensem.
units.tr: The letter, or bull, of Pope Boniface. And from it a disputed question, argued on both sides, for and against papal power. By Giles of Rome, Archbishop of Bourges.

units.la: LITTERA, Siue BVLLA MISSA PER BONIFACIVM S. REGI PHILIPPO PVLCHRO.
units.tr: The letter, or bull, sent by Boniface the Eighth to King Philip the Fair.

units.la: BOnifacius Episcopus, seruus seruorum Dei, Philippo Francorum Regi. Deum time & mandata eius obserua. Scire te volumus quod in spiritualibus nobis subes. Beneficiorum & Præbendarum ad te collatio nulla spectat. Et si aliquorum vacantium custodiam habeas, vsumfructum eorum successoribus reddetis. Et si quæ contulisti, collationem huiusmodi irritam decernimus. Et quantum de facto processerit, revocamus. Aliud autem credentes, haereticos reputamus. Datum Lateran. Non. Decembris Pontificatus nostri, Anno septimo.
units.tr: Boniface, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Philip, King of the Franks. Fear God and keep his commandments. We want you to know that in spiritual matters you are subject to us. The conferring of benefices and prebends does not belong to you. And if you have the custody of any vacant ones, you are to hand over their revenues to the successors. And if you have conferred any, we decree such conferral void. And as far as it has proceeded in fact, we revoke it. Whoever believes otherwise we count as heretics. Given at the Lateran, on the fifth of December, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

units.la: RESPONSIO
units.tr: RESPONSIO

units.la: Regis PHILIPPI PVLCHRI ad Bonifacium, sive Bullam praecedentem.
units.tr: The reply of King Philip the Fair to Boniface, or to the preceding bull.

units.la: PHilippus Dei gratia Francorum Rex, Bonifacio gerenti se pro summo Pontifice, salutem modicam sive nullam. Sciat tua maxima Fatuitas in temporalibus nos alicui non subesse. Aliquarum Ecclesiarum & Praebendarum vacantium collationem ad nos Iure Regio pertinere, & fructus earum nostros facere. Collationes a nobis factas & faciendas, fore validas in praeteritum & futurum. Et earum possessores, contra omnes viriliter nos tueri. Secus autem credentes fatuos reputamus & dementes. Datum &c. Anno 1303.
units.tr: Philip, by the grace of God King of the French, to Boniface, who styles himself supreme Pontiff: little or no greeting. Let your most great Foolishness know that in temporal matters we are subject to no one. The conferral of certain vacant churches and prebends belongs to us by royal right, and we make their revenues our own. Collations made by us, and to be made, shall be valid for the past and the future; and we will vigorously defend their possessors against all men. Those who believe otherwise we consider foolish and demented. Given &c. In the year 1303.

units.la: QVAESTIO
units.tr: QUESTION

units.la: Bene Disputata ad Argumenta, super Debato praecedentium Literarum.
units.tr: A Well-Argued Disputation on the Arguments Concerning the Debate over the Preceding Letters.

units.la: QVaestio est, utrum dignitas Pontificalis & Imperialis, sive Regalis, sint duae Potestates distinctae ad invicem. Et hoc est quaerere, Utrum summus Pontifex plenam Iurisdictionem & ordinariam Potestatem habeat tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus, ita quod omnes Principes temporales subsint ei quantum ad temporalia? Quod sint Potestates distinctae, & quod Papa non habeat Dominium omnium temporalium, probatur; Primo per rationes Physicas. Secundo, per rationes Theologicas. Tertio, per Iura Canonica. Quarto per Iura Ciuilia.
units.tr: The question is whether the Pontifical and the Imperial or Royal dignity are two powers distinct from each other. That is, to ask whether the supreme Pontiff has full jurisdiction and ordinary power both in temporal and in spiritual matters, so that all temporal princes are subject to him as regards temporal matters. That they are distinct powers, and that the Pope does not have dominion over all temporal things, is proved: first, by physical arguments; second, by theological arguments; third, by the canon law; fourth, by the civil law.

units.la: Primo sic arguitur. Philosophus 2. de Anima, dicit quod Potentiae distinguuntur per Actus. Vbi igitur sunt actiones disparatae, ibi sunt necessario potestates disparatae. Sed Regimen temporalium & Spiritualium sunt actiones omnino disparatae; Quae autem sunt disparata, unum non subest alteri. Ergo potestas temporalis non subest spirituali. Item secundum eundem Philosophum Potestates distinguuntur penes obiecta. Quia enim sonus, quod est obiectum auditus, differt a colore, quod est obiectum visus; Ideo audientia & visiua sunt duae potestates distinctae. Sic temporalia & spiritualia sunt omnino distincta, nec sub eodem genere continentur, nec communicant in materia. Ergo temporalis & spiritualis potestates sunt distinctae nec dependentes ab invicem. Item secundum eundem, Actiones & Potentiae distinguuntur penes finem. Quia enim ad alium finem ordinantur Intellectus & Sensus; ideo sunt potentiae in Anima disparatae. Sed ad alium finem ordinatur potestas spiritualis & ad alium temporalis, sicut patet de se, & declarabitur infra in corpore Quaestionis. Ergo &c.
units.tr: The first argument runs thus. The Philosopher, in the second book of On the Soul, says that powers are distinguished by their acts. Where there are acts that are wholly disparate, there must necessarily be disparate powers. But the governing of temporal and of spiritual things are wholly disparate acts; and things that are disparate are not subject one to another. Therefore temporal power is not subject to spiritual power. Likewise, according to the same Philosopher, powers are distinguished by their objects. For since sound, which is the object of hearing, differs from colour, which is the object of sight, hearing and sight are two distinct powers. So temporal and spiritual things are wholly distinct, are not contained under the same genus, and do not share a matter. Therefore the temporal and spiritual powers are distinct and not dependent on one another. Likewise, according to the same, actions and powers are distinguished by their end. For since the intellect and the senses are ordered to different ends, they are disparate powers in the soul. But the spiritual power is ordered to one end and the temporal to another, as is evident of itself and will be declared below in the body of the question. Therefore etc.

units.la: Item probatur hoc idem per rationes Theologicas sic; In principio creavit Deus Caelum & Terram, Genesis 1. Idest, Spiritualem & corporalem creaturam, secundum Beatum Augustinum. Haec est prima & maxima differentia quae possit esse inter creaturas, nec communicant in materia, & diversa requiruntur regimina, quia aliam & aliam ordinationem habent. Ergo Potestates regendi necessario sunt distinctae. Item primo die creationis Mundi, creavit Deus Lucem; & divisit lucem a tenebris. Scilicet, sicut exponunt Augustinus & alii Sancti, per lucem significantur Spiritualia; & per tenebras temporalia. Ergo sic distinguuntur & differunt Spiritualia a temporalibus, sicut differt lumen a tenebris. Ergo & Potestates utriusque Regiminis omnino distinctae sunt. Nam ait Apostolus, quod participatio lucis a tenebris, est quasi nulla. Ite quarta die fecit duo Luminaria magna ad decorem & regimen universi, videlicet Solem & Lunam, quorum utraque officia sunt distincta & diversa; quia Solem ordinavit ut praesset diei, & Lunam ut praesset nocti. Sic per ista duo luminaria, significantur istae duae Potestates, ut per Solem intelligatur Papa, qui praeest Spiritualibus, & per Lunam Imperator, qui praeest in temporalibus, sicut habetur Extra de ma. & obe. c. solite, ubi sic dicitur: Ad firmamentum visibile Ecclesiae fecit Deus duo Luminaria magna, quae sunt Pontificalis auctoritas, & Regalis dignitas. Sicut ergo Sol & Luna immediate sunt producta a Deo, nec unum processit ex alio, licet multum differant claritate: sic utraque potestas Pontificalis & Regalis immediate sunt a Deo, licet differant dignitate. Item in Lege veteri, istae duae Potestates fuerunt distinctae, unde & in ea fuit duplex unctio, Pontificalis & Regia, & habebant officia distincta, ita quod unus non debebat, nec impune poterat officium alterius usurpare. Nec Regalis dignitas suberat Pontificali in temporalibus. Ergo multo magis in Lege nova istae duae Potestates sunt distinctae, ita quod una non subest alteri quantum ad temporalia: Item Lex gratiae maiorem spiritualitatem requirit in Pontificali dignitate; quam Lex vetus. Sic, ne ministri veteris Legis impedirentur a cultu Divino, noluit Deus habere eos Dominium terrenorum. Unde tribus Leui non habuit partem & hereditatem inter alios tribus in divisione Terrae promissionis, sicut in Leui & Iosue; Ergo multo minus Pontifices & alii ministri novae legis, non deberent habere hoc quaerere Dominum terrenorum. Item, sicut ait Saluator, non est discipulus super Magistrum; nec servus maior Domino suo; nec vicarius maiorem potestatem habet, quam ille (cuius vices gerit,) sibi duxerit committendam. Sed Christus, quamuis hæreditario iure Dominus esset omnium, tamen hac potestate vti noluit, sed etiam oblatam penitus recusauit, sicut legitur Ioannis 6. Cum hinc quæreret eum populus vt facerent Regem, fugit, tanquam contemnens, & contemnendam docens insatiabilem voracitatem auaritiæ & ambitionis inexplebilem vanitatem. Spiritualiter suo vicario dans exemplum, non ambiendi & multo fortius non vsurpandi sibi Imperatoriam vel Regiam dignitatem. Item Lucæ 12 scribitur, Quod cum Christo Domino diceret quidam, Domine dic fratri meo vt diuidat meam hæreditatem, respondit, Homo quis me constituit Iudicem & diuidere super vos? Ecce Dei filius super Dominium temporalium recusauit iudicium, qui tamen constitutus est à Deo Iudex viuorum & mortuorum. Ergo vicarius eius de iurisdictione temporali non debet se intromittere. Item successor Petri non habet maiorem potestatem in temporalibus, quam habuit Petrus; primus de Christi vicariis. Sed nec Petro nec cæteris aliis permisit Deus habere Dominium terrenorum. Imo potius eximiam humilitatem præcepit eis tenere & inuiolabiliter obseruare, sicut patet in Euangelio. Ergo successor Petri nullam habet in temporalibus iurisdictionem. Item Dominus interrogatus à Iudæis, vtrum liceret censum dare Cæsari, visa imagine numismatis, respondit; Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei Deo. Ergo quæ sunt Cæsaris, & quæ sunt Dei, sunt distincta. Item in commissione, facta vicario Petro, non legitur potestas temporalis, sed tantum spiritualis, ei fuisse commissa: Tibi, inquit, dabo claues regni cælorum. Non dicit, & Dominium terrenorum; Vnde statim subiungit, (quasi semetipsum exponens, de spirituali tantum potestate dixisse) quodcunque ligaueris super terram, erit ligatum & in cœlo, & quodcunque solueris, &c. Et post resurrectionem suis dixit Apostolis; Accipite spiritum Sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, &c.
units.tr: The same is proved also by theological arguments, thus. "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" (Genesis 1). That is, spiritual and corporeal creation, according to the blessed Augustine. This is the first and greatest difference that can exist between creatures; they do not share a matter, and different governances are required, because they have different and separate orders. Therefore the powers of governing are necessarily distinct. Likewise, on the first day of the creation of the world, God created light and divided the light from the darkness. That is, as Augustine and other saints explain, by light are signified spiritual things, and by darkness temporal things. Therefore spiritual things are thus distinguished and differ from temporal things, as light differs from darkness. Therefore the powers of each government are also wholly distinct. For the Apostle says that the fellowship of light with darkness is as nothing. Again, on the fourth day He made two great lights for the beauty and government of the universe, namely the Sun and the Moon, whose offices are distinct and different: for He appointed the Sun to rule the day, and the Moon to rule the night. Thus by these two lights these two powers are signified: the Sun being understood as the Pope, who presides over spiritual things, and the Moon as the Emperor, who presides over temporal things, as is found in the Extra, De maioritate et obedientia, chapter Solite, where it is said thus: "For the visible firmament of the Church God made two great lights, which are the Pontifical authority and the Royal dignity." Just as the Sun and the Moon were produced immediately by God, and neither proceeded from the other, although they differ greatly in brightness, so each power, Pontifical and Royal, is immediately from God, although they differ in dignity. Again, under the old Law these two powers were distinct; whence there was also a twofold anointing, Pontifical and Royal, and they had distinct offices, so that one ought not, and could not with impunity, usurp the office of the other. Nor was the Royal dignity subject to the Pontifical in temporal matters. Therefore much more in the new Law these two powers are distinct, so that one is not subject to the other as regards temporal matters. Again, the law of grace requires greater spirituality in the Pontifical dignity than the old law did. Thus, lest the ministers of the old Law be hindered from divine worship, God would not have them possess lordship over earthly things. Whence the tribe of Levi did not have a part or inheritance among the other tribes in the division of the land of promise, as in Leviticus and Joshua. Therefore much less should the Pontiffs and the other ministers of the new law seek to have lordship over earthly things. Again, as the Saviour says, the disciple is not above the master, nor the servant greater than his lord, nor does the vicar have greater power than he whose place he holds has thought fit to commit to him. But Christ, although by hereditary right He was Lord of all, yet would not use this power, but even refused it when offered, as we read in John 6. When the people sought to make Him king, He fled, as one despising it, and teaching that insatiable greed of avarice and the boundless vanity of ambition are to be despised; giving spiritually an example to His vicar not to seek after, and much more not to usurp to himself, the imperial or royal dignity. Again, it is written in Luke 12 that when a certain man said to Christ the Lord, "Lord, bid my brother divide the inheritance with me," He answered, "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" Behold, the Son of God refused judgment over lordship of temporal things, though He was appointed by God the Judge of the living and the dead. Therefore His vicar ought not to meddle with temporal jurisdiction. Again, the successor of Peter does not have greater power in temporal matters than Peter had, who was the first of Christ's vicars. But God permitted neither to Peter nor to the others to have lordship over earthly things; rather He commanded them to hold to and inviolably observe a singular humility, as is plain in the Gospel. Therefore the successor of Peter has no jurisdiction in temporal matters. Again, when the Lord was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar, He looked at the image on the coin and answered, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Therefore what is Caesar's and what is God's are distinct. Again, in the commission given to the vicar Peter, there is no mention of any temporal power, but only spiritual power was committed to him: "To you," He says, "I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven." He does not say "and lordship of earthly things"; hence He immediately adds (as if explaining Himself, that He spoke only of spiritual power): "Whatsoever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatsoever you loose," etc. And after the resurrection He said to His Apostles, "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them," etc.

units.la: Item per iura Canonica probatur hoc idem multipliciter. Primo sic, extr. distinct. quoniam idem, &c. vbi ista quodammodo disputantur in glossa. Dicitur sic in textu: Idem mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis, officia potestatis vtriusque propria discreuit. Glossa dicit ibi, quod Christus officia potestatis vtriusque exercuit, vt ostenderet quod vtraq; potestas ab eodem processit, non quod vna persona illa duo officia exerceat, vel gerere debeat. Hæc enim duo dona, imperium & sacerdotium, ab eodem principio sunt; vt in aut b. quomodo oporteat Episcopos, &c. in princ. collat. 3. Item ibidem super verbo, discreuit: Cum ergo ista potestates sunt distinctæ, est hoc argumentum quod imperium non habetur à Papa, & quod Papa non habeat vtrumque gladium, & quod imperium à Deo solo habetur. vt 24. q. 3. c. quæsitum. Alioquin si ab ipso haberetur, licite appellaretur in temporalibus ad ipsum; Quod prohibet Alexander. Et dicit, quod illa non contingunt suam iurisdictionem, vt apparet, extra de appell. cap. si duobus, & extr. qui fil. sunt legit. cap. causam & c. later. Item, quicunque soluit tributum alicui, non videtur præesse in temporalibus, sed magis subesse: Sed soluit Papa tributum Imperatori, vt 11. q. 1. cap. magnum & 23. q. 8. cap. tributum, vbi sic dicitur. Tributum in ore piscis, piscante Petro, inuentum est. Quia de exterioribus suis, quæ palam cunctis apparent, tributum Ecclesia reddit. Et infra de exterioribus Ecclesiæ. Quidem consuetum est antiquitus, pro pace & quiete, quam nos tueri, & defensare debent, Imperatoribus persoluendum est. Item supra dist. quo iure, ait Augustinus; Diuinum ius in diuinis scripturis habemus, humanum ius in scriptis legibus. Vnde, quisquis possidet, quod possidet: nonne iure humano? Nam iure diuino, Domini est terra & plenitudo eius; &c. Pauperes & diuites Deus de vno limo fecit, & vna terra supportat. Iure igitur humano dicitur, hæc villa mea est; Iura autem humana, iura Imperatoris sunt. Quare ipsa iura humana per Imperatores & Reges sæculi, Deus distribuit humano generi.
units.tr: The same is proved in many ways also by the canon law. First, thus: Extra, Distinctio "Quoniam idem," etc., where these matters are somewhat disputed in the gloss. It is said thus in the text: "The same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, by His own acts and distinct dignities separated the offices of each power." The gloss there says that Christ exercised the offices of each power in order to show that both powers proceed from the same source, not that one person ought to exercise or hold those two offices. For these two gifts, the empire and the priesthood, are from the same beginning; as in Authenticum, Quomodo oporteat episcopos, at the beginning, collation 3. Again, on the same passage, at the word discreuit: "Since therefore these powers are distinct, this is an argument that the empire is not held from the Pope, that the Pope does not have both swords, and that the empire is held from God alone," as in 24 q. 3, c. Quaesitum. Otherwise, if it were held from him, it would lawfully be appealed to him in temporal matters; which Alexander forbids. And he says that these matters do not touch his jurisdiction, as appears in Extra, De appellationibus, chapter Si duobus, and Extra, Qui filii sint legitimi, chapter Causam, etc., Lateranense. Again, whoever pays tribute to another does not seem to preside in temporal matters, but rather to be subject. But the Pope pays tribute to the Emperor, as in 11 q. 1, c. Magnum, and 23 q. 8, c. Tributum, where it is said thus: "The tribute was found in the mouth of the fish, when Peter was fishing." Because the Church pays tribute for its external goods, which are plainly apparent to all. And below, concerning the external things of the Church: "Indeed it has been customary from antiquity, for peace and quiet, which they ought to protect and defend, that payment be made to the Emperors." Again, above, Distinctio "Quo iure," Augustine says: "We have divine law in the divine Scriptures, human law in written laws. Whence, whoever possesses what he possesses, does he not do so by human law? For by divine law the earth and its fullness is the Lord's," etc. "God made the poor and the rich from one clay, and one earth supports them. By human law, then, it is said, this estate is mine; but human laws are the laws of the Emperor. Therefore God distributes these very human laws to the human race through emperors and kings of the world."

units.la: Tolle iura Imperatoris; Et quare audet dicere, hæc villa mea est, meus est iste seruus, mea est hæc domus? Et ideo Apostolus voluit seruire omnibus Regibus, voluit honorare Reges & dixit; Regem reueremini. Noli igitur dicere, quid mihi & Regi? Quid tibi ergo & possessioni? Per iura Regum possidentur possessiones. Si autem dicis, quid mihi & Regi? Noli ergo possessiones tuas, dicere tuas; quia ipsa iura renunciasti humana, quibus possessiones possidetur. Istud Decretum S. Bn. attendatur. Magnum terrorem debent memorare, volentibus resistere Regi Franciæ. Item qui confirmat electionem alterius, ei subesse non debet de iure. Sed Regi Franciæ Carolo data sunt potestas à Papa in Synodo, confirmandi Papam & ordinandi sedem Apostolicam. Igitur Rex Franciæ, ei subesse non debet de iure. Probatur 63. dist. c. Adrianus, &c. Vbi sic dicitur de Carolo post debellationem aduersariorum Romanæ Ecclesiæ: Demum Romam reuersus constituit ibi synodum cum Adriano Papa in Patriarchio Lateranensi, in Ecclesia sancti Saluatoris; Quæ Synodus celebrata est, cum centum quinquaginta tribus Episcopis, Religiosis & Abbatibus. Adrianus autem Papa cum vniuersa synodo, tradidit Carolo ius & potestatem eligendi Pontificem, ordinandi sedem Apostolicam: Et dignitatem patriciatus ei concesserunt. Insuper Archiepiscopos & Episcopos per singulas prouincias, inuestituram accipere diffinierunt. Et vt (nisi à Rege laudetur & inuestietur Episcopus) à nemine consecretur: Et quicunque contra hoc Decretum egerit anathematis vinculo cum innodauit, & nisi resipisceret, bona eius publicare præcepit. Hoc idem ostenditur de Carolo & Othone filio eius Imperatore Theutonicorum, 12. dist. s. in synodo: In synodo congregata Romae in Ecclesia sancti Saluatoris, ad exemplum B. Adriani, Apostolicæ sedis & inuestituram Episcoporum concesserunt. Ego quoque Leo, seruus seruorum Dei Episcopus, cum cuncto clero & Romano populo, constituimus, confirmamus, & corroboramus. Et per nostram auctoritatem Apostolicam, concedimus atque largimur Domino Othoni I. Regi Theutonicorum, eiusque successoribus, huius regni Italiæ sibi facultatem eligendi successorem, atque summa sedis Apostolicæ Pontificem ordinandi, ac per hoc Archiepiscopos siue Episcopos, vt ipsi inuestituram accipiant & consecrationem. Et infra: Quod si à clero & populo quis eligatur Episcopus, nisi à supradicto Rege laudetur & inuestiatur, non consecretur. Si quis contra hanc auctoritatem Apostolicam moliatur, huic excommunicationi subiacere decreuimus. Et si non resipuerit, irreuocabili exilio puniri, vel vltimis supplicijs feriri. Ext. de elect. c. venerabilem; super verbo Caroli glossa dicit; Cuius ius Patriciatus siue dignitas collata est, ergo est patronus Romanæ Ecclesiæ, non ergo vi subiicitur. Si dicas quod Ludouicus Imperator, & primus Henricus, & primus Otho, renunciauerunt huic Priuilegio confirmandi Papam, & sedem Apostolicam ordinandi, sicut habetur 63. distinct. per totum. Dicimus e contra, quod non propter hoc subiecerant se Papæ, vel sedi Apostolicæ, quantum ad temporalia. Imo sicut prius, erant non subiecti. Item extra de mai. & obed. cap. solita, dicit Papa; Non negamus quin prædecessor Imperator in temporalibus illos dumtaxat, qui ab eo receperunt temporalia. Sed Papa & Romana Ecclesia, quidquid habent in temporalibus, pro maiori parte perceperunt ab Imperatoribus. Similiter aliæ Ecclesiæ temporalia bona quæ possident, recepe runt à Regibus & Principibus. Ergo, &c. Item extra de foro competent. cap. licet; dicitur: Mandamus si quando laicus Vercellensibus literas super rebus præcipue quæ forum sæculare contingunt, à sede Apostolica contigerit impetrari, sublato appellationis obstaculo, decernas auctoritate nostra, irritas & inanes. Dummodo consules & communitas de se conquerentibus in iudicio sæculari, exhibeant iustitiæ complementum. Ergo nec quo ad Regem Franciæ.
units.tr: Take away the rights of the Emperor, and by what right does a man dare to say, "This estate is mine, this servant is mine, this house is mine"? That is why the Apostle wished to serve all kings, wished to honour kings, and said: "Honour the king" [1 Pet. 2:17]. Do not therefore say, "What have I to do with the king?" Then what have you to do with property? Possessions are held under the laws of kings. But if you say, "What have I to do with the king?", then do not call your possessions yours, since you have renounced the human laws by which possessions are held. Let that decree of St. Bn. be considered. They ought to remember the great terror [inflicted] on those who wished to resist the King of France. Likewise, one who confirms another's election ought not by right to be subject to that person. But power was given by the Pope in a synod to King Charles of France, to confirm the Pope and to ordain the Apostolic See. Therefore the King of France ought not by right to be subject to him. This is proved in dist. 63, c. Adrianus, etc., where it is said thus of Charles, after the defeat of the adversaries of the Roman Church: "At last, returning to Rome, he held a synod there with Pope Adrian in the Lateran patriarchate, in the church of the Holy Saviour. This synod was celebrated with one hundred and fifty-three bishops, religious and abbots. Pope Adrian, with the whole synod, handed over to Charles the right and power of electing the Pontiff and of ordaining the Apostolic See, and they granted him the dignity of patrician. Moreover, they decided that archbishops and bishops throughout each province should receive investiture, and that no one should consecrate a bishop unless he was praised and invested by the King. Whoever acted against this decree they bound with the chain of anathema, and, unless he repented, they commanded that his goods be confiscated." The same is shown of Charles and his son Otto, Emperor of the Teutons, dist. 12, s. In synodo: "In a synod gathered at Rome in the church of the Holy Saviour, after the example of blessed Adrian, they granted to the Apostolic See the investiture of bishops. I too, Leo, servant of the servants of God and bishop, with the whole clergy and the Roman people, establish, confirm and corroborate this. And by our apostolic authority we grant and bestow on the lord Otto I, King of the Teutons, and his successors, the faculty in this kingdom of Italy of electing a successor and of ordaining the highest Pontiff of the Apostolic See, and thereby archbishops or bishops, that they may receive investiture and consecration." And below: "If any bishop is elected by clergy and people, unless he is praised and invested by the aforesaid King, let him not be consecrated. If anyone attempts to act against this apostolic authority, we decree that he shall be subject to this excommunication; and if he does not repent, let him be punished with irrevocable exile or struck down with the final penalties." Ext. de elect. c. venerabilem. On the word "Charles" the gloss says: Whose right of patriciate or dignity was conferred, therefore he is patron of the Roman Church, therefore he is not subject to its power. If you say that Emperor Louis, and the first Henry, and the first Otto renounced this privilege of confirming the Pope and ordaining the Apostolic See, as is held throughout dist. 63, we reply on the contrary that they were not for that reason made subject to the Pope or the Apostolic See as regards temporal matters. Rather, they were not subject, as before. Likewise, extra de maiorit. et obed. c. solita, the Pope says: We do not deny that a predecessor emperor [has power] in temporal matters only over those who have received temporal things from him. But the Pope and the Roman Church, whatever they have in temporal matters, have for the most part received from the emperors. Similarly, other churches hold the temporal goods they possess from kings and princes. Therefore, etc. Likewise, extra de foro competenti c. licet, it is said: "We command that if a layman should ever obtain letters from the Apostolic See concerning the Vercellese, especially those matters which pertain to the secular court, then, the obstacle of appeal being removed, you shall decree by our authority that they are void and empty, provided that the consuls and commune render the fulfilment of justice to those who complain of them in the secular court." Therefore, neither is this so as regards the King of France.

units.la: Item hoc idem probatur per iura ciuilia. In Authentica, Quomodo oporteat Episcopos, &c. in principio collatione prima dicitur: Maxima quidem in omnibus sunt dona Dei, & à superna collata clementia, sacerdotium & imperium; Illud quidem diuinum ministrans, hoc autem humanum præsidens & diuitias gentium exhibens, ex uno eodemque principio utraque procedentia, humanam exornant vitam. Et ita, si sacerdotium inculpabile sit undique & apud Deum fiducia plenum, imperium autem recte & competenter exornet traditam sibi Rempublicam; erit consonantia quædam bona, omne quidquid utile est humano conferens generi. Glossa super verbo Maxima: Vere maxima, quia his ditibus totus regitur mundus. Unde illud: Ecce gladii duo hic. Item Glossa super verbo, conferens: Apparet ergo quod nec Papa in temporalibus, nec Imperator in spiritualibus, se debent immiscere. Si dicas quod rationes & auctoritates præmissæ videntur facere magis pro Imperatore quam pro Rege Franciæ. Et si quæras quare sint hic indutæ? Respondeo, ad probandum iurisdictiones esse distinctas, quarum una est penes Papam & Iudices Ecclesiasticos, & alia penes Imperatorem & Reges. Omnia enim quæ pro Imperatore faciunt, valent nihilominus pro Rege Franciæ, qui Imperator est in regno suo. Specialiter ostendo, quod Rex Franciæ non subest Papæ in temporalibus, extra de iudic. cap. nouit. Vbi dicit sic Innocentius Papa: Non putet aliquis, quod iurisdictionem Illustris Francorum Regis perturbare et minuere intendamus, cum ipse iurisdictionem nostram, nec velit, nec debeat impedire. Gloss. per hoc dicit; Patet quod Ecclesia vel Papa non habet utrumque gladium. Et infra: Non intendimus iudicare de Feudo, cuius ad ipsum spectat Iudicium. Gloss. Iudicium Feudi spectat ad Regem directe, ad Papam ratione Petri. Exprima Authentica concludit quod Rex Franciæ, non est subiectus Papæ in temporalibus. Ex secunda probatur quod subest Papæ primo & principaliter quoad spiritualia, quo ad temporalia vero, non nisi incidenter. Item, non debet de iure dici superior, nisi ille ad quem licet appellare, sed à Iudice sæculari non licet appellare ad Papam in temporalibus. Ergo Iudex sæcularis, non subest Papæ, nec Papa est eius superior in temporalibus, igitur multo minus Regis. Probatur extra de appellat. cap. si duobus: Denique quod quæritur si à ciuili Iudice, non ante iudicium vel post, ad nostram audientiam fuerit appellatum, an huiusmodi teneat appellatio. Respondet Papa; Tenet quidem in his quæ sunt nostra temporalitatis iurisdictioni subiecti; in aliis vero etsi de consuetudine Ecclesiæ teneat, secundum iuris rigorem credimus non tenere. Gloss. Et ita patet, quod iurisdictio temporalis non pertinet ad Ecclesiam, nec de ea se debeat intromittere in præiudicium sæcularis iudicis. supra de iudic. cap. nouit. & 1. qui fil. sunt legit. cap. latoris. & 1. de priuilegiis cap. 20.
units.tr: Likewise, this same point is proved by the civil laws. In the Authentica, Quomodo oporteat Episcopos, etc., at the beginning of the first collation, it is said: The greatest of all God's gifts, bestowed by heavenly mercy, are the priesthood and the empire. The one serves the divine, the other presides over the human and provides the wealth of nations; both proceeding from one and the same source, they adorn human life. And so, if the priesthood is blameless on every side and full of confidence before God, and the empire rightly and fittingly governs the commonwealth entrusted to it, there will be a certain good harmony, conferring everything that is useful to the human race. The gloss on the word Maxima: Truly the greatest, because the whole world is ruled by these two powers. Hence that saying: "Behold, here are two swords" [Luke 22:38]. Likewise the gloss on the word conferens: It appears, therefore, that neither the Pope in temporal matters nor the Emperor in spiritual matters ought to meddle. If you say that the reasons and authorities set out above seem to favour the Emperor rather than the King of France, and if you ask why they have been introduced here, I answer: to prove that the jurisdictions are distinct, one of which lies with the Pope and the ecclesiastical judges, and the other with the Emperor and kings. For all that is done for the Emperor holds equally for the King of France, who is Emperor in his own kingdom. I show specifically that the King of France is not subject to the Pope in temporal matters: extra de iudic. cap. nouit. There Pope Innocent says: Let no one think that we intend to disturb or diminish the jurisdiction of the illustrious King of the French, since he neither wishes nor ought to hinder our jurisdiction. The gloss, on this passage, says: It is clear that the Church or the Pope does not have both swords. And below: We do not intend to judge concerning the fief, the judgment of which belongs to him. Gloss: The judgment of a fief belongs directly to the King, to the Pope by reason of Peter. From the first authority, the Authentica, it follows that the King of France is not subject to the Pope in temporal matters. From the second it is proved that he is subject to the Pope first and principally in spiritual matters, but in temporal matters only incidentally. Likewise, a man ought not rightly to be called superior unless it is permitted to appeal to him, but it is not permitted to appeal from a secular judge to the Pope in temporal matters. Therefore a secular judge is not subject to the Pope, nor is the Pope his superior in temporal matters, and so much less is he the superior of the King. This is proved extra de appellat. cap. si duobus: Finally, as to what is asked, whether such an appeal holds, if it has been made from a civil judge to our hearing, not before or after the judgment. The Pope replies: It does indeed hold in those matters which are subject to the jurisdiction of our temporal power; but in other matters, although by the custom of the Church it may hold, we believe that according to the strictness of law it does not hold. Gloss: And so it is clear that temporal jurisdiction does not belong to the Church, nor ought it to interfere with it to the prejudice of the secular judge. Supra de iudic. cap. nouit; and 1. qui fil. sunt legit. cap. latoris; and 1. de privilegiis cap. 20.

units.la: Item videtur quod Rex Franciæ sit par Imperatori quantum ad libertatem suæ iurisdictionis, quia regnum Francorum prius habuit imperium, quam regnum Theutonicorum. 63. distinct. Ergo Ludouicus. Ibi dicitur in fine, quod tum Papa fuerit consecratus, legati mittuntur ad Imperatores & Reges Francorum, qui inter ipsos amicitiam charitatem & pacem socient. Igitur videtur, quod Imperator & Rex Francorum sunt pares. Glossa ibidem notat imperium prius Francorum fuisse, sed postea Theutonici, virtutibus promeruerunt imperium 28. quæst. 1. cap. omnis. Et hoc ideo quia Romani in eos imperium transtulerunt.
units.tr: Likewise it seems that the King of France is equal to the Emperor as regards the freedom of his jurisdiction, because the kingdom of the Franks had the empire before the kingdom of the Teutons did. dist. 63. Therefore [the same holds for] Louis. There it is said at the end that when the Pope was consecrated, legates were sent to the Emperors and Kings of the Franks, who should join them in friendship, charity and peace. Therefore it seems that the Emperor and the King of the Franks are equals. The gloss on the same passage notes that the empire was first of the Franks, but afterwards the Teutons, by their virtues, earned the empire; 28. quæst. 1, cap. omnis. And this was because the Romans transferred the empire to them.

units.la: Item extra qui filii sunt legit. cap. tantum enim: Nos attendentes quod ad Regem pertinet, non ad Ecclesiam, de alibus possessionibus iudicare, ne videamur Regi Anglorum detrahere, qui ipsorum iudicium ad se adseritpertinere, F. V. mandamus quatenus Regi possessionum iudicium relinquentes, de causa principali plenius cognoscatis. Si hoc dicitur de Rege Angliæ, qui Romanæ Ecclesiæ feudalis est, & censualis, multo magis de Rege Franciæ verum erit, qui in nullo prædictorum penitus est subiectus. Et dicit ibi Glossa; Sic patet quod iurisdictio temporalis & spiritualis distincta est & diuisa. Et sic Papa non habet utramque iurisdictionem. Item extra qui fil. sunt legit. cap. per venerabilem, dixit Papa expresse, quod Rex Francorum in temporalibus superiorem minime recognoscit. Si dicas, prout dicit Glossa, verum est de facto, sed non de iure: Quia de iure debet recognoscere Imperatorem, ut patet 4. quæst. 1. cap. in apibus, & extra de elect. cap. venerabilem. Respondeo, illud factum versum esse in consuetudinem, quæ dat iurisdictionem, ut dicit Innocentius extra de iudic. cap. nouit, super verbo, consuetudinem: Nota, inquit, consuetudinem dare iurisdictionem supra de arbitr. delect. Et ibi præmittitur in Glossa: Nota iurisdictionem pacificari iuri & priuilegio 10. quæst. 3. cap. conquestus. Quia ista etiam consuetudo est approbata & hactenus obseruata pacifice; nec à Papa nec ab Imperatore impugnata, imo iuramentis & pactionibus fœderata; & ex longissimis temporibus iam præscripta.
units.tr: Likewise, in Extra, De filiis qui sunt legitimi, the chapter Tantum enim: We, considering that it belongs to the King and not to the Church to judge concerning other possessions, lest we seem to detract from the King of the English, who asserts that their judgment belongs to him, you, F. and V., are commanded to leave the judgment of the possessions to the King and to examine the principal cause more fully. If this is said of the King of England, who is a feudal and censual vassal of the Roman Church, it will be much more true of the King of France, who is in no respect at all subject to any of the aforesaid. And the Gloss there says: Thus it is clear that temporal and spiritual jurisdiction are distinct and divided. And so the Pope does not have both jurisdictions. Likewise, in Extra, De filiis qui sunt legitimi, the chapter Per venerabilem, the Pope expressly said that the King of France does not recognize any superior in temporal matters. If you say, as the Gloss says, that this is true in fact but not in law: because by law he ought to recognize the Emperor, as appears in 4 q. 1, c. In apibus, and Extra, De electione, c. Venerabilem. I answer that this fact has passed into custom, and custom gives jurisdiction, as Innocent says in Extra, De iudiciis, c. Novit, on the word "custom": Note, he says, that custom gives jurisdiction, see above, De arbitris, De electione. And there the Gloss premises: Note that jurisdiction is established by law and privilege, 10 q. 3, c. Conquestus. For this custom too has been approved and hitherto observed peaceably, challenged neither by the Pope nor by the Emperor, but even confirmed by oaths and agreements, and already prescribed from very long times.

units.la: Ad intelligentiam pleniorem, & clariorem euidentiam propositæ quæstionis, considerandæ sunt quinque, per ordinem & per articulos distinguenda. Primo videndum est, quod utraque potestas spiritualis & temporalis, à Deo est instituente & ordinante.
units.tr: For a fuller understanding and a clearer demonstration of the question proposed, five things are to be considered, to be distinguished in order and by articles.

units.la: Secundo, quod istae duae potestates distinctae sunt & divisae.
units.tr: Second, that these two powers are distinct and divided.

units.la: Tertio, quod Deus spiritualem potestatem instituens, nullum contulit ei Dominium terrenorum.
units.tr: Third, that God, in instituting the spiritual power, gave it no dominion over earthly things.

units.la: Quarto declarabitur, in quibus terrena potestas sit subiecta spiritúali potestati, & in quibus non.
units.tr: Fourth, it will be declared in what respects earthly power is subject to spiritual power, and in what respects it is not.

units.la: Quinto specialiter ostendetur, libertas & exemptio Regis Franciae; quare & qualiter nullum superiorem in temporalibus recognoscit.
units.tr: Fifth, the liberty and exemption of the King of France will be specially shown: why and how he recognizes no superior in temporal matters.

units.la: ARTICVLVS I.
units.tr: ARTICLE I.

units.la: QVOD autem istae duae potestates sint à Deo, de potestate spirituali, quam CHRISTVS Beato Petro successori eius contulit, habetur Matth. 16. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, &c. De temporali potestate dicitur in Auth. 5. collat. sexta. De instrumentorum cautela. §. quia igitur imperium de caelo Deus instituit. Item Proverb. 6. Per me Reges regnant, & legum conditores iusta decernunt. Et distinct. quarta, transfert regna Deus & constituit. Et Apostolus ad Rom. 13. Non est potestas nisi à Deo. De utraque simul, dicitur distinct. 96. cap. in scripturis, & cap. duo. Vbi dicitur: Duo sunt imperia augusta, de quibus principaliter hic mundus regitur, Auctoritas sacra Pontificum, & Regalis potestas. Et in Authent. Quomodo oporteat Episcopos, &c. in principio collatione prima. maxima quidem in omnibus, &c. Require supra 21. argumento. Glossa super verbo imperium: Imo à populo Romano videtur imperium esse, ut Instit. de iure naturali, §. sed & quod Principi. Illud Dei dispositione factum fuit, sine quo factum est nihil. Nec obstat quod primo Exodi legitur, quod contra voluntatem Domini videtur populus petiisse sibi Regem, quia nolebat Dominus populum, quem singulariter praecunctis elegerat, quodam spirituali modo, regere per duces & iudices, viros scilicet mediocres; nec volebat quod alius ex regali, magisterium, per superbiae fastum, super populum efferret. Tamen quando populus, non assentiens dispositioni divinae, omnino voluit Regem habere, Deus (eius precibus condescendens) indicavit ei, quis regnaturus esset, & populus illum elegit quem Deus indicavit. Haec de primo articulo sufficiant.
units.tr: That both these powers are from God: as for the spiritual power, which Christ conferred on the blessed Peter and his successors, it is found in Matt. 16: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church," etc. Concerning temporal power it is said in Auth. 5, Collatio 6, De instrumentorum cautela, §. Quia igitur imperium: God instituted empire from heaven. Likewise Prov. 6: "By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things." And Dist. 4: God transfers kingdoms and establishes them. And the Apostle, Rom. 13: "There is no power but of God." Concerning both together, it is said in Dist. 96, c. In scripturis and c. Duo, where it is said: "There are two august powers by which this world is chiefly governed: the sacred authority of the Pontiffs and the royal power." And in Authentica, Quomodo oporteat episcopos, at the beginning of Collatio 1: "the greatest in all things," etc. See above, argument 21. The Gloss on the word imperium: indeed, empire seems to come from the Roman people, as in Inst. De iure naturali, §. Sed et quod principi; but it was brought about by the disposition of God, without whom nothing was made. Nor does it stand in the way that in the first book of Exodus it is read that the people, apparently against the will of the Lord, asked for a king for themselves; for the Lord did not wish the people, whom he had chosen singularly above all others, to be governed in a certain spiritual manner through leaders and judges, men of middling rank, nor did he wish someone from the royal line to raise himself above the people in the pride of power. Nevertheless, when the people, not assenting to the divine disposition, wholly wished to have a king, God, yielding to their prayers, indicated to them who was to reign, and the people chose the one whom God had indicated. Let these things suffice concerning the first article.

units.la: ARTICVLVS II.
units.tr: ARTICLE II.

units.la: SECVNDO declarandum est, quod istae duae potestates sunt distinctae & ab invicem separatae. Cum enim homo constet ex duobus, scilicet corpore & anima, & duplex sit vita, corporalis, & spiritualis. Propter corporalem vitam obseruandam homo temporalibus indiget; propter spiritualem, spiritualibus opus habet. Imperatores & Reges potestatem habent super corpora & res corporales, ad vitam corpoream pertinentes. Possunt enim, & debent, corporali poena punire reos, & legum imperialium transgressores. Habent etiam Rempub. ordinare, populos sibi subiectos, in pace & tranquillitate servare; defensare patriam & aduersarios debellare. Pontifices autem spiritualem iurisdictionem habent, quae ad regimen & salutem animarum pertinet.
units.tr: Second, it must be declared that these two powers are distinct and separated from one another. For since man consists of two parts, namely body and soul, and life is twofold, bodily and spiritual, man needs temporal things for preserving bodily life, and needs spiritual things for the spiritual life. Emperors and kings have power over bodies and bodily goods, which pertain to bodily life. For they can, and ought to, punish offenders with bodily penalty, and transgressors of imperial laws. They also have to order the commonwealth, to keep the peoples subject to them in peace and tranquillity, to defend the fatherland and to crush its adversaries. But the Pontiffs have spiritual jurisdiction, which pertains to the governance and salvation of souls.

units.la: Rursus, cum duplex sit civilitas, humana videlicet & divina, terrena & caelestis, temporalis & spiritualis, civilem mundanam & temporalem ordinat & disponit imperialis potestas: Spiritualem vero caelestem & divinam in terris regit Pontificalis auctoritas. Ad cuius regimen summus Pontifex habet plenitudinem potestatis. Inferiores autem Praelati, in partem sollicitudinis sunt vocati. Ad utriusque civilitatis regimen Deus duos gladios ordinavit; duas iurisdictiones distinctas & differentes ad invicem, sicut exponunt illud Lucae 22. Ecce gladii duo hic. Et respondit Dominus, satis est. Materiali gladio utuntur Principes, sicut ait Apostolus Roman. 13. Princeps non sine causa gladium portat, Dei enim est minister, & vindex in iram eius qui malum faciunt. De spirituali gladio dicit idem Apostolus Ephes. 5. Galeam assumite & gladium spiritus, quod est verbum Dei. Gladio spirituali utebantur Apostoli, materiali vero nunquam usi esse leguntur; nisi dicatur, quod imminente Christi passione, Petrus cum haberet gladium, exemit, & unius auriculam amputauit.
units.tr: Again, since civility is twofold, namely human and divine, earthly and heavenly, temporal and spiritual, imperial power orders and disposes the worldly and temporal civil life; but the Pontifical authority rules the spiritual, heavenly and divine life on earth. For the governance of this the supreme Pontiff has the fullness of power, while the inferior prelates are called to share in the care. For the governance of each civil life God ordained two swords, two jurisdictions distinct and different from each other, as they explain that passage of Luke 22: "Behold, here are two swords. And the Lord answered: it is enough." The material sword is used by princes, as the Apostle says, Rom. 13: "The prince does not bear the sword in vain; for he is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath upon him who does evil." Of the spiritual sword the same Apostle says, Eph. 6: "Take up the helmet and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God." The apostles used the spiritual sword, but are never read to have used the material sword; unless it be said that, when Christ's passion was at hand, Peter, having a sword, drew it and cut off the ear of one man.

units.la: Distinctae sunt igitur hae potestates, nec debent se mutuo perturbare. Quia sicut Princeps non debet de spiritualibus se intromittere; ita nec Pontifex debet in temporalibus se immiscere, nec iurisdictionem temporalem assumere, nisi in certis casibus determinatis à iure, sicut dicetur. Quod autem nec Princeps Pontificis, nec Pontifex Principis officium debeat usurpare, dicitur expresse distinct. 96. cap. cum ad verum: Vbi dicitur; Cum ad verum ventum fuerit, ultra sibi nec Imperator iura Pontificatus arripuit, nec Pontifex nomen Imperatorium sibi usurpavit; quasi diceret, quidquid disputando vel litigando dicatur, tamen cum ad veritatem diffiniendam ventum fuerit, debent duae potestates remanere distinctae, sicut sunt divinitus institutae. Sequitur in Decreto, primò allegato; Quoniam idem mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis, officia potestatis utriusque discreuit, volens homines medicinali humilitate efferri, non humana superbia ruersum ad inferna demergi, ut & Imperatores pro aeterna vita, Pontificibus indigerent, & Pontifices tantummodo pro cursu temporalium rerum, Imperatorum legibus vterentur, quatenus & spiritualis actio carnalibus insistaret uncursibus. Et Deo militans, non se negotiis saecularibus implicaret; ac vicissim non illerebus diuinis praesidere videretur, qui esset negotiis saecularibus implicatus. Glossa super verbo discreuit, dixit, quod utrumque officium
units.tr: These powers are therefore distinct, and they ought not to disturb one another. For just as the prince should not meddle with spiritual matters, so the pope should not interfere in temporal matters or assume temporal jurisdiction, except in certain cases determined by law, as will be said. That neither the prince should usurp the office of the pope nor the pope the office of the prince is stated expressly in Distinctio 96, the chapter Cum ad verum, where it is said: "When it has come to the truth, neither has the emperor seized for himself the rights of the pontificate, nor has the pope usurped the imperial name," as if to say that whatever is said in disputing or litigating, nevertheless, when it has come to defining the truth, the two powers ought to remain distinct, as they were instituted by God. The decree continues, in the passage cited first: "Since the same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, by his own actions and distinct dignities, separated the offices of each power, wishing men to be raised up by a humility that heals, and not cast down to hell by human pride; so that emperors also would need the pontiffs for eternal life, and the pontiffs would use the laws of the emperors only for the course of temporal affairs; so that spiritual action might not be bound to carnal courses, and one who is serving God should not entangle himself in secular business; and conversely, one who is entangled in secular business should not seem to preside over divine things." The gloss on the word "separated" says that each office...

units.la: ciuum cium gessit per se, vt notaretur quod ex eodem fonte processerunt. Sed melius dici potest, quod CHRISTVS, quam diu fuit viator, temporalem iurisdictionem nunquam exercuit. Nam quod ementes & vendentes eiecit de templo, magis fuit officium Pontificis, cuius est templum mundare, omnes spurcitias eiicere, mercationes & negotiationes terrenas, ab eo prorsus expellere. Et hoc satis patet ex verbis eius, cum dixit; Auferte ista hinc, & nolite facere domum Patris mei; domum negotiationis. Scriptum est enim, Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur, vos autem fecistis illam speluncam latronum. Item Glossa super verbo, sursum efferri; Si haberent aliqui omnia officia, superbirent ita, quod iterum demergentur in inferno. Ex his euidenter apparet & distinctio dignitatum, & ratio distinctionis earum.
units.tr: ...took upon himself the care of the citizens, so that it might be noted that both came from the same source. But it can be said better that Christ, as long as he was a pilgrim, never exercised temporal jurisdiction. For that he cast out the buyers and sellers from the temple was rather the office of the Pontiff, whose task it is to cleanse the temple, to cast out all filth, and to drive out entirely earthly trading and business. This is sufficiently plain from his words, when he said: Take these things hence, and make not my Father's house an house of merchandise. For it is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves. Likewise the Gloss on the words to be lifted up says: If some men had all the offices, they would become so proud that they would again be cast down into hell. From these things it clearly appears both the distinction of dignities and the reason for that distinction.

units.la: ARTICVLVS III.
units.tr: ARTICLE III.

units.la: TErtio declarandum est, quod Christus in institutione spiritualis potestatis, nullam commisit, vel potius promisit Dominium terrenorum. Nam Matth. 16. Vbi Christus vicarium suum instituit, videlicet Beatum Petrum & successores eius ait; Tu es Petrus & super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Et portae inferi non praevalebunt aduersus eam. Et, tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, non dixit, & Dominium terrenorum. Revolve cuncta sacrae scripturae volumina nunquam inuenies Apostolos sedisse vt de temporalibus iudicarent, nec petiisse vt Reges & Principes eis in temporalibus subiacerent, aut de huiusmodi respondere deberent. Item, sicut supra dicebatur, Non est discipulus super magistrum, nec seruus maior Domino suo: Nec vicarius maiorem potestatem habet, quam ille cuius vices gerit. Cum igitur Christus Dominus hac potestate vti noluerit, sed oblatam refugerit, exemplo suo euidenter ostendit, & euidentia facti docuit vicarium suum, talem potestatem refugere, non ambire, nec sibi Imperatoriam Maiestatem, aut dignitatem Regiam vendicare. Ecce Christus Iesus Rex Regum, Dominus dominantium, regale fugit Dominium, & fastuosum fastigium recusauit. Igitur qua ratione vel auctoritate, vicarius eius vendicabit sibi culmen vel nomen Regiae dignitatis?
units.tr: Thirdly, it must be shown that in instituting the spiritual power Christ committed, or rather did not even promise, dominion over earthly things. In Matth. 16. where Christ appointed his vicar, namely Blessed Peter and his successors, he said: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven. He did not say "and dominion over earthly things." Turn over all the volumes of Holy Scripture and you will never find that the Apostles sat in judgment on temporal matters, or asked that kings and princes should be subject to them in temporal affairs, or that they ought to answer about such things. Likewise, as was said above, The disciple is not above the master, nor the servant greater than his lord. Nor does the vicar have greater power than the one whose place he takes. Since Christ the Lord was unwilling to use this power, but refused it when it was offered, he showed by his example, and taught by the plain evidence of his deed, that his vicar should likewise refuse such power, not seek it, and not claim for himself imperial majesty or royal dignity. Behold Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, fled from royal dominion and rejected the proud pomp of rank. By what reason or authority, then, will his vicar claim for himself the height or the name of royal dignity?

units.la: Item, successor Petri non plus habet potestatis, quam Petrus primus Dei vicarius. Sed Christus tam Petro quam caeteris Apostolis, Dominium, potestatem, & iurisdictionem in temporalibus interdixit, cum eis eximiam paupertatem indixit, dicens: Nolite possidere aurum & argentum, &c. Propter quod ipsi Domini sui praecepta inuiolabiliter obseruare volentes, ac magistri documenta sine fictione tenentes, tantum gloriabantur de eximia paupertatis obseruantia, quum solent cupidi, de terrenorum opulentia gloriari. Vnde Petrus iocundanter dicebat, argentum & aurum non est mihi. Omnino elongationem a possessione terrena & Dominio temporali praecepit Christus ipsis, volens eos spirituales esse, & a terrenis, quantum fragilitas humana patitur, elongatos; vacare spiritualibus & aeternis, ac saluti animarum intendere. Quibus omnium Ecclesiarum sollicitudinem committebat. Sciebat enim quod temporalia perturbant, animum distrahunt, intellectum & mentem ad inferiora demergunt, sicut expresse dicitur distinct. 96. cap. cum ad verum, vide supra.
units.tr: Likewise, the successor of Peter has no more power than Peter, the first vicar of God. But Christ forbade both Peter and the other Apostles dominion, power and jurisdiction in temporal things, and enjoined on them extreme poverty, saying: Do not possess gold and silver, etc. For this reason they, wishing to keep their Lord's commands inviolably and holding their Master's teaching without pretence, gloried only in their strict observance of poverty, whereas the greedy are accustomed to boast of the wealth of earthly things. Hence Peter said cheerfully: Silver and gold I do not have. Christ commanded them altogether to keep away from earthly possession and temporal dominion, wishing them to be spiritual and, as far as human frailty allows, removed from earthly things, to be free for spiritual and eternal matters and to attend to the salvation of souls. To them he committed the care of all the Churches. For he knew that temporal things disturb the mind, distract the spirit, and drag the understanding and mind down to lower things, as is expressly said in distinct. 96. cap. cum ad verum, see above.

units.la: Est autem intelligendum, quod cum Christus triplicem habuerit potestatem, videlicet rerum corporalium, animarum, & temporalium facultatum; prima potestate vsus est, secunda vsus est & commisit, tertia nec vti voluit nec commisit. Prima quidem vsus est, infirmitates corporales curando, mortuos suscitando, acin cunctis rebus corporalibus multimoda miracula faciendo. Secunda vsus est, & commisit, videlicet spiritualem quantum est necessarium & expedires ad salutem animarum. Tertia, nec vsus est, sicut patet per exempla praemissa, nec commisit, quin potius eam Petro quam caeteris Apostolis, interdixit, vt dictum est. Attende quid Beatus Bernardus, scribens ad Eugenium Papam, dicat: Et nos, inquit, vt vere sentiamus de nobis, impositum nouimus ministerium, non Dominium datum. Si sapiens es, contentus esto mensura, qua mensura est Deus; quod enim amplius est, a malo est. Discite exemplo Prophetico praesidere, non tam ad imperandum, quam ad faciendum. Discite sarculo opus tibi esse, non regio sceptro, vt opus facias Prophetae, id est, vt euellas & destruas, dispergas & dissipes, & aedifices & plantes; & hac quidem ille. Auditum est hoc supra, ideo non regnatum ascendit, sed extirpaturus. Putasne & tu inuenies ad elaborandum in agro Domini tui? Vtique plurimum. Et infra; Quid tibi dimisi sanctus Apostolus? Quod habeo, inquit, hoc tibi do. Quid illud? Argentum, inquit, & aurum non est mihi, quod autem non habuit, dare non potuit. Esto vt alia quacunque ratione hoc tibi vendidces, sed non Apostolico iure. Quod habuit hoc dedit, sollicitudinem videlicet super omnes Ecclesias. Numquid dominationem? Ipsum audi; Non dominantes (ait) in clero, sed forma facti gregis. Et ne dictum ex sola humilitate putes, non etiam veritate, vos Domini est in Euangelio; Reges gentium dominantur eorum & qui potestatem habent super eos benefici vocantur, vos autem non sic. Planum est quod Apostolis interdicitur Dominatus, igitur & tu tibi vsurpare audes, aut dominans Apostolatum; aut Apostolatus Dominatum? Plane ab alteralitro prohiberis. Si vtramque simul habere voles, perdes vtramque. Alioquin non te exceptum ex illorum numero putes, de quibus conqueritur Dominus, dicens; Ipsi regnauerunt & non ex me, Principes exstiterunt & ego non nouieos. Et sic declaratum est quod summo Pontifici, successori Beati Petri, non est collatum a Deo Dominium terrenorum, neciurisdictio temporalis. Quae igitur est dignitas aut potestas collata summo Pontifici? Quae authoritas Beato Petro vicario Iesu Christi concessa? Profecto, nobilior, sublimior & vtilior quam imperialis. Nam quantum distat Oriens ab Occidente, corpus ab anima, corporalia a spiritualibus, terrena à cœlestibus, tantum distat authoritas summi Pontificis à culmine imperialis aut Regiæ dignitatis. Audi Dominum, vicarium suum instrumentum in Euangelio: Tu es, inquit, Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Et portæ inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam. Et tibi dabo claves regni cœlorum. Ecce, quod, quidquid maius, quidquid sublimius excogitari potuit in hac vita, summo Pontifici diuinitus est collatum. Quid igitur quærit amplius? Nunquid non oculum habere ad hæc inferiora corruptibilia, videtur eius Celsitudini denegare? Patet igitur ex prædictis, quod Pontificalis authoritas, & regalis dignitas, sunt duæ potestates distinctæ, diuinitus institutæ. Et hoc declaratum est in primo articulo. Item quod sunt distinctæ diuisæ & separatæ, ita quod uni non licet iurisdictionem alterius usurpare; & hoc declaratum est in articulo secundo.
units.tr: It must be understood that since Christ had a threefold power, namely over bodily things, over souls, and over temporal resources, he used the first, used and committed the second, and neither used nor committed the third. He did use the first, by healing bodily infirmities, raising the dead, and working many kinds of miracles over all bodily things.
