He used and committed the second, namely the spiritual power, as far as it was necessary and useful for the salvation of souls. The third he neither used, as the examples given above make plain, nor committed; rather, as has been said, he forbade it to Peter and the other Apostles. Consider what Blessed Bernard says in writing to Pope Eugenius: "And we, that we may truly judge ourselves, know that we have been given a ministry, not dominion. If you are wise, be content with the measure by which God is measured; for whatever is more than this is from evil. Learn from the prophetic example to preside, not so much to command as to act. Learn that you need a hoe, not a royal sceptre, to do the work of a prophet, that is, to root up and tear down, scatter and waste, and to build and plant."* So far he. "You have heard this above; therefore he did not ascend to reign but to root out. Do you think you will find work to do in the field of your Lord? Certainly a great deal." And below: "What did the holy Apostle leave to you? 'What I have,' he says, 'I give to you.' What is that? 'Silver and gold I do not have,' he says; but what he did not have he could not give. Grant that you have sold these things to yourself by some other right, but not by Apostolic right. What he had he gave: namely, care over all the Churches. Did he give lordship? Hear him himself: 'Not lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock.' And lest you think this was said from humility alone and not also from truth, listen to the Lord in the Gospel: 'The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors; but you are not so.'" It is plain that lordship is forbidden to the Apostles. So do you dare to claim for yourself either the lordship of an apostle or the apostolate as lordship? Clearly you are forbidden the one by the other. If you wish to have both at once, you will lose both. Otherwise, do not think yourself excepted from the number of those of whom the Lord complains, saying: They have reigned, but not by me; they have been princes, but I did not know them. And so it has been declared that dominion over earthly things, and temporal jurisdiction, were not conferred by God on the supreme Pontiff, the successor of Blessed Peter. What, then, is the dignity or power conferred on the supreme Pontiff? What authority was granted to Blessed Peter, the vicar of Jesus Christ? Surely one nobler, higher and more useful than the imperial. For as far as the East is from the West, the body from the soul, bodily things from spiritual, earthly from heavenly, so far does the authority of the supreme Pontiff stand above the height of imperial or royal dignity. Hear the Lord speaking in the Gospel to his vicar: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Behold, whatever greater, whatever higher, could be imagined in this life has been conferred on the supreme Pontiff by God. What more, then, does he seek? Does it not seem to deny to his Highness the eye for these lower, corruptible things? It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that pontifical authority and royal dignity are two distinct powers, divinely instituted. This was declared in the first article. Likewise, that they are distinct, divided and separate, so that it is not lawful for one to usurp the jurisdiction of the other; and this was declared in the second article.

units.la: Item quod iurisdictio sive Dominium temporalium non est concessa summo Pontifici; Propter quod non se debet intromittere de iurisdictione temporali nisi casualiter. Quia in temporalibus non habet ordinariam potestatem, sicut expresse habetur extra qui filii sunt legit. cap. per venerabilem, ubi sic Papa dicit: Non solum in Ecclesiæ patrimonio, super quo in temporalibus, plenam gerimus potestatem, verum etiam in aliis Regionibus, certis causis inspectis, temporalem iurisdictionem casualiter exercemus. Non quod alieno iuri præiudicare velimus; sed quia (sicut in Deuteronomio continetur) si difficile & ambiguum apud te iudicium esse perspexeris inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, lepram & lepram, & iudicum inter se verba videris variari, veniens ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & ad Iudicem qui fuerit illo tempore, qui iudicabunt tibi iudicii veritatem. Vbi sic dicit Glossa: Quod Papa de temporalibus iudicare potest, cum requiritur, videlicet quando iudicium ambiguum est inter iudices seculares. Et sic declaratus est tertius articulus.
units.tr: Likewise, jurisdiction or dominion over temporal things has not been granted to the supreme Pontiff; for this reason he ought not to meddle in temporal jurisdiction except by chance. For he does not have ordinary power in temporal matters, as is expressly stated in extra qui filii sunt legit. cap. per venerabilem, where the Pope speaks thus: "We exercise full power in temporal matters not only over the patrimony of the Church, but also, in other regions, when certain causes have been examined, we exercise temporal jurisdiction by chance. Not that we wish to prejudice another's right, but because (as is contained in Deuteronomy) if you see that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous before you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and leprosy, and you see the judges disagreeing among themselves, go up to the priests of the Levitical stock and to the judge who is in office at that time, and they will tell you the truth of the judgment." Where the Gloss says thus: That the Pope can judge in temporal matters when he is asked to, namely when the judgment is ambiguous between secular judges. And so the third article has been declared.

units.la: ARTICVLVS IV.
units.tr: ARTICLE IV.

units.la: Quatto declarandum est, in quibus & quomodo potestas temporalis, subiecta est spirituali potestati, & in quibus non. Ad cuius euidentiam notandum est, quod quædam sunt causæ mere spirituales, sicut causæ matrimoniales extra de offic. deleg. cap. causam matrimonii. Item causæ decimarum, extra de Decimis, per totum. Item causæ Simoniæ, extra de Simonia, per totum. Item causæ hæresis, extra de hæreticis cap. ad abolendam, & cap. vergentem, & cap. excom. Item causa Diuortii, extra de procur. Et omnes aliæ causæ matrimoniales sunt spirituales. De quibus dicit Innocentius, extra de iudiciis, super illam Decretalem, Nouit, super verbo Iurament. Nota crimen pacis fractæ & periurii directe pertinet ad Iudicium Ecclesiæ, vt hic in crimine Simoniæ, sacrilegii, vsurarum, hæresis, separationis matrimonii, quantum ad thorum propter adulterium. Causæ mere temporales, sunt causæ feudales, & causæ sanguinis, & huiusmodi. Istas commisit Deus immediate & principaliter Imperatoribus & Regibus, de quibus nec Papa, nec alii Prælati debuerunt se intromittere in Ecclesia primitiua, licet modo consuetudine, de causis personalibus quibusdam & temporalibus ad utrumque Iudicem recurratur. Sed de Feudalibus, in propriis Feudis, non nisi ad Imperatorem, Reges & alios Principes. Vnde in illa Decretali dicit Papa: Non negamus quin Imperator præcellat in temporalibus. Et vt extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit, dicit Papa: Non putes quod iurisdictionem Illustris Regis Francorum perturbare aut minuere intendamus. Et infra qui filii sunt legit. Dicit Papa; Ad Regem non ad Ecclesiam pertinet de talibus possessionibus iudicare. Item extra de foro competent. cap. vero, super verbo de Feudis, dicit Innocentius; Quilibet Dominus quantumcunque villicus vel etiam rusticus, super Feudalibus rebus iurisdictionem habet. Causæ mixtæ, sunt causæ temporales, quæ connexionem quandam habent cum spiritualibus. Sicut causa feudalis quæ de se temporalis est, connexionem potest habere cum iuramento vel pacto. Sicut patet de dissensione mota inter Reges Franciæ & Angliæ, super Comitatu Pictauiensi. Papa quia non poterat directe cognoscere de causa feudali, indirecte ratione iuramenti vel pacti, intromisit se de illa. extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit. Vbi dicit Hostiensis in glossa super verbo, de feudo; Non intendimus cognoscere de feudo, sed tantum ratione peccati, inducendo illum ad pœnitentiam, quia illam non potest agere nisi satisfaciat.
units.tr: Fourthly, it must be explained in what matters, and how, temporal power is subject to spiritual power, and in what matters it is not. To make this clear, it should be noted that some causes are purely spiritual, such as matrimonial causes extra de offic. deleg. cap. causam matrimonii. Likewise, causes of tithes, extra de Decimis, throughout. Likewise, causes of simony, extra de Simonia, throughout. Likewise, causes of heresy, extra de hæreticis, cap. ad abolendam, and cap. vergentem, and cap. excom. Likewise, the cause of divorce, extra de procur. And all other matrimonial causes are spiritual. Of these Innocent says, extra de iudiciis, on that Decretal Nouit, on the words Iurament.: Note that the crime of broken peace and of perjury pertains directly to the judgment of the Church, as here in the crime of simony, sacrilege, usury, heresy, and the separation of marriage as to bed on account of adultery. Purely temporal causes are feudal causes, causes of blood, and the like. God committed these immediately and principally to emperors and kings, and into these neither the Pope nor other prelates ought to have interfered in the primitive Church, although now, by custom, some personal and temporal causes are brought before either judge. But concerning feudal matters, in their own fiefs, only the emperor, kings and other princes may judge. Hence in that Decretal the Pope says: We do not deny that the Emperor excels in temporal matters. And in extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit, the Pope says: Do not think that we intend to disturb or diminish the jurisdiction of the illustrious King of the French. And below, qui filii sunt legit., the Pope says: It belongs to the King, not to the Church, to judge concerning such possessions. Likewise, extra de foro competent. cap. vero, on the words de Feudis, Innocent says: Every lord, however minor a village lord or even a rustic, has jurisdiction over feudal matters. Mixed causes are temporal causes which have some connection with spiritual ones. Thus a feudal cause, which is temporal in itself, can have a connection with an oath or a pact, as is clear from the dispute raised between the kings of France and England over the county of Poitou. Because the Pope could not directly take cognizance of a feudal cause, he intervened in it indirectly, by reason of an oath or pact, extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit. Where Hostiensis, in the gloss on the words de feudo, says: We do not intend to take cognizance of the fief, but only by reason of sin, leading him to repentance, because he cannot be absolved of it unless he makes satisfaction.

units.la: Item causa Dotis per se temporalis est, & ad sæcularem Iudicem pertinet, si de ipsa tantum agatur; tamen quando Iudex Ecclesiasticus cognoscit principaliter de matrimonio, si incidat causa Dotis, tanquam accessoria, cognoscet de illa, sicut de principali cui est annexa, vt patet extra de donat. inter virum & vxorem, cap. de prudentia. Vbi dicit glossa; Quia si non est matrimonium, neque dos. Et ita dos accedet matrimonio. Ideo qui cognoscit de principali, debet cognoscere de accessorio, vt habetur extra de officio delegati cap. preterea, & cap. prudentiam. Sic etiam de hæreditate cognoscit Iudex Ecclesiasticus, ratione incidentis extra qui filii sunt legit. cap. per tuas, & cap. ex tenore. Alii sunt plures casus speciales in quibus Iudex Ecclesiasticus, cognoscit de temporalibus, quos enumerat Hostiensis in glossa extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit. Sic ergo regulariter verum est, quod de causis mere spiritualibus solus Papa & alii Iudices Ecclesiastici, habent cognoscere. De causis vero mere temporalibus, habent cognoscere Reges, Imperatores & alii Iudices seculares. Et sic Rex Franciæ secundum iura non subest summo Pontifici, nec ei tenetur respondere de feudo regni sui; posset tamen ei subiacere incidenter & casualiter, ratione connexionis alicuius causæ spiritualis, sicut habetur extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit. & extra qui filii sunt legit. cap. per venerabilem. Et sic declaratus est quartus
units.tr: Likewise, a cause of dowry is in itself temporal and belongs to the secular judge if it is treated alone; however, when the ecclesiastical judge takes cognizance chiefly of a marriage, if a cause of dowry arises as something accessory, he will take cognizance of it as of the principal to which it is attached, as is clear extra de donat. inter virum & vxorem, cap. de prudentia. Where the gloss says: Because if there is no marriage, neither is there a dowry. And so the dowry accedes to the marriage. Therefore he who takes cognizance of the principal ought to take cognizance of the accessory, as is held in extra de officio delegati cap. preterea, and cap. prudentiam. So too the ecclesiastical judge takes cognizance of inheritance, by reason of an incidental matter, extra qui filii sunt legit. cap. per tuas, & cap. ex tenore. There are several other special cases in which the ecclesiastical judge takes cognizance of temporal matters, which Hostiensis enumerates in the gloss extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit. Thus it is generally true that only the Pope and other ecclesiastical judges are to take cognizance of purely spiritual causes, while kings, emperors and other secular judges are to take cognizance of purely temporal causes. And so the King of France, according to law, is not subject to the supreme Pontiff, nor is he bound to answer to him concerning the fief of his kingdom; yet he could be subject to him incidentally and occasionally, by reason of the connection of some spiritual cause, as is held extra de iudiciis, cap. nouit, & extra qui filii sunt legit. cap. per venerabilem. And so the fourth is declared.

units.la: ARTICVLVS V.
units.tr: ARTICLE V.

units.la: QVINTO declarandum est, à quo Rex Franciæ teneat regnum suum. Vtrum scilicet ab homine, vel à Deo. Et si à Deo, virtum necesse habeat recognoscere ab eius vicario? Ad quod breuiter respondemus, quod à solo Deo immediate tenet & possidet regnum suum, ita quod non ab homine quoquam. A vicario vero CHRISTI non tenet, nec in quantum homo, nec in quantum Christi vicarius. Ad hoc sumamus testimonium summi Pontificis ipsius, videlicet Innocentii, extra qui fil. sunt legit. 6. per venerabilem, de Rege Francorum sic loquentis: Rex Francorum superiorem in temporalibus minime recognoscit. Si dicas, quia etsi non recognoscit, tamen de iure deberet. Respondemus per interemptionem quod non debet. Quia Franci nulli vnquam fuerunt subditi, nec Imperatori, nec aliis, sicut probatur ex antiquis historiis, quod post euersionem Troiæ XII. M. Troianorum ad partes Pannoniæ peruenerunt, vbi ciuitatem Sicambriam construentes, manserunt ibi vsque ad tempora Valentiniani Imperatoris, semper infesti Romano Imperio. Expulsi vero inde ab Imperatore prædicto, pro eo quod tributa Romanis soluere recusarent, iuxta morem aliarum nationum, habitauerunt iuxta Rhenum in confinio Germaniæ & Allemanniæ. Quos cum multis post, idem Valentinianus sibi subiugare tentasset, nec aliquatenus potuisset, appellauit eos Francorum. Et Galliam habitantes, denique, Franciam appellantes, nec Romanis nec aliis quibuscunq; voluerunt esse subditi. Et dato (quod non credo) quod Imperatori vel Papæ fuerunt aliquando subditi; tamen ex tanto tempore præscripserunt, & regnum pacifice possederunt, quod amplius non tenentur alicui respondere. Nam etiam contra Romanam Ecclesiam currit præscriptio centenaria, sicut habetur extra de præscript. c. ad audientiam. in sin. vbi sic dicitur; Contra quam (videl. Romanam Ecclesiam) non nisi centenaria præscriptio currit. Præterea iustæ possessionis & libertatis, iustum titulum, sine recognitione cuiuscunq; superioris, quo dictus Rex nunc possidet regnum suum, & prædecessores eius hactenus possederunt, ac eius successores, omnipotentis Dei dextra protegente, perpetuo possidebunt, rationibus irrefragalibus declaramus.
units.tr: Fifthly, it must be declared from whom the King of France holds his kingdom: whether from man or from God. And if from God, whether he must acknowledge it through God's vicar? To this we briefly answer that he holds and possesses his kingdom immediately from God alone, and not from any man. Indeed, he does not hold it from the vicar of CHRIST, neither as a man nor as Christ's vicar. For testimony on this let us take that of the supreme Pontiff himself, namely Innocent, extra qui fil. sunt legit. 6. per venerabilem, speaking of the King of the French: The King of the French recognizes no superior in temporal matters. If you say that although he does not recognize one, he nevertheless ought by right to, we answer flatly that he ought not. For the Franks were never subjects of anyone, neither of the emperor nor of others, as is proved from ancient histories: after the overthrow of Troy, twelve thousand Trojans came to the parts of Pannonia, where, building the city Sicambria, they remained until the time of the Emperor Valentinian, always hostile to the Roman Empire. Driven out from there by the aforesaid emperor, because they refused to pay tribute to the Romans, as other nations did, they dwelt by the Rhine on the border of Germany and Alemannia. When, many years later, the same Valentinian tried to subdue them and could not do so in any way, he called them Franks. And living in Gaul, and finally calling it France, they wished to be subjects neither of the Romans nor of any others whatsoever. And even granting (which I do not believe) that they were at some time subjects of the Emperor or of the Pope, nevertheless by so long a lapse of time they have prescribed, and have peacefully possessed the kingdom, so that they are no longer bound to answer to anyone. For even against the Roman Church the prescription of a hundred years runs, as is held extra de præscript. c. ad audientiam. in sin. where it is said: Against which (namely the Roman Church) only a prescription of a hundred years runs. Moreover, by irrefutable reasons we declare the just title of just possession and liberty, without recognition of any superior, by which the said King now possesses his kingdom, which his predecessors have hitherto possessed, and which his successors, with the right hand of almighty God protecting them, will possess forever.

units.la: Primo quidem, possessionis huius iustum titulum, probat vnctio sacra, missa diuinitus, qua Reges Franciæ semper, opportunis temporibus, inunguntur. Nonne regnum euidenter approbatur à Deo, cuius Reges diuino munere consecrantur? Secundo, hoc idem probant aperta miracula, vniuerso Orbi manifeste notoria, & notorie manifesta. Vnde Dominus Rex de iusto titulo suo respondens, dicere potest illud in Euangelio, quod respondit Dominus Iesus contra calumnias Iudæorum; Si mihi non vultis credere, operib. credite. Sicut n. hæreditario iure succedit patri filius in adoptionem regni: sic quasi hæreditario iure succedendi, facultatem Deo tradente, alter alteri in simili potestate miracula faciendi. Tertio hoc idem probat bonitas vitæ, claritas famæ, deuotionis feruor, syncieritas fidei Christianæ, quæ semper in Regib. nostris viguit & in regno, præcæteris regnis & Regib. huius mundi. Diximus ergo quod Dominus noster Rex eodem titulo & eodem iure tenet regnum suum & possidet, quo tenuit Beatus Ludouic. quem dieb. nostris sedes apostolica, sanctitatis eius eminentia, promerente, & miraculorum euidentia proclamate, cathalogo sanctorum adscripsit. Ad quæstionem ergo propositam, pro nobis respondeat Beatus Ludouicus, respondeat eius vita sanctissima, quam crebra miracula protestantur.
units.tr: First, indeed, the holy anointing, sent down from God, by which the Kings of France are always anointed at opportune times, proves the just title of this possession. Is not the kingdom evidently approved by God, whose kings are consecrated by divine gift? Second, the same is proved by open miracles, manifestly notorious to the whole world and notoriously manifest. Whence the Lord King, answering concerning his just title, may say what the Lord Jesus answered against the calumnies of the Jews: If you will not believe me, believe the works. For just as by hereditary right a son succeeds his father in the adoption of the kingdom, so, as if by hereditary right of succession, God granting the power, one person succeeds another in the same power of working miracles. Third, the same is proved by the goodness of life, the brightness of fame, the fervour of devotion, and the sincerity of the Christian faith, which has always flourished among our kings and in the kingdom, above other kingdoms and kings of this world. We have therefore said that our Lord King holds and possesses his kingdom by the same title and the same right by which Blessed Louis held it, whom in our own days the apostolic see, his eminent holiness deserving it and miracles being clearly proclaimed, has enrolled in the catalogue of saints. So, to the question proposed, let Blessed Louis answer for us; let his most holy life answer, which frequent miracles attest.

units.la: Contra præmissa arguitur multipliciter, tam per rationes, quam per iura Canonica & ciuilia, probando quod Rex Franciæ, & vniuersaliter omnes Reges, subsint & subesse debeant summo Pontifici, quantum ad temporalia. Primo sic, secundum beatum Dionysium: Militans Ecclesia exempta est, ad similitudinem Ecclesiæ triumphantis, secundum illud Exodi, Inspice, & fac secundum exemplar, quod tibi in monte monstratum est. Sed in Ecclesia triumphante non est nisi vnus solus & summus Hierarcha, cui omnes, tam angeli, quam homines in omnibus obediunt & intendunt, ergo & in Ecclesia militante est vnus solus & summus Hierarcha, cui omnes, tam clerici quam laici, & tam Reges quam alii, tenentur in omnib. spiritualibus & temporalib. obedire. Non est aliquis talis, nisi Papa. Ergo, &c. Respondeo, non est simile de Hierarchia cœlesti & terrena. Quia ille per suam summam persectionem sufficit per seipsum regere totam illam monarchiam cœlestem: Terrenus autem Hierarcha, propter suam imperfectionem, non sufficit per seipsum similiter regere spiritualia. Et propter hoc dicit Apostolus; Nemo militans Deo implicat se negotiis saecularib. Et beatus Ambrosius ait; Qui terrenis occupantur, scire diuina non possunt. Quia videl. terrena distrahunt, & à coelestium contemplatione perturbant. Et hoc probat Beatus Bernardus satis diffuse ad Eugenium Papam. Cum igitur summum Pontificem oporteat & expediat, summe & praecipue, spiritualibus & diuinis intendere, non debet eius animus incurrari ad temporale regimen. Vnde, licet Moyses veteris legislator, fuerit eleuatissimus in contemplatione, & diuinis colloquiis assuetus (loquebatur ei enim Deus, facie ad faciem, sicut dicitur numero 12.) tamen non fuit sufficiens terrenis intendere, sicut dixit Ietro ei; Stulto labore consumeris, vltra vires tuas est hoc negotium, esto populo in his quae ad Deum pertinent, &c. Propter quod Moyses constituit principes, qui temporales causas populi iudicarent. Præterea in illa Hierarchia cœlesti, est summa pax, concordia & vniformitas voluntarum: hic autem sunt dissensiones, lites & discordiæ innumerabiles & fraudes. Ideo non est simile de hac, & illa.
units.tr: The following is argued against the above in many ways, both by reasons and by canon and civil law, proving that the King of France, and all kings in general, are and ought to be subject to the supreme Pontiff in temporal matters. First, according to the blessed Dionysius: The Church militant is modelled on the Church triumphant, according to that text in Exodus, "Look, and make it according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain." But in the Church triumphant there is only one supreme Hierarch, whom all, both angels and men, obey and attend to in all things. Therefore in the Church militant there is also only one supreme Hierarch, whom all, both clergy and laity, and both kings and others, are bound to obey in all spiritual and temporal matters. There is no such person except the Pope. Therefore, etc. I answer: the celestial and the earthly hierarchy are not alike. For the one, by its supreme perfection, suffices by itself to govern that whole celestial monarchy. The earthly hierarch, however, because of his imperfection, does not suffice by himself to govern spiritual matters in the same way. For this reason the Apostle says: No one who serves God entangles himself in secular affairs. And the blessed Ambrose says: Those who are occupied with earthly things cannot know divine things. For earthly things distract and disturb from contemplation of heavenly things. The blessed Bernard proves this quite fully in his letter to Pope Eugenius. Since, then, the supreme Pontiff ought and is expedient to attend above all and especially to spiritual and divine things, his mind must not be burdened with temporal government. Hence, although Moses, the lawgiver of the old covenant, was most exalted in contemplation and accustomed to divine converse (for God spoke with him face to face, as is said in Numbers 12), yet he was not sufficient to attend to earthly affairs, as Jethro said to him: You will wear yourself out with foolish labour; this business is beyond your strength; be for the people in those things which pertain to God, etc. For this reason Moses appointed princes who should judge the temporal causes of the people. Moreover, in that celestial hierarchy there is supreme peace, concord and uniformity of wills; here, however, there are countless dissensions, quarrels, discords and frauds. Therefore the one is not like the other.

units.la: Item secundum eundem Dionysium, omnis multitudo ad vnitatem reducitur, sicut ab vnitate procedit. Ergo omnis multitudo Prælatorum & Principum reducitur ad vnum summum, qui est super omnes Principes & Prælatos. Nullus autem talis est nisi Papa. Ergo, &c. Respondeo dicendum, quod sicut temporalia sunt propter corpus, & corpus propter animam: ita quod hæc omnia inferiora debent ad bonum animæ ordinari. Aliter non recte vteretur homo temporalibus; sed potius abuteretur. Sic potestas temporalis quodammodo ordinatur ad spiritualem, in his quæ ad ipsam spiritualitatem pertinent, id est in spiritualibus. Per istum modum multitudo reducitur.
units.tr: Likewise, according to the same Dionysius, every multitude is led back to unity, as it proceeds from unity. Therefore every multitude of prelates and princes is led back to one supreme person, who is above all princes and prelates. But there is no such person except the Pope. Therefore, etc. I answer that, just as temporal things exist for the sake of the body, and the body for the sake of the soul, so all these lower things ought to be ordered to the good of the soul. Otherwise a man would not use temporal things rightly, but would rather abuse them. In this way temporal power is in some sense ordered to spiritual power, in those matters which pertain to spirituality itself, that is, in spiritual matters. In this manner the multitude is led back.

units.la: Item sicut vnus solus est creator spiritualium omnium & temporalium, à quo omnia procedunt in esse, & vnus finis ad quem omnia (sicut ad finalem terminum) ordinantur, sicut ipse testatur 1. Apocal. Ego sum α. & ω. Id est, Principium & Finis: Sic vnus est omnium gubernator & rector, tam temporalium quam spiritualium. Sed in hoc est differentia, quia in creatione non potest Deus habere vicarium. Ergo vnus solus sub Deo vicarius eius, habens regimen totius vniuersi, & quantum ad temporalia, & quantum ad spiritualia. Respondeo, quando arguitur, vnus est creator, ergo & vnus rector. Dicendum est quod non est simile. Quia creatio est productio de non esse in esse, vbi est infinita distantia. Ideo in creatione requiritur infinita potentia, quæ non potest esse nisi in vno solo principio simplicissimo & potentissimo: in gubernatione autem istorum inferiorum non requiritur infinita potentia, quia omnia sunt finita; tam spiritualia quam temporalia, tamen valde sunt inter se diuersa. Ideo diuersis egent rectoribus, spirituali videl. & terreno. Vel si dicas, quod nec creatio nec vltima perfectio, quæ est per beatitudinem, sunt communicabiles creaturæ, quia vnam requirit & infinitam potentiam ad infinitam bonitatem; gubernatio autem fuit communicabilis. Ideo licet ipse Deus sit principalis rector totius vniuersi, tamen & per angelos suos sanctos, & per homines voluit mundum regi.
units.tr: Likewise, just as there is one sole creator of all spiritual and temporal things, from whom all things proceed into being, and one end to which all things are ordered (as to their final term), as he himself testifies in Revelation 1: I am Alpha and Omega [α & ω], that is, the Beginning and the End; so there is one governor and ruler of all things, both temporal and spiritual. But the difference is this: in creation God cannot have a vicar. Therefore one alone, under God, is his vicar, having the governance of the whole universe, both as to temporal and as to spiritual things. I answer: when it is argued, "there is one creator, therefore also one ruler," it must be said that the two are not alike. For creation is the production of being from non-being, where the distance is infinite. Therefore creation requires infinite power, which can exist only in one most simple and most powerful first principle. But in the governance of these lower things infinite power is not required, because all things are finite, both spiritual and temporal, though they are very different from one another. Therefore they need different rulers, namely a spiritual and an earthly one. Or if you say that neither creation nor the ultimate perfection, which is through blessedness, can be communicated to creatures, because the one requires infinite power for infinite goodness, whereas governance can be communicated: even so, although God himself is the principal ruler of the whole universe, yet he has willed that the world be ruled both through his holy angels and through men.

units.la: Item, in vno corpore naturali tantum est vnum caput, in quo vigent omnes sensus, & omnia membra regit, ergo in corpore Mystico, quod est Ecclesia, vnum tantum erit caput, alioqui monstruosum esset Ecclesiam habere duo capita, sicut esset monstruosum in vno corpore naturali. Respondeo, dicendum, quod totius Ecclesiæ vnum solum est caput, sicut vna est columba Ecclesia. Sed istud caput dicimus esse CHRISTVM, qui solus est proprie caput Ecclesiæ, à quo derivata est vtraque potestas, sicut ait Apostolus, Ephes. 2. Omnia subiecit sub pedibus eius, & ipsum dedit caput super omnem Ecclesiam, quod est corpus ipsius. Potest nihilominus Papa dici caput Ecclesiæ, in quantum est principalis inter ministros Ecclesiæ, à quo dependet tota spiritualis ordinatio, sicut CHRISTI vicarius spirituali principali. Sicut etiam Romana Ecclesia dicitur caput omnium Ecclesiarum, non est autem caput quantum ad regimen temporalium, sed quilibet Rex est caput regni, & Imperator [illegible, ~6 letters].
units.tr: Likewise, in one natural body there is only one head, in which all the senses are active and which governs all the members. Therefore in the mystical body, which is the Church, there will be only one head; otherwise it would be monstrous for the Church to have two heads, just as it would be monstrous in one natural body. I answer that the whole Church has only one head, just as the Church is one dove. But we say that this head is Christ, who alone is properly the head of the Church, from whom both powers are derived, as the Apostle says in Ephesians 2: He subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body. Nevertheless the Pope can be called head of the Church, insofar as he is the principal among the ministers of the Church, on whom all spiritual order depends, as the vicar of Christ in spiritual principality. In the same way the Roman Church is called the head of all churches; yet it is not the head with respect to the government of temporal things. Rather, every king is head of his kingdom, and the Emperor [illegible, about six letters].

units.la: Item secundum Philosophum, in omni genere rerum ordinatorum, ad inuicem ponere est vnum minimum ad quod omnia reducuntur; Ergo in Ecclesia, quæ maxime debet esse ordinata, oportet esse vnum ad quem & per quem omnes alii ordinentur, hoc autem non potest esse nisi Papa. Ergo, &c. Respondeo, illud à quo vniuersitas tota fidelium reducitur reductione vltima, consummatione, & finali, est solus Deus, qui solus potest omnem appetitum humanum terminare, & desiderium adimplere; tamen sub Deo, illud minimum vnitum & indiuisibile, ad quod omnes fideles adspiciunt & intendunt, quantum ad ea quæ sunt necessaria vel expedientia ad salutem, est Papa, videlicet quantum ad spiritualia, sicut Rex in regno quantum ad temporalia.
units.tr: Likewise, according to the Philosopher, in every kind of ordered things, in relation to one another, there is one lowest point to which all things are reduced. Therefore in the Church, which above all ought to be ordered, there must be one to whom and through whom all others are ordered; but this can be none other than the Pope. Therefore, etc. I answer that that from which the whole multitude of the faithful is led back by the final reduction, consummation and end is God alone, who alone can bring every human desire to its goal and fulfil every longing. Yet under God, that one indivisible point of unity, to which all the faithful look and direct their attention as to what is necessary or expedient for salvation, is the Pope, namely in spiritual matters, just as the king in his kingdom is so in temporal matters.

units.la: Item ab exordio mundi humanum genus non nisi vnum rectorem Principem legitur habuisse, sicut patet in diuersis statibus huius mundi. Ergo & modo debet esse vnus Princeps rector. Probatur assumptum; In statu innocentiæ Adam præfuit omnibus, & semper præfuisset, si semper in innocentia perstitisset. Post peccatum vero, in statu legis naturæ, Noë super omnes, suo tempore, præfuit. Postmodum vero Abraham, Isaac & Iacob, quilibet eorum præfuit populo Dei. Fuerunt quoque Sacerdotes hostias Domino offerentes. Similiter Melchisedech Sacerdos Hierosolymis fuit Dei summi. Vnde & ipse CHRISTVS dicitur esse Sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Cui etiam Abraham Patriarcha decimas obtulit, sicut dicitur Genes. 14. in signum quod ei subeiat quantum ad temporalia. Similiter in lege Moysaica, Moyses habuit vtramque potestatem, & vtroque gladio vsus est. Ergo multo fortius in statu legis Evangelicæ debet esse vnus vtramque Potestatem habens. Respondeo, quod istud argumentum multas habet particulas ad sui declarationem; Et propter hoc ad singulas illarum opus speciales responsiones dare.
units.tr: Likewise, from the beginning of the world the human race is read to have had only one ruling prince, as is evident in the various states of this world. Therefore also now there ought to be one prince as ruler. The assumption is proved thus: in the state of innocence Adam presided over all, and would have always presided, had he always remained in innocence. After sin, however, in the state of natural law, Noah presided over all in his time. Afterwards Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, each of them, presided over the people of God. There were also priests offering sacrifices to the Lord. Likewise Melchizedek was priest of the most high God at Jerusalem, and therefore Christ himself is said to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. To him also the patriarch Abraham offered tithes, as is said in Genesis 14, as a sign that he was subject to him in temporal matters. Similarly, under the law of Moses, Moses had both powers and used both swords. Therefore, much more strongly, in the state of the Gospel law there ought to be one who possesses both powers. I answer that this argument has many parts requiring its explanation; and for this reason special answers must be given to each of them.

units.la: Ad primum quod dicitur de Adam in statu innocentiæ; dicendum est quod in illo statu, omnia fuissent communia, nec quisquam dixisset, aliquid esse suum. Fuisset etiam ibi pax & concordia; non fraus, furtum, rapina, iniuria vel iniquitas. Et ideo cum omnes homines essent spirituales, nulla fuisset ibi iurisdictio temporalis. Post peccatum, hon fuit ita, nec modo est; cum multæ fiant iniustitiæ, fraudes & iniquitates abundant. Ideo non est simile. Ibi tamen bene fuisset spiritualis Prælatio, sicut est in angelis sanctis, & fuissent ibi gradus diuersi honoris secundum gradus & ordinationem dignitatis. Quia quantum alius alios præcelluisset in bonitate & sapientia, tantum fuisset amplius honoratus. Ad id quod arguebatur de Noë, dicendum quod Deus ante diluuium fecit omnia per seipsum, & homini; quem formauerat, præcepta dedit, & transgredienti pœnam imposuit, sicut legitur Genes. secundo & tertio. Postmodum alios delinquentes, per seipsum punivit, vsque ad tempus Noë, sicut patet in Caijm & Lamech. In tempore vero Noë & citra, cepit creaturas suas regere per ministros, quorum primus fuit Noë, quod ex eo apparet, quia DEVS commisit ei gubernationem Archæ, per quam figuratur Ecclesia, sicut dicit Beatus Petrus. Deus etiam Noë & filiis eius legem rectoriam commisit In hac autem rectoria successerunt, Patriarchæ, Duces & Iudices, Reges & Sacerdotes, & alii qui pro tempore fuerunt Rectores populi Iudæorum. Tamen usque ad Moysen, proprie loquendo, non fuit verum sacerdotium. Nam Aaron iussu divino, primus summus Sacerdos legitur institutus, & alii inferiores Sacerdotes, institutione divina instituti sunt in lege Moysi. Noë vero, Abraham, Isaac & Iacob, Sacerdotes non fuerunt, licet iubente Deo, altaria construxisse, & Deo hostias obtulisse legantur. Abel, Gedeon, Iephte, Manne, Dauid, & multi alii hostias obtulerunt; de quibus constat quod Sacerdotes non fuerint. De Moyse, nulli est dubium quin frequenter hostias Deo immolavit, & tamen Sacerdos non fuit.
units.tr: As for the first point, that Adam was in the state of innocence: it must be said that in that state all things would have been held in common, and no one would have said that anything was his own. There would also have been peace and concord there, with no fraud, theft, robbery, injury or iniquity. And so, since all men would have been spiritual, there would have been no temporal jurisdiction at all. After the sin it was not so, and it is not so now, since many injustices occur and frauds and iniquities abound. Therefore the comparison does not hold. Even so, a spiritual prelacy would have been fitting there, as it is among the holy angels, and there would have been different degrees of honour according to the grades and ordering of dignity, since the more one excelled the others in goodness and wisdom, the more he would have been honoured. As for the argument about Noah, it must be said that before the Flood God did all things himself, and gave commands to the man he had formed, and imposed a punishment on the one who transgressed, as is read in Genesis 2 and 3. Afterwards he punished other offenders himself, down to the time of Noah, as is clear in Cain and Lamech. But from the time of Noah onwards he began to rule his creatures through ministers, the first of whom was Noah. This is clear from the fact that God committed to him the government of the ark, by which the Church is prefigured, as blessed Peter says. God also committed the law of governance to Noah and his sons. In this governance there succeeded patriarchs, leaders and judges, kings and priests, and others who at various times were rulers of the Jewish people. Yet, strictly speaking, there was no true priesthood until Moses. For Aaron, by divine command, is read to have been the first high priest instituted, and the other, lesser priests were instituted by divine ordinance in the law of Moses. Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were not priests, although they are read to have built altars and offered sacrifices to God at God's command. Abel, Gideon, Jephthah, Manoah, David and many others offered sacrifices, and it is certain that they were not priests. Concerning Moses, no one doubts that he often sacrificed victims to God, and yet he was not a priest.

units.la: Nec obstat quod in Psalmo dicitur; Moyses & Aaron in Sacerdotibus eius. Dicit enim ibi Glossa: Moyses in Dei Sacerdotibus nunculatur, non quia Sacerdos fuerit, sed quia vota sua Deo obtulit; & pro populo supplicavit. Igitur Noë, Abraham, Isaac & Iacob etsi dicantur in populo Dei Principes extitisse, non tamen fuerunt Sacerdotes, ut dictum est, nisi valde large dicatur Sacerdos quicumque offert Deo sacrificium laudis, & spiritus contribulati in altari cordis sui; quod faciunt omnes iusti. Isto modo cunctis fidelibus dicit Beatus Petrus, vos estis genus electum, regale Sacerdotium. Omnes enim Christi fideles in quantum sunt unum cum CHRISTO capite, qui est summus Sacerdos, sunt in ipso Reges & Sacerdotes. Quod autem dicitur de Melchisedech, quod videlicet fuit Rex & Sacerdos; Dico quod verum est, sicut scriptura sacra testatur; Non tamen fuit Monarcha totius mundi, sed solum Rex Salem. Hunc autem præmisit Deus ad præfigurandum CHRISTVM, non solum quantum ad utramque dignitatem, Sacerdotalem & Regiam, sed etiam quantum ad alia multa, sicut ostendit Apostolus Hebræorum quarto, Quia videlicet interpretatur, Rex iustitiæ & Rex pacis. Describitur etiam sine patre, sine matre, sine genealogia, neque initium neque finem vitæ habens, præfigurans CHRISTVM, qui est Rex Regum & per quem Reges regnant. Qui dicitur in Psalmo; Tu es Sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: Nor does what is said in the Psalm stand in the way: Moses and Aaron among his priests. For the gloss there says: Moses is named among the priests of God, not because he was a priest, but because he offered his vows to God and interceded for the people. Therefore Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, even though they are said to have been princes among the people of God, were not priests, as has been said, unless one speaks very loosely and calls a priest anyone who offers to God the sacrifice of praise and of a contrite spirit on the altar of his heart, which all the righteous do. In this sense blessed Peter says to all the faithful: You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood. For all Christ's faithful, insofar as they are one with Christ the head, who is the high priest, are in him both kings and priests. As for what is said of Melchizedek, that he was both king and priest: I say it is true, as holy Scripture testifies. Yet he was not monarch of the whole world, but only king of Salem. God sent him ahead to foreshadow Christ, not only as to both dignities, priestly and royal, but also as to many other things, as the Apostle shows in Hebrews 4, namely that his name is interpreted as King of righteousness and King of peace. He is also described as without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, prefiguring Christ, who is King of kings and through whom kings reign. Of him it is said in the Psalm: You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Isti autem Melchisedech, dedit Abraham decimas; non necessitate censionis, sed ex donatione propriæ voluntatis, cum in nullo legatur fuisse subiectus. Sed forte illuminatus a Deo adorabat CHRISTVM quem intelligebat præfigurari per illum. Ad illud quod arguebatur de Moyse, quod utramque iurisdictionem habuit; & utroque gladio usus est. Dicendum quod vere fuit populi Dux & Princeps, sed non fuit Sacerdos, ut dictum est. Nam antequam vellet a Deo recipere Principatum, adiunctus est ei Aaron in solatium & iuuamen, qui postmodum ex præcepto Dei institutus est summus Sacerdos; unde habuerunt discreta officia, & distincta ad invicem potestates, ita quod unus non usurpabat officium alterius. Quia vero carnalis erat populus Iudæorum, carnalibus utens sacrificiis & non nisi carnalia seu temporalia sapiebat; Ideo principatus temporalis superior sacerdotio videbatur. Unde Aaron obediebat Moysi, & Moyses ipsum in subditum arguebat. Sed in populo Christiano, qui legem non carnaliter, sed spiritualiter intelligit, potestas spiritualis debet iudicari dignior & sublimior temporali.
units.tr: Now to this Melchizedek Abraham gave tithes, not from any necessity of tribute, but from the free gift of his own will, since he is nowhere read to have been subject to anyone. But perhaps, enlightened by God, he was worshipping Christ, whom he understood to be prefigured by him. As for the argument about Moses, that he had both jurisdictions and used both swords: it must be said that he was truly leader and prince of the people, but he was not a priest, as has been said. For before he was willing to receive the principate from God, Aaron was joined to him for comfort and help, and afterwards Aaron was instituted by God's command as high priest. Hence they had distinct offices and powers separate from one another, so that one did not usurp the office of the other. But because the Jewish people was carnal, using carnal sacrifices and savouring only carnal or temporal things, the temporal principate seemed superior to the priesthood. Hence Aaron obeyed Moses, and Moses rebuked him as a subordinate. But in the Christian people, who understand the law not carnally but spiritually, spiritual power ought to be judged worthier and higher than temporal power.

units.la: Item Christus qui est caput Ecclesiæ de tribu sacerdotali & Regia fuit ortus utramque dignitatem in se vniens. Ergo eius vicarius utramque dignitatem habebit, ita quod omnes Reges erunt ei subiecti sicut omnes Pontifices.
units.tr: Likewise, Christ, who is the head of the Church, was born of the priestly and royal tribe, uniting both dignities in himself. Therefore his vicar will have both dignities, so that all kings will be subject to him just as all pontiffs are.

units.la: Item Christus utraque potestate usus est; Temporali, quando vendentes & ementes eiecit de templo, Ioan. 2. Spirituali seu Pontificali, quando semetipsum obtulit hostiam Deo, sicut ait Apostolus Hæb. 2. Cum Christus assistens Pontifex, &c. Ergo & vicarius eius utraque potestate fungetur.
units.tr: Likewise, Christ exercised both powers: the temporal, when he drove the sellers and buyers out of the temple (John 2); the spiritual or pontifical, when he offered himself as a sacrifice to God, as the Apostle says in Hebrews 2: Since Christ, as a high priest standing by, etc. Therefore his vicar also will exercise both powers.

units.la: Respondeo; Dicendum quod Christus ex utraque tribu nasci voluit, quia hæreditario iure Rex erat & Sacerdos, & ab ipso tanquam a capite, deriuanda erat utraque potestas. Sed ea quæ sunt unita in capite, non est necesse unita esse in membris, imo potius ea quæ sunt unita in capite, & in membris distinguuntur, & perfectiones omnes, quæ similiter sunt a Deo. Imo sunt idem, quia Deus per creaturas singulas distribuite, participante ab eis particulariter, & in diversis diversimode distinguit.
units.tr: I answer: it must be said that Christ willed to be born of both tribes, because by hereditary right he was both king and priest, and from him as from the head both powers were to be derived. But those things which are united in the head need not be united in the members; rather, those things which are united in the head are distinguished in the members, as are all perfections, which likewise come from God. Indeed, they are the same, because God distributes them through single creatures, which participate in them particularly, and he distinguishes them in different ways in different things.

units.la: Ad id quod dicebatur, quod Christus utraque potestate usus est; Dicendum, quod ideo hoc fuit, ut ipso facto ostenderet, quod utraque potestas ab eodem fonte procedit. Vel aliter dici potest, quod Sacerdotale quidem officium voluit exercere, & Sacerdotalem instituere dignitatem. Sed temporali usus non est. Quia illa eiectio vendentium & ementium in templo, magis fuit Sacerdotalis officii quam regalis. Ad purgandum scilicet templum a negotiatione rerum venalium, ut dictum est. Unde quando quaerebatur a populo, ut facerent eum Regem, fugiens regale fastigium recusavit. Ut aperte monstraret exemplo, quod eius vicarius, & omnes successores eius, simili modo contemnerent. Non ergo voluit eos Reges esse, nec sibi dignitatem Regiam vendicare.
units.tr: As to what was said, that Christ used both powers: it must be said that this was so in order to show by the very deed that both powers proceed from the same source. Or it can be put otherwise: he willed to exercise the priestly office and to institute the priestly dignity, but he did not use the temporal power. For that casting out of the sellers and buyers from the temple was more a matter of the priestly office than of the royal, namely to cleanse the temple of the trade in saleable goods, as has been said. Hence when the people sought to make him king, he fled from the royal height and refused it, so as to show plainly by example that his vicar and all his successors should likewise despise such things. He therefore did not wish them to be kings, nor did he claim the royal dignity for himself.

units.la: Hoc autem prætermittendum non est, cum Christus in infantia sua, se Regem credi, & ut regem quæri permisit, sicut habetur Matth. 20. ubi est qui natus est rex Iudæorum, & a regib. adorari ibidem; & primus passioni, voluit rex, clamari, & sicut vere rex a populis honorari. Et denique pendens in cruce, regiæ dignitatis titulo insigniri Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudæorum. Volens quidem credi Rex esse secundum fidei veritatem, licet vti noluerit, sed oblatam renuerit Regiam dignitatem. Vnde & in passione sua interrogatus specialiter à Pilato, si esset Rex? Sed tamen vt parenter ostenderet, quod etiam in articulo mortis, vti tali potestate nolebat, Respondit, Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Si de hoc mundo esset Regnum meum, ministri utique mei decertarent ut non traderer Iudaeis.
units.tr: Yet this must not be passed over: in his infancy Christ allowed himself to be believed a king and to be sought as king, as is found in Matthew 2, where is he who is born king of the Jews? and he was worshipped there by kings. And at the beginning of his passion he allowed himself to be hailed as king, and to be honoured by the peoples as truly king. And finally, hanging on the cross, Jesus of Nazareth was marked with the title of royal dignity, King of the Jews. He indeed willed to be believed king according to the truth of faith, though he was unwilling to use it, but he refused the royal dignity when it was offered. Hence also, in his passion, when Pilate asked him specifically, whether he was king? he nevertheless, in order to show plainly that even at the point of death he was unwilling to use such power, answered: My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would surely have fought that I should not be handed over to the Jews.

units.la: Item, vtramque potestatem videtur Christus commisisse Petro, quando dicit, Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Quia, sicut in ædificatione materiali, est vnus lapis primarius & fundamentalis: Sic in Ecclesia debet esse, vnus Princeps principalis, totius Ecclesiæ fundamentum. Respondeo: Dicendum quod hæc Petri firmitas, super quam fundata erat Ecclesia, non est dominatio temporalis, sed immobilis & inviolabilis stabilitas fidei Christianæ, sicut insinuat CHRISTVS dicens: Ego pro te rogavi Petre, ut non deficiat fides tua. De potestate enim temporali nullam fecit mentionem, quando dicit, tu es Petrus; sed solum de potestate spirituali, quæ solum in ligando & absolvendo à peccatis in foro conscientiæ, consistit.
units.tr: Likewise, Christ seems to have committed both powers to Peter when he says, "Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." Just as in a material building there is one primary and foundation stone, so in the Church there ought to be one principal prince, the foundation of the whole Church. Reply: It must be said that this firmness of Peter, upon which the Church was founded, is not temporal dominion but the immovable and inviolable steadfastness of the Christian faith, as Christ indicates when he says: "I have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith fail not." For he made no mention of temporal power when he said "thou art Peter," but only of spiritual power, which consists solely in binding and absolving from sins in the forum of conscience.

units.la: Item tempore Passionis discipuli Christi duos gladios ostenderunt, dicentes; Ecce gladii duo hic. &c. & respondit, satis est. Per quos gladios secundum doctrinam Sanctorum significantur duæ potestates, quæ sunt in Ecclesia penes summum Pontificem principaliter residentes. Qua utraque, contra quoscunque, quando necessitas imminet, potest uti, etiam contra Reges & Imperatores. Ergo. &c. Respondeo, si concedamus duos gladios significare duas in Ecclesia potestates; Dicemus quod revera duæ sunt. Sed unam habent terreni Principes & aliam habet summus Pontifex. Non enim dicuntur duo gladii fuisse Petro, sed unus tantum. Sicut insinuat Dominus dicens ei, Converte gladium tuum in vaginam. Reprehensus est autem Petrus, non quia euaginandus non esset tempore opportuno, quando necessitas imminet; Sed quia euaginavit eum modo & tempore non congruo. Quia non debet Iudex Ecclesiasticus uti eo nisi cum causa, & multa deliberatione, & in magna necessitate.
units.tr: Likewise, at the time of the Passion the disciples of Christ showed two swords, saying, "Behold, here are two swords, etc.," and he answered, "It is enough." According to the doctrine of the Saints, these swords signify the two powers in the Church, which reside chiefly in the supreme Pontiff, and which he may use against whomsoever, when necessity threatens, even against kings and emperors. Therefore, etc. Reply: If we concede that the two swords signify two powers in the Church, we shall say that there are indeed two. But the earthly princes have one, and the supreme Pontiff has the other. For it is not said that Peter had two swords, but only one, as the Lord indicates when he says to him, "Put up thy sword into its sheath." Peter was rebuked, however, not because the sword ought not to be unsheathed when necessity threatens and the time is right, but because he unsheathed it in an unfitting manner and at an unfitting time. For an ecclesiastical judge ought not to use it except with cause, after much deliberation, and in great necessity.

units.la: Item quia Binarius est numerus infamis, quia principium divisionis. Divisio autem fons & origo dissensionis, & divisio causa confusionis. Ergo si essent in Ecclesia duæ potestates distinctæ in duas personas, quarum una non penderet ab altera, esset in Ecclesia maxima confusio. Respondeo, dicendum quod Binarius, sicut secundum unam acceptionem, pro eo quod est principium divisionis, est infamis; Sic secundum aliam, est numerus sacratus, propter duas tabulas Decalogi, in quarum prima continentur præcepta ordinantia ad Deum, in secunda præcepta ordinantia ad proximum. Vel propter duo præcepta charitatis, sicut ait Beatus Gregorius, super illud Lucæ 10. Misit illos binos ante faciem suam: Duo, inquit, sunt præcepta charitatis, Dei videlicet amor, & proximi. Si autem istæ duæ potestates essent omnino distinctæ, ita quod una non penderet ex altera; Ista diversitas esset occasio divisionis. Sed inter eas est mutua dependentia; quia temporalis indiget spiritualis, propter animam; Spiritualis vero indiget temporali, propter temporalium rerum usum. Et hoc expresse habetur 96. dist. c. cum ad verum.
units.tr: Likewise, the number two is an infamous number, being the beginning of division; division is the source and origin of dissension, and division is the cause of confusion. Therefore, if there were in the Church two distinct powers in two persons, one not depending on the other, there would be the greatest confusion in the Church. Reply: It must be said that the number two is infamous in one sense, because it is the beginning of division; but in another sense it is a sacred number, on account of the two tables of the Decalogue, in the first of which are contained precepts ordering us toward God, and in the second precepts ordering us toward our neighbour. Or on account of the two precepts of charity, as Blessed Gregory says on that text of Luke 10, "He sent them two by two before his face": "There are two precepts of charity," he says, "namely the love of God and of neighbour." But if these two powers were wholly distinct, so that one did not depend on the other, that diversity would be an occasion of division. Between them, however, there is mutual dependence: the temporal power needs the spiritual on account of the soul, and the spiritual needs the temporal on account of the use of temporal things. This is expressly stated in Dist. 96, c. Cum ad verum.

units.la: Item hoc idem probatur multipliciter per iura Canonica. Primo sic, 22. distinct. cap. omnes; dicitur; Sic Romanam Ecclesiam solus ille fundavit sub petra fidei, mox nascentem erexit, qui Beato Petro, æterna vita clavigero, terrenæ simul & cœlestis Imperii iura commisit; & illius Privilegio fungitur, cuius authoritate fulcitur. Unde non dubium est, quod quisquis cuiibet Ecclesiæ ius suum detrahit, insultiam facit; Qui autem Romanæ Ecclesiæ privilegium, ab ipso summo omnium Ecclesiarum capite traditum, auferre conatur, hic procul dubio in hæresim labitur, & cum ille vocetur iniustus, dicendus est hæreticus. Responsio: Vbi quæritur de potestate summi Pontificis in temporalibus, efficax est testimonium Imperatorum pro Papa, sed non est multum efficax testimonium Papæ pro seipso, nisi denum fulciatur ratione vel authoritate scripturæ, maxime quando Imperator dicit contrarium, & etiam alii summi Pontifices, sicut est in propositio. Ideo, &c. Potest tamen verbum prædicti Canonis, sane intelligi, pro eo quod Dominus Petro, terreni simul & cœlestis Imperii iura committit, in quantum dedit ei potestatem soluendi & ligandi in terra. Cuius sententia ligationis seu absolutionis, approbatur in cœlo; Et ita exponunt glossa illud verbum sibi dictum, in traditione clavium, Quodcunque ligaueris super terram erit ligatum, &c. Aliter potest dici, quod cum sermones inquirendi sint secundum materiam, sicut ait Apostolus; Et intentio in tota illa Dist. sit, ostendere præeminentiam sedis Apostolicæ ad sedes Patriarchales. Quia sedes Apostolica illas & instituit & authoritatem dedit. Vnde sedes Patriarchales, quidquid potestatis & authoritatis habent, dubium non est, à sede Apostolica emanare. Item Patriarcha authoritatem habet limitatam in aliqua mundi parte; Sedes autem Apostolica, in toto Orbe. Vnde quantum potest se extendere in longum & latum temporalis potestas Imperii: tantum se extendit amplitudo spiritualis potestatis, videlicet Apostolicæ; Et quicunque illud singulare Privilegium conatetur auferre, asserendo, quod sedes Patriarchales potestatem & authoritatem suam à sede Apostolica non haberent & spiritualem potestatem, iste merito dicendus esset hæreticus.
units.tr: Likewise, the same point is proved in many ways by the canon law. First, thus, in Dist. 22, c. Omnes: "Thus he alone founded the Roman Church upon the rock of faith, and raised it up as soon as it was born, he who committed to Blessed Peter, keeper of eternal life, the rights of both the earthly and the heavenly empire, and it enjoys the privilege of him by whose authority it is supported. Whence there is no doubt that whoever takes away the right of any church does an injury; but whoever attempts to take away the privilege of the Roman Church, handed down by the supreme head of all churches himself, undoubtedly falls into heresy, and since the former is called unjust, the latter is to be called a heretic." Reply: Where the question concerns the power of the supreme Pontiff in temporal matters, the testimony of emperors for the Pope is effective, but the Pope's testimony for himself is not very effective, unless it is further supported by reason or by the authority of Scripture, especially when the Emperor says the contrary, and also other supreme Pontiffs, as is the case in the proposition. Therefore, etc. Yet the words of the aforesaid canon can be rightly understood in this sense: the Lord committed to Peter the rights of the earthly and heavenly empire insofar as he gave him the power of loosing and binding on earth. The sentence of binding or absolving pronounced by him is approved in heaven; and so the gloss explains that word spoken to him at the handing over of the keys, "Whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound, etc." Otherwise it can be said that since discourses are to be interpreted according to their subject matter, as the Apostle says, and the intention of that whole Dist. is to show the pre-eminence of the Apostolic See over the patriarchal sees, for the Apostolic See both instituted them and gave them authority, it is beyond doubt that whatever power and authority the patriarchal sees possess emanates from the Apostolic See. Likewise, a Patriarch has limited authority in some part of the world, but the Apostolic See has it in the whole world. Hence, as far as the temporal power of the empire can extend in length and breadth, so far extends the breadth of the spiritual power, namely the Apostolic; and whoever attempts to take away that singular privilege, asserting that the patriarchal sees did not have their power, authority and spiritual power from the Apostolic See, would rightly be called a heretic.

units.la: Item, extra de elect. cap. fundamenta, dicit Bonifacius Papa; Constantinus Imperator quarto die sui Baptismatis, una cum omnibus satrapis, & universo senatu, optimatibusque, & cuncto populo in persona Beati Sylvestri, Romanam concedendam urbem, relinquens ab eo & successoribus eius, per pragmaticum ticum statutum disponendam, esse decernens in ipsa urbe utriusque potestatis. Monarchiam Romanis Pontificibus declaraˢet non iustum arbitrans, ut ubi sacerdotii principatum & Christiana religionis caput Imperator cœlestis instituit, illic Imperator terrenus habeat potestatem. Responsio: Si ex institutione divina Papa dicit se esse Dominum omnium temporalium, necessitas est dicere quod ex donatione Constantini, sit Monarcha utriusque potestatis, in urbe. Si dicat quod hanc Monarchiam Constantinus declaravit (& inde caute dictum est, declararet.) Respondeo, quod ex constitutione divina, Monarchia totius mundi, quantum ad utramque potestatem, non fuit concessa Petro, nec successoribus eius, sicut est superius declaratum. Sed ex dono Constantini potest ibi esse Monarchia, sic intelligendo; Quod cum Papa spiritualem potestatem haberet in urbe & orbe, Constantinus ipse temporalem illam potestatem quam habebat in urbe, transtulit in Papam, ut in ipsa urbe utraque potestas (quæ in duabus personis erat) esset in solo Papa. Sicut dicimus, quod aliquis Episcopus est Dominus temporalis & spiritualis in sua civitate, & sic est ibi Monarcha utrumque obtinens Principatum. Sic ergo concedimus quod Papa habet Monarchiam utriusque potestatis in urbe, non tamen in orbe.
units.tr: Likewise, in Extra, De electione, c. Fundamenta, Pope Boniface says: "Constantine the Emperor, on the fourth day after his baptism, together with all the satraps, the whole senate, the nobles and the entire people, in the person of Blessed Sylvester, granted the city of Rome, to be disposed of by him and his successors through a pragmatic sanction, decreeing that in that same city there should be a monarchy of both powers for the Roman Pontiffs. He did not think it just that where the heavenly Emperor established the principate of the priesthood and the head of the Christian religion, there an earthly emperor should have power." Reply: If the Pope says that by divine institution he is lord of all temporal things, it is necessary to say that by the gift of Constantine he is monarch of both powers in the city. If he says that Constantine merely declared this monarchy (and hence the wording is cautiously "declared"), I reply that by divine constitution the monarchy of the whole world, as far as both powers are concerned, was not granted to Peter nor to his successors, as has been declared above. But by the gift of Constantine there can be a monarchy there, understood thus: since the Pope had spiritual power in the city and the world, Constantine himself transferred to the Pope the temporal power he had in the city, so that in the city itself both powers (which were in two persons) should be in the Pope alone. As we say that some bishop is lord both temporal and spiritual in his city, and so there is a monarch there holding both principates. Thus we concede that the Pope has the monarchy of both powers in the city, but not in the world.

units.la: Item 96. distinct. cap. Constantinus, dicitur sic: Constantinus Imperator coronam, & omnem dignitatem in urbe Romana & in Italia, & in partibus occidentalibus vicario Apostolorum concessit. Item cap. sequenti, unde sumitur quod dictum est in illa decretali, Fundamenta, sic; Decernentes sanctimus ut principatum teneat Sylvester (videlicet Papa) & successores eius, tam super quatuor sedes, quam super omnes in universo orbe Dei Ecclesias. Et Pontifex, qui per tempora, ipsius sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ exiterit, celsior & Princeps sanctus Sacerdotibus, & totius mundi existat. Et infra: Ecce Palatium nostrum & Romanam urbem, & omnes Italiæ, sive occidentalium Regionum Provincias Beatissimo Pontifici Sylvestro concedimus atque relinquimus; & abeo & successoribus eius decernimus disponendum. Itaque iuri Romanæ Ecclesiæ concedimus permanendum. Et infra: Quoniam ubi Principatus sacerdotii & Christiana religionis caput, ab Imperatore nostro cœlesti constitutum est, iustum non est ut illic Imperator terrenus habeat potestatem. Responsio: De ista donatione Constantini dicunt iuristæ communiter, quod non valuit multiplici ratione.
units.tr: Likewise, in Dist. 96, c. Constantinus, it is said: "The Emperor Constantine granted the crown and all dignity in the city of Rome, in Italy, and in the western parts, to the vicar of the Apostles." Likewise the following chapter, from which is taken what was said in that decretal, Fundamenta, reads thus: "We decree and sanction that Sylvester (namely the Pope) and his successors hold the principate, both over the four sees and over all the churches of God in the whole world. And the Pontiff who shall exist in the times of the holy Roman Church himself shall be higher, and prince of the holy priests, and of the whole world." And below: "Behold, we grant and leave our Palace and the city of Rome, and all the provinces of Italy or of the western regions, to the most blessed Pontiff Sylvester, and we decree that they be disposed of by him and his successors. Thus we concede that they remain under the right of the Roman Church." And below: "Since where the principate of the priesthood and the head of the Christian religion has been established by our heavenly Emperor, it is not just that an earthly emperor should have power there." Reply: Concerning this donation of Constantine, the jurists commonly hold that it was not valid, for many reasons.

units.la: Primo quidem, quia ideo dicitur Imperator semper Augustus, quia eius propositum debet esse, semper augere Imperium, non minuere; Et ideo dicta donatio non videtur valuisse, maxime cum nimis excessiva fuerit & immensa.
units.tr: First, because the Emperor is called always Augustus precisely because his purpose ought always to be to increase the empire, not to diminish it; and so the said donation does not seem to have been valid, especially since it was excessive and immense.

units.la: Secundo, quia Imperator est administrator imperii & Reipublicæ, ut dicunt iura.
units.tr: Second, because the Emperor is the administrator of the empire and of the commonwealth, as the laws say.

units.la: Tertio, quia non potuit præiudicare successoribus, quando eam revocare possent, quia non habet imperium par in parem.
units.tr: Third, because he could not prejudice his successors, who could revoke it, since he did not have authority over an equal (par in parem).

units.la: Quarto, quia qua ratione potuit dare unam partem, possent successores eius aliam partem dare, & detruncaretur Imperium. Hæc habentur in Authent. Quomodo oportet Episcopos in primip. collat. 1. in gloss. Dico quod si dicta donatio valuerit, tamen Ecclesia non fuit in possessione, nisi illius portionis terræ, quæ dicitur patrimonium Beati Petri.
units.tr: Fourth, because by the same reasoning by which he could give one part, his successors could give another part, and the empire would be cut to pieces. These points are found in the Authentica Quomodo oportet Episcopos, in the primipilaris collation 1, in the gloss. I say that even if the said donation was valid, nevertheless the Church was not in possession except of that portion of land which is called the patrimony of Blessed Peter.

units.la: Item, non potuit valere quantum ad illos qui non erant subiecti imperio. Quia non potuit dare quod suum non erat; Franci autem non erant ei subiecti ut dictum est supra. Vel dato quod essent subiecti (quod non concedimus) tamen præscriptio longissimi temporis erit contra Imperatorem & Papam, sicut dictum est supra.
units.tr: Likewise, it could not be valid as regards those who were not subject to the empire, because he could not give what was not his own; the Franks, however, were not subject to him, as was said above. Or, granting that they were subject (which we do not concede), nevertheless prescription of very long time would be against the Emperor and the Pope, as was said above.

units.la: Item, Papa potest absolvere vasallos à iuramento fidelitatis debito, Domino temporali; quod non esset, nisi haberet potestatem in temporalibus. Ergo, &c. Responsio: In casu, in quo potest agere contra Principem, potest etiam absolvere vasallos à iuramento fidelitatis, vel absolutos potius declarare; utpote ratione hæresis vel schismatis, vel contumaciæ contra Romanam Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Likewise, the Pope can absolve vassals from the oath of fidelity owed to a temporal lord; this would not be so unless he had power in temporal matters. Therefore, etc. Reply: In the case in which he can act against a prince, he can also absolve vassals from the oath of fidelity, or rather declare them absolved; for instance on account of heresy or schism, or contumacy against the Roman Church.

units.la: Item, Zacharias Papa deposuit Regem Franciæ, sicut habetur 15. quæst. 6. cap. alius. Ergo, &c. Respondeo, nusquam legitur quod Regem Franciæ deposuerit, sed deponendum consuluit, ut dicunt quidam. Interrogatus enim, quis potius regnare deberet, an ille qui agebat regni negotia, an ille qui non agebat? Respondit, quod primus. Quo facto Rex Ylldericus depositus fuit à Baronibus, & Pipinus ordinatus & inunctus in Regem. Vel, sicut alii dicunt, Rex Ylldericus non fuit depositus, sed sponte ingressus monasterium, monachicam vitam assumpsit. Barones autem Regni super electionem Pipini & institutione prædicta hæsitantes, an licitum eis esset, consulunt Papam, quod tamen sine Papa facere potuissent.
units.tr: Likewise, Pope Zachary deposed the King of France, as is found in 15 q. 6 c. alius. Therefore, etc. I answer: nowhere is it read that he deposed the King of France, but he advised that he should be deposed, as some say. For when he was asked who ought rather to reign, he who was conducting the affairs of the kingdom or he who was not, he answered that the first should. Upon this, King Childeric was deposed by the barons, and Pepin was appointed and anointed as king. Or, as others say, King Childeric was not deposed, but of his own accord entered a monastery and took up the monastic life. The barons of the kingdom, however, hesitating over the election of Pepin and the aforesaid installation, as to whether it was lawful for them, consulted the Pope, although they could have done it without the Pope.

units.la: Item, extra lib. sexto de immunitate Ecclesiæ, cap. primo. Non licet hiis qui iurisdictionem obtinent temporalem, vel iustitiam exercent, ipsas Ecclesias vel personas, addistrahendum vel alienandum, aut extra manum suam ponendum acquisita, vel quæ deinceps acquirent, aliquatenus coartare. Sed hoc non posset Papa statuere, nisi Dominus esset omnium temporalium. Ergo, &c. Responsio: Ista Constitutio noua est, nondum à Principibus approbata; quam cum ad discussionem pervenient, nunquam forsitan approbabunt. Quia per istum modum, personæ Ecclesiasticæ tantas possessiones acquirere possent, quod in damnum & præiudicium intolerabile Principibus & Reipub. proveniret.
units.tr: Likewise, Extra, book six, on the immunity of the Church, chapter one: It is not lawful for those who hold temporal jurisdiction or exercise justice to alienate or transfer the Churches or persons themselves, or to place under their hand what has been acquired, or what they shall acquire hereafter, nor in any way to restrict them. But the Pope could not establish this unless he were lord of all temporal things. Therefore, etc. Reply: This constitution is new and has not yet been approved by princes; when it comes to be discussed, perhaps they will never approve it. For in this way ecclesiastical persons could acquire such great possessions that it would result in intolerable loss and prejudice to princes and the commonwealth.

units.la: Item Papa Christi vicarius, Dei locum tenens in terra, dicitur habere plenitudinem potestatis. Sed non haberet plenitudinem, nisi esset dominus temporalium & spiritualium, ut eo ipso vere dicatur: Domini est terra & plenitudo Orbis terrarum. Responsio. Patet per dicta in corpore quaestionis; quod Christus (triplicem potestatem habens; videlicet corporum, animarum, & rerum temporalium) prima vsus est, sed non commisit; tertia nec vti voluit, nec commisit. Ergo Papa nec super humana corpora, nec super res corporales potestatem habet; sed solummodo ligandi animas & soluendi. Nec quantum ad animas dicendus est habere plenitudinem potestatis nisi in ligando & soluendo, claue tamen non errante. Non enim potest animas creare, nec in eas gratiam infundere, nec saluare, nec damnare, nec peccata remittere, nisi ministerialiter. Dicitur igitur plenitudinem habere tantum in spiritualibus, & non absolute, sed in comparatione inseriorum Praelatorum, qui ad partem sollicitudinis sunt vocati.
units.tr: Likewise, the Pope, the vicar of Christ, holding God's place on earth, is said to have the fullness of power. But he would not have the fullness unless he were lord of temporal and spiritual things, so that by that very fact it might truly be said: The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof. Reply: It is clear from what has been said in the body of the question that Christ, having a threefold power, namely over bodies, over souls, and over temporal goods, used the first but did not commit it; the third he neither wished to use nor committed. Therefore the Pope has power neither over human bodies nor over bodily things, but only of binding and loosing souls. Nor, as regards souls, is he to be said to have the fullness of power except in binding and loosing, provided the key does not err. For he cannot create souls, nor infuse grace into them, nor save or damn, nor remit sins, except ministerially. He is said therefore to have fullness only in spiritual things, and not absolutely, but in comparison with the inferior prelates, who were called to share in the care.

units.la: Item, qui potest in maius, potest in minus. Sed spiritualia sunt temporalibus digniora. Ergo, &c. Respondeo, illa maior propositio, qui potest in maius, &c. veritatem habet in rebus eiusdem generis. Vt si potest Rex expugnare ciuitatem, ergo & castrum. Sed non habet veritatem diuersorum generum. Non sequitur, qui potest generare hominum, potest generare muscam. Cum igitur spiritualia & temporalia sint res diuersorum generum, non sequitur: Quod qui habet potestatem in spiritualibus, habeat eam in temporalibus. Rursus dicta propositio non tenet in illis, quae ex sola commissione vel delegatione habentur. Videmus enim quod in curiis Principum, confessoribus commissa est cura & regimen animarum, & medicis cura corporum; nec sequitur, confessor potest in maius, id est, in animas; ergo potest in minus, id est, in corpora. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Likewise, whoever can do more can do less. But spiritual things are more worthy than temporal things. Therefore, etc. I answer: that major premise, whoever can do more, etc., holds true among things of the same kind. For example, if a king can storm a city, he can therefore also storm a castle. But it does not hold true for things of different kinds. It does not follow that whoever can beget men can beget a fly. Since, therefore, spiritual and temporal things are things of different kinds, it does not follow that whoever has power over spiritual things has it over temporal things. Again, the said proposition does not hold in those things which are held only by commission or delegation. For we see that in the courts of princes the care and government of souls is committed to confessors, and the care of bodies to physicians; and it does not follow that the confessor can do more, that is, over souls, therefore he can do less, that is, over bodies. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Item prima Corinth. sexto. Nescitis quoniam Angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis saecularia? Quasi diceret, si possumus spiritualia iudicare, multo magis saecularia possumus & debemus. Ergo, &c. Respondeo, Nuper conuersos ad fidem, reprehendit Apostolus, quia pro negotiis vel controuersiis, quas inter se habebant, super rebus temporalibus; relictis vel contemptis Iudicibus Christianis, remeabant ad Iudices infidelium, quasi non haberent Christianos iudices, sufficientes de huiusmodi iudicare. Ideo ipsos arguendo, dicit Apostolus: Si habetis viros spirituales industrios, sufficientes ad iudicandum maiora & difficiliora, quanto magis sufficient iudicare minora.
units.tr: Likewise, 1 Corinthians 6: Know ye not that we shall judge angels? How much more things that pertain to this life? As if he were saying: if we can judge spiritual things, much more can and ought we to judge secular things. Therefore, etc. I answer: The Apostle rebukes those recently converted to the faith, because, on account of business or disputes which they had among themselves concerning temporal matters, they, having left aside or despised the Christian judges, returned to the judges of unbelievers, as if they had no Christian judges sufficient to decide such matters. Therefore, arguing against them, the Apostle says: If you have spiritual men of industry, sufficient to judge greater and more difficult matters, how much more are they sufficient to judge lesser ones.

units.la: Omnia praemissa & singula, dicta sunt sine praeiudicio sententiae melioris, opinando tantum, non sententiando. Licet autem multae rationes, ad primam partem adductae, sunt solubiles, & necessario non concludant, quia ad istam materiam non possunt demonstrationes adduci; tamen causa breuitatis, eas non soluimus.
units.tr: All the foregoing and each of the points have been said without prejudice to a better opinion, offering only an opinion, not pronouncing a sentence. Although, however, the many arguments adduced for the first part are solvable, and do not necessarily conclude, because demonstrations cannot be brought to bear on this matter, nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, we do not solve them.
