units.la: Explicit Quaestio praedicta edita per bon. memoriam EGIDIVM DE ROMA Ord. Fratrum Heremitarum Sancti Augustini, Sacrae Theologiae eximium Professorem ac Archiepiscopum Bituricensem, secundum quod fertur.
units.tr: Here ends the aforesaid Question, published by the good memory of GILES OF ROME, of the Order of the Hermit Friends of Saint Augustine, eminent Professor of Sacred Theology and Archbishop of Bourges, as it is reported.

units.la: FRATRIS IOHANNIS DE PARISIIS, DOCTORIS THEOLOGI, ORDINIS FRATRVM PRÆDICATORVM; Tractatus. De Potestate Regia & Papali.
units.tr: FRATRIS IOHANNIS DE PARISIIS, DOCTORIS THEOLOGI, ORDINIS FRATRVM PRÆDICATORVM; Tractatus. De Potestate Regia & Papali.

units.la: PROOEMIVM.
units.tr: PROOEMIVM.

units.la: NTERDVM contingit, quod vitare volens aliquem errorem, delabitur in errorem contrarium. Sic enim legimus 16.q.1. nonnullos asserentes quod monachi, quia mundo mortui sunt, non possunt (quia eis repugnat ratione qua monachi sunt) poenitentias dare, nec Christianitatem largiri. Quem errorem aliqui vitare volentes, vel forte ipsum praevenientes, dixerunt: Quod monachis debetur ratione qua perfectionis statum elegerunt, confessiones audire, absolvere, ac poenitentias iniungere salutares. Inter quos duos errores doctrina tamen mediat, ponens quod nec monachis repugnat, nec debetur ratione status. Sed eis convenire poterit, si eis a suis ordinariis committatur: quibus de iure debetur. Sic enim in libro de duabus naturis & una persona Christi, dicit Augustinus, quod fides medium tenet inter duos errores contrarios, scilicet Nestorii & Eutychetis. Modo consimili circa potestatem Ecclesiasticorum pontificum veritas medium ponit inter duos errores: Nam error Vualdensium fuit, successoribus Apostolorum, scilicet Papae & Prælatis Ecclesiasticis, dominium in temporalibus repugnare, nec eis licere habere divitias temporales. Unde Ecclesiam Dei, & successores Apostolorum & veros prælatos Ecclesiae Dei, durasse dicunt tantum usque ad Syluestrum papam: a quo donatione facta Ecclesiae per Constantinum Imperatorem, dicunt incepisse Romanam Ecclesiam, quae modo secundum ipsos non est Dei Ecclesia. Sed Dei Ecclesiam iam defecisse, dicunt nisi quod in ipsis est continuata, & per ipsos reparata. Ad hoc inducunt inter cætera, illud Matthaei sexto: Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra. Et illud prima Timoth. 6. Habentes alimenta, & quibus tegamur, hiis contenti simus. Et illud: Qui volunt divites fieri, & cætera. Et iterum Matth. 6. Non potestis Deo servire, & mammonae. Et ibid. Nolite sollicitari esse animae vestrae, quid manducetis, neque corpori, &c. Et illud: Respicite volatilia coeli. Et illud Matth. 9. Nolite possidere aurum, & cætera. Et illud Lucae 14. Nisi quis renunciaverit omnibus quae possidet, & cætera. Et illud Actuum tertio: Argentum & aurum non est mihi, & cætera. Ex his dicunt, prælatos Ecclesiae Dei, successores Apostolorum, non debere habere dominium in divitiis temporalibus & terrenis.
units.tr: Sometimes it happens that a man who wishes to avoid one error falls into the contrary error. For we read in 16 q. 1 that some asserted that monks, because they are dead to the world, cannot (since this conflicts with the reason why they are monks) give penances or bestow Christian fellowship. Some, wishing to avoid this error, or perhaps anticipating it, said that it belongs to monks, by reason of the state of perfection they have chosen, to hear confessions, to absolve, and to impose salutary penances. Between these two errors, however, sound doctrine takes a middle course, holding that it does not conflict with monks, nor is it due to them by reason of their state. But it can belong to them if it is committed to them by their ordinaries, to whom it is due by right. Thus Augustine, in the book on the two natures and one person of Christ, says that faith holds the middle between two contrary errors, namely those of Nestorius and Eutyches. In a similar way, concerning the power of the ecclesiastical prelates, the truth takes a middle position between two errors. For it was the error of the Waldensians that lordship in temporal affairs is incompatible with the successors of the Apostles, namely the Pope and the ecclesiastical prelates, and that it is not lawful for them to have temporal riches. Hence they say that the Church of God, and the successors of the Apostles and the true prelates of the Church of God, lasted only until Pope Sylvester; from the time of the donation made to the Church by the Emperor Constantine, they say, the Roman Church began, which according to them is now not the Church of God. They say that the Church of God has already failed, except insofar as it has been continued in them and restored through them. To support this they adduce, among other things, the passage of Matthew 6: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth. And the passage of 1 Timothy 6: Having food and covering, let us be content with these. And that: They that will be rich, etc. And again Matthew 6: You cannot serve God and mammon. And in the same place: Take no thought for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, etc. And: Behold the fowls of the air. And Matthew 9: Do not possess gold, etc. And Luke 14: Unless a man renounce all that he possesses, etc. And Acts 3: Silver and gold have I none, etc. From these they conclude that the prelates of the Church of God, the successors of the Apostles, ought not to have lordship over riches that are temporal and earthly.

units.la: Alius vero fuit error Herodis, qui audiens Christum regem natum, credidit ipsum esse regem terrenum. Ex quo deriuari videtur opinio quorundam modernorum, qui intantum supradictum error Vualdensium declinant, ad oppositum totaliter deflexi, ita ut asserant, dominum Papam, in quantum est loco Christi, in terris habere dominium in temporalib. bonis Principum & Baronum, & cognitionem seu iurisdictionem. Dicunt et, quod hanc potestatem in temporalib. habet Papa excellentius, quam princeps secularis: quia Papa habet eam secundum primariam auctoritatem, ut a Deo immediate princeps, aut habet eam a Papa mediate. Et iterum dicunt, quod Papa non habet executionem immediatam, nisi in aliquib. casib. notatis, extra, qui filii sunt legitimi. per venerabilem. princeps autem habet regulariter immediatam executionem. Et qui aliter notauerunt, locuti sunt in fauorem principum, quod verum est deserentes. Et si Papa dicit, se aliquando iurisdictionem temporalem non habere: intelligendum est, quantum ad regularem & immediatam executionem, vel quia vulpeculam principum & Ecclesiae custodire: vel ne prælati sint nimis proni ad intromittendum se de temporalib. bonis & secularib. negociis. Dicunt etiam, quod aliter se habet Papa ad bona temporalia, quam principes & prælati: & solus papa est verus Dominus temporalium, ita quod potest pro libito absoluere usurarium a debito usurae, & auferre ab alio quod alias suum est. Et tenet factum eius, licet peccet, nec debeat hoc facere nisi pro causa rationabili; id est pro defensione Ecclesiae, & aliis huiusmodi. Sed prælati cæteri & principes non sunt domini, sed tutores, procuratores & dispensatores. Hæc autem opinio quantum ad dominium in rebus, non solum ex errore Herodis nascitur: sed videtur intrare Vigilantii errorem. Nam hoc tenent omnes, & tenendum est, quod domino papæ non repugnat ratione status sui, id quod est perfectionis Euangelicæ. Constat autem, quod si papa ratione sui status, in quantum scil. papa, & Christi vicarius, est dominus omnium, abdicatio proprietatis & abiectio dominii in temporalib. ei repugnat ratione sui status, cum oppositum per se coueniat. Paupertas ergo & priuatio dominii in reb. temporalib. siue exterioris, non est perfectionis Euangelicæ, ut dicit Vigilantius: de quo dicit Augustin. in lib. de Agone Christiano, quod sunt qui quæ sua sunt quærunt, quamuis catholici: aut ex ipso Christi nomine gloriam quærentes haeretici. Ex quorum numero olim Vigilantius surrexit in Gallia, quae antea errorum monstris caruerat, paupertati diuitum status æquare præsumens, sicut olim Iouinianus in Italia matrimonium castitati. Videtur etiam haec opinio aliquid habere de supercilio Pharisaeorum, qui populum decimas & sacrificia Deo offerentem, non teneri ad censum reddendum Cæsari prædicabant, ut ab ipsis ditiorib. effecti, pinguiores reciperent portiones, ut dicit Hieron. Haec et opinio in hoc periculosa videtur, quod a conuersis ad fidem, dominium rerum, quod prius habebant, transfert in summum pontificem. Ex quo fides ipsis minus reddetur gratiosa, & ipsi fidei derogatur, cum per eam turbantur iura conditionis Christianæ, vt dicit glossa, 1. Petri 2. Ex hac etiam opinione timendum est, ne dum in domo Domini sic negotiatio ingrediatur, vt Iesus iratus & rigidus non aliter mundet templum suum, nisi flagello adhibito, & de spelunca latronum faciat domum orationis: vt dicit Chrysostomus super Matthæum.
units.tr: The other error was that of Herod, who, hearing that Christ had been born king, believed him to be an earthly king. From this error there seems to derive the opinion of certain modern writers who, while they avoid the aforesaid error of the Waldensians, have swung entirely to the opposite extreme, so that they assert that the lord Pope, insofar as he stands in the place of Christ, has lordship in earthly matters over the goods of princes and barons, together with cognizance or jurisdiction. They also say that the Pope holds this power in temporal matters in a more excellent way than the secular prince, because the Pope has it by primary authority, as a prince receiving it immediately from God, or else he has it from the Pope mediately. And again they say that the Pope does not have immediate execution except in certain noted cases, Extra, Qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem. But the prince ordinarily has immediate execution. Those who have noted otherwise have spoken in favour of princes, deserting what is true. And if the Pope says that he at some time does not have temporal jurisdiction, this must be understood with respect to regular and immediate execution, either because he is guarding the little fox of princes and the Church, or so that the prelates may not be too prone to meddle with temporal goods and secular business. They also say that the Pope stands in a different relation to temporal goods than princes and prelates do, and that the Pope alone is the true lord of temporal things, so that he may at his pleasure absolve a usurer from the debt of usury, and take from one person what is otherwise his own. And his act stands, although he sins, nor ought he to do this except for a reasonable cause, that is, for the defence of the Church and other such purposes. But the other prelates and princes are not lords, but guardians, procurators and dispensers. Now this opinion, as regards lordship over things, arises not only from the error of Herod, but seems to enter into the error of Vigilantius. For all hold, and it must be held, that it is not incompatible with the Lord Pope's state that he should embrace what belongs to evangelical perfection. But it is clear that if the Pope, by reason of his state, insofar as he is the Pope and the vicar of Christ, is lord of all things, then renunciation of property and rejection of lordship over temporal things is incompatible with his state, since the opposite is inherent in it. Poverty, then, and the deprivation of lordship over temporal things, whether external or not, do not belong to evangelical perfection, as Vigilantius says. Of this Augustine speaks in the book On the Christian Contest, that there are some who seek their own things, though they are Catholics, or heretics who seek glory from the very name of Christ. Of this number Vigilantius once arose in Gaul, which before had been free of the monsters of error, presuming to make the poverty of the rich equal in status, just as Jovinian once did in Italy with marriage and chastity. This opinion also seems to have something of the haughtiness of the Pharisees, who taught that the people offering tithes and sacrifices to God were not bound to pay tribute to Caesar, so that, made richer by them, they might receive fatter portions, as Jerome says. This opinion also seems dangerous in that it transfers to the supreme pontiff the lordship over things that converts to the faith previously held. From this the faith itself becomes less welcome to them, and is disparaged, since by it the rights of the Christian condition are disturbed, as the gloss says on 1 Peter 2. From this opinion too one must fear that, while such business enters into the house of the Lord, Jesus, angry and stern, would not otherwise cleanse his temple, unless with the scourge applied, and make of the den of robbers a house of prayer, as Chrysostom says on Matthew.

units.la: Inter has autem opiniones tam contrarias, quarum primam erroneam omnes putant: puto ego quod veritas medium ponit, scilicet quod prælatis Ecclesiæ non repugnat habere dominium in temporalibus, & iurisdictionem, contra primam opinionem. Nec debetur eis per se ratione sui status, & ratione qua sunt vicarii Iesu Christi & Apostolorum successores: sed eis convenire potest, habere talia ex concessione & permissione principum, si ab eis ex devotione aliquid fuerit collatum eis, vel si habuerint aliunde. Protestor autem, quod nihil intendo dicere cum assertione aliqua contra fidem: nec contra bonos mores, vel sanam doctrinam personæ, vel status summi pontificis reverentiam. Et si aliquid huiusmodi occurrerit inter dicta vel dicenda principaliter vel incidenter, volo pro non dicto haberi, volens hanc protestationem valere & currere, ac si eam specialiter resumerem super quolibet dicendorum.
units.tr: Among these opinions, so contrary to one another, of which everyone thinks the first is erroneous, I hold that the truth takes a middle course: namely that it is not incompatible with the prelates of the Church to have lordship over temporal things and jurisdiction, against the first opinion. Nor is this due to them per se by reason of their state, or by reason of their being vicars of Jesus Christ and successors of the Apostles; but it can belong to them to have such things by the concession and permission of princes, if something has been conferred on them out of devotion by these princes, or if they have had it from elsewhere. I protest, however, that I intend to say nothing with any assertion contrary to the faith, nor against good morals, nor against the sound doctrine of any person, nor against the reverence due to the state of the supreme pontiff. And if anything of this kind occurs among the things said or to be said, whether principally or incidentally, I wish it to be held as unsaid; and I wish this protestation to hold and to apply as if I had specially repeated it concerning each of the things to be said.

units.la: In hac autem materia ad declarationem prædictorum, sic proceditur. Primo ostendetur quid sit regnum, & unde habuerit ortum. Secundo ostendetur de sacerdotio. Tertio, de ordine ministrorum ad unum supremum. Quarto, quod sit prius tempore regnum vel sacerdotium. Quinto, quod eorum sit prius dignitate. Sexto, quod sacerdotium non est prius causalitate. Et ibi primo declarabitur, quomodo Papa se habet ad bona exteriora Ecclesiastica, quoad dominium. Septimo, quomodo ipse se habet ad bona laicorum. Octavo, quod ipse non habet iurisdictionem à Christo in bonis laicorum, & quod Christus eam non habuit. Nono, ponentur rationes ad contrarium, & solutiones earum. Decimo ostendetur, quod dato quod Christus habuit eam, tamen ipsam Petro non dedit. Undecimo ponentur quadraginta duæ rationes, dicentium quod Papa habet iurisdictionem in bonis temporalibus laicorum. Duodecimo, præmittentur aliqua ad solutionem prædictorum, & ad intelligendum quam iurisdictionem vel auctoritatem habet Papa in temporalib. bonis, & ibi ponentur auctoritates Petro & aliis Apostolis commissæ à Christo. Decimotertio ostendetur, quod illis auctoritatibus præmissis non habeat prælati Ecclesiastica iurisdictionem in temporalibus, nec ob illas principes eis in temporalibus sunt subiecti. Decimoquarto, ponentur rationes ad primum senarium rationum præmissarum. Decimoquinto, ad secundum senarium. Decimosexto, ad tertium senarium. Decimoseptimo, ad quartum. Decimooctavo, ad quintum. Decimonono, ad sextum. Vicesimo, ad septimum. Vicesimoprimo habebitur de donatione Constantini, & quid Papa propter eam possit. Vicesimosecundo ostendetur, an licitum sit de huiusmodi pertinentibus disputare & iudicare. Vicesimotertio ponentur rationes aliorum, quod Papa non possit resignare. Vicesimoquarto ostendetur, quod potest. Vicesimoquinto, soluentur rationes prædictæ.
units.tr: In this matter, to clarify what has been said, we proceed as follows. First, it will be shown what a kingdom is and whence it has its origin. Second, it will be shown concerning the priesthood. Third, concerning the order of ministers under one supreme head. Fourth, whether the kingdom or the priesthood is prior in time. Fifth, whether one of them is prior in dignity. Sixth, that the priesthood is not prior in causality. And there it will first be declared how the Pope stands with respect to the external ecclesiastical goods, as regards lordship. Seventh, how he himself stands with respect to the goods of the laity. Eighth, that he does not have jurisdiction from Christ over the goods of the laity, and that Christ did not have it. Ninth, the arguments to the contrary will be set out, and their solutions. Tenth, it will be shown that, granting that Christ had it, he nevertheless did not give it to Peter. Eleventh, forty-two arguments will be set out of those who say that the Pope has jurisdiction over the temporal goods of the laity. Twelfth, certain things will be premised for the solution of the aforesaid, and for understanding what jurisdiction or authority the Pope has over temporal goods; and there the authorities committed by Christ to Peter and the other Apostles will be set out. Thirteenth, it will be shown that, with those authorities premised, the ecclesiastical prelates do not have jurisdiction over temporal matters, nor are princes subject to them in temporal matters by reason of those authorities. Fourteenth, the answers will be set out to the first six of the aforesaid arguments. Fifteenth, to the second six. Sixteenth, to the third six. Seventeenth, to the fourth. Eighteenth, to the fifth. Nineteenth, to the sixth. Twentieth, to the seventh. Twenty-first, there will be treatment of the donation of Constantine, and what the Pope may do on account of it. Twenty-second, it will be shown whether it is lawful to dispute and judge about such matters. Twenty-third, the arguments of others will be set out that the Pope cannot resign. Twenty-fourth, it will be shown that he can. Twenty-fifth, the aforesaid arguments will be answered.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CAP. I.

units.la: Quid regnum, & unde habuit ortum.
units.tr: What a kingdom is, and whence it had its origin.

units.la: Circa primum igitur sciendum, quod regnum proprie acceptum, sic potest diffiniri. Regnum est regimen multitudinis perfecta, ad commune bonum ordinatum ab uno. In qua descriptione, regimen ponitur pro genere: multitudinis vero, ponitur ad differentiam regiminis, quo quilibet seipsum regit, vel naturali instinctu, vt contingit in brutis: vel sua ratione, vt in solitariam vitam ducentibus contingit. Perfecta ponitur, ad differentiam multitudinis domesticæ, quæ non est perfecta: quia sibi non sufficit, nisi ad modicum tempus, & non ad totam vitam, sicut ciuitas, secundum Philosophum in primo Politicorum. Ad commune bonum ordinatum, ponitur ad differentiam Tyrannidis, Oligarchiæ & Democratiæ: vbi rector solum intendit bonum suum, & præcipue in tyrannide. Ab uno vero, ponitur ad differentiam Aristocratiæ, id est principatus optimorum, seu optimatum, vbi scilicet pauci dominantur secundum virtutem. Quod regimen vocant aliqui Respónsa prudentum, vel Senatus consulta: ad differentiam Polycratiæ, vel Politiæ, vbi populus denominatur, vel plebiscita. Non est enim rex, nisi qui solus dominatur, dicente Domino per Ezechiel. cap. 37. Servus meus Dauid rex super omnes erit. Est autem tale regimen à iure naturali, & à iure gentium deriuatum. Nam cum homo sit animal naturaliter politicum seu ciuile, vt dicitur in primo Politicorum, quod secundum Philosophum oritur ex victu, vestitu, defensione, in quibus sibi solus non sufficit: & etiam ex sermone qui est ad alterum, quæ homini debentur: necesse est homini, vt in multitudine viuat, & tali multitudine quæ sibi sufficiat ad vitam. Huiusmodi autem non est communitas domus vel vici, sed ciuitatis vel regni. Nam in sola domo vel vico non inueniuntur omnia ad victum, vestitum, vel defensionem necessaria ad totam vitam, sicut in ciuitate vel regno. Omnis autem multitudo, quolibet quærente quod suum est, dissipatur, & in diuersa dispergitur: nisi ad bonum commune ordinetur per aliquem virum, qui curam habeat de bono communi: sicut corpus hominis defluceret, nisi esset aliqua vis communis in corpore, quæ ad bonum commune omnium membrorum intenderet. Propter quod Proverbiorum 11. dicitur, quod vbi non est gubernator, populus corruet. Hoc autem est necessarium, nam non est idem, quod proprium est, & quod commune est. Secundum proprium qui-dem dem differunt homines: per commune autem vtuntur, diuersorum aut diuersæ sunt causæ. Et ideo oportet, præter id quod mouet ad proprium bonum vniuscuiusque, esse aliquid quod moneat ad bonum commune multorum.
units.tr: Concerning the first point, then, it must be understood that a kingdom, taken properly, can be defined as follows: A kingdom is a perfect government of a multitude, ordered to the common good by one ruler. In this description, "government" is placed as the genus. "Of a multitude" is added to distinguish it from the government by which each person rules himself, either by natural instinct, as happens in brute animals, or by his own reason, as happens with those who lead a solitary life. "Perfect" is added to distinguish it from a household multitude, which is not perfect, because it is not sufficient for itself except for a short time and not for a whole life; a city is, according to the Philosopher in the first book of the Politics, sufficient for itself in this way. "Ordered to the common good" is added to distinguish it from tyranny, oligarchy and democracy, where the ruler intends only his own good, above all in a tyranny. "By one" is added to distinguish it from aristocracy, that is, the rule of the best or of the nobles, where a few rule according to virtue. Some call this government the "answers of the prudent" or "decrees of the senate", to distinguish it from polycracy or polity, where the people are named, or from "plebiscites". For there is no king unless he alone rules, the Lord saying through Ezekiel, chapter 37: My servant David shall be king over them all. Such government is derived from the law of nature and from the law of nations. For since man is by nature a political or civil animal, as is said in the first book of the Politics, and as the Philosopher says, arises from food, clothing and defence, in which a man is not sufficient for himself alone, and also from speech directed to another, by which the things due to man are shared, it is necessary for man to live in a multitude, and in such a multitude as can suffice for life. Now a household or a village is not such a community, but a city or a kingdom is. For in a house or a village alone one does not find all the things necessary for food, clothing or defence for a whole life, as one does in a city or kingdom. Moreover, every multitude, when each seeks what is his own, is scattered and dispersed in different directions, unless it is ordered to the common good by some man who takes care of the common good, just as the body of a man would fall apart unless there were some common power in the body directed to the common good of all the members. For this reason it is said in Proverbs 11 that where there is no governor, the people fall. This is necessary, for what is proper and what is common are not the same. Men differ according to what is their own, but they use things in common for diverse and different causes. And therefore, besides that which moves each man to his own good, there must be something which moves him to the common good of many.

units.la: Est autem vtilius regnum multitudinis, per vnum qui præest secundum virtutem, quam per plures, vel paucos virtuosos, quod patet tum ex potentia: nam in vno principante virtus est magis vnica, quam in pluribus, & ideo fortior. Tum ex vnitate & pace, quæ intendi debet in regimine multitudinis, nam plures principantes non seruant pacem multitudinis, nisi fuerint uniti & concordes. Si ergo propter vnumquodque tale, & illud magis, vt dicit Philosophus: vnus princeps seu principans secundum virtutem magis poterit seruare pacem, quam plures, & non tam de facili poterit tui bari pax omnium. Tum etiam, quia princeps vnus intendens ad bonum commune, habet oculum ad magis commune, quam si plures dominentur, etiam secundum virtutem. Et quanto plures excipiuntur, tanto residuum est minus commune: & quanto pauciores, tanto residuum est magis commune. Propter quod dicit Philosophus, quod inter principaliter intendentes suum bonum proprium, tyrannus est peior: quia magis proprium intendit, & contemnit magis commune. Tum quia in naturali regimine videmus totum ad vnum reduci, vt in mixto corpore vnum elementum dominatur: in humano corpore heterogeneo, vnum est principale membrum in toto homine, & anima continet omnia elementa: animalia etiam gregalia, vt apes, & grues, quibus naturale est in societate viuere, & obediunt naturaliter vni regi.
units.tr: Moreover, a kingdom of a multitude is more useful when it is ruled by one who presides according to virtue, than by several or a few virtuous men. This is evident, first, from power: for in one ruler virtue is more unified than in several, and therefore stronger. Second, from unity and peace, which ought to be aimed at in the government of a multitude; for several rulers do not preserve the peace of the multitude unless they are united and of one mind. If therefore each thing of this kind, and that all the more, as the Philosopher says, then one prince or ruler according to virtue will be able to preserve peace more than several, and the peace of all will not so easily be disturbed. Further, because a single prince who intends the common good has his eye on what is more common, than if several ruled, even though they are virtuous. And the more persons are set apart, the less common is what remains; and the fewer they are, the more common is what remains. For this reason the Philosopher says that among those who principally intend their own private good, the tyrant is the worst, because he intends what is more private and despises what is more common. Third, because in natural government we see the whole reduced to one, as in a compound body one element dominates; in the human body, which is made of different parts, one member is the principal member of the whole man, and the soul contains all the elements. Also gregarious animals, such as bees and cranes, which are by nature inclined to live in society, obey one king by nature.

units.la: Ex quibus patet, homini necessarium esse, & vtile, in multitudine viuere: & maxime tali quæ sufficere potest ad totam vitam: vt est ciuitas & regnum, & regio, & præcipue sub vno principante: propter bonum commune, qui rex dicitur. Et patet etiam, quod hoc regimen deriuatur non solum a iure naturali, ex eo scilicet quod homo naturaliter est animal ciuile vel politicum, & sociale in tantum, quod ante Beluß & Ninum, qui primitus regnauerunt, homines non naturaliter, nec vt homines, sed more bestiarum sine regimine viebant: vt narrat quosdam vixisse Orosius primo suo libro contra Paganos. Et Tullius consimilia dicit in principio Veteris rhetoricæ. Et Philosophus dicit de talibus in Politicis, quod non viuunt vt homines, sed vt dii vel bestiæ. Et cum per verba communia ad vitam communem naturaliter eis conuenientem (vt visum est) a vita bestiali non possent huiusmodi homines reuocari, homines magis ratione vtentes, eorum compatientes errori, ad vitam communem sub vno aliquo ordinatum, rationibus persuasoriis reuocare conati sunt, vt dicit Tullius: & ita reuocatos certis legibus ad viuendum communiter ligauerunt: quæ quidem leges hicius gentium dici possunt. Et sic patet, quod huiusmodi regimen a iure naturali & gentium deriuatur.
units.tr: From these things it is evident that it is necessary and useful for man to live in a multitude, and especially in such a multitude as can suffice for the whole of life, such as a city, a kingdom or a region, and above all under one ruler, who is called king, for the sake of the common good. And it is also evident that this government is derived not only from the law of nature, in that man is by nature a civil or political animal, and so social that, before Belus and Ninus, who first reigned, men did not live naturally, nor as men, but like beasts, without government, as Orosius relates that certain people lived, in the first book of his work against the pagans. And Tully says similar things at the beginning of his Rhetoric of old. And the Philosopher says of such people, in the Politics, that they live not as men but as gods or beasts. And since such men could not be recalled from a bestial life by common words to the common life naturally suited to them (as has been seen), men who used reason more, sympathizing with their error, tried to recall them by persuasive arguments to a common life ordered under some one ruler, as Tully says; and having been so recalled, they bound them by certain laws to live in common. These laws may indeed be called the law of nations. And thus it is evident that this kind of government is derived from the law of nature and from the law of nations.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Quid sit Sacerdotium, & unde habuit ortum.
units.tr: What the priesthood is, and whence it had its origin.

units.la: Cæterum est considerandum, quod homo non solum ordinatur ad bonum tale, quod per naturam potest acquiri, quod est viuere tantum secundum virtutem: sed ulterius ordinatur ad finem supernaturalem, quæ est vita æterna, ad quam tota hominum multitudo viuentium secundum virtutem, ordinabilis est: secundum quod patet in Symbolo fidei nostræ, & ideo oportet vnum aliquem esse, qui multitudinem fidelium dirigat ad hunc finem. Et si quidem ad hunc finem posset peruenire virtute naturæ humanæ, necessarium esset, vt ad officium regis humani pertineret, dirigere homines in hunc finem: quia hunc regem humanum diximus, cui commissa est cura summa regiminis in rebus humanis. Sed quia vitam æternam non consequetur homo per virtutem naturæ humanæ, sed diuinæ, secundum illud Apostoli Romanorum 6. Gratia Dei vita æterna: Ideo perducere ad istum finem, non est humani regiminis, sed diuini.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be considered that man is ordered not only to that good which can be acquired by nature, namely to live solely according to virtue, but further he is ordered to a supernatural end, which is eternal life, and to which the whole multitude of men living according to virtue can be directed; as is evident in the Creed of our faith. Therefore it is necessary that there be one who directs the multitude of the faithful to this end. And if indeed this end could be reached by the power of human nature, it would be necessary for it to belong to the office of the human king to direct men to this end; for we have called him the human king, to whom is committed the supreme care of government in human affairs. But because man does not attain eternal life by the power of human nature but by the divine, according to that saying of the Apostle, Romans 6: The grace of God is eternal life, therefore to lead men to that end belongs not to human but to divine government.

units.la: Ad illum igitur regem pertinet hoc regimen, qui non solum est homo, sed etiam Deus: scilicet Christus Iesus, qui homines filios Dei faciens, introducit in vitam æternam, propter quod Rex appellatur, dicente Hieremia: Regnabit rex, & sapiens erit, hoc autem regnum a Deo patre est ei creditum, quod non corrumpetur. Et quia ad curam regis pertinet, remouere impedimenta pertingendi ad finem, & conferre remedia & adiutoria perueniendi: ideo Christus seipsum offerens Deo patri, vt sacerdos simul & sacrificium, impedimentum vniuersale per mortem suam remouit, offensam scilicet Dei patris pro communi peccato generis humani. Et propter hoc sacerdos verus dictus est, pro hominib. ex hominibus assumptus, Hebræorum 5. Verum quia causam vniuersalem oportet coniungi particularibus effectibus, necessarium fuit quædam habere remedia, per quæ illud beneficium generale nobis aliquo modo iungeretur.
units.tr: Therefore this government belongs to that King who is not only man but also God, namely Christ Jesus, who, making men sons of God, brings them into eternal life; for this reason he is called King, as Jeremiah says: A king shall reign, and shall be wise; and this kingdom, which will not be corrupted, has been entrusted to him by God the Father. And because it belongs to the care of a king to remove the hindrances to attaining the end, and to supply the remedies and aids for arriving at it, therefore Christ, offering himself to God the Father as both priest and sacrifice, removed the universal hindrance through his death, namely the offence against God the Father on account of the common sin of the human race. And for this reason he is called the true priest, taken from among men on behalf of men, Hebrews 5. But because the universal cause must be joined to particular effects, it was necessary to have certain remedies through which that general benefit might be joined to us in some way.

units.la: Et illa sunt Ecclesiæ Sacramenta, in quibus specialis virtus passionis Christi continetur, sicut virtus agentis in instrumento. Et ideo ipsa esse sensibilia conueniebat, vt homini prouideretur secundum eius conditionem, quæ est, ad spiritualia & intelligibilia capienda deduci per sensibilia, secundum illud Romanorum 1. Insensibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, &c. Et vt instrumenta ista verbo incarnato (cuius vt principalis agentis virtutem continent) proportionata essent, dum spiritualem virtutem continent sensibilibus signis.
units.tr: These are the Sacraments of the Church, in which the special power of the passion of Christ is contained, as the power of the agent is contained in an instrument. And therefore it was fitting that they be sensible, so that provision might be made for man according to his condition, which is that he is led to grasp spiritual and intelligible things through sensible ones, according to that saying of Romans 1: The invisible things of God are seen through the things that are made, etc. And so that these instruments might be proportioned to the incarnate Word (whose power as principal agent they contain), they contain spiritual power in sensible signs.

units.la: Cæterum quia Christus præsentiam suam carnalem erat Ecclesiæ substracturus, necessarium fuit vt alios ministros instituerct, qui huiusmodi sacramenta hominibus ministrarent: qui ideo sacerdotes dicuntur, quasi sacra dantes, vel sacra docentes homines. Hos autem ministros ideo oportuit non angelos esse, sed homines, spiritualem virtutem sibi collatam habentes. Unde Apostolus Hebr. 5. Omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumptus est, &c. Et hoc, ut minister & ministerium convenirent, in quo est virtus spiritualis sub sensibili elemento, & causa principali salutis hominum, Verbo scilicet incarnato secundum nostram salutem, virtute & auctoritate operatur, in quantum Deus est, & homo.
units.tr: Furthermore, since Christ was about to withdraw his bodily presence from the Church, it was necessary that he appoint other ministers who would administer such sacraments to men; these are called priests, as if giving sacred things or teaching sacred things to men. It was necessary that these ministers be not angels but men, having spiritual power conferred upon them. Hence the Apostle, Hebrews 5: Every high priest is taken from among men, etc. And this so that minister and ministry might correspond, in which there is spiritual power under a sensible element, and the principal cause of the salvation of men, namely the Word incarnate, for our salvation, works by power and authority, insofar as he is God and man.

units.la: Ex his patet, quod sacerdotium definiri potest in hunc modum: Sacerdotium est spiritualis potestas Ecclesiae, ministris Ecclesiae a Christo collata, ad dispensandum fidelibus sacramenta.
units.tr: From these things it is evident that the priesthood can be defined in this manner: The priesthood is the spiritual power of the Church, conferred by Christ upon the ministers of the Church, for dispensing the sacraments to the faithful.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De ordine Ministrorum ad unum summum: quod non est necesse omnes principes ad unum reduci, sicut ministros Ecclesiae ad unum supremum.
units.tr: On the ordering of ministers under one supreme head: that it is not necessary for all princes to be reduced to one, as the ministers of the Church are reduced to one supreme head.

units.la: Æterum quia secundum Apostolum 2. Corinth. 3. haec potestas data est Ecclesiae ad aedificationem: oportet hanc potestatem tamdiu durare in Ecclesia, quamdiu ecclesia aedificatione indiget, scilicet usque ad finem mundi. Et ideo sic fuit data primo Christi discipulis, ut per eos derivari posset ad alios. Inter quos oportet esse aliquos ministros superiores & perfectos, qui huiusmodi sacerdotium aliis conferant ordinando & consecrando.
units.tr: Moreover, since according to the Apostle (2 Cor. 3) this power has been given to the Church for building up, it must last in the Church as long as the Church needs building up, that is, until the end of the world. And so it was first given to Christ's disciples, so that it could be passed down through them to others. Among these there must be some superior and perfect ministers, who confer this priesthood on others by ordaining and consecrating them.

units.la: Et hi sunt episcopi superintendentes: qui licet non excedant simplices sacerdotes, quantum ad verum corpus Christi consecrandum: excedunt tamen in iis quae sunt ad fidem, vel fideles. Nam episcopi sunt sacerdotes magni, & perfecti: quia possunt alios facere sacerdotes, quod non possunt simplices & inferiores. Et quidquid arduum circa fidelem populum est agendum, episcopis reservatur: quorum auctoritate, etiam sacerdotes possunt id quod illis committitur. Et in his quae sacerdotes agunt, utuntur rebus ab episcopis consecratis: ut calice, altari & palliis, ut dicit Dionysius de Ecclesiastica hierar. cap. de Sacerdotalibus perfectionibus. Manifestum est autem, quod licet populi distinguantur per diversas dioeceses & civitates, in quibus praesunt episcopi diversi in spiritualibus: tamen una est omnium fidelium Ecclesia, & unus populus Christianus. Et ideo, sicut in qualibet dioecesi est unus episcopus, qui est caput Ecclesiae in illo loco vel populo: ita in tota Ecclesia, & in toto populo Christiano, est unus summus episcopus, Papa scilicet Romanus, Petri successor: ut sic Ecclesia militans per similitudinem a triumphante deriuetur, ubi unus praesidet, qui praesidet toti universo, Apoc. 21. Ipsi populus eius erunt, & ipse Deus cum eis erit eorum Deus. & Ioelis 1. Congregabuntur filii Iuda, & filii Israel pariter, ut ponant sibi caput unum. Iohan. 10. Fiet unum ovile, & unus pastor. quod quidem de Christo intelligi non potest, sed de aliquo alio ministro qui praesit loco eius. Nam post corporalem subtractionem praesentiae corporalis Christi, convenit interdum circa ea quae sunt fidei, quaestiones moveri, in quibus propter diversitatem opinionum vel sententiarum divideretur Ecclesia: quae ad sui unitatem requirit fidei unitatem, nisi per unius sententiam Ecclesiae unitas servaretur. Hic autem principatum huiusmodi habens, est Petrus, successorque eius: non quidem synodali ordinatione, sed ex ore Domini qui Ecclesiae suae noluit deficere in necessariis ad salutem, ipso dicente Iohannis ultimo, ante ascensionem, Petro singulariter: Pasce oves meas, & Lucae 22. ante passionem: Et tu aliquando conversus, confirma fratres tuos. Hunc autem ordinem ad unum supremum magis invenimus inter ministros Ecclesiae, quam inter principes seculares: quia ministri Ecclesiastici divino cultui specialiter deputati sunt Domino, tanquam populus peculiaris. Et ideo ex divino statuto est ordo omnium ministrorum ad unum. Non sic autem fideles laici sic habent ex iure divino, quod subsint in temporalibus uni monarchae supremo: sed ex naturali instinctu, qui ex Deo est, habent, quod civiliter & in communitate vivant: & per consequens, ut ad bene vivendum in communi rectores eligant diversos quidem, secundum diversitates communitatum. Quod autem ad unam supremam hierarchiam in temporalibus reducantur, nec ex inclinatione naturali, nec ex iure divino habent: nec eis convenit ita, sicut ministris Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: These are the bishops, the superintendents. Although they do not exceed simple priests in consecrating the true body of Christ, they do excel in matters pertaining to the faith, or to the faithful. For bishops are great and perfect priests, because they can make other priests, which simple and lower priests cannot. Whatever is arduous to be done concerning the faithful people is reserved to the bishops, and priests can do what is committed to them only by the bishops' authority. In what priests do, they use things consecrated by bishops, such as the chalice, the altar and the altar-cloths, as Dionysius says in the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, in the chapter "On the sacerdotal perfections." It is clear, however, that although peoples are distinguished by different dioceses and cities, over which different bishops preside in spiritual matters, yet the Church of all the faithful is one, and there is one Christian people. Therefore, just as in each diocese there is one bishop, who is the head of the Church in that place or people, so in the whole Church and the whole Christian people there is one supreme bishop, namely the Roman Pope, the successor of Peter. Thus the Church militant is modelled, by likeness, on the Church triumphant, where one presides who presides over the whole universe (Rev. 21): "They shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, their God." And (Joel 1): "The children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head." (John 10): "There shall be one fold and one shepherd." This cannot be understood of Christ, but of some other minister who presides in his place. For after the bodily withdrawal of Christ's bodily presence, it sometimes happens that questions arise concerning matters of faith, over which the Church would be divided by the diversity of opinions or judgments; and its unity requires unity of faith, unless the unity of the Church were preserved by the judgment of one. Now the one who holds this kind of primacy is Peter and his successor: not by synodal ordinance, but from the mouth of the Lord, who did not wish his Church to fail in what is necessary for salvation. The Lord himself said to Peter alone, at the end of John, before the ascension: "Feed my sheep," and in Luke 22, before the passion: "And you, when once you have turned, strengthen your brothers." We find this ordering under one supreme head more among the ministers of the Church than among secular princes, because ecclesiastical ministers are specially set apart for the Lord's divine worship, as a peculiar people. Therefore, by divine statute, all ministers are ordered under one. The lay faithful, however, do not have this by divine right, that they should be subject in temporal matters to one supreme monarch. By natural instinct, which comes from God, they have it that they live civilly and in community, and consequently, to live well in common, they choose rulers, indeed different ones according to the diversity of communities. But that they should be reduced into one supreme hierarchy in temporal matters, they have neither from natural inclination nor from divine right, nor does it befit them as it befits ecclesiastical ministers.

units.la: Primo quidem, quia sicut in hominibus est diversitas magna ex parte corporum, non autem ex parte animarum, cum omnes sint in eodem gradu essentiali constitutae, propter unitatem speciei humanae: ita seculares potestas plus habet diversitatis secundum secularitatem, & complexionum diversitatem, quam spiritualis, quae minus in talibus variatur. Unde non oportet esse tantam uniustatem in una, sicut in alia.
units.tr: First, because among human beings there is great diversity in their bodies, but not in their souls, since all are constituted in the same essential grade, on account of the unity of the human species. So secular power has more diversity, according to worldly condition and the diversity of temperaments, than spiritual power, which varies less in such matters. Hence there need not be as much unity in the one as in the other.

units.la: Secundo, quia non tantum sufficit unus ad dominandum toti mundo in temporalibus, sicut unus sufficit in spiritualibus: quia potestas spiritualis censuram suam transmutare potest facilitem ad omnes, tam propinquos quam remotos, cum sit verbalis, non potestas secularis, gladium suum cum effectu transmittere tam faciliter potest ad remotos, cum sit manualis, facilius enim est verbum extendere, quam manum.
units.tr: Second, because one alone is not enough to rule the whole world in temporal matters, as one suffices in spiritual matters. Spiritual power can easily send its censure to all, both near and far, since it is verbal; secular power, which is manual, cannot so easily send its sword with effect to distant places. For it is easier to extend a word than a hand.

units.la: Tertio, quia temporalia laicorum non sunt communitatis, sed quilibet est dominus suae rei, tanquam per suam industriam acquisitae, ut infra patebit: & ideo non indigent dispensatore communi, sed quilibet suae rei sit ad libitum dispensator. Bona vero Ecclesiastica communitati sunt collata, ut videbitur infra: & ideo oportet quod sit aliquis unus qui communitati praesit, ut bonorum omnium tum um communis dispensator, non ergo tantum conuenit quod praesit aliquis vnus toti mundo in temporalibus laicorum, sicut in temporalibus clericorum.
units.tr: Third, because the temporal goods of laymen are not held in common, but each is master of his own property, as acquired by his own industry, as will appear below. Therefore they do not need a common steward, but each may be his own steward of his property at will. Ecclesiastical goods, however, have been conferred on the community, as will be seen below. Therefore there must be some one who presides over the community, as the steward of all goods in common. So it is not as fitting that one should preside over the whole world in the temporal affairs of laymen as in the temporal affairs of clerics.

units.la: Quarto, quia omnes fideles conueniunt in vna fide catholica, sine qua non est salus: & saepe conueniunt multae quaestiones oriri de pertinentibus ad salutem seu fidem in diuersis regionibus, sicut regnis. Et ideo ne propter diuersitatem controuersiarum vnitas fidei destruatur, necesse est (vt dictum est) vnum esse superiorem in spiritualibus, per cuius sententiam controuersiae terminentur. Sic autem non est necesse omnes fideles vniri, in aliqua re publica communi: sed possunt secundum diuersitatem climatum, regionum & conditionum hominum, esse diuersi modi viuendi, & diuersae Politiae: & quod est virtuosum in vna gente, non est virtuosum in alia. Sicut de singulis personis dicit Philosophus in secundo Ethicorum, quod aliquid est vni parum, quod alii est nimium. Sicut quod est nimium magistro gymnasiorum, scilicet comedere decem minas seu uncias, esset parum Miloni, qui scilicet vno ictu de pugno, taurum victimam faciebat, vt dicit Commentator. Non est ergo sic necesse mundum regi per vnum in temporalibus, sicut necesse est quod regatur per vnum in spiritualibus: nec ita trahitur a iure naturali, vel diuino. Unde Philosophus in Politicis dicit, generationem regni esse naturalem in singulis ciuitatibus vel regionibus, non autem imperii vel monarchiae.
units.tr: Fourth, because all the faithful agree in one catholic faith, without which there is no salvation; and often many questions arise concerning matters pertaining to salvation or faith in different regions, as in different kingdoms. Therefore, lest the unity of faith be destroyed by the diversity of controversies, it is necessary (as has been said) that there be one superior in spiritual matters, by whose judgment controversies are settled. But it is not necessary for all the faithful to be united in one common commonwealth. Rather, according to the diversity of climates, regions and conditions of men, there can be diverse ways of living and diverse polities, and what is virtuous in one nation is not virtuous in another. As the Philosopher says of individual persons in the second book of the Ethics, something is too little for one person which is too much for another. What is too much for the master of the gymnasium, namely to eat ten minae or ounces, would be too little for Milo, who, as the Commentator says, killed a bull with a single blow of his fist. It is not therefore necessary for the world to be ruled by one in temporal matters, as it is necessary that it be ruled by one in spiritual matters; nor is it derived from natural or divine law in this way. Hence the Philosopher in the Politics says that the generation of a kingdom is natural in individual cities or regions, but not of an empire or monarchy.

units.la: Augustinus etiam quarto de Ciuitate Dei dicit, quod melius & magis pacifice regebatur respublica, cum vniuscuiusque, vel vnumquodque regimen suae patriae terminis finiebatur. Et ibidem etiam dicit, quod causa destructionis imperii Romani fuit ambitio propria dominandi, vel prouocans alienas iniurias: & sic non ita trahitur a iure naturali, quod in temporalibus sit vnus monarcha, sicut in spiritualibus. Nec huic obuiat, quod 7. quaest. 1. In apibus, vbi dicitur quod vnus debet praesse, & non plures: quia ibi loquitur de re vna, vbi non expedit plures ex indistincto dominari: sicut ostendit de Remo & Romulo, qui simul & ex indistincto dominabantur: & ideo vnus in alium fratricidium commisit. Similiter ibidem ostenditur per alia exempla.
units.tr: Augustine too, in the fourth book of The City of God, says that the commonwealth was governed better and more peacefully when the rule of each people was confined within the borders of its own homeland. In the same place he also says that the cause of the destruction of the Roman empire was the proper ambition to dominate, which provoked foreign injuries. So it is not derived from natural law that in temporal matters there should be one monarch, as in spiritual matters. Nor does it stand in the way of this that the decree (7 q. 1, "In apibus") says that one ought to rule and not several. There it speaks of a single thing, where it is not expedient for several to rule indistinctly together, as it shows with Remus and Romulus, who ruled together and indistinctly, and therefore the one committed fratricide upon the other. Similarly, the same place shows this by other examples.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Quid sit prius, Regnum vel Sacerdotium:
units.tr: Which came first, the kingdom or the priesthood?

units.la: NVnc videndum est, quid prius fuit tempore, regnum vel sacerdotium. Ad quod sciendum est, quod de regno loquendo proprie, prout nominant regimen non solum domus, vel vici ciuitatis, sed prouinciae, in qua inuenitur maxime sufficientia eorum, quae pertinent ad totam vitam. Et loquendo de sacerdotio proprie, prius fuit tempore regnum sacerdotio. Nam vt ait Aug. 16. de Ciuitate, cap. 17. primum regnorum fuit regnum Assyriorum, quod longe ante datam legem incepit: quia in Assyria primo regnauit Belus, scilicet 65. annis, quo defuncto, filius eius Ninus regnum amplians per totam Asiam maiorem, etiam in India regnauit 52. annis, 43. annos habens in regno, quando natus est Abraham, anno qui erat circiter 1200. ante Vrbem conditam. Simul ergo cum isto regno incepit regnum Sicyoniorum in Graecia, quod in sui principio non fuit tantum: cuius primus rex fuit Egyaleus, cuius filius fuit Europs.
units.tr: Now we must consider which came first in time, the kingdom or the priesthood. To answer this, it should be understood that, speaking strictly of a kingdom, as the term denotes the government not only of a household or a village or city, but of a province, in which the sufficiency of all things pertaining to the whole of life is found in greatest measure. And speaking strictly of the priesthood, the kingdom came before the priesthood in time. For, as Augustine says in book 16 of the City of God, chapter 17, the first of the kingdoms was the kingdom of the Assyrians, which began long before the giving of the Law. For Belus reigned first in Assyria, for 65 years; when he died, his son Ninus extended the kingdom through all of Greater Asia, and also reigned in India for 52 years, having been 43 years in the kingdom when Abraham was born, in a year which was about 1200 before the founding of the City. Therefore, at the same time as this kingdom began, the kingdom of the Sicyonians in Greece began, which at its beginning was not great. Its first king was Egialeus, whose son was Europs.

units.la: Eodem tempore inueniturde Deum verum colentibus, rex Salem Melchisedech: quem Hebraei dicunt Sem, filium Noe: & dicunt eum vixisse vsq; ad Isaac.
units.tr: At the same time is found, among those who worshipped the true God, King Salem, Melchizedek, whom the Hebrews say was Shem, the son of Noah; and they say he lived until Isaac.

units.la: His autem temporibus iamdudum ante veris regibus existentibus, nondum erat sacerdotium, nec fuit vsq; ad Mediatorem Dei & hominum Christum Iesum. Quod ex hoc patet. Nam apud gentiles si qui sacerdotes dicebantur, non erant veri sacerdotes: quia nec sacrificia offerebant vero Deo, sed aestimato. Deut. 32. Immolauerunt daemoniis, & non Deo.
units.tr: But in these times, when true kings had long since existed, there was not yet a priesthood, nor was there one until the Mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus. This is clear from the following. For among the Gentiles, if any were called priests, they were not true priests, because they did not offer sacrifices to the true God, but to imagined gods. Deut. 32. They sacrificed to demons, and not to God.

units.la: Si vero aliqui Leuitici generis sub lege in Dei populo dicebantur sacerdotes, non erant veri sacerdotes, sed figura verorum sacerdotum, & eorum sacrificium tantummodo figurale: & sacramenta eorum non erant vera, sed figuralia: eo quod a peccato non mundabant: nec coelum aperiebant, sed figurabant, mundando quasdam irregularitates, & aperiendo templum manufactum, per quod apertio templi non manufactiper Iesum Christum figurabatur, nec promittebant spiritualia, nisi sub specie temporalium: secundum quod dicit Apostolus Hebraeorum 11. Vmbram habet lex futurorum bonorum.
units.tr: But if some of the Levitical stock under the Law were called priests among God's people, they were not true priests but figures of true priests, and their sacrifice was merely figurative; and their sacraments were not true but figurative, because they did not cleanse from sin, nor did they open heaven, but only foreshadowed it, cleansing certain ceremonial impurities and opening the temple made with hands. By this opening of the temple made with hands, the opening of the temple not made with hands through Jesus Christ was foreshadowed; nor did they promise spiritual things except under the appearance of temporal ones, as the Apostle says in Hebrews 11. The law has a shadow of the good things to come.

units.la: Ante regem vero inuenitur Melchisedech, sacerdos Dei summi: cuius sacerdotium licet persectius & praestantius esset sacerdotio Leuitico, tamen solum fuit figurale, & non verum. Erat enim perfectius, quia Christi repraesentabat sacerdotium: quantum ad illud, in quo excellebat sacerdotium Christi, sacerdotium Aaron: & sacerdotium Aaron in significando deficiebat a sacerdotio Christi, scilicet quantum ad perpetuitatem: quia non legitur in Scriptura, Melchisedech habere initium vel finem, sicut nec Christus habuit. Et quantum ad multa quae ponit Apostolus Hebraeorum 5. (sed tamen tantum erat figurale, & non verum sicut nec sacerdotium Leuiticum.
units.tr: Before the king, however, we find Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God. His priesthood, although it was more perfect and excellent than the Levitical priesthood, was nevertheless only figurative and not true. For it was more perfect, because it represented the priesthood of Christ, in respect of that in which the priesthood of Christ excelled the priesthood of Aaron; and the priesthood of Aaron, in signifying, fell short of the priesthood of Christ, namely in respect of perpetuity, since it is not read in Scripture that Melchizedek had a beginning or an end, just as Christ had none. And in many respects which the Apostle sets out in Hebrews 5. (but nonetheless it was only figurative, and not true, just as the Levitical priesthood was not).

units.la: Accipiendo ergo verum sacerdotium, non fuit sacerdotium vsque ad mediatorem Dei & hominum Christum Iesum, cuius sacerdotii participes nos effecit.
units.tr: Taking therefore the true priesthood, there was no priesthood until the Mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus, whose priesthood he made us share in.

units.la: Ab aeuo igitur Abraham, ante cuius nativitatem fuerunt reges Assyriorum, Sicyoniorum, Aegyptiorum, & alii quidam, fluxerunt vsque ad Christum, secundum Methodium, duo millia annorum: vel secundum alios, 1150. Manifestum est, ante verum sacerdotium, regnum duratione temporis fuisse: & roges veri erant (licet cum hoc illi qui vngebantur in propositο Dei Christum figurarent) cum officium eorum esset ad vitae humanae ciuilemnecessitatem, sicut modo.
units.tr: From the age of Abraham, before whose birth there were the kings of the Assyrians, the Sicyonians, the Egyptians, and certain others, the kingdoms flowed on until Christ, according to Methodius, for two thousand years, or according to others, 1150. It is clear that before the true priesthood, kingship had existed for a length of time; and the kings were true (although those who were anointed, in God's purpose, also prefigured Christ), since their office was for the civil necessity of human life, as it is now.

units.la: Est tamen sciendum, quod si sacerdotium acciperetur large & improprie, prout legalis sacerdos, vel quilibet alius figuralis vel aestimatiuus sacerdos dicebatur, simul currit & cadit sacerdotium cum regno. Nam in numero Deum colentium Melchisedech simul fuit rex Salem, & sacerdos Dei summi: & ab ipso secundum Hebraeos, & secundum Magistrum inhisferiis, per primogenitos continuatum est sacerdotium vsque ad Aaron.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that if the priesthood were taken broadly and improperly, in the sense in which a legal priest, or any other figurative or imagined priest, was called a priest, then priesthood and kingship would run and fall together. For among the number of those who worshipped God, Melchizedek was at once king of Salem and priest of the Most High God; and from him, according to the Hebrews, and according to the Master of Histories in his histories, the priesthood was continued through the firstborn down to Aaron.

units.la: Iste autem Melchisedech secundum Hebraeos genuit Arphaxat, duobus annis post diluuium, & fluxerunt a diluuio vsque ad septuagesimum annum vitae Abrahae, quando prima promissio ei facta est (vt habetur Genesis 12. secundum planum literae) anni 470. vel secundum alios, 430.
units.tr: Now this Melchizedek, according to the Hebrews, begot Arphaxad two years after the flood; and from the flood to the seventieth year of Abraham's life, when the first promise was made to him (as is found in Genesis 12, according to the plain sense of the letter), there were 470 years, or according to others, 430.

units.la: Apud alios vero, imo simpliciter, primum regnum olim fuit regnum Assyriorum, vt supra dictum est: cuius primus rex fuit Belus. Nullus autem filius eius, ei succedens in regno, patre defuncto idolum fecit nominatum Bel: a quo denominata sunt idola caetera prouinciarum, vt Beelphegor, Beelzebut, & alia huiusmodi: instituitque sacerdotes siue flamines, per quos sacrificia eis offerebantur.
units.tr: But according to others, indeed simply, the first kingdom was long ago the kingdom of the Assyrians, as has been said above; its first king was Belus. Now none of his sons, succeeding him in the kingdom, after his father's death made an idol called Bel; from him the other idols of the provinces were named, such as Baal-peor, Beelzebub, and others of this kind; and he instituted priests or flamens, through whom sacrifices were offered to them.

units.la: Ex his satis patet, regnum concurrisse cum sacerdotio, sic accepto, scilicet aestimato, vel figurali: diu tamen regnum praecessisse sacerdotium verum.
units.tr: From these things it is sufficiently clear that the kingdom coincided with the priesthood, taken in this way, namely the imagined or figurative priesthood; yet the kingdom long preceded the true priesthood.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: Quid sit prius dignitate, regnum vel sacerdotium.
units.tr: Which is prior in dignity, the kingdom or the priesthood.

units.la: EX praedictis patere potest de facili, quid sit prius dignitate, regnum vel sacerdotium. Nam quod posterius est tempore, solet prius esse dignitate, vt perfectum imperfecto, & finis eo quod est ad finem. Et ideo dicimus, potestatem sacerdotalem maiorem esse potestate regali, & ipsam praecellere dignitate: quia hoc semper repertimus, quod illud ad quod pertinet vltimus finis, perfectius est & melius, & dirigit illud ad quod pertinet interior finis. Regnum vero ad hoc ordinatum est, vt multitudo congregata viuat secundum virtutem, vt supra dictum est. Et cum hoc vlterius sacerdotium ordinatur ad altiorem finem, qui est Dei fruitio, cuius directionis cura credita est Christo, cuius vicarii & ministri sunt sacerdotes: & ideo dignior est potestas sacerdotalis regali potestate. Et hoc conceditur communiter, 96. distinctione, capitulo, duo quippe sunt: Non tam preciosius est aurum plumbo, quam regia potestate ordo sacerdotalis est altior. Et extra, de maioritate & obedientia, capit. Solita, dicitur: quia praeferuntur spiritualia temporalibus, sicut sol luna, sic & caetera. Et Hugo de sancto Victore, libro secundo de Sacramentis, parte secunda, capitulo quarto, ait sic: Quantum vita spiritualis dignior est quam terrena, & spiritus quam corpus: ita potestas secularis terrenam potestatem honore & dignitate praecellit. Et Bernardus ad Eugenium Papam, capitulo primo: Quae nam tibi videtur dignitas & potestas, dimittendi peccata, aut praedia diuidendi: sed non est comparatio; quasi dicat: Maior est potestas spiritualis, ea ergo dignitate praecellit. Nec tamen si principe maior est sacerdos dignitate, & simpliciter oportet quod eo sit maior in omnibus. Non enim sic se habet potestas secularis minor ad potestatem spiritualem maiorem, quod ex ea oriatur vel deriuetur: sicut se habet potestas proconsulis ad Imperatorem, qui eo maior est in omnibus, quia potestas sua ab eo derivatur. Sed se habet sicut potestas patris familias ad potestatem magistri militum, quarum vna non est deriuata ab alia, sed ambae a quadam superiori potestate. Et ideo in aliquibus potestas secularis maior est potestate spirituali, scilicet in temporalibus: nec quo ad ista, est ei subiecta in aliquo, quia ab illa non oritur: sed ambae oriuntur ab vna suprema potestate, scilicet diuina immediate: propter quod inferior non est omnino subiecta superiori, sed in his solum in quibus suprema subiecit eam maiori.
units.tr: From what has been said, it can easily be seen which is prior in dignity, the kingdom or the priesthood. What comes later in time is usually prior in dignity, as the perfect is prior to the imperfect and the end to the means to the end. So we say that the priestly power is greater than the royal power and surpasses it in dignity, because we always find that the thing to which the ultimate end pertains is more perfect and better, and directs the thing to which the lesser end pertains. The kingdom is ordained so that the gathered multitude may live according to virtue, as was said above. Furthermore, the priesthood is ordained to a higher end, which is the enjoyment of God, and the care of directing men to it has been entrusted to Christ, whose vicars and ministers the priests are. Therefore the priestly power is more worthy than the royal power. This is commonly granted in Distinctio 96, chapter Duo quippe sunt: Gold is not so much more precious than lead as the sacerdotal order is higher than royal power. And in the Extravagants, de maioritate et obedientia, cap. Solita, it is said that spiritual things are preferred to temporal things, as the sun is to the moon, and so on. Hugh of St. Victor, in the second book of De Sacramentis, part two, chapter four, says this: As the spiritual life is more worthy than the earthly, and the spirit than the body, so secular power surpasses earthly power in honour and dignity. And Bernard, to Pope Eugene, chapter one: What dignity and power do you think it is to forgive sins, or to divide estates? But there is no comparison; as if to say: the spiritual power is greater, and therefore surpasses in dignity. Yet even if the priest is greater than the prince in dignity, it does not follow that he must be greater than him in all things. For the lesser secular power does not stand in relation to the greater spiritual power in such a way that it arises from it or is derived from it, as the power of a proconsul stands to that of the Emperor, who is greater than him in all things because his power is derived from the Emperor. Rather, it stands as the power of the head of a household stands to the power of a master of soldiers, neither of which is derived from the other, but both from some higher power. Therefore in some matters the secular power is greater than the spiritual power, namely in temporal affairs; nor in those matters is it subject to the spiritual power in any way, because it does not arise from it. Both arise from one supreme power, namely the divine power immediately. For this reason the inferior is not wholly subject to the superior, but only in those things in which the supreme power has subjected it to the greater.

units.la: Quis enim diceret, quod quia doctor literarum, vel instructor morum, ordinat omnes de domo ad nobiliorem finem, scilicet ad cognitionem veritatis: ideo & medicus, qui respicit inferiorem finem, scilicet corporum sanitatem, sit ei subiectus, in suis medicinalibus propinandis. Hoc enim non oportet, cum paterfamilias, qui vtrumque in domo constituit, eum, quo ad hoc, non suppose-rit ei.
units.tr: For who would say that, because a teacher of letters or an instructor of morals orders everyone in the household to a nobler end, namely the knowledge of truth, therefore the physician, who looks to a lower end, namely the health of bodies, is subject to him in administering his medicines? This does not follow, since the head of the household, who appoints both within the house, has not placed the one under the other in this respect.

units.la: Est ergo sacerdos in spiritualibus maior principe, & e contrario in temporalibus princeps maior sacerdote: licet simpliciter sacerdos maior sit, quantum spirituale maius est temporali.
units.tr: The priest is therefore greater than the prince in spiritual matters, and conversely the prince is greater than the priest in temporal matters; although, simply speaking, the priest is greater, inasmuch as the spiritual is greater than the temporal.

units.la: Et hoc etiam ostendunt exempla praedictarum auctoritatum. Nam licet aurum sit preciosius plumbo, tamen plumbum non est ex auro causaliter. Hoc etiam expresse dicitur secunda; quaestione septima: nos si incompetenter. Est tamen considerandum, quod illud quod dictum est, intelligatur de vero sacerdotio Christi. Nam sacerdotium gentilium, & totus diuinus cultus eorum erat propter temporalia bona, quae ordinantur ad bonum commune multitudinis, cuius cura regi incumbit. Et ideo sacerdotes gentilium regibus subdebantur, & maius erat sacerdotio regnum: sicut superior est potestas cui incumbit cura de communi bono, quam potestas cui solum incumbit cura de particulari. Similiter in veteri lege sacerdotium solum bona temporalia promittebat immediate, licet non a daemonibus, sed a vero Deo exhibenda. Ideo etiam in veteri lege sacerdotium indignius erat potestate regia, & ei subiectum: quia per sacerdotem non dirigebatur rex ad aliquid alicuius bono multitudinis, cuius cura sibi incumbebat, è conuerso autem est in noua lege. Est autem considerandum, quod mirabiliter ex diuina prouidentia factum est, quod in urbe Romana, quam Deus praeuiderat fore principalem Christiani sacerdotii sedem, iste mos paulatim inualuit ut ciuitatis rectores (etsi non ex debito iustitiae, cum simpliciter essent maiores sacerdotibus) plusquam in caeteris locis voluntarie se subdebant: dicente Valerio, Omnia post religiones ponenda semper nostra ciuitas duxit, etiam in quibus summae maiestatis conspici decus voluit, quapropter non dubitauerunt sacris imperiis seruire: ita se futura humanarum rerum regimen aestimantia, si diuina potentia bene atque constanter fuissent famulata. Quod, quia futurum erat ut in Francia plurimum vigeret religio sacerdotii Christiani, diuinitus est prouisum, quod etiam apud Gallos, gentiles sacerdotes (quos Druydes nominabant) totum Gallicum bellum definirent, ut scripsit Iulius Caesar de Gallico bello. Est igitur Christi sacerdotium dignius regia potestate.
units.tr: The examples of the authorities cited also show this. For although gold is more precious than lead, lead is not caused by gold. This is also expressly stated in secunda, quaestione septima: Nos si incompetenter. It must be considered, however, that what has been said is to be understood of the true priesthood of Christ. For the priesthood of the Gentiles, and their whole divine worship, was for the sake of temporal goods, which are ordered to the common good of the multitude, the care of which falls to the king. Therefore the priests of the Gentiles were subject to the kings, and the kingdom was greater than the priesthood, just as the power to which the care of the common good belongs is higher than the power to which only the care of particular good belongs. Likewise, under the old law the priesthood promised only temporal goods immediately, though these were to be provided not by demons but by the true God. Therefore also under the old law the priesthood was less worthy than the royal power and subject to it, because the king was not directed by the priest to anything for the good of the multitude, the care of which was incumbent on him; the reverse is true under the new law. Now it must be considered that it was wonderfully brought about by divine providence that in the city of Rome, which God foresaw would be the principal seat of the Christian priesthood, the custom gradually prevailed that the rulers of the city (though not from any debt of justice, since they were simply greater than the priests) submitted themselves more willingly than in other places. As Valerius says: Our city has always considered all things to be placed after religion, even those in which it wished the honour of the highest majesty to be seen; therefore they did not hesitate to serve sacred commands, judging that the government of human affairs would be secure if they had served divine power well and steadfastly. Because it was to come about that the religion of the Christian priesthood would flourish greatly in France, it was divinely provided that even among the Gauls the pagan priests (whom they called Druids) should settle the whole Gallic war, as Julius Caesar wrote in de Gallico bello. The priesthood of Christ is therefore more worthy than royal power.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Quod sacerdotium non est prius regno causalitate: & quomodo se habet Papa a- d exteriora bona Ecclesiastica, quoad dominium.
units.tr: That the priesthood is not prior to the kingdom in causality, and how the Pope stands with regard to external ecclesiastical goods, as to ownership.

units.la: ET quia aliqui praeminentiam sacerdotii super regiam potestatem vel dignitatem in tantum extollere volunt, ut dicant sacerdotium non prius solum dignitate, sed etiam causalitate: & potestatem secularem in sacerdotali contineri, & ab ea institui: restat ostendendum, quomodo Papa, qui supremum locum tenet inter Christi sacerdotes, habeat vel non habeat potestatem. Vbi primo ostendetur, quomodo se habeat ad bona exteriora, quoad diuinis in rebus. Secundo, dato quod non sit verus dominus exteriorum bonorum, sed dispensator simpliciter, vel in casu: an saltem habeat radicalem primariam auctoritatem, ut superior, & ut iurisdictionem exercens.
units.tr: Since some wish to raise the pre-eminence of the priesthood above the royal power or dignity so high that they say the priesthood is prior not only in dignity but also in causality, and that secular power is contained within the priestly and instituted by it, it remains to show how the Pope, who holds the highest place among Christ's priests, has or does not have power. Here it will first be shown how he stands with regard to external goods, as far as concerns divine things. Second, granting that he is not the true owner of external goods but simply a dispenser, or a dispenser in certain cases, it will be asked whether he at least has a primary radical authority, as a superior and as one who exercises jurisdiction.

units.la: Circa primum igitur, sciendum est primo, quomodo se habeat ad bona temporalia Ecclesiasticarum personarum, ut Ecclesiasticae sunt. Ad quod sciendum, quod bona Ecclesiastica, ut Ecclesiastica sunt, collata sunt communitatibus ecclesiarum, seu ipsis ecclesiis, & non personae singulari: ita quod in bonis Ecclesiasticis nulla persona singularis habet proprietatem & dominium, sed sola communitas: ut Ecclesia Carnotensis, vel alia huiusmodi est, habens dominium & potestatem in ipsis bonis, ut sibi propriis. Persona autem singularis, non ut singularis, sed ut pars & membrum communitatis, habet in ipsis ius vtendi ad sustentationem, secundum exigentiam & decentiam personae suae, & status: in quo tamen est differentia, quia est aliquod membrum simplex ut simplex canonicus: & illud non habet nisi vsum. Et est aliquod membrum, quod est principale & caput totius communitatis, ut episcopus, nam non esset congregatio vna, nec ordinata, nisi esset vnum caput & membrum principale, & illud non solum habet vsum in bonis communitatis secundum exigentiam sui status, modo praedicto: sed habet administrationem & dispensationem generalem omnium bonorum communitatis, approprians cuilibet quod ei debetur, secundum debitam iustitiae proportionem: dispensans etiam pro communi bono collegii bona fide, ut sibi videtur expedire, & ita est in qualibet Ecclesia cathedrali.
units.tr: Concerning the first point, then, we must first know how he stands with regard to the temporal goods of ecclesiastical persons, insofar as they are ecclesiastical. To understand this: ecclesiastical goods, insofar as they are ecclesiastical, have been conferred on the communities of churches, or on the churches themselves, and not on any single person. So in ecclesiastical goods no single person has property and ownership, but only the community, as the Church of Chartres or any similar body has ownership and power over these goods as its own. An individual person, however, not as an individual but as a part and member of the community, has in them a right of use for his support, according to the needs and fitting standing of his person and rank. Yet there is a difference here: one member is a plain member, such as a simple canon, and he has only use. Another member is principal and the head of the whole community, such as a bishop; for there would be no single or orderly congregation unless there were one head and principal member. He has not only use of the community's goods according to the needs of his rank, in the manner described, but also the general administration and dispensing of all the community's goods, assigning to each what is due to him according to the proper proportion of justice, and also dispensing for the common good of the college in good faith, as seems expedient to him. This is so in every cathedral church.

units.la: Verum quia non solum quaelibet congregatio Ecclesiasticorum virorum est vna in spirituali vnitate, imo omnes Ecclesiasticae congregationes habent quandam generalem vnitatem, in quantum sunt vna Ecclesia, habens connexionem ad vnum principale membrum cui incumbit Ecclesiae cura generalis, scilicet dominum Papam: ideo ipse tanquam principale caput, & principale membrum, & supremum vniuersalis Ecclesiae, est generalis dispensator omnium generaliter bonorum Ecclesiasticorum, spiritualium & temporalium. Non quidem quod sit dominus eorum: sed sola communitas vniuersalis Ecclesiae est domina & proprietaria illorum bonorum generaliter, & singulae communitates & Ecclesiae dominium habent in bonis sibi competentibus. Similiter personae singulares qualitercunque acceptae, dominium non habent: licet principalia membra dispositionem habeant non solum respectu inferiorum, sed etiam quantum faciunt fructus suos ex seruitio pinguiores, secundum exigentiam personae vel status: vel forsan aliquid eis vltra appropriatur ab vniuersali dispensatore sic ordinante, vel discernente seu determinante bona fide, prout iura a papatu condita distinguunt bona Ecclesiastica quadrifariam, 12. q. 2.
units.tr: But since not only is each congregation of churchmen one in spiritual unity, but all ecclesiastical congregations also have a certain general unity, insofar as they are one Church, connected to one principal member to whom the general care of the Church belongs, namely the lord Pope, therefore he, as the principal head, principal member, and supreme member of the universal Church, is the general dispenser of all ecclesiastical goods in general, spiritual and temporal. Not that he is their owner: rather the universal community of the Church alone is the lady and proprietor of these goods in general, and the individual communities and churches have ownership of the goods that belong to them. Likewise individual persons, however they are taken, have no ownership, although the principal members have disposition not only over their inferiors but also insofar as they make their own fruits richer from their service, according to the needs of their person or rank. Or perhaps something more is allotted to them by the universal dispenser, who so orders, discerns, or determines in good faith, as the laws made by the papacy distinguish ecclesiastical goods in a fourfold way (12. q. 2.).
