units.la: Ex his patet, quod male dicunt, qui dicunt, quod nulla persona singularis, alia a Papa, nec collegium vel communitas habet ius & dominium in bonis Ecclesiasticis: sed solus Papa, qui non solum est administrator & dispensator vniversalis, sed verus dominus & proprietarius bonorum Ecclesiae: & de eis ordinare, & ea distrahere potest, prout vult, & tenet factum suum (licet peccet, nisi faciat ex causa rationabili.) Et caeteri praelati, vel etiam principes & communitates non habent dominium: sed solum sunt talium bonorum procuratores, tutores & dispensatores. Hoc patet esse falsum, ex praedictis. Cum dictum sit, quod Papa non sit dominus ecclesiasticorum bonorum generaliter, nec praelati inferiores bonorum sui collegii. Sed Papa est dispositor & dispensator vniuersalis bonorum Ecclesiasticorum: etiam amplius, facit sibi fructus suos de bonis communibus pinguiores, secundum exigentiam sui status, quam praelati inferiores, qui vocati sunt in partem solicitudinis, non in plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: From these things it is plain that those are wrong who say that no single person other than the Pope, nor any college or community, has right and ownership in ecclesiastical goods, but only the Pope, who is not only the universal administrator and dispenser but the true lord and proprietor of the Church's goods; and that he may order them and sell them as he wishes, and his act stands (although he sins unless he acts for a reasonable cause). And that the other prelates, or even princes and communities, do not have ownership but are only procurators, guardians, and dispensers of such goods. This is shown to be false from what has been said. For it has been said that the Pope is not the owner of ecclesiastical goods in general, nor are the lower prelates owners of the goods of their own college. Rather the Pope is the universal disposer and dispenser of ecclesiastical goods; and moreover he makes his own fruits richer from the common goods, according to the needs of his rank, than the lower prelates do, who are called to a share of the care, not to the fullness of power.

units.la: Vnde Augustinus ad Bonifacium, de Praelatis loquens, omnes generaliter includens dicit: Si priuatum vel priuatim possidemus, quod nobis sufficiat, non illa nostra sunt, sed illorum quorum procurationem gerimus: non non ergo proprietatem nobis vsurpatione damnabili vendicemus. Et Apostolus 1. ad Corinth. 4. non excludens Petrum seu Papam: Sic nos existimet homo vt ministros Christi, & dispensatores ministeriorum Dei. Et Bernhardus, loquens de bonis temporalibus, dicit ad Eugenium Papam libro 2. Esto vt alia quacunque ratione hoc tibi vendices, non tamen Apostolico iure: nec illud tibi dare, quod non habuit Petrus, potuit. Argentum, inquit, non est mihi, quod habuit, hoc dedit, scilicet solicitudinem super ecclesias, non (inquit) dominationem. audi ipsum: Non vt dominantes, inquit, in clero: sed forma sancti gregis. Hæc Bernardus. Quod etiam ex hoc euidens est, quia clericis, vt clerici sunt, & monachis, vt monachi sunt, non repugnat habere dominium bonorum exteriorum, saltem in communi: quia ex voto non sunt incapaces, sicut aliqui religiosi. Cum ergo fundatores ecclesiarum intenderunt dominium, & proprietatem bonorum, quae dabant, transferre primo & directe in communitatem collegii, scilicet talis ecclesiae, ad vsum Deo seruientium, & non in dominum Papam: manifestum est, quod communitas ipsa habet immediatum & verum dominium in bonis ipsis, & non Papa vel praelatus alius inferior.
units.tr: Hence Augustine, writing to Boniface about prelates and including all of them generally, says: "If we possess anything privately or as private persons, what suffices for us is not ours but theirs whose stewardship we hold; therefore let us not claim ownership for ourselves by damnable usurpation." And the Apostle in 1 Cor. 4, not excluding Peter or the Pope: "Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." And Bernard, speaking of temporal goods, says to Pope Eugenius in book 2: "Suppose you claim this for yourself on some other ground, but not by apostolic right; nor could he give you what Peter did not have. Silver, he says, I have not; what I had, that I give: namely the care of the churches, not (he says) dominion. Hear him: not as lording it over the clergy, he says, but as a pattern to the holy flock." Thus Bernard. This is also evident from the fact that it is not inconsistent for clerics, as clerics, and monks, as monks, to have ownership of external goods, at least in common, since by vow they are not incapable, as some religious are. Therefore, since the founders of churches intended that the ownership and property of the goods they gave should pass first and directly to the community of the college, namely of such a church, for the use of those who serve God, and not to the lord Pope, it is clear that the community itself has immediate and true ownership of these goods, and not the Pope or any other lower prelate.

units.la: Aliter enim, quoad talia bona, non differret modus viuendi clericorum & monachorum, a modo viuendi fratrum Minorum, qui ex voto suo sunt incapaces dominii talium bonorum in proprio & in communi. Habent enim tantum vsumfructum, vt dicit Nicolaus Papa Quartus. Et ne bona eis collata (quae ex eo quod conferuntur personis ecclesiasticis, sunt facta ecclesiastica) sint vaga & incerta, dominus Papa suscepit in se eius & dominium eorum.
units.tr: For otherwise, as regards such goods, the way of life of clerics and monks would not differ from the way of life of the Friars Minor, who by their vow are incapable of ownership of such goods, either individually or in common. "For they have only the usufruct," as Pope Nicholas IV says. And so that the goods conferred on them (which, because they are conferred on ecclesiastical persons, become ecclesiastical) should not be vague and uncertain, the lord Pope took upon himself both their guardianship and their ownership.

units.la: Sed quaero, per quem potest hoc dominium Papa suscipere, cum non habeat potestatem in temporalibus, nec bona ecclesiae sua sunt, sed communitatis? Absit autem quod ad bona exteriora non aliter se habeant clerici seculares, & alii religiosi: cum etiam dicat Papa Nicolaus in eadem decretali, quod monachus monasterio, & seruus domino acquirit ius & dominium in re aliqua. Non ergo solus Papa dominus est, imo nec dominus, sed dispensator generalis: & Episcopus vel Abbas dispensator spiritualis, & immediatus. Communitas autem dominium verum habet in bonis Ecclesiasticis: amplius non potest dici, quod Papa ius & dominium in talibus bonis habeat, non vt est persona priuata, sed vt est persona publica, & vicarius Christi, cuius sunt omnia talia bona, vt domini principalis: & proprie, vt eius vicarii generalis. Hoc enim dicere non valet, quia Christus secundum quod Deus, est dominus non solum bonorum ecclesiasticorum, sed etiam omnium aliorum: vt autem homo, non habet communitatem & couersationem corporalem cum iis qui sunt in Ecclesia. Nec illi qui conferunt bona ecclesiae, intendunt ius & dominium transferre in Christum, siue secundum quod Deus: quia sic omnia sua sunt: siue secundum quod homo, quia illis nunc non indiget: sed in ministros Christi. & ideo talia bona sunt Ecclesiae, quantum ad proprietatem: sed praelatorum, quantum ad dispensationem, vt dictum est. Ex quo etiam patet, quod Papa non potest ad libitum detrahere seu distrahere bona ecclesiarum, ita quod quicquid ordinet, de ipsis teneat. Hoc enim verum esset, si esset dominus: sed cum sit dispensator bonorum communitatis, in quo requiritur bona fides: non habet sibi collatam potestatem super ipsis, nisi ad necessitatem vel vtilitatem ecclesiae communis. Vnde Apostolus 2. Corinth. 13. Agam secundum potestatem, quam Dominus dedit mihi in aedificationem, & non in destructionem. propter quod si aliter pro libito distrahat Papa, & non bona fide, de iure non tenet: & non solum tenetur ad poenitentiam de peccato, quasi propter abusum rei non suae, sed infideliter agit, & ad restitutionem tenetur, scilicet aliunde de patrimonio, si haberet aliquid, vel acquireret (cum sit fundator rei non suae) Et etiam sicut monasterium posset agere ad depositionem abbatis, vel ecclesia particularis ad depositionem episcopi, si appareret quod dissiparet bona monasterii vel ecclesiae: & quod infideliter non pro bono communi, sed pro priuato ea detraheret seu distraheret. Ita si appareret quod Papa bona ecclesiarum infideliter distraheret seu detraheret, scilicet non ad bonum commune, cui superintendere tenetur, cum sit summus episcopus: deponi posset, si admonitus non corrigeretur, distinct. 40. can. Si Papa, vbi dicitur: Cunctos iudicaturus, a nemine iudicandus est, nisi deprehendatur a fide deuius. vbi dicit glossa: Quod si comprehendatur in quocunque alio vitio, & admonitus non corrigatur, sed scandalizet, vel scandalizaret ecclesiam, idem posset fieri. Sed forte secundum alios hoc fieri posset per solam concilium generale, argumentum 20. t. distinct. can. nunc autem. Et si quidem sciat Papa alios viros Ecclesiasticos vel seculares contra se ob indebitam dispensationem clamantes, eo modo quo possunt & debent, non potest eos de iure mouere, vel deponere ab eis quod ipsorum est qualitercunque, cum ad hoc non habeat auctoritatem a Deo. Et sic dicentes, os ponunt in coelum, & iniuriam faciunt summo Pontifici patri nostro, qui voluntatem suam praedicant sic esse inordinatam (cum praesupponi debeat, voluntatem tanti patris non contrariam iuri) vt scilicet sine causa rationabili vellet auferre alicui quod suum est, cum aliter non possit de iure. Siquidem Deus non vult auferre, vel auferri ab aliquo quod ei dedit, nisi culpa exigente: quia, vt dicitur Roman. 11. sine poenitentia non sunt dona Dei. Propter peccata etiam hominum dixit: Poenitet me fecisse hominem. Propter peccatum Aegyptiorum spolium fecit Hebraeorum. Nihil enim vult auferre vel auferri a viro iusto. Vnde Iob 36. iudicium pauperibus tribuit: & non aufert a iusto oculos suos, & reges in solio suo sedere facit imperpetuum. Et ideo cum Deus dederit Petro vel Papae dispensationem exequendam bona fide, contra Dei voluntatem expressam non potest Papa de iure pro libito, non interueniente culpa manifesta, auferre ius administrationis, quod quis debite & riteerecepit & habet. haec ergo potestas est, quam habet Papa in bonis Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: But I ask: through whom can the Pope take up this dominion, since he has no power over temporal things, and the goods of the Church are not his but those of the community? Far be it from me to say that secular clergy and other religious stand in a different relation to external goods, since Pope Nicholas also says in the same decretal that a monk acquires right and dominion in some thing through his monastery, and a slave through his lord. Therefore the Pope alone is not lord; indeed he is not even lord but a general steward, and the bishop or abbot is a spiritual and immediate steward. The community, however, has true dominion over ecclesiastical goods. Nor can it be said further that the Pope has right and dominion over such goods not as a private person but as a public person and vicar of Christ, to whom all such goods belong as principal lord, and properly as his general vicar. For this cannot hold, because Christ, according as he is God, is lord not only of ecclesiastical goods but of all others; but as man he does not have a bodily community and dealings with those who are in the Church. Nor do those who confer goods on the Church intend to transfer right and dominion to Christ, either according as he is God, since so all things are his, or according as he is man, since he now has no need of them; but they intend them for the ministers of Christ. And so such goods belong to the Church as to ownership, but to the prelates as to dispensation, as has been said. From this it is also plain that the Pope cannot at his pleasure remove or alienate the goods of the churches, so that whatever he ordains about them stands. For this would be true if he were lord; but since he is the steward of the goods of the community, in which good faith is required, he has not been given power over them except for the necessity or advantage of the common Church. Hence the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 13: "We will act according to the power which the Lord has given me for building up, and not for destruction." Therefore if the Pope alienates otherwise at his pleasure, and not in good faith, he does not hold it by right; and he is bound not only to repentance for sin, as if for abusing a thing not his own, but he acts unfaithfully, and he is bound to restitution, namely from elsewhere, from his patrimony if he had any or acquired any (since he is the founder of a thing not his own). And just as a monastery could proceed to the deposition of its abbot, or a particular church to the deposition of its bishop, if it appeared that he was squandering the goods of the monastery or church, and that he was alienating them unfaithfully, not for the common good but for private ends; so, if it appeared that the Pope was unfaithfully alienating or removing the goods of the churches, namely not for the common good, over which he is bound to oversee as supreme bishop, he could be deposed if, when admonished, he did not amend, Distinction 40, canon "Si Papa", where it is said: "He who is to judge all, is to be judged by no one, unless he is caught deviating from the faith." Where the gloss says: "But if he is caught in any other vice, and when admonished does not amend, but scandalizes or would scandalize the Church, the same could be done." But perhaps, according to others, this could be done by a general council alone, see argument 20, t. distinction, canon "nunc autem". And indeed, if the Pope knows that other ecclesiastical or secular men cry out against him for undue dispensation, in the way they can and ought to, he cannot by right move them or depose them from what is theirs in any manner, since he has no authority from God for this. And those who say so set their mouth against heaven, and do wrong to the supreme Pontiff, our father, whom they declare to be of such disordered will (when it ought to be presupposed that the will of so great a father is not contrary to right) that he would wish, without reasonable cause, to take from anyone what is his, since otherwise he could not do so by right. For God does not wish to take away, or have taken away from anyone, what he has given, unless guilt demands it; since, as it is said, Romans 11: "The gifts of God are without repentance." Because of the sins of men too he said: "It repents me that I made man." Because of the sin of the Egyptians he made a spoil of the Hebrews. For he wishes to take nothing away from, or have taken from, a just man. Hence Job 36: "He gives judgment to the poor, and does not take away his eyes from the just, and he makes kings sit on their throne forever." And therefore, since God has given to Peter or to the Pope a dispensation to be carried out in good faith, the Pope cannot by right, against the express will of God, at his pleasure, without manifest fault intervening, take away the right of administration which anyone has duly and rightly received and holds. This therefore is the power which the Pope has over ecclesiastical goods.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Quomodo Papa se habet ad bona laicorum.
units.tr: How the Pope stands in relation to the goods of laypeople.

units.la: EX praedictis patet satis, quomodo Papa se habet ad bona laicorum: quia infirmius habet dominium in bonis exterioribus laicorum, quam clericorum: imo nec in illis est dispensator, nisi forte in vltima necessitate ecclesiae, in qua etiam non est dispensator, sed iuris declarator. Ad quod declarandum, considerandum est, quod exteriora bona laicorum non sunt collata communitati, sicut bona Ecclesiastica: sed sunt acquisita a singulis personis arte, labore & industria propria. Et personae singulares, vt singulares sunt, habent in ipsis ius & potestatem, & verum dominium: & potest quilibet de suo ordinare, disponere, dispensare, retinere, alienare pro libito sine alterius iniuria, cum sit dominus: & ideo talia bona non habent ordinem nec connexionem inter se, nec ad vnum commune caput, quod habeat ea dispensare & ordinare vel disponere, cum quilibet rei suae sit ordinator pro libito. Et ideo nec princeps nec Papa habet dominium vel dispensationem in talibus: verum quia ob talia bona contingit interdum pacem communem turbari, dum aliquis quod est alterius vsurpat: quia etiam homines interdum quę sua nimis amantes, ea non communicant prout necessitati vel vtilitati patriae expedit: ideo positus est princeps a populo, qui in talibus praeest vt iudex, discernens iustum & iniustum, & vt vindex iniuriarum, & vt mensura in accipiendo bona a singulis secundum iustam proportionem pro necessitate vel vtilitate communi. Papa vero quia est supremum caput non solum clericorum, sed generaliter omnium fidelium, vt fideles sunt, tanquam generalis informator fidei & morum in casu summae necessitatis, fidei & morum: in quo casu omnia bona fidelium sunt communicanda, & calices ecclesiarum: habet bona fidelium dispensare, & exponenda decernere, prout expedit necessitati communi fidei: quae alias subuerteretur, propter irruptionem paganorum, aut aliud huiusmodi. & posset esse tanta necessitas, & tam euidens, quod posset exigere decimas vel decimatas portiones a singulis fidelibus, secundum tamen debitam proportionem, ne aliqui plus debito grauarentur quam alii, ad subueniendum communi necessitati fidei, & huius Papae ordinatio non est nisi iuris declaratio. Et posset etiam rebelles & contradictores per censuram Ecclesiasticam compellere: & per talem modum, etiam si de parochia aliqua essent fideles, de novo multiplicati in tantum, quod curato parrochiali non possent sufficere antiqui reddit us, ad quos fideles parrochiae tenebantur, eo quod ad curam parrochiae oporteret sacerdotem de novo tenere capellanos coadiutores: Papa posset ordinare, quod fideles illius parrochiae de bonis suis superaddat vsq; ad debitam sufficientiam: in quo casu, talis ordinatio esset iuris declaratio. Extra vero casus huius necessitatis, pro communi bono spirituali non habet Papa dispositionem bonorum quae terreni tenent, quae scilicet quilibet disponit de suo prout vult, & princeps in casu necessitatis pro communi bono temporali. In casibus vero necessitatis, sed alicuius vtilitatis specialis, vel vbi non constat quod conserant bona exteriora laicorum, tali vtilitati vel necessitati non habet Papa compellere quenquam: sed super hoc posset dare indulgentias pro auxilio ferendo fidelibus, & non est aliud ei collatum, prout puto.
units.tr: From what has been said above it is sufficiently clear how the Pope stands in relation to the goods of laypeople. For he has a weaker lordship over the external goods of laypeople than over those of the clergy; indeed he is not even their steward, except perhaps in the final necessity of the Church, and even then he is not a steward but a declarer of right. In order to declare this, it must be considered that the external goods of laypeople have not been contributed to a community, as Church goods have been, but have been acquired by individual persons through their own skill, labour and industry. And individual persons, as individuals, have in these goods their own right, power and true lordship; each may order, dispose, dispense, retain or alienate what is his at his pleasure, without injury to another, since he is the lord of it. Therefore such goods have no order or connection among themselves, nor any single common head who could dispense, order or dispose of them, since each man is the arranger of his own property at his pleasure. Hence neither the prince nor the Pope has lordship or disposal over such goods. Yet because on account of such goods the common peace is sometimes disturbed, when someone usurps what belongs to another, and because men, loving their own things too much, sometimes do not share them as the need or advantage of the fatherland requires, therefore a prince has been set over the people by the people, who presides in such matters as a judge, distinguishing just from unjust, as an avenger of wrongs, and as a measure in taking goods from individuals according to a just proportion for the common need or advantage. But the Pope, since he is the supreme head not only of the clergy but generally of all the faithful insofar as they are faithful, as the general informer of faith and morals, in a case of the highest necessity of faith and morals, in which case all the goods of the faithful are to be shared, and the chalices of the churches, has the power to dispense the goods of the faithful and to decree what is to be spent, as the common necessity of the faith requires; otherwise the faith would be overthrown by an invasion of pagans or some other such thing. And the necessity could be so great and so evident that he could demand tithes or tithed portions from individual faithful, yet in due proportion, lest some be burdened beyond what is owed compared with others, in order to help the common necessity of the faith; and this ordinance of the Pope is nothing but a declaration of right. He could also compel rebels and contradictors by ecclesiastical censure. And in this way, even if the faithful of some parish had multiplied so greatly that the old revenues, to which the faithful of the parish were bound, could not suffice for the parish priest, because the care of the parish would require the priest to keep assistant chaplains, the Pope could order that the faithful of that parish add from their goods up to due sufficiency; in which case such an ordinance would be a declaration of right. Outside the cases of this necessity, however, the Pope does not have disposal, for a common spiritual good, of the goods that earthly men hold, which indeed each man disposes of as he wishes, and the prince in a case of necessity for a common temporal good. In cases of necessity, however, but of some special advantage, or where it is not clear that external goods of laypeople would be contributed, the Pope cannot compel anyone to such advantage or necessity; but in this matter he could grant indulgences for bringing aid to the faithful, and nothing else has been conferred on him, as I think.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Quod Papa non habet iurisdictionem a Christo in bonis laicorum, quia Christus non habuit eam.
units.tr: That the Pope does not have jurisdiction from Christ over the goods of laymen, because Christ did not have it.

units.la: ET quia non est idem habere proprietatem & dominium in bonis exterioribus, & habere iurisdictionem, id est ius decernendi quid sit iustum vel iniustum in ipsis: sicut habent principes potestatem iudicandi & decernendi seu discernendi in bonis subditorum, licet non habeant dominium in re ipsa: ideo nunc restat videndum, vtrum Papa a Christo habeat iurisdictionem & potestatem huiusmodi, vt aliqui dicunt. Et ad ostendendum, quod non habeat eam a Christo, primo ostendetur, quod Christus vt homo eam non habuit. Secundo ostendetur, quod dato, quod Christus eam habuerit, tamen Petro eam non commisit. Ad primum ergo intelligendum, sciendum est, quod Christus tripliciter potest intelligi. Vno modo secundum quod Deus est vnus cum patre, & sic fuit verus Rex non solum hominum, sed etiam omnium creaturarum: quia ei omnes subditae sunt Ecclesiae, id est, Vnus est creator omnium altissimus, omnipotens rex, & hoc regnum seu hanc potestatem non contulit alicui creaturae. Non enim contulit Petro, quod esset creator. Alio modo potest considerari vt homo Deus: & sic etiam dicitur Rex hominum, in quantum per ea quae in carne egit, nos perduxit ad participationem regni, non quidem mundi, sed altioris, scilicet caeli. & sic non solum sacerdos, sed Rex vocatus est, Heremiae 23. Regnabit rex, & sapiens erit: & sic est ab eo regale sacerdotium deriuatum, secundum illud 1. Petri 2. Vos estis genus electum, regale sacerdotium. & quod amplius est, omnes fideles inquantum sunt membra eius, quasi vnum cum capite Christo, per fidem & charitatem reges & sacerdotes dicuntur, vt innuit glossa ibi. & Apocal.1. dicitur: Fecisti nos Deo nostro regnum & sacerdotes in sanguine tuo, id est, per fidem passionis tuae: in tantum aut amplius, quam alii ministri ecclesiastici huius regalis sacerdotii participes efficiuntur, in quantum non solum sacrificium spiritus contribulati & contriti motus Deo offeruntur, sicut omnes iusti: sed {etiam} exteriora sacrificia, in quibus diuina virtus spirituali modo continetur, offerunt pro se & pro populo, vt dictum est, supra caeteros. Etiam ad participationem regni dirigunt non solum ex charitatis zelo, sed ex officio docendo, & sacramenta ministrando. Si vero tertio modo accipiatur, quod Christus rex fuerit secundum quod homo, rex dico temporalis regni: quasi dominium iurisdictionis, alias directiuum, vel vtile, vel vniuersale habens in temporalibus bonis, omnino falsum est. Accepit enim paupertatem nostram, sicut & caeteros defectus inde tentabiles, vt dicit Iohan. Damascenus lib. 3. vnde Iohan. 18. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. August. in gloss. q. d. Audite gentes & Iudei, non impedio dominationem vestram in hoc mundo. Chrysostomus etiam dicit: quoniam non tenet regnum, vt hic reges principatum, qui non est humanum, sed multo maior & clarior. Et Leo Papa in festo Epiphaniae, magi humano sensu aestimauerunt regem in ciuitate regia esse quaerendum: sed qui formam serui acceperat, & qui ministrare venerat, non ministrari, praelegit sibi Bethleem natiuitati, Hierosolymam passioni. Vnde deceptus Herodes, audiens Regem natum, timuit ne rex esset, qui sibi dominium temporalium vsurparet. Ideo Chrysostomus super Matth. Non consideravit Herodes prophetiam Michea: Et tu Bethleem, terra Iuda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Iuda: ex te enim exibit dux, qui regat populum meum Israel, & dies eius a diebus saeculi. Si ergo integram Prophetiam contulisset, considerans quod non erat rex terrenus, cuius dies a diebus saeculi erant, in tantum errorem non exarsisset. Propter quod etiam Eusebius dicit, quod errant Herodiani dicentes Christum, quia unctus, esse regem temporalium bonorum. quia non est unctus materiali unguento, vt reges huius mundi: sed spirituali oleo laetitiae prae participibus suis. & ideo non est rex huius saeculi, sed illius saeculi, de quo dicit propheta Daniel: Potestas eius, potestas aeterna, &c. & regnum eius, quod non corrumpetur. Et Lucae 2. Regni eius non erit finis. Amplius Lucae 12. ait quidam de turba, Magister, dic fratri meo vt diuidat mecum hereditatem. At ille dicit ei: Homo quis me constituit iudicem aut diuisorem super vos? videte & cauete ab omni auaritia. Et sic patet per sanctos expositores, quod Christus non habuit in temporalibus auctoritatem vel iudicium: sed dare voluit, & dare habuit virtutis documentum. Vnde Bernardus dictam auctoritatem exponens ad Eugenium lib. 2. de Consideratione: Non monstrabitur, inquit, vbi aliquando quispiam Apostolorum sederit index hominum, aut diuersorum terminorum, aut distributor terrarum. Stetisse denique lego Apostolos iudicandos, sedisse iudicantes non lego: erit illud, non fuit. Et infra: Vt sciatis, inquit, quia filius hominis habet potestatem in terra dimittendi peccata, &c. Amplius super illud Matthaei 22. Reddite quae sunt Caesari, Caesari: & quae, &c. dicit Hieronymus, quod soluit tributum pro se & Petro: & Deo reddidit quae Dei sunt, patris faciens voluntatem. Et Hilarius ibidem dicit: Diuitias nostras dare Caesari, Deo autem conscientiam puritatem vel innocentiam seruare iussit. Si dicatur, quod soluere non tenebatur, sed soluit vitare volens scandalum, sicut dicitur de didrachmate census, Matthaei 17. euasio non valet. Illud enim didrachma non soluebatur Caesari, sed templo a primogenitis Israel, propter mortem primogenitorum Aegypti. Et quia putabant Iesum esse primogenitum Ioseph, & Petrum videbant principalem & primum quasi inter Apostolos & Christi discipulos: ideo ab utroque didrachma petebatur. Sed nec Christus tenebatur, cum non esset filius Ioseph: nec Petrus, cum non esset patris sui primogenitus. Ex eo ergo quod principalis discipulus illud didrachma soluit, solum propter vitandum scandalum: secus autem est de tributo soluendo Caesari, quod Christus totiens iussit solui. Vrbanus etiam Papa adducit istam auctoritatem de didrachmate inuento in ore piscis, ad ostendendum, quod omnes clerici & Ecclesiae tenentur soluere tributum Imperatorum, de exterioribus bonis. 23. q. vltra tribu. Ex quibus patet, quod cum Christus, vt homo, non habuerit dominium in temporalibus, quod sacerdos quicunque, vt Christi vicarius, non habet in eis potestatem a Christo, cum eis non contulerit, quod ipse non habuit in se ipso, dicente in Iohan. Amen amen dico vobis, non est seruus maior domino suo, neque Apostolus maior eo qui misit illum. Et Matthaei 10. dicitur: Non est discipulus super magistrum, neque seruus super dominum.
units.tr: Since possessing ownership of external goods is not the same as having jurisdiction, that is, the right to decide what is just or unjust in them (as princes have the power to judge, decide and discern concerning the goods of their subjects, even though they do not own the things themselves), we must now consider whether the Pope has such jurisdiction and power from Christ, as some say. To show that he does not have it from Christ, I will first show that Christ, as man, did not have it. Second, I will show that, even if Christ had it, he did not commit it to Peter. Regarding the first point, we must understand that Christ can be considered in three ways. In one way, as God, one with the Father, and so he was the true King not only of men but of all creatures, since all things are subject to him. He is the Most High Creator of all, the almighty King, and he has not conferred this kingdom or power on any creature. For he did not give Peter the power to be creator. In another way, he can be considered as God-man, and so he is also called King of men, insofar as by what he did in the flesh he led us to share in a kingdom, not of the world but of a higher one, namely heaven. Thus he is called not only priest but King, Jeremiah 23: "A king shall reign, and shall be wise." And so the royal priesthood is derived from him, according to 1 Peter 2: "You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood." What is more, all the faithful, insofar as they are his members, joined as one with Christ their head through faith and charity, are called kings and priests, as the gloss there indicates. Revelation 1 says: "You have made us to our God kings and priests in your blood," that is, through faith in your passion. Ministers of the Church share in this royal priesthood to a greater degree, or at least more than others, insofar as they not only offer to God the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled spirit, as all the righteous do, but also offer, for themselves and for the people, the external sacrifices in which divine power is contained in a spiritual manner, as has been said above. They also lead people into the kingdom, not only from zeal for charity but by the office of teaching and administering the sacraments. But if we take the third way, that Christ was King according to his humanity, king, I say, of a temporal kingdom, as one who holds a dominion of jurisdiction, whether directive, useful or universal, over temporal goods, this is entirely false. For he took on our poverty, along with the other weaknesses that could be tempted by it, as John of Damascus says in book 3. Hence John 18: "My kingdom is not of this world." Augustine, in the gloss, says: "Hear, you nations and Jews, I do not hinder your dominion in this world." Chrysostom also says that he does not hold a kingdom as earthly rulers hold their principality, which is not human but far greater and more splendid. And Pope Leo, on the feast of the Epiphany: the magi, by human reasoning, supposed that the king had to be sought in a royal city; but he who had taken the form of a servant, and who had come to serve and not to be served, chose Bethlehem for his birth and Jerusalem for his passion. Hence Herod, deceived, hearing that a King had been born, feared lest he be a king who would usurp for himself dominion over temporal things. So Chrysostom on Matthew: Herod did not consider the prophecy of Micah: "And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the princes of Judah, for out of you shall come a leader who shall rule my people Israel, and whose days are from the days of eternity." If he had considered the whole prophecy, recognising that he was not an earthly king, whose days were from the days of the world, he would not have been inflamed with such error. For this reason Eusebius also says that the Herodians err in saying that Christ, because he is anointed, is king of temporal goods; for he was not anointed with material ointment as the kings of this world are, but with the spiritual oil of gladness above his companions. Therefore he is not king of this age but of that age, of which the prophet Daniel says: "His power is an everlasting power, etc., and his kingdom is one that shall not be destroyed." And Luke 1: "Of his kingdom there shall be no end." Further, Luke 12: someone from the crowd said, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me." But he said to him: "Man, who made me a judge or divider over you? Take heed and beware of all covetousness." Thus it is clear, through the holy expositors, that Christ had no authority or judgment in temporal matters; he was unwilling to give them, and he had the power to give a lesson in this. Hence Bernard, expounding this authority in his book 2 On Consideration to Eugenius: "It will not be shown," he says, "where any of the Apostles ever sat as judge of men, or of disputed boundaries, or as distributor of lands. I read that the Apostles stood to be judged; I do not read that they sat as judges. That will be a thing that did not happen." And below: "So that you may know," he says, "that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins, etc." Further, on the words of Matthew 22, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and the things that are God's," Jerome says that he paid the tribute for himself and for Peter, and rendered to God what is God's, by doing his Father's will. And Hilary, in the same place, says: he bade us give our riches to Caesar, but to keep our conscience pure and innocent for God. If it is said that he was not bound to pay, but paid to avoid giving offence, as is said of the didrachma of the census in Matthew 17, the evasion does not hold. That didrachma was not paid to Caesar but to the temple, by the firstborn of Israel, on account of the death of the firstborn of Egypt. And because they thought Jesus was the firstborn of Joseph, and saw Peter as the principal and first of the apostles and disciples of Christ, the didrachma was demanded from both of them. But Christ was not bound, since he was not the son of Joseph; nor was Peter, since he was not the firstborn of his father. So the fact that the principal disciple paid that didrachma was done solely to avoid giving offence; but it is otherwise with the tribute to Caesar, which Christ so often commanded to be paid. Pope Urban also cites this authority about the didrachma found in the fish's mouth, to show that all clerics and churches are bound to pay the tribute of emperors on their external goods (23 q. 'Ultra tribu'). From these points it is clear that, since Christ as man did not have dominion over temporal things, no priest, as Christ's vicar, has power over them from Christ, since he did not confer on them what he did not himself have in himself. John 13 says: "Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than him who sent him." And Matthew 10: "A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord."

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Rationes, quod Christus habuit iurisdictionem in bonis laicorum. Et responsiones ad eas.
units.tr: Arguments that Christ had jurisdiction over the goods of the laity, and replies to them.

units.la: SVnt autem forsan contrarium dicentes, ex hoc sumentes argumentum, quod Matthaei 21. legitur, ipsum cum funiculo eiecisse vendentes & ementes de templo: hoc enim non fecisset, nisi auctoritatem habuisset. Vnde dicitur 1. q. 3. ex multis, quod ibi auctoritatem sui praecepti denuncians dixit: Nolite facere domum patris mei, domum negotiationis. Item ipse misit discipulos suos vt tollerent asinam & pullum, & adducerent ad eum, dicentes: Quia Dominus his opus habet. Item Matthaei 8. legitur, quod misit daemones in porcos, qui statim se praecipitauerunt in mare: sed nec Dominum porcorum requisiuit. Item Matthaei vltimo dicitur, quod post resurrectionem dixit: Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo & in terra. Glossa: Qui prius fuerat mortuus, & crucifixus. Amplius assumunt illud Psalmi, vt sit verbum Patris ad filium: Postula, & dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terrae, reges eos, &c. Ex his accipiunt, quod Christus, secundum quod homo, habuit potestatem in rebus temporalibus. Quae omnia de facili soluuntur, si consideretur, quod aliquid debetur Christo vt Deus est, quod ei non conuenit vt est homo: quamuis per singula dici possit. Quod enim primo dicitur de eiectione venditorum: respondetur secundum illud quod dicitur {textit}xtur in Glossa, vbi dicitur, quod Christus quaedam fecit vt Imperator, quaedam vero alia vt sacerdos. de Consecrat. distinct. 2. sacerdos: non quia vna eademque persona illa duo exerceat, vel gerere debeat: sed hoc ideo fecit, vt ostenderet quod vtraque potestas ab eo processit, vt scilicet Deus erat. Haec enim duo, imperium & sacerdotium, ab vno sunt: vt in authent. quomodo oportet episcopos, in principio, collatione 2. Chrysostomus vero super Matthaeum dicit, quod hoc fecit Christus quasi auctoritatem habens in quantum Deus: significans, quod in templo Dei non debent esse ministri nisi spirituales, qui Dei portant imaginem: non qui portant imaginem terreni, vt non sit in domo Domini negociatio, vel donorum cupiditas, ne ingrediatur Iesu iratus & rigidus, & non aliter mundet templum suum nisi flagello adhibito, & de spelunca latronum faciat domum orationis. Similiter quod dicitur de asina, respondetur: quod auctoritatem habuit vt Deus. Unde glossa super illud, Dominus his opus habet, dicit: Dominus dicitur absolute & simpliciter, ad infinitandum, quod non solum erat Dominus iumentorum, sed & hominum: eni iumenta omnia sunt subiecta. Similiter dici potest ad illud, quod dicitur de porcis, quamuis forte porci sylvestres erant, non habentes dominum, pro eo quod de porcis nihil veniebat ad usum hominum: quia carnes porcinas Iudaei non comedebant. Quod vero dicitur, Data est mihi omnis potestas: respondetur secundum Hieronymum, quod cum dicitur, Omnis potestas, intelligenda est non temporalis, sed spiritualis. Unde Hieronymus: In coelo & in terra data est ei omnis potestas, vt qui ante regnavit in coelis, per fidem credentium regnet in terris. Quomodo autem regnet per fidem credentium, dicetur in sequenti argumento. Vel dicendum, secundum Remigium, quod illi, qui mortui fuerat, data erat in incarnatione omnis potestas, scilicet quod Deus esset, qui est omnipotens. & hoc quidem euidens erat in coelo angelis: sed non fuit euidens in terra, nisi post resurrectionem, quando misit praedicatores verbi Dei, annunciantes Christum, & ipsum esse Deum omnipotentem praedicantes. Et ideo tunc fuit sibi data per communicationem idiomatum, omnis potestas in coelo & in terra: non quidem quoad existentiam, quia hanc habuit a principio, sed quoad euidentiam seu innotescentiam. Quod dicitur, Postula a me, &c. respondeo: Loquitur de regno, quod per fidem dirigit nos in coelum. Unde illud, Dabo tibi gentes, &c. exponitur, id est, Gentes per fidem tibi adhaerentes. Similiter illud, Reges eos in virga ferrea: Glossa, Inflexibili iustitia, sc. qua est per fidem, nam iustus ex fide vivit. Et illud, Tanquam vas figuli confringes eos: Glossa, a luto carnalitatis & peccati mundando eos. Sic enim a Christo in membris suis excutitur iugum legis & peccati, secundum glossam. Necesse intelligendum, quod Christus regnet per fidem in hominibus, quasi ex eo, quod aliquis conuertitur ad fidem, sit subditus Christo, vel eius vicario, in temporalibus bonis, sicut solent homines suis regibus subdi: sic enim Christus regnum mutaret aeternum; vt timuit Herodes: sed pro tanto dicitur regnare per fidem, quia id quod in hominibus est supremum & principale, scilicet intellectum, Christo subiiciunt, ipsum in fidei obsequium captivantes, & iste est intellectus sanctorum. Unde Christus per fidem non dicitur regnare in possessionibus, sed in cordibus.
units.tr: Some who hold the contrary, drawing an argument from this, note that in Matthew 21 he drove out with a cord those who sold and bought in the temple; for he would not have done this unless he had authority. Hence it is said in 1 q. 3 (ex multis) that in announcing the authority of his command he said: "Do not make my Father's house a house of trade." Again, he sent his disciples to take the ass and the colt and bring them to him, saying: "Because the Lord has need of them." Again, Matthew 8 relates that he sent the demons into the swine, which immediately rushed into the sea; yet he did not seek out the owner of the swine. Again, at the end of Matthew it is said that after the resurrection he said: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." The gloss: "He who had first died and been crucified." They further take up the verse of the Psalm, as a word of the Father to the Son: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession; you shall rule them," etc. From these they conclude that Christ, as man, had power over temporal things. All of this is easily resolved if it is considered that some things are due to Christ as he is God, which do not belong to him as he is man, although this could be said of each point separately. As to what is first said about the expulsion of the sellers: the answer is according to what the gloss says, where it is stated that Christ did some things as Emperor and some other things as priest (de Consecrat. dist. 2, sacerdos): not because one and the same person exercises or ought to exercise those two offices, but he did this so as to show that both powers proceeded from him, namely as he was God. For these two, empire and priesthood, are from one source, as in authent. quomodo oportet episcopos, in principio, collatione 2. Chrysostom, however, on Matthew, says: Christ did this as having authority in so far as he is God, signifying that in the temple of God there ought to be none but spiritual ministers, who bear the image of God, not those who bear the image of the earthly man; so that there may be no trading in the house of the Lord, nor greed for gifts, and so that Jesus does not enter angry and stern, and cleanse his temple only with the whip applied, and make a house of prayer out of a den of robbers. Likewise, as to what is said about the ass, the answer is that he had authority as God. Hence the gloss on the words "The Lord has need of them" says: "Lord" is said absolutely and simply, to signify without limit that he was not only the Lord of the beasts of burden but also of men, since all beasts are subject to him. Similarly, what is said about the swine may be answered in this way: perhaps they were wild swine, having no owner, because nothing from the swine came into human use, since the Jews did not eat pork. As to the words "All power is given to me": the answer, according to Jerome, is that when it is said "all power," it must be understood not as temporal but as spiritual. Hence Jerome: All power is given to him in heaven and on earth, so that he who before reigned in the heavens may, through the faith of believers, reign on earth. How he reigns through the faith of believers will be explained in the following argument. Or it may be said, according to Remigius, that to him who had died was given at the incarnation all power, namely that he should be God, who is almighty; and this was indeed evident to the angels in heaven, but it was not evident on earth until after the resurrection, when he sent preachers of the word of God, proclaiming Christ and preaching that he is almighty God. And so then, by the communication of attributes, all power in heaven and on earth was given to him, not indeed as to his existence, since he had this from the beginning, but as to its evidence or becoming known. As to the words "Ask of me," etc., I answer: it speaks of the kingdom which through faith directs us to heaven. Hence the words "I will give you the nations," etc., are explained as the nations cleaving to you through faith. Similarly, "You shall rule them with a rod of iron": the gloss says, with unbending justice, namely that which is by faith, for the just lives by faith. And "You shall break them like a potter's vessel": the gloss says, cleansing them from the clay of carnality and sin. For thus the yoke of the law and of sin is shaken off by Christ in his members, according to the gloss. It must be understood that Christ reigns through faith in men not in the sense that, because someone is converted to faith, he becomes subject to Christ or his vicar in temporal goods, as men are wont to be subject to their kings; for in that case Christ would be changing an eternal kingdom into a temporal one, as Herod feared. Rather, he is said to reign through faith because they subject to Christ what is highest and principal in men, namely the intellect, taking it captive to the obedience of faith; and this is the understanding of the saints. Hence Christ is said to reign through faith not over possessions but over hearts.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: Quod Christus non contulit omnem potestatem suam Petro, quam etiam in quantum homo habuit.
units.tr: That Christ did not transfer to Peter all the power he had, including the power he had as man.

units.la: DAto etiam, quod Christus praedictam auctoritatem & potestatem habuerit, eam tamen Petro non commisit. Et ideo Papae, ratione qua est successor Petri, praedicta potestas non debetur, imo sunt potestates distinctae, episcopalis & regalis vel temporalis, non solum re, sed etiam subiecto. Et regalis maior est in temporalibus, non habens super se superiorem, sicut nec Papa in spiritualibus. Quod quidem declarari potest ex comparatione Ecclesiae ad Christum: nam Christus caput est Ecclesia, Ephes. 5. & secundum Ambrosium intelligitur Ecclesiae caput, non solum secundum diuinitatem, sed secundum humanitatem: quae autem sunt indistincta in capite, interdum subiecto distinguuntur in membris. sicut patet, quod omnes sensus sunt in capite, non sic autem in aliquo alio membro. Et hoc quasi regulariter verum est, quod aliqua sunt magis distincta in principiatis, quam in principio: & in effectibus, quam in causa: & in inferioribus, quam in superiore. Et ideo non sequitur, Si Christus secundum quod homo vtranque potestatem habuerit, quod vtranque Petro contulerit: sed spiritualem tantum Petro contulit, & temporalem vel corporalem Caesari dimisit, quam a Deo accepit. Et hoc maiori ostenditur. Nam Christus secundum quod homo, aliquam potestatem habuit in spiritualibus, quam conferre potuit Petro & caeteris ministris Ecclesiae: & tamen non dedit illam, quam potestatem Theologi vocant potestatem excellentiae, quae in solo homine Christo fuit: vt est, effectum sacramenti conferre sine sacramento, sine verbo vocali, vel quod in nomine eius sacramenta conferrentur, vel quod noua sacramenta poterat instituere. Hanc enim potestatem in spiritualibus conferre potuit Petro, & tamen non contulit: vt dicunt omnes Theologi. Et Richardus de sancto Victore, in 6. libro de Remissione peccatorum, dicit, quod Christus potuit peccata dimittere, nos vero non, sed remittere. Igitur multo minus est necesse, si potestatem habuit Christus in temporalibus, quod eam Petro contulerit: & praecipue hoc non est affirmandum, cum hoc non inueniatur expressum: sed de potestate spirituali, qua solum potest soluere a peccatis. Unde omnia argumenta, quae ideo Petro aliquid attribuunt, quia Christus hoc potuit etiam in quantum homo, nullius momenti sunt, nisi inueniatur expressum. Hoc etiam patet
units.tr: Even granting that Christ had the authority and power described above, he did not commit that power to Peter. So the aforesaid power is not owed to the Pope by reason of his being Peter's successor. Indeed, episcopal power and royal or temporal power are distinct, not only in their nature but also in their subject. The royal power is the greater in temporal matters, having no superior above it, just as the Pope has none in spiritual matters. This can be made clear by comparing the Church with Christ. Christ is the head of the Church, Ephes. 5., and according to Ambrose he is understood to be the head of the Church, not only according to his divinity but according to his humanity. Yet things that are undivided in the head are sometimes distinguished by their subject in the members. It is plain that all the senses are in the head, but not so in any other member. And it is generally true that some things are more distinct in what proceeds from a principle than in the principle itself, in effects than in their cause, and in inferiors than in their superior. Therefore it does not follow that, if Christ as man had both powers, he conferred both on Peter. He conferred only the spiritual power on Peter, and left the temporal or bodily power to Caesar, which he had received from God. This is shown by a stronger argument. Christ as man had some power in spiritual matters which he could have conferred on Peter and the other ministers of the Church, and yet he did not give that power which the theologians call the power of excellence, which belonged to Christ the man alone. This is the power to confer the effect of a sacrament without the sacrament, without the spoken word, or to have sacraments conferred in his name, or to institute new sacraments. He could have conferred this spiritual power on Peter, and yet he did not, as all theologians say. Richard of St Victor, in the sixth book on the Remission of sins, says that Christ could forgive sins, but we cannot; we can only remit them. So it is much less necessary, if Christ had power in temporal matters, that he conferred it on Peter. This especially should not be affirmed, since it is not found expressed; it is spiritual power, by which alone one can absolve from sins, that is meant. Hence all the arguments that attribute something to Peter because Christ could do it even as man are of no weight, unless it is found expressed. This also is evident

units.la: ex et perfectione sacrificii Noui Testamenti. nam quanto aliquid habet esse perfectius, tanto magis habet esse distinctum. Sic enim videmus in naturalibus, quod in plantis non est sexus ita perfectus, sicut in animalibus: ideo in eadem planta possunt esse mas & fœmina; & nō distinguuntur subiecto, sicut in animalibus, in quib. habent esse distinctum subiecto (nisi sit error naturæ, vt in hermaphroditis.) In Veteri vero Testamento, in quo erat sacerdotium minus perfectum, erant potestates sacerdotales & regales distinctæ re & subiecto; ergo multo magis Deus voluit eas distinctas esse subiecto in Nouo Testamento. Hoc etiam apparet ex comparatione Ecclesiæ, quæ à Deo est instituta ad opera artis. Videtur enim domus esse imperfecta, & habere penuriam rerum, & non sufficiens sibi in vita, si vna persona ad ministeria diuersa deputetur. Vnde Philosophus dicit sexto Politicorum, quod pauperes, quia non habent copiam seruorum, nec abundant in iis quæ requiruntur ad perfectionem domus, utuntur filiis vt serui, & vxoribus vt ancillis. Ecclesia autem sancta Christi domus dicitur, quæ perfecta est, secundum illud Baruch capite quarto: O Israel, quam magna est domus Dei? Et in Matthæo dicitur: Domus mea, domus orationis vocabitur. Cum igitur à Deo sit sufficienter instituta, & inconueniens est in ea, tam diuersa mysteria vni committi, sacerdotale scilicet officium, & regale dominium: in quo etiam reges Deo ministrant, secundum illud Romanorum decimo tertio: Non sine causa gladium portat, minister enim Dei est. Absit enim, vt in his quæ à Deo instituta sunt, aliud tale ponamus, quale indecorum est ponere in operibus artis & naturæ. Dicit enim Philosophus in priori Politicorum: quod natura nihil facit, quale faciebant fabri, facientes Delphicum gladium, id est, ad duo officia seruientem. Apud Delphos enim fiebant gladii propter pauperes, qui eis ad duo officia seruiebant: Natura autem nihil tale facit, multo minus audor naturæ. Vnde Philosophus dicit, quod vnumquodque organorum optime perficiet opus suum, si non multis operibus sit seruiens. Hoc etiam apparet, si consideremus quare conferens noluit illas duas potestates esse penes vnum. Nam propter duo, voluit istas potestates esse distinctas re & subiecto, vt non essent in vna eademque persona secundum primariam auctoritatem. Vnum est, vt propter mutuam indigentiam & subministrationem membrorum Ecclesiæ, dilectio & charitas seruentur, sine qua membra Ecclesiæ non viuunt: dum princeps indiget sacerdote in spiritualibus, & econuerso sacerdos principe in temporalibus, quod non esset, si vnus utrunque haberet. Et hoc insinuat Apostolus Romanorum duodecimo dicens: Omnes vnum corpus sumus in Christo, singuli autem alter alterius membra habentes, & donationes differentes. Si enim totum esset oculus, vbi esset manus: & si totum esset manus, vbi esset oculus? Aliud est, ne natura temporalis auctoritatis ipsum reddat minus solicitum circa regimen spiritualis. Et hoc tangit Apostolus secundo ad Timotheum secund. dicens: Nemo militans Deo, implicat se negociis secularibus, &c. Vtranque autem rationem tangit Gratianus decima distinctione cap. quoniam idem. Et Nicolaus Papa idem omnino dicit, trigesima distinctione ad vnicum. Item, eandem potestatem acceperunt omnes Apostoli cum Petro, Matthæi decimo octauo. Et habetur vigesima prima distinctione in nouo, vbi dicitur, quod ligandi soluendique potestatem Petrus primus accepit, cæteri vero cum eodem pari consortio honorem & potestatem acceperunt. In collatione huiusmodi Christus non posuit aliquam restrictionem respectu aliorum à Petro: licet ex modo loquendi appareat, quod vellet Petrum Ecclesiæ principaliorem, & caput Ecclesiæ, & hoc propter vnitatem Ecclesiæ conseruandam. Et sic intelligendum est, sic se habere, quod sicut in Apostolis tunc quidquid potuit vnus, sicut Petrus, potuit alius: ita & nunc de iure communi, quidquid potest Papa, potest quilibet episcopus, nisi quod Papa potest vbique, alii vero episcopi in suis diœcesibus tantum. Sed nullus dicit, quod cæteri episcopi, in quantum sunt vicarii Christi, & successores aliorum Apostolorum, habeant auctoritatem & dominium in bonis temporalibus laicorum. Et quod appellari possit à principe in causa temporali ad episcopum illius loci, vel ad presbyterum parrochiæ, quem dicunt aliqui eandem potestatem habere in parrochia sua, quam habet episcopus in diœcesi: sic igitur nullus debet hoc dicere de Papa generaliter. Item, petentibus discipulis quis maior esset futurus in regno Christi (regnum eius, regnum huius mundi intelligentes) respondit, Reges gentium dominantur eorum, &c. Vos autem non sic. Quod verbum exponens Bernardus ad Eugenium Papam libro secundo, dicit: Planum est, quod Apostolu interdicitur dominatus: ergo & tu tibi vsurpare caue aut dominans apostolatum, aut apostolicus dominatum: planum est, quia ab vtroque prohiberis. Si vtrunque similiter habere voles, perdes vtrunque. Alioquin non te exceptum illorum numero putes, de quibus conqueritur Dominus, dicens: Ipsi regnauerunt, & non ex me: principes extiterunt, & non cognoui. Et infra: Forma Apostolica hæc est, dominatio interdicitur, indicitur ministratio. Et infra adhuc: Exi ô Eugeni, exi inquam in mundum. Ager enim mundus est: isque tibi creditus est. Exi in illum non tanquam dominus, sed tanquam villicus, videre & procurare, vnde exigendus es reddere rationem. Non à Christo, vel eius vicario Petro, habes summus Pontifex dominarum. Item idem eodem libro: In criminibus, non in possessionibus potestas vestra: quoniam propter illa, non propter istas, accepistis claues regni cœlorum. Et infra: Habent hæc infima & terrena iudices suos, reges & principes terræ. Quid ergo fines alienos inuaditis? Quid falcem vestram in alienam messem extenditis? Non quia indigni vos, sed quia indignum vos talibus insistere, quippe potioribus occupati. Amplius summi Pontifices dicunt, dictas potestates subiecto esse distinctas, scilicet temporalem & spiritualem. distinctione decima quoniam idem, octog. d. cum ad verum, & cap. duo. Et sic sunt distinctæ, quod vna in aliam non reducitur: scilicet sicut spiritualis immediate est à Deo, ita & secularis. Vnde imperium à solo Deo est, vt habetur vigesima tertia quæstione quarta quæsiuit. Et quia Papa non habet gladium ab Imperatore, nec Imperator habet gladium à Papa. distinct. octog. 6. si Imperator. Nam exercitus facit Imperatorem. distinction. 23. legimus. Et quod à principe in temporalibus non appellatur licite ad Papam. Et quod temporalia non tangunt suam iurisdictionem, vt dixit Alexander extr. de appellationibus, si duobus. & extra, qui filii sunt legitim. causam. Et ab Episcopo appellatur in temporalibus ad principem: extra, de foro competent. verum. Et cognoscitur de his Episcopus tanquam iudex secularis: extra, de iudic. caterum. & Authent. quomodo oport. Episcop. in princ. col. 1. Et ecclesia soluit tributum Imperatori. 10. quaestion. 1. magnum. vbi Ambrosius allegat exemplum de Christo, qui soluit tributum. Et allegat etiam illud Apostoli Romanor. 13. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus sit subiecta. & illud 2. Petri 2. Estote subditi dominis vestris, siue regi quasi praecellenti, &c. Et id eadem quaest. 100. tributum. Et multa consimilia possent adduci, ad ostendendum, dominum Papam non habere vtrunque gladium, nec iurisdictionem in temporalibus, nisi sibi concedatur à principe ex deuotione. Et hoc dicunt expositores iuris Canonici, qui statum in ecclesia habuerunt, etiam in casu in quo minus videtur. Quaerit enim Hostien. extr. de haretic. ca. vergentis, vbi mandat dominus Papa haereticorum confiscari bona, Quid ad Papam de temporalibus? Et respondet cum domino suo Innocentio, Quod reuera nihil ad eum. Sed hoc fecit de assensu Imperatoris, qui tunc Padua praesens concessit. Mirum etiam videtur, quod Constantinus Imperator dedisse dicitur imperium Italicum ecclesiae, & totam iurisdictionem temporalem: & quod ecclesia illud tanquam datum, si hoc habuit, de iure recepit. tunc enim non fuisset facta beato Siluestro donatio: sed redditio eius quod suum erat, cuius contrarium sentit Ecclesia. distinct. 96. Constantinus.
units.tr: and in the perfection of the sacrifice of the New Testament. For the more perfect a thing is, the more distinct it is. We see this in nature: in plants the sexes are not as perfectly separated as in animals, so in the same plant there can be both male and female, and they are not distinguished by subject as they are in animals, where they have a distinct subject (unless it is a mistake of nature, as in hermaphrodites). In the Old Testament, in which the priesthood was less perfect, the priestly and royal powers were distinct both in function and in subject. Therefore God much more wished them to be distinct in subject in the New Testament. This also appears from the comparison with the Church, which God instituted as a work of art. For a household seems imperfect and lacking in resources, and not self-sufficient in life, if one person is assigned to several different duties. Hence the Philosopher says in the sixth book of the Politics that the poor, because they have no abundance of servants, and are not rich in those things that are required for the perfection of a household, use their sons as servants and their wives as maidservants. But the holy Church is called the house of Christ, which is perfect, according to the saying in Baruch chapter four: O Israel, how great is the house of God? And in Matthew it is said: My house shall be called a house of prayer. Since, then, it has been sufficiently instituted by God, and it is unfitting for such different mysteries, namely the priestly office and the royal dominion, to be committed to one person in it (in which kings also minister to God, according to the saying in Romans chapter thirteen: He does not bear the sword in vain, for he is the minister of God), far be it from us to posit in the things instituted by God something of the kind that is indecorous to posit in the works of art and nature. For the Philosopher says in the first book of the Politics that nature makes nothing like the craftsmen who made the Delphic sword, serving two purposes. For at Delphi swords were made for the poor, which served them for two purposes. But nature makes nothing of this kind, much less the author of nature. Hence the Philosopher says that each of the organs will best perform its work if it is not serving many functions. This also appears if we consider why the Council wished those two powers not to be in one person. For it wished these powers to be distinct in subject, for two reasons, so that they would not be in one and the same person as the chief authority. The first is that, through the mutual need and service of the members of the Church, love and charity may be preserved, without which the members of the Church do not live: since the prince needs the priest in spiritual matters, and conversely the priest needs the prince in temporal matters, which would not be the case if one person had both. The Apostle hints at this in Romans chapter twelve, saying: We, being many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another, having different gifts. For if the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing? And if the whole were hearing, where would be the smelling? The second is that the nature of temporal authority should not make a person less concerned about the government of spiritual matters. The Apostle touches on this in the second letter to Timothy, chapter two, saying: No one who serves as a soldier of God entangles himself in worldly affairs, etc. Gratian touches on both reasons in the tenth distinction, chapter Quoniam idem. And Pope Nicholas says exactly the same thing in the thirtieth distinction, ad unicum. Likewise, all the Apostles received the same power as Peter, Matthew chapter eighteen. And it is held in the twenty-first distinction, in novo, where it is said that Peter first received the power of binding and loosing, while the others received honour and power with him on equal fellowship. In conferring this, Christ placed no restriction on the others with respect to Peter, although from his manner of speaking it appears that he wished Peter to be more prominent in the Church and its head, and this for the sake of preserving the unity of the Church. And it must be understood that, as among the Apostles then whatever one, such as Peter, could do, another could do, so now too by common law, whatever the Pope can do any bishop can do, except that the Pope can act everywhere, while the other bishops only in their own dioceses. But no one says that the other bishops, insofar as they are vicars of Christ and successors of the other Apostles, have authority and dominion over the temporal goods of laymen. And as to whether an appeal may be made from the prince in a temporal cause to the bishop of that place, or to the presbyter of the parish, whom some say has in his parish the same power that the bishop has in his diocese: so no one ought to say this of the Pope in general. Likewise, when the disciples asked who would be greatest in the kingdom of Christ (understanding his kingdom as the kingdom of this world), he answered: The kings of the nations lord it over them, etc. But you shall not be so. Expounding this word, Bernard, in the second book to Pope Eugene, says: It is plain that domination is forbidden to the Apostles; therefore beware of usurping for yourself either the dominion of an apostle or the apostolic dominion. It is plain, because you are forbidden both. If you wish to have both alike, you will lose both. Otherwise do not think yourself excepted from the number of those of whom the Lord complains, saying: They have reigned, but not by me; they have become princes, and I did not know it. And below: This is the apostolic form: domination is forbidden, ministry is enjoined. And further below: Go forth, O Eugene, go forth, I say, into the world. For the world is a field, and it has been entrusted to you. Go forth into it not as a lord, but as a steward, to watch over and to care for it, for which you must render an account. You, supreme Pontiff, do not have dominion from Christ or from his vicar Peter. Likewise, in the same book: Your power lies in crimes, not in possessions; for it is for those that you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, not for these. And below: These lowly and earthly matters have their own judges, the kings and princes of the earth. Why then do you invade the territories of others? Why do you stretch your sickle into another's harvest? Not because you are unworthy, but because it is unworthy of you to occupy yourselves with such things, since you are engaged in weightier matters. Furthermore, the supreme Pontiffs themselves say that the said powers are distinct in subject, namely the temporal and the spiritual: distinction ten, Quoniam idem; eighty distinction, cum ad verum; and chapter duo. And they are so distinct that the one is not reduced to the other: just as the spiritual power is immediately from God, so too is the secular. Hence the empire is from God alone, as is held in the twenty-third case, question four, quaesivit. And because the Pope does not have the sword from the Emperor, neither does the Emperor have the sword from the Pope: distinction eighty-six, si Imperator. For the army makes the Emperor: distinction twenty-three, legimus. And that an appeal from the prince in temporal matters does not lawfully lie to the Pope. And that temporal matters do not touch his jurisdiction, as Alexander said: Extra, de appellationibus, si duobus; and extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, causam. And an appeal is made from the bishop in temporal matters to the prince: extra, de foro competenti, verum. And the bishop takes cognizance of these matters as a secular judge: extra, de iudiciis, caeterum; and Authentica, quomodo oportet episcopos, in principio, collatio 1. And the Church pays tribute to the Emperor: question 10, case 1, magnum. where Ambrose cites the example of Christ, who paid tribute. He also cites that saying of the Apostle in Romans chapter thirteen: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; and that saying of Peter in the second letter, chapter two: Be subject to your masters, whether to the king as supreme, etc. And likewise question 100, tributum. Many similar things could be adduced to show that the lord Pope does not have both swords, nor jurisdiction in temporal matters, unless it is granted to him by the prince out of devotion. And this is said by the expositors of canon law who held a position in the Church, even in a case where it seems less so. For Hostiensis asks, extra, de haereticis, cap. vergentis, where the lord Pope commands that the goods of heretics be confiscated: What has the Pope to do with temporal matters? And he answers with his lord Innocent: Indeed nothing to do with him. But he did this with the consent of the Emperor, who was then present and granted it at Padua. It also seems strange that the Emperor Constantine is said to have given the Italian empire and all temporal jurisdiction to the Church; and that the Church, if it had this, received it by right as a gift. For then the donation would not have been made to blessed Silvester, but a restitution of what was his own; the Church holds the contrary. Distinction 96, Constantinus.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Euasiones quorundam, dicentium potestatem secularem esse à Papa, & in Papa, cum eorum reprobatione.
units.tr: Evasions of certain persons, who say that secular power is from the Pope and in the Pope, with a refutation of them.

units.la: SVnt aliqui credentes euadere aliqua praedictorum per breuem distinctionem. Dicunt enim, quod potestas secularis est penes Papam immediate, & secundum primariam auctoritatem. sed non habet Papa executionem immediate, sed eam dat principi. Ita quod secularis princeps, quantum ad ipsam potestatem, recognoscere debet à Papa: sed quantum ad executionem, Papa recognoscit à principe seculari. Et haec sunt verba eorum, per quae soluere niuntur aliqua praedictorum. Sunt vero aliqui sentientes, quod Papa habet à Deo iurisdictionem temporalem secundum primam auctoritatem, sed executionem non habet: sed Imperator executionem habet, non quidem à Papa, sed à Deo. & per hoc volunt soluere aliqua praedictorum. Sed ista euasio est omnino absurda. Nec etiam conuenit dictis ipsorum: quia si ecclesia recognosceret executionem à principe seculari, tunc princeps secularis haberet iudicare de debita executione Papae, & ab eo posset auferre executionem: quod ipsi negant, quia dicunt ipsum à nemine iudicari. Item, si Deus dedit Papae potestatem secularem, secundum primam auctoritatem: sed non executionem, quia ei nō conuenit: quomodo accipit à principe, quod Deus iudicat ei non conuenire? Et quomodo dat ei, quod ab eo reaccipiat? Item, si Papa habet à Deo potestatem secularem immediate, & princeps habet executionem à Papa immediate: ergo princeps est minister Papae, sicut Papa minister Dei vel Christi: quod videtur inconueniens, & contra scripturam Canonicam. dicitur enim Roman. 13. de rege & principe: Si malefecerit, time, non enim sine causa gladium portat. Dei enim minister est, & vindex malorum in ira, &c. & ideo praestatis tributa: minister enim Dei est. non dicit Papae, sed Dei. In hoc enim Christo seruitis. Glossa, sed Deo. Item prius fuit potestas regia secundum se, & quantum ad executionem, quam Papalis: & prius fuerunt reges Franciae in Francia, quam Christiani: ergo potestas regia nec secundum se, nec quantum ad executionem, est à Papa: sed est à Deo, & à populo regem eligente in persona vel in domo: & sic, sicut ante. Dicere enim quod potestas regia prius esset à Deo immediate, & postea à Papa, est valde ridiculosum. Non enim potest hoc esse, nisi Christus Petro dederit potestatem conserendi regiam potestatem: quod non est verum, vt supra dictum est. Indubitanter ergo est à Deo, sicut ante. Vnde glo. super illud 2. Petri 2. Subditi estote omni creaturae, &c. dicit: Fides & religio non turbant iura conditionis. Et Ambrosius in glossa super illud Rom.13. Omnis anima, &c. dicit: Licet omnes fideles vnum sint in Christo, differunt tamen in conuersatione. Amplius etiam, potestas inferiorum Pontificum & curatorum magis videtur esse à Deo mediante Papa, quam regia potestas, eo quod immediatius dependent praelati Ecclesiastici à Papa, quam principes seculares: sed potestas praelatorum inferiorum non est à Deo mediante Papa, sed immediate à Deo, & à populo eligente vel consentiente. Nomen im Petrus (cuius successor est Papa) misit alios Apostolos, quorum successores sunt alii episcopi: nec 72. discipulos, quorum successores sunt presbyteri Curati: sed eos Christus immediate misit. Ioan. 20. & Luce 10. Nec Petrus insufflauit in alios Apostolos, dans eis Spiritum sanctum & potestatem dimittendi peccata, sed Christus. Ioan. 20. & deinde 21. In nouo, dicitur quod omnes à Christo simul eandem & aequalem acceperunt potestatem. Paulus etiam dicit, suum Apostolatum non accepisse à Petro, sed à Christo, seu à Deo immediate. ad Gal. 1. Paulus, inquit, Apostolus non ab hominibus, neque per homines, sed per Iesum Christum, & Deum patrem. & infra: Neque ab homine illud accepi, nec didici. Et infra dicit, quod post vocationem suam ad euangelizandum mundum non viderat Petrum vsque post annos tres, quando venit Hierosolymam videre Petrum. Potestas ergo regia multo minus est à Papa, qualitercunque. Amplius, quia contingit quandoque, quod aliquis habeat potestatem aliquid faciendi. ciendi, & non actum propter impedimenta: verbi gratia, aliquis habet potentiam conficiendi, cui non conuenit actus propter defectum materiæ, quia non habet panem: vel propter suspensionem, vel propter defectum corporalem, quia mutus est, non potens proferre verba ista. Ista tamen sunt impedimenta, superuenientia collationi potestatis. nam nullus sapiens conferret alicui ordinem sacerdotii, dum sciret ipsum habere aliquod impedimentorum prædictorum regulariter. Non ergo videtur dicendum, quod Papa habeat immediate à Deo potestatem gladii secularis, cuius executio ei regulariter non conuenit. Sic enim Deus magis superflueret in suis operibus quam natura, quæ nulli dat virtutem sine actu: quia cuius est potentia, eius est actus, vt dicitur in lib. de Somno & vigilia: & insipientior esset Deus homine. De nullo etiam loco Scripturæ canonicæ possunt accipere prædictam distinctionem: nisi forte velint accipere dictum Bernardi, ponentis quod Papa habet gladium materialem in nutu. Sed dictum hoc, quod non est magnæ auctoritatis, magis est contra eos, quam pro ipsis. Et significanter dicit Bernhardus, quod Papa materialem gladium habet in nutu: quia vbi innuit Papa propter necessitatem boni spiritualis, Imperator debet exercere iurisdictionem sæcularis potestatis. Si tamen nolit, vel non videtur sibi expedire, Papa non habet aliud facere: quia non habet ipsum in iussu, sed Imperator tantum: sicut ipsemet dicit, & infra dicetur magis. Possem etiam ad hoc trahere illudi. Corinth. 6. Secularia iudicia si habueritis, contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia, illos constituite ad iudicandum. Ex quo videtur trahi, quod clerici habeant constituere contemptibiles, id est laicos in causis sæcularibus. Sed istud in nullo est pro ipsis: quia Apostolus non loquitur clericis specialiter, sed loquitur generaliter fidelibus, ipsos scilicet reprehendendo: quia in causis sæcularibus constituebant personas contemptibiles, id est ignaras ad iudicandum, vnde compellebantur fideles recurrere ad iudicium infidelium: quasi inter fideles non esset sapiens aliquis, qui iudicare posset. Vnde illud Constituite, exposuit Glossa non hortatiue dictum, sed ironice q.d. Ita faciitis: constituitis enim tales contemptibiles & ignaros, & ita compellitis fideles recurrere ad iudicium infidelium. Vnde subdit Apostolus: Ad verecundiam vestram dico, quia non sit inter vos sapiens. Et certe ita vult Apostolus, quod fideles etiam laici constituant in causis sæcularibus industrias personas ad iudicandum, & ita nihil est ad propositum. Vel dato, quod loquatur viris Ecclesiasticis: adhuc non est ad propositum, quia non intendit, quia viri Ecclesiastici constituere habeant iudices in sæcularibus iudiciis indistincte, sed solum vbi data est eis iurisdictio à principe in temporalibus bonis. tunc enim debent instituere in talib. contemptibiles, id est laicos, qui iudicent de talibus: & non debent de talibus immediate se intromittere: sicut etiam hodie obseruatur, quia ponunt balliuos sæculares. Vnde Apostolus non dicit, Cum habueritis sæcularia iudicia, &c. sed dicit, Si habueritis: insinuans, quod talia iudicia eis non debentur, nisi eis fuerit concessum vel permissum à principe: & tunc debent iudicare per contemptibiles personas, id est laicos, secundum tenorem legum, & debitum terreni iuris, vt dicit expresse Hugo de Sacramentis, libro 2. parte 2. capite 7. cuius verba sunt hæc: Notandum tamen, quod principes terreni possessionibus, quas in subiectis vel suis subiectis possident, aliquando concedunt ipsi ecclesiæ solam vtilitatem, aliquando vtilitatem & potestatem. Vtilitatem sine potestate concedunt, quando fructum possessionum ad vsum Ecclesiæ transferri decernunt: sed potestatem iustitiæ exercendæ, in ipsa possessione, ad eius iurisdictionem transfire non permittunt. Aliquando autem vtilitatem & potestatem simul tribuunt: potestatem tamen exercendæ iustitiæ, iudicia autem sæcularia per Ecclesiasticas personas exercere non sinunt: possunt tamen habere ministros laicos personas, per quos, vel per quas iura & iudicia ad terrenam potestatem pertinentia, secundum tenorem legum & debitum iuris terreni exercent. Quod vero alii dicebant, quod princeps habet executionem sine potestate à Deo, non à Papa, non videtur rationabile. Non enim videtur rationabile, quod Deus det alicui potestatem sine actu per se vel per alium: & alii executionem sine potestate & auctoritate. Non etiam esset contra nos hæc opinio: quia ad minus secundum eum non appellabitur à principe ad Papam.
units.tr: There are some who believe they can escape some of the aforesaid difficulties by a brief distinction. For they say that secular power resides in the Pope immediately, and according to its primary authority; but the Pope does not have the execution immediately, and he gives it to the prince. Thus the secular prince, as regards the power itself, ought to acknowledge it from the Pope; but as regards the execution, the Pope acknowledges it from the secular prince. These are their words, by which they strive to resolve some of the aforesaid objections. There are indeed some who hold that the Pope has temporal jurisdiction from God according to the first authority, but does not have the execution; rather the Emperor has the execution, not from the Pope but from God. By this they wish to resolve some of the aforesaid objections. But this evasion is entirely absurd, nor does it agree with their own statements: for if the Church acknowledged the execution from the secular prince, then the secular prince would have to judge whether the Pope's execution was due, and could take the execution away from him; which they deny, since they say he is judged by no one. Likewise, if God gave the Pope secular power according to the first authority, but not the execution, because that does not befit him, how does he receive it from the prince, since God judges that it does not befit him? And how does he give to the prince what he takes back from him? Again, if the Pope has secular power from God immediately, and the prince has the execution from the Pope immediately, then the prince is the minister of the Pope, just as the Pope is the minister of God or of Christ; which seems inappropriate and contrary to Canonical Scripture. For it is said in Romans 13 concerning the king and prince: If he does evil, fear; for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is God's minister, an avenger for wrath against evildoers, etc., and therefore you pay tribute; for he is God's minister. It does not say the Pope's, but God's. For in this you serve Christ. The Gloss: but God's. Again, the royal power was prior in itself and as regards execution to the papal power; and the kings of France existed in France before there were Christians. Therefore royal power, neither in itself nor as regards execution, is from the Pope, but is from God, and from the people electing the king in person or in the family; and so it was before. For to say that royal power was first from God immediately and afterwards from the Pope is utterly ridiculous. For this could not be unless Christ had given Peter the power of conferring royal power, which is not true, as was said above. Undoubtedly, then, it is from God, as before.
