Hence the gloss on that passage of 1 Peter 2, Be subject to every creature, etc., says: Faith and religion do not disturb the rights of condition. And Ambrose, in the gloss on Romans 13, Let every soul, etc., says: Although all the faithful are one in Christ, they differ nevertheless in their conduct. Furthermore, the power of inferior bishops and parish priests seems more to be from God through the mediation of the Pope than royal power is, because ecclesiastical prelates depend more immediately on the Pope than secular princes do; yet the power of inferior prelates is not from God through the mediation of the Pope, but immediately from God, and from the people electing or consenting. For Peter (whose successor is the Pope) did not send the other Apostles, whose successors are other bishops, nor the seventy-two disciples, whose successors are the parish elders; but Christ sent them immediately. John 20 and Luke 10. Nor did Peter breathe on the other Apostles, giving them the Holy Spirit and the power of forgiving sins, but Christ did. John 20 and then 21. In the New Testament it is said that all received from Christ together the same and equal power. Paul also says that he did not receive his apostleship from Peter, but from Christ, or from God immediately. To the Galatians 1: Paul, an Apostle, not from men, nor through men, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. And below: Neither did I receive it from man, nor was I taught it. And further below he says that after his calling to preach the gospel to the world he had not seen Peter until three years later, when he came to Jerusalem to see Peter. Royal power, therefore, is much less from the Pope, in whatever manner. Furthermore, it sometimes happens that someone has the power of doing something, and yet does not act because of hindrances: for example, someone has the power of consecrating, but the act does not befit him because of a lack of matter, since he does not have bread; or because of suspension, or because of a bodily defect, since he is mute and unable to pronounce those words. Yet these are hindrances arising after the conferral of the power; for no wise man would confer on anyone the order of priesthood while knowing that he had one of the aforesaid hindrances in the ordinary way. It therefore does not seem right to say that the Pope has immediately from God the power of the secular sword, the execution of which does not ordinarily befit him. For in this way God would be more superfluous in his works than nature, which gives power to no one without act; because whose is the power, his is the act, as is said in the book On Sleep and Waking; and God would be more foolish than man. Nor can they derive the aforesaid distinction from any passage of canonical Scripture, unless perhaps they wish to take the saying of Bernard, who holds that the Pope has the material sword at his nod. But this saying, which is not of great authority, is more against them than for them. And Bernard says significantly that the Pope has the material sword at his nod, because when the Pope signals, on account of the necessity of a spiritual good, the Emperor ought to exercise the jurisdiction of secular power. If, however, he is unwilling, or it does not seem expedient to him, the Pope has nothing else to do; for he does not have it at his command, but the Emperor only, as he himself says, and more will be said below. I could also draw to this point that passage of 1 Corinthians 6: If you have secular judgments, appoint to judge those who are despised in the church. From this it seems to follow that clerics are to appoint the despised, that is, laymen, in secular causes. But this is in no way in their favor; for the Apostle does not speak to clerics specifically, but speaks generally to the faithful, rebuking them indeed; for in secular causes they were appointing despised persons, that is, ignorant ones, to judge, whence the faithful were compelled to resort to the judgment of unbelievers, as if there were no wise man among the faithful who could judge. Hence the Gloss expounds that appoint is said not hortatively but ironically, as if to say: "So you do; for you appoint such despised and ignorant persons, and so compel the faithful to resort to the judgment of unbelievers." Hence the Apostle adds: I say this to your shame, that there is not among you a wise man. And certainly the Apostle wishes that even lay faithful appoint capable persons in secular causes to judge, and so this has nothing to do with the matter. Or granting that he speaks to ecclesiastical men, still it is not to the point, because he does not intend that ecclesiastical men should have judges appointed in secular trials indiscriminately, but only where jurisdiction in temporal goods has been granted to them by the prince. For then they ought to appoint despised persons, that is, laymen, to judge such matters; and they ought not to intrude themselves directly into such matters; as is also observed today, since they appoint secular bailiffs. Hence the Apostle does not say, "When you have secular judgments," etc., but says, If you have, implying that such judgments are not owed to them unless it has been conceded or permitted to them by the prince; and then they ought to judge through despised persons, that is, laymen, according to the tenor of the laws and the due of earthly right, as Hugh expressly says in On the Sacraments, book 2, part 2, chapter 7, whose words are these: It must be noted, however, that earthly princes, in the possessions which they hold in their subjects or among their subjects, sometimes grant to the Church only the use, and sometimes both use and power. They grant use without power when they decree that the fruits of the possessions be transferred to the use of the Church; but they do not permit the power of exercising justice in that very possession to pass to its jurisdiction. Sometimes, however, they grant use and power together; yet they do not allow the power of exercising justice, or secular judgments, to be exercised by ecclesiastical persons; they may, however, have lay ministers, through whom or by whom they exercise the rights and judgments pertaining to earthly power, according to the tenor of the laws and the due of earthly right. But as to the view of others who said that the prince has the execution without power from God, not from the Pope, this does not seem reasonable. For it does not seem reasonable that God should give someone power without act, either by himself or through another, and to another execution without power and authority. Nor would this opinion be contrary to us; for at least according to it there would be no appeal from the prince to the Pope.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Rationes dicentium, Papam habere iurisdictionem in temporalibus bonis exterioribus.
units.tr: Arguments of those who say that the Pope has jurisdiction over external temporal goods.

units.la: NUnc videndum est, quibus innituntur fundamentis, qui dicunt sacerdotes, & præcipue Papam, habere potestatem primariam in temporalibus, & ipsam à summo Pontifice deriuari ad principem sæcularem. Allegant enim illud Hieremiæ 1. & habetur Extra, de magist. & obedientia, cap. solitæ: quod dictum est Hieremiæ sacerdoti de prosapia sacerdotali, non regali, quia de sacerdotibus erat, qui erant in Anathot: Ecce constitui te super gentes & regna, vt euellas & disperdas, & destruas & dissipes, & ædifices & plantes. Ex quo dicunt, Papam, qui supremus est in gradibus ecclesiarum sacerdotum, potestatem habere amouendi reges terræ, & constituendi. Item dictum est Petro Matth. 16. & 18. Quodcumque solueris super terram, &c. quod dictum est indistincte, vt dicunt. Item 1. Corinth. 6. dicitur: Nescitis quoniam angelos vos iudicabitis? Glossa: quanto magis sæculapия? Item, Genes. 1. Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna, solem (scil. Papam) vt præesset diei, vel in spiritualibus & lunam, scil. Imperatorem vel regem, vt præesset nocti, quæ non habet nisi lumen mutuatum à sole. Ergo quod Imperator vel rex præsit in temporalibus, hoc habet per potestatem quam accipit à Papa. Item, Zacharias Papa deposuit regem Francorum, & loco eius substituit Pipinum fratrem eius. 15. q. 6. alias. Item 22. d. c. 1. dicit Nicolaus Papa, quod Christus Petro tam coelestia, quam terreni imperii iura concessit. Item Imperator iurat Papae, ut habetur d.63. tibi domino. Et Papa deponit Imperatorem. 15. qu. 6. alias. Item Papa transtulit imperium de Oriente in Occidens: extra, de electione, cap. venerabilem. Item, à iudice seculari interdum appellatur ad Papam: extra, de foro competenti, liter. Item, Papa absoluit milites à iuramento, quod fecerunt domi-no temporali. Et quandoque omnes Francigenas à iuramento fidelitatis absoluit. 15. q. 6. alias. & 1. q. quia postulatum. Item, Papa habet cognoscere de omnium delicto. Constat autem quod delictum committi potest in temporalibus: vt cum aliquis indebite sibi vendicat alienum, ergo, &c. Item, cum vnus princeps iniuriatur alteri de feudo, potest iniuriam pati sub hoc denunciare summo Pontifici, in quo casu Papa cognoscere habet: extra, de iudiciis, ca. nouit. ergo cognoscere habet de temporalibus.
units.tr: Now we must consider on what foundations they rest who say that priests, and above all the Pope, have primary power in temporal matters, and that this power flows from the supreme Pontiff to the secular prince. They cite Jeremiah 1, and it is found in Extra, de magistris et obedientia, cap. solitae, where the words were spoken to Jeremiah, a priest of priestly and not royal descent, since he was one of the priests who were at Anathoth: Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to root out and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant. From this they argue that the Pope, who is supreme among the grades of priests in the churches, has the power to remove and to appoint kings of the earth. Likewise, it was said to Peter, Matt. 16 and 18: Whatever you shall loose upon earth, etc., which, as they say, was said without distinction. Likewise, 1 Cor. 6 says: "Do you not know that you shall judge angels?" The Gloss adds: "How much more secular things?" Likewise, Gen. 1: "God made two great lights, the sun" (namely the Pope) "to rule the day, or in spiritual things, and the moon" (namely the Emperor or king) "to rule the night," which has no light except what it borrows from the sun. Therefore, that the Emperor or king rules in temporal matters, he has this by the power which he receives from the Pope. Likewise, Pope Zacharias deposed the king of the Franks and put Pepin, his brother, in his place: 15 q. 6 alias. Likewise, in 22 d. c. 1, Pope Nicholas says that Christ granted to Peter the rights of both heavenly and earthly empire. Likewise, the Emperor swears an oath to the Pope, as is found in d. 63, tibi domino. And the Pope deposes the Emperor: 15 q. 6 alias. Likewise, the Pope transferred the empire from the East to the West: Extra, de electione, cap. venerabilem. Likewise, an appeal is sometimes made from a secular judge to the Pope: Extra, de foro competenti, liter. Likewise, the Pope absolves soldiers from the oath they have sworn to their temporal lord, and sometimes absolves all the Franks from the oath of fidelity: 15 q. 6 alias, and 1 q. quia postulatum. Likewise, the Pope has the right to take cognizance of every crime. It is certain, however, that a crime can be committed in temporal matters, as when someone unjustly claims for himself what belongs to another; therefore, etc. Likewise, when one prince wrongs another concerning a fief, the injured party may denounce the injury under this heading to the supreme Pontiff, and in that case the Pope has the right to take cognizance: Extra, de iudiciis, cap. nouit. Therefore he has the right to take cognizance of temporal matters.

units.la: Item, Matt. 18. dicitur: Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, vade, &c. & infra: Quod si te non audierit, dic Ecclesiae; si autem Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. Ecclesia ergo iudicare habet in distinctè, vbi iniuria sibi denunciatur. Item, Theodosius Imperator statuit, & Carolus innouauit, quodcunque litem habens, si in iudicio elegerit sacrosanctae sedis antistitem, illico sine vlla dubitatione, etiamsi pars altera refragetur, ad episcoporum iudicium cum sermone litigantium dirigatur: extra, de iudiciis, cap. nouit. Item, in Deutero. dicitur, & habetur extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem. quod si difficile & ambiguum apud te iudicium esse perspexeris inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, lepram & lepram: & iudicium inter personas videris varium, venies ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & ad iudicantem qui fuerit illo tempore, qui iudicabit tibi iudicii veritatem: & faciesque quaecunque dixerint, qui ibi sunt in loco, quem elegit Deus: sequerisque eorum sententiam, qualiter, &c. Item, Qui potest maius, potest & minus: cum ergo Papa possit in spiritualibus, poterit in temporalibus. Item, temporalia ordinantur ad spiritualia, & interdum eis conferunt: Papa ergo, qui curam gerit de spiritualibus, habet etiam de temporalibus iudicare, & ordinare; saltem in quantum ad spiritualia valent. Item, Papa mutat & transfert ! gata indistincta. Et etiam ad Papam pertinet, restitutiones facere de bonis defunctorum, quando personae ignotae sunt quibus debetur. Et ita ad eum oportet ordinare de temporalibus. Amplius, arguunt aliqui sic: Corporalia reguntur per spiritualia, & ab ipsis dependent, quod ostenduntur ex multis: nam corpora coelestia per angelos administrantur, & in homine anima regit corpus & mouet: quare similiter spiritualis potestas causalitatem habet super temporalem: & temporalis a spirituali, vt a causa dependet, cum talis potestas sit magis propter regimen vitae temporalis. Et rationem hanc videtur tangere Hugo de sacramentis libro secundo, parte 2. capite 4, dicens: quanto vita spiritualis dignior est quam terrena, & anima quam corpus: tanto spiritualis potestas terrenam superat, saecularem potestatem honore ac dignitate praecellit. Nam spiritualis potestas terrenam potestatem & instituere vt sit, & iudicare habet, si bona non fuerit, ipsa vero à Deo primum instituta est: & si deviat a solo Deo iudicari potest. Sic enim scriptum est, spiritualis homo omnia diiudicat, & ipse à nemine iudicatur: & ita spiritualis potestas saecularem instituit & iudicat. Item, idem arguunt ex ordine finium. In artibus enim ordinatis ars, ad quam pertinet vltimus & principalis finis, imperat aliis, ad quos pertinent fines secundarii. Sed saecularis potestas intendit bonum multitudinis, quod est vivere secundum virtutem: ad quod potest venire virtute naturae, per ea quae huic administrantur. Potestas autem spiritualis intendit bonum multitudinis supernaturale, scilicet aeternam vitam vel beatitudinem, & in ipsam dirigit. Finis vero supernaturalis potior est & principalior quolibet alio fine: ergo spiritualis potestas, quae ministris Ecclesiae collata est, superior est non solum dignitate, sed etiam causalitate, potestate saeculari: & ei habet praecipere, qualiter debeat operari. Vlterius ex isto medio concludunt, quod Papa tradit leges Principibus, secundum quas saecularem iurisdictionem exequi & exercere debeant: nec possunt seculares principes aliunde accipere leges, nisi à Papa fuerint approbatae. Dicunt etiam, quod ideo spiritualis potestas dicitur regale sacerdotium: quia Christus rex & sacerdos, & eius vicarius potestatem habet regalem & sacerdotalem: quia per ipsum regalis potestas instituitur, ordinatur, sanctificatur & benedicitur. Propter hoc enim dicunt, quod in Veteri Testamento, vt dicit Hugo, primum à Deo institutum est sacerdotium: postea vero per sacerdotium institutum potestas regalis iubente Domino est ordinata. Et adhuc sacerdotalis dignitas regalem potestatem signicat per benedictionem, & format per institutionem. Ostendunt etiam per Augustinum de Ciuitate Dei libro secundo capite vigesimo primo, vbi dicit: quod sine vera iustitia non potest regi respublica: vera autem iustitia non est, vbi Christus non est rector: & sic non est respublica recta & vera, nisi populi Christiani: in qua non spectat de iure gubernatio, nisi ad Papam, qui est Christi vicarius. Et sic dicunt, Papam vtrumque habere iurisdictionem à Deo immediate. Amplius dicunt sic: Quae à Deo sunt, ordinata sunt. Roman. 8. Vtraque potestas à Deo est: ergo ordine quodam, scilicet saecularis mediante spirituali, & non immediate à Deo. Amplius dicunt, & videtur esse rationabile, cum vna sit Ecclesia, & vnus populus Christianus, & vnum corpus mysticum, quod sit vnum caput, à quo spiritualiter & temporaliter membra dependeant. Ideo dicit, quod potestas in Ecclesia siue saecularis siue temporalis dependet ex vno, apud quem vtraque residet: & iste est Papa, successor Petri, & vicarius Christi. Item adducunt pro se Bernhardum ad Eugenium Papam, libro quarto dicentem sic: Quid tibi denuo gladium vsurpare tentas? quem semel iussus es reponere in vaginam: quem tamen qui tuum negat, non satis videtur attendere verbum. Domini, sic dicentis: Converte gladium tuum in vaginam, tuus est ergo, & vtrumque ipse tuo nutu, etsi non tua manu euaginandus. alioqui si ad te nullo modo pertineret: & is Apostolus dicentibus, Ecce gladii duo hic, non respondisset Dominus, Satis est: sed, Nimis est: vtrumque ergo Ecclesiae est, & temporalis & spiritualis. Sed it quidem pro Ecclesia, ille vero & ab Ecclesia exercendus: ille sacerdotis ore, iste militis manu, sed sine ad nutum sacerdotis, & iussum Imperatoris. Ex quibus patet, Papam immediate habere vtramque iurisdictionem, quam ad primariam auctoritatem, licet executio gladii materialis ad Imperatorem pertineat. Amplius praeter praedicta, arguit quidam Dominus Ioann. de Cremona doctor, vt dicitur, in Decreto, quod Dominus a principio rexit mundum per se: & Euam, Adam, Chaim puniuit, & hoc vsque ad diluuium. Ex tunc vero rexit per Noe; cui praecepit facere arcam, & regere eam & hic Noe sacerdos erat; vt ipse dixit: quia aedificauit altare Domino, & sacrificium obtulit. Postea autem rexit per Abraham & alios patriarchas, qui fuerunt sacerdotes, Deo sacrificia offerentes. vnde Abraham hic Domino aedificauit altare, & fuit presbyter, vt notatur Gen. 4. capite 3. Deinde rexit per Moysem & Aaron, qui punierunt Pharaonem, rexerunt populum Israel & in deserto in temporalibus & spiritualibus, & ii sacerdotes erant, vt in psalmo: Moyses & Aaron in sacerdotibus eius, &c. Videtur ergo, quod sacerdotes nouae legis, cum non sint minoris auctoritatis, habeant regere in vtrisque. Item arguitur sic: Habens dominium super finem, habet etiam in his, quae ordinantur ad finem: sed temporalia ordinantur ad spiritualia vt ad finem; Papa vero habet dominium in spiritualibus, ergo, &c. Item sic: Christus dedit animas Petro: sed corpus est propter animam, & ei subiectum: bona vero exteriora & temporalia sunt propter corpus, & ei sunt subiecta: ergo, de primo ad vltimum omnia exteriora sunt Papae subiecta. Et hoc etiam videtur dicere Apostolus 1. ad Corinth. 3. Nostra sunt omnia, nos autem Christi, Christus autem Dei. Exemplo autem Dei (vt dicit Glossa: quam tamen iste pro se non allegat) omnia quotquot sunt in mundo, nostra sunt. Item dicit iste, quod Imperatores a principio aliquod ius habuerunt in imperio: ipsi tamen propter peccata, quae commiserunt in sanctos, ipsos occidendo, & praecipue summos pontifices, priuati sunt iure imperii, & ius imperii ad Ecclesiam translatum est: quia priuilegium meretur amittere, qui commissa sibi abutitur potestate; vndecima quaestione tertio capite priuilegium. Item dicit iste, quod dominium quod nunc habet Ecclesia, & olim ipsum non habebat: significatum fuit Luca decimoquarto, vbi dicitur, quod pater familias parato conuiuio misit filium suum in vicos & plateas, dicere inutilitatis vt venirent: & cum hoc factum esset, dixit iterum paterfamilias seruo, vt exiret in vicos & saepes, & compelleret omnes intrare, vt impleretur domus tota. In primo significatur Ecclesia, quantum ad statum suum primum, quando non habebat auctoritatem compellendi, quia erat subiecta. Sed in secundo significatur status Ecclesiae modernus, in quo habet auctoritatem plenariam compellendi & imperandi in omnibus: vt expositi Augustinus, & habetur vigesima tertia quaestione quarta cap. displicet. Et consimilia adducunt quidam de illo Psalmo: Quare fremuerunt gentes. fremuisse dicuntur primo gentes & Iudaei contra Christum: in quo significatur primus status Ecclesiae. Postea dicitur, Dirumpamus vincula eorum, &c. & infra, Et nunc reges intelligite: visque, Apprehendite disciplinam, &c. in quo signatur status Ecclesiae modernus, in quo Papa Christi vicarius habet dominium super reges terrae, qui ei debent totaliter esse subiecti, licet a principio hanc potestatem non habuerit. Adiungunt etiam aliqui, quod Dominus a principio Petrum & Andream vocando conuertit: sed vltimum Apostolorum, scilicet Paulum, conuertit ad terram prosternendo: & hoc adaptant modo consimili, sicut & praecedentia. Item adiungunt aliqui ad diminutionem regiae potestatis, & ad exaltationem Papalis dignitatis, quod Dominus populo Israel a principio instituit sacerdotes: sed non instituit eis regem, sed solum permisit eorum arbitrio, dicens Deuteronomio decimoseptimo, Constituam mihi regem super me, &c. Et hoc permisit Dominus, indignatus ad petitionem ipsorum; vt patet per hoc, quod dicit ad Samuelem primo Regum octauo: Non te abiecerunt, sed me, ne regnem super eos. Ex quo patet, regnum sine regimen regale non esse acceptum a Deo, sed ipsum solum permisit indignatus; & magis esset Deo acceptum, quod per solum Pontificem mundus in omnibus regeretur. Vnde Osee octauo dicitur de regibus: regnauerunt, & non ex me: principes extiterunt, & non cognoui eos. Item vt diminuant regiam potestatem, & trahant eam ad Papam, assumunt illud Genes. quadragesimo septimo, quod cum tempore famis cunctorum Aegyptiorum triticum emeret sibi Pharao, atque sub eadem fame suae seruituti subiiceret; sacerdotibus tamen ista necessaria subministrauit, vt nec possessionibus, nec libertatibus nudarentur; quasi Domino ex tunc pronunciante, vel praenunciante, sacerdotes in omni gente liberos esse oportere. Quod verbum sic dictum accipitur ab Vrbano Papa, 24. qu. vltim. cap. tribuunt, ad probandum, quod temporalia clericorum non videntur imperialibus exactionibus subiicienda. Item, si Papa citet episcopos alicuius regionis ad curiam, & rex, a quo tenent feudalia, dicat se eis indigere, & eos retinere velit, tenentur obedire Papae. 23. quaest. 7. ih cap. reprehensibilem. & sic saltem in tali casu non tenentur principi, sed Papa videtur eos eximere. Item dicunt, quod Papa potestate regibus auferre collationem praebendarum, quae sibi competere dicuntur de iure patronatus, & de consuetudine. Quod probant, tum quia collatio beneficiorum est spirituale quoddam, vel spirituali annexum, sicut ius decimarum; & ita non cadit in laicum; tum quia dos Ecclesiae non debet esse onerosa. tum quia consuetudo non praeiudicat iuri priuato: de iure vero priuato competit ordinario beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, & non laicae personae. tum quia consuetudo vel conditio inhonesta, & contraria substantiae contractus, pro non adiecta habetur; & sic cum dicta conditio sit inhonesta, pro non adiecta haberi debet. tum quia Ecclesia gaudet iure minorum; & ideo cum reputet se grauatam de talibus conuentionibus & dissimulationibus, potest restitutionem in integrum; & sic Papa loco Ecclesiae potest repetere praedicta, & inhibere ne amodo reges dicta beneficia conferant. Et ad confirmationem suae sententiae, dicunt isti, quod Papa debet esse perfectus in utraque vita, actiua scilicet & contemplatiua, multo plus quam quilibet alius prælatus. perfectus autem esse non potest in actiua vita, nisi habeat dominium in temporalibus directum & vniuersale: quia ad vitam actiuam pertinet administratio temporalium. Item dicunt, quod clerici plus vigent ratione & intellectu, quam laici: & tales debeant regere in utrisque. Item dicunt, quod contrarium loquentes, dicunt in fauorem principum spe vel timore, & non secundum conscientiam. Item dicit ille de Cremona, quod quasi hæretici vitari debent, & etiam iudicari, dicentes Papam non habere potestatem in temporalibus, quia hoc dicunt, vt ecclesia non possit hæreticos coercere per brachium seculare. Hæc sunt quæ audire vel colligere potui in hanc partem.
units.tr: Again, Matthew 18 says: "If your brother sins against you, go and tell him..." and further: "But if he will not hear you, tell it to the Church; but if he refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector." Therefore the Church has authority to judge wherever an injury is reported to it. Again, the Emperor Theodosius decreed, and Charlemagne renewed, that whoever has a lawsuit and chooses the bishop of the holy see as judge is to have the case sent at once to the bishops' court, with the litigants and their argument, without any doubt, even if the other party objects (Extra, De iudiciis, ch. Novit). Again, Deuteronomy says, and it is cited in Extra, Qui filii sint legitimi, Per venerabilem: "If you find a judgment difficult and ambiguous among you, blood against blood, cause against cause, leprosy against leprosy, and you see that the judgments in the courts vary, you shall go to the priests of the Levitical line and to the judge who is then in office, and they shall declare to you the truth of the judgment; and you shall do whatever they say in the place which God has chosen, and you shall follow their sentence exactly." Again: he who can do the greater can do the lesser. Since the Pope can rule in spiritual matters, he can rule in temporal ones. Again, temporal things are ordered towards spiritual ones and sometimes serve them; therefore the Pope, who has charge of spiritual things, also has to judge and ordain temporal things, at least so far as they bear on spiritual ones. Again, the Pope changes and transfers legacies made indiscriminately. It also belongs to the Pope to make restitution from the goods of the dead when the persons to whom they are owed are unknown; so he must in this way ordain temporal matters. Furthermore, some argue thus: bodily things are governed by spiritual things and depend on them, as is shown by many examples. For the heavenly bodies are administered by angels, and in a human being the soul rules and moves the body. In the same way, then, spiritual power has causal priority over temporal power, and temporal power depends on spiritual power as on its cause, since such power exists chiefly for the governing of temporal life. Hugh touches on this argument in On the Sacraments, book 2, part 2, chapter 4, saying: as spiritual life is more worthy than earthly life, and the soul than the body, so spiritual power surpasses earthly power and excels secular power in honour and dignity. For spiritual power has the right both to establish earthly power, that it may exist, and to judge it, if it is not good; but spiritual power was itself first instituted by God, and if it strays it can be judged by God alone. For it is written: "The spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one" (1 Cor. 2.15); and so spiritual power establishes and judges secular power. Again, they argue the same from the order of ends. In ordered arts, the art to which the ultimate and chief end belongs commands the others, to which the secondary ends belong. But secular power aims at the good of the multitude, which is to live according to virtue, and this can be reached by natural power through the things administered to it. Spiritual power, however, aims at the supernatural good of the multitude, namely eternal life or blessedness, and directs men towards it. A supernatural end is more excellent and more principal than any other end; therefore spiritual power, which has been given to the ministers of the Church, is superior to secular power not only in dignity but also in causal authority, and it has the right to prescribe how the latter ought to act. From this same premise they further conclude that the Pope hands down laws to princes, according to which they ought to carry out and exercise secular jurisdiction, and that secular princes cannot take laws from anywhere else unless they have been approved by the Pope. They also say that spiritual power is therefore called a royal priesthood, because Christ is king and priest, and his vicar has royal and priestly power; for through him royal power is instituted, ordained, sanctified and blessed. For this reason they say that in the Old Testament, as Hugh says, the priesthood was first instituted by God, and afterwards royal power was ordained through the priesthood at the Lord's command. And still the dignity of the priesthood signifies royal power by blessing it, and shapes it by instituting it. They also cite Augustine, On the City of God, book 2, chapter 21, where he says that a commonwealth cannot be governed without true justice, and there is no true justice where Christ is not the ruler; so there is no right and true commonwealth except that of the Christian people, in which the right of governing belongs only to the Pope, who is Christ's vicar. And so they say that the Pope holds both jurisdictions immediately from God. Again they say: "What is from God is ordered" (Rom. 13.1). "Both powers are from God"; therefore they are ordered in a certain way, namely the secular power through the spiritual, and not immediately from God. Again they say, and it seems reasonable, since there is one Church, one Christian people and one mystical body, which has one head, on whom the members depend both spiritually and temporally, that the power in the Church, whether secular or temporal, depends on one person in whom both reside; and this is the Pope, the successor of Peter and vicar of Christ. They also bring forward in their favour Bernard, writing to Pope Eugenius in book 4, who says: "Why do you again attempt to seize the sword, which you were once ordered to return to its sheath? Whoever denies that it is yours does not seem to have paid enough attention to the word of the Lord, who says: 'Put your sword back into its sheath' (Matt. 26.52). It is yours, then, and both are yours to be drawn at your nod, though not by your hand. Otherwise it would not belong to you at all; and the Lord would not have answered the apostles, who said, 'Behold, here are two swords' (Luke 22.38), 'It is enough,' but 'It is too much.' Both, then, belong to the Church, both the temporal and the spiritual sword. But the one is to be drawn for the Church, the other by the Church: the one by the hand of the priest, the other by the hand of the soldier, yet at the nod of the priest and at the command of the emperor." From these words it is clear that the Pope holds both jurisdictions immediately, and that the material execution of the sword, though it belongs to the Emperor, rests on the Pope's primary authority. Furthermore, beyond what has been said, a certain Lord John of Cremona, a teacher in the Decretum, as it is reported, argues that the Lord from the beginning ruled the world himself, and punished Eve, Adam and Cain, and this until the flood. From then on he ruled through Noah, whom he ordered to build the ark and to steer it, and this Noah was a priest, as he himself said, because he built an altar to the Lord and offered sacrifice. Afterwards he ruled through Abraham and the other patriarchs, who were priests offering sacrifices to God; hence Abraham here built an altar to the Lord and was an elder, as is noted in Genesis, chapter 3 of the fourth book. Then he ruled through Moses and Aaron, who punished Pharaoh and governed the people of Israel in the desert in both temporal and spiritual matters; and they were priests, as in the psalm: "Moses and Aaron among his priests" (Ps. 99.6). It seems, therefore, that the priests of the New Law, since they are not of lesser authority, should rule in both spheres. Again the argument runs thus: whoever has dominion over an end has dominion also over the things ordered to that end; but temporal things are ordered to spiritual things as to their end; and the Pope has dominion over spiritual things; therefore, etc. Again: Christ gave souls to Peter; but the body exists for the sake of the soul and is subject to it; and external and temporal goods exist for the sake of the body and are subject to it; therefore, from first to last, all external things are subject to the Pope. The Apostle seems to say this too in 1 Corinthians 3: "All things are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's" (1 Cor. 3.22-23). By the example of God (as the Gloss says, though this writer does not cite it in his favour), all things that are in the world are ours. Again this writer says that the emperors had some right in the empire from the beginning, but that they, because of the sins they committed against the saints by killing them, and especially the supreme pontiffs, were deprived of the right of empire, and the right of empire was transferred to the Church, for he who abuses the power entrusted to him deserves to lose the privilege; 11th question, 3rd chapter, Privilegium. Again this writer says that the dominion which the Church now has, and which it did not have formerly, was signified in Luke 14, where it is said that a householder, when the feast was ready, sent his son into the streets and lanes to tell those invited to come; and when this was done, the householder said again to his servant that he should go out into the streets and hedges and compel all to come in, so that his house might be filled. In the first, the Church is signified in its first state, when it had no authority to compel, because it was subject. But in the second, the modern state of the Church is signified, in which it has full authority to compel and command in all things; as Augustine explains, and as is found in the 23rd question, 4th chapter, Displicet. Some people bring similar arguments from that psalm: "Why do the nations rage?" (Ps. 2.1). It is said that at first the nations and the Jews raged against Christ; and this signifies the first state of the Church. Afterwards it is said: "Let us break their bonds," and further on: "And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth" (Ps. 2.2, 10); and this signifies the modern state of the Church, in which the Pope, Christ's vicar, has dominion over the kings of the earth, who ought to be wholly subject to him, although at the beginning he did not have this power. Some also add that the Lord at the beginning converted Peter and Andrew by calling them, but converted the last of the apostles, namely Paul, by throwing him to the ground; and they apply this in a similar way to what went before. Again some add, to diminish royal power and to exalt the papal dignity, that the Lord at the beginning instituted priests for the people of Israel, but did not institute a king for them; he left this to their own choice, saying in Deuteronomy 17: "I will set a king over me" (Deut. 17.14). And the Lord allowed this, being displeased at their request; as is clear from what he says to Samuel in 1 Samuel 8: "They have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them" (1 Sam. 8.7). From this it is clear that a kingdom without royal rule was not accepted by God, but he merely allowed it in his displeasure; and it would be more acceptable to God if the world were governed in all things by the Pope alone. Hence Hosea 8 says of kings: "They have reigned, but not by me; they have been princes, but I did not know them" (Hos. 8.4). Again, to diminish royal power and draw it to the Pope, they take up Genesis 47, where Pharaoh, in the time of famine, bought wheat for all the Egyptians and at the same time reduced them to his servitude under that same famine; yet he supplied these necessities to the priests, so that they should be stripped neither of their possessions nor of their liberties; as if the Lord at that time were declaring, or foretelling, that priests in every nation ought to be free. This saying, so understood, is taken up by Pope Urban in 24th question, last, chapter Tribuunt, to prove that the temporal goods of clerics do not seem to be subject to imperial exactions. Again, if the Pope summons the bishops of some region to the Curia, and the king, from whom they hold their fiefs, says that he needs them and wishes to keep them, they are bound to obey the Pope (23rd question 7, chapter Reprehensibilem). And so, at least in such a case, they are not bound to the prince, but the Pope seems to release them. Again they say that the Pope may take away from kings the conferment of prebends, which are said to belong to them by right of patronage and custom. They prove this, first, because the conferment of benefices is something spiritual, or annexed to the spiritual, like the right to tithes; and so it does not fall to a layman. Second, because the endowment of the Church ought not to be burdensome. Third, because custom does not prejudice private right; but the private right to benefices of the Church belongs to the ordinary, and not to a lay person. Fourth, because a dishonourable condition or custom, contrary to the substance of the contract, is regarded as not added; and so, since that condition is dishonourable, it ought to be regarded as not added. Fifth, because the Church enjoys the right of minors; and so, since it considers itself burdened by such agreements and dissimulations, it can obtain restitution in full; and thus the Pope, in place of the Church, can recover these things and forbid kings from conferring these benefices from now on. And to confirm their view, these people say that the Pope ought to be perfect in both lives, the active and the contemplative, far more than any other prelate. But he cannot be perfect in the active life unless he has direct and universal dominion over temporal things, since the administration of temporal things belongs to the active life. Again they say that clerics are more vigorous in reason and understanding than laymen, and such men ought to rule in both spheres. Again they say that those who speak against this do so out of hope or fear of princes, and not according to conscience. Again this man of Cremona says that those who deny that the Pope has power over temporal things, because they say this so that the Church may not coerce heretics through the secular arm, ought to be avoided almost as heretics, and even condemned. These are the things that I have been able to hear or gather on this side of the question.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: AD horum vero solutionis euidentiam præmittenda sunt, scil. qualem potestatem acceperunt a Christo, Apostoli & discipuli Domini: & in ipsis episcopi & sacerdotes alii. Nam vt dicit glossa Luc.10. Sicut in Apostolis forma est episcoporum, sic in LXXII. discipulis forma est presbyterorum secundi ordinis, & omnis potestas sacerdotalis ad hos duos ordines reducitur. Est ergo sciendum, quod sicut patuit ex prædictis in 2.ca. Sacerdotium non est aliud quam potestas spiritualis, Ecclesiæ collata ad dispensandum fidelibus sacramenta gratiam continentia, qua ordinant tibi vitam æternam. Sicut autem natura, quæ non deficit in necessariis, ideo non dat alicui potentiam, nisi det sufficientia adiutoria, per quæ potentia illa modo conuenienti possit exire in suam operationem (vnde Philosophus habet pro inconuenienti, quod natura det alicui potentiam aliquam animæ, & non det ei organa, per quæ operatio animæ implicatur) ita Deus, cum minus deficiat quam natura, cum prædicta potestate dat sacerdotibus illa, sine quibus illi prædictam potestatem exercere non possint. Sunt autem quinque talia. Vnum est ex parte sacramentorum, materiæ corporalis sanctificatio, vel consecratio. Nam secundum Hugonem & Magistrum Sententiarum, sacramentum est sensibile elementum, sanctificatum & consecratum per verbum Dei. Duo autem sunt ex parte fidelium, quibus sacramenta ministrantur: quorum vnum est, debita informatio seu eruditio eorum per doctrinam, vt sciant quomodo viuere debeant, vt digne recipiant sacramenta: quia non conferunt, nisi dispositis. Aliud est, contemnentium coercio: vt qui propter turpe quod est in peccato, vel propter monitiones & eruditiones salutares non discedunt a turpi, ipsi per pœnas iudicum terreantur. Ex parte vero ministrorum sacramenta ministrantium, similiter duo requiruntur, vnum est, ipsorum distinctio, & ordinatio debita. Nam si multitudo debita ministrorum non esset ordinata & distincta per vnum, in hoc habente auctoritatem, esset confusio: & negligeretur communis vtilitas, si quilibet ministrorum posset exercere iurisdictionem suam vbique. Nam homines non consueuerunt ita esse solliciti de communi, sicut de sibi appropriato: esset etiam dissensionis materia in populo, & inter ministros, si omnes ministri curam haberent indistincte de omni populo, sicut in primatiua ecclesia erat, vbi vnus dicebat, Ego sum Pauli, alius vero dicebat, Ego sum Apollo. 1.Cor.
units.tr: BEFORE their answers can be made clear, we must first set out what power the Apostles and the disciples of the Lord received from Christ, and in them the bishops and the other priests. For, as the gloss on Luke 10 says, as the form of bishops is in the Apostles, so the form of elders of the second order is in the seventy-two disciples, and all sacerdotal power is reduced to these two orders. It must therefore be understood, as has been shown above in chapter 2, that priesthood is nothing other than the spiritual power conferred on the Church to dispense to the faithful the sacraments that contain grace, by which they are brought to eternal life. Now nature, which does not fail in necessary things, does not give anyone a power without also giving the sufficient aids by which that power can pass into its operation in a fitting way. (Hence the Philosopher holds it an absurdity that nature should give the soul some power and not give it the organs through which the soul's operation is carried out.) So God, since he falls short less than nature does, gives priests, together with the aforesaid power, those things without which they cannot exercise that power. There are five such things. The first, on the side of the sacraments, is the sanctification or consecration of corporeal matter. For according to Hugh and the Master of the Sentences, a sacrament is a sensible element, sanctified and consecrated by the word of God. Two things are required on the side of the faithful, to whom the sacraments are administered. The first is their proper instruction or teaching through doctrine, so that they know how they ought to live and so receive the sacraments worthily, since the sacraments confer grace only on those who are rightly disposed. The second is the restraint of the contemptuous: that those who, because of the shamefulness of sin, or because of salutary warnings and teachings, do not turn away from what is base, be frightened by the punishments of judges. On the side of the ministers who administer the sacraments, two things are likewise required. The first is their proper distinction and due ordering. For if the multitude of ministers were not ordered and distinguished through one man who has authority in this matter, there would be confusion, and the common good would be neglected, if each minister could exercise his jurisdiction everywhere. For men are not accustomed to be as careful about what is common as about what is their own; there would also be a source of dissension among the people and between the ministers, if all the ministers had care indiscriminately of the whole people, as was the case in the primitive Church, where one said, I am of Paul, and another said, I am of Apollos. 1.Cor.

units.la: 1. Et ideo necessaria est distincta ministrorum ordinatio, per aliquem vnum habentem auctoritatem in hoc. Aliud vero est, quo ad necessitatem vitæ, vel sustentationem. Et secundum ista in Euangelio accepimus sex potestates collatas Apostolis & discipulis Domini, & in ipsis successoribus eorum, ministris sc. ecclesiasticis. Prima est potestas consecrationis, quæ interdum dicitur character vel potestas ordinis, quam contulit Dominus in cœna, quando tradens corpus suum sub specie panis, eis dixit: Hoc facite in meam commemorationem. 1.Cor.11. Alia est potestas administrationis sacramentorum, & præcipue sacramenti pœnitentiæ, quæ est potestas clauium vel spiritualis iurisdictionis in foro conscientiæ: & consistit in auctoritate discernendi lepram & non lepram, & in potentia absoluendi a culpa, & commutandi reatum pœnæ æternæ in reatum pœnæ temporalis. Et hæc potestas in spirituali foro promissa fuit Petro Matth.16. vbi dicitur: Tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum. & Matth.18. promissa fuit omnibus, cum dicitur: Quæcunque alligaueritis, &c. Collata vero fuit eis, cum dictum est eis Iohan.20. Sicut misit me Pater, & ego mitto vos. Et cum hoc dixisset, insufflauit dicens: Accipite Spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, &c. Et hæc potestas secundum aliquos cum potestate consecrationis, est vna secundum essentiam potestatis, differens secundum diuersos actus corporis mystici: & est complementum sacerdotalis dignitatis, vel potestatis. Vnde in ordinatione simplicium sacerdotum, & inordinatione episcoporum, qui sunt magni sacerdotes, eadem verba proferuntur: scilicet: Accipite Spiritum sanctum, quorum, &c. Tertia est, scilicet potestas siue auctoritas apostolatus siue prædicationis, quam tradit eis Dominus, dicens Matth.vlt. Euntes prædicate, &c. & Marci vlt. Euntes docete omnes gentes, &c. Quarta potestas est iudiciaria potestas, scil. correctionis in foro exteriori, per quam timore pœnæ peccata corriguntur, præcipue quæ sunt in scandalo Ecclesiæ. Et hæc potestas data est Mat.18. vbi dicitur: Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, &c. vsq; ibi: Quod si te non audierit, dic Ecclesiæ, quod si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. vbi dicit Glossa: Obiurgatio plurimorum ipsum corrigat. Et sequitur: Amen dico vobis, quodcunque alligaueritis, &c. vbi notatur auctoritas discernendi in dicto, data Ecclesiæ, cum dicitur, Dic Ecclesiæ: sc. vt cognoscat. & auctoritas coercendi seu puniendi per ecclesiasticam censuram, cum dicitur, Quod si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus, &c. Cuius confirmationè subiugit dicens: Amen dico vobis, quacunque (vel, quodcunque) alligaueritis, &c. Gloss. Vinculo anathematis. Et est signanter considerandum, quod in istis tribus actibus sacerdotes habent perfectam potestatem hierarchisandi populum fidelium: scilicet illuminandi per doctrinam, purgandi per correctionem, & perficiendi di per sacramentorum administrationem. Potestas quinta est, sc. dispositionis ministrorum secundum quosdam, quo ad determinationem iurisdictionis Ecclesiasticæ, vt viteretur confusio. Et hæc collata est Petro & successoribus eius, Iohan. 21. vbi dictum est ei: Pasce oues meas. Potestas enim clauium, & iurisdictionis potestas, collata erat omnibus æqualiter, & sine determinatione, & poterat quilibet vti ea in quemlibet peccatorem cum effectu: cum peccator sit debita materia, super quam habet cadere iurisdictionis actus: sicut absolutio siue panis triticeus sine determinatione est materia, super quam cadit actus potestatis ordinis. Vnde & B. Paulus vbiq; sine determinatione populum hierarchisabat, vt patet in suis Epistolis. Et quia confusio, vt dictum est, inde sequi poterat: ideo Dominus hæc præuidens, contulit Petro & successoribus eius authoritatem disponendi ministros Ecclesiæ, & determinandi iurisdictionem, dicens, Pasce oues meas: vt scil. pastor generalis, ad quem dispositio & regimen generale ouium & ouilis pertineret. hoc enim nulli alii dictum est. Quidam tamen rationabiliter dicunt, quod non quilibet peccator est materia, super quam debet vel potest cadere cum effectu actus clauium, & potestas iurisdictionis: sed peccator subditus, & ideo prædicta potestas non habet effectū in peccatore, nisi suppositā subiectione, quę facit hominem esse debitam materiam, super quā clauis potest habere actum suum cum effectu: sicut potestas ordinis non habet effectum, nisi super panem triticeum. Et hæc iurisdictio siue prælatio data est Petro super totam Ecclesiam, cum dictum est ei, Pasce oues meas: id est, sis pastor & prælatus, & Ecclesiam tibi vt pastori committo & subdo. Vnde Theophilus, finito prædicto commissionem omnium Petro commendat, & nulli alii. Idem dicit Greg. etiam simile. Et sic, licet vel quamuis omnes Apostoli eandem habuissent à Christo & æqualem potestatem clauium & iurisdictionis: tamen iurisdictionem siue materiam subiectam non habuit nisi Petrus, & cui committere voluit. Et secundum hanc viam per illud verbum, Pasce oues meas, non est data Petro potestas determinandi iurisdictionem prius ab omnibus habitam: sed iurisdictio soli Petro data est. quam tamen postea diuisim Dominus aliis dedit, vocans alios in partem sollicitudinis. Secundum vero primam opinionem, quod quilibet Episcopus non absoluit extra suam dioecesim, est ex ordinatione Petri seu Ecclesiæ determinantis & prohibentis: quia sine prohibitione alias posset: & adhuc si facet, teneret factum, cum habeat potestatem ex sua ordinatione, & materiam debitam, scilicet peccatorem: sed male faceret, transgrediendo Ecclesiæ ordinationem. Sicut Latinus sacerdos, verba sacramentalia proferens super panem fermentatum, conficeret: sed peccaret transgrediendo Ecclesiæ suæ ordinationem, determinantis sibi panem triticeum azymum. Concordat autem dicta positio dominio rerum temporalium, vt sicut appropriatio rerum temporalium est solum per positionem hominum, qua remota non possum dicere, Hoc est meum: sed, Omnia sunt communia, ita amota ordinatione Ecclesiæ, hic populus non plus est istius episcopi quam alterius: sed est cuiuslibet sacerdotis, & indifferenter à quolibet potest absolui. Appropriatio autem facta est per Ecclesiam, ex authoritate data Petro, ibi, Pasce oues meas. Secundum vero opinionem aliam, quod quilibet episcopus non absoluat extra dioecesim, non est ex Ecclesiæ ordinatione tantum, sed propter defectum materiæ: quia extra dioecesim non habet populum subiectum. Vnde intendens absoluere extra dioecesim suam, & verba proferens super peccatorem, non absoluit: sicut nec sacerdos conficeret prosequendo verba consecrationis super lapidem, vel panem non triticeum. Sunt vero tertii, dicentes quod per illud verbum, Pasce oues meas, data est Petro authoritas solum docendi & ædificandi, & prælatis conuenit executio. Executio autem est eis præcepta, cum dictum est: Ite docete, &c. Vnde gloss. Pasce oues meas, verbo & exemplo: non corporali cibo, vel pabulo. Alia vero potestas, quæ sexta est, conuenit eis ex debito præcedentium: scilic. potestas accipiendi necessaria ad congruentem vitæ sustentationem, ab iis quibus spiritualia ministrant: & hæc potestas data est, imo deberi declarata Petro & aliis Apostolis, Matth. 10. vbi postquam dixerat, Euntes prædicate, &c. subiunxit, qualiter ad temporalia se haberent, dicens: Gratis accepistis, gratis date. Glossa: Sicut ego vobis sine precio do talem potestatem, & vos gratis date, ne Euangelii gratia corrumpatur. Et sequitur: Nolite possidere aurum, neque argentum, neque pecuniam in zonis vestris. Glossa: Qui alios ad contemptum hortamini diuitiarum. sequitur, Neque peram in via, neque duas tunicas, neque calciamenta, neque virgam. Glossa: Auxilium baculi prope necessitatis amputat, ne curent de crastino, qui docent omnia regi à Deo. Et subditur potestas eis data, cum dicitur: Dignus enim est operarius cibo suo. Glossa: Ecce quare præcepit eis nil ferre, quia omnia debentur eis. & alia Glossa ibi dicit: Tantum necessaria accipite, quantum ad necessitatem sufficit, vnde sequi melius æternis vacetis. De hac etiam potestate accipiendi necessaria ad suffragationem vitæ, habetur Marci 6. & Luca 10. Hæ igitur sunt potestates, quas acceperunt Apostoli à Christo. Aliam autem potestatem non acceperunt ab eo, vt puto, nisi miracula faciendi ad confirmationem fidei: in qua non necessario succedunt eis episcopi & sacerdotes, propter fidei confirmationem sic manifestam, vt iam non indigeat miraculis confirmari.
units.tr: Therefore a distinct ordering of ministers is necessary, through some one person who has authority in this matter. There is another matter, which concerns the necessities of life and maintenance. In respect of these things, we learn from the Gospel that six powers were conferred on the apostles and disciples of the Lord, and on their successors, namely the ecclesiastical ministers. The first is the power of consecration, which is sometimes called the character or power of orders, and which the Lord conferred at the supper, when, giving his body under the appearance of bread, he said to them: Do this in remembrance of me. 1 Cor. 11. The second is the power of administering the sacraments, and especially the sacrament of repentance. This is the power of the keys, or spiritual jurisdiction in the forum of conscience, and it consists in the authority of discerning leprosy from non-leprosy, in the power of absolving from guilt, and of exchanging the liability to eternal punishment for liability to temporal punishment. This power in the spiritual forum was promised to Peter in Matt. 16, where it is said: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. In Matt. 18 it was promised to all, when it is said: Whatever you shall bind, etc. It was conferred indeed when it was said to them in John 20: As the Father sent me, so I send you. And when he had said this, he breathed on them, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, etc. According to some, this power, together with the power of consecration, is one in essence, differing according to the various acts of the mystical body; and it is the completion of the priestly dignity or power. Hence in the ordination of ordinary priests, and in the installation of bishops, who are the high priests, the same words are spoken: namely, Receive the Holy Spirit, whose, etc. The third is the power or authority of apostleship or preaching, which the Lord handed on to them, saying in Matt. last chapter: Going, preach, etc., and in Mark last chapter: Going, teach all nations, etc. The fourth power is the judicial power, namely of correction in the external forum, by which sins are corrected through fear of punishment, especially those which are a scandal to the Church. This power was given in Matt. 18, where it is said: If your brother sins against you, etc., down to: But if he does not hear you, tell the Church; but if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector. Where the Gloss says: The rebuke of many should correct him. And it follows: Truly I say to you, whatever you bind, etc. Here is noted the authority of discerning, given to the Church in the words Tell the Church, namely that it may know; and the authority of restraining or punishing by ecclesiastical censure, when it is said: But if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen, etc. To confirm this he adds: Truly I say to you, whatever (or whatsoever) you shall bind, etc. Gloss: By the bond of anathema. And it must be carefully noted that in these three acts the priests have full power to govern the faithful people hierarchically: namely to enlighten through teaching, to purify through correction, and to perfect through the administration of the sacraments. The fifth power is, according to some, the power of disposing of ministers, with regard to the determining of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, so that confusion might be avoided. This was conferred on Peter and his successors, John 21, where it was said to him: Feed my sheep. For the power of the keys and the power of jurisdiction had been given equally to all, and without determination, and anyone could use it upon any sinner with effect, since a sinner is the proper matter upon which an act of jurisdiction may fall, just as absolution, or wheaten bread without determination, is the matter upon which an act of the power of orders falls. Hence also blessed Paul everywhere governed the people hierarchically without determination, as is evident in his Epistles. And because confusion, as has been said, could follow from this, the Lord, foreseeing this, conferred on Peter and his successors the authority of disposing the ministers of the Church and of determining jurisdiction, saying, Feed my sheep, namely that he might be the general shepherd, to whom the general disposition and rule of the sheep and the fold would belong; for this was said to no one else. Some, however, reasonably say that not every sinner is the matter upon which an act of the keys and the power of jurisdiction must or can fall with effect, but only a subject sinner; and therefore the aforesaid power has no effect on a sinner unless subjection is presupposed, which makes the man the proper matter upon which the key can exercise its act with effect; just as the power of orders has no effect except upon wheaten bread. And this jurisdiction or prelacy was given to Peter over the whole Church, when it was said to him, Feed my sheep: that is, be shepherd and prelate, and I commit and subject the Church to you as shepherd. Hence Theophilus, having finished the aforesaid, commends the commission of all to Peter, and to no one else. Gregory also says something similar. And so, although all the apostles had from Christ the same and an equal power of the keys and of jurisdiction, nevertheless Peter alone had the subject jurisdiction or matter, and to whomever he wished to commit it. And according to this view, through that word, Feed my sheep, power to determine a jurisdiction previously held by all was not given to Peter; but jurisdiction was given to Peter alone, which the Lord afterwards gave separately to others, calling others into a share of the care. According to the first opinion, however, that no bishop absolves outside his own diocese, this comes from the ordinance of Peter or of the Church, determining and forbidding; for otherwise it would be possible without prohibition. And even if he did so, the act would stand, since he has the power from his ordination and the proper matter, namely the sinner; but he would act wrongly, by transgressing the ordinance of the Church. Just as a Latin priest, pronouncing the sacramental words over leavened bread, would consecrate, but would sin by transgressing the ordinance of his Church, which determines unleavened wheaten bread for him. Moreover, this position agrees with the lordship over temporal goods: just as the appropriation of temporal goods rests solely on the agreement of men, and with that removed I cannot say, This is mine, but rather, All things are common; so, the ordinance of the Church being set aside, this people is no more this bishop's than another's, but belongs to any priest whatever, and can be absolved indifferently by anyone. But the appropriation was made by the Church, by the authority given to Peter there, Feed my sheep. According to the other opinion, however, that no bishop absolves outside his diocese, this is not from the ordinance of the Church alone, but on account of a defect of matter: because outside his diocese he has no subject people. Hence, intending to absolve outside his diocese, and pronouncing the words over a sinner, he does not absolve; just as a priest would not consecrate by pronouncing the words of consecration over a stone, or over bread that is not wheaten. There are, however, third-party writers who say that through that word, Feed my sheep, authority was given to Peter only of teaching and edifying, and that the carrying out belongs to the prelates. The carrying out, however, was enjoined on them when it was said: Go, teach, etc. Hence the gloss: Feed my sheep, by word and example, not by bodily food or fodder. The other power, which is the sixth, belongs to them from the due of those who precede them: namely the power of receiving what is necessary for a fitting maintenance of life from those to whom they minister spiritual things. And this power was given, or rather declared to be due, to Peter and the other apostles, Matt. 10, where, after he had said, Going, preach, etc., he added how they should conduct themselves in temporal matters, saying: You received freely, give freely. Gloss: As I give you such power without price, so you give freely, lest the grace of the Gospel be corrupted. And it follows: Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts. Gloss: You who exhort others to despise riches. It follows: Nor a bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff. Gloss: The help of a staff nearly removes need, so that those who teach that all things are governed by God may not be anxious about tomorrow. And the power given to them is added when it is said: For the labourer is worthy of his food. Gloss: See why he commanded them to carry nothing, because all things are due to them. And another gloss there says: Take only what is necessary, as much as suffices for need, so that you may the better be free for eternal things. Concerning this power also of receiving what is necessary for the support of life, we have it in Mark 6 and Luke 10. These, then, are the powers which the apostles received from Christ. But I think they received from him no other power, except that of working miracles for the confirmation of the faith; and in this bishops and priests do not necessarily succeed them, because the confirmation of the faith is now so manifest that it no longer needs to be confirmed by miracles.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Hīs declaratis, videndum est quid possint in temporalibus, & super principes; episcopi & sacerdotes ex prædictis potestatibus eis commissis. Et videtur quod de nulla dictarum potestatum habent directe potestatem in temporalibus: neque iurisdictionem temporalem super principes, nisi quibus possunt accipere necessaria ad vitæ sustentationem. Quod quidem videndum est per singulas potestates. De prima quidem potestate, quæ est potestas consecrationis, euidens est hoc, cum ipsa sit totaliter spiritualis, & æqualiter in omnibus episcopis & lacerdotibus, & degradatis & suspensis. Quod patet ex hoc, quod reconciliati iterum non ordinantur. Ex quo manifestum est, quod per talem potestatem nihil habent iurisdictionis vel dominii in temporalibus. Secunda vero potestas, scilicet clauium in foro conscientiæ, est spiritualis. unde Ioan. 20. Accipite Spiritum sanctum, &c. Glossa Chrys. dicit. Collata fuit potestas spiritualis tantum dimittendi peccata: nec potest aliquid in temporalibus, nisi cum in foro conscientia, cum ad satisfactionem inducit, sicut & cæteras potestates corporales. Ex quo patet, quod nullus est ei subiectus simpliciter, sed sub multiplici conditione: scilicet si peccauerit, & si pœnitere noluerit: & si quidem obedire noluerit, non potest eum coercere ex prædicta potestate, sicut iudex secularis potest imponere pœnam pecuniariam vel emendam etiam nolenti, & ipsum ad hoc compellere. Tertia vero potestas seu auctoritas, scilicet prædicationis, omnino est spiritualis: nec omnino habet dominium, cum non sit potestas dominii, sed auctoritas magisterii: sicut Apostolus dicit 2. Timoth. 1. Positus sum ego prædicator & apostolus & magister gentium. Bernardus ad Eugenium libro tertio. Apostolis seu viris Apostolicis interdicitur dominatus. & ibidem: Domabis lapos, & non dominaberis ouibus. ësto vt alia quacunque ratione hac tibi vendices: (loquitur de temporalibus) sed non Apostolico iure: neque enim tibi ille dare potuit, quod non habuit: quod habuit, hoc dedit, solicitudinem scilicet super ecclesias. Audi ipsum apostolum Petrum: Non sicut dominantes in clero, sed forma facti gregis. Per hanc tamen auctoritatem docendi indirecte, possunt in temporalibus, in quantum inducunt homines ad pœnitentiam, & restitutionem æris alieni, & ad erogationem temporalium, secundum quod exigit ordo charitatis. De quarta vero potestate, in foro iudiciali exteriori est tota difficultas. propter quod intelligendum est, quod illa duo importat, scilicet auctoritatem discernendi seu corrigendi: quæ significatur, cum dicitur, Dic ecclesiæ: & potestatem coercendi, cum dicitur, Sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. hæc enim sunt duæ claues in foro exteriori. De prima ergo sciendum, quod iudex ecclesiasticus, vt ecclesiasticus est in foro exteriori, non cognoscit regulariter nisi de spiritualibus causis, quæ ecclesiasticæ vocantur: & non de temporalibus, nisi ratione delicti. quod tamen sic intelligitur, quod sit delictum: nec oportet de hoc fieri exceptionem, cum de nullo delicto cognoscat Ecclesia, nisi secundum quod reducitur ad spirituale & ecclesiasticum. Dupliciter enim peccatur in temporalibus: uno quidem modo, peccato oppositionis seu erroris: vt cum tenetur, quod usura non est peccatum mortale: vel tenetur, quod possumus alienum vendicare quocunque titulo: vel cum circa talia aliquis dubitat, an sit licitum vel illicitum secundum Deum. & cum omnia talia determinentur per diuinam legem, secundum quam habet iudicare iudex ecclesiasticus: non est dubium, quod ad solum iudicem Ecclesiasticum pertinet cognitio talium. Alio modo, peccato venditionis detinendo, sive impendendo alienum vt suum: & talium cognitio ad iudicem secularem pertinet solum, qui secundum leges humanas iudicat seu ciuiliter, secundum quas fiunt approbationes rerum, & vendicationes, ne res humanis viribus necessariæ negligantur, si omnibus & singulis essent communes: & ne, si communes essent ex indistincto, non seruaretur pax de facili inter homines. Unde propter hoc facta est rerum huiusmodi approbatio per Imperatores, vt dicit Augustin. super Ioan. vt habetur distinct. 8. cap, quo iure: Tolle, inquit, iura Imperatorum: & non potes ducere, Hæc res mea est. De iure enim naturali est vna omnium libertas, & communis omnium possessio. Et ita de peccato in temporalibus non iudicat vel cognoscit iudex Ecclesiasticus, sed secularis tantum: nisi forte aliunde quam a Christo concessum ei fuerit, vel permissum. Et hoc notauit Bernardus ad Eugenium dicens: Non in possessionibus, sed in criminibus potestas vestra est: vt supra cap. 1ρ. Et super illud Matthæi 18. Et in ore duorum vel trium stet omne testimonium. dicit Glossa, Vt probent illud esse peccatum, si negauerit esse peccatum. sic enim, si non acquiescit, dicendum est Ecclesiæ, & non aliter, quæ iudicat de peccato. Et 26. distinctione cap. duo. vbi Papa loquitur Imperatori, dignosci inter hoc, te ex illorum pendere iudicio; scilicet sacerdotum. Glossa, Quoad spiritualia & hoc etiam notauerunt summi pontifices. extra, qui sunt filii legitimi cap. lator. vbi dicitur, Iudex secularis sive dominus quæstionem de hereditate debet decidere. Et cap. causam debet: Et si attendentes, quod ad regem pertinet, non ad Ecclesiam, de talibus possessionibus iudicare, ne videamur iuris regis Anglorum detrahere, qui ipsorum iudicium ad se asserit pertinere. Extra, de iudiciis, cap. nouit, dicit Papa: Non intendimus iudicare de feudo, cuius ad ipsum regem spectat iudicium, nisi forte iure communi, &c. Et extra, de appellatione, si duobus, dicitur, quod ad Papam non est appellandum a iudice seculari, nisi in terra Ecclesiæ subiecta, vel concessa. Dicere vero quod talia dicunt summi Pontifices ex humilitate, est omnino perniciosum: & hoc est ponere os in cœlum. quia Philosophus hoc attribuit in quarto Ethicorum, peccato ironiæ, quæ opponitur virtuti. Dicit etiam tales humiles non esse virtuosos, sed timidos & blanditores. Et Augustinus in libro de verbis Apostoli, dicit sic: Cum humilitatis causa mentiris, si non eras peccator antequam mentieris, mentiendo peccator efficieris. Et super Iohannem: Non ita timeatur arrogantia, vt veritas relinquatur. Et Gregorius dicit; Incauti sunt humiles, qui se mentiendo illaqueant. De potestate vero correctionis seu censuræ Ecclesiasticæ sciendum, quod non est nisi spiritualis directe: quia nullam pœnam in foro exteriori potest imponere nisi spiritualem, nisi sub conditione & per accidens. Licet enim iudex Ecclesiasticus habeat homines in Deum reducere & a peccato retrahere & corrigere: hoc tamen non habet nisi secundum viam a Deo sibi datam, quæ est separando a sacramentis, & participatione fidelium. & huiusmodi ad censuram Ecclesiasticam pertinent. & dicitur, Nisi sub conditione, scil. si quis pœnitere velit, & pœnitentiam pecuniariam acceptare, non enim potest iudex Ecclesiasticus ratione delicti imponere pœnam corporalem vel pecuniariam.
units.tr: Having made these points clear, we must consider what bishops and priests can do in temporal matters, and over princes, by virtue of the powers committed to them. It seems that they have no direct power in temporal matters from any of these powers, nor any temporal jurisdiction over princes, except in so far as they can receive what is necessary for sustaining life. This must be examined power by power. As for the first power, namely the power of consecration, it is evident that it is entirely spiritual, and equally present in all bishops and priests, whether deposed or suspended. This is clear from the fact that those who are reconciled are not ordained again. From this it is plain that through such a power they have no jurisdiction or dominion whatever in temporal matters. The second power, namely that of the keys in the forum of conscience, is spiritual; hence John 20: "Receive the Holy Spirit, etc." The gloss of Chrysostom says: "The power conferred was only the spiritual power of forgiving sins; it cannot extend to anything temporal, except when, in the forum of conscience, it leads a person to satisfaction, just as with the other, bodily powers." From this it is clear that no one is simply subject to it, but under many conditions: namely, if he has sinned, and if he is unwilling to repent. And if he is unwilling to obey, it cannot coerce him by this power, as a secular judge can impose a fine or penalty in money even on one who is unwilling, and compel him to it. The third power or authority, namely that of preaching, is wholly spiritual; nor does it carry any dominion at all, since it is not a power of lordship but an authority of teaching: as the Apostle says in 2 Timothy 1: "I am appointed a preacher, an apostle and a teacher of the Gentiles." Bernard to Eugenius, book three: "Dominion is forbidden to the Apostles or to apostolic men." And in the same place: "You shall subdue stones, and not lord it over sheep. Suppose you claim these things on some other ground (he is speaking of temporal matters), but not by apostolic right: for he could not give you what he did not have; what he had, he gave, namely care over the churches. Hear the Apostle Peter himself: not as lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock." Nevertheless, through this authority of teaching, they may indirectly exercise influence in temporal matters, in so far as they lead people to repentance, to restitution of debts, and to the giving of temporal goods, as the order of charity requires. As for the fourth power, the whole difficulty lies in the external judicial forum. On this account it must be understood that these two things are involved: the authority of discerning or correcting, which is signified when it is said, "Tell it to the Church"; and the power of coercing, when it is said, "Let him be to you as a heathen and a publican." For these are the two keys in the external forum. Of the first, then, it must be known that an ecclesiastical judge, as ecclesiastical, in the external forum ordinarily takes cognizance only of spiritual causes, which are called ecclesiastical, and not of temporal causes, except by reason of a delict. Yet this is understood in such a way that it be a delict; nor is any exception needed here, since the Church takes cognizance of no delict except in so far as it is referred to the spiritual and ecclesiastical. For one sins in temporal matters in two ways. In one way, by the sin of opposition or error: as when it is held that usury is not a mortal sin, or that we may claim what belongs to another on any ground whatever, or when someone doubts whether such things are lawful or unlawful according to God. And since all such matters are determined by the divine law, according to which the ecclesiastical judge has to judge, there is no doubt that the cognizance of such things belongs to the ecclesiastical judge alone. In another way, by the sin of retaining or spending another's property as one's own; and the cognizance of such things belongs to the secular judge alone, who judges according to human laws, or civilly, by which the appropriation and claiming of things is made, lest the things necessary to human life be neglected, if they were common to all and each, and lest, if they were held in common without distinction, peace among men would not easily be kept. Hence for this reason the approval of such things was made by the emperors, as Augustine says on John, as it is found in Distinction 8, chapter "Quo iure": "Take away, he says, the rights of emperors, and you cannot say, 'This thing is mine.' For by natural law there is a common liberty for all, and a common possession for all." And so the ecclesiastical judge does not judge or take cognizance of sin in temporal matters, but only the secular judge does, unless perhaps it has been granted or permitted to him by some other source than Christ. Bernard noted this in writing to Eugenius, saying: "Your power is not over possessions, but over crimes," as above, chapter 1ρ. And on the words of Matthew 18, "And in the mouth of two or three let every word be established," the gloss says: "So that they may prove it to be a sin, if he denies that it is a sin." For if he does not give way, it must be said to the Church, and not otherwise, since it is the Church that judges concerning sin. And Distinction 26, chapter "Duo," where the Pope speaks to the emperor: "Know that in these matters you depend upon their judgment," namely that of the priests. The gloss: "As to spiritual matters; and the supreme pontiffs have noted this too, Extra, 'Qui sunt filii legitimi,' chapter 'Lator,'" where it is said: "A secular judge or lord ought to decide a question about inheritance." And the chapter "Causam debet": "And if they consider that it pertains to the king, not to the Church, to judge concerning such possessions, lest we seem to detract from the right of the King of the English, who asserts that the judgment of them belongs to him." Extra, "De iudiciis," chapter "Nouit," the Pope says: "We do not intend to judge concerning a fief, the judgment of which belongs to the king himself, unless perhaps by common law, etc." And Extra, "De appellatione," "Si duobus," it is said that "appeal is not to be made to the Pope from a secular judge, except in lands subject or granted to the Church." But to say that such things are said by the supreme pontiffs out of humility is utterly pernicious, and this is to set the mouth against heaven. For the Philosopher attributes this, in the Fourth book of the Ethics, to the vice of irony, which is opposed to virtue. He also says that such persons who feign humility are not virtuous, but timid and flatterers. And Augustine in his book "On the Words of the Apostle" says thus: "When you lie for the sake of humility, if you were not a sinner before you lied, by lying you will become a sinner." And on John: "Let arrogance not be so feared that the truth is abandoned." And Gregory says: "Humble people are unwary who entangle themselves by lying." Concerning the power of correction or ecclesiastical censure, it must be known that it is directly spiritual only: for in the external forum it can impose no penalty except a spiritual one, unless conditionally and incidentally. For although the ecclesiastical judge has the task of bringing men back to God and of withdrawing and correcting them from sin, he has this only according to the way given to him by God, which is by separation from the sacraments and from the fellowship of the faithful; and such things belong to ecclesiastical censure. And I say "unless conditionally": namely, if someone is willing to repent and to accept a penance in money. For the ecclesiastical judge cannot, by reason of a delict, impose a bodily or pecuniary penalty.

units.la: [Marginal line numbers 5 to 60 appear at the right edge and are not reproduced as text.] pecuniariam, sicut facit iudex secularis: sed solum, si ille velit eam acceptare. Si enim non vult eam acceptare, compellet eum iudex Ecclesiasticus per excommunicationem, vel aliam poenam spiritualem, quae est ultima quam potest inferre: nec ultra potest aliquid facere, nisi dico per accidens, quia si esset haereticus & incorrigibilis, & contemptor Ecclesiasticae censurae, posset Papa aliquid facere in populo unde privaretur ille seculari honore, & deponitur a populo. Et hoc faceret Papa in crimine Ecclesiastico, cuius cognitio ad ipsum pertinet excommunicando, sc. omnes qui ei ut domino obedirent: & sic populus ipsum deponeret, & Papa per accidens. Sic etiam econverso, si Papa esset criminosus, & scandalizaret Ecclesiam, & incorrigibilis esset, princeps posset ipsum excommunicare indirecte, & deponere ipsum per accidens, movendo sc. ipsum per se & per cardinales. Et si quidem Papa acquiescere nolet, posset aliquid facere in populo, unde compelleretur cedere, vel deponeretur a populo: quia Imperator posset sub hypotheca rerum, vel poena corporum inhibere omnibus & singulis, ut nullus ei obediret vel serviret Papae, & hoc quidem potest utrerq; in alterum. Nam utrerq;, sc. papa & Imperator, universalem & ubiq; habent iurisdictionem: sed iste spiritualem, & ille temporalem, & tamen in hoc distinctio est adhibenda, quia ubi rex delinqueret in spiritualibus, sc. in fide, matrimonio, & aliis huiusmodi, quorum iurisdictio ad iudicem Ecclesiasticum pertinet, papa habet ipsum monere: & si ipse inveniatur pertinax & incorrigibilis, potest ipsum excommunicare, & ultra non potest plus nisi per accidens: quia si fuerit contemptor, potest facere in populo, ut dictum est. Ubi vero rex peccaret in temporalibus, quorum cognitio ad Ecclesiasticum non pertinet, tunc non habet ipsum corrigere primo, sed Barones & Pares de regno: qui si non possunt, vel non audent, possunt invocare auxilium Ecclesiae: quae requisita a Paribus in iuris subsidium potest monere principem, & procedere contra ipsum modo praedicto. Similiter vero, ubi papa delinqueret in temporalibus, quorum cognitio ad principem saecularem pertinent, ut si mutuaret ad usuram, vel mutuantibus faueret, & praecipue in iis quae per leges civiles sunt prohibita: Imperator si esset, haberet ipsum primo corrigere immediate monendo, & postea puniendo, nam ad principem pertinet omnes malefactores corrigere primo iure. Roman. 13. Non enim sine causa gladium portat, minister enim Dei est, vindex malorum in iram. Glossa super illud Rom. 13. Ideoque tributa praestabis: dicit, quod ad hoc instituti sunt, ut boni laudentur, mali vero puniantur. Et Hieronymus super Hieremiam, & habetur 23. q. 7. Regum officium proprium est facere iudicium & iustitiam, & liberare de manu calumniantium vi oppressos & peregrinos & pupillos & viduas, qui facilius opprimuntur a potentibus. Unde commendabiliter Henricus Imperator duos de papatu altercantes, non solum Canonica censura, sed imperiali auctoritate depoluit: ut legitur in Chronicis Romanorum. Et dicitur, quod primo iure habet Imperator ratione delicti praecipue civilis, papam immediate corrigere: quia de privilegio a principibus indulto, clerici non nisi per suos episcopos iudicantur, quod privilegium primo impetravit Iulius papa, qui secundus fuit post Syluestrum, adhuc Constantino viuente, ut dicitur in Chronicis.
