Quidam tamen dicunt hoc eis deberi iure divino, & non privilegio principum iuxta istud psalmi: Nolite tangere Christos meos, quod ipsi exponunt de sacerdotibus. Alii tamen exposuerunt de regibus, qui tunc vngebantur. Et sic legitur 2. Reg. 2. Dauid interfecit Doec Idumaeum, quia dicebat se interfecisse Christum Domini, id est Saulem. Si vero in spiritualibus delinquat papa, conferendo beneficia Ecclesiastica simoniace, ecclesias dissipando, privando personas Ecclesiasticas & capitula iuribus suis, vel etiam male docendo & sentiendo circa ea quae ad fidem & bonos mores pertinent: tunc primo monendus esset a cardinalibus, qui sunt loco totius cleri: & si incorrigibilis esset, nec possent per se amouere scandalum de ecclesia, tunc in subsidium iuris haberent supplicando invocare brachium seculare: & tunc Imperator requisitus a cardinalibus, cum sit membrum ecclesiae, deberet procedere contra papam, ex quo ecclesia non habet gladium secularem. Alio modo, non quidem manu, nec iussu, sed nutu & supplicatione, ut dicit Bernardus ad Eugenium: sic etiam duo gladii mutuo se iuvare tenentur ex communi charitate, quae membra ecclesiae unit. Colligitur hoc 26. distinct. ad verum. & 24. q. 5. principes. & capitulu sequentibus. Et sic legimus in Chronicis, quod Constantinus secundus, qui post ambitionem papatus cum fecisset multa ecclesiae scandala, per principes est depositus, & zelo fidelium oculis est privatus. Similiter Iohannes XII. cum esset venator, & lubricus, frequenter de sua correctione admonitus, nec correctus, per Imperatorem & clerum de papatu depositus est: cui adhuc viuenti successit Leo papa. Sic etiam 4. Regum legitur, quod cum sacerdotes reciperent oblationes a populo, pro reparatione sartatectorum templi, nec ea repararent: rex Osias prohibuit populo, ne ultra offerrent, & posuit famulos ex parte sua, qui oblata reciperent: & sic de pecunia reparavit sartatecta templi, & pecuniam distribuit operariis. Ex his patet, quod tota censura Ecclesiastica est spiritualis, scilicet excommunicando, suspendendo, interdicendo: nec aliquid ultra potest, nisi indirecte, & per accidens, ut dictum est. Et quod tota censura Ecclesiastica sit spiritualis, patet etiam per hoc quod dicitur Matthaei 18. Si ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus, &c. Glossa: ut obiurgatio plurimorum ipsum corrigat. Et sequitur: Amen dico vobis, quaecunque ligaveritis, &c. Glossa: vinculo anathematis. Chrysostomus ibi dicit: Vide qualiter incorrigibilem duplicem duplicibus alligavit necessitatibus, poena sc. qua est haec, scilicet proiectione ab ecclesia, quam notanter cum dicit, Sit tibi quasi ethnicus & publicanus: & supplicio futuro, quod est, ligatum esse in caelo, ut multitudine iudiciorum corrigatur culpa fratris, haec est sententia Apostoli, 1. Corinth. 5. dicentis: Si qui frater nominatur inter vos, & est fornicarius, aut avarus, aut idolis serviens, aut maledicus, aut ebriosus, aut rapax, cum huiusmodi nec cibum sumite. Ecce quod ultra excommunicationem non procedit Apostolus, etiam in culpis gravibus, & instruens omnes episcopos 1. Timoth. 3. dicit: Hominem haereticum post post vnam & secundam correctionem deuita, sciens quia subuersus est, qui huiusmodi est. Vbi nota, quod non dicit, Comburè: sed, Deuita. Ex quibus patet, quod prædicta potestas est spiritualis: nec principes ratione huius sunt Papæ subiecti, nisi vt supra dictum est. Similiter de potestate Petro tradita, per illud verbum, Pasce oues meas: patet, quod est spiritualis tantum, & nihil ad principes de ea qualitercunque exponatur, scilicet primo vel secundo vel tertio modo. Sexta vero potestas, sc. accipiendi necessaria ad debitam vitæ sustentationem, est temporalis: & magis debet dici ius, quod eis debetur in stipendium vitæ, in quo non sunt principes subiecti, sed debitores, sicut cæteri fideles, qui ab eis spiritualia recipiunt. Et licet hoc sit eis debitum, tamen hoc ius non petebant Apostoli per modum auctoritatis, sed per modum supplicationis: hoc tamen potest Papa decernere debitum eis esse, & ipsi possunt hoc petere secundum debitam facultati possessionem. Et etiam per censuram Ecclesiasticam, potest Papa rebelles compellere ad reddendum.
units.tr: pecuniariam, as a secular judge does, but only if the offender is willing to accept it. If he is unwilling, the ecclesiastical judge will compel him by excommunication or another spiritual penalty, which is the last one he can inflict. He can do nothing further, except indirectly and by accident. For if the offender were a heretic, incorrigible and a despiser of ecclesiastical censure, the Pope could bring it about among the people that he was deprived of secular honour and deposed by the people. The Pope would do this in an ecclesiastical crime, whose cognizance belongs to him, by excommunicating all who obeyed him as their lord; and so the people would depose him, and the Pope would do it by accident. Conversely, if the Pope were a criminal who scandalized the Church and were incorrigible, the prince could excommunicate him indirectly and depose him by accident, namely by moving him through himself and the cardinals. If the Pope were unwilling to submit, the prince could act among the people so that he was compelled to yield or was deposed by the people, since the Emperor could, under pledge of goods or penalty of the body, forbid all and each to obey or serve the Pope. Each of them can do this against the other. For both the Pope and the Emperor have universal jurisdiction everywhere: the one spiritual, the other temporal. Yet a distinction must be applied here. Where a king offends in spiritual matters, namely in faith, marriage and other such things whose jurisdiction belongs to the ecclesiastical judge, the Pope has the right to admonish him; and if he is found obstinate and incorrigible, the Pope can excommunicate him, and he can go no further except by accident, for if he is a despiser, he can act among the people as has been said. But where a king sins in temporal matters, whose cognizance does not belong to the Church, then the Pope does not have the first right to correct him, but the barons and peers of the realm do. If they cannot, or do not dare, they may invoke the aid of the Church; and the Church, having been asked for help by the peers, may admonish the prince and proceed against him in the manner described. Similarly, where the Pope sins in temporal matters, whose cognizance belongs to the secular prince, as if he lent at usury or favoured those who lent at usury, and especially in those things which are forbidden by civil laws, the Emperor, if there were one, would have the first right to correct him directly, by admonishing him and afterwards punishing him. For it belongs first by right to the prince to correct all wrongdoers. Rom. 13. For he does not bear the sword in vain; for he is God's minister, an avenger for wrath upon whoever does evil. The Gloss on that verse of Rom. 13, Therefore you shall pay tribute, says that they were appointed for this, that the good should be praised and the bad punished. And Jerome on Jeremiah, and it is found in 23 q. 7: It is the proper duty of kings to do judgment and justice, and to deliver from the hand of the oppressor those who are wronged by violence, the strangers, the orphans and the widows, who are more easily oppressed by the powerful. Hence Emperor Henry, deserving praise, deposed two men who were contending over the papacy, not only by canonical censure but by imperial authority, as is read in the Chronicles of the Romans. And it is said that the Emperor has, by the first right, especially by reason of civil wrong, the right to correct the Pope directly, because by a privilege granted by princes, clergy are judged only by their own bishops. This privilege was first obtained by Pope Julius, who was the second after Sylvester, while Constantine was still alive, as is said in the Chronicles. Some, however, say that this is owed to them by divine right and not by the privilege of princes, according to the verse of the Psalm: Touch not my anointed ones, which they expound of priests. Others, however, have expounded it of kings, who were anointed at that time. And so it is read in 2 Sam. 2: David slew Doeg the Idumaean, because he said that he had killed the Lord's anointed, that is, Saul. But if the Pope sins in spiritual matters, by conferring ecclesiastical benefices simoniacally, by wasting churches, by depriving ecclesiastical persons and chapters of their rights, or even by teaching and holding wrong opinions about those things which pertain to faith and good morals, then he should first be admonished by the cardinals, who stand in the place of the whole clergy. If he proved incorrigible and they could not themselves remove the scandal from the Church, then, by way of aid under the law, they would have to call upon the secular arm by supplication. Then the Emperor, asked by the cardinals, since he is a member of the Church, ought to proceed against the Pope, since the Church does not have the secular sword. In another way, not indeed by hand or by command, but by nod and supplication, as Bernard says to Eugenius. So too the two swords are bound to help one another by the common charity which unites the members of the Church. This is gathered from Dist. 26, ad verum, and 24 q. 5, principes, and the following chapters. And so we read in the Chronicles that Constantine the Second, who after his ambition for the papacy had caused many scandals in the Church, was deposed by the princes and, by the zeal of the faithful, was deprived of his eyes. Likewise John XII, who was a hunter and dissolute, and was frequently admonished about his correction but was not corrected, was deposed from the papacy by the Emperor and the clergy; and while he was still alive Pope Leo succeeded him. So too we read in 4 Kings that when the priests received offerings from the people for the repair of the roof of the temple, and did not repair it, King Joash forbade the people to offer any more and set servants on his own behalf to receive the offerings; and so he repaired the roof of the temple with the money and distributed the money to the workmen. From these things it is clear that the whole ecclesiastical censure is spiritual, namely excommunicating, suspending, and interdicting; and it can do nothing further, except indirectly and by accident, as has been said. And that the whole ecclesiastical censure is spiritual is also clear from what is said in Matt. 18: If he refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen, etc. The Gloss: so that the rebuke of many may correct him. And it follows: Verily I say to you, whatever you bind, etc. The Gloss: with the bond of anathema. Chrysostom there says: See how he has bound the incorrigible with a double necessity: the penalty, namely the expulsion from the Church, which he marks carefully when he says, Let him be to you as a heathen and a publican; and the future punishment, which is to be bound in heaven, so that the fault of the brother may be corrected by the multitude of judgments. This is the sentence of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 5, saying: If anyone who is named a brother among you is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or an extortioner, with such a one do not even eat. See that the Apostle does not proceed beyond excommunication even in grave faults; and instructing all bishops in 1 Tim. 3, he says: Avoid a heretical man after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a man is subverted. Note here that he does not say Burn, but Avoid. From these things it is clear that the aforesaid power is spiritual, nor are princes subject to the Pope by reason of it, except as has been said above. Similarly, concerning the power given to Peter by the words Feed my sheep: it is clear that it is purely spiritual, and nothing to do with princes, however it is explained, whether in the first, second or third way. The sixth power, namely of receiving what is necessary for a due sustenance of life, is temporal; and it ought rather to be called a right which is owed to them for their stipend of life, in which princes are not subject but debtors, like the other faithful, who receive spiritual things from them. And although this is owed to them, the Apostles did not claim this right by way of authority, but by way of supplication. Nevertheless the Pope can decree that it is owed to them, and they can claim it according to the due faculty of possession. And also, by ecclesiastical censure, the Pope can compel rebels to pay it.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: Quo ponuntur solutiones ad primum senarium rationum præmissarum.
units.tr: In which the solutions are given to the first six of the arguments set out above.

units.la: QVod ergo primo dicitur de Hieremia, Ecce constitui te super gentes & regna: respondetur, Duplicitez exponitur. Aliqui dicunt hoc fuisse dictum in persona Christi, eo quod Hieremias interpretatur excelsus Domini. Sic enim de Salomone multa dicuntur, quæ verificata tamen fuerunt in Christo per Salomonem significato, vt dicit Aug. 18. de Ciuitate Dei, ipse ergo Christus per Hieremiam significatus, positus est super gentes & super regna mundi & diaboli, dum in excelso montis positus, ea sibi oblata contempsit, vel super ea positus est in membris suis, qui fide sibi adhærentibus regum & regnorum sæuitiam vicerunt patiendo, fidei constantia armati, iuxta illud: Sancti per fidem vicerunt regna, & illud Salomonis, Melior est patiens viro forti, vel si de persona Hieremiæ intelligatur, constat quod nullum regem ex quacunque causa de solio depositit. Sed intelligitur positus super gentes & regna: quasi habens auctoritatem super ea, in annunciando & prædicando vera, sicut dictum est de Dauid & Christo in Psalmis: Ego autem constitutus sum rex ab eo super montem, sc. eius, prædicans præceptum eius. Licet etiam positus fuerit super gentes & regna vincendo per patientiam, cum in manu acceperit calicem plenum vini meri, & propinare iussus sit omnibus nationibus. Vnde sequitur, Vt euellas. Glossa: Mala. & destruas & dissipes, intelligitur regna diaboli, & ædifices, intelige Ecclesiam: non scandalizes, & plantes, intellige bona, sic exponitur à sanctis, non de euulsione & destructione regum mundi, & subrogatione aliorum: sed de destructione vitiorum, & plantatione fidei & morum. Sicut accipitur illud 1. Corinth. 3. Dei ædificatio estis, Dei agricultura estis. Et etiam dicitur fuisse de sacerdotibus qui fuerunt in Anathoth, quod interpretatur responsio: quia hoc magis faciunt sacerdotes de fide & moribus respondendo, quam de potentia seculari dominando: ideo etiam ibi præmittitur, quod tetigit Dominus os suum, & dedit verba in ore eius: quia prædicta magis habent facere sacerdotes verbo & doctrina vt magistri, quam manu & potentia vt domini.
units.tr: As for the first point, that Jeremiah was told, Behold, I have set you over the nations and kingdoms: the answer is that this can be explained in two ways. Some say it was spoken in the person of Christ, since Jeremiah means the lofty one of the Lord. In the same way many things are said of Solomon which were in fact fulfilled in Christ, who was prefigured by Solomon, as Augustine says in 18 of the City of God. So Christ himself, prefigured by Jeremiah, was set over the nations and over the kingdoms of the world and of the devil, when, placed on the lofty mountain, he scorned the offers made to him; or he was set over them in his members, who, adhering to him by faith and armed with steadfastness of faith, overcame the cruelty of kings and kingdoms by suffering, according to the words the saints by faith conquered kingdoms, and the saying of Solomon, The patient man is better than the strong man. Or, if it is understood of the person of Jeremiah, it is plain that he deposed no king for any cause from his throne. He is rather understood to be set over the nations and kingdoms as one having authority over them in announcing and preaching the truth, as was said of David and Christ in the Psalms: But I have been set up as king by him over the mountain, that is, of him, proclaiming his decree. He may also be said to have been set over the nations and kingdoms by conquering through patience, since he received the cup full of pure wine in his hand and was commanded to give it to drink to all nations. Hence what follows: To pluck up. The gloss says: Evils, and to destroy and to scatter, is understood as the kingdoms of the devil; and to build, understand the Church; not to scandalise; and to plant, understand good things. This is how the saints explain it, not as the uprooting and destruction of the kings of the world and the substitution of others, but as the destruction of vices and the planting of faith and morals. So also the saying of 1 Corinthians 3 is taken: You are God's building, you are God's field. It is also said to have been spoken of the priests who were at Anathoth, which means answer, because priests do this more by answering on faith and morals than by ruling with secular power. This is why it is also said beforehand that the Lord touched his mouth and gave words into his mouth: because priests ought to accomplish these things more by the word and teaching, as teachers, than by hand and power, as lords.

units.la: Et confirmatur hæc expositio per Bernhardum ad Eugenium Papam secundo libro, vbi exponit qualis est papalis principatus. Accingere, inquit, gladio tuo: gladio scilicet spiritus, quod est verbum Dei, & infra: Sic enim domabis lupos, & non dominaberis ouibus.
units.tr: This explanation is confirmed by Bernard in his second book to Pope Eugenius, where he describes what the papal princedom is like. Gird on your sword, he says, your sword, namely of the spirit, which is the word of God; and further on: For so you will tame the wolves, and you will not lord it over the sheep.

units.la: Quod dicitur secundo, Quodcunque solueritis, &c. respondeo secundum Chrysostomum & Rabanum, per hoc non intelligitur aliqua potestas data, nisi spiritualis, absoluendi scilicet à vinculo peccatorum. Stultum autem esset intelligere, quod per hoc datur potestas absoluendi à vinculo debitorum. Amplius, secundum Hieronymum non est intelligendum, hanc potestatem habere effectum, claue errante. Vnde dicit, quod presbyteri & episcopi potestatem habent: non intelligentes de Pharisæorum supercilio quod assumpserunt, vt vel damnent innocentes, vel soluere se noxios arbitrentur: cum apud Deum non sententia sacerdotum, sed reorum vita quæratur. Et hoc declarat ibidem Hier. per exemplum, quod ponit de sacerdotibus legis, qui non mundabant vel mundos faciebant: sed ex officio suo mundos & immundos iudicabant. Richardus etiam de sancto Victore in lib. de Remissione peccatorum, cap. 8. expedit illud dicens: Non dicit Dominus, Quodcunque voueris & soluere & ligare: sed, Quodcunque ligaueris & solueris, ligat autem & absoluit sacerdos sententia iusta, non iniusta.
units.tr: As to the second point, Whatever you loose, and so on: I answer, following Chrysostom and Rabanus, that by this no power is understood to be given except a spiritual one, namely to absolve from the bond of sins. It would be foolish to understand that by this power is given to absolve from the bond of debts. Moreover, according to Jerome, this power is not to be understood as having effect when the key is faulty. Hence he says that presbyters and bishops have the power, not understanding it in the sense of the pride of the Pharisees, who assumed it so that they might either condemn the innocent or think themselves able to release the guilty, since before God what is sought is not the judgement of priests but the life of the guilty. Jerome himself makes this clear in the same place by the example of the priests of the law, who did not cleanse or make clean, but by virtue of their office judged the clean and the unclean. Richard of St Victor also explains it in his book On the Remission of Sins, chapter 8, saying: The Lord does not say, Whatever you bind and loose, but, Whatever you bind and loose; and the priest binds and absolves by a just sentence, not an unjust one.

units.la: Quod autem tertio dicitur, Nescitis quoniam angelos iudicabitis, &c. Responsio, secundum Ambrosium & alios sanctos expositores: Apostolus loquitur non clericis specialiter, sed generaliter fidelibus: qui eligebant in causis secularibus iudices infideles in scandalum fidei nostræ, & quasi inter fideles non esset sapiens ad iudicandum: & hoc merito reprehendit.
units.tr: As to the third point, Do you not know that you will judge angels, and so on: the answer, following Ambrose and other holy expositors, is that the Apostle is speaking not specially to clergy but generally to the faithful, who in secular causes chose unbelieving judges, to the scandal of our faith, as though there were no wise man among the faithful to judge; and he rightly rebukes this.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur quarto, Fecit Dominus duo luminaria &c. mystica est expositio secundum Dionysium: mystica autem Theologia non est argumentativa, nisi accipiatur eius probatio ex alia Scriptura. Amplius, proprie dicta mystica expositio à sanctis non inuenitur, sed forte contraria. Vnde dicit Isidorus super Genesim in Glossa, quod per solem intelligitur regnum, & per lunam intelligitur sacerdotium. Vnde dicit, Splendor quidem solis significat excellentiam, plebem obtemperantem regi: luna splendor ostendit tanquam synagogam ecclesiæ: principes eius & omnia fundata sunt in regni stabilitate, tanquam in fundamento firmata. Dato etiam quod ita sit, sicut assumitur, pro nobis est, fiant licet luna non illuminet noctem nisi lumine quod accipit à sole, tamen luna habet virtutem propriam à Deo sibi data, quam à sole non habet: ut quod infrigidet & humectet, cuius contrarium facit sol: & in proposito modo, nam princeps illuminationem & informationem de fide habet à Papa & ecclesia: tamen potestatem habet sibi propriam & distinctam, quam non habet à Papa, sed à Deo immediate.
units.tr: As to the fourth point, The Lord made two lights, and so on: this is a mystical exposition according to Dionysius. But mystical theology does not argue, unless its proof is taken from other Scripture. Moreover, a properly mystical exposition is not found among the saints, but perhaps the opposite. Hence Isidore, in the gloss on Genesis, says that by the sun is understood the kingdom, and by the moon is understood the priesthood. He says: The brightness of the sun indeed signifies excellence, the people obeying the king; the moon shows its brightness as the synagogue of the Church; its princes and all things are founded on the stability of the kingdom, as if fixed on a foundation. Even granting that it is as they assume, it is in our favour. Let the moon be made so that it gives no light at night except the light it receives from the sun; yet the moon has its own power given to it by God, which it does not have from the sun, such as to cool and moisten, the opposite of what the sun does. And in the present case the prince has his enlightenment and formation of faith from the Pope and the Church, yet he has a power that is his own and distinct, which he does not have from the Pope but immediately from God.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur quinto, quod Zacharias Papa depositus regem Francorum, & instituit loco eius Pipinum, &c. Glossa ordinaria exponit: Deponentibus consensit. Non enim legitur, quod Zacharias regem Franciae deposuerit. Sed legitur in Chronicis, quod Hildericus regnabat in Francia totus deses & remissus: Pipinus vero solus gubernabat Franciae principatum, & Maior domus dicebatur, Carolo fratre suo existente monacho. Miserunt ergo Barones ad Zachariam Papam, ut discerneret de eorum dubio, quis scilicet potius deberet esse rex: an ille qui otio deditus, solo nomine regebat: an ille, qui omne pondus regni sustinebat? Quibus eum respondisset Papa, quod ille qui regni gubernacula utilius regeret: Franci mox inclusso rege Hilderico & uxore sua in monasterio, sibi Pipinum regem constituerunt: & ipsum sanctus Bonifacius Moguntinus Archiepiscopus unxit in regem, sicut habent Chronica Martini. Aliorum autem Chronica habent, quod postquam Hildericus quatuor annis regnavit, ex devotione in monachum est tonsuratus: & tunc Pipinus princeps in regem est inunctus electione Baronum, & auctoritate Papae decernentis super dubio procerum: quod etiam facere potuisset sine Papae assensu ex causa rationabili. Ex quibus patet, quod Papa nunquam regem Franciae deposuit: nisi exponatur, id est, deponentibus consensit, sicut exponit Glossa. Nec oportet ex talibus factis singularibus, quae interdum ex devotione ad Ecclesiam, vel personam, vel ex favore, vel ex causa alia, & non ex debito iuris fiunt, argumenta sumere: cum legatur in eisdem historiis, quod Bonifacius Romanae ecclesiae misertus, praesidens obtinuit apud Phocam Imperatorem, ut ecclesia Romana esset caput omnium ecclesiarum: quia ecclesia Constantinopolitana scribebat se esse primam omnium. Ex quo posset modo consimili sumi argumentum, quod ad Imperatorem pertinet primatum Ecclesiae transferre, & de ecclesiis ordinare. Legitur etiam à Sozomeno scriptum in Tripartita historia, quod Constantinus Imperator consilio clericorum intererat: quod etiam Eusebius narrat in Ecclesiastica historia, ubi etiam dicit, quod cum ex omnibus fere locis episcopi congregati essent diversis ex causis, & iurgia inter se quaedam detulissent, f equenter appellabatur, & à singulis libelli offerebantur. At ille videns, quod per huiusmodi iurgia causa summi negotii frustraretur, diem certum statuit, qua venusquisque episcoporum, si quam querimoniarum habere videretur, deferret: & hoc facto cum recessissent, suscepit à singulis libellos: quos simul omnes in sinu suo continens, nec in eis quid contineretur aperiens, aut ad episcopos: Deus vos sacerdotes constituit, ac potestatem vobis dedit de nobis iudicandi, & nos recte à vobis iudicamur, vos autem, qui nobis à Deo dati estis dii, non potestis ab hominibus iudicari: quia non est conveniens, quod homo de Deo iudicet: sed Dei inter vos expectare iudicium. De quo scriptum est: Deus stetit in synagoga deorum, &c. His ergo omissis iurgiis, ea quae adhuc sunt distinguite. Cumq; hoc dixisset, omnes simul querimoniarum libellos tulit exuri. Nunquid ergo propter hoc ad principem pertinet, interesse consiliis episcoporum, & dissensiones & causas eorum modo consimili determinare, an non? Hugo etiam Floriacensis libro quinto dicit, quod Constantinus sanxit & instituit in Testamento suo, ut omnia quae ad Ecclesiasticum pertinent ordinem, Romani episcopi iudicio dispositionem recipiant. Et in epistola Constantini ad omnes Catholicos episcopos, quam inscribit beatus Isidorus, dixit Constantinus Imperator: Decernentes sancimus, ut Romana sedes principatum obtineat super quatuor sedes praecipuas, Antiochiam, Alexandrinam, Constantinopolitanam, Hierosolymitanam, & in Testamento eiusdem Constantini, quod ecclesia sancta tam gratanter ampletitur, & in corpore decretorum inseritur, dicit & ordinat, quod pontifex Romanus pro tempore quicunque fuerit, excelsior cunctis mundi sacerdotibus existat: & quaecunque ad cultum Dei vel Christianorum, fidei, stabilitatem procuranda sunt, disponat. Nunquid dicimus propter talia, quod ecclesia Romana habeat ab Imperatoribus primatum ecclesiarum, vel super Ecclesias, & dispositionem earum? Absit. Amplius, in primo concilio Hierosolymitano, quaestione legalium legitur, quod post multam disceptationem hinc inde, postquam Petrus surgens ratione ostendit, iugum legis fidelibus non esse imponendum: Iacobus auctoritate pontificali protulit diffinitivam sententiam, quia quaestio illa mota erat in Ecclesia Hierosolymitana, cuius erat episcopus: nec poterat ad alterum transferri, nisi per appellationem, & ita inquit Iacobus, Iudico, &c. Dicemus ergo, quod licet Romana ecclesia sit caput, quod non habet talem exercere iurisdictionem, nisi in casu appellationis in ecclesiis episcoporum? Legitur etiam, quod tempore Henrici Imperatoris, Romani iurauerunt, non se Papam electuros sine Imperatoris assensu. Est igitur hoc observandum? constat quod non. Haec autem induxi, ut appareat, quia non oportet ex talibus factis singularibus, quae variis causis fieri possunt, argumenta iuris sumere.
units.tr: As to the fifth point, that Pope Zachary deposed the king of the Franks, and set up Pepin in his place, and so on: the ordinary gloss explains it as he consented to those who deposed him. For it is not read that Zachary deposed the king of France. But it is read in the Chronicles that Childeric reigned in France wholly idle and listless, while Pepin alone governed the principality of France and was called Mayor of the Palace, his brother Carloman being a monk. The barons therefore sent to Pope Zachary to decide their doubt: who ought rather to be king, he who was given over to idleness and reigned in name only, or he who bore the whole weight of the kingdom? When the Pope answered that the one who would govern the reins of the kingdom more profitably should reign, the Franks at once shut King Childeric and his wife up in a monastery and made Pepin king for themselves; and Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, anointed him king, as the Chronicle of Martin relates. But the other Chronicles say that after Childeric had reigned four years, he was tonsured a monk out of devotion; and then Pepin, a prince, was anointed king by the election of the barons and by the authority of the Pope, who decided the question raised by the nobles; which he could also have done without the Pope's assent, for a reasonable cause. From these things it is clear that the Pope never deposed the king of France, unless it is explained, that is, he consented to those who deposed him, as the gloss explains. Nor ought arguments to be drawn from such single events, which sometimes happen out of devotion to the Church or to a person, or from favour or some other cause, and not from a debt of right. For in the same histories we read that Boniface, moved with pity for the Roman Church, prevailed upon the Emperor Phocas to make the Roman Church the head of all the churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing that it was the first of all. From this, by a similar argument, one could conclude that it belongs to the Emperor to transfer the primacy of the Church and to ordain churches. It is also read in Sozomen's Tripartite History that the Emperor Constantine took part in the counsel of the clergy; and Eusebius also relates this in his Ecclesiastical History, where he also says that when bishops had gathered from almost all places for various reasons, and had brought certain quarrels among themselves, he was frequently appealed to, and petitions were offered by individuals. He, seeing that the cause of the greatest business was being frustrated by such quarrels, fixed a certain day on which each of the bishops, if he seemed to have some complaint, should bring it forward; and when this was done and they had withdrawn, he received petitions from each one, and, gathering them all together in his lap without opening them or revealing what they contained, said to the bishops: God has appointed you priests and given you power to judge us, and we are rightly judged by you; but you, who are gods given to us by God, cannot be judged by men, since it is not fitting for a man to judge concerning God, but you must await the judgement of God among yourselves. Of this it is written: God stood in the assembly of gods, and so on. These quarrels being therefore set aside, let those things which are still in dispute be settled. And when he had said this, he had all the petitions brought together and burned. Does it therefore belong to the prince, in the same way, to take part in the counsels of bishops and to decide their disputes and causes, or not? Hugh of Fleury also says in his fifth book that Constantine decreed and ordained in his Testament that all matters pertaining to the ecclesiastical order should receive their arrangement by the judgement of the Roman bishop. And in the letter of Constantine to all Catholic bishops, which Saint Isidore inscribes, the Emperor Constantine said: By decree we ordain that the Roman see should hold the primacy over the four principal sees, Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople, Jerusalem; and in the Testament of the same Constantine, which the holy Church so gladly embraces, and which is inserted in the body of the decretals, it says and orders that the Roman pontiff, whoever he may be for the time, should be higher than all the priests of the world, and should arrange whatever has to be provided for the worship of God and for the stability of the faith of Christians. Do we therefore say, on account of such things, that the Roman Church has its primacy over the churches from the Emperors, or its arrangement of them? Far from it. Moreover, at the first council of Jerusalem, in the question about the legalists, we read that after much dispute on both sides, when Peter rose and showed by reason that the yoke of the law was not to be imposed on the faithful, James, by pontifical authority, gave a final sentence, because that question had been raised in the Church of Jerusalem, of which he was bishop; nor could it be transferred to another except by appeal; and so James says: I judge, and so on. Shall we therefore say that although the Roman Church is the head, it does not have the right to exercise such jurisdiction except in the case of an appeal from the churches of bishops? It is also read that in the time of the Emperor Henry, the Romans swore that they would not elect a Pope without the Emperor's assent. Is this therefore to be observed? It is clear that it is not. I have brought these things forward so that it may appear that arguments of right should not be drawn from such single events, which can happen for various causes.

units.la: Quod vero sexto arguitur de Nicolao Papa, dicente quod Christus Petro caelestia terrenique, imperii iura concessit: Respondeo, Ubi quaeritur de potestate Papae in temporalibus, efficax est testimonium Imperatoris pro Papa: & non est multum efficax testimonium Papae pro se ipso, nisi dictum Papae fulciatur auctoritate Scripturae sacrae, vel scripturae Canonicae. Et in materia vbi Imperator dicit contrarium manifeste, etiam caeteri pontifices, ut in proposito, non recipitur tale dictum. Potest tamen verbum Domini Nicolai Papae habere inclusiuam veram multipliciter. Vno modo, quia pro communi utilitate boni spiritualis, modo superius dicto, posset indicere collectam à fidelibus faciendam, non solum de bonis clericorum, sed etiam de bonis laicorum. Secundo modo potest accipi vel intelligi, quod Dominus Petro dedit iura coelestis terrenique, &c. si in quantum dedit ei potestatem absoluendi & ligandi, cuius sententia, absolutio, ligatio, claue non errante appropriatur in coelis: sicut exponitur illud verbum sibi dictum in traditione clauium, Quodcunque ligaueris super terram, &c. Et ita exponunt glossae Matthai 18. Nec videtur, quod Dominus Papa aliunde dictum verbum acceperit, nisi ab illo verbo Domini ad Petrum: Et tibi dabo claues regni coelorum: praecipue cum dicat dominus Papa, Quod beato Petro clauigero regni &c. Quasi alludens verbis, quibus Petro commissa est potestas. Et ideo cum sancti per illud verbum non dent Petro potestatem aliam, quam (vt dictum est) potestatem scilicet spiritualem, vt dicit vniuersitas expositorum ibidem, & Matthai decimo: non est tenendum, quod dominus Papa aliud intendat. Potest etiam aliter tertio verificari dictum domini Papae, quod ideo dicitur Christus dedisse Petro iura coelestis terrenique, & caetera: quia dedit spiritualem potestatem coniungendi ciues terreni regni, ciuibus regni coelestis, sub quo sensu loquitur de Christo Maximinus in Sermone Epiphaniae, dicens: Hic est rex ille magnus, qui venit coelesti imperio sociare terrenum. Inueniuntur etiam quidam Iuristae, verbum Nicolai Papae exponere sic: Petro concessit Christus iura coelestis & terreni imperii: id est, ius imperandi coelestibus & terrenis, clericis & laicis, qui sunt etiam duo parietes ecclesiae, quibus ambobus summus Pontifex in spiritualibus noscitur imperare.
units.tr: As for the sixth argument, which cites Pope Nicholas saying that Christ granted to Peter the rights of the heavenly and the earthly empire: I answer that where the question is about the Pope's power in temporal matters, the testimony of the Emperor counts for the Pope, but the Pope's testimony for himself counts for little, unless his assertion is supported by the authority of Holy Scripture or of the canonical writings. Where an Emperor plainly says the opposite, such a statement is not accepted, and the same holds for other bishops, as in the present case. Nevertheless, the words of the Lord as quoted by Pope Nicholas can be understood in a true sense in several ways. In one way, for the common good of a spiritual benefit, in the manner stated above, he could have ordered a collection to be made from the faithful, not only from the goods of the clergy but also from the goods of the laity. In a second way, the words may be taken or understood to mean that the Lord gave Peter the rights of the heavenly and earthly realm, and so on, insofar as he gave him the power of absolving and binding, whose sentence, absolution and binding, when the key does not err, is ratified in heaven. This is how that word spoken to him at the handing over of the keys is explained: Whatever you bind on earth, etc. The glosses explain Matthew 18 in the same way. Nor does it seem that the Pope took his words from anywhere else than from the Lord's words to Peter: And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; especially since the Pope says that to the blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom, etc., as if alluding to the words by which the power was committed to Peter. Therefore, since the saints do not by that word give Peter any power other than, as has been said, spiritual power, as the whole body of expositors there and Matthew 10 teaches, we must not hold that the Pope intends anything else. In a third way the Pope's statement can also be made true: Christ is said to have given Peter the rights of the heavenly and earthly realm, etc., because he gave him the spiritual power of joining the citizens of the earthly kingdom to the citizens of the heavenly kingdom. In this sense Maximinus speaks of Christ in his Sermon on the Epiphany, saying: This is that great King who came to join the earthly to the heavenly empire. Some jurists also are found to explain the Pope's words thus: Christ granted to Peter the rights of the heavenly and earthly empire, that is, the right to rule over heavenly and earthly things, over clergy and laity, who are also the two walls of the Church, over both of which the supreme Pontiff is known to rule in spiritual matters.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: QVod autem dicitur septimo, quod Imperator iurat Papae: respondeo, Imperator Otho non iurauit Papae, nisi de regno Italiae, quod ab ipso seu ab ecclesia suscepit in feudum. Iurauit etiam reddere terram sancti Petri, si quam tenebat. Sed nihil facit ad caeteras partes mundi, vel quae non sunt de imperio, vel quae non cadunt sub dominatione Constantini.
units.tr: As for the seventh objection, that the Emperor swears an oath to the Pope: I answer that Emperor Otto swore to the Pope only concerning the kingdom of Italy, which he received in fief from him, or from the Church. He also swore to restore the land of St. Peter, if he held any of it. But this has no bearing on the other parts of the world, whether those not belonging to the empire or those not falling under the rule of Constantine.

units.la: Quod dicitur octauo, quod Papa deponit Imperatorem: respondeo, Verum est, illum quem ipse posuit, qui ab ipso accepit feudum, & ex causa rationabili: tamen ista argumenta sunt de facto, & dicunt quid factum, non tamen quid fieri debeat. E contrario autem multa argumenta possunt fieri de facto, vt dictum est in solutione 5. argumenti. Quod vero dicitur, quod Papa transtulit imperium, posset solui sicut prius. Potest nihilominus dici, quod Constantinus nunquam dedit imperium Ecclesiae simpliciter: sed dedit vrbem, & quasdam prouincias occidentales, & signa imperialia, vt de ipsis prouinciis disponeret: sedemque suam transtulit Constantinopolim, cum tota dignitate imperii.
units.tr: As for the eighth objection, that the Pope deposes the Emperor: I answer that it is true, of the one whom he himself set up, who received the fief from him, and for a reasonable cause. Yet these arguments concern what has been done, and say what was done, not what ought to be done. On the other hand, many arguments can be framed from what has been done, as was said in the answer to the fifth argument. As for the objection that the Pope transferred the empire, it could be answered as before. Nevertheless it may be said that Constantine never simply gave the empire to the Church. He gave the city and certain western provinces, and the imperial insignia, so that the Church might dispose of those provinces; and he transferred his own seat to Constantinople, together with the full dignity of the empire.

units.la: Quod vero decimo dicitur, quod postea Papa imperium de Graecis transtulit ad Germanos: responsio. Non transtulit veritatem, sed nomen: quia indignabantur Romani quod imperium vel imperii nomen ab eis Constantinopolim erat translatum: & ideo Carolo, quem pro sua defensione vocauerant, victoriis habitis laudes acclamauerunt, & Imperatoris ei nomen dederunt. Et ex nunc fuit quasi diuisum imperium, dum duo dicerentur Imperatores. Amplius, non fuit factum per solum Papam, sed populo acclamante & faciente, cuius est se subiicere cui vult sine alterius praeiudicio. Ideo hoc fuit factum ex causa necessaria pro sui defensione, contra infideles & paganos, vbi perahum non videbantur posse defendi, quod de iure poterant, nam populus facit regem, & exercitus Imperatorem. Et quid plura? hoc factum est speciali Dei consilio, pro Ecclesiae defensione, vt monstratum fuit, & persuasum Constantinopolitano Imperatori per angelum in specie militis armati sibi apparentem, quae autem lege priuata dicuntur, nulla ratio est vt lege publica constituantur, haec vero omnia ad factum pertinentia declarantur in lib. de Cosmographia, & in Chronicis Hugonis Floracen. lib. quinto, & in Chronicis Sigeberti. Quicquid autem de hoc facto sit, Papa non ordinauit, nisi de eo quod sibi à Constantino collatum fuerat: quod concedo fieri posse de iure.
units.tr: As for the tenth objection, that afterwards the Pope transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Germans: the answer is this. He transferred not the reality but the name. The Romans were indignant that the empire, or the name of the empire, had been transferred from them to Constantinople. And so, when they had called Charles to their defence and he had won victories, they acclaimed him with praise and gave him the name of Emperor. From then on the empire was, as it were, divided, since two were called Emperors. Furthermore, this was not done by the Pope alone, but with the people acclaiming and acting, and it belongs to them to submit themselves to whom they wish, without prejudice to anyone else. This was therefore done out of a necessity for their own defence against unbelievers and pagans, when by themselves they did not seem able to defend what they could rightly claim. For the people makes the king, and the army makes the emperor. And why say more? This was done by the special counsel of God, for the defence of the Church, as has been shown, and it was made clear to the Emperor of Constantinople by an angel who appeared to him in the form of an armed soldier. As for the things that are said to be by private law, there is no reason why they should be established by public law. All these matters concerning the fact are set out in the book de Cosmographia, and in the Chronicles of Hugo of Flavigny, book fifth, and in the Chronicles of Sigebert. Whatever the truth of this deed, the Pope ordained nothing except what had been conferred on him by Constantine, which I concede may be done by right.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur decimo, quod Papa legitimauit in temporalibus: respondeo. Dispensare potest in temporalibus in terra propria, vbi habet iurisdictionem: alibi vero non, nisi per consequentiam, vt notat Ioannes Andreae. Vel melius, quod nec etiam per consequentiam potest, in terra non subiecta sibi. Et ponit Richardus, quod dispensando in spiritualibus dispensat per consequentiam: & indirecte in temporalibus, in terra subiecta, vbi concedendo maius, intelligitur concedere minus, quando vtrumque potest: sed extra non potest, nisi in spiritualibus legitimare. Et sic notat Glossa ordinaria ibidem. Tento tamen, quod si aliqui sunt illegitimati, quia nati ex matrimonio personarum illegitimarum, ad contrahendum matrimonium ex prohibitione Ecclesiae: Papa potest cum talibus vbiq; dispensare, & eos legitimare in spiritualib. & temporalibus, in quantum potest illud matrimonium ratificare, & personas legitimas facere ad contrahendum. Si vero fuerint illegitimi, ex matrimonio personarum illegitimarum ad contrahendum ex iure naturali vel diuino, non potest dispensare vbique cum eis in temporalib. legitimando.
units.tr: As for the tenth objection, that the Pope legitimated in temporal matters: I answer. He can dispense in temporal matters within his own land, where he has jurisdiction; elsewhere he cannot, except by consequence, as John Andreae notes. Or, better, he cannot even by consequence in land not subject to him. Richard holds that in dispensing in spiritual matters he dispenses by consequence, and indirectly in temporal matters, in subject lands, since in granting the greater one is understood to grant the lesser, when he can do both. But outside such lands he can only legitimate in spiritual matters. The ordinary Gloss on the same passage notes this too. I hold, however, that if some are illegitimate because born of a marriage between illegitimate persons, prohibited by the Church from contracting marriage, the Pope may dispense with such persons everywhere, and legitimate them in spiritual and temporal matters, insofar as he can ratify that marriage and make the persons lawful to contract. But if they are illegitimate, born of a marriage between illegitimate persons prohibited by natural or divine law from contracting, he cannot dispense with them everywhere in temporal matters by legitimating them.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur vndecimo, quod Papa aliquando absoluit milites à iuramento fidelitatis, dicitur quod ad hoc est argumentum de facto, quod tanrum introducitur de Francigenis. Respondeo, quod illud fuit magis declaratio iuris, quod sc. iuramentum in tali casu non ligabat: quam absolutio à iuramento fidelitatis. Hoc enim fuit factum de consensu regis, qui forte conscius de sua ineptitudine, volens omnino vacare, monachicam seu monasticam vitam elegit. In quo casu Barones potuerunt ad alterius electionem procedere, prout fuit per Papam declaratum & consultum. Consiederandum detandum tamen est, quod vasallus duplici vinculo obligatus est Domino, naturali scil. ratione rei, quam accipit à Domino, cum honore vasiliæ, & sub determinata conditione, & vinculo iuratorio: à naturali vero vinculo non potest absoluere papa, licet posset declarare quod in tali casu, sc. vbi princeps esset hæreticus, non tenetur vasallus dominium sequi: sed debet se obligare, & reddere feudum. Sed de obligatione iuratoria potest ex causa rationabili, & euidenti, & bona fide, & non aliter tenet obligatio apud Deum: quia papæ, vt dictum est supra, non est collata potestas in destructionem, sed ad ædificationem. Quicquid tamen sit, de iuramento semper manet obligatio naturalis, quæ rem sequitur, nisi reddatur feudum.
units.tr: As for the eleventh objection, that the Pope sometimes absolved soldiers from their oath of fidelity: it is said that the argument from fact is only introduced concerning the French. I answer that this was rather a declaration of law, namely that the oath did not bind in such a case, than an absolution from the oath of fidelity. For this was done with the consent of the king, who, perhaps conscious of his own unfitness and wishing altogether to be free, chose the monastic or cloistered life. In that case the barons could proceed to the election of another, as was declared and advised by the Pope. Yet it must be considered that a vassal is bound to his lord by a double tie: a natural one, by reason of the thing he receives from the lord, together with the honour of vassalage, under a fixed condition; and a sworn bond. From the natural tie the Pope cannot absolve, although he could declare that in such a case, namely where the prince is a heretic, the vassal is not bound to follow his lordship, but ought to renounce it and return the fief. But from the sworn obligation he can absolve, for a reasonable and evident cause and in good faith, and otherwise the obligation before God does not hold; for, as was said above, power was not given to the Pope for destruction but for building up. Whatever the case, however, a natural obligation always remains from the oath, which follows the thing, unless the fief is returned.

units.la: Quod dicitur duodecimo, quod papa habet cognoscere de omni delicto: respondetur, Patet ex prædictis, cap. nono, in principio: quia verum est, vbi quæstio mouetur de peccato, an scilicet hoc sit peccatum, vel non peccatum, licitum, an illicitum, hoc enim determinatur ex naturali vel diuino iure, & sic cognoscit vt Ecclesiasticus. Si autem cognoscat de peccato venditionis, quæ determinatur secundum leges humanas: vel intelligitur papa cognoscere in foro conscientiæ, vbi debet credere confitenti.
units.tr: As for the twelfth objection, that the Pope has to take cognizance of every crime: the answer is clear from what has been said above, chapter ninth, at the beginning. For it is true where the question is raised about sin, whether this is a sin or not a sin, lawful or unlawful; for this is determined by natural or divine law, and so he judges as an ecclesiastic. But if he takes cognizance of the sin of sale, which is determined according to human laws, then either the Pope is understood to take cognizance in the court of conscience, where he ought to believe the one confessing.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: QVod vero dicitur XIII. de denunciatione: ideo respondetur, denunciatio etiam non dat papæ iurisdictionem: quia sic ex toto posset annihilari iurisdictio principum, cum omnis causa papæ posset denunciari aperte: sed vt dicit papa ibidem, non intendit iudicare de feudo, cuius ad ipsum regem Francorum spectat iudicium, nisi forte iuri communi per speciale priuilegium, vel contrariam consuetudinem aliquid sit detractum. Sed decernere de peccato, cuius ad ipsum papam pertinet sine dubitatione censura, sicut ipse dicit: & ad hoc vadunt probationes, quas adducit.
units.tr: As for what is said in the thirteenth chapter on denunciation (de denunciatione), the answer is that denunciation also does not give the pope jurisdiction. If it did, the jurisdiction of princes could be wholly annihilated, since every cause of the pope's could be openly denounced to him. But as the pope himself says in the same place, he does not intend to judge concerning a fief, the judgment of which belongs to the king of the French himself, unless perhaps something has been taken away from the common law by special privilege or contrary custom. But to decide concerning sin, the censure of which, as he himself says, belongs without doubt to the pope himself: and the proofs he adduces are directed to this.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur decimoquarto, Si peccauerit in te, &c. dic Ecclesia: responsio, Chrysostomus exponit Ecclesia, id est iis qui ecclesiæ præsident. Si vero Ecclesia accipiatur non solum pro congregatione clericorum, sed generaliter vocetur Ecclesia communitas fidelium: sic Ecclesiæ præsunt, & Ecclesiasticus iudex in spiritualibus, & secularis in temporalib. Vel potest dici, quod loquitur, quando est quæstio de peccato. Vnde dicit Glossa super illud, Vt in ore duorum vel trium, &c. Si dixerit non esse peccatum, vt probent illud esse peccatum, sic etiam, si non acquieuerit, dicendum est Ecclesiæ: quæ iudicat de peccato.
units.tr: As for what is said in the fourteenth chapter, "If he sins against you, etc., tell it to the Church": the answer is that Chrysostom explains "Church" as "those who preside over the church." But if Church is taken not only for the assembly of clergy, and the community of the faithful is generally called the Church, then the Church is presided over both by the ecclesiastical judge in spiritual matters and by the secular judge in temporal matters. Or it may be said that the passage speaks of the case where the question is about sin. Hence the Gloss on that text, "that in the mouth of two or three witnesses, etc.," says: if he says it is not a sin, let them prove that it is a sin. So too, if he does not acquiesce, it must be told to the Church, which judges concerning sin.

units.la: Quod dicitur decimoquinto, de Theodosio: respondeo, sicut notant Iuristæ, lex illa Theodosiana abrogata est, quia ratio legis viget: cuius rationis notitia vtilis est, vt sciatur quantam deuotionem habuit legislator erga Ecclesiam: & ad hoc ostendendum, inseritur in corpore Decretorum, vndecima, quæstione prima, quicunque. Amplius etiam possumus attendere, quod ex statuto principum contingere potest, quod iudex Ecclesiasticus de talibus cognoscat: sed si de statuto principum ei contingit, non potest concludi, quod ei conueniat secundum se, vt est Christi vicarius: sed magis contrarium posset concludi, & posset dici, quod principes possent, licet non deberent ab Ecclesiasticis iudicibus sua priuilegia & gratias antecessorum suorum reuocare: sicut econuerso pontifices reuocant, vel repocare possunt gratias suas à principibus.
units.tr: As for what is said in the fifteenth chapter, concerning Theodosius: I answer, as the jurists note, that the law of Theodosius has been abrogated, because the reason of the law still holds. Knowledge of that reason is useful, so that one may know how great a devotion the lawgiver had towards the Church; and to show this, it is inserted in the body of the Decretals, Causa 11, question 1, "quicunque." We may further observe that by a statute of princes it may happen that an ecclesiastical judge takes cognizance of such matters. But if this falls to him from a statute of princes, it cannot be concluded that it belongs to him in himself, as Christ's vicar. Rather the contrary could be concluded, and it could be said that princes could, though they ought not, revoke by ecclesiastical judges their privileges and the favours of their predecessors; just as, conversely, popes revoke, or can revoke, their favours from princes.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur decimosexto, de illo verbo Deut. Si difficile, &c. vnus casus est specialis, in quo recurri potest à seculari iudice ad Ecclesiasticum: scilicet seculari dubitante, præcipue vbi est quæstio de peccato: vel dicendum, quod non remittitur ad sacerdotem tantum, sed etiam ad iudicem qui fuerit pro illo tempore, per quem intelligitur iudex secularis: vt vnus iudicet in causis spiritualibus, alius vero in temporalibus. Vnde signanter dicit, ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & ad iudicem, &c. Et ita exponit Glossa.
units.tr: As for what is said in the sixteenth chapter, concerning that word of Deuteronomy, "If it be too hard, etc.": one case is special, in which appeal may be made from the secular judge to the ecclesiastical one, namely when the secular judge is in doubt, especially where there is a question about sin. Or it must be said that the matter is not referred to the priest alone, but also to the judge of the time, by whom the secular judge is understood, so that one judges in spiritual causes and the other in temporal ones. Hence he pointedly says, "to the priests of the Levitical line, and to the judge," etc. And so the Gloss explains it.

units.la: Quod vero decimoseptimo dicitur, papa potest maius, &c. istud est verum in maiori & minori ordinatis per se: vt si episcopus potest ordinare sacerdotem, ergo & diaconum: non autem tenetur in iis quæ sunt diuersi ordinis vel generis: vt si pater meus potuit generare hominem, ergo & canem: vel si sacerdos possit aliquem absoluere à peccato, quod possit eum absoluere à debito pecuniæ.
units.tr: As for what is said in the seventeenth chapter, "the pope can do more, etc.": this is true of things ordered in the greater and the lesser by their own nature. For example, if a bishop can ordain a priest, then he can also ordain a deacon. But the rule does not hold in things of different order or kind: for example, if my father could beget a man, it does not follow that he could beget a dog; or if a priest could absolve someone from sin, it does not follow that he could absolve him from a money debt.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur decimooctauo, quod temporalia ordinantur ad spiritualia, &c. responsio patet ex prædictis supra cap. 7.
units.tr: As for what is said in the eighteenth chapter, that temporal things are ordered to spiritual things, etc.: the answer is clear from what was said above, in chapter 7.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: QVod vero dicitur decimonono, de legatis & restitutionibus: respondeo, legata in quantum sunt ad pias causas, ad ius Ecclesiasticum pertinent: & hoc est spirituale speciale, vt dicunt Ecclesiastici viri, & præcipue quando sunt totaliter indistincta, tunc enim possunt per Ecclesiasticum determinari, iuxta voluntatem expressam testatoris. Quod autem transferri possint, vt si testator legat centum libras pauperibus infra ciuitatem, vel dioecesim Parisiorum, quod possit ratione talis indistinctionis dare pauperibus in Carnotensi dioecesi, non video quod possit de iure voluntatem testatoris mutare. Principi tamen qui vtrique dioecesi præest, ex causa rationabili posset transferri & dari: quia est aliquis dioecesis nominatæ. De restitutionibus autem faciendis, non video quin possint fieri per prouidentiam seu prudentiam quorumlibet virorum bonorum in pios vsus, pro vtilitate terræ, si necessitas immineat, vel vtilitas exposcat: & præcipue per prouidentiam principis, quæ vtilitati communi inuigilat, ex quo pro communi vtilitate vel necessitate erogantur, propter hoc quod personæ sunt ignotæ. Tamen quia licet de culpa vsuræ iudex Ecclesiasticus cognoscat, ratione qua culpa est, & quod restitui debet iudicare habeat: tamen ratione forte facti imponere restitutionem & emendam, ad principem pertinet, qui est iustitia animata, & custos iustitiae: & idem in aliis contractibus, sicut in quo minus videtur convincere haereticos iudicem, ad Ecclesiasticum pertinet, extra, de haereticis, ad abolendam, & cap. sequenti, vergentis, licet principes de negligentia exequendi, a Papa reprehendantur & puniantur: quia, ut notat Innocentius, factum est de Imperatoris praesentis consensu. Tum etiam quia episcopus civitatis habet ab Imperatore facultatem exigendi, & consequendi bona executionis, & exequendi cum testator personam ad exequendum non designauit. C. de sacrosanctis episcopis, nulli liceat: ita tamen, quod cum episcopus huiusmodi pecunias fuerit consecutus, quantitatem & tempus quo eas receperit, apud rectorem provinciae publicare debebit, ut ibidem dicitur. Tum quia lex de petenda hereditate, l. hereditas, ad quam Canonistae per se remittunt, defensionem & executionem piarum voluntatum ultimarum, sicut, &c. quae ad pias causas pertinent, non solum ad pontificem, sed ad principalem pertinere oportet, in fine dicens, quod principali & pontificali, id est principis & pontificis auctoritate compelluntur haeredes ad executionem extremae voluntatis. Tum quia in tali casu, cum sit restitutio aeris alieni, magis videtur pertinere ad iustas causas, quam ad pias. Et ideo puto, quod non oportet quod per solum Ecclesiasticum iudicem talis restitutio fiat: sed magis ad principem pertinet, licet etiam posset fieri per providentiam quorumlibet bonorum virorum.
units.tr: As for what is said in the nineteenth argument, about legacies and restitutions: I answer that legacies, insofar as they are made to pious causes, belong to ecclesiastical law. This is what ecclesiastical writers call a special spiritual matter, especially when they are wholly undefined. In that case they can be determined by the ecclesiastical authority according to the testator's express will. But whether a bequest can be transferred is another matter. Suppose a testator leaves one hundred pounds to the poor within the city or diocese of Paris. I do not see that, because of such lack of definition, it could lawfully be given to the poor of the diocese of Chartres, or that the testator's will could be changed by right. Yet the prince, who presides over both dioceses, could for a reasonable cause transfer and give it, since he is over the named diocese. As for making restitutions, I do not see why they could not be made, by the foresight or prudence of any good men, to pious uses for the benefit of the land, if necessity presses or public advantage demands it. This holds especially through the foresight of the prince, who watches over the common good, since the money is paid out for the common benefit or need, because the persons concerned are unknown. Still, although the ecclesiastical judge takes cognizance of the sin of usury, as a sin, and may judge that restitution must be made, the power to impose restitution and a penalty, by reason of the actual deed, belongs to the prince. He is justice made alive and the guardian of justice. The same holds for other contracts, in which a judge seems less able to convict heretics. Such matters belong to the ecclesiastical authority (Extra, De haereticis, Ad abolendam, and the following chapter, Vergentis), although princes who neglect to carry out such duties are rebuked and punished by the Pope, because, as Innocent notes, the matter was done with the consent of the present Emperor. Also, the bishop of a city has from the Emperor the power to demand and obtain the goods for execution, and to carry out the execution when the testator has not designated a person to carry it out (C. De sacrosanctis episcopis, Nulli liceat). Yet, once such a bishop has received the money, he must make public the amount and the time of receipt before the governor of the province, as it says there. Also, the law on claiming an inheritance (l. Hereditas), to which the canonists themselves refer, states that the defence and execution of pious last wills, as far as they pertain to pious causes, must belong not only to the pontiff but to the civil ruler. It says at the end that heirs are compelled to carry out the last will by the authority of the prince and of the pontiff, that is, of the prince and of the pontiff. Also, in such a case, since it is the restitution of debt, it seems to pertain more to just causes than to pious ones. Therefore I think such restitution need not be made by the ecclesiastical judge alone, but rather belongs to the prince, although it could also be made through the foresight of any good men.

units.la: Quod autem arguitur vigesimo, quod corporalia reguntur per spiritualia, & ab ipsis dependent ut a causa. Responsio. Argumentum, ut sic factum, multipliciter deficit. Primo, quia supponit, quod potestas regalis sit corporalis, & non spiritualis, & habeat curam corporum, & non animarum: quod falsum est, ut patet ex supradictis, cum ordinetur ad bonum commune civium non quodcunque, sed quod est viuere secundum virtutem, unde dicit Philosophus in Ethicis, quod intentio legislatoris est homines bonos facere, & inducere ad virtutem, & etiam in Politicis dicit, quod sicut anima melior est corpore, sic legislator melior est medico: quia legislator habet curam animarum, medicus corporum. Secundo deficit argumentum, quia non quaelibet potestas saecularis a qualibet spirituali instituitur, movetur & dirigitur, nam in domo ordinata doctor literarum, & instructor morum, cuius potestas est spiritualis, non instituit medicum: sed ambo a patrefamilias instituuntur, nec etiam dirigit medicum, in quantum medicus est: sed solum per accidens, in quantum accidit medicum velle castum vel literatum fieri. Sic Papa non instituit regem, sed vterq; est a Deo institutus suo modo: nec eum dirigit per se ut rex est, sed per accidens, in quantum convenit regem fidelem esse, in quo instruitur a Papa de fide, & non de regimine. Unde subiicitur Papae in iis, in quibus subiicit eum potestas suprema, sc. in spiritualibus tantum. Patet etiam, argumentum deficere, & magis esse pro nobis, quam contra nos, si consideremus exemplum: quia licet corpora caelestia moveantur in suum finem, & administrentur per angelos: tamen non sunt producta per angelos, sed immediate a Deo, & ita debet concludi, quod potestas terrena est a Deo immediate, licet ipsa ad beatam vitam dirigatur per potestatem spiritualem.
units.tr: As for what is argued in the twentieth, that bodily things are governed by spiritual things and depend on them as on a cause: I answer that the argument, as it stands, fails in several ways. First, it assumes that royal power is bodily and not spiritual, and that it has care of bodies and not of souls. This is false, as is clear from what was said above. Royal power is ordained to the common good of citizens, not to just any good, but to living according to virtue. Hence the Philosopher says in the Ethics that the intention of the lawgiver is to make men good and to lead them to virtue. And in the Politics he says that just as the soul is better than the body, so the lawgiver is better than the physician, because the lawgiver has care of souls and the physician of bodies. Second, the argument fails because not every secular power is instituted, moved and directed by every spiritual power. In a well-ordered household, the teacher of letters and the instructor of morals, whose authority is spiritual, does not appoint the physician. Both are appointed by the head of the household. Nor does the teacher direct the physician as physician, but only by accident, insofar as it happens that the physician wishes to be chaste or learned. So the Pope does not appoint the king, but each is instituted by God in his own way. Nor does the Pope direct the king as king, but by accident, insofar as it is fitting for a king to be faithful, and in this he is instructed by the Pope concerning faith, and not concerning government. Hence he is subject to the Pope in those things in which the supreme power subjects him, namely in spiritual matters only. It is also plain that the argument fails, and is more on our side than against us, if we consider the example. Although the heavenly bodies are moved to their end and are governed by angels, they were not produced by angels but immediately by God. So it should be concluded that earthly power is from God immediately, although it is directed to the blessed life by spiritual power.

units.la: Quod vero vigesimoprimo dicitur de Hugone, dicente, quod spiritualis potestas instituit temporalem: dici potest, quod dicta Hugonis non sunt autentica, & modicum roboris afferunt. Dici tamen potest, ut dicit Augustinus 1. de Civitate Dei: Mos sacra Scriptura est, dicere rem fieri, quando manifestatur, pro tanto ergo dicit Hugo, quod potestas spiritualis regiam instituit, non quidem ipsam efficiendo ut sit, cum sit a Deo, & Apostolo consentiente & eligente: sed quia in vngendo ipsum institutum & electum manifestat.
units.tr: As for what is said in the twenty-first argument, from Hugo, who says that spiritual power institutes temporal power: it can be said that Hugo's sayings are not authentic and carry little weight. Yet it can be said, as Augustine says in the first book of the City of God, that it is the custom of Holy Scripture to say that a thing is done when it is made manifest. So when Hugo says that spiritual power institutes royal power, he means not that it makes it to be, since it is from God, and by the consent and choice of the Apostle, but that in anointing the one instituted and chosen it makes this manifest.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur 22. quod spiritualis homo omnia diiudicat, & ipse a nemine iudicatur, &c. licet illa auctoritas frequenter assumatur, & in diuersis casibus pro auctoritate domini Papae: tamen non est ad propositum, quia non accipitur ibi homo spiritualis a potestate spirituali, quam habet Ecclesiasticus iudex: cum habens interdum hanc potestatem spiritualem, sit animalis, ut ibi accipitur: sed dicitur animalis homo vita vel sensu. Vita autem animalis dicitur, cum vita alicuius fertur per animalia sciuiam, & non continetur rectore spiritu. Scientia quidem animalis homo est, qui secundum phantasiam corporum, vel legis literam, vel rationem physicam de Deo iudicat. Spiritualis vero dicitur vita & scientia. Vita quidem dicitur spiritualis, qui secundum Deum habens rationem, animam suam regit. Spiritualis autem scientia est, qui non secundum humanum sensum, sed Spiritui sancto subiectus per fidem, de Deo iudicat certissime & fideliter. Unde talis iudicat omnia. Glossa: Certa fide occultorum. Et ipse a nemine iudicatur. Glossa: intelligitur, an bene vel male intelligat, vel a nemine iudicatur, & reprehenditur, & sic exponunt Hieronymus & Augustin. & litera Apostoli hoc ostendit.
units.tr: As for what is said in the twenty-second argument, that the spiritual man judges all things and is himself judged by no one, and so on: although that text is often cited, and in various cases in support of the authority of the lord Pope, it is not to the point. The spiritual man there is not understood as one holding the spiritual power that an ecclesiastical judge has, since a man who sometimes has this spiritual power may be natural, as the word is used there. The natural man is called so by life or by understanding. Natural life is life conducted by natural knowledge alone, not governed by the guiding Spirit. The natural man in knowledge is one who judges of God according to the imagination of bodies, or the letter of the law, or physical reason. The spiritual man, on the other hand, is so in life and in knowledge. In life, one is spiritual who, having reason according to God, rules his own soul. Spiritual knowledge belongs to one who, not according to human sense but subject to the Holy Spirit through faith, judges of God most surely and faithfully. Such a man judges all things (Gloss: by the certain faith of hidden things). And he himself is judged by no one (Gloss: it is understood whether he understands rightly or wrongly). Or he is judged and reproved by no one, and so Jerome and Augustine explain it, and the wording of the Apostle shows this.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur 23. de ordine finium: respondeo: Multipliciter deficit argumentum. Primo quidem, quia ars ad quam pertinet superior finis, movet & imperat arti, ad quam pertinet finis inferior, non quidem simpliciter, sed quantum ei competit ad necessitatem sui finis ultimi, & hoc aliqualiter est concessum superius in proposito. Item plus deficit, quia ars illa superior non semper imperat necessario inferiori, movendo per modum necessitatis, & instituendo eam, sed solum ei imperat per modum dirigentis, & sicut medicus pigmentarium informat, & iudicat de ipso an bene conficiat pigmenta, & debite, sed ipsum non instituit, nec destituit: sed est aliquis superior vtrobique, apud quem est totus ordo civitatis, ut rex vel dominus civitatis: & iste, si pigmentarius non conficiat pigmenta prout medico competit, habet ipsum destituere, sicut & constituere. Et ita est in proposito. Totus mundus est quasi vna civitas, in qua Deus est suprema potestas, quae Papam & Imperatorem
units.tr: As for what is said in the twenty-third argument, about the order of ends: I answer that the argument fails in several ways. First, the art to which the higher end belongs moves and commands the art to which the lower end belongs. It does so not absolutely, but insofar as this is required for the necessity of its ultimate end, and this has been partly granted above in the present discussion. Moreover, the argument fails further, because that higher art does not always command the lower one by necessity, moving it by way of compulsion and establishing it. It commands it only by way of directing. Thus the physician shapes the apothecary and judges whether he prepares the medicines well and properly, but he neither appoints nor removes him. Rather, there is someone above both, under whom the whole order of the city stands, such as the king or lord of the city. If the apothecary does not prepare the medicines as the physician requires, this superior has the power to remove him as well as to appoint him. And so it is in the present case. The whole world is like one city, in which God is the supreme power, who appointed the Pope and the Emperor...

units.la: ratorem tatorem instituit: quare, &c. Tertio deficit argumentum: quia licet aliquid coloris habeat, vbi illud quod pertinet ad artem inferiorem, non habet rationem boni vel appetibilis secundum se: sed solum vt ordinatur ad finem superiorem, quem respicit ars superior. Sicut se habet confectio medicinarum, quam facit pigmentarius, ad sanitatem, quam intendit medicus: tamen dicta ratio nihil coloris habet, vbi illud quod ad inferiorem artem pertinet, habet in se rationem boni & appetibilis secundum se, cuiusmodi est viuere secundum virtutem. Nam multa sunt bona & appetibilia secundum se, quae tamen ad aliud ordinabilia sunt: vt dicitur in 8. Ethicorum, de amicitia: & in 10. dicitur idem de scire & videre, & aliis huiusmodi. Quarto deficit dicta ratio, quia dato quod valeat in aliquibus partibus ordinatis, vbi inferior finis non ducit in superiorem, nisi determinato modo. Et ideo deficere secundum illum determinatum modum, est deficere simpliciter, & inutile remanere respectu illius finis: tamen vbi finis inferior habet diuersos ordines ad superiorem, non oportet, quod si deficiat secundum vnum ordinem, quod potestas constituta in illo, destituatur tanquam inutilis: quia est alius ordo eius ad finem, qui forte, solum notus est supremae potestati: propter quem ordinem vult inferre potestatem manere tanquam vtilem, & sic est de potestate regia: quia secundum eam populus non solum dirigitur in Deum, secundum quod rex ea vitur vt rex est: sed etiam ea vitur vt tyrannus, in quantum scilicet tyrannia principi punitionem peccatorum: vt dicit Iob, quod regnare facit Dominus hypocritam propter peccata, vel in probationem patientiae subditorum, vel in compulsionem eorum, vt ad Deum refugiant, qui solus potest corda regum immutare in melius, dicente Salomone: Cor regis in manu Domini est, & quocumque voluerit inclinabit illud, qui etiam & tyrannos, quos reputat conuersione indignos, potest auferre, secundum illud Salomonis: Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, & sedere fecit mites pro eis. Et per Ezechielem dicit: Liberabo gregem meum de ore eorum, quae pascunt semetipsos.
units.tr: ...rator, instituted the ruler... Therefore, etc. Thirdly, the argument fails: although it has some colour, where that which pertains to the lower art does not have the character of good or desirable in itself, but only insofar as it is ordered to the higher end which the higher art looks to. Thus the compounding of medicines, which the apothecary makes, stands to health, which the physician intends; yet the said argument has no colour where that which pertains to the lower art has in itself the character of good and desirable in itself, such as living according to virtue. For many things are good and desirable in themselves, and yet are ordainable to something else, as is said in the 8th book of the Ethics, concerning friendship; and in the 10th the same is said of knowing and seeing, and other things of this kind. Fourthly, the said argument fails, because even granting that it holds in some ordered parts, where the lower end does not lead into the higher except in a determined manner, to fail in that determined manner is to fail absolutely, and to remain useless with respect to that end. Yet where the lower end has various orders to the higher, it does not follow that if it fails in one order, the power constituted in that is to be deposed as useless; for there is another order of it to the end, which perhaps is known only to the supreme power, on account of which order it wills the power to remain as useful. So it is with royal power: for by it the people is not only directed towards God, insofar as the king uses it as king, but it is also used as tyranny, insofar as tyranny serves the prince for punishing sins, as Job says, that the Lord makes a hypocrite to reign because of sins, or for the testing of the patience of the subjects, or for compelling them to flee to God, who alone can change the hearts of kings for the better, Solomon saying: The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, and he will incline it wherever he wishes; who also can remove even those tyrants whom he judges unworthy of conversion, according to the saying of Solomon: God has overthrown the seats of proud leaders, and made the meek sit in their place. And through Ezekiel he says: I will deliver my flock from the mouth of those who feed themselves.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur 24. quod papa habet facere leges, eo quod princeps non potest facere leges, vel eis vti quousq; fuerint per papam approbatae: Dico quod falsum est, vt dicit expresse Leo papa, scribens Lothario Augusto distinct. 10. de capitulis di. Sic de capitulis & praeceptis imperialibus vestris & praedecessorum vestrorum irrefragabiliter custodiendis & conseruandis, quantum rationem & valemus, Christo propitio & nunc & in aeternum conseruaturos modo omnibus profitemur: & si forte quis libet vobis aliter dixerit, vel dicturus fuerit, sciatis ipsum pro certo mendacem, nec per Canones semper legibus derogatur, nisi quo ad casus spirituales. Nec papa posset leges tollere, nisi quoad suum forum, vt dicit Ioan. & alii. Dicere autem, vt isti magistri dicunt, quod papa tradit leges principibus & quod princeps non potest legem aliunde sumere, nisi per papam fuerint approbatae: est omnino destruere regimen regale & politicum, & incidere in errorem Herodis, timentis & putantis Christum regem destruere terrenum, quia secundum Philosophum in 1. Politicorum, principatus tunc solum dicitur regalis, quando quis praeest secundum leges quas ipse instituit. Cum vero praeest non secundum arbitrium suum, sed secundum leges quas ciues vel alii instituerunt, dicitur principatus ciuilis vel politicus, & non regalis. Si ergo nullus princeps regeret, nisi secundum leges a papa traditas, vel ab eo primo approbatas: nullus principaretur principatu regali vel politico, sed solum papali: quod est regnum destruere, & omnem principatum antiquum euacuare.
units.tr: But as to what is said in the 24th (chapter), that the pope has to make laws, because the prince cannot make laws, or use them until they have been approved by the pope: I say that this is false, as Pope Leo expressly says, writing to the Emperor Lothair, distinct. 10, concerning the capitularies: Thus, concerning the capitularies and imperial precepts of yours and of your predecessors, to be irrefragably observed and preserved, as far as reason allows and we are able, with Christ propitious, we now profess to all, and will preserve for eternity: and if perhaps anyone shall tell you otherwise, or shall be about to, know that he is certainly a liar. Nor are laws always derogated by the Canons, except as to spiritual cases. Nor could the pope abolish laws except as to his own forum, as John and others say.
