But to say, as these masters say, that the pope hands laws down to princes, and that a prince cannot take a law from elsewhere unless it has first been approved by the pope, is entirely to destroy royal and political government, and to fall into the error of Herod, who feared and thought that Christ as king would destroy the earthly one. For according to the Philosopher in the 1st book of the Politics, a principate is then called royal, when someone rules according to laws which he himself has instituted. But when he rules not according to his own will, but according to laws which the citizens or others have instituted, the principate is called civil or political, and not royal. If therefore no prince ruled except according to laws handed down by the pope, or first approved by him, then no one would hold a principate that is royal or political, but only papal; which is to destroy kingship and to empty every ancient principate.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur XXV. quod sacerdotium dicitur regale, quia sacerdotes sunt reges: dicendum, quod sacerdotium, vt patet ex praedictis, dicitur regale a regno, non quidem mundi, sed coeli, ad quod ordinat & dirigit, vel secundum intentionem beati Petri, hoc dicitur omnibus fidelibus iustis: qui in quantum sunt vnum cum Christo capite, in ipso sunt reges & sacerdotes, attribuendo membris quod est capitis, secundum regulam Tyconii. Vel ideo dicuntur regnum, quia in ipsis regnat rex eorum Christus: & sacerdotes dicuntur, quia offerunt Deo sacrificia laudis & spiritus contribulati: quod etiam conferunt omnes iusti.
units.tr: As for what is said at XXV, that the priesthood is called royal because priests are kings: it must be said that the priesthood, as is clear from what has been said above, is called royal from a kingdom, not of the world but of heaven, to which it orders and directs. Or, according to the intention of blessed Peter, this is said of all the just faithful, who, insofar as they are one with Christ the head, are in him kings and priests, attributing to the members what belongs to the head, according to the rule of Tyconius. Or they are called a kingdom because their King, Christ, reigns in them, and they are called priests because they offer to God sacrifices of praise and a contrite spirit, which all the just also offer.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur vicesimo sexto de veteri lege, in qua rex inungebatur per sacerdotem: respondeo, Non est de necessitate potestatis secularis, quod inungatur, cum ante reges inuncti essent populo illo fuerint duces, vt Moyses & Iosua, & successores eorum, de quibus Dominus prouidebat. Non etiam de necessitate regis, qui perfectiorem habet auctoritatem, quod ungatur: cum alias habeant reges habeant, qui non inunguntur. In populo autem illo reges inungebantur in mysterium representationem regis Christi, de populo nasciturí, qui multo oleo gratiae pre participibus suis: oleo (dictio) significato per oleum quo reges de populo vngebantur: quod etiam apud reges Christianos, quia membra Christi profitentur, obseruatur. Non enim est in conuenienti, quod reges in populo sint verireges, & tamen sint figura altioris regis. Augustinus: Hoc vero multis regia fieri praecipit, vt significaretur, quod de populo illo erat nasciturus, qui simul fuerat rex & sacerdos, scilicet quae institutae erant in populo illo, cum pleraque eorum essent figuralia, non sunt ad populum Christianum. Vnde & in novo Testamento non legimus, quod sacerdotes inungi debent reges: nec etiam obseruatur in omnibus regibus Hispaniae. Et ideo argumentum est ad propositum. Augustin. Idem inunctio erat consecratio regum. Consecratae autem secundum papam, est Deo dare. Ex quo patet, quod per hoc non concluditur, quod sacerdotium sit magis temporalibus & cadus saeculi, quam regia potestas, sed solum in causis Dei: sicut per hoc, quod regum peccata oblatione sacerdotis expiabantur, non probatur quod sacerdotium sit maius regia potestate, nisi solum in iis quae a Deo sunt: ut 2.q.6. nos. Quod etiam istud argumentum non concludat, patet: quia in veteri lege sacerdotes qui reges inungebant, indubitanter regibus subdebantur.
units.tr: As for what is said in the twenty-sixth chapter about the old law, in which the king was anointed by the priest: I answer that it is not necessary for secular power that the ruler be anointed, since before there were anointed kings, that people had leaders such as Moses and Joshua and their successors, whom the Lord provided. Nor is it necessary for a king, who has the more perfect authority, to be anointed, since other kings exist who are not anointed. Among that people, however, kings were anointed as a representation of the mystery of the King Christ, who was to be born from the people, who was anointed with the oil of grace above his fellows: the word "oil" being signified by the oil with which kings were anointed from the people; and this is also observed among Christian kings, because they profess to be members of Christ. For it is not inconsistent that kings among the people should be true kings and yet be a figure of a higher King. Augustine: Moreover, he commanded that many things be done in a royal manner, so that it might be signified that he who was to be born from that people would be both king and priest, namely (the things which were instituted among that people, since most of them were figurative), are not binding on the Christian people. Hence, in the New Testament we do not read that priests ought to anoint kings, nor is this observed for all kings of Spain. And so the argument is beside the point. Augustine: The same anointing was the consecration of kings. But to be consecrated according to the pope is to be given to God. From this it is clear that it does not follow from this that the priesthood is greater than royal power in temporal matters and worldly affairs, but only in matters of God; just as, because the sins of kings were expiated by the sacrifice of the priest, it is not proved that the priesthood is greater than royal power, except only in those things which pertain to God, as in 2.q.6, nos. That this argument does not conclude is also clear, because in the old law the priests who anointed kings were undoubtedly subject to the kings.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur XXVII. quod sine Christi iustitia non potest esse respub. dicendum est, quod virtutes morales acquisitae, possunt esse perfectae sine theologicis, nec ab ipsis perficiuntur, nisi quadam accidentali perfectione, ut innuit Augustinus in lib. Sententiarum Prosperi: & ideo sine rectore Christo est perfecta & vera iustitia, quae ad regnum requiritur, cum regnum ordinetur ad viuere secundum virtutem moralem acquisitam, cui accidit quod perficiatur per interiores virtutes quascunque. Vel ideo, dicit Augustinus, quod non est vera iustitia, ubi non est Christus rector: non quia esse non possit, sed quia non erat iustitia etiam moralis acquisita apud illos qui iustitiam seruare credebant, daemonib. & idolis seruientes, contra quos dicit Augustinus quod veram iustitiam non seruabant. Potest etiam esse, quod non regeretur Respub. populi Christiani recte, nisi rector sit papa, qui est Christi vicarius in spiritualib. nec aliter iustitia seruaretur, nisi ei sicut iustum est in spiritualib. obedire tur.
units.tr: As for what is said at XXVII, that without the justice of Christ a commonwealth cannot exist: it must be said that acquired moral virtues can be perfect without the theological virtues, and are not perfected by them except by a certain accidental perfection, as Augustine hints in the book of the Sentences of Prosper. And so, without Christ as ruler, there is perfect and true justice, which is required for a kingdom, since a kingdom is ordered to living according to acquired moral virtue, to which it happens that there is added perfection through whatever inward virtues. Or, as Augustine says, there is no true justice where Christ is not ruler, not because it cannot exist, but because even acquired moral justice was not present among those who believed they kept justice while serving demons and idols; against them Augustine says that they did not keep true justice. It may also be that the commonwealth of the Christian people is not rightly governed unless its ruler is the pope, who is Christ's vicar in spiritual matters; nor would justice otherwise be kept, unless people obey him in spiritual matters as is just.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur XXVIII. quod oportet illas potestates esse a Deo ordine quodam: respondeo. Ordinem habent, ut dictum est, dignitatis, non causalitatis, cum vna non sit ab alia, sicut omnes angeli a Deo sunt producti ordine quodam dignitatis, in quanum vnus in naturalibus semper est nobilior altero: sed non est ibi ordo causalitatis, quo vnus sit ab alio, cum omnes sint a Deo immediate creati. Intentio tamen Apostoli videtur esse de ordine cuiuslibet ad finem suum proprium, & non de ordine cuiuslibet ad alterum. Quod patet ex hoc, quod subiungit de principe, quod minister Dei est in vindictam, &c.
units.tr: As for what is said at XXVIII, that those powers must be from God by a certain order: I answer. They have an order, as has been said, of dignity, not of causality, since the one is not from the other; just as all the angels were produced by God in a certain order of dignity, in which one is always nobler than another in natural things; but there is no order of causality there, by which one would be from another, since all have been created immediately by God. Yet the intention of the Apostle seems to concern the order of each thing to its own proper end, and not the order of one thing to another. This is clear from the fact that he adds concerning the prince that he is the minister of God for vengeance, etc.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur XXIX. de vero capite dici potest, quod vna est Ecclesia, verus populus Christianus, vnutto corpus mysticum: non quidem in Petro, vel Lino, sed in Christo, qui solus proprie & maxime est caput Ecclesiae, a quo distributa est vtraque potestas dicta, quoad diuersos gradus secundum Psal. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Et Ephes. 2. Ipsum dedit caput super omnem ecclesiam, quae est corpus ipsius, vbi dicit Ambrosius, quod Christus est caput Ecclesiae. Potest nihilominus summus pontifex, quantum ad exteriorem ministrorum exhibitionem, dici caput Ecclesiae, quantum ipse est principalis inter ministros, a quo vt a principali Christi vicario in spiritualibus totus ordo ministrorum dependet, vel ab hierarcha & architecto: sicut Romana ecclesia indubitanter est caput omnium ecclesiarum. Non est autem caput, quantum ad regimen in temporalibus, seu dispositionem temporalium: sed quilibet rex est in hoc caput regni sui: & Imperator monarcha si fuerit, est caput mundi. Est etiam hic considerandum, quod ex Ecclesiastica hierarchia, qua oportet habere vnum monarcham summum pontificem, nituntur aliqui ostendere, reges & principes esse subditos papae in temporalibus: ita quod in papa sit vtraque potestas, spiritualis sc. & temporalis, quod ipsi prosequuntur diffuse. Sed in veritate, ex ipsa Ecclesiastica hierarchia secundum beatum Dionysium in infimo gradu sunt laici cum suis regibus, quasi imperfecti: perfectibiles tamen: supra quos sunt perfectiores, vt viri Ecclesiastici: & in supremo est summus monarcha, omnium scilicet dominus papa. Constat autem secundum doctrinam eiusdem Dionysii, quod infimi non reducuntur ad supremos, nisi per medios: neo supremi perficiunt hierarchicae infimos immediate, sed mediantibus mediis. Summus ergo pontifex non habet potestatem generalem & immediatam super laicos, nisi quam habent medii de hierarchia immediatam, & magis contractam, vt episcopi vel abbates. Quamuis enim in angelica hierarchia supremus monarcha, qui est Deus, aliquid possit circa infinitum angelorum, quod circa ipsum no potest aliquis mediorum, vt creare, & in nihilum redigere: tamen hoc non potest in quantum hierarcha, sed in quantum Deus creator. Cum ergo in istis mediis perfectionibus non ponant aliqui vtramq; potestatem, spiritualem sc. & temporalem, sed spiritualem tantum: clarum est ex ista ordinatione Ecclesiasticae hierarchiae, quod summus pontifex vt hierarcha est, non habebit potestatem nisi spiritualem, licet generaliorem, quia vbiq; potentem. Et propter hoc Bernhardus ad Eugenium lib. 4. praedictum ordinem hierarchiacum attendens, nullam potestatem ponit in papa, quam non poterat in praelatis inferioribus, licet in papa ponat summam. Unde dicit sic: Erras, si vt summam, ita & solam a Deo institutam, vestram Apostolicam dignitatem existimas * si nullo sancto * dissentiu ab eo qui ait: Non est potestas nisi a Deo. Proinde quod sequitur, Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit: et si propterea aliter pro nihilo non tamen simpliciter. Deinde idem ait, Omnis anima potestatibus subiecta sit: non ait, Sublimiores tanquam in uno: sed, Sublimiores tanquam in multis. Non tua ergo sola a Domino sunt: & mediocres sunt, & inseriores. Ecce manifeste in isto ordine hierarchico nullam potestatem dat papae, quam non dat aliis praelatis, licet tam in papa ponat summam. Ex quo patet, quod cum dicti medii praelati non habeant potestatem nisi a Christo spiritualem, non potest esse quod papa singulariter habeat temporalem, per hoc quod est totius Ecclesiae summus seu supremus hierarcha. Et hoc dicunt sancti Matt. 16. quod Christus non dedit aliquam potestatem Petro, quam non dedit ceteris apostolis, & episcopis & sacerdotibus ecclesiae: licet Petrus dicatur specialiter claves ecclesiae accepisse propter principalitatem, quam a Christo accepit, vt dicit Rabanus. Et Glossa, propterea hoc etiam quod dictum est Petro soli Matt. 16. dictum est etiam per eandem verba omnibus: Matth. 18. Quodcunq; ligaueris, &c. Et Iohan. 20. dicendum est omnibus: Accipite Spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis, &c. vbi dicit Chrys. quod collata fuit potestas spiritualis tantum. Hanc autem distinctionem hic fecit propter aliquos magnos, qui propter vaitatem Ecclesiasticae hierarchiae nituntur ostendere, papam habere vtramq; gladium. Est etiam considerandum, q ex dicto ordine hierarchiae BernaBernardus vbi supra reprehendit Papam: quia dictum ordinem Ecclesiasticum perturbat, dum abbates & inferiores episcoporum eximit, eos immediate sibi subdens quod in coelesti hierarchia, ad quam extrahitur ecclesiastica, non inuenitur: Quod etiam non posset de iure fieri, sentire videtur, cū Papæ in Moyse dictum sit à Domino: Inspice, & fac secundum exemplar quod tibi à Domino in monte ostensum est: hoc enim dispensationem, non dissipationem indicat: cum tamen papæ non sit credita dissipatio, sed dispensatio. Sed Bernardo sic sentienti, non consentio ex toto.
units.tr: As for what is said at XXIX, concerning the true head, it may be said that there is one Church, the true Christian people, one mystical body: not indeed in Peter or Linus, but in Christ, who alone properly and supremely is the head of the Church, from whom both the aforesaid powers are distributed, as to their various degrees, according to the Psalm: "You have put all things under his feet." And Ephesians 2: "He gave him to be head over all the church, which is his body," where Ambrose says that Christ is the head of the Church. Nevertheless, the supreme pontiff may, as regards the outward exercise of ministers, be called the head of the Church, insofar as he is the principal among the ministers, from whom, as from the principal vicar of Christ in spiritual matters, the whole order of ministers depends, or from the hierarch and architect; just as the Roman Church is undoubtedly the head of all churches. But he is not the head as regards governance in temporal matters, or the disposition of temporal affairs; rather, any king is the head of his own kingdom in this respect, and the emperor, if he is a monarch, is the head of the world. Here it must also be considered that some, from the ecclesiastical hierarchy, which requires that there be one supreme monarch, the supreme pontiff, strive to show that kings and princes are subject to the pope in temporal matters, so that in the pope there is both power, spiritual and temporal, which they pursue at length. But in truth, from the very ecclesiastical hierarchy, according to blessed Dionysius, at the lowest grade are the laity with their kings, as imperfect though capable of being perfected; above them are the more perfect, such as ecclesiastical men; and at the summit is the supreme monarch, namely the lord pope of all. Now it is established, according to the teaching of the same Dionysius, that the lowest are not led back to the highest except through the intermediate ones, nor do the highest perfect the lowest of the hierarchy immediately, but by means of intermediaries. Therefore the supreme pontiff does not have a general and immediate power over the laity, except what the intermediate members of the hierarchy have immediately, but in a more restricted way, such as bishops or abbots. For although in the angelic hierarchy the supreme monarch, who is God, can do some things regarding the infinite number of angels which none of the intermediaries can do, such as to create and reduce to nothing, nevertheless he can do this not as a hierarch but as God the Creator. Since therefore some do not place both powers, spiritual and temporal, in these intermediate perfect ones, but only the spiritual, it is clear from this ordering of the ecclesiastical hierarchy that the supreme pontiff, as a hierarch, will have only spiritual power, though a more general one, because it is powerful everywhere. And for this reason Bernard, in his book 4 to Eugenius, attending to the aforesaid hierarchical order, assigns to the pope no power which he could not have in the lower prelates, although he assigns to the pope the highest. Hence he speaks thus: "You are mistaken if you think your Apostolic dignity, as the highest, is also the only one instituted by God; if this is not so, you dissent from no saint who says: There is no power but from God. Therefore what follows, 'He who resists the power resists the ordinance of God,' is true, even if otherwise for nothing, yet not simply." Then he says the same: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers": he does not say, "to the higher as to one," but "to the higher as to many." Therefore yours alone are not from the Lord; the middling and lower ones are too. Behold, clearly in this hierarchical order he gives the pope no power which he does not give to the other prelates, although he places the highest in the pope. From this it is clear that, since the said intermediate prelates have only spiritual power from Christ, it cannot be that the pope alone has temporal power by the fact that he is the highest or supreme hierarch of the whole Church. And the holy men say this on Matthew 16, that Christ gave Peter no power which he did not give to the other apostles, bishops and priests of the Church, although Peter is said specially to have received the keys of the Church on account of the primacy which he received from Christ, as Rabanus says. And the Gloss: therefore what was said to Peter alone in Matthew 16 was also said to all in the same words, Matthew 18: "Whatever you shall bind," etc. And John 20: it must be said to all: "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive," etc., where Chrysostom says that only spiritual power was conferred. But I have made this distinction here on account of certain great men who, because of the vanity of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, strive to show that the pope has both swords. It must also be considered that from the said order of the hierarchy, Bernard, in the place above, rebukes the pope, because he disturbs the said ecclesiastical order while he exempts abbots and lower bishops, subjecting them immediately to himself, which is not found in the celestial hierarchy, to which the ecclesiastical one is drawn. He seems also to feel that this could not be done rightly, since it was said to Moses by the Lord: "Look, and make it according to the pattern which was shown to you on the mountain"; for this indicates a dispensing, not a dissipating, whereas the pope has not been entrusted with dissipation but with dispensation. But I do not wholly agree with Bernard in his view.

units.la: Quod vero XXX. dicitur de duobus gladiis: respondeo, Non est hic nisi quædam allegatio allegorica, ex qua non potest sumi argumentum: quia secundum Dionysium, mystica Theologia non est argumentativa. Et Aug. dicit in epistola ad Vincentium, quod allegoria non sufficit ad probationem alicuius, nisi tamen eius habeatur aliunde auctoritas manifesta. Possum etiam dicere, quod per illos duos gladios intelligunt omnes mystice verbum Dei, iuxta illud Apost. Ephes. 6. Accipe loricam fidei, & gladium spiritus, quod est verbum Dei. Quod autem dicitur, Duo gladii, propter novum & vetus Testamentum: & per duos gladios intelligunt gladium verbi, & gladium instantis persecutionis. De quo dicitur Lucæ 2. beatæ Virgini, Tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius. Et 2. Regum 12. Non recedet gladius de domo tua: & ii sufficere tunc dicebant. Et horum unus erat Apostolorum passiue, qui ab eis sustinendus, scilicet gladius persecutionis: alius autem erat eorum proprie, quia ab eis pro tempore competenti euaginandus, scilicet gladius verbi Dei. Dato autem quod per illos duos gladios, quos habebant Apostoli, intelligantur duæ potestates, scilicet spiritualis & temporalis: quæ licet dicantur ibi esse, tamen non dicuntur ambæ esse Petri vel alterius Apostoli, nam vnum eorum non tetigit Petrus, sc. secularem, qui suus non erat. Alium vero tetigit, scilicet spiritualem, quem solus Dominus dixit esse suum, & tamen non statim euaginandum à Petro, vnde dictum est ei: Pone gladium tuum in vaginam, quia certe non debet statim, sed cum magna deliberatione, & in necessitate magna, iudex Ecclesiasticus vti suo mucrone spirituali, ne contemnatur. Posito igitur quod per illos duos gladios mysticæ illæ duæ potestates intelligantur, pro nobis est: quia cum essent duo, Petrus non habuit suum nisi vnum, propter quod etiam dicit Deus Matth. 10. Non veni pacem mittere, sed gladium, vel significanter dicit Gladium, non gladios, & in persona Christi dictum est in Psalmo: Accingere gladio tuo super, &c. Et Apoc. 1. de filio sedente in medio candelabrorum, & 19. de illo qui dicitur verbum Dei: dicitur quod ex ore eius exibat gladius, ex vtraq; parte acutus. Ecce ergo quod à Christo non habet nisi vnum. Potest nihilominus dici: quod duo gladii ibi dicuntur fuisse, & ad Apostolos pertinere quia vnus apostolis & eorum successoribus conuenit per se, quem à Christo habent: alius vero suus est aptitudine, quia eis non repugnat: & ex commissione & permissione principum suus erat futurus. Potest etiam dici, quod dicta auctoritas Bernardi pro nobis est, quia dicit quod vtrunque est Ecclesiæ: sed materialis pro ecclesia, spiritualis vero ab ecclesia exercendus: iste sacerdotis, is militis manu, sed sane ad nutum sacerdotis & iussum Imperatoris, vbi signanter dicit, Ad nutum sacerdotis, & non per manum, vel ad iussum eius: quia in hoc non habet auctoritatem iubendi vel compellendi, sed solum inuendi, si voluerit Imperator.
units.tr: As for what is said in the thirtieth point about the two swords, I answer: there is here only an allegorical allusion, and no argument can be drawn from it, because according to Dionysius "mystical theology is not argumentative." And Augustine says in his letter to Vincentius that "an allegory is not sufficient to prove anything unless its authority is otherwise clearly established." I could also say that by those two swords they understand, mystically, the Word of God in all its fullness, in line with the Apostle's words in Ephesians 6: "Take the breastplate of faith, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God." That the text speaks of two swords is said to refer to the New and the Old Testament; and by the two swords they understand the sword of the Word and the sword of impending persecution. Of the latter it is said in Luke 2 to the blessed Virgin, "a sword shall pierce through your own soul," and in 2 Samuel 12, "the sword shall not depart from your house"; and they said that these were then sufficient. Of these, one was the Apostles' passive sword, which they had to endure, namely the sword of persecution; the other was properly theirs, because it was to be drawn by them at the proper time, namely the sword of the Word of God. But even granting that by those two swords which the Apostles had are understood two powers, the spiritual and the temporal, although they are said to be there, it is not said that both belonged to Peter or to another Apostle. For Peter did not touch one of them, the secular, which was not his own; he did touch the other, the spiritual, which the Lord alone said was his own; and yet Peter was not to draw it at once, which is why it was said to him, "Put your sword into its sheath." For certainly the ecclesiastical judge ought not to use his spiritual sword at once, but only after great deliberation and in great necessity, lest it be despised. Granting, therefore, that those two mystical powers are understood by the two swords, it is in our favour: for although there were two, Peter had only one of his own. For this reason God also says in Matthew 10, "I came not to send peace, but a sword," where he says "a sword" in the singular, not "swords" significantly; and of Christ's person it is said in the Psalm, "Gird your sword upon your thigh," etc. And in Revelation 1 of the Son sitting in the midst of the candlesticks, and in 19 of him who is called the Word of God, it is said that "out of his mouth went a sharp sword, on both sides." Behold, then, that he has from Christ only one. Nevertheless it can be said that the two swords are said to have been there and to pertain to the Apostles: one is theirs by its own right, which they have from Christ, the other is theirs by fitness, because it is not opposed to them, and it was to be theirs by the commission and permission of princes. It can also be said that the quoted authority of Bernard is in our favour, since he says that "both are the Church's: the material sword is for the Church, the spiritual sword is to be wielded by the Church; the one by the hand of the priest, the other by the hand of the soldier, yet indeed at the nod of the priest and at the command of the Emperor," where he expressly says "at the nod of the priest," and not "by the hand" or "at the command" of the priest; because in this he does not have the authority to command or compel, but only to grant it, if the Emperor is willing.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: ADXXXI. quod arguit Iohannes de Cremona, respondeo: Quamuis multa iactet se dicturum, tamen absque dubio tam rudia sunt dicta sua, quod mihi non videntur repetitione digna: sed discurramus per singula. Quod ergo primo dicit, quod Dominus principio rexit mundum per semetipsum vsq; ad diluuiū, & postea per sacerdotes Noe, Abraham, Moysem, & alios huiusmodi: dico quod deficit multipliciter. Primo, quia supponit prædictos fuisse sacerdotes: q quidem de Noe falsum est manifeste, cum nec sacerdos fuerit, nec officium aliquod sacerdotis legatur fecisse, non obstante quod legatur quod erexit altare Domino: quia erigere altare Domino, vel orare, seu inuocare Dominum, non sunt actus proprii sacerdotum, cum etiam non sacerdotibus conueniant. Iacobi 5. Orate pro inuicem, vt saluemini. Et si etiam fuisset Noe sacerdos, non ideo dici potest quod mundum rexerit Deus per sacerdotem: quia non legitur Noe ædificasse altare Domino, nisi postquam ædificauerat & rexerat arcam. De Abraham vero & Moyse constat quod nō fuerunt sacerdotes veri, cum nullum sacrificium oblatum fuerit ante veram Christi hostiam, qui primus fuit verus sacerdos, vt supra capit. quarto. patuit: nec etiam fuerunt sacerdotes regales & singulares dignitate & officio, sicut Aaron, cum nondum essent inuncti: nec sacrificia adhuc erant instituta, licet in necessitate, & propter defectum sacerdotum, prædicti aliquos actus sacerdotum fecerint: vt quod Moyses innuxit Aaron, vel aliquid huiusmodi, propter quod Moyses sacerdos dicitur in Psalmo: Moyses & Aaron in sacerdotibus eius. Quod vero Abraham dicitur presbyter, non est ad propositum: quia, sicut dicitur distinct. 94. capit. 3. presbyter vocatur non tantum ætate, sed sapientia. Secundo deficit dicta ratio: quia dato quod fuissent sacerdotes, tamen erant à Deo constituti vt principes: & ideo in temporalibus regebant populum, non vt sacerdotes, sed vt principes. Nec oportet, quod si tunc potestates diuisæ erant simul indistincte in subiecto, quod ita nunc esse debeant in vno: quia hoc erat propter imperfectionem illius sacerdotii, quod tamen voluit Dominus postea magis & magis esse distinctum à potestate seculari, quanto magis accessit ad perfectum. Vnde temporibus regum & iudicum duæ potestates erant subiecto distinctæ, & multo magis nunc esse debent, vt supra dictum est Capitulo decimo.
units.tr: To the thirty-first point, which John of Cremona raises: although he boasts that he will say much, his statements are so crude that I do not think they deserve repetition. Still, let us go through them one by one. He first says that the Lord originally governed the world through himself until the flood, and afterwards through priests such as Noah, Abraham, Moses and others of that kind. I reply that this fails in several ways. First, it assumes that these men were priests. This is clearly false of Noah: he was never a priest, and no priestly office is recorded for him, even though it is written that he built an altar to the Lord. To build an altar to the Lord, or to pray and call upon the Lord, are not proper acts of priests, since these also belong to those who are not priests: Pray for one another, that you may be saved (James 5). Even if Noah had been a priest, it would not follow that God governed the world through a priest, for we do not read that Noah built an altar to the Lord until after he had built and governed the ark. As for Abraham and Moses, it is plain that they were not true priests, since no sacrifice was offered before the true sacrifice of Christ, who was the first true priest, as was shown above in chapter four. Nor were they priests in the royal and singular sense of dignity and office, like Aaron, since they had not yet been anointed. Sacrifices had not yet been instituted, although in necessity, and because of the lack of priests, these men performed some priestly acts, such as Moses anointing Aaron or something of that kind. For this reason Moses is called a priest in the Psalm: Moses and Aaron among his priests. As for the claim that Abraham is called an elder, this has nothing to do with the point, since, as is said in distinct. 94. chapter 3, a man is called an elder not only by age but by wisdom. Second, the argument fails because, even granting that they were priests, they had been appointed by God as rulers, and so they governed the people in temporal matters not as priests but as princes. Nor does it follow that, if the powers were then combined and undivided in one person, they must be so now in one person. That arrangement arose from the imperfection of that priesthood, which the Lord afterwards willed to be increasingly distinguished from the secular power, the more it approached perfection. Hence in the times of the kings and judges the two powers were distinct in their subjects, and they ought to be far more distinct now, as was said above in Chapter ten.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur tricesimo secundo, de habente dominium super finem, & super ea quæ sunt ad finem: patet quod argumentum nullum est, idem enim est modus arguendi, ac si diceretur: Iste est dominus omnium equorum, ergo & omnium frenorum qui fiunt propter equos: quod non sequitur, sicut cuilibet patet. Peccat etiam argumentum in materia, quia non est verum quod papa sit dominus spiritualiū, quia minister est tantū, 1. Cor. 2. Sic nos existimet homo, ut ministros Christi, & dispensatores, scilicet Ecclesiæ. Nō oportet autem, quod si spiritualium & temporalium unus est dominus, q eorū sit tantum unus minister: sed erunt plures, 1. Cor. 12. Diuisiones administrationum sunt, unus autē Dominus: & oēs diuisiones operationum sunt, idem autē Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. Adhæc etiā adaptari possunt rationes, ad argumentum de finibus datæ supra. Quod vero additur, q Deus animas Petro dedit, friuolum est, neque enim ei dedit ut esset dominus earū, sed instructor & defensor contra spirituales lupos. Unde Bernardus ad Eugenium: Domabis lupos, & non dominaberis ouibus. Et Petrus dicit: Non ut dominantes in clero, sed forma facti gregis ex animo. Quod vero subiungit de Apostolo dicente, Vestra sunt omnia: non est ad propositum, quia non loquitur Petro vel papæ singulariter, sed omnibus fidelibus, præcipue iustis: quorum sunt omnia, quantum ad aliquam utilitatem vel operationem in bonum, eo modo quo omnia sunt iustorum, 33. q. 6. cap. 1. vel ideo dicit, quia ut dicit Glo. super illud 1. Corinth. 12. Charitas non quærit quæ sua sunt, quærit omnia communia: ut quod aliquis non habet in se, habeat tamen in alio, cui unum est per charitatem.
units.tr: As for what is said in the thirty-second point, about one who has dominion over the end and over the things that are for the end: it is plain that the argument is no argument at all. The form of reasoning is the same as if one said: This man is lord of all horses, therefore he is lord of all the bridles that are made for horses. That does not follow, as anyone can see. The argument also errs in its subject matter, because it is not true that the pope is lord of spiritual things; he is only a minister, as in 1 Corinthians 4: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ and stewards, namely of the Church. But it does not follow that, if one person is lord of spiritual and temporal things, he must be the only minister of them; there will be several. 1 Corinthians 12: There are diversities of administrations, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who worketh all in all. Moreover, the arguments given above against the argument from ends can also be applied here. What is added, that God gave the souls to Peter, is trifling. He did not give him the souls so that he should be their lord, but so that he should be their teacher and defender against spiritual wolves. Hence Bernard says to Eugenius: You shall tame the wolves, and not lord it over the sheep. And Peter says: not as lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock from the heart. As for what is added about the Apostle saying, All things are yours, this is not to the point, because he is not speaking to Peter or the pope alone, but to all the faithful, especially the just, to whom all things belong, in so far as they are useful or serve for good, in the same way that all things belong to the just, 33. q. 6. chapter 1. Or he says this because, as the Gloss says on 1 Corinthians 12: Charity seeketh not her own, but seeketh all things in common: so that what one does not have in himself, he may still have in another, to whom it is one through charity.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur XXXIII. de peccato Imperatorum, quod propter peccata eorum translatum est ius imperii ad papam: respondeo, hoc totum ridiculosum est, primo, quia ut ostendit Aug. 4. de Ciuitate, regna & imperia vult Deus esse communia bonis & malis, felicitatem non nisi bonis: & ita non est de iure diuino, quod Imperatores propter peccata sua iure imperii priuentur. Secundo, quia non omnes Imperatores prædicta flagitia commiserunt, nec eorum peccata aliis obfuisse debucrunt: & præcipue quia in imperio non succedunt hæredes, sed ab exercitu vel populo rite eliguntur. Tertio etiam, quia aliqui papæ inuenti sunt flagitiosi & hæretici, & iuste depositi: nectamen malitia eorum obfuit aliis successoribus eorum vere & debite electis. Quarto, quia dato quod Imperator culpa sua priuetur iure suo, tamen nihil iuris ex culpa eius papæ in imperio accrescit. Nam ut dicit August. Homo peccando iuste diabolo subditur, non tamen iuste diabolus dominabitur eidem. Et præcipue tenet hoc in proposito, quia dominatio sacerdotibus interdicta est, ut supra patuit. Quinto, quia falsum est quod in fine argumenti insinuatur, sc. quod Imperatoribus debeatur ex priuilegio, hoc enim priuilegium Imperatoribus datum a clericis nusquam audiuimus: sed de iure eis debebatur imperium, populo seu exercitu faciente, ut d. 23. legimus: & Deo inspirante, quia a Deo est. 23. q. 4. quæsitum: & Commentator 8. Eth. c. 10. dicit, quod rex est a populi voluntate: sed cum est rex, quod dominetur est naturale.
units.tr: As for what is said in the thirty-third point, about the sin of the emperors, that because of their sins the right of empire was transferred to the pope, I reply: all of this is ridiculous. First, as Augustine shows in book 4 of The City of God, God wills that kingdoms and empires be common to the good and the bad, and happiness only to the good. So it is not by divine right that emperors are deprived of their imperial right because of their sins. Second, not all emperors committed the crimes mentioned, and their sins ought not to have harmed others, especially since in the empire heirs do not succeed, but are duly chosen by the army or the people. Third, some popes have also been found to be wicked and heretical and were justly deposed, yet their wickedness did not harm their successors, who were truly and duly elected. Fourth, even granting that an emperor is deprived of his right by his own fault, nothing of right in the empire accrues to the pope from the fault of the emperor. For, as Augustine says: A man who sins is justly made subject to the devil, yet the devil will not justly rule over him. This holds especially in the present matter, because dominion is forbidden to priests, as was shown above. Fifth, it is false what is hinted at the end of the argument, namely that the emperors owe the empire by privilege. We have never heard of such a privilege granted to emperors by the clergy. Rather, the empire was owed to them by right, the people or the army making them emperor, as we read in distinction 23, and inspired by God, because it is from God, as is asked in 23. q. 4. And the Commentator, Ethics 8, chapter 10, says that a king is from the will of the people; but once he is king, that he should rule is natural.

units.la: Quod XXXIV. dicitur de maiori potestate quam habet nunc ecclesia, quam haberet in principio respondeo, quantum ad hoc quod argumentum innititur allegoriæ: patet quod nullius est efficacia, quia ut dicit August. in Epistola ad Vincentium: Allegoria non sufficit ad probationem, nisi cum de hoc habeatur auctoritas manifesta. Et ideo dicit, quod mystica theologia non est argumentatiua. Amplius super illud Luc. 14. de parabola conuiuii: & Psalmus, Quare fremuerunt gentes, &c. magis videtur secundum moralem sensum accipi Christi persecutio, quam nunc sustinet in membris suis a malis, & eius dominatores in membris suis in futuro, quando in cœlo omnia ei subiecta erunt, secundum Apost. Heb. 2. quam illud quod isti accipiunt. Si tamen totum accipiatur pro statu militantis Ecclesiæ ad diuersa tempora, ut isti accipiunt, adhuc non est pro eis: quia sicut dicit Aug. de Ver. do. non loquitur Dominus quasi nunc possit Ecclesia compellere Iudeos & gentiles ad fidem: vel quod nunc non fit Ecclesia subiecta in temporalib. regibus & principib. de iure, sicut olim: sed loquitur de hæreticis, qui per sepes intelliguntur. Nam qui sepes construunt, diuisiones quærunt, ii enim de iure sunt ab ecclesia compellendi redire. Sed hoc non faciebat Ecclesia in principio propter defectum potentiæ, eo quod reges & principes non ficerant fauorabiles Ecclesiæ, sicut nunc sunt: & ideo cum fauore principum non possunt. Et sic tractatur ista materia 24. q. & 6.
units.tr: As for what is said in the thirty-fourth point, about the greater power that the Church now has than it had in the beginning, I reply, so far as the argument rests on allegory: it is plain that it has no force at all, because, as Augustine says in his letter to Vincentius: Allegory is not sufficient for proof, unless there is clear authority for it on this point. Hence he also says that mystical theology is not argumentative. Moreover, on the parable of the feast in Luke 14, and on the Psalm, Why do the nations rage, etc., the persecution of Christ, which he now suffers in his members from the wicked, and the rule of his enemies over his members in the future, when all things shall be subjected to him in heaven, according to the Apostle in Hebrews 2, seems to be understood in a moral sense more than what these men take it to mean. Yet even if the whole passage is taken, as they take it, to refer to the state of the militant Church at different times, it still does not apply to their case. As Augustine says in his On True Religion: the Lord does not speak as though the Church could now compel Jews and Gentiles to the faith, or as though the Church were not now subject, by right, to temporal kings and princes, as it was formerly; rather he speaks of heretics, who are understood by the hedges. For those who build hedges seek divisions, and they are by right to be compelled by the Church to return. But the Church did not do this at the beginning, on account of its lack of power, because the kings and princes were not yet favourable to the Church as they now are; and therefore, without the favour of princes, it cannot do so. And this matter is treated thus in 24. q. 6.

units.la: Quod vero obiicitur XXXV. de regis permissione, & Dei indignatione: respondeo, Argumentū deficit, Dominus enim cum sacerdotio vel ante instituit regē in populo illo, licet non cum plena potestate: ut patet in Moyse & Iosue, & successoribus eorum, qui toti illi populo præerant. Unde dicebat Moyses Num. 27. Prouideat Dominus spiritum omnis carnis hominem, qui sit super multitudinem hanc. Et de singulis iudicibus, qui post Iosue fuerunt, legitur quod Deus suscitauit saluatorem, & quod spiritus Dei erat in illis: ut patet Iudic. 2. Erant igitur a Deo instituti, & non iudicio Iudæorum commissi: & erant reges alio modo, in quantum toti populo illi præerant singulariter, vel specialiter, quod est species regni: non erant tantum regimen regium purum, eo quod commiscebatur aristocratiæ, in qua plures dominantur secundum virtutem: & democratiæ, id est principatui populi videbitur, cum etiam postea ad eorum petitionem eis dedit habere regem cum plenitudine potestatis. Adhuc electionem eis non commisit, sed reseruauit: ut patet Deutero. 17. vbi dicitur: Constitues regem, quem Dominus Deus elegerit. Non est etiam contra regiam dignitatem, quod ad petitionem eorum, quasi indignatus, regem concessit, 1. Reg. 7. quia similiter argui posset de sacerdote: quia cum Moyses Domino diceret Exod. 4. Obsecro Domine, mitte quem missurus es: Dominus iratus in Moysem ait: Aaron frater tuus Leuites scit quod eloquens sit, ipse erit tibi in occursum, &c. Sed quare ergo indignatus concessit eis regem? Dicendum, quod non ideo, quia regale regimen ei displiceret simpliciter ut malum: sed ideo, quia illum populum sibi elegerat ut peculiarem, Deuteron. Deutero. 6. & instruxerat eis regimen melius puro regali, saltem illi populo propter duo. Primum est, quia licet regimen regium, in quo vnus simpliciter principatur secundum virtutem, sit melius quolibet alio regimine simplici, vt ostendit Philosophus in 3. Politicorum: tamen si fiat mixtum cum aristocratia & democratia, melius est puro, in quantum in regimine mixto omnes aliquam partem habent in principatu. Per hoc enim seruatur pax populi, & omnes talem dominationem amant & custodiunt, vt dicitur in 2. Politicorum, & tale erat regimen a Deo optime institutum in populo: quia erat regale, in quantum vnus praerat simpliciter omnibus singulariter, vt Moyses vel Iosue. Erat etiam aliquis de aristocratia, qui est principatus aliquorum optimorum principantium secundum virtutem, in quantum sub illo viro eligebantur 72. seniores: Deutero. 5. Erant etiam ibi aliqui de democratia, i. principatu populi, in quantum 72. eligebantur a populo, & de toto populo, vt dicitur ibidem: & sic erat optime mixtum, in quantum omni in regimine illo aliquid habebat, siue aliquam partem. Et sic certe esset optimum regimen Ecclesiae, si sub vno papa eligerentur plures ab omni provincia, & de omni provincia, vt sic in regimine ecclesiae omnes haberent partem suam. Aliud etiam erat, propter quod tale regimen erat melius illi populo, quam purum regale: quia licet regimen regale sit optimum in se, si non corrumpatur, cum propter magnam potestatem, quae regi conceditur, de facili regnum degeneret in tyrannidem, nisi sit perfecta virtus eius cui talis potestas conceditur. Nam, vt dicitur decimo Ethicorum, Viri virtuosi est beneferre bonas fortunas. Haec autem perfecta virtus in paucis reperitur, & praecipue in populo illo, eo quod Iudaei crudeles essent, & ad auaritiam proni, per quae vitia maxime deceditur in tyrannidem. Et ideo Dominus a principio non instituit eis regem cum tanta plenitudine potestatis, sed iudicem & gubernatorem in eorum custodiam modo praedicto: quia sic eis magis competebat. Et ideo, postea ad petitionem eorum regem instituit, quasi indignatus: quia scilicet regimen aliud aliquod eis vtilius abiiciebant. Quod autem in eodem argumento subiungitur de regibus, Osee 8. Regnauerunt, & non ex me: non est ad propositum, quia loquitur de malis praelatis Ecclesiasticis: Qui non intrant per ostium in ouile ouium, vel qui abutuntur accepta auctoritate. Et amplius dici posset, quod dicta auctoritas pro nobis est: quia Bernardus ad Eugenium lib. 2. eam exponit de papa & praelatis Ecclesiasticis, quaerentib. dominatum, dicens: Planum est, Apostolis interdicitur dominatus: ergo tu tibi audes vsurpare aut apostolatus dominatum, aut dominatus apostolatum? plane ab vtroq;, vel ab altero prohiberis, alioquin non te exemptum putes illorum numero, de quibus Dominus conqueritur, sic dicens: Ipsi regnauerunt, & non ex me: principes extiterunt, & non cognoui eos.
units.tr: As for the objection drawn from the XXXV. (question), concerning the king's permission and God's indignation, I answer that the argument fails. The Lord instituted a king over that people together with the priesthood, or before it, though not with full power, as is clear in Moses and Joshua and their successors, who presided over the whole people. Hence Moses said in Num. 27: May the Lord provide a man over the congregation, who may be over this multitude, the spirit of all flesh. And concerning the individual judges who came after Joshua, we read that God raised up a saviour and that the Spirit of God was in them, as is clear from Judg. 2. They were therefore appointed by God and not entrusted to the judgment of the Jews. They were kings in a different way, insofar as they stood singly or specially over that whole people, which is a kind of kingship. Their rule was not pure monarchy, because it was mixed with aristocracy, in which several rule according to virtue, and with democracy, that is, the rule of the people. Afterwards, at their request, he did give them a king with full power. Still, he did not commit the choosing to them but reserved it to himself, as is clear from Deut. 17, where it is said: You shall appoint a king whom the Lord your God shall choose. Nor is it against the dignity of kingship that, at their request, he granted them a king as though in indignation, 1 Sam. 8, for the same could be argued about the priest. When Moses said to the Lord in Exod. 4, Please, Lord, send whom you will send, the Lord, angry with Moses, said: Aaron your brother the Levite knows that he is eloquent; he will come to meet you, and so on. But why then did he, in indignation, grant them a king? The answer is that this was not because kingly rule was simply displeasing to him as evil, but because he had chosen that people as his own special people, Deut. 6., and had ordered for them a form of government better than pure kingship, at least for that people, for two reasons. The first is this: although kingly rule, in which one man rules simply according to virtue, is better than any other simple form of government, as the Philosopher shows in Politics 3, yet if it is mixed with aristocracy and democracy it is better than the pure form, insofar as in a mixed government all have some share in rule. For by this the peace of the people is preserved, and all love and guard such a dominion, as is said in Politics 2. Such was the government God best instituted among that people: it was kingly, insofar as one man, such as Moses or Joshua, stood singly over all as their ruler; it also had an aristocratic element, which is the rule of some best men ruling according to virtue, insofar as under that man seventy-two elders were chosen (Deut. 5); and there were also elements of democracy, that is, rule by the people, insofar as the seventy-two were chosen by the people and from the whole people, as is said in the same place. And so it was best mixed, since in that government every part had some share. And certainly this would be the best government of the Church, if under one pope several were chosen from every province and from every province, so that in the government of the Church all had their share. There was also another reason why such a government was better for that people than pure kingship. Although kingly rule is in itself the best, provided it is not corrupted, yet because of the great power granted to the king, a kingdom easily degenerates into tyranny unless the one to whom such power is granted has perfect virtue. For, as is said in the tenth book of the Ethics, it belongs to a virtuous man to bear good fortune well. Now such perfect virtue is found in few, and especially not in that people, since the Jews were cruel and prone to avarice, and by these vices above all one slides into tyranny. Therefore the Lord did not at the beginning appoint for them a king with such full power, but a judge and governor to keep them in the manner described above, since this suited them better. Afterwards, therefore, at their request, he instituted a king, as though in indignation, because they were rejecting some other form of government more useful to them. As for what is added in the same argument about kings, from Hosea 8: They have reigned, but not by me, this does not bear on the point, for it speaks of bad ecclesiastical prelates, who do not enter by the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, or who abuse the authority they have received. And it could further be said that this authority is on our side, for Bernard, writing to Eugenius, book 2, expounds it of the pope and ecclesiastical prelates who seek dominion, saying: It is plain that dominion is forbidden to the Apostles. Do you then dare to usurp either the dominion of the apostleship or the apostleship of dominion? Clearly you are forbidden either the one or the other; otherwise do not think yourself exempt from the number of those of whom the Lord complains, saying thus: They have reigned, but not by me; they have become princes, but I did not know them.

units.la: Quod vero XXXVI. dicitur de terra sacerdotis, quae sub Pharaone libera erat a tributo & censu: dicendum est, quod per hoc denunciabatur, sacerdotes debere esse liberos, quoad onera principalia, & quoad mansionem siue mansum Ecclesiae, & quoad ea quae eis donantur vt sacerdotes sunt, & ministri Dei pro redemptione animarum: & non quoad ea quae titulo emptionis vel aliter acquiruntur Ecclesiae, quae cum onere suo transeunt ad eos, vt notatur 33. q. vltim. tributum. & alio ca. secundum Canonicam: & hoc est ecclesiis indultum ab Imperatoribus & principibus, vt ibidem dicitur.
units.tr: As for what is said in the XXXVI. (question), concerning the priests' land, which under Pharaoh was free from tribute and tax, it must be answered that by this it was signified that priests ought to be free as regards the principal burdens, and as regards the dwelling or manse of the Church, and as regards those things which are given to them as priests and ministers of God for the redemption of souls. It was not signified as regards those things which the Church acquires by title of purchase or otherwise, which pass to them together with their burden, as is noted in 33. q. ult., tributum, and in the other chapter, Secundum canonicam. This was granted to the churches by the emperors and princes, as is said in the same place.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI.

units.la: Quod autem XXXVII. opponitur de episcopis vocatis a papa, qui remanserunt de mandato Imperatoris, & super hoc reprehenduntur a papa: dicendum, quod sicut notauit Iohannes ibidem, & infra, eadem q. quo supra, istud intelligitur de illis tantum episcopis qui Leuitica portione sunt contenti: de aliis autem regalia tenentibus, vel possessiones alias, cum talia transeant cum suo onere, non intelligitur, imo tales dominis suis obedire tenentur, sicut caeteri, & hanc distinctionem ponit expresse capitulum sequens. Sed notandum, quod hoc etiam videtur persimile, quod monachus transitus ad episcopatum, magis subiectus est archiepiscopo, quam abbati suo, & ei plus debet obedire. Similiter monachus transiens ad curam parrochiae alicuius, in iis quae ad curam illius parrochiae pertinent, magis obedire tenentur episcopo illius loci, quam abbati: & potest episcopus ipsum visitare & corrigere. Sic episcopus accipiens feudalia, praecipue sciente & permittente summo pontifice, magis tenetur obedire temporali domino, quam summo pontifici: imo in casu vbi iam praecipit ei princeps aliquid de pertinentibus ad onera feudorum, videtur exemptus a papa, sicut monachus ab abbate. Ita etiam determinat Hugo de sancto Victore, de sacramen. parte 2. c. 7. dicens, quod principes donantes ecclesiam non possunt in ipsam totaliter transferre dominium sic, quod nihil de dominio retineant, cuius verba sunt haec: Potest ecclesia ministros habere laicas parrochias, per quas iura & iudicia ad terrenam potestatem pertinentia, secundum tenorem legum, & debitum iuris humani exerceat: qui, si ratio postulauerit, & necessitas, & illis ipsa potestas debeat patrocinium, & illi ipsae possessiones debeant in necessitate obsequium. Sicut enim potestas regia patrocinium quod debet alteri, non potest dare: sic ipsa possessio etiam ab Ecclesiastica persona obtenta, obsequium quod regia potestati pro patrocinio debetur, iure negare non potest, sicut scriptum est: Reddite quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari: & quae sunt Dei, Deo. Sed forte dicetur, quod sunt aliqui qui merentur isto iure priuari, quia impediunt spirituale donum, sc. impediendo ne episcopi vadant ad cariam, quando illi sunt vocati pro aliquo negocio spirituali: vel quando oportet eos vel alios ibi ire pro dispensatione super irregularitate, vel pro alia causa huiusmodi, constat enim quod impedire huiusmodi transitum, est impedire bonum spirituale. Amplius, per tales arctationes passuum, & tales leges ne aliqui portent extra regnum pecunias, infertur damnum curiae Romanae: & sic potest papa conqueri legitime, & talia prohibere, & reputare principem talem hostem suum, qui talia facit. Responsio, prohibere simpliciter, & vniuersaliter impedire, ne quacunq; ex causa aliquis transeat, esset impedire spirituale bonum in casu. Sed si prohibeatur cum exceptione, sc. nisi ex causa rationabili & licentia principis, qui causam audiat, non est impedire bonum spirituale. Si etiam per tales attestationes damnificetur curia Romana, quia non accipit consueta seruitia: non ideo debet reputari princeps iniuste agere, & nocere ecclesiae, nisi faciat sola intentione nocendi: quia si faciat hoc pro suo, vel terrae suae commodo, licet inde per consequentiam damnum aliis contingat, sibi est licitum: quia cuilibet licitum est uti iure suo. Argumentum habetur ad hoc: aliquis habet fontem orientem in fundo suo, qui diuersos per riuos rigat hortos vicinorum suorum, iste facit aquam descendere vel currere per diversa loca domus suae, & sic impeditur ne currat ad hortos vicinorum, nunquid hoc est ei licitum? Dicit lex quod sic: licet aliis incommodum euenial, quia utitur iure suo. Esto etiam, quod faciat hoc princeps intentione nocendi, adhuc in casu est ei licitum, sc. si praesentibus probabilib. vel euidentibus argumentis appareat, quod papa ad hoc vocaret praelatos, vt cum ipsis aliquid machinari intenderet contra ipsum, vel contra regnum suum. Est enim licitum principi, abusum gladii spiritualis repellere, eo modo quo potest, etiam per gladium materialem: praecipue vbi abusus gladii spiritualis vergit in malum Reipublicae, cuius cura regi incumbit, aliter enim sine causa gladium portaret.
units.tr: As for what is objected at XXXVII. concerning bishops called by the pope who remained by the emperor's command and were rebuked for it by the pope: it must be said, as John noted in the same place and below, eadem q. quo supra, that this applies only to those bishops who are content with the Levitical portion. It does not apply to those who hold regalia or other possessions, since such things pass together with their burdens. Such bishops are bound to obey their lords like the rest, and the following chapter expressly makes this distinction. But it should be noted that this is also very similar to the case of a monk who passes to a bishopric: he is more subject to the archbishop than to his abbot and owes more obedience to him. Likewise, a monk who passes to the care of some parish is bound, in those matters which pertain to the care of that parish, to obey the bishop of that place rather than his abbot, and the bishop can visit and correct him. So too a bishop who receives feudal holdings, especially with the knowledge and permission of the supreme pontiff, is bound to obey the temporal lord more than the supreme pontiff. Indeed, where the prince already commands him something concerning the burdens of the fiefs, he seems exempt from the pope, as a monk is from his abbot. Hugh of St Victor also determines this, de sacramen. parte 2. c. 7., saying that princes who grant a church cannot transfer the dominion over it entirely, so that they retain nothing of the dominion. His words are these: "The church may have ministers in lay parishes, through whom it may exercise rights and judgments that pertain to earthly power, according to the terms of the laws and the due claim of human right. If reason and necessity require it, that power ought to give protection to them, and those possessions ought to give service in time of need. For just as royal power cannot give the protection it owes to another, so a possession obtained even by an ecclesiastical person cannot by right deny the service owed to royal power in return for protection, as it is written: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." But perhaps it will be said that there are some who deserve to be deprived of this right, because they hinder a spiritual good: namely, by preventing bishops from going to Rome when they have been called for some spiritual business, or when it is necessary for them or others to go there for a dispensation concerning irregularity or some other cause of this kind. For it is clear that to hinder such a journey is to hinder a spiritual good. Moreover, by such restrictions of passage and such laws forbidding anyone to carry money out of the kingdom, loss is inflicted on the Roman curia; and so the pope may lawfully complain and forbid such things, and regard a prince who does them as his enemy. Answer: to forbid absolutely and universally that anyone should pass for any reason would in such a case be to hinder a spiritual good. But if the prohibition is made with an exception, namely unless there is a reasonable cause and the prince's licence, the prince hearing the cause, it is not hindering a spiritual good. Likewise, if the Roman curia is harmed by such restrictions because it does not receive its customary services, the prince ought not therefore to be regarded as acting unjustly and harming the Church, unless he acts from the sole intention of harming it. For if he does this for his own or his land's advantage, then, even though harm to others follows as a consequence, it is lawful for him, because it is lawful for anyone to use his own right. An argument for this: someone has a spring rising in his own ground, which waters the gardens of his neighbours by various channels; if he makes the water flow or run through different parts of his house, so that it does not reach his neighbours' gardens, is this lawful for him? The law says that it is, even though inconvenience comes to others, because he is using his own right. Grant also that the prince acts with the intention of harming; even then it is lawful for him in the case where it appears from probable or evident arguments that the pope summoned the prelates for this purpose, to contrive something against him or against his kingdom. For it is lawful for a prince to repel the abuse of the spiritual sword in the way he can, even by the material sword, especially where the abuse of the spiritual sword tends to the harm of the commonwealth, whose care lies upon the king; otherwise he would bear the sword in vain.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur XXXVIII. de collatione beneficiorum: dicendum, quod collatio ista competere potest laico ex consuetudine, sicut praesentatio de iure scripto, nam non plus repugnat laico vnum, quam aliud, & potest competere de iure patronatus, si hoc fuerit in consuetudine habitum, vel concessum ab ecclesiis. Sicut enim dicitur 8. Ethicorum: Benefacienti, etsi non ex debito iustitiae, ex quo actiones nascuntur inter homines: tamen ex debito honestatis debetur super abundanti honor, indigenti vero retributio lucri, & inde est, quod fundatoribus ecclesiarum, & patronis ratione beneficii accepti, ecclesiae a principio a debito iustitiae non erant obligatae: tamen ex debito honestatis eis voluerunt concedere aliquid honoris, & aliquid vtilitatis. Honoris quidem, praesentando ad beneficia, quod inuenit vt concessum patronis in iure scripto expresse & generaliter, tamen quibusdam excellentioribus patronis, vt magis foueretur eorum devotio ad ecclesias fundandas, est per dissimulationem concessum rationabiliter: & quia illud quod rationabiliter est concessum, licet ex gratia, & non ex debito iustitiae, in longam & praescriptam consuetudinem tractum conuertitur in ius commune, eo quod (vt dicit Plato in Timaeo) Quod semel rationabiliter est institutum, non est diuina voluntatis immutari debere. Ideo dicta praesentatio ad beneficia Ecclesiastica omnibus patronis debetur generaliter: & collatio quibusdam excellentibus, qui hoc ex consuetudine habuerunt, debetur specialiter, & de iure, vt eis auferri non possit sine iniuria: imo si quis auferre vellet eis sine causa euidenti & rationabili, indubitanter non posset, sed semper teneret patroni collatio, quicquid ageretur contra hoc a quocunque. Nam vt dictum est supra, Deus non dedit potestatem Petro vel ministris Ecclesiasticis in bonis ecclesiae, ad ordinandum pro libito: sed pro bona fide, & ad aedificationem, & non ad destructionem, vt dicitur 1. Corinth. Deus enim non vult, quod rite alicui est collatum, ei auferri, nisi culpa intercedente, nam secundum Apostolum Rom. 11. Sine poenitentia sunt dona Dei, & Iob 33. dicitur: Non aufert a viro iusto oculos suos, & reges in solio suo constituit in sempiternum, propter peccata enim fecit vasa Aegyptiorum spolia Hebraeorum. Et ideo ex quo fuit principio patronis concessum expresse vel interpretatiue per longam dissimulationem, & ex causa rationabili: quia ex debito quo benefacienti excellenti honor debetur, etiam vt potentes proniores efficerentur ad dotandas ecclesias, non est dubium, non esse proprie a Christo commissum quod talia reuocari possint sine euidenti & magna culpa: super quam princeps monitus, inueniretur incorrigibilis, & praecipue cum ex hoc ecclesiae sumpserunt magnum emolumentum. Quod ergo arguitur, quod collatio non cadit in laicum, cum sit idem quod spirituale: respondeo, dicendum quod spirituale non dicitur proprie, nisi in habitudine ad spiritum diuinum, per causalitatem, seu per concomitantiam: vnde sacramenta Ecclesiastica sic spiritualia sunt, vt administratio sacramentorum: quia gratiam spiritualem contingunt & causant: spirituali vero annexum dicitur, quod habet ordinem ad dictum spirituale, vel per consequentiam, vt ius decimarum: vel per antecedentiam, vt ius patronatus, & collatio praebendarum. Primum ergo quod est spirituale, proprie non cadit in laicum aliquo modo, nec secundum quod est annexum ei per consequentiam, quia tale dependet ex spirituali officio. Nam ratione spiritualium officiorum competit alicui ius decimarum, & ideo sicut spirituale officium non competit laico: ita nec ius praedictum, licet fructus corporales qui nomine decimarum appellantur, laico competere possunt de concessione ecclesiae. Sed tertium quod annexum est spiritualibus officiis per antecedentiam, vt praesentatio, vel collatio, seu ius conferendi, quia non sic dependet a spirituali, sed conuerso potest competere laico praecipue, & ex concessione ecclesiae, vel ex promissione, & ex longa consuetudine scripta, potest rex sibi ius acquirere, cum sibi non repugnet: quia si ei repugnaret, et non posset conuenire ex concessione cuiuscunque, sicut nec administratio sacramentorum, vel ius decimarum potest competere laico auctoritate cuiuscunque: nec sit onerosa ecclesiis, sed interdum fructuosa, & praecipue ecclesia sciente & permittente. Quod autem dicitur, quod dos non debet esse onerosa: respondeo, ex hoc non fit onerosa, nisi patrono, cui incumbit onus defensionis ecclesiae: nunc vero non est onerosa, cum plus ex hoc habeat commodi, quam incommodi. Et quod dicitur, quod consuetudo non praeiudicat iuri: respondeo, Dicta consuetudo cum non sit damnosa in ministris ecclesiae, sed in plurib. fructuosa, non praeiudicat iuri publico in genere, licet videatur praeiudicare in specie. Nam licet videatur praeiudicare episcopis
units.tr: As for what is said at XXXVIII. concerning the conferring of benefices: it must be said that this conferring can belong to a layman by custom, just as presentation belongs to him by written law. For it is no more repugnant to a layman to have the one than the other, and it can belong to him by right of patronage if this has been customary or granted by the churches. As it is said in the eighth book of the Ethics: To one who does a benefit, even if not by a debt of justice, from which actions arise between men, yet by a debt of honour, honour is owed in abundance, and to one in need a return of gain. Hence it is that founders of churches and patrons, by reason of the benefit they conferred, were not at the beginning bound to the churches by a debt of justice; yet by a debt of honour the churches chose to grant them some honour and some advantage. The honour consisted in presenting to benefices, which is found expressly and generally granted to patrons in written law; yet to some more eminent patrons, so that their devotion to founding churches might be the more encouraged, the conferring was reasonably granted by tacit allowance. And because what has been reasonably granted, though from favour and not from a debt of justice, when drawn into a long and prescribed custom, is turned into common law, since (as Plato says in the Timaeus) what has once been reasonably instituted ought not to be changed by the divine will. Therefore the said presentation to ecclesiastical benefices is owed generally to all patrons, and conferring is owed specially and by right to certain eminent men who have had it by custom, so that it cannot be taken from them without injury. Indeed, if anyone wished to take it from them without an evident and reasonable cause, he could not do so beyond doubt, but the patron's conferring would always hold good, whatever anyone might do against it. For, as was said above, God did not give Peter or the ecclesiastical ministers power over the goods of the church to order them at pleasure, but for good faith and for building up, and not for destruction, as it is said in 1 Corinthians. For God does not wish that what has been rightly conferred on someone be taken from him, unless fault intervenes; for according to the Apostle, Rom. 11, the gifts of God are without repentance, and Job 33 says: He does not take away his eyes from the righteous man, but sets kings on the throne for ever; for on account of sins he made the vessels of the Egyptians the spoils of the Hebrews. Therefore, since from the beginning the patrons had this granted to them expressly or by interpretation through long tacit allowance, and for a reasonable cause, it is beyond doubt that it was not properly committed by Christ that such things could be revoked without evident and great fault. If the prince were warned about this fault and found incorrigible, it would be otherwise; and especially since the churches have derived great advantage from it. As for the argument that conferring does not fall to a layman because it is the same as the spiritual: I answer that the spiritual is not properly so called except in relation to the divine Spirit, by causality or by concomitance. Hence ecclesiastical sacraments are spiritual in that the administration of the sacraments touches and causes spiritual grace. But what is annexed to the spiritual is said to have an order towards that spiritual thing, either by consequence, as the right of tithes, or by antecedence, as the right of patronage and the conferring of prebends. The first, therefore, which is spiritual, does not properly fall to a layman in any way, nor does what is annexed to it by consequence, since that depends on the spiritual office. For by reason of spiritual offices a right of tithes belongs to someone, and so, just as the spiritual office does not belong to a layman, neither does that right; although the bodily fruits called tithes can belong to a layman by grant of the church. But the third, what is annexed to spiritual offices by antecedence, such as presentation, or conferring, or the right of conferring, since this does not depend on the spiritual in this way, but conversely can belong to a layman, especially by grant of the church, or by promise, or by long written custom, a king can acquire the right for himself, since it is not repugnant to him. For if it were repugnant to him, it could not belong to him by anyone's grant, just as neither the administration of the sacraments nor the right of tithes can belong to a layman by anyone's authority; nor is it burdensome to the churches, but sometimes profitable, especially with the knowledge and permission of the church. As for the claim that a dowry ought not to be burdensome: I answer that it is not made burdensome by this, except to the patron, on whom the burden of defending the church falls; but in fact it is not burdensome, since he gains more advantage from it than disadvantage. And as for the claim that custom does not prejudice right: I answer that this custom, since it is not harmful to the ministers of the church but in many cases profitable, does not prejudice public right in general, although in particular it may seem to prejudice the bishops, who are deprived of the conferring of benefices which by common law is owed to them. Yet the churches derive from this a greater advantage, by reason of defence, donation and foundation, and so it does not prejudice absolutely.

units.la: {y} scopis, qui priuantur collatione beneficiorum, quae de iure communi eis debetur: tamen ecclesiae aliunde ex hoc emolumentum accipiunt praeponderans, ratione defensionis & donationis & fundationis, & ideo non praeiudicat simpliciter. Vel ut dicit Philosophus 8. Ethicorum, hoc facimus, quod per amicos facimus: & ideo Ecclesiasticus conferre dicitur, licet non per se, sed per patronum laicum, cui ab eo concessum est rationabiliter: quae concessio non est revocabilis, nisi sicut dixi. Et quod opponitur de consuetudine contraria substantiae contractus, & inhonesta: respondeo, Dicitur quod hic nullus est contractus, nec conditio, quia patroni non dant sub conditione vel modo, sed simpliciter, licet obligatio sequatur collationem iam factam: nec est hic aliquid inhonestum, cum per violentiam non sit ab ecclesiis extortum, sed ab ecclesia sit patronis liberaliter concessum, licet ex debito honestatis, quo cuiusque beneficio excellenti debetur honor, & indigenti retributio lucri, ut dicitur 8. Ethicorum. Si etiam esset contraria substantiae contractus, vel doni, ut dicit argumentum, non ideo sequitur intentum, quod sic pro nunc non adiecta habeatur, & quod donum non manet. Hoc enim convenit in conditione inhonesta, quae non est contraria substantiae contractui: ut, contraho tecum, si occideris hominem. Sed ubi est conditio opposita contraria substantiae doni, donum vel contractus non tenet: ut si dicatur, Contraho tecum, si venenum aut sterilitatem procures, vel aliud huiusmodi: & ideo secundum illud donatio facta ecclesiis non teneret, sed rediret totum ad donatores. Quod vero dicitur, quod ecclesia gaudeat iure minorum, & reputat se deceptam: respondeo, Non sufficit ad restitutionem, quod sit minor, nisi ostendat se laesum. Hoc certe ecclesia facere non posset, cum appareat evidenter, quod ex dicta promissione facta est locupletior. Amplius, secundum magnos iuristas, Ecclesia ponitur in ultimo momento 25. annorum a tempore laesionis facta, ut sic infra quadriennium, quod vocatur tempus utile, tantum restituatur, & non ultra, nisi fraus probetur intervenisse. Alii vero dicunt, quod restituenda sit usque ad 15. annos, ponentes eam in anno 14. Alii autem usque ad 30. ponentes eam in primo die minoris. Amplius, dicit Goffredus, quod ecclesia a minore differt in hoc, quod ecclesia praescribit, & praescribitur contra eam: sed minor semper servatur illaesus, praeterquam in longissima praescriptione, quae quidem contra minorem currit, sed restituitur: contra ecclesiam vero erit praescriptio 40. annorum, nec est restituenda.
units.tr: Bishops, who are deprived of the conferring of benefices that is owed to them by common law: yet the churches gain from this a greater advantage elsewhere, by reason of defence, donation and foundation, and so it does not prejudice the matter absolutely. Or, as the Philosopher says in Ethics 8, we do through friends what we do ourselves; and so the ecclesiastic is said to confer, though not in person but through a lay patron, to whom the right has been reasonably granted by him. That grant cannot be revoked, except as I have said. As to the objection that a custom contrary to the substance of a contract is dishonourable: I answer that here there is no contract and no condition, because patrons do not give under a condition or mode but simply, although the obligation follows the collation already made. Nor is there anything dishonourable here, since it has not been extorted from the churches by violence but has been liberally granted to the patrons by the church, out of the debt of honesty by which honour is owed to one who confers an excellent benefit, and a return of gain to one in need, as is said in Ethics 8. Even if it were contrary to the substance of a contract or of a gift, as the argument says, the conclusion does not follow, namely that the thing would be held as if no addition had been made for the present, and that the gift would not stand. For this holds in a dishonourable condition, which is not contrary to the substance of a contract: for example, "I contract with you, if you kill a man." But where the condition is contrary to the substance of a gift, the gift or contract does not hold: as if it were said, "I contract with you, if you procure poison or sterility, or something of the kind"; and so, according to that principle, a donation made to churches would not stand, but everything would return to the donors. As to the claim that the church enjoys the privilege of minors and regards itself as deceived: I answer that it is not enough for restitution that it is a minor, unless it shows that it has been harmed. The church certainly could not do this, since it is evident that it has been made richer by the said promise. Further, according to the great jurists, the church is placed at the last moment of twenty-five years from the time of the injury, so that it is restored only within the four years, which is called the useful time, and not beyond, unless fraud is proved to have intervened. Others, however, say that it is to be restored up to fifteen years, placing it in the fourteenth year. Others again say up to thirty years, placing it on the first day of minority. Further, Goffredus says that "the church differs from a minor in this: that the church prescribes, and is prescribed against; but a minor is always kept unharmed, except in the very long prescription, which indeed runs against a minor, but he is restored; against the church, however, there will be a prescription of forty years, and it is not to be restored."

units.la: Quod autem dicitur tricesimo nono, quod Papa debet esse perfectus in vita activa: respondeo, Ex hoc solum sibi convenit de rebus suis, & non de rebus alienis: & praedicare aliis, res eorum esse distribuendas, secundum quod exigit ordo charitatis.
units.tr: As to what is said in the thirty-ninth objection, that the Pope must be perfect in the active life: I answer that this belongs to him only in respect of his own things, and not of others' things; and to preach to others that their things are to be distributed, as the order of charity requires.

units.la: Quod XL. opponitur de clericis, qui magis pollent ratione: respondeo, Si sic est, non ideo praecipue debent regere in omnibus, sed in maioribus & in melioribus, scilicet in spiritualibus.
units.tr: As to the fortieth objection, about clerics who excel in reason: I answer that if this is so, they ought not for that reason chiefly to rule in all things, but in the greater and better matters, namely in spiritual ones.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur XLI quod aliter loquentes loquuntur in favorem principum: respondeo, Quamvis in casu aliquo veritas sit subticenda, sicut Moyses reticuit veritatem de repudio uxoris, Matth.19. tamen nulli licitum est in casu quocunque, contra conscientiam docere, vel scribere in doctrina religionis: & ideo dicere quod tanti viri, inter quos aliqui fuerunt summi Pontifices, scripserunt contra conscientiam suam in favorem principum, vel ob timorem eorum, est ponere os in caelum. Magis autem probabiliter posset econtrario dici, quod tales doctores qui sic indebite ampliat auctoritatem Papae, loquuntur timore vel favore ipsius, cum sint personae Ecclesiasticae, qui magis possunt per ipsum promoveri. Et praecipue cum ipsi dicant, licet male, quod summus Pontifex gratiose amplectitur suam potestatem extendentes, & reprimit obloquentes, quod nunc faciunt reges & principes.
units.tr: As to what is said in the forty-first objection, that those who speak otherwise speak in favour of princes: I answer that although in some case the truth may be passed over in silence, as Moses kept silent about the truth concerning the divorce of a wife (Matt. 19), yet it is lawful for no one, in any case, to teach or write against conscience in the doctrine of religion. Therefore to say that so many men, among whom some were supreme Pontiffs, wrote against their conscience in favour of princes, or out of fear of them, is to set one's mouth against heaven.
