Rather, it could be said with greater probability on the contrary that such teachers, who so unduly extend the authority of the Pope, speak from fear or favour of him, since they are ecclesiastical persons who can be advanced more through him. Especially since they themselves say, though wrongly, that the supreme Pontiff graciously embraces those who extend his power and represses those who speak against it, which is what kings and princes now do.

units.la: Quod autem ultimo dicit ille de Cremona, tales pro haereticis habendos, qui dicunt Papam non habere, &c. Dicendum, quod iste est temerarius in iudicando, cum dicit, nos ita dicere, ut ecclesia non possit coercere haereticos. hoc enim falsum apparet, cum ecclesia possit invocare brachium seculare contra haereticos, extra, de haereticis. ad abolendam, & vergentem. Magis autem posset dici, quod iste anathema esset, & non longe ab haeresi, scilicet cum pertinacia suum dictum assereret. Nam Papam habere utrumque gladium, non continetur in sacra Scriptura, quae est regula fidei. & Deuter. 4. dicit Dominus, Non addetis ad verbum quod vobis loquor, neque auferetis ab eo. Et in congestis primae Nicenae synodi dicitur, quod perlecto symbolo Nicena synodi decreuit sancta synodus, aliam fidem nulli licere proferre, vel conscribere, vel componere, praeter diffinitam a sanctis Patribus, qui in Nicena synodo congregati sunt a Spiritu sancto. Et subditur anathematis poena. Et idem recitatur in gestis concilii Chalcedonensis. Amplius, cum fides Christiana sit catholica & universalis, non potest summus Pontifex hoc ponere sub fide sine concilio generali: quia Papa non potest discernere statuta concilii. distinctione 19. Anastasius. nam licet concilium non possit proprie legem imponere, extra, de electione, signasti. & 35. quaestione 6. veniam: tamen non intelligitur in iis quae fidei sunt, eo quod orbis maior est urbe & Papa, concilium maius est Papa solo.
units.tr: As to what that man of Cremona says last, that those who say the Pope does not have [both swords] are to be counted as heretics, etc.: it must be said that he is rash in judging when he says that we speak in such a way that the church cannot coerce heretics. For this appears false, since the church can invoke the secular arm against heretics (Extra, De haereticis, Ad abolendam and Vergentem). But it could rather be said that he himself would be under anathema, and not far from heresy, namely if he maintained his assertion with obstinacy. For that the Pope has both swords is not contained in holy Scripture, which is the rule of faith. And in Deut. 4 the Lord says: "You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor take away from it." And in the acts of the first Nicene synod it is said that, after the creed of the Nicene synod had been read, the holy synod decreed that no one is permitted to put forward, write, or compose any other faith besides that defined by the holy Fathers who were gathered at Nicaea by the Holy Spirit; and the penalty of anathema is added. The same is recited in the acts of the council of Chalcedon. Further, since the Christian faith is catholic and universal, the supreme Pontiff cannot place this under faith without a general council, because the Pope cannot discern the statutes of a council (dist. 19, Anastasius). For although a council cannot properly impose law (Extra, De electione, Signasti, and 35 q. 6, Veniam), yet this is not to be understood in matters that pertain to faith: since the world is greater than the city, and the Pope, a council is greater than the Pope alone.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXII.

units.la: De Donatione Constantini.
units.tr: On the Donation of Constantine.

units.la: Vlso, quid possint viri Ecclesiastici, eo quod sunt Christi vicarii: videndum est quid possint summi Pontifices ex dono Constantini Imperatoris magni. Dicunt enim, quod Sylvestro successoribusque dederit imperium Occidentale, & imperialia signa: ut palatium suum, & coronam, & alia huiusfhuiusmodi. Et ideo voluntaliqui, quod ratione huius doni, summus Pontifex Imperator est, & dominus mundi: & quod potest reges constituere & destituere, sicut Imperator, & praecipue imperio vacante. Vt autem ista melius pateant, praemittenda sunt aliqua ad factum pertinentia, quae in Chronicis & Ecclesiasticis historiis, de hac translatione & donatione leguntur: ut melius videatur, quid per donationem illam possit dominus Papa, praecipue super regem Franciae.
units.tr: Further, what churchmen can do because they are Christ's vicars must be considered. We must consider what the supreme Pontiffs can do by virtue of the gift of the Emperor Constantine the Great. For they say that he gave to Sylvester and his successors the Western empire and the imperial insignia, such as his palace, his crown and other things of this kind. Hence some want to hold that, by reason of this gift, the supreme Pontiff is Emperor and lord of the world, and that he can set up and depose kings as an Emperor can, especially when the empire is vacant. But so that these matters may be clearer, some points concerning the fact must first be laid out, as they are read in the chronicles and ecclesiastical histories about this transfer and donation. Thus it may be seen more clearly what the lord Pope can do by that donation, especially over the king of France.

units.la: Est quidem sciendum de donatione praedicta, quod sicut accipitur ex Chronicis Hugonis Floriacensis, & in libro de Cosmographia, & ex epistola Constantini ad episcopos: & ex Testamento eiusdem, ipse Constantinus non dedit nisi certam provinciam, scil. Italiam cum quibusdam aliis, vbi Francia non includitur: & imperium transtulit ad Graecos, vbi novam Romam aedificauit. Caeterum de translatione a Graecis ad Germanos facta per Romanos, & Papam in persona Caroli Magni, vt dicunt: sciendum est ex Chronicis supradictis, quod non fuit translatio facta, quin remaneret imperium apud Graecos secundum rem, & apud Occidentales secundum nomen: vel quod fuit facta diuisio imperii, vt duo Imperatores dicerentur, Romanus scilicet, & Constantinopolitanus. Eo quod Romani legitur ex triplici causa ab imperio Graecorum recessisse, scil. propter defensionem Reipublicae, quam acceperant a Carolo Magno, Constantino Imperatore negligente: & ex odio Irenae Imperatricis, quae filium suum Constantinum & filios filii exoculauit, vt sola imperaret, provocati, & ex translatione Imperii ad Graecos ab eis per Constantinum Imperatorem facta indignati, & grauiter ferentes imperium Graecorum, laudes imperii Carolo Magno victori declamauerunt. Ex quibus ergo supositis apparet, quod ex dicta donatione & translatione, Papa nihil potest super regem Franciae, propter quatuor.
units.tr: It must indeed be known about the aforesaid donation that, as is gathered from the Chronicles of Hugo of Flavigny, from the book on Cosmography, from Constantine's letter to the bishops, and from his own Testament, Constantine himself gave only a certain province, namely Italy with some other lands, where France is not included; and he transferred the empire to the Greeks, where he built New Rome. As for the transfer from the Greeks to the Germans, said to have been made by the Romans and by the Pope in the person of Charlemagne, it must be known from the chronicles mentioned above that no transfer took place, except that the empire remained with the Greeks in fact and with the Westerners in name; or else a division of the empire was made, so that there were two Emperors, the Roman and the Constantinopolitan. For we read that the Romans withdrew from the Greek empire for three reasons: first, for the defence of the commonwealth, which they had received from Charlemagne while the Emperor Constantine was neglectful; second, from hatred of the Empress Irene, who, to rule alone, had blinded her son Constantine and his sons' sons; and third, being indignant at the transfer of the empire to the Greeks made by the Emperor Constantine, and resenting the Greek empire, they proclaimed the praises of the empire to Charlemagne as conqueror. From these premises, therefore, it appears that from the said donation and transfer the Pope has no power at all over the king of France, for four reasons.

units.la: Primo quidem, quia dicta donatio non fuit nisi de portione determinata, in qua Francia non includebatur, nec translatio fuit facta totius imperii siue monarchiae mundi ad Germanos, cum etiam post translationem praedictam quae magis fuit diuisio Imperii, vel noua imperii appellatio, quam translatio, remanserunt adhuc Imperatores apud Graecos.
units.tr: First, because the said donation was only of a determined portion, in which France was not included; nor was there a transfer of the whole empire or of the monarchy of the world to the Germans, since even after the aforesaid transfer, which was more a division of the empire or a new naming of it than a transfer, Emperors still remained among the Greeks.

units.la: Secundo, quia dicta donatio nihil valuit propter quatuor, quae in Glossa iuris ciuilis ponuntur: & vt Iurisperiti communiter dicunt, quia Imperator ideo dicitur semper Augustus, quia eius est augere Rempublicam & non minuere. & ita dicta donatio non videtur tenuisse, praecipue quia excessiua & immensa, licet alias in remuneratione facta & cum moderatione tenuisset. g. diffinct. tutum, cum plures, & infra primis. Nec obstat quod dicit lex, quod mensura donationis ecclesiae est vniuersalis, vt in authent. de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, finimus. Illud enim intelligitur, quando donatur de patrimonio Caesaris, & non quando donatur de patrimonio fisci, quia pro statu Reipublicae constituendo institutum est, & ab vniuersitate, quae semper debet manere: de quo non potest largiri, nisi cum moderamine, & ex certis causis, in Authentica, quomodo oportet episcopos & clericos, col. 2. Vel intelligitur in principe non donante ecclesiae, sed permutante cum re Ecclesiastica: vbi non est periculum, si res principis sit maior, & non commensurata ab ecclesia acceptae.
units.tr: Second, because the said donation was of no force, for four reasons which are set out in the Gloss on the civil law; and, as the jurists commonly say, the Emperor is therefore called always Augustus, because it is his to increase the commonwealth and not to diminish it. And so the said donation does not seem to have held, especially because it was excessive and immense, although it might have held in a reward given and with moderation. g. dist. tutum, cum plures, and below primis. Nor does it stand in the way that the law says the measure of a gift to the Church is unlimited, as in authent. de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, finimus. For that is understood when the gift is made from the patrimony of Caesar, and not when it is made from the patrimony of the treasury, since that was established for settling the state of the commonwealth and belongs to the whole body, which must always remain; from this it cannot be bestowed except with moderation and for certain causes, as in Authentica, quomodo oportet episcopos & clericos, col. 2. Or it is understood of a prince who does not give to the Church but exchanges with ecclesiastical property, where there is no danger if the prince's property is greater and not out of proportion to what the Church receives.

units.la: Secundo, quia Imperator est administrator Imperii & Reipublicae, vt dicunt iura, per legem regiam ab Hortensio latam: vt de constit. principum l. 1. Si non imperii administrator, est imperii diminutor, non valet. & in tit. proem. Instit.
units.tr: Second, because the Emperor is the administrator of the empire and of the commonwealth, as the laws say, under the royal law proposed by Hortensius, as in de constit. principum l. 1. If he is not an administrator of the empire but a diminisher of it, the gift is not valid; and see in tit. proem. Instit.

units.la: Tertio, quia si donare lex est, C. de donatione inter virum & uxorem. L. donationes. Lex enim facta per vnum, seu ab vno, reuocari potest per successorem: quia par in parem non habet imperium, vt ff. de arbitris, leg. nam & magistratu. Dicta ergo donatio firma non fuit.
units.tr: Third, because if to give is the law, C. de donatione inter virum & uxorem. L. donationes. For a law made by one, or by a single person, can be revoked by a successor, since an equal has no power over an equal, as in ff. de arbitris, leg. nam & magistratu. Therefore the said donation was not firm.

units.la: Quarto, quia eadem ratione qua vnam partem potest dare, & successor potest & aliam, & sic imperium diminueretur & spoliaretur donis suis, quod est inconueniens: quia expedit quod imperii sit locuples. L. legatus. ff. de off. praesidis, & in Auth. vt iudices sine quoquo suffrag. collatione secunda. Ex quibus dicunt Iuristae, quod donatio non valuit.
units.tr: Fourth, because by the same reasoning by which one ruler can give one part, a successor can also give another, and so the empire would be diminished and stripped by its own gifts, which is inconvenient, since it is expedient that the empire be rich. L. legatus. ff. de off. praesidis, & in Auth. vt iudices sine quoquo suffrag. collatione secunda. From these points the jurists say that the donation was not valid.

units.la: Quod vero Deo displicuerit, ex hoc sumitur argumentum, quod legitur in vita B. Syluestri Papae, quod in donatione illa audita est vox angelorum, dicentium in aere: Hodie in Ecclesia venenum effusum est. Item B. Hieron, dicit de isto Constantino, quod ab ipso vsque in praesens tempus, ecclesiarum rapina & totius orbis discordia secuta est. Dicit etiam Hieron. de eodem, quod in tantam crudelitatem postea venisse, vt filium suum Crispum interficeret, & uxorem suam Faustam: extremo etiam tempore vita sua ab Eusebio Nicomediae baptizatus est: & sic bis baptizatus fuit, & amplius in Arianum dogma declinauit. & hoc idem dictum in Chronicis suis multi alii Cronicorum veraces scriptores, & fide digni imitantur. Quod autem aliqui defendere volunt, quod illud de filio suo intelligi debet, patet esse falsum: tum quia B. Hieron. satis postea loquitur de ipso Constantino. Constat autem, quod ab illo Constantino non incepit rapina ecclesiarum, cum ipsius tempore fuerit ecclesiae magna persecutio. Constat etiam ex Chronicis, quod solus Constantinus, & non filius eius, vxorem habuit Faustam nomine. Non inuenitur etiam iste Constantinus familiaris fuisse Eusebio Nicomediae episcopo: sed alius Constantinus, qui mortuus in sua ecclesia est sepultus. & ideo illa scelerosa dicunt Hieronymus & alii de Constantino Magno, quamuis affectus pietatis suae reddiderit eum bonae memoriae apud beatum Greg. in Registro. Graeci etiam ad eum deuotionem conceperunt ex eo, quod ad ipsos Imperium transtulit, & Constantinopolim apud eos fundauit.
units.tr: That it displeased God, however, is argued from what is read in the life of the blessed Pope Sylvester: that at that donation a voice of angels was heard in the air, saying, Today poison has been poured into the Church. Likewise the blessed Jerome says of this Constantine that from him until the present time there has followed the plundering of the churches and discord throughout the whole world. Jerome also says of the same man that later he came to such cruelty that he killed his son Crispus and his wife Fausta; and at the very end of his life he was baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia: and so he was baptized twice, and moreover he inclined to the Arian doctrine. Many other true and trustworthy writers of the chronicles say the same thing in their own chronicles. But that some wish to defend the claim that this should be understood of his son is plainly false: first, because the blessed Jerome speaks afterwards of Constantine himself; and it is certain that the plundering of the churches did not begin with that Constantine, since in his time there was a great persecution of the Church. It is also clear from the chronicles that only Constantine, and not his son, had a wife named Fausta. Nor is it found that this Constantine was a friend of Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia; rather it was another Constantine, who died and was buried in his own church. And so Jerome and others say those wicked things about Constantine the Great, although the affection of his piety has made him, in the register of the blessed Gregory, a man of good memory. The Greeks also conceived devotion to him, because of the fact that he transferred the empire to them and founded Constantinople among them.

units.la: Tertio apparet, quod ex dicta donatione nihil habet Papa super regem Franciae, dato etiam quod valuisset, & generalis de toto imperio fuisset: quia licet Gallici inueniatur tempore Octauiani Augusti in imperio Romano fuisse subiecti, tamen Franci nunquam. Hoc enim legitur in diuersis historiis, quod post excidium duodecim millia Troianorum duce Antenore, à quo primo dicti sunt Antenoridæ, ad partes Pannoniæ iuxta Mæotidas paludes peruenerunt, vbi ciuitatem Sicambriam ædificauerunt, semper Imperio Romano infestißibiq; máseruut vsq; ad tempora Valentiniani Imperatoris, à quo inde expulsi, pro quod tributa Romanis iuxta morem cæterarum gentium soluere recusauerunt: egressi aút inde cum suis ducibus Marcomiro, Symone & Genebaudo, venerunt & habitauerunt iuxta ripam Rheni in confinio Germaniæ & Alemanniæ: quos cum multis prœliis idem Valentinianus postmodum deuincere non potuisset, proprio nomine eos Francos, id est feroces appellauit. Et ab illo tempore virtus Francorum in tantum excreuit, vt totam Germaniam & Galliam usque ad iuga Pyrenæi, & vltra subiugarent: & Galliam habitantes, eamque Franciam nominantes, nullis Romanis, nec aliis quibuscunque fuerunt subiecti.
units.tr: Third, it appears that from the said donation the Pope has nothing over the king of France, even granting that it was valid and extended over the whole empire; for although the Gauls are found to have been subject to the Roman empire in the time of Octavian Augustus, the Franks never were. For it is read in various histories that after the destruction of Troy, twelve thousand Trojans under their leader Antenor, from whom they were first called Antenorides, came to the parts of Pannonia near the Maeotian marshes, where they built the city of Sicambria; and they always remained hostile to the Roman empire until the time of the Emperor Valentinian, by whom they were then expelled, because they refused to pay tribute to the Romans in the manner of the other peoples. Going out from there with their leaders Marcomir, Symon and Genebaud, they came and settled on the bank of the Rhine, on the border between Germany and Alemannia; and when Valentinian could not afterwards subdue them with many battles, he called them by their own name, Franks, that is, fierce. From that time the valour of the Franks grew so great that they subdued all Germany and Gaul as far as the ridges of the Pyrenees and beyond; and those who inhabited Gaul and named it France were subject to no Romans or to any others whatever.

units.la: Quarto, ex dicta donatione dato quod valuerit, & toto imperio facta fuerit, & dato quod Franci tunc fuissent imperio subiecti, q non dicimus: adhuc Papa nihil potest super regnum Franciæ, cum non sit Imperator. Et amplius, dato q esset. Franci præscripserunt contra Imperatorem vsq; ad dies istos. Tenuerunt n. sic regnum Franciæ reges sancti, & tam longo tempore & bona fide, vt patet de B. Ludovico per Ecclesiam meritis suis euidentib. canonizato: qui ita tenuit, & ecclesia canonizando approbauit, quicquid dicant aliqui Theologi: cum iure humano sit appropriatio rerum, & subiectio hominum, secundum Augustinum, iura humana possunt facere comune vel alienum, quod meum est, ex causa rationabili non esse meum, & transferre dominium. Ex quo n. iura imperialia statuerunt, quod aliquid post tñ tempus in præscriptione transferatur, dominium transfertur. Et hoc pro communi vtilitate, vel in odiũ negligentis, & in fauorem bonæ fidei possessoris, & ne lites in infinitum protendantur & multiplicentur: nec in hoc aliquis tenet alienum, sed suum, quod suum factum est præscriptione legitima. Et ideo, dato q regnum Franciæ alias fuisset subiectũ Romano imperio: tñ præscripta est subiectio. Quod etiam patet ex Chronicis Sigisberti & aliorum. Ibi n. legitur: quod Carolus M. totam Italiam sub iure regni Francorum subegit. Legitur etiã in historiis Romanor. quod olim Imperium fuit apud Francos. Et tamen constat, quod Italia nunc non est subiecta Francis: quod non est nisi propter aliquam temporis præscriptionem, quæ in talibus locum habet. Ex prædictis etiam apparet, non valere quod dicunt aliqui Iuristæ de præscriptione iurisdictionis & subiectionis, quod subiectio quæ Imperatori debetur, præscribi non potest: sed illa tantum quæ debetur baronibus inferioribus: ita tamen, quod subiectio remanear ad superiorem. Cuius rationem allegant, quia cum plures dissentiant faciliter, non expedit vt plures regimen habeant, sed quod vnus toti mundo principetur: & ideo ista vtilitas præscriptione tolli non debet. Sed parum valet ista ratio, vt patet ex dictis super 3.ca, quia verũ est, q plures dissentiunt faciliter in re vna: & ideo melius est regimen regũ, q̃ Aristocraticũ: vt supra dictum est ca.1. Meliusautem est, plures pluribus regnis dominari, quam vnum toti mundo.
units.tr: Fourthly, even granting that the said donation was valid and was made for the whole empire, and granting that the Franks were then subject to the empire (which we do not concede), the Pope still has no power over the kingdom of France, since he is not the Emperor. Moreover, even if he were, the Franks have acquired prescriptive title against the Emperor down to the present day. The holy kings have held the kingdom of France so long and in good faith, as is clear from St. Louis, whom the Church has canonized for his manifest merits, and in canonizing him she has approved his possession, whatever some theologians may say. For by human law there is the appropriation of things and the subjection of men, according to Augustine, and human laws can make common or alien what is mine, so that for a reasonable cause it is no longer mine, and can transfer ownership. For the imperial laws have decreed that when something has been held for a certain length of time under prescription, ownership passes. They have done this for the common good, or as a penalty for the negligent owner and in favour of the possessor in good faith, and so that lawsuits do not stretch out and multiply without end. In this case no one holds what belongs to another, but what has become his own by lawful prescription. Therefore, even if the kingdom of France had at some earlier time been subject to the Roman empire, the subjection has nonetheless been prescribed away. This is also clear from the Chronicles of Sigebert and others. For there we read that Charlemagne subdued all Italy under the rule of the kingdom of the Franks. We also read in the histories of the Romans that empire once belonged to the Franks. Yet it is plain that Italy is now not subject to the Franks, and this is due to nothing but some lapse of time, which has force in such matters. From what has been said it also appears that the view of some jurists is worthless, namely that concerning prescription of jurisdiction and subjection: they hold that the subjection owed to the Emperor cannot be prescribed, but only that owed to the lesser barons, provided that subjection remains to the superior. They give as their reason that since many men easily disagree, it is not expedient for many to hold government, but rather for one to rule the whole world; and therefore this advantage ought not to be lost by prescription. But this reason carries little weight, as is clear from what was said above on the third chapter. For it is true that many easily disagree about one matter, and therefore the government of kings is better than aristocracy, as was said above in chapter 1. Yet it is better for many to rule by many kingdoms than for one to rule the whole world.

units.la: Quod ex hoc etiam apparet, quod tempore Imperatorum nunquam fuit mundus in tanta pace, quanta fuit postea, & ante: sed frater fratrem, & mater filium occidebat, & econuerso, & cætera horribilia scelera per mundum currebant, & dissensiones permaximæ, de quibus non oportet modo narrare per singula. Mirum etiam est, si præscribi non possit contra imperium Romanorum, vt dicunt illi, cum ante regnum Romanorum fuerint regna & imperia, scilicet Babyloniorum, quod incepit à Nino, tempore Abrahæ: Carthaginense, tempore Iudith, Macedonum siue Græcorum ab Alexandro tempore Machabæorum: & quodlibet prædictorum est æque à Deo, sicut imperium Romanorum.
units.tr: This also appears from the fact that in the time of the emperors the world was never in such peace as it has been since and before. Rather, brother slew brother and mother slew son, and the reverse, and other horrible crimes ran through the world, and very great dissensions, which there is no need to narrate here one by one. It is also strange, if prescription cannot run against the Roman empire, as those men say, since before the Roman kingdom there were other kingdoms and empires: that of the Babylonians, which began with Ninus in the time of Abraham; the Carthaginian, in the time of Judith; that of the Macedonians or Greeks from Alexander, in the time of the Maccabees. Each of these is from God just as much as the Roman empire is.

units.la: Si igitur, non obstante quod Græci habuerunt imperium à Deo, Romani præscribunt & præscripserunt contra Græcos, & vsurparc tenuerunt Græcos expellendo: quare non possunt alii homines præscribere contra imperium Romanorum, etiam eorum dominium à se abiiciendo: præcipue cum eis se non subiecerunt voluntarie, sed violentia Romanorum? Sicut de Gallicis legitur, quod nunquam, antequam venirent Franci, voluntarie se subiecerunt Romanis: sed semper rebelles fuerunt, prout potuerunt, modo quidem Romanos vincendo, modo econuerso. Si ergo Romani per violentiam acceperunt, nunquid iuste per violentiam etiam abiici potuit dominium eorum, vel etiam contra eos præscribi?
units.tr: If, then, notwithstanding that the Greeks had their empire from God, the Romans prescribed and did prescribe against the Greeks, and held usurped possession by driving the Greeks out, why can other men not prescribe against the Roman empire, casting off its dominion from themselves, especially since they did not submit to it voluntarily but by the violence of the Romans? Just as we read of the Gauls, that before the Franks came they never voluntarily submitted to the Romans, but were always rebels as far as they could be, now conquering the Romans and now the reverse. If, then, the Romans obtained their rule by violence, can their dominion not justly be thrown off by violence as well, or even be prescribed against?

units.la: Si vero aliquis dicat, quod Deo ordinante cessare debuit imperium aliorum, & crescere debuit imperium Romanorum: quare non sic potest dici de Romano imperio, quod cessare debeat Deo ordinante, vt illi qui ante Romanis qualitercunque fuerunt subiecti, amplius non debeant subiici, si discedere velint & possint? imo expressius videtur haberi in Scriptura de imperio Romanorum, quod deficere voluerit, quam de alio. Dicitur enim Num. 24. in prophetia Balaam: Venient in triremibus de Italia, & superabunt Assyrios, vastabunt Hebræos, & ad extremum etiam ipsi peribunt. vbi dicit Magister in historiis: Sicut monarchiam prædixit Romanorum hic, & sic in fine temporum destructionem eorum. Similiter in Danielem, vbi agitur de imagine quadriforma, percussa in pedibus, dicit Glossa: quod regno Romanorum nihil fortius fuit, & nihil in fine debilius aut fragilius erit.
units.tr: But if someone says that by God's ordinance the empire of others had to cease and the Roman empire had to grow, why can it not likewise be said of the Roman empire that by God's ordinance it ought to cease, so that those who were in some way subject to the Romans in earlier times should no longer be subject, if they wish and are able to withdraw? Indeed, Scripture seems to speak more plainly of the fall of the Roman empire than of any other. For it is said in Num. 24, in the prophecy of Balaam: They shall come in galleys from Italy, and shall subdue the Assyrians, and shall afflict the Hebrews, and at the last they also shall perish. On which the Master in the Histories says: Just as he here foretold the monarchy of the Romans, so at the end of time he foretold their destruction. Likewise on Daniel, where the image with four parts, struck on its feet, is discussed, the Gloss says that nothing was stronger than the kingdom of the Romans, and at the end nothing will be weaker or more brittle.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: An licitum sit de pertinentibus huiusmodi disputare & iudicare.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to dispute and judge about such matters.

units.la: NVnc vero inquirendum videtur, si sit reprehensibile iudicare de factis Papæ: & quod aliqui qui dicunt, quod hoc est tangere montem, & ponere os in cœlum. Dicunt etiam, Dioscorum perpetuo condemnatum per concilium generale, quia Papam Leonem reprehendit; & iudicare voluit.
units.tr: Now we must inquire whether it is blameworthy to pass judgment on the acts of the Pope. Some say that this is to touch the mountain and to set one's mouth against heaven. They also say that Dioscorus was condemned in perpetuity by a general council because he rebuked Pope Leo and wanted to sit in judgment on him.

units.la: Sed circa hoc est considerandum, quod contra Papam potest intelligi; esse quadrupliciter discussio & iudicium, scil. de statu, de potestate, de potestatis abusu, & personali defectu. De statu quidem Papæ, scil. an sit Papa, vel non: dico quod discutere licet, cum possit venire in dubium propter defectum electionis: cuius tamen forma est certa, in qua potest error incidere, sicut circa electionem cuiuslibet alterius prælati Ecclesiastici. Et iterum Papa propter defectum personæ, cum interdum possit aliquis esse, quod esset à sede repellendus, ut si esset fœmina vel hæreticus, sicut fuerunt aliqui, qui ob hoc non enumerentur in Catalogo Paparum: & tanto magis est necessarium veritatem istorum requirere, quanto magis periculosum esset in hoc veritatem non agnoscere. Hoc tamen est obseruandum, ut exceptiones in talibus frustratorie & supine non admittantur, quod ex tempore exceptionum factarum, & ex personis excipientibus maxime obseruetur. Si vero contra personam, vel electionem summi Pontificis, post discussionem diligentem à literatis & ab illis, quorum interest, facta, inueniretur aliquid illegitimum contra statuta, non esset dissimulandum, sed monendus cedere: & si nollet, posset excipi, & generale concilium peti, & ad ipsum concilium appellari: imo in tali casu deberet, si pertinax inueniretur cum violentia, aduocato brachio seculari à sede remoueri, ne profanarentur Ecclesiæ sacramenta.
units.tr: But on this point we must consider that there can be four kinds of inquiry and judgment concerning the Pope: about his status, about his power, about his abuse of power, and about his personal defects. As to his status, that is, whether he is Pope or not, I say that it is permissible to examine it, since it may be called into doubt because of a defect in the election. The form of election is certain, but error can creep into it, as with the election of any other ecclesiastical prelate. Likewise the Pope may be called into question because of a defect in the person, since there may sometimes be someone who ought to be removed from the see, for example if he were a woman or a heretic, as some were, who for this reason are not counted in the catalogue of Popes. And the more dangerous it would be to fail to recognise the truth in such cases, the more necessary it is to inquire into them. Yet this must be observed: objections of this kind must not be admitted frivolously or carelessly, and this must be watched most closely with regard to the time at which the objections are raised and the persons who raise them. If, however, after a careful examination by learned men and by those whom it concerns, something illegitimate against the statutes is found concerning the person or the election of the supreme Pontiff, it should not be passed over in silence, but he should be warned to give way. If he refuses, objection may be lodged, a general council may be demanded, and appeal made to that council itself. Indeed, in such a case, if he is found obstinate, he ought to be removed from the see by force, calling in the secular arm, lest the sacraments of the Church be profaned.

units.la: Sic enim legitur in Chronicis Romanorum Pontificum de Benedicto Nono, & Cadelo Portuensi Episcopo, Constantino Secundo, & aliis quibusdam propter intrusionem per brachium seculare commendabiliter à sede depositis: sed quis iudicabit eum hæreticum? Responsio: Si dixerit, & affirmando tenuerit aliquid, quod est contra id, quod est in Symbolo fidei per ecclesiam alias approbato, iam dicitur iudicatus. nam qui non credit, iam iudicatus est. De potestate vero domini Papæ, quid possit, vel quid non possit, credo quod non sit reprehensibile inquirere veritatem, cum ignorantia sit periculosa, & non sit certum in quibusdam: ut, utrum possit dispensare cum bigamo, vel utrum possit dispensare in solemni voto continentiæ, cum inueniatur alius Papa de facto dispensasse aliquando: & cum aliquis Papa dicat, quod non possit: extra, cum de ingredientibus monasterium, & multa etiam alia infinita sunt de potestate Papæ dubia, de quibus est vtile dubitare, & etiam prout per rationes videtur alicui humiliter iudicare. De potestatis vero siue abusu & personali defectu suo, an scilicet præbendas conferat pro communi necessitate Ecclesiæ, vel bono suo priuato: & utrum sit castus, sobrius, vel scelerosus: si non sit euidens aut manifestum, absque dubio non licet iudicare: sed semper in meliorem partem interpretandum est, & trahendum, etiamsi prima facie aliquid mali coloris occurrat. Et minus est licitum de Papa, quam de aliis quibuscunque. Si vero sit factum ex genere suo malum, & manifestum, vt incontinentia vel homicidium, vel ex lege prohibitum, non potest iudicari per modum auctoritatis ab aliquo citando vel excommunicando, cum superiorem non habeat. Vnde Dioscorus, qui Leonem Papam excommunicauit, vt dicitur XXI. per generale concilium est perpetuo condemnatus. Per modum etiam iudicii & correctionis dicunt aliqui, quod non est iudicandus: quia si homicidium Samsonis, quod ex se malum est, interpretamur quod instinctu diuino fuit factum: multo magis omne factum sanctissimi Patris interpretari debemus in bonum. Et si quidem fuerit furtum, vel aliud ex se malum, interpretari debemus, quod diuino instinctu fiat, cuius nutu regitur Ecclesia sancta magis, quam singularis persona. Sed beatus Augustinus latis respondet in primo de Ciuitate Dei. Nam homicidium Samsonis, vt dicitur, interpretatur factum instinctu Dei, qui per ipsum Samsonem alia miracula operabatur. Ideo dicitur, Si Papa errat priuando ecclesias iure suo, dispergendo gregem Domini, scandalizando Ecclesiam ex quocunque facto suo, potest de facto suo iudicari, persuaderi & reprehendi à quocunque: quod si non ex officio, tamen ex charitatis zelo, non pœnam imponendo, sed cum reuerentia exhortando: quia affectus qui personæ debetur, non minus ei debetur ratione maioris status, ad quem assumptus est: & ideo ratione status, sicut populo ad quem assumptus est, non tenetur minus omnibus ad charitatis affectum, licet auctoritate seruata, secundum Augustinum. Ita econuerso, cum aliquid delinquenti teneatur, quilibet ad correctionem fraternam, ex charitatis zelo & debito ipsi facto: Papæ non minus tenetur quilibet impendere charitatis affectum, licet cum humilitate & reuerentia. Vnde Galat. 2. cum venisset Petrus Antiochiam, in facie restitit ei Paulus, quia reprehensibilis erat, nec ideo quis poneret os in cœlum: neque os ponitur in eum, id est contra eum, quando corrigitur. Sed pro eo nec debet aliquis timere de Papa, quod propter hoc scandalizetur, quia scandalum passiuum non cadit in viris perfectis, sed in pusillis tantum: Vnde timere in hoc scandalum Papæ, est in hoc tenere de Papa, quod est pusillus, & minus perfectus quam quilibet alius, quem aliquis audet corripere delinquentem: & ideo tales secundum veritatem ponunt os in cœlum, qui talia prædicant de sanctissimo Patre, quod est vindicatiuus, & quod grauiter portat omnem hominem factâ sua qualiacunque iudicantem: quod certe non est timendum, cum non sit pusillus, sed perfectus, & aliis perfectior. Sed quid si Papa dicat, quod reputat talem hæreticum, qui tenet aliquid de quo sunt opiniones, & dicat hoc sine concilio generali: vel si dicat quod reputat hæreticum omnem hominem asserentem regem Franciæ vel aliquem huiusmodi non esse subiectum? Responsio: Verba summi Pontificis indefinite dicta, semper debent trahi ad aliquem sanum sensum, quantum potest fieri: vnde dicta verba non debent accipi sic, quod non possit ad eum appellari, vel quod sit diuinum habens in rebus ipsis, vel quod Papa se habeat intromittere de tuo & meo: Hoc enim esset manifeste contra Scripturam & contra omnem doctrinam, & novitas quædam: quam non proferret summus Pontifex, nisi cum magna maturitate, & habito prius concilio generali, & discussione facta ubique per literatos. & ideo debet intelligi in sano sensu, scilicet ratione delicti, ubi quæstio movetur de peccato: vel debet intelligi in foro conscientiæ, ut dictum est supra, quo usque super hoc aperuerit intentionem suam. Si vero finaliter aperiat intentionem suam in tam novo & iniurioso sensu (quod absit) debet cum patientia tolerari, quantum potest sine periculo iustitiæ & veritatis. iuxta illud Matthæi quinto, Quicunque angariaverit te mille passus, vade cum illo & alia duo millia: & debet ad eum habere refugium, qui sicut cor regis, ita & cor Papæ habet in manu sua, & potest ipsum quoque si voluerit inclinare & vertere ad ipsum Papam, sicut & regem de sede amovere. Si tamen periculum Reipublicæ sit in mora, quia scilicet trahitur populus ad malam opinionem, & est periculum de rebellione, & Papa commoveat populum indebite per abusum gladii spiritualis. Vbi etiam non speratur quod desistat aliter, puto quod in hoc casu Ecclesia contra Papam debet moveri, & agere in ipsum: princeps vero violentiam gladii Papæ, posset repellere per gladium suum, cum moderamine: nec in hoc ageret contra Papam, sed contra hostem suum, & hostem reipublicæ: sicut Aioth Iudæus, qui Eglom regem Moab interfecit, sagitta infixa in femore eius, eo quod graui seruitute populum Dei premebat, non est reputatus interfecisse rectorem, sed malum & hostem. hoc enim agere, non est contra Ecclesiam agere, sed pro ecclesia. Sic enim commendabiliter populus zelo fidei commotus, Constantinum Papam, qui ecclesiæ in scandalum erat, oculis priuauit, & deposuit. Sic & Henricus Imperator Romam vadens, Benedictum Nonum, & alios duos, qui contentionibus suis scandalizabant ecclesiam, imperiali & canonica censura deposuit, & Clementem Secundum Romanæ ecclesiæ Papam constituit, ut legitur in Chronicis Romanorum.
units.tr: For thus we read in the Chronicles of the Roman Pontiffs that Benedict IX and Cadelus, Bishop of Porto, and Constantine II, and some others, were deposed from their see, with due commendation, by the secular arm because of their intrusion. But who will judge him a heretic? Answer: If he has said, and by affirming holds, something contrary to what is in the creed of faith otherwise approved by the Church, he is already said to be judged, for whoever does not believe is already judged. As to the power of the lord Pope, what he can or cannot do, I think it is not blameworthy to inquire into the truth, since ignorance is dangerous and some points are not settled: for example, whether he can dispense with a bigamist, or whether he can dispense from a solemn vow of continence, since another Pope is found to have dispensed in fact at some time; and since some Pope says that he cannot: Extra, Cum de ingredientibus monasterium. There are also many other questions about the power of the Pope that are doubtful, about which it is useful to doubt, and even, as it seems to someone through reasons, to judge with humility. As to the abuse of power and his personal defects, that is, whether he confers benefices for the common need of the Church or for his own private good, and whether he is chaste, sober, or wicked: if the matter is not evident or manifest, it is unquestionably not lawful to judge it. Rather, it must always be interpreted and drawn to the better side, even if something of an evil appearance presents itself at first sight. And it is less permissible concerning the Pope than concerning anyone else. But if the deed is evil in its own kind and manifest, such as incontinence or homicide, or forbidden by law, it cannot be judged by way of authority, by anyone summoning or excommunicating him, since he has no superior. Hence Dioscorus, who excommunicated Pope Leo, as is said, was condemned in perpetuity by a general council, in the twenty-first. Some also say by way of judgment and correction that he is not to be judged, because if we interpret the homicide of Samson, which is evil in itself, as having been done by divine impulse, much more ought we to interpret every deed of the most holy Father for good. And if it was a theft, or something else evil in itself, we ought to interpret it as done by divine impulse, by whose nod the holy Church is governed more than any single person. But blessed Augustine answers this at length in the first book of the City of God: for the homicide of Samson, as it is said, is interpreted as done by the impulse of God, who worked other miracles through Samson himself. Therefore it is said: if the Pope errs by depriving the churches of their right, by scattering the Lord's flock, by scandalising the Church through any deed of his, his deed may be judged, he may be persuaded and rebuked by anyone. And if this is not done by office, it may nevertheless be done out of zeal for charity, not by imposing punishment but by exhorting with reverence. For the affection owed to a person is owed no less to him by reason of the greater rank to which he has been raised, and therefore, by reason of his rank, as to the people over whom he has been placed, he is no less bound to the affection of charity than all others, although authority is preserved, according to Augustine. Conversely, just as anyone is bound to fraternal correction of a sinner out of zeal for charity and the duty owed to the deed itself, so anyone is bound no less to show the affection of charity to the Pope, although with humility and reverence. Hence in Galatians 2, when Peter had come to Antioch, Paul withstood him to his face, because he was to be blamed; and yet no one therefore set his mouth against heaven, nor is the mouth set against him, that is, against him, when he is corrected. But nor ought anyone to fear, on account of this, that the Pope will be scandalised, because passive scandal does not fall upon perfect men but only upon the little ones. So to fear that the Pope will be scandalised in this matter is to hold of the Pope that he is a little one, and less perfect than any other whom someone dares to rebuke when he sins. Thus, in truth, those set their mouth against heaven who preach such things of the most holy Father as that he is vindictive, and that he bears badly any man who judges his deeds, whatever they may be. This certainly is not to be feared, since he is not a little one but a perfect man, and more perfect than others. But what if the Pope says that he regards as a heretic anyone who holds something about which there are differing opinions, and says this without a general council? Or if he says that he regards as a heretic every man who asserts that the king of France, or someone of that kind, is not subject to him? Answer: The words of the supreme Pontiff, spoken indefinitely, must always be drawn to some sound sense, as far as this can be done. Therefore the words said must not be understood in such a way that one cannot appeal against him, or that he has a divine right over the things themselves, or that the Pope may meddle with what is yours and mine. For this would be plainly contrary to Scripture and to all doctrine, and a kind of novelty, which the supreme Pontiff would not put forward except with great deliberation, after first holding a general council, and after an examination made everywhere by learned men. Therefore it must be understood in a sound sense, namely by reason of the offence, where the question is raised about sin, or it must be understood in the forum of conscience, as has been said above, until he discloses his intention on this point. But if at last he discloses his intention in so new and injurious a sense (which God forbid), it must be borne with patience, as far as this can be done without danger to justice and truth, according to that saying of Matthew 5: Whoever compels you to go a mile, go with him and another two miles. And one must have recourse to him who, as he holds the heart of the king in his hand, so also holds the heart of the Pope, and who can, if he wills, incline and turn even the Pope to himself, just as he can remove a king from his throne. Yet if danger to the commonwealth lies in delay, because the people are being drawn into a bad opinion, and there is danger of rebellion, and the Pope stirs up the people improperly through the abuse of the spiritual sword, and where it is not hoped that he will desist otherwise, I think that in this case the Church ought to be moved against the Pope and act against him. The prince, however, may repel the violence of the Pope's sword with his own sword, with moderation, and in doing so he would not act against the Pope but against his enemy and the enemy of the commonwealth. So Ehud the Jew, who killed Eglon, king of Moab, with a sword thrust into his thigh, because he oppressed the people of God with heavy servitude, was not thought to have slain a ruler but an evil man and an enemy. For to do this is not to act against the Church but on behalf of the Church. Thus the people, moved by zeal for the faith, commendably deprived of sight and deposed Pope Constantine, who was a scandal to the Church. So too the Emperor Henry, going to Rome, deposed by imperial and canonical censure Benedict IX and two others who were scandalising the Church by their contentions, and set up Clement II as Pope of the Roman Church, as is read in the Chronicles of the Romans.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: Quod Papa possit resignare.
units.tr: That the Pope can resign.

units.la: NVnc, quia supponere videbar superius, quod summus Pontifex renunciare potest, & deponi, & viuens potest fieri de Papa non Papa: videndum est, quibus rationibus vsi sunt, qui dicebant Papam non posse resignare voluntarie, nec deponi sola auctoritate inferiorum prælatorum: vt in isto Capitulo ponantur rationes, ad duos articulos distinctæ, superius in isto principio huius Tractatus positos: eo quod sunt multæ rationes, quæ vtrumque concludunt. Sit igitur prima ratio eorum, Quod Papa renunciare non potest: quia papatus à solo Deo est: quæ autem à Deo sunt, vel ab alio superiori alicui committuntur, ab aliquo inferiori remoueri non possunt: & sic papalis dignitas, à nullo inferiori remoueri potest. Secunda ratio est, quod nullus potest auctoritatem vel potestatem auferre, quam conferre non potest: sed auctoritatem papalem nullus potest conferre nisi Deus: ergo nec etiam auferre, quod tamen fieret, si Papa renunciare posset. Tertia ratio est ex decret. inter corporalia, de translatione episcopor. quæ expresse innuit, quod depositio episcoporum, vel translatio episcopatuum soli Papæ reseruatur, & non nisi in quantum Deus, id est Dei vicarius: ergo remouetur Papa ab officio, quia papatus omnes dignitates excellit, per solum superiorem, sicut Deum. Potest fieri quod nulla ratio esse videtur, quod Dominus velit episcopos solum per superiorem Papam, inquantum est Deus, & Papam ipsum posse remoueri per inferiores setimo videtur quod Deus velit, quod ipse solus per seipsum possit Papam amouere, qui solus eo est superior. Quarta ratio est, Summa virtus creata per summam virtutem potest tolli: sed papatus est summa virtus creata: ergo, &c. Quinta ratio est, quia nec Papa, nec tota vniuersitas creaturæ potest facere, quod Pontifex non sit Pontifex: ergo minus potest facere, quod summus Pontifex non sit summus Pontifex. Sexta ratio est, quia Papa non est Papa nisi per legem diuinam, & non per legem creaturæ, nec omnium creaturarum simul: ergo nullo modo videtur, quod Papa possit eximi quin sit Papa. Ex quo enim Papa consensit, & se sponte subiecit, non potest esse non Papa per creaturam aliquam, vel omnes simul. Septima ratio est, quia nullus potest tollere votum alicuius, nisi ille qui est super votum: sed papatus est votum super omnia vota, quia Papa vouet se gerere curam vniversalis Ecclesiæ, & gregis Dominici, & quod de ipso reddet rationem: ergo ab ipso solo potest ab ipsa obligatione absolui. non enim alias alicui superiori obligatus potest seipsum absoluere: sed solus superior eum absoluere potest. Octaua ratio est, nullus videtur seipsum posse absoluere à peccato: ergo nec à papatu: quod esset, si voluntarie renunciare posset. Nona ratio est, quia papalis obligatio non videtur posse tolli nisi per maiorem potestatem, quam sit papalis: qua tamen nulla maior nisi de: ergo, &c. Decima ratio, quia nulla dignitas Ecclesiastica post legitimam confirmationem potest tolli, nisi per eius superiorem: sed Papa non habet superiorem nisi Deum, ergo. Vndecima ratio est, eo quod Apostolus vult, quod Christi sacerdotium est æternum, quia Christus viuit in æternum: ergo nullo modo potest esse vita summi sacerdotis sine summo sacerdotio. quod tamen falsum esset, si Papa renunciare posset.
units.tr: Now, since I seemed above to assume that the supreme Pontiff can resign and be deposed, and that while living a Pope can become a non-Pope, I must consider the reasons used by those who said that the Pope cannot resign voluntarily, nor be deposed by the sole authority of inferior prelates. In this chapter the arguments are set out, divided according to the two points laid down earlier at the beginning of this Treatise, because there are many arguments which prove both. Let the first of their arguments be this: the Pope cannot renounce, because the papacy is from God alone. Those things that are from God, or are committed to someone by another superior, cannot be removed by an inferior; and so the papal dignity cannot be removed by any inferior. The second argument is that no one can take away an authority or power which he cannot confer; but no one can confer papal authority except God; therefore neither can anyone take it away, which nevertheless would happen if the Pope could renounce. The third argument is from the decretal "Inter corporalia" on the transfer of bishops, which expressly implies that the deposition of bishops or the transfer of bishoprics is reserved to the Pope alone, and to him not except as God, that is, as the vicar of God; therefore the Pope is removed from office only by a superior, as God is, since the papacy surpasses all dignities. It may be objected that there seems to be no reason why the Lord should will that bishops be deposed only by the superior Pope, as God, and yet that the Pope himself can be removed by inferiors. Seventhly, it seems that God wills that he alone, by himself, can remove the Pope, since he alone is superior to him. The fourth argument: a supreme created power can be taken away only by a supreme power; but the papacy is the supreme created power; therefore, etc. The fifth argument: neither the Pope nor the whole universe of creatures can bring it about that the Pontiff is not the Pontiff; therefore much less can he bring it about that the supreme Pontiff is not the supreme Pontiff. The sixth argument: the Pope is Pope only by divine law, and not by the law of a creature, nor of all creatures together; therefore it seems in no way possible that the Pope can be freed so as not to be Pope. For once the Pope has consented and voluntarily submitted himself, he cannot cease to be Pope through any creature or all creatures together. The seventh argument: no one can annul another's vow except one who is above that vow; but the papacy is a vow above all vows, since the Pope vows to bear the care of the universal Church and of the Lord's flock, and that he will render an account of it; therefore he can be absolved from this very obligation by none but himself. For he cannot absolve himself from an obligation to any other superior, but only a superior can absolve him. The eighth argument: no one seems able to absolve himself from sin; therefore neither from the papacy, which would follow if he could resign voluntarily. The ninth argument: the papal obligation does not seem able to be removed except by a greater power than the papal one; yet there is no greater power than this; therefore, etc. The tenth argument: no ecclesiastical dignity, once lawfully confirmed, can be removed except by its superior; but the Pope has no superior except God; therefore, etc. The eleventh argument: the Apostle wills that the priesthood of Christ is eternal, because Christ lives for ever; therefore the life of the high priest can in no way be without the high priesthood. This, however, would be false if the Pope could resign.

units.la: Ista sunt media, quæ videre potui ad hanc partem, quod Papa non possit renunciare, vel deponi.
units.tr: These are the means which I have been able to see for the side that the Pope cannot renounce or be deposed.

units.la: NUnc vero ostendendum multipliciter exemplis & rationibus, & auctoritatibus, quod Papa possit renunciare, & inuitus deponi. De renunciatione ponit exemplum de B. Clemente: de quo legitur in gestis Romanorum Pontificum, quod renunciauit, & post Linum & Cletum cathedram recepit, ita quod Clemens fuit immediatus post Petrum, sed eo renunciante receperunt cathedram, Linus & Cletus, post quos fuit quartus à B. Petro. Istud tamen exemplum potest capere calumniam, eo quod Aimo in Christianorum regum memoria & in aliis quibusdã historiis dixisse legitur, quod Linus & Cletus non sederunt Pontifices, sed vt summi Pontificis coadiutores: quibus B. Petrus in vita sua Ecclesiasticarum rerum dispensationem tradidit, ipse vero tantum orationi & prædicationi vacabat. Et ideo prædicti Linus & Cletus tanta auctoritate dotati, meruerunt in catalogo summorum Pontificum reponi. Et sic secundum istos Clemens non renunciauit, sed immediate post Petrum cathedram tenuit usq; ad Anacletum, vel usq; ad Euaristum: puto tamen verius esse primum. & quod ideo forte Clemens resignare voluit, quia Petro adhuc viuente, ab ipso in Papam fuit ordinatus, vt ipse scribit ad B. Iacobum Hierosolymitanum episcopum. Aliud exemplum potest poni de Marcellino, qui fuit tempore Diocletiani: hic renunciauit, vt dicit in Glossa ordinaria, 6. q. 1. ca. non autem. & 21. dist. nō autem dicitur, quod se ipsum deposuit. sua enim renunciatio, fuit quædam depositio. Ipsemet, vt dicit Hugo ex gestis Pontificum, contra seipsum sententiam tulit dicendo, & contra se ipsum eam proferendo, dicens: Ego Marcellinus ob scelus idololatriæ, quod ego infelix commisi, iudico me condemnandum & deponendum: anathematizo etiam, quicunque corpus meum tradiderit sepulturæ. Exemplum etiam potest poni de Cyriaco Papa, de quo legitur, quod cum Vrsula & 11. millibus virginum martyrizatus est. Scribitur etiam de eo, quod nocte quædam sibi relatum est, quod cum illis virginibus esset palmam martyrii recepturus: tunc clero & cardinalibus congregatis, omnibus inuitis, & præcipue cardinalibus, coram omnibus renunciauit & dignitati & officio. Sed iste Cyriacus in catalogo Paparum non annumeratur: quia credebant ipsum non propter deuotionem, sed propter oblectamentum virginum dimisisse episcopatum. Auctoritates etiam sanctorum sunt ad hæc idem, vnde Glossa ordinaria 7. q. 1. non autem, mouet quæstionem in propria forma, nunquid Papa renunciare possit? & dicit quod sic, assignans pro ratione, quod Marcellinus renunciauit, & etiam Clemens. Hugo etiam mouet eandem ibi dist. sed quid de renunciatione Papæ? nunquid renunciare potest, quia vult transfire ad religionem, vel est æger vel senex. Et respondet, quod vtique potest renunciare: assignans pro causa, quod Marcellinus renunciauit, & Clemens. Et similiter 21. distinct. ca. non autem, mouet eandem quæstionem Hugo: & respondet quod sic, si expediret, & alias peccaret.
units.tr: Now, however, it must be shown in many ways, by examples, reasons and authorities, that the Pope can renounce and be deposed against his will. As an example of renunciation, they cite Saint Clement, of whom it is read in the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs that he renounced, and after Linus and Cletus he received the chair; so that Clement was immediately after Peter, but when he renounced, Linus and Cletus received the chair, after whom the fourth was from Saint Peter. This example, however, may be open to challenge, because it is read that Aimo, in the Memorial of the Christian Kings, and in some other histories, said that Linus and Cletus were not Pontiffs but coadjutors of the supreme Pontiff, to whom Saint Peter, during his life, handed over the dispensing of ecclesiastical affairs, while he himself devoted himself only to prayer and preaching. And therefore Linus and Cletus, endowed with such authority, deserved to be placed in the catalogue of the supreme Pontiffs. And so, according to these men, Clement did not renounce, but held the chair immediately after Peter until Anacletus, or until Evaristus; yet I think the first view is truer. And perhaps Clement wished to resign for this reason, that he had been ordained Pope by Peter while Peter was still living, as he himself writes to Saint James, bishop of Jerusalem. Another example can be given of Marcellinus, who was in the time of Diocletian: he renounced, as the ordinary Gloss says, 6. q. 1. c. non autem, and 21. dist. But it is not said that he deposed himself; for his renunciation was a kind of deposition. He himself, as Hugo says from the Deeds of the Pontiffs, pronounced sentence against himself, saying and declaring it against himself: I, Marcellinus, on account of the crime of idolatry which I, unhappy man, have committed, judge myself to be condemned and deposed; I also anathematize whoever shall commit my body to burial. An example may also be given of Pope Cyriacus, of whom it is read that he was martyred together with Ursula and eleven thousand virgins. It is also written of him that on a certain night it was reported to him that he would receive the palm of martyrdom with those virgins; then, with the clergy and cardinals gathered, all being unwilling, and especially the cardinals, he renounced both the dignity and the office before them all. But this Cyriacus is not counted in the catalogue of Popes, because they believed that he gave up the episcopate not out of devotion, but for the pleasure of the virgins. Also the authorities of the saints bear on these matters in the same way; whence the ordinary Gloss, 7. q. 1. non autem, raises the question in its own form, whether the Pope can renounce? and says that he can, assigning as the reason that Marcellinus renounced, and Clement too. Hugo also raises the same question in the same distinction: but what of the renunciation of a Pope? Can he renounce because he wishes to pass over to a religious order, or because he is sick or old? And he answers that he certainly can renounce, assigning as the cause that Marcellinus renounced, and Clement. Likewise 21. dist. c. non autem, Hugo raises the same question, and answers that he can, if it is expedient, and otherwise he would sin.

units.la: Ad hoc etiam possunt adduci rationes ex parte causæ finalis: quia non eligitur aliquis in Papam, nisi propter bonum commune Ecclesiæ & gregis Dominici, ad hoc etiam præest vt prosit. Si ergo postquam fuit in papatu, inuenerit se, vel inuentus fuerit ineptus totaliter, & inutilis, vel superuenia impedimentū: vt insania, vel aliud simile, debet petere cessionem à populo vel à cœtu cardinalium, qui in tali casu est loco totius cleri & totius populi: qua obtenta vel non obtenta cedere tenetur, aliter enim, quod ex charitate institutum est, contra charitatem militaret, si inutiliter & ad malum ecclesiæ & ad damnum animæ suæ residens renunciare non posset. Hoc enim generaliter est verum, quia nulla obligatio facta voluntarie præiudicare potest charitati, vel obligationi: quia quisque tenetur solicitus esse de salute animæ suæ: sicut religiosus, qui determinatam regulam nouit, si videatur sibi & animæ suæ expediens, ad acriorem transire potest, petita licentia à superiore, & ea obtenta vel non obtenta transire potest ad eam libere. 19. q. 2. duæ sunt leges. Qui priuata lege ducitur, nulla ratio est vt lege publica constringatur.
units.tr: Arguments can also be brought forward for this from the side of the final cause: for no one is chosen as Pope except for the common good of the Church and of the Lord's flock; he is set over them also that he may profit them. If therefore, after he has been in the papacy, he finds himself, or is found, to be wholly unfit and useless, or some impediment supervenes, such as madness or something similar, he ought to seek release from the people or from the college of cardinals, who in such a case stand in the place of the whole clergy and the whole people. When this is obtained or not obtained, he is bound to resign; for otherwise what was instituted out of charity would act against charity, if he remained in office uselessly and to the harm of the Church and to the ruin of his own soul, and could not resign. For this is true in general, because no obligation freely undertaken can prejudice charity or a higher obligation; for each one is bound to be solicitous for the salvation of his own soul: just as a religious who knows his determined rule, if it seems to him and to his soul expedient, can pass to a stricter one, having asked leave of his superior; and whether this is obtained or not, he may pass to it freely. 19. q. 2. duae sunt leges. He who is led by a private law, there is no reason why he should be bound by a public law.

units.la: Et ideo si perpendit mollities animi, vel ineptitudo in scandalum Ecclesiæ, vel quod turbet Ecclesiam, seu quod diuidat gregem Domini, faciens diuisiones, & suscitans scandala, & si admonitus non desistat, etiam compellendus est ad cessionem. extr. de renunciatione decendendi: Et, cum inpostulationibus.
units.tr: And so, if his weakness of mind or his unfitness is seen to cause scandal to the Church, or to disturb the Church, or to divide the Lord's flock by making divisions and stirring up offences, and if he does not desist when admonished, he is to be compelled even to resign. Extra, de renunciatione: Et, cum inpostulationibus.

units.la: Non est igitur irrationabile dicere, quod Papa possit cedere inuito populo & reclamante, sicut fecit beatus Cyriacus: & quod ipse inuitus etiam de consensu populi in tali casu possit deponi, quia cum ipse Papa, & quilibet alius prælatus præsit non propter se, sed propter populum vt scilicest prosit, efficacior est consensus populi in hoc casu ad deponendum eum etiam inuitum, si totaliter inuiti iis videatur, & ad eligendum alium, quam eius voluntas ad renunciandum voluntarius vel inuitus populo nolente.
units.tr: It is therefore not unreasonable to say that the Pope can resign even though the people are unwilling and protest, as blessed Cyriacus did, and that in such a case he can be deposed even against his will by the consent of the people. For the Pope, like any other prelate, presides not for his own sake but for the people's, that is, so that he may benefit them. In this case the consent of the people, if they are wholly unwilling to have him, is more effective for deposing him even against his will, and for choosing another, than his own will is for resigning, whether he is willing or unwilling, when the people do not want it.

units.la: In depositione tamen, qua depositur voluntarius, & per populum, eum maiori maturitate est incedendum, quam in cessione vel renunciatione voluntaria: quia ad renunciationem sufficit, quod causam alleget coram collegio cardinalium, quod est in hoc casu loco totius Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Yet in deposition, where a man is deposed against his will by the people, more caution must be used than in a voluntary cession or resignation. For to resign it is enough that he state his cause before the college of cardinals, which in this case stands in place of the whole Church.

units.la: Sed ad deponendum decet, quod fiat per concilium generale: vt patet vigesima prima distinctione, cap. non autem: vbi dicitur, quod conuocatum fuit concilium generale ad depositionem Marcellini. Credo tamen, quod simpliciter sufficeret ad depositionem huiusmodi collegium cardinalium: quia ex quo consensus eorum facit Papam loco ecclesiæ, videtur quod similiter possit eum deponere, siquidem fuerit causa rationabilis, & deponunt eum meritorie. Si vero non fuerit sufficiens peccant. Dicere autem quod aliqua hic adducta non tenent contra Papam, qui non habet superiorem, non valet, vt patebit soluendo argumentum.
units.tr: For deposition, however, it is fitting that it be done by a general council, as is clear from distinction twenty-one, chapter Non autem: where it is said that a general council was convoked for the deposition of Marcellinus. I believe, nevertheless, that a college of cardinals would simply suffice for such a deposition, since, as their consent makes the Pope in place of the Church, it seems that they can similarly depose him, provided the cause is reasonable; and in deposing him they act meritoriously. If the cause is not sufficient, they sin. To say, however, that the things adduced here do not hold against the Pope, who has no superior, is no valid objection, as will be shown in answering the argument.

units.la: Ad primum ergo cum dicitur, quod papatus à solo Deo est, respondeo: Dicendum est, quod potestas Papalis potest dupliciter considerari. Vno modo secundum se, & sic est à solo Deo, quia solus Deus potest hanc potestatem dare hominibus, quod absolutus vel ligatus in terra sit absolutus vel ligatus in coelo. Alio modo potest considerari, vt est in isto vel in illo: & sic est à solo Deo, eo modo quo omnia opera nostra Deo attribuimus. Isaiæ decimo sexto. Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis Domine: ipse enim est, qui operatur omnia in nobis, & velle & perficere: sed quæ sic sunt, à solo Deo sunt: sicut ei soli attribuitur omne opus nostrum. si operamur, non deficimus in opere quod in nobis est, non excludit operationem nostram, nam cooperatores Dei sumus. Igitur licet Papatus sit à solo Deo, in se tamen in hac persona vel illa, est per cooperationem humanam, scilicet per consensum electi & eligentium. & secundum hoc per consensum humanum potest desinere esse in isto, vel in illo: sicut cum anima rationalis sit à solo Deo per creationem, tamen quod sit in hoc corpore, cooperatur humidum radicale, & naturæ dispositio, in disponendo & organizando corpus: & ideo per operationem naturalem potest desinere esse in illo corpore, quando scilicet calor naturalis consumpsit in tantum humidum, quod corpus sit ineptum pro anima rationali. Ad rationem, cum dicitur quod solus Deus potest conferre Papatum, ergo & auferre: dicendum est, vt ad primam, & per idem exemplum potest etiam addi illud exemplum: nam solus Deus dat gloriam, & tamen oportet, quod ibi homo cooperetur: quia qui fecit te sine te, non iustificabit te sine te. Et potest aliquis auferre sibi gratiam suam per actum suum.
units.tr: As to the first point, where it is said that the papacy is from God alone, I answer: it must be said that papal power can be considered in two ways. In one way, in itself, and so it is from God alone, because God alone can give to men this power, that whatever is loosed or bound by them on earth is loosed or bound in heaven. In another way it can be considered as it is in this person or that, and so it is from God alone in the same way that we attribute all our works to God. Isaiah 16. You have wrought all our works in us, O Lord. For he is the one who works in us all, both the willing and the doing. But things that are so are from God alone, just as every work of ours is attributed to him alone. If we work, we do not fail in the work that is in us; this does not exclude our operation, for we are God's co-workers. Therefore, although the papacy is from God alone, in itself, in this person or that, it is by human co-operation, namely by the consent of the one elected and of those electing. In this way, by human consent, it can cease to be in this person or that. So too, although the rational soul is from God alone by creation, yet that it is in this body is brought about by the radical moisture and the disposition of nature in disposing and organizing the body. Therefore by natural operation it can cease to be in that body, namely when natural heat has consumed so much moisture that the body is unfit for a rational soul. As to the argument that because God alone can confer the papacy, he alone can also take it away, the answer is the same as to the first point, and by the same example one may add this: God alone gives glory, and yet there must be human co-operation there, since he who made you without yourself will not justify you without yourself. And a man can take away his own grace by his own act.

units.la: Ad tertiam rationem, de illa decretali, inter corporalia, de translatione episcop. vbi positio, translatio & cessio episcoporum reseruatur soli Papæ: respondeo: Hoc magis est ad concludendum, quod Papa possit sine auctoritate superioris renunciare, quam quod non possit: quod enim exigentia rerum hoc habeat, vt per quem aliquid construitur, per hoc eadem contrario modo se habentia destruantur: sicut fit coniugium quoddam inter prælatum & ecclesiam per consensum eligentium & electi, ita per dissensum dissoluitur. Vnde quilibet episcopus inueniens se mollem & ineptum ad curam & regimen ecclesiæ suæ, allegata causa coram populo vel capitulo suo posset resignare, nisi esset à superiore ei prohibitum, & ei specialiter reseruatum de episcopis & archiepiscopis, per illam decretalem, inter corporalia. Et quia de Papa non inuenitur prohibitum, sicut de episcopis inferioribus: ideo Papa potest resignare & deponi sine auctoritate cuiuscunque superioris. In talibus enim, quæ fiunt secundum exigentiam rei & causæ, hoc est licitum, quod non est prohibitum: in illis vero quæ supra rei & causæ conditionem sunt, non est aliquid licitum, quod non fuerit concessum: vt ordinare de ecclesiis quæ pertinent ad Papam, qui est caput ecclesiæ, est super conditionem episcoporum inferiorum. Vnde nulli eorum est licitum, nisi specialiter sibi fit concessum. Non est igitur simile de Papa, de quo non est reseruatum superiori: nec ei prohibita est resignatio & de inferioribus episcopis, quibus interdicta est, & superiori reseruata. Potest nihilominus aliter responderi ad hoc argumentum, & ad alia quædam, quod vbi apparet manifeste causa rationabilis, sicut vbi est defectus manifestus, supponitur consensus & auctoritas Dei ad renunciationem & depositionem, sicut in eius confirmationem supponitur.
units.tr: To the third argument, concerning that decretal, Inter corporalia, de translatione episcoporum, where the placing, transfer and cession of bishops is reserved to the Pope alone: I answer that this rather serves to show that the Pope can resign without the authority of a superior than that he cannot. For it is in the nature of things that what is built up by certain means is destroyed in the contrary way, by the same means: thus a kind of marriage is made between the prelate and the Church by the consent of the electors and of the one elected, and in the same way it is dissolved by dissent. Hence any bishop who finds himself weak and unfit for the care and government of his church could, after stating his cause before his people or chapter, resign, unless this had been forbidden him by a superior and specially reserved for bishops and archbishops by that decretal, Inter corporalia. And since nothing is found forbidding it for the Pope, as it is for lower bishops, the Pope can resign and be deposed without the authority of any superior. For in matters that are done according to the nature of the thing and the cause, whatever is not forbidden is lawful; but in those matters which go beyond the condition of the thing and the cause, nothing is lawful that has not been granted. Thus, to ordain for churches that belong to the Pope, who is the head of the Church, goes beyond the condition of lower bishops, and so none of them may do it unless it has been specially granted to him. Therefore the case of the Pope is not similar: nothing has been reserved to a superior concerning him, and resignation is not forbidden to him as it is forbidden to lower bishops and reserved to a superior. Nevertheless, this argument and certain others may also be answered otherwise: where a reasonable cause clearly appears, as where there is a manifest defect, God's consent and authority to resignation and deposition are presupposed, just as they are presupposed for his confirmation.

units.la: Est tamen considerandum, quod ex decretali prædicta posset aliquis prædictum argumentum fortificare sic: quia ibi dicitur, quod fortius est vinculum spirituale inter episcopum & ecclesiam, quam carnale inter virum & vxorem suam. Si ergo vinculum carnale inter virum & vxorem nulla humana potestate vel auctoritate, vel consensu quorumcunque interuenienti potest solui: ergo nec vinculum spirituale Papæ ad ecclesiam. In episcopatu enim contrahitur matrimonium spirituale, in electione ratificatur, in confirmatione & consecratione consumatur. Respondeo: Vinculum spirituale dicitur fortius carnali, quia dignius, & non quia durabilius. Potest enim solui spirituale matrimonium etiam post consecrationem, episcopi translatione. 7. quæst. 1. mutationes; & cap. pastoralis depositione vt 1. d. postquam. cessione, vt extra, de renunciatione, in multis locis. Non sic autem matrimonium carnale. Vel ideo dicitur fortius, quia plus adigit & constringit quam carnale: prælatus enim maiorem curam debet habere de ecclesia sua, cum sit bonum commune, quam vir de sua vxore, cum hoc sit bonum particulare. Vel dicitur fortius, quia de se fortius est, quam carnale: quod enim carnale sit durabilius, quia coniuges non possunt separari quamdiu viuunt, hoc potissime habet ex mandato Christi, qui hoc præcepit in Euangelio dicens: Quos Deus coniunxit, homo non separet. propter quod Apostol. primo Corinth. septimo dicit: Præcipio non ego, sed Deus, vxorem à viro non discedere: quod si discesserit, manere innuptam, aut cum viro reconciliari. Ratio autem quare mandauit Deus non solui matrimonium carnale, est, quia ex eius solutione licet interdum posset prouenire bonum personale, tamen hoc esset in malum commune: quia inducerentur homines communiter ad dimittendum vxores, secus vero est de matrimonio spirituali. Si enim persona cum est inutilis & scandalizatiua, non posset resignare depositioni, & alius eligi, hoc esset in malum commune: quia cum talis præesset, hoc esset in bonum particularis personæ, ideo istud non prohibuit. imo si intelligatur ratio legislatoris prohibendo matrimonium carnale non dissolui, præcepit spirituale dissolui: quando manifeste apparet, quod obest bono communi.
units.tr: It must be considered, however, that from the aforesaid decretal one could strengthen the aforesaid argument thus: because there it is said that the spiritual bond between bishop and Church is stronger than the carnal bond between man and wife. If, then, the carnal bond between man and wife cannot be dissolved by any human power, authority, or the consent of anyone intervening, then neither can the spiritual bond of the Pope to the Church. For in the episcopate a spiritual marriage is contracted, in election it is ratified, and in confirmation and consecration it is consummated. I answer: the spiritual bond is said to be stronger than the carnal because it is more worthy, not because it is more lasting. For a spiritual marriage can be dissolved even after consecration, by translation of the bishop, 7. quaest. 1, Mutationes; and chapter Pastoralis, by deposition, as in 1. dist. Postquam, by cession, as in Extra, de renunciatione, and in many places. This is not so with carnal marriage. Or it is called stronger because it binds and constrains more than the carnal: for a prelate ought to have greater care for his Church, since it is a common good, than a husband for his wife, since that is a private good. Or it is called stronger because in itself it is stronger than the carnal. For that the carnal bond is more lasting, so that spouses cannot be separated as long as they live, this it has above all by the command of Christ, who commanded it in the Gospel, saying: What God has joined together, let not man put asunder. Wherefore the Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 7, says: I command, not I but the Lord, that the wife depart not from her husband; but if she depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. The reason why God commanded that carnal marriage not be dissolved is that, although its dissolution might sometimes bring a private good, it would be a common evil, since men would be led generally to dismiss their wives. It is otherwise with spiritual marriage. For if a person is useless and a cause of scandal, and could not resign so that deposition and the election of another might follow, this would be a common evil, since, while such a person presided, it would be a good only for a private individual. Therefore God did not forbid this. Indeed, if the lawgiver's reason is understood, in forbidding carnal marriage to be dissolved he commanded spiritual marriage to be dissolved, whenever it clearly appears that it is harmful to the common good.

units.la: Ad quartam rationem, quæ videtur specialiter probare, quod Papa non possit deponi voluntarius, quia Papatus est summa virtus creata: respondeo, Hic dicerent aliqui, quod argumentum concludit cludit verum : quia licet renunciare possit, tamen inuitus deponi non potest, nisi forte sit haereticus: quia sic pro mortuo habetur, & ita se habens non potest esse caput Christianorum. Et hoc ipsi ostendunt per hoc, quod habetur in d. cap. nunc autem: vbi dicitur, quod nullus rite potest ab his, qui sunt inferiores dignitatis vel ordinis, iudicialibus submitti diffinitionibus. Et ibidem etiam dicitur de Marcellino Papa, quod nullus episcoporum ausus est in eum proferre sententiam: sed sibi dicebant, Non nostro iudicio, sed ore tuo iudica causam tuam. & rursum dixerunt, Non audiri in nostro iudicio, sed collige in sinu tuo causam tuam. Et rursus inquit, Ex ore tuo condemnaberis. propter quod in Legenda eius dicitur, quod seipsum deposuit, & depositus postea est reelectus. Sed istud non intelligitur, quia cum Papa praesit ecclesiae, si potest renunciare nolente ecclesia, vt dictum est de beato Cyriaco: quare non potest voluntarius deponi per ecclesiam, si causa subsit necessaria. Amplius, casu specialis ecclesiae, vbi episcopus nullo tempore ad sanae mentis officium redit: vel etiam si interdum redit, & requisitus cedere noluerit, potest & debet alium eligere. 7. quaestione 1. qualiter. cap. quamuis triste, & ibidem Iohan. & extra de renunciat. cap. quod cedendum. Ergo a simili, collegium cardinalium vice totius Ecclesiae poterit Papam inuitum deponere.
