Item distinctione 40. cap. si Papa, dicitur: Cunctos iudicaturus, a nemine iudicandus, nisi deprehendatur a fide deuius. vbi dicit Glossa, quod si deprehenderetur in quolibet alio vitio, & admonitus non corrigeretur, & ecclesiam scandalizaret, & incorrigibilis esset, inde posset accusari & deponi: quia talis contumacia haeresi aequipollet. Item, si in haeresim lapsus, deponi potest, quia pro mortuo habetur: quare non similiter, si in vitium labatur, de quo non exhibet se corrigibilem, cum talis etiam pro mortuo habeatur: & nihil ei reputetur, dicente Augustino, quod peccatum nihil est, & nihil fiunt homines cum peccant. Pro defectu etiamsi requisitus noluerit renunciare, alius ordinandus est ipso inuito, quia sic videtur malignari.
units.tr: To the fourth argument, which seems specially to prove that the Pope cannot be deposed voluntarily because the papacy is the highest created power: I reply that some would say here that the argument is true in its conclusion. Although he can resign, he cannot be deposed against his will unless perhaps he is a heretic, for then he is regarded as dead and in that condition cannot be head of Christians. They show this from what is found in d. cap. nunc autem, where it is said that no one can properly be subjected to judicial decisions by those who are inferior in dignity or order. And in the same place it is said of Pope Marcellinus that no bishop dared pronounce sentence against him, but they said to him, Judge your own cause not by our judgment but by your own mouth, and again they said, Your cause is not to be heard in our judgment, but gather your cause into your own bosom. And again he says, You shall be condemned by your own mouth. For this reason it is said in his Legenda that he deposed himself, and was afterwards re-elected after being deposed. But this is not understood in that way, because since the Pope presides over the Church, if he can resign while the Church is unwilling, as was said of blessed Cyriacus, then why can he not be deposed voluntarily by the Church, if a necessary cause exists? Further, in the case of a particular church, where a bishop never returns to the office of sound mind, or if he sometimes returns but, when asked to resign, is unwilling to do so, the church can and must elect another: 7. quaestione 1. qualiter. cap. quamuis triste, and there John, and & extra de renunciat. cap. quod cedendum. Therefore by parity, the college of cardinals, in place of the whole Church, will be able to depose the Pope against his will. Likewise, distinctione 40. cap. si Papa says: He is to judge all, and to be judged by no one, unless he is found to have strayed from the faith. Where the Gloss says that if he were found in any other vice, and not corrected when admonished, and scandalized the Church, and were incorrigible, he could be accused and deposed from that, because such obstinacy is equivalent to heresy. Likewise, if he has fallen into heresy he can be deposed, because he is regarded as dead; why then, if he falls into vice, and does not show himself correctable in it, should it not likewise be so, since such a man is also regarded as dead, and nothing is to be reckoned to him, Augustine saying that sin is nothing and that men become nothing when they sin? If, through defect, he is asked and refuses to resign, another must be ordained in spite of him, since otherwise he would seem to be acting maliciously.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur de Marcellino, quod non ausi fuerunt eum condemnare: hoc fuit, quia poenituit, & corrigi voluit. Et quia nihil erat probatum contra eum, nisi quantum ex ore suo voluntarie confitebatur, & ideo ex ore suo iudicatur.
units.tr: As for what is said of Marcellinus, that they did not dare to condemn him: this was because he repented and wished to be corrected. And since nothing had been proved against him except insofar as he freely confessed it from his own mouth, therefore he is judged by his own mouth.

units.la: Quod ergo dicitur in principali argumento, quod Papatus est summa virtus creata, & sic non potest auferri. Respondeo: Licet sit summa virtus in persona, tamen est ei aequalis vel maior in collegio, siue in tota ecclesia. Vel potest dici, quod potest deponi a collegio, vel magis a generali concilio, auctoritate diuina, cuius consensus supponitur & praesumitur ad eum deponendum, vbi apparet manifestum scandalum, & incorrigibilitas ipsius praesidentis.
units.tr: As for what is said in the principal argument, that the papacy is the highest created power and so cannot be taken away: I reply that although it is the highest power in the person, nevertheless it is equal or greater in the college, or in the whole Church. Or it may be said that he can be deposed by the college, or rather by a general council, by divine authority, whose consent is presupposed and presumed for deposing him, where manifest scandal appears and the president himself is incorrigible.

units.la: Ad quintam rationem, vbi dicitur, quod non potest fieri, quin summus Pontifex sit summus Pontifex: sicut quod Pontifex non sit Pontifex: respondeo, Non est simile: quia sacerdos & Pontisex non dicunt, nisi ea quae sunt ordinis, scilicet characterem sacerdotalem, vel potestatem fundatam super ipso charactere, licet diuersimode: quia in sacerdote imprimitur character quasi imperfectus, super quo fundatur potestas conficiendi, sed non faciendi alium sacerdotem sibi similem in potestate conficiendi. Episcopo autem confertur characteris perfectio, in quo fundatur sacerdotalis potestas perfecta: qua potest alium sacerdotem facere, & ita episcopus est vir perfectus, sacerdos vero simplex vt puer. Episcopus etiam est sacerdos non quilibet, sed magnus, & sponsus Ecclesiae: quia potest quasi generare sibi similes, scilicet ordinando sacerdotes. Archiepiscopus vero, Patriarcha, sicut primas, & Papa, non important ex nomine suo vltra sacerdotium & episcopatum, aliquid, quod pertineat ad potestatem ordinis, vel eius augmentum vel perfectionem: sed solum dicunt ex nomine suo gradus iurisdictionis, archiepiscopus quidem in sua prouincia, primas in regno, Papa in tota Ecclesia. Et quia potestas ordinis est indelebilis, & eius perfectio indelebilis, eo quod super characterem, & super characteris perfectionem fundatur: ideo nulla virtute fieri potest, quod sacerdos non sit sacerdos, vel quod episcopus non sit episcopus. Iurisdictio vero sicut potest augeri vel minui, ita & deleri & tolli: & ideo amota iurisdictione Papa definit esse Papa, & summus Pontifex definit esse summus Pontifex, licet non desinat esse Pontifex.
units.tr: To the fifth argument, where it is said that it cannot come about that the supreme Pontiff is not the supreme Pontiff, just as a Pontiff is not a Pontiff: I reply, this is not similar, because priest and Pontiff signify only what belongs to order, namely the priestly character, or power founded upon that character, though in different ways. For in a priest a character is imprinted as it were imperfect, upon which is founded the power of consecrating, but not of making another priest like himself in the power of consecrating. But to a bishop is conferred the perfection of the character, upon which the perfect priestly power is founded, by which he can make another priest; and so the bishop is a perfect man, whereas the simple priest is like a child. The bishop is also a priest not just any priest, but a great one, and the bridegroom of the Church, because he can, as it were, beget priests like himself by ordaining them. The archbishop, however, the patriarch, the primate, and the Pope, do not import by their name anything beyond the priesthood and episcopate that pertains to the power of order, or its increase or perfection; but by their name they signify only grades of jurisdiction: the archbishop in his province, the primate in the kingdom, the Pope in the whole Church. And because the power of order is indelible, and its perfection is indelible, since it is founded upon the character and upon the perfection of the character, therefore by no power can it come about that a priest is not a priest, or that a bishop is not a bishop. Jurisdiction, however, can be increased or diminished, and likewise destroyed and taken away; and therefore, with jurisdiction removed, the Pope ceases to be Pope, and the supreme Pontiff ceases to be supreme Pontiff, although he does not cease to be Pontiff.

units.la: Ad sextam rationem, cum dicitur quod Papa non est Papa, nisi per legem diuinam, & non per legem alicuius creaturae: & quod ex quo subiecit se legi sponte, non potest non esse Papa per aliquam creaturam, vel per omnes: respondeo, Haec ratio duplici innititur fundamento. vnum est, quod Papa est Papa per legem diuinam, quae est immutabilis, & ideo non potest desinere esse Papa. Aliud est quod subiecit se legi sponte, quae est, in ea perpetuari.
units.tr: To the sixth argument, where it is said that the Pope is Pope only by divine law, and not by the law of any creature; and that since he has subjected himself to the law voluntarily, he cannot cease to be Pope through any creature, or through all: I reply that this argument rests on a twofold foundation. The one is that the Pope is Pope by divine law, which is immutable, and therefore he cannot cease to be Pope. The other is that he has voluntarily subjected himself to the law, which is that he remains perpetually in it.

units.la: Quantum ad primum fundamentum, responderi potest, quod non obstante, quod Papa est Papa per legem diuinam, quae est immutabilis, tamen potest non esse Papa: quia licet diuina lex sit immutabilis formaliter & in se, secundum quod inferiora reducuntur in Deum per superiora, & sic inferiores praelati per Papam: tamen mutabilis est materialiter, in isto scilicet vel in illo, vt in Coelestino vel Bonifacio: quia ad hoc cooperatur creatura, vt dictum est supra. Quod ergo Papa sit super omnes, est de lege diuina, & non potest contrarium fieri: sed quod iste vel ille sit Papa, mutabile est, quia ad hoc cooperatur consensus eligentium & electi.
units.tr: As to the first foundation, it can be answered that, notwithstanding that the Pope is Pope by divine law, which is immutable, he nevertheless can cease to be Pope; for although divine law is immutable formally and in itself, insofar as inferiors are led back to God through superiors, and so inferior prelates through the Pope, yet it is mutable materially, in this or that person, as in Celestine or Boniface, because a creature cooperates in this, as was said above. That the Pope is over all is of divine law, and the contrary cannot come about; but that this or that man is Pope is mutable, because the consent of electors and of the elected cooperates in this.

units.la: Quantum ad secundum fundamentum, responderi potest, quod Papa subiecit se legi sponte Ecclesiae, quae est, in ea perpetuari, quantum ad ea quae sunt ordinis: quia semper potest ea facere, quae sunt spiritualia, scilicet ordinare: quia si quem ordinet, ordinatus est. Sed quantum ad ea quae sunt iurisdictionis ex lege sponte, non est perpetuo & immobiliter subditus ecclesiae, quia iurisdictio potest auferri. Ratio autem, quare illa quae sunt ordinis, non possunt auferri, & ea quae sunt iurisdictionis nis auferri possunt, esse potest, quia ea quæ iurisdictionis sunt, non sunt super naturâ & conditionem negocii, & super conditionem hominum: quia non est super conditionem hominis, quod homines prasint hominibus, imo naturale est quodammodo. In talibus autem quod non est prohibitum, est concessum, vt per eandem causas destruatur, per quas construitur, modo contrario se habetes. Et ideo sicut per consensum hominum iurisdictio datur, ita per contrarium consensum tollitur. Ea autem quæ sunt ordinis, sunt super naturam & conditionem negocii & rerum, vt quod ad probationem talium verborum character vel potestas spiritualis imprimatur in anima: & ideo in talibus quod non est expresse concessum, est negatum: unde quia expresse collatum est, quod ad tale verbum talis character imprimatur, ideo sic fit. Sed quia non immediate expresse inuenitur collatum, quod per quemcunque modum auferatur: ideo impressio vel collatio characteris, super quo fundatur potestas ordinis, est indelebilis.
units.tr: As to the second foundation, it can be answered that the Pope has voluntarily subjected himself to the law of the Church, which is that he remains perpetually in it as regards those things that belong to order: for he can always do those things which are spiritual, namely ordain, since if he ordains anyone, that person is ordained. But as regards those things which belong to jurisdiction by voluntary law, he is not perpetually and immovably subject to the Church, because jurisdiction can be taken away. The reason why those things that belong to order cannot be taken away, while those that belong to jurisdiction can be taken away, may be this: that what belongs to jurisdiction is not above the nature and condition of the matter, nor above the condition of men; for it is not above the condition of man that men should preside over men, indeed it is in a manner natural. In such matters, what is not forbidden is permitted, so that things are undone by the same causes by which they are built up, being in the opposite condition. And therefore, just as jurisdiction is given by the consent of men, so by contrary consent it is removed. But those things which belong to order are above the nature and condition of the matter and of things, such as that a spiritual character or power is imprinted on the soul by the pronouncing of such words; and therefore in such matters what is not expressly granted is denied. Hence, because it is expressly granted that such a character is imprinted by such a word, it is so done. But because it is not expressly found granted, immediately, that it may be removed by any means whatever, therefore the impression or conferral of the character, upon which the power of order is founded, is indelible.

units.la: Per hoc ergo quod Papa legi sponte se subiecit, perpetuari habet in ea, quantum ad illa quæ sunt ordinis, vt quantum ad sacerdotium & episcopatum, in quibus imprimitur characteris perfectio: sed quantum ad ea, quæ sunt papatus vel summi pontificatus, cum papatus & summus pontificatus non addant nisi iurisdictionem, non oportet quod perpetuetur, cum iurisdictioni renunciare possit.
units.tr: Therefore, by the fact that the Pope has willingly submitted himself to the law, the following holds for him: as regards those things which belong to orders, that is, as regards the priesthood and the episcopate, in which the character is impressed to its perfection, it is perpetual; but as regards those things which belong to the papacy or the supreme pontificate, since the papacy and the supreme pontificate add nothing but jurisdiction, it is not necessary that it be perpetual, since he can renounce jurisdiction.

units.la: Ad septimam rationem de voto, quod Papa emisit: respondeo, Votum Papæ, quod scil. vniuersaliter habebit curam gregis Dominici, debet intelligi, quamdiu erit in officio, scilicet quamdiu erit Papa. Sic enim illi qui fiunt, potestates communiter iurant se tenere statuta communitatis, & seruare communitates illas in statu bono: quæ omnia intelligenda sunt, quamdiu durat officium eorum. Iuramentum enim quo aliquis iuraret, quod semper esset in officio tali vel Papatu, & simpliciter vel absolute haberet curam de proposito semper, esset illicitum: quia militare posset contra bonum commune, vtpote si videret se insufficientem, & bonum commune languere, & perire sub se.
units.tr: To the seventh argument, concerning the vow which the Pope made: I answer that the Pope's vow, namely that he will universally have the care of the Lord's flock, must be understood as lasting as long as he is in office, that is, as long as he is Pope. For in this way those who are made officials commonly swear that they will keep the statutes of the community and preserve those communities in a good state; and all these things are to be understood as lasting as long as their office lasts. For an oath by which someone swore that he would always be in such an office or papacy, and would simply or absolutely always have the care of the purpose, would be unlawful, because it could work against the common good, for instance if he saw himself to be insufficient and the common good under him languished and perished.

units.la: Ad octauam rationem, quod nullus potest se absoluere à peccato: respondeo, Non est simile: quia absoluere se à peccato, est ascendere: sed se absoluere à papatu, est descendere. Non valet autem argumentum, si aliquis non potest ascendere, quod non possit descendere. Vel potest dici, quod homo absoluit se à culpa in contritione: & quod si teneatur confiteri alii à quo absoluatur, hoc est solum ex Domini præcepto. Iacob. 5. Confitemini alterutrum, &c. Et Luc. 17. dixit Dominus leprosis, per quos peccatores intelliguntur, vt ostenderent se sacerdotibus.
units.tr: To the eighth argument, that no one can absolve himself from sin: I answer that it is not similar, because to absolve oneself from sin is to ascend, but to absolve oneself from the papacy is to descend. Nor does the argument hold, that if someone cannot ascend, he cannot descend. Or it may be said that a man absolves himself from guilt in contrition, and that if he is bound to confess to another by whom he may be absolved, this is only by the Lord's command. James 5: "Confess your faults one to another," etc. And Luke 17: the Lord said to the lepers, by whom sinners are meant, that they should show themselves to the priests.

units.la: Ad nonam rationem, quod Papalis obligatio non potest tolli nisi per maiorem: responsio patet, sicut ad alias: quia Papæ obligatio non est nisi conditionata, scilicet quamdiu est in officio.
units.tr: To the ninth argument, that a papal obligation cannot be removed except by a greater authority: the answer is clear, as to the others, because the Pope's obligation is only conditional, namely as long as he is in office.

units.la: Ad decimam, quod nulla dignitas Ecclesiastica post legitimam confirmationem tolli potest, nisi per superiorem: responsio, Planum est quod hoc intelligitur de dignitate, quæ confirmatur per superiorem: sed ascensus Papæ sine superiore, confirmatio eius est: & ideo descensus eius sine superiore, cessio est.
units.tr: To the tenth, that no ecclesiastical dignity can be removed after lawful confirmation except by a superior: the answer is that it is plain this is understood of a dignity which is confirmed by a superior; but the Pope's ascent without a superior is his confirmation, and therefore his descent without a superior is a cession.

units.la: Ad vndecimam, de sacerdotio Christi æterno: responsio patet ex prædictis. nam sacerdotium Christi fuit æternum, quia Christus viuit in æternum ratione oblationis: & sic concedo de Papa, quod sacerdotium eius durat semper, quamdiu viuit: quia indelebilem habet characterem, & semper erit sacerdos, & poterit offerre in altari: sed papatus eius non necessario est, quamdiu viuit: sed potest cedere, vel ex magna causa deponi: quia papatus vltra episcopatum & sacerdotium nominat iurisdictionem, quæ mutabilis est, & sine hac Papa non potest esse Papa.
units.tr: To the eleventh, concerning the eternal priesthood of Christ: the answer is clear from what has been said. For the priesthood of Christ was eternal, because Christ lives forever by reason of the oblation; and so I concede of the Pope that his priesthood lasts always, as long as he lives, because he has an indelible character and will always be a priest, and will be able to offer on the altar. But his papacy is not necessarily for as long as he lives; it can be resigned, or deposed for a great cause, because the papacy, beyond the episcopate and priesthood, denotes jurisdiction, which is mutable, and without this the Pope cannot be Pope.

units.la: Finit Tractatus de potestate regia & papali, à magistro Iohanne de Parisiis, Ord. Prædicatorum, Doctore Theologo.
units.tr: Here ends the Treatise on royal and papal power, by Master John of Paris, of the Order of Preachers, Doctor of Theology.

units.la: MARSILII MENANDRINI DE PADUA
units.tr: MARSILIUS OF PADUA MENANDRINUS

units.la: TRACTATVS DE TRANSLATIONE IMPERII.
units.tr: A TREATISE ON THE TRANSFER OF THE EMPIRE.

units.la: PRimum capitulum est de intentione narrandorum. Secundum, qualiter Romanum Imperium per triginta tres Imperatores permansit. Tertium, quare Orientales, videl. Persæ, Arabes, Chaldæi, & aliæ confines nationes, à dominio Romani Imperii recesserunt. Quartum, qui fuerint principales populi, qui seditionem huiusmodi ex antedictis occasionib. excitarunt. Quintum, de principio & ordinatione translationis imperii, de Græcis in Francos. Sextum, qualiter Pipinus tempore Zachariæ Papæ de Maiori domus in regem Francorum extitit sublimatus. Septimum, qualiter Pipinus rex Francorum ad petitionem Ecclesiæ Romanæ, adiuit Italiam, aduersus Astulphum regem Lombardorum, ipsumque denicit, & tempora-lia Ecclesiæ Romanæ restituit. Octauum, qualiter tempore Adriani Papæ Carolus M. vrbis Patritius constitutus fuit, ipsiusque sedis Apostolicæ dispositio concessa fuerit. Nonum, qualiter imperii Romani translatio de Græcis in Francos facta fuerit. Decimum, qualiter imperium translatum fuit à Francis seu Gallis, in Germanos. Vndecimum, qualiter Germani Electores Imperii fuerunt instituti. Duodecimum est, Epilogus dictorum.
units.tr: The first chapter concerns the purpose of what is to be related. The second: how the Roman Empire endured through thirty-three emperors. The third: why the Eastern peoples, namely the Persians, Arabs, Chaldeans, and other neighbouring nations, withdrew from the dominion of the Roman Empire. The fourth: which were the principal peoples who stirred up this sedition from the aforementioned occasions. The fifth: concerning the beginning and arrangement of the transfer of the empire from the Greeks to the Franks. The sixth: how Pepin, in the time of Pope Zachary, was raised from the mayoralty of the palace to be king of the Franks. The seventh: how King Pepin of the Franks, at the request of the Roman Church, went into Italy against Aistulf, king of the Lombards, defeated him, and restored the temporal possessions of the Roman Church. The eighth: how, in the time of Pope Hadrian, Charlemagne was appointed Patrician of the city, and the arrangement of the Apostolic See itself was granted to him. The ninth: how the transfer of the Roman empire from the Greeks to the Franks was made. The tenth: how the empire was transferred from the Franks or Gauls to the Germans. The eleventh: how the German Electors of the Empire were instituted. The twelfth is an epilogue of what has been said.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: QVoniam in eo, quę Defensorem pacis habemus, tractatum fecimus de Romani & cuiuslibet alterius principatus institutione, noua translatione, ac alia quauis circa principatū mutatione diximusq; prquem, & quomodo secundum rationem seu de iure fieri debet, & potest: nunc aūt in his perstringere volumus sermonē de sedis imperialis translatione, collectum diligenter ex Chronicis historiis quibusdā per venerabilē Landalphum de Columna, Romanum satrapā, conscriptum. Et quia eius scripturæ in quibusdā nostra sententia dissonat, præsertim in quib. iura læsit imperii secundum sententiā propriam, absq; demonstratione sufficienti. Dicemus igitur de Imperialis Romanæ sedis translatione, per quem vel quos & qualiter de facto processerit à Romanis in Græcos: deinde vero à Græcis in Gallicos, siue Francos: nouissime aūt à Francis in Germanos. Ante tñ oportet attendere, q; Romanum Imperiū in vna sui significatione quandoq; significat Monarchiā, seu regalem principatum Romanę vrbis, siue ciuitatis tñ: qualis fuit ab origine sua, quemadmodū ex sequentib. apparebit. In alia vero acceptione significat Imperium Romanum vniuersalem & generalē totius mundi, vel plurimarum saltē prouinciarum monarchiā: qualis fuit Romanæ vrbis totius orbis principatus, in eius processu. secūdum q; etiam acceptionem de ipsius translatione tractare propositū magis est nobis. A priorib. itaq; secundum ordinem incipientes, narrabimus primo, Romanę vrbis siue ciuitatis originē, eiusq; exordiū monarchiæ. Deinde augmentum ipsius, ad totius orbis monarchiā & principatum supremum, posthæc aūt, ipsius translatione ex sede in sedē, seu ex gente in gentē, secundā tempora describemus.
units.tr: Since in the work that we have titled Defensorem pacis we treated the establishment of the Roman principate and of every other principate, its new transfer, and whatever other change of government there may be, and how and in what manner such changes ought to be and can be made according to reason and right, we now wish in this place to set out a discussion of the transfer of the imperial see. We have compiled it carefully from certain chronicles and histories written by the venerable Landalphus de Columna, a Roman satrap. But since in some points his account disagrees with our opinion, especially where, according to his own view and without sufficient proof, he has violated the rights of the empire, we will speak of the transfer of the Roman imperial see: through whom or by whom, and how, it was actually carried out, first from the Romans to the Greeks, then from the Greeks to the Gauls or Franks, and lastly from the Franks to the Germans. Yet first we must notice that the Roman Empire, in one of its meanings, sometimes signifies the monarchy, or royal principate, of the city of Rome alone, such as it was from its origin, as will appear from what follows. In another sense the Roman Empire signifies the universal and general monarchy of the whole world, or at least of most provinces, such as the rule of the city of Rome over the whole world was in its course; and it is this sense in which we are more inclined to treat of its transfer. So, beginning with the earlier things in order, we shall first tell of the origin of the city of Rome and the beginning of its monarchy; then describe its growth into the monarchy and supreme rule of the whole world; and afterwards, in their order of time, its transfer from see to see, or from nation to nation.

units.la: De Romanę ergo vrbis ortu & patria structuraq; dicturi, ex probatis sumamus historiis, quod Æneas post excidium magnæ Troiæ profugus, per mare Italiam petiit, & in ea Romanum imperiū fundauit, in loco vbi Roma nunc est, & in eo, quia sibi cōplacuit, sementem Romani generis seminauit. Quod quidem semen processu temporis in planta excellentissimam crescens, p vniuersa climata ramos expandit: velut synapis, q; ex minimo super olera reliqua mirabiliter exaltatur. Sub cuius quidē vmbra, plantæ omnes, id est, reges & principes & tyranni, cum populis omnibus, in pacis pulchritudine quiescebant. Romani vero, qui ab Ænea descenderunt, armorum exercitio, disciplina castroru, vsu militiæ, libertate quieta, iustitiæ cultu, legum reuerentia, finitimarum gentium amicitiis, maturitate consiliorum, grauitate verborum & operum obtinuerunt, vt orbem suæ subiicerent ditioni. Nā Romanus populus, à rege Romulo in Cęsarem Augustum per septingentos annos ita per vniuersum orbem virtuose ac potenter arma circumtulit, vt omnia regna mundi sua virtute anteiret: ita vt qui eius magnifica gesta legunt, non vnius populi, sed totius humani generis facta legere videantur: sic etiam vt ad constituendum eius Imperium humana virtus atque fortuna contendisse credantur.
units.tr: Since we are about to speak of the origin, homeland and founding of the city of Rome, let us take it from approved histories: after the destruction of great Troy, Aeneas, a fugitive, sought Italy by sea, and there founded the Roman empire in the place where Rome now stands, and in that place he sowed, as it pleased him, the seed of the Roman race. This seed, as time went on, grew into a most excellent plant and spread its branches through all the climes, like mustard, which from the smallest seed rises wondrously above the other herbs. Under its shade all the plants, that is, the kings, princes and tyrants, together with all the peoples, rested in the beauty of peace. The Romans, descended from Aeneas, won by the practice of arms, the discipline of camps, the usage of warfare, quiet liberty, the cultivation of justice, reverence for the laws, friendship with neighbouring nations, maturity of counsel, and gravity in word and deed, so that they subjected the world to their rule. For the Roman people, from King Romulus down to Caesar Augustus over seven hundred years, carried their arms so virtuously and powerfully through the whole world that they surpassed all the kingdoms of the earth in their valour; so that those who read of their glorious deeds seem to be reading not the deeds of one people but of the whole human race; and so too it is believed that human virtue and fortune strove together to establish their empire.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: IMperium Romanum à Iulio Cæsare secundum quosdam, sed verius ab Octauiano Augusto, primo Romanorum Imperatore sumpsit initium. Nam secundum historiæ veritatem, Iulius Cæsar licet primus fuerit, qui sibi atripuit Romanorum monarchiam, tamen non fuit Imperator, sed potius reipublicę violator & vsurpator. Et propterea non ponitur in catalogo Principum Romanorum. Imperium autem vsq; ad Magnum Constantinum per triginta tres Imperatores, & trecentos quinquaginta quatuor annos & quinq; menses sine mutatione Romæ permansit. Constantinus vero prædictus imperii sui anno vii. sedem mutauit imperii, ipsam in Orientem transferens, apud Byzantium ciuitatem, Constantinopolim nunc nominatam: quæ etiam secundum imperialia iura Romę veteris prærogatiua lætatur, ibiq; sedem imperialem statuit Constantinus, & Romam B. Syluestro tunc Romano Pontifici, eiusq; successoribus disponendam commisit. Et vt in quibusdam narratur Historiis, clericis quoq; Romanæ vrbis ad instantiam B. Syluestri quasdam senatorias dignitates contulisse fertur. Ii vero, qui tunc clerici Romanæ vocabantur Ecclesiæ, nunc Cardinales appellantur. Sed ante Syluestrum simpliciter clerici, seu sacerdotes Romanæ Ecclesiæ vocabantur. Qui tunc, quantum ad decorem & dignitatem, titulos non habebant: sed bene, quantum ad onus, videlicet officium prædicandi, mortuos sepeliendi, baptizandi, & pœnitentias iniungendi, titulos habuerunt. Hæc enim longe ante Syluestrum à temporibus Cleti & Anacleti, Dionysii & Marcellini, fuerant instituta. Sed à tempore Syluestri receperunt dignitatis titulos, & illam prærogatiuam, quam Senatus habebat tempore Constantini. Vtrum autem conuenienter aut non, ex nostro Defensore pacis videbitur intuenti. Cum iis autem attendendum, quod Martinus Polonus ponit in Chronica sua numerum Cardinalium: & dicit, quod sint lii. videlicet vi. episcopi, xxviii. presbyteri, & xviii. diaconi. quorum quidam sunt assidentes summo Pontifici, vt episcopi, qui domino Papæ in solennitatibus assident, & cardidris vtuntur. Quidam sunt assistentes, vt presbyteri, qui per septimanas missis & horis intersunt. Quidam vero sunt insistentes, vt diaconi insistunt ministeriis. Ipsi namq; Papam induunt, & ei circa altare deseruiunt: sed secundum assignationes titulorum factas, primo per Cletum, postea per Anacletum, & demum per Marcellinum, plures inueniuntur. Sed in hoc, quantum ad præsens, vis non est. Quod autem B. Syluester hos clericos primo nominauerit cardinales, communiter dicunt historiarum scriptores. Ante enim, vt iam dictum est, vocabantur presbyteri vrbis Roma, vt patet ex Ecclesiastica historia. Eusebii. Et perid, quod legitur etiam de Nouatiano presbytero Romanæ Ecclesiæ, qui aspirans ad summam Pontificiam, promotionem Cornelii Papæ nisus est impedire.
units.tr: According to some, the Roman Empire took its beginning from Julius Caesar, but more truly from Octavian Augustus, the first Roman Emperor. For according to the truth of history, Julius Caesar, although he was the first who seized the Roman monarchy for himself, was not an Emperor but rather a violator and usurper of the commonwealth. For this reason he is not placed in the list of Roman Princes. The Empire, however, remained at Rome without change until Constantine the Great, through thirty-three Emperors and three hundred and fifty-four years and five months. In the seventh year of his reign Constantine moved the seat of the Empire, transferring it to the East, to the city of Byzantium, now called Constantinople, which, according to the imperial laws, also rejoices in the prerogative of old Rome. There Constantine established the imperial seat, and he entrusted Rome to Blessed Sylvester, then Roman Pontiff, and to his successors to be governed. As some histories relate, he is also said, at the urging of Blessed Sylvester, to have conferred certain senatorial dignities on the clergy of the city of Rome. Those who were then called the clergy of the Roman Church are now called Cardinales. But before Sylvester they were simply called clerici, or sacerdotes Romanae Ecclesiae. At that time they did not have titulos as regards honour and dignity, but they did have titles as regards burden, namely the duty of preaching, burying the dead, baptizing, and imposing penances. For these offices had been instituted long before Sylvester, from the times of Cletus and Anacletus, Dionysius and Marcellinus. But from the time of Sylvester they received the titles of dignity and that prerogative which the Senate had in the time of Constantine. Whether this was fitting or not, the reader may see from our Defensor pacis. Here, however, one should also note what Martinus Polonus gives in his Chronicle as the number of Cardinals: he says there are fifty-two, namely six bishops, twenty-eight elders, and eighteen deacons. Of these, some are assisting the supreme Pontiff, as the bishops, who attend the lord Pope at solemnities and wear the cardinal's dress. Some are assistants, as the elders, who take part in the masses and hours by weeks. Others are ministering, as the deacons minister in their duties. For they clothe the Pope and serve him at the altar. But according to the assignments of titles made first by Cletus, afterwards by Anacletus, and at last by Marcellinus, more are found. But on this point there is no need for us to go into detail at present. That Blessed Sylvester was the first to name these clerics cardinales, the writers of histories commonly say. For before, as has already been said, they were called presbyteri vrbis Roma, as is clear from the Ecclesiastica historia of Eusebius. And this is also evident from what is read of Novatian, a presbyter of the Roman Church, who, aspiring to the supreme Pontificate, sought to hinder the promotion of Pope Cornelius.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: TEnuit quoque Constantinus, eiusque successores Imperatores Romani, pacifice dominium Orientis, vsq; ad XX. annum Imperatoris Heraclii, quo tempore omnes Orientales populi à dominio Latinorum recesserunt. Sed quia causa propter quam recesserunt, & modus, per què recesserunt, comuniter ignorantur: idcirco conueniens iudicaui, causam & modum describere, quib. dicti Orientales se à Græcis & Latinis in dominio & cultu diuinorū diuiserunt. Causa siquidē, quare Orientales, videl. Persę, Arabes, Chaldæi, & aliæ confines nationes à dominio Romani Imperii recesserunt, tyrannicus principatus Heraclii. Nam post magnam victoriā de Persis habita, Heraclius Persas & alias Orientales nationes nimis crudeli dominatu premebat: propter q; rebellandi occasionem còcorditer assumpserunt. Sed vt ab obedientia prædicta recederent firmiter, vt nunq; ad eandem renocarentur amplius, consilio Machometi tunc inter Persas diuitis & potentis, diuersum cultum assumunt, vt tā diuersæ crudelitatis & fidei sectę ad pristinum dominium de caetero non redirent. A Ieroboam forte sumentes exemplum, qui decem tribubus ipsum sequentib. diuersum cultum tradidit, vt in pristinū dominium non redirent. Quod etiam, vel consimiliter Græci fecerunt. Volentes n. ab ecclesiæ Romanæ obedientia separari, acceperunt diuersum cultum siue ritum in Ecclesia ministrandi, & sic in diuersos errores sunt prolapsi scienter. Omnes n. eorū Calogeri, qui conseruant & nutriunt schismata, vel sunt Nestoriani, aut Eutychetistæ, aut Iacobitæ, aut Hebionitæ. Sic ergo factum est de illis populis & nationibus, in quib. iam dicta rebellio & inobedientia cōtigerunt. Nam vt talis esset rebellio duratura, schismata induxerunt: vt non solum ab Imperio, sed etiā à Christianismo recederent, accipientes etiam cōmunia quædam ex lege Moysi, quædam ex lege Euangelii, vt patet in Alcorano. Unde attendendum, quod quædā hæreticorum sectæ multum fuerunt familiares Machometo & legi Saracenorum, sicut in prædicto Alcorano cōtinetur: velut Nestoriani, quos Machometus mandat honorari. Unde Richardus in Chronicis suis narrat, quod quidam monachus Græcus Nestorianus, cui nomen Sergius, longo tempore instruxit Machometum, & hinc est, quod Nestoriani magna habent Monasteria in dominio Sarracenorum.
units.tr: Constantine and his successors, the Roman emperors, also held dominion over the East peacefully until the twentieth year of the Emperor Heraclius, when all the Eastern peoples withdrew from the rule of the Latins. Since the reason for their withdrawal and the manner in which they withdrew are commonly unknown, I have thought it fitting to describe the cause and the manner by which these Easterners separated themselves from the Greeks and the Latins in government and in the worship of God. The cause why the Easterners, namely the Persians, Arabs, Chaldeans and other neighbouring nations, withdrew from the rule of the Roman Empire was the tyrannical government of Heraclius. For after the great victory he had won over the Persians, Heraclius oppressed the Persians and the other Eastern nations with far too cruel a rule, and so they united in agreement to seize the chance to rebel. But so that they might firmly break away from that obedience and never be recalled to it again, they took up, on the advice of Mahomet, then rich and powerful among the Persians, a different form of worship, so that they would never return to their former rule, from such differing cruelty and such a sect of faith. Perhaps they took as their example Jeroboam, who gave a different worship to the ten tribes that followed him, so that they would not return to their former rule. The Greeks also did something similar, or in the same way. For, wishing to be separated from the obedience of the Roman Church, they adopted a different worship, or rite of administering the Church, and so knowingly fell into various errors. For all their Calogeri, who preserve and foster schisms, are either Nestorians, or Eutychians, or Jacobites, or Ebionites. So it happened with those peoples and nations in which the aforesaid rebellion and disobedience occurred. For, in order that the rebellion might last, they introduced schisms, so that they would withdraw not only from the Empire but also from Christianity, taking up certain things common to the law of Moses and certain things from the law of the Gospel, as appears in the Alcoran. Hence it should be noted that certain sects of heretics were very familiar to Mahomet and to the law of the Saracens, as is contained in the aforesaid Alcoran, for example the Nestorians, whom Mahomet orders to be honoured. Hence Richard, in his Chronicles, relates that a certain Greek Nestorian monk, named Sergius, instructed Mahomet for a long time, and hence it is that the Nestorians have many great monasteries in the dominion of the Saracens.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: CAusa igitur & modo præscriptis, quibus Orientales à dominio Græcorum & Latinorum recesserunt, videamus, qui fuerunt principales populi, qui seditionem huiusmodi ex antedictis occasionibus excitarunt: qui etiā non solū rebellionis & inobedientiæ sumpserunt audaciā, sed cum hoc regiones Romani imperii & Imperatori vicinas hostiliter invaserunt. De his Richardus in Chronica sua, Martinus, Isidorus & Admonius de gestis Francor. concorditer dicunt, q; principalis gens in prædicta audaciam elevata, de Arabia & radice montis Caucasi est progressa, quæ gens, secundum Hieronymū in Chronicis, Nabathæa nominatur, à Nabaoth primogenito Ismahelis. Unde nō Sarraceni, sed Agareni, siue Ismahelitæ dici deberent. Hæc natio deuastans regiones Imperii, peruenit vsq; in Syriā & Iudæam, contra quam egressa est innumera militia Imperatoris Heraclii, quæ tota fuit cæsa per hostes, & fuerunt 15000. prostratorū de exercitu Imperatoris prædicti. Verum humanitate hanc hostes fecisse leguntur, quod per legatos omnia spolia Imperatori remiserunt. Heraclius autem spoliis recusatis, in adiutorium accitis Alanis (qui dicuntur de montibus Caspiis exiuisse, secundum historias, ibidem per Alexandrum M. inclusi) exercitum reparauit, & infinitā pugnatorum multitudinem congregauit. Saraceni quoq; duo duces præerat, qui 20000. pugnatorū in bellum instruxerant. Cumq; vterq; exercitus non procul ab inuicem consideret, paratus & instructus nocte quæ diem belli præcesserat, in castris Græcorum 5002. pugnatorum exanimata subito reperta sunt in stratis ipsorum. Quo terrore ac metu percussa exercitus reliqua multitudo, in diuersis fugit locis, totum imperium hostib. relinquens. Heraclius accepto nuncio tantæ cladis, diffidens se posse resistere, præ tristitia in morbum incidit: & quasi desperans in ægritudinem prolabitur animæ: ac secundum quasdā historias Eutycetis cōmaculatur errore: & cum filia sororis suæ, nomine Martina, copulauit se in matrimonio. Aliæ vero historiæ tradunt, quod ante prædictum conflictum, prædicto fuerit maculatus errore. His peractis, multiplicatur exercitus Arabum & Nabathæorum, ex diuersis prouinciis, affinibus videl. Chaldæis, Ammonitis & Moabitis: quibus Machometus adiungitur, qui tenebat in Arabia principatum, vt scribit Richardus in Chronicis. Hic Machometus magicis artibus instructus, vt fertur, sua, vt credo, cum prudentia verius, prætextu contemptus Imperii persuadet, eisdem de modo viuendi ad suum augendum dominiū, populumq; multiplici sua arte deludit & auertit à fide: afferens ipsos principatum tenere non posse, nisi à Christiana fide se diuerterent, & sua documēta sectarentur & seruarent: simulans quoq; aliquid diuini numinis in se habere. sicq; quibusdam præstigiis per ipsum ostensis, homines fallens, tanquā propheta in dicto populo communiter habebatur. Quibus etiā ludibriis quandam nobilem & potentem viduam, nomine Cadigam, Grorozamæ prouinciæ, seduxit intantum, vt eam sibi matrimonio copularet: per quam illius regionis obtinuit principatum. Iudæos etiā multos sic decepit, vt ipsum crederent suum esse Messiam. Iis versutiis, suaq; potentia & ampliatione legis circa venerea, & largis promissionibus circa futura populos seducebat, & armorum potentia ad suam perfidiam compellebat. Lege enim data per Machometum, populi, qui arma sumpserant contra Imperium, si quas regiones occupabant, eas legem Machometi credere compellebant: nolentes vero fateri, neci tradebant. Unde de Arabia intrauerunt in Ægyptum, & ibi populum subuerterunt. Deinde transeuntes in Aphricam, simile fecerunt. Inde etiam in Hispaniam venientes, eam in parte fidem pristinam dimittere coegerunt: & sic multiplicati sunt super numerum plus violentia bolli, quam praedicatione sermonis.
units.tr: The causes and manner, then, by which the Orientals withdrew from the rule of the Greeks and the Latins having been set out above, let us see which were the principal peoples who stirred up this sedition from the aforesaid occasions. These not only took up the boldness of rebellion and disobedience, but also made hostile inroads into the regions of the Roman Empire and those neighbouring the Emperor. Concerning these, Richardus in his Chronica, Martinus, Isidorus and Admonius de gestis Francorum agree in saying that the principal people raised to this audacity came forth from Arabia and from the foot of Mount Caucasus. This people, according to Jerome in Chronicis, is called Nabathaea, from Nabaioth the firstborn of Ishmael. Hence they ought to be called not Saracens but Agarenes, or Ishmaelites. This nation, laying waste the regions of the Empire, reached as far as Syria and Judaea. Against them went out the innumerable army of the Emperor Heraclius, which was wholly cut down by the enemy, and there were 15,000 of the Emperor's army slain. Yet we read that the enemy acted with humanity, for through envoys they sent back all the spoils to the Emperor. Heraclius, however, refused the spoils, and having summoned the Alans (who are said, according to the histories, to have come out of the Caspian mountains, where they had been shut in by Alexander the Great), he rebuilt his army and gathered an infinite multitude of fighting men. The Saracens too had two leaders, who had drawn up 20,000 fighting men for battle. When the two armies were encamped not far from one another, ready and arrayed, on the night before the day of battle, 5,002 fighting men of the Greek camp were suddenly found dead in their beds. Struck by this terror and fear, the rest of the army fled in different directions, leaving the whole empire to the enemy. Heraclius, having received word of so great a disaster and despairing of being able to resist, fell sick from grief, and, as if giving up hope, sank into a mortal illness of the soul; and according to certain histories he was defiled by the error of the Eutychians, and joined himself in marriage to the daughter of his sister, named Martina. Other histories, however, relate that he had been defiled by that error before the aforesaid conflict. After these things, the army of the Arabs and Nabathaeans was multiplied from various provinces, namely from related peoples, the Chaldeans, Ammonites and Moabites; to these Mahomet was joined, who held the principality in Arabia, as Richardus writes in his Chronica. This Mahomet, instructed in magical arts, as is reported, persuades them, under the pretext of contempt for the Empire, with his own prudence (truer, I believe, than his art), concerning their manner of life, in order to increase their dominion; he deceives the people by his manifold craft and turns them away from the faith, asserting that they could not hold the principality unless they turned away from the Christian faith and followed and observed his teachings, pretending also that he had something of the divine power in himself. And so, by certain tricks displayed by him, deceiving men, he was commonly held as a prophet among the said people. By such delusions also he seduced a certain noble and powerful widow named Cadiga, of the province of Grorozama, to such an extent that he joined her to himself in marriage, and through her he obtained the principality of that region. He also deceived many Jews, so that they believed him to be their Messiah. By these wiles, by his power, and by the extension of his law to sensual pleasures, and by large promises concerning the future, he seduced the peoples, and by the might of arms he compelled them to his perfidy. For when the law had been given by Mahomet, the peoples who had taken up arms against the Empire compelled whatever regions they occupied to believe the law of Mahomet; those who were unwilling to profess it they handed over to death. Hence they entered Egypt from Arabia and overturned the people there. Then, passing over into Africa, they did the same. Coming also into Spain, they forced it in part to give up its former faith; and so they multiplied beyond number, more by violence of arms than by the preaching of the word.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: MOrtuo ergo Heraclio, & imperio sic difformato potetia, quantum ad dominium Orientis, remansit sedes Imperialis in Graecia, apud Constantinopolim, usq; ad tempora Constantini VI. & Leonis filii sui, per xxxiii Imperatores, computato M. Constantino, & per 451. annos de Imperio Constantini. Nam tantum a mutata sede de Roma in Graeciam superuixit. Hoc tempore Leonis Papae III. translatio Imperii de Graecis ad Francos, fuit aliqualiter inchoata. Et quoniam historia haec propter scribentium varietatem ignota est communiter, idcirco alias sciendum, quod primitiva causa translationis huius, fuit discordia inter Imperatorem Leonem III. & Romanam ecclesiam, circa venerationem Ecclesiasticarum imaginum. Leo enim III. Imperator dicebat, Christi & sanctorum imagines minime venerandas: quia species idololatriae videbatur. Gregorius vero III. qui tunc Romanae praesidebat ecclesiae, affirmauit, Christi & sanctorum imagines venerandas. In hoc siquidem propositio Leo Imperator praedictus persecuerauit sic, q de Constantinopoli Romam veniens, omnes Christi & sanctorum imagines, quas Romae reperit, abstulit, & secum Constantinopolim asportauit, easq; per sententiam igne cremauit. Propter quod dictus Gregorius, praedictum Leonem anathematizare praesumpsit, & totam Apuliam, totamq; Italiam & Hispaniam ab eius obedientia separari suasit: & quantum in ipso fuit, hoc opere, quamuis minus debite, adimpleuit. Eidem etiam vestigalia, nescio qua authoritate, sed bene qua temeritate, solenniter interdixit: Romaeq; congregans Synodum, venerationem imaginum confirmauit: & violatores huiusmodi, anathemate condemnauit. Demum Leo praedictus in hoc proposito moritur, eiq; successit in imperio filius eius Constantinus V. qui eiusdem propositi cum patre, in nullo Romanae fauebat Ecclesiae. Papa Stephanus II. imperium Romanum de Graecis transferri in Francos aliqualiter ordinauit, viuente Pipino, Francorum postmodum rege, qui dictu Pontificem superuixit. Et ideo quod ab aliquibus dicitur, tempore Stephani translatum fuisse imperium a Graecis in Francos: intelligi debet, quod fuit huiusmodi ordinata translatio, non tamen opere fuit consummata. Igitur huius Papae Stephani tempore, imperii Romani translatio ordinata ad Francos fuit: quorum fauores & beneficia iam Romani clerici sentiebant in multis.
units.tr: Heraclius therefore being dead, and the empire thus reduced in power as far as dominion over the East was concerned, the imperial seat remained in Greece, at Constantinople, until the times of Constantine VI and his son Leo, through thirty-three emperors, counting Constantine the Great, and for 451 years from the reign of Constantine. For it survived the transfer of the seat from Rome to Greece by only so much. At this time the transfer of the Empire from the Greeks to the Franks was in some measure begun under Leo III, Pope. And since this history is commonly unknown because of the variety of writers, it should therefore be known otherwise that the primary cause of this transfer was the dispute between the Emperor Leo III and the Roman Church concerning the veneration of ecclesiastical images. For the Emperor Leo III said that the images of Christ and of the saints were by no means to be venerated, because they seemed a form of idolatry. Gregory III, however, who then presided over the Roman Church, affirmed that the images of Christ and of the saints were to be venerated. In this matter the aforesaid Emperor Leo so persecuted that, coming from Constantinople to Rome, he removed all the images of Christ and of the saints that he found at Rome, carried them off with him to Constantinople, and by sentence burned them with fire. On account of this the said Gregory presumed to anathematize the aforesaid Leo, and advised that all Apulia, all Italy and Spain be separated from his obedience; and so far as lay in him, he accomplished this aim, although less rightly. He also solemnly forbade, by I know not what authority but certainly by what rashness, the payment of tribute to him; and, gathering a synod at Rome, he confirmed the veneration of images and condemned the violators of this with anathema. At length the aforesaid Leo died in this purpose, and his son Constantine V succeeded him in the empire; who, of the same purpose as his father, in nothing favoured the Roman Church. Pope Stephen II in some measure arranged that the Roman Empire should be transferred from the Greeks to the Franks, while Pepin, afterwards king of the Franks, was living, who survived the said Pontiff. And therefore what some say, that in the time of Stephen the empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Franks, must be understood thus: that such a transfer was arranged, but it was not yet carried into effect. Therefore in the time of this Pope Stephen the transfer of the Roman Empire to the Franks was arranged; the favours and benefits of whom the Roman clergy were already experiencing in many ways.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: PIpinus igitur praedictus Caroli Marcelli filius, vir in rebus bellicis strenuus, catholicus, & virtuorum morum honestate praeclarus, secundum cleriorum scripturas, sibi imperialem autoritate vsurpare quaerentium: legitur a Zacharia Papa de Maiori domus, in regni Francorum excellentiam sublimatus. Quod siquidem Zacharias (vt aiunt) regem Francorum Childericum, non tam pro suis iniquitatibus, quam pro eo quod tantae potestati erat inutilis, a regno depoluit, & praedictum Pipinum, Caroli M. patrem, in eius locum substituit: omnesq; Francigenas a iuramento fidelitatis, quo Childerico tenebantur, absoluit. Sed Admonius in gestis Francor. scribit, & verius, Pipinum per Francos legitime in regem electum, & per regni proceres elevatum: per Bonifacium quoq; Remensem archiepiscopum, inunctum Suessione, in monasterio S. Medardi. Childericus vero, qui tunc sub nomine regio in deliciis marcescebat, & otio, fuit in monachum tonsuratus. Unde non illum Zacharias deposuit, sed deponentibus, vt quidam aiunt, consensit. Nam talis depositio regis, & alterius institutio, propter rationabilem causam, non ad episcopum tantummodo, neq; ad clericum aliquem, aut clericorum collegium pertinet, sed ad universitatem ciuium inhabitantium regionem, vel nobilium, vel ipsorum valentiorem multitudinem. Unde Admonii recipiendus est sermo, tanquam verus: clericorum vero scriptura in hoc reiicienda, tanquam Francis praeiudicialis & falsa. Vt autem clarius pateat, quare & qualiter facta fuit a Graecis in Francos Imperii memorata translatio, Pipini praedicti Franciae ac Germaniae regis historiam breuiter prosequamur.
units.tr: Pipin, then, the aforesaid son of Charles Martel, a man vigorous in war, Catholic, and distinguished by the honesty of his virtuous character, was raised by Pope Zachary from the office of Mayor of the Palace to the excellence of the kingdom of the Franks, according to the writings of the clerics, who sought to usurp imperial authority for themselves. Zachary (as they say) deposed King Childeric of the Franks from the kingdom, not so much for his wickedness as because he was useless for so great a power, and put Pipin, father of Charles the Great, in his place. He also absolved all the Franks from the oath of fidelity by which they had been bound to Childeric. But Admonius, in the Deeds of the Franks, writes, and more truly, that Pipin was legitimately elected king by the Franks, raised up by the nobles of the kingdom, and anointed at Soissons, in the monastery of St Medard, by Boniface, archbishop of Reims. Childeric, who then was wasting away in luxury and idleness under the royal name, was tonsured as a monk. Hence Zachary did not depose him but, as some say, consented to those who deposed him. For such a deposition of a king and installation of another, for a reasonable cause, belongs not to a bishop alone, nor to any cleric or college of clerics, but to the whole body of citizens inhabiting the region, or to the nobles, or to the greater part of them. Hence Admonius's account should be accepted as true, and the clerics' writing rejected on this point as prejudicial to the Franks and false. And so that it may be clearer why and how the aforesaid transfer of the empire from the Greeks to the Franks was made, let us briefly follow the history of the aforesaid Pipin, king of France and Germany.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: MOrtuo itaque Zacharia Papa, qui Pipino in regem sublimato consenserat, secundum quosdam (licet etiam absque ipsius assensu Francorum legitimus rex fuerit, vt in praecedentibus apparuit) praedictus Stephanus Secundus natione Romanus ex patre Constantino, anno Domini 770. & ab vrbe condita 1530. in summum Pontificem sublimatus est, vt Admonius scribit in gestis Francorum libro quarto. Grauatus autem a rege Longobardorum Aistulpho, venit in Franciam ad Pipinum regem, pro temporalibus Ecclesiae Romanae recuperandis, quibus eam Aistulphus spoliauerat. Hic autem Papae Romano Pipinus ad miliare tertium occurrit, & vsque ad palatium suum regium eum deduxit. Tunc Papa causam sui aduentus regi exposuit, & iniurias sibi per Aistulphum illatas plenius enarrauit. Cui rex seruire volens, & ipsius satisfacere voluntati, exercitum magnum parat, & cum ipso Papa in Italiam vadit: Aistulphus vero totis viribus regi praedicto obuiat, & Ecclesiae restituere temporalia contradicit. Pugna igitur inter ipsos committitur, in qua Aistulphus cum suis superatur, & sic ad Ecclesiae Romanae temporalia restituendum compellitur: qui datis obsidibus quadraginta, ex melioribus regni sui, Ecclesiae fæ temporalia sub iuramento reddere promisit. Post hoc autem Pipinus rex victor, in Franciam cum gaudio rediit, & Papa Stephanus Romam ad sedem Apostolicam remeauit. Aistulphus vero promissa non seruauit. Ob quam causam rediit Pipinus in Lombardiam, aduersus Aistulphum, ipsumq; in Papia obsedit: & quod promiserat, adimplere coegit. Vadit deinde Pipinus Rauennam, ipsamq; coepit: totamq; Pentapolim Romandiolæ cum Exarchatu, in quo est Bononia, cepit. Quæ omnia Ecclesiæ Romanæ scribitur contulisse de facto. His autem beneficiis Stephanus Papa allectus, & videns illius temporis Imperatoris imbecillitatem, procurauit Romanum Imperium de Græcis transferri in Francos: minime reminiscens beneficiorum, per Imperatores Romanæ ecclesiæ concessorum, in alienos atque remotos imperium transferre satagens, ut Græcis oppressis, Gallicis hæc parum curantibus, posset Papa Italiæ liberius dominari. Sic ergo scripturæ omnes recitantes, quod tempore huius Stephani Papæ, translatum sit Imperium a Græcis in Francos, debent intelligi, scilicet quod tempore suo fuerit ordinata translatio. Tempore namq; alterius Papæ, & Leonis tertii, fuit talis consummata translatio, ut ex sequentibus apparebit.
units.tr: Zachary the Pope having died, who had agreed to Pipin's elevation to king (though, according to some, even without his assent Pipin was the lawful king of the Franks, as appeared above), the aforesaid Stephen II, a Roman by birth, son of Constantine, was raised to the supreme pontificate in the year of the Lord 770 and the 1530th from the founding of the city, as Admonius writes in book four of the Deeds of the Franks. Harassed by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, he came into France to King Pipin to recover the temporalities of the Roman Church, which Aistulf had despoiled it of. Pipin met this Roman Pope three miles out and escorted him as far as his royal palace. Then the Pope explained to the king the reason for his coming and related more fully the injuries inflicted on him by Aistulf. The king, wishing to serve him and satisfy his will, prepared a great army and went into Italy with the Pope himself. Aistulf, with all his strength, opposed the said king and refused to restore the Church's temporalities. Battle was therefore joined, in which Aistulf and his men were defeated, and so he was compelled to restore the temporalities of the Roman Church. Giving forty hostages from the best men of his kingdom, he promised under oath to return the Church's temporalities. After this, King Pipin, victorious, returned to France with joy, and Pope Stephen returned to Rome, to the apostolic see. But Aistulf did not keep his promises. For this reason Pipin went back into Lombardy against Aistulf, besieged him in Pavia, and forced him to do what he had promised. Pipin then went to Ravenna and took it, and took the whole Pentapolis of Romagna together with the Exarchate, in which is Bologna. All these things are written to have been in fact conferred on the Roman Church. Stephen the Pope, enticed by these benefits and seeing the weakness of the emperor of that time, contrived to have the Roman Empire transferred from the Greeks to the Franks, quite forgetting the benefits the Roman Church had received from the emperors. He strove to transfer the empire to foreigners and remote people, so that, with the Greeks oppressed and the Gauls caring little for such matters, the Pope might rule Italy more freely. So when all the writers recount that in the time of this Pope Stephen the empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Franks, they must be understood to mean that the transfer was then ordained, not yet completed. For in the time of another Pope, Leo III, the transfer was completed, as will appear from what follows.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: HOc itaque Papa Stephano secundo mortuo, sub Ecclesiæ Romanæ protectore Pipino: atque Pipino eodem post 18. annum regni sui defuncto, filioq; ipsius à virtutum magnitudine Carolo Magno, nominato, regnante pro patre, tribus pontificibus intermediis (quorum electionem & vitam causa breuitatis omitto) videlicet Paulo primo, Constantino secundo, & Stephano tertio: Adrianus primus natione Romanus, ex patre Theodoro, de regione via lata, Anno Domini 795. & ab Vrbe condita 1547. in summum pontificem eligitur, ecclesiamq; Romanam annis 23. mensibus 10. diebus 18. gubernauit. Hic Carolum Magnum, qui tunc Franciæ ac Germaniæ regna tenebat, in auxilium Romanæ ecclesiæ, contra Longobardos implorauit. Mortuo enim Aistulpho Longobardorum rege, successit ei Desiderius filius eius: qui patris sequens vestigia, temporalibus Romanam priuauit ecclesiam, villasq; videlicet, ciuitates & castra, & reliqua Romanæ Ecclesiæ occupando, Romanos etiam nouis tributis & vectigalibus opprimendo. Ob quam causam misit Adrianus legatum in Franciam, Petrum presbyterum Cardinalem ad supradictum Carolum, eius implorans auxilium. Hic princeps legatum gloriose suscepit, congregatoq; procerum & prælatorum concilio, Adriani petitionibus censuit annuendum. Dicto igitur legato, cum sperato fauore remisso, Carolus rex parat exercitu copiosum, ipsumq; per mare ad iuga montium, in Longobardiam non cum modica difficultate deducit. Veniens igitur in Liguriam & Æmiliam, quæ nunc Lombardia plana vocatur, in circuitu ciuitatis Papiæ sua tabernacula fixit: & castris circumcirca dispositis, ut fidem sequamur historiæ, in eisdem natale Domini celebrauit. Deinde vero exercitu relicto, Romam causa deuotionis accessit, ibiq; cum Adriano Papa Paschha Dominicum simul egit: factaq; solennitate Paschali, ad castra reuertitur circa Papiam, continuataq; obsidione ciuitatem expugnauit. Desiderium Longobardorum regem cum uxore & filiis cepit, quiCaroli subiiciuntur potestati. Ibiq; etiam omnes aduenientes Italici, de singulis ciuitatibus Ambasiatæ & Nuncii, se regis dominio subiecerunt. Quibus sic feliciter expeditis, & inde Romam accedens, temporalia Ecclesiæ Romanæ restituit: simulq; Ducatum Spoletanum & Beneuentum eidem sua libertate de facto donauit. Tunc Adrianus beneficiis temporalibus dicti Principis allectus, 153. episcoporum & abbatum Romæ concilium congregauit. Ibiq; cum uniuersa synodo, glorioso Principi Carolo regi Franciæ ius & potestatem tribuit eligendi Romanum pontificem, & sedem Apostolicam ordinandi: dignitatem quoque Patriciatus eidem concessit, qua olim quasi pater principum videbatur. Insuper Archiepiscopos & Episcopos, per singulas prouincias, ab eo investituram accipere diffiniuit: & ut nisi à rege laudaretur & inuestiretur episcopus, & à nemine consecraretur: omnesq; contra prædicta facientes, anathemate maledixit: & nisi resipiscerent, bonis eos priuari mandauit. Quorum nullam faciendi aut concedendi autoritatem habuit Pontifex, aut alter Episcopus seu clericus, nisi demum Romani populi ordinatione atq; mandato. Prima siquidem concessione, potestate videlicet Romanum pontificem eligendi, & sedem Apostolicam ordinandi, non fuit vsus Carolus memoratus. Quod forte fuit, quia pauci pontifices fuerunt tempore sui regiminis, à concessione prædicta, quod fuit spacium 40. annorum. Soli enim, prædictus Adrianus, & Leo tertius, prædicti temporis spacio Romani pontifices exiterunt, qui 44. annis & mensibus aliquibus Romanæ ecclesiæ præfuerunt. Verum nec ipsum Carolum, tali iuri sibi competenti, ex concessione prædicta renunciasse, ab aliquo reperitur. De secunda vero concessione, videlicet Episcoporum installatione, se aliquotiens intromisit, ut ex ipsius gestis in plerilq; locis apparet: His tamen iuribus sibi competentibus renunciauit Ludouicus, ut fertur: & ut propositum de translatione imperii celerius prosequamur, plura magnificentiæ opera per Carolum gesta omittamus.
units.tr: Pope Stephen II having died, with Pipin as protector of the Roman Church, and Pipin himself having died in the eighteenth year of his reign, his son, named Charles the Great from the greatness of his virtues, reigning in his father's stead, and three popes intervening (whose election and lives I omit for brevity), namely Paul I, Constantine II and Stephen III, Adrian I, a Roman by birth, son of Theodore, of the region Via Lata, was elected supreme pontiff in the year of the Lord 795 and the 1547th from the founding of the city, and governed the Roman Church for 23 years, 10 months and 18 days. He implored Charles the Great, who then held the kingdoms of France and Germany, for aid to the Roman Church against the Lombards. For when Aistulf, king of the Lombards, died, his son Desiderius succeeded him; and he, following his father's footsteps, deprived the Roman Church of its temporalities, occupying its estates, that is, its cities, castles and the rest of its possessions, and also oppressing the Romans with new tributes and taxes. For this cause Adrian sent a legate into France, Peter, presbyter and cardinal, to the aforesaid Charles, imploring his aid. The prince received the legate graciously and, having gathered a council of nobles and prelates, judged that Adrian's requests should be granted. The legate having been dismissed with the favour he hoped for, King Charles prepared a copious army and led it by sea and over the mountain ridges into Lombardy, not without considerable difficulty. Coming then into Liguria and Aemilia, which is now called the Lombard plain, he pitched his tents around the city of Pavia. With the camps set up all around, to follow the history faithfully, he celebrated the Lord's Nativity there. Then, leaving the army, he went to Rome out of devotion, and there celebrated Easter with Pope Adrian. The Easter festivities done, he returned to the camp near Pavia, and by continued siege took the city. He captured King Desiderius of the Lombards with his wife and sons, who were made subject to Charles's power. There also all the Italians who came, ambassadors and messengers from each city, submitted themselves to the king's dominion. With these matters so successfully settled, he went from there to Rome and restored the temporalities of the Roman Church; at the same time he de facto gave the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento to the same Church as a free gift. Then Adrian, enticed by the temporal benefits of the said prince, gathered a council of 153 bishops and abbots at Rome. There, with the whole synod, he granted to the glorious prince Charles, king of France, the right and power of electing the Roman pontiff and of ordaining the apostolic see; he also conceded to him the dignity of Patrician, by which he had formerly seemed like a father of princes. Moreover, he decreed that archbishops and bishops, throughout each province, should receive investiture from him, and that no bishop should be consecrated unless approved and invested by the king, and by no one else. He cursed with anathema all who acted contrary to these things, and ordered that, unless they repented, they be deprived of their goods. The Pope had no authority to make or grant any of these things, nor had another bishop or cleric, except by the ordination and command of the Roman people. Indeed, Charles did not make use of the first concession, namely the power of electing the Roman pontiff and ordaining the apostolic see. Perhaps this was because few popes held office during his reign after the concession, which lasted 40 years: only Adrian and Leo III were Roman pontiffs in that span of time, and they presided over the Roman Church for 44 years and some months. But it is not found that Charles himself renounced such a right, competent to him by the said concession. As to the second concession, namely the installation of bishops, he did at times intrude himself, as appears in many places from his deeds. Louis, as is reported, renounced these rights competent to him. And, to pursue more quickly the matter of the translation of the empire, we omit the many magnificent works done by Charles.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: MOrtuo igitur Adriano prædicto, regnante Carolo Magno, ecclesiæ Romanæ defensore, Leo tertius natione Romanus, ex patre Aistulpho in Romanum pontificem sublimatur, anno Domini 819. & ab vrbe condita 1572. Hic pontifex in Letania captus est in Roma, excæcatus, & lingua truncatus. Qui positus in custodia, nocte per murum euasit, & ad legatos Caroli Girundu abbatē, & Vingisum Spoletanum ducem, cum fiducia magna confugit: & ut Richardus in sua Chronica scribit (cui credat, qui vult) Pontifex restitutis sibi plenarie membris, oculis & lingua, diuina, ut dicitur, virtute ad prædi&tum Carolum, tanquam ad præcipuum Ecclesiæ protectorem, venit in Franciam: qui eum, quo decuit, cum honore suscepit, & cum ipso Romam accedens, iniuriam pontificis & ecclesiæ Romanæ vltus est, iustitia mediante. Admonius quoq; in gestis Francorum, hoc magis copiose describens dicit, Quod postquam rex appropinquauit ad locum qui dicitur Mimentanum, duodecimo lapide ab vrbe Roma, Leo Papa, qui regem præcesserat, cum magno comitatu occurrit eidem: ipsumq; cum esset vrbis patricius, cum summa humilitate & honore suscepit: prandensq; cum ipso in loco prædicto, vt vrbis vtamur historiis, statim Papa ipsum cum sua societate præcesiit ad vrbem, in crastino quoq;, in gradibus basilicæ beati Petri Apostoli stans, missis obuiam Romanæ vrbis vexillis, ordinatisq; per congrua loca tam peregrinorum quam ciuium turmis, quæ venienti regi ad laudem conclamarent, ipse Papa cum turmis & Episcopis equo descendentem regem, & gradus ecclesiæ ascendentem suscepit: factaq; oratione, in basilicam sancti Petri psallentibus cunctis introduxit. Quod est factum 33. anno regis prædicti. Post septem quoq; dies rex, concione vocata, cur Romam venisset, omnibus patefecit: & exinde ad ea propter quæ venerat facienda quotidie operam dedit: & quamuis grauia crimina opponerentur summo Pontifici: tamen quia nullus fuit probator legitimus, idem Pontifex coram toto populo, annuente rege, in basilica beati Petri apostoli Euangelium portans, ambonem conscendit, inuocatoq; sanctæ trinitatis nomine, iureiurando ab obiectis sibi criminibus canonice se purgauit. Aliæ vero historiæ addunt, quod tres Cardinales supra sancta Dei Euangelia ponentes manus, affirmauerunt, omnia esse falsa, quæ summo Pontifici opponebantur. Quæ quidem purgatio a toto clero & populo fuit solemniter approbata, & a dicto Pontifice legitime confirmata. Eadem die vt scribit Admonius in gestis Francorum, quidam abbas Zacharias nomine, cum duobus monachis, vno de monte Oliueti, & alio de Saba in Oriente, Romam venit, quem patriarcha Hierosolymitanus transmisit, qui sepulchri Domini claues, & loci Caluariæ, ac ciuitatis Hierosolymitanæ, cum vexillis detulerunt. Quos Carolus benigne suscipiens, per aliquot dies eos honorando detinuit, humanq; tractauit. Deinde post aliquot dies cum muneribus magnis, regiam maiestatem decentibus, eos in Palæstinam remisit. Tradunt quædam historiæ, quod ex illa legatione motus rex, ad petitionem Constantini Imperatoris, cum magno exercitu transfretauit, totamq; terram Sanctam recuperauit, rege Persarum assentiente, qui tenebat tunc in tota Syria & Palæstina principatum. Iam quoq; per totum Orientem fama celebris gloriosi regis Caroli peruenerat: sic, quod dictus rex Persarum, qui monarchiam in Oriente tenebat, eius habere benevolentiam affectabat, & eidem per solemnes nuncios & legatos preciosa munera destinauit. Rex autem Carolus vbiq; victoriosus, terra sancta recuperata, per Constantinopolim Romam rediit, ibiq; natale Domini cum Leone Papa celebrauit. Ipsa siquidem natiuitatis die, cum rex in Missa ante confessionem beati Petri, surgebat ab oratione deuote: Leo Papa solemniter præordinatis quibuslibet ad tantam solennitatem necessariis, coronam imperialem capiti eius imposuit, & a cuncto Romano populo acclamatum est: Carolo Augusto, a Deo ordinato, magno Imperatori, vita & victoria cœlo ministretur. Hanc siquidem coronationem, per Leonem Papam & imperalium laudum acclamationem per populum, omnes historiæ ponunt. Post prædicta vero, more antiquorum Principum fuit adoratus, & ablato nomine Patricii, Imperator Augustus est ab omnibus acclamatus. Rexit autem Romanum imperium 14. annis. Regna quoq; Franciæ atq; Germaniæ rexerat annis 33. quibus eum Regem solum & Patricium inuenimus ab historiis nominari: sed a tricesimo tertio anno, post imperialem coronam, ipsum Imperatorem Augustum, omnes annales & historiæ, facientes mentionem de ipso, sine aliqua varietate describunt. Quantum autem roboris, iuris ac firmitatis habuit, quod tunc de translatione imperii factum fuit, per nostrum Defensorem pacis vltimo patere potest omnibus euidenter. Durauit autem imperii præscripta translatio, facta de Græcis in Francos, per septem generationes: videlicet per septem Imperatores, annis centum & duobus, quibus mansit apud Francos.
units.tr: After the death of the aforesaid Adrian, while Charles the Great reigned as defender of the Roman Church, Leo III, a Roman by birth and son of Aistulphus, was raised to the Roman pontificate in the year of the Lord 819, and 1572 from the founding of the city. This pontiff was seized in a procession in Rome, blinded, and had his tongue cut out. Placed in custody, he escaped at night over the wall and with great confidence fled to the envoys of Charles, Girundus the abbot and Vingisus the duke of Spoleto. Then, as Richard writes in his Chronicle (let whoever will believe it), the pontiff, with his limbs, eyes and tongue fully restored by divine power, as it is said, came to Charles, the chief protector of the Church, into France. Charles received him with the honour that befitted him, and, going back with him to Rome, avenged the wrong done to the pontiff and the Roman Church, by means of justice. Admonius also, describing this more fully in the Deeds of the Franks, says that when the king drew near to a place called Mimentanum, twelve miles from the city of Rome, Pope Leo, who had gone ahead of the king, met him with a great retinue. Since Charles was patrician of the city, Leo received him with the utmost humility and honour, and after they had dined together in that place, to follow the city's histories, the Pope went ahead of him with his company to the city. On the next day too, standing on the steps of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, with the standards of the city of Rome sent out to meet him, and with throngs of pilgrims and citizens arranged in fitting places to cry out praises as the king came, the Pope himself, with his bands and bishops, received the king as he dismounted and climbed the steps of the church. After a prayer, he led everyone in procession into the basilica of St Peter, singing psalms. This happened in the thirty-third year of the aforesaid king. Seven days later the king called an assembly and made known to all why he had come to Rome, and from then on he worked daily at the business for which he had come. And although serious charges were brought against the supreme Pontiff, yet because there was no lawful accuser, the same Pontiff, with the king's assent, before the whole people, carrying the Gospel in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, went up into the pulpit, invoked the name of the Holy Trinity, and canonically cleared himself of the crimes laid against him by oath. Other histories add that three cardinals, placing their hands upon the holy Gospels of God, affirmed that everything that was charged against the supreme Pontiff was false. This purgation was solemnly approved by the whole clergy and people, and was lawfully confirmed by the said Pontiff. On the same day, as Admonius writes in the Deeds of the Franks, a certain abbot named Zacharias came to Rome with two monks, one from the Mount of Olives and another from Saba in the East, whom the patriarch of Jerusalem had sent; they brought with them, with banners, the keys of the Lord's sepulchre, and of the place of Calvary, and of the city of Jerusalem. Charles received them kindly, detained them for some days, honouring and treating them humanely, and then, after some days, sent them back to Palestine with great gifts befitting the royal majesty. Some histories relate that, moved by that embassy, the king, at the request of the Emperor Constantine, crossed the sea with a great army and recovered the whole Holy Land, with the assent of the king of the Persians, who at that time held the principality over all Syria and Palestine. Already the renown of the glorious king Charles had reached throughout the whole East, so that the said king of the Persians, who held the monarchy in the East, sought to win his goodwill, and sent him precious gifts by solemn messengers and envoys. King Charles, everywhere victorious, having recovered the Holy Land, returned to Rome by way of Constantinople, and there celebrated the Lord's Nativity with Pope Leo. On the very day of the Nativity, when the king rose devoutly from prayer during the Mass before the confession of St Peter, Pope Leo, having solemnly arranged beforehand whatever was needed for so great a solemnity, placed the imperial crown on his head, and the whole Roman people acclaimed him: To Charles Augustus, ordained by God, the great Emperor, may life and victory be granted by heaven. All the histories record this coronation by Pope Leo and the acclamation of imperial praises by the people. After these events, in the manner of the ancient princes, he was adored, and the title of Patrician having been dropped, he was acclaimed by all as Emperor Augustus. He ruled the Roman empire for fourteen years. He had also ruled the kingdoms of France and Germany for thirty-three years, during which we find him named in the histories only as King alone and Patrician; but from the thirty-third year, after the imperial crown, all the annals and histories that mention him describe him without any variation as Emperor Augustus. How much strength, right and firmness the translation of the empire that was then made possesses, can be made plain to everyone by our Defender of the Peace in its final part. The aforesaid translation of the empire, made from the Greeks to the Franks, endured through seven generations, that is, through seven emperors, for a hundred and two years, during which it remained with the Franks.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.
