units.la: IMperator Arnulphus, ultimus de genere Caroli Magni, effœminatus & remissus contra Berengarium tyrannum, qui tunc in Italia Romanam ecclesiam impugnabat: quinimo ipsemet tunc erat Romanæ persecutor ecclesiæ, vt Martinus Polonus scribit, Filio enim Arnulphi prædicti, qui nondum imperialem benedictionem acceperat, a prædicto Berengario Italiæ tyranno deuicto, & apud Victoriam mutilato, genus Caroli defecit omnino in imperio: & coepit dictus Berengarius in Italia dominari, & Romana ecclesia persecutionibus vrgentibus vacillare: cum, quia dictus tyrannus eandem molestabat, tum quia Ecclesiæ non verus Pastor, sed mercenarius præerat: Ioannes videlicet Aberti filius, vt tradit Robertus Cremonensis episcopus, magnus historiarum scriptor. Vnde Cardinales ex communi concordia, anno a natiuitate Christi 905. scripserunt Othoni duci Saxoniæ, qui vir magnæ potentiæ dominabatur super vniuersam Almaniam, qui religiosus erat, fide catholicus, in consilio prouidus, in iudicio iustus, in commisso fidelis, in bellicis strenuus, & vniuersorum morum honestate præclarus, ad Dei ecclesiam deuotus. Huius ergo Principis Cardinales auxilium implorarunt, vt ecclesiam Romanam, quæ procellis impellentibus multis modis vacillabat, protegeret atque iuuaret. Qui magnum parans exercitum, in Italiam transiuit, & cum Berengario pugnauit, ipsumque cum eius exercitu in exilium misit. Postmodum vero Romam pergens, concilium Cardinalium congregauit, & de ipsorum concilio Papam noscens incorrigibilem, monuit, vt Paparui renunciatet. Quem induratum in castro sancti Angeli violenter inclusit, & Papatui ipsum renunciare coegit. Et factus est tunc Romanæ Ecclesiæ pastor, Leo octauus: qui allectus beneficio Romanæ Ecclesiæ per prædictum Othonem collato, tam de Berengario, qui vexabat eandem, quam de reformatione Ecclesiæ facta per ipsum, eisdem dignitates Othoni concessit, quas Carolo contulerat Adrianus: factaque Synodo, & clero ac populo congregato, ipsum Othonem Imperatorem constituerunt, nulla electione precedente, quæ post annos 40. fuit instituta. Sicque facta fai mperii translatio de Francis seu Gallicis, in Germanos. Habuit siquidem hic Otho primus ex ordinatione imperium pacifice. Habuerunt etiam Imperium successiue filius atque nepos, sine contradictione.
units.tr: The Emperor Arnulf, the last of the line of Charlemagne, was effeminate and slack in opposing Berengar the tyrant, who at that time was attacking the Roman Church in Italy. Indeed, Arnulf himself was then a persecutor of the Roman Church, as Martin the Pole writes. For after Arnulf's son, who had not yet received the imperial blessing, was defeated by the aforesaid Berengar, tyrant of Italy, and mutilated at Vittoria, the line of Charlemagne died out entirely in the empire. Berengar began to rule in Italy, and the Roman Church, pressed by persecutions, began to totter, both because that tyrant harassed it and because it was led by a shepherd who was no true shepherd but a hireling: John, the son of Alberic, as Robert, bishop of Cremona, the great writer of histories, relates. Therefore the cardinals, by common agreement, in the year 905 after the birth of Christ, wrote to Otto, duke of Saxony, a man of great power who ruled over all Germany. He was religious, catholic in faith, prudent in counsel, just in judgement, faithful in what was entrusted to him, vigorous in war, and distinguished for the honesty of his whole conduct, and devoted to the Church of God. The cardinals therefore implored the help of this prince, that he would protect and assist the Roman Church, which was tottering in many ways under the pressure of storms. Otto, preparing a great army, crossed into Italy, fought with Berengar, and sent him with his army into exile. Afterwards he went on to Rome and gathered a council of the cardinals. Judging that the pope, with their counsel, was incorrigible, he admonished him to renounce the papacy. When the pope obstinately refused, Otto violently shut him up in the castle of Sant'Angelo and forced him to give up the papacy. Then Leo VIII became shepherd of the Roman Church. Gratefully mindful of the benefit conferred on the Roman Church by Otto, both in the removal of Berengar, who had been troubling it, and in the reform of the Church carried out by him, Leo granted Otto the same dignities which Adrian had conferred on Charlemagne. A synod was held, the clergy and people were assembled, and they made Otto emperor, with no prior election, which was instituted only forty years later. Thus the translation of the empire was made from the Franks, or Gauls, to the Germans. Indeed, this Otto the First had the empire peacefully by ordinance. Afterwards his son and grandson held the empire in succession, without opposition.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: POst hæc autem mortuo tertio Othone sine filio, Gregorius quintus natione Teutonicus, de parentela Othonis in summum Pontificem assumitur. Cuius Pontificis tempore, Imperatoris Electores instituuntur, septem scilicet Principes Almaniæ, quatuor laici, & tres clerici siue prælati, ut Martinus scribit. Quia enim prædicti Othones successiue quasi hæreditario iure obtinuerunt Imperium, fuit pro bono statu Ecclesiæ Dei & populi Christiani ordinatum utiliter, ut tantæ potestatis fastigium, quæ non debetur sanguini, sed virtuti, non per viam successoris, sed per viam electionis procedatur, ut dignissimus eligatur ad dignitatem Imperii gubernandam. Fuit ergo institutum, ut septem Proceres Officiales Imperii regem Romanum eligerent, per Romanum Pontificem imperiali diademate coronandum: quorum, ut dictum est, sunt tres prælati clerici, qui sunt Imperatoris Cancellarii: videlicet Archiepiscopus Moguntinus, qui est Cancellarius Germaniæ: Archiepiscopus Coloniensis, qui est Cancellarius Italiæ: & Archiepiscopus Treuerensis, qui est Cancellarius Galliæ, & quatuor seculares Principes, qui seruiunt Imperatori: scilicet Palatinus Rheni, qui est dapifer Imperatoris: Dux Saxoniæ, qui est Marscalcus eius: Marchio Brandenburgensis, qui est camerarius eius: & rex Bohemiæ, qui pincerna eius. Unde versus est: Moguntinensis, Treuerensis, Coloniensis, Quilibet Imperii sit Cancellarius horum. Est Palatinus dapifer, dux portitor ensis, Marchio præpositus camera, pincerna Bohemus. Hi statuunt Dominum cunctis per secula summum.
units.tr: After this, when the third Otto died without a son, Gregory V, a German and a kinsman of Otto, was raised to the supreme pontificate. In this pope's time the electors of the emperor were instituted: seven princes of Germany, four lay and three clerical or prelates, as Martin writes. For since the aforesaid Ottos had held the empire in succession, almost by hereditary right, it was usefully ordained for the good state of the Church of God and of the Christian people that the summit of so great a power, which is owed not to blood but to virtue, should proceed not by way of succession but by way of election, so that the most worthy might be chosen to govern the dignity of the empire. It was therefore instituted that seven princes, officers of the empire, should elect a King of the Romans, to be crowned with the imperial diadem by the Roman Pontiff. Of these, as has been said, three are clerical prelates who are the emperor's chancellors: namely, the archbishop of Mainz, who is chancellor of Germany; the archbishop of Cologne, who is chancellor of Italy; and the archbishop of Trier, who is chancellor of Gaul. The four secular princes serve the emperor: the Count Palatine of the Rhine, who is his steward; the duke of Saxony, who is his marshal; the margrave of Brandenburg, who is his chamberlain; and the king of Bohemia, who is his cupbearer. Hence the verse: "Mainz, Trier, Cologne, let whichever of these be chancellor of the empire. The Palatine is steward, the duke bears the sword, the margrave is over the chamber, the Bohemian is cupbearer. These appoint as lord the highest one over all, for ever."

units.la: Hæc autem ordinatio facta fuit anno 1004. ut gesta Germanorum tradunt.
units.tr: This ordinance was made in the year 1004, as the German histories relate.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: EX prædictis igitur euidenter apparet, tempore Pipini regis, & Stephani Papæ Romani, ordinatam fuisse translationē imperii Romani de Græcis in Francos, ex occasionibus ante dictis. Tempore vero Adriani, primum Carolum Magnum dispositorem Romanæ Ecclesiæ ac Romani pontificis electorem, & vrbis Romæ patricium ordinatum, tempore vero Leonis tertii, Carolū Magnum Imperatorem Romanum effectum, & etiam ipsius tempore translationem Imperii realiter factam de Græcis in Francos. Demum vero processu temporis, post multas & iam præscriptas reuolutiones annorum, tempore videlicet octaui Leonis papæ, factam esse Romani Imperii translationem de Francis, seu Gallicis principibus in Germanos. Et postmodum tempore Gregorii quinti, electionem Imperatoris Romani septem Principibus Alamaniæ fuisse concessam: qui vsque ad moderna tempora Imperatorem eligunt ad solennitatem, non quidem propter necessitatem aliquam, per Romanum episcopum coronandum. Sic ergo translatum est Romanum Imperium ad Germanos. Præmissa quidem omnia per Romanum pontificem attentata, & cum eis assentientibus consummata, quantum robur habeant in præsenti, ex nostro Defensore pacis, in 12. & 13. & finali capitulo liquide patet, rationabiliter intuenti & attendenti.
units.tr: From what has been said, then, it is plainly evident that in the time of King Pepin and Pope Stephen of Rome, the translation of the Roman empire from the Greeks to the Franks was ordained, for the reasons mentioned above. In the time of Adrian, Charlemagne was first appointed as the disposer of the Roman Church and the elector of the Roman pontiff, and as patrician of the city of Rome. In the time of Leo III, Charlemagne was made Roman emperor, and in his time the translation of the empire from the Greeks to the Franks was actually carried out. Finally, in the course of time, after many revolutions of years already described, namely in the time of Pope Leo VIII, the translation of the Roman empire was made from the Frankish, or Gallic, princes to the Germans. Afterwards, in the time of Gregory V, the election of the Roman emperor was granted to the seven princes of Germany, who, down to modern times, elect the emperor for the solemnity, to be crowned by the Roman bishop, though not indeed out of any necessity. Thus the Roman empire was transferred to the Germans. All these things were undertaken by the Roman pontiff, and carried through with the consent of those who agreed to them. How much force they have at present is plainly clear, from our Defender of Peace, in chapters 12 and 13 and the final chapter, to anyone who considers and weighs them reasonably.

units.la: ADVERSVS VSURPATAM ROMANI PONTIFICIS IVRIS- DICTIONEM, MARSILII DE MENANDRINO PATAVINI, de re Imperatoria & Pontificia liber, qui DEFENSOR PACIS inscri- bitur, tribus partibus, quas ipse Dictiones appellat, sectus, Ad inui- ctissimum & constantissimum Imp. Cæs. Ludouicum Bauaricum, à tribus Romanis Pontificibus indigna perpessum, circa Annum Domini M. CCC. XXIV. conscriptus.
units.tr: AGAINST THE USURPED JURISDICTION OF THE ROMAN BISHOP: A BOOK BY MARSILIUS OF MENANDRINO OF PADUA ON IMPERIAL AND PAPAL AFFAIRS, WHICH IS ENTITLED THE DEFENDER OF PEACE, DIVIDED INTO THREE PARTS WHICH HE HIMSELF CALLS DICTIONES. WRITTEN AROUND THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1324 FOR THE MOST UNCONQUERED AND STEADFAST EMPEROR, LUDWIG OF BAVARIA, WHO SUFFERED UNWORTHY TREATMENT FROM THREE ROMAN BISHOPS.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: De intentione summaria tractandorum, & causa intentionis, & libri diuisione.
units.tr: On the general purpose of the matters to be treated, on the cause of this purpose, and on the division of the book.

units.la: OMni quippe regno desiderabilis debet esse tranquillitas, in qua & populi proficiunt, & vtilitas gentium custoditur. Hæc est enim bonarum artium decora mater. Hac mortalium genus reparabili successione multiplicans facultates protendit, mores excolit. Et tantarum rerum ignarus agnoscitur, qui eam minime quæsisse sentitur. Cassiodorus in prima suarum epistolarum hac serie iam præmissa, tranquillitatis seu pacis ciuilium regiminum commoditates & fructus expressit, vt per hos tanquam optimos, humanum optimum, eius vitæ scilicet sufficientiam explicans, quam sine pace ac tranquillitate nemo consequi potest, ad pacem habendam inuicem, & hinc tranquillitatem, voluntates hominum excitaret. In quo beati Iob sententiæ pronunciauit conformiter, vbi XXII. sui cap. dixit, Habeto pacem, & per hanc habebis fructus optimos. Hanc siquidem propterea CHRISTVS Dei filius, sui novi natalis signum & nunciam fore decreuit, dum militiæ cœlestis oraculo, in eodem voluit decantari: Gloria in altissimis Deo, & in terra pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis. Propter hoc etiam, idem suis discipulis pacem optabat persæpe. Unde Ioannes: Venit IESVS & stetit in medio discipulorum suorum, & dixit, Pax vobis. De pacis inuicem obseruatione monens eosdem, dixit in Marco, Pacem habete inter vos. Nec solum hanc inuicem ipsos habere, verum eandem aliis optare docebat, unde Matthæus: Intrantes autem in domum, salutate eam, dicentes, Pax huic domui. Hæc rursum fuit hæreditas, quam sibi passionis & mortis instante tempore, suis discipulis testamento reliquit, dum Ioannis IX. dixit; Pacem relinquo vobis, pacem meam do vobis. Cuius instar tanquam veri hæredes, & ipsius imitatores Apostoli hanc optauerunt, quibus per ipsorum epistolas euangelica documenta & monita dirigebant, cognoscentes fructus pacis optimos fore, quemadmodum ex Iob inductum est, & per Cassiodorum amplius explicatum.
units.tr: Every kingdom must desire tranquillity, for in it the people prosper and the welfare of the nations is preserved. It is the mother of the good arts. Through it the human race multiplies by a continual succession, extends its resources and improves its morals. Anyone who has not sought it is plainly ignorant of such great goods. In the first of his letters, having already laid down this sequence, Cassiodorus set out the advantages and fruits of tranquillity or peace in civil government. Through these, as the best of things, he explained the highest human good, namely the sufficiency of life, which no one can attain without peace and tranquillity, and he thereby stirred men's wills to hold peace with one another and so to achieve tranquillity. In this he agreed with the sentence of the blessed Job, where in the twenty-second chapter he says: "Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace: thereby good shall come unto thee" (Job 22). Christ, the Son of God, decreed that peace should be the sign and token of his new birth, when he willed that it be sung by the oracle of the heavenly host: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will towards men." For this reason too he often wished peace to his disciples. Hence John: "Jesus came and stood in the midst of his disciples, and said, Peace be unto you." Admonishing them to keep peace among themselves, he said in Mark: "Have peace one with another." He taught them not only to have it among themselves but also to wish it to others. Hence Matthew: "And when ye come into an house, salute it, saying, Peace be to this house." Again, when the time of his passion and death was at hand, he bequeathed this inheritance to his disciples by will, saying in John 14: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you." As true heirs of this and imitators of him, the Apostles desired it, and through their epistles they gave gospel teaching and admonitions, knowing that the fruits of peace are the best, as was brought forward from Job and explained more fully by Cassiodorus.

units.la: Verum quia contraria per se factiua sunt contrariorum, ex opposita tranquillitati discordia, proueniunt ciuili regimini seu regno cuiliber, fructus & incommoda pessima, vt videre sat est, & quasi cuilibet inoccultum, ab Italico regno. Dum enim ipsius incolæ coniuxerunt pacifice, fructus pacis enumeratos pridem suauiter perceperunt. Ex his & in his proficientes in tantum, vt vniuersam habitabilem eorum ditioni subdiderint. Inter ipsos vero discordia seu lite suborta, laboribus & incommodis multimodis vexatum est regnum ipsorum, & alienarum atque inuisarum gentium subiuit imperium. Sicque etiam rursum propter litem laceratum est vndique, quasi solutum, quod occupare volenti, & vtcunque potenti facilis cuilibet ad ipsum iam patet ingressus, nulla siquidem tali eventu admiratione digno; quoniam (in his quæ de Catilina) teste Salustio, Concordia parvæ res crescunt, discordia vero maxima dilabuntur. Ob quam quidem in erroris seducti deuium, vita sufficienti privantur indigenæ, pro quiete quæsita labores graviores, pro libertate vero dura iuga tyrannidum continuae subeuntes, sicque demum cæteris viuentibus ciuiliter infeliciores effecti, vt ipsorum patronymicum nomen, gloriam & immunitatem inuocantibus præbere solitum, in passionem ignominiæ à reliquis nationibus exprobretur eisdem. In has ergo miseri præcipites feruntur tenebras propter discordiam seu litem ipsorum inuicem, quæ velut animalis ægritudo, sic praua ciuilis regiminis dispositio fore dignoscitur. Cuius quidem etsi causæ primitiuæ sint plures & coniunctæ non paucæ, quas solitis modis euenire possibiles, Philosophorum eximius in ciuili scientia, omnes fere descripsit; est tamen extra illas vna quædam & occulta valde, qua Romanum imperium dudum laborauit, laboratque continue, vehementer contagiosa, nil minus & prona serpere in reliquas omnes ciuitates & regna, ipsorumque iam plurima sui auiditate tentauit inuadere. Hanc siquidem eiusque ortum & speciem, nec Aristoteles aut Philosophorum alter, sui temporis vel prioris risconspicere potuit. Est enim hæc & fuit opinio peruersa quædam in posteris explicanda nobis, occasionaliter autem sumpta, ex effectu mirabili post Aristotelis tempora dudum à suprema causa producto, præter inferioris naturæ possibilitatem, & causarum solitam actionem in rebus. Hæc nempe sophistica honesti atque conferentis faciem gerens, hominum generi perniciosa prorsus exstitit, omnique ciuilitati ac patriæ si non prohibeatur, nocumentum tandem importabile paritura. Sunt igitur (vt diximus) pacis seu tranquillitatis fructus optimi, oppositæ vero litis importabilia nocumenta, propter quod pacem optare, non habentes quærere, quæsitam seruare, litemque oppositam omni conamine repellere debemus. Ad ea quoque singuli fratres, eoque magis collegia & communitates se inuicem iuuare tenentur, tam supernæ charitatis affectu, quam vinculo siue iure societatis humanæ: Quod etiam Plato nos admonet, teste Tullio de officiis libro, qui dixit: Non nobis solum nati sumus, ortusque nostri partem patria vendicat, partem amici. Cuius sententiæ subdit Tullius consequenter; Atque, vt Stoicis placet, quæ in terris gignuntur, ad vsum hominum omnia creari, homines autem hominum causa generatos esse. In hoc naturam ducem sequi debemus, communes vtilitates in medium afferre. Quodq; communis vtilitas non parua foret, quinimo necessitas, iam dictæ singularis causæ litium, regnis atq; communitatibus omnibus nocumenta non parua minantis, referare sophisma. Curam vigilem, diligentemque operam, huic præbere tenetur quilibet, commune volens & potens vtile cernere: hoc enim immanifesto, nequaquam pestis hæc euitari potest, nec ipsius perniciosus effectus à regnis seu ciuilitatibus resecari perfecte. Non debet autem curam hanc negligere quispiam timore vel segnitie, aut quouis alio malignitatis spiritu. Nam 2. ad Timotheum.
units.tr: But since contraries by their nature produce contraries, from the opposite of tranquillity, discord, there arise for any civil government or kingdom the worst fruits and disadvantages, as is clear enough and almost hidden from no one, from the example of the Italian kingdom. For while its inhabitants lived together in peace, they long enjoyed sweetly the fruits of peace already enumerated. Advancing by these and in these, they grew so far that they subjected the whole inhabited world to their rule. But when discord or strife arose among them, their kingdom was harassed in many ways by labours and disadvantages, and it came under the rule of foreign and hated peoples. So too, again on account of strife, it was torn apart on every side, as if loosened, so that for anyone who wishes to seize it and is in any way powerful, an easy entrance into it now lies open. Nor is this event at all surprising, since (as Sallust says in his account of Catiline) "by concord small things grow great, by discord the greatest things fall to ruin." Through discord, men led astray into error wander off the path, the native inhabitants are deprived of a sufficient livelihood, and in place of the peace they sought they endure heavier labours, and in place of liberty they constantly bear the harsh yoke of tyrants. So at last they become more wretched in civil life than all other peoples, so that their name, which used to bring them the name, glory and immunity of those who invoke it, is now reproached by the other nations as a cause of shame. Into these shadows the wretched are cast headlong on account of their discord or strife among themselves, which, like a sickness of the body, is recognised as the diseased condition of civil government. Although its primary causes are several and not a few are connected with it, which can arise in the usual ways, the outstanding philosopher in civil science has described almost all of them. Yet beyond these there is one hidden and very dangerous cause, by which the Roman empire has long suffered and continues to suffer, and which, very contagious, creeps into all the other cities and kingdoms, and has already tried in many places to seize them out of its own greed. Neither Aristotle nor any other philosopher of his time or earlier could have discerned its origin and form. For this is, and has been, a perverse opinion, which we must explain later. It was taken up on an occasion from a wonderful effect brought forth long after Aristotle's time by the supreme cause, beyond the capacity of inferior nature and the customary action of causes in things. This sophistry, wearing the face of honesty and usefulness, has proved utterly pernicious to the human race, and unless it is prevented it will in the end bring an intolerable harm to all civil life and to the fatherland. Therefore, as we have said, peace or tranquillity has the best fruits, while the opposite, strife, brings intolerable harms; for this reason we ought to wish for peace, to seek it where we do not have it, to keep it once sought, and to repel strife with every effort. Likewise, individual brothers, and still more colleges and communities, are bound to help one another, both through the affection of supernal charity and through the bond or right of human society. Plato also admonishes us of this, as Cicero records in the book On Duties, where he said: "We are not born for ourselves alone; our country claims a part of our birth, and our friends a part." Cicero adds to this sentiment as follows: "And, as the Stoics hold, all things that grow on earth are created for the use of men, and men are born for the sake of men, so that they may help one another. In this we should follow nature as our guide, bringing common advantages into the midst." And since common advantage would be no small thing, indeed a necessity, it is necessary to unravel this sophism of the aforesaid particular cause of strife, which threatens no small harm to all kingdoms and communities. Every man who wishes and is able to see what is common and useful is bound to give watchful care and diligent effort to this, for unless this is made clear, this plague cannot in any way be avoided, nor can its pernicious effect be completely cut off from kingdoms or civil communities. Yet no one should neglect this care out of fear or sloth, or from any other spirit of malice. For in 2 Timothy:

units.la: 1. Non dedit nobis Deus timoris spiritum, sed virtutis & dilectionis: Virtutis, inquam & dilectionis, propalandæ veritatis, vnde subdit ibidem Apostolus; Noli itaque erubescere testimonium Domini nostri, hoc autem fuit testimonium veritatis, ad quod perhibendum CHRISTVS se venisse dixit in mundum, dum Ioannis 18. inquit: Ego ad hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum, vt testimonium perhibeam veritati; ducenti scilicet humanum genus ad salutem æternam. Ipsius ergo instar, docendæ veritati, qua ciuilium regiminum iam dictæ pestis euitari valeat, ab humano maxime Christicolarum genere, veritati inquam, ad salutem ciuitatis vitæ ducenti, ad æternam quoque proficienti non parum, is magis obligatur intendere, ouium gregarium dator, harum rerum intelligentiam amplius inspirauit, grauiterque velut ingratus, hoc sciens & potens peccat omittens, teste Iacobo suo canonicæ, cap. 4. cum dixit: Scienti bonum facere & non facienti, peccatum est illi. Non aliter enim nequitia hæc humani generis communis hostis succrescetur perfecte, nec perniciosi, quos hactenus produxit, fructus arescent, nisi suæ causæ siue radicis primum pandatur & arguatur iniquitas, hac namque via non alia tute ingredi potest principantium coactiua potestas, ad huius malitiæ patronos improbos, & defensores pertinaces finaliter expugnandos. Præmissis itaque Christi, sanctorum atque Philosophorum monitis, attendens & obsequens Antenorides ego quidam ex intelligentiæ rerum harum, si qua mihi gratia credita est, spiritu quoque confidentiæ ministrato desursum (à quo teste Iacobo suæ canonicæ, primo ca. Omne datum optimum & omne donum perfectum, desursum descendens est à patre luminum) propter dantis reuerentiam, propalandæ veritatis amorem, patriæ ac fratrum charitatis feruorem: oppressorum siquidem misericordiam & reseruationem, opprimentium vero ab erroris deuio reuocationem, eaque permitentium, his tamen obuiare debentium atque potentium excitationem, in re quoque respiciens singulariter, tanquam dei ministrum huic operi finem daturum, quem extrinsecus optat inesse, Inclytissime LVDOVICE, Romanorum Imperator, cui sanguinis antiquo, speciali quasi quodam iure, nec minus singulari heroica tua indole, ac præclara virtute insitus & firmatus est amor hæreses extirpare, catholicam veritatem omnemque aliam studiosam disciplinam extollere atque seruare, vitia cædere, studia propagare virtutum, lites extinguere, pacem seu tranquillitatem vbiq; diffundere ac nutrire: sequentium sententiarum summas post tempus diligentis & intentæ perscrutationis, scripturæ mandauí, ex his arbitrans iuuamentum quoddam euenire posse tuæ vigili maiestati, præscriptis lapsibus atq; contingentibus aliis reliquisq; vtilitatibus publicis prouidere curanti. Est ergo propositum meum, auxiliante Deo, singularem hanc litis causam solummodo pandere. Nam earum quæ per Aristotelem assignatæ fuerunt, numerum atque naturam iterare foret abundans, huius vero quam nec Aristoteles conspicere potuit, nec post ipsum qui potuerit, determinationem alter assumpsit, sic volumus reuelare velamen, vt à regnis seu ciuilitatibus omnibus deinceps facile possit excludi, exclusa vero possint securius studiosi principantes & subditi tranquille viuere, quod est desiderabile propositum in huius operis initio, necessarium debentibus ciuili felicitate frui, quæ in hoc seculo possibiliu homini desideratorum optimum videtur, & vltimum actuum humanorum. Propositum itaq; mihi iam dictum negotium distinguam per tres dictiones, in prima quarum demonstrabo intenta viis certis, humano ingenio adinuentis, constantibus ex propositionibus pe notis cuilibet menti non corruptæ natura, consuetudine, vel affectione peruersa. In secunda vero, quod demonstrasse credidero, confirmabo testimoniis veritatis, in æterna fundatis, auctoritatib. quoq; sanctorum illius interpretum, necnon & aliorum approbatorum doctorum fidei Christianæ: vt liber iste sit stans probationis extrinsecæ. Hinc etiam falsitates determinationibus meis oppositas impugnabo, & ... suis inuolutionibus aduersantium sophismata reserabo. In tertia siquidem ... quasdam, seu perutilia documenta, ciuibus & principantibus quam subiectis obseruanda, inferam, ex prædeterminatis habentia certitudinem euidentem. Vnamquamq; vero harum dictionum per capitula scribo, & capitulum quodlibet diuidam in certas partes, plures res aut pauciores, secundum capituli quantitatem: eritq; dictarum diuisionum vtilitas vna, facilis inueniendi quæsita, in quæ remittentur lectores huius, de dictionibus & capitulis posterioribus ad priora, ex qua sequetur voluminis abbreuiatio vtilitas reliqua. Cum enim contingeret nos in posterioribus dictis assumere veritatem aliquam, vel propter ipsam aut propter alia demonstrandam, cuius probatio aut certitudo in prioribus sufficienter tradita fuerit, absque probationis nugatione remittemus lectorem ad dictionem, capitulum, & partem suæ traditionis, vt sic quæsiti sui certitudinem possit facile reperire.
units.tr: (1) "God hath not given us the spirit of fear, but of power and of love" (2 Tim. 1): of power, I say, and of love, in making known the truth. Hence the Apostle adds in the same place: "Be not therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord"; and this was the testimony of the truth, for the bearing of which Christ said that he had come into the world, when in John 18 he says: "For this cause I was born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth"; namely, to lead the human race to eternal salvation. Therefore, after his example, anyone who teaches the truth, by which the aforesaid plague of civil governments may be avoided, and above all the human race of Christians, I mean anyone who leads to the truth for the salvation of civic life and contributes not a little to eternal life, is more bound to take this task in hand, since the giver of the flock has inspired a greater understanding of these matters. He who knows and is able to do good but omits to do it sins grievously, like an ingrate, as his James in the canonical epistle, chapter 4, testifies: "To him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin." For in no other way will this enmity of the common enemy of mankind be perfectly overcome, nor will the pernicious fruits it has so far produced wither, unless first its cause or root is laid open and the iniquity is exposed; for by no other way can the coercive power of rulers safely proceed to finally overthrow the wicked patrons and the obstinate defenders of this malice. Therefore, having regard to the admonitions of Christ, the saints and the philosophers, and being obedient to them, I, Antenorides, having been given some grace of understanding of these matters, and with the spirit of confidence also supplied from above (from which, as James testifies in the first chapter of his canonical epistle, "every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights"), am moved by reverence for the Giver, by love for making the truth known, and by the fervour of love for fatherland and brothers. For I look especially to the mercy and protection of the oppressed, and to the recall of the oppressors from their wandering in error; and to the stirring up of the powerful, who ought to resist those who permit such things. And I look especially to you, most renowned LUDWIG, Emperor of the Romans, in whom love for uprooting heresies, for exalting and preserving Catholic truth and every other earnest discipline, for striking down vices, for spreading the pursuits of virtue, for extinguishing strife, and for diffusing and nourishing peace and tranquillity everywhere, has been implanted and confirmed by your ancient blood, by a kind of special right, and no less by your heroic character and outstanding virtue. After a long and attentive investigation I have committed to writing the summaries of the following statements, thinking that some help may come from them to your watchful majesty, which takes care to provide against the aforesaid lapses and other contingencies and against other public disadvantages. My purpose, then, with God's help, is to lay open this one particular cause of strife alone. For to repeat the number and nature of those causes which were assigned by Aristotle would be superfluous; but this cause, which Aristotle could not discern and which no one after him could determine, I wish to unveil, so that from all kingdoms and civil communities it may afterwards be easily excluded; and once it is excluded, zealous rulers and subjects can live securely in tranquillity, which is the desirable aim stated at the beginning of this work, necessary for those who ought to enjoy civil happiness, which in this age seems to a man the best of the desirable things possible, and the final end of human actions. I shall therefore divide the matter I have proposed into three Dictiones. In the first of these I shall demonstrate, by sure ways devised by human ingenuity, the things I intend, consisting of propositions known to any mind not corrupted by nature, custom, or perverse affection. In the second I shall confirm what I believe I have demonstrated by testimonies of truth founded in eternity, and also by the authorities of the holy interpreters of it and of other approved teachers of the Christian faith, so that this book may stand firm by external proof. Hence I shall also attack the falsehoods opposed to my conclusions, and I shall unravel the sophisms of my opponents by disentangling their involutions. In the third, I shall set out certain very useful teachings, to be observed by citizens and rulers as well as by subjects, drawn from the things previously established, having evident certainty. I write each of these Dictiones by chapters, and I shall divide each chapter into certain parts, more or fewer according to the length of the chapter. The advantage of these divisions will be one: they make it easy to find what is sought, to which readers are referred from the later Dictiones and chapters back to the earlier ones. From this will follow a second advantage, the shortening of the volume. For when in later passages we happen to take up some truth, either to demonstrate it for its own sake or for the sake of other things, whose proof or certainty has been sufficiently set out earlier, we shall, without unnecessary repetition, refer the reader to the Dictio, chapter and part of its exposition, so that he may easily find the certainty of what he seeks.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De primis quæsitis in hoc libro, & distinctione ac significatorum assignatione huius dictionis Regnum.
units.tr: On the first questions in this book, and the distinction and assignment of the meanings of the term regnum.

units.la: AGgredientes itaq; proposita, primum manifestare volumus, quid sit tranquillitas regni vel ciuitatis, horum autem prius tranquillitatem, hac enim non manifesta in tranquillitatem quid sit, ignorare necesse est. Et quoniam ambæ hæ videntur esse dispositiones ciuitatis aut regni, quod ex Cassiodoro supponatur, continuo declarandum manifestabimus consequenter, quid & propter quid sit regnum aut ciuitas, vnde etiam tranquillitatis & sui oppositi descriptiones apparebunt amplius. Volentes itaq; secundum præmissum ordinem describere tranquillitatem ciuitatis aut regni, ne propter nominum multiplicitatem in proposito eueniat ambiguitas, oportet non latere, quod hæc dictio regnum in vna sui significatione importat pluralitatem ciuitatum seu prouinciarum, sub vno regimine contentarum: secundum quam acceptionem, non differt regnum à ciuitate in politiæ specie, sed magis secundum quantitatem. In alia vero sui acceptione, significat hoc nomen regnum, speciem quandam politiæ seu regiminis temperatis quam vocat Aristoteles monarchiam temperatam, quo modo potest esse regnum in vnica ciuitate sicut in pluribus, quemadmodum fuit circa ortum communitatum ciuilium, quasi enim in pluribus erat rex vnus in vnica ciuitate. Tertia significatio huius nominis & famosior componitur ex prima & secunda. Quarta vero ipsius acceptio est commune quiddam ad omnem regiminis temperati speciem, siue in vnica, siue in pluribus ciuitatibus, secundum quam significationem sumpsit ipsum Cassiodorus in oratione, quam posuimus initium huius Libri, qua etiam vtemur hoc nomine in determinationibus quæsitorum. Debentes itaq; describere tranquillitatem & suum oppositum, suscipiamus cum Aristotele primo & quinto Politica sua capitulis 2. & tertio, ciuitatem esse velut animatam seu animalem naturam quandam. Nam sicut animal bene dispositum secundum naturam, componitur ex quibusdam proportionatis partibus inuicem ordinatis, suaq; opera sibi mutuo communicantibus, & ad totum, sic ciuitas ex quibusdam talibus constituitur, cum bene disposita & instituta fuerit secundum rationem. Qualis est igitur comparatio animalis & suarum partium ad sanitatem, talis videbitur ciuitatis siue regni & suarum partium ad tranquillitatem. Huius vero illationis fidem accipere possumus ex eo quod de ipsarum vtraque comprehenduntur omnes. Existimant enim sanitatem esse dispositionem animalis optimam secundum naturam, sic quoque tranquillitatem dispositionem optimam ciuitatis secundum rationem institutæ. Sanitas autem, vt aiunt peritiores physicorum, describentes ipsam, est bona dispositio animalis, qua potest vnaquæque suarum partium perfecte facere operationes conuenientes suæ naturæ: secundum quam siquidem analogiam, erit tranquillitas bona dispositio ciuitatis aut regni, qua poterit vnaquæq; suarum partium facere perfecte operationes conuenientes sibi secundum rationem, & suam institutionem. Et quia bene dispositiens contraria, consignificat, erit intranquillitas praua dispositio ciuitatis aut regni, quemadmodum infirmitas animalis, qua impediuntur omnes aut aliquæ partes ipsius, facere opera sibi conuenientia, simpliciter, vel in complemento. De tranquillitate quidem igitur & intranquillitate opposita, sic figuraliter sit dictum à nobis.
units.tr: Now, beginning what we have proposed, we wish first to make clear what the tranquillity of a kingdom or state is. Of these two, tranquillity must come first, since without making clear what tranquillity is we cannot know it. And since both of these appear to be dispositions of a state or kingdom, as is presupposed from Cassiodorus, we will immediately and in turn declare what a kingdom or state is and why it exists, whence the descriptions of tranquillity and of its opposite will also appear more fully. Wishing therefore to describe the tranquillity of a state or kingdom in the order we have set out, and lest ambiguity arise in our discussion from the multiplicity of names, we must not conceal that the term regnum in one of its senses signifies a plurality of cities or provinces held under one rule. In this sense a kingdom does not differ from a state in kind of polity, but only in size. In another sense the name regnum signifies a certain species of polity or tempered government, which Aristotle calls monarchiam temperatam, a tempered monarchy. In this sense there can be a kingdom in a single city just as in several, as was the case around the origin of civil communities, for in several cities there was, as it were, one king in each single city. A third meaning of this name, and the more famous, is compounded of the first and second. Its fourth sense is something common to every species of tempered government, whether in a single city or in several cities. It is in this sense that Cassiodorus took the word in oratione, in the oration which we have placed at the beginning of this book, and we too shall use this name in the determinations of the questions. Since we must describe tranquillity and its opposite, let us take up with Aristotle, in primo & quinto Politica sua capitulis 2. & tertio, in the first and fifth books of his Politics, chapters 2 and 3, that a state is as it were an animated or living kind of nature. For just as an animal well disposed according to nature is composed of certain proportioned parts, ordered to one another and mutually communicating their works to one another and to the whole, so a state is constituted of such parts when it has been well disposed and instituted according to reason. Therefore, as the relation of an animal and its parts is to health, so will be the relation of a state or kingdom and its parts to tranquillity. We can accept the truth of this inference from the fact that both are understood in the same way. For they think health is the best disposition of an animal according to nature, and likewise tranquillity is the best disposition of a state instituted according to reason. Health, as the more skilled of the physicians describe it, is a good disposition of an animal by which each of its parts can perfectly perform the operations suited to its nature. By this same analogy, tranquillity will be a good disposition of a state or kingdom by which each of its parts can perfectly perform the operations suited to it according to reason and its institution. And since a good disposition implies its contrary, intranquillity will be a bad disposition of a state or kingdom, just as the infirmity of an animal is when all or some of its parts are hindered from performing their proper works, either altogether or in completeness. Concerning tranquillity, then, and its opposite intranquillity, let this much be said by us in figurative terms.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: De origine communitatis ciuilis.
units.tr: On the origin of civil community.

units.la: QVoniam autem tranquillitatem diximus bonam dispositionem ciuitatis ad partium opus, oportet consequenter intendere quid & propter quid sit ciuitas secundum se, quæ sint & quot primæ partes ipsius, amplius de vniuscuiusque ipsarum conuenienti opere, adhuc de causis & earum ordine inuicem, præ opere enim sunt hæc, ad tranquillitatis & sui oppositi determinationem perfectam.
units.tr: Since we have said that tranquillity is the good disposition of the state for the work of its parts, it is necessary next to consider what the state is in itself, and for what purpose it exists, what its first parts are and how many, and further the proper work of each of them, and also its causes and their order among themselves; for these come before the work, for the complete determination of tranquillity and of its opposite.

units.la: Ante tamen quam de ciuitate, illiusque speciebus aut modis agamus, quæ perfecta communitas est, debemus inducere primo ciuilium communitatum originem, suorumque regiminum & modorum viuendi. Ex quibus tanquam perfectis processerunt homines ad perfectas communitates, regimina, & modos viuendi in eis. Nam ex minus perfectis ad perfectiora semper est naturæ atque artis, suæ imitatricis incessus. Nec homines aliter scire arbitrantur vnumquodque, nisi cum causas illius primas & principia prima cognouerint vsque ad elementa. Secundum hunc itaque modum ingredientes, oportet non latere, quod communitates ciuiles secundum diuersas regiones & tempora, inceperunt ex parvo & paulatim suscipientes incrementum, demum perductæ sunt ad complementum, sicuti ficati euenire iam diximus in omni actione naturæ vel artis. Prima nanque humanarum & minima combinatio, ex qua etiam aliæ prouenerunt, fuit masculi & fœminæ, vt dicit Aristoteles philosophorum eximius primo politica, capitulo primo, apparet hæc amplius ex ipsius Iconomia. Ex hac nempe propagati sunt homines, qui primo repleuerunt domum vnicam, ex quibus ampliores factæ huiusmodi combinationes, tanta hominum propagatio facta est, vt eis non suffecerit domus vnica, & sed plures oportuerit facere domos, quarum pluralitas vocata est vicus, seu vicinia, hæc fuit prima communitas, sicut scribitur etiam vbi supra. Verum quamdiu fuerunt homines in vnica domo, ipsorum actus omnes, maxime quos ciuiles infra vocabimus, regulabantur seniori eorum tanquam discretiore, absq; lege tamen aut consuetudine aliqua, eo quod nondum hæ potuerant inueniri. Nec solum autem vnicæ domus homines regebantur hoc modo, verum etiam quasi eodem prima communitas vocata vicus, licet in aliquibus differenter. Quoniam & si patri familiæ domus vnicæ licuerit remittere vel punire domesticas iniurias, iuxta ipsius votum & beneplacitum omnimode, non tamen illi sic licuisset præsidenti primæ communitati vocatæ vico. In hac enim oportuit seniorem disponere iusta & conferentia rationabili aliqua ordinatione vel lege quasi naturali, vt quia sic omnibus conueniens videbatur, æquitate quadam absque magna exquisitione, solo communi dictamine rationis, & debito quodam societatis humanæ. Huius autem differentiæ causa regiminis in domo vnica & vicinia est & fuit. Quoniam si ex vnica & prima iconomia seu domestica familia, frater occidisset aut aliter offendisset fratrem, absque discrimine inde accidente, licebat patrifamiliæ si volebat delinquentem extremo supplicio non punire, tum quia soli remittenti patri facta videbatur iniuria, tum propter hominum paucitatem, tum etiam quia patrifamiliæ minus erat damni atque tristitiæ, vno carere filio quam duobus, quod etiam fecisse videtur primus auus noster Adam, dum filius eius Chain primogenitus Abel fratrem suum occidit. Non enim est patris ad filium proprie ciuile iustum, vt scribitur quarto Ethicorum, vbi de iustitia tractatus existit. In communitate vero prima, vico siue vicinia non sic facere licuit nec licet, propter dissonantiam prædictorum: quinimo nisi per seniorem vindicta seu æqualitas iniuriarum illatarum facta fuisset aut fieret, contigisset vel contingeret inde pugna & vicinorum separatio. Multiplicatis autem vicis & facta communitate ampliori, quod oportuit crescente propagatione, adhuc regebantur vno, vel propter defectum pluralitatis prudentum, aut aliam quandam alteram causam, vt scribitur tertio Politicæ, capitulo nono, illo tamen qui senior aut melior habebatur, quamuis ordinationibus minus imperfectis, his quibus in vico seu sola vicinia disponebantur. Nec tamen habuerunt communitates illæ primæ tantam partium distinctionem & ordinem, aut necessariarum artium atq; regularum viuendi summam, quanta postmodum successiue reperta est in communitatibus perfectis. Fuit enim quandoque idem homo princeps & agricola seu Pastor outum, veluti Abraam & alii posterorum quam plures, quod tamen in communitatibus perfectis nec expedit, nec liceret.
units.tr: Before we treat of the state and its kinds or forms, which is the perfect community, we must first set out the origin of civil communities, and their governments and ways of living. For men went from these, as from things already perfect, on to perfect communities, governments, and ways of living in them. For the advance of nature and of art, which imitates her, always goes from the less perfect to the more perfect. Nor do men think they know anything otherwise, unless they have first known its first causes and first principles, down to the elements. Proceeding in this way, we must not be unaware that civil communities, according to different regions and times, began small and, gradually gaining growth, were at last brought to completion, just as we have already said happens in every action of nature or art. The first and smallest human combination, from which the others also arose, was that of male and female, as the great philosopher Aristotle says in the first book of the Politics, chapter one; this appears more fully from his Economics. From this union men were propagated, who first filled a single house. From such combinations, as they grew larger, human propagation became so great that a single house no longer sufficed for them, and several houses had to be built; their plurality was called a village, or neighbourhood. This was the first community, as is also written in the place cited above. But as long as men were in a single house, all their actions, especially those which we shall later call civil, were regulated by the eldest among them as the wisest, without any law or custom, since these could not yet have been discovered. Men were governed in this way not only in a single house, but also in what was called the first community, the village, though in some respects differently. For although the head of a single household was entirely free, at his own will and pleasure, to forgive or punish domestic wrongs, the president of the first community, called the village, was not permitted to do so in the same way. In that community the elder had to arrange matters by just and fitting rational ordinance or law, as it were natural, so that it seemed fitting to all, by a certain equity without great inquiry, by the common dictate of reason alone and by a certain duty of human society. The cause of this difference between government in a single house and in the neighbourhood is and was as follows. If in the first single economy or household one brother had killed or otherwise injured another, without any resulting danger, the head of the household, if he wished, was allowed not to punish the offender with the extreme penalty: partly because the wrong seemed done only to the father, who alone could forgive it; partly because of the small number of men; and partly because it was less loss and grief to the father to lose one son than two. It seems that our first forefather Adam also did this, when his firstborn son Cain killed his brother Abel. For, as is written in the fourth book of the Ethics, where justice is treated, there is no properly civil right between father and son. But in the first community, the village or neighbourhood, it was not and is not permitted to act in this way, because of the disagreement mentioned above: indeed, unless vengeance, or an equalising of the wrongs done, had been or were made by the elder, strife and the separation of the neighbours would have followed or would follow. When the villages were multiplied and a larger community formed, as the growing increase of population required, they were still governed by one man, either because of a lack of a plurality of wise men or for some other cause, as is written in the third book of the Politics, chapter nine; but that man was the one who was held to be the elder or the better, and the arrangements were less perfect than those by which affairs were ordered in the village or the single neighbourhood. Nor did those first communities have so great a distinction and order of parts, or so full a store of the necessary arts and rules of living, as was afterwards discovered successively in perfect communities. For it sometimes happened that the same man was both ruler and farmer or shepherd of his flocks, as Abraham and many of his descendants were; yet this is neither expedient nor permitted in perfect communities.

units.la: Augmentatis autem his successiue, auæta hominum experientia, inuentæ sunt artes & regulæ ac modi viuendi perfectiores, distinctæ quoque ampliusque communitatum partes. Demum vero quæ necesse sunt ad viuere & bene viuere, per hominum rationem & experientiam perducta sunt ad complementum, & instituta est perfecta communitas vocata ciuitas, cum suarum partium distinctione, cuius continuo determinationem aggredimur. De ortu itaque ciuilis communitatis tanta sufficiant.
units.tr: As these things were gradually increased, and men's experience grew, more perfect arts, rules and ways of living were discovered, and the parts of communities were more clearly distinguished. At last, what is necessary to live and to live well was brought to completion by human reason and experience, and the perfect community called the state was established, with the distinction of its parts, whose determination we now undertake. So much may suffice on the origin of civil community.

units.la: CAP. IIII. De causa finali ciuitatis, & quaestionum scibilium, & suarum partium distinctione in generali.
units.tr: CAP. IIII. On the final cause of the state, and on the distinction in general of knowable questions and of its parts.

units.la: Est autem ciuitas secundum Aristotelem i. politicæ. c. i. Perfecta communitas omnem habens terminum per se sufficientia, vt consequens est dicere, facta quidem igitur viuendi gratia, existens autem gratia bene viuendi. Quod autem dixit Aristoteles, viuendi gratia facta, existens autem gratia bene viuendi, significat causam finalem ipsius perfectam, quoniam viuentes ciuiliter, non solum viuunt, quod faciunt bestiæ aut serui, sed bene viuunt; vacantes scilicet operibus liberalibus qualia sunt virtutum tam practicæ quam speculatiuæ, animæ. Sic itaque determinata ciuitate propter viuere & bene viuere tanquam finem, oportet de ipso viuere, ac modis eius tractare primū. Est enim vt diximus, cuius gratia ciuitas instituta est & necessitas, omniam quæ sunt & fiunt per hominum communitatem in ea. Hoc ergo statuamus tanquam demonstrandorum omnium principium naturaliter habitum, creditum & ab omnibus sponte concessum: Omnes scilicet homines non orbatos aut aliter impeditos, naturaliter sufficientem vitam appetere, hinc quoque nociua refugere & declinare, quod etiam nec solum de homine, verum de omni animalium genere patet secundum Tullium i. de officiis. c. 3. vbi sic inquit: Principio generi animantium omni a natura tributum est, vt se, corpus, vitamq; tueatur, declinetq; ea quæ nocitura videntur, omnia quæ necessaria sunt ad viuendum, acquirat & paret. Quod etiam ex inductione sensata palam quilibet accipere potest.
units.tr: According to Aristotle, in the first book of the Politics, chapter 1, the state is a perfect community that has every limit sufficient in itself, as it follows to say: it is made indeed for the sake of living, but exists for the sake of living well. When Aristotle said that it is made for the sake of living and exists for the sake of living well, he signified its perfect final cause. For those who live as citizens do not merely live, as beasts or slaves do, but live well, being free for the liberal works of the soul, such as the virtues both practical and speculative. Having thus defined the state as existing for living and living well as its end, we must first treat of living itself and its modes. For, as we have said, the state was instituted for this purpose, and its necessity lies in all the things that are and happen in it through the human community. Let us therefore establish this as the principle of all that is to be demonstrated, a principle naturally held, believed, and freely granted by all: that all human beings, unless they are orphaned or otherwise impeded, naturally seek a sufficient life and therefore shun and avoid what is harmful. This is evident not only of man but of every kind of animal, according to Tully, On Duties, book 1, chapter 3, where he says: At the beginning, nature has granted to every kind of living thing that it protect itself, its body and its life, avoid those things that seem likely to harm it, and acquire and procure all things necessary for living. Anyone can also grasp this plainly from observation by the senses.

units.la: Viuere autem ipsum & bene viuere conueniens hominibus, est in duplici modo, quoddam tempotale siue mundanum, aliud vero æternum siue cœleste vocari solitum. Quodque istud secundum viuere sempiternum scilicet, non potuit Philosophorum vniuersitas per demonstrationem comprehendere, nec fuit de rebus manifestis per se, idcirco de traditione ipsorum quæ propter ipsum sint, non fuerunt solliciti. De vivere autem & bene vivere, seu bona vita secundum primum modum mundanum scilicet; ac de his, quæ propter ipsum necessaria sunt comprehenderunt per demonstrationem philosophi gloriosi rem quasi completam. Unde propter ipsum consequendum conclauerunt ipsi necessitatem civilis communitatis, sine qua viuere hoc sufficiens obtineri non potest. Quorum etiam eximius Aristoteles 1. suæ politicæ cap. 1. dixit: Omnes homines ferri ad ipsam, & secundum naturam impetum propter hoc. Quod quamvis experientia seruata doceat, eius tamen causam quam diximus, inducere volumus distincte magis, dicentes, quod quia homo nascitur compositus ex contrariis elementis, propter quorum contrarias actiones & passiones quasi continue corrumpitur aliquid ex sua substantia: Rursumque quoniam nudus nascitur & inermis ab excessu continentis aeris & aliorum elementorum, passibilis & corruptibilis, quemadmodum dictum est in scientia naturarum, indiguit artibus diuersorum generum & specierum ad declinandum nocumenta prædicta: quæ quoniam exerceri non possunt nisi a multa hominum pluralitate nec haberi, nisi per ipsorum inuicem communicationem, oportuit homines simul congregari, ad commodum ex his assequendum, & incommodum fugiendum. Verum quia inter homines sic congregatos eueniunt contentiones & rixæ, quæ per normam iustitiæ non regulatæ causarent pugnas & hominum separationem, & sic demum ciuitatis corruptionem, oportuit in hac communicatione statuere iustorum regulam, & custodem siue factorem. Et quoniam custos hic habet arcere iniuriosos excedentes, & alios tam intrinsecus quam extrinsecus singulos turbantes, aut communitatem opprimere tentantes, oportuit ciuitatem ad hos habere in se aliquid quo resistat. Rursumque quoniam indiget communitas aliquibus opportunitatibus, reparationibus, & custodiis rerum quarundam, & aliis tempore pacis, aliisque tempore bellico, necesse fuit in ea esse talium prouisores ut communi necessitati, cum expedierit vel oportuerit, succurri possit. Extra hæc autem iam dicta, quæ solum necessitati præsentis vitæ succurrunt, est quo indiget communicantes ciuiliter pro statu futuri seculi, per Dei reuelationem super naturalem humano generi promissio, & vtile etiam pro statu vitæ præsentis, cultus videlicet ac Dei honoratio, & gratiarum actio exhibenda, tam pro receptis in hoc seculo beneficiis, quam recipiendis etiam in futuro: ad quæ docenda & in ipsis homines dirigendos oportuit ciuitatem quosdam determinare doctores. De quibus omnibus & reliquis supra dictis, quæ sint aut qualia, in sequentibus tractatibus exquisite dicetur. Fuerunt igitur homines propter sufficienter viuere congregati, potentes sibi quærere necessaria, numerata pridem, illa sibi communicantes inuicem. Hæc autem congregatio sic perfecta, & terminum habens per se sufficientiæ, vocata est ciuitas, cuius siquidem finalis causa & suarum partium pluralitatis, iam dicta est aliqualiter nobis, & in sequentibus amplius distinguetur. Nam quia diuersa sunt necessaria bene volentibus viuere, quæ per homines vnius ordinis seu officii procurari nequeunt, oportuit esse diuersos ordines hominum seu officia in hac communicatione, diuersa huiusmodi exercentes seu procurantes, quibus pro vitæ sufficientia homines indigent. Hi autem hominum diuersi ordines seu officia, non aliud sunt quam pluralitas & distinctio partium ciuitatis. Quid quidem igitur sit ciuitas, & propter quid facta sit talis communicatio, amplius de suarum partium diuisione sic figuraliter pertransisse, sufficiant.
units.tr: Living itself, and living well, which is fitting for humans, takes two forms: one is called temporal or worldly, the other eternal or heavenly. The philosophers as a whole could not comprehend the second, everlasting life by demonstration, nor was it among things self-evident; therefore they were not concerned with the tradition of those things that are for its sake. But concerning living and living well, or the good life in the first, worldly mode, and concerning the things necessary for it, the glorious philosophers comprehended the matter by demonstration, as if it were complete. Hence, in order to attain it, they concluded that civil community is necessary, without which such a sufficient life cannot be obtained. Among them the outstanding Aristotle said, in the first book of his Politics, chapter 1: All men are drawn toward it, and by natural impulse toward this. Although experience observed teaches this, we wish to set out its cause more distinctly, saying that since man is born composed of contrary elements, by whose contrary actions and passions something of his substance is almost continually corrupted, and since again he is born naked and unarmed, exposed to the excess of the surrounding air and the other elements, passible and corruptible, as has been said in the science of nature, he has needed the arts of various kinds and species to avert the aforesaid harms. These arts cannot be practised or possessed except by a great plurality of men, and only through their mutual sharing; so it was necessary for men to gather together, to obtain advantage from them and to flee disadvantage. But since quarrels and brawls arise among men so gathered, which, not regulated by the rule of justice, would cause fights, the separation of men, and at last the corruption of the state, it was necessary to establish in this communion a rule of justice and a guardian or maker of it. And since this guardian must keep off wrongdoers who exceed their bounds, and others who disturb individuals both within and without, or who try to oppress the community, the state had to have within itself something with which to resist them. Again, since the community needs certain provisions, repairs, and guardianships of certain things, some in time of peace and others in time of war, it was necessary that there be providers of such things within it, so that the common need could be met whenever it was expedient or required. Beyond these matters, which only serve the needs of the present life, there is also what men living as citizens need for the state of the age to come: the promise made to the human race above nature by God's revelation. Also useful for the state of the present life are worship, the honouring of God, and the giving of thanks, both for benefits received in this age and for those to be received in the future. To teach these things and to direct men in them, it was necessary for the state to appoint certain teachers. Of all these matters and the rest mentioned above, what they are and of what kind, will be set out exactly in the following treatises. Men, therefore, gathered together in order to live sufficiently, being able to seek for themselves the necessities already enumerated, sharing them with one another. This gathering, thus perfected and having a limit sufficient in itself, is called the state. Its final cause and the plurality of its parts have been stated to us in some measure, and will be distinguished more fully in what follows. For since there are diverse necessities for those who wish to live well, which men of one order or office cannot procure, it was necessary for there to be diverse orders of men or offices in this communion, exercising or procuring these different things, which men need for a sufficient life. These diverse orders or offices of men are nothing other than the plurality and distinction of the parts of the state. Let this suffice for what the state is, why such a communion was made, and for a general outline of the division of its parts.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: De distinctione ac assignatione partium ciuitatis, & ipsarum inexsistentia ac separationis necessitate, propter finem ab humana inuentione assignari possibilem.
units.tr: On the distinction and assignment of the parts of the commonwealth, and on the necessity of their existence and separation, for the purpose which can be assigned to them from human invention.

units.la: POstquam præmissus est a nobis totalis sermo de partibus ciuitatis in quarum actione & communicatione perfecta inuicem, nec extrinsecus impedita; tranquillitatem ciuitatis consistere diximus, vt earum ampliori determinatione, tam ex operibus seu finibus quam aliis appropriatis causis ipsarum causæ tranquillitatis & sui oppositi manifestentur amplius, de ipsis resumentes, dicimus quod partes seu officia ciuitatis sunt sex generum, vt dixit Aristoteles 7. politica, c. 6. Agricultura, artificium, militaris, pecuniatiua, sacerdotium, & iudicialis seu conciliatiua. Quorum tria, videlicet sacerdotium, propugnatiua, & iudicialis seu conciliatiua simpliciter sunt partes ciuitatis quas etiam in communitatibus ciuilibus honorabilitatem dicere solent. Reliqua vero dicuntur partes large, vt quia sunt officia necessaria ciuitati secundum Aristotelis sententiam 7. politica, c. 7. Et solet horum multitudo dici vulgaris. Sunt igitur hæ partes famosiores ciuitatis seu regni, ad quas omnes aliæ conuenienter reduci possunt. Quarum siquidem necessitas, licet vtcunque dicta fuerit capitulo præcedenti, volumus tamen hanc rursum dicere distincte magis, suscipientes tanquam prius demonstratum ex per se noto, ciuitatem scilicet, communitate esse institutam propter viuere & bene viuere hominum in ea. Quod quidem viuere duobus modis determinauimus prius, Vno nanque, vita seu viuere seculi huius, mundano videl. alio vero, vita seu viuere alterius seculi siue futuri. Ex quibus siquidem viuendi modis, desideratis homini velut finibus, assignabimus necessitate distinctionis partium communitatis ciuilis. Viuere igitur hominis primo modo, mundanum scilicet, quandoque accipitur pro esse viuentium, vt in 2. de anima: Viuere viuentibus est esse, quo modo vita nil aliud est quam anima. Quandoque vero accipitur pro actu seu actione aut passione animæ siue vitæ. Rursum vtrumque, horum duplicitur, quoniam aut in eode esse naturali, vel in consimili, quod dicunt specificum. Et licet viuere vnoquoque modorum dictorum, tam homini proprium quam sibi & cæteris animantium communi dependeat a causis naturalibus, non tamen est ipsius consideratio præsens, in quantum prouenit ab illis, sed in ea quæ de plantis & animalibus scientia naturali: de ipsis autem secundum quod ab arte ac ratione, quibus hominum genus viuit, suscipiunt complementum, est nobis perscrutatio præsens. Et propterea oportet attendere, quod si debeat homo viuere & bene viuere, necesse est, ut ipsius actiones fiant, & bene fiant, nec solum actiones, verum etiam passiones, bene inquam, id est in temperamento conuenienti. Et quoniam ea quibus hæc temperamenta complentur, non accipimus a natura omniquaque perfecte, necessarium fuit homini ultra causas naturales per rationem aliqua formare, quibus compleatur efficientia & conseruatio suarum actionum & passionum secundum corpus & animam.
units.tr: Having set out at length, as we said, the parts of the commonwealth, whose perfect action and mutual communication, not hindered from outside, we declared to be the tranquillity of the commonwealth, we now return to them in order to make clearer, by a fuller determination of them, both from their works or ends and from other appropriate causes, the causes of this tranquillity and of its opposite. We say that the parts or offices of the commonwealth are of six kinds, as Aristotle said in Politics 7, c. 6: agriculture, craft, military, monetary, priesthood, and judicial or conciliatory. Of these, three (priesthood, defence, and the judicial or conciliatory office) are properly called parts of the commonwealth, which in civil communities they are accustomed to call the honourable offices. The rest are called parts in a wider sense, because they are offices necessary to the commonwealth, according to Aristotle's view in Politics 7, c. 7. The multitude of these is commonly called the common sort. These, then, are the more notable parts of the commonwealth or kingdom, to which all the others can fittingly be reduced. Although their necessity was stated in some measure in the preceding chapter, we wish to say it again more distinctly, taking as already demonstrated, from what is self-evident, that the commonwealth was instituted by the community for the living and well-living of the men in it. We determined earlier that this living has two modes: one is the life or living of this age, that is, worldly; the other is the life or living of another age, that is, of the age to come. From these modes of living, which man desires as ends, we shall derive the necessity of the distinction of the parts of civil community. The living of man in the first mode, the worldly, is sometimes taken for the being of living things, as in De anima 2: "To live, for living things, is to be," in which way life is nothing other than the soul. Sometimes it is taken for the act, or the action or passion, of the soul or of life. Each of these is again twofold, since it is either in the same natural being or in a like one, which they call specific. And although living in each of the said modes, as much proper to man as common to him and other animals, depends on natural causes, its consideration is not our present concern insofar as it comes from those causes; that belongs to natural science concerning plants and animals. Our present investigation concerns living insofar as it receives its completion from art and reason, by which the human race lives. Therefore we must note that if man is to live and live well, it is necessary that his actions be done, and done well; and not only his actions but also his passions, well, I say, that is, in a suitable temperament. And since we do not receive perfectly, in every respect, from nature the things by which these temperaments are completed, it was necessary for man, beyond natural causes, to form some things by reason, by which the efficacy and preservation of his actions and passions, both of body and of soul, might be completed.

units.la: Et hæc sunt operum & operatorum genera, & prouenientium a virtutibus & artibus tam practicis quam speculatiuis. Actionum autem humanarum & suarum passionum, quædam proueniunt a causis naturalibus præter cognitionem, quales fiunt per elementorum contrarietatem, nostra componentium corpora propter ipsorum permixtionem. In quo genere reponi possunt conuenienter actiones particulæ nutritiuæ: Quod etiam capitulum mg·ediuntur actiones, quas faciunt elementa nostrum corpus continentia, per alterationem suarum qualitatum: de quorum genere sunt etiam alterationes quæ fiunt ab ingredientibus humana corpora, veluti sunt, cibi, potus, medicinæ, venena, & reliqua similia his. Aliæ vero sunt actiones & passiones a nobis vel in nobis, per virtutes nostras cognoscentes & appetentes, quarum quædam vocantur immanentes, vt quia non transeunt in subiectum a faciente, nec exercentur per aliquod exteriorum organorum seu membrorum motorum secundum locum, vt sunt cogitationes, & hominum desideria seu affectiones. Aliæ vero sunt & dicuntur transeuntes, quia modo altero vel vtroque prædicatorum oppositè se habent immediate prædictis.
units.tr: These are the kinds of works and of workings, and of the things that arise from virtues and arts, both practical and speculative. Of human actions and their passions, some arise from natural causes without knowledge, as those do which come through the contrariety of the elements that compose our bodies by their mixture. Under this kind the actions of the nutritive part may fittingly be placed; the actions which the elements containing our body perform through the alteration of their qualities also belong here. Of this kind too are the alterations made by things entering human bodies, such as food, drink, medicines, poisons, and the like. Others are actions and passions done by us or in us through our powers of knowing and desiring, of which some are called immanent, because they do not pass over from the agent into a subject, nor are they exercised through any external organ or limb moving in place; such are thoughts and human desires or affections. Others are, and are called, transitive, because in one or both of the said respects they stand immediately opposed to the aforesaid.

units.la: Propter has ergo temperandas actiones & passiones omnes atque complendas in eo, ad quod natura producere nequit inuenta fuerunt artificiorum diuersa genera, & reliquarum virtutum, quemadmodum diximus prius, instituriq; sunt homines diuersorum officiorum ad illa exercenda propter supplendam humanam indigentiam, qui ordines nihil aliud sunt, quam partes ciuitatis enumeratæ pridem. Ad temperandos enim atque saluandos actus nutritiuæ partis animæ, quo cessante simpliciter corrumperetur animal secundum individuum & speciem, instituta fuit agricultura camporum, & cura pecorum, ad quas conueniente reducuntur omnes species venatiuæ terrestrium, aquatilium & volatilium animalium, & omnes aliæ artes, quibus acquiritur alimentum commutatione aliqua, vel paratur ad esum: vt per ipsum reparetur tandem, quod deperditur ex substantia nostri corporis, & per id continuetur etiam in esse suo immortali, quantum homini natura permisit.
units.tr: For the sake of tempering all these actions and passions, and of completing them in that to which nature cannot bring them, various kinds of crafts and of the other virtues were devised, as we said before, and men were appointed to exercise different offices for performing them, to supply human need. These orders are nothing other than the parts of the commonwealth listed above. To temper and preserve the acts of the nutritive part of the soul, the cessation of which would simply corrupt the animal both as an individual and as a species, agriculture of the fields and the care of flocks were established. To these are suitably referred all kinds of hunting of land, water, and air animals, and all the other arts by which food is acquired through some exchange or prepared for eating, so that by it is finally repaired what is lost from the substance of our body, and thereby is continued, as far as nature has permitted man, also in his immortal being.

units.la: Ad moderandas vero actiones & passiones nostri corporis, ab his quæ nos extrinsecus continent elementis, & ipsorum impressionibus, inuentum fuit genus mechanicarum, quas Aristoteles 7. Politica, cap. 6. vocat artes, sicuti lanificium, coriaria, sutoriæ, & omnes domificatiuæ species, & aliæ quædam mechanicæ aliis subseruientes officiis ciuitatis, mediate aut immediate. Nec solum moderantes tactus aut gestus, verum etiam aliorum sensuum, quæ magis sunt ad voluptatem & bene viuere, quam ad vitæ necessitatem, velut pictoria cum sibi similibus, de quibus Aristoteles 4. politicæ, cap. 3. inquit: Harum autem artium has ex necessitate opportet existere, has autem ad delicias & bene viuere. Sub quo etiam genere reponitur medicinalis practica, architectonica, quodam modo ad plures prædictarum. Ad moderandos autem excessus actuum qui sunt a virtutibus motiuis secundum locum per cognitionem & appetitum, quos transeuntes diximus, & qui possibiles sunt, fieri ad commodum vel incommodum seu iniuriam alterius a faciente pro statu præsentis seculi: statuta fuit necessario in ciuitate pars aliqua seu officium, per quam excessus talium actuum corrigantur, & ad æqualitatem aut proportionem debitam reducantur, aliter nanque causarentur ex his pugna & inde ciuium separatio, denum ciuitatis corruptio, & vitæ sufficientis priuatio. Hæc autem pars ab Aristotele vocata est iudicialis seu principans & conciliatiua, cum sibi subseruientibus, cuius est, iusta & conferentia communia regulare. Caeterum quia sufficiens vita duci non posset oppressis ciuibus, aut in seruitutem redactis per extrinsecos oppressores, Rursum quoniam iudicum sententias ad iniurios os & rebelles intrinsecos oportet exequi per potentiam coactiuam, necesse fuit in ciuitate militarem seu propugnatiuam partem statuere, cui etiam mechanicarum mul æ subseruiunt. Est enim ciuitas viuendi & bene viuendi gratia constituta, quemadmodum dictum est in cap. precedenti, quod impossibile est ciuibus in seruitutem redactis. Hoc enim dixit eximius Aristoteles esse contra naturam ciuitatis. Unde 4 politicæ, cap. 3. necessitatem assignans, ait: Quantum autem genus quod propugnans, quod his quidem nihilominus necessarium est existere, si debeant non seruire inuadentibus, nihil enim verum impossibili quam dignum esse vocare ciuitatem naturaseruam, per se sufficiens enim est ciuitas; quod autem seruuum, non per se sufficiens. Huius vero partis necessitas propter rebelles intrinsecos habetur ab Aristotele 7. politicæ cap. 6. Seriem autem hic omisimus propter abbreuiationem, & quia ipsam inducemus 14. huius, parte. 8. Rursumq; quoniam in annis mundanis quandoque sunt fructuum fertilitates, quandoque sterilitates, adhuc quia ciuitas quandoque pacifice disponitur ad vicinas, quandoque aliter: suntque ipsius aliæ communes opportunitates, quibus indiget, vt viarum, pontium, & aliorum ædificiorum constructiones aut reparationes, & reliquæ consimiles, quas nec opportunum hic est, nec breue foret enumerare: oportuit pro his parandis conuenienti tempore in ciuitate statuere partem thesaurizantem, quam vocauit Aristoteles pecuniatiuam. Hæc enim pecunias, blada, vina, olea, & reliqua necessaria congregat & custodit, communia conferentia undecunque procurat, & quærit ad succurren-dum dum futuræ necessitati, cui etiam subseruiunt aliarum quædam. Vocavit autem hanc Aristoteles pecuniariam, quoniam pecuniarum custodia videtur thesaurus omnium, eo quod in ipsa omnia communicantur. Superest autem nobis de sacerdotali potestate necessitate dicere, de qua non omnes homines sic senserunt concorditer, ut de necessitate reliquarum partium civitatis. Et causa huius fuit, quoniam ipsius vera & prima necessitas non potuit comprehendi per demonstrationem, nec fuit res manifesta per se. Convenerunt tamen omnes gentes in hoc, quod ipsum conveniens sit instituere propter Dei cultum & honorationem, & consequens inde commodum pro statu præsentis seculi vel venturi. Plurimæ enim legum sive sectarum, honorum præmium & malorum operatoribus supplicium promittunt, in futuro seculo distribuenda per Deum. At extra causas positionis legum, quæ absque demonstratione creduntur, attendunt philosophantes convenienter valde, aliam & pro huius seculi statu, quasi necessariam causam traditionis legum divinarum sive sectarum, ex quibus fuit Hesiodus, Pythagoras, & aliorum antiquorum quamplures. Hæc autem fuit bonitas & humanorum actuum monasticorum & civilium, a quibus quies seu tranquillitas communitatum, & demum sufficiens vita præsentis seculi, quasi tota dependet. Nam licet philosophorum aliqui, talium legum sive sectarum adinuentores, non senserint aut crediderint hominum resurrectionem, & illam vitam quæ vocatur æterna, ipsam tamen esse finxere, & persuaserunt, & in ipsa delectationes atque tristitias secundum qualitates humanorum operum in hac vita mortali, ut ex hoc inducerent hominibus Dei reverentiam & timorem, desiderium fugiendi vitia & colendi virtutes. Sunt enim actus quidam, quos legislator humana lege regulare non potest, ut qui alicui non possunt probari, adesse vel abesse, quos tamen non potest latere Deum, quem finxere ipsi talium legum latorem, & præceptorem observationis ipsarum, sub æternæ pœnæ, vel præmii comminatione bonorum aut malorum operationibus. Unde dixerunt de dissimiliter studiosis in hoc seculo, quod locabantur in firmamento cœli. Et hinc fortasse pervenerunt nomina quibusdam astris & figuris cœlestibus. Agentium vero peruerse quorundam, dixerunt animas diversa brutorum ingredi corpora, puta porcorum, qui intemperati fuerant secundum gustum: hi corum, qui secundum tactum & Venerea, sicque reliquorum in reliqua, iuxta proportiones humanorum vitiorum ad damnabiles eorum proprietates. Sic etiam varia tormentorum assignaverunt genera pravorum operatoribus, quomodo intemperato Tantalo, sitim & famem perpetuam, aquam & poma præsentia, quæ nec bibere aut manducare potest, semper amplius fugientia quam prosequi possit. Dixerunt quoque tartara loca quædam talium tormentorum voraginosa & tenebrosa, terribilibus & contristatiuis quasi omnibus intentionibus, talia describentes. Ex quorum terrore fugiebant homines peruerse agere, ad studiosa quoque operum, pietatis & misericordiæ, excitabantur, ad seipsos atque alios disponebantur bene. Cessabantque propter hæc in communitatibus multæ contentiones & iniuriæ.
