Unde pax etiam & tranquillitas civitatum & vita hominum sufficiens pro statu præsentis seculi difficile minus seruabatur, quod expositione talium legum sive sectarum sapientes illi finaliter intendebant. Fuit ergo gentilium sacerdotum traditio talium præceptorum, ad quæ docenda statuere in suis communitatibus templa, in quibus colebantur ipsorum dii, constituentes etiam doctores dictarum legum seu traditionum, quos sacerdotes vocabant, eo quod templorum sacra tractabant, ut libros, vasa, & huiusmodi reliqua deseruientia cultui divinorum. Hæc siquidem ordinabant decenter iuxta ipsorum credulitates & ritus, nam sacerdotes instituebant non quoscunque, sed cives aliquos studiosos & approbatos, qui fuerant ex officio militari iudiciario vel conciliatiuo, cives inquam qui secularia negotia abdicaverant, excusati iam a muneribus & officiis civilibus propter ætatem. A talibus enim viris iam separatis a passionibus, & quorum dictis propter ætatem, & morum gravitatem amplius credebatur, decebat honorari Deos, & illorum sacra tractari, non a banausis seu mercenariis, qui vilia & maculatiua officia exercuerant. Unde septimo politicæ, cap. septimo: Neque enim agricolam neque banausum, sacerdotem constituendum. Verum quia gentiles & omnium reliquæ leges aut sectæ, quæ sunt aut fuerunt extra catholicam fidem Christianam, aut quæ ante hanc fuit sanctorum patrum credulitatem, & generaliter extra traditionem eorum, quæ in sacro canone, vocata Biblia, continentur, non recte senserunt de Deo, ut quia humanum ingenium secuti sunt, aut falsos prophetas vel doctores eorum: idcoque nec de futura vita, ipsiusque felicitate vel miseria, nec de vero sacerdotio propterea instituto, recte sentire: locuti tamen sumus in ipsorum ritibus, ut eorum a vero sacerdotio Christianorum scilicet differentia & sacerdotalis partis necessitas in communitatibus manifestius appareret.
units.tr: To regulate the actions and passions of our body, arising from the elements that surround us and their impressions, the class of mechanical arts was invented. Aristotle calls these "arts" in Politics 7, chapter 6: weaving, tanning, shoemaking, all the building trades, and certain other mechanical crafts that serve the other offices of the state, directly or indirectly. These arts regulate not only touch and motion but also the other senses, arts that serve pleasure and the good life rather than bare necessity, such as painting and its like. Of these Aristotle says in Politics 4, chapter 3: Some of these arts must necessarily exist, but others serve luxury and the good life. Under this same class falls practical medicine, and in a sense architecture, which serves many of the aforesaid arts. Next, to regulate the excesses of those actions which proceed from the motive powers, namely knowledge and appetite, which we have said pass over to others, and which are possible to occur for the benefit or harm or injury of another by the agent, according to the condition of the present age, it was necessary to establish in the state some part or office by which the excesses of such actions are corrected and brought back to equality or the due proportion. Otherwise, quarrels would arise from them, then division among the citizens, then the ruin of the state and the loss of a sufficient life. Aristotle called this part judicial, or governing and reconciling, together with the parts subordinate to it, whose task is to regulate what is just and what serves the common good. Moreover, since a sufficient life could not be led if the citizens were oppressed, or reduced to slavery by outside oppressors, and since the sentences of judges must be enforced against unjust and rebellious persons within the state by coercive power, it was necessary to establish in the state a military or defensive part, which the many mechanical arts also serve. For the state is constituted for the sake of living and living well, as was said in the preceding chapter, and it is impossible for citizens to be reduced to slavery. For the distinguished Aristotle said this is contrary to the nature of the state. Hence in Politics 4, chapter 3, assigning the necessity of this, he says: The class that defends, which is nonetheless necessary, if they are not to be slaves to invaders. For nothing is more truly impossible than to call a state by nature a slave, since a state is self-sufficient, whereas what is a slave is not self-sufficient. The necessity of this defensive part on account of internal rebels Aristotle treats in Politics 7, chapter 6. I have omitted the sequence here for brevity, and because I shall introduce it in part 14 of this work. Again, since in the years of the world there are sometimes abundant harvests and sometimes barren ones, and since the state is sometimes at peace with its neighbours and sometimes not, and since it has other common needs, such as the construction and repair of roads, bridges and other buildings, and the like, which it would be neither fitting here nor brief to list, it was necessary at the proper time to establish in the state a part that stores up, which Aristotle called financial, to provide for these needs. For this part gathers and keeps money, grain, wine, oil and the other necessities, procures and seeks common advantages from every quarter, and provides for the future needs of the state, and certain other parts serve it in this. Aristotle called it financial because the safekeeping of money seems to be the treasury of all things, since all things are shared in it. It remains for us to speak of the necessity of priestly power, about which not all men have thought alike, as they have about the necessity of the other parts of the state. The reason for this is that its true and primary necessity cannot be grasped by demonstration, nor is it a matter evident in itself. Nevertheless, all nations agree that it is fitting to institute it for the worship and honour of God, and for the advantage that follows from this, both for the present age and the age to come. For most laws or sects promise rewards of honour to the doers of good and punishment to the doers of evil, to be distributed by God in the future age. Beyond the causes for establishing laws, which are believed without demonstration, philosophers, very reasonably, look to another cause, and one that seems almost necessary for the condition of this present age, for the handing down of divine laws or sects. Among these were Hesiod, Pythagoras, and many other ancients. The goodness of human conduct, both in private and in civil life, on which the quiet and tranquillity of communities, and in the end a sufficient life in the present age, almost wholly depend, lies in this cause. For although some of the philosophers who devised such laws or sects did not hold or believe in the resurrection of men and that life which is called eternal, they nevertheless invented it and persuaded people of it, and in it they placed pleasures and sorrows according to the quality of human deeds in this mortal life. They did this so as to instil in men reverence and fear of God, and a desire to flee vices and cultivate virtues. For there are certain acts which a lawgiver cannot regulate by human law, since they cannot be proved to have occurred or not, yet God cannot be hidden from them. They imagined God as the giver of such laws and the enforcer of their observance, with the threat of eternal punishment or reward for good and evil deeds. Hence they said that those who were differently zealous in this age were placed in the firmament of heaven. And perhaps from this the names came to some stars and heavenly figures. Of certain perverse doers they said that their souls entered various brute bodies, for example those of swine who had been intemperate in taste; and others, according to touch and sexual pleasure, and so on for the rest, in proportion to the ratio of human vices to their damnable qualities. So too they assigned various kinds of torments to evil doers. For example, intemperate Tantalus had perpetual thirst and hunger, with water and fruit before him which he could neither drink nor eat, and which always fled from him faster than he could pursue them. They also spoke of Tartarus as places of such torments, gulfs of darkness, describing them in such a way as to be almost wholly terrifying and saddening. From the terror of these, men fled from acting wickedly, and were roused to zealous works of piety and mercy, and were disposed well toward themselves and others. Because of these things, many quarrels and injuries ceased in communities. Hence the peace and tranquillity of states and a sufficient life for men in the present age were kept with less difficulty, which those wise men ultimately aimed at in expounding such laws or sects. Thus there was among the Gentile priests a tradition of such precepts, and for teaching them they set up temples in their communities in which their gods were worshipped. They also appointed teachers of these laws or traditions, whom they called priests, because they handled the sacred things of the temples, such as the books, vessels, and other such things serving the worship of the gods. These they arranged fittingly according to their beliefs and rites. For they did not appoint just anyone as priests, but certain citizens who were zealous and approved, who had served in a military, judicial, or deliberative office, citizens, I say, who had laid aside secular business, now excused from civic duties and offices by reason of age. For it was fitting that the gods be honoured and their sacred things handled by men already separated from the passions, whose words were believed more readily because of their age and gravity of character, and not by mechanics or hired men who had practised base and defiling trades. Hence in Politics 7, chapter 7: For neither a farmer nor a mechanic should be appointed priest. But because the Gentiles and the laws or sects of all the rest, which are or have been outside the Catholic Christian faith, or which existed before the belief of the holy Fathers, and generally outside the tradition of those things contained in the sacred canon called the Bible, did not think rightly about God, since they followed human wit, or their false prophets or teachers, therefore they also did not think rightly about the future life, its happiness or misery, nor about the true priesthood thus instituted. Nevertheless we have spoken of their rites, so that the difference between their priesthood and the true priesthood of Christians, and the necessity of the priestly part in communities, might appear more clearly.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: De finali causa cuiusdam partis civilis sacerdotalis scilicet ex Dei traditione, sive relatione immediata, impossibili tamen humana ratione tamen inveniri.
units.tr: On the final cause of a certain civil-sacerdotal part, namely, which is found by God's tradition or immediate revelation, yet cannot be discovered by human reason.

units.la: Reliquum autem sermonis huius est, dicere de causa finali propter quam fuit verum sacerdotium in communitatibus fidelium institutum. Est enim litteræ moderatio humanorum actuum Imperatorum per cognitionem & appetitum, tam immanentium quam transeuntium, secundum quod ex illis ordinatur genus humanum ad optimum viuere venturi seculi.
units.tr: It remains for this discourse to speak of the final cause for which the true priesthood was instituted in the communities of the faithful. For it is the moderation of human acts by the Emperors through knowledge and desire, both immanent and transient, by which the human race is ordered to live well in the world to come.

units.la: Et propterea oportet attendere, quod licet primus homo Adam videlicet creatus fuerit principaliter propter Dei gloriam, sicut caeterae creaturae, fuit ipse tamen creatus singulariter ab aliis speciebus corruptibilium, quoniam ad imaginem Dei & similitudinem, ut capax & particeps esset felicitatis aeternae post vitam praesentis seculi, fuit etiam creatus in statu innocentiae seu iustitiae originalis & etiam gratiae, ut probabiliter dicunt sanctorum aliqui, & scripturae sacrae quidam doctores praecipui. In quo siquidem permansisset, nec sibi aut suae posteritati necessaria fuisset officium civilium institutio vel distinctio, eo quod opportuna quaeq; ac voluptuosa sufficientiae huius vitae in paradiso terrestri seu voluptatis natura produxisset eidem, absque ipsius poena vel fatigatione quacunque. Verum quia suam corrupit innocentiam seu originalem iustitiam & gratiam in esu prohibiti sibi ligni, divinum in hoc transgrediendo mandatum, repente lapsus est in culpam atq; miseriam siue poenam, poenam inquam privationis felicitatis aeternae, ad quam Dei gloriosi beneficio cum sua posteritate qualibet finaliter fuerat ordinatus. Demeruit etiam ex iam dicti transgressione mandati, omnem sui successionem in libidine propagare, in qua etiam & cum qua quilibet homo postmodum conceptus est & natus, ex hac peccatum contrahens, quod in lege Christianorum originale vocatur, praeter Christum Iesum, qui absque peccato & libidine quibuscunque conceptus fuit de Spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria virgine, quod factum est, dum una trium divinarum personarum, Filius videlicet, verus Deus, unitate sui suppositi, naturam assumpsit humanam.
units.tr: Therefore we must observe that, although the first man, Adam, was created principally for the glory of God, as were the other creatures, he was nevertheless created singularly apart from the other species of corruptible things, because he was made in the image and likeness of God, so as to be capable of, and to share in, eternal happiness after the life of the present world. He was also created in a state of innocence, or original justice, and also of grace, as some of the saints and certain chief doctors of Scripture probably say. Had he persisted in this state, neither the institution nor the distinction of civil offices would have been necessary for him or his posterity, since the nature of pleasure in the earthly paradise would have brought forth for him whatever was suitable and delightful for the sufficiency of this life, without any punishment or weariness on his part. But because he corrupted his innocence, or original justice and grace, by eating of the forbidden tree, transgressing the divine command in this, he suddenly fell into guilt and misery, or punishment, namely the punishment of the loss of eternal happiness, to which, by the glorious benefit of God, he and all his posterity had been ordained as their final end. By the same transgression of the command he also merited that all his successors should be propagated in lust, in which and with which every man is afterwards conceived and born, and from this he contracts sin, which in the law of the Christians is called original sin. The exception is Christ Jesus, who, without sin and without any lust, was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary; this came about when one of the three divine persons, namely the Son, true God, assumed human nature into the unity of his person.

units.la: Ex hac siquidem transgressione primorum parentum infirmata est secundum animam omnis humana successio & infirma nascitur, quae ante creata fuerat in statu sanitatis perfectae, innocentiae atque gratiae, priuata quoque propter delictum, suo finali optimo, ad quod fuerat ordinata. Quodque Dei proprium est, miseri humano generi, factura ac imagini suae, quam praeordinauerat ad beatam & aeternam vitam, voluit, qui nunquam facit frustra quicquam, neque deficit in necessariis, humani casus exhibere remedium, tradendo scilicet praecepta quaedam obedientiae, seruanda homini, quae tanquam contraria transgressioni, sanare debeant aegritudinem culpae, quae prouenit ab illa. Processitque in his ordinate valde a facilioribus ad difficiliora, velut peritus medicus, praecepit namque hominibus primo ritum holocaustorum, de frugum primitiis & primogenitis animalium, quasi poenitentiam & humanam obedientiam experiri vellet, quem ritum seruauerunt antiqui patres in Dei reuerentiam, fidem, obedientiam, & gratiarum actionem usque ad Abrahae tempora.
units.tr: Indeed, by this transgression of the first parents, all human succession is weakened in its soul, and it is born weak, though it had been created before in a state of perfect health, innocence and grace, and deprived also, on account of the offence, of its final good, to which it had been ordained. And since it is proper to God, who never does anything in vain and is never lacking in what is necessary, he willed to provide a remedy for the human fall for the wretched human race, his own handiwork and image, which he had preordained to a blessed and eternal life. He did so by handing down certain precepts of obedience to be kept by man, which, being contrary to the transgression, ought to heal the sickness of guilt that arose from it. In these matters he proceeded in an orderly way, very much from the easier to the more difficult, like a skilful physician. For first he commanded men the rite of burnt offerings, from the firstfruits of the crops and the firstborn of the animals, as if he wished to test their repentance and human obedience; and the ancient fathers kept this rite, in reverence for God, in faith, in obedience and in thanksgiving, down to the time of Abraham.

units.la: Cui siquidem iuxta praedictum, dedit aliud praeceptum gravius, circumcisionis scilicet omnis humani & masculini sexus, in carne praeputii, quasi videretur rursum Deus poenitentiam & humanam obedientiam amplius experiri. Fuerunt autem praecepta haec per aliquos observata usque in tempora Moysi, per quem postmodum tradidit Deus Israelitico populo legem, per quam cum supradictis ampliora praecepta statuit, tam pro statu praesentis seculi quam venturi, ipsiusq; legis ministros etiam statuit sacerdotes atque leuitas. Horum siquidem omnium primorum praeceptorum atque Mosaicae legis observatoribus vtilitas erat, purgatio quaedam peccati siue culpae tam originalis quam actualis seu sponte commissae, Euasio quoque seu praeseruatio quaedam ab aeterna & temporali poena sensus alterius seculi, quam non ex horum observatione non merentur homines felicitatem aeternam. Ad quam tamen quoniam ordinauerat misericors Deus humanum genus, volens ipsum a lapsu reducere seu restituere ad eandem secundum conuenientem ordinem, omnium nouissime humano generi, per filium eius Iesum Christum verum Deum & verum hominem, in suppositi vnitate, tradidit legem Euangelicam, praecepta continentem credendorum, agendorum & fugiendorum, atque consilia eorum: Quorum obseruatione non solum a poena sensus praeseruantur homines, vt per priorum obseruantiam, verum ex ipsius gratiosa ordinatione merentur extalibus, congruitate quadam, felicitatem aeternam. Et propterea lex gratiae vocata est, tum quia per Christi passionem & mortem, redemptum est humanum genus a culpa & poena damni aeternae beatitudinis, quam subiuerat ex lapsu seu peccato primorum parentum: tum quia per illius observationem & sacramentorum cum ipsa institutorum receptione, nobis confertur gratia diuina, collata roboratur, & amissa recuperatur, per quam ex Dei ordinatione, cum merito passionis Christi, congruitate quadam (vt diximus) opera nostra fiunt meritoria felicitatis aeternae. Huius autem meritorum passionis, Christi videlicet, non solum posteriores gratiam susceperunt, qua beatam vitam mereri valeant, verum etiam priorum praeceptorum & Mosaicae legis observatores inde gratiam consecuti sunt aeternae beatitudinis, qua quidem in alio seculo, & in loco quem limbum vocant, priuati manserant vsq; in Christi aduentum, passionem, mortem, & resurrectionem. Per quem repromissionem sibi datam a Deo acceperunt, quamuis in praeceptis prioribus prophetarum & legis Mosaicae, talis gratiae repromissio sub aenigmatico velamine traderetur eisdem, omnia enim illis contingebant in figura, vt dicit Apostolus ad Hebraeos. Fuit autem deductio haec diuina conueniens valde, quoniam de minus perfecto ad magis, & demum ad perfectissimum conuenientem humanae salutis. Nec est opinandum propterea quin Deus potuisset si voluisset, statim a principio lapsus humani tem medium adhiberi perfectum. Sed sic egit, quia sic voluit & decuit, hominum exigente delicto, ut non veniat nimis prompta facilitas praebetet occasionem vlterius delinquendi. Iam dictae vero legis doctores ac sacramentorum secundum illam administratores instituti sunt quidam in communitatibus vocati sacerdotes & diaconi seu levitae, quorum officium est, legis euangelicae Christianae praecepta & consilia docere, in his quae credenda sunt, agenda, & fugienda, finaliter pro statu venturi seculi, beato siquidem consequendo & oppositio deuitando. Sacerdotalis igitur officii finis est, hominum disciplina & eruditio, de his quæ secundum euangelicam legem necessarium est credere, agere, vel omittere propter æternam salutem consequendam & miseriam fugiendam. In hoc autem officium conuenienter veniunt omnes disciplinæ, humano ingenio adinuentæ, tam speculatiuæ quam actiuæ, humanorum actuum moderatiuæ, tam immanentium quam transeuntium, ab appetitu & cognitione proueneintium, quibus bene disponitur homo secundum animam pro statu tam præsentis seculi, quam venturi. Has etenim quasi omnes habemus ex traditione admirabilis Philosophi & reliquorum gloriosorum virorum, enumerare tamen omisimus hic eas propter abbreuiationem sermonis, & quoniam huiusmodi necessitas non habet considerationem præsentem. Debemus autem intelligere de hoc capitulo, & ipsum sequente continuo, alias esse causas officiorum ciuitatis, iuxta quodlibet ipsarum genus, secundum quod sunt habitus corporis, aut mentis humanæ. Nam finales eorum causæ secundum quod habitus corporis, aut humanæ animæ, sunt opera quæ ab illis proueniunt immediate per se, vt nauifactiuæ, nauis: militaris, armorum vsus aut pugna, sacerdotii vero prædicatio legis diuinæ, & secundum illam sacramentorum administratio, & sic conformiter in reliquis omnibus. Ipsorum autem causæ finales secundum quod officia in ciuitate determinata & instituta, sunt commoda & sufficientiæ perfectiuæ actionum & passionum humanarum, proueniêtes ab operibus dictorum habituum, vel quæ sine his haberi nequeunt, quomodo a pugna qui est actus seu finis militaris habitus, hominibus in ciuitate libertas prouenit & seruatur, quæ quidem finis est actuum & operum militaris. Sic etiam a domificatiuæ opere, seu fine qui domus est, prouenit hominibus seu ciuitati defensio, ab aeris impressionibus nociuis, calidi, frigidi, humidi, aut sicci, quæ siquidem defensio causa finalis est, propter quam domificatiuæ officium fuit in ciuitate statutum. Eodemque modo ab obseruatione legis diuinæ, quæ finis est sacerdotii, prouenit hominibus æterna felicitas. Sic quoque de reliquis partibus seu officiis ciuitatis existimare oportet. Hoc etiam modo siue consimili, distinguuntur reliquæ causarum species officiorum dictorum, materialis, formalis, & efficiens, vt ex sequentibus apparebit. De numero quidem igitur partium ciuitatis, ipsarumque necessitate ac distinctione propter finales sufficientias dicta sint tanta.
units.tr: To him, according to what was said above, he gave another, weightier command, namely the circumcision of every human male in the flesh of the foreskin, as if God wished once more to test repentance and human obedience further. These precepts were observed by some down to the time of Moses, through whom God afterwards gave the law to the Israelite people, by which, along with the aforesaid precepts, he laid down weightier commandments, both for the state of the present world and of the world to come, and he also appointed as ministers of this law priests and Levites. Now the benefit for all those who observed these first precepts and the law of Moses was a certain purging of sin or guilt, both original and actual, that is, committed willingly; and also a certain escape or preservation from the eternal and temporal punishment of sense in the other world, which men do not merit eternal happiness without observing. Yet, since merciful God had ordained the human race to this happiness, wishing to lead it back from its fall, or restore it to the same in a fitting order, at last, for the human race, through his Son Jesus Christ, true God and true man, in the unity of his person, he delivered the Gospel law, containing the precepts of things to be believed, done and avoided, and also the counsels of these. By the observance of these, men are preserved not only from the punishment of sense, as by the observance of the former, but by God's gracious ordinance they merit eternal happiness from such things by a certain fitness. And therefore it is called the law of grace: partly because, through the passion and death of Christ, the human race has been redeemed from guilt and from the punishment of the loss of eternal blessedness, which it had incurred by the fall or sin of the first parents; partly because, through the observance of it and the reception of the sacraments instituted with it, divine grace is conferred upon us, strengthened when conferred, and what was lost is recovered, by which, through God's ordinance, together with the merit of Christ's passion, our works become meritorious of eternal happiness by a certain fitness (as we have said). Now not only the later believers received grace from the merit of this passion, namely of Christ, by which they might be able to merit a blessed life, but also the observers of the earlier precepts and of the law of Moses obtained from it the grace of eternal blessedness; yet they had remained deprived of it, in the other world and in the place which they call limbo, until the coming, passion, death and resurrection of Christ. Through him they received the promise given them by God, although in the earlier precepts of the prophets and the law of Moses the promise of such grace was delivered to them under an enigmatic veil, for all things happened to them in a figure, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews. This divine guidance was very fitting, since it proceeded from the less perfect to the more perfect, and at last to the most perfect, suited to human salvation. Nor is it to be supposed that God could not, if he had willed, have applied the perfect means from the very beginning of the human fall. But he acted thus because he so willed and it became him, the sin of men requiring it, so that too ready an ease might not afford occasion for further sinning. The teachers of the aforesaid law and the administrators of the sacraments according to it were instituted in the communities as certain men called priests and deacons or Levites, whose office is to teach the precepts and counsels of the Christian Gospel law, in those things which are to be believed, done and avoided, ultimately for the state of the world to come, namely in order to attain the blessed life and to avoid its opposite. Therefore the end of the priestly office is the discipline and instruction of men in those things which, according to the Gospel law, it is necessary to believe, to do, or to omit, for the sake of attaining eternal salvation and avoiding misery. Into this office all the disciplines devised by human wit, both speculative and practical, that moderate human acts, both immanent and transient, arising from desire and knowledge, by which man is well ordered in soul for the state both of the present world and of the world to come, come together in a fitting way. For we have nearly all of them from the tradition of the admirable Philosopher and of the other glorious men; yet we have omitted to enumerate them here, for the sake of brevity, and because such a need does not call for present consideration. We ought, however, to understand in this chapter, and in the one immediately following, that there are different causes of civil offices according to each kind of them, insofar as they are habits of the body or of the human mind. For their final causes, insofar as they are habits of the body or of the human soul, are the works which proceed from them immediately of themselves, as the final cause of shipbuilding is the ship, of military skill the use of arms or battle, and of the priesthood the preaching of the divine law and, according to it, the administration of the sacraments; and so, similarly, in all the rest. But their final causes, insofar as the offices are determined and instituted in the state, are the advantages and the perfecting sufficiencies of human actions and passions, arising from the works of the aforesaid habits, or which cannot be had without them: thus from the battle, which is the act or end of the military habit, liberty comes to men in the state and is preserved; this is indeed the end of the acts and works of the military. So too from the work of building, or the end which is the house, defence comes to men or to the state against the harmful impressions of the air, whether hot, cold, moist or dry; and this defence is the final cause for which the office of building was established in the state. And in the same way, from the observance of the divine law, which is the end of the priesthood, eternal happiness comes to men. So it is right to think likewise concerning the other parts or offices of the state. In this same manner, or a similar one, the other kinds of causes of the said offices are distinguished, material, formal and efficient, as will appear from what follows. Concerning the number of the parts of the state, and their necessity and distinction on account of their final sufficiencies, let so much be said.

units.la: CAP: VII.
units.tr: CAP: VII.

units.la: De reliquis speciebus causarum inexistentia ac separationis partium ciuitatis, & vnius-cuiusq; speciei diuisione per modos duos ad propositum pertinentes.
units.tr: On the remaining kinds of causes: the inherence and separation of the parts of the commonwealth, and the division of each kind by two modes pertinent to the purpose.

units.la: HIs autem consequens est dicere de reliquis causis officiorum seu partium ciuitatis. Et primum loquemur in causis materialibus & formalibus, deinde vero inquiremus de ipsarum causa mouente: Verum quia in rebus quæ ab humana mente recipiunt complementum, materia formæ præexistit in actu, prius loquamur in causa materiali. Et dicemus, quod materia propria officiorum diuersorum, secundum quod officia nominant habitus animæ, sunt homines ex ipsorum generatione seu nariuitate inclinati ad diuersas artes seu disciplinas. Cum enim natura non deficiat in necessariis, de nobilioribus magis solicita, qualis inter corruptibilia est hominum species, ex qua perfecta, per diuersas artes aut disciplinas, oportet tanquam ex materia, constituere ciuitatem & partes distinctas in ipsa, necessarias ad vitæ sufficientiam consequendam, vt quarto & quinto huius ostensum est. Initiauit ipsa circa generationem hominum distinctionem hanc, quosdam in naturalibus dispositionibus producens aptos & inclinatos ad agriculturam, alios ad militiam, reliquos vero ad aliorum artificiorum & disciplinarum genera, diuersos tamen ad diuersas. Nec solum vnicum individuum ad vnius speciei artem vel disciplinam, sed ipsorum plura in eandem artificii seu disciplinæ speciem inclinauit, veluti sufficientiæ necessitas exigebat. Quosdam ergo genuit aptos prudentiæ, quoniam ex prudentibus in ciuitate statui debet iudicialis pars & conciliatiua. Quosdam vero ad robur & audaciam, quoniam ex talibus conuenienter statuitur militaris. Sic quoque reliquos adaptauit ad operatiuorum & speculabilium habituum genera, quæ sunt ad viuere & bene viuere necessaria seu conuenientia, vt in omnibus scilicet perficeret de diuersitate naturalium inclinationum ad habitus diuersorum generum & specierum, quæ necesse fuit ad diuersitatem partium ciuitatis. Materiales vero causæ officiorum ciuitatis, secundum quod officia nominat partes ciuitatis, iam quasi apparent. Nãhæ sunt homines habituati per artes & disciplinas diuersorum generum & specierum, ex quibus diuersi ordines siue partes statuuntur in ciuitate propter finales sufficientias proueniêtes ab ipsorum artibus & disciplinis, quo modo proprie dicitur partes ciuitatis officia quasi obsequia, quoniam consideratæ, vt statutæ sic sunt in ciuitate, ad humanum obsequium ordinantur. Horum vero formales causæ secundum quod humanæ mentis habitus non aliæ sunt ab huiusmodi habitibus, nam ipsi formæ sunt habentium complectiuæ seu perfectiuæ humanarum inclinationum inexistentium a natura. Vnde 7. politicæ, c. finali: Omnis ars & disciplina quod deficit natura vult supplere. Formales autem officiorum causæ, secundum quod instituta & partes ciuitatis, sunt præcepta mouentis causæ, his tradita seu impressa, qui deputantur in ciuitate ad determinata opera exercenda. Mouentes quidem igitur causæ seu factiuæ officiorum, vt animæ nominant habitus, sunt mentes & voluntates hominum per suas cogitationes & desideria diuisim aut coniunctim indifferenter. Et quorundã etiã cum his principrincipium est motus & exercitium corporalium organorum. Ipsorum vero causa efficiens, secundum quod partes sunt ciuitatis, est humanus legislator frequenter & in pluribus, licet olim raro & in paucissimis cuiusdam aut quarundam causa mouens immediata fuerit Deus absque huiusmodi determinatione, sicuti nono huius dicetur, & 12. & 15. de his amplius apparebit. De sacerdotio vero, diuersa quaedam est institutionis ratio, de qua 15. & 17. secunda dicitur vtiq; sufficienter. De partibus itaque ciuitatis & ipsarum institutionis necessitate à reliquis trium causarum generibus, determinatum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: It follows from this that I should speak of the remaining causes of the offices or parts of the commonwealth. And first we shall treat of the material and formal causes, and then we shall inquire into their moving cause. But because, in things which receive their completion from the human mind, the matter pre-exists the form in actuality, let us speak first of the material cause. And we shall say that the proper matter of the various offices, insofar as offices name habits of the soul, is men inclined by their birth or nativity to various arts or disciplines. For since nature does not fail in necessities, and is more solicitous about the nobler things (such as the human species among corruptible things), it is necessary to constitute the perfect commonwealth, and its distinct parts needed to attain sufficiency of life, out of the various arts or disciplines, as out of matter, as was shown in the fourth and fifth books. Nature itself began this distinction at the generation of men, producing some by their natural dispositions apt and inclined to agriculture, others to war, and the rest to the kinds of other crafts and disciplines, yet each to different ones. Nor did it incline only a single individual to the art or discipline of one species, but it inclined several of them to the same species of craft or discipline, as the necessity of sufficiency demanded. Thus it begot some apt for prudence, since from the prudent the judicial and deliberative part ought to be established in the commonwealth; and others for strength and boldness, since from such the military part is fittingly established. In the same way it also adapted the rest to the kinds of operative and speculative habits, which are necessary or fitting for living and living well; so that, in all things, it might bring about the diversity of natural inclinations toward the habits of the various kinds and species, which was required for the diversity of the parts of the commonwealth. Now the material causes of the offices of the commonwealth, insofar as offices name the parts of the commonwealth, already appear, as it were. These are men habituated through the arts and disciplines of various kinds and species, from whom various orders or parts are established in the commonwealth on account of the final sufficiencies arising from their arts and disciplines. In this way the parts of the commonwealth are properly called offices, as it were services, since, considered as established in the commonwealth, they are ordered to human service. But their formal causes, insofar as they are habits of the human mind, are none other than such habits; for these are the forms which comprehend or perfect the inclinations of the possessors, inherent from nature. Whence in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter last: "Every art and discipline wishes to supply what nature lacks." Moreover, the formal causes of the offices, insofar as they are institutions and parts of the commonwealth, are the precepts of the moving cause, handed down or impressed upon those who are appointed in the commonwealth to exercise determinate works. The moving causes, then, or efficient causes of the offices, insofar as they are habits of the soul, are the minds and wills of men, through their thoughts and desires, separately or jointly and indifferently; and for some, the principle of motion and exercise of the bodily organs is also joined with these. But their efficient cause, insofar as they are parts of the commonwealth, is the human lawgiver, frequently and in many cases; although formerly, rarely and in very few cases, God was the immediate moving cause of some one or some few, without such determination, as will be said in the ninth book, and as will become clearer about these in the twelfth and fifteenth. Concerning the priesthood, however, there is a different reason of institution, about which it is sufficiently said in the fifteenth and seventeenth of the second book. Thus it has been determined in this way concerning the parts of the commonwealth and the necessity of their institution, apart from the other kinds of the three causes.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De generibus politiarum, siue regiminum, Temperato & vitiato, & suarum specierum diuisione.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. On the kinds of polities or governments, sound and corrupt, and the division of their species.

units.la: QVoniam autem in prioribus monstratum est aliqualiter, monstrandum tamen certius institutionem & distinctionem partium ciuitatis ab aliqua mouente causa fieri, quam pridem legislatorem diximus: Quodque legislator idem has partes statuit, distinguit, & separat instar animalis naturae, formando scilicet primum, seu instituendo in ciuitate partem vnam, quam principantem seu iudicialem diximus quinto huius: Per hanc vero reliquas, vt declarabitur amplius 15. huius. Conuenit propterea nobis primum aliquid dicere de natura partis illius: cum enim sit aliarum prima, vt ex sequentibus apparebit, ex ipsius efficientiae manifestatione priori conuenienter ingredimur ad manifestationem institutionis & distinctionis actiuae reliquarum partium ciuitatis. Sunt autem principatiuae partis seu principatuum genera duo, vnum quidem bene temperatum, reliquum vero vitiatum. Voco autem bene temperatum genus cum Aristot. politica, cap. 5. in quo dominium principatum ad commune conferens secundum voluntatem subditorum, Vitiatum vero quod ab hoc deficit. Horum rursum generum, vtrumque diuiditur in tres species, Primum quidem, temperatum scilicet, in regalem monarchiam, aristocratiam, & politiam. Reliquum vero vitiatum scilicet in tres oppositas species diuiditur, tyrannicam monarchiam, oligarchiam, & democratiam. Et vnaquaeq; rursum harum specierum modos habet, de quibus praesentis negotii non est exquisite tractare. De his enim sufficienter tradidit Aristoteles tertio & quarto sua politica. Ad habendam vero ipsarum ampliorem notitiam, quę necesse est aliqualiter propter sequentia declaranda, viamquamque dictarum principatus specierum iuxta intentionem Aristotelis describamus, dicentes primum, quod regalis monarchia est temperatus principatus, in quo dominans est vnicus ad commune conserens, & subditorum voluntatem siue consensum. Tyrannis vero illi opposita, est principatus vitiatus, in quo dominans est vnicus ad conferens proprium praeter voluntatem subditorum. Aristocratia est principatus temperatus, in quo dominatur honorabilitas sola, iuxta subditorum voluntatem siue consensum & commune conferens. Oligarchia vero illi opposita, est principatus vitiatus, in quo dominantur aliqui ditiorum seu potentiorum ad ipsorum conferens, praeter subditorum voluntatem. Politia vero licet in vna significatione sit commune quiddam ad omne genus vel speciem regiminis seu principatus, in vna tamen ipsius significatione importat speciem quandam principatus temperati, in quo ciuis quilibet participat aliqualiter principatu vel consiliatiuo vicissim iuxta gradum & facultatem seu conditionem ipsius, ad commune etiam conferens, & ciuium voluntatem siue consensum. Democratia vero illi opposita, est principatus, in quo vulgus seu egenorum multitudo statuit principatum, & regit sola, praeter reliquorum ciuium voluntatem, siue consensum, nec simpliciter ad commune conferens secundum proportionem conuenientem. Quisquam bene temperatorum principatuum sit optimus, aut quis vitiatorum pessimus, de reliquorum quoque ordine in bonitate vel malitia dicere, non habet praesentem speculationem. Haec tamen de principatuum diuisione in suas species, ipsarumq; descriptione dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Although it was shown in general terms earlier, it must still be shown more precisely that the institution and distinction of the parts of the state comes about through a moving cause, namely the lawgiver whom we mentioned before. The lawgiver establishes, distinguishes and separates these parts as the nature of an animal does: he first forms, or institutes, one part in the state, which we called the ruling or judicial part in book five, and through this he forms the rest, as will be explained more fully in book fifteen. It is therefore fitting first to say something about the nature of that part, since it is the first of the others, as will appear from what follows. By first making clear its efficacy, we proceed properly to an account of the institution and the active distinction of the remaining parts of the state. There are two kinds of the ruling part, or of rulerships: one well tempered, and the other corrupted. I call a kind well tempered, with Aristotle in politica, cap. 5., when the dominium principatum is directed to the common good in accordance with the will of the subjects; and Vitiatum is the kind that falls short of this. Each of these two kinds is in turn divided into three species. The first, the tempered kind, is divided into royal monarchy, aristocracy and polity. The other, the corrupted kind, is divided into three opposed species: tyrannical monarchy, oligarchy and democracy. Each of these species has further modes, which it is not the purpose of the present undertaking to examine exactly, for Aristotle has treated them sufficiently in tertio & quarto sua politica. To gain a fuller knowledge of these species, which must be explained to some degree for what follows, let us describe the course of each of the said species of rulership according to Aristotle's intention. First, royal monarchy is a tempered rulership, in which a single ruler governs for the common good, in accordance with the will or consent of the subjects. Tyrannis, its opposite, is a corrupted rulership, in which a single ruler governs for his own advantage, against the will of the subjects. Aristocratia is a tempered rulership, in which only worth holds sway, according to the will or consent of the subjects, and it serves the common good. Oligarchia, its opposite, is a corrupted rulership, in which some of the wealthier or more powerful rule for their own advantage, against the will of the subjects. Politia, although in one sense it is a common term for every kind or species of government or rulership, in one sense of its own signifies a certain species of tempered rulership, in which each citizen takes some part in rule, either in deliberation, in turn, according to his rank, ability or condition, and which serves the common good and the will or consent of the citizens. Democratia, its opposite, is a rulership in which the common people, that is the mass of the needy, sets up the rule and governs alone, against the will or consent of the other citizens, and does not serve the common good in any proper proportion. Which of the tempered rulerships is best, or which of the corrupted is worst, and what order the others hold in goodness or badness, is not the subject of the present inquiry. Let it suffice to have said this about the division of rulerships into their species and their description.

units.la: CAP. IX. De modis instituendi regalem monarchiam & perfectionis assignatione, de modis quoq; instituendi reliqua regimina, seu politias tam temperatas, quam vitiatas.
units.tr: CAP. IX. On the ways of establishing a royal monarchy and its perfection, and also on the ways of establishing the other forms of government, whether temperate or corrupt.

units.la: DEterminatis autem his, consequens est dicere de modis efficiendi seu constituendi partem principantem. Ex ipsorum namq; natura meliori vel deteriori prouenientibus hinc ciuili regimini tanquam actionibus arguere oportet causam agentē, à qua tam ipsi quam pars principans per ipsos ad politiā vtilius habeant prouenire. Verum quia de causis & actionibus, à quibus secundū plurimū pars principans creari debet, intendimus in hoc libro: antea volumus dicere modum & causam, per quē iam creata fuit pars haec, licet raro, vt hunc modum seu actionem, & ipsius causam immediatam discernamus à modis seu actionibus & ipsarū immediatis causis, per quas huiusmodi pars regulariter & in pluribus creari debet, quas etiā humana demonstratione conuincere possumus: prioris enim modi per demonstrationē certam, comprehensio nequit haberi. Hic autem modus seu actio & ipsius immediata causa, per quam formata est iam pars principans & reliquae partes ciuitatis, praecipue sacerdotium, fuit diuina voluntas, immediate hoc praecipiens alicuius singularis creaturae oraculo terminato, aut per se solam immediate fortassis, quo modo principatum Israelitici populi in persona Moysi & quorundam aliorum iudicum post ipsum. Sacerdotium quoque in persona nam Aaron & ipsius successorum instituit. De qua siquidem causa & ipsius actione libera, tradere dicere, cur sic aut aliter, nec sic esse aut fuisse factum, per demonstrationem nec quicquam dicere possumus, sed simplici credulitate absque ratione tenemus. Alia vero est principatuum institutio, quæ scilicet ab humana mente immediate provenit, licet à Deo tanquam à causa remota, qui omnem principatum terrenum etiam concedit, ut Ioan. 19. habetur, & aperte dicit Apostolus ad Rom. 13. & beatus Augustinus 5. de civitate Dei. c. 21. quod tamen non est immediate semper, quinimo vt in pluribus & vbique quasi hos statuit per hominum mentes, quibus talis institutionis concessit arbitrium. Et de hac causa quæ sit, aut quali actione talia debeat instituere, ex meliori aut deteriori ad politiam, potest per humanam certitudinem assignari. Omisso itaque modo quem per demonstrationem certificare non possumus, modos institutionum principatus per humanam voluntatem immediate factos, narrare volumus primum, deinde vero monstrabimus ipsorum certiorem atque simpliciorem. Postmodum vero ex illius modi natura meliori arguemus causam movientem, à qua prouenire solummodo debet & potest. Ex quibus etiam apparebit consequenter causa movere debens ad institutionem optimam & determinationem reliquarum partium ciuitatis. Demum vero dicemus de principatus vnitate, propter quam apparebit etiam, quæ sit vnitas ciuitatis aut regni. Prosequentes itaque proposita, primum enumerabimus modos institutionis regalis monarchiæ, loquendo scilicet in ipsorum origine. Species enim hæc principatus, videtur quasi cognata nobis, & propinqua statim domesticæ œconomiæ, vt apparet ex dictis, cap. 3. Post huius vero determinationem apparebit consequenter de modis institutionis reliquarum diuisionum principatus. Sunt autem modi siue institutiones regalis monarchiæ quinque numero secundum Aristotelem 3. politi-ca 8. cap. Vnus quidem cum monarcha statuitur ad aliquod vnum opus determinatum, circa regimen communitatis tamen, vt ducatum exercitus, siue cum generis successione, siue pro solius vnicæ personæ periodo, quomodo instituebatur Dux exercitus Agamemnon à Græcis. Vocatur autem officium hoc in communitatibus modernis Capitaneatus aut Constabiliaria. Hic vero exercitus Dux de nullo se intromittebat iudicio tempore pacis, exercitu tamen militante Dominus erat occidendi aut aliter puniendi transgressores. Alius autem modus est, quo quidam in Asia principantur, habentes Dominia ex prædecessoribus per successionem, secundum legem tamen, ad monarchæ conferens magis quam ad commune simpliciter, quasi despotia. Sustinent enim habitatores illius regionis talem principatum nihil contristati, propter ipsorum barbaram & seruilem naturam, & consuetudinis auxilium. Hic siquidem principatus regalis est; quia patrius & voluntarius subditis, vt quia primi habitatores fuerant regionis præcessores monarchæ, aliqualiter tamen tyrannicus propter non esse ipsius leges, ad commune conferens simpliciter, sed monarchæ. Tertius vero modus regalis principatus est, cum quis principatur electus, non ex successione patria sed paterna, secundum tamen legem quæ non est ad commune conferens simpliciter, sed monarchiæ magis, quasi tyrannicam. Propter quod etiam vocauit Aristoteles ibidem hanc speciem principatus, electam tyrannidem. Tyrannidem quidem propter legis despotiam, electam quidem propter quod non erat subditis inuoluntaria. Quartus autem modus est, quo per electionem instituitur aliquis princeps, cum omni suo generis successione, secundum leges quæ sunt simpliciter: id commune conferens. Et hoc vtebantur secundum heroica tempora, vt dicit ibidem. Vocata vero sunt ea heroica tempora, vel quia tunc constellatio tales homines producebat, qui Heroës, id est diuini, credebantur, propter virtutis excessum; aut quia tales statuebantur principes non alii, propter virtutum & suorum beneficiorum excessum, vt quia sparsam multitudinem collegerunt, & in communitatem ciuilem congregauerunt, vel quia per pugnam & armorum strenuitatem liberauerunt regionem ab oppressoribus, aut quia fortasse regionem emerunt, vel alio conuenienti modo acquisiuerunt, & inter subditos diuiserunt. Et (ad vnum dicere) propter magni beneficii collatio nem aut alterius virtutis excessum, ad reliquam multitudinem instituti fuerunt principes cum potestate seu successione tota, sicut etiam dixit Aristoteles 5. politica, cap. 5. Sub hac autem monarchiæ specie fortasse comprehendit Aristoteles eam, ad quam quis eligitur pro sola, sui periodo vel parte periodi, vel eam fecit nos intelligere per hanc, & vocatam tyrannidem electam, eo quod vtrique participer. Quintus vero modus est & fuit, quo principians statuitur omnium Dominus eorum quæ sunt in communitate, sic secundum suam voluntatem realia & personalia disponens, quemadmodum œconomus pro voto dispōnit de his quæ in propria domo sunt. Quod tamen, vt hæc Aristotelis dicta manifesten tur amplius, & etiam modi omnes instituendi reliquos principatus ad capitulum reducantur. Dicemus, quod omnis principatus, vel est voluntarius subditis, vel inuoluntarius. Primum est genus bene temperatorum principatuum, secundum vero vitiatorum. Distinguitur autem vtrunque horum generum in tres species siue modos, sicut dictum est 8. cap. Et quoniam vna species bene temperati principatus, & fortasse perfectior est regalis monarchia: Idcoque præmissa recolligentes ab illius modis inchoemus sermonem dicentes, rex seu monarcha vel instituitur per electionem incolarum, seu ciuium, aut absque ipsorum electione rite obtinuit principatum: Si absque ciuium electione, vel sic est, quia primus inhabitauit regionem aut ipsius prædecessores, ex quibus traxit originem. Vel quia terram & iurisdictionem emit, aut ipsam iusto bello acquisiuit, aut alio quouis licito modo, puta dono sibi de ipsa facto propter impensum seruitium. Participat autem quilibet dictorum modorum tanto amplius de vero regali, quanto magis est ad subditos voluntarios, & secundum legem latam ad commune conferens subditorum. Tanto vero yero amplius tyrannidem sapiens, quanto magis exit ab his, consensu videlicet subditorum, & legead ipsorum commune conferens instituta. Unde 4. politicæ 8. cap. scribitur: Erant autem propterea quod secundum legem, regales (monarchiæ scilicet,) & quia monarchicabant voluntarii, tyrannice autem propter despotice principari & secundum suam sententiam (monarcharum scilicet.) Hæc igitur duo prædicta principatum temperatum & vitiatum separant, vt apparet ex Aristotelis apertα sententia, simpliciter autem aut magis subditorum consensus. Quod si monarcha principans per electionem incolarum fuerit institutus, hoc fieri convenit aliquo horum modorum, quoniam vel instituitur cum sua tota posteritate, seu successore, vel non. Si enim non instituitur cum omni posteritate, hoc contingit pluribus modis, quoniam vel instituitur pro tota vnius vita tantummodo, vel pro vnius & aliquo sui successoris vnius aut plurium. Vel non instituitur ad vitam totam alicuius, nec primi nec successorum, sed solum modo pro aliqua parte temporis terminata, vt annali aut biennali, longiori vel breviori, & rursum vel ad omne iudiciale officium exercendum, vel ad solum vnicum velut exercitus Dux. Conueniunt autem & differunt monarchæ regales, electi cum non electis, quoniam vtrique voluntariis principantur. Differunt autem, quoniam vt in pluribus non electi principantur subditis minus voluntariis, & ipsos disponunt legibus minus politicis ad commune conferens, quales pridem barbaricas diximus. Electi vero magis voluntariis præsunt, cosque disponunt legibus politicis magis, quas diximus latas ad commune conferens. Ex quibus patet, quod & in sequentibus amplius apparebit, genus electum principatus præstantius esse non electo. Est quoque sententia hæc Aristotelis tertio politica, cap. 9. quam induximus supra de his qui statuebantur circa heroica tempora. Rursum hic modus institutionis in communitatibus perfectis permanentior est. Nam omnes alios in hunc quandoque oportet reducere per necessitatem, non econuerso, vt si generis successio defecerit, aut alia de causa fiat genus illud, importabile multitudini ab excessu malitiæ sui regiminis, oportet tunc multitudinem se conuertere ad electionem, quæsiquidem electio deficere nunquam potest, generatione hominum indeficiente. Amplius hoc solo modo institutionis habetur principans optimus. Nam eum expedit optimum esse iis quibus versantur in politia, debet enim regulare actus ciuiles omnium. Modus vero institutionis aliarum specietum principatus temperati, vt plurimum est electio, & quandoque in aliquibus sors absque generis successione continua. Vitiatorum autem principatuum institutiones, vt plurimum sunt fraus, aut violentia, aut vtrumque. Quis vero principatuum temperatorum sit præstantior, an monarcha vel reliquæ duæ species, aristocratia vel politia. Et rursum monarchiarum, an electa vel non electa: adhuc autem electarum, an ea quæ cum omni generis successione statuitur, aut in qua solus statuitur absque tali successione: quæ secatur in duas, vt eam scilicet quæ ad totam periodum alicuius aut aliquorum, vel ad partem solam temporis terminatam, puta annalem, biennalem, longiorem aut breviorem, inquisitionem aut dubitationem rationalem habet, quamuis indubie tenendum secundum veritatem, & Aristotelis apertam sententiam, electionem esse certiorem regulam principatus, vt in 12. 16. & 17. huius certificabitur amplius. Hoc tamen non ignorare debemus, quod alia & altera multitudo, in alia vel diuersa regione ac tempore, dispositæ est ad alteram & diuersam politiam, aliumque aut alterum ferre principatum, vt dicit Aristoteles tertio politica, cap. nono, quæ attendenda sunt a legumlatoribus & principatuum institutoribus. Nam sicut non quilibet homo dispositus est ad optimam disciplinam, & propterea non ad illam acquirendam statuitur a dirigente conuenienter, sed ad quam, bonarum tamen, magis fuerit præparatus, sic fortasse multitudo aliqua, quandoque aut in loco aliquo, non est dispositi ferre optimum principatum. Ideoque ad temperatorum sibi conuenientiorem ipsam prius tentandum reducere. Ante enim Iulii Cæsaris monarchiam, Romanus populus diu ferre noluit monarcham aliquem terminatum, nec cum generis successione, neque etiam ad totam vnius solius monarchiæ periodum. Quod siquidem contingebat illi fortasse, propter heroicorum & principatiorum virorum multitudinem, tam secundum genera seu cognationes, quam secundum indiuidua personarum. Ex his ergo quæ a nobis determinata sunt, manifeste apparet, quod quærentes quis monarcharum sit præstantior ciuitati vel regno, an qui per electionem, vel qui per generis successionem principatur, inconueniter interrogant & quærunt. Sed oportet quærere primum, quis monarcharum sit præstantior, an electus aut non electus. Et si electus, rursum quis electorum, an qui cum omni sui generis successione statuitur, vel qui absque generis successione. Quoniam licet non electus monarcha, quasi semper principatum transmittat hæredi, electus tamen non omnis, sed solum qui cum sui successione omni statuitur principari. De modis itaq; institutionis principatuum & quoniam ipsorum simpliciter præstantior est electio, determinatum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: Having settled these matters, it follows that I should speak of the ways in which the ruling part is brought into being or constituted. For since the good or bad nature of the rulers themselves produces the civil government, as its actions, we must infer from those actions the acting cause, from which both the government itself and the ruling part through them may be expected to come, more usefully for the polity. But because in this book we are concerned chiefly with the causes and actions by which the ruling part is ordinarily to be created, we wish first to speak of the mode and cause by which this part has, though rarely, already been created. We distinguish this mode or action and its immediate cause from the modes or actions and their immediate causes through which such a part is regularly and in most cases to be created, which we can also prove by human demonstration. For the first kind cannot be grasped by certain demonstration. This mode or action, and its immediate cause, by which the ruling part and the other parts of the state, especially the priesthood, were already formed, was the divine will, commanding this directly by the definite utterance of some single creature, or perhaps by itself alone and immediately, as in the case of the rule of the Israelite people through Moses and certain judges after him. The priesthood too it established in the person of Aaron and his successors. Concerning this cause and its free action, we can neither teach by demonstration why it was done thus or otherwise, nor that it was not done so, but we hold it by simple belief, without reason. But the institution of rulers in another way arises immediately from the human mind, although God, as a remote cause, who grants every earthly rule, is its source, as is found in John 19, and as the Apostle plainly says in Romans 13, and as blessed Augustine says in The City of God, book 5, chapter 21. Yet this is not always immediate; rather, in most cases and everywhere, he appoints such rulers through men's minds, to whom he has granted the right of such institution. And concerning this cause, and by what action such rulers ought to be instituted, for better or worse as regards the polity, this can be assigned by human certainty. Therefore, setting aside the mode which we cannot certify by demonstration, we wish first to describe the modes of establishing rule which are made immediately by human will, and afterwards we shall show the more certain and simpler of them. Then from the good nature of that mode we shall argue the moving cause, from which alone it ought and can come. From these things it will also become clear, in due sequence, what cause ought to move men to the best institution and ordering of the remaining parts of the state. Lastly we shall speak of the unity of rule, from which it will also appear what the unity of a state or kingdom is. Pursuing, then, the matters proposed, we shall first enumerate the modes of establishing royal monarchy, speaking of its origin. For this kind of rule seems akin to us and close to domestic economy from the start, as appears from what was said in chapter 3. After the determination of this, it will follow in order to speak of the modes of instituting the other divisions of rule. There are five modes, or institutions, of royal monarchy according to Aristotle, Politics, book 3, chapter 8. In the first, a monarch is set up for some one determined task, yet concerning the governance of the community, such as the leadership of an army, whether by hereditary succession or for the term of a single person alone, as the leader of the army Agamemnon was appointed by the Greeks. In modern communities this office is called the captaincy or the constableship. Yet this leader of the army did not interfere in any judicial matter in time of peace, but while the army was in the field he was lord to kill or otherwise punish transgressors. The second mode is that by which some rule in Asia, holding dominions from their predecessors by succession, yet according to law, conferring more on the monarch than on the common good, as a despotism. For the inhabitants of that region bear such a rule without distress, because of their barbarous and servile nature and the support of custom. This rule is royal, since it is paternal and voluntary to its subjects, as the first inhabitants of the region were the predecessors of the monarch, but in some measure tyrannical because its laws are not conferred on the common good simply, but on the monarch. The third mode of royal rule is when someone rules, chosen not by hereditary succession but by a paternal one, yet according to a law which does not confer on the common good simply, but rather on the monarchy, in a tyrannical manner. For this reason Aristotle in the same place called this kind of rule "elected tyranny": tyranny because of the despotism of the law, elected because it was not involuntary to the subjects. The fourth mode is that by which a prince is established by election, together with his whole line of succession, according to laws which confer simply on the common good. This was practised "in the heroic times," as he says in the same place. Those times were called heroic either because at that time the constellations produced such men as were believed to be "heroes," that is, divine, on account of their excess of virtue; or because such men were set up as princes, not others, on account of the excess of their virtues and benefits, as when they gathered a scattered multitude and brought them together into a civil community, or because by fighting and the vigour of arms they freed the region from oppressors, or because perhaps they bought the region or acquired it by some other fitting means and distributed it among the subjects. And (to say it in one word) on account of the bestowing of a great benefit or the excess of some other virtue, princes were set up over the rest of the multitude with full power or succession, as Aristotle also said in Politics, book 5, chapter 5. Under this species of monarchy Aristotle perhaps comprehends that in which someone is chosen for his own lifetime only, or for part of his lifetime, or else he meant us to understand this by the elected tyranny he mentioned, since both share in it. The fifth mode is and was that by which a ruler is set up as lord of all the things in the community, disposing of both property and persons according to his own will, just as a steward disposes at will of what is in his own house. But so that these sayings of Aristotle may be made clearer, and so that all the modes of establishing the other rules may be brought back to the chapter, we shall say that every rule is either voluntary to the subjects or involuntary. The first is the kind of well-tempered rule, the second of corrupt rule. Each of these kinds is divided into three species or modes, as was said in chapter 8. And since one species of well-tempered rule, and perhaps the more perfect, is royal monarchy, therefore, gathering up what has been said, let us begin our discussion from its modes, saying that a king or monarch is either instituted by the election of the inhabitants or citizens, or has rightly obtained rule without their election. If without the election of the citizens, this is so either because he or his predecessors, from whom he traces his origin, first inhabited the region; or because he bought the land and jurisdiction, or acquired it by a just war, or by any other lawful means, for instance by a gift of it made to him on account of services rendered. Each of the said modes shares more of true royal rule in proportion as it is more voluntary to the subjects and according to a law enacted for the common good of the subjects. But it savours more of tyranny in proportion as it departs from these, namely the consent of the subjects and laws instituted for their common good. Hence it is written in Politics, book 4, chapter 8: "They were royal, because they ruled according to law and over willing subjects; but tyrannical, because they ruled despotically and according to their own opinion (that is, of the monarchs)." These two things, then, separate a well-tempered rule from a corrupt one, as appears from Aristotle's plain judgement: namely, the simple or greater consent of the subjects. But if a monarch who rules has been established by the election of the inhabitants, this ought to happen in one of these modes, since he is instituted either together with his whole posterity or successor, or not. If he is not instituted with his whole posterity, this happens in several ways, since he is instituted either for the whole life of one man alone, or for one man and some successor or successors, one or more. Or he is not instituted for the whole life of anyone, neither of the first nor of the successors, but only for some limited part of time, such as one year or two years, longer or shorter, and again either for the exercise of every judicial office, or for one sole office, like the leader of an army. Elected royal monarchs and non-elected ones agree and differ: they agree because both rule over willing subjects. They differ because, as a rule, non-elected monarchs rule over less willing subjects and govern them by less civil laws, conferring on the common good, such as we have said were barbarian of old. Elected monarchs, however, preside over more willing subjects and govern them by more civil laws, which we have said are enacted for the common good. From these things it is clear, and will become still more apparent in what follows, that the elected kind of rule is more excellent than the non-elected. This is also the judgement of Aristotle in Politics, book 3, chapter 9, which we cited above concerning those who were set up in the heroic times. Again, this mode of institution is more lasting in perfect communities. For all the other modes must sometimes of necessity be brought back to this one, not the reverse: for example, if the succession of a line fails, or for some other reason that line becomes intolerable to the multitude because of the excess of its malice in ruling, then the multitude must turn to election, which can never fail, since the generation of men does not fail. Moreover, only by this mode of institution is the best ruler obtained. For it is fitting that he should be the best for those who live in the polity, since he ought to regulate the civil acts of all. But the mode of institution of the other species of well-tempered rule is for the most part election, and sometimes in some cases by lot, without a continuous hereditary succession. The institutions of corrupt rules are, for the most part, fraud, or violence, or both. Which of the well-tempered kinds of rule is the more excellent, whether monarchy or the other two species, aristocracy or polity? And again, among monarchies, whether the elected or the non-elected; and further, among the elected, whether that which is established with its whole line of succession, or that in which someone is set up alone without such succession, which is divided into two, namely the one which holds for the whole term of one or several men, or for a part of time only, limited, such as one year, two years, longer or shorter. These questions have a rational inquiry or doubt; yet, undoubtedly, we must hold according to the truth and Aristotle's plain judgement that election is the more certain rule of rule, as will be made clearer in books 12, 16 and 17 of this work. Still we ought not to be unaware that one multitude, in one region or at one time, is disposed to one polity and another, or a different one, and to bear one or another rule, as Aristotle says in Politics, book 3, chapter 9. These things must be attended to by lawgivers and by those who institute rules. For just as not every man is fitted for the best discipline, and therefore he is not appointed by a director to acquire it suitably, but rather to that discipline for which he has been better prepared among the good ones, so perhaps some multitude, at some time or in some place, is not disposed to bear the best rule. Therefore it must first be attempted to bring it back to the temperate kind more suited to it. For before the monarchy of Julius Caesar, the Roman people long refused to bear any monarch limited either by hereditary succession or to the whole term of one man's monarchy alone. This perhaps happened to them because of the multitude of heroic and princely men, both according to their lines or kinships and according to the individuals themselves. From these things which we have determined, therefore, it is manifest that those who ask and seek which monarch is more excellent for a city or kingdom, whether the one who rules by election or the one who rules by hereditary succession, ask and seek improperly. Rather, one must first ask which monarch is more excellent, the elected or the non-elected. And if elected, again which of the elected, the one established with his whole line of succession, or the one without succession. For although the non-elected monarch, as it were, always hands his rule on to an heir, yet not every elected monarch, but only the one established to rule with all his succession. Let the account of the modes of establishing rules, and of why election is simply the more excellent, be concluded in this way.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De distinctione ac assignatione significatorum huius nominis lex, & ipsius proprissima, & nobis intenta significatione.
units.tr: On the distinction and assignment of the meanings of this word law, its most proper meaning, and the meaning we intend.

units.la: Quoniam autem electionem diximus perfectiorem, atque præstantiorem modorum instituendi principatum, bene se habet inquirere illius effectiuam causam, a qua scilicet secundum complementum suæ bonitatis habeat prouenire, Nam ex hoc apparebit etiam factiua causa principatus electi, & similiter reliquarum partium politiæ. Verum quia principatus regulare debet actus ciuiles humanos (vt demonstrauimus quinto huius) & secundum regulam, quæ forma est & esse debet principantis, inquantum principans inquirere oportet huiusmodi regulam, si est, quid est, & propter quid. Est enim fortassis eadem ipsius effectiua causa, quæ principantis.
units.tr: Since we have said that election is the more perfect and excellent of the ways of instituting a principate, it is appropriate to inquire into its effective cause, from which it must derive the fullness of its goodness. From this the factive cause of an elected principate will also become clear, and likewise that of the other parts of the polity. But since a principate ought to regulate human civil acts (as we demonstrated in the fifth book), and according to a rule, which is and ought to be the form of the one who rules, insofar as he rules, we must inquire whether such a rule exists, what it is, and on account of what. Its effective cause is perhaps the same as that of the ruler.

units.la: Hanc itaque regulam, quam statutum vel consuetudinem, & communi nomine legem appellant, existere supponentes, quasi per se notum ex inductione in omnibus perfectis communitatibus, Primum ostendemus quid sit; deinde vero ipsius finalem assignabimus necessitatem, demum autem determinabimus per demonstrationem, cuius aut quorum & qualiatione hanc statuere oporteat, quod erit inquirere legislatorem seu causam agentem ipsius, ad quam etiam electionem principaruum pertinere putamus, & per demonstrationem in sequentibus ostendemus. Ex quibus etiam apparebit materia siue subiectum regulæ supradictæ, quam legem diximus. Nam hæc est pars principans, cuius est secundum legem regulare politicos seu ciuiles hominum actus. Ad dicta quidem igitur procedentibus, ne propter nominis multiplicitatem eueniat discolia, distinguere conuenit intentiones seu significata huius nominis Lex, hoc enim nomen de numero multiplicium dictionum importat in vna sui significatione naturalem inclinationem sensitiuam ad actionem aut passionem aliquam, quomodo vocauit eam Apostolus ad Romanos septimo, cum dixit Video autem aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ. In alia vero ipsius acceptione dicitur hoc nomen lex de quolibet habitu operatiuo, & generaliter de omni forma rei operabilis, existente in mente, à qua tanquam exemplari, siue mensura formæ artificiorum proueniunt, quomodo dicitur Ezechielis 43 Hæc ergo lex Domus, ista autem mensura altaris. Tertio vero modo sumitur Lex pro regula continente monita humanorum actuum Imperatorum, secundum quod ordinantur ad gloriam vel pœnam in seculo venturo, secundum quam significationem, Lex Mosaica dicta est lex, quantum ad aliquam sui partem, sic quoque Lex Euangelica secundum se totam lex dicitur. Vnde Apostolus ad Hebr. de hisait; Translato enim sacerdotio, necesse est vt legis translatio fiat. Sic etiam de disciplina Euangelica lex dicitur, Iacobi 1. Qui autem prospexerit in legem perfectam libertatis, & in ea permanserit, &c. Hic beatus in facto suo erit. Hac etiam legis acceptione dicuntur leges omnes sectæ, vt quæ Mahometi aut Persarum, secundum se totas aut aliquas sui partes, licet ex Mosaica & Euangelica, Christiana scilicet, solæ continent veritatem. Sic etiam sectas leges vocauit Aristot. 2. Philosophiæ cum dixit: Quantam vim habeat quod consuetum est, leges ostendunt. Et in 12. eiusdem: Reliqua vero fabulosè iam a ducta sunt ad persuasionem multorum ad leges & conferens. Quarto autem importat hoc nomen lex, & famosè magis scientiam seu doctrinam siue iudicium vniuersale iustorum & conferentium ciuilium, & suorum oppositorum. Et sic accepta lex dupliciter considerari potest, vno modo secundum se, vt per ipsam solum ostenditur quid iustum aut iniustum, conferens aut noxium, & in quantum huiusmodi iuris scientia vel doctrina lex dicitur. Alio modo considerari potest secundum quod de ipsius obseruatione datur præceptum coactiuum per pœnam aut præmium in præsenti seculo distribuenda, siue secundum quod per modum talis præcepti traditur, & hoc modo consideratæ propriissime lex vocatur, & est. Quam etiam sic sumptam diffinit Aristot. 9. Ethicorum 8. cap. duxit: Lex autem coactiua habet potentiam sermonis ab aliqua prudentia & intellectu, politico scilicet, id est ordinatiuo de iustis & conferentibus, & ipsorum oppositis per prudentiam politicam, habens coactiuam prudentiam, id est de cuius obseruatione datur præceptum quod quis cogitur obseruare, seu lata per modum talis præcepti lex est. Vnde iustorum & conferentium ciuilium non omnes verae cognitiones sunt leges, nisi de ipsarum obseruatione datum fuerit præceptum coactiuum, seu latæ fuerint per modum præcepti, licet talis vera cognitio ipsarum necessario requiratur ad legem perfectam. Quinimo quandoque falsæ cognitiones iustorum & conferentium, leges fiunt cum de ipsis datur obseruationis præceptum, seu feruntur per modum præcepti, sicut apparet in regionibus barbarorum quorundam, qui tanquam iustum obseruari faciunt, homicidam absoluiâ culpa & pœna ciuili, reale aliquod precium exhibentes pro tali delicto, cum tamen hoc simpliciter sit iniustum, & per consequens ipsorum leges non perfectæ simpliciter. Esto enim quod formam habeant debitam, præceptum scilicet obseruationis coactiuum, debita tamen carent conditione, videlicet debita & vera ordinatione iustorum. Comprehenduntur autem sub hac legis acceptione, omnes iustorum & conferentium ciuilium regulæ, auctoritate humana institutæ, vt consuetudines, statuta, plebiscita, decretales, & omnes continuiles, quæ scilicet humanæ auctoritati, vt iam diximus, innituntur. Debemus tamen non ignorare, quod tam lex Euangelica, quam Mosaica, & fortasse sectarum reliquæ diuersimodè consideratæ ac comparatæ in toto vel parte ipsarum, ad humanos actus pro statu præsentis seculi vel venturi, quandoque veniunt vel venerunt hactenus, aut venturæ sunt in tertiam legis significationem, & quandoque in vltimam, vt 8. & 9. secunda manifestabitur amplius, quædam quidem secundum veritatem, quædam vero secundum phantasiam fallam, & promissionem inanem. Quod quidem igitur sit regula, seu lex aliqua humanarum actuum ciuilium, & quid sit, exiam dictis palam.
units.tr: Supposing, then, that this rule exists, which they call a statute or custom, and by a common name law, as something known in itself from induction across all well-ordered communities, we shall first show what it is; then we shall assign its final necessity; and finally we shall determine, by demonstration, by whom and in what manner it ought to be established. This will be to inquire into the lawgiver, or efficient cause of law, to which we also think the election of rulers belongs, as we shall show by demonstration in what follows. From these points it will also become clear what the matter or subject of the aforesaid rule is, which we have called law. For this is the ruling part, whose task is to regulate human political or civil acts according to law. Proceeding, then, from what has been said, and so that confusion does not arise from the multiplicity of the term, it is fitting to distinguish the meanings or significations of this word law. This word, being one of many, signifies in one sense the natural sensitive inclination toward some action or passion, as the Apostle called it in Romans 7, when he said: But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind. In another sense the word law is used of any habit of operating, and generally of any form of a thing to be done, existing in the mind, from which, as from an exemplar or measure, the forms of works of art arise; as it is said in Ezekiel 43: This is the law of the house; this is the measure of the altar. In a third sense, law is taken for a rule containing the admonitions of human acts, insofar as they are directed to glory or punishment in the world to come. In this sense the Mosaic law is called a law as to some part of it, and in the same way the Gospel law is called a law in its entirety. Hence the Apostle says of these things to the Hebrews: For the priesthood being changed, there must needs be a change also of the law. So too the discipline of the Gospel is called a law in James 1: But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, &c., this man shall be blessed in his deed. In this sense of law are also called all the laws of sects, such as those of Mohammed or of the Persians, whether wholly or in some of their parts, although only the Christian law, that is, the one drawn from Moses and the Gospel, contains the truth.
