So too Aristotle, in the second book of his Philosophy, called the sects laws when he said: What great force custom has, the laws show. And in the twelfth book of the same work: The rest, indeed, have been already invented as fables for the persuasion of many, and for the laws and for expediency. Fourthly, the word law, and more commonly, signifies the science or doctrine or universal judgment of the just and expedient matters of civil life and of their opposites. Law taken in this sense can be considered in two ways. In one way it can be considered in itself, so that by it alone is shown what is just or unjust, expedient or harmful; and insofar as it is a science or doctrine of this kind, it is called law. In another way it can be considered insofar as a coercive command is given about its observance, to be enforced by punishment or reward in the present world; or insofar as it is handed down by way of such a command. Considered in this way it is most properly called law, and is law. Aristotle, in the eighth chapter of the ninth book of the Ethics, also defined law so taken, saying: Coercive law has the power of speech from some prudence and intellect, namely political prudence, that is, one that orders the just and expedient matters and their opposites; having coercive prudence, that is, a law whose observance is commanded, which one is compelled to observe, or a law laid down by way of such a command. Hence not all true cognitions of the just and expedient matters of civil life are laws, unless a coercive command about their observance has been given, or they have been laid down by way of a command, although such true cognition of them is necessarily required for a perfect law. Indeed, sometimes false cognitions of the just and expedient become laws when a command of observance is given about them, or they are issued by way of a command. This appears in the lands of certain barbarians, who make it be observed as just that a murderer be acquitted of guilt and civil punishment, by paying some sum of money for such a crime, although this is simply unjust; and consequently their laws are not perfect in the absolute sense. For even if they have the due form, namely a coercive command of observance, they lack the due condition, namely the proper and true ordering of what is just. Under this sense of law are included all rules of the just and expedient matters of civil life, instituted by human authority, such as customs, statutes, plebiscites, decretals, and all such things as rest, as we have said, on human authority. We must not, however, be unaware that the Gospel law, as well as the Mosaic law, and perhaps the remaining laws of the sects, considered and compared in various ways, in whole or in part, bear upon human acts for the state of the present or future world; and sometimes they have come, or have hitherto come, or will come, into the third sense of law, and sometimes into the last, as will be made clearer in the eighth and ninth chapters that follow. Some of them do so according to truth, and some according to false fancy and empty promise. What, then, is a rule or law of human civil acts, and what it is, is now clear from what has been said.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: De necessitate Lationis legum in propriissima significatione sumptarum. Et quod nullum principantem quantumcunque studiosum aut iustum expediat absque legibus principari.
units.tr: On the necessity of laws taken in the strictest sense, and that no ruler, however zealous or just, can govern without laws.

units.la: His itaq; legis acceptionibus sic diuisis, eins secundum vltimam & propriissimam significationem, ostendere volumus necessitatem finalem: principaliorem quidem, ciuile iustum & conferens commune, assecutiuam vero quandam principatuum, maxime secundum generis successionem, securitatem & principatus diuturnitatem. Primam ergo necessitatem sic, quoniam illud necessarium est in politia statuere absq; quo ciuilia iudicia simpliciter recte fieri nequeunt, per quod rite feruntur, & a defectu quantum possibile est, humanis actibus preseruantur. Lex est huiusmodi, vt cum secundum ipsam determinatus fuerit principans ferre ciuilia iudicia, ergo legis institutio necessaria est in politia. Prima propositio huius demonstrationis est quasi per se nota, & indemonstrabilibus propinqua valde. Cuius etiam certitudo accipi debet & potest ex quinto huius, parte 7. Secunda vero propositio manifestabitur ex hoc, quoniam ad iudicii complementum in bonitate requiritur affectio recta iudicum, & iudicandorum vera cognitio, quorum opposita, ciuilia corrumpunt iudicia. Nam peruersa iudicantis affectio, vt odii vel amoris, vt auaritiae desiderium iudicantis perurtit. Haec autem a iudicio prohibentur: & ab his preseruatur, dum fuerit iudex seu principans determinatus secundum leges ferre iudicia, propterea quod lex omni caret affectione peruersa, non enim facta est ad amicum aut inimicum vtilem vel nociuum, sed vniuersaliter ad agentem ciuiliter bene aut male. Omnia nanq; reliqua sibi accidunt, & extra legem sunt, non sic autem extra iudicem sunt. Quoniam personae in iudicio constitutae possunt esse amicae vel inimicae iudicanti, vtiles vel nociuae, dando aut aliquid promittendo. Sic quoq; in reliquis intentionibus, quae in iudice causare possunt affectionem, ipsius iudicium peruertentem, propter quod nullum iudicium quantum possibile est, debet committi arbitrio iudicantis, sed lege determinari & secundum ipsam pronunciari.
units.tr: Having thus divided the senses of law, we wish to show the final necessity of law in its last and most proper meaning. The principal necessity is that of civil justice and the common good; a secondary one is that of securing rulers and the lasting tenure of rule, especially across generations. First, then, the necessity is shown as follows. It is necessary to establish in a polity whatever is required for civil judgments to be made rightly at all, so that they are duly rendered and, as far as possible, preserved from human error. Law is of this kind: if the ruler who gives civil judgments is determined by law, then the institution of law is necessary in a polity. The first premise of this demonstration is almost self-evident and very close to indemonstrable principles, and its certainty can and should be drawn from the fifth book of this work, part 7. The second premise will be made clear as follows. For a judgment to be good, the judges must have a right disposition and a true knowledge of the matters to be judged; their opposites corrupt civil judgments. For a perverse disposition in the judge, such as hatred or love, or a desire for greed, pervert his judgment. Law keeps these out of judgment and preserves judgment from them, provided the judge or ruler is bound by law when giving his decisions, because law is free of any perverse affection. It was not made for a friend or an enemy, for one who is useful or harmful, but universally, for one who acts well or badly as a citizen. All other things happen to a person and lie outside the law, but they do not lie outside the judge. Persons brought before a court may be friendly or hostile to the judge, useful or harmful to him, by giving or promising something. So too in other matters which can move the judge to an affection that perverts his judgment. For this reason no judgment, as far as possible, should be left to the will of the one judging; it should be determined by law and pronounced according to it.

units.la: Haec autem fuit sententia diui Aristotelis 4. politica, cap. 9. vbi ex intentione perquirens, an melius sit regi politiam optimo viro absq; lege, vel ab optimis legibus, inquit sic: Valentius autem, (id est praestantius) ad iudicandum, cui non adest quod passionale omnino, (id est affectio quae iudicium peruertere potest,) quam cui connaturale Legi quidem igitur hoc non inest, (passio videlicet siue affectio.) Humanam autem animam necesse hoc habet omne: & dixit omnem, non expediendo quenquam quantumcunque studiosum. Quam siquidem sententiam repetens primo Rhetoricae, cap. 1. sic ait. Omnium quidem maximum queritur, (scilicet nihil absq; lege iudicandum relinqui debet arbitrio iudicantis,) quia iudicium quidem legislatoris, id est lex) non secundum partem, (id est, non est latum propter aliquem hominem particularem,) sed de futuris & vniuersalibus est. Praefectus autem & iudex iam de praesentibus & determinatis iudicant, ad quos & amare & odire, & proprium commodum annexa sunt saepe, vt non adhuc possint videre sufficienter verum, sed attendere in iudicio proprium delectabile aut triste. Hoc etiam dicit eodem. 1. cap. 2 Non enim, inquit, similiter reddimus iudicia tristes & gaudentes, amantes vel odientes. Corrumpitur adhuc iudicium, propter iudicum ignorantiam, esto quod bonae sint affectionis seu intentionis, quod etiam peccatum siue defectus per legem tollitur & suppletur, quoniam in ipsa determinatum est quasi perfecte, quid iustum aut iniustum, conferens vt nociuum, secundum vnumquemque humanum actum ciuile. Hoc autem nequit sic sufficienter fieri per vnicum hominem quantumcunque ingeniosum. Quoniam vnus solus homo, nec fortasse omnes vnius aetatis homines inuenire aut retinere possent omnes actus ciuiles determinatos in lege. Quinimo, q de ipsis dixerunt inuentores primi, & omnes etiam eiusdem aetatis homines, taliu obseruatores, fuit res modica & imperfecta, quae postmodum ex additione posteriorum complementu suscepit. Quod quidem videre sat est experientia nota per additionem & subtractionem ac totaliter in contrariu mutatione quandoq; factam in legibus, secundum diuersas aetates, & secundum diuersa tempora eiusdem aetatis. Testatur autem & hoc Arist 2. politicae. c. 2. cum dixit: Oportet autem non hoc ipsum ignorare, quia oportet attendere multo tempore & multis annis, in quibus non vtiq; lateat si haec bene se habuerunt, quam scilicet statui debent tanquam leges. Idem dicit ipse 1. rhetoricae. c. 1. Deinde, inquit, legislationes quidem ex multo tempore consideratae sunt. Et confirmatur id ratione quoniam legis lationes indigent prudentia, vt pridem ex descriptione legis apparuit, prudentia vero longi eget experientia, haec autem temporis multitudine. Vnde lexto Ethicorum: Signum autem ipsius quod dictum est, & quod Geometri quidem iuuenes & disciplinati fiunt & sapientes talia, prudentes autem non videntur fieri. Causa etiam, & quoniam singularium est prudentia, quae fiunt cognita ex experientia, inuenis autem expertus non est, multitudo enim temporis facit experientiam. Et ideo quod vnus solus homo inuenit, aut scire potest per seipsum, tam in scientia iustorum & conferentium ciuilium, quam in aliis scientiis, est parum aut nihil. Adhuc etiam quod vnius aetatis homines respectu eius quod ex pluribus aetatibus obseruatur, imperfecta res est, propter quod de inuentione veritatis secundum vnamquamque artem & disciplinam, tractans Aristoteles 2. Philosophiae, cap. 1. sic inquit: Secundum vnum quidem inuentorum, (scilicet cuiusuis disciplinae aut artis,) nihil aut parum ei immittere, (id est de ipsa per se solum inuenire,) ex omnibus coarticulatum fieri magnitudinem aliquam. Secundum tamen translationem ex Arabico, magis aperta est haec series, in qua sic habetur: Et vnusquisque eorum, (id est inuentorum cuiusuis artis aut disciplinae,) aut nihil comprehendit de veritate aut aut modicum. Cum igitur congregatum fuerit ex eo ab omnibus qui comprehendere, tunc congregatum erit aliquid quantitatis; quod maxime apparet de Astrologia. Sic ergo per auxilium hominum inuicem, & additionem posterius inuentorum adiuuenta priius, receperunt omnes artes & disciplinæ complementum. Quod figuraliter etiam declarat ibidem Aristoteles circa Musicæ inuentionem, cum dixit: Si Timotheus non fuisset, multam melodiam non haberemus: si autem Phrynes, Timotheus non fuisset, ita perfectus scilicet in melodiis, nisi habuisset prius inuenta per Phrynem. Quæ verba exponens Averrois 2. commento, sic ait: Et quod dicit in hoc cap. (Aristoteles scilicet,) manifestum est. Nullus enim potest inuenire per se artes operatiuas aut consideratiuas, (id est speculatiuas) in maiori parte, quia non complentur, nisi per iuuamentum prioris ad sequentem. Idem dicit 2. elenchorum, cap. finali, de inuentione rhetoricæ & omnium aliarum, quicquid fuerit de Logices inuentione, quam sibi absque prioris alicuius inuentione, seu auxilio perfectam adscribit, in quo singularis inter alios extitisse videtur. Hoc etiam dicit ipse octauo ethicorum cap. primo: Duo, inquit, venientes, (id est conuenientes,) Jagere, intelligere potentiores sunt; supple vno solo. Quod si duo, magis plures duobus, & simul, & successiue, quam solus vnus. Et hoc est quod de proposito dicit tertio politicæ, cap 9 Inconueniens, inquit, forte vtiq; videbitur, si melius percipiat quis duobus oculis & duabus auribus iudicans, & agens duobus pedibus & manibus, quam multi multis. Cum igitur lex sit oculus ex multis oculis, id est comprehensio examinata ex multis comprehensionibus ad errorem euitandum circa ciuilia iudicia, & recte iudicandum, tutius est ea fieri secundum iudicantis arbitrium. Et propter hoc ipsam statui necesse est, si debeant politiæ quantum ad iusta & conferentia ipsarum ciuilia, disponi optime, per ipsam enim ciuilia iudicia præseruantur ab ignorantia, & iudicum affectione peruersa, quæ fuit minor assumptæ demonstrationis, qua ex principio capituli huius, necessitatem legum assignare tentauimus. Quo vero modo subortam litem seu citius lem causam, lege non determinatam, diffinire seu iudicare oportet, dicetur xiv. huius. Sunt ergo leges necessariæ ad excludendum à ciuilibus iudiciis seu sententiis, iudicum malitiam & errorem. Hæc propter consuluit Aristoteles, nulli iudici seu principanti concedere arbitrium iudicandi aut præcipiendi de ciuilibus, absque lege, in quibus lex determinare potuit. Vnde 4. Ethicorum, cap quinto, in tractatu de iustitia dixit Aristoteles: Propter hoc non sinimus principari hominem, sed secundum rationem, id est legem, causam assignans, quam induximus, affectionem peruersam scilicet, quæ in illo cadere potest. Item tertio politicæ, cap. 6. cum dixit: Prima autem dubitatio facit manifestum, nihil sic alterum, quam quod oportet leges recte positas, esse dominas, id est dominari principantes secundum ipsas. Idem eodem cap. 9 dum dixit; Quod quidem intellectum iubet principari, videtur principari iubere Deum & leges, qui autem hominem iubet, (absque lege scilicet, secundum arbitrium proprium,) apponit & bestiam. Parum post subiungens causam, cum dixit; Propter quod sine appetitu intellectus, lex est; quasi dicat, legem intellectum seu cognitionem esse, absque appetitu, id est affectione aliqua. Hanc quoque sententiam repetit primo Rhetoricæ, cap. 1. vbi sic inquit: Maxime quidem igitur conuenit, rectas positas leges quacunque contingit, omnia determinare ipsas, & quam paucissima committere iudicantibus: Assignans huiusmodi pridem adductas cautas, exclusionem scilicet maliciæ atque ignorantiæ iudicum à ciuilibus iudiciis, quæ in lege cadere nequeunt sicut in iudice, quem admodum ostensum est prius. Et his amplius dicit aperte Aristoteles quarto politicæ, cap. quarto: vbi non principantur leges, (id est, vbi principantes non principantur secundum ipsas,) non est politia, (retempera, supple) oportet enim legem quidem principari omnium. Superest autem ostendere, quod principari secundum legem, nec præter ipsam, debent omnes principantes. Horum vero maxime monarchæ, qui cum omni eorum successione principantur, vt ipsorum principatus securiores & diuturniores existant, quæ in huius capituli principio fuerat tanquam secundaria legum necessitas assignata. Hoc autem hic primum videre est, quoniam secundum legem principari, ipsorum iudicia præseruat à defectu, contingente propter ignorantiam & affectionem peruersam. Vnde in seipsis & ad ciues subditos regulati, minus patiuntur seditiones, & per consequens suorum principatuum solutiones, quæ illis contingerent agentibus praue secundum suum arbitrium, sicut patenter dicit Aristoteles quinto politicæ, cap. quinto. Regnum enim, inquit Aristoteles, ab extrinsecis quidem minime corrumpitur, ex ipso autem plurima corruptiones accidunt. Corrumpitur autem secundum duos modos, vno quidem, seditionem facientibus his, qui participant regno, alio autem modo magis tyrannice tentantibus gubernare, quando excegerint esse Domini plurium, & præter legem. Non fiunt autem adhuc regna hunc, sed sic fiunt, Monarchiæ & tyrannides magis. Obicit autem aliquis de optimo viro, quod caret ignorantia & affectione peruersa, nos autem dicamus rarissime id contingere, nec tamen æqualiter ipsi legi, vt pridem induximus ab Aristotele à ratione & sensata experientia, quoniam omnem animam contingit habere hanc, id est affectionem quandoque, siniistran. Quod facile credere possumus ex Danielis 13. Ibi namque scribitur, quod venerunt duo Presbyteri in qua cogitatione aduersus Susannam, vt interficerent eam. Hi autem erant senes & sacerdotes, & populi iudices anno illo, qui tamen falsum testimonium perhibuerunt aduersus eam, propterea quod ipsorum iniquæ concupiscentiæ acquiescere noluit. Et ideo si Presbyteri & senes, quibus nimirum videretur, corrupti fuerunt propter carnalem concupiscentiam, & quanto magis propter auaritiam & reliqua, quid de reliquis lentiendum? neminem certe quantumcunque studiosum sic posse carere passione peruersa & ignorantia, quemadmodum lex. Ideoq; tutius est regulari iudicia ciuilia lege quam arbitrio iudicantis committi quantumcunque etiam studiosi. Esto tamen quamuis rarissimum aut impossibilium quoddam, esse virum aliquem principantem sic heroicum, vt in ipso neque passio neque ignorantia cadat. Quid de natis dicemus, huic dissimiles entibus, qui propter ipsorum excessum in principatu secundum proprium arbitrium committrent, unde principatu priuentur? nisi forte quis dixerit quod pater virorum optimus, His principatum non tradet, quod tamen audiri non debet, tum quia in ipso non est, filios hac successione priuare, ex quo genere principatus per successionem debetur, tum quia si in ipsius potestate foret, principatum in quem vellet transferre, non priuaret eo filios quantumcunq; prauos. Unde Aristoteles tertio politicae, ca. 9. huic respondens obiectioni, sic inquit; Adhuc hoc credere (scilicet patrem priuare filios principatu) difficile est, & maioris virtutis, quam secundum humanam naturam. Propter quod principantibus expedit magis lege regulari & determinari, quam arbitrio proprio iudicia ferre ciuilia, secundum legem enim nil praauum aut reprehensibile agent, unde securior & diuturnior efficietur principatus ipsorum. Hoc autem fuit consilium eximii Aristotelis ad omnes principantes, quod tamen parum aduertunt, cum quinto politicae, ca. 6. dixit: Quanto enim pauciorum fiunt domini (absq; lege scilicet) ampliori tempore necessarium manere omnem principatum, ipsi enim (principantes videlicet) sunt minus dispositi, & moribus aqui magis, & a subditis inuidetur eis minus. Et adducit consequenter testimonium cuiusdam prudentissimi regis vocati Theopompi, qui de potestate sibi concessa dimisit. Unde iudicauimus conuenient, hic seriem Aristotelis inducere propter huius principis singularitatem & virtutem excellentem, & quasi per secula inauditam in alio quoque, dixit ergo Aristoteles: Rursus Theopompo moderante (id est minorante potestatem suam, quae forte videbatur excedens) & in aliis instituente ephororum principatum, a potestate enim auferens (scilicet sua) auxit tempore regnum (id est, fecit durabilius.) Quare modo quodam fecit non minus, sed maius ipsum, qua quidem (id est haec verba) aiunt & ad vxorem respondisse ipsum, quae (scilicet vxor) dixerat: Si nihil (id est, si non) verecundaretur, minus regnum tradens filiis, quod a patre accepit? cui (verba iam dicta) respondit, non oportet hoc dicere, trado enim diuturnius. O vox heroica ex inaudita prudentia Theopompi procedens, & quam notanda his qui extra leges vti volunt plenitudine potestatis in subditos, quam inducentes multi principantium corruerunt. Et nos quidem ex huiusmodi inaduertentia regnorum non minimum, modernis temporibus quasi totum nutare vidimus, dum ipsius princeps quidam insolitam & praeter legem voluit subditis exactionem imponere. Sic itaq; palam ex dictis, in politiis necessarias esse leges, si debeant simpliciter recte disponi, & principatus diutius permanere.
units.tr: This was the view of the divine Aristotle in the fourth book of the Politics, chapter 9, where, inquiring from the standpoint of the end in view whether a state is better governed by the best man without law or by the best laws, he says: "But the more worthy (that is, the more excellent) for judging is the one who has nothing of the passionate element at all (that is, the affection which can pervert judgment), than the one in whom it is inherent. Law, then, does not have this, namely passion or affection. But every human soul necessarily has it." He said "every," not excepting anyone, however zealous. Repeating this opinion in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 1, he says: "Above all, it is to be sought that nothing be left to the judgment of the judge, since the judgment of the lawgiver (that is, the law) is not framed with respect to a part (that is, it is not passed on account of some particular person), but concerns the future and universals. Prefects and judges, however, judge concerning present and determinate matters, to which love and hatred and their own advantage are often attached, so that they cannot yet see the truth sufficiently, but in judgment attend to what is pleasant or painful to themselves." He says the same thing in the same first book, chapter 2: "For we do not render judgments in the same way when we are sad or glad, loving or hating. Judgment is still corrupted through the ignorance of judges, even if their affection or intention is good. The fault or defect is also removed and supplied by law, since in it what is just or unjust, and what is harmful or beneficial, is determined as if perfectly, for every human civil act." But this cannot be done sufficiently by one man, however ingenious. For one man alone, nor perhaps all men of one age, could discover or retain all the civil acts determined in law. Indeed, what the first inventors said about these matters, and what all men of the same age who observed such things thought, was a small and imperfect thing, which afterwards received its completion by the additions of later men. Experience, well known, is enough to show this, through the additions and subtractions, and sometimes total reversals, made in laws according to different ages and different times of the same age. Aristotle also bears witness to this in the second book of the Politics, chapter 2, when he said: "It is necessary not to be ignorant of this very point, that one must observe over a long time and many years, in which it certainly will not remain hidden whether these things have been well arranged, which ought to be established as laws." He says the same thing in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 1: "Then, he says, the enactment of laws has been considered over a long time." And this is confirmed by reason, since the proposing of laws requires prudence, as was shown earlier from the definition of law, and prudence in turn requires long experience, which comes from the multitude of times. Hence in the sixth book of the Ethics: "A sign of what has been said is that young men become geometers and skilled in such things, but they do not seem to become prudent. The cause is also that prudence concerns particulars, which become known through experience, but a young man has no experience, for a multitude of time produces experience." Therefore what one man alone discovers, or can know by himself, whether in the science of justice and civil dealings or in other sciences, is little or nothing. Further, the findings of men of one age, compared with what is observed over several ages, are an imperfect thing. For this reason Aristotle, treating in the second book of the Metaphysics, chapter 1, of the discovery of truth in each art and discipline, says: "According to one of the discoverers (namely of any discipline or art), to add nothing or little to it (that is, to discover it by himself alone), a certain magnitude is produced by joining together the contributions of all. According to the translation from the Arabic, however, this sequence is clearer, in which it is put thus: and each of them (that is, of the discoverers of any art or discipline) comprehends nothing of the truth, or only a little. When therefore there has been gathered from them what all have comprehended, then some quantity will have been gathered." This is especially evident in astrology. So, by the help of men one to another, and by the addition of later discoveries to earlier ones, all arts and disciplines have received their completion. Aristotle declares this figuratively in the same place concerning the invention of music, when he said: "If there had not been Timotheus, we would not have much melody; but if there had not been Phrynis before Timotheus," namely, he would not have been so perfect in melodies unless he had had the inventions of Phrynis before him. Averroes, expounding these words in his commentary on the second book, says: "And what he says in this chapter (namely Aristotle) is manifest. For no one can discover by himself the operative or contemplative (that is, speculative) arts for the most part, because they are not completed except by the help of the earlier man to the later one." He says the same thing in the last chapter of the Sophistical Refutations about the invention of rhetoric and of all the others, whatever may be said of the invention of logic, which he ascribes as perfected without the invention or help of any predecessor, in which he seems to have stood out singularly among others. He says this also in the first chapter of the eighth book of the Ethics: "Two coming together (that is, meeting), he says, are more powerful for acting and understanding; that is, than one alone. But if two, then more than two, both simultaneously and successively, than one alone." And this is what he says on the subject in the ninth chapter of the third book of the Politics: "It would perhaps seem absurd, if a man judged and acted with two eyes and two ears, and two feet and hands, to perceive better than many with many." Since therefore law is an eye made of many eyes, that is, a comprehension examined from many comprehensions, in order to avoid error in civil judgments and to judge rightly, it is safer that these be made according to the judgment of the judge. And for this reason it is necessary that laws themselves be established, if states are to be arranged in the best way as regards the just and beneficial civil matters of their members. For by law civil judgments are preserved from ignorance and from the perverse affection of judges, which was the minor premise of the demonstration we attempted at the beginning of this chapter, by which we sought to assign the necessity of laws. How a dispute or a case that has arisen, and is not determined by law, ought to be settled or judged, will be said in chapter 14 of this book. Laws are therefore necessary to exclude from civil judgments or sentences the malice and error of judges. For this reason Aristotle advised that no judge or ruler be granted the power to judge or command concerning civil matters without law, in those matters which law could determine. Hence in the fourth book of the Ethics, chapter 5, in his treatise on justice, Aristotle said: "For this reason we do not allow a man to rule, but reason" (that is, law), assigning the cause which we have brought forward, namely the perverse affection which can fall upon him. Likewise in the third book of the Politics, chapter 6, when he said: "The first question makes it plain that nothing is so much to be made lord as the rightly established laws", that is, that rulers should rule according to them. The same in the same chapter 9, when he said: "What bids the intellect rule seems to bid God and the laws rule, but he who bids a man rule (namely without law, by his own will) adds also a beast." Shortly after, adding the reason, he said: "For this reason, law is intellect without appetite." As if he were saying that law is intellect or cognition without appetite, that is, without any affection. He repeats this opinion too in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 1, where he says thus: "Therefore it is most fitting that, wherever it is possible, the rightly established laws determine all matters themselves, and that as few as possible be entrusted to judges." He is assigning, as already quoted, the precautions of this kind, namely the exclusion of the malice and ignorance of judges from civil judgments, which cannot fall into the law as they can into the judge, as was shown before. And Aristotle says openly, in addition to these things, in the fourth chapter of the fourth book of the Politics: "Where the laws do not rule (that is, where the rulers do not rule according to them), there is no polity (understand: well tempered), for the law must rule over all." It remains to show that all rulers ought to rule according to law, and not beyond it. Above all this applies to monarchs, who rule throughout their whole succession, so that their rule may be more secure and more lasting; this was assigned at the beginning of this chapter as a secondary necessity of laws. Here it is first to be seen that ruling according to law preserves their judgments from the defect which arises through ignorance and perverse affection. Hence, when they are themselves regulated, and in relation to their subject citizens, they suffer fewer seditions, and consequently fewer overthrows of their rule, which would befall them if they acted wickedly according to their own will, as Aristotle plainly says in the fifth chapter of the fifth book of the Politics: "For a kingdom, says Aristotle, is least of all corrupted from outside, but very many corruptions arise from within it. It is corrupted in two ways: in one, when those who share in the kingdom make sedition; in the other, when they attempt to govern more tyrannically, when they have chosen to be lords of many and beyond the law. Kingdoms, however, do not yet become this way; rather, monarchies and tyrannies become so more." Someone may object concerning the best man, that he lacks ignorance and perverse affection, but we say that this very rarely happens, and not equally to law itself, as we showed earlier from Aristotle, from reason and sensible experience, since it happens to every soul to have this, that is, affection at some time, to its harm. We can easily believe this from the thirteenth chapter of Daniel. For there it is written that two elders came with a plan against Susanna, to kill her. They were old men and priests, and judges of the people in that year, who nevertheless bore false witness against her, because she would not yield to their wicked lust. And therefore, if the elders and presbyters, who would surely seem to be such, were corrupted by carnal lust, and how much more by avarice and the rest, what should we think of others? Certainly no one, however zealous, can be free from perverse passion and ignorance as the law is. Therefore it is safer for civil judgments to be regulated by law than to be committed to the will of the judge, however zealous he may be. Yet suppose that there is some very rare, or almost impossible, ruler so heroic that in him neither passion nor ignorance falls. What shall we say of the sons, who, being unlike him, would by their excess in rule act according to their own will, whereby they might be deprived of their rule? Unless perhaps someone should say that the best of fathers will not hand over the rule to them; but this ought not to be heard, both because it is not in his power to deprive his sons of this succession, by which kind of rule is owed through succession, and because, if it were in his power to transfer the rule to whomever he wished, he would not deprive his sons of it, however wicked they might be. Hence Aristotle, answering this objection in the ninth chapter of the third book of the Politics, says: "It is still difficult to believe this (namely that a father deprives his sons of rule), and it requires more virtue than human nature allows." For this reason it is more advantageous for rulers to be regulated and determined by law than to pass civil judgments by their own will; for by acting according to law they will do nothing depraved or reprehensible, whence their rule will become more secure and lasting. This was the counsel of the distinguished Aristotle to all rulers, which nevertheless they little heed. He said in the sixth chapter of the fifth book of the Politics: "For the fewer the lords (namely without law), the more necessary it is for all rule to last for a longer time; for they themselves (namely the rulers) are less disposed and more unequal in morals, and less envy is directed at them by their subjects." And he consequently adduces the testimony of a certain most prudent king called Theopompus, who gave up the power granted to him. Hence we have judged it fitting to bring in here Aristotle's sequence, on account of this prince's singularity and excellent virtue, almost unheard of through the ages in any other. Aristotle therefore said: "Again, when Theopompus moderated (that is, lessened his power, which perhaps seemed excessive) and established the rule of the ephors among others, by taking away power from himself he lengthened the kingdom in time (that is, made it more lasting). In a certain way he made it not less, but greater. They say that his wife also answered him, when she had said: 'Are you not ashamed to hand on to your sons a kingdom less than you received from your father?' He answered her (these words having been said): 'It is not right to say this, for I hand on one that lasts longer.'" O heroic voice, proceeding from the unheard-of prudence of Theopompus, and how worthy of note for those who wish to act outside the laws with full power over their subjects, a course by which many rulers have fallen. And we ourselves, in modern times, have seen, from this same kind of heedlessness, almost the whole of a kingdom tottering, when a certain prince wished to impose an unusual exaction on his subjects, beyond the law. So, then, it is plain from what has been said that laws are necessary in states, if they are to be arranged rightly in every respect, and rule is to remain for longer.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: De causa legum humanarum effectiua demonstrabili, & de ea etiam, quae per demonstrationem convinci non potest, quod est legis latorem inquirere. Unde etiam apparet, quod electione sola praeter alteram confirmationem datur auctoritas ei, quod per electionem statuitur.
units.tr: On the demonstrable efficient cause of human laws, and on that cause which cannot be proved by demonstration, namely, the need to seek out the lawgiver. From this it also appears that what is enacted by election alone receives its authority without any further confirmation.

units.la: His autem habitum est dicere de causa legum effectiua, quam reddere possumus per demonstrationem, de illa enim institutione, quae Dei opere vel oraculo immediate absq; humano arbitrio fieri possibilis est, aut iam extitit, qualem Mosaicę legis institutionem diximus, etiā quantum ad ea praecepta ciuilium actuum quae in ea sunt, pro statu praesentis seculi, non intendo hic assignationem facere, sed de legum & principatuum institutione tantummodo, quae immediate proueniant ex arbitrio humanae mentis. Ad quam siquidem ingredientes, dicamus, quod legem sumptam quasi materialiter & secundum tertiam significationem, videlicet scientiam iustorum & conferentium ciuilium, inuenire potest ad quemlibet ciuem pertinere, licet inquisitio haec conuenientius fieri possit ex obseruatione potentium vacare, seniorum & expertorum in agibilibus quos prudentes appellant, quam ex mœchanicorum consideratione, qui ad quaerenda vitae necessaria suis operibus habent intendere. Verum quia cognitio seu inuentio vera iustorum & conferentium ac suorum oppositorum, non est lex secundum vltimam significationem & propriam, quae fit mensura humanorum actuum ciuilium, nisi dum de ipsius obseruatione praeceptum coactiuum datum fuerit, seu per modum talis praecepti lata fuerit ab eo, cuius auctoritate transgressores arceri debent & possunt, propterea dicere conuenit, cuius aut quorum sit auctoritas ferendi tale praeceptum, & ipsius transgressores arcendi, quod quidem est inquirere legis latorem siue factorem. Nos autem dicamus secundum veritatem atq; consilium Aristotelis. 3. politicae, ca. 6. legis latorem seu causam legis effectiuam primam & propriam esse populum seu ciuium vniuersitatem, aut eius valentiorem partem per suam electionem seu voluntatem in generali ciuium congregatione per sermonem expressam, praecipientem seu determinantem aliquid fieri vel omitti circa ciuiles actus humanos sub poena vel supplicio temporali: valentiorem inquam partem considerata quantitate in communitate illa super quam lex fertur, siue id fecerit vniuersitas praedicta ciuium aut eius pars valentior per seipsam immediate, siue id alicui vel aliquibus committerit faciendum, qui legis lator simpliciter non sunt, necesse possunt, secundum solum ad aliquid & quandoque, ac secundum primi legis latoris auctoritate. Et dico consequenter huic, quod eadem auctoritate prima non alia debent leges & aliud quodlibet per electionem institutum approbationem necessariam suscipere, quicquid sit de ceremoniis seu solennitatibus quibusdam, quae ad esse non exiguntur electorum, sed ad bene, quibus etiam non factis nil minus electio valida foret, amplius q ab eadem auctoritate debent leges, & alia quae per electionem statuuntur, suscipere ad ditionem aut diminutionem, vel totalem mutationem, interpretationem & suspensionem, secundum exigetiam temporum vel locorum, & reliquarum circumstantiarum, quib. horum aliquid apter commune conferens circa talia fuerit opportunum. Eadem quoq; auctoritate promulgari seu proclamari debent leges post earum institutionem, ne quisquam civis aut advena delinquens in eas, possit per ipsarum ignorantiam excusari. Ciuem autem dico secundum Aristot. 3. politicæ, capitulis 13. & 7. cum qui participat in communitate civili, principatu autem consiliativo vel iudicativo secundum gradum suum. Per quam siquidem descriptionem separantur a civibus pueri, servi, advenæ, ac mulieres, licet secundum modum diversum. Pueri nanq; civium, cives sunt in propinqua potentia propter solum ætatis defectum. Valentiorem vero civium partem oportet attendere secundum politiarum consuetudinem honestam, vel hanc determinare secundum sententiam Aristot. 6. politicæ. c. 2. Sic itaq; determinato cive ac civium valentiore multitudine, ad propositam intentionem redeamus, demonstrare scilicet legum latoris auctoritatem humanam, ad solam civium universitatem, aut eius valentiorem partem pertinere, quod quidem sit primum inferre tentabimus. Quoniam illius tantummodo est legum humanarum lationis seu institutionis autoritas humana prima simpliciter, a quo solum optimæ leges possunt provenire. Hoc autem est civium universitas aut eius pars valentior, quæ totam universitatem repræsentat. Quoniam non facile, aut non possibile, omnium personas in unam convenire sententiam, propter quorundam esse naturam orbatam, aut malitia vel ignorantia singulari discordantem a communi sententia: propter quorum irrationabilem reclamationem seu contradictionem, non debent communia conferentia impediri vel omitti. Pertinet igitur ad universitatem civium, aut eius valentiorem partem tantummodo legum lationis seu institutionis auctoritas. Prima propositio huius demonstrationis est valde probabilis, quamuis eius robur & ultima certitudo sumi possit ex 11. huius. Secundam propositionem probo, videlicet quod ex universæ multitudinis auditu & præcepto tantummodo fieri lex optima, supponendo cum Aristotele 3. politicæ, cap. 7. legem optimam esse, quæ latta est ad communem conferens civium. Unde dixit: Rectum autem fore (in legibus scilicet) ad conferens civitatis, & ad communem civium. Hoc autem fieri optime per civium universitatem tantummodo, aut eius valentiorem partem, quod pro eodem de cætero supponatur, sic ostendo, quoniam illius veritas certius iudicatur, & ipsius communis utilitas diligentius attenditur, ad quod tota intendit civium universitas intellectu & affectu. Aduerrere enim potest magis defectu circa propositam legem statuendam maior pluralitas quacunq; sui parte, cum omne totum corporeum saltem maius sit mole atq; virtute quilibet sui parte seu sum. Adhuc ex universa multitudine magis attenditur legis communis utilitas, eo q nemo sibi nocet scienter. Ibi autem inspicere potest quilibet, an lex proposita magis declinet ad cuiusdam aut quorundam commodum, quam aliorum vel communitatis: & in contrarium reclamare, q non fieret, si per unum aut paucos quosdam, proprium magis quam commune attendentes commodum, lex ipsa feratur. Hanc quoq; sententiam satis adiuuant, quæ de legum necessitate assignauimus in 11. huius.
units.tr: I have already discussed the efficient cause of laws that can be shown by demonstration. For I do not here intend to set out the institution that is brought about immediately by God's work or oracle, without human choice, such as the institution of the law of Moses, which we have described, even as regards those precepts of civil acts that are in it, given the state of the present age. I am speaking only of the institution of laws and principates that comes directly from the judgement of the human mind. Taking up this subject, I say that the law, taken materially and in the third sense, namely the knowledge of what is just and advantageous in civil matters, can be discovered by any citizen. Yet this inquiry can be better carried out by observing the powerful, the elders and those experienced in affairs, whom the wise call prudent, than by considering the mechanics, who must devote themselves to their work to obtain the necessities of life. But because the true knowledge or discovery of what is just and advantageous, and of their opposites, is not law in its ultimate and proper sense, which is the measure of human civil acts, unless a binding precept is given concerning its observance, or it is issued in the form of such a precept by the one whose authority can and must restrain transgressors, it is therefore fitting to say whose authority it is, or whose, to issue such a precept and to restrain its transgressors. This is indeed to inquire who is the lawgiver or maker. Now we say, according to the truth and the counsel of Aristotle, Politics 3, chapter 6, that the lawgiver, or the first and proper efficient cause of law, is the people, or the whole body of citizens, or its more powerful part, by its election or will, expressed by word in a general assembly of citizens, commanding or determining that something be done or omitted concerning civil human acts under penalty or temporal punishment. I say the more powerful part, reckoned by quantity, within that community over which the law is made, whether that whole body of citizens, or its more powerful part, does this itself immediately, or commits it to be done by some person or persons, who are not lawgivers absolutely, but only in a certain respect and at times, and by the authority of the first lawgiver. And I consequently say that, by this same first authority, laws and other things enacted by election do not need any further approval, whatever may be said of certain ceremonies or solemnities, which are not required for the election to exist but for it to be well done, and without which the election would nonetheless be valid. Moreover, by the same authority, laws and other things established by election ought to receive addition, diminution, total change, interpretation and suspension, according to the demands of times and places and of the other circumstances, in which any of these things is opportune and contributes to the common good. By the same authority, laws ought to be promulgated or proclaimed after their institution, so that no citizen or stranger who offends against them may be excused by ignorance of them. I call a citizen, according to Aristotle, Politics 3, chapters 13 and 7, one who takes part in the civil community, and in deliberative or judicial office according to his rank. By this description boys, slaves, strangers and women are separated from the citizens, though in different ways. For the sons of citizens are citizens in potential power, lacking only age. We must consider the more powerful part of the citizens according to the honest custom of the states, or determine it according to the opinion of Aristotle, Politics 6, chapter 2. So, with the citizen and the more numerous part of the citizens thus determined, let us return to our proposed aim, namely to demonstrate that the human authority of the lawgiver belongs solely to the whole body of citizens, or to its more powerful part. This we shall first try to infer. For the primary human authority of making or instituting human laws, the authority from which alone the best laws can arise, belongs simply to that alone. This is the whole body of citizens, or its more powerful part, which represents the whole body. For it is not easy, or not possible, for all persons to agree in one opinion, since some are by nature deprived of reason, or disagree from the common opinion through singular malice or ignorance; and the common advantages must not be hindered or omitted on account of their unreasonable objection or contradiction. Therefore the authority of making or instituting laws belongs only to the whole body of citizens, or to its more powerful part. The first proposition of this demonstration is very probable, although its strength and ultimate certainty can be drawn from the eleventh chapter of this work. I prove the second proposition, namely that the best law is made only by the hearing and command of the whole multitude, supposing with Aristotle, Politics 3, chapter 7, that the best law is that which is enacted for the common advantage of the citizens. Hence he said: What is right (in laws, that is) is what is advantageous for the state and for the common good of the citizens. That this is done best by the whole body of citizens alone, or by its more powerful part, which we shall henceforth assume for the same reason, I show as follows: the truth of a matter is judged more certainly, and its common usefulness is attended to more diligently, by the whole body of citizens, with mind and will alike, toward which it wholly tends. For a greater plurality can more easily notice a defect in the proposed law to be enacted than any single part, since every corporeal whole is at least greater in bulk and power than any one of its parts or some of them. Moreover, the common usefulness of the law is more closely regarded by the whole multitude, because no one knowingly harms himself. And anyone can see there whether the proposed law leans more toward the advantage of one person or of some, than of others or of the community, and can object against it, which would not happen if the law were enacted by one or a few who attend more to private than to common advantage. This view is also greatly supported by what we have said about the necessity of laws in the eleventh chapter of this work.

units.la: Rursum ad principalem conclusionem sic, quoniam illius tantummodo est legum lationis autoritas, per quem latæ melius, aut simpliciter obseruantur. Hoc autem est tantummodo civium universitas, ipsius igitur est autoritas lationis legum. Prima propositio huius demonstrationis est per se notis propinqua valde, ociosa namque lex esset, nisi observaretur. Unde Aristoteles quarto politicæ, cap. 7. Non est autem bona legum institutio, bene poni leges, non obedire autem. Idem 8. eiusdem cap. 9. Nullum profectus est, inquit Aristoteles, sed quidem sententia de iusto, has autem non accipere finem. Secundam propositionem probo, quoniam lex illa melius observatur a quocunque civium, quam sibi quilibet imposuisse videtur, talis est lex lata ex auditu & præcepto universæ multitudinis civium. Prima propositio huius prosyllogismi apparet quasi per se, nam quia civitas est communitas liberorum, ut scribitur 3. politicæ, cap. 4. quilibet civis liber esse debet, nec alterius ferre dominium, id est seruile dominium, hoc autem non contingeret, si vnus aliquis aut pauciores civium legem ferrent autoritate propria supra civium universitatem, sic enim legem ferentes aliorum despotes essent. Et ideo reliqui civium, pars amplior scilicet, talem legem quantumcunque bonam, moleste ferrent, aut nullo modo, & contra illam contemptum passi, reclamarent, & non vocati ad illius lationem, quatenus obseruarent. Latam vero ex auditu seu consensu omnis multitudinis, etiam minus vtilem, quilibet civium faciliter obseruaret & ferret: eo quod hanc quilibet sibi statuisse videtur, ideoque contra illam reclamare non habet, sed æquo animo illam ponis tolerare. Adhuc secundam propositionem primi syllogismi probo ex alio sic. Quoniam illius est potestas obseruationis legum, cuius tantummodo est potentia transgressorum coactiva, hoc autem est universitas, aut ipsius pars valentior, ergo ipsius solius est legum lationis autoritas. Amplius ad principale sic, quoniam illud agibile, in cuius debita institutione consistit maxima pars communis sufficientiæ civium in hac vita, & in cuius prava institutione commune detrimentum imminet per universitatem civium tantummodo debet institui, hoc autem est lex, ergo ad universitatem civium tantummodo illius pertinet institutio. Maior huius demonstrationis est per se notis propinqua & stabiliter in immediatis veritatibus, quæ positæ sunt 4. huius & 7. Conuenerunt enim homines
units.tr: Again, to the principal conclusion, thus: since the authority of making laws belongs only to that by whom laws that are made are better, or indeed only, observed; and this is only the whole body of citizens, therefore the authority of making laws belongs to it. The first proposition of this demonstration is very close to things known in themselves, for a law would be idle unless it were observed. Hence Aristotle, Politics 4, chapter 7: The good institution of laws is not in laying down good laws, but in obeying them. The same, Politics 8, chapter 9: "There is no profit," says Aristotle, "in a sentence about what is just, unless these things receive their end." I prove the second proposition: for a law that has been made by the hearing and command of the whole multitude of citizens is observed better by any citizen than a law which any one of them seems to have imposed on himself. The first proposition of this prosyllogism appears almost self-evident, for since the state is a community of free men, as is written in Politics 3, chapter 4, every citizen ought to be free, and not bear the dominion of another, that is, servile dominion. This would not happen if one or a few of the citizens were to make law by their own authority above the whole body of citizens; for those making the law would thus be the masters of the others. And so the rest of the citizens, that is, the greater part, would bear such a law, however good, with reluctance, or not at all, and would object, having suffered contempt, and not having been called to its making, to observing it. But a law made by the hearing and assent of the whole multitude, even if less useful, any citizen would observe and bear with ease, because each would seem to have made it for himself, and so he has no ground to object against it, but can bear it with an equal mind. I prove the second proposition of the first syllogism also by another route: the power of enforcing the observance of laws belongs to the one whose alone is the coercive power over transgressors; this is the whole body, or its more powerful part; therefore the authority of making laws belongs to it alone. Further, as to the principal matter: that thing which is to be done, in whose proper institution the greater part of the common sufficiency of the citizens in this life consists, and in whose wrongful institution common loss threatens, ought to be instituted by the whole body of citizens alone; this thing is law; therefore the institution of law belongs to the whole body of citizens alone. The major premise of this demonstration is close to things known in themselves and firmly rests on the immediate truths that were laid down in the fourth and seventh chapters. For men have come together, as above, into civil association for the sake of advantage and for obtaining the sufficiency of life, and for avoiding the contrary. Therefore whatever can touch the advantage and disadvantage of all must be known and heard by all, so that they can obtain the advantage and repel the opposite. Such are laws,…

units.la: q. ut supra homines ad ciuilem communicationem propter commodum & vitæ sufficientiam consequendam, & oppositá declinandum. Quæ igitur omnium tangere possunt commodum & incommodum, ab omnibus sciri debent & audiri, vt commodum assequi & oppositum repellere possint. Talia sunt leges, sicut in minori assumebatur. In ipsis enim recte positis totius & omnis humanæ sufficientiæ pars magna consistit. Sub iniquis vero seruitus & oppressio atque miseria ciuium importabiles, ex quibus tandem contingit soluere politiam. Rursum & est hæc quasi abbreuiatio & summa priorum demonstrationum. Aut legum lationis autoritas, ad solam ciuium vniuersi-tatem pertinet, vt diximus, vel ad hominem vnicum aut pauciores, non ad solum vnum, propterea quæ dicta sunt in vndecimo huius & in prima demonstratione, quam in hoc adduximus, posset enim propter ignorantiam vel malitiam aut vtrumq; legem prauam ferre, inspiciendo scilicet magis proprium quam commune, unde tyrannica foret, propter eandem vero causam non pertinet hoc ad pauciores, possent enim peccare in ferendo legem, vt prius ad quorundam (scilicet paucorum) & non commune conferens, quemadmodum videre est in oligarchiis: pertinet hoc igitur ad ciuium vniuersitatem, aut eius partem valentiorem, de quibus est altera & opposita ratio. Quia enim lege debent omnes ciues mensurari secundum proportionem debitam, & nemo sibi scienter nocet aut vult iniustum, ideoq; volunt omnes aut plurimi legem conuenientem comuni ciuium conferenti. Ex eisdem quoque demonstrationibus sola minori extremitate mutata concluditur, legum approbationem, interpretationem, suspensionem, & cætera proposita parte tertia huius, ad solius legis latoris autoritatem tantummodo pertinere. Idemque sentiendum de omni eo quod per electionem statuitur. Cuius enim est autoritas prima eligendi, ipse idem approbat aut reprobat, vel ille cui autoritatem eligendi concesserit, aliter nanq; pars maior esset toto, vel illi saltem æqualis, si ea quæ per totum instituta sunt, autoritate propria dissoluere posset. Modus autem conueniendi ad legum lationem, in sequenti cap. describetur.
units.tr: Since men, as stated above, have come together into civil community for the sake of advantage and for obtaining the sufficiency of life, and for avoiding what is harmful, those things which can affect the advantage and disadvantage of all must be known and heard by all, so that they may be able to obtain the advantage and repel what is harmful. Such are laws, as was assumed in the minor premise. For in laws rightly established lies a great part of all human sufficiency; under unjust laws, on the other hand, there is slavery and oppression, and the misery of citizens becomes unbearable, from which at last it comes about that the commonwealth is dissolved. Again, this is as it were an abridgement and summary of the earlier demonstrations. The authority of enacting laws belongs either to the whole body of citizens alone, as we have said, or to one man or a few, not to one alone; for the reasons stated in the eleventh chapter of this work and in the first demonstration which we have adduced here. For through ignorance or malice, or both, one man could enact a bad law, looking to what is his own rather than what is common, and so it would be tyrannical. For the same reason it does not belong to a few either: they could sin in enacting a law by conferring benefit on some (namely a few) and not on the common good, as may be seen in oligarchies. It therefore belongs to the whole body of citizens, or to its stronger part, and there is a second and opposite argument for this. For since all citizens ought to be measured by laws according to due proportion, and no one knowingly harms himself or wishes what is unjust, all or most therefore wish for a law that agrees with and benefits the common good of the citizens. From the same demonstrations, with only the minor term changed, it follows that the approval, interpretation, suspension of laws, and the other matters set out in the third part of this work, belong to the authority of the lawgiver alone. The same must be held concerning whatever is established by election. For the one whose authority is primary in electing, the same person approves or rejects, or else the one to whom he has granted the authority of electing; otherwise the greater part would be over the whole, or at least equal to it, if it could dissolve by its own authority what has been established by the whole. The manner of coming together for the enactment of laws will be described in the following chapter.

units.la: CAP. XIII. De quibusdam instantiis ad dicta in capitulo præcedenti, & ipsarum solutione, ac propositi amplioris manifestatione.
units.tr: Chapter XIII. Certain objections to what was said in the preceding chapter, their solution, and a fuller statement of the purpose.

units.la: DE quibus tamen diximus dubitabit aliquis, disputans ad ciuium vniuersitatem non pertinere legum lationis seu institutionis autoritatem. Primum quidem, quoniam prauum & indiscretum secundum plurimum non debet legem statuere. Hæc enim duo peccata à legis latore debent excludi, malitia scilicet atque ignorantia, propter quæ etiam in iudiciis euitanda, legis necessitatem accepimus vndecimo huius. Populus autem seu ciuium vniuersitas est huiusmodi, homines enim, vt in pluribus videtur prauì & stulti, nam stultorum infinitus est numerus, vt habetur Ecclesiastes. i. Amplius quoniam difficile valde aut impossibile plurium prauorum & insensatorum concordare sententias, quod non euenit de paucis & studiosis. Est igitur vtilius per paucos legem ferri, quam per ciuium vniuersitatem, & ipsorum superfluam pluralitatem. Rursum in qualibet communitate ciuili sunt pauci sapientes & docti, respectu alterius multitudinis indoctæ. Cum igitur per sapientes & doctos vtilius lex feratur, quam per indoctos & rudes, videtur quod ipsarum lationis autoritas ad paucos pertineat, non ad plures aut omnes. Adhuc frustra fit per plures, quod per pauciores fieri contingit. Cum ergo per sapientes (qui pauci sunt) lex fieri possit, vt dictum est, frustra occuparetur in hoc vniuersa multitudo, aut ipsius pars maior. Non igitur ad vniuersitatem aut ipsius valentiorem partem pertinet legum lationis autoritas. Ex suppositio nobis in prioribus, quasi omnium in hoc libro demonstrandorum principio videlicet. Omnes homines appetere sufficientiam vitæ, & oppositum declinare, per demonstrationem conclusimus ipsorum communitatem ciuilem quarto huius, quoniam per ipsam, sufficientiam hanc adipisci possunt, & præter eam minime, propter quod etiam Aristoteles primo politicæ, cap. primo inquit: Natura quidem igitur in omnibus impetus est, ad talem communitatem, ciuilem scilicet. Ex qua siquidem veritate per necessitatem sequitur alia quædam. & habetur 4. politicæ, cap. 10. videlicet, quod oportet valentiorem esse partem ciuitatis volentem, non volentem manere politiam. Quoniam nihil desideratur per eandem, natura, specie, secundum eius plurimum & immediate cum ipsius corruptione simul, inane nanque foret tale desiderium. Quinimo non volentes manere politiam computantur inter seruos, non inter ciues, vt sunt aduenæ quidam, unde 7. politicæ, cap. 12. Cum subditi enim existunt omnes volentes insolescere, quiper regionem. Et tunc subinfert, Totq; multitudine esse eos in politihemate, (insolentes scilicet, seu non curantes ciuiliter viuere) vt sint valentiores bis omnibus, (videlicet politizare volentibus) vnum impossibilium est, cur autem impossibilium sit, apparet: quoniam hoc esset naturam peccare vel deficere vt in pluribus. Si ergo valentior hominum multitudo vult politiam manere, quemadmodum bene dictum videtur, vult illud etiam, sine quo politia manere non potest. Hoc autem est iustorum & conferentium regula, tradita cum præcepto, vocata lex, eo quod impossibilium est ciuitatem Aristocratizantem, (id est secundum virtutem gubernatam) non bene legibus dispositi, vt habetur 4. politica, cap. 7. & demonstrauimus vndecimo huius. Vult ergo valentior multitudo ciuitatis, legem. Aut contingeret orbatio in natura & arte, secundu plurimum, quod impossibilium supponatur ex scientia naturali. Suscipio rursum cum suprádictis veritatibus ma-nifestis, nifestis, communem animi conceptionem, videlicet. Omne totum maius esse sua parte, quod verum est tam in magnitudine siue molle, quam etiam in actiua virtute & actione. Vnde satis cuidenter, per necessitatem infertur, vniuersitatem ciuium, aut ipsius valentiorem multitudinem, quae pro eodem accipienda sunt, magis posse quid eligendum & quid spernendum discernere, quacunq; sui parte seorsum. His itaq; suppositis tanquam veritatibus inoccultis, facile est repellere instantias, quibus niteretur aliquis convincere, legis lationem non pertinere ad ciuium vniuersitatem, aut eius valentiorem multitudinem, sed ad paucos quosdam. Cum ergo primum dicebatur, ad primum & in pluribus indiscretum non pertinet legum latione auctoritas, concediture. Et cum additur, vniuersitatem ciuium esse huiusmodi, negandum est. Nam ciuium pluralitas neque praua neque indiscreta est quantum ad pluralitatem suppositorum, & in plurali tempore, omnes enim aut plurimi sane mentis & rationis sunt, & recti appetitus ad politiam, & quae necessaria sunt propter eius permanentiam, quemadmodum leges & alia statuta vel consuetudines, sicut prius ostensum est. Quamuis enim non quilibet aut maior multitudo ciuium sit legum inuentor, potest tamen quilibet de inuentis & ab alio sibi propositis iudicare, addendum vel minuendum, aut mutandum discernere. Propterea si, quod in maiori propositione dicitur indiscretum, intelligaturid quod per se inuenire nequit legem secundum plures sui partes vel suppositas, non debere legem statuere, ipsa esset neganda tanquam falsa manifeste, testibus, inductione sensata. & Aristot. tertio politicae, cap. 6. Inductione quidem, quoniam multi de qualitate, picturae domus, aut navis, caeterorumque artificiatorum iudicant recte, qui tamen ea inuenire nescirent. Testatur autem huic Arist. vbi supra, respondens ad propositam instantiam in haec verba: Et quia de quibusdam non solus qui fecit, neque vtique optime iudicabit: inducens hoc in pluribus artificiorum speciebus, idem faciens intelligere de reliquis. Nec obstat quod dicitur, sapientes (qui pauci sunt) magis possunt agibilia statuenda discernere reliqua multitudine: quoniam esto sic verum, non tamen ex hoc sequitur, quod sapientes sciant statuenda discernere magis tota multitudine, in qua comprehenduntur ipsi cum reliquis minus doctis. Omne enim totum maius est sua parte in agendo, & etiam discernendo. Et fuit haec inducbie Aristotelis sententia 3. politicae, ca. 6. cum dixit: Quare iuste dominans maiorum multitudo, id est iuste dominari debet de maioribus, quae sunt in politia multitudo seu ciuium vniuersitas, aut eius pars valentior, quam nomine multitudinis significat, causam huius assignans. Ex multis enim populus & concilium, & praetorium, & honorabilitas, amplior autem horum omnium, quam qui eorum qui secundum vnum, & secundum paucos, principantium magnis principatibus. Vult dicere, quod omnium collegiorum politiae seu ciuilitatis simul sumptorum, amplior est multitudo, siue populus, & per consequens iudicium securius, iudicio alicuius partis seorsum. Sine pars illa sit vulgus, quam hic nomine concilii signauit, veluti agricolae, artifices & huiusmodi; siue sit praetorium, id est qui in praetorio sunt officiales, principantibus subseruientes, vtaduocati seu iurisperiti, atque notarii: Siue sit honorabilitas, id est collegium optimatum, qui pauci sunt; & soli conuenienter eligantur ad maximos principatus: Siue altera pars ciuitatis quaecunq; seorsum accepta. Amplius esto, sicut est secundum veritatem, aliquos minus doctos non aeque bene iudicare de statuenda lege aut alia agibili totidem doctis. Posset tamen in tantum augeri numerus minus doctorum, quod aeque bene vel melius iudicarent de his, paucis doctioribus, quod palam dixit Arist. vbi supra, hanc volens confirmare sententiam: Si sit multitudo non nimis vilis, inquit Arist. vnusquisque quidem erit doctior iudex sui entibus. Omnes autem congregati meliores, aut non deteriores. Ad illud vero quod dicebatur Ecclesi. primo: stultorum infinitus est numerus, oportet dicere, per stultos intelligi minus doctos, vel non vacantes liberalibus operum, qui tamen participant intellectu & iudicio agibilium, licet non aequaliter vacantibus, aut forte significauit ibi sapientes per stultos, infideles, sicut dicit ibidem Hieronymus, qui etiam quantumcunque scientes motus in scientias, sunt stulti simpliciter, secundum illud Apostoli primae ad Corinth. 3. Sapientia huius mundi, stultitia est apud Deum. Secunda vero instantia parum vrget, quoniam licet facilius sit concedare paucorum sententiam, quam plurium, ex hoc non concluditur paucorum seu partis praestantiorem esse sententiam, ea quae totius multitudinis, cuius pauci sunt pars. Nam hi pauciores non aeque bene discernerent neque vellent commune conferens, quemadmodum vniuersa ciuium multitudo. Quinimo in securum esset, sicut ex iam dictis apparuit, paucorum arbitrio committere legis lationem. Respicerent enim in ea fortasse magis conferens proprium, vt personarum vel alicuius collegii quam commune, quod in his qui Decretales clericorum tulerunt, satis apparet. Sicut etiam manifestabimus sufficienter in 8. 2. Ex hoc enim praebeetur oligarchiae via quaedam, veluti dum vni soli legum lationis potestas tribuitur, tyrannidi locus datur, quemadmodum vndecimo huius, parte 4. inductionis ab Aristot. 4. Ethicorum, tractatu de iustitia. Instantia vero tertia ex iam dictis facile repelli potest, quoniam & si per sapientes melius possint leges ferri quam per minus doctos: non tamen ex hoc concluditur, quod per solos sapientes feruntur melius quam per vniuersam multitudinem ciuium, in qua etiam includuntur sapientes praedicti. Verum horum omnium congregata multitudo discernere potest, & vellet amplius commune iustum & conferens, harum partium quacunq; seorsum accepta quantumcunq; prudentium. Vnde non verum enunciant, dicentes minus doctam multitudinem impedire veri aut communis boni electionem & approbationem: quinimo adiuuat in hoc iunctas doctioribus & magis expertis. Nam licet vera & vtilia statuenda per se nesciat inuenire, ea tamen per alios adinuenta & sibi propositas, discernere potest & iudicare, si quid addendum, minuendum, aut totaliter mutandum, vel spernendum in propositis videatur. Multa nanq; comprehendit homo post alterius dictionem, & ad multorum complementum agere potest, ad quorum initia seu inuentionem, per seipsum peruenire nequisset. Sunt enim rerum initia difficillimae inuentionis, unde Arist. 2. elench. ca. sin. Difficillimum est videri principium, s. veritatis & proprium secundum vnamquamq; disciplinam. Hoc autem inuento facile est addere & augere reliquū, propter quod scientiarum & artium & aliarum traditionum inuenire principia, nō est nisi optimorum & acutorum ingeniorum, adinuentis autem addere possunt, etiam humilioris ingenii homines, qui tamē neq; propter hoc indiscreti debent appellari, si ex se talia nequeant inuenire, imo & in bonorum numero comparari debent, vt in. 1. Ethi. 1. ca. dixit Arist. Iste siquidem, inquit, optimus, qui sibi ipse omnia intelligit. Bonus autem rursus & ille, qui benedicenti obedit, ipsum. s. auscultando, illiq; nonabsq; ratione contradicendo. Et propterea iustorum & consentientium ciuilium, & incommodorum seu hominum communium & similium reliquorum, regulas, futuras leges, siue statuta, quaeredas seu inueniendas & examinandas prudentibus & expertis per vniuersitatem ciuium committi, conueniens & peratile est. Sic vt vel seorsum ab vnaquaq; primarum partium ciuitatis, enumeratarum quinto huius, partes, secundum tamen vniuscuiusque proportionem eligantur aliqui, vel ab omnibus simul congregatis ciuibus omnes eligantur experti seu prudentes viri praedicti. Et hic erit conueniens & vtilis modus conueniendi ad legum inuentionem absque documento reliquae multitudinis, minus doctorum scilicet, quae parum proficeret in quaerendis huiusmodi regulis, & a reliquis operibus sibi & aliis necessariis, turbaretur, quod onerosum esset, tam singulis quam communi. Adinuentae vero & examinatae huiusmodi regulae diligenter futurae legis approbandae vel reprobandae in vniuersitate ciuium congregata proponi debent. Vt si cui ciuium videatur quicquam ipsis addendum, aut minuendum, mutandum, aut totaliter spernendum, id dicere possit, quoniam ex hoc poterit lex vtilius ordinari. Possunt enim, vt iam diximus, ciues minus docti quandoque percipere aliquid corrigendum circa propositam legem, qui tamen ipsam inuenire nescirent. Et quoniam sic latae per auditum & consensum vniuersae multitudinis, melius obseruabuntur, nec aduersus eas habebit aliquis reclamare. Publicatis autem iam dictis regulis; futuris legibus, & in vniuersali ciuium congregatione, anditisque ciuibus, qui aliqua circa ipsas rationabiliter dicere voluerunt, eligi debent tursum viri, quales & secundum quem modum praediximus, vel confirmati praedicti, qui vicem & auctoritatem vniuersitatis ciuium repraesentantes, supradictas quaestas & propositas regulas, approbabunt vel reprobabunt in toto vel parte, aut faciet idem si voluerit, vniuersitas ciuium tota simul vel ipsius valentior pars. Postquam siquidem approbationem iam dictae regulae leges sunt, & sic nominari merentur, non antea, quae etiam post ipsarum publicationem seu proclamationem solae humanorum praeceptorum obligat transgressores ad ciuilem culpam & poenam. Quod quidem igitur legumlationis seu institutionis auctoritas, & de ipsarum observatione coactiuum dare praeceptum, ad solam ciuium vniuersitatem, seu ipsius valentiorem partem, tanquam efficientem causam pertineat, aut ad illum vel illos, cui vel quibus auctoritatem hanc concesseris iam dicta vniuersitas, sufficienter ex dictis monstrasse putamus.
units.tr: Someone may doubt what we have said, arguing that the authority to make or establish laws does not belong to the whole body of citizens. First, because a perverse and indiscreet majority ought not to make laws. Two faults must be kept away from the lawgiver, namely malice and ignorance, which is why we have learned, in the eleventh chapter of this work, that the law is needed to avoid them even in judgments. But the people, or the body of citizens, is of this kind: men, as is seen in most cases, are perverse and foolish, for "the number of fools is infinite," as Ecclesiastes 1 says. Further, it is very difficult or impossible for a great number of perverse and senseless men to agree in their opinions, which does not happen with a few studious men. It is therefore more useful for a law to be made by a few than by the whole body of citizens and their superfluous multitude. Again, in every civil community there are few wise and learned men compared with the other, unlearned multitude. Since a law is made more usefully by the wise and learned than by the unlearned and rude, it seems that the authority to make laws belongs to a few, not to many or to all. Moreover, what can be done by a few is done in vain by many. Therefore, since a law can be made by the wise (who are few), as has been said, it would be in vain for the whole multitude, or its greater part, to be occupied with this. So the authority to make laws does not belong to the whole body or to its stronger part. We have proved in the earlier part of this book, as a principle for all that is to be demonstrated here, that all men desire a sufficiency of life and shun its opposite. In the fourth chapter we concluded, by demonstration, that civil community serves this purpose, since through it men can attain this sufficiency and not otherwise. For this reason Aristotle also says in the first chapter of the first book of the Politics: "Nature indeed gives every man an impulse toward such a community, namely the civil one." From this truth there follows of necessity something else, which is found in the fourth book of the Politics, chapter 10: that the stronger part of the city must wish the polity to remain, whether the others wish it or not. For nothing is desired by the same nature, in its species, according to its majority and immediately, except together with its corruption; such a desire would be empty. Indeed, those who do not wish the polity to remain are counted among slaves, not among citizens, as are certain foreigners. Hence in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter 12: "Since all who wish to live insolently are subjects, who are there in the region..." And then he adds that for these people to be in the polity in such numbers (namely insolent men, or men who do not care to live as citizens) that they outnumber all the others (namely those who wish to live politically) is one of the impossibilities. Why it is impossible is clear: it would mean that nature, for the most part, fails or sins. If therefore the stronger multitude of men wishes the polity to remain, as seems rightly said, it also wishes that without which the polity cannot remain. This is the rule of just and useful things, delivered together with a command, and called law; for it is impossible for a city governed as an aristocracy (that is, governed according to virtue) not to be well ordered by laws, as is found in the fourth book of the Politics, chapter 7, and as we have demonstrated in the eleventh chapter. Therefore the stronger multitude of the city wishes a law. Otherwise there would be a failure in nature and in art, for the most part, which is contrary to natural knowledge. I take up again, along with the truths stated above, a common notion of the mind, namely that every whole is greater than its part. This is true both in magnitude or quantity and also in active power and action. Hence it follows quite clearly and necessarily that the body of citizens, or its stronger multitude (which are to be taken as the same), is better able to discern what is to be chosen and what is to be rejected than any part of it taken separately. With these premises, taken as undoubted truths, it is easy to repel the objections by which someone might try to prove that the making of laws does not belong to the body of citizens or its stronger multitude, but to a few. So when it was said first that the authority to make laws does not belong to what is indiscreet in the first place and in most cases, we grant it. But when it is added that the body of citizens is of this kind, this must be denied. For the plurality of citizens is neither perverse nor indiscreet, as regards the number of its members and at any given time; for all, or most, are sound of mind and reason, and have a right desire for the polity and for what is necessary for its permanence, such as laws and other statutes or customs, as was shown before. For although not every citizen, nor the greater multitude of citizens, is the inventor of laws, yet anyone can judge of what has been invented and proposed to him by another, and discern what should be added, diminished, or changed. Therefore, if what is called indiscreet in the major premise is understood to mean that a multitude which cannot by itself invent a law, in most of its parts or subjects, ought not to make laws, that premise must be rejected as manifestly false. Witness the induction drawn from experience, and Aristotle in the third book of the Politics, chapter 6. The induction is this: many people judge rightly of the quality of a house, a ship, or other artifacts, though they could not invent them. Aristotle bears witness to this in the passage cited, answering the objection just made in these words: "And since on some matters not only the maker, nor indeed the best judge, will judge..." By this he illustrates the point with many kinds of craft, and means the same to be understood of the rest. Nor does it stand in the way that is said, "the wise (who are few) are better able to discern what is to be enacted than the rest of the multitude." For even if this is true, it does not follow that the wise discern better what is to be enacted than the whole multitude, in which the wise themselves are included along with the less learned. For every whole is greater than its part, both in acting and in judging. This was also the opinion of Aristotle in the third book of the Politics, chapter 6, when he said: "Wherefore the greater multitude, which rules justly," that is, ought to rule justly over the greater things, which in the polity are the multitude or the body of citizens, or its stronger part, which he signifies by the name of multitude, giving the reason for this: "For from many comes the people, the council, the praetorium, and the honorable class; and the greater of all these, than the one who rules by one or by a few who rule in great principalities." He means that the multitude, or the people, taken together with all the collegia of the polity or civil order, is greater, and consequently its judgment is safer than the judgment of any part taken separately. Whether that part is the vulgus (the common people), which he designates here by the name of concilium, such as farmers, craftsmen and the like; or whether it is the praetorium, that is, those officials in the praetorium who serve the rulers, such as advocates or lawyers and notaries; or whether it is the honorabilitas, that is, the college of the best men, who are few and alone are fittingly chosen for the greatest principalities; or whether it is any other part of the city taken separately. Moreover, let it be granted, as is true, that some less learned men do not judge as well as the equal number of learned men about making a law or any other matter of action. Yet the number of the less learned could be increased so far that they would judge as well as, or better than, the few more learned men about these matters. Aristotle plainly said this, wishing to confirm this opinion: "If the multitude is not too base," says Aristotle, "each one will be a better judge of his own works, and all together, when they are gathered, will be better or no worse." As for what was said in Ecclesiastes 1, "the number of fools is infinite," we must say that by "fools" are meant the less learned, or those not engaged in the liberal arts, who nevertheless share in understanding and judgment about what is to be done, though not equally with those who are so engaged. Or perhaps the wise are signified there by "fools," that is, the unbelievers, as Jerome says in the same place, who, however much they know in the sciences, are simply fools, according to the Apostle's word in 1 Corinthians 3: "The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God."
