The second objection presses little, for although it is easier to agree with the opinion of a few than of many, it does not follow from this that the opinion of a few, or of the stronger part, is better than that of the whole multitude of which they are a part. For these few would not discern as well, nor would they wish the common good as much as the whole body of citizens does. Indeed, as has appeared from what has been said, it would be unsafe to entrust the making of laws to the will of a few. For they would perhaps look more to their own advantage, or that of certain persons or a college, than to the common good; which is quite evident in those who issued the Decretales of the clergy. This we shall also show sufficiently in the eighth chapter of the second book. For this opens a kind of road to oligarchy; just as, when the power of making laws is given to one alone, room is given to tyranny, as in the eleventh chapter of this work, in the fourth part, the induction from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, book 4, treatise On Justice. The third objection can easily be repelled from what has already been said. Even if laws can be made better by the wise than by the less learned, it does not follow that they are made better by the wise alone than by the whole multitude of citizens, in which the said wise are also included. Indeed, the gathered multitude of all these can discern and will more fully the just and useful common good than any one of these parts taken separately, however prudent. Hence those who say that a less learned multitude hinders the choice and approval of what is true or of the common good speak untruly; on the contrary, it helps in this, when joined to the more learned and more experienced. For although it cannot itself find out what is true and useful to enact, it can discern and judge those things that have been invented by others and proposed to it, and see whether anything should be added, diminished, or wholly changed or rejected in what is proposed. For a man comprehends many things after another's teaching, and can carry out the completion of many things to whose beginnings or invention he could not have come by himself. For the beginnings of things are most difficult to discover; hence Aristotle in the second book of the Sophistical Refutations (near the end): "It is most difficult to see the principle," namely of truth, and proper to each discipline. Once this has been discovered, it is easy to add to and enlarge the rest. For this reason, to discover the principles of the sciences, arts, and other traditions belongs only to the best and sharpest minds; but to add to what has been discovered, even men of humbler talent can do, and they ought not on that account to be called indiscreet, if they cannot of themselves discover such things. Rather they ought to be counted among the good, as Aristotle said in the first book of the Ethics, chapter 1: "He indeed is the best, who understands all things for himself. Good again is he who obeys one who advises well," namely by listening to him, and by contradicting him not without reason. And therefore it is fitting and useful that the rules for just and agreed civil matters, and for the common and advantageous things and the like, that is, the future laws or statutes, which are to be sought out or invented and examined, be entrusted by the body of citizens to prudent and experienced men. This may be done either by choosing some men separately from each of the first parts of the city, enumerated in the fifth chapter, parts, in proportion to each part; or by choosing all the experienced or prudent men mentioned above from all the citizens gathered together. This will be a fitting and useful way of making laws, without the help of the rest of the multitude, namely the less learned, who would do little good in seeking out such rules, and would be distracted from their other work, which is necessary for themselves and others, a burden both to each and to the community. Once these rules have been invented and examined, they ought to be proposed to the gathered body of citizens, so that they may be approved or rejected before the future law is made carefully. So that if it seems to any citizen that anything should be added, diminished, changed, or wholly rejected, he may say so, since in this way the law can be framed more usefully. For, as we have said, the citizens who are less learned can sometimes perceive something in the proposed law that needs correcting, though they would not have been able to invent the law itself. Laws thus made, by hearing and the consent of the whole multitude, will be better observed, and no one will have grounds to object to them. Then, when the said rules for the future laws have been published, and in a general gathering of citizens, and after the citizens who wished to say anything reasonable about them have been heard, men must again be chosen, of the kind and in the manner we have described, or men already confirmed, who represent the authority and office of the body of citizens. These men shall approve or reject the aforesaid rules, as proposed, in whole or in part; or the whole body of citizens together, or its stronger part, may do the same if it wishes. For after the aforesaid rules have been approved, they are laws, and deserve to be so called, but not before. And after their publication or proclamation, these alone bind transgressors of human precepts to civil guilt and punishment. Therefore we think we have sufficiently shown from what has been said that the authority to make laws and to establish them, and to give a coercive command for their observance, belongs to the body of citizens alone, or its stronger part, as the efficient cause; or to that one or those whom the said body of citizens has granted this authority.

units.la: CAP. XIV. De qualitatibus seu dispositionibus principantis perfecti, vt sciatur qualem oporteat esse, qui ad principatum debet assumi. Unde apparet etiam conueniens materia siue subiectum humanarum legum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. On the qualities or dispositions of the perfect ruler, so that it may be known what sort of person ought to be taken up into the principate. Whence the suitable matter or subject of human laws also becomes apparent.

units.la: Post haec autem dicere oportet de causa effectiua partis principantis, hoc autem erit ostendere per demonstrationem, cuius sit auctoritas eligendi eam, & consequenter instituendi reliquas partium ciuitatis. De non electae nanque partis principantis institutione, sufficienter dictum est nunc huius, parte quinta. Incipiemus autem primum determinando qualem esse oporteat, qui conuenienter est ad principatum eligendus seu promouendus. Ex hoc enim transibimus certius ad ipsius electionis seu institutionis auctoritatem factiuam. Sunt autem futuri principantis perfecti habitus intrinseci duo, separationem non recipientes in esse, videlicet prudentia & moralis virtus, maxime iustitia. Vnus quidem, vt ipsius in principando dirigatur intellectus, prudentia scilicet. Unde 3. politicae, cap. 2. Prudentia autem propria virtus principi sola; aliás enim videtur conueniens communes subditorum & principum. Reliquus vero habitus est, quo ipsius rectus exter affectus mor-lis, virtus scilicet aliarum maxime iustitia. Unde 4. Ethicorum tractatu de iustitia, inquit Aristoteles: Est autem princeps custos iusti. Est ergo futuro principanti prudentia necessaria, quoniam per ipsam magnifice potest in ipsius opus proprium, iudicio videlicet conferentium & iustorum ciuilium. In quibus namque humanis actibus ciuilibus, actus ipse vel modus non determinatur lege per prudentiam, dirigitur principans in iudicando & etiam exequendo, facto vel modo, aut horum vtroque in quibus ipsum peccare contingeret absque prudentia. Nam (vt in Catilinario Sallustii,) si Consul Cicero complices Catilinae, Romanos ciues atque potentes, aduersus rempublicam coniuratores, proinde mortis reos, secundum legem punisset, loco, tempore, ac modo consuetis: exorta foret inde verisimiliter ciuilis pugna politiae solutiua, propter seditionem per dictos iam coniuratores aduersus consulem & reliquos principantes in populo concitatam, tatam. Hoc siquidem periculum Cicero Consul seu principans vrbis, per suam euasit prudentiam, dum dictos reos tortoribus necandos tradidit, & praecepit in loco carceris, quem forte propterea Tullianum appellant. Sic ergo prudentia diriguntur agibilium consilia, vnde quinto ethicorum, cap. 4. dixit Aristot. Prudentiam habitum verum cum ratione actuum circa hominis bona vel mala, inquantum homo scilicet. Huius autem causa est, quoniam agibilia sunt, circa quae & de quibus plurimis sunt humanae leges, secundum quas debet principans disponere humanos actus ciuiles. Quodque non omnes aut ipsorum modos seu circumstantias quibus inuoluuntur, possibile videtur semper simul lege determinare, propter ipsorum varietatem & differentiam secundum regiones & tempora, vt aperta docet experientia, & testis est Aristoteles primo Ethicorum, cap. 1. cum dixit: Bona autem & iusta de quibus ciuilis intendit, tantam habent differentiam & errorem, vt videantur sola lege esse, non natura, id est quia sic velint homines de ipsis statuere, non quia ipsorum agibilium natura determinata sit, vt videlicet hoc quidem sit iustum, illud vero iniustum. Idemque etiam exprimens amplius 3. politicae, cap. 9. cum dixit: Sed quoniam hac quidem comprehendi legibus contingit, hac autem impossibilia, haec sunt quae faciunt dubitare & quaerere, virum optimam legem eligibilius praeoperari, quam optimum virum: de quibus enim conciliantur (homines scilicet) sunt impossibilium lege statuta esse (omnia supple.) Haec propter oportuit quaedam euenientium in ciuilibus actibus hominum, arbitrio principantium iudicanda committere, quae scilicet secundum se aut modum aliquem sui seu circumstantiam lege determinata non sunt. Nam in his quae lege determinata fuerunt, debitum est principantem sequi legalem determinationem. Et fuit haec Aristotelis sententia 3. politicae, cap. 6. cum dixit: Principem autem, sive vnum sive plures, de his esse dominos, de quibus leges non possunt dicere tertiatim aliter, propterea quod non facile sit determinare de omnibus, quam sententiam replicans 9. eiusdem, inquit: Sunt autem & nunc de quibusdam principatum, dominantes iudicio sicut index, de quibus lex non potest determinare, quoniam de quo potuis, nullum dubitat de his tanquam non vtique optime lex praecipit. Est ergo necessaria principanti prudentia propter talia iudicanda, quae lege determinari non possunt. Hanc siquidem sententiam Aristot. quasi propinquam rebus manifestis per se, certificare potest per demonstrationem, cui eura fuerit per ea quae dicta sunt 2. huius. Est rursum moralis bonitas, virtutis scilicet, earum vero maxime iustitia, principanti necessaria, nam si pertusus fuerit secundum morem, multum laeditur ex eo politis quantumcunque formata legibus. Iam enim diximus, non facile aut non possibile, simul omnia determinare legibus, sed aliqua committi oportere principantis arbitrio, in quibus laedere potest politiam, si fuerit affectionis peruersae. Et haec fuit Aristotelis sententia 2. politicae 8. ca. cum dixit: Magnorum enim dominus constituti, si viles fuerint (id est, more prauî) multum ledunt, & lesuerunt iam ciuitatem Chalcedoniorum. Et quoniam ab hoc praeseruantur per moris virtutem, maxime iustitiam, Idepq; conueniens est si necessaria conueniens dicere liceat, neminem futurum principari carere morali virtute, aliorum vero maxime iustitia. Cui siquidem etiam in principante futuro conueniens est, assequi virtutem quandam, vocatam epieikeiam, qua dirigitur iudex, praecipue secundum affectum, in quibus lex deficit. Vnde Arist. 4. ethicorum, tractatu de iustitia, inquit: Et hoc natura est, quae epieikes directio legis, vbi deficit propter particulare. Quam aestimo, iuristae volunt aequitatem dicere. Est enim haec benigna legis quaedam interpretatio vel moderatio in aliquo casu, quem lex sub rigoris vniuersalitate comprehendit, in quo pro tanto lex deficere dicitur, quia ipsum a regula non excepit, quem tamen si sic futurum attenderet ab vniuersalitate regulae cum aliquo moderamine, vel simpliciter excepisset. Adhuc etiam cum his singularis quidam amor seu beneuolentia futuri principantis, ad politiam & ciues exigitur. Ex hoc nanque principantis actiones ad commune ac singulorum conferens intendunt ur in sollicitudine & bonitate.
units.tr: After these things we must speak of the efficient cause of the ruling part. This will mean showing, by demonstration, whose authority it is to choose it and, consequently, to institute the remaining parts of the state. Concerning the institution of a ruling part that has not yet been chosen, enough has been said now in part five of this work. We shall begin by determining what sort of person ought fittingly to be chosen or promoted to the principate, for from this we shall pass more surely to the authority that makes the choice or institution. The future perfect ruler has two intrinsic habits, which cannot be separated in existence: prudence and moral virtue, above all justice. The first is prudence, by which his intellect is directed in ruling. Whence in the third book of the Politics, chapter 2: Prudence is the proper virtue of the ruler alone; otherwise it would seem that the virtues of subjects and rulers are the same. The other habit is that by which his appetite is rightly disposed in moral matters, namely virtue, and above all justice among the virtues. Whence in the fourth book of the Ethics, in the treatise on justice, Aristotle says: The ruler is the guardian of the just. Prudence is therefore necessary for the future ruler, since through it he can rightly perform his proper work, namely judging between parties and what is just in civil matters. In those civil human acts in which the act itself, or its manner, is not determined by law, the ruler is directed by prudence in judging and also in executing, as to the deed or the manner, or both, in which he could otherwise go wrong without prudence. For (as in Sallust's Catiline) if the consul Cicero had punished the accomplices of Catiline, Roman citizens and powerful men, conspirators against the state and therefore liable to death, according to law, in the usual place, time and manner, a civil war and the dissolution of the commonwealth would probably have arisen, because of the sedition stirred up among the people by those conspirators against the consul and the other rulers. The consul Cicero, ruler of the city, escaped this danger through his prudence, when he handed the accused over to the executioners to be killed, and ordered it done in the prison place which, for that reason, they call the Tullianum. Thus prudence directs the counsels of things to be done. Whence in the fifth book of the Ethics, chapter 4, Aristotle said: prudence is a true habit, with reason, of acts concerning human goods or evils, insofar as one is a man. The reason is that there are things to be done, concerning which and about which there are many human laws, according to which the ruler ought to order men's civil acts. And since it does not seem possible always to determine all of these acts, or the modes and circumstances in which they are involved, at once by law, on account of their variety and difference according to regions and times, as experience plainly teaches, Aristotle bears witness in the first book of the Ethics, chapter 1, when he said: Good and just things, with which civil science is concerned, have such difference and variation that they seem to exist by law alone and not by nature; that is, because men wish to decide about them in this way, not because the nature of the acts themselves is fixed, so that this is just and that unjust. Expressing the same thing more fully in the third book of the Politics, chapter 9, he said: But since some things can be comprehended by laws and others cannot, these are the things that make men doubt and inquire whether the best law or the best man is preferable to be set up; for the things about which men deliberate are those that cannot be fixed by law (all of them, supply). It was therefore necessary to commit to the judgment of rulers certain matters arising in men's civil acts, namely those which are not determined by law either in themselves or in some mode or circumstance. For in matters that have been determined by law, the ruler must follow the legal determination. This was Aristotle's opinion in the third book of the Politics, chapter 6, when he said: The ruler, whether one or several, should be lord over those matters about which the laws cannot speak rightly otherwise, because it is not easy to determine about everything. Repeating this opinion in the ninth book of the same work, he says: There are also now rulers who govern by judgment, like a judge, in matters on which the law cannot determine; for no one doubts what can be determined by law, since the law commands in the best way. Prudence is therefore necessary for the ruler in judging such things as cannot be determined by law. Aristotle's opinion, being close to things manifest in themselves, can indeed be made certain by demonstration, to which attention will be given through what has been said in the second part of this work. Again, moral goodness, namely virtue, and above all justice, is necessary for the ruler. For if he is perverse in his morals, the commonwealth is greatly harmed by him, however well it is formed by laws. For we have already said that it is not easy or possible to determine everything by laws at once, but some matters must be left to the ruler's discretion, and in these he can harm the commonwealth if his disposition is perverse. This was Aristotle's opinion in the second book of the Politics, chapter 8, when he said: For the holders of great offices, if they are base (that is, of bad morals), do great harm, and have already harmed the city of the Chalcedonians. Since the ruler is preserved from this by the virtue of good morals, above all justice, it is fitting, if one may say what is necessary, that no one who is to rule should lack moral virtue, and above all justice among the others. It is also fitting for the future ruler to attain a certain virtue called epieikeia, by which a judge is directed, especially in matters where the law is deficient. Whence Aristotle, in the fourth book of the Ethics, in the treatise on justice, says: And this is by nature, which is the correction of the law where it is deficient because of its particularity. This, I think, the jurists want to call equity. For it is a kind of gentle interpretation or moderation of the law in some case, which the law comprehends under the rigor of its universality. In such a case the law is said to be deficient, because it did not except that case from the rule; yet if the lawgiver had foreseen it, he would either have excepted it from the universality of the rule with some moderation, or simply excepted it. Along with these, a certain singular love or benevolence of the future ruler toward the commonwealth and the citizens is also required. For from this the ruler's actions, directed to the common good and to that of individuals, are carried out with care and goodness.

units.la: Praeter hos autem dictos habitus & dispositiones necessarium est principanti extrinsecum organum quoddam, armatorum videlicet numerus certus, quo suas ciuiles sententias in rebelles & inobedientes per coactiuam potentiam exequi possit. Vnde Arist. 7. politicae cap. 6. Communicantes autem (ciuiliter, supple) necessarium est ipsis habere arma (id est, armatorum multitudinem aliquam) ad principatum inobedientium gratia (id est ad arcendos inobedientes principatibus,) aliter enim leges atque ciuiles sententiae ociosae forent, nisi earum executio posset expleri. Debet autem haec armata potentia principantis determinari per legis latorem, veluti ciuilia reliqua: tanta siquidem vt vniuscuiusque ciuis seorsum aut aliquorum simul excedat potestatem, non tamen eam quae simul omnium aut maioris partis, ne principantem praesumere aut posse contingat violare leges, & praeter, aut contra ipsas despotice principari. Vnde Aristot. 3. politicae, ca. 9. Oportet enim ipsum quidem habere potentiam tantam, vt sit ea quae singulorum, & vnius & simul plurium maior, ea autem quae multitudinis minor. Oportet autem simul plurium intelligere non comparatiue, id est maiorem partem, sed plurium positiue, secundum quod a pluralitate deriuatur, id est a multitudine aliqua, non tamen valentiori ciuium parte. Si enim non sic intelligatur, repugnantia esset in dictis ipsius. Hanc vero coactiuam potestatem, futurum principari, aut ipsius ad principatum electionem, non necessarium est habere, quemadmodum reliquas sui dispositiones intrinsecas, de quibus iam diximus pridem. Sic enim ad principatum nunquam assumerentur studiosi pauperes. Cuius oppositum voluit Aristoteles idem 2. politicae, cap. 8. dum dixit: A principio autem hoc videre est necessariorum, qualiter optimi possint vacare, & nihil dehonestari, non solum principes, sed neque singulariter viuentes. Veruntamen vt quae de principantium dispositionibus, ac reliquis sibi necessariis ad capitulum reducantur, dicamus, quod prudentia & moralis virtus necessariae sunt futuro in principantem eligendo ante ipsius electionem. Armata vero potentia necessaria est principanti, maximum principatum ciuitatis aut regni, tanquam instrumentum seu extrinsecum organum, quo ipsius secundum leges expleantur sententiae, non tamen hanc oportet habere ante ipsius electionem, sed illi simul cum principatu conferre. Amor autem seu benevolentia singularis ad politiam & cives, in suarum actionum ciuilium bonitatem & solicitudinem addit, licet no aequa necessitate cum praedictis exigatur in ipso.
units.tr: Besides these habits and dispositions, the ruler needs an external instrument, namely a certain number of armed men, by which he can enforce his civil sentences against rebels and the disobedient by coercive power. Whence Aristotle, in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter 6: Those who share in the constitution (civilly, supply) must have arms (that is, some multitude of armed men) for the sake of the rulers, that is, to restrain the disobedient to the rulers; otherwise laws and civil sentences would be idle, unless their execution could be carried out. This armed power of the ruler must be determined by the lawgiver, like the other civil matters: so that it exceeds the power of each citizen separately, or of some together, but not that of all or of the greater part together, lest the ruler presume, or happen, to violate the laws and to rule despotically beyond or against them. Whence Aristotle, in the third book of the Politics, chapter 9: For the ruler must have such power that it is greater than that of each single person, or of one and several together, but less than that of the multitude. The phrase "of several together" must be understood not comparatively, that is, as the greater part, but positively, according to what derives from plurality, that is, from some multitude, yet not from the stronger part of the citizens. For if it were not so understood, there would be a contradiction in what he says. But it is not necessary for the future ruler to possess this coercive power, or for it to be a condition of his election to the principate, as it is with the other intrinsic dispositions of which we have spoken before. For in this way poor but studious men would never be taken up into the principate. Aristotle wished the opposite, in the same second book of the Politics, chapter 8, when he said: From the beginning it can be seen what things are necessary, so that the best men may have leisure, and nothing be dishonored, not only rulers but also those who live privately. But, to say what relates to the dispositions of rulers and the other things necessary for them, as they belong to this chapter: prudence and moral virtue are necessary for the future ruler before his election. Armed power, however, is necessary for the ruler of the greatest principate of a city or kingdom, as an instrument or external organ by which his sentences are carried out according to law. Yet it is not necessary to have this before his election; it is to be conferred together with the principate. Singular love or benevolence toward the commonwealth and the citizens adds goodness and care to his civil actions, although it is not required in him with the same necessity as the aforesaid qualities.

units.la: Testatur autem his Aristoteles quinto politicae, cap. 4. dum dixit: Tria autem quedam oportet habere futuros principari principales principatus, primo quidem amorem ad consistentem politiam, deinde potentiam maximorum operum principatus, tertio autem virtutem & iustitiam; per virtutem intelligens prudentiam, quae omnium vinculum est & magistra virtutum. Unde 6. ethicorum, cap. finali Simul enim prudentia vni existenti omnes inerunt. Collocauit autem Aristoteles sub eadem parte divisionis, prudentiam & moralem virtutem, propterea quod in esse non separantur, ut existimasse videtur eodem libro & cap. cum dixit: Manifestum igitur ex dictis, quoniam non possibile bonum esse principaliter sine prudentia, neque prudentem sine morali virtute. Et nominauit Aristoteles 5. politica supra dicto cap. res quas futuro principanti conuenire diximus, fortassis conuerso modo necessitati earum. Ex dictis itaque apparet subiectum proprium seu materia humanarum legum. Hoc enim est principans, cum prudentia & virtute moris, maxime iustitia, praeparatus fuerit sufficienter. Qualis quidem igitur esse debeat futurus principans ciuitatis aut regni, quae etiam sibi necessaria sint & conuenientia, determinatum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: Aristotle bears witness to these things in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 4, when he said: "There are three things that those who are to rule as principal rulers of the principality must have: first, indeed, love of the existing polity; second, the power for the greatest works of the principality; third, virtue and justice." By virtue he means prudence, which is the bond of all things and the mistress of the virtues. Hence in the sixth book of the Ethics, in the last chapter: "For prudence is present in all at once to the one who has it." Aristotle placed prudence and moral virtue under the same heading of division, because they are not separated in being, as he seems to have thought in the same book and chapter, when he said: "It is therefore manifest from what has been said that it is not possible to have good principally without prudence, nor a prudent person without moral virtue." In the fifth book of the Politics, in the chapter cited above, Aristotle named the qualities that we said belong to the future ruler, perhaps reversing the order of their necessity. From what has been said, then, the proper subject, or matter, of human laws becomes clear. For the ruler is the one who has been sufficiently prepared with prudence and the virtue of character, above all justice. What the future ruler of a state or kingdom ought to be, and what qualities are also necessary and fitting for him, has been determined in this way.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: De causa factiua potioris institutionis principatus, unde apparet etiam effectiua causa reliquarum partium ciuitatis.
units.tr: On the efficient cause of the best institution of a ruler, from which the efficient cause of the other parts of the state also becomes clear.

units.la: Consequenter autem dictis restat ostendere principantis factiuam causam, per quam videlicet alicui vel aliquibus datur auctoritas principatus, qui per electionem statuitur. Haec enim auctoritate fit princeps secundum actum, non per legum scientiam, prudentiam, aut moralem virtutem, licet sint haec qualitates principantis perfecti. Contingit enim has, multos habere, qui tamen hac auctoritate carentes, non sunt principes nisi forte propinqua potentia. Adquaesitum ergo redeuntes, dicamus secundum veritatem & sententiam Aristotelis tertio politica cap. 6. Potestatem factiuam institutionis principatus seu electionis ipsius ad legislatorem seu ciuium universitatem, quemadmodum ad eandem legislationem diximus pertinere. 12. huius, principatus quoque correptionem quamlibet etiam depositionem, si expediens fuerit propter commune conferens eidem similiter conuenire. Nam hoc est unum de maioribus in politia, quae ad multitudinem ciuium universam ex dictis Arist. 3. politicae cap. 6. pertinere conclusimus 13. huius, parte. 4. Est enim multitudo dominans maior, ut dicebatur ibidem. Modus autem conueniendi ad institutionem seu electionem praedictam variatur fortasse secundum prouinciarum varietatem. Verum qualitercumque diuersetur, hoc in quolibet obseruandum, ut talis electio seu institutio semper fiat auctoritate legislatoris, quam ciuium universitatem aut eius valentiorem partem persepe diximus. Potest autem & debet conuinci propositum hoc eisdem demonstrationibus, quibus legum lationem, mutationem, & reliqua circa ipsas, ad ciuium universitatem pertinere conclusimus 12. huius. Sola tamen harum demonstrationum minori extremitate mutata, ut videlicet pro termino qui lex dicitur sumatur terminus principantis. Est autem & hoc cum sua veritate probabile valde, si necessariam probabile liceat dicere. Cuius enim est generare formam aliquam, ipsius est determinare subiectum illius, ut in omnibus artibus operatiuis videre est. Unde & Aristoteles. 2. physic. cap. 4. Eiusdem autem scientia est cognoscere speciem & materiam, usque ad hoc, ut medici sanitatem, & coloram, & phlegma, in quibus est sanitas. Similiter autem aedificatoris est speciem domus, & materiam, quoniam lateres & ligna. Sic quoq; in reliquis artificialibus & naturalibus apparet hoc inductione manifesta. Cuius quidem causa est, quoniam formae cum suis operationibus sunt fines & cuius causa materiae sunt aut fiunt, ut eodem libro & cap. dictum est. Cum igitur ad ciuium universitatem pertineat generare formam, secundum quam ciuiles actiones regulari debent, legem scilicet, eiusdem universitatis esse videbitur huius formae determinare materiam seu subiectum. Cuius secundum hanc formam est disponere ciuiles hominum actus, partem scilicet principantem. Et quoniam haec est formarum optima ciuilis communitatis, debet illi determinari subiectum optimum secundum dispositiones, quod etiam in praecedente capitulo probabili ratione conclusimus. Unde conuenienter inferri posse videtur. Electum principantem & absque generis successione, simpliciter non electis, aut his qui cum generis successione statuantur, politiae praestantiori modo praeferri. Huius ergo partis efficiente monstrato, habitum est dicere secundum propositia frequenter a nobis, causam effectiuam, instituentem & determinantem reliqua officiorum seu partium ciuitatis. Hanc autem primam diximus legislatorem, secundariam vero quasi instrumentalem seu executiuam dicimus principantem per auctoritatem huius a legislatore sibi concessam, secundum formam sibi traditam ab eodem legem videlicet, secundum quam semper agere ac disponere debet quantum potest, actus ciuiles, quemadmodum ostensum est cap. precedente. Quamuis enim legislator, tanquam prima causa & appropriata determinare debeat quos, qualia in ciuitate oporteat officia exercere, talium tamen executionem, sicut & caeterorum legalium praecipit, & si oporteat cohibet pars principans. Fit enim per ipsum conuenientius executio legalium quam per vniuersam ciuium multitudinem, quoniam in hoc sufficit vnus aut pauci principantes, in quo frustra occuparetur vniuersa communitas, quae etiam ab aliis operibus necessariis turbaretur. Nam & hoc facientibus his, id facit communitas vniuersa, quoniam secundum communitatis determinationem, legalem scilicet, id faciunt principantes, qui etiam pauci aut vnicus existentes legalia facilius exequuntur. Fuit autem in hoc humana solicitudo conuenienter imitata naturam. Quia enim ciuitas & ipsius partes secundum rationem institutae, analogiam habent animali & suis partibus, perfecte formatis secundum naturam, vt apparet ex Aristotele primo & quinto politica, 2. cap. Qualis igitur est naturae actio in animali perfecte formando, proportionata fuit ea quae humanae mentis ad ciuitatem & ipsius partes instituendas conuenienter. Ad quam siquidem describendam proportionem, ex qua patebit amplius efficientia & determinatio partium ciuitatis, Suscipiemus cum Aristotele in 16. de animalibus. Et a Galieno in suo quodam libro, quem vocauit de exgenia, cum reliquis quoque magis expertis posteriorum, a principio quodam seu causa mouente aliqua sit illud forma materiae aut separata, vel alterum quiddam, virtutem habens generatiuam animalis & partium eius, formari primum tempore atque natura partem quandam organicam animalis, & in ipsa virtutem seu potentiam naturalem cum calore aliquo tanquam actiuo principio, virtutem inquam & calorem vniuersales actiua causalitate, ad formandum & distinguendum vnamquamque reliquarum partium animalis. Et est pars ista primum formata, cor autem cordi proportionalis aliqua, sicut dixit Aristoteles vbi supra, & reliqui philosophorum peritiores, quibus credere oportet propter ipsorum experientiam in hoc, & absque probatione supponere nunc, quoniam id demonstrare non est praesentis inquisitionis. Haec siquidem pars, formata primum, nobilior est & perfectior in suis qualitatibus & dispositionibus caeteris partibus animalis. Statuit enim in ea natura generans virtutem & instrumentum, per quae partes animalis reliquae formantur, ex conuenienti materia, separantur, distinguuntur, & inuicem ordinantur, in suis dispositionibus conseruantur, & a nocumento quantum natura patitur praeseruantur per ipsam: lapsae vero a sui natura propter aegritudinem aut alterum impedimentum, huius partis virtute reparantur.
units.tr: Having said these things, it remains to show the efficient cause of the ruler, namely, through what authority one person or several are given the power of rule, which is established by election. For a ruler becomes such in actuality by this authority, not by knowledge of the laws, by prudence, or by moral virtue, although these are qualities of a perfect ruler. For many may possess these qualities, yet lacking this authority they are not rulers, unless perhaps they have power close at hand. Returning to the question, then, let us say, according to the truth and the opinion of Aristotle in the third book of the Politics, chapter 6, that the power of instituting the ruler, or of electing him, belongs to the lawgiver or to the whole body of citizens, just as we said that the making of laws belongs to the same (12 of this book). Likewise, it is fitting that the correction of the ruler, even his deposition, if it is expedient for the common good, belongs to the same power. For this is one of the greatest matters in the polity, which we concluded, from what Aristotle said in the third book of the Politics, chapter 6, belongs to the whole multitude of citizens (13 of this book, part 4). For the multitude is the greater ruling power, as was said there. The manner of coming together for the aforesaid institution or election perhaps varies according to the variety of provinces. However it differs, this must be observed in every case: such election or institution must always be made by the authority of the lawgiver, which we have often said is the whole body of citizens or its more powerful part. This proposition can and must be proved by the same demonstrations by which we concluded that the enactment, the amendment, and the other matters concerning laws belong to the whole body of citizens (12 of this book). Only the minor term of these demonstrations is changed, so that the term "ruler" is taken in place of the term "law." This too is very probable in its own truth, if it is permitted to call a necessary thing probable. For whoever has the power to generate a certain form also has the power to determine its subject, as can be seen in all productive arts. Hence Aristotle also says, in the second book of the Physics, chapter 4: "It belongs to the same science to know the species and the matter, as the physician knows health, and the humours, and phlegm, in which health resides. Similarly, the business of the builder is the form of the house and its matter, namely bricks and timber." So too in the other artificial and natural things this appears from clear induction. The reason for this is that forms, together with their operations, are the ends and the causes of matter, or come into being for its sake, as was said in the same book and chapter. Since, then, it belongs to the whole body of citizens to generate the form according to which civil actions must be regulated, namely the law, it will seem to belong to that same body to determine the matter or subject of this form. Its function, according to this form, is to arrange the civil acts of men, namely the ruling part. And since this is the best form of a civil community, the best subject must be assigned to it according to its dispositions, which we also concluded by probable reasoning in the preceding chapter. Hence it seems fitting to infer that the ruler who is elected, and not the one who is established without succession by birth, or simply not elected, or those who are set up with hereditary succession, ought to be preferred in the better kind of polity. Having shown the efficient cause of this part, it has been established, as we have often said, that the efficient cause which institutes and determines the other offices or parts of the state is the first, and we call this the lawgiver. The second, which is as it were instrumental or executive, we call the ruler, who acts by the authority granted to him by the lawgiver, according to the form handed down to him by the same lawgiver, namely the law, by which he must always act and order civil actions as far as he can, as was shown in the preceding chapter. For although the lawgiver, as the first and principal cause, ought to determine who should exercise which offices in the state and of what kind, the ruling part both carries out the execution of these offices, as it does of the other legal matters, and restrains them where necessary. For the execution of legal matters is carried out more suitably by the ruler than by the whole multitude of citizens, since one or a few rulers are sufficient for this, whereas the whole community would be occupied in vain with it and would also be thrown into disorder from its other necessary works. For when these rulers act, the whole community also acts, since the rulers, who are few or even one, carry out the laws more easily, in accordance with the determination of the community, namely the law. Now in this matter human care has fittingly imitated nature. For since the state and its parts, according to the rational plan of their institution, bear an analogy to an animal and its parts, which are perfectly formed according to nature, as appears from Aristotle in the first and fifth books of the Politics, chapter 2, the action of nature in perfectly forming an animal was proportionate to the action of the human mind in appropriately instituting the state and its parts. To describe this proportion, from which the efficiency and determination of the parts of the state will become clearer, we shall follow Aristotle in the sixteenth book On Animals, and Galen in a certain book which he called On Semen, together with the other more experienced writers after them. They hold that from some first moving principle or cause, whether this is a separate form or some other thing having the generative power of an animal and its parts, there is first formed, in time and in nature, a certain organic part of the animal. In this part there is a natural power or faculty, together with some heat as an active principle, namely a power and heat which act universally as an active cause to form and distinguish each of the remaining parts of the animal. This part, formed first, is the heart, or something proportional to the heart, as Aristotle said in the passage above, and as the more skilled of the philosophers said, whom we must believe because of their experience in this matter, and whom we now take as given without proof, since to demonstrate this is not the purpose of the present inquiry. This part, formed first, is indeed nobler and more perfect in its qualities and dispositions than the other parts of the animal. For nature has placed in it the generating power and the instrument by which the remaining parts of the animal are formed from suitable matter, separated, distinguished, and ordered among one another, kept in their dispositions, and protected from harm as far as nature allows. And if they fall away from their nature through sickness or some other impediment, they are restored by the power of this part.

units.la: His autem proportionaliter contemplandum in ciuitate conuenienter instituta secundum rationem. Nam ab anima vniuersitatis ciuium aut eius valentioris partis formatur aut formari debet in ea pars vna primum proportionata cordi, in qua siquidem virtutem quandam seu formam statuit cum actiua potentia seu auctoritate instituendi partes reliquas ciuitatis. Haec autem pars est principatus, cuius quidem virtus causalitate vniuersalis lex est, & cuius actiua potentia est autoritas iudicandi, praecipiendi, & exequendi sententias conferentium & iustorum ciuilium, propter quod dixit Aristoteles septimo politicae ca. 6. hanc esse omnium aliarum necessariissimam in ciuitate, causa vero eius est, quoniam sufficientia quae habetur per reliquas partes seu officia ciuitatis, si non existerent, posset aliunde sufficienter haberi, licet non sit faciliter, vt per nam vigilum & reliqua vectigalia. Sed sine principatus inexistentia ciuilis communitas manere, aut diu manere non potest, quoniam necesse est vt scandala veniant, vt dicitur in Matthaeo. Haec autem sunt contentiones propter iniurias hominum inuicem, quae non iudicatae aut mensuratae per iustorum regulam, legem videlicet, & per principantem, cuius est secundum illa talia mensurare, contingeret inde congregatorum hominum pugna & separatio, & demum corruptio ciuitatis & priuatio sufficientis vitae. Debet etiam pars hic in ciuitate nobilior atque perfectior esse in suis dispositionibus, prudentia scilicet atque virtute, modis caeteris partibus ciuitatis. Unde 7. politicae, cap. 12. dixit Aristoteles: Si tantum fuerint differentes alteri ab altera quantum deos & heroes exterminamus ab hominibus differre, confestim primo secundum corpus multam habentes excellentiam, deinde secundum animam, vt indubitata & manifesta sit excellentia principantium respectu subiectorum, palam quidem, quia melius per tosdem, hos quidem principari, hos autem subiici secundum semel, id est secundum virtutem. Statuit etiam principium factiuum ciuitatis, anima videlicet vniuersitatis in hac prima parte virtutem quandam causalitate vniuersalem, legem scilicet, autoritatem quoque seu potestatem agendi & exequendi de his non aliter. Quoniam sicut caliditas innata ipsius cordis tanquam subiecti, per quam cor seu forma eius omnes actiones complet, dirigitur, & mensuratur in agendo per formam cordis seu virtutem, nec aliter ageret ad debitum finem. Ad huc etiam sicut calor, quam spiritum dicunt, tanquam instrumentum ad complendas actiones, per totum corpus ab eadem virtute regitur, nec aliter horum calorum alterutrum ageret ad debitum finem, quoniam deterius agit ignis quam organa, vt in secundo peri generatione & de anima. Sic quoque autoritas principandi alicui hominum data caliditati cordis tanquam subiecti proportionata. Sic etiam ipsius armata seu coactiva potestas instrumentalis, calori quem spiritum diximus, proportionalis, debet regulari per legem in iudicando, praecipiendo, & exequendo de iustis & conferentibus ciuilibus, aliter enim non ageret principas ad debitum finem, conseruationem scilicet ciuitatis, quemadmodum demonstratum est vndecimo huius. Ad huc autem secundum iam dictam virtutem, legem scilicet, autoritatemque sibi datam distinguere debet principans atque statuere partes officia ciuitatis ex conuenienti materia hominibus siquidem habentibus artes (seu habitus ad officia conuenientes. Sunt enim talcs propinqua materia partium ciuitatis, quemadmodum dictum est septimo huius. Est enim haec norma seu lex politiarum bene institutarum, homines statuere ad officia ciuitatis, habentes habitus operatiuos conuenientes ad illa non habentes vero verbi gratia, iuuenes, ad illos ordinare discendos, in quos magis naturaliter inclinantur. Et haec fuit sententia eximii Arist. in hoc vbi primo Ethicorum, cap. primo dixit: Quas enim esse debitum est disciplinarum in ciuitatibus, & quales vnumquemque addiscere, & vsque quo his praerdinat, politica scilicet seu legislatiua prudentia, & consequenter qui secundum legem politiam disponit, principans scilicet. Hoc etiam dixit 7. politicae, cap. 13. Ad omnia quidem igitur, inquit, aspicienti politico leges ferendum, & secum dum partes animae, & secundum passiones ipsarum. Idem quoque 8. eiusdem, cap. 2. dum dixit: Quod quidem igitur legislatorinegociandum circa viuentium disciplinam, nullus vtique dubitabit. Etenim ... hoc, ladet politias. Ex praedictis igitur apparet, ad legislatorem, pertinere determinationem seu institutionem officiorum & partium ciuitatis, eiusque determinationis iudicium, praeceptum & executionem ad principantem secundum legem spectare. Posset autem ... demonstrationibus, quibus ad legumlatorem & principantis institutio- ... huius, & supra. Syllogismorum sola minori extremitate mutata. Propter quod ... est alicui pro libito, sibi assumere officium in ciuitate, maxime aduenis. Non enim debet nec rationabiliter potest pro voto, quilibet se conuertere ad militare vel sacerdotium exercendum. neque debet hoc permittere principans, nam ex hoc contingeret insufficientia ciuitatis eorum, quae per alia officia procurari necesse est. Verum ad talia debet principans determinare personas, partium quoq; seu officiorum ipsorum, quantitatem & qualitatem secundum numerum & potentiam & huiusmodi reliqua, ne propter ipsorum excessum inuicem immoderatum, contingat politiam solui, propter quod quinto politicae c. 2. dixit Arist. Fiunt autem & propter excrescentiam quae pratis proportionem ... politiarum. Sicut enim ex partibus corpus componitur, & oportet augeri proportionaliter vt manet ... ratio. Si autem non corrumpitur. Si enim non solum secundum quantum, sed & secundum ... crescit propter proportionem. Sic & ciuitas componitur ex partibus, quarum saepe latet aliqua excrescens, velut genorum multitudo in democratiis, & sacerdotium in lege Christianorum. Idem dixit etiam tertio politicae, cap. 7. cuius omitto seriem propter abbreuiationem sermonis. Debet rursum pars haec, principans scilicet, auctoritate sua secundum legem praecipere iusta & honesta, & his contraria prohibere, tam opere quam sermone, praemiis aut poenis afficiendo merita vel demerita, obseruantium aut transgredientium praecepta legalia. Quomodo conseruabit se esse debito vnamquamq; partium ciuitatis, & a nocumentis ac iniuriis praeseruabit, quod si partium aliquis agat iniuriam ipsarum aliqua curari debet per principantis actionem, inferens quidem iniuriam, sustinendo poenam. Est enim poena sicut medicina quaedam delicti. Vnde 2. Ethi. ca.
units.tr: In the same way, this must be considered proportionally in a city rightly instituted according to reason. For from the soul of the whole body of citizens, or of its more powerful part, there is formed, or ought to be formed, first one part proportionate to the heart. In this part he places a certain virtue or form, together with the active power or authority of instituting the remaining parts of the city. This part is the principate, whose virtue, as a universal cause, is law, and whose active power is the authority of judging, commanding, and executing the rulings in the disputes of litigants and in civil cases. For this reason Aristotle said in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter 6, that this is the most necessary of all the other parts in the city. Its cause is this: the sufficiency that is had through the remaining parts or offices of the city could, if they did not exist, be had sufficiently from elsewhere, though not easily, as through the night watch and the other taxes. But without the existence of a principate, a civil community cannot remain, or cannot remain long, since, as it is said in Matthew, offences must come. These are the quarrels over the injuries men do one another, which, if they are not judged or measured by the rule of the just, namely the law, and by the ruler, whose task it is to measure such matters according to that law, would lead to fighting and division among the gathered men, and finally to the corruption of the city and the loss of a sufficient life. This part in the city must also be nobler and more perfect in its dispositions than the other parts of the city, namely in prudence and virtue. Hence in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter 12, Aristotle said: "If they differed from one another as much as we say gods and heroes differ from men, first of all in bodily excellence, then in soul, so that the excellence of the rulers over the subjects is undoubted and manifest, it is plain that it is better that some rule and others be ruled according to the one thing, that is, according to virtue." The principate of the city, that is, the soul of the whole body, also establishes in this first part a certain virtue as a universal cause, namely law, and likewise the authority or power of acting and of executing these things, and not otherwise. For just as the innate warmth of the heart itself, as its subject, by which the heart or its form completes all its actions, is directed and measured in acting by the form or virtue of the heart, and would not otherwise act toward its due end; and again, just as the warmth, which they call spirit, as the instrument for completing actions, is ruled throughout the whole body by the same virtue, and neither of these two warmths would otherwise act toward its due end, since fire acts worse than the organs, as in the second book of On Generation and Corruption and in On the Soul; so too the authority of ruling, given to some man, must be proportionate to the warmth of the heart as its subject. Likewise the armed or coercive power, the instrumental power, which is proportional to the warmth we called spirit, must be regulated by law in judging, commanding, and executing concerning just and civil contracts; otherwise the ruler would not act toward its due end, namely the preservation of the city, as has been demonstrated in the eleventh chapter of this work. Moreover, according to the virtue already mentioned, namely the law, and the authority given to it, the ruling part must distinguish and establish the parts and offices of the city from suitable material: men, that is, who have arts, or habits suited to the offices. For such men are the proximate material of the parts of the city, as was said in the seventh book of this work. This is the rule, or law, of well-instituted polities: to appoint men to the offices of the city who have operative habits suited to them, and not to appoint those who lack them, for instance young men, to learn those things toward which they are more naturally inclined. This was also the opinion of the eminent Aristotle in the first chapter of the first book of the Ethics, where he said: For what kinds of studies ought to be in cities, and what sort each one should learn, and up to what point, that is, the prudence of politics or of legislation, and consequently the one who arranges according to the political law, namely the ruler. He also said this in the seventh book of the Politics, chapter 13: For the political man, looking at all things, ought to make laws according to the parts of the soul and according to their passions. Likewise in the eighth book of the same, chapter 2, when he said: That the lawgiver must undertake the training of living people, no one will doubt. Indeed ... this makes polities. From what has been said, then, it is clear that the determination or institution of the offices and parts of the city belongs to the lawgiver, and that the judging, commanding, and executing of this determination belongs to the ruler according to the law. The ... demonstrations by which the institution of the lawgiver and of the ruler ... of this, and above. The syllogisms differ only in the minor term changed. For this reason ... it is up to anyone at pleasure to take on an office in the city, especially newcomers. For no one ought, and no one can reasonably, turn himself to exercising soldiering or the priesthood as he wishes, and the ruler ought not to permit it; for from this would follow insufficiency in the city of those things that must be provided through the other offices. Rather, the ruler ought to assign the persons to such offices, and also determine the quantity and quality of the parts or offices themselves according to their number, power, and the like, lest through their immoderate excess over one another the polity be dissolved. For this reason Aristotle said in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 2: Polities are also altered by the growth that destroys the proportion ... polities. For just as the body is composed of parts, and must grow proportionally so that it remains ... reason. If it is not corrupted. For if not only in quantity but also in ... grows because of proportion. So too the city is composed of parts, of which some excessive one often lies hidden, such as the multitude of the rich in democracies, and the priesthood under the law of the Christians. He said the same also in the third book of the Politics, chapter 7, whose sequence I omit for the sake of brevity. Again, this part, namely the ruler, must by his authority, according to law, command what is just and honourable and forbid the contrary, both by deed and by word, rewarding or punishing with prizes or penalties the merits or demerits of those who observe or transgress the legal precepts. In this way he will keep each of the parts of the city in its due state and protect it from harms and injuries. If one of the parts does an injury to the others, it must be remedied by the action of the ruler: the one who inflicts the injury undergoes punishment. For punishment is, as it were, a medicine for the offence. Hence in the second book of the Ethics, chapter 2:

units.la: 2. Monstrant autem & poenae factae propter hoc, id est propter delectationes quae habentur in male agendo. medicinae enim quaedam sunt. Cui vero illata fuerit iniuria curabitur, emendam recipiendo, quomodo reducentur omnia ad conuenientem aequalitatem aut proportionem. Amplius conseruat haec pars reliquas ciuitatis partes ipsasque adiuuat in ipsarum operibus tam propriis quam communibus exercendis. Propriis quidem vt quae prouenire habent ab officiis earum propriis, communibus vero vt communicationibus quae sunt ipsarum inuicem, quorum vtraq; turbarentur principantis actione cessante a violentorum correptione. Et propterea nunquam debet actio principantis in ciuitate cessare, quemadmodum nec actio cordis in animali, nam licet actiones aliarum partium ciuitatis, aliquo tempore cessare, possint absq; nocumento singularis personae, collegii vel communitatis, vt actio militaris ... pacis similiter quoq; reliquarum partium, huius tamen partis & suae virtutis nunquam cessare potest actio sine nocumento. Quacunque enim hora vel momento durare oportet praeceptu & communem custodiam de licitis & prohibitis secundum legem, & quandocunq; fiat illicitum aut iniustum, oportet principantem talia regulare perfecte, vel illa exercere quae praeuia sunt ad talia regulanda. Ex praedictis autem apparere potest sufficienter ordo partium ciuitatis inuicem, quoniam propter principantem & ad ipsum tanquam omnium primum ... omnes pro statu praesentis seculi. Nam pars illa in ciuili communitate omnium prima est, quae caeteras instituere, determinare, ac conseruare in statu & pro statu praesentis seculi seu fine ciuili, pars autem principans secundum humanam legem est illa, vt iam probabili & demonstratiua ratione conclusimus. Est igitur aliarum omnium prima, & ad ipsam caeterae ordinantur. De causa quidem igitur effectiua electionis partis principantis, similiter autem & reliquarum partium & ciuitatis institutione, ac ipsarum inuicem ordine, determinatum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: 2. Punishments also show, that is, because of the pleasures found in doing wrong, that they are, as it were, medicines. And the one to whom the injury was done will be cured by receiving compensation, whereby all things are restored to a suitable equality or proportion. Moreover, this part preserves the other parts of the city and helps them in carrying out their works, both their own and their common ones: their own, which arise from their proper offices, and their common ones, which are the communications among them. Both would be thrown into confusion if the action of the ruler ceased, from the restraint of the violent. For this reason the action of the ruler in the city must never cease, just as the action of the heart in an animal does not cease. For although the actions of the other parts of the city may cease for some time without harm to an individual person, a college, or a community, as the action of the military ... likewise of the other parts in peace, yet the action of this part and of its virtue can never cease without harm. For at whatever hour or moment, the precept and common guard over what is licit and illicit according to the law must endure, and whenever something illicit or unjust is done, the ruler must regulate such things perfectly, or exercise those acts that precede such regulation. From what has been said it can be sufficiently seen what order the parts of the city have among themselves, since they are for the sake of the ruler, and are ordered to him as to the first of all ... all according to the state of the present age. For that part in the civil community is first of all, which establishes, determines, and preserves the others in the state and for the state of the present age, or the civil end; and the ruling part according to human law is that one, as we have now concluded by a probable and demonstrative reasoning. It is therefore first of all the others, and the others are ordered to it. Concerning the efficient cause of the choice of the ruling part, and likewise of the rest of the parts, and of the institution of the city, and the order of its parts among themselves, let this be determined in this way.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Quod ... quilibet per nouam electionem sigillatim sumendum ... quem ... solum eligere cum omni posteritate ... sua quam ... successionem vocare solent.
units.tr: That each monarch should be chosen by a new election, taken one at a time, and not the one who alone is chosen together with all his posterity, which they are accustomed to call succession.

units.la: ... dubitatio, an videlicet magis expediat ciuiliter viuentibus, monarchiam ... electione praedicentur, hunc statuere principaturum cum omni sua posteritate, q generis successionem vocare solent, vel illum pro sola eius periodo ad principatum assumere, corrupto vero vel aliter a principatu iuste priuato, nouam vicissim semper electionem facere de futuro. Quibusdam quidem .a. visum est potiorem esse prore institutionem propter apparentia quandam. Primum namque propterea quod monarcha succedens ex genere, remp. magis curabit, tanquam sibi quasi propriam & hereditariam, non sic autem monarcha, cui proprium haeredem principaturum fore nosconstat. Unde 2. politicae, ca. primo circa medium inquit Arist. Minime enim curat fortiter quod plurimorum est commune, de propriis enim maxime curant, de communibus autem minus quam quantum unicuique attinet. Et rursum eodem ca. circa finem? Duo enim sunt quae maxime faciunt solicite curare homines & diligere proprium & delectari. Amplius eiusdem 2. ca. inquit. Adhuc autem & ad delectationem inenarrabile, quantum differt putare aliquid proprium esse. Ad quaestum vero principale rursum, quoniam successores monarchae minus despotizare videbuntur subditis, quam nuper electi propter principatum ipsos assuevisse, nilque sibi nouum euenisse putantes, propter quod amplius extolli debeant, & contemnere subditos. Nouiter autem semper electos quemadmodum ditaros nouiter, plerumque superbire contingit. Unde secundo Rhetoricae, ca. 14. Diuitias autem qui assequuntur, mores leuiter est videre omnibus, contumeliosi enim et elati, quod a possessione diuitiarum, tanquam enim habentes omnia bona, sic disponuntur. Amplius ad id quoniam succedentibus in principatu ex genere, magis obedit subiecta multitudo propter assumptam praecessoribus obediendi consuetudinem. Unde 2. philosophiae primae finali cap. Vt consueuimus, ita dignamur. Et secundo Politicae, cap. quinto circa finem. Non tantum proderit qui mutauerit quantum nocebit, principibus rebellare assuescens. Cum aliis quae de consuetudine dicentur 18. huius, parte sexta.
units.tr: The question is whether it is more expedient for those living under civil government that the monarchy be conferred by election, so that the one chosen rules together with all his posterity, which they are accustomed to call hereditary succession, or that the one chosen be raised to the principate only for his own lifetime, so that when he is corrupted or justly deprived of the principate, a new election is held in his place. Some have thought the first method better, because of a certain apparent advantage. First, because a monarch who succeeds by birth will take more care of the commonwealth, as though it were his own and hereditary property. This is not so with a monarch who knows that his heir will not succeed him in the principate. Hence Aristotle says in the second book of the Politics, near the middle of the first chapter: For people take least care of what is common to many, since they care chiefly for what is their own, and care less for common things than is due to each person. And again in the same chapter, near the end: For there are two things which chiefly make men zealous in care and love: what is one's own, and delight. Further, in the same second book he says: Moreover, the difference in pleasure is beyond description between thinking that something is one's own and thinking that it is not. Then, as to gain, which is the principal point: successors in the monarchy by birth are less likely to seem to domineer over their subjects than men recently chosen, who, having grown used to the principate, think that nothing new has happened to them and that they must therefore be raised higher and despise their subjects. Men newly chosen, like men newly enriched, are generally inclined to be proud. Hence in the second book of the Rhetoric, chapter 14: Those who attain wealth are easily seen to have a manner which is insolent and arrogant towards all, for they are disposed as if they possessed all goods. Moreover, with succession by birth in the principate, the subject multitude obeys more readily, because it has adopted the custom of obeying the predecessors. Hence in the second book of the First Philosophy, final chapter: As we are accustomed, so we value. And in the second book of the Politics, chapter 5, near the end: He who has changed will profit no more than he will harm, when he grows used to rebelling against rulers. These matters will be discussed further concerning custom in the sixth part of this work, chapter 18.

units.la: Adhuc etiam ad quaesitum, quoniam genus aliquod tale vel tantum beneficium reliquae multitudini contulisse contingit, aut in tantum reliquos ciues virtute praecellere, vel propter utrumque, ut semper principari, nunquam vero fit subiici dignum. Unde tertio Politicae iuxta capitulo octauo inquit Aristoteles: Quarta autem species monarchiae regalis, quae secundum heroica tempora voluntaria & patria facta secundum legem, quia primi fuerunt benefactores multitudinis secundum artes aut bellum, aut quia collegerunt, aut emerunt regionem, facti fuerunt reges voluntariorum, & successue sumentibus patri, quod etiam expresse magis inducens eiusdem nono inquit: Cum igitur sit genus totum, vel aliorum vnum acciderit esse differentem secundum virtutem tantum, vt excedat quae illius, eam quae aliorum omnium, tunc iustum est genus hoc esse regale, & dominans omnium & regem vnum hunc. Sic etiam quinto politicae, cap. 5. repetens idem, ait. Regnum quidem enim ad auxilium quod a populo episkegis factum est, & instituitur rex Epieikorum, quae secundum excessum virtutis vel actionum quae a virtute, vel secundum excessum talis generis. Amplius per successionem melior princeps habetur, eo quod tales ad virtutem amplius inclinantur, quoniam ex strenuis parentibus prodeunt magis. Unde Aristoteles secundo politicae suae, poetae cuiusdam Theodekti inducens ex egloga sermonem, inquit: Ex ambabus diuinis progenitoribus radicibus, quis utique dignificauit adducere seruum? parum infra subiungens. Dignificare enim quemadmodum ex homine hominem, & ex bestiis fieri bestiam, sic & ex bonis bonum. Et rursum, quoniam talis plerunque meliori consuetudine ductus est. Unde Aristoteles primo Rhetoricae suae, ca. 13. Verisimile enim ex bonis bonum, & sic nutritum talem esse. Rursum ad primum quaesitum, quoniam principatus successoris ex genere, non eas patitur difficultates, quas semper vicissim nuper electus. In hoc enim nouiter electo videlicet, accidit difficultas habendi studiosos electores, quos ad bonam electionem habere necesse est, atque difficile. Amplius & quoniam adinuentos non discrepare inuicem difficile. Sicque discrepantes, dubium est in seditionem vniuersam deducere politiam. Quemadmodum monstrat experientia in electione noua principis Romanorum. Adhuc etiam, quoniam humanae mentes in malum plerunque sunt pronae, propter quod amore vel odio, prece vel precio, aut alterius commodi vel difficultatis spe non semper ab electoribus melior principans, sed fortasse rarius assumetur. Amplius ad primum quaesitum, quoniam monarchae successoris ex genere facilius est morem cognoscere per ciues & consules, quoniam vnicus & determinatus est, quam nouiter eligendi, qui determinatus non est. Plurimi namque sunt ciues, quos per electionem possibile est ad principatum assumi. Facilius autem esse vnici morem nosse quam plurium. Principis vero, cui per consilium aliquid suaderi oportet, ipsumque dirigere quantumcunque prudentem, expedit morem agnoscere. Unde primo Rhetoricae, cap. vndecimo: Morem enim vniuscuiusque maxime persuasionem. Rursum quoniam monarcham per successionem assumere, subditorum ambitionem, temeritatem, seu praesumptionem, atque seditionis concitationem videtur auferre. Scientes nanque sibi nunquam principatum deberi, neque ad illum rationabiliter peruenire se posse, nequaquam ad illud anhelant subditi, nec propter illum obtinendum quicquam machinantur siniestrum, quae tamen sataguntad ipsum rationabiliter peruenire potentes atque credentes, quemadmodum contingit quibus semper monarcha nouus vicissim eligitur. Unde Tullius de officiis, libro primo: Molestum est quod in maximis animis, splendidisque ingenii plerunque existunt honoris, imperii, potentia, & gloria cupiditates. Dignificantes enim hi seipsos principatu propter aliquod vel aliqua bonorum excellentium, procurant eligentium sibi vota, prece vel precio, aut altero quouis illicito modo.
units.tr: Again, as to the question of whether a family has at some time conferred such a great benefit on the rest of the multitude, or excelled the other citizens in virtue so greatly, or both, that it ought always to rule and never be made subject. Hence Aristotle says in the third book of the Politics, following chapter 8: The fourth kind of royal monarchy, which according to the heroic times was voluntary and hereditary, made according to law, because the first men were benefactors of the multitude by their arts, or by war, or because they gathered together or acquired a region, became kings by the consent of the people, and successively passed on to their heirs. He says the same thing more expressly in the ninth book: Since, therefore, the whole kind, or one of the others, happens to be different in virtue only so far as to exceed the virtue of all the rest, then it is just that this kind be royal and rule over all, and that this one man be king. So also in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 5, repeating the same point, he says: For kingship arose from the aid which was given by the people to the best men, and a king is set up over the best men, who excel in virtue or in actions which flow from virtue, or in the excellence of such a family. Further, a better prince is had through succession, because such men are more inclined to virtue, since they come forth more often from vigorous parents. Hence Aristotle, in the second book of his Politics, quoting a verse of a certain poet Theodectes from a play, says: From two divine root-ancestors, who would have been worthy to bring up a slave? And shortly after he adds: For to be ennobled is, as man comes from man, and beast from beast, so also good from good. And again, because such a man has for the most part been brought up in better habits. Hence Aristotle in the first book of his Rhetoric, chapter 13: For it is probable that the good come from the good, and that such a person has been so nurtured. Again, as to the first question: since the principate of a successor by birth does not suffer those difficulties which always attend a newly chosen one, a difficulty arises in the case of a newly chosen ruler, namely that it is hard, and necessary, to have zealous electors who will make a good choice. Moreover, it is difficult that those who are chosen should not disagree among themselves; and if they disagree, it is doubtful whether the whole polity will not be led into sedition. Experience shows this in the new election of the Roman king. Also, since human minds are generally prone to evil, for that reason, through love or hatred, by prayer or price, or by hope of some other advantage or disadvantage, a better ruler will not always be chosen by the electors, but perhaps will be chosen more rarely. Further, as to the first question: it is easier for the citizens and consuls to know the character of a monarch who succeeds by birth, since he is one and determinate, than of one who is to be newly chosen, who is not determinate. For there are very many citizens who could be raised to the principate by election. It is easier, moreover, to know the character of one than of many. And it is fitting that the character of a prince, to whom something must be recommended by counsel, and who must be guided, however prudent he may be, should be known. Hence in the first book of the Rhetoric, chapter 11: For a person's character is his chief means of persuasion. Again, that the succession of a monarch by birth seems to remove the ambition, rashness, or presumption of the subjects, and the stirring up of sedition. For knowing that the principate is never owed to them, and that they can never rightly attain it, the subjects do not long for it, nor devise any wicked scheme to obtain it. But those who think they can rightly attain it, and believe so, do strive for it, as happens to those among whom a new monarch is always chosen in turn. Hence Tully in the first book of On Duties: It is troublesome that in the greatest and most brilliant minds there are often desires for honour, power, influence, and glory. For those who think themselves worthy of the principate because of some excellent good qualities, seek the votes of the electors by prayer or price, or by any other unlawful means.

units.la: Amplius quoniam electus monarcha, non transmittens principatum in posteros, inaudebit iusti[illegible, ~12 letters] potentes, quamuis legem transgressos, & praesertim occidendo vel aliter in corpus [illegible, ~6 letters]do, formidans ipse propriis heredibus, fortasis non principaturis inde odia vel graves [illegible, ~4 letters]icitias & iniurias provenire. Haec autem non habet dubitare monarcha successens ex genere, propter quod secure atq; complete in qualescunq; legum transgressores iustitiam exercebit.
units.tr: Further, since a monarch chosen, who does not hand on the principate to his descendants, will hardly dare to punish the powerful, although they have broken the law, especially by killing or otherwise harming the body; fearing for his own heirs, who perhaps will not succeed him in the principate, hatreds, grave enmities, and injuries may arise from this. But a monarch who succeeds by birth need have no such fear, and therefore he will exercise justice securely and fully against whatever transgressors of the laws.

units.la: Rursum quo plures & in pluribus regionibus ac populis & plurium tempore perfectior est modus assumendi monarcham, quoniam qui magis naturalis, magis perfectus, magis naturale autem quod in pluribus est: Natura namque verum est, quae in pluribus & plurimo tempore inest, ut in tertio caeli & mundi, & 2. physicae etiam scriptum est, ex inductione palam. Sic autem habet modus per generis successionem, assumendi monarcham ad eum aliqui per novam semper electionem futurum assumere, ut in pluralitate monarchatum, regionum & populorum, monstrat inductio, & in temporum descripta per historiographos gesta declarant. Demum vero quoniam principatus monarchae successoris ex genere amplius similis est regimini seu principatui universi cum in universo semper uno intransmutabiliter extet, ut in secundo philosophiae, cap. finali: Unus ergo princeps propter eius [illegible, ~4 letters] dispositionis. Sic autem vbi filius in principatu succedit parenti, euenire vi[illegible, ~5 letters]etur. Et quoniam pater filio eadem quasi persona censetur. Ex determinatis [illegible, ~3 letters] Suppositionem accipientes, oportere futurum monarcham qui[illegible, ~3 letters] prudentem & bonum esse secundum moralem virtutem, praecipue iustitiam, quasi excellenter ad reliquas cines. Amplius cum his suscipientes, quae de diuersitate inclinationum & dispositionum in gentibus & regionib. ad regiminum diuersitatem diximus vono huius parte 10. Credendum opinor, melius esse simpliciter reipub. propter ciuilis vitae sufficientiam, monarcham quemcunq; futurum per novam electionem statuere, quam ipsum per generis successionem assumere. Quoniam secundum hunc quem potiorem diximus modum instituendi monarcham, semper aut raro deficiens erit sumere monacham, haberi tunc posibilium optimum, vel saltem sufficientem simpliciter perfectum. Ab electione nanq; legislatoris humani quasi semper raro deficiens, intenditur & perpetuo commune conferens ciuium, quemadmodum ostensum est 13. huius, quorum quasi maximum est monarchia sufficiens, ut docet experientia, & ratione deductum est 14. huius. Talem autem sic certitudinaliter dare non potest natalis, & plerunq; fortuita successio ut per singula regna sic monarcham suscipientia, ex inductione palam.
units.tr: Again, the method of choosing a monarch is more perfect when it applies to more men, in more regions and peoples, and over more time; for what is more natural is more perfect, and what is natural is what is found in more cases: For that is true by nature which is present in most cases and for most of the time, as is written in the third book of On the Heavens and the World, and in the second book of the Physics, as is clear from induction. Now the method of choosing a monarch to be the one who will be a monarch by succession of kind, and the method by which a monarch is always chosen anew, are so ordered that induction shows the plurality of monarchies, regions, and peoples, and the events recorded by historians over the course of time make this clear. Finally, since the principate of a monarch who succeeds by birth is more like the government or principate of the whole, which always remains in the whole unchanged, as is said in the final chapter of the second book of Philosophy: One prince, therefore, on account of his ... disposition. But this happens where a son succeeds his father in the principate, since a father and son are regarded as the same person. Taking these as determined assumptions, it must be that the future monarch is prudent and good according to moral virtue, especially justice, excelling the other citizens. Further, taking together what we have said about the diversity of inclinations and dispositions in peoples and regions, and their diversity in forms of government, in the tenth part of this work, I believe it is better, simply for the sufficiency of civil life, to establish whatever monarch is to be by a new election, than to have him assume the principate by succession of kind. For according to this method, which we have called the better one for establishing a monarch, it will always, or at least rarely, be lacking when a monarch must be taken; there will then be had the best possible, or at least one simply sufficient and perfect. For the election of a human lawgiver, which almost always rarely fails, aims at and perpetually confers the common good of the citizens, as was shown in the thirteenth part of this work; and the monarchy, which is almost the greatest such good, is sufficient, as experience teaches and as was deduced by reason in the fourteenth part of this work. But hereditary succession, which is often accidental, cannot give such a monarch with certainty, as it receives a monarch in each kingdom, as is clear from induction.

units.la: Amplius quoniam id bonum omne, quod in monarcha simpliciter requisitum, dat generis naturalis successio, nova quasi semper exhibebit electio quamuis econuerso non tñ. Eundem.n. haeredem & successorem monarchae prioris, poterit ciuilis multitudo per electionem assumere, si fuerit studiosus & prudens, qui si non sic dispositus extiterit, studiosum & prudentem alium nova dabit electio[illegible, ~3 letters] tñ successio generis dare non potuit. Rursum propter futuri monarchae [illegible, ~8 letters] reddit praesens amplius diligens ad communem personarum & rerum ciuitatis [illegible, ~3 letters]. Propter virtutem siquidem primum quoniam ex electione hunc talem supponimus, deinde vero metu correptionis per futurum monarcham: Et rursum, vt mereatur ipse pro successoribus electionem futuram: Quos etiam propterea disciplinatos & studiosos efficit magis curabit, ipsiq; hoc attendentes ad virtutes & ipsorum opera intendent amplioni conatu. Vnde verisimile, parenti similes effectos virtute ac propter illius meritum, & eidem ex consuetudine obedientiam praestitam per electionem nouam quamdiu tales successerint, ad principatum assumi. Est autem, quam diximus in hoc sententia philosophi primo 2. 3. & 7. politica capitulis, nono & 8. 2. & 9. atq; 12. Contraria vero his soluere tentantes, ad primum inducebatur, monarcham per generis successionem assumptum, magis curaturum commune conferens siue rem publicam quasi propriam & hereditariam illi: Dicendum id amplius facturum monarcham ex electione nova semper assumptum, quoniam hunc constat saepius esse prudentem, & bonum ut inductione palam. Quem.n. ostendit producit successio, assumere semper potest electio, quamuis econuerso non tamen.
