Idcirco agens secundum suam monasticam & ciuilem virtutem, propter optimum in hoc secundo virtutis opus scilicet, ac propter extrinsecum consequenter honore & famam, sibi & suae memoriae atq; posteritati quaerendam, aeque aut amplius curabit rem publicam siue communem, monarcha successurum per genus, qui praenoscens posteritatem successuram in principatu, si non studiosus extiterit, plerunque talia non attendit, & sui corruptionem, si deliquerit, minus formidat. Et quod addebatur monarcham per generis successionem, suturi despotizare minus, eo qui per nouam electionem vicissim assumitur, negandum vtiq;. Despotia tanque debenti, politice principari, ab imprudentia, malitia vel utroque contingit, Et his adiicere, praesertim cum quis sperat impune malum agere posse. Nunc autem ex nova sumptus electione monarchae [illegible, ~3 letters] prudentior & melior est, eo qui per generis successionem assumitur propter quod amplius seruabit seipsum a malo propter virtutem: Rursum & quoniam id minus impune facere potest, & facilius corrigi, eo cuius est in principatu determinare successiva posteritas. Quod autem de nouiter dictatis exemplum adducitur, nihil ad rationem hanc obuiare. [illegible, ~10 letters] seu aliorum contemptu patiuntur dictati nouiter, ignorantes & more [illegible, ~4 letters] quaedam instrumento, diuinarum scilicet copia, per quod [illegible, ~4 letters] possunt, quamuis diuitiae secundum ipsarum naturam ad bonum & vitae sufficientiam huius saeculi determinatae sint amplius quam ad horum oppositas, vt palam et primo politica, capit. 6. 7. & 8. sic etiam & principatus. Vnde aduenientibus his viris prudentibus & studiosis, quales sæpius noua dabit electio, quam natalis successio, non euenire hinc despotia vel fastus sed opera laudabilia, in quæ non potuit exire studiosus, dum talibus caruit instrumentis. Accidit autem sic opponentibus concedere, à primo electo, quanquam cum illius successione subiectam multitudinem pati despotiam. Ipse enim quoniam electus nouiter à progenitoribus non habuit principatum, ideoque secundum disputantis rationem, patietur ipse de fastu & subditorum contemptu, propter nouæ rei aduentum, quod nouiter patiuntur dictati. Eius tamen oppositum secundum veritatem dicere conuenit aduersantem, quoniam propter huius electi primi excellentem virtutem aut beneficium, impensum ad reliquam multitudinem, successoribus posteris tanquam propter ipsum studiosis conceditur principatus, unde studiosus ipse magis. Semper enim iuxta sapientis gentilis oraculum, Propter quod vnumquodque est, & illud magis. Id vero quod de obedientia subiectæ multitudinis inducebatur, quanquam inter cætera singulariter attendendum nō vrget concedere, futurum monarchā nouiter electū semper minus esse præstantem, eo qui per generis successionem assumitur.
units.tr: Moreover, since the natural succession of a family supplies every good that is required in a monarch, election will always supply something new, although the reverse does not hold. For the civil multitude can, by election, take as heir and successor of the previous monarch the same man, if he is diligent and prudent; and if he turns out not to be so disposed, a new election can give another who is diligent and prudent, which hereditary succession could not give. Again, because of the future monarch, the present one is made more attentive to the common welfare of the persons and goods of the city. For, first, we suppose that by virtue he was chosen through election; and then, through fear of correction by the future monarch, and also so that he may himself deserve a future election for his successors, he will take more care of them, and, making them disciplined and diligent, he will attend to these things and devote himself to their works with greater effort. Hence it is likely that those who succeed, having become like their parent in virtue and on account of his merit, and having from custom rendered obedience to him, will be raised to the principate by a new election for as long as they are such. This is the opinion of the philosopher in what we have said, in the first, second, third and seventh chapters of the Politics, and in the ninth and eighth of the second, and the ninth and twelfth. Those who try to answer the contrary argument are led to the first point, that a monarch assumed by succession of the family will take more care of the common welfare, or of the commonwealth, as if it were his own and hereditary property. It must be said that a monarch always assumed by new election will do more, since it is evident by induction that he is more often prudent and good. For whatever succession brings forth, election can always choose, although the reverse is not always true. Therefore, a man acting according to his moral and civic virtue, for the best work of virtue in this second sense, and on account of the external honour and fame which he seeks for himself, his memory and his posterity, will care for the commonwealth equally or even more than a monarch who is to succeed by family right; that monarch, knowing in advance that his posterity will succeed to the principate, if they are not diligent, is usually not concerned with such things, and fears his own corruption less if he has done wrong. And what was added, that a monarch who succeeds by family right is less likely to play the tyrant in the future than one who is taken up by a new election in turn, must in any case be denied. Tyranny, which ought to rule politically, comes from imprudence, malice, or both, and is added to these especially when someone hopes he can do evil with impunity. Now, however, a monarch taken up by new election is more prudent and better than one who succeeds by family right, because of which he will keep himself more from evil on account of virtue. Again, since he can do wrong less with impunity and more easily be corrected, he is one whose successive posterity has no determined right to the principate. As for the example brought from newly made men, it does nothing to hinder this argument. Newly made men suffer the contempt of others, being ignorant and by custom [...] certain instruments, namely an abundance of riches, by which [...] they can, although riches, according to their own nature, are determined more for the good and sufficiency of life in this age than for the opposite, as is plain at the beginning of the Politics, chapters six, seven and eight; so too the principate. Hence, when these prudent and diligent men come, such as new election will more often give than hereditary succession, tyranny or arrogance does not follow from this, but praiseworthy works, into which a diligent man could not go forth while he lacked such instruments. It happens, however, that when we grant to our opponents that the first elected man, though newly chosen, has the principate from his progenitors, the subject multitude nevertheless suffers tyranny together with his succession. For since he, being newly elected, did not have the principate from his forebears, he himself, according to the reasoning of the disputant, will suffer arrogance and contempt from his subjects on account of the arrival of something new, which newly made men suffer. Yet it is fitting for the opponent to say the opposite of this, according to the truth: because of the excellent virtue or benefit of this first elected man, bestowed on the rest of the multitude, the principate is granted to his posterity as if they were diligent on his account, whence the diligent man himself is more so. For, according to the saying of the wise pagan, For that on account of which a thing is, that thing is all the more so. As for what was introduced about the obedience of the subject multitude, although among other things it must be attended to singularly, it does not compel us to concede that a monarch newly elected will always be less excellent than one who is assumed by succession of the family.

units.la: Quamuis enim ex consuetudine confirmetur obedientia, videmus tamen ex nouitate maiorem admirationem & reuerentiam, præsertim cum ex electione noua fuerit princeps assumptus ex alia regione siue prouincia. Rursumque quoniam obedientiæ consuetudo simpliciter attenditur in comparatione ad leges & principatum, ad personam vero principantem secundum quid: Vnde videmus semper omnes animo & opere reuereri principatum & leges, quamuis animo quandoque propter insufficientiam, personam principantem contemnant, econuerso non tamen. propter quod cum vbique quasi subiecta multitudo assueta sit legibus & principatibus obedire: non tantum nocet personæ principantis mutatio secundum genus, quantum prodest ex electione noua sufficientia eius, ex cuius reuerentia propter virtutem ad principatum & leges obedientia crescit. Signum autem sufficere obedientiam, quæ ad principatum & leges, est quod in ecclesiastica iconomia de Romano papa videmus. Ipsi nanq; subiecta multitudo quasi semper obedientiam debitam, & amplius debita præstat. Cuius quidem causam assignabimus primo 2. parte: Ex qua siquidem abundanti obedientia, principantem despotizare quandoque contingit, propter sperata impunitatem, quemadmodum iam quibusdam dictorum episcoporum euenisse videmus. Et quod dixit Aristot. 2. politicæ: Non tantum proderit qui mutauerit &c. Intentionem habet in his, qui ex occasione qualibet, quamuis leui, mutare quærunt legem aut principem. Ad verbum Arist. tertio politicæ, cap. 9. Quod genus aliquod tam excellens virtute aut beneficio ad reliquam multitudinem reperire contingit, vt idem dignum sit principari, non subiici. Esto idaliquo tempore fortasse etiam alicubi verum esse, quamuis non plerunque vbique hoc reperire contingat. Vnde Arist. 2. Rhetoricæ 14. ca. Generosum autem fuit secundum degenerasse à natura. Quod quidem vt in pluribus non accidit nobilibus: sed sunt multi leuis valoris. Fertilitas enim quædam est in generibus virorum, quemadmodum in his quæ per regiones fiunt, & aliquando si fit bonum genus, fiunt per quoddam tempus viri superstui, (id est, excessiui virtute) & demum iterum suspenduntur, id est deficiunt. Degenerant quoque quidam bene n·to genere in insaniores mores, velut ab Albiado, & qui à Dionysio priore, id est qui descenderunt ab his viris Albiado & Dionysio priore, quamuis illustribus, degenerauerunt: propterea dicendum, quod ex hoc solo genere quandiu suæ nobilitatis durabit fertilitas & legislatori videatur expedient, conuenienter ordinari seu statui potest per electionem: assumi monarchā vicissim tamen nouum, quandocunq; defecerit prior, vt ex eodem genere melior habeatur. Non enim constat, quales monarchæ futuri sint nati, & præsertim primus eorum, quem vbique quasi suscipientes ex successione monarcham ad principatum assumere semper solent. Amplius quoniam & si tale genus illustrium virorum quandoque repertum sit in aliquibus prouinciis, & circa ipsarum originem propter esse paucitatem prudentum studiosorum, eligentium & eligendorum, non tamen id semper videmus, quinimo perducta communitate ad complementum vltimum, vt ea quæ Romanorum apparet principaturum quemcunque ad principatum per nouam electionem assumi debere, tanquam per regulam certiorem & perfectiorem, quamuis enim principatus qui per generis successionem assumitur, quibusdam regionibus etiam si pluribus conuenire videatur, non tamen hæc species institutionis propterea perfectior est, ea quæ nouæ vicissim electionis. Sicut nec quefabrilis habitus quamuis in pluribus reperiatur regionibus aut suppositis, perfectior est medicinali. Ea vero propositione concessa, quod magis ad virtutem inclinatur frequenter & meliori consuetudine ducitur, qui ex strenuis parentibus traxit originem: Dicendum quod his amplius in dispositione assumendi monarchæ dare potest electio noua successione natali, quoniam non solum inclinatum ad prudentiam & virtutem, qualem dat natalis successio, verum etiam iam perfectum & actualiter operantem secundum virtutem, talem autem præstantius est ad principatum assumere, qualem in posse aut agere secundum actum non sit, frequenter exhibet, quæ per genus successio. Quod autem aduersum nouitatem electionis induximus inter cætera singularius formidandum, atque cauendum difficultas scilicet, qua patitur à studiosorum carentia, per quos solummodo debet electio fieri, & hocamplius ipsorum discrepantia, propter quam politiæ seu ciuilitati periculum schismatis imminet. Rursumq; horum affectio siniștra, propter quam quomodocunq; suscepta, concorditer possunt ipsi vel ipsorum pars valentior prauum eligere principantem. Dicendum vtique, quod ea electio per quam principans cum omni sua posteritate seu successione ad principatum assumitur, primam iam dictatum. dictarum difficultatum, iterata electione cuiuslibet monarchae futuri patitur amplius. Eo quod circa politiarum originem, minor est prudentum pluralitas ex quorum siquidem debilitate, contingens error in eligendo, multum laedet politiam quoniam diuturnius. Quae vero schismatis adducitur dubitatio, quamuis super omnes instantias attendenda, non vrget electionem nouam futuri monarchae, minus praestantem ea quae vnica cum omni posteritate principaturum allumit. Quoniam electio semper fit propter commune conferens, quod plerunque quasi semper etiam vult & perficit legislator humanus, vt demonstratum est 13. huius. Ad quem etiam huius electionis autoritas pertinet, quemadmodum certificatum est 12. huius, & cap. praecedenti. Esto rursum cum disputante ad solos & studiosos electionem hanc pertinere. Non est verisimile neque verum in pluribus eos adinuicem discrepare, quoniam prudentes neque cortumpi secundum affectum, quoniam studiosi, quae tertia superextitit difficultas inducta. Id autem exemplum, quod de imperio Romanorum induximus ex difficultate, quam patitur propter electionem nouam, semper fieri de quolibet futuro monarcha: Dicendum difficultatem hanc ab electione tanquam per se causa minime provenire. Sed provenit per se difficultas haec ex quorundam malitia, ignorantia, vel utroque impedientium electionem atque processum principantis praedicti, de quibus quidem per transeundum hic, quoniam de ipsis & eorum actionibus, quibusque modis id hactenus fecerint & faciant, ac facturi sint, & propter quas causas 19. huius. 13. 24. 25. & 26. secunda seriose dicetur. Quae vero fuit obiectio, quoniam facilius & certius bene consuleundo dirigitur monarcha succedens ex genere, quam nova semper electione vicissim assumptus, phantasiam modicam habet, non enim si peruersi moris esset monarcha, debent illi per consiliarios suaderi quae secundum suum morem sunt, vel appetit, sed oppositae magis. Verum monarcha suppositio, qualem expedire in suppositionibus & veris probationibus dixerimus, quae ad politiam seu commune conferens sunt, debent prudentes & studiosi quales nobiles supponi disputans, futuros principantis consiliarios, illi simpliciter suadere. Quinimo dicetur, expediens fortasse magis, ipsos ignorare morem illius, ne ad ipsius illicitum placitum, propter eius gratiam aut fauorem sibi quaerendum, sed verum & communi conferens consulant. Hoc autem sufficienter norunt, habentes politicam prudentiam, propter quod non referent ad hoc monarchae mos qualiscunque; fuerit, debet enim illi semper ad politiam magis expediens suaderi. Amplius, esto, notitiam dispositionum monarchae aliquid consiliariis conferre, propter ipsum certius posse dirigere: Dicendum tamen, non tantum quantum per certitudinem quasi semper studiosum & prudentem habere monarcham, cuius siquidem etiam per consilium dirigendi morem attendendum per se, hoc ipso sufficienter consiliarius quilibet prudens cognoscere poterit. Talem autem certius exhibet noua semper electio quam natalis successio, vt per saepe diximus. Vnde etiam attendendum, quod succedenti monarchae per genus quandoque; peruersio, magis obtemperant assistentes seu consiliatii, minusque increpare audent, aut illius correptionem tentare, propter futuram principari posteritatem ipsius. Et quod inquit Arist. primo rhetoricae: Motem vniuscuiusque maxime persuasiuum ad vnumquemque, potest concedi tanquam verum. Vt quod quisque secundum morem seu inclinationem suam desiderat, vehementius & facilius persuadenti credit id. Quod si tamen peruersum appetat, vt diximus, debet hoc illi minime suaderi.
units.tr: Although obedience is confirmed by custom, we nonetheless see greater wonder and reverence arising from novelty, especially when a prince has been raised by a new election from another region or province. Again, since the custom of obedience is regarded absolutely in relation to the laws and the principate, but only in a certain respect in relation to the person who rules, we always see that all men, in mind and in deed, revere the principate and the laws, although at times they despise the ruling person in their minds on account of his insufficiency, and not the reverse. Therefore, since everywhere the subject multitude is, as it were, accustomed to obey laws and principates, a change of ruler as to lineage does not harm so much as his new election benefits by his sufficiency, from whose reverence, on account of his virtue, obedience to the principate and the laws grows. The sign that obedience to the principate and the laws is sufficient is what we see in the ecclesiastical economy concerning the Roman pope. For the subject multitude renders to him, as it were always, the obedience that is due and even more than is due. We shall assign the cause of this first in part 2. From this abundant obedience it sometimes happens that the ruler becomes despotic, on account of the impunity he hopes for, as we see has already happened to some of the said bishops. And what Aristotle said in the second book of the Politics, that it would not greatly profit whoever changed..., he has in view those who seek, on any occasion, however slight, to change the law or the prince. Word for word, Aristotle in the third book of the Politics, ch. 9: It may happen that some kind is found so excellent in virtue or benefaction, compared with the rest of the multitude, that the same is worthy to rule and not to be subject. Let it be granted that at some time, and perhaps somewhere, this is true, although it does not commonly happen that this is found everywhere. Hence Aristotle in the second book of the Rhetoric, ch. 14: To be of noble birth is to have degenerated from nature. This indeed does not happen in most nobles, but there are many of little worth. For there is a certain fertility in the kinds of men, as in those things that arise by regions; and sometimes, if the kind is good, men of surpassing (that is, excessive, in virtue) appear for a certain time, and at last they are again suspended, that is, they fail. Some also degenerate from a good stock into more insane morals, as from Albiades and from the elder Dionysius, that is, those who descended from these men, Albiades and the elder Dionysius, though illustrious, degenerated. Therefore it must be said that, so long as the fertility of this noble stock endures and seems expedient to the lawgiver, it can be suitably ordered or established by election: yet a new monarch should in turn be chosen whenever the previous one has failed, so that a better one may be had from the same kind. For it is not certain what sort of monarchs will be born, and especially the first of them, whom, as if receiving the monarch by succession, men are always accustomed to take up to the principate. Moreover, although such a kind of illustrious men has sometimes been found in some provinces, and about their origin, because of the scarcity of prudent and studious men who elect and are to be elected, we do not always see this; rather, when the community has been brought to its final perfection, as appears to be the case with the Romans, it should be held that whoever is taken to the principate by new election ought to be taken up by a surer and more perfect rule. For although the principate that is taken up by succession of a kind seems to suit some regions, even if many, this form of institution is not on that account more perfect than that of new election in turn. Just as the habit of the craftsman, although it is found in many regions or conditions, is not more perfect than that of the physician. Now, granting that proposition, that one who has drawn his origin from vigorous parents is more frequently inclined to virtue and led by a better custom, it must be said that new election can give more in the disposition for taking up a monarch than natal succession, since succession by kind frequently offers not only one inclined to prudence and virtue, such as natal succession gives, but also one already perfected and actually operating according to virtue; and it is more excellent to take up to the principate one who is not merely in potency but actually acting according to virtue. As for the difficulty, which we have brought forward against the novelty of election, to be feared and guarded against more particularly than the rest, namely that it suffers from a lack of studious men, by whom alone the election ought to be made, and moreover their disagreement, on account of which there is danger of schism threatening the polity or civil order; and again their sinister affection, on account of which, however they are taken up, the men themselves or their stronger part might agree to elect a wicked ruler: it must be said in every case that that election by which a ruler is taken up to the principate together with all his posterity or succession suffers the first of the difficulties mentioned, namely the repeated election of each future monarch, even more. For around the origin of polities there is a smaller plurality of prudent men, and from their weakness an error in electing, arising from it, will greatly harm the polity, since it lasts longer. But the doubt about schism that is brought forward, although it must be considered above all the other objections, does not press against a new election of a future monarch, which is less excellent than that which takes up a single ruler together with all his posterity. For election is always made for the common benefit, which the human lawgiver nearly always both wills and accomplishes, as was shown in the thirteenth of this work. To him also the authority of this election pertains, as has been established in the twelfth of this work and in the preceding chapter. Granting again, with the disputant, that this election pertains only to the studious and prudent men, it is neither likely nor true that in most cases they disagree among themselves, since the prudent are not corrupted by affection, since they are studious; this is the third difficulty that has been brought forward. As for the example that we brought forward concerning the Roman empire, of the difficulty which it suffers on account of new election, which is always made concerning any future monarch: it must be said that this difficulty does not arise from the election itself as a cause in its own right. Rather, this difficulty arises of itself from the malice, ignorance, or both, of certain men who hinder the election and the process of the aforesaid ruler; about these, we pass over them here in passing, since concerning them and their actions, and by what means they have hitherto done this and do it, and will do it, and for what causes, it will be said at length in the nineteenth of this work and in the thirteenth, twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth of the second part. As for the objection that a monarch succeeding by kind is more easily and more surely directed by good counsel than one always taken up in turn by new election, it has little force. For if the monarch were of a perverse custom, those who advise him ought not to persuade him of what accords with his custom or appetite, but rather of the opposite. But the monarch's supposed character, such as we have said is expedient in suppositions and true proofs, and which concerns the polity or the common benefit, the prudent and studious men, such as the nobles, who are supposed by the disputant to be the future counsellors of the principate, ought to persuade him simply. Indeed it will be said that it is perhaps more expedient that they should not know his custom, lest, for the sake of winning his favour or goodwill, they should counsel in accordance with his unlawful pleasure, but rather counsel what is true and conducive to the common good. Now they know this sufficiently, having political prudence, and therefore they will not refer to this whatever the monarch's custom may be; for to him ought always to be urged what is more expedient for the polity. Moreover, granting that knowledge of the monarch's dispositions contributes something to his counsellors, so that they may direct him more surely: it must be said nonetheless that it does not contribute as much as having a monarch who is, as it were always, studious and prudent, since indeed any prudent counsellor will be able to know sufficiently, by his own counsel, the custom that ought to be observed for directing him. Moreover, a new election always presents such a monarch more surely than natal succession, as we have often said. Hence it must also be observed that when a monarch succeeding by kind is sometimes perverse, those who attend him or are his counsellors more readily obey him, and dare less to reproach him or attempt his correction, on account of the future posterity who will rule after him. And what Aristotle says in the first book of the Rhetoric may be granted as true: The custom of each person is most persuasive to each, so that whatever anyone desires according to his custom or inclination, he believes more eagerly and more readily when it is urged on him. But if he should desire what is perverse, as we have said, this ought by no means to be urged on him.

units.la: Adhuc, quod nec praetereundum silentio, & euenire videmus persaepe, monarcham, si non studiosus extiterit, peruersorum magis quam studiosorum plerumque sequi consilia, propter quod ipsum, quoniam certius studiosum, per electionem nouam sumendam.
units.tr: Further, something that must not be passed over in silence, and which we often see happen: a monarch, if he is not zealous, usually follows the counsels of the perverse rather than of the zealous. For this reason he should be replaced by a new election, since the zealous man is more certain.

units.la: Et quod inducitur es succedente per genus monarcha, ciuium ambitionem, temeritatem, seu praesumptionem, & ambitionem principatus indebitam magis auferri. Dicendum quod non solum indebitum illis aufertur, verum etiam quod secundum rationem debetur, unde illis seditionis mouendae datur occasio. Attendentes enim ciuium plurimi super se monarchizare frequenter minus dignos secundum virtutem, & semper principatu priuari, aut non in tantum vacant virtutibus, quibus principari sint digni, aut vacantes continuo, tamen priuari sibi quandoque debito principatu, iuste seditionem mouebunt: quam siquidem minime tentabunt moeuere, sperantes ad principatum posse per electionem assumi tempore debito. Amplius, quoniam prudentes & studiosi non absque iniuria graui seditionem mouere tentabunt. Hanc autem non illis inferet legislator, aut principans studiosus, qualem semper quasi futurum diximus, qui per nouam electionem assumitur. Plurimum enim studiosus principans & legislator intendunt quod iustum, vt in 13. & 14. huius. Quod autem dixit disputans, ambitionem aut praesumptionem fore cuiusibus appetere principatum, non recte dixit, quoniam studioso & hic bene merito appetere principatum debito tempore, non est ambitio, superbia, neque praesumptio, sed magnanimitatis atque virtutis politicae opus appetere. Propter quod Aristoteles quarto Ethicorum testatur: Magnanimum non inconuenienter aut praeter virtutem appetere magnos honores. Quod autem dixit Tullius de officiis libro primo: Molestum esse, quod in maximis animis, &c. si verum dixerit, veritatem habet, dum talia desiderantur indebite, in quanto vel quali aut ut liquis modis praeter rationis normam & regulam. Quod autem post haec inducebatur, quod non transmittens principatum ad haeredes monarcha, inaudebit iustificare aut punire potentes, personaliter saltem, & extremo supplicio, propter timere ipsorum maleuolentias ad proprios natos. Dicendum non timere propter animo fortem esse talem electum. Et quoniam iustificati potentes, sic-
units.tr: As to the objection that, under succession by birth, the ambition, rashness or presumption of citizens and their undue desire for rule are rather removed: it must be said that not only what is undue is taken from them, but also what is owed to them according to reason, and so they are given occasion to stir up sedition. For most citizens, observing that men less worthy in virtue often become monarchs over them, and that they are always deprived of rule, either are not so lacking in the virtues by which they would be worthy to rule, or, though lacking them, are nonetheless at times deprived of the rule that is rightly theirs; they will justly stir up sedition. Yet they will hardly attempt to stir it, hoping to be taken up to rule by election at the due time. Moreover, prudent and zealous men will not attempt to stir up sedition without grave injury. But the lawgiver or zealous ruler will not inflict this injury on them, such as we have said is always to be expected from one who is taken up by new election, for a zealous ruler and lawgiver chiefly intends what is just, as in chapters 13 and 14 of this work. As for the disputant's claim that it is ambition or presumption for anyone to desire rule, he did not speak correctly, since for a zealous man who has well deserved it to desire rule at the due time is not ambition, pride or presumption, but the work of magnanimity and political virtue. Hence Aristotle testifies in the fourth book of the Ethics: It is not unfitting for the magnanimous man to desire great honours, nor beyond virtue. As for what Tully said in the first book of On Duties: It is troublesome that in the greatest minds, etc., if he spoke truly, it holds insofar as such things are desired undueliy, in whatever measure, quality or manner, beyond the norm and rule of reason. As for what was introduced next, that a monarch who does not pass on his rule to heirs will not dare to condemn or punish the powerful, at least personally and with the extreme penalty, for fear of their ill-will toward his own sons: it must be said that he need not fear this, because the one elected is of a strong spirit. And since the powerful are justly punished in this way,

units.la: Q si secundum legem & ipsorum demerito passi fuerint, aut odium non concipient ad monarchiam & naros illius, aut debile, non quærentes vindictam. Norunt etenim ipsi iustitiam fieri oportere per illum vel alium principantem. Qui si tamen id cum appetitu vindictæ conceperint, propter ipsorum ignorantiam, malitiam, aut utrunq;, ad vindictam non audebunt prorum pere metu legislatoris & reliqui principatis, à quo velut à prædecessore, rursum puniri verisimiliter dubitabunt. Ei vero litigiosæ rationi, quoniam in pluribus regionibus & in plurimo tempore, cum successione generis monarchæ per electionem videntur assumi: Dicendum, fortasse non sic secundum veritatem habere secundum temporis plurimum. Esto tamen sic esse, quemadmodum disputans sumit. Quod autem annectit, principatum hunc eo naturaliorem atque perfectiorem, negandum. Et cum inducit Aristotelis testimonium ex libro tertio cœli & mundi, ac 2. physicæ, quoniam natura rei videtur, qua pluribus & plurimo tempore inest. Dicendum utiq; verum esse, quod naturalius sit ens quam eius priuatio vel orbatio, non tamen naturalius quocunque alio sibi specie diuerso, sic enim faber perfectior esset primo philosopho, & fabrilis prima philosophia vel alia speculatiua quacunque, quod tamen, ut pridem diximus, neq; necessarium est, neque verum. Nunc autem electa semper nouiter monarchia, non est priuatio succedentis ex genere, nec conuerso, sed species inuicem disparatæ, simul in eodem incompossibiles respectu eiusdem multitudinis, seu communitatis perfectæ. Sunt autem & alia fortasse peccata orationis prædictæ, quæ consideranti reliquimus, & assignare omisimus propter abbreuiationem sermonis. Ad eam vero qua omnium nouissime astruebatur, monarcham electum cum omni posteritate præstantiorem, propter eius similitudinem vnitatis ad principem vniuersi. Dicendum, non tantum attendendum huius veritatis similitudinem, quamuis æquiuocam quasi quantum secundum animam, seu animæ habitum, est attendenda perfectionis conformitas. Est enim hæc præcipua causa propter quam debet quis ad principatum assumi, non similitudo generis, secundum quam sūm attenditur vnitas corporalis dispositionis per se, non autem habitus animæ, propter quem per te alicui principatus debetur. Secundum hanc autem perfectionis vnitatem siue similitudinem amplius & sæpius suo præcessori & studioso monarchæ ae enti primo seu principi vniuersitatis entium conformatur electus monarcha singulariter, secundum seipsum quilibet, quam successor ex genere solo & propter alterius electionem, vt palam ex prioribus dictis. Apparebunt autem & apparent fortasse vtrinq; quam plures instantiæ melius & deterius in singulis ad politiam considerare volenti, quas tamen magis attendendas aduertimus in prædictis induximus. De perfectissimo itaque modo instituendi monarcham, sic pertransiuisse sufficiat.
units.tr: if they have suffered according to law and by their own demerit, they will either not conceive hatred toward the monarchy and its heirs, or it will be weak, and they will not seek vengeance. For they know that justice must be done by that ruler or by another. But if they have conceived it with a desire for vengeance, on account of their ignorance, malice, or both, they will not dare to take vengeance for fear of the lawgiver and the other rulers, by whom, as by a predecessor, they will probably fear being punished again. As for that contentious argument, that since in many regions and for a very long time monarchs seem to be taken up by election rather than by succession of stock: it must be said that perhaps it is not so in truth for the greater part of time. Yet let it be so, as the disputant assumes. As for his addition that this rule is more natural and more perfect, that must be denied. And when he adduces Aristotle's testimony from the third book of On the Heavens and the World, and from the second Physics, that the nature of a thing seems to be what belongs to it in most cases and for most of the time: it must be said that it is true that being is more natural than its privation or deprivation, but not more natural than whatever else is specifically different from it. For thus the craftsman would be more perfect than first philosophy, and craft-knowledge more perfect than first philosophy or any other speculative science whatever, which, as we said earlier, is neither necessary nor true. Now, however, when monarchy is always newly elected, it is not a privation of the succeeding by genus, nor the reverse, but mutually disparate species, mutually incompatible in the same respect for the same multitude or perfect community. There are perhaps also other faults in the aforesaid argument, which we have left for the reader to consider and have omitted to assign, for the sake of brevity. As for the last argument, which asserted that an elected monarch, with all his posterity, is more excellent on account of the likeness of his unity to the prince of the universe: it must be said that the likeness of this truth, although somewhat equivocal, is not to be attended to so much as the conformity of perfection in the soul, or in the habit of the soul. For this is the chief cause on account of which someone ought to be taken up to rule, not similarity of stock, in which bodily unity is considered only in itself, not the habit of the soul, on account of which rule is due to someone through himself. But according to this unity or likeness of perfection, more often and more fully, the elected monarch is singly conformed, each one according to himself, to his predecessor, to the zealous monarch, and to the first being, the prince of the universe of beings, than a successor by stock alone and on account of another's election, as is clear from what was said before. Moreover, many instances, better and worse, in individual cases will appear, and perhaps do appear on both sides, to anyone wishing to consider the polity; yet we have set forth those we judge more worthy of attention in what has been said. Let it suffice, therefore, to have passed through the most perfect manner of instituting a monarch in this way.

units.la: CAP. XVII. De numerali vnitate supremi principatus ciuitatis aut regni, & ipsius necessitate, unde etiam apparet vnitas numeralis ciuitatis aut regni, & numeralis vnitas singularium partium primarum, siue officiorum ciuitatis aut regni.
units.tr: CAP. XVII. On the numerical unity of the supreme principate of a city or kingdom, and on its necessity; whence also appears the numerical unity of a city or kingdom, and the numerical unity of its primary parts or offices.

units.la: HIs autem habitum erit dicere de principantis seu principatus vnitate, ad quam siquidem ingredientes, dicamus, quod in ciuitate vnica seu regno vnico, esse oportet vnicum tantummodo principatum, aut si plures numero vel specie, sicut in magnis ciuitatibus expedire videtur, & matime in regno sumpto secundū primam significationem, oportet inter ipsos vnicū numero esse supremū omnium, ad quem & per quem reliqui reducantur & regulentur, & contingentes in ipsis errores per ipsum ét corrigantur. Hunc autem solummodo principatum, supremum sc. dico vnum numero ex necessitate fore nō plures, si debeat regnum aut ciuitas bene disponi. Idemque dico de principante secundum illum, non quidem vnicum numero principantem secundum suppositum humanæ speciei, sed secundum officium. Est enim principatus aliquis vnicus numero supremus & bene temperatus, secundum quem principantur plures homines vno, vt aristocratia & politia, de quibus diximus octauo huius. Verum hi plures sunt vnus principatus numero quantum ad officium, propter numeralem vnitatem cuiuscunq; actionis proueniantis abeis, iudicij, seu sententiæ, vel præcepti. nulla enim talium actionum prouenire potest abipsorum aliquo seorsum, sed ex communi decreto atque consensu eorum, aut valentioris partis secundum statutas leges in his. Et propter talem actionis numeralem vnitatem sic proueniantis, est & dicitur principatus numero vnus, siue vnico regatur homine siue pluribus. Talis vero vnitas actionum non requiritur in aliquo vno reliquorum officiorum seu partium ciuitatis, possunt enim & debent in vnoquoque ipsorum plures actiones consimiles, aut diuersæ speciei, à diuersis in eis suppositis prouenire seorsum. Quinimo talis vnitas actionis in eis esset communitati & singulis, importabilis & nociua. Sic itaque intellecta vnitate numerali principatus aut principantis, concedere volumus, aut vnicum numero tantum modo principatum vel principantem esse in ciuitate vel regno aut si plures, supremam omnium esse vnicum tantum numero, non plures. Hoc autem sic primum monstrabimus, quoniam si principatus essent plures in ciuitate vel regno, & non reducti seu ordinati sub aliquo vno supremo, deficeret iudicium, præceptum, & executio conferentium & iustorum. Et ex his propter inuindicatas iniurias hominum, pugnæ, separatio, & corruptio demum ciuitatis aut regni. Consequens autem istud est inconueniens maxime fugiendum, cuius quidem ad antecedens datum, pluralitatem scilicet principatuum, consequentia potest evidenter ostendi. Primum quidem quoniam legum transgressores iustificari rationabiliter nequeunt nisi vocati coram principante ad quaesitorum seu ipsius obiectorum examinationem. Sed principatuum suppositia pluralitate, non reducta in supremum aliquem vnum, quomodo dicit ipsam disputans, nemo vocatus coram principante sufficienter poterit comparere. Esto nanque, sicut frequenter euenit, quod propter legis transgressionem aliquam, vocetur aliquis respondere a pluribus principatibus, non subinuicem ordinatis, & pro eodem tempore, quoniam eadem ratione tenetur & potest vnus principatuum vocare seu citare reum qua reliquus. Et qua etiam ratione vocatus tenetur coram vno principatum respondere, ne coatumax habeatur. Eadem ratione coram alio vel aliis, si duobus fuerint ampliores, aut igitur coram omnibus simul apparebit, aut coram nullo ipsorum, vel coram quodam quidam sic, coram alio vel aliis minime. Coram omnibus autem simul & eodem tempore non, quoniam hoc est impossibilium natura & arte. Idem enim corpus non potest simul esse in diuersis locis aut pluribus simul loqui vel respondere, diuersa fortasse interrogantibus simul. Amplius esto quamuis impossibile vocatum coram pluribus principatibus comparere, simulque diuersa tacere vel respondere, ab vno tamen fortasse principatuum de eodem crimine damnabitur, ab alio fortasse absoluetur, vel si ab vtroq; damnetur, non aequaliter ab vtroq; propter quod emendare tenebitur & non tenebitur, aut si tenebitur, hoc erit in tanto, & ampliori vel pauciori, & sic in tanto & non in tanto. Unde vel simul contradictoria faciet aut nihil emendabit. Eadem enim ratione vnius principatus & alterius, debet obseruare praeceptum. Coram vno, principatuum comparere magis quam coram reliquo vel reliquis, non habet aliquam rationem. Quod si tn appareat coram vno, reliquis spretis. Et ab illo fortassis absoluatur a culpa & poena ciuili, a reliquis tamen damnabitur propter contumaciam. Sic igitur vocatus seu citatus, nec coram omnibus apparebit simul, nec coram quodam quidem sic, coram quodam quidem non conuenienter poterit apparere. Relinquitur ergo, vt coram nullo principatu vocatus seu citatus debeat comparere, non igitur iustificari poterit. Est quidem igitur impossibilis ciuitati vel regno pluralitas talium principatuum non subordinatorum inuicem, si debeat conseruari ciuile iustum & conferens.
units.tr: Now it will be fitting to speak of the unity of the ruler or principate. Proceeding to this, I say that in a single city or single kingdom there ought to be only one principate, or, if there are several in number or kind, as seems expedient in great cities, and most of all in a kingdom taken in the first sense, there must be among them one supreme principate, numerically one, to which and through which the rest are referred and regulated, and by which the errors that arise in them are also corrected. I say that this supreme principate alone, numerically one and not several, must necessarily exist if a kingdom or city is to be well ordered. The same I say of the ruler according to that principate: not one ruler numerically in the sense of a single individual of the human species, but one according to office. For there is some principate that is supreme and well balanced, numerically one, under which several men rule rather than one, as in aristocracy and polity, of which we spoke in the eighth book of this work. Yet these several men are one principate numerically as regards office, on account of the numerical unity of every action that proceeds from them, whether a judgment, a sentence, or a command. For no such action can proceed from any one of them separately, but only from their common decree and consent, or from the stronger part according to the laws established for these matters. And because of this numerical unity of action, so proceeding, the principate is and is called one in number, whether it is governed by a single man or by several. Such unity of action, however, is not required in any one of the remaining offices or parts of the city, for in each of them many similar or differently kinded actions may and must proceed separately from different individuals who hold them. Indeed, such a unity of action in them would be intolerable and harmful both to the community and to individuals. Having thus understood the numerical unity of the principate or ruler, we wish to grant that in a city or kingdom there is only one principate or ruler numerically, or, if there are several, that there is only one supreme one of all, and not several. Now we shall first show this as follows: if there were several principates in a city or kingdom, not referred or ordered under some one supreme principate, judgment, command and execution of what is useful and just would fail. And from this, because injuries of men go unavenged, there would arise fighting, division, and finally the corruption of the city or kingdom. Now this consequence is to be avoided above all as something unfitting, and the consequence can be clearly shown from the antecedent given, namely the plurality of principates. First, indeed, because law-breakers cannot rightly be judged unless they are summoned before the ruler for the examination of the questions and charges brought against them. But if there is a plurality of principates, not reduced to one supreme, then, as the disputant puts it, no one summoned before the ruler will be able to appear sufficiently. For let it be granted, as often happens, that someone for some breach of law is summoned to answer before several principates, not subordinated to one another, and at the same time. For by the same reason one of the principates is bound and able to call or cite the accused, as is the other. And by the same reason the accused is bound to answer before one principate, lest he be held contumacious. By the same reason, before another or others, if there are more than two, he will either appear before all of them at once, or before none of them, or before some but not others. Before all at once and at the same time he cannot appear, because this is impossible by the nature and art of things: one body cannot be in several places at once, nor speak or answer to several parties at once, even if they ask different things. Furthermore, even if it were impossible for the accused to appear before several principates and to keep silent or answer different things at once, he may perhaps be condemned of the same crime by one of the principates and perhaps acquitted by another; or if he is condemned by both, not equally by both, so that he will be bound and not bound to make amends, or if bound, this will be to such an extent, greater or lesser, and so to this extent and not to that. Hence he will either do contradictory things at once or amend nothing. For by the same reasoning he must obey the command of one principate and of another. To appear before one principate rather than the other or the others has no reasonable ground. But if he should appear before one, neglecting the rest, he may perhaps be absolved by that one of fault and civil penalty, yet will be condemned by the others for contumacy. Thus the summoned or cited man can neither appear before all at once, nor appear suitably before some and not before others. It remains, then, that the man summoned or cited ought to appear before no principate, and so cannot be justified. Therefore a plurality of such principates not subordinated to one another is indeed impossible for a city or kingdom, if civil justice and what is useful are to be preserved.

units.la: Amplius talium principatuum pluralitate suppositia, omnis communis utilitas turbaretur, cum enim principantes frequenter praecipere debeant, ciuium praecipue vacantium congregationem, propter communia conferentia inquirenda & determinanda, vel propter incommoda & emergentia pericula declinanda, vt volentium intrinsecus aut extrinsecus opprimere libertatem communem. Qua quidem enim ratione conuenire tenentur ciues seu subditi vocati ad mandatum, ad locum & horam vnius talium principatuum, eadem propter mandatum ad locum & horam alterius, cuique hora eadem, loca vero possunt esse diuersa. Et rursum quod volet vnus principatuum proponere, diutius forte ab hoc volet alter, cum tamen in locis diuersis esse simul, nec simul diuersa intendere, possibile videatur.
units.tr: Furthermore, if a plurality of such principates were supposed, all common utility would be disturbed. For since rulers must often command the assembly of citizens, especially of those who are at leisure, in order to seek out and determine common advantages, or to avert inconveniences and emerging dangers, lest those who wish to oppress common liberty from within or without should succeed. For the same reason that citizens or subjects are bound to assemble, when summoned by command, at the place and hour of one of these principates, they would be bound by command to the place and hour of another, and at the same hour, though the places might be different. And again, what one of the principates wishes to propose, the other may perhaps wish otherwise, although it seems possible to be in different places at the same time and not to intend different things at the same time.

units.la: Rursum contingeret ex hoc ciuium seu subditorum sectio, & oppositio, pugna & separatio, demumque ciuitatis corruptio, volentibus quibusdam ipsorum vni principatuum obedire, quibusdam vero alteri. Inter principatus quoque inuicem, propter velle supergredi quemcunque ipsorum ad alterum. Adhuc principatuum ad ciues vel subditos sibi recusantes subesse. Et amplius principatibus diffidentibus, aut inuicem contendentibus, & iudice superiori carentibus, oriuntur scandala supradicta.
units.tr: Again, from this there would arise a division and opposition among citizens or subjects, fighting and separation, and finally the corruption of the city, some wishing to obey one principate and some another. Among the principates themselves there would be rivalry, each wishing to surpass the other. Further, principates would have to govern citizens or subjects who refused to be subject to them. And moreover, when principates distrust one another or contend with each other, and lack a superior judge, the aforesaid scandals arise.

units.la: Rursum suppositia pluralitate hac, erit aliquid maximorum secundum rationem & artem, otiosum atque superfluum, nam per vnicum principatum, aut supremum vnicum, perfecte haberi potest quicquid ciuilis utilitatis haberetur ex pluribus, absque nocumentis consequentibus pluralitatem ipsorum.
units.tr: Again, with this plurality supposed, something of the greatest idleness and superfluity would exist, according to reason and art; for through one principate, or one supreme principate, whatever civil utility might be had from several can be had perfectly, without the harms that follow from their plurality.

units.la: Amplius horum sic suppositia pluralitate, nullum regnum aut ciuitas erit vna. Haec enim vnum sunt dicuntur, & propter vnitatem principatus, ad quem & propter quem reliquae partes ciuitatis ordinantur omnes, vt etiam apparebit ex his quae continuo dicturi sumus. Rursumque nullus erit ordo partium ciuitatis aut regni, cum ad nullam primam ordinentur, eo quod nulli subiici teneantur, vt liquido apparuit ex prioribus & supradictis rationibus, eritque ipsarum atque totius ciuitatis confusio: eliget enim sibi quod quisque volet officium, vnum aut plura, nullo regulante nec talia separante. Tot quoque sequerentur ad hoc conuenientia, vt ea non facile aut non possibile sit dinumerare.
units.tr: Furthermore, with such a plurality of principates supposed, no kingdom or city would be one. For those things are said to be one which are one by the unity of the principate, to which and for which all the other parts of the city are ordered, as will also appear from what we are about to say next. Moreover there would be no order of the parts of the city or kingdom, since they would not be ordered to any first part, because they would be bound to be subject to none, as has clearly appeared from the earlier and aforesaid arguments; and there would be confusion of these parts and of the whole city. For each would choose for himself whatever office he wished, one or several, with no one regulating them or separating such offices. Many inconveniences would also follow from this, so many that they could not easily or possibly be enumerated.

units.la: Adhuc sicut in composito animali primum precipiens & mouens ipsum motu, secundum locum est vnum, vt in eo libro qui de motibus animalium apparet, quoniam pluribus existentibus his principiis & contraria vel diuersa simul praecipientibus, necesse foret animal aut in contraria ferri vel omnimodo quiescere, & his carere, quae per motum sibi necessaria quaeruntur & commoda. Sicque in ciuitate conuenienter ordinata, quam animali bene formato secundum naturam proportionaliter habere diximus 15. huius. Ideoque velut in animali taliu principiorum otiosa, quinimo nocua foret pluralitas eodem modo in ciuitate firmiter opinandum. Idem autem videre est, intendere volenti de primo alterante in animali, quemadmodum de moyente secundum locum, & in toto similiter ordine mouentium & motorum. Haec autem praetermittantur, quoniam ad naturale pertinet negotium magis, quantum autem sufficiens est, de ipsis diximus ad praesentem consideratione̅m.
units.tr: Further, just as in a composite animal the first mover, which moves the whole by motion, is one (as is shown in that book which is extant on the motions of animals), so if there were several such principles, commanding contrary or different things at once, the animal would either be carried in opposite directions or remain altogether at rest, and would lack those things which it seeks by motion as necessary and advantageous. And so in a city rightly ordered, which we said in the fifteenth chapter of this work should have proportionally the same arrangement as a well-formed animal according to nature, one must likewise hold firmly that a plurality of such principles would be useless, indeed harmful. The same can be seen in the case of the first alterer in an animal, as with the mover of place, and in the whole similar order of movers and things moved. But these matters may be set aside, since they belong more to natural philosophy; and what we have said of them is enough for the present consideration.

units.la: Amplius, quoniam ars omnino aliquâ quidem perficit, quae natura non potest operari, aliâ vero imitatur, vt in secundo physicae scriptum est. In natura vero entium cum sit vnicum numero primum principans non plura, quoniam entia non volunt male disponi, sicut habitum est 12. phylo sophiae primae. Vnus ergo erit tantum primus principatus secundum rationem, & artem humanum institutus. Cum dictis autem rationibus est hoc videre, verum expediens & necessarium experientia cunctis sensata. Quoniam in quo loco seu prouincia vel hominum congregatione principatus, quomodo diximus, defecerit vnitas: haec impossibile videtur bene disponi, quemadmodum de Romanorum regno quasi omnibus euidenter apparet, & in proemialiter dictis aliqualiter monstrabratur.
units.tr: Furthermore, since art accomplishes some things which nature cannot do, and imitates others, as is written in the second book of the Physics; and since in the nature of beings, there being only one first principle that governs, not many (because beings do not wish to be badly disposed, as was shown in the twelfth book of First Philosophy), there will therefore be only one first principle of rule according to reason, and one instituted by human art. That this is so can be seen from the foregoing arguments, and experience, which is perceived by all, shows that it is both useful and necessary. For in whatever place, province or gathering of men the unity of rule has failed, as we have said, this seems impossible to order well; as is almost evidently plain to all in the case of the Roman empire, and has been shown to some extent in what was said at the outset.

units.la: Vtrum autem vniuersitati ciuiliter viuentium, & in orbe totali vnico numero suprememum omnium principatum habere conueniat, aut in diuersis mundi plagis locorum situ quasi necessario separatis, & praecipue in non communicantibus sermone aut moribus, & consuetudine distantibus plurimum, diuersos tales principatus habere conueniat tempore quodam, ad hoc etiam forte monente causa caelesti, ne hominum superflua propagatio fiat, rationabilem habet perscrutationem, aliam tamen ab intentione praesenti. Videretur enim fortasse alicui naturam per pugnas & epidimias hominum & reliquorum animalium moderasse propagationem, vt ad ipsorum educationem arida sufficiat, in quo maxime sustentarentur, dicentes generationem aeternam. Ad propositam tamen nobis redeuntes intentionem, dicamus, ex his quae dicta sunt iam aliqualiter apparere, quae sit numeralis vnitas ciuitatis aut regni, quoniam haec vnitas est ordinis, non simpliciter vnitas, sed pluralitas aliquorum, quae vna dicitur, vel qui aliquid vnum dicuntur numero, non propter hoc quod vnum numero sint formaliter per aliquam formam, sed vnum numero vere dicuntur, propterea quod ad vnum numero dicuntur, scilicet principatum, ad quem & propter quem ordinantur & gubernantur. Ciuitas enim aut regnum non est vnorum per formam aliquam vnicam naturalem, vt compositionis aut commixtionis, quoniam eius partes seu officia, & harum partium suppositia siue partes, sunt multa in actu & separata inuicem numero formaliter, quoniam loco atque subiecto. Vnde nec sunt vnum per aliquid formaliter inlatens vnum, nec pertangens vnum, aut ea continens velut murus. Roma nanque cum Maguntia & reliquis communitatibus, sunt vnum regnum seu imperium numero, non aliter tamen nisi quia vnaquaeque istarum ordinata est per voluntatem ad vnum numero principatum supremum. Quo etiam quasi modo mundus dicitur vnus numero, non plures mundi, non quidem propter formam aliquam vnicam numeralem formaliter vniuersis entibus inhaerentem, sed propter numeralem vnitatem primi entis, dicuntur omnia entia vnus mundus, quoniam entium quandocunque naturaliter inclinatur, & pendet ab ente primo. Vnde praedicatio qua omnia entia dicuntur vnus mundo numero, non est formaliter alicuius vnitatis numeralis in eis omnibus, neque alicuius vnuei talis dicti secundum vnum, sed est pluralitas quorundam dicta vnum, quia est ad vnum & propter vnum. Sic quoq; vnius ciuitatis aut prouinciae homines dicuntur vna ciuitas aut regnum, quia volunt vnum numero principatum. Nec tamen propter hoc sunt vna pars numero ciuitatis quae sunt vnum regnum aut vna ciuitas numero, quoniam & si hic velint vnum numero principatum, propter quod dicuntur ciuitas aut regnum vnum, quia tamen ad hoc vnum numero per diuersam institutionem actiuam & passiuam referuntur, quae non est aliud quam diuersum praeceptum, eis a principante traditum, per quod diuersum, ad diuersa officia statuuntur. Ex cuius siquidem etiam diuersitate praecepti formaliter sunt isti partes & officia ciuitatis diuersa. Dicitur autem quodlibet officiorum etiam numero vnum vel vna pars ciuitatis numero, non obstante pluralitate numerali suppositorum in ipsis nec quidem per vnum numero inhaerens, sed quoniam ad vnum praeceptum actiuum principantis secundum legalem determinationem referuntur. Ex his aut quae dicta sunt in hoc capitulo nono 12. & 15. huius, concludi potest euidenti demonstratione, nulli personae singulari cuiuscunq; dignitatis aut status existat, neq; collegio cuipiam conuenire principatum seu iurisdictionem aliquam cuiusquam in hoc saeculo coactiuam, nisi per legislatorem diuinum aut humanum immediate sibi tradita fuerit auctoritas ista. Qualis quidem igitur esse debeat vnitas principatus, adhuc aut quae numeralis vnitas ciuitatis aut regni, propter quid et dicatur, & sit numero vnū horum, vnumquodque: amplius de numerali atque specifica vnitate partium seu officiorum ciuitatis ipsarumque ordine, distinctione, ac inuicem separatione, dicta sunt tanta.
units.tr: Whether it is fitting for the whole body of men living in civil society, and throughout the whole world, to have one supreme rule in the single number, or whether it is fitting for them to have several such rulers at a certain time, in different regions of the world which are by their situation almost necessarily separated, and especially among peoples who do not share speech or customs and are very far apart in their habits (perhaps also prompted by some heavenly cause, lest the superfluous propagation of men should occur), is a matter with a reasonable inquiry of its own, but different from our present purpose. For it might perhaps seem to someone that nature has moderated the propagation of men and of the other animals through wars and epidemics, so that the means of their upbringing should suffice, and that by this they should be most sustained, saying that generation is eternal. Returning, however, to the intention we have proposed, let us say that from what has been said it already appears in some measure what the numerical unity of a city or kingdom is: this unity is one of order, not simply unity, but the plurality of certain things which is called one, or which are said to be one in number; not because they are one in number formally through some form, but because they are truly said to be one in number, inasmuch as they are referred to one in number, namely the supreme rule, to which and for the sake of which they are ordered and governed. For a city or kingdom is not one by some single natural form, such as of composition or mixture, since its parts or offices, and the subjects of these parts (or the parts themselves), are many in act and formally separated from one another in number, by place and by subject. Hence they are not one through anything formally inhering in them which makes them one, nor touching them as one, nor containing them like a wall. Thus Rome, together with Mainz and the other communities, is one kingdom or empire in number, yet only in this way: that each of them is ordered by will to one supreme rule in number. In a similar manner the world is said to be one in number, not many worlds; not indeed because of some single numerical form inhering formally in all beings, but on account of the numerical unity of the first being, all beings are said to be one world, since they are always naturally inclined toward and depend upon the first being. Hence the predication by which all beings are said to be one world in number is not a formal numerical unity in all of them, nor a unity of such a kind said of them in respect of one thing, but a plurality of certain things called one, because it is directed to one and for the sake of one. So too the men of one city or province are said to be one city or kingdom, because they will one supreme rule in number. Yet for this reason they are not one part in number of the city, those who together form one kingdom or one city in number; for although they here will one supreme rule, by which they are called one city or kingdom, nevertheless, since they are referred to this one in number through a different active and passive institution, which is nothing other than a different precept handed down to them by the ruler, by which they are appointed to different offices, therefore the parts and offices of the city are formally different from this very diversity of precept. Each of the offices is also called one in number, or one part of the city in number, notwithstanding the numerical plurality of the subjects within them, and not because of any one number inhering in them, but because they are referred to the one active precept of the ruler according to legal determination. From what has been said in this chapter, and from the ninth, twelfth and fifteenth chapters of this work, it can be concluded by evident demonstration that no single person of whatever dignity or status, nor any college whatsoever, is fitting for supreme rule or any coercive jurisdiction in this age, unless that authority has been handed to it immediately by a divine or human lawgiver. What kind of unity of rule ought to exist, and what the numerical unity of a city or kingdom is, why each of these is called one and is one in number: concerning the numerical and specific unity of the parts or offices of the city, and their order, distinction and mutual separation, so much has been said.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: De principantis correctione, & propter quam causam, qualiter, & a quibus, legem transgredientes debet arceri.
units.tr: On the correction of the ruler, and for what cause, in what manner, and by whom those who transgress the law ought to be restrained.

units.la: Dictum est autem a nobis in prioribus, correctiones aut totaliter mutationes principatuum, ad legislatore pertinere quemadmodum institutiones ipsorum de quib. merito dubitabit aliquis, vtrum videlicet principantes expediat corrigere per iudicium & potentiam coactiuam. Et si expediat, vtrum propter excessum qualecunq;, aut solum propter quosdam quidem sic, propter alios vero minime.
units.tr: It has been said by us earlier that the correction, or the total change, of rulers belongs to the lawgiver, just as their institution does; and about these matters someone may rightly doubt whether it is expedient to correct rulers by judgment and coercive power, and, if it is, whether this should be done for any kind of excess, or only for certain excesses and not for others.

units.la: Adhuc etiam cuius aut quorum in ipsos sit talia ferre iudicia, & iudiciorum executiones explere per potentiam coactiuam, cum in prioribus dictum sit ad solos principantes pertinere, ferre ciuiles sententias, legumque transgressores per coactiuam arcere potentiam.
units.tr: Further, there is the question of whose right it is to pass such judgments on rulers and to carry out the execution of those judgments by coercive power; for it was said above that only the rulers themselves have the right to pronounce civil sentences and to restrain the transgressors of the laws by coercive power.

units.la: Nos autem dicamus, quod principans per suam actionem secundum legem & sibi datam autoritatem, regula est atque mensura cuiuslibet ciuilis actus, quemadmodum cor in animali, vt satis ostensum est 15. huius. Quod si principans aliam formam non reciperet praeter legem, autoritatem, & desiderium agendi secundum illam, nunquam minus debitam, aut corrigibilem seu mensurabile ab aliquo faceret actionem. Et ideo tam ipse quam eius actio sic esset mensura cuiusliber ciuilis actus aliorum a se, & nequaquam ab aliis mensuratus, quemadmodum cor bene formatum in animali. Quod quidem, quoniam formam non recipit, per quam inclinetur ad actionem contrariam actioni, quae prouenire habet a virtute sua & calore naturali, semper conuenientem agit actionem naturaliter, contrariam vero minime, propter quod sic regulat & mensurat per suam influentiam seu actionem reliquas partium animalis, quod ab ipsis nullatenus regulatur, nec ipsarum influentiam recipit aliquam. Verum quia principans homo existens, habet intellectum & appetitum, potentes recipere formas alias, vt falsam aestimationem aut peruersum desiderium vel vtrumque, secundum quas contingit ipsum agere contraria eorum, quae lege determinata sunt, propterea secundum has actiones redditur principans mensurabilis ab aliquo habente autoritatem mensurandi, seu regulandi secundum legem, ipsum aut eius actiones legem transgressas, alioquin despoticus fieret quilibet principatus, & ciuium vita seruilis & insufficiens, quod est inconueniens fugiendum, vt exterminatis a nobis apparuit quinto & 11. huius. Debet autem iudicium, praeceptum, & executio cuiuscunque correptionis principantis iuxta illius demeritum seu transgressionem fieri per legislatorem, vel per aliquem aut aliquos legislatoris autoritate statutos, ad hoc, vt demonstratum est 12. & 15. huius. Conuenit etiam pro tempore aliquo, corrigendi principantis officiu suspendere ad illum maxime aut illos, qui de ipsius transgressione debuerint iudicare, ne propter tunc pluralitatem principatus contingeret in communitate schisma, concitatio, & pugna: Et quoniam non corrigitur inquantum principans, sed tanquam subditus transgressor legis. Secundum haec itaque ingredientes ad quaesitas dubitationes dicamus, quod excessus principantis vel grauis est aut modicus adhuc, vel est de possibilibus euenire frequenter, aut raro tantummodo. Amplius vel est de lege determinatis aut non. Si vero grauis fuerit principantis ex- cessus vt in rempublicam, aut insignem vel aliam quamcunque personam, ex quo per correp- tionis omissionem, posset verisimiliter scandalum, aut populi concitatio generari, siue sit euenientium in pluribus siue raro, corrigi debet propter ipsum principans. Ex ipso enim non vindicato possibilis esset in populo concitatio, & politiae turbatio atque solutio. Siquidem lege determinatus, secundum legem corrigendus, si vero non, secundum legislatoris sententiam, & lege debet determinari quantum possibile fuerit, vt ostensum est a nobis undecimo huius.
units.tr: We, however, say that the ruler, by his action according to the law and the authority given to him, is the rule and measure of every civil act, just as the heart is in an animal, as was sufficiently shown in the fifteenth book of this work. If the ruler admitted no other form than the law, the authority, and the desire to act according to it, he would never perform an action that was less than due, or that could be corrected or measured by anyone. And so he himself and his action would thus be the measure of every civil act of others, and in no way measured by others, just as a well-formed heart is in an animal. Since it receives no form by which it could be inclined to an action contrary to the action which arises from its own power and natural heat, it always performs a fitting action naturally, and never a contrary one; and so it regulates and measures the remaining parts of the animal by its influence or action, while it is in no way regulated by them, nor receives any influence from them. But because the ruler, being a man, has intellect and appetite, able to receive other forms, such as a false estimation, a perverse desire, or both, by which it happens that he acts contrary to what is determined by law, on account of these actions the ruler becomes measurable by someone who has the authority to measure or regulate him according to the law, so that he, or his actions, which transgress the law, may be checked. Otherwise every principality would become despotic, and the life of the citizens servile and wretched, which is an inconvenience to be avoided, as was made clear by us in the fifth and eleventh books of this work. Moreover, the judgment, the precept, and the execution of any correction of a ruler, in accordance with his demerit or transgression, must be carried out by the lawgiver, or by someone or some persons appointed by the authority of the lawgiver, as was demonstrated in the twelfth and fifteenth books. It is also fitting, for some time, to suspend the office of correcting the ruler, especially for those who ought to judge his transgression, lest on account of the plurality of rulers at that time there should arise schism, agitation, and strife in the commonwealth; and this because he is not corrected in so far as he is a ruler, but as a subject who has transgressed the law. Accordingly, coming now to the questions raised, we say that an excess of a ruler is either grave or still slight, and that it is either likely to occur frequently or only rarely. Again, it is either determined by law or not. If, however, the excess of the ruler is grave, whether against the commonwealth, or against some notable person or any other person, so that by omitting correction there could probably arise scandal or agitation among the people, then the ruler must be corrected on account of it, whether such an excess occurs in many cases or rarely. For from an unpunished excess there could arise agitation among the people and disturbance and dissolution of the state. If it is determined by law, it must be corrected according to the law; if not, according to the sentence of the lawgiver; and it must be determined by law as far as possible, as we showed in the eleventh book.

units.la: Quod si principantis excessus paruus fuerit, aut est de raro euenientibus & a principante raro commissus, aut est de posibilibus euenire frequenter, & per principantem saepe commissus. Quod si a principante raro committatur aut committi possit, debet potius sub dissimulatione transiri, quam ex eo principans corrigi. Quoniam si ex quolibet excessu raro contingenti & paruo, corrigatur principans, contemptibilis redditur, quod in commune nocumentum non modicum redundans est, eo quod legi & principanti ex hoc eius minus exhibent reuerentiae atque obedientiae. Rursum quoniam nolente principe pro modico quolibet correptionem subire propter id sibi ad paruipensionem reputare, poterit inde oriri scandalum graue, cum tamen tale aliquid non sit in communitatibus refricandum, ex quo euidens utilitas prouenire non potest, sed potius nocumentum.
units.tr: But if the excess of the ruler is slight, and either is of the kind that rarely happens and is rarely committed by the ruler, or is of the kind that can happen frequently and is often committed by the ruler. If it is rarely committed, or can be committed only rarely by the ruler, it ought rather to be passed over with dissimulation than the ruler be corrected for it. For if the ruler were corrected for any slight excess that rarely occurs, he would be rendered contemptible, which would be no small harm to the common good, since people would thereby show less reverence and obedience to the law and to the ruler. Again, if the ruler does not wish to undergo correction for any slight matter, and on that account regards it as a trifle, a grave scandal may arise from it; yet such a thing should not be stirred up in communities, from which no evident advantage can come, but rather harm.

units.la: Haec autem fuit in hoc Aristotelis aperta sententia. 2. politicae, cap. 4. cum dixit: Manifestum, quod sinendum quadam peccata legislatoribus & principibus. Non enim tantum proderit qui mutauerit quantum nocebit, principibus rebellare assuescens. Intellexit autem ibidem per legislatorem latam legem, quam si obseruare consueuerint homines, dicit non esse mutandam propter modicum in eo corrigendum, sed sinendam, eo quod legum frequens mutatio robur ipsarum debilitat, consuetudinem scilicet obediendi atque seruandi, quae praecipiuntur in ipsis. Unde idem eodem libro & cap. Lex nullum robur habet ad persuaderi praeter consuetudinem, vt videlicet a subditis obseruetur, maximum est consuetudo. In quo etiam consimile est de reuerentia & obedientia principantis. Si vero excessus principantis magnitudine modicus sit, possibilis euenire frequenter, lege determinandus est, & in eo saepe delinquens principans per conuenientem poenam debet arceri. Nam excessus huiusmodi quantumcunque modicus saepe commissus, notabiliter laederet politiam sicuti & substantias, id est diuitias paruas expensae consumunt, saepe factae. Verum enim & omnia, non paruum sed componitur ex paruis, vt scriptum est quinto politicae, cap. 4. De correctione itaque principaturi, & quibus ex causis, determinatum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: This was indeed the clear opinion of Aristotle in this matter, in the second book of the Politics, chapter 4, when he said: "It is manifest that certain faults must be tolerated in lawgivers and rulers; for he who changes will not benefit so much as he will harm, by accustoming men to rebel against rulers." He understood there by "lawgiver" the law that has been enacted, which, if men have been accustomed to observe it, he says is not to be changed on account of a small matter to be corrected in it, but is to be tolerated; because frequent change of laws weakens their strength, namely the habit of obeying and keeping what is commanded in them. Hence in the same book and chapter: "A law has no strength to persuade except custom"; for custom is the greatest thing in ensuring that a law is observed by the subjects. In this respect too the case is similar with the reverence and obedience owed to the ruler. But if the excess of the ruler is slight in magnitude, and possible to occur frequently, it must be determined by law, and the ruler, who often offends in it, must be restrained by a suitable penalty. For an excess of this kind, however slight, if often committed, would notably harm the state, just as small expenses, often repeated, consume wealth and substance: "For the whole is not made of small things, but is composed of small things," as is written in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 4. Thus has it been determined concerning the correction of the ruler, and for what causes.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: De causis factiuis tranquillitatis & intranquillitatis ciuitatis aut regni, & ea quæ praeter fo-litos modos singulariter regna conturbat, & de continuatione dictionis prima ad secundam.
units.tr: On the efficient causes of the tranquillity and unrest of a city or kingdom, and on those things which disturb kingdoms in an unusual manner beyond the customary modes, and on the continuation of the discourse from the first part to the second.

units.la: RE liquum autem & vltimum huius dictionis est, ex prioribus determinationibus inferre causas tranquillitatis & sui oppositi in ciuitate vel regno. Hoc enim fuit quæsitorum principale, secundum propositam nobis à principio intentionem. Et primum quidem ostendemus has causas inesse communi, singularem ipsarum determinationem, quæ solito modo proueniunt ab Aristotele in quinto siue in politica, supponentes. His consequenter sermonem faciemus determinatu in specie de insolita causa discordiæ seu in tranquillitatis ciuilium regiminum, quam in dictis procemialiter dudum turbasse diximus vexare atque turbare continuo magis Italicum regnum.
units.tr: It remains, as the final point of this discourse, to infer from the earlier determinations the causes of tranquillity and of its opposite in a state or kingdom. This was the principal object of our inquiry, according to the intention we set out at the beginning. First we shall show that these causes are present in the commonwealth in general, supposing their particular determination, which arise in the usual way, as Aristotle set out in the fifth book, or in the Politics. After these we shall speak in detail about the unusual cause of discord, which we said in the introductory remarks has long disturbed, and continually more and more troubles and harasses the Italian kingdom.

units.la: Resumere autem oportet propter hæc tranquillitatis & sui oppositi descriptiones iam dictas secundo huius. Erit enim tranquillitas bona dispositio ciuitatis aut regni, qua potest vnaquaque suarum partium facere opera conuenientia sibi secundum rationem & suam institutionē. Ex qua quidem descriptione apparet ipsius natura, Cum enim dicitur bona dispositio, notatur ipsius intrinseca quiditas generalis. In eo vero quod per ipsam dicitur vnaquaque partium ciuitatis posse agere sibi opera conuenientia, significatur eius finis, qui etiam ipsius propriam quiditatem seu differentiam intelligere facit: ipsa vero cum forma seu dispositio quædam sit ciuitatis aut regni, nec amplius vna quam regnum & ciuitatem esse diximus 17. huius parte vndecima & duodecima, non habet formalem causam, hoc enim proprium est compositorum, ipsius autem agentem causam facile comprehendere possumus ex dictis 15. huius, & aliis, quæ ipsam necessario consequuntur in ciuitate vel regno, hæc nempe sunt ciuium conuersatio mutua & communicatio ipsorum inuicem suorum operum, mutuumque auxilium atque iuuamentum, generaliterque suorum operum & communium exercendi ab extrinseco non impedita potestas, participatio quoque communium commodorum & hominum secundum conuenientem vnicuique mensurā. Et cum his cætera cōmoda & desiderabilia expressa in oratione Cassiodori, quam posuimus initium huius libri. Quorum quidem omnium aut præcipuorum quorundam contrariam intranquillitatem seu discordiam illi oppositam consequentur.
