Cum igitur actio debita principantis, sit omnium ciuilium commodorum & prædictorum causa efficiens & conseruans, vt demonstratum est 15. huius, parte 11. & 12. erit ipsa tranquillitatis causa factiua, & hoc sensit Apostolus indubie, dum dixit ad Timotheum primæ, cap. 2. Obsecro igitur primum fieri obsecrationes, &c. pro regibus & omnibus qui in sublimitate sunt, vt quietam & tranquillam vitam agamus. Quod vero huius partis actionem per se impediuerit ab eo ciuitatis intranquillitas seu discordia, proueniit tanquam causa factiua. Quæ siquidem genere visa, & si per plures species varietur & modos, de quibus Aristoteles ab actione solita prouenientibus sufficientem, vt dicere est, notitiam fecit in quinto Ciuilis scientia, quam politicam diximus. Est tamen intranquillitatis seu discordiæ ciuitatum seu regnorum insolita causa quædam, occasionaliter sumpta propter effectum à diuina causa productum præter solitam omnem eius actionem in rebus, quem vt in dictis procemialiter tetigisse meminimus, nec Aristoteles aut philosophantium alter sui temporis vel prioris conspicere potuit. Hæc autem dudum hactenus & nunc amplius continuo actionem debitam principantis impediens in Italico regno, ipsum pace seu tranquillitate, cæterisque ipsam consequentibus, & iam dictis commodis priuauit & priuat, omniq; incommodo vexauit & vexat, & quasi omnis generis miseria & iniquitate repleuit. Cuius quidem impedientis singulariter causæ propter consuetudinem malignitatis occultæ secundum nobis à principio propositam intentionem, naturam in specie determinare debentes, reminisci oportet eorum quæ diximus sexto huius, Quod videlicet Dei filius vnā trium personarum verus Deus, propter delictum transgressionis primorum parentum, & consequenter totius humani generis lapsum reparandum, naturam assumpsit humanam, dudum post Aristotelis tempora, Verus homo factus, & idem Deus simul existens, quem Iesum Christum vocatum, adorant Christiani fideles. Hic inquam Christus benedictus Dei filius, Deus & homo simul idem suppositum existens, inter homines iudicii populi ex quibus secundum carnem traxit originem, conuersatus est, veritatem credendorum, agendorum, & fugiendorum, ad vitam æternam hominibus consequendam, & miseriam declinandam docere cœpit: Propter hæc tandem, Iudæorum malitia & insania, sub Pilato Pontio Cæsaris vicario passus & mortuus, resurrexitque à mortuis die tertia suæ mortis, postmodum in cœlos ascendens, ante tamen propter humani generis salutem quosdam sibi, dum viueret corruptibili vita, collegas in veritatis docendæ ministerium, quos Apostolos dicunt, assumplit, & per vniuersum orbem quam docuerat, & ipsos instruxerat, veritatem prædicare præcepit. Vnde Matthæi 28. & vltimo, post sui resurrectionem dixit ad eos: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti, docentes eos seruare omnia quæcunque mandaui vobis. Per hos inquam apostolos, quorum nomina facta nota sunt apud Christi fideles, & alios quosdam, Christus legem euangelicam conscribi voluit, & per ipsorum dictamina conscri-
units.tr: We must also take up again, for this purpose, the descriptions of tranquillity and of its opposite already given in the second book. Tranquillity will be the good disposition of a state or kingdom, by which each of its parts can perform the works that suit it according to reason and its own institution. From this description its nature appears. For when it is called a good disposition, its intrinsic general quiddity is indicated. In what is said through it, that each part of the state can do the works that suit it, its end is signified, which also makes us understand its own proper quiddity or difference. Since it is a kind of form or disposition of a state or kingdom, and, as we said in the eleventh and twelfth parts of the seventeenth chapter of this book, it is not one more than the kingdom and the state are one, it has no formal cause, for that belongs to composite things. We can easily grasp its efficient cause from what was said in the fifteenth chapter of this book, and from other things that necessarily follow it in a state or kingdom. These are the mutual association of citizens and the sharing of their works among one another, mutual aid and assistance, and in general the power of exercising their own and common works unhindered by outside interference, and also the sharing of common goods and advantages according to a measure fitting for each person. With these go the other advantages and desirable things set out in the speech of Cassiodorus, which we put at the beginning of this book. From all of these, or from some of the chief among them, there follows the opposite restlessness or discord. Therefore, since the proper action of the ruler is the efficient and preserving cause of all civic goods and of those mentioned above, as was shown in the fifteenth chapter, parts eleven and twelve, it will itself be an efficient cause of tranquillity. The Apostle undoubtedly understood this when he said to Timothy in the first letter, chapter 2: I exhort therefore that first of all supplications be made, &c., for kings and all who are in high place, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life. That the civic unrest or discord hinders this action of the ruler in itself arises as an efficient cause. This, though seen in its genus, varies through several species and modes, of which Aristotle gave a sufficient account of those arising from the ordinary course of action, as may be said, in the fifth book of the science of civil affairs, which we called the Politics. Yet there is a certain unusual cause of unrest or discord in states and kingdoms, taken occasionally, arising from an effect produced by a divine cause beyond all its customary action in things. As we recall having touched upon it in the introductory remarks, neither Aristotle nor any other philosopher of his time or earlier could observe it. This cause, having long hindered and now continually more and more hindering the proper action of the ruler in the Italian kingdom, has deprived and still deprives it of peace or tranquillity, and of the other things that follow it and of the advantages already mentioned. It has harassed and still harasses it with every kind of disadvantage, and has filled it almost with every kind of misery and iniquity. To determine the nature of this hindering cause in particular, which is in keeping with the intention we set out at the beginning and with the habit of hidden malignity, we must recall what we said in the sixth chapter of this book: that the Son of God, one of the three persons and true God, in order to repair the transgression of our first parents and consequently the fall of the whole human race, took upon himself human nature, becoming true man, long after the time of Aristotle, and at the same time remaining God. Christian believers adore him, calling him Jesus Christ. This Christ, I say, the blessed Son of God, God and man at once, one and the same person, lived among men, among the people of Judaea from whom he took his origin according to the flesh. He began to teach the truth of what is to be believed, done and avoided, so that men might attain eternal life and avoid misery. At length, because of these things, through the malice and madness of the Jews, he suffered and died under Pontius Pilate, vicar of Caesar. He rose from the dead on the third day after his death, and afterwards ascended into heaven. But before this, for the salvation of the human race, while he lived in mortal life, he took to himself certain colleagues in the ministry of teaching the truth, whom they call Apostles, and commanded them to preach throughout the whole world the truth which he had taught them and in which he had instructed them. Hence in Matthew 28, at the end, after his resurrection, he said to them: Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. Through these apostles, I say, whose names are made known among Christ's faithful, and some others, Christ willed the gospel law to be written, and through their dictation it was written.

units.la: {1} 1. Ex parte. conceptum fuit volut pro organa quaedam, ad hoc mota & directa immediate diuina virtute, per quam siquidem legem praecepta & consilia salutis aeternae in ipsius Christi atque apostolorum & euangelistarum ... prehendere valeremus. In qua etiam & secundum quam sacramen-ta culpae originalis ... mundatiua, diuinae gratiae factiua & conseruatiua, illiusque amissae reformatiua, huiusque legis ministrorum institutiua, signauit & statuit. Huius quoque legis doctores, & sacramentorum secundum ipsam ministros primum instituit iam dictos apostolos, ipsis per spiritum sanctum authoritatem huius mysterii conferens, quam sacerdotalem appellant Christi fideles. Per quam siquidem iisdem aut ipsorum successoribus in hoc officio, non aliis, potestatem contulit sub certa forma verborum ab ipsis & eorum singulis dicta, transubstantiandi panem & vinum in verum corpus & sanguinem eius: Cum hoc etiam ipsis authoritatem soluendi atque ligandi homines a peccatis, quam dicere solent clauium potestatem, sibique alios subrogandi cum eadem authoritate concessit. Quam etiam authoritatem apostoli quibusdam contulerunt, aut Deus per ipsos orantes & manus aliis imponentes. Sic quoque reliqui potestatem faciendi susceperunt, & consequenter fecerunt, faciunt, & facient vsque ad seculi consummationem. Quo etiam modo apostolus Paulus Timotheum, Titum, & aliorum plures instituit atque instituere docuit. Vnde primae ad Timotheum quarto: Noli negligere gratiam quae in te est, quae data est tibi per prophetiam cum impositione manuum presbyterii. Et ad Titum primo: Huius gratia reliqui te Creta, vt quae desunt corrigas, & constituas per ciuitates presbyteros, sicut ego tibi disposui. Et est haec authoritas sacerdotalis & clauium siue vnica siue plures, character seu forma quaedam animae per immediatam Dei actionem impressa.
units.tr: {1} 1. From the part. It was conceived as certain instruments, moved and directed immediately by divine power, through which we might be able to grasp the precepts and counsels of eternal salvation in Christ himself and in the apostles and evangelists ... In which law, and according to which, he also appointed and established the sacraments: cleansing from original sin, effecting and preserving divine grace, restoring what had been lost, and instituting the ministers of this law ... He also first instituted the aforesaid apostles as teachers of this law and as ministers of its sacraments, conferring on them through the Holy Spirit the authority of this mystery, which the Christian faithful call priestly. Through it he gave to these men, or to their successors in this office, and to no others, the power, under a certain form of words spoken by them and by each of them, of transubstantiating bread and wine into his true body and blood. With this he also granted them the authority of loosing and binding men from sins, which they usually call the power of the keys, and of substituting others in their place with the same authority. The apostles also conferred this authority on certain men, or God did so through them, as they prayed and laid hands on others. In this way the rest received the power of doing these things, and consequently have done, do now, and will do until the consummation of the age. In the same way the apostle Paul instituted and taught others to institute Timothy, Titus, and many more. Hence in the first letter to Timothy, chapter 4: Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. And in the letter to Titus, chapter 1: For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking, and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you. And this sacerdotal authority and power of the keys, whether one or several, is a certain character or form impressed on the soul by the immediate action of God.

units.la: Est autem et authoritas alia quaedam sacerdotii, humana concessione tradita, ipsoque multiplicato iam numero, propter scandalum euitandum, & haec authoritas est inter ipsos vnius praeminentia super alios dirigendos in templo ad cultum diuinum, debite fiendum & ordinandum seu distribuendum de quibusdam temporalibus, quae ad vsum ministrorum praedictorum statuta sunt. De cuius quidem authoritatis potestate factiua, & unde deriuetur, sufficienter dicetur decimoquinto & decimoseptimo secunda, quoniam non fit haec per Deum immediate, sed per hominum voluntatem & mentem, quemadmodum officia cetera ciuitatis.
units.tr: There is also another authority of the priesthood, handed on by human concession, the number of those holding it having now been multiplied, in order to avoid scandal. This authority consists in the preeminence of one among others in directing the due performance and ordering, or distributing, of divine worship in the temple, and of certain temporal goods that have been appointed for the use of the aforesaid ministers. Concerning the efficient power of this authority, and whence it derives, it will be sufficiently said in the fifteenth and seventeenth chapters of the second book, since this does not come about immediately through God, but through the will and mind of men, just as the other offices of the state do.

units.la: Sicut aque repetito & aliqualiter declarato ministrorum ecclesiasticorum origine, ac ipsorum officii potestate factiua, oportet amplius attendere, quod inter apostolos Christi praedictos, fuit vnus nomine Simon, cognomine vero Petrus, qui a Christo authoritatis clauium promissionem primus accepit, sicut dicit Glossa secundum Augustinum, Matthaei decimosexto super illud Christi oraculum: Et tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, inquit Glossa: Qui prae caeteris confessus est, Iesum Christum sciicet esse verum Dei filium, prae caeteris dotatur clauibus, id est ante caeteros. Hic siquidem apostolus post Christi passionem, resurrectionem, & in coelum ascensionem, peruenit Antiochia, & ibidem factus fuit episcopus per populum, sicuti ex ipsius liquet historia. Inde vero, vt habet historia supra dicta quaecunque causa fuerit praetermissa, quoniam de hoc sunt diuersae sententiae, postmodum Romam profectus est, & ibidem Christi fidelibus praefuit episcopus, tandem vero propter Christi professionem & diuinam praedicationem, obtruncato capite mortuus est, & cum eodem, eadem hora & loco Paulus Apostolus secundum supradictam historiam. Ex praerogativa igitur quam hic discipulus seu apostolus ad alios visus est habere, vt quia prae caeteris dotatus fuit clauibus propter inductam scripturae verba, & alia quaedam Christo singulariter sibi dicta, quae etiam in sequentibus adducentur. Episcoporum aliqui post ipsum in apostolica seu episcopali sede Romana, maxime circa tempora Constantini Romanorum imperatoris, se dicunt & asseruunt praesse quantum ad omnimodam iurisdictionis authoritatem, reliquis omnibus episcopis & presbyteris mundi, & ipsorum moderniores aliqui non solum his, verum etiam omnibus mundi principibus, communitatibus, & singulis personarum, licet hoc non aequaliter de omnibus exprimant, nec explicite dicant, vt de principe Romanorum imperatore vocato, & cuncti prouinciis ac ciuitatibus & personis subiectis eidem. Huius quamuis secundum veritatem dominii, seu coactiuae iurisdictionis in hunc principem expressio singularis, faciem & exordium primum sumpsisse videatur. Ex quodam edicto & dono, quod quidam dicunt per Constantinum fuisse factum beato Syluestro Romano pontifici. Quod quia donum seu priuilegium illud non habet hoc clare, aut quoniam ex post factis expirauit fortasse vel etiam quia inualidum existens, ad reliquos mundi principes, nisi eum qui Romanorum in omnibus prouinciis illius priuilegii seu concessionis ...
units.tr: Having repeated and somewhat explained the origin of the ecclesiastical ministers and the power by which they act, we must also note that among the aforementioned apostles of Christ there was one named Simon, surnamed Peter, who was the first to receive from Christ the promise of the keys of authority. So the Gloss says, following Augustine, on Matthew 16 at Christ's saying: And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. The Gloss says: He who confessed before the others that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God was endowed with the keys before the others, that is, before them. This apostle, after Christ's passion, resurrection and ascension into heaven, came to Antioch and was made bishop there by the people, as his history makes clear. From there, as the history cited above says, for whatever reason (since there are differing opinions on this), he afterwards went to Rome and presided there as bishop over Christ's faithful. At last, on account of his confession of Christ and his divine preaching, he was beheaded and died, and at the same hour and place as Paul the Apostle, according to the history cited. Because of this pre-eminence, this disciple or apostle seems to have had over the others, since he was endowed with the keys before the rest on account of the words of Scripture quoted, and certain other things said to him by Christ alone, which will also be cited in what follows, some of the bishops after him in the apostolic or episcopal see of Rome, especially around the time of Constantine, Emperor of the Romans, say and assert that they preside, with full authority of jurisdiction, over all the other bishops and presbyters of the world. Some of the more recent of them claim this not only over these but also over all the princes of the world, the communities, and each individual person, although they do not all express this equally or state it explicitly, as when they speak of the prince called the Roman emperor and of all the provinces, cities and persons subject to him. Although the express claim to true dominion, or coercive jurisdiction, over this prince seems to have taken its face and first beginning from a certain edict and gift which some say was made by Constantine to the blessed Sylvester, Roman pontiff. Because that gift or privilege does not state this clearly, or perhaps has lapsed through later events, or even because it was invalid, [it does not extend] to the other princes of the world, except to him who is the Roman [prince] in all the provinces of that privilege or grant ...

units.la: Ideoque ... iurisdictionem hanc coactiuam orbi vniuersali; sibi alio quodam omnes comprehendere moderatores Romanorum assumpserunt episcopi, Plenitudinem potestatis videlicet, quae ... per Christum, beato Petro, eiusque successoribus in Romana episcopali sede, vt vicarii. Christus enim vt aiunt & vere, fuit Rex regum & dominus dominantium, super omnium personarum & rerum. Quamuis ex hoc minime sequarur quod volunt intelligere, vt in sequentibus certitudinaliter apparebit. Est igitur huius tituli ... Romanae episcopi, quod sicut Christus plenitudinem potestatis & iurisdictionis ... principes, communitates, collegia, & singulares personas, sic & ipsi qui ... Petri se dicunt vicarios hanc habeant plenitudinem coactiuae iurisdictionis, humana lege nulla determinatam.
units.tr: Therefore ... the bishops of Rome have assumed for themselves this coercive jurisdiction over the whole universal world, and by some other means have claimed to comprehend all rulers, namely the fullness of power, which ... was given by Christ to the blessed Peter and to his successors in the Roman episcopal see, as vicars. For Christ, as they say, and truly, was King of kings and Lord of lords over all persons and things. Yet it does not at all follow from this what they wish to understand, as will clearly appear in what follows. There is therefore, in this title ... of the bishop of Rome, that just as Christ [holds] the fullness of power and jurisdiction over ... princes, communities, colleges, and individual persons, so also those who ... call themselves vicars of Peter have this fullness of coercive jurisdiction, determined by no human law.

units.la: Signum autem huius tituli plenitudinis suæ potestatis, scilicet Romanos episcopos eum quem diximus intendere sensum. Euidens est, quod Clemens quidam nomine, Clementium quintus Rom. episcopus sic eo vtitur in quodam suo edicto seu decretali, de sen. & re iudicata, libro sepsimo, ad Henricum Henricorum 7. diuæ memoriæ Romanorum Imperatorem nouissimum, dum ipsius felicis Henrici quandam reuocādo sententiam, inter cætera protulit seriem, quod diximus de ipsorum sensu circa prædictum titulum exprimentem. Hanc vero inducere omnimus propter rei notitiam, & sermonis abbreuiationem. Et quoniam ad propositum magis, inducemus 15. secunda, parte 18. Cum igitur Christus non magis sit aut fuerit rex, & dominus Romanorum Imperatoris, quam regis aut principis alterius cuiuscunque, quinimo ipsorum æque vel magis, quoniam & tempore Christi, Romanus princeps monarch zabat vbique terrarum, palam est huius tituli sensum ex eiusdem virtute radicis, ad omnes principatus extendi. Quem etiam per ipsum, Episcopos Romanos intendere, manifeste nos docet octaui Bonifacii Romanorum episcopi, contra Philippum Pulchrum claræ memoriæ regem Francorum, attentario contentiosa de his, & inde subiecuta eiusdem Bonifacii decretalis, inducta vigesima huius, parte octaua. Per quam siquidem omnem humanam creaturam coactiua iurisdictione subiectam fore Romano pontifici diffinit esse credendum de necessitate salutis æterna. Hocigitur modo ad hæc ingredientes Romanorum episcopi, primum quidem sub specie quærendæ pacis inter Christi fideles quosdam excommunicauerunt, ipsorum nolentes parere sententiæ, deinde vero in ipsos realem & personalem ferendo sententiam, in quosdam quidem magis expresse, vt qui minus ipsorum potentiæ resistere possunt, velut Italicorum singulares personas & communitates, quorum regnum diuisum & laceratum, in omnibus quasi partibus suis facilius opprimi potest, in quoddam vero remisse magis, veluti reges & principes, quorum resistentiam & coactiuam formidant potentiam. Ad hos tamen paulatim serpunt & serpere continuo tentant in iurisdictionum vsurpatione totum simul inaudentes inuadere, propter quod etiam Romanorum principes, & populos sibi subiectos, hactenus latuit horum subintrans prævaricatio. Paulatim nanque iurisdictionem post aliam occupauerunt episcopi Romanorum, maxime imperiali sede vacante. Sic tamen vt iam sibi totalem supra eundem principem iurisdictionem coactiuam temporalem habere se dicant. Quorum nouissime atque manifestissime modernus iam dictorum episcopus, ad Romanorum principem tam in Italicorum prouinciis quam Germanorum, ad omnes quoque iam dictarum prouinciarum inferiores principes, communitates, collegia, & personas singulares cuiuscunque dignitatis & conditionis existant, ac super omnia iplorum feudalia & reliqua temporalia, supremam iurisdictionem se scripsit habere, ipsorumque principatus dandi & transferendi, potestatem sibi palam ascribens, vt liquido patere potest omnibus, ex huius episcopi quibusdam scripturis, quas vocat edicta siue sententias. Hæcitaque Romanorum quorundam episcoporum existimatio non recta & peruersa fortassis affectio principatus, quem sibi deberi asserunt ex eisdem, vt dicunt, per Christum tradita plenitudine potestatis, causa est singularis illa, quam intranquillitatis, seu discordiæ ciuitatis aut regni factiuam diximus, ipsa enim in omnia regna serpere prona, quemadmodum procemialiter dicebatur infesta sui actione, dudum vexauit Italicum regnum, & à sui tranquillitate seu pace prohibuit, prohibetque continuo: principantis scilicet Imperatoris Romani promotionem seu institutionem, ipsiusque actionem in dicto imperio, sui toto conamine prohibendo. Cuius siquidem actionis cæcentia, iustificationis scilicet ciuilium actuum, iniuriæ ac contentiones euenient facile. Quæ regula iustitiæ siue legis non mensuratæ propter mensurantis abscentiam, pugnas causant, vnde ciuium separationes demumque Italicarum politiarum seu ciuilitatum solutiones contigerunt, quemadmodum diximus. Opinione igitur hac, & affectione fortasse, quam diximus principandi, Romanus episcopus iurisdictione coactiua seu temporali subiectum facere sibi nititur principem Romanorum, qui nec iure debet, vt ex sequentibus palam monstrabitur, nec eidem tali iudicio subiici vult. Vnde tanta lis & discordia suborta est, vt non sine magno discrimine animarum & corporum, ac rerum dispendio possit extingui. Non enim Romano vel alteri episcopo, aut cuiquam spirituali ministro, inquantum huiusmodi, in quenquam, cuiuscunque conditionis, singularem personam, communitatem vel collegium aliquod conuenit officium principatus coactiui, quemadmodum determinatum est 15. & 17. huius. Et hoc de sacerdotio in qualihet lege siue secta, sensit Aristoteles quarto politicæ, cum dixit: Propter quod non omnes, neque electos neque fortiales ponendum principes, puta sacerdotes primo. Hoc enim aliquid præter politicos principatus ponendum, &c. Sunt autem hæc politica curarum, id est officiorum, &c. Et paruum infra subdit: Hæc autem iconomica sunt. Quodque perniciosa pestis hæc humanæ quieti atque felicitati suæ omni aduersans penitus ex eiusdem vitio corruptæ radicis, reliqua mundi regna fidelium Christianorum maxime posset inficere, ipsam repellere omnium necessariissimum arbitror, quemadmodum procemialiter dictum est. Primum quidem opinionis iam dictæ tanquam radicis iam factorum & futurorum malorum, inuolucrum referando, deinde vero ipsius patronos seu inuentores iguaros aut iniustos, ac defensores pertinaces, exteriori opera si oporteat cohibendo. Ad hæc autem obligantur omnes illi obuiare scientes atque potentes, quod etiam negligentes aut omittentes iniusti sunt. Teste Tullio primo de officiis, capitulo quinto, cum dixit: Iniustitia genera duo sunt, vnum eorum qui inferunt, alterum eorum qui ab his, quibus infertur si possunt,
units.tr: The sign of this title of the fullness of his power, that is, of the Roman bishops, [shows] the sense I have described. It is plain that a certain man named Clement, Clement V, Roman bishop, uses it in a certain edict or decretal, on sentence and res judicata, book seven, addressed to Henry, the last Roman Emperor, Henry VII of blessed memory, when, in revoking a certain judgment of that happy Henry, he put forward among other things a sequence which expresses the sense we have described regarding that title. I have cited this, however, for the sake of knowing the matter and for brevity of speech. And since it is more to the point, I will cite it in the second part, section 18. Since Christ therefore is not and has not been more king and lord of the Roman emperor than of any other king or prince whatever, but rather equally or even less so (for in Christ's time the Roman prince held monarchy everywhere on earth), it is plain that the sense of this title, by the force of its root, extends to all principalities. Pope Boniface VIII, of the Romans, clearly teaches us that this is what the Roman bishops mean, in his dispute against Philip the Fair, king of the Franks of renowned memory, and in the following decretal of the same Boniface, cited in the twentieth section of this part, the eighth. By it he defines that every human creature is subject to the Roman pontiff in coercive jurisdiction, and that it must be believed necessary for eternal salvation. Entering upon these matters in this way, the Roman bishops first, under the pretext of seeking peace among Christ's faithful, excommunicated certain persons who were unwilling to obey their sentence; then, pronouncing a real and personal sentence against them, they did so more openly against some, such as the individual persons and communities of Italy, whose kingdom is divided and torn, and can more easily be oppressed in all its parts; and more mildly against others, such as kings and princes, whose resistance and coercive power they fear. Yet they creep gradually toward these and constantly try to creep further, in the usurpation of jurisdictions, daring to invade everything at once. Because of this, the transgression of these men has until now lain hidden even from the princes of the Romans and the peoples subject to them. For the Roman bishops gradually seized one jurisdiction after another, especially while the imperial see was vacant, yet so that they now claim to have full coercive temporal jurisdiction over that same prince. Most recently and most manifestly, the present bishop of these men has written that he has supreme jurisdiction over the Roman prince, both in the provinces of Italy and of Germany, and likewise over all the inferior princes, communities, colleges and individual persons of the aforesaid provinces, of whatever dignity or condition they are, and over all their feudal and other temporal goods, openly ascribing to himself the power of giving and transferring their principalities. This can be clearly seen by all from certain writings of this bishop, which he calls edicts or sentences. This, then, is the opinion of certain Roman bishops, not right but perverse, and perhaps a corrupt desire of rule which they claim is owed to them, as they say, from the fullness of power handed down to them through Christ. This is the particular cause which, as I said, produces unrest and discord in the state or kingdom. For this evil, as I said at the beginning, creeps forward eagerly into all kingdoms, and by its hostile action has long troubled the Italian kingdom, and has prevented and continually prevents its tranquillity and peace, namely by opposing with all its might the promotion and appointment of the ruling Roman emperor, and his action in that empire. For from the blindness of this action, that is, the justification of civil acts, injuries and quarrels will easily arise. This rule of justice, or of a law not measured out because the measurer is absent, causes fights, whence came the separation of citizens and at last the dissolution of the Italian polities or commonwealths, as I have said. Therefore, from this opinion and perhaps from the desire to rule which I have described, the Roman bishop strives to make the Roman prince subject to coercive or temporal jurisdiction, although, as will be plainly shown from what follows, he ought not to be so by right, nor does he wish to be subject to such a judgment. Hence such a great dispute and discord has arisen that it cannot be ended without great danger to souls and bodies and loss of goods. For the office of coercive rule, as has been settled in sections 15 and 17 of this work, does not belong to the Roman bishop, or to any other bishop, or to any spiritual minister as such, over any individual person, community or college whatever its condition. Aristotle also thought this about the priesthood in every law or sect, when in the fourth book of the Politics he said: Wherefore not all, neither the chosen nor the strong, should be placed as rulers, namely priests, first. For this must be placed as something apart from political principalities, etc. These, moreover, are the political cares, that is, offices, etc. And a little below he adds: But these are economic. I think it most necessary, as was said at the beginning, to repel this pernicious pest, which opposes human quiet and happiness in every way and which, from the corrupted root of its own vice, could especially infect the other kingdoms of the Christian faithful. First I will expose the wrapping of the opinion mentioned as the root of evils already done and to come, and then restrain its ignorant or unjust patrons or inventors, and its stubborn defenders, by outward action if need be. Moreover, all those who know and are able to oppose it are obliged to do so, since those who neglect or omit to do so are also unjust. Cicero bears witness to this in the first book of On Duties, chapter five, when he said: There are two kinds of injustice: one of those who inflict injury, the other of those who, when they can, do not ward off the injury from those to whom it is inflicted.

units.la: Marginal line numbers 1–60 appear beside the text, reproduced as the printer's line marks. possint, non propulsare iniuriam. Ecce ergo secundum Tullii sententiam hanc notabilem, quod non solum inuisti sunt qui aliis iniuriam inferunt, verum etiam hi, qui prohibere sciunt & possunt iniuriam aliis inferentes, non prohibent autem, quoniam ad hoc tenetur quilibet alteri, iure quodam quasi naturali, debito videlicet amicitiae, atque societatis humanae. Quod ius, ne siquid: mscienter transgrediens, ipse saltem mihi dicar iniustus, hanc pestem a fratribus Christi fidelibus, doctrina primum & qua valuero exteriori consequenter opera, propulsare propono. Quoniam vt indubitanter videre videor, desuper mihi datum est nosse sophisma & referandi potestas, in quo Romanorum episcoporum quorundam hactenus & in praesertiarum, suorumque complicium obliqua aestimatio, & cum hoc peruersa forsitan affectio, scandalorum iam dictorum parens hactenus inuisa est, & continuo nititur sustentari.
units.tr: possint, non propulsare iniuriam. Behold, then, according to Tully's notable opinion, not only are those unjust who inflict wrong on others, but also those who know how to prevent it and are able to, yet do not prevent the wrong done to others. Everyone is bound to another by a certain natural right, namely the debt of friendship and of human fellowship. Lest I knowingly transgress this right and be called unjust myself, I propose first to ward off this pestilence from the faithful brothers of Christ by teaching, and then, as far as I am able, by outward action. For I seem to see without doubt that the power of exposing and refuting this sophism has been given to me from above. This sophism, the oblique estimation of certain Roman bishops up to the present, and especially of their accomplices, together with what is perhaps a perverse disposition that goes with it, has been odious until now as the parent of the scandals already mentioned, and it constantly strives to sustain itself.

units.la: MARSILII PATAVINI DE RE IMPERATORIA ET PONTIFICIA, DICTIO SEV PARS SECVNDA.
units.tr: MARSILIUS OF PADUA, ON IMPERIAL AND PAPAL AFFAIRS: THE SECOND PART OF THE DISCOURSE.

units.la: CAP. I. De tribus impedimentis siue modis aduersanti veritatibus in hac dictione contentis, intentione tractandorum, & modo procedendi.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. Of the three hindrances, or obstacles opposed to the truths contained in this discourse; of the intention of the treatment, and of the method of proceeding.

units.la: AGRESSVRVS itaque tam arduum, si nequicquam obuium dubitem, quod veritati possit inniti: ex illius tamen tribus infestis hostibus huic operi bella parari video, uno siquidem persecutione violenta potestatis Romanorum episcoporum, suorumque complicum, ipsum etenim, ipsiusque propalatores veridicos, totis viribus niterentur destruere tanquam directo aduersantes, ipsorum proposito detinendi & possidendi temporalia minus iuste, necnon eorum ardenti desiderio principatus. A quibus quidem ipsos revocare sermone iuridico quantumcunque etiam manifesto difficile fiet. Eos tamen misericors Deus per gratiam revocare dignetur, ipsorumque violentam potentiam compescat ipse, compescantque sibi fideles tam principes quam subiecti, quorum omnium profecto inimicantur quieti. Secundo vero veritatis quasi cuiuslibet hoste antiquo paratur huic operi bellum non minus. Consuetudine scilicet audiendi falsa, illaq; credendi, falsa inquam per presbyteros seu episcopos aliquos, reliquosque; ad haec ipsorum suffraganeos, dudum seminata & radicata in animabus plurimorum simplicium Christi fidelium. Hi nanque sacerdotes suis sermonibus & scripturis quibusdam sententiis diuinas & humanas actuum humanorum tam monasticorum quam ciuilium inuoluere implicationes varias, & explicari laboriosa quam multum. Ex tali sententiarum inuolucro, postmodum inferentes, licet indebite sensus aliquos, quibus suam in iustam despotiam induxerunt super Christi fideles, sua simplicitate credentes, ex quibusdam paralogismis horum sacerdotum, & comminatione quadam damnationis aeternae ad talium sophysticorum tam dictorum quam scriptorum observationem, in quibus non propter hoc accidere conclusionem saepe committitur, ordinatione diuina teneri. Harum etenim rerum de quibus quaeritur atque contenditur, suorumque verorum atque simplicium initiorum, de mentibus hominum abolitis veris sententiis horumque vice falsis paulatim suggestis, nunc latet plurimos verorumque discretio. Turbat enim & abducit a veritate non modicum, secundum quamlibet disciplinam auditionum falsarum consuetudo, testis est Arist. philosophiae, finali capite. Propter quam etiam multum impedientur a principio lectores & auditores huius, praecipue qui philosophiae fuerint exortes, & in sacris scripturis inexercitati a comprehensione ac perfecta credulitate veritatum in hoc volumine contentarum. Reliquus autem & tertius veritatis hostis infestus huic doctrinae, impedimentum grande praestabit, liuor siquidem horum etiam qui & si nos vera dixisse crediderint, quia tamen huius verae sententiae, praeter alium explicatorem intelligent eidem detractionis dente clandestino lacerando, vel praesumptionis clamoso latratu aduersus inuidiae id ipsis nequissimo suadente spiritu se opponent.
units.tr: Although I am about to undertake so arduous a task, if I should doubt in vain that it can rest upon the truth, yet I see that war is being prepared against this work by three hostile enemies of the truth. The first is the violent persecution of the power of the Roman bishops and their accomplices, who will strive with all their strength to destroy the author and the truthful publishers of it, as directly opposing their purpose of holding and possessing temporal goods less than justly, and their ardent desire for princely power. It will be very difficult to call them back from these things by any legal argument, however manifest. May merciful God deign to recall them by grace, and may he himself restrain their violent power; and may the faithful, both princes and subjects, restrain it for themselves, since all of them are truly hostile to peace. Secondly, no less a war is prepared against this work by an ancient enemy of the truth, namely the habit of listening to falsehoods and believing them: falsehoods, I say, sown long ago and rooted in the souls of many simple faithful of Christ, by certain elders or bishops and the others subordinate to them. For these priests, in their sermons and writings, wrap the divine and human acts of men, both monastic and civil, in various entanglements of certain sentences, and explain them with great labour. From such a wrapping of sentences they afterwards infer, though improperly, certain meanings by which they have established their unjust lordship over the faithful of Christ, who believe them in their simplicity; by certain paralogisms of these priests, and by some threat of eternal damnation, they are bound by divine ordinance to observe such sophisms, both spoken and written, in which the conclusion is often wrongly assumed not to follow from the premises. Indeed, of the matters in question and disputed, and of their true and simple first principles, the true sense has been abolished from men's minds and false sense has gradually been put in its place, so that the discernment of the truth is now hidden from very many. For the habit of hearing falsehoods, as Aristotle, witness of philosophy, says in the final chapter, disturbs and draws one away from the truth no little, in any discipline. Because of this, the readers and hearers of this work, especially those who have been strangers to philosophy and unpracticed in the holy Scriptures, will be greatly hindered from grasping and perfectly believing the truths contained in this volume. The third and remaining enemy of the truth, hostile to this doctrine, will present a great obstacle: the envy of those who, though they believe we have spoken the truth, nevertheless, apart from another explainer, will understand these true sentences, and will either tear them with the hidden tooth of detraction, or oppose them with the noisy barking of presumption, at the urging of the most wicked spirit of envy.

units.la: Verum a propositis nec principatus ardentium minus debite sacerdotum, quos his scripturis alloquor violentae potentiae terrore desistam. Quoniam dicente Psalmista: Dominus mihi adiutor, & non timebo quid faciat mihi homo. Neque hoc etiam propter obloquentes invidos detractores omittam exprimere, quod expositum tam omnibus prodesse atque neglectum obesse poterit. Et hi quoniam seipsos eruciantes sua sibi malignitate resistent. Nam invidia, ut ait Vgutio bene describens, est in suum autorem reciproca, de bono alterius tabescentis animi cruciatus. Hostili vero consuetudini sufficienter refragabitur dicendarum euidentia veritatum.
units.tr: But I shall not be deterred from my purpose by the terror of violent power, nor by the zeal of the priests, whom I address in these writings. For the Psalmist says: "The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man may do to me." Nor, on account of the envious and detracting contradictors, will I omit to set forth what, once explained, can benefit all and, if neglected, can harm. And since they, tormenting themselves, will resist by their own malice; for envy, as Vegetius describes it well, is turned back upon its author, the torment of a mind wasting away at another's good. The hostile habit will be sufficiently refuted by the plain evidence of the truths to be stated.

units.la: Incedam autem in huius libri dictione secunda, primum adducendo sacri canonis auctoritates, cum quibusdam fidis & alienis quorundam interpretationibus, quibus fortasse videretur posse conuinci Romanorum episcopo iure deberi supremam omnium coactiuarum iurisdictionis seu principatus, ni lege Christianorum praesertim, tam supra Ro. principem quam reliquos omnes principatus, communitates, collegia, & personas singulares etiam seculares, eoq; magis supra presbyteros, seu episcopos diaconos, ipsorumq; collegia & singulares personas cuiuscunq; conditionis existant. Quoniam si qua necessitate ad horum unum ex saecularibus aut clericis concluditur ex virtute verborum scripturae, per eandem quoq; ad reliquos omnes. His etiam consequenter ad iam dictum propositum astruendum quasdam quasi politicas rationes adducam, apparentes valde suppositis quibusdam scripturae sacrae veritatibus, quas etiam omnes concorditer veras, omnes supponere debent. Has inquam adducam, ut sic patenter dissoluam, ne quisquam per illas aut consimiles de caetero falli possit, utque ex earum solutione appareat magis infirmitas aestimationis praedictae, cui dudum hactenus probabilitatis faciem praebuerunt. Post haec autem ex adverso inducam sacri canonis veritates cum sanctorum illius interpretum, non fictis, non alienis aut falsis expositionibus, sed consonis & propriis, demonstrantes aperte Romanum episcopum vocatum papam, aut alium quemlibet presbyterum seu episcopum, vel spiritualem ministrum, communiter aut diuisim, inquantum huiusmodi, nullam iurisdictionem realem aut personalem cuiusquam coactiuam habere, vel habere debere supra presbyterum vel episcopum aut diaconum quenquam, vel ipsorum collegium, eoque minus ipsum, aut ipsorum aliquem communiter vel diuisim talem iurisdictionem habere in quenquam principem seu principatum aliquem, communitatem, collegium, aut personam singularem aliquam cuiuscunque conditionis existat, nisi ea demum iurisdictio per humanum legislatorem in prouincia, presbytero seu episcopo alicui, aut ipsorum collegio concessa foret. Ad quod etiam demonstrandum & confirmandum adduci poterunt & debent, cum alicui fuerit opportunum politicae demonstrationes, quarum principia propria 12. prima 15. & 17. continentur. Has enim iterare non dispoluimus propter abbreviationem sermonis. His consequenter ostendam, quae, quantave sit potestas sacerdotalis & clauium per Christum tradita Romano episcopo & alteri cuilibet sacerdoti. Ex horum enim manifestatione pendet multarum dubitationum solutio, ad veritatem & finem quem producere quaerimus, praebens ingressum. Deinde vero perutile erit dicere ad aliquas innascentes quaestiones ex dictis, cum quibus etiam de priuilegiis Romanorum principum, iam Romanis episcopis concessis, dicemus aliquid expediens ad propositum negotium. Quoniam ex his occasionaliter usurpationes, occupationes, seu detentiones iurisdictionum coactiuarum, quas autoritati proprie Romanorum nunc ascribunt episcopi sumpsere originem, & per consuetudinem, quinimo abusum verius robur acceperunt postmodum, maxime imperiali sede vacante. His enim priuilegiis ab initio, non aliunde in iurisdictionum coactiuarum acquisitione, ac ipsarum conseruatione, sustentati sunt Romanorum episcopi. Posterius vero, vel quia per demeritum priuati sunt illis, vel ne debilitas occasionum & veritas indebite iam per ipsos assumptae iurisdictionis appareat, eorumque ingratitudinem obtegendam, aut etiam fortasse, sicut verisimile ostendimus ultimo primae, quoniam iurisdictionis coactiuae regnorum omnium occupationem intendunt, ad quam sibi nil suffragarentur priuilegia memorata, iisdem non utuntur, sed alio quodam vniuersali ad principantes, & omnes ciuiliter viuentes sibi subiiciendos supradicto titulo, plenitudine scilicet potestatis. Ex qua per Christum, ut asserunt, tradita beato Petro tanquam vicario, coactiuam iurisdictionem supremam omnium hominum & prouinciarum, iam quilibet Romanus episcopus inquantum Petri successor, se dicit habere. Reliquum autem huius dictionis erit ostendere sacri canonis autoritates aduersus eam quam veritatis & scripturae sententiam diximus, nihil suffragari errori praedicto, sed eidem potius aduersari, sicuti manifeste patebit ex sanctorum quorundam expositionibus, necnon & aliorum doctorum approbatorum fidei Christianae, per quem etiam apparebit, quorundam expositiones, imo verius fictiones, scripturam retorquere conantium ad astruendum sensum aestimationis falsae praedictae, violentas esse scripturae alienas atque distortas, sanctorum etiam & peritorum doctorum Christianae fidei sententiae dissonare. Omnium vero nouissime dissoluam rationes, quas quasi politicas dixi, aestimationi falsae saepe dictae, visas aliqualiter suffragari.
units.tr: In the second part of this discourse I shall proceed, first by adducing the authorities of the sacred canon, together with certain trustworthy and not foreign interpretations of some, by which it might perhaps seem possible to prove that the supreme jurisdiction of all coercive power, or dominion, is due by right to the Roman bishop, were it not that by the law of Christians, especially, he is subject to the Roman prince no less than to all the other principalities, communities, colleges and individual persons, even secular ones, and so much more to the elders or bishops, deacons, their colleges and individual persons of whatever condition they may be. For if by necessity it is concluded from the force of the words of Scripture that this holds for one of the secular or clerical persons, by the same reasoning it holds for all the rest. Consequently, to establish the proposition already mentioned, I shall also adduce certain arguments, as it were political, which appear very plausible on the basis of certain truths of Holy Scripture, which all, agreeing, hold to be true and which all ought to presuppose. These I shall adduce, I say, in order to dissolve them openly, so that no one may be deceived by them or similar ones in future, and so that from their solution the weakness of the aforesaid judgment may appear more clearly, to which they have long lent a face of probability. After these things, on the contrary side, I shall bring forward the truths of the sacred canon together with the interpretations of its holy expositors, not fictitious, not foreign or false explanations, but consonant and proper ones, demonstrating clearly that the Roman bishop, called the pope, or any other elder or bishop, or spiritual minister, whether jointly or severally, insofar as such, has no real or personal coercive jurisdiction over any elder, bishop or deacon, nor over their college, and should have none; and still less may he, or any of them, jointly or severally, have such jurisdiction over any prince or principality, community, college, or any individual person of whatever condition, unless that jurisdiction had been granted by the human lawgiver in a province to some elder or bishop, or to their college. To demonstrate and confirm this, political demonstrations can and must be adduced, whenever it is opportune for anyone, whose proper principles are contained in the first, fifteenth and seventeenth chapters. For we have not resolved to repeat these, for the sake of brevity of discourse. After this I shall show what and how great is the sacerdotal power and the power of the keys, handed down by Christ to the Roman bishop and to any other priest. For the solution of many doubts depends on the explanation of these things, and it provides an entrance to the truth and to the end which we seek to bring about. Then, indeed, it will be most useful to speak of some questions arising from what has been said, and with them we shall say something expedient to the proposed matter concerning the privileges of the Roman emperors, already granted to the Roman bishops. For from these occasionally arose the usurpations, occupations, or detentions of coercive jurisdictions, which the Roman bishops now ascribe to their own authority; they took their origin from these, and later received strength through custom, or rather through abuse, especially when the imperial see was vacant. For at the beginning the Roman bishops were supported by these privileges, and by no other means, in acquiring and preserving coercive jurisdictions. Later, either because they have been deprived of them through their own demerit, or so that the weakness of the occasions and the truth of the jurisdiction improperly already assumed by them may not appear, and so that their ingratitude may be covered, or perhaps also, as we have shown probable at the end of the first part, since they intend the occupation of the coercive jurisdiction of all kingdoms, for which the aforesaid privileges would avail them nothing, they do not use them, but instead use some other universal title, namely the plenitude of power, by which they claim to subject to themselves all rulers and all who live as citizens. From this power, they assert, handed down by Christ to the blessed Peter as his vicar, every Roman bishop, insofar as he is the successor of Peter, says he has the supreme coercive jurisdiction over all men and provinces. It remains in this discourse to show that the authorities of the sacred canon, against the opinion we have called false and the sense of the truth and of Scripture, give no support to the aforesaid error, but rather oppose it, as will be clear from the expositions of certain holy men, and also of other approved teachers of the Christian faith. From these it will also appear that the expositions, or rather fictions, of certain men who strive to twist Scripture to establish the sense of the aforesaid false judgment are violent, foreign and distorted, and disagree with the opinions of the holy and learned teachers of the Christian faith. Lastly, I shall dissolve the arguments which I called political, which seem in some measure to support the aforesaid false judgment.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: De distinctione nominum siue dictionum, ex quibus quaesita determinanda componuntur.
units.tr: On the distinction of the names or terms from which the questions to be determined are composed.

units.la: ANte tamen quam de propositis disseramus, ne propter multiplicitatem nominum, quibus in quaesitis principalibus utemur, accidat ambiguitas & implicatio sententiarum, quas volumus aperire, distinguemus significationes ipsorum. Nam, ut in primo Elenchorum. Qui virtutis nominum sunt ignari, paralogizantur & ipsi disputantes, & alios audientes. Nomina vero seu dictiones, quorum multiplicitatem distinguere volumus sunt hae: Ecclesia, Iudex, spirituale, temporale, propterea quod ex inquisitione proposita, scire volumus, utrum ad Romanum aut alium quemuis episcopum seu presbyterum, diaconum, aut ipsorum collegium, qui viri ecclesiastici solent dici, pertineat iudicem esse coactiuum temporalium aut spiritualium, aut utrorumque, vel secundum horum. [illegible, ~20 letters] tum neutrum sint ipsi iudices tales. Haec itaque prosequentes dicamus, quod hoc nomen Ecclesia, vocabulum est ex vsu Graecorum, significans apud ipsos in his quae ad nos peruenerunt, congregationem populi sub vno regimine contenti, quomodo sumpsit ecclesiam Aristoteles secundo politicae, cap. 7. dum dixit: Ecclesia autem participant omnes. Apud Latinos vero vocabulum hoc secundum vulgarem & famosam appellationem, in vna sui significatione importat templum seu domum, in qua Deus communiter a fidelibus colitur, & frequentius adoratur. Sic enim de ecclesia loquebatur Apostolus primae ad Corinth. II. Nunquid domos non habetis ad manducandum & bibendum, aut ecclesiam Dei contemnitis? Vbi Glossa secundum Augustinum: Ecclesiam Dei contemnitis, id est domum orationis, & infra parum subdit: Hoc vsu quotidiano obtinuit, vt in ecclesia prodire vel confugere [illegible, ~10 letters] qui ad locum ipsum, parietesque prodierit vel confugerit. In alia vero significatione importat hoc nomen, Ecclesia, omnes presbyteros seu episcopos, diaconos, & reliquos ministrantes in templo seu ecclesia dicta secundum priorem significationem. Apud modernos maxime importat hoc nomen, ecclesia, ministros illos, presbyteros, seu episcopos, atque diaconos, qui ministrant & praesunt in Metropolitana seu principali, omnium ecclesiarum, quemadmodum hoc ecclesia Romanae urbis dudum obtinuit, cuius ministri & praesidentes sunt Papa Romanus, & Cardinales ipsius, qui iam ex vsu quodam obtinuerunt dici Ecclesia, & ecclesiam aliquid egisse aut recepisse, cum iidem aliquid egerint aut receperint, vel aliter qualiter ordinauerint. Rursum secundum aliam significationem dicitur hoc nomen, ecclesia, & omnium verissime & propriissime secundum primam impositionem huius nominis seu intentionem primorum imponentium, licet non ita famose, secundum tamen vsum de vniuersitate fidelium credentium & invocantium nomen Christi: & de huius vniuersitatis partibus omnibus, in quacunque communitate etiam domestica. Et haec fuit impositio prima huius dictionis, & consuetus vsus eius apud apostolos & in ecclesia primitiua. Vnde Apostolus primae ad Corinthios primo: Ecclesia, quae est Corinthi, sanctificatis in Christo Iesu, vocatis sanctis cum omnibus qui invocant nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Before we discuss the matters proposed, however, we will distinguish the meanings of the names we shall use in the principal questions. Otherwise, because of their many senses, ambiguity and tangled arguments may arise in the opinions we wish to set out. As the author says in the first book of the Elenchi: those who do not know the force of names are led into paralogisms, both the disputants themselves and those who hear them. The names or terms whose multiple senses we wish to distinguish are these: Church, judge, spiritual, and temporal. This is because, from the question proposed, we wish to know whether it belongs to the Roman bishop, or to any other bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or to their college, which are commonly called ecclesiastical men, to be a coercive judge of temporal or spiritual matters, or of both, or according to these [illegible], since they themselves are neither such judges. Pursuing these matters, let us say that the word Church is a term from the usage of the Greeks. In the sources that have come down to us, it signifies among them a gathering of people united under one government, as Aristotle took the church in the second book of the Politics, chapter 7, when he said: But all share in the church. Among the Latins, however, according to the common and familiar usage, this word in one of its senses means a temple or house in which God is commonly worshipped by the faithful and more often adored. So the Apostle spoke of the church in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11: Have you not houses to eat and drink in, or do you despise the church of God? Where the Gloss, following Augustine, says: "The church of God" means the house of prayer. And a little further on it adds: By everyday usage it has come about that to go into the church or to take refuge in it [illegible] means to go to that place and its walls, or to take refuge there. In another sense the word Church means all the presbyters or bishops, deacons, and the rest who minister in the temple or church, which is called by the former meaning. Among the moderns, the word Church chiefly means those ministers, presbyters or bishops, and deacons, who minister and preside in the metropolitan or principal church of all churches, just as the word has long been applied to the church of the city of Rome, whose ministers and presidents are the Roman Pope and his Cardinals. By a certain usage they have come to be called the Church, and it is said that the Church has done or received something when they have done or received something, or ordained it in some other way. Again, in another sense the word church is used, and this is the truest and most proper of all, according to the first imposition of the word or the intention of its first framers. Though it is not so commonly used, it refers to the whole body of believing faithful who invoke the name of Christ, and to all the parts of this body, in whatever community, even a household. This was the first imposition of the term and its customary use among the apostles and in the primitive Church. Hence the Apostle in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1: The church which is at Corinth, sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Vbi Glossa secundum Ambrosium: Sanctificatus in baptismo, & hoc in Christo Iesu. Et secundum hanc intentionem loquebatur Apostolus Actuum 20. ad presbyteros Ephesios, cum dixit: Attendite vobis & vniuerso gregi, in quo vos spiritus sanctus posuit episcopos, vt regeretis ecclesiam Dei, quam acquisiuit sanguine suo. Et propterea viri ecclesiastici secundum hanc verissimam & propriissimam significationem, sunt & dici debent omnes Christi fideles, tam sacerdotes, quam non sacerdotes, quod omnes Christus acquisiuit & redemit sanguine suo. Sicut etiam expresse dicitur in glossa super illud Lucae 22. Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur. Pro vobis, inquit Glossa, non significat pro solis apostolis corpus Christi datum, & sanguinem effusum fuisse, sed causa totius humanae naturae. Sic igitur non pro solis apostolis effusus est Christi sanguis, ergo non soli acquisiti sunt aut fuere per illum, nec per consequens presbyteri aut templorum ministri successores illorum in officio, non igitur sunt ipsi soli Ecclesia, quam Christus suo sanguine acquisiuit. Nec propter eandem causam sunt isti ministri, episcopi, seu presbyteri, & diaconi soli ecclesia, quae sponsa Christi est, sed pars sponsae huius, quoniam Christus pro hac sponsa se tradidit. Vnde Apostolus ad Philip. quinto: Viri diligite vxores vestras, sicut & Christus ecclesiam, & semetipsum tradidit pro ea, nunc vero non pro solis apostolis aut ipsorum in officio successoribus episcopis, seu presbyteris atque diaconis, Christus se tradidit, imo pro tota humana natura. Non igitur sunt ipsi aut ipsorum congregatio tantummodo sponsa, licet abutentium vocabulo ipsorum quaedam congregatio, propter proprium & temporale commodum & aliorum incommodum fraudulenter adipiscendum, se vocet singulariter ecclesiam Christi. Hanc eandem est apprehendere sententiam ex verbis Apostoli prima ad Corinthios primo, Ad Thess. primo, Ad Colossen. 4. & ad Philemonem primo. In omnibus enim Apostolus ecclesiam secundum eam quam eius propriam & verissimam significationem dixit.
units.tr: Here the Gloss, following Ambrose, says: Sanctified in baptism, and this in Christ Jesus. And according to this intention the Apostle spoke in Acts 20 to the elders of Ephesus when he said: Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to rule the church of God, which he purchased with his own blood. Therefore, according to this truest and most proper meaning, all the faithful of Christ, both priests and non-priests, are and ought to be called ecclesiastical men, because Christ purchased and redeemed all of them with his own blood. This is also expressly stated in the gloss on the words of Luke 22: This is my body, which is given for you. "For you," says the Gloss, does not mean that the body of Christ was given and his blood shed for the apostles alone, but for the whole of human nature. So Christ's blood was not shed for the apostles alone, and therefore they alone were not purchased or redeemed by it, nor, consequently, were the presbyters or the ministers of the temples, their successors in office. Therefore these men alone are not the Church which Christ purchased with his blood. For the same reason, these ministers, bishops or presbyters, and deacons are not alone the church, which is the bride of Christ, but a part of this bride, since Christ gave himself up for this bride. Hence the Apostle, in Philippians 5: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the church and gave himself up for her. Now Christ gave himself up not for the apostles alone, or their successors in office, bishops or presbyters and deacons, but for the whole of human nature. Therefore they, or their assembly, are not the only bride, although a certain gathering of those who abuse the name, in order to gain their own temporal advantage and the harm of others by fraud, calls itself by the singular name of the Church of Christ. It is the same understanding we must take from the Apostle's words in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1, the first to the Thessalonians, chapter 1, the Colossians, chapter 4, and the epistle to Philemon, chapter 1. In all of these the Apostle uses the word church in the sense he called its own and truest meaning.

units.la: Huic consequente [illegible, ~10 letters] haec nomina temporale, deinde spirituale, a quorum tamen notationibus inciperet, quod haec dictio temporale in vna sui significatione famosiori dicitur de omnibus rebus quae aliis ab homine, quae aliquo modo in ipsius potestate existentia, ad sui vsum, indigentiam & voluptatem supplendam, ordinantur in statu & pro statu vitae mundanae. Quomodo generalius etiam temporale consueuit dici, omne quod in tempore incipit & definit. Haec enim, vt in quarto Physicae, proprie sunt & dicuntur in tempore. Alio vero modo dicitur temporale de omni habitu, actione aut passione humana in se vel in alterum per hominem operandis, propter finem huius seculi seu vitae praesentis. Adhuc autem minus vniuersaliter dicitur hoc nomen temporale de humanis actionibus & passionibus voluntariis & transeuntibus ad commodum vel incommodum, alterius ab eo qui fecit, de quibus maxime intenduntur humanarum legumlatores.
units.tr: Following this, we must consider the terms temporal and then spiritual. We shall begin with their definitions. In one of its more common senses, the word temporal is applied to all things outside man which, existing in some way within his power, are ordained for his use, need, and pleasure, in the condition and for the condition of worldly life. In this way temporal is also commonly used more generally of whatever begins and ends in time. For these things, as in the fourth book of the Physics, are properly and rightly said to be in time. In another way, temporal is said of every habit, action, or passion of man, whether in himself or in another, which is performed by a man for the sake of the end of this age or present life. Again, in a still less universal sense, this term temporal is applied to the voluntary and transitory human actions and passions which bring advantage or disadvantage to another than the one who did them, and it is these that human lawgivers chiefly concern themselves with.

units.la: Nunc autem distinguere volo significata seu intentiones huius dictionis spiritualis, quod in vna sui acceptione dicitur de omnibus incorporalibus substantiis & ipsarum actionibus. In alia vero significatione dicitur de omni actione aut passione humana virtutis suae, cognoscentis aut appetentis immanente ipsi. Secundum quam etiam intentionem actiones quaedam rerum corporalium in sensus animalium, spirituales dici solent, & sine materia, veluti rerum idola seu phantasmata & species, quae animae sunt aliquo modo ratio cognoscendi, in quo genere reponuntur quibusdam sensibilium actiones, etiam in substantia non animata, vt luminum generationes & quorundam similium. Rursum ad propositum magis dicitur hoc nomen spirituale, de lege divina, de doctrina, & disciplina praeceptorum & consiliorum, secundum ipsam & per ipsam, in quam siquidem etiam significationem, veniunt omnia ecclesiastica sacramenta & ipsorum effectus, omnis gratia divina, virtutes omnes theologicae, atque dona spiritus sancti, ordinantia nos ad vitam aeternam. Sic enim & proprie hoc nomine vtitur Apostolus ad Rom. 15. & primae ad Corinth. nono, cum dixit: Si nos vobis spiritualia seminauimus, magnum est si nos carnalia vestra metamus. Vbi Glossa secundum Ambrosium: Spiritalia, id est ea quae vestrum spiritum vivificant, vel quae a spiritu sancto data sunt, scilicet verbum Dei, & mysterium regni coelorum. Amplius secundum aliam significationem solet hoc nomen accipi pro qualibet actione vel etiam passione humana voluntaria, tam in se quam ad alterum operata, propter meritum beatae vitae futuri seculi, quales sunt Dei contemplationes, dilectiones ipsius & proximorum, abstinentiae, misericordiae, mansuetudines, orationes, oblationes propter pietatem seu cultum divinum, hospitalitates, peregrinationes, corporis proprii castigationes, mundanorum & carnalium voluptatum contemptus & fuga, & generaliter omnia consimilia facta propter finem praedictum. Adhuc autem dicitur hoc nomen, licet non ita proprie, ut secundo & tertio modo, de templo seu ecclesia, dicta secundum secundam significationem, de omnibus vasis & apparatibus quae in eo sunt ordinata propter cultum divinum. Omnium vero novissime inconvenienter & improprie valde, quidam extendunt hoc nomen, ad significandum presbyterorum, seu episcoporum, diaconorum, & aliorum templi ministrorum actiones voluntarias transeuntes; & earum omissiones, quae sunt ad commodum vel incommodum alterius a faciente pro statu vitae mundanae. Extendunt rursum & magis improprie idem nomen ad horum possessiones & temporalia bona, mobilia & immobilia, & ad temporalium proventus quosdam, quos vocant decimas, ut huius praetextu vocabuli, a norma legum & principantium civilium aestimantur. Sed profecto ipsi palam abutuntur vocabulo in his contra veritatem & Apostoli atque sanctorum intentionem & usum, qui talia non spiritualia, sed carnalia seu temporalia vocauerunt. Vnde ad Romanos 15. Quoniam si spiritualium earum participes facti sunt gentiles, debent & in carnalibus ministrare eis. Idem expressius primae ad Corinthios nono: Si nos, inquit Apostolus, vobis spiritualia seminauimus, magnum est si nos carnalia vestra metamus. Vbi Glossa secundum Ambrosium: Quia si nos seminamus vobis spiritualia, id est ea quae spiritum vestrum vivificant, vel quae a spiritu sancto data sunt, scilicet verbum Dei & mysterium regni coelorum, est magnum si nos metamus ad sustentationem, vestra carnalia, id est haec temporalia, quae vita & indulgentia carnis indulta sunt. Ecce quod bona exteriora, quibus praedicatores euangelii sustentari debebant in victu & vestitu, Apostolus & Ambrosius expresse carnalia & temporalia vocant, & sunt secundum veritatem, sive sint decimae, sive praedia, quaestus seu eleemosynae, vel collectae, cuius causam dixit Ambrosius, quoniam vita & indulgentia carnis, id est vitae corruptibilis, indulta sunt. Idem quoque sentiendum indubie de presbyterorum, episcoporum, & diaconorum actionibus quibusdam. Non omnes enim eorum actus spirituales sunt, nec dici debent, quinimo ipsorum sunt multi ciuiles actus contentiosi, & carnales seu temporales. Possunt enim ipsi mutuare, deponere, emere, vendere, percutere, occidere, furari, moechari, rapere, prodere, falsum testimonium perhibere, diffamare, in haeresim cadere, caeteraque committere scelera, crimina, & contentiones, quemadmodum etiam a non sacerdotibus perpetrantur. Propter quod interrogandum conuenienter abeis, si quales diximus actiones ipsorum possibiles, spirituales sint aut dici debeant ab aliquo sana mentis. Et constat quod minime, quin imo carnales & temporales. Vnde Apostolus prima ad Corinth. tertio de talibus actionibus loquens indifferenter ad omnes, inquit: Cum regnet inter vos zelus & contentio, nonne carnales estis, & secundum hominem ambulatis? Cum igitur indubitata demonstret experientia, inter presbyteros inuicem, & ad seculares, euenire zelos & contentiones ex praedictis aut aliis consimilibus actibus, manifestum, huiusmodi sacerdotium & episcoporum actus carnales seu temporales esse, & secundum veritatem non spirituales, nec dici debere. Signum autem, verum esse quod diximus etiam secundum sacerdotum sententiam, quoniam ad huiusmodi tollendas contentiones multae humanae ordinationes, quas Decretales appellant, editae sunt per Romanos pontifices, & ante has, de his leges principum Romanorum. Fiunt enim & fieri possunt per diaconos & presbyteros seu episcopos, actiones multae voluntariae, transeuntes in commodum & iniuriam alterius, pro statu vitae praesentis. Et ideo talium mensura debet esse humana lex, quemadmodum 15. primae dictum est, & dicetur amplius ad propositum octauo huius.
units.tr: Now I want to distinguish the meanings, or senses, of the word spiritual. In one sense it is applied to all incorporeal substances and their actions. In another sense it is applied to every human action or passion that belongs to a power of the soul, whether of knowing or of desiring, and remains within the one who performs it. In this sense, certain actions of corporeal things upon the senses of animals are also commonly called spiritual, as are things without matter, such as the images or phantasms and species of things, which are in some way the means by which the soul knows. Among these are placed certain actions of sensible things, even in inanimate substances, such as the generation of light and similar things. Again, with respect to our purpose, the word spiritual is applied more properly to the divine law, to doctrine, and to the discipline of precepts and counsels, according to it and through it. In this sense all the ecclesiastical sacraments and their effects belong, as do all divine grace, all the theological virtues, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which direct us to eternal life. The Apostle uses the word in this proper sense in Romans 15 and in the ninth chapter of 1 Corinthians, when he says: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things? The Gloss, following Ambrose, explains: Spiritual things, that is, those which quicken your spirit, or which were given by the Holy Spirit, namely the word of God and the mystery of the kingdom of heaven. Further, in another sense this word is usually taken to mean any voluntary human action or passion, whether performed in oneself or toward another, undertaken for the sake of the merit of the blessed life of the age to come. Such are the contemplations of God, love of him and of neighbours, abstinences, acts of mercy, meekness, prayers, offerings made for piety or divine worship, hospitality, pilgrimages, the chastisements of one's own body, the contempt and avoidance of worldly and carnal pleasures, and, in general, all similar deeds done for the aforesaid end. Moreover, the word is also used, though not so properly as in the second and third senses, of the temple or church, taken in the second sense, and of all the vessels and furnishings that are set in it for divine worship. Lastly, and quite inappropriately and improperly, some extend this word to signify the voluntary transitive actions of presbyters, or bishops, deacons, and the other ministers of the temple, and their omissions, which are for the advantage or disadvantage of another, relating to the condition of worldly life. Again, and even more improperly, they extend the same word to their possessions and temporal goods, both movable and immovable, and to certain revenues of temporal things, which they call tithes, so that under the pretext of this word they may be valued by the standard of the laws and of civil rulers. But surely they openly abuse the word in these uses, against the truth and against the intention and usage of the Apostle and the saints, who called such things not spiritual but carnal or temporal. Hence in Romans 15: For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things. The same is said more explicitly in the ninth chapter of 1 Corinthians: If we, says the Apostle, have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things? The Gloss, following Ambrose, says: Because if we sow spiritual things among you, that is, those things which quicken your spirit, or which were given by the Holy Spirit, namely the word of God and the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, it is a great thing if we reap for our sustenance your carnal things, that is, these temporal things, which are granted for the life and indulgence of the flesh. Here we see that the outward goods by which the preachers of the gospel ought to be sustained in food and clothing are expressly called carnal and temporal by the Apostle and by Ambrose, and rightly so. This holds whether they are tithes, estates, earnings, alms, or collections; Ambrose gives the reason, because they are granted for the life and indulgence of the flesh, that is, of corruptible life. Undoubtedly the same must be thought of certain actions of presbyters, bishops, and deacons. For not all of their acts are spiritual, nor ought they to be called so; indeed many of their acts are civil, contentious, carnal or temporal. For they can lend, deposit, buy, sell, strike, kill, steal, commit adultery, rob, betray, bear false witness, defame, fall into heresy, and commit other crimes, offences, and quarrels, just as non-priests also perpetrate them. Therefore they should fittingly be asked whether such actions, of the kind we have mentioned, which are possible for them, are or ought to be called spiritual by anyone of sound mind. And it is plain that they are by no means spiritual, but rather carnal and temporal. Hence the Apostle, speaking of such actions in the third chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, addresses them to all without distinction: Since there is envy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man? Since indubitable experience shows that envies and contentions arise among presbyters themselves, and between them and laymen, from the aforesaid or similar acts, it is manifest that the acts of such priesthood and of bishops are carnal or temporal, and are not, in truth, to be called spiritual. A sign that what we have said is true, even according to the opinion of the priests themselves, is that many human ordinances, which they call Decretals, have been issued by the Roman pontiffs to remove such contentions, and before these, laws concerning them were issued by the Roman princes. For many voluntary actions, which pass over to the advantage or injury of another, are and can be performed by deacons and presbyters or bishops, relating to the condition of the present life. Therefore the measure of such actions ought to be human law, as was said in the fifteenth chapter of the first book, and will be said further in regard to our purpose in the eighth chapter of this book.

units.la: Restat autem distinguere nomina haec iudex atque iudicium, quod illius actionem significat. Sunt enim de numero multiplicium, & in quaesitis difficilis ambiguitatem & impedimentum ipsorum multiplicitate praebentium. Dicitur autem in una significatione iudex de omni discernente seu cognoscente, maxime secundum habitum aliquem speculatiuum aut operatiuum. Et hoc nomen iudicium de cognitione seu discretione talium, quo modo Geometer iudex est, & iudicat de figuris & ipsarum accidentibus, & medicus de sanis & aegris, & prudens de agendis & fugiendis, & domificator de domibus qualiter construendis. Sic quoque omnis sciens aut expertus dicitur iudex & iudicat de scibilibus aut operabilibus suis. Et secundum hanc significationem sumpsit Aristoteles haec nomina primo Ethicorum, cap. primo, cum dixit: Vnusquisque iudicat bene quae cognoscit, & eorum est bonus iudex. Adhuc autem dicitur hoc nomen iudex secundum aliam {a}iam significationem, de habente scientiam iuris politici seu civilis, qui etiam appellatione consulta advocatus nuncupari solet, licet in pluribus prouinciarum & maxime Italicarum index vocetur. Rursum vero dicitur hoc nomen index de principante, & hoc nomen iudicium de principantis sententia, cuius siquidem autoritas est iudicare de iustis & conferentibus secundum leges & consuetudines, latasque per ipsum sententias, praecipiendi & exequendi per potentiam coactiuam. Quomodo iudicium dicitur liber quidam, sacri canonis seu bibliae pars vna quaedam existens. Quomodo etiam de iudice seu principante loquens Aristoteles primo Rhetoricae cap. primo dicit: Praefectum autem & index iam deprehensibus & determinatis iudicant. Sic etiam de principantis iudicio intelligens continue subdit, ad quos (scilicet praefectum seu iudicem) & amare iam & odire, & proprium commodum annexa sunt saepe, ut non adhuc possint videre sufficienter verum. Sed attendere in iudicio proprium dilectabile aut triste. Sunt autem fortassis supradictorum nominum significationes aliae, famosiores tamen inquisitioni propositae magis necessarias, assignasse putamus.
units.tr: It remains now to distinguish these terms judge and judgment, which signifies his action. They belong to the class of many-sensed words, and by their multiplicity they present difficulty and an obstacle of ambiguity in matters under inquiry. In one sense judge is said of anyone who discerns or knows, especially according to some speculative or practical habit. And the word judgment is used of the knowledge or discernment of such a person: thus a geometer is a judge and judges of figures and their accidents, a physician of the healthy and the sick, a prudent person of things to be done and to be avoided, and a builder of how houses are to be constructed. So too, every person who knows or is experienced is called a judge and judges concerning the things he knows or can do. It is in this sense that Aristotle takes these terms in the first chapter of the first book of the Ethics, when he says: Each person judges well what he knows, and he is a good judge of these things. Again, the word judge is used in another sense of one who has knowledge of political or civil law, who is also commonly called by the name of advocate, though in many provinces, and especially in Italy, he is called index. Further, the word index is used of a ruler, and the word judgment of the sentence of a ruler, whose authority is to judge concerning what is just and fitting according to laws and customs, and the sentences passed by him, with the power to command and to enforce them by coercive force.
