Thus judgment is the name of a certain book, being one part of the sacred canon or Bible. Likewise, speaking of the judge or ruler, Aristotle says in the first chapter of the first book of the Rhetoric: But the prefect and the judge judge things already seized and determined. Also, understanding the judgment of a ruler in this way, he continues at once: To whom (namely the prefect or judge) both love and hatred, and their own advantage, are often attached, so that they cannot yet see the truth sufficiently. But in judgment they attend to what is their own pleasant or sad. We think we have assigned perhaps other senses of the aforesaid terms, but those more famous and more necessary for the inquiry proposed.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAP. III.

units.la: De oraculis canonicis & aliis quibusdam argumentationibus, quibus conuinci videtur episcopis siue presbyteris, inquantum huiusmodi principatum coactiuum deberi, etiam absque legislatoris concessione, & Romanorum episcopo siue papa talium omnium principatuum supremum.
units.tr: Concerning the canonical oracles and certain other arguments, by which it seems to be proved that a coercive authority is owed to bishops or presbyters, as such, even without the grant of a lawgiver, and that the bishop of Rome, or pope, is the supreme head of all such authorities.

units.la: HOrum ergo nominum intentionibus, circa quas nostrae plurimum inquisitionis versabitur, sic distinctis, inde secutius ad principale propositum accedentes, adducemus primum auctoritates sacrae scripturae, quibus alicui videri posset, Romanum episcopum vocatum Papam, iudicem esse supremum, & secundum tertiam iudicis seu iudicii significationem, super omnes mundi episcopos seu presbyteros & ecclesiasticos ministros alios, Super omnes quoque huius seculi principantes, communitates, collegia, & singulares personas, cuiusque conditionis existant. Harum autem primam ponamus scripturae seriem, quae habetur Matthaei 16. qua Christus alloquens beatum Petrum, inquit: Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, & quodcunque ligaueris super terram erit ligatum & in coelis; & quodcunque solueris super terram erit solutum & in coelis. Ex hac enim serie, assumpserunt sibi Romanorum episcopi quidam supremae iurisdictionis iam dictae autoritatem. Nam perclaues beato Petro per Christum concessas, intelligi volunt sibi traditam plenitudinem potestatis totius humani regiminis, quam sicut Christus habuit ad omnes reges & principes, ita concessit beato Petro & successoribus eius in episcopali sede Romana, tanquam Christi Vicariis generalibus in hoc mundo. Secunda vero scripturae series ad idem propositum astruendum, sumitur ex verbis Christi Matthaei 11. cum dixit: Omnia mihi tradita sunt a patre meo. Et rursum eiusdem. 23. cum dixit: Data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo & in terra. Cum igitur beatus Petrus & ipsius successores in episcopali sede Romana fuerint & sint Vicarii Christi, sicut hi dicunt, videtur quod omnis potestas seu plenitudo potestatis eidem tradita sit, & consequenter cuiuslibet iurisdictionis autoritas. Tertia vero series ad idem sumitur ex Matthaeo 8. & Marci 5. vbi dicitur: Daemones autem rogabant eum, (Christum scilicet,) dicentes: Si eicis nos, mitte nos in gregem porcorum, & ait illis: Ite, at illi exeuntes abierunt in porcos. Et ecce impetu abiit totum grex per praeceps in mare, & mortui sunt in aquis. Ex quibus verbis apparet, quod Christus de temporalibus disponebat, tanquam de suis omnibus, aliter namque peccasset dissipans gregem porcorum. Christum autem, cuius caro corruptionem non vidit, peccasse, nephas est dicere. Cum igitur beatus Petrus eiusque successores Romanorum episcopi sint & fuerint praecipui Christi Vicarii, vt aiunt quidam, de temporalibus omnibus tanquam tertiae significationis iudices disponere possunt, & ipsorum habent plenitudinem potestatis atq; dominii, sicut Christus. Rursum ostenditur idem per id quod habetur Matth. 21. Mar. 11. Luc. 19. quorum series talis est: Tunc misit (Iesus scilicet,) duos discipulos, dicens eis, Ite in castellum quod contra vos est, & statim invenietis asinam alligatam & pullum eius cum ea. Vel, pullum asina alligatum, cui nemo hominum unquam sedit, vt in Marco & Luca. Soluite & adducite mihi. Ex quibus idem & eodem deductionis modo concludi potest, quid ex immediate praedicta serie conclusum est antea. Amplius arguitur idem ex Luc. 22. vbi habetur haec series: Ecce duo gladii sunt, dixerunt apostoli, respondentes Christo. At ille (Christus scilicet,) respondit, Satis est. Per quae verba, secundum aliquorum interpretationem, debent intelligi quo principatus in mundo praesenti, ecclesiasticus vnus seu spiritualis, & alius temporalis seu secularis. Cum igitur Christus ad apostolos sermonem dirigens dixerit: Satis est. supple vobis de duobus gladiis his, significasse detur vtrumque gladium ad ipsorum auctoritatem pertinere debere, & praesertim beati Petri tanquam principalioris eorum, Nam si temporale gladium ad ipsos pertinere noluisset, dicere debuit, superfluum est.
units.tr: Having thus distinguished the meanings of these terms, which will be the main object of our inquiry, we now come more closely to our principal purpose. First we shall adduce the authorities of Holy Scripture by which someone might think that the Roman bishop, called Pope, is the supreme judge, and, in the third sense of judge or judgment, is over all the bishops or presbyters of the world and all other ecclesiastical ministers, and also over all the princes, communities, colleges and individual persons of this age, whatever their condition. We will set out first the passage of Scripture found in Matthew 16, where Christ, addressing the blessed Peter, says: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. From this passage some Roman bishops have taken to themselves the authority of the supreme jurisdiction just mentioned. For they wish the keys granted to the blessed Peter by Christ to be understood as the handing over of the full power of all human government, which Christ had over all kings and princes, and which he granted to the blessed Peter and his successors in the Roman episcopal see, as the general vicars of Christ in this world. A second passage, to establish the same point, is taken from the words of Christ in Matthew 11, when he said: All things have been delivered to me by my Father. And again in Matthew 28, when he said: All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. Therefore, since the blessed Peter and his successors in the Roman episcopal see were and are the Vicars of Christ, as these men say, it seems that all power, or the fullness of power, has been handed over to them, and consequently the authority of every jurisdiction. A third passage to the same effect is taken from Matthew 8 and Mark 5, where it is said: The demons begged him (namely, Christ) saying: If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine. And he said to them: Go. And they came out and went into the swine. And behold, the whole herd rushed down a steep place into the sea, and they were drowned in the waters. From these words it appears that Christ disposed of temporal things as of his own possessions, for otherwise he would have sinned by destroying the herd of swine. But it is impious to say that Christ, whose flesh did not see corruption, sinned. Therefore, since the blessed Peter and his successors, the Roman bishops, are and have been the chief Vicars of Christ, as some say, they can dispose of all temporal things as judges of the third sense, and they have the fullness of power and dominion, just as Christ had. Again, the same is shown by what is found in Matthew 21, Mark 11 and Luke 19, the sequence of which is this: Then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them: Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find an ass tied and a colt with her; or, a colt tied, on which no man has ever sat, as in Mark and Luke. Loose them and bring them to me. From these words the same conclusion may be drawn, by the same method of inference, as was drawn above from the sequence just cited. Further, the same is argued from Luke 22, where the following passage occurs: Behold, here are two swords, said the apostles, answering Christ. But he (namely, Christ) answered: It is enough. According to the interpretation of some, these words must be understood to mean that in the present world there are two principalities, one ecclesiastical or spiritual and the other temporal or secular. Therefore, since Christ, addressing the apostles, said: It is enough, that is, you have these two swords, it is supposed that he signified that both swords ought to belong to their authority, and especially to the blessed Peter as the chief among them. For if he had not wished the temporal sword to belong to them, he ought to have said: It is superfluous.

units.la: Rursum videtur idem credendum, ex Ioannis 21. vbi dum Christus alloqueretur beatum Petrum, dixit: Pasce oues meas, pasce agnos meos, pasce oues meas, ter eandem seu tentiam replicans, sicut induximus. Ex quibus quidem verbis accipiunt aliqui sensum hunc, videlicet beatum Petrum & ipsius successores Romanos episcopos, simpliciter praefesse debere omnibus quibus Christi fidelibus, scilicet Christianis, horum vero maxime presbyteris atq; diaconis.
units.tr: Again, it seems that the same must be believed from John 21, where Christ, addressing the blessed Peter, said: Feed my sheep, feed my lambs, feed my sheep, repeating the same sentence three times, as we have cited. From these words some draw the following sense: that the blessed Peter and his successors, the Roman bishops, ought simply to preside over all the faithful of Christ, that is, over Christians, and especially over their presbyters and deacons.

units.la: Adhuc videtur h ec aperte sententia beati Pauli primæ ad Corinth. sexto, cum dixit: Nescitis quòniam angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis seculria. Secularium ergo iudicia secundum tertiam significationem, ad presbyteros seu episcopos, ipsorum vero maxime primum, Romanum licet pertinere videntur. Rursum prima ad Corinth. nono, idem sensisse videtur Apostolus cum dixit: Nunquid non habemus potestatem manducandi, &c. Idem prima ad Thessa. 3. in quibus expresse videtur intendere sibi datam à Deo potestatem super temporalia fidelium, & per consequens iurisdictionem eorum.
units.tr: Again, the saying of the blessed Paul in 1 Corinthians 6 seems clearly to support this, when he said: Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more the things of this life? Therefore judgments over secular affairs, in the third sense, seem to belong to the presbyters or bishops, and especially to the first of them, the Roman bishop. Again, in 1 Corinthians 9 the Apostle seems to have had the same meaning when he said: Have we not power to eat and drink? etc. The same is found in 1 Thessalonians 3, where he seems plainly to intend that the power given to him by God extends over the temporal affairs of the faithful, and consequently their jurisdiction.

units.la: Amplius ostenditur idem ex prima ad Timotheum quinto, ad quem dixit Apostolus, Adversus presbyterum noli accipere accusationem, nisi sub duobus aut tribus testibus. Videtur igitur ex hoc quod episcopus saltem iurisdictionem habeat supra presbyteros, diaconos, & reliquos templi ministros, post quam ad eum accusationem ipsorum audire pertinet. De veteri autem scriptura seu testamento ad propositam conclusionem & ipsius oppositam, probationes omittemus inducere, propter quam vero causam, assignabimus nono huius. Ex dictis itaque scripturæ sacræ authoritatibus, & aliis consimilibus, ipsarumque talibus interpretationibus videri posset alicui episcopo Rom. deberi omnium principatum supremum. His consequenter adducere conuenit argumentationes aliquas quasi politicas, quæ fortasse quibusdam phantasiam facerent & credulitatem conclusionis prædictæ, harum autem prima sit hæc. Sicut se habet corpus ad animam, ita princeps corporum ad principem animarum, sed corpus animæ subest quantum ad regnum, ergo & princeps corporum secularis iudex subesse debet regimini iudicis seu principis animarum, & maxime primi omnium, videlicet pontificis Rom. Rursum ex eadem quasi radice, sicut se habent corporalia ad spiritualia, ita princeps corporalium ad eum qui spiritualium. Certum est autem corporalia indigniora & subesse spiritualibus secundum naturam. Igitur corporalium princeps secularis iudex ei qui spiritualium ecclesiastico subesse debet. Amplius sicut finis ad finem, lex ad legem, legislator ad legislatorem, ita iudex seu principans secundum horum alterutrum ad iudicem seu principantem secundum reliquum. Sed finis ad quem dirigit ecclesiasticus iudex, sacerdos seu episcopus, lex secundum quam dirigit legis illius lator, superiores sunt & perfectiores sine lege atque legislatore, ad quæ & secundum quæ dirigit secularis iudex, igitur iudex ecclesiasticus episcopus seu sacerdos, maxime primus, superior est quocunque iudice seculari. Finis enim ad quem dirigit ecclesiasticus iudex est vita æterna, lex secundum quam, diuina, & ipsius lator immediatus est Deus, in quo nec error aut malitia cadere potest, finis vero ad quem secularis iudex intendit dirigere est sufficientia huius vitæ mundanæ, lex secundum quam humana, & ipsius legislator immediatus homo vel homines, in quibus contingit error atque malitia. Sunt igitur hæc inferiora & indigniora prædictis, ergo & secularis iudex, supremus etiam, ecclesiastico sacerdoti supremo. Adhuc cuius actio simpliciter est honorabilior, ipse simpliciter est honorandus, sed actio episcopi seu presbyteri est omnium honorabilissima quæ per hominem fieri possunt in vita præsenti, videlicet consecratio benedicti corporis Christi, ergo & sacerdos quilibet dignior est quolibet non sacerdote. Cum igitur dignius indigniori subesse non debeat, sed præesse, videtur quod iudex secularis non præesse in iurisdictione, sed subesse debeat sacerdoti, & ipsorum maxime primo Romano pontifici. Ostenditur autem idem rursum in specie magis de Romanorum principe, Imperatore vocato, quoniam ille superior est ad Romanorum principem, secundum tertiam significationis iudicium, cuius est auctoritas instituendi principatum hunc, ipsumque de gente in gentem pro libito transferendi, Rom. pontifex se dicit huiusmodi, quoniam ipse hunc principatum transtulit à Græcis in Germanos, sicut expressum est in 7. suarum Decretalium, de iureiur. & idem dicit expressius modernus Romanorum vocatus Episcopus in quodam suo edicto ad Ludovicum Ducem Bavariæ, Romanorum Regem assumptum. Amplius ad idem, quoniam inconveniens videtur, Christi vicarium, Romanum episcopum, aliosque successores Apostolorum episcopos, subesse deberein iurisdictione cuiuspiam principis secularis, cumque etiam secularis princeps peccare possit contra legem diuinam & humanam, unde corrigendus, ut in 18. prima: nec superiorem habeat vel æqualem, qui supremus est omnium secularium, quoniam pluralitas principatuum reprobata est, 17. prima: videbitur in ipsum coactiva iurisdictio ad Romanum episcopum pertinere, nullatenus conuerso. Ex quibus quidem igitur videtur posse convinci, episcopos seu presbyteros, coactivam habere iurisdictionem, ipsorum vero supremo Romanorum pontifici, supremum omnium huius seculi principatum deberi, tam authoritatibus sacræ scripturæ, quam quibusdam quasi humanis & politicis argumentationibus sufficienter appositisse videmur.
units.tr: The same is further shown from 1 Timothy 5, where the Apostle said to Timothy: Do not receive an accusation against an elder except under two or three witnesses. It seems therefore from this that a bishop at least has jurisdiction over the presbyters, deacons and the other ministers of the temple, since it belongs to him to hear accusations against them. We shall omit to bring forward proofs from the Old Testament, or covenant, for the conclusion proposed or its opposite, and for the true cause of this we shall give the reason in the ninth chapter of this work. From the authorities of Holy Scripture just set out, and others like them, and from such interpretations of them, it might seem to someone that the supreme headship of all is owed to the Roman bishop. Next it is fitting to adduce certain arguments that are, as it were, political, which might perhaps lend plausibility and credibility to the conclusion stated above. The first of these is this. As the body is to the soul, so the prince of bodies is to the prince of souls. But the body is subject to the soul as regards rule. Therefore the prince of bodies, the secular judge, ought to be subject to the government of the judge or prince of souls, and above all of the first of them, namely the Roman pontiff. Again, from the same root: as bodily things are to spiritual things, so is the prince of bodily things to him who is over spiritual things. It is certain, however, that bodily things are less worthy and by nature subject to spiritual things. Therefore the secular judge, prince of bodily things, ought to be subject to the ecclesiastical judge, who has charge of spiritual things. Further, as end is to end, law to law, and lawgiver to lawgiver, so the judge or ruler under one of these is to the judge or ruler under the other. But the end toward which the ecclesiastical judge, the priest or bishop, directs, and the law according to which he directs, and the lawgiver of that law, are superior and more perfect than the secular judge's end, law and lawgiver. Therefore the ecclesiastical judge, the bishop or priest, and above all the first of them, is superior to any secular judge. For the end toward which the ecclesiastical judge directs is eternal life; the law according to which he directs is divine; and its immediate lawgiver is God, in whom neither error nor malice can fall. But the end toward which the secular judge intends to direct is the sufficiency of this mundane life; the law according to which he directs is human; and its immediate lawgiver is man or men, in whom error and malice may occur. These, therefore, are inferior and less worthy than the former. Therefore the secular judge, even the supreme one, is subject to the supreme ecclesiastical priest. Again, whose action is simply more honourable, he himself is simply to be honoured. But the action of the bishop or presbyter is the most honourable of all that can be done by man in the present life, namely the consecration of the blessed body of Christ. Therefore every priest is more worthy than any non-priest. Since, then, the more worthy ought not to be subject to the less worthy, but to preside over it, it seems that the secular judge ought not to preside in jurisdiction, but to be subject to the priest, and above all to the first of them, the Roman pontiff. The same is shown again, more particularly, concerning the Roman prince called Emperor, since the one who is superior to the Roman prince, in the third sense of judgment, is he whose authority it is to institute this principality and to transfer it at will from nation to nation. The Roman pontiff says that he is such a one, since he himself transferred this principality from the Greeks to the Germans, as is stated expressly in the seventh of his Decretals, on oaths; and the present-day bishop called Pope says the same more expressly in a certain edict of his, addressed to Ludwig, Duke of Bavaria, styled King of the Romans. Further, to the same effect: since it seems unfitting that the Vicar of Christ, the Roman bishop and the other bishops, successors of the apostles, should be subject to the jurisdiction of any secular prince, and since a secular prince can also sin against divine and human law, and so needs correction, as in the eighteenth prima; and since no one should have a superior or an equal who is supreme over all secular rulers, because plurality of principalities has been condemned, as in the seventeenth prima, it will seem that coercive jurisdiction over the prince belongs to the Roman bishop, and in no way the reverse. From these things, then, it seems that it can be proved that bishops or presbyters have coercive jurisdiction, and that the supreme headship of all the principalities of this age is owed to the supreme Roman pontiff. We seem to have set this forth sufficiently, both from the authorities of Holy Scripture and from certain quasi-human and political arguments.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: De canonicis scripturis, Christi mandatis vel consiliis & exemplis, & sanctorum ac approbatorum doctorum Evangelica legis expositorum, quibus demonstratur evidenter, Romanum aut quemuis Episcopum sive presbyterum vel clericum omnem virtute verborum scripturae, nullum coactivum principatum seu iurisdictionem contentiosam, nedum supremum omnium supra quemquam clericum aut laicum sibi vendicare vel ascribere posse, & quod Christi consilio & exemplo, praesertim in communitatibus fidelium, talem principatum, si eisdem offeratur aut conferatur per auctoritatem eius habentem, debeant recusare: Rursumque quod omnes Episcopi, & indifferenter vocati nunc clerici, subesse debeant coactivo iudicio sive principatui dominantis auctoritate legis lateris humani, praesertim fidelis.
units.tr: On the canonical Scriptures, the commands, counsels and examples of Christ, and the teaching of the saints and approved doctors who expound the Evangelical law. By these it is clearly shown that the Roman bishop, or any bishop, presbyter or clergyman whatever, cannot by the force of the words of Scripture claim or ascribe to himself any coercive principality or contentious jurisdiction, much less the supreme one over all, over any clergyman or layman. It is also shown that, following the counsel and example of Christ, especially in communities of the faithful, they ought to refuse such a principality if it is offered or conferred on them by one who has authority to do so. And again, that all bishops, and indiscriminately all those now called clergy, ought to be subject to coercive judgment or principality exercised by the authority of a human law-giver, especially a faithful one.

units.la: EX adverso autem consequenter adducere volumus veritates scripturae sacrae, praecipientis aut consulentis expresse, tam literali sensu suo, quam mystico, secundum sanctorum interpretationem, ac aliorum approbatorum doctorum Christianae fidei expositionem, Romanum Episcopum vocatum papam, aut aliorum quemlibet episcopum, seu presbyterum, vel diaconum, nullum habere debere principatum seu iudicium vel iurisdictionem coactivam cuiusquam sacerdotis, principantis, communitatis, collegii, vel personae singularis alicuius cuiuscunq; conditionis existat. Intelligendo per coactivum iudicium, id quod secundum tertiam significationem iudicis aut iudicii, secundo huius diximus importari.
units.tr: On the other side, we now wish to adduce in turn the truths of Holy Scripture, which expressly command or counsel, both in its literal sense and in its mystical sense according to the interpretation of the saints and the exposition of the Christian faith by other approved teachers, that the Roman bishop, called the pope, or any other bishop, presbyter or deacon, ought to have no principality, judgment or coercive jurisdiction over any priest, ruler, community, college or single person of whatever condition. By coercive judgment we mean what, in the third sense of judge or judgment, we said above in the second place is implied.

units.la: Verum propter intentionem hanc evidentius explicandam, oportet nos non latere, quod ex hac inquisitione, non quaeritur quid Christus, qui verus Deus & verus homo fuit, habuerit & habeat in hoc seculo potestatis & auctoritatis, nec quid aut quantum horum conferre potuerit beato Petro, & reliquis apostolis, ac ipsorum successoribus, episcopis seu presbyteris, quoniam de his non dubitant Christi fideles in propositis quaestis. Sed volumus & debemus inquirere, quam potestatem & auctoritatem exercendam in hoc seculo, Christus eisdem conferre voluerit, & de facto contulerit, & a qua ipsos exclauserit & prohibuerit consilio vel praecepto. Eos enim talem potestatem & auctoritatem habuisse a Christo, tenemur credere, qualem per verba scripturae sibi traditam conuincere possumus non aliam. Certum enim est omnibus Christi fidelibus, q; Christus, qui verus Deus & verus homo fuit, conferre potuit, nedum apostolis, verum etiam quibuslibet aliis, auctoritatem seu iurisdictionem coactivam in hoc seculo, supra omnes mundi principes seu principatus & singulares personas alias omnes; & hac ampliore fortasse, ut creadi entia, destruendi atq; reparandi coelum & terram, & quae in eis sunt, & etiam angelis simpliciter imperandi, quod tamen nec Christus contulit eis, nec conferre decrevit. Unde Aug. in sermone decimo de verbis domini super Matthaeum, sic inquit: Discite a me non mundum fabricare, non cuncta visibilia & invisibilia creare, non in ipso mundo miracula facere, & mortuos suscitare: Sed quoniam mitis sum & humilis corde. Ideoque secundum praesentem intentionem ostendere sufficit, & ostendam primo, quod Christus ipse non venit in mundum dominari hominibus, nec ipsos iudicare iudicio tertiae significationis, nec principari temporaliter, sed magis subiici secundum statum & conditionem praesentis seculi, quinimo quod a tali iudicio seu principatu, secundum propositum excludere voluit & exclusit seipsum & apostolos ac discipulos etiam suos, ipsorumq; successores consequenter episcopos seu presbyteros ab omni principatu seu mundano regimine tali, coactivo scilicet, exclusit exemplo & per sermonem etiam consilio vel praecepto. Idem quoq; ostendam apostolos praecipuos tanquam Christi veros imitatores fecisse, suosq; successores facere docuisse. Amplius quoq; tam Christum, quam ipsos apostolos voluisse lubesse atq; subfuisse continuo coactivae iurisdictioni principum seculi, realiter & personaliter, aliosq; omnes quibus legem praedicauerunt veritatis, aut per scripturam mandauerunt, idem facere docuisse atq; praecepisse sub poena damnationis aeternae. Deinde vero capitulum faciam de potestate seu auctoritate clauium, tradita per Christum apostolis, & ipsorum in officio successoribus, episcopis & presbyteris, ut tam Romani episcopi, quam aliorum appareat, quae, qualis, quantave sit potestas huiusmodi. Ipsius etenim ignorantia extitit hactenus, & in praesentiarum est, origo multarum quaestionum & damnosarum litium inter Christi fideles, ut in huius dictionis primo aliqualiter tangebatur.
units.tr: But to explain this purpose more clearly, we must not overlook that this inquiry does not ask what power and authority Christ, who was true God and true man, had and has in this world, nor what or how much of these he could have conferred on the blessed Peter, the other apostles and their successors, the bishops or presbyters. Christ's faithful do not doubt these things in the matters proposed. Rather, we want and ought to inquire what power and authority Christ wished to confer on them to exercise in this world, and what he actually conferred, and from what he excluded and forbade them by counsel or precept. For we are bound to believe that they had from Christ only such power and authority as we can prove was handed down to them by the words of Scripture, and no other. For it is certain to all Christ's faithful that Christ could confer, not only on the apostles but also on any others, authority or coercive jurisdiction in this world over all the princes or principalities of the world and all other single persons, and perhaps even a greater one, such as creating, destroying and restoring heaven and earth and whatever is in them, and commanding angels outright; yet Christ neither conferred this on them nor decreed to do so. Hence Augustine, in his tenth sermon on the words of the Lord on Matthew, says: Learn from me not to fashion the world, not to create all things visible and invisible, not to work miracles in the world itself and raise the dead; but learn that I am meek and humble of heart. Therefore, for the present purpose it is enough to show, and I shall show first, that Christ himself did not come into the world to rule over men, nor to judge them with the judgment of the third sense, nor to hold temporal power, but rather to be subject, according to the state and condition of the present age. Moreover, by his purpose he wished to exclude, and did exclude, from such judgment or principality, that is, from all worldly government of a coercive kind, himself, the apostles and his disciples, and consequently their successors, the bishops and presbyters, both by example and by word, by counsel or precept. I shall also show that the chief apostles, as true imitators of Christ, did this, and taught their successors to do the same. Further, I shall show that both Christ and the apostles themselves wished and actually were subject continually, in person and in reality, to the coercive jurisdiction of the rulers of this age; and that they taught and commanded all others to whom they preached the law of truth, or whom they instructed through Scripture, to do the same, under pain of eternal damnation. Then I shall make a chapter on the power or authority of the keys, handed down by Christ to the apostles and to their successors in office, the bishops and presbyters, so that it may appear, both for the Roman bishop and for the others, what this power is, of what kind and how great. For ignorance of it has hitherto been, and still is, the source of many questions and harmful disputes among Christ's faithful, as was touched upon in part at the beginning of this discussion.

units.la: Prosequentes itaq; proposita monstrare volumus, quod ab officio principatus sive contentiosae iurisdictionis, regiminis seu coactivi iudicii cuiuslibet in hoc seculo secundum propositum sive intentionem, sermonem, & operationem, seipsum & apostolos Christus excludere voluit & exclusit. Hoc autem primum apparet indubie per seriem evangelicam Ioannis 18. Dum enim Christus accusatus esset Pontio Pilato Vicario Romani principis in Iudaea, ex eo quod se dixisset regem Iudaeorum, interrogante Pilato, an haec dixisset, aut si se regem diceret, respondit inter cetera Christus ad Pilati quaesitum, verba haec: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, id est regnare non veni regimine seu dominio temporali, quomodo regnant mundani reges, cuius quidem probationem subdit ipsemet Christus per signum euidens, cum dixit: Si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei utique decertarent, ut non traderer Iudaeis. Quasi sicargueret Christus. Si venissem regnare in hunc mundum mundano regimine seu coactiuo haberem ministros huius regiminis, decertatores scilicet, ac transgressorum coactores, quemadmodum caeteri reges habent, sed tales ministros non habeo, vt tu manifeste videre potes. Vnde Glossa interlinearis, apparet quod nullus defendit. Et hoc est quod iterato resumens Christus ait: Nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc, de quo scilicet docere veni. Quas siquidem euangelicas veritates sancti & Doctores exponentes, sic inquiunt, & primum beatus Augustinus in haec verba, dicens: Quod si Pilato interrogante continuo respondisset, non etiam Iudaei, sed solis gentibus hoc de se opinantibus respondisse videretur. Sed post responsionem Pilati tam Iudaeis & gentibus opportunius aptiusque respondit. Quasi diceret: Audite Iudaei & gentes, non impedio dominationem vestram in hoc mundo, quid vultis amplius? venite credendo ad regnum quod non est de hoc mundo, quid enim est regnum eius nisi credentes in eum? Ecce de quo regno docere atque disponere venit, quoniam de actibus quibus peruenitur ad regnum aeternum, fidei scilicet, ac reliquarum theologicarum virtutum: neminem tamen ad hoc cogendo, vt infra patebit. Duo nanque coactiua dominia respectu eiusdem multitudinis non subinuicem posita se impediunt, vt in 7. prima monstratum est. Christus autem horum dominium non venerat impedire, vt dixit Augustinus. Vnde super illud Ioannis eodem: Gens tua & pontifices tui tradiderunt te mihi, quid fecisti? Satis, inquit Augustinus, ostendit illud pro crimine obiectum, tanquam diceret, si te regem negas, quid fecisti, vt tradereris mihi, quasi mirum non esset, sipuniendus iudici traderetur, qui se diceret regem. Ecce secundum Augustinum: quod nimirum, si puniendus fuisset Christus, si se regem secularem dixisset, ignorantibus praeterim ipsum esse Deum, & quod regem se fore negauit, & de quo regno seu regimine coactiuo videlicet legis transgressorum in hoc seculo. Vnde etiam super illud Ioannis eodem: A temetipso dicis hoc, an alii tibi dixerunt? Dixit Christus Pilato, inquit Theophylactes, ac si diceret (Christus scilicet Pilato:) Si hoc ex teipso loqueris, pandesigna mea rebellionis, at si ab aliis percepisti, inquisitionem fac ordinariam. Hoc autem, quod dicit Theophylactes, non debuisset dicere Christus, quod videlicet Pilatus inquisitionem de ipso faceret ordinariam, quinimo dicere debuisset hanc inquisitionem ad ipsum non pertinere, ex quo sibi secundum aduersantium opinionem de iure subiectus non erat vel esse nolebat in iurisdictione siue iudicio coactiuo. Rursum super illud, regnum meum non est hinc, dicit Chrysostomus: Non priuat mundum a sua providentia & prelatione, sed ostendit regnum suum non esse humanum, neque corruptibile. Omne autem regnum in hoc seculo cuiusquam coactiuum, est humanum corruptibile. Amplius super illud Ioannis eodem. Tu dicis quia rex sum ego; inquit Augustinus: Non quia regem se timuit confiteri, sed ita libratum est, vt neque se regem neget, neque regem talem se esse fateatur, cuius regnum putetur esse de hoc mundo. Dictum est enim, tu dicis, ac si diceretur, Carnalis carnaliter dicis de regimine carnali, & actuum temporalium contentiosorum & carnalium secundum tertiam significationem huius nominis temporale: tales enim carnales vocabat Apostolus prima ad Corinth. 3. Apparet igitur ex praedictis quod de carnali seu temporali regimine, vel iudicio coactiuo Christus in mundum disponere non venit neque docere, sed de spirituali regno siue caelesti: de hoc enim solummodo loquebatur, & quasi praedicabat semper, vt ex euangelica serie palam est, tam ex ipsius literali quam mystico sensu. Et propterea saepissime legimus ipsum dixisse: Simile est regnum coelorum. &c. de mundano vero rarissime, aut ipsum docendo spernere. In coelesti nanque regno se praemia vel supplicia daturum promittebat, secundum merita vel demerita operantium, nunquam tamen talia promisit in hoc seculo se facturum, sed magis econtrario huius seculi principantibus agit. Quoniam vt plurimum iustos & bonorum operatores affligit in hoc seculo, vel affligi sinit, & sic ad sui regni praemium perducit. Omnes enim qui placuerunt Deo per multas tribulationes transierunt, vt scribitur Iudith 8. Econtrario vero principes huius seculi seu iudices regni mundani, faciunt & facere debent, seruando iustitiam. Quoniam legum obseruatoribus praemia, & malorum patratoribus supplicia in hoc seculo distribuunt, recte agentes, contraria vero facientes peccaient contra legem humanam atque diuinam. Rursum ad principale per id quod Christus opere seu exemplo monstrauit. Legitur enim Ioannis 6. quod Iesus, cum cognouisset, quia venturi essent vt raperent eum & facerent eum regem, fugiit iterum in montem ipse solus. Vbi Glossa interlinearis: A quo descendit pascere turbas, prospera mundi docens fugere, & contraria erare. Certum est igitur, quod Christus fugiit principatum, aut suo nihil nos docuisset exemplo, quem sensum adiuuat expositio beati Augustini, dicentis, quod fideles Christiani sunt regnum eius, quod modo colitur, modo emitur sanguine Chr.sti. Erit autem aliquando manifestum regnum, quando erit aperta claritas sanctorum eius post iudicium ab eo factum. Discipuli autem & turba credentes in eum putauerunt eum sic euenisse, vt iam regnaret. Ecce quod sancti per regnum Christi in hoc seculo nunquam intellexerunt temporale dominium aut iudicium actuum contentiosorum, & executionem per coactiuam potestatem in legum transgressores in hoc seculo, sed per ipsius regnum; & regnum in hoc seculo intellexerunt doctrinam fidei & regimen secundum ipsam ad regnum coeleste. Quod quidem regnum dicit Augustinus futurum manifestum post eius iudicium in alio seculo. Iterum dicit, quod putare ipsum regnare tunc, quemadmodum turba putabant, erat eum rapere, id est indebite trahere, ac de ipso aestimare. Vbi Chrysostomus etiam. Et propheta iam erat apud eos, (Christus scilicet,) & regem eum inthronizare volebant, propter gulam scilicet, quia pauerat eos, Christus autem fugiit, erudiens nos mundanas contemnere dignitates. Amplius ostenditur idem evidentissime verbo & exemplo Christi, vbi Lucae 12. habetur haec series; Ait autem ei quidam de turba. Magister, dic fratri meo, vt diuidat mecum hereditatem. At ille, (Christus scilicet,) dixit ei. Nemo, quis me constituit iudicem aut divisorem super vos? Quasi diceret, propter hoc officium exercendum non veni, nec ad haec missus sum, per iudicium scilicet lites civiles dirimere, quod tamen nulli dubium est opus propriissimum principantium seu iudicum saeculi. Et licet re vera series Evangelica patentissime contineat & demonstret propositum nostrum, amplius quam glossae sanctorum, eo quod sensum literalem, qualem dicimus, tamque manifestum supponentes, ubique se magis ad allegoricum seu mysticum converterunt, eas tamen induximus ad maiorem propositi confirmationem, & ne temerarie scripturam dicamur exponere. Haec igitur verba Christi beatus Ambrosius exponens ait: Bene ergo terrena declinat, qui propter divina descenderat, nec iudex dignatur esse litium & arbiter facultatum, vivorum habens mortuorumque iudicium, arbitriumque meritorum. Et parum post subdit: Unde non immerito refutatur hic frater, qui dispensatorem caelestium gestiebat corruptibilibus occupare. Ecce quid sentit Ambrosius de Christi officio in hoc saeculo, dicit enim quod bene terrena declinat, id est iudicia contentiosorum agere, qui propter divina, id est spiritualia docenda & ministranda, descenderat, in quo ipsius & suorum successorum signavit officium, caelestia videlicet seu spiritualia dispensare. Spiritualia inquam, de quibus dixerat idem prima ad Corinth. nono, & supra induximus secundo huius in significatione tertia huius nominis spirituale. Nunc vero consequenter restat ostendere, Christum ipsum non solum huius saeculi principatum et coactivum iudicium in hoc saeculo recusasse, propter quod sic agendi apostolis & discipulis suis ac ipsorum successoribus dedit exemplum, verum etiam ipsum sermone docere, ac exemplo monstrasse, cunctos tam sacerdotes quam non sacerdotes subesse debere realiter & personaliter coactivo iudicio principum huius saeculi. Sermone quidem igitur & exemplo sui monstravit Christus hoc primum in realibus, per id quod habetur Matth. 22. nam interrogantibus Iudaeis ab ipso: Dic nobis quid tibi videtur, licet censum dare Caesari an non? His Christus inspecto denario & illius superscriptione, respondens ait: Reddite ergo quae Caesaris sunt Caesari, & quae Dei Deo. Ubi Glossa interlinearis, id est tributum & pecuniam. Ambrosius vero super illud: Cuius est imago & superscriptio haec? inquit sic: Sicut Caesar exigit impressionem suae imaginis, sic & Deus animam, lumine vultus sui insignitam. Attende igitur quid Christus exigere venit in mundum. Chrysostomus autem sic ait: Tu autem cum audieris, redde quae sunt Caesaris Caesari. Illa scito dicere cum solum, quae in nullo pietati nocent, quia si aliquid tale fuerit, non adhuc Caesaris est, sed diaboli tributum. Ecce quod in omnibus Caesari subesse debemus, dum modo non repugnent pietati, id est divino cultui seu mandato. In realibus ergo subiici voluit Christus principi seculari. Haec quoque fuit palam sententia beati Ambrosii, huic Christi sententiae innitens, dixit enim in epistola contra Valentinianum, quae intitulatur. Ad plebem: Solvimus quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, & quae sunt Dei Deo. Tributum Caesaris est, non negatur. Ostenditur autem rursum idem ex Matthaei 17. vbi sic scribitur: Accesserunt qui didrachma accipiebant, ad Petrum, & dixerunt, Magister vester non solvit didrachma? & consequenter paucis interpositis, subditur quod Christus dixit Petro: Ut autem non scandalizemus eos, vade ad mare, & mitte hamum, & eum piscem qui primus ascenderit, tolle & aperto ore eius invenies staterem, illum sumens, da eis pro me & te, nec dixit tantummodo dominus, da eis, sed dixit, da eis pro me & te. Hieronymus autem dicit hic; dominus noster secundum carnem & secundum spiritum, filius regis erat, vel ex David stirpe generatus vel omnipotentis patris verbum. Ergo tributa quasi regum filius non debebat. Et infra subiungit. Quamvis ergo liber esset, quia humiliatam carnu assumpserat, debuit omnem iustitiam adimplere. Origenes autem super illud verbum Christi: Ut autem non scandalizemus eos; magis ad propositum & Evangelistae sententiam, inquit sic. Consequens autem est intelligere, (ex verbis Christi scilicet,) quoniam quoties exurgunt quidam, qui per iniustitiam tollant nostra terrena, Reges huius terrae eos transmittunt ut exigant a nobu quae sunt ipsorum. Et suo exemplo, prohibet dominus aliquod scandalum fieri, etiam huiusmodi hominibus, sive ne amplius peccent, sive ut salvantur. Filius enim Dei, qui nullum opus fecit servile quasi habens formam servi, quam propter hominem suscepit, tributum & censum dedit. Quo igitur modo ex virtute verborum Euangelicae scripturae, sunt exempti Episcopi & presbyteri ab hoc, nec vniversaliter a principum iurisdictione, nisi gratiosa eorum concessione, cum Christus & Petrus exemplum praebentes aliis, tributa solverint? Et licet Christus secundum carnem de stirpe regia, hoc non debuisset fortasse, Petrus tamen de stirpe regia non existens, nec talem exemptionis habebat causam, sicut nec habere voluit. Quod si Christus putasset inconveniens, futuros sibi successores in officio sacerdotali tributa solvere, ac ipsorum temporalia subiecta fore principibus saeculi, potuisset ipse absque mali exempli exhibitione, videlicet subiiciendi sacerdotium iurisdictione principum saeculi, aliter ordinasse atque expediuisse illos exactores didrachmae, utputa remouendo ipsis petendi talia intentionem, aut alio conveniente modo. Sic autem facere non reputavit conveniens, quinimo solvere voluit, singulariter inter Apostolos Petrum sibi assocam in hoc. Qui tamen, secundum quod dicetur decimosexto huius, Ecclesiae praecipuus doctor & pastor futurus erat, ut tali exemplo, aliorum nullus sic facere recusaret. Hinc scripturae seriem ex Matthei decimoseptimo iam adductam, sic intelligens beatus Ambrosius, ut praediximus in epistola, cui titulus, De tradendu basilicu, inquit: Tributum petit (Imperator scilicet,) non negatur, agri ecclesiae soluunt tributum. Et quibusdam interpositis ad propositum magis ait: Solvimus quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, & quae sunt Dei Deo. Tributum Caesaris est, non negatur. Hanc rursum praeinductae scripturae, quam diximus fuisse sententiam, amplius exprimens beatus Bernardus in epistola quadam ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem, sic inquit: Hæc istis (scilicet, qui suggerunt subditos suis superioribus rebellare,) Christus aliter & ipse fit & gessit. Reddite, ait, quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei Deo. Quod ore locutus est, mox opere implere contrauit. Conditor Cæsaris, Cæsari non cunctatus est reddere censum. Exemplum enim dedit vobis, ut & vos ita faciatis. Quando vero Dei sacerdotibus debitam negaret reverentiam, qui hanc quoque secularibus potestatibus exhibere curauit? Et debemus attendere quod dixit Bernardus, Christum curando secularibus potestatibus tradere censum, ipsum exhibuisse debitam reverentiam, non ergo coactam, quoniam huiusmodi census & tributum debetur principibus a quocunque. Ut sequenti capitulo adducemus ex Apostolo ad Romanos 13. & glossa sanctorum atque doctorum ibidem, quamvis forte non omnis census a quibuscunque debeatur ubique, ut illius pedagii quod ab incolis non debebatur, quamvis custodes seu exactores illud quandoque a quibusdam incolis siue terrigenis simplicibus, quales erant Apostoli, minus debite peterent & exigerent. Et propterea conformiter Origeni, quem credo in hac parte magis habuisse intentionem Euangelistæ, quam Hieronymum. Dico, quod consuetum videbatur & fortasse statutum communiter in omnibus regnis, incolas siue indigenas non solvere pedagia, sed alienigenas. Et ideo dixit Christus Petro: Reges terræ a quibus accipiunt tributum? &c. per tributum significans illud pedagium quod exactores didrachmæ colligebant, tributum nanque secundum quod nomen commune est ad omnem censum, Christus non negavit filios terræ indigenas debere, quinimo de tali postmodum dixit, neminem eximendo, Reddite quæ Cæsaris sunt Cæsari, quod etiam Christo conformiter expressit Apostolus ad Romanos 13. dum dixit. Ideo enim tributa praestatis, principib. scilicet, ministri enim Dei sunt. Per filios ergo intellexit Christus filios regnorum, siue terrarum, id est, inde natos siue oriundos, alioquin sermo eius non videretur fuisse ad propositum, nam in plurali locutus est tam pro se quam pro Petro, quem constat non fuisse filium talium regum, de quibus dixit Hieronymus. Amplius, quoniam si Christus erat de stirpe Dauid secundum carnem, sic & alii plurimi Iudaeorum, quamvis fortasse non Petrus. Rursum, quoniam per Dauid nec aliquem ex ipsius semine, tunc exigebatur tributum, sed per Cæsarem, quid ergo dixisset Christus, reges terræ, &c. Ergo filii liberi sunt, de rege caelesti nihil dicens, constat autem etiam Christum neq; Petrum filios fuisse Cæsaris secundum carnem, neque secundum spiritum. Adhuc quid quæsiuisset Christus quæstionem præmissam? omnibus enim constat, filios regum secundum semen, non soluere tributa parentibus. Non igitur fuisse videtur expositio Hieronymi sic consona scripturæ, quemadmodum Origenis. Voluit autem Christus ex verbis prædictis, tributa etiam indebita alicui, & quandoque soluere potius, & apostolos & sibi successores soluenda docere, quam pro talibus contendere. Hæc enim fuit iustitia consilii non præcepti, quam Christus pro humilitate carnis quā sumpserat voluit adimplere ac impleri docere, quod etiam in Christi docebat apostolus fieri. Unde primæ ad Corinthios sexto: Quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? quam ut prædixerat invicem contendatis.
units.tr: Pursuing what we have set out, we want to show that Christ, in purpose, teaching, and action, intended to exclude himself and the apostles from the office of rule, that is, from contentious jurisdiction and from any coercive judgment in this world, and he did exclude them. This appears beyond doubt first from the Gospel narrative of John 18. When Christ was accused before Pontius Pilate, the deputy of the Roman emperor in Judaea, on the ground that he had called himself king of the Jews, Pilate asked whether he had said this. Among other things, Christ answered Pilate's question with these words: My kingdom is not of this world. That is, I did not come to reign by temporal rule or lordship, as worldly kings reign. Christ himself confirms this with a clear sign when he says: If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would surely fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews. It is as if Christ were arguing: if I had come to reign in this world by worldly rule or coercive power, I would have ministers of that rule, namely fighters and enforcers against transgressors, as other kings have. But I have no such ministers, as you can plainly see. Hence the interlinear Gloss: it is clear that no one defends him. And this is what Christ says again when he resumes: But now my kingdom is not from here, that is, the kingdom about which I came to teach. The holy Doctors, expounding these evangelical truths, say so. First blessed Augustine, in these words: If he had answered Pilate's question at once, it would seem that he answered only the Gentiles who held this opinion of him, not the Jews. But after Pilate's answer he replied more fittingly and suitably to Jews and Gentiles alike, as if to say: Hear, Jews and Gentiles, I do not hinder your dominion in this world. What more do you want? Come, believing, to the kingdom which is not of this world. For what is his kingdom but those who believe in him? Here is the kingdom about which he came to teach and to arrange, since it is by the acts by which one reaches the eternal kingdom, namely faith and the other theological virtues, and by compelling no one to them, as will appear below. For two coercive dominions over the same multitude, placed alongside each other, hinder one another, as was shown in the seventh chapter of the first part. But Christ had not come to hinder their dominion, as Augustine said. So also on that same passage of John: Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you to me; what have you done? Augustine says: it sufficiently shows that the charge was made as a crime, as if he meant: if you deny that you are king, what have you done that you should be handed over to me? As if it were not strange that someone who called himself king should be handed over to a judge to be punished. Here is Augustine's view: certainly, if Christ had called himself a secular king, he would have been punishable, especially since the people did not know that he was God, and he denied that he was to be a king, and denied that his kingdom was a coercive rule or kingdom of this age over transgressors of the law. Hence also on that same passage of John: Do you say this of yourself, or did others say it to you? Christ said to Pilate, says Theophylact, as if he said: If you speak this of yourself, you reveal my rebellion; but if you have heard it from others, make an ordinary inquiry. Yet what Theophylact says Christ should not have said, namely that Pilate would make an ordinary inquiry into him. Rather he should have said that this inquiry did not concern him, since, by the opinion of his opponents, he was not subject by right to jurisdiction or coercive judgment, nor did he wish to be. Again, on the words my kingdom is not from here, Chrysostom says: He does not deprive the world of his providence and rule, but shows that his kingdom is neither human nor corruptible. Every coercive kingdom in this age, however, is human and corruptible. Further, on the same passage of John: You say that I am king, Augustine says: not because he feared to confess that he was king, but so balanced that he neither denies being king nor admits being such a king as is thought to have a kingdom of this world. For the words you say are as if it were said: you speak carnally, of carnal rule and of contentious and carnal temporal acts, using the third meaning of the word temporal. For the Apostle called such people carnal in 1 Corinthians 3. It appears, then, from what has been said, that Christ did not come into the world to arrange or teach carnal or temporal rule or coercive judgment, but a spiritual or heavenly kingdom. For he spoke only of this, and was always, as it were, preaching it, as is plain from the evangelical narrative, both in its literal and its mystical sense. That is why we read so often that he said: The kingdom of heaven is like, and so on, but very rarely about worldly kingdoms, or he despised them in his teaching. For he promised that in the heavenly kingdom he would give rewards or punishments according to the merits or demerits of those who act, yet he never promised to do such things in this age. Rather, on the contrary, he deals with those who rule in this age. For for the most part he afflicts, or allows to be afflicted, the just and doers of good in this age, and so leads them to the reward of his kingdom. For all who have pleased God have passed through many tribulations, as is written in Judith 8. On the other hand, the princes of this age, the judges of the worldly kingdom, act, and ought to act, by preserving justice, since they distribute rewards in this age to observers of the laws and punishments to doers of evil, while those who act rightly and those who do the contrary sin against human and divine law. Again, to the main point, from what Christ showed by deed or example. For we read in John 6 that Jesus, when he knew that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, fled again to the mountain by himself. Here the interlinear Gloss says: from which he came down to feed the crowds, teaching us to flee worldly prosperity and to despise its contrary. It is certain, then, that Christ fled from rule, or else he would have taught us nothing by his example. Blessed Augustine's exposition supports this sense, saying that the faithful Christians are his kingdom, which is now worshipped, now bought with the blood of Christ. But his kingdom will be made manifest at some time, when the clear splendour of his saints appears after the judgment he has made. The disciples and the crowd believing in him, however, thought that it had come about already, so that he was now reigning. Here we see that the saints never understood the kingdom of Christ in this age as temporal dominion, or the judgment of contentious acts, or execution by coercive power against transgressors of the laws in this age. They understood it as his kingdom, and they understood the kingdom in this age as the teaching of the faith and the rule according to it toward the heavenly kingdom. Augustine says that this kingdom will be made manifest after his judgment in the other age. Again he says that to think that he was then reigning, as the crowd thought, was to seize him, that is, to drag him unduly and to form judgments about him. Chrysostom also says there: and he was already a prophet among them, Christ that is, and they wished to make him king, for the sake of their belly, since he had fed them; but Christ fled, teaching us to despise worldly dignities. The same is shown most clearly by the word and example of Christ, where Luke 12 contains this passage: And a certain man of the crowd said to him: Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. But he, that is Christ, said to him: Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you? As if he said: I did not come to exercise this office, nor was I sent for this, namely to settle civil disputes by judgment. Yet no one doubts that this is the very proper work of worldly rulers or judges. And although the evangelical narrative in truth contains and most openly demonstrates our purpose, more than the glosses of the saints do, since those who assume that the literal sense is such as we say, and so manifest, have everywhere turned more to the allegorical or mystical sense, nevertheless we have brought them forward to confirm our purpose more strongly, and so that we are not thought to expound Scripture rashly. So blessed Ambrose, expounding these words of Christ, says: He rightly declines earthly things who had come down for divine things, nor does he deign to be the judge of disputes and arbiter of possessions, having the judgment of the living and the dead and the decision of merits. And a little after he adds: Hence this brother, who wished to seize the dispenser of heavenly things for corruptible ones, is not without reason rebuked. See what Ambrose thinks of Christ's office in this age. For he says that he rightly declines earthly things, that is, the judgment of contentious parties, since he had come down to teach and minister divine, that is, spiritual, things. In this he marked the office of himself and his successors, namely to dispense heavenly or spiritual things. Spiritual things, I say, of which the same Apostle spoke in 1 Corinthians 9, and which we brought forward above in the second chapter, in the third meaning of the word spiritual. Now it remains to show in order that Christ not only refused worldly rule and coercive judgment in this age, which is why he gave an example to the apostles, his disciples, and their successors to act in this way, but also that he taught by word and showed by example that all, priests as well as non-priests, ought to be subject, really and personally, to the coercive judgment of the princes of this age. Christ, then, first showed this by word and example in real matters, through what is found in Matthew 22. When the Jews asked him: Tell us what you think: is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not? Christ, having looked at the denarius and its inscription, answered: Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. Here the interlinear Gloss says: that is, tribute and money. Ambrose, on the words Whose is this image and inscription?, says: As Caesar demands the impression of his own image, so God demands the soul, marked with the light of his own countenance. Consider, then, what Christ came into the world to demand. Chrysostom says: But when you have heard, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. Know that you should say this only of things that do no harm to piety, for if anything is of that kind, it is not Caesar's but the devil's tribute. See that we ought to be subject to Caesar in all things, provided they do not conflict with piety, that is, with divine worship or command. Christ, then, willed to be subject in real matters to the secular prince. This was also the plain opinion of blessed Ambrose, who, resting on this saying of Christ, said in his letter against Valentinian, entitled To the People: We render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. Caesar's tribute is owed, it is not refused. The same is shown again from Matthew 17, where it is written thus: Those who received the didrachma came to Peter and said: Does your master not pay the didrachma? And afterwards, with a few words interposed, it is added that Christ said to Peter: But lest we give offence to them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; open its mouth, and you will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and you. The Lord did not say merely, give to them, but said: give to them for me and you. Jerome says here: Our Lord, according to the flesh and according to the spirit, was the son of a king, either born of the stock of David or the Word of the almighty Father. Therefore he ought not to pay tribute as the son of a king. And below he adds: Although, then, he was free, because he had taken on a humbled flesh, he ought to fulfil all righteousness. Origen, however, on the words of Christ, But lest we give offence to them, speaking more to the purpose and to the sense of the Evangelist, says: It follows to understand, from the words of Christ, that whenever certain men arise who unjustly take away our earthly goods, the kings of this earth send them to exact from us what belongs to them. And by his example the Lord forbids that any offence be given, even to such men, either that they may not sin further, or that they may be saved. For the Son of God, who did no servile work, though having the form of a servant, which he took for man's sake, gave tribute and census. By what power of the words of the evangelical Scripture, then, are bishops and elders exempt from this, and not universally from the jurisdiction of princes, unless by their gracious concession, since Christ and Peter, setting an example to others, paid tribute? And although Christ, according to the flesh of royal stock, perhaps ought not to have done this, Peter, who was not of royal stock, had no such ground of exemption, nor did he wish to have one. But if Christ had thought it unfitting that his future successors in the priestly office should pay tribute, and that their temporal goods should be subject to the princes of the age, he could have ordered and arranged things otherwise, without giving an example of evil, namely by subjecting the priesthood to the jurisdiction of the secular princes. He could have dealt with those collectors of the didrachma, for instance by removing from them the intention of demanding such things, or by some other fitting means. But he did not think it fitting to act so; rather he willed to pay it, and singled out Peter among the apostles as his companion in this. Yet Peter, as will be said in the sixteenth chapter of this part, was to be the chief teacher and minister of the Church, so that by such an example none of the others would refuse to do likewise. Hence blessed Ambrose, understanding the passage from Matthew 17 already cited in this way, as we said before, in the letter entitled On Surrendering the Basilicas, says: The Emperor asks for tribute; it is not refused; the fields of the Church pay tribute. And after some words interposed, he says more to the point: We render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. Caesar's tribute is owed, it is not refused. Blessed Bernard, expressing more fully again the opinion we said was that of the Scripture just cited, says in a letter to the Archbishop of Sens: Christ himself acted otherwise than these men do, who stir up subjects to rebel against their superiors. Render, he said, to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. What he had spoken with his mouth he soon took care to carry out in deed. The Creator of Caesar did not hesitate to render the census to Caesar. For he gave you an example, that you too should do likewise. But when would he have denied the reverence due to the priests of God, who took care to show this also to secular powers? We ought to notice what Bernard said: that Christ, by giving the census to secular powers, showed them the due reverence, not a forced one, since such census and tribute is owed to princes by everyone. As we shall bring forward in the following chapter from the Apostle, Romans 13, and the gloss of the saints and doctors there, although perhaps not every census is owed by everyone everywhere, as in the case of the toll that was not owed by the inhabitants, although its guards or collectors sometimes demanded it, less rightly, from certain inhabitants or natives who were simple people, such as the apostles were. Therefore, agreeing with Origen, whom I think had more the intention of the Evangelist in this matter than Jerome did, I say that it seems to have been customary and perhaps commonly established in all kingdoms that inhabitants or natives did not pay tolls, but foreigners did. And so Christ said to Peter: From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute? and so on, meaning by tribute that toll which the collectors of the didrachma gathered. For tribute, according to the common meaning of the name for every census, Christ did not deny that the native sons of the land owed, but rather he afterwards said of such tribute, excepting no one: Render what is Caesar's to Caesar, which the Apostle also expressed in agreement with Christ in Romans 13, when he said: For this reason you pay tributes, namely to the princes, for they are God's ministers. By sons, then, Christ understood the sons of kingdoms or lands, that is, those born or descended there. Otherwise his speech would not seem to be to the point, for he spoke in the plural both for himself and for Peter, who was certainly not a son of such kings as Jerome spoke of. Further, if Christ was of the stock of David according to the flesh, so were very many other Jews, though perhaps not Peter. Again, since no tribute was demanded through David or any of his seed, but through Caesar, what would Christ have meant by saying the kings of the earth, and so on? Then the sons are free, saying nothing of the heavenly King. Yet it is certain that neither Christ nor Peter were sons of Caesar, either according to the flesh or according to the spirit. Moreover, what question would Christ have been answering with the question put before? For everyone knows that the sons of kings by birth do not pay tributes to their parents. The exposition of Jerome, therefore, does not seem to agree with Scripture as well as that of Origen does. Christ wished by these words that tributes, even those not owed to someone, should sometimes be paid rather than contended over, and he taught the apostles and their successors to pay them. For this was the justice of counsel, not of precept, which Christ willed to fulfil for the sake of the humility of the flesh he had taken, and to teach to be fulfilled, which the Apostle also taught was to be done in imitation of Christ. Hence 1 Corinthians 6: Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? That you contend with one another, as he had said before.

units.la: Amplius, acc solum quantum ad realia monstrauit Christus se subesse iurisdictioni ... uæ principis seculi, verum etiam id ostendit in se, quantum ad personalem, qua nullam iurisdictionem maiorem in ipsum aut alium princeps habere potuit, propter quod etiam vocatur hæc iurisdictio a Romano legis latore merum imperium. Hoc autem potest euidenter ostendi ex Matth. 27. nam ut ibidem legitur & apparet, Christus se capi permisit, ad Pilati ducem prætorium, qui vicarius erat Imperatoris Romani, & per ipsum demum tanquam iudicem coactuæ potestatis se sustinuit extremo supplicio iudicari & tradi. Nec contra ipsum tanquam contra non iudicem reclamauit, licet fortasse significauerit se pati minus iustam iudicium. Constat autem quod tale iudicium atque supplicium per sacerdotes subire potuisset si voluisset, si inconueniens iudicasset futuros sibi successores principibus seculi subiici, & per ipsos iudicari. Quod quia sententia hæc seriosius scripta est Ioannis 19. idcirco adducam hic, quod habetur ibidem. Dum ergo Christus ad Pilatum Cæsaris Vicarium esset adductus, accusatus etiam ex eo quod se regem Iudaeorum atque filium Dei dixisset, Pilato quoque interrogante Iesum, Unde es tu? Iesu autem ad hoc ei nullum dante responsum, dixit Pilatus ad ipsum verba consequentia, & nostro propositio atrinentia, quorum series talis est: Dicit ergo ei Pilatus, Mihi non loqueris, nescis quia potestatem habeo crucifigere, & dimittere te? Respondit Iesus. Non haberes potestatem aduersum me vllam, nisi datum esset tibi desuper. Ecce quod Iesus non negauit Pilatum habere potestatem ipsum iudicandi, & in ipsum iudicium exequendi. Nec dixit, hoc non pertinet de iure ad te, imo de facto id facis. Sed addidit Christus banc potestatem Pilatum habere desuper, quomodo desuper? Respondet Augustinus: Discamus ergo quod dixit, (Christus scilicet,) quod & Apostolum docuit, (Paulum videl. ad Romanos 13.) Quid ergo dixit Christus? quid Apostolum docuit quia non est potestas, (id est autoritas iurisdictionis) nisi a Deo, quisquid fit de actu male vtentu ea. Et quia plus peccat, qui innocentem occidendum potestatis liuore tradit quam ipsa potestas sit cum timore alterius potestatis maioris occidit. Talem quippe Deus dederat illi potestatem (Pilato scilicet,) vt effet etiam sub Cæsaris potestate. Fuit ergo iudicialis coactiua potestas Pilati supra Christi personam a Deo, sicut aperte Christus confessus est, & Augustinus palam expressit. Et aperte dixit Bernardus ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem epistola quadam. Cum, vt inquit, Romani præsidis potestatem, Christus super se quoque fateatur calcum ordinatam, loquens de potestate Pilati, & super hunc locum scripturæ. Si ergo Pilati iudiciaria potestas coactiua in Christum fuit a Deo, quanto magis & supra ipsius temporalia seu carnalia bona, si qua Christus possedisset aut habuisset. Quod si supra Christi personam & ipsius temporalia, quanto magis supra personas & temporalia omnium dominium apostolorum, & suorum successorum, omnium episcoporum seu presbyterorum? Fuit autem hoc non solum verbo Christi monstratum, sed operis consummatione firmatum. Nam per Pilatum eundem pro tribunali sedentem, iata fuit in Christum sententia capitalis, & per ipsius autoritatem, illius executio facta sententia, Unde Ioannis eodem habetur haec series: Pilatus ergo cum audisset hos sermones, adduxit foras Iesum, & sedit pro tribunali, & subditur paucis interpositis: Tu ergo tradidisti eis illum, (Iesum scilicet) ut crucifigeretur. Fuit autem de Christo talis Apostoli sententia, dum dixit ad Galatas tertio: At ubi venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere, factum sub lege, ergo & sub iudice, cuius erat iudicare atque praecipere secundum legem, qui tamen non erat episcopus aut sacerdos.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ showed that he was subject to the jurisdiction of the prince of this world not only in temporal matters, but also in his own person, since no prince could hold a higher jurisdiction over him or anyone else. For this reason the Roman lawgivers call this jurisdiction merum imperium. This can be clearly shown from Matth. 27. For, as is read and evident there, Christ allowed himself to be taken to Pilate, the governor, who was the vicar of the Roman Emperor, and through him, as judge with coercive power, he submitted to be judged and handed over to the extreme punishment. Nor did he protest against him as against one who was not a judge, although he perhaps indicated that he suffered an unjust judgment. It is certain that he could have undergone such a judgment and punishment through priests, if he had wished it, had he judged it unfitting for his future successors to be subject to the princes of this world and to be judged by them. Because this passage is written more seriously in John 19., I will cite here what is found there. While Christ was being led to Pilate, the vicar of Caesar, and was accused also because he had said that he was the King of the Jews and the Son of God, Pilate also asked Jesus, Where are you from? When Jesus gave him no answer, Pilate spoke to him the following words, which pertain to our proposition. The sequence is this: Pilate therefore said to him, Do you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have power to crucify you and to release you? Jesus answered, You would have no power against me at all, unless it had been given to you from above. Behold, Jesus did not deny that Pilate had the power to judge him and to carry out that judgment upon him. Nor did he say, "This does not belong to you by right; rather, you do it by force." Instead Christ added that Pilate had this power from above. In what way from above? Augustine answers: Let us learn, therefore, what he said (Christ, that is), which he also taught the Apostle (Paul, namely, in Romans 13): What then did Christ say? What did he teach the Apostle? That there is no power (that is, authority of jurisdiction) except from God, whatever is done by one who misuses it. For he who hands over an innocent man to be killed out of the malice of power sins more than the power itself does when it kills him out of fear of a greater power. For God had given that power to him (to Pilate, namely) so that he might also be under the power of Caesar. Therefore Pilate's judicial and coercive power over Christ's person was from God, as Christ plainly confessed and Augustine openly expressed. Bernard also plainly said in a certain letter to the Archbishop of Sens: Since, as he says, Christ acknowledges that the power of the Roman governor was ordained even over himself, speaking of Pilate's power and upon this passage of Scripture. If, then, Pilate's judicial and coercive power over Christ was from God, how much more would it extend over his temporal or material goods, if Christ had possessed any? And if it extended over Christ's person and his temporal goods, how much more over the persons and temporal goods of all: the dominion of the apostles, of their successors, and of all bishops or presbyters? This was shown not only by Christ's word but confirmed by the completion of the deed. For through the same Pilate, seated on the tribunal, a capital sentence was passed against Christ, and by his authority the sentence was carried out. Thus this sequence is found in John: Pilate therefore, when he had heard these words, brought Jesus out and sat on the tribunal, and a little further on, after some words intervene: Then you handed him over to them (that is, Jesus) to be crucified. Concerning Christ, the Apostle also gave this judgment when he said to the Galatians in chapter three: But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law; therefore also under a judge, whose office it was to judge and to command according to the law, who nevertheless was not a bishop or a priest.

units.la: Necale tantum Christus excludere voluit seculi principatum seu iudicialem coactivam potestatem, verum etiam a suis Apostolis hanc exclusit, tam ipsorum inuicem quam ad alios. Unde Matthaei vigesimo, & Lucae vigesimo secundo habetur haec series. Facta est autem contentio inter eos, (id est apostolos) quis eorum esset maior. Dixit autem eis, (Christus scilicet) Reges gentium dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur. In Matthaeo vero habetur haec clausula sic. Et qui maiores sunt potestate exercent in eos, vos autem non sic. Sed qui maior est in vobis, fiat sicut iunior, & qui praecessor, sicut minister. Nam quis maior est, qui recumbit, an qui ministrat? nonne qui recumbit? Ego autem in medio vestrorum sum sicut qui ministrat. Sed quicunque voluerit inter vos maior fieri, sit vester minister. Et qui voluerit inter vos primus esse, erit vester servus; sicut filius hominis non venit ministrari, sed ministrare, id est servire in temporalibus, non dominari vel par esse. Nam in ministerio spirituali erat primus, non servus in medio apostolorum. Vbi Origines: Scitis quia principes gentium dominantur eorum, id est non contenti tantum regere suos subditos, violenter eis dominari niituntur, id est per potentiam coactivam si oporteat. Inter vos autem qui estis mei, non erunt hoc; Quoniam sicut omnia carnalia in necessitate sunt posita, spiritualia autem in voluntate, sic & qui principes sunt spirituales (id est praelati) principatus eorum in dilectione debet esse positus, non in timore. Chrysostomus autem inter cetera dicit haec quae ad propositum sunt: Principes mundi ideo sunt, ut dominentur minoribus suis, & eos servituti subiiciant & expoliant, (supple, si demeruerint) & usque ad mortem eis vtantur ad suam (id est principantis) utilitatem & gloriam. Principes autem ecclesiae, (id est praelati) fiunt, ut serviant minoribus suis & ministrant eis quaecunque acceperunt a Christo, ut suas utilitates negligant & illorum procurent, & mori non recusent pro salute inferiorum. Primatum ergo ecclesiae cupiscere neque iustum, neque utile. Quis enim sapiens vult ultro subiicere se servituti & periculo tali, ut det rationem pro omni ecclesia? nisi forte qui non timet Dei iudicium, abutens primatu suo ecclesiastico seculariter, ita ut convertat illum in saecularem. Quid ergo de saecularibus iudiciis coactivis habent se intromittere sacerdotes? non enim debent temporaliter dominari, sed servire Christi exemplo & praecepto. Unde Hieronymus: Denique sui proponit exemplum, (Christus scilicet,) ut si dicta (ipsius, supple) parvipenderent (apostoli) erubescant ad opera, temporaliter dominari. Unde Origines super illo: Et dare animam suam redemptionem pro multis, inquit sic. Ecclesiarum ergo principes imitari debent Christum accessibilem, & mulieribus loquentem, & pueris manus imponentem, & discipulis pedes lavantem, ut & ipsi similiter faciant fratribus. Nos autem tales sumus (loquitur de praelatis sui temporis) ut etiam principum mundi excedere superbiam videamur, vel non intelligentes vel contemnentes mandatum Christi, & quaerimus sicut reges, arcies praecedentes & terribiles. Quod quia haec facere, contemnere, vel ignorare Christi mandatum est, primum sunt de hoc monendi praelati, quod faciemus ex hoc contractu, ostendendo quid ipsis autoritatis conveniat, deinde si contempserint, te corrigere, compellendi sunt atque cogendi per seculi principes, ne mores aliorum corrumpant. Haec igitur dicta sunt super Matthaeum. Super Lucam vero dicit Basilius: Decet autem & corporale obsequium ab his, qui praesident, offerri exemplo domini lavantis pedes discipulorum. Dixit ergo Christus, Principes gentium dominantur eorum, vos autem, (scilicet apostoli) non sic. Non igitur Christus rex regum & dominus dominantium eis potestatem exercendi secularia principum iudicia tradidit, neque in quenquam potestatem coactivam. Sed hanc ipsis aperte prohibuit, cum dixit, Vos autem non sic. Et idem consequenter tenendum de omnibus apostolorum successoribus, episcopis sive presbyteris. Hoc est etiam quod beatus Bernardus aperte dicebat ad Eugenium, de consideratione, libro secundo capitulo quarto, tractans illud Christi iam dictum: Reges gentium dominantur eorum, &c. inquit enim inter cetera: Quod habuit apostolus (Petrus videlicet) hoc dedit, solicitudinem, ut dixi, super ecclesias, nunquid dominationem? audi ipsum. Non dominantes, ait, de clero, sed forma facti gregis. Et ne dictum sola humilitate putes, ne etiam veritate, vox domini est in evangelio. Reges gentium dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur. Et infert: Vos autem non sic. Planum est, apostolis interdicitur dominatus, ergo tu usurpare audes, aut dominus apostolatum, aut apostolicus dominatum, plane ab utroque prohiberis si utrumque simul habere voles, perdes utrumque: alioquin non te illorum numero putes exceptum, de quibus quaeritur Deus sic: Ipsi regnaverunt & non per me: principes exiterunt, & non cognovi eos. Ex adductis itaque veritatibus evangelicis, & sanctorum & aliorum approbatorum doctorum interpertatoribus earum, apparere debet omnibus evidenter, Christum seipsum exclusisse seu excludere voluisse, tam sermone quam opere, ab omni principatu seu regimine iudicio coactivo seu potestate mundana, ipsumque seipsum principibus & seculi potestatibus, coactiva iurisdictione voluisse subiectum.
units.tr: Nor did Christ wish only to exclude the princely rule and the judicial coercive power of this world; he also excluded it from his apostles, both among themselves and in their dealings with others. Thus in Matthew 20 and Luke 22 this sequence is found: There arose also a contention among them (that is, the apostles) as to which of them should be greater. And he (Christ, that is) said to them: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. In Matthew the clause reads thus: And those who are great exercise authority over them. But you shall not be so. But whoever is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and he who is chief as the one who serves. For who is greater, he who sits at table or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at table? But I am among you as one who serves. Yet whoever wishes to become great among you, let him be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you, shall be your slave; just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, that is, to serve in temporal matters, not to dominate or to be an equal. For in spiritual ministry he was first, not a servant, in the midst of the apostles. Origen says: You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, that is, not content merely to rule their subjects, they strive to dominate them by force, that is, by coercive power if need be. But among you who are mine it shall not be so; for just as all carnal things are placed under necessity, spiritual things are placed under willingness, so also those who are spiritual princes (that is, prelates) should have their principate based on love, not on fear. Chrysostom, among other things, says what pertains to our purpose: Worldly princes exist so that they may dominate their inferiors, subject them to servitude and despoil them (supply: if they have deserved it) and use them up to death for their own (that is, the ruler's) advantage and glory.
