But the princes of the Church (that is, prelates) are made so that they may serve their inferiors and minister to them whatever they have received from Christ, neglecting their own advantages and seeking those of others, and not refusing to die for the salvation of those beneath them. Therefore to desire the primacy of the Church is neither just nor useful. For what wise man wishes of his own accord to subject himself to such servitude and danger, to give an account for the whole Church? Unless perhaps it is one who does not fear God's judgment, abusing his ecclesiastical primacy in a worldly way, so that he turns it into a secular one. Why then should priests take it upon themselves to meddle in secular judicial matters of coercion? For they ought not to dominate in temporal affairs, but to serve, after the example and precept of Christ. Hence Jerome: Finally, he sets before them his own example (Christ, that is), so that if they should disregard his words (the apostles, that is) they might blush at the deeds of temporal domination. Hence Origen on that passage: And to give his life as a ransom for many, he says thus: The princes of the churches ought therefore to imitate Christ, who was accessible, who spoke with women, who laid hands on children, and who washed the feet of his disciples, so that they too may likewise do these things for their brothers. But we are such (he speaks of the prelates of his own time) that we seem to surpass even the pride of the princes of the world, either not understanding or despising the command of Christ, and we seek, like kings, attendants going before us and terrifying people. Since to do these things, to despise them, or to be ignorant of them is contrary to Christ's command, the prelates must first be warned about this, and we shall do so from this treatise, by showing what authority belongs to them. Then, if they still despise it, they must be corrected and compelled by the princes of this world, lest they corrupt the morals of others. These things, then, have been said on Matthew. On Luke, Basil says: Bodily service also ought to be offered by those who preside, following the example of the Lord who washed the feet of his disciples. Christ therefore said, The princes of the Gentiles lord it over them; but you (namely the apostles) shall not be so. Christ therefore did not hand over to the apostles, the kings of kings and Lord of lords, the power to exercise the secular judgments of princes, nor any coercive power over anyone. Rather, he plainly forbade them this when he said, But you shall not be so. And the same must consistently be held concerning all the successors of the apostles, bishops or presbyters. This is also what blessed Bernard plainly said to Eugene in his book On Consideration, book two, chapter four, treating that saying of Christ already cited: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, etc. For among other things he says: What the Apostle (Peter, namely) had, he gave, as I have said, solicitude over the churches; but did he give domination? Hear him himself: not lording it over the clergy, he says, but being examples to the flock. And lest you think this is said only with humility, it is also said in truth: the voice of the Lord is in the Gospel: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. And he adds: But you shall not be so. It is plain that domination is forbidden to the apostles. Therefore you dare to usurp either lordship in the apostolate or apostolic authority in lordship. Plainly you are prohibited from both if you wish to have both at once; you will lose both. Otherwise do not think yourself excluded from the number of those of whom God complains: They have reigned, but not through me; they have become princes, but I did not know them. From the gospel truths cited, and from the interpretations of them by the saints and other approved teachers, it ought to be evident to everyone that Christ excluded himself, or wished to exclude himself, both by word and by deed, from every principate or government, from coercive judgment or worldly power, and that he himself wished to be subject to the princes and the powers of this world in coercive jurisdiction.

units.la: CAP. V. De canonicis Apostolorum oraculis & expositionibus sanctorum atque doctorum, quibus aperte convincitur idem quod ex capitula precedenti.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the canonical oracles of the Apostles and the expositions of the saints and teachers, by which the same thing is clearly proved as in the preceding chapter.

units.la: RElıquum autem & his habitum est ostendere, hanc eandem fuisse sententiam atque doctrinam præcipuorum Christi apostolorum, Pauli quidem primum, 2. ad Timothium 2. ipsum quem statuerat episcopum seu presbyterum admonentis se mundanis non immiscere negotiis. Inquit enim ipse: Nemo militans Deo implicat se secularibus negotiis. Vbi Glossa secundum Ambrosium: Quia nemo in spiritualibus militans Deo, qui non potest duidis duobus contrariis servis, sicut nemo potest duobus dominis servire, implicat se secularibus negotiis quibuslibet. Et dixit quibuslibet, nullum excipiendo. Cum igitur negotiorum omnium secularissimum sit principatus seu iudicium coactuum contentiosorum actuum, quoniam omnia secularia negotia seu seculares actus humanos, civiles ordinat & regulat, ut demonstratum est decimoquinto primæ, ipsum maxime fugiendum præcipit Apostolus ab eo, qui debet Deo militare, (spiritualia scilicet ministrado, qualis esse debet episcopus & sacerdos quicunque. Hanc autem, quam diximus Apostoli fuisse sententiam aperit ipsius series primæ ad Corinthios 1xxo, cum dixit: Secularia igitur iudicia si habueritis, contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia constituite ad iudicandum. Ibi enim loquebatur Apostolus ad omnes fideles & ecclesiam propriissime dictam secundum ultimam significationem videlicet, quam siquidem Apostoli seriem sic exponit Glossa secundum Ambrosium & Augustinum: Si secularia negotia, &c. Contemptibiles, id est aliquos sapientes, qui tamen sunt minoris meriti (supple, quam presbyteri & doctores evangelii) constituite ad iudicandum. Et redditur causa quare non ministros evangelii: Apostoli enim circumeuntes talibus non vacabant. Sapientes ergo qui in locis consistebant fideles & sancti, non qui hac atque illac propter evangelium discurrebant, talium negotiorum examinatores esse voluit. Aliam vero causam huius assignat Glossa secundum Gregorium in moralibus, & iudicio meo recte ad intentionem Apostoli: Cur enim debent contemptibiles, &c. non episcopi vel sacerdotes ad secularia officia exercenda constituì? inquit Gregorius: Ut videlicet hi terrenas causas examinent, qui exteriorum rerum, id est actuum secularium seu civilium sapientiam perceperunt. Qui autem spiritualibus donis ditati sunt, terrenis non debent negotiis implicari. Ut dum non coguntur inferiora bona disponere, valeant bonis superioribus deservire. Ecce apertissimam Apostoli & sanctorum intentionem esse, quam diximus de officio sacerdotibus per Apostolum interdicto. Quod etiam exprimens Bernardus ad Eugenium de consideratione, libro primo, cap. quinto, sic ait, ad Romanos & reliquos episcopos sermonem dirigens: Ergo in criminibus, non in possessionibus, potestas vestra, propter illa siquidem, & non propter has accepistis claves regni cælorum; prævaricatores itaque exclusuri, non possessiones, ut sciatis, ait, quia filius hominis potestatem habet dimittendi peccata. Et infra subdit: Quæ nam tibi videtur maior dignitas & potestas, dimittendi peccata an prædia dividendi? habent hæc infima & terrena iudices suos reges & principes terræ. Quid fines alienos invaditis? Non pertinet igitur ad officium episcopi sive presbyteri contentiosos actus carnales sive temporalia iudicare iudicio coactivo. quinimo se talibus immiscentes episcopi sive presbyteri alienos fines invadunt, id est alienum perturbant officium & falcem in alienam messem extendunt, secundum Bernardum. Voluit ergo Apostolus eos iudicare coactivo iudicio, qui non sunt ordinati administrandum in evangelio, & qui exteriorum rerum scientiam, id est actuum civilium perceperunt. Cum igitur a tali iudicio, nemo delinquens sit exemptus, apparet tam sacerdotes quam non sacerdotes principantium coactuo iudicio fore subiectos. Et est hic diligenter adurtendum, quod Apostolus generaliter scribens fidelibus de Corintho, sicut ex salutatione apparet, & quia in ecclesia reponit contemptibiles, id est seculares secundum Glossæ interpretationem non dixit, Contemptibiles constituo, nec alium quenquam ad iudicandum secularia negotia quæ habueritis. Nec etiam sui vice aliquem reliquit ibidem ad talia iudicandum, aut tales iudices constituendum. Quod tamen fecisset aut facere debuisset, si hoc ad suum officium & autoritatem pertinuisset, quemadmodum de presbyteris & episcopis fecit. Illos enim in locis fidelium instituebat, & aliorum institutionem eis facere præcipiebat seu committebat, sicut apparet prima ad Timoth. tertio & ad Titum primo. Ad Titum enim ait: Huius gratia reliqui te Creta, ut ea quæ desunt corrigas mala scilicet in peccantibus, & bonum addas, ut dicit Glossa. Et constituas per civitates presbyteros. De secularibus vero iudicibus quoniam hi per humanam electionem habent institui secundum modum quem assignaumus 1 5. prima, dixit Apost. Constituite, ad fideles loquens. Quoniam horum est autoritas hæc, nec dixit alicui episcopo vel sacerdoti, constituas, quemadmodum de sacerdotib. fecit, nec seculares actus per episcopos aut presbyteros iudicari præcepit, sed potius interdixit. Unde Bernardus, ubi supra: Audi tamen Apostolum quid de huiusmodi sentiat. Sic non est sapiens inter nos, ait ille, qui iudicet inter fratrem. Et infert, ad ignominiam vobis dico. Contemptibiliores qui sunt in ecclesia illos constituite ad iudicium. gradum contemptibilium itaque secundum Apostolum indigne tibi vsurpas tu apostolicus officium vile. Unde & dicebat episcopus (Apostolus scilicet) episcopum instruens; nemo militans Deo, implicat se negotiis secularibus. Et subdit, putas ne hæc tempora sustinerent si hominibus litigantibus pro terrena hereditate, & flagitantibus abs te iudicium voce domini respondere; O homines, quis me constituit iudicem super vos? in quale mox iudicium tu venires? Quod diceret homo rusticanus & imperitus, ignoras primatum tuum, ignoras summam & præexcelsam sedem, derogas apostolicæ dignitati. {hyphen-start}initiati. Et tamen non monstrabunt, puto, qui hoc dicerent, vbi aliquando quispiam apostolorum, iudex sederit hominum, aut diuisor terminorum, aut distributor terrarum. Stetisse deniq; lego apostolos iudicandos, sedisse iudicantes non lego. Erit illud non fuit, ita ne imminutor est dignitatis seruus, si non vult esse maior eo qui misit se? Aut filius si non transgrediatur terminos, quos posuerunt patres sui? Quis me constituit iudicem? aut ille magister & dominus. Et eo it iniuria seruo discipulo, nisi iudicet vniuersos? Dixit ergo Bernardus, successorem apostolorum indigne sibi vlurpare officium iudiciale. Et haec rursum subiungens ait: Mihi tamen non videtur aestimator bonus rerum, qui indignum putat apostolis seu apostolicis viris non iudicare de talibus, quibus datum est officium in maiora. Quid ni contemnant iudicare de terrenis possessiunculis hominum, qui in caelestibus & angelos iudicabunt? Praecepit quoq; sanctus Apostolus, omnes indifferenter neminem excipiendo, episcopum, vel sacerdotem, aut diaconum subesse debere in iudicio coactiuo, iudicibus seu principibus secularibus, nec illis resistendum, nisi quicquam contra legem salutis aeternae faciendum perciperent. Vnde ad Romanos 13. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit, non. n. est potestas nisi a Deo. Quae autem sunt a Deo, ordinata sunt. Itaq; qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit: qui resistunt ipsi, sibi damnationem acquirunt. nam principes non sunt timori boni operis, sed mali. Vis autem non timere potestatem, fac bonum, & habebis laudem ex illa. Dei. n. minister est tibi in bonum. si autem malefeceris, time. non. n. sine causa gladium portat. Dei. n. minister est vindex in iram & qui malum agit. Ideo necessitate subditi estote non solum propter iram, sed propter conscientiam. Ideo. n. & tributa praestatis. ministri. n. Dei sunt, in hoc ipsum seruientes. Reddite omnibus debita, cui tributum, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal: cui timorem, timorem: cui honorem, honorem.
units.tr: It remains, in addition to these points, to show that this same view and teaching was held by the chief apostles of Christ, and first by Paul, 2 Timothy 2, who admonishes Timothy, whom he had appointed bishop or presbyter, not to involve himself in worldly affairs. For he says: No one who serves as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular business. Here the Gloss, following Ambrose, says: Because no one who serves God in spiritual matters, who cannot serve two contrary masters, just as no one can serve two lords, entangles himself in any secular business whatsoever. He said "any whatsoever," excepting none. Since, then, the most secular of all business is the exercise of authority or the judgment of compulsory, contentious acts, inasmuch as all secular business, that is, civil human acts, is ordered and regulated by it, as was demonstrated in the fifteenth [chapter] of the first [book], the Apostle most of all forbids that a man who ought to serve God (namely, one who ministers spiritual things, such as every bishop and priest ought to be) should flee from it. That this was the Apostle's view, as we have said, is shown by the sequel of the first [letter] to the Corinthians, chapter 6, where he says: If then you have secular judgments, appoint to judge those who are despised in the Church. For the Apostle was there speaking to all the faithful and to the Church in the strictest sense, namely in its ultimate signification. The Gloss, following Ambrose and Augustine, explains this passage thus: If secular business, etc. Despised, that is, some wise men who nevertheless are of lesser merit (supply: than the presbyters and teachers of the Gospel), appoint to judge. And the reason is given why he did not choose ministers of the Gospel: For the apostles, going about, did not have leisure for such things. Therefore he wanted the wise men who remained in the places of the faithful and the saints, not those who ran here and there on account of the Gospel, to be the examiners of such business. The Gloss, following Gregory in the Moralia, and in my judgment rightly to the Apostle's intention, assigns another reason for this: Why ought the despised, etc., not bishops or priests, be appointed to exercise secular offices? Gregory says: namely so that those who have acquired wisdom in external things, that is, in secular or civil acts, may examine earthly causes. But those who have been enriched with spiritual gifts ought not to be entangled in earthly business, so that, while they are not forced to arrange lower goods, they may be able to serve higher goods. Behold the most evident intention of the Apostle and of the saints, which we have said is forbidden to priests by the Apostle. Bernard, expressing this also, in his To Eugenius on Consideration, book 1, chapter 5, addresses the Pope and the other bishors thus: Therefore your power lies in crimes, not in possessions; for it was for those, and not for these, that you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, to exclude the transgressors, not possessions, as you know, he says, because the Son of Man has power to forgive sins. And below he adds: Which seems to you the greater dignity and power, to forgive sins or to divide estates? These lowly and earthly things have their judges, the kings and princes of the earth. Why do you invade other men's boundaries? It does not belong, therefore, to the office of a bishop or presbyter to judge carnal and temporal contentious acts by coercive judgment. Indeed, bishops or presbyters who involve themselves in such things invade other men's boundaries, that is, they disturb another's office and extend the sickle into another's harvest, according to Bernard. The Apostle therefore wished those to judge by coercive judgment who are not ordained to administer the Gospel, and who have acquired knowledge of external things, that is, of civil acts. Since, then, no one who offends is exempt from such judgment, it is clear that priests and non-priests alike are subject to the coercive judgment of those who rule. And here it must be carefully noted that the Apostle, writing generally to the faithful at Corinth, as appears from the greeting, and because in the Church he sets the despised, that is, according to the Gloss's interpretation, the secular, did not say "I appoint the despised," nor did he leave anyone in his place there to judge the secular business that you have, nor did he appoint such judges. Yet he would have done so, or ought to have done so, if this had belonged to his office and authority, as he did with presbyters and bishops. For he established these in the places of the faithful and commanded or entrusted to them the appointment of others, as appears in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1. For to Titus he says: For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking, namely the evils among those who sin, and add the good, as the Gloss says. And appoint presbyters through the cities. But concerning secular judges, since these are instituted by human election, according to the manner we indicated in the fifteenth [chapter] of the first [book], the Apostle, speaking to the faithful, said: Appoint. Since this authority belongs to them, he did not say to any bishop or priest, "Appoint," as he did about the priests, nor did he command that secular acts be judged by bishops or presbyters, but rather forbade it. Hence Bernard, in the place cited above: Yet hear what the Apostle thinks about such matters. "So there is not a wise man among you," he says, "who can judge between his brothers." And he adds: I speak to your shame. The more despised in the Church, appoint them to judge. So according to the Apostle, you unworthily usurp the office of a judge, a lowly office, you who are an apostolic man. Hence the bishop (the Apostle himself), instructing the bishop, also said: No one serving God entangles himself in secular business. And he adds: Do you think these times could bear it if, when men quarrelling over an earthly inheritance and demanding judgment from you, you answered with the voice of the Lord, "O man, who appointed me judge over you?" What would the rustic and unlearned man say, when you came to such a judgment? "You do not know your primacy, you do not know your high and exalted seat; you detract from the apostolic dignity." [...] And yet, I think, those who said this will not show where any of the apostles ever sat as judge of men, or divider of boundaries, or distributor of lands. I read that the apostles stood to be judged; I do not read that they sat judging. Is that not a diminution of dignity: "A servant is not greater than the one who sent him" [...]? Or the son, if he does not transgress the boundaries which his fathers set? "Who appointed me judge?" says that Master and Lord. Is it an injustice to the servant or disciple that he should not judge everyone? Bernard therefore said that the successor of the apostles unworthily usurps for himself the judicial office. Again adding this, he says: Yet to me he does not seem a good judge of things who thinks it unworthy for apostles or apostolic men not to judge such things, to whom has been given an office in greater matters. Why should they disdain to judge about men's petty earthly possessions, who will judge even angels in heavenly things? The holy Apostle also commanded that every man, without exception, bishop, priest, or deacon, ought to be subject in coercive judgment to secular judges or princes, nor should one resist them unless he perceived that something was being done against the law of eternal salvation. Hence Romans 13: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, for there is no power except from God. Those that exist are ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists the power resists God's ordinance, and those who resist bring condemnation on themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the power? Do good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God's minister to you for good. But if you do evil, fear, for it does not bear the sword in vain. For it is God's minister, an avenger for wrath against him who does evil. Therefore be subject not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay tributes, for they are God's ministers, serving in this very thing. Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour.

units.la: Volui autem super haec apostoli notanda verba, inducere Glossam secundum sanctos atq; doctores catholicos, quoniam ex his quae dixit Apostolus & Glossator, tam aperte demonstratur propositum nostrum esse verum, vt nemo compositae mentis, ipsis inspectis, debeat vlterius dubitare. Dixit ergo Apostolus: Omnis anima &c. nullam excipiendo. Vbi Glossa secundum Aug. primo: Et quandoq; vicissim secundum Amb. inquit sic. Et hic ad humilitatem inuitat. Videbatur. n. quibusdam quod mali domini, & maxime infideles, non deberent fidelibus dominari. Et si boni & fideles essent, bonis & fidelibus essent patres. Quam et superbiam remouet hic Apostolus a parte superiore, id est anima, significans totum hominem. Quid. n. est omnis anima, nisi omnis homo? quasi dicat, omnia praedicta facienda sunt, & si ita perfecti sitis in corpore Christi, tamen omnis anima subdita sit, id est omnis homo subditus sit. Quem nomine anima ideo significo, vt non solum corpore, sed & voluntate seruiatis. Omnis ergo anima subdita sit vt et voluntate seruiat potestatib. secularibus, bonis & malis, scilicet, regibus, principibus, tribunis, centurionibus, & aliis huiusmodi. Ecce ergo quid intelligebat Apostolus per potestates sublimiores, quoniam seculares principes tunc subiungit. Si. n. bonus fuerit qui tibi praest, nutritor tuus est: malus si fuerit, tentator tuus est. Et nutrimenta libenter accipe, & in tentatione approbare. Esto ergo aurum & attende mundum iustum, quasi fornace aurificis. Sic ergo omnis anima subdita potestatib. sublimioribus, id est in hoc quod sublimes sunt, id est in mundanis, vel notatur causa cum dicit, sublimioribus. id est quia sublimiores sunt. (Non est. n.) probat quod debent subiici hoc modo, quia potestas omnis est a Deo. Sed quae a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt, igitur potestas est a Deo ordinata, id est quicunq; habet potestatem, Dei ordinatione habet. Itaq; qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit. Et hoc est quod dicit, quasi ideo debet subiici, quia non est potestas alicui homini bono vel malo, nisi a Deo data. Vnde Pilato dominus ait: Non haberes in me potestatem, nisi datum esset tibi desuper. Quod et Bernardus Archiepis. Senonensis repetens ait Secularior nemo Pilato, cui dominus affixit iudicandum. Non haberes, inquit, in me potestatem, nisi tibi esset data desuper. Ita tunc pro se loquebatur, & in se experiebatur, quod post per apostolos clamavit in ecclesiis, non est potestas nisi a Deo. Et qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit. Et infra paru ibid. subdit. Cum Romani praesidum potestate Christus super se quoq; fateatur coelitus ordinata, &c. Sequitur in glossa. Quae autem sunt, a Deo ordinata sunt, id est rationabiliter a Deo dispositae sunt. Itaq; qui resistit vi vel dolo potestati, id est homini habenti potestatem, in his scilicet, quae ad potestatem pertinent vt in tributo & huiusmodi, Dei ordinationi resistit, id est habetis potestatem Dei ordinatione. Non ergo secundum Dei ordinationem agit. De potestate bona patet, quod ex praecepit Deus rationabiliter: de mala et videri potest, dum & boni per ea purgantur & mali damnantur, & ipsa detrimentum praecipitatur. Et nota, quod nomine potestatis interdum accipitur potestas ipsa, quae data est aliquando a Deo, aliquando ipse homo habens potestatem, quod diligens lector distinguat. Qui autem quasi qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit. Hoc autem tam grave est, quod qui ei resistit, ipsi sibi acquirunt damnationem. Et ideo non debet quis, id est aliquis seu nullus resistere, sed subiici. Si tamen illud iubeat, quod non debet facere, his sane continet potestate, timendo potestatem maiorem. Ipsos humanarum rerum gradus aduerte. Si quid iusserit curator nunquid faciendum est, si contra proconsulem iubeat? Rursus si quid ipse proconsul iubeat, & aliud Imperator iubeat, nunquid dubitatur illo contempto, id est proconsuli, illi, id est Imperatori seruiendum? Ergo si aliud Imperator, aliud Deus iubeat, contempto illo, obtemperandum est Deo.
units.tr: I wish also to bring forward, on these words of the Apostle that deserve notice, the gloss of the holy and catholic doctors. From what the Apostle and the glossator said, our position is so clearly shown to be true that no one of sound mind, having looked at these things, should doubt it any further. The Apostle therefore said: "Let every soul be subject," excepting no one. Here the gloss, first following Augustine and then Ambrose, says: "And here he calls us to humility. For it seemed to some that wicked masters, and especially unbelievers, ought not to rule over believers, and that if they were good and believing, they would be fathers to good and believing people. The Apostle removes this pride here by speaking of the higher part, that is the soul, signifying the whole man. For what is 'every soul' but every man? As if he said: all the things said above are to be done, and even if you are so perfect in the body of Christ, still every soul must be subject, that is, every man must be subject. I name the soul so that you serve not only with the body but also with the will. Every soul, then, must be subject, so that it serves the secular powers with its will, whether good or bad, namely kings, princes, tribunes, centurions, and others of this kind. See, then, what the Apostle understood by the higher powers, since he next subjoins the secular princes: 'If he who rules over you is good, he is your nourisher; if he is bad, he is your tempter. Accept nourishments gladly, and be approved in temptation.' Be therefore gold, and attend to the just world as the goldsmith's furnace. So every soul is subject to the higher powers, that is, in what they are higher in, namely in worldly matters. Or the cause is noted when he says 'higher,' that is, because they are higher. He proves that they must be submitted to in this way, because all power is from God. But what is from God is ordered; therefore power is ordered by God, that is, whoever has power has it by God's ordinance. Therefore whoever resists the power resists God's ordinance. This is what he means: as if one ought for this reason to be subject, because no power is given to any man, good or bad, except from God. Hence the Lord said to Pilate: 'You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above.' Bernard, Archbishop of Sens, repeating this, says: 'No one was more secular than Pilate, to whom the Lord entrusted judgment. "You would have no power over me," he says, "unless it had been given you from above." So then he spoke for himself and experienced in himself what afterwards was proclaimed by the apostles in the churches: there is no power but from God, and whoever resists the power resists God's ordinance.' And a little below in the same place he adds: 'Since Christ himself confesses that the power of the Roman governors was also ordained from heaven,' etc. The gloss continues: 'Those powers which are, are ordered by God,' that is, rationally disposed by God. Therefore whoever resists, by force or by fraud, the power, that is, the man who has power, in those things which belong to power, such as tribute and the like, resists God's ordinance, that is, you have power by God's ordinance. Therefore he does not act according to God's ordinance. That good power is from God is evident, since it rationally commands; that bad power may also be seen, since by it good men are purged and bad men condemned, and it is itself punished. And note that by the name of power sometimes the power itself is understood, which was given at some time by God, and sometimes the man himself who has power; the diligent reader should distinguish these. Whoever resists, therefore, resists God's ordinance. This is so grave that those who resist acquire damnation for themselves. Therefore no one, that is, anyone or no one, should resist, but be subject. Yet if the power commands what one ought not to do, one should indeed refuse in that matter, fearing the greater power. Mark the very degrees of human affairs. If a curator orders something, is it to be done if the proconsul orders otherwise? Again, if the proconsul himself orders something and the Emperor orders something else, is there any doubt that the proconsul is to be despised and the Emperor served? Therefore, if the Emperor orders one thing and God another, the Emperor is to be despised and God obeyed."

units.la: Non randixit Aug. Si aliud Imperator, & aliud episcopus seu papa iubeat, quod tn dicere debuisset, si papa iurisdictionis gradu superior esset, tn voluit Aug. q; si praecepit Imperator aliquid faciendum contra legem salutis aeternae, quae Dei praeceptum est immediatum, in hoc Imperatori non esse obtemperandum, in quo papae praecipienti secundum hanc legem, sc. diuinam magis esset obtemperandum, qua Imperatori praecipienti quicquam agendum contrarium legi diuinae. Sed papae p. ipienti aliquid secundum suas Decretales inquantum huiusmodi, nihil obediendum contra Imperatoris seu legum suarum praeceptum, vt hic aperte liquet, & nono huius amplius deducetur. Tunc Glossa: Quasi merito acquirunt damnationem. na principes boni vel mali non sunt timori boni operis sed mali, id est non sunt ad timore his qui bene operantur, sed his qui male. Si enim bonus est princeps bene operantem non punit, sed diligit. si vero malus, non nocet bono, sed purgat eum. Malus vero debet timere, quia instituti sunt principes vt mala puniant. Principes dicit illos, qui propter corrigendam vitam & prohibenda aduersa creantur, Dei habentes imaginem, vt caeteri sub vno sint. Vobis autem quasi male operantibus sunt timori. Tu autem vis non timere potestatem, quecunq; sit, siue bona, siue mala? Fac bonum, & non est unde timeas, imo habebis laudem ex illa, etiam si mala est, dum tibi causa est maioris corone. Si autem iusta est potestas, habebis laudem ex illa, etiam ipsa laudante. si iniqua est, habebis laudem ex illa, non ipsa laudante, sed ipsa tibi laudis occasionem prabente, vere ex illa habebis laudem. Dei enim minister est tibi in bonum, id est tibi est faciens bonum, siue bonus, siue malus sit, quia tibi datus est in bonum tuum à Deo, vt tueatur te & tua. Manifestum est enim, quod ideo dati sunt à Deo reges, ne malum faciat bonis. si autem quasi bono, non est timendum, est enim, id est quia portat gladium. id est habet iudiciariam potestatem, non sine causa, sed vt malos puniat. Et hoc ostendit subdens, Dei n. minister est id est loco Dei vindicat. Ipse dico existens vindex in iram Dei, id est propter offensam Dei vindicandam, vel in iram Dei, id est futuram ostendendam, id est propter vindictam Dei futuram ostendendam, quia hac punitio iudicat persistentes in malis, grauius puniendos. Dico quod vindex est, & ei, id est ad damnum eius & correctionem, qui malum agit, & quia est minister Dei. Ideoq; subditi estote ei, quasi ex necessitate vel necessitati, id est necessariae ordinationi subditi estote. Et hoc non solum propter iram principis vel Dei vindicandam, sed & propter conscientiam scilicet vt munda sit mens vestra. Pralatum à Deo, id est eum qui sic praeest per Dei ordinationem diligendo. Licet n. omnes fideles, inquantum fideles sunt, vnu sint in Christo, in cuius fide non est distantia. Iudaei, Graeci, domini, & serui, & huiusmodi, differentia tamen est in conuersatione mortali, & eius ordine in huius vitae itinere seruandu esse, apostoli praecipiunt. Alia sunt n. quae seruamus in vnitate fidei, sine vlla distatia, & alia in ordine huius vita tanquam in via ne nomen domini & doctrina blasphemetur. Ideo n. hoc est probatio subiectionis, quare subditi esse debetis, quia & ideo ad ostendendam subiectionem praestatis tributa, quod est signum subiectionis, non ait (spluitis, sed praestatis quasi reddituris, quia reddunt seruiendo in defensione, dum pugnant pro patria, & dum agunt iudicia, praestatis tributa. Vos dico (seruientes Deo in hoc ipsum, id est per hoc ipsum seruitis Deo quod illis tributa datis. Vere per hoc seruitis Deo, ministri n. sunt Dei, ad hoc enim instituti sunt, vt boni laudentur, & mali puniantur. Vel ita, ministri enim, quare debetis praestare tributa, quia ministri Dei sunt, ipsi dico seruientes vobis, dum patriam defendunt, in hoc ipsum, id est propter hoc scilicet, propter tributum seruiunt vobis in defensione patriae, & quia ministri Dei sunt.
units.tr: Augustine did not retract. If the Emperor and a bishop or pope command different things, which he would have had to say if the pope were superior in degree of jurisdiction, nevertheless Augustine meant this: if the Emperor commands anything to be done against the law of eternal salvation, which is the immediate precept of God, then one is not to obey the Emperor in that matter; rather, in that matter the pope commanding according to this law, namely the divine law, is to be obeyed more than the Emperor commanding anything contrary to divine law. But to the pope commanding something according to his own Decretals, as such, nothing is to be obeyed against the command of the Emperor or of his laws, as is clear here and will be further deduced in the ninth [chapter] of this work. Then the gloss: "As if they deservedly acquire damnation. For good or bad princes are not a fear for good works but for bad, that is, they are not a fear to those who act well, but to those who act badly. For if the prince is good, he does not punish the one who acts well, but loves him; if he is bad, he does not harm the good man, but purges him. The bad man, however, ought to fear, because princes are instituted to punish evils. He calls princes those who are created to correct life and to forbid adversities, bearing God's image, so that the rest may be under one. But to you, as those who act badly, they are a fear. Do you wish not to fear the power, whatever it is, whether good or bad? Do good, and you will have no cause for fear; indeed you will have praise from it, even if it is bad, since it is a cause of greater crown for you. If the power is just, you will have praise from it, even with it praising; if it is unjust, you will have praise from it, not with it praising, but with it giving you the occasion for praise; truly you will have praise from it. For it is God's minister for your good, that is, it does good to you, whether it is good or bad, because it has been given to you by God for your good, to protect you and yours. For it is manifest that kings were given by God so that they should not do evil to the good. But if you act as one good, there is no need to fear; for it is, that is, because it bears the sword, not without cause, but has judicial power in order to punish the wicked. And this he shows by adding, 'for it is God's minister,' that is, in God's place it avenges. I say it is an avenger, being in wrath, that is, to avenge God's offence, or in God's wrath, that is, to show the wrath to come, because this punishment judges those who persist in evil to be punished more gravely. I say that it is an avenger, and against him, that is, to his damnation and correction, who does evil, and because it is God's minister. Therefore be subject to it, as by necessity, or to necessity, that is, be subject to the necessary ordinance. And this is not only on account of the prince's wrath or God's vengeance, but also on account of conscience, that is, that your mind may be clean. Be subject to the one set over you by God, that is, to him who so presides by God's ordinance, loving him. For although all believers, as far as they are believers, are one in Christ, in whose faith there is no distinction (Jews, Greeks, masters and slaves, and the like), the Apostles nevertheless command that there is a difference in mortal conversation, and that its order must be kept on the journey of this life, lest the name of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed. For some things we keep in the unity of faith, without any distinction, and others in the order of this life as on a road. For this, then, is the proof of subjection, why you must be subject: that you also, to show subjection, pay tributes, which is the sign of subjection. He does not say 'you pay,' but 'you render,' as those about to give back, because they repay by serving in defence, while they fight for the fatherland and carry out judgments; you pay tributes. I say that you serve God in this very thing, that is, through this very thing you serve God, in that you give them tributes. Truly through this you serve God, for they are God's ministers; for this they were instituted, so that the good may be praised and the wicked punished. Or thus: they are ministers, which is why you must pay tributes, because they are God's ministers; I say they serve you, while they defend the fatherland, in this very thing, that is, for this, namely for tribute they serve you in defence of the fatherland, and because they are God's ministers."

units.la: Ex hac itaq; Apostoli serie, ac sanctorum expositionibus praeinductis non volenti nomen & doctrinam domini blasphemari, tanquam iniustam & contra ciuiles leges praedicantem, vt dixit hic glossa Augustini, & prima ad Timoth. sexto absq; dubitatione aliqua tenendum est, Omnes homines cuiuscunq; statuus aut conditionis existant, realiter & personaliter subesse debere iurisdictioni principum seculi, & eisdem obedire in his omnibus, quae contradicunt legi salutis aeternae, secundum humanas leges maxime, aut consuetudines approbatas & honestas, de his enim loquitur Apostolus aperte, cum dixit: Omnis anima subdita sit, &c. Et quod non sine causa gladium portant, & reliqua, quae de ipsis protulit tam patriae defensione, quam tributorum eidem exhibitione secundum sanctorum expositiones. Haec autem nusquam de quoquam episcopo seu presbytero dixit Apost. Na domini quib. in iurisdictione coactiua obedire tenemur, sunt q per armata potentia defendere debent patriam, q nullo modo conuenit episcopo aut presbytero. Vnde B. Ambr. ad Valentianum, epist. 2. q. intitulatur, Ad plebe, sic inquit: Dolere potero, flere potero, gemere potero, aduersus arma, milites, Gothosque, lachryma mea arma mea sunt, talia enim munimenta sunt sacerdotis, aliter nec debeo nec possum resistere. Rursum domini tales quibus sic obedire tenemur, possent esse infideles, vt dixit glossa circa principium, tales autem non sunt, nec esse possunt episcopi. Et ideo palam omnibus, quod de presbyteris seu episcopis non loquebatur Apostolus, imo de regibus & principibus, sicut dicebat August. Ab hac subiectione etiam neminem Apostolus excipit cum dixit: Omnis anima. Si ergo resistentes huiusmodi potestatibus, etiam infidelibus & malis, sibi damnationem aeternam acquirunt, quanto magis indignationem omnipotentis Dei, & huius apostoli Pauli atq; Petri acquirunt sibi, qui hac Dei & horum apostolorum contempta doctrina, dudum turbauerunt & turbant continuo fideles reges & principes, & maxime ac inexcusabiliter Romanorum. Principes enim ministri sunt Dei, vt dixit Apostolus, nec dixit, ministri nostri sunt, vel Cephae aut alterius apostoli. Et ideo nec in iudicio coactiuo subiecti alicui episcopo vel presbytero sed magis ecouerso. Quod etiam glossa secundum Aug. explicauit, dum dixit: Ergo si aliud Imperator, aliud Deus iubeat, &c. nullum episcopum aut archiepiscopum vel patriarcham nominando in talibus iurisdictionibus, quod tamen fecisset aut facere debuisset, si Christus rex regum & dominus dominantium hanc potestatem sibi concessisset super Imperatorem, vt ipsi fabulantur in suis Decretalibus, quae secundum veritatem nihil aliud sunt, quam ordinationes quaedam oligarchicae, quibus in nullo tenentur obedire Christi fideles, inquantum huiusmodi, quemadmodum ex 12. prima demonstratum est, & in consequentibus specialibus apparebit.
units.tr: From this series of the Apostles and the foregoing expositions of the saints, then, and without any doubt, we must hold (against anyone who is unwilling for the name and doctrine of the Lord to be blasphemed as unjust and as teaching against the civil laws, as the gloss of Augustine here says, and in 1 Timothy 6) that all men, of whatever rank or condition they may be, both in person and in reality ought to be subject to the jurisdiction of the princes of this world and obey them in all those things which do not conflict with the law of eternal salvation, chiefly in accordance with human laws or approved and honourable customs. For the Apostle speaks plainly of these when he says: "Let every soul be subject," etc., and "for they do not bear the sword in vain," and the rest that he said about them, both concerning the defence of the country and the payment of tributes to it, according to the expositions of the saints. Yet the Apostle never said this of any bishop or elder. For those to whom we are bound to obey in coercive jurisdiction are the ones who must defend the country by armed force, and this in no way suits a bishop or an elder. Hence Saint Ambrose, in his second letter to Valentinian, entitled "To the People," says: "I can grieve, I can weep, I can groan against arms, soldiers and Goths; my tears are my arms. For such are the defences of a priest. Otherwise I neither ought nor am able to resist." Again, the lords to whom we are thus bound to obey could be unbelievers, as the gloss on the opening passage says; but such men are not, and cannot be, bishops. And so it is plain to everyone that the Apostle was not speaking of elders or bishops, but rather of kings and princes, as Augustine said. The Apostle excepts no one from this subjection when he says, "Every soul." If, then, those who resist such powers, even unbelieving and wicked ones, win for themselves eternal damnation, how much more do they win the anger of almighty God and of the Apostles Paul and Peter, who, having despised this doctrine of God and of these Apostles, have long troubled and continually trouble the faithful kings and princes, and especially and inexcusably those of the Romans. For princes are "ministers of God," as the Apostle said; he did not say "ministers of ours," or of Cephas or of any other apostle. And so they are not subject in coercive judgement to any bishop or elder, but rather the reverse. The gloss, following Augustine, also explained this when it said: "Therefore if the emperor orders one thing and God another," etc. Nowhere does it name any bishop, archbishop or patriarch in such jurisdictions, though it would have done so, or ought to have done so, if Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, had granted this power over the emperor to them, as they fabricate in their Decretals. These, in truth, are nothing but certain oligarchic ordinances, to which the faithful of Christ are bound to obey in no way, so far as they are such, as has been shown from the twelfth chapter of the first book and will appear in the following special chapters.

units.la: Non tamen ex his dicere volumus, quin doctori seu pastori ecclesiastico debeatur reuerentia & obedientia in his quae praecipit, seu docet obseruanda secundum legem euangelicam, non aliter aut in contrarium, vt Matth. 23 & per Hieronymum ibid. satis apparet, quamuis etiam ipse ad talium obseruatione neminem debeat nec possit arcere in hoc seculo, poena vel supplicio; quoquam reali vel personali. Quoniam talem potestatem arcendi & dominandi cuiquam in hoc seculo, sibi ex euangelica scriptura concessam, non legimus, sed potius interdicta consilio vel praecepto, vt ex hoc & praecedente c. liquet. Talis n. ptas in hoc seculo datur a legibus seu legislatore humano, quae etiam data episcopo vel presbytero ad compellendum homines in his quae sunt dinae legis inutilis esset. Nam coactis nihil tale proficeret ad aeternam salutem. Et haec palam fuit mens Apost. 2. ad Corint. primo cu dixit: Ego aut testem Deu inuoco in animam meam, quod parcens vobis non veni vltra Corinthu, non quia dominamur fidei vestrae, sed adiutores sumus gaudii vestri, na fide statis. Vbi
units.tr: Yet we do not wish to say from this that reverence and obedience are not owed to the ecclesiastical teacher or minister in those things which he commands or teaches to be observed according to the gospel law, provided they are not otherwise or contrary to it, as Matthew 23 and Jerome on that passage make sufficiently clear. Even so, he ought not, and cannot, compel anyone to observe such things in this world by penalty or punishment, whether real or personal. For we do not read that such a power of compelling and ruling anyone in this world has been granted to him by the evangelical Scripture; rather, it has been forbidden by counsel or precept, as is clear from this and the preceding chapter. For such a power in this world is given by human laws or by the human legislator, and if it were given to a bishop or elder to compel men in matters of divine law, it would be useless, since such compulsion would contribute nothing to eternal salvation. This was plainly the mind of the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 1, when he said: "But I call God as witness against my soul that it was to spare you that I did not come again to Corinth; not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy, for in faith you stand." Where

units.la: Glossa secundum Amb. Ego inuoco Deum testem non solum contra corpus, sed etiam in, id est contra animam meam, si mentior de quo loquor. Quod non veni in Corinthum vltra, id est postquam à vobis discessi. Et hoc feci parcens vobis, scilicet ne contristarem multos aspere corripiendo, in quo peperit it eis ne eo asperiore vertantur in seditionem. Vult ergo eos prius mitigari, & ideo non est ex lcuitate vel carnali cogitatione non impleuit qua disposuit.
units.tr: The gloss, following Ambrose: "I call God as witness, not only against my body but also against my soul, that is, against my soul if I lie about what I am speaking of. That I did not come again to Corinth, that is, after I had departed from you. And I did this to spare you, namely so that I would not grieve many by rebuking them harshly, in which case they might be turned to sedition by my harshness. He wills therefore that they first be softened, and so it is not from levity or a carnal purpose that he did not fulfil what he had planned."

units.la: Spiritualis enim tunc dispositum non implet, quando aliquid ad salutem prouidentius meditatur. Et ne indignentur quasi de dominio, eo quod dixerat parcens vobis non veni, subdit, non ideo dico parcens, quia dominemur fidei vestrae, id est, quia dominium & coactionem patiatur fides vestra, quae voluntatis est, non necessitatis. Sed ideo dico, quia adiutores sumus, si vultis cooperari gaudiis vestri aeterni, vel gaudii emendationis vestrae, quia gaudent emendati. Bene dixi quae fidei vestrae, nam fide, per dilectionem operatur statis non dominio. Hanc eandem sententiam ex verbis Apostoli supradictis accepit, & omnib. euidenter expressit B. Ioannes Chrysostomus in suo lib. dialogorum, qui etiam de dignitate sacerdotali intitulatur lib. 2. cap. 3. inquit enim ibidem, postquam induxerat illud Apostoli, Non quia dominamur fidei vestrae, sed adiutores sumus, &c. Hi qui foris sunt iudices, seculares scilicet, malignos quosque cum subdiderint. ostendunt in eis plurimam potestatem, & inuitos eos à priorum morum prauitate compescunt, in ecclesia vero non coactum, sed adquiescentem oportet ad meliora conuerti. Quia nec nobis à legibus data est talis potestas, vt autoritate sententia cohibeamus homines à delictis. Et loquitur in persona omnium sacerdotum, assignans primam causam iam dictam, quare scilicet neminem cogere possint, quia coactiuam in hoc seculo cuiusquam autorem non habent, eo quod à legibus, id est legislatoribus eis data non erat illis temporibus, aut in locis illis siue prouinciis.
units.tr: For the spiritual man does not fulfil what he has planned when he meditates on something more providently for salvation. And lest they be indignant, as though he were speaking of dominion, because he had said "to spare you I did not come," he adds: "I do not say this to spare you because we lord it over your faith," that is, because your faith suffers dominion and compulsion, which belongs to will, not to necessity. "But I say this because we are helpers, if you are willing to co-operate in your eternal joy, or the joy of your amendment, for those who are amended rejoice." He rightly said "of your faith," for faith works through love, not through dominion. Saint John Chrysostom took the same meaning from the words of the Apostle quoted above and expressed it plainly to all in his book of Dialogues, which is also entitled On the Priesthood, book 2, chapter 3. For after citing the Apostle's words, "Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers," etc., he says there: "Those who are judges outside, that is, secular ones, when they have subdued the wicked, show in them very great power, and by compulsion restrain them, unwilling, from the wickedness of their former ways; but in the Church it is necessary that people be turned to better things not by compulsion but by consent. For we have not been given such power by the laws, so that by the authority of a sentence we might restrain men from offences." He speaks in the person of all priests, assigning the first cause already mentioned, namely why they cannot compel anyone: they do not have coercive authority over anyone in this world, because such authority had not been given them by the laws, that is, by the legislators, in those times or in those places or provinces.

units.la: Tunc aliam causam assignans subiungit: Nec si data esset, (talis potestas scilicet) haberemus, (nos videlicet episcopi seu presbyteri,) vbi exerceremus eiusmodi potestatem, cum Deus noster, (Christus scilicet) non necessitate (id est violentia) submotos à peccato, sed propria sese sponte abstinentes remunerabitur sit. Nec tamen ex his dicere volumus inconueniens esse coerceri haereticos aut aliter infideles, sed autoritatem hanc esse solius legislatoris humani. Non igitur conuenit sacerdoti vel episcopo cuiquam coactiua potestas, sed debet tam ipsi quam alii secularibus iudicibus in hac subesse, quemadmodum dictum est. Vnde rursum apostolus primae ad Timot. 2. dixit: Obsecro igitur primum omnium fieri obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus hominibus, pro regibus, & omnibus qui in sublimitate sunt, vt quietam & tranquillam vitam agamus. Vbi Glossa Tim. haec verba dirigens in illo omni ecclesiae formam tradit. Et tunc secundum Aug. subiungit: Pro omnibus hominibus, id est pro hominibus omnis generis, & specialiter pro regibus, & si mali sint, & pro omnibus qui in sublimitate sunt constituti, vt ducibus & comitibus, & si mali sint; cum tamen inter positos in sublimitate seu iudiciaria tali potestate, nunquam Apost. & Aug. episcop. aut presbyterum aliquem nominet, sed solum modo principes seculares. Quare autem, inquit Aug. pro regibus & sublimibus etiam malis orari velit, reddit causam, (Apostolus scilicet, subdens, quia hoc nobis proderit, vt quietam vitam agamus à persecutione & tranquillitate, id est sine inquietatione aliqua. Ecce testimonium eius quod diximus vltimo prima, videlicet q; causa tranquillitatis factiua & conseruatiua est actio principantis debita non impedita. Tunc subiungit Aug. quod est valde ad propositum, dicens: Ideo apostolus ecclesiam orare pro regibus admonuit & omnibus sublimibus eadem Spiritu sancto asslatus, quo & Hieremias, qui misit epistolam Iudaeis, qui erant in Babylone, vt orarent pro vita regis Nabuchodonosor filiorumq; eius, & pro pace ciuitatis, inquiens, quia in pace illorum erit pax vestra. Hoc aut significabat ecclesiam in omnibus sanctis eius, qui sunt ciues coelestis Hierusalem seruituri sub regib. huius seculi. Ideo q; apostolus ea monet pro eis orare, vt quietam agent vitam. Ecce indubie Apostoli atq; Aug. suisse sententiam, quod ecclesia seu Christi fideles omnes subesse debeant principibus seculi, maxime fidelibus & eorum obedire praeceptis, non contrariis legi salutis aeternae. Quod si Apostolus intellexisset, episcopos seu presbyteros principari debere, ac homines realiter aut personaliter coactiuo iudicare iudicio, in statu & pro statu vitae praesentis, dixisset Timotheo quem episcopum constituerat. Obsecro &c. pro regibus & episcopis omnibus, qui in sublimitate sunt.
units.tr: Then, assigning another cause, he adds: "Nor, even if such power had been given, would we have any place in which to exercise such authority, since our God (that is, Christ) will reward those who abstain from sin not by necessity (that is, by violence) but of their own accord." Yet we do not wish to say from this that it is improper for heretics, or unbelievers in other respects, to be restrained; but that this authority belongs only to the human legislator. Therefore coercive power does not belong to a priest or bishop in any way; rather, he must be subject in this matter, both he and others, to the secular judges, as has been said. Hence the Apostle again says in 1 Timothy 2: "I urge therefore that first of all supplications, prayers, petitions and thanksgivings be made for all men, for kings and for all who are in high station, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life." Here the gloss, applying these words to the whole form of the Church, then says, following Augustine: "For all men, that is, for men of every kind, and especially for kings, even if they are wicked, and for all who are placed in high station, such as dukes and counts, even if they are wicked." Yet among those placed in high station or in such judicial power the Apostle and Augustine never name any bishop or elder, but only secular princes. As to why Augustine wishes prayers to be made even for kings and the high-placed, even if wicked, he gives the reason, namely the Apostle, adding: "because this will profit us, that we may lead a quiet life, free from persecution, and a tranquillity, that is, without any disturbance." Here is the testimony to what we said at the end of the first book: that the cause of tranquillity, both producing and preserving it, is the due and unhindered action of the ruler. Then Augustine adds something very much to the point, saying: "Therefore the Apostle admonished the Church to pray for kings and all the high-placed, inspired by the same Holy Spirit by whom Jeremiah also wrote a letter to the Jews who were in Babylon, that they should pray for the life of King Nebuchadnezzar and his sons, and for the peace of the city, saying: 'for in their peace will be your peace.' This, moreover, signified the Church in all its saints, who are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, and who will serve under the kings of this world. Therefore the Apostle advises them to pray for these, that they may lead a quiet life." Here, without doubt, is the view of the Apostles and of Augustine: that the Church, or all the faithful of Christ, ought to be subject to the princes of this world, especially to the faithful ones, and to obey their commands, provided they are not contrary to the law of eternal salvation. But if the Apostle had understood that bishops or elders ought to rule and to judge men in person and in reality by coercive judgement, in the state and for the state of the present life, he would have said to Timothy, whom he had appointed bishop: "I urge, etc., that prayers be made for kings and for all the bishops who are in high station."

units.la: Amplius ad Titum tertio dicebat Apostolus, Admone illos, (quibus praedicas,) subditos esse principibus & potestatibus, non dixit Apostolus, admone seculares tantum, nec rursum dixit, admone illos, subditos esse nobis & principibus, bene enim nouit Apostolus quod nec ipse vel alii episcopi seu presbyteri debent principari aut alios iudicare litigioso seu secularium actuum iudicio, quin imo ipsos à secularibus negotiis quibuslibet reuocauerat, ne dum à principatu seu iudicio tantum, cum dixerat 2. ad Timoth. 1. Nemo militans Deo, implicat se secularibus negotiis. Vnde Ambro. admone &c. quasi: & si tu habes imperium spirituale, id est praecipere de spiritualibus, tamen admone illos subditos esse principibus scilicet regibus, ducibus, & potestatibus minoribus. Quia Christiana religio neminem priuat iure suo. quod pro tanto dixit Ambrosius quia etiam fideles, dominis & principibus infidelibus aut malis voluit & docuit Apostolus subesse, sicut dicit ipse primae ad Timoth. 6. vlt. Quicunque sunt sub iugo serui, &c. Vbi Glossa secundum Augustinum Sciendum quasi semper eduasse, communem omnibus in Christo libertatem esse, quod de spirituali libertate vtique verum est, non de carnali, vt illi intelligebant. Ideo contra eos loquitur hic Apostolus iuben seruos dominus suis subditos esse. Non ergo exigant serui Christiani, quod de Hebraeis dicitur, vt sex annis seruiant & gratis dimittantur liberi, quod mysticum est. Et quare hoc praecipiat Apostolus, supponit, ne blasphemetur nomen domini quasi si lingua loquentis, & doctrina Christiana, quasi iniusta & contra leges praedicet, ciuiles scilicet. Quo igitur modo & qua secundum Deum conscientia vult aliquis sacerdos, quicunq; sit ille, absoluere subditos à iuramento quo dominis fidelibus astringuntur. Est enim haec haeresis manifesta, vt in sequentib. amplius apparebit. Dixit ergo Apostolus, admone illos, subditos esse principibus, non dixit laicos solum, sed indifferenter, quia secundum ipsum, omnis anima subdita est eis in iudicio coactivo seu contentioso. Si vero non, dic mihi, in quo dixit, omnis anima subdita sit &c. Quod si Timotheo & Tito in hoc subiici debuisset, frustra dixisset. Admone illos &c. Kursum si quosdam voluit admoneri subesse potestatibus secularibus, quosdam vero minime, insufficienter fuisset locutus, non faciendo in sermone suo differentiam hanc, quam nusquam in sua scriptura factam reperiret quis, sed oppositum magis dixit enim. Omnis anima subdita sit, &c. in quo inconvenienter & false locutus fuisset Apostolus, quod absit, si qui a talium subiectione fuissent exempti. Haec quoq;conformiter sententia & doctrina B. Petri apostoli prima canonica sua, ca 2. cum dixit: Subiecti estote omni humanae creaturae propter Deum, constitutae videlicet in principatu, de quib. eum intellexisse apparet per exempla quae immediate subiungit, dum dixit: Sive regi quasi praeeminenti, sive ducibus tanquam ab eo missis, ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum, quia sic voluntas Dei est. Glossas autem sanctorum non adduxit super hunc locum, quia totum quod hic dicunt, continetur in Glossa, quam supra induximus ad Apost. Ro. 13. Ecce quod B. Petrus & Paulus conformiter dicunt reges & duces missos a Deo ad vindictam malefactorum, id est ad sumendum de ipsis vindictam per coactivam potentiam in hoc seculo. nusquam vero dixerunt nec ipsi, nec sancti expositores suorum dictorum ad hoc missos esse episcopos aut presbyteros, sed oppositum magis, ut dicto praecipue Chrysost. superius euidenter apparuit. Cum igitur malefactores possint esse presbyteri sicut non presbyteri secundum omnia transgressionum genera, nobis enumerata secundo huius, p necessitatem sequitur, ipsos subesse debere in iudicio coactivo regibus, ducibus, aut aliis principantibus secularibus, quos legislatoris humani auctoritate statuendos ostendimus 15. prima. Hos. n. misit Deus ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum, ut dixit B. Petrus: Sic. n. id est, illis obedite, voluntas Dei est, ut dixit ibidem. Hoc rursum confirmat sermo & exemplum operis manifestum B. Pauli Apost. nam de ipso legitur Actuum 25. ipse refugies sacerdotum iudicium coactivum, dixit aperte: Caesarem appello. Et rursum: Ad tribunal Caesaris sto, ubi me iudicari oportet, dicit Glossa interlinearis, quia hic est locus iudicii. Ergo sacerdotum refugiens iudicium, fassus est se coactivae iurisdictioni Caesaris fuisse subiectum. Sed credendum est non Apostolum fide dixisse, ibi me iudicari oportet, id est apud Caesarem metu mortis, qui iam pro veritate mori elegerat & deliberauerat, ut appareret Act. 21. dum dixit: Ego n. non solum alligari, sed & mori paratus sum in Hierusalem propter nomen domini Iesu Christi. Quis n. demens aestimabit, Apostolum suo verbo tantum crimen commisisse protelandae vitae gratia, ut omne sacerdotium indebite subiiceret sui exemplo & doctrina iurisdictioni principum seculi, si hoc inconveniens & indebitum reputasset? Melius. n. fuerat illi non ascendere in Hierosolymam, qui a nullo compellebatur quam ascendere & mentiri contra seipsum & proximum.
units.tr: Furthermore, in Titus chapter 3 the Apostle says: "Admonish them (to whom you preach) to be subject to principalities and powers." He did not say "admonish the secular people only," nor did he say "admonish them to be subject to us and to princes." For the Apostle well knew that neither he himself nor other bishops or elders ought to rule or to judge others by litigious judgment of secular affairs. Indeed he had rather withdrawn them from all secular business, not only from rule or judgment, when he said in 2 Timothy 2: "No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs." Hence Ambrose: "Admonish etc." as if to say: even if you have a spiritual authority, that is, to command in spiritual matters, nevertheless admonish them to be subject to princes, that is to kings, leaders, and lesser powers. For the Christian religion deprives no one of his right. Ambrose said this because the Apostle wished and taught that the faithful should also be subject to lords and princes who are unbelievers or wicked, as he says himself in 1 Timothy 6 at the end: "As many as are under the yoke of slavery, etc." Where the Gloss, following Augustine, says: "It should be understood that common liberty in Christ has always been the case," which is indeed true of spiritual liberty, not of carnal liberty as those people understood it. Therefore the Apostle speaks here against them, ordering servants to be subject to their masters. Christian servants should not demand, as is said of the Hebrews, that they serve for six years and be released free; that is mystical. And the Apostle presupposes why he commands this, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed, as if the tongue of the speaker and the Christian teaching were teaching things unjust and contrary to the laws, namely civil laws. In what manner, then, and with what conscience before God does any priest, whoever he may be, wish to absolve subjects from the oath by which they are bound to faithful lords? For this is a manifest heresy, as will appear more fully in what follows. The Apostle therefore said, "Admonish them to be subject to princes," not "laymen only," but without distinction, because according to him every soul is subject to them in coercive or contentious judgment. If not, tell me where he said "let every soul be subject," etc. If he had wished Timothy and Titus to be subject in this respect, he would have spoken in vain: "Admonish them," etc. Again, if he had wished some to be admonished to be subject to secular powers, and others not at all, he would have spoken insufficiently, not making in his speech this distinction, which anyone would find nowhere made in his writing; rather he said the opposite: "Let every soul be subject," etc. In which the Apostle would have spoken improperly and falsely, which God forbid, if some had been exempted from such subjection. Likewise, the saint and apostle Peter in agreement with this teaching, in his first canonical epistle, chapter 2, said: "Be subject to every human creature for God's sake," namely those constituted in authority, of whom he is clearly understood to speak through the examples he immediately adds: "whether to the king as supreme, or to leaders as sent by him, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, for so is the will of God." But he did not adduce the glosses of the saints on this passage, because all that they say here is contained in the Gloss which we cited above on Romans 13. Behold, Peter and Paul agree in saying that kings and leaders are sent by God "for the punishment of evildoers," that is, to take vengeance on them by coercive power in this world. Yet neither they nor the holy expositors of their words ever said that bishops or elders were sent for this purpose, but rather the opposite, as was clearly shown above, especially by the saying of Chrysostom. Since therefore evildoers may be elders just as they may be non-elders, according to all the kinds of transgressions enumerated for us in the second chapter, it follows of necessity that they ought to be subject in coercive judgment to kings, leaders, or other secular rulers, whom we have shown to be established by the authority of the human lawgiver in the fifteenth chapter of the first part. For God sent these "for the punishment of evildoers, and the praise of the good," as Peter said: "For so," that is, obey them, "is the will of God," as he said in the same place. This is further confirmed by the word and by the manifest example of the work of the Apostle Paul. For of him we read in Acts 25 that he refused the coercive judgment of the priests and said plainly: "I appeal to Caesar." And again: "I stand at Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be judged," which the Interlinear Gloss explains: "because this is the place of judgment." Therefore, by refusing the judgment of the priests, he confessed that he was subject to the coercive jurisdiction of Caesar. But we must believe that the Apostle did not say "there I ought to be judged" out of fear of death, that is, before Caesar; for he had already chosen and resolved to die for the truth, as appears in Acts 21 where he said: "For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ." For what madman would think that the Apostle, by his word alone, committed such a fault for the sake of prolonging his life, that by his example and teaching he would wrongly subject every priesthood to the jurisdiction of the princes of this world, if he had considered this improper and undue? It would have been better for him not to go up to Jerusalem, since no one compelled him, than to go up and lie against himself and his neighbour.

units.la: Et ideo quia hoc nephas est aestimare de ipso, apparet ipsum id sensisse mente quod ore protulit. Et secundum imitationem magistri sui, quo noluit esse superior, (Christo videlicet,) qui nedum Caesarem, verum etiam Pilatum eius vicarium suum mundanum iudicem recognouit, dum dixit, Io. 19. Non habes potestatem adversum me vllam, nisi datum esset tibi. &c. id est nisi a Dei superna ordinatione, ut supra dicebat Aug. ad Ro. 13. quia non est potestas alicui homini bono vel malo, nisi a Deo data. Quod etiam Bernardus ad episcopum Senonensem amplius explicauit, & supra induximus parte quarta. Cum igitur nulli episcopo iurisdictio seu coactiva cuiusquam potestas in hoc seculo concessa sit lege diuina, sed potius interdicta consilio vel praecepto, ut patenter ostensum est in hoc & praecedenti ca. Nec etiam potestas eiusmodi episcopis seu presbyteris in quantum episcopis conueniat successione patria seu paterna: Per necessitatem sequitur ipsos in hac subiectos esse principibus seculi, sicut ex dictis apostolorum Petri & Pauli & aliorum sanctorum euidenter apparuit. Et ratione demonstrata conuinci potest ex his quae dicta sunt 15. & 17. prima. Nec in quenquam presbyterum aut non presbyterum coactivam in hoc seculo iurisdictionem habere quenquam episcopu siue papam, nisi eadem sibi per humanum legislatorem concessa fuerit, in cuius potestate semper est hanc ab ipsis revocare, inteuenien-te rationabili causa, cuius plena determinatio ad eundem legislatorem, praesertim in communitatib. fidelium pertinere dignoscitur. Quod quidem igitur principatum seu coactivam imiisdictionem cuiuscunq; in hoc seculo Christus abdicauerit, suisq; apostolis ac ipsorum successoribus episcopis seu presbyteris interdixerit consilio vel praecepto, ipsumq; seipsum a apostolos eosdem principum seculi coactivae iurisdictioni subesse voluerit, id quoq; obseruandum docuerit, ac ipsius apostoli praecipui Petrus & Paulus tam opere quam sermone, per euangelicas veritates aeternas testimonia per sanctorum quoq; ac reliquorum approbatorum fidei Christianae doctorum interpretationes seu expositiones, euidenter monstrasse nos credimus.
units.tr: And because it is an abomination to think this of him, it appears that he thought in his mind what he uttered with his mouth. And following the example of his master, who would not be superior (namely Christ), who acknowledged not only Caesar but also Pilate, his vicar and worldly judge, when he said, John 19: "You have no power against me at all, unless it were given you," etc., that is, unless by the supreme ordinance of God, as Augustine said above on Romans 13: "for there is no power to any man, good or bad, unless it is given by God." Bernard explained this further in his letter to the bishop of Sens, which we cited above in the fourth part. Since therefore no bishop has been granted coercive jurisdiction or any power of this kind over anyone in this world by divine law, but rather it has been forbidden by counsel or precept, as has been plainly shown in this and the preceding chapter; nor does such power belong to bishops or elders as bishops by paternal or hereditary succession; it follows of necessity that they are subject in this matter to the princes of the world, as has clearly appeared from the sayings of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the other saints. And this can be demonstrated by reason from what has been said in the fifteenth and seventeenth chapters of the first part. No bishop or pope has coercive jurisdiction in this world over any presbyter or non-presbyter, unless the same has been granted to him by the human lawgiver, in whose power it always remains to revoke it from them when a reasonable cause intervenes, the full determination of which is recognised to belong to that same lawgiver, especially in the communities of the faithful. Indeed, that Christ renounced any rule or coercive jurisdiction of any kind in this world, and forbade his apostles and their successors, the bishops or elders, by counsel or precept; and that he himself willed the apostles to be subject to the coercive jurisdiction of the princes of this world, and taught that this too must be observed; and that the apostles Peter and Paul, the chief of them, showed this both by deed and word, by the eternal truths of the Gospel, we believe we have plainly demonstrated also by the interpretations and expositions of the saints and of the other approved teachers of the Christian faith.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De autoritate clauium Sacerdotalium, & qualem in excommunicando sacerdos aut episcopus habeat potestatem.
units.tr: On the authority of the keys of the priesthood, and what power a priest or bishop has in excommunicating.

units.la: Consequens autem dictis est ostendere, quid potestatis, auctoritatis, & quale iudicium super fideles Christus eisdem apostolis & ipsorum successoribus concedere voluerit, & de facto concesserit ex virtute verborum scripturae factae. Inter caetera vero quae de hoc expressiorem significationem habere videntur, sunt ea quae Christus protulit ad Petrum Matth. 16. Tibi dabo claues regni. Similiter quoq; dicta per eundem Christum ad apostolos omnes, Mat. 18. & Ioan. 20. dum dixit Chri-
units.tr: It follows from what has been said to show what power and authority, and what kind of judgment over the faithful, Christ wished to grant to these same apostles and their successors, and in fact did grant by the force of the words of Scripture. Among the other passages which seem to have a clearer meaning on this point are those which Christ addressed to Peter in Matthew 16: I will give you the keys of the kingdom. Likewise the words spoken by the same Christ to all the apostles in Matthew 18 and John 20, when he said:

units.la: Christus: Quæcunque alligaueritis super terram, ligata erunt & in cælo, & quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, &c. Ex his enim verbis præcipue opinio & titulus plenitudinis potestatis, quem sibi Romanus ascribit episcopus, sumpsit originem. Quorum quidem vt sensus & notitia certius possit haberi, reminisci oportet aliquorum quæ diximus ultimo prima, videlicet quod Christus verus Deus & verus homo venit in hunc mundum, perhibere testimonium veritati, vt idem dixit Io. 18. veritati inquam credendorum agendorum, & ipernendorum ad vitam æternam humano generi consequendam. Quam siquidem etiam sermone docuit, & exemplo monstrauit, in scriptisq; demū tradidit per euangelistarum & suorum apostolorum dictamina, vt per talem scripturam, in ipsius & apostolorum suorum absentia dirigi possemus in his quæ sunt æternæ salutis: & hoc fuit officium quod suis successoribus apostolis exercendum commisit. cum eisdem post resurrectionem quasi omnium nouissime dixit illud Matt. 28. & vltimo: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus sancti, docentes eos seruare omnia quæcunq; mandaui vobis. Verum per baptismi administrationem, quod Christus per apostolos administrari præcepit, fecit eos intelligere etiam aliorum sacramentorum administrationem, quæ propter humanam salutem æternam instituit, quorum est pœnitentiæ sacramentum, quo animæ humanæ actualis culpa mortalis & venialis deletur, & in ipsa propter culpam corrupta Dei gratia reformatur, absq; qua humana opera sic ordinante Deo, meritoria non fierent ad vitam æternam. Vnde ad Ro. 6. Gratia Dei vita æterna. Huius itaq; sacramenti sicuti reliquorum, ministri sunt sacerdotes seu presbyteri, tanquam successores apostolorum Christi, quibus omnibus in persona Petri & reliquorum apostolorum potestas clauium seu conferendi pœnitentiæ sacramentum id est soluendi vel ligandi homines à peccatis, quæ idem sunt, tradita fuisse conuincitur per verba scripturæ prædicta. Vnde Hier. super Mat. 16. Et tibi dabo claues regni cælorum sic inquit: Habent quidem eandem iudiciariam potestatem alii apostoli, quibus post resurrectionem ait: Accipite Spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, & quorum retinueritis retenta sunt. Habet etiam omnis ecclesia in presbyteris & episcopis, sed ideo Petrus eam specialiter accepit, vt omnes intelligant, quod quicunque ab vnitate fidei se separauerit, nec à peccatis absolui, nec cœlum ingredi potest. Et dixit Hieron. Ab vnitate fidei, nec dixit ab vnitate Petri vel Romani episcopi, quoniam ipsorum aliqui poterant hæretici fore, aut aliter peruersi, & iam de facto cooperti sunt tales. Hæc autem iudiciaria potestas est clauiū auctoritas secundū Hier. & Aug. ibidem, dequib. Aug. Claues sunt discernendi scientia & potentia, qua dignos recipere, & indignos excludere debet à regno, sacerdos &c. Qualiter autem recipere, & qualiter excludere possit à regno consequenter patebit: & ex hoc, quæ, quâraue sit harum clauium, per Christum Petro & apostolis concessarum potestas. Primum non oportet attendere quod in anima peccatis mortaliter, generatur culpa, & corrumpitur diuina gratia sibi collata prius. Qua siquidem culpa peccator obligatur debito damnationis æternæ, pro itatu futuri seculi. In qua etiam culpa persistens à consortio fidelium in hoc seculo præciditur per correctionem quandam apud Christi fideles, vocatam excommunicationem. Et econtra debemus aduertere quod peccator per tristitiam sui delicti & exteriorem confessionem factam sacerdoti, de quorum vtroque simul & diuisim dicitur hoc nomen pœnitentia, triplex beneficium consequitur. Primum quidem quoniam ab interioti culpa mundatur, & in ipso Dei gratia reformatur. Secundū vero quoniam à debito damnationis æternæ, ad quam ex culpa obligatus fuerat, absoluitur. Tertium autem, quoniam ecclesiæ reconciliatur, id est fidelium consortio reunitur seu reuniri debet. Hæc igitur in peccatore facere, videlicet à culpa & æternæ damnationis debito soluere vel ligare, quod aliqualiter fieri habet per clauium potestatem sacerdoti concessam, quemadmodum infra dicetur, est sacramentum pœnitentiæ ministrare. His itaq; sic præmissis, ad propositum accedentes, secundum mentem Magistri sententiarum, quinimo scripturæ atq; sanctorum, quorum auctoritate loquitur lib. 4. di. 18. & etiam secundum intentionem Richardi in quodam libello quē fecit intitulatum de clauium sacerdotalium potestate, dicamus, q ad verā pœnitentiā seu sacramentū pœnitētię suscipiendū requiritur primū interior peccatoris cōtritio seu tristitia de commisso siue delicto. Secundo vero requiritur propositum & actus confitendi delictum, ipsum per sermonem exprimendo seu significādo sacerdoti, si sacerdotis facultas affuerit. qui si non adesset, in sic pœnitente seu contrito, sufficit firmum propositum confitēdi delictum sacerdoti cum ipsius primum facultas affuerit. Et ideo intendunt consequenter, quod in peccatore vere pœnitente, id est contrito & habente propositum confitendi, quædam ante confessionem, & omnem sacerdotis actionem, solus Deus operatur. Hæc autem sunt, expulsio culpe, gratia reformatio, & debiti eterna damnationis remissio. Quod autem prædicta Christus operetur, probat Magister li. 4. di. 18. ca. 4. per auctoritatem scripturæ atq; sanctorum. Primum quidem auctoritate psalmistæ, dicentis in persona Dei: Ego solus deleo iniquitates & peccata populi. Rursum auctoritate Ambrosii dicentis: Verbum Dei dimittit peccata, sacerdos & iudex. Sacerdos quidem officium suum exhibet, sed nullius potestatis iura exercet. Adhuc idem Ambr. Ille solus dimittit peccata, qui pro peccatis nostris solus mortuus est. Amplius per August. dicentem: Nemo tollit peccata, nisi solus Christus, qui est agnus tollens peccata mundi. Quod autem hoc faciat Deus ante omnē sacerdotis actionem, deducit Magister ex dictis Augustini, super psalmistæ: Quorū tecta sunt peccata. Ex his .n. inquit Magister aperte ostenditur, quod Deus ipse pœnitentem soluit à debito pœna. Et tunc soluit quando in nus illuminat inspirando veram cordis contritionē. Cui sententiæ ratio suffragatur, & auctoritates attestantur. Nemo .n. de peccato nunc compungitur, habens cor contritum & humiliatum, nisi in charitate, quod autem charitatem habet, dignus est vita. Nemo autē simul dignus est vita & morte. Non est igitur tunc ligatus debito æternæ mortis, filius enim iram esse desiit, ex quo diligere & pœnitere cœpit. Ex tunc igitur solutus est ab ira, quæ non manet super illum qui credit in Christum, sed super illum qui non credit. Non igitur postmodum per sacerdotem cui confitetur ab ira æterna liberatur, à qua liberatus est iam per dominum: ex quo dixit, confitebor. Solus igitur Deus hominem interius mundat à macula peccati, & à debito æternæ pœnæ soluit. Consequenter autem repetit Magister autoritates Psalmistæ atq; sanctorum prius adductas, post quæ etiam epilogans inquit: His aliisq; pluribus testimoniis docetur, Deum solum per se peccata dimittere. Et sicut dimittit quibusdam, ita & aliorum quorundam peccata retinet.
