Exigit in Deus in pœnitente propositum confitendi delicta sacerdoti, cum illius primum facultas affuerit, sicut dicit Magister lib. quarto 17. ca. 4. vbi quærit, an sufficiat soli Deo confiteri peccata & determinat autoritatibus scripturæ, quod non, si facultas affuerit sacerdotis. Quod si non affuerit, sufficit soli Deo confessum esse, habito tñ semper proposito confitendi si possit. Hoc etiam, conformiter Magistro, sensit Ricardus in suo libello prædicto, & ex determinatis ab eo in diuersis capitulis colligitur, quod à vero pœnitente, id est contrito de peccato, Deus ante quodcunque ministerium sacerdotis culpam tollit, debitum quoque æternis soluit æterna, sub conditione tamen quod sacerdoti postmodum debeat confiteri delictum, cum illius primum facultas affuerit. Quam si quidem conditionem vocauit Magister firmum propositum confitendi delicta, cum sacerdotis facultas adesset. Hanc autem sententiam conclusit Magister eodem quarto, di. 18. capitulis quinto & sexto. respondens cum hoc rationabili quæstioni, qua dubitari potest ad quid officium siue actio sacerdotis in pœnitentia requiratur, si solus Deus ante omne illius ministerium culpam tollit, & æternæ damnationis debitum soluit. Et dixit Magister: In hac autem tamen varietate, (quoniam de hoc tam sancti quam doctores dissentire videbantur, licet non in veritate dissentiant,) quod tenendum; hoc sane dicere ac sentire possumus, quod solus Deus dimittit peccata & retinet. Et tamen ecclesia (id est sacerdotibus, qui dicuntur ecclesia, secundum vnam significationem, vt apparuit secundo huius) contulit potestatem ligandi & soluendi. Sed aliter ipse soluit vel ligat, aliter ecclesia id est sacerdotes. Ipse enim per se tantum dimittit ita peccatum, quia & animam mundat ab interiori macula, & à debito æterna mortis soluit, non autem hoc sacerdotibus concessit, quibus tamen tribuit potestatem ligandi & soluendi, id est ostendendi homines solutos vel ligatos. In quo expressit propter quid requiratur in pœnitentia officium seum ministerium sacerdotis, & consequenter id declarans dixit, Vnde etiam dominus leprosum prius sanitati per se restituit, deinde ad sacerdotes misit, quorum iudicio ostenderetur mundatus: ita etiam Lazarum iam vivificatum, obtulit discipulis soluendum, quia & sic quis apud Deum sit solutus, non tamen in facie, id est in notitia ecclesiæ solutus habetur, nisi per iudicium sacerdotis. In soluendis igitur culpis aut retinendis ita operatur sacerdos ecclesiasticus & iudicat, sicut olim legalis in illis qui contaminati erant lepra, quæ peccatum significat. Hanc quoq; sententiam repetit circa finem Ipsamq; confirmat autoritate Hieronymi super illud Matt. 16. Et tibi dabo claves regni cælorum, inquit Hiero. Id iuris & officij habent euangelici sacerdotes, quod olim sub lege habebant legales in curandis leprosis. Hi ergo peccata dimittunt vel retinent, dum dimissa à Deo vel retenta iudicant & ostendunt. Vnde in Leuitico, ostendere se sacerdotibus iubentur leprosi, quos illi non faciunt leprosos vel mundos, sed discernunt qui mundi vel immundi. Requiritur ergo sacerdotis officium ad pœnitentem propter causam prædictam vt per ipsum vide licet ostendatur in ecclesiæ facie, quibus Deus peccata retinuit vel dimisit.
units.tr: Christ says: "Whatsoever you shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven also, and whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them," etc. From these words in particular arose the opinion and the title of "fullness of power," which the Roman bishop claims for himself. To understand their meaning and import more certainly, we must recall some points we made at the end of the first part: that Christ, true God and true man, "came into this world to bear witness to the truth" (John 18), namely the truth of the things to be believed, done and hoped for, so that the human race might attain eternal life. He taught this truth in word, showed it by example, and at last handed it down in writing, through the dictations of the evangelists and his apostles, so that by such Scripture we might be guided in the things of eternal salvation in the absence of himself and his apostles. This was the duty he committed to his apostles and their successors to carry out. After the resurrection, as if the very last thing, he said to them, Matthew 28: "Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." By commanding the apostles to administer baptism, he made them understand that they were also to administer the other sacraments, which he instituted for the eternal salvation of men. Among these is the sacrament of repentance, by which the actual guilt of the human soul, both mortal and venial, is blotted out, and by which the grace of God, corrupted in the soul by sin, is restored; without this grace, since God so ordained, human works could not merit eternal life. Hence Romans 6: "The grace of God is eternal life." The ministers of this sacrament, as of the others, are the priests or presbyters, as successors of the apostles of Christ. It is shown by the words of Scripture quoted above that the power of the keys, that is, of conferring the sacrament of repentance, or of loosing and binding men from their sins (which are the same thing), was given to all of them in the person of Peter and the other apostles. Hence Jerome on Matthew 16, "And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," says thus: "The other apostles indeed have the same judicial power, to whom after the resurrection he said: 'Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained.' Every congregation also has this in its presbyters and bishops; but Peter received it specially so that all might understand that whoever separates himself from the unity of the faith can neither be absolved from sins nor enter heaven." And Jerome said: "From the unity of the faith; he did not say from the unity of Peter or of the Roman bishop, since some of them could become heretics or otherwise perverse, and in fact such men have already been found." Now this judicial power is the authority of the keys, according to Jerome and Augustine in the same place. Of which Augustine says: "The keys are the knowledge and power of discerning, by which one ought to admit the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy," and so on, the priest. But how he may admit and how exclude from the kingdom will become clear afterwards, and from this it will appear what kind and what extent of power over these keys was granted by Christ to Peter and the apostles. First, we must observe that when a person sins mortally, guilt arises in the soul and the divine grace previously bestowed on it is corrupted. By this guilt the sinner is bound to the debt of eternal damnation for the state of the world to come. And while he persists in this guilt, he is cut off in this world from the fellowship of the faithful by a certain correction among the faithful of Christ, called excommunication. Conversely, we must notice that the sinner, through grief for his offence and through outward confession made to the priest (the word "repentance" is applied to both of these together and separately), obtains a threefold benefit. First, he is cleansed of inward guilt, and the grace of God is restored in him. Second, he is absolved from the debt of eternal damnation to which he had been bound by guilt. Third, he is reconciled to the Church, that is, he is, or ought to be, reunited to the fellowship of the faithful. To do these things in the sinner, namely to loose or bind him from guilt and from the debt of eternal damnation, which in some measure is done through the power of the keys granted to the priest (as will be said below), is to administer the sacrament of repentance. With these things thus premised, let us come to our purpose. According to the mind of the Master of the Sentences (indeed, of Scripture and of the saints, by whose authority he speaks in book 4, distinction 18), and also according to the intention of Richard in a little book he wrote entitled On the Power of Priestly Keys, let us say that for true repentance, or for the reception of the sacrament of repentance, the first requirement is the inward contrition or grief of the sinner for the offence committed. Second, there is required the purpose and act of confessing the offence, expressing or signifying it to the priest by speech, if the priest's availability is at hand. If it is not at hand, for a penitent or contrite person a firm purpose of confessing the offence to the priest suffices, once the priest's availability is present. Accordingly they hold that in a sinner who truly repents, that is, is contrite and has the purpose of confessing, certain things happen before the confession and before any action of the priest, and God alone works them. These are: the expulsion of guilt, the restoration of grace, and the remission of the debt of eternal damnation. That Christ works these things is proved by the Master in book 4, distinction 18, chapter 4, by the authority of Scripture and of the saints. First by the authority of the psalmist, who says in the person of God: "I alone blot out iniquities and the sins of the people." Again by the authority of Ambrose, who says: "The Word of God forgives sins; the priest and the judge. The priest performs his office, but exercises no right of power." Again, the same Ambrose: "He alone forgives sins who alone died for our sins." Further, by Augustine saying: "No one takes away sins except Christ alone, who is the Lamb taking away the sins of the world." That God does this before any action of the priest, the Master deduces from Augustine's words on the psalm: "Whose sins are covered." For, says the Master, "from these things it is plainly shown that God himself absolves the penitent from the debt of punishment; and he absolves him when he enlightens him by inspiring true contrition of heart." Reason supports this opinion, and the authorities bear witness to it. For no one is now pricked by sin, having a contrite and humbled heart, unless he is in charity; and whoever has charity is worthy of life; but no one is at once worthy of life and of death. Therefore he is not then bound by the debt of eternal death, for the son has ceased to be under wrath from the moment he began to love and to repent. From that time, then, he is freed from wrath, which does not remain upon him who believes in Christ, but upon him who does not believe. Therefore he is not afterwards freed from eternal wrath by the priest to whom he confesses, since he has already been freed from it by the Lord, from the moment he said, "I will confess." God alone, therefore, cleanses man inwardly from the stain of sin and absolves him from the debt of eternal punishment. Next, the Master repeats the authorities of the psalmist and of the saints adduced before, and afterwards, summing up, he says: "By these and many other testimonies it is taught that God alone forgives sins by himself. And just as he forgives some, so he retains the sins of others." God requires in the penitent the purpose of confessing his offences to the priest when the priest's availability is present, as the Master says in book 4, distinction 17, chapter 4, where he asks whether it is sufficient to confess sins to God alone, and decides by the authorities of Scripture that it is not, if the priest is available. But if he is not available, it suffices to have confessed to God alone, provided there is always the purpose of confessing if one is able. Richard, in agreement with the Master, also held this in his aforesaid little book, and from the determinations he made in various chapters it is gathered that "from the true penitent, that is, one contrite for sin, God, before any ministry of the priest, takes away the guilt and also loosens the debt of eternal punishment, under the condition, however, that he must afterwards confess the offence to the priest when the priest's availability is present." This condition the Master called "a firm purpose of confessing offences when the priest's availability is present." The Master concluded this opinion in the same book 4, distinction 18, chapters 5 and 6, answering with this reasonable question, which may be doubted: to what end is the office or action of the priest required in repentance, if God alone, before any ministry of his, takes away the guilt and loosens the debt of eternal damnation? And the Master said: "In this variety of opinion (since on this point both saints and teachers seem to disagree, although they do not really disagree) what we must hold is this: we may certainly say and think that God alone forgives sins and retains them. And yet the Church (that is, the priests, who are called the Church in one sense, as appeared in the second chapter of this work) has been given the power of binding and loosing. But he himself loosens or binds in one way, and the Church, that is, the priests, in another. For he alone forgives sin in itself, because he both cleanses the soul from inward stain and absolves it from the debt of eternal death; but this he has not granted to the priests, to whom nevertheless he has given the power of binding and loosing, that is, of showing men to be loosed or bound." In this he expressed the reason why the office or ministry of the priest is required in repentance; and consequently, making this clear, he said: "Hence also the Lord first restored the leper to health by himself, and then sent him to the priests, so that by their judgment he might be shown to be cleansed; so too he offered Lazarus, already made alive, to the disciples to be loosed, because, although a man may be loosed before God, yet he is not held loosed before the face, that is, in the knowledge of the Church, except through the judgment of the priest. Therefore in loosing or retaining sins the ecclesiastical priest acts and judges just as in former times the priest under the law did with those who were defiled by leprosy, which signifies sin." He repeats this opinion again near the end, and confirms it by the authority of Jerome on the words of Matthew 16, "And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Jerome says: "Evangelical priests have the same right and office that the priests under the law had in cleansing lepers." Therefore they forgive or retain sins while they judge and show what has been forgiven or retained by God. Hence in Leviticus the lepers are commanded to show themselves to the priests, who do not make them lepers or clean, but discern who is clean or unclean. The office of the priest is therefore required for the penitent, for the aforesaid reason, namely that by him it may be shown, in the face of the Church, whose sins God has retained or forgiven.

units.la: Est aliud etiam quod Deus operatur ad peccatorem, non sine ministerio sacerdotis, vt idem Magister atq; Ricardus senserunt, videlicet commutatio temporalis pœnæ purgatorii, quam pro delictis subiturus erat peccator, quantumcunq; bene pœnitens & confessus, in aliquam huius seculi satisfactionem, vt ieiunium, orationem, aut eleemosynam, peregrinationem, vel consimile aliud. Et secundum hoc iura potestatis in pectore sacerdotis exercet. Vnde Magist. di. 18. ca. 7. sic inquit: Et notandum quia quos satisfactione pœnitentiæ ligant, solutos ostendunt, quia non imponitur aliciui satisfactio pœnitentialis, nisi què sacerdos vere pœnitenti arbitratur, alii non imponit, & eo ipso peccata à Deo retineri iudicat. Commutas quoq; sacerdos pœnas purgatorii peccatori debitas in aliquas huius seculi satisfactiones. Et peccatores post modum ecclesia, id est communioni fidelium reconciliat in quo similiter potestatem in peccatores exercet, si tamen id secundum discretionem egerit. Vnde Magister vbi supra: Ligant quoque sacerdotes satisfactionem pœnitentiæ confitentibus imponunt. Soluunt, cum de ea aliquid dimittunt, vel per eam purgatos ad communionem sacramentorum admittunt, quo modo soluendi scilicet vel ligandi superius Leuitici notauit. Secundum hunc modum dicuntur sacerdotes peccata dimittere vel retinere. Vnde superius Augustinus dixit: Quibus remittunt, remittit Deus, &c. Opus enim iustitiæ exercent in peccatores, cum eos interdum poena ligant, opus misericordiæ, dum de ea aliquid relaxant, vel sacramentorum communionis concedunt, alia opera in peccatores exercere nequeunt. Vnde etiam patet quod iuxta merita pœnitentium, non plus de culpa vel pœna relaxare potest Romanus episcopus, quam alter quicunque sacerdos.
units.tr: There is also another thing that God works in the sinner, not without the ministry of the priest, as the same Master (Peter Lombard) and Richard thought: namely, the commutation of the temporal punishment of purgatory, which the sinner was to undergo for his offences, however truly he repents and confesses, into some satisfaction in this life, such as fasting, prayer, almsgiving, a pilgrimage, or something similar. And in this way the priest exercises the power of the keys. Hence Master (Peter Lombard), Dist. 18, cap. 7, says as follows: And it should be noted that those whom they bind with the satisfaction of penance, they show to be loosed, because no penitential satisfaction is imposed on anyone except what the priest judges suitable for a truly penitent person; he does not impose it on another, and by that very act he judges that sins are retained by God. The priest also commutes the punishments of purgatory owed by a sinner into some satisfactions of this life. And afterwards he reconciles the sinners to the Church, that is, to the communion of the faithful; in this too he similarly exercises power over sinners, if indeed he has acted with discretion. Hence the Master, in the place cited above: Priests also bind sinners by imposing satisfaction of penance on those who confess. They loose when they remit some part of it, or when they admit those cleansed through it to the communion of the sacraments; in the way of loosing and binding, namely, which he noted above from Leviticus. In this way priests are said to forgive or retain sins. Hence Augustine said above: Those whom they remit, God remits, etc. For they exercise the work of justice on sinners when at times they bind them with punishment, and the work of mercy when they relax some of it or grant the communion of the sacraments; they cannot exercise other works on sinners. From this it is also clear that, according to the merits of penitents, the Roman bishop can remit no more of guilt or punishment than any other priest whatever.

units.la: Ex dictis itaq; sanctorum autoritatibus magistri atq; Ricardi, apparet liquido, quod culpa & debitum æternæ damnationis solus Deus peccatori vere pœnitenti remittit absq; opere sacerdotis precedente vel interveniente simul, quemadmodum ostensum est prius. Cuius etiam volo demonstrationem infallibilem assignare secundum scripturam, & iuxta dicta sanctorum atque doctorum. Quoniam solus Deus est, qui non potest ignorare, quibus remittendum, & quib. retinendum sit peccatum. Et solus qui affectione perversa neque monetur neque iudicat quenquam iniuste, Non sic autem ecclesia siue sacerdos, quicunq; sit ille, etiam Romanus episcopus. Potest enim ipsorum qui ibet errare quandoq;, vel inclinari affectione peruersa, vel utroque propter quod, si vere pœnitenti cum debito proposito, aut etiam actu confitendi subsecuto, non retinetur peccatum seu culpa & debitum æternæ damnationis, renitente sacerdote ignorantia, malitia vel utroque periret persæpe fidelis & euangelica Christi promissio, qua bonis præmia æternæ gloriæ, malis vero gehennæ supplicia se dixit datum. Vnde sicut etiam frequenter euenire contingit, Esto peccatorem aliquem fide ac indebite delicta confessum, & sic sacerdotis ignorantia vel malignitate aut vtraq; absolutionem & benedictionem accepisse. Esto rursum alium quendam sufficienter & debite sacerdoti peccata confessum, recusasse quoq; illi sacerdotem, ignorantia, malitia, vel vtraq;, delictorum absolutionem & benedictionem impendere. Nunquid sint fidele confitentis peccata dimissa, & posterioris vere pœnitentis peccata retenta? firmiter & indubie tenendum quod minime. Vnde Chrysost. super illud Ioannis 20. Accipite Spiritum sanctum, & quorum remiseritis peccata, &c. sic inquit: Non enim sacerdos sed neque angelus aut archangelus operari potest aliquid in his, quæ data sunt à Deo. Sacerdos autem suam benedictionem & manum tribuit, non enim iustam est propter alterius malitiam circa symbola nostra salutis ladi eos qui ad fidem veniunt. Idem quoque Hieronymus super illud Matt. 16. Et tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum, &c. sic inquit: Hunc locum quidam non intelligentes aliquid sumunt de supercilio pharisaorum, vt damnare innoxios, vel soluere se putent noxios, cum apud Deum non sententia sacerdotum, sed reorum vita quaeratur. Quibus verbis subiungit Magister dist. 18. capit. 6. seriem hanc notabilem: Ita & hic aperte ostenditur, quod non sequitur Deus ecclesiæ iudicium, quæ per surreptionem & ignorantiam interdum iudicet ecclesiæ, id est sacerdotum in ea. Hoc etiam addens octauo eiusdem: Interdum enim qui foras mittitur, id est extra ecclesiam per sacerdotem esse inducatur intus est: & qui foris est secundum veritatem scilicet, intus retineri videtur, per falsum videlicet iudicium sacerdotum. Hanc etiam de clauium sacerdotalium potestate, sententiam, quam ex dictis sanctorum atque doctorum collegimus & recitauimus pridem, resumens Magister in quarta dist. 18. capit. 8. sic inquit: Iam ostensum est qualiter sacerdotes dimittunt peccata, vel retinent. Et tamen retinuit sibi Deus quandam singularem potestatem dimittendi vel retinendi, quia ipse solus per se debitum æterna mortis soluit, & animam interius purgat. Idem quoque dicit capit. nono atque finali eiusdem distinctionis. Ipsa ergo, inquit, dissimilitudo, qua in est anima ex peccato, & à Deo elongatio, anime macula intelligitur, à qua purgatur in pœnitentia. Hoc autem solus Deus facit, qui solus suscitat animam & illuminat, quod sacerdotes nequeunt, qui sunt medici animarum. Est autem & alius modus ligandi atque soluendi, ad quam similiter requiritur actio sacerdotis, per excommunicationem scilicet. Hæc autem, vt dicit Magister in quarto, dist. 18. capi. 7. Fieri habet, cum quis secundum canonicam disciplinam, tertio vocatus ad emendationem manifesti delicti, & satisfacere volpendens, sententia ecclesia à loco orationis & sacramentorum communione, & fidelium consortio præciditur, vt erubescat, & pudore sceleris conuersus pœniteat, vt spiritus eius saluus sit. Qui si pœnitentiam profitens, respuerit, negata communioni admittitur & ecclesiæ reconciliatur. Hæc autem ecclesiæ anathematizatio hanc pœnam illis, qui digne percelluntur, infligit, quia Dei gratia & protectio illis amplius subtrahitur ac sibi ipsis relinquitur, vt sit eis liberum ruere in interitu peccati, in quos etiam diabolo maior datur sæuiendi potestas. Orationes quoque ecclesiæ & benedictionum ac meritorum suffragia, eis nequaquam suffragari putantur. Circa prædicta quidem, vt sciatur cui is vel quorum sit & secundum quem modum excommunicandi potestas, oportet attendere, quod in excommunicatione iudicatur reus ad pœnam pro statu futuri seculi iudicio quodam, de quo expressius hono huius dicetur, & eidem infligitur pœna quaedam grauis, etiam pro statu vitæ præsentis, vt quia diffamatur publice, sibique interdicitur aliorum consortium. Ex quo etiam ciuili communione atque commoditate priuatur. Et licet primæ pœnæ infl. ctio vt quæ infligitur illi qui percellitur indigne, nihil noceat pro statu futuri seculi, quia Deus non semper sequitur ecclesiæ, id est sacerdotum iudicium, dum scilicet iniuste quenquam iudicant, quemadmodum sufficienter ostensum est prius. Laederetur tamen sic iniuste percussus à sacerdote pro statu vitæ præsentis grauissime quasi, vt quia diffamatur, & ciuili communicatione priuatur. Et propterea dicendum, quod licet ad tale iudicium promulgandum requiratur vox & actio sacerdotis, non tamen ad aliquem solum, aut tantummodo ad ipsorum collegium pertinet iudicium coactiuum & præceptum dare de excommunicandis aut absoluendis: sed talem statuere iudicem, cuius videlicet sit reum vocare ac examinare, iudicare, absoluere, aut condemnare, sic publice diffamandum, aut à fidelium consortio præcidendum, pertinet ad fidelium vniuersitatem in communitate illa in qua debet aliquis tali iudicio iudicari, vel ad superiorem ipsius, vel ad exilium generale veruntamen debet examinatio criminis, si tale fuerit propter quod debeat quis excommunicari nec ne, fieri per talem iudicem habito collegio sacerdotum, aut ex eis peritorum determinato numero secundum leges positas aut consuetudines. Sacerdotes nanque iudicio primæ significationis debent crimina iudicare seu discernere, quibus secundum legem euangelicam, debet quis à fidelium præcidi consortio, ne alios inficiat, quemadmodum medicus aut medicorum collegium, iudicio primæ significationis, iudicare habent de morbo corporali, propter quem debet quis ne alios inficiat leprosus ab aliorum consortio separati. Et rursum debet esse crimen huiusmodi, quod certo testimonio probari possit per aliquē fore commissum. Et propterea, sicut non ad medicum quenquam, aut ipsorum tantummodo collegium, iudicium seu iudicem, cuius est coactiva potestas expellendi leprosos, statuere pertinet, sed ad eiuium fidelium vniuersitatem aut ipsorum partem valentiorem, quemadmodum demonstratum est decimo quinto prima. Sic quoq; propter animæ morbum, vt crimen notorium expellendorum à communi consortio, iudicium aut iudicem, cuius sit horum coactiva potestas, ad nullum sacerdotem solum aut ipsorum tantummodo collegium statuere pertinet in communitate fidelium, quanquam ex ipsorum consilio debeat tale iudicium procedere, quoniam ipsi tenentur scire legem diuinam, in qua determinata sunt crimina propter quæ debet alicui criminoso fidelium non criminosorum interdici consortium. Labia nanque sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & legem requirent ex ore eius, Malachiæ secundo. Vtrum autem huiusmodi crimen commiserit is cui crimen imponitur, non oportet per solum episcopum aut sacerdotem iudicari, sed per fidelium vniuersitatem in communitate illa, vel per iudicem ab eadem institutum ad hoc vel superiorem quemadmodum diximus, siue sacerdotem siue non sacerdotem. Secundum tamen probationes inductas, & si per testes conuictus fuerit, & tale fuerit crimen propter quod debeat excommunicari, in quo solo stari debet iudicio collegii sacerdotum aut sanioris partis illius. Tunc per supradictum iudicem à fidelium vniuersitate illius loci statutum ad hoc, debet sic criminosus excommunicandus per sententiam nunciari. Et fieri debet executio talis sententiæ voce sacerdotis, pro quanto tangit reum etiam pro statu venturi seculi. Demonstrat autem verum esse quod diximus: scriptura, ex qua ortum sumpsisse videtur hæc correctionis species, & est Matthæi decimo octauo, cum dixit Christus: Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, vade & corripe eum inter te & ipsum solum: si te audierit, lucratus eris fratrem tuum: si autem te non audierit, adhibe tecum vnum vel duos testes, vt in ore duorum vel trium testium stet omne verbum. Quod si eos non audierit, dic ecclesiæ. si autem ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. Dixit ergo Christus, dic ecclesiæ, nec dixit, apostolo vel episcopo seu presbytero aut ipsorum soli collegio. Et intellexit ibi Christus ecclesiam fidelium multitudinem aut iudicem ad hæc illius autoritate institutum, quo modo vti sunt hoc nomine apostoli & ecclesia primitiua, sicut plene ostensum est secundo huius. Et quod sic Christus intellexerit ecclesiam, id est credentium seu fidelium vniuersitatem, Et quod huius sit talem iudicem statuere, aut tale iudicium ferre in contumaces, aut taliter criminosos demonstrato per Apostolum prima ad Corinthios quinto, vbi caulam, formam & modum, & per hoc iudicium in quenquam ferri debeat, tradit Apostolus magis expresse, Christi verborum sequens & explanans sententiam, dum dixit: Ego quidem absens corpore, præsens autem spiritu, iam iudicaui vt præsens eum qui sic est operatus in nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi, congregatis vobis & meo spiritu, cum virtute domini Iesu, tradere huiusmodi satanæ. criminosum scilicet quendam, qui patris sui vxorem cognouerat carnaliter. Vbi Glosa secundum Augustinum: Hoc modo iudicaui, vt nos congregati in vnum, absque aliqua dissensione, quibus mea autoritas & virtus Christi cooperabitur, tradatis satanæ huiusmodi. Ecce ergo propter quid, quibus, & qualiter aliquis excommunicandus est secundum intentionem & doctrinam Apostoli, in cuius mandato fortasis magis attenditur consilium quam præceptum, etiam secundum legem diuinam. quoniam esto quod illum criminosum toleraffent inter ipsos conuersari propter ipsorum patientiam quamuis non sine scandalo & periculo infectionis aliorum, nil minus saluari & meritoria opera facere poterant. Amplius, esto quod præceptum stricte sumendo fuisset secundum legem diuinam, non tamen fuit præceptum hoc fieri per solum sacerdotem aut episcopum vel ipsorum tantummodo collegium. Et ideo cum dixit Apostolus: Ego quidem absens corpore, præsens autem spiritu, iam iudicaui, &c. intelligi debet iudicio primæ significationis, non tertiæ. propterea quod subdit, Congregatis vobis & meo spiritu. Vnde & eis formam tradidit, ex qua inter ipsos ex hoc contentio non posset oriri. Quoniam ipsis congregatis in vnum, maxime, si per modum iudicii coactiui hoc fieri debeat, propter quod Augustinus, Vt vos congregati in vnum absque aliqua dissensione, id est de communi consensu per vos fiat vel per iudicem ex communi consensu per vos statuto ad hoc, quod idem est. Et ideo non mandauit hoc Apostolus fieri per presbyterum aliquem, nec alicui episcopo seu presbytero scripsit hoc fiendum per ipsum, tum tamen ad ipsos tunc mitteret Timotheum, qui episcopus erat, vt eadem quarto palam. quod tamen fecisset, si hoc iudicium ad solius sacerdotis autoritatem pertinere nouisset, quemadmodum in aliis fecerat. Quod etiam ex prima ad Timotheum tertio, & ad Titum primo induximus capitulo præcedente. Posset autem, quam tenemus, probabiliter dicta sententia ratione firmari iuxta scripturam. Quoniam certius & absque suspicione magis fit tale iudicium, vt diximus, quam per solam voluntatem vnici sacerdotis aut ipsorum solius collegii, cuius aut quorum iudicium amore vel odio, aut inspecto commodo proprio citius peruerteretur, quam vniuersitatis fidelium, ad quam semper appellare contingit. Quamuis, vt diximus, executio talis sententiæ per sacerdotem fieri debeat, pro quanto inuocatur in hoc seculo diuina virtus ad pœnam aliquam criminoso infligendam in hoc seculo, quæ per hominis potestatem non posset inferri, vt dæmonis vexationem. Et quia pro statu futuri seculi similiter iudicatur ad pœnam, & quoniam priuatur ecclesiæ suffragiis, quod fortasse per solius sacerdotis actionem Deus instituit fieri: Amplius, quoniam si cuiuis episcopo seu presbytero soli, aut cum suo solo collegio clericorum licet quemlibet excommunicare absq; fidelium vniuersitatis consensu, sequitur exeo. sacerdotes aut ipsorum collegium, omnia regna & principatus ab habentibus regibus aut principibus auferre posse. Excommunicato, nanq; quouis principe, subiecta sibi multitudo etiam excommunicabitur, si excommunicato principi obedire voluerit, ficq; cuiuslibet principis erit calla potestas, Cuius oppositum voluit doctor gentium ad Ro. 13. & prima ad Timotheum sexto, & Augustinus ibidem in glossa, quemadmodum induximus quinto huius, parte septima & octava. Instantiae vero quae ad haec determinationem possent apparenter induci, facile repellentur ex dicendis, nono, decimo, decimoquarto & 17. huius. Est rursum auctoritas quaedam sacerdotum, ea qua panis & vinum in corpus Christi benedictum transubstantiatur ad sacerdotis orationem, post certorum verborum ab ipso prolationem. Haec autem auctoritas, character est animae, sicut ea quae clavium. Et dicitur potestas conficiendi eucharistiae sacramentum. Hanc quidem Theologorum quibusdam dicentibus esse ab eodem charactere cum clavium potestate, de qua dictum est prius. Aliis vero, quod diverso charactere, alio etiam tempore atque verbis Christi, collato apostolis, ut his quae ad apostolos protulit Matthaei 26. Marci 14. & Lucae 22. dum dixit ad eos: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur, hoc facite in meam commemorationem, hoc facite, id est hoc faciendi potestatem habete. Qualitercunque tamen de hac diversitate veritas habeat, non refert ad hanc considerationem, quantum enim sufficiens nobis est ad propositum de auctoritatibus seu potestatibus presbyteris seu episcopis per Christum collatis, quod ex scriptura sacra colligi potest, rememorasse putamus. Caeterum quae de clavium sacerdotalium potestate seu auctoritate per Christum apostolis tradita, summam facturi, recolligentes, dicamus quod in peccatore vere poenitente, id est, de peccato commisso dolente aliqua solus Deus operatur etiam absque sacerdotis aliquo praeveniente ministerio, mentis videlicet illuminationem, culpae seu maculae peccati purgationem, & aeternae damnationis remissionem. Alia vero sunt quae Deus in eodem peccatore non secundum se solum operatur, sed per ministerium sacerdotis, sicut ostendere in ecclesiae facie, quis solutus vel ligatus a peccatis habeatur in hoc saeculo, ligandus aut solvendus in alio, id est cuius Deus peccata retinuerit aut dimiserit. Amplius est & illud quod Deus operatur circa peccatorem per ministerium sacerdotis, commutatio scilicet poenae purgatorii debitae peccatori, pro statu futuri saeculi in aliquam satisfactionem temporalem seu saeculi huius, ipsam enim relaxat secundum partem aut totum iuxta satisfactiones iniunctas & poenitentis conditionem, quae omnia per sacerdotem fieri debent, cum clave potestatis secundum discretionem. Sic etiam a sacramentorum communione per sacerdotem excluduntur contumaces & resipientes admittuntur, quomodo dictum est circa finem capituli praecedentis. Haec autem fuit sententia Magistri libro quarto, dist. 18. octavo capitulo, cum dixit: Secundum hos ligandi & solvendi modos, quomodo verum est quod dicitur, Quodcunque solveritis super terram, solutum erit in caelis: & quodcunque ligaveritis super terram, ligatum erit & in caelo. Aliquando enim ostendunt solutos vel ligatos, (presbyteri scilicet) qui non sunt apud Deum, & poena satisfactionis interdum indignos ligant vel solvunt, & indignos sacramentis admittunt, & dignos admisti arcent. Sed intelligendum est in illis quorum merita solvi vel ligari postulant. Quoscunque ergo solvunt vel ligant, adhibentes clavem discretionis reorum meritis, solvuntur vel ligantur in caelis, id est apud Deum, quia divino iudicio sententia sacerdotis sic progressa approbatur & confirmatur. Et dixit Magister consequenter quasi epilogans, Ecce qualis & quantus est usus apostolicarum clavium. Ad cuius etiam euidentiam ampliorem habendam inducemus exemplum seu comparationem ipsius familiarem satis, quae etiam verbis & sententiae Christi atque sanctorum, quorum auctoritates induximus prius, & maxime Ambrosii, multum attinere videtur. Inquit enim ille, quod verbum Dei dimittit peccata, sacerdos quidem officium exhibet suum sed nullius potestatis iura exercet. Nos autem dicamus, quod sacerdos tanquam clavigerr caelestis iudicis, quasi proportionaliter peccatorem liberat clavigero mundani iudicis. Nam sicut per verbum sive sententiam iudicis huius saeculi (principantis scilicet,) damnatur aut absolvitur reus a culpa & poena civili. Sic per verbum divinum aliquis simpliciter solvitur aut ligatur culpa & debito damnationis seu poenae pro statu futuri saeculi. Et sicut actione clavigeri mundani principis nemo a civili culpa vel poena solvitur aut damnatur, per ipsius tamen actionem, qua carcerem claudit vel aperit, reus oftendiatur solutus vel damnatus: sic quasi per sacerdotis actione, nullus solvitur aut ligatur culpa & debito damnationis aeterna, sed ostenditur in ecclesia facie quis solutus aut ligatus habeatur a Deo, dum sacerdotis benedictionem accipit, & ad sacramentorum communionem admittitur, quomodo praedixi-mus circa finem capituli praecedentis. Et ideo sicut clavigeri mundani iudicis aperiendo vel claudendo carcerem, officium suum exhibet, nullius tamen iudiciariae potestatis absolvendi vel damnandi iura exercet, quoniam & si de facto carcerem aperiret alicui reo non absoluto per iudicem, ipsumque populo absolutum sua voce nunciaret, non propter hoc reus solutus esset a poena vel culpa civili. Et e contra, si carcerem aperire recusaret, suoque verbo nunciaret non esse absolutum sed damnatum, quem vere iudex per suam absoluisset sententiam, non propter hoc ille debitor esset culpae aut poenae civilis. Sic proportionaliter sacerdos, clavigera caelestis iudicis officium suum exhibet per absolutionis aut ligamenti seu maledictionis verbalem pronunciationem. Quod si vere damnandos per superum iudicem, aut iam damnatus, sacerdos ipse ignorantia, vel surreptione, aut utroque absoluendos vel absolutos pronunciaret, aut econtra, non tamen propter hoc ellent primi soluti, & secundi damnati, eo quod clavem aut claves cum discretione non adhibuisset reorum meritis. Et ideo suum officium exhibet, sicut dixit Ambrosius. Nullius tamen potestatis iura exercet, quoniam vere solutos aut soluendos apud Deum quandoque in ecclesiæ facie sacerdotes pro futuro seculo ligatos aut ligandos pronunciant & e contra, vt supra diximus auctoritate sanctorum, atque Magistri libro quarto, distinctione decima octaua, & octa-uo capitulo. Et propterea iura potestatis non exercet sacerdos. Sic enim quandoque diuina iustitia & repromissio perire posset. Ille igitur solus iura potestatis exercet in his, & iudex est, coactiuam habens potentiam, qui solus nec falli de humanis cogitationibus & operationibus potest. Nam ad Hebræos 4. Omnia nuda & aperta sunt oculis eius, & qui solus nec quicquam vult peruerse. Quoniam iustus es domine, & omnia iudicia tua iusta sunt, & omnes viæ tuæ, misericordia, & veritas, & iudicium, Tobiæ tertio. ideoque vnicus ipse iudex est talis. Vnde Iacobi quarto. Vnus est legislator & iudex, qui potest perdere & liberare. quod Iacobus nec de ipso aut aliquo dixit apostolorum, cum tamen esset vnus de his tribus, qui videbantur esse columnæ ecclesiæ, vt dixit Apostolus ad Galatas secundo. Voluit autem Christus huiusmodi sententias per ipsum latas aut ferendas in alio seculo, per sacerdotes pronunciari quodam iudicio significationis primæ, quasi prohostico, vt ex hoc peccatores in hoc mundo terreantur & à sceleribus & criminibus reuocentur ad pœnitentiam, ad quod exigitur, & valet multum officium sacerdotum. Quo modo, si medicus corporalis sanitatis, cui docendi & operandi secundum artem medicinæ potestas est data, ex institutione iudicis seu legislatoris humani, de futuris sanis aut morituris iudicium secundum medicinalem scientiam in populo promulgaret, vt ex hoc homines sobriam ducerent vitam, & ab intemperata reuocarentur, propter corporis sanitatem conseruandam, aut acquirendam, præcepta quoque seu documenta talium exhiberet. Præciperet utique talia medicus obseruari & obseruatores futuros sanos & transgressores infirmos vel morituros iudicaret, quos ille neque sanaret, aut infirmaret principaliter, sed naturæ hominum actio, ministerium tamen aliquod exhiberet. Nec rursum posset medicus sui auctoritate sanum aut infirmum ad talia facienda quantumcunque corporali sanitati conferentia compellere, sed solummodo exhortari & docere atque terrere per sui iudicium primæ significationis pronosticum, eis annunciando sanitatem ex quorundam obseruatione, mortem vero aut ægritudinem ex talium transgressione. Sicetiam proportionaliter medicus animarum, sacerdos scilicet, de his quæ ad æternam animæ sanitatem perducunt, vel mortem æternam aut pœnam temporalem pro statu venturi seculi, iudicat & hortatur. Ad quæ tamen iudicio coactiuo neminem arcere potest nec debet in hoc seculo, vt Apostoli & Ambrosii auctoritate probauimus 1. ad Corinth. primo, & supra cum his Chrysostomi sententiam expressam induximus quinto huius, parte sexta. Propter quod sacerdos secundum sui officium non debet similitudinarie corporari iudici tertiæ significationis sed primæ, habenti scilicet auctoritatem docendi aut operandi, quemadmodum medicus, non tamen inquantum per potentiam coactiuam. Sic enim Christus se vocauit medicum, non principem. Vbi Lu. 5. dixit de se loquens: Non egent medico qui sani sunt, sed qui male habent, nec dixit, iudice indigent. Quoniam in mundum de contentiosis coactiuum iudicium exercere non venerat, Vt ex Luca 12. induximus quarta huius, parte octaua. Sed viuos & mortuos tali iudicio iudicaturus est in die illa, de qua dixit Apostolus 2. Timotheum vltimo: In reliquo reposita est mihi corona iustitiæ, quam reddet mihi Dominus in die illa iustus iudex. Tunc enim coactiuo iudicio pœnas infliget his, qui legem latam per ipsum immediate in hoc seculo transgressi fuerint. Et propterea signanter dixit Christus Petro: Tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum. nec dixit, tibi dabo iudicium regni cœlorum. Et inde iam diximus, neque clauigerum mundani iudicis aut superni habere iudicium coactiuum, quod tertiæ significationis vocauimus, eo quod neuter talis potestatis iura exercet, vt de sacerdote palam dixit Ambrosius, & reliquorum etiam sanctorum auctoritate monstratum est satis. De auctoritate itaque sacerdotum seu episcoporum, & apostolicarum clauium potestate per Christum sibi concessa, determinatum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: From the sayings of the saints and the authorities just cited, the Master and Richard, it is clear that God alone remits guilt and the debt of eternal damnation to a sinner who truly repents, without any priestly act going before or accompanying it, as was shown earlier. I also want to set out an infallible proof of this from Scripture and from the sayings of the saints and teachers. God alone cannot be ignorant of whom sin should be remitted to and whom it should be retained from, and God alone neither is moved by a perverse affection nor judges anyone unjustly. The Church or the priest, whoever he is, even the Roman bishop, is not like this. Any of them may at some time err, or be inclined by a perverse affection, or by both together. If, because of this, the guilt and the debt of eternal damnation were not remitted to a truly penitent person who had a firm purpose, or who had even actually confessed, and the priest resisted through ignorance, malice, or both, then the faithful and evangelical promise of Christ, by which he said that rewards of eternal glory are given to the good and punishments of hell to the wicked, would often perish. So, as also happens often, suppose that some sinner has confessed his sins in faith but improperly, and has received absolution and blessing from a priest through the priest's ignorance or malice, or both. Suppose again that another has confessed his sins to a priest sufficiently and properly, but the priest, through ignorance, malice, or both, has refused to give him absolution and blessing. Are the sins of the first confessor remitted, and the sins of the second, truly penitent, retained? We must firmly and undoubtedly hold that by no means is this so. Hence Chrysostom, on the words of John 20, "Receive the Holy Spirit, and whose sins you remit, etc.", says: "For it is not the priest, nor even an angel or archangel, who can do anything in those matters which have been given by God. The priest gives his blessing and his hand, for it is not right that those who come to the faith should be harmed on account of another's malice regarding the symbols of our salvation." Jerome likewise, on the words of Matthew 16, "And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc.", says: "Some, not understanding this passage, take from it a haughty pride of the Pharisees, as if they thought they could condemn the innocent or absolve the guilty, when with God the question is not the judgment of priests but the life of the accused." After these words the Master, in distinction 18, chapter 6, adds this noteworthy sequence: "Thus here too it is clearly shown that God does not follow the judgment of the Church, which through deception and ignorance sometimes judges the Church, that is, the priests in it." He adds this also in the eighth chapter of the same distinction: "For sometimes one who is cast out, that is, put outside the Church by the priest, is in fact inside, and one who is in fact outside is seen to be retained inside, namely through the false judgment of priests." The Master, resuming this opinion about the power of the priestly keys, which we gathered and recited earlier from the sayings of the saints and teachers, says in book 4, distinction 18, chapter 8: "It has now been shown how priests remit or retain sins. Yet God has kept for himself a singular power of remitting or retaining, because he alone himself loosens the debt of eternal death and inwardly cleanses the soul. The same thing he says in the ninth and final chapter of the same distinction: 'That very unlikeness in which the soul is through sin, and its distance from God, is understood as a stain of the soul, from which it is cleansed in repentance. But this only God does, who alone raises the soul and enlightens it, which priests cannot do, for they are physicians of souls.'" There is also another way of binding and loosing, for which the action of a priest is likewise required, namely by excommunication. "This, as the Master says in book 4, distinction 18, chapter 7, is done when someone who, according to canonical discipline, has been called a third time to amendment of a manifest offence, and who refuses to make satisfaction, is cut off by sentence of the Church from the place of prayer, from communion in the sacraments, and from the fellowship of the faithful, so that he may be ashamed and, turned back by the shame of his crime, repent, so that his spirit may be saved. If he professes repentance, he is admitted again and reconciled to the Church, even though communion had been refused him." This anathema of the Church inflicts this punishment on those who are rightly struck down, because the grace and protection of God are withdrawn from them and they are left to themselves, so that it is free for them to fall into the destruction of sin, and over them the devil is given greater power to rage. The prayers of the Church and the suffrages of blessings and merits are also thought not to help them at all. Regarding these matters, so that it may be known to whom, or to which persons, the power of excommunication belongs, and in what manner, we must observe that in excommunication the guilty person is judged to punishment with respect to the judgment of the future age, about which more will be said more fully below, and a certain grave penalty is also inflicted on him for the state of the present life: for he is publicly defamed and forbidden the fellowship of others, and by this he is also deprived of civil communion and advantage. And although the first penalty, which is inflicted on one who is struck down unworthily, does no harm with respect to the state of the future age, because God does not always follow the judgment of the Church, that is, of the priests, when they judge someone unjustly, as has been sufficiently shown before, nevertheless one unjustly struck down by a priest would be gravely harmed, as it were, for the state of the present life, since he is defamed and deprived of civil fellowship. And therefore it should be said that although the voice and action of a priest are required to pronounce such a judgment, nevertheless the coercive judgment and the command to excommunicate or absolve do not belong to any one priest alone, nor merely to their college. But to appoint such a judge, whose task is to summon and examine the accused, to judge, absolve, or condemn him, so that he is publicly defamed or cut off from the fellowship of the faithful, belongs to the whole body of the faithful in that community in which someone is to be judged by such a judgment, or to its superior, or to general exile. Yet the examination of the crime, whether it is such that someone ought to be excommunicated or not, must be made by such a judge, with the college of priests, or a determined number of those skilled among them, taking counsel, according to the laws or customs laid down. For priests, by the judgment of the first signification, ought to judge or discern the crimes for which, according to the evangelical law, someone must be cut off from the fellowship of the faithful, so that he does not infect others, just as a physician or a college of physicians, by the judgment of the first signification, has the duty to judge about a bodily disease, on account of which a leper must be separated from the company of others so that he does not infect them. Again, such a crime must be something that can be proved by sure testimony to have been committed by someone. And therefore, just as it does not belong to any one physician, or merely to their college, to appoint a judgment or a judge who has the coercive power of expelling lepers, but rather to the whole body of the faithful or its more powerful part, as was shown in chapter 15 of the first part, so also, on account of a disease of the soul, the judgment or judge who has the coercive power of expelling from common fellowship a notorious crime does not belong to any one priest alone, or merely to their college, to appoint in the community of the faithful, although such a judgment ought to proceed on their counsel, since they are bound to know the divine law, in which the crimes are determined on account of which a criminal must be forbidden fellowship with the faithful who are not criminals. "For the lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth," Malachi 2. But whether the one charged has committed such a crime, this must be judged not by the bishop or priest alone, but by the whole body of the faithful in that community, or by a judge set up for this by it, or by its superior, as we have said, whether he is a priest or not a priest. Nevertheless, according to the proofs brought forward, and if he has been convicted by witnesses, and if the crime is such that he ought to be excommunicated, then in this case alone the judgment of the college of priests, or of its wiser part, must stand. Then, through the aforesaid judge appointed for this by the whole body of the faithful of that place, the criminal who is to be excommunicated must be notified of the sentence. And the carrying out of such a sentence must be done by the voice of the priest, so far as it touches the guilty person also with respect to the state of the age to come. Scripture, from which this kind of correction seems to have arisen, shows that what we have said is true. It is Matthew 18, where Christ said: "If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two witnesses, so that every word may stand on the mouth of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church. But if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector." Christ therefore said, "Tell it to the Church," and he did not say, "to the apostle or the bishop or the elder, or to their college alone." And there Christ understood the Church to be the multitude of the faithful, or a judge appointed for this by its authority, in the way that the apostles and the primitive Church used this name, as was fully shown in the second part of this work. And that Christ understood the Church in this way, that is, the body of believers or the faithful, and that it belongs to this body to appoint such a judge, or to pronounce such a judgment against the contumacious, or against criminals of this kind, the Apostle shows more clearly in 1 Corinthians 5, where he sets out the cause, the form, the manner, and the judgment to be passed on anyone, following and explaining the sense of Christ's words when he said: "For I indeed, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged as if I were present him who has so acted in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: when you are gathered together, and my spirit is with you, with the power of our Lord Jesus, to deliver such a one to Satan." He meant a certain criminal who had known his father's wife carnally. The Gloss, following Augustine, says: "I have judged in this way, that you, gathered together into one without any dissension, in whom my authority and the power of Christ will cooperate, should deliver such a one to Satan." Behold, then, why, by whom, and how someone is to be excommunicated, according to the intention and teaching of the Apostle, in whose command perhaps more attention is paid to counsel than to precept, even according to the divine law. For suppose they had tolerated that criminal living among them out of their patience, although not without scandal and danger of infecting others, they could nevertheless still be saved and do meritorious works. Moreover, suppose that taking the precept strictly it had been according to the divine law, nevertheless this precept was not given to be carried out by the priest or bishop alone, or by their college alone. And therefore, when the Apostle said: "For I indeed, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, etc." it must be understood in the judgment of the first signification, not the third, because he adds: "when you are gathered together, and my spirit is with you." Hence he also gave them a form by which contention could not arise among them over this. For since they were gathered together into one, this would be done especially if it had to be done by way of coercive judgment, on account of which Augustine says: "That you, gathered together into one without any dissension, that is, by common consent, be done by you, or by a judge appointed for this by common consent among you, which is the same thing." And therefore the Apostle did not command this to be done by any one elder, nor did he write to any bishop or elder that it should be done by him. Yet he would then send Timothy, who was a bishop, to them, so that the same thing might be done, as he says openly in chapter 4. He would have done this if he had known that such a judgment belonged to the authority of the priest alone, as he had done in other matters. This is what we also brought forward from 1 Timothy 3 and from Titus 1 in the preceding chapter. The opinion we hold can also be probably confirmed by reason, according to Scripture. For such a judgment is made more surely and without suspicion, as we have said, when it is made by the will of the whole body, than by the will of a single priest or of his college alone, whose judgment would be perverted more quickly by love or hatred, or by looking to their own advantage, than that of the whole body of the faithful, to which it is always possible to appeal. Although, as we have said, the carrying out of such a sentence must be done by the priest, so far as the divine power is invoked in this age to inflict some punishment on the criminal in this age, which could not be inflicted by human power, such as the harassing of a demon. And because he is likewise judged to punishment for the state of the future age, and because he is deprived of the suffrages of the Church, which God perhaps instituted to be done by the action of the priest alone. Moreover, if it were lawful for any bishop or elder alone, or with his college of clergy alone, to excommunicate anyone without the consent of the whole body of the faithful, it would follow from this that priests or their college could take away all kingdoms and principalities from their rulers. For if any prince were excommunicated, the multitude subject to him would also be excommunicated if they wished to obey the excommunicated prince, and thus the power of every prince would be at the mercy of priests. The teacher of the Gentiles held the opposite, in Romans 13 and 1 Timothy 6, and Augustine in the same place in the gloss, as we brought forward in part 5 of this book, parts 7 and 8. The objections which might seem to be brought against this determination will be easily repelled from what is to be said in sections 9, 10, 14, and 17 of this book. There is again a certain authority of priests, by which bread and wine are changed into the blessed body of Christ at the priest's prayer, after he has spoken certain words. This authority is a character of the soul, as is that of the keys, and it is called the power of consecrating the sacrament of the Eucharist. Some theologians say that this is from the same character as the power of the keys, of which we have spoken before. Others say that it is from a different character, given at another time and with other words of Christ, given to the apostles, as in what he brought forward to the apostles in Matthew 26, Mark 14, and Luke 22, when he said to them: "This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me; do this," that is, have the power of doing this. However the truth stands regarding this difference, it does not affect the present consideration, for we think we have recalled enough for our purpose about the authorities or powers conferred by Christ on the elders or bishops, which can be gathered from holy Scripture. Moreover, as we are about to make a summary, we gather up what has been said about the power or authority of the priestly keys handed on by Christ to the apostles, and we say that in a sinner who truly repents, that is, one who grieves for the sin he has committed, God alone works certain things even without any preceding ministry of a priest: namely the enlightening of the mind, the cleansing of the guilt or stain of sin, and the remission of eternal damnation. But there are other things which God works in the same sinner not by himself alone, but through the ministry of a priest, such as showing in the face of the Church who is regarded in this age as loosed or bound from sins, and who is to be bound or loosed in another, that is, whose sins God has retained or remitted. Moreover, there is also this which God works in the sinner through the ministry of the priest: namely the commutation of the punishment of purgatory owed by the sinner for the state of the future age into some temporal satisfaction, or one of this age. For he relaxes this punishment in part or in whole, according to the satisfactions enjoined and the condition of the penitent, all of which must be done by the priest with the key of power, according to discretion. So also through the priest the contumacious are shut out from communion in the sacraments, and those who come to their senses are admitted, as was said near the end of the preceding chapter. This was the opinion of the Master in book 4, distinction 18, chapter 8, when he said: "According to these modes of binding and loosing, it is true what is said: 'Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.' For sometimes those who are not with God show the loosed or bound (namely the elders), and sometimes they bind or loose the unworthy with the penalty of satisfaction, and admit the unworthy to the sacraments and keep away those who are worthy. But it must be understood in regard to those whose merits require that they be loosed or bound. Therefore whomever they loose or bind, applying the key of discernment to the merits of the guilty, are loosed or bound in heaven, that is, with God, because the sentence of the priest, so pronounced, is approved and confirmed by the divine judgment." And the Master then said, as if summing up: "Behold what and how great is the use of the apostolic keys." To make this even clearer, we shall bring forward an example or comparison which is quite familiar, and which also seems much to fit the words and sentence of Christ and of the saints whose authorities we brought forward earlier, and especially of Ambrose. For he says that "the word of God forgives sins; the priest indeed performs his office, but exercises no right of power. Let us say, then, that the priest, as the keeper of the keys of the heavenly judge, in a proportional way frees the sinner, as the keeper of the keys of the worldly judge does. For just as by the word or sentence of a judge of this age (that is, one who rules) a guilty man is condemned or absolved from civil guilt and punishment, so by the divine word someone is simply loosed or bound from guilt and from the debt of condemnation or punishment for the state of the future age. And just as by the action of the keeper of the keys of the worldly prince no one is loosed or condemned from civil guilt or punishment, yet by his action, by which he locks or opens the prison, the guilty man is shown to be loosed or condemned, so, as it were by the action of the priest, no one is loosed or bound from guilt and from the debt of eternal damnation, but it is shown in the face of the Church who is regarded by God as loosed or bound, when he receives the priest's blessing and is admitted to communion in the sacraments," as we said near the end of the preceding chapter. Therefore, just as the keeper of the keys of the worldly judge, by opening or locking the prison, performs his office, yet does not exercise any right of judicial power to absolve or condemn, since even if he actually opened the prison for a guilty man who had not been absolved by the judge, and announced to the people with his voice that he was absolved, the guilty man would not on that account be loosed from civil punishment or guilt; and conversely, if he refused to open the prison and announced by his word that he was not absolved but condemned, when the judge had truly absolved him by his sentence, this man would not on that account be a debtor of civil guilt or punishment; so in a proportional way the priest, as keeper of the keys of the heavenly judge, performs his office by the verbal pronouncement of absolution, binding, or cursing. But if the priest himself, through ignorance or deception, or both, were to pronounce absolved or to be absolved those who are truly to be condemned by the supreme judge, or who are already condemned, or conversely, they would not on that account be the first loosed and the second condemned, because he had not applied the key or keys with discretion to the merits of the guilty. And therefore he "performs his office," as Ambrose said. Yet he exercises no right of power, since sometimes priests in the face of the Church pronounce bound for the future age those who are truly loosed or to be loosed before God, and conversely, as we said above on the authority of the saints and of the Master, in book 4, distinction 18, chapter 8. Therefore the priest does not exercise the rights of power. For in this way the divine justice and promise could sometimes perish. Therefore he alone exercises the rights of power in these matters, and is the judge who has coercive power, who alone can neither be deceived about human thoughts and actions. For "all things are naked and open to his eyes," Hebrews 4, and he alone wills nothing perversely. "You are just, O Lord, and all your judgments are just, and all your ways are mercy, and truth, and judgment," Tobit 3. Therefore he alone is such a judge. Hence James 4: "There is one lawgiver and judge, who can destroy and deliver." James did not say this of himself or of any one of the apostles, although he was one of those three "who seemed to be pillars of the Church," as the Apostle said to the Galatians, chapter 2. Christ, however, willed that such sentences, pronounced or to be pronounced by him in the other age, should be announced by priests in a certain judgment of the first signification, as it were a prognostic, so that by this sinners in this world may be terrified and called back from their sins and crimes to repentance, for which the office of priests is required and is of great value. In the same way, if a physician of bodily health, to whom the power of teaching and practising according to the art of medicine has been given, by the appointment of a human judge or lawgiver were to announce to the people a judgment, according to medical knowledge, about who would be healthy or about to die in the future, so that by this men might lead a sober life and be called back from intemperance, for the sake of preserving or acquiring bodily health, and were also to set out precepts or instructions of this kind, the physician would certainly command these things to be observed, and would judge those who observe them to be healthy in the future, and those who transgress them to be sick or about to die. Yet he would not principally heal or make sick them, but the action of human nature would do this, though the physician would still provide some ministry. Nor again could the physician, by his own authority, compel the healthy or the sick to do such things, however much they contribute to bodily health; he could only exhort, teach, and terrify by his judgment of the first signification, a prognostic, announcing health to them from the observance of certain things, but death or sickness from the transgression of such things. In the same proportional way, the physician of souls, namely the priest, judges and exhorts about those things which lead to the eternal health of the soul, or to eternal death or temporal punishment for the state of the future age. Yet he cannot, and must not, in this age, bar anyone from these things by a coercive judgment, as we proved by the authority of the Apostle and of Ambrose in 1 Corinthians 1, and above, where with these we brought forward the explicit opinion of Chrysostom in part 6 of section 5 of this book. For this reason the priest, according to his office, must not be likened by analogy to a judge of the third signification, but to one of the first, namely one having the authority of teaching or acting, as a physician has, yet not insofar as he has coercive power. For Christ called himself a physician, not a ruler. Where, in Luke 5, speaking of himself, he said: "Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill," and he did not say that they need a judge. For he had not come into the world to exercise a coercive judgment over the contentious, as we brought forward from Luke 12 in part 8 of section 4 of this book. But he will judge the living and the dead by such a judgment on that day, of which the Apostle spoke in the last chapter of 2 Timothy: "Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day." For then he will inflict punishments by coercive judgment on those who have transgressed the law given by him immediately in this age. Therefore Christ expressly said to Peter: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," and he did not say, "I will give you the judgment of the kingdom of heaven." And hence we have already said that neither the keeper of the keys of the worldly judge nor of the heavenly one has coercive judgment, which we called of the third signification, because neither of them exercises the rights of such power, as Ambrose openly said of the priest, and as the authority of the other saints has sufficiently shown. So let this be settled in this way concerning the authority of priests or bishops, and the power of the apostolic keys conferred on them by Christ.

units.la: CAP. VIII. Qua divisione actuum humanorum, & qualiter referantur ad humanam legem, & iudicem seculi huius.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the division of human acts, how they relate to human law, and the judge of this age.

units.la: Quoniam autem omne iudicium coactiuum est de humanis actibus voluntariis secundum aliquam legem aut consuetudinem, & de his quidem, vel in quantum ad finem huius seculi ordinabilibus vitæ mundanæ scilicet sufficientiam, aut quantum ad finem venturi seculi, quem vitam seu gloriam vocamus æternam, vt amplius appareat distinctio iudicum seu iudicare debentium, & secundum quas leges, quo iudicio, & qualiter de ipsorum actuum differentiis aliqualiter disseramus. Ad priorum etenim dubitatorum solutionem horum determinatio non parum proficiet. Dicamus igitur, quod actum humanorum prouenientium per cognitionem & desiderium, quidam proueniunt absque mentis imperio, alii vero per humanæ mentis imperium. Primo quidem sunt cognitiones, desideria, & dilectiones à nobis & in nobis euenientes absque imperio seu præcepto intellectus aut appetitus de ipsis facto, quales sunt cognitiones & affectiones ad quas eximus dum excitamur à somno vel alitet factæ in nobis absque nostræ mentis imperio. His autem assequuntur cognitiones, consensus, & affectiones aliquae de prioribus actibus continuandis aut quibusdam inquirendis & comprehendendis, vt in actione quae per remenorationem fit, & haec sunt & dicuntur mentis imperia seu praecepta, tum quia nostro imperio fiunt seu eliciuntur, aut ipsis alia quaedam, veluti prosecutiones & fugae.
units.tr: Since every coercive judgment concerns voluntary human acts according to some law or custom, and since these acts are ordered either to the end of this age, namely the sufficiency of worldly life, or to the end of the age to come, which we call eternal life or glory, I shall now treat, in some detail, the distinction between judges, or those who ought to judge, and the laws, the kind of judgment and the manner in which these acts differ. The settling of these points will go a long way toward resolving the earlier doubts. Let us say, then, that human acts arising through knowledge and desire sometimes arise without the command of the mind and sometimes through the command of the human mind. First come the cognitions, desires and loves that occur from us and in us without any command or precept of intellect or appetite concerning them, such as the cognitions and affections we experience when we are roused from sleep, or that otherwise arise in us without the command of our mind. Following these come certain cognitions, consents and affections about continuing earlier acts, or about seeking out and grasping certain things, as in an act performed by recollection. These are, and are called, commands of the mind or precepts, both because they are made or elicited by our command, and because certain other things, such as pursuits and flights, follow upon them.

units.la: Est autem Imperatorum actuum & non Imperatorum differentia, ex eo quod pridem diximus, quoniam non Imperatorum actuum non omnino est in nobis libertas seu imperium vt fiant aut non. Imperatorum vero secundum Christianam religionem potestas in nobis est. Et dixi primorum actuum non omnino potestatem in nobis, quoniam non est in potestate nostra, totaliter horum euentum prohibere, quamuis per secundos actus qui dicuntur imperia, & his consequentes, sic animam disponere possimus, vt non facile sit factiua vel receptiua primorum, videlicet cum horum oppositos fuerit assuetus sibi quisque praecipere, diligere, aut considerare. Imperatorum vero actuum quaedam sunt & dicuntur immanentes, & alii transeuntes. Immanentes autem sunt & dicuntur imperatae cognitiones, affectiones, & horum habitus facti ab humana mente, eo quod in subiectum aliud ab ipso faciente non transeunt. Transeuntes autem sunt & dicuntur omnes prosecutiones desideratorum, & ipsorum omissiones & motus facti per aliquod organorum corporis exteriorum, maxime secundum locum motorum. Rursum transeuntium actuum quidam sunt & fiunt absque nocumento vel iniuria singularis personae, collegii, vel communitatis alterius a faciente, veluti sunt omnium factibilium genera & pecuniarum datio, peregrinatio, & corporis proprii castigatio, verbere seu percussione aut alio quovis modo, & his similes reliqui. Alii vero transeuntium sunt & fiunt, cum opposita circunstantia, nocumento videlicet vel iniuria in alterum a faciente, quales sunt percussio, furtum, rapina, falsum testimonium, & reliqui plures secundum modos & species.
units.tr: There is a difference between acts commanded and acts not commanded, arising from what we said before: over acts not commanded we have no complete freedom or power to make them happen or not happen. Over commanded acts, according to the Christian religion, we do have power. I said that we have no complete power over the first kind of acts, because it is not in our power to prevent their occurrence altogether. Yet through the second kind of acts, which are called commands, and those that follow from them, we can so dispose the soul that it is not easy for it to produce or receive the first kind, provided that a person has been accustomed to command, love or consider the opposites of these. Commanded acts are of two kinds: some are called immanent and others transitive. Immanent acts are cognitions, affections and the habits of these produced by the human mind, and they are called commanded because they do not pass over into any subject other than the one producing them. Transitive acts are all the pursuits of desired things, their omissions, and the motions produced through some of the external organs of the body, above all those that move from place to place. Again, among transitive acts, some occur without harm or injury to any individual person, college or community other than the agent. Such are all kinds of making things, the giving of money, travel, and the chastising of one's own body by beating, striking or any other means, and others like them. Others among the transitive acts occur with the opposite circumstance, namely with harm or injury to another than the agent, such as striking, theft, robbery, false witness, and many more according to their modes and kinds.

units.la: Omnium autem praedictorum actuum ab humana mente scilicet provenientium, Imperatorum maxime, adinuentae sunt quaedam regulae, seu mensurae, vel habitus, quibus conuenienti modo ac debite fiant & proveniant tam pro sufficienti vita huius seculi quam venturi consequendis ex his. Verum istorum habituum seu regularum quaedam sunt, secundum quas docentur & regulantur actus humanae mentis, tam immanentes quam transeuntes in fieri vel omitti absque poena vel praemio operanti vel omittenti distribuentis ab alio per potentiam coactiuam, quales quidem sunt plurimae disciplinae operatiuae, actiuae atque factiuae. Aliae vero dictarum regularum sunt secundum quas praecipiuntur actus huiusmodi fieri vel omitti sub poena vel praemio operantibus aut omittentibus distribuendo per alterius potentiam coactiuam. Harum autem rursum coactiuarum quaedam sunt secundum quas afficiuntur ipsarum obseruatores aut transgressores poena vel praemio in statu & pro statu vitae praesentis, quales sunt omnes leges & humanae consuetudines ciuiles. Aliae vero harum sunt secundum quas pro solo statu & in statu futuri seculi puniuntur aut premiantur operatores. Quales sunt diuinae leges vt plurimum, quae communi nomine sacra vocantur, inter quas vt diximus sexto prima, ea quae Christianorum sola continet veritatem & sufficientiam, pro futuro seculo sperandorum. Est igitur pro vita seu viuere sufficienti huius seculi posita regula humanorum actuum Imperatorum transeuntium fieri possibilium ad commodum vel incommodum, ius aut iniuriam alterius a faciente praeceptina, & transgressorum coactiua supplicio siue poena pro statu praesentis seculi tantum. Quam legem humanam communi nomine diximus in decimo prima. Cuius etiam finalem necessitatem, & causam agentem assignaiimus vndecimo & 12. & 13. prima. Pro vita vero seu viuere in hoc seculo, pro statu tamen futuri seculi tradita & posita est lex per Christum. Quae siquidem lex regula est humanorum actuum Imperatorum, & qui sunt in potestate actiua nostrae mentis, tam immanentium quam transeuntium, secundum quod fieri possunt vel omitti, debite aut indebite in hoc seculo, pro statu tamen siue sine futuri seculi coactiua & distributiua poenae vel praemii, & horum illatiua in futuro seculo non in isto secundum merita vel demerita obseruatorum aut transgressorum illius in vita praesenti. Verum quia leges hae coactiuae tam diuinae quam humanae anima carent & mouente principio iudicatiuo & executiuo indiguerunt habere subiectum seu principium aliquod animatum, quod quidem secundum ipsas humanos actus praecipiat, reguler, seu iudicet, ac etiam exequetur iudicata, & ipsarum arceat transgressores. Hoc aut subiectum aut principium iudex vocatur, quem diximus secundum tertiam significationem secundo huius. Vnde quarto Ethicorum, tractatu de iustitia. Est enim iudex veluti iustum animatum. Secundum humanas ergo leges oportet habere iudicem, qualem iam diximus autoritatem habentem iudicandi tertiae significationis iudicio, de contentiosis hominum actibus exequendi iudicata, & legis transgressorem quemlibet per coactiuam arcendi potentiam. Hic enim index Dei minister est, & vindex in iram, & qui malum agit, vt dixit Apostolus ad Rom. 13. & a Deo missus ad hoc, vt dicitur primae Petri. 2. & dixit Apostolus, qui malum agit, quicunque scilicet fuerit ille, indifferenter hoc intelligens de omnibus. Et ideo cum presbyteri seu episcopi, generaliterque omnes templorum ministri communi nomine vocati clerici, possint committendo vel omittendo malum agere & agunt ipsorum aliqui, vtinam non plurimi quandoque de facto in nocumentum & iniuriam alterius. Sunt & ipsi suppositi vindicta seu iurisdictioni iudicum, quorum est coactiua potentia puniendi legum humanarum transgressores. Quod etiam aperte dixit Apostolus ad Rom. 13. Vnde, omnis anima, inquit, subdita sit potestatibus sublimioribus, regibus, videlicet, principibus & tribunis, secundum sanctorum expositionem. Eadem nanque propria materia debet eiusdem agentis actionem suscipere, quod natum & ordinatum est in illam agere propter finem ad quam apta est, vt appareat in secundo Physica. Sic enim, vt ibidem dicitur, agitur vnumquodque sicut natum est agi, & econuerso. Nunc autem legis transgressor materia est siue subiectum, in quod natus est & ordinatus agere iudex seu principans iustificationem propter æqualitatem siue proportionem faciendam ad pacem seu tranquillitatem & connidum siue congregationem hominum conseruandam, demum propter humanæ vitæ sufficientiam. Et propterea vbicunque talis materia seu subiectum reperiatur in prouincia subiecta iudici, debet illam iustificare. Cum igitur sacerdos possit esse propria seu per se materia talis, verbi gratia, legis humanæ transgressor, debet illius subesse iudicio. Esse enim sacerdotem vel non sacerdotem, accidit transgressori secundum comparationem ad iudicem, sicut esse agricolam aut domificatorem, quemadmodum sanabili aut ægrotabili, musicum aut non musicum esse in comparatione ad medicum. Non enim tollitur id quod est per se, neque variatur per id quod accidit, alioquin essent infinitæ iudicum species atque medicorum. Debet ergo sacerdos seu episcopus quilibet legis humanæ transgressor iustificari & arceri per iudicem, cuius est in hoc seculo transgressorum humanæ legis coactiua potestas. Hic autem est seculi princeps inquantum huiusmodi non presbyter aut episcopus, vt demonstratum est quarto huius & quinto, ergo per principem presbyteros seu episcopos omnes humanæ legis transgressores oportet arceri. Nec solum velut secularis ex transgressione debet plecti sacerdos, seu alter spiritualis minister, sed tanto amplius quanto grauius & indecentius peccat, quoniam magis sciens & eligens, qui præcepta fugiendarum & agendorum amplius nosse debet. Et rursum, quoniam turpius peccatum est debentis docere quam docent. Hoc autem sustinet presbyteri peccatum ad eum qui non presbyteri, peccat igitur grauius sacerdos, & eo amplius puniendus.
