Nec recipi debet instantis termo, qui dicat iniurias verbales, reales, aut personales, & reliqua humana lege prohibita, per sacerdotem in quenquam illata, spirituales fore actiones, & eo non pertinere ad seculi principem in sacerdotem talia vindicare.
units.tr: For all the aforesaid acts that arise from the human mind, and especially the commanded ones, certain rules, measures or habits have been devised, by which they may be done and arise in a fitting and proper manner, both for the sufficiency of this present life and for those things to be gained from them for the life to come. Now some of these habits or rules direct and govern the acts of the human mind, both immanent and transitive, in their doing or omission, without punishment or reward being dealt out to the one who acts or omits by another through coercive power. Such are the many disciplines that are operative, active and productive. Other rules of these kinds prescribe that acts of this sort be done or omitted under penalty or reward, dealt out to those who act or omit by the power of another with coercive force. Again, of these coercive rules, some are those by which their observers or transgressors are visited with penalty or reward in the state and for the state of the present life, such as all laws and human civil customs. Others are those by which doers are punished or rewarded solely for the state of the future age. Such are the divine laws, for the most part, which are commonly called sacred. Among these, as we said, the sixth of the first set out what alone contains the truth and sufficiency of the Christians for the age to come. So for the sufficiency of life, or of living, in this present age, the rule of human commanded acts is established: those transitive acts which can be done, for the advantage or disadvantage, right or wrong, of another than the agent, are prescribed, and those who transgress are subjected to coercive punishment or penalty for the state of the present age only. We called this human law in general terms in the tenth of the first. Its final necessity and efficient cause we set out in the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth of the first. For life, or living, in this age, but with a view to the state of the age to come, the law was handed down and established by Christ. This law is indeed the rule of commanded human acts, and of those which lie within the active power of our mind, both immanent and transitive, insofar as they can be done or left undone, rightly or wrongly, in this age, yet for the state, or with a view to the state, of the age to come, with coercive and distributive penalty or reward, and with the bringing of these things in the future age, not in this one, according to the merits or demerits of those who observe or transgress it in the present life. But because these coercive laws, both divine and human, lack a soul, they needed a living subject or principle to move them, one which would prescribe, regulate or judge human acts according to these laws, and would also carry out the judgments and keep transgressors away from them. This subject or principle is called the judge, whom we described, in the second sense of the second chapter, as of the third signification. Hence in the fourth book of the Ethics, the treatise on justice: For the judge is as it were the just made living. Therefore, according to human laws, there must be a judge of the kind we have already described, who has authority to judge in the third sense of judgment, to execute judgments concerning the contentious acts of men, and by coercive power to restrain any transgressor of the law. For this judge is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath, to him who does evil, as the Apostle said to the Romans, chapter 13, and sent by God for this purpose, as stated in 1 Peter 2. And the Apostle said to him who does evil, whoever he may be, understanding this indifferently of all. And so, since presbyters or bishops, and generally all ministers of the temples, commonly called clergy, can do evil by committing or omitting, and some of them do, would that there were not many who sometimes do so in fact, to the harm and injury of another, they too are subject to the vengeance or jurisdiction of judges, whose coercive power is to punish transgressors of human laws. The Apostle also said this plainly in Romans 13: Let every soul, he says, be subject to the higher powers, namely kings, princes and tribunes, according to the exposition of the saints. For the same proper matter must receive the action of the same agent, which is naturally and ordinately made to act upon it for the end to which it is suited, as appears in the second book of the Physics. For, as is said there, each thing is acted upon as it is naturally made to be acted upon, and conversely. Now the transgressor of the law is the matter or subject upon which the judge or ruler is naturally and ordinately made to act, in order to bring about justification for the sake of equality or proportion, for the preservation of peace or tranquillity and of the community or gathering of men, and finally for the sufficiency of human life. Therefore wherever such matter or subject is found within the province subject to the judge, he ought to justify it. Since, then, a priest can be such matter in himself, for example as a transgressor of human law, he must be subject to that judgment. For being a priest or not being a priest is an accident of the transgressor in relation to the judge, just as being a farmer or a builder, or being able to be healed or sick, or being a musician or not, is in relation to the physician. For what is essential is not removed by what is accidental, nor varied by it; otherwise there would be infinite kinds of judges and physicians. Therefore every priest or bishop who transgresses human law ought to be justified and restrained by the judge, whose office in this age is the coercive power over transgressors of human law. Now this judge is the prince of this age, insofar as he is not a presbyter or bishop, as has been shown in the fourth and fifth of this work. Therefore all presbyters or bishops who transgress human law must be restrained through the prince. Nor should a priest, or any other spiritual minister, be punished merely as a secular person for a transgression, but all the more, insofar as he sins more gravely and more unbecomingly, since he who knows and chooses more ought to know the precepts of what is to be avoided and done more fully. And again, since the sin of one who ought to teach is more shameful than that of those who are taught. Now a presbyter's sin is of this kind compared with one who is not a presbyter; therefore a priest sins more gravely and is to be punished all the more. Nor should we accept the objection of those who say that injuries done by a priest to anyone, whether verbal, real or personal, and other things forbidden by human law, are spiritual actions, and therefore do not belong to the prince of this age to avenge against a priest.

units.la: Quoniam huiusmodi lege prohibita, vt quæ adulterii, percussionis, homicidij, furti, rapinæ, ignominiæ, detractionis, proditionis, fraudis, hæresis, & reliquorum similium per sacerdotem commissa carnalia sunt & temporalia, vt notissimum est experientia, & supra id monstrauimus secundo huius per Apostolum prima ad Corinth. tertio, & ad Rom. 15. Et eo etiam carnaliores atque temporaliores iudicandæ magis quanto secundum ipsa presbyter aut episcopus, grauius & turpius peccat his quos a talibus renocare debet, delinquendi præbens occasionem & facilitatem sui exemplo peruerso. Subest igitur & subesse debet sacerdos quilibet seu episcopus iurisdictioni principum in his quæ præcepta sunt humana lege seruari, quemadmodum cæteri seculares. Nec est exemptus ipse a talium iudicio coactiuo, nec quenquam alium autoritate sua eximere potest, quod demonstro per additionem ad ea quæ dicta sunt 17. prima, deducendo contradicentem ad inconueniens maximum. Quoniam si Romanus episcopus, aut alter quiuis presbyter sic esset exemptus, vt coactiuo principantium iudicio non subesset, sed esset ipse index huiusmodi absque humani legislatoris autoritate, posset que omnes spirituales ministros, quos clericos vocant communi nomine, a principum iurisdictione separare, sibique subiicere, quemadmodum faciunt modernis temporibus Romani pontifices, sequitur per necessitatem, principantium secularium iurisdictionem quasi totaliter annullari, quod reputo graue inconueniens, & omnibus principibus & Communitatibus importandum: quoniam Christiana religio neminem priuat iure suo, vt ex Ambrosio supra illud ad Titum secundo, Admone illos subditos esse principibus & potestatibus, induximus quinto huius. Inconuenientis autem istius consequentiam, sic ostendo, quoniam lege diuina prohibitum non reperitur, quinimo concessum presbyterum aut episcopum esse, qui habet vxorem, præsertim si non vna plures habuerit, vt habitum est prima ad Timoth. 3. Quod autem humana lege seu constitutione statum est eadem autoritate reuocari potest inquantum huiusmodi. Poterit igitur Romanus episcopus, qui se legislatorem facit, aut de suæ plenitudine potestatis, si quis tamen hanc ipsum concedat habere, presbyteris omnibus, diaconis, & subdiaconis vxores concedere: Nec solum his, verum etiam aliis non ordinatis sacerdotio vel diaconatu, aut aliter consecratis, quos clericos tonsura simplici vocant: quinimo & his decentius, quod & de facto Bonifacius octauus fecisse videtur, vt sibi secularem potentiam adaugeret. Omnes enim qui virginem duxerant vxorem & vnicam volentes, ascripsit cœtui clericorum, & per suas ordinationes, quas Decretales appellant, ascribi decreuit, neque adhuc his clausi limitibus, laicos quosdam, quos in Italia Fratres gaudentes, alibi vero Begines appellant, similiter ab humanis legibus ciuilibus rite latis exemptos fecerunt. Sic quoque fratres templariorum hospitaliorum, & reliquos plures huiusmodi ordines, similiter & eos qui de alto passu, sicetiam de cæteris pro libito pari ratione facere possunt. Quod si omnes huiusmodi hoc ipso exempti sunt a principantium iurisdictione secundum Decretales ipsorum (quæ etiam talibus sic exemptis immunitates quasdam onerum publicorum seu ciuilium tribuunt) verisimile valde videtur maiorem hominum multitudinem ad horum collegium declinare, præcipue cum ad hos tam literatos quam illiteratos indifferenter assumant. Est enim quilibet pronus ad commodum proprium prosequendum, & incommodum fugiendum. Maiori vero multitudine seu pluralitate ad clericorum collegium declinante, principantium iurisdictio, & coactiua potestas inualida remanebit, quod est grauissimum inconueniens, & politiæ corruptiuum. Qui enim gaudet honoribus & ciuilibus commodis, vt pace ac tutela legislatoris humani ab oneribus & iurisdictione, non debet eximi absq; determinatione legislatoris eiusdem. Propter quod siquidem cuitandum, fateri oportet secundum veritatem, iurisdictionem in episcopos seu presbyteros & clericos omnes, legislatoris auctoritate principantem habere, ne principatuum etiam pluralitate inordinata politiam solui contingat, quemadmodum determinatum est 17. prime. Numerum quoque certum ipsorum in subiecta sibi prouincia, principantem determinare debere, sicuti & personarum cuiuscuis alterius politiae partis: ne sua excrescentia indebita, potestati coactiuae principantium resistere valeant, aut aliter politiae turbationem inferre, vel sua insolentia & actio necessariorum operum ciuitatem aut regnum priuare commodo, quemadmodum ex secundo quinti Politicae, induximus 15. prime. Sic igitur humana lege ac iudice, qui tertiae significationis regulari habent, actus humani transeuntes in commodum vel incommodum, ius aut iniuriam alterius facientes. Cui siquidem coactiuae iurisdictioni subesse debent omnes seculares & clerici. Sunt autem & alii iudices quidam secundum humanas leges, qui primae significationis iudices dicti sunt, aut secundae, vt ipsarum doctores, auctoritate tamen coactiua carentes, quos in vnica quamuis communitate etiam non subordinatos inuicem, nihil prohibet esse plures.
units.tr: Since such things are forbidden by human law, such as adultery, assault, murder, theft, robbery, insult, slander, treason, fraud, heresy, and the like, when a priest commits them, they are carnal and temporal, as experience makes very plain, and as we showed above in the second chapter of this book through the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 3 and Romans 15. They must therefore be judged all the more carnal and temporal, since a presbyter or bishop, by his own perverse example, sins more gravely and shamefully than those whom he ought to call back from such things, and gives them an occasion and an easy path to sin. Every priest or bishop is therefore, and ought to be, subject to the jurisdiction of princes in those matters that human law requires to be observed, just as other laymen are. Nor is he exempt from the coercive judgment of such a law, and he cannot exempt anyone else by his own authority. I prove this by adding to what was said in the seventeenth [chapter] of the first [book], and by reducing the objector to a very great absurdity. For if the Roman bishop, or any other presbyter, were so exempt that he was not subject to the coercive judgment of rulers, but were himself the judge of such matters without the authority of the human lawgiver, he could separate all the spiritual ministers, whom they commonly call clerics, from the jurisdiction of princes and subject them to himself, as the Roman pontiffs do in modern times. It would follow of necessity that the jurisdiction of secular rulers was almost wholly annulled. I judge this a grave absurdity, one that must be borne by all princes and communities. For the Christian religion deprives no one of his right, as we drew from Ambrose on the words of Titus 2, Remind them to be subject to princes and powers, in the fifth [chapter] of this book. I show the consequence of this absurdity as follows. It is not found forbidden by divine law; rather, it is permitted for a presbyter or bishop to have a wife, especially if he has not had only one, as was shown in 1 Timothy 3. What has been established by human law or constitution can be revoked by the same authority, insofar as it is such. The Roman bishop, who makes himself a lawgiver, or who (if anyone grants that he has it) claims it from the fullness of his power, could therefore grant wives to all presbyters, deacons and subdeacons. Nor would this be limited to them; he could extend it to others who are not ordained to the priesthood or the diaconate, or otherwise consecrated, whom they call clerics with simple tonsure. Indeed, with more propriety he could do so for these, as Boniface VIII seems in fact to have done, in order to increase his secular power. For he enrolled among the body of clerics all who had taken a virgin as wife, and only one, and by his ordinances, which they call Decretals, he decreed that they be enrolled. Nor did he stop at these limits: he likewise made exempt from human civil laws, properly enacted, certain laymen whom they call Fratres gaudentes in Italy and Begines elsewhere. In the same way the Knights Templar, the Hospitallers, and many other orders of this kind, and those of the high step, and others, could be made exempt at pleasure by the same reasoning. But if all such persons are by this very fact exempt from the jurisdiction of rulers, according to their Decretals (which also grant such exempt persons certain immunities from public or civil burdens), it seems very likely that a larger multitude of men would turn aside to join these groups, especially since they admit both the learned and the unlearned to them without distinction. For everyone is inclined to pursue his own advantage and to flee inconvenience. If a greater multitude or plurality should turn aside to the college of clerics, the jurisdiction and coercive power of rulers would remain invalid. This is a most grave absurdity and one that corrupts the commonwealth. For whoever enjoys honours and civil advantages, so as to be free of burdens and jurisdiction under the protection and peace of the human lawgiver, ought not to be exempted without a determination by that same lawgiver. For this reason, if such a thing is to be avoided, we must confess according to the truth that the jurisdiction over bishops, presbyters and all clerics belongs to the authority of the lawgiver, which rules them, lest the commonwealth be dissolved even by an immoderate plurality of principalities, as was determined in the seventeenth [chapter] of the first [book]. The ruler ought also to determine a fixed number of them in the province subject to him, just as he does for persons of any other part of the commonwealth, lest by their undue increase they be able to resist the coercive power of rulers, or otherwise bring disturbance to the commonwealth, or by their insolence and neglect of necessary work deprive the city or kingdom of its benefit, as we drew from the second [chapter] of the fifth [book] of the Politics, in the fifteenth [chapter] of the first [book]. Thus, by human law and by a judge who holds the regular office of the third signification, acts of men that pass over into advantage or disadvantage, that make right or wrong for another, are subject to that coercive jurisdiction, to which all laymen and clerics ought to be subject. There are also certain other judges under human laws, who are called judges of the first signification, or of the second, such as their teachers, yet lacking coercive authority. Nothing prevents there being several of these, even within a single community, not subordinated to one another.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De humanorum actuum relatione ad legem diuinam, & iudicem alterius seculi, Christum videlicet, qualiter etiam ad doctorem legis eiusdem, episcopum siue sacerdotem in hoc seculo comparentur.
units.tr: On the relation of human actions to the divine law and to the judge of the other age, namely Christ; and likewise how they stand toward the teacher of that law, the bishop or priest in this age.

units.la: SEcundum hanc igitur rationem, iudex etiam quidam est, coactiuam habens auctoritatem transgressorum secundum legem diuinam, quam etiam humanorum actuum aliquorum tam immanentium quam transeuntium coactiuam regulam diximus. Hic autem vnicus est, Christus scilicet, nullus alius. Vnde Iacobi quarto: Vnus est legislator & iudex, qui potest perdere & liberare. Verum huius iudicis coactiua potestas in quenquam non exercetur in hoc seculo ad poenam seu supplicium aut praemium distribuenda transgressoribus aut obseruatoribus legislatae per ipsum immediate, quam euangelicam persepe diximus. Voluit enim sui misericordia Christus, vsque ad extremum cuiusque periodum cocedere mereri, & de commissis in ipsius legem poenitere posse, sicut etiam ex sacrae scripturae auctoritatibus in sequentibus ostendetur. Est alius secundum euangelicam scripturam iudex, qui primae significationis proportionaliter humanae legi, sacerdos scilicet, qui doctor est in hoc seculo diuinae legis, & agendorum aut fugiendorum quae sunt ad vitam aeternam consequendam, & poenam declinandam secundum ipsam praeceptorum. Non tamen habens coactiuam potentiam in hoc seculo arcendi quenquam ad praeceptorum secundum ipsam obseruationem. Frustra enim ad haec quenquam cogeret, quoniam obseruatori talium coacto nihil ipsa proficerent ad aeternam salutem, quemadmodum per Chrysostomum, quinimo per Apostolum euidenter ostendimus quinto huius. Ideoq; iudex hic conuenienter assimilatur medico, cui data est auctoritas docendi atq; praecipiendi, & pronosticandi seu iudicandi de his quae sunt vtilia fieri vel omitti, ad corporalem sanitatem consequendam, & mortem aut aegritudinem declinandam. Propter quod etiam Christus in statu & pro statu vitae praesentis vocauit se medicum, non principem atq; iudicem. Vnde Lucae quinto, & supra induximus cap. precedente, de se loquens ad Pharisaeos inquit: Non egent medico qui sani sunt, sed qui male habent. Non enim ordinauit Christus arceri quenquam ad legislatae per ipsum obseruationem in hoc seculo. Et propterea nec iudicem coactiuam habentem potentiam huius legis transgressores arcendi statuit in eodem. Vnde attendendum quod Euangelica lex potest dupliciter comparari ad homines, super quos est lata per Christum, vno quidem modo ad ipsos in statu & pro statu vitae praesentis. Et vt sic rationem habet magis doctrinae speculatiuae aut operatiuae vel vtriusque, quantum ad diuersas sui partes, quam legis dictae secundum propriam & vltimam significationem, quamuis lex possit dici secundum alias legis significationes, vt secundam & tertiam, de quibus diximus decimo primae. Et causa eius quod diximus est, quoniam lex secundum vltimam & proprie dictam significationem, dicitur de regula coactiua, id est secundum quam transgressor arcetur per potentiam coactiuam, traditam secundum ipsam iudicare debenti. Nunc autem per euangelicam doctrinam seu latorem legis ipsius, nemo cogi praecipitur in hoc seculo ad eorum obseruationem, quae in ipsa praecipiuntur in hoc seculo fieri vel omitti. Ideoque ad statum hominis in hoc & pro hoc seculo comparata, dici debet doctrina non lex, nisi secundum quem modum diximus. Et fuit haec Apostoli sententia 2. ad Timoth. 3. cum dixit: Omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata vtilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum, ad erudiendum in iustitia. Nunquam vero dixit Apostolus ad cogendum vel puniendum in hoc seculo. Vnde 2. ad Corinth. primo: Non quia dominamur fidei vestrae, sed adiutores sumus gaudii vestri, quia fide statis. Vbi Ambrosius, & supra induximus quinto huius, hec frequenter iterare piget: Et ne indignentur, (Corinthii scilicet) quasi de dominio, eo quod dixerat Apostolus, Parcens vobis non veni, subdit (Apostolus;) non ideo dico parcens, quia dominamur fidei vestrae, id est, quia dominium & coactio. coactionem patiatur fides vestra, qua voluntatis est, non necessitatis. Sed ideo dico, quia adiutores sumus, si vultis cooperari. Ecce adiutores, per doctrinam scilicet, & si vultis cooperari. Nam fide, qua per dilectionem operatur, status, non dominio. Alio vero modo comparari potest euangelica scriptura seu lex ad homines pro ipsorum statu in alio seculo, in quo solummodo non isto arcebuntur poena vel supplicio, qui eam transgressi fuerint in vita praesenti, & ut sic nomen legis propriissime dictae sortitur. Et qui secundum ipsam iudicabit tunc propriissime iudex, ut qui secundum tertiam significationem coactuam habens potentiam. Sacerdos autem seu episcopus quicunque sit ille, quoniam secundum hanc disponit & regulat homines solummodo in statu vitae praesentis, licet ad futuram vitam, nec sibi secundum ipsam arcere quenquam in hoc seculo concessum est ab illius immediato latore, Christo videlicet, idcirco nec proprie iudex dicitur, ut qui tertiae significationis, coactiuam habens potentiam, nec quenquam tali iudicio in hoc seculo poena reali aut personali potest nec debet arcere. Quo etiam vel proportionali modo doctor aliquis operativus ut medicus se habet ad iudicium sanitatis corporalis hominum absque coactiva cuiusquam potentia, quemadmodum diximus circa principium capituli huius.
units.tr: Accordingly, on this reasoning, there is also a judge who holds coercive authority over transgressors of the divine law, which we have said is also the coercive rule of certain human actions, both immanent and transeunt. This judge is one only, namely Christ, and no other. Hence James 4: There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to save. But the coercive power of this judge is not exercised in this age over anyone, to distribute punishment, penalty or reward to transgressors or observers of the law he has enacted immediately, which we have often called evangelical. For Christ, in his mercy, willed that until the very end of each person's course it should be possible to obtain pardon and to repent of what has been committed against his law, as will also be shown in what follows from the authority of Holy Scripture. According to the evangelical Scripture there is another judge, who in the first sense corresponds proportionally to human law: the priest, namely, who in this age is the teacher of the divine law, and of what is to be done or avoided in order to obtain eternal life and avoid punishment, according to its precepts. Yet he does not have coercive power in this age to compel anyone to observe those precepts. For he would be compelling people in vain, since such compelled observance would profit the one compelled nothing toward eternal salvation, as we have plainly shown through Chrysostom, indeed through the Apostle himself, in the fifth chapter of this book. Therefore this judge is fittingly compared to a physician, to whom authority is given to teach, to command, and to prognosticate or judge which things are useful to do or to omit in order to obtain bodily health and to avoid death or sickness. For this reason Christ also, in the state and for the state of the present life, called himself a physician rather than a prince and judge. Hence in Luke 5, and as we cited above in the preceding chapter, speaking of himself to the Pharisees, he says: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill. For Christ did not ordain that anyone be compelled to observe the law he enacted in this age. And therefore he did not appoint a judge holding coercive power to restrain the transgressors of this law in the same age. Hence we must note that the evangelical law can be related to the men over whom Christ enacted it in two ways. In one way, it is related to them in the state and for the state of the present life; and so it has the character more of speculative or practical doctrine, or of both, according to its various parts, than of law in its proper and ultimate sense, although law can be spoken of in other senses of the word, such as the second and third, of which we spoke in the tenth chapter of the first book. The reason for what we have said is this: law in its ultimate and strictly proper sense is spoken of as a coercive rule, that is, a rule by which the transgressor is restrained through coercive power, entrusted to the one who must judge according to it. But now, through the evangelical doctrine or its giver, no one is commanded to be compelled in this age to observe those things which are commanded to be done or omitted in this age. Therefore, with regard to the condition of man in and for this age, it ought to be called doctrine rather than law, except in the sense we have described. This was the sentiment of the Apostle in 2 Timothy 3, when he said: All Scripture, inspired by God, is profitable for teaching, for reproving, for correcting, for instructing in righteousness. But the Apostle never said "for compelling or punishing in this age." Hence 2 Corinthians 1: Not that we have dominion over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy, for you stand by faith. Where Ambrose, whom we cited above in the fifth chapter of this book, it is tiresome to repeat these things often, says: And lest they (the Corinthians, namely) be offended, as if it were about dominion, because the Apostle had said, "Sparing you I did not come," he adds (the Apostle): I do not say "sparing" because we have dominion over your faith, that is, because your faith should suffer dominion and coercion, which belongs to will, not to necessity. But I say this because we are helpers, if you wish to cooperate. Behold: helpers, namely through doctrine, and if you wish to cooperate. For faith, which works through love, stands, not through dominion. In another way, the evangelical Scripture or law can be related to men with respect to their state in another age, in which, and in which alone, those who have transgressed it in the present life will be restrained by punishment or penalty; and in this way it takes on the name of law in the most proper sense. And he who judges according to it then will be the judge in the most proper sense, as one who holds coercive power in the third sense. But the priest or bishop, whoever he may be, since he arranges and regulates men according to this law only in the state of the present life, although with a view to future life, has not been permitted by its immediate giver, namely Christ, to restrain anyone in this age according to it. Therefore he is not properly called a judge in the sense of the third meaning, holding coercive power, nor can or ought he to restrain anyone in this age by real or personal penalty through such judgment. In the same way, or proportionally, some practical teacher, such as a physician, stands in relation to the judgment of bodily health of men without any coercive power over anyone, as we said at the beginning of this chapter.

units.la: Haec quoque iuxta mentem Apostoli 1. ad Corinth. primo, fuit aperte sententia beati Ioannis Chrysostomi in suo libro Dialogorum, qui etiam de dignitate sacerdotali intitulatur libro 2. cap. 3. Eius vero seriem, quam induximus quinto huius, parte sexta, non reiteravimus hic propter abbreviationem sermonis, sed quod addit ad seriem supradictam subiunximus hic. Inquit ergo Chrysostomus: Propter hoc ergo multum opus est artis auxilio, ut persuadeatur hominibus, & se ultra cum aegrotant, sacerdotum praebeant medicina, nec solum hoc, sed & gratificentur curandi, sive enim aliquis resultet ligatus habet quippe in hoc liberam potestatem, malum suum deterius faciet, sive ea verba quae vice ferri erant pro futura respuerit, altus sibi de contemptu vulnus adiungit, sitque curationis occasio, morbi perniciosioris instrumentum. Non est enim qui curare possit inuitum. Et tunc aliquibus interpositis quae corrigendo, non tamen cogendo debet attendere pastor animarum, infra subiungit: Homo vero si a fide recta fuerit abductus, multum sacerdoti imminet exhortationis, industria & patientia, quia non potest errantem ad talem vi reducere, sed persuadere conabitur, ut ad fidem rectam reuertatur, a qua primitus corruit. Ecce qualiter sanctus iste separat iudicium sacerdotum a iudicio principantium, quoniam sacerdotum iudicium coactiuum nec est nec esse debet, causam quam persaepe diximus assignans. Primum quoniam coactiva potestas a legibus seu legumlatoribus est, quae sacerdotibus suo tempore vel prouincia concessa non erat. Secundo, quoniam si concessa foret eisdem, frustra itaque secundum illam agerent in subditos. Nam coactis nihil spirituale proficit ad aeternam salutem. Idemque dixit supra illud Lucae nono: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum. Seriem autem propter dictarum sufficientiam omisi, & propter abbreviationem. Haec rursum fuit aperte sententia beati Hilarii ad Constantium Imperatorem, in qua epistola inter caetera scripsit eidem: Deus cognitionem sui docuit potius quam exegit, & operationum caelestium admirationem praeceptis suis consilians autoritatem coactiuam confitendi se aspernatus est. Ecce quod vult Deus cognitionem sui & confessionem homines doceri, per fidem scilicet, cogi vero quenquam minime, sed hoc aspernatur. Eadem quoque parum infra repetit dicens: Non requirit Deus coactam confessionem. Rursumque infra eadem in persona omnium sacerdotum, inquit sic: Non possum nisi volentem recipere, nisi orantem audire, nisi profitentem signare. Non vult ergo Deus coactam sui confessionem, nec quenquam ad hoc trahi per violentam alicui actionem seu compulsionem. Unde idem contra Auxentium Mediolanensem episcopum, quem Arrianum reputauit. Et qui per armatam potentiam homines fateri quae suae opinionis erant circa, imo verius contra fidem catholicam, ut dicit, procurabat arceri, ipsumque arguens etiam si vera docuisset, sic ait: Ac primum miserari licet nostra aetatis laborem, & praesentium temporum stultas congemiscere opiniones, quibus patrocinari Deo, humana creduntur, & ad tuendam Christi ecclesiam, ambitione saeculari laborat. Rursus ad eundem ibidem: At nunc prob dolor diuinam fidem suffragia terrena commendant, inopsque virtutis sua Christus, dum ambitio nomini suo consiliatur, arguitur. Terret exilii & carceribus ecclesia, credique sibi cogit, qua exilii & carceribus credita est. Et loquitur de ecclesia pro collegio sacerdotum seu episcoporum, & reliquorum templi ministrorum, quos vocant clericos. Hoc etiam Ambrosius ad Valentinianum Imperatorem epistola secunda, quae intitulatur Ad plebem, sensit aperte, cum dixit: Dolere potero, flere potero, gemere potero aduersus arma, milites, Gothos quoque, lachryma mea arma mea sunt, talia enim munimenta sunt sacerdotis, aliter nec debeo nec possum resistere. Ecce quod non debet, esto quod posset, arma vel potentiam coactiuam in quenquam mouere aut moueri, iubere vel exhortari sacerdos, maxime contra Christi fideles, cuius oppositum contra documentum sacri canonis & sanctorum omnis iste mundus, de quibusdam sacerdotibus sentire potest. Secundum veritatem igitur & apertam intentionem Apostoli atque sanctorum, qui doctores ecclesiae seu fidei extiterunt, aliorum praecipui, nemo cogi praecipitur in hoc seculo poena vel supplicio ad legis euangelicae praecepta seruanda, per sacerdotem praecipue, nedum fidelis, verum etiam nec infidelis: propter quod huius legis ministri, episcopi seu presbyteri, nec quenquam iudicare possunt in hoc seculo, tertiae significationis iudicio, nec quenquam ad praeceptorum diuinae legis obseruationem, praesertim absque humani legislatoris autoritate, quoniam tale iudicium secundum legem diuinam in hoc seculo exerceri non debet, aut eius executio fieri, sed in futuro tantummodo. Unde Matth. 19. Iesu autem dixit illis, id est apostolis: Amen dico vobis, quod vos, qui secuti estis me in regeneratione, cum sederit filius hominis in sede maiestatis suae, sedebitis & vos super sedes duodecim, iudicantes tantes duodecim tribus Israel. Ecce quando sessuri erant apostoli cum Christo tanquam iudices tertiæ significationis, quoniam in alio seculo, non in isto. Vbi Glossa, in regeneratione, id est quando mortui resurgent incorrupti. Vnde secundum Gloss. duæ sunt regenerationes, Prima ex qua & spiritu sancto, secunda in resurrectione. Vnde sedebitis & vos, dicit Glossa secundum Aug. Forma serui qua iudicata est, (Christi scilicet, qui in hoc seculo iudicatus fuit coactiuo iudicio,) non iudicans, cum iudiciariam exercuerit potestatem (in resurrectione scilicet,) eritis & vos mecum iudices. Ecce ergo secundum Christi oraculum euangelicum, & sanctorum expositionem, quod Christus non exercuit in hoc seculo iudiciariam potestatem, coactiuam scilicet, quam tertiæ significationis diximus. Sed potius in forma serui existens, ab alio iudicatus est tali iudicio, & quod talem iudiciariam potestatem coactiuam, cum exercuerit in alio seculo, tunc apostoli cum ipso sedebunt ad iudicandum tali iudicio non antea.
units.tr: This also was clearly the opinion of Blessed John Chrysostom, in accordance with the mind of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 1, in his book of Dialogues, which is also entitled On the Priesthood, book 2, chap. 3. I did not repeat the whole sequence that I quoted in part 6 of the fifth book here, for the sake of brevity, but I have added here what he adds to that sequence. Chrysostom says: "Therefore, for this reason, there is great need of the help of art, so that men may be persuaded that, when they are sick, they should of their own accord offer themselves to the priests for medicine. And not only this, but they should also be willing to be cured. For if someone struggles while bound, since he has free power in this matter, he will make his evil worse; or if he rejects the words which were in place of the knife for the future, he adds to himself another wound through contempt, and the occasion of healing becomes an instrument of a more deadly disease. For there is no one who can cure an unwilling person." Then, after some intervening remarks which the pastor of souls ought to heed by correcting, not by compelling, he adds below: "But if a man has been led away from the right faith, the priest has great need of exhortation, diligence and patience, because he cannot bring the one who has gone astray back by force, but he will try to persuade him to return to the right faith from which he first fell." See how this holy man separates the judgment of priests from the judgment of rulers, since the coercive judgment of priests neither is nor ought to be, assigning the reason which we have often stated. First, because coercive power belongs to laws or lawgivers, and it was not granted to priests in his time or in his province. Second, because even if it were granted to them, they would act in vain toward their subjects by means of it. For nothing spiritual profits the coerced toward eternal salvation. He said the same above on that passage of Luke 9: "If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself." I have omitted the sequence, because what has been said is sufficient, and for the sake of brevity. This again was clearly the opinion of Blessed Hilary in his letter to the Emperor Constantius, in which, among other things, he wrote to him: "God taught the knowledge of himself rather than exacted it, and, while he encouraged the admiration of heavenly works by his precepts, he disdained to use coercive authority to make confession." See, God wants the knowledge of himself and confession to be taught to men, namely through faith, but that no one be compelled at all; this he disdains. The same he repeats shortly after, saying: "God does not require a forced confession." And again, a little further on, in the person of all priests, he says thus: "I cannot receive anyone unless he is willing, hear anyone unless he is praying, or seal anyone unless he professes faith." Therefore God does not want a forced confession of himself, nor for anyone to be drawn to this by violent action or compulsion of any kind. Hence the same writer, against Auxentius, bishop of Milan, whom he judged an Arian, and who, by armed power, was procuring that men should be prevented from professing what was relevant to their opinion, or rather, as he says, against the Catholic faith; and rebuking him, he says, even if he had taught true things: "And first it is permitted to pity the labour of our age, and to lament the foolish opinions of the present times, by which men believe that they defend God, and labour by worldly ambition to protect the Church of Christ." Again to the same, in the same place: "But now, alas, divine faith is commended by earthly supports, and Christ, poor in power, is accused while ambition takes counsel for his name. The Church terrifies with exile and prisons, and she compels men to believe in her, by whom exile and prisons were believed." And he speaks of the Church as the college of priests or bishops and of the rest of the ministers of the temple, whom they call clerics. Ambrose also clearly held this, in his second letter to the Emperor Valentinian, which is entitled To the People, when he said: "I can grieve, I can weep, I can groan against arms, soldiers, and even Goths; my tears are my arms, for such are the defences of a priest; otherwise I neither ought nor am able to resist." See, a priest ought not, even if he were able, to stir up or be stirred to arms or coercive power against anyone, or to command or urge it, especially against the faithful of Christ; and the whole of this world may think the opposite of some priests, contrary to the teaching of the sacred canon and the saints. Therefore, according to the truth and the clear intention of the Apostle and of the saints, who were the teachers of the Church or of the faith and the chief of others, no one is ordered to be compelled in this age by punishment or torture to keep the precepts of the gospel law, especially by a priest, and not only the faithful but not even the unbelieving; for which reason the ministers of this law, bishops or presbyters, can judge no one in this age with the judgment of the third sense, nor compel anyone to observe the precepts of the divine law, especially without the authority of a human lawgiver, since such a judgment according to the divine law ought not to be exercised in this age, nor its execution carried out, but only in the future. Hence Matt. 19: "But Jesus said to them, that is, to the apostles: Truly I say to you, that you who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." See, when the apostles were to sit with Christ as judges of the third sense, namely in the other age, not in this one. Where the Gloss says: "in the regeneration, that is, when the dead shall rise incorruptible." Hence, according to the Gloss, there are two regenerations: the first by water and the Holy Spirit, the second in the resurrection. Hence, "you also shall sit," the Gloss says, following Augustine: "The form of the servant by which he was judged (namely Christ, who was judged in this age by coercive judgment) not judging, since he exercised judicial power (namely in the resurrection), you will be judges with me as well." See, therefore, according to the evangelical oracle of Christ and the exposition of the saints, Christ did not exercise judicial power in this age, namely coercive power, which we have called the power of the third sense. Rather, existing in the form of a servant, he was judged by another by such judgment; and when he exercises such coercive judicial power in the other age, then the apostles will sit with him to judge by such judgment, and not before.

units.la: Vnde admiratione dignum est valde, cur sibi assumat episcopus seu presbyter aliquis quicunque sit ille, maiorem aut aliam autoritatem quam Christus aut eius apostoli habere voluerint in hoc seculo, ipsi enim in forma seruorum iudicari sunt per seculi principes, eorum vero successores presbyteri, principibus non solum subesse recusant contra Christi & apostolorum exemplum atque præceptum, verum etiam principibus & potestatibus supremis coactiua iurisdictione præesse se dicunt, cum tamen dixerit Christus Matth. 10. Et ad reges & ad præsides ducemini propter me, nec dixit præsides aut reges eritis. Et infra subiungit, non est discipulus supra magistrum, nec seruus super dominum suum. Nullum ergo iudicium, principatum, seu dominium coactiuum potest aut debet in hoc seculo presbyter seu episcopus aliquis, inquantum huiusmodi exercere. Fuit etiam hæc aperte sententia Aristot. 4. Politicæ, cap. 12. inquit enim: Propter quod non omnes neque electos neque sortiales ponendum principes, puta sacerdotes primo: Hos enim aliquid præter politicos principatus ponendum, adhuc & distributores & præcones. Eligantur autem & legati. Sunt autem hæc quidem politica currarum vel omnium ciuium ad quandam operationem. Et parum infra subdit, hæ autem œconomicæ sunt.
units.tr: Hence it is very much to be wondered at why any bishop or presbyter, whoever he may be, should assume for himself greater or different authority than Christ or his apostles willed to have in this age. For they themselves were judged in the form of servants by the princes of this world, while their successors, the presbyters, not only refuse to be subject to princes, contrary to the example and precept of Christ and the apostles, but also say that they preside over princes and supreme powers with coercive jurisdiction, although Christ said in Matt. 10: "And you shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake," and he did not say, "you shall be governors or kings." And below he adds: "The disciple is not above the master, nor the servant above his lord." Therefore no bishop or presbyter whatsoever can or ought in this age to exercise any judgment, principality or coercive lordship, insofar as he is such. This was also clearly the opinion of Aristotle in the fourth book of the Politics, chapter 12, for he says: "Therefore, not all, neither the chosen nor those appointed by lot, are to be placed as rulers, for example priests first. For these must be placed apart from the political rulers, and also the distributors and heralds. Envoys too are to be chosen. These offices indeed are political, of the chariots or of all citizens for a certain operation." And a little below he adds: "but these are economic."

units.la: Testatur autem dictis, quoniam si voluisset Christus sacerdotes nouæ legis iudices esse secundum ipsam tertiæ significationis iudicio coactiuo videlicet contentiosos hominum actus in hoc seculo per talem definiendo sententiam, tradidisset vtique in lege huiusmodi specialia præcepta talium, quemadmodum Moysi fecit in antiqua lege, quem oraculo suo & non per hominem, Deus principem & Iudæorum iudicem coactiuum instituit. Sicut habetur Actuum septimo, propter quod etiam illi legem Deus tradidit obseruandorum in statu vitæ præsentis, ad contentiones hominum dirimendas, præcepta talium specialiter continentem, & in hoc proportionaliter se habentem humanæ legi quantum ad aliquam sui partem. Ad quæ siquidem obseruanda compellebantur & arcebantur homines in hoc seculo per Moysen & ipsius substitutos iudices coactiuos, pœna vel supplicio, minime non per sacerdotem aliquem, sicut Exodi 18. euidenter apparet. Verum huiusmodi præcepta in euangelica lege non tradidit Christus, sed tradita vel tradenda suppositit in humanis legibus, quas obseruari & principantibus secundum eas omnem animam humanam obedire præcepit, in his saltem quæ non aduersarentur legi salutis. Vnde Matth. 22. & Marci 11. Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, per Cæsarem significans quemlibet principantem. Sic etiam Apostolus ad Rom. 13. nec reiterare piget: Omnis anima subdita sit potestatibus sublimioribus. Sic etiam primæ ad Timoth. vltimo, Etiam dominis infidelibus. & ibidem Glossa secundum Augustinum, quam quinto huius induximus, parte octaua. Ex quibus apparet liquido intentionem Christi, Apostoli, & sanctorum fuisse humanis legibus, & secundum ipsas iudicibus cunctos homines subesse debere.
units.tr: He bears witness to this in his words: if Christ had wished priests to be judges of the New Law, in the sense of the third signification, namely judges with coercive power who by such a sentence settle the contentious acts of men in this world, he would surely have handed down in that law special precepts of this kind, just as he did for Moses in the old law, whom God, not through a man but by his own oracle, appointed as prince and coercive judge of the Jews, as is found in Acts 7. For this reason God also gave that people a law which contained specifically precepts of this kind for settling the disputes of men in the state of the present life, and which in this respect stood in proportion to human law as to some part of it. Men were compelled and restrained in this world to observe these precepts through Moses and the judges he appointed, with punishment or torture, and not at all through some priest, as Exodus 18 plainly shows. But Christ did not hand down precepts of this kind in the Gospel law; rather he left them to be supplied by the human laws, whether already handed down or yet to be handed down, and he commanded every human soul to observe these laws and to obey those who rule according to them, at least in those matters which do not conflict with the law of salvation. Hence Matthew 22 and Mark 12: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's," where "Caesar" signifies any ruler whatever. So also the Apostle in Romans 13, and I am not ashamed to repeat it: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers." So too in 1 Timothy at the end: "even to unbelieving masters," and in the same place the Gloss following Augustine, which we cited in the fifth part of this book, in the eighth section. From these things it is clear that the intention of Christ, the Apostles and the saints was that all men should be subject to human laws, and that all should be subject to judges according to them.

units.la: Amplius ex his palam, quoniam non omnia quæ in lege seu testamento veteri Iudaico populo consulta vel custodiri præcepta fuerunt, obseruare tenentur Christi fideles. Quinimo quorundam est ipsis obseruatio interdicta, vt quæ ceremoniarum sub pœna perditionis aeternæ, quemadmodum docet Apostolus ad Rom. 3. & 7. ad Gal. 2. & 5. ad Ephe. 2. & ad Heb. 7. & 10. Cuius etiam assequentes sententiæ beati Hieron. & Augustini, in ipsorum mutuis epistolis 11. & 13. concorditer in hoc dicentes, asserunt talium ceremoniarum obseruatores, siue veros siue simulatos post publicationem euangelicæ legis fore in diaboli baratrum deuolutos: Ad legalium quoque similiter obseruationem minime tenentur Christi fideles, vt apparet per Apostolum vbi supra. & per August. super illud prædictum primæ ad Timoth. vltimo, cum dixit: Non ergo exigant, id est, quia non exigere possunt serui Christiani, quod de Hebreis dicitur, &c. Cum igitur nec in lege gratiæ tradita sint præcepta, specialiter pro contentiosis actibus hominum in hoc seculo dirimendis, relinquitur talia diffiniri debere per humanas leges tantummodo, & iudices secundum has ab humano legis latore autoritatem habentes. Fuerunt autem & alia quædam in lege Mosaica obseruari præcepta pro statu tentum seculi, veluti ea quæ sacrificiorum aut hostiarum seu oblationum quorundam pro redemptione peccatorum, maxime occultorum, quæ per immanentes actus committuntur. Ad quæ implenda nemo cogebatur pœna vel supplicio præsentis seculi. Et his proportionaliter habent omnia nouæ legis tam consilia quam præcepta, eo quod ad talium obseruationem in hoc seculo neminem Christus voluit nec præcepit arceri, licet legum humanarum institutA generali mandato præcipiat obseruari, sub pœna tamen aut supplicio in alio seculo transgressoribus infligendo. Vnde transgressor humanæ legis, quasi vt in pluribus peccat in legem diuinam, licet econuerso non sic. Quoniam multi sunt actus, in quibus committens aut omittens peccat contra legem diuinam, quæ de his præcipit, de quibus humana lex frustra præciperet: quales sunt quos pridem diximus immanentes, qui alicui adesse vel non inesse probari nequeunt, cum tamen Deum latere non possint. Et ideo de talibus debite faciendis aut omittendis lex diuina lata fuit conuenienter propter hominum melioritatem, tam in præsenti seculo quam venturo.
units.tr: Further, it is plain from these things that the faithful of Christ are not bound to observe all the precepts which were given or kept in the law or covenant of the old Jewish people. Indeed, the observance of some of them is forbidden to them, namely the ceremonies, under pain of eternal perdition, as the Apostle teaches in Romans 3 and 7, Galatians 2 and 5, Ephesians 2, and Hebrews 7 and 10. Following this opinion, the blessed Jerome and Augustine, in their mutual letters 11 and 13, agree in saying that the observers of such ceremonies, whether genuine or feigned, after the publication of the Gospel law will be cast down into the pit of the devil. Likewise the faithful of Christ are by no means bound to observe the legal precepts, as appears from the Apostle in the passage cited above, and from Augustine on the aforementioned words of 1 Timothy at the end, when he said: "Let them not therefore demand," that is, because Christian servants cannot demand what is said of the Hebrews, etc. Since, therefore, precepts specifically for settling the contentious acts of men in this world have not been handed down even in the law of grace, it follows that such matters must be defined through human laws alone, and through judges who hold authority under these laws from the human lawgiver. Yet there were also certain other precepts in the Mosaic law to be observed for the state of this world only, such as those concerning sacrifices, or certain victims or offerings for the redemption of sins, especially hidden sins, which are committed through immanent acts. No one was compelled to fulfil these with punishment or torture of the present world. And in proportion to these, all the counsels and precepts of the New Law stand alike, since Christ willed and commanded that no one be restrained from observing such things in this world, although he commands by a general mandate that the human laws be observed, inflicting punishment or torture on transgressors in another world. Hence the transgressor of human law, as for the most part, sins against the divine law, though conversely this is not always so. For there are many acts in which the one who commits or omits sins against the divine law, which commands about those matters concerning which human law would command in vain; such are the immanent acts we mentioned earlier, which cannot be shown to be present or absent in anyone, though they cannot be hidden from God. Therefore the divine law was rightly given concerning such acts to be done or omitted, for the betterment of men, both in the present world and in the world to come.

units.la: Obiiciet autem aliquis imperfectionem euangelicæ legi, si per ipsam, vt diximus sufficienter regulari nequeant actus humani contentiosi pro statu & in statu vitæ præsentis. Nos autem dicamus, quod per legem euangelicam sufficienter dirigimur in agendis aut declinandis in vita præsenti, pro statu tamen venturi seculi seu æternæ salutis consequendæ, aut supplicii declinandi propter quæ lata est non quidem pro contentiosis actibus hominum ciuiliter reducendis ad æqualitatem aut commensurationem debitam pro statu seu sufficientia vitæ præsentis, eo quod Christus in mundum non venit ad huiusmodi regulandos pro vita præsenti, sed futura tantum modo. Et propterea diuersa est temporalium & humanorum actuum regula, diuersimode dirigens ad hos fines. Vna enim, diuina scilicet, nullo modo docet contendere aut repetere in iudicio, licet non prohibeat: Ideoque nec de talibus specialia tradit præcepta, vt diximus. Reliqua vero horum actuum regula hæc docet, tradit & transgresso res arceri præcipit, humana lex scilicet, propter quod Lucæ 12. petenti à Christo humanum iudicium inter se & fratrem suum, respondit ipse: Homo, quis me constituit iudicem aut diuisorem inter vos? quasi diceret, non veni ad tale iudicium exercendum. Vnde Glossa: Non dignatur esse iudex litium, non arbiter facultatum, qui viuorum & mortuorum habet iudicium, & mortuorum arbitrium. Non ergo per diuinam vel euangelicam legem commensurari possent sufficienter actus humani pro fine præsentis seculi. Quoniam nec regulæ talium actuum commensurationis ad proportionem, quam volunt homines & licite pro statu vitæ præsentis, sunt in ea traditæ, sed ab humanis legibus suppositæ, vel traditæ vel etiam tradendæ sine quibus etiam propter defectum iustitiæ contingeret ex hominum scandalo seu contentione ipsorum pugna & separatio, ac humanæ vitæ mundanæ insufficientia, quam quasi omnes refugiunt secundum naturam. Nō potest ergo propterea dici secundum veritatem, euangelica lex siue doctrina imperfecta: quoniam non est nata habere perfectionem quam non habeat. Est enim lata vt per ipsam dirigamur immediate de his & in his quæ sunt æternæ salutis hominibus consequendæ & miseriæ declinandæ, in quibus est valde sufficiens & perfecta. Non autem lata fuit nec est ad ciuilia litigiosa negotia dirimenda, propter finem quem volunt homines & licite in vita mundana. Si enim ex hoc diceretur imperfecta, æque conuenienter imperfecta dici posset, quoniam per ipsam medicari corporales ægritudines aut mensurare magnitudines vel oceanum navigare nescimus. Quamuis hoc sane concedi posset, quod ipsa non simpliciter est perfecta, quia non est tale aliquid ens nisi vnicum, Deus ipse. Huic quidem sententiæ tanquam indubie veræ testatur glossa secundum Gregorium super sextum primæ ad Corinthios, vbi sic ait: Ad reuerentiam vestram dico: vt videlicet hi terrenas causas examinent, qui exteriorum rerum sapientiam perceperunt, qui autem spiritualibus donis dotati sunt, terrenis non debent negociis implicari. Quod si per sapientiam rerum exteriorum & terrenarum causarum seu contentionum intellexisset sacram scripturam, non dixisset, qui autem spiritualibus donis dotati sunt; id est scriptura sacra, terrenis non debent negociis implicari, nec tales secundum has doctrinas inuicem separasset. Amplius, quia talem sapientiam habentes, exteriorum rerum videlicet, prius vocauerat Apostolus & sancti secundum vnam expositionem, contemptibiles in ecclesia, quod tamen nec Apostolus aut sancti exponentes eius seriem, senserunt de doctis in sacra scriptura. Quot quidem igitur, & quales sunt actus legales humani, quibus etiam legibus atque iudicibus, qualiter & quando, & per quos regulandi & corrigendi, sufficienter ad intentionem propositam monstrasse putamus.
units.tr: Someone will object that the Gospel law is imperfect, if through it, as we have said, the contentious human acts cannot be sufficiently regulated for the state and condition of the present life. We, however, reply that through the Gospel law we are sufficiently directed in doing or avoiding things in the present life, with a view to the state of the world to come, or to attaining eternal salvation, or to avoiding the punishment for which it was given; but not indeed for regulating contentious human acts civilly, bringing them to equality or the due proportion for the state or sufficiency of the present life, since Christ did not come into the world to regulate such things for the present life, but for the future only. And therefore the rule of temporal and human acts is different, directing these ends in different ways. For the one, the divine, teaches in no way to contend or to bring suit in judgment, although it does not forbid it; and therefore it hands down no special precepts about such matters, as we have said. The other rule of these acts, the human law, teaches this, hands down this, and commands that transgressors be restrained; for this reason, when in Luke 12 a man asked Christ to settle a human judgment between himself and his brother, he answered: "Man, who made me a judge or divider between you?" as if to say, I did not come to exercise such judgment. Hence the Gloss: "He does not deign to be a judge of lawsuits or an arbiter of property, who has the judgment of the living and the dead, and the decision of the dead." Therefore human acts could not be sufficiently measured by the divine or Gospel law with respect to the end of the present world. For the rules of such measuring of acts, to the proportion which men wish and lawfully wish for the state of the present life, are not handed down in it, but are supplied by human laws, whether already handed down or yet to be handed down; without these, through lack of justice, there would result from men's scandal or contention strife and separation among them, and the insufficiency of human life in the world, which almost everyone naturally shuns. It cannot therefore be said in truth that the Gospel law or doctrine is imperfect, since it was not born to have a perfection which it does not have. For it was given so that by it we might be directed immediately concerning, and in, those things which concern the attainment of eternal salvation for men and the avoidance of misery, in which it is wholly sufficient and perfect. But it was not given, nor is it, for settling civil litigious affairs, with respect to the end which men wish and lawfully pursue in worldly life. For if it were called imperfect on this account, it could just as fairly be called imperfect, since we do not know how to cure bodily sicknesses through it, or measure magnitudes, or sail the ocean. Although it could certainly be conceded that it is not simply perfect, because the only thing which is perfect in this absolute sense is one being, God himself. This opinion, as undoubtedly true, is attested by the Gloss following Gregory on the sixth chapter of 1 Corinthians, where he says: "I speak to your shame: that those who have acquired the wisdom of external things should examine the earthly causes, but those who are endowed with spiritual gifts ought not to be involved in earthly business." But if by the wisdom of external things and of earthly causes or disputes he had meant Holy Scripture, he would not have said, "but those endowed with spiritual gifts," that is, Scripture, "ought not to be involved in earthly business," nor would he have separated such persons from one another according to these teachings. Moreover, since the Apostle and the saints, according to one exposition, had earlier called those who possess such wisdom, namely of external things, contemptible in the Church, the expositors of his sequence did not think this of the learned in Holy Scripture, though the Apostle did not. How many, and what kinds, of human legal acts there are, by what laws and judges, in what way and when, and through whom they are to be regulated and corrected, we believe we have sufficiently shown for the purpose proposed.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De coactiuo hæreticorum iudice, cuius videlicet sit ipsos iudicare in hoc seculo, arcere, ac pœnas reales aut personales illis infligere, exigere, & cui de- beant applicari.
units.tr: On the coercive judge of heretics: namely, who has the right to judge them in this age, to exclude them, to inflict real or personal penalties on them and exact these, and to whom such penalties ought to be applied.

units.la: SEd de quibus diximus, merito dubitatur. Nam si arcendorum omnium in vita præsenti, iudicio coactiuo ac realium aut personalium pœnarum inflictio & exactio principanti tantum modo legislatoris autoritate pertineat iurisdictio, quemadmodum in prioribus ostensum est. Hæreticorum igitur aut aliter infidelium vel schismaticorum iudicium coactiuum, realis quoque ac personalis pœnæ inflictio, exactio, ac applicatio ad principem huiusmodi pertinebit, quod siquidem inconuenientis faciem habere videtur. Cum enim eiusdem autoritatis appareat delictum cognoscere, iudicare atque corrigere. Sacerdotis autem presbyteri seu episcopi sit hæresis discernere crimen, nullius alterius ad sacerdotem seu episcopum solum videbitur, vtrique huius criminis & consilium, iudicium coactiuum & correctio pertinere. Amplius ad illum videtur iudicium & pœnæ delinquentis exactio pertinere, in quem seu cuius legem delinquens peccauerit.
units.tr: But the question arising from what we have said is rightly disputed. For if the jurisdiction over excluding all persons in the present life, by coercive judgment and by the infliction and exaction of real or personal penalties, belongs only to the authority of the ruler as lawgiver, as has been shown above, then the coercive judgment over heretics, or over other unbelievers or schismatics, and likewise the infliction, exaction and application of real or personal penalties, will belong to such a prince. This seems to have the look of an absurdity. For it appears that the same authority is needed to recognise, judge and correct an offence. But it seems that to discern whether an offence is heresy belongs to the priest, that is, the presbyter or bishop, and to no one else, so that counsel, coercive judgment and correction in this crime also belong to the priest or bishop. Further, it seems that the judgment on the offender and the exaction of his penalty belong to the one against whose law the offender has sinned.

units.la: Mention of numbered line markers: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60 printed in right margin. cauerit, hic autem presbyter est seu episcopus. Est enim legis diuinæ minister & iudex, in quam per se peccat hæreticus, schismaticus, aut aliter infidelis sit peccans, collegium aut singularis persona. Relinquitur igitur hoc fore iudicium sacerdotis, principantis vero nequaquam. Et videtur hæc aperte sententia beati Ambrosii ad Valentinianum Imperatorem epistola prima, & quia quasi per totam illius epistolæ seriem id sentire apparet, tam inducere omisi propter abbreuiationem.
units.tr: ...is a presbyter or bishop. For he is the minister and judge of the divine law, against which the heretic, schismatic, or other unbeliever sins, whether he be a body or a single person. It follows, therefore, that this judgment belongs to the priest, and in no way to the ruler. And this opinion seems to be plainly that of the blessed Ambrose, in his first epistle to the Emperor Valentinian; and since it appears to be his view throughout nearly the whole course of that letter, I have omitted to quote it at length for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Nos autem dicamus, quod peccans quilibet in legem diuinam, iudicandus est secundum illam, corrigendus & arcendus, verum secundum ipsam duplex est iudex. Vnus quidem qui tertiæ significationis coactiuam habens potentiam, transgressores huius legis arcendi, & ab ipsis exigendi supplicia: & hic vnicus est Christus scilicet, quemadmodum ex Iacobi quarto induximus capitulo præcedente. Qui tamen omnes huius legis transgressores voluit & ordinauit iudicari iudicio coactiuo in seculo venturo, & in eodem tantummodo arceri pœna vel supplicio non in isto, vt ex præcedenti capitulo sufficienter apparuit. Alius vero iudex est secundum hanc legem, presbyter videlicet seu episcopus, non quidem tertiæ significationis, vt ipsius sit arcere quenquam huius legis transgressorem in hoc seculo, pœnam aut supplicium exigere per potentiam coactiuam, quemadmodum quinto huius, & cap. præcedente autoritate Apostoli atque sanctorum aperte monstratum est, ac inuincibili ratione ipsorum. Iudex tamen est ipse secundum primam significationem, cuius est docere, exhortari, arguere, atque corripere delinquentes seu transgressores illius, ipsosque terrere iudicio futuræ sibi damnationis & pœnæ infligitionis per iudicem coactiuum, Christum scilicet in seculo venturo, quemadmodum declarauimus sexto huius & 7. in quibus agebatur de clauium sacerdotalium potestate, & in capitulo præcedente, vbi medico corporum comparauimus sacerdotes, qui medici sunt animarum, vt dixit Augustinus auctoritate prophetæ, & recitat Magister in quarto, distin. 18. cap. nono. Cum igitur hæreticus, schismaticus, aut infidelis alter, quicunque transgressor sit euangelicæ legis, in eo perfistens crimine per eum iudicem punietur, cuius est transgressores diuinæ legis arcere, inquantum huiusmodi, cum suum videlicet iudicium exercebit. Hic autem iudex Christus est, qui iudicaturus est vivos, & iam mortuos & morituros, in futuro tamen seculo, non in isto. Quoniam vsque ad vltimum ex hoc seculo transituin, mortem scilicet, misericorditer peccatoribus posse mereri & pœnitere concessit. Per reliquum vero iudicem, pastorem scilicet, episcopum seu presbyterum, docendus & exhortandus est homo in vita præsenti, arguendus, corripiendus peccator, atque terrendus, iudicio seu pronostico futuræ gloriæ, vel damnationis æternæ, nequaquam vero cogendus, vt ex priori capitulo palam. Quod si humana lege prohibitum fuerit hæreticum aut aliter infidelem in regione manere, qui talis in ipsa repertus fuerit, tanquam legis humanæ transgressor, pœna vel supplicio huic transgressioni eadem lege statutis, in hoc seculo debet arceri. Et per eum iudicem, quem legislatoris autoritate humanæ legis demonstrauimus esse custodem 15. prima. Si vero hæreticum, aut aliter infidelem, commorari fidelibus eadem prouincia non fuerit prohibitum humana lege, quemadmodum hæreticis ac semini Iudæorum iam humanis legibus permissu n exturit, etiam temporibus Christianorum populorum, principum atque pontificum, dico cuiquam non licere hæreticum aut aliter infidelem quenquam iudicare vel arcere pœna vel supplicio, ealiaut personali prostatu vitæ præsentis. Et causa eius generalis est: quoniam nemo quantumcunque peccans contra disciplinas speculatiuas aut operatiuas quascunque punitur vel arcetur in hoc seculo præcipe inquantum huiusmodi, sed inquantum peccat contra præceptum humanæ legis. Sed enim inebriati aut calceos facere vel vendere cuiuscunque modi, prout possit aut velit quilibet, medicari & docere, ac similia reliqua officiorum opera exercere pro libito, quoniam non esset humana lege, nequaquam arceretur ebriosus aut aliter peruersè agens in operibus reliquis. Et propterea oportet attendere, quod in quolibet huius seculi iudicio coactiuo, antequam absolutionis vel damnationis feratur sententia, quantum pertinet ad propositum secundum ordinem inquirenda sunt aliqua. Vnum quidem, si dictum aut factum alicui tanquam reo impositum sit, quale dicitur. Hoc autem est præscire quid est quod commissum dicitur. Secundum vero an huiusmodi sit humana lege prohibitum fieri. Tertium autem an accusatus id commiserit. Hæc autem sequitur iudicium seu sententia damnationis in reum vel absolutionis, verbi gratia. Si aliquis accusatus tanquam hæreticus, aut vasorum aureorum, vel metallorum falsator alterius, debet, antequam per sententiam coactiuam damnetur aut absoluatur, inquiri an dictum aut factum impositum illi sit hæreticum, aut non. Secundo vero, an sic tale aliquid dicere, humana lege prohibitum. Tertio vero, an tale aliquid crimen commissum sit per eum cui crimen imponitur. Demum vero ad hæc sequitur absolutionis vel damnationis iudicium coactiuum. De primo quidem horum certificari debet principans per eos qui periti sunt secundum vnamquamque disciplinam, quorum est considerare per se quiditatem seu naturam eius dicti vel operis, quod accusato imponitur, quoniam hi sunt iudices primæ significationis talium, quemadmodum diximus secundo huius, & ipsorum naturam scire tenentur, quibus docendi, ut operandi talia in ciuitate per principantem data est auctoritas, quam in disciplinis liberalibus consuetio vocabulo licentiam appellamus, quod & in aliis omnibus artibus factiuis seu rebus humanis proportionaliter habet, vt demonstratum est 15. prima. Sic enim medicus nosse debet leprosos & non leprosos secundum corporis habitum, sic sacerdos sermonem seu doctrinam
units.tr: But we say that anyone who sins against the divine law is to be judged according to it, and corrected and excluded. Yet according to that law there are two judges. The first is the one who holds coercive power in the third sense, to exclude the transgressors of this law and to exact punishments from them; and this one is Christ alone, as we have adduced from James chapter four in the preceding chapter. He willed and ordained that all transgressors of this law be judged by coercive judgment in the age to come, and be excluded by penalty or punishment in that age only and not in this one, as has sufficiently appeared from the preceding chapter. The other judge according to this law is the presbyter or bishop; not indeed of the third sense, so that it belongs to him to exclude any transgressor of this law in this age, or to exact penalty or punishment by coercive power, as has been plainly shown by the authority of the Apostle and the saints, and by their unconquerable reasoning, in the fifth book and the preceding chapter. Yet he is a judge in the first sense, whose office it is to teach, exhort, reprove and rebuke offenders or transgressors of the law, and to terrify them with the judgment of the damnation and punishment that awaits them from the coercive judge, namely Christ in the age to come, as we declared in the sixth and seventh chapters of this book, where we treated of the power of priestly keys, and in the preceding chapter, where we compared priests to physicians of bodies, who are physicians of souls, as Augustine said on the authority of a prophet, and as the Master recites in the fourth book, distinction 18, chapter nine. Therefore, when a heretic, schismatic, or any other unbeliever who transgresses the gospel law persists in that crime, he will be punished by that judge whose office it is to exclude transgressors of the divine law, insofar as they are such, when he exercises his judgment. This judge is Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, yet in the future age and not in this one. For he has mercifully granted sinners the possibility of earning repentance up until the last passage out of this age, that is, death. Through the other judge, namely the minister, bishop or presbyter, a man in the present life is to be taught and exhorted, and the sinner reproved, rebuked and terrified by the judgment or foreshadowing of future glory or eternal damnation; but he is by no means to be compelled, as is plain from the previous chapter. But if it has been forbidden by human law for a heretic or other unbeliever to remain in a region, then whoever is found there, as a transgressor of human law, ought to be excluded in this age by the penalty or punishment that the same law has established for this transgression. This is done through that judge whom we have shown, on the authority of the lawgiver, to be the guardian of human law, in the fifteenth chapter of the first book. But if human law has not forbidden a heretic or other unbeliever to dwell in the same province with the faithful, just as human laws have already permitted this to heretics and to the seed of the Jews, even in the times of Christian peoples, princes and pontiffs, I say that it is not lawful for anyone to judge or exclude a heretic or other unbeliever by penalty or punishment, or by personal restraint in the present life. The general reason for this is that no one, however much he sins against any speculative or practical disciplines, is punished or excluded in this age simply as such, but insofar as he sins against a precept of human law. For if a drunkard, or one who makes or sells shoes of whatever kind, or who practises medicine and teaches, or performs the other similar works of trades, did so as he pleased or as he was able, with no human law forbidding it, then the drunkard or one who otherwise acted perversely in his other work would not be excluded. And therefore it is necessary to observe that in every coercive judgment of this age, before a sentence of acquittal or condemnation is pronounced, several things must be inquired into, as far as they pertain to the matter in hand, and in this order. The first is whether a deed or word has been imputed to someone as a defendant, and of what kind it is said to be; for this means knowing beforehand what is said to have been committed. The second is whether such a thing is forbidden by human law. The third is whether the accused has actually committed it. After these comes the judgment, or sentence of condemnation or acquittal, against the defendant; for example, if someone is accused of being a heretic, or of being a counterfeiter of gold vessels or of other metals, then before he is condemned or acquitted by coercive sentence, it must be inquired whether the word or deed imputed to him is heretical or not. Second, whether it is forbidden by human law to say such a thing. Third, whether such a crime has been committed by the one to whom it is imputed. Finally, after these comes the coercive judgment of acquittal or condemnation. The ruler ought to be informed of the first of these by those who are skilled in each discipline, whose task it is to consider in themselves the quiddity or nature of the word or work imputed to the accused; for these are the judges of the first sense in such matters, as we said in the second chapter of this book, and they are bound to know their nature, to whom the authority to teach or to practise such things in the city has been given by the ruler, which in the liberal disciplines we commonly call licence. The same holds proportionally in all the other productive arts or human affairs, as has been shown in the fifteenth chapter of the first book. For a physician ought to know lepers from non-lepers according to the condition of the body; so a priest ought to know the doctrine, whether heretical or catholic, of a sermon...

units.la: T ătrinam hæreticam & catholicam, sicaurifex seu argentarius de metallis, sic etiam de mutuis aut depositis & aliis consimilibus actibus ciuilibus iurisperitus seu doctor. Talia enim principans inquantum huiusmodi, non tenetur cognoscere quamuis secundum legislatorem, si lex perfecta fuerit, debet certificari de natura sermonum, operum & actuum per disciplinarum doctores aut operatores. Tunc ad propositum quæsitum dico, quod an crimen impositum alicui sit hæresis vel non, iudicare potest & debet, primæ tamen significationis iudicio quilibet diuinarum scripturarum doctor, qualis est aut esse debet sacerdos quicunque. Vnde Malachiæ secundo: Labia enim sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & legem, (diuinam scilicet,) requirent ex ore eius. Tales enim esse debent apostolorum successores episcopi seu presbyteri, quibus dictum est à Christo Matth. 28. Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes &c. docentes eos seruare omnia quæcunque mandaui vobis. Sic etiam primæ ad Timoth. 3. oportet ipsum inter cætera, doctorem esse, sacræ legis scilicet. Sic etiam ad Titum primo, oportet episcopum esse amplectantem eum qui secundum doctrinam est fidelem sermonem, vt potens sit exhortari in doctrina sancta, & eos qui contradicunt arguere. Sunt enim multi seductores, quos oportet redargui. Secundum vero, an scilicet tale commissum sit lege prohibitum aut non, nosse oportet principantem ex lege dicta secundum vltimam & propriam significationem, secundum quam legislatoris autoritate principari quis debet. Tertium autem quod scire oportet, est, an crimen dicti vel operis hæretici, dixerit aut exercueritis, cui crimen imponitur. Et hoc quidem iudicium per sensus exteriores & interiores consequenter tam à doctis quam ab indoctis iudicari potest, quos testes vocare solent. Post hæc autem per principantem ferendum est iudicium seu sententiam damnationis aut absolutionis pœnæ aut supplicii, exactio quoque vel relaxatio illius ab eo qui ex crimine delatus fuerat, fienda. Non enim propterea quod in legem diuinam tantum modo peccat quis, à principante punitur. Sunt enim multa peccata mortalia & in legem diuinam, vt fornicationis, quæ permittit etiam scienter legislator humanus, nec coactiua potentia prohibet, nec prohibere potest aut debet episcopus vel sacerdos. Sed peccans in legem diuinam hæreticus, scilicet tali peccato etiam humana lege prohibito, punitur in quantum peccans in legem humanam. Est enim hæc causa præcisa seu per se prima, cur aliquis arceatur pœna vel supplicio præsentis seculi, quoniam posita ponitur effectus, & remota remouetur. Sicut e contrario, peccans in legem humanam peccato aliquo, punietur in alio seculo non in quantum peccans in legem humanam: multa enim sunt humana lege prohibita, quæ sunt diuina lege permissa. Vt si non restituerit quis mutuum statuto tempore propter impotentiam, casu fortuito, obliuione, ægritudine, vel aliquo quodam impedimento, non punietur ex hoc in alio seculo per iudicem coactiuum secundum legem diuinam. Qui tamen per iudicem coactiuum secundum legem humanam in hoc seculo iuste punitur. Et ideo peccare in legem diuinam est per se prima causa, quæ in philosophia, secundum quod ipsa dici solet, quoniam ipsi posita ponitur, & remota remouetur effectus pœnæ vel supplicii pro statu & in statu futuri seculi.
units.tr: ...doctrine, whether heretical or catholic; so a goldsmith or silversmith knows metals; so too a jurist or teacher knows loans, deposits and other similar civil acts. For the ruler, as such, is not bound to know these things, although, according to the lawgiver, if the law is complete, he ought to be informed of the nature of words, works and acts by the teachers or practitioners of the disciplines. Then, as to the question asked, I say that whether the crime imputed to someone is heresy or not, any teacher of the divine Scriptures can and must judge by the judgment of the first sense, as must any priest who is or ought to be such. Hence in Malachi chapter two: For the lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law (namely the divine law) at his mouth.
