For such ought the successors of the apostles, the bishops or presbyters, to be, to whom Christ said in Matthew 28: Go ye therefore and teach all nations, etc., teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. So also in 1 Timothy 3, the bishop ought among other things to be a teacher, namely of the sacred law. So too in Titus 1, a bishop ought to be holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers. For there are many seducers, whose mouths must be stopped. Second, as to whether such a thing is forbidden by law or not, the ruler must know from the said law, in its ultimate and proper sense, according to which anyone ought to be ruled by the authority of the lawgiver. Third, what must be known is whether the crime of the word or deed, which the heretic has said or practised, is imputed to him. This judgment can then be made through the external and internal senses by the learned as well as by the unlearned, whom they are accustomed to call witnesses. After this, the ruler is to pronounce the judgment or sentence of condemnation or acquittal, and the penalty or punishment is to be exacted, or remitted, by him who had been accused of the crime. For a man is not punished by the ruler merely because he sins against the divine law. There are many mortal sins against the divine law, such as fornication, which even a human lawgiver knowingly permits and does not forbid by coercive power, nor can or ought a bishop or priest forbid them. But a heretic who sins against the divine law, namely by a sin also forbidden by human law, is punished insofar as he sins against human law. For this is the immediate and primary cause why someone is excluded by penalty or punishment in the present age: when this is posited, the effect is posited, and when it is removed, the effect is removed. Conversely, one who sins against human law by some sin will be punished in the other age not insofar as he sins against human law; for many things are forbidden by human law that are permitted by divine law. For example, if someone does not repay a loan at the appointed time because of inability, by chance, by forgetfulness, by sickness, or by some other hindrance, he will not on that account be punished in the other age by a coercive judge according to divine law. Yet he is justly punished in this age by a coercive judge according to human law. And therefore to sin against the divine law is the primary cause in itself, which in philosophy, as it is usually called, is such that when it is posited the effect of penalty or punishment is posited, and when it is removed the effect is removed, with respect to the condition and state of the future age.

units.la: Est igitur in hæreticos schismaticos aut aliter infideles quoscunque iudicium & arcendi ac exigendæ ab ipsis pœnæ vel supplicii temporalis, sibique aut communitati non alteri applicandi potestas, solius principantis autoritate legislatoris humani, non autem presbyteri seu episcopi cuiusquam, propterea quod in legem diuinam peccent, quæ ad homines comparata in statu & pro statu vitæ præsentis, lex est, non quidem secundum vltimam significationem coactiuam habens cuiusquam potentiam in hoc seculo, vt palam est ex capitulo precedenti & quinto huius. Sed lex est dicta secundum tertiam legis, significationem, vt apparuit ex decimo prima. Secundum quam etiam in hoc seculo sacerdotes iudices sunt secundum primam iudicis aut iudicii significationem, nullam coactiuam habentes potentiam, vt ex quinto huius ostensum est, & per Apostolum, Ambrosium, Hilarium, & Chrysostomum, capitulo precedente. Si nanque suerent ipsi iudices coactiui seu principantes in hæreticos, quia tales peccant in eam disciplinam, cuius sunt ipsi doctores, & secundum ipsam aliquorum operatores in alios, sic esset aurifaber, falso fabricantis aurea sculptilia, iudex coactiuus & principans, quod absurdum est valde. Sic quoque medicus prave agentes secundum artem medicinæ possent arcere, foretque tanta principantium multitudo quot & officiorum ciuitatis in quæ peccare contingit, cuius tamen impossibilitas aut superfluitas ostensa est 17. prima. Non enim arcerentur sic peccantes in officia ciuitatis, aut punirentur propterea, nisi aliud intervenirent, verbi gratia legislatoris seu legis humanæ præceptum. Si enim peccata huiusmodi non essent humana lege prohibita, ea committentes nequaquam punirentur. Est autem quod diximus in exemplo familiari videre, esto nanque humana lege prohibitum leprosos aliis ciuibus commanere, nunquid medicus qui horum ægritudinem solus iudicare potest secundum ipsius disciplinam, vtrum scilicet leprosi sint aut non, quos leprosos esse iudicauerit primæ significationis iudicio, poterit per coactiuam potentiam autoritate propria, vt qua doctor est medicinalis scientiæ ab aliorum arcere consortio vel conuictu, & constat quod minime. Sed hoc is solummodo potest, cui legis humanæ coactiuæ custodia commissa est, principans scilicet. Non enim priuate populo aut collegio cuiquam licet quenquam iudicare aut arcere, vel pœnam exigere, sed soli principanti. Qui tamen de impositis maculis, criminibus, seu peccatis, & ipsorum natura iuxta legis determinationem si de hoc dixerit, erit si fuerit lex pfecta, vel per suam prudentiam, si lege omissum fuerit, vti debet & credere iudicio peritorum in disciplinis quæ talium operum, actuum, aut sermonum tractant naturam, vt medici de leprosis aut non leprosis, Theologi de criminosis, qui per leprosos figurantur in sacra scriptura secundum sanctorum expositionem. Similiter quoque de vasorum metallicorum sophismate credere debet aurifabro, & in consimilibus cuilibet docto, secundum reliqua operabilium & agibilium genera. Sicigitur de hæreticis aut aliter infidelibus iudicare debet medicus animarum, sacerdos scilicet, iudicio siquidem primæ significationis, discernendo videlicet sermonem aut actum hæreticum à non hæretico. De his vero iudicare tertiæ significationis iudicio, damnando scilicet vel absoluendo accusatos supplicio aut pœna temporali, ipsosque arcere ad talia persoluenda, qui damnati fuerint, sollus est principantis humana lege: exactas quoque pœnas si reales fuerint, quemadmodum eas quæ propter alia crimina exiguntur, applicare secundum legislatoris seu legis humanæ determinationem. His autem quæ diximus testatur scriptura in Actibus apostolorum, capitulo 25. Dum enim Apostolus à Iudæis accusatus esset tanquam hereticus, licet falso, causæ suæ inquisitio, deductio, applicatio, & diffinitio illius facta est coram iudice ad iudicem & per iudicem humani legislatoris autoritate statutum ad hoc, quemadmodum ad reliquos actus contentiosos siue ciuiles. Contraria vero his non est difficile soluere, cum enim dicebatur, ad eum tanquam iudicem hæretici iudicium pertinere, cuius est hæresis cognoscere crimen. Hæc distinguenda est propter multiplicitatem huius dictionis iudex aut iudicium, & secundum vnum sensum vera est, acceptis scilicet his nominibus secundum primam eorum significationem: si vero secundum tertiam sumatur, falsa est. Ideoque nihil contra nostram determinationem ex hoc prallegato concluditur. Ad reliquum vero, quod subiungebatur, ad illum spectare iudicium delinquentis, & exactionem pœnæ, ac illius si realis fuerit ubi applicationem, contra quem seu in cuius legem peccat delinquens, verum est si in ipsum tanquam tertiæ significationis iudicem, & in ipsius legem dictam secundum vltimam legis significationem, coactiuam scilicet. Et cum assumitur quod hæreticus peccat in legem diuinam, concedendum. Et ideo iudicabitur per iudicem tertiæ significationis secundum ipsam, Christum scilicet, in alio tantummodo seculo non isto, iuxta ipsius legislatoris ordinationem, quæ talis fuit. Per ipsum etiam arcebitur pœna vel supplicio, aut præmiabitur secundum legis præceptorum & consiliorum obseruationem vel transgressionem. Talis autem iudex huius legis, diuinæ scilicet, non est episcopus aut sacerdos aliquis, sed primæ significationis tantummodo quasi doctor, maxime comparata lege hac ad homines in statu & pro statu vitæ præsentis. Rursum maiori huius syllogismi suppositia tanquam vera, secundum quem diximus sensum, ad eum scilicet tanquam iudicem coactiuum pertinere iudicium transgressoris, in quem aut in legem cuius custos est, peccat transgressor, legem inquam etiam dictam secundum vltimam legis significationem tantummodo: tunc subsumenda est hæc propositio vera, videlicet quod in iudicem huius seculi dictum secundum tertiam iudicis significationem & legem cuius est custos, dictam etiam secundum vltimam eius & propriam significationem, coactiuam scilicet tantummodo, non in aliam in hoc seculo coactiuam legem aut iudicem peccat hæreticus. Et ideo per talem in hoc seculo iudicandus iudicio coactiuo, sic huius legis ordinante latore, ab eodem quoque transgredi per eundem iudicem pœna exigenda, quæ si realis fuerit applicanda per hunc iudicem ei, cui legislator humanus illam in lege statuit applicandam. Vel distinguendum est maiorem secundum æquiuocationem, vt in priori paralogismo. Sic igitur non inferre per necessitatem, aliquis damnandus aut iudicandus est tanquam hereticus in hoc & pro hoc seculo iudicio coactiuo realiter aut personaliter, vel vtroque modo. Ergo per sacerdotem aut episcopum quenquam, nisi fortasse vt diximus primæ significationis iudicio. Nec sequitur etiam propter hoc, ergo damnari tanquam hæreticì carnalia seu temporalia bona, quæ ab eodem exiguntur tanquam pœna vel pars pœnæ delicti, applicari debent episcopo seu presbytero cuiquam. Sicut nec sequitur, hi ciudicandus est tanquam monetæ falsarius, ergo per monetarios, nisi fortasse primæ significationis iudicio, non quidem tertiæ, coactiuo videlicet. Nec etiam sequitur, quod temporalia quæ ab illo exiguntur in pœnam, debeant monetariis applicari, collegio aut singulari personæ, sed coactiuo iudicio iudicari debet per principantem, & applicari pœna secundum legis humanæ determinationem.
units.tr: There is therefore power to judge heretics, schismatics, and other unbelievers of any kind, and to restrain them and exact from them a temporal penalty or punishment, and to apply it to themselves or to the community and not to another. This power belongs to the authority of the ruling human legislator alone, not to any presbyter or bishop. This is because they sin against the divine law, which, though it is set before men for the state and condition of the present life, is law, not in its final, coercive sense, which gives anyone power in this age, as is plain from the preceding chapter and the fifth of this book. Rather, law is taken in the third sense of "law," as appeared from the tenth of the first book. In that sense too, priests in this age are judges according to the first sense of "judge" or "judgment," with no coercive power, as was shown in the fifth of this book and by the Apostle, Ambrose, Hilary, and Chrysostom, in the preceding chapter. For if they were coercive or ruling judges over heretics, because such men sin against that discipline of which the priests are teachers, and by which they act upon others, then the goldsmith, who falsely makes golden idols, would also be a coercive and ruling judge, which is very absurd. Likewise, a physician could restrain those who act badly according to the art of medicine, and there would be as many rulers as there are offices in the state in which it is possible to sin. Yet the impossibility or superfluity of this was shown in the seventeenth of the first book. Those who sin in the offices of the state would not be restrained or punished for that reason, unless something else intervened, such as the command of the legislator or of human law. For if sins of this kind were not forbidden by human law, those who committed them would by no means be punished. We can see what we have said in a familiar example. Suppose human law forbids lepers to live among other citizens. Could the physician, who alone can judge these diseases according to his discipline, namely whether a man is a leper or not, and who has judged those he finds to be lepers by the judgment of the first sense, by his own authority restrain them from the company or company's fellowship of others, as one who is a teacher of medical science? It is clear that he cannot. Only the one to whom the custody of human coercive law has been entrusted can do this, namely the ruler. A private people or any collegium may not judge, restrain, or exact a penalty from anyone, but only the ruler may. Yet if he speaks about the stains, crimes, or sins imposed, and about their nature according to the determination of the law, he will do so either if the law is complete, or, if something has been left out of the law, by his own prudence, and he ought to use and trust the judgment of those skilled in the disciplines that treat the nature of such works, acts, or words. So physicians judge concerning lepers and those who are not lepers, and theologians concerning criminals, who are signified by lepers in Holy Scripture according to the exposition of the saints. Likewise, he ought to trust the goldsmith about the sophistry of metal vessels, and in similar matters anyone learned, according to the other kinds of things that are made and done. Thus the physician of souls, namely the priest, ought to judge concerning heretics and other unbelievers by the judgment of the first sense, that is, by distinguishing a heretical word or act from one that is not heretical. But to judge concerning these by the judgment of the third sense, namely by condemning or absolving the accused to punishment or temporal penalty, and to restrain those who have been condemned from paying such penalties, belongs solely to the ruler by human law. The exacted penalties, if they are real, are to be applied just as those exacted for other crimes are applied, according to the determination of the legislator or human law. Scripture bears witness to what we have said in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 25. When the Apostle was accused by the Jews as a heretic, though falsely, the inquiry, conveyance, application, and decision of his case were made before the judge, to the judge, and through the judge, by the authority of the human legislator, as set down for this, just as for other contentious or civil acts. It is not hard to answer what is contrary to this. When it was said that the judgment of a heretic belongs to him as judge, whose office it is to know the crime of heresy, this must be distinguished, because of the many meanings of the words "judge" and "judgment." In one sense it is true, namely when these words are taken in their first sense. But if it is taken in the third sense, it is false. Therefore nothing against our determination follows from this prior argument. As for what follows, that the judgment of the offender and the exaction of the penalty, and its application if it is real, belong to him against whom, or against whose law, the offender sins, this is true if it refers to him as a judge of the third sense, and to his law taken in the final sense of law, namely the coercive sense. And when it is assumed that the heretic sins against the divine law, this is to be granted. Therefore he will be judged, according to that law, by the judge of the third sense, namely Christ, in the other age only and not in this one, according to the ordinance of the lawgiver himself, which was of this kind. By him too he will be restrained with punishment or penalty, or rewarded, according to the observance or transgression of the precepts and counsels of the law. Such a judge of this law, namely the divine law, is not a bishop or any priest, but only a teacher in the first sense of the word, especially since this law is given to men for the state and condition of the present life. Again, we take the major premise of this syllogism as true in the sense we have described: that the judgment of a transgressor belongs to him as coercive judge, against whom the transgressor sins, or whose law he keeps, the law, I say, taken only in its final sense. Then this proposition is to be assumed as true: that the heretic sins against a judge of this age, taken in the third sense of "judge," and against the law of which he is the keeper, also taken in its final and proper sense, namely only the coercive sense, and not against another coercive law or judge in this age. Therefore he is to be judged in this age by such a coercive judgment, as the legislator of this law has ordained, and the penalty for transgression is to be exacted by the same judge, and if it is real, it is to be applied by this judge to the one to whom the human lawgiver has stated in the law that it is to be applied. Or the major premise must be distinguished by equivocation, as in the earlier argument. Thus it does not follow by necessity that anyone is to be condemned or judged as a heretic in this age and for this age by coercive judgment, whether really or personally, or in both ways. Therefore it does not follow that anyone is to be judged by a priest or bishop, except perhaps, as we have said, by the judgment of the first sense. Nor does it follow for this reason that the carnal or temporal goods of a heretic, which are exacted from him as the penalty or part of the penalty for his offence, ought to be given to any bishop or presbyter. Just as it does not follow that one who is judged as a counterfeiter of coin should be judged by moneyers, except perhaps by the judgment of the first sense, and not of the third, namely the coercive. Nor does it follow that the temporal goods exacted from him as a penalty ought to be given to moneyers, a collegium, or a single person. Rather, he ought to be judged by coercive judgment by the ruler, and the penalty applied according to the determination of human law.

units.la: Ad beatum Ambrosium dicendum, quod intellexit hæreticum seu crimen hæresis ad sacerdotum seu episcoporum iudicium pertinere, iudicio primæ significationis, non tertiæ. Hoc enim iudicio, autoritate propria nunquam vsus est episcoporum seu pontificum aliquis circa statum ecclesiæ primitiuæ, quamuis postmodum ad talia processerint occasionaliter ex quibusdam concessionibus principum sibi factis. Ideoque talium vera considerantibus initia, quæ nunc exabusione robur & faciem iuris habere videntur, velut somniorum phantastica videbuntur.
units.tr: As for blessed Ambrose, the answer is that he understood that the heretic, or the crime of heresy, belongs to the judgment of the bishops or priests in the first sense of judgment, not the third. For no bishop or pontiff ever used this judgment by his own authority in the state of the early Church, although afterwards they occasionally went beyond this through certain concessions made to them by princes. Therefore those who consider the true beginnings of these things, which now, through abuse, seem to have the force and face of law, will see them as the fantasies of dreams.

units.la: De iudice itaque, ac iudicio, & coactiua potestate infidelium & hæreticorum, determinatum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: Thus let it be determined concerning the judge, the judgment, and the coercive power over unbelievers and heretics.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De quibusdam signis, testimoniis, & exemplis tam ex canonica quam humana scriptura, quibus ostenditur verum esse, quod determinatum est quarto huius, & quinto, octavo, nono, & decimo tertio, circa statum episcoporum & generaliter sacerdotum: & cur Christus ipsorum statum, paupertatis scilicet, a statu principantium separauit.
units.tr: Concerning certain signs, testimonies and examples, drawn from canonical as well as human writings, by which it is shown that what was determined in the fourth, fifth, eighth, ninth and thirteenth chapters of this work is true, concerning the state of bishops and of priests in general; and why Christ separated their state, namely poverty, from the state of rulers.

units.la: QVoniam autem ex prioribus demonstratum est nobis tam canonicae scripturae autoritatibus, quam aliis quasi politicis evidentibus argumentis quibusdam, nulli episcopo aut presbytero vel alteri clerico iurisdictionem cuiusquam coactiua in hoc seculo convenire, Nunc volumus id declarare signis & testimoniis manifestis: quorum evidens est, quia nec Christum aut ipsius apostolorum aliquem unquam aut usquam quenquam iudicem aut ipsorum vicarium pro tali regimine seu iudicio faciendo instituisse legimus: cum tamen tam necessarium in humano conuictu, nec ipsum ignorasse aut neglexisse, nec ipsius apostolos, verisimile videatur. Si hoc ad ipsorum officium pertinere nouissent, & si ad suos successores episcopos aut presbyteros id spectare voluissent, super hoc praeceptum aut consilium tradidissent, verum de instituendis spiritualibus ministris, episcopis, presbyteris & diaconis formam tradiderunt & modum. Et hoc ad ipsorum officium pertinere, satis noscitur ex Apostoli sententia prima ad Timotheum tertio, ad Titum primo, & in aliis pluribusque scripturae locis apparet. Separauit autem Christus presbyterorum seu episcoporum officium ab eo quod principum, cum tamen potuisset ipse si voluisset, statum principis & officium sacerdotis exercere, & apostolos idem facturos similiter ordinasse. Sed sic noluit, imo tanquam conuenientius, qui simpliciter melius cuncta disposuit, haec officia suppositio & ratione distingui voluit. Quia etiam humilitatem & huius seculi contemptum Christus docere venerat, tanquam viam meriti salutis aeternae, ut prius humilitatem & mundi seu rerum temporalium contemptum exemplo quam verbo doceret. In summa quidem humilitate ac temporalium contemptu hunc mundum ingressus est, sciens ipse, quod non minus, imo magis opere seu exemplo docentur homines quam sermone. Unde Seneca epistolarum nona: Quid faciendum, a faciente discendum. Voluit igitur Christus, ut suo nos prius exemplo quam sermone doceret, in summa humilitate ac mundi contemptu seu paupertate nasci. Unde Lucae secundo: Pannis cum inuoluit, beata virgo scilicet, & reclinauit eum in praesepio. Ecce quod in aliena domo, ecce quod in praesepio, nisi scilicet bestiae locus erat & pabulum. Et verisimile quod alienis pannis, quia beata Virgo & Ioseph peregrini & viatores erant ibidem, pauper etiam natus, pauper vixit aetate proiectus. Unde loquens de sui paupertate Matthaei octavo, & Lucae nono dixit: Vulpes foueas habent & volucres caeli nidos, filius hominis non habet vbi reclinet caput. Et hunc statum, tanquam eum qui perfectionis, caeteris obseruatis vt decet praeceptis atque consiliis, docuit Christus eligere eos, qui sui volus esse discipuli & imitatores praecipui, & maxime successores ipsius in officio, quod in mundum venerat exercere. Unde Matthaei 19. Marci decimo, & Lucae 18. cuidam interroganti ab ipso, Magister bone, quid faciens, vitam aeternam possidebo? Dixit autem ei Iesus, Mandata nosti? Non occides, &c. qui ait; Haec omnia custodiui a iuuentute mea, quo audito, Iesus ait ei: Adhuc vnum tibi deest, vt si vis esse perfectus, vt dicitur in Matth. Omnia quaecunque habes vende & da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in caelo. Rursus eiusdem Lucae 14. dicebat discipulis. Sic ergo inquit Christus, Omnis ex vobis qui non renunciauerit omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus.
units.tr: Since it has been shown from what has gone before, both by the authority of canonical Scripture and by certain other evident political arguments, that no jurisdiction of coercion in this world belongs to any bishop, presbyter or other cleric, we now wish to declare this by clear signs and testimonies. It is plain that we never read that Christ, or any of his apostles, at any time or in any place, appointed any judge, or his own vicar, for such governing or judging. Yet this is so necessary in human society that it is not likely Christ was ignorant of it or neglected it, or that his apostles did. If they had known that this belonged to their office, and had wished it to pertain to their successors the bishops or presbyters, they would have handed down a precept or counsel about it. Instead they handed down the form and manner of appointing spiritual ministers: bishops, presbyters and deacons. That this belongs to their office is sufficiently clear from the apostle's words in the first letter to Timothy, chapter three, and in Titus, chapter one, and it appears in many other passages of Scripture. Christ separated the office of presbyters or bishops from that of princes, although he could have exercised the state of a prince and the office of a priest himself, had he wished, and could have ordained the apostles to do the same. But he did not wish this. Rather, as the more fitting course, since he arranged all things in the best way, he willed that these offices be distinguished by their very nature and reason. Christ had also come to teach humility and contempt for this world, as the way to the merit of eternal salvation. So he taught humility and contempt for the world, or for temporal things, by example before teaching by word. He entered this world in the greatest humility and contempt for temporal things, knowing that men are taught no less, indeed more, by deed or example than by speech. Hence Seneca, in the ninth of his letters: "What is to be done, is to be learned from one who does it." Christ therefore willed to teach us by his example before his word, and so to be born in the greatest humility and contempt for the world, that is, in poverty. Hence Luke, chapter two: "She wrapped him in swaddling cloths," namely the blessed virgin, "and laid him in a manger." Behold, in another's house, behold, in a manger, unless indeed it was the place and fodder of beasts. And it is likely that he was wrapped in borrowed cloths, since the blessed Virgin and Joseph were strangers and travellers there. Born poor, he also lived poor, and advanced in years. Hence, speaking of his own poverty in Matthew chapter eight and Luke chapter nine, he said: "Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head." And this state, as the state of perfection, Christ taught us to choose, while the other precepts and counsels are kept as is fitting. He taught that those who wished to be his disciples and chief imitators should choose it, and above all his successors in the office which he came into the world to exercise. Hence Matthew 19, Mark 10, and Luke 18, where Jesus is asked by a certain man: "Good Master, what shall I do to possess eternal life?" Jesus said to him: "Do you know the commandments? You shall not kill, etc." He answered: "All these things I have kept from my youth." When Jesus heard this he said to him: "One thing is still lacking to you. If you wish to be perfect, as it is said in Matthew: sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven." Again, in Luke chapter 14, he said to his disciples: "So then, Christ says, whoever of you does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple."

units.la: Ecce ergo quod status paupertatis & mundi contemptus decet omnem perfectum, praecipue Christi discipulum & successorem in officio pastorali, quinimo quasi necessarius est debenti suadere aliis mundi contemptum, si sua doctrina seu praedicatione proficere velit. Nam si talis diuitias possideat & principatus ambiat, qui eos quos alloquitur haec spernere docet, ipse quidem sui actione sermonem proprium manifeste redarguit. Vnde Chrysostomus contra tales in libro de compunctione cordis, inquit: Dicere & non facere, non solum lucri nihil, sed & damni plurimum. Grandis quidem enim condemnatio est componenti sermonem suum, vitam vero negligenti. Hoc etiam resonat philosophorum eximius decimo Ethicorum, cap. primo dicens: Cum enim dissonent, (sermones scilicet), ab his quae secundum sensum, (id est ab operibus dicentis, quae opera sententiunt) credenti, (id est componenti sermones,) verum interimunt. Et paulo post subdit: Conuenientes enim opera credentur, sermones scilicet. Et ideo qui nouit omnia qualiter fienda conuenientius, Christus scilicet, volens sermones credibiles fieri, quibus mundi docetur contemptus, vanitatum & carnalium voluptatum spretus & fuga, opera monuit sermonibus conformari. Vnde ad omnes talium futurous doctores in apostolorum persona, dicebat Matth. 5. Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, id est doctrina, quae luci comparatur. Sic, inquam, luceat, vt videant opera vestra bona. Vbi Glossa: Opera requirit vt videantur, & sic confirmetur doctrina: aliter enim sermonibus & doctrinae parum creditur. Vnde Glossa super illud Matthaei decimo, Nolite possidere aurum neque argentum: huius causam reddens, inquit: Si haec habeant, viderentur non causa salutis praedicare, sed lucri.
units.tr: Behold, then, the state of poverty and contempt for the world befits every perfect person, especially a disciple of Christ and a successor in the pastoral office. Indeed, it is almost necessary for one who wishes to persuade others to despise the world, if he wishes to make progress by his teaching or preaching. For if he possesses such riches and seeks dominion, while he teaches those whom he addresses to despise these things, he plainly refutes his own words by his own conduct. Hence Chrysostom, against such men, in his book on compunction of heart, says: "To speak and not to act is not only no gain but a great loss. For the condemnation is great for one who composes his words and neglects his life." The distinguished philosopher also echoes this in the first chapter of the tenth book of the Ethics, saying: "For when words (namely) disagree with the things that accord with the sense (that is, with the deeds of the speaker, which give the sense), they destroy the true belief (that is, the belief of those who compose the words)." And a little later he adds: "For words will be believed when deeds agree with them." And therefore Christ, who knows how all things are best done, wishing his words to be believable, by which contempt for the world, and the flight from and rejection of vanities and carnal pleasures, is taught, admonished that his deeds be conformed to his words. Hence, in the person of the apostles, he said to all future teachers of this kind in Matthew 5: "So let your light shine before men," that is, your teaching, which is compared to light. "So, I say, let it shine, that they may see your good works." Where the Gloss says: "Works demand to be seen, and so the teaching is confirmed; otherwise little credit is given to words and teaching." Hence the Gloss on that passage of Matthew 10, "Do not possess gold or silver," giving the reason for this, says: "If they had these things, they would seem to preach not for the cause of salvation but for gain."

units.la: Talia enim possidentes aliorum doctores siue pastores, magis destruunt hominum fidem & deuotionem suis oppositis operibus & exemplis, quam sermonibus confirment, eo quod his opera manifeste opponunt, ad quæ magis attendunt homines quam ad verba. Et formidandum valde, quin demum fidelem populum deducant suis peruersis exemplis operum ad desperationem futuri seculi. Talia nanque operantur quasi omnes ecclesiarum ministri, episcopi seu presbyteri & reliqui clerici consequenter. Manifestius autem ipsorum, qui super maiores thronos ecclesiæ sedent, vt futurum Dei iudicium in alio seculo nullatenus credere videantur. Qua enim, dicant quæso secundum Deum, conscientia, & si futurum credunt venturi seculi iustum Dei iudicium, Romani pontifices plurimi, & ipsorum Cardinales, aliique presbyteri seu episcopi, ad curas animarum & ecclesiastica temporalia pauperibus distribuenda præfecti, reliqui quoque quasi omnes, diaconi & clerici quilibet secundum sui facultatem ex furto vel rapina temporalium, quæ per devotos fideles statuta sunt & legata propter euangelizantium, & reliquorum pauperum sustentationem, quantas possunt denariorum summas, tradunt viuentes aut legant morientes non egentibus, sed sibi sanguinis affinitate coniunctis, aut aliis quibuslibet, eisdem bonis nullis dubium pauperes spoliantes? Qua etiam secundum Christianam religionem conscientia flagito, dicant viuentes ipsi temporaliter, qui propter euangelii ministerium contenti debent esse alimentis & his quibus tegantur secundum Apostolum prima ad Timotheum ultimo, in tot præternecessariis bona pauperum consumunt, equis, familiis, conuiuiis, ac reliquis vanitatibus & voluptatibus manifestis & occultis? Quæ vero de ecclesiasticorum officiorum & beneficiorum seu temporalium distributione fiunt inconuenientia perstranseo. Nam ipsorum plurima prece vel fauore potentum seculi obtinendis, aut pretio si phas sit dicere distributoribus aut intercessoribus Magi Symonis ministris oblato talia conferuntur ignorantibus, criminosis, pueris, incognitis, & inanis ac idiotis manifeste secundum totius vulgi sententiam. Cum tamen Apostolus prima ad Timotheum tertio præcipiat, officiales ecclesiasticos debere cognosci tanquam probatos & perfectos vita seu moribus & doctrina. Vnde vbi supra: Oportet autem illum, id est presbyterum seu episcopum, & testimonium habere bonum ab his qui foris sunt, quanto magis & ab his qui sunt intra ecclesiam? Et infra parum eodem: Diaconos similiter pudicos. Et hi autem probentur primum, & sic ministrent, nullum crimen habentes. Verumtamen hoc conuenienter poterit dicere quis, quod bene probantur horum plurimi vt nouit mundus, quantum scilicet pretium aut precem valeant exhibere. Quod ne singula inconuenientium denumerare tentemus tanquam impossibilium aut difficillimum valde, de presbyterorum seu episcoporum, cæterorumq; templi ministrorum quasi omnium actibus summam facientes, coram Christo testamur, eius si mentimur iudicium inuocantes, præfatos episcopos & reliquos fere omnes modernis temporibus, omnium quasi opposita perpetrare, quæ secundum doctrinam euangelicam aliis prædicant obseruanda. Voluptates, nanque vanitates, temporalia & seculi principatus exardent, & omni conamine, non iure, sed iniuria, occulta & manifesta prosequuntur & occupant, quæ tamen omnia Christus & veri eius imitatores apostoli spreuerunt & spernere docuerunt & præceperunt, eos maxime qui aliis euangelizare debent mundanorum contemptum. Poterat enim Christus si voluisset, si euangelizanti expedire vidisset, seruasse statum principis in hoc seculo, & in eo statu pati similiter. Sed fugit in montem vt statum talem abiiceret & abijci doceret; sicut ex Ioanne sexto supra inductum quarto huius. Talem enim statum gerere non decet euangelizantes ipsius contemptum, sed potius subiectorum & humilium, qualem in hoc seculo tam ipse quam ipsius apostoli seruauerunt. Econtra status paupertatis exterioris & abiectus nō decet principantem, quoniam expedit illi statum quem boni subditi reuereantur, & mali vereantur, per quem etiam si oporteat rebelles legum transgressores valeat coercere: quod nec facere posset conuenienter, si statum pauperem & deiectum haberet, propter quod etiam illi non conuenit euangelizantis officium. Si enim principans sin pulo suaderet statum paupertatis & abiectum, adhuc si quod percussus in vna maxilla percutienti offerat aliam: & rursum quod auferenti sibi tunicam, det quis pallium potius quam aduersus iniuriantem contendat iudicio, talia nec sibi faciliter crederentur, quia statu quem decet ipsum & quem gerit, suo repugnaret sermoni: amplius, sic inconuenienter ageret. Cum enim sua interesset per pœnam iniurias arcere, id etiam non requirentibus passis iniuriam, si prædicaret iniurias remittendas iniuriosis & prauis occasionem quandam amplius delinquendi præberet: & offensis seu passis iniustum, dubitationem aut suspicionem iustitiæ consequendæ, propter quod Christus qui omnia semper meliori modo disposuit, officia principantium & sacerdotum in eodem supposito coniungi noluit, sed potius separari. Hæc autem videtur beati Bernardi expressa sententia de consideratione ad Eugenium papam libro secundo cap. quarto, vbi sic ait: Ergo tu & tibi vsurpare aude, aut dominus apostolatum, aut apostolicum dominatum, plane ab vtroque prohiberis, si vtrunque simul habere voles, perdes vtrunque: Alioquin non te exceptum illorum numero putes, de quibus queritur Deus sic: Ipsi regnauerunt, & non per me, principes extiterunt & ego nō cognoui eos. Testantur autem dictis Decreta seu Historiæ quædam Romanorum pontificum, ipsis enim inscriptum reperitur, & ab eisdem approbatum priuilegium quoddam Constantini Romanorum Imperatoris, quo beato Syluestro Romano pontifici concessit iurisdictionem coactiuam super omnes mundi ecclesias, reliquosque presbyteros seu episcopos omnes. Cumque concessionem eam fuisse validam fateatur quilibet papa Romanus, & cum eo presbyterorum seu episcoporum reliquus coetus, consequenter ipsis concedendum est eundem Constantinum hanc iurisdictionem seu potestatem in eos primitus habuisse, præterea cum ad ipsos viuæ verborum scripturæ sacræ nulla talis iurisdictio in quenquam clericum aut laicum pertinere noscatur. Et hoc est quod beatus Bernardus dicit expresse ad Eugenium de consideratione libro & cap. quarto, inquit enim ibi: Petrus hic est, qui nescitur praecessisse aliquando, vel gemmis ornatus, vel sericis, nec tectus auro, nec vectus equo albo, nec stipatus milite, nec circumstrepentibus septus ministris. Absque his tamen satis credidit posse implere sali[ut]are mandatum. Si amas me, pasce oves meas. In his enim, secularibus videlicet apparatibus & potestatibus, successisti non Petro, sed Constantino. Principantium igitur officium non est sacerdotale inquantum huiusmodi, nec econuerso, de quorum tamen differentia rememoratum sit hoc modo:
units.tr: For men who possess such things, the teachers or pastors of others do more to destroy the faith and devotion of people by their contrary works and examples than they build up by their sermons, because their works plainly contradict their words, and people attend to deeds more than to words. It is greatly to be feared that they will at last lead the faithful people, by their perverse examples of conduct, to despair of the life to come. For nearly all the ministers of the churches, bishops or elders and the rest of the clergy in turn, act in just this way. Still more openly, those who sit on the highest thrones of the Church seem in no way to believe in the future judgement of God in the next life. For what conscience, I ask them, do they have before God? If they believe in the just judgement of God in the age to come, how can so many Roman pontiffs, and their Cardinals, and other elders or bishops appointed to the cure of souls and to distributing the temporal goods of the Church to the poor, and nearly all the rest, deacons and clergy of every kind, according to their means, out of the theft and plunder of temporal goods, which devoted faithful have set aside and bequeathed for the support of those who preach the gospel and of the other poor, hand over, while living, or bequeath, when dying, sums of money as large as they can, not to the needy, but to men joined to them by blood-relationship, or to others whoever they may be, undoubtedly robbing the poor of those same goods? With what conscience too, according to the Christian religion, I ask, do they themselves, who for the ministry of the gospel ought to be content with food and clothing, as the Apostle says in the last chapter of 1 Timothy, spend the goods of the poor on so many superfluous things: horses, households, feasts, and the other vanities and pleasures, open and hidden? As for the improprieties that occur in the distribution of ecclesiastical offices and benefices, or of temporal goods, I pass them over. For most of these are conferred, by the entreaty or favour of worldly powers, or, if it is lawful to say so, by a price offered to the distributors or intermediaries, the ministers of Simon Magus, upon people who are ignorant, criminal, boys, unknown, empty-headed and uneducated, plainly by the judgement of the whole common people. Yet the Apostle commands, in the third chapter of 1 Timothy, that church officers must be known as proved and perfect in life, morals and teaching. Hence, as above: It is necessary that he, that is, the elder or bishop, should have a good testimony from those who are outside; how much more from those who are within the Church? And a little further on in the same place: Likewise the deacons must be chaste. And let these also first be proved, and then let them minister, having no crime. Yet someone may fairly say that most of these men are well proved, as the world knows, in how much money or entreaty they can offer. Lest we attempt to list the individual improprieties, as if they were impossible or extremely difficult, we bear witness before Christ, calling on his judgement if we lie, and by summing up the acts of the elders or bishops and of nearly all the other ministers of the temple, that the bishops in question and nearly all the rest in modern times commit the opposite of everything they preach to others as to be observed according to the gospel teaching. For pleasures, vanities, temporal things and worldly dominion burn fiercely in them, and with every effort, not by right but by wrong, they pursue and seize them, both secretly and openly. Yet Christ and his true imitators, the apostles, despised all these things, and taught and commanded others to despise them, especially those who ought to preach the gospel to others, that they should scorn worldly things. For Christ could, if he had wished, and if he had seen it expedient for the one preaching the gospel, have kept the state of a prince in this world, and suffered in that state in the same way. But he fled into the mountain so that he might reject such a state and teach that it should be rejected; as is shown above from John 6, cited in chapter 4 of this book. For it does not befit those who preach the gospel to hold such a state, in contempt of him, but rather the state of the subject and the humble, which both he himself and his apostles kept in this world. On the contrary, a state of outward poverty and abasement does not befit a ruler, since it is expedient for him to have a state which good subjects revere and bad subjects fear, by which he may restrain even rebellious transgressors of the laws; and he could not do this fittingly if he had a poor and humble state, for which reason the office of preaching the gospel does not suit him either. For if a ruler were to persuade his people to a state of poverty and abasement, and to turn the other cheek to one who strikes them, and to give the cloak as well to one who takes their tunic, rather than contend against the injurer in court, such teaching would not easily be believed, because it would conflict with the state which befits him and which he holds, and with his own speech; moreover, he would act improperly in this way. For since it is his concern to restrain injuries by punishment, even when the injured do not ask for it, if he preached that injuries should be forgiven to the injurers, he would give a certain occasion for further wrongdoing to the wicked and perverse; and to the offended or injured he would cause injustice, and doubt or suspicion about obtaining justice. For this reason Christ, who has always arranged all things in the best way, did not wish the offices of rulers and priests to be joined in the same person, but rather separated. The clear opinion of blessed Bernard seems to be this, in his book On Consideration, addressed to Pope Eugenius, book 2, chapter 4, where he says: Therefore dare you to usurp either the lordship of an apostle or the apostolic lordship; you are plainly forbidden from both; if you wish to have both at once, you will lose both. Otherwise do not think yourself excepted from the number of those of whom God complains thus: They have reigned, but not by me; they have been princes, and I have not known them. Moreover, certain Decrees or Histories of the Roman pontiffs bear witness to these words, for there is found in them a certain privilege of Constantine, Emperor of the Romans, inscribed to them and approved by them, by which he granted to blessed Sylvester, Roman pontiff, coercive jurisdiction over all the churches of the world and all the other elders or bishops. Since every Roman pontiff admits that this grant was valid, and with him the rest of the company of elders or bishops, it follows that it must be conceded that the same Constantine first had this jurisdiction or power over them; moreover, since no such jurisdiction over any clergyman or layman is known to pertain to them by the living words of Holy Scripture. And this is what blessed Bernard says expressly, in to Eugenius, On Consideration, book and chapter 4; for he says there: This is Peter, who is not known ever to have gone before, either adorned with jewels or with silk, nor covered with gold, nor carried on a white horse, nor attended by a soldier, nor surrounded by a noisy crowd of ministers. Yet without these he believed that he could fulfil the command: If you love me, feed my sheep. For in these secular trappings and powers you have succeeded not Peter, but Constantine. The office of rulers, therefore, is not priestly insofar as it is such, nor conversely; and the difference between them has been recalled in this way:

units.la: CAP: XII.
units.tr: CAP: XII.

units.la: De distinctione quarundam dictionum necessaria propter determinationem quaestorum, circa statum paupertatis suprema.
units.tr: On the distinction of certain terms necessary for settling the questions about the highest state of poverty.

units.la: Sic igitur singulariter nobis ostenso, Christum & ipsius Apostolos viatores, statum paupertatis & humilitatis docuisse atque seruasse: certumque tenendum sit fidelibus, doctrinam seu consilium omne Christi & apostolorum aeternae vitae meritorium aliqualiter extitisse: Conuenienter utique inquirendum videtur de ipsorum paupertate, quae, qualis, quantaque fuerit, ne imitari volentes eosdem, hanc lateat viatores.
units.tr: Since we have thus shown plainly that Christ and his Apostles, as wayfarers, taught and observed a state of poverty and humility, and since it must be firmly held by the faithful that all the teaching and counsel of Christ and the apostles was in some way meritorious of eternal life, it seems fitting to inquire into their poverty: what kind it was and how great, lest it remain hidden from wayfarers who wish to imitate them.

units.la: Huiusmodi ergo tentantes inquisitionem, primum dicturi sumus, quid est quod dicitur, & quot modis paupertas aut pauperem esse, similiter autem & diutem esse. Videntur enim haec inuicem opponi quandoque velut habitus & priuatio, quandoque ut contraria: deinde vero nominum horum utrumque distinguemus in suos modos, & ipsorum descriptiones subiungemus. Vt si qua sit paupertas meritoria, & ipsius modorum aliquis perfectionis ordo inuicem, quisque aliorum summus aut primus nobis appareat. Et quoniam diuitem omnes eum dicunt, qui licitam seu de iure potestatem habet vel dominium aut possessionem rerum temporalium, quas vocant diuitias in proprio vel communi, aut utroque modo. Pauperem autem vocant illum, qui bonis talibus priuatus est, ne propter usus varietatem quorundam iam dictorum nominum, quibus ad propositum nostrum indigebimus vt sententia, quam explicare volumus, extet ambigua. Distinguemus primum significata seu modos eorum. Sunt autem nomina haec, ius, dominium, possessio, proprium, & commune, diues, & pauper.
units.tr: In undertaking this inquiry, we shall first say what is meant by the term, and in how many ways one is poor, and likewise rich. For these terms sometimes seem to be opposed to each other as a state (habitus) and its privation, and sometimes as contraries. Then we shall distinguish each of these names into its modes and append their descriptions, so that, if there is some meritorious poverty, and some order of perfection among its modes, the highest or first of each may appear to us. Now, everyone calls rich the one who has lawful or rightful power, or ownership, or possession of temporal goods, which they call riches, whether as private or common, or in both ways. They call poor the one who is deprived of such goods. So that the opinion we wish to explain may not remain ambiguous, because of the variety of usage of some of the names mentioned, which we shall need for our purpose, we shall first distinguish their meanings or modes. These names are: right, dominion, possession, property, common, rich, and poor.

units.la: Incipiemus autem distinguere significata iuris, quoniam ipsis indigebimus in aliorum assignationibus & distinctionibus, non econuerso. Ius igitur in vna sui significatione dicitur de lege dicta secundum tertiam & ultimam legis significationem, de qua fuit habitum decimo primae, quae siquidem duplex est, vna quidem humana, reliqua vero diuina, quae etiam secundum aliquod tempus & modum venit in vltimam legis significationem, vt dictum est vbi supra. De harum vero legum natura & qualitate, ipsarumque conuenientia & differentia sufficienter diximus octauo huius & nono.
units.tr: We shall begin by distinguishing the meanings of right, since we shall need it in the assignments and distinctions of the others, and not the reverse. Right, then, in one of its senses, is said of law, taken according to the third and last meaning of law, which was discussed in the tenth chapter of the first book. This law is twofold: one human, the other divine. And it also, according to some time and manner, comes to the last meaning of law, as was said above. Of the nature and quality of these laws, and of their agreement and difference, we have spoken sufficiently in the eighth and ninth chapters of this book.

units.la: De quibus etiam resumentes ad propositum, dicamus ipsarum conuenientiam in eo primum, quod utraque lex est praeceptum vel prohibitio aut permissio actuum qui prouenire tunc nati ab imperio mentis humanae. Differunt autem, quoniam primum coactiuum est in hoc secundo transgredientium illud: secundum vero, diuinum scilicet minime, sed in futuro tantummodo. Dicitur autem praeceptum dupliciter, vno quidem modo actiue, de actu scilicet praecipientis, quomodo solemus dicere, velle aliquod imperantis expressum esse praeceptum, vt regis aut alterius principantis. Alio modo dicitur praeceptum de ipso volito peractum praecipientis, quo modo solemus dicere seruum fecisse praeceptum domini, non quidem quod actum domini qui est praecipere aut imperare fecerit seruus, sed quoniam volitum fieri per actum seu imperium domini fecit seruus. Et propterea quoties hoc nomen praeceptum refertur ad praecipientem, idem est quod actus imperandi: quoties vero ad subditum, idem est quod volitum fieri per actum imperandi, passiue dictum.
units.tr: Returning to our purpose, let us state first how they agree: each law is a command, prohibition, or permission of acts that arise from the will of the human mind. They differ in that the first is coercive, binding those who transgress it, whereas the second, namely the divine law, is not coercive at all, but only in the future. The word command is used in two ways. In one way it is active, that is, it refers to the act of the one commanding, as we commonly say that a king or other ruler has issued an express command. In the other way, command is said passively of the thing commanded, as we commonly say that a servant has carried out his master's command. Not that the servant performed the master's act of commanding or ordering, but that by the master's act or order the servant brought about the thing willed. Therefore, whenever this word command is referred to the one commanding, it means the act of commanding; whenever it is referred to the subject, it means the thing willed to be done through the act of commanding, used passively.

units.la: Hoc ergo nomen praeceptum actiue sumptum & communiter dicitur de ordinatione seu statuto legislatoris tam affirmatiuo quam negatiuo ad poenam obligante transgressorem, secundum tamen vsum modernum proprie sumitur pro statuto affirmatiuo. Quoniam statutum affirmatiuum non habet ex vsu nomen proprium, sed nomen commune sibi retinuit. Statutum vero negatiuum sibi nomen habet proprium, quoniam prohibitum dicitur.
units.tr: This word command, taken actively, is commonly applied to the ordinance or statute of a lawgiver, whether affirmative or negative, binding the transgressor to a penalty. According to modern usage, however, it is properly taken for an affirmative statute, since an affirmative statute has no proper name by usage but has kept the common name for itself. A negative statute, on the other hand, has its own proper name, for it is called prohibited.

units.la: Voco autem affirmatiuum statutum, quo fieri aliquid ordinatur; negatiuum quo aliquid ordinatur non fieri, & si fuerit talis ordinatio affirmatiua obligans transgressorem ad poenam, vocatur praeceptum. Si vero negatiua sit, etiam obligans vocatur prohibitum, quod siquidem prohibitio duplicit er dicitur actiue atque passiue, quemadmodum & praeceptum. Hae autem duae ordinationes obligatae ad poenam scilicet, vt plurimum in legibus sunt expressae, vel secundum proprium speciem, vel secundum similem aut proportionalem. Alio vero modo sumitur praeceptum magis stricte in lege diuina, similiter & prohibitum pro eo solo statuto, siue affirmatiuo siue negatiuo, quod obligat ad poenam aeternam, quomodo vsus ipsorum est apud Theologos, dicentes praecepta sunt de necessitate salutis, id est obseruan-da. danecessario, si debeat quis saluari. Unde Lucæ 18. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata, i.e. præcepta. Sunt autem aliæ quædam ordinationes expressæ vel intellectæ tantum in legibus, tam affirmatiuæ quam etiam negatiuæ, siue circa eundem actum, siue circa diuersum facientem aut omittentem, non obligantes ad pœnam, vt actum liberalitatis exercere vel omittere. Similiter & aliorum plurimorum quorundam. Et talia proprie dicuntur lege permissa, quamuis hoc nomen permissum communiter sumptum, quandoque dicatur de statutis obligantibus ad pœnam. Nam omne quod lege fieri præcipitur, fieri permittitur, licet non econuerso. Sic etiam quod lege prohibetur fieri, lege permittitur non fieri. Horum vero rursum permissorum proprie, nō obligatium scilicet, quædam sunt meritoria secundum legem diuinam & vocantur consilia, quædam vero minime, absolute nomine vocata permissa, quæ etiam sic sumpta & proprie dupliciter dicuntur actiue atque passiue, quemadmodum prohibita & præcepta. Hæc tamen vt plurimum secundum suam speciem non exprimuntur in legibus, præsertim humanis propter eorum multitudinem, & quoniam ipsorum ordinatio generali sufficiens est in hoc. Omne .n.quod lege non est præceptum aut prohibitum, intelligitur legislatoris ordinatione permissum. Est igitur præceptum secundum legem in propria significatione statutum affirmatiuum, obligans ad pœnam transgressorem illius: Prohibitum vero proprie statutum negatiuum ad pœnam obligans est: Permissum vero proprie dicitur ordinatio legislatoris ad pœnam neminem obligans, iuxta quas significationes, proprias scilicet, his nominibus vtendum est. Ex his autem conuenienter apparere potest, quid est quod licitum dicitur, quoniam omne factum iuxta legis præceptum aut permissionem, vel omissum iuxta legis prohibitionem vel permissionem licite factum vel omissum est, & licitum dici potest, eius vero contrarium seu oppositum illicitum. Hinc etiam nobis apparere potest, quid est quod phas appellari solet: est enim phas in vna significatione id quod licitum quasi conuertibiliter. In alia vero significatione importat hoc nomen phas, id quod legislator in aliquo casu permisisse rationabiliter præsumitur, quamuis tale aliquid sit absolute prohibitum seu regulariter, vt pet alienum agrum transire quandoque, aut rem alienam contrectare absque domini expresso consensu phas est, licet non sit ius dictum regulariter secundum aliquem dictorum modorum. Nam alicuius rei contrectatio regulariter prohibita est, in casu tamen phas est, in quo rei domi nus rationabiliter præsumitur consentire, quamuis hoc non concedat expresse propter quod in talibus quandoque opus est epieikeia. Sic igitur secundam vnam significationem ius idem est quod lex diuina vel humana, seu secundum has præceptum aut prohibitum & permissum. Est autem & alia quædam iuris & proprie humani diuisio in ius naturale atque ciuile. Et dicitur ius naturale secundum Aristot. quarto Ethicorum, tractatu de iustitia, statutum illud legislatoris, in quo tanquam bonitto & obseruando quasi omnes conueniunt, vt Deum esse colendum, parentes honorandos, humanas proles vsque ad tempus parentibus educandas, nemini iniuriandum, iniurias licite repellendum, & similia reliqua: quæ licet sicut ab humana institutione pendentia transumptiue iura dicuntur naturalia, quoniam eodem modo creduntur apud omnes regiones licita, & eorum opposita illicita, quemadmodum actus naturalium non habentium propositum conformiter apud omnes proueniunt, velut ignis qui sic ardet hic, sicut in ipsis.
units.tr: I call an affirmative statute one by which something is ordained to be done, and a negative one by which something is ordained not to be done. If such an affirmative ordinance binds the transgressor to a penalty, it is called a command. If it is negative and likewise binds, it is called a prohibition, and this prohibition, like command, is said in both an active and a passive sense. These two ordinances that bind to a penalty are for the most part expressed in laws, either in their proper species or in a similar or proportional one. In another and stricter sense, however, command is used in divine law, and likewise prohibition for that statute alone, whether affirmative or negative, which binds to eternal punishment. This is how the theologians use the terms, saying that commands are necessary for salvation, that is, they must be observed if one is to be saved. Hence Luke 18: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments, that is, the commands. There are also other ordinances, expressed or only understood in laws, both affirmative and negative, whether concerning the same act or concerning a different act of the doer or omitter, which do not bind to a penalty, such as to exercise or to omit an act of liberality, and likewise many others of this kind. Such things are properly called permitted by law, although the word permitted, taken in its common sense, is sometimes applied to statutes that do bind to a penalty. For everything that the law commands to be done is also permitted to be done, though not conversely. Likewise, what the law forbids to be done is permitted by the law not to be done. Of these permitted things, properly speaking (that is, those that do not bind), some are meritorious according to divine law and are called counsels, while others are not, and are simply called permitted. These too, so taken and properly speaking, are said in two ways, actively and passively, just as prohibited and commanded are. Yet these for the most part are not expressed in laws according to their species, especially human laws, on account of their number, and because a general ordinance suffices for them. For whatever is neither commanded nor forbidden by law is understood to be permitted by the ordinance of the lawgiver. Therefore, according to law in its proper meaning, a command is an affirmative statute binding the transgressor to a penalty; a prohibition is properly a negative statute binding to a penalty; and permission is properly an ordinance of the lawgiver binding no one to a penalty. These names are to be used in these proper senses. From this it can fitly be seen what is meant by lawful: whatever is done in accordance with a legal command or permission, or omitted in accordance with a legal prohibition or permission, is done or omitted lawfully, and may be called lawful; its contrary or opposite is unlawful. From this too it can be seen what is usually called phas. In one sense phas is, as it were, interchangeable with what is lawful. In another sense the word phas means that which the lawgiver is reasonably presumed to have permitted in some case, although such a thing is absolutely or generally prohibited. For example, to cross another's field at times, or to handle another's property without the owner's express consent, is phas, although it is not right in the usual sense of any of the modes mentioned. For the handling of a thing is generally prohibited, yet in the case where the owner is reasonably presumed to consent, though he does not expressly grant it, it is phas; and in such matters there is sometimes need of [ἐπιείκεια] epieikeia, that is, equity. Thus, in one sense, right is the same as divine or human law, or, according to these, the command, prohibition, and permission. There is also another division of right, properly human, into natural and civil right. According to Aristotle in the fourth book of the Ethics, in the treatise on justice, natural right is that statute of the lawgiver in which almost all agree as good and to be observed, such as that God is to be worshipped, parents honoured, human offspring, until they come of age, to be educated by their parents, no one is to be wronged, wrongs may lawfully be repelled, and the other similar things. Although these, being dependent on human institution, are called natural rights in a transferred sense, it is because they are believed to be equally lawful in all regions, and their opposites unlawful, just as the actions of natural things that have no purpose arise uniformly everywhere, as fire burns here just as it does there.

units.la: Sunt tamen quidam, qui ius naturale vocant, rectæ rationis agibilium dictamen, quod sub iure diuino collocant, propterea quod omne factum secundum legem diuinam, & secundum rectæ rationis consilium simpliciter est licitum. Non tamen omne factum secundum leges humanas, quoniam in quibusdam a recta ratione deficiunt, verum naturale hic & supra æquiuocedicitur. Multa enim sunt secundum rectæ rationis dictamen, vt quæ videlicet non omnibus sunt per se nota, & per consequens neque confessa, quæ non ab omnibus nationibus concedantur tanquam honesta. Sic etiam secundum legem diuinam sunt quædam præcepta prohibita vel permissa, quæ se habent in hoc conformiter humanæ legi, quod quia notum est in pluribus, exempla prætermisi propter abbreuiationem sermonis.
units.tr: There are, however, some who call natural law the dictate of right reason concerning things to be done, and they place it under divine law, because every act done according to divine law and the counsel of right reason is simply lawful. Yet not every act done according to human laws is lawful in this way, since in some cases they fall short of right reason. The word natural is used equivocally here and above. For there are many things that accord with the dictate of right reason but are not known per se to all, and consequently are not admitted by all nations as honourable. Likewise, according to divine law, there are certain precepts, prohibitions or permissions that agree with human law in this respect: since they are well known to most people, I omit the examples for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Et inde etiam est, quod quædam licita sunt secundum legem humanam, quæ non licent secundum legem diuinam, & econuerso. Veruntamen licitum & illicitum simpliciter attendenda sunt secundum legem diuinam potius quam humanam, in quibus dissonant præceptis prohibitis aut permissis. Dicitur autem ius secundo modo de omni humano actu, potestate vel habitu acquisito, imperato, interiori vel exteriori, tam immanente quam transeunte in rem aliquam exteriorem, aut in rei aliquid, puta vsum aut vsufructum, acquisitionem, detentionem, seu conseruationem, aut commutationem, & reliqua similia, conformiter iuri dicto secundum priorem significationem. Quod autem sit rei vsus aut vsufructus cum aliis rei licitis contrectationibus seu de iure a scientia ciuilium actuum supponatur ad præsens.
units.tr: Hence it also follows that some things are lawful according to human law which are not lawful according to divine law, and conversely. Nevertheless, what is lawful and unlawful in the absolute sense must be judged according to divine law rather than human law, wherever they disagree in their prohibitions or permissions. Law, however, is used in a second sense of every human act, power or acquired habit, commanded, inward or outward, whether immanent or transeunt, directed at some external thing or at some aspect of a thing, such as use or usufruct, acquisition, holding or preservation, or exchange, and other similar things, in accordance with law as understood in the first sense. Whether the use or usufruct of a thing, together with other lawful dealings with it, is to be taken as a matter of right, is presupposed for the present from the science of civil acts.

units.la: Secundum hanc quidem significationem soliti sumus dicere, hoc ius aliquando esse, cum rem aliquam iuri primo modo dicto conformiter vult aut tractat. Unde talis contrectatio vel voluntas ius dicitur, quoniam iuri conformatur in eo quod præcipit, prohibet, aut permittit: quemadmodum columna dextra dicitur aut sinistra, cum animalis dextro vel sinistro secundum situm propinquior extiterit. Ius igitur dictum hoc modo secundo, nil aliud est quam volitum præcepto, vel prohibitione aut permissione actiua legislatoris, quod quasi præceptum prohibitum aut permissum passiue pridem diximus. Et est
units.tr: In this second sense we are accustomed to say that this is a right at some time, when someone wills or deals with a thing in conformity with law in the first sense. Hence such a dealing or will is called a right, because it conforms to the law in what it commands, forbids or permits, just as a column is called right or left when it stands nearer to the right or left side of an animal. Law taken in this second sense is therefore nothing other than what is willed by the active command, prohibition or permission of the lawgiver, which we earlier called a precept, prohibition or permission passively. And this is

units.la: T hoc etiam quod prius licitum dicebamus. Importat autem tamen hoc nomen ius sententiam iudicantium secundum legem seu iudicia ipsorum secundum ius dictum iuxta primam significationem quomodo dicere solent iudicem seu principatem ius alicui fecisse aut reddidisse, dum ipsum per sententiam legalem damnavit aut soluit. Dicitur autem amplius ius de actu aut habitu particularis iustitiae, quomodo iustum velle dicimus eum, qui æquale aut proportionale vult in commutationibus aut distributionibus.
units.tr: also what we earlier called the lawful. The word law also signifies, however, the sentence of those who judge according to law, or their judgments according to law in the first sense, in the way that we are accustomed to say that a judge or ruler has done or rendered right to someone when he condemned or acquitted him by a legal sentence. Furthermore, law is said of an act or habit of particular justice, as when we call a man just who wills what is equal or proportionate in exchanges or distributions.

units.la: Hinc vero habitum est distinguere modos seu signata dominii: quod quidem significat stricte sumptum, potestatem principalem vendicandi rem aliquam quæsitam iure dicto secundum primum modum: potestatem inquam scientis & non dissentientis in hoc, volentis etiam nemini alteri licere rem illam contrectare absque sui dominantis scilicet, dum illi dominatur, expresso consensu. Hæc autem potestas nil aliud est quam actuale aut habituale velle sic habendi rem iure quæsitam, ut diximus: quæ siquidem alicuius ius dicitur, quoniam iuri primo modo dicto conformis, secundum quem modum etiam columnam dextram aut sinistram esse iam diximus, cum ad animalis dextera aut sinistra secundum propinquitatem vere fuerit comparata. Dicitur autem rursum hoc nomen communiter magis de potestate iam dicta, sive fuerit in rem tantum, sive in usum aut usumfructum tantum, sive in hæc omnia simul. Dicitur amplius idem nomen de potestate iam dicta, non tamen scientis aut consentientis, neq; dissentientis expresse seu renunciantis: quo modo infanti & absenti aut alteri cuilibet ignoranti, capaci tn, acquiri potest res aliqua vel ei aliquid cum dominio seu potestate ipsam mendicandi ab auferre seu auferre volente per se vel alium coram iudice coactiuo. Dictum est autem non dissentientis, quoniam expresse dissentienti seu renuntianti rei aliquam aut rei aliquid, non acquiruntur talia, neq; ipsa vendicandi dominii aut potestas. Potest. n. quilibet renunciare licite iuri pro se introducto secundum humanas leges, neq; ad iuris beneficium compellitur quis invitus secundum legem aliquam. Sunt autem iam dicta dominia legalia, quoniam legis seu ipsius latoris ordinatione, ac hominum electione acquiruntur seu acquisibilia sunt. Adhuc dicitur nomen dominii de humana voluntate seu libertate secundum se, cum ipsius executiua seu motiua organica potestate non impedita. His enim possumus in actus aliquos & ipsorum oppositos, propter quod etiam dicitur homo inter animalia cætera, suorum actuum habere dominium: quod siquidem a natura inest homini, non voluntarie seu electione quæsitum.
units.tr: From this it has been customary to distinguish the modes or senses of dominion. In its strict sense it signifies the principal power of claiming for oneself some thing acquired by law in the first sense: the power, I say, of one who knows of it and does not dissent, and who also wills that no other person may handle that thing without the express consent of his owner, that is, of the one who holds dominion over it. This power is nothing other than an actual or habitual will to hold the thing thus acquired by right, as we have said. It is called a person's right because it conforms to law in the first sense, in which sense we have already said that a column is right or left when it has been truly placed in relation to the right or left side of an animal according to nearness. This name is commonly applied more widely to the power just mentioned, whether it extends only to the thing, or only to its use or usufruct, or to all of these together. The same name is applied further to the power just mentioned when the person does not know of it or consent to it, nor expressly dissent or renounce it: thus a thing, or something belonging to it, may be acquired for an infant, for an absent person, or for anyone else who is ignorant but nevertheless capable, with dominion or the power of claiming it from one who wishes to take it away, whether by himself or through another before a coercive judge. It is said "who does not dissent," because such things, or the power of claiming dominion over them, are not acquired for one who expressly dissents or renounces the thing or something belonging to it. For anyone may lawfully renounce a right introduced for himself under human laws, and no one is compelled against his will to accept the benefit of a law. The dominions just mentioned are legal, because they are acquired, or are capable of being acquired, by the ordinance of the law or of its very author, and by the choice of men. Finally, the name of dominion is also applied to human will or liberty in itself, when the power that executes or moves its bodily organs is not impeded. For by this we can have dominion over certain acts and their opposites; this is why man, among the other animals, is said to have dominion over his own acts. This dominion is indeed inborn in man from nature and is not acquired by will or choice.

units.la: Consequenter distinguendum est hoc nomen possessio, quod quidem sumptum large significat uno modo idem quod dominium dictum secundum primam aut secundam significationem vel tertiam, aut rem temporalem aliquam in comparatione ad sic habentem & habere volentem, quemadmodum dictum est in duabus prioribus dominii significationibus. Unde Gen. 13. Erat autem dives valde in possessione auri & argenti, & eiusdem 17. Dabo tibi & semini tuo omnem terram Chanaam in possessionem æternam. Alio modo & magis stricte dicitur possessio de dominio iam dicto cum actuali contrectatione corporali, præsenti vel præterita, rei vel usus aut usufructus ipsius, quo modo nomine hoc utuntur plurimum in scientia civilium actuum. Amplius dicitur hoc nomen de licita contractione corporali rei suæ, vel etiam alienæ. Unde Actuum quarto: Nec quisquam eorum quæ possidebat aliquid suum esse dicebat, sed erant illis omnia communia. Dicitur autem rursum possessio, licet improprie de re detentione illicita in præsenti vel præterito, per se vel alium corporaliter contrectata.
units.tr: Next we must distinguish the term possession, which, taken broadly, signifies in one way the same as dominion in the first, second or third sense, or some temporal thing in relation to one who has it and wishes to have it, as was said of the two earlier senses of dominion. Hence Gen. 13. "And Abram was very rich in possession of gold and silver," and in the same book, chapter 17: "I will give to thee and to thy seed after thee all the land of Canaan for an everlasting possession." In another and stricter sense, possession is said of the dominion just described together with actual bodily handling, present or past, of the thing or its use or usufruct; this is the sense in which the term is chiefly used in the science of civil acts. Further, the term is applied to lawful bodily handling of one's own thing, or even of another's. Hence Acts 4: "Neither did any of them say that aught of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common." Possession is also said, though improperly, of an unlawful holding of a thing, present or past, which has been bodily handled by oneself or another.

units.la: Nunc autem sequitur distinguere nomen proprii & communis. Dicitur autem proprium proprietas vno modo de dominio dicto secundum primam significationem, quomodo utuntur ipso in scientia civilium actuum. Dicitur rursum magis large sumedo, et de dominio dicto secundum eius significationem tam primam quam secundam, quomodo usus eius est apud Theologos, etiam in sacra scriptura plerunque. Amplius dicitur hoc nomen proprium & proprietas famose magis apud Theologos de singularitate personæ vel rei, aut rei aliquo pertinentibus ad unica personam tantum, non cum alia. Sic enim sumunt proprium, distinguentes ipsum contra commune, qui quærunt, utrum perfectius seu magis meritorium æternæ vitæ sit habere temporalia in proprio, id est singulariter quam habere talia cum alio vel aliis in communi. Dicitur autem rursum hoc nomen proprium sive proprietas de accidente alicui subiecto inhærente per se quo modo utuntur philosophi nomine hoc, in eo tamen famosius quod convertitur cum subiecto. Hoc autem nomen commune quantum ad propositum pertinet, sumitur oppositæ duabus significationibus proprii posterius dictis.
units.tr: We must now distinguish the terms proper and common. "Proper" (proprium) or "property" (proprietas) is used in one way of dominion in the first sense, as they use it in the science of civil acts. It is used again, more broadly, of dominion in both its first and second senses, as it is customarily used by theologians, and very often in Holy Scripture. Further, the term "proper" and "property" is more famously used by theologians of the singularity of a person or thing, or of something belonging to a thing, that pertains to one person only and not to another. For in this sense they take "proper," distinguishing it from "common," when they ask whether it is more perfect, or more meritorious of eternal life, to have temporal goods as one's own, that is, singularly, than to have them in common with another or others. Finally, the term "proper" or "property" is also used of an accident inhering per se in some subject, as philosophers use the word; but in this sense it is most famously applied to what is convertible with the subject. The term "common," as far as our purpose is concerned, is taken in opposition to the two senses of "proper" stated last.

units.la: Reliquum vero nobis est distinguere modos horum nominum pauper & dives. dicitur autem hoc nomen dives famose magis de habente sibi superabundantiam rerum temporalium quas vocant divitias simul pro quolibet tempore: præsenti atq; futuro & licite. Alio vero dicitur dives de habente sibi licite res prædictas solum sufficientes simul pro quolibet præsenti atque futuro. Dicitur autem adhuc dives dupliciter & magis proprie, primum quidem de habente res iam dictas superabundantes etiam ut dictum est, vel sic eas habere volente, alio rursum modo de habente iam dictas res sufficienter solum ut etiam dictum est in secundo modo, vel sic eas habere volente. His autem quasi oppositæ privatiue duobus prioribus modis dicitur pauper: vno quidem, qui primatus est superabundantibus solum: alio vero modo, qui etiam sufficientia pro quolibet tempore non simul habet. Tertio vero modo dicitur pauper oppositæ diviti, quasi contrarie, primum quidem. lato qui sponte vult primariis abundantibus pro quolibet tempore. Quarto vero modo de eo qui etiam sufficientes pro quolibet praesenti atque futuro, non vult simul habere, sed ipsis vult quandoque sponte carere. debes autem attendere, quod inus iuxta secundum & 4. modum pauperis est iuxta primum & 3. paupertatis modum. Unde non quilibet modus paupertatis & pauperis opponitur cuilibet modo divitis indifferenter. Nec oportet omittere, quod sententiarum pauperum, sunt quidam abdicantes temporalia propter finem honestum, & convenienti modo. Alii vero talia videntur abdicare, non propter hoc, sed propter inanem gloriam, aut aliam aliquam mundanam fallaciam committendam. Est etiam cum his attendendum, quod rerum temporalium, quas vocant divitias, quaedam sunt quae sui & communi hominum institutione vnico aliquo actu vel usu consumptibiles sunt, quemadmodum cibi, potus, medicinae, ac reliqua similia: quaedam vero sunt quae manentia pluribus visibus deseruire sunt nata, vt ager & domus, securis & vestis, equus aut seruus. Sunt autem iam dictorum nominum significationes aliae fortasse, famosiores tamen ipsarum & modos nostro proposito magis attinentes, enumerasse putamus: quas siquidem secernere atque describere vel diffinire proprie, difficile est propter vsus eorum varietatem apud diversos & eosdem etiam artifices loca & tempora. Fere autem igitur nomina vnumquodq; dicitur multifariam, vt in De generatione scribitur lib. primo.
units.tr: It remains for us to distinguish the senses of the terms poor and rich. The word rich is most famously applied to one who has for himself a superabundance of temporal things, which they call riches, at once for every time, present and future, and lawfully. In another sense, one is called rich who lawfully has for himself such things merely sufficient, at once for every time, present and future. Again, one is called rich in two ways and more properly: first, of one who has the aforesaid things superabundant, as has been said, or who wills to have them thus; and second, of one who has the aforesaid things merely sufficient, as also has been said in the second sense, or who wills to have them thus. Opposed to these two former senses, as privations, is the term poor: in the first sense, of one who has only superabundant things at the first; and in the second sense, of one who does not have at once what is sufficient for every time. In the third sense, one is called poor in direct opposition to the rich, as contrary: namely, one who of his own accord wishes to have, at first, abundance for every time. In the fourth sense, one is called poor who, though he has what is sufficient for every present and future time, does not wish to have it all at once, but at times wishes to be voluntarily without it. You should note that the lesser in the second and fourth senses of poor is in accordance with the first and third senses of poverty.
