Hence not every mode of poverty and of the poor is opposed indifferently to every mode of the rich. Nor must we omit that among the opinions of the poor there are some who renounce temporal things for an honourable end and in a proper manner, while others seem to renounce such things not for that reason, but out of empty glory or for some other worldly deceit. Along with these things we must also note that among the temporal things which they call riches, some are consumed by a single act or use, by their own nature and by human institution, such as food, drink, medicines and other similar things; others are by nature such that, remaining, they serve many uses, such as a field and a house, an axe and a garment, a horse or a slave. We think we have listed the other senses of these terms, perhaps, and the more famous ones, and those that more closely bear on our purpose; but to separate, describe or properly define them is difficult, because of their variety of use among different people, and even among the same craftsmen at different places and times. Indeed, nearly every word is said in many ways, as is written in the first book of De generatione.

units.la: CAP. XIII. De statu iam dicta paupertatis, quem evangelicam perfectionem dicere solent, & quod hunc Christus & ipsius apostoli seruauerunt.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the state of poverty mentioned above, which they are accustomed to call evangelical perfection, and that Christ and his apostles observed it.

units.la: HIs itaq; modis & significationibus doctorum nominum sic distinctis, conclusiones aliquas inferemus, primam quidem quod rem aliquam temporalem aut rei aliquid, puta vsufructus aut similia in proprio vel communi suam vel alienam, non potest aliquis licite contrectare sine iure seu non habens in ea vel eius aliquo ius dictum secundum primam & secundam iuris significationem. Nam omne factum, non praeceptum aut permissum iure fieri, est non licitum, vt ex diffinitione liciti cuilibet euidenter apparet: nec oportet immorari ad hoc probandum, quoniam omnibus quasi per se notum est. Secundo possumus ex dictis inferre, quod rem aliquam aut eius aliquid potest aliquis licite contrectare secundum vnam legem, puta diuinam, & illicite secundam aliam, vt humanam. Similiter e conuerso. Rursum idem facere licite aut idem etiam illicite facere secundum vtrunque. Hoc autem videre non est difficile, quoniam praecepta, prohibita, & permissa quandoque diuersantur & dissonant in his legibus inuicem, quandoque conueniunt. Et ideo secundum vnius praeceptum aut permissionem operans licite operatur secundum illam, quod si alia lege prohibitum extet, idem illicite secundum legem aliam operatur: Quod si tale aliquid vtraque lege permissum fuerit, secundum vtrumque licite operatur. Si vero vtraq; prohibitum fuerit, idem operatur illicite secundum vtrunque. Vtrum aut secundum legem diuinam sit permissum quicquam fieri vel omitti, quod humana lege praeceptum aut prohibitum extet, quemadmodum e conuerso, considerandum relinquitur, non est enim hoc praesentis inquisitionis. Certum est autem multa fore permissa humana lege, quemadmodum fornicationes, ebrietates, & reliqua quaedam peccata, quae lege diuina prohibita sunt. His consequenter ostendere volo, quod rem quamcunque temporalem, aut eius aliquid siue vnico aliquo vsu consumptibilem, siue non propriam alicuius iuxta tertium modum proprii, siue communem sibi cum alio vel aliis suam, id est, sibi iure acquisitam vel alienam, ex consensu tamen eius, cui iure primo modo dicto quaesita est. Potest aliquis contrectare in proprio dicto secundum tertiam significationem, vel etiam cum alio in communi habet possidere secundum tertiam possessionis significationem, atque corrumpere licite absque omni eius rei, aut eius alicuius dominio secundam primam, secundam, vel tertiam dominii significationem. Hoc autem demonstro sic. Quoniam rem illam temporalem, aut eius aliquid secundum omnem eius dictum modum potest quis licite contrectare atque corrumpere absq; dominio secundum iam dictos tres modos, tam in proprio quam communi, quam contrectat vel habet absq; iam dictis dominiis secundum legem diuinam aut humanam, vel vtranq; Sed rem aliquam suam, & rei aliquid ac alienam consentiente illo, cuius res illa fuerit, potest aliquis contrectare secundum leges, vt dictum est absque omni praedicto domino, ergo licite sine ipso. Prima propositio huius deductionis per se nota est ex licito diffinitione. Secundam probo ratione sumpta ex inductione, primum quidem in re sua seu alicui iure quaesita facto suo vel alieno in proprio, vel sibi cum alio in communi, vt dono vel legato, venatione, piscatione, aut altero sui labore seu opere licito. Esto enim rem aliquam sic alicui esse quaesitam. Certum est igitur ipsum ea vti & eam contrectare posse secundum leges, quoniam modi praedictis secundum legem acquiritur res, vt ex inductione palam. Constat etiam quod quilibet aptus licite potest renunciare iuri pro se introducto, quoniam beneficium non conferatur inuito, secundum legem humanam atque diuinam. Poterit igitur cui rei vel eius vsus dominium acquiri potest facto suo vel alieno tali dominio renunciare. Cum igitur eidem si voluerit acquiratur tam potestas vtendi licite, quam etiam potestas rem vendicandi & ab altero prohibendi, potest licite renunciare potestati vendicandi, seu rem aut eius aliquid ab altero prohibendi, quae nihil aliud est quam dominium dictum secundum tres priores modos legales, non renunciata potestate vtendi re aut eius aliquo, quae siquidem potestas cadit sub iuris dicto iuxta secundam eius significationem. Et vocari solet ab aliquibus simplex facti vsus sine iure vtendi per ius vtendi sumenatibus dominium, secundum aliquam iam dictarum trium significationum. Am-
units.tr: Having distinguished the meanings of these terms in this way, I will draw some conclusions. The first is that no one can lawfully handle a temporal thing, or any part of a thing (for example, the usufruct or something similar), whether it is his own or another's, held privately or in common, unless he has a right to it, in the first or second sense of right. For every act that is not commanded or permitted by law is unlawful, as is plain to anyone from the definition of the lawful. There is no need to dwell on proving this, since it is known to everyone almost of itself. Second, from what has been said we may infer that someone may lawfully handle a thing, or part of it, under one law, such as the divine law, and unlawfully under another, such as the human law, and the reverse holds too. Again, the same act may be lawful, or equally unlawful, under both. This is not hard to see, since commands, prohibitions and permissions sometimes differ and clash between these laws and sometimes agree. So whoever acts under the command or permission of one law acts lawfully according to that law; if another law forbids the same act, he acts unlawfully according to that other law; but if both laws permit such a thing, he acts lawfully according to both; and if both forbid it, he acts unlawfully according to both. Whether, according to the divine law, it is permitted to do or omit something that the human law commands or forbids, or conversely, is left for consideration; it is not part of the present inquiry. It is certain, however, that the human law permits many things that the divine law forbids, such as fornication, drunkenness and certain other sins. From this I wish to show next that any temporal thing, or part of it, whether consumable by a single use or not, whether belonging to someone in the third sense of the term "his own," or held in common with another or others, and whether it is one's own (that is, acquired by right) or another's, but with the consent of him to whom it was first acquired by right in the sense already stated, can be handled and used up lawfully by someone without any ownership of it in the first, second or third sense of ownership. I demonstrate this as follows. Whatever temporal thing, or part of it, a person can lawfully handle and use up in every one of the senses mentioned, without ownership in the three senses just given, whether as his own or in common, and which he handles or holds without these ownerships according to the divine or human law, or both, is lawful for him. But someone may handle a thing that is his own, or part of it, or another's with the consent of its owner, according to the laws, as has been said, without any of the aforementioned ownership; therefore it is lawful for him without that ownership. The first premise of this argument is known of itself from the definition of the lawful. I prove the second by reasoning drawn from induction: first, for a thing acquired by right, whether by one's own act or another's, as one's own or in common with another, such as by gift or bequest, hunting, fishing, or some other lawful labour or work. Suppose, then, that some thing has been acquired by someone in this way. It is certain that he can use it and handle it according to the laws, since a thing is acquired by law in the ways mentioned, as induction makes plain. It is also agreed that anyone competent may lawfully renounce a right introduced in his favour, since under both human and divine law a benefit is not conferred on an unwilling person. So he who may acquire ownership of a thing, or of its use, by his own act or another's, can renounce that ownership. Since, if he wishes, the power of using it lawfully is acquired for him together with the power of claiming the thing and forbidding others to touch it, he can lawfully renounce the power of claiming it, or of forbidding others to touch the thing or any part of it. This is nothing other than the ownership described under the three earlier legal senses, while the power of using the thing, or some part of it, is not renounced, and this power falls under the term "right" in its second sense. Some who take the right of use as the right to use a thing call the bare use of a thing, without the right of use, a kind of ownership in one of the three senses already mentioned.

units.la: Amplius re quæ in nullius bonis est, potest aliquis licite uti secundum leges, sed aliquatenus eius potestatem vendicandi & ab altero prohibendi renunciauit quis, potest esse in nullius bonis, ergo ipsa potest quis licite uti. Cum igitur renuncians potestati prædictæ non habeat rei dominium, apparet quod rem aliquam potest quis licite contrectare, ac ea uti absque omni legali iam dicto dominio.
units.tr: Furthermore, a thing that belongs to no one may be lawfully used by someone according to the laws. But if someone has renounced in part the power of claiming it and of forbidding others to touch it, the thing can be in no one's goods; therefore a person can lawfully use it. Since the one renouncing that power does not have ownership of the thing, it is clear that someone can lawfully handle a thing and use it without any of the ownership mentioned above.

units.la: Rursum illa separantur inuicem, quorum unum per licitum votum abdicari potest pro quolibet tempore, reliquum vero minime. Sed iam dictum rei dominium seu vendicandi & prohibendi rem temporalem aut eius aliquid potestas per licitum votum abdicari potest pro quolibet tempore. Habere vero rem licite seu eius simplicem vsum, non pro quolibet tempore abdicari potest per licitum votum, ergo hæc ab invicem separatare conuenit. Prima propositio huius deductionis est per se nota ex liciti diffinitione: non enim potest idem secundum eandem legem simul licitum & illicitum esse. Secundam propositionem probo quantum ad utrangi sui partem: & primo quod abdicatio dominii per votum licita sit pro quolibet tempore, quoniam de Christi consilio potest emitti licitum votum: sed talis abdicatio est Christi consilium, vbi Matthæi 20. dixit: Omnis qui dimisit domum aut agros, &c. propter nomen meum centuplum accipiet, & vitam æternam possidebit. Idem habetur Matthæi quinto & Lucæ sexto, cum dixit Christus: Et ab eo qui aufert tibi vestimentum, etiam tunicam noli prohibere. Et ei qui vult tecum iudicio contendere, & tunicam tuam tollere, remitte ei & pallium. vbi Augustinus si pro necessariis imperat, id est consulit non contendere, quanto magis pro superfluis? Iuxta quam etiam Christi sententiam dixit Apostolus primæ ad Corinthios sexto: Iam quidem, inquit, omnino delictum est in vobis quod iudicia habetis inter vos: quare non magis iniuriam accipitis, quare non magis fraudem patimini? supple, quam iudicio, etiam iusto aduersus quenquam contendere, pro rei temporalis vendicatione? vbi Glossa secundum Augustinum inducit euangelium in locis prælsignatis. Et tunc addit hoc, id est contendere iudicio, iuste scilicet, secundum veniam infirmis concedit Apostolus, cum sint in ecclesia talia iudicia fieri inter fratres fratribus iudicantibus. Consequenter propter quoddam dictum August. dubium subdit Glossa: Vt autem predicta verba Augustini, quibus ait, peccatum est iudicium habere contra fratrem, sane intelligantur, dicendum est hic quid in huiusmodi conueniat perfectis & quid non, & quid liceat infirmis & quid non. Perfectis igitur licet repetere sua simpliciter scilicet sine causa, sine lite, sine iudicio, sed non conuenit eis inde mouere causam ante iudicem. Infirmis vero licet & sua repetere mouendo causam ante iudicem, & iudicium habendo contra fratrem. Potest igitur de abdicatione dominii licitum votum emitti. Quod si etiam perfectis non est licitum contendere coram iudice coactiuo, ergo potestatem licite vendicandi non habent, quæ dominium est iam dictum: tali enim potestati iam per votum renunciauerunt contra quod eis vllo tempore venire non licet, præcipue stante voto. Quod autem rei vel eius vsus, habitus licitus seu simplex facti vsus abdicari nequeat pro quolibet tempore, satis apparet, quia nullum prohibitum lege diuina potest licite cadere sub voto, sed talis abdicatio est prohibita lege diuina, eo quod species quædam homicidii. Talis enim votum obseruans seipsum fame aut frigore vel siti perimeret scienter, quod lege diuina prohibetur expresse vt Mat. 19. Mar. 10. Luca 18. vbi Christus aliqua præcepta legis antiquæ confirmans ait: Non occides, &c. Separatur igitur rei scilicet vsus simplex seu habere licitum ab omni iam dicto dominio seu vendicandi & prohibendi rem aut eius aliquid potestate.
units.tr: Again, those things are separable from one another of which one may be given up at any time by a lawful vow, and the other not at all. But the ownership of a thing, or the power of claiming and forbidding others to touch a temporal thing or part of it, can be given up at any time by a lawful vow. But to hold a thing lawfully, or to have its simple use, cannot be given up at any time by a lawful vow. Therefore these ought to be separated from one another. The first premise of this argument is known of itself from the definition of the lawful, for the same thing cannot be both lawful and unlawful at once under the same law. I prove the second premise with regard to each of its parts; and first, that the giving up of ownership by a vow is lawful at any time, since a lawful vow can be made in accordance with Christ's counsel. Such a giving up is Christ's counsel, where in Matthew 20 he said: "Everyone who has left house or fields, &c., for my name's sake shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life." The same is found in Matthew 5 and Luke 6, where Christ said: "And from him who takes away your coat, do not withhold even your tunic. And to him who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, give up also your cloak." Where Augustine, if he commands for necessities, that is, counsels not to contest, how much more for superfluities? In accordance with this saying of Christ the Apostle also said in 1 Corinthians 6: "Now indeed, he says, there is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather be defrauded?" That is, why do you not rather bear it than contend against anyone in a lawsuit, even a just one, for the recovery of a temporal thing? Here the Gloss, following Augustine, brings in the gospel in the places already indicated. Then it adds: that is, to contend in judgment, justly of course, the Apostle grants to the weak by way of indulgence, since such lawsuits are allowed in the Church, with brothers judging brothers. Afterwards, because of a certain doubtful saying of Augustine, the Gloss adds: "But so that the words of Augustine just cited, in which he says it is a sin to have a lawsuit against a brother, may be rightly understood, it must be said here what befits the perfect in such matters and what does not, and what is permitted to the weak and what is not. The perfect may therefore recover their own things simply, that is, without cause, without strife, without judgment, but it does not befit them to bring a case before a judge. The weak, however, may both recover their own things by bringing a case before a judge, and have a lawsuit against a brother." Therefore a lawful vow of giving up ownership can be made. And if it is not lawful even for the perfect to contend before a judge with coercive power, then they do not have the lawful power of claiming, which is the ownership mentioned; for they have already renounced such power by a vow, and it is not lawful for them at any time to return to what they have renounced, especially while the vow stands. That the lawful possession of a thing, or its use, or the bare use of the thing, cannot be given up at any time, is quite plain, because nothing forbidden by the divine law can lawfully fall under a vow; but such a giving up is forbidden by the divine law, since it amounts to a kind of murder. For one who keeps such a vow would knowingly kill himself by hunger, cold or thirst, which the divine law expressly forbids, as in Matthew 19, Mark 10 and Luke 18, where Christ, confirming certain precepts of the old law, says: "You shall not kill," &c. Therefore the bare use of a thing, or having it lawfully, is separated from all the aforementioned ownership, that is, from the power of claiming and forbidding others to touch the thing or any part of it.

units.la: Ex quo etiam per necessitatem sequitur manifeste, insanam hæresim esse, asserentis rem aut eius vsum haberi non posse absque iam dicto dominio. Sic enim dicens, nil aliud sentit quam Christi consilium adimpleri non posse, quod apertum mendacium est, & vt diximus tanquam peruersum & hæreticum fugiendum. Nec obstat sermo dicentis, quod de actu contentioso possit abdicatio licita per votum fieri, non tñ de habitu seu actiua potestate legali ad vendicandū & prohibendū rem ab alio coram iudice coactiuo, quam pridem tale dominium esse diximus, hoc n. falsum est, quoniam omnis habitus seu potestas legalis acquisita vel acquisibilis, cuius habitus per licitum votum abdicari potest, eodem modo abdicabilis est, sicut inductione apparet in omnibus consultis sub voto cadentibus. Nam vouens castitatem aut obedientiam, non solum per votum abdicat actus, verum etiam potestatem licitam ad tales actus sibi iure primo modo dicto conuenientem prius. Rursum inconsonum veritati est dicere quenquam habere licitam potestatem ad actus qui oes sunt illiciti, cum potestas non dicatur licita vel illicita, nec aliter harum differentia cognoscatur, nisi per actus licitos aut illicitos prouenientes, aut prouenire posibiles ab eadem. Cum igitur oes actus licitæ potestatis, quam quis habuit ante votum, sint post votum illiciti, apparet quod eorum nulla potestas licita remansit apud vouentem. Deinde ostendo quod rei aut eius vsus alienæ quantum ad omne dominium supradictum, potest aliquis habere vsum licitum, rem ipsam etiam consummante. Si hunc vsum consentiente domino in rem exerceat absque omni tali dominio supradicto. Namex quo supponitur esse omnino in alterius dominio seu potestate vendicandi, certum est quod tale dominium non transfertur in alium, nisi facto domini & expresso consensu, non dissentiente etiam, in quem rei talis aut eius vsus, tale dominium seu iuuicandi potestas transferri debet. Esto igitur dominum non velle transferre rei vel eius vsus tale dominium in alium quenquam. Esto etiam alium dissentire in tale dominium, vt qui expresso voto temporaliter omnium iam dictum abdicauit dominium, sicut perfectis conuenit. Esto amplius dominum consentire perfectum aliquare sua vti etiam vsque ad rei consumptionem, perfectum quoque seu qui omnis rei domi
units.tr: From this it also follows by necessity that it is a manifest heresy to assert that a thing, or its use, cannot be had without the aforesaid dominion. For whoever says this understands nothing other than that Christ's counsel cannot be fulfilled, which is a plain falsehood and, as we have said, must be shunned as perverse and heretical. Nor does it help the claim that the renunciation of a contentious act may be made lawfully by vow, but not the habit or active legal power to claim and forbid a thing against another before a judge with coercive authority, which we said above is such a dominion. For this is false: every legal habit or power that is acquired, or can be acquired, and whose habit may be renounced by a lawful vow, is renounceable in the same way, as induction shows in all the counsels that fall under a vow. For one who vows chastity or obedience renounces not only the acts but also the lawful power to such acts that belongs to him by the first right already described. Again, it is inconsistent with the truth to say that anyone has lawful power to acts that are all unlawful, since a power is not called lawful or unlawful, and the difference between them is known only through the lawful or unlawful acts that arise from it, or that can arise from it. Therefore, since all the acts of the lawful power that someone had before the vow are unlawful after the vow, it is evident that no lawful power over them remains with the one who vows. Next I show that someone may have lawful use of a thing, or of another's thing, free of all the aforesaid dominion, even if he consumes the thing itself. This is so if he exercises that use with the owner's consent and without any such dominion. For since it is supposed that the thing is wholly in the dominion or power of another to claim, it is certain that this dominion is not transferred to another except by the owner's deed and express consent, and the recipient, to whom the thing or its use and this dominion or power to claim ought to be transferred, must not dissent. Grant, then, that the owner does not wish to transfer such dominion over the thing or its use to anyone else; grant also that the other dissents from such dominion, as one who by express vow has renounced for a time all the aforesaid dominion, as is fitting for the perfect; grant further that the owner consents that the perfect man use his own things even to the consumption of the thing, and the perfect man, too, who has renounced all dominion of the thing...

units.la: {1} Ad 1 ordinem cit. ex contrarium uoluit dominium abdicauit tali re velle vti consentiente domino, dico sic vtentem re illa licite vti ea, & tamen illius aut eius vsus nullum supradictum penitus habere dominium. Quod autem nullum rei aut eius vsus habeat dominium, apparet ex praemissis hypothesibus, tā ex habentis domini voluntate, quam ex recepturi rei vsum conditione, qui talia simpliciter abdicauit dominia. Quod autem ea licite vtatur, apparet ex liciti diffinitione, quoniam lege permissum est vnicuiq; vti aliena re etiam vsq; ad eius consumptionem, si ad hoc interueniat dominantis eam consensus expressus. Quod si sumatur dominium vltimo modo, pro voluntate scilicet seu libertate humana, cum ipsa motiua potentia naturali non acquisita, sed connata nobis: dico quod rem aliquam aut eius aliquid neq; licite neq; illicite contrectare possumus sponte sine tali dominio, neq; tale dominium abdicare possumus. Et quia hoc secundum se quasi notum est omnibus, quoniam sine potestatib. his nemo in esse manere potest absq; probatione aliqua, de hoc pertranseo propter abbreviationem sermonis. Ex his itaq; apparere potest, quod non omnis rei temporalis aut eius vsus potestas licita seu de iure primo aut secundo modo dicto vel vtroq; sit dominium, quamuis econuerso dominium omne licitum secundum iam dictos tres modos legales in rem vel eius vsum aut vtrumque sit potestas licita, seu de iure iam dicto. Unde sic inferens, Est potestas in rem aut eius vsum licita seu de iure, igitur est in rem aut eius dominium licitum seu de iure, paralogismum incidit consequentis. Est enim rem licite habere & contrectare tam suam in proprio vel communi quam etiam alienam, domino vel eo cui quaesita licite fuerit consentiente absq; omni legali dominio acquisito. His ergo praemissis ad propositum ingredientes amplius, primum dicimus pauperem aut pauperem aliquem fore quasi per se notorum, & in scriptura repertum plerunque, sic vt ex omnibus de hoc vnum inducere sufficiat, ex Marc. 12. vbi Christus: Amen dico vobis, quoniam mulier haec pauper plus omnibus misit. Deinde ostendo similiter per scripturam, paupertatem meritoriam esse ad vitam aeternam. Quoniam dixit veritas Lucae 6. Beati pauperes, quia vestrum est regnum Dei, merendo scilicet, quia nemo praeter Christum in hac vita beatus efficitur sed meretur.
units.tr: {1} In reply to the first objection cited in order: the one who, on the contrary, has renounced dominion by vow wishes to use such a thing with the owner's consent. I say that one so using the thing uses it lawfully, and yet has no dominion whatever over it or its use. That he has no dominion over the thing or its use is evident from the aforesaid hypotheses, both from the will of the owner who has it and from the condition of the one who is to receive the use of the thing, who has simply renounced such dominions. That he uses it lawfully is evident from the definition of the lawful, since by law it is permitted to each person to use another's thing even to its consumption, if the express consent of the one who holds it intervenes. But if dominion is taken in the last sense, namely for the human will or liberty, with its natural motive power not acquired but innate in us, I say that we can neither lawfully nor unlawfully handle any thing or any part of it spontaneously without such dominion, nor can we renounce such dominion. And since this is in itself almost known to all, because without these powers no one can remain in existence without some proof, I pass over it for the sake of brevity. From these points it can therefore be seen that not every power over a temporal thing or its use that is lawful, or lawful by the first or second right described, or by both, is a dominion; although conversely every lawful dominion over a thing or its use, or over both, according to the three legal modes already mentioned, is a lawful power, or power by the right already mentioned. Hence one who infers thus, "There is a lawful power over a thing or its use, or by right; therefore there is a lawful or rightful dominion over the thing or its dominion," commits the fallacy of the consequent. For it is lawful to have and handle a thing, both one's own, whether private or common, and another's, with the consent of the owner or of the one to whom it was lawfully entrusted, without any acquired legal dominion. With these points laid down, let us proceed further to our purpose. First we say that a poor man, or the poor, is something known in itself and found very often in Scripture, so that it suffices to cite one passage from all of them, Mark 12, where Christ says: "Verily I say unto you, this poor widow has cast in more than all." Next I show similarly from Scripture that poverty is meritorious for eternal life, since the truth says in Luke 6: "Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God," that is, by merit, since no one in this life is made blessed except Christ, but merits it.

units.la: Et ex hoc sequitur per necessitate, paupertatem esse virtutem, si ex multis actibus, sic volendi carere temporalib. bonis habituata fuerit, aut actu virtutis factiuo aut elicitum a virtute, qa omne meritorium virtus est aut actus eius. Rursum omne Christi consilium pertinet ad virtute per se, paupertas est huiusmodi, vt Matt. quinto, 19. & aliis plerisque locis euangelicae scripturae satis apparet.
units.tr: And from this it follows of necessity that poverty is a virtue, if by many acts of willing to lack temporal goods it has become a habit, whether as an act producing virtue or as an act elicited by virtue, since everything meritorious is either virtue or an act of virtue. Again, every counsel of Christ pertains to virtue in itself, and poverty is of this kind, as is sufficiently clear in Matthew 5 and 19 and in many other places of the evangelical Scripture.

units.la: Ex quo sequitur per necessitatem, hanc esse paupertatem spontaneam dictam secundum tertium & quartum modum paupertatis, eo quod non est virtus aut eius opus sine electione, electio vero non sine consensu, vt ex secundo & tertio Ethicorum satis apparet. Cuius et confirmatio sumi potest ex Matth. 5. vbi Christus Beati pauperes spiritu, intelligens per spiritum voluntatem seu consensum, quamuis aliqui sanctorum exponant per spiritum superbiam, quod tamen non multum est ad propositum, quoniam in eadem serie subiungitur immediate, beati mites. Quicquid tamen sit de huius loci expositione, nemini dubium, & secundum sententiam sanctorum, quod paupertas si meritoria sit regni coelorum, quemadmodum Christus ait, oportet hanc esse non exteriorem, temporalium priuationem principaliter, sed interiorem mentis habitum, quo quis vult talibus sponte priuari propter Christum. Unde Basilius super illud Lucae sexto. Beati pauperes, &c. inquit: Non omnis quem paupertas premit, beatus est. Plures enim pauperes sunt in subsidiis, auaritissimi vero secundum affectum, quos non saluat paupertas, sed damnat affectus, nihil enim involuntariorum beatificale est, eo quod omnis virtus libero designatur arbitrio. Est ergo paupertas meritoria virtus & spontanea per consequens, non autem exterior priuatio secundum se virtus est, quoniam talis non saluat sine affectu debito, posset enim quis talibus priuari coactus & inuitus: & propter horum tamen inordinatum affectum damnari. Sic etiam de hoc sensit Apostolus 2. ad Corinth. 8. cum dixit: Si enim voluntas prompta est secundum id quod habet, accepta est, id est, meritoria. Debet etiam haec electio priuationis temporalium fieri propter Christum, si futura sit meritoria. Unde veritas Matth. 19. Et omnis qui reliquit domum, &c. propter nomen meum. Vbi Hieronymus, Qui carnalia pro saluatore reliquit, spiritualia recipiet, quae merito & comparatione sui, quasi paruo numero centenarius numerus comparantur. Et infra: Qui propter fidem Christi ad euangelii praedicationem, omnes affectus contempserint, atq; diuitias & saeculi voluptates, centuplum accipient, & aeternam vitam possidebunt. Rursum quod opponitur auaritiae per se meritorium existens virtus essentialiter est, paupertas spontanea propter Christum est huiusmodi, auaritia enim vitium est. Proportionem autem habet virtus haec ad moralem liberalitatem, quamuis a b ipsa sine differat & rei medio saltim specieseius perfectior quaedam, vt ex sequentibus apparebit: propter quod ambae in eadem atoma specie reponi non possunt. Ex his quidem igitur apparere potest, quod paupertas meritoria virtus est, qua quis propter Christum priuari vult & carere bonis omnibus temporalibus, quae diuitiae vocari solent, supereffluis suae sufficientiae. Unde etiam sequitur manifeste, virtutem hanc non esse habitum aut actum charitatis, quod visi sunt quidam opinari. Quoniam habitus aut actus non est hic, qui Dei odio actuali aut habituali per se primum opponatur, eo quod tunc vni opponerentur plura primo. Nam quamuis charitati repugnet vitium oppositum vniuscuiusque virtutis theologicae, non tamen propter hoc ipsa est virtus omnis theologica, quoniam nec talia sibi primum opponuntur.
units.tr: From this it follows of necessity that this is the poverty called voluntary, according to the third and fourth modes of poverty, because virtue or its work is not without choice, and choice is not without consent, as is sufficiently clear from the second and third books of the Ethics. Its confirmation can also be drawn from Matthew 5, where Christ says, "Blessed are the poor in spirit," understanding by spirit the will or consent, although some of the saints explain spirit as pride; yet this does not greatly matter to our purpose, since in the same series it is immediately added, "blessed are the meek." Whatever the explanation of this passage, it is beyond doubt, and according to the judgment of the saints, that if poverty is meritorious of the kingdom of heaven, as Christ says, it must be not chiefly an external deprivation of temporal goods but an inner habit of mind, by which one wishes to be spontaneously deprived of such things for Christ's sake. Hence Basil, on the words of Luke 6, "Blessed are the poor," etc., says: "Not everyone whom poverty oppresses is blessed. For many are poor in means, but the most greedy in affection, whom poverty does not save but affection condemns; for nothing involuntary is beatifying, since every virtue is referred to the free will." Poverty is therefore a meritorious virtue and, consequently, voluntary; but external deprivation, in itself, is not a virtue, since it does not save without the due affection. For someone could be deprived of such things by compulsion and against his will, and yet be condemned on account of the disordered affection of these same people. The Apostle also thought this way in 2 Corinthians 8, when he said: "For if the willingness is ready, it is accepted according to what one has," that is, it is meritorious. This choice of deprivation of temporal goods must also be made for Christ's sake if it is to be meritorious. Hence the truth in Matthew 19: "And everyone who has left house, etc., for my name's sake." Where Jerome says: "He who has left carnal things for the Saviour will receive spiritual things, which are compared with it by merit and proportion, as the number a hundred is compared with a small number." And below: "Those who for the faith of Christ, in preaching the gospel, have despised all affections, and riches and the pleasures of the world, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life." Again, what is opposed to avarice is a virtue existing by itself and meritorious in its essence; voluntary poverty for Christ's sake is of this kind, for avarice is a vice. This virtue has a proportion to moral liberality, although it differs from it in its own way and is in species at least somewhat more perfect, as will appear from what follows; for which reason both cannot be placed in the same lowest species. From these things it can therefore be seen that poverty is a meritorious virtue, by which one wills, for Christ's sake, to be deprived of and to lack all temporal goods, which are commonly called riches, beyond the surplus of his sufficiency. Hence it also clearly follows that this virtue is not a habit or act of charity, as some seem to think. For this is not a habit or act that is opposed first and per se to the hatred of God, actual or habitual, since then several things would be opposed to one thing first. For although the opposite vice of each theological virtue is contrary to charity, it does not follow that charity is every theological virtue, since such things are not first opposed to it.

units.la: Nec obstat, sermo dicentis, eandem esse virtute essentialiter qua in Deum tendimus p dilectione, & qua recedimus ab inordinato rerum temporalium desiderio, velut motum eandem essentialiter fore, quo aliquis tendit ab aliquo termino & in oppositum tendit. Cum ergo charitate per tendamus in Deum, eadem igitur non alia virtute ab amore temporalium exire videntur. Ex iam enim praemisso nobis sermone patere potest huius deductionis infirmitas: Quoniam & si charitate per se primo tendamus in Deum per dilectionem, eadem ipsa eximus ab huius oppositio per se primo, quod quidem odium Dei est, non amor illicitus rerum temporalium; quamuis quandoque ad charitatem sequitur hic exitus, propterea quod ad ipsum sequitur illa diosa paupertas, quae talis temporalium est per se primo abdicatio spontanea, ad quam per necessitatem sequitur exitus ab oppositio per se primo, scilicet ab amore illicito temporalium rerum. Si enim disputantis sermo verum inferret, ex veris concluderet sic, charitatem esse quasi omnem virtutem, quoniam ad charitatem plurimae sequuntur per necessitatem, ut tides & spes, quibus per se primum eximus ab haeresi & desperatione. Amplius charitas non cadit sub voto quia praeceptum est. Iam dicta paupertas praecipue quarto modo dicta, cadit sub voto, non igitur est charitas essentialiter studiosa paupertas nec ecclesiae, quamuis haec sequatur charitatem sicut aliarum theologicarum plurimae. Huius autem virtutis summum modum aut speciem esse dico votum viatoris expressum, quo propter Christum renunciando primari & carere vult tam in proprio quam etiam in communi omni legali iam dicto domino acquisito seu potestate vendicandi & ab alio prohibendi coram iudice coactivo res temporales quas vocant divitias. Votum inquam etiam, quo propter Christum tam in proprio, quam etiam in communi priuari vult & carere omni potestate, habitu, & contrectatione vel iussu ipsorum superfluo in quanto & quali praesenti sufficientiae. Nec talia bona quantumcunque sibi licite advenientia, pro pluribus futuris necessitatibus seu indigentiis supplendis propter se solum, nec propter se cum aliquo vel determinatis aliquib. in communi vult habere simul, sed unica tantum simul ut immediate instante quali praesente indigentia alimenti atque tegmenti. Hoc tamen duntaxat excepto, si hic vouens in loco, tempore, aut sui dispositione tali, ut vicissim successive singulis diebus sibi de temporalibus tantum quaerere possit, quo suam indigentiam iam dictam, solum tamen unicam simul, non plures supplere possit. Hic siquidem modus aut species meritoriae paupertatis status est, quem ad evangelicam perfectionem necessarium dicere volunt, ut ex sequentibus aperte patebit. Quem etiam iam dictum modum meritoriae paupertatis siue habetis in proprio tertio modo dicto, siue etiam cum alio in communi modo communis huic opposito, deinceps propter abbreviationem vocabimus summam paupertatem, sic vero habere volentem more Theologorum perfectum dicemus. Quod autem iam dictus modus paupertatis meritoriae sit aliorum summus, ostendi potest ex hoc, quoniam secundum ipsum aliorum maxime omnia Christi meritoria consilia obseruantur. Omnia nanque primum temporalia abiici possibilia viatori per votum abdicantur, plurima diuinae charitatis sic vouentibus amouentur impedimenta pluribus seculi passionibus & ignominiis, ac sustinendis incommodis disponuntur, pluribus quoque ipsius voluptatibus & vanitatibus sponte priuantur: & ad vnum dicere, ad obseruanda Christi tam praecepta quam consilia omnia maxime se disponunt. Quod autem temporalia simpliciter & quantum viatori possibile ac licitum est, abdicet sic vouens, euidens est, quoniam nihil nisi quod praesenti aut quasi praesenti alimenti atque tegmenti supplendae indigentiae vnicae necessarium fuerit, habere vult simul, minus autem habere non licet alicui viatori fideli, quoniam si minus habere vellet sibi necessario ad vitae sustentationem sui esset homicida scienter, quod diuina saltim lege non licet alicui. Qui ergo sic habere vult temporalia, quod eorum minus non licet habere, minimum vult ex ipsis: Et qui tantum abdicat ex eis, quod amplius abdicare non licet maximum abdicat. Sic autem facit viator secundum iam dictum modum meritoriae paupertatis, quem summum diximus. Quod autem sit hoc secundum Christi consilium apparet, nam de hoc voto consilium dedit. Lucae 14. cum dixit: Sic igitur quicunque non renunciat omnibus quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus.
units.tr: Nor does the argument of the objector stand, that the same virtue essentially by which we tend toward God through love is also that by which we withdraw from the disordered desire for temporal things, just as a motion by which someone tends away from one terminus and toward its opposite is essentially the same motion. Since, then, we tend toward God through charity, it seems to follow that the same virtue, not another, goes out from love of temporal things. The weakness of this inference can already be seen from what we have said: although through charity we tend primarily toward God by love, we go out, by that same charity, from its opposite, which is primarily hatred of God and not unlawful love of temporal things. Yet sometimes this departure follows upon charity, because there follows upon it that holy poverty, which is primarily a voluntary renunciation of temporal goods, and from which, of necessity, there follows a departure from its primary opposite, namely the unlawful love of temporal things. For if the objector's argument proved what it claims, it would conclude from true premises that charity is virtually every virtue, since many things follow of necessity from charity, as faith and hope, by which we primarily depart from heresy and despair. Furthermore, charity does not fall under a vow because it is commanded. But the poverty just described, especially as described in the fourth way, does fall under a vow; therefore poverty studied in this way is not essentially charity, nor is it the Church's, although it follows upon charity just as many other theological virtues do. I maintain, moreover, that the highest mode or form of this virtue is the express vow of a wayfarer, by which, for Christ's sake, he wishes to renounce and be without, both in what is his own and in what is held in common, every legal ownership already mentioned, that is, the lordship over acquired goods, and the power of claiming them and of forbidding others, before a coercive judge, of temporal things, which they call riches. I say, moreover, the vow by which, for Christ's sake, he wishes to be deprived of and to lack, both in what is his own and in what is held in common, every power, possession, and handling or disposal of what is superfluous, in whatever amount and quality is present sufficiency. Nor does he wish to have at once, for the sake of supplying many future needs or wants, goods of this kind, however lawfully they may come to him, whether for their own sake or, for their own sake, together with some or certain others in common; but only one thing at a time, as the immediately impending or present need of food and clothing requires. This is the only exception: if the one vowing, by place, time, or such disposition of his own, is able in turn, successively, day by day, to seek for himself only temporal goods by which he may supply his said need, yet only one at a time and not several. This mode or form of meritorious poverty is the state which they wish to call necessary for evangelical perfection, as will clearly appear from what follows. And this mode of meritorious poverty just named, whether it is had in what is one's own in the third mode mentioned, or also with another in common in the mode opposed to this, we shall henceforth, for brevity, call supreme poverty, and one who wishes to have it we shall, after the manner of the theologians, call perfect. That this mode of meritorious poverty is the highest of all may be shown from this: that according to it, above all, all the counsels of Christ that merit are observed. For first, all temporal goods that are possible for a wayfarer are renounced by the vow; by such vowing, many hindrances to divine charity are removed; many sufferings and disgraces of the world are embraced, and many inconveniences are willingly borne; and many of its pleasures and vanities are voluntarily given up. In a word, those who vow thus most fully dispose themselves to observe all of Christ's precepts as well as all his counsels. That the one vowing thus renounces temporal goods absolutely and as far as is possible and lawful for a wayfarer is evident, since he wishes to have at once nothing more than what is necessary to supply the one present or almost present need of food and clothing; but it is not lawful for any faithful wayfarer to have less, since if he wished to have less than what is necessary for the sustenance of life, he would knowingly be a murderer of himself, which is not lawful for anyone by divine law at least. Therefore, he who wishes to have temporal goods in such a way that it is not lawful to have less of them, wishes to have the least of them; and he who renounces so much of them that it is not lawful to renounce more, renounces the most. And so the wayfarer does, according to the mode of meritorious poverty just named, which we have called supreme. That this is the counsel of Christ appears, for he gave counsel about this vow in Luke 14, when he said: So therefore whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.

units.la: Quod autem plurima charitatis diuinae sibi amoueat impedimenta euidens est, quoniam amor & voluntas conseruandi temporalia conuertit hominem ad ipsa, & per consequens magis a conuertit in tantum ab amore seu Dei dilectione. Vnde veritas Matthaei sexto: Vbi thesaurus tuus, ibi & cor tuum. Nec valet excusatio dicentis, quod habens has, non conuertet suum amorem ad illas. Nam audi Christum Matth. 13. & Marci quarto dicentem, quod fallacia diuitiarum suffocat verbum. Vbi Hieronymus: Blanda enim sunt diuitiae aliud agentes, aliud pollicentes, propter quod etiam ipsas simpliciter abdicare, volenti perfectum esse. Christus consuluit Lucae 18. cum dixit: Omnia quaecunque habes vende, & da pauperibus. Vbi Beda: Quicunque ergo perfectus esse voluerit, debet vendere quae habet: non ex parte, sicut Ananias fecit & Saphyra, sed totum. Et ibidem quod est ad propositum, subdit Theophylactus: Summam paupertatem suadet, si quid enim restituerit, (temporalium scilicet,) illius seruus est, supple, qui seruat talia propter se. Sunt enim huiusmodi nata inordinate mouere detinentis affectum. Eidem quoque sententiae Rabanus super idem Christi oraculum Matth. 19. addit, quod est ad propositum valde. inquit enim: Inter pecunias habere, & pecunias amare nonnulli distantia est. Tutius autem est, non habere, nec amare diuitias. Quoniam, ut ibidem subdit Hieronymus: Diuitiae habita difficile contemnuntur. Sunt enim visco viscosiores, ut dicit Thomas Luc. 18. super eodem Christi consilio. Plurima ergo ubi sibi charitatis impedimenta subtrahit, qui diuitias quantum viatori possibile ac licitum est, subtrahit. Pluribus etiam seculi pasionibus, ignominiis, & incommodis exponit (e pluribus voluptatibus & mundanis commodis sponte se priuat. Hoc autem quamuis per se notum sit, experientia sensata, dicit tamen Sapiens Ecclesiastes decimo: Pecunia enim, inquit, obediunt omnia, id est habenti pecunias. Ex opposito autem Prouer. 15. Omnes dies pauperis mali. quoniam pauper afflictionibus abundat, vt Glossa dicit ibidem. Rursum eiusdem 19. ait: Diuitiae addunt amicos plurimos, a paupere autem & hi quos habuerit separantur. Quod autem tristia sustinere in hoc seculo, & a delectabilibus abstinere propter Christum, sic meritorium & consultum, apparet euidenter, Matt. quinto, & 19. ac Luc. 6. vnde quantum ad tristium tolerantiam: Beati pauperes, Beati qui lugent, Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur, Beati qui esuritis, cum caeteris quae ibidem annumerantur his: quantum vero ad delectationum abstinentiam: Quoniam omnis qui reliquit domum aut fratres, cum reliquis ibidem annumeratis, centuplum accipiet, & vitam aeternam possidebit. Hanc eandem sententiam explicant ibidem Glossae sanctorum, quas omisi propter abbreuiationem sermonis, & eo quod res haec est nota satis. Haec quoque fuit Apostoli sententia ad Rom. 6. Existimo enim, inquit, quod non sunt condigna passiones huius temporis ad futuram gloriam quae revelabitur in nobis. ergo meritoriae sunt aduersitates huius seculi tolerantibus sponte. Idem 2. ad Corinth. primo, cum dixit: Quoniam sicut socii passionum estis, sic eritis & consolationis. Vbi Ambr. Quia aequa gloria labori vestro retribuetur, id est proportionalis. Ad haec autem seculi tristia & incommoda sustinenda non se omniquaq; sic disponunt collegia personarum habentium dominium temporalium in communi, quinimo minus multis pauperibus in seculo coniugatis, habentibus quandoque propria, eis tamen quae ad vitae sufficientiam saepius egentibus his qui talia solum possidunt in communi. Quod autem secundum hunc modum paupertatis meritoriae, quem supremum diximus aliorum, maxime omnia praecepta & Christi consilia obseruari possint, aparebit discurrenti per seriem euangelicam, praecipue in ... tulis assignatis. Qui enim talem pauperrimum elegit, quomodo erit auarus aut superbus, qualiter incontinens aut intemperatus, ambitiosus, immisericors, & curiniustus, timidus, accidiosus, aut inuidus, cur etiam mendax, impatiens, & alteri propter quid malitiosus? quinimo ad omnes virtutes sic dispositio, ianua reserata videtur ad omnia quoque praecepta & consilia aequanimiter adimplenda. Quod quia palam sit inducenti, probare omitto propter abbreuiationem sermonis. Sic igitur summus modus aut species meritoriae paupertatis est, quem prius descripsimus: quoniam secundum ipsum possunt amplius & securius omnia Christi praecepta & meritoria consilia obseruari. Ex qua si quidem descriptione primum apparet, quod temporalia quantum ad dominium per votum expressum renunciare debet perfectus, tum quia Christi consilium, vt ex Luca 14. pridem induximus, tum quia ex hoc suam paupertatem notificans, se amplius in aliorum conspectu contemptibilem reddit, & seculari. honorib. magis caedit. Vnde Lucae nono: Si quis vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum. Ex quo sequitur amplius, quod nemo summam paupertatem obseruare potest ante perfectum rationis visum. Sequitur etiam ex hac descriptione, quod perfectus existens nihil habere neque quaerere debet aut conseruare propter se, ad futuram scilicet suam necessitatem supplendam, nisi instantem quasi praesentem: excepto duntaxat in casu quem pridem in descriptione diximus. Vnde Matth. 7. Nolite ergo solliciti esse in crastinum. Crastinus enim dies solicitus erit sibiipsi. Vbi Glossa, in crastinum, id est, in futurum. de praesentibus concedit, de futuris quae diuina procurat ordinatio, non conuenit solicitari, sed praesentia grate suscipientes, curam futurorum quia incerta est, Deo relinquimus: Cui de nobis cura est. Idem eodem septimo, cum dixit Christus ad discipulos: Respicite volatilia caeli, quoniam non serunt, neque metunt, neque congregant in horrea, & pater vester caelestis pascit illa. Et parum infra subiungit: Nolite ergo solliciti esse, dicentes: quid manducabimus, aut quid bibemus, aut quo operiemur? haec enim omnia gentes inquirunt. Diximus autem perfecto nihil licere propter se ad crastinum custodire, non quidem intelligentes sic, vt si quid ex eo quod illi aduenit ex quaestu diurno licito, residuum fuerit, id reiicere debeat & nullo modo custodire, sed quod tale residuum non debeat sibi sic custodire, quin illud pauperibus sibi occurrentibus & prius indigentibus quam ipse proponat firmiter tribuere atque dispensare conuenienter. Vnde Lucae tertio: Qui habet duas tunicas, det non habenti: & qui esca, similiter faciat. Intelligens per duo vestimenta & esca, id vel de eo quod superest indigentiae praesentis proprio supplemento. Cuilibet autem dictum est, quoniam communitas seruantium aut habentium pro aliquibus determinatis solum: vt quae monachorum & canonicorum & similium, non est perfecta communitas, perfecta enim, vt quae Christi & apostolorum ad omnes fideles extitit, vt apparet Actuum quarto. Et si ad infideles in casu se extenderet, adhuc fortasse magis meritoria foret, iuxta illud Lucae sexto: Benefacite his qui oderunt vos. Potest autem licite perfectus custodire residua & debet: ea tamen intentione seu proposito firmo quod diximus. Vnde Ioannis sexto: colligite quae superauerunt fragmenta, ne pereant. Collegerunt ergo & impleuerunt duodecim cophinos fragmentorum. Sicetiam sentit Glossa super Matthaei 18. Staterem illum assumens, &c. inquit enim: Tanta paupertatis fuit dominus, vt unde daret tributa non haberet. Iudas quidam communia in loculis habebat. Sed res pauperum in suos visus convertere nephas duxit. Ecce quod reseruata erant pauperum, id est ea intentione custodiebantur. Et ex hoc apparet illos errare, qui dicunt attinere perfectioni votum nihil recipiendi ad distribuendum dum pauperibus infirmis aut aliter quærere sufficientia impotentibus. Nam hunc quæstum exercuit Apostolus, & licite ac meritorie nulli dubium, quemadmodum palam est secunda ad Corinth. capite nono. Et apparet etiam ex Glossa super illud Ioan. 21. Pasce oves meas. &c. Series autem horum omitto propter abbreviationem. Sequitur etiam ex iam dicta descriptione nec sfario, quod perfectus nullam rem immobilem, ut domum aut agrum in sua potestate existentem seruare aut retinere debet nec potest nisi firmo proposito, cum primum potuerit id alienandi seu commutandi ad pecuniam vel rem aliam conuenienter pauperibus immediate distribuibilem. Nam quia domus aut ager non possent immediate distribui pauperibus conuenienter, quin in eo contingeret peccare per superabundantiam & defectum, in talibus est Christi consilium attendendum, dum dixit Mathæi decimonono, Lucæ decimooctauo, & Marci decimo: Vade & vende: Nec dixit, omnia quæ habes da pauperibus: nec dixit, omnia quæ habes dimitte deperdi, sed vade & vende, quoniam vendendo conuenientior distributio fieri potest: sic etiam fieri consulebant apostoli. Et quibus consulebatur, sic etiam faciebant, sua volentes pauperibus distribuere conuenienter. Unde Actuum quarto: Quotquot enim possessores agrorum domorum erant, vendentes afferebant pretia eorum. Dividebantur autem singulis, prout cuique opus erat. Apparet etiam ex iam dictis, quod nullius rei temporalis dominium acquisitum, iuxta primam, secundam, & tertiam dominii significationem iam dictam perfecto conuenire potest, ut ex Matthæi quinto, & Lucæ sexto probauimus prius. Et per Apostolum idem confirmauimus prima ad Corinth. sexto. Idem q; per Augustinum & Glossam ibidem patefecimus sufficienter: quorum series omisimus inducere propter rei euidentiam & sermonis abbreviationem. Nec est auscultandus sermo dicentis, immobilia licite a perfecto iste seruari posse: ut ex ipsis prouentus annui pauperibus distribuantur: quoniam amplioris est meriti propter Christi dilectionem & proximi misericordiam distribuere pauperibus rem simul & prouentum quam alterum tantum. Et adhuc magis rem solam quam solum eius prouentum: Quoniam sic pluribus pauperibus ac ~gentibus simul subuenire potest, qui fortasse ante futurum rei prouentum propter defectum incurrerent ægritudinem aut mortem, stuprum, furtum, aut aliud inconueniens. Rursum quoniam infra tempus futuri rei prouentus fortasse morietur, qui eam reseruauit, & sic ex ea nunquam merebitur quod mereri poterat. Idem penitus tendendum de mobilibus quibuscunque, quæ etiam sic retenta cum aliis similiter inordinate mouere sunt nata detinentis affectum. Quod si tamen hæc virtus charitas esse credatur, ut quidam sentire videntur nulli, dubium, quin hic modus charitatis, cum summa scilicet pauperitate perfectior sit habitu dominii rei temporalis in proprio vel communi, ut ex prioribus rationibus palam.
units.tr: That the love and desire for temporal goods turns a man toward them, and so turns him away from the love of God, is plain. This is why the truth of Matthew 6 holds: "Where your treasure is, there is your heart also." Nor does the excuse of the man who says, "Though I have these things, I do not turn my love to them," carry any weight. Hear Christ in Matthew 13 and Mark 4, saying that the deceitfulness of riches chokes the word. Jerome says there: "Riches are flattering, promising one thing and doing another; for this reason, one who wishes to be perfect must give them up altogether." Christ counselled in Luke 18: "Sell all that you have and give to the poor." Bede says there: "Whoever therefore wishes to be perfect must sell what he has, not in part, as Ananias and Sapphira did, but all of it." And Theophylact, in the same place and to the point, adds: "He urges the greatest poverty; for if he keeps back anything of temporal goods, he is its slave," that is, of those who keep such things for their own sake. Things of this kind are by nature apt to stir the affection of the one who holds them in disordered ways. Rabanus, on the same saying of Christ in Matthew 19, adds something very much to the point: "There is a considerable difference between having money and loving money. It is safer neither to have nor to love riches." For, as Jerome adds in the same place, "riches, once possessed, are hard to despise." They are stickier than birdlime, as Thomas says on Luke 18, on the same counsel of Christ. So one who withdraws from riches, as far as it is possible and lawful for a wayfarer to do so, withdraws from very many hindrances to charity. He also voluntarily deprives himself of many pleasures and worldly advantages, exposing himself to many sufferings, dishonours and inconveniences of this age. Although this is known in itself, and confirmed by experience, the wise man says in Ecclesiastes 10: "Money, he says, obeys all things, that is, for the one who has money." On the other side, Proverbs 15 says: "All the days of the poor are evil, since the poor man abounds in afflictions," as the Gloss says there. Again, in chapter 19 he says: "Riches add many friends, but from the poor even those he had are separated." That to endure the sorrows of this age, and to abstain from pleasant things for Christ's sake, is meritorious and advisable, is plainly shown in Matthew 5, 19 and Luke 6. Thus, as regards the endurance of sorrows: "Blessed are the poor; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who suffer persecution; blessed are those who hunger," together with the other things listed there; and as regards the abstaining from pleasures: "everyone who has left house or brothers," together with the others listed there, "will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life." The holy Glosses there explain the same point, which I have omitted for brevity, since the matter is well enough known. This was also the view of the Apostle in Romans 8: "For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed in us." Therefore the adversities of this age are meritorious for those who voluntarily bear them. The same Apostle in 2 Corinthians 1 says: "For as you are partners in the sufferings, so you will be in the comfort also." Ambrose there: "Because an equal glory will be repaid to your labour," that is, proportionate to it. Yet the communities of persons who hold dominion over temporal goods in common are not so arranged as to bear these sorrows and inconveniences of the world. Indeed, many poor people living in marriage in the world, who sometimes have private property, but often lack what is needed for life, are in a better position in this respect than those who possess such things only in common. That the precepts and counsels of Christ can be observed most fully according to this kind of meritorious poverty, which we have called the highest of the others, will appear to anyone who runs through the Gospel series, especially in the passages assigned. For one who has chosen such extreme poverty, how can he be covetous or proud, incontinent or intemperate, ambitious, merciless, dishonest and quarrelsome, timid, slothful, envious, or, again, lying, impatient and malicious toward another for some reason? Indeed, a disposition of this kind seems to open the door to all virtues, so that the precepts and counsels can also be fulfilled with equanimity. Since this is plain to the one who considers it, I omit the proof for brevity. Thus the highest mode or species of meritorious poverty is the one we described earlier, since by it all the precepts of Christ and his meritorious counsels can be observed more fully and more securely. From this description it first appears that the perfect person ought to renounce temporal goods as regards dominion by an express vow, both because of Christ's counsel, which we have already quoted from Luke 14, and because by declaring his poverty in this way he makes himself more contemptible in the sight of others and is more exposed to worldly dishonours. Hence Luke 9: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself." From this it follows further that no one can observe the highest poverty before he has the perfect use of reason. It also follows from this description that the one who is perfect ought to have, to seek or to keep nothing for his own sake, namely to supply his future need, except what is present and pressing, apart only from the case we mentioned earlier in the description. Hence Matthew 6: "Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself." On this the Gloss says: "About tomorrow, that is, about the future. It is right to take what is present with thanks; about the future, which divine providence arranges, one should not be anxious, but commit the care of the future, since it is uncertain, to God, to whom our care belongs." In the same chapter 6 Christ said to the disciples: "Look at the birds of the air, for they do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them." And a little below he adds: "Therefore do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed? For the Gentiles seek all these things." We have said, however, that it is not lawful for the perfect person to keep anything for tomorrow for his own sake. We do not mean by this that, if something remains of the lawful daily gain that has come to him, he must reject it and in no way keep it. Rather, he should not keep such a remainder for himself in such a way that he does not firmly intend to give it away and distribute it fittingly to the poor who meet him and are in need before he himself is. Hence Luke 3: "He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none; and he who has food, let him do likewise." By "two garments and food" he understands what is left over beyond the person's own provision for present need. Yet it has been said that a community of those who keep or hold goods only for certain specified persons, such as those of monks, canons and the like, is not a perfect community. For the perfect community was that of Christ and the apostles, which extended to all the faithful, as appears in Acts 4. And if it were extended to unbelievers in some case, it would perhaps be even more meritorious, according to the saying of Luke 6: "Do good to those who hate you." The perfect person may lawfully keep what is left over, and indeed should do so, but with the intention or firm purpose that we have described. Hence John 6: "Gather up the fragments that remain, so that they may not perish. So they gathered them and filled twelve baskets with the fragments." The Gloss on Matthew 17 also thinks the same, on the words "taking that stater, etc." For it says: "The Lord was so poor that he had nothing from which to pay the tribute. Judas, however, kept common funds in a purse. Yet to turn the goods of the poor to his own use he thought a sin." See, then, that the goods of the poor were kept for them, that is, they were kept with that intention. From this it appears that those are in error who say that a vow to receive nothing, except to distribute it to the poor, or to seek what is sufficient for those unable to support themselves, belongs to perfection. For the Apostle exercised this kind of gain, and that it was lawful and meritorious is beyond doubt, as is plain in 2 Corinthians 9. It also appears from the Gloss on John 21: "Feed my sheep," and so on. I omit the series of these passages for brevity. It also follows from the description just given, and not obscurely, that the perfect person ought not to keep or retain any immovable thing, such as a house or field, in his own power, nor can he do so, except with a firm purpose to alienate or exchange it for money or another thing that can be fittingly distributed immediately to the poor, as soon as he is able to do so. For since a house or a field cannot be fittingly distributed immediately to the poor without sinning by excess or by deficiency, in such cases the counsel of Christ must be attended to, when he said in Matthew 19, Luke 18 and Mark 10: "Go and sell." He did not say, "Give to the poor all that you have," nor "Let go all that you have to be lost," but "Go and sell," because by selling a more fitting distribution can be made. So the apostles also advised doing this, and those who were so advised did it, being willing to distribute their goods fittingly to the poor. Hence Acts 4: "For as many as were owners of fields or houses sold them and brought the prices of them. And they were distributed to each as anyone had need." It also appears from what has been said that the dominion over any temporal thing, acquired in the first, second or third sense of dominion mentioned above, cannot belong to the perfect person, as we proved earlier from Matthew 5 and Luke 6. We confirmed the same by the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 6. We have also sufficiently shown the same through Augustine and the Gloss there, whose series I have omitted to adduce, for the sake of the clarity of the matter and the brevity of the discourse. Nor should we listen to the argument of one who says that the perfect person may lawfully keep immovable goods, so that the yearly yield from them may be distributed to the poor. For it is of greater merit, on account of love for Christ and mercy toward one's neighbour, to distribute to the poor both the thing and its yield together, than to distribute only an equal amount. And it is still more meritorious to give the thing alone than only its yield. For in this way one can help many poor and needy people at once, who might perhaps, before the future yield of the thing, fall into sickness or death, debauchery, theft, or some other unfitting course because of want. Again, because within the time of the future yield the one who kept it may perhaps die, and so he will never merit from it what he could have merited. The same must be understood entirely of any movable goods, which, when retained in this way along with other things, are likewise by nature apt to stir the affection of the one who holds them in disordered ways. But if this were believed to be charity itself, as some seem to think, there is no doubt that this way of charity, namely with the highest poverty, is more perfect than the possession of temporal goods in private or in common, as is plain from the earlier arguments.

units.la: Nunc autem ad principale propositum accedentes, ostendere volumus, Christum viatorem summam meritoriæ pauperitatis speciem vel modum seruasse: quoniam primum in vnoquoque aliorum est maximum, Christus autem sub noua lege primus viatorum merentium vitam æternam: fuit ergo aliorum perfectione maximus, ergo statum hunc ad temporalia obseruauit, cum absque ipso mereri maxime, secundum legem communem impossibile sit. Rursum si hunc non obseruasset modum paupertatis, fuisset alter viator, esset, vel esse posset Christo secundum communem legem perfectior in merendo, quod nephas est credere. Hoc enim Christus ad perfectionem meriti asseruit pertinere, cum dixit vbi supra: Si vis perfectus esse, omnia quæcunque habes vende & da pauperibus. nec addit proprium aut commune, sed hoc vniuersaliter intellexit, propter quod etiam significatum vniuersale geminauit, dicens: Omnia quaecunque. Nam qui habet in communi cum aliquo vel aliquibus dominium aut reseruationem temporalium extra modum dictum non abdicauit temporalium omne abdicari possibile, nec tot passionibus seculi exponitur, aut commodis priuatur, sicut temporalibus renuncians vtroq; modo, nec sic ab horum solicitudine liberatur, nec omnia Christi consilia seruat æqualiter omnimode abdicanti.
units.tr: Now coming to our main proposition, we wish to show that Christ, as a wayfarer, observed the highest kind or mode of meritorious poverty. The first in each class is the greatest, and Christ under the new law was the first of the wayfarers meriting eternal life. He was therefore the greatest of all in perfection, and so he observed this state with regard to temporal things, since under the common law it is wholly impossible to merit most of all without it. Again, if he had not observed this mode of poverty, he would have been another wayfarer, and would be, or could be, more perfect than Christ in merit under the common law, which it is wicked to believe. For Christ affirmed that this pertains to the perfection of merit when he said above: If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor. He adds neither "proper" nor "common" but understood it universally, and for that reason he also doubled the universal sense, saying: All that you have. For whoever holds dominion or reservation of temporal goods in common with someone or others, beyond the mode described, has not renounced every temporal thing that can be renounced. Nor is he exposed to so many sufferings of the world, nor deprived of its comforts, as one who renounces temporal goods in both ways. Nor is he so freed from anxiety about them, nor does he observe all Christ's counsels equally, as one who renounces in every way.

units.la: Post hæc ostendere volo Christum habuisse aliquid in proprio, & etiam in communi, summam tamen pauperta tem seruando in proprio quidem dicto secundum tertiam significationem per id quod habetur Marci secundo: Erant autem multi qui sequebantur eum scribæ & pharisæi videntes quia manducauerat cum publicanis & peccatoribus. Certum est autem ipsum licite ac sibi proprium seu singulariter habuisse quod ori suo applicabat & manducabat. Amplius & vestimenta sibi propria seu singulariter habuit, vt ex Matthæi 27. Marci 15. Lucæ 23. & Ioannis 19. satis apparet. Unde in Matthæo vbi supra: Exuerunt eum chlamide, & induerunt eum vestimentis eius. Sic et in Marco & Luca, quorum series omittantur propter decurtationem sermonis: Temporalia igitur in proprio Christus habuit licite seu de iure summam etiam pauperta tem obseruans, & talia voluit habere & velle debuit, alioquin mortaliter peccaturus, quia verus homo existens eluniit, vt apparet ex Matthæi 21. & Marci decimo octavo. Ideoque cibo indiguit, quem non sumens; sumere potens peccasset graviter, scilicet fame videlicet perimendo scienter. In communi quoque Christus habuit licite, summam etiam pauperta tem obseruans. Unde Ioannis 12. Dixit autem hoc Iudas, non quia de egenis pertinebat ad eum, sed quia fur erat & loculos habens, communes scilicet Christo & apostolis, & pauperibus reliquis, quod apparet ex eo quod de his Christus iussit distribui famescentibus pauperum tuum, vt Matthæi decimoquarto satis apparet. Loculi autem erant repositoria, in quibus pecunia eleemosynaria sibi data reseruabatur. Idem rursum eiusdem 14. Quidam autem putabant quia loculos habebat Iudas. Idem etiam Glossa super illud Matth. 18. Statere illum sumens, &c. Iudas, inquit Glossa, communia in loculis habebat. Sic etiam apostoli post
units.tr: Next I wish to show that Christ had something in his own right and also in common, yet observed the highest poverty, taking "in his own right" in the third sense, from what is written in Mark 2: Many publicans and sinners sat down with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes and Pharisees, when they saw that he ate with publicans and sinners. It is certain that he lawfully had as his own, and singly, what he applied to his mouth and ate. Moreover, he had garments as his own and singly, as is sufficiently clear from Matthew 27, Mark 15, Luke 23 and John 19. Hence in Matthew, above: They stripped him of his cloak and put his own garments on him. So too in Mark and Luke, whose passages are omitted for brevity. Christ therefore had temporal goods in his own right, lawfully and by right, while still observing the highest poverty. He willed to have such things and ought to have willed it, since otherwise he would have sinned mortally; for, being a true man, he hungered, as appears from Matthew 21 and Mark 18. Therefore he needed food, and had he not taken it, though able to take it, he would have sinned gravely, namely by knowingly bringing about his own death by hunger. Christ also had things in common lawfully, still observing the highest poverty. Hence John 12: Judas said this, not because he cared for the needy, but because he was a thief and had the money box, that is, the common funds of Christ, the apostles and the other poor. This is clear from the fact that Christ ordered these funds to be distributed to the hungry poor, as is sufficiently clear from Matthew 14. The money boxes were containers in which alms money given to them was kept. Again in the same chapter 14: Some thought that Judas had the money box. The Gloss on Matthew 18 also says the same: Taking that coin, etc. Judas, says the Gloss, had the common funds in the money box. So too the apostles, after

units.la: {f} Ad propositum facit notatio, ut sequitur. post Christi resurrectionem communia inuicem & cum aliis pauperibus habuerunt, summam paupertatem seruantes. Unde Actuum quarto: Erant autem illis omnia communia. Propria quoq; similiter habuerunt, victum scilicet atque vestitum, quos sibi proprie applicuerunt, quemadmodum Christus.
units.tr: The note bears on the matter, as follows: after Christ's resurrection they had things in common among themselves and with other poor, observing the highest poverty. Hence Acts 4: And all things were common to them. They likewise had things of their own, namely food and clothing, which they applied to themselves in their own right, just as Christ did.

units.la: Deinde tanquam principale intentum ex hoc & precedente atque immediate sequente capitulo inferre volo per necessitatem Christum viatorem, summam perfectionis praecipue monstrantem, non habuisse dominium aliquod acquisitum, secundum primam vel secundam aut tertiam dominii significationem, dictum in proprio vel cum alio in communi rei alicuius temporalis aut eius visus. Quoniam tale dominium sibi assumens non omnia consilia, & praecipue summam paupertatem viatori possibilem, seruasset, Christus autem haec omnia perfectissime viatorum seruauit. Non igitur tale dominium temporalium Christus habuit, nec habere voluit, quod scriptura possessionem plerunq; nominauit, ut in Lucae 14. Qui non renunciat omnibus quae possidet. Sic etiam Matthaei decimo: Nolite possidere aurum, neq; argentum, neq; pecuniam in zonis vestris, id est, conseruare nolite, nisi forte in casu licito, ea scilicet intentione atq; necessitatibus, quas pridem diximus, ut propter impotentes pauperes, quemadmodum fecit Paulus, aut temporis vel loci & personae dispositionis necessitate urgente, de quibus in sequenti capitulo amplius apparebit. Quamuis tamen dominium iam dictum, etiam in praedictis casibus summe pauperi habere non liceat: quoniam tale dominium per necessitatem circa summam paupertatem excludit Christi consilium. Non habuit ergo Christus temporalium dominium iam dictum, nec habere potest eius aliquis imitator, summam scilicet paupertatem seruare volens. His consequenter dico, quod ex scriptura sacra convinci non potest Christum quantumcunque condescendentem infirmis, habuisse temporalium iam dictum dominium seu possessionem in proprio vel communi, quamuis hoc credantur sensisse sanctorum aliqui. Pari nanq; ratione concludi posset, Christum exercuisse omnia permissa, ne statum talia exercentium damnasse videretur. Sic ergo saeculi principatum seu saeculare iudicium contentiosum acceptasset ac exercuisset, cuius oppositum ostensum est irrefragabiliter quarto huius. S.c coniugium, sic actionem contentiosam coram iudice coactiuo, sic reliqua permissa omnia: Quae Christum exercuisse nemo per scripturam convincere potest, sed oppositum magis. Non enim talia ipsum oportuit aut decuit exercere, ne statum exercentium, quos vocant infirmos, damnasse videretur: Quoniam non sequitur, Christus non fuit coniugatus, ergo statum coniugatorum visus fuit damnare, similiter & in reliquis. Nam ipse sufficienter expressit differentiam inter ea, quae sunt de necessitate salutis fienda vel omittenda, praecepta vel prohibita, & ea quae non sunt de necessitate salutis apud sanctos vocata supererogationis. Cum enim interrogatus fuisset a quodam de necessariis ad salutem aeternam, respondit Christus: Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata. Interroganti vero iterum de his quae sunt supererogationis, non respondit Christus, si vis ad vitam ingredi, sed dixit illi, si vis perfectus esse. In quibus verbis Matth. 19. Luc. 18. & Marci 10. Christus expresse fecit intelligere, quod observatio mandatorum sufficiebat ad vitam aeternam; cum de hoc interroganti nil aliud respondit quam serua mandata, si vis ad vitam ingredi. Idcoque non omnia permissa Christum oportuit aut decuit exercere, ne statum eiusmodi exercentium damnasse videretur, quia iam expresserat ipsos ex solis mandatis seu praeceptis, communiter sumendo praeceptum affirmatiuum & negatiuum, posse saluari, sed magis decuit ipsum consiliorum exercitium, ut summam paupertatem seruare, coniugium omittere propter talium exercitii reliquis omnibus praebendum exemplum, quemadmodum ipsum de facto fecisse atque dixisse legimus in scriptura. Nam Matth. 8. Lucae nono de sua paupertate loquens, ait: Vulpes foueas habent, volucres caeli nidos: filius autem hominis non habet vbi reclinet caput. vbi Glossa, Cum ita sit pauper vt nec hospitium habeam quod meum sit. Tantae enim paupertatis fuit dominus, vt vnde daret tributa non haberet, secundum Gloss. super illud Matth. 18. Staterem illum assumens, da eis pro me & te. Nusquam tamen legimus ipsum habuisse castra vel agros, aut cumulos thesaurorum, ne statum sic habentium visus damnare fuisset.
units.tr: Then, as the principal aim to be drawn from this and the preceding and immediately following chapters, I wish to infer by necessity that Christ, as wayfarer, showing above all the highest perfection, did not have any acquired dominion in the first, second or third sense of dominion, namely of some temporal thing or its use, held singly or in common with another. For had he assumed such dominion, he would not have observed all the counsels, and above all the highest poverty possible to a wayfarer; but Christ observed all these most perfectly. Therefore Christ neither had nor wished to have such dominion over temporal things, which Scripture often calls possession, as in Luke 14: Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses. So too Matthew 10: Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts, that is, do not keep them, except perhaps in a lawful case, namely with that intention and for those necessities which we have said before, such as for impoverished poor, as Paul did, or when the necessity of the time, place and person's situation presses, as will appear more fully in the following chapter. Yet such dominion as described is not lawful even in these cases for one who wishes to be most poor, since such dominion through necessity excludes the counsel of Christ concerning the highest poverty. Christ therefore did not have the dominion over temporal things described, nor can any imitator of his who wishes to observe the highest poverty have it.
