Consequently I say that from Holy Scripture it cannot be proved that Christ, however much he condescended to the weak, had such dominion or possession of temporal things, singly or in common, although some of the saints are believed to have held this view. By the same reasoning one could conclude that Christ exercised all things permitted, lest he seem to have condemned the state of those who exercise them. Thus he would have accepted and exercised secular rule or contentious secular judgment, the opposite of which was shown irrefutably in book four of this work; likewise marriage, likewise a lawsuit before a judge with coercive power, and likewise all the other permitted things. No one can prove from Scripture that Christ exercised these; rather the opposite. For it was not fitting or proper for him to exercise such things, lest he seem to have condemned the state of those who exercise them, whom they call weak. For it does not follow that because Christ was not married, he therefore seemed to condemn the state of married people; and likewise in the other cases. For he sufficiently expressed the difference between those things which must be done or omitted for necessary salvation, the commanded or forbidden, and those which are not necessary for salvation and are called works of supererogation among the saints. For when a certain man asked him about what is necessary for eternal life, Christ answered: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. But when he asked again about what belongs to supererogation, Christ did not answer, If you wish to enter into life, but said to him, If you wish to be perfect. In these words, Matthew 19, Luke 18 and Mark 10, Christ clearly made it understood that observing the commandments was sufficient for eternal life, since to the man asking about this he answered nothing else than keep the commandments, if you wish to enter into life. Therefore Christ neither ought nor was it fitting for him to exercise all permitted things, lest he seem to have condemned the state of those who exercise them, because he had already expressed that they can be saved by commandments alone, taking precept affirmative and negative in the common sense. Rather it was fitting for him to practise the counsels, such as keeping the highest poverty and omitting marriage, so as to provide an example to all the rest for the exercise of such counsels, just as we read that he actually did and said in Scripture. For in Matthew 8 and Luke 9, speaking of his poverty, he says: Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head. Here the Gloss says: He is so poor that he does not even have a lodging that is his own. For the Lord was of such poverty that he had nothing from which to pay the tribute, according to the Gloss on Matthew 18: Taking that coin, give it for me and you. Yet we nowhere read that he had camps or fields, or heaps of treasure, lest he seem to condemn the state of those who have such things.

units.la: Quod si tamen Christus exercuisset permissa, potuisset hoc facere nil minus omnibus consiliis pariter obseruatis, quoniam ipse qui legislator erat, poterat huiusmodi exercere, ne statum exercentium reprobare videretur, unde talia non voluisset simpliciter, quemadmodum volunt infirmi qui ea volunt propter suum commodum, sed ea Christus voluisset propter aliud, & ea quodam modo nolens, quia non propter se sed propter iam dictam causam. Reliqui vero perfecti tale dominium nullo modo possunt velle convenienter, summam consiliorum obseruantes. Non enim id possunt velle, ne statum aliorum damnare videantur: quoniam ad eos statum approbare vel damnare non pertinet, eo quod legislatores non fuerunt nec sunt aut erunt. Si ergo tale dominium vellent, id vellent quemadmodum infirmi, non tanquam perfecti, licuisset ergo Christo si voluisset haec exercere permissa, summam omnium consiliorum obseruans, quod tamen alteri ab ipso minime licere potest propter causam iam dictam. Quod si quaeratur, quis tam perfectus esse valeat, vt nihil timol temporal um velit habere, nisi sufficiens indigentiae praesenti aut immediate instanti, quasi praesenti. Dico, quod Christus & alii quicunq; volentes quamuis tales pauci sunt, quoniam via lata arta est & angusta, & pauci ingrediuntur per eam, vt scribitur Matthaei septimo. Et dicitur tu quaeso: Quot sint martyres voluntarii temporibus his? quot viri heroici? quot Catones, Scipiones, atque Fabritii?
units.tr: But if Christ had exercised the permitted things, he could have done so without in any way neglecting the sum of all the counsels, since he himself, being the lawgiver, could exercise such things without seeming to condemn the state of those who do exercise them. Therefore he would not have wished such things simply, as the weak wish them for their own advantage; rather Christ would have wished them for another reason, and in a certain way unwillingly, because he did not do so for his own sake but for the cause already mentioned. The rest of the perfect, however, cannot in any way fittingly wish such dominion, since they keep the sum of the counsels. For they cannot wish it without seeming to condemn the state of others, since it does not belong to them to approve or condemn a state, inasmuch as they were not, are not, and will not be lawgivers. If therefore they wished such dominion, they would wish it as the weak do, not as the perfect. So it was permitted to Christ, if he had wished, to exercise these permitted things while still keeping the sum of all the counsels; but this cannot by any means be permitted to anyone else, for the reason already mentioned. But if someone asks who can be so perfect as to wish to have nothing of temporal things beyond what suffices for present need, or for need immediately impending, as if present, I say that Christ and others who are willing are such, although they are few, since "the way that leads to life is narrow, and few find it," as it is written in Matthew chapter seven. And I ask you: how many voluntary martyrs are there in these times? how many heroic men? how many Catos, Scipios, and Fabricii?

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: De quibusdam instantiis ad determinata in cap. precedenti & ipsarum solutionibus, ac confirmatione dictorum in eodem capitulo.
units.tr: On certain objections to the points made in the previous chapter, their solutions, and the confirmation of what was said in this chapter.

units.la: AD dicta vero sic intendentibus obiiciet aliquis, quoniam si ministrantes evangelium, statum perfectioris etiam seruare volentes episcopi atque presbyteri nihil seruare possint propter suam futuram necessitatem supplendam, quin illud firmo proposito velle debeant tribuere pauperi, vel pauperibus occurrentibus primum & magis indigentibus cum reliquis quæ in descriptione summæ paupertatis iam diximus. Quomodo poterunt intendere prædicationi verbi Dei, & quotidianam vitam procurare, quod necessarium videtur si nihil illis pro futuro sibi seruare liceat? Videntur enim hic simul fieri difficilia vel impossibilia quædam. Unde Actuum sexto: Non est æquum nos derelinquere verbum Dei & ministrare mensis. Innuentes apostoli quod duo hæc, simul fieri nequeunt. Licitum est ergo perfectis propter suam necessitatem futuram supplendam temporalia reseruare. Amplius ostenditur idem ex alia: quoniam Ioannis 14. super illud: Quia loculos in quibus oblata seruabantur, &c. dicit Glossa: In quo forma datur ecclesiæ seruandi necessaria. Cum igitur in hoc loco ecclesiæ nomine intelligantur perfectius, præcipue sacerdotes & episcopi, videtur quod necessaria pro futuro sibi licite seruare possint. Rursum supra illud Matth. 7. Nolite solliciti esse in crastinum, dicit Glossa: Sed nemo debet scandalizari, si quem iustorum viderit hæc necessaria sibi suisque procurare, ne indicet eum de crastino cogitare, quia ille qui hoc præcepit, cui ministrabant angeli, propter hoc exemplum dandum, loculos habuit, unde necessaria vitibus præbebat. Adhuc firmatur idem ex Ioannis decimo quarto, vbi dicitur sic: Quidam autem putabant quia loculos habebat Iudas, quod dixisset ei Iesus, Eme ea quæ opus sunt nobis ad diem festum. ergo pecuniam reseruatam habebant Christus & Apostoli, unde talia emere poterant. Adhuc ostenditur idem ex alio, quoniam Matthæi sexto, super illud: Respicite volatilia cæli, &c. dicit Glossa, Non prohibet providentiam & laborem, sed sollicitudinem: ut tota spes nostra sit in Deo. Perfectis igitur de futuris sibi necessariis prouidere licet. Amplius ostenditur idem ex Matthæi 14. Marci sexto & octavo, & Lucæ decimo. Dixit enim Christus ad apostolos: Quot panes habetis? Qui dixerunt, septem. Hos autem seruauerant extra præsentem necessitatem, ergo perfectis pro futuro sibi temporalia seruare licet.
units.tr: To those who understand these things in this way, someone will object: if bishops and elders, who minister the Gospel and wish to keep to the more perfect state, cannot keep anything because of the future need they must supply, then they must firmly resolve to give to the poor, or to the poor who come along, first and most of all to those in need, along with the rest, as we have already said in describing supreme poverty. How will they be able to devote themselves to preaching the Word of God and to provide for daily life, which seems necessary, if they may keep nothing for the future? For here some things seem to be difficult or impossible to do together. Hence Acts 6: It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables, the apostles implying that these two cannot be done at the same time. It is therefore lawful for the perfect to keep temporal goods in reserve to supply their future need. The same is shown further from another passage: John 14, on the words because they kept the purses in which the offerings were stored, etc., the Gloss says: In this a pattern is given to the Church for keeping what is necessary. Since in this place the name of the Church is understood of the more perfect, especially priests and bishops, it seems that they may lawfully keep necessities for the future. Again, on Matthew 7, Take no thought for the morrow, the Gloss says: But no one should be scandalized if he sees one of the righteous providing these necessities for himself and his own, lest he judge him for thinking about tomorrow, because he who gave this command, whom the angels served, had a purse, for the sake of giving this example, from which he supplied the necessities of life. The same is further confirmed from John 14, where it is said: Some thought that, because Judas had the purse, Jesus had told him, Buy what we need for the feast. So Christ and the apostles had money kept in reserve, from which they could buy such things. The same is shown from another passage, Matthew 6, on the words Behold the birds of the air, etc., the Gloss says: It does not forbid foresight and labour, but anxiety, so that our whole hope may be in God. It is therefore lawful for the perfect to make provision for what they will need in the future. The same is shown further from Matthew 14, Mark 6 and 8, and Luke 9. For Christ said to the apostles: How many loaves have you? They said, seven. Now they had kept these beyond the present need; therefore it is lawful for the perfect to keep temporal goods for the future.

units.la: Deinde ostenditur per necessitatem, quod perfecti habeant vel habere possint etiam perfecti manentes, dominium dictum secundum primam aut secundam vel tertiam speciem dominii rerum temporalium vel visus earum in proprio aut cum alio vel aliis in communi, & maxime rerum quæ vnico aliquo visu consumptibiles sunt. Primum quidem apparet hoc ex Lucæ 22. cum loquens Christus ad Apostolos ait: Et qui non habet, vendat tunicam suam & emat gladium: sed qui emit aut vendit aliud, dominium rei vel pretii transfert in alterum, nullus autem in alterum transfert quod prius non habuit. Dominium igitur habuerunt Christus & Apostoli supradictum. Deinde ostendo idem ex alio sic: quoniam qui habuit visum licitum alicuius rei ab illius dominio iam dicto inseparabilem ex necessitate habuit rei dominium, sed Christus & apostoli talium rerum habuerunt visum, ergo per necessitatem ipsarum dominium: prima propositio huius deductionis famosa est, secunda vero probatur, ex eo visu rerum consumptibilium, quem Christus & apostoli habuerunt: Quoniam vel habuerunt visum rei suæ de iure, vel non suæ, de iure. Si visum rei suæ de iure, ergo habuerunt simul cum visu rei dominium. Si vero rei non suæ aut ergo alienæ, aut rei quæ in nullius bonis erat ante visum eius. Si rei quæ in nullius bonis erat, cum talis occupanti concedatur de iure: Christus autem & apostoli per necessitatem prius aut simul tempore cum visu rem occupauerunt, ergo ipsius dominium ante visum vel simul cum visu habuerunt. aeq; presbyteris. Vnde Ambrosius in epistola de tradendis basilicis, ait: Agri ecclesiae soluunt tributum, ergo agros & immobilia possidebant viri perfecti, qui etiam ecclesiae nomine designantur aut designari debent, praecipue sacerdotes. Ostenditur autem hoc de Christo in speciali primum quidem: quoniam secundum leges etiam humanas, qui aliquem redimit a morte, illius dominus efficitur, & per consequens omnium suorum temporalium, sed Christus nos a morte redemit, non quacunque, sed ab aeterna, ergo nostrorum corporum & temporalium acquisiuit dominium. Rursum Apocalypsis decimonono scribitur de ipso, quod habebat scriptum in vestimento, rex regum, & dominus dominantium. Vbi glossa: in vestimento scilicet humanitatis. Cum igitur rex & dominus omnium eorum habeat dominium, apparet quod Christus in rebus temporalibus hoc habuerit.
units.tr: Next, it is shown from necessity that the perfect have, or can have, even while remaining perfect, the dominion (as said, of the first, second or third kind of dominion over temporal things) or the use of such things, either as their own or with another or others in common, and especially of things that are consumed by a single use. The first point appears from Luke 22, where Christ, speaking to the apostles, says: And he who has no sword, let him sell his garment and buy one. But whoever buys or sells something transfers the ownership of the thing or the price to another, and no one transfers to another what he did not first have. Christ and the apostles therefore had the aforesaid dominion. Next I show the same from another point as follows: whoever has the lawful use of a thing, which is by necessity inseparable from the aforesaid dominion over it, has of necessity the ownership of the thing. But Christ and the apostles had the use of such things; therefore by necessity they had the ownership of them. The first premise of this argument is well known; the second is proved from the use of consumable things that Christ and the apostles had. For either they had the use of a thing that was their own by right, or of one that was not their own by right. If the use of their own thing by right, then they had the ownership together with the use. But if of a thing not their own, then it was either another's, or a thing that belonged to no one before they used it. If it belonged to no one, since such a thing is granted by right to whoever takes possession of it, and Christ and the apostles of necessity took possession of the thing either before or at the same time as they used it, then they had its ownership before or together with its use. The same holds for the elders. Hence Ambrose, in his letter on handing over the basilicas, says: The fields of the Church pay tribute; therefore the perfect men, who are or ought to be designated by the name of the Church, especially the priests, possessed fields and immovable property. This is shown of Christ in particular, first of all because, even according to human laws, whoever redeems someone from death becomes his lord, and consequently lord of all his temporal goods. But Christ redeemed us from death, not from any death but from eternal death; therefore he acquired dominion over our bodies and temporal goods. Again, Revelation 19 says of him that he had written on his garment, King of kings and Lord of lords. The Gloss there: on his garment, that is, of his humanity. Since therefore he has the dominion of a king and lord over all these things, it appears that Christ had this dominion over temporal things.

units.la: Ex prius autem diffinitis a nobis de summa paupertate temporalium atque dominio respondeti poterit conuenienter his quae obiecta sunt ex praesenti capitulo, secundum Christi tamen & Apostoli sententiam; primum apponentes, quod ministri euangelii, presbyteri seu episcopi, cum reliquis inferioris ordinis, contentari debent alimento quotidiano, & necessario tegumento statum perfectionis seu summam paupertatem custodire volentes. Vnde 1. ad Tim. vltimo: Habentes autem alimenta & quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Quae siquidem euangelizantibus ministrare tenentur secundum legem diuinam saltem, quibus euangelica praedicatio ministratur. Hoc enim figuraliter dictum Deuteronomii 24. Non alligabis os bouis triturantis in area fruges tuas. Exponens Paulus primae ad Corinthios nono; tanquam dictum propter suturos euangelii doctores atque ministros, sic ait: Nunquid de bobus cura est Deo, an propter nos utique dicit? Idem apparet ex Matthaei decimo, dum ad hoc & propter hoc propositum dixit Christus: Dignus est operarius cibo suo. Debent ergo suscipientes euangelium, victum quotidianum, atque vestitum euangelizanti ministrare si possint. Et hoc tanquam debitum ex lege diuina petere possunt euangelizantes licite, quamuis non in iudicio coactiuo praesentis seculi, idque quibus euangelium ministratur si possint exhibere recusantes, in legem diuinam committunt. Vnde primae ad Corinthios nono: Ita & dominus ordinauit his qui euangelium annunciant de euangelio viuere. Sicut qui pascit gregem, de lacte gregis manducat: & qui plantat vineam de fructu eius edit. Ad aliam vero, decimam aut partem aliquam suorum prouentuum nemo fidelium euangelizantibus, secundum scripturam tenetur. Quod si quibus euangelium ministratur, tantae paupertatis essent, vt euangelizantis sufficientiam, victus atque vestitus ministrare nequi ent: non obligantur ad hoc lege diuina, sed debet ipse aliunde sibi quaerere necessaria vitae, vt alia doctrina vel arte operatiua si quam nouerit exercere, aut alio quodam honesto & conuenienti modo. Sic enim faciebat Apostolus, ne pauperibus quibus euangelizabat onerosus redderetur. Vnde Actuum 20. de se loquens ait: Aurum & argentum aut vestem nullius concupiui, ipsi scitis, quoniam ad ea quae mihi opus erant, & his qui mecum sunt, laborauerunt manus istae. Idem dixit secundae ad Thessalonicenses vltimo: Neque, inquit, panem gratis manducauimus ab aliquo, sed in labore & fatigatione, nocte & die operantes, ne quem vestrum grauaremus. Verum autem iam fidelium deuotorum numero, & praecipue temporibus his, nec laborare manibus neque mendicare necesse est doctrinae sacrae ministros. Nam statuta sunt & ordinata in fidelium communitatibus, tam per legis humanae latorem, quam personas aliquas singulares prouentus quidam, tam ex mobilibus, quam ex immobilibus, ex quibus sufficienter, quinimo abundanter ministrantes euangelium sustentari possunt. Interrogabit autem aliquis, cuius aut quorum sit horum temporalium, praecipue immobilium iam dictum dominium seu vendicandi potestas coram iudice coactiuo praesentis seculi, cum tale dominium ministris euangelicis perfectis existentibus conuenire non possit, secundum determinationem capituli praecedentis. Nos vero dicamus dominium temporalium, quae sunt pro ministrorum euangelicorum sustentatione statuta, legislatoris esse aut eius vel eorum qui per legislatorem ad hoc fuerint deputati, vel per eos qui talia dederunt, si fuerint singulares personae, quae supradicta temporalia dederint & ordinauerint ex bonis suis ad vsum praedictum: qui siquidem sic statuti ad ecclesiasticorum temporalium defensionem & vendicationem vocari solebant ecclesiarum patroni. Nam antiquitus viri sancti atque perfecti ministri euangelici, Christum imitari volentes, contra nullum voluerunt contendere iudicio. Denique nec temporalium dominium assumpserunt, sed solum vsum necessariam ad vitae praesentis & impotentium pauperum sustentationem. Si n. immobilia temporalia habuissent in ipsorum potestate alienandi, etiam sine dominio aliquo seu vendicandi proposito, & ea non alienauerunt ad pauperibus occurrentibus statim distribuendum, minime seruassent Christi consilium, in quo dixit: Vade & vende omnia quaecunque habes, & da pauperibus, siue talia fuissent alueis habita in proprio siue etiam in communi. Hoc tamen est opinandum, quod huiusmodi patroni, quos dominus vendicandi talia diximus, habeant potestatem alienandi ea, vel ad vsus alios conuertendi, quoniam peccarent in legem diuinam saltem, & in humanam forte, quoniam eis non est ad hoc concessum dominium, sed solummodo prohibendi & vendicandi coram iudice coactiuo ab auferentibus aut auferre vel aliquid contrectare volentibus. Et propterea si prouentuum custodia distributio concedatur alicui perfectorum per legislatorem, aut personam singularem, cuius fuerit potestas huiusmodi, dico perfectum summam paupertatem seruando, licite posse quinimo meritorie hanc curam suscipere propter proximi charitatem, & misericordiam exercendam in eum. Sed dicet alius perfectum sibi prouidere de crastino aut de crastinis multis, quoniam suum annuum victum, atq; vestitum suscipit & suscipere intendit ex sibi concesso proventu. Et dicendum est quod talia tempora sic sibi distribuenda concedeuntur, vt ex eis reseruetur quod sufficiat euangelizanti singulis diebus ad victum & vestitum decentem, residuum vero illi committitur distribuendum pauperibus. Et quoniam perfectus propter communem fidelium vtilitatem ad æternam salutem statutus vel electus est ad euangelizandum super certum populum & in loco certo, seu determinato, inquantum euangelizans proponit conuenienter sing ꝟ iis diebus vnicam simul tantum sumere sufficientiam quam deseruit; non autem proponeret simul plures aut successiue sumere ex eadem re quæsita simul si posset vacare quæstui quotidiano, & simul euangelizare, sed quia simul hiis vacare non potest, oportet ipsum ex eadem re intendere plures sufficientias quotidianas cibi & potus sumere, successiue tamen ex eadem re. Nam si quod superest vni suæ sufficientiæ, distribueret pauperibus, non haberet in crastino vnde sumeret sufficientiam vitæ, quam quærere coactus necessario haberet mittere assumptam populi curam, in quo peccaret mortaliter, faciendo commune detrimentum animarum. Deinde vero in eo quod aliena distribueret præter, imo contra intentionem eorum qui talia sibi distribuenda commiserunt. Quia ergo secundum decretum fidelium, quorum est autoritas ordinandi, visum est expediens, determinatum populum habere determinatum ministrum euangelii atque sacramentorum, qui eis ministrare debens in his, alendus est per eos, non conseruat ipse ad crastinum ex intentione propria propter se aliquid quod in sua potestate sit distribuere. Rursum, quoniam non est in dispositione, secundum quam quotidianam vitam sibi quærere possit propter iam dictam causam, perfectus permanens, potest ex re commissa suæ custodiæ plures sufficientias sumere, semper tamen cum proposito id distribuendi quod sibi superest præsenti suæ sufficientiæ, si foret in sua potestate, foret q; ipse in dispositione sibi acquirendi futurum quotidianum victum, quemadmodum etiam dicebatur in summæ paupertatis descriptione. Sufficere debet igitur euangelico ministro victus atq; vestitus quotidiani sufficientia, quam sibi ministrare tenentur suscipientes illius ministerium. Et hanc iure diuino sibi debitâ licite petere potest, quauis non humano iure vendicare sibi debeat hanc coram iudice coactiuo, etiam si iure humano id foret præceptum. Vnde in Glossa secundum Aug. super eodem 2. ad Tim. 3. Nemo militans Deo, &c. dicitur sic: Hoc ideo dicit apostolus, scribens Timotheo ne forte cum indigeret Timotheus, & nollet victu quotidiano sustentari ab eis quibus euangelium ministrabat, nec in opere corporis laborare posset aliqua negotia sibi quaereret, quibus animus eius implicaretur intento, ex quo sibi relinquebatur mendicandum. Ecce ergo, quod si noluissent Timotheo ministrare victum, non dixit eos cogendos, nec quod ipse hoc requirere deberet coram iudice eoactiuo. Quoniam auferenti tuni-cam dandum est & pallium, iuxta Christi consilium, Matth. 5. & Lu. 6. potius quam in iudicio contendendum. Sic etiam dicebat Apostolus secundæ ad Corinth. 8. & nono, pro pauperibus petens ab ipsis, Non quasi imperans dico: & infra, in hoc consilium do. talem collectam appellans gratiam, propter quod etiam lignans eam spontaneam, dixit: Vnusquisq; aut prout destinauit in corde suo, non ex tristitia vel necessitate.
units.tr: From the points we have already settled about the utmost poverty of temporal goods and about ownership, a reply can be given fittingly to the objections raised in the present chapter, yet according to the teaching of Christ and the Apostle. First we set forth that the ministers of the gospel, presbyters or bishops, together with the rest of the lower order, ought to be content with daily food and necessary clothing, if they wish to keep the state of perfection or the utmost poverty. Hence 1 Tim. last: Having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content. Those to whom the gospel is preached are bound, at least by the divine law, to supply these things to those who preach the gospel. For this was said figuratively in Deuteronomy 24: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. Paul, expounding this in 1 Corinthians 9, as said on account of the future teachers and ministers of the gospel, says: Doth God take care for oxen, or does he say it altogether for our sake? The same appears from Matthew 10, where Christ, speaking to this purpose and for this reason, said: The workman is worthy of his food. Those who receive the gospel therefore ought to supply daily food and clothing to the one who preaches it, if they are able. And those who preach may lawfully ask for this as a debt owed by divine law, although not by the coercive judgment of the present age; and those to whom the gospel is preached, if they refuse to provide it when they are able, offend against the divine law. Hence 1 Corinthians 9: So also the Lord ordained that they who preach the gospel should live of the gospel. Who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof? Who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock? But no believer is bound by Scripture to give a tenth or any part of his income to those who preach the gospel. If, however, those to whom the gospel is preached were so poor that they could not supply the food and clothing of the one preaching, they are not bound to this by divine law; the preacher must seek the necessities of life elsewhere, by exercising some other teaching or manual skill he may know, or by some other honest and fitting means. For so the Apostle did, that he might not be a burden to the poor to whom he preached. Hence Acts 20, speaking of himself: I have coveted no man's gold, or silver, or apparel. You yourselves know that these hands have ministered to my own needs and to the needs of those who are with me. He said the same in 2 Thessalonians, last: Neither, he says, did we eat bread freely of any man, but in labour and toil, working night and day, that we might not burden any of you. But now, since the number of the faithful is devoted, and especially in these times, the ministers of sacred teaching need neither labour with their hands nor beg. For in the communities of the faithful, both by the framer of human law and by certain individual persons, certain revenues, both from movable and from immovable goods, have been established and ordained, from which those who minister the gospel can be sustained sufficiently, and indeed abundantly. Someone will ask, however, whose these temporal goods are, especially the immovable ones, and to whom the said ownership or power of claiming them belongs before the coercive judge of the present age, since such ownership cannot belong to perfect evangelical ministers, according to the determination of the preceding chapter. We reply, however, that the ownership of the temporal goods established for the support of evangelical ministers belongs to the lawgiver, or to those whom the lawgiver has appointed for this purpose, or, if they are individual persons who gave and ordained these temporal goods from their own property for the aforesaid use, to those persons. Those so established for the defence and claiming of ecclesiastical temporal goods were commonly called the patrons of the churches. For in ancient times holy men and perfect evangelical ministers, wishing to imitate Christ, were unwilling to contend in judgment against anyone. Indeed, they did not even assume ownership of temporal goods, but only their use, as far as necessary for the present life and the support of the poor who could not help themselves. For if they had held immovable temporal goods in their own power to alienate, even without any ownership or intention of claiming them, and had not alienated them to be distributed at once to the poor who came to them, they would not have kept the counsel of Christ, in which he said: Go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, whether such goods had been held in private or in common. Yet it must be held that such patrons, whom we have said have the power of claiming such goods, have no power to alienate them or turn them to other uses, because they would sin at least against the divine law and perhaps against human law, since ownership has not been granted to them for this, but only the power of forbidding and of claiming before the coercive judge from those who take them away or who wish to take away or touch anything. And therefore, if the custody and distribution of the revenues are committed to one of the perfect by the lawgiver, or to an individual person who has such power, I say that the perfect man, while keeping the utmost poverty, may lawfully, and indeed meritoriously, undertake this care for the sake of love of neighbour and for the exercise of mercy toward him. But someone else will say that the perfect man provides for himself for tomorrow, or for many tomorrows, since he receives and intends to receive his yearly food and clothing from the revenue granted to him. It must be said that such revenues are granted to him to distribute in such a way that what suffices for the evangelist each day for decent food and clothing is kept back, and the remainder is committed to him to distribute to the poor. And since the perfect man has been appointed or chosen for the eternal salvation of the common good of the faithful, to preach to a certain people in a certain and determined place, insofar as the preacher intends to take each day, as is fitting, only one sufficiency which he has set aside, he would not propose to take several at once or successively from the same property acquired at once, if he could be free from daily gain and preach at the same time. But since he cannot be free for both at once, he must intend to take several daily sufficiencies of food and drink from the same property, yet successively. For if he distributed to the poor what remains over from one sufficiency of his own, he would not have from which to take the sufficiency of life for tomorrow; compelled to seek it, he would necessarily have to abandon the care of the people he has undertaken, and in this he would sin mortally, causing the common loss of souls. Further, he would be distributing what belongs to others, indeed against the intention of those who committed such goods to him for distribution. Since therefore, according to the decree of the faithful, whose authority it is to ordain, it has seemed expedient that a determined people should have a determined minister of the gospel and of the sacraments, who ought to serve them in these things, he must be supported by them. He does not keep anything for himself for tomorrow from his own intention, so that it would be within his power to distribute. Again, since it is not in his disposal, for the reason already given, to seek his daily life for himself, the perfect man who remains in his office may take several sufficiencies from the goods committed to his custody, always with the purpose of distributing what is left over from his present sufficiency, and, if it were in his power, of acquiring for himself the daily food for the future, just as was also said in the description of the utmost poverty. The evangelical minister, therefore, ought to have a sufficiency of daily food and clothing, which those who receive his ministry are bound to supply to him. And he may lawfully ask for this as due to him by divine right, although he ought not to claim it for himself by human right before the coercive judge, even if human law had prescribed it. Hence in the Gloss, following Augustine, on the same passage, 2 Tim. 3, No man that warreth for God, etc., it is said thus: The Apostle says this, writing to Timothy, lest perhaps Timothy, when he was in need and unwilling to be supported with daily food by those to whom he preached the gospel, and unable to labour with his body, should seek for himself some business by which his mind would be occupied with what it was intent upon, and from which he would be left to beg. See then, that if they had been unwilling to supply Timothy with food, he did not say that they should be compelled, nor that he himself ought to demand this before the coercive judge, since it is better to give the tunic and the cloak to the one who takes away, according to the counsel of Christ, Matt. 5 and Luke 6, than to contend in judgment. So also the Apostle said in 2 Corinthians 8 and 9, asking the faithful for the poor: Not as commanding I say this; and below, In this I give counsel. Calling such a collection a grace, and on that account marking it as voluntary, he said: Let every man do according as he has determined in his heart, not with sadness or of necessity.

units.la: Nunc autem restat singulariter dicere ad præmissas instantias. Ad eam ergo primum, quæ inducebatur ex Actuum sexto; Non est æquum nos derelinquere verbum Dei, &c. dicendum est hoc dixisse apostolos, nō qa vellent quicq; sibi acquiri temporaliū reseruandū ꝑ futuro nisi quo dixim' in summæ paupertatis descriptione, sed qa splentis aut immediate instantis quasi splentis simul vnicâ sibi quæ-. volebant p aliquos necessitatis sufficientiam, eo q; hoc per se ipsos facere non poterant debentes simul insistere pdicationi euangelicæ. Ad alia q inducebatur ex Glos. super Io. 14. q ecclesia datur for-ma seruandi necessaria, &c. Dico ecclesiæ, i. e. viris pfectis tam in ꝑpnio q ét in cómuni, datam esse formam seruandi, q superest præsenti aut quasi præsenti sufficientiæ, si superfluum aliquid eis licite aduenìat vt datum, aut corporis proprii opere seu labore quæsitum. Et hoc perfectis licitum est ex causa & intentione, quas diximus in summæ paupertatis descriptione, quamuis non debeant pfeᵭi ex intentione propter se quiequâ superfluum præsenti aut quasi splenti necessitati quærere: Quod in licite aduenit superfluum, potius custodire aut aliis custodiendū & distribuendum cō-mittere, quos ad hoc nouerint magis idoneos quam reiicere debent. Vnde super id Matth. decimo: Dignus est operarius cibo suo inquit Hieron. Ergo necessaria tantum accipite, vt inde securi æternis mi-tius vaceris. Deinde vero super idem, inquit Augustin. Illa loquebatur apostolis (Christus scilicet,) vt securi non possiderent neque portarent huic vitæ necessaria, nec magna ac minima, offendens à fidelibus omnia deberi ministris suis nulla superstua requirenibus. Et ideo si decimæ frugum nō sint necessariæ ad ipsorum sustentationem sed superstuæ in toto vel parte, quod ex eis supersluit virtute verborum sacræ scripturæ, nequaquam exigere possunt euangelici ministri, nec ad eius exhibitionem tenentur Christi fideles. Quod autem intellexerit Christus eos posse petere solum quæ sunt præsentis necessitatis, victus aut vestitus vel quasi præsentis apparet, eodem super id, neque duas tunicas. Vbi B. Hieron. In duabus tunicis duplex mihi videtur innuere vestimentum, non quod in locis Scythiæ & glaciali ni-ue rigentibus vna quis tunica debeat esse contentus: Sed quod in vna tunica vestimentum intelligamus, ne alio vestitu, aliud nobis futurorum timore reseruemus. Prohibet ergo duas tunicas simul, id est duplicia vestimenta, quorum alterum seorsum sufficiat pro tempore. Idemque de victu & eadem ratione intelligendum secundum determinationes scripturæ atque sanctorum expositiones in prioribus adductas.
units.tr: Now it remains to answer the preceding objections one by one. To the first, which was brought from Acts 6, "It is not right that we should leave the word of God," etc., it must be said that the apostles said this not because they wished to acquire temporal goods to be reserved for the future, beyond what we spoke of in the description of extreme poverty, but because, for the sake of present or immediately impending need, they were seeking some sufficiency through certain persons, since they could not do this themselves while they were also obliged to devote themselves to the preaching of the gospel. To the other objection, brought from the gloss on John 14, that to the Church is given a form of preserving necessities, etc., I say: to the Church, that is, to perfect men both in private and in common, is given a form of preserving what suffices for present or quasi-present need, if some superfluity lawfully comes to them as a gift, or is acquired by the work or labour of their own bodies. And this is lawful for the perfect, on account of the cause and intention we spoke of in the description of extreme poverty, although they ought not to seek, intentionally and for its own sake, any superfluity beyond present or quasi-present necessity. Whatever superfluity comes to them lawfully they should rather keep, or commit to others to keep and distribute, namely to those whom they know to be more fit for this, than reject it. Hence, on Matthew 10, "the workman is worthy of his food," Jerome says: "Therefore receive only necessities, so that you may be free and at leisure for the eternal." Then, on the same passage, Augustine says: "Christ was speaking to the apostles, so that they would not possess securely nor carry the necessities of this life, neither great nor small, showing that from the faithful everything is owed to his ministers, who seek no superfluities." And so, if tithes of the fruits are not necessary for their sustenance but superfluous in whole or in part, the evangelical ministers cannot by the force of the words of Holy Scripture demand what is superfluous, nor are Christ's faithful bound to hand it over. But that Christ meant they could ask only for what is of present necessity, food or clothing, or quasi-present, appears from the same gloss on "nor two tunics." There blessed Jerome says: "In the two tunics a double garment seems to me to be hinted at, not that in the regions of Scythia and icy snow one ought to be content with a single tunic, but that we understand by one tunic a garment, lest with one garment we reserve another out of fear of future things. He forbids therefore two tunics at once, that is, double garments, of which one alone suffices for the time." The same is to be understood of food, by the same reasoning, according to the determinations of Scripture and the expositions of the saints adduced above.

units.la: Non conuenit igitur perfectis Christi & apostolorum successoribus in suo dominio sibi reseruare agros, ciuitates, aut castra, nec vnquam opere seu exemplo Christi aut apostolorum fuit data forma ecclesiæ, i.e. euangelicis ministris habendi dominium immobilium nec ipsa reseruandi ad futurum in ipsorum existentia potestate. Sed oppositum huius bene reperimus in scriptura ex Christi consilio, dum dixit: Vade & vende. Et rursum: Nolite possidere aurum &c. Amplius & Actuum quarto: Vendentes offerebant pretia. Datur ergo forma ecclesiæ seruandi acquisita mobilia propter causas iam dictas, immobilia vero nequaquam, quæ in sui dominio vel simplici potestate alienandi fuerint, quin ea debeant alienando commutare, cum primum potuerint. Hæc etiam fuit sententia Bedæ super illud Lucæ 22. Quando misi vos sine sacculo &c. Non eadem, inquit Beda, vivendi regula perfectionis, qua pacis tempore discipulos informat. Missi quidem discipuli ad prædicandum, ne quid tollerent in via, id est secum portarent, præcepit: ordinans, ut qui euangelium nunciat, de euangelio viuat. Iustante vero mortis articulo & tota illa gente fi-mul pastorem & gregem persequente, congruam temporis regulam decernit, permittens, ut tollant necessaria victui, donec sopita persecutorum insania tempus euangelizandi redeat. Quo sic tempore non indigent tollere seu portare aliqua pro necessitate futura, eo quod a suscipientibus euangelium sustentari debent, & hoc ab ipsis licite quotidie petere possunt. Si ergo quolibet tempore licuisset apostolis & ipsorum successoribus pro futuro quolibet necessaria reseruare, frustra & inconuenienter dedisset eis aliam regulam temporis quietis, & aliam in casu, tempore persecutionis. Et hoc est, quod in summa paupertate descriptione iam diximus, perfectis videl. non licere temporalium reseruationem, si fuerint in loco, tempore, ac sui dispositione tali, quod quotidianum victum sibi successiue conuenienter quærere possint. Ad aliam instantiam quæ inducebatur ex Glos. super Matt. 7. cum dixit: Sed nemo debet scandalizari &c. dicendum, quod necessaria & suis ad instante aut immediate instantem quasi præsentem necessitatem, persectus licite procurare potest. Residuum vero si quod fuerit ex quæsito pauperibus reseruando, absque tamen omni proposito dominii, & hoc magis expediens ac meritorium est quam illud deperdi sine re, misericordiæ enim opus est hoc & supererogationis. vnde Matth. 5. Beati misericordes. Et cum subiungitur in eadem Glossa, quod Christus habuit loculos, vnde necessaria vsibus præberet, concedendum vtique, sed talia in loculis reseruari fecit, vt quia loci vel temporis conditio, ac reliquæ adiicientiæ hoc exigebant, vel vt pauperibus occurrentibus inde prouideret. Sicut expresse patet ex Glossa super illud Matth. 18. Staterem illum assumens &c. Tanta enim, inquit, paupertatis fuit dominus, vt vnde daret tributa non haberet. Iudas quidem communia in loculis habebat, sed res pauperum in suos vsus conuertere nephas dixit. Ecce quod res illæ seruatæ pauperum erant, id est, propter pauperes, nec intelligas ex pauperibus solos apostolos, sed alios quoscunque, præcipue fideles, quibus etiam ipse cum apostolis præbebant de reseruatis manducare, sicut apparet Matthei decimo, Marci sexto & 8. & Ioan. 6. Vnde ait Christus: Date vos illis manducare. Sic etiam, vt ibidem, quæ superfuerunt, reseruari præcepit, ne deperirent. vnde Ioannis sexto: Colligite quæ superauerunt fragmenta ne pereant. Collegerunt ergo (apostoli videlicet) & impleuerunt duodecim cophinos fragmentorum.
units.tr: It therefore does not befit the perfect successors of Christ and the apostles to reserve for themselves, as their own lordship, fields, cities, or castles; nor was a form of the Church ever given by the work or example of Christ or the apostles that evangelical ministers should hold lordship over immovable property, or reserve it for the future in their own power. Rather we find the opposite of this plainly in Scripture, from Christ's counsel, when he said: Go and sell. And again: Do not possess gold, etc. Further, Acts 4: Those who sold offered the prices. Therefore a form of the Church is given for preserving acquired movable goods, for the reasons already stated, but not immovable goods, which were in their lordship or in their simple power of alienation, since they ought to convert them by alienating them as soon as they could. This was also the opinion of Bede on Luke 22, When I sent you without purse, etc. "The rule of living of perfection," says Bede, "is not the same as that by which he instructs the disciples in time of peace. He commanded the disciples sent to preach not to take anything on the way, that is, not to carry it with them, ordaining that he who proclaims the gospel should live from the gospel. But at the moment of death, when the whole nation persecutes the shepherd and the flock together, he decrees a rule suited to the time, permitting them to take what is needed for food until the madness of the persecutors subsides and the time for preaching the gospel returns." At such a time they do not need to take or carry anything for future necessity, since they ought to be supported by those who receive the gospel, and they may lawfully ask this from them daily. If therefore at any time it had been lawful for the apostles and their successors to reserve necessities for any future time, he would have given them in vain and inappropriately one rule for a time of quiet and another for a case of persecution. And this is what we have already said in the description of extreme poverty: that for the perfect it is not lawful to reserve temporal goods, namely if they are in such a place, time, and disposition that they can successively seek their daily food suitably. To the other objection, brought from the gloss on Matthew 7 where it said But no one ought to be scandalized, etc., it must be said that the perfect can lawfully procure for themselves what is necessary for their immediately impending or quasi-present need. But whatever remains of what has been sought should be reserved for the poor, yet without any intention of lordship; and this is more expedient and meritorious than that it should perish uselessly, for this is a work of mercy and of supererogation. Hence Matthew 5: Blessed are the merciful. And when the same gloss adds that Christ had a purse, from which he provided necessities for use, this must certainly be granted, but he had such things kept in the purse either because the condition of place or time, and other circumstances, required it, or so that he might provide from it for the poor who came to him. This is clearly shown by the gloss on Matthew 18, Taking that stater, etc. For, it says, the Lord was so poor that he had nothing from which to pay tribute. Judas indeed had common funds in the purse, but he said it was wicked to turn the goods of the poor to his own uses. See, those goods were kept for the poor, that is, on account of the poor; nor should you understand by "the poor" only the apostles, but any others whatever, especially the faithful, to whom he himself with the apostles gave to eat from what was reserved, as appears in Matthew 10, Mark 6 and 8, and John 6. Hence Christ says: You give them to eat. So too, in the same place, he commanded that what was left over be reserved, lest it perish. Hence John 6: Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they perish. They gathered therefore (namely the apostles) and filled twelve baskets with the fragments.

units.la: Ad reliquam vero instantiam ex Glossa super Matth. 7. cum dixit: Non prohibet prouidentiam Labores, ad eam quoque inducatam ex Ioannis 14. Quidam autem putabant &c. rursum ad eas quæ inducebantur ex Matth. 14. Marci sexto & octauo, ac Lucæ nono, cum dixit Christus ad apostolos: Quot panes habetis? &c. dicendum per omnia similiter, quemadmodum ad priorem immediatam instantiam dictum fuit. Ad eas vero instantias quibus deducebatur, perfectum summam paupertatem etiam obseruantem, rerum temporalium habere posse iam dictum dominium in proprio vel cum alio in communi, dicendum consequenter. Ad earum igitur primam, quæ sumpsit exordium ex Lucæ 22. cum dicebatur: Omnis qui emit & vendit, vel emere aut vendere potest aliquid rei alicuius temporalis & eius pretii, habet dominium de necessitate. Hanc nego, & cum probatur, quia omnis emens aut vendens transfert rei vel pretii alicuius dominium. Hoc nego ab omnibus viris perfectis, quamuis enim per se rem licite transferant aut commutent in pretium aut econuerso, non propter hoc transferunt in alios, aut in se suscipiunt dominium rei alicuius, nisi forte secundum accidens trasferre dicantur, vt quia ipsis rem licite transferentibus, dominii fiunt in quos transfertur, aliude tn per se, vt infra patebit, dominium autem nullo modo suscipiunt, nec suscipere possunt perfecti manentes.
units.tr: To the remaining objection from the gloss on Matthew 7, when it said Providence does not forbid labours, and to that also brought from John 14, Some indeed thought, and again to those brought from Matthew 14, Mark 6 and 8, and Luke 9, where Christ said to the apostles How many loaves do you have? etc., it must be said in every respect similarly to what was said of the former immediate objection. To those objections by which it was argued that the perfect, even while observing extreme poverty, can have the aforesaid lordship over temporal goods, either privately or in common with another, it must be answered in turn. To the first of these, which took its start from Luke 22, where it was said: Everyone who buys and sells, or who can buy or sell anything of some temporal thing and its price, of necessity has lordship. I deny this; and when it is proved because every buyer or seller transfers the lordship of the thing or of the price, I deny this of all perfect men. For although they lawfully transfer or exchange a thing for a price, or the reverse, they do not on that account transfer lordship over anything to others, nor take it upon themselves, unless perhaps they are said to transfer it by accident, namely because, when they lawfully transfer the thing, lordship passes to those to whom it is transferred; otherwise, per se, as will be made clear below, they take up lordship in no way, nor can they take it while remaining perfect.

units.la: Sed dicet disputans, qui emit rem a perfecto, vel vendit, suscipit quod transfertur a perfecto, & nihil aliud, similiter autem & imperfectum transfert quod habebat, cum igitur emens suscipiat rei quam emit dominium aut eius quam perfecto vendit, prius habebat & nunc desinat habere dominium, per necessitatem sequitur perfectum rei venditæ per ipsum prius habuisse dominium, aut emptæ iam dominium habere posterius. Primam vero propositionem huius paralogismi concedo, si intelligatur per nihil aliud, id est nullam rem aliam. Et similiter quod perfectus suscipit ab alio rem quam transfert, & habere desinit vendens, sed cum additur. Emens suscipit rei dominium, ergo a perfecto transfertur in emptorem, committitur figura dictionis, quoniam suscipere rei dominium aut rem cum dominio, non est suscipere quod, sed quomodo. Vnde similis est paralogismus ei quem format Aristot. in secundo Elenchorum iuxta locum sophisticum, qui dicitur figura dictionis. Est autem hic: Quoniam tradidisti mihi solum denarium, solum denarium non habuisti, ergo tradidisti quod non habuisti. differt tamen hic ab illo, quoniam in præsenti mutatur quid in aliquid, in eo vero quem format Aristot. econuerso. Veruntamen vt amplius satisfiat quæstioni, quoniam quærentis sophisma dissolutum est, & propter minus doctos in arte sophistica. Dico quod dum perfectus rem aliquam vendit, commutando, rem licite transfert in alterum, quoniam rem sibi iure quaesitam, & contrectari lege concessam, cuius tamen nunquam habuit dominium. Quoniam ex praecedente capitulo monstratum est, quod rei alicuius aut eius usus vel utriusque simul, convenit habere potestatem licitam seu de iure, primo & secundo modo dicto, etiam rei corruptiuam absque dominio, dicto secundum tres saepe dictas significationss, & ideo licitam potestatem habet rem sibi iure quaesitam commutandi, dum tamen illa in nullius alterius sit dominio. Tu dices, unde acquirit emens illius dominium? Dico quod iuris primo modo dicti permissione tam humani quam divini. Nam quae in nullius bonis sunt, occupanti & volenti conceduntur quantum ad dominium, quanto ergo magis, quae sunt in bonis alicuius aliquo modo? ut iure primo & secundo modo dicto, quamuis non domino eo concedente ac consentiente possunt accipienti & volenti acquiri quantum ad dominium iure primo modo dicto, & translatione perfecti, secundum accidens tamen. Sic etiam econverso dico quod dum perfectus aliquid emit, rei potestatem licitam accipit, non tamen dominium, neque per se, neque secundum accidens, esto quod dominium desinat in vendente, acin quolibet alio.
units.tr: But the objector will say: whoever buys a thing from a perfect person, or sells one, takes up what is transferred by the perfect person and nothing else; likewise the imperfect person transfers what he had. Therefore, since the buyer takes up the ownership of the thing he buys, or of the thing the perfect person sells, and the perfect person ceased to have ownership, it follows of necessity that the perfect person had ownership of the thing sold before, or that the buyer afterwards has ownership of the thing bought. I grant the first premise of this paralogism, if "nothing else" is understood as "no other thing." Likewise I grant that the perfect person takes from another a thing that he transfers, and that the seller ceases to have it. But when it is added, "the buyer takes up the ownership of the thing, therefore it is transferred from the perfect person to the buyer," the fallacy of figure of speech is committed, since to take up the ownership of a thing, or the thing together with its ownership, is not to take up what but how. Hence this paralogism is similar to the one Aristotle sets out in the second book of the Elenchi, under the sophistic topic called figure of speech. The example there is: Since you gave me only a denarius, and you did not have only a denarius, therefore you gave what you did not have. This differs from the present case, however, because here one thing is changed into another, whereas in Aristotle's example the reverse happens. Yet, so that the question may be satisfied more fully, since the sophism of the questioner has been dissolved, and for the sake of those less learned in the art of sophistry, I say this: when the perfect person sells some thing by way of exchange, he lawfully transfers the thing to another, since it is a thing he acquired by right and may lawfully handle, though he never had ownership of it. For it was shown in the preceding chapter that for a thing, or its use, or both together, it is fitting to have a lawful power, or power by right, in the first and second senses stated, even of a thing that is consumable, without ownership, in the sense of the three meanings often stated; and so he has a lawful power to exchange a thing acquired by right, provided that it is not in the ownership of any other person. You will ask: whence does the buyer acquire ownership of it? I answer: by the permission of law in the first sense stated, both human and divine. For things that belong to no one are granted to the one who takes them and wishes to have them, as far as ownership goes; how much more, then, things that are in someone's goods in some way, as by law in the first and second senses stated, may be acquired, even without the owner's granting and consenting, by the one who takes them and wishes to have them, as far as ownership goes under the first sense stated, and by the transfer of the perfect person, though only indirectly. So too, conversely, I say that when the perfect person buys something, he receives a lawful power over the thing, but not ownership, neither directly nor indirectly, even though ownership ceases in the seller and passes to some other person.

units.la: Sed dices, ergo licite res venalis aut alia quaelibet potest auferri a perfecto, etiam actualiter ipsa indigente, quoniam in nullius bonis est, ex quo in nullius dominio, seu vendicandi potestate, similiter autem pretium aut res empta per ipsum, quod absurdum videtur. Ad hoc dicendum, quod res in nullius bonis existens, occupanti iure conceditur: & cum dicitur rem quam habet seu tenet perfectus, in nullius bonis esse, quoniam in nullius dominio de iure praesertim humano. In hoc committitur paralogismus consequentis, quoniam non sequitur, hoc non est in dominio alicuius de iure, ergo non est in bonis alicuius de iure: potest enim ut diximus, aliquid acquiri alteri iure primo modo dicto, absque omni iam dicto dominio. Quod si tamen humana iura hoc permitterent, videlicet ut res quae in nullius est dominio iam dicto, in nullius bonis intelligatur, & consequenter quod iure occupanti concedatur: Dico, quod rem quamcunque apud perfectum existentem potest quilibet capax occupare, ac suam facere licite secundum ius humanum primo modo dictum, quod apparet ex liciti diffinitione, quamuis ipsam non consentiente perfecto, praesertim indigente, licite secundum ius divinum illam nequeat occupare aut suam facere, quinimo peccat sic faciens mortaliter, committens lege divina prohibitum sub poena damnationis aeternae. Possunt autem haec simul contingere, ut secundum unam legem scilicet aliquid liceat quod secundum alteram prohibitum est. Sunt enim fornicationes solutorum humana lege permissae, propter aliquid maius incommeniens declinandum, quae tamen lege divina prohibitae sunt cum poena iam dicta. Ad aliam instantiam qua dicebatur: qui habuit licitum usum alicuius rei a domino eius inseparabilem, per necessitatem habuit rei dominium. Haec concedenda est si referatur inseparabilitas dominii ab usu in personam utentis, quo modo dominium actiue dicitur, ut videlicet quod ad omnem utentem sequatur dominium. Si vero haec inseparabilitas referatur ad rem quo modo passiue dicitur, eiusdem rei omnino potest esse usus & dominium, non tamen propter idem est dominus & utens. Potest enim aliquis licite uti re non sua consentiente domino rei, ut ex praecedente capitulo palam fuit, & ideo in hoc sensu neganda est. Secundum primum ergo sensum concessa propositione, sicut etiam videtur intendere disputans, ad minorem qua dicitur Christum & apostolos quarundam rerum habuisse usum licitum, quarum dominium non separabatur ab usu in utente scilicet: hanc nego tanquam haereticam, sumendo dominium secundum tres priores iam dictas significationes. Et cum additur, aut habuerunt usum rei suae de iure, aut non sua de iure: dico, quod utrarumque, ut quandoque suarum de iure, quandoque alienarum consentientibus earum dominis. Et cum dicitur, si suarum de iure, cum usu igitur earum habuerunt dominium: paralogismus consequentis committitur hic, ut pridem diximus. Non enim sequitur, hoc est alicui iure quaesitum vel eius usus, ergo ipsius est dominium, quamuis bene sequatur, dominium rei, aut dominium usus eius est alicui iure quaesitum, ergo res vel ipsius usus sua seu sibi iure quaesita est. Et cum ulterius dicitur, sine non sua utitur, aut ergo aliena vel ea quae in nullius bonis est. Dico quod utraq; licite potest uti, aut simul aut successiue. Et cum destruitur utraque pars consequentis dicendo primo, quod re in nullius bonis existente perfectum uti non posse sine dominio, eo quod prius aut simul cum usu oportet ipsum rem occupare, & sic ipsius habere dominium. Dico perfectum eiusmodi rem prius occupare, cum vero infertur, ergo eius sit dominus, Paralogismus consequentis est ut prius: posset enim piscem capere perfectus atque comedere, cum expresso tamen prius voto, nunquam praedictum piscem aut rem aliquam temporalem vendicandi contentiose coram iudice coactiuo. Tu dices, occupanti concedit rei dominium: dico quod verum est volenti, non volenti autem non, quia spernere dominium vnicuique permissum est lege divina & etiam humana, ut expriori capitulo palam. Deinde ad alteram partem consequentis, videlicet, quod in rem alienam non conuenit usus perfecto absque rei iam dicto dominio: Quoniam dicet aliquis disputans, aut concedente domino rei seu consentiente vel non; Dicendum, quod consentiente domino, aliter enim illicitus esset usus, maxime si dissentiret licite vel expresse: Si vero consentiente domino, dicet disputans, aut ipso concedente dominium ipsi perfecto vel non concedente; Dico quod utroque modo licite contingere potest, etiam in re unico usu consumptibili. Esto quidem igitur usum concessum alicui perfecto, quem exercet in rem, esse usum, rem consumentem, si concesso sibi dominio rei cum usu vtatur, ergo [illegible, ~12 letters] vsu habet perfectus iam dictum dominium: Dico paralogismum consequentis committi vt prius, quoniam non sequitur: hic concedit alicui vsum & dominium alicuius rei, ergo cui conceditur efficitur dominus rei, quia potest vnum acceptare, vt potestatem licitam vsus, & alterum renuere, aut dudum renuisse per votum, puta dominium. Dicet ergo disputans aliquis, cuius est ergo rei dominium? Dico quod domini cuius erat ante concessionem expressam quam fecerat perfecto, non volenti suscipere, vel nullius: si tali expressa concessione, priuetur dominus de iure humano rei dominio, potest tamen nihilominus perfectus re vti vsu etiam consumente & licite tanquam sibi iure quaesita, quamuis illius dominio in nullius bonis existente. Quod si dicatur dominum rei perfecto alicui concessisse vsum rei suae etiam consumentem absque dominio: Adhuc dico Christum & apostolos & vnumquemque perfectum in summa paupertate manentem, licite posse in rem illam exercere vsum eam consumentem & destruentem. Et cum dicitur vsum licitum fieri, quia priuat dominum sine facto suo, rei suae dominio. His attendendum, quod dominus rei alicuius vnico consumptibilis vsu, perfecto concedit, vsum & concedere potest licite cum proposito sibi retinendi rei dominium quam diu res extat, sed quam cito definit siue in fieri, siue in facto esse, non intendit sibi seruare dominium, sed illi renunciat ex nunc prout extunc solum non antea, quod etiam faciunt concedentes eleemosynam persectis, ne aliqui maligni ab ipsis auferant, eo quod potestate talia repetendi contentiose seu coram iudice coactiuo priuati sunt, quamuis sponte perfecti. Si enim dominus rei semper rei suae dominium intenderet habere, nunquam concederet aut concedere deberet perfecto vsum destruentem eam nisi esset insanus: Quoniam rei non existentis, nemo dominus esse potest. Similiter etiam perfectus talem vsus concessionem non suscipERET, si hanc domini fore nosset intentionem. Et ideo dico, quod rei dominus facto suo priuatur rei dominio in fieri vel facto esse, dum res consumitur aut perfecte consumpta est, quia sic priuari vult & exprimit. Et ideo nullam patitur iniuriam, propter quod etiam vsus perfectorum in res alienas, sic volentibus rerum dominis, nequaquam illicitus est, quinimo sanctus & honestus, & tamen sic eis licite vruntur absque iam dicto dominio. Ad sequentem vero instantiam iam perfecte dictum est in solutione primae instantiae circa finem. Ad aliam instantiam sumentem originem ex primae ad Timoth. 3. & ad Titum secundo, quod oportet episcopum hospitalem esse. Supponendo semper & vbique episcopum summe pauperem seu perfectum esse debere, si Christi & apostolorum imitator perfectus existit, dico, quod oportet vel necesse est episcopum &c. potest dupliciter intelligi, & secundum mentem Apostoli Vno modo necessitate simpliciter & absolute. Alio modo ex conditione. Rursum vel quantum ad affectum seu firmum propositum, vel quantum ad affectum & exteriorem effectum. Si ergo intelligatur necessitate absoluta, quod oportet episcopum hospitalem esse secundum affectum, dico verum esse, sicque Apostolum intellexisse. Si vero intelligatur, quod oportet &c. quantum ad exteriorem effectum, dico quod oportet siue debet non absolute, sed ex conditione, vt si habuerit vnde possit hospitalitatem exhibere. Quod si ad hospitalitatem quantum ad exteriorem effectum teneretur episcopus absolute per necessitatem oporteret ipsum habere atque intendere consetuare temporalia, & per consequens sibi vendicare contentiose atque talibus dominari, sed non tenetur ad hoc absolute, sed ex conditione. Nam summus pontificum secundum exteriorem effectum quandoque hospitalitatem non tenuit, cum dixit: Filius hominis non habet vbi reclinet caput, & quoniam, vt supra induximus, Tanta paupertatis sua dominus, vt unde daret tributa non haberet. De quo igitur & in quo tunc seruasset hospitalitatem secundum exteriorem effectum, quamuis secundum interiorem affectum illam semper obseruauerit. Et ideo ad maiorem syllogismi dicendum, quod qui ex conditione debet hospitalitatem exteriorem vel absolute interiorem, non oportet fieri dominum alicuius rei temporalis, prouisorem autem futurorum aut reseruatorem omnem episcopum esse oportet ex conditione si potuerit, non tamen propter se, sed propter pauperes, sicut apparet ex Glossa super illud Iohannis 21. Pasce oves meas. Ad aliam cum dicebatur, episcopos sanctos immobilium habuisse dominium, vt ex epistola beati Ambrosii de tradendis basilicis supra inductam est, Dico quod sancti episcopi, vt Ambrosius & alii, agros & reliqua quae dixerunt ecclesiae, non dixerunt ecclesiae, quia in dominio vendendi, alienandi; aut vendicandi potestate fuerit episcoporum in proprio vel communi, qui ecclesiae nomine signantur persaepe, si statum summae paupertatis obseruauerunt; quod ad praesens supponimus, sed pro tanto dicti sunt agri ecclesiae, quoniam prouentus inde venientes, ad cultum Dei & sustentationem ministrorum euangelicorum atque templorum statutus erat per legislatorem aut alium donatorem, in quorum scilicet statuentium remanebat dominium defendendi & vendendi, a quocunque aliter talia contractare volenti, quemadmodum dictum est circa principium huius. Et haec erat intentio praedictorum sanctorum, unde Ambrosius eadem epistola post praeinducta verba, sic ait: Si agros desiderat Imperator, potestatem habet vendicandorum. Nemo nostrum, (id est presbyterorum seu episcoporum,) interrumpit, potest pauperibus collatio populi redundare, non faciat de agris invidiam, tollat eos si libitum est: Imperatori non dono, sed non nego. Non sic autem dicerent episcopi modernorum, & tamen si sciuisset se peccare mortaliter in non defendendo seu non negando agros: Imperatori certum est quod ipsos sibi negasset, praecipue si ad hospitalitatem exteriorem fuisset simpliciter obligatus, quemadmodum quidam somniasse videntur, qui tamen in Israel magistri sunt, nec talia ignorare deberent, nec fortasse ignorant, sed magis homini quam Deo placere student. Quod autem offendebatur de Christo in speciali, eo quod secundum leges humanas, qui aliquem redimit a morte, illius dominus efficitur ac suorum temporalium: Christus autem omnes homines a morte redemit, Dico ad primam propositionem, quod non est vniversaliter vera, etiam secundum leges civiles, nisi apponatur volens. Esto nanq; iure permissum omni redemptori alterius fieri dominum eius, qui a morte redimitur & suorum temporalium. Dico quod redimens aliquem a morte non necessario fit eius dominus, verbi gratia si non voluerit aut renunciauerit, propter quod etiam esto Christum omnes homines sic a morte redemisse, vt dicunt humanae leges, & per consequens omnium posse dominum effici. Dico tamen quod Christus perfectus existens, dominus non fuit temporalis, maxime humano seu etiam acquisito dominio, eo quod omni tali dominio Christus renunciauit, tam in personis quam in rebus, vt ex quarto huius, & etiam immediate praecedenti capitulo satis apparet. Vel dicendum, quod Christus pro eo statu omnium dominus efficitur, pro quo nos a morte redemit: hoc autem est pro statu alterius seculi & non praesentis, non enim redemit nos a morte huius seculi, de qua etiam leges humanae loquuntur. Et ideo pro statu seculi huius ex sua redemptione non acquisivit dominium hominum, nec suorum temporalium. Quo enim modo dixisset verum Christus, dum dixit de seipso Matth. 8. & Lucae nono: Filius autem hominis non habet vbi reclinet caput, si dominus erat omnium humanorum temporalium? Et ideo vel nunquam acquisivit tale dominium, vt in secunda solutione dicitur, vel si acquirere potuisset, noluit & renunciauit, quemadmodum facere posset etiam quilibet alter perfectus. Aut apertum dixisset mendacium, quod nephas est credere. Ad vltimam instantiam, ex Apoc. 19. vbi accipiebatur de Christo, quod habebat scriptum in vestimento, Rex regum &c. & hoc in vestimento humanitatis, secundum Glossam. Dico quod scriptum habuit hoc Christus in vestimento humanitatis, quia verbum Dei iunctum fuit cum pelle humana, ratione cuius illud dominium sibi debebat sicut verbum scriptum est cum pelle ovina similitudinarie, ratione cuius pellis aliquid habet venerandum, vt disciplinam signare, aut aliam veritatem quamcunque. Vel dicendum quod de tali dominio, scilicet temporali, non sensit ibi beatus Ioannes, imo de dominio regni aeterni, vel quantum ad regnum aeternum. Vnde Glossa subdit, Rex regum, id est super omnes sanctos. Non igitur error, nec secum alios errare faciat Rom. Papa vel alter episcopus, quoniam si temporalia possidere quaerit hisque dominari, hoc licite fortasse poterit, etiam in statu salutis existens, non tamen summae paupertatis seu perfectionis, instar Christi & apostolorum statum obseruans. Quid quidem igitur sit paupertas meritoria, quaeve summus eius modus seu perfectissima species, & quod hunc Christus, ipsumque imitantes apostoli seruauerint in via, ex dictis sufficienter determinasse putamus.
units.tr: But you will say: then a saleable thing, or any other thing whatever, may lawfully be taken from the perfect man, even when he is actually in need, since it belongs to no one's goods, and so to no one's dominion or power of claiming it. Likewise the price, or a thing bought by him, would belong to no one, which seems absurd. To this I answer that a thing which belongs to no one's goods is granted by right to the one who occupies it. When it is said that a thing which the perfect man has or holds belongs to no one's goods, because it is in no one's dominion, especially by human right, the fallacy of the consequent is committed here. It does not follow that because a thing is not in someone's dominion by right, it is not in someone's goods by right. As I have said, something can be acquired by another by the first mode described, without any of the dominion just mentioned. But if human laws did permit that a thing which is in no one's dominion in the sense just mentioned should be understood to belong to no one's goods, and consequently should be granted by right to the occupant, then I say that any capable person may occupy whatever thing is in the possession of a perfect man, and make it his own lawfully according to human law, in the first mode described. This is clear from the definition of the lawful. Yet, if the perfect man does not consent, especially when he is in need, he cannot lawfully occupy it or make it his own according to divine law. Indeed, one who does so sins mortally, transgressing a prohibition of divine law under the penalty of eternal damnation. These things may happen together, so that by one law something is lawful which by another law is forbidden. For the fornications of unmarried persons are permitted by human law, to avoid some greater inconvenience, and yet they are forbidden by divine law under the penalty just mentioned. To the other objection, which said: one who has lawful use of a thing from its owner, inseparable from it, by necessity has the dominion of the thing: this is to be granted if the inseparability of dominion from use is referred to the person of the user, in which sense dominion is called active, namely that dominion follows every user. But if this inseparability is referred to the thing, in which sense it is called passive, then the same thing can certainly have both use and dominion, yet not on account of the same thing is one both owner and user. For a person may lawfully use a thing which is not his, with the consent of its owner, as was made plain in the preceding chapter. Therefore in this sense the proposition must be denied. Accordingly, I grant the proposition in the first sense, as the disputant also seems to intend. To the minor premise, which says that Christ and the apostles had lawful use of certain things, of which the dominion was not separated from the use in the user, I deny it as heretical, taking dominion in the three senses already mentioned earlier. And when it is added: either they had use of a thing that was theirs by right, or of a thing not theirs by right, I say of both: sometimes of things that were theirs by right, sometimes of things belonging to others, with the consent of their owners. And when it is said: if of things that were theirs by right, then with the use of them they had dominion: the fallacy of the consequent is committed here, as I said before. For it does not follow: this is acquired by right by someone, or its use is, therefore the dominion of it is his. Though it does follow well: the dominion of a thing, or the dominion of its use, is acquired by right by someone, therefore the thing or its use is his own, or acquired to him by right. And when it is further said: or else he uses what is not his, either what belongs to another or what is in no one's goods: I say that either may be used lawfully, either together or in succession. And when both parts of the consequent are refuted, first by saying that a perfect man cannot use a thing that is in no one's goods without dominion, because he must first occupy the thing, or at the same time as using it, and so have dominion of it: I say that the perfect man occupies such a thing first. But when it is inferred: therefore he is its owner, the fallacy of the consequent is as before. For the perfect man could catch a fish and eat it, though with a prior express vow that he would never claim that fish, or any temporal thing, by contentious suit before a judge with coercive power. You will say: the grant of dominion of a thing goes to the one who occupies it. I say that this is true for one who is willing, but not for one who is unwilling, because every person is permitted by divine law and also by human law to reject dominion, as was made plain in the earlier chapter. Next, as to the other part of the consequent, namely that use of another's thing does not belong to the perfect man without dominion of the thing, as I have said: someone may ask whether this is with the consent of the owner of the thing or without it. It must be said that it is with the owner's consent, for otherwise the use would be unlawful, especially if he lawfully or expressly dissented. But if it is with the owner's consent, the disputant will ask whether the owner grants dominion to the perfect man or does not grant it. I say that either way it can happen lawfully, even in a thing consumed by a single use. Granted, then, that a use granted to some perfect man, which he exercises on a thing that is consumed by use, is a use consuming the thing: if, with the dominion of the thing granted to him, he uses it with the use, then [illegible] the perfect man has the said dominion by that use. I say the fallacy of the consequent is committed here as before, for it does not follow: here someone grants to another the use and the dominion of a thing, therefore the one to whom it is granted becomes the owner of the thing. For he may accept one of these, namely the lawful power of use, and refuse the other, or have refused it earlier by vow, namely dominion. The disputant will then say: whose, then, is the dominion of the thing? I say that it belongs to the owner who was before the express grant he made to the perfect man, who was unwilling to take it, or else to no one. If by such an express grant the owner is deprived, by human right, of the dominion of the thing, nevertheless the perfect man may still use the thing, even by a use that consumes it, and lawfully, as something acquired to him by right, although the dominion of it is in no one's goods. But if it is said that the owner of the thing granted to some perfect man the use of his thing, even one consuming it, without dominion: I still say that Christ, the apostles, and every perfect man remaining in the highest poverty may lawfully exercise on that thing a use that consumes and destroys it. And when it is said that the use becomes lawful because the owner, without any act of his own, is deprived of the dominion of his thing, to this it must be noted that the owner of a thing consumed by a single use, who grants that use to a perfect man, can lawfully grant it while intending to keep the dominion of the thing for as long as the thing exists. But as soon as it ceases, whether in becoming or in being made, he does not intend to keep the dominion for himself, but renounces it from now on, to take effect then and not before. Those who give alms to the perfect also do this, so that some wicked people may not take it from them, since they have been deprived of the power to reclaim such things by contentious suit or before a judge with coercive power, although they have done so of their own accord, being perfect. For if the owner of a thing always intended to keep dominion of his thing, he would never grant, or ought never to grant, to the perfect man a use that destroys it, unless he were insane. For no one can be the owner of a thing that does not exist. Likewise the perfect man would not accept such a grant of use if he knew that this was the owner's intention. And so I say that the owner of a thing is deprived of dominion of it by his own act, in becoming or in being made, while the thing is consumed or has been wholly consumed, because he wishes and expresses that he be so deprived. Therefore he suffers no wrong. For this reason the use by perfect men of other people's things, when the owners are willing, is by no means unlawful, but rather holy and honourable, and yet they use these things lawfully without the dominion just mentioned. As for the following objection, it has already been fully answered in the solution to the first objection, near its end. To the other objection, drawn from 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 2, that a bishop must be hospitable: supposing always and everywhere that a bishop ought to be most poor, or perfect, if he is a perfect imitator of Christ and the apostles, I say that "a bishop must, or it is necessary that he..." can be understood in two ways, according to the mind of the Apostle: in one way, by simple and absolute necessity; in another way, conditionally. Again, this may be as regards the disposition or firm resolve, or as regards both the disposition and the outward effect. If it is understood as absolute necessity, that a bishop must be hospitable in disposition, I say this is true and that the Apostle so understood it. But if it is understood that he must, or ought, as regards the outward effect, I say that he ought not absolutely, but conditionally, that is, if he has the means by which he can show hospitality. For if a bishop were absolutely bound by necessity to hospitality as regards the outward effect, he would have to possess temporal goods and intend to keep them, and consequently to claim them by contentious suit and to rule over such things. But he is not bound to this absolutely, only conditionally. For the chief of the pontiffs did not, as regards the outward effect, always keep hospitality, when he said: "The Son of man has nowhere to lay his head," and, as we have brought forward above, "The Lord was so poor that he had no means to pay tribute." In what, then, would he have kept hospitality as regards the outward effect, though he always kept it as regards the inward disposition? Therefore, to the major premise of the syllogism it must be said that the one who is bound conditionally to outward hospitality, or absolutely to inward hospitality, need not become the owner of any temporal thing.
