But every bishop must be a provider of future needs and a keeper of reserves, conditionally, if he is able, not for his own sake but for the sake of the poor. This appears from the Gloss on John 21: "Feed my sheep." To the other objection, where it was said that holy bishops had dominion of immovable goods, as was adduced above from the letter of the blessed Ambrose, On Handing Over the Churches: I say that the holy bishops, as Ambrose and others, did not call the fields and other things belonging to the Church "the Church's" because the power of selling, alienating, or claiming them lay with the bishops, whether in their own or in common, the bishops who are often named by the name of the Church, if they kept the state of highest poverty (which we now suppose). Rather, they were called "the fields of the Church" because the revenues coming from them were appointed by the lawgiver or some other donor for the worship of God, and for the support of the evangelical ministers and of the temples. The dominion of defending and selling them remained with those who made such appointments, against anyone else who wished to deal with them in another way, as was said near the beginning of this work. And this was the intention of those holy men. Hence Ambrose, in the same letter, after the words quoted above, says: "If the Emperor desires the fields, he has the power of claiming them. None of us (that is, of the priests or bishops) resists. The gift of the people may overflow to the poor. Let him not make the fields a source of hatred; let him take them if he pleases. I do not give them to the Emperor, but I do not deny them." The bishops of our own time would not speak thus. And yet, if they knew that they would sin mortally by not defending or denying the fields, it is certain that they would have denied them to the Emperor, especially if they were simply bound to outward hospitality, as some seem to have dreamed. Yet they are teachers in Israel, and they ought not to be ignorant of such things, nor perhaps are they ignorant; but they are more eager to please men than God. As for the objection made about Christ in particular, that according to human laws whoever redeems someone from death becomes the owner of that person and of his temporal goods, and that Christ redeemed all men from death: to the first proposition I say that it is not universally true, even according to civil laws, unless the word "willing" is added. For although it is permitted by law that any redeemer becomes the owner of the one who is redeemed from death, and of his temporal goods, I say that one who redeems someone from death does not necessarily become his owner, for example if he is unwilling or renounces it. For this reason, even if Christ redeemed all men from death in the way human laws speak of, and so could become owner of all, I say nevertheless that Christ, being perfect, was not an owner of temporal things, least of all by human or acquired dominion, since he renounced every such dominion, both over persons and over things, as is sufficiently clear from the fourth chapter of this work and from the chapter immediately preceding. Or it must be said that Christ becomes Lord of all for the state for which he redeemed us from death. But this is for the state of another age and not of the present one, for he did not redeem us from the death of this age, of which human laws also speak. Therefore, for the state of this age, he did not acquire dominion over men or their temporal goods by his redemption. For how would Christ have spoken truly when he said of himself in Matthew 8 and Luke 9: "The Son of man has nowhere to lay his head," if he were the owner of all human temporal goods? Therefore either he never acquired such dominion, as is said in the second solution, or if he could have acquired it, he did not wish to and renounced it, as any other perfect man could also do. Otherwise he would have spoken an open lie, which it is impious to believe. To the last objection, from Revelation 19, where it was taken of Christ that he had written on his garment: "King of kings," etc., and this on the garment of humanity, according to the Gloss: I say that Christ had this written on the garment of humanity because the Word of God was joined with human skin, by reason of which that dominion was owed to him, just as a word is written on sheepskin in a figurative sense, by reason of which the skin has something to be revered, as to signify discipline, or any other truth whatever. Or it must be said that the blessed John did not mean by it such temporal dominion there, but rather the dominion of the eternal kingdom, or in respect of the eternal kingdom. Hence the Gloss adds: "King of kings," that is, over all the saints. Therefore let the Roman Pope, or any other bishop, not err, nor make others err with him, for if he seeks to possess temporal goods and to rule over them, he may perhaps do so lawfully, even while in a state of salvation, but not while observing the state of the highest poverty or perfection, after the example of Christ and the apostles. What meritorious poverty is, and what its highest mode or most perfect kind is, and that Christ and the apostles who imitated him observed this on the way, we think we have determined sufficiently from what has been said.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: De sacerdotalis officii, per essentialem & accidentalem, separabilem & inseparabilem aucto- ritatem divisione, & quod in essentiali dignitate quicunq; presbyter epi- scopo non sit inferior, sed in accidentali tantummodo.
units.tr: On the division of the priestly office into its essential and accidental authority, separable and inseparable, and that every presbyter is not inferior to a bishop in essential dignity, but only in accidental dignity.

units.la: ESt autem his habita quaestio difficilis, & ad considerandum necessaria valde. Dictum est enim nobis 15. prima, & aequaliter rememoratum octavo huius in fine, legislatorem humanum ipsum secundum se aut per partem principantem, causam agentem esse institutionis omnium officiorum seu partium ciuitatis, cum his quoque meminimus nos dixisse in ultimo primae, Sacerdotium seu sacerdotale officium nouae legis a solo Christo primum institutum fuisse, quem tamen omnem seculi principatum, omneque temporalium dominium abdicasse monstrauimus quarto & 11. 13. & 14. huius, & neque humanum legislatorem fuisse duodecimo & 13. prima: qua propter non eundem esse cuiuslibet officii ciuitatis institutorem, & humanum legislatorem aut principem, dixisse videmur; vnde merito dubitabit aliquis ex his, cuius quidem sit auctoritas instituendi sacerdotium, & in communitatibus fidelium maxime, quoniam inuicem iam dicta de hoc repugnare videntur. Hanc itaq; dictorum apparentem contrarietatem amouere tentantes, rememorabimus primum eorum quae diximus sexto & septimo primae, videlicet alteras esse causas cuiuslibet officiorum ciuitatis, secundum quod officia nominant habitus animae, alterasq; ipsorum secundum quod partes sunt ciuitatis institutae propter sufficientias habendas ex his, quod etiam proportionaliter oportet attendere in sacerdotio, quemadmodum in reliquis officiis ciuitatis. Nam sacerdotii secundum quod animae nominat habitum quendam, quem characterem vocant sacrae scripturae doctores causa efficiens per se immediata seu per se factor est Deus, hunc imprimens in animam, humano tamen quodam praevio ministerio, quasi praeparante. Cuius exordium in noua lege fuit a Christo; ipse enim qui verus Deus & verus homo fuit inquantum humanus sacerdos ministerium exhibuit, quod subsequentes nunc exhibent sacerdotes; Inquantum vero Deus characterem impressit in animas eorum, quos sacerdotes instituit, quo modo primum sanctos apostolos instituit tanquam successores suos immediatos, sicq; consequenter reliquos sacerdotes omnes, per ministerium tamen apostolorum, & reliquorum sibi succedentium in hoc officio. Nam apostolis aut reliquis sacerdotibus manum aliis imponentibus, & debita verba seu orationes ad hæc proferentibus, Christus in quantum Deus hunc habitum seu characterem sacerdotalem digne suscipere volentibus, imprimit. Et similiter opinandum est in reliquorum ordinum collatione, ex quibus character aliquis imprimitur in animam suscipientis. Hic siquidem character sacerdotalis sit unus aut plures, potestas est, per quam sacerdos consecrare potest ex pane & vino, corpus & sanguinem Christi benedictum cum certa verborum pronunciatione ac reliqua ecclesiastica sacramenta ministrare, per quem etiam soluere potest & ligare homines à peccatis.
units.tr: This question is difficult and very necessary to consider. For we said in 15. prima, and recalled in equal measure at the end of the eighth chapter of this book, that the human lawgiver, either in himself or through the governing part, is the efficient cause of the institution of all the offices or parts of the state. We also recall saying at the end of the first book that the priesthood, or the priestly office of the new law, was first instituted by Christ alone. Yet we showed in the fourth, eleventh, thirteenth and fourteenth chapters of this book that he renounced all secular rule and all temporal lordship, and in the twelfth and thirteenth chapters of the first book that he was not a human lawgiver. Therefore it seems we have said that the institutor of any office of the state is not the same as the human lawgiver or ruler. From this, someone may rightly doubt whose authority it is to institute the priesthood, and especially in the communities of the faithful, since what we have said on this point seems to contradict itself. Trying, then, to remove this apparent contradiction, we shall first recall what we said in the sixth and seventh chapters of the first book: that there are two kinds of cause for any office of the state. One is the cause of the offices as they name habits of the soul; the other is the cause of them as they are parts of the state instituted for the sake of having the necessary abilities. The same must be observed proportionally in the priesthood, as in the other offices of the state. For the priesthood, insofar as it names a certain habit of the soul, which the teachers of Holy Scripture call the character sacerdotalis, has as its efficient cause, immediately and in itself, God, who imprints it upon the soul, though with a certain prior human ministry that prepares the way. Its beginning in the new law was with Christ. For he, who was true God and true man, exercised the ministry as human priest, which the priests who follow now exercise. Insofar as he is God, he impressed the character upon the souls of those whom he appointed as priests, just as he first appointed the holy apostles as his immediate successors, and consequently all the other priests, yet through the ministry of the apostles and of those who succeeded them in this office. For when the apostles or the other priests lay hands on others and pronounce the due words or prayers for this purpose, Christ, as God, imprints this priestly habit or character on those who desire to receive it worthily. We should think the same of the conferral of the other orders, by which some character is imprinted on the soul of the recipient. This priestly character, whether it be one or several, is the power by which a priest can consecrate the blessed body and blood of Christ from bread and wine, with a certain pronouncement of words, and administer the other ecclesiastical sacraments, and by which he can also absolve and bind men from their sins.

units.la: Huncautem characterem seu potestatem susceperunt apostoli secundum quorundam sententiam, cum dixit eis Christus, quod scriptum est Matth. 26. Marci 14. & Luc. 22. Quod quia series huius perfectius apparet in Luca, ipsam adducamus ibidem, ut habetur sic, Accepto pane, gratias egit & fregit, (Christus scilicet,) & dedit eis, (apostolis videlicet,) dicens, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur, hoc facite in meam commemorationem. hoc facite, id est, hoc faciendi potestatem habete. Quibuldam vero visum est, hanc auctoritatem apostolis fuisse datam, per id quod scriptum est Ioannis 20. dum dixit Christus ad eos. Accipite Spiritum sanctum: & quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: & quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt. Alii autem dicunt hoc factum fuisse per id quod habetur Matth. 16. dum dixit Christus ad eos in persona Petri: Tibi dabo claves regni cælorum &c. Vel per id quod dictum est eis à Christo, eiusdem 18. Amen dico vobis: quaecunque alligaveritis super terram, erunt ligata & in cælo: & quaecunque solveritis super terram, soluta erunt & in cælo. Alii vero rursum dicunt, duas esse potestates seu auctoritates sacerdotales prædictas: Unam quidem, qua sacramentum eucharistiæ conficere possunt: Reliqua vero, qua ligare vel absoluere possunt homines à peccatis. Quasi quidem etiam diuersis temporibus & Christi sermonibus dicunt apostolis fuisse collatas. Quod tamen horum probabilius existat, non refert ad præsentem intentionem. Nam qualitercunque aut quandocunque huius officii facta fuerit institutio in apostolos, constat, ipsis per Christum hanc potestatem fuisse traditam: sic quoque ipsorum ministerio iam dicto, & suorum successorum conferri cæteris, qui ad hoc officium assumuntur. Unde primæ ad Timoth. 4. Noli negligere gratiam quæ in te est, quæ data est tibi per prophetiam, per impositionem manuum presbyteri. Eodemque modo, suum quendam characterem recipiunt diaconi per impositionem manuum presbyteri.
units.tr: Now some hold that the apostles received this character, or power, when Christ said to them what is written at Matt. 26, Mark 14 and Luke 22. Since the sequence of this appears more fully in Luke, let us cite it there, as it reads: "Taking bread, he gave thanks and broke it," (Christ, that is,) "and gave it to them," (namely the apostles,) "saying, This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me." "Do this," that is, have the power of doing this. Others, however, have thought that this authority was given to the apostles through what is written at John 20, when Christ said to them: "Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them; and whose you retain, they are retained." Others say that this took place through what is found at Matt. 16, when Christ said to them in the person of Peter: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," etc. Or through what was said to them by Christ in the same chapter 18: "Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven." Still others say that there are two of the aforesaid sacerdotal powers or authorities: one by which they can consecrate the sacrament of the Eucharist, and the other by which they can bind or absolve men from sins. They say these were conferred on the apostles at different times and by different words of Christ. Which of these opinions is the more probable does not bear on the present purpose. For however or whenever the institution of this office was made in the apostles, it is certain that this power was handed down to them by Christ; and in the same way it is conferred, through the ministry of the apostles just mentioned and of their successors, on the others who are taken up into this office. Hence 1 Tim. 4: "Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the elder." And in the same way deacons receive their own character through the laying on of the hands of the elder.

units.la: De quibus Actuum sexto: Hos, (scilicet diaconos futuros,) statuerunt ante conspectum apostolorum, & orantes imposuerunt eis manus. Hunc siquidem sacerdotalem characterem siue unum siue plures, quem diximus potestatem conficiendi sacramentum eucharistiæ seu corporis & sanguinis Christi, ac potestatem soluendi atque ligandi homines à peccatis, & quem etiam deinceps appellabimus auctoritatem essentialem seu inseparabilem presbytero, inquantum presbyter est: probabiliter mihi videtur, quod omnes sacerdotes habent eundem specie, nec ampliorem habet hunc Romanus episcopus, aut alter aliquis quam simplex dictus sacerdos quicunque. Nam in hac auctoritate siue una siue plures extent, episcopus à sacerdote non differt, teste Hieronymo, imo verius Apostolo, cuius etiam est aperta sententia, ut infra patebit. Inquit enim Hieronym. super illud Matth. 16. Et quodcunque ligaveris super terram &c. Habent quidem eandem iudiciariam potestatem alii apostoli, (supple, quam habuit Petrus,) quibus post resurrectionem ait, (Christus scilicet,) Accipite spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, &c. Habet omnis ecclesia, presbyteris & episcopis; præponens in hoc presbyteros, quoniam auctoritas hæc debetur presbytero inquantum presbyter primo & secundum quod ipsum. De potestate vero sacramenti eucharistiæ nemo contendit quin æqualis sit in quouis sacerdote illi, quæ Romani pontificis. Ideoque mirandum est, cur contendant aliqui pertinaciter asserentes, minus tamen rationabiliter, Romanum pontificem reliquis sacerdotibus ampliorem clauium à Christo potestatem habere, cum id ex scriptura convinci nequeat, sed oppositum magis. Propter quæ etiam euidentius intuenda, debet vos non latere, quod hæc nomina presbyter & episcopus in primitiua ecclesia fuerunt synonyma, quamuis à diuersis proprietatibus eidem impositta fuerint. Nam presbyter ab ætate nomen impositum est, quasi senior; episcopus vero à dignitate seu cura super alios, quasi superintendens. Unde Hieronymus in epistola quadam ad Euandrum presbyterum, quæ intitulari solet, qualiter presbyter & diaconus d sferant, inquit sic: Presbyter & episcopus aliud ætatis, aliud dignitatis est nomen. Unde & ad Titum & ad Timotheum de ordinatione episcopi & diaconi dicitur, de presbyteris omnino recitetur, quia in episcopo presbyter continetur. Hoc etiam manifeste apparet per apostolum ad Philippenses primo, cum dixit: Omnibus sanctis in Christo Iesu, qui sunt Philippis, cum episcopis & diaconibus. Ecce quod sacerdotes non aliter nominauit quam episcopos. Certum enim est, quod episcopi plures in vnica ciuitate non aliter erant, nisi quia plures sacerdotes. Idem rursum palam per eundem ad Titum primo, cum dixit: Huius rei gratia reliquite Creta, ut ea quae desunt corrigas, & constituas per ciuitates presbyteros, sicut ego tibi dispensi, si quis sine crimine est. Et immediate subiungens constituendorum presbyterorum qualitatem ait: Oportet enim episcopum sine crimine esse, sicut Dei dispensatorem. Ecce quod constituendum presbyterum non nisi episcopum vocauit. Idem Actuum 20. loquens ad vnius ecclesiæ sacerdotes, Ephesi videlicet, inquit: Attendite vobis & vniuerso gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus posuit episcopos regere ecclesiam Dei, quam acquisiuit sanguine suo. Ecce quod in ecclesia vnius municipii, videlicet Ephesi, plures allocutus est apostolus tanquam episcopos, quod non fuit nisi propter sacerdotum pluralitatem, qui omnes episcopi dicebantur, propter hoc quod superintendentes esse debebant populo, quamuis hoc nomen in posteriori ecclesia sibi solum retinuerit qui primus sacerdotum eiusdem ciuitatis aut loci, per reliquos sacerdotes & populum instituebatur. Vocabat autem Apostolus eos magis episcopos quam presbyteros, vt ad eorum memorias reduceret, curam & solicitudinem quam habere debent reliquorum fidelium. Seipsum presbyterum vocabat, non episcopum propter humilitatem, vt apparet ex praeinducta serie primae ad Timotheum quarto, cum dixit: Noli negligere gratiam &c. Sic etiam Petrus atque Iohannes se vocarunt seniores, id est presbyteros, quoniam nomen hoc ab aetate impositum fuit. Unde primae Petri quinto: Seniores ergo qui in vobis sunt obsecro consenior, & testis Christi passionum. Et 2. Iohannis primo: Senior electa domina & natis eius. Et rursum eiusdem 3. primo: Senior Caio charissimo. Verum vbi communis litera canonis habet senior aut consenior, beatus Hieronymus in epistola praedicta vbique habet presbyter aut conpresbyter, quoniam his nominibus tanquam synonymis vtebantur apostoli. Post haec autem apostolorum tempora numero sacerdotum notabiliter aucto, ad scandalum & schisma euitandum elegerunt sacerdotes vnum ex ipsis, qui alios dirigeret & ordinaret quantum ad ecclesiasticum officium & seruitium exercendum, & oblata distribuendum, ac reliqua disponendum conuenientiori modo, ne istud quolibet pro libito faciente iconomia & seruitium templorum turbaretur, propter affectionum diuersitates. Hic siquidem electus ad alios sacerdotes regulandos, ex posteriorum consuetudine retinuit sibi soli nomen episcopi quasi superintendentis, eo quod non solum fideli populo superintendens erat, propter quod omnes sacerdotes in ecclesia primitiua dicebantur episcopi, verum etiam quia superintendebat reliquis cum presbyteris suis, propter quod talis Antiochiae sibi soli nomen episcopi retinuit, exteris sibi postmodum simplex nomen retinentibus sacerdotis. Verum iam dicta electio seu institutio per hominem, sic electio nihil amplioris meriti essentialis seu sacerdotalis autoritatis, aut prius dictae potestatis tribuit, sed solum ordinationis iconomicae in domo Dei seu templo potestatem quandam, alios sacerdotes, diaconos, & officiales reliquos ordinandi & regulandi quomodo Priori datur potestas in monachos temporibus his, potestas inquam non coactiua cuiusquam, nisi quantum de hoc sic electo concessum fuerit per legislatorem humanum, vt quarto huius & octavo demonstratum est, & in sequenti capitulo amplius apparebit, neque aliqua intrinseca dignitas alia siue potestas. Hoc etiam modo militantes in bellicis sibi eligunt capitaneum quem praeceptorem seu imperatorem antiquitus solebant dicere, quamuis nomen hoc, Imperator scilicet, ad regalis monarchiae modum quendam aut speciem, aliarum quasi supremam translatum fuerit, & taliter his temporibus vtitentur. Sic quoque diaconi ex ipsis archidiaconum eligunt, cui meritum essentiale seu sacrum ordinem diaconatu ampliorem talis electio minime tribuit, sed solum qualem quandam, vt diximus, humanam potestatem ordinandi seu regulandi diaconos reliquos. Vnde non plus sacerdotalis autoritatis essentialis habet Roman. episcopus quam alter sacerdos quilibet, sicut neque beatus Petrus amplius ex hac habuit caeteris apostolis. Omnes enim hanc eandem autoritatem a Christo susceperunt aequaliter & immediate, vt dictum est prius autoritate Hieronymi super illud Matth. 16. Et tibi dabo claues regni caelorum, & amplius declarabitur capitulo consequenti. Fuit autem haec aperte sententia beati Hieronymi epistola supradicta, in qua postquam ex multis apostolorum praedictorum autoritatibus demonstrauerat eundem esse penitus in essentiali dignitate a Christo data presbyterum & episcopum in ecclesia primitiua seu apostolorum tempore, reddens causam dictorum, inquit: Quod autem vnus electus est, qui caeteris praeponeretur, in schismatis remedium factum est, ne vnusquisque ad se trahens, Christi ecclesiam rumperet. Nam & Alexandria a Marco euangelista vsque ad Heraclam & Dionysium episcopos presbyteri semper vnum de se electum in excelsiori gradu collocatum, episcopum nominabant, quomodo, si exercitus Imperatorem faciat, (id est praeceptorem seu capitaneum secundum modernum vsum, non quidem secundum quod Imperator modum monarchae dicit vsu moderno:) aut eligant diaconi de se quem industrium nouerint & archidiaconum vocent. quid enim facit excepta ordinatione episcopus, quod presbyter non faceret? quantum scilicet ad actus essentialis autoritatis: Non enim intellexit ibi Hieronymus per ordinationem potestatem conferendi, seu collationem sacrorum ordinum, quoniam praeter hanc multa faciunt, & faciebant etiam suis temporibus episcopi, quae non faciunt sacerdotes, quamquam ad omnia sacramenta conferenda diuina potestate sic possit sacerdos quilibet sicut episcopus. Sed intellexit ibi per ordinationem potestatem iconomicam, de qua diximus prius, ab homine vel hominibus sibi datam immediate, quod etiam confirmo ratione cum eiusdem Hieronymi autoritate: Ratione quidem, quoniam iam multi fuerunt electi episcopi a tota plebe, sicut beatus Clemens, beatus Gregorius, beatus Nicolaus, & reliqui multi sanctorum, quibus constat per plebem aut etiam sibi compresbyteros maiorem sacrum ordinem non fuisse collatum, aut intrinsecum characterem aliquem: sed solam potestatem ordinandi ecclesiae ritum, atque personas regulandi, quantum ad exercitium diuini cultus in templo seu domo Dei: propter quod etiam tales electi ad alios sacerdotes dirigendum in templo, & populum instruendum in his quae sunt fidei vocati episcopi, ab antiquis legumlatoribus, vt a Iustiniano & Romano populo, tunc vocabantur iconomi reuerendi, quorum etiam supremus vocatus est iconomus reuerendissimus ab eisdem. Et ideo secundum veritatem & intentionem Hieronymi non aliud est est Episcopus quam archipresbyter. Quod autem non altera sit essentialis dignitas Episcopi quam Sacerdotis, neque inuicem episcoporum seu sacerdotum amplior, expressit etiam Hieronymus epistola praedicta, cum dixit: Nec altera Romanae urbis Ecclesia, & altera totius orbis existimanda est, & Galliae, & Britanniae, & Africa, & Persis, & Orientis, & India, & omnes barbarae nationes unum Christum adorant, unam observant regulam veritatis. Si autoritas quaeritur, orbis maior est urbe. Vbicunque fuerit Episcopus siue Romae, siue Eugubii, siue Constantinopolis, siue Regii, siue Alexandriae, siue Rachanis: eiusdem sunt meriti, eiusdem sunt sacerdotii. Potentia diuitiarum, & paupertas humilitas vel sublimiorem vel inferiorem episcopum facit, caeterum omnes Apostolorum successores sunt. Alia vero quaedam aut aliae sunt sacerdotalium officiorum institutiones non essentiales, qualem quandam iam dictam electionem diximus, qua vnus ex ipsis ad aliorum ordinationem seu gubernationem assumitur, quantum ad ea quae diuino cultui attinent, quales etiam sunt ipsorum quorundam electiones & institutiones ad docendum & instruendum, ac novae legis sacramenta ministrandum certo populo & in determinato loco maiori aut minori, similiter quoque ad dispensandum tam sibi; quam reliquis pauperibus temporalia quaedam, per legislatorem aut singulares personas statura & ordinata pro sustentatione pauperum euangelizantium in certa provincia vel communitate, nec non propter aliorum etiam pauperum sibi sufficere, impotentium, propter aetatem aut infirmitatem vel alteram miserabilem causam, sustentationem, ex eo tamen quod superest euangelizantium sufficientiae; quae siquidem temporalia sic statuta vocantur ex vsu moderno ecclesiastica beneficia, de quibus habitum est decimo quarto huius. Haec enim templorum ministris dispensanda committuntur in vsus praedictos, ministris inquam ad haec statutis, electis, & ordinatis in certa prouincia, per eam enim autoritatem essentialem, qua successores sunt Apostolorum, non magis determinantur ad vnum locum aut populum instruendum, & sacramenta nouae legis ministrandum quam ad reliquum, quemadmodum nec Apostoli omnino fuerunt determinati, quibus dictum fuit Matthaei vltimo: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes. Non determinat eos Christus ad loca, sed ipsi postmodum iter sibi condixerunt populos & prouincias; in quibus verbum Dei seu legem Euangelicam annunciarent, quandoque vero reuelatione diuina id etiam perceperunt. Vnde etiam ad Galatas secundo: Dexteras dederunt mihi & Barnabae societatis, (Iacobus videlicet, Cephas, atque Ioannes,) vt nos in gentes, ipsi autem in circumcisionem. Sic igitur ex praedictis apparet, a quo tanquam efficiente sit institutio sacerdotii & aliorum ordinum, quos sacros appellant, quoniam a Deo seu Christo immediate, quamuis praeuio quasi praeparante quodam humano ministerio, vt manuum impositione atque verborum pronunciatione, quae ad hoc fortasse nihil efficiunt, sed sic praemittuntur ex quodam pacto seu ordinatione diuina. Apparet etiam ex iam dictis, quod alia est quaedam humana institutio, qua sacerdotum vnus aliis praefertur, qua etiam sacerdotes ad certas prouincias & populos erudiendos & instruendos in lege diuina, & ministrandis sacramentis, ac dispensandis temporalibus, quae beneficia ecclesiastica diximus, statuuntur.
units.tr: From Acts 6: Whom they set before the apostles (namely, those who were to be deacons), and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them. This priestly character, whether one or several, which I have said is the power of consecrating the sacrament of the Eucharist, that is, the body and blood of Christ, and the power of loosing and binding men from sins, and which I will henceforth call the essential or inseparable authority of the presbyter as presbyter, seems to me probably the same in species in all priests. The Roman bishop has no greater share of it than any ordinary priest. For in this authority, whether one or many hold it, a bishop does not differ from a priest, as Jerome witnesses, and more truly the Apostle, whose clear opinion will appear below. For Jerome says on the words of Matthew 16, And whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth, etc.: The other apostles indeed have the same judicial power (namely, that which Peter had), to whom Christ said after the resurrection, Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted unto them, etc. Every church has presbyters and bishops, placing presbyters first in this, since this authority is owed to the presbyter first and as presbyter. As for the power over the sacrament of the Eucharist, no one disputes that it is equal in any priest to that of the Roman pontiff. It is therefore to be wondered at why some persist in asserting, though less reasonably, that the Roman pontiff has a greater power of the keys from Christ than the other priests, since this cannot be proved from Scripture, but rather the opposite. For this reason you should also see more clearly that these names presbyter and bishop were synonyms in the primitive Church, although they were given to the same men from different qualities. For presbyter was given as a name of age, as if "elder"; but bishop from dignity or care over others, as if "overseer." Hence Jerome, in a certain letter to the presbyter Evagrius, which is usually entitled How a presbyter and a deacon differ, says: Presbyter and bishop are names of age and of dignity respectively. Hence, where Titus and Timothy are told about the ordination of a bishop and a deacon, the presbyters are not named at all, because the presbyter is included in the bishop. This also appears plainly from the Apostle to the Philippians, chapter 1, where he said: To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons. See, he named the priests only as bishops. For it is certain that there were several bishops in a single city only because there were several priests. Again, the same thing is plain from the same Apostle to Titus, chapter 1, where he said: For this cause I left you in Crete, that you should correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I have directed you, if anyone is blameless. And immediately adding the qualification of the presbyters to be appointed, he says: For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God. See, he called the presbyter to be appointed nothing but a bishop. The same appears in Acts 20, where he speaks to the priests of one church, namely at Ephesus: Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood. See, the Apostle addressed several as bishops in the church of a single town, namely Ephesus, and this was only because of the plurality of priests, who were all called bishops, because they were to oversee the people. Although the name was afterwards kept for himself alone by the one who was first among the priests of the same city or place, and was installed over the other priests and the people. The Apostle called them bishops rather than presbyters, so as to recall to their minds the care and concern they ought to have for the other faithful. He called himself a presbyter, not a bishop, out of humility, as appears from the aforementioned passage of 1 Timothy 4, where he said: Neglect not the grace, etc. So also Peter and John called themselves elders, that is, presbyters, since this name was given from age. Hence 1 Peter 5: The elders who are among you I beseech, as a fellow elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ. And 2 John 1: The elder to the elect lady and her children. And again the same, 3 John 1: The elder to Gaius the beloved. But where the common text of the canon has senior or consenior, the blessed Jerome in the aforementioned letter everywhere has presbyter or fellow presbyter, since the apostles used these names as synonyms. After the time of the apostles, however, when the number of priests had notably increased, the priests chose one of their own, to avoid scandal and schism, who would direct and ordain the others as regards the performance of ecclesiastical office and service, and the distribution of offerings, and to arrange the remaining matters in a more fitting manner, so that the stewardship and the service of the temples would not be thrown into confusion by each man acting as he pleased, because of the diversity of feelings. This man, chosen to rule the other priests, by the custom of later times retained for himself alone the name bishop, as one who oversees, because he not only oversaw the faithful people, for which reason all priests in the primitive Church were called bishops, but also because he oversaw the other priests with his presbyters. For this reason, the one at Antioch retained the name bishop for himself alone, while the others afterwards kept the simple name of priest. Yet this election or institution by men, as I have said, confers on the one elected no greater merit of essential or priestly authority, nor of the power previously mentioned, but only a certain power of ordering the house of God or the temple as steward, of ordaining and regulating the other priests, deacons and remaining officials, just as in these times a prior is given power over monks. I say this is a power not coercive over anyone, except as far as it is granted to the one so elected by the human lawgiver, as has been shown in Book 4 and Book 8, and will appear more fully in the following chapter, and it carries no other intrinsic dignity or power. In the same way, soldiers in war choose a captain for themselves, whom in ancient times they used to call praeceptor or imperator, although this name, imperator, has been transferred to a certain kind or form of royal monarchy, as it were a supreme one among others, and is used in that way in these times. Likewise, the deacons choose from among themselves an archdeacon, to whom such an election by no means gives an essential or sacred merit greater than the diaconate, but only a certain human power, as we have said, of ordaining and regulating the other deacons. Hence the Roman bishop has no more essential priestly authority than any other priest, just as the blessed Peter did not have more of it than the other apostles. For all received this same authority from Christ equally and immediately, as was said earlier on the authority of Jerome on the words of Matthew 16: And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and this will be declared more fully in the following chapter. Now this was the plain opinion of the blessed Jerome in the letter cited above, in which, after he had shown from many passages of the aforementioned apostles that presbyter and bishop were entirely the same in essential dignity given by Christ in the primitive Church, or in the time of the apostles, giving the reason for this, he says: That one was chosen to be set over the others was done as a remedy for schism, so that no one, drawing the Church of Christ to himself, would break it. For also at Alexandria, from Mark the evangelist down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always named as bishop one of their own, placed in a higher rank, just as if an army should make an emperor (that is, a commander or captain, according to present usage, not in the sense in which the emperor is called a monarch by present usage), or if the deacons should choose from among themselves whom they knew to be diligent and call him archdeacon. For what does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter would not do? Clearly as regards acts of essential authority. For Jerome did not there understand by ordination the power of conferring, or the bestowal of sacred orders, since apart from this bishops did many things, and in his own times did things which priests do not do, although any priest can confer all the sacraments by divine power just as a bishop can. But he there understood by ordination the stewardly power, of which we spoke earlier, given immediately to him by a man or men. I confirm this also by reason, together with the authority of Jerome himself. By reason, indeed, because many bishops were already elected by the whole people, such as the blessed Clement, the blessed Gregory, the blessed Nicholas, and many other saints, and it is known that to them, by the people or even by their fellow presbyters, no greater sacred order was conferred, nor any intrinsic character, but only the power of ordering the rite of the Church and of regulating persons as regards the exercise of divine worship in the temple or house of God. For this reason, such men chosen to direct the other priests in the temple and to instruct the people in the matters of faith were called bishops, and by the ancient lawgivers, such as Justinian and the Roman people, they were then called reverend stewards, and their highest was also called by them the most reverend steward. And so, according to the truth and intention of Jerome, a bishop is nothing other than an archpresbyter. That the dignity of a bishop is not a different essential dignity from that of a priest, nor greater than that of one bishop or priest over another, Jerome also expressed in the aforementioned letter, when he said: Nor should the Church of the city of Rome be thought one thing and the Church of the whole world another, nor Gaul, Britain, Africa, Persia, the East, India and all barbarian nations: they all worship one Christ and keep one rule of truth. If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city. Wherever there is a bishop, whether at Rome, at Eugubium, at Constantinople, at Rhegium, at Alexandria, or at Tanis, they are of the same merit and of the same priesthood. Wealth or poverty and humility make a bishop higher or lower, but all are the successors of the apostles. Other institutions of priestly offices, however, are not essential, such as the election we have mentioned, by which one of them is taken to order or govern the others in matters pertaining to divine worship; such also are their own elections and appointments to teach and instruct a certain people, and to administer the sacraments of the new law, in a larger or smaller place; likewise to distribute certain temporal goods, both to themselves and to the other poor, which are fixed and ordained by the lawgiver or by particular persons, for the support of the poor who preach the gospel in a certain province or community, and also for the support of other poor who are unable, because of age or infirmity or another wretched cause, but only from what remains over and above what is sufficient for those who preach the gospel. Such temporal goods, so established, are now usually called ecclesiastical benefices, about which we treated in Book 14. For these are committed to the ministers of the temples to be distributed for the uses mentioned, to ministers, I say, appointed, elected and ordained for these purposes in a certain province. For by that essential authority by which they are the successors of the apostles, they are not more bound to one place or people to instruct, or to administer the sacraments of the new law, than to another, just as the apostles themselves were not wholly bound to any place, to whom it was said in the last chapter of Matthew: Go therefore and teach all nations. Christ did not bind them to places, but they afterwards arranged their own journeys to peoples and provinces in which they would announce the word of God or the Gospel law, and sometimes they perceived this even by divine revelation. Hence also Galatians 2: They gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (namely James, Cephas and John), that we should go to the Gentiles, but they to the circumcision. So from what has been said it appears from whom, as the efficient cause, the institution of the priesthood and of the other orders, which they call sacred, comes, namely from God or Christ immediately, although with a certain human ministry going before as a kind of preparation, such as the laying on of hands and the pronouncing of words, which perhaps effect nothing in this, but are so put first by a certain covenant or divine ordinance. It also appears from what has been said that there is another, human institution, by which one of the priests is preferred to the others, and by which priests are appointed to particular provinces and peoples, to be taught and instructed in the divine law, to administer the sacraments, and to distribute the temporal goods which we have called ecclesiastical benefices.

units.la: Apparuit rursum ex his, quoniam in autoritate prima, quam ex principio essentialem diximus, omnes Sacerdotes aequales sunt merito atque sacerdotio, quemadmodum Hieronymus dixit in epistola praedicta, causam assignans; quoniam omnes Episcopi Apostolorum successores sunt. In quo innuere videtur, omnes Apostolos aequalis autoritatis fuisse: sicque consequenter, neminem ipsorum singulariter in alterum aut supra reliquum vel reliquos autoritatem habuisse, nec quantum ad essentialem institutionem, quam primam diximus, nec quantum ad secundarias institutiones.
units.tr: It appears again from these points that, in the first authority, which we called essential at the beginning, all priests are equal in merit and in priesthood, as Jerome said in the letter mentioned above, giving the reason: because all bishops are successors of the Apostles. In this he seems to suggest that all the Apostles had equal authority; and so, consequently, that none of them had authority over another singly, or above the rest, neither as to the essential institution, which we called the first, nor as to the secondary institutions.

units.la: Vnde etiam similiter opinandum videtur de ipsorum successoribus inuicem, ad quos siquidem & in quos, vnde perueniant institutiones huiusmodi, quas secundarias & autoritate humana factas iam diximus; quaeue rationabiliter sit earum effectiua causa, determinandum vtique restat.
units.tr: Hence it seems likewise to be thought of the Apostles' successors among themselves. It remains, of course, to determine to whom and from whom such institutions come, which we have already called secondary and made by human authority, and what is rightly their effective cause.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: De Apostolorum aequalitate in officio siue dignitate quacunque, per Christum illis immediate col- lata, vnde probatur quod de successorum omnium aequalitate dictum est capitulo praecedente, & qualiter Episcopi omnes indifferenter successores sint Apostoli cuiuscunque.
units.tr: On the equality of the Apostles in office or in whatever dignity, conferred on them immediately by Christ. From this it is proved that what was said in the preceding chapter about the equality of all successors is true, and how all bishops indifferently are successors of any apostle.

units.la: A Prioribus itaque inchoantes, in hoc ostendemus primum Apostolorum neminem ad alios habuisse praeeminentiam in essentiali dignitate sacerdotali scilicet sibi datam a Christo; deinde vero quod in nulla institutione alia, quam secundariam diximus, & eo minus in iurisdictione aliqua coactiua, quamuis hoc proximum sufficienter demonstratum fuerit quarto huius & quinto. Ex quibus etiam per necessitatem deducemus, Episcoporum sibi successorum, neminem singulariter autoritatem seu potestatem aliquam iam dictarum in reliquos sibi coepiscopos seu compresbyteros habere, nec oppositum huius virtute verborum scripturae, sed magis propositum posse conuinci. Demum vero ex hoc quod & praecedenti capitulo finaliter intendimus, deducemus per necessitatem ad humanum legislatorem fidelem pertinere has institutiones, quas secundarias saepe vocauimus, tanquam ad causam per se factuam illarum, sicuti & aliarum partium ciuitatis. Primum quidem igitur propositorum conuincitur, ex Luca 22. Nam tribuens Christus Apostolis stolis potestatem ad eucharistiæ sacramentum, inquit ad eos: Hoc est enim corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur, hoc facite in meam commemorationem, id est, hoc faciendi potestatem habetis, proferendo tamen verba consimilia, quando actum hunc exercere debetis, videlicet: Hoc est enim corpus meum. Nec dixit hæc verba plus ad beatum Petrum quam ad alios. Non enim dixit Christus, fac & aliis apostolis sic faciendi potestatem tribuas; sed dixit, facite, in plurali & omnibus indifferenter. Idem quoque per omnia sentiendum de clavium potestate, sive his eisdem verbis tradita fuerit apostolis sive aliis, aut alio tempore, ut his quæ habentur Ioannis vigesimo. Postquam enim Christus dixit Apostolis, Sicut misit me pater, ita & ego mitto vos. Insufflavit & dixit eis, Accipite spiritum Sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, & quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt. Dixit ergo Christus, Mitto vos, sicut pater me misit, nec dixit Petro aut alteri Apostolo singulariter, Mitto te sicut pater, &c. & tu alios mitte. Nec rursum dicitur, Christus insufflavit ei, sed dixit eis, non uni per alterum. Nec dixit Christus ad Petrum, accipe spiritum Sanctum & aliis postmodum tribue, sed dixit, accipite, in plurali & indifferenter omnibus loquens. Et hoc est etiam quod habetur Matthæi ultimo, dum dixit Christus ad eos: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, & dixit euntes pluraliter & indifferenter, non dicens Petro, vade ergo & aliis mitte. Quod amplius exprimens Apostolus ad hanc quæstionem diffiniendam, ut videlicet nemo crederet aliquem Apostolorum hanc habuisse prærogatiuam seu autoritatem super alios, eam expresse remouens à Petro, de quo fortasse videbatur hoc magis, propter aliqua sibi à Christo singulariter dicta, & quia senior cæteris erat, secundo ad Galatas inquit sic: Mihi n. qui videbantur esse aliquid, nihil contulerunt, sed e contra, cum vidissent quod creditum est mihi euangelium præputii sicut Petro circumcisionis. Qui n. operatus est Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est & mihi inter gentes. Et cum cognovissent gratiam quæ data est mihi, Iacobus, & Cephas, & Ioannes, qui videbantur columnæ esse, dexteras dederunt mihi & Barnabæ societatis, &c. Qui ergo fuit operatus Petro in apostolatum, operatus fuit & Paulo, hic autem fuit Christus, ergo huiusmodi officium non suscepit à Petro, & similiter nec apostoli reliqui. Vbi etiam Glossa secundum Aug. hoc amplius exprimens, inquit: Illi qui videbantur esse aliquid, scil. Petrus & alii qui fuerunt cum domino, nihil contulerunt, id est, addiderunt mihi, in quo patet, quod non illis inferior sum, qui à domino, à Deo perfectus sum, ut nihil esset quod in collatione mea perfectioni adderent. Ecce quod Paulus non fuit inferior Petro nec aliis. Consequenter ad hanc intentionem subiungit Glossa: Cum vid essent, quod euangelium præputii creditum est mihi ut fideli, ita principaliter, sicut & Petro euangelium circumcisionis. Ecce ǫ æque principaliter missus fuit Paulus quemadmodum & Petrus, & non à Petro aut apostolorum aliquo, sed à Christo immediate, quod amplius exprimens Apostolus eadem primo, sic ait: Paulus Apostolus non ab hominib. neq; per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum & Deum patrem. vbi Glossa secundum Ambr. Paulus apostolus non electus vel missus ab hominib scil. ab Anania, ut quidam dicebant, vel ab aliis, ut quidam ab apostolis electi & missi fuerunt. Deinde parum infra subdit secundum Augustt. Ceterum apostoli videbantur esse maiores, quia priores, iste minimus, quia novissimus. Sed inde apparet dignior, quia priores constituti sunt per Christum adhuc ex parte hominem, id est mortalem. Novissimus vero Paulus per Christum iam totum Deum, id est, ex omni parte immortalem, & Deum patrem qui hominem per filium, atq; ut aperiret, cur dixerit neq; per hominem, subdit, qui suscitavit eum à mortuis. Et ita dignius constituit me per immortalem Christum, quam alios per mortalem. Rursum confirmans hoc apostolus infra eodem ait: Notum n. vobis facio euangelium quod evangelizatum est à me, quia non est secundum hominem, neq; n. ego ab homine accepi illud neq; didici, sed per revelationem Iesu Christi. Vbi Glossa secundum Augustin. Notum n. vobis facio euangelium, fratres quod evangelizatum est à me, quia non est secundum hominem docemi me, & vere non est ab homine. Neq; n. accepi illud neq; didici ab homine, ut homo me eligeret ad evangelizandum, vel mihi iniungeret, neq; didici ab homine doctus me, sed per revelationem Iesu Christi. Ecce ǫ neq; Petrus neq; alius apostolorum aut homo quisquam elegit, misit, aut iniunxit Paulo ministerium euangelii. Idem quoq; iudicandum est de apostolis reliquis. Nulla ergo potestatem, eoq; minus coactiua iurisdictionem habuit Petrus à Deo immediate sup apostolos reliquos, neq; instituendi eos in officio sacerdotali, neq; segregandi eos seu mittendi ad officium prædicationis, nisi ǫ hoc sane concedi potest, ipsum fuisse priorem aliis æratè vel officio fortasse secundum tempus, aut apostolorum electione qui eum propterea reuerebantur merito. quamuis hanc electionem ex scriptura nemo convincere potest. Signum autem verum est, quod dixinus, est, quoniam beatus Petrus nullam sibi assumpsisse singulariter autoritatem supra reliquos apostolos, inuenimus ex scriptura, sed magis cum ipsis æqualitatem seruasse. Non n. sibi assumpsit autoritatem determinandi, quæ dubia erant circa euangelii prædicationem, quod pertinet ad doctrinam. Sed quæ dubia fuerunt in hoc, ex communi deliberatione apostolorum & aliorum fidelium magis doctorum determinabantur, non Petri aut alterius apostoli seorsum determinatione. Vnde Actuum decimo quinto, dissentione orta inter prædicatores euangelii, an oporteret circuncidere incircuncisos fideles ad salutem æternam consequendam; Quibusdam dicentibus oportere, Paulo vero & Barnaba reclamantibus contra hoc, conuenerunt Apostoli & seniores videre de verbo hoc, super quo locuti sunt Petrus & Iacobus non oportere, quorum sententiæ seniores & reliqui consenserunt Apostoli, unde subditur infra: Tunc placuit Apostolis & senioribus cum omni Ecclesia eligere viros, & mittere Antiochiam, &c. scribentes per manus eorum. Et fuit modus scribendi modo deliberandi conformis & talis: Apostoli & seniores fratres hu qui sunt Antiochiæ, & Syriæ, & Ciliciæ fratribus ex gentibus, salutem, &c. Simile etiam habetur infra eodem continuata sententia, cum dicitur: Placuit ergo nobis collectis in unum eligere viros & mittere ad vos. Rursum idem eodem in fia parum: Visum est enim spiritui Sancto & nobis, nihil ultra imponere vobis oneris. Non ergo determinauit Petrus suprasupendita dubia circa fidem de plenitudine potestatis, quam quidam somniantes magistri in Israel habere dicunt Romanum Episcopum, qui pronunciauerunt in non scriptis dogmatibus, ipsum per seipsum, quod non audit Petrus, ea quae circa fidem dubia sunt, determinare posse, quod falsum apertum est, & scripturae dissonans palam, de quo etiam sequenti capitulo & huius vigesimo diffuse dicemus. Deliberauit ergo, dubium determinauit, elegit, & scripsit fidelium doctorum congregatio. Et hac autoritate validum fuit sic determinatum atque mandatum. Congregatio enim Apostolorum amplioris fuit autoritatis, quam solus Petrus, aut alter Apostolus. Vnde ab ipsa Petrum legimus missum in Samariam, vt apparet Actuum octauo: Cum autem audissent Apostoli qui erant Hierosolymis, quia recepit Samaria verbum Dei, miserunt ad eos Petrum & Ioannem. Cur ergo & unde assumunt adulatores sacrilegi quidam, dicere quenquam Episcopum habere a CHRISTO plenitudinem potestatis, etiam in clericos, nedum in laicos, cum Beatus Petrus aut alter Apostolus nunquam talem sibi potestatem ascribere praesumpserit opere vel sermone? Hoc enim asserentes deridendi sunt, nihil credendi, minusque timendi, cum scripturae oppositum clament in literali & manifesto sensu ipsarum. Nam Beatus Petrus nunquam super Apostolos aut alios talem habuit potestatem, sed cum ipsis potius, vt iam diximus, aequalitatem iuxta Christi praeceptum seruauit. Vnde Matthaei vigesimo tertio: Nolite vocari rabbi. Vnus est enim magister vester Christus: Omnes autem vos fratres estis, id est aequales. Et dixit omnes, excipiendo neminem. Confirmatur autem sententia haec per Apostolum ad Galatas secundo, vbi sic ait: Ascendi autem secundum revelationem, & contuli cum illis Euangelium quod praedico in gentibus, vbi Glossa secundum Augustinum: Et non didici ab illis tanquam maioribus, (a Petro scilicet, nec ab aliis principalioribus Apostolorum, de quibus infra dicetur) sed contuli cum eis tanquam amicis & paribus. Idem rursum infra eodem, cum dixit Apostolus: Cum autem venisset Cephas Antiochiam, in faciem ei restiti, quia reprehensibilis erat, &c. vbi Glossa secundum Hieronym. Ipsi nihil mihi contulerunt, sed ego contuli Petro. Et subiungitur consequenter: Ego restiti eis, tanquam par. Hoc enim non auderet facere nisi sciret se non imparem fore. Ecce ergo quod Paulus fuit par officio & dignitate, Petro non inferior, licet Petrus fuerit aetate senior & tempore prior pastor.
units.tr: Beginning with the earliest examples, we will first show that none of the Apostles had pre-eminence over the others in the essential sacerdotal dignity given to them by Christ. Then we will show that none had it in any institution other than what we have called secondary, and still less in any coercive jurisdiction, although this has already been sufficiently demonstrated in the fourth and fifth of this work. From these points we will also deduce by necessity that none of their successors as bishops has, individually, any of the authority or power mentioned above over the other bishops, his fellow-bishops or fellow-presbyters. Nor can it be proved that the opposite follows from the force of the words of Scripture; rather, the contrary is what they show. Finally, from what we intend in the preceding chapter and in this one, we will deduce by necessity that these institutions, which we have often called secondary, belong to the human lawgiver, as to their proximate efficient cause, just as do other parts of the commonwealth. The first of our propositions is proved from Luke 22. For when Christ gave the Apostles power over the sacrament of the Eucharist, he said to them: This is my body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me. That is, you have the power of doing this, but you must use similar words when you are to perform this act, namely: This is my body. Nor did he speak these words to blessed Peter more than to the others. Christ did not say, "Give the other apostles the power of doing this as well," but he said do, in the plural and addressed indifferently to all. The same must be understood throughout concerning the power of the keys, whether it was given to the apostles in these same words or in others, or at another time, as in what is found in John 20. For after Christ said to the Apostles, As the Father has sent me, so I also send you. And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained. So Christ said, I send you, as the Father sent me; he did not say to Peter or to any other apostle singly, "I send you as the Father sent me, etc., and you send the others." Nor is it said that Christ breathed on him; rather he said to them, not to one through another. Nor did Christ say to Peter, "Receive the Holy Spirit and afterwards give it to the others," but he said receive, speaking in the plural and indifferently to all. This is also what is found in the last chapter of Matthew, where Christ said to them: Go therefore and teach all nations; and he said go in the plural and indifferently, not saying to Peter, "Go, then, and send the others." The Apostle, expressing this more fully in order to settle the question, so that no one would believe that any of the Apostles had this prerogative or authority over the others, expressly removed it from Peter, who might seem to have it more than the rest, because of certain things Christ said to him singly and because he was senior to the others. In the second chapter to the Galatians he says: For those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me; but on the contrary, when they saw that the gospel of uncircumcision was committed to me, as the gospel of circumcision was to Peter; for he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also in me among the Gentiles. And when they had known the grace that was given to me, James, and Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, etc. Therefore, he who worked in Peter for the apostleship worked also in Paul, and this was Christ; so this office was not received from Peter, and likewise not from the other apostles. Here the Gloss, following Augustine, expresses this further, saying: Those who seemed to be something, namely Peter and the others who were with the Lord, contributed nothing, that is, they added nothing to me; in which it is clear that I am not inferior to them, since I have been made perfect by the Lord, by God, so that they had nothing to add to my perfection. See, then, that Paul was not inferior to Peter or to the others. Following this line of thought, the Gloss continues: When they saw that the gospel of uncircumcision was committed to me, as to one faithful, so principally, just as the gospel of circumcision was to Peter. See, then, that Paul was sent just as principally as Peter was, and not by Peter or by any of the apostles, but immediately by Christ. Expressing this more fully, the Apostle says at the beginning of the same letter: Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. Here the Gloss, following Ambrose: Paul the apostle was not chosen or sent by men, namely by Ananias, as some said, nor by others, as some said that apostles were chosen and sent by apostles. Then a little further on, the Gloss adds, following Augustine: Moreover, the apostles seemed to be greater because they were earlier; this one seems least because he was last. But from this it appears that he is more worthy, because the earlier ones were appointed by Christ while still in part man, that is, mortal. But Paul, the last, was appointed by Christ, who is now wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect, and by God the Father, who raised him from the dead, the man through the Son. And to show why he said "not through man," he adds: who raised him from the dead. And so he has appointed me, through the immortal Christ, more worthily than the others through the mortal one. Again confirming this, the Apostle says a little further in the same chapter: For I make known to you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached by me is not according to man. For I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came through the revelation of Jesus Christ. Here the Gloss, following Augustine: For I make known to you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached by me is not according to man, and truly it is not from man. For I did not receive it from man, nor was I taught it by man, so that a man should choose me to preach or enjoin it on me; nor was I taught by man, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ. See, then, that neither Peter nor any other of the apostles, nor any man at all, chose, sent, or enjoined on Paul the ministry of the gospel. The same must be judged of the other apostles. Therefore Peter had no power from God immediately over the other apostles, still less coercive jurisdiction; nor did he have the power to appoint them to the sacerdotal office, nor to separate them or send them to the office of preaching. Unless one may indeed concede that he was prior to the others in rank or perhaps in office, according to the order of time, or by the choice of the apostles who for this reason rightly revered him. Yet no one can prove this choice from Scripture. The sign, however, that we have mentioned is true: we find from Scripture that blessed Peter never claimed for himself any authority singly over the other apostles, but rather kept equality with them. For he did not claim the authority of determining doubtful matters concerning the preaching of the gospel, which pertains to doctrine. Rather, whatever questions arose in this matter were settled by the common deliberation of the apostles and of other faithful who were more learned, not by the decision of Peter or of any other apostle alone. Hence in Acts 15, when a dispute arose among the preachers of the gospel as to whether the uncircumcised believers had to be circumcised in order to obtain eternal salvation, some saying that they must, while Paul and Barnabas objected to this, the Apostles and elders met to consider this question, and Peter and James spoke, saying that they should not. Their opinion was agreed to by the elders and the rest of the apostles. Hence it is added further on: Then it seemed good to the apostles and elders, with the whole Church, to choose men and send them to Antioch, etc., writing by their hands. And the manner of writing was in accordance with this manner of deliberating, and was of this kind: The apostles and elders, brethren, who are at Antioch, and in Syria and Cilicia, to the brethren from among the Gentiles, greeting, etc. Something similar is found further on in the same passage, where it is said: It has therefore seemed good to us, being assembled together, to choose men and send them to you. Again, a little further in the same place: For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden. Therefore Peter did not determine the doubtful matters of faith by the fullness of power, which some dreaming teachers in Israel say the Roman Bishop has, who have pronounced that in unwritten dogmas he by himself, which Peter did not claim, can determine what is doubtful in faith. This is plainly false and clearly contrary to Scripture, and we will speak of it at length in the following chapter and in the twentieth of this work. Therefore the assembly of faithful teachers deliberated, settled the doubtful matter, chose, and wrote; and by this authority the decision and command were valid. For the assembly of the Apostles had greater authority than Peter alone or any other single apostle. Hence we read that Peter was sent by them into Samaria, as appears in Acts 8: Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John. Why, then, and from what source do some sacrilegious flatterers claim that any bishop has from Christ the fullness of power, even over the clergy, not to mention the laity, when blessed Peter or any other apostle never presumed to ascribe such power to himself by deed or word? Those who assert this are to be mocked, not believed, and feared still less, since they cry out against the plain and manifest literal sense of Scripture. For blessed Peter never had such power over the apostles or others, but rather, as we have said, he kept equality with them according to Christ's command. Hence Matthew 23: Do not be called rabbi; for one is your master, Christ; but you are all brethren, that is, equals. And he said all, excepting no one. This opinion is further confirmed by the Apostle in Galatians 2, where he says: And I went up by revelation, and conferred with them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, where the Gloss, following Augustine: And I did not learn from them as from greater men (namely from Peter, nor from the other chief apostles, of whom it will be said below), but I conferred with them as with friends and equals. Again, a little further in the same chapter, when the Apostle said: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I withstood him to his face, because he was to be blamed, etc., where the Gloss, following Jerome: They contributed nothing to me, but I contributed to Peter. And it is consequently added: I withstood them as an equal. For he would not have dared to do this unless he knew that he was not unequal. See, then, that Paul was equal to Peter in office and dignity, not inferior to him, although Peter was older in age and earlier in time as a minister.

units.la: Similiter apparet, Beatum Petrum aut alium Apostolorum neminem super reliquos habuisse praeeminentiam seu potestatem in distribuendis temporalibus oblatis ecclesiae primitiuae, vnde Actuum 4. Quotquot enim possessores agrorum & domorum erant, vendentes offerebant pretia eorum, & ponebant ante pedes Apostolorum, diuidebantur autem singulis, prout cuique opus erat. Ecce quod dispositio temporalium oblatorum ecclesiae fiebat per Apostolos communiter non a solo Petro. Non enim dicitur, ponebant ante pedes Petri, sed Apostolorum. Nec dicitur, diuisit autem Petrus, sed diuidebantur.
units.tr: Similarly, it appears that Blessed Peter, or any other of the apostles, had no pre-eminence or power over the rest in distributing the temporal offerings of the primitive church. Acts 4: "For as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them down at the apostles' feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need." Behold, the disposal of the church's temporal offerings was made by the apostles jointly, not by Peter alone. For it is not said that they laid them at Peter's feet, but at the apostles' feet. Nor is it said that Peter distributed them, but that distribution was made.

units.la: Dicigitur mihi, vnde Romano Episcopo venit autoritas talia pro voto distribuendi, vel legata in hominum testamentis ad pias causas, aliis tamen commissa conseruari aut distribui, tanquam sibi soli debita repetendi, cum nec sibi soli aut cum alio liceat diuino aut humano iure talia petere, quae aliorum fidei custodiae per leges rationabiles commissa sunt, vt testantium aut sic ordinantium voluntate? Dicat enim testator, de suo scilicet, & lex erit, sicut in aliis scriptum est. Non enim potest ratio sumi ex scriptura sacra, fidem faciens, hanc potestatem Romani aut cuiusquam alterius Episcopi fore, sed oppositi magis. Quod si haec legata commissa fuerint ecclesiae distribuenda determinatae dioecesis, ad eos pertinebit Episcopos, qui sic determinatae dioecesi praesunt, ad Romanum vero nequaquam. Huius autem causa est, quoniam Romanus Episcopus supra reliquos sibi coepiscopos aut compresbyteros nullam habet a Christo, nec habuit potestatem aut autoritatem, quod erat vnum propositorum ex principio capituli huius. Nam sicut Petrus hanc non habuit supra reliquos Apostolos, ita nec Petri successores in episcopali sede Romana supra successores reliquorum Apostolorum. Non enim habuit Petrus potestatem, sacerdotium, apostolatum, aut episcopatum illis conferendi, quoniam omnes a Christo potestatem seu autoritatem hanc immediate non per Petri ministerium plusquam econuerso sumpserunt, quemadmodum ex scriptura patenter probauimus supra. Quod etiam expresse dicit Augustinus de quaestionibus noui & veteris Testamenti, q. 84. vbi sic ait: Eodem die, (id est pentecosten,) lex lata est, quo & spiritus Sanctus decidit in discipulos, vt autoritatem caperent, ac scirent euangelicum ius praedicare.
units.tr: Let someone tell me: whence does the Roman bishop derive the authority to distribute such things at his pleasure, or to reclaim bequests made in people's wills to pious causes, as though owed to himself alone, when those bequests have been entrusted to others to be kept or distributed? Neither alone nor with another may anyone seek, by divine or human right, things which by reasonable laws have been committed to the safekeeping of others, according to the will of the testators or of those who so ordained. Let the testator say what is his own, and that shall be the law, as is written in other cases. For no reasoning drawn from holy Scripture can make it plain that this power belongs to the Roman bishop or to any other bishop; rather the opposite. If such bequests have been committed to the church of a particular diocese for distribution, they will belong to the bishops who preside over that diocese, and not at all to the Roman bishop. The reason is this: the Roman bishop has from Christ no power or authority over his fellow bishops or co-elders, which was one of the propositions set out at the beginning of this chapter. For just as Peter did not have this over the other apostles, so neither do the successors of Peter in the Roman episcopal see have it over the successors of the other apostles. Peter did not have the power to confer on them the priesthood, the apostleship, or the episcopate, since all of them received this power or authority immediately from Christ, not through Peter's ministry, any more than the reverse, as we have plainly proved from Scripture above. Augustine also says this expressly in De quaestionibus novi et veteris Testamenti, q. 84, where he writes: On the same day (that is, Pentecost) the law was given, on which the Holy Spirit also descended upon the disciples, so that they might receive authority and know how to preach the gospel law.

units.la: Amplius sicut Petrus Antiochiae legitur electus in Episcopum per fidelium multitudinem, aliorum Apostolorum confirmatione non indigens: sic & Apostolorum reliqui praefuerunt in aliis prouinciis absq; Petri scientia, institutione, vel consecratione aliqua, fuerant enim per Christum consecrati sufficienter, propter quod similiter opinandum horum Apostolorum successores non indiguisse aliqua confirmatione successorum Petri, quinimo multi successores aliorum Apostolorum fuerunt electi & instituti Episcopi rite, ipsorumq; prouincias sancte rexerunt absq; alia institutione vel confirmatione de ipsis facta per successores Petri. Et exitit hoc sic legitime obseruatum vsq; quasi ad tempora Constantini Imperatoris, qui quandam praeeminentiam & potestatem tribuit Episcopis & Ecclesiae Romanorum super caeteras mundi ecclesias seu presbyteros omnes. Hanc siquidem Petri & Apostolorum aequalitatem significauit Apostolus ad Galat. 2. cum dixit: Dextrae dederunt mihi & Barnabae societatis, Iacobus, Petrus, atq; Ioannes, vt nos in gentes, ipsi autem in circumcisionem. Dexterae societatis ergo & aequalitatis, vt ex Glossa secundum Aug. factis osteasum est supra, quamuis in hoc dictum Apostoli sic sit apertum, vt Glossa non egeat, quod etiam supra induximus ex epistola Hieronymi ad Euandrum, dicentis omnes Episcopos sive Romæ sive alibi, eiusdem sacerdotii atque meriti seu potestatis à Christo collatæ.
units.tr: Moreover, just as Peter is read to have been elected bishop of Antioch by the multitude of the faithful, without needing confirmation by the other apostles, so too the other apostles presided in their provinces without any knowledge, appointment, or consecration by Peter, for they had been sufficiently consecrated by Christ. Hence we should similarly suppose that the successors of these apostles did not need any confirmation by the successors of Peter. Indeed, many successors of the other apostles were lawfully elected and installed as bishops, and governed their provinces holily, without any other installation or confirmation made by Peter's successors. This was legitimately observed right up to about the time of the Emperor Constantine, who granted a certain pre-eminence and power to the bishops and the church of Rome over the other churches of the world, or over all the elders. The Apostle indicated this equality of Peter and the apostles when he said in Galatians 2: "And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision." The right hands, then, signify fellowship and equality, as has been shown above from the Gloss according to Augustine. Yet in this saying of the Apostle the meaning is so plain that the Gloss is hardly needed. We also cited above Jerome's letter to Evangelus, which says that all bishops, whether at Rome or elsewhere, have the same priesthood and merit, and the same power conferred by Christ.

units.la: Quod si tamen beatus Petrus à quibusdam sanctorum princeps Apostolorum scribatur, dictum est large, ac improprie sumendo vocabulum principis, etiam si sic aperte contra Christi sententiam & oraculum, vbi Matth. 20. & Lucæ 22. inquit: Principes gentium dominantur eorum, vos autem non sic: Ideoque dicendum sic sanctos locutos fuisse, non propter potestatem aliquam à Christo super Apostolos sibi datam: sed forte quia ætate senior, aut quia Christum prius confessus est, fuisse verum Dei consubstantialem filium, vel quia fortasse fuit in fide feruentior atque constantior, aut quia cum Christo conuersatus & frequentius vocatus in consiliis & secretis. Vnde Apostolus ad Galat.
units.tr: But if Blessed Peter is nevertheless called by some of the saints "prince of the apostles," the term "prince" has been used broadly and improperly. This is plainly contrary to the saying and oracle of Christ in Matthew 20 and Luke 22: "The princes of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; but ye shall not be so." Therefore it should be said that the saints spoke thus not because of any power given him by Christ over the apostles, but perhaps because he was older in years, or because he confessed earlier that Christ was the true, consubstantial Son of God, or perhaps because he was more fervent and steadfast in faith, or because he had conversed with Christ and was more often called into his counsels and secrets. Hence the Apostle in Galatians:

units.la: 2. Iacobus & Cephas, (id est Petrus) & Ioannes, qui videbantur columnæ esse. vbi Glossa secundum Ambrosium, Quia honoratiores erant in Apostolis, quia semper in secretis cum domino fuerunt. Cuius rei exemplum conueniens sumi potest ex principantibus seculi, qui nec præsunt sibi inuicem aliqua potestate, vt Comites eiusdem regni, quorum vnus alteri non subest iurisdictione vel autoritate, sed omnes immediate regi. Cum tamen quandoque inter alios vnus aut plures cæteris honoratiores habeantur, vt quia seniores aut aliqua vel aliquibus virtutibus excellentiores, vel magis obsequiosi regi aut regno, propter quod à rege vel populo magis diliguntur, & reverentiores habentur. Quo etiam modo debemus opinari de Apostolis inuicem & ad Christum. Omnes enim sub Christi potestate & autoritate fuerunt, immediate ab ipso suam institutionem sacerdotii & apostolatus suscipientes non ab inuicem, vt in aperto clamat vbique scriptura, & sancti sequentes ipsam, quamuis inter eos beatus Petrus honoratior fuerit propter iam dictas causas, non tamen propter aliquam sibi à Christo super reliquos traditam potestatem. Hanc enim eis inuicem interdixit, vt supra induximus ex Matth. 23. cum directe ad propositam hunc intentionem dixit eis: Nolite vocari Rabbi, vnus est enim magister vester, vos autem omnes fratres estis.
units.tr: 2. "James and Cephas" (that is, Peter) "and John, who seemed to be pillars." Here the Gloss according to Ambrose says: Because they were more honoured among the apostles, since they were always with the Lord in private. A fitting example of this can be taken from secular rulers, who do not preside over one another by any power. Such are the counts of the same kingdom, of whom one is not subject to another in jurisdiction or authority, but all are ruled immediately by the king. Yet sometimes among them one or more are held in higher honour than the rest, either as being older, or more excellent in some virtue or virtues, or more obedient to the king or kingdom, and for this reason they are loved more by the king or the people and held in greater reverence. In the same way we ought to think of the apostles among themselves and in relation to Christ. For all were under the power and authority of Christ, receiving their institution to the priesthood and apostleship immediately from him, not from one another, as Scripture everywhere plainly proclaims and the saints who follow it affirm. Although among them Blessed Peter was more honoured for the reasons already mentioned, it was not because of any power handed to him by Christ over the rest. For Christ forbade this among them, as we cited above from Matthew 23, when he said to them directly, with this very purpose in view: "Be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren."

units.la: Similiter autem neq; iurisdictionem coactiuam habuit in reliquos apostolos plusquam econuerso, nec per consequens ipsorum successores inuicem. Hanc enim sibi Christus penitus interdixit Matth. 20. & Luc. 22. ad propositas intentiones directe. Cum enim facta esset contentio inter eos, quis eorum esset maior, dixit eis Christus: Reges & principes gentium dominantur eorum, & qui maiores sunt, potestatem exercent in eos, vos autem non sic, nec posset Christus hoc magis aperte negare. Cur ergo credet aliquis de hoc magis humanæ traditioni, siue sancti siue non sancti, quam apertissimo Christi eloquio? Contra talem n. vel tales loquitur Christus Marci septimo, cum dixit directe ad propositam intentionem: In vanum autem me colunt docentes doctrinas & præcepta hominum. Relinquentes enim mandatum Dei tenetis traditiones hominum. Et parum infra: Bene irritum facitis præceptum Dei, vt traditionem vestram seruetis, quod faciunt docentes humanas Decretales, quæ Romano Episcopo dicunt conuenire potestatem & dominium temporalium non solum ecclesiasticorum, verum etiam & imperialium atque regalium, facientes irritum Dei præceptum, vt ex decimo quarto demonstratum est, & ex præsenti capitulo liquet aperte, vt suam traditionem de bonis temporalibus ad ipsorum commodum seruent. Quod si tamen Apostoli beatum Petrum tanquam sibi Episcopum elegissent, aut principaliorem propter ipsius ætatem & sanctitatem acquisitam, excellentiorem, vt haberetur ex quodam Anacleti Papæ Decreto, in Isidori codice contento, cuius series est: Ceteri vero Apostoli cum eodem, (Petro scilicet,) pari consortio honorem & potestatem acceperunt, ipsumque principem eorum esse voluerunt: Non tamen ex hoc sequeretur, quod ipsius successores in Romana sede vel alia, si alibi fuit Episcopus, hanc prioritatem habeant super aliorum successores, nisi à reliquorum successoribus eligerentur ad hoc, maioris enim virtutis fuerunt aliqui successores aliorum quibusdam successoribus Petri, quamuis proprie quilibet Episcopus indifferenter sit successor cuiuslibet Apostoli quantum ad officium, licet non locum. Rursum cur magis conuenieret hoc successoribus eius in sede Romana, quam in Antiochena vel Hierosolymitana vel alia, si Episcopus in pluribus extitisset? Amplius quilibet Episcopus quantum ad intrinsecam dignitatem, inseparabilem scilicet, indifferenter successor est cuiuslibet Apostoli, & eiusdem meriti siue perfectionis, quantum ad dignitatem prædictam siue characterem, quoniam omnes hunc habent eundem ab vno efficiente siue datore secundum numerum immediate, videlicet à Christo, non ab eo qui manus imposuit. Neque refert quis Apostolorum manus imposuerit.
