Vnde primæ ad Corinth. tertio: Nemo in hominibus glorietur siue Paulus siue Apollo, siue Cephas, &c. vos baptizauerit, vel aliter, manus imposuerit, non refert. Vnde subdit, vos autem Christi estis, id est, interius signaculum habetis à Christo. Vbi Glossa: Vos autem Christi non hominum, in creatione vel recreatione, quæ per sacramentum fit, (supple.)
units.tr: Likewise, Peter had no coercive jurisdiction over the other apostles, any more than they had over him, and consequently neither did their successors have it over one another. Christ utterly forbade this to them, as Matthew 20 and Luke 22 directly declare to the matter in question. For when there was a dispute among them as to which of them should be greatest, Christ said to them: "The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors. But ye shall not be so." Christ could not have denied this more openly. Why then would anyone believe human tradition, whether of saints or of non-saints, rather than the most open word of Christ? For Christ speaks against such people in Mark 7, when he addressed directly the question in hand: "Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men. For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men." And a little further on: "Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition." This is what those do who teach the human Decretals, which say that power and dominion over temporal matters belong to the Roman bishop, not only ecclesiastical but also imperial and royal, thereby making God's commandment void, as has been shown in the fourteenth chapter and is clear from the present chapter, so that they may keep their tradition concerning temporal goods for their own advantage. But suppose the apostles had chosen Blessed Peter as their bishop, or as their chief, more excellent on account of his age and acquired holiness, as is held from a decree of Pope Anacletus contained in Isidore's collection, whose wording is: The other apostles, with the same (namely Peter), received honour and power in equal fellowship, and wished him to be their prince. Even so, it would not follow that his successors in the Roman see, or elsewhere if he was bishop elsewhere, hold this priority over the successors of the others, unless they were chosen for it by the successors of the rest. For some successors of the other apostles were of greater virtue than some successors of Peter; although, properly speaking, any bishop is indifferently the successor of any apostle as to office, though not as to place. Again, why would this apply more to his successors in the Roman see than to those in Antioch or Jerusalem or elsewhere, if he had been bishop in several places? Further, any bishop, as to intrinsic dignity, namely the inseparable dignity, is indifferently the successor of any apostle, and of the same merit or perfection as to that dignity or character, since all have the same one from one efficient cause or giver, numerically and immediately, namely Christ, and not from the one who laid on hands. Nor does it matter which of the apostles laid on hands. Hence 1 Cor. 3: "Therefore let no man glory in men, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, etc.... whether he baptized you, or otherwise laid on hands, it does not matter." Hence he adds, "and ye are Christ's," that is, you have the inward seal from Christ. The Gloss says: "And ye are Christ's," not of men, in creation or re-creation, which is effected through the sacrament (supply: "is effected").

units.la: Amplius propter manuum impositionem Romanus Episcopus non est aut dici debet singulariter beati Petri successor, quoniam Romanum Episcopum esse conuenit, cui non imposuit manus beatus Petrus, nec mediate nec immediate: nec rursum propter sedem siue loci determinationem, primum quidem, quia nullus Apostolorum lege diuina determinatus fuit omnino ad populum aliquem vel locum, nam Matthæi vltimo dictum est omnibus: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes. Amplius quoniam Beatus Petrus prius legitur Antiochiæ fuisse quam Romæ. Rursum quoniam si Roma fieret inhabitabilis, non propterea periret Petri successio. Adhuc quia neq; lege diuina, neq; scriptura, quanquam de necessitate salutis ad sui credulitatem inuitante, conuinci potest per Christum, aut Apostolorum aliquem vel ipsorum collegium fuisse statutum, episcopum alicuius determinatæ prouinciæ siue diocesis debere vocari vel esse Petri aut alterius apostoli singulariter successorem, cæterisque priorem, esto quantumcunque apostolos autoritate impares extitisse, sed ille vel illi magis sunt aliquo modo beati Petri & reliquorum apostolorum successores, qui vitæ & ipsorum sanctis moribus amplius conformantur. Tales enim, responderent beati apostoli, fore successores suos interrogati de his, instar Christi eorum magis, qui Matth. 12. respondens, dicenti sibi: Mater tua & fratres tui foris stant, quærentes te, ait: Qua est mater mea & fratres mei? Quicunque enim fecerit voluntatem patris mei qui in cœlis est, ipse meus frater, & soror, & mater est. Quis ergo episcoporum aut sacerdotum magis meretur Apostolorum dici successor? is certe, qui eos amplius moribus & operibus imitatur.
units.tr: Furthermore, because of the laying on of hands, the Roman bishop is not, and ought not to be called, the sole successor of the blessed Peter. For it would have to be the case that the Roman bishop was someone on whom blessed Peter had not laid his hands, neither mediately nor immediately. Nor is he so because of the seat or the designation of a place. The first reason is that no Apostle was by divine law assigned absolutely to any particular people or place, for at the end of Matthew it is said to all: Go therefore and teach all nations. Moreover, blessed Peter is read to have been at Antioch before he was at Rome. Again, if Rome were to become uninhabitable, Peter's succession would not thereby perish. Further, neither by divine law nor by Scripture, though Scripture invites us to believe it as necessary to salvation, can it be proved that Christ or any of the Apostles, or their college, ever ordained that the bishop of a particular province or diocese should be called, or should be, the sole successor of Peter or of any other apostle above the rest. Even if the Apostles were in authority no more than equal to one another, those men are in some measure the successors of blessed Peter and of the other apostles who conform more closely to their holy manner of life. For the blessed Apostles, when questioned about this, would answer that such are their successors, after the example of Christ, who, Matt. 12., answering the man who said to him: Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you, said: Who is my mother and who are my brothers? For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother. Which of the bishops or priests therefore deserves more to be called the successor of the Apostles? Surely he who imitates them more closely in morals and works.

units.la: Quod si dicatur, Episcopum aliquem eo fieri Beati Petri singulariter & principaliter successorem, quia per Romanum clerum, aut per ipsum cum reliquo populo ad episcopatum eligitur: & eo fieri Episcopum vniuersalis Ecclesiæ, quanquam specialius ciuitatem Romanam respiciat, quam diu extiterit ipsa. Dicendum quod, quamuis hoc dictum multiplices possit pati calumnias, vnico tamen modo sufficienter repelli potest, quoniam ex sacra scriptura conuinci non potest, sed oppositum magis, quemadmodum supra monstratum est, & immediate sequenti capitulo amplius ostenditur. Propter quod eadem vel consimili facilitate qua dicitur, negari potest. Vnde tamen & propter quid principalitas peruenerit, si debeatur Episcopo & Ecclesiæ Romanorum super cæteras, 22. huius seriose dicetur. Iam dictis autem audiri desuetis mirabilius est, quia desuetum amplius & inopinabile fortassis videbitur, si non falsum: Quod ex certo scripturæ testimonio conuinci potest, Romanos Episcopos magis esse successores quantum ad prouinciam & gentem, Apostoli Pauli quam Petri, præsertim in episcopali sede Romana: Rursumque quod iam dicto super admirabilius videbitur, quod per scripturam probari nequit, Romanos Episcopos successores esse singulares beati Petri, propter sedis siue prouinciæ determinationem, sed propter hoc potius eos, qui sederunt aut sedent in episcopali Antiochena sede, quam Romanos.
units.tr: But if it is said that some bishop becomes the sole and principal successor of blessed Peter because he is chosen to the episcopate by the Roman clergy, or by them together with the rest of the people, and that by this he becomes bishop of the universal Church, though he regards the Roman city more especially for as long as it exists, I answer as follows. Although this claim may suffer many calumnies, it can be sufficiently refuted in one way only, namely, that it cannot be proved from Holy Scripture, but rather the contrary, as has been shown above and is shown more fully in the next chapter. For this reason it can be denied with the same or like ease with which it is asserted. Yet how and on what ground primacy has come to the Roman bishop and Church over the rest, if it is due to them, will be discussed at length in chapter 22 of this work. Now, though these things are to be heard as unfamiliar, it is more remarkable that what I am about to say will perhaps seem even more unfamiliar and unexpected, if not false: that it can be proved from clear testimony of Scripture that the Roman bishops are more the successors of the Apostle Paul than of Peter, as regards the province and the people, especially in the Roman episcopal see. And again, what will seem even more wonderful after what has been said, is that it cannot be proved from Scripture that the Roman bishops are the sole successors of blessed Peter by reason of the determination of the see or province; rather, for this reason, those who have sat or sit in the Antiochene episcopal see are more so than the Romans.

units.la: Prioris autem nunc dictorum fides esse potest ex eo quod, quamuis beatus Paulus generaliter missus fuerit ad omnes nationes, quemadmodum apostolorum quilibet reliquorum (vnde Actum 9. Vas electionis est iste mihi, vt portet nomen meum coram gentibus & regibus & filiis Israel) singulariter tamen & principaliter fuit Apostolus gentium, quemadmodum Petrus Iudæorum, tam per reuelationem quam secundum Apostolorum inuicem ordinationem. Vnde ad Galatas secundo.
units.tr: The truth of what I have just said can be seen from the fact that, although blessed Paul was sent generally to all nations, as was each of the other apostles (whence Acts 9: This man is a chosen vessel to me, to bear my name before the Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel), nevertheless he was singularly and principally the Apostle of the Gentiles, just as Peter was of the Jews, both by revelation and by the mutual arrangement of the Apostles. Whence Galatians 2.

units.la: 30 Cum vidissent Iacobum, Petrus, & Ioannes, quod creditum est mihi Euangelium præputii, (id est gentium,) sicut Petro circumcisionis, id est Iudæorum; & intendit Apostolus vtrobique tam Petro quam sibi principaliter, quoniam & Petrus gentibus & Paulus Iudæis poterant prædicare, si causa vel necessitas extitisset, quamuis principalitas in gentibus per dispensationem esset Pauli & ad Iudæos esset beati Petri, sicut Glossa secundum August. exponit ibidem. Rursum Act. 22. dictum est Paulo in stupore mentis suæ per reuelationem: Vade, quoniam in nationes longe mittam te. Amplius Act. 28. & vltimo: Et sic venimus Romam. Et infra parum loquens Apostolus Iudæis in Roma, inquit: Notum ergo sit vobis, quoniam gentibus missum est hoc salutare Dei, & ipsi audient, manßit autem biennio toto in suo conductu, & suscipiebat omnes qui ingrediebantur ad eum prædicans regnum Dei. Rursum testatur hoc ipse magis specialiter ad Rom. 11. Vobis enim, inquit, dico gentibus, quam diu quidem ego sum apostolus gentium, ministerium meum honorificabo, si quomodo ad æmulandum provocem carnem meam, id est, licet quandoque etiam Iudæos exhortet ad hoc, principaliter tamen ad gentiles apostolus sum. Adhuc ad Galatas 2. Iacobus, & Cephas, & Ioannes, qui videbantur columnæ esse, dextras dederunt mihi & Barnabæ societatis, vt nos in gentes, (id est ad Gentiles,) ipsi autem in circumcisionem, id est ad Iudæos irent Euangelium prædicandum. Postremo vero legitur idem prima ad Timoth. 2. & 2. ad eundem primo, & series omisi propter abbreviationem.
units.tr: 30 When James, Cephas and John saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed to me, as to Peter the gospel of the circumcision, that is, of the Jews; and the Apostle intends in both cases that it was principally to Peter and to himself, since both Peter could preach to the Gentiles and Paul to the Jews, if cause or necessity had arisen, although primacy among the Gentiles was by the dispensation of Paul, and among the Jews was blessed Peter's, as the Gloss, following Augustine, explains there. Again, Acts 22: Paul was told in a revelation while he was in a trance: Go, for I will send you far away to the nations. Further, Acts 28, at the end: And so we came to Rome. And a little further on, the Apostle, speaking to the Jews in Rome, says: Be it known therefore to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will hear it. He remained two whole years in his own hired lodging, and received all who came in to him, preaching the kingdom of God. Again, he bears witness to this more particularly in Romans 11: For I say to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will magnify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy, that is, although he sometimes exhorts the Jews to this also, nevertheless he is an apostle principally to the Gentiles. Further, Galatians 2: James, and Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision, that is, to the Jews, to preach the gospel. Lastly, the same is read in 1 Timothy 2 and 2 Timothy 1, and I have omitted the sequence for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Cum igitur per scripturam constet euidenter, Paulum Romæ fuisse biennio, & ibidem omnes suscepisse Gentiles conuerti volentes, idemque prædicasse, constat ipsum fuisse Romanum episcopum specialiter, eo quod ibidem officium pastoris exercuit, autoritatem huius habens a Christo, & reuelatione mandatum, & apostolorum aliorum electione consensum. De beato vero Petro 50 in quo secundum propositorum apparebit, dico per scripturam sacram conuinci non posse ipsum fuisse Romanum episcopum, & quod amplius est, ipsum vnquam Romæ fuisse. Admirandissimum nanque videtur, si secundum quandam vulgatam ecclesiasticam legendam sanctorum beatus Petrus præuenerit Romam beatum Paulum, ibidem prædicans verbum Dei, & postmodum captus, deinde quod beatus Paulus in suo aduentu Romam, vna cum beato Petro tot conflictus habuerint cum Simone Mago, & simul tantum pro fide certarunt aduersus Imperatores & ipsorum ministros: demumque secundum eandem historiam, quod ambo simul capite priuati, propter Christi confessionem dormierunt in domino, & sic Romanam Christo consecrauerunt ecclesiam. Admirandissimum, inquam, dico, quod beatus Lucas, qui actum apostolorum scripsit, & Paulus Apostolus de beato Petro nullam prorsus mentionem fecerunt. Amplius quod beatus Petrus Romam non 60 præuenerit eos, credere facit probabiliter valde, quod Actum vltimo scribitur. Dum enim Paulus in suo aduentu primo alloqueretur Iudæos inter cætera, sui aduentus Romam volens assignare causam, inquit: Contradicentibus autem Iudæis coactus sum appellare Cæsarem. At illi dixerunt ad eum: Nos neque litteras accepimus de te a Iudæa, neque veniens aliquis fratrum nuncians aut locutus est quid de te malum. Rogamus autem a te audire quæ sentis, nam de secta hac notum est nobis, quia vbique ei contradicitur. Dicat ergo mihi veritatis inquisitor, non quærens contendere solum si probabile sit alicui beatum Petrum Romam prævenisse Paulum & nihil nunciasse de Christi fide, quam Iudæi loquentes ad Paulum sectam vocabant? Amplius Paulus in reprehendendo ipsos de incredulitate, si nouisset Cephaм ibidem fuisse & prædicasse, quomodo non dixisset aut ipsum huius testem induxisset negotii, qui resurrectionis Christi testis extiterat? vt apparet Actuum tertio. Et rursum, de quo iam diximus quis opinabitur, quod biennio existens ibidem Paulus nunquam conuersationem collationem aut contubernium habuerit cum beato Petro? Et si habuisset, quod de ipso nullam penitus mentionem fecisset, qui Actuum scripsit historiam? In aliis enim locis minus famosis, dum Paulus Petrum inuenit, mentionem de ipso fecit, & cum eo conuersatus est, vt in Corintho. prima ad Corin. tertio, & in Antiochia, vt ad Galatas secundo, & sic de reliquis plerisque locis: In Roma vero inuentum, quomodo non nominasset, quæ omnium vrbium famosissima erat, & in qua secundum iam dictam historiam beatus Petrus præerat tanquam episcopus? Sunt enim hæc incredibilia quasi, propter quod historia illa siue legenda non videtur in hac parte probabiliter posse teneri, & cum apocryphis computari debere. Sed per scripturam sacram indubitanter tenendum, beatum Paulum fuisse Romanum Episcopum: & si quis alter cum ipso Romæ fuerit, tamen Paulum singulariter & principaliter propter causas prædictas fuisse Romanum Episcopum, beatum vero Petrum Antiochiæ, vt apparet ad Galatas secundo. Romæ vero non contradico, sed verisimiliter teneo ipsum in hoc non prævenisse Paulum, sed potius econuerso. Quod autem omnium maxime attendendum propter propositum principale, est: quoniam & si aliquæ sint congruentiæ, propter quas appareant quomodocunque singulariter vocati successores Beati Petri, successoribus aliorum reuerentiores, & præcipue in episcopali sede Romana: nulla tamen, vt eisdem subiecti credantur secundum aliquam potestatem iam dictam aliorum Apostolorum successores, sacræ scripturæ necessitas vocat. Esto adhuc Apostolos auctoritate impares extitisse. Non habuit ergo beatus Petrus aut Apostolus alter virtute verborum scripturæ super alios potestatem instituendi aut deponendi, neque quantum ad sacerdotalem dignitatem quam essentialem diximus, neque ad eorum missionem seu determinationem ad locum aut populum, neque ad scripturæ seu fidei catholicæ interpretationem, neque quantum ad coactiuam cuiusquam in hoc seculo iurisdictionem. Unde per necessitatem sequi videtur, quod nec virtute verborum scripturæ, successor aliquis ipsorum alicuius singulariter quomodocunque vocatus, in successores reliquorum aliquam supradictarum habeat potestatem. Potest autem hoc patenter astrui auctoritate Hieronymi, quam ex epistola ipsius ad Euandrum circa finem quarta capituli præcedentis induximus.
units.tr: Since therefore it is evident from Scripture that Paul was at Rome for two years, and there received all who wished to be converted from the Gentiles, and preached the same, it follows that he was the Roman bishop in a special sense, because he there exercised the office of pastor, having authority from Christ, a mandate by revelation, and the consent of the election of the other apostles. But concerning blessed Peter, in whom, as will appear according to my purpose, I say it cannot be proved from holy Scripture that he was the Roman bishop, and, what is more, that he was ever at Rome at all. For it seems most astonishing, if according to a certain common ecclesiastical legend of the saints blessed Peter came to Rome before blessed Paul, preaching the word of God there, and was afterwards taken; then that blessed Paul, on his coming to Rome, together with blessed Peter, had so many conflicts with Simon Magus, and that they struggled together so much for the faith against the emperors and their ministers; and finally, according to the same story, that both were deprived of their heads together for the confession of Christ, fell asleep in the Lord, and so consecrated the Roman Church to Christ. It is astonishing, I say, that blessed Luke, who wrote the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apostle Paul, made absolutely no mention of blessed Peter. Furthermore, the fact that blessed Peter did not come to Rome before them makes it very probable, as is written in the last chapter of Acts. For when Paul, on his first arrival, addressed the Jews, among other things, wishing to give the reason for his coming to Rome, he said: But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar. They said to him: We have received no letters from Judea concerning you, nor has any of the brethren come and reported or said anything evil of you. But we ask to hear from you what you think, for concerning this sect it is known to us that it is spoken against everywhere. Let the inquirer into truth tell me this, not merely seeking to dispute whether it is plausible that blessed Peter came to Rome before Paul and announced nothing of the faith of Christ, which the Jews speaking to Paul called sect. Furthermore, if Paul knew that Cephas had been there and preached, when reproaching them for unbelief, why would he not have said so, or brought forward as witness of the matter the one who had been a witness of Christ's resurrection, as appears in Acts 3? And again, who will suppose that Paul, being there for two years, never had conversation, conference or fellowship with blessed Peter? And if he had, why would he, who wrote the history of the Acts, have made no mention of him at all? For in other places, less famous, when Paul found Peter, he did mention him and associated with him, as at Corinth in 1 Corinthians 3, and at Antioch, as in Galatians 2, and so in most other places. But at Rome, if he had found him there, how would he not have named him, since Rome was the most famous of all cities, and since, according to the history just mentioned, blessed Peter presided there as bishop? These things are almost incredible, and therefore that story or legend does not seem able to be held as probable on this point, and ought to be reckoned among the apocryphal writings. But by holy Scripture it must be held beyond doubt that blessed Paul was the Roman bishop; and even if someone else was at Rome with him, yet Paul was the Roman bishop singularly and principally, for the reasons already given, while blessed Peter was at Antioch, as appears in Galatians 2. As for Rome, I do not contradict it, but I think it probable that he did not come there before Paul, but rather the reverse. What must be most of all considered for the principal purpose is this: although there may be some fitness by which, in whatever way, those called the sole successors of blessed Peter appear more reverend than the successors of others, especially in the Roman episcopal see, nevertheless no necessity of Scripture calls them to be believed subject to the others, in virtue of any power just mentioned, as successors of the other Apostles, even granting that the Apostles were no more than equal in authority. Therefore blessed Peter, or any other apostle, did not have, by the force of the words of Scripture, a power over the others of instituting or deposing, neither as regards the sacerdotal dignity, which we have called essential, nor as regards their mission or assignment to a place or people, nor as regards the interpretation of Scripture or of the Catholic faith, nor as regards any coercive jurisdiction in this world. Hence it seems to follow of necessity that neither by the force of the words of Scripture does any successor of theirs, however singularly called, have any of the aforesaid powers over the successors of the rest. This can be clearly established by the authority of Jerome, which we cited from his letter to Evangelus near the end of chapter 4 above.

units.la: CAP. XVII. De autoritate instituendi Episcopos & alios curatos, ac reliquos Ecclesiæ ministros quantum ad vtranque dignitatem siue officium separabilem siue inseparabilem.
units.tr: CAP. XVII. On the authority to institute bishops and other pastors, and the rest of the Church's ministers, as regards both the separable and the inseparable dignity or office.

units.la: DE primæ quidem igitur sacerdotalis autoritatis, quam essentialem diximus, factiua causa iam dictum est nobis. De reliqua vero, qua scilicet certis sacerdotibus aut populo vel vtrisque in certa prouincia seu loco præferuntur ipsorum aliqui, amplius unde conueniat eisdem temporalia quædam, iam vocata ecclesiastica beneficia, dispensare: unde etiam rursum ad ipsos seu ipsorum quosdam coactiuæ iurisdictiones peruenerint, ad quem etiam, aut quos, & qualiter conuenientius sacræ scripturæ dubios sensus, in his præcipue quæ ad salutis necessitatem attinent, determinare pertineat, reliquum nobis est diffinire. Sufficienter enim manifestatis his, apparebit quod ab huius operis initio propositum manifestare fuerat.
units.tr: Concerning the first, sacerdotal authority, which we have called essential, we have already said what its efficient cause is. Concerning the remaining authority, by which certain of the priests, or the people, or both, set some of their number over a particular province or place, and by which these men are then able to dispense certain temporal goods, now called ecclesiastical benefices, and by which some of them come to hold coercive jurisdiction, it remains for us to define to whom, and by whom, and in what manner it more fittingly belongs to determine the doubtful senses of Holy Scripture, especially in those matters that pertain to the necessity of salvation. For once these points are sufficiently made clear, it will be apparent what we promised at the beginning of this work to show.

units.la: Ante tamen quam hic proposita singulariter prosequamur, expedit hartare primum institutionis & determinationis Episcoporum seu presbyterorum modum circa statum & initium ecclesiæ primitiuæ, unde cætera postmodum deriuata sunt. Horum autem omnium principium, accipiendum est à Christo, qui caput est & petra, super quam fundata est Ecclesia catholica, secundum quod dicit Apostolus ad Ephesios quarto & quinto: & prima ad Corinthios decimo. Quod etiam dicit Glossa quædam super illud Matthæi decimo sexto: Super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Hoc, inquam, caput Ecclesiæ petra & fundamentum, Christus scilicet, Apostolis contulit sacerdotium & autoritatem episcopalem super omnes gentes & populos cuilibet seorsum neminem ad certum locum seu populum determinando sic, quin etiam sibi liceret vbilibet prædicare, quamuis aliquai mag s d-putati fuerint in gentes, alii vero in circumcisionem ipsorum inuicem, aut spiritus Sanctu ordinatione. Quod etiam videtur sentire Glossa super illud secundæ ad Galatas: Et cum cognouissent gratiam quæ data est mihi, intergentes. Inquit enim Glossa: Christus enim dedit Paulo vt ministraret gentibus, qui etiam Petro dederat vt ministraret Iudæis. Ita tamen dispensatio distributa est illa, vt & Petrus gentibus prædicaret, si causa fuisset, & Paulus Iudæis. Quod similiter videtur Apostolus intellexisse ad Romanos vndecimo, cum dixit: Ministerium meum honorificabo, si quo modo ad æmulandum prouocem carnem meam, (id est, Iudeos,) ex quibus natus erat secundum carnem, vt Glossa dicit ibidem. Ex quibus verbis sentiendum videtur, quod ea potestate seu characterc, qua quis sacerdos instituitur, indifferenter habet potestatem vbique ministrandi, & super omnem populum, quamuis diuina reuelatione, vel humana quadam ordinatione quidam ad certum locum aut populum magis determinentur, quam ad reliquum præcipue temporibus his. Hæc autem videtur scripturæ ac rationi consona. Nam generalem vnicuique Apostolorum tradens Christus administrationem, Matthæi vigesimo octauo dixit Apostolis indifferenter: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, neminem determinando ad locum aut populum. Quandoque vero ad speciale gentem aut populum diuina reuelatione determinati fuisse videntur, cum dicat Apostolus de se Actuum 22. Factum est autem reuertenti mihi in Hierusalem, & oranti in templo fieri me in stupore mentis, & videre illum, (Christum scilicet,) dicentem mihi: Festina & exi velociter ex Hierusalem, quoniam non recipient testimonium tuum de me. Et parum infra subiungitur sibi dictum à Christo: Vade, quoniam in nationes longe mittam te. Ecce quod per reuelationem accepit quandoque Paulus aliquam loci & populi determinationem, sic etiam eandem suscepit determinationem ipse cum aliis Apostolis, humana quadam ordinatione.
units.tr: Before we take up the points proposed here one by one, it is useful first to treat the manner in which bishops or elders were instituted and determined, with respect to the state and beginning of the primitive Church, from which the rest was afterwards derived. The principle of all these things must be taken from Christ, who is the head and the rock upon which the catholic Church is founded, as the Apostle says to the Ephesians, chapters four and five, and in the first to the Corinthians, chapter ten. A certain Gloss also says this on the text of Matthew 16: Upon this rock I will build my Church. This head of the Church, the rock and foundation, namely Christ, I say, conferred on the Apostles the priesthood and episcopal authority over all nations and peoples, without assigning any one of them separately to a fixed place or people, so that each was also free to preach anywhere, although some were appointed more to the Gentiles and others to the circumcision, by the ordering of the Holy Spirit. The Gloss on the text of 2 Corinthians appears to hold the same view: And when they had known the grace that was given to me, they gave me the right hand of fellowship. For the Gloss says: Christ gave Paul the task of ministering to the Gentiles, and had given Peter the task of ministering to the Jews. Yet that distribution was so arranged that Peter should also preach to the Gentiles if there were cause, and Paul to the Jews. The Apostle seems to have understood this in the same way in Romans 11, when he said: I will magnify my ministry, if by any means I may provoke to emulation my flesh (that is, the Jews), among whom I was born according to the flesh, as the Gloss says there. From these words it seems we should conclude that by the power or character through which a man is instituted a priest, he has authority to minister everywhere indifferently and over every people, although by divine revelation or some human ordinance certain men are more specifically assigned to a particular place or people than to the rest, especially in these times. This view also seems consonant with Scripture and reason. For when Christ gave each of the Apostles a general commission, he said to them all alike in Matthew 28: Go therefore and teach all nations, assigning no one to a place or people. Yet at times they seem to have been designated to a special nation or people by divine revelation, as the Apostle says of himself in Acts 22: And it came to pass, that when I had returned to Jerusalem, and while I was praying in the temple, I was in a trance, and saw him (namely Christ) saying to me: Make haste, and get quickly out of Jerusalem, for they will not receive your testimony concerning me. And a little further on it is added that Christ said to him: Go, for I will send you far away to the nations. Here we see that Paul at times received by revelation a designation of place and people; and in the same way he also received such a designation by human ordinance, together with the other Apostles.

units.la: Unde ad Galatas secundo dixit: Dexteras dederunt mihi & Barnabæ societatis, Iacobus, Cephas, atque Ioannes, ut nos in gentes, ipsi autem in circumcisionem. Ecce determinationem Apostolorum ad certum populum & prouincias, humana ordinatione factam immediate. Constat autem, quod ex tali determinatione sine facta immediata Dei reuelatione, siue ipsorum inuicem ordinatione, ipsos non recepisse perfectionem per spiritum Sanctum, quam prius non habuissent. Apparet hoc siquidem ratione, quoniam esto, Episcopum aut alium curatum quemlibet determinatum ad aliquam prouinciam aut populum, extra prouinciam sibi commissam exiuisse, sicut frequentius quam oporteat, euenire videmus, obuiet autem casu aliquo vel à proposito etiam alicui non fideli neque baptizato, baptizari tamen petenti per se vel alium, si quidem hunc baptizet, seruata forma sacramenti, constat hunc vere baptizatum esse, quamuis forte moraliter peccet sic baptizans in non sibi subiecta seu commissa prouincia. Non ergo determinatus est quisquam ex episcopali seu sacerdotali potestate, quam essentialem diximus, ad locum aut populum, sed indifferenter respicit omnes. Determinata fuerunt tamen huiusmodi quandoque diuina reuelatione, vt in Ecclesia primitiua, frequentius tamen humana ordinatione præcipue modernis temporibus. Et hoc ad scandalum euitandum inter Episcopos & sacerdotes inuicem, & propter alias euidentes vtilitates, quas in sequentibus assignabo.
units.tr: Hence he said in Galatians 2: James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision. Here is a designation of the Apostles to a particular people and provinces, made directly by human ordinance. It is certain, however, that without such a designation made by an immediate revelation of God, or by their own mutual ordering, they did not receive from the Holy Spirit a perfection which they had not had before. This is clear by reason. For even if we see that a bishop or any other pastor assigned to a particular province or people has, more often than is proper, gone outside the province committed to him, and if by some chance, or even by design, he meets some unbeliever who is not baptized but asks to be baptized, either by himself or by another, and if he baptizes him, keeping the form of the sacrament, it is certain that the man has truly been baptized, even though the one who baptized him may perhaps sin morally by baptizing in a province not subject to him or not committed to him. No one, therefore, is determined by episcopal or sacerdotal power, which we have called essential, to a place or people; it regards all men indifferently. Nevertheless, such determinations have sometimes been made by divine revelation, as in the primitive Church, but more often by human ordinance, especially in modern times. This is done to avoid scandal between bishops and priests, and for other obvious advantages, which I shall set out in what follows.

units.la: His itaque sic præmissis ad proposita in principio huius capituli singulariter accedentes, ostendemus primum determinatæ institutionis Apostolorum ad certos populos atque prouincias causam factiuam conuenientiorem immediatam fuisse Christi reuelationem, aut ipsorum inuicem concordem ordinationem: Deinde vero quod suorum successorum primorum ante populi conuersionem, determinatæ institutionis causa factiua immediata fuit expressa voluntas omnium Apostolorum aut plurium, si omnes aut plures præsentes fuerunt simul in loco seu prouincia, in qua sacerdotem aut Episcopum oportebat statuere, vel ipsorum Apostolorum vnicus secundum loci & populi ac temporis dispositionem: Demum vero quod post mortem Apostolorum aut in ipsorum absentia, episcoporum & aliorum Ecclesiæ seu spiritualium ministrorum institutio secundaria modorum conuenientissimo possibilium humanæ conuersationi, facta est per vniuersitatem fidelium in loco siue prouincia, super quam iam dicti ministri debent institui, quam per aliquod singulare collegium aliud vel personam. Sicque postmodum ostendentur reliqua consequenter. Horum ergo primum apparere potest, quod videlicet non alia conuenientior huius determinationis causa potest assignari quam diuina reuelatio, aut ipsorum conueniens deliberatio, quoniam in harum neutra error aut malitia interuenisse videtur. De diuina siquidem reuelatione nemini dubium, de Apostolorum autem electione videtur probabile, atque credendum, quoniam spiritu Sancto inspirati erant, vt ex Ioannis vigesimo pridem induximus.
units.tr: Having laid down these points, we now come to the matters proposed at the beginning of this chapter one by one, and we shall show, first, that the immediate efficient cause of the Apostles' particular designation to certain peoples and provinces was most fittingly Christ's revelation, or their own harmonious ordering among themselves. Second, that the immediate efficient cause of the particular institution of their first successors, before the conversion of the people, was the express will of all the Apostles or of several of them, if all or several were present together in the place or province where a priest or bishop had to be set up, or of a single one of the Apostles themselves, according to the disposition of place, people and time. Finally, that after the death of the Apostles, or in their absence, the secondary institution of bishops and other ministers of the Church or of spiritual office, made in the most fitting way possible for human life, was carried out by the whole body of the faithful in the place or province over which these ministers were to be instituted, and not by some separate college or other person. In this way the remaining points will be shown in order. Of these, the first can be seen to be this: that no more fitting efficient cause of this determination can be assigned than divine revelation, or their own fitting deliberation, since neither error nor malice seems to have intervened in either. For concerning divine revelation there is no doubt; and concerning the election of the Apostles it seems probable and to be believed, since they were inspired by the Holy Spirit, as we have already shown from John 20.

units.la: Deinde dico quod suorum successorum primorum, maxime ante populorum conuersionem, institutionis secundariæ seu determinationis causa factiua immediata fuerunt & esse debuerunt omnes aut plures Apostolorum vel ipsorum vnicus secundum modum prædictum, vt si simul omnes, aut ipsorum plures aut vnicus tantum reperti fuerint ibidem. Hoc autem conuincitur primum ex scriptura, nam ipsos sic egisse legimus Actuum sexto in diaconorum institutione, etiam quantum ad primam institutionem, quam essentialem iam diximus, vnde: Hos statuerunt ante conspectum Apostolorum, & orantes, (Apostoli scil.) imposuerunt eis manus. Non ergo adduxerunt eos ad Petrum solum, sed ante conspectum Apostolorum. Nec solus Petrus sibi assumpsit singulariter auctoritatem imponendi eis manus, sed Apostoli imposuerunt eis manus, est autem & hoc rationi consonum.
units.tr: Next I say that the immediate efficient cause of the secondary institution or determination of their first successors, especially before the conversion of the peoples, was, and ought to have been, all or several of the Apostles, or a single one of them according to the manner described above, so that whether all, or several, or only one was present there. This is proved first from Scripture. For we read that they acted in this way in Acts 6, in the institution of deacons, even as regards the first institution, which we have already called essential: Whom they set before the Apostles, and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them. They did not therefore bring them to Peter alone, but before the Apostles. Nor did Peter alone take to himself the authority to lay hands on them; rather the Apostles laid hands on them. This also agrees with reason.

units.la: Verisimile enim est omnes aut plures Apostolorum simul certius deliberasse, ac minus errasse circa personam promouendam siue ad sacerdotium siue ad alium sacrum ordinem, quolibet ipsorum seorsum accepto, quemadmodum supra induximus cap. precedente, ipsos propter hoc simul conuenisse cum aliis senioribus ad diffiniendum dubium circa legem euangelicam in facto circumcisionis. Rursum ex hoc collebatur scandali & contentionis materia, quæ verisimiliter inter eos orta fuisset, si quis eorum in aliorum præsentia potestatem aut prioritatem præter reliquos assumere voluisset, quam Christo viuente inter ipsos ortam ex hoc Christus diffiniuit, ipsorum exprimens æqualitatem, vt ex Matth. 22. & Luca 22. induximus, per Apostolum quoq; ac sanctorum expositiones, id amplius manifestauimus cap. precedente. Amplius rationabilius licet agere fuit, vt ex hoc omnibus suis successoribus præsumptionem huius singularitatis auferens, & similiter faciendi exemplum præberent, vt ex Glossa super Act. 6. monstrabitur infra parte nona.
units.tr: For it is likely that all or several of the Apostles together deliberated more securely, and erred less, about the person to be promoted, whether to the priesthood or to another sacred order, than any one of them alone would have done. As we brought out above in the preceding chapter, they came together for this purpose with the other elders to settle a doubt about the gospel law in the matter of circumcision. Again, from this there would have arisen a matter of scandal and contention, which would likely have arisen among them if any one of them had wished, in the presence of the others, to assume power or precedence above the rest. Christ himself, while he lived, settled such a dispute that had arisen among them, expressing their equality, as we have shown from Matthew 22 and Luke 22; and we have further made this plain from the Apostle and the expositions of the saints, in the preceding chapter. Moreover, it was more reasonable for them to act in this way, so that by it they would take from all their successors the presumption of this singular authority and would give them an example of acting likewise, as will be shown below in the ninth part from the gloss on Acts 6.

units.la: Quod si tamen non simul omnes aut plures fuissent, vbi Episcopum multitudini alicui fidelium lium custodiendæ ac seruandæ in fide oportebat præficere? Dicendum sane hoc ipsorum vnicum licite facere potuisse, maxime vbi multitudo fidelium pauca erat, rudis & imperita discernere conuenientiorem personam ad episcopatus officium, & præcipue vbi sufficientium personarum ad hoc officium quasi nulla pluralitas erat, quemadmodum Paulo & suis successoribus primis saepe contigit propter causas prædictas, vt ex Actibus Apostolorum & suis epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum satis apparet. Quod autem per ipsorum vnicum talis institutio fieri potuerit & debuerit licite ostendi potest, quoniam ex hoc eligebatur melior & conuenientior pastor. Aut enim præficere se aliis in ministerio Euangelii, licitum erat vnicuique pro voto, aut hoc fieri debebat per electionem subiectæ multitudinis, aut per Apostolorum aliquem ibi præsentem. Ex primo modo scandalum & error contingere potuisset, scandalum quidem, si duo vel plures hanc sibi auctoritatem assumere voluissent. Error quidem seu pastoris insufficientia similiter: quoniam vt plurimum stulti aut ambitiosi præsidatum appetunt & assumere tentant amplius studiosis & sapientib. viris. Ex secundo vero modo, videl. ex illius multitudinis electione constituisse prælatum, error & insufficientia verisimiliter contigisset, propter multitudinis illius imbecillitatem in quanto & quali, rudes enim erant à principio in pluribus prouinciis, præsertim extra Iudæam, & facile seducibiles, vt ex tota epistola ad Galatas & pluribus aliis satis apparet. Vnde Apostolus primæ ad Corinthios tertio: Et ego fratres non potui vobiscum loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus, tanquam parvulis in Christo lac potum dedi, nondum enim poteratis, sed nec nunc quidem potestis, adhuc enim carnales estis. Tutius ergo & sanius fuit hanc institutionem fieri electione seu determinatione alicuius Apostolorum, cuius vita & sapientia præponderans & amplior erat (propter habitum sancti Spiritus) ea quæ simul omnium in tali multitudine, quamuis non sit negandum, expediens fuisse Apostolum consuluisse multitudinem de moribus præferendi.
units.tr: But if all or several had not been together, where would it have been necessary to set a bishop over some multitude of the faithful, to guard and keep them in the faith? It must certainly be said that one of them alone could have done this lawfully, especially where the multitude of the faithful was small, rude and unskilled in discerning the more suitable person for the office of bishop, and above all where there was, as it were, no plurality of persons sufficient for this office. This often happened to Paul and his first successors, for the reasons stated, as is sufficiently clear from the Acts of the Apostles and his epistles to Timothy and Titus. That such an appointment could lawfully and properly be made by one of them can be shown, since by this means a better and more suitable minister was chosen. For either a man might set himself over others in the ministry of the Gospel at his own pleasure, or this had to be done by the election of the multitude subject to him, or by some one of the Apostles present there. From the first way, scandal and error could have arisen: scandal indeed if two or more wished to assume this authority to themselves; error too, or insufficiency of the minister, in the same way, since for the most part fools or the ambitious seek and attempt to assume the leadership, rather than the more studious and wise men. From the second way, namely by the multitude of that people electing a prelate, error and insufficiency would likely have occurred, because of the weakness of that multitude in quantity and quality, for they were rude at the beginning in many provinces, especially outside Judea, and easily led astray, as is sufficiently clear from the whole Epistle to the Galatians and many others. Hence the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 3: "And I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal, as to babes in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, nor are you even now able, for you are still carnal." It was therefore safer and more wholesome that this appointment be made by the choice or decision of one of the Apostles, whose life and wisdom outweighed and exceeded those of all together in such a multitude (by reason of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit), although it cannot be denied that it was expedient for the Apostle to consult the multitude about the morals of the man to be preferred.

units.la: His consequenter ostendere volo, quod post tempus Apostolorum & priorum patrum, sibi quasi prope succedentium in officio, & præcipue communitatibus fidelium iam perfectis huius institutionis seu determinationis præsidis siue maioris, quem vocant Episcopum, siue minoris, quos curatos sacerdotes appellant, simul & reliquorum minorum, causa factiua immediata sit & esse debeat vniuersa eius loci fidelium multitudo per suam electionem seu voluntatem expressam, aut ille vel illi, cui vel quibus iam dicta multitudo harum institutionum auctoritatem concesserit. Et quod eiusdem auctoritatis sit, vnumquemque iam dictum officialem ab huiusmodi officiis licite amouere siue priuare, ac ad illius exercitium compellere, si expediens videatur. Veruntamen oportet attendere, quod quamuis in potestate cuiuslibet sacerdotis sic sit suum exhibere ministerium, vt alterum quemlibet fidelem volentem, promouere possit ad sacerdotium, ipso ministrante quasi præparante, Deo autem simpliciter & immediate sacerdotalem potestatem seu characterem imprimente. Dico tamen id sibi pro voto non licere conferre cuiilibet, neque diuina neque humana lege in communitatibus fidelium iam perfectis, vt diximus, quinimo criminoso aut aliter insufficienti cooperans peccat plectibiliter contra legem diuinam & humanam. Quod autem contra legem diuinam plectibiliter peccet, apparet per Apostolum primæ ad Timotheum tertio, & ad Titum primo: Quoniam Episcopum oportet esse sine crimine esse, cum reliquis sufficientiis ibidem enumeratis, idemque aut proportionale de diaconis opinandum, vnde ad Timotheum vbi supra: Diaconues similiter pudicos, &c. Quod autem contra humanam legem delinquat plectibiliter sic insufficientem promouens ad ecclesiasticum ordinem, apparet ex his quæ ostensa sunt octauo huius. Committit enim aliquid transiens in alterius nocumentum pro statu præsentis & etiam futuri seculi simul, quod sibi probari potest in esse, id etiam ipso negante, promouendo scilicet ad publicum officium talem, qui aliorum vtriusque sexus, fœminini maxime, vitam & mores corrumpere potest, aut quantum expedit & necesse est pro statu tam præsentis quam futuri seculi, mores hominum formare nequit, qualis est peruersus vel aliter insufficiens diaconus aut sacerdos.
units.tr: Following on from this, I wish to show that after the time of the Apostles and the first Fathers, who succeeded them, as it were, in the office, and especially once the communities of the faithful were already established, the immediate efficient cause of this institution or determination of the leader or greater one, whom they call the Bishop, or of the lesser one, whom they call the parish priests, and likewise of the other lesser ministers, is and ought to be the whole multitude of the faithful of that place, by its election or expressed will, or he or those to whom the said multitude has granted the authority of these appointments. And it belongs to the same authority to remove or deprive lawfully any such officer from these offices, and to compel him to exercise them, if this seems expedient. Yet we must observe that although it lies within the power of any priest so to offer his ministry that he can promote any other faithful man who wishes it to the priesthood, he ministering as it were preparing, while God simply and immediately imprints the priestly power or character, I say nevertheless that it is not lawful for him to confer this at his own pleasure on anyone, neither by divine nor by human law, in communities of the faithful already established, as we have said; rather, if he cooperates with a criminal or otherwise insufficient person, he sins punishably against both divine and human law. That he sins punishably against divine law appears from the Apostle in 1 Timothy 3 and in Titus 1: "For a bishop must be without crime," together with the other qualifications listed there; and the same, or something proportionate, must be thought of deacons, whence in 1 Timothy, loc. cit.: "Deacons likewise must be chaste, etc." That he who promotes an insufficient man to the ecclesiastical order offends punishably against human law appears from what was shown in the eighth part of this work. For he commits an offence, passing into the harm of another, both for the state of the present and also of the future age at once, which can be proved in fact, even if he himself denies it, namely by promoting to a public office a man who can corrupt the life and morals of others, especially of women, or who cannot form the morals of men as far as is fitting and necessary for the state of both the present and the future age; such is a perverse or otherwise insufficient deacon or priest.

units.la: Ex his amplius per necessitatem inferre volo, quod in communitatibus fidelium iam persectis ad legislatorem humanum solummodo seu fidelium multitudinem eius loci, super quam intendere debet promouendus minister, pertineat eligere, determinate, ac præsentare personas promouendas ad ecclesiasticos ordines. Et quod nemini sacerdoti vel Episcopo singulariter, neque ipsorum soli collegio cuiquam cooperari liceat ad huiusmodi suscipiendos ordines absque legislatoris humani vel ipsius auctoritate principantis licentia. Hoc autem primum ex scriptura sacra demonstrabo, demum vero ratione probabili confirmabo, auctoritate siquidem scripturæ hoc apparet ex Act. sexto. Indigentes enim sancti Apostoli diaconis pro ministerio ipsorum & populi, requisiuerunt fidelium multitudinem tanquam eam, cuius erat personas huiusmodi eligere, ac etiam determinate, vnde vbi supra: Conuocantes autem duodecim multitudinem discipulorum, (id est fidelium, qui tunc discipuli vocabantur omnes; vt habetur in Glossa,) dixerunt; Non est aequum nos derelinquere verbum Dei, & ministrare mensis. Considerate ergo fratres, viros ex vobis boni testimonii septem plenos spiritu Sancto & sapientia, quos constituamus super hoc opus. Nos vero orationi & ministerio verbi instantes erimus. Et placuit sermo coram omni multitudine. Et elegerunt Stephanum virum plenum fidei & spiritu Sancto, & Philippum, reliquosque similiter. Quod si præsentibus apostolis talis electio commissa fuit multitudini; minus perfecta, vt certius eligerentur magis apti, quoniam tota multitudo aliquid scire potest, præcipue de moribus & vita vnius hominis, quod vnus multum doctus ignorat persæpe, quanto magis electio sacerdotum, qui amplioris necessitatis sunt in virtute ac sapientia diaconis & absentibus talibus prælatis, quæ es fuerunt Apostoli in communitate fidelium perfecta, debet electio hæc vniuersitati commit’ vt de promouendo amplius & certius testimonium habeatur: Conuocantes ergo duodecim, non sol. Petrus, vbi Glossa, de communi consensu. Multitudinem discipulorum, vbi Gloss. Consensum querunt multitudinis, quod in exemplum debet assumi. Hos statuerunt, &c. vbi Rabanus; Hic ordo seruandus est in ordinandis. Eligat populus, ordinet Episcopus, & hoc est, quod etiam dicit Apostolus aperte primæ ad Timotheum tertio: Oportet autem illum, (id est presbyterum) testimonium habere bonum ab his qui foris sunt, id est extra Ecclesiam, vnde Glossa: Non solum à fidelibus, sed etiam ab infidelibus. Vbi etiam de diaconibus parum infra dicitur: Et hi autem probentur primum & sic ministrent. Nunc autem ratione probabili, si necessarium probabile liceat dicere, ostendere volo, promouendi cuiuslibet ad sacrum ordinem, electionem, atque approbationem pertinere ad iudicium tertiæ significationis, sententiam scilicet humani legislatoris in communitatibus fidelium iam perfectis: & cum hoc simul secundariam eius institutionem, qua scilicet fideli populo alicui & incerto loco præficitur Episcopus aut curatus, sicque in reliquis minoribus ecclesiasticis officiis, ab ea quoque remotionem seu priuationem, ad exercitium quoque secundum eam ecclesiasticos si oporteat arcere ministros. Deinde vero monstrabitur ad quem vel quos ecclesiastica temporalia, vocata beneficia, distribuere pertineat. Primum quidem conuinci potest eisdem aut consimilibus demonstrationibus qualibus 12.13. & 15. prima ad vniuersitatem ciuium legumlationem & principantium institutionem ostendimus pertinere, sola demonstratione mutata extremitate minori, vt videlicet electio seu personæ ad ordinem sacrum promouendæ approbatio, ipsiusque institutio seu determinatio ad certæ plebis atque prouinciæ præsidatum, eiusque priuatio sine remotio ab eisdem propter delictum vel rationabilem alteram causam assumantur in demonstrationibus pro termino legis, aut principantis institutione. Est autem & in his tanto euidentior necessitas talium fiendorum per legislatorem seu ciuium vniuersitatem, quanto periculosior est error circa propriam in sacerdotali aut altero ecclesiastico gradu atque præsidatus officio statuendam, quam circa humanam legem aut principaturum secundum ipsam instituendum. Nam si ad sacerdotium promoueatur peruersus more & ignorans aut vtrinq; deficiens, sicque curando & dirigendo fideli populo præferatur, ex eo periculum imminet populo mortis æternæ siquidem, quoniam ipsius est docere atque dirigere in his & de his quæ attinent ad necessitatem æternæ salutis. Vnde Malachiæ secundo; Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & legem requirent ex ore eius: diuinam scilicet, in qua continentur præcepta, & prohibita obseruari aut omitti, de quibus transgredien s non excusaretur per ignorantiam aut malitiam sacerdotis. Ideoque discernere debet populus, qualem sibi præferat pastorem, eo quod ex ipsius officio vnicuique commodum aut incommodum atque periculum euenire potest. Cuius quidem discretionis seu cautelæ, populus fidelis habet & rationabiliter habere debet potestatem, aliter nanque inconueniens hoc euitare non posset. Est autem quam diximus, plane Augustini sententia in libro de pœnitentia, quinimo & Christi verius, cuius auctoritate loquitur, & affirmat quod dicit. Inquit enim, & recitat Magister sententiarum libro quarto, decimoseptimo, dist. cap. sexto. Qui vult peccata confiteri vt inueniat gratiam, quærat sacerdotem, qui sciat ligare & soluere: ne cum negligens circa se extiterit, negligatur ab illo, (Christo scilicet,) qui eum misericorditer monet & petit, ne ambo in foueam cadant, quam stultus cuitare noluit. Est ergo vel esse debet in potestate cuiuslibet, ministrum pœnitentiæ conuenientem eligere, similiter & aliorum sacramentorum, vt dicit etiam Magister ibidem. Cum igitur electio præstantior fieri possit per fidelium vniuersitatem quam per vnicum, apparet quod ad ipsam magis quam ad vnicam singularem personam, aut singulare collegium talis electio seu præsidis institutio debeat pertinere. Amplius potest hoc esse ad ciuile incommodum grande, quoniam sacerdotes confessionis titulo, mulierum habent persæpe secreta colloquia. Quod quia facile seducibiles sunt, præsertim ipsarum iuuenes tam virgines quam etiam coniugatæ (vt apparet Genef. 4. & inducit Apostolus primæ ad Timotheum tertio: Adam enim seductus non fuit, sed mulier in prevaricatione) sacerdos peruersus existens, ipsarum mores & pudicitiam facile corrumpere poterit, quod etiam frequenter his temporibus propter sacerdotum qualitatem euenire videmus, hoc autem est ciuile incommodum non modicum, considerare volenti, quæ sequuntur ex hoc inconuenientia. Vnde & Arist. 1. Rhetoricæ, octauo capitulo: Quibuscunque enim ea qua secundum mulieres sunt prava, quemadmodum Lacedæmonii fere secundum dimidium vitæ non sunt felices. Mulier enim est quasi domus medietas, vt apparet ex illius Icenomia. Vnde si propter temporale commodum assequendum per legislatorem, expedit determinari personas ad reliqua ciuitatis officia promouendas, ac etiam principantis institutes seu determinare personam, vt potior fiat electio, & propterea conuenientior ad officium assumatur, quemadmodum demonstratum credimus 15. primæ: videtur eo magis ad eundem legislatorem humanum, seu fidelium vniuersitatem pertinere determinationem promouendorum ad officium sacerdotis, & sacerdotum institutionem in officio præsidatus. Quoniam & si peruersus princeps afferre possit graue incommodum pro statu præsentis sæculi, puta temporalis mortis, sacerdotis & peruersi ecclesiastici pastoris actio eo grauius inducere potest, quoniam mortis æternæ. Sic etiam propter periculum cogendus est & rationabiliter per humanum legislatorem aut principem cogi potest ecclesiasticus minister ad exhibenda & ministranda sacramenta, quæ sunt de necessitate salutis, vt baptismum, si peruersus existens hoc facere recusaret. Possunt autem confirmari prædicta de promouendis ad sacros ordines, & instituendis ad animarum curas maiores siue minores, per ea quæ de Isidori codice induximus 11. huius parte. quarta & quinta. Testantur autem dictis institutionesgloriosissimorum sanctorum, factæ secundum modum quem diximus, vt Beati Gregorii & Nicolai; ac reliquorum plurimorum, quemadmodum ex ipsorum legendis & approbatis apparet historiis.
units.tr: From these points I wish to draw a further conclusion by necessity: that in communities of the faithful already perfected, it belongs to the human lawgiver, or to the multitude of the faithful of that place over which the minister to be promoted is to preside, alone to choose, determine and present the persons to be promoted to the ecclesiastical orders; and that no priest or bishop singly, nor the college of them alone, may cooperate in receiving such orders without the licence of the human lawgiver or of the ruling authority itself. I shall demonstrate this first from Holy Scripture, and then confirm it by probable reasoning. By the authority of Scripture it appears from Acts 6. For the holy Apostles, needing deacons for their ministry and for the people, called together the multitude of the faithful, as those to whom it belonged to choose such persons, and also to determine them. Hence, as above: Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples together (that is, of the faithful, who were then all called disciples, as is found in the Gloss), and said: It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables. Wherefore, brethren, look out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. But we will give ourselves continually to prayer and to the ministry of the word. And the saying pleased the whole multitude. And they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and the others likewise. If, while the apostles were present, such a choice was committed to the multitude, so that the more fit might be chosen with greater certainty (since the whole multitude can know something, especially about the morals and life of a man, which one very learned man often does not know), how much more ought the choice of priests, who are needed in greater measure for strength and wisdom than deacons, and in the absence of such leaders as the Apostles were, to be committed to the whole community of the perfected faithful, so that there may be more certain testimony concerning the one to be promoted. Calling therefore the twelve: not Peter alone, where the Gloss says by common consent. The multitude of the disciples: where the Gloss says: They sought the consent of the multitude, which ought to be taken as an example. They appointed these, etc.: where Rabanus says: This order is to be kept in ordinations: let the people elect, let the bishop ordain. And this is also what the Apostle plainly says in 1 Timothy 3: Moreover he must have a good report of those who are outside, that is, outside the Church; whence the Gloss: not only from the faithful, but also from the unbelievers. Where also, a little further on, it is said of deacons: And let these first be proved, and then let them minister. Now, by probable reasoning, if it is permitted to say what is probable, I wish to show that the election and approval of anyone promoted to holy orders belongs to the judgment of the third kind of signification, namely the decision of the human lawgiver in communities of the faithful already perfected; and together with this, its secondary institution, by which a bishop or pastor is set over some faithful people and some fixed place, and likewise the removal or deprivation from that office, and, if need be, the exclusion of ecclesiastical ministers from its exercise, in the other lesser ecclesiastical offices. Then it will be shown to whom or to whom the distribution of ecclesiastical temporalities, called benefices, belongs. First, this can be proved by the same or similar demonstrations by which, in 12, 13 and 15 of the first part, we showed that the making of laws and the institution of rulers belong to the community of citizens; only the minor term of the demonstration is changed, so that the election, or approval of the persons to be promoted to holy orders, and the institution or determination of these to the governance of a certain people and province, and their deprivation or removal from the same for fault or some other reasonable cause, are taken in the demonstrations as the subject of law or of the institution of the ruler. Moreover, the necessity that such things be done by the lawgiver or by the community of citizens is all the more evident in these matters, the more dangerous is the error in appointing someone to the priesthood or another ecclesiastical grade and the office of governance, than in establishing a human law or a ruler to be set up according to it. For if someone who is perverse, ignorant, or deficient in both respects is promoted to the priesthood, and so is set over the faithful people to care for and direct them, danger of eternal death threatens the people from this; for it is the priest's task to teach and direct them in those things and about those things which pertain to the necessity of eternal salvation. Hence in Malachi 2: The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth: namely the divine law, in which are contained the commands to be kept and the prohibitions to be avoided or omitted, and those who transgress them are not excused by the ignorance or malice of the priest. Therefore the people ought to discern what sort of minister they set over themselves, since from his office advantage or disadvantage and danger can come to each one. Of this discernment or caution the faithful people has, and ought reasonably to have, the power; otherwise this inconvenience could not be avoided. Moreover, what we have said is plainly the opinion of Augustine in his book On Penance, and indeed of Christ more truly, by whose authority he speaks and whose words he affirms. For he says, and the Master of the Sentences recites it in Book 4, distinction 17, chapter 6: He who wishes to confess his sins that he may find grace, let him seek a priest who knows how to bind and to loose, lest, if he has been careless about himself, he be neglected by him (that is, by Christ), who mercifully warns him and asks that both should not fall into the pit which the fool refused to avoid. It is therefore, or ought to be, within the power of each person to choose a suitable minister of penance, and likewise of the other sacraments, as the Master also says in the same place. Since, then, the choice can be made more excellent by the community of the faithful than by one man, it appears that such choice or institution of a governor ought to belong to that community rather than to a single person or a single college. Further, this may be a great civil inconvenience, since priests, under the title of confession, often have secret conversations with women. Because these are easily seduced, especially the young women, both virgins and married (as appears from Genesis 4, and as the Apostle brings forward in 1 Timothy 2: For Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression), a wicked priest will easily be able to corrupt their morals and chastity; and we see this happen frequently in these times on account of the character of the priests. This is no small civil inconvenience for one who wishes to consider the disadvantages that follow from it. Hence Aristotle, Rhetoric 1, chapter 8: For in whatever matters the things that concern women are base, as the Lacedaemonians are scarcely happy for half of their life. For the wife is, as it were, half the household, as appears from the Economics of Icenomus. Hence, if for the sake of obtaining a temporal advantage it is expedient that persons be determined by the lawgiver for promotion to the other offices of the state, and also that the ruler's institution or appointment of a person be determined, so that the choice may be better and so that the more suitable man is assumed to the office, as we believe was demonstrated in 15 of the first part, it seems all the more to belong to the same human lawgiver, or to the community of the faithful, to determine those to be promoted to the office of priest and to institute priests in the office of governance. For although a wicked prince may bring serious harm to the present state of the world, such as temporal death, the act of a wicked priest or ecclesiastical pastor can bring a harm all the more grievous, namely eternal death. So too, on account of danger, an ecclesiastical minister may be compelled, and can reasonably be compelled by the human lawgiver or prince, to administer and dispense the sacraments which are necessary for salvation, such as baptism, if he, being wicked, refused to do so. What has been said may also be confirmed concerning those promoted to holy orders and those instituted to the greater or lesser cares of souls, by what we have adduced from the code of Isidore in the fourth and fifth parts of the eleventh book. Moreover, the institutions of the most glorious saints, made in the manner we have described, bear witness, such as those of Blessed Gregory and Nicholas, and of very many others, as appears from their lives and from approved histories.

units.la: Nec obstat, quod sacerdotes aut ipsorum collegium, de promouendorum sufficientia, tam ad sacerdotium quam ad officium pastoratus & reliqua minora, magis nouè intiudicare. Similiter & reliquæ consimiles instantiæ adductæ 13. prime, qualibus argui videbatur ad ciuium vniuersitatem, legumlationem, aut principantium institutionem, minime pertinere, potest enim ad has, quemadmodum ibidem consimiliter respondetur. Quoniam, esto sacerdotes de talib. amplius & certius habere iudicium, reliqua ciuium multitudine quod tamen fallit his diebus plerunque, non tamen ex hoc inferri potest solum collegium sacerdotum, horum certius habere iudicium tota multitudine, cuius pars existunt, unde reliquæ multitudini coniuncto sacerdotum collegio, certius & securius habebitur iudicium, quam ex solo seorsum. Veruntamen hoc sane tenendum, quod bene posita lex conformiter legi diuinæ statuere debet, principantem de hoc credere; iudicio sacerdotum, aut legis diuinæ doctorum & aliorum honestorum virorum, quemadmodum de promouendis in reliquis disciplinis, tam de disciplina, quam de moribus iudicio peritorum & approbatorum debet examinevti, Iudicio inquam peritorum dicto secundum primam iudicis aut iudicii significationem. Quoniam iudicio tertiæ significationis, autoritate legislatoris habet principans approbare vel reprobare personas statuere vel remouere ab officiorum exercitio, quemadmodum ostensum est decimoquinto prima. Secus autem tot essent in communitate vnica principantes supremi, quot iudicantes primæ significationis iudicio, de sufficientia vel defectu, secundum vnum quodq; officiorum ciuitatis, quod est inconuenientium & impossibilium si debeat manere ciuitas, & recte disponi, velut demonstratum est decimo huius & decimoseptimo prima.
units.tr: Nor is it an objection that priests, or their college, judge more newly about the fitness of candidates, both for the priesthood and for the office of pastor and the other lesser offices. Likewise the similar arguments cited in the thirteenth chapter of the first part, by which it seemed to be argued that such matters do not belong to the whole body of citizens, to legislation, or to the appointment of rulers, can be answered in the same way as was answered there. For although priests have a fuller and surer judgment about such things than the rest of the citizens, which nevertheless often fails in these days, it cannot be inferred from this that the college of priests alone has a surer judgment of these things than the whole multitude of which they are a part. Hence the judgment of the whole multitude, together with the college of priests, will be surer and safer than that of the priests alone and apart. Yet this must certainly be held: that a well-established law, which ought to agree with the divine law, should in this matter trust the judgment of priests, or of the teachers of the divine law and other honest men, just as candidates for the other disciplines, both for their learning and for their morals, ought to be examined by the judgment of the skilled and approved. I mean the judgment of the skilled, taken in the first sense of the word judge or judgment. For by judgment in the third sense, the ruler has, on the authority of the legislator, the power to approve or disapprove persons, and to appoint or remove them from the exercise of offices, as was shown in the fifteenth chapter of the first part. Otherwise there would be as many supreme rulers in the one community as there are judges in the first sense, deciding on the sufficiency or insufficiency of persons for each office of the state. This is inconvenient and impossible if the state is to remain and be rightly ordered, as was demonstrated in the tenth chapter of this part and the seventeenth of the first.

units.la: Sunt ergo legislatoris, aut eius autoritate principantis sententia seu iudicio, tertiæ significationis approbandæ vel reprobandæ personæ ad ecclesiasticos ordines promouendæ. Instituendæ quoque vel remouendæ, à cura seu præsidatu maiori vel minori, & ab exercitio eius prohibendæ; aut etiam, si ex malitia desisterent ab officii exercitio, exercere cogendæ, ne sui peruersitate possit aliquis incidere periculum mortis æternæ, vt defectu baptismatis vel alterius sacramenti. Quod sane intelligendum est in communitatibus fidelium iam perfectis. Nam in quo loco legislator & eius autoritate principans infideles existerent, quemadmodum erat in communitatum plurimis, & quasi omnibus circa statum ecclesiæ primitiuæ, personarum promouendarum ad ecclesiasticos ordines, approbatio vel reprobatio cum reliquis institutionibus iam dictis, & officiorum exercitiis sacerdoti vel Episcopo cum saniori parte fidelis multitudinis existentis ibidem aut illi soli, si solus esset, autoritas hæc conueniret absque consensu vel scientia principantis, vt ex huiusmodi promotione, ac prælatorum seu curatorum institutione, fides Christi & doctrina salutaris diuulgaretur, quæ legis custodis autoritate, studio vel præcepto non fierent sed magis prohiberentur, quo et modo, id fecerunt apostoli, circa initium Ecclesiæ Christi. Et facere tenebantur præcepto diuino, & tenerentur ipsorum successores, in legislatoris defectum. Unde Apostolus primæ ad Corinthios nono: Nam si euangelizauero, non est mihi gloria; necessitas enim mihi incumbit. Væ mihi, si non euangelizauero. Vbi tamen legislator fidelis, & legis custos, talia volunt fieri dico ipsorum esse autoritatem, secundum iam dictum modum, propter assignatas causas seu probationes, tam ex scriptura sacra, quam ex humana, probabili & necessaria ratione.
units.tr: Therefore the judgment or decision of the legislator, or of the ruler acting on his authority, in the third sense, is what approves or rejects persons to be promoted to the ecclesiastical orders; it is also what institutes or removes them from the care or charge, greater or lesser, and forbids them the exercise of it, or even compels them to exercise it if through malice they cease from the duties of their office, lest by their perversity anyone should fall into the danger of eternal death, as by the lack of baptism or of another sacrament. This must certainly be understood of communities of the faithful that are already established. For where the legislator and the ruler acting on his authority were unbelievers, as was the case in most of the communities, and almost all of them, at the time of the primitive Church, the approval or rejection of persons to be promoted to the ecclesiastical orders, together with the other appointments already mentioned and the exercise of offices, would belong to the priest or bishop, with the sounder part of the faithful multitude living there, or to him alone if he were alone. This authority would be exercised without the consent or knowledge of the ruler, so that through such promotions and the institution of prelates or pastors the faith of Christ and the saving doctrine might be spread abroad. These things were not done by the authority, zeal or command of the guardian of the law; rather they were forbidden by him. The apostles did so at the beginning of the Church of Christ, and they were bound to do it by divine command, as their successors would be bound in the absence of a legislator. Hence the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 9: "For if I preach the gospel, I have no ground for boasting, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel." Yet where the legislator is faithful and a guardian of the law, and wishes such things to be done, I say that the authority belongs to them, in the way already described, on account of the causes or proofs assigned, both from holy Scripture and from human, probable and necessary reasoning.

units.la: De distributione vero temporalium, quæ beneficia ecclesiastica vocari solent, oportet præscire, quod talia temporalia, vel ordinata sunt per legislatorem, ad sustentandum euangelicos ministros & reliquas personas miserabiles, de quibus diximus 14. & 15. huius, vel ordinata sunt ad hunc vsum, per personam aliquam, aut collegium aliquod singulare. Quod si huiusmodi temporalia ex dono, & legislatoris ordinatione sic statuta fuerint, dico, quod de ipsis distribuendis, autoritatem cui vult & quando, licite secundum legem diuinam committere potest: Et ex causa, cum voluerit, autoritatem ab eo vel eis, cui vel quib. personæ singulari vel collegio comiserat, reuocare, nec posset huius oppositum, sed magis propositum ex scriptura conuinci. Sicut etiam autoritate Ambrosii ex epistola de tradendis basilicis supra monstrauimus 14. huius. Nec solum talium temporalium autoritatem distribuendi, ab eo vel eis cui commiserat, reuocare potest licite, secundum legem diuinam legislator fidelis, verum etiam, vendere aut aliter alienare, propter rationabilem causam superuenientem, quoniam sua sunt & in ipsius semper potestate de iure, nisi fortasse rem ipsam simpliciter, aut etiam cum dominio in alterius collegii, aut personæ singularis transtulerit potestatem. His tamen semper adiiciendo, secundum omne euentum fidelem populum lege diuina obligari, si potens fuerit, ad euangelicorum ministrorum sustentationem, in victu & tegmento decenti, quib. contenti debet esse, vt ex prima ad Timotheum vltimo monstratum est. Si vero huiusmodi temporalia statuta fuerint ad pia opera ex dono vel legato personæ, vel personarum singularum, dico talia debere conseruari, custodiri, atq; distribui, secundum donantis aut legantis intentionem. Quod si quis error, in distributoribus horum correctione indigens, appareat iuxta donantis vel legantis intentionem, debet error huiusmodi per humanum legislatorem, aut eius autoritate principante corrigi. Quinimo id sciens & potens, peccat omittens, quoniam non pertinet hoc, aut fieri debet per collegium aut personam aliam singularem aliquā cuiuscunq; conditionis existant, excepto duntaxat, sic casi talium correctio per donatorem aut legatorem alicui personae vel collegio commissa foret, quorum etiam error si contingeret, tandem corrigi debet per principantem. Quamuis etiam persona singularis aut collegium basilicam construere, ibiq; legis evangelicae quemquam ministrum statuere nequeat, absque legislatoris concessione, propter pridem assignatas causas. Amplius, proposita de ministrorum ecclesiasticorum institutione, ac temporalium seu beneficiorum distributione vel collatione ostendere volo, auctoritate catholicorum Franciae Regum, non spernenda, sed potius attendenda. Asserunt enim ipsi de iure, quod etiam de facto usque in praesens tempus volunt & faciunt immutabiliter observari, aliquorum officiorum ecclesiasticorum & temporalium seu beneficiorum ad se sic pertinere auctoritatem institutionis & distributionis, ut a nemine singulari vel collegio mortalium cuiuscunq; conditionis existat, in ipsos aut ad ipsos haec auctoritas deriuetur. Non enim lege divina prohibitus est legislator aut princeps, ab horum institutione, collatione, seu distributione. Quinimo auctoritas haec in perfectis fidelium communitatibus ex legislatoris concessione deriuata est, si licita fuerit, non subdole usurpata in personas aut collegia sacerdotum. Unde in legibus principum Romanorum status est modus & forma eligendi seu instituendi Episcopos, curatos, decanos; & reliquos ordinandi ceterorum ministros, numerus quoq; ipsorum determinatus & praefinitus. Hoc enim ad humanum legislatorem & principantem pertinet, ut denostratum est octavo huius, & decimoquinto prima.
