Sic etiam de modo tractandi ecclesiastica temporalia seu beneficia, & actuum contentiosorum inter presbyteros inuicem, & ad quoscunque alios, leges statutae sunt, contra quas priores Romani antistites, sancti & suae libertatis conscii, non ignari, minime reclamarunt, sed illis fuerunt & esse voluerunt, sicut etiam & iuste debuerunt, sponte subiecti. Ut etiam vicesimoprimo huius, parte secunda declamabitur amplius, usque in octavam. Unde vero tanta peruenerit alietas, ut sacerdotale collegium, non solum legibus & principum seculi consuetudinibus se dicat exemptum, vetum etiam super illos, iam se legislatorem constituat, idque pertinaciter asserat & defendat, posterius dicturi sumus. Rursum etiam ex praemissis, nos latere non debet, humanum legislatorem, aut eius auctoritate principantem, ex temporalibus ecclesiasticis, praesertim prouentibus immobilium quae beneficia diximus, si qua residua fuerint sufficientiae ministrorum euangelicorum, tallias & collectas suscipere posse licite secundum legem humanam atque diuinam, pro patriae defensione, aut captiuorum in fidei obsequium redemptione, vel supportandis oneribus publicis, ac aliis rationabilibus causis, secundum legis latoris fidelis determinationem. Non enim qui talia temporalia, legato vel dono ad pias causas statuit, & alicui vel aliquibus distribuenda committit, ea potuit cuiquam collegio, vel singulari personae cum immunitate maiori tribuere, quam habuerit dum extiterunt in ipsius potestate. Sed pro tunc nunquam fuerunt a publicis oneribus immunia, ergo nec postquam per donatorem aut institutorem translata fuerint cuiusuis alterius potestatem. Hucautem testatur Ambrosius in epistola de tradendis basilicis, cum dixit: Soluimus quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari: & quae sunt Dei Deo. Tributum Caesaris est, non negatur. Et rursum eadem: Si tributum petit imperator, non negamus. Agri Ecclesiae soluunt tributum. Quod tamen Imperatori negasset, si hoc sibi iure non deberi credidisset, quemadmodum sibi templa negauit, seu sacerdotum institutionem in eis propterea quod Arianis videbatur fauere, etiam contra plebis sententiam, de quo amplius in sequentibus dicturi sumus est. Idem dicit Hugo de sancto Victore tractatu de sacramentis. Inquit enim: Ecclesia licet fructum terrena possessionis in vsum accipiat, potestatem tamen exercenda iustitiae per ecclesiasticas personas aut iudicia secularia exercere non potest. potest tamen ministros habere, laicas personas, per quas iura & iudicia ad terrenam potestatem pertinentia secundum tenorem legum & debitum iuru terreni exerceantur, sic tamen vt & ipsum quod potestatem habet, a principe terreno se habere cognoscat, & ipsas possessiones nunquam ista a regia potestate elongare posse intelligat, quia si ratio postulauerit & necessitas, & illius ipsa potestas debeat patrocinium: & illi, ipsae possessiones debeant in necessitate obsequium. Sicut enim regalis potestas patrocinium, quod debet alii, non potest non dare, sic ipsa possessio ab ecclesiastica, &c.
units.tr: As to the distribution of temporal goods, which are usually called ecclesiastical benefices, we must first understand that such temporal goods are either ordained by the legislator for the support of the gospel ministers and the other wretched persons of whom we spoke in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters of this part, or are ordained for this use by some person or a particular college. If such temporal goods have been established by gift and by the ordinance of the legislator, I say that he may lawfully commit the authority to distribute them, to whomever he wishes and whenever he wishes, according to the divine law. For a cause, when he wishes, he may recall the authority from the person or persons, or from the individual or college, to whom he committed it; nor could anyone prove the opposite, but rather the proposition is convicted by Scripture. Thus also, on the authority of Ambrose, in his letter on the surrender of the basilicas, we showed above in the fourteenth chapter of this part. Nor may a faithful legislator, according to the divine law, only recall lawfully from the person to whom he committed it the authority to distribute such temporal goods, but also sell or otherwise alienate them, on account of a reasonable cause that arises. For they are his own, and are always in his power by right, unless perhaps he has simply transferred the thing itself, or even with its dominion, into the power of another college or of a particular person. Yet always adding this: that according to every event the faithful people, if able, is bound by the divine law to support the gospel ministers with food and decent clothing, with which they ought to be content, as was shown from the last chapter of the first letter to Timothy. But if such temporal goods have been established for pious works by the gift or bequest of a person or of individual persons, I say that such goods ought to be preserved, guarded and distributed according to the intention of the giver or testator. If any error appears among the distributors that needs correction, according to the intention of the giver or testator, such error ought to be corrected by the human legislator, or by the ruler acting on his authority. Indeed, whoever knows of it and is able, and neglects it, sins; for this does not pertain to, nor ought it to be done by, a college or any other individual, of whatever condition they may be, except only in the case where the correction of such things had been committed by the donor or testator to some person or college. If an error were to occur there too, it must in the end be corrected by the ruler. Although a particular person or a college cannot build a basilica and set up any minister of the gospel law there without the concession of the legislator, for the causes assigned earlier. Furthermore, having proposed the matter of the institution of ecclesiastical ministers and the distribution or conferral of temporal goods or benefices, I wish to show it by the authority of the Catholic kings of France, which is not to be despised but rather to be considered. For they assert, by right, and wish and do, which they have maintained unchanged up to the present time, that the authority of appointing and distributing certain ecclesiastical and temporal offices or benefices belongs to them, so that this authority does not derive from any single person or college of mortals, of whatever condition, into them or to them. For the legislator or prince is not forbidden by the divine law from their institution, conferral, or distribution. Rather this authority, in communities of the faithful that are perfect, has been derived from the concession of the legislator, if it has been lawful, and not craftily usurped by persons or colleges of priests. Hence in the laws of the Roman princes the manner and form of electing or instituting bishops, pastors, deans, and of ordaining their other ministers, and also their number, was fixed and prescribed. For this belongs to the human legislator and ruler, as has been shown in chapter eight of this part, and chapter fifteen of the first. So too laws were enacted concerning the manner of handling ecclesiastical temporal goods or benefices, and of disputed matters between presbyters among themselves and with any others. The earlier Roman bishops, holy men who were conscious of their freedom and not ignorant of it, did not protest against these laws, but were, and wished to be, willingly subject to them, as they also rightly ought to have been. This will be argued further in the twenty-first chapter of this part, in the second section, up to the eighth. But from what cause such a great alienation came about, that the priestly college not only claims to be exempt from the laws and customs of secular princes, but also sets itself up as a legislator over them, and stubbornly asserts and defends this, we shall speak of later. Again, from what has been said above, it should not be hidden from us that the human legislator, or the ruler acting on his authority, may lawfully, according to human and divine law, take tallies and collections from ecclesiastical temporal goods, especially from the income of the immovable property which we have called benefices, if any surplus remains beyond the sufficiency of the gospel ministers, for the defence of the fatherland, or for the ransom of captives in the service of the faith, or for bearing public burdens, and for other reasonable causes, according to the determination of the faithful legislator. For one who has established such temporal goods by bequest or gift for pious causes, and has committed them to be distributed to one or more persons, could not grant to any college or individual a greater immunity than he had while they were in his own power. For at that time they were never free from public burdens; therefore neither are they after they have been transferred by the donor or founder into the power of another. Ambrose bears witness to this in his letter On the Surrender of the Basilicas, when he said: Render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. The tribute to Caesar is not denied. And again in the same place: If the emperor demands tribute, we do not deny it. The fields of the Church pay tribute. Yet he would have denied it to the emperor if he had believed that it was not due to him by right, just as he denied him the churches, or the appointment of priests in them, because it seemed to favour the Arians, even against the opinion of the people, about which we shall speak more in what follows. Hugh of Saint Victor says the same in his treatise on the sacraments. For he says: The Church, although it receives the fruit of earthly possessions for its use, cannot however exercise the power of administering justice through ecclesiastical persons or secular courts. It may, however, have ministers, lay persons, through whom laws and judgments pertaining to earthly power are exercised according to the tenor of the laws and the due right of the earthly realm; yet in such a way that it also recognises that the power it has, it has from the earthly prince, and understands that these possessions can never be removed from the royal power, because if reason and necessity demand, that power ought to give protection to it, and it ought to give its possessions for service in necessity. For just as royal power cannot withhold the protection which it owes to another, so the possession itself from the ecclesiastical, etc.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: De origine ac statu primo Ecclesiae Christianae, & unde Romanus Episcopus & Ecclesia praedictam auctoritatem, ac super caeteros sibi quendam primatum assumpsit.
units.tr: On the origin and first state of the Christian Church, and whence the Roman Bishop and Church assumed the aforesaid authority and a certain primacy over the rest.

units.la: NUNC autem restat ex propositis intentionibus manifestare ortum & initium, ex quibus iurisdictio coactiua & omnium sacerdotalium institutionum secundariarum, non essentialium vocatarum, ecclesiasticorum quoque temporalium omnium distribuendi potestas in Episcopos seu presbyteros aliquos peruenerit, talium quoque potestatum supremam unde sibi Papa Romanus ascribat. His consequenter adiiciendum, cuius aut quorum scripturae sensus dubios interpretari, & interpretatos fidelibus credendos & obseruandos tradere atque praecipere sit iusta potestas. Supponentibus igitur primum ex determinatis a nobis decimoquinto & decimoseptimo prima, quarto, quinto, octavo, nono & decimo huius, ad nullum Episcopum, aut presbyterum, vel ministrum ecclesiasticum aliquem, inquatum huiusmodi, iurisdictionem aliquam cuiusquam coactiuam in hoc seculo pertinere. Rusumque monstratum sufficienter decimoquinto, decimosexto, & decimoseptimo huius, nullum Episcopum aut presbyterum immediata ordinatione Christi, alteri Episcopo vel presbytero subesse quantum ad aliquam sacerdotalium potestatum essentialem, aut non essentialem iam dictam, id quoq; quod de temporalium ecclesiasticorum distributione iam diximus capitulo precedenti: sufficienter patere posset insipientibus solutio quæsitorum, verumtamen ad horum dissolutionem accedere volumus singulariter magis, propter minus introductorum in talibus tarditatem.
units.tr: Now it remains, from the intentions we have set out, to show the origin and beginning from which coercive jurisdiction, and the power of distributing all secondary sacerdotal institutions (called non-essential) and all ecclesiastical temporal goods, came to bishops or certain presbyters, and from what source the Roman Pope claims for himself the supreme authority over such powers. To these must be added the question of whose authority it is to interpret the doubtful senses of Scripture, and to hand down and prescribe the interpreted senses for the faithful to believe and observe. We assume first, from what we have determined in the fifteenth and seventeenth chapters, and in the first, fourth, fifth, eighth, ninth and tenth of this book, that no coercive jurisdiction of any kind in this age belongs to any bishop, presbyter or ecclesiastical minister as such. And it has been sufficiently shown in the fifteenth, sixteenth and seventeenth of this book that no bishop or presbyter, by the immediate ordination of Christ, is subordinate to another bishop or presbyter in respect of any essential or non-essential sacerdotal power mentioned above. Likewise, what we said in the preceding chapter about the distribution of ecclesiastical temporal goods could sufficiently make the solution of the questions raised clear to the unlearned; nevertheless, we wish to deal with their solution more particularly, on account of the slowness of those less instructed in such matters.

units.la: Quæsita ergo proposita reddere tentaturis oportebit de ipsis intendere primum quatenus processerunt de facto, & circa ipsorum origines. Deinde vero quantum iuri diuino & humano, ac recte rationi sic facta, conformiter se habuerint aut habere debuerint, quæ etiam his contrarie atq; difformiter, vt demum conformia tanquam probanda & obseruanda, difformia vero velut notoria seculo & fidelium quieti ac licite detestanda & declinanda noscamus. De his autem quantum de facto & iure processerint, principium quærendum est ex canone sacro. De consequentibus vero colligere possumus ex approbatis historiis. Harum autem plurimum ex Isidori codice supradicto, & demum aliqua recitare, quæ disciplinarum experientia magistra nos docuit. A sacro itaque canone tanquam à fonte veritatis quæsitæ facientes exordium, suscipiemus oraculum Christi, Ioannis vigesimo, quo siquidem sacerdotalem auctoritatem aut clauium potestatem vel vtrumq; indifferenter apostolis tribuit, dum eisdem dixit insufflans: Accipite Spiritum Sanctum: quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis. Huic quoque adiicientes mandatum eiusdem, quo indifferenter etiam prædicationem euangelicam per vniuersum orbem iniunxit eis, cum ad eos Matthæi vltimo dixit: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, &c. Quibus siquidem postmodum immediata sui vocatione adiunxit Paulum tanquam vas electum, spiritus Sancti videlicet, vt ex Actuum nono satis apparet. Hic autem, simul & alii iam dictum Christi mandatum exequentes Apostoli, vt ex ipsorum actibus & epistolis palam, in Iudaea primum nunciauerunt & docuerunt Euangelium seu fidem Christianam, ad quam multos etiam converterunt ibidem. Deinde vero revelatione diuina & ipsorum ordinatione inuicem ipsorum quidam in Iudaea remanserunt. Reliqui vero diuisim ad diuersos se transtulerunt populos, in quibus confidenter & constanter prædicantes Euangelium, profecit in personarum vtriusque sexus conversione, quantum potuit & Deo placuit vnusquisque, velut in ipsorum legendis seu de ipsis approbatis Historiis recitatur, quamuis inter cæteros sua prædicatione notabiliter profecerint ipsorum duo beati scilicet Petrus & Paulus, qui siquidem Paulus, quamuis ex duodecim non fuerit, à Christo nil minus vocatus & missus fuit æque immediate ac principaliter, sicut aliorum Apostolorum quicunq;, quemadmodum apparet Actuum nono & ex secundo ad Galatas, cum dictis sanctorum exponentium, sufficienter ostensum est decimosexto huius. Ab his, inquam, duobus Apostolis Petro & Paulo primum, quamuis tamen secundum canonis seriem à Paulo manifestius, & præsertim ad Gentiles (Augustinus 14. de ciuitate Dei, capitulo nono) Ecclesiæ Christianæ deriuatus est ritus: nam & ipse Paulus principalis & primus Apostolus fuit ad gentes, siue Gentiles, seu præputium, quemadmodum Petrus in circumcisionem, vt apparet secundo ad Galatas, & Romanos vndecimo. Ex Glossa quoq; sanctorum ibidem, & aliis plerisq; scripturæ locis. Hi vero apostoli duo cum reliquis omnibus suum magistrum imitantes, Christum videl. sub principum seculi coactiua iurisdictione vixerunt, & alios sic viuere docuerunt, vt aperte monstratum est quarto huius & quinto. Sic quoq; vixerunt ipsorum successores presbyteri seu Episcopi, cum suis diaconib. & reliquis ministris euangelicis successiue vsq; ad tempora primi Constantini Rom. Imperatoris, vt ex prædicto Isidoris codice satis apparet. Ita quod nemo Episcoporum per omne tempus illud, in alios Episcopos coactiuam iurisdictionem exercuit. Quamuis tamen aliarum provinciarum Episcopi plures, in quibus dubitabat, tam de scriptura sacra, quam de ritu ecclesiastico, non audentes se publice congregare, consuluerunt Episcopum & Ecclesiam fidelium existentem Romæ, propter maiorem ibidem forte fidelium multitudinem, & magis peritiorem, eo quod studia scientiarum omnium tunc multum Romæ vigebant. Vnde ipsorum episcopi & sacerdotes peritiores, & in tali numero plus cæteris abundabat ipsorum ecclesia. Erant etiam & reuerentiores, tum quia beatus Petrus apostolorum senior, meritis perfectior & reuerentior ibidem tanquam episcopus sedisse legitur, & beatus Paulus similiter, de quo amplius constat, quemadmodum apparuit decimosexto huius. Tum etiam propter Romanæ vrbis principalitatem & famositatem amplioREM ad certas mundi prouincias. Vnde etiam prouinciarum aliarum fideles, sufficientia personarum carentes, ad ipsorum ecclesias gubernandas ab episcopo & Ecclesia Romana fidelium postulabant personas, sibi ad episcopatum præficiendas, eo quod ecclesia fidelium Romæ personis talibus, vt iam diximus, amplius abundabat. Episcopi vero & ecclesia Romanorum sic requisiti consilium & auxilium, tam circa fidem, quam circa ecclesiasticum ritum & personarum prouisionem indigentib. & requirentib. charitatiue atq; fraterne subueniebant in his, episcopos scil. eis mittendo, qui vix inueniebantur acceptare volentes. Ordinationes etiam, quas super ecclesiasticum ritum sibi fecerant, aliis communicando prouinciis, & quandoq; etiam in aliis prouinciis contentionem aut schisma fidelium inter se audientes charitatiue mouendo. Hæc autem aliarum prouinciarum ecclesiæ grate suscipiebant, vt ex quibusdam historiis & serie prædicti codicis à Clemente Papa, qui primus ibid. scribitur episcopus Petri vel Pauli aut vtriusq; successor vsq; ad tempora iam dicti Constantini, satis apparet. Hoc etiam modo vel consimili quasi suscepit à Græcis Rom. populus gratuite non coacte leges quasdam vocatas decem tabularum, à quib. tanquam ab origine leges reliquæ Romani populi processerunt. Et tamen constat Rom. populum, Græcis nulla iurisdictione vel auctoritate subiectum. Sic et qui librum hunc in lucem deduxit, Studiosorum Vniuersitatem Aurelianis degentē vidit, audiuit, & sciuit per suos nuncios & epistolas requirentem & supplicantē Parisien. vniuersitati tanquam famosiori & veneratiori, pro ipsius habendis regulis, privilegiis, atque statutis, cum tamen Parisien. vniuersitati, nec ante nec post esse in autoritate apostolica vel iurisdictione subiecta. Ex iam dicta vero quasi consuetudinaria prioritate, aliarum Ecclesiarum consensu spontaneo, Romanorum Episcopi secundum ipsorum vlteriorem a principio processum, autoritatem quandam. Decreta, seu ordinationes constituendi super vniuersalem Ecclesiam, quantum ad ecclesiasticum ritum & actus etiam sacerdotum, & illarum obseruationem praecipiendi amplioerem sumpserunt vsque ad tempora Constantini praedicti, vtrum autem id facere potuerint Romanorum Episcopi sola ipsorum autoritate, an aliorum oportuerit ad haec interuenire consensum, in sequentibus dicturi sumus. Constantinus vero praedictus, vt ex iam dicto Codice, capitulo de primitiis Ecclesiae, in concilio Nicaeno narrat Isidorus, & in edicto domini Constantini Imperatoris inscripto patitur continetur, primus fuit Imperator, qui fidem Christi, ministerio beati Syluestri tunc Papae Romani patenter adeptus est: Et qui sacerdotium a iurisdictione coactiua principum exemisse videtur: qui etiam per praedictum edictum, Ecclesiae Romanae ac ipsius Episcopo similiter tribuisse videtur autoritates & potestates super alios Episcopos & Ecclesias omnes, quas sibi conuenire nunc asserunt aliunde, vt decimonono prima, parte octaua & nona supra narrauimus. Cum his quoque iurisdictiones coactiuas super eosdem agros, praedia, & possessiones plurimas cum quarundam etiam prouinciarum seculari dominio, vt palam se offert inspicienti praedictum edictum. Hic etiam, vt supra legitur, primus Imperator fuit, qui Christianis concessit licentiam se publice congregandi, templa seu Ecclesias construendi, & cuius praecepto primum concilium Nicenum extitit congregatum. De quo siquidem cum reliquis quae facta sunt in processu Ecclesiae ab Apostolorum vsque in praesentia tempora, consequenter in suis locis quantum proposito nostro conueniet, tangemus & inducemus historias. Ex ipsis quidem quae legi diuinae ac rectae rationi consona fuerint, recipientes: quae vero dissona, reiicientes. Qualiter autem & quae facta sunt se habere tradentes. Sic itaque dissiniendorum a sui origine aliqualiter recitato progressu, ad ipsorum determinationem ingredientes amplius, Suppositionem cum Apostolo faciemus indubiam, fidem catholicam vnam esse, non plures, vnde ad Eph. 4. Vnus dominus, vna fides. Hanc quoque rursum in vnitate secundum eundem sensum, videlicet credendam & ab omnibus confitendam, vt vbi supra, parum post inquit Apostolus. Donec occurramus omnes in vnitate fidei, & agnitionem filii Dei. Ex quibus quidem per necessitatem inferemus primum, quod legis diuinae praesertim euangelicae dubios sensus atq; sententias, & si quae fuerint inter doctores ipsius contentiones vel controuersiae probabiles, quemadmodum quorundam ignorantia vel malignitate aut vtrisque iam euenisse legimus iuxta Christi & Apostoli prophetiam, expedit terminare: huicautem per necessitatem assequi mostrabimus, ad solum generale concilium, fidelium omnium vel eorum, qui omnium fidelium autoritatem habuerint, determinationem hanc tantummodo pertinere. Deinde ostendam, secundum legem diuinam & rationem rectam, quod generale concilium conuocare, idq; si expediat per coactiuam potentiam congregare, ad solius humani fidelis legislatoris superiore carentis, autoritatem pertineat, non autem ad personam aliquam aut collegium aliquod singulare, cuiuscunq; dignitatis aut conditionis existant, nisi eidem aut eisdem, per supradictum legislatorem, autoritas concessa foret. Amplius ostendam per certitudinem nihil statui posse circa ecclesiasticum ritum & humanos actus, quod omnes homines ad obseruationem obliget sub aliqua poena, pro statu praesentis seculi vel venturi, nisi per solum generale concilium seu supremum legislatorem fidelem immediate, aut inde sumpta prius autoritate. Ex quo etiam monstrabitur consequenter, quod nullus princeps, prouincia vel communitas aliqua, interdici aut excommunicari possit nec debeat per aliquem sacerdotem quicunque sit ille, nisi secundum modum, per supradictum generale concilium ordinatum. Deinde monstrabitur euidenter, ad nullius vnici siue solius Episcopi vel alterius vnicae singularis personae aut particularis vnici collegii cuiusquam autoritatem pertinere, in eunctis mundi ecclesiasticis officiis personas instituere, neque pro eisdem ecclesiastica temporalia, vocata beneficia, distribuere seu conferre, sed autoritatem hanc, solius esse fundatoris seu donatoris, vel vniuersalis legislatoris fidelis, aut eius vel eorum, cui vel quibus & secundum quam formam & modum, idem donator aut legislator hanc concesserit potestatem. Deinde vero monstrabitur, qui vnicum Episcopum & Ecclesiam, quales & quorum autoritate; aliorum principaliorem sine caput, conueniens est instituere. Cuius quidem cum ipsius Ecclesia sit insinuare, reliquis omnibus Episcopis & ecclesiis ea, quae per generalia concilia circa ritum ecclesiasticum & alios humanos actus ad communem fidelium vtilitatem, tranquillitatem, & quietem ordinata fuerint & apparebunt ordinanda. Demum vero ex his per necessitatem inferemus, tam determinata circa scripturam & fidem catholicam, quam circa ritum ecclesiasticum, cum reliquis institutis per generale concilium, solius generalis concilii autoritate, non autem alterius particularis collegii vel personae singularis alicuius immutari posse, augeri, minui, vel suspendi, aut totaliter reuocari. Ex quibus quidem omnibus ad vniuscuiusque, quasi sensatam notitiam deducetur, Romanum Episcopum aut ipsius Ecclesiam vel quemuis alium Episcopum aut Ecclesiam; in quantum huiusmodi, nullam potestatem aut autoritatem iam dictarum habere, super reliquos Episcopos & Ecclesias, diuino vel humano iure, nisi quae sibi simpliciter vel ad tempus concessa fuerit per supradictum concilium generale. Propter quod etiam apparebit, Romanum Episcopum aut quemuis alium incongrue, minus debite, ac praeter, imo contra scripturarum diuinarum & humanarum demonstrationum tionum sententiam, sibi ascribere, super principem, communitatem aut personam aliquam singularem, plenitudinem potestatis. Et quod ab ipsius sibi attributione, idem Episcopus & alter quicunque penitus est, etiam per monitionem & coactiuam potestatem, si oporteat, ab humanis legumlatoribus, seu ipsorum autoritate principantibus, cohibendus.
units.tr: Those who would answer the questions raised must therefore first consider them as they have actually developed and as to their origins. Then they must consider how far these developments have conformed, or ought to have conformed, to divine and human law and to right reason. Conversely, we must recognise which developments were contrary and unlike these, so that we may approve and observe the conforming ones as things to be proved, and may detest and avoid the unlike ones as known to disturb the peace of the world and of the faithful and as unlawful. As to how far these things have proceeded in fact and in law, our starting point must be sought in the sacred canon. What followed from them we may gather from approved histories, chiefly from the Codex of Isidore mentioned above, and then we shall recite some things which the experience of church discipline, as its teacher, has taught us. Taking our beginning from the sacred canon, as from the fountain of the truth we seek, we shall take up the oracle of Christ in John 20, where he gave the apostles priestly authority, or the power of the keys, or both alike, when he breathed on them and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them." To this we add his command, by which he likewise enjoined on them the preaching of the gospel throughout the whole world, when he said to them at the end of Matthew: "Go therefore and teach all nations, etc." To these commands he afterwards joined, by his own immediate calling, Paul as a chosen vessel, namely of the Holy Spirit, as is sufficiently clear from Acts 9. Now the apostles, carrying out this command of Christ together with the others, first announced and taught the gospel, or the Christian faith, in Judea, as is plain from their acts and epistles, and they converted many there to that faith. Then, by divine revelation and by their own mutual appointment, some of them remained in Judea, while the rest went off separately to different peoples. Among these they preached the gospel confidently and steadily, and each of them made progress, as far as he could and as God pleased, in converting persons of both sexes, as is recounted in their writings and in the approved histories about them. Yet among the rest, the two blessed apostles Peter and Paul made notable progress in their preaching. Paul, though he was not one of the twelve, was called and sent by Christ no less immediately and principally than any of the other apostles, as appears in Acts 9 and in Galatians 2, and as has been sufficiently shown with the words of the holy expositors in chapter 16 above. From these two apostles, I say, Peter and Paul, the rite of the Christian Church was derived first, though in the order of the canon it comes more clearly from Paul, and especially for the Gentiles (Augustine, City of God 14, chapter 9). For Paul himself was the principal and first apostle to the nations, or Gentiles, or the uncircumcised, just as Peter was to the circumcision, as appears in Galatians 2 and Romans 11, and from the gloss of the holy fathers there and from many other passages of Scripture. These two apostles, with all the rest, imitating their master Christ, lived under the coercive jurisdiction of the princes of this age, and they taught others to live the same way, as has been clearly shown in chapters 4 and 5 above. In the same way their successors, the elders or bishops, lived with their deacons and the other evangelical ministers in succession, down to the time of the first Constantine, Roman emperor, as is sufficiently clear from the Codex of Isidore mentioned above. So during all that time none of the bishops exercised coercive jurisdiction over other bishops. Yet many bishops of other provinces, when they doubted about the holy Scripture or the ecclesiastical rite, and did not dare to gather publicly, consulted the bishop and the body of the faithful at Rome, perhaps because there was a larger and more skilled multitude of the faithful there, since the study of all the sciences then flourished greatly at Rome. Hence the bishops and priests there were more skilled, and in such numbers the Church there abounded more than the rest. They were also more venerable, both because the blessed Peter, the senior of the apostles, is read to have sat there as bishop, more perfect in merit and more reverend, and because the blessed Paul likewise, of whom more is known, as appeared in chapter 16 above, and also on account of the principality and fame of the city of Rome, which extended to certain regions of the world. Hence also the faithful of other provinces, lacking persons sufficient for governing their churches, asked the bishop and the faithful Church of Rome for persons to be set over them as bishops, since the Church of the faithful at Rome, as we have said, abounded more in such persons. The bishops and the Church of Rome, thus asked, gave help and counsel charitably and fraternally to those who needed and asked for it, whether concerning the faith, the ecclesiastical rite, or the provision of persons, by sending them bishops, though these could scarcely be found willing to accept. They also communicated to other provinces the ordinances they had made concerning the ecclesiastical rite, and sometimes, when they heard of contention or schism among the faithful in other provinces, they charitably stirred themselves to deal with it. The churches of the other provinces gladly received these things, as is sufficiently clear from certain histories and from the series in the said Codex, from Clement, the Pope who is first written of there as bishop and successor of Peter or Paul or both, down to the time of the Constantine already mentioned. In this same way, or something similar, the Roman people freely and without compulsion took from the Greeks certain laws called the Laws of the Ten Tables, from which, as from their origin, the rest of the laws of the Roman people proceeded. Yet it is established that the Roman people were not subject to the Greeks in any jurisdiction or authority. So too, he who brought this book to light saw, heard and knew that the university of students living at Orléans, through its messengers and letters, asked and begged the University of Paris, as more famous and more venerable, for rules, privileges and statutes to be had, although the University of Paris was neither before nor after subject to it in apostolic authority or jurisdiction. From this so-called customary priority, and by the voluntary consent of the other churches, the Bishops of Rome, according to their further progress from the beginning, gradually assumed a certain authority: to issue decrees or ordinances over the universal Church concerning the ecclesiastical rite and even the acts of priests, and to command their observance, and they grew in this authority down to the time of the Constantine mentioned above. Whether, however, the Bishops of Rome could do this by their own authority alone, or whether the consent of others had to intervene, we shall say in what follows. This Constantine, as Isidore relates from the said Codex, chapter on the first-fruits of the Church, at the Council of Nicaea, and as is contained in the edict of the lord Emperor Constantine inscribed as it is, was the first emperor who openly obtained the faith of Christ through the ministry of the blessed Silvester, then Pope of Rome. He seems also to have removed the priesthood from the coercive jurisdiction of princes. Through the said edict he seems likewise to have granted to the Church of Rome and to its bishop authorities and powers over all other bishops and churches, which they now claim for themselves from other sources, as we related in the nineteenth of the first part, eighth and ninth above. Along with these he granted coercive jurisdictions over the same fields, estates and many possessions, together with the secular lordship of certain provinces, as is plainly seen by anyone who inspects the said edict. This Constantine, as is read above, was also the first emperor who granted Christians the liberty to gather publicly, to build temples or churches, and by whose command the first Council of Nicaea was assembled. Concerning this, together with the other things that were done in the progress of the Church from the apostles down to the present time, we shall touch upon and introduce histories in their proper places, as far as our purpose requires. Accepting from them whatever agrees with the divine law and right reason, and rejecting what disagrees, we shall set out what was done and how it stands. Having thus recounted in some measure the progress of these matters from their origin, we now proceed further to their determination. We shall make the undoubted supposition, with the Apostle, that there is one catholic faith and not several, whence Ephesians 4: One Lord, one faith. Again, in the same unity, in the same sense, that is, to be believed and confessed by all, the Apostle says a little after, as above: "until we all come together in the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God." From these things we shall infer, first of necessity, that the doubtful senses and opinions of the divine law, especially of the gospel, and whatever contentions or probable controversies have arisen among its teachers, ought to be settled, as we read has happened through the ignorance or malice of some, or both, according to the prophecy of Christ and the Apostle. But we shall show by necessity that this determination pertains only to a general council of all the faithful, or of those who have the authority of all the faithful. Then I shall show, according to the divine law and right reason, that to summon a general council, and, if it is expedient, to gather it by coercive power, belongs to the authority of a human legislator who is faithful and has no superior, and not to any person or particular college, of whatever dignity or condition they may be, unless authority has been granted to them or to them by the said legislator. I shall further show with certainty that nothing can be established concerning the ecclesiastical rite and human acts which binds all men to observance under any penalty, for the state of the present or future world, except through a general council alone, or the supreme faithful legislator immediately, or by authority previously taken from these. From this it will then be shown that no prince, province or community can be interdicted or excommunicated by any priest, whoever he may be, except in the manner ordained by the said general council. Next it will be clearly shown that it belongs to the authority of no single bishop, or other sole individual person, or any particular single college whatever, to institute persons in all the ecclesiastical offices of the world, nor to distribute or confer for them the ecclesiastical temporalities called benefices, but this authority belongs only to the founder or donor, or to the universal faithful legislator, or to him or them to whom the same donor or legislator has granted this power, and in the form and manner he has laid down. Then it will be shown which single bishop and Church, of what kind and by whose authority, it is fitting to appoint as the chief and head of the others. Since it is the business of his Church to make known to all the other bishops and churches those things which have been or shall be ordained by general councils concerning the ecclesiastical rite and other human acts, for the common benefit, tranquillity and quiet of the faithful. Finally, from these things we shall infer of necessity that the determinations made concerning Scripture and the catholic faith, as well as those concerning the ecclesiastical rite and the other institutions of the general council, can be altered, increased, diminished, suspended or wholly revoked only by the authority of a general council alone, and not by the authority of any other particular college or any single person. From all these things it will be drawn out for each one, as if by a sound understanding, that the Bishop of Rome, or his Church, or any other bishop or church, as such, has no power or authority over the other bishops and churches of the kinds mentioned above, by divine or human law, except what has been granted to him simply or for a time by the said general council. On account of this it will also appear that the Bishop of Rome, or any other, unseemly, improperly and beyond what is due, indeed against the judgment of the divine and human demonstrations of the Scriptures, ascribes to himself fullness of power over a prince, community or any single person. And that this bishop and any other whatever, by such self-attribution, must be wholly restrained, even by admonition and coercive power if necessary, by human legislators or those ruling by their authority.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Depravatio quodam propter determinationem autoritatis & primatus iam dicti, cui videlicet dicto vel scripto veritatis sit praestanda credulitas atque confessio de necessitate salutis aeternae.
units.tr: The corruption arising from the determination of the aforesaid authority and primacy, namely, to whom, by word or writing, the belief and confession of truth is to be given as necessary to eternal salvation.

units.la: ANte vero quam ad demonstranda propolita procedamus, oportet attendere perutile quiddam quin imo necessarium, ad eorum omnium certitudinem quae in sequentibus dicturi sumus. Est autem hoc, quod nullam scripturam irreuocabiliter veram credere vel fateri teneantur de necessitate salutis aeternae, nisi eas, quae canonicae appellantur, vel eis quae ad has ex necessitate sequuntur, aut scripturarum sacrarum sensum dubium habentium, eis interpretationibus seu determinationibus, quae per generale fidelium seu catholicorum concilium essent factae, in his praesertim, in quibus error damnationem aeternam induceret, quales sunt articuli fidei Christianae.
units.tr: Before we proceed to demonstrate the propositions, it is very useful, indeed necessary, to attend to one point, for the certainty of all those things which we are about to say in what follows. It is this: that men are not bound, as necessary to eternal salvation, to believe or to confess as irrevocably true any Scripture except those which are called canonical, or those which necessarily follow from these, or, where the sense of the holy Scriptures is doubtful, those interpretations or determinations which have been made by a general council of the faithful or of the Catholics, especially in those matters in which error would bring eternal damnation, such as the articles of the Christian faith.

units.la: Quod autem sacris scripturis firma sit veritatis praestanda credulitas, & confessio, per se notum supponitur omnibus Christianis, quod quia probari non posset aliter quam ipsarum autoritatibus, series praetermisi propter abbreuiationem. Quod vero ipsarum interpretationibus sic factis, vt diximus, eadem sit praestanda credulitas, satis apparet: quoniam ab eodem spiritu nobis reuelatas, pie tenendum videtur. Quod etiam ex scriptura, & in ipsa infallibili deductione firmata, ostendere possumus. Ex scriptura quidem, dicente veritate Matth. 28. & vltimo: Et ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, vsque ad seculi consummationem. Vbi Rabanus; Ex hoc intelligitur quod vsque in finem seculi non sunt d futuri in mundo, qui diuina mansione & inhabitatione sunt digni. Quibus scilicet, ad fidei conseruationem, spiritum Sanctum pie tenendum est semper adesse, vnde Hieronymus: Quamdiu vsque ad consummationem seculi cum discipulis se esse promittit, & illos ostendit semper esse victuros, & se numquam a credentibus recessurum. Idem aperte concincitur ex Actuum 15. ostendente Apostolorum & fidelium congregatione, post ambiguitatis illius determinationem: Visum est enim spiritui Sancto & nobis. Asseruerunt enim & asserit scriptura ipsorum determinationem, in dubietate illa circa fidem, sed tamen esse a spiritu Sancto. Cum igitur fidelium congregatio seu concilium generale per successionem, vere repraesentet congregationem Apostolorum & seniorum ac reliquorum tunc fidelium, in determinandis scripturae sensibus dubiis, in quibus periculum maxime aeternae damnationis induceret error verisimile. Quinimo certum est, deliberationi vniuersalis concilii, spiritus Sancti dirigentis & reuelantis adesse virtutem. Hoc etiam deductione infallibili ex scriptura vim sumente, patere potest: quoniam frustra dedisset Christus legem salutis aeternae, si eius verum intellectum, & quem credere fidelibus est necessarium ad salutem, non aperiret eisdem hunc quaerentibus, & pro ipso inuocantibus simul, sed circa ipsam fidelium pluralitatem errare sineret. Quinimo talis lex non solum ad salutem foret inutilis, sed in hominum aeternam perniciem tradita videretur. Et ideo pie tenendum, determinationes conciliorum generalium in sensib. scripturae dubiis a spiritu Sancto, quae veritatis originem sumere. Ab humano vero legislatore, vt in sequentib. ostendetur, suae obseruationis in confessione, autoritatem coactiuam, promulgationem vero & doctrinam earum a sacerdotibus & euangelicis ministris, horum veram maxime ab eo, quem ad hoc principalem statuerit fidelis legislator humanus superiore carens, aut concilium generale. Quod autem scripturis aliis, quae scilicet humano spiritu reuelatae sunt & tradite, nemo certam credulitatem aut veritatis confessionem praebere teneatur, apparet. Quoniam nulli scripturae falsum significare potenti, tenetur quis firmiter credere, aut ipsam tanquam veram simpliciter confiteri. Hoc autem patiuntur scripturae innitentes humanae inuentioni singularis personae aut collegii partialis. Possunt enim a veritate deficere, vt experientia palam, & habetur Psalmo cxv. Ego autem dixi in excessu meo, omnis homo mendax. Scripturae vero canonicae non sic, quia non sunt ab humana inuentione, sed immediata Dei traditae inspiratione, qui nec falli potest, nec fallere vult. Hanc autem quam diximus sententiam & differentiam humanarum & diuinarum scripturarum, aperte confirmat Augustinus 13. epistolarum ad Hieronymum, cum dixit: Ego enim fateor sanctitati tuae: solum enim scripturarum libris, quae iam canonicae appellantur, didici hunc honorem timorem tamquam deferre, vt nullum earum auctorem scribendo aliquid errasse, firmissime credam. Nisi aliquid in eis offendatur litteris, quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud, quam vel mendosum esse codicem, vel interpretem non assecutum esse quod dictum est, vel me minime intellexisse, non ambigam. Alios autem sanctitate doctrinae prepolleant, non ideo verum putem, quia ipsi ita senserunt. Sed quia mihi, sed illos autores canonicos vel probabili ratione, quod a vero non aberret persuadere potuerint. Hocidem rursus & admonet in prologo terriii de Trinitate, cum dixit: Noli, (lector scil.) meis litteris quasi scripturis canonicis inseruire, sed in illis, (id est canonicis,) & quod non credis, cum inueneris, incuncti inter credenda ipsis quae certum non habeas, nisi certum intellexeris, noli firmiter tenere. Idem quoq; dixit in epistola ad Fortunatianum, & aliis pleriisq; libris, quorum series omisi propter abbreuiationem. Id quoq; videtur sensisse Hieronymus, in expositione catholicae fidei, cum dixit. [illegible, ~40 letters] in Novo & veteri Testamento recipimus in eo librorum numero, quem sancta catholica Ecclesia tradidit auctoritate. Intellexit ergo Beatus Augustinus per canonicas scripturas, eas solas, quæ in volumine Bibliæ continentur, non quidem Decretales aut Decreta Romani Pontificis, & suorum collegii clericorum, quos Cardinales appellant, neq; alia quavis humana statuta de humanis actibus aut contentionibus, & humano spiritu adinventa. Canon enim regula est & mensura, mensura vero, quoniam certa, quod solius divinæ scripturæ inter cæteras proprium est, ut ex Augustin. induximus pridem. Ideoque Augustinus idem scripturas proprias à canonicis separavit necipse qui tantæ fuit sanctitatis, auctoritatis, & scientiæ, suas traditiones, canonicas appellare præsumpsit. Hoc enim impium est, & sacrilegii genus quidam, quoniam in humana traditione dicta vel scripta, error & falsum continere potest, quod in canone secundum veritatem dicto aut ejusmodi, quam per generale concilium canonicæ scripturæ interpretationem factam diximus, nullatenus evenire contingit. Probatur quod deinde ex concilio Carthaginensi tertio prohibitum reperitur rationabiliter valde, ne sub nomine horum, canonicarum scilicet, alia quam scriptura legatur. Unde legitur ibidem, & in Isidoro prædicto codice continetur series hæc: Item placuit, ut præter scripturas canonicas nihil in Ecclesia legatur sub nomine divinarum scripturarum. Sunt autem canonicæ scripturæ, Genesis, & cæteræ, quæ de volumine Bibliæ numerantur ibidem.
units.tr: That firm belief and confession are to be given to the holy Scriptures is taken as self-evident by all Christians; since it could not be proved except by their own authority, I have passed over the series of proofs for the sake of brevity. That the same belief is to be given to their interpretations, made as we have said, is sufficiently clear: since it seems right to hold piously that they were revealed to us by the same Spirit. This we can also show from Scripture, and from infallible deduction drawn from it. From Scripture indeed, when the Truth says in Matthew 28, at the end: And behold, I am with you all days, even unto the end of the world. Where Rabanus says: From this it is understood that until the end of the world there will not be lacking in the world those who are worthy of the divine dwelling and indwelling. To these, for the preservation of the faith, the Holy Spirit is piously to be held as always present; whence Jerome: He promises that he will be with his disciples until the consummation of the world, and shows that they will always be living, and that he will never withdraw from believers. The same is openly gathered from Acts 15, showing the assembly of the Apostles and the faithful after the determination of that doubt: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. For they asserted, and Scripture asserts, that their determination in that doubt concerning the faith was from the Holy Spirit. Since therefore the assembly of the faithful, or a general council, through succession truly represents the assembly of the Apostles, the elders and the rest of the faithful of that time, in determining doubtful senses of Scripture in which error would most probably bring the danger of eternal damnation. Indeed it is certain that the power of the Holy Spirit, directing and revealing, is present in the deliberation of a universal council. This too can be made clear by infallible deduction, drawing its force from Scripture: for Christ would have given the law of eternal salvation in vain, if he did not disclose its true meaning, which it is necessary for the faithful to believe for salvation, to those who seek it and call upon him for it, but allowed them to err concerning this very plurality of the faithful. Indeed such a law would not only be useless for salvation, but would seem to have been handed down to the eternal destruction of men. And therefore it is to be held piously that the determinations of general councils concerning doubtful senses of Scripture come from the Holy Spirit, and derive their origin from truth. But from the human lawgiver, as will be shown in what follows, they receive coercive authority over the observance of the confession; and their promulgation and teaching by priests and evangelical ministers, and above all by him whom the faithful human lawgiver, having no superior, or a general council, has appointed as principal for this purpose. That no one is bound to give firm belief or assured confession of truth to other writings, which have been revealed and handed down by the human spirit, is also clear. For no one is bound to believe firmly, or to confess simply as true, any writing that is able to signify falsehood. But this is the case with writings that rest on the human invention of a single person or a partial college. For they can fall away from the truth, as experience openly shows, and as is said in Psalm 115: I said in my excess, every man is a liar. Canonical Scriptures, however, are not so, because they are not from human invention, but were handed down by the immediate inspiration of God, who can neither be deceived nor wishes to deceive. Augustine openly confirms this opinion which we have stated, and this difference between human and divine Scriptures, in his thirteenth letter to Jerome, when he said: For I confess to your holiness: for I have learned to pay this honour and reverence only to the books of Scripture which are now called canonical, so that I most firmly believe that none of their authors has erred in writing anything. If anything in them shall offend the letter as seeming contrary to the truth, I do not doubt that either the codex is faulty, or the interpreter has not grasped what was said, or I myself have not understood it at all. But other writers, however much they excel in the holiness of their teaching, I do not therefore hold to be true because they thought so, but because they could persuade me, either by probable reasoning or because they did not depart from the truth, of that which is canonical. He gives the same admonition again in the prologue of the third book On the Trinity, when he said: Do not, (reader, that is,) serve my letters as if they were canonical Scriptures, but in those (that is, the canonical ones), and what you do not believe, when you have found it, do not firmly hold among the things to be believed, which you do not know for certain, unless you have understood it for certain. He also said the same in his letter to Fortunatianus, and in many other books, whose series I have omitted for brevity. Jerome also seems to have held this view, in his Exposition of the Catholic Faith, when he said: [illegible, about 40 letters] we receive in the New and Old Testament, in that number of books which the holy Catholic Church has handed down by authority. Blessed Augustine therefore understood by canonical Scriptures those alone which are contained in the volume of the Bible, and not indeed the Decretals or Decrees of the Roman Pontiff and of his college of clerics, whom they call Cardinals, nor any other human statutes concerning human acts or disputes, devised by the human spirit. For a canon is a rule and measure; and a measure, since it is certain, is peculiar to divine Scripture alone among the rest, as we have shown above from Augustine. And so Augustine himself separated his own writings from the canonical ones, and he, of such holiness, authority and learning, did not presume to call his own traditions canonical. For this is impious, and a kind of sacrilege, since in human tradition, whatever is said or written can contain error and falsehood; which does not in any way happen in the canon, which is said according to truth, or in that kind of canon, which we have said was made an interpretation of canonical Scripture by a general council. This is further proved by the fact that the Third Council of Carthage forbade, very reasonably, that under the name of these, that is, the canonical ones, anything other than Scripture should be read. Hence it is read in the same place, and the following passage is contained in the aforesaid codex of Isidore: Likewise it has been decided that, besides the canonical Scriptures, nothing shall be read in the Church under the name of divine Scriptures. The canonical Scriptures are, however, Genesis and the others which are numbered in the volume of the Bible in that place.

units.la: Nec obstat his, quod dicit Augustin. contra Manichæos in epistola fundamenti, inquit enim: Ego non crederem Evangelio, nisi me catholica Ecclesia commoveret auctoritas, in quo humanam auctoritatem videtur auctoritati scripturæ. Semper enim propter quod unumquodque est, & illud magis dictum, quod aliud est credere sermonem aut scripturam aliquam esse traditionis ab aliquo factam: & aliud est credere illam esse veram, utilem vel nociuam, observandam, aut evitandam. Unum quidem enim horum recipere potest quis ex hominum testimonio secundo, & econverso, & utrunq; similiter quandoq;. Velut oblatam & sibi præsentem aliquam, credet quis esse patriam legem ab incolarum communi testimonio, quam esse veram, observandam, & non transgrediendam addiscere potest signo sensibili aliquo, aut pœna quam illius transgressoribus infligi videt sua ratiocinatione recta, præter hominum persuasionem aut dictum. Sic etiam econverso, videns aliquem hominem librum aut domum construere, vel alterum aliquid, credet ex se absq; hominum testimonio, librum aut domum ab hoc esse constructum. Quod autem in libro contenta sint vera vel falsa, utilia vel nociva, prosequenda vel fugienda, ab hominum, præsertim fide dignorum testimonio credere potest. Rursum & utrunq; quandoq; ab hominum testimonio suscipere potest quis, ut quod hic sit Hippocratis liber atq; doctrina, credet qui nunquam viderit Hippocratem ab hominum testimonio. Quod autem in eo contenta seu scripta sint vera vel falsa, servanda vel omittenda propter sanitatem consetudinem, & egritudinem declinandam; suscipiet idem à testimonio peritorum. Eodem quoq; vel quasi consimili modo scripturam aliquam in Biblia contentam, Dei credere traditionem, seu legem à Christo editam esse vel dictam, potest accipere quis ex fidelium communi testimonio seu ecclesiæ catholicæ, qui tamen nec Christum vidit nec audivit, aut alio exteriori sensu percepit. Hanc tamen scripturam veram esse vel observandam, credet ex fide vel signo aliquo sensibili, puta miraculo, absque testimonio cuiusquam, quemadmodum Paulus, qui legem quam persequebatur prius, Christi fuisse doctrinam credebat ex prædicantium quos persequatur testimonio, nec eam propterea verum cotinere credebat. Credidit autem postmodum veram esse, primum ex sensibili miraculo, consequenter ex fide quam habuit. Similiter autem & utrunq; quandoq; suscepta est ab humano testimonio, ut hanc scripturam esse legem à Christo traditam & latam, in ipsa quoq; contenta vera esse, ac observanda propter æternam salutem consequendam, & miseriam fugiendam, creditur & credendum est à multis, nec Christum viderunt, aut exteriori sensu cognoverunt, nec unquam aliquod signum de hoc sensibile perceperunt.
units.tr: Nor does what Augustine says against the Manichaeans in the letter On the Foundation stand in the way of these points; for he says: I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me, in which he seems to set human authority above the authority of Scripture. For it is always the case that the thing on account of which anything is, is the more to be said; and it is one thing to believe that a discourse or some writing is a tradition made by someone, and another to believe that it is true, useful or harmful, to be observed or to be avoided. For one of these two things a man can receive from the second-hand testimony of men, and conversely, and sometimes both alike. As when, seeing some native law present to him, a man will believe from the common testimony of the inhabitants that it is the law of his country, but he can learn by some sensible sign, or by a punishment which he sees inflicted on its transgressors, by his own right reasoning, apart from the persuasion or saying of men, that it is true, to be observed and not to be transgressed. So too conversely: seeing a man build a book or a house, or something else, a man will believe from himself, without the testimony of men, that the book or house was built by this man. But that what is contained in a book is true or false, useful or harmful, to be pursued or to be shunned, a man can believe from the testimony of men, especially of trustworthy men. Again, a man can sometimes receive both alike from the testimony of men: as one who has never seen Hippocrates will believe from men's testimony that this is the book and doctrine of Hippocrates. And that what is contained or written in it is true or false, to be kept or omitted for the sake of health, and for avoiding sickness, he will receive from the testimony of experts. In the same way, or in a quite similar way, a man can receive from the common testimony of the faithful, or of the Catholic Church, that some writing contained in the Bible is God's tradition, or a law given or spoken by Christ, though he has neither seen nor heard Christ nor perceived him by any other outward sense. Yet he will believe that this Scripture is true and to be observed by faith or by some sensible sign, for instance a miracle, without the testimony of anyone; just as Paul, who previously persecuted the law, believed from the testimony of the preachers whom he persecuted that it was the doctrine of Christ, yet did not for that reason believe it to be true. He afterwards believed it to be true, first from a sensible miracle, and consequently from the faith which he had. Likewise both are sometimes received from human testimony: that this Scripture is the law given and brought by Christ, and that what is contained in it is true and to be observed for the sake of obtaining eternal salvation and fleeing misery, is believed and must be believed by many who have neither seen Christ nor known him by outward sense, and never perceived any sensible sign of this.

units.la: Quod ergo dicit Beatus Augustinus: Non crederem Evangelio, &c. potest secundum prædicta secundum habere, unum quidem, quia scripturam illam credidit evangelium esse, id est ex testimonio ecclesiæ catholicæ sive universalis, quamvis hanc scripturam verum continere principalius crediderit ex miraculo fortasse, vel revelatione aliqua quam Christus manifestavit esse verum Deum, & per consequens omnem eius traditionem. Possunt autem habere Augustini verba prædicta, ut testimonio catholicæ ecclesiæ primum accepit & credidit. Licet ipsius sensus sententia primo magis convenire videatur, non enim dicta Christi sive Dei vera quidem sunt, sed testimonium ecclesia catholica vero testimonio: sed testimonium ecclesiæ dicta Christi vera, propter veritatem dictorum Christi, unde nos aut angelus de cœlo evangelizet vobis præterquam quod evangelizavimus, anathema sit. Et consequenter intelligendum, si tota Ecclesia aliud evangelizasset, illud non fuisset verum, & credendum, quia sibi constabat, illud Evangelium esse ... , sed revelationem, in qua falsitas esse non poterat, quamvis ex necessitate consequentiæ & à posteriori bene sequatur: Ecclesia catholica dixit hanc orationem, Deus est trinus in personis, esse veram, ergo est vera, vel de quo nunc alio Christi dicto sive præcepto, quod dicat esse servandum, eo quod dicta ecclesiæ Catholicæ in his quæ circa fidem versantur, a Spiritu Sancto immediate revelata fore, pie tenendum est, ut apparuit ex promissis. Et ideo secundum quemvis sensum,
units.tr: Therefore, when Blessed Augustine says, "I would not believe the Gospel," etc., this can be understood in line with what has been said above. First, he believed that Scripture was the Gospel, that is, on the testimony of the Catholic or universal Church, although he perhaps believed principally that this Scripture contains truth from a miracle or from some revelation by which Christ showed that he is the true God, and consequently all his teaching. Augustine's words can also mean that he first received and believed it on the testimony of the Catholic Church. Yet the sense of his statement seems to fit the first reading better. The words of Christ or of God are true in themselves, not because of the Church's testimony, but the Church's testimony is true because of the truth of Christ's words: "But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1:8). It follows that if the whole Church had preached something else, that would not have been true, and it would not have been believed, since it was plain that this was the Gospel... but a revelation, in which falsehood could not exist. Yet it follows well, by necessity of consequence and a posteriori, that the Catholic Church has said this statement, "God is triune in persons," is true, therefore it is true. Or, concerning another saying or precept of Christ, which bids us keep it, since the statements of the Catholic Church in matters pertaining to faith are to be held with piety as revealed immediately by the Holy Spirit, as appears from the promises. And therefore, in whatever sense the words of Augustine are proposed,

units.la: {Y} Scripturas Sanctas... sensum expònantur Augustini verba proposita, non aduersantur sententiae quam dixi-mus: niam dicit Ecclesiae de his quae circa fidem sunt credere, magis est credere spiritui Sancto, homini. Dicit autem Augustinus prorsus se credere Euangelio propter Ecclesiae Catholicae auctoritatem, quia suae credulitatis initium inde sumpsit, quam spiritus Sancto dirigenuit. Fides quandoque incipit ex auditu. Voco autem catholicam ecclesiam eam, quae propriissime atque verissime dicitur ecclesia secundum ultimam significationem ecclesiae, dictam secundo huius.
units.tr: Holy Scriptures... the words of Augustine that are put forward are explained in a way that does not conflict with the opinion I have stated. For he says that to believe the Church in those matters that pertain to faith is to believe the Holy Spirit rather than a man. Augustine indeed says plainly that he believes the Gospel on account of the authority of the Catholic Church, because he took the beginning of his belief from there, which the Holy Spirit guided. "Faith sometimes begins from hearing." I call the Catholic Church that which is most properly and most truly called the Church in the last signification of the word, as said second in this.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: Cuius sit vel fuerit auctoritas diffiniendi seu determinandi dubias scripturae sacrae sententias.
units.tr: Whose authority it is, or has been, to define or determine the doubtful sentences of Holy Scripture.

units.la: His itaque sic praemissis concludenda iam proposita resumentes, ostendere volumus, quod debios sensus siue sententias scripturae sacrae iam exortas aut orituras, cum ortae fuerint, praesertim circa fidei articulos, praecepta & prohibita, sit expediens & necessarium terminare, quoniam expediens est, quinimo necessarium sine quo fidei unitas minime saluaretur, error & schisma contingeret circa fidem inter Christi fideles. Hoc autem est determinatio dubiarum, & quandoque contrariarum sententiarum doctorum quorundam circa legem diuinam. In hac enim opinionum diuersitates aut contrarietates, diuersas sectas inducerent, schismata & errores, sicut ex iam dicto Isidori codice capitulo, intitulato, Incipit prefatio Niceni concilii, recitatur. Quodam enim Alexandrino presbytero, Arrio nominato, Christum sic Dei filium esse dicente, ut ipsum existimaret pure creaturam existere, & per consequens pati Deo inaequalem atque minorem. Huius erroris diuulgatione, numerosa multitudo Christianorum labefacta fuit, suisseque amplior, nec ab errore reuocata, nisi verus in hoc scripturae sensus a falso determinatus fuisset. Sic quoque in spiritum Sanctum, & circa personae ac essentiae unitatem & pluralitatem in Christo, insanas quidam protulere sententias, propter quarum discretionem a veris & ipsarum reprobationem ac damnationem conuocatae ac congregatae sunt quatuor primae Synodi, Nicena, Constantinopolitana, Ephesina, & Calcedonensis. Has etenim controuersias inter ecclesiae Christianae doctores, veros aut simulatos fideles, propheta uit Christus, Luca 21. & Apostolus prima ad Timoth. 4. & secunda ad eundem tertio, quorum series praetermisi propter ipsarum notitiam, & abbreuiationem sermonis. Huic consequenter ostendo, quod huius determinationis auctoritas principalis, mediata vel immediata soli-us sit generalis concilii Christianorum, aut valentior pars ipsorum vel eorum quib. ab vniuersitate fidelium Christianorum autoritas haec concessa fuerit, sic videlicet, ut omnes mundi prouinciae seu communitates notabiles secundum sui legislatoris humani, determinationem siue unici siue pluris & secundum ipsarum proportionem in quantitate ac qualitate personarum viros eligant fideles, presbyteros primum, & non presbyteros consequenter, idoneos tamen, ut vita probatiores, & in lege diuina peritiores, qui tanquam iudices secundum iudicis significationem prima vicem vniuersitatis fidelium repraesentantes, iam dicta sibi per vniuersitates auctoritate concessa, conueniant ad certum orbis locum, conuenientiorem tamen secundum plurimae partis ipsorum determinationem, vel suorum legislatorum, in quo simul ea quae circa legem diuinam apparuerint dubia, vtilia, expedientia, & necessaria terminari, diffinient: & reliqua circa ritum ecclesiasticum seu cultum diuinum, q futura sint et ad quietem & tranquillitatem fidelium, habeant ordinare. Ociose nanq; ac inutiliter ad congregationem hanc conuenire multitudo fidelium imperita, inutiliter autem, quonia turbaretur ab operib. necessariis ad vitae corporalis sustentationem, q onerosum ei esset, aut importabile forte. Quamuis ad hanc congregationem, fideles omnes obligentur lege diuina propter finem praedictum, licet diuersimode, sacerdotes quidem n. eo q ipsorum officium sit legem docere secundum ipsius verum sensum, & ea procurare quae ad ipsius iynceritatem pficere possint errores contrarios reprobare, ab ipsis quoq; suis exhortationibus, arguitionibus, & increpationibus homines reuocate. Vnde Matth. vlt. ad sacerdotes omnes in persona tantum Apostolorum ait veritas: Euntes docete omnes gentes, propter quod in persona omnium Apostolorum loquens Apostolus prima ad Corinth. 9. dicebat: Necessitas mihi incumbit, vae mihi si non euangelizauero. Obligantur autem sacerdotibus consequenter amplius reliqua multitudine, qui periti fuerint in lege diuina, debent enim his aliquos excitare & conuenire cum sacerdotibus, praesertim si sufficienter adhaec requisiti fuerint vel mandati. Quoniam scienti bonum facere, & non facienti, peccatum est illi, ut scribitur Iacobi 4. Pro reliquis etiam diffiniendis extra legem diuinam, quae sunt ad fidelium communem utilitatem & pacem, interesse possunt & debent concilio, qui ad hoc statuti fuerint per humanum legislatorem fidelem. Legislatores vero ad hoc etiam obligantur, eligendo personas idoneas ad concilium integrandum, eisq; de necessariis temporalibus prouidendum: & venire recusantes, ad hoc tamen idoneos & electos, tam sacerdotes quam non sacerdotes propter vtilitatem publicam, si oportuerit, compellendum. Quod solius generalis iam dicti concilii sit auctoritas praedicta diffiniendi & ordinandi secundum modum, nullius vero alterius personae singularis, aut alterius particularis collegii, conuinctionis demonstrationib. & scripturae sacrae autoritatibus conuinci potest, qualib. legum latorum & ecclesiasticorum institutionem secundariam, 11. prima, & 17. huius monstrauimus pertinere, nola demonstrationum minori extremitate mutata, vt videlicet circa legem diuinam determinatio diffiniendi dubia cum reliquis circa ritum ecclesiasticum siue cultu diuinum ac fidelium pacis & vnitate ordinandis assumantur pro termino legis aut officiorum ecclesiasticorum secundariae institutionis. Tanto ampliori necessitate attendenda in his, quanto de lege seu fide tenenda, & his quae omnibus fidelibus proficere vel nocere possunt, discretio & cura diligentior est habenda. Sic nanque fecerunt Apostoli cum senioribus, de his quae dubia circa Euangelium occurrerunt, vt apparet Act. 15. & seriose induximus 16. huius. Non enim dubium illud de circumcisione beatus Petrus aut alter Apostolus, seorsum aut singulariter diffiniuit, sed conuenerunt super his omnes apostoli & seniores siue peritiores in lege. Signum autem verum esse quod diximus, est, quoniam & conciliis principalib. in diffiniendis scripturae dubiis, aderant Imperatores & Imperatrices fideles cū suis officialib. vt ex Isidori saepe dicto codice satis apparet, vbi sequenti c. induximus ipsum à secunda in octaua, quis eo tempore non tanta vocaret necessitas, non sacerdotum praesentiam, quanta moderno propter instantium sacerdotum & episcoporum turbam maiorem, diuinae legis, quantum oporteret, ignaram. Vnde sacerdotib. inuicem diffidentib. de credendis ad salutem aeternam, de iplorum saniori parte, fidelium pars valentior habet iudicare, quis ipsis omnib. concordantib. credendum sit in praedictis, sic tamen promotis ad ordines, quemadmodum diximus 7. huius. Propter ea etiam ostendere volo rursum determinationem hanc nullatenus ad solum Rom. episcopum pertinere, neq; ad ipsum et cum solo Cardinalium coetu, & consequenter ex hoc, quod ad nullum episcopum alium vnicum siue solum, siue ipsum & aliud aliquod particulare collegium. Esto nanq; sicut euenire contingit, haereticum aliquem ad Rom. Pontificem assumi, vel postquam assumptus fuerit, si non antea, in hanc cadere labem, ignorantia vel malitia, vel vtriusq;, quales iam quidem assumpti leguntur, videl. Liberius, nativitate Romanus. Siquidem solus hic Pontifex, aut cum solo suo coetu Cardinalium, quos sui complices erroris verisimiliter fore continget, quia sibi quales vult absq; cuiusquam determinatione assumit & se dicit assumere posse: aliquid determinauerit circa dubiam aliquam scripturae sententiam: nunquid huius Episcopi aut eius & sui solius collegii sententia standum erit, qui forte ignorantia vel malitia cupiditate aut ambitione vel alia quauis erunt affectione sinistra seducti? De quo ne longe petatur exemplum, id contigisse videmus cuidam Papae Romano. Ipse enim per se singulariter, aut cum solo suorum Cardinalium coetu, ne summam Christi paupertatem & perfectionis statum deserere videretur, cum hoc volens temporalia etiam immobilia in suo vendicandi retinere dominio & seculariter principari, edictum emisit circa summae paupertatis siue perfectionis statum, cuius sententia per falsam interpretationem Christi Euangelio contradicit, sicut palam ostendimus 13. & 14. huius. Propter quod soli cuiuis Episcopo aut sibi & suo soli collegio clericorum hac autoritate concessa fidelium vniuersitas naufragii circa fidem periculo subiacebit, vt ex iam dictis atque dicendis compositae mentis quilibet intelligere poterit. Amplius si solius Romani Papae, aut alterius cuiusquis solius Episcopi, quemadmodum dictum est, talis esset autoritas; vel si secundum Isidorum praedicto Codice, capitulo, cui titulus, Praefatio Isidori in sequenti opere: epistolae siue decreta Romani Pontificis aequalia vel non imparia forent autoritate, his, quae determinata & diffinita sunt per concilium generale, omnes seculi principatus omnia regna & mundi prouincias, ac personas singulares cuiuscunque dignitatis, praeeminentiae, vel conditionis existant, antistiti Romano primo forent coactiua iurisdictione subiecti. Decreuit enim hoc octauus Bonifacius Papa Romanus, per ipsius epistolam siue decretum quoddam, cuius initium: Vnam sanctam catholicam Ecclesiam, eius vero finis: Porro subesse Romano pontifici omnem humanam creaturam, declaramus, dicimus, & diffinimus omnino esse de necessitate salutis. Cum igitur semel determinata circa scripturam per concilium generale rite vocatum, congregatum, & secundum formam debitam celebratum, & consummatum, praesertim quae ad salutem aeternam vera credere necessarium sit, immutabilis & infallibilis veritatis existant, quemadmodum demonstratum est circa principium 19. huius. Obtineret igitur epistola haec Bonifaciana certam & indubiam ac irrevocabilem veritatem. Nunc autem eam ab initio nunc & semper constat esse falsam, erroneam, cunctisque civiliter viuentibus praeiudicialissimam omnium excogibilium falsorum, sicut indubie demonstratum est quarto, quinto, & nono huius.
units.tr: Having laid these things down, and now returning to the conclusions proposed, I wish to show that doubtful senses or opinions of Holy Scripture, which have already arisen or will arise, once they have arisen, especially concerning the articles of faith and the commands and prohibitions, ought to be settled and must be settled. This is expedient, indeed necessary, since without it the unity of faith could not be preserved, and error and schism about the faith would arise among the faithful of Christ. Such settling is the determination of doubtful and sometimes contrary opinions of certain teachers concerning the divine law. For these differences or contrarieties of opinion would produce diverse sects, schisms and errors, as is recited from the chapter already cited from Isidore's codex, entitled "Here begins the preface of the Nicene Council." There, a certain Alexandrian presbyter named Arius said that Christ was the Son of God in such a way that he thought him to be merely a creature, and consequently unequal to God and less than God. By the spread of this error a large multitude of Christians was shaken, and it would have grown larger, nor would it have been recalled from error, unless the true sense of Scripture had been separated from the false by determination. Likewise, some put forward insane opinions concerning the Holy Spirit, and concerning the unity and plurality of person and essence in Christ. For the distinguishing of these from the true, and their rejection and condemnation, the four first synods were called and assembled: Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon. Christ foretold these controversies among the teachers of the Christian Church, whether true or pretended faithful, in Luke 21, and the Apostle in 1 Timothy 4 and in 2 Timothy 3; I have passed over the list of them for the sake of brevity. Next, I show that the principal authority for this determination, whether mediate or immediate, belongs solely to a general council of Christians, or to the greater part of them, or to those to whom the authority has been granted by the whole body of the faithful. This would be done in such a way that all the provinces or notable communities of the world, according to the determination of their human lawgiver, whether one or several, and in proportion to the number and quality of their people, choose men who are faithful, first elders and then, in turn, non-elders, yet suitable: men more approved in life and more skilled in the divine law. These, as judges (in the sense of the word "judge"), representing first the whole body of the faithful, having received the authority granted to them by the communities, should meet at a certain place in the world, one more convenient according to the determination of the greater part of them or of their lawgivers. There, they shall define whatever doubts appear concerning the divine law, which are useful, expedient and necessary to settle, and they shall arrange the remaining matters concerning ecclesiastical rite or divine worship, which are to be for the peace and tranquillity of the faithful. For it would be idle and useless for an unskilled multitude of the faithful to gather at this assembly, useless too because they would be distracted from the labours necessary for the support of bodily life, which might be burdensome or even intolerable for them. Although all the faithful are bound by the divine law to take part in this assembly for the aforesaid end, they are bound in different ways: priests, because their office is to teach the law according to its true sense and to take care of the things that can help its sincerity, to reject contrary errors, and to recall men from them by their exhortations, rebukes and reproofs. Hence the Truth said, in Matthew's last chapter, to all priests, in the person of the Apostles alone: "Go and teach all nations." For this reason the Apostle, speaking in the person of all the Apostles, said in 1 Corinthians 9: "Necessity is laid upon me; woe is me if I do not preach the gospel." Moreover, the rest of the multitude who are skilled in the divine law are bound to follow the priests; for they ought to rouse some of their number and meet with the priests, especially if they have been sufficiently asked or commanded for this. "To him who knows how to do good, and does not do it, it is sin," as is written in James 4. For the other matters to be settled outside the divine law, which concern the common utility and peace of the faithful, those who have been appointed to this by a faithful human lawgiver may and should take part in the council. Lawgivers too are bound to this, by choosing suitable persons to form the council, and by providing for them the necessary temporal things; and those who refuse to come, though they are suitable and chosen, whether priests or non-priests, shall be compelled, if necessary, for the public benefit. That the aforesaid authority to define and ordain according to this manner belongs to the general council alone, and to no single person or particular college, can be demonstrated by the proofs of reason and by the authorities of Holy Scripture, by which we have shown, in the eleventh and seventeenth chapters of this work, that the secondary institution of lawgivers and ecclesiastical persons pertains to it. The minor premise of the demonstrations is not changed: namely, that the determination of doubtful matters concerning the divine law, together with the remaining matters concerning ecclesiastical rite or divine worship, and to be arranged for the peace and unity of the faithful, are taken as the limit of the law or of ecclesiastical offices of secondary institution. The more necessary it is to attend to these things, the more carefully must discernment and diligence be exercised, since they concern the law or faith to be held, and what can benefit or harm all the faithful. For so the Apostles did with the elders concerning the doubts that arose about the gospel, as appears in Acts 15, and as I have set out at length in the sixteenth chapter of this work.
