For the blessed Peter, or another Apostle, did not define that doubt about circumcision alone or singly; rather, all the Apostles and elders, or those more skilled in the law, met together about these things. The sign that what we have said is true is that at the principal councils for the definition of doubtful points of Scripture, Christian emperors and empresses were present with their officials, as is clear enough from the often-cited codex of Isidore, where in the following chapter I have quoted it from the second to the eighth. At that time, such necessity did not call for the presence of priests in such numbers as now, when, because of the greater crowd of importuning priests and bishops, the multitude is more ignorant of the divine law than it ought to be. Hence, when priests disagree among themselves about what must be believed for eternal salvation, the more sound part of the priests, and the stronger part of the faithful, have the duty to judge which of them, when all agree, is to be believed in the matters aforesaid; provided, however, that they have been promoted to orders as I said in the seventh chapter of this work. For this reason I also wish to show again that this determination in no way belongs to the Roman bishop alone, nor to him with only the college of Cardinals; and consequently not to any single bishop, whether alone or with some other particular college. For suppose, as may well happen, that some heretic is chosen as Roman Pontiff, or, after being chosen, falls into this stain, whether through ignorance or malice, or both, as is read of some who were indeed chosen, namely Liberius, a Roman by birth. If this Pontiff alone, or with only his college of Cardinals (who will probably be accomplices of his error, since he chooses them as he likes, without anyone's determination, and says he may do so), should determine something about some doubtful sentence of Scripture, shall we have to abide by the opinion of this bishop, or of him and his college alone, who may perhaps have been led astray by ignorance, malice, greed, ambition, or some other sinister affection? Lest we seek an example from far off, we see that this has happened with a certain Roman Pope. For he, acting alone or with only the college of his Cardinals, wishing not to seem to abandon the supreme poverty of Christ and the state of perfection, while nevertheless willing to keep temporal and immovable goods in his own ownership and to rule secularly, issued an edict concerning the state of supreme poverty or perfection; its opinion, through a false interpretation, contradicts the gospel of Christ, as we have plainly shown in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters of this work. Therefore, if this authority were granted to any bishop alone, or to himself and his own college of clergy alone, the whole body of the faithful would be exposed to the danger of shipwreck in the faith, as anyone of sound mind may understand from what has been said and what is to be said. Furthermore, if such authority belonged to the Roman Pope alone, or to any other single bishop, as has been said; or if, according to Isidore in the aforesaid codex, in the chapter entitled "Preface of Isidore to the following work," the letters or decrees of the Roman Pontiff were equal or not inferior in authority to those things which are determined and defined by a general council, then all the princes of the secular world, all kingdoms and provinces of the world, and individual persons of whatever dignity, eminence or condition, would first be subject to the Roman prelate by coercive jurisdiction. For Boniface VIII, Roman Pope, decreed this by a certain letter or decree of his, which begins: "We, holy Catholic Church, one," and ends: "Moreover, we declare, say and define that it is altogether necessary to salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff." Since, therefore, what has once been determined about Scripture by a general council rightly called, assembled, celebrated according to the due form and completed, especially what it is necessary to believe as true for eternal salvation, is of unchangeable and infallible truth, as has been demonstrated near the beginning of the nineteenth chapter of this work, then this Boniface letter would hold a certain and undoubted and irrevocable truth. But now it is established that it is false from the beginning, and now and always erroneous, and most prejudicial to all who live civilly of all falsehoods that can be devised, as has been indubitably demonstrated in the fourth, fifth and ninth chapters of this work.

units.la: Quam etiam falsam esse, ac dictum Isidori, nisi fortassis illud pia interpretatione iuuetur, manifeste demonstrat quinti Clementi successoris eiusdem Bonifacii epistola siue decretum, cuius initium: Meruit charissimi filii nostri Philippi Regis Francorum Illustris, eius vero finis: Tanquam tam ad Ecclesiam, quod etiam quo ad regem & regnum superius nominatos. Hac enim dictus Clemens exprimit diffiniendo Bonifacianam epistolam, in nullo praeiudicare regi aut regno praedicto. Cum ergo nec Rex praedictus, nec illius successor aliquis vel regnicola suus quisquam, iuxta dicti Clementis conscientiam, ac omnium Christianorum scientiam verum crediderint, aut creditur fuerint, sed falsum apertum esse, quod continet epistola supradicta in eo articulo, quo cunctos sibi subiicit principatus & regna per necessitatem sequitur, quod credere id, non sit de necessitate salutis, nam si sic, praeiudiciale foret vtriq; non credenti. Amplius consideranti, videbuntur tales epistolae siue decreta insaniae quaedam. Nam ea quae Bonifacii verum continente, ad ipsius credulitatem omnes mundi principes & populos obligat, ea vero quae Clementis, non omnes, quoniam ab hac credulitate Francorum princeps cum suis regnicolis solus eximitur. Sunt igitur aliqua de necessitate salutis, autoritate scripturae quibusdam credenda, quibusdam vero minime. Non ergo vnus dominus, nec vna fides, nec Christo in vnitate fidei, omnes tenentur occurrere, cuius oppositum dicit aperte doctorum ad Ephes. 4.
units.tr: This is also shown to be false, and Isidore's saying as well (unless perhaps it is helped by a pious interpretation), by the letter or decree of Clement, successor of the same Boniface, in the fifth place, whose opening runs: "Our most beloved son Philip, the illustrious King of the Franks, has deserved..." and whose end reads: "as much towards the Church as also towards the king and kingdom named above." For in this decree Clement, defining Boniface's letter, expresses that it prejudices in no way the aforesaid king or kingdom. Since, then, neither that king nor any successor of his, nor any of his subjects, has believed it to be true, according to the conscience of Clement and the knowledge of all Christians, but it is manifestly false, what the letter quoted above contains in that article, where it subjects all principalities and kingdoms to itself, it follows of necessity that to believe this is not necessary for salvation; for if it were, it would be prejudicial to all who do not believe it. Considering further, such letters or decrees will seem to be a kind of madness. For those things in Boniface's letter which are held to be true bind all the princes and peoples of the world to belief in them, whereas those of Clement do not bind all, since the prince of the Franks, with his subjects, alone is exempted from this belief. There are therefore some things necessary for salvation, to be believed on the authority of Scripture by some, but by others in no way. Not therefore one Lord, nor one faith, nor are all bound to meet Christ in the unity of faith, the opposite of which the teachers openly state on Ephesians 4.

units.la: Y 3 E ij Est rursum interrogandum Clementi, secundum quem sanum intellectum ex sua fide merito potuit Francorum Rex, cum populis sibi subiectis, non obligari credere, quæ credenda sunt de necessitate salutis. Aut igitur ex fide meruerunt hæretici & infideles fieri, aut epistola Bonifaciana continet apertum mendacium, & sic ista quæ à veritate non veniunt, plerunque etiam nulle impellente, seipsa subvertunt, ut dicit Augustinus 7 de ciuitate Dei, cap. 16.
units.tr: Again, Clement must be asked, according to what sound understanding from his own faith the King of the Franks, with the peoples subject to him, could rightly not be bound to believe what must be believed of necessity for salvation. Either, then, by faith heretics and unbelievers have deserved to become such, or the letter of Boniface contains a manifest lie, and so those things which do not come from the truth, very often even without any compelling cause, subvert themselves, as Augustine says in book 7 of the City of God, chapter 16.

units.la: Amplius dignum est admirari cæteros reges & populos, ipsisq; conuenienter quærendum, quis locus aut sensus scripturæ, ipsos præter Francorum Regem constituat Romano Papæ iurisdictione subiectos, cuius illud unus reliquo magis ad suæ salutis necessitatem credere teneatur. Hoc enim velut figmento simile multa fuit & est irrisione dignum: & ex talia proferentium ambitione, ac principandi secularitor ardore ac supradicti Francorum Regis Illustrissimi terrore procedens.
units.tr: Furthermore, it is worthy of wonder that other kings and peoples, and it must be asked fittingly, what place or sense of Scripture establishes them, apart from the King of the Franks, as subject to the jurisdiction of the Roman Pope, such that one more than another should be bound to believe this for the necessity of his salvation. For this, being like a fiction, has been and is worthy of much mockery; and it proceeds from the ambition of those who put forward such things, from the zeal of secular rule, and from the terror of the aforesaid most illustrious King of the Franks.

units.la: Quod autem prædiximus, generale concilium etiam per bon sacerdotes integrari posse, deliberandis quoque per concilium conuenienter una cum sacerdotibus suum apposituri & interposituri decretum, suadebimus primum ex Isidori prædicto codice, capitulo, cui titulus, Incipiunt Canones, id est regulæ ecclesiasticæ. Continentur enim in eo inter cætera series hæc: Deinde ingrediantur laici, qui electione concilij interesse meruerunt. Multo magis igitur qui fuerint literati, & in lege diuina periti, quamquam non sacerdotes existant. Sic nō fecerunt apostoli cum senioribus, ut prudem induximus. Unde oportet attendere, quod in ecclesia primitiua & antiquis temporib. præsertim ante tempora Constantini soli sacerdotes & quasi omnes erant, si ut soli tenentur, & esse debent, legis diuinæ doctores, iuxta illud Malachiæ 2. Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & legem (diuinā scil.) requirent ex ore eius. Unde etiam Apostolus 1. ad Tim. 3 & ad Titum 1. Oportet Episcopum, id est sacerdotem, doctorem esse, amplectentem cum qui secundum doctrinam est fidelem sermonem, ut potens sit exhortari in doctrina sana, & eos qui contradicunt, arguere. Propter quod soli tales existentes sacerdotes, ad dissicilia vel dubia circa scripturam & fidem interpretanda & diffinienda, quasi soli conuenire solebant.
units.tr: As for what we said before, that a general council can also be made up of good priests, and that, with the priests, it may appropriately deliberate and set down and insert its own decree, we shall first argue for it from the aforesaid code of Isidore, the chapter entitled Here begin the Canons, that is, the ecclesiastical rules. For in it, among other things, this sequence is contained: Then let the laymen enter, who have deserved to take part in the council by election. Much more, therefore, those who are learned and skilled in the divine law, although they are not priests. So the apostles did not act with the elders, as we have shown above. Hence it must be observed that in the primitive Church, and in ancient times, especially before the time of Constantine, all, or nearly all, were priests; and if priests alone are held and ought to be the teachers of the divine law, according to that of Malachi 2: The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law (namely the divine law) at his mouth. Hence also the Apostle, 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1: A bishop, that is a priest, ought to be a teacher, holding fast the faithful word which is according to doctrine, that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to convict those who contradict. On account of which, those who alone were such priests were accustomed to gather, as if alone, to interpret and define matters difficult or doubtful concerning Scripture and faith.

units.la: Nunc vero propter ecclesiastici regiminis corruptionem, plurima pars sacerdotum & episcoporum in sacra scriptura periti sunt parum. & si dicere liceat insufficienter, eo quod temporalia beneficiorum, quæ assequuntur officiis ambitiosi, cupidi, & causidici quidam obtinere volunt & obtinent obsequio prece vel pretio, vel seculari potentia. Et Deo teste ac fidelium multitudine, sacerdotes plurimos, abbates & ecclesiasticos Prælatos quosdam me vidisse at audiu esse memini adeo diminutos, ut etiam nec grammatice congruum scirent proferre sermonem.
units.tr: But now, on account of the corruption of ecclesiastical government, the greater part of priests and bishops are little skilled in Holy Scripture, and, if it be permitted to say so, insufficiently, since the temporal benefices, which ambitious, greedy and litigious men pursue, wish to obtain and do obtain by servility, by entreaty, by money, or by secular power. And, God being witness and a multitude of the faithful, I remember having seen and heard of many priests, abbots and certain ecclesiastical prelates so diminished that they did not even know how to speak grammatically correct Latin.

units.la: Et quod amplius horrendum est, in ecclesiastico ritu sciui & vidi hominem citra vigesimum ætatis suæ annum diuinæ legis ignarum quasi penitus, cui tamen in famosa & populosa ciuitate commissa est episcopalis cura, eo non solum sacerdotali ordine carenti, verum etiam diaconatus & subdiaconatus exorti, quod quidam asseruit se licite posse. Hoc etiam & quasi consimile inconueniens de facto persæpe faciens, propter potentum fauorem sibi quærédum, qui super ecclesiasticorum officiorum institutionem, & beneficiorum distributionem, Romanus Episcopus habere se dicit, velut Christi vicarium plenitudinem potestatis. A quo siquidem conuenienter interrogandum, cur talis episcoporum & sacerdotum in generali concilio congregabitur turba? Et qualiter in dubiis circa scripturas determinare noverit veros sensus a falsis, propter quod in horum defectum, non sacerdotes approbatos fideles, iuxta fidelis legislatoris determinationem scripturæ sacræ doctos sufficienter, vita & moribus etiam talibus episcopis & sacerdotibus præpollentes, perutile quinimo necessarium legi diuinæ, ac rectæ rationi consonum est tali concilio interesse, ipsorumq; deliberatione cum reliquis, dubia circa fidem & quæsita cætera diffiniri.
units.tr: And what is still more horrible, in the ecclesiastical rite I have known and seen a man younger than twenty years of age, almost wholly ignorant of the divine law, to whom nevertheless the episcopal care of a famous and populous city was entrusted, he not only lacking the priestly order but having risen to the diaconate and subdiaconate, which some asserted he could lawfully do. He also did this, and very often did similar improper things, in order to seek the favour of the powerful, who say that the Roman Bishop holds, over the institution of ecclesiastical offices and the distribution of benefices, the fullness of power as Christ's vicar. To him, indeed, it must fittingly be asked why such a crowd of bishops and priests should be gathered in a general council; and how they would know how to determine in doubtful matters about Scripture the true senses from the false. For which reason, in their default, it is most useful, indeed necessary, and consonant with the divine law and right reason, that approved faithful non-priests, learned sufficiently in Holy Scripture according to the determination of the faithful lawgiver, and also excelling in life and morals beyond such bishops and priests, should take part in such a council, and that, by their deliberation together with the rest, doubtful matters concerning faith and other questions be defined.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Cuius sit vel fuerit autoritas hactenus coactiua congregandi generale concilium sacerdotum, & Episcoporum, ac reliquorum fidelium, cuiusue sit autoritas in ipso aliquid statuendi quod fideles obliget ad pœnam aut culpam pro statu præsentis seculi vel venturi, & cuius rursum sit in hoc seculo statutorum aut diffinitorum in generali concilio, quemlibet transgressorem arcere, amplius quod nullus Episcopus aut sacerdos excommunicare potest principem aut populū interdicere quenquam, nec ecclesiastica temporalia beneficia, vel decimas, aut disciplinarum cuiquam conferre licentias, nec officia ciuilia quenquam, nisi iuxta generalis concilii aut legislatoris, vel utriusq;, determinationem atq; concessionem.
units.tr: Whose authority has hitherto been, or been, to compel the convening of a general council of priests, bishops and other faithful; and whose authority it is to decree within that council anything that binds the faithful to punishment or guilt for the state of the present or future world; and whose again it is, in this world, to restrain by force any transgressor of the statutes or decisions of a general council. Further, that no bishop or priest can excommunicate a prince or place a people under interdict, nor grant to anyone ecclesiastical temporal benefices, tithes, or licences of discipline, nor civil offices to anyone, except according to the determination and grant of a general council or of the lawgiver, or of both.

units.la: Nunc autem ostendere volo, ad solius humanis legislatoris fidelis superiore carentis, autoritatem pertinere, aut eius vel eorum, cui vel quibus per iam dictum legislatore potestas hæc committa fuerit generale concilium conuocare, personas ad hoc idoneas determinare, ipsumq; congregari, celebrari & secundum formam debitam facere consumari, rebelles quoq; ad conueniendum & iam dicta necessaria & vtilia faciendum, determinatorum quoq; ac ordinatorum in dicto concilio transgressores tam sacerdotes quam non sacerdotes, clericos aut non cleticos licite secundum diuinam & humanam legem, per coactiuam arcere potentiam. Quæ quamuis demonstrata sint 15.1.4.5.9.46 11.huius in quib.per demonstrationem ostensum est, & autoritate scripturæ certificatum amplius iurisdictiones coactiuas super omnes indifferenter sacerdotes & non sacerdotes, personarum determinationes & approbationes, officiorum quoq; institutiones omnium, ad solius lius humani legislatoris fidelis autoritatem, minime vero ad sacerdotalis collegii solius, inquantum huiusmodi pertinere, volumus tamen nunc ea persuadere per iam dictum Isidori codicem plerisque locis, maxime vero in quibus ea quæ facta sunt, legi diuinæ ac recte rationi consona recitat. Primum quidem igitur, in capitulo, cui titulus, Incipit prefatio Niceni concilii, vbi sic inquit: Ibiq; Arium ccccxviii. residentibus Episcopis adesse iubet, (Constantinus videlicet,) ac de eius propositionib. indicare, Episcopos scilicet. Ecce quod iussu legislatoris congregati fuerunt Episcopi & Sacerdotes in concilio supradicto. Idem rursum in capitulo, cui titulus, Incipit concilium 630. Episcoporum, vbi sic inquit: Sancta & magna & venerabilis synodus, quæ secundum gratiam Dei ex decreto pißimorum Imperatorum Valentiani & Marciani congregata est: Amplius ex capitulo, cui titulus, Explicit concilium Toletanum septimum, incipit octauum: vbi sic inquit; Anno vero orthodoxi atque gloriosi, & vera clementia dignitate pracipuis Recesuinthi Regis, cum omnes nos diuina ordinatio voluntatis, eiusdem Principis Serenissimo iussu, in basilica sanctorum Apostolorum ad sacrum Synodi coegisset aggregari conuentum. Idem adhuc ex capitulo cui titulus Explicit concilium Toletanum vndecimum, incipit 12. Idem rursum ex eo, cui titulus, Explicit concilium Bracharense primum, incipit secundum. Amplius idem ex epistola Leonis Papæ Romani ad Ephesinam synodum. Idem rursum ex epistola Leonis Papæ Romani, ad Theodosium Imperatorem. Adhuc idem ex epistola Leonis Episcopi Marciano Augusto, cuius initium est, Poposceram. Idem amplius in epistola ad Marcianum augustum, cuius initium est: Multa mihi in omnibus. Idem in aliis plerisque locis, dicti codicis & epistolis, quarum series propter rei notitiam & sermonis abbreuiationem omisi.
units.tr: Now I wish to show that this authority belongs solely to the human lawgiver who is faithful and has no superior, or to him or to those to whom this power has been committed by the said lawgiver: to convene a general council, to determine suitable persons for it, to gather it, to celebrate it and bring it to completion in due form; and also to restrain by coercive power rebels who refuse to assemble and to do the necessary and useful things mentioned, and likewise transgressors of the decisions and ordinances made in the said council, whether priests or non-priests, clerics or non-clerics, lawfully according to divine and human law. Although these matters have been demonstrated in 15, 1, 4, 5, 9, 46 and 11 of this work, where by demonstration it has been shown, and certified by the authority of Scripture, that coercive jurisdiction over all priests and non-priests alike, the determination and approval of persons, and the institution of all offices belong to the authority of the sole human lawgiver who is faithful, and not to the college of priests alone as such, nevertheless we now wish to persuade of these things also by the said Codex of Isidore, in many places, especially where it recounts things done that are consonant with divine law and right reason. First, then, in the chapter entitled Here begins the preface of the Council of Nicaea, where it says: There, with 318 bishops in attendance, he orders Arius to appear (namely Constantine) and to give an account of his propositions, namely the bishops. Behold, by command of the lawgiver the bishops and priests were gathered in the aforesaid council. Again, in the chapter entitled Here begins the council of 630 bishops, where it says: The holy, great and venerable synod, which by the grace of God was gathered by the decree of the most pious emperors Valentinian and Marcian. Further, from the chapter entitled Here ends the seventh Council of Toledo, here begins the eighth, where it says: In the year of the orthodox and glorious King Recesuinth, distinguished by true clemency and dignity, when the divine ordering of his will, by the most serene command of the same prince, had gathered all of us in the basilica of the holy Apostles into a synod. Likewise from the chapter entitled Here ends the eleventh Council of Toledo, here begins the twelfth. Likewise from the one entitled Here ends the first Council of Braga, here begins the second. Further, likewise from the epistle of Leo, Roman Pope, to the Synod of Ephesus. Likewise again from the epistle of Leo, Roman Pope, to the Emperor Theodosius. Also likewise from the epistle of Leo the Bishop to the Emperor Marcian, beginning I had asked. Likewise in the epistle to the Emperor Marcian, beginning Many things to me in all. Likewise in many other places of the said codex and its epistles, the series of which I have omitted for the sake of brevity and because the matter is known.

units.la: Quod autem ad solum Romanum Episcopum vel ipsum & suorum Cardinalium solum collegium, non pertineat autoritas supradicta, suaderi potest cum prædictis, ex eo, quod si reus esset ipse aut cum suo collegio, criminis alicuius propter quod expediret huiusmodi concilium conuocare, verisimile est, ipsum talem congregationem quantum posset differre vel auferre totaliter, quod in grande fidelium grauamen & præiudicium redundaret. Hoc autem fideli legislatori seu fidelium vniuersitati, sic euenire non potest, eo quod ipsa vel ipsius valentior pars non sic seducibilis est, neq; in ciuilibus, quemadmodum ostendimus decimotertio primæ, neq; in spiritualibus, præsertim circa fidem, vt ostensum est 19. & 20. huius.
units.tr: That the aforesaid authority does not belong to the Roman bishop alone, or to him and his college of cardinals alone, can be persuaded along with the foregoing: if he himself, or he with his college, were guilty of some crime for which it would be expedient to convene such a council, it is likely that he would delay such a gathering as long as he could, or prevent it altogether, which would be a great burden and prejudice to the faithful. But this cannot happen with the faithful lawgiver, or with the whole body of the faithful, since that body, or its more powerful part, is not so easily seduced, neither in civil matters, as we showed in the thirteenth of the first book, nor in spiritual matters, especially concerning faith, as was shown in 19 and 20 of this work.

units.la: Quod vero diffinitorum seu iudicatorum, & reliquorum ordinatorum primæ significationis iudicio per generale concilium, obseruationis coactiuum ferre præceptum seu dare Decretum super omnes indifferenter, tam Sacerdotes quam non Sacerdotes eiusque præcepti siue decreti transgressores arcere poena reali aut personali vel utraque, in hoc etiam seculo transgressoribus infligenda, sit autoritas humani legislatoris fidelis, superiore carentis, suadere volumus primum ex his quæ rationabiliter acta sunt. Et recitat Isidorus codice prædicto plerisque locis. Est enim hoc videre palam ex capitulo, cui titulus: Edictum Marciani Imperatoris in affirmatione concilii Calcedonensis, in quo continetur inter cætera series hæc: Nemo itaque, vel clericus militans & alterius conditionis, de fide Christiana, publice tettminata, coadunatis & audientibus tractare conetur in posterum, ex hoc tumultus & perfidiae occasionem requirens. Vbi etiam parum infra subiungitur: Nam in contemptoribus huius legis poena non deerit. Et infra rursum: Igitur si clericus erit, qui publice tractate de religione aliquis fuerit, a consortio clericorum remouebitur. Si vero militia praditus fit, singulo militiæ expoliabitur; & sic de reliquis consequenter statuit. Idem apparet rursum ex capitulo immediate subnixo, cuius titulus; Incipit sacra Valentiniani & Martiani augustorum post concilium Calcedonense, in confirmatione eiusdem concilii, & damnatione haereticorum; in qua series talis habetur: Hac lege decernimus eos qui Euticetis errore decipiuntur ad exemplum Apollinaristarum, quos Eutices secutus est, quos venerabiles patrum regule, (id est ecclesiastici canones,) & diuorum principum sacratissimae sanctiones condemnant, nullum episcopum, nullum presbyterum, nullos clericos vel appellare ecclesiasticos, ipsumq; Eutychen nomine presbyteri, quo indigne vtens expoliatus est, in totum carere. Si quis tamen contra diffinita nostra episcopos, presbyteros, caterosq; clericos ausi fuerint ex hac creare, tam facientes quam factos, vel praesumentes sibi clericorum honorum amissione, periculo subiacere exilii perpetui praecipimus. Ex hoc autem apparet verum esse, quod de promouendis ad sacerdotium & reliquos ordines sacros, ad fidelis legislatoris aut principis autoritatem diximus pertinere. Amplius idem ex habito huic immediate capitulo, cui titulus: Item alia Martiani Imperatoris contra eosdem haereticos. Adhuc idem ex capitulo, cui titulus: Edictum regis de confirmatione concilii, vbi hoc inter cætera continetur: Si quis ergo clericus aut laicus harum sanctionum obediens esse noluerit, si Episcopus, presbyter, diaconus, aut clericus fuerit ab omni concilio excommunicationi subiaceat. Si vero laicus & honestioris loci persona fuerit, medietatem facultatum suarum amittat, fisci iuribus profuturam. Ex quo etiam manifeste apparet, quod poenas personales atque reales haereticis infligere, ipsasque exigere, sibiq; applicare licite possunt & solebant principes siue legislatores humani, quemadmodum diximus decimo huius. Hoc rursum ex capitulo, cui titulus: Explicit concilium Toletanum 13. cuius initium est: Charitatis instinctu, & aliis plerisque locis, de quibus perrransco propter abbreuiationem, & quoniam præinducta sufficiunt. Nec solum de obseruandis his quæ per concilium diffinita fuerant, coactiuum ferre decretum ad humanum legislatorem seu ipsius autoritate principantem pertinet, verum etiam formam & modum, Romanam sedem apostolicam ordinandi, seu Romanum eligendi pontificem statuere. Quod etiam ab Imperatore Romanum pontificem cum instantia postulasse legimus, non reclamasse, vt ex eiusdem Codicis capitulo, cui titulus; Incipiunt Decreta Bonifacii Papa. Epistola deprecatoria ad Honorium Augustum, vt constituatur a principe in vrbe Romana, quatenus per ambitum nunquam Pontifex ordinetur. ordinetur.Et ex capitulo immediate subiuncto, cui titulus: Constantini, Honorii Imperatoris ad Bonifacium Papam missa, ut si denuo Roma duo Episcopi ordinati fuerint, ambo ciuitate pellentur, cuius initium: Victor Honorius inclytus triumphator semper augustus, sancto ac venerabili Bonifacio Papa urbis Roma. In quo siquidem decreto dictus Imperator parum infra subinfert: Illud autem pietatis nostrae satis placuisse cognoscite, quod sanctimonia tua de ecclesiarum aut populi perturbatione solicita est. Quae ne aliqua ratione possit euenire, satis clementia nostra credidit esse prouisum. Denique praedicante beatitudine tua, id ad cunctorum clericorum notitiam volumus peruenire, ut si quid forte religioni tuae (quod non optamus) humana sorte contigerit, sciant omnes ab ambitionibus esse cessandum. At si dato forte contraphas, temeritate certantium fuerint ordinati, nullum ex eis penitus futurum sacerdotem, (id est Romanum Episcopum.) Sed illum in sede apostolica permansurum, quem ex numero clericorum noua ordinatione diuinitum iudicium, & vniuersitatis consensus elegerint. Ex quo etiam apparet verum esse quod diximus 17. huius, ad vniuersitatem fidelium siue humanum legislatorem fidelem pertinere institutionem secundam, sacerdotum, episcoporum, & reliquorum ministrorum Ecclesiae ad curas animarum maiores siue minores.
units.tr: As to whether the human faithful lawgiver, who has no superior, has the authority to lay down a coercive precept for observing the decisions, judgments and other ordinances of the first signification made by a general council, and to issue a decree binding alike on priests and non-priests, and to restrain transgressors of that precept or decree by penalty, real or personal or both, to be inflicted on them even in this age: we wish first to persuade this from things that were rightly done. Isidore recounts this in the aforesaid codex in many places. For it can plainly be seen from the chapter entitled Edict of the Emperor Marcian in confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon, in which, among other things, the following passage is contained: Therefore let no one, whether a serving cleric or of any other condition, attempt in future to discuss publicly, in gatherings and before hearers, the Christian faith which has been settled, seeking from this an occasion of tumult and perfidy. Where a little further it is added: For there will be no lack of penalty for those who despise this law. And again below: Therefore, if he is a cleric who has publicly discussed religion, he shall be removed from the fellowship of clerics. If he is a man of military rank, he shall be stripped of his military office; and so he consequently decrees for the rest. The same appears again from the chapter immediately following, entitled The sacred [edict] of the Emperors Valentinian and Marcian after the Council of Chalcedon, in confirmation of that council and condemnation of heretics, in which the following passage is found: By this law we decree that those who are deceived by the error of the Eutychians, after the example of the Apollinarists whom Eutyches followed, and whom the venerable rules of the Fathers (that is, the ecclesiastical canons) and the most sacred sanctions of the divine princes condemn, shall be wholly deprived of any bishop, any presbyter, any clerics, or of those who call themselves ecclesiastics, and of Eutyches himself, who has unworthily used the name of presbyter, from which he has been stripped. But if anyone should dare, against our decisions, to create bishops, presbyters or other clerics from these, we command that both those who make and those who are made, and those who presume to claim the honours of clerics, shall be liable to perpetual exile and the loss of their clerical honours. From this it appears true that, as we said, the promotion to the priesthood and the other sacred orders belongs to the authority of the faithful lawgiver or prince. Likewise again from the chapter immediately following this one, entitled Another edict of the Emperor Marcian against the same heretics. Again from the chapter entitled Edict of the King on the confirmation of the council, where this is contained among other things: If therefore any cleric or layman is unwilling to obey these sanctions, if he is a bishop, presbyter, deacon or cleric, let him be subject to excommunication from every council. But if he is a layman and a person of more honourable rank, let him lose half of his property, which shall go to the rights of the treasury. From which it also clearly appears that human lawgivers or princes could and used to inflict personal and real penalties on heretics, and to exact them and apply them to themselves lawfully, as we said in the tenth of this work. This again from the chapter entitled Here ends the Council of Toledo 13, whose beginning is By the impulse of charity, and from many other places, which I pass over for brevity, since those already cited are sufficient. Nor does it belong only to the human lawgiver, or to one ruling by his authority, to issue a coercive decree on observing what has been decided by the council; it also belongs to him to establish the form and manner of ordaining the apostolic Roman see, or of electing the Roman pontiff. We read that the Roman pontiff even urgently asked this of the Emperor, and that the Emperor did not object, as appears from the chapter of the same Codex entitled The Decrees of Pope Boniface begin. Epistle of entreaty to the Emperor Honorius, that it be ordained by the prince in the city of Rome that a pontiff never be ordained through ambition. And from the chapter immediately subjoined, entitled Letter of Constantine and of the Emperor Honorius sent to Pope Boniface, that if two bishops should again be ordained at Rome, both shall be driven from the city, whose beginning is: Victor Honorius, illustrious triumphant ever Augustus, to the holy and venerable Boniface, Pope of the city of Rome. In which decree the said Emperor adds a little further: Know that it has pleased our piety that your holiness is anxious about the disturbance of the churches or of the people. Lest this should happen by any means, our clemency has thought it sufficiently provided for. Finally, at your blessedness's proclamation, we wish this to come to the notice of all the clerics, so that if anything should happen by human chance to your religion (which we do not wish), all may know that ambition must cease. But if, by chance, two should be ordained through the rashness of those contending for it, then none of them shall ever be priest, (that is, Roman bishop) but he shall remain in the apostolic see whom the divine judgment and the consent of the whole body have chosen from the number of the clerics by a new ordination. From which it also appears true what we said in the seventeenth of this work: that the second institution of priests, bishops and the other ministers of the Church, whether with greater or lesser cure of souls, belongs to the whole body of the faithful or to the human faithful lawgiver.

units.la: Amplius proposita suadere possumus ex epistola, cui titulus: Item ad Martianum Augustum gratias agens, quod eius industria per Calcedonense concilium pax Ecclesiae reddita sit, cuius initium est: Leo Episcopus Martiano augusto. Multa mihi in omnibus clementia vestra literis causa gaudii est. In qua etiam circa finem legitur, quod idem Leo ait: Quia vero omnibus modis obediendum est pietati vestrae & religiosissimae voluntati, constitutionibus synodalibus, quae mihi de confirmatione fidei catholicae, & de haereticorum damnatione placuerunt, libens adiecti meam sententiam. Quae ut in notitiam omnium sacerdotum, ecclesiarumque peruenient, vestra clementia praeceptio ordinare dignabitur. Ecce quod suam sententiam siue iudicium primae significationis adiecit Romanus Pontifex diffinitis per concilium, praeceptionem tamen observationis ad Ecclesias & Sacerdotes supplicans fieri per Romanum Principem, quod tamen non fecisset, si haec illius non fuisset auctoritas. Ex quo etiam apparet verum esse, quod diximus quarto, quinto, & nono huius, auctoritatem scilicet coactiuam, tam in sacerdotes quam non sacerdotes ad humanum legislatorem seu eius auctoritate principantem pertinere, neque contra hoc reclamauerunt Romani Pontifices antiquis temporibus, sed pro talibus sibi dandis regulis siue legibus per Imperatores potius supplicabant. Eadem rursum euidenter apparet sententia ex capitulo, cuius principium: Imperatores, Caesares, Theodosius & Valentinianus. In quo parum infra subiicitur: Quoniam igitur in praesenti subita emergente dubitatione ad catholica & apostolica doctrinae ac nostrae fidei custodiam. Qua ut sit diuersis sententiis impugnata conturbat & confundit hominum sensus & animas, intolerabile duximus huiusmodi delictum contemnere, ne per talem negligentiam, ipsi Deo inferri contumelia videretur. Ideoque sanctissimos in vnum sanctissimos & Deo placitos conuenire viros, quibus proprietate catholica, atque vera fide plurimum ferme est, ut vniuersa quidem talis & vana dubitatio subtilis propositio & inquisitione soluatur. Vera autem & Deo amica catholica fides firmetur. Igitur & tua sanctitas, sumpta secum decem reuerendissimi Metropolitani qui sub tua degunt dioecesi, & alius similiter decem sanctae Episcopi, sermone & vita ornatu, qui in doctrina & scientia recta & immaculata fidei, pro cunctis apud cunctos eminent proximus Kal. Augusti Ephesum, Metropolim Asiae, conuenire absque vlla dubitatione fistinent: nullo scilicet alio prater praedictos viros sanctam synodum molestante, quatenus vniuersis, sanctissimi & beatissimi Episcopi, quos conuenire per sacras nostras epistolas sanctimus ad praedictam concurrentibus ciuitatem, & subtilissime inuestigantibus & quarentibus, omnis de medio error contrarius auferatur, catholica autem doctrina & orthodoxa fidei saluatoris nostri Christi amicissima solidetur & consueta fulgeat, quod vniuersi in posterum incontestum Deo propitio & intemeratum custodiant. Si quis vero tam necessariam & vere Deo amicam synodum praetermiserit, & omni virtute secundum praedictum tempus adpraefinitum locum non peruenerit, nullam excusationem neque apud Deum neque apud nostram inueniet pietatem. Sacerdotalem enim conuentum, non nisi quis mali propria conscientia fauctatus euitat. Theodoretum sane Episcopum Syriae ciuitatis, quem pridem iussimus sua sola vacare Ecclesia, sanctimus, non prius ad sanctam Synodum conuenire, nisi vniuerso complacuerit conuenienti concilio & ipsum concurrere, & pariter interesse. Si vero aliqua discordia de eo emerserit, absque illo sanctam synodum conuenire & qua iussa sunt, ordinare praecipimus. Ex hoc autem edicto attendenti apparet intentio trium conclusionum iam propositarum vnius quidem, quod dubia: quae circa legem diuinam fuerint, expedit diffinire. Secundae diffinitionis haec non ad singularis personae vel collegii auctoritatem pertinet, sed ad concilium generale. Tertiae quidem, quod huiusmodi conuocare seu praecipere concilium, & per ipsum diffinita & ordinata seruari statuere, statutorum quoque transgressores arcere in statu & pro statu praesentis seculi, auctoritas sit solius humani legislatoris fidelis, seu eius auctoritate principantis.
units.tr: Further, we can argue our proposition from the letter entitled Item ad Martianum Augustum gratias agens, quod eius industria per Calcedonense concilium pax Ecclesiae reddita sit, which begins: Leo Episcopus Martiano augusto. Multa mihi in omnibus clementia vestra literis causa gaudii est. Near the end of it Leo also says: Since we must in every way obey your piety and most religious will, I have gladly added my opinion to the synodal decrees that have pleased me concerning the confirmation of the Catholic faith and the condemnation of heretics. So that these may come to the knowledge of all priests and churches, your clemency will deign to order it. Here the Roman Pontiff added his own opinion, or judgment, of the first kind to the matters defined by the council, yet he begged that the order to observe them be issued to the churches and priests by the Roman Emperor. He would not have done this if the authority had not belonged to the Emperor. From this it also appears that what we said in the fourth, fifth and ninth points of this chapter is true: coercive authority over priests and non-priests alike belongs to the human lawgiver, or to the one ruling by his authority. The Roman Pontiffs in ancient times did not object to this, but rather begged the Emperors to give them such rules or laws. The same view is evidently found again in the chapter that begins: Imperatores, Caesares, Theodosius & Valentinianus. Slightly further on it says: Since, therefore, in the present sudden doubt, which for the guarding of the Catholic and apostolic doctrine and of our faith, is attacked by diverse opinions, confounds and disturbs the minds and souls of men, we have thought it intolerable to disregard a crime of this kind, lest through such negligence an insult seem to be offered to God himself. Therefore we have ordered the most holy men, most pleasing to God, who excel in the Catholic propriety and true faith, to gather together, so that such an empty doubt may be dissolved by a subtle proposal and inquiry, and the true faith, friendly to God, may be strengthened. Therefore your holiness, taking with you ten most reverend metropolitans who live within your diocese, and ten other holy bishops adorned in speech and life, who stand out in sound doctrine and knowledge and the immaculate faith before all, should hasten without any doubt to come to Ephesus, the metropolis of Asia, on the nearest first of August; with no one else disturbing the holy synod except the men named. The purpose is that all the most holy and most blessed bishops, whom we command by our sacred letters to gather in the aforesaid city, may, by investigating and inquiring most carefully, have every contrary error removed from the midst, and that the Catholic doctrine and the orthodox faith of our Saviour Christ may be made firm, most friendly to us, and shine as usual, so that all may keep it henceforth, by God's favour, uncontested and unspoiled. If anyone, however, neglects so necessary a synod, one truly friendly to God, and does not with all diligence arrive at the appointed place at the time fixed, he will find no excuse either before God or before our piety. For only one who is conscious of having wrongdoing avoids a gathering of priests. Indeed, we decree that Theodoret, bishop of a city in Syria, whom we earlier ordered to stay only in his own church, is not to come to the holy synod unless it has pleased the whole council to have him come and be present together with it. If, however, any dispute about him arises, we order the holy synod to meet without him and to ordain what has been commanded. From this edict, to one attending to it, the intention of the three conclusions already proposed appears: the first, that doubtful matters concerning the divine law are to be defined; the second, that this definition belongs not to the authority of a single person or of a college, but to a general council; the third, that to summon or order such a council, and to decide that what is defined and ordained by it be kept, and to restrain the transgressors of its statutes in the state and for the state of the present age, is the authority of the human faithful lawgiver alone, or of one ruling by his authority.

units.la: His consequenter ostendere conuenit, nihil per hominem aliquem singularem cuiuscunque dignitatis aut conditionis existat, statui posse circa ecclesiasticum ritum, quod homines ad observationem obliget sub aliqua poena pro statu praesentis seculi vel venturi, nisi per generale concilium immediate, aut inde sumpta prius auctoritate: ad haec etiam fidelis humani legislatoris primi, aut eius auctoritate principantis, interueniente decreto, nihilque circa humanos actus alios, velut ieiunia, esus carnium, abstinentias, sanctorum canonizationes ac venerationes, operum mochanicorum aut aliorum quorumcunque prohibitiones seu vacationes (Augustinus decimo quinto de ciuitate Dei, capitulo decimosexto) matrimoniorum copulas infra certos cognitionis gradus, ordines quoque siue collegia religiosorum approbare vel reprobare, reliquaque similia lege diuina licita seu permissa, statuere sub aliqua ecclesiastica censura, ut interdicti vel excommunicationis aut alterius poenae consimilis maioris aut minoris, eoque minus ad ea quenquam obligare posse sub poena
units.tr: Next, it is fitting to show that no single man, of whatever dignity or condition, can establish anything concerning ecclesiastical rite that binds men to observe it under some penalty for the present or future age, unless this is done immediately by a general council, or by authority first taken from it; and likewise by the decree of the faithful first human lawgiver, or of one ruling by his authority. Nor can he establish anything concerning other human acts, such as fasts, eating of meat, abstinences, canonizations and veneration of saints, prohibitions or exemptions of mechanical works or of any others (Augustine, De civitate Dei, book fifteen, chapter sixteen), the joining of marriages within certain degrees of kinship, or approve or reprove religious orders or colleges, or other similar things permitted or lawful under divine law, under some ecclesiastical censure, such as interdict, excommunication, or another penalty of greater or lesser kind like these. Still less can he bind anyone to them under a penalty

units.la: poena tali vel personali in statu praesentis saeculi exigenda, absque iam dicti legislatoris auctoritate, cuius liquidem licita solius potestas est infligere ac exigere tales poenas, ut ex decimoquinto prima ac decimo huius sufficienter apparet. Haec autem eisdem demonstrationibus & auctoritatibus supponendum probata, quibus & dubiorum legis divinae sensuum determinationem ad supradictum concilium, reliquosque humanos actus circa ritum ecclesiasticum per coactiva decreta ordinare, ad fidelem legislatorem humanum supra monstravimus pertinere, sola rationum minori extremitate mutata. Adhuc quoniam lege divina permissa, non prohibentur nec illicita sunt, nisi per legislatorem humanum. Amplius quoniam nullus Episcopus in alium auctoritatem habet aliquam a Christo immediate, quemadmodum demonstratum est decimoquinto & decimosexto huius, neque coactivam invicem aut aliquos iurisdictionem, ut quarto, quinto, & nono huius ostendimus prius; ex quibus etiam deduci potest & convenit ad solius iam dicti concilii, non autem ad solius Episcopi aut presbyteri vel alicuius eorum particularis collegii auctoritatem pertinere, principem, provinciam, aut communitatem aliam civilem excommunicare, vel divinorum officiorum usum interdicere. Ignoranter enim aut inique volente presbytero seu Episcopo vel particulari aliquo illorum collegio principem aut provinciam excommunicare vel interdicere, magnum inde scandalum pacis & quietis fidelium omnium eunire contingit. Quod etiam quasi nuissime iam rerum experientia magistra monstravit, dum Octavus Bonifacius Papa Romanus claram memoriam philosophum pulcherrimum Francorum Catholicum Regem excommunicare tentavit, eiusque regnum cum sibi adhaerentibus ecclesiasticorum officiorum interdictis supponere, reclamante praedicto Rege adversus narrationem quandam scriptam, cui principium, Vnam sanctam Catholicam Ecclesiam, emissam a praedicto Bonifacio, aut ab eodem cum suorum Cardinalium coetu, inter cetera continentem, quinimo finaliter concludentem, omnes mundi principes, communitates, & singulares personas Romano Pontifici coactiva iurisdictione subiectos. Quamvis etiam temporibus illis proponeret idem Bonifacius adversus iam dictum principem & sibi subditos ac adhaerentes singulariter tendere, reliquosque quos potuisset adversus illum principes & populos fideles, teste immortali veritate, ac viventium plurimorum memoria concitare, nisi de medio sorte mortalium sublatus fuisset. Haec aut consimilis alterius maligna concitationis tempestas potius quam potestas grandis schismatis atque periculi fidelibus allatiua, rescecanda prorsus est, temperandaque. Interdictorum & excommunicationum huiusmodi forma soli Christianorum generali concilio relinqui debet, cuius iudicium dirigente sancto Spiritu, ignorantia vel malignitate aliqua, pervertI non potest. His autem semper necessitatem sequitur ordinata & diffinita tam circa fidem, sive legis euangelicae sensum, quam circa ecclesiasticum ritum sive cultum divinum & reliqua omnia per concilium generale statuta, mediate vel immediate, implicite vel explicite, aut alio quovis modo, auctoritate ac ordinatione nullius Episcopi, aut alterius particularis collegii, concilii, vel congregationis, eoque minus personae singularis cuiuscunque conditionis aut dignitatis extet, posse immutari, augeri, minui, vel suspendi, aut interpretationem recipere, praesertim in arduis, aut penitus revocari: sed quae sic ordinata fuerint, fiad immutandum aut simpliciter revocandum vocet necessitas evidens, ad supradictum concilium convocandum debere referri. Hoc autem eisdem rationibus & auctoritatibus convincendum, quibus per solum iam dictum concilium eiusmodi ordinanda, diffinienda, & statuenda monstravimus.
units.tr: or personal penalty to be exacted in the state of the present age, without the authority of the aforesaid lawgiver, whose lawful power alone it is to inflict and exact such penalties, as is sufficiently clear from the fifteenth of the first book and the tenth of this chapter. These things are to be assumed as proved by the same demonstrations and authorities by which we have shown above that the determination of the meanings of doubtful points of divine law by the aforesaid council, and the ordering by coercive decrees of other human acts concerning ecclesiastical rite, belong to the faithful human lawgiver, the only difference being a change in the lesser premise of the arguments. Further, since things permitted by divine law are not forbidden and are not unlawful except by a human lawgiver. Moreover, since no bishop has any authority over another immediately from Christ, as has been shown in the fifteenth and sixteenth of this chapter, nor any coercive or other jurisdiction over one another, as we first showed in the fourth, fifth and ninth of this chapter; from these things too it can be deduced, and it is fitting, that the authority to excommunicate a prince, a province, or another civil community, or to forbid the use of divine offices, belongs to the aforesaid council alone, and not to a bishop or presbyter alone, or to any particular college of them. For when a presbyter or bishop, or some particular college of them, out of ignorance or injustice, wishes to excommunicate or interdict a prince or a province, great scandal arises and the peace and quiet of all the faithful is disturbed. Experience, the teacher of affairs, has shown this quite recently, when Boniface VIII, Roman Pontiff of illustrious memory, tried to excommunicate that most excellent philosopher, the Catholic King of the Franks, and to place his kingdom and his adherents under an interdict of ecclesiastical offices. The said King objected to a certain written document beginning Unam sanctam Catholicam Ecclesiam, issued by the aforesaid Boniface, or by him with the body of his Cardinals, which contained, among other things, and finally concluded, that all princes, communities and single persons of the world are subject to the Roman Pontiff in coercive jurisdiction. Yet in those times the same Boniface also proposed to move against the said prince and his subjects and adherents individually, and to stir up against him the other princes and faithful peoples whom he could, as immortal truth and the memory of many living men bear witness, had he not been removed from the midst by the lot of mortals. This storm of malicious agitation, or of another similar one, brought to the faithful a great schism and danger rather than a power, and must be wholly cut off and restrained. The form of such interdicts and excommunications ought to be left to the general council of Christians alone, whose judgment, with the Holy Spirit directing it, cannot be perverted by any ignorance or malice. Necessarily it follows from these things that what has been ordained and defined by a general council, whether concerning the faith or the sense of the gospel law, or concerning ecclesiastical rite or divine worship, and all other things established by the general council, mediately or immediately, implicitly or explicitly, or in any other way, cannot be changed, increased, diminished, suspended, admit of interpretation, especially in difficult matters, or be wholly revoked by the authority or ordinance of any bishop, or of another particular college, council or congregation, and still less of any single person of whatever condition or dignity. But what has been so ordained, if clear necessity calls for its change or outright revocation, ought to be referred to the aforesaid council for convening. This must be proved by the same reasons and authorities by which we showed that such matters are to be ordained, defined and established by the aforesaid council alone.

units.la: Exeildem quoque cum scripturae auctoritatibus & humanis rationibus demonstrari potest & convenit, ad nullius solius Episcopi vel personae singularis aut particularis alicuius collegii auctoritatem pertinere, absque iam dicti generalis concilii vel fidelis humani legislatoris determinatione, in aliquibus mundi ecclesiasticis officiis personas instituere seu praefecere, neque pro eisdem officiis quenquam ecclesiastica temporalia, vocata beneficia, distribuere, neque vocatas disciplinarum licentias, notariatus, aut reliqua officia publica seu civilia conferre cuiquam, nisi auctoritate iam dicta. Quae quamvis decimoquinto prima, ac huius decimoseptimo secundum modum aliquem ostensa sint convenienter, ea tamen amplius explicandum & confirmandum ex immediate praedictis & aliis quibusdam probabilibus argumentis in hac parte decrevimus. Nam illud non est, necesse debet auctoritas Romani vel alterius cuiusuis Episcopi, aut particularis cum ipso collegii clericorum. Propter quod omnia regna omnesque politiae maiores sive minores haereses & dissolutionis exponuntur periculo. Sic autem fit Romano aut alteri soli cuius Episcopo, absque determinatione vel legislatoris, vel concilii generalis tali potestate permissa. Esto nanque, ut supraiam diximus, haereticum aliquem aut necromanticum, cupidum, & superbum, aut aliter criminosum, quales quidam in episcopos Romanos praefici visum est, & leguntur assumpti. Siquidem criminosus hic auctoritatem habeat absque determinatione legali aliqua generalis concilii aut fidelis legislatoris mortalis in omnibus ecclesiasticis officiis personas statuere, qualescunque voluerit, verisimile valde videtur, eiusmodi pontificem eos in ecclesiasticis officiis, praecipue maioribus, ut cardinalatu, episcopatu aut presbyteratu praeferre, quorum criminum complices noverit, & suis peruersis omnib. fauere votis. Erit igitur inde grex fidelium expositus periculo subversionis a fide, quemadmodum etiam aliquando ostensum est undecimo huius. Et hoc praesertim, si haeresi labefactus ignorantia, vel malitia interpretationis divinae legis habeat potestatem, sicut etiam pridem induximus vigesimo huius, & praesentium memoria & constitutio de duobus Romanis Episcopis omnibus liquet. Rursum a Romano Episcopo divina vel humana lege non repetitur concessa potestas, sed potius interdicta instituendi sibi successorem in episcopali sede Romana. Cum tamen ex ea provincia magis nosse possit & debeat sufficientias personarum, & quid eidem provinciae magis expediat. Cur igitur Episcoporum aut aliorum Praelatorum, curatorum, & etiam ministrorum in alienis & remotis provinciis, quibus expedientia minus notiit, & ex ipsis sufficientias personarum successores instituendi, potestas siue autoritas eidem Episcopo permittitur.
units.tr: These things can also be demonstrated and are fitting, both from the authority of Scripture and from human reasoning, that it does not belong to the authority of any single bishop or any individual person, or of any particular college, without the determination of the aforesaid general council or of a faithful human lawgiver, to institute or appoint persons to any ecclesiastical offices in the world, nor to distribute to anyone for those offices ecclesiastical temporalities, called benefices, nor to confer on anyone the licences of the disciplines, notaryships, or other public or civil offices. Although these matters have been shown fittingly in some measure in the fifteenth chapter of the first part, and the seventeenth of this, we have resolved to explain and confirm them further in this part, from the arguments immediately set out above and certain other probable arguments. For it is not necessary that the authority of the Roman bishop, or of any other bishop, or of a particular college of clergy with him, be the rule. On account of this, all kingdoms and all greater and lesser polities are exposed to the danger of heresies and dissolution. Yet this happens when the power is granted to the Roman bishop or to some other single bishop without a determination either by a lawgiver or by a general council empowered for this. For suppose, as we said above, that he is a heretic, a necromancer, covetous and proud, or otherwise criminal, such as some have been thought fit, and are read, to be raised to the Roman episcopate. If this criminal has authority, without any legal determination of a general council or a faithful mortal lawgiver, to appoint whomever he wishes to all ecclesiastical offices, it seems very likely that such a pontiff will prefer to ecclesiastical offices, especially the greater ones such as the cardinalate, the episcopate or the presbyterate, those whose accomplices in his crimes he knows, and will favour all his perverse wishes. The flock of the faithful will therefore be exposed to the danger of subversion from the faith, as has also been shown at times in the eleventh of this. And this especially if, weakened by heresy, he has power over the interpretation of divine law through ignorance or malice, as we also brought forward in the twentieth of this, and as the record and decision of the present time concerning the two Roman bishops make plain to all. Again, the power granted by divine or human law is not withdrawn from the Roman bishop, but rather he is forbidden to institute a successor to himself in the Roman episcopal see. Yet he could and ought to know better from that province the sufficiency of persons and what is more useful to that same province. Why, then, is power or authority granted to this same bishop to institute bishops or other prelates, curates, and even ministers, in foreign and distant provinces, about whose needs he knows less, and to institute successors from among them according to their sufficiency?

units.la: Amplius, cuius Episcopo soli, aut etiam cum solo particulari aliquo clericorum coetu conferendi omnia mun[?]ecclesiastica temporalia; vocata beneficia, pro suo voto absque iuris dicta determinatione legali [?]generalis concilii & humani legislatoris vel fidelis principantis autoritate sibi concessa, omnia regna & omnes politiae maiores & minores solutionis exponantur periculo. Rursumque ritus hic ad ecclesiarum siue animarum regimen ditiores & excellentiores seculari potentia vel fauore, quantumcunque ignorantes & more perverso, pauperibus, iustis & humilibus quantumcunque doctis & vita pollentibus praeferri faciet. Esto enim Romanum Episcopum superbum aut aliter criminosum, volentem etiam seculariter principari. Quales eos & qualia sectari videmus modernis temporibus ipsorum quam plures. Propter suam liquidem avaritiam insatiabilem & explenda reliqua sua vota pervertsa iam dicta, & propterea potentum fauores & gratias acquirendis ecclesiastica officia & beneficia venalia ponet. Ipsa quoque potentibus, violentis & bellicosis, aut iuxta ipsorum requisitionem, cognatis, affinibus, & amicis eorum conferet, quos ad sua pravita desideria perficienda suffragari tam velle quam posse putabit. Haec autem, ut diximus, sic evenire possibile, non solum argumenta probant, verum etiam sic evenisse dudum ac evenire continuo, experientia rerum magistra docet, quasi fidelibus omnibus inoccculta. Rursum haec illi officiorum institutionis, & temporalium seu beneficiorum distributionis, generali & immoderata potestate permissa, regna & politiae omnes solutionis aut immensae perturbationis periculo subiacent, si talis Episcopus seculares principatus sibi subiicere quaerat, quos omnes secundum suam narrationem scriptam, decretalem vocatam nobis praemissam, Octavus Bonifacius, sic Romanum [?]libet Episcopo coactiva iurisdictione subiectos expressit, ut id credere fidelibus pertinaciter fortasse asseruit de necessitate salutis. Idemque in suis edictis aduersus inclytum Ludovicum ex Ducibus Bavariae Romanorum regem assumptum, implicet quidam vocatus Papa Romanus, quamuis hoc solum exprimere videatur de regno [?] imperio Romanorum. Reliqua tamen omnia comprehendens per eum, quod sibi hoc cum aliis rationibus praemissum ascribit titulum plenitudinem scilicet potestatis, hoc enim titulo non magis superest coactiva iurisdictione principi Romanorum quam reliquis regibus, quemadmodum evidenter ostensum est ultimo primae. Hic inquam ergo Episcopus hanc super principes seculi iurisdictionem, quamuis minus debite quaerens talium temporalium seu beneficiorum & decimarum, quae ad omnia regna mentem convertentium quasi factae sunt inestimabilis: pars distributione seu donatione seditionem magnam concitare potest, & de facto hactenus concitavit & concitat, praecipue in universo Romanorum imperio, quemadmodum magis in sequentibus seriose dictari tumus.
units.tr: Furthermore, if all ecclesiastical temporalities, called benefices, are to be conferred by a bishop alone, or even with one particular gathering of clergy, at his own will, without the legal determination of the general council and the authority of a human lawgiver or a faithful ruler granted to him, then all kingdoms and all greater and lesser polities are exposed to the danger of dissolution. Moreover, this practice will cause those who are richer and more eminent in worldly power or favour, however ignorant and perverse in their habits, to be preferred to the poor, the just and the humble, however learned and strong in virtue, for the government of churches or of souls. Suppose the Roman bishop is proud or otherwise criminal, and wishes to rule even in secular affairs. We see many of them in modern times of such a kind, and pursuing such aims. Because of his clear insatiable greed and the perverse fulfilment of his other wishes mentioned above, he will put ecclesiastical offices and benefices up for sale, so as to win the favours and graces of the powerful. He will also confer them on the powerful, the violent and the warlike, or, at their request, on their relatives, kinsmen and friends, whom he thinks both willing and able to help him carry out his wicked desires. That these things can happen, as we have said, not only do the arguments prove, but experience, the teacher of things, teaches that it has happened long ago and goes on happening continually, as if hidden from no faithful person. Again, if this power of appointing offices and distributing temporalities or benefices is granted to him in a general and unrestrained way, then all kingdoms and all polities are subject to the danger of dissolution or of immense disturbance, if such a bishop seeks to subject secular principalities to himself. Boniface VIII, in his written account called the decretal, which we have set before you, expressed all of them as subject to the Roman bishop with coercive jurisdiction, so that he stubbornly asserted, perhaps, that the faithful must believe this of necessity to salvation. The same man, the so-called Pope of Rome, in his edicts against the famous Louis, of the Dukes of Bavaria, taken up as king of the Romans, seems to express this only concerning the kingdom and empire of the Romans; yet by the title that he attributes to himself, together with the other arguments set out above, namely fullness of power, he embraces all the rest. For by this title there is no more coercive jurisdiction left to the prince of the Romans than to other kings, as has been clearly shown at the end of the first part. Therefore this bishop, seeking this jurisdiction over secular princes, though less rightly, through the distribution or donation of such temporalities or benefices and tithes, which are almost infinite for all kingdoms that turn their minds to them, can stir up great sedition, and has in fact stirred it up and still stirs it up until now, especially throughout the whole Roman empire, as we shall set out more fully in what follows.

units.la: Et propterea oportet humanum legislatorem aut ipsius autoritate principantem attendere in decimarum & reliquorum temporalium ecclesiasticorum acceptione, sive assumptione, an huiusmodi ecclesiastica temporalia superfluant sufficientiae pauperum, Euangelii ministrorum, & reliquorum etiam pauperum impotentium, propter quos statuta sunt talia, vel non superfluant. Et rursum attendere debet, an talibus bonis de necessitate indigeat ad rempublicam defendendam, aut aliter sustentandam, vel non necessario his egeat propter finem iam dictum. Quod si egerit his temporalibus ex necessitate propter finem praedictum, superflúis omnibus sufficientiae iam dictorum ministrorum & pauperum vti, & autoritate propria sumere possunt licite secundum legem divinam legislatores sive principantes, nulla obstante contradictione sacerdotum aut talium ministrorum, nec solum decimas, verum etiam quartas & tertias, & ad unum dicere, ipsorum & pauperum impotentium sufficientiae quodcunque superfluum. Alimenta enim & his quibus tegantur contenti sine sacerdotes, ut dicit Apostolus prima ad Timoth. sexto. Quod si huiusmodi bonis advsum sive finem praedictum non egent, peccant mortaliter suscipientes, sibique consentientes vel ipsos inducentes ad hoc. Non est igitur ecclesiasticorum temporalium potestas soli Romano Episcopo vel alteri permittenda, nec sibi & suo collegio sacerdotum, ne tali potestate seculares maiores in praeiudicium principum & populorum sibi quaerere possint, & inter Christi fideles inde contentiones & scandala suscitare. Ad haec enim sibi non modicum, quinimo magnum instrumentum est tam dicta potestas, eo quod plurimi, quamuis seducti, credentes talia per ipsum sic posse distribui, seq; ipsa suscipere iuste, ad acquisitionem & receptionem ipsorum faciliter inclinantur. Propter quod illi Episcopo & alteri cuicunq; per generale concilium & legislatorem humanum [?]lium haec quieti perniciosa potestas penitus subtrahenda est, aut debite moderanda, praesertim eum eidem lege divina ministrorum [?]sed, sicut est, fuerit potius interdicta, quemadmodum ostensum est sufficienter decimas [?] & decimas septimo huius.
units.tr: For this reason, the human lawgiver, or the ruler acting by his authority, ought to consider, in the receiving or taking up of tithes and other ecclesiastical temporalities, whether such ecclesiastical temporalities exceed the sufficiency of the poor, of the ministers of the gospel, and of the other poor who are unable to work, for whose sake such things were established, or whether they do not exceed it. And again he ought to consider whether he needs such goods of necessity to defend the commonwealth or to sustain it in some other way, or whether he does not need them of necessity for the end just mentioned. If he does need these temporalities of necessity for the said end, then the lawgivers or rulers may lawfully and by their own authority, according to divine law, use and take all that exceeds the sufficiency of the said ministers and poor, and, to put it simply, whatever exceeds the sufficiency of them and of the poor who are unable to work, not only tithes but also quarters and thirds, no contradiction from priests or such ministers standing in the way. For having food and clothing, let us be content with these, as the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 6. But if they have no need of such goods for the aforesaid purpose or end, then those who receive them, and who consent to them or induce others to do so, sin mortally. Therefore the power over ecclesiastical temporalities must not be granted to the Roman bishop or to any other, nor to himself and his college of priests, lest by such power secular greaters could seek for themselves, to the prejudice of princes and peoples, and thence stir up quarrels and scandals among the faithful of Christ. For this power, as we have said, is no small but a great instrument for them, because many, though deceived, believing that such things can be distributed by him in this way, and that they themselves can justly receive them, are easily inclined to their acquisition and receipt. For this reason that harmful power over the peace must be entirely withdrawn from that bishop and from any other, by a general council and a human lawgiver, or else duly moderated, especially since, by the divine law of the ministers, it has rather been forbidden to him, as it is, as has been sufficiently shown concerning tithes in the seventeenth of this part.

units.la: Propter eandem quidem igitur causam [?]lendi licentias in discipliinis, iam dicto Episcopo, & alteri cuicunq; presbytero ac ipsorum [?]collegio debeat ac licite potest revocari potestas. Est enim hoc [?]mini legislatoris aut eius autoritate principantis officium, quoniam haec ad commune ius [?]commodum aut incommodum [?] possunt pro statu praesentis seculi, quemadmodum
units.tr: For the same reason, therefore, the power of granting licences in the disciplines may and rightly ought to be withdrawn from the aforesaid bishop, and from any other presbyter, and from their college. For this is the office of the human lawgiver, or of the ruler acting by his authority, since these matters pertain to the common right, and can be harmful or beneficial to the commonwealth according to the state of the present age, as has been shown in the fifteenth chapter of the first part. In the same way we ought to think about the institution of the canonization or veneration of saints. For this can be harmful or beneficial to the community of the faithful citizens; for a perverse bishop, relying on this power, could proclaim certain men to be sanctified, so that by their sayings...

units.la: {?} modum demonstratum est decimoquinto prima. Eodemq; modo sentiendum est de sanctorum canonizatione seu veneratione instituenda, potest enim haec nociua vel proficua sore communitati fidelium ciuium, posset nanq; peruersus Episcopus hac potestate fretus quosdam pro nunciare sanctificatos, vt ipsorum dictis aut scriptis suas roboraret opiniones peruersas in praeiudicium aliorum, propter quod autoritas haec est soli generali concilio fidelium committenda. Sic enim Gregorius quartus ex assensu Ludovici Imperatoris & omnium Episcoporum instituit, vt festa omnium sanctorum celebrarentur, unde etiam de consimilibus omnibus similiter sentiendum. Rursum, quoniam hac sibi temporibus antiquis per legislatorem autoritate concessa propter ipsorum vitae sanctitatem, & doctrinae sufficientiam, vt ex scientia ciuilium actuum euidenter apparet, in oppositas temporibus his qualitates conuersi literatorum collegia sibi subiiciunt & seculi principantibus subtrahunt, ipsisque tanquam non modicis instrumentis, quinimo maximis in suis acquirendis & defendendis vsurpationibus aduersus seculi principantes vtuntur Episcopi supradicti. Nolentes enim aut dubitantes viri literati suorum Magistrorum titulos perdere appetitu commodi & gloriae consequentis, hosque sibi Episcoporum autoritate aduenisse non aliunde credentes, votis horum assequuntur, & quam arbitrantur, eorum autoritati contradicentib. aduersantur tam seculi principibus quam subiectis. Verum quia eiusmodi autoritas conferendi disciplinarum licentias est humani legislatoris, aut illius autoritate principantis, ne literatorum & sapientum fauore careant, sed hunc, qui super auxilia extrinseca quaeque ad suos stabiliendos & defendendos principatus & politias, praeponderandus est, acquirent & seruent iam dictas soli debent & licite praesunt autoritate propria conferre licentias notariatuum & reliquorum magistratuum siue officiorum ciuilium titulos, hoc enim priuatae personae cuiuscunque dignitatis, aut conditionis, vel collegio particulari cuiquam competere nequit, inquantum huiusmodi, quemadmodum demonstratum est decimoquinto & 17 prima.
units.tr: This has been shown in the same way as in chapter fifteen of the first book. The same view must be taken of the institution of the canonization or veneration of saints, for this can be harmful or beneficial to the community of the faithful. A wicked bishop, relying on this power, could declare certain people sanctified, so that by their sayings or writings he might strengthen his own perverse opinions to the prejudice of others. For this reason, the authority must be committed to the general council of the faithful alone. Thus Gregory IV, with the assent of the emperor Louis and of all the bishops, established that the feast of All Saints should be celebrated, and the same must be thought of all similar matters. Again, since in earlier times this authority to confer the licences of the disciplines was granted by the lawgiver because of the holiness of life and the sufficiency of learning of those who held it, as is plainly evident from the knowledge of civil affairs, the aforementioned bishops, now that these qualities have been reversed, subject the colleges of the learned to themselves and withdraw them from the rulers of the state. They use them as instruments, and indeed as very great instruments, in acquiring and defending their usurpations against the rulers of the state. For the learned men, unwilling or afraid to lose the titles of their masters, drawn on by the desire for advantage and glory that follows, and believing that these titles have come to them from no source but the authority of the bishops, accomplish the bishops' wishes, and they oppose, both to the princes of the state and to the subjects, whatever they think is contrary to the bishops' authority. But since the power of conferring licences in the disciplines belongs to the human lawgiver, or to the ruler who holds his authority, then, so that the learned and wise do not lack favour, but acquire and preserve this favour, which must be given the greatest weight above all external aids for establishing and defending their principalities and polities, the rulers ought to confer by their own authority the licences of notaries and the titles of the other magistrates or civil offices. For this cannot belong to any private person of whatever dignity or condition, or to any particular college, insofar as they are such, as was shown in chapters fifteen and seventeen of the first book.

units.la: CAP. XXII. Qualiter Romanus Episcopus & ipsius Ecclesia sit caeterarum caput & principalior, & propter quam autoritatem hoc illis conueniat.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII. How the Roman bishop and his Church are the head of the rest and more principal, and on account of what authority this belongs to them.

units.la: DETERMINATIS autem his, ostendere volumus consequenter, expediens & perutile, fore vnicum Episcopum & vnicam Ecclesiam siue collegium sacerdotum aliarum caput siue principaliorem statuere. Primum tamen oportet diuidere modos & intentiones, quibus vnicam Ecclesiam aut Episcopum aliorum omnium esse caput, intelligi potest, vt ipsorum conuenientem ab inconuenientibus & expedientibus separemus. Esse autem vnicum Episcopum aut Ecclesiam omnium aliarum caput, vno modo intelligi potest, vt videlicet secundum ipsorum diffinitionem & determinationem scripturae sacrae sensum, in quibus dubia fiunt, praecipue de credendis & observandis de necessitate salutis, omnes mundi ecclesiae ac personae singulares credere teneantur, rituque ecclesiasticum siue cultum diuinum, secundum ipsorum ordinationem seruare. Iuxta quem sensum siue modum, nullus Episcopus aut Ecclesia vnica cuiusquam prouinciae, inquantum huiusmodi siue collegium sacerdotum caput aliarum ex statuto diuinae legis, nec secundum exemplum ecclesiae primitiuae, talem aliquam vnicam expedit esse. Neq; similiter legislatoris humani fidelis ordinatione aliqua seu decreto. Sic enim cum reliquis inconuenientib. quae sequuntur ad haec, ex necessitate salutis credere tenerentur omnes principes, communitates, & populi, secundum octauam Bonifacii diffinitionem, sefore Romano Papa coactiua iurisdictione subiectos. Rursum q; secundum cuiusdam, vocati Papae Romani, constitutiones non esse Christi consilium, spernere seu renunciare in communi & proprio temporalium, quae ad praesentem necessitatem superfluunt, possessioni siue dominio seu potestati licite contendendi pro talibus, aut talia sibi vendicandi coram iudice coactiuo, quorum vnum falsum horrendissimum est; secundum vero tanquam haereticum declinandum, quemadmodum ex 13.14.16. & vigesimo ac 21. huius clare visum est prius.
units.tr: Having settled these points, we next wish to show that it is expedient and very useful for a single bishop, or a single church or college of priests, to be appointed head or more principal over the others. First, however, we must distinguish the ways and senses in which it can be understood that a single church or bishop is the head of all the others, so that we may separate what is fitting from what is unfitting and inexpedient. That there be a single bishop or church that is the head of all the others can be understood in one way: that, according to its definition and determination of the sense of Holy Scripture, in matters where doubts arise, especially concerning what must be believed and observed of necessity for salvation, all the churches of the world and all individual persons are bound to believe, and to keep the ecclesiastical rite or divine worship according to its ordinance. In accordance with this sense or manner, no single bishop or church of any province, as such, or college of priests, ought to be head of the others, either by a statute of divine law or according to the example of the primitive church. Nor likewise by any ordinance or decree of a faithful human legislator. For then, along with the other absurdities that follow from this, all princes, communities and peoples would be bound to believe, of necessity for salvation, according to the eighth definition of Boniface, that they are subject to the Roman Pope by coercive jurisdiction.
