Again, according to the constitutions of a certain man called the Roman Pope, it is not the counsel of Christ to renounce or give up, in common and in particular, the possession, lordship or power over temporal goods that exceed present need, or to lawfully contend for such goods or claim them for oneself before a coercive judge. Of these, the one is a most horrible falsehood, and the other must be avoided as heretical, as has been clearly shown above from 13, 14, 16, 20 and 21 of this work.

units.la: Alio rursum modo existimare est vnicum Episcopum & Ecclesiam siue collegium caput siue principaliorem cunctis aliis, sicut omnes mundi clerici siue collegia clericorum sibi sint iurisdictione coactiua subiecti, quod etiam nulli Episcopo vel Ecclesiae lege diuina conuenit, sed magis interdicitur consilio vel praecepto, quemadmodum ostensum est sufficienter 4.5.8.9. & 11. huius. Alio quoque modo intelligi potest prioritas haec sic, vt ad vnicum episcopum aut ecclesiam siue collegium pertineat omniu officialium ecclesiasticorum institutio, & temporalium beneficiorum distributio, depositio, & oblatio, quo et modo lege diuina conuinci non potest, episcopum aliquem aut ecclesiam aliq caeteris esse priorem, sed oppositum magis. Et ad vnum dicere, virtute verborum scripturae conuinci non potest, quod aliquis episcopus secundum vllam autoritatem siue potestatem, aut ecclesia sit caput siue principalis aliorum aut aliarum, quemadmodum ostensum est ex 17. 18. 17. & vigesimo huius, & in capitulo praecedente. Vnde neque aliqum episcopum plus excommunicare potest, aut sibi commisso populo siue prouinciae diuina interdicere sacramenta vel officia quam econuerso, neque autoritatis plus habet in alterum aut sibi commissum populum, quam econuerso, nisi per generale concilium aut fidelem legislatorem humanum super alium aut alios autoritas siue potestas haec concessa foret. Omnes ipsi Episcopi aequalis meriti sunt & autoritatis, inquantum Episcopi sunt, vt ex epistola Hieronymi ad Euangelum inducimus decimoquinto huius. Nec perfectior est aut fuit cui perfectior Apostolus aut Episcopus manus imposuit, ut apparet primæ ad Corinth. tertio. Nemo enim, inquit Apostolus, in hominibus glorietur. Omnia enim vestra sunt, sive Paulus, sive Apollo, sive Cephas, &c. vos autem Christi, vbi Glossa: Vos autem Christi non hominum in creatione vel recreatione. Propter quod non refert ad aliquod sacramentum, an perfectior vel minus perfectus presbyter manus imponat, dummodo autoritatem habeat, quia solus Deus effectum dat sacramenti. Vnde eadem & eodem, inquit Apostolus, soluens ad dubitationem hanc: Ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit, sed Deus incrementum dedit. Sicut plantans arborem aut irrigans, non est qui germinare seu opera vitæ facere tribuit, sed qui dat animam vegetantem plantæ: ita vult Apostolus, quod imponentes manus, docentes aut benedicentes, non dant opera meritoria, sed qui dat characterem aut gratiam interiorem. Deus ipse, qui minis & hi adiuuent, quemadmodum irrigantes. Et quoniam vnus est dator interioris autoritatis & characteris eiusdem speciei & gratiæ, Deus ipse, ideoque omnes Episcopi siue sacerdotes æqualis sunt autoritatis & meriti à Deo dati, secundum quemmodum Hieron. intellexit. Non est igitur Episcopus aliquis aut Ecclesia caput siue principalior aliorum inquantum huiusmodi virtute verborum scripturæ. Caput enim Ecclesiæ simpliciter & fidei fundamentum Dei ordinatione immediata, secundum scripturam siue veritatem vnicum est Christus ipse, non aliquis Apostolus, Episcopus, aut sacerdos, vt aperte dicit Apostolus ad Ephesios quarto & quinto, ad Colossenses primo, & prima ad Corinthios decimo. Vnde omnes Apostolos, prophetas, doctores, reliquosque fideles dicit constituere corpus Christi, quod est Ecclesia, tanquam reliqua membra; neminem autem sicut caput, nisi solum Christum. Vnde ad Ephesios quarto: Et ipse dedit quosdam quidem Apostolos, quosdam autem prophetas, alios vero euangelistas, alios autem pastores & doctores ad consummationem sanctorum in opus ministerii, in ædificationem corporis Christi, donec occurramus omnes in vnitatem fidei, &c. Et parum infra subiungit: Vnitatem autem facientes in charitate, crescamus in illo per omnia, qui est caput Christus. Ex quo totum corpus compactum & connexum per omnem iuncturam subministrationis, secundum operationem in mensuram vniuscuiusq; membri, augmentum corporis facit, in ædificationem sui in charitate. Rursum quinto: Quoniam vir caput est mulieris, sicut Christus est caput Ecclesiæ, ipse saluator corporis. Sicut ecclesia subiecta est Christo, ita & mulieres viris suis in omnibus. Nusquam tamen Cephaм dixit ecclesiæ caput, nec ecclesiam illi tanquam capiti fore subiectam, cum tamen hæc dicta fuerint, postquam Christus surrexit à mortuis, & super cœlos ascendit. Vnde parum infra eodem, in persona omnium fidelium loquens Apostolus, ait: Nemo enim vnquam carnem suam odio habuit, sed nutrit & fouet eam, sicut & Christus ecclesiam, quia membra sumus corporis eius. Amplius ad Colossenses primo: Et ipse est caput corporis ecclesiæ, qui est principium primogenitus ex mortuis, vt sit in omnibus ipse primatum tenens. Idem dixit aperte beatus Petrus prima canonica sua, capitulo 5. Et cum apparuerit princeps pastorum, (Christus scil.) percipietis immarcescibilem gratiæ coronam. Est rursum & fuit Christus solus ecclesiæ siue fidei fundamentum & petra. Vnde primæ ad Corinth. 3. Fundamentum enim aliud nemo ponere potest præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Et rursum eiusdem decimo, Petra autem erat Christus. Et hæc palam fuit Augustini sententia decimo de ciuitate Dei, cap. sexto & vigesimo. Idem decimo tertio, cap. vigesimo tertio. Idem 17. capitulo quarto, nono, duodecimo, decimo octauo, & vigesimo. Idem 18. cap. 45. & 52. Idem vigesimosecundo, capitulo decimo octauo, & aliis plerisque locis, de quibus pertranseo propter abbreuiationem sermonis. Alio vero modo Episcopum aliquem aut ecclesiam esse vel statui caput, & cæteris principaliorem, autoritate generalis concilii, aut fidelis legislatoris humani, conuenienter intelligi potest, sicut videlicet ipsius sit officium, cum suo tamen collegio sacerdotum, quos sibi fidelis lator aut generale concilium ad hoc asseciare voluerit, deliberatione præhabita, si casus emerserit fidei, aut fidelium euidens necessitas, sibi delatus, propter quem expediens omnino videatur generale concilium conuocare, id insinuare atque significare debeat fideli legislatori, superiore carenti, iuxta cuius coactionem præceptum id debeat, quemadmodum diximus, congregari cuius etiam officium sit in dicto concilio, inter episcopos & clericos primam sedem seu locum tenere, deliberanda proponere, deliberata in præsentia totius concilii recolligere in scriptis sub sigillis authenticis, & tabellionum signaculis redigi facere. cunctis requirentibus ecclesiis, talia communicare atq; insinuare: ea quoq; scire, docere, ac de talibus respondere: deliberatorum quoq; tam circa fidem quaritum ecclesiasticum siue cultum diuinum, & reliquorum ordinatorum ad pacem atq; fidelium vnitatem, transgressores per ecclesiasticam aliquam arcere censuram, vt excommunicationis vel interdicti, aut alterius pœnæ consimilis, secundum concilii tamen determinationem, & per ipsius autoritatem, nequaquam vero potestate aliqua coactiua pœnæ realis aut personalis inflictiua pro statu & in statu præsentis seculi. Cuius etiam, cum sibi per legislatorem videl. dati & instituti collegii parte valentiori siue maiori iudicare sit super episcopos & ecclesias, non subiunctem positas de contentionib. spiritalib. proprie dictis, iuxta secundam scil. ac tertiam huius nominis spirituale significationem, assignatis secundo huius. In quibus cadunt ea quæ circa ritum ecclesiasticum ordinata fuerint per concilium obseruari, quamuis eiusmodi Episcopo Ecclesiæ siue collegio circa tale officium secundum apertam, verisimilem, & quasi communem aliarum ecclesiarum sententiam, peruerse nimis aut negligenter habente licitum sit ecclesiis reliquis humanum legislatorem fideletm appellare, si per legislatorem aut ipsius autoritate principantem corrigi possit conuenienter, vel generale concilium requirere, si casus ille per reliquarum ecclesiarum ampliorem partem, & legislatoris iudicium exigat concilium huiusmodi congregari.
units.tr: In another way one may think that a single bishop and church or college is the head or more principal than all the others, as if all the clergy of the world, or colleges of clergy, were subject to it by coercive jurisdiction. This too does not belong to any bishop or church by divine law, but is rather forbidden by counsel or precept, as has been sufficiently shown in 4, 5, 8, 9 and 11 of this work. In another way this priority can also be understood: that the appointment of all ecclesiastical officials, and the distribution, deposition and conferral of temporal benefices, belong to a single bishop or church or college. This too cannot be proved by divine law to make any bishop or church prior to the others; the opposite is rather the case. Nor can it be proved, by the force of the words of Scripture, that any bishop, by any authority or power, or any church, is the head or principal of the others, as has been shown from 17, 18, 17 and 20 of this work and in the preceding chapter. Hence no bishop can excommunicate more people than the reverse, nor forbid the sacraments or the offices of divine worship to the people or province committed to him any more than conversely; nor has he more authority over another, or over the people committed to him, than conversely, unless this authority or power over another or others were granted by a general council or a faithful human legislator. All bishops are of equal merit and authority, insofar as they are bishops, as we have adduced from Jerome's letter to Evangelus in 15 of this work. Nor is anyone more perfect, or was he more perfect, on whom a more perfect apostle or bishop laid hands, as appears from 1 Corinthians 3. For, says the Apostle, let no one glory in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, etc. But you are Christ's, where the Gloss says: "You are Christ's, not men's," in creation or re-creation. Therefore it makes no difference to any sacrament whether a more perfect or a less perfect presbyter lays on hands, provided he has authority, because God alone gives the effect of the sacrament. Hence the same Apostle, resolving this doubt, says: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase." As one who plants a tree or waters it is not the one who gives it the power to germinate or to produce the works of life, but the one who gives the vegetating soul to the plant, so the Apostle wills that those who lay on hands, teach or bless do not give meritorious works, but He who gives the character or inner grace. God himself, who gives the increase, helps through these ministers, like those who water. And since there is one giver of inner authority, and of the character of the same kind and of grace, namely God himself, therefore all bishops or priests are of equal authority and merit, given by God, as Jerome understood. Therefore no bishop or church is the head or more principal of the others, as such, by the force of the words of Scripture. For the head of the Church absolutely, and the foundation of faith, by God's immediate ordinance, according to Scripture or truth, is one: Christ himself, not any apostle, bishop or priest, as the Apostle plainly says to the Ephesians 4 and 5, to the Colossians 1, and 1 Corinthians 10. Hence he says that all apostles, prophets, teachers and the other faithful constitute the body of Christ, which is the Church, as its remaining members; but no one as the head except Christ alone. Hence Ephesians 4: "And he gave some apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others ministers and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, until we all come into the unity of faith," etc. And a little below he adds: "But doing the truth in love, let us grow up in him in all things, who is the head, Christ. From whom the whole body, compacted and joined together by every joint of supply, according to the working in due measure of each member, makes increase of the body, to the edifying of itself in love." Again, in chapter 5: "For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the Saviour of the body. As the Church is subject to Christ, so also wives to their husbands in all things." Yet nowhere did he call Peter the head of the Church, nor say that the Church would be subject to him as head, although these things were said after Christ rose from the dead and ascended above the heavens. Hence a little below, in the same place, speaking in the person of all the faithful, the Apostle says: "For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also the Church, because we are members of his body." Further, Colossians 1: "And he is the head of the body of the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he himself may hold the primacy." The blessed Peter said the same plainly in his first Epistle, chapter 5: "And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory." Again, Christ alone is and was the foundation and rock of the Church or of faith. Hence 1 Corinthians 3: "For no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ." And again, in chapter 10: "But the rock was Christ." This was clearly also the opinion of Augustine: in the tenth book of the City of God, chapters 6 and 20. The same in book 13, chapter 23. The same in 17, chapters 4, 9, 12, 18 and 20. The same in 18, chapters 45 and 52. The same in book 22, chapter 18, and in many other places, which I pass over for the sake of brevity. In another way, however, a bishop or church may suitably be understood, by the authority of a general council or of a faithful human legislator, to be set up as head and more principal than the others. This would be on the basis that it is his office, together with his own college of priests whom the faithful legislator or general council wishes to associate with him for this purpose, after prior deliberation, if a case of faith arises, or a plain necessity of the faithful is brought to him, on account of which it seems altogether expedient to convene a general council, to signify and make this known to the faithful legislator who has no superior, by whose coercion, as we said, such a council ought to be assembled. It is also his office, in the said council, to hold the first seat or place among bishops and clergy; to propose matters for deliberation; to gather together in writing, under authentic seals and with the signatures of notaries, what has been deliberated in the presence of the whole council; and to communicate and make known such things to all the churches that ask; to know and teach these things, and to answer concerning them. Also, to keep off, by some ecclesiastical censure such as excommunication, interdict, or another similar penalty, those who transgress the decisions taken concerning faith, ecclesiastical rite or divine worship, and the other ordinances for peace and the unity of the faithful; but this is to be done according to the determination of the council and through its authority, and never by any coercive power or by inflicting a real or personal penalty for the state and condition of the present age. It is also his to judge, with the more powerful or greater part of the college given and instituted by the legislator, over bishops and churches not subject to him, concerning spiritual disputes properly so called, according to the second and third meanings of this word "spiritual" assigned in the second [chapter] of this work. Among these fall those things which have been ordained by the council to be observed concerning ecclesiastical rite. Although, for a bishop, church or college that holds such an office, if it is perversely or negligently following an opinion that is plain, probable, and almost common among the other churches, it is lawful for the remaining churches to appeal to the faithful human legislator, if the matter can suitably be corrected by the legislator or by one ruling under his authority; or to request a general council, if that case, by the judgment of the greater part of the remaining churches and of the legislator, requires such a council to be convened.

units.la: Hoc igitur solo & vltimo modo Episcopum aut Ecclesiam aliquam vnicam statuere aliarum caput seu principaliorem in cura pastorali, absque iurisdictione coactiva, quamuis non sit lege divina præceptum, quoniam & sine hoc fidei vnitas, licet non sic faciliter salvaretur, expedire dico ad hanc vnitatem facilius & decentius observandam. Deinde vero monstrandum erit nobis, qualem Episcopum, Ecclesiam, siue collegium sacerdotum & clericorum. Et ex qua dicecesi siue prouincia conuenientius expediat aliorum caput siue principaliorem statuere. Demum vero monstrabimus cuius aut quorum sit auctoritas huius institutionis, correctionis, & depositionis etiam, si visum fuerit expedire. Horum autem primum videl. quod tale caput ecclesiarum vnicum expediat instituere, supposita necessitate, conuocandi quandoq; generale fidelium concilium & sacerdotum propter vtilitates prædictas circa ecclesiasticum ritum siue fidem & cultum diuinum suaderi potest ex eo quod frustra occuparentur plures Episcopi aut ecclesiæ in officio quod per vnicum Episcopum aut ecclesiam, æque conuenienter exerceri potest, atq; compleri. Nunc autem insinuatio conciliorum prædicta cum reliquis, quæ ad huius capitis ecclesiæ officium diximus pertinere, æque conuenienter aut conuenientius per vnicum exerceri possunt & perfici quam per plures. Amplius & huiusmodi capitis siue principalioris super episcopos & ecclesias institutione, contentio tollitur, & scandalum oriri possibile. Nam in generali concilio congregato, agendorum dare formam & modum oportet. Hæc autem ordinare aut præcipere, si quilibet indifferenter posset & veller, inter eos verisimiliter suscitaretur scandalum, confusio atq; contentio, & rursum quoniam in generali concilio congregato attenditur ordo loci: vt in sedendo vel stando, sermonis etiam, vt in proponendo & deliberando, & aliqua præcipere quandoq;, vt nimis garrulis, silentium imponendo. Amplius quoniam & per concilium deliberatare colligere oportet, ac in scriptis per tabelliones redigi facere, sub certis & authenticis signaculis & sigillis, expediens fuit vnum esse aliorum priorem cuius sit autoritas cæteros ordinandi, & reliqua expedientia præcipiendi circa concilium celebrandum & debite consumandum, ne propter talium diuersitatem & quandoq; contrarietatem publicam fidelium turbetur aut differatur vtilitas. Adhuc videtur id expedire propter consuetudinem ecclesiæ Christianæ, in hoc. Et quoniam ex eo fidei vnitas magis apparet sensibili signo.
units.tr: In this one final way, then, a bishop or a single church may be set up as the head or chief of the others in pastoral care, without coercive jurisdiction. Although this is not commanded by divine law, since without it the unity of the faith could still be preserved, though not so easily, I say it is expedient for keeping this unity more easily and more becomingly. Next we must show what kind of bishop, church, or college of priests and clergy this should be, and from which diocese or province it is more fitting to appoint the head or chief of the others. Last, we will show whose authority this institution, correction, and even deposition belongs to, if it seems expedient. Of these, the first point, namely that it is expedient to appoint such a single head of the churches, given the necessity of sometimes calling a general council of the faithful and of priests, can be argued from the following: for the sake of the advantages mentioned above, concerning ecclesiastical rite, faith, and divine worship, several bishops or churches would be needlessly busied with a task that a single bishop or church can carry out and complete just as becomingly. Now the aforesaid convening of councils, together with the other duties we have said belong to the office of this head church, can be exercised and performed just as becomingly, or more becomingly, by one as by many. Moreover, by such an institution of a head or chief over bishops and churches, contention is removed and the possibility of scandal arising is lessened. For when a general council has been gathered, it is necessary to give a form and method to its business. If anyone at all could and would issue these orders or commands, strife, confusion, and contention would probably arise among them. Again, since in a gathered general council the order of place is observed, both in sitting or standing and in speaking, as in proposing and deliberating, and sometimes some commands must be given, such as imposing silence on the overly talkative, it is also necessary that the council's deliberations be collected and drawn up in writing by notaries, under certain authentic seals and signatures. Therefore it was expedient that one of them be the first among the others, whose authority is to order the rest and to command what else is useful for holding the council and bringing it properly to completion, lest the public good be disturbed or delayed through the diversity, and sometimes the open contrariety, of such men. It seems further that this is expedient on account of the custom of the Christian Church in this matter, and because unity of faith appears more clearly by a visible sign.

units.la: Quem vero episcopum & qualem cuiusq; prouinciæ siue diœcesis ecclesiam, sic caput aliarum instituere magis conueniat, qualem primum assignates, dicamus secundum veritatem eum qui cæteris vita & sacra doctrina, cunctis præpollet, in quo tamen est bonæ vitæ potius attendendus excessus, cuius autem loci siue puncta ecclesiæ præferri debeat, dicendum eam, cuius sacerdotale ue clericorum collegium, & vt plurimum honestioris vitæ ac lucidioris doctrinæ sacræ, viris abundat. Quamuis cæteris parib. aut non multum distantib. etiam Romanus Episcopus & ipsius Ecclesia, quam diu locus habitabilis extet, plurib. congruentiis videatur merito præferri. Primum quidem, propter Episcopi sui primi beati Petri aut Pauli, vel virtusq; excellentem fidem & charitatem, famositatem, & per Apostolos reliquos illis impensam reverentiam: deinde vero propter Romanæ vrbis solennitatem, & quam dudum super cæteras obtinuit principalitatem & abundantiam in ipsa virorum Illustrium, sanctorum atq; doctorum fidei Christianæ, secundum temporis piurimum ab initio ecclesiæ constitutæ, qui aliarum ecclesiarum in augmento fidei & eius vnitate ser- uanda, curam diligentem atq; laborem assiduum præbuerunt, rursum etiam propter sui populi ac principis generalem tunc monarchiam & auctoritatem coactiuam super reliquos omnes mundi principantes & populos, qui de observatione fidei & eorum quæ per generalia diffiniebantur consilia, toti poterant omnibus coactiuum ferre præceptum, & illius vbilibet transgressores arcere, sic quoque fecerunt & ecclesiam ex modico in tem magnam auxerunt, quanquam ab ipsorum aliquibus postmodum persecutionem fideles sint passi quandoq; propter quorundam malitiam etiam sacerdotum. Demum vero congruit Episcopo Romano & illius Ecclesiæ principalitas hæc pro- pter consuetudinem, eo quod hunc Episcopum & Ecclesiam fideles omnes præceteris dixerunt seu consuenerunt amplius reuereri, & illius exhortationibus atque monitionibus ad virtutes & reuerentiam excitari, eiusq; arguitionibus seu increpationibus & comminationibus æternæ damnationis à vitiis & scelcribus reuocari.
units.tr: But which bishop, and what kind of church of each province or diocese, it is more fitting to set up as head of the others, as the first to be designated, we shall say according to the truth: it is the one who excels the rest in life and in sound doctrine, in all things; yet in this one ought chiefly to be considered an excellence of good life. As to what place or city the church ought to be preferred, we say it is the one whose college of priests or clergy abounds in men of more honourable life and more brilliant sacred learning. Yet, even with others being equal or not much different, the Roman bishop and his Church, for as long as the habitable world stands, seem rightly to be preferred on many grounds. First, indeed, because of the eminent faith and charity of Peter or Paul, the first bishop of that church, or of both together, their fame, and the reverence shown to them by the other apostles. Then, because of the dignity of the city of Rome and the primacy it long ago won above the rest, and the abundance there of illustrious, holy, and learned men of the Christian faith, who for most of the time since the church was founded gave diligent care and constant labour to the increase of the faith in other churches and to keeping its unity. Again, because of the then general monarchy and coercive authority of its people and prince over all the other rulers and peoples of the world, who, concerning the observance of the faith and of what was defined by general councils, could issue a coercive command to all and restrain wherever transgressors of it appeared. They acted in this way too, and enlarged the church from a small beginning into a great one, although the faithful at times suffered persecution from some of these rulers, sometimes because of the malice of certain priests. Lastly, this primacy suits the Roman bishop and his Church because of custom, in that all the faithful have been accustomed to revere this bishop and Church more than others, and to be stirred to virtue and reverence by his exhortations and admonitions, and to be called back from vices and crimes by his rebukes, reproofs, and threats of eternal damnation.

units.la: Cuius autem sit auctoritas instituendi prioritatem hanc: Dicendum, quod generalis concilii aut secundarie vs d'ramen fidelis legislatoris humani superiore carentis. Ad quos etiam pertinet determinare primum illum clericorum cœtum siue collegium, secundum quem modum Romanæ vrb. quam diu extiterit, obtinemque ad hoc non appoluerit populus ille, propter beatorum Petri & Pauli reverentiam, & quas pridem diximus conuenientias poterit licite ac debebit iam dicta principalitas in Episcopo & Ecclesia continue seruari.
units.tr: As for whose authority it is to institute this primacy, we say: it belongs to a general council, or to a secondary authority of a faithful human lawgiver who has no superior. To these also belongs the determination of that college or assembly of clergy by which the aforesaid primacy in the bishop and church may lawfully and must continually be kept, in the manner in which the Roman city, for as long as it has existed and holds it, has not been appointed to this by that people, but by reverence for the blessed Peters and Paul, and by the fitnesses we have mentioned above.

units.la: Hanc autem fore legislatoris quam diximus potestatem, testatur edictum primi Constantini Romanorum Imperatorum, insertum codici Isidori supradicto, in quo continetur inter cætera series hæc: Atque decernentes sancimus, (nos videlicet, Imperator Romanus,) vt principatum teneat (ecclesia Rom. scilicet,) tam super quatuor præcipuas sedes, Antiochenam, Alexandrinam, Constantinopolitanam, & Hierosolymitanam, atque etiam super omnes in vniuerso orbe terrarum Dei Ecclesias. Et pontifex, qui pro tempore ipsius sacrosanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ extiterit, celsitudine principalis sacerdotibus totius mundi existat. Et eius iudicio, quæque ad cultum Dei, vel fidei stabilitatem procurandam fuerint, disponentur. Dixit autem signanter, procurandam per ipsum fidei siue legis diuinæ stabilitatem; nec dixit secundum suam aut suæ solius ecclesiæ siue collegii sententiam determinandam. Quoniam vt pridem diximus solicitari & inquiri, reor opiniones emergentes circa scripturam & fidem, quæ schisma vel aliud scandalum afferre possunt, & fidelium quietem ac vnitatem turbare, idque denunciare fideli legislatori, aut illius autoritate principanti, & ab ipso concilium requirere propter huiusmodi determinanda, & si expediens fuerit, corrigenda, ad sui pertinet officii prioritatem, quam diximus. Sic igitur principalitatem hanc tribuit Constantinus Episcopo & Ecclesiæ Romanorum: & cum principalitate hac propter devotionem, autoritates alias quam plurimas etiam coactiuas, ad quarum collationem eidem diuino vel humano iure minime tenebatur. Hanc siquidem etiam principalitatem iam dictam ab Episcopo & ecclesia Romanorum, revocatam fortasse per successores aliquos Constantini, restituit Augustus Phocas ecclesiæ supradictæ, vt ex Chronica Martini de Romanis Pontificibus & Imperatoribus euidenter apparet: Vbi legitur inter cætera, Bonifacium quartum natum Marsorum, &c. & parum infra: Hic obtinuit ab Augusto Phoca Imperatore, vt Ecclesia beati Petri Apostoli caput esset omnium ecclesiarum, quia Constantinopolitana primam omnium se scribebat.
units.tr: That this is the power of the lawgiver we have described is attested by the edict of the first Constantine, Emperor of the Romans, inserted in the aforesaid code of Isidore, in which among other things this sequence is contained: "And decreeing, we (namely, the Roman Emperor) sanction that the Church of Rome shall hold primacy both over the four chief sees, Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople, and Jerusalem, and also over all the churches of God in the whole world. And the pontiff who for the time shall be of that most holy Roman Church shall be the chief of all priests of the whole world, and by his judgment whatever is to be done for the worship of God or for the procuring of the stability of the faith shall be arranged." He said expressly "the stability of the faith or divine law to be procured through him," and did not say "to be determined according to his own opinion or that of his church or college alone." For, as we said before, I hold that the opinions arising concerning Scripture and the faith, which can bring schism or other scandal and disturb the peace and unity of the faithful, ought to be sought out and examined, and that this be reported to the faithful lawgiver, or to one ruling by his authority, and a council be requested from him to determine such matters and, if expedient, to correct them; this belongs to the aforesaid primacy of his office. Thus Constantine granted this primacy to the bishop and Church of the Romans, and along with this primacy, because of their devotion, many other authorities, even coercive ones, to whose bestowal he was in no way bound by divine or human law. This same primacy, which had perhaps been revoked by some successors of Constantine, was restored to the aforesaid Church of the Romans by the Emperor Phocas, as is clearly shown in the Chronicle of Martin concerning the Roman Pontiffs and Emperors, where among other things we read: "Boniface the Fourth, son of the Marsi, etc.," and a little lower: "He obtained from the Emperor Phocas that the Church of the blessed Apostle Peter should be the head of all churches, because the Church of Constantinople had been writing itself first of all."

units.la: Huius autem rursum institutionis autoritatem esse legislatoris humani fidelis, iuxta consilium & determinationem generalis concilii, coiunci potest eisdem rationib. & autoritatib. quib. ostensum est 21. huius, ad ipsum autoritatem pertinere generale concilium conuocare, rebelles ad conueniendum sacerdotes & non sacerdotes omnes, ac ordinatorum per concilium transgressores, licite per coactiuam arcere potentiam, sola rationum mutata extremitate minori. Ex quib. eisdem per necessitatem sequitur, eiusdem forte autoritatis, iam dictum Episcopum principalem, & Ecclesiam sine collegium corrigere, ab officio suspendere ac priuare seu deponere licite, si visum fuerit rationabiliter expedire. Non est autem prætereundum silentio, quod sub infidelib. legislatorib. siue horum autoritate principantib. constituti fideles, tam sacerdotes quam non sacerdotes, qui fuerint in lege diuina periti, eadem diuina lege videlicet obligantur, si congrue possint conuenire ad eius sensus dubios diffiniendum, & determinandum, ac reliqua ordinandum, quæ ad fidei & fidelium augmentum & vnitatem atq; communem vtilitatem spicere possint, quamuis ad hoc ampliùs obligentur sacerdotes, & debeant alios excitare. Quoniam ipsorum officium est alios docere, exhortari, arguere, & si oportuerit increpare. Tenentur etiam consequenter ad hoc, qui docti fuerint in lege diuina, & per sacerdotes ad hoc requirendi sunt, quoniam scienti bonum facere, & non facienti peccatum est illi, vt scribitur Iacobi 4. Quemadmodum enim ad ciuilem libertatem defendendam per pugnam corporalem tempore necessitatis, humana lege non solum obligantur qui assignati sunt officio militari, pedestri aut equestri, verum etiam qui ex aliis officiis ciuitatis extiterint. Et amplius qui ad hoc sunt magis idonei, præcipue cum per militares aut ipsorum ducem fuerint requisiti. Sic etiam ad fidei defensionem & declarationem & reliquum ritum ecclesiasticum ordinandum, non soli sacerdotes obligantur lege diuina, verum etiam qui non sacerdotes, periti tamen in ea, præsertim cum ad hæc per sacerdotes fuerint requisiti, quamuis hoc sit proprium sacerdotum officium.
units.tr: The authority of this institution, again, belongs to the faithful human lawgiver, in accordance with the counsel and determination of a general council, and it can be joined with the same reasons and authorities by which it was shown in chapter 21 of this work that it belongs to him to convene a general council and to restrain lawfully, by coercive power, all rebellious priests and non-priests who refuse to attend, and transgressors of what has been ordained by the council, the only difference being in the minor premise of the arguments. From these same considerations it follows of necessity that the same authority may lawfully correct, suspend from office, deprive, or depose the aforesaid principal bishop and Church or college, if it seems reasonably expedient. Nor is it to be passed over in silence that the faithful, both priests and non-priests, who are learned in divine law, living under unfaithful lawgivers or under rulers acting by their authority, are bound by that same divine law to come together, if they can conveniently do so, to define and determine its doubtful senses and to order the rest, which may serve the increase and unity of the faith and of the faithful and the common good. Priests are more strongly bound to this and ought to stir up others, since their office is to teach, exhort, rebuke, and, if necessary, reprove. Those also who are learned in divine law are bound to this in consequence, and must be called upon for it by the priests, since "to him who knows to do good and does not do it, it is sin," as written in James 4. For just as, for the defence of civil liberty in time of need, by bodily fighting, not only those assigned to military service, on foot or on horse, are bound by human law, but also those from other offices of the state, and especially those who are more fit for it, above all when they have been called upon by the soldiers or their leader; so too, for the defence and declaration of the faith and for ordering the rest of the ecclesiastical rite, not only priests are bound by divine law, but also non-priests, provided they are learned in it, especially when they have been called upon for these things by the priests, although this is the proper office of priests.

units.la: Quo vero conuocante sacerdotum collegium & reliquorum fidelium idoneorum congregabitur, merito quæret vtiq; quis, cum nullus sacerdotum aut reliquorum fidelium, lege diuina sit cæteris prior secundū determinata pri, neq; humana, eo q legislator humanus vbiq; supponitur infidelis. Nos autem dicamus iuxta scripturæ sensum, per nullum episcopum siue sacerdotem habentem super alios sacerdotes & episcopos autoritatem, futuram conuocationem aut congregationem prædictam, nisi forsitan eo casu, quo per iam dictam fidelium pluralitatem huiusmodi autoritas alicui sacerdotum concessa foret. Esto igitur neminem sic aliis omnibus per sacerdotem & reliquorum fidelium multitudinem fuisse prælatum, sed præferendum expedire, aut aliud quid circa fidem & ecclesiasticum ritum expediens ordinandum. Dico vocationem congregationis huius vel ab omnibus sacerdotibus prouenturam, si fortasse tantæ charitatis fuerit vnusquisq;, quod propter fidem conseruandam & augendam velit alios excitare, sic, vt hoc sibi condicentibus & consentientibus omnibus, nulli dubium ipsos facilitèr congregari. Aut si forte non omnes tantæ fuerint charitatis, vt seipsos & alios ad dictam congregationem monere velint, ab aliquo vel aliquib. reliquis feruentioribus amore diuino proueniet, aliis vero presbyteris aut non presbyteris obtemperantib. sibi tanquam benedicentibus & cósalentibus recte. Quo etiam alterutro dictorum modorum conuenerunt apostoli & seniores videre, an oporteret ad salutem æternam incircumcisos fratres circumcidi, sicut apparet Actuum 15. Nusquam legitur, quod vocante apostolorum aliquo per suam autoritatem alii conuenerint. Sed solum hoc, quod conuenerunt apostoli & seniores videre de verbo hoc. Et rursum quod conuocantes duodecim multitudinem discipulorum. Quis vero apostolorum primus exeitator seu exhortator fuerit ad huius congregationes fiendas, ex scriptura non habetur expressum. Esto tamen hunc fuisse beatum Petrum propter ampliorem in ipso charitatem, non propterea sequeretur ex hoc, ipsum habuisse super apostolos alios autoritatem aliquam, nisi eam forte quam sibi per ipsorum electionem super cæteros tribuissent, quemadmodum supra ostensum est 15. & 16. huius. Sunt enim in claustris & ciuilitatibus plurimi, merito vitæ atq; doctrinæ sacræ perfectiores, aut virtute politica præstantiores, qui tamen minus perfectiorum non sunt principes aut prælati, sed plerunque subiecti, quod in sacerdotalibus officiis, nescio vel fortasse noui, quapeste frequenter euenit temporibus his. Amplius, sicut quandoque in ciuili congregatione studiosioribus, antiquioribus, & magis approbatis vitis à suis ciuibus, nulla sibi tamen autoritate subiectis, sed propter solam reuerentiam quæ ampliori virtuti & ætati deberi videtur prærogatiua sedendi, loquendi, & deliberandi conceditur, & in aliis honorationibus defertur quam plaribus, pluribus, sic verisimile valde ac iuxta scripturae seriem, propterea dictas causas, caeteri Apostoli Petro deferebant. Primus enim inter alios propositum legitur, unde fortassis a quibusdam sanctis, dictas est es & vertex collegii Apostolorum, quamuis nulla forent sibi auctoritate subiecti, nisi secundum eam quam pridem diximus ipsorum electionem, si ipsum sic sibi praeferre sponte voluerint abbatem aut priorem monachi & praesidem populi. Secundum itaq; iam dictos modos, conocationem & congregationem fidelium fuisse possibilem, rationabile valde. Sicut enim ad civilem communitatem & legem ordinandam convenerunt homines a principio, ipsorum valentiori parte concordante in his quae sunt ad vitae sufficientiam, non quidem vocati per singularem hominem, aut per plures aliquos habentes auctoritatem coactiuam in reliquos, sed suasione & exhortatione prudentum & facundorum virorum, quos natura inter alios produxit inclinatos ad hoc, ex se postmodum proficientes suis exercitiis, & alios dirigentes, ad quam etiam homines naturaliter inclinati, obtemperaverunt suadentibus facile, quemadmodum ex primo Politicae c. 1. & quarto eiusdem cap. decimo, & ex septimo illius capitulo 12. induximus tertio, quarto, septimo & 13. prima. Sic quoque proportionaliter opinandum, multitudinem apostolorum atque fidelium convenisse, suadente fortasse apostolorum aliquo vel aliquibus charitate feruentioribus, reliqua quoq; multitudine spiritus Sancti gratia, & inclinatione obtemperante faciliter. Quo etiam modo post apostolorum tempora sub infidelibus legislatoribus sive principibus, fortasse fecerunt Episcoporum sive sacerdotum aliqui charitate Christi & proximi magis abundantes, cum quibus se mansurum usq; ad seculi consummationem, Christus promisit Matth. ultimo & novissimo verbo. Hi enim sunt, de quib. Rabanus dicit ibidem; quod usque in finem seculi non sunt defuturi in mundo, qui divina manistone & inhabitatione sunt digni, quamuis ad hoc ex officio teneatur quilibet sacerdotum, si congrue possit. Omnibus enim hoc datum est praeceptum in apostolorum persona Matth. ultimo, dum ad eos dixit Christus; Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes. Quod attendens apostolus primae ad Corinth. 9. dicebat: Vae mihi si non evangelizavero, necessitas enim mihi incumbit. Cuius exemplum, sollicitudinem & laborem circa fidei augmentum & unitatem servandam moderni pastores ecclesiae Romanae, parum attendunt, Christi fideles ad litem & discordiam invicem excitantes, ut eisdem possint securius, quamuis illicite ac indebite, seculariter principari.
units.tr: Who, then, will summon the college of priests and the other suitable faithful to assemble? Surely someone will ask this, since no priest or other faithful person has priority over the rest by divine law, as determined above, nor by human law, because a human lawgiver is always assumed to be an unbeliever. But we say, according to the sense of Scripture, that no bishop or priest who holds authority over other priests and bishops will summon that assembly or gathering, unless perhaps in the case where such authority has been granted to someone among the priests by the plurality of the faithful already mentioned. Suppose then that no one has been set above all the others by a priest and the multitude of the other faithful, but that someone should be put forward, or something else concerning the faith and ecclesiastical rite needs to be settled. I say that the summons to this gathering will come either from all the priests, if each of them has so much charity that he wishes to rouse the others for the sake of preserving and increasing the faith, so that, with all agreeing and consenting to this, there is no doubt that they will easily assemble. Or, if perhaps not all have such charity as to wish to warn themselves and others about that gathering, it will come from some one or several of the others who are more fervent in the love of God, and the other elders or non-elders will obey them readily, as those who bless and rightly counsel. In one or other of these ways, the apostles and elders came together to consider whether the uncircumcised brethren had to be circumcised for eternal salvation, as appears in Acts 15. It is nowhere read that they gathered at the summons of one of the apostles by his own authority. But only this is read: the apostles and elders came together to consider this matter. And again: calling together the twelve, the multitude of the disciples. Who among the apostles was the first to stir up or urge the holding of these gatherings is not expressly stated in Scripture. Yet even if we grant that this was blessed Peter, on account of his greater charity, it would not follow from this that he had any authority over the other apostles, except perhaps that which they had given him over the rest by their own choice, as was shown above in sections 15 and 16 of this work. For in monasteries and in civil communities there are many who are more perfect in the merit of life and sacred teaching, or more outstanding in political virtue, yet they are not the rulers or superiors of those who are less perfect, but are for the most part subject to them; and this, I know not or perhaps I do know, very often happens in ecclesiastical offices in these times. Furthermore, just as sometimes in a civil assembly the more studious, the older, and those whose lives are more approved by their fellow citizens, though they have no authority over them, are granted the precedence of sitting, speaking and deliberating, and receive other marks of honour from the majority, out of mere reverence which seems due to greater virtue and age, so it is very likely and in keeping with the order of Scripture that for these reasons the other apostles deferred to Peter. For he is read to have been named first among the others, whence he is perhaps called by some holy writers thou art the summit and head of the college of the Apostles, although they were not subject to him by any authority, except according to that choice of theirs which we mentioned earlier, if they had voluntarily wished to set him over themselves as abbot or prior of a monastery and leader of a people. Accordingly, by the methods already mentioned, the calling and gathering of the faithful was possible, and very reasonable. For just as men from the beginning came together to establish a civil community and law, the more capable part of them agreeing on what is needed for a sufficient living, summoned not by a single man, nor by several who held coercive authority over the rest, but by the persuasion and exhortation of wise and eloquent men, whom nature had brought forth among the others as inclined to this, who afterwards advanced by their own exercises and directed the others; to these men, too, naturally inclined, the people obeyed readily as they persuaded, as we have shown from the first book of the Politics, chapter 1, and the fourth of the same, chapter 10, and from the seventh of that work, chapter 12, and from the third, fourth, seventh and thirteenth [chapters] of the first [book]. So too we should think in a similar way that the multitude of apostles and faithful came together, perhaps at the urging of some one or several of the apostles who were more fervent in charity, and the rest of the multitude, by the grace of the Holy Spirit and with an inclination to obey, readily followed. In the same way, after the time of the apostles, under unbelieving lawgivers or princes, perhaps some of the bishops or priests who abounded more in the charity of Christ and of neighbour did so, those with whom I shall remain until the end of the age, as Christ promised in the last words of Matthew. For these are the ones of whom Rabanus says in the same place that until the end of the age there will be those in the world who are worthy of the divine indwelling and habitation, although every priest is bound by his office to do this, if he can do so fittingly. For this command was given to all in the person of the apostles in Matthew's last chapter, when Christ said to them: Go therefore and teach all nations. The apostle, heeding this, said in 1 Corinthians 9: Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel, for necessity is laid upon me. Of this example, the concern and labour for increasing and keeping the faith in unity, the present ministers of the Roman church pay little attention, stirring up Christ's faithful to strife and discord with one another, so that they may rule more securely in worldly fashion, though unlawfully and undeservedly.

units.la: Ex dictis itaq; patet, Romanum episcopum, & ipsius ecclesiam aliarum hactenus extitisse principaliorem & caput, & in quibus esse debuit & debeat esse caput, sufficienter ostensum est. Unde vero ad ipsum, & secundum quem modum peruenerit auctoritas haec, & usq; ad quantum de facto, quamuis indebite acillicite subreptitie sit protensa, resumentes dicamus, quod Episcopus & Ecclesia Romanorum, secundum ea quae induximus 18. huius, parte 5. 6. & 7. ab initio sui usq; ad tempora Constantini obtinuit licite prioritatem hanc ex aliarum ecclesiarum, quasi electione praebentium eidem consensum & obedientiam, sponte tamen, non quidem, quia eidem aliqua forent auctoritate subiectae, sed propter apostolorum Petri & Pauli praeeminentiam charitatis, & in fide constantiam, & rursum propter multitudinem solennium personarum in ea, honestate praepollentium atq; doctrina. Qui etiam propter ipsorum charitatem immensam, curam & sollicitudinem assumpserunt, aliarum ecclesiarum praelatos & singulares fideles alios instruere, ac fraterne monere. His autem ipsorum monita tanquam doctiorum, suscipientib. ipsorum etiam ordinationes circa ecclesiasticum ritum, quoniam vtiles videbantur & iustae, postmodum susceperunt, & demum ipsorum mandatis sub ecclesiastica censura excommunionis vel interdicti, propter fidelium unitatem servandam obedierunt, quae siquidem obedientia spontanea, per longam consuetudinem obtinuit vim electionis cuiusdam. Unde licet circa initium Ecclesiae, reliqui Episcopi & Ecclesiae fidelium neque divina neq; humana lege aliqua obligarentur obedire mandatis aut institutis Ecclesiae vel Episcopi Romanorum, plusquam econuerso, inualescente tamen hac vtili & rationabili consuetudine, qua fideles in unitate amplius servabantur, eo q; tunc fideli carmerunt legislatore ipsos ad ordinem redacente ac in unitate seruante, obligati fuerunt posteri lege divina ad huiusmodi obedientiam in licitis & honestis, ac si dictum Episcopum & Ecclesiam per electionem sibi iudicem statuissent circa ecclesiarum ritum, & hoc praesertim vsq; in ea tempora quib. possent publice congregari, & de statu ecclesiastico perfectius ordinare. De contentiosis autem actib. altera quidem ratio est, in illis iudicandis inter fideles, sive sacerdotes sive non sacerdotes aliud consilium dedit apostolus, secundum quod ex 1. ad Cor. 6. induximus aliqualiter 9. huius, & eiusdem 29. explicabimus amplius. Hoc n. noluit Apostolus esse officium sacerdotis seu episcopi cuiusquam, aut solius ipsorum collegii, sicut ex Apostoli serie ac sanctorum expositionib. euidenter apparet ibid. Sic ergo Romanus Episcopus & ipsius Ecclesia prioritatem licite a principio, per quandam sui charitatidam sollicitudinem obtinere coepit, q postmodum propter consuetam deuotionem, reuerentiā, & obedientiam spontaneam electionis quasi robur assumpsit. Nusquam n. ex scriptura colligi potest, q praecepto Christi vel consilio aut alicuius apostolorum, ecclesiae vel Episcopi reliqui, subesse deberent Ecclesiae vel Episcopo Romanorum etiam in ecclesiastico ritu. Quod si tamen necessitatis fuisset debitum ad salutem fidelium, quemadmodum asserunt iam quidam Rom. Episcopi, nec solum circa ecclesiasticum ritum, verum etiam in iurisdictionib. coactiuis, non tantum super clericos, verum et seculares principatus quoslibet, quomodo existimabile est, Christum & ipsius apostolos hoc praetermisisse tradendum. Sed quoniam tam Christus q ipsius apostoli aperte statuerunt oppositum, plerium in iurisdictionib. coactiuis, ut ex scriptura palam ostensum est 4. huius, 5, & 9. debet sic sermo dicentium cum apocryphis fabulis computari. Tempore vero Constantini I. Rom. Imperatoris, qui patenter Christi fide & baptismo assumpsit, primum fideles inceperunt publice congregari, & dubia circa fidem diffinire, ac ecclesiasticum ritum ordinare, vt ex Isidori pdicto codice apparet, capitulo, de primitiva ecclesia, in synodo Nicena, ab hoc liquide Constantino per editum imperiale iuxta praedicta laudabile & antiquam consuetudinem obtinuit episcopus & ecclesia Rom. prioritatem, q sibi super alias determinauimus conuenire. Et vltra prioritatem hanc prouinciarum quarundam possessiones atq; dominia, quamuis ante tempora Constantini & post etiam Rom. Episcopi quidam suis epistolis siue decretis quibusdam prioritatem, q super aliosillis conuenire monstrauimus electione vel constitutionib. principum sibi singulariter absq; requisitione vel consensu legislatoris humani fidelis, collegii cuiusquam vel personae singularis cuiuscuis praeeminentiae aut auctoritatis exstat, innuerunt diuina lege deberi, cuius tamen oppositum monstratum est sufficienter capitulo praecedente. Post tempora vero Constantini I. & praecipue imperiali sede vacante, hanc sibi deberi prioritatem quandoq; lege diuina, quandoq; vero concessione principum suis epistolis expresserunt Rom. Episcopi quidam. In quibus autem & qualibus haec sit attendenda prioritas, quam pluribus ipsorum insinuantibus & aliqualiter exprimentib. hanc esse circa legis euangelicae interpretationem, & circa ordinationem ecclesiastici ritus, tam circa diuinum cultum quam circa ministros, quantum ad omnem ipsorum institutionem, inseparabilem siue primariam quam essentialem diximus, siue secundariam ac ipsius priuationem, quam separabilem siue accidentalem dicebamus. Hanc etiam extendentes auctoritatem in omnes episcopos, & ecclesias, populos & singulares personas, ad sententiam excommunicationis & interdicti diuinorum officiorum, tam subditis, quam ecclesiarum ministris siue praelatis, alterius cuiuslibet ecclesiasticae censurae consimilis, vt anathematis in supradictos fideles ferendum. Consequenter vero ipsorum aliis idem intendentib. de omni iurisdictione seu coactiua potestate, super omnes ecclesiarum mundi ministros & ipsorum collegia, ea quidem vtentes tanquam sibi conuenienti ex concessione principum, quam diu potens exstat Romanorum princeps, ipsiusq; regnum integrum, & plena sedes. Hoc vero deducto in seditione, & praecipue imperiali sede vacante, per temporum interualla, freti sunt hac potestate, tanquam sibi diuina lege concessa. Quod cur tam varie contigerit, sequenti cap dicturi sumus. Sic etiam suis epistolis expresserunt, sibi conuenire temporalium omnium ecclesiasticorum dispensationem seu distributionem, p voto absq; collegii cuiusquam aut personae singularis cuiuscunq; dignitatis vel auctoritatis requisitione consensus. Quibus etiam ipsorum moderniores excessib. non contenti, suis expresserunt Epistolis siue Decretis, auctoritatem siue iurisdictionem coactiuam supremam super omnes mundi principatus, populos & singulares personas, sibi lege diuina deberi: sic quidem, vt nullus principantium iam dictorum, iurisdictionem hanc coactiuam, quam vocant ipsi gladium temporalem praeter aut contra ipsorum consensum siue dictamen, licite valeat exercere, praeter autem aut contrarium facientes, principantes & populos excommunicationis vel interdicti sententiae vocaliter pronunciando subiectos, asserunt enim se solos in mundo Christi vicarios, qui fuit Rex regum & dominus dominantium, hic latenter intendentes per eum quem sibi debitum dicuntitulum plenitudinis potestatis, propter quod etiam ad suam auctoritatem pertinere dicunt omnia mundi regna & principatus conferre, ac auferre licite posse, regibus & caeteris principantibus, ipsorum mandata transgredientibus, quamuis impia sint secundum veritatem & illicita saepe. Hoc autem inter caeteros Romanos Episcopos, non minus temerarie quam praeiudicialiter & contra scripturae sensum literalem, metaphysicis eius expositionibus innisus Octauus Bonifacius, intantum expressit & asseruit, vt hanc Romanis Episcopis deberi potestatem decreuerit ab omnibus tenendum & confitendum esse de necessitate salutis aeternae. Cuius sententiam assecuti sunt successores eius Clemens quintus, & dicti Clementis vocatus Ioannes immediate successor, quamuis hoc solum explicite videantur dicere de solo imperio Romanorum. Quod quia id asserunt inuisi titulo supradicto, plenitudinis videlicet sibi datae potestatis a Christo, indubium est, potestatem hanc siue auctoritatem, si qua talis ex hoc illis conueniat, omnia mundi regna & principatus ex aequo respicere, quemadmodum Christi potestas, sicuti seriose satis ostendimus decimonono, & vltimo prima.
units.tr: From what has been said, it is plain that the Roman bishop and his church have hitherto been the principal one and the head of the others, and it has been sufficiently shown in what matters they ought to be the head. Now, taking up again the question of where this authority came from, by what manner it reached the bishop, and how far it has been extended in fact (though unlawfully, illicitly and surreptitiously), we say that the bishop and church of Rome, according to what we have set out in chapters 18, 5, 6 and 7 of this part, from the beginning until the time of Constantine, held this priority lawfully. The other churches, as if by election, freely gave it their consent and obedience, not because the Roman church was subject to them by any authority, but on account of the pre-eminence of charity belonging to the apostles Peter and Paul, their constancy in the faith, and also because of the large number of distinguished persons there, outstanding in honour and learning. Out of their immense charity they took on the care and concern of instructing the prelates of other churches and individual faithful, and of admonishing them as brothers. The others received their admonitions as coming from the more learned; and afterwards they also accepted their ordinances concerning ecclesiastical rite, since these seemed useful and just. At last they obeyed their commands, under the ecclesiastical censure of excommunication or interdict, in order to keep the faithful united. This obedience, being freely given, by long custom acquired the force of a kind of election. Hence, although at the beginning of the Church the other bishops and churches of the faithful were bound by neither divine nor human law to obey the commands or institutions of the Roman church or bishop, any more than the reverse, nevertheless, as this useful and reasonable custom grew, by which the faithful were more firmly preserved in unity, and since at that time they lacked a faithful lawgiver to bring them into order and keep them in unity, their successors came to be bound by divine law to such obedience in lawful and honourable matters, as if they had by election appointed that bishop and church as judge over the rite of the churches. This held especially until such times when they could meet publicly and put the ecclesiastical state in better order. As for contentious matters, there is another reason: in judging disputes among the faithful, whether priests or not, the apostle gave a different counsel, as we have briefly set out from 1 Corinthians 6 in chapter 9 of this part, and we shall explain it further in chapter 29. For the apostle did not wish this to be the office of any priest or bishop, or of their college alone, as is clearly seen from the sequence of the apostle's words and the expositions of the saints. Thus the Roman bishop and his church began lawfully, from the beginning, to obtain priority through a certain zeal of charity; afterwards, on account of the customary devotion, reverence and spontaneous obedience of election, this priority gained, as it were, its strength. For it can nowhere be gathered from Scripture that, by a precept of Christ, or by the counsel of any apostle, the other churches or bishops ought to be subject to the church or bishop of Rome, even in ecclesiastical rite. But if it had been necessary for the salvation of the faithful, as some Roman bishops now assert, not only in ecclesiastical rite but also in coercive jurisdictions, not only over clergy but also over any secular principalities whatever, how can it be thought that Christ and his apostles would have passed this over without teaching it? But since both Christ and his apostles plainly laid down the opposite, most of all in coercive jurisdictions, as has been shown from Scripture in chapters 4, 5 and 9 of this part, the speech of those who say otherwise must be counted with apocryphal fables. Now, in the time of Constantine I, the Roman emperor, who openly took up the Christian faith and baptism, the faithful first began to meet publicly, to settle doubtful matters concerning the faith, and to order ecclesiastical rite, as appears from the aforementioned code of Isidore, in the chapter On the Primitive Church, at the Council of Nicaea. From this same Constantine, by imperial edict and in accordance with the aforesaid praiseworthy and ancient custom, the bishop and church of Rome obtained the priority which we have determined belongs to them above the others. And beyond this priority, the possessions and dominions of certain provinces, although some Roman bishops, both before the time of Constantine and afterwards, in their letters or certain decrees, implied that they were due to them by divine law, which we have shown belongs singularly to the Roman bishop by election or by the constitutions of princes, without the requirement or consent of any human lawgiver, believer, college, or any individual of whatever pre-eminence or authority. But the contrary has been sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding chapter. After the time of Constantine I, and especially while the imperial see was vacant, some Roman bishops expressed in their letters that this priority was due to them, at one time by divine law, at another by the concession of princes. Regarding in what and of what kind this priority is to be understood, many of them have made clear, and have to some extent stated, that it lies in the interpretation of the gospel law and in the ordering of ecclesiastical rite, both concerning divine worship and concerning ministers, with respect to every institution of theirs, whether we called it inseparable or primary and essential, or secondary and its privation, which we called separable or accidental. They extended this authority also over all bishops and churches, peoples and individual persons, to the sentence of excommunication and of interdict from divine offices, against subjects and against ministers or prelates of the churches alike, and to any other similar ecclesiastical censure, such as anathema against the aforesaid faithful. Consequently, others who intended the same thing claimed for them every jurisdiction or coercive power over all the ministers of the churches of the world and their colleges, using it as if it were fitting for them, by the concession of princes, for as long as the Roman prince, his whole kingdom and his full see remained powerful. But once this was carried into rebellion, and especially while the imperial see was vacant, over intervals of time they relied on this power as if it had been granted to them by divine law. Why this came about in so many different ways, we shall discuss in the following chapter. In the same way they expressed in their letters that the dispensing or distribution of all temporal ecclesiastical goods belonged to them by their own will, without the requirement or consent of any college or individual of whatever dignity or authority. Not content even with these excesses, the more recent of them expressed in their letters or decrees that supreme authority or coercive jurisdiction over all the principalities, peoples and individual persons of the world was due to them by divine law. And so, none of the aforesaid rulers may lawfully exercise this coercive jurisdiction, which they call the temporal sword, except with their consent or judgment, and, if anyone does otherwise or against it, they declare the rulers and peoples subject to the sentence of excommunication or interdict, pronounced aloud. For they assert that they alone are the vicars of Christ in the world, who was King of kings and Lord of lords, secretly intending by this the title of fullness of power which they claim is owed to them. On account of this they also say that it belongs to their authority to be able lawfully to confer and to take away all the kingdoms and principalities of the world, from kings and other rulers who transgress their commands, even though those commands are often impious and unlawful in truth. Among the other Roman bishops, Boniface VIII, relying not less rashly than prejudicially, and against the literal sense of Scripture, on its metaphysical expositions, asserted this so strongly that he decreed this power was due to the Roman bishops and must be held and confessed by all as necessary to eternal salvation. His successors, Clement V, and John, who was called immediate successor of the said Clement, followed his opinion, although they seem to say this explicitly only of the Roman empire. Because they assert it under the title mentioned above, namely the power given to them by Christ in fullness, there is no doubt that this power or authority, if any such belongs to them, extends equally over all the kingdoms and principalities of the world, just as the power of Christ does, as we have shown fully enough in the nineteenth chapter and the last of the first part.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIII.

units.la: De modis plenitudinis potestatis, & secundum quem modum & ordinem, hos sibi assumpserit Romanus Episcopus, & summarie, qualiter hu vsus sit & vtatur.
units.tr: On the modes of the plenitude of power, and in what mode and order the Roman Bishop has assumed them to himself, and in summary how he has used and still uses them.

units.la: DE quantis quidem igitur & qualibus potestatibus sacerdotum, determinatum est 6.7.9.&11. huius. Amplius de ipsorum inuicem potestatis & dignitatis aequalitate habitum est 15.&16. huius. Et rursum de vnius Episcopi, Ecclesiae siue collegii sacerdotum & clericorum super caeteros omnes expedienti & conuenienti prioritate seu principalitate ipsiusq; initii atq; processus, adhuc autem de illius indisconuenientem sibi prioritatis formam & speciem latenti transitu, atq; serpigine, vlq; quasi ad grauissimum & importabilem secularium potestatum occupationis excessum, immoderatumq; amplius & intolerabile futurum penitus eorum desiderium principandi, vocaliter iam expressum, dictum est aliqualiter capitulo praecedente. Quodq; tam in occupatis quam etiam occupandis secularibus potestatibus & principatib. ad quos, vt omnium quasi sensibus euidenter apparet, omni conanimine tendunt Episcopi Romanorum, quamuis indebite, non modicum exemexemplum fuerit, exter futurusque sit eis locus ille sophisticus, quem sibi videlicet ascribunt titulum plenitudinis potestatis. Unde etiam paralogismus, quo reges & principantes ac singulos coaétos sibi iurisdictione subiectos, niuntur concludere traxit originem, bene se habet perscrutari de huiusmodi plenitudine potestatis. Primum quidem separando seu distinguendo modo illius, deinde vero inquirendo, an Romano pontifici vel alteri cuiquam episcopo, secundum aliquem vnū aut plures modos, plenitudo conueniat potestatis. Post haec autem secundum quā significationū, hunc titulum Romanus episcopus sibi primum assumpsit. Demum vero qualiter ex hac in alias assumendas acceptiones non vt deceptiones principantib. & subiectis omnibus ciuiliter viuentibus praeiudiciales se transtulit. Et qualiter & in quib. eis vsus fuerit & vtatur idem pontifex, & nisi prohibeatur, verisimiliter sit vsurus. Verum quia plenitudo potestatis, vniuersalitatem quandam importare videtur, & de voluntariis potestatib. propositum sit intendere solum, distinguendum nobis est plenitudinem potestatis in modos, penes vniuersalis voluntatiæ potestatis distinctionem. Est igitur & intelligi vere potest vno modo potestatis plenitudo secundum significationem siue virtutem termonis, ea quae cuiuslibet actus possibilis & in rem quamlibet voluntarie factiua est, nō habens hiperbolem, quae soli hominum Christo conuenire videtur, vnde Matth. vlt. Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra. Secundo vero modo intelligi potest plenitudo potestatis, ad propositum magis, ea secundum quam liceat homini exercere quemlibet suum actum voluntarium imperatum, in quemlibet hominē & rem quamlibet exteriorem existentem, in hominum potestate, siue ordinabilem ad vsum eorum. Vel ea rursum secundum q̄ quidem liceat in omnem actum iam dictum, quis non super quemlibet hominem aut rem omnem, humanae potestati subiectam, vel amplius ea secundum quam liceat, non omnem actum exercere sed determinatum specie, siue modo, secundum tamen omnem volentis impetum quemlibet super hominem & rem omnem humanæ subditam potestati. Tertio vero modo intelligi potest plenitudo potestatis, ea quæ supremæ iurisdictionis coactiuæ super omnes mundi principatus, populos, communitates, collegia, & singulares personas, aut rursum in aliqua horum, secundum tamen omnem impetum voluntatis. Quarto vero modo intelligi potest, ea quæ iam dicta est, aut secundum dictum modum super omnes clericos tantum, ipsosq; omnes ad ecclesiastica officia instituendi, priuandi, seu deponendi, & ecclesiastica temporalia siue beneficia distribuendi, aut secundum modum iam dictum. Quinto autem potest intelligi, vt ea quæ sacerdotum omnimode ligandi & soluendi homines à culpis & poenis excommunicandi, interdicendi, & reconciliandi, de qua dictum est 6. huius, & 7. Sexto quidem intelligi potest, ea qua manus imponere liceat omnib. ad ecclesiasticos ordines suscipiendos, & ecclesiastica sacramenta conferendi vel prohibendi, de qua dictum est et 16. & 17. huius. Septimo vero intelligi potest, ea quæ sit interpretandi scripturæ sensus, præsertim in his quæ sunt de necessitate salutis, & veros à falsis, sanos ab insanis distinire seu determinare, ritumq; omnem ecclesiasticum ordinandi, & ordinatorum obseruationis coactiuum vel sub anathemate generaliter ferre præceptum. Octauo vero & vltimo modo quantum proposito nostro attinet, intelligi potest plenitudo potestatis, ea quæ curæ pastoralis, animarum generalis ad omnes mundi populos atq; provincias, de qua dictum est 9. & 21. huius. Posset autem rursum plenitudo potestatis intelligi secundum vnamquamque diuisionum dictarum, ea quæ nulla sit determinata lege, non plena vero, quæ foret determinata per leges humanam aut diuinam, sub qua etiam recta ratio potest conuenienter comprehendi. Sunt autem fortasse modi quidam & combinationes aliæ plenitudinis potestatis, quæ tamen omnes ad intentionem propositam pertinent, enumerasse videmur. His itaq; potestatis plenæ diuisionibus sic præmissis: Dico plenitudinem potestatis secundum iam dictos duos priores modos episcopo Rom. vel alteri cuiquam sacerdoti, præter Christum siue Deum minime conuenire. De quibus siquidem, propter rei euidentiam, & quoniam certificatum est ex diuina & humana sapientia, & omni morali scientia, pertranseo etiam propter abbreuiationem. De tertio quidem & quarto modo plenæ potestatis per demonstrationem ostensum est 15. prima, per scripturæ sacræ testimonium infallibile quarto, quinto, & 8. huius, amplius confirmatum 15. 16. 17. ac 21. eiusdem firmissime roboratum, quoniam sacerdoti aut episcopi inquantum huiusmodi super clericum aut non clericum quenquam absolute, nedum cum plenitudine aliqua lege diuina nulli conueniunt. Vtrum autem humana lege sit clerico cuiquam, episcopo, vel sacerdoti vel non sacerdoti, talis potestatis plenitudo concessa, secundum aliquem modum possibilis quidem concedi, & ex causa rationabili legislatoris humani iudicio reuocari, certificandum est & humanis legibus & rescriptis seu priuilegiis legislatoris eiusdem. De reliquis autem quinto & sexto modo, plenæ potestatis scil. ostensum est sexto huius & septimo, quoniam potestas ligandi atq; soluendi à culpis & poenis, similiter eaq; anathematizandi seu excommunicandi publice quenquam, non est absolute siue cum plenitudine sacerdoti concessa, sed lege diuina determinata, sic vt neq; innoxios apud Deum damnare, neq; noxios soluere possit. Et rursum, quoniam excommunicandi quenquam publice, præcipue principantem aut communitatem aliquam interdicendi cuilibet episcopo & sacerdoti humana ordinatione conuenienter debet determinari potestas, quemadmodum ostensum est sexto, 7. & 21. huius. Amplius eandem potestatem ad ecclesiasticos ministros instituendos per manuum impositionem, docendum & prædicandum, ac ecclesiastica sacramenta in communitatibus fidelium ministrandum, monstratum est 17. huius, non sic episcopis aut sacerdotibus cum plenitudine conuenire, quia diuina & humana lege determinatus sit eis modus conueniens agendi secundum illam. De residuis autem septimo & octauo modo plenitudinis potestatis, ostensum est 10. 21. & 22. huius, eps nulli Episcopo aut sacerdoti cum plenitudine conuenire, sed secundum determinationem tam diuinæ quam humanæ legis. Non igitur Episcopo Romanorum aut alteri sacerdoti cuiquam plenitudo conuenit potestatis, inquantum huiusmodi, nisi eam fortasse velint appellare plenitudinem potestatis, prioritatem seu principalitatem, quam Episcopo supradicto & ipsius Ecclesiæ super reliquas omnes, fidelis legislatoris humani auctoritate, 22. huius monstrauimus conuenire. Unde vero & à qua significatione per Romanum Pontificem primum exordium sumptum est huius ascribendi sibi tituli plenitudinis potestatis, cum tamen vere secundum nullam dictarum significationum illi competeniat, consequenter dicendum. Videtur autem titulus hic à Romano Pontifice secundum significationem octauam primum assumptus, & suæ cuiusdam apparentis conuenientiæ, originem extitisse id Christi oraculum, quod habetur Ioannis 21. dum beatum Petrum alloquens, inquit, Pasce oues meas. Amplius ex eo quod Matth. 16. ad eundem singulariter, Tibi dabo claves regni cœlorum, &c. Rursum ex eo quod Ioannis 18. Converte gladium in vaginam. Amplius ex discipulorum responso ad Christum: Ecce duo gladii. Ex quibus siquidem secundum suas interpretationes, quidam intelligi volunt vniuersitatem totam & totius orbis ouium, id est Christifidelium, soli Petro fuisse commissam, & sic cuiibet Romano Pontifici, tanquam beati Petri vicario singulari: reliquis vero apostolis & ipsorum successoribus Episcopis, non totam & totius orbis vniuersitatem ouium, sed singularis determinatum & singulum gregem atque prouinciam gubernandam, fuisse commissam. Quorum beatus Bernardus, sic intelligens oraculum Christi prædictum, ad Eugenium Papam Romanum de consideratione libro secundo, sic ait: Nec modo ouium, sed & pastorum tu modo vnus omnium. Unde id probem, quia ?et verbo Domini. Cui enim, non dicta Episcoporum, sed etiam Apostolorum sic absolute & indiscrete, tota commissa sunt oues? Si me amas Petre, pasce oues meas, nihil excipitur, vbi nihil distinguitur. Parum etiam infra subiungens: Inde est, quod alii singulis ... plebes scientes sacramentum. Denique Iacobus, qui videbatur vna esse columna Ecclesiæ, vna contentus est Hierosolyma, Petro vniuersitatem cedens. Consequenter autem propositum inferens inquit sexto; iuxta canones tuos, alii in partem sollicitudinis, tu in plenitudinem potestatis vocatus es. Intellecta fuit igitur ab initio plenitudo potestatis, administratio seu cura generalis omnium animarum.
units.tr: Concerning how great and what kind of powers belong to priests, we have settled this in chapters 6, 7, 9 and 11 of this work. Further, we have treated the equality of power and dignity among priests themselves in chapters 15 and 16. Again, we have discussed in the preceding chapter, to some extent, the suitable and fitting priority or pre-eminence of one bishop, or of a church or college of priests and clergy, over all the others, and its origin and development; and also how that priority, by a hidden and creeping passage, has slid into an unfitting form and character, until it reached the most grave and intolerable excess of seizing secular powers, and their desire to rule, now openly spoken, became ever more immoderate and unbearable. Since the Roman bishops strive with all their effort, as is plainly evident to everyone, to seize and also to acquire secular powers and principalities, though without right, this has been no small example, and that sophistical ground which they claim for themselves under the title of plenitude of power will in the future be a further example to them. Hence the fallacy, by which they try to conclude that kings and rulers, and all the individuals subject to their jurisdiction, also had its origin. It is well, therefore, to examine this plenitude of power. First, by separating or distinguishing its modes; then by inquiring whether plenitude of power belongs to the Roman pontiff, or to any other bishop, according to one or more of these modes. After that, in what sense the Roman bishop first took this title to himself; and finally, how from this he passed over, without deceiving rulers and subjects alike who live as citizens, to other meanings that he has assumed, which are prejudicial to all; and how and in what matters this same pontiff has used it and still uses it, and, unless he is prevented, will probably continue to use it. But since plenitude of power seems to import a certain universality, and our intention is only to treat of voluntary powers, we must distinguish the plenitude of power into modes, according to the distinction of universal voluntary power. There is therefore one mode in which the plenitude of power can truly be understood, according to the meaning or force of the word: that which is capable of any possible act and is voluntarily effective upon any thing whatever, without exaggeration, which seems to belong to Christ alone among men. Hence Matthew at the end: All power is given to me in heaven and in earth. In a second mode, more to our purpose, the plenitude of power can be understood as that by which a person may exercise any of his voluntary commanded acts upon any man and any external thing existing in human power or capable of being directed to their use. Or again, as that by which one may exercise every such act upon every man or every thing subject to human power; or further, that by which one may exercise not every act, but an act determined in kind or manner, yet with every impulse of the will, upon every man and every thing subject to human power. In a third mode the plenitude of power can be understood as that which is the supreme coercive jurisdiction over all the principalities, peoples, communities, colleges and individual persons of the world, or over any of these, yet with every impulse of the will. In a fourth mode it can be understood as the same as what has just been described, or, in the same manner, over all clerics only, to institute, deprive or depose all of them from ecclesiastical offices, and to distribute ecclesiastical temporalities or benefices, or in the manner already stated. In a fifth sense it can be understood as the power of priests to bind and loose men from faults and punishments in every way, to excommunicate, to interdict and to reconcile, of which we spoke in chapters 6 and 7. In a sixth sense it can be understood as the permission for all to lay on hands for taking up ecclesiastical orders, and of conferring or forbidding ecclesiastical sacraments, of which we have spoken in chapters 16 and 17. In a seventh sense it can be understood as the power to interpret the sense of Scripture, especially in those matters which are necessary to salvation, and to distinguish or determine true from false and sound from insane; and to lay down generally, under anathema, a coercive precept for ordering all ecclesiastical rites and for observing those who are ordained. In the eighth and last mode, as far as our purpose is concerned, the plenitude of power can be understood as that of the general pastoral care of souls over all the peoples and provinces of the world, of which we have spoken in chapters 9 and 21. Again, the plenitude of power could be understood, according to each of the divisions mentioned, as that which is under no determined law, but is not full if it is determined by human or divine law, under which right reason may also fittingly be included. There are perhaps other modes and combinations of the plenitude of power, but all of them, it seems to us, pertain to our proposed intention, and we have enumerated them. With these divisions of full power thus set out, I say: according to the two first modes just mentioned, the plenitude of power belongs to no bishop of Rome or any other priest, but to Christ or God alone. Of these I shall pass over the matter for the sake of brevity, since the thing is evident, and it is certain from divine and human wisdom and from all moral knowledge.
