As to the third and fourth modes of full power, it has been shown by demonstration in chapter 15 of the first book, and by the infallible testimony of Holy Scripture in chapters 4, 5 and 8 of this work, further confirmed in chapters 15, 16, 17 and 21 of the same, and most firmly established, since a priest or bishop, as such, does not hold any absolute power over a cleric or non-cleric, much less with plenitude under any divine law. Whether, however, by human law, a plenitude of such power may be granted to any cleric, bishop, priest or non-priest, in some mode, it may possibly be granted, and may be revoked by the judgment of the human lawgiver for a reasonable cause; this must be ascertained from human laws and from the rescripts or privileges of the same lawgiver. As to the remaining fifth and sixth modes of full power, it has been shown in chapter 6 and chapter 7 of this work, that the power of binding and loosing from faults and punishments, and likewise of publicly anathematizing or excommunicating anyone, is not granted absolutely or with plenitude to a priest, but is determined by divine law, so that he can neither condemn the innocent before God nor absolve the guilty. And again, since the power of publicly excommunicating anyone, especially a ruler, or of interdicting any community, must be suitably determined for any bishop or priest by human ordinance, as has been shown in chapters 6, 7 and 21 of this work. Further, it has been shown in chapter 17 of this work that the same power of appointing ecclesiastical ministers by the laying on of hands, of teaching and preaching, and of administering ecclesiastical sacraments among the faithful communities, does not belong to bishops or priests with plenitude in this way, because a fitting mode of acting according to it is determined for them by divine and human law. As to the remaining seventh and eighth modes of the plenitude of power, it has been shown in chapters 10, 21 and 22 of this work that they belong to no bishop or priest with plenitude, but according to the determination of both divine and human law. Therefore the plenitude of power does not belong to the Roman bishop or to any other priest, as such, unless perhaps they wish to call by the name of plenitude of power that priority or pre-eminence which we have shown in chapter 22 of this work belongs to the aforesaid bishop and to his Church over all the rest, by the authority of a faithful human lawgiver. Now, from what meaning and by whom the Roman Pontiff first took the beginning of this title of plenitude of power, which he ascribes to himself, although it truly belongs to him in none of the said meanings, we must consequently say. It seems that this title was first assumed by the Roman Pontiff in the eighth meaning, and that the origin of its apparent fitness is that oracle of Christ which is found in John 21, where, addressing the blessed Peter, he says: Feed my sheep. Further, from what is said to him alone in Matthew 16: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc. Again, from John 18: Put up your sword into the sheath. Further, from the disciples' answer to Christ: Behold, here are two swords. From these texts, according to their own interpretations, some wish it to be understood that the whole universality of the sheep of the whole world, that is, of the faithful in Christ, was committed to Peter alone, and thus to any Roman Pontiff as the sole vicar of the blessed Peter; but that to the other apostles and their successors, the bishops, was committed not the whole universality of the sheep of the world, but a particular and determined flock and province to govern. Blessed Bernard, understanding the aforesaid oracle of Christ in this way, writes to Pope Eugenius in the second book of his De consideratione, as follows: "Not only of sheep, but also of shepherds, you alone are the one of all. I prove this by the word of the Lord. For to whom have the sheep been committed absolutely and indiscriminately, not only of bishops but even of apostles? 'If you love me, Peter, feed my sheep': nothing is excepted, where nothing is distinguished." A little further on he adds: "Hence it is that the others each... the peoples knowing the sacrament. Finally, James, who seemed to be one pillar of the Church, was content with one Jerusalem, yielding the universality to Peter." Then, drawing the consequence of his proposition, he says in the sixth book: "According to your canons, the others were called to a part of the care, but you to the plenitude of power." Therefore the plenitude of power was understood from the beginning as the general administration or care of all souls.

units.la: Secundum hanc quidem significationem assumpta sibi prædicatione tituli huius, quamvis non secundum verum scripturæ sensum, quem admodum 28. huius sufficienter monstrabitur: ex præsumptione transiuit in aliam Romanus Episcopus, fortasse quæstus gratia, vel alterius commodi aut excellentiæ super alios vsurpandæ, assumendo videlicet, ac publice prædicando se solum singulariter à pœnis debitis seu infligendis pro statu futuri seculi, iuxta peccatorum demerita, suo verbo vel satisfactionis in hoc seculo, quo sibi libeat modo taxato simpliciter eximere peccatores & absoluere posse.
units.tr: In keeping with this meaning, the Roman Bishop assumed for himself the title's wording, although not according to the true sense of Scripture, as will be sufficiently shown in chapter 28 of this book. From presumption he passed on to another claim, perhaps for the sake of gain, or to seize some other advantage or preeminence over others, namely by assuming and publicly proclaiming that he alone could simply release sinners from the punishments owed or to be inflicted for the state of the future age, according to the demerits of their sins, by his word or by satisfaction in this age, in whatever manner pleased him, once that manner had been prescribed.

units.la: His autem sic sumptis sub quadam pietatis & misericordiæ specie: Prima quidem, vt ex caritate solicitari & curare de omnibus videantur: secunda vero, vt omnibus misereri posse ac velle credantur, priuilegiis & concessionibus principum fulti, præcipue Imperiali sede vacante, titulū hunc consequenter extenderunt Episcopi Romanorum. Primum quidem ad ordinandum circa ecclesiasticum ritum lationes legum quasdam in clericos ab initio vocata Decreta. Deinde vero per modum rogationum seu exhortationum ordinationes quasdam laicis suaserunt, vt ieiuniorum & caeteris temporib. abstinentiæ ciborum quarundam propter diuinum suffragium, & misericordiam impetrandam, ad quasdam tollendas tunc ab hominib. epidemias, & aerias tempestates, sicut ex legenda beati Gregorii, & aliorum quorundam sanctorum satis apparet. Has autem suscipientib. laicis sponte, ac propter devotionem obseruantib. inueterata talium consuetudine, ordinationes in dictas rogationes per modum præcepti coeperunt indicere, sic vt earum transgressores sui sint absque humani legislatoris licentia, vocalis sui anathematis seu excommunicationis, sub pietatis tamen, seu diuini cultus specie, terrore ferire. Crescente autem consequenter ipsis appetitu amplius dom. inandi, attendentib. etiam devotos fideles huiusmodi verbis terreri propter ignauiam & diuinæ legis imperitiam, qui ad ea quæ per sacerdotes indicebantur, obligari credebant, metu damnationis æternæ præsumpserunt vlterius Episcopi Romanorum cum suo clericorum coetu oligarchica quædam edicta siue ordinationes circa ciuiles actus statuere, quib. seipsos, ac ipsorum ordinem siue officium clericatus assumentes quoslibet, etiam mere laicos pronunciauerunt exemptos ab omnibus publicis, ad hoc promouentes officium, seculares etiam coniugatos, qui facile sint allecti, vt immunitatib. gaudeant onerum publicorum, vnde non modicam ciuilis multitudinis sibi subiecerunt particulam, subtrahentes principantium potestati. Rursumq; ampliorem subtrahere studentes, aliis pronunciauerunt edicta, anathematis pœna feriri eos qui personales iniurias quales cunq; intulerint his, qui clericorum collegio sunt ascripti, sic quoq; clericis iniuriam inferentes per excommunicationem in templis publice diffamantes, nec minus propterea persequentes eosdem, requirunt humanarum legum pœnis arceri. Horum autem detestabilius & sacerdotum officio execrabile valde, quod Romanorum & Episcopi reliqui, vt suam amplient iurisdictionem, & per hanc sibi q. stum turpissimum in Dei contemptum & principantium præiudicium manifestum, tam laicos quam clericos, vel negligentes aut etiam impotentes quædam persoluere debita pecuniaria, quib. ad certum temporis terminum persoluendis fuerant ciuiliter obligati, excommunicant & excludunt ab ecclesiasticis sacramentis quos Christus & sancti apostoli multis exhortationib. pœnis, & laboribus ac deacciderunt suis martyriis & pretiosis sanguinibus infra Ecclesiam posuerunt, non enim sic fecit qui omnib. omnia factus est, vt omnes lucrifaceret. Sed propter sola crimina gravia voluit peccatores à reliquorum fidelium praecidi consortio, vt ex prima ad Cor. 5. induximus 7. huius. Quibus etiam non contenti, sed secularium contra Christi & apostolorum praeceptum aut consilium pertentes fastigia in legumlationes seorsum ab iis quae civium vniversitatis proruperunt, omnem clerum ab his decernentes exemptum, civile schisma & principatuum supremorum pluralitatem inducentes ex ipsis quidam velut impossibilem humanae quieti, certam huius experientiam inducentes, demonstrarunt 17 prima. Haec n. pestilentiae Italici regni radix est & origo, ex qua cuncta scandala germinaverunt, prodeunt, & qua stante, nunquam civiles ibidem cessabunt discordiae, potestatem etenim hanc ad quam paulatim & latenti praevaricatione subintravit ex consuetudine aut abusione versus, dudum detinuit Romanorum Episcopus, eademque sibi per principem revocari formidans, & merito propter commissos excessus, creationem, atq; promotionem Romani principis omni maligna solicitudine vetat, & in tantam demum ipsorum quidam prorupit audaciam, vt in suis edictis expresserit, Romanum principem sibi iuramento fidelitatis astringi, tanquam coactiva iurisdictione subiectum, vt ex suarum narrationum, quas Decretales appellant, derisibili & contemnendo prorsus simulacro septimo, de sententia & re iudicata, palam se inspicientibus offert. Cui praecipiti temeritati adnuere recusans Christianissimus Imperator ille, virtutum omnium vir, per omne tempus, locum & statum, singulariter inter caeteros principes approbatus, felicis & diuae memoriae 7. Henricorum, tanquam praestiti iuramenti se immemorem simulans, illius transgressor describitur per fallam non minus quam temerariam narrationem quandam, decretalem vocatam, cui titulus de iureiurando: quamuis potius de iniusta iniuria & illata diuo Imperatori, suisq; successoribus & affinibus omnib. contumelia, intitulari merito possit. Nam a canonum vocatis conditoribus, quoniam periurium pronunciatum mis. Qui etiam eius claram memoriam, si calumniatorum huiusmodi maculari posset verbis aut scriptis, denigrare sunt nisi. Has siquidem oligarchicas ordinationes non auserunt Episcopi Romanorum cum suis cardinalib. vocare leges, sed decretales appellarunt, quamuis eisdem hominess ad poenam obligare intendant pro statu praesentis seculi & per potentiam coactinam, quemadmodum haec intendunt legislatores humani. Id autem vocabulo legum à principio inauserunt exprimere, formidantes resistentiam & correctionem legislatoris praedicti, quoniam ex hoc in principantes & legislatores commiserunt crimen laesae Majestatis, vocaverunt rursum huiusmodi ordinationes à principio iura canonica, vt ex vocabuli colore, quamuis impie appositi, magis habeantur authenticae, iplarumq; credulitatem & reverentiam atq; obedientiam fidelibus imprimant amplius. Sic igitur paulatim clanculum se transferentes, vt omnia concludamus, sex posteriores significationes plenitudinis potestatis de se praedicant Romanorum Episcopi, per has quam plurima in civili ordine monstruosa committentes contra legem diuinam & humanam, ac rectum iudicium cuiuslibet rationem habentis. De quorum aliquibus, quamuis non omnibus, singulariter saltem, rememorationem fecimus capitulo praecedenti.
units.tr: Having taken these things up under a certain appearance of piety and mercy, the Bishops of Rome afterwards extended this title, supported by the privileges and grants of princes, especially while the Imperial see was vacant. The first aim was that they might seem to be concerned and to take care of all out of love. The second was that they might be believed both able and willing to show mercy to all. At first they issued certain laws, called decrees from the beginning, to regulate ecclesiastical rites for the clergy. Then, by way of requests or exhortations, they urged certain ordinances upon the laity: fasts and abstinence from certain foods at set times, in order to win divine favour and mercy, and to remove certain epidemics and pestilential storms then afflicting mankind, as is sufficiently clear from the legend of blessed Gregory and of some other saints. When the laity accepted these freely and observed them out of devotion, and the custom of such practices had grown old, they began to issue these ordinances in the form of commands, under the appearance of piety or divine worship, so that their transgressors would be struck with terror by their own vocal anathema or excommunication, without the permission of any human lawgiver. Then, as their appetite for domination grew, and as they saw that devout faithful people, lacking skill in divine law and fearing eternal damnation, were frightened by such words and believed themselves bound by what the priests prescribed, the Bishops of Rome, together with their college of clergy, further presumed to enact certain oligarchic edicts or ordinances concerning civil acts. By these they declared that they themselves, and their order or office of clergy, and whoever they admitted, even purely lay persons, were exempt from all public burdens. They promoted this office even to secular men, including married men, who were easily enticed to enjoy the immunities from public burdens. In this way they subjected to themselves no small part of the civil multitude, withdrawing it from the power of those who rule. Still wishing to withdraw a larger part, they issued other edicts declaring that those who inflicted personal injuries of any kind on members of the clerical college should be struck with the penalty of anathema. Likewise, those who did wrong to clergy were publicly defamed by excommunication in the churches, and, no less on that account, they persecuted the same people, and demanded that they be restrained by the penalties of human laws. Yet more detestable, and utterly abominable to the office of priests, is this: the Bishop of Rome and the other bishops, in order to enlarge their jurisdiction, and by this means to gain for themselves a most shameful profit, to the manifest contempt of God and the prejudice of the rulers, excommunicate and shut out from the ecclesiastical sacraments both laymen and clergy who are negligent, or even unable, to pay certain monetary debts by which they had been civilly bound to pay within a fixed term. Yet Christ and the holy apostles placed these people within the Church by many exhortations, punishments, labours, and even by their deaths and precious blood. For he who became all things to all men did not act in this way, so that he might gain all. But for grave crimes alone he willed that sinners be cut off from the fellowship of the other faithful, as we have shown from 1 Corinthians 5, in chapter 7 of this book. Not content even with these things, but striving for the heights of secular power against the precept or counsel of Christ and the apostles, they broke forth into lawmaking separate from those things which belong to the whole body of citizens. Decreeing that all the clergy were exempt from these, they introduced a civil schism and a plurality of supreme principalities. Some of them, by introducing a certain experience of this, showed what seems impossible to human peace, as shown in chapter 17 of the first book. For this is the root and origin of the pestilence of the Italian kingdom, from which all scandals have sprung and come forth, and while it stands, civil discords will never cease there. For the Bishop of Rome has long held this power, which by gradual and hidden transgression he entered by custom or abuse of a word. Fearing that it would be revoked by the prince, and rightly so on account of the excesses he had committed, he forbids with every malicious care the creation and promotion of a Roman prince. At last some of them broke out in such audacity that in their edicts they declared that the Roman prince is bound to them by an oath of fidelity, as one subject to coercive jurisdiction. This appears plainly, in a manner ridiculous and utterly contemptible, from their so-called Decretals, in the book of narratives of theirs, in Decretales, title 7, concerning sentence and res judicata, to all who look at it. The most Christian Emperor, a man of all virtues, approved singularly above other princes in every time, place and condition, of blessed and divine memory, Henry VII, refused to assent to this headlong rashness. Feigning forgetfulness of the oath he had given, he is described as its transgressor, through a certain narrative no less false than rash, called a decretal, which bears the title de iureiurando. Yet it could more rightly be entitled an unjust injury, and a contumely inflicted on the divine Emperor, his successors and all his relatives. For it is declared perjury by the so-called founders of the canons. They also strove to blacken his clear memory, if it could be stained by the words or writings of such calumniators. Indeed, the Bishops of Rome with their cardinals did not wish to call these oligarchic ordinances laws, but named them decretals. Yet they intend to bind men to punishment for the state of the present age by coercive power, just as human lawgivers intend. But at the beginning they avoided expressing this by the word laws, fearing the resistance and correction of the aforesaid lawgiver, since by this they would have committed the crime of treason against the rulers and lawgivers. Again, they called such ordinations from the beginning canon law, so that by the colour of the word, though impiously applied, they might be held more authentic, and might impress upon the faithful greater belief, reverence and obedience to them. Thus, gradually transferring themselves secretly, to sum up: the Bishops of Rome claim for themselves the last six meanings of fullness of power. By these they commit very many monstrous things in the civil order, contrary to divine and human law and to the right judgment of anyone who has reason. We have recalled some of these, though not all, but at least individually, in the preceding chapter.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIV.

units.la: Qualiter in speciali Romanus Episcopus vsus sit assumpto primatu & plenitudine potestatis infra ecclesiasticos limites sive sacerdotalem iconomiam.
units.tr: How the Roman Bishop, in particular, has used the primacy and fullness of power assumed within ecclesiastical limits, or sacerdotal stewardship.

units.la: AD haec autem consequens est manifestare, qualiter & in quibus plenae potestatis sibi modis assumptis vsi fuerint hactenus Romanorum Episcopi, vtantur, & nisi vetentur, verisimiliter sint visuri: & primum quidem in ecclesiasticis officialibus statuendis & beneficiis, seu temporalibus dispensandis tam in ecclesiasticos ministros, quam alias miserabiles personas, propter quas etiam, vt in 14. huius, ecclesiastica temporalia tradita sunt & statuta fuere sic per ministros ecclesiasticos dispensanda. Deinde vero monstrandum, qualiter his plenis potestatibus vsi sint hactenus & vtantur ac deinceps vsuri ad eos qui civiliter viuunt tam principes quam subiectos. Secundum hanc itaque plenitudinem potestatis hactenus & in praesentiarum Romanis Episcopis actione permissa, Christi corpus omne mysticum infecerunt, & si dicere liceat, corruperunt. Electionem namque, modum potiorem, quinimo in quo solo securitas est simpliciter bene instituendi officialem quemcunque, diminuerunt, corruperunt & demum quasi totaliter extinxerunt, cum tamen hac Apostoli cum reliqua fidelium multitudine diaconorum institutionem essecerunt, vt habetur Actuum sexto. Diminuerunt quidem primo, in solum clerum convertendo quod per vniuersam fidelium multitudinem fieri solebat & debet, quemadmodum ostensum est 17. huius. Corruperunt autem rursum diminuendo, vt in quorundam imperitorum & exorti num legis diuinae iuvenes, quos Canonicos vocant, exclusis provinciae sacerdotibus, eligendi Episcopum auctoritatem transferendo, nisi forte casu contingeret, quod rarum est & in pauciori bus, eundem esse sacerdotem atque canonicum, ad solius vnius Ecclesiae sive templi clericos in provincia, determinantes electionis autoritatem, quae saltim per omnem provinciae clerum fieri deberet, & per sacerdotes praecipue, quos debitum est esse diuinae legis doctores, vt vbi supra monstravimus. Extinxerunt autem quasi finaliter, quoniam omnium fere praelationum ecclesiasticarum, nec non horum, verum mediocrium & minorum officiorum, et quae mere laicis convenire possunt, propter templorum custodiam, collectionem & p his temporalium seu beneficiorum distributionem, immediate mediate suæ potestati reseruant episcopi Romanorum. Qua siquidem reseruatione, irritas & inanes esse decernunt electiones quaslibet, quamuis rite factas, de sufficientib. & approbatis personis horum vice institutentes de suæ plenitudine potestatis ignorantis aut affectæ precio vel prece, odio vel amore, terrore, obsequio exhibito, aut obtinendo fauore, vel pertersæ aliter, diuinarum literarum ignaros, idiotas & indisciplinatos, & plerunq; homines mente corruptos & notorie criminosos, qui plebibus etiam quib. præficiuntur, non communicant idiomate seu sermone. Vnde respondeat ipse Christo Ioannis decimo, qui contra vel post factas aut fiendas electiones inter cætera monstra, quæ fecit & facit, de lingua sua Occitana duos instituit episcopos, vnum Guintonien-sem in Anglia, reliquum Londensem in Dacia, cum populis illis nullo communicantes sermone, quales autem doctrina & moribus, non mea referre interest, quamuis Londensis, vt in Dacia liquet, ecclesia & dioecesis, spoliata omnium armentorum gregibus necessariis ad agrorum culturam, secundum exigentiam patriæ, per venditionem collectis inde thesauris & ecclesia destituta, abfugerit, reuersus in regionem suam. Respondeat, inquam, Romanus Episcopus, quomodo pastor hic proprias oues vocabit nominatim, mores ipsarum cognoscendo per ipsorum confessiones, & quos arguere oportet reprehendendo aut quomodo sequentur illum oues, eius vocem prædicationis & doctrinæ intelligendo? Nec modo propter necessitatem siue defectum hominum, qualis erat antiquis temporibus, oportet ex alienis prouinciis mendicare pastores. Erant enim in Anglia viri præstantiores vita, & sacra doctrina doctiores eo qui vocum seu sermonum significationis ipsorum expers nec sacræ scripturæ doctor sed causidicus quidam præfectus est illis, sic & in Dacia, & in reliquis prouinciis de quibus in errore consimili, inocculta possent induci testimonia plurima, quæ tamen perransfeo propter abbreuiationem. Quis enim non admirabitur aut stupebit, diuinarum scripturarum ignaros iuniores, morum conuenienti grauitate carentes, inexpertes indisciplinatos & quandoque notorie criminosos, ad maiores ecclesiæ thronos esse præfectos Simoniaca pravitate, vel prece potentum, non dico quandoq; terrore, obsequio vel sanguinis affinitate, repulsis aut neglectis scripturæ sacræ doctoribus, viris honestate probatis. Ficta ne loquor aut falsa, ab numeranti quippe prouinciarum Episcopos aut archiepiscopos, patriarchas & reliquos inferiores prælatos, Sacræ Theologiæ Doctor, aut in ipsa sufficienter instructus, non reperitur vnus ex decem. Et quod referre pudet, quamuis non pigeat quia verum, Episcopi modernorum neque prædicare populo verbum Dei, nec hæreticorum, si qui apparuerint, nouerunt erroris aduersari doctrinis, sed in prædictis euentibus impudenter mendicant aliorum doctrinas, cum tamen dicat Doctor gentium primæ ad Timoth. tertio, quod oportet Episcopum esse doctorem, amplectentem eum qui est secundum doctrinam, fidelem sermonem, vt potens sit exhortari in doctrina sana, & eos qui contradicunt arguere, vt idem scripsit ad Titum primo. De reliquis vero Prælatis inferioribus, abbatibus & prioribus ac reliquis Ecclesiarum curatis, testem inuoco Deum, immortalem veritatem, numerosam ipsorum multitudinem, vitæ atque doctrinæ sufficientis exortem, sic etiam, vt grammatice nesciant ipsorum quam plures congruum proferre sermonem. Sed quibus rursum dicam de plenitudine potestatis, plerunq; concedunturmaiores Ecclesiæ dignitates, & qui ad has gubernandas sufficientes putantur, causidici sunt. Hos enim tanquam vtiles significat Romanus pontifex, & Ecclesiæ defensores, qui pro temporalibus conseruandis vel amplius vsurpandis, contendere norunt. Sacræ vero theologiæ doctoribus tanquam inutilibus reiectis ab eo, simplices enim sunt, vt inquit ille, cum suorum Cardinalium coetu, & ecclesiam dilapidare sinerent, cum tamen ecclesia non sint temporalia sed Christi fideles, pro qua non pro temporalib. iuxta Christi consilium & apostoli, contendere debet Episcopus, vt in Ioannis decimo, ac ex apostolo, vbi supra, & aliis innumerosis scripturæ locis, quæ inducere omitto propter euidentiam & sermonis abbreuiationem. Non enim sunt temporalia hæreditas apostolorum, quam conseruandam successoribus suis Episcopis dimiserunt. Nec sunt iura sponsæ Christi, fastigia imperialia & secularia dominia, quæ sub huiusmodi verborum sophistice, modernus Romanorum Episcopus se, vt defendat, imo potius vt offendat, opposuit iniquissime inclyto Ludouico ex Bauariæ ducibus Romanorum Regi. Vnde Bernardus ad Eugenium de consideratione libro secundo, capitulo quarto, cum de animarum seu Ecclesiarum solicitudine locutus fuerat, quam sancti Apostoli successoribus dimiserunt, inquit: Nam quid aliud sanctus dimisit Apostolus? quod habeo, inquit, hoc tibi do, quid illud? vnum scio, non est aurum neque argentum, cum dicat ipse, Argentum & aurum non est mihi. Et infra parum subdit: Esto vt alia quacunque ratione hac tibi vendices, (temporalia scilicet,) sed non apostolico iure. Et infra rursum: Quod habuit hoc dedit, solicitudinem, vt dixi, super Ecclesias. Quid autem de dominio seu principatu audi adiicientem Bernardum; Nunquid dominationem? audi ipsum. Non dominantes, ait, de clero, sed forma facti gregis. Et ne dictum sola humilitate putes, ne etiam veritate, vox domini est in Euangelio, Reges gentium dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur. Et infert: Vos autem non sic. Planum est, apostolis interdicitur dominatus. Et quod amplissima omnium admiratione ac attentione dignum, & per principes tanquam Dei ministros ad formam debitam reducendum in concilio generali, est de summi Pontificis & suorum fratrum, Cardinalium scilicet, institutione quos caput & principaliores cæteris constituendos diximus, principaliter ad fidei veritatem & vnitatem seruandam atque docendam iuxta determinationem concilii supradicti. Ad hunc enim dignitatis apicem non semper, imo rarius eligitur, qui sacræ scripturæ Doctor præfuerit, sed plerunque assumitur ex causidicorum collegio, quod sacræ scripturæ inconsonum est omnino, rectæ rationi dissonum, & in omnium Ecclesiarum facie pudentissimum
units.tr: Next, it follows that I should show how and in what matters the Bishops of Rome have hitherto used and exercised the modes of full power they have assumed, and how, unless they are restrained, they will likely go on using them. First, I will take up the appointment of ecclesiastical officials and the disposal of benefices or temporal goods, both to ecclesiastical ministers and to other needy persons. For these persons, as we said in chapter 14 of this work, ecclesiastical temporal goods were given and established to be dispensed by ecclesiastical ministers. After that, it must be shown how they have hitherto used these full powers, and how they will use them in future, against those who live in civil society, both princes and subjects. By this fullness of power, which has hitherto been allowed to the Bishops of Rome and is still permitted to them in their actions, they have infected the whole mystical body of Christ and, if one may say so, corrupted it. For they have diminished, corrupted, and at last almost wholly extinguished election, which is the better method, indeed the only method in which security lies for appointing any official rightly. Yet the Apostles, with the whole multitude of the faithful, made the institution of deacons by this method, as is found in Acts chapter six. They diminished it first by transferring to the clergy alone what used to be, and ought to be, done by the whole multitude of the faithful, as was shown in chapter 17 of this work. They corrupted it further by diminishing it again: they transferred the authority of electing a bishop away from the priests of the province, to the so-called canons, young men inexperienced and ignorant of divine law. This is so unless, by chance (which is rare and happens in few cases), the same man is both priest and canon. They fixed the authority of election in the clergy of a single church or temple in the province, whereas it should be exercised at least by the whole clergy of the province, and especially by the priests, who ought to be teachers of divine law, as we showed above. They have almost finally extinguished it, because the Bishops of Rome reserve to their own power, directly or indirectly, nearly all ecclesiastical prelacies, as well as the lesser and middling offices, and those that can be given to mere laymen, such as the care of churches, the collection of revenues, and the distribution of temporal goods or benefices. By this reservation they declare void and empty any elections whatever, even though made duly, of suitable and approved persons to these offices. In the fullness of their power they appoint, out of ignorance, or moved by money or entreaty, hatred or love, fear, servility shown, or favour sought, or otherwise corrupted, men ignorant of the Scriptures, untrained and undisciplined, and often morally corrupt and notoriously criminal, who do not even share a language or speech with the peoples over whom they are set. Hence the Bishop of Rome answers to Christ, John chapter ten, who, against or after elections made or to be made, among other monstrosities which he has done and does, appointed from his own Occitan tongue two bishops: one of Guinton in England, and the other of London in Denmark, with peoples with whom they had no shared speech. How they were in doctrine and morals is not my concern. Still, as is clear in Denmark, the church and diocese of London, stripped of the flocks of cattle needed for cultivating the fields according to the needs of the country, its treasures gathered by sale, and left without a church, fled back to its own region. I say the Bishop of Rome must answer: how will this pastor call his own sheep by name, knowing their morals through their confessions, and rebuke those whom he ought to rebuke, or how will the sheep follow him, understanding the voice of his preaching and teaching? Nor, as in ancient times, because of a need or lack of men, must pastors be begged from foreign provinces. For in England there were men more outstanding in life and more learned in sacred doctrine than this one, who lacked knowledge of the meaning of their words and speech, and who was set over them not as a teacher of Holy Scripture but as a certain pleader. So also in Denmark, and in the other provinces concerning which very many testimonies of a similar error could be brought forward, but I pass them over for the sake of brevity. For who would not marvel or be astonished that the Bishops of Rome set over the greater thrones of the Church men ignorant of the divine Scriptures, younger, lacking the fitting gravity of conduct, inexperienced, undisciplined, and sometimes notoriously criminal, by simoniacal depravity or the entreaty of the powerful, I do not say sometimes by fear, servility, or ties of blood, while teachers of Scripture, men proven in honesty, are rejected or neglected? Am I speaking fictions or falsehoods? Counting up the bishops or archbishops of the provinces, the patriarchs and the other lower prelates, not one in ten is found to be a Doctor of Sacred Theology, or sufficiently instructed in it. And what it shames one to report, though I am not ashamed to say it because it is true: the bishops of today know neither how to preach the Word of God to the people, nor how to oppose the errors of heretics, if any appear. Instead, in these matters they shamelessly beg the doctrines of others. Yet the teacher of the Gentiles says in the first letter to Timothy, chapter three, that "a bishop must be a teacher, holding to the faithful word which is according to doctrine, that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to convince those who contradict," as he also wrote to Titus, chapter one. As for the other lower prelates, abbots and priors, and the rest who have the care of churches, I call God and immortal truth to witness that a great number of them lack sufficient life and doctrine, and that many of them cannot even speak correct grammatical Latin. But again, to speak of the fullness of power: the greater dignities of the Church are commonly granted to those who are thought fit to govern them, and these are pleaders. For the Roman pontiff regards such men as useful and as defenders of the Church, since they know how to contend for preserving or even seizing more temporal goods. Teachers of sacred theology, on the other hand, are cast aside by him as useless, "for they are simple," as he, together with the company of his Cardinals, once said, "and would allow the Church to be squandered." Yet the Church consists not of temporal goods but of the faithful of Christ, for whom a bishop ought to contend, not for temporal goods, according to the counsel of Christ and the Apostle, as in John chapter ten, and from the Apostle as above, and from countless other passages of Scripture, which I omit to cite for the sake of clarity and brevity. For temporal goods are not the inheritance of the Apostles, which they left to their successors, the bishops, to be preserved. Nor are the rights of the bride of Christ imperial dignities and secular dominions, which the present Bishop of Rome, under such sophistical words, has most unjustly set against the illustrious Ludwig of Bavaria, King of the Romans, so that he might defend himself, or rather so that he might injure. Hence Bernard, in his book On Consideration, to Eugenius, book two, chapter four, when he had spoken of the care of souls or churches, which the holy Apostles left to their successors, says: "For what else did the holy Apostle leave? 'What I have,' he says, 'I give you; what is that? I know one thing: it is not gold nor silver,' since he himself says, 'Silver and gold I do not have.'" And a little further he adds: "Suppose you claim these by some other reason, namely temporal goods, but not by apostolic right." And further again: "What he had, he gave: care, as I said, over the Churches." What about dominion or principality? Hear Bernard again adding: "Is it domination? Hear him. 'Not lording it,' he says, 'over the clergy, but being examples to the flock.' And lest you think this said from humility alone, consider that it is also the truth: it is the voice of the Lord in the Gospel, 'The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. But you are not so.' It is plain that domination is forbidden to the Apostles." And, worthy of the greatest admiration and attention of all, and to be reduced to the due form by princes as God's ministers in a general council, is the appointment of the supreme Pontiff and of his brothers, the Cardinals, whom we said were to be set up as the head and principal members over the rest, chiefly to keep and teach the truth and unity of the faith, according to the determination of the aforesaid council. For to this height of dignity there is not always, indeed more rarely, chosen one who has been a teacher of Holy Scripture, but commonly one is taken from the college of pleaders. This is wholly inconsistent with Holy Scripture, dissonant with right reason, and most shameful in the face of all the Churches.

units.la: tissimum rissimum omnium. Sic quoque conuenienter, nec quasi minus aduertendum de Cardinalium cætu, quoniam ad hoc assumuntur lasciui iuuenes, & diuinarum literarum indocti quam plutes: Cum tamen Episcopus hic & Ecclesia siue collegium omnium aliorum esse debeat exemplar & forma, horumque consilio fretus, non aliter, præsertim in arduis, Romanus Pontifex habeat vniuersalem Ecclesiam gubernare. Sed de his hactenus, vnde sermo venerat, redeuntes dicamus, quod Romanus Pontifex de plenitudine potestatis, ampliorem multitudinem prælationum maiorum, mediocrum & minorum conferet idiotis aut diuinarum literarum ignaris, non vtinam criminosis, tam sibi cognitis quam ignotis, pueris & infantibus etiam Simoniaca prauitate sui, vel intercessoris, aut alia quauis plerunque affectione sinistra. Maioribus ergo ac principalioribus sedibus sic infectis ex talium promotione, quinimo intrusione, cæterae minores curæ siue officia ad collationem horum pertinentia, contagione polluta redduntur. Gaudentes enim similibus, quemadmodum homine homo, & equus equo, iuxta sapientis gentilis oraculum, ad ecclesiastica officia eam, qua symoniæ aut alterius peruersæ viæ ianuam ingressi sunt, referant idiotis & more peruersis. Nam volentes agere secundum habitum proprium, quem non mutauit dignitas, sed plerunque monstrauit sanctos & iustos ac doctos, qui per talem semitam domum Dei intrare non quærunt, tanquam sibi inimicos odiunt & reiiciunt, declinant, & premunt. Quoniam, vt inquit veritas, qui male facit odit lucem. Nec tacco quod supradictus Episcopus, fauore ac gratia potentum sibi quærendis, & cum his etiam inde fortassis receptis pecuniis, quosdam iuuenes diuinæ legis & aliarum disciplinarum indoctos, nec in sacrum quenquam ordinem promotos, adhuc in famosis vrbibus ad episcopatus promouit, cum tamen ad Euandium dicat Hieronymus, presbyterum in Episcopo continere. Ecclesiastico igitur regimine sic infecto, vniuersum corpus Christi mysticum ægrotat nimirum. Omittentibus enim ecclesiarum Prælatis reliquis curatis exhortationes, obsecrationes & increpationes secundum sanam doctrinam, committentibus autem detestanda & abominanda, palam scandalizatur populus ipsorum exemplo. Quia velut signum sagittatoribus, sic plebi constituuntur exemplum, quod veritas attendens Matthæi quinto inquit: Sic lucet lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant opera vestra bona. Et hinc est modernorum morum radix & prima peruesitas, ad quam demum sequitur æterna damnatio. Quoniam, vt ait Christus Matthæi quinto: Si cæcus cæco ductatum præstet, ambo in foueam cadunt. Quid autem de temporalium dispensatione dicemus, cum debeant ecclesiasticorum ministrorum sufficientiæ residua pauperibus impotentibus, aliisque personis miserabilibus dispensari? quod neminem quasi latet: conuertuntur in eos vsus, & verius abusus dixero, de quibus sermo fuit vndecimo huius: quibus adiice nouum eleemosynæ modum, quod in mercenarios milites, equites, & pedites, horum plurima consumuntur ad pugnas inter Christi fideles concitandas, & continue nutriendas, vt eos suæ tandem subiicere valeant tyrannicæ potestati. Sic igitur ex prædictis apparet, propter plenitudinem potestatis corpus Ecclesiæ mysticum, secundum materiam siue membra principalia, maxime (verbi causa) Prælatos vndique infectum, & corruptioni propinquum.
units.tr: most shameful of all. Likewise, it should not be overlooked that the college of cardinals is equally tainted, since lascivious young men are admitted to it, many of them more ignorant of the divine writings than others. Yet the bishop and the Church, or the college of all the others, ought to be the pattern and model, and the Roman Pontiff, relying on their counsel, should not otherwise govern the universal Church, especially in difficult matters. But let us return to the point from which this discussion began. The Roman Pontiff, by virtue of his fullness of power, confers the greater, middling and lesser prelacies in great number on the unlearned and those ignorant of the divine writings, and I wish they were not also criminals, whether known to him or unknown, boys and infants included, for reasons of simony and depravity on his own part or that of an intercessor, or for some other, usually sinister, affection. The chief and principal sees are thus infected by the promotion, or rather the intrusion, of such men, and the other, lesser cures and offices that depend on their conferral are polluted by the same contagion. For like delights in like, man with man and horse with horse, as the saying of the wise pagan has it, so these men refer to the ecclesiastical offices the same entrance by which they came in, through simony or some other perverse way, and they bring their own perverse manners with them. For those who wish to act according to their own habit, which dignity has not changed but has rather shown to be the habit of saints, the just and the learned, who do not seek to enter the house of God by such a path, hate them as enemies, reject them, shun them and oppress them. For, as Truth says, he who does evil hates the light. Nor do I pass over the fact that the aforesaid bishop, seeking the favour and grace of the powerful, and perhaps also with money received from them, has promoted to episcopates in notorious cities certain young men ignorant of the divine law and of other disciplines, and not even advanced to any sacred order, although Jerome says to Euangelus that the presbyter is to be contained in the bishop. With the ecclesiastical government thus infected, the whole mystical body of Christ is surely sick. For when the prelates of the churches neglect the exhortations, entreaties and rebukes according to sound doctrine that are owed to the remaining parish clergy, and instead commit detestable and abominable acts, the people are openly scandalized by their example. For, as a mark is set for archers, so these men are set as an example for the common people, and Truth, looking to Matthew 5, says: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works. And hence comes the root and first perversity of present-day morals, to which eternal damnation at last follows. For, as Christ says in Matthew 5: If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit. What shall we say of the dispensing of temporal goods, when the surplus of the ministers' livelihoods ought to be distributed to the impotent poor and other wretched persons? That is no secret to anyone: those funds are turned to uses, or rather, I would call them abuses, of which we spoke in the eleventh chapter of this book. To these add a new kind of almsgiving, by which much of the money is spent on mercenary soldiers, horsemen and foot soldiers, to stir up and continually feed fights among the faithful of Christ, so that they may finally bring them under their tyrannical power. Thus, from what has been said, it is evident that, by reason of the fullness of power, the mystical body of the Church, in its principal matter or members, and especially (for instance) its prelates, is infected everywhere and near to corruption.

units.la: Nunc autem de corporis huius forma dictaris, quæ in suorum membrorum ordine, ac situ debito consistere debet. Hoc ipsum tanquam inuenustum ac deforme monstrum videbitur diligenter inspectum. Quis enim animalis corpus, cuius singula membra suo capiti nexu immediate iunguntur, monstruosum & inutile ad operationes conuenientes esse non æstimet. Digitus nanque vel manus, si capiti immediate nectatur, situ sibi debito carens, virtute, motu & opere conueniente carebit. Non sic autem, si digitus manui, manus brachio, brachium humero, humerus ceruici, ceruix vero capiti, per conuenientes nectantur iunctuas. Sic enim corpus redditur sua forma decens, sic eius caput membris reliquis conuenientem virtutem vni per reliquum secundum eorum naturam & ordinem immittere potest. Et ipsa quidem hinc sibi conuenientes operationes perficere. Quam siquidem formam & modum in ecclesiastico, necnon & ciuili quolibet regimine oportet attendere. Non enim potest vniuersalis pastor aut princeps immediate in omnibus prouinciis singulorum singulos actus inspicere, & immediate dirigere, sed oportet, si decenter, si sufficienter hæc perfici debeant, secundum ordinem debitum substitutis & specialibus ad ea iuuari ministris, sic enim ordinatum permanere potest & crescere corpus Ecclesiæ. Quod sentiens doctor gentium Paulus ad Ephesios quarto, sic inquit: Crescamus in illo, qui per omnia caput est Christus, ex quo totum corpus compactum & connexum per omnem iunctuam subministrationis, secundum operationem in mensuram vnius cuiusque membri augmentum corporis facit. Verum de plenitudine potestatis Romano permissa Pontifici, omnis hic ordo seu forma sublata est, absoluit n. ipse à potestate seu cura & correctione superiorum, inferiores prælatos & ordines, vt à patriarchis archiepiscopos, ab archiepiscopis episcopos, ab episcopis vero suorum capitula seu collegia clericorum, & rursum abbates & monachorum priores, nouissime autem, non vtinam pessime, religiosos qui pauperta‑tis ordines appellantur. Hos q; omnes ordine perturbato suæ curæ atq; immediatæ correctioni submittens, nulla quidem euidenti vtilitate, sed notoria potius sibi lites accumulandi auiditate, in pecuniarum confluxum, ac in Prælatorum expoliationem, & ipsorum ampliorem subiugationem intendens. Quanta tamen inde subsecuta insolentia, quasi nullus ignorat. Carentes etenim hi superiori cura sibi præsenti, contumaces, inobedientes & irreuerentes fiunt, quibus merito subesse deberent, ad seipsos & alios facultatem peccandi liberius, hinc etiam assumentes. Quibus vero cura taliam esse deberet, sibi debita potestate priuatis, torpendi & negligendi præbetur occasio, vnde vexavationes fidelium tot, tantaque contingunt inconvenientia, eo quod ea diffusius enumerare non valeo: ipsorum incomprehensibilem quasi varietatem & numerum, particulariter describere prætermisi. Quamuis ipsorum plurima, si volentib. indagare, facilitèr offerant. Id quidem pertranseo, iam ex abusu faciem gerens honesti, quod mensarum ministros diaconos quosdam, Cardinales vocatos, sede ac reverentia episcopis & sacerdotib. præferre patitur, nihil attendens scripturam in hoc, nec quantum detestabile sit illud secundum Hieron. ad Euandrum epistola, de qua supra 15. huius. Et his adiice novum germen iam dicti radicis, quod Romanus Episcopus ex hac plenitudine potestatis, beneficium ecclesiasticum obtinentib. ubique locorum, absque sui licentia, interdixit condere testamenta, & intestatorum simpliciter, aut licet suam sedem immediate decreuit bona denoluì & debere deferri. Et quod amplius a malo est, quoniam Simonia, quamuis post factum explicatur, amplissima est, quod eadem potestate redditus & proventus beneficiorum omnium & ubique, quo primum anno vacantia fuerint, sibi reseruat, secundum hunc modum sibi congregans omnes mundi thesauros, & eisdem omnia regna spolians, atque prouincias in quib. distribui debent ministris euangelicis & personis miserabilibus, aut in reipublicæ, de qua sumuntur, subsidium, si oportet conuerti, quoniam ad hoc statuta & ordinata fuerunt. Hoc rursum intolerabilius, quod legata in testamentis fidelium laicorum, pro vltramarino transitu vel alias pias causas, secundum determinatarum personarum dispositionem, quas Commissarios vocare solent, ad sui ordinationem pertinere dicit, eadem plenitudine potestatis: nec mirum, cum eadem omnium regum, principum & regnorum, se quidam ipsorum asseruerit habere dominium, vt induximus 10. huius, cum tamen prædictorum omnium nullum ad sui pertineat potestatem, vt ostensum est 15. prima, & 17. huius. Ab eodem quoq; radice his ampliora & graviora contingent, quæ omnia narrari nequeunt, propter ipsorum tam variam esse naturam. Vno enim inconvenienti dato, præsertim eo, in quo cætera cogitabilia circa ciuiles actus humanos, inconvenientia continentur alia quaecunq; contingere, nihil difficile, iuxta gentilis sapientis oraculum. Hac enim sibi debita potestate plena, illi sequitur licere quod libet, propter quod humanas omnes ordinationes & leges, etiam per generale concilium ordinatas, secundum sui votum suspendit & reuocat, quod tanquam vltimum inconvenientium in omni mundano regimine, tam sancti q; philosophi refugerunt, vt in undecimo primæ p demonstrationem, & quinto huius, autoritate Augustini, 1. ad Tim. 6. fuit amplius confirmatum. Sic igitur ex sibi permissa plenitudine potestatis vniuersum corpus ecclesiæ infectum est. Omnis ecclesiasticæ iconomiæ prævaricatus est ordo, & omne ciuile regimen impeditum simpliciter, aut in parte turbatum, cum tamen huius Episcopi, & ipsius Ecclesiæ siue collegii sermones & opera constituta sint velut exemplum omnium aliorum. In quos siquidem, velut quæso, fideles conuertant lumina, quodam dudum honestatis sophisticæ plurimorum ex ipsis obumbrata velamine, cernent se ipsis lympide, qui Romanæ curiæ, imo verius cum veritate dicam, domus negociationis, & ea quæ latronum horribilioris speluncæ limina visitarunt, aut qui ab hac abstinuerunt, numerosæ fide dignorum multitudinis relatione discent, eam pene scelleratorum omnium & negotiatorum, tam spiritualium quam temporalium receptaculum esse factam. Quid n. aliud ibi, quam Simoniacorum undecunq; concursus? quid aliud q; causidicorum strepitus & calumniatorum insultus, & iustorum impulsus? Ibi periclitatur innocentum iustitia, vel in tantum differtur, si eam pretio redimere nequeant, vt tandem exhausti innumeris fatigati laboribus iustas & miserabiles ipsorum causas cogantur deserere. Ibi namque alte intonant leges humanæ, silent, aut rarius resonant diuinæ doctrinæ, ibi tractatus & scrutinia inuadendi prouincias Christianorum, & per armatam & violentam potentiam obtinendi & eripiendi ab his, quorum custodiæ licite sunt commissæ. Acquirendarum animarum nulla solicitudo neq; consilia. Et addeq ibi nullus ordo, sed sempiternus horror inhabitat. Qui vero vidi & affui, videre videor, quam Dan. 2. Nabuchodonosor terribilem statuam in somnio recitatur vidisse, caput siquidé habentem aureum, brachia vero & pectus argentea, ventrem autem & femora ærea, tibias quidem ferreas pedumq; partem vnã ferream, & reliquam fictilem. Quid n. aliud ingens hæc statua, quæ status personarum curiæ Romanæ seu summi pontificis, q; olim peruersis hominum terribilis, nunc vero cunctis studiosis horribilis est aspectu. Huius n. statuæ superiora membra caput, pectus & brachia, quid sunt aliud in conspectu, in affectu & in amplexu quam aurum & argentum & opera manuum hominum? Eius vero venter & femora, quid aliud, quam sæcularium litium seu causarum calumniarum ve, ac Simoniacarum negotiationum, tam spiritalium quam carnalium rerum sonitus & tumultus? Nec modo dicæ excommunicationum & anathematum, tam vocalium quam literalium, tonitrua & fulmina in Christi fideles Romano pontifici & ipsius ecclesiæ sæcularitèr subiici, & ipsorum carnalia siue temporalia, quamuis iuste reculantes tribuere. Quid aliud dic qso enea femora, quam voluptatum, luxus & vanitatum quasi omnium, etiam laicis indecentium, apparatus pomposus, quem sensib. hominum imprimunt, qui cæteris esse debent castitatis & honestatis exemplum? Ipsius autem ferreæ tibiæ ac pedes & digiti, quibus statua figitur, secundum partem fictiles & testei, in quid aliud tendunt, quam sæcularium principatuum, regnorum & prouinciarum vsurpationem, inuasionem & occupationem, per armatorum seu ferreatorum violentam potentiam, secum portantes in hoc superiora membra, auri & argenti exhibitionem, armatos ad hoc inuitantes, ventrem quoq; ac femora ænea talium, sonora promissione ac peccatorum & pœnarum vocali, quamuis fallaci, absolutione, ppriam vero libertatem defendentium, suisq; principib. debitam fidem obseruare volentium, iniusta, quamuis Deo protegente prorsus innocua, condemnatione ac maledictio-ne [illegible, ~12 letters] vero bases & digitis testei, fictiles & proinde fragiles, quid aliud repraesentant, quam inconstantiam Romanae curiae? quid aliud notant quam quibus innititur Romanus Pontifex adversum Christi fideles opprimendos, occasionum debilitatem, non modo dicam falsitatem & iniquitatem omnibus manifestam? Verum eodem testante propheta, super hanc statuam casurus est lapis sine manibus abscissus de monte, id est, Rex, quem de hominum universitate per suam gratiam electum suscitabit Deus, illi scilicet conferendo potestatem, & cuius regnum alteri non tradetur, hic inquam magis virtute siue gratia trinitatis quam opere seu potestate manuum hominum, huius terribilis & horribilis ac monstruosae statuae primum conteret atq; comminuet testeam partem, pedes videlicet, quib. inconvenienter innititur, falsas scil. ac iniquas causas, & occasiones caluas vetius dixero cum poeta, omnib. populis, & principib. ipsarum reserato sophismate ac humanis demonstrationibus impugnato, & scripturae sacrae veritatib. annullato, innotescere faciendo, deinde vero ferrum ipsius, scil. atrocem & impiam potestatem arcendoras autem consequenter, id est maledicendi, quam sibi praesumpsit in principes & populos, auctoritatem: secularium quoq; iurisdictionum vsurpatarum & proinde causarum & vexationum tumultum silere ac obmutescere faciet: luxus quoq; voluptatum & pompas vanitatum cessare: Demum vero argentum & aurum, id est, auaritiam & rapinam Romani Pontificis & superiorum membrorum curiae Romanae compescet, temporalium quoq; usum moderamine debito sibi concedet. Sicq; pariter secundum prophetam conterentur ferrum, testa, argentum & aurum, omnia scil. supradictae curiae vitia & excessus extinguentur, quasi redacta in fauillam aestiuae areae, quae rapta sunt vento. Quod enim tam contra naturam, legem humanam atq; divinam & omnem rationem est, diu permanere non potest.
units.tr: Now consider the form of this body, as it is set out in the order and proper arrangement of its members. This will appear a hideous and deformed monster when examined closely. Who would not judge a body, whose individual members are joined directly to its head, to be monstrous and unfit for its proper functions? A finger or a hand, if it is attached directly to the head, lacks its proper position and will lack the strength, movement and work that belong to it. It is otherwise if the finger is joined to the hand, the hand to the arm, the arm to the shoulder, the shoulder to the neck, and the neck to the head, through fitting joints. In that way the body keeps its becoming form, and the head can send to the other members the strength suited to each, according to their nature and order, so that they can perform their own proper operations. This form and order ought to be observed in the ecclesiastical government, and in any civil government as well. For the universal pastor or the prince cannot inspect each single act of each individual in every province and direct it immediately. If these things are to be done properly and sufficiently, they must be aided by subordinate and specially appointed ministers, arranged in due order; in this way the body of the Church can remain ordered and grow. The teacher of the Gentiles, Paul, perceiving this, says in Ephesians 4: Let us grow up into him who is in all things the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every joint of supply, according to the working in due measure of each individual part, makes the body increase. But by the fullness of power granted to the Roman Pontiff, all this order and form has been removed. For he has freed himself from the power, care and correction of his superiors, and he subjects the lower prelates and orders to his own immediate care and correction: patriarchs to himself rather than archbishops, archbishops rather than bishops, bishops rather than the chapters or colleges of their clergy, and in turn abbots and the priors of monks, and last of all, and would that it were not the worst, the religious who are called orders of poverty. He subjects all of these, with the order thrown into confusion, to his own care and immediate correction. He does this not for any plain advantage, but rather from a notorious greed for piling up lawsuits, aiming at a flow of money, at the despoiling of the prelates, and at their more complete subjection. Yet how great an insolence has followed from this, scarcely anyone is ignorant. For these men, lacking the superior care that should be present to them, become stubborn, disobedient and irreverent, and they are rightly subject to those who should have command over them; they take for themselves and for others a freer license to sin. Those to whom such care ought to belong, being deprived of the power due to them, are given an occasion for sloth and neglect. From this come so many and so great troubles for the faithful, which I cannot list at greater length. I have passed over describing in detail their almost incomprehensible variety and number, although many of them, if anyone wishes to search, are easily found. I pass over this too: the abuse, already wearing the face of honour, by which he allows certain deacons, the servants of the tables, called Cardinals, to be placed before bishops and priests in rank and reverence. He pays no attention to Scripture on this point, nor to how detestable it is according to Jerome in his letter to Evangelus, which I mentioned above in chapter 15 of this book. To these add the new shoot of the same root: from this fullness of power the Roman Bishop has forbidden anyone who holds an ecclesiastical benefice anywhere, without his licence, to make wills; and when people die intestate he has simply decreed, or at least ordered, that their goods should fall to his see. What is worse still, and it is very great, since the Simony, though it is explained after the deed, is enormous: by the same power he reserves to himself the revenues and income of all benefices everywhere, for the first year in which they fall vacant. In this way he gathers to himself all the treasures of the world, despoiling all kingdoms and provinces, and the funds that ought to be distributed to evangelical ministers and to needy persons, or, if necessary, turned to the support of the commonwealth from which they are drawn, since they were established and ordained for these purposes. More intolerable still, he claims that by the same fullness of power the legacies in the wills of lay believers, for passage overseas or for other pious causes, belong to his own disposal, according to the arrangement of certain persons whom they usually call Commissioners. This is no wonder, since one of these men has asserted that he holds dominion over all kings, princes and kingdoms, as I showed in chapter 10 of this book, although none of all these things belongs to his power, as has been shown in chapter 15 of the first book and chapter 17 of this one. From the same root there follow still greater and more serious evils, which cannot all be related, because of their very great variety. For once one inconvenience is granted, especially that in which all other conceivable inconveniences in human civil affairs are contained, it is not difficult for any other inconvenience whatever to follow, according to the saying of the pagan sage. For once he has been given this full power, it follows that he may do whatever he pleases. On this ground he suspends and revokes all human ordinances and laws, even those enacted by a general council, according to his own will. This, as the last of all inconveniences in every worldly government, both holy men and philosophers have shunned, as was shown in chapter 11 of the first part and chapter 5 of this one, and was further confirmed by the authority of Augustine on 1 Timothy 6. Thus the whole body of the Church has been infected by the fullness of power granted to him. The order of all ecclesiastical stewardship has been violated, and all civil government has been either altogether hindered or in part disturbed, although the teachings and deeds of this Bishop, and of the Church or college itself, are set up as the example for all others. If the faithful turn their eyes towards these men, the covering of a sophistical honour, long since cast over many of them, will be seen through; they will see clearly for themselves what the Roman court is, or rather, to speak the truth, a house of trade. Those who have visited it, the threshold of the most horrible den of robbers, or those who have kept away from it, will learn from the reports of a large number of trustworthy witnesses that it has been made almost a refuge for all criminals and dealers, both spiritual and temporal. For what else is there there but a gathering of Simoniacs from every quarter? What else but the clamour of advocates, the assaults of slanderers, and the pressing of the unjust? There the justice of the innocent is put in danger, or is so delayed, if they cannot buy it back with money, that at last, exhausted and worn down by endless labours, they are forced to abandon their just and wretched causes. There human laws thunder loudly, while the voices of divine doctrine are silent or sound only rarely. There plans and schemes are devised to invade the provinces of Christians, and to seize and take them by armed and violent power from those to whose custody they were lawfully committed. There is no concern or counsel for winning souls. And there no order dwells, but an everlasting horror. I who have seen and been present seem to see what Nebuchadnezzar, in Daniel 2, is said to have seen in a dream: a terrible statue, with a golden head, arms and breast of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, shins of iron, and part of its feet iron and the rest clay. For what else does this huge statue represent but the state of the persons of the Roman court or of the supreme pontiff, which was once terrible to wicked men, and now is horrible to the sight of all who are zealous? For the upper members of this statue, the head, breast and arms, what are they in sight, in desire and in embrace but gold and silver and the works of human hands? Its belly and thighs, what are they but the sound and tumult of secular lawsuits, cases and slanders, and of simoniacal dealings in spiritual and carnal matters? Nor should I speak only of the thunders and lightnings of excommunications and anathemas, both spoken and written, which are hurled at the faithful of Christ, so that they are made subject to the Roman Pontiff and to his Church in secular matters, and so that they are obliged to yield up their carnal or temporal goods, even when they justly refuse. What else do the bronze thighs signify but the pompous display of pleasures, luxury and vanities of every kind, even unbecoming to laymen, which they impress on the senses of men, although they ought to be an example of chastity and honour to others? As for the iron shins and the feet and toes of the statue, in which it is fixed, partly clay and earthen, where do they point but to the usurpation, invasion and seizure of secular principalities, kingdoms and provinces by the violent power of armed and iron-clad men? They carry the upper members with them, offering the display of gold and silver, inviting armed men to this. They also carry the bronze belly and thighs, with the sonorous promise and the spoken, though deceptive, absolution of sins and punishments, and with the unjust condemnation and curse, though by God's protection altogether harmless, of those who defend their own freedom and wish to keep the faith owed to their princes. But the clay bases and the earthen toes and fingers, fragile for that very reason, what else do they represent but the inconstancy of the Roman court? What else do they mark but the weakness of the grounds on which the Roman Pontiff leans in order to oppress the faithful of Christ, I will not say the falsehood and iniquity that are plain to everyone? But as the prophet testifies: a stone shall strike the statue, cut out without hands from the mountain, that is, the King whom God will raise up from the whole human race, chosen by his grace, to whom he will certainly give power, and whose kingdom shall not be handed over to another. This one, I say, by the power or grace of the Trinity rather than by the work or power of human hands, will first crush and grind to pieces the earthen part of this terrible, horrible and monstrous statue, namely the feet on which it unfittingly rests: the false and unjust causes, and, to speak with the poet, the empty pretexts, exposed to all peoples and princes, the sophistry being laid bare and assailed with human demonstrations, and annulled by the truths of holy Scripture. Then he will break its iron, that is, the atrocious and impious power, and in turn the authority to curse, which it has presumed to use against princes and peoples. He will also cause the uproar of secular jurisdictions seized, and therefore of lawsuits and vexations, to be silenced and made dumb. The luxury of pleasures and the pomp of vanities will also cease. Lastly, he will restrain the silver and gold, that is, the avarice and plunder of the Roman Pontiff and of the higher members of the Roman court, and he will grant them the use of temporal goods under due moderation. So, according to the prophet, the iron, clay, silver and gold will equally be crushed, that is, all the vices and excesses of the aforesaid court will be extinguished, like chaff from a summer threshing floor that is carried off by the wind. For what is so contrary to nature, to human and divine law, and to all reason, cannot remain for long.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAP. XXV.

units.la: Qualiter in speciali praedictis sit usus Romanus Episcopus extra ecclesiasticos limites ad laicos siue civilia.
units.tr: How the Roman Bishop has in particular used the aforesaid powers outside ecclesiastical limits, over laymen and in civil matters.

units.la: SVperest autem nobis exquirere, qualiter & in quibus plenitudine sibi potestatis assumpta extra limites ecclesiasticos usi sint hactenus & vtantur Episcopi Romanorum, rememorabimur tamen primum Ecclesiae primitiuae ritus eiusq; processus a sui principio & capite quod est Christus, & a primis suis promotoribus, apostolis sanctis. Hic enim, Christus videlicet, venit in mundum, sacerdotale siue pastoris animarum officium instruere, ac etiam exercere. Legis namque lator aeternae, salutis existens, sacramentorum ritum & exercitium praecepta quoque atque consilia credendorum, agendorum & spernendorum ad merendam simpliciter aut excellenter felicem seu beatam vitam, quam vocamus aeternam, sub eadem lege perstrinxit, iudicium quidem ciuilium actuum siue principatus officium huius seculi abdicans & eidem expresse renuntians; & consimiliter abdicare praecipiens aut consulens, omnes apostolos & sui ac ipsorum alios successores in officio supradicto, seipsumq; subiectum exprimens ordinatione diuina, iudicio seu coactiuae potestati principantium huius seculi, sic quoq; suos apostolos, sic ipsi seipsos tam opere quam sermone, quemadmodum euidenter ostensum est ex scriptura, cum sanctorum & doctorum expositionib. & auctoritatib. 4. huius & 5. Et humanis rationib. 8. & 9. eiusdem aliqualiter declaratum. Eas vero potestates exercens & apostolis ac ipsorum successoribus in eorum persona exercendas concedens, de quib. etiam dictum est 6.7.15. & 16. huius, summamque rursum paupertatem obseruans, ipsisq; ac ipsorum successoribus seruare docens, praecipiens, aut consulens secundum rememoratum & declaratum a nobis modum 13. & 14. huius. Hanc siquidem formam & modum viuendi, & iam dictum officium exercendi, secundum potestates praedictas, obseruauerunt apostoli, tanquam obedientiae filii, obseruauerunt etiam Romanorum Episcopi & Apostolorum caeteri successores plurimi, quamquam non omnes, usque quasi ad tempora Constantini primi Romanorum Imperatoris, ipsorum n. quidam praedia possederunt quorum primus legitur fuisse primus Vrbanus, Romanus Episcopus, vsq; in cuius tempus vixerat ecclesia siue sacerdotale collegium instar vitae Christi & apostolorum, quam meritoriam & summam diximus paupertatem. Hoc quamuis fortasse faciens principaliter praedictus Vrbanus propter pietatem & pauperum subuentionem seu misericordiam, vt ipsius intentionem q; pie possumus referamus ad bonum, si tamen huiusmodi praediorum aut ex ipsis prouenientium coram iudice coactiuo, vendicandi potestatem assumpsit, vel ipsa vendendi & precium distribuendi pauperib. habuit potestatem, nec vendidit & distribuit, a summa paupertate iam dicta siue perfectionis statu scienter aut ignorantes haec fecerit, indubie declinauit. Quemadmodum etiam secuti sunt Rom. Episcoporum quam plures in hoc vsq; in tempora Constantini. Quo siquidem interuallo, quemadmodum diximus 8. 10. & 12. huius, ordinationes quasdam circa ritum ecclesiasticum, vt cultum diuinum, & statum honestum sacerdotalis collegii sibi statuerint cum suo collegio Romanen. Episcopi. Et eas tanquam vtiles communicauere reliquis ecclesiis requirentibus, maxime has, caeteratum quoq; mundi ecclesiarum iuxta possibilitatem propter pietatem & charitatem, curam, diligentiam assumpserunt, eo quod rectoribus, siue pastoribus, sufficientibus carebant frequentius, propter quod aliarum personas exhortabantur atq; monebant in his quae pertinebant ad honestatem & fidem. Eorum vero monitiones grate ac sponte sumebant ecclesiarum reliquae propter causas assignatas 18. & 22. huius. In quibus quidem etiam ecclesiis, quandoq; discolis existentibus sacerdotum seu Episcoporum aut diaconorum vel reliquarum personarum aliquibus, neque ab aliorum turbatione circa mores aut fidem, fraterna præsentium monitione cessantib. procedebant fortasse ipsorum discretiores, ac pie volentes in Christo viuere, per Romanum Episcopum & ipsius Ecclesiam, quorum monita propter iam dictas causas magis verebantur fideles, excommunicationes seu anathemata ferri, & mandari super rebelles & aliorum turbatores vel aliter criminosos, vel id per seipsos zelo fidei fecerunt episcopi Romanorum. In aliis ergo locis, fideles existentes, secundum plurima partem ipsorum, concordauerunt obedire Rom. episcopo, & ipsius ecclesiæ, propter fidei vnitatem & ipsorum inuicem quietem seruandam, quoniam hæc potestate coactiua nec modo conuenientiori alio seruare poterant, eo quod infidelis esset quasi vbiq; tunc legislator humanus.
units.tr: It remains for us to inquire how, and in what matters, the bishops of Rome have hitherto used and still use the fullness of power they have assumed beyond ecclesiastical limits. First, however, we shall recall the rites of the primitive Church and its progress from its beginning and head, which is Christ, and from its first promoters, the holy apostles. For Christ came into the world to teach and also to exercise the priestly office, or the office of minister of souls. As the giver of the eternal law, the author of salvation, he prescribed the rite and practice of the sacraments, and also the precepts and counsels concerning what is to be believed, done and despised, in order to merit simply or in a more excellent way the happy or blessed life which we call eternal. Under this same law he bound his followers. He renounced the judgment of civil acts, that is, the office of government in this age, and expressly disowned it. Likewise he commanded or counselled the apostles, and their successors in the aforesaid office, to renounce it. He himself declared himself subject, by divine ordinance, to the judgment or coercive power of the rulers of this world. He taught his apostles, and they themselves, both by deed and by word, as is clearly shown from Scripture, together with the expositions and authorities of the holy and learned men cited in 4. huius and 5, and partly explained by the human arguments in 8 and 9 of the same. Exercising those powers, and granting that they be exercised by the apostles and their successors in their persons (of which things it has also been said in 6, 7, 15 and 16 of this chapter), he likewise observed the highest poverty, and taught, commanded or counselled his followers to observe it, according to the manner recalled and explained by us in 13 and 14 of this chapter. The apostles observed this form and manner of living, and of exercising the aforesaid office according to the powers described, as obedient sons. Also the bishops of Rome and many, though not all, of the other successors of the apostles observed it, almost down to the time of Constantine the First, Emperor of the Romans. For some of them possessed landed estates. The first of these is read to have been Urban, bishop of Rome, and until his time the Church, or priestly college, lived in the manner of Christ and the apostles, which we have called the meritorious and supreme poverty. Although Urban may perhaps have done this chiefly out of piety and for the relief and mercy of the poor, so that we may fairly refer his intention to good, nevertheless, if he assumed the power of claiming such estates, or of their produce, before a judge with coercive power, or had the power of selling them and distributing the price to the poor, and did not sell and distribute them, he undoubtedly departed from the supreme poverty already mentioned, or from the state of perfection, whether he did this knowingly or in ignorance. Many bishops of Rome also followed him in this, down to the time of Constantine. In this interval, as we have said in 8, 10 and 12 of this chapter, the bishops of Rome with their college made certain regulations concerning the ecclesiastical rite, such as divine worship and the honourable state of the priestly college. They shared these with the other churches as useful when they asked for them. Above all, they took upon themselves, so far as possible, the care and diligence of the other churches of the world out of piety and charity, because those churches often lacked sufficient rulers or pastors. For this reason they exhorted and admonished the persons of other churches in matters that pertained to honesty and faith. The remaining churches gladly and willingly accepted their admonitions, for the reasons assigned in 18 and 22 of this chapter. Moreover, when some priests, bishops, deacons or other persons in those churches were disorderly, and did not cease from disturbing others in matters of morals or faith despite brotherly admonition in the present, the more prudent among them, who wished to live piously in Christ, perhaps proceeded through the bishop of Rome and his Church. Because the faithful feared his admonitions more, for the reasons already given, excommunications or anathemas were pronounced and ordered against the rebels and disturbers of others, or against those otherwise guilty of crimes. Either the bishops of Rome did this themselves, out of zeal for the faith. In other places, then, the faithful, for the most part, agreed to obey the bishop of Rome and his Church, in order to keep the unity of the faith and their mutual peace. For they could not keep these things by coercive power, or in any more fitting way, since the human lawgiver was then almost nowhere to be found who was faithful.

units.la: Adueniente vero tempore Constantini I. Rom. Imperatoris, q primus Romanorum principū permisit & concessit, fideles Christi publice congregari: facta sunt primum concilia generalia sacerdotum seu episcoporum, præcepto & autoritate principis supradicti: Quibus quidem conciliis definiti sunt & determinati scripturæ sacræ sensus ambigui, & ipsorum veri à falsis & erroneis sequestrati. Quos siquidem falsos & insanos sacerdotum aliqui, quandoq; quidem propter ignorantiam & plerunq; propter superstitionem atq; malitiam seminauerant inter Christi fideles. In quib. rursum concitiis, factæ sunt ordinationes circa ecclesiasticum ritum, vt circa cultū diuinum, diaconorum & sacerdotum honestate & disciplina, ipsorumq; ad officia ecclesiastica, tam inseparabilia, q vocant ordines, q separabilia, q vocant prælationes, siue curas animarum, & huiusmodi reliqua, in certis locis siue punciis promouendi, et temporalia seu beneficia, vt oblationes ac reliqua quæ sibi propter ministerium euangelii tradebantur, tam mobilia quam immobilia distribuendi, determinatus siue statutus est modus & forma. De quo siquidem obseruando legislator humanus seu principans eius autoritate, præceptum coactiuum siue legem tulit, obligantem quemlibet sacerdotem aut non sacerdotem, secundum exigentiā cuiusq; poena reali vel personali, p statu & in statu præsentis seculi transgressoribus infligenda.
units.tr: But when the time of Constantine the First, Emperor of the Romans, came, who was the first of the Roman rulers to permit and grant that the faithful of Christ might assemble publicly, the first general councils of priests or bishops were held by the command and authority of the aforesaid prince. In these councils the ambiguous senses of Holy Scripture were defined and determined, and their true meanings were separated from the false and erroneous ones. Some priests had sown these false and mad opinions among the faithful of Christ, sometimes out of ignorance, but more often out of superstition and malice. In these councils again, regulations were made concerning the ecclesiastical rite, such as divine worship, and the honesty and discipline of deacons and priests. Also determined and fixed were the manner and form in which persons were to be promoted to ecclesiastical offices, both those inseparable from them, which they call orders, and those separable, which they call prelacies or cures of souls, and similar matters in certain places or points. Likewise fixed was the manner of distributing temporal goods or benefices, such as the offerings and other things given to them for the ministry of the gospel, both movable and immovable. To secure the observance of these things, the human lawgiver, or the ruler by his authority, enacted a coercive precept or law, binding every priest or non-priest, with a real or personal penalty, according to the nature of each case, to be inflicted in this present age and state on transgressors.

units.la: Ferebantur n. huiusmodi leges in sacerdotes & episcopos magis quam in alios, quoniam & ipsi tunc erant, qui frequentius causam dabant talibus edictis: nec aduersus legislatorem humanum reclamantib. episcopis Romanorum, aut aliis quibuscunq; tanquam non subiectis principum legib. & edictis, sed instanter supplicantib. ad principes pro legib. ferendis huiusmodi, quemadmodum ex codice Isidori supradicto, & aliis approbatis apparet historiis, de quib. induximus plures vigesimo primo huius. Amplius per eosdem principes statuebantur & statutæ sunt leges de ipsorum numero certo secundum prouincias, & de ipsorum temporalibus siue carnalibus bonis, tam mobilibus quam immobilibus, quæ sibi per prædictum Constantinum donata fuere, ac per reliquos principes Romanos aut alios, & successiue etiam per personas aliquas singulares: rursumque de ciuilibus seu contentiosis ipsorum actibus, quamuis specialibus ex humani legislatoris gratia moderatæ fauoribus.
