Attendentes nanque legislatores sacerdotalis charactetis dignitatem & reuerentiam, quoniam per ipsum secundum veritatem, Christi repræsentatur officium, attendentes etiam grauitatem morum, & simplicitatem ac innocentiam personarum, quæ tunc in euangelio ministrabant, & iam dictum gerebant officium etiam in consimilib. actibus leges minus rigorosas pro his statuebant, ipsisq; quam plurima priuilegia concedentes, ne à laicis calumniatoribus, vexarentur, vel à diuinis officiis turbarentur. Erant n. numero pauci deuoti, & propter humilitatē facile causidicorum cedentes insultib. nec violenta seu armata propter sui defensionem aut aliorum offensionem vallati potentia. Nam clericos, præsertim sacerdotes aut Episcopos ... re, vel per se sumi iubere, grande nephas, & quasi monstrum ciuile visum fuisset prisci vnde Ambrosius, vbi supra induximus nono huius: Dolere potero, flere potero, gemere potero, mili-tes, Gothos quoque, lachryma mea irrumpe mea sunt, ratio enim munimenta sunt sacerdotis, aliter nec debeo nec possum resistere.
units.tr: Such laws were indeed directed more against priests and bishops than against others, since they were then the ones who most often gave occasion for such edicts. Nor did the bishops of Rome, or any others, protest against the human lawgiver, as though they were not subject to the laws and edicts of princes. Rather they urgently petitioned the princes to enact laws of this kind, as appears from the aforesaid code of Isidore and from other approved histories, from which we have cited many in 21 of this chapter. Moreover, by the same princes laws were enacted and established concerning the fixed number of clergy according to provinces, and concerning their temporal or carnal goods, both movable and immovable, which had been given to them by the aforesaid Constantine, and by the other Roman or other princes, and afterwards also by certain individuals. Laws were also made concerning their civil or contentious acts, though these were moderated by the special favours of the grace of the human lawgiver. For the lawgivers, attending to the dignity and reverence of the priestly character, because through it the office of Christ is truly represented, also attending to the gravity of morals and the simplicity and innocence of the persons who then ministered in the gospel and performed the aforesaid office, enacted less rigorous laws for them even in similar acts. They granted them very many privileges, so that they should not be harassed by lay calumniators or disturbed in their divine offices. For they were few in number, devout, and because of their humility they easily gave way to the insults of the pleaders. They were not fortified with violent or armed power for their own defence or for the injury of others. For to order clerics, especially priests or bishops, [...] to be seized, or to be taken by force, would have been a great impiety, and would have seemed a sort of civic monstrosity. Hence Ambrose, cited above in 9 of this chapter, says: "I can grieve, I can weep, I can groan; soldiers and Goths too... my tears are my weapons. For reason is the bulwark of the priest; otherwise I neither ought nor am able to resist."

units.la: Propter quod fauoribus & priuilegiis specialibus indigebant; ad quiete agitare viuendum, & calumniatorum vexationes cuadendum, quamuis moderniis temporibus ipsorum ad laicos in hoc conuersio facta sit in oppositam qualitatem. Sic ergo sub legibus & ordinationibus ciuilibus principum vixerunt antiquis temporibus & dadum totum sacerdotale collegium ab eisdem & à populo collationes, confirmationes, & inuestituras suorum officiorum separabilium, vt prælationum, curarum & reliquorum similium, aut minorum: ac temporalium seu beneficiorum distribuendi & dispensandi potestatem suscipientes, nec propter huiusmodi subiectiones contendebant pastores antiqui Romanorum episcopi aduersus principes Romanorum, neq; aduersus populum aut singulares personas ecclesiarum patronos; quoniam ad hoc nouerant diuina & humana lege, quemadmodum quarto, quinto, & octauo huius, in decimo spectant scripturam & humanas rationes sufficienter ostendimus. Sic enim legimus de Symachio, Vatinante Sardo. Hic enim Laurentio cuidam coelectus discorditer per Theodoricum regem, facto iudicio confirmatus est in Papam Romanum. Sic etiam scribit Martinus de beato Gregorio: Hic, inquit, in Papam eligitur, & ipse, (Mauritius videlicet Imperator,) imperialibus litteris suum affirmat consensum. Sicetiam suorum priuilegiorum confirmationem, ab Imperatoribus petere solebant Episcopi Romanorum, vt de Vitelliano, natiuitate Signeno, & Constantino, natiuitate Syro, & aliis plerisque Romanis Pontificibus legitur, quinimo pro his & aliis supplicationib. & suis confirmationibus impetrandis ad Imperatores per loca distantia plurimum personaliter solebant accedere, vt de ipsorum quam pluribus legitur in chronicis & approbatis historiis. Et quod amplius est, Iohannes duodecimus per Ottonem primum Romanum Imperatorem suis exigentibus demeritis, consentiente omni populo, tam clero quam laicis, à papatu depositus est, sicetiam vbi de nono Benedicto dicto agitur in chronica Martini, legitur de duobus electis contentiose, atque depositis Imperiali censura per Henricum tunc principem Romanorum. Eiusdem enim auctoritatis primae est aliquid statuere, ac id cum expediens fuerit destituere: cum igitur Episcopus quilibet per principem & omnem populum eligi debeat, ipsorum auctoritate destitui sive deponi potest, quemadmodum certificatum est decimoseptimo huius. Instar ergo Christi & Apostolorum vixerunt Romani, & caeterarum provinciarum Episcopi & sacerdotes, ac clericorum omne collegium, sub regimine coactivo principantium auctoritate legislatoris humani. Verum suadente ac stimulante huius mundi principe, superbiae, ambitionis primo parente, reliquorum quoque vitiorum omnium suggestore diabolo, in alienam viam, ab ea quae Christi & Apostolorum, deducti sunt, quinimo seducti versus Romanorum Episcopi quidam. Nam ipsorum animos inuadens cupiditas & avaritia, inde foris expulit, quam Christus in Ecclesia tertio modo dicta, plantaverat & statuerat, summam meritoriam paupertatem. Rursumque inuadens eosdem superbia & ambitio seculariter principandi, expulit inde summam humilitatem, quam Christus indixerat, & observare mandaverat eidem Ecclesiae sive universo coetui sacerdotum. Quorum quidem primus hoc passus, si eo prior in hoc non alter exiterat, fuisse legitur Simplicius quidam, Tibertinus cognomine, Romanus Episcopus. Hic enim, unde sibi nescio auctoritate sumpta, quamuis certissime noverim, nisi per ignorantiam excusetur, unde temeritate praesumpta statuit nullum clericum inuestituram a laico debere suscipere. Inuestituram siquidem intelligendo beneficiorum & officiorum, de quib. diximus prius, quamuis tamen ex ipsius statuto significetur manifeste, praedecessores suos humilitatem & reverentiam debitam principibus exhibere volentes, inuestituras praedictas a laicis recipere soluisse. Huius siquidem rursum successor, quamuis non immediatus, Pelagius primus statuit, ut haeretici per seculares potestates punirentur. De quo etiam statuto mirandum, quoniam nolatuit illum huiusmodi legem tempore Iustiniani Romani principis in haereticos latam fuisse. Et quoniam suae non erat auctoritatis ferre huiusmodi leges in quantum Episcopi, nisi forte hoc sibi auctoritate humani legislatoris foret indultum, quemadmodum duodecimo & decimo tertio primae ostensum est, & vigesimo primo huius. Ideo quemadmodum iam dictus Simplicius in alienam messem falcem iniecit, auctoritatem sibi, videlicet quae alterius, usurpando. Cui rursum Adrianus tertius, licet non immediate, successit in usurpatione praedicta. Statuit enim, ut nullus Imperator se intromitteret, & de electione Papae, ut dicti Martini verbis vtamur. Quod siquidem statutum omnino nullum, eo qua carente tali auctoritate legislativa scilicet, emanauit. Apertum etiam inconueniens continebat, quemadmodum ex decimo septimo huius ostensum est, fueratque illius oppositum longa & laudabili consuetudine roboratum. Quamuis enim dicat Martinus, vbi legit de Leone decimo, quod Romanie x prava consuetudine petebant ab Imperatore pontificem sibi dari; consuetudinem confessus, quod verum concedimus, pravam tamen auctoritate propria dicens, quantum petens usurpationes praedictas Romanorum pontificum, & iura principum sive humani legislatoris obfuscans, magis homini quam Deo & veritati placere nisus, non verum dicit. Sed huius rei ortum & mysterium sibi clausum fuisse demonstrat. Nam licet ad principem aut alteram personam singularem, inquantum huiusmodi, non conveniat divino vel humano iure, nec aliqua laudanda consuetudine, secundum ipsius solius imperium ad officium aliquod instituere seu determinare personam, maxime ad Romanorum episcopatum, quemadmodum decimoquinto primae, ac decimoseptimo & vigesimo huius sufficienter ostensum est: ad principem tamen auctoritate legislatoris humani sibi concessa secundum certam formam & modum determinatum a lege, ut videlicet usuro collegii sacerdotalis & aliorum sapientum, & studiorum consilio, ipsorumque valentioris partis determinationi crediturò poterit licite valde Romani Pontificis institutio pertinere. Nec in hoc Martino credendum est, quoniam ipse, cum sui ordine usurpationis huiusmodi particeps erat, obtinuerunt namque; vel obtinuisse credunt ordines, quos paupertatis fratres appellant, a Romanis Pontificibus exemptionem, ut videlicet suis pastoribus Episcopis aut aliis superioribus praelatis nulla sint iurisdictione subiecti, quamuis exemptionem, quae a principum iurisdictione obtineant ex solis privilegiis, quibus clerus ab humano legislatore reperitur exemptus.
units.tr: Therefore they needed special favours and privileges, to lead a quiet life and to escape the harassment of slanderers, although in more recent times the situation has been turned around by them towards laymen, into the opposite condition. So, in ancient times, the whole priestly college lived under the laws and civil ordinances of princes, and for a long time both the emperors and the people granted, confirmed and invested them with their separable offices, such as prelacies, cures and similar or lesser ones, and received the power to distribute and dispense temporal goods and benefices. Nor on account of such subjection did the ancient pastors, the Roman bishops, contend against the Roman princes, nor against the people or the individual patrons of the churches; for they knew from divine and human law, as we have sufficiently shown in the fourth, fifth and eighth chapters of this book, and as the tenth treats from Scripture and human reasons, that this was right. For thus we read about Symmachus, a Sardinian, son of Vatinas. He, having been elected together with a certain Laurentius, in a disputed way, was confirmed as Roman Pope by Theodoric the king, after a judgement had been made. So also Martin writes of the blessed Gregory: "He, says he, is elected Pope, and he himself (namely, the Emperor Maurice) affirms his consent by imperial letters." Likewise the Roman bishops were accustomed to seek confirmation of their privileges from the emperors, as is read of Vitalian, of Sisinnius the Syrian-born, of Constantine the Syrian-born, and of many other Roman pontiffs; indeed, to obtain these and other petitions and their confirmations they often went in person to the emperors over long distances, as is read of very many of them in the chronicles and approved histories. And what is more, John XII was deposed from the papacy by Otto I, the first Roman emperor, for his demerits, with the consent of the whole people, clergy and laity alike; likewise, where the ninth Benedict is discussed in Martin's chronicle, we read that two contentiously elected men were deposed by the imperial censure of Henry, then prince of the Romans. For it belongs to the same authority first to establish something and, when expedient, to remove it. Therefore, since any bishop ought to be elected by the prince and the whole people, he can be removed or deposed by their authority, as was certified in the seventeenth chapter of this book. Thus the Romans, and the bishops and priests of other provinces, and the whole college of clergy, lived after the pattern of Christ and the Apostles, under the coercive rule of princes by the authority of the human lawgiver. But, at the persuasion and incitement of the prince of this world, Satan, the first parent of pride and ambition, and the instigator of all the other vices, some of the Roman bishops were led and seduced away from the way of Christ and the Apostles into another path. For covetousness and avarice, invading their minds, drove out from there that meritorious poverty, the highest poverty, which Christ had planted and established in the Church, as mentioned in the third way. And again, pride and the ambition to rule in a worldly manner, invading the same men, drove out from there the highest humility, which Christ had ordained and commanded to be observed by the same Church, or the whole assembly of priests. The first of these to suffer this, if he was not the first to do so in this respect, is read to have been a certain Simplicius, surnamed Tiburtinus, Bishop of Rome. For he, by an authority I know not from where, though I know most certainly that, unless it is excused by ignorance, he presumed with rashness to decree that no cleric ought to receive an investiture from a layman. For by "investiture" he meant the investiture of benefices and offices, of which we spoke before; yet although his decree clearly signifies that his predecessors, wishing to show due humility and reverence to princes, were accustomed to receive those investitures from laymen, Pelagius I, not his immediate successor, next decreed that heretics should be punished by secular powers. Concerning this decree it is also remarkable, since it has escaped notice that such a law against heretics had been passed in the time of the Roman emperor Justinian. And since it was not within his authority, as bishop, to make such laws, unless perhaps this had been granted to him by the authority of the human lawgiver, as was shown in the twelfth and thirteenth chapters of the first part and in the twenty-first chapter of this book. Therefore, just as the aforementioned Simplicius cast his sickle into another's harvest, usurping for himself an authority which belonged to another. To him in turn Adrian III, though not immediately, succeeded in the aforesaid usurpation. For he decreed that no emperor should interfere in the election of the Pope, to use the words of Martin. This decree was entirely null, since it issued from one lacking such legislative authority. It also contained an evident impropriety, as was shown from the seventeenth chapter of this book, and its opposite had been strengthened by long and praiseworthy custom. For although Martin, where he reads about Leo X, says that "the Romans, by a bad custom, used to ask the emperor to give them a pontiff," and he admits that it was a custom, which we grant to be true, yet by his own authority calling it "bad," he, striving to please man rather than God and the truth, obscuring the usurpations of the Roman pontiffs and the rights of princes or the human lawgiver, does not speak the truth. But he shows that the origin and mystery of this matter were hidden from him. For although it is not fitting, by divine or human law, nor by any praiseworthy custom, for a prince or any other single person, merely by his own command, to institute or appoint a person to any office, especially to the Roman episcopate, as has been sufficiently shown in the fifteenth chapter of the first part and in the seventeenth and twentieth chapters of this book; yet it may be most lawful for the institution of the Roman Pontiff to belong to the prince, granted to him by the authority of the human lawgiver, according to a certain form and manner determined by law, namely, with the counsel of the college of priests and other wise men, and of their studies, and to be entrusted to the determination of the more powerful part. Nor is Martin to be believed in this, since he himself was a sharer in such usurpation with his order: for the orders which they call "brothers of poverty" have obtained, or believe they have obtained, exemption from the Roman pontiffs, so that they are subject to no jurisdiction of their pastors, bishops or other superior prelates; although the exemption which they hold from the jurisdiction of princes rests only on the privileges by which the clergy is found exempt from the human lawgiver.

units.la: Unde tamen venit sermo prius, non prava neq; illaudabilis consuetudo fuit per Imperatores, ut diximus, ecclesiae Romanae pastores instituti. Hanc n. auctoritatem & ampliori modo iam dicto legimus, & concedunt qui tecum Martine veritati huic aduersari niuntur per omnem Romanum populum, ut per Episcopum, clerum, & alias seculares personas Carolo Magno, & OttHoni I. Regi Theutonicorum, & Romanorum Imperatori postmodum fuisse concessam. Unde in approbatis legitur historia, & verum est, ed:itum hoc emanasse de populi Romani consensu communi: Leo Papa in synodo congregata Romani Ecclesia sancti Salvatoris ad exemplum beati Adriani apostolicae sedis Episcopi, qui domino Carolo victoriosissimo Regi Francorum & Longobardorum patriciatus dignitatem ac ordinationem apostolicae sedis & inuestituram concessit. Ego quoq; Leo servus servorum Dei Episcopus cum cunctio clero, ac populo Romano constituimus, confirmamus, & roboramus, & per nostram apostolicam auctoritatem concedimus atque largimur domino Ottoni primo Regi Theutonicorum, eiusque successoribus huius regni Italiae in perpetuum, tam sibi facultatem eligendi successorem, quam summae sedis apostolicae pontificem ordinandi, ac per hac Archiepiscopos seu Episcopos, ut ipsi ab eo inuestituram suscipiant, consecrationem autem unde debent, exceptis his quos Imperator Pontifici & Archiepiscopis concessit. Et nemo deinceps huiusquisque sit dignitatis vel religiositatis eligendi vel patrium sive Pontificem summae sedis apostolicae vel quantumcunque Episcopum ordinandi habeat facultatem absque consensu consensu ipsius Imperatoris, qui tamen fiat absque omni pecunia, & vt ipse sit patritius & Rex. Quod si a clero quis Episcopus eligatur, nisi a supradicto rege laudetur & investietur, non consecretur. Si quis contra hanc auctoritatem aliquid moliatur, hunc excommunicationi subiacere decreuimus: & nisi resipuerit irrevocabili exilio puniri, vel ultimo supplicio puniri. Hoc siquidem edictum confirmauit Stephanus Papa, prædicti Leonis successor, & Stephani successor quidam Nicolaus, ipsumque sub terribilis anathematis poena seruari præcipiens, vt videlicet eius violatores seu transgressores cum impiis, qui non resurgent, debeant computari. Ex hoc autem edicto singulariter notandum est, quod auctoritas hæc, quam de investitura Romanus Episcopus cum vniuerso populo in Imperatorem transtulit, quantum erat ex parte Papæ, fuit renunciatio quædam, quoniam auctoritas huius prima fuit & est principis siue legislatoris humani, qui hanc auctoritatem, inuestiendi scil. Episcopos & Archiepiscopos iam Papæ concesserat, eo quod omnia temporalia per quemcunq; translata fuerint in quamuis Ecclesiam, quantum ad hoc subiecta fuerant & sunt legislatoti humano, prouinciæ, in qua sita sunt. Signatur autem hoc ex edicto prædicto, vbi dicitur, exceptis his, quos Imperator Pontifici & Archiepiscopis concessit. Sic etiam sedis apostolicæ Pontificem instituere, pertinet ad Romani principis & populi potestatem, vt decimoseptimo huius ostensum est. A quo siquidem populo non excluditur sed includitur clerus cum pars sit illius, quam quidem potestatem seu autoritatem, si transferre voluerunt in principem, aut simpliciter, aut cum determinatione legali, eam princeps Romanus licite sumpsit, nec ab ipso per Decretalem siue legem cuiusquam Romani Pontificis, absq; decreto populi potuit licite reuocari. Non enim Romano populo, vel sibi cum clero tantummodo in communitate fidelium conuenit leges aut decretales aliquas condere, quenquam obligantes ad poenam, vt ex decimo tertio prime, ac vigesimo primo huius ostensum est. Has tamen ferre ac promulgare, licet indebite, tam in ipsa latione, quam in legibus latis, iurisdictionem populorum & principum vsurpantes tentauerunt Rom. Episcopi quidam, & paulatim in his processerunt, maxime imperiali sede vacante, quemadmodum deduximus vigesimo secundo huius. Hinc autem plurimum, & propter temporalium quorundam occupationem, quantum ex chronicis siue approbatis historiis comprehendi potest, suscitatæ sunt lites inter Romanorum Imperatores & ipsorum Episcopos, quamuis contra Christi & Apostolorum consilium aut præceptum in hoc egerint, qui sibi succedere debent in apostolatu siue sacerdotis officio, summam pauperratem & humilitatem seruare debentes, qui quidem in aliam quandam & illi oppositam diuertentes viam ignorantia vel malitia vel vtrisq;, vt ex præmissis ostendimus, hanc inierunt aduersus iam dictos principes immortalem contentionem & pugnam, quam inter cæteros magis aggressus est Rom. Episcopus quidam, nomine Paschalis contra Henricum IV. Theutonicorum regem. Hunc enim secundum historias prohibuit dictus Episcopus ad imperialem apicem scandere, aduersus illum concitans Romanum populum, vsque quo præfatus Henricus in Tuscia existens per nuncios & literas inuestituras episcoporum, abbatum, & omnium clericorum quasi coactus eidem concessit Episcopo. A quo rursum postquam ingressus est vrbem, super extortis ab ipso iuramentum expetens Papa prædictus, cum suorum Cardinalium coetu captus est: Et demum liberatus pacem habuit cum Imperatore prædicto, cui rursum suscitans pristinam litem, tandem contendendo, laboriose finiuit.
units.tr: Whence, however, the earlier practice arose, which was neither a wicked nor a blameworthy custom, that the pastors of the Roman Church were appointed by the emperors, as we have said. For we read this authority, and in a broader form than already mentioned, and those who strive with you, Martin, against this truth concede that it was granted to Charlemagne, and afterwards to Otto I, King of the Germans and Emperor of the Romans, by the bishop, the clergy and other secular persons throughout the whole Roman people. Hence it is read in the approved history, and it is true, that the edict issued from the common consent of the Roman people: "Pope Leo, in a synod gathered in the Roman Church of the Holy Saviour, after the example of the blessed Adrian, bishop of the apostolic see, who granted to the most victorious lord Charles, King of the Franks and Lombards, the dignity of patrician, and the ordering of the apostolic see, and investiture. I also, Leo, servant of the servants of God, bishop, together with all the clergy and the Roman people, establish, confirm and strengthen, and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow on the lord Otto the First, King of the Germans, and on his successors in the kingdom of Italy for ever, both the power of choosing a successor and of ordaining the pontiff of the supreme apostolic see, and thus the archbishops or bishops, so that they receive investiture from him, and consecration from whomever they ought, except those whom the Emperor has granted to the Pontiff and archbishops. And henceforth let no one, of whatever dignity or religious order, have the power of choosing or ordaining a patriarch, or the pontiff of the supreme apostolic see, or any bishop whatever, without the consent of the Emperor himself, which shall nevertheless be given without any payment, and so that he may be patrician and king. But if anyone is elected bishop by the clergy, unless he is approved and invested by the aforesaid king, he shall not be consecrated. If anyone attempts anything against this authority, we decree that he shall be subject to excommunication; and unless he repents, he shall be punished with irrevocable exile or with the final punishment." This edict was confirmed by Stephen, Pope, successor of the aforesaid Leo, and by a certain Nicholas, successor of Stephen, who ordered it to be kept under the penalty of a terrible anathema, so that its violators or transgressors should be counted with the impious who shall not rise again. From this edict it must be especially noted that this authority, which the Roman bishop with the whole people transferred to the Emperor concerning investiture, was, so far as it lay on the part of the Pope, a certain renunciation, since the authority of this was first, and is, that of the prince or human legislator, who had already granted to the Pope this authority of investing bishops and archbishops; for all temporal things, by whomsoever transferred to any church, were and are subject, so far as this goes, to the human legislator of the province in which they are situated. This is indicated by the aforesaid edict, where it says: "except those whom the Emperor has granted to the Pontiff and archbishops." Thus also to appoint the pontiff of the apostolic see belongs to the power of the Roman prince and people, as was shown in the seventeenth chapter of this work. From this people the clergy is not excluded but included, since it is a part of it; and if they wished to transfer this power or authority to the prince, either simply or with a legal determination, the Roman prince lawfully took it up, and it could not lawfully be revoked by him through a decretal or law of any Roman Pontiff without the decree of the people. For it does not belong to the Roman people, or to the clergy alone within the community of the faithful, to enact any laws or decretals binding anyone to punishment, as was shown in the thirteenth and twenty-first chapters of this work. Yet some Roman bishops attempted to issue and promulgate such laws, although improperly, both in the enactment itself and in the laws enacted, usurping the jurisdiction of peoples and princes, and they gradually advanced in this, especially while the imperial see was vacant, as we have shown in the twenty-second chapter of this work. From this, and on account of the occupation of certain temporal goods, as far as can be gathered from the chronicles or approved histories, quarrels arose between the Roman emperors and their bishops; yet in this they acted against the counsel or precept of Christ and the Apostles, since those who ought to succeed them in the apostolate or the priestly office should keep the utmost poverty and humility. Turning instead into another way, opposed to this, through ignorance, malice, or both, as we have shown above, they entered upon this immortal contention and fight against the said princes, which among the others was pursued most of all by a certain Roman bishop named Paschal against Henry IV, King of the Germans. For according to the histories, this bishop prevented Henry from ascending to the imperial summit, stirring up the Roman people against him, until the aforesaid Henry, while staying in Tuscany, by messengers and letters, as if compelled, granted to the same bishop the investitures of bishops, abbots and all clerics. Afterwards, when Henry had entered the city, the aforesaid Pope, demanding an oath concerning the things extorted from him, was seized together with the company of his cardinals; and at last, once freed, he made peace with the aforesaid Emperor, but, renewing the former quarrel against him, he finally ended it with difficulty after a long contention.

units.la: Huius vero successori Calixto cuidam, narrat Martinus, Imperator prædictus ad cor rediens, vt Martini verbis vtamur, inuestituram Episcoporum & aliorum prælatorum per annulum & baculum libere resignauit, & concessit per omne imperium in omnibus Ecclesiis, canonicam fieri electionem, possessiones & regalia beati Petri, quæ propter suam vel aliam cum Ecclesia discordiam alienata fuerant, Romanæ Ecclesiæ restituit, & aliàs possessiones tam clericorum quam laicorum eisdem occasione guerræ sublatas, restitui fideliter disposuit. Has siquidem postmodum concessiones & priuilegia ex causa forsan legitima reuocare volentes, aut reuocantes simpliciter aut in parte, Otto quartus & Fredericus secundus Romanorum Imperatores, Episcoporum & cleri Romani plurimas insidias, persecutiones, & impedimenta sunt passi, & eorum prædecessores aliqui minus adiuti per populos subditos propter ipsorum aut suorum officialium & ministrorum regimen, quandoque fortassis tyrannidem sapuisse. Est igitur, vt iam diximus, & fuit fomes hic primus præsentis litis atque discordiæ inter Imperatores & Romanos Pontifices. Hisque propter legem diuinam, & quorundam principum hæresim contentionibus extinctis omnino. Volunt enim Romanorum Episcopi minus debite ac excessiue temporalia possidere, nec legibus & edictis subesse principum seu legislatoris humani contra Christi & Apostolorum exemplum atque doctrinam, vt in quarto huius, & quinto, & decimo quarto eiusdem ostensum est prius, cum tamen in his quæ sua non sunt, suis existentibus potius cedere quam contendere debeant iuxta consilium Apostoli ad omnes fideles primæ ad Corinthios sexto: Sic non est, inquit, inter vos sapiens quisquam, qui possit iudicare inter fratrem suum, sed frater cum fratre iudicio contendit, & hoc apud infideles. Iam quidem omnino delictum est in vobis: quid iudicia habetis inter vos? Quare non magis iniuriam accipitis? Quare non magis fraudem patimini? Et subdit, quod potest ad Romanos Episcopos & reliquos clericos quasi omnes conuenienter dici: Sed vos iniuriam facitis & fraudatis, & hoc fratrib. An nescitis, quia iniqui regnum Dei non possidebunt? Nolite errare, neq; fornicarii, neq; idolis seruientes, neq; adulteri, neq; molles, neq; masculorum concubitores, neq; fures, neq; auari, neq; ebriosi, neq; maledici, neq; rapaces regnum Dei possidebunt. Quod parum attendentes Romani Episcopi cum reliquis aliis, in quando per Romanos principes sibi videantur grauari per decimarum aut tributorum talium temporalium sumptionem, ad suos milites sustentandos, instante necessitate bellorum, pro suscepta causa ...
units.tr: Under his successor, a certain Calixtus, as Martin relates, the aforesaid Emperor, coming to his senses, to use Martin's words, freely resigned the investiture of bishops and other prelates by ring and staff, and granted throughout the whole empire that in all churches the election should be canonical; he restored to the Roman Church the possessions and regalia of blessed Peter which had been alienated on account of his own or another's discord with the Church; and he faithfully arranged that the possessions both of clergy and of laymen, taken away on the occasion of the war, should be restored. Afterwards, Otto IV and Frederick II, Roman Emperors, wishing to revoke these concessions and privileges, perhaps for a legitimate cause, or revoking them either wholly or in part, suffered many snares, persecutions and hindrances from the bishops and clergy of Rome; and some of their predecessors, being less supported by their subject peoples, because of the rule of their officials and ministers, perhaps at times savoured of tyranny. Therefore, as we have already said, this was and is the first spark of the present strife and discord between the Emperors and the Roman Pontiffs; and it was utterly extinguished by the divine law and by the heresy of certain princes. For the Roman bishops wish to possess temporal goods in a manner that is undue and excessive, and not to be subject to the laws and edicts of princes or of the human legislator, against the example and teaching of Christ and the Apostles, as was shown earlier in the fourth, fifth and fourteenth chapters of this work; whereas in matters which are not their own, they ought rather to yield than contend, as they have it, when they are their own, according to the counsel of the Apostle to all the faithful in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter six: "So there is not among you a wise man who can judge between his brethren, but brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers. Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, that you go to law with one another. Why do you not rather take wrong? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? But you do wrong and defraud, and that to your brethren. Do you not know that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived; neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with mankind, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God." Heedless of this, the Roman bishops, together with the rest, when they seem to be burdened by the Roman princes through the taking of tithes or such temporal tributes, to sustain their soldiers, in pressing need of wars, for the cause they have undertaken...

units.la: {y} Calixto] Calixtus II, 1119–1124. cepta gratia, & beneficio carnalium rerum quas sibi cotulerunt gratiose Romani principes, in superbiam elati, suae conditionis ignari, & ingratissimis omnib. magis ingrati, effrenata quadam praesumptione in horribiles blasphemias & anathemata proruperunt tam in principes quam ipsis subditos Christi fideles, quamuis in ipsorum animas infelices & corpora potius redeuntes, quam in principes & innocentem gregem fidelium transeuntes.
units.tr: {y} Calixto] Calixtus II, 1119–1124. Having received grace and the benefit of worldly goods that the Roman princes had generously bestowed on them, they were puffed up with pride, forgetful of their own station, and more ungrateful than any people. With an unbridled presumption they broke out into horrible blasphemies and anathemas, against the princes and against the faithful subjects of Christ alike. Yet these curses fell back more upon their own unhappy souls and bodies than upon the princes and the innocent flock of the faithful.

units.la: Nec sibi per principes concessis temporalibus contenti propter eorum esse insatiabilem talium appetitum, multa temporalium ad imperiale ius pertinentium provinciarum, ut quae Romandiolae civitatum, ut quae Ferrariae atque Bononiae, ac plurium aliarum possessionum, nec non etiam praediorum & aliarum iurisdictionum occuparunt, maxime imperiali sede vacante. Et quod omnium civilium inconvenientium est extremum, principes & legislatores se constituerunt, ut reges & populos in suam, quamuis intolerabilem & turpissimam servitutem redigere valeant. Eorum enim plurimi ex humili plebe trahentes natalia, dum ad statum pontificalem summuntur, praesidarum saeculi nescientes, quemadmodum neq; diuitias, indiscreti nuper ditati, fidelibus omnibus importabiles fiunt.
units.tr: Not content with the temporal goods granted them by the princes, and with an insatiable appetite for more, they seized many provinces that belonged to the imperial right, such as the cities of Romagna, Ferrara and Bologna, and many other possessions, estates and jurisdictions, especially while the imperial see stood vacant. And the greatest of all civil evils: they made themselves princes and lawgivers, so that they might reduce kings and peoples to their own intolerable and most shameful servitude. For most of them, being born of the humble plebs, when they are raised to the pontifical state, know nothing of the prudence of the world. Having lately grown rich without discernment, they become unbearable to all the faithful.

units.la: Amplius credentes sibi licere quodlibet de plenitudine potestatis, quam sibi debitam asserunt, ordinationes quasdam oligarchicas, Decretales vocatas, statuerunt & statuunt, quibus ea quae suo & suorum clericorum ac reliquorum laicorum, de quorum exemptione diximus 8. huius, temporali commodo conuenire credunt, quamuis in principantium & reliquorum fidelium grande praeiudicium seruanda decernunt. Inobedientes vero his suo, quemadmodum praediximus anathemate ferientes, vocaliter aut in scriptis, in tantam quoq; dementiam demum & insaniam prorumpentes ipsorum aliqui, ut omnes mundi principes & populos, his decretalibus pronunciaverunt sibi coactiua iurisdictione subiectos. Et hoc credere tanquam verum fore cuilibet de necessitate salutis aeternae. Quod tamen quanta sit irrisione dignum, supra monstrauimus 20. huius, 8. in 13.
units.tr: Believing moreover that they may do whatever they like by the fullness of power that they claim is due to them, they have laid down, and still lay down, certain oligarchic ordinances called Decretales. By these they decree that whatever they believe conduces to the temporal advantage of themselves, their clergy and the other laity (whose exemption we discussed in the eighth chapter of this book) is to be observed, even though it greatly prejudices princes and the other faithful. Those who disobey these decrees they strike with their anathema, as we said before, and some of them, breaking out into such madness and frenzy, have declared by word of mouth or in writing that all the princes and peoples of the world are subject to them by coercive jurisdiction. And they demand that this be believed by everyone, as true and necessary to eternal salvation. How worthy of ridicule this is, we showed above in the twentieth chapter of this book, in the eighth part of the thirteenth section.

units.la: Hos itaq; quos narrauimus per Rom. Episcopos cum suorum clericorum coetu in cunctos principes & populos patratos excessus, quamuis amplius & manifestius in Italicos populos & principes Romanorum conseruare volentes ipsi, & pertinaciter velut obstinati defendere. Nec hos tantummodo, sed proceptos & optatos eosdem aut ampliores in reliqua regna sibi quaerere volunt, omniqué solicitudine tendunt, & quam audent omnium ad hoc exteriorem operam praebent. Sane tamen attendentes atq; noscentes, quamuis hoc dissimulent, & quibusdam verborum poeticis boatibus & inuolucris, tam obscurate quam negare conentur humani legislatoris eiusdem esse auctoritatem, priuilegia & concessiones quascunq; conferre & auferre. Cum id iudicauerit expedire, Romani principis creationem atq; promotionem omni solicitudine maligna & conamine prohibet, suae vel praedecessorum suorum ingratitudinis & demeritorum conscii, priuilegia & concessiones renocari & auelli sibi per Romanum principe formidantes, & inde merita disciplinas subire. Rursumq; propter iam dictam formidinem, & quoniam priuilegiis suprad dictis ad aliorum ignorum dominia, iurisdictiones & possessiones occupandas, non sine calumnia sibi parere ingressi, reclamantib. fortasse quibusdam principum exemptionem a principe Romano aliquam astuta incditatione ad haec quaesierunt intrare. Assumpserunt n. titulum quem de se praedicant, & huiusmodi nequitiae instrumentum facere studeant, plenitudinem videl. potestatis, quam a Christo in persona beati Petri aiunt sibi tanquam huius apostoli successoribus singulariter fore concessam. Quo siquidem execrabili titulo & oratione sophistica secundum equiuocum, omnibusq; fidelib. nihilominus tanquam falsa secundum omnem eius sensum semper & vbiq; neganda: paralogizauerat haec tenus, paralogizant & ampliss paralogizare nituntur, & in ipsorum seruitutem redigere omnes mundi principes & populos, collegia & singulares personas. In co nanq; sensu, secundum quem plenitudo potestatis signare videtur vniuersalem animarum curam seu pastoratus vniuersalitatem, & rursum secundum quem sensum potestatem importat: omnes n. homines singulariter absoluendi a culpis & poenis sub specie pietatis, charitatis, & misericordiae dicto titulo plenae potestatis per Rom. Episcopos sibi primum assumpto: ex his paulatim atq; latenter, ut deduximus vigesimotertio huius, transierunt, & demum sibi sumpserunt hunc titulum in eam & secundum eam significationem, qua potestatis plenitudo per ipsos intelligitur auctoritas vniuersalis & suprema iurisdictio siue principatus coactiuus, omnium principum, populorum, & temporalium rerum. Eius quidem transitus & praesumptionis inde, quamuis inconvenienter, per metaphoricas expositiones suscipientes exordium, vnde diximus vigesimo tertio huius parte 5. Signum autem omnibus inoccultum, Romanos Episcopos iuxta sensum hunc de se praedicare plenitudinem potestatis, supremae scilicet iurisdictionis seu coactiui principatus auctoritatem sibi velle super omnes principes, populos, & singulares personas ex hac potestatis plenitudine convenire. Quoniam in suarum narrationum, quas Decretales appellant, inuolutro septimo, de sententia & re iudicata, Clemens quintus Papa Romanus, qui conditor eius praescribitur, & qui postmodum propalauit, eiusdem vocatus successor, quantum in ipsis extitit, reuocantes sententiam quandam dini Henrici septimi Romanorum Imperatoris inter caetera ipsorum iam solito more praemissis quamplurimis contumeliae, ignominiae ac irreuerentiae verbis in praefatum Henricum, tam vocaliter quam in scriptis protulerunt hanc seriem: Nos tam ex superioritate, quam ad imperium non est dubium nos habere, quam ex potestate, in qua vacante imperio, Imperatori succedimus, & nihilominus ex illius plenitudine potestatis, quam Christus rex regum & dominus dominantium, nobis, licet immeritis, in persona beati Petri concessit, sententiam & processus praedictos, & quicquid ex eis secutum est, vel occasione ipsorum de fratrum nostrorum. rum consilio declaramus fuisse, sic esse omnino irritos & inanes. Quod ne deinceps lateat horum Episcoporum fallacia, tanquam veritatis preco, clamo valenter, & vobis dico, regibus, principibus, populis, tribubus, & vniuersis linguis per Romanos Episcopos cum suorum clericorum seu Cardinalium coetu, hac ipsorum scriptura, secundum omnem eius suppositionem apertissime falsa, summum omnium praeiudicium fieri. Vos enim tentant in sua red gere subiectionem, si eam manere passi fueritis, praesertim vim ac robur legis habere. Attendite nanq; per necessitatem sequi, habentem autoritatem primam cuiuslibet principis siue iudicis reuocandi sententiam, super eum habere iurisdictionem & coactiuum principatum, potestatem quoq; sui principatus instituendi & deponendi. Hanc autem Rom. Episcopus sibi autoritatem ascribit super omnes principes mundi & principatus indifferenter: quoniam ab ea potestate plena, quam sibi Christum in persona beati Petri concessisse asserit, sententiam ciuilem reuocauit Henrici praefati. Quam siquidem etiam potestatem, per necessitatem sequitur non sibi minus fuisse concessam super reliquos omnes mundi reges & principes, quam super principem Rom. quoniam Christus non minus est vel fuit, aut erit rex aut dominus aliorum regum & principum, quam regis aut principis Rom. Quod etiam ipsorum sermo siue scriptura restatur aperte, dum dicunt aut scribunt, rex regum, & dominus dominantium. Si enim ipsorum sermo vel scriptum habuisset singulariter, quod de plenitudine potestatis sibi concessae per Christum regem & dominum, regis siue Imperatoris Romani, &c. posset ex eo reliquorum regum atq; regnorum aliqualiter exceptio comprehendi. Nunc autem, quoniam pluraliter, absolute ac indifferenter orationem protulerunt, quemadmodum ab Euangelista scribitur, quamuis non ad eam quam Episcopi Rom. intendunt sententiam, nulla potest ex ea regis aut principis exceptio fieri, sicut nec ipsi quenquam ab hoc exceptum intelligunt, sed conceptum quemlibet, validibi praedecessor ipsorum octauus Bonifacius distincte protulit, & induximus 20. huius, parte 8. Ad quos tamen ne propter ipsorum sermonem vel scripturam quisquam infestus animo maneat. Quod quanquam verum dixerit Euangelista, Christum enuncians regem regum, & dominum dominantium, etiam si addidisset omnium creatorum: falsum tamen & apertum mendacium contra Christi & Apostolorum Petri, Pauli, & Iacobi manifestam sententiam dixit & scripsit, qui potestatem principatus seu coactiuae iurisdictionis aliquam, ne dum plenam asseruit fore traditam in persona beati Petri aut alterius cuiuslibet apostoli, Romano vel alteri Episcopo cuiquam. Sed est, fuit & erit Episcopo Romano, & reliquis omnibus in Apostoli cuiuscunque persona, talis per Christum interdicta potestas, quemadmodum indubie certificauimus per scripturam, & sanctorum autoritates, 4. 5. & 9. huius. In ea vero noua, & prius semper inaudita fictione Romanus Episcopus non minus salsc, quam temerarie contra suam mentem & omnium quasi fidelium, consideratione hac participantium, non veretur enunciare palam, dum pertinaciter asserit non esse dubium se superioritate, quam coactiuae iurisdictionis siue principatus intendit, ad Imperatorem Romanum habere: tursum que vacante Imperio, sed succedere Imperatori predicto. His enim manifeste monstratur iniqua & iniusta vsurpatio iurisdictionum imperialium, quam hactenus Episcopi Romanorum exercuerunt, & in praesentiarum exercent, vt diximus, maxime imperiali sede vacante. Quis enim tam effrons siue verecundia proferret indubium verum esse, quod nunquam a seculis est auditum, neque diuina vel humana lege aut recta ratione firmatum, & cuius oppositum secundum has semper est conceptum & enunciatum, tanquam signum omnibus creditae veritatis? Unde proportionaliter medicorum proverbio, sicut plures sanat ille, de quo plures confidunt, sic reuera dicere possumus: Plures seducere vult & fallere, cui plurima credulitas, modernis temporibus adhibetur.
units.tr: These things, then, which we have related, the Roman bishops together with the company of their clergy have perpetrated against all princes and peoples. They wish to preserve them, and to defend them stubbornly, like obstinate men, more fully and openly against the Italian peoples and the princes of the Romans. Nor do they seek only these things, but they wish to obtain the same or greater ones, both proclaimed and desired, in the other kingdoms; they strive with all their care, and they give all the outward effort they dare to this end. Yet they pay attention and know, although they dissemble this, and with certain poetic bombast and wrappings of words they try to hide, as obscurely as possible, that the authority to confer and to take away privileges and concessions of whatever kind belongs to the same human lawgiver. Whenever he judges it expedient, the Roman prince's creation and promotion is forbidden by them with all their malicious care and effort. Conscious of their own ingratitude and demerits, or those of their predecessors, they fear that their privileges and concessions will be revoked and torn away from them by the Roman prince, and that they will thereby undergo deserved discipline. Again, out of this fear already mentioned, and because they have entered upon the privileges mentioned above, not without calumny, to seize the dominions, jurisdictions and possessions of others, they have sought by some cunning device to bring within this scope some exemption from the Roman prince, perhaps for certain princes who object. For they have adopted the title that they proclaim of themselves, and they strive to make of it an instrument of such wickedness, namely the fullness of power (plenitudinem potestatis), which they say was granted to them singularly by Christ in the person of blessed Peter, as successors of that apostle. Indeed, by this execrable title and sophistical speech, which is equivocal, and which must always and everywhere be denied as false in every sense by all the faithful, they have hitherto deceived, they do deceive still, and they strive to deceive still more, and to reduce all the princes and peoples of the world, collegiate bodies and individual persons, to their servitude. For in that sense in which fullness of power seems to signify the universal care of souls or the universality of pastoral office, and again in that sense in which it imports power, namely absolving all men singly from guilt and punishments under the appearance of piety, charity and mercy, under the title of full power first assumed by the Roman bishops for themselves, they have passed gradually and secretly from these meanings, as we showed in the twenty-third chapter of this book. At last they have taken this title in that sense and according to that meaning by which the fullness of power is understood by them as universal authority and supreme jurisdiction, or coercive principality, over all princes, peoples and temporal things. The passage and presumption of this, though improperly, took its beginning from metaphorical expositions, as we said in part five of the twenty-third chapter. It is, however, a sign hidden from no one that the Roman bishops, according to this sense, proclaim of themselves the fullness of power, that is, they wish the authority of supreme jurisdiction or coercive principality to belong to them over all princes, peoples and individual persons by this fullness of power. For in the narrative of their Decretals, in the seventh book, On sentence and res judicata, Pope Clement V, who is named as its compiler and who afterwards made it public, being the successor of the same man, revoking, so far as in him lay, a certain sentence of the lord Henry VII, Roman Emperor, and having prefaced it, as is their custom, with very many words of insult, dishonour and disrespect against the said Henry, both by word of mouth and in writing, brought forth this series: We, both by the superiority which there is no doubt we have over the empire, and by the power by which, when the empire is vacant, we succeed the Emperor, and likewise by the fullness of that power which Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, has granted to us, though unworthy, in the person of blessed Peter, declare, with the counsel of our brethren, that the aforesaid sentence and proceedings, and whatever has followed from them, or on account of them, were altogether void and empty. That their deceit may not hereafter lie hidden, I cry out vigorously, as a herald of the truth, and I say to you, kings, princes, peoples, tribes and all tongues, that by the Roman bishops, together with the company of their clergy or cardinals, the greatest prejudice is done to all of you by this writing of theirs, which, on every supposition of it, is most manifestly false. For they try to reduce you to their subjection, and if you allow it to remain, especially to have the force and strength of law. Note well that it follows of necessity that whoever has the first authority to revoke the sentence of any prince or judge has jurisdiction and coercive principality over him, and also the power to institute and depose his principality. But the Roman bishop ascribes this authority to himself over all the princes of the world and all principalities indifferently, since from that full power which he asserts Christ granted to him in the person of blessed Peter, he revoked the civil sentence of the aforesaid Henry. And from necessity it follows that this same power was granted to him no less over all the other kings and princes of the world than over the Roman prince, since Christ is and was and will be no less the king or lord of other kings and princes than of the king or prince of Rome. This their speech or writing also openly confirms, when they say or write King of kings and Lord of lords. For if their speech or writing had said singly that the fullness of power granted to them by Christ, the King and Lord, extends over the king or emperor of Rome, and so on, some exception of the other kings and kingdoms might in some way be understood from it. But now, since they have expressed the phrase in the plural, absolutely and indifferently, as it is written by the Evangelist, though not in the sense which the Roman bishops intend, no exception can be made from it of any king or prince, just as they themselves understand no one to be excepted, but every one included, as their predecessor Boniface VIII plainly stated, and as we have brought forward in the twentieth chapter of this book, part eight. Yet lest anyone be hostile to them because of their speech or writing: although the Evangelist spoke truly in naming Christ King of kings and Lord of lords, even if he had added of all creatures, they have spoken and written a false and manifest lie against the plain opinion of Christ and of the Apostles Peter, Paul and James. They have asserted that any power of principality or coercive jurisdiction, let alone full power, was delivered in the person of blessed Peter or of any other apostle to the Roman bishop or to any other bishop whatever. But such power is, was and will be forbidden by Christ to the Roman bishop and to all others in the person of any apostle, as we have indubitably shown by Scripture and by the authorities of the saints, in the fourth, fifth and ninth chapters of this book. In this new and hitherto always unheard-of fiction, the Roman bishop, no less falsely than rashly, against his own mind and that of almost all the faithful who share in this consideration, does not hesitate to declare openly, while he stubbornly asserts that there is no doubt that he has superiority over the Roman Emperor (which he means as coercive jurisdiction or principality), and likewise when the empire is vacant, that he succeeds the aforesaid Emperor. For by these words the unjust and unrighteous usurpation of imperial jurisdictions is plainly shown, which the Roman bishops have hitherto exercised, and at present exercise, as we have said, especially while the imperial see stands vacant. For who would be so shameless or so lacking in modesty as to put forward as an undoubted truth what has never been heard of in past ages, has been confirmed neither by divine nor human law nor by right reason, and whose opposite has always been conceived and declared in these ways, as a sign of truth believed by all? Hence, by a proportion to the proverb of physicians, that as he heals many in whom many trust, so we may truly say: he wishes to deceive and mislead many, to whom great credulity is given in these modern times.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXV.

units.la: Qualiter eisdem specialitas sit vsus Rom. Episcopus in principem & Romanum Imperium.
units.tr: How the Roman Bishops have used the same plenitude of power against the prince and the Roman Empire in particular.

units.la: IAM dicta quidem igitur plenitudine potestatis, & in deterius continuo secundum processum sic hactenus vsi sunt Romanorum Episcopi & vruntur, magis tamen aduersus principem & principatum Romanum. Quoniam in eum amplius hanc suam, sibi scilicet submittendi principatus, possunt exercere nequitiam, propter regnicolarum inuicem, & aduersus eorum principem per hos vocatos pastores, seu patres sanctissimos, suscitatam hactenus, & continuo suscitari atque nutriri discordiam. Et rursum, quoniam hoc principatu submisso ipsis, facile credunt, ad subiuganda reliqua regna patere ingressus, quamuis principi & principatui Romanorum ex susceptis beneficiis amplius & singulariter, vt notum est omnibus, obligentur. Verum ne vlli rem incognitam aut nostrae vocis egentem loquamur, cupiditate seu auaritia, superbia & ambitione percussi, ingratitudine peiores effecti quam mali, omnimode quaerunt prohibere Romani principis creationem, ipsiusque demum quaerentes soluere principatum, aut in aliam formam sibi subiectam amplius transferre tentantes, ne per iam dicti principis potestatem corrigantur, quos in imperium patrauerunt excessus, & inde meritas subeant disciplinas. Quod quamuis ea, quam diximus, intentione patenter obicem ponant vndecunq; principi supradicto: id tamen dolose praetendentes, se facere aiunt vt sponsa Christi, ecclesiae videlicet, iura defendant, quanquam sophistica pietas haec derisibilis sit. Quoniam temporalia vel eorum cupiditas, iurisdictionis aut principatus ambitio sponsa Christi non est, neq; hanc Christus sibi matrimonio copulauit, sed tanquam alienam repudiauit expresse, quemadmodum ex diuinis scripturis ostensum est quarto & quinto, 13. & 14. huius. Non est haec etiam Apostolorum hæreditas, quam suis veris non fictis successoribus reliquerunt, vt aperte dicit beatus Bernardus ad Eugenium Papam, de consideratione libro, & cap. quarto: Petrus hic est, inquit Bernardus, qui nec situr processisse aliquando vel gemmis ornatus vel serico: nec vt ditius auro, vel vectus equo alto, nec stipatus milite, nec circumstrepentibus septus ministris, absque hu tamen credidit satis posse adimplere salutare mandatum: Si amas me, pasce oves meas. In his (auro, vel gemmis & reliquis, temporalibus scilicet,) successisti non Petro, sed Constantino. Sic igitur propter temporalia contendendo, non vere defendunt sponsa Christi. Eam enim quae vere Christi sponsa est, catholicam fidem & fidelium multitudinem, non defendunt modérni Romanorum Pontifices, sed offendunt, illiusque pulchritudinem, vnitatem videlicet, non seruant, sed fœdant, dum zizania & schismata seminando, ipsius membra lacerant, & ab invicem separant, Christi quoque veras comites, paupertatem, & humilitatem, dum non admittunt, sed excludunt penitus, se sponsi ministros non ostendunt, sed potius inimicos. Hunc ergo principatum quaerentes subuertere Romanorum Episcopi, supponunt quod ex suis narrationibus pridem induximus, se diuino vel humano iure, aut utroque fortassis, superioritatem habere ad Romanum principem seu Imperatorem, siue creatum siue creandum, Imperialem quoque potestatem, siue iurisdictionem illis conuenire, vacante imperio. Quae tamen suppositiones apertissime sunt falsae, & nullo iure diuino vel humano, aut recta ratione firmatae, sed oppositum per demonstrationem ostensum est 12. prima, quarto, quinto, & nono huius, per scripturam amplius confirmatum. Fuit autem cum aliis iam dictis harum suppositionum, imo verius praesumptionum occasio, superflua dicam deuotio quaedam: Voluerunt enim Romanorum principum quidam citra tempora Constantini, electionem de se factam amicabiliter signare Romanis Pontificibus, vt in eorum persona Christo singularem reverentiam exhibentes, ab eo per Pontificum intercessionem ampliorem benedictionem & gratiam ad suum gubernandum imperium obtinerent: eodemque aut consimili quasi modo, propter suae intronizationis solennitatem & signum, & ampliorem Dei gratiam obtinendam, Romanorum quidam Imperatores, diadema regium imponi sibi fecerunt per Romanos Pontifices: quam siquidem impositionem Pontifici Romano plus auctoritatis tribuere super Romanum principem, quam Remensi archiepiscopo super regem Francorum, quis dicet? Non enim conferunt huiusmodi solennitates auctoritatem, sed habitam vel collatam significant. Ex hac quidem igitur reverentia sic sponte per Romanos principes exhibita, quae rentes saepius quae sua non sunt, Episcopi Rom. induxerunt consuetudinem, & abusum verius pro prior principum simplicitatem, non modo dicam ignauiam, laudationem electae personae ac benedictionem, quam super illam mittebant vocaliter aut in scriptis vocare confirmationem electionis praedictae. Nec attendentibus olim Romanis principibus, quae sub hac appellationis figura praeiudicialis latebat intentio, sic ipsam successiue subinduxerunt: latenter, nunc vero patenter Rom. Pontifices, vt nullus quantumcunque conuenienter electus in Romanorum regem, Rex vocari debeat, neque regi Romanorum auctoritatem habeat aut exerceat, nisi per Romanum Episcopum fuerit approbatus. Quae siquidem approbatio in Episcopi Romani solius mera voluntate consistit, vt dicit, quoniam in terris superiorem neminem aut aequalem in tali iudicio recognoscit, neque suorum fratrum, quos Cardinales appellant, consilium in hoc aut aliis, quamuis eo vtatur imitari tenetur, sed oppositum agere se posse in quibuscunque, si voluerit de suae plenitudine potestatis. Verum in hoc secundum suum morem falsum ex veris, & malum ex bonis concludit Romanus Episcopus, non enim ex hacilli per Romanum principem propter deuotionem sponte impensa reuerentia, significando sibi suam electionem, & ipsius postulando benedictionem, & apud Deum intercessionem, sequitur electionem Rom. principis ab ipsius voluntate pendere. Non nesciet hoc aliud quam Romanum soluere principatum, & principis creationem perpetuo phibere. Nam si electi regis auctoritas penderet a solius Ro. episcopi voluntate inane penitus est officium eligentium quoniam per ipsos electus, neque rex est, neque rex vocari debeat antequam per suam voluntatem siue auctoritatem, quod vocat sedem apostolicam, confirmetur, neque regalem auctoritatem aliquam sic electus exercere potest, quinimo neque nedum pati, verum etiam audire onerosum est valde, nemini licebit electo ex puentib. imperii absque huius episcopi licentia, quotidianos sibi sumere sumptus. Quid ergo aliud sibi tribuit auctoritatis principum electio quam nominationem, ex quo ipsorum determinatio ab vnius solius alterius voluntate dependet? Tantam n. septem tonsores aut lippi possent Romano regi auctoritatem tribuere. Ne tamen hoc in contemptum ipsorum, sed ipsos auctoritate sibi debita priuare volentis irrisionem dixerimus. Ignorat n. ipsi, quod sit electionis virtus & ratio, & propter quid in valentiore parte debentium eligere, consistat potestas ipsius. Et quoniam eius effectus ab alicuius vnius voluntate solius dependere non debet nec potest, si fuerit rationabiliter instituta, sed a solo legislatore, super quem principans debet institui: vel ab his tantum modo, quibus idem legislator talem auctoritatem concesserit, quemadmodum certificatum est per demonstrationem 12. & 13. prima. Sic igitur Romanus Episcopus palam destruere vult officium electorum, quamuis ipsos miranda versutia excaecare ac circumuenire nitatur. Inquit n. suis quibusdam sermonib. atque scripturis, quod nullus electus in Romanorum regem, rex est, nec rex vocari debet ante confirmationem, cuius auctoritatem ad suam libertatem potestatem pertinere asserit, (& electorum etiam institutionem ad eandem non minus intelligit pertinere:) Quoniam imperium a Graecis in personam magni Caroli translatum in Germanos, vt asserit idem Episcopus. In aliis vero quibusdam edictis pronunciando, quendam per ipsos electum a Christo & a sua sede priuatum esse omni auctoritate, quam electores illi tribuere potuerunt, subdole subdit: Ac per hoc nullum volumus electoribus, seu ipsorum officio praiudicium generari, manifeste tamen illis praeiudicando, quinimo verius ipsorum penitus officium annullando, dum praedixit per ipsorum electionem nemini regalem Romanorum auctoritatem conferri. Et dum per ipsos electum absque ipsorum consensu & determinatione priuat electionis iure per ipsos impensio. Sicq; ipsis illudens, non aliter praeiudicat, quam eruens alterius oculum, id patienti noceat, quamuis sic agens dicat se illi nocere non velle. Est rursum, hanc sibi Romani regis electi confirmationem ascribere, acabsq; ipsa, regem non esse quenquam, nec regem vocari debere, neq; regalia ministrare, nil aliud quam dicti principis creationem & promotionem perpetuo prohibere vel iam dictum principatum in Rom. episcopi totalem redigere seruitutem. Quoniam Rom. episcopus neminem electum Romanorum regem, si non voluerit approbabit aut confirmabit, cum se omnib. superiorem asserat, & in hoc nulli subesse collegio vel singulari personae: volet autem neminem semper, eo q; ab electo rege certa pacta & iuramenta, priusquam approbet, exigere vult, & inter caetera iuramentum, quo Ro. Imperator se illi episcopo asserat & exprimat fidelitate seu temporali siue coactiua iurisdictione subiectum, & quarundam pluinciarum occupationes illicitas & iniustas conseruari vult sibi per dictum electum, idq; promitti, & ipsius electi iuramento firmati. Quae siquidem illicita pacta & iuramenta, nec salua conscientia regiae Majestatis, & licito iuramento praestito in sui creatione, ad libertates imperij conseruandas fieri possibilia, neq; facta teneri, nullus unquam electus, nisi mulier mollior, & manifeste talia iurando vel promittendo periurus, Romano vel alteri cuiquam praestabit Pontifici, propter quod electorum regum nullum unquam in regem Rom. creabitur, aut vocem imperii merebitur, si ab Episcopo Romano regalis seu imperialis auctoritas electorum pendeat, quam diu enim dictas Episcopus, quamuis hoc iniquissime agens, & quae sua non sunt, quaerens, ipsos poterit impedire ac prohibere, impediet tam opere quam sermone.
units.tr: Thus far the Roman Bishops have used and still use the plenitude of power in the way already described, and it has grown steadily worse. They have used it most of all against the prince and the principate of Rome. In that realm they can exercise their wickedness more freely, by stirring up and constantly fostering, as they have done until now, discord among the subjects of the realm and against their prince, through those whom they call pastors or most holy fathers. Again, once that principate is made subject to them, they easily believe that the way lies open for subduing the remaining kingdoms, although the Roman prince and principate have, as everyone knows, laid upon them the most particular and singular obligations for the benefits they have received. But so that we may not speak of a matter unknown to anyone or in need of our voice, struck by greed, avarice, pride and ambition, and made worse than wicked by ingratitude, they seek in every way to prevent the creation of the Roman prince. Some of them, seeking to dissolve the principate itself or trying to transfer it into another form subject to themselves, do so so that the prince already mentioned may not correct the excesses they have committed against the empire and so suffer the discipline they deserve. Although they openly place this obstacle before the aforesaid prince, in every quarter, for the purpose we have described, they pretend deceitfully that they do so as defenders of the rights of the Bride of Christ, namely the Church, though this sophistical piety is laughable. For temporal things, or the greed for them, and the ambition for jurisdiction or principate, are not the Bride of Christ. Christ did not join this bride to himself in marriage, but expressly rejected her as a stranger, as has been shown from the divine Scriptures in the fourth and fifth chapters and in 13 and 14 of this work. Nor is this the inheritance of the Apostles, which they left to their true, not feigned, successors, as the blessed Bernard clearly says to Pope Eugenius in his book On Consideration, chapter four: "Here is Peter," says Bernard, "who never went forth adorned with jewels or silk, nor richer in gold, nor carried on a high horse, nor surrounded by soldiers, nor hemmed in by ministers making a noise about him; yet he believed without these things that he could fulfil the saving command: 'If you love me, feed my sheep.'" You have succeeded, in these things (gold, jewels and the rest, that is, temporal things), not to Peter but to Constantine. Thus, by contending for temporal things, they do not truly defend the Bride of Christ. For the modern Roman Pontiffs do not defend her who is truly the Bride of Christ, the catholic faith and the multitude of the faithful; rather they offend her. They do not preserve her beauty, namely unity, but defile it, while by sowing tares and schisms they tear her members and separate them from one another. They also do not admit, but completely exclude, the true companions of Christ, poverty and humility; so they show themselves not ministers of the Bridegroom but rather his enemies. The Roman Bishops, then, who seek to overthrow this principate, assume, as we earlier argued from their own accounts, that by divine or human right, or perhaps by both, they have superiority over the Roman prince or Emperor, whether already created or yet to be created, and that imperial power or jurisdiction belongs to them while the empire is vacant. Yet these assumptions are most manifestly false, and are confirmed by no divine or human right or sound reason. The opposite has been shown by demonstration in the twelfth chapter of the first part, and in the fourth, fifth and ninth chapters of this work, and has been further confirmed from Scripture. Moreover, along with the other assumptions already mentioned, there was, I would rather call it, a presumption, the occasion of a certain superfluous devotion. For some Roman princes, before the time of Constantine, wished to signify to the Roman Pontiffs, in a friendly way, the election made of themselves, so that by showing singular reverence to Christ in the person of the Pontiffs, they might obtain through the Pontiffs' intercession a fuller blessing and grace from him for governing their empire. In the same or a similar way, some Roman Emperors, for the solemnity and sign of their enthronement and for obtaining a fuller grace of God, had the royal diadem placed upon them by the Roman Pontiffs. Who would say that this imposition gives the Roman Pontiff more authority over the Roman prince than the Archbishop of Reims has over the king of the Franks? Such solemnities do not confer authority, but signify that it has been held or conferred. From this reverence, freely shown by the Roman princes, who were often giving what was not their own, the Roman Bishops introduced a custom, and an abuse rather, of taking advantage of the simplicity, I will not say the indolence, of the earlier princes: that is, the praise and blessing of the chosen person, which they sent over him by voice or in writing, they called the confirmation of the aforesaid election. Since the earlier Roman princes did not notice what prejudicial intent lay hidden under this figure of speech, the Roman Pontiffs gradually introduced it, at first secretly, but now openly, so that no one, however lawfully elected as king of the Romans, should be called king, nor have or exercise royal authority, unless he has been approved by the Roman Bishop. This approval rests, so he says, solely on the mere will of the Roman Bishop, since he acknowledges no superior or equal on earth in such a judgment, and is not bound to follow the counsel of his brethren, whom they call Cardinals, in this matter or in others, though he may use it; he claims he may act otherwise in any matter, if he wishes, by the fullness of his power. But in this, according to his custom, the Roman Bishop infers falsehood from truth and evil from good. For it does not follow from that reverence freely offered by the Roman prince out of devotion, signifying to him his election and asking his blessing and his intercession with God, that the election of the Roman prince depends on the Bishop's will. This would be nothing else than dissolving the principate and forbidding the creation of the prince forever. For if the authority of the elected king depended on the will of the Roman Bishop alone, the office of the electors would be utterly empty, since the one elected by them is neither king, nor ought he to be called king, before he is confirmed by the will or authority of him whom they call the apostolic see. Nor can the elected man exercise any royal authority; indeed, it is very burdensome even to suffer, or to hear, that no one of the electors of the empire may take daily expenses for himself without the Bishop's permission. What authority, then, does the election of princes grant them, other than a nomination, if their determination depends on the will of one other person alone? Seven barbers or men with sore eyes could grant royal authority to the Roman king in this way. Yet I would not say this in contempt of the electors, or to mock them, as one who wishes to deprive them of the authority due to them. For he does not know what the force and reason of election is, and on what its power rests, namely in the more powerful part of those entitled to elect. Since its effect ought not, and cannot, depend on the will of any one person alone, if it has been rationally instituted, but only on the lawgiver, over whom the ruler ought to be established, or on those alone to whom that same lawgiver has granted such authority, as has been established by demonstration in the twelfth and thirteenth chapters of the first part. Thus the Roman Bishop openly wishes to destroy the office of the electors, although he strives to blind and circumvent them with remarkable cunning. For in certain sermons and writings he says that no one elected as king of the Romans is king, nor ought to be called king, before confirmation, whose authority he asserts belongs to his own liberty and power; and he understands the institution of the electors to pertain to the same authority no less. He says that the empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Germans in the person of Charlemagne, as the same Bishop asserts. In certain other edicts he declares that a certain man elected by them has been deprived by Christ and by his see of all the authority which those electors could have conferred, and he slyly adds: "And therefore we do not wish any prejudice to be brought upon the electors or their office," while clearly prejudicing them, or rather utterly annulling their office, since he has said that "no royal authority of the Romans is conferred by their election." And in depriving the man elected by them, without their consent and determination, of the right of election that belongs to them, he mocks them. Thus, in mocking them, he prejudices them no less than one who, plucking out another's eye, says he does not wish to harm the one who suffers it, although he claims to act without such intent. Again, to ascribe to himself this confirmation of the elected Roman king, and to hold that without it no one is king, nor ought to be called king, nor should administer royal functions, is nothing other than forbidding forever the creation and promotion of the said prince, or reducing the principate itself to total servitude under the Roman Bishop. For the Roman Bishop will approve or confirm no one elected as king of the Romans if he does not wish to, since he claims to be superior to all and subject to no college or single person in this matter. He will also always want to exact from the elected king certain pacts and oaths before he approves him. Among the other oaths is one by which the Roman Emperor declares and acknowledges himself subject to that Bishop in temporal, or even coercive, jurisdiction, and he wishes certain illicit and unjust occupations of provinces to be preserved for him by the said elected man, and this promised and confirmed by the oath of the same elected man. Such illicit pacts and oaths can be made neither consistently with the conscience of the royal Majesty, nor with the lawful oath taken at his creation, which required the preservation of the liberties of the empire; nor is any elected man, unless he is a softer woman, and one who manifestly perjures himself by swearing or promising such things, going to render them to the Roman Pontiff or to anyone else. For this reason none of the electors' kings will ever be created king of the Romans, nor will he deserve the title of empire, if royal or imperial authority depends on the electors while the Roman Bishop is able to hinder and prohibit them. For as long as this Bishop, acting most unjustly and seeking what is not his own, is able to hinder and prohibit them, he will hinder them by deed as well as by word.

units.la: His autem grauius praeiudicium & importabile nocumentum assequitur cunctos principes, communitates, & singulos Romano subiectos imperio. Cum n. vacante eodem, asserat iam dict. Episcopus se in officio succedere Imperatori praedicto, per necessitatem sequitur, ad ipsi autoritate pertinere, iuramenta fidelitatis a cunctis principib. & foedatariis imperialib. reliquis exigendi, ipsosq; compellendi ad praestandum iuramenta praedicta: necnon ab eisdem petendi tributa & reliqua seruitia, per eosdem Romanis principib. fieri consueta, cum hisdem q; ultra consuetudinem sibi debita fingere voluerit iam dictus Episcopus, de sua, quam de se praedicat, plenitudine potestatis. Collationem quoq; principatuum, foedorum & aliorum iurium, quae propter defectum masculorum haeredum aut alia quauis ratione vel causa princeps Romanus conferre potest ad auctoritatem huius episcopi, vacante imperio, similiter pertinere. Ampli horum praeiudicialissimum & summe molestum, quod vacante imperio, iuxta Rom. episcoporum potentiam & solicitudinem, ut diximus, in perpetuum vacaturo: contendentes inuicem ciuiliter principes, collegia, communitates, & singulares personae, imperio Romano subiectae, per interpositas appellationes aut de ipsis ad curiam Romani Episcopi delatis querelis, tam realib. quam personalib. iam dicti episcopi per ipsius citationes adire curiam & subire ciuile iudicium compellentur. Nullam quoq; sententiam poterit princeps, communitas aut iudex Romano subiectus imperio, executioni mandare ad Ro. curiam ab ipsorum sententiis ciuilib. appellationes semper interponentib. condemnatis. Nolentes autem imperio Romano subiecti, iam dicto Episcopo parere aut in praedictis subesse, quemadmodum nec tenerentur, per anathematum seu blasphemiarum, excommunicationum, haeresum, interdictorum, & demum temporalium priuationis seu amissionis vocatas sententias, eiusmodi temporalia publicando, & concedendo quomodocunq; potentib. rapere, ipsosq; persequentib. cum sibi subditis & adhaerentibus, qualitercunq; etiam occidentib. cuiuslibet culpae aut poenae veniam, inanem quamuis, atq; fallacem concedendo, subditos eorum a iuramentis sibi praestitis aut praestandis, haeretice quamq; absoluendo, incessanter & omni suo maligno ac proteruo natu, saepe dictus Episcopus persequitur. Quod si dixerit Rom. Episcopus more solito, curam plebis & pietatem praetendens, eo pertinere ad se Romani principis electionem confirmare, siue probare, ne fortassis ad imperialem apicem haereticus scandere valeat, communitati fidelium inde quam plurimum nociturus. Illi respondendum utiq; conuenienter, propter quod talis electio sui probatione non eget, cum eadem celebretur & fiat p tres solennes Archiepiscopos Christianos, quorum quilibet aequale a Christo suscepit auctoritatem episcopalem seu sacerdotalem Rom. Pontifici, quemadmodum ostensum est 15. & 16. huius. Et rursum per quatuor fideles principes seculares, cum quib. una conuenientib. praedictis religiosis pastoribus, siue praelatis, electio praedicti Ro. principis consumatur. Hos autem septem non est verisimile sic errare, aut intentione peruersa moueri, sicut solius Ro. Episcopi voluntatem, qui suo inniti soli iudicio sibi credit de iure licere, per ea, q; sibi ascribit incongrue, plenitudine potestatis. Sicn. quencunq; p voto posset haereticum iudicare, ac electionis iure priuare, unde principum diligentium officium redderetur nullum, & electi creatio atque promotio prohibita semper, propter causas praedictas. Esto tamen secundum aduersantem Romanum principem ante vel post sui electionem in haereticam incidisse, aut incidere labem, idq; latuisse vel sciuisse principes electores, dicendum, nequaquam propterea iudicium aut correptionem ipsius, ad solum Romanum Episcopum pertinere. Nec rursum erit autoritas haec illius solius Episcopi, aut cum solo suorum clericorum coetu vel synodo, sed concilii generalis, eorum qui sub imperiali regimine continentur, propter iam dictas causas & alias assignatas 21. huius. Nam & cardinales ipsi praedictae vsurpationi plerunq; consenconsenserunt, consentiunt, atq; participant, propter quod insecurum est, electionem hanc, talium subesse iudicio. Amplius quaetendum, cur etiam non aliorum regum sufficientias personarum suo dictoiudicio & approbationis potestati subesse, pro quibus spondeo, sic ipsos intendere, quamuis hoc nondum audeant attentare, sed eius sibi congruum tempus observent, de quo etiam fortassis aliquid dicturi sumus. Ex dictis itaq; suppositionibus falsis viam erroris & iniquitatis ingredians, iam omnium novissime modernus quidam, vocatus Papa Romanus, totis suis studiis & nisibus impedit & prohibet inclyti Ludovici, ex Bavariae Ducibus Romanorum regis assumpti, processum ad possessionem quietam apicis imperatoriae dignitatis. Interimit enim & merito dictus Ludovic⁹ tam verbo quam facto, suppositiones Episcopi supradicti.
