Nam quamuis nondum per illius verba vel scripta, confirmatus aut approbatus extitit, sicut pridem evidenter ostendimus, nec indiget confirmatione ab electionis de se factae & publicatae per electores tempore citra se regem Romanorum continuo, sicut secundum veritatem fuit, & est, scribi ac nominari facit, ac fecit. Imperialia quoque sive regalia quaeque, quod etiam de iure tenetur, & potest, in omnibus administrat. Unde adversus ipsum, quamuis tamen per ipsum, seu praedecessores ipsius, calefactus coluber in suis praedecessoribus, iuxta Esopi attendendam, & huic proposito conuenientem apologum, ex quanta paupertate, deiectione, oppressione, opprobriis, ac persecutione, per Romanos principes, ad temporalium abundantiam, throni sublimitatem, & honorem, potestatem, & tranquillitatem releuat, non velut habens apostolorum, sed tanquam ingratus & immemor, Romanus hic vocat episcopi se erexit. Primum quidem suo peruerso & solito more in dictum principem expuens, verba ignominiae ac irreuerentiae quam plurima protulit, hoc tamen sub melle venenum porrigens, speciem pietatis secundum suam consuetam praetendit fallaciam, dum inquit in suis quibusdam epistolis, quas vocat edita, (e talia scribere vel proferre, ut dictum Ludovicum ab erroris deuio, ad callem sive semitam veritatis & salutis reducat. seipsum qui loquitur, quid loquitur, & cui loquitur non attendens. Ad quem tanquam deuium ab omni tramite veritatis & cuiuslibet aequitatis exortem, conuenienter & cum veritate verissime dici potest illud Matthaei 7. & Lucae 8. Quid autem vides festucam in oculo fratris tui, & trabem in oculo tuo non vides? aut quo modo dicis fratri tuo, frater sine eiciam festucam de oculo tuo, & trabs est in oculo tuo? Hypocrita eiice primum trabem de oculo tuo, & tunc videbis eiicere festucam de oculo fratris tui. Non est arbor bona quae facit fructus malos, neque arbor mala faciens fructum bonum, una quaeque arbor de fructu suo cognoscitur. Quid igitur hypocrita hic, arbor pessima, fructus omnis malitiae, ac seditionis, & discordiae portans ubique, ut sensatum est omnibus, virum virtutum, insontem, catholicum, & probatum suis ignominiae verbis sub falsa pietatis & charitatis specie nititur diffamare. Eiiciat n. primo a sui mente caliginosa & quasi caeca trabem, summam scil. ignorantiam & errorem, & a sui affectione peruersa, quasi obstinata & indurata, malitia & furorem: tuncq; aliorum minutias peccatorum cernere valebit, & per suas exhortationes & monitiones poterit aptius & conuenientius expurgare. Deinde vero, qui non correptionem hominis, sed mortem ciuilem his sermonibus dolosis & fictis intendit, in supradictum principem Christianissimum, venena quae credidit illi mortifera ciuilis vitae, supradictus episcopus effudit & sparsit, dum ipsum cum sibi singulariter adhaerentibus excommunicauit, & communitatibus fidelium, eidem tanquam regi Rom. praestantib. aut praestituris auxilium, consilium aut fauorem, diuinorum officiorum exercitium interdixit: parum aut nihil attendens, quod monet Ambrosius in libro, qui de sacerdotali dignitate intitulatur. Tractans enim illud primae ad Timotheum tertio: Si quis episcopatum desiderat, inter caetera 8. dicti libri capitulo inquit: Non litigiosum, id est non linguam ad conuicium relaxet Episcopus, ne per eandem linguam, per quam laudes referet Deo, & diuina libat officia, litium venena proferat. Quia non decet de ore Episcopi benedictionem simul & maledictionem egredi, ne per eandem linguam qua Deus laudatur, homo maledicatur, quia non potest de uno fonte dulcem & amaram producere aquam. Demum vero suae malitiae aculeum, quem in nocumentum & exterminatione credit extremum, foras emittet fortassis, in praedictum principem figere credens, blasphemiam videl. suam quandam, ab ipso vocatam sententiam, licet re vera supremam dementiam, qua supradictum principem cum adhaerentibus, aut obedientibus, & fauentibus sibi omnibus tanquam regi, pronunciauit haereticos & ecclesiae inimicos sive rebelles, suorumq; temporalium omnium, mobilium & immobilium iure priuauit, ea quidem per iam dicta sententiam indigne vocata, publicando, ipsa quoq; occupare volentib. & occupantib. concedendo, & hoc licite fieri posse, per suas voces atq; membranas inscriptas, per se vel pseudo quosdam praedicatores alios, in omnibus prouinciis nunciando, Ipsosq; rursum morte damnando, & occidentib. aut inuadentibus, culparum atq; poenarum omnium conuitiorum criminum, veniam concedendo. Et si viui capiantur vbicunq; fuerint, in seruitutem capientium redigendo. Amplius officia ecclesiastica maiora, ut episcopatus, archiepiscopatus, atq; patriarchatus, mediocria & minora concedit, ecclesiastica quoq; temporalia, beneficia iam vocata, thesauros, atq; pecunias effundit, ut aduersus dictum principem in inuidiam atq; rebellionem, & guerram atq; discordiam concitet vniuersos, cum tamen supradictorum cuiusquam ad hui9 episcopi auctoritatem nulla pertineat proferre sententiam, ut 4.5.6.7.8.&10.ac20.huius euidenter ostendimus. Praeter has autem malignitates horrendas nonum genus exercet nequitiae, quod manifeste videtur haereticam sapere labem. Concitat n. aduersus iam dictu catholicum principe in rebellionem eius subditos atq; fideles, per sua qdam dicta vel scripta diabolica, q tamen apostolica vocat, ipsos absoluendo a iuramentis fidelitatis, quib. saepe dicto principi fuerant & sunt secundum veritatem astricti. Talesq; absolutiones vbiq; diuulgat prædicat per quosdam ministros facinorum, ex tali exercitio sperantes, per iam dictum episcopum, ad ecclesiastica officia & beneficia promoveri. Hoc siquidem non op° apostolicum, sed diabolicum esse extat: quoniam secundum hoc & ex hoc episcop° iste cum omnib. sibi complicib. ordinatorib. consensorib. & executorib. sermone, scriptura, vel opere, cœci existentes cupiditate, avaritia, superbia, cum ambitione, summaq;, vt omnib. constat, iniquitate repleti, ducatum præbent sibi credentib. & assequentib. opere, in omnib. supradictis ipsorum sermonib. atq; scripturis ad casum & præcipitationem in foveam mortalium peccatorum. Primum quidem in periurium manifestum, deinde vero in proditionem & iustitiam omnib. inoccultam, consequenter autem in rapinam, homicidium, & omnia quasi scelerum genera incidere faciunt, in quib. morientes nec pœnitentes, perhunc sanctissimum patrem, & illi° seducti ministros, nec propter ipsorum crassam fuisse ignorantiam excusabiles apud Deum, præcipitantur & submerguntur in gehennam ignis, foveam videl. perpetuo damnatorum. Nam certum est & esse debet vnicuique rationem habenti, & ea vti potenti, neque Romanum Episcopum aut alium sacerdotem ab huiusmodi & quouis alio licito iuramento præstito siue promisso quenquam absq; causa rationabili absoluere posse. Nunc autem vnicuiq; constat, qui proprie conscientiæ stare voluerit, & quem sinistra non perturbat affectio, causam quam Romanus prætendit episcopus aduersus pium principem Ludovicum, & alium quemcunque in casu consimili, rationabilem minime fore, sed iniquam, præcipitem & iniustam. Vnde ducatus siue doctrina & exhortatio huius Episcopi & sibi ministrantium in talib° cauendus est, & omnino spernendus tanquam is qui ad æternum animarum perducit interitum. Sanæ n. doctrinæ ac verbis & sententiæ Apostoli ad Romanos 13. ad Ephesios sexto, prima ad Timotheum sexto, 2. ad Titum 2. & 3. repugnat palam. Aperte namque vbi supra, præcipit Apostolus, subditos obedire debere dominis suis carnalibus, non tantum bonis & modestis, sed etiam discolis, vt beatus Petrus dicit prima canonica sua, secundo capitulo. Quanto igitur magis cum fuerint illis per iuramentum astricti? quod etiam Glossæ secundum sanctos ibidem amplius explicant, manifeste dicentes, quod dominis etiam infidelibus & quantumcunque malis obedire tenentur & debent subiecti. Hoc sane tamen intelligendo, in quibus obedientia non repugnet sermone vel opere legi diuinæ. Indubium autem est, sermones & opera, quibus Romanus Episcopus aduersus Romanum principem inuehitur & procedit, nec diuinæ legis fore mandata, neq; illi consona, sed dissona potius & repugnantia manifeste, quemadmodum per scripturam monstratum est, capitulo quarto, quinto, & nono huius. Hæc rursum docenti seu prædicanti Romano aut alteri cuiuis Episcopo credere vel obtemperare, nihil aliud est quam omnium principatuum radicem succidi sinere, vinculum & nexum cuiuscunq; ciuilitatis & regni dissolui. Non n. radicem & nexum huiusmodi arbitror alium, nisi mutuum iuramentum & fidem subditorum & principum. Hæc enim, fides scil. vt inquit Tullius de officiis, libro primo, Omnis est fundamentum iustitiæ, quam inter principantes & subditos soluere nitens, nil minus sibi quærere tentat, quam pro sui libito principatuum omnium potestatem euertere posse, & hinc eos in suam redigere seruitutem. Et hoc etiam ciuiliter viuentium omnium pacem seu tranquillitatem turbare, ac inde præsentis seculi sufficienti vita priuate, denumq;, vt iam diximus, sic animo dispositos finaliter perducere ad æternam perniciem animarum: Propter quod huius Episcopi & suorum complicum peius quam Pharisæorum veniæ promissionem inanem, perniciosam & insanam doctrinam, quinimo seductionem animarum verius dicam, omnes Christiani contemnant & caveant, attendentes Christum id° consulentem aut præcipientem, Matthei 15. dum ad vniuersos fideles, in Apostolorum persona tamen, ait: Sinite illos, id est, Pharisæos, qui tunc Mosaicæ legis doctores putabantur: erroneæ tamen sentientes in ea, & Christo aduersantes quasi continuo. Per quos siquidem significabantur & intelligebantur omnes sophistici & falsi doctores sacræ scripturæ, quales sunt hi persecutores Romani principis & aliorum innocentum vere fidelium, in quorum persona etiam hi nequam Christum persequuntur, & illi aduersantur. Subdit autem causam Christus, quare hos falsos doctores spernere debemus, dum inquit, cœci sunt, & duces cœcorum: cæcus autem si cæco ducatum præstet, ambo in foveam cadunt. Sic igitur iuxta præceptum dominicum sinendi & sper- nendi sunt hi falsi doctores, tanquam cœci cupiditate, avaritia, superbia, & ambitione, cœcorum, anarorum scilicet, ac superborum & rebellium duces. Qui etiam non attendentes aut attendere non volentes præceptum apostolicum, quinimo diuinum, sine metaphora, dicentis aperte ad Romanos decimo tertio: Omnis anima subdita sit potestatibus sublimioribus, docent & prædicant subditos aduersus ipsorum principes esse rebelles. Tales enim sicrebelles & alios ad rebellionem suis dolosis & iniquis persuasionibus inducentes, ordinationi Dei resistunt. Nam Apostolus vbi supra, qui potestati, id est, secularitec principanti, resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. de quibus prophetauit idem primæ ad Timoth. quarto, & eundem secundo, tertio, dum dixit: Hoc scito, quod in nouissimis diebus instabunt tempora periculosa. Et erunt homines seipsos amantes, cupidi, elati, superbi, blasphemi, parentibus non obedientes, sub parentibus principes comprehendens, unde Tullius de officiis, libro primo: Principes sunt patria, sunt parentes, quorum maximis beneficiis obligamur. Parentibus ergo siue principibus non obedientes, ingrati, scelesti, infideles, pactum non custodientes, sine affectione, (supple bona,) sine pace, criminatores, incontinentes, immites, sine benignitate, proditores, precaces, proterui, tumidi, voluptatum amatores magis quam Dei, habentes quidem speciem pietatis, (id est, apparentes agere quæ faciunt, propter cultum Dei, reuerentiam, & amorem,) virtutem autem eius, (scilicet talis pietatis,) abnegantes. Quod de facile omnibus cognoscere est ab ipsorum operib. iuxta illud Matthæi septimo: Attendite vobis, te vobis, inquit, a falsis Prophetis, qui veniunt ad vos in vestimentis ouium, intrinsecus autem sunt lupi rapaces, a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos. Et subdit Apostolus conformiter Christi consilio vel praecepto praemisso: Et hos deuita, id est, his noli credere, neque in talibus obedire. Sed proh dolor, quod propter hanc speciem pietatis, in tantum homines seduxerunt, vt iam violenta freti potentia, quam sub specie pietatis obtinuerunt gratis in parte, plurimum vero latenter vsurpauerunt, & nunc patenter atq; violenter vsurpant, denuitari non possunt, violentiam Christi fidelib. inferentes. Qui et ingrati, superbi, sine pace, ac inuites, & reuera quales eos per omnia descripsit Apostolus, Ponentes bonum malum, & lucem tenebras, secundum illud Esaiae 5. Ecclesiasticorum officiorum, maiorum, mediocrium, & minorum, collatione, ac temporalium seu beneficiorum, tam rerum mobilium, q; immobilium; ac decimarum, q; propter bonum finem statuta fuerunt, exhibitione, promissione, ac horum pri' interueniente conuentione nephanda: concitant aduersus fideles principes sibi subditos, & affines etiam nō subiectos. Quod quamuis cum sibi coplicib. nec solum aduersus Rom. principem facere videantur, illius tamen exemplo, qui Rom. Episcopo, & ipsius Ecclesiae, in tantum beneficus extitit, caeteri principes discant, eadem sibi probabiliter contingere posse, & aduersus eosdem, eadem satagare praedictum Episcopum, sine affectione bona in quemlibet existentem, dum se illi huius insultus facultas offeret. Asserens n. ipse, tam suis sermonib. quam scripturis pridem inductis, propter suae, quam sibi, quamuis inconuenienter ascribit plenitudinem potestatis, omnes principes & populos suo principatui siue iurisdictioni coactiuae subiectos. Hoc etiam ad effectum perducere cupiens & anhelans, obseruat tempora quib. principum fidelium inuicem aut populorum inuicem schismata & contentiones, aut subditorum aduersus ipsorum dominos rebelliones appareant, quas etiam nonnunquam concitari procurat, vt sic altera dissidentium inuicem partium, debilior vel aduersanti resistere nequiens suum cogatur implorare subsidium & subire dominium. Quamuis n. sub ficta specie pietatis ac misericordiae videatur impotentes, iniq; fortassis oppressos, aliquando protegere, illisq; fauorem secularem impendere, non tamen hunc praestat, nisi prius ipsi constituerit sui fauoris egentes, eumq; requirentes, suum subituros principatum seu seculare dominium: Sperans inde demum per mutuam oppressionem & inuidiam, vtrunq; sic aduersantium ipsius potestatem cogi subire, propter q; cauendae sunt contentiones & actiones, quae suorum fauorum cuiquam necessitatem inducant, quoniam tandem conuertuntur in libertatis perniciem & eos suscipientium seruitutem. Secundum hunc igitur modum per regna mundi successiue reperit episcopus hic, vt omnes tandem, quos incessanter ardet, principatus sibi subiicere valeat. In omnib. nanq; vel plurib. simul inault huiusmodi tentare processus, sed paulatim sibi tantum expectat seculatem subcreuisse potentiam, vt reliquorum residuam videat & posse credat absq; sui discrimine superare. Tunc n. fiducialiter aperiret super reliqua regna, sensum praesumpti a se rituli plenitudinis potestatis. Et quemadmodum eum qui Romanorum, sic reliquos principatus explicite proferret suo dominio seu coactiuae iurisdictioni fore subiectos, sibiq; subiici, quanquam licite recusantes per blasphemias & cosimiles iam praemissis sententias in Rom. principem & sibi fideles, p violentam quoq; siue armata vsq; ad attritionem & exterminium persequeretur potentiam. His igitur modis & viis iam dict' episcopus cum sibi complicib. quasi omnes Italiae principatus, communitates & populos in contentionem ac schisma seduxit, idemque in Alamania iam facere coepit, & continuo perficere studet. Quosdam n. subditorum, pditores & sceleratos, fauoribus secularib. vt officiorum ecclesiasticorum collationib. decimarum & pecuniarum exhibitione in rebellionem aduersus Ro. principem concitauit, & indesinenter quoscunq; potest maiores, medios, & minores concitare, procurat, eosq; q sic per ipsum seducti fuerint, & eidem obtemperauerint, ecclesiae filios & vere fideles appellat & vocat: qui vero in debita fidelitate suo principi obedientes persistunt, & persistere volunt, schismaticos & haereticos nominat; & tanq; ecclesiae inimicos persequitur, blasphemando, quantum in ipso est, diffamando, excommunicando, & per sententiam secularem personas atq; realiter condemnando, cu tamen nullum tale iudicium illi taliter debeatur, inquantum huiusmodi diuina vel humana lege, vt ex praecedentibus patet, & rememoratum est prius. Est autem, de quo pridem aliquid diximus, omnium nequissimum & grauissimum nocumentum generaliter inferens, nec taceri potest a lege charitatis excidere non volenti, q videl. Romanus exercens episcopus, omnes Christi ones, quas ad pascendum salutari doctrina sibi dicit fore comissas, aeternaliter confundit & deuorat. Ponens n. rursum malum bonum, & lucem tenebras, concedit ipse vocaliter in scriptis absolutionem culpa ac poenae cuiuslibet militantibus omnibus tempore certo, equitibus aut pedibus aduersus iam dictos Christi fideles, Romano principi subditos, & constanter illi tanquam regi obedientes & obedire volentes, quos etiam velut haereticos, & crucis Christi rebelles impugnare quomodocunque licitum esse spoliare ac exterminare finaliter, per se vel alios, scripto tamen scripto, quam non scripto pronunciat. Et quod horret auditus, id praedicat, & per quosdam falsos & pseudofratres, sitientes ecclesiasticas dignitates, tanquam Deo sit acceptum, quemadmodum in transmarinis partibus expugnare paganos; praedicari facit vbique. Quam signam fallacem veniam concedit similiter dictus Episcopus, non potentibus propter ... ad scelus explere, si ad proprios ipsorum sumptus, id per alios vsq; in idem tempus perpetrari; aut summam illam ad hoc sufficientem exhibuerint nephariis exactoribus suis. Cum tamen secundum catholicam religionem nulli dubium esse debeat, sic militantib, atq; pugnanti-bus bus hanc detisibilem & inanem absolutionem nihil proficere, sed nocere. Sic tamen fallit simplices ad explenda sua impia desideria, quod in sui potestate non est vocaliter concedendo, quinimo sic ipsos deducit atq; seducit ad æternam perniciem animarum. Alienæ nanq; patriæ invasores existentes, & expugnatores iniusti pacis, & quietis innocentum fidelium turbatores, quos etiam non ignorant vere catholicos fore, sed propriæ patriæ defensores, & iplorum vero & legitimo domino fidelitatis observatores spoliando & occidendo, vel aliter impugnando, non sunt Christi, sed diaboli pugiles. Rapinas enim, incendia, furta, homicidia, fornicationes, adulteria, cætera quoq; quasi omnia criminum genera inciduunt & committunt. Unde constat indubie, non ipsos mereri veniam, sed eo potius reos & debitores fieri damnationis æternæ: ad quæ tamen patranda seducuntur ipsi per illius oraculum atq; scripturas, qui, quamuis non existat, se Christi vicarium dicit in tertis. Neque his tam horrendis suo imperio vel inductione per laicos exerceri contentus, vir sanguinum hic & dolosus quendam presbyterum ex suis fratribus, sive complicibus, quos Cardinales appellant, cum equitum & peditum numerosa caterua, transmisit in provinciam Lombardiæ, similiter quoq; abbatem, monachum quendam, in Marchia quadam Italiæ q cognominatur Anchone propter impugnandos & exterminandos Christi fideles, quos suis impiis & iniquis iussib. aduersus ipsorum principem parere nolentes, iam dictis persecutionib. omnimodis incessanter infestat, ipsorumque pium principem Ludovicum prædictum, illis compatientem, ipsosq; pro posse fouentem, fautorem haereticorum ob hoc solita temeritate, in suis dictis & scriptis appellare præsumpsit. In quos siquidem atq; consimiles usus ecclesiastica temporalia, quæ devoti fideles tam principes quam subiecti, communitates & singuli statuerunt ad sustentationem ministrorum euangelii & subuentionem pauperum impotentum, episcopus hic consumit atq; converit: & in testamentis ad pias causas legata temporalia, ut ultra marinum transitum, captiuorum per infideles redemptionem, & similia reliqua, tanquam suæ potestatis existentia iniuste vendicans, convertere quærit. Cum tamen apostolicum & sacerdotale opus non sit, neq; sacerdotem aut virum Deo dedicatum decet arma movere vel moveri iubere inter Christi fideles, & inique præsertim, sed eosdem potius, si discordes aut diffidentes inuicem fuerint, per conuenientes exhortationes, ad concordiam revocare, quemadmodum per Apostolum, Chrysostom & Hilarium, atq; Ambrosium sufficienter ostensum est 5. huius & 9. Non est igitur de cætero permittendum huic Episcopo, vel alteri cuiquam, sic generalem absolutam & tantam potestatem ecclesiastica ipsi alia conferendi, & distribuendi, sed per principes & legislatores, vel hanc simpliciter revocandum ab ipso, vel moderandum, sic, ut quæ ad salutem fidelium præsentem atq; futuram statuta, & ordinata sunt hactenus, statuuntur & ordinantur continuo, vel in futurum ordinabuntur, non cedant in continuam ipsorum vexationem temporalem, & demum in perpetuum cruciatum. Talibus quoq; processibus sic laudabilibus, & Deo gratis, quantum vnusquisq; sanctmentis neq; peruersus affectu comprehendere potest, modernis temporibus processit, & continuo procedit, vocatus modernus Papa Romanus cum suis ministris, quos legatos appellat, aduersum sæpe dictum Ludovicum Rom. regem: sic quoq; aduersus eiusdem vicarios, & fideles subditos, maxime in provincia Lombardiæ, Thusciæ, ac Anchonitanæ Marchiæ processerunt. Quorum tamen singularius persecutus est hactenus generosum, nobilem, & illustrem virum catholicum, morum honestate, ac gravitate inter cæteros Italicos singularem, bonæ recordationis Matthæum Vicecomitem imperiali autoritate Mediolanensem vicarium cum plurima sibi adhærentium multitudine fidelium populorum. Hunc n. quamuis iniquissime, prædictus episcopus suis prophanis sermonibus & scripturis damnatæ vitæ fuisse, ac damnatæ memoriæ fore pronunciat: verum non ille Matthæus, sed ipse per quem scandala veniunt, & qui profert de suæ thesauro malitiæ semper mala, damnatæ pœnitentiæ apud Deum & homines patenter habetur, estq; amplius ante mortem & post mortem futurus haberi, id sibi comminante veritate, Matthæi 18. dum inquit: Væ homini per quem scandalum venit. Et rursum eodem: Qui autem scandalizauerit unum de pusillis istis, qui in me credunt, expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo eius, & demergatur in profundum maris. Quæ etiam non attendens, sicut nec cætera monita Christi, qui pertinax & impœnitens est, indesinenter persequitur, blasphemat viros alios quamplures clarissimos, fidelitatis atque constantiæ ad ipsorum iam dictum Romanorum principem sectatores. Quorum famam apud Deum & homines redolentem prædictis suis prophanationibus atq; blasphemiis nititur maculare. Hic enim est Episcopus, cuius & ipsius Ecclesiæ non sequitur iudicium Deus, quoniam per surreptionem & ignorantiam iudicat, sicut dicit Magister sententiarum, libro quarto, dist. 18. capitulo sexto. Et huius causam reddit Hieronymus super illud Matthæi 16. Et tibi dabo claves regni cœlorum. Inquit enim, quod nec repetere piget: Hunc locum quidam non intelligentes, (sicut, supplendum, nec Episcopus iste,) aliquid sumunt de supercilio Pharisæorum, ut damnare innoxios, vel soluere se putent noxios. Et subdit ad propositum: cum apud Deum, non sententia sacerdotum, sed reorum vita quaeratur. Non igitur sequitur Deus talis sacerdotis seu Episcopi vel Ecclesiæ iudicium tam iniquum. Propter quod ipsius ac suorum complicum blasphemiæ verendæ non sunt, nec ab aliquo fideli timendæ, quemadmodum diximus, quoniam non transeunt in fidelium gregem, sed prorumpentium in has fœda corpora (celeratas & infelices animas, diuina virtute referre potius didicerunt. Sunt igitur quæ iam narrauimus quæsitorum initia vera. Et quæ etiam tam debite quam indebite processerunt post hæc, vel ab his, quamuis propter temporis longitudinem, hominum ignauiam & inadvertentiam, exciderint ab ipsorum conspectibus sine memoriis, horumque vice propter consuetudinem tudinem audiendi falsa siue figmenta quædam in animabus fidelium plurimorum subinducta sint & inserta veritatis oppositą. Quorum siquidem origo & fomes, auaritia, siue cupiditas, & ambitio siue superbia fuit. Incrementi vero atque horum tutelæ non parum instrumentum, execrabilis illa opinio & enunciatio, qua Romanus Episcopus & suorum clericorum cœtus siue collegium eidem asserunt, in persona tamen beati Petri apostoli, à Christo fore traditam plenitudinem potestatis. Verum post multam diligentem atq; laboriosam perscrutationem, & exquisitionem scripturarum, diuinas ab humanis separantes, quas Romani pontifices quidam in vnum cōfuderant, credentes ex permixtione hac communicare suis propriis institutis, eam q; soli sacro canoni debetur auctoritas enunciationis iam dictæ seu tituli, sensus determinauimus, & sufficienter aperuimus vigesimo tertio huius omnibus ratione vtentibus, saltem quos sinistra non perturbat affectio fallos esse, aliorum vero maxime eum sensum ad quem vltimo prædictam orationem transtulit Romanus Episcopus, ex ea sibi videlicet ascribendo vniuersalem siue supremam iurisdictionem coactiuam, quam sub verborum metaphora vocat gladium temporalem super omnes mundi principes, communitates, & populos. Quamuis, vt diximus, & quibus ex causis in solum principem Romanorum nunc explicet titulum hunc. In omnes tamen reliquos explicaturus eundem, dum in ipsorum regnus seditionem prospexerit, ea quoque vsurpandi & occupandi violentam sibi videri potestatem adesse. Sic ergo plenitudine potestatis propter ignauiam permissa Romanis Episcopis, circa seculares actus ciuiles vt sunt hactenus, vtuntur continuo, sunt & in deterius, nisi prohibeantur vsuri. Leges enim oligarchicas statuerunt, quibus videlicet clericorum collegium & aliorum coniugatorum quosdam à legibus ciuilibus rite latis exemerunt in principum & populorum præiudicium summum. Nec his contenti limitibus, iam laicos citari faciunt coram suis vocatis officialibus siue iudicibus, & iustificare volunt, in hoc principantium iurisdictionem punitus destruentes. Hæc autem litis seu ciuilis discordiæ causa est singularis & occulta in sui origine valde, quam ex principio proponebamus ostendere. Propter diuinarum enim & humanarum scripturarum inuolucrum paralogizati fidelium plures inducti sunt credere, Romanum Episcopum cum suis clericis, quos Cardinales appellant, super fideles statuere posse quod volunt, ad id quoque seruandum omnes obligari lege diuina, transgredientes vero reos fieri damnationis æterne, quod tamen in prioribus, & præcipue duodecimo & decimo tertio prima, ac huius vigesimoprimo, parte octaua monstrauimus per certitudinem non esse verum, nec vero propinquum, sed veritatis oppositum manifeste. Hæc rursum causa est, vt proœmialiter diximus, qua regnum Italicum dudum laborauit, laboratque continuo vehementer contagiosa nil minus & prona serpere in reliquas omnes ciuilitates & regna, & ea omnia iam infecit vtcunque, demumque nisi prohibeatur, ea totaliter velut Italicum infectura, propter quod principibus omnibus & populis per generale concilium, vt prædiximus conuocandum. Expedit hunc titulum interdicere, ac simpliciter prohibere Romanorum Episcopo, & alteri cuicunque, ne propter consuetudinem audiendi falsa, de cætero populus seducatur. Reuocandaq; sibi est potestas, ecclesiastica officia, & temporalia siue beneficia conferendi & distribuendi. Quoniam his abutitur Episcopus hic in dispendium corporum, & animarum damnationem fidelium Christianorum. Ad hæc enim obligantur omnes iurisdictionem habentes, præcipue reges, lege diuina. Quoniam propter hoc constituti sunt, vt faciant iudicium & iustitiam, quod etiam negligentes facere, deinceps inexcusabiles sunt, cum scandalum ex huiusmodi omissione proueniens, non ignorent. Qui vero Romanus Episcopus cum sibi successoribus in sede prædicta, omnesque reliqui sacerdotes atque diaconi & spirituales ministri: ad quos sermones hi sunt, non tanquam inimicos, testem inuoco Deum in animam & corpus meum, sed potius patres, & fratres in Christo, studeant imitari Christum & Apostolos, seculares principatus & temporalium dominia simpliciter abdicando. Eos enim peccantes coram omnibus, iuxta doctrinam Christi & Apostoli argui & increpaui palam. Et ad veritatis callem præco veritatis existens, per diuinarum & humanarum scripturarum concordiam tentaui reducere, vt cauere possint, maxime Romanus Episcopus, qui amplius tamen deuiasse videtur, eam indignationem omnipotentis Dei & Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, quam ipse singulariter cæteris persæpe comminatur.
units.tr: A still graver prejudice and an unbearable injury also fall upon all the princes, communities and individuals subject to the Roman Empire. For if the aforesaid bishop claims that, while the Empire is vacant, he succeeds the Emperor in his office, it follows of necessity that the authority to demand oaths of fidelity from all princes and the other imperial vassals belongs to him, and that he may compel them to swear those oaths. It follows too that he may demand the tributes and other services that these same vassals have customarily paid to the Roman princes, and that the bishop, by the fullness of power he claims for himself, may invent further demands beyond the customary dues. It likewise follows that the conferral of principalities, fiefs and other rights, which the Roman prince can grant because of the lack of male heirs or for any other reason or cause, belongs in the same way to this bishop's authority while the Empire is vacant. Even more prejudicial and most troublesome is this: while the Empire is vacant, as we have said, it would remain vacant forever under the power and solicitude of the Roman bishops. The princes, colleges, communities and private persons subject to the Roman Empire, contending with one another in civil matters, whether by appeals lodged or by complaints about them brought before the court of the Roman bishop, will be compelled by the aforesaid bishop's summonses, both in real and in personal actions, to come to his court and submit to civil judgement. Nor can a prince, community or judge subject to the Roman Empire carry out any sentence, since appeals from their civil sentences are always lodged at the Roman court and the condemned parties always appeal. Those subject to the Roman Empire who refuse to obey the aforesaid bishop, or to be subject to him in the matters mentioned (as they would not be bound to be), are constantly and with all his malignant and insolent nature persecuted by the same bishop, through what he calls sentences of anathema or blasphemy, of excommunication, of heresy, of interdict and finally of the deprivation or loss of temporal goods. By publishing these temporal goods and granting them in whatever way to the powerful who seize them, and by granting to those who persecute these men, together with their subjects and adherents, and even to those who kill them in any manner, forgiveness of any fault or penalty (though it is an empty and deceptive forgiveness), and by absolving their subjects heretically from the oaths they have sworn or are to swear to him, the said bishop persecutes them without ceasing. If the Roman bishop should say, as is his custom, under the pretext of concern for the flock and of piety, that it pertains to him to confirm or approve the election of the Roman prince, lest perhaps a heretic should climb to the imperial summit, to the great harm of the community of the faithful, the answer must be given that such an election needs no approval of his, since it is celebrated and completed by three solemn Christian archbishops, each of whom has received from Christ an episcopal or priestly authority equal to that of the Roman Pontiff, as was shown in the fifteenth and sixteenth chapters of this work. Again, the election of the said Roman prince is completed by four faithful secular princes, together with the religious pastors or prelates who agree with them. It is not likely that these seven would err in this way or be moved by a perverse intention, as the will of the Roman bishop alone would be, since he trusts that by his own judgement alone he may rightly do what he pleases, by the fullness of power that he unsuitably ascribes to himself. For thus he could judge anyone heretical at his pleasure and deprive him of the right of election, so that the diligent office of the princes would be rendered void, and the creation and promotion of the elected man would always be prohibited, for the reasons already given. Yet even granting, according to the opposing claim, that the Roman prince, before or after his election, has fallen into heresy or is falling into a stain, and that the electing princes knew of it or concealed it, it must be said that by no means does the judgement or correction of him belong to the Roman bishop alone. Nor again will this authority belong to that bishop alone, or to the assembly or synod of his clergy alone, but to a general council of those who are contained under the imperial government, for the reasons already given and for others assigned in the twenty-first chapter. For the cardinals themselves have often consented to, do consent to, and take part in the aforesaid usurpation; therefore it is unsafe that this election should be subject to the judgement of such men. Furthermore, one may ask why the fitness of other kings' persons should not also be subject to his judgement and to the power of approval. To this I answer that they intend this, although they do not yet dare to attempt it, but they watch for a time suitable to them, about which we will perhaps also say something. So, setting out on the path of error and iniquity from the said false suppositions, the present man, lastly and most recently called the Roman Pope, with all his efforts and endeavours hinders and prohibits the illustrious Louis, of the dukes of Bavaria, chosen King of the Romans, from proceeding to the peaceful possession of the imperial dignity. For the said Louis, rightly, both by word and by deed, overturns the suppositions of the aforesaid bishop. For although he has not yet been confirmed or approved by his words or writings, as we have clearly shown before, and although he needs no confirmation of the election made in his favour and published by the electors at the time, he has had himself written and named, and continuously does so, as King of the Romans, as he truly was and is. He also administers all imperial and royal affairs, as he is also held and able to do by law. Against him, however, the Roman who calls himself bishop has set himself up, though he has been raised up by him and by his predecessors from such poverty, abasement, oppression, reproach and persecution, to the abundance of temporal goods, the lofty throne, honour, power and tranquillity, by the Roman princes. He is like the frozen snake in the fable of Aesop, which must be taken into account and suits this purpose; and he does not act as one who has the spirit of the apostles, but like an ungrateful and forgetful man. First, in his perverse and customary way, he spits upon the said prince, and utters many words of disgrace and irreverence; yet under honey he offers poison, and under the appearance of piety, in his usual deceit, he pretends, saying in certain letters of his, which he calls edita, that he writes and utters such things so that he may lead the said Louis back from the wandering path of error to the track or footpath of truth and salvation, not considering who he is who speaks, what he says, and to whom he speaks. To this man, who is turned aside from every path of truth and lacks all fairness, can most fittingly and most truly be applied that saying of Matthew 7 and Luke 8: Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, brother, let me take the speck out of your eye, when there is a beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit; every tree is known by its own fruit. What then is this hypocrite here, a most evil tree, bearing everywhere the fruit of all malice, sedition and discord, as is perceived by all? Under the false appearance of piety and charity, he strives to defame with his words of shame a man of virtue, blameless, catholic and approved. For let him first cast out of his own clouded and almost blind mind the beam, namely his very great ignorance and error, and from his perverse affection, as if obstinate and hardened, malice and rage; then he will be able to see the smaller sins of others, and will be able to purge them more aptly and fittingly by his exhortations and admonitions. But further, he who by these deceitful and feigned words intends not the correction of a man but his civil death, has poured out and scattered upon the said most Christian prince the poisons which he believed deadly to his civil life. He has excommunicated him together with those who adhere to him alone, and has forbidden the communities of the faithful, which obey or will obey the same Louis as King of the Romans, to give him aid, counsel or favour, and forbidden the exercise of divine offices. He pays little or no attention to what Ambrose advises in the book entitled On the Sacerdotal Dignity. For in treating of the saying in 1 Timothy 3, If anyone desires the episcopate, he says, among other things, in the eighth chapter of the said book: The bishop should not be quarrelsome, that is, he should not let his tongue loose in insults, so that the same tongue with which he offers praise to God and performs the divine offices should not pour out the poison of strife. For it is not fitting that blessing and cursing should come out of the same mouth of a bishop, lest by the same tongue by which God is praised, man should be cursed; for one fountain cannot produce both sweet and bitter water. At last he will perhaps send out the sting of his malice, which he believes to be the final means of harm and destruction, thinking to strike the said prince with it: that is, his blasphemy, which he calls a sentence, though in truth it is the supreme madness, by which he has pronounced the said prince, with his adherents, or all who obey or favour him as king, to be heretics, enemies of the Church or rebels, and has deprived them of all their temporal goods, movable and immovable, by publishing, through the aforesaid sentence unworthily so called, and by granting these goods to those who wish to seize them and who do seize them, and by declaring through his voices and written parchments, through himself or through certain pseudo-preachers, that this may lawfully be done, announcing it in all provinces; and by condemning them again to death, and by granting forgiveness of all faults, penalties and crimes to those who kill or attack them. And if they are taken alive wherever they are, he reduces them to the slavery of their captors. Moreover, he grants the greater ecclesiastical offices, such as bishoprics, archbishoprics and patriarchates, and the middling and lesser ones, and he pours out ecclesiastical temporal goods, the benefices as they are called, treasures and money, so that he may stir up everyone against the said prince to hatred, rebellion, war and discord, although none of these things belongs to the authority of this bishop to pronounce, as we have clearly shown in chapters 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 20 of this work. Beyond these horrible malignancies he practises a ninth kind of wickedness, which plainly seems to savour of heretical stain. For he stirs up the subjects and faithful of the said Catholic prince to rebellion against him, by certain diabolical sayings or writings which he calls apostolic, absolving them from the oaths of fidelity by which they had often been, and in truth are, bound to the said prince. And such absolutions he spreads and proclaims everywhere through certain ministers of crimes, hoping by such practice to be promoted by the said bishop to ecclesiastical offices and benefices. For this is plainly not an apostolic work but a diabolical one. Accordingly, this bishop with all his accomplices, ordainers, consenters and executors, blind by greed, avarice and pride, and filled with ambition and with the greatest iniquity, as is known to all, by speech, writing or deed, offers guidance to those who believe him and follow him, in all the aforesaid words and writings of theirs, leading them to fall and be cast down into the pit of mortal sins. First they make them fall into manifest perjury, then into treachery and injustice hidden from none, and consequently into robbery, homicide and almost every kind of crime; and dying in these without repentance, they and those seduced by this most holy father and his ministers, not excused before God for their gross ignorance, are hurled and plunged into the pit of the fire of hell, the pit of the eternally damned. For it is certain, and must be certain to everyone who has reason and can use it, that neither the Roman bishop nor any other priest can absolve anyone without reasonable cause from an oath of this kind or from any other lawful oath or promise sworn. Now it is clear to everyone who wishes to stand by his own conscience, and whom a sinister affection does not disturb, that the cause which the Roman bishop alleges against the pious prince Louis, and against any other in a similar case, is by no means reasonable, but unjust, headlong and unrighteous. Hence the leading and the teaching and the exhortation of this bishop and of those who serve him in such matters are to be guarded against and utterly rejected, as leading to the eternal destruction of souls. For this is plainly contrary to the sound doctrine and words and sentence of the Apostle in Romans 13, Ephesians 6, 1 Timothy 6, and 2 Titus 2 and 3. For the Apostle clearly commands, in the passages above, that subjects must obey their earthly masters, not only the good and gentle but also the froward, as the blessed Peter says in the second chapter of his first Epistle. How much more, then, when they are bound to them by oath? The Glosses, following the saints, explain this further in the same place, plainly saying that subjects are bound and ought to obey even unbelieving masters, however wicked they may be; yet this must be understood only where obedience does not contradict the divine law in word or deed. Now there is no doubt that the words and deeds by which the Roman bishop rails against and proceeds against the Roman prince are not the commands of the divine law, nor consonant with it, but rather plainly dissonant and contrary, as has been shown by Scripture in the fourth, fifth and ninth chapters of this work. Again, to believe or obey the Roman bishop or any other bishop who teaches or preaches such things is nothing other than to allow the root of all principalities to be cut down, and the bond and tie of every civil society and kingdom to be dissolved. For I think there is no other root and tie of this kind than the mutual oath and faith of subjects and princes. For this faith, as Tully says in the first book of On Duties, is the foundation of all justice; whoever strives to dissolve it between rulers and subjects seeks nothing less than to be able, at his pleasure, to overturn the power of all princes, and thereby to reduce them to his own slavery. And he also disturbs the peace and tranquillity of all who live in civil society, and thereby brings men, in the private life sufficient to this present age, and at last, as we have said, so disposed in mind, finally to eternal destruction of souls. For this reason all Christians should despise and guard against the promise of this bishop and his accomplices, a vain promise worse than that of the Pharisees, a pernicious and insane doctrine, or rather, to speak more truly, a seduction of souls; they should heed Christ, who counsels or commands this in Matthew 15, when he says to all the faithful, though in the person of the Apostles: Let them alone, that is, the Pharisees, who were then thought to be the teachers of the law of Moses, yet who thought erroneously in it and were almost always opposed to Christ. For by them were signified and understood all the sophistical and false teachers of Holy Scripture, such as those persecutors of the Roman prince and of other truly faithful and innocent men are, in whose person those wicked men also persecute Christ and set themselves against him. Christ then gives the reason why we ought to despise these false teachers, saying: They are blind, and leaders of the blind; and if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch. So, according to the Lord's precept, these false teachers are to be let alone and despised, as blind men, blinded by greed, avarice, pride and ambition, and as leaders of the blind, that is, of the ignorant, and of the proud and rebellious. Those who do not heed, or do not wish to heed, the apostolic precept, or rather the divine precept, which speaks plainly and without metaphor in Romans 13: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, teach and preach that subjects are rebels against their princes. For such men, who, by their deceitful and wicked persuasions, lead both themselves and others into rebellion, resist the ordinance of God. For the Apostle in the passage above says that whoever resists the power, that is, the secular ruler, resists the ordinance of God. Of such men the same Apostle prophesied in 2 Timothy 3 and 4, when he said: Know this, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, and under parents he includes princes; whence Tully, in the first book of On Duties: Princes are our country, they are our parents, to whose greatest benefits we are obliged. Therefore those who are disobedient to parents or princes are ungrateful, wicked, faithless, not keeping covenant, without natural affection (supply: good), without peace, slanderers, incontinent, fierce, without kindness, traitors, headstrong, arrogant, puffed up, lovers of pleasures rather than of God; having indeed a form of godliness (that is, appearing to do what they do for the worship, reverence and love of God), but denying its power (that is, of such godliness). This can easily be known to all from their works, according to the saying of Matthew 7: Beware of false prophets, he says, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves; you shall know them by their fruits. And the Apostle, in agreement with the counsel or precept of Christ, adds: And avoid these, that is, do not believe them, nor obey them in such matters. But alas, because of this appearance of godliness they have so deceived men that now, relying on the violent power which they have obtained under the appearance of piety, partly freely but mostly by secret usurpation, and now openly and violently usurp, they cannot be dislodged, and they inflict violence on Christ's faithful people. They are ungrateful, proud, without peace, and unjust, and indeed such as the Apostle has described them in every respect: putting bad for good and light for darkness, according to the saying of Isaiah 5. By the conferral of ecclesiastical offices, greater, middling and lesser, and of temporal goods or benefices, both movable and immovable, and of tithes, which were established for a good end; by the giving and promising of these, and by a wicked agreement made beforehand, they stir up against the faithful princes subject to them, and even against neighbouring princes who are not subject to them. Although they seem to do this not only against the Roman prince together with their accomplices, yet by his example, who has been so beneficent to the Roman bishop and to his Church, the other princes should learn that the same things may probably happen to themselves, and that the aforesaid bishop will strive by the same means against them, without good will towards anyone, whenever the opportunity of such an assault presents itself to him. For he himself asserts, by his words and by the writings previously adduced, on account of his own fullness of power, which he unsuitably ascribes to himself, that all princes and peoples are subject to his principality or to his coercive jurisdiction. Desiring and longing to bring this also to effect, he watches for the times when schisms and contentions appear between faithful princes or between peoples, or rebellions of subjects against their lords, and he sometimes takes care to stir these up, so that one of two disagreeing parties, too weak to resist its opponent, is forced to implore his aid and submit to his dominion. For although under a feigned appearance of piety and mercy he seems at times to protect those who are perhaps powerless and unjustly oppressed, and to grant them secular favour, yet he gives this only after first making them needy of his favour and seeking it, so that they will submit to his principality or secular lordship. He hopes thus at last, through mutual oppression and envy, to force each of the two opposing parties to submit to his power. For this reason contentions and actions must be guarded against, which bring anyone to the necessity of such favours, since at last they turn to the destruction of liberty and to the slavery of those who accept them. In this way, then, the bishop finds by degrees, throughout the kingdoms of the world, the means by which he may at last bring under himself all the principalities he burns to subject. For he does not attempt such procedures in all or several at once, but he waits for secular power to grow in each by degrees, so that he may see the remainder of the others and believe he can overcome them without danger to himself. Then he would openly, with confidence, unfurl over the rest of the kingdoms the banner of the fullness of power which he has presumed for himself. And just as he would openly declare that those of the Roman Empire are subject to his dominion or coercive jurisdiction and must be subject to him, so would he declare the other principalities also; and though they lawfully refuse, he would pursue them with blasphemies and sentences like those already mentioned against the Roman prince and against those faithful to him, and by violent or armed power he would pursue them to destruction and extermination. By these means and ways, then, the said bishop together with his accomplices has led almost all the principalities, communities and peoples of Italy into contention and schism, and he has now begun to do the same in Germany and constantly strives to complete it. For he has stirred up to rebellion against the Roman prince some of his subjects who are wicked and criminal, by secular favours, by conferring ecclesiastical offices, tithes, and the payment of money; and without ceasing he endeavours to stir up all whom he can, greater, middling and lesser. Those who have been seduced by him in this way and have obeyed him, he calls and names sons of the Church and truly faithful; but those who persist, and wish to persist, in the fidelity due to their prince, he names schismatics and heretics, and persecutes them as enemies of the Church, blaspheming, defaming and excommunicating them as far as in him lies, and condemning them by secular sentence both as persons and in their property, although no such judgement is due to him in such matters, as far as concerns such matters, either by divine or human law, as is clear from what has gone before and has been recalled earlier. But there is one thing, of which we have said something before, which inflicts the most wicked and grievous harm of all in general, and which cannot be passed over by anyone who does not wish to fall from the law of charity: namely, that the Roman bishop, exercising his office, eternally confounds and devours all the sheep of Christ, which he says have been committed to him to feed with wholesome doctrine. For putting evil for good and light for darkness, he himself openly grants in his writings absolution of every fault and penalty to all who fight, on horse or on foot, for a certain time against the said faithful of Christ, subject to the Roman prince and constantly obedient, or willing to obey, to him as king. Those whom he also attacks as heretics and rebels against the cross of Christ, he declares may lawfully be plundered and finally exterminated in any way, by himself or by others, whether in writing or otherwise. And what horrifies the hearer, he preaches this, and causes it to be proclaimed everywhere through certain false and pseudo-brothers, thirsting for ecclesiastical dignities, as if it were pleasing to God, just as the pagans are to be attacked in the lands beyond the sea. The said bishop likewise grants a fallacious forgiveness, to those who are unable, on account of ... to carry out the crime, if they are to commit it at their own expense, through others, at the same time; or if they have paid the sum sufficient for this to his wicked collectors. Yet according to the Catholic religion there ought to be no doubt that for those who thus fight and make war this detestable and empty absolution profits nothing, but harms. Nevertheless, by granting it openly, he deceives the simple into fulfilling his impious desires, which are not in his power to grant, and so leads and seduces them to the eternal destruction of souls. For those who are invaders of a foreign country, and unjust disturbers of the peace and quiet of innocent faithful, whom they also know to be truly Catholic, and who are the defenders of their own country and the faithful keepers of their allegiance to their true and lawful lord, by despoiling and killing them, or attacking them in other ways, are not soldiers of Christ but of the devil. For they commit and fall into robberies, arsons, thefts, homicides, fornications, adulteries, and almost every other kind of crime. From this it is certainly clear that they do not deserve forgiveness, but are rather made liable and debtors to eternal damnation; and yet they are seduced to commit these things by the oracle and writings of him who, although he is not Christ's vicar, calls himself Christ's vicar on earth. Not content to have these horrible things carried out by laymen under his command and inducement, that man of blood and deceit has sent a certain priest, one of his brothers or accomplices, whom they call Cardinals, with a numerous band of horsemen and foot soldiers, into the province of Lombardy; and similarly an abbot, a certain monk, into a certain march of Italy called Ancona, to attack and exterminate the faithful of Christ who refuse to obey his impious and unjust commands against their prince. They are constantly harassed by him with the aforesaid persecutions in every way, and this same bishop has presumed, in his sayings and writings, with his usual rashness, to call the pious prince Louis, who sympathises with them and supports them as far as he can, a favourer of heretics. Against these and like persons this bishop consumes and turns to his own uses the ecclesiastical temporal goods which devout faithful, princes as well as subjects, communities and individuals, have established for the support of the ministers of the gospel and the relief of the poor and helpless. He also seeks to convert to such uses the temporal legacies bequeathed to pious causes in wills, such as those for passage across the sea, for the ransom of captives by infidels, and the like, claiming them unjustly as if they were in his own power. Yet the apostolic and sacerdotal task is not this, nor does it befit a priest or a man dedicated to God to take up arms or to order them to be taken up among the faithful of Christ, and this especially unjustly; rather, if they are at odds or distrust one another, he should call them back to concord by fitting exhortations, as has been sufficiently shown by the Apostle, Chrysostom, Hilary and Ambrose, in the fifth and ninth chapters of this work. It is therefore not to be permitted from now on to this bishop, or to anyone else, to have such a general, absolute and great power of conferring and distributing ecclesiastical goods; but either this power must be simply revoked from him by princes and legislators, or it must be moderated, so that what has been established and ordained up to now for the present and future salvation of the faithful, and what shall be established and ordained henceforth, do not turn to the continual temporal vexation of the same men, and at last to everlasting torment. Also, the present Roman Pope, so-called, with his ministers, whom he calls legates, has in our times proceeded, and continues to proceed, against the aforesaid Louis, the Roman king, in a manner that any man who is not perverse in his affection can see is laudable and pleasing to God. So too the legates have proceeded against his vicars and faithful subjects, especially in the province of Lombardy, Tuscany and the march of Ancona. Yet he has hitherto persecuted with particular bitterness the noble, distinguished and illustrious Catholic man, singular among the other Italians for the honesty and gravity of his character, Matteo Visconti of good memory, vicar of Milan by imperial authority, together with a great multitude of faithful peoples who adhered to him. For although the aforesaid bishop, most unjustly, pronounces this man to have lived a condemned life and to be of condemned memory, by his profane sayings and writings, yet it is not that Matthew but he himself, through whom scandals come, and who brings forth evil things from the treasure of his malice, who is and will be openly held, both before God and men, and more so before and after death, to be of condemned repentance; and the truth threatens him with this in Matthew 18, when it says: Woe to the man through whom scandal comes. And again in the same place: But whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hung about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea. Not heeding this, as he does not heed the other warnings of Christ, being obstinate and impenitent, he ceaselessly persecutes and blasphemes many other most illustrious men, followers of the said Roman prince, in fidelity and constancy. He strives to stain with his profane defamations and blasphemies their reputation, which is sweet-smelling before God and men. For this is the bishop whose judgement, and that of his Church, God does not follow, since he judges by surreption and ignorance, as the Master of the Sentences says, in book four, distinction 18, chapter six. And Jerome gives the reason for this on the saying of Matthew 16: And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For he says, and I am not sorry to repeat it: Some, not understanding this passage (as, it must be added, this bishop does not), take up something from the haughtiness of the Pharisees, so that they think they can condemn the innocent or absolve the guilty. And he adds to the point: since before God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the guilty that is sought. God therefore does not follow the judgement of such a priest or bishop, or of the Church, which is so unjust. Because of this, the blasphemies of this bishop and of his accomplices are not to be feared, nor are they to be dreaded by any faithful man, as we have said, since they do not pass into the flock of the faithful, but have learned by divine power to fling back these wicked and unhappy souls which rush upon these foul bodies. Therefore the beginnings of the inquiries we have now narrated are true. And the things that were done afterwards, both rightly and wrongly, or by these men, though because of the length of time, the sloth and inattention of men, they have passed out of their sight without being remembered, and in their place, through the custom of hearing falsehoods, certain fictions have been introduced and inserted into the souls of very many faithful, opposed to the truth. The origin and fuel of these falsehoods is avarice or greed, and ambition or pride. But the great instrument for their growth and protection is that detestable opinion and assertion, by which the Roman bishop and the body or college of his clerics affirm that the fullness of power was handed down by Christ to the blessed apostle Peter in person. Yet after a long, diligent and laborious examination and search of the Scriptures, separating the divine from the human, which certain Roman pontiffs had mixed together, believing that by this mixture they could lend authority to their own institutions, we have determined the sense of the said saying or title, which belongs only to the sacred canon, and we have sufficiently explained it in the twenty-third chapter of this work, to all who use reason, at least to those whom a sinister affection does not disturb, and who are shown to be false. But that sense, especially, to which the Roman bishop has lately turned the said prayer, namely ascribing to himself by it universal or supreme coercive jurisdiction, which by a metaphor of words he calls the temporal sword over all the princes, communities and peoples of the world. Although, as we have said, and for the reasons given, he now applies this title only to the prince of the Romans; yet he intends to apply it to all the rest, whenever he sees sedition in their kingdoms, and to think that he has the violent power to seize and occupy them too. Thus, through the negligence that has allowed it, the Roman bishops, by this fullness of power, now use it continually in secular and civil affairs, as they have hitherto done, and they go even further to the worse, unless they are prevented from exercising it. For they have established oligarchic laws, by which, to the very great prejudice of princes and peoples, they have exempted from the civil laws duly enacted a college of clerics and certain other married men. Not content with these limits, they now have laymen cited before their own summoned officials or judges, and wish them to be brought to justice, thereby destroying in this matter the jurisdiction of rulers. Now the cause of this strife or civil discord is singular and very hidden in its origin, which we proposed at the beginning to show. For many of the faithful have been induced, by the wrapping of divine and human Scriptures, into the paralogism that the Roman bishop, together with his clerics whom they call Cardinals, can set up over the faithful whatever they will, that all are bound by divine law to observe it, and that those who transgress become liable to eternal damnation. Yet in the earlier chapters, and especially in the twelfth and thirteenth of the first part, and in the twenty-first of this part, eighth section, we have shown that this is not true with certainty, nor even near the truth, but is plainly the opposite of the truth. This again is the cause, as we said in the preface, by which the kingdom of Italy has long laboured, and continues to labour most grievously, a contagion which creeps no less, and readily, into all other communities and kingdoms; and it has already infected all of them in some measure, and unless it is prohibited, it will at last infect them wholly, as it has Italy. Therefore all princes and peoples should be summoned to a general council, as we have said before. It is expedient to forbid this title, and simply to prohibit it to the Roman bishop and to anyone else, lest because of the custom of hearing falsehoods the people be seduced from now on. And the power of conferring and distributing ecclesiastical offices and temporal goods or benefices must be taken back from him, since this bishop abuses it to the loss of bodies and to the damnation of the souls of Christian faithful. For all who have jurisdiction are bound by divine law to these duties, especially kings. For they are appointed for this purpose, that they may do judgement and justice; and those who neglect to do this are from now on inexcusable, since they are not ignorant of the scandal that arises from such an omission. As for the Roman bishop with his successors in the said see, and all the other priests and deacons and spiritual ministers, to whom these words are addressed, not as enemies, I call God to witness upon my soul and body, but rather as fathers and brothers in Christ, let them strive to imitate Christ and the Apostles, simply renouncing secular principalities and the lordship of temporal goods. For those who sin, as Christ and the Apostle taught, are to be openly rebuked and reproved before all. And I, a herald of the truth, have tried, through the harmony of divine and human Scriptures, to bring them back to the path of truth, so that they may take care, especially the Roman bishop, who seems to have strayed further, to avoid that indignation of almighty God and of the Apostles Peter and Paul, with which he himself so often threatens others above all.

units.la: Vnde attendat ordinem charitatis, sicut ipsam sibi præcauens, alios cauere doceat consequenter. Ipse enim non ignorat, vel ignorabit de cætero, quod præter, quinimo contra Christi & Apostolorum consilium aut præceptum, Romanum aggreditur principatum, & principem minus iuste prohibet atque perturbat. Neque rursum ignorat, quod propter scandalū per suos quosdam prædecessores & ipsum in Italia concitatum, bellicæ pugnæ sunt ortæ, unde violenta morte tot millia fidelium sunt extincta quos æternæ damnationis reos extitisse verisimiliter præsumi potest, eo quod subita morte præuenti sunt ipsorum plurimi fratrum odio & maliuolentia pleni, eorumque superstites infelices, nisi medica diuina manus adiuuet, eundem, quasi consimilem periculosum casum & exitum miserabilem expectantes. Ipsorum enim animos inuasit odium, lis atq; contentio, unde postmodum pugnæ sequuntur, honestis quoq; iam corruptis moribus, & disciplinis virtutisq; sexus mentes & corpora, vitiorum, dissolutionum, scelerum, & errorum quasi omnia generatotaliter occupatrunt. Recisa est ipsis reparatiua successio prolis, consumptæ substantiæ, dirruptæ domus, atq; subuersæ ciuitates quam magnæ atq; famosæ, vacuæ, suis incolis destitutæ, inculti agri & iam deserti delitucrunt reddere solitos fructus. Et q; omnium deflendissimum est, diuinus nus cultus quasi omnino ibidem cessauit abolitus, & Ecclesiæ siue templa in solitudinem destitutæ rectoribus seu animatum curatoribus remanserunt. Ad quæ omnia miserabilia instigauit & instigat continuo miseros incolas vndecunque, propter odium & discordiam ipsorum inuice mente cæcos, draco ille magnus, serpens antiquus, qui digne vocari debet diabolus & satanas, quoniam omnino seducit & seducere tentat vniuersum orbem.
units.tr: Let him therefore heed the order of charity: having first taken care of himself, let him then teach others to take care. For he does not know, or will not know from now on, that he lays claim to the Roman principate beyond, indeed against, the counsel or command of Christ and the Apostles, and unjustly hinders and disturbs the prince. Nor again does he fail to know that because of the scandal stirred up in Italy by some of his predecessors and by himself, wars have arisen, and through them so many thousands of the faithful have been killed by violence, who may reasonably be presumed to have been liable to eternal damnation, since very many of them were cut off by sudden death, full of hatred and ill will toward their brothers; and their unhappy survivors, unless a divine healing hand helps them, await the same dangerous fate and a miserable end. For hatred, strife and contention have invaded their minds, and fighting follows from them. With honest customs and discipline already corrupted, the minds and bodies of both sexes have been almost wholly taken over by vices, dissolutions, crimes and errors of every kind. The reparative succession of offspring has been cut off, substances have been consumed, houses have been destroyed, and cities once so great and famous have been overthrown, emptied and deprived of their inhabitants; uncultivated and now deserted fields have ceased to yield their accustomed fruits. And what is most lamentable of all, divine worship has there almost wholly ceased and been abolished, and the churches or temples, left desolate, remain without rectors or spiritual curators. To all these miseries that great dragon, the old serpent, who rightly ought to be called the devil and Satan, has incited and continually incites the wretched inhabitants from every side, their minds blinded toward one another by hatred and discord, since he entirely seduces, and tries to seduce, the whole world.

units.la: Quis igitur tam agrestis huius patriæ siue matris tam pulchræ olim & nunc adeo deformis & laceratæ, filius hæc cernens, sciens & potens aduersus sic ipsam trahentes & lacerantes iniuste, silere poterit & clamoris spiritum ad dominum continere? Huic nanq; cum Apostolo dicetur verissime, quod fidem negauit, & omni foret deterior infideli De plenitudine quidem igitur potestatis, & modis ipsius, adhuc autem de illius origine atque progressu, amplius secundum quos modos & qualiter eam sibi sumpserit Romanus Episcopus, & eadem sit vsus, tam circa ecclesiasticum ritum quam circa seculares hominum actus ciuiles, determinarum sit hoc modo.
units.tr: What son, however lacking in feeling for this country or mother, once so beautiful and now so deformed and torn, who sees these things, knows them, and has the power to act against those who thus unjustly drag and tear her apart, could keep silent and restrain the spirit of outcry before the Lord? For to him it will be said most truly, with the Apostle, that he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever [1 Tim. 5.8]. Concerning the fullness of power, and its modes, and further its origin and progress, and in what manner and how the Roman Bishop has assumed it for himself and how he has used it, both in ecclesiastical rite and in the civil acts of secular men, the matter is to be determined more fully as follows.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: De quibusdam instantiis ad determinata in decimoquinto huius, & in reliquis capitulis consequenter.
units.tr: On certain instances bearing on what was determined in the fifteenth chapter of this book, and so on consecutively in the remaining chapters.

units.la: VErum de quibus diximus 15. huius, & sic in reliquis capitulis consequenter, merito quis dubitans, primum ostendet ampliorem & alteram esse speciem dignitatem episcopi, ea quæ simpliciter siue tantummodo sacerdotis, nec solum humana institutione, quam separabilem diximus, verum etiam ordinatione diuina, quam essentialem vocauimus prius. Videtur autem id posse coniunci ex Luc. 10. vbi series hæc habetur: Post hæc autem designauit dominus & alios 72. & misit illos binos ante faciem suam. Vbi Beda: Sicut autem duodecim Apostolos formam Episcoporum præmonstrare, nemo est qui dubitet, sic & hos 72. figuram presbyterorum secundi ordinis sacerdotum gessisse. Amplius ostenditur idem ex primæ ad Timotheum quinto, cum dixit Apostolus: Aduersus presbyterum noli accipere accusationem, nisi sub duobus aut tribus testibus. Ergo Timotheus erat dignitate superior presbyteris aliis, non tamen presbyterorum, aut fidelium multitudinis electione, igitur ordinatione diuina. Rursum apparet idem ex epistola Clementis Papæ, ad Iacobum fratrem Domini superscripta. Videtur autem & hæc fuisse sententia quasi omnium Episcoporum, qui beato Petro aut Paulo successisse dicuntur in episcopali sede Romana, vt ex Isidori codice supradicto euidenter apparet.
units.tr: Now, concerning the matters we spoke of in the fifteenth chapter of this book, and so on consecutively in the remaining chapters, one may reasonably doubt, and I shall first show that the dignity of bishop is a broader and different kind from that of the priest simply or merely, one that rests not only on human institution, which we said can be separated, but also on divine ordination, which we called essential earlier. This may be gathered from Luke 10, where the sequence reads: After these things the Lord also appointed seventy-two others, and sent them two by two before his face. Bede says there: No one doubts that just as the twelve Apostles prefigured the form of bishops, so these seventy-two bore the figure of the presbyters, the priests of the second order. The same is shown further from 1 Timothy 5, where the Apostle said: Do not receive an accusation against an elder except under two or three witnesses. Therefore Timothy was superior in dignity to the other elders, yet not by the election of the elders or of the multitude of the faithful, and so by divine ordination. Again, the same appears from the epistle of Pope Clement, superscribed to James the brother of the Lord. Moreover, this seems to have been the opinion of nearly all the bishops who are said to have succeeded Saint Peter or Paul in the Roman episcopal see, as is clearly evident from the aforementioned codex of Isidore.

units.la: Deinde vero videtur ostendi posse, beatum Petrum potestate siue autoritate per Christum immediate, non per hominem aut homines alios sibi tradita, superiorem fuisse cæteris Apostolis, & per consequens successores ipsius successoribus aliorum. Videtur autem hoc primum ex Matthæi 16. dum ad ipsum Christus singulariter inquit: Et ego dico tibi, quia tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferi non prævalebunt aduersus eam: & tibi dabo claues regni cælorum, &c. Per quæ verba Christus expressisse videtur, beatum Petrum futurum caput & fundamentum Ecclesiæ, præsertim mortuo Christo. Vbi Glossa: specialiter etiam, (scilicet potestatem,) Petro concessit, vt ad vnitatem nos inuitaret. Ideo enim eum principem Apostolorum constituit, vt Ecclesia vnum principalem Christi haberet vicarium, ad quem diuersa membra Ecclesiæ recurrerent, si forte inter se dissentiret. Quod si diuersa capita in Ecclesia essent, vnitatis vinculum rumperetur. Amplius ostenditur idem ex Lucæ 22. cum ad ipsum specialiter Christus inquit: Ego autem rogaui pro te Petre, vt non deficiat fides tua, & tu aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Suorum ergo fratrum, apostolorum scilicet, ac aliorum fidelium prima cura pastoralis & confirmatio beato Petro commissa fuit, propter suæ fidei firmitationem, pro qua, ne deficeret, singulariter Christus orasse videtur, ne deficeret inquam in ipso, neque in ipsius aliquo successore. Vbi Glossa: Confirma fratres tuos, cum te principem Apostolorum constituerim. Hoc autem non solum intelligendum de apostolis, qui tunc erant, vt roborarentur a Petro, sed de omnibus fidelib. Et parum infra subdit: Per pœnitentiam obtinuit, (Petrus scil.) vt esset antistes mundi. Rursum ostenditur idem Ioan. 21. inquit n. ad ipsum Christus singulariter, Pasce oues meas, Pasce agnos meos, Pasce oues meas, ter replicans idem verbum. Non determinatis igitur ouibus, primus & vniuersalis omnium pastor immediate à Christo institutus fuisse videtur. Vbi Chrysostomus etiam inquit sic: Eximius n. apostolorum erat Petrus, & os discipulorum, & vertex collegii, vnde negatione deleta, committit ei prælationem fratrum. Demum confirmatur hoc autoritate plurimorum sanctorum, super illud Ioannis 21. Sic eum volo manere, donec veniam, quid ad te? tu autem sequere me. Inquit enim Augustinus: Duas vitas sibi diuinitus prædicatas nouit Ecclesia, quarum vna est in fide, alia in spe. Ista, (scil. in fide,) signata est per Apostolum Petrum propter sui apostolatus primatum. Rursum Theophylactus ibid. cunctorum fidelium prælaturam ei instituit. Chrysostomus autem: Si vero dixerit quis, qualiter igitur Iacobus thronum assumpsit Hierosolymorum? id rtiq; dicam, Quoniam Petrum orbis terrarum in throniz auit magistrum. Et infra inquit idem: Huic, (scil. Petro,) & præpositura fratrum credita est. Amplius idem, Quia igitur ei magna prædixerat dominus, (Petro videl.) & orbem terrarum commisserat. Et rursum Theophylactus super illud Ioan. 21. Sic eum volo manere, inquit sic: Tenan nunc dimitto ad orbis pontificatum, & in hoc sequere me. Amplius, quoniam si Christus ecclesiæ caput non instituisset, in ipsius absentia ipsam acephalam reliquisset, nec videretur ipsam ordinasse, secundum meliorem dispositionem aut optimam; nunc autem ipsam optime dispositam & ordinatam eum reliquisse credendum, ergo & illi caput aliquod instituisse tenendum, non aliud conuenientius beato Petro. Igitur fuit ipse Christi determinatione immediate, cæteris apostolis autoritate superior.
units.tr: Next, it seems it can be shown that the blessed Peter, by power or authority given immediately by Christ, not through man or other men, was superior to the other Apostles, and consequently his successors to the successors of the others. This seems first to follow from Matthew 16, where Christ speaks to him alone: And I say to you, that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it: and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc. By these words Christ seems to have indicated that the blessed Peter would be the head and foundation of the Church, especially after Christ's death. The Gloss says there: He granted this power to Peter in particular, so as to invite us to unity. For he appointed him prince of the Apostles so that the Church might have one principal vicar of Christ, to whom the various members of the Church would resort if perhaps they disagreed among themselves. But if there were various heads in the Church, the bond of unity would be broken. Further, the same is shown from Luke 22, where Christ speaks to him specially: But I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail, and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren. Therefore the first pastoral care and the strengthening of his brethren, that is, of the Apostles and of the other faithful, was committed to the blessed Peter, on account of the firmness of his faith, for which Christ seems to have prayed specially, that it might not fail, I say, in him or in any of his successors. The Gloss there: Strengthen your brethren, since I have made you prince of the Apostles. This is to be understood not only of the Apostles who were then present, that they might be strengthened by Peter, but of all the faithful. And a little below it adds: By penance he (Peter, that is) obtained that he should be the bishop of the world. Again, the same is shown in John 21, where Christ speaks to him alone: Feed my sheep, feed my lambs, feed my sheep, repeating the same word three times. Therefore, without specifying which sheep, he seems to have been appointed immediately by Christ as the first and universal shepherd of all. Chrysostom also says there: Peter was the outstanding one among the Apostles, the mouth of the disciples and the head of the college, and so, his denial being wiped out, he entrusts to him the leadership of the brethren. Finally, this is confirmed by the authority of many saints, on the words of John 21: So I will have him remain until I come; what is that to you? You follow me. For Augustine says: The Church knows that two lives have been divinely foretold to her, of which one is in faith, the other in hope. The first (that is, in faith) was signified by the Apostle Peter, on account of the primacy of his apostleship. Again, Theophylact on the same passage: He appointed him the leadership of all the faithful. Chrysostom, however: But if someone should say, how then did James take the throne of Jerusalem? I will answer this: because the teacher of the world had set Peter on the throne. And a little below the same author says: To him also was entrusted the oversight of the brethren. Again the same: Because the Lord had foretold great things to him (Peter, that is), and had committed the world to him. And again Theophylact on John 21, So I will have him remain, says: I now dismiss you to the papacy of the world, and in this follow me.
