Moreover, if Christ had not appointed a head of the Church, he would have left it headless in his absence, and it would not seem that he had arranged it in the best or most excellent way; but since it must be believed that he left it in the best and well-ordered condition, it must also be held that he appointed some head for it, and none more fitting than the blessed Peter. Therefore he was, by Christ's determination, immediately, and by authority, superior to the other Apostles.

units.la: Deinde vero idem in specie conuincere possumus, ostendentes Paulum beato Petro dignitate siue autoritate non fuisse parem. Ad Galatas enim secundo habetur haec series: Deinde, inquit Paulus, post annos tres veni Hierosolymam videre Petrum, & mansi apud eum diebus quindecim. Et parum infra eodem subdit: Deinde post annos quatuordecim iterum ascendi Hierosolymam cum Barnaba assumpto Tito, ascendi autem secundum revelationem, & contuli cum illis Euangelium quod praedico in gentibus, seorsum autem his, qui videbantur esse aliquid, ne forte in vacuum currerem, aut cucurrissem. Vbi Glossa: Ostendit, Paulus scilicet, se non habuisse securitatem Euangelii, nisi esset auctoritate Petri confirmatum, & aliorum roboratum. Cum igitur Paulus securitatem Euangelii sumpserit a Petro secundum Glossam, apparet ipsum non suisse parem Petro in auctoritate. Unde per necessitatem sequi videtur tam ex hoc, quam aliis supra dictis, reliquos omnes Episcopos mundi Romano Episcopo tanquam singulari successori B. Petri din uina ordinatione fore subiectos, Ecclesiam quoq; Rom. esse aliarum omnium caput & primam, propter ipsius Episcopi Beati Petri successoris in ea authoritate, & omnium aliorum esse iudice & pastorem, & amplius exprimens Isidorus in codice suprādicto, capitulo, cuius titulus, Incipit praefatio Nicaeni concilii, sic ait: Sciendum est sane ab omnibus catholicis, quoniam Sancta Ecclesia Romana nullis synodicis decretis praelata est, sed Evangelica voce Domini & Salvatoris nostri primatum obtinuit, ubi dixit Beato Petro Apostolo, Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, & tibi dabo claves regni caelorum &c. Quo siquidem primatu, absq; principum concessione aliqua, visi sunt hactenus omnes Episcopi Romani a tempore Beati Petri usq; ad tempora Constantini primi Romanorum Imperatoris, condendo scilicet canones, & illorum observationem, per omnem praecipientes Ecclesiam, ut ex serie iam dicti codicis patenter apparet. Hoc rursum ratione confirmo, quoniam fides una est secundum Apostolum ad Ephesios quarto, ergo & Ecclesia una: non autem est aliter una, nisi propter unum caput atque principium, quo nullum convenientius aut aeque conveniens est Episcopo Romanorum singulari successori Beati Petri, qui petra fuit, super quam Christus se dixit suam Ecclesiam fundaturum. Confirmatur autem hoc ex eo, quoniam velut temporalia in unum reducuntur principium, puta in principatum, sic & spiritualia in aliquod unum primum videntur debere reduci, puta Episcopatum. Amplius ex alio, quoniam sicut in unico templo vel unica dioecesi oportet unicum Episcopum esse, ne ibidem sacerdotum unusquisq; ad se trahens, Christi rumpat Ecclesiam, ut ex Epistola Hieronymi ad Euandrum induximus decimo quinto huius: sic eo magis necessarium est in universa Christi Ecclesia unicum esse caput, propter fidelium unitatem seruandam. Quanto enim communius est bonum eiusdem modi, tanto diuinius & eligibile magis. Unde Ioannis decimo: Et fiet unum ouile & unus pastor. Hic quidem pastor, & hoc quidem caput aliorum conuenientissimum videtur Romanus Episcopus propter causas in prioribus assignatas. Ex praedictis autem per necessitatem sequi videtur Romanum Episcopum solum causam effectiuam primam esse institutionis secundariae omnium aliorum, tam mediate quam immediate propter ipsius vniuersalem auctoritatem super reliquos omnes Episcopos, Presbyteros, & alios Ecclesiarum siue templorum ministros. Cui siquidem sententiae suffragatur auctoritas Ambrosii, de tradendis Basilicis, vbi sic ait: Ecclesia Dei est, Caesari vtiq; non debet ascribi. Ius Caesaris esse non potest Dei templum, nec per consequens institutio sacerdotum in eo, quam secundariam ipsorum auctoritatem vocauimus decimo quinto huius. Quod si Basilicarum traditio ius Caesaris esse non potest, eo minus alterius cuiusuis principantis. Erit igitur auctoritas haec illius, qui caput est, & primus omnium sacerdotum, Romani pontificis auctoritate diuina, si nullius principis ius esse potest. Hinc etiam necessario sequi videtur ipsius auctoritatem fore distribuendi seu conferendi beneficia, seu Ecclesiastica temporalia, quoniam propter exercenda officia conferuntur huiusmodi. Ex supradictis etiam inferri posse videtur, eiusdem Episcopi primi fore iurisdictionem coactiuam super reliquos omnes Episcopos mundi & alios templorum ministros. Sunt enim ordinatione diuina sibi subiecti, vt ex prioribus rationibus palam. Quod etiam potest astrui ex praedicto Isidori codice atque capitulo. Inter caetera nanque ibidem scripsit hanc seriem: Sed in eo concilio admirabile factum principis non puto reticendum. Etenim cum ex omnibus pene locis Episcopi conuenissent, & vt fieri solet, diuersis ex causis inter se quedam iurgia detulissent, interpellabatur frequenter, a singulis offerebantur libelli, culpae offerebantur, & magis ad hoc quam ad id pro quo venerant fuerat, animos dabant. At ille videns, quod per huiusmodi iurgia causa summi negotii frustraretur, diem certum statuit, quo vnusquisque Episcoporum, si quid querimonia habere videretur, deferret. Cumque recedisset, suscepit a singulis libellos, quos simul omnes in suo sinu continens, nec in eis quid contineretur aperiens: Ait ad Episcopos, Deus vos constituit sacerdotes, & potestatem vobis dedit, de nobis quoque iudicandi, & ideo nos a vobis recte iudicamur, vos autem non potestis ab hominibus iudicari, propter quod Dei solius inter vos expectate iudicium. Et vestra iurgia quaecunque sunt, ad illud diuinum referuntur examen. Vos etenim nobis a Deo datis estis dii. Conueniens non est, vt homo iudicet Deos. Ad eum ergo, qui talium Deorum Deus est in terris, videtur Romanum Episcopum pertinet in eos iurisdictionis auctoritas.
units.tr: Next, we can prove the same in particular, showing that Paul was not equal to the blessed Peter in dignity or authority. In Galatians 2 this sequence occurs: "Then," says Paul, "after three years I came to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I stayed with him fifteen days." And a little further on he adds in the same chapter: "Then after fourteen years I went up to Jerusalem again with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up according to a revelation, and I laid before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should run, or had run, in vain." The Gloss there: Paul, that is, shows that he did not have the security of the Gospel unless it had been confirmed by the authority of Peter and strengthened by the others. Since, then, according to the Gloss, Paul received the security of the Gospel from Peter, it appears that he was not equal to Peter in authority. Hence it seems to follow of necessity, both from this and from the other reasons stated above, that all the other bishops of the world are subject by divine ordination to the Roman bishop as the unique successor of the blessed Peter, and that the Roman Church is the head and first of all the others, on account of the authority of that bishop, the successor of the blessed Peter, and that he is the judge and shepherd of all the others. Isidore, expressing this more fully in the aforementioned codex, in the chapter whose title is "Here begins the preface of the Nicene council," says: "It must certainly be known by all Catholics that the holy Roman Church has been placed above no synodal decrees, but has obtained the primacy by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Saviour, when he said to the blessed Peter the Apostle: 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,' etc. By this primacy, apart from any grant by princes, all the Roman bishops from the time of the blessed Peter down to the times of Constantine the first, Emperor of the Romans, have been seen to hold it, namely by framing canons and by requiring their observance throughout the whole Church, as is plainly evident from the sequence of the said codex." I confirm this also by reason: since faith is one, according to the Apostle to the Ephesians chapter four, so the Church is one; but it is not one in any other way than through one head and beginning, and none is more fitting or equally fitting for this than the Roman bishop, the unique successor of the blessed Peter, who was the rock upon which Christ said he would found his Church. This is further confirmed by the fact that just as temporal things are reduced to one beginning, namely a principate, so spiritual things seem to have to be reduced to some one first, namely an episcopate. Again, from another point: just as in one temple or one diocese there must be one bishop, lest each priest drawing to himself break the Church of Christ, as we brought out from Jerome's letter to Evangelus in the fifteenth chapter of this book, so it is all the more necessary that there be one head in the whole Church of Christ, for the sake of preserving the unity of the faithful. For the more widely a good of the same kind is shared, the more divine and the more worthy of choice it is. Hence, John 10: "And there shall be one fold and one shepherd." This one shepherd and this one head of the others seems most fitting to be the Roman bishop, for the reasons assigned earlier. From the foregoing it seems to follow of necessity that the Roman bishop alone is the first efficient cause of the secondary institution of all the others, both mediately and immediately, on account of his universal authority over all the other bishops, elders, and the other ministers of the churches or temples. To this opinion the authority of Ambrose, in his treatise on surrendering the basilicas, lends support, where he says: "The Church is God's, and certainly must not be ascribed to Caesar. The temple of God cannot be under the right of Caesar, nor consequently the institution of priests in it, which we called the secondary authority of these in the fifteenth chapter of this book. But if the surrender of basilicas cannot be under Caesar's right, much less under that of any other ruler. This authority, therefore, will belong to him who is the head and first of all priests, the Roman pontiff, by divine authority, if it cannot belong to the right of any prince." Hence it also seems to follow necessarily that his authority is to distribute or confer benefices, or ecclesiastical temporalities, since such things are conferred for the sake of exercising offices. From the foregoing it may also seem to be inferred that the same first bishop has coercive jurisdiction over all the other bishops of the world and the other ministers of the temples. For they are subject to him by divine ordination, as is clear from the earlier arguments. This can also be supported from the aforementioned codex of Isidore and its chapter. For among other things he wrote there the following sequence: "But in that council I do not think a remarkable act of the prince should be passed over in silence. For when the bishops had assembled from nearly all places, and, as usually happens, had brought various quarrels against one another for various reasons, they were frequently importuned, petitions were offered by individuals, accusations were presented, and they were spurred on more to these matters than to the one for which they had come. But he, seeing that the chief business was being frustrated by such disputes, fixed a certain day on which each of the bishops, if he seemed to have any complaint, should lay it before him. And when he had withdrawn, he received the petitions from each, and holding them all together in his bosom, without opening them or revealing what was in them, he said to the bishops: 'God has appointed you priests and has given you power to judge even us, and therefore we are rightly judged by you, but you cannot be judged by men; so wait among yourselves for the judgement of God alone. Whatever your quarrels are, let them be referred to that divine examination. For you are gods given to us by God. It is not fitting that a man should judge gods.'" Therefore it seems that the authority of jurisdiction over those bishops pertains to the Roman bishop, to him who is God's representative on earth of such gods.

units.la: Ex iisdem quoque videtur eiusdem Episcopi auctoritatem fore, generalia sacerdotum concilia conuocare atque praecipere, in ipsis etiam proponere ac determinare, quae sibi proponenda & determinanda videntur circa legem diuinam & Ecclesiasticum ritum. De auctoritate siquidem congregandi concilii loquens Isidorus in praefatione operis iam dicti codicis, inquit sic: Synodorum vero congregandarum auctoritas, Apostolicae sedi priuata potestate commissa est, nec vllam synodum ratam esse legimus, quae eius non fuerit auctoritate congregata vel fulta. Haec Canonica testatur auctoritas, haec ecclesiastica roborat historia, haec sancti patres confirmant. De ea vero potestate siue auctoritate determinandi siue diffiniendi Scripturae sensum, loquens idem, eodem codice atque cap. dicit: Deinceps diuersorum concilio- rum liorum Græcorum ac Latinorum, siue quæ ante vel postmodum facta sunt, sub ordine numerorum ac temporum capitulis suis distincta sub huius voluminis aspectu locauimus, subiicientes etiam reliqua decreta prasulum Romanorum usque ad sanctum Gregorium, & quasdam Epistolas ipsius, in quibus pro calmine Sedis Apostolicæ non impar conciliorum extat auctoritas. Potest igitur summus pontifex sui autoritate solus id determinare, quod potest autoritas concilii generalis, ex quo non impar est eius autoritas, ei quæ concilii generalis, secundum Isidorum. Potest autem & debet autoritas generalis concilii scripturæ Sacræ dubias determinare, diffinire, ac interpretari sententias, quemadmodum ostensum est vigesimo huius. Eadem quoque videtur in hoc fuisse sententia Hieronymi in Epistola intitulata, de expositione Catholicæ fidei, vbi sic inquit: Hæc fides est, papa beatissime, quam in Catholica Ecclesia edidicimus quam semper tenuimus, in quasi minus perite aut parum occulte aliquod forte positum est, emendari cupimus à te, qui Petri & fidem & sedem tenes. Sin autem hac nostra confessio Apostolatus tui iudicio comprobatur, quicunque me maculare voluerit, se imperitum vel maleolum, vel etiam non catholicum, non me hereticum comprobabit.
units.tr: From the same passages it seems that it also belongs to the authority of the same Bishop to convene general councils of priests, to command, to propose in them, and to determine what seems to be proposed and determined for them concerning the divine law and the ecclesiastical rite. Isidore, speaking of the authority to convene a council in the preface to the work already mentioned, says: "The authority to convene synods has been committed by private power to the Apostolic See, nor do we read of any synod being valid that was not convened or supported by its authority. This the canonical authority attests, this ecclesiastical history confirms, and the holy fathers affirm." Concerning that power or authority to determine or define the sense of Scripture, the same Isidore, speaking in the same book and chapter, says: "Next, I have set out the various councils of the Greeks and Latins, whether held before or after, arranged under their own chapters in the order of numbers and times under the view of this volume, adding also the remaining decrees of the Roman prelates down to Saint Gregory, and certain letters of his, in which, for the support of the Apostolic See, the authority of the councils is not inferior." Therefore the supreme pontiff alone can by his own authority determine what the authority of a general council can determine, since, according to Isidore, his authority is not inferior to that of a general council. Moreover, the authority of a general council can and ought to determine doubtful passages of Holy Scripture, to define and interpret its meanings, as has been shown in the twentieth chapter of this work. The same opinion seems to have been held by Jerome in the letter entitled On the Exposition of the Catholic Faith, where he says: "This is the faith, most blessed Pope, which we learned in the Catholic Church and have always held. If anything in it has been put rather unskilfully or not clearly enough, we wish it to be corrected by you, who hold the faith and the see of Peter. But if this our confession is approved by the judgment of your Apostleship, whoever wishes to stain me will prove himself unskilled or ill-disposed, or even not Catholic, and will not prove me a heretic."

units.la: De potestate vero statuendi, quæ ad Ecclesiasticum ritum & æternam salutem pertinent, apparet ex oraculo Christi Lucæ decimo. Inquit enim Apostolis, & in ipsorum persona cunctis Episcopis siue Presbyteris: Qui vos spernit, me spernit: qui autem me spernit, spernit eum qui me misit. Sunt ergo de necessitate salutis sacerdotum obseruanda statuta. De his quidem igitur potestatibus assignatis Romano pontifici, & eis ampliioribus, collectionem faciens Beatus Bernardus ad Eugenium Papam, de consideratione libro secundo, sic ait: Nunc iam repetenda reliquia, si quasfunt, loci quem diseruimus. Age indagemus adhuc diligenter quis sis, quam geras videlicet pro tempore personam in Ecclesia Dei. Quis es? Sacerdos magnus, summus pontifex. Tu princeps Episcoporum: Tu hares Apostolorum, tu primatu Abel, gubernatu Noe, Patriarchatu Abraam, ordine Melchisedech, dignitate Aaron, autoritate Moses, iudicatu Samuel, potestate Petrus, vnctione Christus. Et subdit infra eodem continua sententia: Nec modo ouium, sed & pastorum, tu vnus omnium pastor. Vnde id probem quaeris? ex verbo Domini. Cui enim? non dico Episcoporum, sed etiam Apostolorum sic absolute & indiscrete, tota commissa sunt oues? Si me amas Petre, pasce oues meas. Et parum infra subiungit: Cui non planum, non designasse oues? nihil excipitur, vbi distinguitur nihil. Et infra rursum eodem, Inde est quod alii singuli singulas sortiti sunt plebes, scientes sacramentum: denique Iacobus, qui videbatur columna vna Ecclesiæ, vna contentus est Hierosolyma, Petro vniuersitatem cedens. Deinde vero concludens, ait sexto: Iuxta canones tuos, alii in partem sollicitudinis, tu in plenitudinem potestatis vocatus es, aliorum potestas certis arctatur limitibus, tua extenditur & in ipsos qui potestatem super alios acceperunt. Nonne si causa extiterit, tu Episcopo cœlum claudere, tu ipsum ab Episcopatu deponere, etiam & tradere Sathanae potes? Stat ergo inconcussum priuilegium tuum tibi, tam in datis claubis, quam in ouibus commendatis. Neque solum in Ecclesiasticos ministros, vt Episcopos, sacerdotes & inferiores ordines reliquos, autoritatem dixit Bernhardus habere Romanum pontificem, verum etiam & coactiuam iurisdictionem super omnes principantes, quam temporalem gladium idem Bernhardus sub metaphora vocat, eidem Episcopo videtur ascribere. Vnde idem ad eundem Eugenium libro quinto, capitulo quarto sic ait: Quid tu denuo vsurpare gladium tentes, quem semel inssus es reponere in vaginam? qui tamen, qui tuum negat, non satis mihi videtur attendere verbum Domini dicentis sic: Conuerte gladium tuum in vaginam. Tuus ergo & ipse forsitan tuo nutu, si non tua manu euaginandus. Alioquin, si nullo modo ad te pertineret, & his dicentibus Apostolis: Et ecce gladii duo hic, non respondisset Dominus, satis est, sed nimis est. Vterque ergo Ecclesia, & spiritualis scilicet gladius & materialis, sed is quidem pro ecclesia, ille vero & ab ecclesia exercendus, ille sacerdotis, is militis manu, sed sane ad nutum sacerdotis & iussum Imperatoris. Sunt autem ad supradicta firmanda sanctorum aliæ autoritates quam plures, harum tamen seriem inducere omisi, propter eandem aut consimilem earum esse cum inductis virtutem & eundem aut consimilem modum soluendi, & propter abbreuiationem sermonis. Amplius videntur hæc posse firmari per Decretales & decreta quædam pontificum Romanorum. His enim cauetur omnia officia Ecclesiastica, & propter hoc instituta beneficia, per Episcopum Romanum & alios, nequaquam vero per humanum legislatorem, aut eius autoritate principantem, statui vel conferri debere. Cauetur & rursum eisdem Decretalibus & Decretis, sacerdotes & clericos non debere subire iudicium coactiuum iam dicti legislatoris aut principantis, sed potius econuerso. Eisdem quoque astruitur omnes potestates conuenire Romano pontifici, quas eidem in suis sermonibus ascribit Bernhardus.
units.tr: Concerning the power to enact what pertains to ecclesiastical rite and eternal salvation, it appears from the saying of Christ in Luke 10. For he says to the Apostles, and in their person to all bishops or presbyters: "He who despises you despises me, and he who despises me despises him who sent me." Therefore the statutes of the priests must be observed as a matter of necessity for salvation. Gathering these powers assigned to the Roman pontiff, and greater ones, Blessed Bernard, in his second book On Consideration, addressed to Pope Eugenius, says: "Now let us take up again the remaining points, if any, of the place we have discussed. Come, let us examine more carefully who you are, what person you bear for the time in the Church of God. Who are you? A great priest, the supreme pontiff. You are the prince of bishops; you are the heir of the apostles; by primacy you are Abel, by government Noah, by patriarchate Abraham, by order Melchizedek, by dignity Aaron, by authority Moses, by judgment Samuel, by power Peter, by anointing Christ." He adds a little below, in the same continuous passage: "Not only of the sheep but also of the shepherds, you alone are the shepherd of all. Whence do you seek to prove this? From the word of the Lord. To whom, I ask, not of bishops but even of apostles, were all the sheep entrusted so absolutely and without distinction? 'If you love me, Peter, feed my sheep.'" And a little further: "To whom is it not plain that the sheep were not assigned? Nothing is excepted where nothing is distinguished." And again further on in the same work: "Hence it is that the others each received single peoples, knowing the sacrament; finally James, who seemed the one pillar of the Church, was content with Jerusalem alone, yielding the universality to Peter." Then, concluding, he says in the sixth book: "According to your canons, others are called to a part of the care, but you to the fullness of power. The power of others is restricted within fixed limits, but yours extends even over those who have received power over others. If there is cause, can you not shut heaven against a bishop, depose him from the episcopate, and even hand him over to Satan? Your privilege therefore stands unshaken, both in the keys given and in the sheep committed." Nor did Bernard say that the Roman pontiff has authority only over ecclesiastical ministers, such as bishops, priests and the remaining lower orders, but also coercive jurisdiction over all rulers, which he calls by metaphor the temporal sword, and which he seems to ascribe to the same bishop. Hence the same Bernard, writing to the same Eugenius in the fifth book, chapter four, says: "Why do you again try to seize the sword, which you were once ordered to put back into its sheath? He who denies that it is yours does not seem to me to heed sufficiently the word of the Lord saying: 'Put your sword into its sheath.' Therefore it is yours too, to be drawn at your nod, if not by your own hand. Otherwise, if it did not pertain to you in any way, the Lord, when the Apostles said, 'Behold, here are two swords,' would not have answered 'It is enough,' but 'It is too much.' Both swords, then, belong to the Church, the spiritual and the material; but the one is to be wielded for the Church, the other by the Church; the one by the hand of the priest, the other by the hand of the soldier, but indeed at the nod of the priest and at the bidding of the emperor." There are also many other authorities of the saints to confirm the above, but I have omitted to set out their series, since they have the same or a similar force as those brought forward and the same or a similar way of answering them, and for brevity's sake. Further, these things seem capable of being confirmed by certain Decretals and decrees of the Roman pontiffs. For by these it is provided that all ecclesiastical offices, and on this account the benefices instituted, are to be established or conferred by the Roman bishop and others, and in no way by a human lawgiver or a ruler exercising his authority. It is also provided, again, by these same Decretals and Decrees, that priests and clergy ought not to submit to the coercive judgment of the aforesaid lawgiver or ruler, but rather the reverse. By the same Decretals it is also asserted that all the powers which Bernard ascribes to the Roman pontiff in his sermons belong to him.

units.la: De responsionibus ad prædictas instantias.
units.tr: On the answers to the aforementioned objections.

units.la: RESiduum autem huius dictionis est, Scripturæ siue canonis autoritates conuenienter exponere, ac humanas rationes dissoluere, quæ tertio huius, & capitulo præcedente inductæ, nostris determinationibus contrariæ videbantur. Ante tamen bene se habet reminisci, quod diximus decimo nono huius, iuxta sententiam beati Augustini & infallibilem rationem in scriptura firmatam, videlicet, quod nulli sermoni vel scripturæ siue credulitatem certam, aut confessionem veritatis præstare tenemur de necessitate salutis, nisi eis, quæ canonica appellantur. idest quae in volumine Bibliae continentur, & in eis quae ad has per necessitatem sequuntur, & scripturarum sacrarum dubium sensum habentium eis interpretationibus, quae per generale fidelium seu catholicorum concilium essent factae, praesertim in his clausulis, in quibus error damnationem aeternam induceret, quales sunt articuli fidei Christianae, cum suis interpretationibus, factis in conciliis generalibus rationabiliter convocatis, celebratis, & consummatis. Propter quod auctoritates canonis sacri sive Scripturae, quae mystica expositione non egent, secundum ipsarum sensum literalem manifestum sequemur omnino, in quibus vero mystica expositione indigent sanctorum, probabiliori adhaerebo sententiae. Quas vero ipsorum auctoritate propria praeter scriptura protulerunt sententias, Scripturae sive canoni consonas, recipiam. Quas vero dissonas reverenter abiiciam: non tamen aliter quam auctoritate scripturae, cui semper innitar, quoniam & ipsi quandoque; circa scripturam & praeter scripturam sententiis ad invicem dissident, ut Hieronymus & Augustinus super illud 2. ad Galat. Cum autem venisset Cephas Antiochiam, in faciem ei restiti, quia reprehensibilis erat. Et rursum Ambrosius cum Hieronymo de virginitate Ioseph. Amplius & idem ipsi sibi sanctorum aliquis quandoque; dissona profert, ut ex sequentibus manifeste patebit. Hinc ergo primum ad instantias, quae inductae sunt capitulo praecedenti. Cum enim ex Luca decimo sumebatur, Episcopos esse maioris dignitatis quam simplices sacerdotes, ex eo quod ibidem habetur: Post haec autem designavit Dominus & alios 72. per quos secundum Bedam figuratur ordo Presbyterorum, quem secundum appellat, post episcoporum ordinem scilicet. Dicendum, quod iuxta sententiam Apostoli, & ea quae de sanctis inducta sunt 15. huius, convenientius figuratur per 72. Diaconorum ordo, quam sacerdotum. Vel potest dici convenienter, quod non propter hoc sequitur Episcopu, ordinem essentialem ampliorem habere Presbytero. Unde illa missio, qua Christus eos misit in mundum, significavit electionem sive institutionem humanam, qua unus eorum caeteris praeferretur in Ecclesiastica oeconomia. Non enim contulit Christus eis, cum dixit, Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, dignitatem essentialem, sed prius tradiderat. Et esto quod simili tempore utranque tradidisset, dico quod illa missio non addidit intrinseca perfectionem, quam prius non habuissent cum sacerdotium per Spiritum sanctum receperunt. Fuit autem de Apostolis super reliquos futuros sacerdotes, facta per Christu haec institutio secundaria, quoniam nulla tunc erat multitudo fidelium, per quam posset huiusmodi electio celebrari. Nec si fuisset, adhucque convenienter fieri potuisset per aliquam multitudinem, sicut per Christum. Unde Apostoli etiam post Christi passionem & resurrectionem, ad electionem in diuidendis prouinciis se reduxerunt. Namad Galatas secundo legitur: Dexteras dederunt mihi & Barnabae societatis, ut nos quidem in gentes, ipsi vero in circumcisionem, Iacobus, Cephas, & Ioannes. Et ideo esto quod figura fuisset, qualem dixit Beda de statu sacerdotii. Dico quod intrinsecam dignitatem sive perfectionem aut characterem a Deo immediate, non habet amplior Episcopus quam sacerdos, & horum ratio sufficiens assignata est 15. huius. Ad reliquam vero instantiam exprimae ad Timoth. quinto: Adversus Presbyterum. &c. Dico quod secundam institutionem non essentialem acceperat ab Apostolo super Presbyteros alios in illa provincia, cuius siquidem Apostoli voluntas & institutio, electioni aequivalebat propter defectum & insufficientiam, sive ruditatem multitudinis fidelium. Unde Apostolus primae ad Corinthios 3. Et ego fratres non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus. Tanquam parvulis in Christo vobis lac potum dedi non esca. Nondum enim poteratis, sed ne nunc quidem poteritis, adhuc enim estis carnales. Hoc autem explicauimus amplius 17. huius, parte 7. Quod autem inducebatur de Clementis Epistola, quae intitulatur ad Iacobum fratrem Domini, non recipio tanquam certum, nam Epistolam fuisse Clementis, valde suspectum est, propter plura in ipsa contenta. Rursum suspecti sunt hi canones seu Epistolae, quoniam in ea quae de sacramentis, vestibus & vasis ad Iacobum fratrem Domini, & in ea quae de communi Apostolorum vita intitulantur, scribitur, ac si Clemens Iacobo narret ea quae Christus cum Apostolis egit. Haec autem fuisset magna ignorantia; non modo dicam praesumptio Clementis, quod ea quae tantum audiuerat, significare vellet, quasi per modum doctrinae, illi qui praesens interfuerat, & Christum cum Apostolis, quorum unus fuerat, ipse viderat. Quis enim discipulos, qui Hierosolymis erant, melius instruere poterat de vita Christi & Apostolorum, quis de ritu Ecclesiastico plus nosse debuit, an Apostolus aut successor Apostoli, nemo est qui dubitet, propter quod ipsae sunt cum Apocryphis computandae. Sed esto quod Clementis fuerint, ut quidam asserunt, fabularibus innisi sermonibus, etiam prorumpentes in tantum; ut Clementem dicant, quia Romanus erat Episcopus, maioris auctoritatis in Ecclesia Dei, Apostolo Iacobo. A quibus quaerendum conuenienter, cur Epistola Clementis in contextu Sacri Canonis positae non sunt, sicut ea quae Iacobi? Dicemus tamen ad ea quae in dictis Epistolis conuenientia videbantur Christi & Apostolorum sententiae, cum auctoritates scripturae tractabimus, quibus inniti videntur. Ad id autem quod dicebatur, hanc fuisse sententiam omnium Episcoporum, qui Beato Petro successerunt in Episcopali sede Romana, dicendum est, quemadmodum diximus ad primam instantiam, sic eos intellexisse, si vero aliter, ipsis relictis; sequimur Apostolum & Hieronymum 15. & 16. huius.
units.tr: The remaining part of this discussion is to set out properly the authorities of Scripture or the canon, and to dissolve the human arguments which were introduced in the third chapter of this work and the preceding chapter and seemed contrary to our conclusions. Yet first it is well to recall what we said in the nineteenth chapter of this work, following the opinion of blessed Augustine and the infallible reasoning established in Scripture, namely that we are bound by necessity of salvation to give certain belief or confession of truth to no speech or writing, except to those things which are called canonical, that is, those contained in the volume of the Bible, and to those things which follow from these of necessity, and to the interpretations of doubtful passages of the sacred Scriptures which were made by the general council of the faithful or Catholics, especially in those articles in which error would bring eternal damnation, such as the articles of the Christian faith, together with their interpretations made in general councils rightly convoked, celebrated and concluded. For this reason we shall follow altogether the plain literal sense of the authorities of the sacred canon or Scripture, which do not need mystical exposition; where they do need mystical exposition, we shall cleave to the more probable opinion of the saints. But the opinions which they have put forward on their own authority apart from Scripture, I shall accept if they agree with Scripture or the canon; those which disagree I shall reverently reject, yet not otherwise than by the authority of Scripture, on which I shall always rest, since the saints themselves sometimes disagree with one another, both about Scripture and beyond Scripture, as Jerome and Augustine did on that passage of Galatians 2, But when Cephas had come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. And again Ambrose disagreed with Jerome on the virginity of Joseph. Moreover, one and the same saint sometimes puts forward conflicting views, as will be clearly seen from what follows. Let me therefore first take up the objections which were brought forward in the preceding chapter. When it was argued from Luke 10 that bishops are of greater dignity than simple priests, because it is there written, After these things the Lord appointed also seventy-two others, by whom, according to Bede, the order of the presbyters is figured, which he calls the second order, namely after the order of bishops, I answer: according to the opinion of the Apostle, and what has been said of the saints in the fifteenth chapter of this work, the order of the seventy-two is more fitly figured as the order of deacons than of priests. Or it may fitly be said that it does not follow from this that a bishop has a higher essential order than a presbyter. That mission by which Christ sent them into the world signified a human election or appointment, by which one of them was set above the others in the ecclesiastical economy. For Christ did not confer on them an essential dignity when he said, Go therefore and teach all nations; he had given it to them earlier. And even if he had conferred both at the same time, I say that that mission did not add any inward perfection which they had not possessed before, when they received the priesthood through the Holy Spirit. Now this secondary institution, by which some of the Apostles were set over the other future priests, was made by Christ, since at that time there was no multitude of the faithful by which such an election could be carried out. Nor, even if there had been, could it fittingly have been done by a multitude, as it was done by Christ. Hence the Apostles too, even after Christ's passion and resurrection, reverted to election in the division of provinces. For it is read in Galatians 2: They gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision: James, Cephas, and John. And so, even if it were a figure of the kind Bede spoke of concerning the state of the priesthood, I say that the bishop has no greater inward dignity or perfection or character from God immediately than the priest, and the sufficient reasons for this were given in the fifteenth chapter of this work. As for the other objection, from the words of 1 Timothy 5, Against an elder, etc., I say that he had received from the Apostle a secondary, non-essential institution over the other elders in that province, and the Apostle's will and institution in that matter amounted to an election, on account of the defect, insufficiency, or rudeness of the multitude of the faithful. Hence the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 3: And I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal. As to babes in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able, nor even now are you able, for you are still carnal. I have explained this more fully in the seventeenth chapter of this work, part 7. As for what was brought forward from the epistle of Clement, which is entitled To James the brother of the Lord, I do not accept it as certain, for that it was written by Clement is very doubtful, on account of many things contained in it. Likewise these canons or epistles are suspect, since in the writings entitled On the sacraments, vestments and vessels, addressed to James the brother of the Lord, and in the one entitled On the common life of the Apostles, it is written as if Clement were relating to James what Christ did with the Apostles. Yet this would have been great ignorance, not to say presumption on Clement's part, that he should wish to set forth, as a teaching, to one who had been present, what he had only heard, and about Christ and the Apostles, of whom one had been, whom he himself had seen. For who could better instruct the disciples who were at Jerusalem about the life of Christ and the Apostles? Who ought to know more about ecclesiastical rite than an Apostle, or a successor of an Apostle? No one can doubt this, and therefore these writings are to be counted among the Apocrypha. But even if they were Clement's, as some assert, relying on fabulous discourses, and even breaking out to such a degree that they say Clement, because he was bishop of Rome, had greater authority in the Church of God than the Apostle James, one must fairly ask them why the epistles of Clement have not been placed in the context of the sacred canon, as those of James have been? We shall nevertheless say, when we treat the authorities of Scripture on which they seem to rest, what agrees in those epistles with the opinions of Christ and the Apostles. As for what was said, that this was the opinion of all the bishops who succeeded blessed Peter in the Roman episcopal see, it must be said, as we said in answer to the first objection, that they understood it in this way; but if otherwise, we set them aside and follow the Apostle and Jerome, in the fifteenth and sixteenth chapters of this work.

units.la: Ad eas vero canonis auctoritates, quibus videtur ostendi, beatum Petrum superiorem dignitate caeteris Apostolis, non solum humana electione, verum etiam immediata Christi ordinatione, cum primo inducebatur ex Matthaei 16. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam: & tibi dabo claves regni caelorum, &c. Per quae verba Christus ipsum videretur instituisse in sui saltem absentia, caput & fundamentum Ecclesiae; dico caput & fundamentum Ecclesia unicum esse & fuisse ordinatione immediata Dei: & hoc Christum, Apostolorum vero neminem, etiam in absentia Christi, quemadmodum per scripturam indubie convincimus in sexto & 22. huius. Ad canonem ergo, cum dicitur, super hanc petram &c. dico secundum Glossam, super hanc petram, id est super Christum, in quem credit. Vbi Glossa interlinearis addit, Tu es Petrus, id est à me petra, ita tamen ut mihi retineam fundamenti dignitatem. Petrum autem vocavit eum Christus, id est constantem in fide, quod non negamus. Esto enim quod aliis constantior & merito perfectior, non propter hoc dignitate prior, nisi tempore forte, ut evidentior per scripturam probavimus, ubi supra. Eum autem quem diximus fuisse scripturae sensum, adiuvat expositio beati Augustini super hunc locum, inquit enim Augustinus, & sumptum est ex libro Retractationum: Dixi in quodam loco de Apostolo Petro, quod in illo tanquam in petra aedificata sit Ecclesia, sed scio me postea sapientissime expositisse, quod a Domino dictum est, Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, ut super hunc intelligeretur, quem confessus est Petrus, dicens, Tu es Christus filius Dei vivi, ac si Petrus ab hac petra appellatus, personam Ecclesiae figuraret, quae super hanc petram aedificatur. Non enim dictum est illi, tu es petra, sed tu es Petrus, petra autem erat Christus, quem confessus Simon. Sicut ei, (Christo scilicet) tota Ecclesia confitetur delus est Petrus. Et potest huius ratio assignari secundum scripturam, quoniam Petrus quamdiu viator extitit, errare potuit & peccare per sui arbitrii libertatem, unde Christum negasse legitur, & quandoque ad veritatem Evangelii ambulasse non recte: tale autem non poterat esse fundamentum Ecclesiae, sed ille solus fuit Christus, ut appareat prima ad Cor. 3. qui aberrare non potuit, eo quod ab instanti suae conceptionis impeccabilis fuerit confirmatus. Unde Apostolus ubi supra: Fundamentum enim aliud nemo ponere potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Et quod addebatur, tibi dabo claves regni caelorum, nullam Petro super reliquos Apostolos auctoritatem tribuit, quoniam hanc eandem iudiciariam potestatem ceteris Apostolis tribuit, secundum Hieron. & Rabanum, quorum Glossas induximus sexto huius, parte 3. Amplius, quoniam Christus potestatem clavium illi non videtur tradidisse per haec verba, inquit enim, tibi dabo, quod sonat futurum, dixit, Dom. Sed Iohan. vigesimo indifferenter omnibus dixit: Accipite Spiritum sanctum, & quorum remiseritis peccata, &c. Esto tamen quod Petrus his verbis potestatem hanc recepisset, non concluditur ex hoc, nisi quod tempore prius fuerit pastor institutus, & quod illi singulariter has tradiderit Christus claves, signare voluit Ecclesiae unitatem in fide, ad quam fideles invitavit Christus per singularem clavium traditionem sive promissionem, ut Glossa dicit: vel fortasse, quia Christum Dei Filium esse primum constanter & manifeste confessus est, primum tempore dotatur clavibus & honoratur aut honorari promittitur, ut sic etiam confitendi Christum palam & constanter per huiusmodi praemium promissum, ceteris praeberetur exemplum, non tamen propter hoc convincitur, ipsum fuisse ceteris dignitate sive autoritate priorem, quamvis hoc plures Glossatorum dicere videantur a se, non habentes hoc ex Scriptura. Significat autem infallibiliter nos verum dicere sequens Evangelii series, quae habetur eiusdem Matth. vigesimo vbi Christus quaesitum hoc aperte diffiniens, dixit, nullum illorum esse superiorem aliis. Facta enim erat contentio inter eos, quis eorum esset maior. Idemque 22. ad quos sic inquit Christus: Vos autem (invicem, supple,) nolite vocari rabbi, unus est enim magister, vester omnes autem vos fratres estis. Omnes autem fratres, id est aequales, non ergo excepit aliquem. Et est mirandum, si magis credere debeamus auctoritati Glossatoris quam Christi, quicunque fuerit ille Glossator etiam sanctus, & maxime, cum hoc non dicat tanquam Glossator, sed proprio sensu. Series enim scripturae tam manifesta est, quod Glossa non eget in hoc. Amplius, quoniam & ipsae Glossae oppositum dicunt, ad Galatas exponentes secundum, sicut apertum est 16. huius. Tractavimus autem istud sufficienter & iterum 4. & 16. huius, nec reiteravimus omnes probationes propter rei notitiam & abbreviationem sermonis. Ad aliam vero canonis auctoritatem sumptam ex Luca vigesimo secundo, Dixit enim Christus beato Petro, Ego autem rogavi pro te Petre, ut non deficiat fides tua, & tu aliquando conversus, confirma fratres tuos. Ex qua quidem serie inferunt aliqui duo: unum quod solius Ecclesiae Romanae fides deficere nequit, eo quod de fide Petri Christus intellexit etiam fidem successorum, & consequenter Episcopum sibi successorem, aliorum primum: secundum vero quod ex hoc Christus ipsum reliquorum Apostolorum praelatum fecerit. Dico neutrum sequi ex verbis Christi per virtutem sermonis. In hac enim consequentia stat oppositum consequentis cum antecedente. Secundo probo per scripturam neutrum sequi, & per verba Christi, non alia. Primum quidem iam dictorum non sequitur, propterea quod omnibus dixit Christus Matth. ultimo, Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes &c. Et, ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus ad usque ad consummationem saeculi. Si Christus ergo ispospondit se cum aliis futurum, usque in saeculi consummationem omnibus diebus, ergo intellexit etiam de aliorum successoribus, si de successoribus Petri hoc debet intelligi. Amplius, quoniam si successor beati Petri singulariter dicatur Romanus Episcopus, constat haereticum quendam aut quosdam in sede illa tanquam Episcopum fuisse praefectum, ut de Liberio & quibusdam aliis ostensum est 28. huius Rufsum quia 16. huius monstratum est, Romanum Episcopum non esse singulariter successorem beati Petri, propter causas secundum scripturam assignatas ibidem. Reliqua consequentia similiter nulla est, quod probo etiam per scripturam. Contulit enim Paulus Petro in Evangelio, non contra, ut ex 2. ad Galatas induximus satis 16. huius. Et quod evidentius est, huius consequentiae destructionum est sermo Christi pridem inductus, ex Matth. vigesimo, & Luc. vigesimo secundo, per quem ex aperto sui sensu determinavit Christus & diffinivit oppositum. Unde Glossa exponens hunc locum.
units.tr: As for the canonical texts by which it seems to be shown that blessed Peter was superior in dignity to the other Apostles, not only by human election but also by the immediate ordination of Christ, the first is Matthew 16: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc. By these words Christ would seem to have appointed him, at least in Christ's own absence, the head and foundation of the Church. I say that the head and foundation of the Church is and has been one only, by the immediate ordination of God, and that this is Christ, and not any of the Apostles, even in Christ's absence, as we prove beyond doubt from Scripture in chapters 6 and 22 of this work. So when it is said upon this rock, etc., I say, according to the Gloss, upon this rock, that is, upon Christ, in whom he believes. The interlinear Gloss adds: You are Peter, that is, a rock from me, yet so that I keep for myself the dignity of the foundation. Christ called him Peter, that is, steadfast in faith, which we do not deny. For even if he was steadfaster than the others and rightly more perfect, he was not on that account superior in dignity, except perhaps in time, as we have shown more clearly from Scripture above. The sense of Scripture that we have stated is also supported by the exposition of blessed Augustine on this passage. For Augustine says, and it is taken from the Book of Retractations: I said in a certain place about the Apostle Peter that the Church was built on him as on a rock; but I know that I afterwards explained, most wisely, what the Lord said, You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church: that it be understood as upon him whom Peter confessed, saying, You are Christ, the Son of the living God. As if Peter, named from this rock, represented the person of the Church, which is built upon this rock. For it was not said to him, you are the rock, but you are Peter; the rock, however, was Christ, whom Simon confessed. Just as the whole Church confesses him (Christ, that is), so Peter, who confessed him, is named Peter. A reason for this may also be given from Scripture: while Peter was a wayfarer he could err and sin through the freedom of his own will, whence we read that he denied Christ, and at times did not walk rightly in the truth of the Gospel. Such a man could not be the foundation of the Church; only Christ was, as appears from 1 Cor. 3., who could not go astray, because he was confirmed in sinlessness from the moment of his conception. Hence the Apostle, in the place cited: For no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. As for the added words, to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, they grant Peter no authority over the other Apostles, since Christ gave the same judicial power to the other Apostles as well, according to Jerome and Rabanus, whose Glosses we cited in chapter 6 of this work, part 3. Moreover, Christ does not seem to have given him the power of the keys by these words, for he said to you I will give, which signifies the future, but in John 20 he said indifferently to all: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, etc. Even if Peter had received this power by these words, it would not follow from this unless he was appointed a minister earlier in time, and unless Christ gave the keys to him alone in order to signify the unity of the Church in faith, to which Christ invited the faithful through the singular giving or promise of the keys, as the Gloss says. Or perhaps, because he was the first to confess constantly and openly that Christ is the Son of God, he was first endowed with the keys in time and was honoured, or was promised honour, so that the others might be given an example of confessing Christ openly and constantly through such a reward promised. Yet it is not thereby proved that he was superior to the others in dignity or authority, although several of the Glossators seem to say this on their own, not having it from Scripture. The following series of the Gospel infallibly shows that we speak the truth, in which Christ, clearly settling this very question, said that none of them was superior to the others. For a contention had arisen among them as to which of them was the greatest. The same thing is found in chapter 22, where Christ says to them: But you (one to another, understand) do not be called rabbi; for one is your teacher, and all of you are brothers. All are brothers, that is, equals; therefore he excepted no one. And it is to be wondered at, if we ought to believe the authority of a Glossator rather than that of Christ, whoever that Glossator may be, even if holy, and especially since he does not say this as a Glossator but in his own sense. For the sequence of Scripture is so plain that the Gloss is not needed here. Moreover, the Glosses themselves say the opposite, explaining the second passage in Galatians, as is clear in chapter 16 of this work. We have treated this sufficiently, and again in chapters 4 and 16 of this work, and we have not repeated all the proofs, for the sake of brevity and of the reader's acquaintance with the matter. Next, the other canonical text, taken from Luke 22: Christ said to blessed Peter: But I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers. From this series some infer two things: first, that the faith of the Roman Church alone cannot fail, since Christ meant by Peter's faith also the faith of his successors, and consequently of the bishop who succeeds him, the first of the others; second, that by this Christ made him the prelate of the remaining Apostles. I say that neither follows from the words of Christ by the force of the statement. For in this inference the opposite of the consequent stands with the antecedent. Second, I prove from Scripture, and from the words of Christ alone, that neither follows. The first of the things just mentioned does not follow, because Christ said to all at the end of Matthew: Go therefore and teach all nations, etc. And: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age. If Christ therefore promised that he would be with the others all days until the consummation of the age, then he intended this also of the successors of the others, if it must be understood of the successors of Peter. Moreover, if the successor of blessed Peter is to be called singularly the Roman bishop, it is plain that some heretic or heretics were set over that see as bishop, as has been shown of Liberius and certain others in chapter 28 of this work. Again, since it was shown in chapter 16 of this work that the Roman bishop is not singularly the successor of blessed Peter, for the reasons assigned from Scripture in that place. The second consequence is likewise null, which I prove also from Scripture. For Paul withstood Peter in the Gospel, not the reverse, as we sufficiently cited from Galatians 2 in chapter 16 of this work. And what is more evident: the words of Christ, cited above from Matthew 20 and Luke 22, destroy this consequence, by which Christ, from the plain sense of his own words, determined and defined the opposite. Hence the Gloss, explaining this passage:

units.la: (Second, marginal numerals as printed.) locum inquit, Sicut ego te orando protexi ne deficeres, sic tu infirmiores fratres exemplo tuae poenitentiae conforta, ne de venia desperent, intelligens per fratres indifferenter fideles. Quod etiam dicens Petro fecit, alios Apostolos intelligere facturos. Unde Marci decimo tertio: Quod uni dico, vel secundum aliam litteram, sensum tamen eundem, quod vobis dico, omnibus dico. Aut fortasse id Petro singulariter dixit, sicut etiam Glossa sentire videtur; quoniam praesciebat Christus Petrum se negaturum. Unde, tu conversus aliquando, id est, exemplo tuae poenitentiae, eo quod verbo & sui exemplo, qui veniam meruerat, infirmos in fide singularius confortare seu confirmare volebat; ne scilicet de venia desperarent. Ad reliquam autem canonis auctoritatem sumptam Ioan. vigesimo primo, per quam idem quod prius quidam nituntur convincere; ex eo quod Christus beato Petro dixit, Pasce oves meas, pasce agnos meos, &c. Dicendum primo secundum Glossam huc esse sensum huius seriei, quod pascere oves est credentes ne deficiant confortare, terrena subsidia si necesse est, subditis providere, exempla virtutum praebere, adversarios obsistere, fidei scilicet, peccantes corrigere Et subditur in Glossa, & cum tertio audit a Petro se diligi, iubet pascere oves, trina negatione redditur trina confessio; ne minus amori lingua serviat, quam timori. Ex hoc autem non convincitur, nisi quod ipsum pastorem ovium Christus instituit: non tamen ex hoc sequitur quod ipsum super reliquos Apostolos auctoritate vel dignitate priorem: nec rursum sequitur ex hoc, alios Apostolos non fuisse institutos pastores. Oppositum enim utriusque; consequentis iam dicti stat cum antecedente, videlicet cum sermone Christi praedicto. Testatur autem dictis, quod Ecclesia Catholica cantat de omnibus Apostolis indifferenter, Vere dignum & iustum est, aequum & salutare, te quidem omni tempore supplicitier exorare, ut gregem tuum pastor aeternus non deseras, sed per beatos Apostolos tuos continua protectione custodias. Ut eisdem rectoribus gubernetur, quos operis tui vicarios eidem contuisti praesse pastores. Ecce Apostolos in plurali, rectores, vicarios, & pastores, per Christi collationem immediatam. Non autem solum aliquem rectorem, vicarium, aut pastorem constitutum per Christum: Interroganti vero, cur Christus hoc Petro singulariter dixit, dicendum vitique, quod Christus quandoque sermonem dirigebat ad hominem in persona propria, ut in remissione peccatorum, sanatione infirmorum, & suscitatione mortuorum, quandoque; vero dirigebat sermonem ad alterum in persona omnium aut plurium, ut in Ioan 5. Vade & amplius noli peccare, ne deterius tibi contingat. Unde id officium Christus committendo Petro, illi loquebatur in persona omnium Apostolorum, sicut ipsemet testatur huc modum loquendi suum; Marci 13. cum dixit; Quod autem uni vel vobis dico, omnibus dico Specialiter tamen ad Petrum sermonem direxit, quia senior erat, vel quia charitate ardentior, vel ut significaret Ecclesiae futurae quales debeant pastores institui, quoniam aetate maturi, ex qua signatur prudentia, seu scientia, & charitate pleni, ex qua significatur cura & diligentia quas debent habere pastores, aut fortasse ne videretur abiectior, quia Christum negaverat, quod sapere videtur Glossa, cum dixit, trina negatione redditur trina confessio, ne minus amori lingua serviat quam timori. Hoc enim certissime constat, quod omnibus, Matt. vi. dictum est indifferenter. Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, necdixit Petro, Vade & alios mitte, in quo significavit omnibus autoritatis aequalitatem, sicut etiam ex Matt. 13. pridem induximus, dum ad eos inquit Christus, Nolite vocari Rabbi, sulple inuicem aut unus super reliquum vel reliquos. Unum enim est magister vester, vos autem omnes fratres estis. Aut dicendum & valde probabiliter, atque secundum veritatem mihi videtur quod pro tanto dixit Petro; Pasce oves meas, ut sibi specialiter propter sui constantiam committeret populum Israel, qui & duae cervicis populus fuit versus Deum, ut apparet Exodi 33. Et inducit Apostolus per Esaiam Actuum ultimo Et quoniam propter hunc populum convertendum & salvandum principaliter venerat Christus. Unde Matt. 15. Non sum missus nisi ad oves quae perierunt domus Israel. Non sum missus, principaliter, supple. Idcirco huius populi curam beato Petro specialiter commississe videtur, cum dixit, Pasce oves meas. Et videtur haec fuisse Apostoli aperta sententia, cum ad Gal. 2. dixit; Cum vidissent quod creditum est mihi Evangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis &c. vbi Glossa secundum Aug. Cum vidissent quod Evangelium praeputii creditum est mihi ut fideli, ita principaliter, sicut Petro Evangelium circumcisionis. Christus enim dedit Paulo, ut ministraret gentibus, qui etiam dederat Petro ut ministraret Iudaeis, ita tamen dispensatio distributa est illis, ut & Petrus gentibus praedicaret, si causa fecisset; & Paulus Iudaeis. Nec video quod Paulus, vel alter sanctus aliunde sumere potuerit ex scriptura, populum Iudaicum specialiter & principaliter fuisse Petro commissum, nisi ex eo quod Christus dixit illi, Pasce oves meas. Cum dicat Paulus ad Gal. 2. fili creditum Evangelium praeputii, quemadmodum Petro circumcisionis. Si namque creditum erit Petro Evangelium vniuersaliter plusquam Paulo, vel alius; inconvenienter utique dixisset Paulus verba praedicta, quinimo totus eius sermo fuisset inanis, & comparatio quam fecit in eo ad glossas sanctorum & reliquorum doctorum. Super haec tria puncta scripturae iam dicta dicemus in fine capituli huius, ne idem saepius iterare contingat. Ad dictum vero Apostoli ad Gal. 2. per quod videbatur ipsum auctoritate fuisse minore Apostolo Petro, per id quod dixit; Contuli cum illis Evangelium quod praedico in gentibus, ne forte in vacuum currerem aut cucurrissem &c. dicendum primo secundum Glossam Aug. super hunc locum, Inquit enim, & non didici ab illo tanquam maioribus; sed contuli cum eis tanquam amicus & paribus. Quod autem secundum Hieron. Glossa inducit super id, Ne in vacuum currerem &c. Ostendit, inquit Glossa secundum Hieronymum; se non habuisse securitatem Evangelii, nisi etiam auctoritate Petri confirmatum & aliorum roboratum. Dico cum reverentia, haec Glossa vel sibi contradiceret, in eo quod infra dicitur secundum eundem Hieronymum si sic intelligatur; quemadmodum qui adversatur sententiae, quam dicimus, videtur intendere. Vel oportet Glossam hanc secundum Hieron. intelligi, secundum id quod in ea subditur secundum Aug. Non enim fuit ista causa collationis, quia ipse dubitaret se non habere certitudinem Euangelii, sed hæc vt magis ab audientibus crederetur, cum dicebat se contulisse cum illis qui cum Christo fuissent conversati, quorum testimonium probabilius erat. Vnde verbum illud, Ne in vacuum currerem, aut cucurrissem, non debet referri ad defectum Apostoli secundum se, nec ad dubitationem quam haberet in Euangelio, quoniam hoc, neq; ab homine neq; per hominem accepit aut didicit, sed per Dei revelationem immediatam, vt ipsemet dicit ad Gal. 1. Amplius ad Gal. 2. de hac collatione faciens memoriam, inquit Apostolus, Mihi autem qui videbantur esse aliquid, nihil contulerunt, sed e contra. Vbi Glossa secundum Aug. Mihi enim (vel autem,) quasi ideo ad priora non recurro, quia qua modo fiunt, sufficiunt mihi ad commendationem, scilicet quod illi qui videbantur esse aliquid, scilicet Petrus & alii qui fuerunt cum Domino, nihil contulerunt, id est, addiderunt mihi, in quo patet quod non illis inferior sum, qui a Domino a Deo perfectus sum, vt nihil esset quod in collatione mea perfectioni adderent. Qui enim illis tribus imperitis tribuit sensum, dedit & mihi. Et infra dicit Glossa secundum Hieronymum, Ipsi mihi nihil contulerunt, sed ego contuli Petro. Et infra rursum, Ego restiti enim, tanquam par. Hæc enim non auderet facere nisi sciret se non imparem fore. Debet igitur illud verbum, Ne in vacuum currerem &c. referri ad audientes qui forte sibi non credidissent, aut non tantum, & ideo vacui remansissent. Et ipse similiter in eis vacuus fuisset, id est, propositum frustratum habuisset in eis, quoniam non generasset in eis fidem, quam suæ prædicationis curfugenerare intendebat. Et hoc est etiam quod in Glossa secundum Augustinum subditur infra: Apostolus enim Paulus, post Christi ascensionem de cælo vocatus, si non cum Apostolis communicaret, & cum eis Euangelium non conferret, quo eiusdem societatis esse appareret, Ecclesia illi omnino non crederet. Sed cum cognouisset eum hoc annunciare quod illi, & in eorum communione & unitate viuentem, accedentibus etiam per eum talibus signis qualia & illi operabantur, ita enim Domino commendante autoritatem meruit, vt verba illius sic audiantur in Ecclesia tanquam in illo Christus, sicut ipse verissime dixit, locutus audiatur. Metuit ergo Paulus autoritatem Christo commendante ipsum siue approbante simpliciter, non dixit, Petro vel aliis Apostolis ipsum commendantibus.
units.tr: (Second, marginal numerals as printed.) He says, As I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail, so you, when you have returned, strengthen your weaker brothers by the example of your repentance, so that they do not despair of pardon. By "brothers" he understands the faithful in general. He said this to Peter, and it means that the other Apostles would do the same. So in Mark 13: What I say to one, or, according to another reading, with the same sense, what I say to you, I say to all. Or perhaps he said this to Peter alone, as the Gloss also seems to think, because Christ foresaw that Peter would deny him. Hence when you have returned, that is, by the example of your repentance, since he had obtained pardon both by word and by his own example, Christ wished him to strengthen or confirm the weak in faith more particularly, so that they would not despair of pardon. As for the other authority, taken from John 21, by which some try to prove the same point as before, namely that Christ said to the blessed Peter, Feed my sheep, feed my lambs, etc.: first, according to the Gloss, the meaning of this sequence is that to feed the sheep is to strengthen believers so that they do not fail; to provide for the subjects in temporal needs if necessary; to offer examples of virtues; to resist adversaries of the faith; and to correct sinners. And the Gloss adds: And when he hears from Peter the third time that he is loved, he bids him feed the sheep. The threefold denial is answered by a threefold confession, so that the tongue serves love no less than fear. From this passage, however, it is proved only that Christ appointed Peter the shepherd of the sheep. It does not follow from this that he was superior to the other Apostles in authority or dignity, nor does it follow that the other Apostles were not appointed as shepherds. Each is the opposite of the other: the consequent I have just mentioned stands with the antecedent, namely with the saying of Christ quoted above. Moreover, the Catholic Church sings of all the Apostles without distinction: It is truly meet and just, right and salutary, that we should always and everywhere pray to you, eternal Shepherd, that you would not forsake your flock but keep it under continual protection through your blessed Apostles, so that it may be governed by those same rulers whom you appointed as vicars of your work and shepherds to preside over it. See, the Apostles are called in the plural rulers, vicars and shepherds, by the immediate appointment of Christ. Christ did not constitute only one ruler, vicar or shepherd. But if someone asks why Christ said this to Peter alone, the answer must be that Christ sometimes addressed a person in his own person, as in the forgiveness of sins, the healing of the sick and the raising of the dead; and sometimes he addressed another in the person of all or of several, as in John 5: Go and sin no more, lest something worse befall you. Therefore, in committing that office to Peter, Christ spoke to him in the person of all the Apostles, as he himself testifies to this manner of speaking in Mark 13, when he said: What I say to one, or to you, I say to all. Yet he addressed the words specially to Peter, either because he was the older, or because he was more ardent in love, or to signify what sort of men ought to be appointed as ministers of the future Church, namely men mature in age, which signifies prudence or knowledge, and full of charity, which signifies the care and diligence that ministers ought to have. Or perhaps it was so that Peter would not seem too abject, because he had denied Christ, which the Gloss seems to imply when it says: The threefold denial is answered by a threefold confession, so that the tongue serves love no less than fear. For this is quite certain: what was said in Matthew 28 was said to all without distinction: Go therefore and teach all nations. He did not say to Peter, Go and send the others. By this he signified the equality of authority among all, as we have already shown from Matthew 23, where Christ says to them: Do not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher, and you are all brothers; do not claim to be above one another or above the rest. Or, and this seems very probable and true to me, he said to Peter, Feed my sheep, in order to commit to him in particular the people of Israel, because of his steadfastness; that people was a stiff-necked people towards God, as appears from Exodus 33. The Apostle also brings this forward through Isaiah at the end of Acts. And because Christ had come principally to convert and save this people: I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15). I was sent principally, supply. Therefore he seems to have committed the care of this people especially to the blessed Peter when he said, Feed my sheep. And this seems to have been the Apostle's plain meaning when he said in Galatians 2: When they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed to me, as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter, etc., where the Gloss, following Augustine, says: When they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed to me as to a believer, so principally, as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter. For Christ gave Paul the task of ministering to the Gentiles, and had given Peter the task of ministering to the Jews; yet the dispensation was so distributed that Peter would also preach to the Gentiles if the case required it, and Paul to the Jews. Nor do I see how Paul or any other saint could have derived from Scripture that the Jewish people was committed to Peter especially and principally, except from the fact that Christ said to him, Feed my sheep. For Paul says in Galatians 2: the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed to me, just as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter. If the gospel had been committed to Peter in general more than to Paul or to anyone else, Paul would have spoken inappropriately in those words, indeed his whole saying would have been empty, and the comparison he made would have been pointless with regard to the glosses of the saints and other teachers. We shall deal with these three points of Scripture just mentioned at the end of this chapter, so that we need not repeat the same thing too often. As for the Apostle's saying in Galatians 2, by which it seemed that he was inferior in authority to the Apostle Peter, because he said: I laid before them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain, etc. First, according to the Gloss on this passage, which is that of Augustine: He says, I did not learn it from him as from my elders, but I conferred with them as a friend and an equal. And what the Gloss cites according to Jerome on the words lest I should run in vain etc., the Gloss says, following Jerome, shows that he did not have the certainty of the gospel unless it was also confirmed by the authority of Peter and strengthened by the others. I say, with respect, that this Gloss would contradict itself if it were understood in the way the opponent of the view we defend seems to intend, since it is further said, according to the same Jerome. Either the Gloss according to Jerome must be understood in accordance with what it adds according to Augustine: For this was not the reason for the conference, as if he doubted that he had certainty of the gospel, but so that it might be believed more readily by the hearers, since he said that he had conferred with those who had lived with Christ, whose testimony was more credible. Hence those words, lest I should run, or had run, in vain, should not be referred to any defect in the Apostle himself, nor to any doubt he had about the gospel, since he received this not from man nor through man, but by the immediate revelation of God, as he himself says in Galatians 1. Again, in Galatians 2, recalling this conference, the Apostle says: But from those who seemed to be something, they added nothing to me, but on the contrary. Here the Gloss, following Augustine, says: For I (or rather, as if I do not have recourse to earlier things, because what is now done suffices to commend me) does not need recourse; namely, that those who seemed to be something, that is Peter and the others who were with the Lord, added nothing to me. In this it is evident that I am not inferior to them, for I was perfected by the Lord and by God, so that there was nothing they could add to my perfection in the conference. For whoever attributes sense to those three unlearned men also gives it to me. And a little further the Gloss says, following Jerome: They themselves added nothing to me, but I conferred with Peter. And again further on: For I withstood him as an equal. He would not have dared to do this unless he knew that he was not unequal. Therefore those words, lest I should run in vain etc., must be referred to the hearers who perhaps had not believed him, or not fully, and so would have remained empty. And he himself would likewise have been empty among them, that is, his purpose would have been frustrated in them, since he would not have begotten in them the faith which he intended to produce by the course of his preaching. This is also what the Gloss, following Augustine, adds below: For the Apostle Paul, called from heaven after the ascension of Christ, if he had not communicated with the Apostles and had not conferred the gospel with them, by which it would appear that he was of the same fellowship, the Church would not have believed him at all. But when they knew that he preached the same thing as they did, and lived in their communion and unity, and when, through him, signs such as they performed also came about, then, since the Lord commended him, he earned such authority that his words are heard in the Church as if Christ were speaking in him, just as he himself most truly said, Since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me. Therefore Paul feared that his authority would be commended or approved simply by Christ, not by Peter or the other Apostles commending him.

units.la: Et subditur infra parum in Glossa secundum eundem. Vnde contulit cum illis Euangelium & dextras accepit, quia idem verbum cum eis etsi non per eos habuit. Ipsa enim collatio vnam doctrina speciem, excussa omni lepra varietate, monstrauit. Hæc igitur fuit causa collationis, vt varietatis doctrinæ scrupulus tolleretur ab auditoribus. Et hoc est quod supra dixerat Glossa secundum Augustinum inquit enim, Iterum ascendi Hierosolymam, &c. Ascendi dico cum Barnaba, qui de Iudæis erat, assumpto Tito, qui de gentibus, quasi hinc inde testes habui, quibus pateret falsum esse me aliud gentibus, aliud Iudæis prædicare.
units.tr: And a little further on the Gloss says, following the same author: Hence he conferred with them about the gospel and received their right hands, because he had the same word with them, though not through them. For the conference itself showed the one form of doctrine, with all variety of leprosy cast out. The reason for the conference, then, was that the scruple of varied doctrine might be removed from the hearers. This is also what the Gloss said above, following Augustine: "Again I went up to Jerusalem," etc. I say I went up with Barnabas, who was of the Jews, taking Titus with me, who was of the Gentiles, so that I had witnesses on each side, by whom it would be plain that it is false that I preach one thing to the Gentiles and another to the Jews.

units.la: Ascendi aut non solum ea dispositione, sed secundum revelationem Dei, & non didici ab illis tanquam maioribus, sed contuli cum eis tanquam amicis & paribus Euangelium Christi, quod prædico in gentibus. Hoc fecit pro assertione prædicationis, quia multis erat scrupulus in doctrina Apostoli, perturbantibus Iudæis, quem scilicet scrupulum Deus voluit tollere, Et ideo non humana deliberatione, sed Dei revelatione Apostolus ad conferendum cum illis Euangelium ascendisse se dixit, non quidem propter dubitationem quam in Euangelio haberet Apostolus, sed vt ab auditoribus iam dictus scrupulus tolleretur.
units.tr: I went up, however, not only by this arrangement but by a revelation of God, and I did not learn from them as from my elders, but I conferred with them as friends and equals about the gospel of Christ, which I preach among the Gentiles. He did this to confirm his preaching, because the doctrine of the Apostle was a scruple to many, since the Jews were disturbing them; God wished to remove that scruple. And so the Apostle said that he went up to confer the gospel with them not by human deliberation but by the revelation of God, not indeed because the Apostle had any doubt about the gospel, but so that the scruple mentioned might be removed from the hearers.

units.la: Quod vero inducebatur ex Glossatore ad Gal. 2. quod posterior pastor fuit Paulus beato Petro Apostolo, dicendum, Glossatorem fuisse locutum proprie, quoniam beatus Paulus posterius tempore vocatus fuit ad Apostolatum, & ideo posterior tempore, sed non propter hoc inferior autoritate, nec hoc Glossa expressit, sed oppositum magis. Sic igitur ex prædictis apparet, neq; Petrum aut Apostolorum alium fuisse maiorem Paulo, sed amicum & parem autoritate per Christum illis immediate collata. Si qua vero fuerit inter eos prioritas, attendenda est ex ipsorum inuicem electione fortasse, aut secundum quem modum beatum Petrum cæteris priorem Apostolis diximus 16. huius.
units.tr: As for what is drawn from the Gloss on Gal. 2, that Paul was a later minister than the blessed Apostle Peter, it must be said that the Gloss spoke properly, since the blessed Paul was called to the apostleship later in time, and so was later in time; but this does not make him inferior in authority, and the Gloss did not express this, but rather the opposite. Thus it is clear from what has been said that neither Peter nor any other of the Apostles was greater than Paul, but a friend and equal in authority, conferred on them immediately by Christ. If there was any priority among them, it should perhaps be judged from their mutual choice, or according to the manner in which we said the blessed Peter was prior to the other Apostles, in chapter 16 of this book.

units.la: Ad dictum vero sumptum ex Codice Isidori cap. cui titulus: Incipit prefatio Niceni concilii, cum inquit; Sciendum est sane ab omnibus catholicis, quoniam sancta Romana Ecclesia nullis synodicis Decretis prælata est, sed Euangelica voce Domini & Saluatoris nostri primatum obtinuit, sic quoq; intelligendo de ipsius Episcopo. Negandum est Isidori & cuiuslibet alterius extra canonem sic dicentis sermonem Nam Romana Ecclesia ex Decretis Romanorum principum est aliarum principalior institutia, & ex aliarum Ecclesiarum consensu, quasi electione quadam, secundum quem modum diximus, 18. & 22. huius.
units.tr: As to the saying taken from the Codex of Isidore, in the chapter titled: Here begins the preface of the Council of Nicaea, where it says: It must certainly be known by all Catholics that the holy Roman Church has been placed before no synodal decrees, but has obtained the primacy by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Saviour, this too is to be understood of its bishop. The statement of Isidore, and of anyone else outside the canon who says so, that the Roman Church is more principal in institution than other churches, because it is from the decrees of the Roman princes, and by a kind of election from the consent of the other churches, must be denied, according to the manner we spoke of in chapters 18 and 22 of this book.

units.la: Amplius ex præmissa canonis autoritate, non sequitur, quod infert Isidorus, sed repelli potest eius illatio & cuiuslibet sic dicentis, per determinata nobis 15. huius, parte 8. & 16. parte 13. & 14. Ad id vero per quod hæc astruere nititur, ex Matth. 16. Tues Petrus & super hanc petram &c. iam dictum est prius, & manifestata fuit huius Isidori sententiæ debilitas 22. huius. Ad eam vero rationem, qua deducebatur, Ecclesiam vnam esse, & vnum esse primum Episcopum propter fidei unitatem, secundum Apostolum ad Ephes. 4. dicendum, sumendo Ecclesiam in propria significatione pro fidelium multitudine, sic esse vnam Ecclesiam, sicut fides est vna. Et quoniam fides non est vna numero in omnibus fidelibus, sed specie vel genere, iccirco non concludit argumentum, Ecclesiam aliter esse vnam. Et cum additur, Ecclesiam non esse vnam, nisi per unitatem numeralem alicuius Episcopi cæteris superiorem, hanc nego, & si concederem ipsam ad aliam illationem, quod hoc principium siue caput est Romanus Episcopus institutione diuina immediate, nego illationem hanc cum suis probationibus.
units.tr: Furthermore, from the authority of the aforesaid canon it does not follow what Isidore infers, and his inference, and that of anyone who speaks thus, can be refuted, as we have settled for ourselves in chapter 15 of this book, part 8, and in chapter 16, part 13 and 14. As to the passage from Matt. 16, "You are Peter, and upon this rock," etc., by which he tries to establish these things, it has been said before, and the weakness of this opinion of Isidore was shown in chapter 22 of this book. As to the argument by which it was deduced that the Church is one, and that there is one first bishop because of the unity of faith, according to the Apostle in Eph. 4, it must be said that, taking Church in its proper sense for the multitude of the faithful, the Church is one just as the faith is one. And since the faith is not one in number in all the faithful, but in kind or genus, the argument does not conclude that the Church is one in some other way. And when it is added, "the Church is not one unless through the numerical unity of some bishop set above the others," I deny this; and even if I were to concede the principle to another inference, namely that this principle or head is the Roman bishop by immediate divine institution, I deny this inference together with its proofs.

units.la: Quoniam nec Petrus Apostolus fuit petra, super quam fundata est Ecclesia, sed Christus, sicut pridem & 16. huius, per Scripturam ostensum est. Et quoniam Romanus Episcopus institutione diuina immediate, non sic est singulariter Beati Petri aut aliorum Apostolorum successor, quod illi propter hoc, ad reliquos superior autoritas debeatur, vt vbi supra monstratum est.
