Sed si qua illi singularitas insit, sibi conuenit per institutionem seu electionem humanam, vt 22. huius. sufficienter ostendimus. Ad huius vero confirmationem, quoniam sic vnum episcopum aut episcopatum oportet esse, tanquam spiritualium principium, quemadmodum vnum principem aut principatum, temporalium omnium primum, potest negari comparatio, quoniam primi principantis aut principatus vnitas numeralis necessaria est propter contentiosos hominum actus, vt demonstratum est 17. prima. Quae siquidem vnitas non est necessaria in aliquo vel reliquorum officiorum ciuitatis aut regni. Amplius concessa comparatione secundum similitudinem seu proportionem, quae primum assumitur ad id quod subiungitur, vnum esse primum principem aut principatum, dici potest quod verum est humana institutione, non aliqua Dei siue legis diuinae ordinatione, seu statuto immediate. Quo modo conclusimus etiam 22. huius, expediens fore vnum episcopum aliquem & vnum ecclesiam, secundum certam formam, & ad certum opus instituere omnium aliarum principaliorem & caput. Ad aliam vero ratiocinationem, quoniam vt in vnico templo est vnus episcopus, sic in orbe vniuerso fidelium. Dicendum primo in vnico templo, neque de necessitate salutis, neque legis diuinae praecepto est vnus episcopus, imo possent esse plures, sicut 15. huius ex Actuum 20. & aliis plerisque locis per Apostolum, & ex epistola Hieronymi ad Euandrum monstrauimus. Quod vero vnicus in vnico templo vel dioecesi posteriori tempore instituatur episcopus anthonomatice in iconomia templi praeferendo illum proueniunt ex humana institutione immediate: non quidem, vt diximus ex necessitate imposita per legem diuinam. Neque si esset talis imposita necessitas, lege diuina teneret simile. Non enim eadem necessitas est vnius iconimi numero in vnica domo, & in tota ciuitate aut prouinciis pluribus, quoniam non existentes in eadem familia domestica, non egent vnitate numerali cuiusquam iconomi, eo quod sibi inuicem cibos & reliqua victui necessaria mansionem accubitum & reliqua non inuicem participant, nec in tali vnitate, sicut qui sunt eiusdem domesticae familiae insimul conuersantur. Concluderet enim ratio haec, pariter oportere vnum numero esse iconomum in orbe vniuerso, quod non est expediens neque verum. Sufficiunt enim ad conuictum humanum quietum, vnitates numerales principatuum secundum prouincias, quemadmodum diximus 17. prima. Vnu autem esse iudicem coactiuum omnium, nondum demonstratu videtur esse de necessitate salutis aeternae, cum tamen huius amplior videatur necessitas inter fideles, quam vnius vniuersalis episcopi, eo quod vniuersalis princeps magis in vnitate potest conseruare fideles, quam vniuersalis episcopus. Antiquis nanque temporibus per principes coacti sunt schismatici ad fidei vnitatem seruandam, quemadmodum ostensum est 21. huius. Per episcopos autem cogi non poterant, eo quod auctoritate coactiua carebant, quae nec ipsis debetur in quantum huiusmodi, quemadmodum demonstratum 15. prima, & per scripturam & sanctorum auctoritates & alias rationes, amplius confirmatum, quarto, quinto, octauo, nono & decimo huius. Vnitatem vero numeralem atq; principalitatem episcopi & ecclesiae siue collegii clericorum, & secundum quem modum instituendam, expedire monstrauimus 22. huius, quamuis vt diximus determinatus sacerdos nullus, neq; collegium ad hoc institutum sit lege diuina, sed humana electione seu institutione talis determinatio facta fuerit, quemadmodum 22. huius veraciter & euidenter ostendimus. Quod vero addebatur ex Ioannis decimo, & fiet vnum ouile & vnus pastor, dicendum, quod loquebatur Christus de seipso. Ipse enim solus fuit vniuersalis pastor, & princeps pastorum, non alius post ipsum, sicut ipse solus fuit caput, & fundamentum ecclesiae, quemadmodum 16. huius monstrauimus, & aliis plerisq; locis repetiuimus. Et fuit haec aperta & literalis sententia beati Petri, inquit enim sua canonica prima capitulo quinto: Cum venerit princeps pastorum, (de Christo loquens,) percipietis immarcescibilem gloriam. Haec etiam est sententia sanctorum super hunc locum: Inquit enim Glossa secundum Gregorium, Qui ex duobus gregibus vnum ouile efficit, quia Iudaicum & Gentilem populum in sua fide coniungit. Ecce qualiter ouile fit vnum, quoniam in fidei vnitate. Non dixit Gregorius vnum ouile fieri, quia sub episcopo Romano vel alio vnico praeter Christum omnes fideles sint positi. Adhuc secundum Theophylactum: Idem namque omnibus est baptismi signaculum, vnus pastor, verbum Dei. Attendant ergo Manichaei, quoniam vnum ouile & vnus pastor est noui & veteris testamenti. Nusquam enim nominatus est ad hanc vnitatem ouilis Petrus aut Paulus, vel alter Apostolus, sed sola fidei vnitas, & Christi persona, qui solus ordinatione immediata Dei caput est & fundamentum, & omnium princeps Pastorum, vt ex praemissis diximus, & per certitudinem ostendimus 16. huius. Ad aliam vero illationem, qua concludebatur, Romanum episcopum solum, aut cum suorum clericorum solo collegio esse primam causam effectiuam institutionis secundariae omnium aliorum ministrorum ecclesiae, & eisdem assignare seu determinare templa in ipsius potestate mediata vel immediata, vel vtraq; fore, negando respondeo. Et dum confirmatur per Ambrosium, de tradendis basilicis, qui sacerdotes ad templa siue basilicas determinare siue instituere, dicit ius Caesaris esse non posse, quoniam ecclesia Dei est. Dicendum sane, quod hoc propterea dixit Ambrosius, quoniam temporibus illis non erat tutum, talia officia, scil. animarum curas, permittere Romanis principib. conferenda, & qp nondum erat in fide confirmati sufficienter, quinimo ipsorum principum quidam magis fauebat quadoq; sacerdotibus haereticis, quam vere fidelibus, velut idem Valentinianus Imperator, ad quem epistolam dirigebat Ambr. Veruntamen fide radicata & firmata, tam in subditis, quam in principatibus, & tali existente communitate: tutius, & vtilius, & magis conformiter legi diuinae fit episcoporum & aliorum animarum curatorum electio siue institutio, per auctoritate vniuersitatis fidelium, quae per vnicum & partiale ciuitatis seu communitatis collegii, vel per vnius solius hominis voluntate, qp prece aut pretio, amore, vel odio, aut alia quauis affectione sinistra, leuiter & quasi quotidie videmus peruerti. Cōuenimus ergo cū beato Ambr. in hoc, qp curatores animarum, episcopos aut sacerdotes reliquosq; tèplorū ministros instiinstituere, non sit ius Cæsaris, inquantum persona talis, aut alterius singularis personæ, sed vniuersitatis fidelium, aut illius vel illorum, cui fidelium vniuersitas autoritatem huiusmodi sponte tradiderit, neque hoc negauit ipse. Vnde aduersus Imperatores semper recurrebat ad plebem fidelem, per quam etiam idem ipse fuerat institutus episcopus, secundum quem modum determinauimus 17. huius. Neq; vnquam dixit autoritatem hanc fuisse Romani aut alterius cuiusquam pontificis, sed propter causam prædictam dixit, Ecclesiam siue templum solius Dei esse, ac ipsius fidelium multitudinis tanquam ecclesiæ principaliter & primo dictæ; cuius ecclesiæ caput est Christus, &ius, id est possessionem de iure Cæsaris esse non posse. Omnia enim quæcunq; sint illa temporalia possessionis Cæsaris siue fidelis, siue infidelis esse possunt. Sed templum siue institutio sacerdotum in eo, ad solius multitudinis fidelium autoritatem pertinet, quemadmodum ostensum est 17. huius. Huius autem signum propterea solum contendisse Ambrosium, tanquam pastorem fidelium, vt scilicet malo seu hæretico sacerdoti grex fidelium non committeretur regendus, quod dixit ad Valentinianum epistola prima. Inquit enim: Atque vtinam liquido mihi pateret, quod Arriani ecclesiæ minime traderetur, sponte me offerrem tuæ pietatis arbitrio. Quod autem sic ipsum intellexisse oporteat circa basilicarum traditionem, vt nunc diximus, & 17. huius manifeste demonstrauimus. Quoniam si basilicam occuparet in communitate fidelium, qui hæresis labe factus existeret episcopus aut sacerdos credere nolens, constat huiusmodi iuste compelli posse per iudicem coactiuum & armatam potentiam, secundum leges humanas. Hoc autem coactiuum iudicium atque potentia nullius est sacerdotis autoritas, vt idem & vere testatur Ambrof. in epistola, quæ intitulatur ad plebem, inquit enim: Aduersus Gothos, milites quoq;, lachryma mea arma mea sunt. Talia enim munimenta sunt sacerdotis, aliter nec debeo nec possum resistere: quamuis hoc etiam demonstratione conclusum sit 15. & 17. prima, & autoritate scripturæ atq; sanctorum cum aliis quoq; probationibus confirmatum quarto, quinto, octauo, & nono huius. Et ideo sane tenendum sic sensisse Ambrosium, vt diximus, nam & Apostolus Cæsarem appellauit, vt ex Actuum 25. induximus prius. Vnde vel sic dicendum, in communitatibus fidelium, aut singulos permittendum de fide docere quod volunt, sicut videtur sensisse Hilarius ad Constantium, epistola quadam. Sic igitur ad fidelis vniuersitatis autoritatem vel principantis secundum eius ordinationem pertinere videtur, basilicas siue templa disponenda tradere, ac sacerdotes in illis statuere, quod etiam catholici Francorum reges faciunt in quibusdam Ecclesiis; nullum sacerdotem seu episcopum recognoscentes, à quo deriuetur ad eos autoritas hæc. Sic etiam beatum Ambrosium intellexisse, & si vere intelligere oportuisse credimus. Et si contrarie huic, quam canonis scimus & credimus esse sententiam senserit, eius opinione relicta, quam credere non compellimur ad salutem, cum ipsius scriptura canonica non sit, scripturis canonicis inhærentes, eam quam diximus, tanquam veram tenemus sententiam. Et cum ab eadem autoritate Ambrosii videbatur inferri ad Romanum Episcopum pertinere, autoritate diuina immediate supremam iurisdictionem ecclesiasticorum temporalium, quæ propter officia ministris euangelicis conferuntur. Apparet ex dictis illationem invalidam fore, sicut etiam 17. huius sufficienter conclusimus, quam in hoc etiam sententiam confirmat Ambrosius iam dicta epistola de tradendis basilicis, vbi sic inquit; Si tributum petit, Imperator scilicet, non negamus, agri ecclesiæ soluunt tributum. Si agros desiderat Imperator, potestatem habet vindicandorum, nemo nostrum interuenit, potest pauperibus collatio populi redundare, non faciant de agris inuidiam, tollat eos si libitum est, Imperatori non dono, sed non nego. Sed forte obiiciet, qui semper agros defendere quærit, dicens hos esse iura sponsa Christi, parum curans de vera sponsa, fide scilicet catholica defendenda, vt rex & regnum Armeniæ sibi manifeste testificari potest, quod beatus Ambrosius dixit hæc, non quia agri ecclesiæ de iure debeant tributum, sed quia per vim & oppressionem Imperatorum exigebatur ab ipsis. Hæc profecto falsa expositio est, qua quidam etiam Romani episcopi cum suis complicibus ad effugiendam & declinandam coactiuam principum iurisdictionem, frequenter vtuntur, dicentes se de facto violenter, non iure in seculare deductos iudicium, quoniam oppositum dixit Christus, Iohan. 19. & supra induximus, 4. huius, & hoc est quod iuxta sententiam quam secundum canonem tenemus, subdit Ambrosius, Soluimus, inquit, quæ Cæsaris sunt Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei Deo. Tributum Cæsaris est, non negatur. Ecclesia Dei est, Cæsari vtique non debet adscribi, sed fideli supple sacerdoti, secundum iudicium fidelis multitudinis, quemadmodum pridem diximus, & 17. huius euidenter astruximus. Est igitur tributum & iurisdictio principantis super ecclesiastica temporalia non violenter, sed de iure. Ad aliam vero illationem qua videbatur concludi, omne collegium clericorum Romano episcopo coactiua iurisdictione subiectum, eo quod diuina ordinatione sit omnium princeps, negandum est antecedens. Ostensum enim est prius, quod nullus episcopus aut sacerdos immediata Dei ordinatione seu lege diuina inferior est aut subditus episcopo Romanorum, autoritate aliqua, essentialiter aut accidentaliter debita sacerdoti. Et quod inducitur consequenter ex Isidori codice, de verbis Constantini, dicendum, quod verbum fuit exhortationis & monitionis, quo siquidem deuotus Constantinus ostendit, quales esse deberent episcopi & sacerdotes, tales enim esse deberent inuicem & ad alios, quod in seculari iudicio non oporteret ipsos contendere, secundum doctrinam Apostoli primæ ad Corinth. 6. Quare, inquit, non magis iniuriam accipitis, quare non magis fraudem patimini, quam inter vos habere iudicia? Et quod additur ex dicto Constantini, vobis Deus dedit de nobis iudicandi &c. Dicendum, quod verum est iudicio primæ significationis, nullius in hoc seculo coactiuo, de quo siquidem dictum est sufficienter 6. 7. 8. & 9. huius. Nec tamen ex prædicta serie, quam inducit Isidorus siue dicta à Constantino, siue non dicta, sequitur, reliquos episcopos Romano fore iurisdictione subiectos. Inquit enim Constantinus, Dei solius inter vos expediate iudicium, & vestra iturgia quacunque sunt, ad id diuinum reseruentur examen, non dixit ad iudicium vel examen Romani pontificis. Et quod additur, Romanum episcopum esse vicem Dei gerentem in terris, dicendum, quod ordinatione diuina immediate non plus ipse vicem Dei gerit, quam alter episcopus, vt saepe dictum & ostensum est prius. Neque si vicem Dei gereret in terris, quam ad spiritualia docenda & ministranda, propter hoc Dei vicem gerit, quam ad iudicium coactiuum, super quenquam clericum aut laicum, vt ex 4. & 5. huius, & aliis plerisque locis ostensum est prius, sed in hoc ministri Dei sunt principes, quemadmodum dixit Apostolus Paulus ad Romanos 13. & beatus Petrus prima canonica, cap. 2. Adhuc esto quod Constantinus hoc asserendo aperte dixisset esse verum, negarem ipsius dictum, quoniam nec canonicum est, nec ad canonicum consequens. Quod si hoc per modum statuisset edicti, id obseruari expediret, sicut reliquas humanas leges, non tanquam Dei ordinatione immediate statutum. Verum ex ipsa Isidori serie liquet aperte, cunctos episcopos Romano principi coactiua iurisdictione subiectos. Ad ipsius enim iudicium, non autem Romani pontificis, spontanei, non coacti suas contentiones & iurgia detulerunt, ipsius interpellantes examen atque iudicium, vt Isidorus narrat ibidem. Et cum infertur viterius ex eisdem antecedentibus, ad solius Romani episcopi, aut eius cum suo solo collegio sacerdotum autoritatem pertinere, generalia conuocare concilia sacerdotum & aliorum fidelium, & reliqua ordinare in eisdem, de quibus in argumentatione praediximus. Neganda est illatio tum suo antecedente. Nam antecedentis & consequentis oppositum est 16. & 21. huius. Ad confirmationes horum innisas autoritati siue sententiae Isidori, quoniam interpretationem non patiuntur, eo quod hanc expressit sententiam. Dico, negando eas omnes tanquam canoni sacro, & demonstrationi super hunc firmatae dissonas, quemadmodum 20. 21. & 22. huius seriose ac manifeste deduximus, & ex his etiam quae ipsemet inducit codice supra dicto. Id autem quod dixit Hieron. in expositione catholica fidei, in qua sermonem dirigens ad Romanum episcopum, inquit, Emendari cupimus a te, qui fidem & sedem tenes, in quibus videtur innuere, Romanum episcopum singulariter beati Petri successorem. Dicendum, pro tanto dixisse Hieronym. Romanorum episcopum tenere fidem & sedem Petri, quia in Romana ecclesia haec statuto humano aliarum est caput, ipsam & suum episcopum denominat successorem ab Apostolo digniore siue perfectiore, quamuis immediata Dei ordinatione non fuerit, autoritate aliqua sibi per Christum immediate collata, superior reliquis Apostolis, vt supra induximus & plene probauimus 16. huius. Et quod addit Hieronymus, Sin autem haec nostra confessio apostolatus tui iudicio comprobatur &c. In quo videtur innuere Hieronymus, ad solius Romani pontificis autoritatem pertinere, legis diuinae, etiam in articulis fidei, dubias diffinire seu determinare sententias. Dicendum, nec istud sensisse Hieronymum, sed haec pro tanto dixit, quoniam ad Romanum episcopum pertinebat dare responsum de his quae circa fidem catholicam, dubia & citra itum ecclesiasticum diffinita seu determinata erant per concilium generale. Nam Romanus episcopus & ipsius ecclesia propter hoc instituta erat caput siue principalior aliarum, secundum quem modum diximus 22. huius. Signat autem, quod dicimus, intellex se Hieronymum, quoniam in epistola ad Euandrum, vbi reprehendens quosdam ritus circa Diaconos ecclesiae Romanae, dixit expresse: Si autoritas quaeritur, orbis maior est vrbe, id est, autoritas omnium ecclesiarum orbis maior est ea quae vibis Romanae. Per illam ergo solam autoritatem, quae aliarum maxima est & certissima, debent circa fidem dubia diffinire, quemadmodum ostensum est 20. huius. Vnde & idem Hieron. in expositione catholica fidei plane sequitur quae sunt approbata per generalia concilia, ea vero delinat & reprobat, quae sunt per eadem concilia reprobata. Quod si tamen sensisset Hieron. solius Romani pontificis autoritatem esse iam dictam, ipsius declino sententiam, tanquam non canonicam, neque per canonicam ex necessitate deductam. Non enim, vt in prioribus diximus atque probauimus, nec repetere piget, beatus Petrus aut alter Apostolus per solum, autoritatem assumpsit, quae dubia circa fidem esse poterant diffinire. Sed pro talibus conuenerunt Apostoli & seniores, vt Actum 15. inspicienti se offert. Quod vero inducetur ex Lucae 10. Qui vos audit, me audit &c. Dicendum, Qui vos audit &c. verum est, vt, id est, generale concilium, quod solum repraesentat Christum legis aeternae latorem vel Apostolorum & iplorum ecclesiae congregationem. Diuisim vero, Qui vos audit &c. verum est, loquentes secundum legem diuinam, non blasphemantes iniuste. Quomodo dixit Christus de Pharisaeis, Quae dicunt, facite, quae dicunt secundum legem, diuinam videlicet, vt inquit Hieronymus, Matth. 23. super praemissum immediate Christi oraculum. Vel sic, Qui vos audit &c. in praeceptis aut prohibitis lege diuina, obligatur. In conciliis vero, qualia sunt iciunia, non obligatur, nisi fidelium omnium, aut valentioris partis in generali concilio intercedente consensu. Ad rationes autem Bernhardi, & primum ad eam quae ad Eugenium est, de consideratione lib. 2. Quis es? inquit Bernhard. & idem respondens, ait, Sacerdos magnus, summus pontifex. Dicendum, quod si intellexerit hoc immediata Dei ordinatione, aut legis diuinae praecepto, neganda est eius responsio, quoniam sic non esset sacro canoni consona, nec deductis per necessitatem ex ipso 16. & 22. huius. Si vero intellexerit hunc primatum illi conuenire humana electione siue institutione, concedenda est sua responsio, secundum quem modum dictum est 22. huius. Et cum addit: Tu princeps Episcoporum, ) verum est, accipiendo principem large, id est, principaliorem institutione praedicta, stricte vero accipiendo principem non est concedenda Bernhardi oratio. nam & ipse idem ab eodem Eugenio, & consequenter à quolibet episcopo principatum negat, vt ab eodem Bernhard. ad eundem Eugenium libro primo, capitulo quinto supra induximus quinto huius. Tu heres Apostolorum, sic & alii episcopi quamuis hic principalius, secundum modum dictum quinto, 16. & 22. huius. Tu primatu Abel, (verum est assumptus pro illo, humana tamen electione, vel propter illius reuerentiam, qui tempore fuit apostolus. Gubernatu Noe,) verum est in ministrandis spiritualibus tantum, & humana institutione. Tu omnium patrum spiritualium pater. Ordine Melchisedech,) verum est quantum ad sacerdotium, quod figuratum est per illum de Christo, quomodo & caeteri sacerdotes omnes, non autem quantum ad regnum. Quoniam secundum hoc solum Christum & nullum alium sacerdotem figurauit Melchisedech, qui rex simul & sacerdos erat, nec tamen Christum figurauit hic quantum ad regnum mundanum, quia nec sic Christus regnare venit aut voluit, vt in 4. huius ostenditur, sed ille Melchisedech simul sacerdos & mundanus rex, Christi sacerdotium, & coeleste regnum non mundanum figurauit, & eo minus in aliquo sacerdote vel Episcopo, tale enim regnum negat ab Episcopo Romano Bernhardus, vbi supra, & magis expresse, neque etiam quantum ad primatum sacerdotii, quenquam alium à Christo figurauit Melchisedech, sed hic primatus in aliis est, vt diximus ab humana institutione. Dignitate Aaron) verum est quantum ad similitudinem primatus inter sacerdotes, differenter tamen vt diximus, quoniam Aaron immediate institutione Dei, sed non sic quisquam Romanus aut alter Episcopus Apostolorum successor. Autoritate Moses) huius oppositum aperte dixit idem, vbi supra de consideratione libro primo, capitulo quinto & libro 3. capitulo primo. Moses enim princeps fuit secundum legem coactiuam, vt apparet Actum 7. quod Bernhardus negauit à quolibet Apostolorum successore, vbi supra. Rursum Moses hoc habuit Dei ordinatione immediata, & super omnem Israel. Romanus autem episcopus hoc immediata habet humana concessione solum, & super solos euangelicos siue templorum ministros. Iudicatu Samuel, verum est ad similitudinem, differenter tamen dupliciter, primo quidem, quoniam non immediata Dei ordinatione, quemadmodum Samuel: Secundo quoniam super solos sacerdotes, & reliquos euangelicos inferiores ministros. Samuel autem super omnem populum Israel indifferenter. Potestate Petrus, verum est essentiali & immediate Dei actione, & sic etiam quilibet alter episcopus aut sacerdotes, primatum tamen super alios sola humana institutione immediate obtinet quilibet Romanus episcopus, siue hunc beatus Petrus habuerit immediate institutione Dei siue non, sed apostolorum electione, quod credimus secundum scripturam, si tamen hunc etiam sic habuerit, quemadmodum ostensum est 16. huius. Unctione Christus, si unctionem intendat gratiae, vel Spiritus sancti, quae datur cum sacerdotali charactere; verum est, quamquilibet Sacerdos etiam suscipit. Si vero per unctionem intelligat primatum super omnem ecclesiam, immediata Dei non hominum institutione, quem Christus solus habuit super omnes sacerdotes, ipsius declino sententiam propter Apostolum dicentem oppositum, in plerisque scripturae locis, quemadmodum ostensum est 16. huius. Quod vero subdit, non modo ouium, sed & pastorum tu vnus omnium pastor: si intelligeret humanam institutione immediate, concederem; si autem Dei ordinatione seu legis diuinae statuto, quemadmodum videtur intendere, ipsius declino sententiam, quoniam non est canonica nec ex canone per necessitatem deducta, sed oppositum magis. Et cum eam ex canone nititur astruere, subiungens: Vnde id probem quaeris? ex verbo Domini, Sime amas Petre, pasce oues meas. Cui enim, inquit, non dico episcoporum, sed etiam apostolorum, sic absolute & indiscrete totae commissa sunt oues? Cui non planum, non designasse oues? Nihil excipitur, vbi distinguitur nihil. Dicendum, & cum reuerentia semper, quod miranda est interrogatio haec, quae quaerit, cui apostolorum, non modo dicit episcoporum, sic absolute & indiscrete totae commissae sint oues. Dico quod omnibus apostolis communiter & diuisim. Vnde id probem quaeritis? ex verbo Domini euidentius quam ipse. Nam Matthaei vltimo, & omnium quasi praeceptorum nouissime dixit Christus ad apostolos omnes, Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes &c. Euidentius autem dico, quoniam Iohan. 21. dixit, Pasce oues, nec addit omnes. Certum est autem, quod plures comprehendit oues, qui omnes tradit uniuersaliter, quam qui solum indefinite, dicens, Pasce oues. Propter quod rursum cum reuerentia, videtur scriptura, quam inducit Bernhardus, aliam & magis scripturae conuenientem interpretationem recipere, quam supra tetigimus parte nona, nec repetere piget. Nam Christus Matth. 15. dixisse legitur, Non sum missus, nisi ad oues quae perierunt domus Israel. Quod siquidem oraculum, iuxta sanctorum interpretationes debet intelligi, non quidem, vt inquit Hieronymus, quin & ad gentes missus, sed quod primum ad Israel missus est &c. Remigius vero & magis ad propositum & literae consonum: Specialiter missus est ad salutem Iudaeorum, vt etiam corporali praesentia eos doceret. Quamuis ergo secundum sanctorum expositionem, Christus missus fuerit ad salutem omnium, specialiter tamen & primum ad salutem Iudaeorum, sicut etiam sonant verba Christi secundum Matthaeum, dum dixit, Non sum missus nisi ad oues &c. Has igitur oues inter caeteras sibi appropriauit, cum subdit, Quae perierunt domus Israel. Et quoniam hic populus semper fuit durae ceruicis, vt apparet Exodi 32. & prophetarum occisor, vt veritas ipsamet dixit Lucae 13. Petrum vero quoniam Christus nouerat constantiorem fide, ac charitate sui & proximi feruentiorem, eidem singulariter has oues recommendauit, dum dixit, Si amas me, pasce oues meas, id est, insiste specialiter ad docendum populum Israel. Signat autem hoc verum esse, quod scribitur ad Galatas 2. Cum vidissent quod creditum est mihi euangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis &c. Nec aliunde per euangelium posset dictum apostoli confirmari. Et rursum, Dextras dederunt mihi & Barnabae societatis, vt nos in gentes, ipsi vero in circumcisionem, id est, ad Iudaeos. Non igitur ex hoc quod dixit Christus: Pasce oves meas, beato Petro generaliorem curam commisit, imo specialiorem alicuius populi. Ea enim, quae dedit omnibus Apostolis, Matthaei ultimo, & Iohan. 20. dum dixit, Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes &c. Et, accipite Spiritum sanctum, & quorum remiseritis peccata remittuntur &c. nulla generalior esse potest. His enim verbis auctoritatem & curam pastoralem acceperunt omnes Apostoli, & ad omnes indifferenter, quemadmodum etiam dixit Aug. de quaestionibus novi testamenti q. 94. & supra inductus 16. huius. Quam etiam dicat Bernhard. generaliorem curam commisit Christus alicui, ea quam Paulo actuum 9. dum dixit? Vas electionis est mihi ille, ut portet nomen meum coram gentibus & regibus & filiis Israel. Et quod infra subdit Bernhard. Inde est, quod alii singuli singulas sortis sunt plebes, apparet scripturae dissonum, nec id consentit leries epistolarum Pauli, nisi posset ex scriptura convinci, sed oppositum, ut pridem ostendimus. Et quod infra subiungit 6. iuxta canones tuos, alii in partem felicitatis &c. Si intellexerint immediata institutione Dei, ipsorum dicta declino, tam scilicet Eugenii scripturam, quam sibi consentientis Bernhardi, eo quod canonicae non sunt, nec vocari debent, nisi scripturae, de quibus diximus. 19. huius, & quoniam oppositum eius quod dicunt, saepe probavimus per scripturam. Si vero intellexerint humana institutione immediate plenam illam potestatem, secundum quem modum diximus 22. huius. Ecclesiarum curam universalem concedimus eius dictum. Et rursum quod addit: Aliorum potestas certis arctatur limitibus, tua extenditur & in ipsos quoque efficatem super alios acceperunt, nonne si causa exiterit, tu episcopo caelum claudere? Tu ipsum &c. Dicendum, ut prius, quod Dei ordinatione immediata non plus habet Rom. episcopus aut quivis alter autoritatis in reliquos quam econuerso. Non enim ex crimine potest Rom. episcopus alium episcopum excommunicare vel deponere auctoritate sibi per Christum immediate collata, magis quam econuerso, ut 15. & 16. huius, per scripturam ostensum est, & pridem etiam repetitum. Si vero intelligat Bernh. hunc primatum ab humana concessione immediate, tunc illum habet super reliquos episcopos, in spiritualibus ministrandis, qui sibi per generale concilium concessus fuerit: & in temporalibus eum qui eidem super reliquos per mortalem legislatorem concessus extiterit. Et quod additur ultimo, quantum ad hanc orationem, Stat ergo inconcussum privilegium tuum tibi &c. Dicendum quod verum est, nam potestatem ligandi & soluendi homines a peccatis ipsosque docendi & sacramenta legis aeternae salutis ministrandi potestatem habet Romanus episcopus & sacerdos. Si vero per privilegium intelligat Bernhardus, primatum aliquem Romano episcopo lege divina seu Dei ordinatione immediata super reliquos episcopos debitum, eius velut prius, & propter assignatas causas declino sententiam. Ad aliam vero eiusdem Bernhardi orationem, qua libro & capitulo 4. ad eundem Eugenium innuere videtur, ad Romanum episcopum pertinere iurisdictionem coactivam, quam sub metaphora temporalem gladium appellavit, non modo super clericos, verum etiam super laicos, cum dixit, Quem tamen (gladium scilicet,) qui tuum negat, non satis mihi videtur attendere verbum Domini &c. Et in fine concludens inquit, uterque ergo ecclesia spiritualis (scilicet gladius) & materialis: cum reverentia nec minus cum admiratione dicendum, quod idem Bernhardus sibi de hac materia dissone, quinimo contrarie pronunciavit aperte, inquit enim de hac auctoritate seu potestate loquens, ubi supra immediate: Quid tu denuo (papa scilicet) usurpare gladium tentes, quem semel iussus es reponere in vaginam? Constat autem, quod quis usurpat, ad suam auctoritatem minime pertinere. Sed dicet Bernhardus aut eius interpres, iuxta id quod dixit in fine sermonis huius, quod quamvis auctoritas iam dicta ad sacerdotem pertineat, tamen executio per ipsum fieri non debet, quod exercere materialem gladium dixit. Verum responsio haec non est ad intentionem scripturae. Non solum enim banc gladii materialis extractionem Christus a se negavit, verum etiam & iudicium id, atque praeceptum de illo exerendo, dum dixit Lucae 12. petenti ab ipso tale iudicium: Homo, quis me constituit iudicem aut divisorem super vos? Quod verbum cum quibusdam aliis, tam Christi quam Apostolorum, tractans Bernhardus ad Eugenium de consideratione libro primo, capitulo quinto, & supra induximus quinto huius, sic ipsum exponentis in hoc loco interpretationem interimit. Inquit enim ad eundem Papam: Audi Apostolum quid de huiusmodi auctoritate, scilicet temporalia iudicandi, sentiat, & est primo ad Corinth. 6. Sic non sapiens inter vos, ait ille, qui iudicet inter fratrem et fratrem. Et infert, Ad ignominiam vobis dico, contemptibiliores qui sunt in Ecclesia, illos constituite ad iudicium. Itaque secundum Apostolum indigne tibi usurpas tu Apostolicus officium vile, gradum contemptibilium. (Attende quod de officio loquitur, non de executione.) Unde & dicebat episcopus (Paulus scilicet,) episcopum instruens, (Timotheum videlicet,) Nemo militans Deo, implicat se negotiis saecularibus, ego autem parco tibi. Non enim fortia loquor, sed possibilia. Putas ne haec tempora sustinerent, si hominibus lucrantibus pro terrena hereditate, flagitantibus abs te iudicium voce Domini respondere, ut homines quis me constituit iudicem super vos. In quale moxiudicium tu venires, quid diceret homo rusticanus & imperitus? Ignoras primatum tuum, inhonoras summam & praeexcelsam sedem, derogas apostolicae dignitati. Et tamen non monstrabunt puto, qui haec dicent, ubi aliquando quispiam Apostolorum iudex sederit hominum, aut divisor terminorum, aut distributor terrarum. Steriasse deniq; lego Apostolosiu dicandos, sedisse iudicantes non lego, erit illud, non fuit. Ita ne imminutor est dignitatis servus, si non vult esse maior Domino suo, aut discipulus si non vult esse maior, eo quod se misit, aut filius, si non transgreditur terminos quos posuerunt patres suis? Quum me constituit iudicem, ait ille magister & Dominus, & erit iniuria servo, discipulo, nisi iudicet vniversos? Non solum ergo remouet Bernh. quinimo verius Christus & Apostoli a successoribus sacerdotibus & episcopis, executionem saecularis iudicii, verum etiam officium, sueque auctoritatis de talibus iudicandi, propter quod infra subiungitur idem. Habent hac infima & terrena iudices suos, reges & principes terrae. Quid fines alienos invaditis? quid falcem vestram in alienam messem extenditis? Hanc rursum sententiam repetit & confirmat, libro 2. capitulo 4. & supra induximus quinto, 11. & 22. huius. Vbi ad propositam intentionem, sic inquit: Nunquid dominationem, (supple reliquit Apostolus Petrus,) successoribus suis? audi ipsum, (Petrum videlicet,) Non dominantes, ait, de clero, sed forma facti gregi. Et ne dictum sola humilitate putes, ne etiam veritate, vnx Domini est in Evangelio, reges gentium dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur. Et infert, Vos autem non sic. Planum est, Apostolis interdicitur dominatus. Ergo tu, & tibi vsurpare audas aut Dominus apostolorum, aut apostolicus dominatum, plane ab utroque prohiberis, supple simul habendo, & hoc est quod subdit ibidem Bernar. Si utrumque simul habere voles, perdes utrumque, & aliquin non receptum illorum numero putes, de quibus queritur Deus sic, Ipsi regnaverunt & non per me, principes extiterunt, & non cognovi eos. Amplius eandem profert sententiam in epistola quadam ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem, vbi sic inquit: Haec ipsi suggestores, (inobedientiae scilicet,) sed Christus aliter & iussit & gessit: Reddite, ait, quae sunt Caesari Caesari, & quae sunt Dei Deo. Quod ore locutus est, mox opere implere curavit. Condiderat Caesari non cunctatus est Caesari reddere censum. Exemplum enim dedit vobis, vt & vos ita facuritis. Quomodo vero Dei sacerdotibus debitam negaret reverentiam, qui hanc quoque saecularibus potestatibus exhibere curavit? Noluit ergo Christus principibus huius saeculi temporaliter dominari, sed subiici, & debitum illis censum atque reverentiam reddere, id faciendi cunctis eius successoribus, apostolis primum, deinde sacerdotibus, & episcopis praebens exemplum. Adhuc expressius eandem sententiam infra subiungens, ait: Quid igitur vos, o monachi, sacerdotum gravat auctoritas, metuitis infestationem? sed si quid patimini propter iustitiam, beatissecularitatem contemnitis, id est, principantes in saeculo. Sed saecularior nemo Pilato cui Dominus aptitudinem indicandum. Non haberes, inquit, in me potestatem, nisi tibi data esset desuper. Iam tunc pro se loquebatur, & in se experiebatur, quod post per apostolos clamavit in ecclesia, non est potestas, nisi a Deo. Et qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit. Ite nunc ergo resistere Christi vicario, cum nec suo aduersario Christus resisterit, aut dicite si audetis, sui praesulis Deum ordinationem nescire, cum Romani praesidis potestatem Christus quoque super se fatetur fuisse caelitus ordinatam. Vsurpat ergo episcopus alienum officium & in alienam messem falcem extendit, dum se iudicio saecularium actuum ingerit inter homines, cuiuscunque conditionis existant. Et quod addit Bernhardus in praemissa instantia: Quem tamen qui tuum negat, non satis mihi videtur attendere verbum Domini, &c. Dico quod nullus quem viderim aut audiuerim, id negavit aut negare potest expressius, vt ex ipsius praeinductis orationibus liquet. Quibus etiam adiungendum, cum reverentia, semper convenientiorem esse aliorum sanctorum expositionem super hunc locum. Fuit enim (vt omnes concordant) locutio Christi metaphorica, dum dicentibus discipulis, Ecce duo gladii, respondit Dominus, satis est. Unde Chrysost. Equidem si humano volebat tos vti praesidio, nec centum sufficerent gladii. Quod si nolebat eos vti humano subsidio, etiam duo superuacui sunt. Vnde apparet verborum Christi sensum fuisse mysticum, quod etiam signat manifeste ipsius sermo, dum Matt. 26. & Ioan. 18. tempore defensionis, si qua per illos gladios fieri debuisset, inquit Petro, Converte gladium tuum in locum suum, vel in vaginam, in quo significatur se non praecepisse, munitionem fieri per apostolos gladiorum, sed mystice fuisse locutum, secundum quem sensum sufficienter attendens verbum Domini, beatus Ambrosius exponit verba praedicta, sic inquiens: Duo gladii permittuntur, vnum nouum, alter veteris testamenti, quibus aduersus Diaboli munimur insidias. Et dicitur, satis est; quia nihil defuit ei, quem vtrumque testamenti doctrina munierit. Verum, quia ad vsurpandos principatus sacerdotes anhelant, & toto exteriori conamine, licet indebite, tenduntur: peregrinas expositiones Scripturae, quae ipsorum opinionem corruptam & affectionem perversam sapere videantur, libenter recipiunt. Quod si tamen literaliter verba Christi sumantur, nihil sunt contra nostram sententiam, quoniam gladius materialis non est principatus neque iudicium saecularium actuum, neque etiam secundum metaphoram, iuxta Christi sententiam, principatum sive officium saecularis iudicii, quod Christus Petro aut alteri Apostolo commiserit, significare potest, vt idem Bernhardus probavit alibi manifeste, vbi supra induximus, & etiam per Scripturam indubie monstratum. 4 huius & quinto. Et quod subiungit, Forsitan tuus, & tuo nutu exercendus, dico quod dixit forsitan, quamuis non debuisset in hoc dubitare, nisi fortasse hoc sane intelligat, quod princeps in exercendo gladium ad nutum sacerdotis, id est, ad consilium sacerdotis in generali vel speciali consilio secundum exigentiam factionis emergentis attendere debet: vt in movendo bellum, dubitans vtrum iuste secundum legem divinam, debet vti consilio sacerdotum, ne mortale peccatum incurrat, sicut & in reliquis suis actibus monasticis & civilibus, praesertim etiam in quibus dubitat per ignorantiam mortale peccatum incurrere, non quidem quod propterea sacerdoti subiiciatur in tali officio. Sic enim in conferendis disciplinarum licentiis & expellendis a civitate leprosis, vt debet consilio peritorum, quibus in iurisdictione non subiicitur; quemadmodum diximus decimo huius. Unde Bernhar. in fine sermonis iam dicti ait, quod nutu sacerdotis & iussu Imperatoris hic gladium exeri debet, non ergo per nutum intellexit Imperium, sive auctoritatem coactivam, sed consilium, quoniam hoc ad Imperatorem sive principem expressit pertinere, quamvis Romanus episcopus hunc gladium exeri persaepe etiam inter Christi fideles adversus invicem minus iuste praecipiat. Et ad unum dicere, si Bernhardus ex his verbis intelligat tale officium sive iudicium ad sacerdotis sive episcopi cuiusquam auctoritatem pertinere, tanquam in hoc superiorem alicui principanti, secundum tertiae significationis iudicium in hoc saeculo: Dico quod in manifesto, tam sibi quam Scripturae sacrae quam inducit, contradicit aperte, vt ex praedictis apparet, propter quod simpliciter eius in hoc loco, sitalis fuerit, declino sententiam, tanquam non canonicam sed canoni dissonam atq; contrariam. Ad dicta vero sanctorum atq; doctorum, & praecipue super scripturam inductam ex Matth. 16. Tu es Petrus & super hanc petram &c. Et rursum super illud Lucae 22. Ego autem rogavi pro te Petre &c. Amplius & super illud Iohan. 21. Si amas me, pasce oves meas. Quibus utique dictis videntur intendere, beato Petro per Christum immediate super reliquos Apostolos traditam potestatem seu auctoritatem, ipsum vocantes apostolorum principem, & universalem pastorem, & ipsorum quidam caput ecclesiae. Dicendum (cum reverentia tamen) quod auctoritatem nullam essentialem, quam sacerdotalem diximus, neq; accidentalem aliquam pastoratus praeexcellentiam super reliquos Apostolos Christus immediate beato Petro tradidit, sed ab illo & caeteris invicem removit, ut 16. huius per scripturam & sanctorum atq; doctorum expositionem evidenter ostendimus. Et modo quodam repetiimus circa principium capit. huius. Unde Christum & Apostolum & ipsorum quorundam alibi dicta sequentis, quam super inducta iam scripturae loca & alia quaecunq; similia dicere videntur sententiam de tali primatu seu principalitate, aliter quam 16. & 22. huius, dixerimus, declino. Quoniam canonica nec est, nec canonicam sequitur, quinimo ipsorum aliqui oppositum dixerunt alibi, exponendo scripturam. Hic autem talia proferunt extra scripturam ex propria sententia, sequentes consuetudinem, & magis attendentes quaedam dicta famosa, quam verba scripturae. Quis enim non admirabitur, contendentibus Apostolis, quis eorum esset maior, Christum respondisse, semper inter ipsos aequalitatem & prioritatem auctoritatis ab ipsorum quocunq; negasse, si intendebat beatum Petrum inter ipsos principaliorem & caput? Quid etiam Christus non dabat reliquis mandatum, ut Petro subessent in officio pastorali, ne tantum mysterium lateret eos & ipsorum successores, quantum erat caput ecclesiae? Nusquam enim legitur in scriptura tale mandatum fuisse datum Apostolis. Quomodo etiam dexteras dedit Petrus Paulo societatis? imo mandatum dare debuit tanquam superior. Et ad unum dicere, tota scriptura, ubi tangitur materia haec, huius sententiae oppositum clamat aperte. Esto amplius, quod tamen secundum scripturam negavimus beato Petro, per Christum immediate fuisse commissam curam pastoralem aliorum Apostolorum, non tamen propterea per scripturam convinci posset, Romanum aut alium quemuis episcopum post mortem beati Petri esse Pastorem omnium aliorum immediata Christi ordinatione, sed convenit alicui talis auctoritas per electionem humanam immediate, quemadmodum 16. 17. & 22. huius ostendimus prius. Et cum inducebatur, ecclesiam acephalam esse, neq; fuisse ordinatam a Christo secundum optimam dispositionem, si eam absque capite in sui absentia reliquisset, possumus dicere secundum Apostolum ut prius, quod Christus semper caput remanlit ecclesiae: omnesq; Apostoli & ecclesiastici ministri, membra, ut plane patet ad Ephesios 4 & aliis plerisq; locis, de quibus sufficienter induximus 22. huius, parte quinta. Et hoc etiam Christus ipse manifeste significavit Matthaei ultimo, dum dixit, Ego autem vobiscum sum usq; in seculi consummationem. Et dicat disputans, nunquid etiam sit acephala, mortali capite vacante ab episcopo, Romana sede plerunque; & constat quod sic. Nec tamen propterea concedendum eam inordinatam, aut praue dispositam a Christo relictam; propter quod redire oportet ad praedicta, & ea quae in solutione sequentis instantiae dicturi sumus. Rationi vero quae apparens est, ut amplius satisfaciat dicamus in forma. Cum enim ex ipsa deducitur & infertur, Christum non ordinasse ecclesiam secundum optimam dispositionem, si caput mortale determinatum, in sui absentia non reliquisset idem. Neganda est illatio. Et cum videtur id astrui, propterea quod ecclesia est in meliori dispositione per huius capitis institutionem, concedendum utq; credo, meliorem ecclesiastici ritus & observandae fidei dispositionem, per huiusmodi capitis mortalis institutionem, non tamen immediate fiendam per Christum. Quoniam si sic, tunc semper, vel ut in pluribus hoc modo provenire deberet, ex Christi ordinatione. Sed melius fuit determinandum & eligendum per fidelium institutionem, & hanc fuisse optimam dispositionem a Christo traditam ecclesiae militanti, ut hic ad exemplum traherentur imposterum; & scandali materia tolleretur; tam ab Apostolis quam reliquis eorum successoribus atq; fidelibus. Quoniam Romanae urbis aut cuiusuis alterius, fortasse non semper sunt clerici sacra scriptura & vita praestantiores, caeteris mundi collegiis, ut in ipsorum comparatione ad Parisiensis universitatis & cleri collegium satis appareat, propter quod reliquendo fidelibus institutionem talis capitis ecclesiae quemadmodum diximus 22. huius, parte 8. & 9. Christus eam in optima convenientium humanae conversationi, dispositione reliquit, quo modo do fortasse Apostoli Petrum caput instituerunt ecclesiae, quemadmodum ex Anacleti decreto induximus 16. huius, parte duodecima. Quod autem dixit Augustinus, super illud Iohan. 21. Sic eum volo manere) quod vita quae est in fide, significata est per Apostolum Petrum propter sui Apostolatus primatum. Dico Christium intellexisse tempore, quoniam inter caeteros ad Apostolatum per Christum vocatus est prius, sicut etiam clavium promissionem tempore primus accepit, secundum eundem Matth. 16. super illud, Tibi dabo claves regni caelorum. Vita enim quae est in fide, videlicet corruptibilis huius seculi, praecedit tempore illam, quae est in spe incorruptibilem alterius seculi. Ad eam vero confirmationem obiectionum, quae inducebatur ex Decretis sive Decretalibus pontificum Romanorum, dicendum generaliter ad omnes huiusmodi scripturas atque sermones, non quales diximus 19. huius, quod ipsis veritatis credulitatem non tenemur praestare, neque in quibus sententiarum praedicatarum, quas tum scriptura tenemus, oppositum continent, sed eas, quamuis cum reverentia, declinamus, & aperte negamus. Et quod singulariter concludere volunt, ad Romanum Episcopum solum; aut cum suo clericorum collegio, pertinere auctoritatem instituendi personas ad ecclesiastica officia, & pro illis temtemporalia siue beneficia conferendi. Dicendum, quod si per officia ecclesiastica intelligantur sacri ordines & characteres, qui cum his imprimuntur in anima velut habitus quidam. Haec inquam ossicia, per solos episcopos siue pastores posse conferri, siue à Deo per ministerium eorum tantummodo, & nullius alterius collegii, vel singulariis personā. Et hoc credendum de necessitate salutis, vel non ipsius oppositum, quia sic ordinatum reperitur lege diuina, non quidem quoniam sic statutum est, per humanas aliquas Decretales siue Decreta. Quamuis tamen vt diximus 17. huius, personarum habilitatis ad haec suscipienda officia examen & determinatio, non sine legislatoris fidelis autoritate, vel eius principantis fieri debeat, vt vbi supra monstrauimus, & 15. prima. Si vero per officia ecclesiastica intelligantur determinationes seu institutiones presbyterorum & aliorum iam dictorum officialium ad curas animarum, maiores aut minores, in certis locis & ad certos populos gubernandos, talia instituere officia, siue personarum ad haec determinationes facere, & pro his ecclesiasticis temporalia distribuere seu conferre, ad fidelem legislatorem pertinet, secundum quem modum diximus 17. huius. Idq; generaliter & vbiq; nullius vnici episcopi, aut collegii sacerdotum, autoritatis esse nec expedire, quemadmodum 17. & 21. huius ostensum est. Quod ergo obiicitur nobis oppositum horum, ex Decretis & Decretalibus Romanorum pontificum: Dicendum, quod quamuis huiusmodi Decretales siue Decreta, & quaecunq; aliae scripturae siue sermones consimiles, no quales diximus 19. huius, possint continere plurima documenta & consilia, etiam vtilia, tam pro statu praesentis seculi, quam venturi inquantum ab episcopo Romano, etiam cum suo collegio clericorum, praeter licentiam fidelis legislatoris aut Principis, aut aliter seu contra formam dictam 21. huius, statuta huiusmodi neminem obligare ad culpam vel poenam, & praecipue temporalem. Sic nanq; disponuntur eiusmodi ferentes traditiones, quemadmodum Pharisaei & scribae, ad quos Christus Marci 7. inquit, In vanum autem me colunt, docentes doctrinas & precepta hominum. Relinquentes enim mandatum Dei, tenetis traditiones hominum. Et parum infra, Bene irritum facitis praeceptum Dei, vt traditionem vestram seruetis; Decretales atq; Decreta videlicet de temporalibus vsurpandis. Non enim sunt Decretales in quantum huiusmodi, leges diuinae aut humanae, sed narrationes aut documenta, & in pluribus obligarchica quaedam statuta. Propter quod talium ordinatores, contra formam, & praeter autoritatem iam dictam, ad ipsorum quoq; obseruationem quenquam inducentes verbis subreptitiis, quasi cogentes, comminando simplicibus eorum transgressoribus, damnationem aeternam, aut blasphemias siue anathemata, vel alias maledictiones inferentes in quenquam verbo vel scripto corporaliter sunt extremo puniendi supplicio, tanquam conspiratores & ciuilis schismatis concitatores. Est enim haec grauissima species criminis laesae maiestatis. Quoniam in principatum directe committitur, ad eius etiam supremi pluralitatem, & consequenter per necessitatem ad solutionem cuiuslibet politiae perducens.
units.tr: Since neither the Apostle Peter was the rock on which the Church is founded, but Christ, as has already been shown from Scripture above and in chapter 16 of this book; and since the Roman bishop, by divine institution and immediately, is not so singularly the successor of Blessed Peter or of the other Apostles that for this reason supreme authority over the rest is owed to him, as was shown above; but if he has any such singularity, it belongs to him through human institution or election, as we have sufficiently shown in chapter 22 of this book. As for the confirmation of this, that there must be one bishop or one episcopate as the principle of spiritual things, just as there must be one prince or one principate, the first of all temporal things, the comparison may be denied, since the numerical unity of the first ruler or principate is necessary because of the contentious acts of men, as was demonstrated in chapter 17 of the first part. Indeed, this unity is not necessary in any of the other offices of a state or kingdom. Furthermore, even if the comparison is granted according to the likeness or proportion by which the assumption is made, that there is one first prince or principate, it can be said that this is true by human institution, not by any ordinance or statute of God or divine law immediately. In this way we also concluded in chapter 22 of this book that it is expedient to appoint one bishop and one church, according to a certain form and for a certain work, as the principal and head of all the others. As for the other argument, that as there is one bishop in one temple, so there is one over the whole world of the faithful: it must be said, first, that in one temple there is not of necessity for salvation, nor by a precept of divine law, one bishop; indeed there could be several, as we have shown from Acts 20 and from many other places by the Apostle, and from the letter of Jerome to Evangelus. That in one temple or in a later diocese one bishop is set up as the single head in the economy of the temple, this comes immediately from human institution, not indeed, as we have said, from a necessity imposed by divine law. Nor, even if such a necessity had been imposed, would divine law require the same thing. For the necessity of a single steward in one house is not the same as that of a single steward in a whole city or several provinces, since those who do not live in the same household do not need the numerical unity of any one steward, because they do not share with one another food and the other necessities of life, lodging, couches and the rest, nor do they live together in such unity as those who belong to the same household. For this argument would conclude that there must likewise be one numerically single steward over the whole world, which is neither expedient nor true. For numerical unities of principates, according to provinces, suffice for the peaceful life of human society, as we said in chapter 17 of the first part. But that there should be one coercive judge over all is not yet shown to be necessary for eternal salvation, although the necessity of such a thing seems greater among the faithful than that of one universal bishop, since a universal prince can preserve the faithful in unity more than a universal bishop can. For in ancient times schismatics were compelled by princes to keep the unity of the faith, as was shown in chapter 21 of this book. But they could not be compelled by bishops, because bishops lacked coercive authority, which is not owed to them as such, as was demonstrated in chapter 15 of the first part, and was further confirmed by Scripture, by the authority of the saints and by other arguments, in chapters 4, 5, 8, 9 and 10 of this book. As for the numerical unity and principality of a bishop, and of the Church or college of clergy, and in what manner they ought to be established, we showed in chapter 22 of this book that it is expedient; although, as we said, no determinate priest or college is so established by divine law, but such determination was made by human election or institution, as we have truly and evidently shown in chapter 22 of this book. As for what was added from John 10, "and there shall be one fold and one shepherd", it must be said that Christ was speaking of himself. For he alone was the universal shepherd and the prince of shepherds, and no other after him, just as he alone was the head and foundation of the Church, as we showed in chapter 16 of this book and repeated in many other places. And this was the plain and literal meaning of Blessed Peter, for he says in his first canonical epistle, chapter 5: "When the Prince of shepherds (speaking of Christ) shall appear, you shall receive the unfading crown of glory." This is also the view of the saints on this passage. For the gloss, following Gregory, says: "He who makes one fold out of two flocks, because he joins the Jewish and the Gentile people in one faith." Here is how the fold becomes one: by the unity of faith. Gregory did not say that the fold becomes one because all the faithful are placed under a Roman bishop or under some other single person besides Christ. Again, according to Theophylact: "For there is one seal of baptism for all, one shepherd, the word of God." Let the Manichaeans therefore note that one fold and one shepherd belong to both the New and the Old Testament. For nowhere is Peter or Paul or any other Apostle named as the one who brings about this unity of the fold, but only the unity of faith and the person of Christ, who alone by the immediate ordinance of God is the head and foundation, and the prince of all shepherds, as we have said from what precedes and shown with certainty in chapter 16 of this book. As for the other inference, by which it was concluded that the Roman bishop alone, or he with the single college of his clergy, is the first efficient cause of the secondary institution of all the other ministers of the Church, and that he, either mediately or immediately, or both, has the power of assigning or determining churches to them, I answer by denying it. And when it is confirmed by Ambrose, in his treatise On Surrendering the Basilicas, who says that the Emperor's right cannot extend to determining or establishing priests for temples or basilicas, because the Church is God's, it must be said that Ambrose said this because at that time it was not safe to allow such offices, namely the cure of souls, to be conferred by the Roman princes, and because the people were not yet sufficiently confirmed in the faith. Indeed, some of the princes themselves at times favoured heretical priests rather than truly faithful ones, as did the same Emperor Valentinian, to whom Ambrose was writing that letter. Nevertheless, when the faith has taken root and been established both in subjects and in princes, and when the community is of such a kind, the election or institution of bishops and of other pastors of souls by the authority of the whole body of the faithful is safer, more useful and more in conformity with divine law, than by a single and partial college of the city or community, or by the will of one man alone, who can easily and almost daily be seen to be corrupted by prayer or price, by love or hatred, or by any other sinister affection. We therefore agree with the blessed Ambrose in this, that the institution of pastors of souls, of bishops or priests and of the other ministers of the temples, is not the right of Caesar, insofar as such a person, or any single person, belongs to it, but the right of the whole body of the faithful, or of that person or those persons to whom the whole body of the faithful has freely committed such authority; and Ambrose himself did not deny this. Hence against emperors he always appealed to the faithful people, by whom he himself had been instituted bishop, according to the manner we determined in chapter 17 of this book. Nor did he ever say that this authority belonged to the Roman pontiff or to any other pontiff, but for the reason stated he said that the Church or temple belongs to God alone, and to the multitude of the faithful itself, as the Church properly and first so called, whose head is Christ, and that it cannot be "of Caesar's right", that is, a possession of Caesar's right. For all those things that are temporal possessions can belong to Caesar, whether he be faithful or unfaithful. But the temple, or the institution of priests in it, belongs to the authority of the multitude of the faithful alone, as was shown in chapter 17 of this book. Ambrose contended for this sign alone, as the pastor of the faithful, so that the flock of the faithful should not be committed to be governed by an evil or heretical priest; and he said this in his first letter to Valentinian. For he says: "And would that it were clear to me that the church is not to be handed over to the Arians, I would willingly offer myself to the judgment of your piety." And that Ambrose must be understood to have meant this concerning the surrender of basilicas, as we have just said, and as we clearly demonstrated in chapter 17 of this book: for if someone in the community of the faithful were to seize a basilica, and the bishop or priest who had become stained by the blemish of heresy were unwilling to believe, it is plain that such a man may justly be compelled, according to human laws, by a coercive judge and armed power. But this coercive judgment and power belong to no priest's authority, as the same Ambrose truly testifies in his letter entitled "To the People": "Against the Goths, and against soldiers too, my tears are my arms. For such are the defences of a priest; otherwise I neither ought nor am able to resist." Although this too has been concluded by demonstration in chapters 15 and 17 of the first part, and confirmed by the authority of Scripture and the saints, and by other proofs, in chapters 4, 5, 8 and 9 of this book. And therefore it must surely be held that Ambrose thought as we have said; for the Apostle also appealed to Caesar, as we previously adduced from Acts 25. Hence it must be said in this way too: that in communities of the faithful, individuals are to be permitted to teach about the faith whatever they wish, as Hilary seems to have thought in a certain letter to Constantius. Thus it seems to belong to the authority of the whole body of the faithful, or to the ruler according to its ordinance, to hand over basilicas or temples for disposal and to appoint priests in them; and this the Catholic kings of the Franks also do in certain churches, recognising no priest or bishop from whom this authority is derived for them. Thus we believe that Blessed Ambrose also understood it, and if we must believe that he understood it truly. And if he held an opinion contrary to this, which we know and believe is the view of the canon, we leave that opinion aside, since we are not compelled to believe it for salvation, and since it is not part of the canonical Scripture; and adhering to the canonical Scriptures, we hold the view we have stated as true. And when it seemed that from the same authority of Ambrose it could be inferred that it belongs to the Roman bishop, by divine authority immediately, to have supreme jurisdiction over the temporal possessions of the clergy, which are conferred on the evangelical ministers for the sake of their offices, it appears from what has been said that the inference is invalid, as we also sufficiently concluded in chapter 17 of this book. Ambrose confirms this same view in the letter already cited, On Surrendering the Basilicas, where he says: "If the Emperor asks for tribute, we do not deny it; the fields of the Church pay tribute. If the Emperor desires the fields, he has the power of claiming them; none of us will interfere. The gifts of the people may overflow to the poor. Let them not stir up hatred over the fields; let him take them if he pleases. I do not give them to the Emperor, but I do not deny them." But perhaps someone who always seeks to defend the fields will object, saying that these are "the rights of the Bride of Christ", caring little for the true bride, namely the defence of the Catholic faith; as the king and kingdom of Armenia can clearly testify to him. Ambrose said these things, not because the fields of the Church owe tribute by right, but because it was being exacted from them by violence and oppression of the Emperors. This is indeed a false interpretation, which certain Roman bishops, with their accomplices, frequently use in order to escape and avoid the coercive jurisdiction of princes, saying that they have been violently, not lawfully, dragged into secular judgment. For the opposite was said by Christ, as we cited from John 19 and above, chapter 4 of this book. And this is what Ambrose adds, according to the view we hold in accordance with the canon: "We render what is Caesar's to Caesar, and what is God's to God. Tribute is Caesar's and is not denied. The Church is God's; it certainly ought not to be ascribed to Caesar," but to the faithful, that is, to the priest, according to the judgment of the faithful multitude, as we said above and clearly argued in chapter 17 of this book. Therefore the tribute and jurisdiction of the ruler over the temporal possessions of the Church is exercised not by violence but by right. As for the other inference, by which it seemed to be concluded that every college of clergy is subject to the coercive jurisdiction of the Roman bishop, because by divine ordinance he is the prince of all, the antecedent must be denied. For it has been shown before that no bishop or priest is, by the immediate ordinance of God or by divine law, inferior to or subject to the Roman bishop, by any authority owed to a priest either essentially or accidentally. And as for what is brought up next from the Isidorian collection, from "the words of Constantine", it must be said that these were words of exhortation and admonition, by which the devout Constantine showed what bishops and priests ought to be, for they ought to be such toward one another and toward others; and that they ought not to contend in secular judgment, according to the teaching of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 6: "Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? But you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and that your brethren." And as for what is added from the saying of Constantine, "God has given you to judge us," it must be said that this is true in the judgment of the first signification, which is not coercive in this world, as was sufficiently said in chapters 6, 7, 8 and 9 of this book. Nor does it follow from the aforesaid sequence which Isidore brings forward, whether or not these were words of Constantine, that the other bishops are subject to the jurisdiction of the Roman bishop. For Constantine says: "Let the judgment of God alone be carried out among you, and let whatever your affairs are be reserved to the divine examination." He did not say "to the judgment or examination of the Roman pontiff." And as for what is added, that "the Roman bishop acts as the vicar of God on earth", it must be said that by immediate divine ordinance he does not act as God's vicar any more than any other bishop, as has often been said and shown before. Nor, even if he did act as God's vicar on earth, should it follow from this that he acts as God's vicar in coercive judgment over any cleric or layman any more than in teaching and administering spiritual things. As was shown above from chapters 4 and 5 of this book and from many other places, in this matter the ministers of God are rulers, as the Apostle Paul said to the Romans, chapter 13, and Blessed Peter in his first canonical epistle, chapter 2. Even if Constantine, in asserting this, had clearly said that it was true, I would deny his statement, since it is neither canonical nor consequent upon the canon. But if he had laid it down in the manner of an edict, it would be expedient for it to be observed, like other human laws, but not as something established immediately by the ordinance of God. Indeed, it is plain from the very sequence in Isidore that all the bishops are subject to the coercive jurisdiction of the Roman prince. For it was to his judgment, and not to that of the Roman pontiff, that they brought their disputes and quarrels, voluntarily and not under compulsion, calling upon his examination and judgment, as Isidore relates in the same place. And when it is further inferred from the same antecedents that it belongs to the authority of the Roman bishop alone, or of him with his single college of priests, to convene general councils of priests and other faithful, and to order the other matters in them, of which we spoke in the argument, the inference must be denied together with its antecedent. For the opposite of the antecedent and consequent is shown in chapters 16 and 21 of this book. As for the confirmations of these points, resting on the authority or opinion of Isidore, since they do not admit of interpretation, because they express this opinion, I say, denying them all as dissonant from the sacred canon and from the demonstration founded upon it, as we have seriously and manifestly argued in chapters 20, 21 and 22 of this book, and also from those things which he himself brings forward in the aforesaid collection. As for what Jerome said in his Exposition of the Catholic Faith, where, addressing his speech to the Roman bishop, he says: "We wish to be corrected by you, who hold the faith and the see," in which words he seems to imply that the Roman bishop alone is the successor of Blessed Peter, it must be said that Jerome said that the Roman bishop holds the faith and the see of Peter for this reason: because in the Roman Church, by human statute, this one is the head of the others; and he calls it and its bishop the successor of the more worthy or more perfect Apostle, although not by the immediate ordinance of God, nor by any authority conferred immediately on him by Christ, superior to the other Apostles, as we cited above and fully proved in chapter 16 of this book. And as for what Jerome adds: "But if this our confession is approved by the judgment of your apostolate," etc., in which Jerome seems to imply that it belongs to the authority of the Roman pontiff alone to define or determine doubtful opinions even in articles of faith, by divine law, it must be said that Jerome did not think this either. He said this for this reason only: because it belonged to the Roman bishop to give a response concerning those matters of Catholic faith which were doubtful, and which had been defined or determined without ecclesiastical process by a general council. For the Roman bishop and his Church were established as the head, or the more principal of the others, for this reason, in the manner we said in chapter 22 of this book. Jerome himself indicates what we say, since in his letter to Evangelus, where he rebukes certain rites of the deacons of the Roman Church, he said expressly: "If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city"; that is, the authority of all the churches of the world is greater than that of the city of Rome. Therefore by that authority alone, which is the greatest and most certain of all the others, doubtful matters of faith ought to be defined, as was shown in chapter 20 of this book. Hence Jerome himself in his Exposition of the Catholic Faith plainly follows those things which have been approved by general councils, and rejects and condemns those which have been rejected by the same councils. But even if Jerome had thought that the authority of the Roman pontiff alone is the one just mentioned, I would decline his opinion as not canonical, and not necessarily deduced from the canon. For, as we said and proved earlier, and it is no trouble to repeat it, Blessed Peter or another Apostle did not assume by his sole authority the power to define doubtful matters of faith. Rather, for such matters the Apostles and elders came together, as is evident to anyone who looks at Acts 15. As for what will be brought forward from Luke 10: "He who hears you, hears me," etc., it must be said that "He who hears you," etc., is true when "you" means a general council, which alone represents Christ, the giver of the eternal law, or the Apostles and the congregation of the Church itself. But taken separately, "He who hears you," etc., is true when they speak according to divine law, not when they blaspheme unjustly. Thus Christ said of the Pharisees: "What they say, do; but what they say according to the law," that is, the divine law, as Jerome says on Matthew 23, on the oracle of Christ immediately preceding. Or it may be taken in this way: "He who hears you," etc., is bound in the precepts or prohibitions of divine law. But in councils, such as the fasts, he is not bound unless by the consent of all the faithful, or of the stronger part, in a general council. As for the arguments of Bernard, and first the one addressed to Eugenius, in On Consideration, book 2: "Who are you?" says Bernard, and answering himself, he says: "A great priest, the highest pontiff." It must be said that if he meant this by immediate ordinance of God, or by precept of divine law, his answer must be denied, since in that case it would not agree with the sacred canon, nor be deduced of necessity from it, as shown in chapters 16 and 22 of this book. But if he meant that this primacy belongs to that man by human election or institution, his answer must be granted, in the manner stated in chapter 22 of this book. And when he adds, "You are the prince of bishops," it is true if the word prince is taken broadly, that is, more principal by the aforesaid institution; but if the word prince is taken strictly, Bernard's speech must not be granted. For he himself denies this same thing to Eugenius, and consequently to any bishop whatever; as Bernard, in the first book, chapter 5, of the same work addressed to the same Eugenius, was cited above in chapter 5 of this book. "You are the heir of the Apostles": so too other bishops, although here the one more principal, in the manner stated in chapters 5, 16 and 22 of this book. "You are the primate of Abel": this is true, taken for him, but by human election, or on account of the reverence of him who was an apostle in time. "You are the governor of Noah": this is true only in ministering spiritual things, and by human institution. "You are the father of all spiritual fathers." "In the order of Melchizedek": this is true as far as the priesthood is concerned, which was prefigured by him for Christ, as it is for all other priests, but not as far as kingship is concerned. For Melchizedek prefigured only Christ, and no other priest, in this respect, since he was at the same time king and priest; nor did he prefigure Christ here as regards worldly kingship, because Christ did not come or wish to reign in that way, as is shown in chapter 4 of this book; but that Melchizedek, at once priest and worldly king, prefigured the priesthood of Christ and his heavenly, not worldly, kingdom; and still less does he prefigure it in any priest or bishop. For Bernard himself denies such a kingdom to the Roman bishop in the passage above, and more expressly. Nor did Melchizedek prefigure anyone other than Christ even as regards primacy of priesthood; but this primacy in others, as we have said, comes from human institution. "In the dignity of Aaron": this is true as regards likeness of primacy among priests, but differently, as we said, since Aaron was instituted immediately by God; but no Roman or other bishop is in this way the successor of the Apostles. "In the authority of Moses": the same Bernard plainly said the opposite of this in the passage above, in On Consideration, book 1, chapter 5, and book 3, chapter 1. For Moses was a prince according to coercive law, as appears in Acts 7; and Bernard denied this of any successor of the Apostles, in the passage above. Again, Moses had this by the immediate ordinance of God, and over all Israel; but the Roman bishop has this only by human concession, and over only the evangelical ministers of the temples. "In judgment, Samuel": this is true by likeness, but differently in two ways: first, because it was not by immediate ordinance of God as in Samuel's case; and second, because it is over only priests and the other lower evangelical ministers, whereas Samuel was over the whole people of Israel without distinction. "In power, Peter": this is true by essential and immediate action of God, and so too is any other bishop or priest; but the primacy over others is obtained by any Roman bishop only by human institution immediately, whether or not Blessed Peter had it immediately by the institution of God, but by the election of the Apostles, which we believe according to Scripture, if indeed he had it in this way, as shown in chapter 16 of this book. "Christ by anointing": if he means the anointing of grace or of the Holy Spirit, which is given with the priestly character, this is true, as every priest also receives it. But if by anointing he means primacy over the whole Church, by immediate institution of God and not of men, which Christ alone had over all priests, I decline his opinion because of the Apostle who says the opposite, in many passages of Scripture, as was shown in chapter 16 of this book. As for what he adds, "not only of sheep but also of shepherds you alone are the one shepherd of all": if he meant by human institution immediately, I would grant it; but if by ordinance of God or statute of divine law, as he seems to intend, I decline his opinion, since it is neither canonical nor deduced by necessity from the canon, but rather the opposite. And when he strives to establish it from the canon, adding: "You ask whence I prove this? From the word of the Lord: 'Simon, Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.' To whom, I ask, not only of bishops but even of apostles, were the sheep so absolutely and indiscriminately committed as a whole? Is it not plain that he did not designate the sheep? Nothing is excepted where nothing is distinguished." It must be said, and always with reverence, that this question is astonishing, which asks to which of the Apostles the sheep were so absolutely and indiscriminately committed as a whole, not only of bishops. I say that they were committed to all the Apostles, both jointly and severally. You ask whence I prove this? From the word of the Lord, more evidently than he himself. For at the end of Matthew, and almost the last of all the precepts, Christ said to all the Apostles: "Go therefore and teach all nations," etc. And I say more evidently, because in John 21 he said, "Feed my sheep," and did not add "all." But it is certain that he who gives all the sheep universally embraces more sheep than he who speaks only indefinitely, saying "Feed my sheep." For this reason, again with reverence, the passage which Bernard cites seems to admit of another interpretation, more agreeable to Scripture, which we touched on in the ninth part, and it is no trouble to repeat it. For we read that Christ said in Matthew 15: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." This oracle, according to the interpretations of the saints, must be understood not in the sense, as Jerome says, that he was not also sent to the Gentiles, but that he was first sent to Israel, etc. Remigius, more to the point and more consistent with the letter: "He was sent specially for the salvation of the Jews, that he might also teach them by his bodily presence." Therefore, although according to the exposition of the saints Christ was sent for the salvation of all, he was sent specially and first for the salvation of the Jews, as the words of Christ in Matthew also sound, when he said, "I was not sent except to the sheep," etc. These sheep, therefore, he appropriated to himself among the others, when he added, "which are lost of the house of Israel." And since this people has always been stiff-necked, as appears in Exodus 32, and a killer of the prophets, as the truth itself said in Luke 13; and since Christ knew Peter to be steadfast in faith and more fervent in love for himself and his neighbour, he commended these sheep to him especially, when he said, "If you love me, feed my sheep," that is, devote yourself especially to teaching the people of Israel. This is confirmed as true by what is written to the Galatians 2: "When they had seen that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed to me, as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter," etc. Nor could the Apostle's saying be confirmed by the gospel in any other way. And again: "They gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles, but they to the circumcision," that is, to the Jews. Therefore it is not from the fact that Christ said "Feed my sheep" that he committed to Blessed Peter a more general care, but rather a more special care of one people. For those things which he gave to all the Apostles, in the last chapter of Matthew, and in John 20, when he said, "Go therefore and teach all nations," etc., and "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven," etc., cannot be more general. For by these words all the Apostles received authority and pastoral care, and this was given to all indifferently, as Augustine also said in his Questions on the New Testament, question 94, and as cited above in chapter 16 of this book. Or what more general care did Christ commit to anyone, as Bernard says, than that which he committed to Paul in Acts 9, when he said: "He is a chosen vessel to me, to bear my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel"? And as for what Bernard adds below, that "each of the others has his own portion of people," this appears to be inconsistent with Scripture, nor does the series of Paul's epistles agree with it, unless it could be proved from Scripture; but the opposite is true, as we have shown earlier. And as for what he adds below in his sixth point, "according to your canons, others in part of felicity," etc.: if they meant it by immediate institution of God, I decline their words, namely both the writing of Eugenius and that of Bernard who agrees with him, since they are not canonical, nor should they be called so, except the Scriptures of which we have spoken in chapter 19 of this book; and because we have often proved from Scripture the opposite of what they say. But if they meant by human institution, immediately, that full power, in the manner we stated in chapter 22 of this book, we grant his statement concerning the universal care of the churches. And again, as to what he adds: "Other men's power is restricted within certain limits, yours is extended even to them, and they have received efficacy over others. Would you not, if the cause arose, shut heaven against a bishop? You, him," etc. It must be said, as before, that by immediate ordinance of God the Roman bishop or any other has no more authority over the others than they have over him. For the Roman bishop cannot excommunicate or depose another bishop on account of a crime, by authority conferred on him immediately by Christ, any more than the reverse, as was shown from Scripture in chapters 15 and 16 of this book, and was repeated earlier. But if Bernard means that this primacy is immediately from human concession, then he has it over the other bishops in ministering spiritual things, as granted to him by a general council; and in temporal things he has what has been granted to him over the others by a mortal lawgiver. And as for what is added last, as to this speech: "Your privilege therefore stands unshaken for you," etc. It must be said that this is true, for the Roman bishop and priest have the power of binding and loosing men from sins, and of teaching them and administering the sacraments of the law of eternal salvation. But if by privilege Bernard means some primacy owed to the Roman bishop over the other bishops by divine law or immediate ordinance of God, then, as before and for the reasons assigned, I decline his opinion. As for another speech of the same Bernard, in which in book 4, chapter 4, addressed to the same Eugenius, he seems to imply that the coercive jurisdiction, which he called the temporal sword under a metaphor, belongs to the Roman bishop, not only over clerics but also over laymen, when he said: "Yet he who denies that it is yours does not seem to me to heed sufficiently the word of the Lord," etc.; and concluding at the end he says: "Both, therefore, the spiritual church (namely the sword) and the material": it must be said with reverence, and no less with wonder, that the same Bernard pronounced on this matter in a way inconsistent with himself, indeed plainly contrary to himself.
