For he says of this authority or power, speaking in the passage above immediately: "Why do you again attempt to seize the sword, which you were once ordered to put back in its sheath?" But it is clear that whoever usurps something does not belong to its authority at all. But Bernard, or his interpreter, will say, in accordance with what he said at the end of this sermon, that although the aforesaid authority belongs to the priest, its execution must not be carried out by him, since he called the exercise of the material sword that. But this answer does not match the intention of Scripture. For Christ not only refused this drawing of the material sword from himself, but also refused the judgment and the command concerning its use, when he said in Luke 12 to one who asked him for such a judgment: "Man, who made me a judge or divider over you?" Bernard, dealing with this word together with certain others of Christ and of the Apostles, in On Consideration, book 1, chapter 5, and cited above in chapter 5 of this book, destroys in this passage the interpretation of it he himself sets forth. For he says to the same Pope: "Hear what the Apostle thinks of such an authority, namely of judging temporal matters, and it is in 1 Corinthians 6: 'Is there not among you one wise man who can judge between brother and brother?' And he adds: 'I say this to your shame; are the least esteemed in the Church the ones you appoint to judge?' So according to the Apostle you unworthily usurp the base office of the Apostolic, the rank of the despised." (Note that he speaks of the office, not of its execution.) Hence the bishop, Paul himself, also instructing the bishop, namely Timothy, said: "No one who serves God entangles himself in secular affairs; but I spare you. For I speak not of the things that are hard, but of the things that are possible. Do you think these times could endure it, if men who gain by earthly inheritance, pleading before you for judgment, were to answer in the voice of the Lord, 'Who made me judge over you?' What would a rustic and unlearned man say if you came to such a judgment? You do not know your primacy, you dishonour the highest and most exalted see, you detract from the dignity of the Apostles." And yet, I think, those who say these things will not show where any of the Apostles ever sat as judge of men, or divider of boundaries, or distributor of lands. I read that they were sent to preach, I do not read that they sat as judges; that will be the answer, "it was not." Is a servant made less when he does not wish to be greater than his lord? Or a disciple, if he does not wish to be greater than the one who sent him? Or a son, if he does not overstep the bounds which the fathers have set for his own? "Since he made me judge," says that master and lord, "will it be an injury to a servant or disciple unless he judges all?" Therefore Bernard, or rather Christ and the Apostles, removes from the successors of the Apostles, the priests and bishops, not only the execution of secular judgment, but also the office and the authority of judging such matters; on account of which he adds below: "Such lowly and earthly things have their own judges, kings and princes of the earth. Why do you invade other men's territory? Why do you stretch your sickle into another's harvest?" He repeats and confirms this same opinion in book 2, chapter 4, and as above, cited in chapters 5, 11 and 22 of this book. There, coming to the point at issue, he says: "Did the Apostle Peter leave dominion to his successors? Hear him, namely Peter: 'Not lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock.' And do not think that this was said from humility alone, but also from truth: there is a word of the Lord in the Gospel: 'the kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors.' And he adds: 'But you are not so.' It is plain that domination is forbidden to the Apostles. So you, do you dare to usurp either the lordship of the Apostles or the Apostolic domination? You are plainly forbidden both; that is, to hold them both at once. And this is what Bernard adds in the same place: 'If you wish to have both at once, you will lose both; and otherwise you may think yourself not received among those of whom God complains: They reigned, and not through me; they became princes, and I did not know them.'" He further offers the same opinion in a certain letter to the Archbishop of Sens, where he says: "These suggesters of disobedience, but Christ both commanded and acted otherwise: 'Render,' he said, 'to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.' What he said with his mouth, he soon took care to fulfil in deed. He did not hesitate to pay the tribute to Caesar, for he gave you an example that you too should act so. But how would he deny due reverence to God's priests, who also took care to show it to the secular powers? Christ therefore did not wish to rule temporally over the princes of this world, but to be subject to them, and to render to them the due tribute and reverence, giving an example of doing this to all his successors, first to the Apostles, then to priests and bishops." Still more expressly, adding the same opinion below, he says: "Why then, you monks, does the authority of priests weigh upon you, and do you fear annoyance? But if you suffer anything for righteousness' sake, you despise worldliness, that is, the princes of the world. But no one is more worldly than Pilate, to whom the Lord showed the fitness of his judgment. 'You would have no power over me,' he said, 'unless it had been given to you from above.' Already at that time he was speaking for himself, and experiencing in himself what afterwards the Apostles proclaimed in the Church: 'There is no power except from God, and whoever resists power resists the ordinance of God.' Go now and resist Christ's vicar, since Christ himself did not resist his adversary; or say, if you dare, that God's ordinance is unknown to your prelate, since Christ also confessed that the power of the Roman governor was ordained from heaven over himself." Therefore the bishop usurps another's office and stretches his sickle into another's harvest, when he thrusts himself into the judgment of secular affairs among men, of whatever condition they may be. And as for what Bernard adds in the instance premised: "Yet he who denies that it is yours does not seem to me to heed sufficiently the word of the Lord," etc.: I say that no one whom I have seen or heard has denied this, or can deny it more expressly, as is clear from the speeches of his own cited above. To these, with reverence, must always be added that the interpretation of other saints on this passage is more agreeable. For the speech of Christ was (as all agree) metaphorical, when, the disciples saying, "Behold, here are two swords," the Lord replied, "It is enough." Whence Chrysostom: "Certainly, if he wished them to use human protection, even a hundred swords would not suffice. But if he did not wish them to use human help, even two are superfluous." Whence it appears that the meaning of Christ's words was mystical, as his own speech also clearly indicates, when in Matthew 26 and John 18, at the time of the defence, when some defence ought to have been made with those swords, he said to Peter: "Put your sword back into its place, or into its sheath," in which it is signified that he had not commanded that protection be made by the Apostles with swords, but that he spoke mystically. According to this meaning, attending sufficiently to the word of the Lord, Blessed Ambrose expounds the words cited above, saying: "Two swords are permitted, one new and the other of the Old Testament, by which we are defended against the snares of the Devil. And it is said, 'It is enough,' because nothing was lacking to him whom the teaching of both Testaments had defended." But because priests pant after the usurping of principates, and are stretched out with all their outward effort, though undue, they willingly accept foreign interpretations of Scripture, which seem to savour of their corrupt opinion and perverse affection. But if the words of Christ are taken literally, they are nothing against our view, since a material sword is not a principate, nor the judgment of secular affairs, nor, according to metaphor and the sentence of Christ, can it signify the principate or office of secular judgment which Christ committed to Peter or to another Apostle, as Bernard himself clearly proved elsewhere, as cited above, and as indubitably shown also by Scripture in chapters 4 and 5 of this book. And as for what he adds: "Perhaps yours, and to be exercised at your nod," I say that he said "perhaps," although he should not have doubted this at all, unless perhaps he means this rightly: that a prince, in exercising the sword at the priest's nod, that is, at the counsel of the priest in a general or special council, according to the exigency of the faction that arises, ought to attend; as in moving war, when he doubts whether it is just according to divine law, he ought to use the counsel of priests, lest he incur mortal sin; as also in his other monastic and civil acts, especially those in which he doubts that through ignorance he may incur mortal sin. Yet he is not thereby made subject to the priest in such an office. Thus in granting licences for schools and in expelling lepers from the city, he ought to act on the counsel of experts, to whom he is not subject in jurisdiction, as we said in chapter 10 of this book. Hence Bernard, at the end of the sermon already cited, says that the sword must be drawn here at the priest's nod and the Emperor's command. He did not therefore understand by nod the empire or coercive authority, but counsel, since he expressed that this belongs to the Emperor or prince; although the Roman bishop very often orders this sword to be drawn even among the faithful of Christ against one another, and that less justly. And to say in one word: if Bernard from these words understood that such office or judgment belongs to the authority of a priest or bishop, as superior in this to any ruler in the third sense of judgment in this world, I say that in manifest contradiction he contradicts himself, and the sacred Scripture which he himself cites, as appears from what has been said; on which account I decline his opinion in this passage simply, as not canonical but contrary and discordant with the canon. As for the sayings of the saints and doctors, and especially on the Scripture cited from Matthew 16: "You are Peter, and upon this rock," etc.; and again on that of Luke 22: "But I have prayed for you, Peter," etc.; and further on that of John 21: "If you love me, feed my sheep": by these sayings they seem to intend that power or authority was given immediately by Christ to Blessed Peter over the other Apostles, calling him "prince of the Apostles and universal shepherd," and some of them "head of the Church." It must be said, with reverence nonetheless, that Christ did not immediately give Blessed Peter any essential authority, which we have called sacerdotal, nor any accidental preeminence of pastorate over the other Apostles; rather he removed these from him and from the others, as we clearly showed from Scripture and from the exposition of the saints and doctors in chapter 16 of this book, and repeated in a certain manner near the beginning of chapter 22 of this book. Hence I decline the opinion of Christ and of the Apostles, and of certain of them elsewhere, which they set forth in sayings following the aforesaid passages of Scripture and any other similar ones, which seem to say something about such a primacy or principality otherwise than as we said in chapters 16 and 22 of this book. For these are neither canonical nor follow the canon; indeed some of them said the opposite elsewhere, in expounding Scripture. But these men here put forward such things outside Scripture, from their own opinion, following custom, and attending more to certain famous sayings than to the words of Scripture. For who would not wonder that, when the Apostles were disputing which of them was the greater, Christ answered by denying among them any equality or priority of authority from any of them, if he meant Blessed Peter to be the principal and head among them? Again, why did Christ not give the others a command that they should be subject to Peter in pastoral office, lest so great a mystery should be hidden from them and their successors, namely how great a head of the Church he was? For nowhere is it read in Scripture that such a command was given to the Apostles. Why too did Peter give the right hand of fellowship to Paul? Rather he ought to have given a command as a superior. And to say in one word: the whole of Scripture, wherever this matter is touched upon, plainly cries out the opposite of this opinion. Moreover, even if we have denied, according to Scripture, that the pastoral care of the other Apostles was committed by Christ immediately to Blessed Peter, it could not on that account be proved from Scripture that the Roman bishop or any other bishop after the death of Blessed Peter is the pastor of all the others by the immediate ordinance of Christ; but such authority belongs to someone by human election immediately, as we showed earlier in chapters 16, 17 and 22 of this book. And when it was brought forward that the Church is headless, and that Christ did not establish it according to the best arrangement, if he left it without a head in his absence, we can say, according to the Apostle, as before, that Christ always remained the head of the Church, and all the Apostles and ecclesiastical ministers are members, as is plain from Ephesians 4 and from many other places, of which we have sufficiently cited in chapter 22 of this book, part 5. Christ himself also clearly signified this in the last chapter of Matthew, when he said: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." And the disputant may say, is it then also headless, with its mortal head absent from the bishop, which is often the Roman see? And it is agreed that it is so. Yet it must not therefore be conceded that it was left by Christ in disorder or badly arranged; for which reason we must return to what has been said above, and to what we are about to say in the solution of the following objection. As for the argument which seems to be valid, so that I may satisfy it more fully, let us state it in form. For when from it is deduced and inferred that Christ did not establish the Church according to the best arrangement, if he had not left a determinate mortal head in his absence, the inference must be denied. And when it seems to be argued that the Church is in a better arrangement through the institution of this head, I grant, and I believe, that a better arrangement of ecclesiastical rite and of the faith to be observed comes through the institution of such a mortal head; but it was not to be made immediately by Christ. For if so, then always, or in most cases, this would have to come about by the ordinance of Christ. But it was better that it should be determined and chosen by the institution of the faithful, and that this should have been the best arrangement handed down by Christ to the militant Church, so that it might serve as an example hereafter, and the occasion of scandal be removed, both by the Apostles and by their other successors and by the faithful. For the clergy of the city of Rome, or of any other city, are perhaps not always more excellent in Scripture and in life than the other colleges of the world, as appears sufficiently in comparison with the college of the University of Paris and of its clergy. For this reason, by leaving to the faithful the institution of such a head of the Church, as we said in chapter 22 of this book, parts 8 and 9, Christ left it in the best disposition suited to human life. In the same way the Apostles perhaps instituted Peter as head of the Church, as we cited from the decree of Anacletus in chapter 16 of this book, part 12. As for what Augustine said on the words of John 21, "So I wish him to remain," that the life which is in faith is signified by the Apostle Peter because of the primacy of his apostleship, I say that Christ meant it in time, since among the others he was first called to the apostleship by Christ, just as he first received the promise of the keys in time, according to the same Matthew 16, on the words "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." For the life which is in faith, namely of this corruptible world, precedes in time that which is in hope of the incorruptible life of the other world. As for that confirmation of objections which was brought from the "Decrees or Decretals of the Roman pontiffs", it must be said generally of all such writings and discourses, not of the kind we described in chapter 19 of this book, that we are not bound to give them credence as to truth, nor, where they contain the opposite of the aforesaid opinions which we hold from Scripture, but we decline them, though with reverence, and plainly deny them. And as for what they wish to conclude singularly, that the authority of instituting persons for ecclesiastical offices, and of conferring temporal goods or benefices for them, belongs to the Roman bishop alone, or to him with his college of clergy: it must be said that if by "ecclesiastical offices" are meant the sacred orders and characters, which are impressed with these upon the soul as a kind of habit, then I say these offices can be conferred only by bishops or pastors, or by God through their ministry alone, and by no other college or single person. And this must be believed as necessary for salvation, or else the opposite; because it is so ordained by divine law, and not indeed because it has been so decreed by any human Decretals or Decrees. Nevertheless, as we said in chapter 17 of this book, the examination and determination of the fitness of persons to receive these offices must be made not without the authority of the faithful lawgiver, or of the ruler, as was shown above and in chapter 15 of the first part. But if by "ecclesiastical offices" are meant the determinations or institutions of presbyters and of the other officials already named, for the cures of souls, greater or lesser, in certain places and to govern certain peoples, and to establish such offices, or to make determinations of persons for these, and to distribute or confer temporal goods for these ecclesiastical purposes, this belongs to the faithful lawgiver, in the manner we stated in chapter 17 of this book; and that this is not the authority of any single bishop or college of priests, in general and everywhere, nor is it expedient, as was shown in chapters 17 and 21 of this book. As for the opposite of these points which is objected to us from the Decrees and Decretals of the Roman pontiffs, it must be said that although such Decretals or Decrees, and all other writings or discourses of similar kind, not of the kind we described in chapter 19 of this book, may contain many lessons and counsels, even useful ones, both for the state of the present world and of the world to come, insofar as they come from the Roman bishop, even with his college of clergy, without the licence of the faithful lawgiver or the prince, or otherwise or against the form stated in chapter 21 of this book, such statutes do not bind anyone to fault or penalty, and especially not temporal penalty. For such makers of traditions are disposed in the same way as the Pharisees and scribes, to whom Christ says in Mark 7: "In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men. For you lay aside the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men." And a little further on: "You make void the commandment of God well enough, that you may keep your tradition." The Decretals and Decrees, namely concerning the usurping of temporal things, are of this kind. For Decretals, as such, are not divine or human laws, but narrations or documents, and in many cases certain oligarchic statutes. On which account those who issue such things, against the form and beyond the authority already named, who by deceptive words, as if compelling, bring anyone to observe them as well, threatening simple transgressors of them with eternal damnation, or inflicting blasphemies or anathemas, or other curses, upon anyone by word or in writing, are to be punished with extreme corporal punishment, as conspirators and instigators of civil schism. For this is the most grievous kind of the crime of treason, since it is directly committed against the principate, and also, to its supreme plurality, and consequently by necessity leads to the dissolution of every polity.

units.la: CAP. XXIX. De solutione instantiarum, ex scriptura inductarum tertio huius, ad ostendendum iurisdictionem coactiuam episcopis, & supremam Romano episcopo in quantum huiusmodi, conuenire.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX. On the answer to the objections drawn from Scripture in the third part of this book, which are meant to show that coercive jurisdiction belongs to bishops, and supreme jurisdiction to the Roman bishop as such.

units.la: AD reliquas vero instantias ex scriptura inductas tertio huius, propter quas fortassis alicui videretur posse conuinci, Romanum Papam vel alium quemuis episcopum, iudicem esse secundum tertiam significationem super omnes clericos, aut indifferenter super reliquos omnes, absq; tamen humani legislatoris institutione, sed Dei ordinatione immediata. Dicendum, & primo ad eam quae sumebatur ex Matth. 16. dum dixit Christus beato Petro, Tibi dabo claues regni caelorum &c. quod ex his verbis non aliam potestatem beato Petro aut alteri Apostolo tradidit Christus, quam ligandi & soluendi homines à peccatis, sicut expresse dicit beatus Bernhard. ad Eugenium de consideratione libro primo cap 5. & supra induximus quinto huius, parte secunda, de qua etiam seriose dictum est 6. huius & 7. Nec illius plenitudinem aliter quam dictum sit 23. huius. Unde propter haec verba, Romanus aut alter episcopus vel sacerdos, in Apostoli aut Apostolorum persona, coactiuam in hoc seculo autoritatem siue iurisdictionem in quenquam clericum aut laicum non accepit à Christo. Dictum enim est, Tibi dabo claues regni caelorum, ad differentiam regni mundani. Ab huiusmodi namq; regimine sui exemplo Christus vnumquenq; Apostolum & eorum successorem episcopum siue praesbyterum significauit exclusum, dum dixit Lucae 12. Homo, quis me constituit iudicem, terrenorum videlicet? Idemq; per alia praeinducta 4. & 5. huius. Eodem quoq; siue consimili modo dicendum est ad autoritates sumptas ex canone, Matth. 18. & Ioh. 20. dum dixit Christus Apostolis, Quaecunque alligaueritis super terram &c. Et quorum remiseritis peccata &c. Non enim ex his verbis aliam, quam iam dictam & secundum quem modum diximus, Christus illis tradidit potestatem. Ad aliam quae sumebatur ex Matth. 11. dum dixit Christus, Omnia mihi tradita sunt à patre meo. Dicendum quod non sequitur, Omnia mihi tradita sunt à patre meo, ergo potestatem omnium Apostolo vel Apostolis tradidi, sicut etiam diximus 4. huius. Non enim ex hac inquisitione dubitatur, quid Christus tradere potuerit potestatis & autoritatis, Apostolo vel Apostolis, & ipsorum successoribus, sed quid tradere voluerit & de facto tradiderit, & à qua ipsos prohibuerit consilio vel praecepto. Haec n. ostensa sunt sufficienter 4. 5. & 6. ac 9. huius. Unde Bernhard. etiam hoc intendens ad Eugenium de consideratione lib. 3. capit. primo sic inquit, Non enim reor omnem modum, sed sane quodammodo, vt mihi videtur, dispensatio tibi super illum credita est, (videlicet super orbem) non data possessio. Si pergis vsurpare huuc, contradicit tibi qui dicit, Meus est orbis terra & plenitudo eius. Non tu ille de qui quo propheta, Et erit omnis terra possessio eius. Christus hic est, qui possessionem sibi vendicat, & iure creationis & merito redemptionis. Et plura subiungit ad propositum, quae omisi propter sufficientiam praemissorum & abbreviationem sermonis. Non igitur Christus omnia, & secundum modum sibi tradita, tradidit Apostolo, vel Apostolis, sed certa solum & secundum certum modum. Amplius secundum Gloss. omnium sanctorum super hunc locum, intendebat Christus, hanc traditionem sibi factam secundum diuinitatem, qua Dei filius aeternus erat :quod nulli Apostolorum aut successorum conuenire potuit. Propter quod hic sermo Christi nec etiam appareat, aliquid infert contra sententiam quam tenemus. Ad eam vero quae sumebatur Matth. 28. & vltimo, dum dixit Christus, Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo & in terra. Dicendum, sicut diximus ad immediate praemissam. Non enim propter hoc sequitur, esto etiam quod secundum humanitatem omnem potestatem susceperit in terris, quod omnem potestatem Apostolo vel Apostolis tradiderit, sed solum eam, de qua dictum est Matth. vltimo, & Ioh. 20. quam etiam explicauimus 6. huius & 7. Quoniam & secundum hanc solum regnare venit Christus, unde Hieron. super hunc locum: In caelo autem & in terra potestas data est, vt qui ante regnabat in caelo, per fidem credentium regnet in terris. Quod autem ex Matth. 8. & Marc. 5. sumebatur, Daemones autem rogabant eum, dicentes &c. Dicendum, nec id dictum obuiare sententiae, quam tenemus. Esto nanque, sicut verum est, Christum habuisse si voluisset, etiam secundum humanitatem, dominium, & omnem potestatem temporalium, non ex hoc per necessitatem potest inferri, eum tradidisse Apostolo vel Apostolis, aut ipsorum successoribus consimilem potestatem, quinimo, tam opere quam sermone Christus illis monstrauit, temporalium fugere possessionem atque dominium, sic etiam iurisdictionem coactiuam cuiusquam in hoc seculo, siue iudicium, vt 4. huius & 5. monstratum est, & repetitum cap. precedente. Quod si tamen Christus aliquando vsus fuerit talium potestate siue dominio, non tamen humani principantis seu iudicis modo, sed miraculose ac raro valde diuina potestate potius quam humana, vt in proposito & in arefactione ficulnea, suis Apostolis ex hoc significare volens sui diuinitatis naturam, unde ipsos amplius in fide firmaret, vel etiam propter aliquod melius, occultum homini & inoccultum sibi, sicut dicunt ibidem Chrysost. & Hieron. Vt sit, inquit Hieron. saluris hominum occasio per porcorum interfectionem. Et ideo Christus, nec ipsos miracula facere docuit, vt ex Aug. de verbis Domini, super Matth. sermone 10. supra inducimus 4. huius. Eoque minus ipsos voluit exercere potestatem in alienam iacturam & scandalum propter quod talia non exercuit, vt ipsi talia exercere deberent, sed vt illis se verum Deum ostenderet esse. Ei vero instantiae, quae inducebatur ex Matth. 22. Marc. 11. & Lucae 19. Tunc misit duos discipulos, dicens eis Iesus, Ite in castellum quod contra vos est, & inueniets asinam alligatam &c. similiter dicendum est, quemadmodum instantiae immediate praemissae. Ea vero quae de duobus gladiis, sumpta Luc. 22. & quae de pastu ouium ex Ioan. 21. nil contradicunt, aut contradicens inferunt necessario sententiae, quam tenemus; sicut seriose monstrauimus praecedenti cap. Non n. ex his B. Petro vel alteri Apostolo, aut ipsorum successori coactiuam in hoc seculo cuiusquam iurisdictionem tradidit, siue iudicium, sed officium pastoratus, de quo traditum est sufficienter 9. huius. Quod autem inquit Apostolus primae ad Corinth. 6. Nescitis quoniam Angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis saecularia? nec contradictorium est sententiae quam tenemus, nec contradictorium infert. Non enim sermone seu scriptura praedicta, monebat seu alloquebatur Apostolus, sacerdotes tantum modo, sed generaliter omnes fideles de Corintho. Nam iisdem generaliter, vt ex salutatione patet, scripsit epistolam. Contendebant enim inuicem de saecularibus & ciuilibus, coram infidelibus iudicibus se trahentes, propter quod monebat ipsos Apostolus, tanquam pastor ipsis consulendo, vt ex coetu fidelium sibi iudices constituerent, non quidem sacerdotes aut episcopos, sed alios ab his. Propter quod immediate subdit Apostolus: Saecularia igitur iudicia, si habueritis contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia, illos constituite ad iudicandum, ad verecundiam vestram dico, si non est inter vos sapiens quisquam, qui possit iudicare inter fratrem suum? sed frater cum fratre contendit iudicio apud infideles. Quam siquidem Apostoli seriem exponens Gloss. secundum Aug. Ambr. & Greg. inquit sic. Saecularia igitur &c. Sicut iam reprehendit eos, quia causas agebant apud infideles contemptu fidelibus, ita nunc reprehendit eos, quod contemptibiles iudices, licet fideles, constituebant, qui, & quia debetis iudicare. Igitur si habueritis saecularia iudicia, ideo dicit, si habueritis, quia nec habendi sunt, sed potius sunt contemnenda, si inquam habueritis, constituite ad iudicandum illos contemptibiles, id est, ind-scretos & viles, qui sunt in ecclesia, quid hoc est, quod vos fecistis. Vnde coacti fratres recurrerent ad illos, id est, ad infideles. Hoc redarguit in eis Apostolus, ironice eis loquens, & quia non decet fieri, adiecit, ad verecundiam vel ad reuerentiam vestram dico, non imperio, sed memoro, vt verecundemini, & debetis erubescere, quia non est inter vos quisquam sic, id est, adeo sapiens, quod possit iudicare inter fratrem suum, vt ita necesse sit, vt stultos statuatis iudices. Et hi tamen potius statuendi sunt, quam ad infideles iudices eatur, si desint sapientes, sic inquam non est sapiens, sed frater cum fratre contendit in iudicio, quod malum est, etiam apud infideles, quod peius est, vel ita. Saecularia igitur, quia dixerat Apostolus, eos posse de his minimis iudicare, determinat, qui ad huiusmodi diffinienda negotia sunt constituendi, scilicet contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia. Maiores enim spiritualibus intendere debent, qui, & quia iudicare debetis, igitur hoc modo facite, si saecularia negotia habueritis, illos constituite ad iudicandum, qui sunt in ecclesia contemptibiles, id est, aliquos sapientes, qui tamen sunt minoris meriti, Apostolis enim praedicando circumeuntes talibus non vacabant. Sapientes ergo qui in locis considebant fideles & sancti, non qui hac ataa illac propter euangelium discurrebant talium negotiorum examinatores esse voluit. A quibus nos excusare non possumus & si velimus. Christum enim testem inuocc, quoniam mallem per singulos dies certis horis manibus aliquid operari, ri, & certas horas habere liberas ad legendum & orandum, vel ad agendum aliquid de diuinis literis, quam tumultuosas perplexitates causarum pati de negotiis secularibus, vel iudicando dirimendis, vel interueniendo prae-cidendis. Dico contemptibiles constituite, hoc autem ad reuerentiam vestram dico, vt videlicet, hi terrenas cau-sas examinent, qui exteriorum rerum sapientiam perceperunt, qui autem spiritualibus donis ditati sunt, terrenis non debent negotiis implicari, vt dum non coguntur inferiora bona disponere, valeant bonis superioribus deseruire. Sed tamen curandum magno opere est, vt hi qui donis spiritualibus emicant, nequaquam proximorum infirmantium negotia funditus deserant, sed haec alii, quibus dignum est tractanda committant, vel per se gerant. Sunt autem haec Apostoli & sanctorum scripta notanda. Apparet enim ex ipsis primo, quod omnes contentiones inter quascunque personas, de his quae non pertinent ad legem diuinam, sunt seculares & non spirituales, & ad seculare iudicium pertinentes. Nam generaliter locutus est Apostolus, & sancti super hunc locum, non facientes differentiam, sicut nec est, inter contentiones temporales seu ciuiles, quae sunt presbyterorum inuicem, & generaliter clericorum, aut quae sunt inter presbyteros & laicos, & inter eas quae sunt seculariuм inuicem. Dicat n: quasi sophista & vocabulorum abusor, qui spirituale vocat, quod est simpliciter seculare, secundum Apostoli & sanctorum appellationem, si presbyter iniuriam inferens fratri, sacerdoti, siue non sacerdoti, verbo vel facto, facit iniuriam spirituale, magis ea quam laicus intulerit, hoc n. dicere derisio est, credere vero summa vesania, quippe, quoniam carnalior seu secularior & detestabilior est iniuria, quae per sacerdotem infertur illata per laicum. Nam turpius peccat & grauius qui aliud docere tenetur, tam opere quam sermone, iniuriam non inferre, quemadmodum seriosius ostensum est 8. huius. Quod autem seculares, non spirituales sint, & dici debeant huiusmodi clericorum actus, aperte testatur Aug. in praedicta Glossa, dum causas contentiosas presbyterorum & clericorum, quae coram ipso agebantur, qui episcopus erat, vocauit, tumultuosas perplexitates causarum de negotiis secularibus, non faciens harum causarum siue contentionum differentiam, propter personarum conditiones. Haec n. differentia, presbyteri scilicet, ac non presbyteri, quantum ad hoc accidentalis est, veluti ea quae circuli per aureum & argenteum, qua nullus artifex assignat, eo quod distinctione non efficit in effectu per se. Apparet secundo quod hoc u actui iudicii, aut iudicie esse, non est sacerdotum, & quod talem iudicem instituere non plus, imo fortasse minus, ad ipsorum auctoritate pertinet, quam reliquorum fidelium, sed pertinet hoc ad fidelium vniuersitatem, quemadmodum ostensum est 15. prima. Et propterea dixit Apostolus, constituite, nec dixit alicui episcopo vel sacerdoti, Constitue. Vbi namque agebatur aliquid pertinens ad officium sacerdotis seu episcopi, id facere mandabat singulariter illi non multitudini fidelium, sicut presbyteros seu episcopos, aut diaconos constituere, aut euangelium praedicare, ac reliqua exercere officia, quae propria sunt presbytero aut pastori. Unde ad Titum primo: Huius gratia reliquit te Creta, vt ea quae desunt corrigas, quantum videlicet ad doctrinam salutarem & mores. Et constitutas per ciuitates presbyteros, sicut ego disposui, non tamen dixit illi, Constitue iudicem negotiorum secularium examinatorem. Nec Corinthiis scribens, dixit, Vobis constituet episcopus vel sacerdos, sed dixit Apostolus ad vniuersam fidelium multitudinem, Constituite, non quidem imperans, sed consulens sine memorans. Unde Glossa super illud, Ad reuerentiam vestram dico, inquit, quasi non impero, sed memoro, vt verecundemini. Bene n. nouerat Apostolus, tales iudices instituere, ad suum officium minime pertinere, & eo minus, ad sacerdotem seu episcopum alium. Nec rursum ad huiusmodi officium exercendum assumi consuluit presbyterum aut episcopum quenquam, sed oppositum magis, quoniam nemo, vt inquit, militans Deo implicat se secularibus negotiis. Sed consuluit statui iudices, contemptibiles in ecclesia, id est, de numero fidelium, eos qui non erant idonei ad euangelizandum, quamuis non omnes sed secundum Glossam sanctorum, illos terrenas causas examinare voluit apostolus siue consuluit, qui exteriorum rerum scientia perceperunt, qui autem spiritualibus donis dotati sunt, non debent terrenis negotiis implicari, quod manifeste docebat beatus Bern. ad Eugenium, de consideratione lib. 1. c. 5. & pridem induximus 7. precedenti. Obiicit autem aliquis Aug. dictum, in superioribus Glossis. Inquit n. ille, de secularium contentiosorum actuum iudiciis loquens, a quibus nos excusare non possumus, et si velimus. Cuius etiam sententia ibid. confirmas Greg. addit: Sed tamen curandum magno opere est &c. sed haec (scil. iudicia secularium actuum,) quibus dignum est, tractanda committant episcopi, vel per se gerant. Sic talia iudicare ac talium iudices constituere, ad episcopos seu presbyteros, in quantum huiusmodi pertinere videtur, ex quo ab his secundum sanctorum sententiam excusari non possunt, & ipsis hoc magno curandum est opere. Nos autem ad haec obiecta, & reliqua cosimilia dicta sanctorum aut doctorum, dicamus, quod antiquis temporibus & iam doctorum sanctorum propter status sacerdotalis reuerentiam, & ipsorum moris siue virtutis confidentiam, ac reliquas causas, de quibus diximus 25. huius parte 5. concessum fuit per fideles legislatores & principes, iudiciale officium tertiae significationis episcopis & principalibus animarum pastoribus supra clericorum personas, & temporalia, vt minus vexarentur, aut turbarentur a diuinis officiis, & honestius in causis secularibus tractantur. Et quoniam iam doctorum sanctorum aliqui constituti erant episcopi in prouinciis siue locis, quorum principes aut incolae supradictum iudiciale officium illis contulerant, nisi episcopatui renunciassent, ab huiusmodi gerenda causarum secularium inter clericos cura, excusari non poterant rursum. Sed rursum dubitabit aliquis merito quaerens, cur viri sancti, vt beatus Siluester, & aliorum plurimi iudicia & potestates seculares, ac temporalium possessione & ad ministrationem assumpserint, si talia presbyterorum, episcoporum, & reliquorum euangelizantium officio non conueniunt neq; conuenerint. Dicendum arbitror, secundum veritatem inductas prius, praesertim 17. & 25. huius, quod fidelium ecclesia seu multitudo, modica existens circa principium & consequenter, etiam tepore multo, a principatibus & subditis infidelibus, persecutiones plurimas usq; ad mortalia martyria patiebatur frequenter & in multa pauper tate viuebat. Propter quod sancti episcopi veri pastores, pro gregis salute, augmentu, conservatione & sustentatione nem ab Imperatoribus fidelibus, deuotis, & sibi propitiis, gratias, & fauores, concessiones, seu priuilegia impetrabant, aut oblatas suscipiebat, non quidem vt penlent, sed vt possent, & fidelem prote-
units.tr: As for the remaining objections drawn from Scripture in the third part of this book, by which someone might think the Roman Pope or any other bishop could be convicted of being a judge, in the third sense, over all clergy, or indifferently over all others, yet without any institution of a human lawgiver and by the immediate ordinance of God, the answer is as follows. First, to the objection taken from Matthew 16, where Christ said to the blessed Peter, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc.: Christ did not give blessed Peter, or any other Apostle, by these words any power other than that of binding and loosing men from sins, as blessed Bernard expressly says, to Eugenius, On Consideration, book 1, ch. 5, and as we cited above, in the fifth part of this book, part two, which was also discussed at length, in the sixth and seventh parts of this book. Nor was its fullness different from what was said in the twenty-third part of this book. Therefore, on account of these words, the Roman bishop or another bishop or priest did not receive from Christ, in the person of the Apostle or the Apostles, coercive authority or jurisdiction in this age over any clergyman or layman. For it is said, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, in contrast to a worldly kingdom. For by his own example Christ showed that every Apostle, and their successor bishop or presbyter, was excluded from such government, when he said in Luke 12, Man, who made me a judge?, namely over earthly things. The same is shown by the other passages cited above, in the fourth and fifth parts of this book. In the same or a similar way one must answer the authorities taken from the canon, Matthew 18 and John 20, where Christ said to the Apostles, Whatsoever you bind on earth, etc., and whose sins you remit, etc. For from these words Christ gave them no other power than the one already mentioned and in the manner we have described. To the other objection, taken from Matthew 11, where Christ said, All things have been delivered to me by my Father: it does not follow that, because all things have been delivered to me by my Father, he therefore handed over the power of all things to an Apostle or the Apostles, as we also said in the fourth part of this book. For the question here is not what power and authority Christ could have handed over to the Apostle or the Apostles and their successors, but what he wished to hand over and in fact did hand over, and from what he forbade them by counsel or command. For these points have been sufficiently shown in the fourth, fifth, sixth and ninth parts of this book. Hence Bernard, also aiming at this in his To Eugenius, On Consideration, book 3, chapter 1, says thus: For I do not think the whole world, but in some sense, as it seems to me, the stewardship over it has been entrusted to you (namely over the world), not possession given. If you go on to usurp it, he contradicts you who says, The earth is mine and the fullness thereof. You are not that one of whom the prophet says, And all the earth shall be his possession. Christ is he who claims possession for himself, by the right of creation and by the merit of redemption. And he adds more to the point, which I have omitted on account of the sufficiency of what has been put forward and for brevity of speech. Therefore Christ did not hand over to the Apostle or the Apostles all things, nor in the manner in which they were delivered to him, but only certain things and in a certain manner. Moreover, according to the Gloss of All Saints on this passage, Christ intended that this delivery made to him was according to his divinity, by which he was the eternal Son of God; and this could not belong to any Apostle or successor. For this reason this saying of Christ, not even apparently, brings anything against the opinion we hold. As for the objection taken from Matthew 28 and the last chapter, where Christ said, All power is given to me in heaven and on earth: the answer is as we said to the objection immediately preceding. For it does not follow, even if according to his humanity he received all power on earth, that he handed all power over to the Apostle or the Apostles; only that power of which it is said in the last chapter of Matthew and in John 20, which we also explained in the sixth and seventh parts of this book. For Christ came to reign only in this sense. Hence Jerome on this passage: But power has been given in heaven and on earth, so that he who before reigned in heaven may reign on earth through the faith of believers. As for the objection taken from Matthew 8 and Mark 5, And the demons begged him, saying, etc.: the answer is that this saying does not run counter to the opinion we hold. For even if, as is true, Christ had, if he had wished, dominion and all temporal power even according to his humanity, it cannot be inferred from this of necessity that he handed a similar power over to an Apostle or the Apostles or their successors. Rather, Christ showed them by deed as well as by word that they should flee the possession and dominion of temporal things, and likewise any coercive jurisdiction or judgment in this age over anyone, as in the fourth and fifth parts of this book has been shown, and as was repeated in the preceding chapter. But if Christ at some time made use of such power or dominion, he did so not in the manner of a human ruler or judge, but miraculously and very rarely, by divine power rather than human, as in the case in question and in the withering of the fig tree; wishing thereby to signify to his Apostles the nature of his divinity, so as to confirm them further in the faith, or also on account of something better, hidden from man and not hidden from him, as Chrysostom and Jerome say in the same place. So that, says Jerome, there might be an occasion for the salvation of men through the killing of the swine. And therefore Christ did not teach the Apostles to work miracles, as we cited above in the fourth part of this book, from Augustine On the words of the Lord, on Matthew, sermon 10. Still less did he wish them to exercise power to the loss and scandal of others; for which reason he did not exercise such things, so that they ought to exercise such things, but so that he might show himself to them to be the true God. As for the objection brought from Matthew 22, Mark 11 and Luke 19, Then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, Go into the village that is over against you, and you will find an ass tied, etc., the answer is similar to that for the objection immediately preceding. As for what is drawn from Luke 22 about the two swords, and what is drawn from John 21 about feeding the sheep, these contradict nothing, nor do they of necessity bring anything contrary to the opinion we hold; as we have shown in detail in the preceding chapter. For from these words Christ did not give blessed Peter, or another Apostle, or their successor, any coercive jurisdiction or judgment over anyone in this age, but the office of pastoral care, which has been sufficiently treated in the ninth part of this book. As for what the Apostle says in the first letter to the Corinthians, 6. Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more things of this life?, this is neither contrary to the opinion we hold, nor does it bring anything contrary. For the Apostle did not address or admonish, in the aforesaid speech or writing, only priests, but in general all the faithful of Corinth. For he wrote the letter to all of them in common, as the greeting makes clear. For they were quarrelling among themselves about secular and civil matters, dragging each other before unbelieving judges; and for this reason the Apostle admonished them, as a pastor advising them, that from the assembly of the faithful they should appoint judges for themselves, not indeed priests or bishops, but others apart from these. Therefore the Apostle immediately adds: If then you have secular judgments, set those who are of no account in the Church to judge; I say this to your shame. Is there not among you one wise man who is able to judge between his brothers? But brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers. Explaining this sequence of the Apostle, the Gloss, following Augustine, Ambrose and Gregory, says this: If then you have secular judgments, etc. As he has already rebuked them because they were pleading their causes before unbelievers, contemptuous of the faithful, so now he rebukes them because they were appointing contemptible judges, though faithful, who, since you ought to judge... Therefore, if you have secular judgments, he says, if you have, because they ought not to be held, but rather despised; if, I say, you have them, appoint to judge those contemptible, that is, undiscerning and worthless, who are in the Church. What is this that you have done? Hence the brothers, compelled, went to those, that is, to unbelievers. The Apostle rebukes them for this, speaking to them ironically, and because it ought not to be done, he added, I say this to your shame or reverence, not by command, but by reminding, that you may be ashamed, and ought to blush, because there is not among you anyone so wise, that is, so wise that he could judge between his brother, that it is so necessary for you to set foolish men as judges. And yet these ought rather to be appointed than that one should go to unbelieving judges, if wise men are lacking. Is there not, I say, one wise man, but brother goes to law with brother, which is an evil even before unbelievers, and which is worse, or thus. Therefore secular, because the Apostle had said that they could judge in these least matters, he determines who ought to be appointed to decide such affairs, namely those who are contemptible in the Church. For the greater ones ought to attend to spiritual matters; and because you ought to judge, therefore do it in this way: if you have secular business, appoint to judge those who are contemptible in the Church, that is, some wise men who are nevertheless of lesser merit, for those who went about preaching as Apostles were not free for such things. Therefore he wished the examiners of such matters to be wise men who sat in places among the faithful and holy, not those who ran here and there for the sake of the gospel. From these matters we cannot excuse ourselves, even if we should wish to. For I call Christ to witness that I would rather work with my hands for certain hours each day, and have certain free hours for reading and praying, or for doing something from the divine letters, than suffer the tumultuous perplexities of causes concerning secular affairs, either in settling them by judgment, or in intervening to cut them short. I say: appoint those who are contemptible; but this I say to your reverence, namely that those who have perceived the wisdom of external things should examine earthly causes, while those who are enriched with spiritual gifts ought not to be entangled in earthly business, so that, while they are not compelled to arrange lower goods, they may be able to serve higher goods. Yet it must be carefully attended to that those who shine with spiritual gifts by no means utterly abandon the affairs of weak neighbours, but commit these to others who are worthy to handle them, or manage them themselves. These writings of the Apostle and of the saints ought to be noted. For it appears from them, first, that all disputes between any persons concerning matters that do not pertain to the divine law are secular and not spiritual, and belong to secular judgment. For the Apostle spoke in general terms, and the saints on this passage likewise made no distinction, just as there is none, between temporal or civil disputes, which are between presbyters among themselves, and generally between clergy, or those which are between presbyters and laymen, and those which are between secular persons among themselves. For let someone say, like a sophist and an abuser of words, who calls spiritual what is simply secular according to the usage of the Apostle and the saints: if a presbyter, doing an injury to a brother, whether a priest or not, by word or deed, does an injury that is spiritual, more so than a layman would have inflicted it. For to say this is mockery, and to believe it is the height of madness; indeed, because an injury inflicted by a priest is more carnal or more secular and more detestable than one inflicted by a layman. For he sins more shamefully and more gravely who is bound to teach, both by deed and by word, not to inflict injury, as was shown more seriously in the eighth part of this book. That the actions of such clergy are secular and not spiritual, and ought to be called so, Augustine clearly testifies in the aforesaid Gloss, when he called the contentious causes of presbyters and clergy, which were being pleaded before him, since he was a bishop, tumultuous perplexities of causes concerning secular affairs, making no distinction of these causes or disputes on account of the conditions of the persons. For this difference, namely between presbyters and non-presbyters, is accidental as far as this matter is concerned, like those things that are distinguished by gold and silver, which no craftsman assigns, because the distinction does not produce an effect in itself. Second, it appears that this act of judging, or the function of a judge, does not belong to priests, and that to appoint such a judge belongs to their authority no more, indeed perhaps less, than to that of the remaining faithful; but it pertains to the whole body of the faithful, as has been shown in the fifteenth [section] of the first part. And therefore the Apostle said, appoint, and did not say to any bishop or priest, appoint. For wherever something pertaining to the office of a priest or bishop was at issue, he commanded that to be done not by the multitude of the faithful, but to that one person alone, as to appoint presbyters or bishops or deacons, or to preach the gospel, and to exercise the other offices that are proper to a presbyter or pastor. Hence to Titus in the first chapter: For this cause I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking, namely as regards sound doctrine and morals; and appoint presbyters in the cities, as I have directed you; yet he did not say to him, appoint a judge of secular business, an examiner. Nor, writing to the Corinthians, did he say, let a bishop or priest appoint for you, but the Apostle said to the whole multitude of the faithful, appoint, not indeed commanding, but advising or reminding. Hence the Gloss on the words, I say this to your reverence, says: as if I do not command, but remind, that you may be ashamed. For the Apostle well knew that to appoint such judges did not pertain at all to his office, and still less to a priest or other bishop. Nor again did he advise that any presbyter or bishop be taken up to exercise such an office, but rather the opposite, since, as he says, no one who serves God entangles himself in secular business. But he advised that contemptible men in the Church, that is, from the number of the faithful, be set up as judges, those who were not fit to preach the gospel; though not all, but according to the Gloss of the saints, the Apostle wished or advised that those who have perceived the knowledge of external things should examine earthly causes, while those who are endowed with spiritual gifts ought not to be entangled in earthly affairs; which the blessed Bernard clearly taught to Eugenius, On Consideration, book 1, ch. 5, and which we cited earlier in the seventh part of the preceding. But someone may object the saying of Augustine in the Glosses above. For he, speaking of judgments concerning secular contentious acts, from which we cannot excuse ourselves even if we wish, says so. Gregory, confirming the same opinion in the same place, adds: Yet it must be carefully attended to, etc., but these (namely judgments of secular acts) the bishops should commit, to those worthy to handle them, or manage them themselves. Thus, to judge such matters and to appoint judges of them seems, so far as it is in the nature of such things, to pertain to bishops or presbyters, since, according to the opinion of the saints, they cannot be excused from it, and they must attend to it with great care. But we, to these objections and to the other similar sayings of the saints or doctors, reply that in ancient times, and already in the time of the holy doctors, on account of the reverence due to the priestly state, and the confidence in their character or virtue, and the other reasons of which we spoke in the twenty-fifth part of this book, part five, the judicial office of the third sense was granted by faithful lawgivers and princes to bishops and principal pastors of souls over the persons of clergy and over temporal matters, so that they might be less harassed or disturbed in their divine offices, and that causes of a secular kind might be more honourably handled. And since some of the holy doctors were already appointed bishops in provinces or places, whose princes or inhabitants had conferred the aforesaid judicial office upon them, they could not again be excused from the care of managing secular causes among clergy, unless they had renounced the episcopate. But again someone will rightly ask, wondering why holy men, such as blessed Sylvester and very many others, took up secular judgments and powers, and the possession and administration of temporal goods, if such things do not and did not agree with the office of presbyters, bishops and the other evangelists. I think it must be said, according to the truth set out earlier, especially in the seventeenth and twenty-fifth parts of this book, that the Church or multitude of the faithful, being small at the beginning, and consequently also very lukewarm, suffered very many persecutions, even to death by martyrdom, from princes and subjects who were unbelievers, and frequently lived in great poverty. For this reason the holy bishops, true pastors, for the salvation, increase, preservation and support of the flock, obtained or accepted from faithful, devoted and favourable emperors thanks, favours, grants or privileges, not indeed that they might rule, but that they might be able to protect and cherish the faithful people to pro-

Sic ergo iudicia secularium actuum inter clericos precipue, propter iam dictas causas sancti episcopi susceperunt. Sic etiam quorundam temporalium administrationem absq; possessione siue dominio, seu autoritate vendicandi, curam acceperunt, vt posset hoc in fideles pauperes redundare. Unde Ambr. de tradendis basilicis, vbi supra: si agres desiderat Imperator, potestatem habet vendicandorum, nemo nostrum interuenit, potest pauperibus collatio populi redundare. Nemo ergo sacerdotum seu episcoporum interueniebat pro agris, quoniam Christū & Apostolos imitantes, horum abdicabant dominium, pro fide vero agonizabant constanter vsque ad mortem, quamuis moderni episcopi & precipue Romanorum, pro agris & secularibus dominiis fortissime pugnent, & pugnas vndiq; inter Christi fideles concitent, dicentes se in hoc iura sponsae Christi defendere, cum tamen ipsius iura non sint, sed iniuriae, veram sponsam, fidem videlicet, doctrinam & mores defendere, ne per prauos vsus aut actus, aut infidelium impetum corrumpatur, quasi totaliter negligentes, quemadmodum diximus 22. huius. His ergo de causis, antiquis temporibus, huiusmodi officia & beneficia susceperunt sanctorum aliqui, quibus siquidem conuenienter renunciare possent moderni, ad minus in comunitatibus fidelium. Sufficienter n. per principantes ab oppressionibus defenditur clerus, quinimo vix ab offensionibus in aliquos reprimi possunt. Verum talibus renunciare secularibus officiis, possessioni atque dominio temporalium non est propositum modernorum pastorum, sed pro huiusmodi etiam armata pugnare potentia, non solum habitis conseruandis, verum etiam pro reliquis vsurpandis, sicut quilibet quantumcunq; rudis sensu, si non alio, doceri possunt: vniuersitatem fidelium etiam quamplurimum scandalizantes, ex hoc ambitionis exemplo, non attendentes Christi comminationem, Matth. 18. dum dixit, Qui scandalizauerit vnum de pusillis istis &c. Vbi Glossa secundum Hieron. Et quanquam generaliu possit esse sententia aduersus omnes, qui aliquem scandalizant, tamen iuxta consequentiam sermonis etiam contra Apostolos dictum intelligi potest, qui interrogando, quis maior esset, videbantur inter se de dignitate contendere. Et si in hoc vitio permansissent, poterant eos quos ad fidem vocabant, per suum scandalum perdere, dum Apostoli viderent inter se de honore pugnare. Quod autem de Apostolis Hieron. dixit, intelligendum est etiam de ipsorum successoribus omnibus, episcopis siue presbyteris. Qui si tamen sponte huiusmodi officia iudicialia, & autoritatem distribuendi temporalia relinquere nolint, ipsisq; abutantur, secundum diuinam & humanam legem, licite possunt & debent principantes aut fideles legislatores eadem ab ipsis renocare, quemadmodum demonstratum 15. prima, 17. & 21. huius. Quod autem obiiciebatur ex Apostolo primae ad Corinth. 9. & 2. Thess. 3. Nunquid non habemus potestatem &c. dissolutum fuit 14. huius. Talis enim potestas, vt tibi dicebatur, non est iurisdictionis, sed licite petendi secundum legem diuinam, quamuis tamen non in iudicio coactiuo, alimentum & tegumentum sibi debitum propter euangelii ministrationem a potentibus exhibere. Ei vero quae inducebatur ex 1. ad Timoth. 5. dum dixit Apostolus: Aduersus presbyterum noli accipere accusationem &c. Dicendum, hic Apostolum intellexisse, si debeat sacerdos publice increpari a suo superiori, pastore siue doctore, non enim iurisdictionem coactiuam alicui sacerdoti vel episcopo in quenquam exercere mandauit, quoniam & hoc ad suam & cuiuslibet sui successoris autoritatem non pertinere nouit Apostolus. Significauit autem Apostolus, correptionem quae ad Pastorem pertinet, solum esse verbalem; in eo quod subdit, Peccantes coram omnibus argue, vt caeteri timorem habeant, nec dixit cape vel incarcera, sed incorrigibiles sermone docuit euitari. Unde ad Tit. 3. haereticum hominem post primam & secundam correptionem deuita, cum sit proprio iudicio condemnatus.
units.tr: Those holy bishops, the true ministers, accepted judicial cases of secular affairs, especially those involving clergy, for the reasons already mentioned, so that they might protect and cherish the people of their flock. They likewise accepted the administration of certain temporal goods, without possession or lordship, and without any authority to claim them, so that the benefit might flow to the faithful poor. Hence Ambrose, On Handing Over the Basilicas, above: If the Emperor desires land, he has the power to claim it; none of us intervenes. The gift of the people can flow to the poor. So no priest or bishop intervened for lands, since, imitating Christ and the Apostles, they renounced such lordship and struggled constantly for the faith, even to death. Yet today's bishops, and especially those of Rome, fight most fiercely for lands and secular lordships, and stir up wars everywhere among the faithful of Christ, claiming that in this they defend the rights of the Bride of Christ. Yet these are not her rights but wrongs. She is the true Bride, namely the faith, the doctrine and the morals, and these they neglect almost entirely, so that they may be defended against corruption by bad practices or deeds, or against the assault of unbelievers, as we said in the 22nd chapter of this book. For these reasons, in ancient times, some of the saints accepted such offices and benefices, which today's bishops could suitably renounce, at least in the communities of the faithful. For the clergy are sufficiently defended from oppression by the rulers; indeed they can scarcely be restrained from injuring some people. But it is not the purpose of today's pastors to renounce such secular offices, possession and temporal lordship. Instead they fight with armed power for these things, not only to keep what they have but also to seize the rest. This can be taught to anyone, however dull in understanding, if by no other means. They also cause great scandal to the whole body of the faithful by this example of ambition, not heeding the warning of Christ, Matth. 18., when he said, Whoever shall offend one of these little ones, etc. Here the Gloss, following Jerome: Although this sentence could be general against all who offend anyone, it can nevertheless be understood, from the sequence of the discourse, as spoken also against the Apostles, who, when they asked who was greater, seemed to contend with one another about dignity. If they had persisted in this vice, they could have lost those whom they called to the faith through their scandal, while the Apostles were seen fighting with one another over honour. What Jerome said of the Apostles must be understood also of all their successors, bishops or presbyters. If, however, they are unwilling to give up such judicial offices and the authority to distribute temporal goods of their own accord, and abuse them, then the rulers or the faithful lawgivers may lawfully and must, according to divine and human law, revoke these from them, as shown in the 15th, 17th and 21st chapters of this book. As for the objection drawn from the Apostle, 1 Cor. 9. and 2 Thess. 3., Have we not the power? etc., it was answered in the 14th chapter. Such power, as was said to you, is not a power of jurisdiction, but a lawful right, under divine law, to demand from the powerful, though not by coercive judgment, the food and clothing due to those who minister the gospel. As for the passage brought from 1 Tim. 5., where the Apostle says, Do not receive an accusation against an elder, etc., it must be said that the Apostle here means this: if a priest ought to be publicly rebuked by his superior, his pastor or teacher. For he did not command that any priest or bishop should exercise coercive jurisdiction over anyone, since the Apostle knew that this did not belong to his own authority or to that of any successor of his. The Apostle indicated, however, that the correction which belongs to the pastor is only verbal, in what he adds: Rebuke those who sin in the presence of all, so that the rest may have fear. He did not say to seize or imprison, but taught that the incorrigible are to be avoided by word. Hence in Titus 3: Avoid a heretical man after the first and second admonition, since he is condemned by his own judgment.

units.la: De solutione rationum eodem tertio ad idem etiam inducatarum, & imperii Romani, ac alterius cuiuslibet principatus translatione, quantum secundum rectam rationem fieri debet & potest.
units.tr: On the solution of the arguments adduced in the same third section for the same point, and on the transfer of the Roman empire and of any other principality, as far as it ought and can be done according to right reason.

units.la: Reliquum vero & vltimum huius dictionis, est soluere rationes, quas etiam 3. huius induximus, ad astruendum errorem dicentium, iurisdictiones coactiuas ad presbyteros siue episcopos, ipsarumq; supremam omnium in hoc seculo, ad Romanum episcopum, in quantum huiusmodi pertinere. Ad earum ergo primam, cum dicebatur, Sicut se habet corpus ad animam, sic princeps corporis ad principem animae. Haec propositio falsa est vniuersaliter sumpta. Nam quamuis anima distinguatur a corpore, quoniam anima non est corpus, nullus tamen est corporis princeps, quin sit etiam animae aliquo modo princeps, & econuerso, sumendo principem proprie, quemadmodum apparet 8. & 9. huius. Si vero per Principem corporis, secundum metaphoram intelligatur medicus, qui eius curam gerit tanquam doctor operatiuus; & quantum ad actus qui sunt particulae rationalis & nutritiuae: per principem autem animae, eum qui medicus est & doctor siue praeceptor operatiuus, quantum ad actus partis rationalis & appetitiuae tam in statu & pro statu praesentis seculi, quales sunt humanarum scientiarum vel disciplinarum doctores, quam pro statu futuri seculi, quales sunt pastores & sacerdotes, posset iam dicta propositio indefinite sumpta concedi, quoniam vniuersaliter sumpta semper instantiam multiplicem pateretur. Anima enim ad corpus, rursum rationalis ad irrationalem, multas habet differentias, quas doctor aut curator secundum vnam, non habet ad doctorem seu curatorem secundum aliam. Etenim rationalis ad imaginem trinitatis est syllogizans, irrationalis vero minime, nec tamen inter harum curatores seu doctores est huiusmodi differentia, sic & in aliis. Ea ergo in aliquo sensu concessa, vt videlicet sicut anima rationalis & appetitiua nobilior est corpore, id est, animato secundum nutritiuam, in quantum huiusmodi, ita doctor vel curator animæ rationalis &c. dignior est eo qui curator & doctor irrationalis: siue etiam fiat comparatio hæc, inter doctorem animæ rationalis pro statu seu fine præsentis seculi tantum ad eum qui eiusdem doctor est, principaliter pro statu, seu fine futuri seculi. Esto sic inquam, alterum altero perfectiorem esse, non ex hoc sequitur, ipsorum perfectiorem iudicē esse super imperfectiorē iudicio coactiuo, sic n. mathematicus princeps esset coactiuus medici, & plurima manifeste inconuenientia sequerentur ex hoc. Quod si per principem corporum intelligatur principans siue iudex hominum coactiuus, seu tertiæ significationis, in statu & pro statu siue fine præsentis seculi tantum, aut principaliter: per principem vero animarum eum qui iudex est secundum tertiam significationem principaliter pro statu seu fine venturi seculi, sicut videtur intendere disputans, posset concedi coparatio siue proportio secundum aliquē sensum, seu indefinite sumpta, quoniam vniuersaliter, vt prædiximus, multas pateretur instantias. Et cum assumitur corpus subest animæ vel irrationale omnino, aut secundum modum aliquē subest animæ, id est rationali, simpliciter concesso secundum perfectionem subesse, non ex hoc sequitur subesse secundum iurisdictionē, sic n. inferens peccaret secundū consequens. Esto tamen, quamuis non propter argumentationē hanc principem corporum, id est, hominum iudicem coactiuū pro statu præsentis seculi tantum, subesse secundum iurisdictionem iudici animarum coactiuo pro statu venturi, non propter hoc sequitur, quenquam huius seculi principem, siue iudicem coactiuū, subesse secundū iurisdictionem alicui episcopo vel sacerdoti. Quoniā nullus episcopus aut sacerdos, inquantum huiusmodi est princeps, seu iudex coactiuus cuiusquā pro statu præsentis seculi vel venturi, quemadmodū 4.5.& 9. huius ostensum est. Iudex n. coactiuus animarum siue pro statu futuri seculi Christus est solus, vnde Iacobi 4. quod nec repetere piget, Vnus est legislator & iudex, qui potest perdere & liberare. Hic autem neminem mortalem statuit iudicare irreuocabiliter, neminemq; punit aut præmiat in hoc seculo, sed punire aut præmiare in vēturo tantūmodo statuit, vt diximus & per scripturam probauimus 9. huius. Romanus a. episcopus cum reliquis etiā pastoribus est animarū doctor, quemadmodū medicus, non iudex coactiuus aut princeps, vt vbi supra monstrauimus per seriem euangelicam, per Apostolū, Hilarium, atq; Chrysostomum, & ratione cogente. Quæ vero amplius inducebatur ratio, quoniam sicut corporalia spiritualibus comparantur, sic princeps corporalium ad eum qui spiritualium, quia eidem quasi radici cum priore innititur, quasi eodem aut consimili modo repellenda est, maior n. instantias patitur plurimas ad minorē, qua dicitur, Corporalia subdi spiritualibus, si accipiatur, subdi, pro esse minus perfecto, debet concedi iuxta proprias significationes horum nominum, temporale & spirituale. Cum vero subiungebatur, Romanū episcopū esse principē siue iudicē spiritualiū, si iudex sumatur secundū primā iudicis significationem, vtq; horū iudicator, speculatiuus aut operatiuus, verū est, Romanum episcopū & aliū quemlibet huiusmodi iudicē esse vel esse debere, & ex hoc concluditur, q perfectior est eo qui iudicat tali iudicio de corporalibus tantū, præsertim propter bonitatem iudicatarū rerum, sed propter hoc non sequitur, iudicē spiritualium talem superiorē esse altero iurisdictione seu iudicio coactiuo. Sic n. qui animalia speculatur princeps esset siue iudex coactiuus astrologi vel geometræ vel ecōuerso, cum tamen neutrum sit nec necessarium neq; verum. Si vero intendatur, Romanum aut quemuis aliū episcopum, iudicem esse spiritualium secundū tertiam significationē, videlicet coactiuum, neganda est tanquam manifeste falsa, vt ex Iacobi 4. pridem induximus, & 9. huius. Solus n. Christus huiusmodi iudex est, cui iudicem huius seculi quantum ad coactiuā iurisdictionem pro statu futuri seculi, nusquam negauimus neque negamus subesse. Unde Apostolus ad Ephes. 6. & Colloss. vltimo. Illorum & vester dominus est in cœlo. Vbi tunc nullus erat Apostolus, aut sacerdos novæ legis, alter à Christo. Propter q ab hoc iudice solo, iudicio coactiuo, iudicabuntur huius seculi iudices, & qui demeruerint arcebuntur per pœnam coactiuam, in alio seculo tamen secundum suam legem, vt apparuit 9. huius, per æquiuocationem ergo huius nominis iudex, fallebat iam dictus paralogismus. Ei autē argumentationi, quoniā sicut finis ad finem, lex ad legem &c. sic iudex ad iudicem negari posset, vniuersaliter sumpta. Ea tamen indefinite concessa, cū minore adiuncta, concluditur fortasse propter materiā, iudicē coactiuum secundū legem diuinam superiorem esse ad iudicē coactiuum secundum humanam legem, q concessimus prius. Quod si assumatur, Romanum aut alium quemuis episcopū iudicem esse secundum legem diuinam, distinguenda est oratio, secundum æquiuocationē huius dictionis iudex & interimenda in sensu, secundū quā disputans concludere quærit, Romanū aut alium quenquā episcopū iudicē esse coactiuū in hoc seculo vel futuro secundū legem diuinam. Quæ vero ratio accipit, eum cuius actio nobilior est siue perfectior, non debere illi subiici secundum iurisdictionem coactiuam, cuius actio minus nobilis est, siue minus perfectus: hoc a. iustinet episcopi seu presbyteri actio, ad eam quæ principantis. Est n. nobilius & perfectius cucharistiā consecrare, cætera quoq; ministrare sacramenta ecclesiæ, quod est opus episcopi, siue sacerdotis, quā de ciuilibus seu contentiosis actibus humanis iudicare atq; præcipere, quod opus est principantis seu iurisdictionem actiuam habentis solummodo, in quantum huiusmodi. Primam propositionem, recipit fallam negandā vniuersaliter sumptā, quoniā nec aliter ratiocinatio formā conueniente haberet. Minor etiā vniuersaliter sumpta, similiter pro quocunq;, scil. sacerdotio vel sacerdote, pateretur instantiā. Non n. actio sacerdotū in aliis legibus nobilior est actione principantis, eius n. oppositū ostensum est 15. primæ, sed in sola lege Christianorū actio sacerdotū est aliarū perfectissima, quod tamen sola fide tenemus. Est igitur huius argumentationis prima propositio falsa, nihil enim prohibet, nobiliorem seu perfectiorem simpliciter habens actionem quantum ad aliquid, dependere ab habente minus perfectam, & sic quod ad quid esse imperfectius. Corpus enim humanū, quod est perfectius simpliciter omni corpore simplici aut mixto, generabili salte, quantū ad aliquid positū est, & minus perfectum, multis mixtis atq; simplicibus. Est etiam hic videre in partibus eiusdem totius. Nam quauis oculus sit membrum siue pars perfectior manu vel pede, quoniam perfectiorem efficit actionem, nihil minus ab eis pendet & recipit aliquam actionem aut motum, e quoq; conuerso, haec ipsa dependent ab oculo, quoniam in finem ad quem mouent aut mouentur, diriguntur per ipsum. Sic etiam dicebat Apostolus primae ad Cor. 12. Non potest autem oculus dicere manui, opera tua non indigeo. Quo siquidem igitur seu proportionali modo, principatus etiam dependet ac recipit aliqua, per actiones aliquarum & inferiorum partium ciuitatis, de quibus diximus quinto primae, quamuis non secundum iudicium coactiuum, cum tamen ipse secundum aliquid melius & perfectius a principatu dependeant & coactiuum iudicium, vt ostensum est 15. primae. Sic ergo sacerdotium a principatu dependet ac recipit, & principatus a sacerdotio. Recipit enim sacerdotium a principatu iustificationem suorum ciuilium actuum, & custodiam ab iniuria, ne siquidem hanc inferat alteri, nec illi ab altero inferatur in statu & pro statu praesentis seculi, quoniam hoc est officium principantis & nullius alterius partis ciuitatis, quemadmodum demonstratum est 15. prime. Quod etiam expressit Apostolus ad Roman. 13. & prius induximus quinto huius, hoc etiam ad Tim. prima, quinto cap. sensit cum dixit: Obsecro igitur primum fieri obsecrationes &c. pro regibus & omnibus qui in sublimitate sunt, vt quietam & tranquillam vitam agamus, id est, habeamus. Conuersa vice indiget ac pendet principatus ab actione sacerdotii, recipit enim ab hoc, doctrinam videlicet cum sacramentis disponentibus homines in hoc seculo & contraria remouentibus ad salutem seu beatitudinem aeternam pro statu venturi seculi. Verum differenter inuicem has agunt & recipiunt actiones, quoniam princeps iudex coactiuus existens in hoc seculo Dei ordinatione, quamuis immediate humani legislatoris aut alterius cuiusuis humanae voluntatis institutione suam actionem, per coactiuam potestatem, supplicium vel poenam inferendo imprimere potest licite in sacerdotem, etiam non volentem, si legis humanae, non contrariae diuinae legi transgressor exiterit, vt demonstratum est quinto, & 8. huius, & 15. prima. Episcopus autem siue sacerdos quoniam secundum legem diuinam non est iudex coactiuus cuiusquam in hoc seculo, vt 15. prima, quarto, quinto, & nono huius ostensum est, sed Iudex est secundum primam iudicis significationem, quasi doctor operatiuus, vt medicus per suam actionem siue praeceptum neminem cogere potest, nec debet poena vel supplicio reali aut personali, secundum vitam praesentem. Sic igitur falsa fuit prima propositio iam dictae argumentationis, qua sumebatur, Omne quod perfectiorem efficit actionem, secundum iurisdictionem non debere subesse minus perfectam actionem agenti. Cum dictis enim ad ipsam sequitur per necessitatem aliud manifestum inconueniens, falsum videlicet, nullum speculatiuum artificem, aut saltem primum Philosophum, seu Metaphysicum subesse iurisdictioni principantis secundum legem humanam, cum nullus habituum operatiuorum aliorum a fide in principante vel alio, aut actio proueniens ab iis, sint aeque perfecti habitui Philosophi primi, aut actioni puenienti per illum, quo tamen carere contingit principante sufficientem & recte etiam institutum. Quod autem posterius obiiciebatur, inconueniens videri, vicarium Christi singularem Romanum Episcopum, aut quemuis Apostolorum successorem alium, subesse debere iudicio coactiuo principantis secundum legem humanam. Dicendum, nullum inconueniens, vicarium alicuius, illi vel consimili subesse iudici, cui Dominus eiusdem vicarii sponte subesse decreuit, propter conueniente seculi huius ordinationem obseruandam. Christus enim Deus & homo, sub Pilati Pontii, principantis secundum legem humanam, vicarii iudicium coactiuum sponte subiuit, sic etiam & Apostoli sancti fecerunt, & alios facere praeceperunt secundum legem diuinam, quemadmodum liquide ostensum est per scripturam & dicta sanctorum atq; aliorum doctorum 4. & 5. huius, & in 28. repetitum. Vnde etiam cum seruus non sit maior Domino, nec Apostolus eo, qui misit illum, vt ex scriptura per Bernh. induximus, 28. huius (Bernhardus enim haec inter caetera ad Eugenium de consideratione li. primo, c. 5. Ita ne, inquit, imminutor est dignitatis seruus, si non vult esse maior Domino suo? aut discipulus, si non vult esse maior eo qui se misit? aut filius, si non transgreditur terminos, quos posuerunt patres sui? Quis me constituit iudicem? ait ille magister & Dominus, & erit iniuria seruo discipulo, nisi iudicet vniuersos?) nullum inconueniens, sed valde conueniens, quinimo necessarium ad ciuilitatis, seu politiae quietem, omnem Episcopum atq; Presbyterum & clericum subesse iudicio coactiuo principantium secundum legem humanam, huius vero contrarium, inconueniens omnino est & impartibile, sicut demonstratum est decimo septimo prima, & vbi supra in hac pridem confirmatum testamentis aeternis. Adhuc quoniam Romanus aut quiuis Episcopus, non est Christi vicarius, seu minister ad omne officium exercendum in hoc seculo, sed secundum determinatu, vera causa, Sacerdotium, in quo siquidem inquantum huiusmodi, non attenditur coactiuum iudicium inferius aut superius secundum ipsum, vt ex Aristotele induximus palam, 9 huius, parte 3. principans vero secundum legem humanam Dei vicarius seu minister est, secundum principatus officium, in quo superius & subiectum attenditur quantum ad coactiuam potestatem, vnde ad Romanos 13. neminem excipiens Apostolus, Episcoporum aut Presbyterorum, inquit, Omnis anima subdita sit potestatibus sublimioribus, causam subiungens, Dei enim minister est. Ecce vicarium Dei, non violentum, sed coactiuum malorum, in hoc seculo. Vnde subdit, Vindex in iram & qui malum agit. Sed malum agere potest Episcopus aut sacerdos, quibus nunquam Christus aut Apostolus aliquis, opere seu exemplo vel sermone, alium iudicem assignauit, vt in hac, vbi supra monstrauimus.
units.tr: What remains of this discourse, and the last part, is to solve the arguments which we also introduced in the third section of this work to support the error of those who say that coercive jurisdictions belong to the elders or bishops, and that the supreme power of all these in this age belongs to the Roman bishop, insofar as such. Against the first of these, when it was said, "As the body stands to the soul, so the prince of the body stands to the prince of the soul," I answer that this proposition is false when taken universally. For although the soul is distinguished from the body, since the soul is not a body, yet there is no prince of the body who is not in some way also a prince of the soul, and conversely, if "prince" is taken properly, as appears in the eighth and ninth sections of this work.
