But if by the prince of the body is meant, in a figurative sense, the physician, who takes care of it as an operative teacher, and in respect of those acts which belong to the nutritive and rational parts; and by the prince of the soul is meant the one who is physician and operative teacher or instructor in respect of the acts of the rational and appetitive part, both in and for the state of the present age, such as the teachers of human sciences or disciplines, and also for the state of the future age, such as the ministers and priests, then the said proposition, taken indefinitely, could be granted, since taken universally it would suffer many counterexamples. For the soul in relation to the body, and again the rational in relation to the irrational, has many differences, which a teacher or curator has in respect of one but not of another. Indeed the rational soul, being an image of the Trinity, reasons, while the irrational does not; yet there is no such difference between their curators or teachers. So too in other cases. Therefore, granting it in some sense, namely that just as the rational and appetitive soul is nobler than the body, that is, than the body as animated by the nutritive power insofar as such, so the teacher or curator of the rational soul, etc., is more worthy than the curator and teacher of the irrational; or even if this comparison is made between the teacher of the rational soul for the state or end of the present age, as compared with him who is principally its teacher for the state or end of the future age; granting, I say, that one is more perfect than the other, it does not follow that the more perfect of them is judge over the less perfect in coercive judgment. For so the mathematician would be the coercive prince of the physician, and many manifest absurdities would follow from this. But if by the prince of bodies is understood the ruler or coercive judge of men, or judge in the third signification, in and for the state or end of the present age only, or principally; and by the prince of souls is understood the judge in the third signification, principally for the state or end of the future age, as the disputant seems to intend, then the comparison or proportion could be granted in some sense, or taken indefinitely, since, as we said before, taken universally it would suffer many counterexamples. And when it is assumed that the body is subject to the soul, either wholly irrational or in some way subject to the soul, that is, to the rational, the subjection is granted in respect of perfection; but it does not follow from this that it is subject in respect of jurisdiction. For one who inferred so would commit the fallacy of the consequent. Nevertheless, even granting that the prince of bodies, that is, the coercive judge of men for the state of the present age only, is subject in jurisdiction to the coercive judge of souls for the state of the future age, it does not follow from this argument that any prince or coercive judge of this age is subject in jurisdiction to any bishop or priest. For no bishop or priest, insofar as such, is a prince or coercive judge of anyone, either for the state of the present age or of the future, as has been shown in the fourth, fifth and ninth sections of this work. For the coercive judge of souls, whether for the state of the future age, is Christ alone, whence in James 4, which I am not ashamed to repeat: There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to save. Here he has not appointed any mortal to judge irrevocably, nor does he punish or reward anyone in this age, but he has appointed to punish or reward only in the coming age, as we have said and proved from Scripture in the ninth section. The Roman bishop, however, together with the other ministers, is a teacher of souls, like a physician, not a coercive judge or prince, as we showed above through the gospel sequence, through the Apostle, Hilary, and Chrysostom, and by compelling reason. As for the further argument that, since bodily things are compared to spiritual things, the prince of bodily things stands to him who has spiritual things as to the same root on which the former rests, and must be repelled in a similar or the same manner: this has very many counterexamples in the minor premise, which says, "Bodily things are subject to spiritual things." If "subject" is taken to mean being in a less perfect state, it must be granted according to the proper meanings of these terms, temporal and spiritual. But when it was added that the Roman bishop is the prince or judge of spiritual things, if "judge" is taken in the first signification of judge, as one who discerns these things, speculatively or operatively, it is true that the Roman bishop and any other such judge is, or ought to be, a judge; and from this it is concluded that he is more perfect than the one who judges with such judgment only concerning bodily things, especially on account of the goodness of the things judged. But it does not follow from this that the judge of spiritual things is superior to the other in coercive jurisdiction or judgment. For so the one who studies animals would be the prince or coercive judge of the astrologer or geometer, or the reverse, although neither is either necessary or true. But if it is meant that the Roman bishop or any other bishop is judge of spiritual things in the third signification, namely coercive, this must be denied as manifestly false, as we previously cited from James 4 and in the ninth section. For Christ alone is such a judge, to whom we have never denied, nor do we deny, that the judge of this age is subject in coercive jurisdiction for the state of the future age. Whence the Apostle in Ephesians 6 and at the end of Colossians: Their Lord and yours is in heaven. There was then no apostle or priest of the new law other than Christ. Therefore it is by this one judge alone, in coercive judgment, that the judges of this age will be judged, and those who have deserved it will be shut out by coercive punishment, yet in another age according to its own law, as appeared in the ninth section. The aforesaid paralogism therefore failed through the equivocation of the word judge. As for that argument, that since as the end is to the end, law to law, etc., so judge to judge, this could be denied when taken universally. Yet if it is granted indefinitely, with the minor premise added, it may perhaps be concluded, on account of the matter, that the coercive judge according to divine law is superior to the coercive judge according to human law, which we conceded before. But if it is assumed that the Roman bishop or any other bishop is judge according to divine law, the statement must be distinguished according to the equivocation of the word judge, and the sense in which the disputant seeks to conclude that the Roman bishop or any other bishop is a coercive judge in this age or the future according to divine law must be rejected. But the argument which holds that the one whose action is nobler or more perfect ought not to be subject in coercive jurisdiction to the one whose action is less noble or less perfect: this argument is supported by the action of the bishop or elder compared with that of the magistrate. For it is nobler and more perfect to consecrate the Eucharist, and also to administer the other sacraments of the Church, which is the work of a bishop or priest, than to judge and command in civil or contentious human acts, which is the work of a prince or of one who has only active jurisdiction, insofar as such. The first proposition of this argument is received as false when taken universally, since otherwise the reasoning would not have the proper form. The minor premise, also taken universally, would likewise suffer a counterexample for any priesthood or priest. For the action of priests under other laws is not nobler than the action of the magistrate; indeed the opposite was shown in the fifteenth section of the first part. But under the sole law of the Christians the action of priests is the most perfect of all, which, however, we hold by faith alone. Therefore the first proposition of this argument is false. For nothing prevents one who has a nobler or more perfect action, simply speaking, from depending in some respect on one who has a less perfect action, and so being in some respect less perfect. For the human body, which is simply more perfect than any simple or mixed body, at least of those that can be generated, is in some respect placed below many mixed and simple bodies. The same may be seen among the parts of the same whole. For although the eye is a member or part more perfect than the hand or the foot, because it produces a more perfect action, nevertheless it depends on them and receives some action or motion from them; and conversely, these depend on the eye, because they are directed through it to the end toward which they move or are moved. So too the Apostle said in 1 Corinthians 12: The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. Therefore in the same or a proportional way, the principate also depends on and receives some things through the actions of certain lesser parts of the commonwealth, of which we spoke in the fifth section of the first part, although not in coercive judgment; yet these in turn depend on the principate in some better and more perfect respect, and in coercive judgment, as was shown in the fifteenth section of the first part. So the priesthood depends on the principate and receives from it, and the principate depends on the priesthood and receives from it. For the priesthood receives from the principate the justification of its civil acts and protection from injury, so that it does not inflict injury on another, nor is injury inflicted on it by another, in the state and for the state of the present age, since this is the office of the prince and of no other part of the commonwealth, as was demonstrated in the fifteenth section of the first part. The Apostle also expressed this in Romans 13, and we cited it earlier in the fifth section of this work; he also meant this in 1 Timothy 2, in the fifth chapter: I urge therefore that first of all supplications be made, etc., for kings and all who are in high place, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life, that is, that we may have it. Conversely, the principate in turn needs and depends on the action of the priesthood, for it receives from the latter the teaching, namely, and the sacraments that dispose men in this age and remove what is contrary to their salvation or eternal blessedness in the state of the future age. Yet these actions and receptions differ between them, since the prince, being a coercive judge in this age by God's ordinance, although he exercises his action immediately by the institution of a human lawgiver or of some other human will, can lawfully impose upon a priest, even one unwilling, by coercive power, by inflicting torture or punishment, if he has transgressed a human law that is not contrary to divine law, as was shown in the fifth and eighth sections of this work and in the fifteenth section of the first part. But a bishop or priest, since according to divine law he is not a coercive judge of anyone in this age, as was shown in the fifteenth section of the first part, and in the fourth, fifth and ninth sections of this work, but is a judge according to the first signification of judge, like an operative teacher, as a physician who by his action or precept cannot compel anyone, nor ought he to, by real or personal punishment or torture, according to the present life. Thus the first proposition of the aforesaid argument, which assumed that whatever produces a more perfect action ought not, in jurisdiction, to be subject to the agent of a less perfect action, was false. For from what was said about it there follows of necessity another manifest absurdity, namely that no speculative craftsman, or at least no first philosopher or metaphysician, would be subject to the jurisdiction of the prince according to human law, although the habits of the operative arts other than faith, in the prince or another, or the actions proceeding from them, are not equally perfect as the habit of the first philosopher, or as the action proceeding through him, which the prince nonetheless may lack, and which is also sufficient and rightly instituted. As for the objection that followed, that it seems inconvenient that the Roman bishop, the unique vicar of Christ, or any other successor of the Apostles, should be subject to the coercive judgment of the prince according to human law: I answer that there is no inconvenience in a vicar of anyone being subject to that judge, or to one of the same kind, to whom his lord has willingly decided to be subject, in order to observe the arrangement of this age. For Christ, God and man, under Pontius Pilate, the prince according to human law, willingly underwent the coercive judgment of a vicar; so also the holy Apostles did, and they commanded others to do so according to divine law, as has been clearly shown by Scripture and by the sayings of the saints and other teachers, in the fourth and fifth sections of this work, and repeated in the twenty-eighth. Whence also, since the servant is not greater than his lord, nor the apostle than him who sent him, as we cited from Scripture through Bernard in the twenty-eighth section of this work (for Bernard, among other things, in his letter to Eugenius On Consideration, book one, chapter five, says: "Does the servant, he asks, lose any dignity if he does not wish to be greater than his lord? Or the disciple, if he does not wish to be greater than him who sent him? Or the son, if he does not overstep the boundaries which his fathers have set? 'Who appointed me judge?' says that master and Lord; and will it be an injury to the servant or disciple, unless he judges everyone?"), there is no inconvenience but rather the greatest convenience, indeed a necessity for the peace of the civil order or polity, that every bishop, elder and cleric be subject to the coercive judgment of the princes according to human law; but the contrary is wholly inconvenient and impossible, as was demonstrated in the seventeenth section of the first part and, as confirmed above, by eternal testimonies. Again, since the Roman or any other bishop is not the vicar or minister of Christ for the exercise of every office in this age, but only in a determinate respect, namely the priesthood, in which, insofar as such, no inferior or superior coercive judgment is considered in relation to it, as we clearly drew from Aristotle in the ninth section of this work, part three; while the prince who rules according to human law is the vicar or minister of God in respect of the office of the principate, in which the superior and the subject are considered in regard to coercive power. Whence in Romans 13 the Apostle, excepting no one, neither bishop nor elder, says: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, giving the reason: for he is God's minister. Behold the vicar of God, not violent but coercive of evils in this age. Whence he adds: an avenger for wrath, and to him who does evil. But a bishop or priest can do evil, and to them Christ or any apostle never assigned another judge, by work, example or word, as we have shown above in this section.

units.la: Ei vero, quae per modum conclusionis proponitur, instantiae, quod si expediat principantes secundum autoritatem humanam corrigere, dum delinquent in diuinam aut hominum legem, non videri nos corrigi posse conuenienter, cum superiore careant in politia, primi saltem, aut primus ipsorum. Et propterea eos subiici debere sacerdotum, aut Episcoporum iudicio coactiuo. Dicendum, quod principans delinquens in diuinam aut humanam legem corrigi potest & debet, conuenienter per ministrum Ecclesiasticum, Episcopum, siue Presbyterum per sermonem exhortatorium aut increpatorium, modestum tamen, iuxta doctrinam Apostoli, secunda ad Timoth. 2. & 4. & Chrysostomi explicationem, quam induximus nono huius: per coactiuam vero potestatem nequaquam. Quoniam haec ad Episcopum vel sacerdotem inquantum huiusmodi, super quenquam in hoc seculo minime pertinet, vt saepe probatum & repetitum est in prioribus dictis. Corrigere vero principantem propter excessum in leges, & inquantum in legem humanam; vt in decimo huius diximus, secundum legem tamen humanam, & arcere quoq; si oporteat, poena vel supplicio temporali, ad solius humani legislatoris autoritate pertinet, vel ad hoc statutorum ab illo, vt 18. prima sufficienter ostensum putamus.
units.tr: As for the objection put forward as a conclusion, that if it is expedient to correct rulers by human authority when they offend against the divine or human law, we do not seem to be properly corrected, since they have no superior in the polity, at least the first of them, or the first among them; and that therefore they ought to be subject to the coercive judgement of priests or bishops: I answer that a ruler who offends against the divine or human law can and should be properly corrected by an ecclesiastical minister, a bishop or presbyter, by an exhortatory or rebuking speech, yet a modest one, according to the teaching of the Apostle, 2 Timothy 2 and 4, and the explanation of Chrysostom which we brought forward in the ninth [chapter] of this book; but by coercive power, by no means. For this does not pertain to a bishop or priest, as such, over anyone in this world, as has often been proved and repeated in what was said before. But to correct a ruler for excess in the laws, insofar as he offends against human law, as we said in the tenth [chapter] of this book, and to restrain him, if necessary, by temporal penalty or punishment, pertains to the authority of the human lawgiver alone, or to what has been sufficiently shown by his statutes, as in 18 of the first [discourse], we think.

units.la: Quae autem finaliter addebatur deductio, quoniam secundum iurisdictionem ille superior est ad Romanum Imperatorem, ipsumq; de iure instituere atq; deponere potest, qui translulit Imperium a Graecis in Germanos in persona Magni Caroli, vt iam dictum est. Hic autem Papa Romanus, ergo Imperatore superior, ipsumq; instituere atq; deponere de iure potest. Dicendum, quod si maior indefinite sumatur, ex ipsa cum minore nihil infertur, propter non fieri syllogismum similem ex indefinita cum particulari. Si vero sumatur vniuersaliter, vt dicatur, Omnis translator Imperii Romani a Graecis in Germanos, superior est &c. nisi determinetur subiectum, quam plures haberet haec propositio veras instantias. Si enim quis de facto & non de iure translulisset imperium, aut si aliena, ceu sibi ab altero tuc data potestate ad hoc, tanquam procurator vel quasi, qui sic inquam translulisset, non propter hoc solus superiorem iurisdictionem haberet, nec potestatem iustam, Romanum principem instituendi aut deponendi.
units.tr: As for the deduction that was added at the end, namely that he is superior to the Roman Emperor in jurisdiction and can by right institute and depose him, he who transferred the Empire from the Greeks to the Germans in the person of Charles the Great, as has already been said; and that the Roman Pope is therefore superior to the Emperor and can by right institute and depose him: I answer that if the major premise is taken indefinitely, nothing follows from it with the minor, because no similar syllogism arises from an indefinite with a particular. But if it is taken universally, so as to say, "Every transferrer of the Roman Empire from the Greeks to the Germans is superior, etc.", then unless the subject is specified, this proposition would have very many true counterexamples. For if someone had transferred the empire in fact but not by right, or had done so with a power that belonged to another, given to him by someone else for this purpose, as a procurator or the like, such a man, I say, would not on that account alone have superior jurisdiction, nor a just power, to institute or depose the Roman prince.

units.la: Sic vero determinata iam dicta priori propositione, vt omnis mortalis qui translulit aut transferre potest Romanum Imperium a Graecis in Germanos iuste, autoritate propria, non sibi concessa per alterum, superior est secundum coactiuam iurisdictionem ad Romanum principem, ipsumq; iuste instituere atq; deponere potest, sic ipsa concessa. Quae huic annectitur secunda, videl. Romanus Episcopus siue Papa est qui translulit imperium, vt dictum est, negauda est tanquam omnino falsa. Nam eius oppositum demonstrata est 15. prima, & iursum tam ipsius quam ex ipsa illatae conclusionis oppositum, per scripturam & dicta sanctorum atq; catholicorum doctorum certificatum est 4. huius & quinto, & repetitum in aliis plerisq; locis: sicq; obseruatum de facto sine reclamatione fuisse per antiquos patres & pastores Romanos Episcopos, persuasimus 21. huius ex approbatis historiis.
units.tr: But when the earlier premise is specified in this way, namely that every mortal who has transferred, or can justly transfer, the Roman Empire from the Greeks to the Germans, by his own authority and not granted to him by another, is superior in coercive jurisdiction to the Roman prince and can justly institute and depose him, to the extent that this power is granted to him: the second premise joined to it, namely that the Roman bishop or Pope is the one who transferred the empire, as has been said, must be rejected as wholly false. For its opposite was demonstrated in 15 of the first, and the opposite of it, as well as of the conclusion drawn from it, has been established by Scripture and by the sayings of the saints and catholic teachers in 4 of this [book] and the fifth, and repeated in many other places. And thus we have shown, in the twenty-first [chapter] of this book, from approved histories, that it was observed in fact, without objection, by the ancient fathers and the Roman bishops who were pastors.

units.la: Quod autem scribitur in septimo quarundam narrationum, quas Decretas appellant, de iureiurando, & in Epistola quadam vocati iam Papae Romani, ad inclytum Ludovicum ex Bauaria ducibus Romanorum regem assumptum, per Sedem Apostolicam siue Romanum Papam vel solum, aut cum suorum collegio clericorum, Romanum Imperium a Graecis ad Germanos, in persona Magni Caroli fuisse translatum rationabiliter siue iuste, supponatur ad praesens, quamuis non ipsorum autoritate propria, hac enim translatione quantum de facto praecesserit, dicturi sumus in altero quodam ab hoc tractatu seorsum. Esto igitur imperii translationem a Graecis in Germanos iuste factam. Dico tamen q; non autoritate Romani Papae solius, aut cum suo solo collegio clericorum, vt pridem diximus.
units.tr: But as for what is written in the seventh [book] of certain collections, which they call Decretals, on the oath, and in a certain Epistle of a Roman pope, now so called, to the illustrious Louis of Bavaria, assumed as king by the Romans, that the Roman Empire was reasonably or justly transferred from the Greeks to the Germans in the person of Charles the Great, through the Apostolic See or the Roman Pope alone, or with his college of clerics: let this be supposed for the present, although not by their own authority. For how far this transfer actually went forward, we shall speak of in another separate work from this treatise. Let it be granted, then, that the transfer of the empire from the Greeks to the Germans was justly made. Yet I say that it was not done by the authority of the Roman Pope alone, or with his college of clerics alone, as we said earlier.

units.la: Et propterea oportet attendere secundum demonstrationes inductas 12. 13. & 15. prima, quod eiusdem est autoritas prima, secundum rationem rectam intendentibus leges humanas statuendi, principatum instituendi, principem assumendi, autoritate mi illi concedendi, & haec omnia mutandi, destruendi, augendi, vel minuendi, suspendendi, corrigendi, deponendi, transferendi, reuocandi, & reliqua faciendi circa ea, quae iam dictam autoritate habenti principaliter non ab altero expedire videntur, & per suam expresserit voluntatem.
units.tr: And therefore one must attend, according to the demonstrations adduced in 12, 13 and 15 of the first, that the primary authority of making human laws, of instituting a principality, of choosing a prince, of granting authority to him, and of changing, destroying, increasing or diminishing, suspending, correcting, deposing, transferring and revoking all these things, and of doing the rest concerning those matters which seem expedient, belongs to the one who, in the view of right reason, holds the aforesaid authority principally, not from another, and who has expressed it by his will.

units.la: Cuius autem sit autoritas supradicta, determinatum est duodecimo, & 13. primae. Propter quod vbicunq; legatur & a quocunq; dicatur translatum fuisse imperium, aut alter quicunq; principatus vel princeps aliquis q per electionem assumitur, institutus per Papam vel aliam personam singularem, aut per collegium singulare aliquod prouinciae siue regni. Si vera debeat esse scriptura vel sermo & valida seu iusta institutio, siue translatio talis, oportet fieri aut factam esse autoritate legislatoris primi in prouincia vel prouinciis, super quas, a quibus, & ad quas debet institutio aut translatio fieri aut facta fore. Ideoq; si translatio Imperii Romani vel Imperatoris alicuius institutio, dicatur aut scribatur rite facta fuisse per Papam Romanum solum, aut per ipsum cum suo solo collegio clericorum, & verum sit huiusmodi dictum aut scriptum, oportet translationem aut institutionem iam dictam per ipsos intelligere factam, p auto ritatem illis concessam ad hoc a Romani Imperii legislatore humano supremo, per medium, aut sine medio, vel ab eis quidem non factam simpliciter, sed modo quoda, vt publicatam vel pronunciata, autoritate tamen praedicta.
units.tr: Whose authority the aforesaid is has been determined in the twelfth and thirteenth [chapters] of the first [discourse]. Therefore, wherever it is read, and by whomever it is said, that the empire has been transferred, or that any other principality or prince is instituted, who is chosen by election, instituted by the Pope or by some other single person, or by some single college of a province or kingdom: if the writing or the saying is to be true, and the institution or transfer valid or just, it must have been done, or must be done, by the authority of the first lawgiver in the province or provinces over which, by which, and to which the institution or transfer ought to be or to have been made. Hence, if it is said or written that the transfer of the Roman Empire or the institution of some emperor was rightly made by the Roman Pope alone, or by him with his college of clerks alone, and if such a saying or writing is true, it must be understood that the aforesaid transfer or institution was made by them through an authority granted to them for this purpose by the supreme human lawgiver of the Roman Empire, either through an intermediary or without one. Or else it was not made by them simply, but in a certain way, as published or proclaimed, yet still by the aforesaid authority.

units.la: Transtulit enim fortasse aut instituit circa imperium aliquid legislator praedictus, quod postmodum soli Papae Romano tanquam reuerentiori personae vniuersitatis humanae, vel sibi cum suis sacerdotibus, velut venerabiliori clericorum collegio pronunciandu & publicandum commisit, non quidem propter facti vel fiendi necessitatem, sed solennitatem tantum modo, cu translationes principatus legum & principantiu institutiones, similiter & officia ciuilia reliqua, inquantu huiusmodi quantum ad eorum robur, ex sola legislatoris iam dicti electione seu ordinatione dependent, vt demonstratum est 12. & 13. prima, ac 26. huius, parte quinta, cum declaratione quadam no inutiliter repetitu. Sic quoq; per omnia sentiendum, de institutione officii principum eligentium Imperatorem Romanum, non enim aliam in hoc; neq; ab alio habent autoritate, neq; ab ipsis per alium suspendi vel reuocari potest, quam a supremo Imperii Romani humano legislatore praedicto.
units.tr: For the aforesaid lawgiver perhaps transferred or instituted something concerning the empire, which he afterwards entrusted to the Roman Pope alone, as the more reverend person of the human community, or to himself with his priests, as the more venerable college of clerics, to be proclaimed and published. This was not for the sake of the necessity of the deed done or to be done, but for solemnity only. For transfers of principality, the institution of laws and princes, and likewise the other civil offices, insofar as they are such, depend for their force solely on the election or ordinance of the said lawgiver, as has been demonstrated in 12 and 13 of the first, and 26 of this [book], part five, with a certain declaration, not uselessly repeated. So too must it be understood in all respects concerning the institution of the office of the princes who elect the Roman Emperor. For they hold it by no other authority in this matter, nor can they be suspended or revoked by anyone other than the aforesaid supreme human lawgiver of the Roman Empire.

units.la: De propositis quidem igitur dubitationibus tertio & 27. huius, sic pertransisse sufficiat. Et finem imposuisse quaesitis.
units.tr: Concerning the doubts proposed, then, in the third and the twenty-seventh [chapters] of this book, let it suffice to have passed through them in this way, and to have brought the questions to an end.

units.la: LIBRI SECVNDI FINIS.
units.tr: END OF THE SECOND BOOK.

units.la: DEFENSORIS PACIS DICTIO, SEV PARS TERTIA, QVÆ EST INDEX PRÆMISSORVM.
units.tr: THE DEFENDER OF PEACE: THE THIRD PART, WHICH IS AN INDEX OF THE PREMISES.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: De recapitulatione principaliter intentorum & determinatorum, dictione prima & secunda, & dictorum cum dicendis consequentia quaedam.
units.tr: On the recapitulation of what was principally intended and determined in the first and second parts, and certain consequences of what has been said for what is still to be said.

units.la: Quoniam autem in prioribus regnorum & communitatum quarundam singularem civilis discordiae, seu intra qualitatis iam existentem assignauimus causam, omniumque reliquarum, nisi prohibeatur, futuram existimationem, desiderium, atque conatum, quibus Romanus Episcopus & suorum coetus clericorum, singulariter ad seculares tenduntque principatus, & temporalia possidenda superflue. Quorum etiam suprem[?] omnium sibi vendicare nititur memoratus Episcopus ex eidem praecipue, vt asserit, concessa per Christum, in persona beati Petri, plenitudine potestatis, vt in ultimo primaeximus, & in plerisque; Dictionis secunda capitulis non inconuenienter extitit repetitum: Cum tamen nullus principatus seu cuiusquam coactuum iudicium in hoc seculo, nedum supremus omnium illi conueniat, nec alteri cuiquam Episcopo, sacerdoti vel clerico, inquantum huiusmodi, communiter aut diuisim: Veluti viis certis humanis demonstrauimus duodecimo, 13. & 15. prima. Idemque quarto & quinto secunda firmauimus testimoniis veritatis aeternae, nec non sanctorum eius interpretum expositionibus, ac plurimorum approbatorum eiusdem doctorum, postque etiam sexto & septimo Dictionis secunda assignauimus ex scripturis & rationibus certis; quae, quantaue sit, ac in quibus sacerdotum, seu Episcoporum potestas. Quibus omnibus etiam aut ipsorum alicui, ostendimus eiusdem 2nec communiter vel diuisim, quam sibi sumpserant, praesertim Romanus Episcopus, conuenire plenitudinem potestatis. Propter quae malignitatis illius singularis in dictis proemialiter saepius nominatae sufficienter radices succisae videntur. Nunc, vt quos hactenus pestilentia haec regnis, & communitatibus palmites, & germina discordiae siue litis adduxit, nec inducere cessat, arescant citius, & de caetero propagari non valeant: ex iam praemissis dictionibus, reliquam & tertiam producemus: Quae nil aliud erit, quam ex antea positis per se notis vel demonstratis necessaria & explicita illatio conclusionum quarundam, quibus adhibita diligentia attentione meditationis & operae, supradicta pestis, eiusque sophistica causa, non difficulter excludentur a regnis, ipsisque deinceps ad ea, reliquasque ciuilitates praeludetur ingressus.
units.tr: Since in the earlier parts we have assigned the particular cause of civil discord in certain kingdoms and communities, or of discord already existing within them, and of all the rest that will arise unless it is prevented: the desire, the ambition, and the effort by which the Roman Bishop and his company of clerics aim singularly at secular principalities and seek to possess temporal goods beyond measure. The said Bishop also strives to claim for himself supreme power over all of these, which he asserts was granted to him above all, through Christ, in the person of the blessed Peter, as a "fullness of power." As we have shown at the end of the first part and in many places, and as was not unfittingly repeated in the chapters of the second part, no principality or judgment of any coercive power in this age, much less supreme power over all, belongs to him, nor to any other bishop, priest or cleric, as such, either jointly or severally. This we demonstrated in the twelfth, thirteenth and fifteenth chapters of the first part, by certain human ways. We also confirmed the same in the fourth and fifth chapters of the second part, by the testimonies of eternal truth, by the explanations of its holy interpreters, and by the approved teachings of many of its doctors. Afterwards, in the sixth and seventh chapters of the second part, we set out from Scripture and from sound reasons how great, and in what respects, the power of priests or bishops is. To all of these, or to any one of them, we have also shown that the fullness of power, which the Roman Bishop in particular has claimed for himself, does not belong, either jointly or severally. For these reasons the roots of that singular malignity, so often named in the preface, seem sufficiently cut away. Now, so that the shoots and sprouts of discord or strife which this pestilence has brought forth in kingdoms and communities, and does not cease to bring forth, may wither more quickly and be unable to spread further, we will produce from the foregoing parts a third and last part. This will be nothing other than the necessary and explicit inference of certain conclusions from what has been set down or shown before through things known in themselves. If these are attended to with diligence, careful thought and effort, the aforesaid pestilence and its sophistical cause will not be difficult to exclude from kingdoms, and an entrance will thereafter be prepared for it into those and other communities.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De Conclusionum quarundam explicita illatione, ad determinata in prioribus dictionibus de necessitate sequentium, quarum attentione facilius assequi possunt principantes & subditi sinem per hunc librum intentum.
units.tr: On the explicit inference of certain conclusions, which follow of necessity from what was determined in the earlier parts. By attending to these, rulers and subjects can more easily attain the end intended by this book.

units.la: Harum autem inferendarum conclusionum hanc primam ponemus.
units.tr: We shall put forward the first of these conclusions to be inferred.

units.la: CONCLVS. I.
units.tr: CONCLUSION I.

units.la: Solam diuinam seu canonicam scripturam, & ad ipsam per necessitatem sequentem quamcunque, ipsiusque interpretationem ex communi concilio fidelium factam, veram esse, ad aeternam beatitudinem consequendam necesse credere, si alicui debite proponatur. Huius siquidem certitudo est, & iumi potest 19. secunda.
units.tr: That it is necessary to believe the divine or canonical Scripture alone, together with whatever follows from it of necessity, and its interpretation made by the common council of the faithful, to be true, in order to attain eternal blessedness, if it is duly proposed to someone. Its certainty is established, and can be proved, in the second part, chapter 19.

units.la: CONCLVS. II.
units.tr: CONCLUSION II.

units.la: Legis diuinae dubias diffinire sententias, in his praesertim, qui Christianae fidei vocantur articuli, reliquisque credendis de necessitate salutis aeternae, solum generale concilium fidelium, aut illius valentiorem multitudinem, siue partem determinare debere, nullumque aliud partiale collegium, aut personam singularem cuiuscunque conditionis existat, iam dictae determinationis auctoritatem habere. Huius autem certitudo habetur vigesimo secunda.
units.tr: That to define doubtful opinions of the divine law, especially in those matters called the articles of the Christian faith and in the other things to be believed of necessity for eternal salvation, belongs only to a general council of the faithful, or to its more powerful multitude or part. No other partial college, nor any single person of whatever condition, has authority to make the aforesaid determination. Its certainty is held in chapter 22.

units.la: CONCLVS. III.
units.tr: CONCLUSION III.

units.la: A Dobseruanda praecepta diuinae legis, poena vel supplicio temporali, seu praesentis seculi nemo Euangelica scriptura compelli praecipitur. nono secunda.
units.tr: That no one is commanded by the Gospel Scripture to compel the observance of the precepts of divine law by penalty or temporal punishment, that is, of the present age. Ninth, second part.

units.la: CONCLVS. IV.
units.tr: CONCLUSION IV.

units.la: Solius nouae legis diuinae praecepta, vel ad ipsa per necessitatem sequentia, & quae secundum rectam rationem fieri aut omitti conuenit, propter aeternam salutem necesse seruari, antiquae vero legis nequaquam omnia, nono secunda.
units.tr: That only the precepts of the new divine law, or those that follow of necessity from them, and those which it is fitting to do or omit according to right reason, must be observed for the sake of eternal salvation. Not all of the old law must be so observed. Ninth, second part.

units.la: CONCLVS. V.
units.tr: CONCLUSION V.

units.la: IN diuinis noux legis præceptis, aut prohibitis, neminem mortalem dispensare posse, permissa vel prohibere, obligando ad culpam aut pœnam pro statu præsentis seculi vel venturi, solum posse generale concilium, aut fidelem legislatorem humanum, nullumq; aliud partiale collegium, vel singularem personam cuiuscunq; conditionis existat.duodecimo prima, & 9. secunda, & 21. secunda.
units.tr: That in the precepts or prohibitions of the new divine law no mortal can dispense, by permitting or forbidding, so as to oblige to guilt or penalty for the state of the present or the future age. Only a general council, or a human legislator who is a believer, can do this, and no other partial college or single person of whatever condition exists. Twelfth chapter of the first part, and ninth and twenty-first of the second part.

units.la: CONCLVS. VI.
units.tr: CONCLUSION VI.

units.la: LEgislatorem humanum, solam ciuium vniuersitatem esse, aut valentiorem illius partem, duodecimo & 13. prima.
units.tr: That the human legislator is only the whole body of citizens, or its more powerful part. Twelfth and thirteenth of the first part.

units.la: CONCLVS. VII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION VII.

units.la: DEcretales vel Decreta Romanorum, aut aliorum quorumlibet pontificum, communiter aut diuisim absq; concessione legislatoris humani constituta, neminem obligare pœna, vel supplicio temporali, seu seculi huius, duodecimo prima, & 28. secunda.
units.tr: That decretals or decrees of the Romans, or of any other pontiffs, enacted jointly or severally without the grant of a human legislator, do not oblige anyone by penalty or temporal punishment, that is, of this age. Twelfth of the first part, and twenty-eighth of the second part.

units.la: CONCLVS. VIII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION VIII.

units.la: IN humanis legibus solum legislatorem vel illius autoritate alterum dispensare posse. duodecimo prima.
units.tr: That in human laws only the legislator, or another by his authority, can dispense. Twelfth of the first part.

units.la: CONCLVS. IX.
units.tr: CONCLUSION IX.

units.la: PRincipatum electum aut alterum qualecunq; officium, à sola electione autoritatem habentis ad illam, nullaq; alia confirmatione seu approbatione pendere. duodecimo prima, & 26. secunda.
units.tr: That an elected prince, or any other office, depends solely on the election by those who have authority to make it, and on no other confirmation or approval. duodecimo prima, & 26. secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. X.
units.tr: CONCLUSION X.

units.la: CViuslibet principatus aut alterius officii, per electionem instituendi, præcipue vim coactiuam habentis, electionem à solius legislatoris expressa voluntate pendere. duodecimo prima, & 15.
units.tr: That the election of anyone who is to be installed by election into a prince's office, or any other office, especially one carrying coercive power, depends on the express will of the lawgiver alone. duodecimo prima, & 15.

units.la: CONCLVS. XI.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XI.

units.la: SOlum vnum numero supremum principatum esse debere in ciuitate vel regno, decimoseptimo prima.
units.tr: That there must be only one supreme prince in a state or kingdom, numerically speaking. decimoseptimo prima.

units.la: CONCLVS. XII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XII.

units.la: PErsonas & ipsarum qualitatem ac numerum ad officia ciuitatis, sic quoq; ciuilia omnia determinare, ad principantis fidelis autoritatem secundum leges aut probatas consuetudines, tantummodo pertinere. duodecimo & quintodecimo prima.
units.tr: That the determination of persons, their qualifications and their number for all civic offices, including all civil matters, belongs only to the authority of the faithful ruler, according to the laws or approved customs. duodecimo & quintodecimo prima.

units.la: CONCLVS. XIII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XIII.

units.la: NVllum principantem, eoq; minus collegium partiale vel singularem personam cuiuscunque conditionis existat, alienorum actuum monasticorum aut ciuilium absq; mortalis legislatoris determinatione, imperii plenitudinem seu potestatis habere. vndecimo prima, & vigesimo tertio secunda.
units.tr: That no ruler, still less a partial college or any single person of whatever condition, has the fullness of power or authority over the affairs of others, whether monastic or civil, without the determination of a mortal lawgiver. vndecimo prima, & vigesimo tertio secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XIV.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XIV.

units.la: PRincipatum seu iurisdictionem coactiuam, supra quenquam clericum aut laicum, etiam si hereticus extet, nullum Episcopum vel sacerdotem, inquantum huiusmodi, vllam habere. decimoquinto prima, quarto, quinto, & nono, ac decimo secunda.
units.tr: That no bishop or priest, as such, has any coercive principate or jurisdiction over anyone, clergy or laity, even if he is a heretic. decimoquinto prima, quarto, quinto, & nono, ac decimo secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XV.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XV.

units.la: SVper omnem singularem personam mortalem cuiuscunq; conditionis existat, atq; collegium laicorum ac clericorum, autoritate legislatoris solum modo principem iurisdictionem tam realem quam personalem, coactiuam habere. decimo quinto, ac decimo septimo prima, quarto, quinto, octavo, ac vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: That over every single mortal person, of whatever condition, and over every college of laity and clergy, the prince alone, by the authority of the lawgiver, holds coercive jurisdiction, both real and personal. decimo quinto, ac decimo septimo prima, quarto, quinto, octavo, ac vigesimo primo secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XVI.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XVI.

units.la: EXcommunicare quenquam aut diuinorum officia interdicere, absq; fidelis legislatoris autoritate, nulli Episcopo vel sacerdoti aut ipsorum collegio licere. sexto & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: That no bishop or priest, or their college, may excommunicate anyone or forbid divine services without the authority of the faithful lawgiver. sexto & vigesimo primo secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XVII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XVII.

units.la: OMnes Episcopos æqualis autoritatis esse immediate per Christum, neq; secundum legem diuinam conuinci posse, in spiritualibus aut temporalibus præesse inuicem vel subesse. decimo quinto & decimo sexto secunda.
units.tr: That all bishops have equal authority immediately from Christ, and it cannot be proved from divine law that they preside over or are subject to one another, either in spiritual or in temporal matters. decimo quinto & decimo sexto secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XVIII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XVIII.

units.la: AVtoritate diuina, legislatoris humani fidelis interveniente consensu, seu concessione, sic alios Episcopos communiter aut diuisim excommunicare posse Romanum Episcopum, & in ipsum autoritatem aliam exercere, quemadmodum è conuersa. sexto, 15. & 16. secunda.
units.tr: That, by divine authority, with the consent or grant of the faithful human lawgiver intervening, the Roman bishop may in this way excommunicate other bishops, either together or separately, and exercise other authority over them, and conversely. sexto, 15. & 16. secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XIX.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XIX.

units.la: COniugia seu matrimonia diuina lege, noua præsertim, prohibita, per mortalem neminem dispensari posse, humano vero lege prohibita, ad solius legislatoris, vel per ipsius principantem autoritatem pertinere. duodecimo prima, & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: That marriages, which are forbidden by divine law, especially the new ones, cannot be dispensed by any mortal; but what is forbidden by human law belongs to the authority of the lawgiver alone, or of the prince acting by his authority. duodecimo prima, & vigesimo primo secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XX.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XX.

units.la: NAtos non ex legitimo thoro seu matrimonio, legitimos facere, sic, vt hæreditarie succedere possint, aliaq; suscipere ciuilia & Ecclesiastica officia & beneficia ad solum fidelem legislatorem noscitur pertinere. Vbi supra immediate.
units.tr: That it is known to belong only to the faithful lawgiver to make those born outside a lawful bed or marriage legitimate, so that they may inherit by right of succession, and to admit them to civil and ecclesiastical offices and benefices. Above, immediately.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXI.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXI.

units.la: AD Ecclesiasticos ordines promouendos, ipsorumq; sufficientiam iudicare iudicio coactiuo, ad solum legislatorem fidelem spectare, ac sine ipsius autoritate quenquam promouere ad hoc, cuiquâ sacerdoti vel Episcopo non licere. decimo quinto prima, & decimo septimo, & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: That the promotion of men to ecclesiastical orders, and the judgment of their fitness by coercive judgment, belongs to the faithful lawgiver alone, and that no priest or bishop is permitted to promote anyone to this without his authority. decimo quinto prima, & decimo septimo, & vigesimo primo secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXII.

units.la: NVmerum Ecclesiarum siue templorum, ac in ipsis ministrare debentium, sacerdotum, Diaconorum, & reliquorum officialium, ad solum principantem secundum leges fidelium pertinet mensurare. Vbi supra immediate.
units.tr: That the number of churches or temples, and of the priests, deacons and other officials who must minister in them, belongs to the prince alone to determine, according to the laws of the faithful. Above, immediately.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXIII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXIII.

units.la: ECclesiastica officia separabilia solius fidelis legislatoris autoritate debere conferri, & similiter auferri posse, sicut quoq; beneficia, & propter pias causas reliqua constituta. decimo quinto prima, decimo septimo, & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: That ecclesiastical offices which can be separated ought to be conferred by the authority of the faithful lawgiver alone, and likewise can be taken away, as can benefices and the other things established for pious causes. decimo quinto prima, decimo septimo, & vigesimo primo secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXIV.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXIV.

units.la: NOtarios aut alios officiales publicos ciuiles statuere, ad nullum Episcopum pertinere, inquantum huiusmodi, communiter aut diuisim. decimo quinto prima, & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: That the appointing of notaries or other public civil officials belongs to no bishop, as such, either together or separately. decimo quinto prima, & vigesimo primo secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXV.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXV.

units.la: DOcendi aut operandi publice secundum artem aut disciplinam aliquam, neminem Episcopum communiter aut diuisim, inquantum huiusmodi, licentiam concedere posse, sed hoc ad legislatorem saltem fidelem aut eius autoritate principantem, tantummodo pertinere. Vbi supra immed.
units.tr: That no bishop, as such, either together or separately, can grant permission to teach or to practise publicly any art or discipline; this belongs only to the faithful lawgiver, or to the prince acting by his authority. Above, immediately.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXVI.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXVI.

units.la: PRomotos ad Diaconatum aut sacerdotium, reliquosq; Deo irrevocabiliter consecratos in Ecclesiasticis officiis & beneficiis, caeteris non sic consecratis debere praeferri. decimo quarto secunda.
units.tr: That those promoted to the diaconate or priesthood, and the others irrevocably consecrated to God for ecclesiastical offices and benefices, ought to be preferred over others who are not so consecrated. decimo quarto secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXVII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXVII.

units.la: ECclesiasticis temporalibus, expleta sacerdotum & aliorum Euangelii ministrorum, & his quae ad cultum diuinum pertinent, ac impotentum pauperum necessitate, licite ac secundum legem diuinam, pro communibus seu publicis utilitatibus, aut defensionibus uti posse legislatorem humanum totaliter & in parte. decimo quinto prima, & decimo septimo & 21. secunda.
units.tr: That the human lawgiver may lawfully and according to divine law use ecclesiastical temporal goods, wholly or in part, for common or public utilities or defences, once the needs of priests and other ministers of the Gospel, of what pertains to divine worship, and of the poor who cannot support themselves have been met. decimo quinto prima, & decimo septimo & 21. secunda.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXVIII.
units.tr: CONCLUSION XXVIII.

units.la: CVncta temporalia quae ad pias causas seu misericordiae opera statuta sunt, ut quae testamentis legantur pro vltramarino transitu ad resistendum infidelibus, aut pro captiuorum ab ipsis redemptione, vel pauperum impotentium sustentatione, caeterisq; similibus, ad solum principantem secundum legislatoris determinationem ac legantis, vel aliter largientis intentionem, disponere pertinet. Vbi supra immediate.
units.tr: That it belongs to the prince alone to dispose of all temporal goods established for pious causes or works of mercy, such as those bequeathed in wills for passage overseas to resist the unbelievers, or for the ransoming of captives, or the support of the poor who cannot support themselves, and similar things, according to the lawgiver's determination and the intention of the testator or other donor. Above, immediately.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXIX.
units.tr: Conclusion XXIX.

units.la: COllegii cuiuscunq; vel religionis vacationem concedere, iplamq; approbare vel reprobare, ad autoritatem pertinet solius legislatoris fidelis. decimo quinto prima, decimo septimo, & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: The power to grant an exemption from any college or religious community, and to approve or disapprove of it, belongs to the authority of the faithful legislator alone. first part, 15th, 17th; second part, 21st.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXX.
units.tr: Conclusion XXX.

units.la: HAereticos, omnesq; delinquentes, & arcendos poena vel supplicio temporali, iudicare iudicio coactiuo, poenasq; personales infligere, ac reales exigere, iplasq; applicare, ad solius principantis autoritatem pertinet, secundum legislatoris humani determinationem. decimo quinto prima, octauo, decimo, & 21. secunda.
units.tr: To judge heretics and all offenders, and those to be restrained by temporal penalty or punishment, by a coercive judgment, to inflict personal penalties, to exact property penalties, and to apply them to their own use, belongs to the authority of the ruling power alone, according to the determination of the human legislator. first part, 15th, 8th, 10th; second part, 21st.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXI.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXI.

units.la: NEminem subditum & per iuramentum licitum alteri obligatum, absq; causa rationabili per fidelem legislatorem tertiae significationis iudicio iudicanda, per Episcopum aut Presbyterum aliquem solui posse, huiusq; oppositum aduersari sanae doctrinae. sexto, septimo, & vigesimo sexto secunda.
units.tr: No subject who is bound by a lawful oath to another, and whose case is not a matter of reasonable cause to be judged by a judgment of the third kind by the faithful legislator, can be released by any bishop or presbyter; and to hold the contrary is to oppose sound doctrine. second part, 6th, 7th, 26th.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXII.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXII.

units.la: EPiscopum, aut Ecclesiam aliquam metropolitanam simpliciter omnium statuere, atq; priuare seu deponere ab huiusmodi officio, ad solum generale concilium fidelium omnium pertinere. vigesimo secundo secunda.
units.tr: To appoint a bishop or any metropolitan church over all others, and to deprive or depose such a person from office, belongs simply to the general council of all the faithful alone. second part, 22nd.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXIII.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXIII.

units.la: GEnerale concilium, aut partiale sacerdotum & Episcoporum, ac reliquorum fidelium per coactiuam potestatem congregare, ad fidelem legislatore aut eius autoritate principantem in communitatibus fidelium tantummodo pertinere, necin aliter congregato determinata vim aut robur habere, ad obseruationem quoq; neminem obligare temporali aut spirituali poena vel culpa. decimo quinto, & decimo septimo prima, & octauo, & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: To call together by coercive power a general council, or a partial one of priests and bishops and of the other faithful, belongs only to the faithful legislator, or to the ruler acting by his authority, in the communities of the faithful; and a determination made by an assembly not so convened has no force or strength, nor does it bind anyone to its observance under any temporal or spiritual penalty or guilt. first part, 15th, 17th, 8th; second part, 21st.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXIV.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXIV.

units.la: IEiunia & aliquorum ciborum prohibitiones, solius generalis concilii fidelium, seu fidelis legislatoris autoritate fieri debere. Opera quoq; mechanicarum artium ac doctrinas disciplinarum, quae lege diuina, nulla dierum exerceri prohibita fuerint, solum praedictum concilium seu legislatorem praedictum, interdicere posse, ad obseruationem quoque talium, atcere poena vel supplicio temporali, solum legislatorem fidelem, aut eius autoritate principantem. decimo quinto prima, & vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: Fasts and prohibitions of certain foods ought to be made only by the authority of the general council of the faithful, or of the faithful legislator. Likewise, only the aforesaid council or the aforesaid legislator can forbid the works of the mechanical arts and the pursuits of the disciplines which have not been prohibited to be practised on any day by divine law; and only the faithful legislator, or the ruler acting by his authority, can enforce the observance of such prohibitions by temporal penalty or punishment. first part, 15th; second part, 21st.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXV.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXV.

units.la: Canonizari, aut tanquam sanctum adorari quempiam per solum generale concilium statui & ordinari debere. vigesimo primo secunda.
units.tr: That anyone be canonized, or adored as a saint, ought to be decreed and ordained by the general council alone. second part, 21st.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXVI.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXVI.

units.la: Episcopis, aut Presbyteris aliisq; templorum ministris, si vxores interdicere conuenit, reliquaq; circa Ecclesiasticum ritum, per generale solum fidelium concilium id statui & ordinari, aut illud solum collegium aut personam in hoc cum prædictis dispensare posse, cui data fuerit eius auctoritas per concilium supra dictum. Vbi supra immediate.
units.tr: That bishops, or presbyters, or the other ministers of the churches be forbidden to marry, and that other matters concerning the ecclesiastical rite be decreed and ordained by the general council of the faithful alone; and that only that council, or a college or person to whom its authority has been given by the aforesaid council, can grant dispensation in these matters. Immediately as above.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXVII.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXVII.

units.la: A Iudicio coactiuo, Episcopo vel sacerdoti concesso, semper ad legislatorem contendentem licet appellare, vel ad eius autoritate principantem. decimo quinto prima, & 22. secunda.
units.tr: From a coercive judgment granted to a bishop or priest, it is always lawful to appeal to the contending legislator, or to the ruler acting by his authority. first part, 15th; second part, 22nd.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXVIII.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXVIII.

units.la: PErfectionem Euangelicam summæ paupertatis seruare debentem, nihil immobilium in sua potestate habere posse absq; determinato proposito, quodlibet tale habitum vendendi, cum primum potuerit, precium q; pauperibus tribuendi; mobilis autem, aut immobilis rei nullius habere Dominium seu potestatem, cum proposito scilicet vendicandi eam coram iudice coactiuo ab auferente vel auferre volente. decimo tertio, & 14. secunda.
units.tr: A person who must keep the evangelical perfection of the highest poverty cannot have any immovable property in his power without a fixed purpose; he must sell any such property he holds as soon as he can and give the price to the poor. As for movable or immovable things, he cannot have ownership or power over anything, unless he intends to claim it before a coercive judge from the one who takes it or wishes to take it. first part, 13th; second part, 14th.

units.la: CONCLVS. XXXIX.
units.tr: Conclusion XXXIX.

units.la: EPiscopis, reliquisq; ministris Euangelicis quæ ad alimentum & tegumentum necesse fuerint, saltem quotidiana vitæ; quæ ministrat Euangelium, multitudo vel persona singularis secundum legem diuinam & suam possibilitatem exhibere tenetur, decimas vero vel alterum quid aliud, si superfuerit dictorum ministrorum necessitati supplendæ, nequaquam. decimo quarto secunda.
units.tr: The multitude or any single person is bound, according to divine law and their ability, to supply to the bishops and the other evangelical ministers what is necessary for food and clothing, at least for the daily life of those who minister the Gospel; but tithes or anything else, if any remain over to meet the needs of those ministers, are by no means owed. second part, 14th.

units.la: CONCLVS. XL.
units.tr: Conclusion XL.

units.la: LEgislatorem fidelem, aut eius autoritate principantem, in subiecta sibi prouincia cōpellere posse tam Episcopos quam reliquos Euangelicos ministros, quibus de sufficientia victus & tegumenti prouisum est ad diuina officia celebranda & sacramenta Ecclesiastica ministranda. decimo quinto prima, & octauo secunda.
units.tr: The faithful legislator, or the ruler acting by his authority, can compel in the province subject to him both the bishops and the other evangelical ministers, who have been provided with sufficient food and clothing, to celebrate the divine offices and to administer the ecclesiastical sacraments. first part, 15th; second part, 8th.

units.la: CONCLVS. XLI.
units.tr: Conclusion XLI.

units.la: EPiscopum Romanum & alium quemlibet Ecclesiasticum, seu spiritualem ministrum, secundum legem diuinam per solum fidelem legislatorem, aut eius autoritate principantem, vel fidelium generale concilium ad officium Ecclesiasticum separabile promoueri debere, ab eodem quoq; suspendi atq; priuari, exigente delicto. decimo quinto prima, & vigesimo secundo secunda.
units.tr: The Roman bishop and any other ecclesiastical or spiritual minister must, according to divine law, be promoted to a separable ecclesiastical office only by the faithful legislator alone, or by the ruler acting by his authority, or by the general council of the faithful; and, when the offence requires it, he may likewise be suspended and deprived by the same authority. first part, 15th; second part, 22nd.

units.la: CONCLVS. XLII.
units.tr: Conclusion XLII.

units.la: POssent autem aliæ quamplures & utiles conclusiones ex prioribus diuisionibus per necessitatem inferri, quas tamen deduximus, contenti sumus, quoniam ad prædictam pestem cum ipsius causa succidendam facilem atq; sufficientem præbent ingressum.
units.tr: Many other useful conclusions could indeed be drawn of necessity from the earlier divisions, but we have been content with those we have set forth, since they offer an easy and sufficient entry for cutting out the aforesaid plague together with its cause.

units.la: DEFENSORIS PACIS TERTIÆ DICTIONIS FINIS.
units.tr: END OF THE THIRD PART OF THE DEFENDER OF THE PEACE.

units.la: LICENTII EVANGELI SACERDOTIS:
units.tr: Licence of the Evangelical Minister:

units.la: Ad Lectorem operis probatio.
units.tr: Approval of the work, to the reader.

units.la: HAbes, candidissime Lector, Opus, etsi imperitum fortasse sermones, non tamen aspernanda prudentia, quod ipsi eius autori, Defensorem pacis placuit inscribere, eo quod in illo collegerit atq; digesserit, haud quaquam otiose omnes eas rationes, quibus potissimum Imperia, seu quæuis alia ciuilis hominum inter se societates optime continentur atq; fœderentur, perpetuam quandam magistratuum, multitudinisq; gratia, citra vllum seditionis & discordiametum firmata, vtriusq; iuribus suis veluti limitibus certis se continentibus, & neutri aliquid, præter id quod legibus licet sibi arrogantibus. Quæ vna consensio inter ordines, plus æquo negligenter habita, dum alteri alteros licentius ledunt, quantum malorum, procellarumq; semper exciuerit, non in rebus modo prophanis, verum etiam Ecclesiasticis, cum maiorum nostrorum, tum etiam hæc tempora præsentia multis ob hoc agitata incommodis, palam probant. Quibus malis, vtinam ante deploratam penitus salutem, mederentur, qui merito deberent, & possent. Tu vero, optime Lector, (hunc hortor,) Defensorem pacis, studiose euolias, inuenies in eo expressissimam horum temporum imaginem, & eadem Romanistarum tyrannide, quam nunc gemantur omnes boni, non sine funesta reipublicæ iniuria, diuexatos, iactatosq; etiam antehac, optimos quosq; perpetuo
units.tr: You have here, most candid reader, a work which, though perhaps unskilled in its language, is not to be despised for its wisdom. Its author was pleased to title it Defender of the Peace, because in it he gathered and set in order, not idly at all, all those principles by which empires, or any other civil societies of men, are best held together and bound in covenant: a lasting kind of concord of magistrates and multitudes, firmly established without any cause of sedition or discord, with each party's rights fixed as it were within certain limits, so that neither claims anything beyond what the laws allow. This one agreement between the orders, when it is too carelessly neglected, while each party injures the other more freely, has always stirred up as much evil and turmoil, not only in secular affairs but also in ecclesiastical ones. Our elders and our present times, troubled on this account by many misfortunes, plainly prove it. Would that those who ought and are able to do so had remedied these evils before our salvation was utterly despaired of. And you, best reader, I urge you to read the Defender of the Peace diligently; you will find in it a most express image of our times, and of the same tyranny of the Romanists, by which all good men now groan, to the grievous harm of the commonwealth, and by which, even in former times, the very best Caesars were harassed and battered continually.

units.la: Cæsares. Anno Dom. M. D. XXII.
units.tr: Caesars. In the year of our Lord 1522.

units.la: PHILALETHES AD LIBRVM.
units.tr: PHILALETHES TO THE BOOK.

units.la: VAde liber manibus passim voluende bonorum, Et facili cunctis excipiende sinu, Quis sedet & fixum est, iustum verumq; tueri, Et stabilem contra sistere iniqua pedem. Hi tibi tam placidis occurrent mentibus omnes, Quam Roma insano saucia felle gemet.
units.tr: Go, book, to be turned over by the hands of good men everywhere, and easily received into every bosom: those who sit firm to defend what is just and true, and to set a steadfast foot against what is wrong. All of these will meet you with minds as calm as Rome, wounded by its mad gall, will groan.

units.la: MAGISTRI GVLIELMI OCCAMI, MONACHI FRANCISCANI EX ORDINE MINORUM, DOCTORIS FAMOSISSIMI, OPERA DE ECCLESIASTICA ET POLITICA POTESTATE.
units.tr: MASTER WILLIAM OCCAM, FRANCISCAN FRIAR OF THE ORDER OF MINORS, MOST FAMOUS DOCTOR: WORKS ON ECCLESIASTICAL AND POLITICAL POWER.

units.la: MAGISTRI GVILHELMI DE OCKAM SVPER Potestate Summi Pontificis, Octo Quæstionum decisiones, scriptæ circa annum M. CCC. XXVI.
units.tr: THE WORKS OF MASTER WILLIAM OF OCKHAM ON THE POWER OF THE SUPREME PONTIFF: Decisions on Eight Questions, written around the year 1326.

units.la: Iodocus Badius Ascensius, F. Marco Alexandreo de Beneuento, Coelestinorum ordinis Diui Benedicti obseruantissimo, artiumq; bonarum Professori inter eos, quos Nominales vocant, peritissimo, salutem dicit.
units.tr: Jodocus Badius Ascensius greets Fr Marcus Alexander of Benevento, of the Celestine order of Saint Benedict, a most devoted observer of it, and a professor of the liberal arts, most skilled among those whom they call the Nominalists.

units.la: RECTE mediusfidius atq; prudenter, suauissime ac longe venerande pater Marce, vitam tuam instituisse mihi comprobaris, qui tuis sacris lucubrationibus omnes artium bonarum Professores longe lateq; demeruisti. Enimuero nihil ista ætate tua dignius effici posses, quam ut optimo cuiq; viro facile charissimus euadas: & ætati adhuc imbecilliori ad virtutem incumbenti, ex editiori quodam loco dexteram miseratus porrigas. Quas res abundantissime depleuisti, non solum quia optimos auctores aut hominum negligentia aut temporum saevitia pene laceros & situ victos, integros nitidosq; ac omnibus ex parte castigatos in lucem effers: verum etiam, atq; eo quidem candidius, quod coadiutores tuos pro merita laude undecunq; extollere conaris. Inter quos M. Ioannes Trechsel artis impressoriæ studiosissimus non minimam sibi partem agnoscit, quem tuis classicis bonisq; cohortationibus usq; adeo incensum reddidisti, ut non sit fere terrarum angulus, quo pro comperiendis professionis istius operibus non transmiserit. Beneficentia autem tua, qua laborum ac studiorum tuorum amplissimam gloriam in Expositionem veteris artis Magistri Guilhelmi de Ockam nomini ipsius dedicasti, sane rubicundum atq; anxium dedisti. Rubicundum quidem, quod se tali nequaquam dignetur honore: anxium vero, quia dignus satis gratias paternitati tuæ referre non possit. Novit enim vir ille prudentissimus, quæ in amicitia seruanda sint leges: quippe qui more feracium agrorum longe plus, quam acceperit, reddidisse velit. Quocirca patienter ferre non potest, quod hactenus saltem paria ac tantundem retulisse datum non sit. Veretur enim pessime, ne forte ingratitudinis vitium, quod non modo barbararum gentium, sed etiam ferarum plurimæ devitarunt, incurrisse censeatur. Caterum tametsi quam plurima tua beneficentia iam pridem parens cudatq; munuscula, uno tamen atq; eo quidem exiguo, sed non contemnendo opusculo Marcum suum interea donatum voluit. Impatiens etenim morarum sui arumq; præceps semper ingenuus conspicitur amor. Atq; adeo nec te suspensum teneam, cum hisce diebus, Summam de Ecclesia Domini Ioannis de Turrecremata Cardinalis sancti Sixti, cum 73. quæstiunculis ex sancto Thoma per eundem collectis, tertius pro veteri more compressisset: in qua quidem summa multa de Romani Pontificis Conciliorumq; vniuersali potestate atq; dignitate fideliter disquiruntur, in mentem venit opusculi octo quæstionum super Apostolica atq; Imperiali maiestatibus a supradicto Magistro Guilhelmo de Ockam Nominalium (vt aiunt) inceptore atq; principe, & docte & vafre compositi. In quo calliditate atq; acumine ingenii sui fretus, nonnullis imperitioris turbæ hominibus labyrintheas fere ambages struxisse visus est, vt nesciant (quid enim sciant?) unde ingressi reditum petant. Nam & auctor ipse in quam sententiam eat, vti in Dialogo ita in hoc quoq; opusculo, latere voluit: Verum ne quis errore isto deterritus pedem referat, Trechselnoster Dædalea & arte & pietate præditus filum, quo cacarregant vestigia, ingressuris præbuit; atq; ( ne ipse quoq; labyrinthum facere videar ) argumentationibus suas quibusq; solutiones consignatas dedit. Et quantam maximam potuit diligentiam adhibuit, vt castigatius emitteret. Quod quidem opusculum, tametsi norit Marco suo quam charissimum fore, ne tamen ab imperitioribus, qui molem non satis librorum emunt propter exilitatem vilipendatur, admonitos facere ipsum, vti compluria optimi maximi rerum artificis Dei nostri ornamenta, maiorem saepe gratiam maiusq; precium in oculis hominum obtineant, quod parvo & exili sint corpore. Nam & unciones exiguos longe pluris haberi conspicimus,
units.tr: Rightly and wisely, by my faith, most gracious and deeply revered Father Marcus, you are shown to me to have ordered your life, since by your learned labours you have served all professors of the liberal arts far and wide. Indeed, at your age nothing could be done more worthily than that you should become most dear to every good man, and, reaching out your right hand from some higher place, lend a helping hand to a younger generation still weak and striving for virtue. You have fulfilled these duties most abundantly, not only by bringing into the light the best authors, who had been nearly torn to pieces and worn out by the neglect of men or the cruelty of the times, now whole, bright and corrected in every respect; but also, and all the more graciously, because you strive to raise your fellow workers to the praise they deserve from every quarter. Among them, Master Johann Trechsel, most devoted to the art of printing, rightly claims no small part for himself, whom you have so inflamed with your classical and good encouragements that there is scarcely a corner of the earth to which he has not sent men to seek out the works of this profession. Your kindness, moreover, by which you dedicated the ample glory of your labours and studies to the name of Master William of Ockham in the Exposition of the Old Art, has indeed made him blush and feel anxious. He blushes because he does not deserve such an honour; he is anxious because he cannot repay your fatherhood worthily enough. For that most prudent man knows the laws to be observed in friendship: he wishes, like fertile fields, to give back far more than he has received. Therefore he cannot bear patiently that it has not been granted him to return even equal and matching gifts so far. For he greatly fears lest he be judged to have fallen into the vice of ingratitude, which not only barbarian peoples but very many wild beasts have avoided. Yet, although your kindness has long been producing and polishing many small gifts, meanwhile he wished to give to his Marcus this one small but not contemptible little work. For an eager love, always generous, is seen to be impatient of delay and rushes ahead. And so that I may not keep you in suspense any longer: since in these days I had, as is my custom, published the third edition of the Summa on the Church by Lord John of Torquemada, Cardinal of St Sixtus, with the 73 small questions gathered from Saint Thomas by the same author, in which many matters concerning the power and dignity of the Roman Pontiff and the universal authority of Councils are faithfully examined, there came to mind the little work of eight questions on the Apostolic and Imperial majesties, written learnedly and cunningly by the aforesaid Master William of Ockham, the originator and prince, as they say, of the Nominalists. Relying on the cleverness and sharpness of his wit, he seems to have built nearly labyrinthine windings for some men of the untrained crowd, so that they do not know (for what could they know?) where, having entered, they may seek the way back. For the author himself wished to conceal in what direction he was heading, as in his Dialogue, so also in this little work. But lest anyone, frightened by this error, should turn back, our Trechsel, endowed with Daedalean skill and devotion, has provided a thread for those about to enter, by which they may guide their steps; and so that I too may not seem to make a labyrinth, he has set down, with each argument, its own solutions. And he has applied the greatest care he could, so that he might publish it more correctly. This little work, although he knows it will be most dear to his Marcus, nevertheless, lest it be despised by the less learned, who do not buy a bulk of books because of its slightness, he admonishes that, as many of the adornments of our God, the best and greatest craftsman of things, often gain greater favour and greater price in the eyes of men because they have a small and slender body. For we see that small figures are held in far higher esteem,

units.la: Ac saepe ingentes solido de marmore Ianos,
units.tr: And often huge Janus figures of solid marble,

units.la: Aut etiam excisos paria de rupe Colossos:
units.tr: Or even Colossi cut in pairs from the rock:

units.la: Sed haec missa facio. Te vero Doctissime Marce exoratum velit, ut hoc tenue donum humanio- ri fronte suscipias, longe maiora sub nominis tui dexteritate ab ipso propediem imprimenda opitulaturus. Nam (sit modo vita comes) efficere pretendit, ut Marcus suus, qui non modo Bononiensi Gymnasio, sed vel toti Italiae multo est ornamento, amplissimis Germaniae, Gallia-rum, Hispa- niarumq; regionibus olim iam notissimus, suis praeconiis (quod ad eius fieri potest) multo reddatur notior. Quod quia effectum quam dictum malit, finem facio. Vale. Ex Lugduno ad Calendas Octobris, Anno salutis nostrae M. CCCC. XVI.
units.tr: But I set these aside. And I wish, most learned Marcus, that you be prevailed upon to receive this slight gift with a more gentle brow, since he himself intends, before long, to publish under the sponsorship of your name far greater works, aided by you. For he undertakes (if life only accompanies him) to make his Marcus, who is a great ornament not only to the Bolognese Gymnasium but to all of Italy, long since most famous in the most ample regions of Germany, France and Spain, much better known through his praises (as far as this can be done). Since he prefers this to be done rather than said, I make an end. Farewell. From Lyons, on the Kalends of October, in the year of our salvation 1516.

units.la: OCTO QVÆSTIONVM SVPER PO- TESTATE AC DIGNITATE PAPALI OPVSCVLI ARGV- TISSIMI, quod M. Guilhelmo de Ockam adscribitur, incipit ipsius Autoris praefa- tio, in qua institutum ac intentum suum explanat.
units.tr: Eight Questions on the Papal Power and Dignity, a Very Subtle Little Work Ascribed to Master William of Ockham. Here begins the Author's own preface, in which he explains his plan and purpose.

units.la: Sanctum canibus nullatenus esse dandum: & margaritas non esse mittendas ante porcos, diuinum ac sanctum eloquium testatur: ne videlicet margaritae conculcentur a porcis, & mittentes ac dantes sanctum canibus ab eis dirumpantur: quo velut probabili a sensu contrario, innuitur, non solum margaritas (scilicet sanos sermones & iustos) propter canes & porcos, a fidelibus iustitiam & veritatem zelantibus non subtrahendas sed etiam coram ipsis porcis & canibus taliter esse spargendas, si fieri potest, ut verisimiliter praesumatur quod ab ipsis non debeant turpiter conculcari, nec spargentes periculose disrumpi. Ea propter, quia sequens opusculum, ut desidero, ad manus forte perveniet aemulorum, qui odio stimulante, etiam quae ipsis vera videntur (si dicerem) damnare; vel ad periculosum sensum trahere molirentur; tali modo in eo conabor procedere, ut ex modo loquendi non quis dicit, sed quid dicitur coacti attendere, meiq; odium nisi ipsos malitia vexauerit, inaudita-m nequaquam nequiter lanient veritatem: personam enim biuiam recitabo, & saepius opiniones contrarias pertractabo: non solum eas quibus aduersor, sed etiam quibus mente adhaereo, hoc tamen nullatenus exprimendo: interdum scienter pro eis tentatiue sive sophistice allegando in persona confirmantium aliorum, ut pro utraq; per te allegationibus intellectis, veritatis sincerus amator, purae orationis verum a falso habeat discernendi occasionem.
units.tr: Holy scripture, the divine and holy word, testifies that what is holy must by no means be given to dogs, and that pearls must not be cast before swine, lest the pearls be trampled underfoot by the swine and those who cast or give what is holy to the dogs be torn apart by them. From this, as it were by a plausible contrary sense, it is implied that not only should the pearls (namely sound and just words) not be withheld from dogs and swine by the faithful who zealously pursue justice and truth, but that they should also be scattered in their very presence, if it can be done, so that it may reasonably be presumed they will not be shamefully trampled by them, nor will those who scatter them be dangerously torn apart. Therefore, since the following little work, as I wish, may perhaps fall into the hands of rivals who, goaded by hatred, would seek to condemn even what seems true to them (I would say), or to twist it to a dangerous sense, I will try to proceed in such a way that, from the manner of speaking, they must attend not to who speaks but to what is said. And so that, unless their malice has troubled them, they will in no way wickedly mangle the truth, which is unheard of, out of hatred for me. For I will present a wavering speaker, and I will often treat opposing opinions: not only those I oppose, but also those to which I adhere in my mind, though I will nowhere express this. Sometimes I will knowingly argue for them tentatively or sophistically, in the person of others who confirm them, so that, with both sides' arguments understood, you, a sincere lover of truth, may have an occasion to distinguish the true from the false in pure discourse.

units.la: De causa scribendi.
units.tr: On the cause of writing.

units.la: Vir quidam venerabilis, octo tradidit mihi quaestiones, quarum a me solutionem dignatus est humiliter flagitare. Ego autem scientiae meae penuriam non ignorans, non solum soluendi, sed etiam sarcinam discutiendi easdem, ad praesens quaerere declinare, si non seruire cuperem deprecanti. In illo ergo habens fiduciam, qui nonnunquam reuelat parvulis, quae a sapientibus & prudentibus absconduntur, ipsas breuiter conferendo tractare curabo: vel saltem occasionaliter aliis fructificans quaedam eorum excitabo ingenia.
units.tr: A certain venerable man handed me eight questions, and deigned to ask me humbly for their solution.
