I, however, not unaware of the poverty of my learning, wished, if not to serve the one who asks, at least not to shrink from seeking not only to solve these questions but also to examine the burden of them. Trusting therefore in him who sometimes reveals to little ones what is hidden from the wise and prudent, I will take care to treat them briefly, setting them side by side; or at least, bearing some fruit for others incidentally, I will stir up some of their minds.

units.la: QVÆSTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: QUESTION I.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Probat quod suprema potestas spiritualis & potestas suprema laicalis ex natura rei non possunt cadere in eundem hominem, & probatur quinq; rationibus, ad quas respondetur infra, capitulo quinto & decimo octauo.
units.tr: Shows that the supreme spiritual power and the supreme lay power cannot, by the nature of the thing, fall to the same man. This is proved by five arguments, which are answered below in chapters five and eighteen.

units.la: Primo igitur quaeritur, Vtrum potestas spiritualis suprema, & laicalis suprema, ex natura rei, in tantum ex opposito distinguuntur, quod non possint formaliter simul cadere in eundem hominem. Circa hanc quaestionem, sunt vel esse possunt contrariae opiniones, quarum vna est, quod duae potestates praedictae simul in eundem hominem cadere minime possunt: pro qua potest taliter allegari, quae ex opposito diuiduntur, in tantum distinguuntur ex natura rei, quod simul in eodem esse non possunt: sed potestas spiritualis suprema, & laicalis suprema, ex opposito diuiduntur; potestas enim humana coactiua, primo diuiditur in potestatem spiritualem & laicalem; ergo spiritualis potestas suprema, & laicalis potestas suprema, in tantum distinguuntur ex natura rei, quod simul in eodem esse non possunt. Amplius, potestates illae quae duo capita diuersorum corporum constituunt, simul in eodem esse non possunt, sicut nec idem homo potest simul esse duo capita diuersorum corporum: Potestas autem spiritualis suprema & laicalis suprema constituunt duo capita diuersorum corporum, scilicet Imperatorem & summum Pontificem, quae sunt duo capita diuersorum corporum, scilicet clericorum & laicorum, qui distincti debent esse, ex verbis Hieronymi, quae ponuntur duodecim quaest. prima, cap. duo, & aliis sacris canonibus colligi potest. ergo non possunt cadere in eundem hominem. Rursus, potestas laicalis suprema, ex natura rei includit dominationem, unde & Imperator est Dominus mundi: & iure Imperatorum ac regum unusquisq; possidet quod possidet. 8. di. c. quo iure. Sed suprema potestas spiritualis, dominatione excludit, sicut & omnis prælatio Ecclesiastica, testante Petro, qui in epistola sua prima cap. 5. vniuersis prælatis Ecclesiæ ait: Pascite qui in vobis est gregem Dei. Et post: Neque vt dominantes in clero, sed forma facti gregis ex animo: ergo istæ duæ potestates in eundem cadere non possunt: Preterea, idem ex natura respectu eiusdem non potest esse pater & filius; fungens autem laicali potestate suprema, est filius Ecclesiæ, si est fidelis, vt dicitur di. 96. Si Imperator. Si autem est infidelis, neque filius est Ecclesiæ, neque pater: summus autem Pontifex, pater est vniuersalis Ecclesiæ: ergo istæ duæ potestates non possunt cadere in eundem: Item, idem homo non est sibiipsi subiectus, nec esse potest ex natura rei: sed fungens suprema potestate laicali, est subiectus & inferior Papa: cum etiam Episcopo inferiori ipse submittat caput; distinct. 63. cap. Valentinianus, ergo istæ duæ potestates non possunt cadere in eundem hominem.
units.tr: First, then, the question is whether the supreme spiritual power and the supreme lay power are, by the nature of the thing, so opposed and distinct that they cannot formally fall to the same man together. On this question there are, or can be, opposing opinions. One is that the two powers cannot in any way fall to the same man together. It may be argued thus: things that are divided as opposites are so distinct by nature that they cannot be in the same subject together. But the supreme spiritual power and the supreme lay power are divided as opposites, for human coercive power is first divided into spiritual and lay power. Therefore the supreme spiritual power and the supreme lay power are by nature so distinct that they cannot be together in the same subject. Again, those powers which constitute the two heads of different bodies cannot be together in one subject, just as one man cannot at the same time be the two heads of different bodies. But the supreme spiritual power and the supreme lay power constitute the two heads of different bodies, namely the Emperor and the supreme Pontiff, who are the two heads of different bodies, namely of clergy and laity, who ought to be kept distinct, as can be gathered from the words of Jerome given in Dist. 12, qu. 1, ch. 2, and from other sacred canons. Therefore they cannot fall to the same man. Again, the supreme lay power by its nature includes lordship, whence the Emperor is also "Lord of the world," and by the law of emperors and kings each one possesses what he possesses (8 dist. ch. "Quo iure"). But the supreme spiritual power excludes lordship, as does every ecclesiastical prelacy, as Peter attests in his first epistle, chapter 5, where he says to all the prelates of the Church: "Feed the flock of God which is among you." And after: "Neither as lords over the clergy, but being examples to the flock from the heart." Therefore these two powers cannot fall to the same man. Moreover, by nature the same man cannot be father and son with respect to the same person. But one who holds the supreme lay power is a son of the Church, if he is a believer, as is said in Dist. 96, "Si Imperator." If he is an unbeliever, he is neither son nor father of the Church. The supreme Pontiff, however, is father of the universal Church. Therefore these two powers cannot fall to the same man. Likewise, the same man is not subject to himself, nor can he be, by the nature of the thing. But one who holds the supreme lay power is subject to and inferior to the Pope, since he himself submits his head even to an inferior bishop (Dist. 63, ch. "Valentinianus"). Therefore these two powers cannot fall to the same man.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Ponit opinionem tenentem quod Papa habeat plenitudinem potestatis tam in spiritualibus, quam in temporalibus: & huc rationibus nouem, ad quas respondetur infra, ca. 7. & seqq. vt ad singulas annotabitur.
units.tr: Sets out the opinion holding that the Pope has the fullness of power both in spiritual and in temporal matters, and sets out nine arguments for it, which are answered below in chapter 7 and following, each being noted in turn.

units.la: ALia opinio est, quod de facto potestas spiritualis suprema, & potestas laicalis suprema, cadunt in eundem hominem, scilicet in supremum Pontificem, non quod idem homo sit summus pontifex, scilicet Papa & laicus: sed quia idem homo possit fungi potestate spirituali suprema, & tanta potestate vel maiori respectu secularium tam rerum quam personarum, quantam Imperator, vel quicunq; laicus habet, & habere potest respectu earundem. Hoc vt videtur habent dicere illi qui ponunt, quod Papa in spiritualibus & temporalibus habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit, quæ non sunt expresse contra legem diuinam, nec contra ius gentium, ciuile & canonicum: in tantum, quod licet interdum ipse faciendo vel iubendo quæcunq; ex natura rei indicta sunt & non sunt ex natura rei contra legem Dei, ad quam tenentur Christiani in noua lege, nec contra legem naturæ peccaret, vel propter intentionem corruptam, vel propter ignorantiam affectatam, vel crassam, & supinam: vel ex quacunq; alia causa: tamen ista, quæ de facto faceret, tenerent, & ista, quæ iuberet, essent ab alijs adimplenda: nam multa fieri non debent, imo absq; peccato fieri nequaquam possunt, & tamen facta renent: vt testantur canonicæ sanctiones. Extra de re. & tran. ad reli. c. ad Apostolicam. Qui enim in temporalibus habent talem plenitudinem potestatis, habent tantam potestatem super temporalia, quantam habet quicunq; laicus super quamcunque personam vel rem temporalem. Si ergo papa habeat huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis, potestas laicalis suprema cadit in papam, quamuis non sit laicus, vt vere rem potestatis imperialis possideat, quamuis sibi nomen huiusmodi non assumat. In papam autem cadit potestas spiritualis suprema. Ergo quantum ad rem cadunt in eundem duæ potestates prædictæ.
units.tr: Another opinion is that in fact the supreme spiritual power and the supreme lay power fall to the same man, namely the supreme Pontiff. This does not mean that the same man is both supreme pontiff, that is Pope, and layman; rather, the same man can exercise the supreme spiritual power and, with respect to secular things and persons alike, as much power, or more, as an Emperor or any layman has or can have over them. This, it seems, is what those hold who maintain that the Pope, in spiritual and temporal matters, has such fullness of power that he can do everything that is not expressly contrary to divine law, nor to the law of nations, civil or canon law. So much so that, although at times, by doing or commanding things which by their nature are not forbidden and are not contrary to the law of God (which Christians under the new law are bound to observe), and which do not offend against the law of nature, he might sin, either through a corrupt intention, or through deliberate or gross and careless ignorance, or from some other cause, nevertheless what he actually did would stand, and what he commanded would have to be carried out by others. For many things ought not to be done, and indeed cannot be done without sin, and yet, once done, they stand, as the canonical sanctions testify (Extra, De regulis iuris, and De translatione ad religionem, ch. "Ad Apostolicam"). For those who have such fullness of power in temporal matters have as much power over temporal things as any layman has over any person or temporal thing. If therefore the Pope has such fullness of power, the supreme lay power falls to the Pope, even though he is not a layman, so that he truly possesses the substance of imperial power, although he does not assume this name for himself. But the supreme spiritual power falls to the Pope. Therefore, as far as the thing itself goes, the two powers mentioned fall to the same man.

units.la: Restat ergo ostendere quoad opinionem illam, quod papa habet in temporalibus huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis, quod videtur posse probari multis modis. Christus enim nihil excipiendo nec quoad temporalia, nec quo ad spiritualia, dedit vel promisit beato Petro, & per consequens successoribus suis plenitudinem potestatis, vt habetur Matth. 16. Tu es Petrus &c. Et post: quodcunq; ligaueris super terram, erit ligatum & in cœlo. Ergo nec nos ab eius potestate debemus aliquid excipere: Papa ergo non solum habet in spiritualibus, sed etiam in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis. Hæc videtur expresse sententia Inno. 3. qui vt legitur extra. de maio. & obe. ca. Solita, ait: dixit Dominus ad Petrum, & dixit in Petro ad successores ipsius: Quodcunque ligaueris super terram, erit ligatum & in cœlis.
units.tr: It remains, then, to show, on the opinion that the Pope has such fullness of power in temporal matters, that this can be proved in many ways. For Christ, excepting nothing either as to temporal or as to spiritual matters, gave or promised to the blessed Peter, and consequently to his successors, the fullness of power, as is found in Matthew 16: "Thou art Peter," etc. And after: "Whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven." Therefore we too ought to except nothing from his power. The Pope therefore has fullness of power not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters. This seems to be the express view of Innocent III, who, as is read in Extra, De majoritate et obedientia, ch. "Solita," says: "The Lord said to Peter, and in Peter to his successors: Whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound also in the heavens."

units.la: Rursus ille qui ordinatione diuina nihil excipiendo constituitur super omnes gentes & regna, in temporalibus habet plenitudinem potestatis, vel saltem tantam quantam habet quicunq; laicus. Sed ordinatione diuina, nihil excipiendo, constituitur Papa super omnes gentes & regna. Nam si sacerdoti in veteri lege fuit dictum immediate à Deo, Ecce constitui te super gentes & regna: Hieremiæ 1. non distinguendo inter has gentes & alias, nec inter hæc regna & alia, multo magis credendum est hoc esse dictum supremo sacerdoti nouæ legis. Igitur papa habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis absq; omni exceptione, omnia possit quæ non sunt contra legem diuinam nec contra ius naturale: cum sic sibi dictum est: Ecce constitui te super gentes & regna vt euellas, & dissipes, & disperdas, & ædifices, & plantes. Quibus verbis cum nulla addatur exceptio, quantum ad agenda & non agenda, plenitudo potestatis sibi videtur à Domino concessa.
units.tr: Again, he who by divine ordinance, with nothing excepted, is set over all nations and kingdoms, has fullness of power in temporal matters, or at least as much as any layman has. But by divine ordinance, with nothing excepted, the Pope is set over all nations and kingdoms. For if it was said to the priest in the old law, immediately by God: "Behold, I have set thee over the nations and the kingdoms" (Jeremiah 1), without distinguishing between these nations and others, or between these kingdoms and others, much more must it be believed that this was said to the supreme priest of the new law. Therefore the Pope has in temporal matters such fullness of power, without any exception, that he may do all things which are not contrary to divine law or to natural law, since it was said to him: "Behold, I have set thee over the nations and the kingdoms, to root up, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to build, and to plant." Since no exception is added to these words, as to what is to be done and not to be done, the fullness of power seems to have been granted to him by the Lord.

units.la: Hoc expresse videtur velle Innocentius tertius extra. de maio. & obedientia. c. solita. In qua quidem sua decretali ait: Non minoris quidem, sed longe maioris autoritatis est, ad credendum æternum Christi Pontificium in fundatissima Petri sede sub gratia reuelatum: quam inueteratum illud quod antiquis legibus temporaliter seruiebat, & tamen dictum est à Deo illius temporis Pontificatu fungenti: ecce constitui te super, &c.
units.tr: Innocent III seems expressly to wish this in Extra, De majoritate et obedientia, ch. "Solita." In that decretal of his he says: "It is of no lesser, but of far greater authority, to believe that the eternal Pontificate of Christ was revealed under grace on the most firmly founded see of Peter, than that old institution which served temporarily under the ancient laws, and yet was spoken by God to him who then held the pontificate: Behold, I have set thee over, etc."

units.la: Amplius qui absq; omni exceptione habet seculuria iudicare, habet in secularibus & temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis: Papa autem absq; omni exceptione habet secularia iudicare; Apostolus enim prima Cor. 6. non distinguendo nec excipiendo pro prælatis spiritualibus, & præcipue pro supremo pontifice ait: Nescitis quoniam angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis secularia? Ergo Papa habet in secuseculariḃus plenitudinem potestatis. In hoc etiam se fundare videtur Innocentius 3. verbis superius allegatis. Sed Ecclesia gentium hanc plenitudinem non restringendam ostendit dicens: An nescitis quod angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis seculária? Innuens ad temporalia quoque, potestatem datam eidem, qui in Angelos haberet potestatem, ut his intelligantur minora subesse, quibus subdita sunt maiora.
units.tr: Moreover, he who has authority to judge secular matters without any exception has full power in secular and temporal affairs. But the Pope has authority to judge secular matters without any exception. For the Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 6, not distinguishing or excepting spiritual prelates, and especially the supreme pontiff, says: "Know ye not that we shall judge angels? How much more things that pertain to this life?" Therefore the Pope has full power in secular affairs. Innocent III also seems to rest on this, in the words cited above. But the Church shows that this fullness is not to be restricted, saying: "Know ye not that we shall judge angels? How much more things secular?" Hinting that the power given to him extends also to temporal matters, since he who has power over angels is understood to have the lesser things made subject to him, to whom the greater things are subject.

units.la: Item, quod Papa quo ad temporalia sit superior Imperatore, & ratione consimili quoliber alio fungente potestate laicali, & per consequens quoad rem, potestas suprema laicalis cadit in Papam, quod multiplicitèr conantur probare. Nam tam in Veteri Testamento apud Iudaeos, quàm etiam apud Tureas Pontificalis auctoritas praeferebatur dignitati regali, & reges honorem pontificibus detulerunt, quibus etiam subiecti fuerunt. Unde Samuel Saulem unxit in regem & sibi omnem quam habuit, contulit potestatem: qui etiam David postea reprobato Saule regem constituit. Ioiada etiam sacerdos, occisa Athalia Ioas regem constituit. Alexander etiam Magnus reverentiam Ioiadae Pontifici Iudaeorum exhibuit. Totila rex Gothorum ob reverentiam Leonis Papae, de Italia, quam coeperat devastare, recessit. Imperatores etiam devoti super alios Constantinus, Iustinianus, & Carolus Magnus Ecclesiae devoti & subiecti fuerunt. Ergo Papa est superior, & Imperator inferior, quo ad potestatem temporalem.
units.tr: Likewise, that the Pope is superior to the Emperor in temporal matters, and by a similar reason to any other holder of lay power; and consequently, as to the thing itself, the supreme lay power falls to the Pope. They try to prove this in many ways. For both in the Old Testament among the Jews, and also among the Turks, pontifical authority was placed above royal dignity, and kings have paid honour to pontiffs, and have been subject to them. Hence Samuel anointed Saul as king and conferred on him all the power he had; and afterwards, when Saul was rejected, he appointed David king. Also the priest Jehoiada, after Athaliah was slain, set up Joash as king. Alexander the Great showed reverence to Jehoiada, the high priest of the Jews. Totila, king of the Goths, out of reverence for Pope Leo, withdrew from Italy, which he had begun to devastate. Also the devout emperors above others, Constantine, Justinian, and Charlemagne, were devoted and subject to the Church. Therefore the Pope is superior, and the Emperor inferior, as to temporal power.

units.la: Praeterea Christus non solum fuit sacerdos, sed etiam rex supremus habens in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis: tota autem iurisdictio Christi concessa est vicario eius: ergo Papa habet talem in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis, quod nec aliquis Imperator habet aliquam iurisdictionem in temporalibus, nisi ab ipso: ergo potestas laicalis suprema, quantum ad rem, cadit in Papam, sicut dicit Innocentius tertius ubi prius, quod cum Imperator coronam recipit à summo Pontifice, recipit enim in vagina, quem Imperator eximens & vibrans, innuit se habere omnem potestatem à Papa.
units.tr: Furthermore, Christ was not only priest but also supreme king, having full power in temporal affairs; but all the jurisdiction of Christ has been granted to his vicar. Therefore the Pope has such fullness of power in temporal affairs that no emperor has any jurisdiction in temporal affairs except from him. Therefore supreme lay power, as to the thing itself, falls to the Pope, as Innocent III says in the place cited above, that when the Emperor receives the crown from the supreme Pontiff, he receives it in its sheath, which the Emperor, drawing it out and brandishing it, signifies that he has all his power from the Pope.

units.la: Amplius sicut anima se habet ad corpus, sic spiritualia se habent ad temporalia: sed anima vitatur corpore sicut instrumento, ergo fungens suprema potestate spirituali, vitur suprema potestate laicali, tanquam instrumento solummodo: & per consequens, quantum ad rem, suprema potestas laicalis cadit in eundem, in quem cadit suprema potestas spiritualis.
units.tr: Moreover, as the soul is related to the body, so spiritual things are related to temporal things. But the soul uses the body as an instrument. Therefore he who exercises supreme spiritual power uses supreme lay power merely as an instrument. And consequently, as to the thing itself, supreme lay power falls to the same person to whom supreme spiritual power falls.

units.la: Rursus, in eo qui omnibus legibus secularibus est solutus, & cuius leges non dedignantur quaecunque leges laicorum seu secularium imitari, cadit quo ad rem, potestas suprema laicalis: Papa autem legibus quibuscunque positivis est solutus, & eius sacros canones, leges imitari minime dedignantur: quia leges Imperiales, quae supremae sunt inter leges secularium, non dedignantur Sacros Canones imitari, de iudic. c. clerici: Ergo potestas suprema laicalis cadit in Papam.
units.tr: Again, in him who is released from all secular laws, and whose laws do not disdain to imitate any laws of laymen or secular men, supreme lay power falls as to the thing itself. But the Pope is released from all positive laws, and his sacred canons do not disdain at all to be imitated as laws: because the imperial laws, which are supreme among secular laws, do not disdain to imitate the sacred canons, De iudiciis, c. clerici. Therefore supreme lay power falls to the Pope.

units.la: Adhuc, ille cui oportet universitatem fidelium, spiritualium, & temporalium, vel secularium, absque omni exceptione in omnibus obedire, fungitur suprema potestate laicali, quo ad rem: Papae autem oportet universitatem fidelium spiritualium & secularium obedire in omnibus, absque omni exceptione, prout colligitur evidenter, ut videtur ex sacris Canonibus & legibus civilibus, ut habetur di. 12. c. praeceptis Apostolicis. & Dist. 19. in memoria. & c. enim nero. & c. ita Dominus, & aliis multis locis in numeris. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Further, he to whom it is fitting that the whole body of the faithful, spiritual and temporal or secular, obey in all things without any exception, exercises supreme lay power as to the thing itself. But it is fitting that the whole body of the faithful, spiritual and secular, obey the Pope in all things, without any exception, as is evidently gathered, as it seems, from the sacred canons and the civil laws, as is found in Dist. 12, c. praeceptis Apostolicis, and Dist. 19, in memoria, and c. enim nero, and c. ita Dominus, and in many other places in the same numbers. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Item, in illum cadit potestas laicalis suprema, de cuius quocunque iudicio nemini licitum est iudicare, & à cuius sententia & iudicio aut facto, nulli penitus est licitum appellare: quia in omni causa ab illo qui suprema non fungitur potestate, sed habet superiorem, si male iudicaverit, licet appellare. 2. q. 6. can. placuit. 1. de iudicio autem Papae, nemini est licitum iudicare vel appellare. 9. q. 3. c. potest. & c. ipsi sunt. c. cuncta. 17. q. 4. qui autem. & c. nemini autem. Ergo in Papam cadit potestas laicalis suprema, &c.
units.tr: Likewise, supreme lay power falls to him from whose judgment it is lawful for no one to judge, and from whose sentence, judgment, or act no one at all may lawfully appeal; for in every cause one may appeal from one who does not exercise supreme power but has a superior, if he has judged badly. 2 q. 6, can. placuit; 1; but concerning the judgment of the Pope, it is lawful for no one to judge or to appeal. 9 q. 3, c. potest, and c. ipsi sunt, c. cuncta; 17 q. 4, qui autem, and c. nemini autem. Therefore supreme lay power falls to the Pope, etc.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Probat quod potestas secularis suprema, & spiritualis suprema possunt cadere in eundem hominem, quantum ex natura rei.
units.tr: He proves that the supreme secular power and the supreme spiritual power can fall upon the same man, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned.

units.la: Alia est opinio quodammodo media via inter praedictas opiniones incedens, in quibusdam concordans, in nonnullis discrepans ab utraque. Tenet enim consentiens primae quod de facto, potestas spiritualis suprema, & laicalis suprema, non cadunt nec cadere possunt simul in eundem hominem: sed recedit ab eadem dicens, quod istae duae potestates, non in tantum ex natura rei distinguuntur, quin formaliter simul cadere possint in eundem, & in hoc concordat cum opinione secunda, à qua tamen discordat, affirmans quod istae duae potestates, non cadunt in eundem hominem, scilicet in supremum Pontificem seu Papam: Primo ergo probare conantur, quod istae duae potestates, quantum ex natura rei, cadere possunt in eundem simul.
units.tr: There is another opinion, walking in a sort of middle way between the aforementioned opinions, agreeing with some points and differing from both in others. For it holds, with the first, that in fact the supreme spiritual power and the supreme lay power neither fall, nor can fall, together upon the same man; but it departs from that view by saying that these two powers are not distinguished so far by the nature of the thing that they cannot formally fall together upon the same man. In this it agrees with the second opinion, from which, however, it differs by affirming that these two powers do not fall upon the same man, namely upon the supreme Bishop or Pope. First, then, they try to prove that these two powers, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned, can fall together upon the same person.

units.la: Nam omnis potestas spiritualis, quae competit fungenti potestate spirituali: aut competit sibi ratione ordinis, aut ratione administrationis: sed potestas laicalis nec ordini, nec administrationi repugnat: Ergo, quantum ex natura rei, simul cadere possunt in eundem, puta in illum in quem cadit potestas spiritualis suprema. Quod enim ipsa ordini non repugnat, apparet. Nam potestas laicalis suprema, quantum est ex parte rei, maiorem repugnantiam non videtur habere ad ordinem sacerdotalem, vel quemcunque alium, quam non suprema: sed potestas laicalis non suprema, quantum est ex natura rei; nullam repugnantiam habet ad quemcunque ordinem; alioquin si aliquis rex vel aliquis laicus fieret sacerdos, Episcopus, vel Papa, ipso facto amitteret omnem potestatem temporalem, quam habuisset super quamcunque rem vel personam, quod videtur absurdum.
units.tr: For every spiritual power that belongs to one who exercises spiritual power belongs to him either by reason of his order or by reason of his administration. But lay power conflicts neither with order nor with administration. Therefore, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned, they can fall together upon the same person, namely upon the one upon whom the supreme spiritual power falls. That it does not conflict with order is evident. For supreme lay power, as far as the thing itself goes, does not seem to have any greater conflict with the priestly order, or any other order, than non-supreme power has. But lay power that is not supreme, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned, has no conflict with any order whatever. Otherwise, if some king or some layman were made a priest, bishop, or Pope, he would by that very fact lose all temporal power he had over any thing or person, which seems absurd.

units.la: Item, matrimonium ipsi non repugnat, unde & in primitiva Ecclesia, sacerdotes & Episcopi licite habuerunt uxores. Quantum est ergo ex natura rei, potestas laicalis etiam suprema, quantum ad rem potestati spirituali non repugnat: cum matrimonium ad actum carnalem magis distantem à spiritualibus, quam potestas laicalis in temporalibus, ordinetur.
units.tr: Likewise, marriage does not conflict with it, whence in the primitive Church priests and bishops lawfully had wives. Therefore, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned, even supreme lay power does not conflict, as regards the matter, with spiritual power, since marriage, which is directed to a carnal act further removed from spiritual things, is ordered to something more distant than lay power is from temporal things.

units.la: Item, ordo, & potestas laicalis, non magis repugnant quam spiritus & corpus, quae reperiuntur in eodem homine: ergo non est ratio, quare ordo & potestas laicalis, sive in temporalibus etiam suprema, non possint, quantum est ex natura rei, cadere in eundem.
units.tr: Likewise, order and lay power conflict no more than spirit and body, which are found in the same man. Therefore there is no reason why order and lay power, even supreme lay power in temporal matters, should not be able, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned, to fall upon the same man.

units.la: Item, actus ordinis qui videtur esse potestas quaedam, & actus potestatis laicalis etiam suprema, non habent repugnantiam, quantum est ex parte rei, quin possint cadere in eundem hominem: ergo multo magis ipsae potestates, quantum ex natura rei possunt cadere in eundem. Assumptum probatur, quia nullus est actus potestatis supremae laicalis, qui actui consecrandi corpus Christi, clericos ordinandi, virgines consecrandi, ligandi vel soluendi, vel alii cuicunque repugnat ex natura rei. Iudicare enim secularibus criminibus irretitos, maxime videtur ordini repugnare: & tamen non repugnat, cum actus huiusmodi, etiam de facto & de iure, propter negligentiam iudicis secularis, debeat iudici Ecclesiastico conuenire. Iudex enim Ecclesiasticus, supplet negligentiam iudicis secularis, extra de foro compet. c. licet & sequenti. Videtur ergo, quod potestas laicalis non repugnet fungenti spirituali propter ordinem quem habet. Nec sibi repugnat propter administrationem: Tum quia, potestas laicalis minus distat ab administratione, quam ab ordine: Tum quia, maior spiritualitas est in ordine quam in administratione: Tum quia nullus actus potestatis supremae laicalis, repugnat cuicunque actui administrationis quam habet fungens potestate spirituali suprema. Iudicare enim criminosos, maxime videtur repugnare, cum tamen non repugnet, cum sicut dictum est, Ecclesiasticus debeat supplere negligentiam iudicis secularis. Ex praedictis concluditur, quod potestas laicalis suprema, & potestas suprema spiritualis, quantum est ex natura rei, possit cadere cum alia in eundem virum.
units.tr: Likewise, the act of order, which seems to be a certain power, and the act of supreme lay power, do not conflict, so far as the thing itself is concerned, so that they cannot fall upon the same man. Therefore much more so the powers themselves can, by their nature, fall upon the same man. The assumption is proved, because there is no act of supreme lay power which conflicts by its nature with the act of consecrating the body of Christ, ordaining clerics, consecrating virgins, binding or loosing, or any other such act. For to judge those entangled in secular crimes seems especially to conflict with order; yet it does not conflict, since acts of this kind, both in fact and by law, on account of the negligence of the secular judge, ought to belong to the ecclesiastical judge. For the ecclesiastical judge supplies the negligence of the secular judge, Extra, De foro competenti, c. Licet, and the following chapter. It seems, therefore, that lay power does not conflict with the one who exercises spiritual power, on account of the order he holds. Nor does it conflict with him on account of administration: both because lay power is less remote from administration than from order; and because there is greater spirituality in order than in administration; and because no act of supreme lay power conflicts with any act of administration which the one who exercises supreme spiritual power holds. For to judge criminals seems especially to conflict, yet it does not conflict, since, as has been said, the ecclesiastical judge ought to supply the negligence of the secular judge. From what has been said it is concluded that supreme lay power and supreme spiritual power, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned, can fall upon the same man together with one another.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Probat secundam partem opinionis in praecedenti capitulo recitata, scilicet quod illae potestates non cadunt, nec cadere debent in eundem hominem, & probatur tribus rationibus, quae soluuntur cap. 19. per totum.
units.tr: This chapter proves the second part of the opinion recited in the previous chapter, namely that those powers do not and ought not to fall to the same man. It is proved by three arguments, which are answered throughout chapter 19.

units.la: Secundo, tenet ista opinio, quod istae duae potestates non cadunt, nec cadere debent in eundem hominem: quod quidem non accidit ex natura rei, sed ex ordinatione Dei, & iure diuino, quo cautum est ne ordinarie & regulariter idem homo praesit omnibus secularibus, & etiam diuinis: licet casualiter fungens potestate spirituali suprema, ea quae sunt potestatis laicalis supremae, valeat exercere: ita tamen quod potestas suprema ordinata in ipsum non cadat: de potestate autem praedicto modo ordinaria & regulari non casuali, praedictas negatiuas intelligunt. Et quod sic istae duae potestates non cadant, nec cadere debeant in eundem, multis modis nituntur ostendere.
units.tr: Second, this opinion holds that these two powers do not and ought not to fall to the same man. This is not the result of the nature of the thing but of God's ordinance and divine law, by which it is provided that, ordinarily and regularly, the same man should not preside over both secular and sacred affairs. Although a man who holds supreme spiritual power may by chance exercise the functions of supreme lay power, the supreme power ordained for him does not thereby fall to him. These negative propositions are understood of power that is held in this ordinary and regular way, not by chance. And they strive to show in many ways that these two powers do not and ought not to fall to the same man.

units.la: Primo, Fungens enim potestate laicali suprema ordinaria, debet se secularibus negociis implicare. dist. decim. c. imperium. dist. nonagesim. sext. c. Si Imperator nono. q. 1. Sicut. Fungens enim potestate spirituali, se debet minime secularibus negotiis implicare: cum etiam alii inferiores se talibus implicare non debeant, teste beato Paulo, qui 2. ad Timoth. 2. cap. ait: Nemo militans Deo implicare debet se secularibus negotiis, ut ei placeat cui se probauit. Hoc idem Petrus in Epistola Clementis, prout legitur 21. q. 1. cap. te quidem, patenter videtur asserere, dicens; Te quidem oportet irreprehensibiliter viuere & summo studio niti, ut omnes occupationes huius vitae abiicias, ne fideiussor existas, ne aduocatus litium fias, ne vel aliqua occupatione prorsus inneniaris mundani negocii occasione perplexus, neque enim iudicem, neque cognitorem secularium iudiciorum hodie te ordinare vult Christus. 9. q. 1. sicut enim, ait, Impietatis crimen tibi est, o Clemens, neglectu verbi Dei studiis, sollicitationes seculares suscipere. Hoc etiam canon ab Apostolis editus, iubet in haec verba, ut legitur di. 88. can. Episcopus: Episcopus, aut Sacerdos, vel Diaconus, nequaquam seculares curas assumat, sin aliter, deiiciatur. His concilium Cartag. 4. ut legitur eadem di. can. Episcopus, videtur alludere, dicens, Episcopus nullam rei familiaris curam ad se reuocet, sed electioni, & orationi, & verbo praedicationis tantummodo vacet. Hoc etiam in aliis sacris canonibus & decretalibus continetur expresse, ut 21. q. 3. cap. ultimo. & extra. ne clerici, vel monachi, secularibus negotiis se immisceant. cap. 1. & c. nec. & c. clericis. Ergo istae duae potestates, secundum iura diuina fundata, iure diuino in eundem hominem cadere minime debent.
units.tr: First, a man who holds ordinary supreme lay power must involve himself in secular business (dist. 10, c. Imperium; dist. 96, c. Si Imperator; C. 1, q. 1, Sicut). But a man who holds spiritual power must by no means involve himself in secular business, since even other inferiors ought not to involve themselves in such things, as the blessed Paul witnesses in 2 Timothy 2, where he says: "No one who serves as a soldier of God gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him." Peter also plainly seems to assert the same in the Epistle of Clement, as it is read in C. 21, q. 1, c. Te quidem, saying: "You ought to live blamelessly and strive with the utmost zeal to cast off all the occupations of this life, so that you do not become a surety, nor an advocate of lawsuits, nor are found wholly entangled in some worldly business. For Christ does not want you today to appoint yourself a judge or an overseer of secular courts." (C. 9, q. 1, Sicut enim.) "For," he says, "it is a crime of impiety, O Clement, to take up worldly cares and neglect the study of the Word of God." The canon issued by the Apostles also commands, in these words, as read in dist. 88, c. Episcopus: "A bishop, or priest, or deacon, must in no way take up secular cares; otherwise let him be deposed." The Council of Carthage IV, as read in the same dist. c. Episcopus, seems to allude to this, saying: "A bishop shall not take on himself any care of household affairs, but shall devote himself only to election, prayer and the preaching of the Word." This is also expressly contained in other sacred canons and decretals, as in C. 21, q. 3, c. ultimo, and Extra, De clericis vel monachis, ne se secularibus negotiis immisceant, cc. 1, Nec, and Clericis. Therefore these two powers, being founded on divine law, ought by divine law by no means to fall to the same man.

units.la: Amplius potestates istae, quas Deus voluit esse distinctas, & distinctis personis competere, non debent cadere in eandem. Christus autem voluit potestatem laicalem supremam, & spiritualem supremam, esse distinctas, & distinctis personis competere, quod Cyprianus, vt legitur distin. 10 c. quoniam, & Nicholaus Papa, vt legitur distin. 96. c. cum ad verum, fere sub eisdem verbis testatur. Videtur autem huius rationes (quare hoc voluit) assignare, sic enim scribit Nicholaus; Cum ad verum ventum est, vltra sibi neq; Imperator, iura pontificatus arripuit, nec Pontifex nomen Imperatorium sibi vsurpauit: quoniam idem mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis, officia potestatis vt iusta discreuit, propria volens homines medicinali humilitate sursum efferri, non humana superbia rursus in inferno demergi: vt & Christiani Imperatores pro aeterna vita pontificibus indigerent, & pontifices pro cursu temporali tantummodo rerum, Imperialibus legibus venerentur: quatenus spiritualis actio a carnalibus distaret in curribus, & Deo militans se negociis secularibus minime implicaret: vt nec vicissim, homo ille rebus diuinis praesidere videretur, qui esset negotiis secularibus implicatus. Ex quibus verbis videtur patenter haberi, quod sicut Imperator sibi non debet vsurpare potestatem spiritualem, ita Papa non debet sibi vsurpare potestatem laicalem supremam. Et hoc ordinauit Christus, cuius ordinationem nemini transgredi licet: ne sibi damnationem acquirat, iuxta sententiam Apostoli ad Roman. decimo tertio. Triplex autem inuenitur ratio, quare Christus ordinauit istas duas potestates supremas distinctis debere competere personis, prima est, ne si Imperator vel pontifex haberet vtramque, superbiret, & hic Glossa ait: Primus homo per superbiam cecidit, unde in infernum omnes demergebantur; sed Christus humilitate sua sursum erexit: sed si haberent omnes eadem officia, superbirent, ita quod iterum demergerentur in infernum. Secunda ratio est, vt distinctae personae distinctas potestates supremas habentes, scilicet Imperator & pontifex, se inuicem deberent indigere. Tertia quae in Scriptura sacra (sicut & allegatio praecedentium) fundari videtur, est vt militans Deo secularibus negotiis se non implicet, & secularibus intentus negotiis, supremam in spiritualibus non habeat potestatem. Ex quibus concluditur, quod secundum ordinationem Christi, illae duae potestates supremae non debent cadere in eundem.
units.tr: Furthermore, these powers, which God willed to be distinct and to belong to distinct persons, ought not to fall to the same one. But Christ willed that supreme lay power and supreme spiritual power be distinct and belong to distinct persons. Cyprian testifies to this almost in the same words, as read in dist. 10, c. Quoniam, and Pope Nicholas, as read in dist. 96, c. Cum ad verum. Nicholas also seems to assign the reasons why he willed this, for he writes: "When it came to the truth, the Emperor no longer seized the rights of the pontificate, nor did the Pontiff usurp the imperial title for himself. For the same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, by his proper acts and distinct dignities, separated the offices of power as just, wishing men, raised up by medicinal humility, to be lifted up on high, and not again plunged into hell by human pride. So that Christian emperors might need the pontiffs for eternal life, and the pontiffs be honoured by imperial laws only for the temporal course of affairs; so that spiritual action might be distinct from carnal in its courses, and one who serves God might not involve himself in secular business; and so that, conversely, that man should not seem to preside over divine things who was entangled in secular business." From these words it plainly appears that just as the Emperor ought not to usurp spiritual power for himself, so the Pope ought not to usurp supreme lay power for himself. Christ ordained this, and no one is permitted to transgress his ordinance, lest he bring damnation on himself, according to the saying of the Apostle in Romans 13. There is a threefold reason found why Christ ordained that these two supreme powers ought to belong to distinct persons. The first is that, if the Emperor or the Pontiff had both, he would become proud. And here the Gloss says: "The first man fell through pride, whereby all were plunged into hell; but Christ by his humility raised them up on high. But if they all had the same offices, they would become proud, so that they would again be plunged into hell." The second reason is that distinct persons holding distinct supreme powers, namely the Emperor and the pontiff, ought to need each other. The third, which seems to be founded in Holy Scripture (as well as in the citation of the preceding), is that one who serves God should not involve himself in secular business, and one intent on secular business should not hold supreme power in spiritual matters. From these things it is concluded that, according to Christ's ordinance, these two supreme powers ought not to fall to the same person.

units.la: Rursus, ad potestatem laicalem supremam, spectat armis intendere, & iudicium sanguinis exercere, teste Apostolo ad Roma. decim. tertio. Non frustra gladium portat, Dei enim minister est, vindex in iram ei qui malum facit. Hinc Cyprianus, vt habetur 23. quaest. v. can. rex: ait, rex debet furta cohibere, adulteria punire, impios de terra perdere, homicidas, & periuros non sinere viuere. hinc Augustin. contra Manichaeos, vt habetur 23. quaest. prima. can. quid culpatur; vult, quod belli suscipiendi auctoritas penes principes sit. Et per consequens primo est penes principem secularem supremum: quod enim ibi loquitur de principe seculari, patet per illud quod subiungit dicens, Vir iustus si forte etiam sub rege homine sacrilego militet, recte potest illo iubente bellare. Hinc Salomon Prouerb. 20. cap. ait: Rex qui sedet in solio iudicii, dissipat omne malum intuitu suo. Et iterum, Impios dissipat rex sapiens, & incurvat super eos fornicem: Armis autem intendere, & sanguinis iudicia exercere, Christus verbo & exemplo, Vicario suo & aliis Praelatis spiritualibus interdixit. Dixit enim Petro, vt legitur Iohan. decimo octauo. Mitte gladium tuum in vaginam. & Matth. vigesimo sexto. Converte gladium tuum in locum suum, omnes qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit. Non solum autem Petrum, sed alios Apostolos ab vsu gladii prohibuisse videtur, teste Luca vigesimo secundo. Videntes autem qui circa ipsum erant, quod futurum erat, dixit ei Petrus, Domine, si percutimus in gladio, & percussit prunus ex illis seruum principis sacerdotum & amputauit auriculam eius dexteram. Respondens autem Iesus dixit: Smite vsque huc: Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Christus Petro & aliis Praelatis, potestatem gladii interdixit: & per consequens, voluit vt ab effusione sanguinis abstinerent: quod etiam eis inhibuit, cum dixit eisdem, vt legitur Matt. vigesimo. Scitis quod gentium principes dominantur eorum, & qui maiores potestatem exercent in eos, non ita erit inter vos, sed quicunque voluerit inter vos fieri maior, erit vester seruus. sicut filius hominis non venit ministrari, sed ministrare. Ex quibus verbis duo colliguntur, Primum est, quod Christus Apostolis supremam potestatem secularem inhibuit, aliquam enim potestatem eis inhibuit, non omnem: Tum quia voluit quod inter alios maiores essent & primi, quia ipsis praecepit, vt potestatem aliquam super alios exerceant, cum dixit Petro, Pasce oues meas, & cum dixit vniuersis Apostolis Iohan. 2. Sicut misit me pater & ego mitto vos, & post, quorum remiseritis peccata remittuntur eis, & quorum retinueritis retenta sunt: ergo supremam potestatem secularem Christus Apostolis interdixit, sed non omnem.
units.tr: Again, it belongs to supreme lay power to attend to arms and to exercise judgement over blood, as the Apostle witnesses in Romans 13: "He does not bear the sword in vain; for he is God's minister, an avenger to execute wrath on him who does evil." Hence Cyprian, as found in C. 23, q. 5, c. Rex, says: "A king ought to restrain thefts, punish adulteries, root out the impious from the earth, and not allow murderers and perjurers to live." Hence Augustine, against the Manichaeans, as found in C. 23, q. 1, c. Quid culpatur, holds that the authority to undertake war rests with princes. And consequently it rests first with the supreme secular prince; that he speaks there of a secular prince is evident from what he adds: "If a just man should perhaps serve under a king who is a sacrilegious man, he may rightly make war at that king's command." Hence Solomon, in Proverbs 20, says: "A king who sits on the throne of judgement scatters all evil with his gaze." And again: "A wise king scatters the wicked and brings the vault down upon them." But Christ, by word and example, forbade his Vicar and other spiritual prelates to attend to arms and exercise judgements over blood. For he said to Peter, as read in John 18: "Put your sword into its sheath." And in Matthew 26: "Put your sword back into its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword." Christ seems to have forbidden not only Peter but the other Apostles the use of the sword, as Luke 22 witnesses: "When those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, 'Lord, shall we strike with the sword?' And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus answered, 'No more of this!'" From these words it is gathered that Christ forbade Peter and the other prelates the power of the sword, and consequently willed that they abstain from the shedding of blood. He also forbade this to them when he said to them, as read in Matthew 20: "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are great exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you; but whoever would be great among you must be your servant; even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve." From these words two things are gathered. The first is that Christ forbade the Apostles supreme secular power, for he forbade them some power, though not all power. Since he willed that among them some should be greater and first, he commanded them to exercise some power over others, when he said to Peter, "Feed my sheep," and when he said to all the Apostles in John 20: "As the Father sent me, so I send you," and afterwards, "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained." Therefore Christ forbade the Apostles supreme secular power, but not all power.

units.la: Secundo, colligitur ex verbis praedictis, quod Christus voluit, quod Apostoli imitarentur ipsum, in abdicatione exercendae potestatis super alios: cum seipsum proponat eis in exemplum dicens: sicut filius hominis non venit ministrari, sed ministrare, quasi diceret, facite sicut facere me vidistis, vt non maiorem potestatem exerceatis in alios, quam me exercere vidistis: Christus autem, inquantum homo mortalis is, suo vicario exemplum praebens, quomodo gubernare debet sibi subiectos, nunquam iudicium m sanguinis, aut secularem potestatem exercuit, sed omnem potestatem, etiam occasione sibi data am ab aliis declinauit. Nam sicut legitur Ioh. 8. adduxerunt Scribae & Pharisaei mulierem adulteram, & statuerunt eam in medio & dixerunt, magister hac mulier modo deprehensa est in adulterio: in lege autem in Moysess mandauit huiusmodi lapidari, tu igitur quid dicis? ipse se intromittere de causa sanguinis in tantum renuit, vt nec interrogantibus vellet, quae secundum legem a se vel ab alio iudice esset in ipsam ferenda sententia, respondere. Etiam cum discipuli eius Iacobus & Iohannes, vt habetur Luc 29. cuperent poena mortis contemptum Samaritanorum, quem in Iesum fecerant, non recipiendo eum, vindicari: ipse increpans illos dixit, nescitis cuius spiritus estis: filius hominis non venit animas perdere, sed salvare, quasi diceret, non dico quin contemptus Samaritanorum est dignus morte non tamen inferam eam: quare? non veni in quantum homo mortalis pro quocunq; crimine vitam corporalem auferre, sed conservare. Tres enim mortuos suscitauit, sed nullum quantumcunq; sceleratum, morte aut membri truncatione puniuit, licet nonnunquam in quosdam aliquam aliam poenam inferret corporalem: nam sicut scribitur Ioh. 11. facto flagello de funiculis vendentes oues & boues deiecit de templo: & nummulariorum effudit mensas. Ipse etiam cum traheretur ad mortem se defendere recusauit: unde dicit Petro, ut legitur Matth. 26. Putas quia modo non possum rogare Patrem meum, & exhibebit mihi plusquam duodecim legiones angelorum? & tamen hoc facere nullo modo volebat: licet itaq; Christus exemplo docuerit, quod praelati ecclesiae spirituales, poena leui corporali corrigere valeant scelerator: facto tamen ostendit, quod non debent armis uti: nec mortem nec truncationem membrorum inferre: quod sacri canones, Christi sequentes vestigia praecipere, & detestari videntur, sicut 23. q. 8. cap. Hii a quibus, &c. Si quis & extra. ne clerici vel monachi se negotiis secular. &c. c. clericis, &c. sententiam sanguinis, & extra. de excessibus praelatorum. cap. ex litteris. & 23. q. v. c. 1. & c. poena, & c. unum, & c. incestuosi, & can. sunt quidam. Ex quibus & aliis quamplurimis colligitur, quod armis intendere, & causam sanguinis agitare, ad solos laicos, non ad praelatos pertinet spirituales. Quare concluditur, quod potestas laicalis suprema, & potestas spiritualis suprema in eundem cadere minime debent, ut patuit.
units.tr: Secondly, it follows from the words quoted above that Christ wished the Apostles to imitate him in giving up the exercise of power over others, since he sets himself before them as an example, saying: just as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve. It is as if he were saying: do as you have seen me do, so that you do not exercise greater power over others than you have seen me exercise. Christ, as a mortal man, gave his vicar an example of how he ought to govern those subject to him. He never exercised judgment of blood or secular power, but turned aside from all power, even when the occasion was offered to him by others. For we read in John 8 that the scribes and Pharisees brought an adulterous woman, set her in the midst, and said: Master, this woman was taken in adultery, in the very act; now Moses in the law commanded us that such should be stoned; what do you say? He refused so firmly to interfere in a case of blood that he would not even answer those asking whether a sentence of death was to be pronounced on her, either by himself or by another judge, according to the law. Again, when his disciples James and John, as we find in Luke 9, wished to avenge by death the contempt the Samaritans had shown toward Jesus by refusing to receive him, he rebuked them and said: You do not know what spirit you are of. The Son of Man came not to destroy men's lives, but to save them. It is as if he were saying: I do not deny that the Samaritans' contempt deserves death, yet I will not inflict it. Why? Because I have not come, as a mortal man, to take away bodily life for any crime, but to preserve it. For he raised three dead persons, yet he punished no one, however wicked, with death or the mutilation of a limb, although sometimes he inflicted some other bodily punishment on certain persons. Thus we are told in John 2 that, having made a whip of cords, he drove the sellers of sheep and oxen out of the temple and overturned the tables of the money-changers. Moreover, when he was being led to death he refused to defend himself; hence he says to Peter, as we read in Matthew 26: Do you think that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he will send me more than twelve legions of angels? Yet he was in no way willing to do this. Although, therefore, Christ taught by example that spiritual prelates may correct wrongdoers with a light bodily penalty, by his deed he showed that they ought not to use arms, nor inflict death or the mutilation of limbs. The sacred canons seem to enjoin and condemn this, following the footsteps of Christ, as in 23. q. 8. cap. Hii a quibus, etc.; Si quis and extra, ne clerici vel monachi se negotiis secularibus, etc.; c. clericis, etc.; the sentence of blood, and extra, de excessibus praelatorum, cap. ex litteris; and 23. q. v. c. 1., and c. poena, and c. unum, and c. incestuosi, and can. sunt quidam. From these and very many other passages it is gathered that to bear arms and to take up matters of blood belongs only to laymen, not to spiritual prelates. Hence it is concluded that supreme secular power and supreme spiritual power ought by no means to fall upon the same person, as has been shown.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Soluit rationes opinionis prima capitulo primo recitata.
units.tr: He resolves the arguments of the first opinion, recited in chapter 1.

units.la: Quia autem in hoc opusculo, tensui solummodo recitando & allegando procedere narrandum est, quomodo secundum praedictas opiniones, ad allegationes eis contrarias potest respondéri: & quomodo secundum tertiam opinionem, ea quae prima adducit opinio, dissoluuntur.
units.tr: Since in this little work we must proceed only by reciting and citing, I shall set out how, according to the aforesaid opinions, the authorities that oppose them can be answered, and how, according to the third opinion, those things which the first opinion adduces are dissolved.

units.la: Ad quorum primum dicitur, quod quamuis ea quae ex opposito distinguuntur tanquam contraria ex natura rei, non possunt idem subiectum supremum habere, licet possint cadere in diuersas personas eiusdem subiecti: tamen saepe ista quae distinguuntur ex opposito, tanquam diuersae species, aut aliquo modo ex opposito inter se distincta, & ideo licet non secundum idem, tamen possunt cadere in eandem personam: immo nonnunquam in idem subiectum, primum patet, namo ordo sacer & ordo non sacer, quodammodo ex opposito diuiduntur: & tamen in eundem hominem cadunt, imo in eandem animam, quae est subiectum primum utriusque: Sic etiam virtus intellectualis & moralis, aliquo modo ex opposito diuiduntur, & tamen cadunt in eundem hominem, & sic de aliis: quare ex hoc, quod potestas primo diuiditur in potestatem spiritualem & laicalem, non potest concludi, quod non possunt cadere in eundem hominem: licet ex hoc possit comunici, quod non sunt eadem potestas. Et ita videtur esse dicendum de potestate spirituali suprema, & de potestate laicali suprema: quia licet eo quod aliquo modo ex opposito diuiduntur, possit ostendi quod non sunt, nec esse possunt eadem potestas: non tamen quod non possint cadere in eundem hominem simul, quantum est ex natura rei.
units.tr: To its first point I reply: although things that are distinguished in opposition, as contraries by the nature of the thing, cannot have the same supreme subject, they may fall to different persons of the same subject. Yet often things distinguished in opposition, as different species, or distinguished from one another in some way in opposition, can fall to the same person, though not in the same respect. Indeed sometimes they fall to the same subject. This is shown first by the fact that holy orders and non-holy orders are divided in some way in opposition, and yet they fall to the same man, indeed to the same soul, which is the primary subject of both. So too intellectual and moral virtue are divided in some way in opposition, and yet they fall to the same man, and so on for other cases. Therefore from the fact that power is first divided into spiritual and lay power, it cannot be concluded that they cannot fall to the same man; it can only be concluded from this that they are not the same power. And it seems that the same must be said of supreme spiritual power and supreme lay power: although from the fact that they are divided in some way in opposition, it can be shown that they are not, and cannot be, the same power, it does not follow that they cannot fall to the same man at the same time, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned.

units.la: Ad secundum dicitur, quod potestas spiritualis suprema, & potestas laicalis suprema, ex natura rei non constituunt duo capita corporum diuersorum, clericorum & laicorum: tamen, quia clerici & laici sunt unum corpus, iuxta illud Apostoli ad Roma. 12. Omnes unum corpus sumus in Christo, tum quia licet debeant esse distincti clerici & laici, sunt tamen unum corpus propter multitudinem Christianorum quae nunc est, & fuit tempore beati Hieronymi: tamen putant quidam, quod non est possibile clericos & laicos auerti a fide: & quod solum remaneret unum genus ipsorum, respectu quorum, posset, quantum est ex natura rei, idem homo habere tam potestatem supremam spiritualem, quam laicalem.
units.tr: To the second point I reply: supreme spiritual power and supreme lay power do not by their nature constitute two heads of two different bodies, of clergy and of laity. Nevertheless, because clergy and laity are one body, according to that saying of the Apostle in Rom. 12: "We, being many, are one body in Christ"; and although the clergy and laity ought to be distinct, they are nonetheless one body on account of the multitude of Christians that now exists, and existed in the time of blessed Jerome. Yet some think that it is not possible for clergy and laity to be turned away from the faith, and that only one kind of them would remain, with respect to whom the same man could, so far as the nature of the thing is concerned, hold both supreme spiritual power and lay power.

units.la: Ad tertium respondetur uno modo, quod licet papatus & quaelibet praelatio ecclesiastica, a se excludat dominationem, quae est respectu non liberorum, ita ut nullus praelatus ecclesiae, ex vi praelationis seu potestatis spiritualis sit tali dominatione dominus Christianorum quorumcunque, qui Graece vocatur Despotes secundum Aristotelem in politicis, ex ordinatione Christi non est despoticus, sed magis assimilatur principatui regali, iuxta illud primae Petri. 2. Vos autem genus electum regale sacerdotium. Et illud Apocal. 1. Fecit nos regnum sacerdotale, tamen praelatio ecclesiastica, dominationem (quae est respectu liberorum, quemadmodum rex est dominus sibi subditorum) a se non excludit. Beatus autem Petrus in verbis praeallegatis, excludit a Pastoribus dominationem primam, non secundam, cum dicit: non dominantes in clero: & si dicatur quod hoc repugnet sacris canonibus, secundum quos praelati ecclesiae sunt Domini respectu seruorum, quae ecclesia seruos habet. Respondetur secundum quosdam, quod nullus est seruus ecclesiae ex vi praelationis ecclesiasticae institutae a Christo: sed quicunque est seruus ecclesiae, est seruus ex ordinatione humana: unde & nonnulli sunt serui ecclesiae, qui a Dominis suis dati sunt ecclesiae.
units.tr: To the third point it is answered, in one way, that although the papacy and every ecclesiastical prelacy excludes from itself the lordship that is exercised over those who are not free, so that no prelate of the Church, by virtue of his prelacy or spiritual power, is by such lordship lord of any Christians whatever (which in Greek is called despotes [δεσπότης], according to Aristotle in the Politics, and by Christ's ordinance he is not despotic but rather resembles regal principality, according to that saying of 1 Pet. 2: "But you are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood"; and that of Rev. 1: "He has made us a kingdom of priests"), nevertheless ecclesiastical prelacy does not exclude from itself dominion (which is exercised over free persons, as a king is lord over his subjects). Now blessed Peter, in the words cited above, excludes the first kind of lordship from ministers, not the second, when he says: "not lording it over the clergy." And if it be said that this is repugnant to the sacred canons, according to which the prelates of the Church are lords with respect to servants, since the Church has servants, it is answered, according to some, that no one is a servant of the Church by virtue of the ecclesiastical prelacy instituted by Christ; rather whoever is a servant of the Church is a servant by human ordinance. Hence some are servants of the Church who have been given to the Church by their lords.

units.la: Aliter respondetur ad tertium motivum pro prima opinione, quod licet praelatio & clericatura, iuxta auctoritatem Petri, imo iuxta verba Christi (qui voluit quod praelati ecclesiae essent serui, & ministri aliorum) dominationem talem, qualem habet potestas laicalis suprema, a se excludat, (quare potestas suprema nec est huiusmodi dominatio, nec habet eam necessario annexam) tamen non excludit eam a persona in qua est: & ideo licet secundum beatum Petrum talem dominationem non debeat habere qui fungitur potestate spirituali, tamen sibi tali dominatio non repugnat, & ideo posset cadere in eandem personam cum potestate spirituali suprema, si aliud non obstaret. Ad quartam respondetur, quod quia Imperator non debet esse summus prælatus spiritualis, ideo si est fidelis, est filius Ecclesiæ, sed hoc non est ex natura potestatis supremæ quam habet: & ideo quantum est ex natura rei illius potestatis supremæ, posset esse pater & non filius Ecclesiæ, decretum autem loquitur secundum modum, qui seruari debet circa Imperatorem, non qui conuenit ex natura rei.
units.tr: Otherwise it is answered to the third argument for the first opinion: although prelacy and the clerical office, by the authority of Peter, and indeed by the words of Christ (who willed that the prelates of the Church should be servants and ministers of others), exclude from themselves such lordship as supreme lay power has (so that supreme power is neither such lordship nor has it necessarily annexed to it), nevertheless they do not exclude it from the person in whom it is. Therefore, although according to blessed Peter the one who exercises spiritual power ought not to have such lordship, yet such lordship is not repugnant to him, and so it could fall to the same person together with supreme spiritual power, if nothing else stood in the way. To the fourth point it is answered that, since the Emperor ought not to be the supreme spiritual prelate, if he is faithful he is a son of the Church; but this does not arise from the nature of the supreme power which he has. Therefore, so far as the nature of that supreme power is concerned, he could be a father and not a son of the Church; the decree, however, speaks according to the manner which must be observed concerning the Emperor, not according to what belongs to the nature of the thing.

units.la: Ad vltimum dicitur, quod Imperator habens supremam potestatem laicorum, non est subditus Papæ ex natura illius potestatis: sed qui illam potestatem supremam laicalem haberet; deberet carere potestate spirituali suprema, quam habet summus pontifex: & ideo de facto minor est supremo pontifice: non autem ex natura potestatis.
units.tr: Lastly it is said that the Emperor, having supreme lay power, is not subject to the Pope by the nature of that power; but whoever had that supreme lay power would have to lack the supreme spiritual power which the supreme pontiff has. And so, in fact, he is less than the supreme pontiff, but not by the nature of the power.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Arguit contra opinionem adductam supra, capitulo secundo, & hoc octo motiuis, probans illam opinionem esse haereticam.
units.tr: He argues against the opinion stated above in chapter two, with eight arguments, and proves that opinion to be heretical.

units.la: RESTAT nunc, secundum opinionem tertiam, respondere ad motiua opinionis secundæ, quorum nonnulla fundantur in hoc, quod Papa habet plenitudinem potestatis, tam in spiritualibus, quam in temporalibus; quod intellectum, vt nonnulli intelligunt, quidam reputant haereticum. Dicere enim, quod Papa talem habet (siue in spiritualibus, siue in temporalibus) plenitudinem potestatis, vt vniuersa (absq; omni exceptione) possit, quæ non sunt contra ius diuinum, quod Christiani de necessitate salutis seruare tenentur: hoc est, contrarius naturale indispensabile & immutabile scripturæ diuinæ; iuri humano canonico, & ciuili, at evidenti rationi repugnat: vt illi multis modis probare nituntur. Aliqua motiua breuiter tangendo, absque prolixa discussione duxi præsentibus inserenda.
units.tr: It remains now, according to the third opinion, to answer the arguments of the second opinion. Some of these rest on the claim that the Pope has the fullness of power, both in spiritual and in temporal matters. Some regard this claim as heretical, at least as some understand it. For to say that the Pope has such a fullness of power, whether in spiritual or in temporal matters, that he can do everything without exception which is not contrary to divine law (which Christians are bound to observe of necessity for salvation), is to say that he can act against the natural, indispensable and immutable [law] of Divine Scripture, against human canon and civil law, and against evident reason. Those who hold this try to prove in many ways. I have thought fit to insert here a few of their arguments, touching on them briefly and without lengthy discussion.

units.la: Primum autem quod aliqui fortius arbitrantur, tale est secundum literas sacras, lex euangelica est lex libertatis respectu Mosaicæ legis; quod saltem debet necessario intelligi, vt non sit tantæ seruitutis, neque in temporalibus, neque in spiritualibus, quoad ceremonias & observantias exteriores quantæ fuit lex Mosaica: ita quod quamuis Christiani quidam, vel omnes per se aut per alios ex causa de nouo emergente, seruituti possint subiugari tantæ vel maiori: tamen communitas fidelium per legem Euangelicam nequaquam tanta seruitute teneretur: nec aliquis mortalis virtute euangelicæ legis, præsertim sine culpa, & causa manifesta at rationabili, potest eam tantæ subdere seruituti: etsi quicunq; hoc tentare præsumpserit, quod facit, ipso facto, & iure diuino nullû est. Sed si Papa haberet talem plenitudinem potestatis a Christo & Euangelica lege, lex Euangelica esset intolerabilis seruitutis, & multo maioris quam lex Mosaica: omnes enim essent per ipsam serui Papæ, ita quod Papa haberet tantam potestatem super Christianos, quantam vnquam habuit, vel habere potuit quicunq; dominus super seruos: & Papa posset quoscunq; reges dare & vendere, & quorumcunq; subdere seruitutibus: posset etiam Papa ceremonias & observantias exteriores imponere communitati fidelium, quæ fuerunt statutæ in veteri lege: Et ita lex euangelica esset incomparabiliter maioris seruitutis; quam lex Mosaica, quod nonnullis apparet haereticum: relinquitur ergo quod Papa non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: The first argument, which some find the strongest, runs as follows. According to the sacred letters, the gospel law is a law of liberty in comparison with the Mosaic law. This must at least be understood to mean that it does not impose such a heavy servitude, either in temporal or in spiritual matters, as to outward ceremonies and observances, as the Mosaic law did. Thus, although some Christians, or all of them, may through their own fault or that of others, or for some newly arisen cause, be brought under an equal or greater servitude, the community of the faithful is by the gospel law in no way bound to such servitude. Nor can any mortal, by the power of the gospel law, especially without fault and without a manifest and reasonable cause, subject them to such servitude. And if anyone presumes to attempt this, what he does is by that very fact null by divine right. But if the Pope had such a fullness of power from Christ and by the gospel law, the gospel law would be of intolerable servitude, and of far greater servitude than the Mosaic law. For all would be slaves of the Pope through it, so that the Pope would have as much power over Christians as any lord has ever had, or could have, over his slaves. The Pope could give and sell any kings, and subject them to whatever servitudes he pleased. He could also impose on the community of the faithful the ceremonies and outward observances which were established in the old law. The gospel law would then be incomparably of greater servitude than the Mosaic law, which seems heretical to some. It follows, therefore, that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power.

units.la: Circa istud motiuum, non restat nisi ostendere, quod lex Euangelica, est lex libertatis: quod quidam tam per sacram scripturam; quam per sacros canones asserunt posse aperte probari: hoc enim, vt dicunt, testatur beatus Iacobus in Canonica sua cap. 1. & Apostolus Paulus 1. Corinth. 3. & ad Galat. 3. 4. & 5. capit. & in pluribus textibus Bibliæ. Item Vrbanus Papa 19. q. 2. capit. 2. & Inno. 3. extr. de regularibus cap. licet. & beatus Aug. ad inquisitiones Ianuarii, & habetur di. 12. c. omnia. Has autem auctoritates gratia breuitatis non adduco, ex quibus, & quam pluribus aliis, dicunt apertè patere, legem euangelicam esse legem libertatis, respectu veteris legis.
units.tr: On this argument, it remains only to show that the gospel law is a law of liberty. Some assert that this can be clearly proved both from Sacred Scripture and from the sacred canons. As they say, the blessed James testifies to this in his canonical epistle, chapter 1, and the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 3 and in Galatians 3, 4 and 5, and in many other passages of the Bible. Likewise Pope Urban, 19 q. 2 c. 2; Innocent III, extra, de regularibus, c. licet; and the blessed Augustine, in his letters to Januarius, and it is found in dist. 12 c. omnia. I do not cite these authorities here for the sake of brevity. From these and many other authorities they say it is plainly evident that the gospel law is a law of liberty in comparison with the old law.

units.la: Amplius, licet Christus inquantum Deus, omnem habuit plenitudinem potestatis, tamen inquantum homo mortalis, abdicauit talem plenitudinem potestatis, cum dicit Ioh. 16. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, intendens per verba ista negare se esse regem in temporalibus; alioquin per verba ista nequaquam apud Pilatum exclusisset actionem Iudæorum accusantium ipsum, quod diceret se esse regem in præiudicium Cæsaris, vt cum sic legitur Lucæ 23. Postquam Iudæi accusauerunt Christum, quod dixerit se regem, Pilatus dixit; nullam inuenio in ipso causam, aduertens quod Christus non dixerat se esse regem in temporalibus: sed alio modo quam in temporalibus, quemadmodum non reputabat Cæsari aduersari: & ideo non damnauit Christum, tanquam conuictum quod fecerat se regem in temporalibus; sed propter importunitatem Iudæorum petentium vt crucifigeret eum, teste Luca vbi prius, & dicente; ille autem, scilicet Pilatus, tertio dixit ad istos, quid enim mali fecit ille? nullam enim causam mortis inuenio in eo, corripiam ergo eum, & dimittam: at illi instabant vocibus magnis postulantes vt crucifigeretur & invalescebant voces eorum: & Pilatus adiudicauit fieri petitionem eorundem: & Iesum vero tradidit voluntati eorum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Pilatus non reputauit per verba eorum Christum conuictum de crimine, ac dignum morte, quod tamen fecisset, si Christus conuictus fuisset, vel confessus se temporale regnum habere siue ab hominibus, siue a Deo, siue in Iudæa, vbi Cæsar noluit esse aliquem regem, nisi qui esset constitutus ab eo: Pilatus vero victus mira improbitate perentium & incutientium timorem, ne falso accusaretur apud Cæsarem a Iudæis, quod faueret alicui in Iudæa dicenti se regem in temporalibus, qui non esset à Cæsare constitutus, præsertim cum contra eum clamarent & dicerent illud Iob. 19. Si hunc dimittis non es amicus Cæsaris; omnis enim qui se regem facit contradicit Cæsari; cótra conscientiā & etiam iustitiā, tradidit Iesum petentibus vt crucifigeretur: sciens quod licet Christus dixerit sibi, rex ego sum, tamen intellexerit aliter regem quam illo modo quo intellexerunt Iudæi, quando accusauerunt eum, quod faceret se regem: unde stupent nonnulli, quod istum sensum aduertit Pilatus homo mundanus & sine fide ex verbis Christi de regno suo; & tamen ipsum non perpendunt Christiani quidam, qui etiam volunt esse legis doctores: cuius vt ipsis videtur, non est alia causa, nisi quia sunt mala affectione cæcati. Papa autem ex ordinatione diuina, præcise non habet maiorem potestatem in temporalibus, quam habuit Christus, inquantum erat mortalis; cuius est vicarius: ergo Papa non habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: Further, although Christ, as God, had the whole fullness of power, yet as a mortal man he renounced such a fullness of power. When he says in John 16, My kingdom is not of this world, he means by these words to deny that he is a king in temporal matters. Otherwise, by these words he would not have at all rebutted before Pilate the charge of the Jews who accused him of saying that he was a king to the prejudice of Caesar. So Luke 23 reads: after the Jews accused Christ of saying that he was a king, Pilate said, I find no cause in him, noticing that Christ had not said he was a king in temporal matters, but in some other way than in temporal matters, just as he did not regard himself as opposed to Caesar. Therefore he did not condemn Christ as convicted of having made himself a king in temporal matters. Rather, because of the importunity of the Jews who asked that he be crucified, Pilate, as Luke says in the same place, said: He said to them the third time, "Why, what evil has he done? I find no cause of death in him; I will therefore chastise him and let him go." But they insisted with loud voices, asking that he be crucified, and their voices prevailed. And Pilate adjudged that their request should be granted; and he delivered Jesus to their will. From these words it is gathered that Pilate did not, from their words, regard Christ as convicted of a crime worthy of death. He would have done so if Christ had been convicted, or had confessed that he had a temporal kingdom, whether from men, from God, or in Judea, where Caesar would allow no king except one appointed by himself. But Pilate, overcome by the marvellous wickedness of those who demanded and instilled fear, lest the Jews falsely accuse him before Caesar of favouring someone in Judea who said he was a king in temporal matters without being appointed by Caesar, especially since they cried out against him and said the words of John 19, If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend; for everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar, against his conscience and also against justice, delivered Jesus to those who asked that he be crucified. He knew that, although Christ had said to him, I am a king, Christ had understood kingship in another way than the Jews understood it when they accused him of making himself a king. Hence some are amazed that Pilate, a worldly man without faith, perceived this sense from Christ's words about his kingdom, and yet some Christians, who also want to be teachers of the law, do not consider it. As it seems to them, the only cause of this is that they are blinded by evil affection. But the Pope, by divine ordinance, has precisely no greater power in temporal matters than Christ had as a mortal man, whose vicar he is. Therefore the Pope does not have such a fullness of power in temporal matters.

units.la: Rursum quod Papa non habeat in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, sacri canones testari videntur: nam ille non habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, cuius iurisdictioni temporali aliquæ terræ sunt subiectæ, & aliquæ non: Papæ autem, quo ad iurisdictionem temporalem, aliquæ terræ sunt subiectæ, & non omnes. extra, de hereticis, capit. vergentis; ergo, &c.
units.tr: Again, that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power in temporal matters seems to be attested by the sacred canons. For he who has such a fullness of power in temporal matters is not one over whose temporal jurisdiction some lands are subject and others not. But over the Pope's temporal jurisdiction some lands are subject and not all. Extra, de hereticis, c. vergentis. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Item, contra illum, qui habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, non currit præscriptio; contra autem Papam, quo ad temporalia, currit præscriptio, saltem centenaria, extr. de præscriptionibus, si diligenti, ergo, &c.
units.tr: Likewise, prescription does not run against one who has such a fullness of power. But prescription does run against the Pope in temporal matters, at least a prescription of a hundred years. Extra, de praescriptionibus, si diligenti. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Præterea, ille non habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, qui feuda & alia bona temporalia sibi deputata alienare non potest: Papa autem alienare non potest bona ratione ecclesiæ. 12. q. 2. can. non liceat, ergo, &c. Adhuc quod Papa non habeat talem plenitudinem potestatis videtur posse probari per iura ciuilia: Nam si Papa haberet talem plenitudinem potestatis, omnia regna mundi, & imperium essent à Papa, quod canonibus obuiare videtur, cum dicant, imperium esse à Deo, in authentica, quomodo omnes episcopi, in principio, Col. 1. vbi sic legitur: maxima in omnibus hominibus sunt dona Dei, superna collata clementia, sacerdotii & imperii: illud quidem diuinis mysteriis, hoc autem humanis præsidens, ac diligentiam exhibens: ex uno eodemq; principio, utraq; præcedentia humanam exornant vitam. Et C. de veteri iure enuc. lib. 1. vbi habetur, Deo auctore nostrum gubernante imperium, quod nobis à cœlesti maiestate traditum est: ergo Papa super imperium non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: Moreover, he does not have such a fullness of power in temporal matters who cannot alienate fiefs and other temporal goods assigned to him.
