But the Pope cannot alienate goods held by the church. 12 q. 2 can. non liceat. Therefore, etc. It also seems that it can be proved by civil law that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power. For if the Pope had such a fullness of power, all the kingdoms of the world and the empire would be from the Pope. This seems to contradict the canons, which say that the empire is from God. In authentica, quomodo oportet episcopos, in principio, Collatio 1, where it is read thus: The greatest gifts of God among all men are the priesthood and the empire, bestowed by supreme mercy: the former presides over divine mysteries, the latter over human affairs and takes care of them. From one and the same principle, both adorn human life. And in C. de veteri iure enucleando, lib. 1, where it is found: God, the author, guiding our empire, which has been handed down to us from the heavenly majesty. Therefore the Pope does not have such a fullness of power over the empire.

units.la: Quod etiam ratione (vt quibusdam videtur) euidenti probatur, nam principatus Apostolicus siue spiritualis, non minus respicit fidelium vtilitatem subditorum, quam principatus seculares. Sed secundum Aristotelem in politicis, principatus secularis temperatus, rectus, & iustus, est institutus principaliter propter bonum commune subditorum: ergo multo magis principatus Apostolicus est institutus principaliter à Christo propter bonum commune omnium fidelium: Sed si Papa haberet talem plenitudinem potestatis, principatus ipsius non esset propter bonum commune, sed propter bonum proprium Papæ.
units.tr: This is also clearly proved by reason, as it seems to some. For the apostolic or spiritual principality looks no less to the usefulness of the faithful subjects than do secular principalities. But according to Aristotle in the Politics, a secular principality that is moderate, upright and just is instituted chiefly for the common good of its subjects. Therefore the apostolic principality, much more, has been instituted by Christ chiefly for the common good of all the faithful. But if the Pope had such a fullness of power, his principality would not be for the common good, but for the Pope's own good.

units.la: Tum quia per talem principatum, magis esset prouisum Papæ, quam subditis: & esset magis dicendus mercenarius qui quærit proprium lucrum quam pastor: Tum quia talis principatus esset periculosus subditis: quia si Papa haberet talem plenitudinem potestatis, quamuis ipse omnes Christianos extra casum necessitatis extremæ vniuersis libertatibus spoliaret, & laboribus, seruitutibus & oneribus, & pœnis illos immensis subiiceret, tamen non liceret eis Papæ resistere: sed tenerentur de necessitate parere, quod eis periculosum existeret. Restat igitur, quod Papa non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: Furthermore, because through such a principality more provision would be made for the Pope than for the subjects, and he would rather be called a hireling who seeks his own gain than a minister. And because such a principality would be dangerous to the subjects. For if the Pope had such a fullness of power, then even though he, outside the case of extreme necessity, stripped all Christians of all their liberties and subjected them to immense labours, servitudes, burdens and penalties, still it would not be lawful for them to resist the Pope; rather, they would be bound of necessity to obey, which would be dangerous for them. It remains, therefore, that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power.

units.la: Amplius plenitudo potestatis, id est, totalis quæ est in omnibus supremis pontificibus, est illa scilicet, quam habent à Christo ratione papatus: sed aliqui fuerunt supremi pontifices, & adhuc possunt esse, qui non erant capaces prædictæ plenitudinis potestatis, puta monachi, & alii religiosi de religionibus perfectis assumpti; quare religiosi huiusmodi non sunt capaces proprietatis & dominii, neq; temporalium rerum proprium, principaliter, cum per votum paupertatis, à quo absoluti possunt, extra, de statu monachorum, capit. cum ad monasterium, tale proprietatem abdicauerint: quæ tamen in prædicta plenitudine potestatis necessario includitur: ergo nullus Papa ex potestate sibi concessa à Christo, huiusmodi habet plenitudinem potestatis. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod monachus vel alter religiosus ad papatum assumptus, est simpliciter absolutus à voto paupertatis; quod probatur, quia ita necessitatio annexum est religioni perfectæ votum obedientiæ, sicut votum paupertatis: sed religiosus ad papatum assumptus, est totaliter absolutus à voto obedientiæ, quare non plus tenetur prælatis religionis suæ propter votum abdicationis, quā pro voto obedientiæ, & sic non tenetur pro voto paupertatis. Respondetur quod religiosus assumptus ad papatum, non est totaliter absolutus à voto obedientiæ, nec est ita liber, sicut si semper fuisset secularis: & ideo licet tempore papatus sui non teneatur obedire prælatis ordinis sui, tenetur tamen obedire regulæ quam vouit, quoad aliqua, & illa quæ non impediunt officium ad quod est assumptus: tum quia esto quod voto obedientiæ non respiciat proprie illa quæ præcipiuntur solum modo aut præcipi possunt à prælatis, tamen religiosus factus Papa non est ita liber, sicut si fuisset secularis: quare si talis Papa efficeretur hæreticus, vel aliquo crimine diffamatus, in quo appareret incorrigibilis, & scandalizaretur ecclesia, & deponeretur per sententiam, vel sponte renunciaret papatui: ipso facto, & iure, efficeretur de obedientia prælatorum ordinis sui: & ita, quia Papa talis potest effici, ideo Papa non est ita liber ab obedientia prælatorum ordinis sui, sicut si nunquam fuisset religiosus, & ideo non est simpliciter à voto obedientiæ absolutus: quare absque nouo voto, potest & tenetur ad obedientiam prælato: unde recurrit: nec mirum, quia vnaquæque res, de facili ad naturam suam reuertitur. Cum igitur votum paupertatis sit de substantia perfectae regulae, & exercitium pontificalis officii nequaquam impediat, tenendum videtur, quod religiosus ad Papatum assumptus, proprietatem habere non potest, praesertim extra casum necessitatis. Unde, esto quod aliquis casus posset accidere, in quo necesse esset Papam religiosum alicuius rei temporalis proprietatem in speciali assumere: tamen extra casum huiusmodi non licet proprietatem habere.
units.tr: Again, the fullness of power, that is, the total power which is in all the supreme pontiffs, is that which they have from Christ by reason of the papacy. But some have been supreme pontiffs, and there may still be some, who were not capable of the aforesaid fullness of power, for example monks and other religious taken from the perfect religious orders. Such religious are therefore not capable of property and ownership, chiefly not of temporal goods as their own, since by the vow of poverty, from which they can be absolved (extra, de statu monachorum, capit. cum ad monasterium), they have renounced such property; and yet this is necessarily included in the aforesaid fullness of power. Therefore no Pope, by the power granted to him by Christ, has such a fullness of power. But perhaps someone would say that a monk or other religious raised to the papacy is wholly absolved from the vow of poverty. This is proved because the vow of obedience is attached to a perfect religious life of necessity just as the vow of poverty is; but a religious raised to the papacy is wholly absolved from the vow of obedience; therefore he is no more bound to the prelates of his religious order by reason of the vow of renunciation than by the vow of obedience, and so he is not bound by the vow of poverty. The reply is that a religious raised to the papacy is not wholly absolved from the vow of obedience, nor is he as free as if he had always been a secular. And therefore, although during his papacy he is not bound to obey the prelates of his order, he is still bound to obey the rule he vowed in certain respects, namely those which do not hinder the office to which he has been raised. This is so because, even if the vow of obedience does not properly regard those things which are or can be commanded only by prelates, nevertheless a religious made Pope is not as free as if he had been a secular. Hence, if such a Pope became a heretic, or was defamed by some crime in which he appeared incorrigible and the Church was scandalised, and he were deposed by sentence or voluntarily resigned the papacy, then by the very fact and by right he would fall again under the obedience of the prelates of his order. And so, since such a Pope can come to be, a Pope is not as free from the obedience of the prelates of his order as if he had never been a religious; and therefore he is not wholly absolved from the vow of obedience. Hence, without a new vow, he can and is bound to obey his prelate, to whom he returns; nor is this surprising, since each thing readily returns to its own nature. Since, then, the vow of poverty is of the substance of a perfect rule and does not in any way hinder the exercise of the pontifical office, it seems to be held that a religious raised to the papacy cannot have property, especially outside the case of necessity. Hence, even if some case could arise in which it was necessary for a religious Pope to take on specifically the ownership of some temporal thing, nevertheless outside such a case it is not lawful for him to have property.

units.la: CAP: VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Respondet primae rationi supra capitulo secundo adductae.
units.tr: He answers the first argument adduced above in the second chapter.

units.la: Viso quomodo quidam tenentes opinionem tertiam, probare conantur quod Papa istam non habet plenitudinem potestatis, quae exposita est superius: videndum est, quomodo ad rationes in contrarium respondere nituntur. Ad quarum primam dicitur, quod Christus per illa verba quodcunque ligaueris super terram &c. non dedit nec promisit Petro talem plenitudinem potestatis: & ideo talem etiam non dedit nec promisit Papae in beato Petro, talis enim potestas, nec Papae nec subditis expediret, sed periculosa esset vtrisq;: Esset enim periculosa Papae, quia ipsum in superbia nimis efferret, & esset sibi occasio mala nimia perpetrandi: Esset etiam periculosa subditis, quia cum inter fideles multi sunt spiritualiter debiles & infirmi: pluresque sunt, qui onera quae eis absque culpa sua, & sine causa, Papa posset imponere, absque maxima difficultate sufferre non possent, (quia tale iugum nimis periculosum existeret) timendum esset ne potius iugum obedientiae omnino abiicerent, quam tamen gravia sustinerent. Cum igitur Christus non dedit Papae aliquam potestatem sibi periculosam & aliis: sibi talem non contulit plenitudinem potestatis. Aliam ergo sibi dedit plenitudinem potestatis. Dicunt enim quidam, quod Christus per verba praemissa non dedit beato Petro vel promisit aliquam potestatem, nisi respectu peccatorum, respectu quorum solummodo dedit potestatem conferendi poenitentiae sacramentum & potestatem ligandi atque soluendi homines a peccatis; non quidem expellendo culpam, vel gratiam conferendo, ac remittendo debitum damnationis aeternae (quia hoc solus Deus operatur) sed solummodo ostendendo homines esse solutos, vel ligatos in facie ecclesiae, & aliquam satisfactionem in hoc seculo imponendo: puta orationem, vel ieiunium, vel aliquid aliud consimile; ac peccatores communioni fidelium reconciliando; & etiam interdum promulgando peccatores esse excommunicationi subdendos, non coactiuum iudicium exercendo.
units.tr: Having seen how those who hold the third opinion try to prove that the Pope does not have that fullness of power which was explained above, we must now see how they strive to answer the arguments on the other side. To the first of these it is said that Christ did not give or promise Peter such fullness of power by the words whatsoever you shall bind on earth, &c., and therefore he did not give or promise such power to the Pope in the person of blessed Peter either. For such power would be expedient neither for the Pope nor for his subjects, but dangerous to both. It would be dangerous to the Pope, because it would puff him up excessively with pride and give him a great occasion of committing wrong. It would also be dangerous to subjects, since among the faithful there are many who are spiritually weak and infirm, and many who could not bear, without the greatest difficulty, burdens which the Pope might lay on them without fault on their part and without cause (for such a yoke would be far too dangerous). It would be feared that they would rather cast off the yoke of obedience altogether than bear heavy burdens. Since therefore Christ did not give the Pope any power that was dangerous to himself and to others, he did not confer on him such fullness of power. He therefore gave him another fullness of power. For some say that Christ, by the words quoted, did not give or promise blessed Peter any power except with respect to sins, and with respect to these alone he gave the power of conferring the sacrament of penance and the power of binding and loosing men from sins. This is not by expelling guilt or conferring grace, or remitting the debt of eternal damnation (for God alone works this), but only by showing that men are loosed or bound in the face of the Church, by imposing some satisfaction in this life, such as prayer, or fasting, or something else of the kind, by reconciling sinners to the communion of the faithful, and sometimes also by declaring that sinners are to be subjected to excommunication, without exercising a coercive judgment.

units.la: Alii putantes non vacuum esse restringere potestatem Papale. Dicunt quod Christus per verba ista, aut saltem per illa pasce oues meas, dedit vel promisit beato Petro & in ipso Papae, omnem potestatem necessariam regimini fidelium, ad adipiscendo vitam aeternam; saluis iuribus & libertatibus rationabilibus honestis, vel etiam licitis aliorum quorumcunque; non delinquentium manifeste, nec perpetrantium scelus pro quo deberent iuribus aut libertatibus suis iuste priuari. Dicunt enim potestatem necessariam regimini fidelium, non concessam esse Papae ad excludendum potestatem non solum perniciosam aut periculosam; sed etiam in casu vtilem, non tamen necessariam in eodem casu: propter quod Papa ex sola ordinatione Christi, non habet potestatem super fideles respectu illorum quae inter opera supererogationis sunt extra casum necessitatis & vtilitatis, quae parificari debeat necessitati: Dicunt autem pro adipiscenda vita aeterna, ad excludendam potestatem spiritualem respectu illorum, quae ad vitam aeternam non disponunt: & propter hoc Christus dixit Petro, Tibi dabo claues &c. quasi dicat omnis potestas, quam tibi dabo, est tibi vel aliis fidelibus necessaria ad adipiscendum regnum coelorum: propter quod supra temporalia nulla habet potestatem spiritualem sibi data a Christo, nisi in casu in quo aliquo modo potest dici necessario respicere regnum coelorum: puta in casu in quo necessarium esset quod Papa de aliquibus temporalibus disponeret pro peccato aut periculo necessario euitando vel aliquo opere de necessitate agendo. Dicunt autem quidam, salua iuribus & libertatibus &c. vnde notandum est, quod Papa per nullam potestatem sibi data a Christo potest tollere iura & libertates regum, aut imperatorum, aut aliorum quorumcunque; clericorum, aut laicorum, ipsis inuitis sine culpa, & absque causa, extra casum necessitatis & vtilitatis, quae valeat parificari necessitati: dumodo libertates & iura huiusmodi non sint contra legem diuinam, ad quam Christiani tenentur, quia quamuis essent contra illa quae in veteri lege (ad quae Christiani minime tenentur vel obligantur) ipsis gaudere deberent, nec contra ius naturae, praesertim si sint consonae iuri diuino, naturae vel gentium vel ciuili: quia se essent cohtra ius gentium, vel ciuile, ipsis vti non deberent. Dicunt autem, non delinquentium nec perpetrantium scelus &c. Ad hoc est notandum, quod Papa a Christo habet potestatem infligendi poenam debitam Christianis pro omni scelere, quando necessarium est bono communi fidelium talem poenam infligi, saluo iure iudicum aliorum, suam non negligenter, nec damnabiliter exercentium potestatem: quia si alii iudices, ad quos spectat punire reos, parati fuerint facere iustitiae complementum: Papa de eorum subditis puniendis, in praeiudicium eorundem, se intromittere nullatenus potest per potestatem sibi collatam a Christo. Si etiam subditi, vel quicunque, in sublimitate constituti, nequaquam suis iuribus aut libertatibus abuntur, Papa extra casum necessitatis ipsos priuare non debet, sic ergo secundum istos, habet Papa plenitudinem potestatis, ita quod ista potestas nec boni communi, nec proprio cuiuscunque non delinquentis praeiudicet. Si autem in vindictam malefactorum communi per ipsum consulitur & per consequens Papae (qui caeteros homines meritis & sapientia debet praecellere) si talis poterit reperiri, videtur merito tribuendam: quia ista potestas videtur esse ad aedificationem, non ad destructionem boni: quam Apostolus 2. ad Corinth. vltimo loquens in persona omnium praelatorum ecclesiae) dicit cit sibi esse concessam: quia plenitudo non exeundo fines ipsius, vigere debet in Papa: tum quia debet velle prodesse non præesse secundum Augustin. 19. de ciuit. Dei, & habetur 8. q. 1. qui episcopatum: Et tali potestate dicitur esse contentus, vt secundum maiorem inuitis fidelibus non vsurpet, licet capax sit maioris: etiam si in ipsum alii ampliorem voluerint sponte transferre, præsertim si maiorem per votum abdicauerit. Isti igitur respondentes ad allegationem præscriptam dicunt, quod licet verba Christi, quodcunq; ligaueris, aliter proferantur, non tamen debent generaliter, sicut quidam volunt, ab omni penitus exceptione intelligi, cum ipsimet dicant q; aliquas exceptiones debent habere. Illa n. quæ sunt contra legem diuinam & euangelicam, & contra legem naturæ excipiuntur, vt illa Papa non possit, vnde concedunt quod prædicta sint excipienda à potestate Papæ. Sic etiā, quamuis Christus, quando protulit ista verba, vocaliter nihil exceperit, tamen omnia ista sunt excipienda, quæ Christus verbo & exemplo excipienda docuit: & Apostoli scripturis canonicis, quorum verba, vt verba Christi recipienda sunt: quia à Spiritu sancto inspirati locuti sunt, & per eos debere recipi meruerunt: Christus autem & Apostoli esse excipienda prædicta omnia innuebant: potestatem enim non necessariam regimini fidelium esse excipiendam insinuat Christus, cum dominium modum regendi à potestatibus seculi obseruandum, Apostolis interdixit, & ad humilitatem induxit, sicut ex Matth. 20. & Marc. 10. & Luc. 22. colligitur. Quod etiam Petrus secutus Christū fecit cum dixit: non dominantes in clerum. Si enim aliquis præceperit alicui cui non tenetur: omni durationis munere careret. Qui enim de re aliqua vel persona facit quid vult, se aliquo modo esse Dominum ipsius ostendit. Potestates etiam iura & libertates aliquorum sine culpa & absq; causa esse excipienda à potestate Petri insinuauit Christus verbo pariter & exemplo: verbo quidem, cum dicit, vt habetur Matth. 22. reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari: quæ verba non tantum de illis, quæ debentur Cæsari, debent intelligi, sed de omnibus, quibuscunq; debentur: quod Apostolus, sequens doctrinam Christi ad Romanos, 13. manifestat, cum loquens de potestatibus infidelium, dicit: reddite omnibus debita, cui tributum tributum, cui vectigal vectigal, cui timorem timorem, cui honorem honorem. Si autem debita sunt reddenda, & iura & libertates sine culpa, & absq; causa tolli nō debent: quod etiā ostendit Christus exemplo, cū tributū soluit, ad q; minime tenebatur, vt patet Matt. 17. c. quo facto dedit exemplū Petro, & aliis volentibus sequi perfectionē vitæ ipsius, vt ad scandalū euitandū cedant iuri suo: quare multo magis monstrauit exemplo, ne Petrus tolleret iura aliorum & libertates ipsis inuitis: quia hoc absq; scandalo (quod Petrū oportuit vitare) minime fieri potuisset. Quis n. non scandalizatur, cui inuito suæ libertates & iura tolluntur? Ex prædictis & aliis quasi innumeris, quę quidā ad idē adducunt, concluditur quod Christus voluit prædicta esse excipienda à potestate, quā sub generalibus verbis indulsit Petro. Ex quo infertur q; nec Petrus nec alius successor eius habuit à Christo, præsertim in temporalibus illam plenitudinē potestatis, quæ expo-sita est supra secundo capite cum verbis insinuauerit atq; factis, q; vicarius eius tale plenitudinē potestatis nō debuit exercere virtute alicuius potestatis ab ipso sibi concessæ, extra casum necessitatis: cum n. ipse dixerit Petro & omnibus aliis Apostolis, vt legitur, Matth.17. Non est discipulus super magistrum, neq; seruus super Dominum suum, & Ioh. 13. Non est seruus maior eo, qui misit eum, & ipso facto tale potestate recusauerit exercere: quia legitur Ioh. 6. Cum cognouisset quia venturi erant, vt raperent eum, & facerent eum regem fugit in montem, qui etiā cuidā petenti vt iudicū in temporalibus faceret inter se & fratrē suū, respondit, put legitur Luc. 12. homo quis me constituit iudicē aut Dominū super vos? quasi dicat, nullus: testante Glossa ibid. non dignabatur iudex esse litiū nō arbiter facultatū: manifeste vt apparet cōuincitur, q; vicarius eius tale potestate in temporalibus nō potest regulariter exercere: casualiter posset, secundū q; Innocen. 3. insinuare videtur, vt habetur extr. qui filii sunt legitimi. Per venerabilem.
units.tr: Others, thinking it not idle to restrict the papal power, say that Christ, by those words, or at least by the words feed my sheep, gave or promised blessed Peter, and in him the Popes, all the power necessary for governing the faithful in order to attain eternal life, saving the reasonable and honest rights and liberties, or even the lawful ones, of anyone whatever, provided they are not manifestly offending and not committing a crime for which they would justly be deprived of their rights or liberties. For they say that the power necessary for governing the faithful was not granted to the Pope so as to exclude a power that is not only harmful or dangerous, but even useful in a given case though not necessary in that case. Hence the Pope, by Christ's ordinance alone, has no power over the faithful with respect to those things which belong to works of supererogation, outside a case of necessity and of utility that ought to be equated with necessity. They say, moreover, that it was for attaining eternal life that the spiritual power was given, so as to exclude power over those things which do not dispose one to eternal life. And for this reason Christ said to Peter, I will give you the keys &c., as if to say: every power that I shall give you is necessary for you or for other faithful people in order to attain the kingdom of heaven. Therefore he has no spiritual power over temporal things given him by Christ, except in a case in which it can in some way be said to bear necessarily on the kingdom of heaven: for example, in a case in which it would be necessary for the Pope to dispose of some temporal things in order to avoid a sin or danger that must necessarily be avoided, or to do some work that must necessarily be done. Some say, moreover, saving the rights and liberties &c. Hence it must be noted that the Pope, by no power given him by Christ, can take away the rights and liberties of kings, emperors, or anyone else whatever, clerics or laymen, against their will, without fault and without cause, outside a case of necessity or utility that can be equated with necessity; provided that such liberties and rights are not contrary to the divine law, to which Christians are bound. For although they might be contrary to those things which belong to the old law (to which Christians are in no way bound or obliged), they ought to enjoy them; nor are they contrary to the law of nature, especially if they agree with the divine law, the law of nature, the law of nations or the civil law; for if they were contrary to the law of nations or the civil law, they ought not to be used. They say, moreover, not of those who offend or commit a crime &c. On this it must be noted that the Pope has from Christ the power of inflicting the punishment due to Christians for any crime, whenever it is necessary for the common good of the faithful that such punishment be inflicted, saving the right of other judges who do not negligently or culpably exercise their power. For if other judges, to whom it belongs to punish offenders, are ready to render the full measure of justice, the Pope can in no way interfere, by the power conferred on him by Christ, in punishing their subjects to their prejudice. Likewise, if subjects, or whoever is placed in a high position, do not in any way abuse their rights or liberties, the Pope ought not, outside a case of necessity, to deprive them of these. Thus, according to these men, the Pope has a fullness of power such that this power prejudices neither the common good nor the private good of anyone who does not offend. If, however, for the punishment of wrongdoers, he is consulted by the community, and consequently the Pope (who ought to surpass other men in merit and wisdom, if such a man can be found), then he is rightly thought to be entitled to it, because this power seems to be for building up and not for destroying the good; and the Apostle, speaking in 2 Cor. at the end in the person of all the prelates of the Church, says that it has been granted to him. For fullness, not going beyond its limits, ought to flourish in the Pope, both because he ought to wish to benefit rather than to rule, according to Augustine, 19 de civitate Dei, and it is found in 8 q. 1, qui episcopatum: and he is said to be content with such power that, against the will of the greater part of the faithful, he does not usurp more, although he is capable of more; even if others have voluntarily wished to transfer a greater power to him, especially if he has renounced the greater power by vow. These men, therefore, answering the aforesaid allegation, say that although the words of Christ, whatsoever you shall bind, are worded in this way, they ought not to be understood, as some wish, in an absolutely unqualified sense, since these very men say that there must be some exceptions. For those things which are contrary to the divine and evangelical law and to the law of nature are excepted, so that the Pope cannot do them; hence they concede that the aforesaid things are to be excepted from the power of the Pope. Likewise, although Christ, when he uttered these words, expressly excepted nothing, nevertheless all those things are to be excepted which Christ taught by word and example to be excepted, and which the Apostles in the canonical Scriptures, whose words are to be received as the words of Christ, because they spoke inspired by the Holy Spirit and have deserved to be received through them, showed to be excepted. Christ and the Apostles were indicating that all the aforesaid things were to be excepted; for Christ intimates that power not necessary for governing the faithful is to be excepted, since he forbade the Apostles to dominate and taught them the manner of ruling to be observed, unlike the powers of the world, and led them to humility, as is gathered from Matt. 20, Mark 10 and Luke 22. Peter, following Christ, did this too when he said, not lording it over the clergy. For if someone commands another to whom he is not bound, he would be without any office of duration. For whoever does what he wants with a thing or a person shows that he is in some way the lord of it. Christ also indicated by word and likewise by example that the powers, rights and liberties of certain people, without fault and without cause, are to be excepted from the power of Peter: by word indeed, when he says, as is found in Matt. 22, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, which words ought to be understood not only of those things which are owed to Caesar, but of all things to which anything is owed; as the Apostle, following the teaching of Christ, makes plain in Romans 13, when, speaking of the powers of the unbelievers, he says: render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is owed, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour. If, then, what is owed must be rendered, rights and liberties must not be taken away without fault and without cause. Christ also showed this by example, when he paid tribute, to which he was in no way bound, as is clear from Matt. 17, and by this deed he gave an example to Peter and to others who wish to follow the perfection of his life, that they should yield their right to avoid scandal. Therefore he showed by example much more that Peter should not take away the rights of others and their liberties against their will, since this could not have been done without scandal, which Peter had to avoid. For who is not scandalized when his liberties and rights are taken from him against his will? From the aforesaid and from other almost countless arguments which some bring forward for the same point, it is concluded that Christ wished the aforesaid things to be excepted from the power which he granted to Peter under general words. From this it follows that neither Peter nor any other successor of his had from Christ, especially in temporal matters, that fullness of power which was set out above in the second chapter, since by word and deed he indicated that his vicar ought not to exercise such fullness of power in temporal matters by virtue of any power granted to him by Christ, outside a case of necessity. For when he himself said to Peter and all the other Apostles, as we read in Matt. 17, the disciple is not above the master, nor the servant above his lord, and in John 13, the servant is not greater than he who sent him, and by the very fact he refused to exercise such power, since we read in John 6, when he knew that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, he fled to the mountain; and to a certain man who asked him to act as judge in temporal matters between himself and his brother, he answered, as we read in Luke 12, man, who made me a judge or divider over you? as if to say: no one. As the Gloss on that passage bears witness, he did not deign to be a judge of disputes or an arbiter of goods; it is clearly shown, as is apparent, that his vicar cannot ordinarily exercise such power in temporal matters; he could do so occasionally, as Innocent III seems to suggest, as is found in Extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, Per venerabilem.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Dat duas replicas contra responsionem datam supra cap. precedenti quæ etiam soluuntur.
units.tr: He gives two objections against the answer given in the preceding chapter, which are also answered.

units.la: INter præscripta sunt duo, quæ præcipue posse impugnari videntur: quorū primū est, quod talis plenitudo potestatis esset periculosa subiectis, quod non videtur verum, quia obediētia perfecta etiam cum voto, non est periculosa: sed ad obedientiam perfectam spectat, quod prælatus habeat talem plenitudinem potestatis: ergo talis plenitudo potestatis in Papa non est periculosa fidelibus. Secundū est, quod Papa potest tale potestate in temporalibus casualiter exercere: Hoc n. superioribus obuiare videtur, nam si vt allegatū est, Non est discipulus &c. & nec Christus in temporalibus etiā casualiter exercuit huiusmodi potestate; sequitur q; Papa nō debet potestate huiusmodi casualiter exercere. Ad primū illorum respondetur, quod sicut quædā sunt saluberrima bonis, quæ tamē sunt mortifera malis: sic quædam sunt perfectis expedientia, & periculo euitando carentia, quæ tamen imperfectis noscuntur periculosa: periculis, quæ ab imperfectis sunt euitanda implicita. Martyrium n. non habet annexum periculū, quod fugiendo non debeat ipsum perfectus sumere & suscipere: & tamen periculo coniuncto martyrio, nō debet se exponere imperfectus: teste Beda, qui super illud Matt. 26. Discipuli relicto eo omnes fugerunt, ait; discipuli qui articulum comprehensionis fugiendo prævenerunt, cautelam fugiendi docent eos, qui se ad supplicia minus senserint idoneos: quando tutius est latere, quam se discrimini exponere: sic est de tali plenitudine potestatis, quia esto quod talis plenitudo potestatis in supremo pontifice non esset periculosa perfectis voluntate obedientiæ perfectissimæ se subdentibus, esset tamen periculosa multis imperfectis: quibus etiā ad obedientiā perfectissimā obligari discriminosum esse videtur. Cum ergo in congregatione fidelium multi imperfecti existant, non expedit vt Papa, respectu omnium, talem habeat plenitudinem potestatis: quare talis potestas est periculosa, saltem imperfectis, quos etiam certum est ad obedientiam perfectissimam non magis teneri, quam ad perferēda onera & pericula, quæ Papa de iure (si huiusmodi haberet plenitudinem potestatis) malitiose vel indiscrete posset iniungere, obligare. Ad secundum dicitur, quod Christus talem potestatem in temporalibus non exercuit, quia non accidit casus in quo expediret fidelibus, Christum potestatem huiusmodi exercere: qui tamen ab executione huiusmodi non abstinuisset in casu, in quo fuisset necessarium ipsam exercere. Ad q; tamen forte insinuandum quaedam fecit, vel secundum potentiam deitatis vel secundum potentiam humanitatis non regularem, sed casualem, quae ad talem in temporalibus potestatem spectare videntur: sicut quando dixit daemonibus, ut intrarent porcos aliquorum, quos suffocarent in aquis, & quando interdixit ne facerent aliis: & ideo Papa non regulariter sed casualiter in casu necessitatis habet in temporalibus, etiam quandam (licet non praedictam) plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: Among the points set down above, two seem chiefly open to challenge. The first is that such a fullness of power would be dangerous to subjects. This does not seem true, because perfect obedience, even when it is bound by a vow, is not dangerous. Perfect obedience requires that the prelate have such fullness of power, so such fullness of power in the Pope is not dangerous to the faithful. The second is that the Pope may sometimes exercise such power in temporal matters. This seems to conflict with what has been said above. For if, as was alleged, The disciple is not above his master, etc., and Christ never exercised this kind of power in temporal matters, not even occasionally, it follows that the Pope ought not to exercise such power even occasionally. To the first, the answer is that just as some things are most wholesome for good people and yet deadly for the wicked, so some things are fitting for the perfect and free from danger that may still be known to be dangerous for the imperfect. The dangers that the imperfect must avoid are implicit. Martyrdom has no danger attached to it that the perfect person ought not to take up and undergo by fleeing; yet, with martyrdom threatening, the imperfect person ought not to expose himself to it. Bede bears witness to this, who, on the words of Matthew 26, The disciples all forsook him and fled, says: The disciples who fled before the moment of arrest teach caution in flight to those who judge themselves less fit for punishment, when it is safer to lie hidden than to expose oneself to peril. It is the same with this fullness of power. Even if such fullness of power in the supreme pontiff were not dangerous to the perfect, who submit themselves to him with the most perfect will of obedience, it would still be dangerous to many imperfect people, for whom it seems perilous to be bound even to the most perfect obedience. Therefore, since many imperfect people exist in the congregation of the faithful, it is not expedient that the Pope, with respect to all of them, should have such fullness of power. Hence such power is dangerous, at least to the imperfect, who are certainly not more bound to the most perfect obedience than to bear the burdens and dangers that the Pope, if he had such fullness of power, could by right impose or oblige them to bear, whether maliciously or indiscreetly. To the second, it is said that Christ did not exercise such power in temporal matters, because no occasion arose in which it would have been expedient for the faithful that Christ exercise such power. Yet he would not have refrained from exercising it in a case where its exercise was necessary. Nevertheless, to perhaps hint at this, he did certain things, either by the power of his deity or by the power of his humanity, not as a rule but occasionally, which seem to belong to such power in temporal matters. Such was his command to the demons that they enter the swine of certain men, whom they then drowned in the waters, and his forbidding them to do so to others. Therefore the Pope has, in temporal matters, not as a rule but occasionally, in a case of necessity, a certain fullness of power too, though not the one mentioned above.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Respondet ad confirmationem, capitulo secundo pro prima ratione, adductam.
units.tr: He answers the confirmation brought forward in the second chapter for the first argument.

units.la: REstat igitur respondere ad verba Innocentii 3. quae contra praedicta videntur expressius militare: ad quae dicitur, q; nisi violenter & contra intellectum, quem prima facie sonant, exponantur, sapiunt haeresim manifestam: sicut & nonnulla alia verba eiusdem Innocentii, quae insuper etiam aliis verbis ipsius contraria videntur. Cunq; n. dicit, extra. Qui filii sunt legitimi capit. per venerabilem, cum Deuteronomium lex secunda interpretetur, ex vi vocabuli, corroboratur, ut quod ibi decernitur, in novo testamento debeat observari, &c. quibus verbis, si intelligit quod sint observanda in novo testamento, quo ad superficiem literae, quomodo observanda erant in veteri testamento, quo ad multa, est erroneum reputandum, quia ibidem sunt multa caerimonialia, sicut patet cap. 13. & in multis aliis, quae non observantur in nova lege, nec illo modo servanda sunt illa quae 3. Deuter. decernuntur, plusquam illa quae decernuntur in aliis libris Moysi: aut intelligit, quod observanda sunt secundum intelligentiam mysticam vel moralem, & sic non solum servari debent illa quae in Deuteronom. sed etiam omnia alia quae in aliis libris Moysi decernuntur, ut legitur in decret. Dist. 6. cap. Hu itaq, &c. Cum igitur in his praemissis verbis innuit Innocentius quod magis observari debent illa quae decernuntur in Deuteronomio, quam quae decernuntur in aliis libris legis, praesertim cum verba praescripta omnino impertinentia essent ad conclusionem, quam probare intendit, sequitur quod verba nisi sanius interpretentur haeretica sunt censenda.
units.tr: RIt remains, then, to answer the words of Innocent III, which seem to militate more expressly against what has been said. To these it is replied that, unless they are explained forcibly and against the sense they seem to bear at first sight, they savour of manifest heresy, as do several other words of the same Innocent, which moreover seem to contradict his other words. For when he says, Extra, Qui filii sunt legitimi, cap. Per venerabilem: since Deuteronomy, the second law, is interpreted from the force of its name, it is confirmed that what is decreed there ought to be observed in the New Testament, etc., if he means that those things must be observed in the New Testament according to the surface of the letter, in the way they were observed in the Old Testament, this must be held erroneous, because there are many ceremonial matters in that book, as is clear from cap. 13. and in many other places, which are not observed under the New Law, nor are those things decreed in the third chapter of Deuteronomy to be kept in that manner, any more than those decreed in the other books of Moses. Or else he means that they must be observed according to a mystical or moral understanding, and in that case not only those things in Deuteronomy but all the other things decreed in the other books of Moses must be kept, as is read in Decretum, Dist. 6, cap. Hu itaque, etc. Since, then, in the words quoted above Innocent hints that the things decreed in Deuteronomy ought to be observed more than those decreed in the other books of the law, especially since the words cited were wholly irrelevant to the conclusion he intends to prove, it follows that, unless they are interpreted more soundly, they must be judged heretical.

units.la: Cum extra. de elect. capit. venerabile dicit: Idem etiam contra proprium iuramentum, super quo nec consilium de fide apostolica requisivit, ambitionis vitio regimen sibi usurpare praesumsit, cu super illo iuramento, prius Romana ecclesia consulere debuisset: nec valet ad plena excusatione ipsum, si iuramentum illud dicatur illicitum, cum nihilominus super eo nois prius consulere debuisset. Quae omnia, nisi contra intentionem (quam verba sonare videntur,) exponantur, absurditates haereticales videtur includere: cum verba ista praetendant, quod nemo debeat venire contra iuramentum suum illicitum, antequam consulat summum pontificem: ex quo absurditates innumerae contra bonos mores sequi videntur. Sequitur enim, quod si aliquis iuraret illicite se nolle abstinere a fornicatione, furto, homicidio, vel aliquo alio quocunq; peccato ab huiusmodi peccato nequaquam abstineret antequam Papam consuleret.
units.tr: When Extra, De electione, cap. Venerabile says: He also, against his own oath, about which he did not seek the counsel of the apostolic faith, presumed through the vice of ambition to usurp rule for himself, since he ought first to have consulted the Roman Church about that oath; nor does it avail him as a full excuse if that oath is said to be unlawful, since nevertheless he ought first to have consulted the Roman Church about it. All these things, unless they are explained against the intention which the words seem to express, appear to contain heretical absurdities, since these words hold that no one ought to act against his own unlawful oath before consulting the supreme pontiff. From this, countless absurdities against good morals seem to follow. For it follows that if someone had sworn unlawfully that he would not abstain from fornication, theft, murder, or any other sin of the kind, he would in no way abstain from such sin until he had consulted the Pope.

units.la: Sequitur etiam si aliquis iuraret se non laudare Deum vel proximum diligaturum, aut non redditurum aliena, vel aliam rem; quod huiusmodi nec laudare Deum, nec diligere proximum, nec reddere aliena deberet, antequam consuleret Romanam ecclesiam, quae videtur haeresim sapere manifestam, & fomentum peccatis & iniquitati ministrare. Insuper verba praedicti Innocentii allegata pro praedicta plenitudine potestatis Papalis, aliis verbis eius, nisi saniusexponantur, repugnare videtur: cu, ut legitur extra. qui filii sunt legitimi. capit. causam dicat: Nos attendentes quod ad regem pertinet non ad ecclesiam de talibus possessionibus iudicare, &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ad Papam, qui est ecclesia, vel caput ecclesiae, non pertinet de possessionibus iudicare, & per consequens non habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, q; etiam ex pluribus decretalibus eiusdem Innocentii patenter potest colligi, unde dicitur, q; sane exponenda sunt verba Innocentii Quodcunq; ligaveris &c. cu dicit, q; Christus nihil excepit, cu dixit Petro, & ne deprehendatur in haeresi manifesta, dupliciter ad sensum catholicum exponunt, uno modo intelligat q; Christus tunc quando dixit Petro, quodcunq; ligaveris &c. nihil excepit vocaliter & expresse; alibi tamen, & aliis verbis & exceptis, ostendit excepta esse plura, & ita illa excepta sunt a nobis. Alio modo dicitur, q; Christus nihil excepit de his quae sunt necessaria regimini fidelium, & non praeiudicant iuribus & libertatibus aliorum: & ideo per ista verba, Christus nullam potestatem permisit Petro nō necessariam regimini fidelium, nec praeiudicialem aliis praesertim notanter seu notabiliter non abutentibus iuribus & libertatibus suis, nec damnabiliter negligentibus ius suum vnicuiq; exhibere &c.
units.tr: It also follows that if someone swore that he would not praise God or would not love his neighbour, or would not restore what belongs to others, or any other thing, then he ought not to praise God, love his neighbour, or restore what belongs to others until he had consulted the Roman Church, which seems to savour of manifest heresy and to supply fuel to sin and iniquity. Moreover, the words of the aforesaid Innocent quoted in support of the said fullness of papal power seem to conflict with his other words, unless they are more soundly explained, since, as is read in Extra, Qui filii sunt legitimi, cap. Causam, he says: We, considering that it pertains to the king and not to the Church to judge about such possessions, etc. From these words it is gathered that it does not pertain to the Pope, who is the Church or the head of the Church, to judge about possessions, and consequently he does not have such a fullness of power in temporal matters. This can also be clearly gathered from several decretals of the same Innocent. Hence it is said that the words of Innocent, Whatever you shall bind, etc., when he says that Christ excepted nothing when he spoke to Peter, must rightly be explained, and that, lest he be caught in manifest heresy, they explain them in two ways in a Catholic sense. In one way, one understands that Christ, when he said to Peter, Whatever you shall bind, etc., excepted nothing in words and expressly; yet elsewhere, and in other words, and with exceptions, he shows that many things were excepted, and so those exceptions are to be made by us. In another way, it is said that Christ excepted nothing that is necessary for the government of the faithful and that does not prejudice the rights and liberties of others; and therefore by these words Christ permitted Peter no power that is not necessary for the government of the faithful, nor prejudicial to others, especially to those who do not abuse their rights and liberties in a notable or considerable way, nor culpably neglect to render to each his due, etc.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Respondet rationi secundae capitulo secundo adductae, quam probat sophistice.
units.tr: He replies to the second argument adduced in chapter two, which he proves to be sophistical.

units.la: AD secundam rationem adductam supra capitulo secundo pro plenitudine potestatis, quae in hoc fundatur, quia ut probatur auctoritate. Hieremiae, Deus nihil excipiendo constituit Papam super omnes gentes & regna. Respondetur quod huiusmodi ratio propter multa est sophistica recipienda: Primo, quia summo sacerdoti nullatenus fuit dictum, ecce constitui te super omnes gentes & regna: Dictu n. fuit Hieremiae, qui non erat summus sacerdos. Secundo quia licet Hieremias fuit sacerdos, tamen non sibi inquantum sacerdos erat, sed inquantum Propheta, dicta fuerunt verba praedicta: unde & ibidem promisit Dominus, Prophetam in gentibus dedit te. Tertio, Hieremias nequaquam talem exercuit potestatem, nec dixit populis se recepisse potestatem talem a Deo. Quomodo vult ergo concludere per ista verba, quod Papa habet talem potestatem à Deo, & quod quilibet sacerdos, & omnis Propheta habet à Deo talem plenitudinem potestatis, quam tamen non videtur concludere allegatio supradicta? quia licet ea, quæ ad spiritualia & ad cœlestia spectant, plenius debent refulgere in supremo Pontifice nouæ legis, tamen non congruenter matrimonio uterentur: & sicut in veteri lege summus sacerdos, armis, bellis, necibus hominum, truncationibus membrorum, vindictæ sanguinis, immiscuit se decenter: ita etiam decteret, ut summus sacerdos nouæ legis se huiusmodi implicarer; quæ tamen omnia & similia absurda sunt censenda: quamobrem ex potestate & dominio, quod habuit in temporalibus summus sacerdos veteris legis, concludi non potest, quod Papa in temporalibus aliquam habeat potestatem, quæ nec sibi nec aliis necessaria est credenda, & ideo non concludit: quia licet in illis verbis non addatur exceptio, ex aliis tamen verbis scripturæ colligi potest, quod alia est exceptio addenda.
units.tr: As for the second argument adduced above in chapter two in support of the fullness of power, which rests on the authority of Jeremiah, that God without exception has set the Pope over all nations and kingdoms: the answer is that this kind of argument must be rejected as sophistical for many reasons. First, the words "Behold, I have set you over the nations and kingdoms" were by no means spoken to the high priest, for they were spoken to Jeremiah, who was not the high priest. Second, although Jeremiah was a priest, these words were not addressed to him insofar as he was a priest, but insofar as he was a prophet; hence the Lord also promised in the same place, I have given you as a prophet to the nations. Third, Jeremiah never exercised any such power, nor did he tell the people that he had received such power from God. How, then, do they wish to conclude from these words that the Pope has such power from God, and that every priest and every prophet has from God such fullness of power? The above allegation does not seem to prove this. For although those things which pertain to spiritual and heavenly matters ought to shine more fully in the supreme pontiff of the new law, nevertheless it would not be fitting for him to engage in worldly affairs. Just as in the old law the high priest fittingly involved himself in arms, wars, the slaughter of men, the mutilation of limbs and the vengeance of blood, so too it would be unseemly for the high priest of the new law to become entangled in such things. Yet all these things and the like must be judged absurd. Therefore, from the power and dominion which the high priest of the old law had in temporal affairs, it cannot be concluded that the Pope has any power in temporal affairs, which neither he nor others need be believed to have; and so the argument does not follow. For although no exception is added in those words, it can nevertheless be gathered from other words of Scripture that another exception must be added.

units.la: Ad Innocentium diuersi diuersè respondent, quidam enim (ut videtur eis) verba eius sane intelligunt, dicentes eum intendere quod æternû Christi Pontificium longè maioris potestatis est, etiam in temporalibus casualiter, quamuis non regulariter, quam Pontificium veteris legis: & ideo si dictum est Pontifici veteris legis; Ecce constitui te super gentes, &c. ut euelleret, hoc est ut casualiter etiam in temporalibus, super gentes & regna, iurisdictionem exerceret, ut sit tamen iurisdictionem assignans non in præiudicium regum, ac etiam principum, sua legitimè utentium potestate. Quod hæc fuerit intentio sua, colligitur ex verbis suis quæ sequuntur, cum ait, Relinquitur igitur Romanum Pontificem etiam casualiter exercere Pontificale iudicium, in quemlibet Christianum, cuiuscunque conditionis existat, maxime ratione peccati: ut peccatorem quemcunque, postquam in profundum vitiorum venerit, propter contemptum, tanquam publicanum & ethnicum, haberi constituat à fideli corporealienum: quibus verbis innuitur, quod non nisi casualiter Pontifex Romanus super omnes Christianos temporale exercet iudicium: ex quo concluditur, quod Papa non habet regulariter prædictam plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: Different men answer Innocent differently. Some (as it seems to them) understand his words in a sound sense, saying that he meant that the pontifical office of Christ is of far greater power, even in temporal matters, occasionally though not as a rule, than the pontifical office of the old law. And so, if it was said to the pontiff of the old law, "Behold, I have set you over the nations," etc., in order to pluck up, that is, so that he might exercise jurisdiction over nations and kingdoms occasionally even in temporal matters, nevertheless he was assigning jurisdiction without prejudice to kings and princes who use their power lawfully. That this was his intention is gathered from his following words, where he says: "It follows, therefore, that the Roman Pontiff exercises pontifical judgment even occasionally over any Christian whatever his condition, chiefly by reason of sin, so that he may appoint any sinner, once he has fallen into the depths of vices, to be held on account of his contempt as a publican and a heathen, and to be cut off from the faithful." By these words it is implied that the Roman Pontiff exercises temporal judgment over all Christians only occasionally; from which it is concluded that the Pope does not as a rule have the aforesaid fullness of power.

units.la: Alii non curant prædictum Innocentium excusare, præsertim cum videtur ipsis in eadem decretali sua hæresim manifestam inexcusabilem asserere & affirmare, dicens, quod extra ecclesiâ, nulla est à Deo ordinata potestas aut iurisdictio, & quod non est concessa, sed permissa tantum modo, & quod nulla potestas temporalis regiminis extra ecclesiam potest reperiri: quæ omnia, ut isti dicunt, sunt hæretica reputanda: quod ut in aliis allegatis operibus quamplurimis numero nituntur ostendere, de quibus pauca perstringam. Ad euidentiam tamen allegationum ipsorum, est primo obseruandum, quod secundum ipsos ante aduentum Christi, & post apud infideles, fuit verum dominium temporalium rerum, & vera ac legitima & ordinata potestas, & gladii materialis vera iurisdictio temporalis, non tantum permissa à Deo, qualiter Deus permisit tyrannos, prædones, & inuasores alienarum rerum, etiam iurisdictionis sibi potestatem & dominium usurpare: sed concessso quod quamuis talem potestatem habentes apud infideles illegitime & inordinate usi fuerint semper aut frequenter: sed abusus utentis, & legitima potestas eam habentis in nullo sibi obuiant & repugnant: sed simul in eodem tempore & in eundem hominem cadere possunt, teste August. qui ut legitur 14. q. 5. can. neque enim, ait, Neque tyrannica factionis peruersitas laudabilis erit, si regia clementia tyrannus subditos tractet: neque vituperabilis ordo regiæ potestatis, si rex crudelitate tyrannica seuiat: aliud namque est iniusta potestate velle iuste uti & iusta potestate iniuste velle uti. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod iusta potestas & abusus eiusdem potestatis, iuste compatiuntur se in eodem, quia esto, quod omnes ædificarent extra ecclesiam ad gehennam, & quod infideles penitus abuterentur omni potestate, non posset tamen ostendi, quod nullam haberent veram & legitimam potestatem.
units.tr: Others do not trouble to excuse the aforesaid Innocent, especially since it seems to them that in the same decretal he asserts and affirms a manifest and inexcusable heresy, saying that outside the Church there is no power or jurisdiction ordained by God, that it is not granted but merely permitted, and that no temporal power of government can be found outside the Church. All these things, as they say, are to be regarded as heretical. They strive to show this in many of the other works they cite, of which I will touch on a few. However, to make their allegations clear, it must first be observed that, according to them, before the coming of Christ and after it, among unbelievers there was true dominion over temporal things, and a true, lawful and ordained power, and a true temporal jurisdiction of the material sword, not merely permitted by God, in the way that God permitted tyrants, robbers and invaders of other men's property to usurp for themselves power and dominion even over jurisdiction. Rather, it is granted that although those who held such power among unbelievers have always or often used it unlawfully and disorderly, the abuse of one who uses power and the lawful power of one who holds it do not in any way oppose or contradict each other, but can fall together at the same time and in the same man. Augustine bears witness to this, as is read in 14 q. 5, can. "Neque enim," he says, "the perverseness of a tyrannical faction will not be praiseworthy if a tyrant treats his subjects with royal clemency; nor will the order of royal power be blameworthy if a king rages with tyrannical cruelty; for it is one thing to wish to use unjust power justly, and another to wish to use just power unjustly." From these words it is plain that just power and the abuse of that same power can justly exist together in the same person. For even if all men were building towards hell outside the Church, and unbelievers were wholly abusing all power, it still could not be shown that they had no true and lawful power.

units.la: Quod ergo etiam ante aduentum Christi & post, apud infideles fuit vera potestas gladii materialis, & verum dominium rerum temporalium, tali modo probatur. Dominium rerum determinatis hominibus sic datum est à Deo, quod ab eis illud auferre aliis etiam minime licet: est enim verum dominium, non solum permissum, sed etiam concessum ab illo, qui verum & legitimum dominiû concedere & dare potest: Dominus autem, ut habetur in Deuter. d. lit filiis Esau & filiis Moab, & filiis Amon, qui erant infideles, terras & regiones, quas ab eis auferre fidelibus non licebat: ergo ipsi, quamuis essent infideles, habuerunt verum & legitimum dominium temporalium rerum, quantumcunque abuterentur eodem. Amplius, qui præcepto spirituali diuino in regem vngitur, non solum ad hoc habet potestatem gladii materialis permissam, sed etiam concessam (quod uictio regalis legitima non est sine potestate) Deus autem præcepit Hellæ propter hoc, ut legitur 3. Reg. 19. ut vngeret Asahel regem super Syriam, qui tamen infidelis erat. Ergo Asahel legitimam habuit potestatem, de quo ibidem subiungitur: Et erit, quicunque fugerit gladium Asahel, occidet eum Iehu. Rursus, ille verum habet dominium temporalium rerum, & non solum permissum, cui fideles (illa quæ dicit) sua reddere obligantur (quia præmia quæ tyrannus aut prædo vendicat vel inuasor, non tenetur alius sibi dare) sed Christus voluit & præcepit fidelibus, ut redderent Cæsari illa, quæ sua esse dicebat, dicens: reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei Deo: ergo Cæsar ille Tiberius, qui extitit infidelis, habuit verum & legitimum dominium temporalium rerum. Adhuc, ille cui fideles non solum propter periculum euitandum, sed etiam propter conscientiam debent esse subiecti, habet veram & legitimam potestatem: potestatibus autem infidelibus debuerunt, tempore Apostolorum, Christiani esse subiecti, non solum propter periculum euitandum, sed propter conscientiam, teste Apostolo ad Rom. 13. cum dicit; ideoque necessitate subditi estote non solum propter periculum, sed propter conscientiam: ergo infideles veram
units.tr: That, therefore, even before and after the coming of Christ, among unbelievers there was true power of the material sword and true dominion over temporal things, is proved in the following way. Dominion over things has been given by God to certain men in such a way that it is not lawful for others to take it away from them. For it is true dominion, not merely permitted but also granted by Him who can grant and give true and lawful dominion. Now the Lord, as is recorded in Deuteronomy, gave to the sons of Esau, the sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon, who were unbelievers, lands and regions which it was not lawful for believers to take from them. Therefore they, although unbelievers, had true and lawful dominion over temporal things, however much they abused it. Furthermore, one who is anointed king by a divine spiritual command has power of the material sword not merely permitted but also granted (for a royal anointing is not lawful without power). God commanded Elijah for this purpose, as is read in 3 Kings 19, to anoint Hazael king over Syria, who was nevertheless an unbeliever. Therefore Hazael had lawful power, of whom it is added in the same place: "And it shall come to pass that whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall slay him." Again, one who has true dominion over temporal things, and not merely permitted, is one to whom the faithful are bound to render what is theirs (for a tyrant, robber or invader who claims booty for himself is not owed anything by another). But Christ willed and commanded the faithful to render to Caesar those things which he said were his own, saying: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Therefore that Caesar Tiberius, who was an unbeliever, had true and lawful dominion over temporal things. Further, one to whom the faithful must be subject not only to avoid danger but also for conscience' sake has true and lawful power. But at the time of the Apostles Christians were bound to be subject to unbelieving powers not only to avoid danger but for conscience' sake, as the Apostle testifies in Romans 13, when he says: "Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath, but also for conscience' sake." Therefore unbelievers

units.la: E e veram & legitimam potestatem habuerunt: Et cp Apostolus sub potestatibus sublimioribus comprehedit infideles, patet per illud quod scripsit 1. Tim. 6. dicēs, Quicunq; sunt sub iugo serui dominos suos omni honore dignos arbitrentur, ne nomen Domini & doctrina blasphemetur. Qui autem fideles habent Dominos, non contemnant quia fratres sunt, sed magis seruiant, quia sunt fideles: vbi apte insinuat, cp dominorum verorū quidam erant fideles, & quidā infideles, & quod seruiendum est vtrisque, quare etiā cum dicit Rom. 13. 5 Omnia anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: voluit fideles esse subiectos etiā potestatib. infidelibus, quia dicit; non est potestas nisi à Deo: quae autem sunt, à Deo ordinata sunt: intellexit aperte, cp potestas, quae erat apud infideles, erat ordinata à Deo, & non solum permissa: quia dicit; Qui autem resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit: quod non de potestate permissa, sed de concessa habet intelligi. Non n. Patres in Veteri Testam. qui saepe infidelibus habentib. super eos potestatem permissam à Deo restiterunt, Dei ordinationi restiterunt: quia resistendo illis nequaq; sibi damnationem acquisierunt: sed laudabiles & digni praemio extiterunt. Sic etiā Christiani, qui infidelibus opprimentib. eos, & potestate permissam habentibus resistere tentauerūt, nullatenus ordinationi Dei restiterunt. Extra ecclesiam igitur apud infideles, potest potestas legitima & concessa (& non permissa) solummodo reperiri: quia infideles, vt frequenter illa potestate legitima abutuntur, quemadmodum nonnulli fideles peccatores habentes tñ potestatem legitimā, sepius ea abutuntur. Hanc sententiā de potestate data aut concessa à Deo, tam infidelibus q; fidelibus malis, tenere videtur, & asserit August. 19. de ciuit. Dei. Isti ergo putant Innocentium praedictū super praedicto errore excusari non posse, nec verba ipsius praescripta, ad aliū intellectum q; sonant, reputant intelligenda; quinimmo dicunt ipsa irrationabilia esse, & euidenter ostendunt inuentorem eorum pariter in Scripturis sacris fuisse ignarum ac inexpertum, quare non 20 sequitur, quod Pontificium summum sub gratia ordinatum fuerit longe maioris potestatis in temporalibus quam sacerdotium Aaron: immo regulariter est minoris potestatis in temporalibus, nam & temporalia plura & maiora, ex ordinatione diuina assignata fuerunt sacerdotio veteris legis, quam sacerdotio nouae legis. Tum quia Pontificium Petri non fuit aequalis potestatis cum Pontificio Christi. Christus enim auctoritate sui Pontificii, noua potuit instituere sacramenta, quod nequaquam potuit Petrus, potuit etiam Christus in multis dispensare, in quibus Petrus dispensandi non habuit potestatem. Tum quia Pontificio fungenti, non erat dictum à Deo, ecce constituit te super &c. quia Hieremias non erat Pontifex, sed de sacerdotibus inferioribus, &c.
units.tr: had true and lawful power. And that the Apostle includes unbelievers under the "higher powers" is plain from what he wrote in 1 Timothy 6, saying: "Whoever are under the yoke of slavery, let them count their masters worthy of all honour, lest the name of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed. But those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brethren, but rather serve them the more, because they are faithful and beloved." There he aptly insinuates that some of the true masters were believers and some unbelievers, and that both are to be served. Likewise when he says in Romans 13, "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers," he wished the faithful to be subject even to unbelieving powers; for he says, "There is no power but of God; the powers that exist are ordained of God," and he clearly understood that the power which was among unbelievers was ordained by God and not merely permitted; for he says, "Whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God," which must be understood of granted, not merely permitted, power. For the Fathers in the Old Testament, who often resisted unbelievers who had power over them permitted by God, did not resist the ordinance of God, since by resisting them they did not acquire damnation for themselves, but were praiseworthy and worthy of reward. So too Christians who tried to resist unbelievers oppressing them, and holding power permitted by God, did not in any way resist the ordinance of God. Outside the Church, therefore, among unbelievers, lawful and granted power (and not merely permitted) can be found; for unbelievers often abuse that lawful power, just as some faithful sinners, though holding lawful power, quite often abuse it. This opinion, that power is given or granted by God both to unbelievers and to wicked believers, seems to be held and asserted by Augustine in book 19 of The City of God. Those men therefore think that the aforesaid Innocent cannot be excused of that error, nor can the words written above be understood in any other sense than they sound; indeed they say that they are irrational, and they plainly show that their author was equally ignorant and inexperienced in the holy Scriptures. Therefore it does not follow that the supreme pontificate under grace was ordained to have far greater power in temporal matters than the priesthood of Aaron. On the contrary, as a rule it has less power in temporal matters; for by divine ordinance more and greater temporal possessions were assigned to the priesthood of the old law than to the priesthood of the new law. Also, the pontificate of Peter was not of equal power with the pontificate of Christ. For Christ, by the authority of his pontificate, could institute new sacraments, which Peter could by no means do; Christ could also dispense in many matters in which Peter had no power to dispense. Also, to the one holding the pontificate it was not said by God, "Behold, I have set you over, etc.," since Jeremiah was not a pontiff, but one of the lower priests, etc.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Respondet ad allegationem tertiam, cap. 2. adductam.
units.tr: He responds to the third argument, adduced in chapter 2.

units.la: AD tertiam rationem adductam superius respondetur, quod Apostolus dicens, nescitis quoniā angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis secularia? non loquebatur in persona propria, aut summi Pontificis, vel etiam clericorum: sed in persona omnium fidelium clericorum & laicorum, quia de coetu fidelium constituendi sunt iudices, qui debet secularia iudicare, saluo iure iudicum infidelium, non negligentiū iustitiam facere in his quae spectant ad eos, anteq; iuste sua iurisdictione priuentur. Nō quidem de necessitate in aliquo casu episcopus, vel sacerdos, sed magis aliquis laicus idoneus constitui debet, vel clericus idoneus, qui necessitate vrgente valeat secularia iudicare: nullus tamen debet constitui, qui in omni casu sine omni exceptione, habeat secularia taliter iudicare, vt super ea habeat talem plenitudinē potestatis: quia quemcunq; mortale, talem potestatē habere super oēs fideles, esset periculosū comunitati fidelium. Vnde tale potestatem, nec Papa, nec Imperator habere debet sup comunitatem fidelium: quia nullus eorū valet tollere iura & libertates inferiorum, sine culpa, & absq; causa, nisi in casu necessitatis: cū igitur dicitur cp Papa absq; omni exceptione habet secularia iudicare, hoc negaf: & cū probatur, quia Apostolus nō distinguendo nec excipiendo p praelatis spiritualib. & praecipue p supremo Pontifice ait; Nescitis quod angelos iudicabimus, quanto magis secularia? Respondetur, cp Apostolus nō dicit ista verba p praelatis spiritualib. tantūmodo, nec praecise pro Pontifice supremo, nisi casualiter: sed dicit ista in psona communitatis fidelium, modo quo dictum est: qui quamuis nō distinxerit, nec exceperit, tamen voluit exceptiones quas alibi posuit, subesse intelligendas, ne sibiipsi inueniretur contrarius, imo etiam Christo: qui constituit Petrum supremum Pontificem cunctorum fidelium non ad dominandum, sed ad pascendum fideles, non propter vtilitatem, & exaltationē vel honorem Petri, sed principaliter propter vtilitatem fidelium: & ideo nullam constituit sibi potestatem, nisi ad aedificationem non ad destructionem, nec voluit propter multa pericula euitanda esse fideles subditos successoribus Petri, nisi in necessariis (saluis libertatibus & iuribus, non solum fidelium, sed etiam infidelium) nisi ex causa rationabili & manifesta propter culpam aliquam specialem: à principe laico, catholico clerico, vel in casu ecclesiastico iuste suis iuribus & libertatibus priuarentur: propter quod Apostolus in pluribus locis praecepit fidelibus, vt potestatibus etiam infidelibus, obedientiam & reuerentiam, ac subiectionem impenderent: manifeste insinuans quod cum dicit prima Corinth. sext. quod fideles debent secularia iudicare, non intelligit quod absque omni exceptione deberent fideles à fidelibus iudicari, & quod non esset potestas apud infideles. Dicit ergo quod Apostolus intendit hortari Corinthios vt faciant, quemadmodum ordinatur secundum canonicas sanctiones. Nam semper vt habetur s. quaest. 2. cap. primates, distinctione nonagesim. studendum, extra de simonia cap. querelam. 23. quaestione quarta. Si illic. Iudex debet partes prius concordare, quam ad iudicium veniant, si potest: quemadmodum melius faciunt immediate subiecti alicui iudici, vel principi seculari, vel ecclesiastico, inter se causas habentes, quae possunt per arbitros expediexpediri absque iudicio superioris: si antequam venirent ad iudicem superiorem negocia sua inter se per arbitros vel iudices ecclesiasticos à partibus diffinitos negociis suis studuerint debitum finem imponere: sicut ipsi Corinthii, & eadem ratione fideles alii, habentes negocia etiam secularia inter se, si non tenerentur iniuriam sustinere & eandem pati, & vellent ius suum, si non possent aliter, per iudicium obtinere, si constituerent inter se iudices fideles, inter quos, vel apud iudices infideles ius suum acquirant absque praeiudicio illicito iudicum infidelium, quibus fuerunt subiecti. Et ideo in tribus casibus poterant fideles Corinthii, apud infidelem licite iudicium exposcere. Primus est, si infideles in casibus, in quibus erant subiecti, ipsos ad iudicium infidelium protrahebant: Secundus, si reus fidelis coactus ab actore fideli, licet iniquo in hoc, in iudicium infidelium trahebatur: Tertius, si actor tenebatur acquirere ius suum, quod non potest nisi per iudices infideles solummodo obtinere. In aliis casibus voluit Apostolus, quod iniuriam utrumque acciperet & pateretur fraudem, vel quod iudicarentur apud fideles iudices à fidelibus constitutis: & ut inquantum licite possunt, vitarent apud infideles cum scandalo iudicari: ne infideles scirent fraudes & iniurias, quas Christiani mali & iniqui non verebantur facere Christianis: & si occasionem haberent, non solum Christianos, sed etiam doctrinam Dei blasphemandi.
units.tr: To the third argument adduced above, the answer is that the Apostle, saying Know ye not that we shall judge angels? how much more things that pertain to this life?, did not speak in his own person, nor in that of the chief Pontiff, or even of the clergy, but in the person of all the faithful, clergy and laity alike. For judges who are to decide secular matters must be appointed from the body of the faithful, saving the right of unbelieving judges, and not neglecting to do justice in those matters which belong to them, before they are justly deprived of their jurisdiction. Not indeed of necessity should a bishop or priest be appointed in every case; rather some suitable layman, or suitable cleric, should be appointed who, in urgent necessity, may be able to judge secular matters. Yet no one should be appointed who, in every case and without any exception, has such authority to judge secular matters that he holds such fullness of power over them. For it would be dangerous to the community of the faithful for any mortal to have such power over all the faithful. Hence neither the Pope nor the Emperor ought to have such power over the community of the faithful, since neither of them can take away the rights and liberties of inferiors without fault and without cause, except in a case of necessity. Therefore, when it is said that the Pope, without any exception, has to judge secular matters, this is denied. And when it is proved because the Apostle, without distinguishing or excepting spiritual prelates, and especially the supreme Pontiff, says Know ye not that we shall judge angels, how much more secular things?, the answer is that the Apostle does not say these words of spiritual prelates only, nor precisely of the supreme Pontiff, except by chance. He says them in the person of the community of the faithful, in the way already explained. Although he did not distinguish or except, he nevertheless wished the exceptions which he set down elsewhere to be understood as still in force, lest he be found contrary to himself, and even to Christ. Christ appointed Peter supreme Pontiff of all the faithful, not to lord it over them but to feed them, not for the usefulness, exaltation or honour of Peter, but chiefly for the usefulness of the faithful. Therefore he set up for himself no power except for building up, not for destroying. Nor did he will, in order to avoid many dangers, that the faithful should be subject to the successors of Peter except in necessary matters, saving the liberties and rights not only of the faithful but also of unbelievers, and unless, for a reasonable and manifest cause on account of some special fault, they should be justly deprived of their rights and liberties by a lay prince, a Catholic cleric, or, in an ecclesiastical case, by an ecclesiastical authority. On this account the Apostle in many places commanded the faithful to render obedience, reverence and subjection even to unbelieving powers, plainly hinting that when he says in 1 Cor. 6. that the faithful ought to judge secular matters, he does not mean that the faithful should without any exception be judged by the faithful, or that there should be no authority among unbelievers. He means, therefore, that the Apostle intends to exhort the Corinthians to act as is ordained by the canonical sanctions. For, as is held in 2 Quaest. 2 cap. Primates; dist. 90 Studendum; extra de Simonia cap. Querelam; 23 Quaest. 4 Si illic, a judge ought first to reconcile the parties before they come to judgment, if he can. Those who are immediately subject to some judge, whether secular or ecclesiastical prince, and who have causes between themselves that can be settled by arbitrators without the judgment of a superior, do better if, before they come before a higher judge, they strive to bring their affairs to a due end among themselves through arbitrators or ecclesiastical judges chosen by the parties. The Corinthians themselves did this, and for the same reason other faithful persons, having secular affairs between themselves, should do likewise, provided they were not bound to suffer injury and to endure the same, and if they wished to obtain their right by judgment, if they could not otherwise, they should appoint faithful judges among themselves, or obtain their right before unbelieving judges without unlawful prejudice to the unbelieving judges to whom they were subject. And so in three cases the faithful Corinthians could lawfully seek judgment before an unbeliever. The first is if unbelievers, in cases in which the faithful were subject to them, dragged them before an unbelieving court. The second is if a faithful defendant, compelled by a faithful plaintiff (though unjust in this), was dragged before a court of unbelievers. The third is if the plaintiff was bound to recover his right, which could be obtained only through unbelieving judges. In other cases the Apostle wished that both parties should accept the injury and suffer the fraud, or else be judged before faithful judges appointed by the faithful; and that, so far as they lawfully could, they should avoid being judged before unbelievers, lest it cause scandal. For unbelievers would learn of the frauds and injuries which wicked and unjust Christians did not hesitate to inflict upon Christians, and if they had the occasion, they would blaspheme not only the Christians but also the doctrine of God.

units.la: Ad verba Innocentii Tertii adducta in fine allegationis praescriptae, Dicunt quidam, quod exponenda sunt ad bonam sensum, ut scilicet potestas Papae sit restringenda, quantum ad ea, quae regulariter necessaria sunt regimini fidelium, (saluis praexpositio modo iuribus & libertatibus aliorum) vel etiam casualiter sit minime restringenda, quantum ad necessaria agenda, quando non est alius qui velit, & possit, & debeat quod necesse est fieri expedire. Quidam aliter exponunt dictum Innocentii, quod ex aliis verbis eius patenter habetur, quod secundum ipsum, Christus in Apostolica sede regalem constituit monarchatum, propter quod nulla est potestas regulariter extra ecclesiam, quod haereticum arbitrantur: quia contra Scripturam esse putant, ut superius est probatum. Dicunt igitur, quod Innocentius saepe dictus erraVit aperte, primo in hoc, quod dicit Apostolum ostendere huiusmodi plenitudinem non restringendam, cum Apostolus ipsam in pluribus locis voluerit esse restringendam, ut prius putatur esse probatum. Secundo dicunt cum errare, cum dicit quod intelliguntur minora subesse, quibus subiecta sunt maiora: quia hoc non est universaliter & absque omni exceptione verum, licet sit verum in multis. Nam episcopi regulariter subiecti sunt archiepiscopo suo: & tamen subditi episcoporum non sunt illi subiecti nisi in casibus. Saepe etiam maiora decent aliquos, quo minora non decent, teste Gregorio, 19. moralium, qui tractans ista verba Apostoli: Secularia iudicia, &c. dicit sic, Contemptibiles illi qui sunt in ecclesia, & nullis magnorum donorum virtutibus praediti, ipsi de terrenis negociis iudicent: Et post: Qui autem spiritualibus deputati sunt, profecto non debent secularibus negociis implicari: ut dum coguntur inferiora bona iudicare, non valeant bonis superioribus deservire. Ex quibus verbis conduditur, quod nequaquam regulariter, quibus subdita sunt maiora, eisdem subdita sint minora. Quod Apostolus innuit evidenter, cum dicit: Nemo militans Deo implicet se secularibus negociis: Et Petrus hoc etiam dicit aperte, ut habetur 11. quaest. 1. can. te quidem oportet, &c. sicut allegatum est supra. Nequaquam ergo ex hoc, quod Papa est iudex in spiritualibus, inferri potest quod habet regulariter secularia iudicare. Ex hoc tamen concludi potest, quod in casu, si non esset alius inferior gradus, qui non ex officio possit & velit iuste secularia iudicare, potest Papa se huiusmodi immiscere iudicio: quemadmodum unum membrum corporis naturalis, officium alterius membri ipso deficiente, vel non valente actum suum habere, si potest, assumit. Qui enim non potest pedibus ambulare, manibus conatur, & qui non potest manu cadente percutere, dentibus mordere conatur.
