units.tr: As for the words of Innocent III, cited at the end of the aforesaid allegation, some say they are to be explained in a good sense: namely, that the power of the Pope is to be restricted as regards those things which are ordinarily necessary for the governance of the faithful (saving the rights and liberties of others, as set out above), or even that it is by no means to be restricted, as regards necessary acts, when there is no one else who is willing, able and obliged to do what must needs be done. Others explain Innocent's saying differently, since it is plainly evident from other words of his that, according to him, Christ in the Apostolic see established a royal monarchy, on account of which there is no power ordinarily outside the Church. They consider this heretical, because they think it is contrary to Scripture, as has been proved above. They say, therefore, that Innocent, often mentioned, clearly erred. First, in this: that he says the Apostle shows such fullness is not to be restricted, when the Apostle wished it to be restricted in many places, as was thought proved earlier. Second, they say he erred when he says that the lesser things are understood to be subject to those to whom greater things are subject, because this is not universally and without any exception true, although it is true in many cases. For bishops are ordinarily subject to their archbishop, yet the subjects of bishops are not subject to him except in certain cases. Often, too, greater things befit some men which lesser things do not befit. Gregory testifies to this in the nineteenth book of the Moralia, where, treating those words of the Apostle, "secular judgments" and so on, he says: "Those who are in the Church, contemptible and endowed with none of the virtues of great gifts, let them judge about earthly business." And after: "But those who are assigned to spiritual things ought certainly not to be entangled in secular business, so that, while they are forced to judge lower goods, they may not be able to serve the higher goods." From these words it follows that by no means are those to whom greater things are subject regularly subject to lesser things as well. The Apostle evidently hints at this when he says: "No one serving God entangles himself in secular business." Peter also says this plainly, as is found in C. 11 q. 1 c. Te quidem oportet, as was alleged above. Therefore it cannot be inferred from the fact that the Pope is judge in spiritual matters that he regularly has to judge secular matters. From this, however, it can be concluded that in a case where there is no other lower rank which, by its office, can and rightly wishes to judge secular matters, the Pope may interpose himself in such a judgment. This is just as one member of the natural body takes up the office of another member when that member fails or is not able to perform its act, if it can. For he who cannot walk on his feet tries with his hands, and he who cannot strike with a falling hand tries to bite with his teeth.

units.la: CAP. XII. Respondet rationi quartae cap. secundo posita.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. Answers the fourth argument set out in chapter two.

units.la: AD quartam allegationem inductam capite secundo, quae quidem specialiter probare conatur, quod Papa auctoritate & potestate temporali praeminet aliis, quibuscunque potestatibus sive dominationibus, multipliciter respondetur. Vno modo, esto quod in veteri lege Pontificalis auctoritas praelata fuisset etiam in temporalibus dignitati regali; non tamen esset praeferenda in nova lege: quia auctoritas Pontificalis in nova lege spiritualior est, & magis a terrenis negociis elongata, quam fuerit auctoritas Pontificalis in veteri lege: quemadmodum lex nova magis est spiritualis, quam lex vetus. Sed praedicti videntur hanc rationem velle improbare dicentes, quod scripturae Veteris Testamenti, actus, & quaecunque opera euangelica imitantur. quare ad Roman. 15. unde sequitur, quod qualiter se habuit in Veteri Testamento rex ad Pontificem; sic se debeat habere rex in Novo Testamento ad Papam. Sed respondetur, quod illa allegatio haereticalis est, quia sequitur ex ipsa, quod circumcisionem, discretionem ciborum, & alia cerimonialia & iudicialia veteris legis deberet etiam imitari. Quia tunc sicut sacerdos veteris legis intendebat armis, & iudicium sanguinis exercebat: Ita deberet Papa in talibus occupari, quae haereticalia sunt. Nequaquam ergo actus & opera, quae fecerunt Patres in veteri lege, imitari tenentur: nisi quo ad moralia, ad quae omnes homines indifferenter obligari noscuntur. Cum autem allegatur Apostolus: Respondeo, Quod quaecunque scripta sunt, ad nostram, &c. non vt illa omnia ad litteram faciamus, sed vt per patientiam et consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus, & illa secundum spiritualem non carnalem intelligentiam impleamus.
units.tr: To the fourth argument put forward in chapter two, which tries especially to prove that the Pope surpasses all other powers or dominions in authority and temporal power, there are several replies. First, even granting that in the Old Law the priestly authority was set above the royal dignity even in temporal matters, it would not follow that it should be preferred in the New Law. The priestly authority of the New Law is more spiritual and further removed from earthly affairs than was the priestly authority of the Old Law, just as the New Law is more spiritual than the Old. Yet these opponents seem to want to reject this reasoning, saying that the Scriptures of the Old Testament, the acts and all the works of the Gospel imitate one another, and they cite Romans 15 for this. From this it follows that the king should now relate to the Pope in the New Testament as the king related to the high priest in the Old Testament. But the reply is that this argument is heretical, because it would follow from it that we ought also to imitate the circumcision, the distinction of foods, and the other ceremonial and judicial matters of the old law. For then, just as the priest of the Old Law engaged in arms and exercised judgment over blood, so the Pope ought to be occupied in such things, which are heretical. Therefore the acts and works which the Fathers performed under the Old Law are by no means bound to be imitated, except as to the moral matters, to which all men are known to be equally bound. As for the appeal to the Apostle, I reply: "Whatever things were written, were written for our instruction, &c." not so that we should do all those things literally, but so that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we may have hope, and fulfil them according to a spiritual and not a carnal understanding.

units.la: Secundo respondetur ad allegationem praedictam, quod in Veteri Testamento, sacerdotalis gradus non praeferebatur dignitati regali in temporalibus regulariter disponendis, & iurisdictione temporali regulariter exercenda: licet praelatus fuerit, quantum ad sacrificia Deo offerenda, & ea quae ad cultum divinum spectabant: per quem modum in noua lege auctoritas Pontificalis dignitati regali praefertur, non quoad iurisdictionem & regimen temporale. Isti enim nequaquam negant potestatem Pontificalem esse praeferendam omni seculari potestati: sed dicunt ipsam non esse praeferendam in temporalibus extra articulum necessitatis, quando laici potestatem sibi commissam rite & legitime ministrant. Cum vero acceperunt allegantes praedicti, quod Samuel cum esset summus Sacerdos & Pontifex in Israel, Saul de communi genere, regem instituit, & ipsum propter delictum regno deposuit: & Deus Dauid assumpsit in regem, multipliciter etiam errant contra sacram Scripturam, & eius, sit sic allegant, omnes videntur ignari. Primo, quia Samuel non erat summus Pontifex, nec sacerdos in Israel, sed Iudex tantummodo; imo etiam non fuit de genere Aaron: & per consequens, nec sacerdos, nec summus Pontifex, nec maior, vt colligitur ex primi Paralipom. capite sexto. Secundo, quod Samuel non constituit Saul regem tanquam pollens gradu & dignitate eminentiore, praesertim in temporalibus, quam sit dignitas regalis: sed tanquam diuino praecepto obediens, cui parere deberet etiam si esset infimus, nulla potestate puta ecclesiastica vel seculari praefulgens: quemadmodum vt habetur quarto Regum nono, quidam de filiis prophetarum ad mandatum Helisaei vnxit Iehu in regem Israel: & tamen, nec iste, nec ille, scil. Helisaeus propheta, maiori, praesertim in temporalibus, dignitate eminuit, quam sit dignitas regalis. Ex quo euidenter concluditur, quod per vnctionem haberi non potest, quod Imperator vel quicunque rex in Nouo Testamento sit inferior illo qui vngit. Et similiter ex hoc, quod Samuel solummodo vnctus fuerit in ducatu, qui est inferior dignitate regali: nec etiam, esto quod Samuel deposuisset de mandato Dei Saulem propter delictum, fuisset eo quantum ad publicam potestatem & iurisdictionem temporalem superior: quia non deposuisset eum tanquam superior quo ad regimen temporale, sed quo in hoc exercens & exequens mandatum & praeceptum Dei, qualiter rusticus de potestate Dei posset Imperatorem, imo Papam deponere, quamuis nulla alia potestas, neque in temporalibus neque in spiritualibus darctur eidem a Deo. Errant tertio allegantes praedicti, cum dicunt, quod Samuel Saulem propter delictum a regno deposuit. nam in libro Regum non legitur, quod Samuel deposuit Saulem: sed quod Deus eum deposuit: & quod hoc Samuel executus fuit & nunciauit Sauli, quamuis legitur, quod constituerit eum regem, cum dicit Dominus Samueli, vt legitur 1. Reg. 8. Audi vocem eorum & constitue super eos regem, & ipsum vnxit in Regem, de depositione enim leguntur haec verba 1. Regus 15. capitulum isti allegant, quae dicit Samuel ad Saul: Pro eo quod abiecisti sermonem Domini, abiecit te Dominus ne regnes. Et post Samuel ad Saul: & non reuertar tecum, quia proiecisti sermonem Domini: & proiecit te Dominus ne sis rex super Israel. & post: Scidit Dominus regnum Israel a te hodie. Et cap. 16. sic scribitur, dixit Dominus ad Samuelem: Vsque quo tu luges Saul, cum ego proieceram eum ne regnet super Israel. Ex quibus non habetur, quod Samuel deposuerit Saulem: sed quod nunciator fuit depositionis a Deo. Et ideo de ista depositione a Deo concludi non potest, quod Papa de plenitudine potestatis potest Imperatorem vel quemcunque alium regem ad libitum suum deponere, nisi in casu: & hoc quando propria officia debite exercere nollet vel non posset, & propterea ex iniquitatibus suis regno vel regali seu imperiali potestati inutilis esset, propter quod Zacharias Papa (de quo legitur 15. q. 6. c. alius) deposuisse dicitur regem Francorum quia deponentibus consensit vt dicit glossa. Quod autem adducunt de Ioiada sacerdote, qui, vt legitur 4. Regum 11. fecit & vnxit Ioas regem, non concluditur quod Ioiada fuerit superior rege, praesertim, quo ad iurisdictionem temporalem: quia saepe videtur in scripturis diuinis & aliis, quod aliqui fecerunt & constituerunt reges, qui tamen regibus superiores non fuerunt; imo erant subiecti constitutis ab eis. Nam filii Israel constituerunt Ieroboam regem, 3. Regum 16. vbi dicitur, fecit sibi regem omnis Israel: Et post: media pars populi sequebatur Thebni filium Gineth, vt constitueret eum regem, &c. & 4. Regum cap. 21. sic scribitur: Percussit autem populus ille omnes, qui coniuraverant contra regem Amon, & constituerunt sibi regem Iosiam filium eius pro eo. Hieron. etiam ad Euandrum, & habetur dist. 93. c. legimus, dico quod Imperatorem exercitus facit. Ex quibus & aliis innumeris colligitur, quod inferiores constituunt & faciunt regem, cui sunt subiecti. quare ex hoc, quod Ioiada vnxit & fecit Ioas regem, inferri non potest, quod Ioiada fuit, quoad iurisdictionem temporalium, eo superior. Nam & alii quam Ioiada fecerunt & constituerunt omnes regem, de quibus dicitur: fecerunt que regem & vnxerunt & plaudentes manu dixerunt: viuat rex. Nec valet si dicatur, quod Ioiada ostenditur esse ex hoc superior, quod occidit Athaliam, quae sibi vsurpauerat regnum.
units.tr: Second, I reply to the aforesaid argument that under the Old Testament the priestly rank was not preferred to royal dignity in the ordinary arrangement of temporal affairs and in the ordinary exercise of temporal jurisdiction, although the priest was set above the king as to the offering of sacrifices to God and the matters that pertained to divine worship. In this way, under the New Law, the priestly authority is preferred to royal dignity, but not as to jurisdiction and temporal government. For these men by no means deny that the papal power is to be preferred to every secular power; they say only that it is not to be preferred in temporal matters outside the case of necessity, when laymen duly and lawfully administer the power committed to them. But when the aforesaid opponents assert that Samuel, although he was the chief priest and high priest in Israel, appointed Saul, a man of the common people, as king, and deposed him from the kingdom for his sin, and that God took David up as king, they err in many ways against Holy Scripture, and all who cite them in this way seem ignorant. First, because Samuel was not the high priest or priest in Israel, but only a judge; indeed he was not even of the line of Aaron, and consequently neither priest, nor high priest, nor greater, as is gathered from 1 Chronicles chapter 6. Second, Samuel did not appoint Saul king as one who excelled in rank and a higher dignity, especially in temporal matters, than the royal dignity itself, but as one obeying a divine command, which he ought to obey even if he were the lowliest, shining with no power, ecclesiastical or secular. Just as we read in 4 Kings chapter 9 that one of the sons of the prophets, at the command of Elisha, anointed Jehu king over Israel, and yet neither the one nor the other, that is Elisha the prophet, stood out in a greater dignity, especially in temporal matters, than the royal dignity. From this it is plainly concluded that by anointing it cannot be established that the emperor or any king in the New Testament is inferior to the one who anoints him. And similarly, from the fact that Samuel was anointed only as a leader, which is inferior to royal dignity, nor even if Samuel had deposed Saul for his sin by God's command, would he have been superior to him in public power and temporal jurisdiction. For he would not have deposed him as a superior in temporal government, but as one carrying out and executing the command and precept of God. In the same way a peasant, by the power of God, might depose an emperor, indeed a Pope, although no other power, either in temporal or spiritual matters, had been given to him by God. Third, the aforesaid opponents err when they say that Samuel deposed Saul from the kingdom for his sin. For in the Book of Kings it is not read that Samuel deposed Saul, but that God deposed him, and that Samuel carried this out and announced it to Saul. Although it is read that he appointed him king, when the Lord said to Samuel, as we read in 1 Samuel 8: Hearken unto their voice and make them a king, and he anointed him king, the words about deposition are found in 1 Samuel chapter 15, which these opponents cite, where Samuel says to Saul: Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord hath rejected thee from being king. And afterwards Samuel says to Saul: I will not return with thee, for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. And later: The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day. And in chapter 16 it is written: The Lord said to Samuel, How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him from reigning over Israel. From these passages it does not follow that Samuel deposed Saul, but that he was the announcer of the deposition by God. Therefore from this deposition by God it cannot be concluded that the Pope, by the fullness of power, may depose the emperor or any other king at his pleasure, except in the case where a king would not or could not duly perform his proper office and, because of his iniquities, became useless to the kingdom or to the royal or imperial power. For this reason Pope Zacharias (of whom we read in Decretum 15, q. 6, c. alius) is said to have deposed the king of the Franks, because, as the gloss says, he consented to those who deposed him. As for what they adduce about the priest Jehoiada, who, as we read in 4 Kings 11, made and anointed Joash king, it does not follow that Jehoiada was superior to the king, especially as to temporal jurisdiction. For it often appears in the divine Scriptures and elsewhere that some made and appointed kings who were nevertheless not superior to them; indeed they were subject to those whom they had appointed. For the sons of Israel appointed Jeroboam king, 3 Kings 16, where it is said: All Israel made him king. And afterwards: Half the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, etc. And in 4 Kings chapter 21 it is written thus: The people of the land slew all those who had conspired against King Amon, and made Josiah his son king in his place. Jerome also, in his letter to Evander, and it is found in Distinctio 93, c. legimus, says that the army makes the emperor. From these and countless other examples it is gathered that inferiors appoint and make a king, to whom they are subject. Therefore from the fact that Jehoiada anointed and made Joash king, it cannot be inferred that Jehoiada was superior to him as to temporal jurisdiction. For others besides Jehoiada made and appointed a king, all of whom are described as having made him king, and anointed him, and clapping their hands said: Long live the king. Nor does it help if it is said that Jehoiada is shown to be superior in this respect, that he slew Athaliah, who had usurped the kingdom for herself.

units.la: Nam hoc non fecit in quantum superior rege: sed in quantum tutor, rector & institutor consiliarius vel vicarius regis, qui tunc, eo quod non esset nisi septem annorum, per seipsum regere non valebat. Quod vero dicitur de Alexandro, qui fecit reuerentiam Ioiadae sacerdoti, nullam apparentiam habere videtur, quia non fecit sibi reuerentiam tanquam superiori in temporalibus, sed quia sacerdos erat supremus, quemadmodum Imperatores & reges ac principes etiam spiritualibus sacerdotibus religiosis & secularibus reuerentiam in missis exhibent genu flectentes. {blurred}sestendo & osculando manus eorum: quos tamen superiores in temporalibus minime recognouerunt. Sic etiam Totila non recessit ab Italia ob preces Leonis Papæ, quia ipsum dominum suum in temporalibus reputabat: sed quia ipsum virum sanctum habebat: & ideo ipsum timebat offendere, vnde nonnulli mirantur, quod quicunque fideles literati per gentiles & ethnicos probare nituntur Papam etiam in temporalibus superiorem Imperatore: cum apud omnes ethnicos & gentiles, Imperatores & reges, qui non erant sacerdotes gentilium, semper se super sacerdotes reputauerunt: præsertim quo ad ea disponenda, quæ ad cultum Deorum suorum minime pertinebant & honorem: & tamen multi eorum modicam reuerentiam sacerdotibus exhibebant. Nam quidam eorum interdum in honorauerunt sacerdotes & templa & ritus eorum sacerdotii: sicut legitur de Pompeio, qui reuerentiam debitam templo Dei & sacerdoti non exhibuit: & ideo non immerito prosperitatem extunc non habuit consuetam.
units.tr: For he did this not as being superior to the king, but as the king's guardian, ruler, instructor, counsellor, or vicar, since at that time, being only seven years old, the king could not rule by himself. As for what is said of Alexander, who showed reverence to the priest Joiada, this seems to have no real force, because he did not show reverence to him as a superior in temporal affairs, but because the priest was supreme in sacred matters. In the same way, emperors, kings and princes also show reverence to priests, both religious and secular, at Mass by kneeling, stretching out their hands and kissing them, yet they did not acknowledge those priests as their superiors in temporal affairs. Likewise Totila did not withdraw from Italy because of the entreaties of Pope Leo, since he did not regard the Pope as his lord in temporal matters, but because he held him to be a holy man and therefore feared to offend him. This is why some are astonished that certain learned believers try to prove from the Gentiles and heathens that the Pope is superior to the Emperor even in temporal matters, when among all the heathen Gentiles the emperors and kings, who were not priests of the Gentiles, always reckoned themselves above the priests, especially in arranging those things which did not pertain to the worship and honour of their gods; and yet many of them showed only modest reverence to the priests. For some of them occasionally honoured priests, temples and the rites of their priesthood, as is read of Pompey, who did not show the due reverence to the temple of God and to the priest, and for that reason, not without good cause, he did not afterwards enjoy his usual prosperity.

units.la: Quod vero praedicti Constantinum, Iustinianum & Carolum Magnum in exemplum adducunt, contra eos militare videtur. Nam licet isti Imperatores devoti exiterunt non solum summis Pontificibus, sed etiam sacerdotibus & clericis vniuersis, nequaquam tamen se subiectos in temporalibus clero putabant: sed pro superioribus eis se gestabant. Et de Constantino quidem hoc expresse videtur, per istud sumptum ex gestis Siluestri Papæ, quod ponitur in decretis distinctione nonagesima sexta. cap. Constantinus. Ex quo videtur haberi patenter, quod nequaquam vt dicit; immo Imperator Constantinus nunquam potestatem, qua prius vtebatur, ecclesiæ resignauit; nec aliquam potestatem secularem aut temporalem, siue iura, siue res, à Siluestro recepit: sed aliquam potestatem & prædia sibi tribuit & concessit: cum vocabulum restringendum seu recipiendum aut æquipollens ibi non valeat reperiri: sed verbum tribuendum & æquivalens, quoad significationem ibidem sæpius inferatur. Vbi sic legitur: Constantinus Imperator quarto die sui baptismi priuilegium Romanæ ecclesiæ Pontifici contulit, vt in toto orbe Romano Pontifices vel sacerdotes (alias seculares) ita hunc (alias hanc) caput habeant sicut iudices regem, & ita tribuentes ei potestatem dignitatem & vigorem & honorificentiam imperialem (alias temporalem) atque determinate (alias decernentes) sancimus vt principatum teneat tam super quatuor sedes Alexandrinam, Antiochenam, Hierosolymitanam, Constantinopolitanam, quam etiam super omnes in vniuerso orbe terrarum Dei ecclesias. Et infra: Ecclesiis beatorum Apostolorum Petri & Pauli pro continuatione luminariorum possessionum prædia contulimus & rebus diuersis eas ditauimus. Et infra: Ecce tam palatium nostrum, quam Romanam vrbem, & omnes Italiæ siue Occidentalium regionum prouincias, loca, ciuitates, beatissimo Pontifici & Papæ Siluestro concedimus atque relinquimus: & ab eo & à successoribus eius per pragmaticum constitutum decreuimus disponenda: atque iuri sanctæ Romanæ ecclesiæ concedimus peragenda (alias permanenda.) Et infra: Haec omnia vero quæ per hanc imperialem iussionem sacram: & per alia diualia decreta statuimus & confirmauimus vsque in finem mundi illibata & inconcussa manere decreuimus. Quibus verbis (vt videtur) patenter habetur, quod Constantinus non intendebat quæcunque temporalia summo Pontifici, tanquam quæ ab eo prius possessa seu vsurpata fuerant quomodolibet resignare, aut tanquam ad summum Pontificem spectarent de iure restituere seu reddere: sed intendebat sibi illa, de quibus mentionem fecit, de nouo conferre, concedere, donare & tribuere. Ex quo infertur, quod Constantinus Papa & clericis, quibus ista temporalia conferebat, se superiorem in talibus reputauit. Quare si ita verba eiusdem Constantini legantur, vt videantur innuere, quod Constantinus se inferiorem Papa reputauit: de inferioritate in spiritualibus debet intelligi, ne sibiipsi contrarius reputetur, quod ipse insinuare videtur cum dicitur, vbi prius: Et Pontifex, qui per tempora ipsius sacrosanctæ ecclesiæ Romanæ extiterit, celsior & princeps cunctis sacerdotibus & totius mundi existat: & eius iudicio qua ad cultum Dei & fidem Christianorum vel vnitatem & stabilitatem procuranda fuerint, disponantur. Quibus verbis, per argumentum contrario sensu, videtur innuere, quod Papa pure temporalia omnia regulariter dispensare non debebat. Ex quo habetur, quod non habebat in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: As for the examples which these men bring forward, namely Constantine, Justinian and Charlemagne, these seem to tell against them. For although these emperors were devoted not only to the supreme Pontiffs but also to all priests and clergy, they nevertheless did not think themselves subject to the clergy in temporal matters, but conducted themselves as their superiors. Concerning Constantine this is clearly the case from what is taken from the acts of Pope Silvester, which is set down in the Decretum, distinction 96, chapter "Constantinus". From this it seems plainly to follow that he did not, as they say, resign to the Church the power he had previously exercised; rather, Emperor Constantine never handed over to Silvester any secular or temporal power, whether rights or property, but granted and bestowed certain power and estates upon him, since the word "restrict", "receive" or an equivalent cannot be found there, but the word "bestow" and its equivalent occur again and again in the same sense. There it is read thus: Emperor Constantine, on the fourth day after his baptism, conferred a privilege on the Pontiff of the Roman Church, so that throughout the Roman world the Pontiffs or priests (otherwise secular men) should have him as head just as judges have the king, and, bestowing on him power, dignity, vigour and imperial (otherwise temporal) honour, we decree and sanction (otherwise deciding) that he shall hold the primacy both over the four sees of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople, and also over all the churches of God in the whole world. And further on: To the churches of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, for the maintenance of their lights, we have conferred estates and enriched them with various properties. And further: Behold, we grant and leave to the most blessed Pontiff and Pope Silvester our palace as well as the city of Rome and all the provinces, places and cities of Italy and of the Western regions, and we have decreed that they be disposed of by him and his successors by a pragmatic constitution, and we grant that they be carried out by the right of the holy Roman Church (otherwise remain in force). And further: All these things which we have established and confirmed by this sacred imperial command and by other divine decrees, we have decreed shall remain unimpaired and unshaken until the end of the world. By these words (as it seems) it is plainly shown that Constantine did not intend to resign to the supreme Pontiff, as if they had previously been possessed or usurped by him in any way, all the temporal things, nor to restore or give back to the supreme Pontiff as things that rightly belonged to him; rather he intended to confer, grant, give and bestow anew upon him those things which he mentioned. From this it follows that Constantine, in conferring these temporal goods on the Pope and clergy, regarded himself as their superior in such matters. Therefore, if the words of Constantine are read in such a way as to seem to suggest that Constantine regarded himself as inferior to the Pope, this must be understood of inferiority in spiritual matters, lest he be thought to contradict himself, which he seems to hint at when he says, earlier in the same text: And the Pontiff who shall be in the time of the most holy Roman Church shall be higher and the prince of all priests and of the whole world, and by his judgment whatever shall be needful for the worship of God, the faith of Christians, or the procuring of unity and stability, shall be arranged. By these words, by argument from the contrary sense, he seems to imply that the Pope ought not ordinarily to dispose of all purely temporal matters. From this it is clear that he did not have the fullness of power in temporal matters.

units.la: De Iustiniano autem nonnulli mirantur, quod adducitur ab istis in exemplum, quibus videtur, quod isti allegatores leges ipsius Iustiniani non legerunt, cum nullus Imperator fuerit Christianus, nec ante Iustinianum nec post, qui ita expresse tam magnam superioritatem & iurisdictionem & potestatem super res & personas Papæ, & clericorum, etiam super illa, quæ Papa vendicat ex collatione siue resignatione Constantini, magis sibi attribuat, quam Iustinianus in legibus ab eo editis, & per vniuersum orbem tanquam seruandis & recipiendis ab omnibus promulgatis. Ad superiorem autem spectat aliis statuere legem, quanto tempore subiecti res alienas possessas ab eis possint præscribere & subiectis mandare vt eandem legem obseruent. Hoc autem facit Iustinianus circa Papam & alios & clericos & res Romanæ ecclesiæ, vel etiam ecclesiarum aliarum, vt habetur in autenti. vt ecclesia Romana centum annorum gaudeat præscriptione. collat. secunda. igitur Iustinianus reputauit se superiorem in temporalibus, etiam Papa, quo ad res Romanæ ecclesiæ deputatas. Item superioris est scire, quæ regulæ vim legis debeant obtinere: hoc autem fecit Iustinianus de regulis generalibus, qui in quatuor conciliis generalibus, quo ad condendum legem pro superiori se gessit. Item ad superiorem & super clericos potestatem habentem spectat statuere, ordinare, præcipere & iubere, quid iuris debet esse clericorum in ecclesia; à quibus immunes debent esse ecclesiæ: & à quibus etiam liberæ esse non debent, neres quæcunque ecclesiæ alienentur; quantas liceat vnicuique donationes conferre ecclesiis; in quibus locis clerici debeant ordinari; qui punire debeant clericos delinquentes; quas mulieres valeant clerici secum retinere, & quas norint sibi interdictas; quæ res clericorum decedentium non condito testamento debeant ecclesiis assignari, & quæ aliis; quod clerici non proficiscantur sine litteris ad vrbem alienam; Vbi sancta crux & reliquiæ martyrum debeant obseruari; quando episcopus & quando alius facultatem habeat exigendi ea, quæ pro redemptione captiuorum à testatoribus sunt relicta; qua pœna debeat puniri, qui ambitiose & pecuniæ interuenitu fuerit episcopalem sedem adeptus; coram quibus iudicibus debeant clerici litigare; qui episcopi habere debeant immunitatem tutelæ siue testamentariæ, siue legitimæ, siue datiuæ; qualiter puniri debeat clericus, qui ante diffinitiuam sententiam frustratoriæ dilationis causa ad appellationis auxilium conuolat; quod nec cogatur inuitus coram iudice litigare; quis debeat punire antistitem, iterantem sacramentum Baptismi. Hæc autem & plura alia, quæ ad habeatem iurisdictionem spectant. Iustinianus in suis legibus ordinauit, iussit & præcepit, primum habetur C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, & rebus & priuilegiis earum. l. non plures. Secundum in l. placet. eo tit. Tertium. e. tit. in lege ad instructiones. & l. iubemus: & l. neminem. Quartum. e. tit. l. iubemus. Quintum. e. tit. l. illud. Sextum habetur C. de episcop. & cleric. l. in ecclesiis. Septimum. eo tit. l. quicunque. Nonum. e. tit. l. si qua per calumniam. Octauum & Decimum. e. tit. l. decernimus. Vndecimum & Duodecimum. e. titulo l. nulli. Decimum tertium. eo. tit. l. si quenquam. Decimum quartum. e. titul. l. omnes. Decimumquintum. eo. tit. l. generaliter. Decimumsextum. C. de episcop. audi. si clericus. Decimumseptimum. e. tit. l. decernimus. Decimumoctauum. C. nec sacrum baptisma iteretur l. i. Iustinianus igitur leges condendo priuatas & alias multas de clericis & rebus eorum, ac eis libertatem & immunitates & priuilegia indulgendo indicauit aperte, quod se superiorem Papa & clericis reputauit.
units.tr: But some are amazed that these men cite Justinian as an example, since it seems they have not read Justinian's own laws. For no emperor, either before Justinian or after him, was a Christian who so expressly attributed to himself such great superiority, jurisdiction and power over the goods and persons of the Pope and clergy, even over those things which the Pope claims from the grant or resignation of Constantine, as Justinian did in the laws he issued and promulgated throughout the whole world to be observed and accepted by all. For it belongs to a superior to lay down a law as to how long subjects may acquire by prescription the property of others that has come into their possession, and to order subjects to observe the same law. Yet Justinian does this with regard to the Pope, others, clergy and the property of the Roman Church, or indeed of other churches, as is found in the Authentica "ut ecclesia Romana centum annorum gaudeat praescriptione", Collatio secunda. Therefore Justinian regarded himself as superior in temporal matters, even over the Pope, as regards the property assigned to the Roman Church. Again, it belongs to a superior to know which rules ought to have the force of law; and Justinian did this regarding the general rules, and in the four general councils he acted as one who lays down law. Again, it belongs to one who has power over the clergy to decree, ordain, command and order what the rights of clergy in the Church should be; from what burdens churches ought to be free, and from what they ought not to be free, nor should any church property be alienated; how great a gift each person may lawfully make to churches; in what places clergy ought to be ordained; who ought to punish delinquent clergy; what women clergy may keep with them and which they know to be forbidden to them; what goods of deceased clergy, who die without a written will, should be assigned to churches and what to others; that clergy should not set out for a foreign city without letters; where the holy cross and the relics of martyrs ought to be kept; when a bishop and when another has the power to exact what has been left by testators for the ransom of captives; by what penalty he who has obtained an episcopal see through ambition and by means of money should be punished; before what judges clergy ought to bring lawsuits; what immunity bishops ought to have from guardianship, whether testamentary, lawful or appointed; how a cleric who, to delay a final sentence, rushes to the aid of an appeal for the sake of frustrating delay should be punished; that he should not be compelled to plead before a judge against his will; who should punish a bishop who repeats the sacrament of baptism. Justinian, then, in his laws ordered, commanded and prescribed these and many other matters that pertain to jurisdiction. The first is found in C. "de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, et rebus et privilegiis earum", law "non plures". The second in law "placet", same title. The third, same title, in the law "ad instructiones", and laws "iubemus" and "neminem". The fourth, same title, law "iubemus". The fifth, same title, law "illud". The sixth is found in C. "de episcopis et clericis", law "in ecclesiis". The seventh, same title, law "quicunque". The ninth, same title, law "si qua per calumniam". The eighth and tenth, same title, law "decernimus". The eleventh and twelfth, same title, law "nulli". The thirteenth, same title, law "si quenquam". The fourteenth, same title, law "omnes". The fifteenth, same title, law "generaliter". The sixteenth, C. "de episcopis audientia", law "si clericus". The seventeenth, same title, law "decernimus". The eighteenth, C. "ne sacrum baptisma iteretur", law 1. Justinian, therefore, by enacting private laws and many others concerning clergy and their property, and by granting them liberties, immunities and privileges, has clearly shown that he regarded himself as superior to the Pope and the clergy.

units.la: De Carolo Magno etiam non legitur, quod se reputauit in temporalibus inferiorem supremo Pontifice, cuius signum est, quod reges Franciæ qui dicunt se successores ipsius, superiorem in temporalibus minime recognoscunt, extra, qui filii sunt legitimi. cap. per venerabilem. Nec obstat capitulum eiusdem Caroli, quod ponitur in decretis, distinctione decimanon. in memoriam, vbi dicit, quod licet vix ferendum ab illa sancta sede imponatur iugum, tamen ferendum est. Ex quibus verbis videtur haberi, quod idem Carolus inferiorem se supremo Pontifice reputauit: sed non arbitratur Carolus, quod apostolica sedes poterat sibi indicere vel aliquid magnum inuito in temporalibus imponere, sed in spiritualibus, quod in eodem capite insinuare videtur cum præmittit: In memoriam beati Petri honoremus sanctam Romanam ecclesiam & apostolicam sedem, vt qua nobis sacerdotalis iuris & dignitatis esse debeat & magistra rationis. Quibus verbis videtur, quod in spiritualibus apostolica sedes est iudex & magistra, ergo si argumentum a contrario sensu tenet, in temporalibus non est iudex & magistra.
units.tr: It is also not read of Charlemagne that he regarded himself as inferior to the supreme Pontiff in temporal matters. A sign of this is that the kings of France, who say they are his successors, by no means acknowledge any superior in temporal matters: extra, qui filii sunt legitimi. cap. per venerabilem. Nor does a chapter of the same Charles, which is placed in the Decretum, distinctione decimanon. in memoriam, stand in the way, where he says that although the yoke imposed by that holy see can hardly be borne, yet it must be borne. From these words it seems to be concluded that Charles likewise regarded himself as inferior to the supreme Pontiff. But Charles did not think that the apostolic see could impose on him any great burden against his will in temporal matters, but only in spiritual ones, which he seems to hint at in the same chapter when he begins: In memory of blessed Peter let us honour the holy Roman church and the apostolic see, which ought to be for us the mistress and teacher of priestly right and dignity. By these words it seems that in spiritual matters the apostolic see is judge and mistress; therefore, if the argument from the contrary sense holds, in temporal matters it is not judge and mistress.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Respondet quintæ rationi secundi capituli.
units.tr: Ad quintam rationem secundi capituli respondet. (Answer to the fifth argument of the second chapter.)

units.la: AD quintam allegationem adductam supra capitulo 2. quæ maiorem tractatum requireret, quam breuitas permittat istius opusculi, propter hoc quod plures allegationes, vt quibusdam appareret, affirmant errorem. Breuiter respondetur, quod deficit primo, eo quod Christus, in quantum erat homo mortalis, non erat rex in temporalibus, nec habebat regulariter talem plenitudinem potestatis: licet in quantum Deus habuit plenissimam potestatem: & in quantum homo, puta inquantum erat iustificator nouæ legis, in spiritualibus habuit plenitudinem potestatis. Secundo deficit allegatio supra scripta: quia non Petro, nec alicui supremo Pontifici concessit Christus omnem, quam habuit potestatem. Nam etiam inquantum homo & prælatus cunctorum sacramenta nouæ legis instituit: quam potestatem nulli concessit. Potest etiam contra statuta à seipso edita dispensare; quod tamen non potest Papa quicunque. Potest etiam absque culpa illa, quæ supererogationis sunt, sibi subiectis imponere; quæ Papa non potest regulariter, & ita Christus multa potest, quæ non potest Papa: quia sicut etiam inquantum homo fuit Dominus veteris legis, quod insinuare videtur cum dicit Matthæi duodecimo. Dominus est filius hominis etiam Sabbati. Item, etiam fuit Dominus nouæ legis, cuius tamen Dominus non est Papa. Falsum ergo accipit allegatio memorata, cum dicit, quod tota iurisdictio Christi concessa est vicario eius. Raro enim aut nunquam Dominus totam iurisdictionem committit vicario suo: immo nonnulla ex necessitate fit, quod vicarius est minor potestate, quam ille, cuius est vicarius. Et si dicatur, quod Christus faciendo Petrum vicarium suum, & committendo sibi potestatem suam, nihil excepit: ergo totam iurisdictionem sibi concessit, videtur quibusdam, quod hoc patenter exclusum est per prædicta verba, cum ostensum sit, quod Christus verbis & exemplis multa excepit. Cum igitur Papa non habet in temporalibus rebus potestatem, sequitur quod in ipsum potestas laicalis extrema minime cadit. Ad minorem respondetur; quod cum Imperator coronetur à supremo Pontifice, non ideo recipiens ensem in vagina eximit & vibrat eum, vt ostendat se in temporalibus inferiorem Papa: cū non teneatur, nisi sponte voluerit, ensem in vagina à Papa recipere, sicut nec ab ipso, nisi voluerit coronari tenetur, nam & multi fuerunt veri Imperatores, qui à summo pontifice minime coronati fuerunt: imo supremum pontificem omni honore reputauerunt indignum, (sed Imperatori, quando placuit coronari à papa, etiam placuit vaginam & gladium suscipere, & ipsum eximere & vibrare, ut monstraret se paratum, quando oporteret mediante materiali gladio facere iustitiæ complementum, & alios, præcipue Christianos, in iustitia defendere.
units.tr: To the fifth argument, adduced above in chapter 2, which would need a longer treatment than the brevity of this little work allows, since several arguments of this kind, as some think, assert error, a brief reply is given. First, it fails because Christ, insofar as he was a mortal man, was not king in temporal matters, and did not ordinarily have such a fullness of power. He had the most complete power as God, and as man, that is, insofar as he was the lawgiver of the new law, he had fullness of power in spiritual matters. Second, the argument written above fails, because Christ did not grant to Peter, or to any supreme Pontiff, all the power he himself had. For even as man and prelate of all, he instituted the sacraments of the new law, a power he granted to no one. He can also dispense from statutes he himself has enacted, which no Pope whatsoever can do. He can also impose on his subjects, without fault, things that belong to works of supererogation, which the Pope cannot ordinarily do. So Christ can do many things that the Pope cannot. Just as, even as man, he was Lord of the old law, which he seems to hint at when he says in Matthew 12, The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath, so too he was Lord of the new law, of which the Pope is not Lord. The argument cited above therefore takes as true something false when it says that the whole jurisdiction of Christ was granted to his vicar. For the Lord very rarely, or never, commits his whole jurisdiction to his vicar. Indeed, of necessity, the vicar is in some respects less powerful than the one whose vicar he is. And if it is said that Christ, in making Peter his vicar and committing his power to him, excepted nothing, and so granted him the whole jurisdiction, this seems to some to be plainly excluded by the words above, since it has been shown that Christ, by words and examples, made many exceptions. Since therefore the Pope has no power in temporal affairs, it follows that the extreme lay power does not fall under him at all. To the minor premise it is answered: when the Emperor is crowned by the supreme Pontiff, he does not, by receiving the sword in its scabbard, draw it out and brandish it to show that he is inferior to the Pope in temporal matters. He is not bound to receive the sword in its scabbard from the Pope, unless he freely wishes to, just as he is not bound to be crowned by him unless he wishes. For there were many true Emperors who were never crowned by the supreme Pontiff at all; indeed, they regarded the supreme Pontiff as unworthy of all honour. (But when it pleased the Emperor to be crowned by the Pope, it also pleased him to receive the scabbard and sword, and to draw it out and brandish it, to show that he was ready, when it was required, to accomplish the fulfilment of justice by means of the material sword, and to defend others, especially Christians, in justice.)

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: Respondet sexta rationi secundi capituli.
units.tr: He replies to the sixth argument of the second chapter.

units.la: AD sextam allegationem secundi ca. respondetur quod quantum ad multa sicut anima se habet ad corpus, ita spiritualia se habent ad temporalia: sed non quantum ad omnia, quia sicut anima est nobilior corpore, ita spiritualia temporalibus sunt digniora. Et sicut anima, quantum ad multa, regit corpus: ita temporalia in multis sunt secundum exigentiam spiritualium disponenda. Et sicut anima rationalis non habet plenitudinem potestatis super corpus, quia complures operationes habet corpus, quæ non sunt in potestate animæ rationalis: ita habens potestatem in spiritualibus non habet plenissimam potestatem in temporalibus, & ideo in papam, qui habet plenissimam potestatem in spiritualibus non cadit nec debet suprema potestas laicalis, licet in multis laici à prædicta potestate regi debeant ab habente supremam in spiritualibus potestatem.
units.tr: To the sixth allegation of the second chapter, the reply is this: as far as many things are concerned, spiritual matters stand to temporal matters as the soul stands to the body; but not as far as all things are concerned, because just as the soul is nobler than the body, so spiritual matters are more worthy than temporal ones. And just as the soul, in many respects, governs the body, so temporal matters, in many respects, are to be ordered according to the requirements of spiritual ones. And just as the rational soul does not have full power over the body, because the body has many operations which are not within the power of the rational soul, so one who has power in spiritual matters does not have the fullest power in temporal ones; and therefore the supreme lay power does not, and must not, fall to the pope, who has the fullest power in spiritual matters, although in many respects laymen ought to be ruled in that power by the one who holds supreme power in spiritual matters.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Respondet septimæ rationi secundi capituli.
units.tr: He replies to the seventh reason of the second chapter.

units.la: AD septimam respondetur, quod papa non est absolutus absq; omni exceptione quibuscunq; legibus positiuis: licet sit absolutus quibuscunq; mere positiuis à supremis pontificibus institutis: quia nulla illarum ligare potest ipsum, cum non sit imperiû paris in parem. Solutus est etiam legibus quibuscunq; generalium conciliorum, ac Imperatorum regum & quorumcunq; illorum, quæ conditæ erant super his quæ ad eius pertinent potestatem, & non super his quæ ad propria iura & libertates pertinent aliorum. Quæcunq; enim statuta essent à conciliis generalibus, & aliis quibuscunque, super his quæ in spiritualibus de necessitate facienda sunt pro regenda congregatione fidelium, papa dicitur solutus huiusmodi legibus positiuis; quia non tenetur eas seruare & posset abrogare, annullare easdem, & alias statuere, & in huiusmodi papa maior est generali concilio, imo toto residuo congregationis fidelium. Legibus autem institutis super his, quæ iura ac libertates & res respiciunt aliorum non est papa prædicto modo duplici solutus, nam cum de se non fuerint iniquæ, papa non potest abrogare eas; & ipsas nonnunquam, saltem conditionaliter, seruare tenetur. Si etiam Imperator vel rex aut princeps aut alius iura vel res proprias papæ tribuerit, certas leges & pacta rationabilia imponendo, easdem leges, si papa res illas aut iura voluerit recipere, seruare & tenere astringetur: eo quod quilibet in introductione rei suæ legem, quam vult, potest imponere: & tamen tradit rem ecclesiæ, 18. q. 2. Eleutherius, extra. de condi. appo. c. verum. Cum autem dicitur in allegatione prædicta, quod leges temporales non deignantur sacros canones imitari. Respondeo: q hoc non est de necessitate verum, nisi cum statueret leges super his, quæ ad pontificalem pertinent potestatem, super quibus si aliquid fuerit constitutum ab Imperatore vel alio, etiam quod papæ vel clericorum vel aliorum quorumcunque respiciat commodum vel fauorem, nullam continet firmitatem, nisi à summo pontifice fuerit approbatum. Aliæ autem leges absq; canonibus stabilem habent firmitatem: nec opus quod sacros canones imitentur: dum modo rationabiles sint & iustæ, si vero essent iniquæ possunt per iustos canones abrogari, & ideo licet papa casualiter habeat de legibus iudicare, regulariter tamen leges abrogare non potest, & ideo suprema potestas laicalis non cadit in papam, nec cadere debet: licet cadere posset, si per legem Dei iam non esset contrarium ordinatum.
units.tr: To the seventh, it is answered that the Pope is not absolute without any exception from positive laws of any kind, although he is absolute from all merely positive laws instituted by the supreme pontiffs, since none of those can bind him, for there is no power of an equal over an equal. He is also released from whatever laws have been enacted by general councils, by emperors, kings, or any others, which were framed concerning those matters that pertain to his power, and not concerning those matters that pertain to the rights and liberties of others. For whatever statutes have been passed by general councils or by any others concerning those things in spiritual matters which must of necessity be done for governing the congregation of the faithful, the Pope is said to be released from such positive laws, because he is not bound to observe them and can repeal, annul and enact others; and in such matters the Pope is greater than a general council, indeed than the whole remaining body of the faithful. But with laws instituted concerning those matters which concern the rights, liberties and property of others, the Pope is not released in the twofold manner just described; for since they are not unjust in themselves, the Pope cannot repeal them, and at times he is bound to observe them, at least conditionally. Likewise, if an emperor or king or prince or anyone else has granted rights or property to the Pope, imposing certain laws and reasonable conditions, the Pope will be bound to observe and keep those same laws, if he is willing to accept those things or rights; because whoever introduces his own property may impose whatever law he wishes; and yet he hands the property over to the Church, 18. q. 2. Eleutherius, extra. de condi. appo. c. verum. But when it is said in the aforesaid allegation that temporal laws do not deign to imitate the sacred canons, I answer: this is not necessarily true, except when they enact laws concerning those matters which pertain to the pontifical power; if anything has been established about these by an emperor or another, even if it concerns the advantage or favour of the Pope or of the clergy or of any others whatever, it has no firmness unless it has been approved by the supreme pontiff. Other laws, however, have stable firmness without the canons, nor is there any need that they imitate the sacred canons, provided only that they are reasonable and just; but if they were unjust, they can be abrogated by just canons. And therefore, although the Pope may in a particular case have to judge concerning laws, nevertheless as a rule he cannot repeal laws; and so the supreme lay power does not, and ought not, fall to the Pope, although it could fall to him if, by the law of God, it were not already ordained to the contrary.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: Respondet octaua rationi capit. 2.
units.tr: Answer to the eighth argument of chapter 2.

units.la: AD octauam allegationem adductam supra, c. 2. respondetur, quod non est necesse vniuersitatem fidelium sine omni exceptione in omnibus obedire papæ: sed necesse est sine omni exceptione obedire sibi in his quæ necessaria sunt congregationi fidelium, saluis iuribus & libertatibus aliorum. Et si quæratur, quis habet iudicare quæ sint illa necessaria congregationi fidelium? respondetur quod hoc iudicare per simplicem notitiam vel doctrinam spectat ad sapientes in lege diuina peritos, & in huiusmodi scientiis & rationis iudicio eminentiam habentes, quicunq; sint, siue subditi, siue prælati, siue seculares, siue religiosi, siue magistri, siue pauperes, siue diuites & potentes. Hoc autem auctoritatem (vt videtur) iudicare principaliter spectat ad supremum pontificem de consilio sapientum: qui si in iudicio errauerit, sapientes, imo quicunq; errare cognouerint, resistere obligantur pro loco & tempore & aliis circumstantiis: & quantum licet vnicuique pro gradu suo & statu suo, quia aliter debent ei resistere eruditi: aliter prælati: aliter reges: aliter principes: & aliter simplices & temporali potentia destituti.
units.tr: To the eighth argument adduced above, in chapter 2, the answer is this: it is not necessary that the whole body of the faithful obey the Pope in all things without any exception; but it is necessary to obey him without any exception in those things which are necessary for the assembly of the faithful, the rights and liberties of others being preserved. And if it be asked, who has the authority to judge what those necessary things are for the assembly of the faithful? The answer is that to judge this, by plain knowledge or teaching, belongs to the wise who are skilled in the divine law and eminent in such sciences and in the judgment of reason, whoever they may be: whether subjects, prelates, laymen, members of religious orders, teachers, poor men, or the rich and powerful. Yet the chief authority to judge this (as it seems) belongs principally to the supreme pontiff, with the counsel of the wise; and if he has erred in his judgment, the wise, or rather whoever perceives the error, are bound to resist him according to place, time and other circumstances, and as far as each person is permitted by his rank and station; for learned men must resist in one way, prelates in another, kings in another, princes in another, and ordinary folk who lack temporal power in yet another.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Respondens 9. & ultima rationi secundi capituli, ostendit quibus modis Papa habeat superiorem.
units.tr: Answering the ninth and last argument of the second chapter, he shows in what ways the Pope has a superior.

units.la: AD aliam allegationem ibidem inductam respondetur, quod in casu est licitum etiam de iudicio summi pontificis & potestate iudiciaiiter per sententiam iudicare; & ab eo etiam appellare. Quod enim de iudicio summi pontificis licet in casu iudicare, quidam tali ratione nituntur probare. Licet in casu iudicare de persona papæ: ergo & de iudicio eius. Antecedens patet per decretum Bonifacii martyris, quod ponitur di. 40. c. si papa. Unde tribus casibus tenetur papa humanum subire iudicium secundum quosdam: primo in casu hæresis, sicut dicitur per allegatum capitulum, sed refert in rei veritate an sit hæreticus, quia tunc ipso facto & iure, scilicet tam divino quam humano, est papatu priuatus & omni dignitate ecclesiastica destitutus. Quod enim sit divino iure priuatus papatu, quidam multis rationibus demonstrationis (ut eis videtur) ostendunt. Pro quibus omnibus unam auctoritatem & rationem sufficiat nunc tangere. Unde Apostolus in epistola ad Ti. 3. testari videtur cum dicit: hereticum hominem post primam & secundam correptionem devita: sciens quia subuersus est qui huiusmodi est & delinquit cum sit proprio iudicio condemnatus. Item ille qui non est de corpore ecclesiæ, non est verū caput ecclesiæ, licet putaretur ab omnibus, omnes enim tunc errarent, uniuersalis enim ecclesia, licet in his, quæ iuris sunt, præsertim diuini, errare non possit: tamen errare potest in his quæ facti sunt, sicut errat, quando papa in rei veritate est peccator, & tamen sanctus ab omnibus reputatur, papa igitur verus, si postea efficiatur hæreticus, diuino iure secundū q infidelis est, abscissus & resectus de corpore ecclesiæ, papatu priuatur, qui etiā iure canonico omni dignitate ecclesiastica est priuatus, nam omnes hæretici quibuscunque nominibus censentur, sunt à generali concilio (quod etiam supra papam hæreticum habet iudiciariam potestatem) damnati, extra de hereticis, c. excommunicamus. Cum igitur papa hæreticus non excipiatur à canone supradicto: nec nos ipsum debemus excipere, si autem papa est de hæresi primo solummodo diffamatus: propterea non est ipso facto aliqua dignitate priuatus. Si tamen facto conuincitur, & in eum fertur sententia, si non appellat, in rem iudicatam transire videtur. Si quæreret aliquis coram quo iudice posset vel debeat papa ab hæresi conuinci vel accusari: huic respondent quidam dicentes, quod papa coram dicecesano suo, in cuius dicecesi moratur, potest de hæresi accusari: cum papæ hæretico nullum priuilegium speciale ultra alios episcopos legatur in iure concessum: & aliquis sortitur forum ratione delicti, sicut alii episcopi, quæ inueniuntur hæretici in dicecesi alicuius episcopi, iudicari possent ab episcopo, quamuis non solenniter de gradari: ita & papa si efficiatur hæreticus, præsertim notorius, si moratur in Romana dicecesi, potest ab eo iudicari, q si episcopus, in cuius dicecesi manet, aut non vult aut non potest audire accusatores papæ hæretici: tunc alii episcopi fidei zelo accensi ipsos audire debent, quod exemplo quidam probare conantur, nam cum beatus Marcellus, in papatu idololatriam notorie commisisset: & ideo merito non conuictus, sed suspectus de hæresi haberetur: conuenerunt episcopi, ut habetur di. 21. nunc autem, ad inquirendum de ipso: quem quia non inuenerunt hæreticum, sed solummodo idolatram, & correctum, ipsum iudicare nolebant, nequaquam autem inquisitionem fecisset huiusmodi, nisi superiores ipso se putassent, si coram ipsis conuictus fuisset de hæresi, quare in hoc casu episcopi super papam hæreticum obtinent potestatem. Si autem episcopi vel noluerint vel nequiuerint papam hæreticum iudicare, alii catholici, maxime Imperator, si catholicus fuerit, ipsum iudicare valebit, nam no. gloss. di. 18. super c. de concilii. vbicunque deficit ecclesiastica potestas, semper recurritur ad brachium seculare: quia quicunque canones, qui inferiores sunt iure naturali & diuino, sonantes quod papa eo quod clericus vel episcopus nequiuerit coram seculari iudice conueniri, exponendi sunt per epibatam hoc casu: ut quia sicut habetur, ff. de legi. l. non possunt. Legumlatores non possunt omnes articulos prævidere: & per consequens omnes casus non possunt comprehendi sigillatim in legibus, videtur ergo iuxta naturalem æquitatem ratione fultam & literis sacris: quod nequaquam debent intelligi de papa hæretico, quando per impositam malitiam vel negligentiā damnabilem constat eum ecclesiasticam vsurpare potestatem, in hoc enim casu non debet se defendere per eam, unde sicut habetur in Gloss. 11. q. 4c. præsul. non requiruntur tot testes contra papā, quot requiruntur contra episcopos & cardinales Romanæ ecclesiæ: imo duo sufficiunt: & in hoc est deterioris conditionis: quia ipse magnus sine comparatione aliorum creatus est: & ideo sine spe venia condemnatus est vt diabolus: vt dicitur de pæn. di. 2. circa princi. hoc Gloss. Sic in casu hæresis propter magnitudinem periculi, q imminet vniuersali ecclesiæ, si papa efficiatur hæreticus: vtpote qui propter auctoritate & potestate tam spirituales quam temporales, quibus alios putatur excellere, plurimos ad suam hæresim & nequitiam trahere valeret, rationis igitur est vt papa in hoc potius deterioris quam melioris conditionis existat: vt specialissime de illo Epiotes canones dirigendo dicat: quod de ipso canones in hoc casu non debent intelligi: quia canonum conditores si de hoc casu cogitassent & ipsum timuissent venturum esse, ipsum excepissent omnino. Nec mirum, quia quemadmodum (ut habetur extra de electi. c. licet) in Romana ecclesia aliquid statuitur, quia in multis casibus non poterit ad superiorem recursus haberi: sic circa papam hæreticum, quia vltra omnes nocere potest toti congregationi fidelium, non irrationabiliter statuetur aliquid speciale cum aliquis papali dignitate præditus in prauitatem hæreticam laberetur, quia vt habetur extra de electione. c. vbi. li. 6. vbi periculum intenditur ibi proculdubio cautius est consulendum, sicut & in magnis rebus est diligenter inquisitio & per dominos prouisio facienda l.4.2.c. nuper. Secundo tenetur papa humanum subire iudicium, quandocunq; crimen eius est notorium; & inde scandalizaretur ecclesia, & ipse sit incorrigibilis, vt dicit Gloss. dist. 40. super papa. Si quaereret aliquis coram quo iudice posset papa accusari in hoc casu, respondent quidam quod propter reuerentiam officii, quo fungitur, est ipso facto exhortandus primo exemplo Leonis papae de quo habentur 2. q. 1. nos, vt alicui viro sapienti & prouido neq; aliis neq; sibi suspecto se submittat. Si autem noluerit, ex quo eius crimen notorium est, non opus adhibere testem, sed dicendum est ecclesiae: & primo quidem videtur dicendum ecclesia, id est congregationi Romanorum, quorum est quodammodo proprius episcopus, vt arguatur coram ipsis, qui possunt facilius convenire ad iudicandum. Si autem Romani noluerint aut nequiuerint iudicare ipsum, tunc potestas iudicandi devolvitur ad quemcunque catholicum, qui tanta sit praeditus potestate, vt per temporale potentiam ipsum valeat coercere, praesertim si papae crimen vergit in periculum congregationis fidelium, quod multis rationibus fundatis in legibus tam diuinis, quam humanis probare conantur, quas duxi ad praesens abbreviationis gratia supprimendas. Tertio vt dicunt quidam tenetur subire humanum iudicium, si res aut iura aliorum inuadit aut detinet minus bene. Et si quaeratur ab eis, coram quo in hoc casu respondere tenetur? respondetur dicendo, quia aut committit iniuriam in eum qui superiorem non habet in temporalibus, sicut Imperatores: aut in eum, qui habet superiorem. Si primo modo, tenetur se submittere alicuius iudicio neutri parti suspecti, aut eligere arbitros de voluntate alterius partis, qui inter eos potestatem habeant iudicandi. Si autem neutrum facere voluerit, Imperator propter culpam papae potest vel ipsum iudicare vel delegare alteri qui super ipsum in hoc casu habeat potestatem. Si vero inuadit aut detinet rem vel ius superiorem habentis: conueniri potest coram superiore ipso. Haec & plura alia, quae tangunt illam materiam nonnulli multis modis nituntur ostendere, quae omnia gratia breuitatis pertranseo. Ex hoc patet, quod papa in casibus supra dictis tenetur humanum subire iudicium, quod moliuntur ostendere, quia in casu licet appellare a papa & agente sua pro papa: & extra iudicium, prouocare ipsum ad causam ne aliquid faciat in praeiudicium appellantis vel prouocantis, quia ab omni illo, qui humanum tenetur subire iudicium, licet appellare tam a sententia, si male iudicauerit, quam a grauamine & praeterito & futuro, siue appellans siue prouocans reputet ipsum iudicem siue reputet ipsum non iudicem. Nam omnis oppressus, vel probabiliter opprimi metuens, ab illo appellare potest in omni casu, in quo accusari potest, cum appellatio sit oppressorum releuamen, extra de app. cum spirituali, cum ergo in tribus casibus suprascriptis papa valeat accusari: sequitur quod in ipsis est licitum appellare ab ipso, dicunt ergo isti, quod si papa factus haereticus gerat se pro papa, ab omni sententia, quam tulerit in omni causa & quocunq; grauamine quod intulerit vel comminatus fuerit, licet omni homini appellare, cuius interest ranquam a non iudice & nullam habente ecclesiasticam potestatem omnino: quia omnis haereticus quantumcunq; occultus iure diuino est omni potestate ecclesiae priuatus; licet non esset iure eodem priuatus dignitate seculari, si q̄ haberet: quia ecclesiastica dignitate nemo potest habere, nisi saltem sit de numero congregationis fidelium, seculare tamen dignitate supremam potest in infidelis habere, sicut de facto ille vere habuit tempore Christi vel Apostolorum, & hinc est, q̄ de iure diuino potest quilibet cuius interest in omni causa appellare a papa, si efficiatur haereticus: sed non oportet propter hoc iure diuino appellare, si Imperator aut rex efficiatur haereticus, ab ipso, tanq̄ a non iudice seculari, licet secundum quosdam hoc fiat iure humano canonico, non enim haeretici ipso facto priuantur iure diuino rebus temporalibus communibus, q̄ data sunt communitati fidelium: vt sunt omnia bona & iura temporalia, q̄ ecclesiastica ab ecclesia, non q̄ est a papa, appellantur, denominantur enim ecclesiastica ab ecclesia, non q̄ est papa, aut congregatio clericorum: sed ab ecclesia, quae est congregatio fidelium, q̄ clericos & laicos, & viros, & mulieres comprehendit. Illa enim ecclesia post Deum primo & principaliter est domina omnium bonorum & iurium temporalium ecclesiasticorum: nisi aliqui concedentes bona sua & iura aperte expresserint: vel verisimile sit eos voluisse bona illa & iura alicui personae vel collegio ecclesiastico appropriari debere, nam in concessione rerum suarum & iurium possunt laicique voluerint pacta & conditiones imponere, quae personis recipientibus congruant: & non sunt iuribus, ad quae seruanda tenentur dantes & recipientes, approbata. In causa autem fidei licet cuilibet catholico a papa haeretico appellare: quia eius interest: quia causa fidei omnes tangit & ad omnes omnino pertinet Christianos, dist. 96. c. vlt. nam licet in hoc casu non sit simpliciter necesse appellare a papa haeretico: etiā si contra dignitatem ecclesiasticā & diffinitiuā veritate, pferat sententiam: quia omnia sententia talis eo q̄ esset contra ius diuinū, nulla esset ipso facto: licet non esset appellatione suspensa: ideo in hoc casu sufficeret papa haereticum accusare, ideo si non reperiretur iudex: maxime qui volentem accusare vellet vel auderet audire: sufficeret coram quocunq; verbo vel scripto papa esse haereticū putare: causam vel causas, quare esset haereticus allegando: contra quē tamen opari deberet huiusmodi publicatio de iure diuino & naturali: ad q̄ obligantur oēs catholici, quantū in quacunq; alia causa contra quemcunq; & a quocunq; iudice appellare. Huiusmodi enim publicationi in fauore fidei Christianæ & catholicæ oēs catholicæ in tantū quod appellatione deferre deberent & publice nisi de friuola publicatione conuiceretur, legitime cōuincent sē vere vel friuole, p papa & oēs publicātes vel cōplices eī defendere tenerentur de necessitate salutis & cōgruo statui ipsoq̄ cuiuslibet. Verumtamē dicunt isti, q̄ in hoc casu, propter iuris diuini & humani ignaros solennitas appellationis nō obesset, sed posset valeret, ampliū dicūt isti, q̄ in secundo casu, sc. quādo crime papę quā cunq; esset notoriū & de ipso scādalizaretur ecclesia & esset incorrigibilis, sufficeret cuilibet accusare ipsū, nisi esset tale crime, ex quo aliqs grauari timeret: & sic p talis extra iudicū à futuro grauamine appellare: nisi aliqs faceret in preiudicū eī, in aliis et casib ad hunc articulum spectantibus appellare licet, quos nunc exprimere non intendo, in hoc etiam casu secundum istos cum si papa inuaderet vel detineret iniuste res vel iura aliquorum, quandoque licet appellari ipsum & quandoq; appellare ab ipso: scilicet de hoc superseedendum est ad praesens, vbi praedicta itaque & ipsa contingentia diffinitiue isti probare conantur, patet secundum eos, quia in casu licet, imo regulariter licitum est, & de persona propria papae & de eius iudicio iudicare: & ab ipso etiam appellare, & ideo ex his probari non potest quod potestas laicalis suprema cadat in ipsum de facto vel de iure diuino, ad omnes autem canones, qui in contrarium possunt adduci, dicunt quod canones veri, quales sunt canones antiquorum patrum, licet nonnullas decretales quorundam posteriorum haereticales existimant, debent intelligi, quod regulariter in his, quae spectant ad supremum pontificem, de cuius iudicio iudicare non licet: nec regulariter licet appellare ab ipso, scilicet casualiter tantum: iudicari tamen regulariter licet, nam cuilibet iudicare licet de manifestis eius criminibus quibuscunque, quae bene fieri minime possunt, non quidem iudicialem sententiam proferendo; sed ipsa cordialiter detestando & nullatenus excusando; & multo minus illicite defendendo, ad hoc allegari potest Beda extra, de reg. iur. c. estote, & Hieron. ii. q. 3. cap. si quis dixerit, & c. si quis hominem, & gloss. di. 15. super c. nos non.
units.tr: To the other argument brought forward there, the reply is that in some cases it is also lawful to judge, by sentence and judicial power, even the judgment of the supreme pontiff, and to appeal from him. Some try to prove that it is lawful in certain cases to judge the judgment of the Pope by the following reasoning: it is lawful in certain cases to judge the person of the Pope, therefore also his judgment. The antecedent is clear from the decree of Boniface the martyr, which is found in di. 40. c. si papa. According to some, the Pope is bound to submit to human judgment in three cases. First, in the case of heresy, as the cited chapter says; but whether he is in truth a heretic is a matter to be decided, because then, by the very fact and by right, both divine and human, he is deprived of the papacy and stripped of all ecclesiastical dignity. Some, by many demonstrative arguments (as it seems to them), show that he is deprived of the papacy by divine right. Of all these arguments it is enough now to touch on one authority and one reason. Thus the Apostle seems to testify in his epistle ad Ti. 3. when he says: Avoid a heretical man after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a man is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment. Likewise, one who is not of the body of the Church is not the true head of the Church, even though he is thought to be so by all; for then all would be in error, since the universal Church, although it cannot err in matters of law, especially divine law, can err in matters of fact, as it errs when the Pope is in truth a sinner and yet is regarded by all as holy. Therefore, if the Pope, being a true pope, afterwards becomes a heretic, then by divine right, insofar as he is an unbeliever, he is cut off and removed from the body of the Church and deprived of the papacy. By canon law too he is deprived of all ecclesiastical dignity, for all heretics, under whatever names they are called, are condemned by a general council (which also has judicial power over a heretical pope), extra de hereticis, c. excommunicamus. Since, then, a heretical pope is not excepted from the canon cited above, neither should we except him. But if the Pope has merely been publicly reported as a heretic, he is not thereby deprived of any dignity; yet if he is convicted in fact and sentence is passed against him, and he does not appeal, he seems to pass into a judged matter. If anyone asked before what judge the Pope could or should be convicted or accused of heresy, some answer that the Pope may be accused of heresy before his own diocesan in whose diocese he dwells, since no special privilege beyond other bishops is granted to a heretical pope in law, and anyone has a forum by reason of a crime. Just as heretics found in the diocese of some bishop could be judged by that bishop, though not solemnly deposed, so also the Pope, if he becomes a heretic, especially a notorious one, if he dwells in the Roman diocese, can be judged by that bishop. But if the bishop in whose diocese he dwells either does not wish or is unable to hear the accusers of the heretical pope, then the other bishops, kindled with zeal for the faith, ought to hear them. Some try to prove this by example: when blessed Marcellus had notoriously committed idolatry while pope, and was therefore rightly regarded not as convicted but as suspected of heresy, the bishops assembled, as is recorded in di. 21. nunc autem, to inquire into him. Since they did not find him a heretic, but only an idolater, and one who had been corrected, they were unwilling to judge him. Yet they would never have made such an inquiry unless they had considered themselves his superiors, had he been convicted of heresy before them. Therefore in this case bishops have power over a heretical pope. But if the bishops either will not or cannot judge a heretical pope, other Catholics, especially the Emperor, if he is a Catholic, will be able to judge him. For the gloss di. 18. super c. de concilii notes: wherever ecclesiastical power fails, recourse is always had to the secular arm. For the canons which are inferior to natural and divine law, and which seem to say that the Pope cannot be brought before a secular judge because he is a cleric or bishop, must be explained in this case by equity. For, as is held in ff. de legi. l. non possunt, legislators cannot foresee all the articles, and consequently all cases cannot be individually comprehended in laws. It therefore seems, according to natural equity grounded in reason and in the sacred writings, that such canons ought by no means to be understood of a heretical pope, when it is clear, through wicked obstinacy or damnable negligence, that he is usurping ecclesiastical power. For in this case he ought not to defend himself by that power. Hence, as is held in the gloss on Gloss. 11. q. 4c. præsul. Not so many witnesses are required against the Pope as are required against the bishops and cardinals of the Roman Church; indeed two suffice; and in this he is of worse condition, because he was created great beyond comparison with the others, and therefore was condemned without hope of pardon, like the devil, as is said in de pæn. di. 2. circa princi. This is the gloss. Thus in the case of heresy, on account of the greatness of the danger that threatens the universal Church if the Pope becomes a heretic (for he, by the authority and power both spiritual and temporal with which he is thought to excel others, could draw very many to his heresy and wickedness), it is reasonable that the Pope should be in a worse rather than a better condition in this matter. This is why Epiotes, in directing the canons, says especially of him that the canons ought not to be understood of him in this case, because the framers of the canons, if they had thought of this case and feared that it would come to pass, would have excepted him altogether. Nor is this surprising, for just as (as is held in extra de electi. c. licet) something is laid down in the Roman Church because in many cases recourse cannot be had to a superior, so concerning a heretical pope, who can harm the whole congregation of the faithful more than anyone, it is not unreasonable that something special be laid down when a man endowed with papal dignity falls into heretical depravity. For, as is held in extra de electione. c. vbi. li. 6. where danger threatens, there beyond doubt greater caution must be taken; and as in great matters diligent inquiry and provision must be made by the lords, l.4.2.c. nuper. Second, the Pope is bound to submit to human judgment whenever his crime is notorious, and the Church is thereby scandalized, and he is incorrigible, as the gloss dist. 40. super papa says. If anyone asked before what judge the Pope could be accused in this case, some answer that, out of reverence for the office he holds, he is by the very fact to be urged, following the example of Pope Leo, recorded in 2. q. 1. nos, to submit himself to some wise and prudent man, suspect neither to others nor to himself. But if he is unwilling, since his crime is notorious, there is no need to bring in a witness, but the matter must be declared to the Church, that is the congregation of the Romans, of whom the bishop is in some sense the proper bishop, so that the case may be argued before them, since they can more easily assemble to judge. But if the Romans are unwilling or unable to judge him, then the power of judging devolves upon any Catholic who is endowed with such power that he can restrain the Pope by temporal power, especially if the Pope's crime tends to the danger of the congregation of the faithful. They try to prove this by many arguments grounded in laws both divine and human, which I have for the present chosen to omit for the sake of brevity. Third, some say, the Pope is bound to submit to human judgment if he invades or unjustly holds the goods or rights of others. And if they are asked before whom in this case he is bound to answer, the answer is given by saying that either he commits the injury against one who has no superior in temporal matters, such as the Emperors, or against one who has a superior. In the first case, he is bound to submit himself to the judgment of someone suspect to neither party, or to choose arbiters by the will of the other party, who may have the power of judging between them. But if he is unwilling to do either, the Emperor, on account of the Pope's fault, may either judge him or delegate to another who has power over him in this case. But if he invades or holds a thing or right belonging to one who has a superior, he may be sued before that superior himself. These and many other things that touch this matter some labour to show in many ways, all of which I pass over for the sake of brevity. From this it is clear that in the cases stated above the Pope is bound to submit to human judgment, which they strive to show. For in such a case it is lawful to appeal from the Pope, and to summon him to the cause outside the judgment, so that he does nothing to the prejudice of the appellant or the summoner; for from every person who is bound to submit to human judgment, one may appeal, both from a sentence if he has judged badly, and from a grievance, both past and future, whether the appellant or summoner regards him as judge or does not regard him as judge. For every oppressed person, or one who fears being probably oppressed, may appeal from him in every case in which he can be accused, since appeal is the relief of the oppressed, extra de app. cum spirituali. Therefore, since in the three cases written above the Pope can be accused, it follows that in them it is lawful to appeal from him. These men therefore say that if a Pope who has become a heretic acts as Pope, then from every sentence he passes in any cause, and from every grievance he inflicts or threatens, it is lawful for any man whose interest is involved to appeal, as from one who is not a judge and has no ecclesiastical power at all, because every heretic, however hidden, is by divine right deprived of all power of the Church. Yet he would not on that account be deprived of secular dignity, if he had any, by the same law; for no one can have ecclesiastical dignity unless he is at least of the number of the congregation of the faithful, whereas an unbeliever can hold supreme secular dignity, as in fact that man truly did in the time of Christ or the Apostles. Hence it is that by divine right anyone whose interest is involved may in every cause appeal from the Pope, if he becomes a heretic. But it is not necessary on this account to appeal by divine right from an Emperor or king if he becomes a heretic, as from one who is not a secular judge. Although some hold that this is done by human canon law, heretics are not by the very fact deprived by divine right of the common temporal goods which have been given to the community of the faithful, such as all the goods and temporal rights which are called ecclesiastical, not from the Pope, but from the Church. They are called ecclesiastical not from the Church as the Pope or as the congregation of clerics, but from the Church, which is the congregation of the faithful, comprising clerics and laymen, men and women. For that Church, after God, is first and principally the lady of all ecclesiastical goods and temporal rights, unless some who grant their goods and rights have expressly stated otherwise, or it is probable that they wished those goods and rights to belong to some person or ecclesiastical college.
