For in granting their possessions and rights, laymen may, if they wish, impose agreements and conditions suited to the persons who receive them; and these are not approved as rights which the givers and receivers are bound to observe. In a matter of faith, however, any Catholic may appeal from a heretical pope, because his interest is involved, since a matter of faith touches all and pertains altogether to all Christians, dist. 96. c. vlt. For although in this case it is not simply necessary to appeal from a heretical pope, even if he pronounces sentence against the ecclesiastical dignity and against the defining truth, since any such sentence, being contrary to divine law, would be null by the very fact, though it would not be suspended by appeal, therefore in this case it would be enough to accuse the heretical pope. Thus, if no judge could be found, especially one who would or dared to hear the accuser who wished to accuse, it would be enough, before anyone, by word or writing, to hold that the Pope is a heretic, by alleging the cause or causes why he is heretical. Against him such a publication ought to be made by divine and natural right, to which all Catholics are bound, as in any other cause they are bound to appeal against anyone and from any judge. For all Catholics ought, in favour of the Christian and Catholic faith, to bring such a publication to appeal and to make it publicly, unless they were convicted of a frivolous publication; and if they prove legitimately, truly or frivolously, the Pope and all who publish or are accomplices of it would be bound to defend them by necessity of salvation, according to the proper state of each. Nevertheless these men say that in this case the solemnity of appeal would not be an obstacle, on account of those ignorant of divine and human law, but would be valid. Moreover, these men say that in the second case, namely when the crime of the Pope is notorious, the Church is scandalized by him, and he is incorrigible, it would be enough for anyone to accuse him, unless it were such a crime that someone feared to be harmed by it; and thus, outside judgment, one may appeal against a future grievance, unless someone acted to his prejudice. In other cases relating to this article, which I do not now intend to set out, it is lawful to appeal. In this case too, according to them, if the Pope unjustly invades or holds the goods or rights of some, it is sometimes lawful to appeal against him and sometimes to appeal from him. But this must be deferred for the present. Where these men try to prove definitively the aforesaid points and that very contingency, it appears, according to them, that in the case it is lawful, indeed ordinarily lawful, both to judge the person of the Pope himself and his judgment, and also to appeal from him. Therefore it cannot be proved from these points that supreme lay power falls upon him, either in fact or by divine right. As to all the canons which can be adduced to the contrary, they say that the true canons, such as the canons of the ancient Fathers, though some of the decretals of later men they consider heretical, must be understood as follows: in matters that concern the supreme pontiff, on whose judgment it is not lawful to judge, nor ordinarily lawful to appeal from him, that is, only in a casual way; yet it is ordinarily lawful to judge him. For it is lawful for anyone to judge his manifest crimes of whatever kind, which by no means can be done well, not indeed by pronouncing a judicial sentence, but by detesting them from the heart and in no way excusing them; and still less by defending them unlawfully. For this, Bede may be cited extra, de reg. iur. c. estote, and Jerome ii. q. 3. cap. si quis dixerit, & c. si quis hominem, & gloss. di. 15. super c. nos non.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Ostendit quomodo secunda opinio respondet argumentis contra se factis capit. primo huius prima quaestionis.
units.tr: Shows how the second opinion answers the arguments brought against it, in the first part of the first question.

units.la: VIso quomodo opinio 3. ad ea quae supra primo & secundo capitulis adducta sunt, contra ipsam nititur resurgere & respondere: videdum est quomodo opinio secunda ad illa quae adducuntur contra ipsam, i. 2. 3. & 4. c. valeat respondere. Ad primum itaque quod adductum est, c. 1. responderi potest, quod potestas spiritualis suprema dupliciter accipi potest, vno modo potest accipi pro tota potestate, quae a supremo spirituali concessa est, id est a Christo: & sic secundum ipsos potestas spiritualis suprema & potestas laicalis suprema ad rem ex opposito minime diuiduntur: scilicet potestas laicalis suprema, quantum ad rem, est pars potestatis spiritualis supremae: ita quod potestas respectu temporalium non est simpliciter suprema: quia illa potestas, quae est in Imperatore, est minor illa quae est in papa: & est quidam effectus spiritualis potestatis primo modo dicto. Aliter accipi potest potestas spiritualis suprema pro potestate solummodo, quae respicit spiritualia & non temporalia: & potestas laicalis suprema pro potestate quae solummodo respicit temporalia & non spiritualia: & sic potestas spiritualis suprema & potestas laicalis suprema, hoc est potestas suprema solummodo respicientes temporalia, & non spiritualia, aliquo modo diuiduntur ex opposito: quae tamen possunt cadere in eandem personam: secundum quod declaratum existit per opinionem secundam supra c. 2. Ad secundam dicitur quod istae duae potestates non constituunt duo capita duorum corporum diuersorum: sed vnum habens duplicem potestatem praedictam. Ad tertium dicitur, quod papatus non dominationem includit, sed excludit dominationem tyrannicam & iniustam, de qua loquitur beatus Petrus epistola sua prim. c. 5. Ad quartum dicitur, quod fungens potestate laicali suprema praecise & non potestate spirituali, est filius ecclesiae, si est fidelis & ideo imperator, qui pollet solummodo potestate laicali, si est fidelis, est filius ecclesiae, sed pollens potestate suprema super temporalia & spiritualia, est caput omnium fidelium. Ad quintum dicitur, quod Imperator vocari potest vel ille, qui inter laicos supremam obtinet potestatem absque suprema potestate spirituali: & sicille est inferior papa, & ille vocatur communiter Imperator, vel qui super omnes laicos supremam habet etiam in spiritualibus potestatem: & ille non est inferior papa: quamuis papa communiter non vocerur hoc nomine, sed quodam alio nomine digniori, sc. apostolicus, papa supremus pontifex vel sacerdos.
units.tr: Having seen how the third opinion strives to rise again against the arguments set out above in the first and second chapters, and to answer them, we must now see how the second opinion can answer those arguments brought against it in the second, third and fourth chapters. To the first argument, set out in the first chapter, it can be answered that the "supreme spiritual power" may be understood in two ways. In one way it may be taken for the whole power granted by the supreme spiritual authority, that is, by Christ; and so, according to them, supreme spiritual power and supreme lay power are not divided in substance as opposites. Supreme lay power, in substance, is a part of supreme spiritual power, so that the power in respect of temporal matters is not simply supreme, because the power that lies in the Emperor is less than that which lies in the Pope; and it is a certain effect of spiritual power in the first sense just described. In another way, supreme spiritual power may be taken for the power which concerns only spiritual things and not temporal ones, and supreme lay power for the power which concerns only temporal things and not spiritual ones. So taken, supreme spiritual power and supreme lay power, that is, supreme power concerning only temporal and not spiritual things, are in some respect divided as opposites; yet they can fall into the same person, as has been declared by the second opinion above in the second chapter. To the second argument it is said that these two powers do not constitute two heads of two different bodies, but one head having the twofold power just mentioned. To the third it is said that the papacy does not include domination, but excludes tyrannical and unjust domination, of which the blessed Peter speaks in his first epistle, chapter 5. To the fourth it is said that one who exercises supreme lay power alone, and not spiritual power, is a son of the Church, if he is faithful; and therefore the emperor, who is endowed only with lay power, if he is faithful, is a son of the Church; but one who holds supreme power over temporal and spiritual things is the head of all the faithful. To the fifth it is said that "Emperor" may be applied either to one who holds supreme power among laymen without supreme spiritual power, and such a one is inferior to the Pope, and he is commonly called Emperor; or to one who has supreme power over all laymen, including power in spiritual matters, and such a one is not inferior to the Pope; although the Pope is not commonly called by this name, but by another, more worthy name, namely apostolic, supreme pontiff or priest.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Respondet argumentis factis c. 4. pro secunda parte opinionis tertia.
units.tr: He answers the arguments put forward in chapter 4 for the second part of the third opinion.

units.la: SEcundum etiam istam opinionem respondetur ad illa, quae supra ca. 4. pro opinione tertia sunt adducta: quae contra istam opinionem secundam militare videntur. Dicitur autem ad primum quod papa non debet regulariter per seipsum negocia secularia exercere, secundum apostolum & canones sacros: sed huiusmodi negocia aliis debet committere, multi enim multa facere debent per alios quae non debent ipsimet facere per seipsos, s. q. 3. vl. di. 88. c. episcopus guber. 12. q. 1. praecipimus, quae tamen si fecerit per seipsos, tenent: licet faciendo peccent, & saepe mortaliter, sic saepe papa si in temporalibus aliquid fecerit, quicquid illud sit, nisi sit contra legem diuinam nec contra ius naturale, etiam de iure tenet: poterit tamen hoc faciendo peccare mortaliter: quia facit per seipsum quod debet facere per alium. Ad secundum dicitur quod illae duae potestates sunt distinctae, tamen in eandem cadere possunt & cadunt de facto: licet non cadant nec cadere debeant in eundem regulariter quo ad exercitium: quia ille, in quem cadit potestas spiritualis suprema, non debet per seipsum aliam exequi potestatem, nisi forte casualiter. Ad tertium dicitur, quod armis intendere & iudicium sanguinis exercere papa non debet per seipsum: hoc tamen potest aliis committere & debet: & ideo Christus vicario suo vsum gladii materialis regulariter interdixit: non autem potestatem hoc aliis committendi, & illo modo intelligunt & exponunt omnes canones & auctoritates alias, quæ in contrarium sonare videntur.
units.tr: According to this opinion too, replies are given to those arguments which were adduced above in chapter 4 for the third opinion and which seem to tell against this second opinion. As to the first, it is said that the Pope ought not, as a rule, to exercise secular business himself in person, according to the Apostle and the sacred canons; rather he ought to commit such business to others. For many men ought to do through others many things which they ought not to do with their own hands (Secunda quaestio 3, distinctio 88, canon Episcopus; causa 12, quaestio 1, canon Praecipimus). Yet if they do them in person, those acts still hold good in law, although they sin in doing them, and often mortally. So too the Pope, if he does anything in temporal matters, whatever it may be, holds it binding in law, unless it is contrary to divine law or to natural law; yet in doing it he may sin mortally, because he does in person what he ought to do through another. To the second it is said that those two powers are distinct, yet they can fall upon the same man, and in fact do so; though they do not, and ought not, as a rule, fall upon the same man as regards their exercise, because he upon whom the supreme spiritual power falls ought not to exercise the other power himself, except perhaps by chance. To the third it is said that the Pope ought not himself to engage in arms or to exercise judgment of blood; he may and ought, however, to commit these to others. Accordingly Christ, as a rule, forbade his vicar the use of the material sword, but not the power of committing it to others; and all the canons and other authorities which seem to say the contrary are understood and explained in this sense.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Penes solutiones earum de prima opinione ad argumenta, quæ adducta sunt contra eam, cap. 2. & 3.
units.tr: Replies to the arguments brought against the first opinion, in chapters 2 and 3, and their solutions.

units.la: ULtimo videndum est, quomodo prima opinio ad illa quæ in cap. 2. & 3. contra illam adducuntur, niti tur respondere. Ad illa enim, quæ adducuntur ex cap. 4. pro opinione tertia, forsan respondetur, sicut respondent illi de opinione tertia, ad illa quæ adducuntur, cap. 3. ad probandum quod istæ duæ potestates licet non debent, tamen possunt cadere in eundem: dupliciter respondetur: quia sicut potestas laicalis suprema repugnat habenti potestatem spiritualem supremam ratione statuς papalis: ita etiam repugnat potestati laicali supremæ: quamuis non repugnat omni potestati laicali: & hoc quia ad plura repugnantia statui papali se extendit potestas laicalis suprema, ad quæ non omnis potestas laicalis se potest extendere, propter hoc si aliquis rex fieret papa, amitteret potestatem laicalem supremam, licet non laicalem interiorem seu minorem, eidem etiam statui papali repugnat matrimonium: licet non repugnat ordini sacerdotali, unde licet in primitiua ecclesia tam sacerdotes quam episcopi habuerunt vxores & vsi fuerunt matrimonio: non tamen legitur quod aliquis papa vsus fuerit & papatu & matrimonio. Status autem papalis & potestas laicalis suprema repugnant magis quam spiritus & corpus: quemadmodum plus repugnant quam spiritus & mulier: & ideo quamuis corpus & spiritus valeant reperiri in eodem: status tamen papalis tam mulieri quam potestati laicali supremæ repugnat, inferre etiam mortem corporalem iudicialem statui papali repugnat: qui tamen est actus potestatis laicalis supremæ, & ita licet potestas laicalis suprema non repugnet pollenti potestate spirituali suprema: nec ratione ordinis sacerdotalis nec ratione administrationis, repugnant tamen sibi ratione status papalis, qui non patitur secum plures actus iudiciales spectantes ad potestatem laicalem supremam: licet compatiatur secum eosdem actus quantum ad substantiam actuum: quemadmodum non compatitur secum concubitum coniugalem: licet statui quantum ad substantiam actus non repugnat: Et sic finis primæ quæstionis, incipit secunda quæstio.
units.tr: Lastly, we must see how the first opinion attempts to answer those arguments which are brought against it in chapters 2 and 3. As for those things which are adduced from chapter 4 in favour of the third opinion, perhaps the answer will be the same as the adherents of the third opinion give to those things which are adduced in chapter 3 to prove that these two powers, although they ought not to, nevertheless can fall into the same person. The answer is given in two ways. First, just as supreme lay power is incompatible with holding supreme spiritual power by reason of the papal state, so also it is incompatible with supreme lay power, although it is not incompatible with every lay power. This is because supreme lay power extends to many things that are repugnant to the papal state, to which not every lay power can extend. For this reason, if some king were made pope, he would lose supreme lay power, although not inferior or lesser lay power. Likewise, marriage is repugnant to the papal state, although it is not repugnant to the sacerdotal order. Hence, although in the primitive Church both priests and bishops had wives and made use of marriage, yet we do not read that any pope both held the papacy and used marriage. Now the papal state and supreme lay power are repugnant to one another more than spirit and body are, just as they are more repugnant than spirit and woman. And so, although body and spirit can be found in the same subject, the papal state is nevertheless repugnant to a woman as well as to supreme lay power. To inflict judicial bodily death is likewise repugnant to the papal state, yet it is an act of supreme lay power. Thus, although supreme lay power is not repugnant to one who wields supreme spiritual power, neither by reason of sacerdotal order nor by reason of administration, it is nevertheless repugnant to him by reason of the papal state, which does not admit many judicial acts belonging to supreme lay power alongside it, although it tolerates the same acts as to their substance. Just as it does not tolerate conjugal intercourse alongside it, although as to the substance of the act it is not repugnant to the state. And so the end of the first question; the second question begins.

units.la: QVÆSTIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: THE SECOND QUESTION.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Caput primum secundæ quæstionis proponit ipsam quæst. & circa eam duas opiniones recitat: circa quarum secundam ponuntur distinctiones de potestate propria, & de immediatione quæ quidem accipitur à Deo.
units.tr: The first chapter of the second question sets out the question itself and recounts two opinions on it. Concerning the second of these, distinctions are offered about proper power and about immediacy, which is understood to come from God.

units.la: SEcunda quæstio est, vtrum suprema potestas laicalis proprietatem sibi propriè propriâ habeat immediatè à Deo. Circa autem hanc q. sunt duæ opiniones contrariæ. Vna est quod suprema potestas laicalis proprietatem sibi propriè propriam non habet immediatè à Deo: quia habet eam à Deo mediante papali potestate, papa vero habet plenitudinem potestatis tam in spiritualibus q̄ in temporalibus & ideo nemo habet aliquâ proprietatē nisi ab ipso. Pro hac opinione adduci possunt illa q̄ allegata sunt, supra q. 1. c. 2. Alia est opinio quæ per distinctiones respondet: quarum vna est q̄ proprietas propriæ propria alicuius potest dupliciter accipi, vno modo vt proprietas propriæ propria alicuius vocetur illa, q̄ est proprietas propriissime & strictissime accipiendo nomen proprietatis: aliter vt proprietas propriæ propria alicuius vocetur illa q̄ siue fuerit proprietas propriissime accipiendo nomen proprietatis siue large accipiendo, magis propriæ convenit alicui q̄ aliqua alia. Secunda distinctio est q̄ aliq̄ proprietatē sicut & aliq̄ potestatē esse immediatè à Deo tripliciter potest intelligi, vno modo vt detur à Deo solo sine donatione vel ministerio creaturæ, p quē modum Moyses habuit ducatu à Deo immediatè & filii Israel proprietatē terræ promissionis, & Petrus summū sacerdotium, & 11. apostoli apostolatum, secundo potest esse aliquid immediatè à Deo: quia à solo Deo datur, tamen ministerio creaturæ: p quē modū summus pontifex quilibet post Petrū pontificem, pontificium habet à Deo immediatè: quia quis non habeat potestatē illam absq; electione humana: electores tamen illi sibi potestatē suā non tribuunt, sed solus Deus: sicut qui baptizatur gratiam accipit à solo Deo, non tamen sine ministerio baptizantis: & tamen baptizans non est creans gratiā illā: sicut plebanus habet ecclesiā à solo episcopo, & tamen non sine præsentatione patroni, hoc modo potest intelligi, aliquis habens potestatē vel proprietatem aliq̄ à solo Deo: quia licet eā à principio habuerit cum concessione, donatione vel resignatione alterius, postq̄ sibi data est & resignata, à solo Deo dependet: ita q̄ solus Deus quantum ad huiusmodi potestatē vel proprietatem est eo superior: sic secundū quosdā papa dicitur habere dominiū siue proprietatē rerum temporaliū, quæ concessæ sunt à fidelibus Romano pontifici immediatè à solo Deo: quia licet primo receperit ex largitate fideliū: tamē postq̄ illas recepit, nullus alius quicq̄ iuris habet nisi solus Deus, ita q̄ prædia & civitates & alias res, quas sibi dederunt fideles, nō ab homine sed à solo Deo tenet: ita q̄ superiorē in huiusmodi temporalibus post Deū nullo modo recognoscit: sicut etiā quādo erat solus Noe cū filiis & vxoribus res quas habebat tunc siue iure hæreditario siue donatione aliorum aut quouis alio modo à Deo tenebat: nec in huiusmodi tunc superiorē habebat: licet habuisset ante diluuiū in his superiorē, regem, s. aut aliū dominū principalē, quo fuisset inferior.
units.tr: The second question is whether supreme lay power has its own proper possession immediately from God. There are two opposing opinions on this question. One is that supreme lay power does not have its own proper possession immediately from God, because it has it from God through papal power, and the pope has the fullness of power both in spiritual and in temporal matters, so that no one has any possession except from him. The arguments cited above in question 1, chapter 2, can be adduced in support of this opinion. The other opinion answers by way of distinctions. The first distinction is that the proper possession of anyone may be taken in two ways. In one way, that is called the proper possession of someone which is a possession in the most proper and strictest sense of the word "possession." In the other way, that is called the proper possession of someone which, whether it is a possession in the most proper sense or in a broader sense, belongs to a person more fittingly than some other thing does. The second distinction is that something, like some power, can be understood to be immediately from God in three ways. In one way, it is given by God alone, without the gift or ministry of a creature. In this manner Moses had leadership immediately from God, and the sons of Israel had the land of promise, and Peter had the high priesthood, and the eleven apostles had the apostleship. In a second way, something can be immediately from God because it is given by God alone, yet through the ministry of a creature. In this manner, any supreme pontiff after Peter has the pontificate immediately from God, because no one can have that power without human election; yet those electors do not confer their power on him, but God alone does. Just as the one who is baptized receives grace from God alone, yet not without the ministry of the one baptizing, and yet the baptizer is not the creator of that grace; or as the parish priest has his church from the bishop alone, and yet not without the presentation of the patron. In this manner it can be understood that someone who has some power or possession is dependent on God alone, because although he had it at the start with the concession, gift, or resignation of another, once it has been given and resigned to him, it depends on God alone, so that God alone is superior to him as regards such power or possession. Thus, according to some, the pope is said to have the lordship or possession of temporal goods which have been granted to the Roman pontiff by the faithful immediately from God alone. For although he first received them from the bounty of the faithful, yet after he has received them, no one else has any right over them except God alone, so that he holds the estates, cities, and other things which the faithful have given him not from man but from God alone; and so he recognises no superior in such temporal matters after God in any way. Likewise, when Noah was alone with his sons and wives, the things he then possessed, whether by hereditary right, by the gift of others, or in any other way, he held from God, and he had no superior in such matters then, although before the flood he had had a superior in these things, a king or some other principal lord, to whom he would have been inferior.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Secunda q. recitat duas alias opiniones, ortas ex distinctionibus circa secundam opinionem positis.
units.tr: The second question: it recites two other opinions, arising from the distinctions laid down with regard to the second opinion.

units.la: HIs distinctionibus visis videndum, quomodo non omnes tenētes imperium esse à papa, eodem modo respondēt ad propositum quæstionis. Dicunt enim quidam, quod quamuis ille, qui habet potestatem laicalem supremam, habeat eam ex alio quam ex suprema potestate spirituali: proprietatem tamen proprie propriā potest habere, sc. primo modo capiendo nomen proprietatis propriissime & strictissime: quia huiusmodi potestatem habere potest in bonis, quæ habuit antequam haberet vel obtineret supremam potestatem laicalem, & in aliis quæ postea acquireret per se & non dignitati seu supremæ laicali potestati: tamen propriissime & strictissime accipiendo nomen proprietatis suprema potestas laicalis nullam habet proprietatem: quia de proprietate strictissime sumpta potest habēs eam facere quod vult, l. q. i. eos, quicquid enim fecerit de ea, eam sc. bene vel male exponendo, donando, legando, vel quomodolibet alienando: quamuis cum graui peccato talia facere valeat, tamen ad restitutionem non tenetur: sed sufficit quod aliis modis Deo satisfaciat de peccato, hoc autem faciens Imperator, qui summam potestatem continet laicalem de iuribus & rebus imperii & boni communis: ipse de bonis propriis obligatur restituere: & ideo secundum illos potestas suprema laicalis: sicut nec suprema potestas spiritualis: nec mediate nec immediate à Deo, nec ab aliquo habet proprietatem sibi propriam illo modo. Cuius ratio assignatur: quia potestas suprema laicalis est principatus eiusdem perfectissimus: cuiusmodi est regalis, qui à principatu tam tyrannico quam despotico supreme distinctus hoc habet inter alia, vt instituatur propter bonum commune subiectorum & non propter bonum proprium principatus, de tali enim regimine dicit Arist. lib. 8. Ethicorum, vtilia ergo sunt alia sibiipsi: quædam non vtiq, sed subditis. Aut ergo finaliter bona imperii sunt à Deo concessa propter commune bonum subditorum, quare non potest ea expendere, nisi propter bonum commune seu vtilitatem omnium subditorum: & aliter si ea expendit ad restitutionem tenetur, nam qui bona concessa ab aliquibus ad certos vsus in aliis vsibus contra concedentium voluntatē consumpserit, restituere, si potest, eadem astringatur. Alia est opinio, quod potestas laicalis suprema habet aliquam proprietatem sibi proprie propriam modo prædicto accipiendo nomen proprietatis, nam constitutus in suprema potestate & eadem illis bonis abundare debet, quibus virtutum actus politicarum valeat exercere, hinc dicit Arist. 8. ethi. quod non est rex, qui per se non sufficit & omnibus bonis, superexcellens, inter virtutes autem politicas necessarias in suprema potestate laicali constituto virtus liberalitatis nequaquam est minima, nam vt dicit Arist. 8. Ethi. principatus & potestates & potentatus possessionibus maxime necessariae sunt amici, quia, vt dicit ibidem, bona fortuna quanto maior, tanto minus secatur, nam sic habetur extra de accusationibus qualiter & quando 2. Prælati ecclesiastici odium multorum frequenter incurrunt & insidias patiuntur: sic etiam reges & principes, quia interdum iudicium sanguinis habent inter potentes & diuites exercere: multi eis libenter parant insidias, quare pro sua defensione & potestate etiam in malos intrepide exercenda sæpissime indigere noscuntur amicis, amici autem maxime acquiruntur & conseruantur per liberalem munificentiam: teste Salomone, qui prouer. 9. ait: multi colunt personā potentis & amici sunt dona tribuentis, & etiam diuitiæ adducunt amicos plurimos, igitur actus virtutis liberalitatis est actus necessarius constitutis in suprema potestate laicali: quia cum potestas laicalis suprema debeat esse sibiipsi & fungenti sufficiens, tantis abundare debet vt præeminens ea actus liberalitatis valeat exercere, cuius actus est dare, dare autem spectat ad proprietatem habentem: quia suprema potestas proprietatem strictissimam propriissime accepto vocabulo debet habere.
units.tr: Having seen these distinctions, we must consider how those who do not all hold that the empire comes from the pope answer the question put forward in the same way. For some say that although the one who holds supreme secular power has it from something other than the supreme spiritual power, he can nevertheless have a property that is properly his own, taking the word property in the first sense, most properly and most strictly. For he can have such power over goods which he possessed before he held or obtained the supreme secular power, and over others which he afterwards acquires by himself and not by virtue of his dignity or of the supreme secular power. Yet, taking the word property most properly and most strictly, the supreme secular power has no property at all. For over property taken in the strictest sense, its holder may do what he wishes (l. q. i. eos): whatever he does with it, whether by spending it well or badly, giving it away, bequeathing it, or alienating it in any way, although he may do such things, even with grave sin, he is not bound to make restitution; it is enough that he make satisfaction to God for the sin by other means. But the emperor, who holds the supreme secular power, does not do this with the rights and goods of the empire and of the common good; he is bound to restore such things from his own goods. And therefore, according to them, the supreme secular power, like the supreme spiritual power, has no property of its own in that sense, neither mediately nor immediately from God, nor from anyone else. The reason assigned for this is that the supreme secular power is the most perfect kind of principality; of this kind is kingly rule, which, being supremely distinct from principality both tyrannical and despotic, has this among other features: that it is instituted for the common good of the subjects and not for the good of the ruler. For Aristotle, in book 8 of the Ethics, says of such government: therefore some things are useful to themselves, but others are not so, but to subjects. Therefore either the goods of the empire are given by God finally for the common good of the subjects, so that the ruler cannot spend them except for the common good or the advantage of all the subjects; otherwise, if he spends them otherwise, he is bound to make restitution, for whoever has consumed goods granted by some for certain uses in other uses, contrary to the will of the grantors, is bound, if he can, to restore the same. There is another opinion: that the supreme secular power does have some property that is properly its own, taking the word property in the aforesaid sense. For one placed in supreme power ought to abound in those goods by which he may be able to exercise the acts of political virtues. Hence Aristotle says in Ethics 8 that he is not a king who by himself is not sufficient and superexcellent in all goods. Among the political virtues necessary for one set in supreme secular power, the virtue of liberality is by no means the least. For, as Aristotle says in Ethics 8, principalities, powers and dominions most need possessions and friends, and because, as he says in the same place, the greater the good fortune, the less it is sought after. For thus it is held in the Extra, de accusationibus, qualiter et quando, chapter 2: ecclesiastical prelates frequently incur the hatred of many and suffer plots; so also kings and princes, since they sometimes have to exercise the judgment of blood among the powerful and rich, and many readily lay snares for them. Therefore, for their defence and for the exercise of their power even against evil men, they are very often known to need friends. Friends, moreover, are acquired and kept most of all through liberal generosity, as Solomon witnesses, who says in Proverbs 9: many court the person of the powerful, and they are friends of the one who gives gifts; riches also bring many friends. Therefore the act of the virtue of liberality is a necessary act for those set in supreme secular power, because, since the supreme secular power ought to be sufficient for itself and for the one who exercises it, it must abound so greatly, and be so pre-eminent, that it can exercise acts of liberality, whose act is to give; but giving pertains to the one who has property. For the supreme power must have property in the strictest and most proper sense of the word.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Huius secunda quæstionis primo ponit declarationem opinionis dicentium quod suprema potestas laicalis sit à Deo. Deinde probatis quibusdam opinionibus probat 10. ratio- nibus, quod imperium est à Papa, ad quas, vt annotabitur, suis locis respondetur.
units.tr: In this second question he first sets out the view of those who hold that the supreme lay power is from God. Then, after setting out some opinions, he proves with ten arguments that imperial power is from the Pope. He replies to these arguments in their proper places, as will be noted.

units.la: POrro opiniones ambæ præcedentes in hoc concordant, quod suprema potestas laicalis habet proprietatem sibi proprie propriam secundo modo: quia alia bona temporalia sic sunt appropriata potestati laicali supremæ quod ad alterius proprietatem vel dominium minime spectant. Sed nō ambæ eodem modo tenent, quod istam proprietatem habeat immediate à Deo: quia nullus eorum habuit huiusmodi potestatem. Quidam tamen dicunt, quod istam proprietatem non habent immediate à Deo primo modo, sicut nec aliquis papa post beatum Petrum habuit potestatem spiritualem papalem immediate à Deo: quia nullus eorum habuit huiusmodi potestatem absque electione illius vel illorum, ad quem vel ad quos spectat eligere summum pontificem: cum potestas laicalis habet proprietatem propriam sibi primo modo vel secundo modo immediate à Deo, quomodo supremus pontifex habet auctoritatem sibi propriam immediate à Deo. Sicut enim quando papa eligitur eligentes ipsum nullam sibi tribuunt potestatem: sed celebrata electione & electo consentiente Deus immediate confert sibi omnem potestatem, quam habet: ita celebrata electione Imperatoris eligentes nihil conferunt sibi, sed ipso consentiente omnem potestatem, quæ propria est Imperatoris dignitatis, sibi solus Deus confert. Hæc videtur opinio Glossæ di. 96. sup. c. si imperator, quæ super verbo diuinitus ait: Non ergo à papa imperium, sed à solo Deo est, vt 23.q.4.c. quæsitum. Nam à cœlesti numine (aliis maiestate) habet gladii potestatem. C. de ve. in. enu. lib. 1. in principio, quod concedo de vero Imperatore. Pro ista opinione potest taliter allegari. Imperator non habet ab homine potestatem & proprietatem propriam potestatis laicalis suprema: ergo habet eam à solo Deo, consequentia videtur manifesta, antecedes probatur: quia si haberet eam ab homine, aut ab electore, aut à coronatore, aut à confirmatore. Non ab electoribus, quia generaliter electores, quando sunt præcise electores, non dant electo dignitatem, ad quam eligitur, quando electio non indiget ab homine confirmari: & sic nec potestatem immediatam, sed solum capacitatem recipiendi dignitatem, ad quam eligitur, à Deo, sicut quando electo supremo pontifice non indiget ab homine confirmari, electores non dant sibi potestatem papalem, sed solummodo capacitatem immediatam recipiendi à Deo huiusmodi dignitatem: quia secundum ordinationem Dei à se solo non est capax huius dignitatis Imperator, ergo ab electoribus neq; potestatem neq; proprietatem recipit. Nec habet eam à coronatore, nam non dat coronator proprietatem alicuius rei temporalis, sicut nec consecrator dat consecrato aliq; proprietatem vel etiam administrationem alicuius rei spiritualis, ergo Imperator à coronatore, qui non est confirmator, nullam recipit proprietatem. Nec habet eam à confirmatore, quia confirmatore non indiget, sicut isti supra ponunt. Hic propter rationes adductas, 6. c. quod papa in temporalibus habet huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis, dicendum est, quod imperium est ab ipso. Ex quo inferri potest, quod potestas laicalis suprema, sc. imperialis, habet proprietatem sibi propriam à papa, & non immediate à Deo, sed habet ab eo potestatem à quo est. Restat ergo probare, quod imperium est à papa, quod multis modis ostenditur, primo sic: Ab illo est imperium, cui datæ sunt cœlestis & terreni Imperii claues: sed Petro & successoribus suis sunt datæ claues cœlestis & terreni imperii, di. 22. c. 1. ergo impium erit à papa. Amplius: Impium est ab illo & in eius potestate perfectissime est imperium, qui ex ordinatione Dei cœlestis caput primum & iudex supremus cunctorum mortalium: papa aut & non Imperator ex ordinatione Dei est caput primum & iudex supremus cunctorum mortalium: ergo imperium est à papa. Rursus, ab illo est imperium, qui potest imperatorem deponere: papa aut potest imperatorem deponere, 15.q.5.c. aliud: ergo impium est à papa. Item ab eo est imperium, qui potest transferre imperium de una gente ad aliam: hoc autem potest papa, ext. de electis c. venerabile. ergo imperium est à papa. Item ab illo est imperium, à quo imperator postq; electus est, examinatur, inungitur, consecratur, & coronatur: ergo imperium est à papa. Item ab illo est imperium cui Imperator iurat tanq; vasallus: sed Imperator tanquam vasallus præstat papæ iuramentum fidelitatis & subiectionis dist. 63. tibi domino, ergo imperium est à papa. Item ab illo qui habet utrumq; gladium materialem & spiritualem est imperium papa autem habet utrumq; gladium, igitur imperium est à papa. Hæc videtur sententia Innocentii quarti qui in quadam decretali asserit quod in gremio fidelis ecclesiæ ambo gladii administrationis utriusq; habentur repositi, unde q; si quis ibidem non fuerit neutrum habet, uterq; creditur iure Petri cū de materiali eidem non dixerit: mitte: sed converte gladium tuum, ut imperium videlicet per te ipsum non exerceas: in vaginam tuam, signanter vbi exprimitur huius potestas gladii materialis apud ecclesiam esse implicita: sed per imperatorem qui eam recipit explicatur. Item ab illo est impium ad quem se habet imperator sicut filius ad patrem: sicut discipulus ad magistrum: sicut plumbum ad aurum, sicut luna ad solem: sed has comparationes habet imperator ad papam di. 46. si imperator & c. quis dubitet, &c. Duo sunt extra dema. & obe. c. solita ergo imperium est à papa. Item ab illo est imperium cui imperator tenetur caput submittere, papæ autem hoc tenetur, di. 63. Valentinianum di. 46. nunquam ergo imperium est à papa. Item ab illo est imperium à quo ex auctoritate propria & non ordinatione imperatoris vel alterius hominis regi habet imperium ipso vacante, hoc autem facto papa vacante imperio, ergo imperium est à papa.
units.tr: Both of the preceding opinions agree on this point: the supreme lay power has its own property in the second sense, because other temporal goods are so appropriated to the supreme lay power that they do not belong to anyone else's property or dominion. But they do not hold the same view on whether it has this property immediately from God, since neither of them had such a power. Some, however, say that it does not have this property immediately from God in the first sense, just as no pope after the blessed Peter had spiritual papal power immediately from God, because none of them had such power apart from the election of the person or persons whose task it is to elect the supreme pontiff. Yet the lay power has its own property, in the first or the second sense, immediately from God, just as the supreme pontiff has authority of his own immediately from God. For when a pope is elected, the electors confer no power on him; rather, once the election has been completed and the one elected consents, God alone immediately confers on him all the power he has. Likewise, when an emperor has been elected, the electors confer nothing on him; rather, with his consent, God alone confers on him all the power that belongs to the imperial dignity. This seems to be the opinion of the Gloss on di. 96, on the chapter "si imperator", which says at the words "super verbo diuinitus": "Therefore the empire is not from the Pope but from God alone, as in 23 q. 4 c. quaesitum. For he has the power of the sword from the heavenly divinity (others read majesty). C. de vet. jur. enuc. lib. 1 in principio", which I grant of the true emperor. For this opinion the following argument may be made. The emperor does not have from a human being the power and the proper property of the supreme lay power; therefore he has it from God alone. The inference seems plain, and the antecedent is proved as follows: if he had it from a human being, it would be from an elector, or from one who crowns him, or from one who confirms him. Not from the electors, because electors, when they are merely electors, do not give the elected person the dignity to which he is elected when the election does not need to be confirmed by a human being. In that case they give him not the power itself but only the capacity to receive the dignity to which he is elected, from God. Just as, when a supreme pontiff has been elected and needs no confirmation from a human being, the electors do not give him papal power but only the immediate capacity to receive this dignity from God, so too, by God's ordinance, the emperor is not capable of this dignity by himself; therefore he receives neither power nor property from the electors. Nor does he have it from the one who crowns him, for a coronor does not give ownership of any temporal thing, just as a consecrator does not give the consecrated person any property or even administration of any spiritual thing. Therefore the emperor receives no property from the coronor, who is not a confirmer. Nor does he have it from a confirmer, since, as those above maintain, he does not need one. For the reasons adduced here, and because of the sixth chapter, "quod papa in temporalibus habet huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis," it must be said that the empire is from him. From this it can be inferred that the supreme lay power, namely the imperial power, has its own property from the Pope, and not immediately from God, but it has power from him from whom it is. It remains, therefore, to prove that the empire is from the Pope, which is shown in many ways. First, as follows: the empire is from him to whom the keys of the heavenly and the earthly empire were given; but the keys of the heavenly and earthly empire were given to Peter and his successors, dist. 22 c. 1; therefore the empire will be from the Pope. Further: the empire is from him, and is perfectly in his power, who by God's ordinance is the first head of heaven and the supreme judge of all mortals; but the Pope, and not the emperor, is by God's ordinance the first head and supreme judge of all mortals; therefore the empire is from the Pope. Again, the empire is from him who can depose the emperor; but the Pope can depose the emperor, 15 q. 5 c. aliud; therefore the empire is from the Pope. Likewise, the empire is from him who can transfer the empire from one nation to another; but the Pope can do this, Extra, de electis, c. venerabile; therefore the empire is from the Pope. Likewise, the empire is from him by whom the emperor, once elected, is examined, anointed, consecrated and crowned; therefore the empire is from the Pope. Likewise, the empire is from him to whom the emperor swears as a vassal; but the emperor, as a vassal, gives the Pope an oath of fidelity and subjection, dist. 63 "tibi domino"; therefore the empire is from the Pope. Likewise, the empire is from him who has both the material and the spiritual sword; but the Pope has both swords; therefore the empire is from the Pope. This seems to be the view of Innocent IV, who in a certain decretal asserts that in the bosom of the faithful Church both swords, of either administration, are kept stored, and that therefore, if someone is not there, he has neither; both are believed to belong by right to Peter, since he did not say of the material sword, "Put it away," but "Turn your sword," namely so that you may not exercise the empire yourself, "into your scabbard." This is especially so where the power of the material sword is stated to be implicit in the Church, but is made explicit through the emperor who receives it. Likewise, the empire is from him to whom the emperor stands as a son to a father, as a disciple to a master, as lead to gold, as the moon to the sun; but the emperor has these comparisons to the Pope, dist. 46 "si imperator" etc., "quis dubitet" etc. "Duo sunt" extra de maiorit. et obed. c. solita; therefore the empire is from the Pope. Likewise, the empire is from him to whom the emperor is bound to submit his head; but this is what the emperor is bound to do to the Pope, dist. 63 "Valentinianum", dist. 46 "nunquam"; therefore the empire is from the Pope. Likewise, the empire is from him by whose own authority, and not by the ordinance of the emperor or of another human being, the empire is ruled when it is vacant; but this happens when the Pope has the empire vacant; therefore the empire is from the Pope.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Recitat tres opiniones diversimode opinantium de modo, quo imperium sit à Papa.
units.tr: He recounts three opinions, differing in their manner, on how the empire is from the Pope.

units.la: Orro licet quidam dicant concorditer imperium esse à papa: non tamen omnino in modo ponendi concordant, nec ex eadem ratione mouentur. Una est opinio, q; propter hoc, q; dicitur papam habere tam in spiritualibus quã in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis, de qua dictum est supra, q.1.c.1. ponit & concedit imperium & omnia alia regna taliter esse à papa, quod de plenitudine potestatis, quãdocunq; voluerit, possit absq; causa & sine culpa ad suum libitum destituere institutum, & eidem alium subrogare, & sibi ipsi imperium retinere, qualem etiã potestatem (vt dicunt) super omnia alia habet regna, aliter enim non haberet plenitudinem potestatis, sed haberet potestatem per alia iura quam p diuina & per naturalia limitatu. Alii autem, quamuis putent opinione prædictam saperehæresim manifestam: tamen dicunt, imperiu esse à papa: propter hoc quod secundum eos papa habet quandã aliam plenitudinem potestatis, quia licet (vt dicunt) imperium est à papa: tamen papa non possit omnia sine exceptione, quæ non sunt prohibita: neq; per ius diuinum neq; per ius naturale: quia illa, q superogationis sunt, non pōt præcipere, nec aliquē priuare iure suo sine culpa: & nisi subsit causa, non potest illa, quæ ad regendū mortales minime dignoscuntur necessaria, licet p seipsum vel sibi instutos officiales ab ipso, etiam sine exceptione potest, q constant esse necessaria regimini subditorum. Unde licet reges & principes iā iuste regentes & principatus habentes, absq; culpa, nisi subsit causa, nequaquam potest regnis suis & principatibus priuare de plenitudine potestatis suæ: tamen si esset aliquis papa, qui regeret principem aut caput in temporalibus nō haberet (licet non solū expediens sed etiã necessarium sit cuilibet papæ esse in temporalibus caput, à quo de necessitate regatur) tunc habere posset papa de plenitudine potestatis absq; electione nominationem & sine consensu eorum ipsis caput praeficere maiorem vel minorem dignitatem vel potestatem tribuendo eidem, in similibus circa potestatem similiter est dicendum. Ex ista plenitudine potestatis, vt dicit ista opinio, habet papa potestatem super Imperatorem & imperium, non quod possit imperatorem, nisi sit causa necessaria, priuare sine culpa imperio: nec quod possit imperium ad libitum transferre de gente in gentem: sed quia pro culpa & ex causa necessaria potest imperatorem quibuscunq; aliis minime requisitis deponere: si hoc sit necessarium vtilitati communi, & non solum tanq; expediens de plenitudine potestatis, & non requisitis aliis quibuscunq;, de gente in gentem, vel de dominio in dominium, vel de persona in personam transferre imperium: sed etiam ex aliqua causa euidenti, si necessarium fuerit bono communi, vt nullus ad regnum vel imperium eligatur, potest ordinare & praecipere quandiu necessarium fuerit, quod huius electio differatur, & isto modo imperium est a papa: non ga papa in ipso habet plenitudinem potestatis, de qua dictum est, q. 1. c. 2. quam etiam habet supra omnia regna & super quecunq; temporalia, nec differt ista opinio a secunda, quae recitata est super, q. 1. c. 2. quod secundum istam opinionem papa potest corrigere imperatorem, quando corrigendus est, & omnia facere circa temporalia quaecunq; necessaria sunt bono communi: licet non possit aliquem priuare iure suo sine culpa, nisi subsit causa, illa consequentia tenet: quia papa in temporalibus praeterq; iure exigente, nullam habet potestatem a Christo: nisi salvis non solum iuribus sed etiam libertatibus aliorum: ideo papa illa, quae etiam necessaria sunt reipub. etiam in temporalib. minime potest, quamdiu sunt alii, qui ipsa possunt & volunt vtiliter expedire. Et ideo si esset aliquis populus, qui rectores in temporalibus non haberet, papa non deberet nec posset super eos rectores constituere, si ipsimet vellent sibi ipsis rectorem constituere siue praeficere idoneum eligendo: sic etiam quando corrigendus esset Imperator, vel rex, aut princeps alius, aut etiam deponendus propter defectum aut crimen, qui vel quad spiritualia minime pertineret: papa auctoritate eius siue potestate concessa Christo se intromittere non deberet nisi propter negligentiam & malitiam laicorum, vnde videtur veri similiter (dicunt isti) quod vt papa spiritualibus totaliter vacet, atq; etiam ne aliquo modo ad hoc se insufficientem inueniat: se temporalib. quibuscunq; non debeat implicare negociis, quamdiu inueniuntur laici, qui ea velint & possint iure & legitime expedire, hoc habetur 11. q. 1. te quidem. Alia est opinio, quod imperium non est a papa de iure diuino: sed ex iure humano, ex voluntaria sc. successione vel concessione Romanorum, qui omnem potestatem, quam habuerunt super imperium, supremo pontifici concesserunt, vel praescriptione humana, qua summus pontifex ius & potestate sui imperii acquisiuit, & hinc est, q. licet iure diuino papa in nullo maiorem potestatem habet super imperium, q. super regna quaecunq;: tamen iure humano maiore super ipso obtinet potestatem: quia nec populus aliquorum regnorum potestatem suam dedit papae, nec ipse contra alia regna praescripsit legitime. Licet ergo opiniones praedictae discordant, q. ponunt imperium esse a papa, vel iure humano vel iure diuino, & ideo concedunt, quod potestas laicalis vel suprema imperialis sibi proprium habet proprietatem a papa & non immediate a Deo: quia ab illo habet proprietatem propriam sibi, a quo est imperium: sed illud est a papa, vt patuit: ergo &c.
units.tr: Furthermore, although some say with one accord that the empire is from the Pope, they do not agree at all in the way of putting it, nor are they moved by the same reasoning. One opinion holds that, because the Pope is said to have a fullness of power both in spiritual and in temporal matters, of which it was said above (dist. 1, c. 1), he both asserts and concedes that the empire and all other kingdoms are from the Pope in such a way that, by the fullness of his power, whenever he wishes, he may without cause and without fault remove the appointed ruler at his pleasure, substitute another in his place, and keep the empire for himself. They say he has this same power over all other kingdoms, for otherwise he would not have a fullness of power but only a power limited by other laws than the divine and natural ones. Others, although they think the aforesaid opinion smacks of manifest heresy, nevertheless say that the empire is from the Pope, because, in their view, the Pope has a certain other fullness of power. For although (they say) the empire is from the Pope, the Pope cannot do everything without exception that is not forbidden either by divine law or by natural law; for he cannot command or deprive anyone of his right without fault those things which are matters of supererogation. Nor, unless there is a cause, can he do those things which are not known to be necessary for governing mortals, though he may do them through himself or through officials appointed by himself. Without exception, he may do those things which are plainly necessary for the government of subjects. Hence, although the Pope cannot, without fault and unless there is a cause, deprive kings and princes who already rule justly and hold principalities of their kingdoms and principalities by the fullness of his power, yet if there were a Pope who did not have a ruler or head in temporal affairs (although it is not only expedient but necessary for every Pope to have a head in temporal matters, by whom he is governed of necessity), then the Pope could, by the fullness of his power, without election or nomination and without their consent, set over them a head, bestowing on him a greater or lesser dignity or power; and the same is to be said similarly with regard to power in like cases. From this fullness of power, as this opinion says, the Pope has power over the Emperor and the empire, not in the sense that he may deprive the emperor of the empire without fault, unless there is a necessary cause, nor that he may transfer the empire at his pleasure from nation to nation; but because, for a fault and for a necessary cause, he may depose the emperor by any means whatsoever, if this is necessary for the common good, and not merely as expedient; and, without any other requirements whatsoever, he may transfer the empire from nation to nation, from lordship to lordship, or from person to person. He may even, for some clear cause, if it is necessary for the common good, order and command that no one be chosen to a kingdom or empire, and for as long as it is necessary he may defer that election. In this way the empire is from the Pope, not because the Pope has in it that fullness of power, which was spoken of (dist. 1, c. 2), and which he also has above all kingdoms and over all temporal things; nor does this opinion differ from the second, which was recited above (dist. 1, c. 2), namely that according to this opinion the Pope can correct the emperor when he must be corrected, and do all things in temporal matters that are necessary for the common good; although he cannot deprive anyone of his right without fault unless there is a cause. That consequence holds, because the Pope has no power from Christ in temporal matters beyond what the law requires, except saving not only the rights but also the liberties of others. Therefore the Pope can least of all do, even in temporal matters, those things which are also necessary for the commonwealth, as long as there are others who can and are willing to carry them out usefully. And so, if there were any people who had no rulers in temporal matters, the Pope ought not, and could not, set over them rulers, if they themselves wished to appoint for themselves a ruler, or to set over themselves a suitable man by election. Likewise, when the emperor, or a king, or another prince, must be corrected, or even deposed on account of incapacity or crime, which would not pertain at all to spiritual matters, the Pope, by the authority or power given to him by Christ, ought not to interfere, unless on account of the negligence and malice of the laity. Hence it seems likely (these men say) that, so that the Pope may be wholly free for spiritual matters, and so that he may not find himself in any way insufficient for this, he ought not to entangle himself in any temporal business whatever, as long as there are laymen who wish and are able to carry these things out lawfully and rightfully; this is held in 11, q. 1, te quidem. The other opinion is that the empire is not from the Pope by divine right, but by human right, namely by the voluntary succession or concession of the Romans, who granted to the supreme pontiff all the power they had over the empire, or by human prescription, by which the supreme pontiff acquired the right and power of his empire. And hence it is that, although by divine right the Pope has no greater power over the empire than over any kingdoms whatever, yet by human right he holds greater power over it, because neither the people of some kingdoms have given their power to the Pope, nor has he lawfully prescribed against other kingdoms. Therefore, although the aforesaid opinions disagree in that they hold the empire to be from the Pope, either by human right or by divine right, and thus concede that lay or supreme imperial power has its own ownership from the Pope and not immediately from God, because a thing has its own proper ownership from that from which it has its empire; but the empire is from the Pope, as has been shown; therefore etc.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: Recitat quartam opinionem circa dictum modum, cuius opin. duo membra seu puncta seorsum probat.
units.tr: It recites the fourth opinion on this mode, and proves its two parts or points separately.

units.la: ALia est opinio tenens, q. nec primo modo nec secundo habet potestas laicalis suprema potestate aliq; sibi propriam a Deo his modis, sed bene tertio modo solum: quia licet etiam habeat ea a donatione papae, & non ex sola donatione Dei, papa. n. non solum modo de imperio ordinauit, quod esset vna suprema potestas laicalis, nec populus eligit imperatorem, quomodo cardinales eligunt solum modo papa, nullam sibi de bonis, proprii temporalia tribuendo, sc. ordinauerunt & statuerunt potestate supremam laicalem certa ei temporalia de suis proprijs largiendo, q. dignitati & non personae dederunt, & ideo imperator, nisi in casibus, alienare illa non potest, sed ad restitutionem, si alienauerit, obligatur: & successor ipsius potest ipsa & debet cuicunq; data fuerit reuocare. Ista itaq; consideratio duo dicit, primum est q. potestas suprema non habet proprietatem a Deo primo modo vel secundo, & q. habet ea immediate a Deo, tertio mo. Pro primo potest taliter allegari. Nō est dicendum q. aliqua dignitas vel persona habeat proprietatē sibi proprium a Deo immediate a Deo primo modo vel secundo: nisi de hoc indubitanter per reuelationem diuinam constiterit: eo q. per rōem naturalem vel experientiam constare non pōt. Cum .n. per scripturam diuinitus reuelatā: vt habetur Gen.1. constet q. Dominus Deus dedit humano generi dominium temporalium rerum, & non est necesse q. appropriatio quarumcunq; rerum specialiter fiat a solo Deo absq; assensu & voluntate illorum quib. datum est cōe dominium, ergo sequitur q. nō est tenendū aliq; appropriatione talē facta esse a solo Deo absq; voluntate illoī quib. erat datū dominiū in cōi: nisi de hoc constet per reuelationē diuinā, p quem modum constat q. Deus primauit Cananeos terra, promissionis, & ipsam specialiter contulit filiis Israel, p quem et modum scimus q. Deus aliās terras dedit specialiter filiis Israel, Esau, Aaron, & Moab: sicut patet Deut. 1. Sed per nullam reuelationem diuinam constat nobis, q. Deus specialiter aliq bona dedit seu appropriauit imperio seu supremae potestati laicali: nec etiā q. iusserit, quod specialiter aliquod sibi appropriari deberet: nec q. haberet imperium aliq. proprietatem a solo Deo plusquā alia regna, quae ante imperium extiterunt: qa de hoc in scripturis diuinis, in quib. donationes diuinae scribuntur, nihil habemus, ergo tenendū est, quod imperium non habet aliq. proprietatē a Deo immediate primo modo & secundo modo. Sed forte diceret aliquis, q. imperium habere proprietatē tali modo a Deo immediate in euangelio inuenitur dictum à Christo. Matt. 22. Reddite quæ sunt Cæsari Cæsari &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Christus, qui est verus Deus, aliqua speciali ter iussit dare Cæsari: ergo illa habuit Cæsar immediate à Deo, quia à Christo, hic respondetur, quod per illa verba Christus nihil dedit specialiter Cæsari, sed iussit illa, quæ prius fuerunt donata per humanam ordinationem Cæsari, sibi reddi: & ideo non dixit, date Cæsari, sed reddite, illi quæ sua sunt quæ sc. sibi ab hominibus collata fuerunt. Illi enim, qui constituerunt ipsum Imperatorem vel prædecessorem suum, ordinauerunt vel iure naturali vel iure humano, quæ ratione potestatis laicalis supremæ vendicare debebat, & hoc Christus approbauit, qui autem approbat, nihil novum constituit: sicut qui confirmat, nullum nouum ius tribuit, extra. de fi. instru. inter dilectos. extra de confirma. uti. c. cum dilecta. & c. examinata. Secundum quod tenet ista opinio, est, quod potestas laicalis suprema habet potestatem sibi propriam immediate à Deo, tertio modo: quia licet in principio institutionis potestatis laicalis supremæ Deus immediate nec per seipsum nec per aliquod mandatum spirituale miraculose revelatum quibuscunq; hominibus, sed per homines æquitatem naturalem sequentes, considerantes reip. expedire unum principem in spiritualibus, aliis præsidere, potestati laicali supremæ determinata temporalia tribuit: quibus traditum sibi officium exercere valeat: ita quod tunc nō à solo Deo, sed etiam ab hominibus proprietate recepit: eorum tamen post traditionem illam à solo Deo tenuit ea: & quantum ad illa solum Deum habuit recognoscere superiorem, assignans omnem proprietatem illam & omne ius positiuum, quod habebat in ipsis, in potestatem supremam institutam à Deo per ipsos transferebat. Pro ista opinione taliter potest allegari. Si suprema potestas laicalis non esset illo modo immediate à Deo, haberet aliquem hominem vel communitatem in temporalibus superiorem, à quo vel à qua temporalia sua teneret: sed suprema potestas laicalis, nec ab homine nec à communitate tenet temporalia sua. Quod non ab homine, patet: quia si ab homine teneret, & nō posset alius assignari q; papa: ergo teneret ea à papa. Quod ostenditur esse fallum etiam de Imperatore fideli & Christiano: quia successor gaudet eodem iure, quo prædecessor, extra de regu. iuris. qui in iu. lib. 6. non enim esset vera successio, si verus successor minus quam prædecessor haberet. Imperator autem fidelis succedit Imperatori infideli: ergo illo iure, quo vtebatur infidelis, & fidelis vti debet, sed Imperator infidelis non tenebat temporalia sua à papa, cum ante fuerat Imperator quam papa. Tum quia Imperator infidelis tempore Christi non tenebat temporalia à Christo: quia Christus non venit tollere dominium regum seu Imperatorum, beato Aug. teste, qui super Ioh. ait loquens regibus mundi in persona Christi: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, id est, non impedio dominationem vestram in mundo, vt vane sæuiatis & timeatis. Cui concordat Leo papa, dicens: Dominus mundi temporale non quærit regnum, qui præstat æternum, quod ecclesia testari videtur, cum canit de Christo. Non eripit mortalia qui regna dat cælestia. Tum quia religio Christiana nulli infideli tollit ius suum, teste beato Ambro. qui supra epistolam ad Cy. ait: Admone illos principibus & potestatibus subditos esse di.q.d. Si habes Imperium, spirituale tamen, admone illos subditos esse principibus, ducibus & potestatibus minoribus: quia Christiana religio nemine m priuat suo iure. Tum quia ante Christum & religionem Christianam fuit Imperator, quo tempore nullum superiorem habuit in temporalibus, ergo necaliquis successor eius habet aliquem hominem superiorem in temporalibus: & per consequens non est vasallus papæ. Unde si aliquis Imperator subiiceret se papæ recognoscendo tanquam vasallus papam superiorem in temporalibus, eo ipso renunciaret Imperio & potestati supremæ laicali; nec posset dici successor primi Imperatoris, nec Augustus vocari deberet, quia non augeret Imperium, sed quantum in eo esset destrueret. Quod autem Imperator proprietatem propriam supremæ potestati laicali non teneat ab alia potestate, posset hic apparentiam aliqualem habere: quia non videtur eam posse tenere de alia communitate quam de communitate Romanorum: de qua non potest veritatem habere: quia idem respectu eiusdem non potest esse vasallus & Dominus: præsertim eadem ratione vel causa, Romani autem inferiores & vasalli Imperatorum sunt, quorum ipse est Dominus: ergo nulla temporalia tenet ab eis immediate, ergo à Deo tertio modo habet proprietatem proprie propriam potestati supremæ laicali.
units.tr: There is another opinion, which holds that the secular power, the supreme power, has no property of its own from God in either the first or the second way, but only in the third way. For although it does have its rights through the gift of the Pope, and not from God's gift alone, the Pope did not merely ordain the empire as one supreme secular power, and the people do not elect the emperor, as the cardinals elect the Pope. He gave it nothing from his own goods. Rather, he ordained and established a supreme secular power and bestowed on it certain temporal goods from his own possessions. He gave these to the office, not to the person. Therefore the emperor cannot alienate them, except in certain cases, and if he does alienate them he is bound to restore them. His successor may and must recall them from whomever they were given. This consideration therefore contains two claims. The first is that the supreme power does not have its property from God in the first or second way, and that it has it immediately from God in the third way. For the first claim the following argument can be made. It must not be said that any office or person has property of its own immediately from God in the first or second way, unless this has been established beyond doubt by divine revelation, because it cannot be established by natural reason or experience. For since it is established by Scripture divinely revealed, as is found in Genesis 1, that the Lord God gave to the human race dominion over temporal things, and since it is not necessary that the appropriation of any things at all be made specifically by God alone without the consent and will of those to whom common dominion was given, it follows that we must not hold that any such appropriation was made by God alone without the will of those to whom common dominion had been given, unless this is established by divine revelation. In this way it is established that God set apart the land of the Canaanites as the land of promise and specifically bestowed it on the sons of Israel. In the same way we know that God gave other lands specifically to the sons of Israel, to Esau, to Aaron and to Moab, as is clear from Deuteronomy 1. But by no divine revelation is it established for us that God specifically gave or appropriated any goods to the empire or the supreme secular power, nor that he commanded that anything be specially appropriated to it, nor that the empire had any property from God alone beyond other kingdoms that existed before the empire. For we have nothing on this in the divine Scriptures, in which the divine gifts are recorded. Therefore we must hold that the empire does not have any property from God immediately in the first or second way. But perhaps someone would say that the empire's having property in this way from God immediately is found in the Gospel, where Christ said, Matthew 22: Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, etc. From these words it is gathered that Christ, who is true God, specifically commanded that certain things be given to Caesar; therefore Caesar had those things immediately from God, since they came from Christ. To this it is answered that by those words Christ gave nothing specifically to Caesar, but commanded that those things which had previously been granted to Caesar by human ordinance be returned to him. For this reason he did not say give to Caesar, but render, namely those things which are his own, that is, which had been conferred on him by men. For those who established him as emperor, or his predecessor, ordained by natural law or by human law what he ought to claim by reason of the supreme secular power, and Christ approved this. Now whoever approves establishes nothing new, just as whoever confirms grants no new right: see extra. de fi. instru. inter dilectos; extra de confirma. uti. c. cum dilecta, and c. examinata. The second claim this opinion holds is that the supreme secular power has power of its own immediately from God in the third way. For although at the beginning of the institution of the supreme secular power, God did not, either in person or by any spiritual command miraculously revealed to any men, but through men following natural equity, who considered that it was expedient for the commonwealth that one prince should preside over others in temporal matters, assign certain temporal goods to the supreme secular power, by which it might be able to exercise the office entrusted to it. So then it received the property not from God alone but also from men. Yet after that transfer it held those goods from God alone, and in respect of them it acknowledged God alone as superior. Assigning all that property and all the positive right which it possessed in them, it transferred them to the supreme power instituted by God through them. For this opinion the following argument can be made. If the supreme secular power were not immediately from God in this way, it would have some man or community superior to it in temporal matters, from whom or from which it held its temporal goods. But the supreme secular power holds its temporal goods neither from a man nor from a community. That it does not hold them from a man is clear: for if it held them from a man, and no other man could be named except the Pope, then it would hold them from the Pope. That this is false is shown even of the faithful and Christian emperor: for a successor enjoys the same right as his predecessor, see extra de regu. iuris, qui in iu. lib. 6. For it would not be a true succession if a true successor had less than his predecessor. But the faithful emperor succeeds an unfaithful emperor. Therefore he ought to use the same right that the unfaithful one used. But the unfaithful emperor did not hold his temporal goods from the Pope, since he was emperor before there was a Pope. Also, in the time of Christ the unfaithful emperor did not hold temporal goods from Christ, because Christ did not come to abolish the dominion of kings or emperors, as blessed Augustine testifies, who in his commentary on John, speaking to the kings of the world in the person of Christ, says: My kingdom is not of this world, that is, I do not hinder your dominion in the world, so that you may rage and fear in vain. Pope Leo agrees with this, saying: The Lord of the world, who gives the eternal kingdom, does not seek a temporal kingdom, which the Church seems to bear witness to when it sings of Christ: He who gives heavenly kingdoms does not snatch away mortal ones. Also, the Christian religion takes away no unbeliever's right, as blessed Ambrose testifies, who in his commentary on the epistle to Titus says: Admonish them to be subject to princes and powers, and: If you have an empire, though spiritual, admonish them to be subject to princes, leaders and lesser powers, because the Christian religion deprives no one of his right. Also, before Christ and the Christian religion there was an emperor, who at that time had no superior in temporal matters. Therefore some successor of his also has no man superior to him in temporal matters, and consequently is not a vassal of the Pope. Hence if any emperor were to submit himself to the Pope, acknowledging the Pope as his superior in temporal matters as a vassal, he would by that very act renounce the empire and the supreme secular power. He could not be called successor of the first emperor, nor ought he to be called Augustus, because he would not increase the empire but, as far as in him lay, would destroy it. That the emperor does not hold his own property of the supreme secular power from another power might seem somewhat doubtful here, since it does not seem that he can hold it from any community other than the community of the Romans. But this cannot be true, since the same person cannot be both vassal and lord of the same thing, especially for the same reason or cause. The Romans, however, are inferiors and vassals of the emperors, of whom he is lord. Therefore he holds no temporal goods immediately from them. Therefore he has property of his own in the supreme secular power from God in the third way.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Respondet primæ rationi cap. tertii.
units.tr: He replies to the first argument of chapter three.

units.la: VIsis rationibus in supradictis cap. præmissis, videndum est ad illa, quæ in contrarium allegantur, & primo ad illa, quæ supra, cap. 4. contra istam opinionem ultimam sunt adducta, ad quæ dicitur, quod imperium non est à papa: quia ab eodem fuit Imperium post adventum Christi & ante: sed ante non fuit Imperium à papa, sicut allegatum est supra, ergo nec vnquam postea fuit à papa. Sed ad primum argumentum, cum dicitur quod Christus dedit potestatem siue commisit beato Petro in terreni & cœlestis imperii. Ad 2. secundum Anthærium papa respondetur, quod verba Nicolai papæ aliter, quam prima facie sonare videntur, exponenda sunt, ne hæresim sapere videantur: quemadmodum & quædam alia eiusdem in e. c. cum sc. ait, illam, (scilicet Romanam ecclesiam) solam ipse instituit & fundauit & supra Petram fidei mox nascentis erexit. Et cum dicit: Omnes siue Patriarchæ cuiuslibet apicem, siue metropoleos primatus, aut episcopatuum cathedras, vel ecclesias cuiusque ordinis dignitatem confirmat Romana ecclesia, illam vero solus ipse fundauit: & supra Petram fidei mox nascentis erexit, &c. quæ Verba nisi sanius intelligantur, scripturis diuinis & sanctorum Patrum obuiare videntur: quia Christus non fundauit Romanam ecclesiam supra Petram fidei mox nascentis: quia Romana ecclesia non fuit fundata in principio fidei, nec ipsa alias fundauit ecclesias, ante enim Romanam ecclesiam fundatæ fuerunt plures ecclesiæ: ante etiam plures fuerunt ad ecclesiasticas dignitates assumpti. Nã ante Romanam ecclesiam fuit beatus Matthias ad apostolatus dignitatem electus, actor. 1. etiam Diaconi ante Romanam ecclesiam ab apostolis electi fuerunt, ibi ca. 6. ante Romanam ecclesiam beatus Paulus & Barnabas de præcepto Dei ad dignitatem apostolatus fuerunt sublimati, actuum 13. antequam Romana ecclesia potestatem haberet eligendi prælatos, Paulus & Barnabas per singulas ecclesias constituerunt presbyteros actor. 14. Romana ecclesia antequam aliquam auctoritatem haberet, Apostoli & seniores constituerunt concilium, actor. 15. Antequam Romana ecclesia potestatem instituendi prælatos haberet, dicit beatus Paulus, ut habetur actu. 20. maioribus natu, quos vocauerat de Epheso: Attendite vobis & vniuerso gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus posuit episcopos regere ecclesiam Dei, antequam Romana ecclesia primatum haberet, multiplicatæ fuerunt ecclesiæ Antiochiæ discipuli: ita ut primo Christiani vocarentur ibidem act. 11. Vnde & beatus Petrus ibidem habuit sedem, antequam Romæ, 24. q. 1. c. regamus, & ita ecclesia Antiochena prius instituit ecclesias & dignitates ecclesiasticas, quam Romana. Interpretationem itaque sanam opus adhibere verbis præscriptis Nicolai papæ, ut non contradicant aperte scripturis diuinis. Et consimiliter alia eius verba, q sequuntur, de iuribus terreni simul & cœlestis imperii commissis Petro, sane exponenda sunt, ne videantur sapere hæresim manifestam. Si vero intelligantur ut prima facie sonant, ex ipsis duo sequuntur errores, primus est, quod cœleste imperium est a papa: quia dicit Nicolaus, quod Christus iura cœlestis & terreni imperii commisit Petro. Sed constat quod dicere cœleste imperium esse a papa: maxime illo modo, quo quidam dicunt propter auctoritatem Nicolai papæ: aut terrenum imperium esse a papa, sic sc. quod habens terrenum imperium, tenet ipsum a papa in feudum, est erroneum: quia hæreticum esset dicere, quod aliquis tenet cœleste imperium a papa, sicut a domino, sicut isti dicunt: quia terrenum dominium est a papa, sicut a domino, cum papa sit solummodo clauiger cœlestis imperii, & nullatenus dominus. Secundus error qui sequitur ex verbis Nicolai est, sicut ipsa intelliguntur, quod omnia regna sunt a papa, quod in præiudicium omnium regum non facientium homagium papæ, multipliciter redundare dignoscitur, videretur enim Rex Franciæ periculose errare in fide, cum in temporalibus minime recognoscat superiorem, extra qui sit sunt le. c. per venerabilem. Dicunt itaque isti, quod aliter, quam sonant, intelligenda sunt verba Nicolai præscripta, unde dicunt quod secundum Gregor. in homelia communi de virginibus, quod regnum cœlorum non nunquam ecclesia militans debet intelligi, sic etiam per cœleste imperium specialiter boni in ecclesia militante possunt intelligi, quare etiam per terrenum imperium designantur specialiter mali in ecclesia: & sic, vt dicunt, intelligi debent verba prædicta: ut sc. Christus commiserit beato Petro potestatem aliquam super bonos & super malos in ecclesia. Aliter dicunt quidam, quod Nicolaus papa per cœleste imperium intelligit spirituales, quorum conuersatio est in cœlis: & per terrenum imperium terrenos secularibus negotiis implicitos, & super vtrosq; habet papa potestatem. Aliter dicunt, q Christus commisit Petro iura cœlestis imperii, in quantum habet in spiritualibus potestatem supra viatores prædestinatos sc. ad cœleste imperium, commisit iura terreni imperii, in quantum constituit eum superiorem in spiritualibus Imperatore terreno, quem etiam casualiter coercere potest. Sed sicut cœleste imperium nullus tenet a papa in feudum: ita etiam nullus tenet ab ipso terrenum imperium in feudum.
units.tr: Having set out the arguments in the chapters above, we must now turn to those objections that are brought against them. First, we take those that were raised above in chapter 4 against this last opinion, to which it is answered that the empire is not from the pope, because it was from God both after the coming of Christ and before it, yet before Christ it was not from the pope, as was shown above, and so it was never afterwards from the pope either. As for the first argument, where it is said that Christ gave or committed to the blessed Peter the power over the earthly and heavenly empire, and as for the second, which pope Anthærius (that is, Nicholas) answers, the words of Pope Nicholas must be explained differently from how they first seem to sound, lest they appear to savour of heresy. The same is true of certain other words of his in the same passage, where he says that the Roman Church alone was instituted and founded by him and set up upon the Rock of the newly born faith. And when he says: "The Roman Church confirms all, whether the summit of any patriarch, or the primacy of a metropolis, or the seats of bishoprics, or the dignity of churches of any order; but she alone was founded by him and set up upon the Rock of the faith as soon as it was born," and so on: unless these words are understood more soundly, they seem to oppose the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers. For Christ did not found the Roman Church upon the Rock of the newly born faith, since the Roman Church was not founded at the beginning of the faith, nor did it found other churches; for several churches were founded before the Roman Church, and several men were raised to ecclesiastical dignities before it.
