Before the Roman Church, the blessed Matthias was chosen to the dignity of the apostleship (actor. 1.); deacons too were chosen by the apostles before the Roman Church (ibi ca. 6.); before the Roman Church, the blessed Paul and Barnabas were raised by God's command to the dignity of the apostleship (actuum 13.); before the Roman Church had the power of choosing prelates, Paul and Barnabas appointed elders in each church (actor. 14.); before the Roman Church had any authority, the apostles and elders constituted a council (actor. 15.); and before the Roman Church had the power of appointing prelates, the blessed Paul said, as is recorded in actu. 20., to the elders whom he had called from Ephesus: Attendite vobis & vniuerso gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus posuit episcopos regere ecclesiam Dei (Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to feed the church of God). Before the Roman Church had the primacy, the churches of the disciples at Antioch were multiplied, so that the believers were first called Christians there (act. 11.). Hence also the blessed Peter had a see there before he had one at Rome (24. q. 1. c. regamus,). Thus the church of Antioch founded churches and ecclesiastical dignities before the Roman Church did. A sound interpretation is therefore needed for the words of Pope Nicholas quoted above, so that they do not plainly contradict the divine Scriptures. Likewise his other words that follow, about the rights of the earthly and heavenly empire together committed to Peter, must certainly be explained, lest they seem to savour of manifest heresy. But if they are understood as they first sound, two errors follow from them. The first is that the heavenly empire is from the pope, since Nicholas says that Christ committed the rights of the heavenly and earthly empire to Peter. But it is plain that to say the heavenly empire is from the pope, especially in the way that some say on the authority of Pope Nicholas, or that the earthly empire is from the pope, so that one who holds the earthly empire holds it from the pope in fief, is erroneous, because it would be heretical to say that anyone holds the heavenly empire from the pope as from a lord, as these men say; for earthly lordship is from the pope as from a lord, whereas the pope is only the keeper of the keys of the heavenly empire and by no means its lord. The second error that follows from Nicholas's words, if they are taken as they stand, is that all kingdoms are from the pope. This is seen to redound in many ways to the prejudice of all kings who do not perform homage to the pope, for the King of France would seem to err dangerously in the faith, since he acknowledges no superior in temporal matters (extra qui sit sunt le. c. per venerabilem.). These men therefore say that the words of Nicholas quoted above must be understood otherwise than they sound. Hence they say that, according to Gregory (in homelia communi de virginibus,), the kingdom of heaven must sometimes be understood as the church militant; so also the heavenly empire may be understood to mean specifically the good in the church militant, and for that reason the earthly empire designates specifically the wicked in the church. And so, they say, the foregoing words must be understood: namely, that Christ committed to the blessed Peter some power over the good and over the wicked in the church. Others say differently: that Pope Nicholas by the heavenly empire means spiritual persons, whose conversation is in heaven, and by the earthly empire the earthly people entangled in secular affairs, and that the pope has power over both. Others again say that Christ committed to Peter the rights of the heavenly empire insofar as the pope has power in spiritual matters over the pilgrims predestined to the heavenly empire, and committed the rights of the earthly empire insofar as he made him superior in spiritual matters to the earthly emperor, whom he can also coerce on occasion. But just as no one holds the heavenly empire from the pope in fief, so likewise no one holds the earthly empire from him in fief.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Respondet secundæ rationi tertii capituli.
units.tr: He replies to the second argument of the third chapter.

units.la: AD secundam allegationem, quæ in hoc consistit: quod papa ex ordinatione Christi, & non Imperator est caput primum, & supremus iudex cunctorum mortalium. Respondetur, quod hoc non continet veritatem. Cum quia contradicit scripturæ sacræ, dicēte Apostolo, 1. Cor. 5. in persona cunctorum fidelium: Quid enim mihi de his qui foris sunt iudicare. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod saltem papa est supremus iudex cunctorum fidelium: ergo papa est Imperatoris Iudex, si est fidelis. Hic triplicitêr respondetur. Vno modo dicitur, quod papa non est iudex cunctorum fidelium, nisi in spiritualibus, quæ ad eius pertinent potestatem: & ideo si auctoritate papali extra necessitatis casum & vtilitatis (quæ parificari debeat necessitati) aliquam sententiam tulerit in temporalibus, vel super temporalia, sententia nulla est ipso iure, tanquam a non suo iudice lata: quia in talibus non est Iudex: & si talia faceret, nulla esset illo iudice vel iure, iuxta regulam extra, de regulis iuris, libro sexto: Ea quæ à iudice sunt, si ad eius non spectant officium, viribus non subsistunt, non ergo papa, sed Imperator, non solum cunctorum fidelium sed etiam vniuersorum mortalium in his est Iudex supremus: ita etiam quod in his papa non est iudex, quia enim religio Christiana neminem priuat iure suo, vt dicit Ambro. secundum quod allegatum est supra: & fundatur in dicto Apostoli, qui primæ ad Cor. 7. ait, vnusquisq;, in qua vocatione vocatus est in ea permaneat, seruus vocatus es, nō sit tibi cura. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, q religio Christiana seruos infidelium à seruitute nō liberat, ne nomē Domini & doctrina blasphemetur, vt dicit Apostolus 1. Tim. 6. Multo fortius religio Christiana nō liberat assumptū ad papatum à subiectione, q fideli Domino tenebatur: qa, sicut dicit Apostolus, 1. Tim. 6. qui fideles habent dominos, nō contemnant, quia sunt fratres sed magis seruiant quia fideles sunt & dilecti &c. Imperator ergo Romanus est Iudex papæ, sicut & fuit ante papatum ipsius. Neque enim papa, neq; clerici alii exempti sunt à iurisdictione Imperatoris: & ita iure diuino remanent subiecti Imperatori, sicut prius, in his quæ Christianæ religionis obseruantiam & exercitationem officiorum, ad quæ assumuntur, non impediunt. In huiusmodi enim, quia magis oportet obedire Deo quam hominibus: sicut in potestatibus societatis humanæ maior potestas minori ad obediendum præponitur, ita Deus hominibus, dist.8. c. vlt. Nec conuersi Domino infideli: nec papa aut clerici Imperatori, vel alii infideli Domino, sunt subiecti. In aliis autem quantum est de iure diuino, subiecti sunt: & ideo libertatem maiorem, quam gaudent, habent ex iure humano solummodo. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod ista responsio contradictionem implicat, quod scilicet in casu necessitatis papa est iudex Imperatoris, & Imperator est iudex papæ, quæ sibiipsis sunt contraria: quia sequitur, quod idem respectu eiusdem sit superior & inferior: eo quod nemo potest iudicari nisi à superiori, dist.21.c.inferior. & c.submittitur. Hic respondetur, quod inconueniens est eundem eadem ratione respectu eiusdem rei esse pariter superiorem & inferiorem, sed eundem eodem modo regulariter esse inferiorem, & casualiter superiorem, non debet inconueniens reputari. Rex enim superior est toto regno: & tamen in casu est inferior regno: quia in casu necessitatis potest regem deponere & in castro detinere, hoc enim habetur ex iure naturali, sicut ex iure naturali habetur quod vim vi repellere licet: sicut etiam in multis religionibus prælati supremi sunt superiores cunctis fratribus ordinis sui, & tamen in aliquibus casibus generalia eorum capitula sunt superiora prælatis supremis; ita quod ipsos possunt absoluere, & ideo sicut in iure reperitur expresse, quod in multis casibus minor supplet negligentiam maioris: ita non est inconueniens, quod idem sit eodem regulariter inferior & casualiter superior: sicut delegatus sæpe ordinatione inferior est episcopo suo, qui tamen in casu delegato à papa potest esse superior. Et taliter respondetur ad illud, quod circa principium illius capituli assumitur, quod sc. papa est Iudex cunctorum fidelium. Dicitur enim, quod in temporalibus nemo est Iudex cunctorum fidelium, nemine excepto, quamuis enim Imperator sit supremus Iudex multitudinis fidelium: non tamen est Iudex supremus personæ papæ in temporalibus propter reuerentiam officii, quo fungitur papa, propter quod papa in spiritualibus est superior Imperatore, & modicum detrimentum est, si persona papæ non sit ei subiecta: eo quod modicum quid non nocet, nam modica res non inducit simoniam, extra, de simonia, & si quæstiones, iuri enim diuino congruit, etiam naturali, vt Imperator non sit iudex ordinarius papæ, & papa non est Iudex ordinarius in temporalibus Imperatoris, ideo in hoc nemo est Iudex summus siue supremus cunctorum fidelium, nemine excepto.
units.tr: To the second allegation, which holds that the Pope, by the ordinance of Christ and not the Emperor, is the first head and supreme judge of all mortals, the reply is that this is not true. First, it contradicts Holy Scripture, where the Apostle speaks in the person of all the faithful: 1. Cor. 5. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? But someone might say that at least the Pope is supreme judge of all the faithful, and therefore the Pope is judge of the Emperor, if the Emperor is faithful. Here there is a threefold answer. In one way it is said that the Pope is judge of all the faithful only in spiritual matters, which fall within his power. So if, by papal authority, outside the case of necessity and of utility (which must be treated as equal to necessity), he pronounces some sentence on temporal matters or concerning temporal things, that sentence is void in law, as pronounced by one who is not his judge, since in such matters he is not judge. If he did such things, they would have no force from that judge or from the law, according to the rule extra, de regulis iuris, in the sixth book: Those acts of a judge which do not belong to his office have no force. Therefore it is not the Pope but the Emperor who is supreme judge in these matters, not only of all the faithful but of all mortals. So too the Pope is not judge in these matters, because the Christian religion deprives no one of his right, as Ambrose said, as was cited above. This rests on the saying of the Apostle, who says in 1 Cor. 7: Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called; were you a slave when called? Let it not concern you. From these words it is gathered that the Christian religion does not free the slaves of unbelievers from servitude, lest the name of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed, as the Apostle says in 1. Tim. 6. Much more strongly, the Christian religion does not free one raised to the papacy from the subjection he owed to a faithful lord, since, as the Apostle says, 1. Tim. 6. Those who have faithful masters should not despise them, because they are brethren, but should rather serve them, because they are faithful and beloved, etc. Therefore the Roman Emperor is judge of the Pope, as he was also before the Pope's papacy. Neither the Pope nor other clergy are exempt from the Emperor's jurisdiction. So by divine right they remain subject to the Emperor, as before, in those matters which do not hinder the observance of the Christian religion and the exercise of the offices to which they are raised. In such matters we ought to obey God rather than men, just as in the powers of human society the greater power is set over the lesser for obedience; so God is set over men, dist.8. c. vlt. Neither a convert with an unbelieving lord, nor the Pope or clergy, are subject to the Emperor or to any other unbelieving lord. In other matters, however, they are subject by divine right, and so the greater liberty they enjoy they have from human law alone. But perhaps someone would say that this answer implies a contradiction: in a case of necessity the Pope is judge of the Emperor and the Emperor is judge of the Pope, which are contrary to each other, since it follows that the same person is both superior and inferior with respect to the same thing, because no one can be judged except by a superior, dist.21. c. inferior, & c. submittitur. Here it is answered that it is inconsistent for the same person to be equally superior and inferior to the same thing on the same ground. But for the same person to be inferior in the same way as a general rule, and superior in a particular case, should not be counted an inconsistency. A king is superior to the whole kingdom, and yet in a case he is inferior to the kingdom, because in a case of necessity it is lawful to depose the king and keep him in prison. This follows from natural law, just as it follows from natural law that force may be repelled by force. Likewise in many religious orders the supreme prelates are superior to all the brethren of their order, and yet in some cases their general chapters are superior to the supreme prelates, so that they can absolve them. And just as the law expressly provides that in many cases the lesser makes up for the negligence of the greater, so it is not inconsistent that the same person should be inferior as a rule and superior in a particular case. A delegate, for instance, is often by ordinary arrangement inferior to his bishop, yet in a case delegated by the Pope he can be superior. This is also the answer to what is assumed near the beginning of that chapter, namely that the Pope is judge of all the faithful. It is said that in temporal matters no one is judge of all the faithful, with no exception. For although the Emperor is supreme judge of the multitude of the faithful, he is not supreme judge of the person of the Pope in temporal matters, on account of the reverence due to the office the Pope holds. For this reason the Pope is superior to the Emperor in spiritual matters, and it is a small loss if the Pope's person is not subject to him, since a small matter does no harm; a trifling thing does not make simony, extra, de simonia, & si quæstiones. It is in accordance with divine law, and even natural law, that the Emperor should not be the ordinary judge of the Pope, nor the Pope the ordinary judge of the Emperor in temporal matters. Therefore in this matter no one is the highest or supreme judge of all the faithful, with no exception.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Respondet tertiæ rationi cap. tertii.
units.tr: Answer to the third argument, cited in chapter 3.

units.la: AD tertiam allegationem adductam supra, cap. 3. cum accipitur, quod papa potest Imperatorem deponere. Respondetur quod sicut papa regulariter deponere alios reges non potest à potestate concessa sibi à Christo: ita non potest regulariter deponere Imperatorem, quantumcunq; sit dignus deponi propter defectum quemcunq; vel crimen, quod non est inter spiritualia diuina computandum. Et ideo si Imperator committat crimen dilapidationis vel destructionis imperii aut damnabilis negligentiæ in periculum imperii tyrannidis, vel quodcunque aliud deponere dignissimum, Romani vel illi, in quos suam potestatem Romani dederunt, debent ipsum deponere, & non papa, nisi illi, ad quos spectat, sibi suam potestatem tribuerunt, vel nisi illi ad quos spectat, nollent vel non possent facere iustitiæ complementum: & talis immineret casus, in quo necesse esset talem circa Imperatorem iustitiam exerceri. Illud autem decretum, 15. q. 6. c. alius, non facit ad propositum, vt videtur: quia non loquitur de Imperatore, sed de rege Franciæ, qui tamen superiorem in talibus minime recognoscit: quia non solum rex, sed regnicolæ communiter tenent, quod papa auctoritate propria non possit regem eorum extra casum necessitatis aliis non negligentibus deponere: & ideo papa, vt dicitur, proprie non deposuit regem Francorum, sed, vt dicit Glos. dicitur deposuisse, quia de ponentibus consensit, laudando eorum factum & propositum, & consulendo vt non timerent in hoc potestatem suam contra regem pro communi vtilitate omnino exercere. Illi igitur Franci dubii forsitan de propria potestate papam tanquam sapientiorem, quam ipsi essent seu haberent, (nondum enim erat studium Parisius) consulebant & interrogabant, an eis secundum Deum liceret suum regem deponere. Nostris autem temporibus quidam de potestate sua nullatenus dubitantes regem suum deposuerunt, papa nullatenus requisito. Vt enim dicunt isti, nec instituere nec destituere regem spectat ad papam: quando ipsis circa institutionem, destitutionem regum suorum non interueniunt pericula: nec sunt damnabiliter negligentes. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod Innocentius 3. Ottonem quartum & Innoc. 4. deposuit Fridericum Imperatorem. Hic triplíciter respondetur, quidam enim dicunt, quod Innoc. 3. & Innoc. 4. illas depositiones fecerunt auctoritate Romanorum, ad quos spectat correctio Imperatoris. Idcirco quod Principes Alemanniæ, quibus datum est ius eligendi Imperatores à Romanis, circa Imperatoris correctionem fuerunt damnabiliter negligentes. Alii dicunt quod simpliciter Innoc. 4. auctoritate concilii generalis deposuit Fridericum, quia in casu hæresis simpliciter habet potestatem super omnes Christianos. Alii dicunt, quod vterque male processit vsurpando sibi potestatem, quam non habuit: sicut saepe faciunt Romani pontifices, vt dicit Gloss. de foro compe. super c. si clericus, dicens in haec verba, papa, siue sint negligentes laici siue non, quotidie concedit literas clericis contra laicos supra quacunque quaestione: & ita vsurpat iurisdictionem aliorum: contra illud quod dicitur supra cap. proximo. nouit. in principio, propter quam vsurpationem dicunt ordinem Christianitatis esse confusum: quia omnis ordo confunditur, si vnicuique sua iurisdictio non seruatur, vt testantur canonicae sanctiones, ii. q. i. peruenit. Ex ista enim vsurpatione dicunt populorum strages, vastationes regionum, ciuitatum & terrarum & alias desolationes auctoritate praedicti Innocentii 4. in Italia accidisse, de quo, quicquid fuerit de Friderico, sc. siue haereticus siue laicus fuerit, dicunt quod contra Fridericum ediderit decretalem vel scripturam compluribus contra fidem erroribus inexcusabilibus firmatam. Quod autem dicunt quidam a centum annis & citra in regionibus Galliae siue Hispaniae & in maiori Britannia per supremum pontificem a gente in gentem dominia esse translata, apertissimum est mendacium, non enim in maiori Britannia, neque quoad ipsam neque quo ad Scotiam eidem subiectam, facta est per ipsum quaecunque translatio: nec etiam illi de maiori Britannia in aliqua translatione vel destitutione, nec institutione supremum pontificem requirere voluerunt: & multa alia, quorum quaedam ecclesiae libertatibus & clericorum derogare videntur, quae contra expressas diffinitiones, ordinationes & statuta summorum pontificum in maiori Britannia fiunt, vt nonnullis apparet. Quod autem in Hispania de translatione regni Aragoniae per supremum pontificem extitit attentatum, iniquum fuisse putatur a multis, & nullatenus potuit ad effectum produci.
units.tr: As for the third argument adduced above in chapter 3, when it is taken that the Pope can depose the Emperor, the answer is this. Just as the Pope cannot as a rule depose other kings by the power given to him by Christ, so he cannot as a rule depose the Emperor, however worthy he may be of deposition on account of some defect or crime, since such a matter is not to be reckoned among things divine and spiritual. Therefore, if the Emperor commits the crime of squandering or destroying the empire, or culpable negligence to the peril of the empire, or tyranny, or any other thing deserving of deposition, it is the Romans, or those to whom the Romans have given their power, who ought to depose him, and not the Pope, unless those to whom the matter belongs have granted him their power, or unless those to whom it belongs are unwilling or unable to carry out the full measure of justice; and if such a case were imminent, in which justice would have to be exercised against the Emperor in this way. But that decree, 15 q. 6 c. alius, does not seem to bear on the point, because it does not speak of the Emperor but of the king of France, who nevertheless recognises no superior in such matters: for not only the king but also the subjects of the kingdom commonly hold that the Pope, by his own authority, cannot depose their king outside a case of necessity where the others are not negligent. And so the Pope, as is said, did not properly depose the king of the French, but, as the Gloss says, is said to have deposed him, because he consented to those deposing, praising their deed and purpose, and advising them not to fear to exercise his power entirely against the king for the common good. Those Franks, perhaps doubting about their own power, consulted and asked the Pope, as wiser than themselves or than they were (for there was not yet a university at Paris), whether it was lawful for them before God to depose their king. In our own times, however, certain men, in no way doubting their power, deposed their king, without any request to the Pope at all. For as they say, it does not belong to the Pope either to install or to remove a king, when no dangers arise for them concerning the installation or deposition of their kings, nor are they culpably negligent. But perhaps someone would say that Innocent III deposed Otto IV and Innocent IV deposed the Emperor Frederick. Here there is a threefold answer. Some say that Innocent III and Innocent IV made those depositions by the authority of the Romans, to whom the correction of the Emperor belongs; and that the princes of Germany, to whom the right of electing emperors had been given by the Romans, were culpably negligent in the correction of the Emperor. Others say that Innocent IV simply deposed Frederick by the authority of a general council, because in a case of heresy he has power over all Christians without qualification. Others say that both proceeded wrongly, usurping a power they did not have; as the Roman pontiffs often do, as the Gloss says on de foro competenti, super c. si clericus, saying in these words: "the Pope, whether the laity are negligent or not, every day grants letters to clerics against laymen on whatever question; and so he usurps the jurisdiction of others, contrary to what is said above in the chapter next before, nouit, at the beginning." On account of this usurpation, they say, the order of Christendom is thrown into confusion, because every order is confused if each one's jurisdiction is not preserved, as the canonical sanctions attest, ii q. i peruenit. From this usurpation, they say, came the slaughter of peoples and the devastation of regions, cities and lands, and other desolations in Italy, by the authority of the aforesaid Innocent IV; concerning whom, whatever may be said of Frederick, whether he was a heretic or a layman, they say that against Frederick he issued a decretal or writing confirmed with many inexcusable errors against the faith. As for what some say, that for a hundred years and more in the regions of Gaul or Spain and in Greater Britain, dominions have been transferred from people to people by the supreme pontiff, this is most manifestly a lie: for in Greater Britain, neither in respect of itself nor of Scotland, which is subject to it, has any such transfer been made by him; nor did those of Greater Britain ever wish to ask the supreme pontiff for any transfer, deposition or installation; and there are many other things, some of which seem to detract from the liberties of the Church and of the clergy, which are done in Greater Britain contrary to the express definitions, ordinances and statutes of the supreme pontiffs, as seems clear to some. As for what was attempted in Spain concerning the transfer of the kingdom of Aragon by the supreme pontiff, it is thought by many to have been unjust, and it could in no way be brought into effect.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Respondet quartae rationi cap. tertii.
units.tr: Replies to the fourth argument of the third chapter.

units.la: AD quartam allegationem inductam cum dicitur, quod papa potest transferre imperium de vna gente in aliam: diuersimode respondetur. Vno modo, quod papa potest hoc casualiter, quia non est alius. Aliter dicitur, quod distinguendum est, quia aut imperium transferendum est a gente in gentem propter aliquod crimen speciale gentis, a qua est imperium transferendum: puta si gens illa inficiatur prauitate haeretica vel ad legem Iudaeorum, ad ritum vel sectam gentilitatis, vel sectam aliam conuertatur, aut propter aliud simile: vel populi, qui crimen seculare aut negligentiam vel desectum alium, propter quod etiam iudicio sapientum gentilium vel non Christianorum gens illa non esset digna alios gubernare. Si transferendum sit imperium propter crimen aliquod speciale; dicunt quidam, quod papa potest ex iure diuino transferre imperium, cum ipse in spiritualibus & annexis eis habeat plenitudinem potestatis, quantum ad ea quae sunt de necessitate facienda. Alii dicunt, quod papa in hoc casu non potest transferre imperium, nisi laici fuerint damnabiliter negligentes vel fauentes genti, a qua necesse est transferre imperium: sed in hoc casu ad papam spectat de crimine speciali cognoscere vel denunciare eis ad quos spectat vt ipsum deponant, nisi ipsi voluerint committere papae potestatem suam in hac parte. Si autem illi noluerint, vel non potuerint transferre imperium, in hoc casu iure diuino devoluta est potestas transferendi imperium ad summum pontificem, ex hoc quod ipse plenitudinem habet potestatis quantum ad omnia, quae de necessitate sunt facienda, saluis iuribus & libertatibus aliorum non negligentium ea, quae ad ipsos spectant in dispendium boni communis, papa autem iuxta canonem illum, ii. quaestione. i. te quidem, qui specialiter loquitur de papa, & plures alii, qui in scriptura Dei sunt fundati: & exemplis Christi & Apostolorum roborati: de secularibus negotiis, nisi propter defectum laicorum, se intromittere nullatenus deberet. Et hinc est, vt quaedam assertio dicit, si a Romanis esset imperium transferendum ex causa manifesta, ista translatio facienda esset per laicos, non per papam; nisi laici essent damnabiliter negligentes: quod tamen admonere deberet; quia admonitio simplex, non multum eum a spiritualibus curis distraheret. Si vero imperium transferendum esset a gente in gentem propter crimen aliquod speciale, vel damnabilem negligentiam, vel propter defectum quemcunque seculararem, papa auctoritate propria talem translationem non potest facere, nisi Romani omnes essent damnabiliter negligentes. Qualiter autem fuit processum per papam, cum imperium fuit translatum a Romanis de Graecis, in Germanos, an iuste an iniuste processerit, posset per certitudinem iste solus scire, quia acta temporis illius haberet: & tunc per processum, quantum ad omnia quae concernebant translationem, cognosceret: licet pro facto papae praesumendum sit, quod non possit probari contrarium: quemadmodum pro quocunque iudice praesumendum sit donec probetur contrarium, extra de renun. in praesentia. propter hoc dicunt quidam, qui dictam decretalem non viderunt, quod papa absque iusta causa vel auctoritate, cum non ex commissione neque propter negligentiam translationem facere potuit: nec ex iusta causa eam facere attentauit, falcem suam praesumpsit damnabiliter in messem mittere alienam. Si autem causa manifesta exigens eam fecerit ex commissione vel assensu vel auctoritate Romanorum, vel ipsi Romani in faciendo eam fuerunt damnabiliter negligentes, iuste processit: quia in tanta necessitate poterat supplere negligentiam eorundem, & ita solummodo casualiter & non regulariter potest transferre imperium, licet sit imperium transferendum. Quod autem dicunt quidam, tenentes Papam regulariter posse transferre non solum imperium, sed etiam omnia alia regna. Respondetur quod in Gallia non videtur talis translatio fuisse facta à quingentis annis & citra, &c.
units.tr: To the fourth argument, where it is said that the pope can transfer empire from one nation to another, answers are given in different ways. One way is this: the pope can do so by accident, because there is no one else who can. Another way holds that a distinction must be made. Either the empire is to be transferred from one nation to another on account of some special crime of the nation from which it is to be transferred, for example if that nation is infected with heretical depravity, or is converted to the law of the Jews, to the rite or sect of the Gentiles, or to some other sect, or on account of something similar; or on account of a people's secular crime, or negligence, or some other defect, by reason of which that nation, even in the judgment of wise Gentiles or non-Christians, would not be worthy to govern others. If the empire is to be transferred on account of some special crime, some say that the pope can transfer it by divine right, since in spiritual matters and those connected with them he has the fullness of power, so far as things that must of necessity be done are concerned. Others say that in this case the pope cannot transfer the empire, unless the laity are culpably negligent or favour the nation from which the empire must be taken. In this case, however, it belongs to the pope to take cognizance of the special crime, or to denounce it to those to whom it belongs, so that they may depose the offender, unless they themselves are willing to commit their power to the pope in this matter. If, however, they are unwilling or unable to transfer the empire, then in this case the power to transfer it has devolved by divine right upon the supreme pontiff, because he has the fullness of power in all things that must of necessity be done, saving the rights and liberties of others who are not negligent in those matters that belong to them, to the detriment of the common good. The pope, however, according to that canon, ii. quaestione. i. te quidem, which speaks specifically of the pope, and several others founded in the Scripture of God and confirmed by the examples of Christ and the Apostles, ought in no way to meddle in secular affairs, except on account of the default of the laity. Hence a certain assertion says that if the empire were to be transferred from the Romans for a manifest cause, the transfer would have to be made by the laity, not by the pope, unless the laity were culpably negligent; and even then he ought to admonish them, since a simple admonition would not greatly distract him from spiritual cares. But if the empire were to be transferred from nation to nation on account of some special crime, or culpable negligence, or any secular defect whatever, the pope cannot make such a transfer by his own authority, unless all the Romans were culpably negligent. As for how the proceeding was carried out by the pope when the empire was transferred from the Romans, from the Greeks, to the Germans, and whether it proceeded justly or unjustly, one could know this for certain only by having the records of that time; through those proceedings one would learn everything that concerned the transfer. Yet for a pope's act it must be presumed that the contrary cannot be proved, just as for any judge it must be presumed until the contrary is proved, extra de renun. in praesentia. For this reason some, who have not seen the said decretal, say that the pope, lacking a just cause or authority, since he could make the transfer neither by commission nor on account of negligence, and did not attempt it for a just cause, presumed culpably to put his sickle into another's harvest. But if he made it, prompted by a manifest cause, by commission, assent or authority of the Romans, or if the Romans themselves were culpably negligent in making it, he proceeded justly: because in so great a necessity he could supply their negligence, and so he can transfer the empire only by accident and not as a rule, although the empire is to be transferred. As for what some say, holding that the pope can as a rule transfer not only the empire but all other kingdoms, the answer is that in Gaul no such transfer seems to have been made for five hundred years and more, etc.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Respondet quintae rationi capituli tertii.
units.tr: Answer to the fifth argument of the third chapter.

units.la: AD quintam allegationem 3. cap. cum dicitur, ab illo est imperium, à quo Imperator postquam electus est examinatur & inungitur, consecratur & coronatur: dicitur hic, quod hoc non continet veritatem: quia nec per examinationem nec per consecrationem potest ostendi, quod imperium sit à Papa: nec quod in temporalibus Imperator sit inferior Papa, nec quod propter confirmari à Papa sit dicendus inferior in temporalibus. Sed an existimandus sit indigere confirmari à Papa, diversimode dicitur à diversis. Dicunt enim quidam, quod electio personae electae in regem Romanorum ad ecclesiam pertinet: non ad hunc finem, ut approbetur vel reprobetur electio vel electi persona: vel etiam ad hunc finem, ut possit approbatione ab eadem ecclesia habita administrare: cum ex electione concordi, vel à maiori parte principum electione sibi facta illud sibi competat, sed ad finem ut corrigat eum de criminibus notoriis, praesertim gravibus à se commissis, de quibus poenitentiam non egit: & si correctionem contempserit nolendo agere poenitentiam de peccatis seu criminibus eius ad requestam ecclesiae tunc denegare potest unctionem & coronationem imperialem, vel aliter contra ipsum procedere: Sed quando quis electus est à minore parte principum, tunc Papa posset reprobare talem electionem & ipsum electum: hoc est, declarare ipsum non habere ius, alii dicunt, quod examinatio illa non fit à Papa ad hunc finem: puta propterea, ut Papa corrigat electum de criminibus quibuscunque, nisi forte per accidens & ex consequenti: sed ut sciat an debeat ipsum pro Imperatore habere: ut sciat aliis, si necesse fuerit, per certitudinem indicare, quod ei sicut vero Imperatori obedire teneantur: non ut ei aliquam tribuat potestatem, sed coronam imperialem tantummodo, si electus eam voluerit ab ipso recipere. Quemadmodum illi, ad quos mittitur legatus, examinat litteras eius: & tamen legato nullam conferunt potestatem, nec de alio quo crimine corrigunt eum: sed ut sciant solummodo an debeant ei obedire, ut colligi potest ex canon. 97. distinctione. nobilissimus. ubi dicit Glossa: legati sine periculo non recipiuntur. unde maior in eis est facienda examinatio. sic etiam, ut habetur extra de crimine falsi, ad falsariorum, qui litteras Papales recipiunt, illas examinare debent, non tanquam ut superiores approbent vel reprobent eas, vel aliquid tribuant eis potestatis vel vigoris, sed ut sciant isti an sint verae; ne in periculum suum litteris falsis vtantur. Sicut quando electio supremi Pontificis representabatur examinanda Imperatori. Frustra enim esset repraesentatio illa, nisi ut examinaret Imperator electionem summi Pontificis non ut eam tanquam superior in hoc approbaret: nec ut aliquam tribueret potestatem, quantum ad illa, quae commisit Christus beato Petro, sed ut sciret an esset vere & rite electus: & an ipsum tanquam verum Papam deberet ab haereticis & schismaticis & aliis malevolis defensare, teste Gratiano, qui distinctione 63. ait: principibus vero aut Imperatoribus electiones Romanorum Pontificum atque aliquorum episcoporum referendas usus & constitutio in ecclesia tradidit, pro schismaticorum atque haereticorum dissensionibus, quibus nonnunquam ecclesia Dei commissa periclitabatur, contra quos legibus fidelissimorum Imperatorum ecclesia munita legitur. Sic ergo videtur quibusdam, quod alii reges inunguntur consecrantur & coronantur ab episcopis, vel archiepiscopis, à quibus tamen regna sua tenent minime, &c.
units.tr: As for the fifth citation from chapter 3, where it is said, "The empire is from him by whom the Emperor, after he has been elected, is examined and anointed, consecrated and crowned": it is said here that this does not contain the truth, because neither by the examination nor by the consecration can it be shown that the empire is from the Pope, nor that in temporal matters the Emperor is inferior to the Pope, nor that he is to be considered inferior in temporal matters because he is confirmed by the Pope. But whether he is to be thought to need confirmation by the Pope, different people speak differently. For some say that the choosing of the person elected as King of the Romans pertains to the Church, not for this purpose, that the election or the person of the elected be approved or rejected, nor even for this purpose, that he may be able to administer by the approval received from the same Church, since that belongs to him by a harmonious election or by the election made for him by the greater part of the princes; but for the purpose that it may correct him for notorious crimes, especially grave ones committed by him, for which he has not done repentance; and if he has despised the correction, refusing to do penance for his sins or crimes at the request of the Church, then it may refuse him the imperial anointing and coronation, or otherwise proceed against him. But when someone has been elected by the lesser part of the princes, then the Pope could reject such an election and the one elected, that is, declare that he has no right. Others say that this examination is not made by the Pope for this purpose, namely so that the Pope may correct the elected man for any crimes whatsoever, unless perhaps by accident and as a consequence; but so that he may know whether he ought to hold him as Emperor, so that he may be able to indicate to others, if it is necessary, with certainty, that they are bound to obey him as the true Emperor; not that he may confer on him any power, but only the imperial crown, if the elected man is willing to receive it from him. Just as those to whom a legate is sent examine his letters, and yet they confer on the legate no power, nor do they correct him for any other crime, but only so that they may know whether they ought to obey him, as can be gathered from the canon 97, distinction "Nobilissimus", where the Gloss says: legates are not received without danger; hence a greater examination is to be made of them. So too, as is found in the title on forgery, concerning those who receive papal letters, the forgers ought to examine them, not as superiors who approve or reject them, or grant them any authority or force, but so that they themselves may know whether they are genuine, lest they use false letters to their own peril. Just as when the election of the supreme Pontiff was presented to the Emperor to be examined. For that presentation would be pointless, unless the Emperor examined the election of the supreme Pontiff not so that he might approve it as superior in this matter, nor so that he might confer any power upon him as to those things which Christ committed to the blessed Peter, but so that he might know whether he had truly and duly been elected, and whether he ought to defend him as the true Pope against heretics, schismatics and other ill-disposed persons; as Gratian witnesses, who in distinction 63 says: "Yet to princes or emperors the usage and constitution in the Church have handed down that the elections of the Roman Pontiffs and of certain bishops are to be referred, on account of the dissensions of schismatics and heretics, by which at times the Church of God was endangered, against whom the Church is read to have been fortified by the laws of the most faithful emperors." Thus it seems to some that other kings are anointed, consecrated and crowned by bishops or archbishops, from whom nevertheless they do not hold their kingdoms at all, etc.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Respondet ad sextam rationem cap. 3.
units.tr: Responds to the sixth argument, chapter 3.

units.la: AD sextam allegationem 6. 3. Respondetur diversimode à diversis. Quidam enim dicunt, quod Imperator non tenetur iurare tanquam vasallus Imperatori: praesertim pro praediis, civitatibus, castris & villis, & omnibus aliis quae superabundant ultra illa, quae sibi necessaria sunt pro sua sustentatione honorifica & executione sui officii, de quibus etiam caeteri clerici tenentur tributum reddere Imperatori. Nam ab imperiali dignitate huiusmodi immunitatem obtinent, quam dare potest Imperator, si non fuerit in notabile imperii detrimentum, omnibus sacerdotibus. Dixit enim Christus Matthaei 22. Reddite quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari. Et Apostolus Romanor. 13. universis praecepit fidelibus: Reddite omnibus debita: cui tributum, tributum; cui vectigal, vectigal, &c. Aliter dicitur, quod nec Imperator Papae, nec Papa Imperatori iuramentum fidelitatis & homagii praestare tenetur. Ad illud autem quod adducitur 63. dist. c. tibi Domino. Respondetur, quod illud iuramentum non erat iuramentum fidelitatis & homagii, sed fidelis defensionis; quale iuramentum praestant alii reges in regnis suis iurantes ք fideliter defendet ecclesiam, qui tamen ab ecclesia non tenent sua regna in feudum. Sed quaereret aliquis, an Imperator teneatur huiusmodi iuramentum fidelis defensionis praestare? Quidam dicunt, ք Imperator in coronatione sua vel ante, tale iuramentum summo Pontifici tenetur pbere: aliis tenentibus quod ad hoc nō tenetur. Etsi fecerit ex devotione vel simplicitate vel alia causa quacunque, successores suos ad hoc non poterit obligare, cum non habeat imperium par in parem, licet enim Imperator sit Papalis advocatus, id est defensor Romanæ ecclesiæ, sicut & patroni ecclesiæ vel ecclesiarum sunt advocati, id est defensores earum, tamen in nullo est Imperator magis subiectus Papæ quam alii. Alii autem reges ad hoc iuramentum minime obligantur, ergo nec Imperator. Ulterius sic, vnus qui succedit alteri, iure eo vti debet, quo succedit alterius dignitati: & libertatibus gaudere debet, quibus ille gaudebat. Sed Imperator Romanus succedit in iuribus Romanorum Imperatorum, tam fidelium quam infidelium, qui hac libertate gaudebant: & hoc iuramentum præstare non tenebantur, ergo & Imperator nunc huiusmodi iuramentum nullatenus tenetur exhibere, vt satis iam ostensum videtur.
units.tr: Responses to the sixth objection (6.3) vary from one writer to another. Some say that the Emperor is not bound to swear as a vassal to the Emperor (that is, the Pope), especially for estates, cities, castles, villages and all other possessions beyond those that are necessary for his honourable maintenance and the discharge of his office; the other clergy too are bound to pay tribute to the Emperor for these. For they hold such immunity from the imperial dignity, which the Emperor can grant to all priests, provided it is not to the notable detriment of the empire. For Christ said in Matthew 22: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's"; and the Apostle in Romans 13 commanded all the faithful: "Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom," etc. Others say that neither the Emperor is bound to give an oath of fealty and homage to the Pope, nor the Pope to the Emperor. As for what is adduced from Dist. 63, c. Tibi Domino, the answer is that this oath was not an oath of fealty and homage but of faithful defence, such as other kings swear in their kingdoms, promising to defend the Church faithfully, though they do not hold their kingdoms in fief from the Church. But someone might ask whether the Emperor is bound to make such an oath of faithful defence? Some say that the Emperor is bound to make this oath to the supreme Pontiff at his coronation or before it; others hold that he is not bound to it. Even if he has done so out of devotion, simplicity or some other cause whatever, he cannot oblige his successors to it, since he has no authority over an equal, for although the Emperor is the Papal advocate, that is, defender of the Roman Church, just as the patrons of a church or churches are their advocates, that is, their defenders, nevertheless the Emperor is in no way more subject to the Pope than others are. Other kings are not bound at all to this oath; therefore neither is the Emperor. Furthermore: one who succeeds another ought to use the right by which he succeeds to the other's dignity, and ought to enjoy the liberties which that man enjoyed. But the Roman Emperor succeeds to the rights of the Roman Emperors, both faithful and unfaithful, who enjoyed this liberty and were not bound to make this oath; therefore the Emperor now is in no way bound to render such an oath, as has now been sufficiently shown.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Respondet septimæ allegationi capituli tertii.
units.tr: He responds to the seventh argument of the third chapter.

units.la: AD septimam rationem adductam tertio cap. dicitur, quod Papa non habet regulariter vtrumque gladium materialem, scil. temporalem & spiritualem: licet habet vtrumque in casu. Nec ad hoc probandum sufficiunt verba illa Luc. 22. Ecce gladii duo hic, quod proferentes ista verba intelligebant ea de duobus gladiis materialibus secundum literam, quia intelligere ipsa de gladio materiali & spirituali esset mystice interpretari ipsa, sensus autem mysticus non est proprie intellectus aliquorum verborum Scripturæ diuinæ. Et ad confirmandum ea, quæ in contentione veniunt, adduci non possunt nisi per alia verba scripturæ, vel per aliam rationem euidentem aperte probetur. Ad probandum autem, quod Papa habet gladium vtrumque, aliam probationem oportet inuenire. Ad Innocentii Tertii adductionem dicitur, quod eius verba admitti non debent, cum errorem contineant manifestum, scilicet quod nemo, nisi qui intra ecclesiam est, aliquem gladium, id est aliquam potestatem habet, eo quod potestas gladii materialis vere & de iure non solum intra, sed etiam extra ecclesiam valet reperiri. Verè enim infideles potestatem gladii materialis habebant, licet ea fuerunt frequenter abusi: sed abusus potestatis veram & legitimam potestatem non excludit. Neq; valet dicere, quod Imperator ipse accipit gladium à summo Pontifice in vagina, quem eximit & vibrat: quod hoc facere non tenetur: quia quamuis non faceret, verus Imperator existeret. Nec valet dicere, quod Dominus dicit Petro: Converte gladium tuum in vaginam, non alienam, sed tuam. Non enim propter hoc quod dicitur vaginam tuam, innuitur quod Petrus habuit gladium materialem, licet per seipsum non debuit exercere: quod illa verba Christi ad literam debent intelligi de gladio, quem Petrus per seipsum exercuerat, antequam esset Pontifex supremus: & per consequens nisi per alium locum Scripturæ ac rationem insolubilem aperte probetur, ad auctoritatem de Gratiano confirmandam adduci non potest.
units.tr: To the seventh argument adduced in the third chapter it is said that the Pope does not ordinarily possess both swords, the material, namely the temporal, and the spiritual, although he does possess both in a particular case. Nor are those words of Luke 22 sufficient to prove this: "Behold, here are two swords." Those who uttered these words understood them literally, of two material swords, because to understand them of a material and a spiritual sword would be to interpret them mystically, and a mystical sense is not the proper meaning of certain words of divine Scripture. Moreover, to confirm points that are in dispute, nothing can be adduced except by other words of Scripture, or else it must be clearly proved by some other evident reason. But to prove that the Pope possesses both swords, another proof must be found. As to the citation from Innocent III, it is said that his words ought not to be admitted, since they contain a manifest error, namely that no one except one who is within the Church has any sword, that is, any power; for the power of the material sword truly and by right can be found not only within but also outside the Church. Indeed, the unbelievers truly had the power of the material sword, although they frequently abused it; but the abuse of a power does not exclude a true and lawful power. Nor is it valid to say that the Emperor himself receives the sword from the supreme Pontiff in its scabbard, and draws it out and brandishes it, which he is not bound to do; for even if he did not do so, he would still be a true Emperor. Nor is it valid to say that the Lord says to Peter: "Put up your sword into its sheath," not someone else's sheath, but your own. For it is not implied by the words "your sheath" that Peter had a material sword, although he ought not to have wielded it himself; those words of Christ must be understood literally of the sword which Peter himself had wielded before he became the supreme Pontiff. Consequently, unless it is clearly proved by another passage of Scripture and by an unanswerable reason, it cannot be adduced to confirm the authority drawn from Gratian.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Respondet octavæ & nonæ allegationibus capitulo tertio adductis.
units.tr: He answers the eighth and ninth arguments adduced in the third chapter.

units.la: AD octavam rationem eiusdem capituli respondetur, quod nequaquam ab illo est imperium, ad quem se habet Imperator, vt filius ad patrem, sicut discipulus ad magistrum, sicut plumbum ad aurum, quia has comparationes non habet Imperator, ad quemcunque hominem purum propter suum terrenum imperium, vel saltem propter temporalia, sed propter spiritualia, in quibus ipse subiectus est. Consimiliter respondetur ad nonam negando, quod imperium est ab illo, cui tenetur Imperator caput submittere, vnde si per verba Valentiniani probari posset, quod imperium esset à Papa, probaretur per ipsum, quod imperium est ab episcopo Mediolanensi, quod de illo protulit Valentinianus verba illa.
units.tr: To the eighth argument of that same chapter it is answered that the empire is by no means from him to whom the Emperor stands in the relation of a son to a father, of a disciple to a master, or of lead to gold; for the Emperor does not hold these comparisons toward any man as such, on account of his earthly empire, or at least on account of temporal things, but on account of spiritual things, in which he himself is subject. Likewise, to the ninth, it is answered by denying that the empire is from him to whom the Emperor is bound to submit his head. Hence, if it could be proved by the words of Valentinian that the empire was from the Pope, it would be proved by the same words that the empire was from the bishop of Milan, concerning whom Valentinian uttered those words.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: Respondet decimæ & vltimæ rationi cap. tertii.
units.tr: Answers the tenth and last argument of chapter three.

units.la: AD decimam rationem respondetur, quod Papa vacante imperio, præsertim si non fuerit vicarius alius imperii ab Imperatore, vel etiam Romanis, vel ab illis quibus Romani contulerunt potestatem, assumpsit, quam tamen assumere debuisset, maxime tempore fidelium, qui non minus, quam modo, ecclesiæ & summo Pontifici in his, quæ debebant, parati fuerunt humiliter obedire, si potestas huiusmodi ad Papam ex ordinatione Christi spectasset, cum secundum beatum Cyprianum, vt habetur 8. q.1. quam periculosum sit in diuinis rebus, vt quis cedat suo iuri & potestati. Sed forte aliquis diceret, quod secundum Innocentium Tertium, vt habetur extra de fo. compe. licet. Vacante imperio recurrendum est ad summum Pontificem pro iustitia obtinenda. Ergo ad ipsum spectat de imperio se intromittere, quando vacat. Respondetur, quod Innocentius intelligit ad Papam habere recursum vacante Imperio, quando non est aliquis vicarius imperii, qui in temporalibus facit iustitiam his qui opprimuntur iniuste, quod insinuare videtur cum dicitur, appellandum ad Papam, quando vacante imperio ad iudicem secularem recurrere nequeunt, qui a superioribus opprimuntur, &c.
units.tr: To the tenth argument it is answered that when the empire is vacant, the Pope has assumed a power which he ought not to have assumed, especially in a time of faithful people, who were no less ready than they are now to obey humbly the Church and the supreme Pontiff in those matters which they owed, if such power had belonged to the Pope by the ordinance of Christ. For, according to blessed Cyprian, as it is found in 8 q.1, it is very dangerous in divine matters for anyone to yield his right and power. But perhaps someone might say that according to Innocent III, as it is found in extra de foro competenti, Licet: When the empire is vacant, recourse must be had to the supreme Pontiff to obtain justice. Therefore it belongs to him to intervene in the empire when it is vacant. It is answered that Innocent means that recourse is to be had to the Pope when the empire is vacant and there is no vicar of the empire who does justice in temporal matters for those who are unjustly oppressed. This seems to be hinted at when he says: an appeal is to be made to the Pope when, the empire being vacant, those who are oppressed by their superiors cannot have recourse to a secular judge, etc.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Potest solutiones alterius opinionis adea, quae in contrarium adducta sunt, cap. 5. circa finem eius ad probationem secundi membri.
units.tr: Solutions can be given to the arguments of the other opinion, which were brought forward in the contrary sense, at the end of chapter 5, in support of the second member.

units.la: Dictum est, quomodo secundum opinionem tenentem, supremam potestatem laicalem tenere temporalia sibi appropriata a solo Deo ad illa, quae sunt adducta in contrarium respondetur. Nunc dicendum est, qualiter secundum opinionem dicentem, potestatem laicalem supremam tenere temporalia appropriata sibi a supremo Pontifice: respondetur ad illa, quae circa finem quinti ca. in contrarium adducta sunt. Unde ad primum, cum dicitur, quod Imperator infidelis non tenebat temporalia sua a Papa. Respondetur, quod Imperatores infideles tenebantur recognoscere Papam suum superiorem in temporalibus: licet de facto non faciebant. Et cum dicitur, quod ante fuit Imperator q Papa. Respondetur dupliciter. Uno modo, quod ante Christum, qui fuit primus Papa & summus Pontifex, non fuit Imperator: quia nullus Imperator ante ipsum habuit verum dominium temporalium rerum, sed solummodo fuit possessor bonae fidei, cum ipsi per bonam fidem tempore durante licuit uti reb. propriis. Sed ista responsio videtur sapere haeresim manifestam, eo quod apud infideles fuit verum dominium temporalium: licet plures illud tenerent ex intentione corrupta, sed intentio corrupta in accipiendo verum dominium non excludit. Emens enim ex intentione corrupta rem alienam a vero domino, verum dominium acquirit. Aliter respondetur, quod verum Imperium fuit ante Papam, & etiam ante Christum, quo tempore Imperator a nullo homine tenebat Imperium, sed postquam Christus venit, cui Deus dedit dominium temporalium rerum, Imperator tenebatur ab ipso recognoscere Imperium, & cum abesset, a generali vicario eius sc. supremo Pontifice. Sed forte diceret aliquis, Imperator, qui fuit tempore Christi, successit Imperatori qui fuit ante Christum, ergo isto iure, quo ille usus est, debuit uti & iste, qui fuit tempore Christi: ergo sicut iste non tenebatur recognoscere ab homine imperium, ita nec ille, qui fuit tempore Christi. Respondetur qui in ius alterius succedit eo iure uti debet, quo & alter, nisi per superiorem aliter ordinetur. Deus autem, qui est supremus omnium Imperatorum ordinavit dando Christo dominium temporalium rerum, ut Imperator succedens Imperatori, qui fuit ante Christum, subiectus esset Christo & vicario eius. Et cum dicitur, quod Christus non venit tollere, nec etiam impedire imperium regum seu Imperatorum. Respondetur ad argumentum, q Christus non impediuit dominationem regum, quando libere, sicut prius, iuste dominationem praecedentem exercuerunt, licet dominationem ipsorum voluit depedere ab ipso. Et ad auctoritatem Leonis Papae respondetur, q Christus non quaerebat temporale regnum, ut ipsum a temporalibus regnis auferret: sed voluit quod omne regnum temporale sibi esset subiectum. Sic etiam respondetur ad illud, quod canit ecclesia: non eripit mortalia, &c. q Christus non venerit eripere alicui mortalia, licet voluerit omnia mortalia sibi esse subiecta & a se recognosci. Per idem ad Ambrosium respondetur, quod religio Christiana neminem primat suo iure absque culpa & sine causa: iura tamen, quae prius erant aliena, dimittendo ea eis, quorum erant sibi subiecit ut recognoscerentur ab ipso. Et p praedicta respondetur ad illud, quod dicitur, quod ante Christum & religionem Christianam fuit Imperator, qui tunc nullum superiorem habuit in temporalibus: quia illo tempore Imperator nulli homini fuit subiectus in temporalibus: quia tunc nullus erat homo, cui Deus in cuius sinu omnia sunt, dedit principaliter dominium temporalium rerum, postea fuit Christus inquantum homo factus Dominus principalis eorum.
units.tr: We have said how, according to the opinion that holds the supreme lay power keeps the temporal things appropriated to it by God alone, the objections brought on the other side are answered. Now it must be said how, according to the opinion that holds the supreme lay power keeps the temporal things appropriated to it by the supreme Pontiff, the objections brought on the other side near the end of the fifth chapter are answered. So, to the first, when it is said that an unbelieving Emperor did not hold his temporal possessions from the Pope: it is answered that unbelieving Emperors were bound to acknowledge the Pope as their superior in temporal matters, although in fact they did not. And when it is said that there was an Emperor before there was a Pope, it is answered in two ways. In one way, that before Christ, who was the first Pope and supreme Pontiff, there was no Emperor, because no Emperor before him had true dominion over temporal things, but was only a possessor in good faith, since for the time being it was lawful for him by good faith to use things as his own. But this answer seems to savour of manifest heresy, since among unbelievers there was true dominion over temporal things, although many held it with a corrupt intention; yet a corrupt intention does not exclude the acquiring of true dominion. For one who buys from a corrupt intention a thing belonging to another, from the true owner, acquires true dominion. In another way it is answered that true empire existed before the Pope, and even before Christ, at which time the Emperor held his empire from no man; but after Christ came, to whom God gave dominion over temporal things, the Emperor was bound to acknowledge his empire from him, and, when he was absent, from his general vicar, namely the supreme Pontiff. But perhaps someone would say: the Emperor who was in the time of Christ succeeded the Emperor who was before Christ; therefore by the same right which the earlier one used, the one in Christ's time ought to use it too; therefore, just as the earlier one was not bound to acknowledge his empire from a man, so neither was the one in Christ's time. It is answered that whoever succeeds into the right of another must use that right which the other used, unless it is otherwise ordained by a superior. But God, who is the supreme over all Emperors, ordained, by giving Christ dominion over temporal things, that the Emperor succeeding the Emperor who was before Christ should be subject to Christ and to his vicar. And when it is said that Christ did not come to take away, nor even to hinder, the empire of kings or Emperors: it is answered to the argument that Christ did not hinder the rule of kings, when they freely, as before, justly exercised the rule that preceded, although he willed that their rule should depend upon him. And to the authority of Pope Leo it is answered that Christ did not seek a temporal kingdom, so as to take it away from temporal kingdoms, but willed that every temporal kingdom should be subject to him. Likewise it is answered to that which the Church sings, he does not snatch away mortal things, etc., that Christ did not come to snatch away mortal things from anyone, although he willed that all mortal things should be subject to him and acknowledged by him. By the same reasoning it is answered to Ambrose that "the Christian religion deprives no one of his right without fault and without cause"; yet by giving back those rights, which were previously another's, to those whose they were, he made them subject to himself so that they would be acknowledged by him. And by the aforesaid it is answered to what is said, that before Christ and the Christian religion there was an Emperor who then had no superior in temporal matters, because at that time the Emperor was subject to no man in temporal matters, since at that time there was no man to whom God, in whose bosom are all things, had principally given dominion over temporal things; afterwards Christ, made principal Lord of them as man, did so.

units.la: QVAESTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: QUESTION III.

units.la: CAP. I
units.tr: CHAPTER I

units.la: Primum caput tertiae quaestionis proponit ipsam quaestionem, & circa eam primam opinionem, quae tenet, quod omnis iurisdictionis auctoritas dependeat a Papa, quam quidem multis rationibus stabilire conatur.
units.tr: The first chapter of the third question sets out the question itself. It takes up the first opinion, which holds that all authority over jurisdiction depends on the Pope, and tries to establish it by many arguments.

units.la: Tertio quaeritur, utrum Papa & Romana ecclesia ex institutione Christi habeant, quod committant Imperatori & aliis principibus saecularibus iurisdictiones temporales: sic ut ipsi aliter non habeat exercere. Circa istam quaestionem sunt opiniones contrariae, quarum una est, quod ecclesia Romana & Papa ex ordinatione Christi habet Imperatori & aliis principibus iurisdictiones temporales committere, & sine commissione eius iurisdictiones illas debere temere nullatenus exerceri. Hanc opinionem, ut videtur, debent tenere isti, qui asserunt quod Papa habet tam in spiritualibus quam in temporalibus illam plenitudinem potestatis, quae dicta est supra quaest. 1. ca. 2. ut ex ordinatione Christi possit omnia, quae non sunt contra ius naturale aut spirituale, aut contra ius divinum de necessitate salutis tempore gratiae observanda. Quod vero secundum alios Papa possit committere Imperatori & aliis principib. iurisdictiones temporales, videtur aperte posse probari, si Papa talem habeat potestatem seu plenitudinem scilicet potestatis eum posse iurisdictiones temporales committere talis plenitudo potestatis includat: eo quod hoc posse nec iuri obviat naturali, nec legi divinae repugnat. Quod etiam tales iurisdictiones, cum ipsas per seipsum non valeat exercere, committere teneatur, ostendiostenditur: quia aliter opus Dei sibi à Deo commissum facere negligeret: nec imitaretur Christum dicentem Ioh. 18. Opus consummaui quod dedisti mihi vt facerem. Si autem ex ordinatione diuina Christi omnia posset, oportet quod omnia exequatur & faciat, vt quæ nequit exequi per seipsum, per alios studeat adimplere. Quod vero secundum illos Imperator & alii principes seculares huiusmodi iurisdictiones temporales, nisi vt sic committantur à Papa, non debeant exercere, videtur posse probari. Nam qui assumit officium & administrationes dignitatis & honoris etiam secularis absq; principe, ad quem spectat de huiusmodi officiis ordinare, de ambitione merito est notandus. Ambitio autem etiam respectu secularium dignitatum siue iurisdictionum à legibus etiam humanis improbatur. Si ergo ad Papam ex institutione Christi spectat de huiusmodi officiis ordinare, non licite sine Papa exerceret eadem. Item sicut habetur extra, de regulis iuris. non est licitum: Non est sine culpa qui rei quæ ad se non pertinet, se immiscet. sed si ad Papam pertineat huiusmodi iurisdictiones Imperatori & aliis committere, ad nullum eorum spectat sine Papa, & per consequens illicite se immiscet. Quare nullus sine Papa debet huiusmodi iurisdictionem exercere. Rursus secundum Apostolum ad Heb. 6. nemo sumat sibi honorem, quod non tantummodo de spirituali vel etiam ecclesiastico: sed etiam de seculari debet intelligi, quod etiam ex ratione, quam ibidem tangit Apostolus, videtur probari. Nam nemo potest magis sibi assumere honorem secularem quam spiritualem, seu ecclesiasticum, cum nemo sit dignior honore seculari, quam Christus spirituali, quia Christus, vt testatur Apostolus, non semetipsum clarificauit vt Pontifex fieret, sed qui locutus est ad eum: filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. ergo nemo debet sibi assumere honorem secularem absque Papa, nec ad Imperatorem spectat huiusmodi honores, cui voluerit, committere. aliter enim per ostium, id est per institutionem legitimam non intrabit, qui fur erit & latro, & non Imperator aut princeps, sed tyrannus & inuasor. Istam opinionem habent tenere illi, qui dicunt, quod licet Papa nō habeat illam plenitudinem potestatis, de qua dictum est: q. i.c.i. ne lex Christiana sit maioris seruitutis, quam sit lex Mosaica, tamen habet plenitudinem potestatis, quantum ad omnia quæ necessaria sunt pro communitate fidelium gubernanda, & licet non possit quæ sunt supererogationis: tamen potest omnia sine quibus vniuersitas fidelium regi non potest. Et ita si Papa habeat plenitudinem talem potestatis ex institutione Christi, ad ipsum spectabit huiusmodi iurisdictiones temporales committere. Quare qui absque ipso sibi sumeret huiusmodi iurisdictionem, illicite sibi sumeret ipsam, & illicite eandem exerceret. Pro ista opinione potest sic argui. Communitas volentium communionem habere adinuicem, in qua omnes vel plurimi ad discordias, dissensiones & lites sunt proni, non est optime ordinata, nisi vni supremo rectori iudici & capiti, à quo iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependeat, sit subiecta. Istud videtur posse probari. Nam vnus populus, si est bene ordinatus, vni gubernatori & non pluribus debet esse subiectus, quod Salomon insinuare videtur Proverb. 11. Vbi non est gubernator, populus corruet. Quod enim non dicit, vbi non sunt gubernatores, sed vbi non est gubernator, videtur innuere, quod vni populo vnus supremus debet esse gubernator, & non plures. Totum autem genus humanum vnus populus est, non enim ad vnitatem populi requiritur, quod vnam ciuitatem aut villam inhabitent. Nam vt legitur 2. Paral. 18. ibi dicit rex Achab ad Iosaphat regem: Sicut populus tuus, ita & populus meus: & tamen nec vnius regis, nec alterius populus inhabitauit solummodo vnam ciuitatem aut villam. Ergo si totum genus humanum optime gubernaretur, oporteret quod vni supremo gubernatori esset, quod ad omnia subiectum, à quo iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependeat. Hoc etiam Saluator Ioh. 10. videtur innuere dicens: Fiat vnum ouile & vnus pastor. Ex quo sequitur & datur intelligi, quod vni regi & vni communitati quantumcunque magnæ debet vnus supremus pastor præesse. Hoc etiam Hieron. videtur sentire in epistola ad Rusticum monachum, vt habetur 7. q. i. cap. in apibus, vbi videtur asserere, quod in omni communitate debet esse supremus pastor, rector & iudex: quia secundum ipsum Imperator est vnus iudex, vnius prouincia vnus est: singularum ecclesiarum singuli sunt episcopi. ergo ratione consimili totius orbis debet esse vnus princeps, à quo omnium iurisdictio aliorum dependeat. Hoc etiam ratione probatur: quia si in toto orbe non esset summus Pontifex seu rector seu iudex, à quo iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependeat, ergo sunt vel esse debent plures superiores non habentes superiorem. Sed hoc optimo modo regendi obuiare videtur: quia si sunt plures superiorem non habentes, aut præsunt eidem, aut diuersis, si eidem, quemadmodum si multis in regno aliquo vel provincia eadem saltem præest laicis rex & iudex secularis, & patriarcha aut episcopus vel alius ecclesiasticus, quamuis vnus in secularibus & alius in spiritualibus, videtur quod talis communitas non est bene ordinata: quia illa communitas non est optime gubernata, in qua subditi suo superiori in his, quibus tenentur obedire non possunt: sed si eidem præsint plures superiorem non habentes, eo facto subditos à se existentes in diuersis locis tempore eodem vocabunt. Non poterunt autem obedire cuilibet, ergo necesse erit, vt sint alterius vel illorum aliquibus inobedientes. Quare illa communitas non est optime ordinata. Restat ergo, quod nulla communitas est bene ordinata, nisi vni capiti subsit, à quo iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependeat. Vniuersitas autem mortalium est communitas quædam volentium communionem habere adinuicem, in qua plurimi ad discordias sunt proni. Ergo non est optime ordinata, nisi vni capiti subsit, à quo iurisdictio omnium dependeat: sed nullus potest esse alius, quam supremus Pontifex, cuius iurisdictio saltem quantum ad ea, quæ ad fidem & religionem Christianam spectant, à solo Deo dependet. Ergo à solo supremo Pontifice iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependet. Si vero præsunt diuersis plures superiorem non habentes, quemadmodum diuersi reges regnant in diuersis regnis, non potest dici, quod tota communitas sit optime disposita, non enim tota communitas comprehendens subditos diuersorum non habentium superiorem, est optime ordinata: quia cum natura humana est prona ad dissentiendum inter diuersos superiorem non habentes, leuiter poterit oriri discordia, quæ per superiorem sedari non poterit. Discordia autem inter maiores superiorem non habentes periculosa est, secundum Aristotelem 6. politic. cap. 9. qui, vt dicit ibidem, in signum dissensionis coassumere faciunt totam ciuitatem. quando enim tales dissentiunt, totam communitatem scindunt & diuidunt, sed talis communitas non est optime gubernata. Si autem iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependet à summo Pontifice, nec Imperator, nec alius princeps debet iurisdictionem temporalem exercere, nisi sibi à supremo Pontifice committatur.
units.tr: Third, it is asked whether the Pope and the Roman Church have, by the institution of Christ, the power to commit temporal jurisdictions to the Emperor and other secular princes, so that these princes may not exercise them otherwise. On this question there are opposing opinions. One is that the Roman Church and the Pope, by Christ's ordinance, have the power to commit temporal jurisdictions to the Emperor and other princes, and that without their commission these jurisdictions must on no account be exercised rashly. Apparently those who assert that the Pope has, in both spiritual and temporal matters, that fullness of power which was described above in question 1, chapter 2, must hold this opinion. By that power he may, by Christ's ordinance, do everything that is not contrary to natural or spiritual law, or to divine law that must be observed for salvation in the time of grace. As for the view of others, that the Pope can commit temporal jurisdictions to the Emperor and other princes, it seems clearly provable, if the Pope has such power, or fullness of power, that the power to commit temporal jurisdictions is included in such fullness. This power is neither opposed to natural law nor repugnant to divine law. It is also shown that he is bound to commit such jurisdictions, since he cannot exercise them himself. Otherwise he would neglect the work committed to him by God, and would not imitate Christ, who says in John 18: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do. If, however, by the divine ordinance Christ could do all things, it is necessary that he carry out and perform all things, so that what he cannot carry out himself he may strive to accomplish through others. That the Emperor and other secular princes ought not to exercise such temporal jurisdictions unless they are so committed by the Pope, seems capable of being proved. For whoever takes upon himself the office and administration of a secular dignity and honour, without the prince to whom it belongs to appoint to such offices, is rightly to be noted for ambition. Ambition, even with respect to secular dignities or jurisdictions, is condemned also by human laws. If therefore it belongs to the Pope, by the institution of Christ, to appoint to such offices, then no one could lawfully exercise them without the Pope. Likewise, as it is held in the Extra, De regulis iuris: "He is not without fault who thrusts himself into a matter that does not pertain to him." But if it belongs to the Pope to commit such jurisdictions to the Emperor and others, then it pertains to none of them without the Pope, and so he who meddles without the Pope meddles unlawfully. Therefore no one ought to exercise such jurisdiction without the Pope. Again, according to the Apostle in Hebrews 5 (6): "No one takes this honour upon himself", which must be understood not only of spiritual or ecclesiastical honour but also of secular honour. This is also shown by the reasoning the Apostle touches on there. For no one can take to himself secular honour more than spiritual or ecclesiastical honour, since no one is worthier of secular honour than Christ is of spiritual honour. For Christ, as the Apostle testifies, did not glorify himself to be made a high priest, but he that said unto him: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. Therefore no one ought to take secular honour to himself without the Pope, and it does not belong to the Emperor to commit such honours to whomever he wishes. Otherwise, he who enters not by the door, that is, by lawful institution, will be a thief and a robber, and not an emperor or prince but a tyrant and usurper. Those who say that, although the Pope does not have that fullness of power of which we have spoken (Q. 1, c. 1: that Christian law should not be of greater servitude than the Mosaic law), he nevertheless has fullness of power in all things necessary for governing the community of the faithful, and although he cannot do what is supererogatory, he can do all things without which the body of the faithful cannot be ruled, must hold this opinion. So, if the Pope has such fullness of power by the institution of Christ, it will belong to him to commit such temporal jurisdictions. Therefore whoever took such jurisdiction to himself without him would take it unlawfully and would exercise it unlawfully. For this opinion one may argue thus: a community of those willing to have fellowship with one another, in which all or most are prone to discords, dissensions and quarrels, is not best ordered unless it is subject to one supreme ruler, judge and head, on whom the jurisdiction of all the others depends. This seems provable. For one people, if it is well ordered, ought to be subject to one governor and not to several, which Solomon seems to hint at in Proverbs 11: Where there is no governor, the people falls. For he does not say "where there are no governors" but "where there is no governor", which seems to suggest that one people ought to have one supreme governor and not several. Now the whole human race is one people, for unity of a people does not require that they inhabit one city or village. Thus we read in 2 Chronicles 18, where King Ahab says to King Jehoshaphat: As thy people is, so is my people; and yet the people of neither king lived only in one city or village. Therefore, if the whole human race were best governed, it would have to be subject to one supreme governor, subject in all things, on whom the jurisdiction of all others depends. The Saviour also seems to hint at this in John 10, saying: Let there be one fold and one shepherd. From this it follows, and is made clear, that one king and one community, however large, ought to be governed by one supreme shepherd. Jerome also seems to think this in his letter to the monk Rusticus, as it stands in Distinction 7, chapter In apibus, where he seems to assert that in every community there must be a supreme shepherd, ruler and judge, because according to him, the Emperor is the one judge, the one province has one, each single church has its own bishops. Therefore, by like reasoning, there ought to be one prince of the whole world, on whom the jurisdiction of all others depends. This is also proved by reason: if in the whole world there were no supreme Pontiff, ruler or judge, on whom the jurisdiction of all others depends, then there are, or ought to be, several superiors who have no superior. But this seems to hinder the best manner of governing, because if there are several who have no superior, they either preside over the same people or over different ones. If over the same people, as when in some kingdom or province the same people have a secular king and judge over the laity, and a patriarch or bishop or other ecclesiastic over them, one in secular matters and another in spiritual, it seems that such a community is not well ordered, because that community is not best governed in which subjects cannot obey their superior in those matters in which they are bound to obey. But if several who have no superior preside over the same people, then they will at the same time summon subjects who are in different places. They will not be able to obey each one, so it will be necessary that they be disobedient to some of them. Therefore that community is not best ordered. It remains, then, that no community is well ordered unless it is subject to one head, on whom the jurisdiction of all others depends. The community of mortals is a certain community of those willing to have fellowship with one another, in which most are prone to discord. Therefore it is not best ordered unless it is subject to one head, on whom the jurisdiction of all depends. But no one can be this other than the supreme Pontiff, whose jurisdiction, at least as regards those matters that pertain to the Christian faith and religion, depends on God alone. Therefore the jurisdiction of all others depends on the supreme Pontiff alone. But if several who have no superior preside over different peoples, as different kings reign in different kingdoms, it cannot be said that the whole community is best disposed. For a whole community, comprising subjects of different persons who have no superior, is not best ordered, because since human nature is prone to disagree among different persons who have no superior, discord may easily arise which cannot be settled by a superior. Discord among greater persons who have no superior is dangerous, according to Aristotle, Politics 6, chapter 9, who says there that they cause the whole city to take up arms as a sign of dissension. For when such persons disagree, they split and divide the whole community, but such a community is not best governed. If, then, jurisdiction of all others depends on the supreme Pontiff, neither the Emperor nor any other prince ought to exercise temporal jurisdiction unless it is committed to him by the supreme Pontiff.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Capitulum secundum tertia quaestionis ponit opinionem secundam, tenentem oppositum superioris opinionis, cuius etiam probationes adducit, quae soluentur cap. 8. huius quaestionis.
units.tr: The second chapter, on the third question, sets out a second opinion, which holds the opposite of the previous opinion. It also adduces its proofs, which will be answered in chapter 8 of this question.

units.la: ALia est opinio, quod nec Papa nec Romana ecclesia habet ex institutione Christi, quod regulariter committat Imperatori & aliis principibus secularibus iurisdictiones temporales, & quod ipsi eas absque eo possunt exercere.
