Sed circa hanc assertionem sunt diuersi modi ponendi. Vnus est, quod nec Papa nec Romana ecclesia hoc habet à Christo seu ex institutione Christi. Et sic quod Romana ecclesia nullam habet potestatis plenitudinem penitus coactinam, nisi sibi à Papa vel Imperatore, vel aliquo alio inferiore Imperatore committatur, & quod Imperatori aut populo in temporalibus est Papa subiectus, & si aliquod crimen siue spirituale siue seculare commiserit, subiectus poena debita realiter est coercendus, & quod Imperator & alii principes seculares absque hoc, quod ex institutione eis aliquid à Papa committitur, iurisdictiones temporales habeant exercere. Alius modus ponendi est, quod ex institutione Christi habet Papa, vt tam spirituales censurae criminales, quam aliae ad ipsum pertineant, in quibus potestatem obtineat coactiuam. Sed de temporalibus nec regulariter nec casualiter habet se intromittere, nisi sibi à populo vel Imperatore vel seculari alio committatur. Tertius modus ponendi est, quod Papa regulariter non habet, sed solummodo casualiter ex institutione Christi, quod iurisdictiones scilicet temporales committat Imperatori & aliis principibus, & quod in casu ipsi eas aliter non debeant exercere. Concordantes itaque isti ponentes in hoc, quod nec Papa nec Romana ecclesia habet ex institutione Christi, quod regulariter committat Imperatori, nec aliis principibus secularibus iurisdictiones seculares siue temporales, & quod ipsi eas regulariter absque commissione valeant exercere. Pro quo taliter allegari potest. Nemo quocunque modo iurisdictionem temporalem domino suo committere potest: Imperator autem est summus dominus summi Pontificis, cum Papa sit vasallus eius scilicet Imperatoris, cui tributum debet, nisi ab imperiali dignitate immunitatem obtineat 11. quaest. 1. cap. Si tributum. Quod Vrbanus Papa, vt legitur 23. quaest. 8. cap. tributum, fateri videtur, qui loquens de tributo dando Cæsari pro se & aliis clericis dicit: De exterioribus ecclesia, quod constitutum est antiquitus, pro pace & quiete, quae nos tueri & defendere debent, Imperatoribus persoluendum est. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Papa debet Imperatori dare tributum, quod est approbatio subiectionis, extra, de censibus cap. omnis anima: ergo Imperator est dominus summi Pontificis, unde & nonnunquam supremi Pontifices Imperatorem dominum suum appellauerunt, 11. quaestion. 1. cap. sacerdotibus, distinctione 63. cap. nobis dominus, & cap. Salonitana. Amplius, res transit cum onere suo, extra, de pignoribus, ex litteris, igitur Papa recipiens dignitatem & praedia, quae tributum & seruitium debent Imperatori, ratione rerum huiusmodi est Imperatori subiectus. Rursus, religio Christiana à seruitute neminem liberat, sicut allegatum est supra, ergo si Papa ante Papatum fit subiectus Imperatori, remanet Imperatori subiectus & seruus, nisi Imperator libertatem & immunitatem ei concesserit. Sed diceret aliquis, quod seruus ante Papatum assumptus in fauorem Christianae religionis liberatur à seruitute, & etiam ab omni subiectione; sicut seruus factus presbyter à seruitute. Respondetur, quod in fauorem ecclesiae nihil iniustum statui debet: quia praetextu pietatis non est facienda impietas, 14. quaestion. 6. cap. fur autem, & 1. quaest. 1. non est putanda. cum igitur iniustum sit & iniquum, quod aliquis sine culpa priuetur iure suo, Ecclesia non potest statuere, vt Imperator vel alius priuetur iure, quod habuit in personam Papae antequam esset ad Papatum assumptus, ne (vt dicit Apostolus prima Timoth. 6.) nomen Domini & doctrina blasphemetur. Cuius doctrinam Gelasius Papa, vt habetur distinct. 54. cap. generali, sequi videtur, affirmans quod serui dominorum fuerum iura sub obtentu religionis fugere minime debent: ne per Christiani nominis institutum aut aliena iura videantur persuadi (alias perimi) aut publica disciplina subuerti. Videtur ergo, quod si seruus fiat presbyter vel summus Pontifex, neque iure diuino neque iure naturali eripitur à seruitute. Nec à seruitute eripi potest iure canonico. Quia iura canonica leges seculares nequaquam tollere possunt, ergo si seruus Papa vel presbyter in libertatem eripitur, oportet quod ipsam à iure humano in posterum assequatur.
units.tr: There is another opinion, that neither the Pope nor the Roman Church has from the institution of Christ the regular power to commit temporal jurisdictions to the Emperor and other secular princes, and that they may exercise them without such a commission. There are, however, different ways of stating this assertion. One is that neither the Pope nor the Roman Church has this from Christ or by the institution of Christ. On this view the Roman Church has no fullness of power that is wholly coercive, unless it is committed to it by the Pope, or by the Emperor, or by some other authority inferior to the Emperor. The Pope is subject to the Emperor or the people in temporal matters, and if he commits any crime, whether spiritual or secular, he is to be really restrained by the punishment due to a subject. The Emperor and other secular princes may exercise temporal jurisdictions without anything being committed to them by the Pope through an institution. Another way of stating it is that the Pope has from the institution of Christ that spiritual censures and criminal matters, as well as other matters, belong to him, and that in these he has coercive power. But he may not intervene in temporal matters, either as a regular or as an occasional thing, unless they are committed to him by the people, the Emperor, or some other secular authority. A third way of stating it is that the Pope does not have this regularly, but only occasionally, by the institution of Christ: namely, that he commits temporal jurisdictions to the Emperor and other princes, and that in such a case they ought not to exercise them otherwise. Those who hold these views therefore agree that neither the Pope nor the Roman Church has from the institution of Christ the regular power to commit secular or temporal jurisdictions to the Emperor or to other secular princes, and that they may regularly exercise them without a commission. For this position the following argument may be made. No one can in any way commit temporal jurisdiction to his lord. But the Emperor is the supreme lord of the supreme Pontiff, since the Pope is his vassal, that is, the Emperor's, to whom he owes tribute, unless he obtains immunity from the imperial dignity, 11. quaest. 1. cap. Si tributum. Pope Urban seems to acknowledge this, as is read in 23. quaest. 8. cap. tributum, where, speaking of the tribute to be given to Caesar for himself and other clerics, he says: What is due to the church from external sources, which was established long ago, is to be paid to the Emperors for the peace and quiet which they ought to protect and defend. From these words it is gathered that the Pope ought to give tribute to the Emperor, which is an acknowledgment of subjection, extra, de censibus cap. omnis anima: therefore the Emperor is lord of the supreme Pontiff. Hence the supreme Pontiffs have sometimes also called the Emperor their lord, 11. quaestion. 1. cap. sacerdotibus, distinctione 63. cap. nobis dominus, and cap. Salonitana. Moreover, a thing passes with its burden, extra, de pignoribus, ex litteris, so the Pope, in receiving the dignity and the estates which owe tribute and service to the Emperor, is subject to the Emperor by reason of such things. Again, the Christian religion frees no one from servitude, as was said above. Therefore if the Pope was subject to the Emperor before he became Pope, he remains the Emperor's subject and slave, unless the Emperor has granted him liberty and immunity. But someone might say that a slave taken up before the papacy is freed from servitude, and from all subjection, in favour of the Christian religion, just as a slave made a presbyter is freed from servitude. The answer is that nothing unjust ought to be established in favour of the Church, because impiety is not to be committed under the pretext of piety, 14. quaestion. 6. cap. fur autem, and 1. quaest. 1. non est putanda. Since it is unjust and iniquitous that anyone be deprived of his right without fault, the Church cannot decree that the Emperor or anyone else be deprived of the right he had over the person of the Pope before he was raised to the papacy, lest (as the Apostle says, 1 Timothy 6) the name of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed. Pope Gelasius, as is found in distinct. 54. cap. generali, seems to follow this teaching, affirming that the slaves of their masters ought by no means to flee their rights under the pretext of religion, lest by the institution of the Christian name the rights of others be seen to be overturned (or destroyed) or public discipline subverted. It seems therefore that if a slave becomes a presbyter or the supreme Pontiff, he is not rescued from servitude either by divine right or by natural right. Nor can he be rescued from servitude by canon law, because canon laws cannot in any way abolish secular laws. Therefore if a slave who is Pope or a presbyter is rescued into liberty, it must be that he attains it afterwards by human law.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Respondet allegationi ad medium primi capituli posita.
units.tr: It answers the argument placed at the middle of the first chapter.

units.la: HIs opinionibus breuiter recitatis videndum est, quomodo secundum eas allegationes cōtra eas inductas, respondetur. Secūdum autem opinionem vltimo recitatam ad allegationem inductā supra c.1. pro opinione prima diuersimode respondetur. Dicitur vno modo respondendo, quod nulla communitas est optime ordinata, nisi vni supremo sit subiecta, & ideo conceditur, quod omnium mortalium, si optimo regimine debeant gubernari, debet esse vnus supremus Iudex per electionem vniuersitatis mortalium vel sanioris vel maioris partis constitutus, qui non debet esse Papa, sed alius, qui supremo sacerdotio non fungatur: cui Papa, & omnes alii in omnibus, qui ad supremum spectat officium, sint subiecti, ita vt Papa ex institutione Christi nullam iurisdictionem aut potestatem neq; regulariter neque casualiter, neque in spiritualibus habeat coactiuam, quamuis a Christo habeat potestatem absoluendi in foro poenitentiae a peccatis, ac caetera ecclesiastica sacramenta ministrandi, & docendi qualiter sit viuendum, vt vita perpetua acquiratur. Haec responsio in diuinis scripturis fundari videtur, quia in eis legitur (vt dicunt) quod Christus Apostolis omnem potestatem coactiuam interdixit, cum dicit Matth. 20. Scitis quod principes gentium dominantur eorum, & qui maiores sunt potestatem exercent in eos: non ita erit inter vos. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Apostoli nullam habuerunt potestatem in alios exercere. Quod de potestate coactiua praecipue debet intelligi, quod nec Papa successor Petri ex institutione Christi p hoc potestatem habet coactiuam aliquā. Hoc etiam per hoc videtur posse probari, quod Christus, cuius Papa est solummodo vicarius, nullam vnquam potestatem exercuit coactiuam, sed a iudice seculari voluit iudicari: ergo nec eius vicarius habet potestatem coactiuam aliquam, sed in omnibus iudici seculari subditus est. Aliter respondetur, quod Papa habet plenam potestatem in spiritualibus coactiuam, & alius Iudex habet solummodo in temporalibus, & tamen communitas mortalium, hoc non obstante, poterit esse optime regulata, & ideo negatur illa: Nulla communitas potest esse optime ordinata, nisi vni supremo Iudici sit subiecta. Aliter dicitur secundum secundam opinionem superius recitatam, quod nulla communitas discordias inter se habere valentium est optime regulariter ordinata, etiam si in omni casu vni supremo iudici esset subiecta: quia in tali communitate posset iste supremus Iudex in perniciem totius communitatis delinquere, & optimae ordinationi communitatis cuiuscunque repugnare. Rursus optimae ordinationi communitatis obuiat, quod aliqui alii a supremo Iudice potestatem regularem etiam habeant coactiuam, qui non sunt praeiudiciales potestati supremi Iudicis. Ex his infertur, quod optimae ordinationi communitatis non repugnat, quod supremus Iudex & alii inferiores ipso alicui alteri, quā supremo Iudici, casualiter sint subiecti, qui super eos potestatem habeant coactiuam. Adhuc optimae ordinationi communitatis non obuiat, quod aliquis a iurisdictione coactiua supremi iudicis regulariter sit exemptus. Ad allegationem supradictam dicitur, quod nulla communitas dissentire valentium est optime ordinata, nisi tota vni supremo iudici sit subiecta, vel regulariter vel casualiter, ita vt nullus alius a supremo iudice sit casualiter ab eius potestate exemptus, vt in nullo casu liceat supremo Iudici coercere eundem: sed quod a potestate supremi iudicis aliquis regulariter sit exemptus, & in casu necessitatis sit subiectus eidem, optimae ordinationi communitatis generalis vel specialis non repugnat, nec etiam vt supremus in eadem communitate regulariter sit exemptus a potestate totius communitatis: & tamen quod in casu necessitatis sit eidem communitati subiectus, & ideo vniuersitas mortalium non est optime ordinata, nisi vni supremo Iudici praedicto modo sit subiecta, licet in casu expediat ab huiusmodi optima ordinatione saltem ad tempus recedere.
units.tr: Having briefly recited these opinions, we must see how, according to them, answers are given to the arguments brought against them. Now, according to the opinion recited last, the argument brought above in chapter 1 in support of the first opinion is answered in different ways. In one way it is answered: no community is best ordered unless it is subject to one supreme authority; and so it is granted that, if all mortals are to be governed by the best government, there must be one supreme judge, constituted by the election of the whole body of mankind, or of its wiser or greater part, who ought not to be the Pope but someone else who does not hold the supreme priesthood. To him the Pope and all others are subject in all matters that pertain to the supreme office; so that by the institution of Christ the Pope has no jurisdiction or power, neither regularly nor occasionally, nor in spiritual matters, of coercive force, although he has from Christ the power of absolving from sins in the forum of repentance and of administering the other ecclesiastical sacraments, and of teaching how one must live so that eternal life may be attained. This answer seems to be grounded in the divine Scriptures, because in them it is read (as they say) that Christ forbade the Apostles all coercive power, when he says in Matthew 20: "You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them; it shall not be so among you." From these words it is gathered that the Apostles had no power to exercise over others. This ought to be understood especially of coercive power: that neither the Pope, the successor of Peter, has by the institution of Christ any coercive power by this means. This also seems provable from the fact that Christ, of whom the Pope is only the vicar, never exercised any coercive power, but willed to be judged by a secular judge; therefore neither does his vicar have any coercive power, but in all things is subject to the secular judge. In another way it is answered: the Pope has full coercive power in spiritual matters, and another judge has it only in temporal matters; and yet the community of mortals, notwithstanding this, can be best regulated; and therefore that proposition is denied: no community can be best ordered unless it is subject to one supreme judge. Another answer is given according to the second opinion recited above: no community whose members can disagree among themselves is best regularly ordered, even if in every case it were subject to one supreme judge; for in such a community that supreme judge could offend to the ruin of the whole community, and oppose the best ordering of any community whatever. Again, what obstructs the best ordering of a community is that some others besides the supreme judge also have regular coercive power, who are not prejudicial to the power of the supreme judge. From these things it follows that it is not repugnant to the best ordering of a community that the supreme judge and other inferiors should, occasionally, be subject to some other than the supreme judge, who have coercive power over them. Moreover, the best ordering of a community is not obstructed by the fact that someone is regularly exempt from the coercive jurisdiction of the supreme judge. To the aforesaid argument it is said: no community whose members can disagree is best ordered unless the whole of it is subject to one supreme judge, either regularly or occasionally, so that no one else is occasionally exempt from his power, such that in no case may the supreme judge be permitted to coerce him. But that someone be regularly exempt from the power of the supreme judge, and in a case of necessity be subject to him, does not repugnant to the best ordering of the general or particular community; nor does it follow that the supreme man in the same community is regularly exempt from the power of the whole community; and yet, since he is in a case of necessity subject to the same community, the body of mortals is not best ordered unless it is subject to one supreme judge in the aforesaid manner, although in a case it may be expedient to depart from such optimal ordering, at least for a time.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Pro declaratione solutionis data in cap. precedenti ostendit, quae principatui supremo compossibilia, & quae incompossibilia sint dicenda, & hoc primo medio.
units.tr: To explain the solution given in the preceding chapter, he shows which things are compatible with supreme government and which are to be called incompatible with it, and he does so by the first means.

units.la: PORRO quia ista videntur non vlquequaque clare dicta, sed obscure, ita vt quaeliter intelligi debeant, aliquis valeat dubitare, vt lucidius eorum pateat intellectus, ac per hoc an sit verus an falsus magis appareat, breuiter est dicendum secundum istam opinionem, quae ad optimum principatum rectoriam seu regimen requiruntur, quae sibi repugnant, & quae sibi compossibilia possent reputari. Dicitur itaque, quod ad optimum principatum exigitur, quod sit propter bonum commune subditorum, non propter principantis proprium institutus. Per hoc enim optimus principatus, tam generalis omnium mortalium, quam specialis, qui est respectu quorundam, non solum differt a principatu illicito discolo & iniusto, verum etiam a principatu despotico, id est dominatione propter bonum proprium principantis, & ab omni alio etiam illicito, qui non ordinatur ad commune bonum, talis autem principatus est Papalis & episcopalis, quantum est ex ordinatione Christi: quod Christus insinuasse videtur, quando beatum Petrum ordinauit in Papam dicendo ei: pasce oues meas, quasi diceret, super oues meas principem te constituo, vt non tollas ab eis lac & lanam, nisi pro necessitacessitatibus suis, iuxta illud primæ ad Corinth. 9. Quis pascit gregem & de lacte gregis non manducat? sed ad pascendum non ad exhauriendum eandem. Eandem etiam potestatem videtur Christus commisisse Petro, quando dicit eidem, ut habetur Matth. 16. Tu es Petrus; & super hanc Petram ædificabo ecclesiam meam: & porta inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam. Et tibi dabo claves regni cælorum, quasi diceret, ad ædificandam ecclesiam meam, non ad dominandum ei, ut ipsemet Petrus in sua canonica prima capite quinto innuit dicens: Neque ut dominantes in clero, & ut introducas eas ad regnum cælorum, cæteris te proponam & præferam, & ideo per verba Christi, quæ sequuntur, Quæcunque ligaveris super terram erunt ligata & in cælis, intelligitur, Petro fuisse permissa potestas super sibi subiectos, non super alios, quæ esset ad ædificationem & non ad destructionem ipsorum: qualem potestatem Apostolus 1. ad Corinth. ultimo super sibi subiectos dicit sibi datam a Domino, non a Papa. Etiam beatus Petrus nullam potestatem recepit a Christo, nisi propter bonum sibi subiectorum ad obtinendum regnum cælorum, ut nihil eis valeret imponere per præceptum, nisi quod esset eis necessarium ad consequendum regnum cælorum, & ideo iura & libertates fidelium sunt a Deo & natura concessa, ut nihil eis nisi auctoritate Christi valeat iniungere: quia ad ædificationem, non ad destructionem iurium & libertatum a Deo & natura fidelibus concessarum recepit potestatem a Christo, ne ipsorum non solummodo pastor & servus: sed & dominus videretur, contra illam doctrinam, qua ipse & alios episcopos informavit dicens: Pascite qui est in vobis gregem Dei: providentes non coacte sed spontanee secundum Deum: neque turpis lucri gratia, sed voluntarie, neque ut dominantes in clero, sed forma facti gregis ex animo, propter quod si beatus Petrus, qui iura & libertates fidelium extra casum necessitatis & utilitatis, quæ necessitati comparari valet, aliquid in communi vel in speciali iniuriam...
units.tr: Since these points may seem not to be stated altogether clearly but obscurely, so that someone may doubt how they ought to be understood, I shall briefly say, following this opinion, which things are required for the best principality, rule or government, which things are opposed to it, and which may be regarded as compatible with it, so that its meaning may be clearer and it may appear more plainly whether it is true or false. It is said, then, that the best principality requires that it be instituted for the common good of the subjects, not for the advantage of the ruler himself. For by this the best principality, both the general one over all mortals and the particular one that exists over certain people, differs not only from an unlawful, disorderly and unjust principality, but also from a despotic principality, that is, a lordship exercised for the ruler's own good, and from every other unlawful principality that is not ordered to the common good. Such a principality is papal and episcopal, so far as it rests on the ordinance of Christ. Christ seems to have hinted at this when he appointed blessed Peter as Pope, saying to him: Feed my sheep, as if he were saying: I set you as a prince over my sheep, so that you do not take from them their milk and wool except for their needs, according to that saying of 1 Corinthians 9: Who feeds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock? The point is to feed the flock, not to drain it. Christ also seems to have committed the same power to Peter when he says to him, as we read in Matthew 16: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. It is as if he said: to build up my church, not to lord it over it. Peter himself hints at this in his first canonical epistle, chapter five, saying: Neither as lording it over the clergy, but that you may be examples to the flock, and so through the words of Christ that follow, Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, it is understood that a power was granted to Peter over those subject to him, not over others, and that it was for their building up and not their destruction. The Apostle, in the last chapter of 1 Corinthians, says that he was given such a power over those subject to him by the Lord, not by the Pope. Blessed Peter also received no power from Christ except for the good of those subject to him, in order to attain the kingdom of heaven, so that he could impose on them by command nothing except what was necessary for them to attain the kingdom of heaven. Therefore the rights and liberties of the faithful have been granted by God and by nature, so that nothing can be enjoined on them except by the authority of Christ. For Peter received his power from Christ for the building up, not the destruction, of the rights and liberties granted to the faithful by God and nature, lest he should seem not only the pastor and servant of those people but also their lord. This runs against the teaching by which he himself instructed the other bishops, saying: Feed the flock of God that is among you, taking the oversight not by constraint but willingly, according to God; not for filthy lucre, but voluntarily; nor as lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock from the heart. Therefore, if blessed Peter had attempted anything against the rights and liberties of the faithful, whether in common or in particular, outside the case of necessity and of usefulness that may be set on a par with necessity,

units.la: fisset, huiusmodi iussio neminem obligasset. Etiam si in contradicentes sententiam aliquam protulisset, tanquam a non suo iudice lata, ipso iure nulla fuisset, iuxta regulam, extra, de regulis iuris libr. (lext. ea quæ fiunt a iudice, si ad eius non spectant officium, viribus non subsistunt. Si enim quod a prælato exigitur, a sibi subiecto est liberum denegare (extra, de excessibus prælatorum, cum ad querundam, in glossa expressa, quod accipi videtur ex textu) multo magis quod Petrus exegisset a sibi subiecto contra libertatem sibi a Deo & natura concessam, liberum extitisset eidem subiecto denegare: & sententia Petri contra priuilegium Dei sic etiam nulla fuisset, tanquam a non suo iudice lata. Nam quantum ad libertates fidelibus a Deo & a natura concessas, omnes a iurisdictione Petri exempti fuerunt, quia cum priuilegia & exemptio, quæ conceduntur a Deo & natura, magis debeant vnicuique seruire, quam quæ indulgentur a Papa vel a beato Petro: Iequi videtur, quod omnis sententia Petri contra libertatem huiusmodi, tanquam a non suo iudice lata, ipso iure nulla fuisset, licet huiusmodi principatum, quæ bonum solummodo respicit subditorum, non proprium principantis, nisi inquantum in bono communi concluditur aliorum, Christus Apostolis minime interdixit: sed eis præceptorie vel consultorie imposuit, ut ab omni principatu propter honorem & commodum proprium abstinerent: dicens ad eos, ut habetur Matth. vigesimo. Scitis quia principes gentium dominantur eorum, & qui maiores sunt potestatem exercent in eos: non ita est inter vos, sed quicunque voluerit inter vos maior fieri, sit sicut minister: & qui voluerit inter vos primus esse, erit vester seruus, sicut filius hominis non venit ministrari, sed ministrare. Quibus verbis Christus Apostolis non omnem potestatem interdixit: sed magis aliquid appetendum ab eis ostendit, cum dicit: quicunque voluerit inter vos maior fieri: & quicunque voluerit inter vos primus esse, nam maioritas & primitas in principatu haerere noscuntur: quod etiam non ignorans doctor gentium ianuit manifeste, primæ ad Timotheum decimo tertio dicens, si quis episcopatum desiderat, bonum opus desiderat. Qualem autem principatum Christus voluit ab Apostolis appeti, patefecit dum subdit: Sicut filius hominis non venit ministrari, honorem & munera, tributa & seruitia, præsertim non necessaria, præceptis, pœnis vel timoribus exigendo, qualia petunt principes sæculi, qui obtinentes ius principandi, modum nullatenus ampleduntur. Nam a subiectis talia exigunt & extorquent, sæpius etiam violenter, sed ministrare venit non tantummodo corporaliter etiam pedes discipulorum suorum humiliter abluendo: sed etiam spiritualiter credentes in ipsum propter eorum utilitatem, non suam, ex nimia charitate docendo, monendo, ac præceptis & prohibitionibus, quæ ad principatum spectare noscuntur, saluberrime dirigendo, teste evangelio Matthæi decimo, vbi dicitur: Hos duodecim misit Iesus præcipiens eis & dicens: In viam gentium ne abieritis, & in civitates Samaritanorum ne intraveritis: sed potius ite ad oves, qua perierunt domus Israel, &c. Et post: nolite possidere aurum, &c. Quod etiam in compluribus aliis locis evangelicæ doctrinæ explicite inuenitur Christus præcepisse, ergo non obstat, quod dicit, se venisse non ministrari sed ministrare. Nequaquam enim omnem prælationem seu principatum a se remouet, sed solummodo propter utilitatem propriam, gloriam vel honorem, sicut ipse sæpe testatus est, quamobrem cum ipse voluerit, quod ipsi essent imitatores sui fidelium utilitatem procurando, nullatenus ipsos ab omni principatu prohibuit: sed ipsos præcepto vel consilio informavit, ut præcipiendo fidelibus non dominari propter propriam utilitatem, gloriam & honorem appeterent: qualiter principes sæculi semper vel frequenter quærere dinoscuntur. Huiusmodi autem principatus puritate propter bonum aliorum facti sunt Apostoli: sed secundum quosdam ad puritatem huiusmodi principatus absque omni promotione cuiuslibet alterius principatus, qui propter bonum proprium, gloriam & honorem assumitur, principatus successorum Apostolorum de necessitate salutis minime astringuntur, nisi aliqui, qui per votum veluramentum
units.tr: such a command would have bound no one. Even if he had pronounced some sentence against those who resisted, as passed by a judge who was not his own, it would by law itself have been void, according to the rule in the Decretals, De regulis iuris, in the Liber Extra: What is done by a judge, if it does not belong to his office, has no force. For if what a prelate demands may be refused by a subject as free (Extra, De excessibus praelatorum, Cum ad quorundam, with the gloss expressly stating this, which seems to be drawn from the text), much more would it have been open to that subject to refuse what Peter demanded against the liberty granted to him by God and nature. Peter's sentence, passed against the privilege of God, would likewise have been void, as passed by a judge who was not his own. For as regards the liberties granted to the faithful by God and nature, all of them were exempt from the jurisdiction of Peter, because privileges and exemptions granted by God and nature ought to serve each person more than those granted by the Pope or by blessed Peter. Hence it seems that every sentence of Peter against such liberty would, as passed by a judge who was not his own, have been void by law itself. Yet Christ did not at all forbid the Apostles a principality of this kind, which regards only the good of the subjects and not the good of the ruler, except insofar as it is included in the common good of others. Rather, he laid down for them, by precept or by counsel, that they should abstain from every principality undertaken for their own honour and advantage. He said to them, as we read in Matthew 20: You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are great exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you; but whoever would be great among you, let him be your minister; and whoever would be first among you, let him be your servant; even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister. By these words Christ did not forbid the Apostles all power; rather, he showed that something was to be sought by them, when he says: whoever would be great among you, and whoever would be first among you, for greatness and primacy are known to belong to principality. The teacher of the Gentiles, not ignorant of this, plainly indicated it in 1 Timothy 3, saying: If anyone desires the office of a bishop, he desires a good work. But what kind of principality Christ wished the Apostles to seek he made clear when he added: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, that is, not to exact honour and gifts, tributes and services, especially those that are not necessary, by commands, punishments or fears, as worldly princes seek to do, who, having obtained the right to rule, do not at all embrace the manner of ruling that is proper to it. For they demand and extort such things from their subjects, often even by violence. But he came to minister, not only bodily, by humbly washing the feet of his disciples, but also spiritually, by teaching and admonishing the believers in him for their benefit, not his own, out of exceeding charity, and by guiding them most salutarily with precepts and prohibitions, which are known to belong to principality. This is attested in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter ten, where it is said: These twelve Jesus sent out, charging them, saying: Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into any city of the Samaritans enter not; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, etc. And afterwards: Provide neither gold, etc. Christ is found explicitly to have given such precepts in many other places of the evangelical teaching as well. Therefore his statement that he came not to be ministered unto, but to minister is no obstacle. He by no means removes from himself every pre-eminence or principality, but only that which is for his own advantage, glory or honour, as he himself often testified. Wherefore, since he wished his followers to imitate him by promoting the advantage of the faithful, he did not forbid them every principality at all. Rather, he instructed them by precept or counsel that, in commanding the faithful, they should not seek to lord it over them for their own advantage, glory and honour, as worldly princes are always or frequently known to seek. The Apostles were made into such a principality, of purity for the good of others. But according to some, the successors of the Apostles are not bound, by the necessity of salvation, to the purity of this kind of principality, free from any promotion of any other principality that is assumed for one's own good, glory and honour, unless some of them, by vow or oath, should renounce every principality of this kind. Although the assertion of some holds that those who succeed the Apostles in principality are bound to such purity of principality.

units.la: Gg tum à se omnem principatum huiusmodi abdicarent, licet quorundam assertio asserat, quod ad talem puritatem principatus illi, qui in principatu succedunt Apostolis, obligentur.
units.tr: ...then renounce from themselves all such principality, although some people assert that those who succeed the Apostles in their principality are bound to that same purity of principality.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Cap. 5. tertia quaestionis ostendit alie medio, quid ad optimum principatum requiritur: ostenditq; primum uno argumento, quod principatus monarchicus praecellit ceteros, & hoc circa principium cap. deinde circa medium intentum probat.
units.tr: Chapter 5 of the third question shows, in the middle, what is required for the best government. It first demonstrates by one argument that monarchical government excels the others, which it does near the start of the chapter, and then proves the point further on in the middle of the chapter.

units.la: SEcundo ad optimum principatum tam generalem respectu cūctorum mortalium, quam speciale respectu quorundam secundum opinionem praescriptam requiritur, quod principans sit una persona, sicut principatus est unus, quapropter secundum philosophos principatus regalis, quo una persona refulget, tam principatum aristocraticum quam politicum, quorum utriq; praesident plures, superat & praeexcellit. Pro quo posset triplicitér allegari: sed ad praesens unam sufficiat allegationem adducere, quae talis est. Ille principatus est optimus & caeteris praestantior reputandus, quo inter subditos charitas, amicitia, pax & concordia potissime procuratur, multiplicatur, crescit & seruatur: & quo seditio seu discordia, quae est cuiuslibet communionis corruptio, praecipue deuitatur, propter hoc enim omnis principatus bonae communioni expediens principaliter est institutus: & ita summo conatu plantare debet princeps & fouere in suis subiectis, unde & princeps pacis Christus, super cuius humerum factus est optimus principatus corporaliter, ab Apostolis & caeteris fidelibus recessurus ipsis dilectionem & amicitiam singulariter imponebat, dicens: hoc est praeceptum meum, ut diligatis invicem. Qui etiam ipsis pacem, quae est caritatis & amicitiae effectus, optauit saepius, & praecepit illis inter se seruare, & aliis dare docebat. Dicit enim eis, ut habetur Iohannis 14. pacem relinquo vobis: pacem meam do vobis, & 16. ait: Inme pacem habeatis. Matt. 9. pacem habete inter vos, & Iohannis 20. sic legitur: venit Iesus & stetit in medio discipulorum & dixit: pax vobis. Et Matthaei decimo dixit Apostolis: intrantes domum salutate eam dicentes: Pax huic domui. Quod autem ex discordia, corruptio & destructio cuiuslibet communitatis peruenit, & per consequens ex concordia constructio communitatis optima: omnis communitatis bonae auctor & rector Christus declarat dicens, ut habetur Matthaei duodecimo. Omne regnum diuisum contra se desolabitur. His sola ratione coactus concordat Aristoteles, qui quinto libro politicorum ait: amicitiam putamus maximum esse bonum ciuitatibus: sic enim utique sibi minime seditiones faciunt, & septimo libro ethicorum dicit: videtur autem & ciuitates continere amicitia, & legis positores magis circa ipsam studeant, quam circa iustitiam. Concordia enim simile aliquid amicitiae videtur esse: hanc autem maxime appetunt. Ex quibus probatur, quod principatus ad seruandam amicitiam, pacem & concordiam, & ad tollendum discordiam inter subditos principi potissime ostenditur. Hoc autem magis fit, si princeps fuerit una persona, quam si plures existant, quemadmodum existit in aristocratia. Nam si unus solus fuerit summus principans, nulla poterit omnino a capite discordia prouenire: nemo enim dissentit a seipso. Si vero fuerint plures supremi principantes, siue diuersi sint viri aristocratice vel politice praesidentes, inter rectores totius communitatis poterit amicitia & pax dissolui: ac discordia & seditio suboriri: quae omnibus discordiis inter subditos & minus potentes gravior & periculosior esse dignoscitur. Omnis enim discordia inter minus potentes & subditos per principantem vel principantes sedari potest & sanari. Sed si inter principantes supremos fuerit suborta discordia, etiam ad omnes alios faciliter se diffundet: quia, ut testatur Aristoteles quinto politicorum capite nono. Totaliter insignium assumere faciunt dissensiones totam ciuitatem: propter quod subditos oportet vereri talia & dissolui ne praesidentium & potentium sint dissensiones, unum scilicet principem, si commode potest, omnibus praeficiendo. In principio enim, id est principantibus, sit principatus in periculum & perniciem omnium, si fuerit dissidentes. Principium autem dicitur esse dimidium totius: & ideo si inter principes discordia est, in tota communitate periculosissima reputatur, ergo ad principatum simpliciter optimum requiritur, quod persona principantis sit una & unica, ut principatus est unus. Plura alia ad principatum optimum requiruntur: sed ista ad praesens breuiter & grosse tractare sufficiat. Restat ergo inquirere, quae optimo principatui per opinionem praescriptam debeant compossibilia reputari: & quae ad eius essentiam nequaquam pertineant vel sibi possunt conuenire vel adesse. Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur ante omnia, quod licet ad principem multa pertineant, plura tamen sunt, quae statui eius repugnant, ut optimo principatui, de quibus perstringenda sunt pauca, quorum primum est, quod sibi repugnat habere seruos sibi subditos. Primo nonnullis apparet, quod non stat cum potestate optimi principatus quemcunque subditum, praesertim inuitum, abiq; culpa sua esse seruum. Nam principatus optimus propter bonum subditorum principaliter est institutus: principatus autem seruorum, qui despoticus nominatur, est principaliter propter bonum principantis: sed huiusmodi principatus non est optimus iudicandus. Amplius principatus, qui institutus est contra naturam, non est optimus aestimandus: sed iniustum est & contra naturam, quam quis maioribus aut aequalibus & sibi similibus, vel de quibus spes probabilis esse potest: quia futuri sunt maiores aut aequales & sibi similes virtute & sapientia; principetur tanquam seruis: ut Aristoteles tertio politicae aperte videtur asserere, quod etiam Hieronymus testari videtur, cum dicit, vt tangitur in decretis distinct. 25. §. nunc autem: Talis eligatur in principem & prælatum, cuius comparatione cateri grex dicantur, & I. q. I. cap. vilissimus, habetur sic: vilissimus reputandus est nisi præcellat scientia & sanctitate, qui est honore præstantior. hinc Sapiens Ecclesiastic. 32. rectores & principes instruens & informans ait: Rectorem te posuerunt, noli extolli: esto in illis quasi unus ex ipsis. Quare optimo principatui repugnare videtur, vt omnes subditi vnius principantis sint serui. Ad quod etiam probandum videtur sufficere ratio Aristotelis primo politica, qua probare conatur, quod melior est principatus liberorum quam seruorum: quia melior est principatus, qui est meliorum subditorum; sicut melior est principatus hominum quam bestiarum, liberi autem sunt meliores quam serui, quare principatus seruorum non est optimus iudicandus. Sed contra illud forte aliquis obiiceret, dicens, quod optimo principatui non repugnat perfecta obedientia in subditis, tunc enim optimus principatus non posset in religione perfectissima, quæ obedientiam perfectissimam permitteret, reperiri. Sed perfectissima est seruorum obedientia, quia qui perfectissimam obedientiam permittit & vouet, permittit in omnibus obedire: ad quod tenentur serui. Ergo principatus seruorum principatui optimo non repugnet. Hic respondetur, quod religio perfectissima non permittit simpliciter in omnibus obedire: sicut tenentur serui in omnibus obedire. Tunc etiam posset prælatus religiosum huiusmodi cogere vitam ducere secularem, perfectissima autem religio permittit obedire in omnibus, quæ non sunt contra Deum & regulam suam, præsertim in his quæ ad Deum & ad mores & vitam pertinent regularem.
units.tr: Second, for the best government, both in general for all mortals and in particular for certain peoples, according to the opinion set out above, it is required that the ruler be one person, just as the government is one. Hence, according to the philosophers, royal government, in which one person shines forth, surpasses and excels both aristocratic and political government, over which several preside. This could be argued in three ways, but for now it is enough to adduce one argument, which runs as follows. That government is the best and must be judged superior to the others in which charity, friendship, peace and concord are chiefly promoted, multiplied, increased and preserved among the subjects, and in which sedition or discord, which is the corruption of every community, is especially avoided. For every government is established principally for the good of a well-ordered community, and so the prince must with the greatest effort plant and foster these things among his subjects. This is why Christ, the Prince of Peace, upon whose shoulder the best government rested in bodily form, when about to depart from the Apostles and the other faithful, laid upon them especially love and friendship, saying: This is my commandment, that you love one another. He also often wished them peace, which is the effect of charity and friendship, and commanded them to keep it among themselves and teach it to others. For he says to them, as we read in John 14: Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you, and in John 16 he says: In me you may have peace. Matthew 9: Have peace among yourselves. And in John 20 we read: Jesus came and stood in the midst of the disciples and said: Peace be to you. And in Matthew 10 he said to the Apostles: When you enter a house, greet it, saying: Peace be to this house. That the ruin and destruction of any community come from discord, and consequently the best building up of a community from concord, Christ, the author and ruler of every good community, declares, saying, as we read in Matthew 12: Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste. Aristotle, compelled by reason alone, agrees with this, for in the fifth book of his Politics he says: We consider friendship to be the greatest good for states, for thus they are least liable to factions; and in the seventh book of his Ethics he says: Friendship seems also to hold states together, and lawgivers care more for it than for justice. For concord seems to be something like friendship, and this they especially seek. From these things it is proved that government is chiefly shown to serve the preservation of friendship, peace and concord, and the removal of discord among the subjects. This happens more fully if the ruler is one person than if there are several, as is the case in aristocracy. For if there is one sole supreme ruler, no discord can arise at all from the head, for no one disagrees with himself. But if there are several supreme rulers, whether they be different men presiding in aristocratic or political fashion, friendship and peace may be dissolved among the rulers of the whole community, and discord and sedition may arise, which is recognised as more grievous and more dangerous than all discords among subjects and lesser men. For every discord among lesser men and subjects can be calmed and healed by the ruler or rulers. But if discord arises among the supreme rulers, it will also spread easily to all the others, because, as Aristotle testifies in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 9: Dissensions among the notables make the whole city take sides; so subjects ought to beware of such things and of the dissensions of those who preside and hold power, by setting over all, if it can conveniently be done, a single prince. For the beginning, that is the rulers, is the government, and it is a danger and ruin to all if they are at odds. Now the beginning is said to be half of the whole; therefore, if there is discord among the princes, it is judged most perilous for the whole community. Therefore, for the simply best government it is required that the person of the ruler be one and single, as the government is one. Many other things are required for the best government, but it is enough for now to treat these briefly and roughly. It remains, then, to inquire which things, according to the opinion set out above, may be regarded as compatible with the best government, and which by no means belong to its essence, or can be attached to it or be present in it. To make this clear, it must first be said that, although many things pertain to the prince, there are nevertheless several which are repugnant to his office and to the best government. Of these a few must be set out, and the first is that it is repugnant to him to have slaves as subjects. At first it appears to some that it does not agree with the power of the best government that any subject, especially one unwilling, should be a slave without fault of his own. For the best government is established principally for the good of the subjects, but the government of slaves, which is called despotic, is principally for the good of the ruler; but such a government is not to be judged best. Further, a government which is instituted against nature is not to be esteemed best; but it is unjust and against nature for someone to rule as over slaves those who are greater or equal to him and like him, or of whom there is a reasonable hope that they will be greater, equal and like him in virtue and wisdom. As Aristotle seems plainly to assert in the third book of the Politics, which Jerome also seems to attest when he says, as is touched upon in the Decretum, Dist. 25, §. Nunc autem: Let such a man be chosen as prince and prelate that the rest of the flock are called in comparison with him; and C. 1, q. 1, cap. Vilissimus, it reads thus: The most worthless man is to be considered, unless he excels in learning and holiness, who is more distinguished in honour. Hence the wise man, instructing and forming rulers and princes, says in Ecclesiasticus 32: They have made you a ruler; do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them. Therefore it seems repugnant to the best government that all the subjects of one ruler should be slaves. The reason of Aristotle in the first book of the Politics also seems sufficient to prove this, by which he attempts to show that the government of free men is better than that of slaves, because a government of better subjects is better, just as the rule of men is better than the rule of beasts, and free men are better than slaves; therefore the government of slaves is not to be judged best. But someone might perhaps object to this, saying that perfect obedience in subjects is not repugnant to the best government, for then the best government could not be found in the most perfect religious order, which permits the most perfect obedience. But the obedience of slaves is most perfect, because whoever permits and vows the most perfect obedience permits obedience in all things, to which slaves are bound. Therefore the government of slaves is not repugnant to the best government. Here it is answered that the most perfect religious order does not permit obedience simply in all things, as slaves are bound to obey in all things. Otherwise a prelate could also compel such a religious to lead a secular life; but the most perfect religious order permits obedience in all things which are not against God and its rule, especially in those matters which pertain to God and to the morals and regular life.

units.la: Ex isto secundum opinionem præfatam videtur principatui optimo repugnare, quod princeps illam habeat plenitudinem potestatis, quæ descripta est supra q. 1. cap. 6. vt sc. de iure si voluerit omnia possit percipere & imponere subditis, quæ nec iuri naturali indispensabili, nec iuri diuino ad quod omnes catholici obligantur, obuiant vel repugnant, nam omnes subditi habenti huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis super eos sunt serui ipsius, secundum strictissimam significationem vocabuli serui. Nam hac potestate nullus dominus super seruos potest habere maiorem de iure, ergo optimo principatui repugnat, quod omnes subiecti sint serui, ergo etiam repugnat, quod habeat huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: From the same opinion set out above, it seems repugnant to the best government that the prince should have that fullness of power which is described above in q. 1, cap. 6, namely that by right he may, if he wishes, be able to take and impose everything on the subjects, provided it does not oppose or conflict with indispensable natural law or with divine law, to which all Catholics are bound. For all subjects under a ruler having such a fullness of power over them are his slaves, according to the strictest meaning of the word "slave." For no lord over slaves can by right have greater power than this. Therefore it is repugnant to the best government that all subjects should be slaves, and therefore it is also repugnant that he should have such a fullness of power.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Ostendit, quod optimo principatui debeant compossibilia reputari. Et inferuntur quaedam corrolaria notatu dignissima.
units.tr: He shows that certain things ought to be regarded as compatible with the best principate. And some corollaries worth especial note are drawn.

units.la: Consequenter restat inquirere, quæ secundum opinionem prædictam optimo principatui debeant compossibilia reputari: licet ad essentiam eius nequaquam pertinent, sed sibi adesse valet & deesse. Ad cuius evidentiam ante omnia est sciendum, quod licet ad principatum, de quo est sermo, multa pertinent, videlicet vnicuique sua iura tribuere & seruare: leges condere necessarias atque iustas: iudices inferiores & alios officiales constituere: quales artes & a quibus in communitate sibi subiecta debeant exerceri: omniumque virtutum actus præcipere, & alia multa: tamen ad hoc videtur esse principalissime constitutus, vt corrigat & puniat delinquentes. Si enim in aliqua communitate nullus pro delicto seu culpa puniri deberet, monitor ad bonum & doctor sufficeret: & princeps superfluus omnino videretur, quod ex Scripturis colligitur. Ad illud enim lex & principes principalissime videtur institui. Lex quidem, quoniam non propter bonos sed malos coercendos & puniendos instituitur, teste Apostolo, qui I. Timoth I. ait: Lex iusto non est posita, sed iniustis & non subditis. Et ad Galat. 5. ait, si spiritu (id est ratione) ducimini (nihil contra rationem & bonos mores agendo) non estis sub lege, & 2. ad Corinth. 3. ait: vbi spiritus Domini, ibi libertas: vt scilic. lex alterius principis ligare non valeat. Unde habe caritatem & fac quod vis, & per consequens nulla lege teneberis, si caritate, quae non agit perperam, fueris munitus. dist. 4. c. factae sunt leges, vt coerceatur humana audacia, & Aug. 23. qu. 5. ca. ad fidem, ait, legibus benefacere non cogimini: sed malefacere prohibemini, ergo similiter principans principaliter non propter bonos sed propter malos coercendos præsse debet, quod Apostolus ad Roman. 4. expresse videtur asserere, dicens, principes non sunt timori boni operis sed mali. & post: si enim malefeceris, time: non enim sine causa gladium portat. Dei enim minister est, vindex in iram ei qui male agit. quod etiam Sapiens Eccles. 7. videtur innuere dicens: noli quaerere fieri Iudex, nisi valeas virtute dissumpere iniquitates.
units.tr: It remains to inquire, following the opinion stated above, which things ought to be regarded as compatible with the best principate. They do not belong to its essence at all, but it can have them or lack them. To make this clear, it must first be known that although many things belong to the principate in question (namely: to render to each his rights and to preserve them; to enact necessary and just laws; to appoint lower judges and other officials; which arts are to be practised in the community subject to it, and by whom; to command the acts of all the virtues; and many other things), yet it seems to have been established chiefly for this purpose: to correct and punish offenders. For if in some community no one ought to be punished for a crime or fault, a teacher and adviser toward the good would suffice, and the prince would seem wholly superfluous; this is gathered from the Scriptures. For law and princes seem to have been instituted principally for this end. Law indeed is instituted not for the good but for the restraint and punishment of the wicked, as the Apostle witnesses, who says in 1 Timothy 1: "The law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust and the disobedient." And in Galatians 5 he says: "If you are led by the Spirit (that is, by reason, doing nothing against reason and good morals), you are not under the law"; and in 2 Corinthians 3 he says: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty," so that the law of another prince may not bind. Hence "Have charity and do what you will," and consequently "you will be bound by no law, if you are fortified by charity, which does not act amiss." Dist. 4, c. "Factae sunt leges": laws were made so that human audacity might be restrained; and Augustine, 23 qu. 5, c. "Ad fidem," says: "You are not compelled to do good by laws, but you are forbidden to do evil." Therefore likewise the ruler ought principally to preside not for the good but for the restraint of the wicked, which the Apostle in Romans 13 seems plainly to assert, saying: "Rulers are not a terror to good works but to evil. And afterward: If you do evil, fear; for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is God's minister, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil." The Wise Man also seems to hint at this in Ecclesiastes 7, saying: "Do not seek to be made a judge, unless you are able by strength to break down iniquities."

units.la: His visis dicitur, quod optimo principatui non repugnat, sed est compossibile nonnunquam iurisdictionem seu potestatem alicuius vel aliquorum ex istis de communitate illa supremo principe eiusdem communitatis minime dependere, seu non institui ab eodem, dummodo per hoc nullus delinquens in illa communitate iustam debitamq; debeat effugere vltionem, non obuiat. Nam illud, quod non derogat bono communi, licet aliquis de honore principantis vel potestate dirimat, non videtur optimo principatui repugnare, cum ille, qui optimo fungitur principatu, non potestatem propriam vel honorem, sed bonum commune & aliorum quaerere teneatur, vt videatur Apostolum imitari, qui primæ ad Corinth. 10. sic ait: non quærens quod vtile mihi, sed quod multis, qui ad Philip. 2. ait: Non quae sunt sua singuli considerantes, sed quae aliorum. Nec mirum, quoniam caritas, quae vigere debet in principe ad subditos, non quærit quae sua sunt, 1. ad Corint. 13. quod Imperator insinuat de se ipso dicens, voluntarios labores appetimus vt quietem aliis praeparemus, in autenticis vt diuina iussiones subscriptionem nem habeant gloriosissimi quaestores, in principio, coll. 8. Et, nolłei ducimus insomnes, vt subiecti sub omni quiete subsistant, in autenticis, vt iudices sine quoquo suffragio, in principio collat. 2. aliquam igitur iurisdictionem, praesertim a superiori vel potestatem, vel officium esse in aliqua communitate vel institui & no dependere a supremo principe communitatis eiusdem, dummodo per hoc nullus delinquens debitam euadat vltionem, bono communi non obuiat nec repugnat. Nam cum talis iurisdictio vel potestas bono communi debeat expedire, non refert, a quo instituatur, dummodo iuste exerceatur, & rite & nullatenus negligenter, quae cuncta implentur, si nullus delinquens in eadem communitate punitionem supremi iudicis vel alterius subterfugere queat. Non enim refert ad commune bonum, a quo legitime instituatur exercitus seu princeps militiae, dummodo pro salute reipublicae prudenter & strenue bellagerat. Nec ad bonum commune distat, a quo legitime Iudex instituatur inferior, dummodo legitime, quod iustum est, exequatur bene, & hoc in omni communitate seruari videmus. Nam cum quis super aliquam communitatem, supremam accipit potestatem seu principatum, nequaquam omnino, qui in eadem communitate, iurisdictione, potestate vel officio sint functuri, de nouo instituit: sed quos a praedecessore suo inuenit institutos, sua dimittit officia exercere, & nonnullos, si est consuetudo vel lex, ab aliis de nouo institui permittit. Et sicut dictum est bono communi non derogat, a quo quis legitimam habeat potestatem; dummodo quae bono communi expediunt, per potestatem acceptam exerceat diligenter, quare potestatem ali quam vel iurisdictionem in aliqua communitate a supremo principante non dependere non repugnat: dummodo per hoc bonum commune nullatenus malo exponatur, quod accideret si fungens huiusmodi potestate deliquerit, & valeat correctionem necessariam euitare, & caetera multa, vt patet.
units.tr: Having seen these things, it is said that it is not repugnant to the best principate, but is sometimes compatible with it, that the jurisdiction or power of some one or of some of those in that community should in no way depend on the supreme prince of that same community, or should not be instituted by him, provided that by this no offender in that community may escape the just and due vengeance. For that which does not detract from the common good does not seem to be repugnant to the best principate, even if it diminishes somewhat the honour or power of the ruler; since he who discharges the best principate is bound to seek not his own power or honour, but the common good and that of others, so that he may seem to imitate the Apostle, who says in 1 Corinthians 10: "Not seeking what is profitable to me, but what is profitable to many," and who says in Philippians 2: "Each looking not to his own things, but to the things of others." Nor is this surprising, since the charity which ought to flourish in the prince toward his subjects "does not seek its own" (1 Corinthians 13), which the Emperor indicates of himself, saying: "We seek voluntary labours that we may prepare quiet for others" (in the Authentics, that divine commands may have the subscription of the most glorious quaestors, in the beginning, coll. 8); and "we do not wish to sleep, that the subjects may live in all quiet" (in the Authentics, that judges be without any favour, in the beginning, coll. 2). Therefore some jurisdiction, especially one held from a superior, or some power or office, to exist in a community and to be instituted there without depending on the supreme prince of that same community, provided that by this no offender escapes due vengeance, neither obstructs nor is repugnant to the common good. For since such jurisdiction or power ought to serve the common good, it does not matter by whom it is instituted, provided it is exercised justly, duly, and in no way negligently; and all these conditions are fulfilled if no offender in the same community can escape the punishment of the supreme judge or of another. For it does not matter to the common good by whom a lawful army or general of the forces is appointed, provided he wages war prudently and vigorously for the safety of the commonwealth. Nor does it make a difference to the common good by whom a lower judge is lawfully appointed, provided he lawfully carries out what is just and does so well; and we see this observed in every community. For when someone receives supreme power or principate over some community, he by no means newly appoints all those who are to exercise jurisdiction, power or office in that same community; but those whom he finds instituted by his predecessor he lets remain in the exercise of their offices, and he permits some to be newly instituted by others, if there is custom or law to that effect. And, as has been said, it does not detract from the common good by whom one holds lawful power, provided he diligently exercises through the power received what serves the common good. Hence it is not repugnant that some power or jurisdiction in a community should not depend on the supreme ruling prince, provided that thereby the common good is in no way exposed to harm, which would happen if one holding such power offended and could avoid the necessary correction; and many other things, as is evident.

units.la: Ex praedictis infertur, quod optimo principatui non repugnat aliquem in aliqua communitate a potestate coactiva principantis supremi regulariter esse exemptum, dum tamen casualiter, ne delinquere valeat, existat principanti supremo subiectus, quia talis exemptio bono communi non derogat: ex quo sic exemptus, si deliquerit, necessariam bono communi punitionem non valeret euadere.
units.tr: From what has been said it follows that it is not repugnant to the best principate that someone in a community should, as a rule, be exempt from the coercive power of the supreme ruling prince, provided that, by chance, so that he may not be able to offend, he is subject to the supreme ruling prince; because such an exemption does not detract from the common good. From this it follows that one so exempted, if he offended, would not be able to escape the punishment necessary for the common good.

units.la: Ex hoc concluditur vlterius, quod principatui optimo non repugnat correctionem seu punitionem taliter exempti a potestate supremi principantis ad alium vel alios, quam ad principatum supremum spectare, dummodo difficilius & inconuenientius, siue per malitiam, siue per impotentiam, siue negligentiam damnabilem, saltem casualiter per supremum puniri valeat principantem: quia hoc bono communi non derogat. Nihil enim refert bono communi, a quo delinquentes legitime puniantur, cum enim princeps maiorem habes quam doctor & monitor potestatem, sit principalissime institutus ad corrigendum & puniendum legitime delinquentes, vt humana coerceatur audacia: & ut sint inter improbos innocentes, licet fiat talis exemptio: infertur quod optimo principatui non repugnet, cum propterea delinquentes in principantem, impunitatem periculosam bono communi nullatenus valeant obtinere.
units.tr: It is further concluded from this that it is not repugnant to the best principate that the correction or punishment of one so exempted from the power of the supreme ruling prince should belong to another or others rather than to the supreme principate, provided that, more difficultly and less conveniently, whether through malice, impotence, or culpable negligence, at least by chance he can be punished by the supreme ruler. For this does not detract from the common good. For it does not matter to the common good by whom offenders are lawfully punished, since, as the prince has greater power than teacher and adviser, he is chiefly instituted to correct and lawfully punish offenders, so that human audacity may be restrained, and so that among the wicked the innocent may be safe, even if such an exemption is made. It follows that it is not repugnant to the best principate, since on this account offenders against the ruler can by no means obtain a dangerous impunity to the common good.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Ostendit, quomodo ea, quae de optimo principatu dicta sint, non semper locum habeant, quia dabilis est casus, quo ex tali principatu malum sequatur: non autem dabilis est contra eum praescriptio.
units.tr: Shows how the things said about the best government do not always hold, because a case can arise in which harm follows from such a government; and prescription cannot be pleaded against it.

units.la: SANE licet praescripta opinio praedicta omnia teneat de optimo principatu tam generali respectu diuersorum mortalium, quam speciali respectu quorundam, dicitur tamen, quod huiusmodi optimus principatus non est semper instituendus, neq; in tota communitate cunctorum mortalium, neque in speciali: quia sicut saepe sunt aliqua simpliciter bona, & tamen multa sunt aliqua mala propter indispositionem illorum (bibere enim vinum & comedere carnes sunt bona: & tamen sunt mala aegrotis) ita optimus principatus non est simpliciter omnibus optimus, imo aliquibus est nocius, & nonnunquam inducitus corruptionis & periclitationis boni communis. Quod accidere potest tam ex malitia subiectorum, quam ex malitia & insufficientia huiusmodi assumentis. Quanquam enim subiecti ex ambitione cupientes indebite principari, vel aliqua alia malitia meritari principatum optimum nullatenus sustinerent: sed ante seditiones & discordias corrumpentes rempublicam excitarent. Nonnunquam etiam persona sufficiens in bonitate & discretione inueniri non posset: & tunc aliquis alius principatus, puta aristocraticus vel politicus, quo funguntur simul plures, deberet ad tempus institui, quia illud est pro tempore statuendum, quod pro tempore magis proficit ad commune bonum de voluntate Dei: qui secundum congruentiam temporum cuncta disponit. Vnde regnum filiorum Israel, quod fuit prius vnum, postea fuit in duo regna diuisum. Si tamen optimus principatus cunctorum mortalium, siue aliquorum semel fuit institutus, non est postea sine causa vrgente destruendus: tamen in multis casibus corrumpi posset. Ex quibus tamen destitutio non valeret, propter quod ad destruendum ipsum non valet praescriptio: quia omnis praescriptio, quae est contra optimum principatum, videtur iniqua. Et ideo si contra multa minora non currit praelcriptio: multo magis non debet currere contra optimum, licet currere debeat pro ipso: sicut non contra libertatem, quia fauor libertatis est habendus, extra, de coniug. seruorum. c. licet.
units.tr: Certainly, although the opinion stated above holds all these things about the best government, both in its general application to the various mortals and in its particular application to certain people, it is nevertheless said that this kind of best government is not always to be instituted, neither in the whole community of all mortals nor in a particular one. For just as there are often things that are good in themselves yet are harmful to some because of their condition (drinking wine and eating meat are good, and yet they are harmful to the sick), so the best government is not best for everyone without qualification; indeed, for some it is harmful, and sometimes it leads to the corruption and endangering of the common good. This can happen both through the wickedness of the subjects and through the wickedness and insufficiency of the one who is put in power. For although subjects who, through ambition, desire to rule unduly, or who deserve the government by some other wickedness, would by no means tolerate the best government, they would stir up seditions and quarrels that corrupt the commonwealth. Sometimes too a person sufficient in goodness and judgement cannot be found; and then some other form of government, such as aristocratic or polity, in which several rule together, ought to be instituted for a time, because that must be established for the time which, for the time, better advances the common good by the will of God, who arranges all things according to the fitness of the times. Hence the kingdom of the sons of Israel, which was first one, was afterwards divided into two kingdoms. Yet if the best government of all mortals, or of some, has once been instituted, it is not afterwards to be destroyed without a pressing cause; nevertheless, in many cases it could be corrupted. Yet prescription would not be valid for its destruction, because every prescription that runs against the best government seems unjust. And therefore, if prescription does not run against many lesser things, much more ought it not to run against the best, although it ought to run in its favour, just as it does not run against liberty, since the favour of liberty is to be held (Extra, de coniug. servorum, c. licet).

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAP. VIII.

units.la: Respondet iuxta opinionem vltimo positam ad allegationes primi capituli circa medium eius positas. Ostenditque circa medium capituli: an iurisdictio Romani Pontificis à solo Deo dependeat.
units.tr: He answers, according to the opinion placed last, the arguments of the first chapter placed about its middle. He shows, about the middle of the chapter, whether the jurisdiction of the Roman Pontiff depends on God alone.

units.la: PEr scripta, puta per opinionem memoratam & illa quæ dicta sunt c. 4. clarescere videtur, totam allegationem adductam capite primo exsufflari. Nam cum primo accipitur, quod communitas volentium communionem habere adinuicem, in qua omnes vel plurimi ad discordias, dissensiones & lites sunt proni, non est ordinata, nisi vni supremo rectori, iudici, & capiti, à quo iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependeat, sit subiecta. Dicitur quod non est necesse ad communitatem optime ordinatam, quod omnis iurisdictio à supremo rectore dependeat, iuxta illa quæ dicta sunt supra c. 6. & 7. Cum autem probatur per illud Prou. 11. vbi non est gubernator, populus corruet. Respondetur, quod per hoc probaretur, quod totum genus humanum non est simpliciter optime ordinatum, nec super ipsum est simpliciter optime principatus institutus, cum non vni supremo principanti sit subiectus, à quo quilibet alius in aliquo casu, saltem si delinqueret, sit subiectus, sed quod aliqui populi sint subiecti optimo principatui, non requiritur quod omnium aliorum iurisdictio à primo principante dependeat: quia aliquis potest esse exemptus in omni casu à punitione inferenda per principantem supremum tanquam per supremum principatum totius communitatis. Per idem respondetur ad illud Ioh. 10. fiet vnum ouile & vnus pastor: à quo cum aliquis potest esse exemptus in aliquo casu, in illo videlicet cuius exemptio non derogat bono communi. Et cum similiter debet intelligi Hieron. quod in omni communitate debet esse vnus supremus Iudex & rector, à quo tamen absque derogatione optimi principatus potest aliquis quantum ad aliquem esse exemptus. Cum autem secunda ratione probatur, quod oportet vnum esse supremum, à quo iurisdictio omnium aliorum dependeat: quia si in toto orbe non est vnus, & supremus. Ergo vel sunt vel esse debent plures superiorem non habentes, quod optimo videtur reginimi obuiare: quia aut præessent eidem aut diuersis, quorum vtrumque esse inconueniens videtur. Respondetur, q; si totus mundus optimo principatu regeretur, quauis non esset necesse, q; vnus sc. supremus sit, à quo quantum ad institutionem & commissionem aliorum omnium iurisdictio dependeret, oporteret tamen q; esset supremus principatus, cui tamen principanti supremo omnis alius casualiter ratione alicuius delicti esset subiectus, q; quis non ratione cuiuslibet, &non in omni casu, etiā non essent plures superiorem non habentes, si vnus esset simpliciter primus respectu omnium quantumcunq; diuersi, possunt diuersimode esse sibi subiecti: quia vnus illorum potest esse in multis exemptus absq; periculo boni communis, & alii tali exemptione carere valerent. Ille etiam vnus exemptus posset absq; prætudicio boni communis magnam potestatem habere etiā coactiuam à simpliciter supremo principante regulariter nullatenus dependentem: cui sufficeret ratione alicuius delicti esse illi supremo tanq; principanti subiectus: & ita non essent plures simpliciter supremi superiorem non habentes, quare ratio adducta ad probandum, q; optimo principatui cuiusq; communitatis repugnat, q; in eadem communitate sint plures superiore non habentes, siue præsint eisdem siue diuersis: secundū istum modum dicendi non procedit. Sed in contrarium forte obiiciet aliquis, quod imaginatio illa ideo contra modum hunc opinandi procedit: quia si est vnus supremus & habet supra multos potestatem etiā coactiuam, prædictus exemptus à supremo, & subiecti illi exempto sunt exempti à iurisdictione illius supremi aut non, si sint exempti à iurisdictione ipsius supremi principantis: ergo supremus nequaq; omnibus principatur, & p consequens respectu totius communitatis non est optimus principatus. Si aut non sunt exempti à iurisdictione principantis supremi, procedit ratio supradicta, quia poterit contingere, q; supremus principans & ille exemptus eodem tempore eosdem subiectos ad tribunalia sua vocabunt siue citabunt. Respondetur, quod aut in vocatione huiusmodi vocantes exprimunt causam vocationis, aut non exprimunt, si non exprimunt, ad summum principantem ire debent: quia taliter exempto non tenentur obedire, nisi saluo omnium aliorum iure: quemadmodū laici non tenentur obedire Papæ, nisi saluo iure principantis secularis: ita taliter exempto non irrogat iniuriam subditi sui in tali casu, si ad eum non accedant; quemadmodum episcopus vocatus ad synodum, non facit iniuriam vocanti, si præceptione regia impeditur. dist. 18. c. si episcopus, vbi notat Glossa, quod hic defertur regiæ dignitati. 12. q. 2. de rebus. Nam auctoritas maiorum excusat, vt notat Glossa 63. dist. s. Salanitana. Si autem sic, hoc est si vocantes eodem tempore causam vocationis expresserint, non potest dari regula generalis pro omni casu, ad quem debent accedere, eo quod sæpe casus vocatum ad superiorem excusat: & sæpe vocatus minime excusatur: propter quod sæpe vocatum à superiori excusat nece ssitas, quem tamen vocatum ab inferiori non excusat: quia nulla apparet necessitas, qua valeat excusari, quapropter coram quo debet apparere, debeat prudētum discretioni relinqui: quia in talibus propter multiplices, qui possunt accidere, casus, regula generalis dari, quæ nunquam sallat, non potest. Causa est, quia semper debet coram supremo principe comparere: nisi ratio dictet, quod non potest propter quādam cogentem necessitatem, puta propter maius negocium vel aliud simile, & non comparendo coram illo & non coram alio excusetur. Sed forte diceretad hæc aliquis, si taliter exemptus solummodo casualiter est sic supremo principanti subiectus ratione delicti alicuius sequitur, quod nō plus est sibi subiectus quā supremus principans sibi, qui etiam ratione alicuius delicti
units.tr: From what has been written, namely the opinion mentioned and what was said in chapter 4, it seems clear that the whole argument adduced in the first chapter is blown away. For when it is taken first that a community of those who wish to have fellowship with one another, in which all or most are prone to discords, dissensions and quarrels, is not well ordered unless it is subject to one supreme ruler, judge and head, on whom the jurisdiction of all others depends, it is said that it is not necessary for a community to be optimally ordered that all jurisdiction depend on a supreme ruler, as was said above in chapters 6 and 7. But when it is proved by that text of Proverbs 11, "where there is no governor, the people fall," the reply is that by this it would be proved that the whole human race is not simply optimally ordered, nor is a supreme government simply optimally instituted over it, since it is not subject to one supreme ruler, from whom every other person is subject in some case, at least if he should offend. But that some peoples are subject to the optimal government does not require that the jurisdiction of all others depend on the first ruler, because someone can be exempt in every case from punishment to be inflicted by the supreme ruler, as by the supreme government of the whole community. By the same reasoning, the reply is made to John 10, "there shall be one fold and one shepherd": since someone can be exempt in some case, namely in that case whose exemption does not detract from the common good. And Jerome must be understood in the same way, when he says that in every community there ought to be one supreme judge and ruler, from whom, nevertheless, someone may be exempt in some respect without detriment to the optimal government. But when it is proved by the second reason that there must be one supreme, on whom the jurisdiction of all others depends, because if in the whole world there is not one supreme, then there are, or ought to be, several who have no superior. This seems to be repugnant to the best government, because they would either be over the same people or over different ones, and both seem inconvenient. The reply is that if the whole world were governed by an optimal government, although it would not be necessary that there be one supreme from whom the institution and commission of all others depend, it would nevertheless be necessary that there be a supreme government, to which every other is subject by chance, on account of some offence, not on account of any and not in every case. Even if there were several who had no superior, if one were simply first with respect to all, they could be subject to him in different ways, since one of them could be exempt in many matters without danger to the common good, and the others could lack such exemption. And that one exempt person could, without prejudice to the common good, have great power, even coercive, which regularly does not depend at all on the simply supreme ruler; it would suffice that he be subject to that supreme ruler as to a ruler, on account of some offence. And so there would not be several simply supreme without a superior. Therefore the argument adduced to prove that it is repugnant to the optimal government of any community that there be in the same community several who have no superior, whether they preside over the same or different people, does not hold according to this way of speaking. But perhaps someone will object to this on the contrary: that this imagined idea is refuted by this way of thinking, because if there is one supreme who has power over many, even coercive, the aforesaid person exempt from the supreme, and the subjects of that exempt person, are either exempt from the jurisdiction of that supreme or not. If they are exempt from the jurisdiction of the supreme ruler himself, then the supreme does not in any way rule over all, and consequently with respect to the whole community he is not the optimal government. But if they are not exempt from the jurisdiction of the supreme ruler, the aforesaid argument holds, because it can happen that the supreme ruler and that exempt person summon or cite the same subjects to their tribunals at the same time. The reply is that either in such a summons those who summon state the cause of the summons, or they do not state it.
