If they do not state it, the summoned person must go to the supreme ruler, because they are not bound to obey the person exempt in this way except saving the right of all others, just as laymen are not bound to obey the Pope except saving the right of the secular ruler. Thus the exempt person does not do wrong to his subject in such a case if the subject does not come to him, just as a bishop summoned to a synod does no wrong to the one summoning him if he is prevented by a royal command. Dist. 18, c. si episcopus, where the Gloss notes that here it is deferred to royal dignity; 12 q. 2, de rebus. For the authority of the greater excuses, as the Gloss notes on 63 dist., s. Salanitana. But if it is so, that is, if those summoning at the same time have stated the cause of the summons, no general rule can be given for every case to which the summoned must come, because the circumstance of the case often excuses the person summoned by a superior, and often the summoned person is not excused at all. Hence necessity often excuses the person summoned by a superior, though it does not excuse the one summoned by an inferior, because no necessity appears that could excuse him. Therefore, before whom he must appear should be left to the discretion of the prudent, because in such matters, on account of the many cases that can arise, a general rule that never fails cannot be given. The reason is that he must always appear before the supreme prince, unless reason dictates that he cannot do so on account of some compelling necessity, for instance on account of a greater business or something similar; and by not appearing before that one and not before another he may be excused.

units.la: licti licêti posset principantem supremum punire, quando sc. omnes alii deficerent, & correctio seu punitio principantis supremi non posset sine periculo totius reipublicæ sub silentio vel dissimulatione transiri. Respondetur, quod magis esset sic exemptus principanti supremo subiectus, quam ecouerso: quia primus principans haberet punire sic exemptum non solum de necessitate deficientib. omnibus sibi subiectis, sed etiam ratione principatus supremi, sic autem exemptus ex sola necessitate non ratione officii sui haberet deficientibus omnib. aliis corrigere principantem supremum. Cum autem accipitur in minore allegationis prædictæ, quod iste vnus supremus iudex seu principas non debet esse alius, quam supremus Pontifex, dicitur quod si vniuersitas mortalium esset optime ordinata & principatui optimo esset subiecta, stante ordinatione Christi, qua disposuit Pontificem supremum & cæteros clericos negociis secularibus, extra casum necessitatis nullatenus implicari, ille vnus supremus principans sue iudex non deberet esse vnus supremus Pötifex, sed princeps Christianus secularis & laicus. Quod n. laicus esse deberet & non supremus Pontifex nec clericus, probatur per hoc, quod probatur supra q.1. vbi probatur, quod clerici extra casum necessitatis & vtilitatis, quæ necessitati valeat cöparari, debent esse à negociis secularibus alieni. Quod autem deberet esse Christianus, patet per hoc: quod si aliter bonum cömune spirituale non fouere, sed destruere niteretur; quod optimo principatui vniuersitatis mortalium obuiat & repugnat. Cum vero dicitur, quod iurisdictio supremi Pontificis, præsertim in his, quæ ad fidem & religionem Christianam spectant, à solo Deo dependet. Respondet, quod quemadmodum aliqualiter tactum est supra, baptismum & alia sacramenta dependere à solo Deo, diuersimode potest intelligi, & hoc quantum ad prius tripliciter. Vno modo, quod supremus Pontifex absq; ministerio humano accipiat iurisdictionem suam à Deo, vt in nullo casu neq; institui neq; destitui debeat ab homine, & sic non dependet iurisdictio eius à solo Deo, quia nullus post Petrum absque electione fuit ad Papam assumptus. Aliter potest intelligi, quod huiusmodi iurisdictio dependeat à solo Deo, quantum ad institutionem humano ministerio sc. electione canonica concurrente, & sic præcedit ista opinio, quod iurisdictio Papæ, quæ habet ex ordinatione Christi, dependet à solo Deo. Tertio quod non solum sic, sed etiä quantum ad destitutionē à solo Deo dependeat, vt Papa à nemine in quocunq; casu, nisi à solo Deo, possit destitui, & sic non dependet à solo Deo: quia ipsemet seipsum destituit. Nam tam prauitatem hæreticam, quæ per renunciationem spontaneā seipsum destituere potest. Potest etiā ab homine accusari, de quocunq; crimine, si notorium sit, & inde scandalizetur ecclesia, & incorrigibilis sit, vt notatur in gl. dist. 40 sup. c. si Papa. ita potest in casu huiusmodi ab homine iudicari & destitui & deponi. Omnis n. accusatio est coram iudice facienda. Nec de hoc debet Papa perturbari, ne præsse nō prodesse quærere videatur: ne contra doctrinā Christi Apostolis pro se & pro prælatis ecclesiæ traditam velit, tanq; sal infatuatum mitti foras, & ab hominibus conculcari: ne contra præceptum eiusdem velit, pro salute eius corporis mystici vt membrū putridum amputari: ne desideret ipse potestatem, quæ ex caritate correptum, quis etiam ecclesiam non audiret, tanquam ethnicus & publicanus, nō sinat se & carnes putridas reseccari: & vt ouem scabiosam repellendum à stabulis: & expurgādum vt fermētum, quod totam massam corrumpit: sed velit vt sibi parcatur, vt vniuersa ecclesia ad interitū adducatur, quæ omnia à desiderio Papæ, qui animam suam tenetur pro subditis ponere, conuenit exularI. Papa ergo secundum opinionem istam, licet in his, pro quæ habet omnium saluti spicere, ne à quoq; in eis valeat retardari, à potestate & iurisdictione principantis summi non immerito sic sit exeptus: contra quam exemptionem supremus principatus, si pdesse cupit non præsse, nullo modo attentare, sed laudare tenetur, cum ratione delicti non cuiuscunq; naturæ ipsius auctoritas contemptibilis videatur: & ne pro paruo commisso forsitan eius dominatio ab vtilitate communi valeat impediri: sed grauis & enormis præsertim sæpius iterati & in discrimen notabile præcipue boni communis editi, hoc expedit, vt Papa humano iudicio destitui valeat: & hoc maxime, si appareat incorrigibilis & de ipso scandalizetur ecclesia. Videtur autem rationabile, vt huiusmodi Papæ iudicium spectaret primo ad aliquas certas personas de clero, quibus deficientibus siue per malitiam siue per negligentiam damnabilem ad principantem pertineat, si fidei & Christianæ religionis sincerus est & feruidus æmulator, ipso autem deficiente siue per malitiam, siue per damnabilem negligentiam destitutio Papæ, vel saltem detentio aut prohibitio, ne insolescat, optime pertinet vel ad vniuersalem congregationem fidelium: vel ad quoscunque fideles, qui tantam super ipsum temporalem habere valeant potestatem: vt scilicet contra peccatum cuiuslibet Christiani siue parui, siue magni congruum remedium in ecclesia valeat reperiri, iuxta illud Apostoli, primæ ad Corinth. sext. Auferte malum à vobis ipsis Qui etiam ait: Expurgate vetus fermentum: nisi potestas deficiat temporalis, in quo casu seruandum est consilium Hieronym. quod habetur vndec. quæstion. 3. cap. quando igitur, scilicet vt taceant Christiani etiam intelligentes atque prudentes, ne dent sanctum canibus, & mittant margaritas ante porcos, qui conuersi conculcent eas, & imitentur Hieremiam dicentem: solus sedebam quod amaritudine plenum eram. Signum autem, quod ratione delicti Papa in aliquo casu sortiatur forum principantis primi supremi, qui debeat esse laicus, ex diuinis Scripturis accipitur, in quibus legimus, Christum & Apostolos, cum essent de criminibus accusati, à secularibus iudicibus etiam infidelibus iudicatos. Nec legimus, quamuis crimina imposita sibi negarent, quod asserent vel protestarentur se in tali casu non teneri coram huiusmodi iudicibus respondere: imo magis in tali casu sibi subiectos innuisse viderentur: dixit enim Christus Pilato, vt legitur Iohannis decimo nono: Non haberes in me potestatem vllam, nisi tibi datum esset desuper. Quibus verbis Christus infinuasse videtur, quod Pilatus in illo casu super eum ordinariam habuit potestatem, sibi datam desuper à Deo, secundum expositionem quorundam Doctorum, vel ab Imperatore, secundum expositionem aliorum, quia super ipsum habuit Pilatus in illo casu non permissam & usurpatam, sed concessam & datam potestatem, quod etiam de se Apostolus, cum de criminibus accusaretur coram iudicibus infidelibus, insinuasse videtur, ut legitur actuum 24. ubi dicit ad praesidem: Ex multis annis te iudicem huic genti sciens, bono animo pro me satis faciam. Non dicit coram te non teneor respondere, sed dicit pro me (alias per me) satisfaciam, quare videtur facto & verbo recognouisse in illo casu iudicem suum. Et hoc habetur cap. 25. eiusdem, ubi dixit praesidi: Ante tribunal Caesaris sto: ibi me oportet iudicari. Iudaeis non nocui sicut tu melius nosti: si cui nocui, aut dignum morte aliquid feci, non recuso mori. Si vero nihil est eorum, quae isti accusant: nemo potest me illis donare. Caesarem appello. Quibus verbis Paulus tam Festum quam Caesarem, suum iudicem recognouit, cum ergo nephas sit dicere, Paulum facto vel verbo fuisse mentitum, vere Caesar erat iudex Pauli. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod ex hoc manifesta absurditas sequeretur, quod scilicet imperator etiam infidelis in causa fidei esset iudex papae: quia causa Pauli, quae coram iudice tractabatur, erat causa fidei, nam propter Christianam fidem accusabatur a Iudaeis. Hic respondetur, quod causa fidei coram imperatore fideli, deficientibus aliis, esset rite tractanda, quia, ut habetur distinct. 46. Vbinam, quaestio fidei non tantum ad clericos, verum etiam ad laicos & ad omnes pertinet Christianos. Coram autem imperatore infideli causa fidei non in quantum respiceret solummodo veritatem revelatam, sed in quantum posset tangere mores reipublicae, derogare etiam bono communi aut alicui personae iuriam irrogare, videtur posse tractari. Quorum utrumque prudenter innuisse videtur proconsul Achaiae Gallio, qui, ut dicit actor. 18. cum Paulus accusaretur a Iudaeis, dicit ad eos: Si iniquum quidem esset aliquid aut facinus pessimum, o viri Iudaei, vos recte sustinerem. Si vero quaestiones sunt de verbo & de nominibus legis vestrae, vos ipsi videritis. Iudex ego horum nolo esse. Sic ergo dicitur, quod in casu ratione delicti papa imperatori est subiectus. Ad omnes vero canones & authoritates alias, ex quibus colligitur, quod papa est a nemine iudicandus, dicitur, quod non debent intelligi sine omni exceptione, sed cum exceptionibus suis: quemadmodum aliae regulae in iure, & etiam authoritates quamplurimae divinae scripturae, quamvis non solum modo indifinite, sed etiam in verbis generalibus & cum signis universalibus sint prolatae, debent intelligi, unde & glo. 9. q. 3. sup. 6. nemo, aliquas exceptiones enumerat, si tamen submittit se. vt. 2. & 7. nos si. & cum submittit se confessori suo, & etiam in casu haeresis, & hanc ultimam ponit glossa. dist. 40. sup. c. si papa: addens aliam comprehendentem innumeras, de qua dictum est superius, scilicet si crimen eius quodcunque esset notorium, & ipse incorrigibilis, & deo scandalizetur ecclesia. Sed inter exceptionem de haeresi & aliis criminibus est magna differentia attendenda, quod propter haeresim, quantumcunque occulta est, ipso iure sit sine omni sententia humana papatu & omni ecclesiastica praelatione priuatus: tanquam de congregatione fidelium secundum veritatem tam merito quam numero praecisus existens: licet secundum opinionem nescientium esse haereticum, caput ecclesiae reputatur: imo quod plus est, ipso iure excommunicationis sententiam & alias poenas omnes a sacris canonibus & pontificibus contra haereticos, praesertim episcopos, indistincte prolatas incurrit, hinc dicit glo. 24. quaest. 1. c. Achatius: hic est casus in quo papa papam ligare potest: in quo papa in canonem lata sententia incurrit, nec huic obuiat regula illa: quia par parem soluere vel ligare non potest, quia si papa haereticus est, in eo quod haereticus, est minor quolibet catholico: quia lex factum notat etiam sine sententia. Sed propter alia crimina papa non est ipso iure papatu priuatus; sed per sententiam est priuandus.
units.tr: ...could lawfully punish the supreme ruler, namely when all others failed, and the correction or punishment of the supreme ruler could not be passed over in silence or ignored without danger to the whole commonwealth. The answer is that such a person would be more subject to the supreme ruler than the reverse, because the former ruler would have the right to punish the exempt person not only when all his subjects failed, but also by reason of his supreme office. But one who is exempt only by necessity, and not by reason of his office, would have no right to correct the supreme ruler when all others failed. As for the minor premise of the aforesaid argument, that this one supreme judge or ruler ought to be none other than the supreme Pontiff, the reply is this: if the whole human race were perfectly ordered and subject to the best government, then, given Christ's ordinance by which he appointed the supreme Pontiff and the other clergy not to be entangled in secular affairs except in a case of necessity, this one supreme ruler or judge would not have to be the supreme Pontiff, but a Christian secular prince and layman. That he ought to be a layman and not the supreme Pontiff or a cleric is proved by what is proved above in question 1, where it is shown that clerics, outside the case of necessity and of usefulness that can be compared to necessity, ought to keep away from secular affairs. That he ought to be a Christian is clear: for if he tried to harm rather than foster the common spiritual good, he would oppose and resist the best government of the human race. When it is said that the jurisdiction of the supreme Pontiff, especially in those matters that concern the faith and Christian religion, depends on God alone, the answer is that, just as was touched on above, baptism and the other sacraments depend on God alone, this can be understood in different ways, and first as regards institution in three ways. In one way, that the supreme Pontiff receives his jurisdiction from God without any human ministry, so that in no case ought he to be instituted or deposed by man; and so his jurisdiction does not depend on God alone, because no one after Peter was raised to the papacy without election. In another way it can be understood that such jurisdiction depends on God alone as regards institution, with human ministry, namely canonical election, concurring; and in this sense that opinion holds good, that the jurisdiction of the Pope, which he has by Christ's ordinance, depends on God alone. Thirdly, it depends on God alone not only in this way but also as regards deposition, so that the Pope can be deposed in no case by anyone except God alone; and in this sense it does not depend on God alone, because he himself deposes himself. For a heretical depravity, which can depose him by voluntary renunciation, can also be brought against him by a man, on any crime whatever, if it is notorious, and if the Church is thereby scandalized and he is incorrigible, as is noted in the gloss on distinction 40, above chapter "si Papa." So in a case of this kind he can be judged, deposed and removed by a man. For every accusation must be brought before a judge. Nor should the Pope be disturbed about this, lest he seem to seek power rather than benefit; lest he wish to act against the doctrine of Christ delivered to the Apostles, and for himself and the prelates of the Church, to be cast out as salt that has lost its savour and trodden under foot by men; lest he wish, against the same Lord's command, to have a putrid member cut off for the salvation of that mystical body; lest he desire power that would not allow him, when corrected in love, and even if the Church does not hear him, to be treated as a heathen and a publican, and not allow his putrid flesh to be cut away; and lest he be driven from the stalls like a scabby sheep, and purged out like leaven that corrupts the whole lump. Rather, he should wish that he be spared, so that the whole Church is brought to ruin; all of which is unfitting to the desire of the Pope, who is bound to lay down his soul for his subjects. The Pope, therefore, according to this opinion, although in those matters where he ought to look to the salvation of all, so that he may not be hindered in them by anyone, is not unjustly exempt from the power and jurisdiction of the supreme ruler. Against this exemption the supreme government, if it wishes to benefit and not to harm, is bound in no way to attempt anything, but to praise it, since the authority of a person is not thought contemptible by reason of a crime of whatever kind, and lest his domination be hindered from serving the common good for some small offence. But if the offence is grave and enormous, especially one repeated and bringing notable danger to the common good, it is expedient that the Pope be capable of being deposed by human judgment; and this especially if he appears incorrigible and the Church is scandalized by him. It seems reasonable that the judgment of such a Pope should belong first to certain persons of the clergy, and if they fail, whether through malice or culpable negligence, it should pertain to the ruler, if he is a sincere and fervent defender of the faith and of the Christian religion. But if the ruler too fails, whether through malice or culpable negligence, the deposition of the Pope, or at least his detention or prohibition from growing insolent, belongs best either to the universal assembly of the faithful, or to any faithful who may have such temporal power over him that a fitting remedy may be found in the Church against the sin of any Christian, whether small or great, according to that saying of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 5: "Put away the evil from among yourselves"; and again he says: "Purge out the old leaven." Unless temporal power fails, in which case the counsel of Jerome must be kept, which is found in question 3 of cause 11, chapter "Quando igitur": namely that Christians, even those who understand and are prudent, should keep silent, lest they give what is holy to dogs and cast their pearls before swine, who, turning, trample them underfoot; and they should imitate Jeremiah saying: "I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness." A sign that, by reason of a crime, the Pope in some case falls under the court of the first supreme ruler, who ought to be a layman, is taken from the divine Scriptures, in which we read that Christ and the Apostles, when they were accused of crimes, were judged by secular judges, even unbelieving ones. Nor do we read that they, although they denied the crimes laid against them, asserted or protested that in such a case they were not bound to answer before such judges; rather, in such a case they seem to have indicated that they were subject to them. For Christ said to Pilate, as we read in John 19: "You would have no power at all over me, unless it were given you from above." In these words Christ seems to have hinted that Pilate in that case had ordinary power over him, given to him from above by God, according to the interpretation of some doctors, or from the Emperor, according to the interpretation of others; because Pilate in that case had over him not a usurped power but a granted and given power. The Apostle also seems to have hinted at the same thing about himself, when he was accused of crimes before unbelieving judges, as we read in Acts 24. where he says to the governor: "Knowing that you have been for many years a judge to this nation, I shall answer for myself with good courage." He does not say "I am not bound to answer before you," but says "I shall answer for myself (otherwise, through myself)," wherefore he seems by deed and word to have acknowledged his judge in that case. And this is found in chapter 25 of the same book, where he said to the governor: "I stand before Caesar's tribunal; there I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. If I have wronged anyone, or done anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die. But if none of those things is true of which these men accuse me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar." In these words Paul acknowledged both Festus and Caesar as his judge. Since, therefore, it is wicked to say that Paul lied in deed or word, Caesar truly was Paul's judge. But perhaps someone might say that from this a manifest absurdity would follow, namely that an emperor, even an unbeliever, would be the judge of the Pope in a matter of faith; because Paul's case, which was being handled before the judge, was a matter of faith, for he was accused by the Jews on account of the Christian faith. Here the answer is that a matter of faith could properly be handled before a believing emperor, when others failed, because, as is found in distinction 46, "Ubinam," the question of faith pertains not only to clerics but also to laymen and to all Christians. But before an unbelieving emperor a matter of faith may seem capable of being tried, not insofar as it concerns only the revealed truth, but insofar as it can touch the morals of the commonwealth, or derogate from the common good, or inflict injury on some person. It seems that the proconsul of Achaia, Gallio, prudently indicated both of these, who, as Acts 18 says, when Paul was accused by the Jews, said to them: "If it were some wrong or some grave crime, O Jews, I would rightly bear with you. But if these are questions about a word and about names and your law, see to it yourselves. I do not wish to be a judge of these things." So, then, it is said that in a case involving a crime the Pope is subject to the Emperor. As for all the other canons and authorities from which it is gathered that the Pope is to be judged by no one, it is said that they ought not to be understood without every exception, but with their own exceptions; just as other rules of law, and indeed very many authorities of divine Scripture, though they are pronounced not only indefinitely but also in general terms and with universal signs, must be understood with exceptions. Hence also the gloss on 9. q. 3. sup. 6, "Nemo," lists some exceptions, if he submits himself, as in 2 and 7, "Nos si," and when he submits himself to his confessor, and also in the case of heresy; and the gloss on dist. 40, above chapter "si papa," puts this last one, adding another that comprehends countless cases, of which it was said above: namely, if his crime, of whatever kind, were notorious, and he were incorrigible, and the Church were scandalized by him. But between the exception concerning heresy and the exception concerning other crimes there is a great difference to be noted: for on account of heresy, however hidden it may be, the Pope is by the law itself deprived of the papacy and of every ecclesiastical prelacy, without any human sentence, as one who by the truth, both in merit and in number, is already cut off from the assembly of the faithful; although, according to the opinion of those who do not know that he is a heretic, he is still reputed the head of the Church. Indeed, what is more, by the law itself he incurs the sentence of excommunication and all the other penalties, pronounced indiscriminately against heretics, especially bishops, by the sacred canons and Popes; hence the gloss on 24. q. 1, chapter "Achatius," says: "This is the case in which a pope can bind a pope; in which a pope incurs a sentence pronounced by the canon." Nor does that rule stand in the way: that an equal cannot loose or bind an equal; for if the Pope is a heretic, in that he is a heretic he is less than any Catholic, since the law marks the deed even without a sentence. But for other crimes the Pope is not deprived of the papacy by the law itself; he must be deprived by sentence.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: Capite ultimo tertia quaestionis respondet ad rationes supra positas capitulo secundo, pro approbatione secundae opinionis post prin- cipium capituli.
units.tr: In the last chapter of the third question he answers the arguments set out above in chapter two, in support of the second opinion, after the opening of the chapter.

units.la: Visso quomodo secundum opinionem supra cap. 2. recitatam, respondetur ad allegationem adductam primo cap. Videndum est quomodo respondetur secundum primam opinionem ad illa, quae pro secunda opinione cap. 2. allegantur. Ad primum, cum dicitur quod imperator est Dominus supremi pontificis, dicitur quod non est verum, quia papa non est vasallus imperatoris, nec ei de iure tributum debet, nisi forte propter scandalum euitandum. Alii autem clerici habentes ab imperatore praedia, villas & superabundantes possessiones imperatori sunt subiecti, ut dicitur praeallegato 2. cap. quoniam sic intelligitur decretum Vrbani. 23. quaest. 8. c. tributum, cum autem dicitur, quod aliqui supremi pontifices Imperatores Dominos suos appellauerunt, dicitur quod ex humilitate hoc fecerunt.
units.tr: Now that it has been shown how, according to the opinion recited above in cap. 2., the argument adduced in primo cap. is answered, we must see how, according to the first opinion, the points alleged for the second opinion in cap. 2. are answered. To the first point: when it is said that the emperor is Lord of the supreme pontiff, we reply that this is not true, because the pope is not the vassal of the emperor, nor does he owe him tribute by right, except perhaps to avoid scandal. But other clerics who hold estates, farms and surplus possessions from the emperor are subject to the emperor, as is said in the 2. cap. cited above; for this is how the decree of Urban is to be understood, 23. quaest. 8. c. tributum. As for the claim that some supreme pontiffs called the emperors their Lords, we say that they did so out of humility.

units.la: Ad secundum autem cum dicitur quod res transit cum onere suo. Respondetur secundum illos, qui dicunt quod papa habet illam plenitudinem potestatis, de qua tactum est supra quaest. 1. hoc est verum, quando res transit de dominio in dominium: vel de iure in ius nouum alterius. Sed illo modo nulla res temporalis potest transire in dominium papae: quia papa est Dominus omnium temporalium rerum cuiuscunque, quae de permissione ipsius possidentur: & ideo secundum opinionem istam nullus Imperator, aut rex, aut alius potest proprie loquendo dare possessionem vel rem quamcunque supremo pontifici: sed si rem de permissione papae possidet, resignare potest eidem: quemadmodum secundum Innocent. 4. Constantinus illam inordinatam potestatem, qua fortassis antea illegitime utebatur, humiliter resignavit. Secundum vero illos, qui illam plenitudinem potestatis negant a papa: sed illam, qua posset omnia, quae necessaria sunt pro communitate fidelium gubernanda sibi attribuunt. Respondetur, quod res transit cum onere suo, nisi in favorem fidei papae aut ecclesiae aut alicuius alterius specialiter a suo onere liberetur: quemadmodum servus presbyter in favorem clericalis ordinis liberatur, ita tamen ut peculii amissione multetur, di. 54. ex antiquis. Cum autem accipitur, quod religio Christiana neminem a servitute liberat, dicitur quod hoc non est verum. Cum vero dicitur, quod in favorem ecclesiae nihil iniustum statuitur, concedit: sed dicitur, quod non est semper iniustum & iniquum, quod aliquis sine culpa privetur iure suo, quando subest causa: & quando ius huiusmodi est totaliter in potestate superioris: quemadmodum omnia iura sua sunt in potestate papae. Ad Gelasium respondetur, quod Gelasius intendit servos dominorum suorum iura sub obtentu religionis fugere non debere absque auctoritate supremi pontificis: & ita hoc iure canonico est statutum. Et cum dicitur, quod iura canonica leges seculares & iura secularia nequaquam tollere possunt. Respondetur secundum opinionem, quae papae illam plenitudinem potestatis attribuit, de qua dictum est supra: quod iura canonica omnes leges seculares & omnia iura secularium principum tollere possunt & subuertere, & ea dare cui placuerit, & ita ut etiam omnia regna & quaecunque alia iura ac res temporales vniuersas pro suo libito voluntatis de iure posset papa tollere ab his qui possident eas, & sibi retinere, & aliis quibuscunque conferre: ita quod quamuis hoc faciendo peccaret, tamen cum factum esset de iure teneret: ac reges & omnes alii sibi tenentur in hoc obedire. Secundum vero aliam opinionem, quae dicit, quod papa habet huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis, sc. illam qua possit omnia, quae necessaria sunt pro communitate fidelium gubernanda: respondetur, quod iura canonica leges seculares & iura secularia tollere possent ex causa, sed non absque causa rationabili & manifesta electione.
units.tr: To the second point, when it is said that a thing passes with its burden, we reply, according to those who hold that the pope has that fullness of power of which we spoke above in quaest. 1., that this is true when a thing passes from one ownership to another, or from one right to a new right of someone else. But in that way no temporal thing can pass into the ownership of the pope, since the pope is Lord of all temporal things of whatever kind that are possessed by his permission; and so, according to this opinion, no emperor, king or anyone else can properly speak of giving possession or any thing whatever to the supreme pontiff. But if he holds a thing by the pope's permission, he can surrender it to him, just as, according to Innocent IV, Constantine humbly surrendered that disordered power which he perhaps had been using illegitimately before. According to those, however, who deny that fullness of power to the pope, but attribute to him that power by which he can do all things that are necessary for governing the common body of the faithful, we reply that a thing passes with its burden, unless it is specially freed from its burden in favour of the faith, of the pope, of the Church or of someone else; just as a servant who becomes a presbyter is freed in favour of the clerical order, yet in such a way that he is punished by the loss of his property, di. 54. ex antiquis. When it is taken that the Christian religion frees no one from servitude, we say this is not true. When it is said that nothing unjust is decreed in favour of the Church, we grant it; but we say that it is not always unjust and iniquitous for someone to be deprived of his right without fault, when there is a cause for it, and when a right of this kind lies wholly in the power of a superior, just as all their rights lie in the power of the pope. As for Gelasius, we reply that Gelasius meant that servants should not flee from their masters' rights under the pretext of religion without the authority of the supreme pontiff, and that this is what canon law has so decreed. And when it is said that canon laws can by no means override secular laws and secular rights, we reply, according to the opinion which ascribes to the pope that fullness of power of which we have spoken above, that canon laws can override and subvert all secular laws and all the rights of secular princes, and give them to whomever he pleases; indeed the pope could by right take all kingdoms and all other rights and temporal things from those who possess them at his whim, keep them for himself and confer them on whomever he likes, so that although he would sin in doing so, the act would nonetheless hold good in law, and kings and all others are bound to obey him in this. According to the other opinion, which holds that the pope has such a fullness of power, namely that power by which he can do all things necessary for governing the common body of the faithful, we reply that canon laws, secular laws and secular rights could indeed be overridden for a cause, but not without a reasonable cause and a manifest election.

units.la: QVAESTIO QVARTA.
units.tr: QUESTION FOUR.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Quaestionis quarta capitulum primum proponit ipsam quaestionem: & circa eius solutionem primo incidentaliter disquiritur, an inter Imperatorem & regem Romanorum sit distinctio. Et ponit diversas opiniones, primam hic, & aliam capite sequenti. Ad primam autem probationes respondebitur capitulo 7. Sed capitulo 8. procedit ad principalis quaestionis decisionem.
units.tr: The first chapter of this question sets out the question itself. In working towards its solution, it first inquires incidentally whether there is a distinction between the Emperor and the King of the Romans. It sets out various opinions, the first here and another in the following chapter. The arguments for the first opinion will be answered in chapter 7, and in chapter 8 it proceeds to the decision of the main question.

units.la: QVarto quaeritur, Vtrum electio alicuius in regem Romanorum vel Imperatorem sibi det plenam administrationem, ex quo sua potestas est immediate a Deo. Haec quaestio quandam aliam videtur supponere, quod inter regem Romanorum & Imperatorem sit aliqua distinctio. Circa quam sunt opiniones diversae: quarum una est, quod inter regem Romanorum & Imperatorem realis est distinctio, & quod primo est electus Rex Romanorum, quam sit Imperator. Nam Rex est postea in Imperatorem promouendus, di. 23. in nomine Domini. & extra, de electione, venerabilem, quod non esset verum, si non esset realis distinctio inter regem Romanorum & Imperatorem: sed verbalis tantum modo, quod videtur absurdum: quia tunc lex esset imposita verbis & non rebus: & distinctio nominum non declararet distinctionem rerum, quod est contra iura di. 21. Dicitur ergo, quod promotio ad imperium, quae fit per unctionem & coronationem imperialem, nou fit propter nomen imperatorii tantummodo consequendum: sed Imperator post unctionem & coronationem consequitur potestatem imperialem in omnibus regnis & etiam in populis, praesertim occidentalibus, qui non fuerunt sub iurisdictione & potestate Caroli Magni ante tempus translationis imperii, & adhuc sunt sub potestate imperii: & de facto in Italia & in aliis terris & prouinciis, quae ante unctionem & coronationem imperialem subiectae erant Carolo Magno, primo habet Rex Romanorum eandem potestatem ante unctionem imperialem, quam est postea habituri; & ideo Imperator non tenet a papa prouincias & terras subiectas regno & Imperio, quas tenuit Carolus, sine iure haereditario, siue iure belli, ante translationem imperii in ipsum factam per papam. Sed Imperator tenet a papa nomen imperatoris & iura imperialia seu potestatem imperialem in aliis prouinciis & terris, quae non erant sub potestate Caroli ante tempus translationis imperii: & ratione illius nominis Imperii ac iurium huiusmodi recipit ab eo unctionem & coronationem imperialem. Sic etiam potestas eligendi Imperatorem, ut electus ab eis consequatur nomen Imperatoris & potestatem aestatem imperialem, seu potestatem actus Imperatori reservatos exercendi in aliis provinciis & terris, quæ non subsunt regno & Imperio Romanorum, & quas non habuit Carolus tempore translationis imperii, pervenit ad principes electores per ecclesiam, & quoad ista consequenda Rex Romanorum petere consuevit a papa & Romana ecclesia, post electionem suam sibi vnctionem & coronationem impendi.
units.tr: Fourthly, it is asked: whether the election of someone as King of the Romans or Emperor gives him full administration of power, since his power comes immediately from God. This question seems to presuppose that there is some distinction between the King of the Romans and the Emperor, and opinions on this differ. One opinion holds that there is a real distinction between the King of the Romans and the Emperor, and that a man is first elected King of the Romans and only afterwards Emperor. For the King is later to be promoted to the empire (di. 23, In nomine Domini; extra, de electione, Venerabilem). This would not be true if the distinction between King of the Romans and Emperor were not real but merely verbal. That seems absurd, since then the law would be imposed on words and not on things, and a distinction of names would not declare a distinction of things, which is contrary to the law in di. 21. It is therefore said that promotion to the empire, which takes place through anointing and imperial coronation, is not undertaken merely to obtain the name of emperor. Rather, after anointing and coronation the Emperor acquires imperial power over all kingdoms, and also over peoples, especially western peoples, who were not under the jurisdiction and power of Charlemagne before the time of the translation of the empire, and who are still under the power of the empire. In fact, in Italy and in other lands and provinces which were subject to Charlemagne before imperial anointing and coronation, the King of the Romans already has, before imperial anointing, the same power that he will afterwards have. Therefore the Emperor does not hold from the pope the provinces and lands belonging to the kingdom and Empire which Charles held, by hereditary right or by right of war, before the translation of the empire made to him by the pope. But the Emperor does hold from the pope the name of emperor and the imperial rights, or imperial power, in other provinces and lands which were not under Charles's power before the time of the translation of the empire; and by reason of that title of the Empire and such rights he receives from the pope anointing and imperial coronation. Likewise, the power of electing an Emperor, so that the one elected obtains from the electors the name of Emperor and imperial power, or the power of exercising acts reserved to the Emperor in other provinces and lands which do not belong to the kingdom and Empire of the Romans, and which Charles did not have at the time of the translation of the empire, passed to the electoral princes through the Church. And in order to obtain these things, the King of the Romans has customarily asked the pope and the Roman Church, after his election, to bestow anointing and coronation upon him.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Recitat contrariam fore opinionem opinioni capituli precedentis.
units.tr: Sets out the opinion contrary to that of the preceding chapter.

units.la: ALia est opinio, quæ videtur dicere, optimum principatum Germaniæ, de quo notatur extra, de verb. sig. super quibusdam hoc velle, quod inter regem Romanorum & Imperatorem, seu inter regnum & Imperium solummodo est verbalis distinctio: ut sint diversorum nominum, sed eiusdem officii & potestatis: quemadmodum dicitur de primatibus & patriarchis, dist. 99. provincia, unde Imperatores antiquitus, antequam esset aut dubitatio, aut distinctio inter regem Romanorum & Imperatorem, aliquando vocabantur reges: aliquando Imperatores, & eorum dominium, aliquando regnum, aliquando imperium vocabatur: sicut patet ex lib. Iudi. c. 1. & 2. & libro Hester. c. 1. Pro ista opinione potest taliter allegari. In initio imperii Romanorum, & per longa tempora post, inter imperatorem & regem illorum, seu inter imperium & regnum Romanorum nulla erat distinctio: sed ista erant nomina eiusdem potestatis, ergo & nunc sunt nomina eiusdem potestatis, antecedens non videtur aliqua probatione indigere, nam in novo testamento, in quo semper de regno Romanorum & Imperio fit mentio, nec in scripturis aliis, fere usque ad tempora moderna, nulla insinuatur nec implicite nec explicite inter imperium & regnum Romanorum distinctio, nec legitur in antiquis scripturis de hoc dubitatione etiam modicam fuisse motam. Consequentia probatur: quia reges Romanorum & Imperatores posteriores usque ad tempora ista fuerunt successores eorum, qui primo non solummodo reges, sed Imperatores Romanorum facti fuerunt: scilicet Iulii Cæsaris, Augusti & cæterorum, quia ab illis vocabantur Cæsares & Augusti. Et in signum, quod sunt illorum successores, omnes isti successores usque ad tempora ista Augusti & Cæsares vocabantur, & omnes scripserunt se Augustos. Rex autem, qui alteri regi in regno aliquo succedit, eodem iure, quo ille, uti debet, extra, de regu. iuris. si quis lib. 6. Aliter enim successor minus haberet, quam prædecessor: & sic non esset vera successio, ut arguit glo. in simili casu, extra, de constitutionibus, super cap. cum omnes, quare multi reges Romanorum usi fuerunt omni iure in temporalibus, quo Imperator post unctionem & coronationem utitur, ergo ultimi reges Romanorum & omnes futuri, qui illorum regum, qui fuerunt primi Imperatores, fuerunt veri successores, obtinuerunt omnem potestatem, & habebant, quam Imperator habet, post quantamcunque unctionem & coronationem.
units.tr: There is another opinion, which seems to hold that the best principality of Germany, which is noted in extra, de verb. sig. in the passage on certain matters, wishes this: that between the king of the Romans and Emperor, or between the kingdom and the Empire, there is only a verbal distinction, so that they are different names for the same office and power, as is said of primates and patriarchs in dist. 99. provincia. Hence, in ancient times, before there was any doubt or distinction between the king of the Romans and the Emperor, the rulers were sometimes called Imperatores, sometimes kings, and their dominion was sometimes called regnum and sometimes imperium, as is clear from lib. Iudi. c. 1. & 2. & libro Hester. c. 1. For this opinion the following argument can be made. At the beginning of the Roman empire, and for a long time afterwards, there was no distinction between the Emperor and the king of the Romans, or between the Roman imperium and regnum; these were names of the same power. Therefore they are names of the same power now too. The antecedent does not seem to need any proof, for in the New Testament, where the kingdom and Empire of the Romans are always mentioned, and in other writings almost up to modern times, no distinction between imperium and regnum of the Romans is hinted at, either implicitly or explicitly, and nowhere in the ancient writings is it read that any doubt about this was even slightly raised. The consequence is proved thus: the later kings of the Romans and Emperors, up to these times, were successors of those who first were made not only kings but Emperors of the Romans, namely Julius Caesar, Augustus and the others, since they were called Cæsares & Augusti after them. And as a sign that they are the successors of those men, all these successors up to the present time were called Augusti & Cæsares, and all of them styled themselves Augustos. But a king who succeeds another king in some kingdom ought to use the same right as that king, extra, de regu. iuris. si quis lib. 6. For otherwise the successor would have less than the predecessor, and so there would not be a true succession, as the gloss argues in a similar case, extra, de constitutionibus, super cap. cum omnes. Therefore many kings of the Romans have enjoyed in temporal matters every right which the Emperor exercises after unction and coronation. Consequently the last kings of the Romans, and all future ones, are true successors of those kings who were the first Emperors; they have obtained every power, and have whatever power the Emperor has, after however much unction and coronation.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Deducit prædictas opiniones, ostendens, in quo discordent: & quid verisimilitudinis habeant. Multa præterea de regno Franciæ, an usurpatitium sit, inseruntur. Et diversarum opinionum discordia iterum ostenditur. Et quomodo secundum secundam opinionem imperium Romanorum non distinguitur à regno Romanorum. Ponuntur etiam exceptiones, quibus gerentes iusta bella non efficiuntur domini expugnatorum.
units.tr: He sets out the aforementioned opinions, showing where they differ and what plausibility each has. Much is also said about the kingdom of France, and whether it was usurped. The disagreement between the various opinions is shown again, and how, according to the second opinion, the Roman empire is not distinguished from the Roman kingdom. Exceptions are also laid down, by which those who wage just wars do not become lords of the conquered.

units.la: VErum, quia primam opinionem munitam allegationibus & declaratam a quodam venerabili Doctore inueni, non autem secundam, quæ videtur fuisse principum Germaniæ, ut ex collatione secundæ ad primam inveniendi vel investigandi veritatem etiam circa iura imperii detur occasio: absque assertione tantummodo recitando fore utile iudicium aliqua, quæ exprimat prima opinio, breviter absque assertione pertractare. In quibus apparet, quod secunda opinio secundum intentionem principum Germaniæ sive præter intentionem eorum contrariatur ei: quia integram pronunciationem eorum nescio indicare. Contrariantur autem opinio prima & secunda in multis. Discordant enim prima, quia primo opinio
units.tr: But since I have found the first opinion supported by arguments and set out by a certain venerable Doctor, while the second, which seems to have been held by the princes of Germany, is not, I will briefly treat the first opinion here without offering any assertion, merely reciting its judgment, so that the comparison of the second with the first may give occasion to find or investigate the truth, even concerning the rights of the empire. In these matters it appears that the second opinion, whether according to the intention of the princes of Germany or contrary to their intention, is opposed to the first, since I cannot tell what their complete pronouncement was. The first and second opinions differ in many respects. For first, the first opinion

units.la: videtur asserere quod Imperatores, qui fuerunt post Carolum Magnum, nihil iuris habent in regno & imperio, nisi in quantum sunt eiusdem Caroli successores: eius scilicet successores non solum in quantum fuit Imperator, sed etiam in quantum fuit Francorum Rex hereditarie succedens patri suo Pipino, qui depositio Childerico Rex Francorum subrogatus fuit: & in quantum idem Carolus per bella sibi iusta & licita sibi multas terras & provincias subiugauit; & regno Francorum adiunxit.
units.tr: seems to assert that the Emperors who came after Charlemagne have no right in the kingdom and empire, except insofar as they are successors of Charlemagne himself: namely, his successors not only as Emperor, but also as King of the Franks, succeeding hereditarily his father Pepin, who was made king of the Franks in place of Childeric, once he had been deposed; and insofar as the same Charlemagne, by just and lawful wars, subjected to himself many lands and provinces and joined them to the kingdom of the Franks.

units.la: Secunda opinio tenet, quod Imperatores & reges Romanorum, qui fuerunt post Carolum Magnum, fuerunt principaliter successores primorum imperatorum & regum Romanorum, quorum nonnulli fuerunt temporibus Christi & Apostolorum eius. Non fuerunt autem in quantum Imperatores & reges Romanorum successores Caroli, nisi in quantum Carolus fuit successor primorum Imperatorum & regum Romanorum, & aliorum qui fuerunt post primos, licet quidam successores Caroli erant successores illius, non solummodo in quantum erat successor primorum Imperatorum, nec in quantum erat Imperator, sed in quantum erat Rex Francorum, vel alicuius partis regni Francorum: quemadmodum si filius Imperatoris ad imperium electi & assumpti posset fieret Imperator, dupliciter succederet patri. In quantum enim pater eius, antequam esset Imperator, fuerat Dux Bauariae, succederet patri in Ducatum ut patri. In quantum vero pater eius Imperator erat, succederet ei in imperiu ut Imperatori. Ex hoc siquidem, quod Imperatores post Carolum fuerunt successores primorum Imperatorum & regum Romanorum, praesertim illorum, qui fuerunt tempore Christi & Apostolorum, in quo fundata est allegatio adducta in praecedenti capi. apparet quod Imperatores & reges Romanorum, multo magis stabilitatem & vigorem habere videntur, quam ex hoc quod sunt successores Caroli Magni. Ratio est, quia magis notum est, quod infideles erant veri Imperatores & reges Romanorum, quam quod Carolus fuit verus Imperator & Rex Romanorum: quia de illo vero Imperio sive regno testimonium magis habemus: cum testimonium Dei maius sit, quam testimonium hominum: ut habetur in Iohan. Nam de vero Imperio sive regno illorum Imperatorum infidelium habemus testimonium Christi sive Spiritus sancti, qui in Iohanne Baptista & Luca Euangelista loquebatur & Apostolis, dicit enim Christus de Tiberio Caesare: Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, non dicit: reddite, quae Caesar dicit esse tua: sed dicit, quae sunt Caesaris. Iohannes etiam Baptista: ut legitur Luc. 3. dixit publicanis & militibus, qui officium & stipendium a Tiberio Caesare acceperunt, nihil amplius faciatis quam statutum est vobis. Contenti estote stipendiis vestris. Ex quibus colligitur, quod iste Tiberius & Rex Romanorum erat & verus Imperator. De Octauiano vero primo Augusto dicit Lucas Euangelista, euangelii sui secundo. Exiit edictum a Caesare Augusto, ut describeretur universus orbis. Et de alio quodam loqui videtur Petrus, dicens, 1. canonica sua, cap. 2. Subiecti estote omni humanae naturae sive regi, quasi praecellenti. Et iterum, regem honorificate. Et beatus Paulus de Nerone actuum 25. ait, ad tribunal Caesaris sto: ibi oportet me iudicari, & iterum, Caesarem appello. Tantum autem testimonium non habemus de Carolo Magno: sed longe minus de vero Imperio sive regno quocunque ipsius habemus, praesertim quantum ad regnum Francorum. Unde etiam quidam ex historiis & Chronicis conantur probare, quod non est verum regnum, sed tantummodo usurpatum, cum primi reges Francorum, in quorum locum successit Carolus Magnus, eiusdem regni fuerint invasores, aut successores eorum, qui terras eiusdem regni aut provincias contra obedientiam, quam Imperatori debebant, sibi contumaciter vsurpauerunt. Nam legitur in chronica Eusebii, quod Sicambri, qui a quibusdam profugis traxerunt originem, propter victoriam, quam habuerunt de Alemannis, de Valentiniano Imperatore per decem annos facti liberi omni tributo, & Franchi vocati post expletum decennium tributum soluere recusantes, missos ab Imperatore ad recipiendum tributum occiderunt: & postea ab Imperatore & exercitu rebellantes venerunt in Turingiam, & primo post Rhenum transgressi Romanos, qui eo tempore in Gallia per suos magistratus usque ad Rheni fluuium imperabant, bello aggressi partim ipsos occiderunt & partim fugauerunt. Postea captis urbibus Tornaco & Cameraco, atque paulatim aggressi & regressi Remis, Suessionem, Aurelianam, & Coloniam, quae dicebatur tunc Agrippina, & Treuerim, ac postremo totam Galliam ab Aquitania usque ad Bauariam sibi vendicant atque subiiciunt. Ex iis, qui mixti sunt cum Teuthonicis, proprio vocabulo Franci: qui vero per connubia a Gallis sunt geniti, Francigenae appellati sunt. Primus autem Rex Francorum fuit Pharamundus, nepos Priami, sub quo & cum duce suo Antenore fuit predicta victoria de Alemannis, & regnauit ipse anno domini 426. & ab illo tempore Germani vocantur. Franci vero a tempore praedicti Pharamundi fuerunt reges Francorum usque ad tempora Hilderici regis, qui fuit vltimus de genere illo, quo deposito Pipinus pater Caroli Magni substitutus est eidem. Ex quo patet, quod regnum Francorum ex tyrannico incepit initio, & videtur saltem antequam Carolus Magnus factus est Imperator nunquam fuisse verum & iustum regnum, sed tyrannicum & vsurpatum, quia si factum fuit legitimum, iustum & verum regnum, aut hoc fiebat per praescriptionem, aut electionem & consensum seu voluntatem populi Francorum, aut per substitutionem Pipini Hilderico regi iam depositi. Non per praescriptionem legitimam. Tum quia possessor malae fidei nullo tempore praescribit, extra de reiudic. possessor. lib. 6. extra de praescript. vigilanti. Franci autem in principio bonam fidem acquirendo sibi regnum minime habuerunt, cum per violentiam terras subiectas Imperio inuaserunt & possederunt, quare origo praescriptionis exitit vitiosa: & per consequens praescriptio vera non fuit. Cum quia contra consuetam obedientiam vel subiectionem contra publicam vtilitatem, contra res principis non currit praescriptio: sed Franci con-
units.tr: The second opinion holds that the Emperors and Roman kings who came after Charlemagne were chiefly successors of the first emperors and Roman kings, some of whom lived in the times of Christ and his Apostles. They were not, however, successors of Charlemagne as Emperors and Roman kings, except insofar as Charlemagne was himself a successor of the first Emperors and Roman kings, and of the others who came after the first. Yet some successors of Charlemagne were also successors of his in another respect, not merely as successor of the first Emperors, nor as Emperor, but as King of the Franks, or of some part of the kingdom of the Franks. It is as if the son of an Emperor, once elected and assumed to the empire, could become Emperor, and so would succeed his father in two ways: insofar as his father, before he was Emperor, had been Duke of Bavaria, he would succeed him in the duchy as a son; but insofar as his father was Emperor, he would succeed him in the empire as Emperor. From the fact that the Emperors after Charlemagne were successors of the first Emperors and Roman kings, especially of those who lived in the time of Christ and his Apostles (on which the argument brought forward in the preceding chapter is founded), it appears that the Emperors and Roman kings seem to have much greater stability and force than they have from being successors of Charlemagne. The reason is that it is better known that the infidels were true Emperors and Roman kings than that Charlemagne was a true Emperor and Roman king, since we have more testimony concerning that true empire or kingdom. For the testimony of God is greater than the testimony of men, as is found in John. Indeed, concerning the true empire or kingdom of those infidel Emperors we have the testimony of Christ, or of the Holy Spirit, who spoke through John the Baptist, Luke the Evangelist, and the Apostles. For Christ says of Tiberius Caesar: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; he does not say: render what Caesar says is yours, but he says the things that are Caesar's. John the Baptist too, as we read in Luke 3, said to the tax collectors and soldiers, who had received their office and pay from Tiberius Caesar: Do nothing more than what is appointed for you. Be content with your wages. From these words it is gathered that this Tiberius was both the Roman king and the true Emperor. Concerning Octavian, the first Augustus, the Evangelist Luke says in the second chapter of his Gospel: A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. And Peter seems to speak of another, saying in 1 Peter, chapter 2: Submit yourselves to every human ordinance, whether to the king as supreme. And again: Honour the king. And the blessed Paul, speaking of Nero in Acts 25, says: I stand before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be judged, and again: I appeal to Caesar. But we have no such testimony concerning Charlemagne, and far less do we have testimony concerning any true empire or kingdom of his, especially as regards the kingdom of the Franks. Hence some, from histories and chronicles, try to prove that it is not a true kingdom but merely usurped, since the first kings of the Franks, in whose place Charlemagne succeeded, were invaders of that kingdom, or successors of those who stubbornly usurped for themselves the lands or provinces of that kingdom against the obedience they owed to the Emperor. For we read in the chronicle of Eusebius that the Sicambri, who derived their origin from certain fugitives, on account of the victory they had over the Alemanni, were made free of all tribute for ten years by the Emperor Valentinian; and when, after the ten years were completed, the Franks, who had been so called, refused to pay the tribute, they killed the men sent by the Emperor to collect it; and afterwards, rebelling against the Emperor and his army, they came into Thuringia, and first crossing the Rhine they attacked the Romans, who at that time governed Gaul through their magistrates as far as the river Rhine, and in war they partly killed them and partly put them to flight. Afterwards, having captured the cities of Tournai and Cambrai, and gradually advancing and retreating, they attacked and claimed for themselves and subjected to their rule Reims, Soissons, Orléans, Cologne, which was then called Agrippina, and Trier, and finally the whole of Gaul from Aquitaine as far as Bavaria. Those who were mixed with the Teutons were called Franks by their own name; but those who were born of Gauls through intermarriage were called Gallo-Franks. The first King of the Franks, however, was Pharamond, grandson of Priam, under whom and with his leader Antenor the aforesaid victory over the Alemanni was won; he reigned in the year of the Lord 426, and from that time they are called Germans. The Franks, moreover, from the time of the aforesaid Pharamond, were kings of the Franks down to the time of King Childeric, who was the last of that line, and after whose deposition Pepin, the father of Charlemagne, was put in his place. From this it is clear that the kingdom of the Franks began in tyranny, and seems, at least before Charlemagne became Emperor, never to have been a true and just kingdom, but a tyrannical and usurped one. For if it was made a legitimate, just and true kingdom, this happened either by prescription, or by election and the consent or will of the people of the Franks, or by the substitution of Pepin in place of the already deposed King Childeric. Not by lawful prescription; first, because a possessor in bad faith never prescribes at any time (Extra, de reiudicatis, possessor, lib. 6; Extra, de praescriptionibus, vigilanti). The Franks, moreover, at the beginning, in acquiring the kingdom for themselves, by no means had good faith, since they invaded and possessed by violence lands subject to the Empire; therefore the origin of the prescription was vicious, and consequently no true prescription arose. Secondly, prescription does not run against the customary obedience or subjection, against the public benefit, or against the property of the prince; but the Franks, by setting up a king for themselves, became disobedient to the Emperor and acted against the public benefit, which is so public and so useful a right of the empire, by diminishing the property and lands of the prince, that is, the Emperor, by usurping them unjustly for themselves. Therefore the kingdom of the Franks was not made by lawful prescription.

units.la: 60 stimendo sibi regem inobedientes Imperatori fuerunt & contra publicam vtilitatem fecerunt ius imperii, quod est tam publicum & vtilissimum minuendo ac res ac terras principis, scilicet Imperatoris, sibi vsurpando iniuste, quare regnum Francorum per praescriptionem legitimam factum non fuit verum regnum. Nec per electionem & consensum seu voluntatem populi Francorum poterat fieri verum regnum: quia quamuis populus non habens superiorem seu regem, si careat rege, possit constituere regem proprium de iure gentium: tamen populus habens de iure quamuis non de facto superiorem seu regem, non potest constituere alium regem, populus autem Francorum de iure habuit superiorem, scilicet imperatorem, cuius est reges constituere in terris subiectis imperio. Habuerunt etiam regem, scilicet imperatorem: ergo populus Francorum absque auctoritate imperatoris non poterat constituere sibi regem: & ita regnum Francorum non fuit de iure verum regnum, etiam per voluntatem populi Francorum. Nec fuit verum regnum per substitutionem, quia aut illa substitutio facta fuit a populo Francorum, aut a papa. Si a populo Francorum, nulla fuit; quia licet populus Francorum potest sibi constituere regem; non tamen potest aliquem substituere alteri in regem. Sed populus Francorum, vt probatum est, propter hoc, quod de iure subiectus fuit imperatori, non potest sibi constituere regem: ergo nec substituere. Si autem illa substitutio fieret a papa de iure, nulla fuit. Tum quia sicut papa tollere iura imperatorum non potest: ita nec exercere, vt papa testatur, extra, de iudiciis, nouit. Tum quia de secularibus negotiis se intromittere non debet, iuxta illud Apostoli, 2. Timoth. 2. Nemo militans Deo implicat se secularibus negotiis. Cum quia consimili ratione posset in quocunque regno constituere regem: & ita imperatores, ad quos solummodo pertinet conferre regiam dignitatem, sibi vsurpare non possent cuius contrarium habetur act. 6. Sed forte aliquis diceret, quod licet papa regulariter non possit constituere regem: potest tamen casualiter, scilicet in casu necessitatis, qualis fuit, quando Pipinus fuit constitutus Rex Francorum.
units.tr: 60 By making themselves kings, they became disobedient to the Emperor and acted against the public good. They took to themselves, unjustly, a right of the empire that is so public and so very useful, thereby diminishing the property and lands of the prince, namely the Emperor. Therefore the kingdom of the Franks, made by legitimate prescription, was not a true kingdom. Nor could it become a true kingdom through election, or through the consent or will of the Frankish people. For although a people that has no superior or king may, if it lacks a king, establish its own king by the law of nations, a people that has by right, though not in fact, a superior or king cannot set up another king. The Frankish people by right had a superior, namely the Emperor, whose office it is to appoint kings in lands subject to the empire. They also had a king, namely the Emperor. Therefore the Frankish people could not establish a king for themselves without the Emperor's authority, and so the kingdom of the Franks was not by right a true kingdom, even through the will of the Frankish people. Nor was it a true kingdom through substitution, because that substitution was made either by the Frankish people or by the Pope. If it was made by the Frankish people, it was null. Although the Frankish people can establish a king for themselves, they cannot substitute someone else in place of a king. But the Frankish people, as has been proved, because by right they were subject to the Emperor, cannot establish a king for themselves; therefore neither can they substitute one. If, on the other hand, that substitution was made by the Pope with right, it was null. First, because just as the Pope cannot abolish the rights of emperors, so neither can he exercise them, as the Pope himself testifies in Extra, De iudiciis, and he knows it. Second, because he ought not to meddle in secular affairs, according to that saying of the Apostle, 2 Timothy 2: "No one who serves as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs." Third, because by similar reasoning he could set up a king in any kingdom whatever; and thus emperors, to whom alone it belongs to confer royal dignity, could not usurp it for themselves, whereas the contrary is found in Acts 6. But perhaps someone would say that although the Pope cannot normally appoint a king, he can do so occasionally, namely in a case of necessity, such as when Pepin was made King of the Franks.

units.la: Hic dici posset, quod esto, quod papa possit in casu necessitatis constituere regem: tamen non posset in praeiudicium illius vel illorum, ad quem vel ad quos spectat constitutio regum: praesertim illo vel illis inconsulto vel inconsultis, hoc etiam non potest, quando per alium modum possunt pericula praecaueri: vt si communis vtilitas nunc procurat. Ita concurrebat, quando Pipinus factus fuit rex, quia institutio tunc pertinebat ad imperatorem: qui etsi fuisset negligens, tamen potestas constituendi regem non deuoluebatur ad papam: qui iuxta auctoritatem Apostoli praeallegatam, & canones sacros, se non debet implicare secularibus negociis: sed deuoluebatur ad Romanos: si autem ipsi fuerunt negligentes, deuoluta fuisset ad Francos in casu necessitatis; quibus omnibus deficientibus, deuoluta fuisset ad eos, qui in casu necessitatis supplere possent negligentiam eorum, ad quos prius pertinet potestas aliquid faciendi. Item per alium modum, quam instituendo regem, qui inter actus reseruatos Imperatori vel Romanis, deficiente imperatore, videtur esse praecipuus, vel de praecipuis, poterat in terris Francorum per illos praecaueri, & procurari vtilitas communis, igitur tunc non fuit casus, in quo papa habuit potestatem constituendi regem. Sane praedicta de regno Francorum secundum opinionem secundam tantummodo allegando siue arguendo sunt dicta: quia opinio secunda haec tenet. Licet haec dicat, eo quod imperatores magis gloriari possunt se esse imperatorum successores & regum Romanorum, qui tempore Christi & Apostolorum eius fuerunt, quam Caroli Magni propter testimonia Christi & Apostolorum intelligendo de vero regno & imperio eorum, non de moribus eorundem, quibus debent succedere non in infidelitate & prauis moribus, sed in imperiali siue regia potestate, non permissa tantummodo, sed concessa & a Deo pro pace publica ordinata, quod etiam ille rex magnus Artaxerxes, quamuis infidelis sensisse videtur, cum vt habetur Hester vltimo, dicat, maximi semperque viuentis Dei, cuius beneficio & patribus nostris & nobis regnum est traditum & vsque hodie custoditur. Quibus verbis, & illis quae habentur Hester. 13. capit. insinuauit, quare traditum esset sibi regnum dicens, cum plurimis gentibus imperem, & vniuersum orbem mea ditioni subiugassem, volui nequaquam abuti potentia magnitudine, sed clementia & lenitate gubernare subiectos, vt absque vllo terrore vitam silentio transfigentes optata cunctis mortalibus pace fruerentur. Sed forte aliquis contra ista obiiceret, dicens, quod imperatores fideles iniuste gloriarentur in auctoritate, se esse imperatorum infidelium successores, illorum scilicet, qui nihil possent possidere: cum apud infideles nullum sit iustum dominium. Sed quomodo sit isti respondendum, secundum opinionem istam poterit studiosus colligere ex iis, quae tractata sunt superius.
units.tr: Here it could be said that, even granting that the Pope could appoint a king in a case of necessity, he still could not do so to the prejudice of the one or those to whom the appointment of kings belongs, especially without consulting him or them. Nor can he do it when dangers can be averted by some other means, as when the common good already provides for them. This was the situation when Pepin was made king, since the appointment then belonged to the Emperor. Even if the Emperor had been negligent, the power of appointing a king would not have devolved upon the Pope, who, according to the authority of the Apostle quoted above and the sacred canons, ought not to involve himself in secular affairs. It would have devolved upon the Romans. If they too had been negligent, it would have devolved upon the Franks in a case of necessity. And if all these had failed, it would have devolved upon those who, in a case of necessity, could make up for the negligence of those to whom the power of acting belongs first. Likewise, the common good in the lands of the Franks could have been secured and provided for through these persons by some means other than appointing a king. Among the acts reserved to the Emperor or the Romans when the emperor is absent, this seems to be the chief one, or one of the chief ones. Therefore at that time there was no case in which the Pope had the power to appoint a king. Indeed, what has been said above about the kingdom of the Franks has been put forward only by way of argument or objection, according to the second opinion, because the second opinion holds this. Although it says that emperors may glory more in being successors of the Roman kings who lived at the time of Christ and his Apostles than of Charlemagne, it does so on the testimony of Christ and the Apostles, understood of their true kingdom and empire, not of their morals. The emperors ought to succeed to these not in unbelief and wicked morals, but in imperial or royal power, which was not merely permitted but granted and ordained by God for public peace. This is also what that great king Artaxerxes seems to have felt, though he was an unbeliever, when, as is found in the last chapter of Esther, he says: "of the greatest and ever-living God, by whose benefit the kingdom was handed down to us and to our fathers, and is preserved even to this day." By these words, and by those found in Esther chapter 13, he hinted why the kingdom had been handed down to him, saying: "Since I rule over very many nations and have subjected the whole world to my dominion, I resolved by no means to abuse the greatness of my power, but to govern my subjects with clemency and gentleness, so that, living without any terror in quiet, they might enjoy the peace desired by all mortals." But perhaps someone would object to these things, saying that faithful emperors unjustly boast of their authority in being successors of unbelieving emperors, namely of those who could possess nothing, since among unbelievers there is no just dominion. How this is to be answered, the diligent reader will be able to gather, according to this opinion, from what was treated above.

units.la: Quod autem discordent opinio prima & secunda ex hoc patet, quod opinio prima tenet, sicut pro parte recitatum est supra cap. 1. quod rex Romanorum ante vnctionem & coronationem imperialem eandem potestatem non habet in omnibus terris & prouinciis, quam habet imperator post vnctionem & coronationem imperialem, quia ante coronationem imperialem & vnctionem licet ex electione principum eandem habet potestatem, quam habet imperator in Italia & in aliis etiam terris, subiectis hodie regno & imperio: tamen non habet eandem potestatem, quam habet imperator, in omnib. regnis & prouinciis, praesertim occidentalibus, quae sub potestate Caroli Magni non erant ante tempus translationis imperii in ipsum, & adhuc non sunt sub potestate imperiali: de facto Imperator post vnctionem & coronationem imperialem in huiusmodi regnis potest spurios legitimare, quo ad temporalia, infames ad famam restituere: leges condere: & in iis consimilia facere, quae de iure sunt solis Imperatoribus reseruata. Item potest a regibus & principibus eorundem regnorum & prouinciarum subiectionem exercere, quod ante vnctionem & coronationem imperialem facere non poterat, nisi in iis terris & prouinciis, quae erant sub dominio dicti Caroli ante tempus dictae translationis, & quae adhuc hodie subiectae sunt imperio, in iis autem potest potestatem imperialem exercere & praemissa facere ante vnctionem & coronationem imperialem saltem virtute consuetudinis ex iure, quo illud potuit Carolus. Secunda autem opinio distinguens inter regnum Romanorum & regnum Francorum, & inter regem Romanorum & regem Francorum, tenet, quod licet praedicta saltem pro parte veritatem possent habere de rege Francorum: & de Carolo, in quantum fuit Rex Francorum: tamen veritatem non habent de rege Romanorum: nec de Carolo in quantum fuit Rex Romanorum. Carolus enim ante coronationem & vnctionem imperialem & translationem imperii in ipsum, fuit Rex Francorum, & Patritius Romanorum, sicut patet distinct. 63. cap. Adrianus & cap. infynodo. non fuit autem Rex Romanorum: & in quantum iam Rex Romanorum, omnes in potestate habuit, quos habuit in quantum imperator: nec ante fuit Rex Romanorum, quam Imperator. Ergo successores eius non aliam potestatem habent in quantum reges Romanorum: & in quantum imperatores: sicut nec Carolus Magnus habuit aliquam potestatem in quacunque terra, in quantum erat imperator, quam non habuit in eadem in quantum Rex Romanorum: quia quantum ad ipsum nec quantum ad rem, nec quantum ad appellationem: vt scilicet prius vocaretur Rex Romanorum, quam Imperator: aut prius nominaretur electus in regem Romanorum, quam in imperatorem: aut quam aliqua solennitas fieret specialis circa ipsum in quantum erat Rex Romanorum, nam in quantum imperator, nulla fuit distinctio, igitur & in successoribus eius quantum ad potestatem, nulla debet esse distinctio inter regem Romanorum & Imperatorem.
units.tr: That the first and second opinions disagree is clear from this. The first opinion holds, as was stated in part above in chapter 1, that the King of the Romans before anointing and imperial coronation does not have the same power in all lands and provinces that the emperor has after anointing and imperial coronation. Before imperial coronation and anointing, although by election of the princes he has the same power that the emperor has in Italy and in other lands too, now subject to the kingdom and empire, he does not have the same power that the emperor has in all kingdoms and provinces, especially the western ones. These were not under the power of Charlemagne before the time of the transfer of the empire to him, and still are not under imperial power. In fact, the emperor after anointing and imperial coronation can in such kingdoms legitimate bastards as far as temporal matters go, restore the infamous to good repute, make laws, and do similar things that by right are reserved to emperors alone. Likewise he can exercise subjection from the kings and princes of those same kingdoms and provinces, which before anointing and imperial coronation he could not do, except in those lands and provinces that were under the dominion of the said Charles before the time of that transfer and are still subject to the empire today. In those lands he can exercise imperial power and do the aforesaid things even before anointing and coronation, at least by virtue of custom, by the right by which Charles could do so. The second opinion, however, distinguishes between the kingdom of the Romans and the kingdom of the Franks, and between the king of the Romans and the king of the Franks. It holds that although the aforesaid things may be true, at least in part, of the king of the Franks, and of Charles insofar as he was King of the Franks, they are not true of the king of the Romans, nor of Charles insofar as he was King of the Romans. For Charles, before imperial coronation and anointing and the transfer of the empire to him, was King of the Franks and Patrician of the Romans, as is clear from Dist. 63, chapters Adrianus and In synodo; he was not King of the Romans. And insofar as he was now King of the Romans, he had over all those whom he had as emperor the same power; nor was he King of the Romans before he was emperor. Therefore his successors do not have a different power as kings of the Romans and as emperors. Just as Charlemagne himself had no power in any land as emperor that he did not have in the same land as King of the Romans, since as regards the thing itself and as regards the title there was no difference. He was called King of the Romans before he was called Emperor, or he was named elected king of the Romans before emperor, or some special solemnity was held concerning him insofar as he was King of the Romans; for insofar as he was emperor there was no distinction. Therefore also in his successors, as regards power, there ought to be no distinction between the king of the Romans and the Emperor.

units.la: Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod saltem quantum ad terras, quas obtinuit, antequam esset imperator: & quantum ad alias, aliqua debet esse distinctio: quia habuit regiam potestatem in illis terris & prouinciis antequam esset imperator, ergo etiam successores eius, antequam sint imperatores, in prouinciis, quas tenuit Carolus, antequam esset imperator, habent regiam potestatem.
units.tr: But perhaps someone might say that, at least as regards the lands which he held before he was emperor, and as regards others, there ought to be some distinction; because he had royal power in those lands and provinces before he was emperor, therefore his successors too, before they become emperors, have royal power in the provinces which Charles held before he was emperor. ## Response to the objection

units.la: Huic respondetur secundum opinionem secundam, quod Carolus, antequam esset imperator, aliquas terras & prouincias occupauit in quantum Rex Francorum haereditario iure: & aliquas occupauit in quantum expugnator & debellator detentorum iniustorum quarundam prouinciarum & terrarum, quae propter tyrannides & iniurias, quas contra innocentes potentes exercebant, digni erant a quocunque temporali praevalente potentia, licito bello priuari & penitus extirpari. In quibus terris & prouinciis Carolus habuit regiam potestatem illo iure, quo alii reges in regnis suis, qui potestate regia decorantur. In illis tamen terris, vt nonnullis apparet, Carolus, antequam esset Imperator, non habuit regiam potestatem. Licet enim iusta bella gerentes saepe faciant sua, quaecunque capiunt ab hoste vel adiutoribus suis: tamen illud non est vniuersaliter verum, cum aliquas exceptiones habeat. Quarum prima est secundum quosdam, quod cum habens iustum bellum, tantum accepit ab hostibus, quod secundum bonam conscientiam est sibi satisfactum de omni dato damno & labore & operibus tam suis quam suorum. Alia est, quando ille, contra quem geritur iustum bellum, offert ius & vult satisfacere. Alia est, quando qui gerit bellum iustum, non habet iurisdictionem super illos, quibus ingerit bellum iustum, sed tantummodo pugnat, & alii eum inuadunt, tunc enim licet nec bona nec personam aduersam capere, nec inuasorem detinere: sed potest ille, qui iuste pugnat, res, quibus spoliatus est, vendicare & recuperare. Alia potest esse, quando habens iustum bellum capit rem alterius ab hoste iniuste detentam. Res enim vel seruus innocentis, aut etiam innocens homo, si detinetur ab hoste, & post capiatur a iuste pugnante, non transit in dominium capientis. Alia potest esse, quando subditi vel vasalli alicuius Domini ex causa siue auctoritate Domini pugnant contra inuasores vel detentores rerum, siue sint mobilia siue immobilia, aut homines Domini sui: & capiunt res & homines Domini sui de manu detinentium siue occupantium. Non enim tale bellum iustum habentes faciunt sua, illa quae capiunt: quia per hoc Dominus eorum non perdit dominium rerum suarum & hominum. Carolus itaque licet per bella iusta occupauit multas prouincias & terras, non potuit per huiusmodi bella iusta facere eas suas; quia pertinebant ad dominium & ius imperatoris. Et forte aliquae illarum ad ius & dominium aliorum, qui non poterant per Carolum priuari iure, quod habebant in eis: venantames Carolus poterat illas terras licite occupare, & fructus accipere quousque; sibi satisfactum esset de laboribus & expensis & operibus suis & suorum: praesertim si veri Domini illarum terrarum ipsis modo debito minime repetebant. Sicut autem per huiusmodi occupationem non potuit illorum dominium acquirere saltem principale: ita nec per ea in eis potuit dignitatem regiam adipisci: sed post quam fuit imperator, nactus fuit in eis imperialem & regiam potestatem, quamobrem quia Imperatores successores Caroli non succedebant Carolo inquantum erat rex Francorum, nec in quantum per iusta bella terras aliquas occupauit: aliquas assignauit Imperio, vt Imperator successor suus omnes illas eodem iure possideret. Aliquas autem attulit cuidam filio suo aut nepoti: ideo Imperatores Romanorum seu successores Caroli eodem iure vel diuerso possident omnes terras sibi subiectas, quo possidebat Carolus inquantum Imperator erat: & quas possidere debent inquantum reges seu Imperatores Romanorum. Vt autem sciatur, quare dicitur eodem iure vel diuerso, est notandum, quod Carolus, sicut & quidam alius Imperator, non habebat omnino idem ius seu potestatem in omnibus terris sibi subiectis.
