Quædam enim erant solummodo Imperii, non alicuius alterius regis aut principis, aut domini: quæ quidem quasi stipendia erant Imperatori, quas pro Imperialibus laboribus, ac etiam pro his exequendis, quæ ad Imperiale spectant officium, assignauit, de quibus habebat potestatem faciendi quæcunq; volebat: præsertim vbi videret reipublicæ expedire: & in destructionem seu mutilationem aut diminutionem Imperii nullatenus redundare. Aliæ vero terræ erant aliquorum regum vel principum ac dominorum: in quibus eo quod alii reges & principes ac domini non erant serui Imperatoris, sed erant liberi, propter quorundam aliorum vilitatem: Imperium, si erat optimus principatus sic principaliter institutus, non habuit tantam potestatem, vt vltra illud, quod erat constitutum, facere posset de eis, & in eis quæ vellet: quia si Imperium fuit optimus principatus secularis, vltra debitum ordinatum non poterat de iure accipere aliquid ab inimicis: nisi pro vtilitate publica procuranda. Ex quibus colligitur, quod Carolus, antequam esset Imperator, non habuit regularem in Italia potestatem: & ideo Italia nunquam fuit a dominio regni Germaniæ regnum quasi accessorium principali, præsertim si Italia comprehendit etiam Romam, quæ est caput Imperii: sed aliquo tempore tam Italia quam Germania fuit prædictis causis imperio deputata ad onera Imperii sufferenda.
units.tr: To this it is answered, according to the second opinion, that Charles, before he was emperor, occupied some lands and provinces as King of the Franks by hereditary right, and some he occupied as conqueror and vanquisher of unjust holders of certain provinces and lands, which, because of the tyrannies and injuries they inflicted on the innocent, deserved to be deprived by just war and utterly rooted out by whatever temporal power prevailed against them. In those lands and provinces Charles had royal power by the same right by which other kings hold power in their own kingdoms, who are adorned with royal authority. Yet in those lands, as some think, Charles, before he was emperor, did not have royal power. For although those who wage just wars often make their own whatever they take from the enemy or their allies, this is not universally true, since it has some exceptions. The first of these, according to some, is when one who has a just war has taken from the enemies only so much that, in good conscience, he has been compensated for every loss, toil and expense, both his own and those of his men. Another is when the one against whom a just war is waged offers right and is willing to make satisfaction. Another is when the one who wages a just war has no jurisdiction over those against whom he wages it, but merely fights, and others attack him; for then, although he may not seize the goods or the person of the adversary, nor detain the aggressor, yet he who fights justly may claim and recover the things of which he has been despoiled. Another can be when one who has a just war takes the property of another which was unjustly held by the enemy. For a thing, or a slave of an innocent man, or even an innocent man, if he is held by the enemy and afterwards seized by one who fights justly, does not pass into the ownership of the captor. Another can be when the subjects or vassals of some lord fight, for a cause or by the authority of their lord, against invaders or holders of property, whether movable or immovable, or against the lord's own men, and they recover the goods and men of their lord from the hands of those who detain or occupy them. For those who wage such a just war do not make their own the things they seize, because by this their lord does not lose the ownership of his goods and men. Therefore Charles, although by just wars he occupied many provinces and lands, could not by such just wars make them his own, because they belonged to the dominion and right of the emperor. And perhaps some of those lands belonged to the right and dominion of others, who could not be deprived of the right they had in them by Charles; so Charles could lawfully occupy those lands and take their fruits until he was satisfied for his labors, expenses and works, and those of his men; especially if the true lords of those lands did not seek them back in the due manner. But just as by such occupation he could not acquire their principal ownership, so neither could he obtain royal dignity over them by these means; but after he became emperor, he obtained imperial and royal power over them. Wherefore, since the emperors who succeeded Charles did not succeed him as King of the Franks, nor in respect of the lands he had taken by just wars, but assigned some lands to the Empire so that each successor emperor might possess all of them by the same right, and gave some to a son or grandson of his, therefore the Emperors of the Romans, or Charles's successors, possess all the lands subject to them either by the same right or by a different one, by which Charles possessed them as emperor, and which they ought to possess as kings or emperors of the Romans. So that it may be known why it is said "by the same right or a different one," it should be noted that Charles, like some other emperor, did not have altogether the same right or power over all the lands subject to him. For some were only of the Empire, not of any other king, prince or lord; these were, as it were, stipends for the emperor, which he assigned to him for imperial labors, and also for carrying out those things which belong to the imperial office, and over which he had power to do whatever he wished, especially where he saw it expedient for the commonwealth, and which in no way tended to the destruction, mutilation or diminution of the Empire. But other lands belonged to certain kings, princes or lords; and in these, because the other kings, princes and lords were not servants of the emperor but free, on account of the baseness of certain others, the Empire, if it was an optimal principate instituted in this way as a principal one, did not have so much power that it could do with them and in them whatever it wished beyond what was ordained; for if the Empire was the best secular principate, it could not lawfully take anything from enemies beyond the due order, except for the public advantage to be promoted. From these things it is gathered that Charles, before he was emperor, did not have a regular power in Italy; and therefore Italy was never a kingdom, as something accessory to the principal, subject to the lordship of the kingdom of Germany, especially if Italy included also Rome, which is the head of the Empire; but at some times both Italy and Germany were assigned to the Empire, for the aforementioned causes, to bear the burdens of the Empire.

units.la: Monet contra prædicta pro secunda opinione obiectionem, in cuius solutione ostenditur an regnum Francorum in Carolo Magno defit: & qui fuerunt eiusdem successores.
units.tr: The author raises an objection against the foregoing, in support of the second opinion, and in answering it shows whether the kingdom of the Franks ceased with Charlemagne, and who his successors were.

units.la: Sed adhuc dicet aliquis contra istam secundam opinionem, quod secundum illam sequeretur, quod regnum Francorum cessasset post Carolum Magnum, quia videtur quod in regnum Francorum nullus sibi successit, nisi Imperator. Sed vt dicit opinio prædicta, nullus successit prædicto Carolo inquantum erat rex Francorum: sed solummodo inquantum erat Imperator: ergo regnum Francorum tunc cessasset. Hic respondetur, quod illud regnum Francorum, quod sic primitus vocabatur, cuius caput & principium fuit in Theutonia: & super quod primo, antequam esset Imperator, fuit Carolus rex, post mortem Caroli defit esse regnum: & inde per multa tempora postea nullus fuit Francorum rex. Carolus enim non solum regnum Francorum, sed etiam Imperium pro parte diuisit (alias dimisit.) Nam, vt in chronicis nonnullis habetur, Carolus Magnus, dum morbo & senectute aggrauaretur: congregatis solenniter de toto regno Francorum proceribus, Ludouicum filium suum acquitauit: eumq; cunctorum consilio consortem sibi totius regni ac Imperialis nominis heredem sub anno domini octingentesimo vigesimotertio constituit: impositoque capiti eius diademate Imperatorem & Augustum appellari iussit. Post hoc ille Ludouicus mortuo patre suo generalem conuentum Aquisgrani sub Anno Domini 827. habens, filium primogenitum Lotharium nominis atque Imperii consortem constituit, & cateros reges appellatos vnum Aquitaniæ scil. Pipinum, alterum Bauariæ, scil. Ludouicum, prefecit: quarto vero filio, scil. Carolo, Alemanniam, Graciam & Burgundiam post concessit. Idem vero Lotharius post mortem Ludouici Imperatoris, assumpto sibi Pipino, filio fratris sui Pipini, cum Ludouico & fratribus suis occasione discordia inter ipsos super diuisione regni Francorum suborta, sub anno domini 841. apud pagum Altisiodorensem, in loco qui dicitur Fonchauich, bellum grauissimum commisit: cum Ludouicus & Carolus sine graui dispendio suorum vicerunt. Post hoc autem bellum supradicti fratres inter se pacificati imperium & regnum Francorum sub anno Domini 842. diuiserunt hoc modo: Carolus habuit regnum occidentale Francorum a Britannia maiore vsque ad Mosam fluuium: & vocatus fuit rex Gallia. Ludouicus habuit Orientale regnum Francorum: scil. totam Germaniam vsque ad Rheni fluuium & nonnullas ciuitates cum adiacentibus pagis trans Rhenum: & vocatus est rex Germaniæ & Pannoniæ, Poloniæ, Bohemiæ & Moraviæ inclusis. Lotharius vero primogenitus, Imperator vocabatur, & a Mosa vsque ad Rhenum fluuium Belgicam, quasi medius inter duos incedens sortitus est, quæ vsque hodie Lotharingia ex eius nomine sortita est nomen. Habuit etiam prouincias & omnia regna Italiæ cum vrbe Romana. Sed Pipino prædicto filio fratris ipsorum Aquitania cessit. Post hac vero Lotharius Imperator prædictus, conuocatis primatibus regni filio suo Ludouico sub anno Domini 855. Italiam tradidit: & Imperatorem constituit. Lothario vero fratri regnum Lotharingiæ, quod ex nomine suo sic vocatur, concessit. Ex his aliisque quamplurimus colligitur, quod regnum Francorum cessauit esse regnum, & quod terræ, quæ immediate erant subiectæ Carolo tam vt imperatori quam vt regi Francorum, multis modis diuisæ fuerunt: & ideo nec in regno Francorum, nec in aliqua eius parte, aliquis successit Carolo inquantum Carolus fuit rex Francorum: sed vnus filiorum successit ei inquantum erat Imperator in partem Imperii: & in regnum vel in partem regni Francorum: non tamen vocabatur. batur rex Francorum: sed tantummodo Imperator, vel iam Imperator, iam Rex Acquitaniæ, propter hoc quod prius fuerat Rex Acquitaniæ, quam Imperator. Alter vero filius Caroli vel nepos successit Carolo in partem, quæ fuerat imperii, inquantum Carolus erat Imperator, habens potestatem separandi partem imperii ab imperio, & quæ non immediate sed mediate esset subiecta Imperatori. Italia vero, quæ prius erat pars imperii immediate subiecta Imperatori, nullum alium regem habens Dominum, tunc fuit data Bernhardo Bosonii, nepoti Caroli, qui fuit rex super Italiam constitutus. Postea vero regnum Francorum fuit aliis modis divisum, sicut patet per prædicta: ita tamen, quod in multis annis postea nullus vocabatur rex Francorum: & Italia, quæ prius fuerat à terris Imperatori immediate subiectis separata, postea fuit unita.
units.tr: But someone may still object to this second opinion that, according to it, the kingdom of the Franks would have ceased after Charlemagne, since it seems that no one succeeded him in the kingdom of the Franks except as Emperor. For the aforesaid opinion says that no one succeeded the said Charles insofar as he was king of the Franks, but only insofar as he was Emperor; therefore the kingdom of the Franks would then have ceased. To this it is answered that the kingdom of the Franks, which was first so called, whose head and beginning was in Germany, and over which Charles was king before he became Emperor, ceased to exist after the death of Charles; and for many times afterwards there was no king of the Franks. For Charles divided not only the kingdom of the Franks but also the Empire, or (as others have it) dismissed part of it. For, as is found in some chronicles, when Charles Magnus was weighed down by sickness and old age, he assembled the nobles of the whole kingdom of the Franks solemnly, associated his son Louis with himself, and with the counsel of all appointed him co-ruler of the whole kingdom and heir to the imperial name in the year of the Lord 823; and placing the diadem on his head, he ordered that he be called Emperor and Augustus. After this, Louis, his father having died, held a general assembly at Aachen in the year of the Lord 827, and made his firstborn son Lothair partner in name and in Empire, and appointed the other sons, called kings, one over Aquitaine, namely Pepin, and another over Bavaria, namely Louis; and afterwards he granted Alemannia, Greece and Burgundy to his fourth son, Charles. Lothair himself, after the death of the Emperor Louis, took to himself Pepin, the son of his brother Pepin, and with Louis and his brothers, a very grievous battle was fought at a place called Fontenoy near the village of Auxerre in the year of the Lord 841, the discord between them over the division of the kingdom of the Franks having arisen; Louis and Charles conquered without heavy loss to their own men. After this battle, the aforesaid brothers, having made peace among themselves, divided the Empire and the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the Lord 842 in this way: Charles had the western kingdom of the Franks from Greater Britain as far as the river Meuse, and was called king of Gaul. Louis had the eastern kingdom of the Franks, namely all Germany as far as the river Rhine and some cities with the adjacent districts beyond the Rhine, and was called king of Germany, and of Pannonia, Poland, Bohemia and Moravia included. Lothair the firstborn was called Emperor, and he obtained the Low Countries from the Meuse to the river Rhine, advancing as it were between the two, which to this day has taken its name from him as Lotharingia. He also had the provinces and all the kingdoms of Italy with the city of Rome. But Aquitaine was ceded to the aforesaid Pepin, the son of their brother. Afterwards, the aforesaid Emperor Lothair, having summoned the chief men of the kingdom, handed Italy over to his son Louis in the year of the Lord 855 and made him Emperor. To his brother Lothair he granted the kingdom of Lotharingia, which is so called from his name. From these and very many other things it is gathered that the kingdom of the Franks ceased to be a kingdom, and that the lands which were immediately subject to Charles, both as Emperor and as king of the Franks, were divided in many ways; and therefore neither in the kingdom of the Franks nor in any part of it did anyone succeed Charles insofar as Charles was king of the Franks; but one of his sons succeeded him insofar as he was Emperor, in a part of the Empire, and in the kingdom or a part of the kingdom of the Franks; yet he was not called king of the Franks, but only Emperor, or now Emperor, now king of Aquitaine, because he had been king of Aquitaine before he was Emperor. Another son or grandson of Charles succeeded him in that part which had belonged to the Empire, insofar as Charles was Emperor, having the power to separate a part of the Empire from the Empire, and which was subject not immediately but mediately to the Emperor. Italy, which had earlier been a part of the Empire immediately subject to the Emperor, and had no other king as lord, was then given to Bernard, son of Bosonus and grandson of Charles, who was appointed king over Italy. Afterwards the kingdom of the Franks was divided in other ways, as is clear from what has been said; yet in the following many years no one was called king of the Franks; and Italy, which had earlier been separated from the lands immediately subject to the Emperor, was afterwards united.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Monet & soluit tres quæstiunculas incidentes ex dictis in superioribus capitulis.
units.tr: Showing and resolving three minor questions arising from what was said in the earlier chapters.

units.la: Circa prædicta possunt fieri quæstiones. Quarum prima est, quomodo Carolus, ex quo dictus fuit Augustus ab augendo, poterat diuidendo minuere imperium.
units.tr: Several questions may be raised about the above. The first is how Charles, who was called Augustus from augeo (to increase), could diminish the empire by dividing it.

units.la: Secunda, qua potestate aut iure poterat filium suum constituere Imperatorem. Tertia est an quilibet Imperator successor Caroli habuit vel habeat eandem, quantum ad illa, potestatem. Ad primam illarum quæstionum respondetur secundum opinionem secundam, quod Carolus, in quantum erat Imperator habuit tam plenam administrationem in rebus imperii, ut non posset solummodo facere pro suo arbitrio voluntatis, quicquid conferret ad bonum commune, sed etiam ut posset facere de eis quicquid non esset in dispendium boni communis. Et ideo quia separatio Italiæ ab aliis terris & prouinciis immediate subiectis Imperatori non erat in dispendium boni communis: quin immo separatio Italiæ ab aliis terris & prouinciis, prout fortassis vidit Carolus, erat expediens bono communi. Ideo potuit eam ab aliis terris separare: præsertim cum ipse subiecisset regnum Francorum immediate Imperatori, quod primo non erat ei subiectum immediate: & ita poterat Augustus ab augendo Imperium merito appellari; non obstante, quod Italiam, quæ erat parua respectu aliarum separasset. Unde sicut ciuitates aliquas potuit facere liberas absque detrimento imperii: ita potuit Italiam tali modo ab aliis prouinciis immediate subiectis Imperatori separare.
units.tr: The second is by what power or right he could appoint his son as Emperor. The third is whether each Emperor who succeeded Charles had, or has, the same power in these matters. To the first question, following the second opinion, the answer is that Charles, as Emperor, had such full administration of the affairs of the empire that he could not only do at his own will whatever served the common good, but could also do with them whatever was not to the detriment of the common good. Since the separation of Italy from the other lands and provinces immediately subject to the Emperor was not to the detriment of the common good, but indeed, as Charles perhaps saw, was expedient for it, he could separate it from the other lands. This is especially so because he himself had placed the kingdom of the Franks immediately under the Emperor, which before had not been immediately subject to him. Thus Augustus could rightly be called so from augeo, even though he had separated Italy, which was small compared with the others. Just as he could make some cities free without harm to the empire, so he could separate Italy in this way from the other provinces immediately subject to the Emperor.

units.la: Ad secundam quæstionem respondetur, quod Carolus illo iure & illa potestate potuit filium suum constituere Imperatorem, quo & qua Iulius Cæsar & Octauius primus Augustus, & alii quam plurimi successores eorum quandoque filios suos, quandoque alios fecerunt interdum successores, & nonnunquam consortes imperii. Ex quo enim translatum fuit Imperium in Germanos & personam Caroli Magni, omnem eius & omnem potestatem, quod & quam habuerunt primi Imperatores, habuit & Carolus Magnus. Et si dicatur, quod Imperium Romanum non fuit translatum in Carolum Magnum: quia si fuisset translatum, remansisset apud Græcos: quod tamen non remansit apud eos. Unde & in quadam Chronica sic legitur: Imperatores Constantinopolitani Nicephorus, Michael & Leo ultro & amicitiam & societatem eius expetentes, complures ad eum misere legatos, conquerentes ipsum suspectum à se Imperatorem nominari. Et ob hoc quasi Imperium eis capere vellet, eum habere suspectum: cum quibus tamen fœdus firmissimum statuit, ut nulla inter partes cuiuslibet scandalis remaneret occasio. Et infra de eodem sic habetur: Romam veniens & Carolus Magnus propter recuperandum, quod minus circa ecclesiam statum, ibi hyemis tempore egerat: quo tempore Imperatoris & Augusti nomen accepit. Quod primo tamen auersatus est, ut affirmaret se eo die, quo prima festiuitas esset, ecclesiam non intraturum, &c. Et paulo post: Inuidiam tunc suscepti nominis, illis Romanis Imperatoribus super hoc indignantibus magna iniuria patientia: vicitque eorum contumaciam magna virtute, qua eis procul dubio longe præstantior erat mittendo ad eos crebras legationes: & in epistolis eos fratres appellando. Ex hoc videtur haberi, quod Imperatores, qui in Constantinopoli morabantur, non solum fuerunt Imperatores Constantinopolitani, sed Romani Imperatores, postquam Carolus factus fuit Imperator: & per consequens Romanum Imperium non fuit translatum de Græcis in Carolum: quia quod transfertur ab vno, non manet post translationem apud illum, de quo transfertur. Respondetur, quod Imperium Romanum fuit vere translatum de Græcis in Carolum, & ideo Carolus fuit postea verus Imperator Romanus, & non Græci: licet forte aliqui nomine, non re fuerunt postea Imperatores Romani: & ideo Imperatores priores prædicta translatione priuati fuerunt iure & potestate, quam primi Imperatores habuerunt in vniuerso orbe: & Carolus per dictam translationem ius & illam potestatem adeptus fuit. Ad illud, quod adducitur per chronicam supradictam de amicitia, societate & confœderatione Caroli cum Imperatoribus Constantinopolitanis siue Romanis: & de crebris legationibus inter ipsos: Respondetur, quod Carolus propter scandala & inconuenientia multa vitanda tolerauit Constantinopolitanos in Græcia, immo Græciam possidere & se vocare Imperatores Romanos. Et propter hanc causam votam voluit cum eis amicitiam & societatem habere: cum ipse solus sit verus Imperator Romanus, habens omne ius & potestatem, quod & quam habuerunt primi Imperatores, & alii successores eorum ante Carolum. Si quaeratur, authoritate cuius facta sit huiusmodi translatio? Respondetur, circa hoc sunt opiniones diversae. Una est, quod dicta translatio facta fuit a Papa. A quo autem Papa facta fuit, sunt diversae opiniones. Haec opinio fulcitur per decretalem, venerabilem. Extra, de electione.
units.tr: To the second question the answer is that Charles could appoint his son Emperor by that right and that power by which Julius Caesar and Octavius, the first Augustus, and many other successors of theirs, sometimes made their sons, sometimes others, and at times successors and sharers of the empire. For from the time the empire was transferred to the Germans and to the person of Charles the Great, Charles the Great had all the power and whatever right the first Emperors had. And if it is said that the Roman empire was not transferred to Charles the Great, because if it had been transferred it would have remained with the Greeks, which it did not do, then in a certain chronicle we read thus: "The Emperors of Constantinople, Nicephorus, Michael and Leo, of their own accord seeking his friendship and alliance, sent many envoys to him, complaining that he had been named Emperor by them as a suspect. And because of this, as if he wished to seize the empire from them, they held him suspect; yet with them he made a most firm covenant, so that no occasion for scandal should remain between the parties." And below, concerning the same, it is written thus: "Charles the Great, coming to Rome to recover what he had lost in the church during the winter, there received the name of Emperor and Augustus. At first, however, he shrank from it, so that he affirmed that on the day of the first festival he would not enter the church," etc. And a little later: "He bore the odium of the name he had then received with great patience, since the Roman Emperors were indignant at this, and he overcame their obstinacy by great virtue, in which he was undoubtedly far superior to them, by sending them frequent embassies and calling them brothers in his letters." From this it seems to follow that the Emperors who dwelt in Constantinople were not only Emperors of Constantinople but Roman Emperors, after Charles had been made Emperor; and consequently the Roman empire was not transferred from the Greeks to Charles, because what is transferred from one does not remain with the one from whom it is transferred. The answer is that the Roman empire was truly transferred from the Greeks to Charles, and therefore Charles was afterwards the true Roman Emperor, and not the Greeks; although perhaps some who were afterwards Roman Emperors were so in name, not in reality. Thus the earlier Emperors, by that transfer, were deprived of the right and power which the first Emperors had over the whole world, and Charles through that transfer obtained that right and that power. As to what is adduced from the aforementioned chronicle concerning the friendship, alliance and confederation of Charles with the Emperors of Constantinople or Romans, and the frequent embassies between them: the answer is that Charles, to avoid many scandals and inconveniences, tolerated the Constantinopolitans in Greece, indeed allowed them to possess Greece and to call themselves Roman Emperors. For this reason he was willing to have friendship and alliance with them, although he alone is the true Roman Emperor, having all the right and power which the first Emperors and their other successors before Charles had. If it is asked by whose authority such a transfer was made? The answer is that opinions differ on this. One is that the said transfer was made by the Pope. By whom the Pope made it, opinions differ again. This opinion is supported by the decretal Venerabilem. Extra, de electione.

units.la: Alii autem dicunt, quod translatio ista fuit facta principaliter a populo Romano, cuius Papa est pars, & etiam clerus, quod quaedam chronica insinuare videtur, in qua sic legitur: Ille die sacratissima natali Domini, cum rex missam ante confessionem (alii confessionem) sancti Petri Apostoli audisset, & ab oratione surgeret; Leo Papa coronam capiti eius imposuit: & a cuncto Romanorum populo acclamatum est: Carolo serenissimo, Augusto a Deo coronato, vt pacifico Imperatori, vita & victoria. Quae verba videntur innuere, quod Leo Papa Carolum coronavit de voluntate & ordinatione populi Romani, ad quem spectabat de imperio ordinare, & sic translatio imperii de Graecis in Germanos facta fuit a populo Romano, non exclusis Papa & clero. Quod taliter videtur posse probari. Ad illos spectat translatio principaliter imperii, si transferri debet, a quibus fuit imperium institutum: ergo a Romanis & non a Papa, nisi quantum a parte, quando esset pars Romanorum, debet fieri imperii translatio, quae ad potestatem pertinet temporalem. Papa autem inquantum Papa de temporalibus, saltem regulariter, se intromittere nullatenus debet, ne videatur iuribus derogare. Quamvis ergo Papa teneatur, deficientibus Romanis, vel si nollent, transferre posset imperium: tamen vbi ipsi Romani ex necessitate essent promti pro bono communi transferre imperium, non debent: sed vna cum aliis Romanis, inquantum Romanus, posset transferre imperium. Cum igitur, vt patet ex praeallegata chronica, Romani tunc fuerunt parati imperium transferre: Papa tunc authoritate propria imperium transferre non potuit. Et ad decretalem, venerabilem, Respondetur, quod illa verba Innocentii 3. sicut & alia plura verba eius ibi & alibi sunt exponenda, ne verbis eius in aliis contraria demonstrentur. Potest itaq; dici, q; ideo dicit, q; Apostolica sedes Romanum Imperium in personam magnifici Caroli a Graecis translatum in Germanos: quia Papa authoritate Romanorum coronavit Carolum Imperatorem: vel quia populus Romanus Papae, tanquam eminentiori personae, potestatem tribuit ad transferendum: vel quia Papa & clerus cum aliis Romanis transtulerunt imperium: vel quia Papa persuasit & consuluit translationem illam fieri in Germanos. Quare autem facta fuit dicta translatio, non est tractandum. Quis autem fuerit effectus dictae translationis, non opus modo exquisite disquirere, sed sufficit nunc secundum opinionem illam breviter dicere, q; per dictam translationem Carolus non solum exemptus fuit ad obedientia & subiectione Imperatoris praedecessoris sui: a cuius obedientia & subiectione, quamvis non habuisset eum pro superiore, tamen non fuit exemptus: quia non habere superiorem pro Imperatore non eximit aliquem a subiectione: sed etiam si filius sit Dominus ipsius, qui Imperator fuit ante eum, & omnium regnorum terrarumq; & prouinciarum, quarum Domini fuerunt illi, qui tenuerunt monarchiam imperii: & ideo Carolus per talem translationem habuit potestatem de iure, licet non de facto, in omnibus, quae Octavio Augusto subiectae fuerunt: & in prouinciis etiam, quas ante per bella licita subiugauit, habuit potestatem Imperialem, in quibus prius de iure nec Imperialem nec regalem potestatem habuerat. In terris autem & prouinciis, quas ex successione paterna possidebat, nactus est potestatem Imperialem: sed ante ea solummodo habuit potestatem regalem. Pro omnibus istis vna videtur allegatio talis, quae ex praecedentibus implicite potest adduci. Antequam Carolus fuit ad Imperiale fastigium sublimatus, nequaquam fuit Romanum Imperium consecutus: sed tale fuit natus imperium, quale ipsum processit. Aliter imperium non fuisset de aliquo nec de aliquibus translatum in ipsum: ergo omnem potestatem in quibuscunq; terris, quas habuerunt praecedecessores sui, ipse per talem translationem obtinuit: quia in vniuersum orbe Imperialem potestatem acquisiuit. Sed forte aliquis quaereret, quomodo fuit Imperium translatum in Germanos: nonne sic, quod nullus deberet esse Imperator, nisi Germanus? Hic respondetur, quod sicut Romanum imperium non fuit translatum de Graecis sic, quod nullus nisi Graecus debeat esse Imperator: sic etiam non fuit sic translatum in Germanos, quod nullus deberet esse Imperator, nisi Germanus. Talis enim ordinatio seu translatio optimo modo prouidendi imperio de Imperatore obuiaret, ac potestati Imperatoris non modicum derogaret: quia tunc non habuisset Carolus potestatem, nec aliquis alius promouendi alium in Imperatorem, quam Germanum: cum tamen de facto aliqui alii, quam Germani electi fuerunt. Fratres enim Henrici Reges Angliae, proavi Erbrardi, qui modo regnat in Anglia, electus & coronatus fuit in regem Romanorum seu Imperatorem. Alphonsus etiam rex Castellae fuit electus; quorum neuter fuit Germanus. Sed translatum fuit in Germanos, quia Carolus, qui tunc fuit Imperator, factus erat natione Germanus. Ad tertiam quaestionem propositam in principio istius capituli, dicitur, quod secundum praedictam opinionem quilibet Imperator successor Caroli eandem habuit potestatem, quam habuit Carolus, vel quicunque praedecessor Caroli: tum quantum ad dandum aliquam partem Imperii alii, dummodo remanerent Imperio sufficientes terrae & prouinciae ad omnia onera Imperii sustinenda: tum quantum ad potestatem constituendi filium suum vel alium Imperatorem. Vtrumque probatur per allegationem, quae ad alia quaestionem adducta est. Nam qui in ius succedit alterius, eodem iure, quo ille, vti debet: aliter enim non est vera successio. Ergo quilibet Imperator successor Caroli, tam quantum ad illa duo, sicut quantum ad alia quaecunq;, potest vti eodem iure & potestate, quo & quae Carolus vel quicunque praedecessorus vsus fuit. Et specialiter probatur de potestate constituendi Imperatorem per hoc, quod saepe de facto, quod per rationem reprobari non potest, successores Caroli tam ante institutionem principum Electorum, quam post filios suos & alios constituerant Imperatores consortes Imperii vel successores: sicut in Chronica Ottonis: & in aliis quibusdam gestis Imperatorum usque post Fredericum vltimum legitur & habetur. Nam Ludouicus Pipini filius fecit Lotharium filium suum Imperatorem: & idem Lotharius Ludouicum filium suum constituit Imperatorem, qui simul fuerunt Augusti: vt habetur dist. 63. in rubro. Conradus omnium electione 79. ab Augusto, regimen scil. Romanorum accepit: & Henricus Dux Saxoniae filius Ottonis Ducis in regnum prouehitur.
units.tr: Others, however, say that this transfer was made chiefly by the Roman people, of whom the Pope is a part, and also by the clergy. A certain chronicle seems to suggest this, and in it we read as follows: On that most sacred day of the Lord's Nativity, when the king had heard Mass before the confession (others read confessio) of the holy Apostle Peter, and was rising from prayer, Pope Leo placed a crown on his head; and by the whole Roman people it was acclaimed: To Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, the peaceful Emperor, life and victory. These words seem to imply that Pope Leo crowned Charles by the will and ordinance of the Roman people, to whom it belonged to appoint the empire. On this view, the transfer of the empire from the Greeks to the Germans was made by the Roman people, without excluding the Pope and the clergy. This may be shown in the following way. The transfer of the empire, if it ought to be transferred at all, belongs chiefly to those by whom the empire was instituted. Therefore it is the Romans, and not the Pope, who should make the transfer, except insofar as the Pope is a part of the Romans; for the transfer of the empire pertains to temporal power. The Pope, however, as Pope, ought in no way to meddle in temporal affairs, at least as a rule, lest he seem to infringe on the rights of others. Although, then, the Pope could transfer the empire if the Romans failed or were unwilling, nevertheless, where the Romans themselves were ready of necessity to transfer the empire for the common good, he ought not to do so; rather, together with the other Romans, insofar as he is a Roman, he could transfer it. Since, then, as is clear from the chronicle cited above, the Romans were at that time ready to transfer the empire, the Pope could not at that time transfer it by his own authority. As for the decretal Venerabilem, it is answered that those words of Innocent III, like many of his other words here and elsewhere, must be explained so that they are not shown to contradict his other words. It may therefore be said that he says that the Apostolic See transferred the Roman Empire to the Germans in the person of the great Charles for one of these reasons: either because the Pope, by the authority of the Romans, crowned Charles Emperor; or because the Roman people gave the Pope, as the more eminent person, the power to transfer it; or because the Pope and clergy, together with the other Romans, transferred the empire; or because the Pope persuaded and advised that the transfer be made to the Germans. Why this transfer was made need not be discussed here. As to what its effect was, there is no need to inquire carefully now; it is enough, according to that opinion, to say briefly that by this transfer Charles was not only freed from the obedience and subjection of his predecessor the Emperor, from whose obedience and subjection he had not been freed even though he did not regard him as his superior (for not regarding someone as one's superior does not free one from subjection), but also that he became lord of his predecessor, who had been Emperor before him, and of all the kingdoms, lands and provinces of which those had been lords who held the monarchy of the empire. Therefore Charles, through such a transfer, had power by right, though not in fact, over all the things that had been subject to Octavian Augustus; and in the provinces also which he had previously subdued in lawful wars, he had imperial power, whereas before he had had neither imperial nor royal power there by right. In the lands and provinces which he possessed by paternal succession, he obtained imperial power; before this he had had only royal power. For all these points one argument, which can be implicitly drawn from what has gone before, seems to suffice. Before Charles was raised to the imperial dignity, he had by no means obtained the Roman Empire; but the empire was of such a kind as it had come forth, and otherwise the empire would not have been transferred to him from anyone or from any persons. Therefore, through such a transfer, he obtained all the power in whatever lands his predecessors had held, because he acquired imperial power over the whole world. But perhaps someone might ask how the empire was transferred to the Germans: was it not so that no one ought to be Emperor except a German? Here it is answered that just as the Roman Empire was not transferred from the Greeks in such a way that no one except a Greek ought to be Emperor, so it was not transferred to the Germans in such a way that no one ought to be Emperor except a German. For such an ordinance or transfer would stand in the way of the best way of providing for the empire, and would not a little diminish the power of the Emperor; for then Charles would not have had the power, nor anyone else, to promote anyone as Emperor other than a German, whereas in fact some others than Germans have been elected. For the brothers of Henry, Kings of England, great-grandfathers of Edward, who now reigns in England, were elected and crowned king of the Romans or Emperor; Alfonso also, king of Castile, was elected; neither of these was a German. But the empire was said to be transferred to the Germans because Charles, who was then Emperor, had become German by nation. As to the third question proposed at the beginning of this chapter, it is said that according to the aforesaid opinion every Emperor who succeeded Charles had the same power that Charles, or any predecessor of Charles, had, both as to giving some part of the empire to another, provided that enough lands and provinces remained in the empire to sustain all the burdens of the empire, and as to the power of appointing his son or another as Emperor. Both are proved by the argument that was brought forward for the other question. For whoever succeeds another in his right must use the same right that the other used; otherwise the succession is not true. Therefore every Emperor who succeeded Charles, as to those two points as well as to all others, can use the same right and power that Charles or any predecessor used. And specifically the power of appointing an Emperor is proved by this: that often in fact, which cannot be disproved by reason, the successors of Charles, both before the institution of the Electoral princes and afterwards, appointed their sons or others as Emperors, partners in the empire or successors; as is read and found in the Chronicle of Otto, and in some other deeds of the Emperors down to Frederick the last. For Louis, son of Pepin, made his son Lothar Emperor; and Lothar in turn made his son Louis Emperor, and they were both Augusti at the same time, as is found in dist. 63, in rubro. Conrad, by the election of all, 79th from Augustus, received the rule of the Romans; and Henry, son of Otto, Duke of Saxony, was raised to the kingdom.

units.la: Item de Ottone primo legitur sic: Ottho primus ab Augusto. 89. filium suum Ottonem impuberibus annis regem constituit. Item de quodam alio Conrado sic legitur: Conradus 85. ab Augusto secundo regni sui anno filium de iure regem fecit. Item de Henrico sic legitur: Henricus Conradi tertii Imperatoris filius dadum patre viuente rex constitutus 86. ab Augusto patri succedit: filium quoque suum Henricum Romani pontificis cum electorum, pontificum & principum regni electione regem constituit. De Henrico quarto sic legitur: Henricus quartus Henricum filium suum regem constitui fecit. Item de quodam Conrado 90. ab Augusto legitur, quod filio suo sedem regni reliquit.
units.tr: Likewise, concerning Otto the First, we read as follows: Otto the First, 89th from Augustus, appointed his son Otto king while still in his boyhood. Likewise, concerning another Conrad, we read as follows: Conrad, 85th from Augustus, in the second year of his reign, rightfully made his son king. Likewise, concerning Henry, we read as follows: Henry, son of the Emperor Conrad III, having been made king a little while earlier while his father was still living, 86th from Augustus succeeded his father; he also appointed his son Henry king, by the election of the Roman pontiff, of the electors, the pontiffs and the princes of the kingdom. Concerning Henry IV we read as follows: Henry IV caused his son Henry to be made king. Likewise, concerning a certain Conrad, 90th from Augustus, we read that he left the seat of the kingdom to his son.

units.la: De Frederico primo, sic legitur, Fredericus primus 91. regum, regnum accepit magis ex delegatione patrui sui, quam ex electione principum, qui filium Henricum suum designauit fieri Imperatorem, qui de consensu principum coronari Aquisgrani incepit. Ista haec procurant principes Alemanniae pene omnium paruulum ipsius, (scil. Fredericum) adhuc in cunis vagientem in regno assumpserunt & ei fidelitatem iurauerunt. Vnde postea: Principes Alemanniae, rex videlicet Bohemiae, Dux Hauftriae, Dux Bauariae, & Landtgrauius Turingiae, & alii quamplures Comites eundem Fredericum regem Siciliae elegerunt Imperatorem coronandum, cui etiam olim cum adhuc in cunis esset iuramentum & fidelitatem fecerunt. De Henrico filio Friderici sic legitur: Henricus vnicus filius Friderici circiter octo annos habens quorundam ministrallium & aliorum principum interuentu a patre suo & principibus rex constituitur, & Aquisgrani coronatur cum patre suo Imperium adepturus. Ex his colligitur, quod Imperatores post Carolum alios creauerunt Imperatores, tanquam habentes eandem potestatem in omnibus, quam habuit Carolus Magnus & praedecessores sui, qui quamplures Imperatores fecerunt. Nam ab Imperatoribus fuerunt in fia scripti Imperatores, Reges, Caesares & Augusti creati. Octauius seu vt nunc dicunt, Octauianus, qui fuit primus Augustus, Anthonius, Lepidus, Drusus, Caius, Piso, Lucius, Marcus, Lucius Commodus, Anthonius, Alexander, Decius, Volusianus, Galienus, Cornelius, Claudius, Coruinus, Maximianus, Constantinus, Galienus, Maximus, Seuerus, Constantinus, Lucius, Crispus, Lixinianus, Maxentius, Constantinus, Dalmacius, Gallus, Vitalianus, Valerius, Gratianus, Valentinianus, Leo, Anthonius, Theodoricus, Martianus, Iustinianus, Tiberius, Constantinus, Mauritius, Germanus, Theodosius, Tiberius, Constantinus, Heraclius, Tiberius. Quibus ergo Imperator, si est verus Imperator Romanorum, Imperio succedens primis Imperatoribus: & est nunc tale Imperium, quale ab initio fuit, alios potest creare Imperatores, vel vt secum regnent & imperent: vel vt sint sui solummodo successores: & utroque modo fuerunt per Imperatores alii Imperatores constituti.
units.tr: Concerning Frederick I, this is what is written: "Frederick I, the 91st king, received the kingdom more by the appointment of his uncle than by the election of the princes, who designated his son Henry to be made emperor, who began to be crowned at Aachen with the consent of the princes. The princes of Germany, almost all of them, procured these things for his little son (namely Frederick), still crying in the cradle, and they took him up into the kingdom and swore fealty to him." Then afterwards: "The princes of Germany, namely the king of Bohemia, the duke of Austria, the duke of Bavaria, and the landgrave of Thuringia, and many other counts, elected this same Frederick, king of Sicily, to be crowned emperor, and to him too, when he was still in the cradle, they once gave an oath and fealty." Concerning Henry, son of Frederick, this is what is written: "Henry, the only son of Frederick, being about eight years old, was made king by his father and the princes through the intervention of certain ministerials and other princes, and was crowned at Aachen with his father, so that he might obtain the empire." From these things it is gathered that the emperors after Charles created other emperors, as though they had the same power in all things which Charles the Great and his predecessors had, who made many emperors. For in the written records, emperors, kings, caesars and augusti were created by emperors. Octavius, or as they now call him, Octavian, who was the first Augustus; Antony, Lepidus, Drusus, Gaius, Piso, Lucius, Marcus, Lucius Commodus, Antony, Alexander, Decius, Volusianus, Gallienus, Cornelius, Claudius, Corvinus, Maximian, Constantine, Gallienus, Maximus, Severus, Constantine, Lucius, Crispus, Licinius, Maxentius, Constantine, Dalmatius, Gallus, Vitalianus, Valerius, Gratian, Valentinian, Leo, Antony, Theoderic, Marcian, Justinian, Tiberius, Constantine, Maurice, Germanus, Theodosius, Tiberius, Constantine, Heraclius, Tiberius. Therefore, to these the emperor, if he is the true emperor of the Romans, succeeding to the empire of the first emperors, and since the empire now is such as it was from the beginning, can create other emperors, either so that they may reign and rule with him, or so that they may be only his successors; and in both ways other emperors have been appointed by emperors.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Quarta quaest. contra ea, quae in superiori cap. dicta sunt, duo obiicit & soluit: in quorum solutione inquiritur, an Imperator possit per successionem fieri: & an possit ordinare Apostolicam sedem.
units.tr: The fourth question, against what was said in the preceding chapter: he raises and resolves two objections. In the resolution of these it is asked whether the Emperor can be made by succession, and whether he can appoint the Apostolic See.

units.la: SEd contra praedicta dupliciter obiicitur. Primo, quia secundum ista Imperatores fuere per successionem, & non per electionem: quod repugnat optimo principatui in prouidendo: & per consequens repugnat optimo principatui prouidendo de Imperatore: & per consequens repugnat optimo principatui, qualis debet esse principatus Imperialis.
units.tr: But the foregoing is objected to in two ways. First, because according to these views the Emperors came to power by succession and not by election; this is contrary to the best principle in providing for a ruler, and consequently contrary to the best principle in providing for the Emperor, and so contrary to the best principle by which an imperial sovereignty ought to be constituted.

units.la: Secundo obiicitur: quia secundum ista Imperator posset ordinare Apostolicam sedem, & facere Papam, & Archiepiscopos, & episcopos: quia illam potestatem habuit Carolus Magnus, vt dist. 63. cap. Adrianus. Ad primam istarum obiectionum respondetur secundum opinionem secundam, quod optimus modus prouidendi simpliciter de Imperatore est per electionem, & non per successionem: & ideo non legitur, quod aliquis fuerit aliter quam per electionem constitutus Imperator. Vnde etiam filii Imperatorum per electionem facti fuerunt Imperatores: sed non semper per electionem illorum, quibus regulariter data erat eligendi potestas, vacante Imperio: sed semper per electionem ipsorum Imperatorum. Nam ipsimet Imperatores habentes potestatem eligendi, elegerunt saepe proprios filios vel alios: quia non minorem habet Imperator potestatem eligendi, quam quicunque alii inferiores eo. Ad secundam obiectionem diuersimode respondetur: dicitur enim vno modo, quod quilibet Imperator post Carolum & post Ottonem primum habuit potestatem eligendi summum pontificem: quia potestas ordinandi Apostolicam sedem pertinet ad ius publicum: sed ius publicum est in sacris & sacerdotii sacerdotibus & magistratibus: per consequens in Imperatoribus, quæ inter magistratus supremum locum obtinere noscuntur. Sed iuri publico derogari non potest: neq; potest quis renunciare iuri publico. Extra, de foro compet. si diligenti. Quare Imperatores posteriores tali iuri minime renunciare potuerunt. Aliter dicitur, quod illud priuilegium Caroli & Ottonis fuit personale: vel saltem quod imperatores poterant renunciare priuilegio illi. Finaliter dicitur, quod nec Carolus nec Ottho habuerunt potestatem eligendi supremum pontificem, inquantum erant imperatores: quia primi Imperatores, quorum Carolus & Ottho fuerunt successores, potestatem illam nullatenus habuerunt: & ideo potestas eligendi Papam non competiit eis, inquantum erant imperatores, sed in quantū Romani Christiani ipsis commiserunt vices suas. Eodem modo dicitur de investitura episcoporum & archiepiscoporum, quod specialiter secundum opinionem quandam veritatem habet, qualiter ad collationem temporalem, quam facere habet Imperator, præsertim in terris immediate sibi subiectis, & non Papa. Quæ istarum responsionum maiorem euidentiam habeat, non est dicendum ad præsens: quia magnam requirit discussionem.
units.tr: Second, it is objected: according to these views the Emperor could appoint the Apostolic See, and make the Pope, the archbishops and the bishops, because Charlemagne had that power, as in dist. 63, chapter "Adrianus." To the first of these objections it is answered, according to the second opinion, that the best way of providing for the Emperor, absolutely speaking, is by election and not by succession; and therefore we do not read that anyone was constituted Emperor otherwise than by election. Hence also the sons of Emperors became Emperors by election; yet not always by the election of those to whom the power of electing was ordinarily granted when the Empire was vacant, but always by the election of the Emperors themselves. For the Emperors, possessing the power of electing, often chose their own sons or others; since an Emperor has no less power of electing than any inferior persons whatever. To the second objection the answer is given in different ways. In one way it is said that every Emperor after Charlemagne and after Otto I had the power of electing the supreme pontiff, since the power of ordaining the Apostolic See belongs to public law; but public law resides in sacred matters and in the priests of the priesthood and in the magistrates, and consequently in the Emperors, who are known to hold the highest place among the magistrates. But public law cannot be set aside, nor can anyone renounce public law (Extra, de foro competenti, "si diligenti"). Therefore the later Emperors could by no means renounce such a right. In another way it is said that the privilege of Charlemagne and Otto was personal, or at least that the Emperors could renounce that privilege. Finally it is said that neither Charlemagne nor Otto had the power of electing the supreme pontiff in so far as they were emperors, since the first Emperors, of whom Charlemagne and Otto were successors, had no such power at all; and therefore the power of electing the Pope did not belong to them as emperors, but in so far as they were Roman Christians, to whom the Romans had entrusted their functions. The same is said of the investiture of bishops and archbishops: that, according to a certain opinion, it holds true especially as regards the temporal conferral which the Emperor has to make, particularly in lands immediately subject to him, and not the Pope. Which of these answers has greater clarity is not to be said at present, since it requires lengthy discussion.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Ponit solutiones, quas illi de secunda opinione dicant ad argumenta facta pro prima opinione superius cap. primo.
units.tr: The solutions which the holders of the second opinion give to the arguments advanced for the first opinion above, in chapter one.

units.la: IN multis aliis opiniones prima & secunda superius recitatæ discordant, de quibus non est nunc tractandum: licet a quibusdam eorum in posterum breuiter tractaturus sum. Modo autem sufficiat dicere, quomodo opinio secunda respondeat ad ea, quæ superius primo capitulo pro opinione prima sunt adducta. Cum enim dicitur, quod rex Romanorum est postea in imperatorem promouendus: dicitur, quod hoc non est proprie dictum. Sed ideo dicitur, quod rex Romanorum est imperator postea appellandus: cuius appellatio ex consuetudine non multum rationabili ante unctionem & coronationem posterioribus temporibus & non ab initio fuit admissa. Primi enim imperatores & successores eorum usque ad multa tempora post Carolum magnum non vocabantur reges Romanorum, priusquam Imperatores. Quare autem postea caperunt prius reges Romanorum, quam imperatores appellari, forte nescitur: & ideo supersedendum est ad tollendum dubitationes periculosas, quæ ex huiusmodi appellationibus exoriri valerent. Multa enim sunt constituta (ut scribit Aug. & habetur dist. 12. c. omnia) quorum omnino vix aut nunquam inueniri causa possint, quas in eis constituendis homines secuti sunt: quæ vbi facultas tribuitur, sine aliqua dubitatione æstimat resecanda. Concluditur ergo, quod proprie loquendo rex Romanorum est imperator: licet non sic appelletur semper. Quod igitur dicitur, dist. 23. c. in nomine, de rege Henrico Romanorum quod futurus sperabatur imperator, intelligi debet quantum ad appellationem, vt sic communiter appellaretur, qualiter tunc non appellabatur communiter, non quantum ad aliquam potestatem iurisdictionis, vel ius de nouo accipiendam vel accipiendum. Quemadmodum electus in Papam si antea fuit episcopus, ex ipsa electione ante omnem inthronisationem seu coronationem & omnem potestatem & iurisdictionem habet, quam per inthronisationem in Apostolicam sedem vel coronationem aut quamcunq; aliam solennitatem dep-turus est. Nam Papa non nisi duplicem potestatem habet, scil. ratione ordinis & ratione potestatis, vt innuit Gloss. dist. 23. in nomine. Sed Papa si prius est episcopus, per coronationem nihil iurisdictionis seu potestatis consequitur, quam uis ante vocetur electus. Quod etiam probatur per hoc, quod beatus Petrus statim, quando fuit factus a Christo Papa omnem statim habuit potestatem, nec aliquam de nouo post accepit. Sed electio Papæ de nouo, respectu successoris Petri, succedit in locum institutionis Petri a Christo, sine omni ministerio humano. Ergo Papa, si est episcopus (quemadmodum Petrus fuit) antequam Papa, per electionem omnem habuit potestatem, quam habuit post. Si autem aliquis, qui non est sacerdos vel episcopus, eligatur in Papam: oportet quod consecretur in sacerdotem vel in episcopum, antequam habeat potestatem, quantum ad illa quæ ordinis sunt. Rex igitur Romanorum non est proprie in imperatorem promouendus: & ideo promotio talis magis verbalis quam realis est. Et si dicatur, quod hoc videtur absurdum & ridiculosum: Respondetur quod non: quemadmodum multa fiunt, quæ magis ad solennitatem spectant, quam ad veritatem: sicut patet in matrimoniis, extra, de sponsalibus. cap. primo. Et in ordinibus clericorum & consecrationibus episcoporum, & etiam in missa, & in multis aliis: quæ tamen non sunt absurda & ridiculosa: quia facere in talibus, præter illa quæ sunt de substantia rei aliqua quæ sunt ad solennitatē & decorem & ad ipsam magnificandam in mentibus eorum; vt in maiori admiratione, venerationc, deuotione & reuerentia habeantur: non est absurdum & ridiculosum, sed sæpe necessarium, vtile & decorum: quamuis secundum opinionem in casu præsenti esset vtile & expediens: quod dimissa dilatione imperialis nominis rex Romanorum statim titulum imperialem assumeret sine mora, & pro imperatore se gereret, ne aliqui ambitiosi, bono communi priuatum præferentes honorem, ex dilatione huiusmodi occasionem accipiant in damnum reipublicæ: asserendo quod rex Romanorum non statim habet imperialis plenitudinem potestatis. Et cum dicitur, quod tunc lex esset impositia verbis, & non rebus: & distinctio nominum non declaret distinctionem rerum. Respondetur, quod nonnunquam nomina imponuntur non ad declarandum differentiam secundum substantiam rei: sed ad declarandum solennitatem vel differentias solennitatum, quæ sunt circa substantiam rei: sicut patet de Papa, qui cum habeat eandem potestatem, primo vocat se electum; & postea ipse vocatur Papa. Sic & Imperatores vocati sunt primo reges Romanorum: Postea nominantur Imperatores: postea etiam aliquando Augusti, aliquando Cæsares appellantur. Et ista nomina nullam differentiam potestatis habent: quare potius mens consideranda est quam verba, quæ deserviunt intentioni; & non e contrario. Extra, de verbo. signi. intelligentia. Licet rex Romanorum non statim vocetur Imperator; nulla est sibi offerenda potestas: quia sic rei lex imposita est, non verbis. Et sic intelligenda sunt verba, ut res verbis non pereat, sed valeat: quia non sermoni res, sed rei debet esse sermo subiectus. Ut extra, de verborum significatione. c. intelligentia. Et ideo, quia non mediocriter periret respublica, si rex Romanorum non statim esset imperator, propter hoc quod prius se vocat regem, quam Imperatorem, ex consuetudine quadam forte minus rationabili. Non est dicendum, quod quantum ad rem, sit differentia inter regem Romanorum & imperatorem. Et sic de quæstione principali est dicendum.
units.tr: The first and second opinions recited above disagree on many other points, but these need not be treated now, though I shall deal briefly with some of them later. For now it is enough to say how the second opinion answers the arguments adduced for the first opinion in the first chapter above. When it is said that the King of the Romans is afterwards to be promoted to emperor, the reply is that this is not properly stated. Rather, the King of the Romans is to be called emperor later. This title, by a custom not very reasonable, was not admitted from the beginning but only in later times, before anointing and coronation. For the first emperors and their successors, down to many centuries after Charlemagne, were not called Kings of the Romans before they were emperors. Why they later began to be called Kings of the Romans before emperors is perhaps not known, and so one must refrain from it, to remove the dangerous doubts that such titles could give rise to. For many things have been established (as Augustine writes, and it is found in dist. 12, c. omnia) whose causes can scarcely or never be found, which men followed in establishing them; where the opportunity is given, these are judged without any doubt to be cut away. It is concluded, therefore, that properly speaking the King of the Romans is emperor, although he is not always so called. What is said in dist. 23, c. in nomine, about King Henry of the Romans, that he was expected to be future emperor, must be understood with respect to the appellation, so that he would be commonly so called, as he was not then commonly called; it does not refer to any power of jurisdiction, or to a right to be newly received. Just as an elected pope, if he was previously a bishop, has from the election itself, before any enthronement or coronation, all the power and jurisdiction which he is about to receive through enthronement in the apostolic see, or coronation, or any other solemnity. For the Pope has only a twofold power, namely by reason of order and by reason of authority, as the Gloss hints at dist. 23, in nomine. But if the Pope was previously a bishop, he gains through coronation no jurisdiction or power, although he is called elect beforehand. This is also proved by the fact that blessed Peter, as soon as he was made pope by Christ, immediately had all power and afterwards received none anew. The election of a pope, with respect to the successor of Peter, succeeds to the place of Peter's institution by Christ, without any human ministry. Therefore the Pope, if he is a bishop (as Peter was) before he is pope, has by election all the power which he has afterwards. If, however, someone who is not a priest or bishop is elected pope, he must be consecrated priest or bishop before he has power in those matters which belong to order. The King of the Romans, therefore, is not properly to be promoted to emperor, and so such a promotion is more verbal than real. And if it is said that this seems absurd and ridiculous, the answer is no: many things are done which pertain more to solemnity than to truth, as is clear in marriages (Extra, de sponsalibus, c. primo), in the orders of clergy and consecrations of bishops, and also in the mass, and in many other things. These are nevertheless not absurd and ridiculous, because doing such things, beyond those which belong to the substance of the matter, for the sake of solemnity and decorum, and to magnify the matter in men's minds so that it may be held in greater admiration, veneration, devotion and reverence, is not absurd and ridiculous but often necessary, useful and fitting. Although, according to this opinion, in the present case it would be useful and expedient that, setting aside the delay in the imperial name, the King of the Romans should at once assume the imperial title without delay and conduct himself as emperor, lest some ambitious men, preferring private honour to the common good, take occasion from such a delay to the harm of the commonwealth, by asserting that the King of the Romans does not immediately have the fullness of imperial power. And when it is said that the law would then be imposed on words and not on things, and that a distinction of names does not declare a distinction of things, the answer is that names are sometimes imposed not to declare a difference in the substance of the thing, but to declare the solemnity, or the differences of solemnities, which concern the substance of the thing. This is clear of the Pope, who, although he has the same power, first calls himself elect and afterwards is called Pope. So also emperors were first called Kings of the Romans, afterwards named Emperors, and afterwards sometimes called Augusti and sometimes Caesars. These names make no difference in power; wherefore the intention is to be considered rather than the words, which serve the intention, and not the reverse (Extra, de verborum significatione, c. intelligentia). Although the King of the Romans is not at once called Emperor, no power is thereby offered to him or withheld, because the law is imposed on the thing, not on the words. Words are therefore to be understood so that the thing does not perish through the words but has its force, because speech is not subject to the thing; rather, the thing must be subject to speech (as in Extra, de verborum significatione, c. intelligentia). And therefore, since the commonwealth would not a little suffer if the King of the Romans were not at once emperor merely because he first calls himself king rather than emperor, owing to some custom perhaps not very reasonable, it is not to be said that, as regards the thing, there is any difference between the King of the Romans and the emperor. And so the principal question is to be answered in this way.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Redit ad discussionem principalis quæstionis in principio propositæ. Circa quam recitatis diversis opinionibus probat secundam.
units.tr: He returns to the discussion of the principal question proposed at the beginning. Having recited the various opinions on it, he proves the second.

units.la: NUnc tractandum est, utrum electio alicuius in regem Romanorum vel Imperatorem sibi det plenam administrationem: ex eo quod illa potestas est immediate a Deo. Circa hæc est opinionum diversitas. Quarum una tenet partem negativam propter hoc, quod ipsa ponit potestatem regis Romanorum seu Imperatoris non esse immediate a Deo: quia tenet quod potestas sua est a Papa, secundum quod tenet opinio, quæ recitata est 2. q. c. f. & ideo huiusmodi electio non habet plenam administrationem: sed oportet quod confirmetur a Papa.
units.tr: Now it must be considered whether the election of someone as King of the Romans or Emperor gives him full administration, on the ground that this power comes immediately from God. On this point there is a diversity of opinions. One of them takes the negative side, because it holds that the power of the King of the Romans or the Emperor does not come immediately from God, since it holds that his power comes from the Pope, according to the opinion recited in 2. q. c. f. Therefore such an election does not give full administration, but it must be confirmed by the Pope.

units.la: Secunda opinio, de qua modo tractatum est: quæ videtur dicere, quod electio alicuius in regem Romanorum dat sibi administrationem in Italia & aliis terris & provinciis, quæ subiectæ fuerunt Carolo ante unctionem & coronationem imperialem. Et hoc quia potestas sua in illis terris est immediate a Deo: quia rex Romanorum illas provincias & terras non tenet a Papa. Sed electio alicuius in regem Romanorum vel imperatorem non dat sibi plenam administrationem in provinciis, quæ non erant subiectæ Carolo magno ante coronationem imperialem: quia alias terras & provincias tenet a Papa: & quantum ad alias tacite illo facto confirmatur a Papa: ex eo scilicet quod Papa ipsum ungit & coronat. Porro quia illa opinio declarata est a quodam reverendo Doctore, transeo ad opinionem secundam, quæ tractata est supra c. 2. quæ sic dicit. Quod inter regem & Imperatorem, seu inter regnum Romanorum & imperium nulla est differentia. Ita etiam tenet quod potestas regni seu imperatoris immediata est a Deo, de quo dictum est, 1. cap. Quemadmodum Papatus immediate est a Deo. Rex enim Romanorum seu Imperator in quibuscunque terris vel provinciis nullum superiorem habet in temporalibus: nec quascunque terras seu provincias tenet ab alio quam a Deo. Et ideo dicitur, quod electio alicuius in regem seu Imperatorem dat sibi plenam administrationem, quæ sibi competit de iure in quibusdam terris & provinciis. Non enim eandem plenitudinem habet in omnibus terris & provinciis: quia de iure plenior habet administrationem immediate in terris subiectis Imperio, quam in aliis: Sic & primi Imperatores pleniorem habuerunt potestatem & administrationem in terris immediate sibi subiectis, quæ ad Imperium deputatæ erant ad onera Imperii perferenda, quam in aliis terris. Pro ista assertione prædictæ opinionis secundæ potest taliter allegari, sicut allegatum est prius. Quia illi, qui alteri in imperio vel regno succedunt, eodem iure, quo ille, uti debent. Sed electus in regem seu Imperatorem succedit Imperatoribus, qui fuerunt tam ante Carolum magnum, quam etiam Constantinum. Ergo eodem iure, quo illi, uti debet. Electio autem dedit illis Imperatoribus plenam administrationem, quæ competebat eis de iure in quibuscunque terris & provinciis. Ergo & modo electio dat plenam administrationem electo in regem Romanorum seu Imperatorem. Aliter enim vel rex Romanorum seu Imperator non esset successor Imperatorum illorum seu regum: aut modo per electionem non succederet in ius electionis vel electionum priorum. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod ista allegatio supponit falsum, scilicet quod Imperatores sen per fiant per electionem: cum multi fuerunt Imperatores per successionem generis tam ante Carolum magnum, quam post. Hic respondetur, quod nunquam aliquis fuit factus Imperator Romanorum nisi per electionem: non proprie loquendo per successionem generis. Illi enim Imperatores, qui facti videntur imperatores per generis successionem, per electionem praeuiam suorum vel aliorum ad Imperii fastigium promoti fuerunt. Unde Ludovici Caroli filius non iure primogenituræ, nec aliquo iure proprio, sed per electionem patris fuit factus Imperator. Unde si pater decessisset, & nullū ad Imperium elegisset, Ludovicus, si fuisset primogenitus, quamuis habuisset ius vendicandi regnum Francorum iure primogenituræ: quo iure in regnis occidentalibus succedunt primogeniti patribus: non tamen habuisset ius vendicandi Imperium seu regnum Romanorum. In hoc enim, quod Imperium seu regnum Romanorum nemo assequeretur per successionem, sed per electionem: ipsum optimo modo regalis monarchiæ magis appropinquat, quam regnum, quod per generis successionem quæreretur.
units.tr: The second opinion, of which we have just treated, seems to say that the election of someone as King of the Romans gives him administration in Italy and the other lands and provinces that were subject to Charles before his anointing and imperial coronation. This is because his power over those lands is immediately from God, since the King of the Romans does not hold those provinces and lands from the Pope. But the election of someone as King of the Romans or Emperor does not give him full administration in the provinces that were not subject to Charles the Great before his imperial coronation, because he holds those other lands and provinces from the Pope, and, as to the others, he is tacitly confirmed by the Pope through that very act, namely because the Pope anoints and crowns him. Since that opinion was set forth by a certain reverend Doctor, I pass to the second opinion, which was treated above in c. 2., and which says this: that between the king and the Emperor, or between the kingdom of the Romans and the empire, there is no difference. It likewise holds that the power of the kingdom or of the Emperor is immediate from God, of which it was said in 1. cap., just as the papacy is immediately from God. For the King of the Romans, or the Emperor, in whatever lands or provinces, has no superior in temporal matters, nor does he hold any lands or provinces from anyone other than God. And so it is said that the election of someone as king or Emperor gives him full administration, which belongs to him by right in certain lands and provinces. For he does not have the same fullness in all lands and provinces, because by right he has a fuller administration in the lands immediately subject to the Empire than in others. So too the first Emperors had a fuller power and administration in the lands immediately subject to them, which had been assigned to the Empire to bear its burdens, than in other lands. In support of this assertion of the said second opinion, one may argue as follows, as was argued before. Those who succeed others in an empire or kingdom ought to use the same right that the one they succeed used. But the one elected as king or Emperor succeeds those Emperors who existed both before Charles the Great and before Constantine. Therefore he ought to use the same right that they used. Now the election gave those Emperors full administration, which belonged to them by right in whatever lands and provinces. Therefore now too the election gives full administration to the one elected as King of the Romans or Emperor. Otherwise the King of the Romans or the Emperor would not be a successor of those Emperors or kings, or else by election he would not succeed to the right of the earlier election or elections. But perhaps someone would say that this argument assumes something false, namely that the Emperors were made by election, since many were Emperors by succession of blood both before and after Charles the Great. Here it is answered that no one was ever made Emperor of the Romans except by election, not properly speaking by succession of blood. For those Emperors who seem to have been made emperors by succession of blood were promoted to the summit of the Empire by a prior election of their own or of others. Hence Louis, the son of Charles, was made Emperor not by right of primogeniture, nor by any right of his own, but by the election of his father. Therefore, if his father had died and had elected no one to the Empire, Louis, if he had been the firstborn, although he would have had the right to claim the kingdom of the Franks by right of primogeniture (which right in the western kingdoms passes from fathers to firstborn sons), would still not have had the right to claim the Empire or kingdom of the Romans. For the Empire or kingdom of the Romans would be attained by no one through succession, but by election; and in this respect it comes closer to the best form of royal monarchy than a kingdom which would be sought by succession of blood.

units.la: Secundo ad prædictam quæstionem taliter allegatur. Imperator tenet à Papa, quæ non erant subiecta Carolo Magno ante vnctionem Imperialem ipsius, & non alia. Ergo istæ terræ & reliquæ sunt subiectæ iurisdictioni & potestati Papæ: non iure naturali: quia vna terra iure naturali non est magis subiecta Papæ quam alia. Iure enim naturali omnia sunt communia, & communis omnis possessio est, & omnium est vna libertas, id est ius naturale. Nec iure diuino aliquæ terræ sunt magis subiectæ Papæ quam aliæ. Tum quia, sicut dicit Augustinus super Iohan. & recitatur distinct. octau. quo iure: Iure diuino, Domini est terra & plenitudo eius: pauperes & diuites vna terra portat: Tum quia ius diuinum in scripturis diuinis habemus. distinct. octau. quo iure. in scripturis autem diuinis nullatenus inuenitur, quod Deus magis subiugauerat iurisdictioni Papæ terras, quæ non erant subiectæ Carolo ante coronationem Imperialem, quam alias: tum quia plures illarum nec de iure nec de facto nunquam Christianorum fuerunt, quia incolæ eorundem nunquam fuerunt conuersi ad fidem: & per consequens Papa super ipsos nullam habuit iurisdictionem, iuxta illud Apostoli primæ ad Cor. 5. Quid ad nos iudicare de his qui foris sunt? Nec iure humano terræ illæ magis sunt subiectæ iurisdictioni Papæ, quam aliæ: Nec iure Ciuili: nec iure Canonico. Non de iure Ciuili: quia de hoc in iure Ciuili nihil habetur. Nec iure Canonico, quia Papa, cuius est condere Canones, non habet potestatem, vt huiusmodi regna & prouincias possit sibi subiicere. Tunc enim posset quodcunq; regnum subiicere iurisdictioni suæ, & omnium Regnorum iura potestati suæ subiicere; & sic omnia iura & regna turbare, quod tamen non debet. Extra de iudiciis c. nouit. Item, illæ terræ, quæ non erant subiectæ Carolo ante coronationem Imperii, nec iure scripto nec non scripto erant subiectæ iurisdictioni Papæ. Quod non iure scripto, patet: quia tale ius scriptum minime inuenitur. Nec iure non scripto, scilicet consuetudine rationabili ac approbata aut scripta, quia super hæc nulla consuetudo præcessit. Imperatores enim prædecessores Caroli non magis recognoscebant à Papa illas terras, quæ non erant subiectæ Carolo, quam alias. Nec inuenitur, quod aliquas tenuerint à Papa. Quia minus videtur quod tenuerunt alias à Papa terras, quæ non erant subiectæ Carolo Magno, quam Italiam & alia Occidentalia Regna, quæ erant subiecta Carolo: quia capitulum illud Constantinus. dist. 96. sonare videtur, quod Constantinus dedit Papæ Syluestro & successoribus eius omnes Italiæ & Occidentalium Regionum prouincias & ciuitates & loca, & non Orientalium Regionum: quia si prædecessores Caroli tenuerunt à Papa potissime Italiam, etiam Occidentalia regna debuerunt tenere à Papa. Sed forte diceres, quod virtute translationis Imperii in Carolum Magnum per Papam Carolus tenuit à Papa illas terras, quæ prius non erant sibi subiectæ. Et ideo in illas habuit solum modo potestatem Imperialem per translationem Imperii factam à Papa, & non in alias. Hic diuersimode respondetur. Vno modo, quod illa translatio non fuit à Papa, sed à Romanis, quorum ab initio fuit Imperium & à quibus Imperator primo accepit Imperium: qui omnem suam potestatem regendi propter bonum commune transtulerunt in Imperatorem, non tamen in ipsam potestatem dominandi seu regendi despotice, necà se abdicauerunt omnem potestatem casualiter dispon endi de Imperio. Si enim hoc fecissent, seruos se fecissent Imperatoris strictissime accipiendo vocabulum serui: & reuera nullatenus liberi remansissent: & per consequens Imperator non habuisset principatum regalem, sed pure despoticum: quia secundum istam responsionem Imperator virtute illius translationis Imperii nullas terras tenet à Papa. Aliter respondetur, quod esto quod illa translatio sit à Papa: tamen ex hoc non sequitur, quod Imperator quascunq; terras ab illo debeat tenere: quia secundum sic opinantes: sicut Papa transtulit Imperium de Græcis in Carolum, ita transtulit regnum Francorum de Hylderico in Pipinum patrem Caroli: quia vt dicunt, illum deposuit, & istum substituit: & tamen non obstante tali translatione regnum Francorum non tenetur à Papa. Ergo similiter propter translationem Imperii à Papa non est dicendum, quod Imperator quascunq; terras teneat à Papa. Sed diceret aliquis: omnis transferens de iure rem aliquam de vno in alium habet de iure potestatem aliquam super eandem rem. Si ergo Papa de iure Imperium transtulit de Græcis in Carolum Magnum: habuit aliquam potestatem de iure super Imperium. Quare Carolus debuit recognoscere Imperium à Papa: & per consequens tenuit aliquas terras à Papa. Hic respondetur, quod omnis transferens de iure casualiter vel regulariter habet aliquam potestatem super eandem rem. Et ideo si Papa transtulit Imperium, habuit saltem casualiter aliquam potestatem super Imperium. Sed ex hoc non sequitur quod Imperator debeat tenere Imperium vel alias terras à Papa: quia ita poterit res transferri de vno in alium, vt à transferente minime teneatur, postquam translata est de vno in alium. Sicut patet de venditione & donatione: per quam sæpe translatio terrarum fit & iurium, quæ postea à transferente non tenentur. Si ergo Papa fecit debitam translationem, Carolus debuit recognoscere Imperium à Papa: tanquam ab illo, à quo primo habet Imperium: non tanquam ab illo, à quo tenet Imperium, vel aliquas terras eius: quemadmodum donatarius, si vult esse gratus, tenetur recognoscere rem donatam à donatore. Et sic non valet illud vltimum: & per consequens quæstio principalis taliter confirmatur. Verbum indiffinite prolatum generaliter debet intelligi, & non est aliqualiter restringendum. dist. 19. si Romanorum. Sed in chronicis & in decretis, extra de electione. venerabilem. indiffinite dictum est, quod Imperium translatum est de Græcis in Carolum Magnum. Ergo generaliter debet intelligi, vt non restringatur ad modū talem transferendi in aliquas terras & prouincias, q Imperator à Papa non teneat alias. Ergo Imperator vel omnes terras Imperii tenet à Papa: vel nullas. Sed non omnes terras: ergo nullas. Sed aliquis diceret, quod non solū verba indiffinite prolata, sed etiam generaliter plata debent restringi: sicut non solum per iura ciuilia & canonica, sed etiam per scripturas diuinas posset aperte probari, quare verba de translatione Imperii indiffinite prolata debent restringi. Isti possunt dicere, quod quamuis verba etiam prolata generaliter debeant saepe restringi, tamen quia fauores conuenit ampliari, extra de Regul. Iur. c. odia. li. 6. super re fauorabili prolata indiffinite magis ampliari debent, quam restringi, nisi restrictio per rationem vel authoritatem, quam negare nō licet, possit euidenter ostendi. Imperium autem est res fauorabilis, quae ad vtilitatem omnium mortalium instituitur: quare verba indiffinite prolata in fauorem Imperii ampliari debent, non restringi. Et si dicat quis, quod talis restrictio probari potest per rationem: quia aliter promotio ad imperium esset verbalis. Respondetur, quod esto, quod rex Romanorum, quando coronatur corona Imperiali, nisi aliquam potestatem de nouo acciperet, huiusmodi promotio esset tantum verbalis, non tamen ex hoc posset probari, quod Carolus Magnus aliquas terras tenebat à Papa, antequam esset Imperator, quia non prius fuit rex Romanorum, quam Imperator.
units.tr: Secondly, the question above is argued in the following way. The emperor holds from the Pope those lands which were not subject to Charlemagne before his imperial anointing, and no others. Therefore those lands and the rest are subject to the jurisdiction and power of the Pope. Not by natural law, because one land is no more subject to the Pope by natural law than another. For by natural law all things are common, all possession is common, and there is one liberty for all, that is, natural law.
