Nor is any land more subject to the Pope than another by divine law: first, because Augustine says, super Iohan. and it is quoted in distinct. octau. quo iure: By divine law the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord; the earth bears rich and poor alike; and second, because we have divine law in the divine Scriptures, and nowhere in the divine Scriptures is it found that God subjected to the jurisdiction of the Pope those lands which were not subject to Charlemagne before the imperial coronation more than others. Furthermore, many of those lands were never Christian, neither by right nor in fact, because their inhabitants were never converted to the faith; and consequently the Pope had no jurisdiction over them, according to the saying of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 5: What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Nor by human law are those lands more subject to the jurisdiction of the Pope than others: neither by civil law nor by canon law. Not by civil law, because nothing on this is found in civil law. Nor by canon law, because the Pope, whose office it is to make canons, has no power to subject such kingdoms and provinces to himself. For then he could subject any kingdom whatever to his jurisdiction and bring all the laws of all kingdoms under his power, and so disturb all laws and kingdoms, which he ought not to do: Extra de iudiciis c. nouit. Likewise, those lands which were not subject to Charlemagne before the coronation of the empire were subject to the jurisdiction of the Pope neither by written nor by unwritten law. That they were not subject by written law is evident, because no such written law is found. Nor by unwritten law, that is, by reasonable custom approved or written down, because no custom preceded in this matter. For the predecessors of Charlemagne did not acknowledge those lands, which were not subject to Charlemagne, as held from the Pope any more than others, nor is it found that they held any lands from the Pope. For it seems less likely that they held from the Pope other lands, which were not subject to Charlemagne the Great, than Italy and the other Western kingdoms, which were subject to Charlemagne; because that chapter, Constantinus. dist. 96., seems to say that Constantine gave to Pope Sylvester and his successors all the provinces, cities and places of Italy and the Western regions, and not of the Eastern regions. For if the predecessors of Charlemagne held Italy above all from the Pope, they ought to have held the Western kingdoms from the Pope as well. But perhaps you would say that by virtue of the translation of the empire to Charlemagne by the Pope, Charlemagne held from the Pope those lands which had not previously been subject to him, and so he had only imperial power over those lands by the translation of the empire made by the Pope, and not over others. Here there are different answers. In one way: that translation was not made by the Pope but by the Romans, from whom the empire originally came and from whom the emperor first received it. They transferred all their power of ruling for the common good to the emperor, but not the power of ruling despotically, and they did not strip themselves of all power of disposing of the empire at their pleasure. For if they had done this, they would have made themselves slaves of the emperor, taking the word slaves in the strictest sense; and in truth they would not have remained free at all; and consequently the emperor would not have had a royal principate but a purely despotic one. For according to this answer, the emperor by virtue of that translation of the empire holds no lands from the Pope. In another way it is answered that, even granting that the translation was made by the Pope, it does not follow from this that the emperor must hold from him any lands whatever; for according to those who think so, just as the Pope transferred the empire from the Greeks to Charlemagne, so he transferred the kingdom of the Franks from Hilderic to Pepin, the father of Charlemagne, because, as they say, he deposed the one and set up the other; and yet, notwithstanding such a translation, the kingdom of the Franks is not held from the Pope. Therefore, similarly, on account of the translation of the empire by the Pope, it should not be said that the emperor holds any lands whatever from the Pope. But someone might say: whoever rightfully transfers a thing from one person to another has some power by right over the same thing. If therefore the Pope rightfully transferred the empire from the Greeks to Charlemagne the Great, he had some power by right over the empire. Hence Charlemagne ought to have acknowledged the empire from the Pope, and consequently he held some lands from the Pope. Here it is answered that whoever rightfully transfers something, whether occasionally or as a rule, has some power over the same thing. And therefore, if the Pope transferred the empire, he had at least occasional power over the empire. But it does not follow from this that the emperor ought to hold the empire or other lands from the Pope, because a thing can be so transferred from one person to another that it is not held from the one who transferred it once it has been transferred. This is clear in the case of sale and gift, by which the transfer of lands and rights often takes place, and which are afterwards not held from the one who transferred them. If therefore the Pope made a due translation, Charlemagne ought to have acknowledged the empire from the Pope, as from him from whom he first had the empire, but not as from him from whom he held the empire or any of its lands; just as a donee, if he wishes to be grateful, is bound to acknowledge the gift as from the donor. And so that last point does not hold, and consequently the principal question is confirmed in this way. A word spoken indefinitely ought to be understood generally, and is not to be restricted in any way: dist. 19. si Romanorum. But in the chronicles and in the decrees, extra de electione. venerabilem., it is stated indefinitely that the empire was transferred from the Greeks to Charlemagne the Great. Therefore it ought to be understood generally, so that it is not restricted to a mode of transferring it to some lands and provinces such that the emperor does not hold others from the Pope. Therefore the emperor holds either all the lands of the empire from the Pope, or none. But not all; therefore none. But someone might say that not only words spoken indefinitely but also words spoken generally ought to be restricted, just as it could be clearly proved from the civil and canon laws, and even from the divine Scriptures, why words about the translation of the empire spoken indefinitely ought to be restricted. These men can say that although even words spoken generally often ought to be restricted, nevertheless, since it is proper to enlarge favours, extra de Regul. Iur. c. odia. li. 6., in a favourable matter words spoken indefinitely ought to be enlarged rather than restricted, unless a restriction can be clearly shown by reason or authority, which it is not lawful to deny. But the empire is a favourable matter, which is instituted for the benefit of all mortals; therefore words spoken indefinitely in favour of the empire ought to be enlarged, not restricted. And if someone says that such a restriction can be proved by reason, because otherwise the promotion to the empire would be merely verbal, the answer is this: even granting that the King of the Romans, when he is crowned with the imperial crown, received no new power, such a promotion would be merely verbal; yet it could not thereby be proved that Charlemagne held any lands from the Pope before he was emperor, because he was not King of the Romans before he was emperor.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: Caput vltimum huius quartae quaestionis, ostendit, quam potestatem consequatur electus in Romanorum Regem, ponens argumenta, quorum solutiones ad superiora remittuntur capitula.
units.tr: The last chapter of this fourth question shows what power the elected man acquires as King of the Romans, setting out the arguments, whose solutions are referred back to the preceding chapters.

units.la: TEnet itaq; opinio ista, quod quamuis non sit necesse de natura electionis cuiuslibet, quod electores etiam modicam dent administrationem, nedum plenam. Nam multi electi etiam canonice atq; rite ante confirmationem, nullam administrationem habent omnino. Et ideo poterat ordinari, quod electio alicuius in regem Romanorum vel in Imperatorem non daret sibi plenam administrationem, imo nullam: sed quod approbatio expeteretur alicuius vel aliquorum, qui vim confirmationis habent, vel quod ante certum tempus electus non adipisceretur administrationem. Unde & nonnulli Imperatores aliquos videntur ad imperium elegisse, sic tamen, quod eis succederent, & eligentibus viuentibus nullam administrationem haberent. Tamen quia non habetur, nec constat, quod electio & potestas eligendi regem Romanorum seu Imperatorem principibus electoribus tali modo data fuerit vel concessa: sed quod absolute & indiffinite fuerit eis eligendi data potestas: ideo dicit ista opinio, quod cum potestas regis Romanorum seu Imperatoris sit immediate à Deo, isto modo tamen, quod imperium tenetur à solo Deo, ita quod in temporalibus superiorem non habet. Ideo electio alicuius in regem Romanorum vel Imperatorem dat electo plenam administrationem isto modo, quod electus statim, cum legitime constiterit se esse electum, absq; alia confirmatione vel approbatione vel examinatione aut coronatione seu vnctione habet plenam potestatem administrandi, quae regi Romanorum vel Imperatori post quamcunq; vnctionem seu coronationem de iure debetur: in tantum quod nulla consuetudo in hoc electo derogare valeret, quin de plenitudine potestatis sic posset de iure talem consuetudinem auferre, & venire contra eam. Nec est distinguendum inter terras & prouincias sibi subiectas, vel inter terras sibi vel Imperio vel immediate subiectas, quin omnem habeat potestatem administrandi, quam de iure habet Imperator, postquam vnctionem & coronationem suscepit: tamen potestatem maiorem habet electus in terris immediate subiectis Imperio, quam in aliis, quia plura potest de iure in illis terris, quam in aliis, quae regibus & aliis principibus ac Dominis sunt immediate subiectae, pro eo quod reges & alii principes sunt liberi, & non sunt puri serui Imperatorum. Imo secundum nonnullos, si principatus Imperialis esset pure regalis principatui despotico & omni alii principatui humanitus instituto, taliter imperans nullum purum seruum (cum quilibet esset liber) haberet: nisi aliquis fieret seruus eius propter culpam: quamuis haberet multos seruos dictos à seruiendo seu ministrando: de qua seruitute loquitur Arist. primo politi. cum dicit quosdam esse naturaliter seruos. Quod ergo electio alicuius in regem vel Imperatorem aliquo modo det electo plenam administrationem, multis modis videtur posse probari. Primo sic: Verbis indiffinite prolatis vel concessis est interpretatio rationabilior & commodior seu vtilior applicanda. Tum quia sicut benigniora sunt praeferenda, ff. de Reg. Iur. l. semper, sic etiam rationabiliora & vtiliora sunt praeferenda. Tum quia in obscuris sic fieri debet interpretatio, vt prosit praesertim bono communi. Sed rationabile est & vtile, vt electio alicuius in regem Romanorum seu Imperatorem sic fiat, vt electus non habeat superiorem in temporalibus. Quare rationabile est, vt aliquid speciale constituatur circa electionem ipsius: vt scilicet ipse electus nulla confirmatione indigeat: sed statim habeat plenam & liberam administrationem: quemadmodum propter haec, cum Papa non habeat superiorem, ad quem possit haberi recursus, statim cum est electus, debet Pontifex Romanus haberi. Extra de electionibus. c. licet. Hoc enim commodum est & vtile, ne propter expectationem confirmationis, approbationis, vnctionis & coronationis, dissensiones & guerrae vel alia mala proueniant in quacunq; parte Imperii: quae, si electus statim plenam potestatem haberet, vel cessarent totaliter, vel possent facilius & citius extirpari vel sedari. Per ipsius etiam electi prouidentiam possent multa vtilia procurari: quae per talem expectationem aut impedirentur omnino; aut necesse esset ea saepe periculose differri. Quia igitur non constat, quod electoribus sit data limitata eligendi potestas, vt electus non habeat statim plenam administrationem: ideo intelligenda est eis esse data eligendi potestas, propter vtilitatem communem, vt electus statim habeat plenam administrationem. Confirmatur haec allegatio: quia non minus plena est interpretatio fundata in indulgentiis seu concessionibus, seu priuilegiis, quae propter bonum commune conceduntur, quam in beneficiis. Sed in beneficiis est plena interpretatio facienda extra, de donationibus cum dilecti. ergo priuilegium principum electorum, quo concessum est, vt propter bonum commune ius habeant eligendi regem Romanorum aut Imperatorem, est plene interpretandum, vt secundum ius habeant istam electionem faciendi: cum qua electione detur plena administratio. Secundo ad idem etiam sic allegatur. Rex Romanorum seu Imperator fidelis non debet esse deterioris conditionis, quam fuerat rex Romanorum seu Imperator infidelis, cui succedit. Sed Imperatores infideles, statim facta electione habebant plenam administrationem: Ergo & Imperatores fideles statim habebunt plenam administrationem. Item, non minus dat electio Imperatori, quam successio generis, quae dat aliis regibus plenam administrationem. Contra praedicta, multa possunt opponi: sed quomodo ad ipsa ista opinio secunda responderet, patere potest ex his, quae dicta seu recitata sunt Secunda quaestione speciliter capitulo 6. sequentibus. & q 3. ca. 4. & quibusdam sequentibus.
units.tr: This opinion holds that, although it is not necessary by the nature of any election that the electors give the one elected even a small measure of administration, let alone full administration (for many who are elected canonically and duly have no administration at all before confirmation), it could nonetheless be ordained that the election of someone as King of the Romans or as Emperor would not give him full administration, indeed none at all, but that the approval of some person or persons who have the force of confirmation would be sought, or that the elected man would not obtain administration until a certain time had passed. Hence some Emperors also seem to have chosen men for the empire in such a way that these succeeded them, while the men had no administration during the lifetime of the electors. Yet since it is not held or established that the power of electing a King of the Romans or Emperor was granted or conceded to the prince-electors in such a manner, but rather that the power to elect was given to them absolutely and without limitation, this opinion says that, since the power of the King of the Romans or Emperor comes immediately from God, it is held in such a way that the empire is held from God alone, so that he has no superior in temporal matters. Therefore the election of someone as King of the Romans or Emperor gives the elected man full administration in this way: as soon as it is lawfully established that he has been elected, without any further confirmation, approval, examination, coronation or anointing, he has full power to administer, which by right is owed to the King of the Romans or Emperor after any anointing or coronation. So far is this so that no custom could derogate from this elected man, but by the fullness of his power he could thus by right remove such a custom and act against it. Nor must a distinction be drawn between lands and provinces subject to him, or between lands subject to him or to the Empire immediately, so that he would not have all the power of administration which the Emperor has by right after receiving anointing and coronation. Nevertheless the elected man has greater power in lands immediately subject to the Empire than in others, because he can by right do more in those lands than in others, which are immediately subject to kings, other princes and lords, since kings and other princes are free and are not mere slaves of the Emperors. Indeed, according to some, if the Imperial principality were purely royal, like a despotic principality and every other principality instituted by human authority, one who ruled in that way would have no pure slave (since everyone would be free), unless someone became his slave on account of a fault, although he would have many slaves, so called from serving or ministering; Aristotle speaks of this servitude in the first book of the Politics, when he says that some are slaves by nature. That the election of someone as King or Emperor gives the elected man full administration in some way seems capable of being proved in many ways. First, thus: for words spoken or granted indefinitely, the more reasonable, more convenient or more useful interpretation is to be applied; since, as the more kindly things are to be preferred (ff. de Reg. Iur. l. semper), so also the more reasonable and more useful things are to be preferred. Again, in obscure matters the interpretation must be made so as to benefit above all the common good. But it is reasonable and useful that the election of someone as King of the Romans or Emperor be made in such a way that the elected man has no superior in temporal matters. Therefore it is reasonable that something special be established concerning his election, namely that the elected man himself need no confirmation, but at once has full and free administration; just as, for this reason, since the Pope has no superior to whom appeal can be made, the Roman Pontiff must be regarded as such as soon as he is elected (Extra de electionibus, c. licet). For this is convenient and useful, so that because of waiting for confirmation, approval, anointing and coronation, dissensions, wars or other evils do not arise in any part of the Empire; which, if the elected man had full power at once, would either cease altogether or could be more easily and quickly uprooted or calmed. Through the foresight of the elected man himself, many useful things could also be secured, which either would be wholly hindered by such waiting or would have to be deferred, often dangerously. Since therefore it is not established that the electors were given a limited power of electing, so that the elected man would not have full administration at once, it must be understood that the power of electing was given to them for the common benefit, so that the elected man would at once have full administration. This argument is confirmed: for an interpretation founded on indulgences or concessions or privileges, which are granted for the common good, is no less full than one applied to benefices. But in benefices the interpretation must be full (Extra, de donationibus, cum dilecti). Therefore the privilege of the electing princes, by which it was granted that they should have the right to elect the King of the Romans or Emperor for the common good, must be fully interpreted, so that they may have this election according to law, with which election full administration is given. Second, the same is argued thus: a faithful King of the Romans or Emperor ought not to be in a worse condition than the unfaithful King of the Romans or Emperor whom he succeeds. But unfaithful Emperors had full administration as soon as they were elected; therefore faithful Emperors will also have full administration at once. Likewise, election gives the Emperor no less than succession of birth gives other kings, which gives them full administration. Many objections can be raised against what has been said; but how this second opinion answers them can be seen from what was said or recited in the Second Question, especially chapter 6 and following, and Q. 3, ch. 4, and certain following passages.

units.la: QVÆSTIO QVINTA.
units.tr: QUESTION FIVE.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Primo c. V. q. proposita quaestione recitat circa eam duos articulos principales, de quorum primo, qui in tres partiales diuiditur, tractatur in quatuor primis capitulis. Nam in hoc primo recitatur circa primum articulum partialem prima opinio, ad cuius probationes respondetur capitulo 3. De secundo autem articulo principaliter videbitur cap. 7. & seqq.
units.tr: At the start, the fifth chapter, having set out the question, recites two principal articles concerning it. The first of these, which is divided into three partial articles, is treated in the first four chapters. In this first chapter, the first partial article is set out with the first opinion about it, and the proofs for that opinion are answered in chapter 3. The second principal article will be dealt with mainly in chapter 7 and following.

units.la: QVinto quaeritur, vtrum rex haereditarie succedens accipiat aliquam potestatem super temporalia, ex eo quod a persona Ecclesiastica inungitur, consecratur & coronatur: vel solum ex hoc aliquam consequatur gratiam doni spiritualis. Ista quaestio articulos duos principales includit. Primus est de potestate super temporalia. Secundus est de gratia doni spiritualis. Circa primum possunt formari tres articuli: quorum primus est; An rex haereditarie succedens aliquam potestatem accipiat super temporalia ex eo quod a persona Ecclesiastica inungitur: Secundus, an ex eo quod consecratur: Tertius, an eo quod coronatur. Circa primum est vna opinio, quod rex haereditarie succedens aliquam accipit potestatem super temporalia, ex eo quod a persona Ecclesiastica inungitur. Pro qua opinione potest taliter allegari. Sic se habet vnctio regalis ad regem, sicut vnctio sacerdotalis ad sacerdotem; & Episcopalis ad Episcopum. Sed per vnctionem sacerdotalem & Episcopalem aliqua potestas acquiritur. Ergo per consequens etiam per vnctionem regalem. Sed non potestas spiritualis; per consequens temporalis. Ergo rex eo quod sic inungitur, accipit aliquam potestatem super temporalia. Item, sicut natura nihil facit frustra; ita rationabiliter operans nihil facit frustra. Sed frustra heret & ridiculose, nisi rex per ipsam aliquam potestatem acciperet super temporalia. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Fifthly, it is asked whether a king who succeeds by inheritance receives any power over temporal affairs from being anointed, consecrated and crowned by an ecclesiastical person, or whether he obtains only some grace of spiritual gift from this. This question contains two principal articles. The first concerns power over temporal affairs; the second concerns the grace of spiritual gift. Three articles can be formed on the first: the first is whether a king who succeeds by inheritance receives any power over temporal affairs from being anointed by an ecclesiastical person; the second, whether he does so from being consecrated; the third, whether he does so from being crowned. On the first there is one opinion, that a king who succeeds by inheritance does receive some power over temporal affairs from being anointed by an ecclesiastical person. This opinion may be argued thus: royal anointing stands to the king as priestly anointing stands to the priest, and episcopal anointing to the bishop. But through priestly and episcopal anointing some power is acquired; therefore, by consequence, also through royal anointing. But it is not a spiritual power; therefore it is a temporal one. So the king, by being anointed in this way, receives some power over temporal affairs. Again, just as nature makes nothing in vain, so a reasonably acting agent does nothing in vain. But the anointing would be pointless and ridiculous unless through it the king received some power over temporal affairs. Therefore, etc.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Recitat secundam opinionem contrariam prima: cuius duas conclusiones ponit & probat: quarum probationibus respondebitur capitulo 4. huius quaestionis.
units.tr: He recites the second opinion, contrary to the first, and sets out and proves two conclusions of it; answers to these proofs will be given in chapter 4 of this question.

units.la: ALia est opinio, quod rex haereditarie succedens non accipit aliquam potestatem super temporalia, ex eo quod a persona Ecclesiastica inungitur, quae duas conclusiones tenet: quarum prima est haec. Rex non accipit aliquam potestatem super temporalia, ex eo quod inungitur. Secunda, quod non ex eo, quod coronatur a persona Ecclesiastica, siue consecratur.
units.tr: There is another opinion, that a king who succeeds by inheritance does not receive any power over temporal affairs from being anointed by an ecclesiastical person. This holds two conclusions. The first is this: a king does not receive any power over temporal affairs from being anointed. The second is that he does not receive it from being crowned or consecrated by an ecclesiastical person.

units.la: Pro prima taliter allegatur. Omnes reges in eodem regno haereditarie sibi succedentes habent eandem super temporalia potestatem in eodem regno. Aliter enim vnus non esset verus successor & verus haeres alterius. Sed in multis regnis fuerunt sibi plures haereditarie succedentes: quorum aliqui fuerunt infideles & pagani, qui non fuerunt inuncti: quia reges Paganorum non inunguntur. Ergo per hoc, quod haereditarie rex succedens inungitur, non recipit super temporalia potestatem. Quod non ex eo quod a persona Ecclesiastica iniungitur, taliter allegatur. Eadem vnctio a quocunque conferatur, habet eundem effectum: sicut baptismus, siue conferatur a persona Ecclesiastica, siue a laico, siue etiam a muliere, habet eundem effectum. Ergo vnctio regalis habet eundem effectum, siue conferatur a persona Ecclesiastica, siue ab alia. Ergo vnctio ex hoc quod confertur a persona Ecclesiastica, non habet vnctus aliquam super temporalia potestatem. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod vnctio regalis non potest conferri nisi a persona Ecclesiastica: sicut nec vnctio sacerdotalis vel Episcopalis. Hic forte diceretur, quod vnctio regalis potest conferri a persona non Ecclesiastica: quia vnctio regalis introducta est ex Veteri Testamento. In Veteri autem Testamento aliquando vnctio regalis conferebatur a sacerdote vel Leuita tantum, quibus in Nouo Testamento succedunt personae Ecclesiasticae. Nam Samuel qui fuit Leuita, vnxit de praecepto Dei Saulem & Dauid in regem: & Sadoch sacerdos vnxit in regem Salomonem. Nonnunquam vero vnctio regalis fiebat ab aliis. Præceptum enim fuit Heliæ, vt vngeret Azael regem super Syriam, & Iehu filium Namsi regem super Israel. Quidam etiam adolescens puer Prophetæ, vt legitur, 4. Reg. 9. vnxit Iehu regem super Hierusalem. Quare & nunc posset à persona non Ecclesiastica rex inungi.
units.tr: For the first it is argued thus: all kings who succeed one another by inheritance in the same kingdom have the same power over temporal affairs in that kingdom. Otherwise one would not be the true successor and true heir of another. But in many kingdoms there have been several who succeeded by inheritance, some of whom were unbelievers and pagans, who were not anointed, since pagan kings are not anointed. Therefore, by the fact that a king who succeeds by inheritance is anointed, he does not receive power over temporal affairs. As for the second conclusion, that he does not receive it from being anointed by an ecclesiastical person, it is argued thus: the same anointing has the same effect, whoever confers it, just as baptism has the same effect whether it is conferred by an ecclesiastical person, a layman, or even a woman. Therefore royal anointing has the same effect whether it is conferred by an ecclesiastical person or by another. Therefore the anointed man does not acquire any power over temporal affairs from its being conferred by an ecclesiastical person. But perhaps someone would say that royal anointing can be conferred only by an ecclesiastical person, just as priestly or episcopal anointing can. To this it might perhaps be replied that royal anointing can be conferred by a person who is not ecclesiastical, since royal anointing was introduced from the Old Testament. In the Old Testament, however, royal anointing was sometimes conferred only by a priest or a Levite, whose successors in the New Testament are ecclesiastical persons. For Samuel, who was a Levite, anointed Saul and David as king by God's command, and Zadok the priest anointed Solomon as king. Sometimes, however, royal anointing was performed by others. For Elijah was commanded to anoint Hazael king over Syria and Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel. Likewise a young man, a disciple of the prophet, as we read in 4 Reg. 9., anointed Jehu king over Jerusalem. Hence now too a king could be anointed by a person who is not ecclesiastical.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Respondet rationibus pro prima opinione capitulo primo factis.
units.tr: It answers the arguments made for the first opinion in the first chapter.

units.la: Ista opinio respondet ad motiua primæ opinionis. Dicit namq; ad primum, quod non est necesse, quantum ad omnia, quod ita se habeat vnctio regalis ad regem, & vnctio sacerdotalis ad sacerdotem & Episcopalis ad Episcopum. Vnctio enim sacerdotalis & Episcopalis est ex institutione diuina. Vnctio vero regalis, licet fuerit in Veteri Testamento ex institutione legis, in Nouo tamen est ex institutione humana. Et ideo nullam potestatem super temporalia dat vnctio, nisi hoc per voluntatem humanam fuerit voluntarie ordinatum. Quod si per ordinationem humanam non est sic institutum, vt vnctio regalis det potestatem super temporalia, nullam sibi dabit.
units.tr: This opinion replies to the arguments of the first opinion. For it says, to the first point, that it is not necessary, in every respect, that royal anointing stand to the king as priestly anointing stands to the priest, and episcopal anointing to the bishop. For priestly and episcopal anointing is by divine institution. Royal anointing, however, although under the Old Testament it was instituted by the law, under the New Testament is by human institution. And therefore anointing gives no power over temporal matters, unless this has been voluntarily ordained by human will. But if it has not been so instituted by human ordinance that royal anointing confers power over temporal matters, it will give no such power.

units.la: Ad secundum dicitur, quod vnctio regalis non fit frustra, quamuis nullam det super temporalia potestatem, sicut nec illa, quæ fit solummodo ad solennitatem, fit frustra, quamuis nullam conferat potestatem. Potest enim fieri vnctio regalis, vt rex maiori veneratione & reuerentia habeatur, quemadmodum in vnctione & coronatione fiunt conuiuia magna & solennitates magnæ, vt reges in maiori amore habeantur, & vt regalis magnificentia ostendatur, sicut rex Assuerus, vt habetur Hester primo, fecit grande conuiuium, vt ostenderet diuitias gloriæ regni sui ad magnificentiam atque iactantiam potentiæ suæ.
units.tr: To the second point it is said that royal anointing is not done in vain, although it confers no power over temporal matters, just as that anointing which is done only for solemnity is not done in vain, although it confers no power. For royal anointing can be performed so that the king may be held in greater veneration and reverence, just as at the anointing and coronation great feasts and great solemnities are held, so that kings may be held in greater affection, and so that royal magnificence may be displayed; as King Ahasuerus, as we read in Esther chapter one, made a great feast to show the riches of the glory of his kingdom, for the magnificence and boasting of his power.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Respondetur ad motiua cap. secundo pro secunda opinione adducta.
units.tr: Responses to the arguments adduced in chapter two for the second opinion.

units.la: Secundum opinionem primam respondetur ad motiua adducta capitulo secundo pro opinione secunda. Ad primum enim, cum accipitur, quod in multis regnis fiunt plures reges sibi succedentes, quorum aliqui fuerunt uncti, & aliqui non fuerunt uncti. Respondetur diuersimode. Uno modo enim dicitur, quod reges Pagani, qui non fuerunt uncti, nec fuerunt reges veri: quia vt dicit Innoc. 4. Extra Ecclesiam non est Dominum, nec per consequens potestas ordinata & concessa, sed permissa tantummodo. Aliter dicitur, quod reges pagani, qui non fuerunt uncti, fuerunt veri reges. Quia, sicut pagani non tenentur ad constitutiones Ecclesiasticas. Extra de diuortiis. c. gaudemus: sic etiam consuetudinibus regum Christianorum non attantur: tamen Christiani non possunt fieri veri reges, nisi vngantur: quia ex eo quod sunt Christiani, ad consuetudines Christianorum obligantur, siue consuetudines Ecclesiasticas seruare tenentur. Ad secundum quando probatur, quod rex hereditarie succedens nullam habet super temporalia potestatem, ex eo quod a persona Ecclesiastica inungitur, per hoc quod vnctio regalis potest conferri ab alia persona quam ab Ecclesiastica. Dicitur, quod vnctio regalis non potest fieri ab alia persona quam ab Ecclesiastica: quia illa, quæ sunt propria legi diuinæ, non debent fieri nisi a ministro legis diuinæ. Cuiusmodi fuerunt Sacerdotes & Leuitæ in Veteri Testamento, & personæ Ecclesiasticæ in Nouo. Et quando dicitur, quod Helias debuit vngere aliquos in reges, & similiter filius Prophetæ, qui non erat Sacerdos nec Leuita, vnxit Iehu regem super Israel. Respondetur, quod non habetur in Canone Bibliæ Heliam & filium Prophetæ supradictum non fuisse Sacerdotes nec Leuitas.
units.tr: In accordance with the first opinion, I reply to the arguments adduced in chapter two for the second opinion. To the first, which is that in many kingdoms several kings succeed one another, some of whom were anointed and some not, the answer is given in different ways. In one way it is said that the pagan kings who were not anointed were not true kings, because, as Innocent IV says, "Outside the Church there is no lordship" (Extra Ecclesiam non est Dominum), and consequently they had no power ordained and granted, but only permitted. In another way it is said that the pagan kings who were not anointed were true kings. For just as pagans are not bound by ecclesiastical constitutions (Extra, De divortiis, c. Gaudemus), so neither are they bound by the customs of Christian kings. Yet Christians cannot become true kings unless they are anointed, because by the very fact that they are Christians they are bound to the customs of Christians and are obliged to observe ecclesiastical customs. To the second argument, which proves that a king who succeeds by hereditary right has no power over temporal affairs because he is anointed by an ecclesiastical person, on the ground that royal anointing can be conferred by a person other than an ecclesiastical one, the reply is this: royal anointing cannot be performed by any person other than an ecclesiastical one, because those things which belong properly to the divine law ought not to be done except by a minister of the divine law. Such were the priests and Levites in the Old Testament, and ecclesiastical persons in the New. And when it is said that Elijah ought to have anointed some as kings, and that likewise the son of the prophet, who was neither a priest nor a Levite, anointed Jehu king over Israel, the answer is that it is not found in the canon of the Bible that Elijah and the son of the prophet mentioned above were not priests or Levites.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Ostenso cur de secundo articulo partiali parum sit dicendum: de tertio articulo recitat & probat primam opinionem eiusdem.
units.tr: Having shown why little needs to be said about the second partial article, he sets out and proves the first opinion on the third article.

units.la: Secundus articulus circa primam partem quæstionis principalis est, an rex hereditarie succedens aliquam percipiat super temporalia potestatem, ex eo quod consecratur à persona Ecclesiastica: circa quæ fiunt diuersæ opiniones: sicut circa primum, quæ fere eadem & consimilia motiua possunt habere. Propter quod ad tertium articulum, qui est, an rex hereditarie succedens aliquam percipiat super temporalia potestatem ex eo quod à persona Ecclesiastica coronatur. Duxi breuiter hoc transeundum: quia videtur habere difficultatem, propter hoc, quod reges non solum Christiani & fideles coronantur, sed etiam pagani & infideles. Circa quem articulum est opinionum diuersitas: quaram prima est; quod rex succedens hereditarie, accepit aliquam potestatem super temporalia ex hoc quod à persona Ecclesiastica coronatur. Pro quo potest taliter allegari. Quanto maior est dignitas, tanto in adeptione eius debet adhiberi maior solennitas, sine qua haberi non potest. Sed dignitas regalis est maior quam militia: circa autem militiam, quando quis adipiscitur eam, debet aliqua solennitas adhiberi, sine qua nullus potest esse miles. Ergo multo magis quando quis fit rex, aliqua solennitas bitas debet fieri circa eum, sine qua nemo potest esse rex. Illa autem solennitas est coronatio: quia sola coronatio videtur illa esse solennitas, quæ est communis omnibus regibus, quæ exhibetur sibi contra omnes paganos. Ergo ex eo, quod aliquis coronatur, aliquam accipit potestatem super temporalia.
units.tr: The second article, concerning the first part of the principal question, is whether a king who succeeds by hereditary right receives any power over temporal matters from the fact that he is consecrated by an ecclesiastical person. Various opinions are held on this, and as with the first article, they can have almost the same and similar grounds. Therefore, as to the third article, which asks whether a king who succeeds by hereditary right receives any power over temporal matters from the fact that he is crowned by an ecclesiastical person, I have thought it best to pass over it briefly, since it seems to present a difficulty: kings are crowned not only when they are Christian and faithful but also when they are pagan and unbelieving. On this article there is a diversity of opinions. The first is that a king who succeeds by hereditary right receives some power over temporal matters from being crowned by an ecclesiastical person. This may be argued as follows. The greater the dignity, the greater the solemnity that must be used in attaining it, without which it cannot be had. But royal dignity is greater than knighthood, and in the case of knighthood, when someone receives it, some solemnity must be used, without which no one can be a knight. Therefore, much more, when someone becomes king, some solemnity must be performed over him, without which no one can be king. Now that solemnity is coronation, because coronation alone seems to be the solemnity that is common to all kings and is given to them in contrast to all pagans. Therefore, from the fact that someone is crowned, he receives some power over temporal matters.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Prosequitur tertium articulum minus principalem, recitando secundam eius opinionem, circa quam de diversitate succedendi & de iure eius multa disquiruntur.
units.tr: It pursues the third, less principal article, by setting out the second opinion on it, around which much is debated concerning the diversity of succession and its right.

units.la: Alia est opinio, quod rex hereditarie succedens non necessario aliquam potestatem super temporalia habet ex hoc, quod coronatur à persona Ecclesiastica, quasi ex hoc acciperet aliquam potestatem super temporalia. Ad cuius evidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod licet sint diversi modi principatus regales; sicut docet Arist. in politi. Nullus tamen principatus regalis assimulatur in multis principatui naturali. De differentia autem principatuum patet: quia quidam leguntur facti institutione divina: quidam vero humana. De divina autem institutione legitur in libris Regum, unde 1. Reg. 8. habemus, quod Deus per Samuelem instituit principatum regalem: pandendo, quod deberet esse ius regis, qui constituendus erat. De humana patet tam in Veteri Testamento, quam in aliis Historiis atq; gestis, in quibus legitur, quod multi fuerunt per voluntatem hominum facti reges. Propter quod ad sciendum, qualiter & quando & unde rex hereditarie succedens super temporalia habeat potestatem: considerandum est, si est possibile, quomodo principatus regalis ab initio institutus fuerit. Nam si sit memoria de institutione laudabili, & non iniqua: tunc ea debet seruari in succedentibus. Si vero non est memoria, quomodo huiusmodi regnum fuerit ab initio institutum, addenda est consuetudo, de qua est memoria; & illa est seruanda: dummodo, ut prius, non sit iniqua, nec contra leges superiorum: ad quas conseruandas rex huiusmodi tenetur. Si vero ex aliquo euentu ignoraretur haec consuetudo: vel etiam primus rex moreretur, antequam per constitutionem ab initio constituisset legem pro se & suis haeredibus: si modo licito acquisiuisset regnum: vel antequam ordinasset, quem modum rex hereditarie succedens seruare deberet: accipiendum & seruandum esset illud: quod rationabilius & vtilius esset pro bono communi totius regni. Quia sicut benigniora & vtiliora, ita rationabiliora in huiusmodi sunt praeferenda: nisi forte rex hereditarie succedens vellet & posset cedere iuri, quod posset rationabiliter vendicare. Ex isto habetur, quod ad principatum regalem humanitus institutum: cuiusmodi est omnis principatus, qui in politica habetur; qui pendet & procedit ex ordinatione humana; qui ex causa rationabili variari potest: non est necesse, quod rex hereditarie succedens aliquam percipiat super temporalia potestatem, ex hoc quod coronatur siue à persona Ecclesiastica, siue ab alia. Tripliciter enim potest principatus regalis institui. Vno modo per voluntatem & ordinationem populi: quia quilibet populus carens rege proprio, qui non est subditus Imperatori, vel alteri regi, potest de iure gentium constituere sibi regem. Alio modo potest institui principatus regalis per Imperatorem vel regem, qui diuersos populos habet subiectos. Imperator enim potest nouos facere reges in prouinciis, quae non habent reges. Rex etiam habens sub se diversas prouincias sic per ordinationem latiuam populi vel predecessoris sui minime prohiberi potest creare nouos reges. Tertio modo potest institui principatus regalis per acquirentem plenum dominium super regionem, quae conuenienter posset habere regem. Si enim aliquis potens, per emptionem vel bellum iustum vel alio modo acquirit dominium super prouinciam aliquam, si per superiorem suum minime prohibetur, potest sibi nomen & rem regis assumere super eandem prouinciam vel alteri dare. Si primo modo institutur principatus regalis: sicut in voluntate populi est ordinare, an reges fiant per generis successionem, an per electionem: sic in voluntate ipsius populi, si ordinauerit regem hereditarie successurum, est ordinare quod defuncto rege filius successurus statim ante omnem coronationem vel quamcunque solennitatem habeat omnem debitam super temporalia potestatem: vel quod solummodo huiusmodi potestatem accipiat per coronationem vel aliam solennitatem fiendam circa ipsum, cuius coronatio est: quia quilibet in traditione seu donatione rei suae potest imponere pactum vel legem, quam vult: quia in re propria quisq; est moderator & dispositor & arbiter. L. in re mandata. Cod. mandati. Ergo instituentes voluntate principatum regalem, ac sponte se subdentes regi & successoribus eius, possunt ponere legem, quam volunt: dummodo non sit irrationabilis & iniqua, nec contra ius superioris: quia populus subdens seipsum alicui regi & haeredibus suis, potest imponere legem, quod quilibet rex hereditarie successurus statim defuncto praedecessore habeat omnem, quam habiturus est super temporalia potestatem absq; omni solennitate. Poterit etiam ponere legem; vt rex hereditarie successurus non habeat sine coronatione super temporalia potestatem. Et propter eandem rationem dicitur, quod siue aliquis constituat in alio regno regem: siue acquirens super aliam regionem dominium, legitime potest imponere successoribus vnam legem vel aliam: vt sibi rex hereditarie succedens statim habeat omnem, quam habiturus est super temporalia potestatem. Et ita per coronationem vel mediante coronatione potest conferri; vel potest non conferri aliqua potestas super temporalia. Et si per ipsam coronationem nulla conferatur potestas: tunc ipsa non fit.
units.tr: There is another opinion, that a king who succeeds by hereditary right does not necessarily have any power over temporal matters from the fact that he is crowned by an ecclesiastical person, as though he would receive some power over temporal matters from this. To make this clear, it must be noted that although there are different kinds of royal government, as Aristotle teaches in the Politics, no royal government is in many respects like natural government. The difference between governments is clear, because some are said to have been established by divine institution, and others by human. We read in the books of Kings of the divine institution, whence in 1 Sam. 8 we have that God through Samuel established royal government, laying down what the right of the king should be who was to be appointed. The human institution is clear both in the Old Testament and in other histories and deeds, in which we read that many were made kings by the will of men. For this reason, to know how, when and from what source a king who succeeds by hereditary right has power over temporal matters, we must consider, if possible, how the royal government was first instituted. For if there is a record of an institution that was praiseworthy and not unjust, then it ought to be kept by those who succeed. But if there is no record of how such a kingdom was first established, the custom of which there is record must be added, and that is to be kept, provided, as before, it is not unjust nor contrary to the laws of superiors, which such a king is bound to preserve. But if this custom were unknown through some event, or if the first king died before he had by constitution, from the beginning, laid down a law for himself and his heirs (if he had acquired the kingdom lawfully), or before he had ordained what manner a king who succeeds by hereditary right should observe, then whatever is more reasonable and more useful for the common good of the whole kingdom should be accepted and kept. For as the more benign and useful, so the more reasonable things are to be preferred in such matters, unless perhaps the king who succeeds by hereditary right wished and were able to yield a right that he could reasonably claim. From this it follows that for a royal government instituted by human authority, such as every government which is treated in politics, which depends on and proceeds from human ordinance, and which may be varied for a reasonable cause, it is not necessary that a king who succeeds by hereditary right should receive any power over temporal matters from being crowned, whether by an ecclesiastical person or by another. For a royal government can be instituted in three ways. In one way, by the will and ordinance of the people: for any people lacking its own king, who is not subject to the Emperor or to another king, may by the law of nations set up a king for itself. In another way, a royal government can be instituted by an Emperor or king who has various peoples subject to him. For an Emperor can make new kings in provinces that have no kings. A king who has various provinces under him likewise cannot be prevented from creating new kings by the broad ordinance of the people or of his predecessor. In a third way, a royal government can be instituted by one who acquires full dominion over a region that could fittingly have a king. For if some powerful man, by purchase, or by a just war, or in some other way, acquires dominion over some province, and is not forbidden by his superior, he may assume for himself the name and office of king over that province, or give it to another. If a royal government is instituted in the first way, then just as it lies in the will of the people to ordain whether kings are made by succession of birth or by election, so it lies in the will of that same people, if it has ordained a king who will succeed by hereditary right, to ordain that the son who is to succeed, on the death of the king, has at once, before any coronation or any solemnity whatever, the full power over temporal matters which is due to him; or that he receives such power only through the coronation or another solemnity to be performed on him, of which the coronation consists. For anyone, in handing over or giving away his own property, may impose whatever condition or law he wishes, since in his own property each person is the governor, disposer and arbiter. L. in re mandata. Cod. mandati. Therefore those who by their will institute a royal government, and voluntarily submit themselves to the king and his successors, may lay down whatever law they wish, provided it is not unreasonable and unjust, nor contrary to the right of the superior. For a people submitting itself to a king and his heirs may impose the law that every king who succeeds by hereditary right shall, at once on the death of his predecessor, have all the power over temporal matters that he is to have, without any solemnity whatever. It may also lay down the law that a king who succeeds by hereditary right shall not have power over temporal matters without a coronation. And for the same reason it is said that whether someone appoints a king in another kingdom, or acquires dominion over another region, he may lawfully impose on his successors one law or another, so that the king who succeeds by hereditary right has at once all the power over temporal matters that he is to have. And so power over temporal matters can be conferred through the coronation, or by means of a coronation, or it can be conferred without one. And if no power is conferred through the coronation itself, then the coronation is not made.

units.la: Ad. sit, nisi ad solennitatem, vt rex in maiori honore & amore habeatur. Hoc probatur: quia foeminae coronantur, sicut reginae; & tamen per huiusmodi coronationem nullam recipiunt super temporalia potestatem. Ergo hoc est de natura coronationis, q; per ipsam detur aliqua potestas super temporalia. Et per idem probatur, quod per vnctionem & coronationem seu consecrationem nulla datur potestas super temporalia: quia Reginae vnguntur & consecrantur: & tamen per vnctionem & coronationem & consecrationem nullam recipiunt potestatem super temporalia. Imo secundum leges ab omnibus quibuslibet officiis, etiam publicis, sunt remotae. Vnde non possunt esse iudices, nec magistratus gerere, nec adoptare, nec postulare, nec fidem docere, nec praedicationes facere, nec arbitrium: licet per consuetudinem in aliquibus regionibus valeant iudicare.
units.tr: It may be replied that it is for nothing but solemnity, so that the king may be held in greater honour and love. This is proved because women are crowned, as queens are; and yet through such a coronation they receive no power over temporal matters. Therefore it is not of the nature of coronation that power over temporal matters is given through it. And by the same reasoning it is proved that through anointing and coronation or consecration no power over temporal matters is given: for queens are anointed and consecrated, and yet through anointing, coronation and consecration they receive no power over temporal matters. Indeed, by the laws they are excluded from all offices, even public ones. Hence they cannot be judges, nor hold magistracies, nor adopt, nor plead, nor teach the faith, nor preach sermons, nor give arbitration; although by custom in some regions they may hold judgment.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: Chapter VII.

units.la: Huius quinta quaestionis prosequitur secundum articulum principalem quaestionis: cuius primam opinionem recitat & probat rationibus, quibus respondetur cap. 9.
units.tr: Here the fifth question pursues the second principal article of the question. It sets out the first opinion on it and proves that opinion with arguments, to which answer is given in chapter 9.

units.la: CIrca secundum articulum principalem quaestionis propositae: an rex haereditarie succedens ex hoc quod a persona Ecclesiastica inungitur & consecratur & coronatur, gratiam consequatur doni spiritualis: sunt opiniones diversae. Vna tenet, quod rex per vnctionem & consecrationem & coronationem consequitur gratiam doni spiritualis. Pro qua potest taliter allegari. Nulli debetur reuerentia timoris spiritualis vel honoris; nisi propter eminentiam corporalem seu spiritualem, seu secularem. Sed regi consecrato & vncto debetur spiritualis reuerentia, timor & honor; teste Dauid rege, qui, vt habetur 1.Reg.24. noluit mittere manum & occidere regem Saul, quia erat vnctus Domini, dicens: Propitius sit mihi Dominus, ne faciam rem hanc Domino meo Christo, vt mittam manum meam in eum, quia Christus Domini est. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod ideo reuerebatur, quia erat vnctus Christi Domini. Vnde & propter hoc eum habuit in tanta reuerentia, quod percussit cor suum, eo quod abscidisset oram chlamydis Saulis. Propter hoc etiam occiditadolescentem, qui dixit se occidisse Saul, vt habetur 2. Reg.1. dicens: Quare non timuisti mittere manu tuam & occidere Christum Domini? Vocansq; Dauid vnum de pueris suis ait: Accedens irrue in eum: qui percussit illum, & mortuus est. Et ait ad illum Dauid: Sanguis tuus super caput tuum. Os enim tuum locutum est aduersum te dicens: Ego interfeci Christum Domini. Et si dicatur, quod non habuit Dauid Saul in reuerentiam & honorem, nec voluit habere eum in timore, quia per vnctionem factus fuit rex: sed propter regiam dignitatem, talem sibi exhibuit reuerentiam, & ab aliis voluit exhiberi. Hoc excludit ista opinio, dicens, quod Dauid non propter regiam dignitatem, sed propter vnctionem ipsam, inquantum erat diuinitus instituta, censuit Sauli talia exhibenda; secundum quod verba praeallegata sonare videntur. Quod etiam probatur per hoc, quod Dauid aliis regibus, qui erant solummodo reges, non vncti, non exhibuit talia, nec reputauit ab aliis exhibenda, quia nonnullos censuit occidendos. Secundo pro opinione ista potest taliter allegari. Naturalis curatio aegritudinis corporalis, est gratia Dei spiritualis. Quibusdam autem regibus, scilicet Franciae & Angliae, sicut fertur, per vnctionem regalem confertur potestas curandi & sanandi specialiter scrophulas patientes. Ergo per huiusmodi vnctionem rex consequitur gratiam doni spiritualis.
units.tr: Concerning the second principal article of the question proposed, namely whether a king who succeeds by hereditary right obtains a gift of spiritual grace from being anointed, consecrated and crowned by an ecclesiastical person, opinions differ. One holds that a king obtains a gift of spiritual grace through anointing, consecration and coronation. This opinion may be argued as follows. No one is owed reverence of spiritual fear or honour except on account of some eminence, whether bodily, spiritual or secular. But spiritual reverence, fear and honour are owed to a king who has been consecrated and anointed. David the king bears witness to this: as we read in 1 Sam. 24, he refused to lay hands on and kill King Saul because he was the Lord's anointed, saying: "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my lord, the LORD's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed." From these words it appears that David revered Saul because he was the Lord's anointed. For this reason he held him in such great reverence that his heart smote him because he had cut off the skirt of Saul's robe. For the same reason he also put to death the young man who said he had killed Saul, as we read in 2 Sam. 1: "How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?" And David called one of his young men and said: "Go near, and fall upon him." And he smote him so that he died. And David said to him: "Thy blood be upon thy head; for thy mouth hath testified against thee, saying, I have slain the LORD's anointed." And if it is said that David did not show Saul such reverence and honour, nor wished him to be feared, because he had been made king by anointing, but that he showed him this reverence and wished it to be shown by others on account of the royal dignity, this opinion rejects that claim, saying that David judged such reverence due to Saul not on account of the royal dignity but on account of the anointing itself, insofar as it was divinely instituted, as the words quoted above seem to indicate. This is also proved by the fact that David did not show such reverence to other kings who were merely kings and not anointed, nor did he think others ought to show it to them, since he judged some of them deserving of death. Secondly, this opinion may be argued as follows. The natural cure of a bodily sickness is a spiritual grace of God. Now to certain kings, namely those of France and England, as is reported, the power of curing and healing those suffering from scrofula is conferred specially through royal anointing. Therefore through such anointing the king obtains a gift of spiritual grace.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: Chapter VIII.

units.la: Recitat & probat secundam opinionem duabus rationibus, quibus respondetur cap.10.
units.tr: Sets out and proves the second opinion by two arguments, to which a reply is given in chapter 10.

units.la: ALia est opinio, quod per vnctionem, consecrationem & coronationem regalem rex haereditarie succedens non consequitur aliquam gratiam doni spiritualis. Pro qua potest taliter allegari. Per sola Sacramenta diuinitus instituta, non humanitus, consequitur aliquis gratiam doni spiritualis. Vnctio autem, consecratio & coronatio regales, quae circa reges haereditarie succedentes fiunt, non sunt diuinitus, sed humanitus institutae: quia nec sunt constitutae in Veteri Testamento: quia tunc etiam exercens talia officia iudicaret. Nec institutae in Nouo Testamento: sicut patet perlegenti totum Nouum Testamentum. Ergo non consequitur aliquis gratiam doni spiritualis. Secundo pro eadem sic allegatur: Per vnctionem, quae in Veteri Testamento fiebat, non consequebatur rex aliquam gratiam doni spiritualis: ergo multo magis per consecrationem & coronationem, quae per ordinationem humanam, & non de precepto Dei, fiunt circa reges, non consequitur rex haereditarie succedens gratiam doni spiritualis. Consequentia videtur manifesta: quia minus consequitur quis gratiam doni spiritualis per ordinationem humanam, quam per diuinam. Vnctio autem in Veteri Testamento de precepto Dei fiebat etiam circa regem infidelem. Nam vt allegatum est supra cap. 2. Deus praecepit Heliae Prophetae vt vngeret Azael infidelem super Syriam. Ergo in Veteri Testamento per vnctionem non consequebatur rex gratiam doni spiritualis.
units.tr: There is another opinion, that through the anointing, consecration and coronation of a king who succeeds by inheritance, he does not obtain any grace of a spiritual gift. It may be argued for in this way. A person obtains a grace of a spiritual gift only through the sacraments instituted by God, not by men. But the anointing, consecration and coronation of kings, which are performed over kings who succeed by inheritance, were not instituted by God but by men. They were not established in the Old Testament, for then the one exercising such offices would also be judged. Nor were they instituted in the New Testament, as is plain to anyone who reads through the whole New Testament. Therefore no one obtains a grace of a spiritual gift through them. Second, it is argued in the same way: through the anointing that was performed in the Old Testament, the king did not obtain any grace of a spiritual gift. Therefore much more so, through the consecration and coronation, which are performed over kings by human ordinance and not by the command of God, the king who succeeds by inheritance does not obtain a grace of a spiritual gift. The consequence seems plain, because a person obtains a grace of a spiritual gift less through a human ordinance than through a divine one. But in the Old Testament the anointing was performed by God's command even over an unbelieving king. For, as was alleged above in chapter 2, God commanded the prophet Elijah to anoint Hazael, an unbeliever, over Syria. Therefore in the Old Testament a king did not obtain a grace of a spiritual gift through anointing.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Respondetur ad rationes prima opinionis cap. septimo inductas.
units.tr: Response to the arguments of the first opinion, cited in chapter seven.

units.la: SEcundum istam opinionem respondetur ad motiua pro opinione prima. Ad primum enim dicitur, quod in Veteri Testamento debebatur reuerentia spiritualis, timor & honor regi vncto. Responspondetur, quòd huiusmodi reuerentia, timor & honor non debebatur propter gratiam doni spiritualis, quam sibi conferebat vnctio. Nam quamuis ponatur; quod Saul, eo quod fuit vnctus, recepisset huiusmodi gratiam: tamen quia fuit datus in reprobum sensum, & exagitatus à spiritu maligno, perdidisset eandem: & tamen Dauid postea voluit ipsum in reuerentia & honore habere, & haberi debebat. Ergo sibi reuerentia & honor debebantur, non propter gratiam doni spiritualis; sed quia huiusmodi vnctionem recepit de praecepto Dei: & quia per ipsam sibi dignitas regia deferebatur, à qua non erat depositus, quamdiu vixit. Quod enim dixit Samuel 1. Reg. 15. ad Saulem; pro eo quod abiecisti sermonem Domini, abiecit te Dominus ne sis rex: & consimilia verba, non sic debent intelligi, vt Saul fuerit tunc regno priuatus: sed sic, quod tunc fuerit lata sententia, vt eius progenies non regnaret post ipsum. Sic etiam exponitur illud, quod sequitur: Scidit Dominus regnum Israel à te hodie, id est, à progenie tua. Unde etiam quod immediate sequitur. Et tradidit illud proximo tuo meliori te: non debet intelligi, vt tunc, quando Samuel protulit illa verba, fuerit regnum traductum de facto in Dauid, sed quia ordinatum fuit in praedestinatione diuina, quod tradendum esset ipsi Dauid post mortem Saul totaliter auferendum. Quin etiam verba consimiliter procedentia debet sic intelligi, quod filii Saul non erant regnaturi post mortem Saul. Ergo secundum ordinationem Dei regnaturus erat, quamdiu viueret: & propter hoc Dauid eum in reuerentia habuit & honore, quod per ipsum non debuit regno priuari nec occidi. Quidam autem alii reges Dei iudicio interfici debuerunt: & ideo illos non habuit in reuerentia tali & honore. Ad secundum motiuum respondetur, quod si reges Angliae & Franciae habent gratiam curandi de scrophulis, non habent potestatem propter vnctionem regalem: quia multi alii reges, quamuis inunguntur, huiusmodi gratia non decorantur: sed sunt digni huiusmodi gratia propter alia causam, quae nec licet, nec potest ab homine iudicari. Tenet igitur ista opinio, quod quamuis ex bona intentione & proposito, quod rex vnctus, consecratus & coronatus intendit ista sustinere ad honorem Dei & beatitudinem populi sibi subiecti, meretur, si est in charitate: tamen ista non habent spiritualiter conferre donum spirituale: sed propter bonam intentionem prodesse possunt etiam spiritualiter: quemadmodum omnes solennitates, etiā corporales, quae fiunt circa nouos milites, nuptias, inthronizationes praelatorum, etiam secularium potestatum; circa magistros quando magistrantur, & circa quaecunque alia, quae cum solennitate fiunt, prodesse possunt etiam spiritualiter, si absque permixtione vanitatis dissolutionis & nequitiae fiant, cum debitis circumstantiis, ad honorem Dei, & vt talia, quae laudabilia vel vtilia & necessaria sunt censenda, in deuotione & veneratione debita habeantur.
units.tr: According to this opinion, a reply is given to the arguments advanced for the first opinion. To the first, it is said that in the Old Testament a spiritual reverence, fear and honour were owed to the anointed king. I reply that such reverence, fear and honour were not owed on account of the grace of the spiritual gift which anointing conferred. For although it be granted that Saul, because he had been anointed, received such grace, yet, since he was given over to a reprobate mind and tormented by an evil spirit, he lost it; and nevertheless David afterwards wished to have him in reverence and honour, and was bound to be held in them. Therefore reverence and honour were owed to him not on account of the grace of the spiritual gift, but because he had received that anointing by the command of God, and because by it the royal dignity was conferred upon him, from which he was not deposed as long as he lived. For what Samuel said to Saul in 1 Kings 15, "Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, that you should not be king," and similar words, must not be understood to mean that Saul was then stripped of the kingdom, but that a sentence was then pronounced that his posterity should not reign after him. So too is explained what follows: "The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day," that is, from your posterity. Hence also what immediately follows, "And he has given it to your neighbour, who is better than you," must not be understood as if, at the moment Samuel uttered those words, the kingdom was actually transferred to David, but because it was ordained in the divine predestination that it would be handed over to David and wholly taken away from Saul after his death. Indeed, the words that follow in a similar way must be understood to mean that the sons of Saul were not going to reign after Saul's death. Therefore, according to the ordinance of God, Saul was to reign as long as he lived; and for this reason David held him in reverence and honour, because through him he ought not to be deprived of the kingdom nor killed. Other kings, however, had to be put to death by the judgement of God, and so David did not hold them in such reverence and honour. To the second argument it is replied that if the kings of England and France have the gift of healing scrofula, they do not have this power on account of the royal anointing, since many other kings, although they are anointed, are not adorned with this gift; rather they are worthy of it on account of some other cause, which a man may neither lawfully nor able judge. This opinion therefore holds that although, from good intention and purpose, the anointed, consecrated and crowned king intends to undertake these things for the honour of God and the blessedness of the people subject to him, he merits (if he is in charity) reward; yet these things do not confer a spiritual gift by themselves, but can benefit even spiritually on account of the good intention: just as all solemnities, even bodily ones, which are performed for new soldiers, weddings, the enthronement of prelates, even of secular powers, for teachers when they are installed as teachers, and for any other things which are performed with solemnity, can benefit even spiritually, provided they are done without any admixture of vanity, dissolute conduct and wickedness, with the due circumstances, for the honour of God, and are regarded, as things which are to be considered praiseworthy, useful and necessary, as held in due devotion and veneration.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: In hoc capite ad rationes pro secunda opinione factas cap. 7. respondetur.
units.tr: In this chapter the arguments brought forward for the second opinion in chapter 7 are answered.

units.la: Vtrum quomodo secunda opinio respondet ad allegationes pro prima opinione adductas: nunc videndum est, quomodo prima opinio respondeat ad allegationes pro secunda opinione adductas. Ad primam dicitur, quod per sacramentum seu sacramentalia humanitus instituta potest quis consequi gratiam doni spiritualis. Nam aspersio aquae benedictae videtur solummodo humanitus instituta: & tamen per ipsam consequitur quis gratia doni spiritualis. Similiter per exorcismum & catechismum assequitur quis catechizatus fidei indumenta: & per exorcismum expellitur ab exorcizato potestas diaboli. Unde de catechismo dicit Rabbanus & Magister sententiarum recitat li. 4. di. 6. ante baptismum catechizandi debent in homine praeuenire officium: vt fidei catechumenus accipiat indumentum: & sciat cui debitor deinceps fiat de exorcismo. Vt recitat idem Magister, dicit Augustinus: parvuli insufflantur & exorcizantur, vt ab eis pellatur diaboli potestas, ne iam contendat eos auertere, ne baptismum consequantur. Similiter per subdiaconatum & accolitatum, cum sint Ecclesiastici ordines, consequitur quis gratiam doni spiritualis, & tamen non sunt diuinitus, sed solummodo humanitus instituti. Unde in c. 1. dist. 21. sic habetur: Leuitas autem ab Apostolis ordinatos legimus: quorum maximus fuit beatus Stephanus. Subdiaconos & accolitos procedente tempore Ecclesia sibi constituit. Sed contra textum obiicit ibidem Gloss. dicens: Non videtur verum dicere, quod tempore Apostolorum aliqui non fuerunt subdiaconi, vt habetur 35. dist. c. Episcopus, quia illud capitulum est canon Apostolorum. Et respondens dicit: sed dic, quod subdiaconatus tunc fuit, sed non fuit sacer ordo adhuc: extra de aeta. & qualit. c. a multis. Si dicatur, ex illo cap. videtur haberi, quod subdiaconatus non humanitus, sed diuinitus institutus est: Dici potest secundum opinionem istam, quod Deus non immediate, sed mediate sibi subdiaconatum instituit, licet fuerit tempore Apostolorum: quia potuit ab aliis praelatis constitui, Apostolis non contradicentibus, sed approbantibus. Potuit etiam ab ipsis Apostolis institui, non in quantum hoc spiritualiter erat eis inspiratum diuinitus, sicut constitutio Leuitarum non erat eis spiritualiter inspirata, sed in quantum per humanam prouidentiam, qua pollebant, considerabant, quod hoc Ecclesiae conueniens esset. Et ideo constitutio subdiaconorum non est tantae auctoritatis, nec eis est aequalis veneratio exhibenda. Sicut non omnia dicta & scripta Apostolica sunt eiusdem auctoritatis, nec eis eundem timorem & honorem est necesse inferre. Quaedam enim dicta & scripta eorum in canone Bibliae continentur: quaedam vero, ibidem non habentur. Ista autem scripta, quae sunt in canone Bibliae, maioris auctoritatis sunt, quam illa quae alibi, sicut habetur di. 16. per totum. quare dicta & scripta Apostolorum, de quibus solet esse dubitatio & altercatio, an sint & qualiter sint recipienda: sicut patet di. 16. non sunt tantae auctoritatis, sicut alia dicta & scripta ipsorum. Quare humanae prouidentiae, & non immediatae inspirationi divinæ possunt attribui. Ad secundam allegationem adductam pro opinione secunda cap. 8. respondetur, quod per unctionem regalem in Veteri Testamento consequebatur rex gratiam doni spiritualis si non ponebat obicem, maxime infidelitatem vel contemptum, propter quod reges fideles consequebantur huiusmodi gratiam, & non infideles.
units.tr: Now that we have seen how the second opinion answers the allegations brought forward for the first opinion, we must see how the first opinion answers the allegations brought forward for the second. To the first it is said that a person can obtain the grace of the spiritual gift through a sacrament or sacramentals instituted by human authority. For the sprinkling of holy water seems to be instituted only by human authority, and yet through it a person obtains the grace of the spiritual gift. Similarly, through exorcism and catechism a catechumen obtains the garment of faith, and through exorcism the power of the devil is driven out of the one exorcised. Hence Rabanus says about catechism, and the Master of the Sentences records it in book 4, dist. 6: before baptism, catechists ought to anticipate the office in the man, so that the catechumen may receive the garment of faith and know to whom he will thereafter be bound by exorcism. As the same Master records, Augustine says: infants are breathed upon and exorcised, so that the power of the devil may be driven out of them, lest he now strive to turn them away from obtaining baptism. Similarly, through the subdiaconate and the acolyteship, since they are ecclesiastical orders, a person obtains the grace of the spiritual gift, and yet they are not instituted by divine authority but only by human authority. Hence in c. 1, dist. 21, it is stated as follows: We read that the Levites were ordained by the Apostles, the greatest of whom was the blessed Stephen. In the course of time the Church established subdeacons and acolytes for itself. But the Gloss, in the same place, objects against this text, saying: It does not seem true to say that at the time of the Apostles there were no subdeacons, as is found in dist. 35, c. Episcopus, because that chapter is a canon of the Apostles. Answering this, it says: but say that the subdiaconate then existed, but was not yet a holy order: Extra, de aetate et qualitate, c. A multis. If it is objected that this chapter shows the subdiaconate to have been instituted by divine rather than human authority, it can be said, according to this opinion, that God instituted the subdiaconate not immediately but mediately, and that although it existed in the time of the Apostles, it could have been established by other prelates, the Apostles not contradicting but approving. It could also have been instituted by the Apostles themselves, not insofar as this was spiritually inspired in them by God, just as the constitution of the Levites was not spiritually inspired in them, but insofar as through the human foresight they possessed they judged that this would be fitting for the Church. And therefore the constitution of the subdeacons does not have such authority, nor is equal reverence to be shown to it. Just as not all the sayings and writings of the Apostles have the same authority, nor is it necessary to bring the same fear and honour to them all. For some of their sayings and writings are contained in the canon of the Bible; others are not found there. Those writings which are in the canon of the Bible are of greater authority than those which are elsewhere, as is found throughout dist. 16. Wherefore the sayings and writings of the Apostles about which there is usually doubt and dispute, whether and how they are to be received, as is clear in dist. 16, are not of such authority as their other sayings and writings. Hence they can be attributed to human foresight, and not to immediate divine inspiration. To the second allegation brought forward for the second opinion, in chapter 8, it is answered that through royal anointing in the Old Testament the king obtained the grace of the spiritual gift if he did not place an obstacle in the way, above all unbelief or contempt; on account of this, faithful kings obtained such grace, and not unbelieving ones.

units.la: QVÆSTIO SEXTA.
units.tr: QUESTION SIX.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Capitulo primo VI. q. propositæ quæstione recitat & probat circa eam primam opinionem.
units.tr: In the first chapter, on the sixth question proposed, he recites and proves the first opinion concerning it.

units.la: EXto quæritur, Vtrum rex hæreditarie succedens sit coronatori in aliquo subiectus. Circa quam possunt esse opiniones contrariæ. Quarum prima est, quod rex hæreditarie succedens suo coronatori in aliquo est subiectus. Pro qua potest taliter allegari. Rex hæreditarie succedens est in aliquo subiectus ei, ad quem spectat examinatio ipsius regis. Quia examinatio personæ alicuius non spectat ad inferiorem, nec ad parem, sed ad superiorem. Examinatio autem regis seu personæ regiæ hæreditarie succedentis pertinet ad coronatorem, teste Innoc. 3. qui, ut legitur extra de elect. c. venerabilem, ait: Est enim regulariter ac generaliter observatum, ut ad eum examinatio personæ pertineat, ad quem impositio manus. Cum igitur ad ipsum spectet examinatio personæ, sequitur per consequens quod huiusmodi rex suo coronatori aliquo modo est subiectus.
units.tr: Sixthly, it is asked whether a king who succeeds by inheritance is in any way subject to his crowner. On this question there can be opposing opinions. The first is that a king who succeeds by inheritance is in some respect subject to his crowner. This can be argued as follows. A king who succeeds by inheritance is in some respect subject to the one whose duty it is to examine the king himself. For the examination of a person does not belong to an inferior or to an equal, but to a superior. Now the examination of a king, or of a royal person who succeeds by inheritance, belongs to the crowner, as Innocent III attests, who, as we read in extra de elect. c. venerabilem, says: For it is regularly and generally observed that the examination of a person belongs to the one whose office it is to lay on hands. Since, then, the examination of the person belongs to him, it follows that such a king is in some way subject to his crowner.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Recitat & probat secundam opinionem.
units.tr: He recites and proves the second opinion.

units.la: ALia est opinio, quod rex hæreditarie succedens suo coronatori in nullo est subiectus. Pro qua potest taliter allegari. Illi rex hæreditarie succedens in nullo est subiectus, qui nihil iuris aut potestatis tribuit regi hæreditarie succedenti: sed coronator est huiusmodi: ergo &c. Item, rex hæreditarie succedens non tenet regnum suum a coronatore suo. Tum quia non est vasallus suus, cum non præstet sibi iuramentum homagii. Tum quia prædecessores, quibus tales reges hæreditarie succedunt in pluribus regnis, Francorum Anglicorum, & multis aliis, non tenebant regna sua ab aliquo coronatore: ergo nec isti. Aliter enim non essent veri successores primorum; & deterioris conditionis essent reges fideles, quam infideles. Ergo hæreditarie succedentes in nullo sunt subiecti coronatoribus suis. Item, nullus est subiectus illi, a quo subiectionis & fidelitatis recipit iuramentum. Coronator autem regis hæreditarie succedentis, sicut cæteri Episcopi eiusdem regni, iuramentum subiectionis & fidelitatis pro temporalibus, quæ a rege tenent, præstant ipsi regi. Ergo rex coronatori suo in nullo est subiectus. Item, coronari non est magis subiectionis, quam vngi, consecrari & ordinari, quæ non sunt subiectionis probatio: quia Papa, si non est lacerdos vel Episcopus, quando eligitur, postea vngitur & consecratur, coronatur & ordinatur: & tamen consecratori suo in nullo est subiectus. Metropolitanus etiam consecratur a Suffraganeis suis, quibus non est subiectus. Multi etiam clerici habentes literas dimissorias ab illo Episcopo suo, & a non Episcopo suo ordinantur, cui non sunt subiecti. Pueri seu liberi regum, & aliorum tam nobilium quam non nobilium, baptizantur & vnguntur a Presbyteris, quibus non sunt subiecti. Ergo multo magis coronari non est subiectionis probatio. Item, Imperatores multi sunt coronati a suis inferioribus, quibus non erant subiecti: ergo per hoc, quod rex hæreditarie succedens ab aliquo coronatur, non potest probari, quod eidem sit subiectus. Item, minus iuris & potestatis tribuit coronator regi coronato, quam electores electo; & facientes Imperatorem aut regem Imperatori: sed quamvis electus non habeat ius nisi per electores, tamen non est eis subiectus. Non enim Papa, qui nullum ius habet, nisi eligatur canonice, electoribus est subiectus. Similiter Episcopus vel alius prælatus vel potestas seculares sæpe aliquod ius non habent; nisi eligantur rite; & tamen electoribus minime sunt subiecti. Imperator etiam, inquantum populus transtulit suam potestatem, non habet ius Imperiale nisi a populo: & tamen populo non erit subiectus.
