Similiter primi reges diuersorum regnorum qui a populo voluntarie facti fuerunt reges, non habuerunt ius regale nisi a populo. Et tamen postea populis suis non fuerunt subiecti. Ergo multo minus, imo nullatenus rex hæreditarie succedens coronatori suo est subiectus.
units.tr: The other opinion is that a king who succeeds by inheritance is in no way subject to his crowner. This can be argued as follows. A king who succeeds by inheritance is subject to no one who grants no right or power to that king: but the crowner is of this kind; therefore etc. Likewise, a king who succeeds by inheritance does not hold his kingdom from his crowner. This is because he is not his vassal, since he does not render him the oath of homage; and because the predecessors, whose successors such kings are in many kingdoms (of the French, the English, and many others), did not hold their kingdoms from any crowner; therefore neither do these. Otherwise they would not be true successors of the first kings, and kings who are faithful would be in a worse condition than unbelievers. Therefore kings who succeed by inheritance are subject to their crowners in nothing. Likewise, no one is subject to the one from whom he receives the oath of subjection and fealty. But the crowner of a king who succeeds by inheritance, like the other bishops of that kingdom, renders the oath of subjection and fealty to the king himself for the temporal goods that they hold from him. Therefore the king is subject to his crowner in nothing. Likewise, being crowned is no more a proof of subjection than being anointed, consecrated and ordained, which are not proofs of subjection: for the Pope, if he is not a priest or bishop when he is elected, is afterwards anointed and consecrated, crowned and ordained, and yet he is subject to his consecrator in nothing. A metropolitan too is consecrated by his suffragans, to whom he is not subject. Also many clergy who have letters dimissory from their own bishop are ordained by a bishop who is not their own, to whom they are not subject. Children or offspring of kings, and of other nobles as well as non-nobles, are baptized and anointed by presbyters, to whom they are not subject. Therefore, much more, being crowned is no proof of subjection. Likewise, many emperors have been crowned by their inferiors, to whom they were not subject; therefore from the fact that a king who succeeds by inheritance is crowned by someone, it cannot be proved that he is subject to that person. Likewise, a crowner grants less right and power to the crowned king than electors grant to the elected, and those who make an emperor or king make him emperor; yet although the elected has no right except through the electors, he is nevertheless not subject to them. For the Pope, who has no right unless he is canonically elected, is not subject to the electors. Similarly, a bishop or other prelate, or secular authorities, often have no right unless they are duly elected; yet they are in no way subject to their electors. The emperor too, insofar as the people have transferred their power to him, has imperial right only from the people; yet he will not be subject to the people. Likewise, the first kings of various kingdoms, who were made kings voluntarily by the people, had royal right only from the people; yet afterwards they were not subject to their peoples. Therefore, much less, indeed in no way, is a king who succeeds by inheritance subject to his crowner.

units.la: QVÆSTIO SEPTIMA.
units.tr: QUESTION SEVEN.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Primo capitulo VII. q. proponit primo quæstionem. Deinde resolvit eam, tum eius primam opinionem recitat, & finaliter eandem probat.
units.tr: In the first chapter of Question VII he first proposes the question, then resolves it: he sets out its first opinion and finally proves that same opinion.

units.la: SEptima quæstio, vtrum si talis rex coronetur ab aliquo altero Archiepiscopo, quam ab eo qui antiquitus coronare consueuit, vel sibiipsi coronam imponeret, per hoc perderet titulum vel potestatem regalem? Quæstio ista solummodo est, an rex si coronaretur ab alio, quam ab eo, qui consueuit coronare ipsum, ipso facto absque sententia perdat titulum vel potestatem regalē? Circa quam
units.tr: The seventh question is whether, if such a king were crowned by some other archbishop than the one who has customarily crowned him, or if he placed the crown on his own head, he would thereby lose his title or regal power. This question is only whether a king who is crowned by someone other than the one who has customarily crowned him loses his title or regal power by the very fact itself, without a sentence. Concerning which

units.la: {1} vel potestatem regalem: Cica quam sic intellectam non videtur esse tanta difficultas, quanta esset, si quæreretur, an propter hoc deberet vel mereretur per sententiam perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem? Et ideo, vt inuestigandæ veritatis maior detur occasio, inuestigandum est, an propter talem culpâ esset rex talis dignus priuari titulo vel potestate regali. Et est vna opinio, quod sic. Pro qua potest taliter allegari. Qui non per ostium ad aliquam dignitatem ascendit, nihil iuris acquirit. Unde symoniaci symoniacæ dignitates Ecclesiasticas adipiscentes, quia non intrant per ostium, nihil iuris habent. Sed qui coronatur ab alio, quam ab illo, qui antiquitus coronare constituit vel consueuit, non per ostium ad regiam dignitatem ascendit. Ergo nihil iuris habet: & per consequens, quia de facto pro rege se gerit, de facto debet regia dignitate priuari. Item, si quis aliquid de iure Ecclesiæ alienare tentauerit, debet honoris sui amissione multari. 17. q. 4. quicunq; sed talis rex aliquid alienaret de iure Ecclesiæ illius Archiepiscopi, à quo coronari consueuit: quia tolleret illud ius Ecclesiæ. Ergo debet honoris sui amissione multari. Item qui perpetua debet damnari infamia, & incarcerari, & in exilium deportari, perdere debet titulum vel potestatem regalem. Sed rex talis, cum sit sacrilegus iura Ecclesiæ minuendo aut auferendo, debet perpetua infamia condemnari, & incarcerari, & in exilium deportari. 17. q. 4. attendendum. 17. q. 4. quicunq. Ergo debet perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem.
units.tr: {1} regal power. Understood in this way, the question does not seem to be as difficult as it would be if one asked whether, on account of this, he ought, or deserves, to lose his title or regal power by a sentence. Therefore, so that a greater opportunity for investigating the truth may be given, we must inquire whether a king of this kind is deserving of being deprived of his title or regal power on account of such a fault. And there is one opinion that he is. It may be argued for in this way. Whoever does not ascend to a dignity through the door acquires no right. Hence simoniacs who obtain ecclesiastical dignities, since they do not enter through the door, have no right. But whoever is crowned by someone other than the one who was accustomed or appointed of old to crown him does not ascend to the royal dignity through the door. Therefore he has no right, and consequently, since he acts as king in fact, he ought to be deprived of the royal dignity in fact. Likewise, if anyone has attempted to alienate anything from the right of the Church, he ought to be punished by the loss of his honour (17. q. 4. Quicunque). But such a king would alienate something from the right of that archbishop by whom he is customarily crowned, because he would take away that right of the Church. Therefore he ought to be punished by the loss of his honour. Likewise, whoever ought to be condemned to perpetual infamy, imprisoned and sent into exile, ought to lose his title or regal power. But such a king, since he is a sacrilegious man who diminishes or removes the rights of the Church, ought to be condemned to perpetual infamy, imprisoned and sent into exile (17. q. 4. Attendendum; 17. q. 4. Quicunque). Therefore he ought to lose his title or regal power.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Capitulo 2, & vltimo huius septimæ quæstionis, primo ponit secundam opinionem, pro cuius declaratione deinde ponit tres distinctiones. Post quas vltimo loco protredit per quatuor articulos sane diligenter notandos.
units.tr: Chapter 2, the last of this seventh question, first sets out the second opinion and then explains it through three distinctions. After these, it finally proceeds through four articles, which should be noted carefully.

units.la: ALia est opinio, quæ non dicit ita districte talem regem post huiusmodi factum esse dignum priuari titulo vel potestate regali: sed duas ponit distinctiones, iuxta quas respondet ad quæstionem propositam. Prima distinctio est, quod Archiepiscopus aliquis aut coronat aliquem regem de iure, aut de pura gratia. Hæc distinctio probatur per hoc, quod Archiepiscopû aliquem coronare regem quemcunq; non competit sibi ex iure diuino vel iure naturali: quia quantum ad ius diuinum, omnes Episcopi sunt pares & æquales. Ius etiam naturale commune est omnibus. di. 1. ius naturale. Iure autem diuino, quod est in scripturis sacris, inter Episcopum & Archiepiscopum non reperitur distinctio. Et si aliquis Archiepiscopus coronat licite aliquem regem, aut haberet à se, aut ab alio. Non à se: quia qua ratione vnus Archiepiscopus hoc posset facere, eadem & alius, quia non est maior ratio de vno, quam de alio; cum omnes Archiepiscopi (præsertim si non vnus est sub alio) sunt pares. Si autem hoc habet ab aliis: siue hoc habet à rege coronato vel coronando, vel à populo regni, siue ab Imperatore, vel ab alio rege. Sic rex coronatus in hoc sit subiectus: siue à quocunq; homine, vel populo, seu collegio, vniuersitate, vel communitate hoc habere potest de pura gratia, qua ad libitum concedentis valeat reuocari. Si tamen concedens talem habeat potestatem concedendi huiusmodi ius, vt nec ipse nec successor valeat reuocare. Circa hoc enim possunt esse opiniones, præsertim de Imperatore & Papa, quia secundû vnam opinionê nec Imperator nec Papa potest concedere alicui aliquod priuilegium, ius vel libertatem, quod successor reuocare non possit. Secundum aliam opinionem, sicut Imperator, similiter & Papa, potest res temporales dare, quas successor reuocare non potest: sic non potest concedere priuilegia & libertates, quæ & quas successor reuocare non potest. Siue igitur ius vel auctoritas coronandi regem sic possit dari alicui, quod à nullo valeat libere reuocari, siue non possit sic dari: sic tamen potest dari, quod à nullo inferiore donante potest reuocari, & absq; noua donatione vel gratia tempore opportuno potest vti huiusmodi donatione, nisi à concedente prohibeatur tali modo, quod non posset dicere se debere coronare regem, & tunc noua gratia indigeret. Et sic non obstante varietate opinionum de potestate concedendi ius coronandi regem patet prædicta distinctio: quia scilicet Archiepiscopus coronat regem de pura gratia vel de iure. Secunda igitur distinctio, quod rex talis coronatus ab alio tali Episcopo, quam ab eo, qui antiquitus coronare consueuit, vel sibi coronam imponés, potest sic coronari sine culpa vel cum culpa. Hæc distinctio patet ex præcedenti: quia si talis Archiepiscopus ex pura gratia & donatione regum coronatorum maxime cum protestatione conuenienti præmissa: vel etiam ex pura gratia Imperatoris, vel populi, aut perius, qui de coronatione habent ordinare, reges præcedentes coronauit: rex succedens potest sine culpa ab aliis coronari. Item, si non esset amplius talis sedes Archiepiscopalis: vel sedes vacaret, & non posset de Archiepiscopo conuenienti tempore prouideri: vel Archiepiscopus esset absens, vel infirmus, vel alio impedimento legitimo impeditus, quod non posset congruo tempore coronare regem: posset rex absq; culpa ab alio coronari. Non enim in fauorem Archiepiscopi deberet coronatio regis per tempus nimium prolixum differri; maxime si esset talis rex, quod ante coronationem suam non potest potestatem regiam exercere: quia talis fauor esset iniquus & iniustus, & reipublicæ periculosus ac perniciosus. Quare de iure concedi non posset: Sine culpa autem talis rex posset ab aliquo alio coronari. Si vero Archiepiscopus habet ius coronandi ipsum, & non apparet rario, quare potestate coronandi regem etiam illa vice priuari deberet, tunc rex non esset sine culpa, si ab alio coronaretur. Quia non est sine culpa, qui sine culpa & absq; causa priuat aliquem iure suo, quod maxime non est ab ipso priuante.
units.tr: There is another opinion, which does not say so strictly that such a king, after this kind of deed, deserves to be deprived of his royal title or power. It instead offers two distinctions, according to which it answers the question proposed. The first distinction is that a certain archbishop crowns a king either by right or by pure grace. This distinction is proved as follows. That an archbishop should crown any king does not belong to him by divine right or by natural right. As to divine right, all bishops are equal and alike. Natural right is also common to all (Dist. 1, "Ius naturale"). But by divine right, which is found in the holy Scriptures, no distinction is found between a bishop and an archbishop. And if some archbishop lawfully crowns a king, he has this either from himself or from another. Not from himself, because for whatever reason one archbishop could do this, another could too, since there is no greater reason for one than for another, given that all archbishops (especially if none is subordinate to another) are equal. But if he has it from others, whether from the crowned or to-be-crowned king, from the people of the realm, from the Emperor, or from another king, then the crowned king is in this respect subject. And it can be had from any person, people, college, university or community by pure grace, which may be revoked at the pleasure of the one granting it. Yet if the grantor has the power of granting such a right, so that neither he nor his successor can revoke it, then there can be differing opinions about this, especially concerning the Emperor and the Pope. For according to one opinion, neither the Emperor nor the Pope can grant anyone any privilege, right or liberty which a successor cannot revoke. According to another opinion, just as the Emperor, so also the Pope can give temporal goods which a successor cannot revoke; but he cannot grant privileges and liberties which a successor cannot revoke. Therefore, whether the right or authority of crowning a king can be given to someone in such a way that it can be freely revoked by no one, or cannot be given in this way, it can still be given in such a way that it cannot be revoked by any inferior giver, and that without a new donation or grace the recipient can at the proper time use this donation, unless he is prohibited by the grantor in such a way that he could not say that he ought to crown the king, and then he would need a new grace. And so, notwithstanding the variety of opinions about the power of granting the right to crown a king, the aforesaid distinction is evident: namely, that an archbishop crowns a king either by pure grace or by right. The second distinction, therefore, is that a king crowned by another bishop than the one who used to crown him from of old, or who places the crown on him himself, may be so crowned without fault or with fault. This distinction follows from the preceding one. For if such an archbishop crowned the preceding kings by pure grace and by the donation of the crowned kings, especially with a suitable protest made beforehand, or also by the pure grace of the Emperor or of the people, or of those above who have the right to ordain the coronation, then a succeeding king can be crowned by others without fault. Likewise, if there were no longer such an archiepiscopal see, or the see were vacant and a suitable archbishop could not be provided in good time, or the archbishop were absent, or sick, or hindered by some other lawful impediment, so that he could not crown the king in due time, then the king could be crowned by another without fault. For the coronation of a king should not be deferred for too long a time out of favour to an archbishop, especially if the king were such that before his coronation he cannot exercise royal power; for such favour would be unjust and unfair, and dangerous and pernicious to the commonwealth. Wherefore it could not be granted by right. But such a king could be crowned by someone else without fault. If, however, the archbishop has the right of crowning him, and no reason appears why he should be deprived of the power of crowning the king even on that occasion, then the king would not be without fault if he were crowned by another. For he is not without fault who deprives someone of his right without fault and without cause, least of all when it is not his own to take away.

units.la: Tertia distinctio est, quod rex talis, qui non sine culpa coronatur ab alio, quam ab illo Archiepiscopo, piscopo, qui antiquitus coronare consueuit, aut est incorrigibilis aut corrigibilis. Iuxta istas distinctiones possunt formari diuersi articuli, de quibus habet dicere, quid sibi videtur ista secunda opinio.
units.tr: The third distinction is that such a king, who is not crowned without fault by another than that archbishop who used to crown him from of old, is either incorrigible or corrigible. According to these distinctions, various articles can be formed, on which he must say what this second opinion seems to him to be.

units.la: PRIMVS ARTICVLVS est, an si rex coronaretur ab alio Archiepiscopo, quam ab illo, qui antiquitus de pura gratia & non de iure coronare consueuit, per hoc perderet vel dignus esset perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem? Ad quod dicitur, quod non: quia cum denegatur alicui illud, quod habuit de gratia duntaxat, nullum fit ei praeiudicium. Nam sua auctoritate quis potest detinere, quod de iure non praestitit, licet illud diu soluerit. Cod. de agri. & cens. litibus. vt notat Glos. 10. quaest. c. quia cognouimus. Tempus enim non inducit obligationem, extra, de censibus. cap. peruenit. & quod quis dat de gratia, potest reuocare, vt colligitur extra, de postul. praelat. bona memoria, secundo. Nemo enim tenetur facere gratiam nisi velit: quia nemo inuitus cogitur de suo facere beneficium. 10. q. 2. precaria. quia si aliquis Archiepiscopus solummodo de gratia consueuit coronare regem, rex si coronaretur ab alio, non esset dignus perdere aliquid propter hoc. Sed quaereret aliquis, quid si aliquis Archiepiscopus consueuit coronare talem regem, & nesciretur an de gratia, an de iure coronauerit eundem: nunquid rex tenetur coronari ab eodem? hic potest responderi, quod tenetur rex coronari ab illo Archiepiscopo.
units.tr: THE FIRST ARTICLE is: if a king were crowned by an archbishop other than the one who used to crown him from of old by pure grace and not by right, would he thereby lose, or be worthy of losing, his royal title or power? To this it is answered that he would not, because when something is refused to someone which he had only by grace, no prejudice is done to him. For by his own authority a person can retain what he did not render by right, even though he has paid it for a long time (Cod. de agri. & cens. litibus, as the Gloss notes, 10. quaest. c. quia cognouimus). For time does not create an obligation (extra, de censibus, cap. peruenit); and what someone gives by grace he can revoke, as is gathered from extra, de postul. praelat., Bona memoria, secundo. For no one is bound to do a favour unless he wishes to, because no one is compelled against his will to confer a benefit from his own goods (10. q. 2, Precaria). Therefore, if some archbishop has customarily crowned the king only by grace, the king, if he were crowned by another, would not be worthy of losing anything on that account. But someone might ask: what if an archbishop has customarily crowned such a king, and it were not known whether he crowned him by grace or by right; is the king then bound to be crowned by the same man? Here it can be answered that the king is bound to be crowned by that archbishop.

units.la: SECVNDVS ARTICVLVS potest esse. Si Archiepiscopus de iure habeat coronare talem regem, an pro culpa an ex causa possit priuare Archiepiscopum tali iure coronandi? Et circa hoc potest esse opinionum diuersitas. Vna est, quod rex pro culpa & ex causa potest priuare Archiepiscopum huiusmodi iure coronandi. Quia propter culpam, probatur hoc modo. Idem ius videtur esse de reuocatione iuris donati, & de reuocatione rei donatae: quia eadem ratio est de vtroq;. Vbi autem est eadem ratio, ibi debet esse idem ius: vt notatur extra, de constit. translato. sed res donata alicui propter culpam & ingratitudinem reuocari potest. extra, de donat. cap. vlt. igitur similiter ius coronandi propter culpam & ingratitudinem potest reuocari a rege. Alia est opinio, quod ius huiusmodi reuocari non potest a rege. Quia sacrilegus est, qui reuocare vult ea, quae Ecclesiis sunt concessa. 17. q. 4. sunt qui. & cap. sacrilegium. Alia opinio responderet per distinctionem, quod aut Archiepiscopus talis habet ius coronandi regem a regibus praedecessoribus talis regis, aut a populo, vel a superiori, scilicet Imperatore, vel ab alio, cui tales reges sunt subiecti. Si habet ius coronandi a regibus eiusdem regni, rex pro culpa Archiepiscopi, praesertim a pluribus Episcopis vel Archiepiscopis iterata, maxime si ex aliquibus appareat probabiliter, quod successores erunt culpae praedecessorum imitatores, poterit Archiepiscopum huiusmodi iure priuare, ius huiusmodi, quod a praedecessoribus fuit oblatum, liberaliter reuocando: praesertim si praedecessores regis potestatem reuocandi ius coronandi in Papam vel in alium transferendo a se nullatenus abdicauerunt: quia si priuatus potest rem donatam reuocare propter certas culpas: multo magis rex, qui est in suprema dignitate seculari post Imperatorem, poterit res & iura donata reuocare propter certas culpas. Si autem Archiepiscopus non habet ius coronandi a regibus talis regni, sed ab Imperatore vel aliquo, cui tales reges sunt subiecti: rex non potest ius huiusmodi reuocare, sed Imperator vel alius superior rege tali propter culpam potest huiusmodi ius reuocare. Et consimiliter ex causa potest a rege vel Imperatore, vel ab alio superiore rege reuocari ius coronandi. Quia sicut aliquis propter culpam priuatur iure suo: ita etiam absque culpa ex causa priuatur quis iure suo: sicut in legibus & canonibus expresse habetur. Ad allegationem pro secunda opinione praescripta adducam, cum dicitur, quod sacrilegus est qui vult reuocare ea, quae Ecclesiis sunt concessa: variis modis respondetur. Vno modo dicitur, quod ille est sacrilegus, qui sine causa & sine culpa vult reuocare ea, quae ecclesiis sunt concessa. Nam quantumcunq; aliqua sunt concessa, si incipiunt esse nociua, extirpari debent. Si enim quod ratione caret extirpandum est, dist. 67. corepisc. multo magis quod perniciosum est & nociuum seu noxium extirpari oportet. Praeterea si illa, quae concessa sunt Ecclesiis, siue iura siue priuilegia, siue libertates, si incipiunt esse onerosa, extirpari debent. Nam, vt Glossa super allegato cap. corepisc. dicit: A quocunq; auctore aliquid sit institutum, & quantumcunq; diu obtentum: si non subest causa, vel si onerosum est, extirpandum est: extra. de censi. c. peruenit. vnde etiam 63. dist. c. Quia secundam. §. verum. sic legitur: Magna auctoritas ista habenda est in Ecclesia: vt si nonnulli ex maioribus & praedecessoribus nostris fecerunt aliqua quae illo tempore potuerunt esse sine culpa, & postea vertuntur in errorem & superstitionem, sine tarditate aliqua & cum magna auctoritate a posteris destruantur. Vnde dicit Glossa super verbo destruantur. Argu. successores debere mutare instituta antecessorum etiam bona, si viderint ea esse perniciosa. Ex quo arguitur consimiliter. Si illa, quae sunt in Ecclesiis, incipiunt esse perniciosa, reuocari debent & possunt. Item priuilegium meretur amittere, qui permissa sibi abutitur potestate. 11. quaest. 3. cap. priuilegium. extra, de regularibus. cap. licet. Si igitur Ecclesiae abuntuntur priuilegiis eis concessis, ipsę merentur ea amittere. Item, persona Ecclesiastica propter culpam debet perdere clericale priuilegium. Ergo consimiliter Ecclesia propter culpam potest perdere priuilegium: quia idem ius est in toto & in parte. Item, Ecclesia propter fauorem alterius Ecclesiae potest perdere priuilegium & ius suum, 22. distinct. renouantes. Ergo multo plus propter culpam potest perdere priuilegium suum: cum multo magis sit quis priuandus iure suo propter culpam propriam, quam propter honorem aut fauorem alterius. Sicut enim locupletari non debet aliquis cum alterius iniuria vel iactura. extra, de Regul. Iuris. locupletari. lib. 6. Et si non potest alteri subueniri nisi alter laedatur: commodius est neutrum iuuari, quam grauari alterum. decimo quarto. quaest. sexto. denique. & nulli est cum alterius iniuria consulendum.22.q.2.c.1. Similiter cum alterius dehonoratione non est alius honorandus: quia licet non obstante, quod nec Ecclesia nec persona propter fauorem alterius debeat regulariter priuari iuribus & priuilegiis: tamen casualiter priuari debet: multo fortius tamen regulariter puniendæ sunt culpæ & non solummodo casualiter. Ergo Ecclesiæ propter culpam pœ sunt licite atq; debent in casu priuari priuilegiis, iuribus & libertatibus sibi concessis. Item, illis sunt priuilegia detrahenda, qui præceptis superiorum obuiare non timent, extra, de priuilegiis. c. dilecti: vbi dicit Glos. super verbo decurrabimus: Non sunt ei iura sua seruanda, qui ius alienum violare non metuit. Ecclesiæ ergo propter culpam inobedientiæ & irreuerentiæ priuari possunt priuilegiis sibi concessis. Item, communitas secularis propter culpam priuari potest iuste priuilegio & honore sibi concessis. Ciuitas enim propter occisionem Episcoporum suorum priuatur dignitate Episcopali. 95.q.2. ita nos. in quo casu etiam ipsa Ecclesia priuata fuit honore Episcopali non propter delictum Ecclesiæ cathedralis, sed propter delictum ciuitatis. Ergo multo fortius Ecclesia propter delictum proprium potest priuari sibi concessis. Item frustra petit debitum, qui quod debet non impendit: vt allegando dicit Glos. dist. 95. esto. Ad quod probandum diuersos canones allegat. Sic Ecclesiæ laicis, si non impendunt quod debent frustra petunt ab eis iura sua seruari. Item, laici, præsertim reges, Imperatores, principes ac personæ aliæ eminentes, qui Ecclesias honoribus, priuilegiis & libertatibus illustrarunt, ex sola donatione non magis quantum ad ius Ecclesiis sunt subiecti, quam subditi dominis suis: quia Ecclesiæ non dominantur huiusmodi laicis, iuxta illud Petri: non dominantes in clero. Et per consequens minus in populo: sed vt dicit Glos. 22. quæst. vltima. super c. de forma fidelitatis. in fine: Eadem fide tenetur quis subditus suo sicut subditus Domino. vt 95. distinct. esto subiectus. extra, de iureiurando. perunuit. & 22. quæst. 6. nihil minus. Et si non fecerit, priuatur illo dominio, quod habet in vasallo: & transit feudum ad superiorem: vt in lib. de feudis. qualiter feudum amittatur. Ergo multo magis Ecclesiæ, si non fuerint fideles laicis, quæ eis honores, iura, libertates & priuilegia concesserunt, possunt iure priuari & iuste sibi concessis. Item, hosti non seruanti fidem, non est fides seruanda. Cum etiam fide seruata contra idem versetur. extra, de iureiurando perunuit: si igitur Ecclesiæ non seruando fidem laicis incipiant hostiliter persequi: eis non est fides seruanda: & per consequens priuari possunt illis, quæ sunt concessa sibi. Sed aliquis vno modo istis omnibus respondebit dicens, quod quamuis persona Ecclesiastica potuit committere culpam, tamen Ecclesiæ non possunt aliquam culpam incurrere: quia scilicet Ecclesia non potest culpa aliqua inquinari, cum sit sine macula, malitia & sine dolo. Sed hæc ratio impugnatur, quia quauis Ecclesia vniuersalis, quæ est congregatio generalis cunctorum fidelium, non sic possit errare contra fidem, nec culpa maculari mortali, vt nullus omnino sit in vera fide & charitate: tamen Ecclesiæ particulares possunt taliter contra fidem & bonos mores errare, ita etiam vt sint à catholicis defrenda, teste beato Ambrosio, qui, vt habetur 24.q.1.c. quæ dignior ait: si qua Ecclesia est, quæ fidem respuat, vel Apostolicæ prædicationis fundamenta non possidet, ne quam Iubem perfidia possit aspergere, deserenda est. Ecclesiæ igitur propter culpam possunt priuari eis, quæ concessa sunt eis. Aliter dicitur, quod licet nulla Ecclesia debeat priuari eis, quæ concessa sunt sibi, tamen quælibet persona de Ecclesia propter culpam debet priuari his, quæ Ecclesiæ sunt concessa. Et idem quilibet Archiepiscopus propter culpam potest priuari iuste potestate coronandi regem, licet Ecclesia huius potestate priuari non debet.
units.tr: The second article may be this: if an Archbishop has by right the power to crown such a king, may the king, for fault or for cause, deprive the Archbishop of this right of crowning? On this there may be a diversity of opinions. One is that the king may, for fault and for cause, deprive an Archbishop of this right of crowning. It is proved as follows, on the ground of fault. The same law seems to hold for the revocation of a granted right as for the revocation of a granted thing, since the reason is the same in both. Where the reason is the same, the law must also be the same, as is noted in extra, de constit. translato. But a thing granted to someone may be revoked for fault and ingratitude, extra, de donat. cap. vlt. Therefore likewise the right of crowning may be revoked by the king for fault and ingratitude. Another opinion holds that a right of this kind cannot be revoked by the king, because he is a sacrilegious person who wishes to revoke what has been granted to the Churches, 17. q. 4. sunt qui. & cap. sacrilegium. A third opinion answers by distinction: either the Archbishop has this right of crowning from the kings predecessors of this king, or from the people, or from a superior, namely the Emperor, or from another to whom such kings are subject. If he has the right of crowning from the kings of the same kingdom, then the king, on account of the Archbishop's fault, especially if it has been repeated by several Bishops or Archbishops, and most of all if it appears probable from some evidence that the successors will imitate the faults of their predecessors, may deprive the Archbishop of this right by freely revoking the right which was conferred by the predecessors. This holds especially if the predecessors of the king did not at all renounce their power of revoking the right of crowning by transferring it to the Pope or to someone else. For if a private person can revoke a granted thing for certain faults, much more can the king, who holds the highest secular dignity after the Emperor, revoke granted things and rights for certain faults. But if the Archbishop does not have the right of crowning from the kings of this kingdom, but from the Emperor or from someone to whom such kings are subject, then the king cannot revoke this right; rather the Emperor or another superior to the king can revoke it for such a fault. Likewise the right of crowning may be revoked for cause by the king, or by the Emperor, or by another superior to the king. For just as someone is deprived of his right for fault, so also without fault someone may be deprived of his right for cause, as is expressly stated in the laws and canons. As to the allegation brought against the second opinion, namely that he is sacrilegious who wishes to revoke what has been granted to the Churches, it is answered in various ways. In one way it is said that he is sacrilegious who wishes to revoke, without cause and without fault, what has been granted to the churches. For however much something has been granted, if it begins to be harmful, it ought to be rooted out. For if what lacks reason ought to be rooted out, dist. 67. corepisc. much more ought what is pernicious and hurtful or noxious to be rooted out. Moreover, if what has been granted to the Churches, whether rights or privileges or liberties, begins to be burdensome, it ought to be rooted out. For, as the Gloss on the cited corepisc. says: Whatever has been instituted by any author, and however long it has been held, if no cause underlies it, or if it is burdensome, must be rooted out, extra, de censi. c. peruenit. Hence also in 63. dist. c. Quia secundam. §. verum. it is read thus: This authority is to be held in the Church: that if some of our ancestors and predecessors did certain things which at that time could have been without fault, and afterwards they turn into error and superstition, they are to be destroyed by their successors without any delay and with great authority. Hence the Gloss on the word destruantur says: successors ought to change the institutions of their predecessors, even good ones, if they see them to be pernicious. From this it is argued in the same way: if those things which are in the Churches begin to be pernicious, they ought to be and can be revoked. Likewise, one who abuses the power granted to him deserves to lose the privilege, 11. quaest. 3. cap. priuilegium. extra, de regularibus. cap. licet. If therefore the Churches abuse the privileges granted to them, they deserve to lose them. Likewise, an ecclesiastical person ought to lose a clerical privilege on account of fault. Therefore likewise the Church may lose a privilege on account of fault, because the same law holds for the whole as for a part. Likewise, the Church may lose a privilege and its right on account of the favour of another Church, 22. distinct. renouantes. Therefore much more may it lose its privilege on account of its own fault, since a person is much more to be deprived of his right on account of his own fault than on account of the honour or favour of another. For just as no one ought to be enriched at another's injury or loss, extra, de Regul. Iuris. locupletari. lib. 6. and if one cannot be helped unless another is harmed, it is better that neither be helped than that the other be burdened, decimo quarto. quaest. sexto. denique. and no one is to be provided for at the injury of another, 22. q. 2. c. 1. Similarly, no one is to be honoured at the dishonour of another. For although, as a general rule, neither a Church nor a person ought to be deprived of rights and privileges on account of another's favour, nevertheless in some case they ought to be deprived; much more, then, must faults be punished as a general rule, and not only in particular cases. Therefore the Churches may lawfully, and ought in some case, to be deprived, on account of their fault, of the privileges, rights and liberties granted to them. Likewise, privileges are to be taken away from those who do not fear to resist the commands of their superiors, extra, de priuilegiis. c. dilecti, where the Gloss on the word decurrabimus says: Those are not to have their rights preserved who do not fear to violate the right of another. Therefore the Churches may be deprived, on account of the fault of disobedience and irreverence, of the privileges granted to them. Likewise, a secular community may justly be deprived of a privilege and honour granted to it on account of its fault. For a city is deprived of episcopal dignity on account of the killing of its Bishops, 95. q. 2. ita nos. In that case the Church itself was also deprived of episcopal honour, not on account of the fault of the cathedral Church but on account of the fault of the city. Therefore much more may a Church be deprived of what has been granted to it on account of its own fault. Likewise, one who does not render what he owes asks in vain for what is due to him, as the Gloss says when arguing by allegation, dist. 95. esto, and it cites various canons to prove this. So too, if the laity do not render what they owe, the Churches ask in vain that their rights be preserved by them. Likewise, laymen, especially kings, emperors, princes and other eminent persons who have adorned the Churches with honours, privileges and liberties, are not by the mere gift made subject to the Churches in respect of right any more than subjects are to their lords; for the Churches do not rule over such laymen, according to the saying of Peter: not lording it over the clergy. And consequently still less over the people. But, as the Gloss says on 22. quaest. ultima, on the chapter concerning the form of fealty, at the end: One is bound to his subject by the same fidelity as a subject is to his lord, as in 95. distinct. esto subiectus. extra, de iureiurando. perunuit. and 22. quaest. 6. nihil minus. And if he does not do so, he is deprived of the lordship which he has over the vassal, and the fief passes to the superior, as in the book on fiefs concerning how a fief is lost. Therefore much more the Churches, if they are not faithful to the laymen who granted them honours, rights, liberties and privileges, can rightly be deprived of what has been granted to them. Likewise, faith is not to be kept with an enemy who does not keep faith; nor is faith to be kept when keeping it works against the same. extra, de iureiurando perunuit. If therefore the Churches, by not keeping faith with the laity, begin to persecute them as enemies, faith is not to be kept with them, and consequently they may be deprived of what has been granted to them. But someone will answer all these things in one way, saying that although an ecclesiastical person may have committed a fault, nevertheless the Churches cannot incur any fault, because the Church cannot be stained by any fault, since it is without spot, malice and deceit. But this argument is attacked, because although the universal Church, which is the general congregation of all the faithful, cannot so err against the faith, nor be stained by mortal fault, that no one at all is in true faith and charity, nevertheless particular churches can err against the faith and good morals in such a way that they must be shunned by Catholics, as the blessed Ambrose says, cited in 24. q. 1. c. quae dignior: If there is any Church which rejects the faith, or does not possess the foundations of apostolic preaching, it must be abandoned lest any stain of perfidy spread to us. Therefore Churches may on account of fault be deprived of what has been granted to them. Otherwise it is said that although no Church ought to be deprived of what has been granted to it, nevertheless any person of the Church ought on account of fault to be deprived of those things which have been granted to the Churches. And so any Archbishop may justly be deprived, on account of fault, of the power of crowning the king, although the Church ought not to be deprived of this power.

units.la: TERTIVS ARTICVLVS potest esse, An rex talis, qui non absque culpa sua coronaretur ab altero Archiepiscopo, quam ab eo, qui antiquitus coronare consueuit: sibi ipsi coronam imponens, per hoc perderet vel dignus esset perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem: quamuis obstinatus & etiam incorrigibilis in culpa nullatenus appareret? Et tenet prædicta opinio, quod non: quia talis culpa regis esset sacrilegium, non quidem ratione personæ, quale sacrilegium committit quis, cum verberat aut occidit clericum vel religiosam personam, sed solummodo sacrilegium ratione iuris publici: quia si talis rex in hoc facto esset transgressor iuris publici, & consistit in sacris & sacerdotibus, di.1.ius publicum, quia videlicet auferret Archiepiscopo, qui consueuit coronare regem, ius suum. Pœna autem huius sacrilegii neque secundum leges, neque secundum canones est depositio à regno. Igitur rex talis, si est corrigibilis, non est dignus propter huiusmodi culpam perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem, sicut ace propter aliquas species vel modos sacrilegii est dignus maxima & grauissima pœna. QVARTVS ARTICVLVS potest esse: An rex propter huiusmodi culpam si est incorrigibilis, sit dignus huiusmodi pœna. Et est vna assertio, quod sic, pro qua potest taliter allegari: vt dicitur Glos. distinct. 40. super capitulo, si Papa: Si notorium est crimen eius quodcunque & inde scandalizetur Ecclesia, & incorrigibilis sit, inde accusari potest. Et per consequens, si potest accusari sic vt criminalis accusatio, quæ ad diminutionem capitulo 1. ad degradationem intenditur: nisi legitima præcedat inscriptio, nullatenus dimittatur. extra, de accusatoribus qualiter & quando. multo magis quilibet alius siue regalis siue quacunque alia dignitate præfulgeat, pro quocunque crimine, si est incorrigibilis, est dignus à dignitate deponi. Ex quo concluditur, quod rex talis pro huiusmodi sacrilegio, si est incorrigibilis, dignus est perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem. Ergo sequitur, quod quilibet siue laicus siue clericus & cuiuscunq; fuerit status, etiam Papa, propter hæresim est dignitate sua deponendus. De aliis enim à Papa dicit Glossa, extra, de hæreticis, super c. excommunicamus: Papa propter hæresim potest deponere omnes tam laicos quam clericos à dignitatibus suis. Sed rex talis propter huiusmodi sacrilegium est ex communicatus, vel excommunicari potest, si est incorrigibilis: & si in excommunicatione extra annum persistat postquam fuerit { } rit inter hæreticos computandus, præsertim si fuerit excommunicatus à Papa, & sit incorrigibilis, inter schismaticos erit cōputandus. Schismaticus autē in schismate perseuerans censetur hæreticus, vt ex Glossa colligitur 24.q 1. super capitulo primo in fine, vbi dicit: eadem dic de schismatico, maxime cum schisma non possit esse sine haresi, nisi forte in summo pontifice: vt si duo crearentur, & vterq; crederet Ecclesiam apud se esse. Hæc videtur esse beati Hieron. intentio; qui, vt habetur eadem causa. quæst. 3. c. inter schismaticos ait: Nullum schisma est, nisi sibi aliquā haresim confingat vt recte ab Ecclesia recessisse videatur. Vbi dicit Glossa: Potest dici, quod hæc sit differentia inter haresim & schisma, quæ est inter dispositionem & habitum. Primo enim dicitur schisma: sed cum post tempus pertinaciter adhaeserit suæ sectæ, dicitur hæresis. dicit etiam Glossa: assignans rationem, quare, vt dictum est, pro quocunq; crimine notorio, si inde scandalizetur Ecclesia, & sit incorrigibilis, potest accusari: nam contumacia dicitur hæresis. Ex quibus colligitur, quod talis rex per huiusmodi sacrilegium, si fuerit incorrigibilis, & in excommunicatione, præsertim lata à Papa perstiterit, est inter hæreticos computandus. Quare dignus est perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem.
units.tr: The third article may be raised: whether a king who could not be crowned by another archbishop without his own fault, rather than by the one who has customarily crowned kings, would by this act lose, or deserve to lose, his royal title or power, even though he shows no obstinacy and no incorrigibility in his fault. The aforementioned opinion holds that he would not. For such a fault on the king's part would be sacrilege, not by reason of the person, as when someone strikes or kills a cleric or a religious person, but only by reason of public law. For if such a king in this act were a transgressor of public law, which concerns sacred things and priests (dist. 1, ius publicum), he would be taking away from the archbishop who customarily crowns the king his right. But the penalty for this sacrilege, according to neither the laws nor the canons, is deposition from the kingdom. Therefore such a king, if he can be corrected, does not deserve to lose his royal title or power on account of this kind of fault, just as, for some kinds or modes of sacrilege, he deserves the greatest and most severe penalty. The fourth article may be raised: whether a king who is incorrigible in such a fault deserves such a penalty. There is one assertion that he does, and it may be argued thus, as the Gloss says on dist. 40, on the chapter si Papa: if a crime of his, of whatever kind, is notorious, and the Church is scandalized by it, and he is incorrigible, he can be accused of it. And consequently, if he can be accused in the manner of a criminal accusation, which aims at diminution (chapter 1) or degradation, it must in no way be dropped unless a lawful written charge precedes it (extra, de accusatoribus, qualiter et quando). Much more, then, any other person, whether he shines in royal or in any other dignity, if he is incorrigible in whatever crime, deserves to be deposed from his dignity. From this it follows that such a king, for such sacrilege, if he is incorrigible, deserves to lose his royal title or power. Therefore it follows that anyone, whether layman or cleric and of whatever rank, even the Pope, is to be deposed from his dignity on account of heresy. For the Gloss says of others besides the Pope (extra, de haereticis, on the chapter excommunicamus): the Pope may depose from their dignities on account of heresy all, both laymen and clerics. But such a king, on account of this sacrilege, is excommunicated, or can be excommunicated, if he is incorrigible; and if he persists in excommunication for more than a year after it has been pronounced, he is to be counted among the heretics, especially if he has been excommunicated by the Pope and remains incorrigible, he will be counted among the schismatics. And a schismatic who perseveres in schism is considered a heretic, as is gathered from the Gloss on 24 q. 1, on the first chapter, at the end, where it says: the same is to be said of a schismatic, especially since schism cannot exist without heresy, except perhaps in the case of the supreme pontiff, as when two are created and each believes that the Church is with him. This seems to be the intention of blessed Jerome, who, as is found in the same cause, question 3, chapter inter schismaticos, says: there is no schism unless one invents for himself some heresy so that he may seem to have rightly withdrawn from the Church. On this the Gloss says: it can be said that the difference between heresy and schism is the difference between disposition and habit. For first it is called schism, but when after a time one has obstinately clung to his sect, it is called heresy. The Gloss also says, giving the reason why, as has been said, for any notorious crime, if the Church is scandalized by it and he is incorrigible, he can be accused: for contumacy is called heresy. From these things it is gathered that such a king, through such sacrilege, if he is incorrigible and has persisted in excommunication, especially one pronounced by the Pope, is to be counted among the heretics. Therefore he deserves to lose his royal title or power.

units.la: Alia est opinio, quod rex pro tali sacrilegio, quamuis sit incorrigibilis, non potest perdere titulum vel potestatem regalem. Pro qua potest taliter allegari. Talis rex incorrigibilis absq; grauissimo scandalo eius deponi non potest à dignitate sua: sed pro scandalo euitando cessat rigor iudicii, cum etiam propter scandalum sit desistendum de iure. extra, de prescriptio. nihil. Cum propter hoc etiā scandalum fugiendus cibus, qui magis necessarius est, quam vt talis rex incorrigibilis perdat titulum vel potestatem regalem sit dimittendus, dicente Apostolo 1. Cor. 7. Si esca scandalizat fratrem: non manducabo carnem in æternum, ne fratrem meum scandalizem. Ergo quamuis talis rex esset dignus titulum vel potestatem regalem perdere: ipsum tamen perdere non debet. Sed forte hic aliquis respondebit dicens, quod quando scandalum nascitur non ex ignorantia vel infirmitate, quod est scandalum pusillorum: sed ex malitia, quod est scandalum perfectorum: non sunt temporalia propter scandalum dimittenda. Nam propter scandalum, quod ex malitia oritur; non est rigor iustitiæ dimittendus: quia hoc noceret bono communi: quia daret malis audaciam delinquendi. Nam facilitas veniæ incentiuum tribuit delinquendi. extra, de vita & honestate clericorum. c. vt clericorum. Sed si talis rex esset incorrigibilis, scandalum aliquod ex malitia oriretur: quare tunc non esset talis punitio omittenda. Sed ista responsio impugnatur: quia, vt habetur dist.50. vt constitueretur; videtur quod vbi per graues dissensionum scissuras non huius aut illius hominis periculum, sed populorum strages iacet, detrahendum est aliquid seueritati, vt maioribus malis sanandis charitas sincere subueniat. Siue ergo scandalum ex ignorantia & infirmitate, siue ex malitia oriatur, seueritas punitionis debet dimitti. Si ergo populorum strages iacet, quia magis debemus diligere vitam populorum, quam vnius mali punitionem, vel pauca vel parua temporalia bona. Illud autem, quod minus diligendum est, est dimittendum propter illud quod magis est diligendum, quando simul haberi non possunt. Si, inquam, ex depositione talis regis à titulo vel potestate regali emineret populorum strages, propter scandalum, quantumcunq; ex malicia oriretur, talis seueritas dimittenda est.
units.tr: There is another opinion, that a king, for such sacrilege, although he is incorrigible, cannot lose his royal title or power. It may be argued thus. An incorrigible king cannot be deposed from his dignity without very grave scandal on his account; but for the avoiding of scandal the rigour of judgment ceases, since even on account of scandal one must refrain from what is lawful (extra, de praescriptionibus, nihil). Since for this same reason, to avoid scandal, food which is more necessary must be given up, so that an incorrigible king should not lose his royal title or power, the Apostle saying in 1 Cor. 8: If food gives scandal to my brother, I will eat no flesh for ever, lest I scandalize my brother. Therefore, although such a king would deserve to lose his royal title or power, nevertheless he must not be deprived of it. But perhaps someone here will answer, saying that when scandal arises not from ignorance or weakness, which is the scandal of the little ones, but from malice, which is the scandal of the perfect, temporal things are not to be given up on account of scandal. For the rigour of justice is not to be set aside on account of scandal arising from malice, because this would harm the common good, since it would give the wicked boldness to offend. For the ease of pardon offers an incentive to offend (extra, de vita et honestate clericorum, chapter ut clericorum). But if such a king were incorrigible, some scandal would arise from malice; therefore such punishment would not then be to be omitted. But this answer is opposed, because, as is found in dist. 50, ut constitueretur, it appears that where, through the grave rendings of dissensions, not the danger of this or that man, but the slaughter of peoples lies, something must be taken away from severity, so that sincere charity may come to the aid of greater evils to be healed. Therefore whether scandal arises from ignorance and weakness or from malice, the severity of punishment ought to be set aside. If, then, the slaughter of peoples lies at stake, we ought to love the lives of peoples more than the punishment of one wicked man, or a few or small temporal goods. But that which is less to be loved is to be given up for the sake of that which is more to be loved, when both cannot be had together. If, I say, from the deposition of such a king from his royal title or power there would arise a slaughter of peoples on account of scandal, however much it might arise from malice, such severity is to be set aside.

units.la: QVÆSTIO OCTAVA.
units.tr: QUESTION EIGHT.

units.la: CAP. I,
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Caput primum Octaua & vltima quæstionis, proponit ipsam quæstionem; circa quam recitat & probat primam opinionem, & duos eius modos ponendi. Quæ etiam probat: ad quorum probationes respondetur ex ordine.
units.tr: The first chapter of the eighth and last question sets out the question itself. It recites and proves the first opinion, and its two ways of stating it, and also gives the proofs for it. The replies to those proofs follow in order.

units.la: Octauo & vltimo quæritur, Vtrum canonica electio principum electorum, seu eligentium, ex natura tantum det electo in regem Romanorum, quantum dat legitima successio regi hereditarie succedenti. Quantum ad istam quæstionem, quæ multum videtur esse vicina quæstioni quartæ est opinionum diuersitas. Vna est tenens partem negatiuam, circa quam sunt diuersi modi ponendi. Vnus est, quod canonica electio principum electorum illius, non dat electo in regem Romanorum tantum, quantum dat successio regi hereditarie succedenti: quia huiusmodi electio nullam dat electo administrationem, nisi per Papale confirmationem vel comprobationem seu nominationem vel coronationem. Ad fulcimentum istius modi deduci possunt multæ allegationes, quæ hic solummodo sunt tangendæ, pro eo quod qualiter confirmari & declarari potest, studiose ex præcedentibus quæstionib⁹ apparere poterit. Quod ergo non electio, sed confirmatio vel approbatio nominatio aut coronatio à Papa adhibenda det administrationem electo in regem Romanorum: Patet primo ex hoc; quod electus huiusmodi est vasallus Papæ, & ei iuramentū fidelitatis & homagiū præstare tenetur. Item per hoc, quod Imperium est à Papa. Similiter per hoc, quod electus in regem Romanorum nihil petere tenetur à Papa. Item per hoc, quod Papa potest deponere Imperatorē & per consequens constituere: quia licet aliquis potest solus aliquando dare honorem, qui eū non posset solus auferre. extra, de translatione. inter corporalia: tamen qui potest auferre honorem, potest dare eundem. Item per hoc, quod Papa habet plenitudinem potestatis tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus. Item per hoc, quod in vniuerso mundo debet esse vnum caput, à quo omnis iurisdictio & potestas dependeat: quod non est aliud, nisi Papa, cum ipse à solo Deo habeat potestatem. Item per hoc, quod Papa habet vtrumq; gladium, scil, (spiritualem & temporalem. Alius modus ponendi istam negationem dicit sic: Quod imo canonica electio principum electorum non dat tantum electo in regem Romanorum, quantum dat legitima successio regi hæreditarie succedenti : quia potestas eligendi data est electoribus à supremo pontifice. Extra. de elect. venerabilem. Et ideo sicut inspicienda sunt priuilegia ad hoc, vt sciatur, quam potestatem habeant, siue quid contineatur in eis. Extr. de priuilegiis cap. porro &c. recepimus: ita vt sciatur, quam potestatem eligendi habeant electores, & quam potestatem ex eorum electione consequantur, inspiciendæ essent literæ, quibus data est electoribus potestas eligendi. Quod si non reperiuntur, ipsius summi pontificis est declarare, quam potestatem ex eorum electione electus obtinet: quia eius est interpretari legem, cuius est condere, extr. de priui. si Papa in 6. Papa vero habet alios iudicare. Extr. de iudiciis, cum venissent. Cum ergo Papa declararet, quod electus in regem Romanorum debeat examinari per Papam: & per consequens declarat, quod ex sola electione non est aliquis rex Romanorum aut Imperator: sequitur quod eligens non dat electo in regem Romanorum plenam administrationem, nec regalem titulum, vel potestatem Imperialem; quæ omnia tamen dat legitima successio, regi hæreditarie succedenti. Pro isto modo ponendi istam negatiuam, quæ fundatur principaliter in hoc, quod electio principum dat tantam potestatem electo, quantam Papa vult per eam sibi dari, potest multipliciter allegari. Et primo specialiter quo ad regna & prouincias, quæ de facto regi Romanorum seu Imperatori obediunt. Nam Papa super omnia regna occidentalia, quorum aliqua Imperatori sunt de facto subiecta, habet eandem potestatem, quam habuit Constantinus Magnus super totius Imperii Monarchiam: quia ipsa Constantinus Magnus reliquit Siluestro & eius successoribus disponenda. dist. 96. c. Constantinus. Constantinus autem pro suæ voluntatis arbitrio potuit ampliare & restringere potestatem electorum, vt electio ab eis facta legitime maius vel minus daret electo: ergo & Papa hoc potest saltem quoad occidentalia regna. Amplius, qui potest regem alicuius regni vel regnorum deponere; & fideles ipsius à iuramento fidelitatis absoluere; & quibus vult ius eligendi regem, & eiusdem regni vel regnorum dominia tribuere; & regem constituere; huiusmodi etiam quantum electio alicuius in regem debeat dare electo, potest instituere. Papa autem omnia suprardicta potest, specialiter quantum ad occidentalia regna: quia non videtur, quod neq; à Deo neque ab homine habeat maiorem potestatem super regnum Francorum, quam super alia regna occidentalia præscripta. Potest autem exercere primo super regnum Francorum, & omnes prouincias ab Aquitania vsq; ad Bauariam. Comprehendit namq; illas propter Hildericum (aliis Ildericum) regem Francorum, tam Orientalium (scil. Germaniarum) quam Occidentalium: & regem deponit, & sibi subiectos iuramento fidelitatis absoluit: & Pipinum patrem Caroli Magni in eius loco substituit. 15. q. 6. alius. Electoribus etiam regis Romanorum ius tribuit eligendi. Extr. de elect. venerabilem. ergo Papa potest instituere, quantum tali electo dare debeat electio. Ruursus, qui potest alium cui regi potestatem dare eligendi sibi successorem: habet statuere, quando & quantam electus habere debeat administrationem: an mortem opus alterius expectare. Papa autem potest dare regi Romanorum seu Imperatori potestatem eligendi Imperatorem successorem, quo ad regnum Italiæ. distinct. 63. in synodo. Et similiratione quo ad alia regna, scil. Occidentalia: ergo potest statuere quando & quantum electio dare debeat electo. Item electio illa, quæ indiget confirmatione ad hoc, quod electus habeat administrationem, non tantum dat electo, quantum legitima successio debet regi hæreditarie succedenti: quia rex hæreditarie succedens nulla indiget confirmatione ad hoc quod ad ministret. Sed electio canonica principum electorum indiget confirmatione papali ad hoc quod electus habeat administrationem. Item illa electio, virtute cuius electus non est rex, non dat tantum electo, quantum legitima successio dat regi hæreditarie succedenti.
units.tr: The eighth and last question is whether canonical election by the electing princes, or electors, gives the one elected as King of the Romans, by nature alone, as much as lawful succession gives to a king who succeeds by inheritance. On this question, which seems very close to the fourth question, opinions differ. One party holds the negative, and there are different ways of stating it. One way is that the canonical election by those princes does not give the elected as much as succession gives to a king who succeeds by inheritance, because such an election gives the elected no administration except through papal confirmation, approval, nomination or coronation. Many arguments can be brought in support of this view, which need only be touched on here, since how it may be confirmed and declared can be seen in detail from the preceding questions. That it is not the election but the confirmation, approval, nomination or coronation by the Pope that gives administration to the one elected King of the Romans is shown, first, by this: that the one so elected is a vassal of the Pope and is bound to swear an oath of fidelity and to do homage to him. Likewise, because the Empire is from the Pope. Similarly, because the one elected King of the Romans is not bound to ask anything of the Pope. Also, because the Pope can depose an Emperor and consequently appoint another; for although someone can sometimes alone give an honour which he could not alone take away, yet whoever can take away an honour can also give the same. extra, de translatione. inter corporalia: Also, because the Pope has the fullness of power both in temporal and in spiritual matters. Also, because there ought to be one head in the whole world, on whom all jurisdiction and power depend; and this is none other than the Pope, since he alone has his power from God. Also, because the Pope has both swords, namely the spiritual and the temporal. The other way of stating this negative says: On the contrary, the canonical election by the electing princes does not give the one elected King of the Romans as much as lawful succession gives to a king who succeeds by inheritance, because the power of electing was given to the electors by the supreme pontiff. Extra. de elect. venerabilem. And so, just as privileges must be inspected to learn what power they confer, or what is contained in them, so to learn what power the electors have of electing, and what power they obtain from their election, the letters by which the power of electing was given to the electors would have to be inspected. Extr. de priuilegiis cap. porro &c. recepimus But if these are not found, it is for the supreme pontiff himself to declare what power the elected obtains from their election, because it belongs to him to interpret a law whose it is to enact it. extr. de priui. si Papa in 6. The Pope, moreover, has power to judge others. Extr. de iudiciis, cum venissent. Since, therefore, the Pope declares that the one elected King of the Romans must be examined by the Pope, and consequently declares that by election alone no one is King of the Romans or Emperor, it follows that the electing does not give the elected full administration, nor the royal title or imperial power; yet lawful succession gives all of these to a king who succeeds by inheritance. For this way of stating the negative, which rests chiefly on the view that the election of princes gives the elected only as much power as the Pope wishes to be given to him through it, many arguments can be made. And first, specifically as regards the kingdoms and provinces which in fact obey the King of the Romans or Emperor. For the Pope, over all the western kingdoms, some of which are in fact subject to the Emperor, has the same power that Constantine the Great had over the monarchy of the whole Empire, because Constantine the Great left it to Sylvester and his successors to dispose of. dist. 96. c. Constantinus. Constantine, however, by his own will could extend and restrict the power of the electors, so that an election made by them lawfully gave more or less to the one elected; therefore the Pope can also do this, at least as regards the western kingdoms. Furthermore, whoever can depose the king of a kingdom or kingdoms, absolve their subjects from the oath of fidelity, grant the right of electing a king and the lordship of that kingdom or those kingdoms to whomever he wishes, and appoint a king, can also establish how much the election of anyone as king ought to give the elected. The Pope can do all the things mentioned above, especially as regards the western kingdoms, because it does not appear that he has greater power over the kingdom of the Franks, whether from God or from man, than over the other western kingdoms just listed. He can exercise this first over the kingdom of the Franks and all the provinces from Aquitaine as far as Bavaria. For he included these, on account of Childeric (others read Ildericus), king of the Franks, both the Eastern (namely the Germanies) and the Western; he deposed the king, absolved his subjects from the oath of fidelity, and put Pippin, father of Charlemagne, in his place. 15. q. 6. alius. He also granted to the electors of the King of the Romans the right of electing. Extr. de elect. venerabilem. Therefore the Pope can establish how much such an election ought to give the elected. Again, whoever can give another the power to choose a successor to a king has the right to determine when and how much the elected ought to have as administration, whether he must wait for another's death. But the Pope can give the King of the Romans or Emperor the power of electing an Emperor as successor, as regards the kingdom of Italy. distinct. 63. in synodo. And by similar reasoning as regards the other kingdoms, namely the western ones; therefore he can determine when and how much the election ought to give the elected. Also, that election which needs confirmation in order for the elected to have administration does not give the elected as much as lawful succession ought to give to a king who succeeds by inheritance, because a king who succeeds by inheritance needs no confirmation in order to govern. But the canonical election by the electing princes needs papal confirmation in order for the elected to have administration. Also, that election by virtue of which the elected is not yet king does not give the elected as much as lawful succession gives to a king who succeeds by inheritance.

units.la: Virtute autem electionis principum electus in regem Romanorum non est rex, sed tantum electus in regem, teste Ioh. 22. qui in processu contra Dominum Ludouicum de Bauaria, quem aliqui Bauari Imperatorem appellant, ait: Præfatus Ludouicus à nobis, ad quem sua electionis sicut præsumitur, in discordia celebrata, ac persona ipsius examinatio & admissio, repulsio & approbatio noscitur pertinere: electione prædicta nequaquam approbata, nec eius admissa persona, sicut vulgari fama innotuerat, & publica facti evidentia manifestat: non quarens vt deberet peroptime regni seu Imperii conscendere dignitatis fastigium, sed potius aliunde nescimus quo ductus seu potius seductus consilio, præfati nomen sibi & titulum regis vsurpauit; quamuis, priusquam alterius eorum per sedem Apostolicam fuisset approbata persona, vel reprobata, neutri electorum ipsorum assumere licuit nomen vel titulum præsumptum: cum nec interim Romanorum reges extiterint, sed in reges electi, nec sint habendi pro regibus: nec reges etiam nominandi &c. Virtute vero successionis legitimæ hæreditarie succedens in aliquo regno statim est rex: nec personæ ipsius examinatio, approbatio vel admissio spectat ad Papam: ergo electio in regem Romanorum non dat electo tantum, quantum dat legitima successio regi hæreditarie succedenti. Aliæ plures allegationes ad prædictam assertionem possunt adduci: de quibus in discussione istarum forte tangetur.
units.tr: By virtue of the election of the princes, however, the one elected King of the Romans is not yet king, but only elected as king, as John XXII says in the process against Lord Louis of Bavaria, whom some Bavarians call Emperor: The aforesaid Louis, to whom, as is presumed, the choice of his election belongs in the disputed assembly, and whose person's examination and admission, rejection and approval are known to pertain to us, the said election having in no way been approved, nor his person admitted, as has become known by common report and is shown by the public evidence of the fact, not seeking to mount the summit of dignity of the kingdom or Empire in the proper way, but rather, led or rather seduced by some counsel we know not whence, usurped for himself the name and title of king; although, before either of those persons had been approved or rejected by the Apostolic See, it was not lawful for either of the electors to assume the presumed name or title, since in the meantime they had not been Kings of the Romans but elected as kings, and are not to be regarded as kings, nor even to be called kings, etc. But by virtue of lawful hereditary succession, the one succeeding in some kingdom is at once king; nor does the examination, approval or admission of his person belong to the Pope. Therefore election as King of the Romans does not give the elected as much as lawful succession gives to a king who succeeds by inheritance. Many other arguments can be adduced for the aforesaid assertion, some of which may perhaps be touched on in the discussion of these.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Recitat & probat secundam opin. de cuius probationibus pauca dicentur, cap. septimo.
units.tr: He sets out and proves the second opinion, whose proofs will be discussed briefly in chapter seven.

units.la: ALia est opinio, dicens, quod canonica electio principum electorum tantum dat electo in regem Romanorum in terris & prouinciis quæ subiectæ erant Carolo Magno ante coronationem Imperialem, quantum legitima successio dat regi haereditarie succedenti. Prima pars illius opinionis probatur sic. Electio, quae dat electo in aliquibus regnis & prouinciis siue terris plenam administrationem, virtute cuius licet electo nomen regis assumere: tantum dat electo in terris illis, quantum dat legitima successio haereditarie succedenti: quia legitima successio non plus dat regi haereditarie succedenti, nisi quia potest licite sibi nomen regis assumere, ac iura & bona regni administrare. Sed canonica electio dat electo in regem Romanorum seu Imperatorem in prouinciis & terris, quae erat subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem imperialem, plenam administrationem, & virtute electionis electus potest sibi nomen regis assumere: igitur &c. maior, ut videtur, probatione non indiget. Minorem probat quidam Doctor venerabilis, de quo in praecedentibus facta est mentio: cuius verba, quamuis sint prolixa, absque omni immutatione propter reverentiam dicentis, quia solo sincero veritatis & iustitiae amore (ut arbitror) exquisitius, quam multi alii, conatus est iura Imperii declarare, duxi praesentibus inserenda, & breviter pertractanda, ut ex ipsa discussione veritas elimatior discutiatur vel intelligatur: quia quaerendo, opponendo & soluendo, ac diuersas artes & responsiones recitando, melius veritas inuenitur: & quod a pluribus quaeritur, facilius inuenitur, dist. 20. de quibus. Dicit igitur praedictus Doctor in haec verba: Electus in regem: siue Imperatorem in concordia potest statim ex ipsa electione nomen regis assumere, & iura & bona regni & Imperii in Italia & in aliis prouinciis eius administrare. Ad huius articuli approbationem praemitto, quod Carolus Magnus rex Francorum, ut patet ex his quae dicta sunt in primo cap. huius tractatus, Francorum regnum, quod protendebatur ab Aquitania usque Bauariam, habuit ex successione paterna more & consuetudine quasi generali omnium aliorum regnorum occidentalium, qua tunc, sicut & nunc, per successionem generis ut plurimum debebantur: & in hoc regno sibi suisq; successoribus Italiam & multas alias prouincias & terras per bellum licitum acquisiuit: ex eo videlicet, quod reges & principes & possessores illarum prouinciarum contra ecclesias Christianas, multimodas, ut ex diuersis historiis & chronicis apparet, tyrannides suis temporibus exercebant: & hoc poterat facere idem Carolus de iure gentium, ex quo bella sunt indicta: ut patet, ff. de iusti. & iur. l. ex hoc iure. Instit. de iure na. gen. & ci. §. ius autem & §. ius gentium. Et contenti prouincias & terras huiusmodi eodem modo fecit suas: ea enim, quae in bello iusto capimus, iure gentium nostra fiunt, ut patet, ff. de acquirendo rerum Dominio. l. naturalem. §. vlt. Insti. de rer. diui. §. item ea quae ex hostibus. ad idem 23. q. v. dicat. & q. 6. si qua de rebus. Et primus dictus Carolus elapsis pluribus annis, ut patet supr. c. 1. vnctus & coronatus fuit in Imperatorem Romanorum. Unde notatur in constitutione Frederici Imperatoris hac edicta. §. iniuria. in Gloss. secundum leges. colla. 10. quia Carolus stetit 10. annis rex Franciae & Lombardiae, antequam haberet Imperium: nec reperitur nisi fecisse 9. leges in Lombardia contentas, postquam fuit Imperator, ut ibi notatur. Qui Carolus reliquit regnum & Imperium cum puinciis licite acquisitis virtute dicta generalis consuetudinis filio suo Ludouico, recepta Italia, quam reliquit Bernhardo nepoti suo: & sic deinceps reges Imperatores de gratia dicti Caroli exeuntes habuerunt per successionem regnum Francorum seu partem eiusdem regni per diuisionem eiusdem cum Italia & Imperio eodem iure & titulo, quo illa Carolus tenebat usque ad tempora Ludouici tertii, cuius tempore Italia defecerit a fidelitate sua. Regna autem Germania habuerunt reges de genere dicti Caroli descendentes, quousque defecit genus vel saltem potentia generis ipsorum in dicto regno. Quo genere deficiente principes & natu maiores Francorum, Alemanorum, Bauarorum & Saxonum, qui repraesentabat totum populum Germaniae, elegerunt Henricum Ducem Saxoniae in regem Germaniae a Francorum, ut ex prius dictis in cap. 2. apparet. Quod facere poterant ex iure gentium: ex quo iura & regna condita sunt: scil. quilibet populus potest sibi eligere regem: ut patet ex his quae leguntur & notantur ff. de iusti. & iuri. l. ex hoc iure. Et deinde Otthonem primum, filium eiusdem Henrici (ut etiam visum est superius in eodem capitulo) recuperauit Italiam ipsi regno Germaniae: a quo & a cuius societate defecerat, & factus fuit postea Imperator, & ex iterato incepit regnum cum Italia & Imperio deberi ex successione generis usque ad tempora Ottonis tertii, cuius tempore fuit institutum, per certos principes Germaniae, scil. per Officiatos Imperii, eligeretur Imperator: ut etiam ex superius dictis plane patet. His itaq; praemissis, probo veritatem dicti articuli generaliter de administratione omnium prouinciarum regni & Imperii. Secundo principaliter de administratione regni Germaniae. Primum sic probatur: quilibet populus habens rege potest sibi regem eligere de iure gentium: ex quo iure regna condita sunt, ut supra dictum est per l. ex hoc iure: quod non est aliud, quam nomen regis assumere & bona & iura illius regni administrare, ut de se patet. Sed in regno & Imperio (cum non habeat locum hodie successio generis) mortuo rege & Imperatore populus Germaniae, Italiae & aliarum prouinciarum regni & Imperii, carentium rege: & principes & electores iam dicta institutionis habent eligere regem seu Imperatorem, repraesentantes omnes principes & populum Germaniae, Italiae & aliarum prouinciarum & terrarum regni & Imperii, quasi vice omnium eligendo: ut ex dicendis infra cap. prox. clarius apparebit. Igitur concluditur, quod electus per eos concorditer ex electione huiusmodi potest de iure gentium licite nomine & re ipsa regnare. Quod non videtur aliud, quam nomen regis assumere, ac iura & bona regni & Imperii administrare: ut praedixi. Et ex his iure gentium credo verificari dictum beati Hieron. dicentis, quod exercitus facit Imperatorem, ut patet in canone 93. dist. legimus: quia exercitus seu Romanus populus eo tempore repraesentabat totum populum Romanum Imperio subiectum. Unde facere poterat Imperatorem. Sicut hodie principes electores ratione institutionis populi huiusmodi repraesentant. Secundo potest idem probari aliunde sic. Illud quod subrogatur & succedit in locu alterius rei, debet recipere & imitari ius & naturam illius rei, in cuius locu succedit & subrogatur, ut patet ff. de con. &. & demon. l. filia. ad idem extr. de vo. & vo. redemp. magna. De Baptismo. Maiores: cum suo concordantiis. Et hoc etiam cum sit certum iure canonico & ciuili, satis dicitur Ratio naturalis, apud omnes enim non potest dici aliquid proprie succedere in locu alterius rei, si non haberet ius & naturam illius rei, in cuius locum succedit & subrogatur, ut de se notum est, & sic illud videtur esse de iure gentium. Quod enim ratio naturalis dictat, apud omnes idem est, ut ff. de iusti. & iur. l. omnes Instit. de iure na. gen. & ciuil. §. quod vero, sed electio regis & Imperatoris, quae fit per principes electores succedit, & est subrogata in locu successionis generis, quae per multa tempora fuit in regno & Imperio, videlicet supr. in c ap. 2. retinebit ergo illa electio ne & maturam successionis generis, qua per multa tempora fuit in regno & Imperio. Sed tunc filius statim mortuo patre ex ipsa generis successione assumpsit nomen regis, & administrauit bona & iura Imperii in Italia & in aliis prouinciis regni & Imperii: immo interdum simili ter cum patre administrauit ex ipsius patris dispositione, vt ex superius dictis in cap. 2. patet: velsi non esset filius regis aut Imperatoris: tunc, eo decedente, alius de genere decedentis succedebat eidem regno & Imperio nomen regis assumendo, & bona & iura ipsius Imperii & regni iuxta consuetudinem generalem aliorum regnorum occidentalium; in quibus habet locum successio generis in administrando, vt etiā ex superius dictis satis patet. Igitur similiter & nostro tempore electus a principibus electoribus concorditer ex tali electione, qua subrogata est de regno & Imperio, loco successionis generis, potest statim licite nomen regis assumere, ac iura & bona Imperii administrare. Deinde illud probo specialiter de administratione regni & Imperii in Germania, scil. quod in ea posset electus a principibus in concordia ex electione huiusmodi licite administrare, dato sed non concesso, quod in Italia hoc non posset: & hoc modo. Nam apparet ex praedictis Chronicis omnibus, quod postquam defecit successio generis Caroli Magni in regno Germaniae, Henricus primus ex electione principum & natu maiorum Germaniae statim assumpsit nomen regis, & administrauit bona & iura dicti regni. Post hoc iterum deficiente successione eiusdem Henrici in regno Germania, instituuntur certis principibus ad eligendum reges: Henricus fundator secundus Ecclesiae Bambergensis, ex electione principum sic assumpsit statim nomen regis, & administrauit iura & bona dicti regni. Post hunc etiam deinceps (vt ex chronicis praedictis patet) idipsum potuerunt alii eorundem regnum successores in reges a principibus electi concorditer assumpti. Praeterea satis patet ex praedictis, quod Germania post diuisionem regni & Imperii Francorum, de qua supr in c. 2. dictum est, fuit regnum per se, sicut regnum Galliae Occidentalis, quod hodie regnum Franciae nuncupatur: & est regnum per se. Et hoc regnum Germaniae Ludouicus frater Lotharii Imperatoris & Caroli regis Galliae in portione hereditatis obtinuit: & post mortem eius filii sui tres, Carolus Magnus, Ludouicus, & Carolus: quorum vnus, scil. Carolus, Italiam & Imperium, & post eum Arnulphus, filius Caroli magni praedicti, Italiam simul cum Imperio obtinuit. Quam Italiam Ottho primus rex Germaniae per Berengarium tertium postea recuperauit eam ad potestatem regni Germaniae reducendo, & Imperator factus est, vt visum est in d. cap. 2. Ex hoc autem non debet esse deterior conditio regni & Imperii in Germania: quia reges ipsius fuerunt Italiam & Imperium assecuti: sed melior. Virtutibus enim reges ipsius promeruerunt Imperium. Virtutibus autem praemia debentur, in C. de statu. & Imm. l. vl. & ff. de Iusti. & iur. l. 1. Imperium autem dispendia ex hoc sequi non debent, vt ex fideiussore proueniet. Sed constat, si electus ad Imperium non posset administrare bona & iura Imperii & regni in Germania statim ex ipsa electione: sed haberet rationē Italiae expectare coronationem, nominationem & approbationem ecclesiae Romanae, quod ipsius Germaniae & constitutio facta Italia per reges Francorum deterior esset. Magna enim possent dispendia populo Germaniae ex tali expectatione per guerras, ex quibus solent sequi caedes hominum, rapina & incendia generari, quae per administrationem regis de facili cessare possent: vt de se notum extitit. Quare concluditur, quod electus concorditer a principibus, dato etiā quod in Italia non posset administrare: id tamen in Germania facere poterit & debebit. Nec obstat, si iuxta praemissam suppositionē dicatur, quod licet electus in regē a principibus possit administrare in Germania, considerata ipsa Germania per se: & hoc ex electione principum electorum: tamen cum Italia accedere videtur Germania, hoc non poterit ex electione huiusmodi, sed potius ex ecclesia Romana approbatione: vt sic accessorium sortiatur naturā sui principalis Extr. de reg. iur. accessoriū lib. 6. & cū concordantiis ibi notatis. Vnde ex hoc electus a principibus non rex Germaniae sed rex Romanorum appellatur, quod fieri videtur ratione Italiae, in qua sita est Roma. Quia ad hoc respondendo dicitur, quod Germania seu regnum Germaniae non fuit accessorium regno Italiae. Regnum enim Germaniae etiam post diuisionem regni Francorum, cum adhuc regnum Germaniae erat de genere Caroli Magni obtinuerunt duo reges Germaniae, scil. Carolus tertius & Arnulphus. Ipsum quod regnū Italiae Ottho primus aliquamdiu regno Germaniae vi ablatū recuperauit; vt patet ex dictis supr. c. 2.
