Reges vero Italiae, qui ante tempora Caroli Magni fuerunt Longobardi, nunquam regnum Germaniae & Francorum sibi, vt ex supradictis chronicis patet, subiugasse noscuntur. Quod autem electus a principibus in regem Rex Romanorum appellatur: illud non est factum ratione Italiae, cum ipsa regno Germaniae accesserit, vt est dictum: sed credo quod illud introductum est, tum propter reuerentiam sacrosanctae Romanae ecclesiae, quae omnium ecclesiarum primatum & magistratum obtinet, vt patet dist. 16. quam dist. c. 1. & 2. extra, de summa trini. & fide catho. damnamus: cū similibus. Vt & Imperator asserit, Papa senioris Romae esse primū omnium sacerdotum, in auten. de eccl. ti. in princ. collati 9. Tum etiā propter honorem vrbis Romanae, cuius populus olim tenuit monarchiam Imperii. Sed postquam translatum est Imperium ipsum Imperatore confirmauit, vt patet de iure natu. gentium & ciuili. Sed & quod principi. ratione de administratione regni & Imperii in Germania: idem dico de administratione regni & Imperii in Gallia Belgica, seu regno quondam Lotharii sito inter Mosam & Rhenum fluuios. De quo regno fit mentio in canone 63. dist. porro. Hoc enim Lotharii seu Lothariense regnum post mortem Lotharii regis, filii Lotharii Imperatoris, de quo multoties fit mentio in decretis, vt dixi supra cap. 2. Ludouicus secundus rex Germaniae, & Carolus rex Galliae Occidentalis, fratres inter se aequaliter anno Domini 871. diuiserunt. Post vero Ludouici mortem variis contentionibus super eodē regno inter regem Germaniae & regem Galliae habitis, Ludouicus & Carolus adolescentes regis Caroli praedicti nepotes, in portionem dicti regni Lotharii, Ludouico Regi occidentali Franciae filio regis Ludouici iam dicti, ex integro successerunt. Postea vero deficiente genere Caroli in Regno Germaniae, quidam rex Galliae occidentalis, Carolus nomine, Henrico, qui primo de genere Saxonum coepit regnare in Germania, confaederatus; eidē Henrico sub anno domini 974. reddidit dictum regnum, de post mortem eiusdem Henrici, variis discordiis contra Otthonem primum, filium dicti Henrici, pro regno Lotharii habitu, tandem regnum Lotharii totum fuit ad dictum regem Otthonem conuersum, & omnes reges Theutonici Belgicam Galliam ac regnum huiusmodi sine contradictione quolibet tenuerunt, prout in praedictis Francorum & Godefredi chronicis plenius enarratur. Idem etiam ex causa primi dicta ex omnibus aliis prouinciis & terris, quae tempore diuisionis fuerunt adiuncta regno Germaniae vel quae post diuisionem regni Francorum praedicto regno Germaniae in montanis partibus accesserunt, intelligo repetendum. Haec sunt verba praedicti Doctoris, quibus probat & declarare conatur, quod electus in regem seu Imperatorem Romanorum a principibus electoribus in concordia potest statim ex ipsa electione licite nomen regis assumere: & iura & bona regni & Imperii & in aliis provinciis eiusdem regni & Imperii, quae subiectae erant Carolo Magno ante coronationem Imperialem, administrare. Et haec sententia est pars minoris rationis, positae in principio istius capituli: ad probandum primam partem opinionis recitatae: videlicet quod canonica electio principum electorum dat tantum electo in regem Romanorum in terris & provinciis, quae erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem imperialem, quantum legitima successio generis dat regi haereditarie succedenti. Secunda pars opinionis, secundum quod canonica electio principum electorum non dat tantum electo in regem Romanorum in terris & provinciis, quae non erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem Imperialem, quantum legitima successio generis dat regi haereditarie succedenti, probatur: quia si electus in regem Romanorum virtute electionis ius haberet tantum in illis terris & provinciis, quantum habet rex haereditarie succedens virtute successionis legitimae, tunc promotio regis in Imperatorem esset verbalis, & non realis, sicut dictum est quaestione quarta, cap. 9.
units.tr: There is another opinion, which holds that a canonical election by the electoral princes gives the elected man, as king of the Romans, as much right in the lands and provinces that were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation as lawful succession gives a king who succeeds by inheritance. The first part of this opinion is proved as follows. An election that gives the one elected full administration in some kingdoms, provinces or lands, by virtue of which he may lawfully take the name of king, gives him in those lands as much as lawful succession gives one who succeeds by inheritance, because lawful succession gives the hereditary successor nothing more than the right to take the name of king lawfully and to administer the rights and goods of the kingdom. But a canonical election gives the one elected as king of the Romans or Emperor full administration in the provinces and lands that were subject to Charlemagne before the imperial coronation, and by virtue of the election the elected man may take the name of king. Therefore, etc. The major premise, as it seems, needs no proof. The minor premise is proved by a certain venerable teacher, who was mentioned in what precedes. Although his words are lengthy, I have thought fit to insert them here without any alteration, out of respect for the speaker, since he has tried, from a sincere love of truth and justice alone (as I believe), to set out the rights of the Empire more carefully than many others. I have briefly examined them so that the truth may be refined and understood through the discussion itself, since truth is found better by asking, objecting and answering, and by reciting the various arguments and replies; and what is sought by many is more easily found (dist. 20. de quibus.). The aforementioned teacher therefore says these words: The one elected king, or Emperor, in harmony may at once, from the election itself, take the name of king and administer the rights and goods of the kingdom and Empire in Italy and in the other provinces. To approve this article I first set out that Charles the Great, king of the Franks, as appears from what was said in the first chapter of this treatise, held the kingdom of the Franks, which extended from Aquitaine to Bavaria, by paternal succession, according to the custom almost universal among all the other western kingdoms, in which at that time, as now, rule for the most part passed by succession of the family. In this kingdom he acquired for himself and his successors Italy and many other provinces and lands by lawful war, namely because the kings, princes and possessors of those provinces were, as various histories and chronicles show, exercising manifold tyrannies against the Christian churches in their times; and Charles could do this by the law of nations, from the time when wars were declared, as appears in D. de iust. et iur., l. ex hoc iure; Inst. de iure nat. gen. et civ., §. ius autem and §. ius gentium. And having held these provinces and lands, he made them his own in the same way, for those things that we take in a just war become ours by the law of nations, as appears in D. de acquirendo rerum dominio, l. naturalem, §. ult.; Inst. de rer. div., §. item ea quae ex hostibus; ad idem 23 q. 5 dicat. and q. 6 si qua de rebus. And this Charles, after several years had passed, as appears above in c. 1, was anointed and crowned Emperor of the Romans. Hence it is noted in the constitution of the Emperor Frederick, the edict Iniuria, §. in gloss. secundum leges, col. 10, that Charles was king of France and Lombardy for ten years before he had the Empire, and that he is not found to have made more than nine laws in Lombardy, those contained there, after he became Emperor, as is noted there. This Charles left the kingdom and the Empire, with the provinces lawfully acquired by virtue of the said general custom, to his son Louis, having received Italy, which he left to his nephew Bernhard; and thus afterwards the kings and Emperors descending from the family of the said Charles had by succession the kingdom of the Franks, or part of the same kingdom by division, together with Italy and the Empire, by the same law and title by which Charles held them, until the time of Louis III, in whose time Italy revolted from its allegiance. The kings of Germany, however, were kings descended from the family of the said Charles, until the family, or at least the power of that family, failed in the said kingdom. When that family failed, the princes and the elders of the Franks, Alemanni, Bavarians and Saxons, who represented the whole people of Germany, elected Henry, Duke of Saxony, as king of Germany, from the Franks, as appears from what was said earlier in c. 2. They could do this by the law of nations, from which laws and kingdoms were established: namely, any people may choose its own king, as appears from what is read and noted in D. de iust. et iur., l. ex hoc iure. Then Otto the First, son of the same Henry (as was also seen above in the same chapter), recovered Italy for the kingdom of Germany, from which and from whose association it had fallen away; and he afterwards became Emperor, and from then on the kingdom together with Italy and the Empire was again owed by succession of the family, until the time of Otto III, in whose time it was instituted that the Emperor should be elected by certain princes of Germany, namely by the officials of the Empire, as is also quite clear from what has been said above. Having set out these things, I prove the truth of the said article in general concerning the administration of all the provinces of the kingdom and Empire; secondly, principally, concerning the administration of the kingdom of Germany. The first is proved thus: any people having a king may choose a king for itself by the law of nations, from which law kingdoms were established, as was said above by the law ex hoc iure; and this is nothing other than to take the name of king and to administer the goods and rights of that kingdom, as is evident in itself. But in the kingdom and Empire (since hereditary succession now has no place), when the king and Emperor has died, the people of Germany, Italy and the other provinces of the kingdom and Empire, lacking a king, and the princes and electors, by the said institution, have the right to elect a king or Emperor, representing all the princes and the people of Germany, Italy and the other provinces and lands of the kingdom and Empire, electing as it were on behalf of all; as will appear more clearly below in the following chapter. Therefore it is concluded that the one elected by them in harmony, by such an election, may lawfully, by the law of nations, reign both in name and in fact. This seems to be nothing other than to take the name of king and to administer the rights and goods of the kingdom and Empire, as I said before. And by this law of nations I believe the saying of the blessed Jerome is verified, that the army makes the Emperor, as appears in c. 93 dist. Legimus, because the army, or the Roman people at that time, represented the whole Roman people subject to the Empire. Hence they could make an Emperor, just as the electoral princes today represent such a people by virtue of its institution. Secondly, the same can be proved from elsewhere, thus. What is substituted for and succeeds in the place of another thing must receive and imitate the right and nature of that thing in whose place it succeeds and is substituted, as appears in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. filia; ad idem extra de voto et voti redemptione, Magna; De baptismo, Maiores, with its concordances. And since this is certain both by canon and civil law, it is sufficiently called natural reason; for among all men nothing can properly be said to succeed in the place of another thing unless it has the right and nature of that thing in whose place it succeeds and is substituted, as is known in itself; and so this seems to be by the law of nations. For what natural reason dictates is the same among all, as in D. de iust. et iur., l. omnes; Inst. de iure nat. gen. et civ., §. quod vero. But the election of king and Emperor, which is made by the electoral princes, succeeds and is substituted in the place of the succession of the family, which for many ages was in the kingdom and Empire, as above in c. 2. It will therefore retain that election and the nature of the succession of the family, which for many ages was in the kingdom and Empire. But then the son, immediately on his father's death, by the very succession of the family, assumed the name of king and administered the goods and rights of the Empire in Italy and the other provinces of the kingdom and Empire; indeed sometimes he administered jointly with his father, by his father's disposition, as appears from what was said above in c. 2; or, if he was not the son of the king or Emperor, then on his death another of the family of the deceased succeeded to the same kingdom and Empire, assuming the name of king, and the goods and rights of the same Empire and kingdom, according to the general custom of the other western kingdoms, in which succession of the family has its place in administration, as is also sufficiently clear from what was said above. Therefore, in the same way, in our own time the one elected by the electoral princes in harmony, by such an election, which has been substituted for hereditary succession in the kingdom and Empire, may at once lawfully assume the name of king and administer the rights and goods of the Empire. Next I prove this specially concerning the administration of the kingdom and Empire in Germany: namely, that in Germany the one elected by the princes in harmony could lawfully administer by such an election, granting, but not conceding, that this could not be done in Italy; and in this way. For it appears from all the aforementioned chronicles that, after the family succession of Charles the Great had failed in the kingdom of Germany, Henry the First, by election of the princes and elders of Germany, at once assumed the name of king and administered the goods and rights of that kingdom. After this again, when the succession of the same Henry in the kingdom of Germany had failed, certain princes were appointed to elect kings; Henry the Second, founder of the church of Bamberg, by election of the princes, at once assumed the name of king in this way and administered the rights and goods of the said kingdom. After him also, afterwards (as appears from the aforementioned chronicles), the other successors of the same kingdom, chosen and assumed as kings by the princes in harmony, could do the same. Moreover it is sufficiently clear from what has been said that Germany, after the division of the kingdom and Empire of the Franks, of which it was spoken above in c. 2, was a kingdom in itself, just as the kingdom of Western Gaul, which is today called the kingdom of France, is a kingdom in itself. And Louis, brother of the Emperor Lothar and of Charles, king of Gaul, obtained this kingdom of Germany in his share of the inheritance; and after his death his three sons, Charles the Great, Louis and Charles, held it; of whom one, namely Charles, obtained Italy and the Empire, and after him Arnulf, son of the aforesaid Charles the Great, obtained Italy together with the Empire. Otto I, king of Germany, afterwards recovered this Italy from Berengar III, bringing it back under the power of the kingdom of Germany, and became Emperor, as was seen in the said c. 2. But from this the condition of the kingdom and Empire in Germany ought not to be worse: for its kings obtained Italy and the Empire, but rather better. For its kings earned the Empire by their virtues. But rewards are owed to virtues (C. de stat. et imm., l. ult.; and D. de iust. et iur., l. 1.), while the Empire should not bring losses on that account, as will come from a surety. But it is plain that if the one elected to the Empire could not administer the goods and rights of the Empire and kingdom in Germany at once by that election, but had to wait for Italy's coronation, nomination and approval by the Roman church, the constitution of Germany would be worse, made so by the kings of the Franks in Italy. For great losses could come to the people of Germany from such waiting, through wars, from which slaughter of men, plunder and burning tend to arise, which could easily cease through the administration of a king, as is known in itself. Therefore it is concluded that the one elected in harmony by the princes, even though he could not administer in Italy, will be able and ought to administer in Germany. Nor does it stand in the way if, following the supposition stated above, it is said that although the one elected king by the princes can administer in Germany considered in itself, by the election of the electoral princes, yet Germany seems to be attached to Italy, and this cannot be done by such an election, but rather by the approval of the Roman church, so that the accessory takes the nature of its principal (Extra, de reg. iur., accessorium, lib. 6, and with the concordances noted there). Hence the one elected by the princes is called not king of Germany but king of the Romans, which seems to be done on account of Italy, in which Rome is situated. To this it is answered that Germany, or the kingdom of Germany, was not an accessory to the kingdom of Italy. For the kingdom of Germany, even after the division of the kingdom of the Franks, while it was still of the family of Charles the Great, had two kings of Germany, namely Charles III and Arnulf. Indeed, that the kingdom of Italy was for some time taken from the kingdom of Germany by force and recovered by Otto I is plain from what was said above in c. 2. But the kings of Italy, who before the time of Charles the Great were the Lombards, are never known, as appears from the aforesaid chronicles, to have subjected the kingdom of Germany and the Franks to themselves. As for the one elected by the princes being called king of the Romans, this was not done on account of Italy, since Italy had become attached to the kingdom of Germany, as has been said; rather I believe it was introduced both on account of the reverence due to the most holy Roman church, which holds the primacy and rule over all churches, as appears in D. 16, which D. c. 1 and 2 extra de summa trinitate et fide catholica, damnamus, with similar passages; and also because the Emperor himself asserts that the Pope of old Rome is the first of all priests, in Auth. de eccl. tit. in princ., collat. 9. And also on account of the honour of the city of Rome, whose people once held the monarchy of the Empire. But after the Empire was transferred, it confirmed the same Emperor, as appears from the law of nature and nations and the civil law. But also concerning the prince, on account of the administration of the kingdom and Empire in Germany, I say the same of the administration of the kingdom and Empire in Belgic Gaul, or the former kingdom of Lothar, lying between the rivers Meuse and Rhine. Of this kingdom mention is made in c. 63 dist. Porro. For this kingdom of Lothar, or Lotharingia, after the death of King Lothar, son of the Emperor Lothar, of whom mention is made many times in the decretals, as I said above in c. 2, was divided equally between Louis II, king of Germany, and Charles, king of Western Gaul, brothers, in the year of the Lord 871. But after the death of Louis, following various disputes over the same kingdom between the king of Germany and the king of Western Gaul, Louis and Charles, young nephews of the aforesaid King Charles, succeeded entirely to the share of the said kingdom of Lothar, Louis, king of Western France, son of the aforesaid King Louis. Afterwards, when the family of Charles failed in the kingdom of Germany, a certain king of Western Gaul, named Charles, allied with Henry, who first of the Saxon family began to reign in Germany, and in the year of the Lord 974 he gave the said kingdom back to the same Henry; and after the death of the same Henry, with various discords against Otto I, son of the said Henry, over the kingdom of Lothar having been held, at last the whole kingdom of Lothar was turned to the said King Otto, and all the Teutonic kings held Belgic Gaul and this kingdom without any contradiction, as is more fully told in the aforesaid chronicles of the Franks and of Godfrey. I understand the same for the same reason to be repeated concerning all the other provinces and lands that were joined to the kingdom of Germany at the time of the division, or that came to the aforesaid kingdom of Germany in the mountainous parts after the division of the kingdom of the Franks. These are the words of the aforesaid teacher, by which he proves and tries to make clear that the one elected king or Emperor of the Romans by the electoral princes in harmony may at once, from the election itself, lawfully assume the name of king, and administer the rights and goods of the kingdom and Empire, and in the other provinces of the same kingdom and Empire which were subject to Charles the Great before the imperial coronation. And this opinion is the part of the minor premise, laid down at the beginning of this chapter, for proving the first part of the opinion recited: namely that a canonical election by the electoral princes gives the one elected as king of the Romans, in the lands and provinces which were subject to Charles the Great before the imperial coronation, only as much as lawful succession of the family gives a king who succeeds by inheritance. The second part of the opinion, according to which a canonical election by the electoral princes does not give the one elected as king of the Romans, in lands and provinces which were not subject to Charles the Great before the imperial coronation, as much as lawful succession of the family gives a king who succeeds by inheritance, is proved thus: if the one elected as king of the Romans, by virtue of the election, had a right in those lands and provinces only as much as a king who succeeds by inheritance has by virtue of lawful succession, then the promotion of the king to Emperor would be verbal and not real, as was said in question four, c. 9.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Ponit tertiam opinionem & eius motiva, de quibus videbitur cap. ultimo.
units.tr: He sets out the third opinion and its grounds, which will be considered in the last chapter.

units.la: ALia est opinio, quae videtur fuisse opinio Principum Germaniae provinciae, et rex Romanorum post electionem concordem principum, vel a maiori parte illorum, de facto habet eandem potestatem omnino & simpliciter, quantum habet Imperator: & et electio canonica principum electorum tantum, imo plus, quoad aliquid, dat electo in Regem Romanorum, quantum legitima successio regi haereditarie succedenti. Primo enim sic dicentes probare conantur, quod pronunciatio praedicta principum Germaniae est consona veritati, quod quamvis liqueat, ut videtur ex his, quae dicta sunt, q.4.c.2.&3.&9. ubi probatum est, quod inter regem Romanorum & Imperatorem nulla est realis differentia, & quod electio alicuius in regem Romanorum dat sibi plena administrationem, & quod Imperator nullas terras tenet a Papa: sive non esse dicendum, Imperatorem aliquas terras ab eo tenere: tamen nunc quasi replicando plura, quae tacta sunt ibi, dicendum est; quomodo per fundamenta probationum, quibus praefatus Doctor conatur probare, quod electus in regem seu Imperatorem a principibus electoribus regni & Imperii in concordia potest statim ex ipsa electione nomen regis assumere: & iura & bona regni & Imperii in Italia & aliis provinciis eiusdem regni & Imperii, quae scil. erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem imperialem, administrare, videtur posse probari pronunciatio principum Germaniae, scil. quod rex Romanorum post electionem eorundem principum, vel a maiori parte eorum de se facta, habet eandem potestatem omnino & simpliciter, quam habet Imperator. Nam quilibet populus carens rege potest sibi regem eligere de iure gentium, ex quo iure regna condita sunt, ff. de iust. & iur. l. ex hoc iure. Ex consequenti potest electus talis eodem iure ex tali electione populi regnare nomine & re, quod non est aliud quam nomen regis assumere & bona & iura ipsius regni administrare. Sed in regno & in Imperio, cum non habeat locum successio generis, mortuo rege & Imperatore, populus Germaniae, Italiae, Indiae, Persidiae, Africae, Graeciae & aliarum provinciarum, quae de iure regno & Imperio Romanorum sunt subiectae, caret rege supremo & Imperatore illo, scil. qui solus super omnes populos praedictarum provinciarum debet esse rex & Imperator. Et principes electores ratione institutionis, qua instituti sunt electores supremi regis & Imperatoris, habent eligere Imperatorem repraesentantes in hoc omnes principes & populum Germaniae, Italiae, Indiae, Africae, Graeciae & aliarum provinciarum, quae de iure regno & Imperio Romanorum sunt subiectae, quasi vice omnium eligendo. Ergo electus per eosdem concorditer ex electione huiusmodi potest de iure gentium nomine & re ipsa regnare. Quod non videtur aliud, nisi nomen regis assumere, ac iura & bona regni omnium provinciarum, quae sunt de iure subiectae Romanorum Imperio, administrare, quare praedicta pronunciatio principum Germaniae continet veritatem. Sed forte huic allegationi diceretur, quod principes electores non repraesentant nisi populum Germaniae, Italiae & aliarum provinciarum, quae subiectae erat Carolo Magno ante coronationem Imperialem. Et ideo electio in Imperatorem virtute electionis non habet eandem potestatem omnino, quam habet Imperator: nec habet administrationem nisi in illis provinciis, quarum principes & populos repraesentant. Sed haec responsio impugnatur: quia illi, qui repraesentant solum partem alicuius populi, maxime si repraesentant paruam partem alicuius populi, non possunt eligere regem seu Imperatorem, nisi super illum populum, quae praesentant. Aliter enim sequitur, quod repraesentantes principes & populum vel partem cuiuscunque populi possent eligere regem seu Imperatorem super totum mundum. Si igitur principes electores non repraesentant, nisi principes & populum Germaniae, Italiae & aliarum provinciarum, quae erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem Imperialem: sequitur quod principes electores possunt eligere solum modo regem seu Imperatorem super illas provincias, & non super alias provincias. Et etiam quidam Doctor tenet, quod principes electores non habent eligere Imperatorem Romanorum, sed quendam alium, qui de iure non est Imperator, nisi illarum provinciarum, quae erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem Imperialem. Quod non est consonum dictis istius Doctoris. Item qua ratione populus Germaniae, Italiae & aliarum provinciarum, quae erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem imperialem, possunt sibi eligere regem de iure gentium, quando caret rege, eadem ratione residua pars mundi, quae est in temporalibus maior quam Germania, Italia & aliae provin-ciae, cia, quae erant subiectae. Carolo magno ante coronationem Imperialem, mortuo rege supremo eorum & Imperatore possunt de iure gentium sibi eligere regem & Imperatorem, qui potius tanquam electus a maiori parte erit Rex & Imperator Romanorum, quam electus ab illis. Igitur duo possunt eligi in reges Romanorum & Imperatores, quod est absurdum. Quare relinquitur, quod nisi principes electores repraesentet principes & populos vniuersos subiectos Romano Imperio, non possunt eligere Imperatorem Romani Imperii. Videtur igitur concludendum, quod principes electores repraesentat principes & vniuersos populos subditos vniuerso Romano Imperio, vel Romanos tanquam caput omnium aliorum. Et sic infertur, quod electio huiusmodi non plus dat electo administrationem in illis prouinciis, quam in aliis prouinciis, quae non erant subiectae &c. Sic igitur per fundamentum primae allegationis praefati Doctoris videtur posse probari, quod rex Romanorum post electionem concordem habet eandem potestatem omnino & simpliciter, quam habet Imperator: & hoc idem probatur per fundamentum secundae allegationis ipsius.
units.tr: There is another opinion, which seems to have been held by the princes of the German provinces. It holds that a king of the Romans, after a concordant election by the princes, or by the greater part of them, actually has the same power in every respect and without qualification as the Emperor has. It holds also that the canonical election made by the electoral princes alone gives the one elected as King of the Romans as much as legitimate succession gives a king who succeeds by inheritance, and even more in some respects. First, those who hold this view try to prove that the aforementioned declaration of the princes of Germany agrees with the truth. Although it is clear from what has been said (q. 4, cc. 2, 3 and 9), where it was proved that there is no real difference between the King of the Romans and the Emperor, that the election of someone as King of the Romans gives him full administration, and that the Emperor holds no lands from the Pope (or, as some say, that the Emperor does not hold any lands from him), nevertheless, by restating several points already touched on there, it must be said how the declaration of the princes of Germany may be shown to be true, on the basis of the arguments by which the aforesaid author tries to prove that a man elected as king or emperor by the electoral princes of the realm and the Empire, acting in agreement, can at once, by that very election, assume the name of king and administer the rights and goods of the realm and Empire in Italy and the other provinces of the same realm and Empire, namely those which were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation. The declaration can be shown to hold: that the King of the Romans, after the election made by those princes or by the greater part of them, has exactly the same power, in every respect and without qualification, as the Emperor has. For any people lacking a king may by the law of nations choose a king for itself, and it is by this law that kingdoms have been founded (Dig. de iustitia et iure, l. ex hoc iure). It follows that a man so elected by the people may by the same law reign, in name and in fact, which is nothing other than assuming the name of king and administering the goods and rights of that kingdom. But in the realm and in the Empire, since no succession by birth applies, when a king and Emperor dies the people of Germany, Italy, India, Persia, Africa, Greece and the other provinces which by right are subject to the realm and Empire of the Romans are left without a supreme king, that is, without that Emperor who alone ought to be king and Emperor over all the peoples of the aforesaid provinces. And the electoral princes, by the institution under which they were made electors of the supreme king and Emperor, have the right to elect the Emperor, representing in this all the princes and people of Germany, Italy, India, Africa, Greece and the other provinces which by right are subject to the realm and Empire of the Romans, electing as it were on behalf of all. Therefore the one elected by them in concord, by such an election, can by the law of nations reign in name and in fact. This seems to be nothing other than assuming the name of king and administering the rights and goods of the realm of all the provinces which are by right subject to the Roman Empire; therefore the aforesaid declaration of the princes of Germany contains the truth. But perhaps someone might answer this argument by saying that the electoral princes represent only the people of Germany, Italy and the other provinces which were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation. Therefore an election to the Empire, by virtue of the election, does not have the same power in every respect as the Emperor has, nor does it have administration except in those provinces whose princes and peoples the electors represent. But this answer is refuted: for those who represent only a part of some people, especially if they represent a small part of it, cannot elect a king or emperor except over that people which they represent. Otherwise it would follow that those representing princes and a people, or a part of any people, could elect a king or emperor over the whole world. If, then, the electoral princes represent only the princes and people of Germany, Italy and the other provinces which were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation, it follows that the electoral princes can elect a king or emperor only over those provinces and not over other provinces. And indeed a certain author holds that the electoral princes are not to elect an Emperor of the Romans, but some other man who is not by right Emperor except of those provinces which were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation; but this does not agree with the statements of that author. Likewise, by the same reasoning by which the people of Germany, Italy and the other provinces which were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation may choose a king for themselves by the law of nations when they lack a king, the remaining part of the world, which is greater in temporal matters than Germany, Italy and the other provinces which were subject, could, when their supreme king and Emperor has died, choose for themselves a king and Emperor by the law of nations. Such a man, chosen by the greater part, would be King and Emperor of the Romans rather than one chosen by those provinces. Thus two men could be chosen as kings of the Romans and Emperors, which is absurd. Hence it follows that unless the electoral princes represent the princes and all the peoples subject to the Roman Empire, they cannot elect the Emperor of the Roman Empire. It seems therefore necessary to conclude that the electoral princes represent the princes and all the peoples subject to the whole Roman Empire, or the Romans as the head of all the others. And so it follows that an election of this kind gives the one elected no more administration in those provinces than in other provinces which were not subject. Thus by the foundation of the first argument of the aforesaid author it seems possible to prove that the King of the Romans, after a concordant election, has exactly the same power in every respect and without qualification as the Emperor has; and the same is proved by the foundation of his second argument.

units.la: Nam illud, quod subrogatur & succedit in locum alterius, debet recipere & imitari ius & naturam illius rei, cui succedit & subrogatur, vt ff. si quis cautionibus. l. si eum. §. qui iniuriarum & ff. de condit. & demon. l. filia. §. Titia. Ad idem extra, de voto & vo. re. magne, de baptismo, maiores. Et magis expresse videtur Extr. vt lite pendente. c. ecclesia. 1. Vbi dicit Glos. super verbo successerunt: est hoc argum. quod res quae succedit in locum alterius eodem iure censetur cum illa. Et hoc etiā ratio naturalis dictat, quod non posset proprie dici aliquid succedere in locum alterius, si non haberet ius & naturam illius rei, in cuius locum succedit & subrogatur. Sed electio regis & Imperatoris, quae nunc per principes electores succedit, subrogata est in locum successionis vel electionis, quae quondam fiebat per populum Romanum, seu per exercitu, qui populus Romanus seu exercitus tunc repraesentabat totum populum Romano Imperio subiectum, secundum istum Doctorem: igitur electio, quae modo fit per principes electores, retinebit ius & naturam electionis, quae fiebat per populum Romanum seu exercitum. Sed per illam electionem, quae fiebat a populo Romano vel exercitu, electus statim assumpsit nomen regis seu Imperatoris, & administrauit iura & bona regni & Imperii in omnibus prouinciis subiectis de iure imperio, & eandem omnino habuit potestatem in quantum rex Romanorum. Igitur & modo electus a principibus & electoribus concorditer a tali electione, subrogata, quae est in locum illius electionis, quae fiebat a populo Romano vel exercitu, habet omnino eandem potestatem in quantum rex Romanorum, & in quantum Imperator, ac posset licite nomen regis & Imperatoris assumere, & iura & bona Imperii non solum in Germania & Italia & in aliis prouinciis, quae erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem imperialem: sed etiam in aliis modo congruo administrare, scil. in prouinciis sibi mediate vel immediate subiectis. Sed forte huic allegationi respondebitur, quod electio, quae modo fit per principes electores, non succedit nec subrogata est in locu alterius electionis, quae fiebat a populo Romano vel exercitu, sed in locum successionis generis, quae erat post tempora Caroli tertii. Et ideo non retinebat ius & naturam illius electionis prioris, sed successionis generis. Sed haec responsio impugnatur, quia si electio, quae fit per principes electores, non succedit immediate illi electioni, quae fiebat antiquitus per populum Romanum seu exercitu, tamen successit illi mediate, & in locu illius subrogata est mediate electione, quae tempore multo post fiebat per imperatore, vel mediante successione generis. Secundum illum Doctorem semper Imperator Romanorum ante Caroli fiebat per successionem generis, vel per electionem factam per Imperatorem. Quare illa successio tempore Caroli sic fuit aut nulla: & quorundam successorum suorum secundum illum Doctorem: vel electio facta per Imperatorem secundum alios successit aliter alii modo constituendi regem seu Imperatorem Romanorum: & per consequens recipit ius & naturam illius & ille modus alius, quae per successionem generis, constituendi regem seu Imperatorem, erat electio a populo Romano vel exercitu: vel successit illi electioni. Igitur retinuit ius & naturam illius electionis, quae facta fuit antiquitus a populo Romano vel exercitu, secundum illum Doctorem. Electio quae modo fit per principes electores, recipit ius & naturam successionis generis, in cuius locum subrogata est successio generis secundum illum Doctorem ex quo secundum ipsum successio generis subrogari potest in locu electionis illius. Ex quo sequitur, q; sicut praedictu est in praecedenti allegatione, principes electores, qui modo sunt, non tantum modo repraesentant principes & populu Germaniae, Italiae & aliarum prouinciarum, quae erant subiectae Romano Imperio ante coronarione Imperiale, sed etiā repraesentant populos & principes aliarum prouinciarum, quae non erant subiectae Carolo Magno ante coronationem Imperiale, sed erant subiectae Romano Imperio. Nam principes, qui modo sunt electores, quamuis tñ immediate, tamen mediate in eligendo succedunt populo Romano vel exercitur. Ergo in eligendo retinet ius & naturā illius populi, scil. Romani, vel exercitus. Sed eligendo & secundu potestate eligendi repraesentabant totu populu Romano Imperio subiectu, vt etiā dicit iste Doctor. Igitur & principes electores nunc repraesentat totu populu Romano Imperio subiectu. Ex quo patet, quod sicut antiquitus Imperator electus per populu Romanu vel exercitum habuit plena potestatem supra totu Imperiu: ita & nunc habeat eandem potestate omnino & simpliciter inquantu rex Romanorum & inquantu Imperator. Tertio per fundamentu motiui, quo probat iste Doctor, q; electus per principes ex ipsa electione statim potest licite assumere nome regis in Germania, ac iura & bona regni Germaniae administrare, probatur, q; quo ad alia prouincia electus per principes electores habet omnino eandem potestate, inquantu rex & inquantu Imperator, & statim post iura & bona prouinciae eiusdem modo competenti sibi, mediate vel immediate administrare. Na nulla est prouincia siue regnum, quae vel quod, antequam esset Romanum imperium, non habuit rege vel Imperatorem, qui statim, quod possit esse rex constitutus siue per electionem siue per successionem, haberet potestatem administrandi modo competenti sibi iura & bona provinciae eiusdem siue regni. Sed ex hoc, quod eadem provincia subdebatur Romano imperio, non debuit esse deterioris conditionis: sicut nec conditio regni & Imperii in Germania, secundum illum Doctorem est deterior ex hoc, quod reges ipsius assecuti fuerunt Italiam & imperium. Sed si electus per principes electores ad Romanum Imperium non posset statim modo sibi competenti mediate vel immediate administrare bona & iura ipsius provinciae, siue regni, sed expectare oporteret coronationem Imperialem, quae ex causa longo tempore differri valeret: conditio provinciae esset deterior ex hoc, quod esset subiecta Romano imperio: quia propter huiusmodi expectationem per guerras & discordias possent mala quamplurima provenire, quae per administrationem electi cessare valent. Relinquitur igitur quod electus in Imperatorem ne conditio regni alicuius vel provinciae fiat deterior propter hoc, quod est subiecta Romano Imperio, statim habet de iure administrationem sibi competentem, scilicet mediatam vel immediatam. Videtur igitur quod pronunciatio principum Germaniae quod scil. rex Romanorum post electionem eandem habet potestatem omnino, quam habet Imperator, a veritate non discrepat, quia statim virtute electionis habet in provinciis Romano Imperio subiectis administrationem competentem sibi mediatam, vel immediatam. Quod adhuc tali modo probatur. Eadem res dicitur eodem iure censeri, licet secundum diversas partes posset diverso iure censeri: vt scilicet Romanum Imperium est vnum & idem, licet habeat diversas partes. Ergo licet diversae partes Imperii Romani possent diverso iure censeri, vt scil. electus in Imperatorem in vna parte Imperii idem homo prius habeat super illam potestatem regalem, & postea potestatem Imperialem. Quare rex Romanorum habet omnino eandem potestatem, quam habet Imperator super totum Imperium: & licet non habet eandem potestatem omnino super vnam partem, quam habet super aliam. Dicitur itaq; secundum istam opinionem ne oporteat concedere, quod Carolus Magnus fuit factus Imperator super nouum Imperium, vt antiquum Romanum Imperium a primis Imperatoribus & successoribus eorum possessum non fuit translatum in ipsum & qp Carolus Magnus non habuit omnem potestatem Imperialem, quam habuerunt ante ipsum Imperatores Romani.
units.tr: For whatever is substituted for another and succeeds to its place must receive and imitate the right and nature of the thing to which it succeeds and in whose place it is substituted: see ff. si quis cautionibus, l. si eum, §. qui iniuriarum, and ff. de condit. et demon., l. filia, §. Titia. To the same effect, Extr. de voto et voto redemptione, magne, de baptismo, maiores. And more expressly, Extr. ut lite pendente, c. ecclesia, 1. Where the Gloss says, on the word successerunt, this is an argument that a thing which succeeds to the place of another is judged by the same law as that thing. Natural reason also dictates this, that one could not properly say that something succeeds to the place of another unless it had the right and nature of the thing in whose place it succeeds and is substituted. But the election of the king and Emperor, which now takes place through the electoral princes, is substituted in the place of the succession or election which was formerly made by the Roman people, or by the army, which Roman people or army then represented the whole people subject to the Roman Empire, according to this Doctor. Therefore the election which is now made by the electoral princes will retain the right and nature of the election which was made by the Roman people or the army. But by that election, which was made by the Roman people or the army, the one elected at once assumed the name of king or Emperor, and administered the rights and goods of the kingdom and Empire in all the provinces subject by right to the Empire, and had altogether the same power as king of the Romans. Therefore the one now elected by the princes and electors in harmony, by such an election substituted in the place of that election which was made by the Roman people or the army, has altogether the same power as king of the Romans and as Emperor, and could lawfully assume the name of king and Emperor, and administer the rights and goods of the Empire not only in Germany, Italy and the other provinces which were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation, but also in the other provinces, in a manner fitting for him, namely in provinces subject to him either mediately or immediately. But perhaps it will be answered to this argument that the election now made by the electoral princes does not succeed to, nor is substituted in the place of, the other election which was made by the Roman people or the army, but in the place of the succession by blood which existed after the time of Charles III. And so it did not retain the right and nature of that earlier election, but of the succession by blood. But this answer is refuted, because if the election made by the electoral princes does not succeed immediately to that election which was formerly made by the Roman people or the army, nevertheless it succeeded to it mediately, and in its place is substituted, mediately, the election which, long afterwards, was made by the Emperor, or by succession by blood. According to that Doctor, the Roman king before Charles was always made either by succession by blood or by election made by the Emperor. Hence that succession in Charles's time was either null, or (according to that Doctor) that of some of his successors; or else the election made by the Emperor, according to others, succeeded to another mode of constituting a king or Emperor of the Romans, and consequently receives the right and nature of that mode; and that other mode of constituting a king or Emperor, which was by succession by blood, was an election made by the Roman people or the army, or succeeded to that election. Therefore it retained the right and nature of that election which was formerly made by the Roman people or the army, according to that Doctor. The election which is now made by the electoral princes receives the right and nature of the succession by blood, in whose place, according to that Doctor, succession by blood is substituted, since according to him succession by blood can be substituted in the place of that election. From this it follows that, as was said in the preceding argument, the electoral princes who now exist not only represent the princes and people of Germany, Italy and the other provinces which were subject to the Roman Empire before the imperial coronation, but also represent the peoples and princes of other provinces which were not subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation, but were subject to the Roman Empire. For the princes who are now electors, although immediately, nevertheless mediately, in electing succeed the Roman people or army. Therefore in electing they retain the right and nature of that people, namely the Roman people, or of the army. But in electing, and by the power of electing, they represented the whole Roman people subject to the Empire, as this same Doctor also says. Therefore the electoral princes now also represent the whole people subject to the Roman Empire. From this it is plain that, just as formerly an Emperor elected by the Roman people or the army had full power over the whole Empire, so now he has altogether the same power, simply, both as king of the Romans and as Emperor. Thirdly, by the foundation of the motive by which this Doctor proves that one elected by the princes may at once lawfully assume the name of king in Germany and administer the rights and goods of the kingdom of Germany, it is proved that, as regards the other provinces, the one elected by the electoral princes has altogether the same power, as king and as Emperor, and immediately afterwards may administer the rights and goods of the province in a manner fitting to him, mediately or immediately. For there is no province or kingdom which, before there was a Roman Empire, did not have a king or Emperor who, as soon as he could be constituted king, whether by election or by succession, had the power to administer the rights and goods of that same province or kingdom in a manner fitting to him. But from the fact that the same province was subject to the Roman Empire, it ought not to be of worse condition; just as the condition of the kingdom and Empire in Germany, according to that Doctor, is not worse because its kings obtained Italy and the Empire. But if the one elected by the electoral princes to the Roman Empire could not at once administer the goods and rights of that province or kingdom, mediately or immediately, in a manner fitting to him, but had to wait for the imperial coronation, which could be deferred for a long time for some cause, the condition of the province would be worse because it was subject to the Roman Empire; for on account of such waiting, many evils could arise through wars and discords, which cease through the administration of the elected man. It remains, therefore, that the one elected as Emperor, so that the condition of any kingdom or province does not become worse on account of its being subject to the Roman Empire, has by right at once the administration due to him, that is, mediate or immediate. It seems, therefore, that the declaration of the princes of Germany, namely that the king of the Romans after election has altogether the same power as the Emperor, does not depart from the truth, because at once, by virtue of the election, he has in the provinces subject to the Roman Empire the administration due to him, mediate or immediate. This is further proved in this way: the same thing is said to be judged by the same law, although in different parts it could be judged by different law; as the Roman Empire is one and the same, although it has different parts. Therefore, although different parts of the Roman Empire could be judged by different law, as, for example, the same man, elected Emperor, may first have royal power over one part of the Empire and afterwards imperial power. Hence the king of the Romans has altogether the same power as the Emperor over the whole Empire, even if he does not have altogether the same power over one part as he has over another. Therefore, according to this opinion, it is said that we need not concede that Charlemagne was made Emperor over a new Empire, as if the ancient Roman Empire, possessed by the first Emperors and their successors, had not been transferred to him, and that Charlemagne did not have all the imperial power which the Roman Emperors had before him.

units.la: Et quod Romanum Imperium ab illo tempore, quo mundus fuit sibi subiectus, quod fuit tempore natiuitatis Christi, pro ea quod tunc tota vniuersitas mortalium vni regi seu Imperatori subdebatur, qp est vnum de potissimis, quae ad principatum optimum requiruntur: non potuit de iure distrahi nec diminui, nec per praescriptionem nec per consuetudinem, nec per diuisionem nec per translationem, nec per aliquam ordinationem humanam, nisi forte singuli mortales huiusmodi distractioni vel diuisioni praeberet consensum. Nec potuit prouideri de Imperatore aliter quam per electionem: quia modus prouidendi per electionem potior est & melior, quam per generis successionem. Et ideo principes cunctorum mortalium per electionem non per generis successionem debent principatu supremum adipisci. Ius autem & potestas eligendi supremum principe vniuerso mortalium principaliter est apud Imperatorem: quia populus huiusmodi ius & potestatem condendi leges transtulit in imperatorem. Vnde & in principio Romani Imperii, & per multa tempora post, Imperator elegit consortem Imperii vel successorem. Si igitur Imperator habuit ius eligendi, vel alteri committendi ius eligendi, quando ipsemet non eligeret. Si autem Imperatore mortuo, & non substituto per ipsum Imperatore, cum nulli vel nullis commisisset in spirituali ius Imperatore eligendi, populus Romanus vel exercitus Romanus tanquam caput totius Imperii, haberet ius eligendi Imperatorem, qui non solum posset tunc eligere Imperatorem, sed etiam aliis vices suas committere. Quam commissionem Romanorum potest Imperator electus tunc approbare & confirmare, & illi tanquam repraesentantes vniuersitatem mortalium habent ius eligendi Imperatore, quando Imperator nullu elegit. Imperator insuper hanc habet potestatem, vt possit diuidere imperium, non quidem separando vnam partem ab Imperio, vt non subsit imperio vel Imperatori: sed potest diuidere Imperium in illam partem Imperii: quae immediate subiecta est Imperatori, & quae deputata est Imperatori ad onera Imperii sustinenda, vt aliqua pars illius partis non Imperatori, sed alicui inferiori Imperatore sit immediate subiecta, & Imperatori solummodo mediate: ita quod talis diuisio non redundet in detrimentum enorme Imperii.
units.tr: And that the Roman Empire, from the time when the world was made subject to it, which was at the time of the birth of Christ, since at that time the whole multitude of mortals was subject to one king or emperor (which is one of the chief requirements of the best principality), could not by right be divided or diminished, neither by prescription nor by custom, neither by partition nor by transfer, nor by any human ordinance, unless perhaps each of the mortals gave consent to such dismemberment or division. Nor could provision be made for the emperor otherwise than by election, because the mode of providing by election is more excellent and better than by succession of birth. And therefore the rulers of all mortals ought to obtain the supreme principate by election, not by succession of birth. The right and power of electing the supreme prince of all mortals, however, belongs principally to the emperor, because the people transferred this right and power of enacting laws to the emperor. Hence also at the beginning of the Roman Empire, and for many times afterwards, the emperor chose a partner in the Empire or a successor. If, therefore, the emperor had the right of electing, or of committing to another the right of electing, when he himself did not elect... But if, the emperor having died and no one having been appointed by him, since he had committed to no one or to no persons the right of electing an emperor in his place, the Roman people or the Roman army, as the head of the whole Empire, had the right of electing an emperor, who could not only then elect an emperor but also commit his own powers to others. The emperor elected may then approve and confirm this commission of the Romans, and they, as representatives of the whole multitude of mortals, have the right of electing the emperor when the emperor has elected no one. Moreover, the emperor has this power, that he may divide the empire, not indeed by separating one part from the Empire so that it would no longer be subject to the Empire or the emperor; but he may divide the Empire into that part of the Empire which is immediately subject to the emperor and which is assigned to the emperor for bearing the burdens of the Empire, so that some part of that part is immediately subject not to the emperor but to some inferior ruler, and to the emperor only mediately; provided that such a division does not turn to the enormous detriment of the Empire.

units.la: Et sicut potest tali modo diuidere Imperium, ita potest terras & regna, quae ex casu desinunt habere iustum regem & dominum, applicare & adiungere Imperio, hoc est illi parti Imperii, quae deputata est Imperatori ad onera communia Imperii perferenda: qui etiam posset regna, terras & provincias, quae & quas habuit iuste antequam esset Imperator, adiungere & applicare tali modo Imperio. Pro illis omnibus & singulis posset allegari multipliciter, sed causa brevitatis transeo. Iuxta ista dicitur, quod ista, quae narrant capitula chronicae & historiae, quas saepe dictus Doctor allegat, vera sunt. Sed dicitur, quod quaedam eorum possunt male intelligi. Verum enim est, quod Carolus Magnus reliquit regnum & Imperium Ludovico filio suo, sed non virtute consuetudinis Regnorum occidentalium, quae per generis successionem debentur: sed virtute potestatis Imperialis, qua potuit sibi successorem suum eligere, vel consortem Imperii: qua potestate Italiam seperauit ab aliis partibus, quas deputauit Imperatoribus pro oneribus Imperii perferendis: ita tamen Imperatori non immediate, sed mediate esset subiecta. Vnde quia Carolus Magnus tunc volens ex iusta causa habere pacem cum Graecis, qui occupabant terras plures & fere omnes quae erant subiectae immediate Imperatorib. successoribus suis, terras omnes praeter Italiam, quas habuit, cum esset Imperator, subiecit immediate Imperatori pro oneribus Imperii perferendis. Imo illae terrae & provinciae non erant de regno Francorum pro tunc: sed de regno seu Imperio Romanorum, licet quaedam pars illarum terrarum postea per Imperatorem habentem Imperiale potestatem eandem, quam habuit Carolus Magnus. magnus facta fuerit regnum per se vocatum Lothariense, & quædam pars alia fuit vocata regnum Germaniæ, quemadmodum Boemia quam tenuit Carolus magnus, quæ tunc non erat regnum per se, modo est regnum per se. Et sicut illa facta fuerunt de terris immediate subiectis imperatori: ita nunc consimilia fieri possent ex causa de terris immediate subiectis imperatori. Et de his, quæ desinunt habere dominos proprios immediatos, dummodo non essent in detrimentum enorme imperii: sed de terris immediate subiectis imperio, quæ habent dominos immediatos alios, non posset hoc facere imperator, nisi pro culpa vel ex causa rationabili apparenti propter bonum commune posset priuare dominos terris huiusmodi. quia quamuis omnia sint imperatoris, tanquam supremi domini, tamen non omnia sunt imperatoris isto modo, quo bona servi sunt domini. 10 quia subiecti imperatori non sunt servi imperatoris, sed sunt liberi; propter vtilitatem & commodum etiam principatus imperialis, si est vere regalis principaliter institutus. Sicut autem filius Caroli magni successit Carolo magno in imperio non virtute consuetudinis regnorum occidentalium, quæ iure successionis debetur, sed per electionem Caroli magni, qui specialiter filium elegit in imperatorem, & constituit eum imperatorem: ita etiam filius illius eodem modo successit illi, & omnes filii imperatorum siue primogeniti siue alii, qui patribus in imperio successerunt, non successerunt iure primogeniturę vel iure successionis. vnde & aliquando non habuerunt terras, quas habuerunt patres: sed successerunt tanquam electi à patribus suis vel aliis, qui nō eligentibus patribus imperatoribus habebant ius & potestatem eligendi. Et propter id verum est, quod dicunt historiæ & chronicæ, quod licet aliquando Italia fuerit separata à Germania, tamen postea fuit sibi vnita, non tamen sic quod Italia accederet tanquam regnum accessorium principali respectu alterius; sed vniebatur sic, quod vtrunq; accedebat vrbi Romanæ tanquam capiti; quia ipsa erat caput mundi. In cuius signum imperator non vocatur communiter imperator Germanorum vel Italorum, sed Romanorum. Si igitur aliquando inuenitur, quod filius successit in imperio patri suo iure hereditario, non debet sic intelligi, quod filius habuit ius vendicandi imperium absq; electione speciali patris, qua specialiter constitueretur imperator, quemadmodum in regnis & principatibus pluribus ac dominiis filius patri etiam de bonis suis specialiter ordinanti successit. Sed propter hoc diceretur filius iure hereditario successere patri, quod pater eligendo filium ad imperium, & constituendo eum imperatorem & successorem suum, quodammodo ipsum specialiter heredem suum instituit dando scilicet sibi in imperio ius, quod habet. Quod enim sic constitutus imperator ab imperatore potest vocari heres imperatoris, quamuis nihil iuris penitus haberet in imperio, nisi specialiter eligeretur & constitueretur imperator per imperatorem; probatur per hoc, quod heres nihil penitus haberet in imperio iuris aliunde, quam successio in vniuersum ius, quod defunctus habuit. ff. de re. iuris. nihil. Vnde illo modo quilibet imperator à quocunq; vel à quibuscunq; eligatur, posset dici heres imperatoris defuncti, cum succeðat in vniuersum ius, quod defunctus habuit. Et illo modo legitur in chronicis Otthonis Frisingensis, quod Iulius Cæsar Octavianum nepotem suum adoptauit in filium, & nomen suum ferre iussit.
units.tr: And just as he can divide the Empire in this manner, so he can annex and attach to the Empire lands and kingdoms which by chance cease to have a lawful king and lord, that is, to that part of the Empire which is assigned to the emperor for bearing the common burdens of the Empire; he who could also annex and attach in this manner to the Empire kingdoms, lands and provinces which he had lawfully held before he became emperor. Many arguments could be brought forward for all and each of these points, but for the sake of brevity I pass them over. In accordance with these things it is said that those things which the chronicles and histories, which the aforesaid Doctor often cites, relate, are true. But it is said that some of them can be wrongly understood. It is true that Charles the Great left the kingdom and the Empire to his son Louis, but not by virtue of the custom of the western kingdoms, which are owed by succession of birth, but by virtue of the imperial power by which he could choose his successor or partner in the Empire; by which power he separated Italy from the other parts, which he assigned to the emperors for bearing the burdens of the Empire, yet in such a way that it would be subject to the emperor not immediately but mediately. Hence, since Charles the Great then, wishing for peace with the Greeks for a just cause, who occupied many lands and nearly all those which were subject immediately to him and his successors, made all the lands which he held, except Italy, while he was emperor, immediately subject to the emperor for bearing the burdens of the Empire. Indeed those lands and provinces were not then of the kingdom of the Franks, but of the kingdom or Empire of the Romans, although some part of those lands was afterwards made by an emperor possessing the same imperial power that Charles the Great had into a kingdom called by itself Lotharingia, and another part was called the kingdom of Germany, just as Bohemia, which Charles the Great held, which was then not a kingdom by itself, is now a kingdom by itself. And just as those were made from lands immediately subject to the emperor, so now similar things could be done for a cause from lands immediately subject to the emperor. And this applies to those things which cease to have their own immediate lords, provided they were not to the enormous detriment of the Empire; but for lands immediately subject to the Empire which have other immediate lords, the emperor could not do this, unless, on account of a fault or for a reasonable apparent cause for the common good, he could deprive the lords of such lands. For although all things belong to the emperor as supreme lord, yet not all things belong to the emperor in the same way that the goods of a slave belong to his master. For those subject to the emperor are not slaves of the emperor, but are free; for the advantage and benefit also of the imperial principate, if it is truly instituted as royal in its primary character. But just as the son of Charles the Great succeeded Charles the Great in the Empire, not by virtue of the custom of the western kingdoms, which is owed by right of succession, but by the election of Charles the Great, who specially chose his son as emperor and appointed him emperor: so also the son of that one succeeded him in the same way; and all sons of emperors, whether firstborn or others, who succeeded their fathers in the Empire, did not succeed by right of primogeniture or by right of succession. Hence also they sometimes did not have the lands which their fathers had, but succeeded as chosen by their fathers or by others who, when the emperor-fathers did not elect, had the right and power of electing. And therefore it is true, what the histories and chronicles say, that although at times Italy was separated from Germany, yet afterwards it was united to it, not however in such a way that Italy was joined as a kingdom accessory to the other as principal; but it was united in such a way that both were joined to the city of Rome as to a head, because it was itself the head of the world. As a sign of this, the emperor is commonly called not emperor of the Germans or of the Italians, but of the Romans. If therefore it is sometimes found that a son succeeded his father in the Empire by hereditary right, it should not be understood as meaning that the son had the right to claim the Empire without a special election by the father, by which he was specially constituted emperor; just as in many kingdoms, principalities and dominions a son succeeded his father who had specially provided for him even in regard to his goods. But for this reason it would be said that the son succeeded his father by hereditary right, because the father, by electing his son to the Empire and constituting him emperor and his successor, in a certain manner specially instituted him as his heir, namely by giving him in the Empire the right which he himself holds. For that the emperor so constituted can be called heir of the emperor, although he would have no right at all in the Empire unless he were specially elected and constituted emperor by the emperor, is proved by this: that an heir would have no right at all in the Empire from any other source than the succession to the whole right which the deceased had. ff. de re. iuris. nihil. Hence in that way whoever is elected emperor by whomsoever or by whatsoever persons could be called heir of the deceased emperor, since he succeeds to the whole right which the deceased had. And in that way it is read in the chronicles of Otto of Freising that Julius Caesar adopted his nephew Octavian as son and ordered him to bear his name.

units.la: CAP. IV. Secundum opinionem ca. tertio recitatam dat solutionem ad principalem quæstionem, & similiter ostendit, vter præstantiorem conditionem habeat, an electus in regem, an hereditarie sucedens.
units.tr: CAP. IV. According to the opinion recited in the third chapter, he gives a solution to the principal question, and likewise shows which of the two has the better condition: the one elected king, or the one succeeding by hereditary right.

units.la: Viso, quomodo opinio recitata superius ca. præcedenti propter motiua ante dicti doctoris, sicut & propter quædam alia, quorum aliqua hic reticentur, non solum ti, quod electus in regem seu imperatorem Romanum à principibus electoribus potest ex ipsa electione statim nomen regis assumere, & iura ac bona regni & imperii in Italia & in aliis prouinciis eiusdem regni, quæ erant subiectæ Carolo magno, ante coronationem imperialem administrare: sed etiam ti, quod potest statim nomen regis assumere, nisi forte sit solummodo propter aliquod scandalum euitandum, acíura & bona totius imperii in Italia, Græcia, Francia, India, aliisq; prouinciis Romani imperii modo competenti subiectis imperiali potestati mediate vel immediate de iure administrare, propter quod pronunciationem præscriptam principum Germaniæ arbitrantur consonam veritati. Videndum est, quomodo ista opinio respondet ad formam propositæ quæstionis. dicitur igitur, quod canonica electio principum electorum ex natura rei electionis, quę est ordinata, quis minus rationabiliter posset alia ordinari, dat electo in regem Romanorum in terris & prouinciis, quæ tempore electionis sunt immediate subiectæ imperio, quæcunq; sint illæ, quantum dat legitima successio regi hereditarie succeðenti, præsertim si regnum regis hereditarie succeðentis non plus suo modo deficiat ab optimo modo monarchiæ regalis, vel ei plus appropinquet quam regnum regis per electionem succeðentis, puta si subiecti huiusmodi regis hereditarie succeðentis sint servi eius, vel magis appropinquent conditioni servili, quam subiecti imperio, qui illo modo sunt liberi, quo subiecti optimo modo monarchiæ regalis sunt facti liberi: vel minus appropinquent conditioni servili, quam subiecti huiusmodi regis: tunc canonica electio principum electorum, quantum ad aliquid, daret minus electo in regem Romanorum, quam legitima successio regi hereditario succeðenti, imo quantum ad aliquid daret sibi minus, quā dat legitima successio.
units.tr: Having seen how the opinion recited in the previous chapter stands, on the reasons of the said doctor and on certain others, some of which are passed over here, I hold not only that the one elected king or Roman emperor by the prince-electors can at once, from the election itself, take the name of king and administer the rights and goods of the kingdom and empire in Italy and in the other provinces of that kingdom which were subject to Charlemagne before the imperial coronation. I hold also that he can at once take the name of king, unless perhaps this is withheld solely to avoid some scandal, and can lawfully administer, by right, the rights and goods of the whole empire in Italy, Greece, France, India, and the other provinces subject to the Roman empire in the present manner, whether mediately or immediately subject to imperial power. For this reason they judge the aforesaid declaration of the princes of Germany to agree with the truth. It must now be considered how this opinion corresponds to the form of the question proposed. It is said, then, that the canonical election of the prince-electors, from the nature of the act of election, which is so ordered that it could hardly be ordered otherwise by reason, gives to the one elected king of the Romans, in the lands and provinces which at the time of the election are immediately subject to the empire, whatever they may be, as much as lawful succession gives to a king succeeding by hereditary right. This holds especially if the kingdom of the king succeeding by hereditary right falls short of the best form of royal monarchy no more than the kingdom of the king succeeding by election does, or comes closer to it. Suppose, for example, that the subjects of such a king succeeding by hereditary right are his slaves, or come closer to the condition of slavery than the subjects of the empire do (for these are free in the way that the subjects of the best form of royal monarchy have been made free), or come less close to the condition of slavery than the subjects of such a king do. Then the canonical election of the prince-electors would, in some respects, give less to the one elected king of the Romans than lawful succession gives to a king succeeding by hereditary right; indeed, in some respects it would give him less than lawful succession gives.

units.la: K k cesio militi vel alicui habenti seruos puros hereditario iure. quia plus potest in multis despotes seu dominus super seruos; quia quicquid acquirunt, domino suo acquirunt; & dominus pro libito suo potest eos de iure dare vendere & legare modisq; aliis alienare; ꝭ non posset imperator super sibi subiectos: si quidem imperium continetur sub optimo modo monarchiae regalis, & optimi principatus natura, qui in hoc consistit, quod est constitutus propter commune bonum subiectorum, & non propter utilitatem & gloriam principantis, nisi forte ex continenti & secundario. & imo quanto subiecti gaudent maiori libertate, quae non est corruptio tranquillitatis & pacis, nec repugnat bono communi subiectorum, tanto principatus est melior & nobilior. unde imperator vel rex optimo praeeminens principatu, qui sit omni alii principatui impermixtus, habet subiectos tam liberos, ut ipsi de iure absq; culpa eorum, nisi causa fuerit manifesta, non possint priuari rebus & libertatibus suis vel iuribus; nec quicquid acquirunt, regi vel imperatori acquirunt, sic ut pro libito suo de iure posset taliter acquisitum accipere & retinere vel dare, cui sibi placuerit: quamuis tamen secundario ex casu multa potest, quae dominus potest super eos, qui sibi sunt conditione seruili subiecti. veruntamen hoc non obstante, canonica electio principum electorum plus quantum ad aliqua dat electo in regem Romanorum, quam dat legitima successio regi hereditarie succedenti, etiam si regnum Romanorum non sicut aliud regnum continentur sub optimo modo monarchiae regalis. & hoc supposito, quod aliud regnum sit subiectum regno seu imperio. quia multae causae in regno hereditarie successentis per appellationem vel alio modo possent deferri ad imperatorem, in quibus imperator seu electus in regem Romanorum haberet potestatem iudicandi, & non rex hereditarie succedens; sed tales causae in terris immediate subiectis imperio non possent oriri. ita igitur quantum ad potestatem huiusmodi electio canonica principum electorum plus dat electo in regem Romanorum, quam legitima successio regi hereditarie succedenti, propter hoc, quod rex Romanorum non habet superiorem, & rex hereditarie succedens habet superiorem super se. quantum vero ad terras, quae sunt immediate subiectae imperatori, electio in regem canonica electorum principum, quantum ad aliquid minus dat electo in regem Romanorum, quae legitima successio regi hereditarie succedenti, & quantum ad aliquid dat sibi plus minus. n. sibi dat, quantum ad administrationem bonorum & iurium aliarum terrarum, quae constituunt in recipiendis fructibus earum, in instituendis iudicib. officialibus, in eisdem conferendis, & aliis pluribus ad iurisdictionem & principatum regalem & interiorem spectantibus. quantum ad aliquid plus dat electio canonica principum electo in regem Romanorum, quae dat legitima successio regi hereditarie succedenti, eum dictum sit, quod imperator seu electus in regem Romanorum habet potestatem diffiniendi causas in ipso regno regis hereditarie succedentis: quia non potest diffinire ipse rex hereditarie succedens. potest etiam electus in regem Romanorum quosdam actus reseruatos imperatori exercere in terris non sibi immediate subiectis, quos non potest exercere rex hereditarie succedens, nisi ex concessione imperatoris vel consuetudine collata ab imperatore; quare quantum ad huiusmodi actus reseruatos imperatori, ipsa electio canonica plus dat electo in regem Romanorum, quam dat legitima successio regi hereditarie succedenti.
units.tr: K k [the signature mark is omitted here] grant to a soldier, or to anyone holding pure slaves by hereditary right. For a despot [δεσπότης] or master can do more over slaves in many respects, since whatever they acquire they acquire for their master, and the master may by right, at his pleasure, give, sell, bequeath, and alienate them in other ways. An emperor could not do so over his subjects, since the empire is contained under the best form of royal monarchy, and the nature of the best principality, which consists in this, is that it is established for the common good of the subjects, and not for the advantage and glory of the ruler, except perhaps incidentally and secondarily. Indeed, the more the subjects enjoy greater liberty, which is no corruption of tranquillity and peace and does not oppose the common good of the subjects, the better and nobler the principality is. Hence an emperor or king who excels in the best principality, which is unmixed with any other principality, has subjects so free that by right they cannot, without their fault, unless the cause is manifest, be deprived of their goods, their liberties, or their rights; nor whatever they acquire do they acquire for the king or emperor, so that he could by right take or keep such acquisitions at his pleasure, or give them to whomever he likes. Yet by accident he may secondarily do many things that a master may do over those who are subject to him in servile condition. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, the canonical election of the prince-electors gives more in some respects to the one elected king of the Romans than lawful succession gives to a king succeeding by hereditary right, even though the kingdom of the Romans is not contained under the best form of royal monarchy as other kingdoms are. And this holds on the supposition that another kingdom is subject to the kingdom or empire, because many causes in the kingdom of the king succeeding by hereditary right could be brought before the emperor by appeal or in some other way, in which the emperor, or the one elected king of the Romans, would have the power of judging, and not the king succeeding by hereditary right; but such causes could not arise in lands immediately subject to the empire. So, as regards this power, the canonical election of the prince-electors gives more to the one elected king of the Romans than lawful succession gives to a king succeeding by hereditary right, because the king of the Romans has no superior, whereas the king succeeding by hereditary right has a superior over him. As regards the lands that are immediately subject to the emperor, the canonical election of the prince-electors to the kingship gives the one elected king of the Romans in some respects less than lawful succession gives to a king succeeding by hereditary right, and in some respects more or less. For it gives him, as regards the administration of the goods and rights of the other lands, what consists in receiving their revenues, in appointing judges and officials, in conferring those offices, and in many other matters pertaining to jurisdiction and to royal and internal authority. In some respects the canonical election of the prince-electors gives more to the one elected king of the Romans than lawful succession gives to a king succeeding by hereditary right, since it has been said that the emperor, or the one elected king of the Romans, has the power of determining causes in the very kingdom of the king succeeding by hereditary right, because the king succeeding by hereditary right cannot determine them himself. The one elected king of the Romans can also exercise certain acts reserved to the emperor in lands not immediately subject to him, which the king succeeding by hereditary right cannot exercise except by a grant of the emperor or by custom conferred by the emperor. Therefore, as regards such acts reserved to the emperor, the canonical election itself gives the one elected king of the Romans more than lawful succession gives to a king succeeding by hereditary right.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Ponit solutiones ad probationes positas primo ca. pro prima opinione, quo ad utrumque modum ponendi. deinde recitat errores in extravagantibus Io. 22. positos.
units.tr: He gives the answers to the arguments put forward for the first opinion, in respect of both ways of putting it, and then recites the errors set out in the Extravagants of John XXII.

units.la: HIs opinionib. recitatis, secundum eas respondendum est ad allegationes, quae contra eas militare videntur. Primo autem videndum est, quomodo per istam opinionem respondetur ad ea quae supra primo cap. pro prima opinione adducta sunt. Unde ad primum, cum probatur quod non electio, sed confirmatio vel approbatio seu nominatio vel coronatio a Papa habenda dat administrationem electo in regem Romanorum, cum fit vasallus Papae & ei iuramentum fidelitatis & homagii praestare teneatur. Respondetur negando assumptum. non enim est vasallus Papae, nec praestare tenetur huiusmodi iuramentum. Quod si praestaret sibi fidelitatis & homagii iuramentum, eo ipso faceret se non imperatorem Romanorum: quia non posset uti eo iure, quo poterant uti antiquitus imperatores Romani, & per consequens extunc non deberet reputari successor eorum. Ad secundum, cum dicitur, imperium est a Papa, negatur: quia sicut a principio non fuit ita, & nunc non est a Papa, quia idem est nunc quod fuit ab initio.
