Ad tertium cum dicitur, electus in regem Romanorum nihil petere tenetur a Papa: Respondetur, quod electus nihil tenetur petere a Papa de necessitate: sed tamen tenetur sequi informationes eius consonas fidei Christianae, & ministrare sibi carnalia necessaria sibi. Ad quartum cum dicitur, quod Papa potest deponere imperatorem, dicitur quod non potest regulariter deponere Imperatorem: sed si imperator deponendus est, hoc est per illos, qui repraesentant populos Romano imperio subiectos, siue sint Romani, siue sint principes electores, siue quicunque; alii casualiter aut posset Papa deponere imperatorem. deficientib. omnib. aliis, ad quos prius depositio imperatoris spectaret. sed si imperator esset deponend, & illi, ad quos pertinet depositio ei, deficerent siue per ignorantiam siue per malitiam aut per negligentiam dabilem. abilem, rex quicunque alius habens potestatem temporalem sufficientem in aliquo casu licite ipsum deponeret. Liceret etiam alicui nulla prædito dignitate occidere talem imperatorem in aliquo casu. Non est autem vniuersaliter sine omni exceptione verum, quod qui potest aliquē deponere de aliqua dignitate, potest sibi eandem restituere. Nam imperator, & similiter Papa, potest seipsum deponere de dignitate imperiali vel papali, & tamen non potest seipsum instituere. Similiter archiepiscopus in causa potest alicui episcopo prælato inferiori auferre prælaturam, quam tamen sibi non potest conferre. Ad quintum, cum accipitur, quod Papa habet plenitudinem potestatis tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus; Respondetur negando assumptum, sicut dicunt plures opiniones ex præcedentibus quæstionibus recitatæ. Ad sextum cum dicitur, quod in vniuerso mundo oporteat esse vnum caput, habens potestatem à Papa, cum ipse à solo Deo habeat potestatem; Respondetur, quod regulariter & rationabiliter poneretur vnum supremum caput ad iuste coercendum omnes malefactores. illud tamen caput non debet esse Papa, quia Imperator per potentiam diuinam est exclusus, quia præceptum est, ne regulariter temporalibus negotiis se intromittat, sicut superius multipliciter est probatum, licet casualiter aliis deficientibus se posset huiusmodi negotiis implicare, quando vrgens necessitas vel euidens vtilitas, quæ necessitati valeat comparari, hoc poposcit, quia sicut in corpore naturali vno membro deficiente aliud, si aliquo modo potest, supplet defectum ipsius: qui enim non potest pedibus ambulare, aliter se portat vel voluit se vt potest: & mancus ore, accipit de terra vel alio loco, si potest, cibum necessarium sibi: & qui non potest culcello scindere panem suum, scindit aut diuidit dentibus si potest. Sic in corpore mystico, & in collegio seu vniuersitate, vno deficiente, alius si habet potentiam, supplet defectum eius. vbi autem non sunt milites, rustici pugnant pro patria, si possunt: & deficientibus viris, mulieres, si valeant, patriam & seipsas defendunt. Sic Papa & clerici, deficientibus laicis, se debent secularibus reipublicæ necessariis immiscere, ab aliis tamen, quæ possunt à laicis expediri, abstinere tenentur. Ad septimum cum dicitur, quod Papa habet vtrunq; gladium: dicitur, quod regulariter Papa non habet vtrunque sed tantummodo à Christo gladium spiritualem, saluis iuribus & libertatibus aliorum omnium, quæ & quas absq; culpa & sine causa minime tollere potest. casualiter autem vrgente necessitate vel euidenti vtilitate potest Papa aliquo modo per se vel per alios vti vtroq; gladio. nec mirum, quia et casualiter posset rusticus vti gladio materiali contra imperatorem. regulariter igitur ex ordinatione Christi Papa gladium materialem non habet, sed oportet eum à negociis secularibus abstinere. ita etiam ex ordinatione Christi iura & libertates quorumcunq; non debet diminuere vel turbare, nec etiam de rebus eorum vltra necessitates suas pro victu & vestitu & pro exercendo suo officio vendicare. Sed pro huiusmodi potest & hoc de illis rebus, quas laici voluerunt ad prædicta deputare, dummodo ipsius Papæ necessitatibus satis fit. Omnia autem, quæ vltra illa, quæ sibi necessaria sunt, possidet, sc. ciuitates, castra, aplas possessiones & superabundantes, & iurisdictionem temporalem quamcunq;, sicut & omnem gloriam mundanam, qua Papa nunc rutilat, vel habet ex largitate imperatorum, regum vel aliorum fidelium, vel sibi tyrannice & damnabiliter contra Deum & rationem ac bonos mores vsurpat. vn in his, quæ licite possidet, non Petro sed Constantino & aliis imperatoribus ac regibus & aliis fidelib. qui Papæ hæc contulerunt, succedit: non tñ sic succedit eis vt tanquam plenum ius in reb. & iuribus sibi datis possideat, sicut illi qui dederūt. quia res supra has virtutes ex pura largitate fidelium sibi concessas tenetur de necessitate salutis ad intentionem dantium dispensare. Et si dispensauerit aliter, committendo furtum imo peculatum, si habet vñ, ad restitutionem tenetur.
units.tr: With these opinions recited, we must now answer, in line with them, the arguments that seem to tell against them. First, then, we must see how, on this opinion, the points raised above in the first chapter for the first opinion are answered. As to the first: when it is proved that the one elected King of the Romans receives the administration not from his election but from confirmation, approval, nomination or coronation by the Pope, since he becomes the Pope's vassal and is bound to swear fealty and homage to him, the answer is to deny the assumption. He is not the Pope's vassal, nor is he bound to take such an oath. Indeed, if he did swear fealty and homage to the Pope, he would by that very act cease to be Emperor of the Romans, because he could not exercise the rights which the Roman emperors could exercise in former times, and consequently from then on he could not be regarded as their successor. As to the second: when it is said that the empire is from the Pope, this is denied, because it was not so from the beginning, and it is not from the Pope now either, since what it is now is what it was from the start. As to the third: when it is said that the one elected King of the Romans is not bound to ask anything of the Pope, the answer is that the elected king is not bound of necessity to ask anything of the Pope; yet he is bound to follow his instructions, so far as they agree with the Christian faith, and to supply him with the carnal necessities that he needs. As to the fourth: when it is said that the Pope can depose the Emperor, the answer is that he cannot ordinarily depose the Emperor; but if the Emperor is to be deposed, this must be done by those who represent the peoples subject to the Roman empire, whether they be Romans, or princes electors, or whoever else; and only by chance could the Pope depose the Emperor, when all the others to whom the deposition of the Emperor would first belong were lacking. But if the Emperor were to be deposed, and those to whom the deposition belongs were to fail, whether through ignorance or malice or culpable negligence, then any other king who had sufficient temporal power could lawfully depose him in some case. In some case, too, anyone at all, even without any dignity, could lawfully kill such an emperor. It is not, however, universally and without any exception true that whoever can depose someone from a dignity can restore the same dignity to him. For the Emperor, and likewise the Pope, can depose himself from imperial or papal dignity, and yet cannot institute himself. Similarly, an archbishop in a cause can take the prelacy from a lower bishop who is subject to him, though he cannot confer it on himself. As to the fifth: when it is taken that the Pope has the fullness of power both in temporal and in spiritual matters, the answer is to deny the assumption, as the several opinions recited in the preceding questions maintain. As to the sixth: when it is said that there must be one head in the whole world, having power from the Pope, since he himself has power from God alone, the answer is that one supreme head would ordinarily and reasonably be appointed to restrain all evildoers justly; yet that head ought not to be the Pope, because the Emperor is excluded by divine power, since it has been commanded that he should not ordinarily meddle with temporal affairs, as has been proved above in many ways. Still, when the others are lacking, he may by chance involve himself in such affairs, when pressing necessity or evident advantage, which may be weighed against necessity, calls for it. For just as in the natural body, when one member fails, another supplies its defect in whatever way it can: he who cannot walk on his feet carries himself as best he can or wishes to; and one who is maimed in the mouth takes from the ground or elsewhere the food he needs, if he can; and one who cannot cut his bread with a knife cuts or divides it with his teeth, if he can. So too in the mystical body, and in a college or university, when one fails, another, if he has the power, supplies his defect. Where there are no soldiers, the country folk fight for their homeland, if they can; and when men are lacking, women, if they are able, defend the homeland and themselves. So the Pope and the clergy, when laymen are lacking, ought to involve themselves in the secular necessities of the commonwealth, yet they are bound to abstain from those matters which can be dispatched by laymen. As to the seventh: when it is said that the Pope has both swords, the answer is that ordinarily the Pope does not have both, but only the spiritual sword from Christ, saving the rights and liberties of all others, which he can by no means take away without fault and without cause. By chance, however, when pressing necessity or evident advantage calls for it, the Pope may in some way, himself or through others, use both swords. Nor is this strange, since by chance a country man could also use a material sword against the Emperor. Ordinarily, therefore, by the ordinance of Christ, the Pope does not have the material sword, but he ought to abstain from secular business. So too, by the ordinance of Christ, he ought not to diminish or disturb the rights and liberties of anyone whatever, nor claim for himself the goods of others beyond his needs for food and clothing and for the exercise of his office. But for such purposes he may use those goods which laymen have wished to assign to these ends, provided that the needs of the Pope himself are sufficiently met. All that he possesses beyond what is necessary for him, namely cities, castles, ample possessions and superabundant wealth, and any temporal jurisdiction whatever, as also all the worldly glory in which the Pope now shines, he either has from the bounty of emperors, kings or other faithful people, or usurps for himself tyrannically and culpably against God, reason and good morals. Thus, in those things which he lawfully possesses, he succeeds not Peter but Constantine and the other emperors and kings and faithful persons who conferred these things on the Pope; yet he does not so succeed them as to possess these things and rights given to him as if he held full right over them, as those who gave them did. For he is bound, as a matter of necessity for salvation, to dispense the goods conceded to him beyond these needs, from the pure bounty of the faithful, according to the intention of the givers. And if he has dispensed them otherwise, committing theft or indeed peculation, if he has the means, he is bound to restitution.

units.la: Hæc & quamplura alia ad materiam istam spectantia videntur manifeste probari per beatum Bernard. qui li. de consid. ad Eugenium Papam ait: In criminibus non in possessionibus est potestas vestra propter illa siquidem & non propter has accepistis claues regni cælorum. Et in eodem ait: quid tibi aliud dimisit Petrus nisi, quod habeo, inquit, hoc tibi do. Quid illud fuit scio: non est aurum & argentum: cum ipse dicat aurum & argentum non est mihi. Esto vt alia quacunq; ratione hos tibi vendises sed non apostolico iure. Nec n. ille dare tibi potuit, quod non habuit. dedit sollicitudinem super ecclesias, nunquid dominationem? Audi ipsum: Non dominantes ait in clero sed forma facti gregis ex animo. Et ne putes hoc dictum sola humilitate, non in veritate: lex est Domini in euangelio: Reges gentium dominantur eorum: & qui potestatem habent, benefici vocantur: vos autem non sic. Planum est igitur, quod apostolis interdixit dominationem eorum: quo ergo tu vsurpare audes aut dominatus apostolatum aut apostolatus dominatum? planum est, quod ab vtroq; simul prohiberis. si vtrunq; simul habere voles, perdes vtrunq;. alioquin non te exceptū illorum numero putes, de quibus conqueritur Deus: Ipsi regnauerunt & non ex me: principes exiterunt, & ego non cognoui eos. si interdictum habemus: audiamus edictum: Qui maior est vestrum fiat sicut minor & qui præcessor est sicut qui ministrat. Forma apostolica hoc est dominatio interdicitur, conceditur administratio. Item in eodem ait: Errasti vt supremam, ita & solam institutam à Deo vestram apostolicam potestatem existimas. si hoc sentis dissentis ab eo qui ait: Non est potestas nisi à Deo. ad Rom. 13. quod sequitur: Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Denique idem ait: Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita est. non ait, sublimiori, tanquam in vno, sed sublimioribus. tanquam in multis. Item in eodem ait: Nō monstrabunt puto, qui hoc dicunt, vbi quispiam apostolorum iudex sedit hominum. Et infra: Stetisse denique lego apostolos iudicados: sed sse iudicates non lego. Item in eodem ait: Quis mihi det vt videa ecclesiam Dei sicut in diebus antiquis, quando apostoli laxabat retia sua in capturam non aurei: sed in capturam animarum. Quis mihi det vt audiā vocem tuam, vocem illam virtutis: petunia tua tecum sitim in perditionem. Item in eodem ait: Abiectus eram de domo Dei mei: quale est hoc depauperē & abiecto, leuor super gentes & reges, & ita sicut & propheta cū similiter leuaretur audiuit, vt tuellas destruas, & dissipes, & edifices & plantes: qua horū fastū sonant: rustica magis vita sonant, in quib. labor spiritualis expressus est. Et nos igitur, vt multum sentiamus de nobis: impositum sentiamus ministerium non dominium datum. Et ita disce sarculo opus esse modo suscepto vt opus facias propheta. Item in eodem ait: Non es tamen ille, qui propheta: Et omnis terra possessio eius. Christus est qui possessionem sibi vendicat, & hoc iure creationis & meritò redemptionis & merito patris, cui alteri dictum est: Postula à me & dabo tibi gentes, &c. An possessionem & dominium considere habuit vt curam illius habeas? Pars tua hęc plenitudine extendas manum tuam vt prasis, sed procura vt sernias & prouideas: prasis vt prosis vt fidelis seruus & prudens quem constituit dominus super familiam suam. Ad hoc enim prelatus es vt dispenses non vt impereś. Hoc fac & dominari ne affectes omnibus hominibus, vt non dominetur homo cum omni iniustitia, ergo si te cognoscis debitorem, non dominatorem putandum summopere est. Ex his verbis B. Bernardi aliisq; compluribus eiusdem, quæ ex auctoribus noui testamenti dictisque sanctorum colliguntur: quidam credunt, quod omnino erroneum est dicere, quod Papa ex ordinatione Christi regulariter habeat vtrumq; gladium, & quod habet plenitudinem potestatis tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus, vt omnia possit, quæ non sunt contraria diuinum, & omnes obliget orthodoxos. Quorum quidam ex eis conantur concludere, quod Papa ex ordinatione Christi nullam habet potestatem coactiuam omnino. alii autem hoc non concedunt; sed ex scripturis diuinis & auctoribus sanctorum & sacris canonibus credunt se demonstratiue colligere, quod Papa ex ordinatione Christi habet principatum principaliter institutum propter vtilitatem & commodum subiectorum, saluis iuribus & libertatibus aliorum, vt apostolicus principatus principatus mundanos præcellat in duobus. primo quia spiritualia administrat non temporalia, nisi casualiter & ex necessitate. Secundo quia apostolicus principatus institutus à Christo quantum ad hoc institutus est propter vtilitatem & profectum subiectorum excluso omni principatu despotico, & qui non est optimus, nec est omnino impermixtus. Et sic de illo principatu dominatiuo, qui vocabulo sumpto ex idiomate græco vocatur despoticus, nihil penitus habeat. Et hoc voluit (secundum istos) Bern. dicens: forma apostolica hęc est. dominatio interdicitur, & scilicet, nobis sentiamus ministerium non dominium datum. Et quando dicit, dominari ne affectes omnibus hominibus. sed & sic intelligenda sunt secundum illos verba B. Petri, non dominantes in clero. verùtamen istos damnare oporeat omnes summos pontifices, qui multum de principatu despotico habuerunt, nec omnem principatum despoticum abdicauerunt: quia in hoc B. Petrum & quosdam alios principales nequaquam imitati fuerunt. Dicunt, quod verba B. Bern. prędicta, & similia tam ipsius quam aliorum patrum, sicut & verba scripturæ diuinæ, in quibus fundantur, sane debeant intelligi, vt scilicet Christus instituerit prędictum apostolicum statum & principatum, vt summi pontifices, qui ipso in sua potestate absq; omni permixtione cuiuslibet alterius principatus vellent esse contenti, laudem & gloriam acquirerent singularem, & essent remunerandi in vita beatâ præmio spirituali: qui autem nollent ad hoc nō essent astricti: & quantum ad illos, qui se ad illud nequaquam voto astrinxerunt, magis est lex consilii quam præcepti: quia quamuis Christus nullam principatum despoticum imposuerit vicario suo, non tamen sibi per præceptum interdixit, sed sub conditione. si in hoc eius vellet seruare consilium. Et sic potest intelligi illud verbum B. Bern. Dominatio interdicitur, scilicet volentibus sequi consilium Christi & apostolos, qui se sponte inuitauerunt ad dictum consilium imitari Christum.
units.tr: These and many other points bearing on this subject seem clearly to be proved by the blessed Bernard, who in his book On Consideration, addressed to Pope Eugenius, says: "It is over crimes, not over possessions, that your power extends; for it is for the former, and not for the latter, that you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven." And in the same place he says: "What else did Peter leave you but what he had? 'Such as I have,' he says, 'I give you.' What that was I know: 'Silver and gold I have not,' since he himself says, 'silver and gold are not mine.' Suppose you have bought these for yourself by some other right; still it is not by apostolic right. For he could not give you what he did not have. He gave you care over the churches; did he give you dominion? Hear him: 'Not lording it over the clergy,' he says, 'but being examples to the flock from the heart.' And do not think this said only in humility and not in truth: the law of the Lord in the Gospel is: 'The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power are called benefactors; but you are not so.' It is plain, then, that he forbade the apostles dominion over them. Why, then, do you dare to usurp either lordship in the apostolate or apostolate in lordship? It is plain that you are forbidden both together. If you want to have both together, you will lose both. Otherwise do not think yourself excepted from the number of those of whom God complains: 'They have reigned, but not by me; they have become princes, and I did not know them.' If we have the prohibition, let us hear the command: 'Let the greater among you become as the lesser, and the one who goes before as the one who serves.' The apostolic form forbids dominion; it allows administration. Again in the same place he says: 'You have erred in thinking your apostolic power supreme and the only one instituted by God. If you think so, you disagree with him who says, "There is no power but from God" (Rom. 13), and what follows: "Whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God." Finally, the same writer says: "Every soul is subject to the higher powers." He does not say "to a higher power," as if to one, but "to higher powers," as to many.' Again in the same place he says: 'I think those who say this will not show where any of the apostles sat as judge over men.' And a little later: 'Finally, I read that the apostles stood to be judged, but I do not read that they sat as judges.' Again in the same place he says: 'Who will give me to see the Church of God as in the ancient days, when the apostles let down their nets, not for a catch of gold, but for a catch of souls? Who will give me to hear your voice, that voice of power: "Your sheep are with you in thirst unto destruction"?' Again in the same place he says: 'I was cast down from the house of my God. What is this, to be lifted up over the nations and kings, from one who is poor and cast down? And so the prophet, when he was similarly lifted up, heard: "to pluck up and destroy, and to scatter, and to build and to plant" (Jer. 1). Those words sound of rustic rather than of lofty life, in which spiritual labour is expressed. So we too, however highly we think of ourselves, should feel that a ministry has been laid upon us, not a dominion given us; and so learn that the work of the hoe is needed, that you may do the prophet's work in the office you have taken up.' Again in the same place he says: 'Yet you are not that prophet. "And all the earth is his possession." It is Christ who claims possession for himself, by the right of creation and the merit of redemption and the merit of the Father, to whom it was said of another: "Ask of me and I will give you the nations," etc. Did he have possession and dominion in view, that you should have care of it? Your part is this: stretch out your hand in fullness to help, but take care to serve and to provide; help to benefit, as the faithful and wise servant whom the lord has set over his household. For you are appointed a prelate to dispense, not to rule. Do this, and do not aim at lordship over all men, so that no man lords it over others with all injustice. Therefore, if you know yourself a debtor, you must by all means not think yourself a lord.' From these words of Bernard, and from many others of the same man, which are gathered from the writers of the New Testament and the sayings of the saints, some believe (and it is wholly erroneous to say so) that the Pope by Christ's ordinance regularly holds both swords, and that he has the fullness of power both in temporal and in spiritual matters, so that he can do all things that are not contrary to the divine law, and that he binds all orthodox believers. Some of these try to conclude from this that the Pope, by Christ's ordinance, has no coercive power at all. Others do not concede this; but they believe that from the divine Scriptures, the writings of the saints and the sacred canons they can demonstrate that the Pope, by Christ's ordinance, has a principate instituted principally for the usefulness and advantage of the subjects, with the rights and liberties of others preserved; so that the apostolic principate excels worldly principates in two respects. First, because it administers spiritual, not temporal, matters, except by chance and of necessity. Second, because the apostolic principate, as instituted by Christ, is instituted for the usefulness and progress of its subjects, with every despotic principate excluded; and a principate that is not the best, and is not wholly unmixed, is not of this kind. Thus the Pope should have nothing at all of that dominative principate which, from a word taken from the Greek idiom [δεσποτικός], is called despoticus. And this, according to them, is what Bernard meant when he said: The apostolic form is this: dominion is forbidden, and, we should feel, a ministry, not a dominion, has been given to us. And when he says: Do not aim at lordship over all men, so also, according to them, should the words of St. Peter be understood: not lording it over the clergy. Yet they say we would have to condemn all the supreme pontiffs who held much of despotic principate and did not renounce all despotic principate, because in this they by no means imitated St. Peter and certain other leading men. They say that the aforesaid words of the blessed Bernard, and similar words of his own and of other Fathers, as well as the words of divine Scripture on which they rest, ought to be understood soundly, namely that Christ instituted the aforesaid apostolic state and principate, so that the supreme pontiffs who wished to be content with it alone, in his power, without any mixture of any other principate, would win singular praise and glory, and would be rewarded with a spiritual prize in the blessed life; but those who did not wish this were not bound to it. As for those who have in no way bound themselves to it by vow, it is more a law of counsel than of precept; for although Christ imposed no despotic principate on his vicar, he did not forbid it to him by precept, but under a condition: if he wished to keep Christ's counsel in this. And thus that saying of the blessed Bernard, dominion is forbidden, can be understood as addressed to those who wish to follow the counsel of Christ and of the apostles, who of their own accord invited themselves to imitate Christ in the said counsel.

units.la: Secundum istam opinionem respondetur etiam ad motiua adducta superius ca primo, quib. probatur. quod electio principum electorum dat electo in regem Romanorum tantam potestatem, quantâ Papa vult per eam sibi dari, & nō maiorem. Ad primum, quod consistit in hoc, quod Papa super ciuitatibus regna occidentalia habet eandem potestatem, quam habuit Constantin. magnus super monarchiam totius imperii: Respondetur quod Constantinus non dedit talem potestatem Papæ super regna occidentalia, sicut dictum est supra. q. 1. a. 12. nec etiam dare potuit sibi talem potestatem super occidentalia regna. quamuis enim Imperator posset dare Papæ sicut alteri personæ, potestatem eligendi imperatorem super totum imperium: quamuis etiam imperator possit facere imperatorem deputando sibi imperii administrationem, quamdiu imperator esset, non tamen posset alicui cum successione absque omni noua electione dare aliquam partem imperii, ita vt obtinens eam fit verus imperator. quamuis enim imperator (si non redundaret in detrimentum ipsius: sed forte esset ad vtilitatem ipsius. quia sic habetur in auth. vt iudi. sine quoquo suffragio colla 2. imperium abundabit vtens subiectis locupletib. sic per similem rationem imperium est potens vtens subiectis potentib.) posset dare alicui personæ pro se & filiis suis aliquod regnum, etiam immediate subiectum imperio, non tamen posset ordinare, quod talis rex cum successione generis sui teneret imperium: quia hoc optimum mō puidendi ipso. (s. per electionem, repugnaret. Ad secundum motiuum ibidem adductum dicitur, quod Papa non deposuit regem Francorum, nec aliū eidem substituit potestate concessa sibi à Christo, sed vel hoc non fecit, vel fecit potestate sibi concessa à Francis. Papa. n. non absoluit Francos à iuramento præstito sidelitatis Hilderico regi; sed declarauit & indicauit eis, quia forte de hoc dubitabant, quod illi iuramento post depositionem regis non erant astricti. Ad tertium respondetur q proprie loquendo non dedit nec concessit Othoni potestatem eligendi sibi successorem in Italia: sic tamen concessit, quod non intendebat eū super electione h moi perturbare. Ad quartum dicitur, q electio alicuius in regē romanorum non indiget aliqua confirmatione sicut est supra in diuersis locis pbatū. Ad qntū dupliciter sindetur. Vno modo, q lo. 22. intellexit de electione in regē romanorū in discordia, sicut verba eius videtur præ-tendere, tendere. Aliter quidam respondent dicentes, quod processus ille Iohannis. 22. contra Ludouicum de Bauaria non est recipiendus, nec taliter allegandus principaliter propter tria. primo quia factus est ab haeretico manifesto. secundo quia continet intolerabilem errorem. tertio quia non est à suo iudice factus, quia nec etiam, vt dicunt si Iohan. 22. fuisset catholicus & verus papa, ipse non fuisset in illa causa iudex domini Ludouici, licet in quibusdam aliis fuisset iudex eius.
units.tr: According to this opinion, a reply is also given to the arguments adduced above in chapter one, by which it is proved that the election of the electors gives the elected man as King of the Romans as much power as the Pope wishes to be given to him through it, and no more. To the first, which consists in this, that the Pope has over the Western kingdoms the same power that Constantine the Great had over the monarchy of the whole empire: it is replied that Constantine did not give the Pope such power over the Western kingdoms, as was said above (q. 1, a. 12); nor could he have given him such power over the Western kingdoms. For although the emperor could give the Pope, as to any other person, the power of electing an emperor over the whole empire, and although the emperor could also make an emperor by assigning to him the administration of the empire for as long as he himself was emperor, yet he could not give any part of the empire to anyone with succession, without any new election, so that the one obtaining it would be a true emperor. For although the emperor (if it were not to his own detriment, but perhaps to his advantage, as is held in the Authentica, ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio, collatio 2: the empire flourishes when it uses rich subjects, and so by a similar reasoning the empire is powerful when it uses powerful subjects) could give to some person, for himself and his sons, some kingdom even immediately subject to the empire, yet he could not ordain that such a king should hold the empire with succession of his own line; because this is the best way of providing for it, namely by election, and that would be contrary to it. To the second argument adduced there, it is said that the Pope did not depose the King of the Franks, nor substitute another in his place by a power given him by Christ; or else he did not do this, or he did it by a power given him by the Franks. For the Pope did not absolve the Franks from the oath of fidelity they had sworn to King Childeric; but he declared and indicated to them, since perhaps they doubted it, that after the king's deposition they were not bound by that oath. To the third it is replied that, properly speaking, he did not give or grant to Otto the power of electing a successor for himself in Italy; yet he granted it in such a way that he did not intend to disturb him over such an election. To the fourth it is said that the election of anyone as King of the Romans does not need any confirmation, as has been proved in various places above. To the fifth there are two replies. In one way: John XXII understood the election of a King of the Romans in a time of discord, as his words seem to suggest. Otherwise some reply, saying that the process of John XXII against Louis of Bavaria is not to be received, nor to be principally alleged in this way, for three reasons. First, because it was made by a manifest heretic. Second, because it contains an intolerable error. Third, because it was not made by his judge; for even if John XXII had been a Catholic and true pope, they say, he would not have been the judge of Lord Louis in that cause, although in certain other matters he would have been his judge.

units.la: Ad praesens autem tantummodo dicendum vel potius tangendum est breuiter, quare praedicti dicunt Iohan. 22. fuisse haereticum manifestum. Circa quod sciendum est, quod dicunt ipsum fuisse haereticum tum propter errores, quos in decretalibus suis sub bulla redegit: tum propter errores, quos solummodo publice asseruit & domatizauit, quae (vt dicunt) ad minus sunt circiter 90. de quibus dicunt aliquos tam ridiculosos esse & tam fantasticos, vt mirentur, quomodo vnquam homo potuit eos opinari. quos tamen dicunt haereticales propterea, quod sacris literis contradicunt. De assertionibus autem Iohan. praedicti, quas isti dicunt esse erroneas et quas (vt dicunt) ad destruendum introduxit & damnandum regulam fratrum Minorum cum declaratione Nicolai tertii super eam, cuius verba quasi impugnanda ponit in principio primae suae decretalis de hac materia quae incipit: ad conditorem. paucas absque improbatione causa breuitatis duxi praesentibus inserendas. Prima itaque assertio hic ponenda, quam putant erroneam, est, quod vsus facti in rebus vsuconsumptibilibus non potest a proprietate & dominio separari. hanc ponit in decretali quae incipit, ad conditorem, in his verbis: dicere siquidem, quod in talibus rebus vsus iuris vel facti separatus a proprietate rei seu dominio possit constitui, repugnat iuri & obuiat rationi. Secunda est, quod nec simplex vsus facti, qui est seruitus, nec ius vtendi in talibus rebus potest constitui vel haberi: hanc ponit sub eisdem verbis in decretali sua praedicta. Tertia est, quod vtire nihil aliud est, quam percipere rei fructum, quae potest ex ipsa salua eius substantia prouenire, quam ponit sub his verbis: Cum enim vti re nihil aliud sit proprie quam fructum rei seu vtilitatem aliquam in solidum vel pro parte recipere, quae ex causa pateat salua substantia prouenire. restat quod illa re vtiquis nequeat, ex qua salua eius substantia nulla sibi prouenire potest vtilitas, quare res vsu consumptibiles esse constant. Quarta est, quod ius vendendi non potest in rebus vsuconsumtibilibus constitui vel haberi. Quinta est, quod vsus facti in rebus vsuconsumptibilibus haberi non potest. quia nullus talis actus haberi potest. hanc ponit in eadem decretali sub his verbis. Praeterea quod simplex vsus rei sine iure vtendi a proprietate seu dominio separatus in rebus vsuconsumptibilibus haberi nequeat. sic probatur: si enim haberi posset vsus talis, aut ante ipsum actum, aut in ipso actu, aut post completum actu huius habere- tur. Quod autem hoc nequeat fieri, ex hoc patet: quia quod non est, haberi nequaquam potest. patet autem, quod actus ille, antequam exerceatur vel postquam factus est, in rerum natura non est. ex quo sequitur, quod haberi minime potest. licet enim ante actum ipsum quis facultatem habeat ipsum exercendi, post hoc tamen actus ipse in rerum natura, nisi in potentia, non existit. cum enim actus est in fieri, nec adhuc est in rerum natura, quod rem perfectam significat, quamdiu est in fieri, non potest actu conuenire. quod enim de actu, quae est in fieri, praeteriit, iam non est. quod autem fit, instantaneum seu momentaneum est, & tale quid haberi non potest nisi pro momento quodam magis intelligitur quam sensu percipi potest adhuc post actum completum: licet (si ex facto ipso producta res alia fuit, res ipsa facta haberi valeat) factum tamen ipsum, quod iam transit, non habetur. Sexta est, quod haereticum est dicere, quod scripturae diuinae contrarium est, Christum & apostolos non habuisse in rebus, quas habebant, ius vtendi, vendendi, donandi & ex ipsis alia acquirendi. Septima est, quod actus vtendi est iniustus, nisi vtens habeat ius vtendi, vendendi, donandi, & ex ipsis alia acquiredi. & has duas ponit in decretali sua, Cum inter nonnullos: sub his verbis: pertinaciter affirmare quod redemptori nostro praedicto eiusque apostolis in his quae eos habuisse sacra scriptura testatur nequaquam ius vendendi competierit: nec ipsi illa vendendi seu donandi ius habuerint, aut ex ipsis alia acquirendi, quae tamen ipsos de praemissis fecisse sacra scriptura testatur, seu ipsos potuisse facere supponit expresse, cum talis assertio ipsorum vsum & gesta euidenter imitudit in praemissis non iusta, quae utique de vsu gestis seu factis redemptoris nostri Dei & bonis sentire nephas est, & scripturae sacrae contrarium, & doctrinae catholicae inimicum: assertionem ipsam pertinacem censendam merito & haereticam censemus de fratrum eorundum concilio deinceps erroneam declaramus. Octaua est, quod ordo fratrum Minorum (ratione consimili, vt isti dicunt, orthodoxa ecclesia tam vniuersalis quam particularis, ac quaecunque communitas, vniuersitas, multitudo aut collegium) non potest aliquem actum realem habere vel exercere. Nona est, quod quia persona imaginaria repraesentata potest habere ius vtendi, sed non facti vsum: ideo est, quod ordo fratrum Minorum & ratione consimili orthodoxa ecclesia, & omnis persona imaginaria est repraesentata & imaginaria. huiusmodi assertiones ponit in decretali sua, Quia quorundam, edita contra appellationem domini Ludouici de Bauaria supradicti dicens sic: cum enim dicatur in decretalibus supradictis quod ordo vsum rerum habebat praemissarum, ad vsum iuris necesse est hoc referri: sacra siquidem, quae singulorum sunt, personam exiguunt veram & requirunt. Ordo autem vera persona non est: sed repraesentata & imaginaria potius est censenda. quare quae factis sunt sibi conuenire nequeunt, licet eis possint congruere, quae sunt iuris. Decima est, quod habere ius proprietatis & dominii seu aliqua in communi quomodo habet aliqua communitas specialis, quae est solummodo pars totius congregationis fidelium, non diminuit de altissima paupertate. Vndecima est, quod regulae & statuto fratrum Minorum non repugnet nec obstat habere aliquid in communi proprium sibi. Duodecima est quod non bene dixit Innocen. 5. dicendo, altissimam paupertatem esse, quae nihil habet in hoc mundo nec in proprio nec in communi. has tres assertiones ponit in decretali praedicta, Quia quorundam, in haec verba Nec hoc (scilicet habere in communi) et quoad proprietatem aliquam derogat iuxta dictum Greg. 9. praedicti altissimae paupertati, quae in quadam sua decretali dicitur expresse. extra de excess. prael. c. vnicis prauis. Praedicatores & Minores in altissima paupertate Christo famulari: & tamen constat ipsos Praedicatores habere in communi quoad proprietatem aliqua eorum regula & statuto non repugnat. Et ita non obstat, quod dicunt Innoc. 3. praedecessorem nostrum dixisse, altam paupertatem esse habere pauca propria propter Deum: altiorem, quae nulla habet propria, tamen habet in communi: altissimam quae nihil habet in hoc mundo nec in communi nec in proprio. dicimus enim quod hoc dixerit non ut Papa sed ut Petrus de Tarentasia in quadam postilla sua. quare dicta praemissorum pontificum sunt praeferenda.
units.tr: For the present I need only say briefly, or rather touch on, why these men claim that John XXII was a manifest heretic. On this point it should be understood that they say he was a heretic both for the errors he set down under seal in his decretals, and for the errors he publicly asserted and taught, which (they say) number at least about ninety. Some of these they regard as so ridiculous and fantastical that they wonder how any man could ever have held them. They nonetheless call them heretical because they contradict the sacred letters. Of the assertions of the said John which these men call erroneous, and which (they say) he introduced in order to destroy and condemn the rule of the Friars Minor, together with Nicholas III's declaration upon it, I have thought it right, for the sake of brevity and without taking exception, to insert a few in this work. The words of Nicholas are set out as if for refutation at the start of John's first decretal on this matter, which begins ad conditorem. The first assertion to be quoted here, which they consider erroneous, is that the use of fact in consumable goods cannot be separated from ownership and dominion. He states this in the decretal that begins ad conditorem, in these words: For to say that in such things a use of right or of fact can be established separately from the ownership or dominion of the thing is contrary to law and opposed to reason. The second is that neither a bare use of fact, which is servitude, nor a right of using such things, can be established or held. He states this in the same words in the aforesaid decretal. The third is that to use a thing is nothing other than to receive the fruit of a thing, or some benefit that can arise from it while its substance remains intact. He states it in these words: For since to use a thing properly means nothing other than to receive, wholly or in part, the fruit of the thing or some advantage that clearly arises from it while its substance remains intact. It follows that no one can use a thing from which, while its substance remains intact, no advantage can accrue to him; hence it is agreed that such things are consumable. The fourth is that the right of selling cannot be established or held in consumable goods. The fifth is that the use of fact in consumable goods cannot be held, because no such act can be held. He states this in the same decretal in these words: Furthermore, a bare use of a thing, separated from the right of using it and from ownership or dominion, cannot be held in consumable goods. It is proved thus: if such a use could be held, it would be held either before the act itself, or in the act itself, or after the act has been completed. That this cannot happen is clear, because what does not exist can by no means be held. It is plain that the act, either before it is exercised or after it has been done, does not exist in the nature of things. From this it follows that it cannot be held at all. For although before the act someone has the power of exercising it, after the act itself does not exist in the nature of things, except potentially. For while the act is in process of becoming, it does not yet exist in the nature of things, which signifies a completed thing; as long as it is in becoming, it cannot be actually present. What has passed away from the act that is in becoming no longer exists. What is done is instantaneous or momentary, and such a thing cannot be held, except for a moment, and is grasped more by the mind than perceived by the senses, even after the act is completed. Although the thing produced by the deed may be held if it is some other thing, the deed itself, which is already past, is not held. The sixth is that it is heretical to say what is contrary to divine Scripture: that Christ and the apostles had no right, in the things they possessed, to use, sell, give away, and acquire other things from them. The seventh is that the act of using is unjust unless the user has the right to use, sell, give away, and acquire other things from them. He states these two in his decretal Cum inter nonnullos, in these words: to affirm stubbornly that to our aforesaid Redeemer and his apostles, in those things which sacred Scripture testifies they had, the right of selling in no way belonged; nor did they have the right to sell or give them away, or to acquire other things from them; although sacred Scripture testifies that they did these things, or expressly implies that they were able to do them; since such an assertion clearly ridicules their use and deeds in these matters as unjust, which indeed it is wicked to think of the use, deeds or acts of our Redeemer God and his good works, and is contrary to sacred Scripture and hostile to Catholic doctrine: we rightly judge that assertion to be stubborn and heretical, and by the counsel of the brethren we declare it erroneous henceforth. The eighth is that the order of Friars Minor (by a similar reasoning, as these men say, the orthodox Church, both universal and particular, and any community, university, multitude or college) cannot have or exercise any real act. The ninth is that because a represented imaginary person can have a right of use but not the use of fact, therefore the order of Friars Minor, and by similar reasoning the orthodox Church, and every imaginary person, is represented and imaginary. He states these assertions in his decretal Quia quorundam, issued against the appeal of the aforesaid Lord Louis of Bavaria, saying: For since it is said in the aforesaid decretals that the order had the use of the aforementioned things, this must be referred to the use of right: for sacred things, which belong to individuals, require and demand a true person. But the order is not a true person; rather it is to be judged represented and imaginary. Therefore things that pertain to facts cannot belong to it, although those that pertain to right may suit it. The tenth is that to have a right of ownership and dominion, or anything in common, in the way any particular community has it, which is only a part of the whole congregation of the faithful, does not detract from the most lofty poverty. The eleventh is that the rule and statute of the Friars Minor do not oppose or stand in the way of having something of their own in common. The twelfth is that Innocent V did not speak well in saying that the most lofty poverty is that which has nothing in this world, neither as its own nor in common. He states these three assertions in the aforesaid decretal Quia quorundam, in these words: Nor does this (namely, having in common) and, as to any ownership, detract from the most lofty poverty, according to the saying of Gregory IX, which he expressly states in a certain decretal of his: Extra, de excess. prael., c. Vnicis prauis: that the Preachers and Minors serve Christ in the most lofty poverty; and yet it is agreed that the Preachers have something in common as to ownership, and their rule and statute do not oppose this. And so it is no obstacle that they cite our predecessor Innocent III as having said that a high poverty is to have a few possessions for God's sake; a higher poverty is to have none of one's own but to have things in common; the most lofty is to have nothing in this world, neither in common nor as one's own. For we say that he said this not as Pope but as Peter of Tarentaise in a certain postil of his. Therefore the sayings of the aforesaid pontiffs are to be preferred.

units.la: Decima tertia est, quod domus, agri & quaecunque immobilia, quae credentes, de quibus Act. 2. & 4. fit mentio, in speciali vendebant pro fidelibus sustentandis, priusquam vendebantur fuerunt effecta totius communitatis credentium iure proprietatis seu dominii, quod possessores eorum in eis habebant. hanc ponit in decretali sua, quae incipit: Quia vir reprobus, sub his verbis: Illis (scilicet credentibus) omnia quae possidebant erant communia inter eos, & quod communia quoad dominium seu proprietatem intelligi debeant ex eo patet, quod illud, quod prius ante conversionem eorum ipsis fuerat proprium postquam credentes facti sunt, fuit inter eos communicatum. Constat autem quod illa, quae possidebant ante conversionem, et erant illis, quantum ad dominium propria. aliter enim illa communicare non poterant. quare sequitur, quod fuerunt quo ad proprietatem seu dominium inter eos communicata. quia de rebus non consumptibilibus scriptura praedicta Act. 4. aperte dicit, nisi violentia sibi fiat cum n. dixisset: Nec quisquam eorum, quae possidebat, aliquid esse suum dicebat, sed erant eis omnia communia. Ex quo sequitur quod nec quisquam egens erat inter ipsos: & huiusmodi volens reddere rationem subdit: Quotquot enim erant possessores agrorum aut domorum vendentes afferebant pretia eorum quae vendebant & ponebant ante pedes apostolorum. Cum igitur prius dicit, quod inter credentes erant omnia communia, & post subiungit quod agri vendebantur & domus, evidenter apparet, quod illa communia, antequam venderentur, erant effecta.
units.tr: The thirteenth is that houses, fields and all immovable property which the believers mentioned in Acts 2 and 4, when they sold them specifically to support the faithful, had already become the property of the whole community of believers, by the right of ownership or lordship which their former possessors held in them before they were sold. He sets this out in his decretal that begins Quia vir reprobus, in these words: They (namely the believers) held all their possessions in common, and that these things were common as to ownership or property may be understood from the fact that what had earlier belonged to each of them before their conversion, after they became believers, was shared among them. It is certain, however, that what they possessed before their conversion was theirs as property, as to ownership, for otherwise they could not have shared it. It follows, therefore, that as to property or ownership these things were shared among them. This is clearly stated in the aforementioned Scripture of Acts 4 concerning movable goods, which are not consumed, when it says: "Nor did anyone of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common." From this it follows that there was no one in need among them. Wishing to give the reason for this, it adds: "For as many as were possessors of fields or houses sold them and brought the prices of what they sold and laid them at the apostles' feet." Since it first says that all things were common among the believers, and afterwards adds that fields and houses were sold, it plainly appears that those common goods had become common before they were sold.

units.la: Aliter enim sequeretur, quod remanssissent eorum, quorum prius fuerunt, propria. & per consequens, quod ipsi post illorum venditionem remansissent proprietarii, cuius tamen contrarium dicit sacra scriptura praedicta cum dicit: nec quisquam eorum quae possidebat aliquid suum esse ducebat. Decimaquarta est, quod apostoli post missionem sancti Spiritus pro aliquo tempore habuerunt praedia in Iudaea quoad dominium seu proprietatem in communi: & quod licuit eis postea habere & retinere proprietatem agrorum seu praediorum. Hanc ponit in decretali praedicta sub his verbis: Si quaeratur, quare agros apostoli non tenebant & domus in Iudaea, sed potius vendiris illis habebant pretia in commune: Respondet Melchiades P.P. ad hoc dicens, futuram id est transituram ecclesiam ad gentes apostoli praeviderant. Idcirco praedia in Iudaea minime sunt adepti.
units.tr: Otherwise it would follow that the goods would have remained the property of those whose they formerly were, and consequently that after their sale those people would have remained owners, whereas the aforementioned Holy Scripture says the contrary, when it says: "Nor did anyone of them consider that anything he possessed was his own." The fourteenth is that after the sending of the Holy Spirit the apostles, for some time, held lands in Judaea in common as to ownership or property, and that it was afterwards lawful for them to hold and retain ownership of the fields or estates. He sets this out in the aforementioned decretal in these words: If it is asked why the apostles did not hold fields and houses in Judaea, but rather had the prices of what was sold in common, Pope Melchiades answers this, saying that they had foreseen that the Church would be future, that is, would pass, to the Gentiles. For this reason they did not acquire estates in Judaea.

units.la: Et si dicatur, quod Melchiades videtur supponere, quod credentes etiam ante venditionem praediorum illa nequaquam habuerunt in communi: cum dicat, quod illa in Iudaea minime sunt adepti. Dicimus, quod Melchiades pro tanto dicit apostolos in Iudaea non esse adeptos praedia, quia non adepti fuerunt illa, ut ea sibi intenderent retinere. & ideo, quia non retinebant, non videbantur ea fuisse adepti: cum is qui rem adipiscitur ut eam in continenti abdicare debeat adeptus proprie non dicatur. Ex praedictis patet quod apostolis fuit licitum in Iudaea, si voluissent, praedia retinere: nec voto compulsi sunt, quia illa non retinuerunt, sed voluntate propria quae se non contrariuros mora sed transituros praeviderant ad gentes. Decimaquinta est, quod B. Petrus & apostoli post missionem Spiritus sancti fuerunt proprietarii, habentes in speciali proprietatem seu dominium pecuniarum & aliarum rerum. hanc ponit in decretali praedicta sub his verbis: videtur etiam quod probabiliter posset dici, quod post distributionem bonorum usu consumptibilium quae fiebat inter apostolos & credentes, unusquisque portionis sibi assignatae proprietarius & dominus posset dici: cum hoc scriptura actum videtur expresse supponere, cum dicit. Nec quisquam egens erat inter illos, & quare hoc, reddit rationem dicens: Quotquot enim possessores res agrorum & domorum erant vendentes afferebant pretia eorum & ponebant ante pedes apostolorum. dividebant autem singulis prout cuique opus esset. Cum igitur daretur ab illis qui dare poterant, scilicet apostolis: & illis, qui recipere poterant ea quae ad vita humana sustentationem pertinebant, videtur quod quilibet fuerit dominus eius portionis, quae sibi fuerat assignata. aliter non videtur verum quod dicitur, quod egentes non essent, nisi post divisionem haberent proprietatem in assignata sibi portione. Praeterea constat, quod vestimenta quotidiana inter res usu consumptibiles computatur per conclusionem nunc praedictam, in qua fit mentio in dict. c. act. 4. Item in actibus legitur quod angelus Petro dixit: praecingere & calcia te caligas tuas. Item dixit ei: circumda tibi vestimentum tuum &c. ubi clare supponit angelus, quod caligae & vestimentum assignata Petro propria quo ad dominium erant Petri. Quare pecunia, panis, vinum, & res aliae consumptibiles dividebantur pro vitae sustentatione assignatae simpliciter eius essent.
units.tr: And if it is said that Melchiades seems to suppose that the believers did not hold those things in common even before the sale of the estates, since he says that the apostles did not acquire estates in Judaea, we reply that Melchiades says the apostles did not acquire estates in Judaea only to this extent: they did not acquire them in order to intend to keep them. And therefore, because they did not keep them, they were not seen to have acquired them, since one who acquires a thing in order to renounce it immediately is not properly called an acquirer. From what has been said it is clear that it was lawful for the apostles in Judaea, if they had wished, to retain estates; nor were they compelled by any vow, because they did not retain them, but by their own will, which had foreseen that they would not be opposed to them by delay but would pass to the Gentiles. The fifteenth is that Blessed Peter and the apostles, after the mission of the Holy Spirit, were owners, holding in particular ownership or lordship of money and other goods. He sets this out in the aforementioned decretal in these words: It also seems that it could probably be said that after the distribution of goods consumable by use, which was made among the apostles and the believers, each one could be called owner and lord of the portion assigned to him. This Scripture seems expressly to suppose in the act it describes, when it says: "Nor was there anyone in need among them." And it gives the reason for this, saying: "For as many as were possessors of fields or houses sold them and brought the prices of them and laid them at the apostles' feet. And they distributed to each one as anyone had need." Since, then, things were given by those who could give, namely the apostles, and were received by those who could receive what pertains to the sustenance of human life, it seems that each was the lord of that portion which had been assigned to him. Otherwise what is said, that there were no needy persons, does not seem true unless after the division each had ownership of the portion assigned to him. Moreover, it is established that everyday clothing is counted among goods consumed by use, by the conclusion just stated, in which mention is made of the said chapter, Acts 4. Likewise in the Acts it is read that an angel said to Peter: "Gird yourself and put on your sandals," and again said to him: "Wrap your garment around you," etc., where the angel clearly supposes that the sandals and garment assigned to Peter were Peter's own as to ownership. Therefore money, bread, wine and other goods consumed by use, which were distributed for sustenance of life, were simply theirs to whom they were assigned.

units.la: Decima sexta est quod voluntas vivendi sine proprio non se extendit ad illa, quibus necessario indiget vita humana. hanc ponit sub eisdem verbis in decretali praedicta. Decimaseptima, quod Christus, in quantum homo, viator passibilis & mortalis, non solum paucarum & parvarum & viliū rerum in speciali dominium habuit seu proprietatem, sed etiam in speciali regni temporalis & viliter omnium temporalium rerum.
units.tr: The sixteenth is that the will to live without property does not extend to those things which human life necessarily requires. He sets this out in the same words in the aforementioned decretal. The seventeenth is that Christ, as man, a wayfarer, passible and mortal, had in particular ownership or property not only a few, small and cheap things, but also, in particular, the kingdom of the temporal realm and, in a cheap sense, of all temporal things.

units.la: Decimaoctava est, quod Christus fuit Dominus omnium rerum temporalium, in quantum crucifixus. Decimanona est quod Christi regnum est vile dominium, dominus enim ille fuit inquantum Deus ab æterno, eo ipso quod Deus pater genuit ipsum inquantum homo ex tempore, scilicet ab instanti conceptionis, scilicet ex Dei dono. Vigesima est, quod Christus nihilominus habuit dominium aliquarum rerum non ab instanti suæ conceptionis, sed postea successive modis aliis, utpote ex collatione fidelium & emptione acquisitarum. Vigesimaprima est, quod Christus non potuit renunciare regno ac dominio rerum temporalium: quia si hoc fecisset, contra ordinationem patris fecisset. Vigesima secunda est, quod non carentia dominii fecit Christum egenum & pauperem, sed potius carentia fructus & obtentionis rerum quarum dominus erat. Vigesimatertia erat, quod nudum dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rerum habentem non fecit divitem. Vigesimaquarta est, quod dominium omnium temporalium ab omni perceptione commodi temporalis in perpetuum separatum est inutile reputandum. Vigesimaquinta est, quod Christus, quo ad præceptionem fructuum regni & temporalium rerum in quibusdam palam gessit se pro rege & domino. Has assertiones, quarum aliquas dicunt prædicti inter se repugnare, dicit Iohannes 22. in decre. prædicta. Quia vir, in hæc verba: Secundo quaeritur, utrum Christus aliquium rei temporalis habuit dominium & quale. Quod autem dominium rerum temporalium habuit, sacra scriptura tam in veteri testamento quam in novo multis locis testatur. multi quidem eum regem futurum populi Israelitici & per consequens habere regni dominium prophetarum, dicentes: Ecce dominus iudex noster, ipse veniet & salvabit nos, & ita cum Pilatus interrogaret, utrum esset rex Iudeorum, respondit, regnum meum non est hinc. non dicit: non est hic, sed dicit, non est hinc, quasi diceret, regnum meum a mundo non habeo, sed nec habebat, imo a Deo, sicut angelus eius genitrici prædixerat dicens Luc. 1. Dabit ei Dominus sedem David patris eius. & itaque rex & dominus factus est, inquantum crucifixus: & crucifixus fuit, inquantum homo, sequitur, quod regnum & dominium, inquantum hominis, Deus sibi concessit: & ita iuxta premissa patet, quod regnum & vtile dominium habuit dominus Iesus, inquantum Deus ab æterno, eo ipso quod Deus pater genuit, similiter inquantum homo ex tempore, scilicet ab instanti suæ conceptionis ex Dei dono, & nihilominus habuit dominium aliquarum rerum temporalium non ab instanti conceptionis, sed postea successive modis aliis, utpote ex oblatione fidelium vel emptione acquisitarum, & ita cum ex his evidenter appareat, ipsum regno & dominio non renunciasse prædicti, imo videtur quod non potuisset renunciare, & fecisset contra ordinationem patris, dicendum est, quod non carentia dominii fecit eum pauperem & egenum, sed potius carentia perceptionis fructus & obventionis rerum, quarum erat dominium. Nudum enim dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rerum, habentem non fecit divitem: cum sit inutile reputandum. unde habens tale dominium potest egenum & pauper merito reputari. Et ita Christus rex regum & dominus dominantium, quo ad perceptionem fructus regni & rerum temporalium, nisi in valde paucis pro rege & domino se non gessit. propter quod merito pauper dici potuit voluntarius & egenus, non propter dominii carentiam sine regni, sed propterea quia se fructibus rerum & proventibus non intromittebat. Vigesimasexta assertio est, quod Christus non aliam legem vivendi dedit apostolis, quam quibuscunque aliis discipulis suis sive viris sive mulieribus. Hanc ponit in decretali prædicta in hac verba: De discipulis autem constat, quod habuerint aliqua temporalia. de Ioseph ab Arimathia legitur Iohannis 19. quod erat discipulus Iesu. Matth. autem 27. dicitur, quod erat dives homo & discipulus Iesu. Item constat quod Symon leprosus erat discipulus Iesu, & tamen legitur Matth. 27. quod Iesus erat in Bethania in domo eius. Item Lazarus, Martha & Maria Magdalena, qui erant discipuli eius, habebant multa bona: unde de eis legitur Iohan. 11. quod castrum dictum Bethania erat Maria Magdalene, & Martha: & quod in Bethania fecerunt sibi magnam cenam, in qua Martha ministrabat: Lazarus autem erat unus de discumbentibus cum eo: Maria vero accepit librum unguentum nardi pistici, & unxit pedes Iesu, & tersit capillis suis pedes eius. Thabita autem, quae interpretatur Dorcas, quam Petrus suscitavit a mortuis, legitur act. 9. quod erat discipula & plena bonis operibus & eleemosynis, quas faciebat illis Dorcas. Ex quibus patet, non obstante, quod ista esset discipula, tamen temporalia habebat, de quibus faciebat eleemosynas prædictas. nec reperimus, quod Iesus dominus noster aliam legem vivendi discipulis suis dederit, & aliam apostolis suis: immo beatus Clemens in quadam epistola sua, cuius pars recitatur. 12. quaest. 1. cap. dilectissimis, expresse dicit, quod eadem erat apostolorum & discipulorum vita, dicens. Communis vita omnibus est necessaria, & maxime his, qui vitam apostolorum imitari & eorum discipulorum volunt. nec cum ipsos apostolos ex discipulis fecit, videtur eis indixisse vitam aliam, quam prius habuerunt, sed potestatem aliam eis tribuisse. unde cum Apostolos eos ordinavit, legitur Matth. 10. sic dixisse: Et convocatis. 12. discipulis dedit illis potestatem spiritum &c.
units.tr: The eighteenth is that Christ was Lord of all temporal things, insofar as he was crucified. The nineteenth is that Christ's kingdom is a base dominion, for he was Lord insofar as he was God from eternity, by the very fact that God the Father begot him, and insofar as he was man from time, namely from the moment of conception, by the gift of God. The twentieth is that Christ nevertheless had dominion over some things, not from the moment of his conception but afterwards, successively, by other means, as for instance things acquired from the contributions of the faithful and by purchase. The twenty-first is that Christ could not renounce the kingdom and dominion of temporal things, because if he had done so he would have acted against the ordinance of the Father. The twenty-second is that it was not the lack of dominion that made Christ needy and poor, but rather the lack of the enjoyment and income of the things of which he was Lord. The twenty-third is that bare dominion, permanently separated from every enjoyment of the benefit of things, does not make a man rich. The twenty-fourth is that dominion over all temporal things, permanently separated from every enjoyment of temporal benefit, must be regarded as useless. The twenty-fifth is that Christ, in respect of receiving the fruits of the kingdom and of temporal things, in some matters openly acted as king and lord. John 22, in the aforesaid decretal, sets out these assertions, some of which the aforesaid critics say are mutually contradictory. The decretal Quia vir says in these words: Secondly, it is asked whether Christ had dominion over any temporal thing, and of what kind. That he had dominion over temporal things, holy Scripture witnesses in many places, both in the Old Testament and in the New. Indeed many prophets said that he would be the king of the people of Israel and consequently would have dominion of the kingdom, saying: "Behold, our judge, the Lord himself, will come and save us." And so when Pilate asked whether he was the king of the Jews, he answered: "My kingdom is not from hence." He does not say "is not here," but "is not from hence," as if to say: I do not have my kingdom from the world; yet neither did he have it from himself, but from God, as his angel had foretold to his mother, saying (Luke 1): "The Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father." And so he was made king and lord insofar as he was crucified, and he was crucified insofar as he was man. It follows that the kingdom and dominion, insofar as he is man, God granted to him. Thus, according to the premises, it is clear that the Lord Jesus had a kingdom and a useful dominion insofar as he is God from eternity, by the very fact that God the Father begot him; likewise insofar as he is man from time, namely from the moment of his conception, by the gift of God. And nevertheless he had dominion over some temporal things not from the moment of conception but afterwards, successively, by other means, as things acquired by the offering of the faithful or by purchase. And since it is thus plainly evident that he did not renounce the kingdom and dominion, as the aforesaid critics say, but rather it seems that he could not have renounced them, and would have acted against the ordinance of the Father, it must be said that it was not the lack of dominion that made him poor and needy, but rather the lack of the enjoyment and income of the things of which he was Lord. For bare dominion, permanently separated from every enjoyment of the benefit of things, does not make a man rich, since it must be regarded as useless. Hence one who has such dominion can rightly be regarded as needy and poor. And so Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, in respect of enjoying the fruits of the kingdom and of temporal things, acted as king and lord only in very few matters. For this reason he could rightly be called a voluntary and needy poor man, not because he lacked dominion over a kingdom, but because he did not concern himself with the fruits and revenues of things. The twenty-sixth assertion is that Christ did not give the apostles a different rule of living from that given to his other disciples, whether men or women. He sets this out in the aforesaid decretal in these words: "It is agreed that the disciples had some temporal goods. Of Joseph of Arimathea we read in John 19 that he was a disciple of Jesus; Matthew 27 says that he was a rich man and a disciple of Jesus. Likewise it is agreed that Simon the leper was a disciple of Jesus, and yet Matthew 26 reads that Jesus was in Bethany in his house. Likewise Lazarus, Martha and Mary Magdalene, who were his disciples, had many goods; so of them we read in John 11 that the village called Bethany belonged to Mary Magdalene and Martha, and that in Bethany they made him a great supper, at which Martha served, while Lazarus was one of those reclining with him; Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair. Tabitha, who is interpreted Dorcas, whom Peter raised from the dead, is read in Acts 9 to have been a disciple, full of good works and almsdeeds, which Dorcas did. From these things it is plain that, although she was a disciple, nevertheless she had temporal goods, from which she gave the aforesaid alms. Nor do we find that Jesus our Lord gave his disciples one rule of living and his apostles another. Indeed blessed Clement, in a certain epistle of his, part of which is cited in 12 q. 1 c. Dilectissimis, expressly says that the life of the apostles and of the disciples was the same, saying: 'A common life is necessary for all, and especially for those who wish to imitate the life of the apostles and to be their disciples.' Nor when he made the apostles out of the disciples does he seem to have prescribed for them a different life from the one they had before, but rather to have granted them a different power. Hence, when he ordained them apostles, we read in Matthew 10 that he said: 'And calling together the twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits,' etc.
