units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Premissa detestatione eorum, qui Ioan. 22. adhaerebant, ponit alios errores ab eo in aliis operibus eius positos.
units.tr: Having first set out a detestation of those who adhered to John XXII, he sets forth other errors which he put forward in his other works.

units.la: HÆ assertiones, quas prædicti erroneas arbitrantur, in eiusdem decretalibus continentur, & multæ aliæ, quas non minus erroneas & culpabiles existimant, vt dicunt, quia nunquam viderunt aliquam scripturam assertiue prolatam, neque paganorum, neque hæreticorum, in quas paucæ veritates falsitatibus non essent admixtæ. Reputant enim, quod in omnibus decretalibus supradictis paucissima verba dicentis sunt consona veritati, propter quod mirantur, quod multitudo Christianorum, & maxime virorum literatorum, præcipue in iure canonico & theologia, ipsas approbat & confirmat: cum sint tam fantastica & absurda, quam esto quod non essent contra fidem & bonas mores, vilipendi omnino deberent. Sed beati Pauli sententia nunc locum habet, qui 2. Timoth. 4. air: Erit tempus cum sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt, sed ad desideria sua coacervabunt sibi magistros prurientes auribus, & a veritate quidem auditum auertent: ad fabulas autem conuertentur. Quia vbi de potestate vel etiam de voluntate papæ sit sermo, non curant Christiani scire his diebus, quid Christus docuit, nec quod apostoli senserunt & sancti patres, quamuis ratione manifesta hoc docetur: sed quod placet papæ, timore vel amore aut cupiditate carnis amplectuntur, & ad fabulas quas somniauerunt, scripturas & prophetias student trahere repugnantes, & sic ad papæ transferre videntur honorificentiam creatoris, fidem Christianam contra apostolum in sapientia vel potius voluntate papæ, non voluntate scripturæ ponentes: cum dicant isti se legisse in historiis & chronicis fide dignis circiter 28. a tempore beati Siluestri sedem apostolicam occupasse, qui non solum dicunt Iohannem 22. in prædictis errasse contra fidem & bonos mores, sed etiam dicunt ipsum inter hæreticos computandum, licet aliquis alius posset ea erronea opinari absque hoc quod esset hæreticus iudicandus: pro eo quod ea sub bulla redigendo & per totam Christianitatem promulgando conatus est cogere præceptis & minis universos Christianos ad ipsa pertinaciter defendenda, sic errori suo pertinaciam adiungendo & cum eis non errorem tantummodo sed etiam prauitatem hæreticam incurrendo. Præter autem istas assertiones, quas Iohannes 22. in suis decretalibus affirmauit, quas isti censent erroneas, dicunt isti ipsum alios prædicasse errores, propter quos etiam hæreticus est iudicandus. Quorum primus est (vt dicunt) quod animæ sanctorum in cœlo non vident nec videbunt diuinam essentiam vsque ad diem iudicii generalis. Secundus est, quod animæ damnatorum nec sunt nec erunt in inferno, nec cruciabuntur pœna æterna vsque ad diem iudicii. Tertius est quod dæmones non puniuntur nec punientur ante diem iudicii. Quartus est, quod Deus de potentia absoluta non potest aliud facere, nec aliter quam facit. Quintus est, quod Christus non regnabit post vltimum iudicium. Propter ista & alia dicunt æpe isti istum esse inter hæreticos numerandum, nec, vt dicunt, potest excusari de hæretica prauitate, si dicatur quod ista dixit solummodo conferendo & recitando, quia (vt affirmant) si fieret debita inquisitio, inueniretur per testes legitimos & legitima documenta, quod ista dixit asserendo. Nec iterum (vt dicunt) de istis & aliis, quæ in decretalibus suis inseruit, excusari potest per hoc, quod in fine vitæ suæ reuocauit, quicquid male dixisset: tum quia illa reuocatio fuit conditionalis, qualem faceret quilibet hæreticus quantumcunque pertinax, tum quia quamuis fuisset sufficiens reuocatio, & per consequens excusasset eum de hæretica prauitate post præfatam reuocationem, vt ex tunc non fuisset reputandus hæreticus, tamen pro tempore precedenti dictam reuocationem ipsum nullatenus excusasset: quin dicendus esset hæreticus ante dictam reuocationem. De Iohanne 22. & assertionibus eius sunt hæc dicta, vt literati solerter legentes præsens opusculum diligenter aduertant, an impugnantes decretales prædictas sint hæretici aggregandi, & an processus illius Ioannis 22. a tempore, quo primo edidit decretalem de prædicta materia, quæ incipit, ad conditorem, contra dominum Ludouicum de Bauaria & alios principantes, sunt censendi de iure tenere: & sunt recipiendi vel allegandi, tanquam a vero & catholico papa compositi atque facti.
units.tr: These assertions, which the aforementioned men judge to be erroneous, are contained in his decretals, and many others, which they think no less erroneous and blameworthy, as they say, because they have never seen any writing, whether of pagans or heretics, put forward as assertions in which a few truths are not mixed with falsehoods. For they consider that in all the aforesaid decretals there are very few words that agree with the truth. So they wonder that the multitude of Christians, and especially learned men, above all in canon law and theology, approve and confirm them, since they are so fanciful and absurd that, even if they were not contrary to the faith and good morals, they ought to be utterly despised. But the saying of the blessed Paul applies here, who says in 2 Timothy 4: "The time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but will heap up for themselves teachers tickling their ears, and will turn their hearing away from the truth, and will be turned to fables." For when the question is about the power or even the will of the pope, Christians these days do not care to know what Christ taught, or what the apostles and holy Fathers thought, although this is taught by clear reason. Instead, what pleases the pope they embrace, from fear, love or fleshly desire, and they strive to drag Scriptures and prophecies, which resist, to the fables they have dreamed up. In this way they seem to transfer to the pope the honour due to the Creator, placing the Christian faith not in the wisdom of Scripture but in the wisdom, or rather the will, of the pope, contrary to the apostle. These men say they have read in trustworthy histories and chronicles that, about twenty-eight times since the time of the blessed Sylvester, the apostolic see has been occupied by men of this kind. They say not only that John XXII erred in the aforesaid matters against the faith and good morals, but also that he must be counted among the heretics. Yet someone else might hold those erroneous opinions without being judged a heretic, for the reason that he attempted to commit them to writing under a bull, to publish them throughout all Christendom, and to compel all Christians by precepts and threats to defend them stubbornly. Thus he added obstinacy to his error, and by this he incurred not only error but heretical depravity. Besides these assertions which John XXII affirmed in his decretals, and which these men judge erroneous, they say that he preached other errors as well, on account of which he too must be judged a heretic. The first of these, as they say, is that the souls of the saints in heaven do not see, and will not see, the divine essence until the day of the general judgment. The second is that the souls of the damned neither are nor will be in hell, and will not be tormented with eternal punishment until the day of judgment. The third is that demons are not, and will not be, punished before the day of judgment. The fourth is that God, by his absolute power, cannot do otherwise than he does, nor do anything other than what he does. The fifth is that Christ will not reign after the last judgment. On account of these and other matters, these men often say that he is to be numbered among the heretics. Nor, as they say, can he be excused of heretical depravity if it is said that he uttered these things only by way of discussion and recital, because (as they affirm) if due inquiry were made, it would be found, through lawful witnesses and lawful documents, that he uttered them by way of assertion. Nor again, as they say, can he be excused regarding these and the other matters he inserted in his decretals on the ground that at the end of his life he retracted whatever he had said wrongly. For that retraction was conditional, the kind any heretic, however obstinate, would make. And although it would have been a sufficient retraction, and consequently would have excused him of heretical depravity after the said retraction, so that from then on he would not have been regarded as a heretic, nevertheless it would in no way have excused him for the preceding time. Indeed, he would have to be called a heretic before the said retraction. These things have been said about John XXII and his assertions, so that learned readers, reading this little work carefully, may consider diligently whether those who attack the aforesaid decretals are to be counted as heretics, and whether the proceedings of that John XXII, from the time when he first issued the decretal on this matter, which begins "To the Founder," against Lord Louis of Bavaria and the other princes, are to be regarded as lawfully maintained, and are to be received or cited as the work and act of a true and catholic pope.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Pauca quæ secundam opinionem positam c. 2. respiciunt, tangit nihil dis- cutiendo.
units.tr: A few points touching the second opinion stated in chapter 2, touched on without discussion.

units.la: TEnentes opinionem prædictam non æstimant, quod eos oporteat ad motiua secundæ opinionis adducta supra c. 2. respondere. Nam secundum ipsos motiua pro prima parte eiusdem opinionis secundæ verum concludunt, quod scilicet electus in regem Romanorum potest statim ipsa electione nomen regis assumere, & bona & iura regni & imperii in Italia & in aliis provinciis, quæ erant subiectæ Carolo magno, ante coronationem imperialem administrare, tamen secundum istam vltimam opinionem, vt patere ex fundamentis motiuorum illorum videtur, potest concludi, quod virtute electionis prædictæ possit electus in regem Romanorum in omnibus terris & prouinciis, quæ ante & post coronationem imperialem erant subiectæ Carolo magno & prædecessoribus eius. Ad motiua pro secunda parte eiusdem, quod scilicet electus in regem Romanorum manorum non poterit virtute electionis illa statim in aliis tertiis, quæ non erant subiectæ Carolo magno ante coronationem imperialem, responsum est supra. q. 3. c. 6. Responsiones autem pro secunda opinione, ad ea quæ dicta sunt & adducta ab opinione prima & tertia, quæ contra ipsam militare videntur: quia ipsius auctor superstes est, & homo non mediocris scientiæ, decreui ipsius iudicio relinquere. Sufficiens enim est ad suam opinionem contra contrarias defendendam.
units.tr: Those who hold the opinion just mentioned do not think they need to answer the arguments adduced for the second opinion above in chapter 2. For, according to them, the arguments for the first part of that second opinion truly conclude that one elected king of the Romans may at once, by that very election, assume the name of king and administer the goods and rights of the kingdom and empire in Italy and in the other provinces that were subject to Charlemagne before his imperial coronation. Yet, according to this last opinion, as is evident from the foundations of those arguments, it may be concluded that by virtue of that election the elected king of the Romans may do so in all lands and provinces that were subject to Charlemagne and his predecessors both before and after the imperial coronation. As for the arguments for the second part of the same opinion, namely that the elected king of the Romans cannot by virtue of that election at once rule over other lands that were not subject to Charlemagne before the imperial coronation, an answer was given above in question 3, chapter 6. The replies on behalf of the second opinion to the points raised and adduced by the first and third opinions, which seem to tell against it, I have resolved to leave to the judgement of its author, who is still alive and a man of no small learning. For he is sufficient to defend his own opinion against its opponents.

units.la: CAP. OCTAVVM,
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII,

units.la: Et vltimum, octava & vltima quæstionis, respondet rationibus secundo & tertio cap. positis.
units.tr: The last one, the eighth and final question, answers the arguments put forward in the second and third chapters.

units.la: POrro tenentes opinionem primam sunt multi, qui exquisite ad illa, quæ adducta sunt pro opinione secunda & tertia, diuersimode responderent, & forte nullatenus concordarent, proinde aliquas responsiones ad ipsas, quas ipsi vel aliqui ipsorum, vt alii cogitare possunt, breuiter recitabo, quid de ipsis sentiam ad præsens minime exprimendo. Ad primum enim monuunt pro opinione secunda adductum c. 2. cum dicit quod quilibet populus carens rege potest sibi regem eligere de iure gentium, ex quo iure regna condita sunt: Forte aliqui responderent, quod hoc intelligitur de populo non habente superiorem, ad quem spectat constituere regem super populum, sicut fuit de multis populis, antequam mundus haberet verum dominium, tunc enim pertinebat ad populum super se constituere regem. Sed postquam Papa factus est dominus totius mundi, habes plenitudinem potestatis tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus, non est verum: quia ex tunc no ad populum carentem rege, sed ad Papam pertinuit constituere regem super populum. Ad legem adductam dicent aliqui, quod nulla lex potest derogare plenitudini potestatis papalis. Ad secundum, cum dicit quod tempore successionis generis in regno & imperio filius statim mortuo patre ex ipsa generis successione assumpsit nomen regis, & administrauit bona & iura imperii: Posset aliquis respondere, quod hoc fuit ex permissione Papæ; quia placuit Papæ etiam, quia electio regis & imperatoris quæ fit per principes electores succedit & subrogata est in locum prædictæ successionis generis. Si placet Papæ, dat electo administrationem prædictam & potestatem assumendi nomen regis; & si non placet Papæ, non dabit electo administrationem. Habet enim ius & naturam illius successionis, cuius natura fuit, quod dedit prædicta, quia placuit Papæ; & si non placuisset, non dedisset. Et quod innuitur, quod successio prædicta dabit illi iuxta consuetudinem regnorum occidentalium, non habet vim, nisi quia scienter toleratur a Papa, quæ quidem consuetudo nihil iuris daret, si ipsam Papa habens plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus reuocaret. Per prædicta potest responderi ad tertium. Ex his patet, quomodo responderi potest ad illa quæ c. 3. pro opinione ultima inducuntur, quia in quantum sunt contra opinionem primam, non aliam difficultatem habere videntur, quam illa, quæ allegata sunt pro opinione secunda, ad quæ responsum est c. precedenti.
units.tr: Now, there are many who hold the first opinion, and who have answered in detail the arguments adduced for the second and third opinions in various ways, and perhaps not at all in agreement with one another. Therefore I shall briefly recite some of the responses to them, which they themselves, or some of them, or others as they may think, have given, while not at present expressing what I think of them. For first, they warn about the argument adduced for the second opinion in chapter 2, where it says that any people lacking a king can by the law of nations choose a king for itself, and by that law kingdoms were founded. Perhaps some would reply that this is to be understood of a people not having a superior, to whom it belongs to set up a king over the people, as was the case with many peoples before the world had a true lordship; for then it belonged to the people to set up a king over themselves. But since the Pope became lord of the whole world, having the fullness of power both in temporal and in spiritual matters, that is not true: because from that time it has belonged, not to a people lacking a king, but to the Pope, to set up a king over the people. To the law adduced, some will say that no law can derogate from the fullness of papal power. As to the second point, where it says that at the time of hereditary succession in a kingdom or empire, a son, immediately upon his father's death, by the very succession of the line assumed the name of king and administered the goods and rights of the empire: someone could reply that this came about by permission of the Pope, because it pleased the Pope that the election of a king or emperor made by the electing princes succeeds to and has been substituted in the place of that hereditary succession. If it pleases the Pope, he gives the elect the aforesaid administration and the power of assuming the name of king; and if it does not please the Pope, he will not give the elect the administration. For it has the right and nature of that succession, whose nature it was that he gave the aforesaid things, because it pleased the Pope; and if it had not pleased him, he would not have given them. And as for the hint that the aforesaid succession gives this to him according to the custom of the western kingdoms, it has no force, except that it is knowingly tolerated by the Pope; and indeed that custom would give no right at all if the Pope, having the fullness of power in temporal matters, were to revoke it. By what has been said, a reply can be made to the third point. From these things it is clear how replies can be given to those things which are brought forward in chapter 3 for the last opinion, because insofar as they are against the first opinion, they seem to have no other difficulty than those alleged for the second opinion, to which a reply was given in the preceding chapter.

units.la: Peroratio auctoris.
units.tr: The author's peroration.

units.la: Hæc breuiter pro exigentia materiæ conferendo, allegando & disputando de prædictis sunt dicta; non vt aliqua certa veritas in dubium reuocetur, sed propter exercitium, vt aliqua habeatur occasio, qualiter valeat veritas confirmari, & falsitas confutari. Quid autem sentiam de prædictis, non expressi; quia hoc (vt puto) nequaquam veritati prodesset; & si crederem, quod veritati quam reputo, non noceret, hoc promere vtique non differrem. Illum autem dominum mihi quamplurimum venerandum, qui hoc opus componere suis precibus me induxit, rogo & obsecro, vt mihi indulgeat, si præscriptas quæstiones ad intentionem suam sim minime prosecutus, quare eas discutiendas voluit, & mihi tradidit, & porrexit. Et si quid inuenerit, ex quo valuerit occasionem indagandi vel intelligendi veritatem accipere, Deo gratias agat; quæ autem confuse, obscure vel aliter inordinate prolata compererit, non malitiæ sed imperitiæ meæ; aut si dignabitur benignius excusare, distractioni mentis vel festinantiæ aut inanimaduertentiæ deputet & ascribat. Et sic finis huius negocii.
units.tr: These things have been briefly said, as the nature of the subject required, by comparing, alleging and disputing about the aforesaid matters; not so that any certain truth should be called into doubt, but for the sake of exercise, so that there may be an occasion of how truth may be confirmed and falsehood refuted. What I think of the aforesaid matters I have not expressed; because this (as I think) would in no way benefit the truth; and if I believed that it would not harm the truth which I hold, I would certainly not delay in setting it forth. I beg and beseech that most venerable gentleman, who by his prayers induced me to compose this work, that he may pardon me if I have by no means pursued the stated questions to his intention, for which he wished them to be discussed, and handed and presented them to me. And if he finds anything from which he may have been able to take an occasion of searching out or understanding the truth, let him give thanks to God; but whatever he finds stated confusedly, obscurely, or otherwise disorderly, let him impute and ascribe it not to malice but to my inexperience; or, if he deigns to excuse it more kindly, let him attribute it to distraction of mind, or haste, or inattention. And so ends this business.

units.la: DIALOGVS MAGIST- RI GVILLERMI DE OCKAM DOCTORIS FAMOSISSIMI.
units.tr: DIALOGUE OF MASTER WILLIAM OF OCKHAM, A MOST FAMOUS TEACHER OF THEOLOGY.

units.la: Anno Christi 1318.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1318.

units.la: RELIGIOSISSIMO ATQVE DOCTISSIMO VIRO, IOHANNI DE TRITTENHEM, ABBATI Spanhemensi ordinis sancti Benedicti de Obseruantia Bursfeldensi, præsidio suo atq; de- cori dulcissimo, salutem plurimam dicit
units.tr: To the most religious and learned man, John of Trittenheim, Abbot of Spanheim of the Order of St Benedict of the Bursfeld Observance, his most sweet protector and ornament, sends very many greetings.

units.la: IOANN. BABT. ASCENSIVS.
units.tr: JOANNES BAPTISTA ASCENSIUS.

units.la: VI priscam illam laudatissimam tempestatem, qua literarum studia maximopere floruerunt, cum hac nostra, vir dignissime, conferre voluerit, haud facile diiudicarit, illa ne huic, an hac illi plus debere convincatur. Siquidem uti in illa oppido quâ multa & sane egregia literarum volumina excogitata atq; consummata fuere: quorum tamen plurima superioris seculi negligentia aut certe bellorum saevitia interciderunt: ita in hac nostra præter noua, quæ quotidie excuduntur compluria, uetera (qua quidem extant) omnia, indelibili quadam diuturnitate donantur. Enimuero ex quo diuina imprimendi facultas inuenta aut (ut verius dicam) in meliorem formam renocata est, pretiosissima librorum supellex paulo ante hac situ victa, & pene (proh Iupiter) è medio mortalium sublata, in pristinum nitorem, cum multa noxiorum operum foetura rediit. tantumq; abest, ut boni libri diluuio bellorum obruantur, ut extra omnem temporis edacitatem, incendii oblivionisq; aleam, dum rerum mortalium ornamentum (quem mundum vocamus) persisteret, sese in tutum receperint. Quo factum est, ut tanta librorum copia studiosissimo cuiq; nunc parvo medius fidius pretio à bibliopolis vulgo obiiciatur, quantam nemo excentos ab hinc annos, ne sperare quidem vel maximo pecuniarum pondere quiverit. Proinde quandoquidem quæ superioribus annis propter librorum penuriam etiam summos (ut in illa tempestate) viros latuerunt, nunc iuuenes mediocri ingenio freti perinde ac digitos suos callent. idcirco argutissimi (qui nunc complures sunt viri) subtilissima quaq; scripturarum indagantes non cessauerunt quotidiana ferme flagitatione integerrimum & in hac arte solertissimum virum, Magistrum Ioannem Trechselisinc (de Germania loquor) oriundum, cohortari, immo improbiusculè sollicitare, ut ingeniosissimi viri Magistri Guilhelmi Ockam Dialogos quamprimum impressioni mandaret. quippe in quo eruditionis bona & argutiarum non contemptibilium immensum pelagus compererint. Scilicet (quod vigilem diligentiam tuam minime fugit) vir ille acri ingenio & incredibili animositate praeditus fuit, ut qui ea disertissime & cum summa fiducia disquisierit, de quibus alii fere vel modicum mutire piaculum duxerant. Siquidem de inæstimabili & summi pontificis & maximi imperatoris maiestate, quonam usq; potentiarum sese utraq; protendit, tanta subtilitate in varias sententias disputauit, ut nescias (si quid nescire possis) doctiusne an cautius illud effecerit. nam ne in haeresim, de qua illi plurimum sermo est, innocuus quispiam incidisse calumnietur: hac via cauit, quâ se nihil assertiue, sed omnia disputatiue discussurum protestatus est. multa tamen sic itu dignissima non obscura verborum ambage resoluit, usque adeo, ut neq; eius sententiarum desideratissima volumina, neq; alia multa sine Dialogi huius lectione quisquam intellexerit. Qua re perspecta cum docti illi viri vrgentius & sine intermissionibus instarent, cepit praefatus Trechsel ad imprimendum eum paulatim adduci. Ante tamen (ut vir diligens est) curauit opus ipsum per doctos viros examinari: atq;, ubi compertum est, mutilum & mancum esse, neq; omnes, qui praelibantur, tractatus haberi: territus tantisper pedem retraxit, dum intelligeret industria & dedita opera à prioris impressionis artifice tractatulos aliquot praetermissos. Nam constanter aiebant, quicquid bonæ frugis in toto illius operis non mediocri campo desideretur, in hiis, quæ vides, iugeribus contentum: in reliquis autem defensiones & accusationes amariores, quam ut vulgo legerentur, conspersas. Neq; vero hanc tam bonam tamq; fructiferam partem propterea cotemnendam, sed veluti à pictoribus & statuariis, Apellis, Lisippi, Phidiae, Zeuxis, & id genus laudatorum opificum, Veneres, Alexandri, Herculis Iunones, cateraq; insignia, si qua adhuc extarent, non ideo minus amarentur, quod naso aut crure altero aut brachio aliaue parte manca conspicerentur, sed eo auidius contemplarentur reliquam faciem: Ita sese hanc reliquam Dialogi partem non minori affectione complexuros, ac humanitatis studiosi, Liuianas decadas & Plautinas comoedias, quamuis bona pars in illis deperierit, complectitur. His itaq; persuasus iam secundo loco prædictus Iohann. Trechsel. quanta maxima potuit diligentia opus hoc per studiosos & disertos Parisiensis gymnasii viros fideliter castigatum, ac terssissime impressum, cum quæstionum principalium totius operis repertorio ac (ut dicunt) tabula alphabetica præmissis: dignitati tuæ, vir excellentissime, destinatum voluit. Cognouit enim cum ex complurium laudatorum hominum testimonio, tum ex nostro (quantulum est) præconio, ut sis vir optimus, atq; studiosorum omnium unicus amator: necnon & summis Germaniæ proceribus charissimus, & præter cæteros prauenerando in Christo patri domino Bertholdo Moguntinensi ecclesiæ Archiepiscopo & Romani imperii Electori prudentissimo, summa obseruatione & benevolentia devinctissimus. Quocirca nihil ambegerit Dialogon hunc tuo auspicio atq; præsidio fretum sane multis, etiam principibus viris, fore quam gratissimum. hæc summa est. Vale literarum decus.
units.tr: When you compare that old and most celebrated age, in which the study of letters flourished greatly, with our own, most worthy sir, one would hardly judge which of the two owes more to the other. For just as in that age many excellent and truly outstanding volumes of literature were devised and brought to completion, most of which were lost through the neglect of the previous century or certainly through the savagery of wars, so in our own age, besides the many new works that are printed daily, all the old ones that survive are preserved with a certain lasting durability. Indeed, since the art of printing was invented, or (to speak more truly) restored to a better form, the most precious stock of books, which a little while ago lay ruined by neglect and was almost removed from among mortals (good heavens!), has returned to its former brightness, along with a crop of many harmful works. So far is it from being the case that good books are buried under the flood of wars, that they have withdrawn into safety, beyond all the consuming power of time and the hazard of fire and oblivion, for as long as the ornament of mortal things, which we call the world, endures. As a result, such a great abundance of books is now offered by the booksellers to every eager scholar at a low price, by my faith, as no one could have hoped for even with the greatest weight of money some five hundred years ago. Therefore, since in earlier years, because of the scarcity of books, even the most eminent men (as in that age) remained unknown, now young men of moderate talent know them as well as their own fingers. Hence the most keen-witted men (of whom there are now many) who investigate the most subtle points of Scripture have not ceased, almost daily, to urge and even somewhat importunately to press that most upright man, most skilled in this art, Master John Trechsel, a native of Germany, to bring out as soon as possible the Dialogues of the most ingenious Master William of Ockham. For in them they have found an immense sea of learning and of no contemptible subtleties. Indeed (as your watchful diligence does not miss) that man was endowed with a keen mind and incredible boldness, so that he investigated with great eloquence and the utmost confidence those matters which others had hardly dared to murmur about even a little. For concerning the inestimable majesty of the supreme pontiff and the greatest emperor, and how far the power of each extends, he disputed in various opinions with such subtlety that you would not know (if you could know anything) whether he did this more learnedly or more cautiously. For, lest some innocent man should be accused of falling into the heresy about which he speaks at length, he took care in this way: he declared that he would discuss nothing assertively but everything disputatively. Yet he resolved many matters, which deserve to be known, without obscure verbal circumlocution, to such an extent that no one could understand his most desired volumes of opinions, or many other works, without reading this Dialogue. When this had been observed, and those learned men pressed more urgently and without intermission, the aforementioned Trechsel began gradually to be brought to print. Yet first (as a diligent man he is) he took care that the work itself be examined by learned men; and when it was found to be mutilated and incomplete, and that not all the treatises announced were contained in it, he drew back for a while, fearing lest he should learn that some little treatises had been deliberately and purposely omitted by the printer of the earlier edition. For they constantly said that whatever good fruit is wanting in the whole of that work, which is no small field, is contained in those furrows which you see; but in the remaining parts the defences and accusations were scattered too bitterly to be read by the public. Yet this so good and so fruitful part is not on that account to be despised; rather, as painters and sculptors of renown, such as Apelles, Lysippus, Phidias, Zeuxis and that sort of celebrated craftsmen, were not loved the less for the fact that their Venuses, Alexanders, Herculeses and Junos, and other famous works, if any still survived, were seen to be lacking a nose, a leg, an arm, or some other part, but were all the more eagerly contemplated in the rest of the face; so too, lovers of humane letters will embrace this remaining part of the Dialogue with no less affection, just as they embrace the Decades of Livy and the comedies of Plautus, though a good part of those has perished. Persuaded therefore, in the second place, by these considerations, the aforementioned John Trechsel, with the greatest diligence he could, wished this work, faithfully corrected by the learned and eloquent men of the Parisian academy and most neatly printed, to be dedicated to your dignity, most excellent sir, with a table of the principal questions of the whole work and (as they say) an alphabetical index prefixed. For he has learned, both from the testimony of many praiseworthy men and from our own (however slight) commendation, that you are a most excellent man and the sole lover of all students; and that you are also most dear to the chief men of Germany, and, above all others, bound by the greatest respect and goodwill to the most reverend father in Christ, Lord Berthold, Archbishop of the Church of Mainz and most prudent Elector of the Roman Empire. Wherefore he has no doubt that this Dialogue, placed under your auspices and protection, will be most welcome to many, even to princely men. This is the sum. Farewell, glory of letters.

units.la: Ex Lugduno pridie Idus Septembrias, huius anni 1444.
units.tr: Written at Lyons, the day before the Ides of September, in this year 1444.

units.la: IODOCI BADII ASCENSII, UT BONI IVVENES AD LITERARVM STVDIA frequentius incumbant, Cohortatio; cum quadam huius operis, & Clarissimi Viri Ioannis de Trittenhem Abbatis in Spanhem commendatiuncula.
units.tr: Exhortation of Jodocus Badius Ascensius, that good young men should apply themselves more often to the study of literature; with a short commendatory note on this work by the most distinguished man, John of Trittenheim, Abbot of Sponheim.

units.la: INgenui iuuenes fatis melioribus orti, Quis acre ingenium Iuppiter ipse dedit: Pellite segnitiem, veteresq; reuoluite libros, Quorum instar licitum est condere cuiq; nouos. Edite, quo noscant vixisse aliquando minores: Triste etenim totum est morte migrare virum. Nec mihi tam ignaua quisquam formidine dicat, Quid faciam, quando facta perisse sciam? Scilicet egregii periere volumina Grispi, Et bona pars Plauti, diaq; verba Titi. Denique si veterum repetas monumenta virorum; Heu quota quaque extet portio codicibus! At nihil excuses transacti obliuia secli, Nec belli rabiem, nec rapidi astra poli. Perpetuum siquidem cunctis extantibus aeuum Mira impressores arte dedere libris. Ecce modo arguti liber optatissimus Ockam, In quo de variis quaritur haresibus: Et maiestates Papalis & Imperialis Pensantur trutina lancibus aquifera. Atque incredibili panduntur dexteritate, Vnde aliis visum est hiscere grande nephas. Is liber, inquam, olim iam multum optatus, amicum In Spanhemensis ouat Patris abire sinum. Nempe viri auspicio tam magni praditus, orbem Terrarum exigua sperat obire die. Nam neque Germanis studiosis charior alter, Nec magis Heroum dignus amicitia. Illum & Magnifici Proceres mirantur, & omnis Vt patria patrem Religiosus amat. Proinde morer minime, quin nostro multa laboris Illius accedant commoda praesidio.
units.tr: Noble young men, born under better fates, to whom Jupiter himself gave a keen mind: drive off sloth and turn over the old books, following whose pattern each man is free to compose new ones. Publish your works, so that later and lesser men may know that you once lived, for it is a sad thing for a man to depart from life leaving nothing behind. Let no one say to me with such lazy fear, "What shall I do, since I know that deeds have perished?" Indeed the outstanding volumes of Crispus have perished, and a good part of Plautus, and the divine words of Titus. Finally, if you seek out the monuments of the ancient men, alas, how small a portion of each survives in the codices! But you cannot blame the oblivion of a past age, nor the rage of war, nor the swift turning of the heavens. For wonderful printers, by their art, have given a perpetual life to the books that survive. Behold now the most desired book of the clever Ockham, in which he inquires into various heresies, and in which the majesties of Papal and Imperial power are weighed in the balance of scales. They are unfolded with incredible skill, for which others have thought it a great sin even to open their mouths. This book, I say, long desired, rejoices to pass into the friendly bosom of the Father of Sponheim. Surely, endowed with the patronage of so great a man, it hopes to traverse the whole earth in a short day. For there is no other more dear to studious Germans, nor more worthy of the friendship of heroes. The magnificent nobles marvel at it, and every religious man loves it as a country loves its father. Therefore I will not delay at all, lest many advantages of this work be added to our labour under its protection.

units.la: PROLOGVS IN DIALOGVM
units.tr: PROLOGUE TO THE DIALOGUE

units.la: NOn omnibus curiosus existis, nec me definis infestare. Quamuis enim ob multos editos laboriose tractatus scias me hon modicum fatigatum: quoddam tamen opus insolitum postulas importune. Nam vt de controuersia, quæ de fide catholica & multis incidentibus inter Christianos nunc vertitur quæstio: quam tibi summam expohàm; impudenter exposcis, & audacter formam procedendi, modumque loquendi mihi (vt dicis) intendis imponere. Sane cum tuam fuerim importunitatem frequenter expertus, non eo quod amicus meus es, sed propter improbitatem tuam voluntati tuæ parere conabor. Quale ergo opus & cuiusmodi desideras manifesta.
units.tr: You are not a curious man in every matter, and you ought not to harass me. Although you know that I have been not a little worn out by the many laborious treatises I have published, you unreasonably demand a work of an unusual kind. For you shamelessly demand that I set out for you the sum of the controversy about the Catholic faith and the many matters arising from it, which is now being debated among Christians, and you boldly try to impose on me, as you say, the method of proceeding and the manner of speaking. Indeed, since I have often found your importunity troublesome, I will try to comply with your wishes, not because you are my friend, but because of your impudence. Now make clear what kind of work you want and of what sort.

units.la: DISCIP. Vehementer exulto, quod tu meis supplicationibus acquiescis. teneo ergo firmissime, quod opus futurum occasionem inueniendi veritatem quamplurimas toti Christianitati perutiles mihistrabit. Quod opto in tres distingui partes. quarum prima de hæreticis: secunda de dogmatibus Iohann. 22. tertia de gestis contra fidem altercantium orthodoxam; volo vocari. Totum vero opus Dialogum censeo appellandum. Peto enim, vt per interrogationem & per responsionem fiat. volo enim te interrogare; & tu mihi respondebis. Persona autem mea nomine discipuli: tua vero homine magistri vocetur. In quo personam recitantis assumas: nec tantum vnam, sed plures quando tibi videbitur, ad eandem interrogationem narra sententias. Sed quod tua sapientia sentit, mihi velis nullatenus indicare. Quamis enim velis omnino, vt cum diuersas & aduersas assertiones fueris discursurus, tuam conclusionem minime prætermittas: quæ tamen tua sit, nullatenus manifestes. ad quod perendum moueor ex duobus.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I rejoice greatly that you yield to my entreaties. So I hold firmly to the view that the work will provide an occasion for finding out many truths, very useful to the whole of Christendom. I wish it to be divided into three parts: the first concerning heretics; the second concerning the doctrines of John XXII; the third concerning the proceedings of those who dispute against the orthodox faith. I want the whole work to be called a Dialogue. For I ask that it be carried on by question and answer: I wish to question you, and you will reply to me. Let my role be called that of the disciple, and yours that of the master. In this, you may take up the role of whoever you are reporting, and not only one but several, whenever it seems good to you, setting out opinions on the same question. But what your own wisdom thinks, you must on no account reveal to me. For although you wish, as you will be running through diverse and opposing assertions, that you by no means omit your own conclusion, you must never make clear what it is. I am moved to ask this for two reasons.

units.la: Primum est, quia tantam de tua doctrina æstimationem obtineo; quod propter sententiam, quam te omnino scirem asserere, intellectum proprium cogerer captiuare. In his autem, quæ modo gestio indagare, nolo auctoritate moueri: sed quid in me possint rationes & auctoritates, quas quis adduceret aut meditatio propria, experiri.
units.tr: First, because I hold your learning in such high esteem that, if I knew for certain what view you were going to assert, I would feel compelled to take my own understanding captive to it. But in the matters I am now eager to investigate, I do not want to be moved by authority; I want to test what effect the arguments and authorities that anyone might adduce, or my own reflection, have upon me.

units.la: Secundum est, quia cum amor & odium, superbia, ira, & inuidia, nec non aliæ animæ passiones ab inquisitione veritatis humanum impediant, immo & peruertant iudicium. Si sententiam tuam & etiam nomen occultare volueris, nec amici opus futurum plusquam debeant amplectentur: nec plusquam oporteat despicient inimici. Sed hi & illi non quis est alicuius sententiæ auctor: sed quid dicitur attendentes remotis zeli oculis, scribenda respicient & insistent sincerius indagare veritatem. propter quam etiam rationem in hoc opere quid de domino summo pontifice, ac de doctrina eius, suisque æmulis sentias, nunquam aperias. quod vt magis abscondas, cum de personis loqueris, eorum nomina supprimas officiorum, & primis litteris nominum propriorum appellā. Vnde dominum Papam, dominum Iohann. Bauariæ dominum B. Fratrem Michaelem Generalem Fratrum Minorum. MAGIST. Fratrem Gerardum Othonis, Fratrem G. cura vocate. A te autem specialiter hoc opus effagito; non solum quia te reputo præ aliis eruditum: sed etiam quia te video circa controuersiam præfatam singulariter occupatum.
units.tr: Second, because love and hatred, pride, anger and envy, and other passions of the soul, hinder the search for truth and even pervert judgment. If you wish to conceal your opinion and even your name, then friends will not embrace the work more than they ought, nor will enemies despise it more than is fitting; but neither group will attend to who is the author of any opinion, only to what is said, and, with the eyes of zeal set aside, they will look at what is written and apply themselves more sincerely to the search for truth. For this same reason, in this work, you must never reveal what you think about the lord supreme pontiff, or about his doctrine, or about his rivals. To conceal this more thoroughly, when you speak of persons, suppress their names and their offices, and refer to them by the initial letters of their proper names. Hence: the lord Pope; the lord John of Bavaria; the lord B.; Brother Michael, Minister General of the Friars Minor; MASTER: call him Brother G. of Otto; Brother G. ... I particularly ask you for this work, not only because I count you more learned than others, but also because I see that you are singularly occupied with the aforesaid controversy.

units.la: Omnes enim libellos & opera aduersariorum contra dominum summum pontificem mitetis congregare: in quibus sine intermissione studes. Ita vt aliquando occasionem habeam suspicandi, quod aliqua dubitatio in corde tuo de summo pontifice eiusque doctrina nascatur. Quia tamen a me (quem scis eiusdem domini summi pontificis sinceritissimum zelatorem, & quod aduersationes complicesque eorum valde detestor) de prædictis nihil abscondis: mihi præbes materiam opinandi, quod ad reprobandum tempore opportuno omnia opera colligis æmulorum. Venitamen propter motiua præscripta ante huius operis consummationem mihi mentem tuam minime pandas, nec propter hoc putes te culpam aliquam incursurum.
units.tr: For you are busy gathering all the little books and works of the opponents against the lord supreme pontiff, and you study them without intermission. So much so that at times I have reason to suspect that some doubt about the supreme pontiff and his doctrine has arisen in your heart. Yet, since you conceal nothing of these matters from me (you know that I am a most sincere zealot for the same lord supreme pontiff, and that I greatly detest his adversaries and their accomplices), you give me material for supposing that you are collecting all the works of his rivals in order to refute them at the proper time. Nevertheless, for the reasons stated above, do not lay open your mind to me before this work is finished, and do not think that you will incur any blame for this.

units.la: Primam ergo partem de hæreticis acceleres inchoate: materiam in septem diuide libros, quorum primus inuestiget ad quos (theologos videlicet vel canonistas) pertinet principaliter diffinire, quæ assertiones catholicæ, quæ hæreticæ: qui etiam hæretici & catholici debeant reputari.
units.tr: So, hasten to begin the first part, on heretics: divide the subject matter into seven books. The first should investigate to whom it belongs chiefly to define (that is, to theologians or to canonists) which assertions are Catholic and which heretical, and also who ought to be regarded as heretics and who as Catholics.

units.la: Secundus inquirat, quæ assertiones hæreticæ, quæ catholicæ sunt censendæ. Tertius principaliter consideret, quis erratus inter hæreticos est computandus. Quartus quomodo de pertinacitate & prauitate hæretica debeat quis conuinci. Quintus, qui possunt prauitate hæretica maculari. Sextus agat de punitione hæreticorum, & maxime Papæ si efficiatur hæreticus. Septimus tractet de credentibus, fautoribus, defensoribus & receptoribus hæreticorum.
units.tr: The second should inquire which assertions are to be judged heretical and which Catholic. The third should chiefly consider what error is to be counted among heresies. The fourth, how someone ought to be convicted of pertinacity and heretical depravity. The fifth, who can be stained by heretical depravity. The sixth should treat of the punishment of heretics, and especially of the Pope, if he should become a heretic. The seventh should deal with those who believe in, favour, defend and harbour heretics.

units.la: MAGIST. Affectas (ut video) quatenus ex serie dicendorum nemo possit colligere, quam partem dissentientium circa fidem catholicam teputem iustiorem, quod tuę satisfaciens voluntati una cum aliis, quæ vel efflagitas vel affectas, seruare curabo. Primo tamen cum opus futurum per interrogationem & responsionem fieri roges, responsionem autem interrogatio antecedit, tuum erit incipere. Quod ergo tibi placet, interroga.
units.tr: MASTER. You aim (as I see) at a sequence of topics from which no one could gather which side of those who dissent from the Catholic faith you judge more just; I will take care to observe this, satisfying your will together with the other things you ask for or aim at. But first, since you request that the work be carried out by question and answer, and the question comes before the answer, it will be your task to begin. So ask whatever pleases you.

units.la: INCIPIT LIBER PRIMVS, QVI QVÆRIT, AD QVOS SPECTAT, SCILICET SIVE AD THEOLOGOS SIVE AD CANONISTAS, PRINCIPALITER DIFFINIRE, QVÆ ASSER- TIONES catholicæ & quæ hæreticæ, siue qui hæretici seu catho- lici sint censendi. CAP. I.
units.tr: THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS, WHICH ASKS PRINCIPALLY TO WHOM IT BELONGS, NAMELY TO THE THEOLOGIANS OR TO THE CANONISTS, TO DEFINE WHICH ASSERTIONS ARE CATHOLIC AND WHICH ARE HERETICAL, AND WHETHER THOSE WHO HOLD THEM ARE TO BE JUDGED HERETICS OR CATHOLICS. CHAPTER I.

units.la: In quo proponitur quæstio, ad quam respondetur sub distinctione huius termini diffinire, & probatur quod hoc principaliter spectat ad canonistas tribus rationibus, ad quas respondetur capitulo tertio.
units.tr: In this chapter the question is put, and it is answered under a distinction of the term "to define." It is proved that this belongs principally to the canonists, by three reasons, which are answered in the third chapter.

units.la: DISCIP. Quoniam occasione dissensionis, quam in Christianitate conspicio, de assertionibus hæreticis & catholicis, acriter de personis hæreticis & orthodoxis, sum indagaturus quamplurimum, in primis duxi quærendum, ad quos (theologos videlicet vel ad canonistas) principaliter pertinet diffinire, quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica est censenda: MAG. Ad interrogationem tuam propositam respondetur, quod hoc verbum diffinire plures habet significationes. de quibus ad propositum duæ videntur pertinere. Contingit enim aliquid diffinire auctoritate officii. & sic diffinire, quæ est assertio hæretica, quæ catholica est censenda, ad summum pontificem spectat & concilium generale. Aliquando contingit diffinire per modum doctrinæ, quo modo Magistri in scholis quæstiones diffiniunt & determinant. & sic accepto secundo modo diffiniendi circa propositam quæstionem diuersimode sentiunt literati. DISCIP. Ad præsens accipio verbum diffiniendi secundo modo. & sic accepto vocabulo diuersas sententias cum motiuis earum audire desidero.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Since, on account of the dispute I see in Christendom over heretical and Catholic assertions, and over heretical and orthodox persons, I am going to inquire into this at great length, I first thought it right to ask: to whom (that is, to the theologians or to the canonists) does it principally belong to define which assertion is to be judged Catholic and which heretical? MASTER. To your question, as put, the answer is that this word "to define" has several meanings, of which two seem relevant to the point. For one may define something by the authority of an office, and in this sense it belongs to the supreme pontiff and to a general council to define which assertion is to be judged heretical and which Catholic. At other times one defines by way of teaching, as masters in the schools define and determine questions. In this second sense of defining, learned men hold differing views on the question before us. DISCIPLE. For the present I take the word "defining" in the second sense, and with that understanding I wish to hear the various opinions and the reasons behind them.

units.la: MAGIST. Quorundam opinio est, quod ad canonistas principaliter spectat, quæ assertio est catholica, quæ hæretica iudicare, pro qua tribus rationibus videntur posse moueri. Quarum prima est hæc. Ad illam scientiam principaliter spectat diffinire & discernere, quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica est censenda, quæ principaliter tractat de approbatione veritatum catholicarum, & reprobatione hæresum damnatarum. huiusmodi est scientia canonistarum, & non theologia. igitur. Secunda ratio est hæc. Ad istam scientiam pertinet diffinire, &c. cuius fides, quantum ad credibilia, principalius adhibetur. sed quantum ad ea, quæ sunt fidei, magis credendum est canonistarum scientiæ, quam theologiæ. igitur. probo minorem, quia magis credendum est ecclesiæ, per quam edita est canonistarum scientia, quam euangelio, teste Augustino, contra epistolam fundamenti, qui videtur asserere, maiorem esse ecclesiæ auctoritatem, quam euangelii. quia nec euangelio crederem, inquit, nisi ecclesia auctoritas compulisset. ergo &c. Tertia ratio. Ad illam scientiam principaliter spectat discernere, quæ assertio &c. cuius auctor habet symbolum fidei ordinare, & articulos fidei rite diffinire. sed hoc spectat ad summum pontificem, qui auctor est scientiæ canonistarum. ergo ad scientiam canonistarum, & per consequens ad ipsos principalius, quam ad theologos pertinet diffinire, quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica debeat reputari.
units.tr: MASTER. Some hold that it belongs principally to the canonists to judge which assertion is Catholic and which heretical, and three reasons seem to support this view. The first is this. To that science belongs principally the defining and discerning of which assertion is to be judged Catholic and which heretical; it principally treats of the approval of Catholic truths and the rejection of condemned heresies. Such is the science of the canonists, and not theology. Therefore (it follows). The second reason is this. To that science belongs the defining, etc., whose credibility, as far as matters of faith go, is more principally relied upon. But as far as things that belong to faith are concerned, more credence is to be given to the science of the canonists than to theology. Therefore. I prove the minor premise: more credence is to be given to the Church, through which the science of the canonists was issued, than to the gospel, as Augustine says against the letter of Manichaeus (the "Fundamental Epistle"), who seems to assert that the authority of the Church is greater than that of the gospel, since, he says, "I would not believe the gospel itself unless the authority of the Church had compelled me." Therefore, etc. The third reason. To that science belongs principally the discerning of which assertion, etc., whose author has the power to draw up the creed and rightly define the articles of faith. But this belongs to the supreme pontiff, who is the author of the science of the canonists. Therefore it belongs principally to the science of the canonists, and consequently to them rather than to the theologians, to define which assertion ought to be regarded as Catholic and which as heretical.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: Vbi probatur per octo rationes, quod ad solos theologos spectat talis diffinitio per modum doctrinæ.
units.tr: Where it is proved by eight arguments that such a definition, by way of doctrine, belongs only to the theologians.

units.la: MAGISTER Porro alii indubitanter tenent, quod ad theologos spectat, non per modum diffinitionis authenticæ: sed per modum doctrinæ principaliter diffinire, quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica sit censenda. & quod ad canonistas non pertinet, nisi inquantum eorum scientia aliqua ad fidem pertinetia a theologia dignoscitur mendicare. hanc autem suam assertionem rationibus confirmare nituntur.
units.tr: THE MASTER: Others, however, hold without doubt that it belongs to the theologians to determine, not by way of authoritative definition but principally by way of doctrine, which assertion is to be regarded as Catholic and which as heretical. They hold that it does not belong to the canonists, except insofar as their science is seen to borrow some points pertaining to faith from theology. They try to confirm this assertion of theirs by reasons.

units.la: Quarum prima hæc est. Ad illius scientiæ Doctores (propter quam solummodo dicitur quæcunque assertio catholica vel hæretica) principaliter pertinet diffinire per modum doctrinæ, quæ assertio est catholica reputanda. sed propter theologiam solummodo quæcunque assertio est catholica huncupanda. illius enim assertio, quæ sola est consona theologiæ, est vere theologica. illa vero sola, quæ theologiæ noscitur aduersari, hæretica esse dignoscitur. Si enim aliqua assertio aliquibus decretis summorum pontificum vel etiam generalium conciliorum ac etiam legibus imperatorum inueniretur aduersa, si theologiæ nullatenus obuiaret, (quamuis falsa & erronea vel iniqua posset haberi) non tamen deberet inter hæreses computari: ergo ad theologiæ tractatores principaliter pertinet diffinire per modum doctrinæ, quæ assertio catholica & quæ hæretica est censenda.
units.tr: The first of these is this. It belongs principally to the teachers of that science, for the sake of which alone any assertion is called Catholic or heretical, to determine by way of doctrine which assertion is to be considered Catholic. But only for the sake of theology is any assertion called Catholic at all. For that assertion alone is truly theological which agrees with theology, and only that which is known to oppose theology is recognised as heretical. For if some assertion were found to conflict with some decrees of the supreme pontiffs, or even of general councils, or with the laws of emperors, yet if it did not in any way oppose theology, it could be held false, erroneous, or unjust, but it should not be counted among the heresies. Therefore it belongs principally to the students of theology to determine, by way of doctrine, which assertion is to be considered Catholic and which heretical.

units.la: Secunda ratio. Ad illius scientiæ Doctores pertinet diffinire &c. quæ tractat regulas fidei, quæ tractantur in alia scientia, & plures alias, & non econtra. huiusmodi est scientia theologiæ, non canonistarum. Multa enim, quæ ad fidem nostram spectant, in theologia reperiuntur explicite, de quibus in scientia canonistarum mentio non habetur. Nihil autem spectans ad regulam fidei in eorum scientia poterit reperiri, nisi quod a theologia recipiunt. ergo ad theologos talis diffinitio principaliter noscitur pertinere. ad canonistas autem non spectat, nisi quantum aliqua theologica noscuntur a theologis mendicare.
units.tr: The second reason. It belongs to the teachers of that science, which treats the rules of faith, which are treated in another science, and many others, and not the reverse, to make such determinations. Such a science is theology, not the science of the canonists. For many things pertaining to our faith are found explicitly in theology, and no mention of them is made in the science of the canonists. Nothing pertaining to the rule of faith could be found in their science except what they borrow from theology. Therefore such a definition is known to belong principally to the theologians. It does not belong to the canonists, except insofar as they are known to borrow some theological matters from the theologians.

units.la: Tertia ratio est hæc. De assertionibus, quas scientia superior & inferior tractare noscuntur, habet scientia superior principaliter iudicare. sed de quibusdam assertionibus catholicis & hæreticis theologia, quæ est superior, & scientia canonistarum, quæ est inferior, aliquomodo tractant. ergo ad theologiam pertinet principaliter de assertionibus catholicis & hæreticis iudicare: & per consequens ad theologos principalius pertinet diffinire, & per modum doctrinæ quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica est censenda.
units.tr: The third reason is this. The higher science has the principal right to judge the assertions which the higher and the lower science are known to treat. But theology, which is the higher science, and the science of the canonists, which is the lower, both treat certain Catholic and heretical assertions in some way. Therefore it belongs principally to theology to judge concerning Catholic and heretical assertions, and consequently it belongs more principally to the theologians to determine, by way of doctrine, which assertion is to be considered Catholic and which heretical.

units.la: Quarta ratio est hæc. Ad illius scientiæ tractatores, per quam plures assertiones catholicæ explicite sub forma propria pertractantur, pertinet &c. huiusmodi est theologia, non scientia canonistarum, in quibus pauca veritates catholicæ sub forma propria pertractantur. ergo talis diffinitio ad theologos dignoscitur principaliter pertinere.
units.tr: The fourth reason is this. It belongs to the teachers of that science, through which many Catholic assertions are treated explicitly in their proper form, to make such determinations. Such a science is theology, not the science of the canonists, in which few Catholic truths are treated in their proper form. Therefore such a definition is known to belong principally to the theologians.

units.la: Quinta ratio est hæc. Ad tractatores illius scientiæ per quam antequam esset canonistarum scientia, viri catholici veritates catholicas approbauerunt, prædicauerunt, ac occulte & publice docuerunt, doctrinasque hæreticales, & auctores earum confutauerunt, reprobauerunt & etiam damnauerunt, principaliter pertinet diffinire, quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica est censenda. huiusmodi autem est theologia. nam antequam canones condrentur, apostoli aliique discipuli Iesu Christi, tanquam viri theologi, veritates catholicas approbauerunt, prædicauerunt ac occulte & publice docuerunt, doctrinasque hæreticales & auctores earum confutauerunt, reprobauerunt ac etiam damnauerunt. Vnde & beatus Paulus, sicut legitur ad Timoth. 3. hæreticum hominem post primam & secundam correctionem deuitandum docuit. Prima etiam ad Timoth. 4. docuit manifeste doctrinam prohibentium nubere, abstinere a cibis quos Deus creauit ad percipiendum cum gratiarum actione fidelibus ad spiritum erroris & doctrinam daemoniorum, & per consequens ad prauitatem haereticam pertinere. ergo ad theologiam, & per consequens ad theologos, principaliter pertinet diffinitio talis.
units.tr: The fifth reason is this. It belongs principally to the teachers of that science, through which, before there was a science of the canonists, Catholic men approved, preached, and taught Catholic truths both privately and publicly, and refuted, condemned, and even damned heretical doctrines and their authors, to determine which assertion is to be considered Catholic and which heretical. Such a science is theology. For before the canons were compiled, the apostles and the other disciples of Jesus Christ, as theologians, approved, preached, and taught Catholic truths both privately and publicly, and refuted, condemned, and even damned heretical doctrines and their authors. Hence also the blessed Paul, as we read in 1 Tim. 3, taught that a heretical man is to be avoided after the first and second correction. In 1 Tim. 4 he also plainly taught that the doctrine of those who forbid marriage and abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful is a spirit of error and a doctrine of demons, and consequently pertains to heretical depravity. Therefore such a definition belongs to theology, and consequently to the theologians, principally.

units.la: Sexta ratio est hæc. Ad tractatores illius scientiæ, cui quantum ad illa, quæ fidei sunt, omnes alii cedunt, principaliter per modum doctrinæ pertinet diffinire, quæ assertio catholica &c. huiusmodi est scientia scripturæ diuinæ, quæ theologia vocatur, vt patet ex decretis di. 9. per totum & specialiter capitul. noli. & capitul. negare. & capitul. ego solum. & capitul. quis nesciat. & capitul. nobis. & capitul. neque, colligitur euidenter, quod ad theologos principaliter talis diffinitio spectat. Septima ratio est hæc. Ad tractatores illius scientiæ, cuius auctor immediatus Deus est, a quo est tota fides nostra, principaliter pertinet diffinitio aute dicta. talis autem est theologia: quia scriptores scripturæ diuinæ nihil penitus conscripserunt ex humano ingenio, sed solum ex diuina inspiratione, teste Petro, qui
units.tr: The sixth reason is this. It belongs principally, by way of doctrine, to the students of that science, to which all others yield in matters of faith, to determine which assertion is Catholic. Such a science is the science of divine Scripture, which is called theology, as is clear from the decrees of Dist. 9, throughout, and especially from the chapters Noli, Negare, Ego solum, Quis nesciat, Nobis, and Neque. From this it is evidently gathered that such a definition principally pertains to the theologians. The seventh reason is this. It belongs principally to the definition mentioned above to belong to the students of that science whose immediate author is God, from whom all our faith comes. Such a science is theology, because the writers of divine Scripture wrote nothing at all from human talent, but only from divine inspiration, as Peter bears witness,

units.la: {1} Marks in margin refer to the numbered sections of the argument. qui in prima canonica sua ait: Spiritu sancto inspirati locuti sunt sancti Dei omnes. propter quod docet ibidem, quod prophetia scripturae divinae propria interpretatione non fit. non enim voluntate humana allata est aliquando prophetia, ergo ad theologos principaliter pertinet diffinitio ante dicta.
units.tr: {1} Marginal marks refer to the numbered sections of the argument. who in his first Epistle says: Holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit. For this reason he teaches in the same place that prophecy of divine Scripture does not come about by private interpretation. For prophecy was never brought forth by the human will. Therefore the definition mentioned above principally pertains to the theologians.

units.la: Octava ratio est haec: Ad tractatores illius scientiae principaliter pertinet diffinitio saepe fata, cui non licet aliquid addere nec auferre. huiusmodi est autem theologia, Moyse in persona Dei dicente Deuteron. cap. 4: Non addetis ad verbum quod vobis loquor, nec auferetis ab eo. cui correspondet Salomon Proverb. 30. de sermone Dei loquens ait: ne addas quicquam verbis illius, et arguaris inveniarisque mendax. hinc addentibus et auferentibus aliquid ex scriptura divina, spiritus sanctus per beatum Iohann. Euangelistam Apocal. ultimo terribiliter comminatur dicens: Si quis apposuerit adhuc super haec, apponet super eum Deus plagas quae sunt in libro isto. Et si quis diminuerit de verbis prophetiae libri huius, auferet Deus partem eius de libro vitae et de civitate sancta. Ex quibus omnibus evidenter colligitur, quod ad sacram scripturam nihil est addendum, nec aliquid auferendum ex ea. ergo ad theologos scripturae sacrae tractatores principaliter pertinet diffinire per modum doctrinae, quae assertio catholica, et quae haeretica est censenda. Ecce ad interrogationem tuam assertiones contrarias recitavi: et in fulcimentum utriusque partis rationes tetigi fortiores. nunc vero ergo considera, quae probabilior tibi videtur.
units.tr: The eighth reason is this. It belongs principally to the students of that science, to which it is often said that nothing may be added or taken away, to make the definition. Such a science is theology, Moses speaking in the person of God in Deut. 4: You shall not add to the word which I speak to you, nor take away from it. To this Solomon corresponds in Prov. 30, speaking of the word of God: Add nothing to his words, lest you be reproved and found a liar. Hence the Holy Spirit terribly threatens those who add to or take away anything from divine Scripture, through the blessed evangelist John in the last chapter of Revelation: If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues that are written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God will take away his part from the book of life and from the holy city. From all of these it is evidently gathered that nothing is to be added to sacred Scripture, nor anything taken away from it. Therefore it belongs principally to the theologians, the students of sacred Scripture, to determine by way of doctrine which assertion is to be considered Catholic and which heretical. Behold, in answer to your question I have recited the contrary assertions, and in support of each side I have touched on the stronger arguments. Now, therefore, consider which seems more probable to you.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationem primam in primo capitulo factam primo contra canonistas innuendo.
units.tr: In which the first argument, raised in the first chapter against the canonists, is answered by first hinting at the canonists' position.

units.la: DISCIP. Quamuis ex rationibus pro assertione secunda adductis mihi tribus occasionem multa quaerendi: fateor tamen, quod ipsa mihi videtur consona veritati. Licet ad rationes pro prima assertione nesciam respondere mihi metipsi: Unde peto ut tu ad eas respondeas.
units.tr: DISCIP. Although the reasons adduced for the second assertion have given me occasion to ask many questions, I confess that it seems to me consonant with the truth. Yet I cannot answer the reasons for the first assertion myself, so I ask you to answer them.

units.la: MAGIST. Tu videris tibi ipsi contrarius. In principio enim petisti, ut quid de interrogationibus tuis sentirem, nullatenus indicarem: nunc autem poscis, ut ad aliquas rationes respondeam. Ex quo conuinci potest, quod desideras, quatenus quid teneam in corde aperiam.
units.tr: MAGIST. You seem to be contradicting yourself. At the beginning you asked me not to tell you what I thought of your questions, and now you demand that I answer some reasons. From this it can be shown that you want what you wish to have, namely that I should disclose what I hold in my heart.

units.la: DISCIP: Quicquid petitio mea ex vi vocis insinuet, nullo modo volebam, quod quid mente habeas indices: sed petere intendebam, ut responsiones aliorum, quae cogitari possunt ab aliis rectiores, nullatenus exprimendo an eas rationabiles vel irrationabiles putes esse censendas.
units.tr: DISCIP. Whatever my request may seem to imply by the force of its words, I never wanted you to indicate what you hold in your mind. I only meant to ask that you set out the replies others might think of, which are more correct, without saying whether you consider them reasonable or unreasonable.

units.la: MAGIST. Ex quo tuam petitionem concipio, faciam quod hortaris. Imprimis autem volo te scire, quod auctores theologi moderni temporis canonistas, tanquam non intelligentes, praesumptuosos, temerarios, fallaces, deceptores, cavillatores, et ignaros in cordibus suis valde despiciunt, reputantes quod sacrorum canonum intellectum ignorent. pro quo tali ratione moventur. Sacrorum canonum dictatores viri acutissimi in scientia naturali, morali, et theologia fuerunt: neque per nullam absque praedictis scientiis canones tam certae tamque profundae veritatis aliqualiter conscripsissent. Cum ergo canonistae moderni scientias ante dictas ignorent, quamuis valeant canonum sacrorum retinere memoriam, ad intellectum tamen eorum nequeunt pervenire.
units.tr: MAGIST. Since I understand your request in this way, I will do what you urge. First, however, I want you to know that the modern theologians hold the canonists in great contempt in their hearts, as men who do not understand, presumptuous, rash, deceitful, deceivers, quibblers and ignorant, reckoning that they are ignorant of the meaning of the sacred canons. They are moved to this by the following reason. The compilers of the sacred canons were most acute men in natural science, moral philosophy and theology; nor could they have drawn up canons of such certain and profound truth without those sciences. Since, therefore, the modern canonists are ignorant of the sciences just mentioned, although they can retain the sacred canons in memory, they cannot come to understand them.

units.la: DISCIPL. Nostri temporis canonistas non reputo contemnendos. Licet forte scire canonum sacrorum intellectum (illorum praecipue, qui ex theologia vel ratione naturali accipiuntur, et non sunt pure positivi) magis ad theologos, quam ad canonistas pertineat: sed circa hoc quaeso hic nullatenus immoreris: quia forte de ista materia quaestionem habebo. Ad rationes ergo praefatas accede.
units.tr: DISCIP. I do not think the canonists of our time are to be despised. Yet perhaps the understanding of the sacred canons (especially those that are drawn from theology or natural reason and are not purely positive) belongs more to the theologians than to the canonists. But I ask you not to linger on this point here, because I may perhaps have a question on this matter. Now come to the reasons mentioned before.

units.la: MAGIST. Quia in hoc opere non sensum meum, sed tuam voluntatem sequi promisi, rationes praedictas incipiam pertractare. Unde ad primam nonnulli respondent theologi, dicentes; quod ad theologiam, non ad scientiam canonistarum principaliter spectat de approbatione veritatum theologicarum catholicarum; et reprobatione haeresum damnatarum tractare. Cuius rationem assignant dicentes, quod assertio veritatis est approbatio veritatis. qui enim aliquod dictum asserit esse verum, approbat idem dictum tanquam verum. Assertio enim veritatis est contraria reprobatio falsitatis. quia qui aliquam approbat veritatem, per consequens reprobat contrariam falsitatem; sicut qui praecipit unum contrariorum, et per consequens prohibet aliud, ut notat Gloss. in decret. capitulo primo. Assertio ergo veritatum catholicarum per quandam consequentiam est reprobatio omnium haeresum contrariarum. Cum ergo per theologiam principaliter veritates catholicae asseruntur, sequitur quod approbatio veritatum catholicarum et reprobatio seu damnatio haeresum principaliter ad theologiam pertinet.
units.tr: MAGIST. Since I promised in this work to follow your wish rather than my own opinion, I shall begin to deal with the reasons mentioned. Some theologians answer the first of them by saying that the approval of Catholic theological truths and the condemnation of condemned heresies belong principally to theology, not to the science of the canonists. They give this reason: the assertion of a truth is the approval of that truth. For whoever asserts that some statement is true approves the same statement as true. And the assertion of a truth is the opposite of the rejection of falsehood, because whoever approves one truth consequently rejects the contrary falsehood, just as whoever commands one of two contraries consequently forbids the other, as the Gloss notes in the Decretum, chapter one. Therefore the assertion of Catholic truths is, by a certain consequence, the rejection of all contrary heresies. Since, then, Catholic truths are principally asserted through theology, it follows that the approval of Catholic truths and the rejection or condemnation of heresies belong principally to theology.

units.la: LI
units.tr: LI

units.la: DISCIP. Ista ratio videtur mihi satis probabilis: velle tamen scire, quare dicunt isti, quod talis approbatio & damnatio principaliter pertinent ad theologiam. Ex quo insinuare videntur, quod non tantum pertinent ad eam.
units.tr: DISCIP. This argument seems to me quite probable. Yet I want to know why these men say that such approval and condemnation belong principally to theology. By this they seem to imply that they do not belong to theology alone.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad istam tuam quaestionem respondent isti dicentes: quod ad scientiam canonistarum pertinent libri decretorum & decretalium, & aliae constitutiones summorum pontificum & epistolae: licet in praedictis libris minime sint insitae. In praedictis autem libris, in nonnullis constitutionibus & epistolis summorum pontificum quaedam veritates theologicae asseruntur, & nonnullae haereses reprobantur. Licet tam istae veritates quam haereses sint paucae respectu illarum, quae in theologia habentur. & ideo non tantum ad theologiam, sed etiam ad scientiam canonistarum spectat aliquas catholicas veritates approbare, & aliquas haereses licet paucas reprobare. ad theologiam autem spectat omnes veritates catholicas approbare, & omnes haereses reprobare. quare licet principaliter approbatio & reprobatio ad theologiam pertineant: pertinent tamen secundario nihilominus ad scientiam canonistarum. Aliam autem rationem adducunt dicentes: quod theologia veritates catholicas approbando, & haereses reprobando, a canonistatum scientia nihil omnino recipit; nihil mendicat. canonistarum vero scientia veritates catholicas approbando, & haereses reprobando a theologia omnia mendicando procedit. quare ad theologiam haec principaliter & utiliter pertinere noscuntur: ad canonistarum vero scientiam secundario & particulariter tantum.
units.tr: MAGIST. To this question of yours these men answer, saying that the books of the Decretum and the Decretals, and the other constitutions and letters of the supreme pontiffs, belong to the science of the canonists, although they are not at all concerned with the arts of the theologians in these books. In the said books, however, in some constitutions and letters of the supreme pontiffs, certain theological truths are asserted and some heresies are rejected. Although both these truths and these heresies are few compared with those held in theology, it therefore belongs not only to theology but also to the science of the canonists to approve some Catholic truths and to reject some heresies, though few. It belongs to theology to approve all Catholic truths and reject all heresies. So although approval and rejection belong principally to theology, they nonetheless belong secondarily to the science of the canonists. They also offer another reason, saying that theology, in approving Catholic truths and rejecting heresies, takes nothing at all from the science of the canonists and begs nothing from it, whereas the science of the canonists proceeds in approving Catholic truths and rejecting heresies by borrowing everything from theology. Therefore these things are known to belong principally and usefully to theology, but to the science of the canonists only secondarily and in a limited way.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad secundam rationem capitulo primo factam.
units.tr: In which the second argument made in the first chapter is answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Haec responsio videtur mihi probabilis: quare rationem secundam pertractat. MAGIST. Ad secundam rationem respondetur, quod quantum ad ea, quae fidei sunt, magis credendum est theologiae, quam cuicunque alteri scientiae: nullisque scriptoribus quarumcunque scientiarum ita oportet credere, sicut scriptoribus theologiae sacrae. Auctoritas beati Augustini, quae adducitur, ut nonnulli dicunt, frequenter a multis contra intellectum textus Augustini allegatur. ad cuius intellectum dicunt esse sciendum: quod nomen Ecclesiae aequivoce in locis variis scripturarum accipitur. Aliquando enim accipitur pro loco corporali divinis officiis deputato. Aliquando accipitur pro aliquo speciali collegio clericorum. Aliquando pro toto collegio clericorum omnium. Aliquando pro aliqua multitudine speciali cleri & Papae. Aliquando pro tota congregatione fidelium simul in hac vita mortali degentium. Aliquando vero nomen Ecclesiae non solum totam congregationem catholicorum viuentium, sed etiam fideles mortuos comprehendit.
units.tr: DISCIP. This answer seems to me plausible, so let us go on to deal with the second argument. MAGIST. To the second argument the reply is this: where matters of faith are concerned, more credit is to be given to theology than to any other science, and one ought to believe the writers of no other discipline as one ought to believe the writers of sacred theology. The authority of blessed Augustine that is cited, as some say, is frequently alleged by many against the true sense of Augustine's text. For its understanding, they say, we must know that the name Church is used equivocally in various places of Scripture. Sometimes it is taken for a place set apart for divine services. Sometimes it is taken for some particular college of clergy. Sometimes for the whole college of all the clergy. Sometimes for some particular multitude of the clergy and the Pope. Sometimes for the whole congregation of the faithful living together in this mortal life. But sometimes the name Church embraces not only the whole congregation of living Catholics but also the faithful dead.

units.la: Et isto modo ultimo accipit ecclesiam beatus Augustinus in li. contra Manichaeos & recitatur. 2. di c. palam. Qui ait: palam est quantum in re dubia ad fidem & certitudinem valeat catholica ecclesiae auctoritas, quae ab ipsis fundatissimis sedibus apostolorum, usque ad hodiernum diem, succedentibus sibimet episcoporum serie & tot populorum concessione & assertione firmatur. vbi ecclesia catholica episcopos & populos a tempore apostolorum usque ad hodiernum diem sibimet succedentes importat. Et sic accipit nomen Ecclesiae Augustinus cum asserit, quod non crederet euangelium, nisi eum auctoritas ecclesiae compelleret. Ista enim ecclesia scriptores euangelii & omnes apostolos comprehendit, sicut probatum est. Quare ex auctoritate Augustini sane intellecta inferri non potest, quod magis sit credendum summo pontifici canonum conditori, quam euangelio. Et per consequens probari non potest, quod maior fides exhibenda sit sacris canonibus, quam euangelio sancto. Conceditur tamen, quod magis credendum est ecclesiae, quae est multitudo catholicorum omnium, qui fuerunt a temporibus prophetarum & apostolorum usque modo, quam euangelio: non quia de euangelio sit aliqualiter dubitandum, sed quia totum maius est sua parte. Ecclesia ergo, quae maioris auctoritatis est, quam euangelista, est illa ecclesia, cuius auctor euangelii pars esse dignoscitur.
units.tr: It is in this last sense that blessed Augustine takes the Church in his book against the Manichaeans, and it is cited in dist. 2, c. Palam. He says: "It is plain how much the authority of the Catholic Church avails in a doubtful matter concerning faith and certainty, an authority which, from the very firmest seats of the apostles down to the present day, is confirmed by the succession of bishops in an unbroken line and by the consent and assent of so many peoples." Here the Catholic Church means the bishops and peoples succeeding one another from the time of the apostles down to the present day. And Augustine takes the name Church in this same sense when he asserts that he would not believe the gospel, unless the authority of the Church compelled him.
