For that Church embraces the writers of the gospel and all the apostles, as has been proved. Therefore it cannot be inferred from Augustine's authority, rightly understood, that more credit is to be given to the supreme pontiff, the author of the canons, than to the gospel. And consequently it cannot be proved that greater faith is to be shown to the sacred canons than to the holy gospel. It is granted, however, that more credit is to be given to the Church, which is the multitude of all Catholics who have lived from the times of the prophets and apostles until now, than to the gospel; not because the gospel is in any way to be doubted, but because the whole is greater than its part. The Church, therefore, which has the greater authority than the evangelist, is that Church of which the author of the gospel is known to be a part.

units.la: Non est autem mirum, si maior est auctoritas totius, quam partis. Et ideo maiorecт auctoritas totius congregationis comprehendentis euangelistas & omnes alios orthodoxos usque ad haec tempora, quam unius vel etiam plurium personarum congregationis eiusdem. Quod autem conditor canonis non sit maioris auctoritatis, quam euangelium, sed multo minoris, ipsimet canonum conditores testantur aperte.
units.tr: Nor is it surprising if the authority of the whole is greater than that of a part. And so the authority of the whole congregation, which comprises the evangelists and all other orthodox believers down to these times, is greater than that of one or even several persons of the same congregation. That the author of a canon is not of greater authority than the gospel, but of much less, the authors of the canons themselves openly testify.

units.la: Vrbanus enim Papa, & habetur vigesimaquinta quaest. 1. c. sunt quidem, ait: Sciendum vero summopere est, quia inde novas leges potest condere pontifex (supple Romanus,) unde euangelistae nequaquam dixerunt, ibi vero aperte dominus vel eius discipuli veleius sequaces sancti patres sententialiter aliquid dixerunt, ibi non novam legem Romanus pontifex dare potest: sed potius quod praedictum est, usque ad animam & sanguinem confirmare debet. Si enim, quod docuerunt apostoli & prophetae, destruere
units.tr: For Pope Urban, found in 25 q. 1, c. Sunt quidem, says: It must be carefully noted that the pontiff (namely the Roman) can make new laws only where the evangelists have said nothing; but where the Lord, or his disciples, or his holy followers the fathers, have said something clearly in a judgement, there the Roman pontiff cannot give a new law, but ought rather to uphold what has been said, even unto blood. For if he were to try to destroy what the apostles and prophets taught

units.la: {y} Ecclesia etc. nitere (quod dixit) niteretur, non sententiam dare, sed errare magis convinceretur. Ex his verbis colligitur evidenter, quod conditor canonum multo minoris auctoritatis est quam evangelium sacrosanctum, contra quod novam legem nequaquam condere potest, sed ipsum defendere usque ad animam & sanguinem sane obligatur. Contra quod si novam legem daret praesumeret, esset de errore per catholicos convincendus. His Fabianus Papa concordat, qui ut habetur 13. q. 3. c. quiomnipotentem, ait: qui omnipotentem Deum metuit, nec contra euangelium Christi, nec contra apostolos, nec contra prophetas, nec contra sanctorum patrum instituta agere aliquid ullo modo consentit. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod conditor canonum si omnipotentem metuit, nihil contra euangelium praesumit statuere. Et ita non maioris, sed minoris auctoritatis quam euangelium esse dinoscitur.
units.tr: {y} the Church, etc. ... were he to strive (as he said) to strive, he would be shown not to be giving a judgement but rather to be convicted of error. From these words it is clearly gathered that the author of the canons is of much less authority than the most holy gospel, against which he can by no means make a new law, but is bound to defend it even unto blood. If he were presumptuous enough to give a new law against it, he would be convicted of error by Catholics. Pope Fabian agrees with this, who, as is found in 13 q. 3, c. Qui omnipotentem, says: "He who fears almighty God consents to do nothing in any way against the gospel of Christ, nor against the apostles, nor against the prophets, nor against the institutions of the holy fathers." From these words it is plainly held that the author of the canons, if he fears almighty God, presumes to lay down nothing against the gospel. And so he is known to be of less, not greater, authority than the gospel.

units.la: Quod ex plurimis regulis in libro decretorum insertis clarius luce constat, sicut ex dist. 9. c. 4. noli. & c. ego solus. & c. quis nesciat. & c. noli. & c. neque & 2 dist. c. consuetudinem. & ex dist. 14. ca. sicut. & 5. q. 3. sis qui praesunt. Aliae auctoritates quam plurimae, quas longum esset enarrare seu recitare, hoc idem asserunt manifeste. & propter easdem rationes dicunt, quod haec tota multitudo Christianorum nunc vita mortali viventium non est maioris auctoritatis, quam sit euangelium sanctum: quia multitudo gentium viventium euangelium debet, usque ad animam & sanguinem defendere.
units.tr: This is made plainer than the light by very many rules inserted in the book of Decrees: as from dist. 9, c. 4 Noli, c. Ego solus, c. Quis nesciat, c. Noli, c. Neque, and 2 dist., c. Consuetudinem, and from dist. 14, c. Sicut, and 5 q. 3, Sis qui praesunt. Very many other authorities, which would be tedious to recount or recite, openly assert the same thing. And for the same reasons they say that this whole multitude of Christians now living this mortal life is not of greater authority than the holy gospel, because the multitude of living peoples ought to defend the gospel even unto blood.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad tertiam rationem factam capitulo primo.
units.tr: In which the third argument made in the first chapter is answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Ad istam secundam rationem mihi videtur quod responsionem totalem recitasti: nunc autem referas mihi (quaeso) quomodo ad tertiam rationem respondetur. MAG. Ad tertiam rationem respondent nonnulli dicentes, quod summus pontifex debet sacrarum literarum habere noticiam, & in sacris canonibus debet esse peritus. & ideo symbolum ordinare, & articulos fidei recte distinguere, spectat ad ipsum; praecipue cum consilio & consensu concilii generalis etiam in symbolum ordinando & articulos fidei distinguendo, & eadem ratione in diffiniendo authentice, quae assertio est catholica, & quae haeretica reputanda, theologiae principaliter debet inniti: secundario autem in sacris canonibus poterit se fundare. Et ideo ex illa ratione concludi potest, quod ad theologos principaliter spectat diffinire docendo vel legem aliis imponendo, quae assertio inter catholicas, & quae inter haereticas debeat numerari. DISCIP. Puto quod quicunque intelligens haec quae scripsisti, perlegerit, tenebit indubie, ad canonistas non pertinet de multis assertionibus iudicare, an catholicae vel haereticae sint censendae, & de quibuscunque assertionibus canonistae diffiniant, an inter catholicas vel haereticas debeant numerari, necesse est eos ad theologiam recurrere, si voluerint ad profunda resolvere; praesertim cum nulla assertio vere catholica, vel haeretica sit habenda, nisi quia theologiae consonat vel repugnat. quare non arbitror, quod aliquis literatus qualitercunque opinetur, quod ad canonistas, qui non sunt theologi, pertineat principaliter diffinitio saepe facta.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. To this second argument, it seems to me, you recited a complete response; now, I beg you, tell me how the third argument is answered. MASTER. Some answer the third argument by saying that the supreme pontiff ought to have knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and be skilled in the sacred canons. Therefore it belongs to him to order the creed and rightly to distinguish the articles of faith; especially with the counsel and consent of a general council, both in ordering the creed and in distinguishing the articles of faith, and by the same reasoning, in authoritatively defining which assertion is catholic and which must be regarded as heretical, this must rest principally upon theology; secondarily, however, it may be grounded in the sacred canons. And so from this reasoning it can be concluded that it belongs chiefly to the theologians to define, by teaching or by imposing a rule on others, which assertion is to be counted among the catholic and which among the heretical. DISCIPLE. I think that anyone who understands what you have written and reads it through will undoubtedly hold that it does not pertain to the canonists to judge of many assertions whether they are to be deemed catholic or heretical; and concerning whatever assertions the canonists define, whether they should be counted among the catholic or the heretical, they must of necessity have recourse to theology, if they wish to resolve deep questions; especially since no assertion is to be held truly catholic or heretical, except because it agrees or disagrees with theology. Wherefore I do not think that any learned person, however he may hold, supposes that the definition so often made belongs chiefly to the canonists, who are not theologians.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Invehit contra canonistas ostendens quid pertineat ad eos.
units.tr: He attacks the canonists, showing what belongs to them.

units.la: MAGIST. Multa nimis ignoras. Scio enim quosdam canonistas, qui theologos deridere praesumunt, cum inuestigare nituntur de multis assertionibus, an debeant inter haereses comparari; dicentes: quod talis inuestigatio ad canonistas, non ad theologos noscitur pertinere.
units.tr: MASTER. You are very much mistaken about many things. I know some canonists who presume to mock the theologians when they try to investigate many assertions, whether they ought to be classed as heresies. They say that such an investigation belongs to the canonists, not to the theologians.

units.la: DISCIP. De hoc quod dicis vehementer admiror, quia dictum huiusmodi nullam videtur probabilitatem habere. narra tamen, si pro se aliquam rationem huiusmodi assertores allegant. MAGIST. Audivi quod ex hoc motientur tantummodo, quia theologi, cum in quibusdam alii de haeresi accusantur, vel aliquos accusare conantur, libellos accusationis, responsionis, appellationis & huiusmodi componere nesciunt nec formare: sed ad canonistas oportet eos habere recursum. quare dicunt, quod ad canonistas, non ad theologos spectat discernere, quae assertio catholica vel haeretica sit censenda.
units.tr: STUDENT. I am greatly surprised by what you say, since this claim seems to have no plausibility at all. Still, tell me whether those who make it offer any reason in its support. MASTER. I have heard that they are moved only by this: when theologians are accused of heresy in certain matters, or try to accuse others, they do not know how to compose or frame the documents of accusation, answer, appeal and the like, so they must have recourse to the canonists. Therefore they say that it is for the canonists, not the theologians, to decide which assertion is to be judged catholic or heretical.

units.la: DISCIP: Ista ratio apparet mihi tam frivola, quod responsione non indigeat. Aliud enim est discernere, quae assertio est catholica, & quae haeretica est censenda. Et aliud est scire formulas accusationum & modum agendi contra haereticos; ac etiam modum defendendi dendi in iudicio accusatos de haeresi. Primum ad theologos; secundum ad iuristas noscitur pertinere. Quemadmodum aliud est cognoscere denarios veros a falsis, aurum ab auricalco, equos sanos ab aegris, arma fortia & tabefacta ab aliis. & aliud est scire si aliquid de aliquo praedictorum voluerit aliquem in iudicio accusare, & accusatus nihil se fuerit defendere, quomodo libelli accusationis, responsionis, appellationis, & huiusmodi, quibus fuerit optimum uti in iudicio, confici debeant & formari. Primum ad monetarios, aurifabros, ferrifabros, & fabricatores armorum pertinere dinoscitur. Secundum vero ad iuristas non est dubium pertinere. Unde per istam probationem probare contingeret, quod ad iuristam pertineret discernere, quod aurum est verum, & quod falsum: qui panni artificialiter sint facti, & qui non: quae aedificia sunt utilia, & quae non & ut breviter concludam, de omnibus mechanicis & rebus naturalibus universis, quae in usum hominis veniunt, habent iuristae principaliter discernere, qualia essent secundum naturam suam vel artem, quoniam de omnibus huiusmodi contingit in iudicio litigare. in quo casu necesse est litigatores pro libellis accusationis, responsionis, & appellationis ad iuristas habere recursum, constat autem, quod iuristae periti de rebus minimis an sint talia quales debent esse secundum naturam vel artem, a qua fiunt, nesciunt iudicare, qui tamen de talibus rebus recuperandis vel defendendis in iudicio, ordinant & formant libellos & alia, quae spectant ad formam agendi vel defendendi coram iudice. Mag. Ecce interrogationem tuam iuxta formam, quam mihi praefixisti, breviter pertractavi: nunc autem propone aliam, vel quiescere me permittas.
units.tr: STUDENT. That reason seems to me so flimsy that it does not even need an answer. It is one thing to discern which assertion is to be judged catholic and which heretical; it is another to know the forms of accusations and the method of proceeding against heretics, and also the method of defending those accused of heresy in court. The first belongs to the theologians; the second is known to belong to the jurists. It is like the difference between knowing true coins from false, gold from brass, healthy horses from sick ones, or sound weapons from broken ones, and knowing how the documents of accusation, answer and appeal, which it is best to use in court, ought to be drawn up and framed, in case someone wishes to accuse another of one of these things in court and the accused does not defend himself. The first belongs clearly to moneyers, goldsmiths, ironsmiths and makers of arms; the second, beyond doubt, belongs to the jurists. So by this same argument it would follow that it belongs to the jurist to decide whether gold is genuine or false, which cloths have been artificially made and which not, which buildings are useful and which not. And, to conclude briefly, the jurists would have to decide principally about all crafts and all natural things that come into human use, what they are by their nature or art, since disputes about all such things can arise in court. In that case, litigants would have to have recourse to jurists for the documents of accusation, answer and appeal. Yet it is certain that skilled jurists cannot judge about the smallest things whether they are such as they ought to be according to the nature or art by which they are made, though they do arrange and frame the documents and the other things that pertain to the form of proceeding or defending before a judge in order to recover or defend such things in court. Master. Behold, I have briefly treated your question according to the form you set before me. Now either propose another, or allow me to rest.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: In quo movetur dubitatio ad quos principaliter & profundius spectat habere intellectum eorum quae in decretis continentur. & arguitur, quod ad canonistas.
units.tr: In which the question is raised as to whom it principally and more deeply belongs to understand those things contained in the decretals. It is argued that this belongs to the canonists.

units.la: DISCIP. Quia aliqui canonistae putant, ut dicis, quod ad ipsos principaliter spectat inter assertionem catholicam & haereticam discernere, cum tamen (ut mihi videtur) falcem suam in messem mittant alienam, si hoc absque theologia attemptare praesumpserint, eo quod nec absque theologia capitula decretis inserta, quae de haeresibus loquuntur, intelligere valeant. Dic mihi obsecro parum a principali proposito disgrediendo, quid sentiunt literati de intellectu illorum, quae in decretis habentur, ad quos sc. principalius & profundius pertinet illorum intellectum cognoscere. M A G. Circa quaestionem propositam inveniuntur opiniones contrariae. Canonistae enim sentire videntur, quod ipsi non solum habent memoriam maiorem eorum, quae in libris iuris canonici inserunt, sed etiam ista clarius & magis profunde, & quis sit intellectus ipsorum, ad ipsos spectat principaliter iudicare saltem per modum doctrinae. Pro hac autem opinione videtur tali ratione moveri iuxta sapientis sententiam, quisquis bene iudicat de his quae novit, & horum est bonus iudex: canonistae autem magis cognoscunt illa, quae in libris eorum habentur quam alii. Igitur ad ipsos de intellectu eorum pertinet principaliter iudicare. Item pro ista opinione alia ratio posset adduci. Quoniam ad nullos magis spectat aliquorum notitia, quam ad tractatores illius scientiae, quae ipsa considerat: igitur ad nullos magis spectat notitia illorum, quae in iure canonico habentur, quam ad tractatores iuris canonici, cuiusmodi sunt canonistae. ergo ad ipsos principaliter spectat de intellectu eorum discernere.
units.tr: DISCIP. Because some canonists think, as you say, that it belongs principally to them to distinguish between a Catholic and a heretical assertion. Yet (as it seems to me) they put their sickle into another man's harvest if they presume to attempt this without theology, since without theology they cannot understand the chapters inserted in the decretals that speak of heresies. I beg you, digressing a little from our main purpose, tell me what learned men think about the understanding of those things contained in the decretals, that is, to whom it belongs more principally and more deeply to know their meaning. M A G. Regarding the question proposed, opposing opinions are found. For the canonists seem to think that they not only have a greater memory of those things which they insert in the books of canon law, but also that they understand these more clearly and more deeply, and that it belongs principally to them, at least by way of teaching, to judge what their meaning is. In support of this opinion, the argument seems to be moved by the saying of the wise man, whoever judges well of the things he knows is a good judge of them: canonists, however, know those things which are contained in their books better than others do. Therefore it belongs principally to them to judge of their meaning. Likewise, another argument could be adduced for this opinion. For the knowledge of certain things belongs to no one more than to the writers of the science that considers them. Therefore the knowledge of those things which are contained in canon law belongs to no one more than to the writers of canon law, such as the canonists. Therefore it belongs principally to them to discern their meaning.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: In quo recitatur opinio canonistarum asserentium, quod ad eos spectat de his quae in libris eorum continentur maiorem habere memoriam, & praesertim de positivis.
units.tr: In which is set out the opinion of the canonists, who assert that it belongs to them to have a greater memory of what is contained in their books, and especially of positive matters.

units.la: DISCIP. Narra aliam opinionem. M A G. Aliis minime placet ista opinio. Dicunt enim, quod ad canonistas spectat de multis, quae reperiuntur in libris eorum, maiorem habere memoriam. De pluribus autem tenaciorem memoriam & profundiorem intellectum oportet theologos habere si perfecti fuerint. Nonnulli vero saecularium legum periti & profundius intelligunt & non minori commendant memoriae. Quidam autem naturali praediti ratione, & in philosophia morali eruditi, ac scientiae naturalis nequaquam ignari, & plenius intelligunt, & non minus noscuntur memoriae imprimere. Nonnulli vero canonistae intelligunt profundius, licet non propter maiorem multorum memoriam: quia sicut aliquoties intellectus quorundam promptius valet explicare, ad quae alii tardius, licet profundius, cum magno labore & studio perveniunt.
units.tr: DISCIP. Tell me another opinion. MAG. This opinion does not please others at all. They say that canonists ought to have a greater memory of many things found in their books. Theologians, if they are to be perfect, must have a more tenacious memory and a deeper understanding of many things. Some experts in secular law also understand more deeply and retain no less in memory. Some who are endowed with natural reason, learned in moral philosophy, and by no means ignorant of natural science, understand more fully and are known to fix things in memory no less. Some canonists, however, understand more deeply, though not because of a greater memory of many things; for just as the understanding of some people can more readily explain certain matters, others reach those same matters more slowly, though more profoundly, and only with great labour and study.

units.la: Si autem aliqui canonistae in scientia naturali & philosophia morali, iure civili & in theologia plenius essent instructi, ad illos principalissime pertinerent illud quod habetur in libris eorum rum & tenaciori memoria retinerent, & de iplorum intelligentia promptius & perfectius indidicarent. Ad evidentiam autem praedictorum dicunt isti esse notandum, quod libri canonistarum non sunt nisi quaedam collationes ex auctoritatibus Bibliae & originalibus theologorum & sanctorum, & ex quibusdam legibus imperialibus, & ex constitutionibus, diffinitionibus seu determinationibus conciliorum generalium & summorum pontificum, in quibus quaedam theologica pure explicantur & declarantur, sicut in illis, in quibus haereses damnantur & veritates theologicae approbantur, ut patet extra de summa trin. & fi. catho. c. i. & c. damnamus. & extra de haeretic. cum Christus. & in pluribus aliis capitulis decretis insertis. Quaedam vero pure moralia traduntur in eis, quae nulla possunt ratione muniri, sicut patet in multis capitulis decretorum & decretalium.
units.tr: But if some canonists were more fully instructed in natural science, moral philosophy, civil law and theology, then it would belong most principally to them to hold in tenacious memory what is contained in their books, and to learn their meaning more readily and more perfectly. To make the foregoing clear, these people say that it should be noted that the books of the canonists are nothing but collections drawn from the authorities of the Bible, the originals of theologians and saints, certain imperial laws, and the constitutions, definitions or determinations of general councils and the supreme pontiffs, in which some theological matters are purely explained and declared, as in those in which heresies are condemned and theological truths approved, as is evident from extra de summa trin. & fi. catho. c. i. & c. damnamus. & extra de haeretic. cum Christus. and in many other chapters inserted into the decrees. Some purely moral matters are also handed down in them, which cannot be supported by any reasoning, as is evident in many chapters of the decrees and decretals.

units.la: Quaedam autem praecipiuntur in eis & prohibentur, quae sunt mere positiva ex humana voluntate dependentia, quae pro necessitate & utilitate possunt rationabiliter variari & penitus abrogari, ut patet extra de consanguinitate & affinitate, c. non debet & di. 9. sicut quidem. Ex his discunt, quod de theologicis in libris canonistarum intuentis tam quantum ad memoriam quam quantum ad intellectum, theologi, si sint perfecti, canonistas excedunt, licet nunquam oporteat theologos illorum verborum memoriam, sub quibus sententia pure theologica in determinatione ecclesiae explicatur, habere.
units.tr: Some things are also commanded and forbidden in them, which are purely positive, depending on human will, and which for reasons of necessity and utility can reasonably be varied and entirely abrogated, as is evident in extra de consanguinitate & affinitate, c. non debet & di. 9. sicut quidem. From these things they learn that, as regards the theological matters found in the books of the canonists, both as to memory and as to understanding, theologians, if they are perfect, surpass the canonists, although theologians ought never to have the memory of those words under which a purely theological sense is explained in the determination of the Church.

units.la: Quo ad leges autem imperiales, quae in libris praefatis reperiuntur, sicut patet 2. q. 6. c. propter superfluam, & in multis capitulis sequentibus, & in multis aliis locis, nec quantum ad memoriam, nec quantum ad intellectum, sunt canonistae praeferendi peritis in iure civili. Quantum vero ad moralia, quae nulla possunt ratione muniri, si universalia sunt nec in memoria nec in intellectu, possunt canonistae naturali ratione praeditos & in philosophia morali instructos & in scientia naturali perfectos excedere quoquo modo.
units.tr: As for the imperial laws found in the aforesaid books, as is evident in 2. q. 6. c. propter superfluam, and in many following chapters and in many other places, the canonists are to be preferred neither in memory nor in understanding to those skilled in civil law. As for moral matters, which cannot be supported by any reasoning, if they are universal, then the canonists, whether in memory or in understanding, can in no way surpass those endowed with natural reason, instructed in moral philosophy and perfect in natural science.

units.la: De illis vero quae particularia sunt, & tamen nequaquam dispensationem seu mutationem recipiunt, canonistae maiorem possunt habere memoriam, ac etiam de intellectu eorum promptius iudicare, sed ad alios, scilicet theologos, profundius, quia per principia priora, licet tardius & cum maiori labore, pertinet de intellectu eorum discernere. Illa vero quae pure positiva sunt, & quae ex causa possent variari, canonistae magis in memoria retinent, sed non habent profundius iudicare.
units.tr: As for those matters which are particular, and yet do not admit of any dispensation or change, the canonists can have a greater memory of them and can also judge their meaning more readily; but to others, namely theologians, it belongs to discern their meaning more profoundly, since this is done through prior principles, though more slowly and with greater labour. Those things, however, which are purely positive and which could be varied for a reason, the canonists retain more in memory, but they do not have the ability to judge them more profoundly.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: In quo primo obiicitur contra quoddam dictum capitulo praecedenti, quod etiam postea probatur rationibus & exemplo, scilicet quod ad theologos profundius spectat cognoscere, quae in canonibus continentur.
units.tr: In which, first, an objection is raised against a certain statement in the preceding chapter, which is afterwards also proved by arguments and an example, namely that it belongs more deeply to theologians to know what is contained in the canons.

units.la: DISCIP. Istam secundam opinionem pro parte liberiter attendo: quia quantum ad illa, quae dicit de theologicis & legibus imperialibus, & puris moralibus ac naturalibus, omnino videtur rationalis aestimanda. Quantum vero ad moralia particularia & pure positiva, quae in libris canonistarum sunt solummodo tradita, non apparet probabilitatem habere. Unde posset arguí tali ratione. Nullus enim non dico profundius, sed nec aliquo modo potest iudicare de illis, quae non novit. Cum igitur talia ad noticiam tractatorum aliarum scientiarum nequaquam pertineant, ad ipsos nullo modo spectat iudicare de ipsis. Veruntamen vellem scire, si pro illa assertione aliquae rationes apparentes valeant cogitari.
units.tr: DISCIP. I willingly attend to this second opinion, in part: for as far as it concerns theological matters, imperial laws, and purely moral and natural matters, it seems entirely reasonable to judge. But as regards particular moral matters and purely positive ones, which are only handed down in the books of the canonists, it does not appear to have probability. Hence one could argue with this reasoning. For no one can judge in any way, let alone more deeply, about things he does not know. Since such matters by no means belong to the knowledge of the experts in the other sciences, it does not belong to them in any way to judge about them. Nevertheless I should like to know whether any plausible arguments can be devised in support of that assertion.

units.la: MAGIST. Assertionem praefatam nonnulli ratione & exemplo probare nituntur. Ratione sic. Scientia superior de traditis in scientia inferiori subordinata sibi certius potest & profundius iudicare, quam scientia inferior. Sed scientia canonistarum, quantum ad multa moralia particularia, & quae valent variationem recipere, est scientia inferior subordinata theologiae, etiam quantum ad multa subordinata est morali philosophiae, sicut particularia subordinantur universalibus, igitur de talibus potest theologia & moralis philosophia certius iudicare, quam canonistarum scientia.
units.tr: MAGIST. Some people try to prove the aforesaid assertion by reason and example. By reason, thus. A superior science can judge more certainly and more profoundly about the matters handed down in a subordinate inferior science than the inferior science can. But the science of the canonists, as regards many particular moral matters which admit of variation, is an inferior science subordinate to theology, and also, as regards many things, subordinate to moral philosophy, just as particulars are subordinate to universals. Therefore theology and moral philosophy can judge about such matters more certainly than the science of the canonists.

units.la: Secundo sic de illis agilibus particularibus, quae variari possunt, potest illa scientia certissime iudicare, per quam, si fuerit aliquid inique statutum, debet omnimode reprobari, & contra quam nihil valet in particulari ordinari vel statui. Huiusmodi autem est theologia & philosophia moralis respectu agibilium particularium, & quae mutari possunt in iure canonico repertorum, ergo de illis theologia & philosophia moralis habent certissime iudicare. Maior videtur habere evidentiam: minor tali ratione probatur.
units.tr: Secondly, thus: concerning those particular practical matters which can be varied, that science can judge most certainly through which, if something has been unjustly enacted, it must be rejected in every way, and against which nothing can validly be ordained or established in particular. Now theology and moral philosophy are of this kind with respect to particular practical matters, and to those found in canon law which can be changed; therefore theology and moral philosophy can judge about them most certainly. The major premise seems to be evident; the minor is proved by this reasoning.

units.la: Constitutio ecclesiastica non est minoris auctoritatis, dignitatis aut firmitatis quam ecclesiastica consuetudo. Sed omnis consuetudo tam veritati scripturae divinae quam etiam iuri naturali, quod non solum in lege & evangelio, sed etiam in vera philosophia morali habetur, cedit, si ei inveniatur adversa, & per consequens si aliqua consuetudo fuerit theologiae & verae philosophiae morali contraria, est omnimode reprobanda. Igitur, si quaecunque consuetudo ecclesiastica alteri scientiarum praedictarum probetur adversa, damnata est. Ex quo infertur quod de omnibus talibus habet theologia & vera philosophia moralis certissime iudicare. Confirmatur firmarur auctoritate beati Cypriani, qui vt habetur 8. d. c. consuetudo, ait: consuetudo, quae apud quosdam irrepserat, impedire non debet, quo minus veritas praevaleat et vincat: nam consuetudo sive veritate aut veritati contraria vetustas erroris est. Ex qua auctoritate & aliis quae in eadem d. ponuntur in c. veritati. & 64. pro consuetudine & contra qui contempta. & c. fructus. & c. si solus, colligitur, quod omnis consuetudo veritati contraria, ubicunque repetiatur, sive in theologia sive in philosophia morali, est penitus contemnenda. Ex quo sequitur, quod etiam omnis constitutio ecclesiastica, si veritati fuerit inimica, debet repudiari & damnari. Hinc Gratianus 8. d. c. dignitate, ait: dignitate vero ius naturale praevalet similiter consuetudini & constitutioni quaecunque enim de moralibus acepta sunt, vel in scripturis comprehensa, si naturali iuri fuerint adversa, nulla & irrita sunt, sunt censenda. & 9. d. c. 1. ait: liquido igitur apparet, quod consuetudo iuris naturali postponitur. Quod autem consuetudo iuri naturali postponitur, multiplici auctoritate probatur per eundem, qui g. d. c. vl. ait: Cum igitur in naturali iure nihil aliud praecipiatur, quam quod Deus vult fieri, nihilque vetetur quam quod Deus prohibet fieri; denique cum in canonica scriptura nihil aliud, quam quod in divinis legibus inveniatur: divinae vero leges in illa consistunt, patet quod quaecunque divinae voluntati seu catholicae scripturae contraria probantur, eadem iuri naturali inveniuntur adversa. unde quaecunque divinae voluntati seu catholicae scripturae seu divinis legibus postponenda censentur, eisdem naturale ius praeferri oportet. Ex his patenter habetur, ut istis apparet, quod quaecunque in iure canonico theologiae & naturali iuri, quod non solum est in theologia, sed etiam in moralii philosophia, inuenirentur contraria, per alteram scientiarum praedictarum essent penitus reprobanda; cum inceperit ab exordio rationalis creaturae, ut habetur 6. d. bis continetur igitur utraque de talibus habet certissime iudicare, & eo certius scientiarum huiusmodi tractatores haberent de talibus iudicare, quam canonistae; quo principiis dignioribus, certioribus, prioribus & vniuersaliorib. vti noscuntur. Secundo principaliter isti moliuntur suam assertionem exemplo ostendere, referentes, quod cum Commentator librorum Dionysii de multis articulis a suis aemulis, qui Papam & cardinales muneribus corruperant, accusatus cogeretur in consistorio respondere, ipse tanquam purus philosophus & theologus omnis iuris ignarus a Papa petiit advocatum. qui Papa respondit: absit ut tibi, qui inter omnes clericos, mundi literatior reputaris, hanc confusionem facias, ut alius pro te loquatur, pro te ipso loquaris. Qui cernens malitiam recepta copia obiectorum & acceptis ad deliberandum trium dierum induciis quarta die respondit ad omnium legum civilium & iuriun canonicorum complurium contra ipsum allegatorum obiecta, quibus aduersarii insolubiliter (ut putabant) suam intentionem fundaverant, per theologiam & rationem naturalem ita patenter pro se intellectum affigians, quod iudicio omnium intelligentium omnes leges & iura quae contra ipsum fuerant allegata pro ipso liquide concludebunt. unde ut fere cardinales sibi contrarii postmodum eius aemulos, arguentes dixerunt; vos dixistis istum philosophum nescire leges & iura; & ipse scit principia, radices & causas omnium iurium & legum. Ex quibus isti concludunt, quod iste theologus, qui est magnus philosophus, multo certius, profundius & clarius iudicavit de intellectu iurium, quorum antea nullam habuerat scientiam & memoriam; quam theologiae & rationis naturalis legiari; qui tamen ab infantia in illis fuerant enutriti.
units.tr: An ecclesiastical constitution is not of less authority, dignity or firmness than an ecclesiastical custom. But every custom yields, if it is found to be opposed, both to the truth of divine Scripture and to natural law, which is contained not only in the law and the gospel but also in true moral philosophy. Consequently, if any custom is shown to be contrary to theology and true moral philosophy, it must be rejected in every way. Therefore, if any ecclesiastical custom is shown to be opposed to either of the aforesaid sciences, it is condemned. From this it follows that theology and true moral philosophy can judge most certainly about all such matters. This is confirmed by the authority of blessed Cyprian, who, as is found in 8. d. c. consuetudo, says: a custom which has crept in among some people ought not to hinder truth from prevailing and conquering; for custom, whether set against truth or opposed to it, is the antiquity of error. From this authority and from others which are set out in the same distinction, in c. veritati, and in 64. pro consuetudine and contra qui contempta, and c. fructus, and c. si solus, it is gathered that every custom opposed to truth, wherever it is practised, whether in theology or in moral philosophy, is to be utterly despised. From this it follows that every ecclesiastical constitution also, if it is hostile to truth, ought to be repudiated and condemned. Hence Gratian, in 8. d. c. dignitate, says: by right, natural law prevails over custom and constitution alike; whatever has been accepted concerning moral matters, or contained in the Scriptures, if it is opposed to natural law, is to be regarded as null and void. And in 9. d. c. 1. he says: it is therefore clear that custom is placed below natural law. That custom is subordinate to natural law is proved by many authorities through the same man, who in g. d. c. vl. says: since in natural law nothing else is commanded than what God wills to be done, and nothing is forbidden except what God prohibits; finally, since in canonical Scripture nothing is found other than what is contained in the divine laws, and the divine laws consist in those things, it is plain that whatever is proved contrary to the divine will or catholic Scripture is found to be contrary to natural law. Therefore whatever is judged to be subordinate to the divine will, or catholic Scripture, or the divine laws, natural law must needs be preferred to them. From these things it is plainly held, as it appears to these men, that whatever in canon law is found contrary to theology and to natural law, which exists not only in theology but also in moral philosophy, must be entirely rejected by one or other of the aforesaid sciences; since it has begun from the beginning of rational creation, as is held in 6. d. bis continetur. Therefore both of these sciences have the most certain judgement about such matters, and the teachers of these sciences would judge about such matters more certainly than the canonists, in proportion as they use more worthy, more certain, prior and more universal principles. Secondly, and chiefly, these men labour to show their assertion by an example, reporting that when the Commentator on the books of Dionysius was accused by his rivals of many articles, namely that they had corrupted the Pope and the cardinals with bribes, and was compelled to answer in consistory, he, like a pure philosopher and theologian ignorant of all law, asked the Pope for an advocate. The Pope replied: far be it that you, who are reckoned the most learned of all the clergy in the world, should create such confusion that someone else should speak for you; speak for yourself. He, perceiving the malice, having received a copy of the charges and been granted three days' delay for deliberation, on the fourth day answered the objections of all the civil laws and of many canons alleged against him, by which his adversaries had (as they thought) founded their case insolubly; he so clearly applied his mind to his own defence through theology and natural reason that, in the judgement of all intelligent men, all the laws and rights which had been alleged against him were clearly concluded in his favour. Whereupon, as nearly all the cardinals, who were opposed to him, afterwards said to his rivals when they argued against him: you said that this philosopher did not know the laws and rights; and yet he knows the principles, roots and causes of all rights and laws. From these examples they conclude that this theologian, who is a great philosopher, judged the meaning of the rights much more certainly, profoundly and clearly, although he had previously had no knowledge or memory of them, than the lawyers who had been brought up in them from infancy.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAP. X.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationem factam in principio capituli noni.
units.tr: In which an answer is given to the argument made at the beginning of chapter nine.

units.la: DISCIP. Nunc aduerto, quod assertiones, quae apparent prima facie falsae, non sunt penitus condemnandae. Assertionem enim, pro qua fortiter allegasti in principio, omnino irrationabilem arbitrabar; nunc autem non videtur mihi omni probabilitate carere. unde ad rationem contra eam, quam retigi, qualiter ipsius respondeant defensores enarta. MAG. Rationem illam valde despiciunt, dicentes, quod est illorum, qui nullam originem & ordinem scientiarum noverunt. aiunt enim, quod quemadmodum aliquis iudicat optime de metaphysicis & aliis, quae tamen fere nescit, sicut multi, qui pingere, scribere, arma, naves, & alia artificialia fabricare ignorant, melius quam ipsi artifices iudicare noscuntur; ita scientiae superiores, tractantes causas & principia istorum, quae in istis inferioribus considerantur, certius & clarius valent iudicare de illis, si eis proponantur, quam istae scientiae inferiores. unde & habentes perfectam notitiam scientiae subalternantis certius iudicant de conclusionibus scientiae subalternatae; ita theologi & veri philosophi propositis illis quae in iure tractantur canonico, profundius & certius poterunt iudicare de illis, quamuis saepe tamen cum maiori labore.
units.tr: STUDENT. Now I notice that assertions which seem false at first sight are not to be wholly condemned. I had thought the assertion you argued for so strongly at the beginning entirely unreasonable, but now it does not seem to me to lack all probability. So please explain how its defenders answer the argument against it that I touched on. MASTER. They scorn that argument greatly, saying that it comes from people who know nothing of the origin and order of the sciences. For they say that just as someone judges very well about metaphysics and other matters which he almost does not know, as many people who are ignorant of painting, writing, making weapons, ships and other artificial things are known to judge better than the craftsmen themselves, so the higher sciences, which treat the causes and principles of the things considered in these lower fields, can judge about them more certainly and clearly, if they are put before them, than the lower sciences can. Hence also those who have perfect knowledge of the subalternating science judge more certainly about the conclusions of the subalternated science. So theologians and true philosophers, when the matters treated in canon law are put before them, will be able to judge about them more deeply and certainly, although often with greater labour.

units.la: DISCIP. Video quod responsio quaerit de scientia solummodo, quae non est alteri subalternata nec subordinata. nam ut euidenter aspicio, de scientia, cui alia scientia superior principiatur, sicut de frenifactiva respecta equestris, & de illis quae architectonicae subiiciuntur, de quibus in libr. ethi. & in li. politico. fit mentio, & de [illegible, ~3 letters] cuius principia in scientia superiori traduntur, apparentiam non videtur habere. & ideo de theologia & scientia canonistarum dinoscitur colore carere, quia scientia canonistarum à theologia recipit sua principia, testante Innocentio tertio, qui ut habetur, extra de accusationibus, qualiter & quando, asserit manifeste, quod ex auctoritatibus novi & veteris testamenti processerunt postea canonicae sanctiones. quamvis ego de istis possem quaerere multa: quia tamen canonistae aliarum scientiarum terminos ignorantes eorum intellectum non caperent. Cupio autem in hoc opere quantum poteris, sic terminos proprios aliarum scientiarum à theologia & scientia canonistarum evites, quod omnia canonistae intelligant. Idcirco illa, quae dicta sunt de illa materia, sufficiant: nec curo, quod ad rationes pro prima opinione respondeas; quia modo valde debiles mihi videntur, & qualiter ad eas responderi potest per praedicta satis apparet. MAGIST. Considero quod si praedictam materiam exquirentius indagares, ad multas assertiones, quas aliquando facillimas reputasti, posses faciliter inclinari. Unde si aliquid circa praedicta adhuc animum tuum anxerit, si placet propone.
units.tr: STUDENT. I see that the answer concerns only a science which is neither subalternated to another nor subordinate to it. For as I clearly see, a science to which a higher science supplies its principles, such as horsemanship with respect to bridle-making, and those sciences which are subordinated to architectonic, mentioned in the Ethics and the Politics, and [illegible] whose principles are handed down in a higher science, do not seem to have this appearance. And so theology and the science of the canonists are known to lack this colour, because the science of the canonists receives its principles from theology, as Innocent III testifies, who, as is held, in extra de accusationibus, qualiter & quando, clearly asserts that the canonical sanctions afterwards proceeded from the authorities of the New and Old Testaments. Although I could ask many questions about these matters, since the canonists, ignorant of the terms of the other sciences, would not grasp their meaning, I wish in this work, as far as you can, to avoid the proper terms of other sciences from theology and the science of the canonists, so that the canonists understand everything. Therefore what has been said on that matter is enough. Nor do I care that you answer the arguments for the first opinion, since they now seem to me very weak, and how they can be answered is sufficiently clear from what has been said. MASTER. I consider that if you had investigated the aforesaid matter more closely, you could easily be inclined toward many assertions which you once thought very easy. So if anything about the aforesaid still troubles your mind, propose it, if you please.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: In quo perituractatur, an ad theologos vel canonistas spectet inter haereticos & orthodoxos discernere, & recitantur duae opiniones contrariae.
units.tr: In which it is discussed whether it belongs to the theologians or the canonists to distinguish between heretics and orthodox, and two contrary opinions are recited.

units.la: DISCIP. Si omnia illa, quae vellem in animo, tibi proponerem; & tu ad omnia respondères, sicut coepisti, librum maximum faceremus. ideo illis omissis ad aliam interrogationem praememoratam accede. Saepe audivi, quod assertio haereticalis alicuius dicitur, & tamen ipse inter haereticos minime computatur. Ex quo videtur quod ad alios poterit pertinere: & ad alios, quis haereticus est, & quis catholicus est censendus, & quae assertio catholica, & quae haereticalis discernere. Quamobrem interrogo, an ad theologos vel ad canonistas spectat inter haereticos & orthodoxos discernere.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. If I were to put to you all the things I have in mind, and you were to answer every one as you have begun, we would be making a very large book. So let those be set aside, and let me come to the other question mentioned earlier. I have often heard that someone's assertion is called heretical, and yet he himself is not counted among the heretics. From this it seems that it can belong to some people, and to others, to judge who is a heretic and who is to be regarded as Catholic, and to distinguish which assertion is Catholic and which heretical. Wherefore I ask whether it belongs to the theologians or to the canonists to distinguish between heretics and orthodox.

units.la: MAGIST. Aliqui canonistae tenere videntur, quod ad eos spectat inter haereticos & catholicos iudicare, pro qua opinione potest sic argui. Ad illos principaliter spectat inter catholicos & haereticos diiudicare, qui de haereticis exquisitius & magis de intentione considerant. huiusmodi sunt canonistae, unde in libro decretalium speciális titulus satis prolixus de haereticis est insertus. In decretis etiam de haereticis saepe diffuse tractatur, in theologia autem raro de haereticis fit mentio, unde & nomen haeretici solummodo in uno loco Bibliae sc. ad Timoth. 3. inveniter.
units.tr: MASTER. Some canonists seem to hold that it belongs to them to judge between heretics and Catholics, and for this opinion the following argument can be made. It belongs chiefly to those to distinguish between Catholics and heretics who examine heretics more closely and more carefully with regard to intention. Such are the canonists; hence in the Book of Decretals a special title, quite lengthy, On Heretics, has been inserted. In the Decretum too, heretics are often treated at length, whereas in theology mention of heretics is rare; hence also the name "heretic" is found in only one place in the Bible, namely at 1 Timothy 3.

units.la: quare ad canonistas pertinet principaliter haereticos discernere ab orthodoxis. Sed alii opinionem praedictam reputant omnino falsam, dicentes, quod ad theologos spectat, quis reputari debeat haereticus, & quis catholicus iudicare: sed canonistae habent ostendere, quod poena postquam aliquis fuerit factus haereticus, debeat secundum canonica iura puniri, quemadmodum iudex secularis (licet nesciat aliquem convincere esse haereticum, postquam tamen sibi fuerit tanquam haereticus ab ecclesia derelictus.) non ignorat, quod poena secundum iura civilia fit plectendus. Iudex ergo ecclesiasticus si aliquis coram eo fuerit ranquam haereticus accusatus, habet primo consulere theologos, quomodo oportet talem convincere, & postmodum per canones habet eum condignae poenae subiicere. Quia autem theologi principaliter super haereticos & orthodoxos discernant, isti ostendunt dicentes: quia nullus est haereticus habendus, nisi qui haeresi pertinaci animositate adhaeret. Sed ad theologos non solum, quae assertio inter haereses est numeranda, sed etiam qui autor eius debet pertinax aestimari, principaliter spectat discernere. ergo &c.
units.tr: Therefore it belongs chiefly to the canonists to distinguish heretics from the orthodox. But others judge the aforesaid opinion to be wholly false, saying that it belongs to the theologians to judge who ought to be reckoned a heretic and who a Catholic; but the canonists have to show that the penalty, once someone has been made a heretic, must be imposed according to the canonical laws, just as a secular judge (although he may not know how to convict someone of being a heretic, yet once he has been abandoned by the Church to him as a heretic) knows that the punishment is to be inflicted according to the civil laws. The ecclesiastical judge, therefore, if someone has been accused before him as a heretic, must first consult the theologians as to how such a person ought to be convicted, and afterwards, by the canons, subject him to the appropriate penalty. Since, however, the theologians chiefly discern between heretics and orthodox, these men argue as follows: no one is to be held a heretic except one who clings to heresy with stubborn obstinacy. But it belongs chiefly to the theologians to discern not only which assertion is to be numbered among the heresies, but also who its author ought to be judged to be, that is, obstinate. Therefore etc.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: In quo recitatur opinio canonistarum tenentium quod ad ipsos spectat iudicare, quis pertinax sit censendus, & hoc probatur tribus rationibus, quae solvuntur capitulo 14.
units.tr: In which is recited the opinion of the canonists, who hold that it belongs to them to judge who is to be considered obstinate; and this is proved by three reasons, which are answered in chapter 14.

units.la: DISCIP. Licet mihi videatur probabile, quod ad theologos pertineat principaliter iudicare, quae assertio catholica, quae haeretica est censenda. adhuc tamen ignoro, an ad ipsos principaliter spectet quis pertinaciter, quis non pertinaciter adhaeret pravitati haereticae, diffinire, & ideo nescio, an ad eos principaliter pertineat inter haereticos & orthodoxos diffinire, quia error absque pertinacia errantis non reddit haereticum. de hoc ergo velis disserere.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. Although it seems to me probable that it belongs chiefly to the theologians to judge which doctrine is to be considered Catholic and which heretical, I am still uncertain whether it belongs chiefly to them to define who clings to the heretical perversity obstinately and who does not, and therefore I do not know whether it belongs chiefly to them to define between heretics and orthodox, since error without the obstinacy of the one who errs does not make a heretic. Please, then, discourse on this matter.

units.la: MAGIST. de hoc quidem canonistae à theologis discordare videntur, dicentes; quod ad theologiam principaliter non pertinet iudicare; quis est pertinax, indicandus. Ad quod ponendum rationibus infra scriptis videntur posse moveri. Quarum prima talis est: nullus errans contra fidem catholicam est pertinax iudicandus; nisi qui corrigendus à suo praelato suum defendit errorem. Ad quos ergo spectat determinare, quomodo errantes corripi debeant à prælatis, ad illos principaliter spectat discernere, quis est pertinax iudicandus. Sed ad canonistas principaliter spectat determinare, quomodo errantes corripi debeant à prælatis; quia ipsorum est scire, quando & quomodo prælati debeant contra errantes procedere; quia ad theologos minime spectat. Canonistæ enim, non theologi, de accusationibus, denunciationibus, inquisitionibus pravitatis hæreticæ; & etiam de citationibus, interrogationibus, & examinationibus hæreticorum, & de aliis quæ spectant ad iudiciarium ordinem circa errantes servandum, debent cognoscere. ergo ad canonistas pertinet principaliter scire, quis est pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus.
units.tr: MAGISTER. On this point the canonists seem to disagree with the theologians, saying that it does not belong chiefly to theology to judge who is to be declared obstinate. To support this view, the following reasons seem able to be brought forward. The first is this: no one who errs against the Catholic faith is to be judged obstinate, unless he defends his error when he is to be corrected by his prelate. Therefore, to those whose task it is to determine how those who err ought to be corrected by prelates, it belongs chiefly to discern who is to be judged obstinate. But it belongs chiefly to the canonists to determine how those who err ought to be corrected by prelates, because it is their office to know when and how prelates ought to proceed against those who err, which in no way belongs to the theologians. For it is the canonists, not the theologians, who must know about accusations, denunciations, inquisitions into heretical perversity, and also about the citations, interrogations and examinations of heretics, and about the other matters which pertain to the judicial order to be observed with regard to those who err. Therefore it belongs chiefly to the canonists to know who is to be judged obstinate and heretical.

units.la: Secunda ratio est hæc: pertinacia est quædam contumacia, secundum Gregorium ut innuit, & habetur di. 15. c. non licuit: & per beatum Augustinum, ut legitur. 24. q. 3. ca. Qui in ecclesia. de contumacia autem principaliter tractant canonistæ; cum contumacia attendatur vel respectu non venientis vel respectu non restituentis, vel rectum non respondentis, vel respectu recedentis, vel respectu exhibentis: quæ omnia citationem præsupponunt ad hoc quod aliquis contumax reputetur. De citationibus autem in his, quæ ad iudiciarium ordinem pertinere noscuntur, non theologi, sed canonistæ considerant. ergo ad ipsos principaliter spectat scire, quis est contumax & hereticus iudicandus.
units.tr: The second reason is this: obstinacy is a kind of contumacy, according to Gregory, as he hints, and it is found in Dist. 15, c. Non licuit; and according to blessed Augustine, as is read in C. 24, q. 3, c. Qui in ecclesia. But the canonists treat chiefly of contumacy, since contumacy is judged either with respect to one who does not come, or to one who does not make restitution, or does not answer rightly, or to one who withdraws, or to one who offers obedience; all of which presuppose a citation, so that someone may be regarded as contumacious. But concerning citations in those matters which are known to pertain to the judicial order, it is not the theologians but the canonists who consider them. Therefore it belongs chiefly to them to know who is to be judged contumacious and heretical.

units.la: Tertia ratio est hæc: ad quem spectat alicuius criminis punitio, ad eundem spectat eiusdem criminis puniendi cognitio; quia crimen incognitum puniri non debet. sed ad canonistas principaliter spectat, quomodo pro pertinacia quis debeat puniri. ergo ad eosdem spectat principaliter, quis est pertinax, iudicare.
units.tr: The third reason is this: whoever has the punishment of a crime belongs also to the knowledge of that same crime to be punished, since an unknown crime ought not to be punished. But it belongs chiefly to the canonists to know how someone ought to be punished for obstinacy. Therefore it belongs chiefly to the same men to judge who is obstinate.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: In quo pertractatur opinio theologorum scilicet, quod ad theologos spectat princi- paliter huiusmodi discernere.
units.tr: In which the opinion of the theologians is examined, namely that it belongs chiefly to theologians to discern such matters.

units.la: DISCIP. Narra assertionem contrariam cum motivis eiusdem. MAG. Alii dicunt, quod ad theologos spectat scire principaliter, quis pertinax est habendus.
units.tr: STUDENT. State the opposing assertion together with its grounds. MASTER. Others say that it belongs chiefly to theologians to know who is to be held obstinate.

units.la: Primum autem motivum eorum est tale. ad theologos pertinet principaliter tractare de illis criminibus, quæ directe committuntur in Deum. quia cum theologia sit de Deo, sicut de principali subiecto, ipsa principaliter habet considerare crimina, quæ committuntur in ipsum. pertinacia autem pravitatis hæreticæ directe in Deum committitur. ergo ad theologos principaliter pertinet de pertinacia perscrutari.
units.tr: Their first argument is this. It belongs to theologians to treat chiefly of those crimes that are committed directly against God. For since theology is about God, as its principal subject, it must chiefly consider the crimes committed against him. Now the obstinacy of heretical depravity is committed directly against God. Therefore it belongs chiefly to theologians to inquire into obstinacy.

units.la: Secundum motivum est tale. eadem est scientia contrariorum. nam idem est iudex veri & obliqui. fides autem & hæretica pravitas sunt contraria, igitur ad theologos principaliter pertinet considerare de fide. ergo ad eosdem pertinet considerare de pravitate hæretica, & per consequens de pertinacia, sine qua hæretica pravitas minime reperitur.
units.tr: The second argument is this. The science of contraries is one and the same, for it is the same judge who decides on what is straight and what is crooked. Faith and heretical depravity are contraries, so it belongs chiefly to theologians to consider faith. Therefore it belongs to them also to consider heretical depravity and, consequently, obstinacy, without which heretical depravity is never found.

units.la: Tertium motivum est. quando scientia superior & inferior considerant de eodem: notitia illius principalius spectat ad scientiam superiorem quam inferiorem: quia cognoscit per causas superiores & per prima principia. sed de pertinacia hæresis considerat tam theologia quam scientia iuristarum. igitur cum theologia sit scientia superior, scientia vero canonistarum sit inferior: ergo ad theologiam principalius spectat, &c. maior est certa, ut videtur; minor ostenditur. nam quod de pertinacia consideret scientia canonum, est notum, & ipsi concedunt. Quod vero theologia consideret de eodem, patet aperte, cum apostolus ad Tim. 3. doceat hæreticum deuitandum. & in evangelio pertinaciam Iudæorum volentium credere Christo, ipsamet veritas reprehendit.
units.tr: The third argument is this. When a higher and a lower science consider the same thing, knowledge of it belongs more chiefly to the higher science than to the lower, because the higher science knows through higher causes and first principles. But both theology and the science of the lawyers consider the obstinacy of heresy. Theology is the higher science and the science of the canonists is the lower; therefore it belongs more chiefly to theology, and so on. The major premise is certain, as it seems; the minor is shown thus. That the science of the canons considers obstinacy is well known, and the canonists themselves concede it. That theology considers the same thing is plainly clear, since the apostle in 1 Tim. 3 teaches that a heretic is to be avoided. And in the gospel the truth itself rebukes the obstinacy of the Jews who were unwilling to believe in Christ.

units.la: DISCIP. In toto evangelio de pertinacia mentio non habetur: quomodo dicunt isti, quod Christus Iudæorum pertinaciam reprehendit. MAG. ad hoc respondetur, quod licet de hoc nomine pertinacia vel pertinax nulla in evangelio mentio fiat, tamen de re significata fecit Christus sæpe mentionem vel sermonem. DISCIP. Ubi? MAGIST. Ioan. 15. ubi ait de Iudæis: si non venissem & locutus fuissem, peccatum non haberent. nunc autem excusationem non habent de peccato suo. ubi Christus declarat Iudæos fuisse in erroribus suis pertinaces, quia sibi credere noluerunt. unde subdit: si opera non fecissem in eis, quæ nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent. nunc autem & viderunt & oderunt me & patrem meum. ubi eos pertinaces ostendit, quia operibus credere noluerunt, maliciam & pertinaciam Iudæorum indicans (in communitate tamen) ut habetur Matthæi 11. exprobrat civitatibus, quæ sibi credere noluerunt.
units.tr: STUDENT. In the whole gospel there is no mention of obstinacy, so how can these men say that Christ rebuked the obstinacy of the Jews? MASTER. To this it is answered that although the word obstinacy or obstinate is nowhere mentioned in the gospel, Christ often made mention of, or spoke of, the thing signified. STUDENT. Where? MASTER. John 15, where he says of the Jews: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin." Here Christ declares that the Jews were obstinate in their errors, because they were unwilling to believe him. Hence he adds: "If I had not done among them works that no one else did, they would have no sin; but now they have both seen and hated me and my Father." Here he shows them to be obstinate, because they were unwilling to believe the works, thereby indicating the malice and obstinacy of the Jews (in the community as a whole). Likewise, as found in Matthew 11, he reproaches the cities that were unwilling to believe him.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: In quo ponuntur responsiones ad rationes Canonistarum in capitulo 12.
units.tr: In which replies are given to the arguments of the canonists in chapter 12.

units.la: Discipul. Quantum ad hoc, intelligo, vel plus placet mihi assertio ista secunda, & ideo indica, quomodo isti ad rationes tres contrarias respondere nituntur. Magist. Ad primam nonnulli respondent dicentes: quod licet in genere Theologi principaliter debeant scire, quis est pertinax iudicandus: tamen aliquem modum speciale m errantem de pertinacia convincendi magis ex intentione propter aliquas circumstantias considerant Canonistae. Licet etiam si de tali modo inter Canonistas dubitatio oriretur, ad Theologos videretur applicandum, qui sciunt universalia ac particularia profundius & certius iudicare: licet forte cum investigatione & deliberatione prolixa & magna. Unde dicunt, quod multi sunt modi deveniendi ad notitiam pertinaciae alicuius errantis contra fidem, quorum aliqui respiciunt ordinem iudiciarium, puta si errans citatus ad iudicium venire recusat, si veniens renuerit respondere & subterfugere iudicium & examinationem malitiose molitur. Similes autem modos convincendi haereticos, quantum ad circumstantias multas ordinem iudiciarium respicientes explicite magis tractant Canonistae quam Theologi. In genere tamen & quantum ad multos alios modos convincendi de pertinacia, magis spectat ad Theologos pertractare. Discipul. Potest aliquis convinci de pertinacia extra iudicium? Magist. Nemo convincitur auctoritate iudicii extra iudicium vel sine iudicis auctoritate, aliquis tamen extra iudicium convincitur, quantum ad hoc, quod eius malitia propter evidentiam rei ad notitiam pervenit aliorum, in tantum ut liceat absque temeritate ipsum pertinacem haereticum reputare. Discipul. Dic ad formam rationis illius opinionis. Magist. Ad formam dicitur, quod cum accipitur, quod nullus errans contra fidem est pertinax iudicandus, nisi qui corrigendus a suo praelato suum defendit errorem, quod hoc est manifeste falsum, quia sunt alii modi extra omnem iudicium deprehendendi errantem in pertinacia manifesta, nam qui iuraret se in perpetuum aliquam haeresim defensare vel defensurum, de qua in decretis & in tota scientia Canonistarum nulla fit mentio, sed in Theologia duntaxat: Theologi, non Canonistae talem deprehenderent in pertinacia manifesta. Ad secundam rationem dicitur, quod omnis contumacia est pertinacia, sed non econtra, nec omnis pertinacia est sub vocabulo contumaciae reputanda, & ideo licet Canonistae de contumacia principaliter considerarent, non sequitur, quod de pertinacia principaliter perscrutarentur: quia saepe scientia superior de universalibus, & inferior de particularibus tractant, nec Greg. & Augustin. dicunt, quod omnis pertinacia est contumacia: sed intellexerunt, quod saepe haeretici pro contumacia sunt iudicialiter condemnandi. Ad tertiam rationem respondetur, quod ad quem spectat alicuius criminis punitio, ad eundem spectat eiusdem criminis aliqualis cognitio, saltem generalis & confusa vel accepta ab alio, sed non oportet quod ad ipsum principaliter spectet eiusdem criminis perscrutatio scientialis vel subtilis & specialis cognitio & profunda. Ad iudicem namque secularem spectat ultima punitio haeretici a suo errore resilire nolentis, postquam fuerit seculari relictus iudicio: & tamen ad iudicem secularem non spectat principaliter scire profunde, quis sit haeretibus reputandus. Iudices etiam seculares falsarios monetarum & mechanicos contra artes suas falsa opera facientes condigna poena plectere debent: tamen monetarii & mechanici falsitatem monetae & opera aliorum acutius quam iudices deprehendunt: sic licet Canonistae considerent, quomodo pertinaces in errore contra fidem oportet iuste puniri, Theologi tamen multo fortius & certius errantes pertinaciter deprehendunt: quemadmodum tortores melius sciunt, quam iudices, quomodo debeant suspendi latrones: gravitatem tamen latrocinii minus cognoscunt.
units.tr: Pupil: So far as this goes, I understand, or I like this second assertion better; so tell me how these men try to answer the three contrary arguments. Master: Some reply to the first by saying that, although theologians are chiefly obliged to know who is to be judged obstinate, the canonists consider more closely, from their intention and because of certain circumstances, a particular way of convicting an erring person of obstinacy. And even if a doubt about such a way arose among the canonists, it would seem to belong to the theologians, who know how to judge universals and particulars more deeply and more certainly, though perhaps only after long and thorough investigation and deliberation. So they say that there are many ways of coming to know that someone erring against the faith is obstinate. Some of these relate to the judicial order: for example, if the accused, summoned to judgment, refuses to appear; if, having appeared, he refuses to answer and maliciously contrives to evade judgment and examination. The canonists treat such ways of convicting heretics explicitly and at greater length than the theologians, insofar as they concern many circumstances that relate to the judicial order. In general, however, and as regards many other ways of convicting someone of obstinacy, it is more the business of the theologians to treat them. Pupil: Can someone be convicted of obstinacy outside a trial? Master: No one is convicted by the authority of a court outside a trial, or without the authority of a judge; yet someone may be convicted outside a trial in the sense that his malice, because the fact is evident, comes to the knowledge of others, so that one may, without rashness, regard him as an obstinate heretic. Pupil: Tell me the form of the argument of that opinion. Master: As to its form, it is said that when it is assumed that no one erring against the faith is to be judged obstinate unless, when corrected by his prelate, he defends his error, this is manifestly false, because there are other ways of detecting an erring person in manifest obstinacy outside any trial at all. For instance, someone who swore that he would for ever defend, or would defend, some heresy, of which there is no mention in the decrees or in the whole science of the canonists, but only in theology, would be detected in manifest obstinacy by theologians, not by canonists. To the second argument it is said that every contumacy is obstinacy, but not conversely, and not every obstinacy is to be reckoned under the name of contumacy. So although the canonists considered contumacy chiefly, it does not follow that they examined obstinacy chiefly, because a higher science often treats universals and a lower one particulars. Nor do Gregory and Augustine say that all obstinacy is contumacy; they understood that heretics are often to be condemned judicially for contumacy. To the third argument the answer is that whoever is charged with the punishment of a crime is also charged with some knowledge of that same crime, at least a general and confused knowledge, or one received from another; but it is not necessary that the scientific examination of that same crime, or a subtle and special and profound knowledge of it, belong chiefly to him. For it belongs to the secular judge to inflict the final punishment on a heretic who refuses to return from his error, once he has been handed over to the secular judgment; yet it does not belong chiefly to the secular judge to know thoroughly who is to be reckoned a heretic. Secular judges too ought to punish with fitting penalty those who counterfeit coinage and craftsmen who make false work contrary to their own arts; yet moneyers and craftsmen detect the falsity of coin and of the work of others more keenly than judges do. So although canonists consider how those obstinate in error against the faith ought to be justly punished, theologians detect erring persons who are obstinate much more strongly and more certainly. Just as executioners know better than judges how robbers ought to be hanged, yet know less of the gravity of the robbery.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: In quo summarie quasi recapitulando narrantur ea, quae spectant ad Canonistas in materia, qua agitur de discussione pravitatis haeretica.
units.tr: In which, summarily, as if by way of recapitulation, are set out those things that pertain to the Canonists in the matter concerning the investigation of heretical depravity.

units.la: Discipul. Dic breviter quae sunt illa secundum assertores istos, quae habent Canonistae de haereticis indagare. Magist. Dicunt isti, quod non solum Canonistae habent disserere, qua poena secundum iura canonica oportet haereticos castigare: Sed qualiter sit contra haereticos iudicialiter procedendum, quomodo scilicet contra haereticos formandi sunt libelli accusatorii, & alii: quomodo producendi sunt testes: & alia quae ad iudiciarium ordinem spectant, oportet eos cognoscere, propter etiam multas haereses, quae in libris eorum reperiuntur damnatae, possunt de multis discernere an sint haeretici iudicandi, licet de hoc valeant Theologi profundius iudicare. Licet enim in Biblia de haereticis sub nomine illo raro mentio habeatur: sancti tamen Bibliae tractatores de haereticis semper per principia in sacra scriptura tradita, quomodo sit aliquis haere-
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me briefly what those advocates say the Canonists have to inquire into concerning heretics. Master. They say that the Canonists have not only to discuss what punishment heretics ought to suffer according to the canon law, but also how one must proceed judicially against heretics: namely, how accusatory libels are to be drawn up against them, and so on; how witnesses are to be produced; and the other matters that belong to the judicial order. They must also know these things. Moreover, because many heresies condemned in their books are found there, they can distinguish in many cases whether people are to be judged heretics, although theologians may judge this more profoundly. For although the Bible rarely mentions heretics under that name, the holy interpreters of the Bible have always written great treatises on how a heretic is to be recognised, by the principles handed down in Holy Scripture. Many of these are inserted into the books of the Canonists, besides the determinations of the Church, which are founded on divine Scripture. Their books often declare, not who is to be held a heretic, but how one is to proceed in judgment against heretics and with what penalties they are to be struck, as is plainly evident in the title On Heretics, which is inserted in the book of Decretals. Now these matters, because they are positive, particular, and depend on human invention, are not the concern of the theologians, who do not principally consider such things. Nevertheless, it belongs to them to judge by universal principles, where the prudence of the Canonists fails, whether the ecclesiastical laws that extend to heretics in certain ways, and the mode of proceeding against them, are contrary to the divine Scriptures. For if such laws were in conflict with Holy Scripture, they should not be tolerated in any way.

units.la: Mm hæreticus cognoscendus, magnos tractatus efficiunt. De quibus in libris Canonistarum plurima inseruntur, præter quæ & determinationes ecclesiæ in scriptura diuina fundatas sepe omnia alia de hæreticis in libris eorum inuenta, non quis sit habendus hæreticus, sed quomodo sit contra hæreticos in iudicio procedendum, & qua debeant pœna feriri declarant, quod in titulo de hæreticis, qui in libro decretalium est insertus, patenter apparet. Prædicta autem, quia sunt positiua particularia & ex inuentione pendent humana, non sunt de consideratione Theologorum, qui talia principaliter non considerant: per rationes tamen vniuersales ad ipsos pertinet iudicare, vbi deficeret Canonistarum prudentia, an leges ecclesiasticæ de hæreticis certis modis extendis, & modo procedendi contra eosdem scripturis sint aduersæ diuinis, quia si leges huiusmodi contrariarentur scripturæ sacræ, non essent aliter tolerandæ.
units.tr: How a heretic is to be recognised, they produce great treatises. In the books of the Canonists a great deal of this is inserted, along with the determinations of the Church founded on divine Scripture, and almost all the other things about heretics found in their books. These works do not set out who is to be held a heretic, but how one is to proceed in judgment against heretics and with what penalties they are to be struck, as is plainly apparent in the title On Heretics, which is inserted in the book of Decretals. These matters, however, because they are positive, particular and dependent on human invention, are not the concern of the theologians, who do not principally consider such things. Nevertheless, it belongs to them to judge by universal principles, where the prudence of the Canonists falls short, whether the ecclesiastical laws that extend to heretics in certain ways, and the mode of proceeding against them, are contrary to the divine Scriptures. For if laws of this kind were at odds with Holy Scripture, they could not be tolerated in any way.

units.la: EXPLICIT LIBER PRIMVS. INCIPIT LIBER SECVNDVS, QVI DOCET, QVÆ assertiones sint catholicæ, vel hæreticæ iudicandæ. CAP. I.
units.tr: END OF THE FIRST BOOK. HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK, WHICH TEACHES WHICH ASSERTIONS ARE TO BE JUDGED CATHOLIC OR HERETICAL. CHAPTER I.

units.la: In quo primum proponitur quæstio, quæ veritates sint catholicæ credendæ, ad quam respondetur secundum vnam opinionem, dicentem: quod illæ solæ veritates sunt catholicæ & de necessitate salutis tenendæ, quæ in canone Bibliæ explicite vel implicite continentur sub propria forma: aut ex contentis consequentia formali & necessaria sequuntur.
units.tr: In this chapter the first question is put: which truths are to be believed as catholic. According to one opinion, which answers it, only those truths are catholic and must be held as necessary to salvation which are contained in the canon of the Bible, either explicitly or implicitly, in their own proper form, or which follow from what is contained there by a formal and necessary consequence.

units.la: Discipulus. Quæ recitasti circa quæsita, ad præsens sufficiunt mihi, & ideo ad aliud, quod magis cordi habeo, festino. Volo enim de hæresibus multa inquirere, sed quia nonnunquam cognitio vnius contrariorum ad cognitionem alterius conferre dignoscitur, quæro primo, quæ veritates sunt catholicæ credendæ. Magist. Quæstio tua vnum videtur supponere, & aliud quærere, videtur enim supponere, quod non omnes veritates sunt catholicæ iudicandæ, quod beatus Augustin. in Enche. expresse determinat. Quærit autem, quæ sunt illæ veritates, quæ catholicæ sunt credendæ. Discipul. Cum beato Augustin. illud, quod supponit, firmiter teneamus, & circa quæsitum sententiam vnam vel plures enarra. Magist. Circa quæsitum sunt diuersæ & aduersæ sententiæ. Quarum vna est: quod illæ solæ veritates sunt catholicæ reputandæ & de necessitate salutis credendæ, quæ in canone Bibliæ explicite vel implicite asseruntur: ita quod si aliquæ veritates in Biblia sub forma propria minime continentur, ex solis tamen contentis in ea consequentia necessaria & formali possunt inferri, sunt inter catholicas connumerandæ. Sicut hæc veritas: Christus est verus Deus & verus homo: in tota scriptura diuina sub hac serie verborum nullatenus inuenitur: quia tamen ex contentis in scriptura sacra consequentia necessaria & formali concluditur, catholica est censenda, & eam credere est necessarium ad salutem, omnes autem aliæ veritates, quæ nec in Biblia sunt insertæ, nec ex contentis in ea consequentia formali & necessaria possunt inferri, licet in scripturis sanctorum & in diffinitionibus summorum pontificum asserantur, & etiam ab omnibus fidelibus teneantur, non sunt catholicæ reputandæ: nec est necessarium ad salutem eis per fidem firmiter adhærere vel propter eas rationem vel humanum intellectum captiuare. Hanc suam sententiam rationibus & auctoritatibus confirmare nituntur. Auctoritas prima est Salomonis Prouerbio. 30. omnis sermo Dei ignitus clypeus est omnibus sperantibus in se, ne addas quicquam verbis illius, & argu-aris inueniarisque mendax. Ex quibus colligitur, quod verbis diuinis, quæ in diuina scriptura habentur, nihil penitus est addendum, tanquam necessarium ad credendum. Hoc etiam testari videtur Moyses Deuteron. quart. capit. & beatus Iohann. Apocal. vltim. quorum verba, cap. secund. sunt adducta primi libri. Ex quibus datur intelligi, quod sicut de scriptura sacra nihil penitus est auferendum, ita nihil est penitus addendum tanquam necessarium ad salutem.
