Hanc sententiam auctoritate Augustin. conantur ostendere, vnde Augustin. in quadam epistola ad Hieronymum, & recitatur in decretis distinctio. 9. capit. Ego, ait: Ego solis scripturarum libris (qui iam canonici appellantur) didici hunc timorem honoremque deferre vt earum nullum auctorem aliquid errasse firmissime credam. Si aliquid autem in eis inuenero quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud quam mendosum codicem esse vel non esse assecutum interpretem, quod dictum est vel minime me intellexisse non ambigam: alios aualias autem ita lego, vt quantalibet sanctitate, quanta ve doctrina polleant, non ideo verum putem, quia ita ipsi senserint: sed quia per alios auctores vel canonicas vel probabiles rationes quod a vero non aberrent, mihi persuaderi potuerunt. His verbis colligitur, quod solum canonibus, qui in Biblia continentur, necesse est fidem certissimam adhibere: & quod assertionibus aliorum non est necessarium ad salutem firmiter adhaerere. Item hoc idem August. in lib. de vnica Baptismo, vt recitatur dist. 9. cap. quis nesciat, aperte sentire videtur, ait enim, Quis nesciat sanctam Scripturam canonicam tam veteris quam noui testamenti certis terminis suis contineri eamque posterioribus omnibus episcoporum libris ita praponi, vt de illa omnino dubitari & disceptari non possit, vtrum verum vel vtrum rectum sit, quicquid in ea scriptum esse constiterit, episcoporum autem litteras, quae post confirmatum canonem vel scripta sunt vel scribuntur, & per sermonem forte sapientiorum cuiuslibet in ea reperitur: & per aliorum episcoporum grauiorem auctoritatem doctioremque prudentiam, & per concilia reprehendi licere, si quid in eis forte a veritate est deuiatum. Ex his verbis colligitur, quod de sola sacra scriptura noui & veteris testamenti est illicitum dubitare, vtrum sit verum vel rectum, quicquid in ea scriptum esse constiterit. Ergo de omnibus scripturis conciliorum generalium, & continuatium, & quorumcunque aliorum expositorum scripturae diuinae, ac etiam Romanorum pontificum, & quorumlibet historiographorum, post canonem editis confirmatum, non est illicitum dubitare & discrepare, an a veritate exorbitent, quaecunque scriptura constiterit in eis, antequam scripturae noui & veteris testamenti consona demonstretur. Item Aug. in epistola ad Vincentium, & allegatur di. praedicta. ca. noli, loquens de scripturis posterioribus nouo & veteri testamento, ait: hoc genus litterarum ab auctoritate canonis distinguendum est, non enim sic leguntur, tanquam ex ea ita testimonium praeferatur, vt contra sentire non liceat, vbi forte aliter sapuerint quam veritas postulat. Ex his habetur, quod contra omne genus litterarum post canonem Bibliae licet sentire. His concordare videtur August. in epistola ad Fortunatum, & habetur dist. prefata. c. Neque, qui ait: neque quorumlibet disputationes, (id est, exponens secundum glo. quamuis catholicorum & laudatorum hominum) velut scripturas canonicas habere debemus, vt nobis non liceat (salua honorificentia, quae illis debetur hominibus) aliquid in eorum scriptis improbare atque respuere, si forte inueniremus, quod aliter sensepunt, quam veritas habet diuino adiutorio vel alii intellecta, vel a nobis. Ex his concluditur, quod nullis assertionibus quorumcunque quae in scripturis canonicis non habentur, firmiter assentire quis constringitur.
units.tr: Student. What you have recited about the questions raised is enough for me at present, so I hurry on to another matter that lies closer to my heart. I wish to inquire at length about heresies, but since knowledge of one of two opposites is often seen to help the knowledge of the other, I first ask: which truths are to be believed as catholic? Master. Your question seems to presuppose one thing and to ask another. For it seems to presuppose that not all truths are to be judged catholic, which blessed Augustine expressly determines in the Enchiridion. Yet it asks which are the truths that must be believed as catholic. Student. Since we hold firmly to what blessed Augustine presupposes, please set out one opinion or several on the question. Master. On the question there are diverse and opposing opinions. One of them holds that only those truths are to be reckoned catholic and must be believed as necessary to salvation which are asserted in the canon of the Bible, either explicitly or implicitly, so that if some truths are not contained in the Bible in their proper form, but can be inferred from what is contained in it by a necessary and formal consequence, they are to be counted among the catholic truths. Take this truth: Christ is true God and true man. This sequence of words is nowhere to be found in the whole of divine Scripture; yet because it is concluded by a necessary and formal consequence from what is contained in Holy Scripture, it is to be considered catholic, and it is necessary to salvation to believe it. But all other truths, which are neither inserted in the Bible nor can be inferred from what is contained in it by a formal and necessary consequence, although they are asserted in the writings of the saints and in the decisions of the Roman pontiffs, and are even held by all the faithful, are not to be reckoned catholic, nor is it necessary to salvation to adhere firmly to them by faith, or to captivate the reason or human understanding on their account. The advocates of this opinion try to confirm it by arguments and authorities. The first authority is Solomon, Proverbs 30: "Every word of God is fire-tried; he is a shield to those who trust in him. Add nothing to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar." From these words it is gathered that nothing at all is to be added to the divine words contained in divine Scripture as necessary for belief. Moses seems to testify the same in Deuteronomy, chapter 4, and blessed John in the last chapter of the Apocalypse, whose words have been cited in the second chapter of the first book. From these it is to be understood that, just as nothing at all is to be taken away from Holy Scripture, so nothing at all is to be added as necessary to salvation. They try to show this opinion by the authority of Augustine, whence in a certain letter of Augustine to Jerome, and in the Decretum, distinction 9, chapter Ego, it is quoted: "I have learned to give this reverence and honour to the books of Scripture alone, which are now called canonical, so that I firmly believe that none of their authors has erred. If I find anything in them that seems contrary to truth, I do not doubt that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator has not grasped the meaning, or I myself have not understood what was said. But other writers I read in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning, I do not therefore hold them true because they have so judged, but because they have been able to persuade me, through other authors, whether canonical or probable arguments, that they do not stray from the truth." From these words it is gathered that only the canonical books contained in the Bible must be given the most certain faith, and that it is not necessary to salvation to adhere firmly to the assertions of others. Likewise the same Augustine, in his book On the One Baptism, as quoted in distinction 9, chapter Quis nesciat, seems plainly to hold the same. For he says: "Who does not know that holy Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is contained within its fixed limits, and that it is so placed above all the later books of bishops that it is wholly impossible to doubt or dispute whether whatever is written in it is true or right; but that the letters of bishops, whether written or to be written after the canon was confirmed, may be censured both by the words of any wiser person who might find something in them, and by the weightier authority and more learned judgment of other bishops, and by councils, if perchance something in them has deviated from the truth." From these words it is gathered that it is unlawful to doubt whether whatever has been shown to be written in Holy Scripture alone, of the Old and New Testaments, is true or right. Therefore, concerning all the writings of general and continuing councils, and of whatever other expositors of divine Scripture, and also of the Roman pontiffs, and of whatever historians, published after the canon was confirmed, it is not unlawful to doubt and to dissent, whether they stray from the truth, in whatever writing is found in them, before it is shown to agree with the writings of the Old and New Testaments. Likewise Augustine, in his letter to Vincentius, cited in the same distinction, chapter Noli, speaking of writings later than the Old and New Testaments, says: "This kind of writing must be distinguished from the authority of the canon; for it is not read as though testimony were so brought from it that it is not lawful to think otherwise, where perhaps they have judged differently from what the truth requires." From this it is established that, against every kind of writing after the canon of the Bible, it is lawful to think otherwise. Augustine seems to agree with this in his letter to Fortunatus, and it is found in distinction prefixed, chapter Neque, where he says: "We ought not to hold the disputations of anyone whatever (that is, of Catholic and praiseworthy men, as the gloss explains) as canonical Scripture, so that it is not lawful for us (saving the honour due to those men) to disapprove and reject anything in their writings, if perchance we find that they have thought otherwise than the truth has been understood, either by divine help or by someone else, or by us." From these things it is concluded that no one is constrained to assent firmly to any assertions whatever that are not contained in the canonical Scriptures.

units.la: Item de veritatibus, quas docuit August. Quod nullus teneatur eas de necessitate salutis recipere, nisi in scripturis canonicis habeantur, secundum eundem August. ostendunt. Nam in libro de trinit. vt in di. 19. recitatur ca. noli, ait: Noli meis litteris quasi canonicis scripturis inserire: sed in illis quae non credebas, sine dubio, incunctanter crede. In ipsis autem quod certum non habeas (nisi certum intellexeris) noli firmum tenere. Et in epistola ad Vincentium Victorem. libro 2. & habetur dist. 9. cap. negare, ait: negare non possumus debeo, sicut in ipsis mei oribus est, ita esse multa in tam multis opusculis meis quae possunt iusto iudicio & nulla temeritate culpari. Ex his concluditur, quod scripturis beati Augustini non est necesse incunctanter adhaerere. Ergo eadem ratione nec scripturis aliorum quotumcunque, qui inter scriptores Bibliae non habentur.
units.tr: Likewise, that no one is bound to receive, as necessary to salvation, the truths taught by Augustine unless they are found in the canonical Scriptures, they show from Augustine himself. For in the book On the Trinity, quoted in distinction 19, chapter Noli, he says: "Do not insert my writings as though they were canonical Scripture; but in those things which you did not believe, believe without hesitation, undoubtedly. But in those things where you have no certainty (unless you have understood them with certainty), do not hold them firmly." And in his letter to Vincentius Victor, book 2, which is found in distinction 9, chapter Negare, he says: "We cannot deny, nor ought we, that, just as there is in my own mouth, so there are many faults in my many small works, which may be justly blamed and without rashness." From these it is concluded that one need not adhere without hesitation to the writings of blessed Augustine. Therefore, by the same reasoning, nor to the writings of any others whatever who are not counted among the writers of the Bible.

units.la: Sententiam memoratam etiam rationibus moliuntur ostendere. Quarum prima est haec. Extra illam scripturam nulla catholica veritas inuenitur, in qua omnis veritas vtilis ad salutem habetur, & omnis falsitas inimica saluti damnatur. Sed secundum August. in scriptura diuina quicquid vtile est inuenitur: & quicquid noxium vel nociuum est, damnatur, ergo extra sacram scripturam nulla veritas catholica reperitur. Secunda ratio est haec: Nō minus sufficiens pro fidelibus Christianis est nouum testamentum vna cum veteri, quam fuit solummodo vetus testamentum pro Hebraeis, sed tota fides, ad quam astringebantur Hebraei, fuit expressa in veteri testamento, ergo & tota fides, ad quam de necessitate salutis Christiani tenentur & arcentur, in nouo testamento & veteri continetur, ergo Christianus de necessitate salutis non tenetur ad credendum nec credere, quod nec in Biblia continetur, nec ex solis contentis in Biblia potest consequentia necessaria & manifesta inferri. Tertio sic. Illud, quod eadem facilitate contemnitur, qua probatur, ad fidem catholicam minime spectat, esto quod sit verum, non debet inter veritates catholicas numerari, sed secundum Hieronym. de scripturis diuinis loquentem: quod de scriptura auctoritatem non habet, eadem facilitate contemnitur, qua probatur, ergo nulla auctoritas, quae ex Scripturis auctoritatem non habet, est inter veritates catholicas computanda.
units.tr: They also set out to show the same opinion by arguments. The first of these is this. Outside that Scripture no catholic truth is found, in which every truth useful for salvation is held and every falsehood hostile to salvation is condemned. But according to Augustine, whatever is useful is found in divine Scripture, and whatever is harmful or hurtful is condemned; therefore outside Holy Scripture no catholic truth is to be found. The second argument is this: the New Testament together with the Old is no less sufficient for Christian believers than the Old Testament alone was for the Hebrews; but the whole faith to which the Hebrews were bound was set out in the Old Testament; therefore the whole faith to which Christians are bound and held, of necessity for salvation, is contained in the New Testament and the Old. Therefore a Christian is not necessarily bound, for salvation, to believe or to hold anything which is not contained in the Bible, nor which can be necessarily and plainly inferred from the things contained in the Bible alone. Thirdly, thus: that which is despised as easily as it is proved does not belong to the catholic faith at all, and even if it is true, it ought not to be counted among catholic truths. But, speaking of divine Scripture, Jerome says: "What does not have authority from Scripture is despised as easily as it is proved." Therefore no doctrine which does not have its authority from Scripture is to be reckoned among catholic truths.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: In quo ponitur opinio precedenti contraria, distinguens diuersas veritates: sed magis & minus ad fidem catholicam pertinentes: qua etiam capitulo sequenti probatur.
units.tr: In which the opinion contrary to the preceding one is set out, distinguishing different truths, some pertaining more and some less to the Catholic faith; this is also proved in the following chapter.

units.la: Magister. Sed alii isti sententiae nequaquam consentiunt, dicentes: quod multae sunt veritates catholicae & fidem sapientes catholicam, quae nec in diuinis scripturis habentur explicite necex solis contentis in eis possunt inferri: quibus tamen fidem indubiam explicitam vel implicitam tam adhibere est necessarium ad salutem. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod praeter veritates, circa quas licitum est sic vel aliter opinari, veritates, quas quilibet catholicus certa credulitate explicite vel implicite tenere astringitur, possunt in triplici differentia reperiri. Quaedam enim sunt de Deo & Christo secundum humanitatem, ex quibus principaliter salus nostra dependet, sicut quod unus est Deus & tres sunt personae: quod Christus est verus Deus & verus homo, passus & mortuus, & quod resurrexit & ascendit &c.
units.tr: Master: But others do not at all agree with that opinion. They say that there are many Catholic truths, and truths savouring of the Catholic faith, which are not found explicitly in the divine Scriptures, nor can they be inferred from the contents of Scripture alone, and yet it is necessary for salvation to hold them with firm and undoubted faith, explicitly or implicitly. To make this clear, they say that one must know that, apart from the truths on which it is lawful to hold this or that opinion, there are truths which every Catholic is bound to hold, explicitly or implicitly, with certain belief, and these can be found in three kinds. For some concern God and Christ according to his humanity, on which our salvation chiefly depends, such as that there is one God and three persons, that Christ is true God and true man, that he suffered and died, and that he rose and ascended, and so on.

units.la: Aliae sunt veritates, ex quibus non ita principaliter pendet salus humana: ea tamen oportet firma fide tenere: quia ex revelatione vel approbatione Dei (cui nullus debet catholicus dissentire) ad orthodoxorum notitiam pervenerunt: quibus mediantibus eas fideles posteri susceperunt, huiusmodi veritates sunt complures in canone confirmato contentae, in quo etiam multae habentur de creaturis, etiam de infidelibus hominibus, quae non directe sed indirecte quodammodo ad salutem humani generis pertinere noscuntur, sicut quod Pharao, Madianitae, Chananei, & alii infideles quamplurimi multas terras occupaverunt, & filios Israel multipliciter afflixerunt, nonnullae etiam veritates huiusmodi extra praedictum canonem continentur: quae tamen per revelationem & approbationem divinam mediantibus Apostolis ad catholicos pervenerunt: quia Christus dum viueret in carne mortali cum Apostolis, multa docuit eos & fecit coram eis, quae tamen in Biblia non habentur. Ex revelatione etiam Spiritus sancti (qui secundum promissionem Christi docturus erat Apostolos omnem veritatem) multa, quae non habentur in sacris literis, didicerunt, quae postea catholicos docuerunt. Omnes veritates praedictas & quae ex eis consequentia necessaria omni tempore necessitatem habente possunt inferri, dicunt isti catholicas esse tenendas. Praeter veritates vero praedictas dicunt esse quasdam veritates alias, quae ex solis contentis in scriptura divina & veritatibus, quae ad nos per Apostolos pervenerunt, concludi non possunt, quae tamen ex praedictis veritatibus, vel aliqua earum & quibusdam aliis veris, quae in facto consistunt, quae vera negari non possunt, manifeste sequuntur. Et de talibus veritatibus, quae ad notitiam pervenerunt, exemplificare nituntur, dicentes, quod talis veritas est illa; Regulae a sanctis Patribus; scilicet Basilio, Benedicto, Augustino, & Francisco institutae, sunt licitae, meritoriae & perfectae: quia licet ista veritas ex solis contentis in scriptura sacra & veritatibus, quas ab Apostolis ecclesia universalis accepit, inferri non possit, cum de istis sanctis & gestis ac regulis institutis ab eis, nulla in praedictis veritatibus mentio habetur, illa tamen veritas simul ex scripturis divinis & gestis & actibus praedictorum sanctorum, de quibus gestis & actibus Christiano rationali sufficienter potest fieri fides, videtur evidenter. Tales etiam veritates sunt illae: fides, quam tenuit beatus Augustin. fuit & est catholica putanda. Symbolum Athanasii est catholicum reputandum & fidele. Sancta quatuor concilia generalia rite celebrata veritatem catholicam diffinierunt: & huiusmodi multae, quae ex solis contentis in divina scriptura & doctrina Apostolica inferri non possunt: cum Augustin. & Athanasius tunc non fuerunt in rerum natura: nec tunc illa concilia fuerunt celebrata, ex contentis tamen in illis veris evidenter possunt concludi. Tales veritates dicunt esse quamplurimas. Quarum aliquae doctrinis authenticis sunt insertae: nonnullae vero in scripturis non habentur. Istas veritates dicunt non esse catholicas, accipiendo vocabulum catholica stricte: sed dicunt esse sapere catholicam veritatem, etiamsi ex veris aliis inferantur. Et ideo, ut dicunt, large accipiendo veritates catholicas, possunt veritates catholicae nuncupari, & illas veritates, quas dicunt sapere catholicam veritatem, existimant ab omni fideli tenendas, saltem implicite. Adhuc sunt aliae veritates, quas dicunt solummodo in facto consistere: cuiusmodi sunt veritates de gestis ecclesiae & sanctorum, quae in gestis, cronicis & historiis fide dignis habentur: quas etiam asserunt a fidelibus minime respuendas. Ex his omnibus isti concludunt, quod multae sunt veritates catholicae, quae nec in scriptura sacra continentur explicite, nec ex solis contentis in ea possunt inferri. Et multae etiam sunt veritates aliae, quas oportet certa fide tenere.
units.tr: Other truths are those on which human salvation does not so chiefly depend, yet they must be held with firm faith, because they have come to the knowledge of the orthodox by the revelation or approval of God (to which no Catholic ought to dissent), and through these the faithful posterity received them. Of this kind there are many contained in the confirmed canon, in which there are also many things said about creatures, even about unbelieving men, which are known to pertain to the salvation of the human race not directly but in some indirect way: for example, that Pharaoh, the Midianites, the Canaanites and very many other unbelievers occupied many lands and afflicted the sons of Israel in many ways. There are also some truths of this kind contained outside the aforesaid canon, which nevertheless reached Catholics through divine revelation and approval, by means of the Apostles, because Christ, while he lived in mortal flesh with the Apostles, taught them many things and did many things before them, which are nonetheless not found in the Bible. Through the revelation also of the Holy Spirit (who, according to Christ's promise, was to teach the Apostles all truth), they learned many things that are not found in the sacred letters, and afterwards taught them to Catholics. All the aforesaid truths, and whatever follows from them by necessary consequence and can be inferred at any time when there is need, these men say are to be held as Catholic. Beyond the aforesaid truths, they say there are certain other truths which cannot be concluded from the contents of divine Scripture and the truths that have come down to us through the Apostles alone, but which nevertheless follow manifestly from those truths, or from some of them together with certain other true facts which cannot be denied. And they try to give examples of such truths that have come to our knowledge, saying that this truth is one: the rules instituted by the holy Fathers, namely Basil, Benedict, Augustine and Francis, are lawful, meritorious and perfect. For although this truth cannot be inferred from the contents of sacred Scripture alone and from the truths which the universal Church received from the Apostles, since there is no mention of these holy men, their deeds, or the rules instituted by them in the aforesaid truths, yet that truth evidently appears from the divine Scriptures together with the deeds and actions of the aforesaid saints, from which deeds and actions a rational Christian can be sufficiently persuaded. Such truths also are these: the faith which blessed Augustine held was and is to be considered Catholic; the Creed of Athanasius is to be regarded as Catholic and faithful; the holy four general councils, lawfully celebrated, defined Catholic truth; and many such truths, which cannot be inferred from the contents of divine Scripture and apostolic doctrine alone, since Augustine and Athanasius were not then in existence, nor were those councils then held, but which can nevertheless be evidently concluded from the contents of those true things. These men say there are very many such truths. Some of them have been inserted into authentic doctrines, but some are not found in the Scriptures. These truths, they say, are not Catholic when the word Catholic is taken strictly, but they say they savour of Catholic truth, even if they are inferred from other true things. And therefore, as they say, if the word is taken broadly, these truths can be called Catholic truths, and they hold that those truths which they say savour of Catholic truth must be held by every faithful person, at least implicitly. There are still other truths which they say consist only in fact: such as truths about the deeds of the Church and of the saints, which are found in deeds, chronicles and trustworthy histories, and which they likewise affirm are not to be rejected by the faithful. From all these things they conclude that there are many Catholic truths which are neither contained explicitly in sacred Scripture nor can be inferred from its contents alone. And there are also many other truths which must be held with certain faith.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: In quo probatur opinio posita capitulo praecedenti auctoritatibus & quinque rationibus.
units.tr: In which the opinion stated in the preceding chapter is proved by authorities and five reasons.

units.la: Discipulus. Satis diffuse narrasti illam secundam sententiam, sed vellem scire, an pro illa aliquae auctoritates vel rationes valeant allegari, ad probandum scilicet, quod oporteat ad salutem aliquibus veritatibus adhaerere, quae nec in literis sacris habentur, nec ex solis contentis in eis necessario argumento possunt inferri. Verum autem tales veritates stricte loquendo catholicae debeant reputari, non curo quod inquiges. Magister. Assertio de qua interrogas, multis auctoribus & rationibus videtur posse probari, hoc enim Innocen. tertius, vt habetur extra de ce. mif. ca. Cum Martha, testari videtur, ait enim multa tam de verbis, quam de factis domi-nicis, inuenimus ab Euangelistis omissa, quæ Apostoli vel supplesse vel facto expressisse leguntur. Et infra idem: Credimus ergo quod formam verborum, sicut in canone reperitur, & à Christo Apostoli, & ab ipsis eorum accepe-runt successores. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod quamuis forma conficiendi sacramentum eucharistiæ nequaquam reperiatur secundum le totam in scriptura diuina: tamen quod illam formam Christus tradiderit est credendum, hoc etiam beatus August. sicut allegatum est supra, expresse sentire videtur, cum dicit: palam est quod in re dubia ad fidem & certitudinem valeat catholicæ ecclesiæ auctoritas, quæ ab ipsis fundatissimis Apostolorum sedibus usque in hodiernum diem succedentium sibimet episcoporum serie & totius populorum assertione firmatur, his verbis datur intelligi, vt videtur, quod ad faciendam fidem sufficeret auctoritas ecclesiæ absque scriptura diuina. Item Agato papa, vt habetur di. 19. c. Sic omnes, ait, sic omnes apostolicæ sedis sanctiones accipienda sunt, tanquam ipsius diuina voce Petri firmata. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod omnes sanctiones apostolicæ sedis sunt eiusdem auctoritatis cum scripturis beati Petri, quæ inter scripturas diuinas censentur, ergo eis fides æqualiter est præbenda, sed in sanctionibus sedis apostolicæ veritates plures habentur, quæ in scripturis diuinis minime sunt inserte, ergo pluribus aliis veritatibus est firmiter adhærendum. Item Nicolaus papa, vt habetur dist. 22. cap. 1. ait: Qui autem Romana ecclesia priuilegium ab ipso summo omnium ecclesiarum capite traditum auferre conatur: hic procul dubio in hæresim labitur, & parum post: hic est dicendus hereticus. Ex quo datur intelligi, quod qui non vult hæreticus reputari, necessario credere debet, quod Romana ecclesia su-per omnes alias ab ipso Christo primatum accepit, de quo tamen in sacra scriptura nulla fit mentio, ergo veritates aliquæ sunt credendæ, licet ex scripturis sacris inferri non possint. In fulcimentum autem assertionis eiusdem isti rationes adducunt, quarum prima ducit ad inconueniens, quia si solis scripturis diuinis, & his qui ex solis contentis in eis possunt inferri, adstringerentur Christiani fidem indubiam adhibere: sequeretur, quod negare liceret Apostolos symbolum condidisse, beatum Petrum Romanum pontificem fuisse, sedem beati Petri de Antiochia Romam fuisse translatam, Romanos pontifices Petro successisse: cum de his in scripturis diuinis nil legatur, has tamen veritates vniuersalis ecclesia hactenus tenuit, probauit & docuit, & per consequens ecclesia vniuersalis errasset; quod omnis catholicus ecclesiasticus pro inconueniente debet habere. Secunda ratio est hæc. Non minus tenentur catholici determinationibus & diffinitionibus Romanorum pontificum (cum nihil contra fidem diffiniunt catholicam) credulitate indubia adhærere, quam eorum statutis, quando nihil contra Dei voluntatem præcipiunt, obedire, sed omnibus statutis Romanorum pontificum, quando nihil contra Dei voluntatem præcipiunt, oportet cum omni humilitate & reuerentia obedire, sicut per sacros canones habetur dist. 11. cap. 1. & etiam cap. præceptis. Et alibi in decretis cap. innumeri. constat aperte, ergo determinationibus & diffinitionibus Romanorum pontificum, quando constat eos nihil contra fidem diffinire catholicam, oportet certissime adhærere. Sed Romani pontifices multas veritates quæ ex solo canone confirmato probari non possunt, diffiniunt firmiter esse tenendas, ergo de necessitate salutis oportet nonnullis veritatibus, quæ ex solis scripturis diuinis probari non possunt, fidem indubiam adhibere. Discipul. Affecto scire, an isti assertores ponant exemplum de aliqua veritate, quæ firmiter sit tenenda: quæ tamen nec in scripturis diuinis habetur, nec ex solis scripturis diuinis illis potest aperte probari. Magist. Multa exempla eorum iam tibi monstraui, videlicet quod Apostoli symbolum condiderunt, quod beatus Petrus fuit Romanus pontifex, quod sedes beati Petri fuit de Antiochia Romam translata, quod beato Petro Romani pontifices successerunt. Aliud etiam ponunt exemplum de principatu Romanæ ecclesiæ, de quo in scriptura diuina nulla fit mentio: quia licet de papatu beati Petri scriptura sacra expresse loquatur, quod tamen beatus Petrus Romanam rexit ecclesiam, in eadem scriptura minime reperitur: & ita de papatu Romanæ ecclesiæ nihil per solam eandem scripturam potest ostendi: & tamen firmiter tenere debemus, quod Romana ecclesia papatum habet super alias vniuersas. Discipul. De illo papatu Romanæ ecclesiæ superseдe; quia de ipso postea tibi aliquas quæstiones mouebo. Sed si isti assertores in aliqua alia ratione se fundant enarra. Mag. Adhuc aliis rationibus satagant se munire, vnde tertia ratio eorum est ista. Non in minori reuerentia & honore debet haberi Apostolorum doctrina, quam eorum canones & statuta, sed canones & statuta Apostolorum, siue ea quæ in scripturis redegerunt, siue solo verbo quæ ipsi seruari mandauerunt, firmiter sunt seruanda, ergo & omnes veritates, quas scripto vel verbo Apostoli docuerunt, tanquam verissimæ sunt habendæ, Apostoli autem plurima docuerunt, quæ in scripturis minime reliquerunt, ergo aliquæ veritates, quæ in scripturis canonicis non habentur, verissimæ sunt censendæ, quibus per consequens oportet adhæsione certissimâ consentire. Quarta ratio est hæc. Vniuersalis ecclesia non potest errare, ipsa testante veritate, quæ ait Apostolis Matthæo vltimo, vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem seculi, quæ etiam pro fide Petri rogauit, ne vnquam deficeret, imo quicunque diceret ecclesiam vniuersalem errare in articulo fidei, in sanctam ecclesiam catholicam vehementer impingeret. Ecclesia autem vniuersalis multas prædicat veritates, quæ nec in scripturis diuinis habentur: nec ex eis solis possunt inferri, sicut per exempla præta&a patet, igitur huiusmodi veritates firmiter sunt tenendæ. Quinta ratio est hæc. Non minoris auctoritatis sunt scripta summorum pontificum & sanctorum doctorum, quæ pro suis dogmatibus conscripserunt, quam sint quæcunque chronicæ & historiæ siue fidelium, siue infidelium, quæ extra sacram scripturam habentur, sed omnino fatuus censetur, qui omnes cronicas & historias extra canonem Bibliæ reprobaret vel eas diceret minime approbandas, tunc enim liceret ea, quæ enarrantur de summis pontificibus, imperatoribus, regibus, regnis & aliis quibusque qui non inueniuntur in Biblia, respuere & negare: quod inconueniens est censendum, ergo multo magis scriptis summorum pontificum & sanctorum, quæ pro suis dogmatibus conscripserant? quæ non inueniuntur in Biblia, est firmiter adhærendum. Discipul. Rationes & authoritates, quas pro secunda sententia adduxisti, fortes mihi videntur. Et quamuis nolim, quod in toto hoc opere manifestes, quæ sit tua assertio, quando contrarias opiniones recitas & aduersas, veruntamen in generali cupio scire, an scilicet, quando illam assertionem, quæ tua est rationibus & authoritatibus munire conaris, existimes omnes authoritates & rationes, quas allegas, conclusionem tuam demonstratiue probare. Magist. Pro sententia, quam reputo veram, motiua quandoque demonstratiua, interdum probabilia tantum, nonnunquam solummodo apparentia, propter aliquos exercitandos aut probandos seu tentandos allego.
units.tr: Disciple. You have set out that second opinion at considerable length, but I would like to know whether any authorities or reasons can be cited in its support, namely to prove that for salvation it is necessary to adhere to certain truths which are not found in the sacred writings, nor can be necessarily inferred from the contents of those writings alone. As for whether such truths should strictly be counted as catholic, I do not care what you will inquire into. Master. The assertion you ask about seems to be capable of being proved by many authors and reasons. For Innocent III, as found in extra de cel. mis. cap. Cum Martha, seems to bear witness to it, for he says: "We find many things, both of the words and of the deeds of the Lord, omitted by the Evangelists, which the Apostles are read to have either supplied or expressed by deed." And further on the same: "We believe therefore that the form of words, as it is found in the canon, was received both from Christ by the Apostles and from them by their successors." From these words it is gathered that, although the form for consecrating the sacrament of the Eucharist is nowhere found in the divine Scripture as such, nevertheless we must believe that Christ handed down that form. Blessed Augustine also seems to hold this expressly, as was cited above, when he says: "It is plain that in a doubtful matter the authority of the catholic Church, which is confirmed from the very most firmly founded seats of the Apostles down to the present day by the succession of bishops succeeding one another and by the assent of the whole people, carries weight for faith and certainty." By these words it is given to understand, as it seems, that the authority of the Church without divine Scripture is sufficient to create faith. Likewise Pope Agatho, as found in dist. 19, cap. Sic omnes, says: "In this way all the sanctions of the apostolic see are to be received, as though confirmed by the divine voice of Peter himself." From these words it is given to understand that all the sanctions of the apostolic see have the same authority as the writings of blessed Peter, which are counted among the divine Scriptures; therefore faith is equally to be given to them. But many truths are contained in the sanctions of the apostolic see which are not at all inserted in the divine Scriptures; therefore one must firmly adhere to many other truths. Likewise Pope Nicholas, as found in dist. 22, cap. 1, says: "Whoever tries to take away the privilege handed down to the Roman Church by the very highest head of all churches, he undoubtedly falls into heresy," and a little after: "such a one is to be called a heretic." From this it is given to understand that whoever does not wish to be reckoned a heretic must necessarily believe that the Roman Church has received the primacy over all others from Christ himself. Yet there is no mention of this in holy Scripture; therefore some truths are to be believed although they cannot be inferred from the sacred Scriptures. In support of this same assertion they adduce these reasons. The first leads to an absurdity: for if Christians were bound to give undoubted faith only to the divine Scriptures and to those things which can be inferred from the contents of them alone, it would follow that it would be lawful to deny that the Apostles drew up the creed, that blessed Peter was Roman pontiff, that the seat of blessed Peter was transferred from Antioch to Rome, and that the Roman pontiffs succeeded Peter. Yet nothing about these matters is read in the divine Scriptures, and the universal Church has hitherto held, proved and taught these truths; and consequently the universal Church would have erred, which every catholic and churchman must regard as absurd. The second reason is this. Catholics are no less bound to adhere with undoubting belief to the determinations and definitions of the Roman pontiffs (since they define nothing contrary to the catholic faith) than to obey their statutes when they command nothing contrary to the will of God. But all the statutes of the Roman pontiffs, when they command nothing contrary to the will of God, must be obeyed with all humility and reverence, as is laid down in the sacred canons, dist. 11, cap. 1, and also cap. Praeceptis; and it is plainly stated elsewhere in the Decretals, cap. Innumeri. Therefore the determinations and definitions of the Roman pontiffs, when it is clear that they define nothing contrary to the catholic faith, must be adhered to most certainly. But the Roman pontiffs define that many truths which cannot be proved from the canon alone are firmly to be held; therefore of necessity for salvation one must give undoubted faith to some truths which cannot be proved from the divine Scriptures alone. Disciple. I want to know whether these advocates put forward an example of some truth which must be firmly held, which nevertheless is not found in the divine Scriptures and cannot clearly be proved from the divine Scriptures alone. Master. I have already shown you many of their examples, namely that the Apostles drew up the creed, that blessed Peter was Roman pontiff, that the seat of blessed Peter was transferred from Antioch to Rome, and that the Roman pontiffs succeeded blessed Peter. They also give another example, concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, of which no mention is made in the divine Scripture: for although holy Scripture expressly speaks of the papacy of blessed Peter, it is nowhere found in that same Scripture that blessed Peter governed the Roman Church; and so nothing about the papacy of the Roman Church can be shown from Scripture alone; and yet we must firmly hold that the Roman Church has the papacy over all others. Disciple. Set aside that papacy of the Roman Church for now, since I shall later raise some questions about it. But if these advocates rest on some other reason, relate it. Master. They still strive to fortify themselves with further reasons, of which their third reason is this. The doctrine of the Apostles ought to be held in no less reverence and honour than their canons and statutes; but the canons and statutes of the Apostles, whether those which they drew up in writing or those which they ordered to be observed by word alone, must be firmly observed; therefore all the truths which the Apostles taught either in writing or by word must be held as most true; and the Apostles taught very many things which they did not leave in the Scriptures; therefore some truths which are not contained in the canonical Scriptures are to be considered most true, and to these one must consent with most certain adherence. The fourth reason is this. The universal Church cannot err, the truth itself attesting it, which said to the Apostles in the last chapter of Matthew, "I am with you even to the end of the age," and which also prayed for the faith of Peter that it might never fail; indeed whoever said that the universal Church errs in an article of faith would strike violently against the holy catholic Church. But the universal Church preaches many truths which are neither contained in the divine Scriptures nor can be inferred from them alone, as is plain from the examples set forth above; therefore truths of this kind are to be firmly held. The fifth reason is this. The writings of the supreme pontiffs and holy teachers, which they composed in support of their doctrines, are of no less authority than any chronicles and histories, whether of believers or unbelievers, which are found outside sacred Scripture. But he would be thought utterly foolish who would reject all chronicles and histories outside the canon of the Bible, or who would say that they are not to be approved; for then it would be lawful to reject and deny whatever is related about the supreme pontiffs, emperors, kings, kingdoms and any others who are not found in the Bible; which must be judged absurd. Therefore much more must one firmly adhere to the writings of the supreme pontiffs and holy men, which they composed in support of their doctrines, which are not found in the Bible. Disciple. The reasons and authorities which you have adduced for the second opinion seem strong to me. And although I would not wish you to make clear throughout this whole work what your own assertion is, when you recite and oppose contrary opinions, nevertheless in general I want to know whether, when you try to fortify with reasons and authorities that assertion which is your own, you think all the authorities and reasons you allege demonstrably prove your conclusion. Master. For an opinion which I consider true I sometimes allege demonstrative arguments, at other times merely probable ones, and sometimes only apparent ones, for the sake of exercising, testing or trying some readers.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: In quo reiiciuntur duæ opiniones, quibus scilicet assertionibus sit assentiendum, & qui libri, seu sanctorum opuscula sint tanquam catholica habenda, de quibus ponuntur duæ conclusiones, quæ etiam pro- bantur.
units.tr: In which two opinions are rejected: namely, to which assertions one should assent, and which books or short writings of the saints are to be held as catholic. Two conclusions are laid down on these matters, and they are also proved.

units.la: Discipulus. Modus ille valde mihi placet: quia per hoc sæpe scientiam instatorum experiar, porro cum quæsiuerim, quibus veritatibus oporteat firmiter assentire, super quo diuersas opiniones diuersorum referasti, quarum prima habet consequenter dicere, quod solummodo sacrarum scriptoribus literarum est fides firmissima adhibenda. Secunda vero, quæ mihi placet magis, concedere debet etiam quod aliquid aliud est credendum. Magist. Ad interrogationem tuam à diuersis diuersimode respondetur, quidam enim dicunt vniuersis conciliis generalibus & omnibus summis pontificibus in his quæ diffiniunt, esse credendum, & omnibus sanctis scripturæ sacræ tractatoribus credere esse necesse; licet ea, quæ dicantur, per sacram scripturam nequeant demonstrare. Pro hac assertione videtur esse, quod legitur dist. 15. cap. 1. vbi de conciliis generalibus recipiendis habetur aperte. Et etiam cap. sicut, & cap. sancta Romana. De assertionibus summorum pontificum recipiendis habetur dist. 19. c. si Romanorum. Et in pluribus aliis, de traditionibus autem sanctorum habetur dist. 15. c. sanctam. Alii vero prædictæ assertioni non vsquequaque consentiunt, asserentes quod licet assertionibus generalium conciliorum sit vniuersaliter adhærendum, licet etiam multis decretis seu etiam decretalibus ac diffinitionibus summorum Romanorum pontificum, ac pluribus opusculis sanctorum doctorum, pro eo quod omnia quæ inueniuntur in eis constat esse consona catholicæ veritati, oporteat catholicos consentire: non tamen eo ipso, quod Romani pontifices vel sancti tradunt aliquid esse tenendum, est huiusmodi (tanquam consonum veritati) necesse accipere. Discipul. De generalibus conciliis & summis pontificibus intendo aliqua postea ad materiam istam spectantia indagare: & ideo hic nihil loquaris de ipsis, sed de sanctis obsecro resera, quid prædicti sentiunt assertores. Magist. De sanctis duas conclusiones affirmant. Quarum prima est, quod non eo ipso, quod aliquis sanctus aliquid opinatur esse credendum, est à cunctis fidelibus tanquam veritati consonum approbandum. Secunda conclusio, quod non omnibus sententiis, quæ inueniuntur in sanctorum opusculis iam per ecclesiam diuulgatis, est firmiter adhærendum.
units.tr: Disciple. That method pleases me greatly, because through it I shall often test the knowledge of those being instructed. Further, when I asked which truths one ought to assent to firmly, you reported the differing opinions of various people on this. The first of these consequently holds that the firmest faith is to be given only to the writers of the holy letters. The second, which pleases me more, must also concede that something else is to be believed. Master. Different people answer your question in different ways. Some say that one must believe all general councils and all the supreme pontiffs in what they define, and that one must believe all the holy writers who treat of Sacred Scripture, even though what they say cannot be demonstrated from Sacred Scripture. For this assertion there seems to be support in what is plainly stated in dist. 15. cap. 1., where the reception of general councils is discussed. Also in cap. sicut, and cap. sancta Romana. On the reception of the assertions of the supreme pontiffs, see dist. 19. c. si Romanorum. And in many other places. On the traditions of the saints, see dist. 15. c. sanctam. Others, however, do not agree with the aforesaid assertion in every respect. They maintain that, although one must universally adhere to the assertions of general councils, and Catholics ought to agree with many decrees or even decretals, with the definitions of the supreme Roman pontiffs, and with many writings of the holy teachers (because everything found in them is agreed to be consonant with Catholic truth), it does not follow that, merely because the Roman pontiffs or the saints teach that something is to be held, one must necessarily accept it as consonant with the truth. Disciple. I intend to investigate later some matters relating to this subject, concerning general councils and the supreme pontiffs. So do not speak of them here, but please explain to me what the aforesaid advocates think about the saints. Master. Concerning the saints, they affirm two conclusions. The first is that it does not follow, merely because some saint holds that something is to be believed, that it must be approved by all the faithful as consonant with the truth. The second is that one must not firmly adhere to every opinion found in the writings of the saints that have already been published by the Church.

units.la: Prima conclusio probatur authoritatibus Augustin. quæ ponuntur distinct. 9. cap. noli & cap. negare & cap. Ego & cap. noli & cap. neque. In quibus manifeste asserit Augustin. quod nonnulla in opusculis sanctorum & suis inserta licet fidelibus iusto modo absque omni temeritate culpare.
units.tr: The first conclusion is proved by the authorities of Augustine that are cited at distinct. 9. cap. noli, cap. negare, cap. Ego, cap. noli, and cap. neque. In these places Augustine clearly asserts that certain things inserted in the writings of the saints and in his own may be blamed by the faithful, in a just manner and without any rashness.

units.la: Hoc etiam ratione moliuntur ostendere, nam non est necesse, putare aliquid esse verum propter hoc, quod illi, qui possunt errare, hoc sentiunt; nam propter solam existimationem illorum, qui possunt asserere falsum pro vero, non est eo ipso aliquid asserendum pro vero, quia tales sic sentiunt. Sed sancti, stante sanctitate, possunt errare, etiam contra catholicam veritatem, igitur hoc, quod sancti aliquid sentiunt esse verum, non est efficaciter adhærendum. Maior est aperta, minor exemplo & ratione probatur. Exemplo quidem de beato Augustin. qui sanctus existens plurima scripsit & docuit contra veritatem catholicam, quorum aliqua postmodum reuocauit, hoc etiam ratione probatur.
units.tr: They also try to show this by reason. It is not necessary to think that something is true merely because those who are capable of error hold it. For the mere opinion of those who can assert what is false as true does not, for that reason alone, oblige us to assert something as true because such people think so. But the saints, while remaining saints, can err, even against catholic truth. Therefore, that the saints hold something to be true is not something we must firmly adhere to. The major premise is obvious; the minor is proved by example and by reason. By example, indeed, from the blessed Augustine, who, though a saint, wrote and taught very many things against catholic truth, some of which he afterwards retracted. This is also proved by reason.

units.la: Nam error, qui pertinaciam non habet annexam, non obuiat sanctitati. Sed contingit aliquem errare contra catholicam veritatem absque pertinacia, ergo non est inconueniens affirmare sanctos stante sanctitate posse errare contra catholicam veritatem absque pertinacia, & ita non est necesse omnibus, quæ sancti dicunt firmiter adhærere. Secunda conclusio probatur, nemo debet contrariis assentire: sed sancti in suis opusculis iam per ecclesiam diuulgatis inter se inueniuntur contrarii, etiam in his, quæ ad fidem & doctrinam Apostolicam pertinere noscuntur, nam vt habetur distinct. 26. circa doctrinam beati Pauli dicentis, quod oportet episcopum vnius vxoris esse virum & non plurium, Hieronymus & Augustinus sententias contrarias protulerunt, hinc est quod Gloss. distinct. prædicta c.1. dicit, male sentit hic Hieronymus, unde Augustinus eum corrigit in proximo. Isti etiam sancti multi, sicut patet in eorum epistolis, & recitat Gloss. ad Gal. 2. de reprehensione, qua B. Paulus dixit B. Petrum esse reprehensibilem, contraria sentiebant. Beatus etiam Cyprianus de baptismo haereticorum aliter quam B. Augustinus scripsit, unde & B. Augustin. eundem sanctissimum Cyprian. redarguit, loquens enim de sancto Cypriano & aliis, vt habetur de consec. dist. 4. c. quomodo ait, non obaliud visum est etiam quibusdam egregiis viris & antistitibus Christi, inter quos precipue beatus Cyprianus eminebat, non esse posse apud haereticos vel schismaticos baptismum Christi: vbi quia non distinguebat sacramentum ab effectu vel vsu sacramenti, & quod sacramentum atque eius vsum in liberatione a peccatis & cordis rectitudine apud haereticos non inueniebat, ipsum quoque sacramentum illic non esse putabat. Haec autem est sententia Cypriani de sacramentis haereticorum, cuius contrarium Augustin. ibidem dicit & asserit. Manifeste ergo sancti circa sacramenta ecclesiae contraria dogmatizant, hinc dist. 33. c. adhuc sciendum, legitur: Sciendum vero quod canones Apostolorum, quorum omnium auctoritate orientalis ecclesia & ex parte Romana vtitur, & insignis martyr Cyprianus & omnes episcopi cum eodem baptismum haereticorum lanacrum diaboli appellat. Stephanus vero & Cornelius martyres & Pontifices Romani, & venerabilis Augustin. in libro de baptismate eundem Cyprianum & praefatos episcopos ob hanc causam vehementer redarguerunt, affirmantes baptisma siue ab haretico, siue a schismatico, ecclesiastico more, traditum siue celebratum, esse ratum. Ex his colligitur, quam Cyprianus & Augustin. de sacramento ecclesiae contraria tradiderunt, quae etiam reperiuntur in scripturis eorum, sicut ex praedictis, & ca. eiusdem Cypriani, quod habetur 1. q. c. si quis, patet aperte, non ergo omnibus assertionibus in operibus sanctorum inuentis debet catholicus adhaerere. Discip. De sanctorum libris tam aperte probasti, quod non sunt in omnibus approbandi, quod nequeo dissentire. Ex quo sequitur, quod nihil auctoritatis remansit in eis, quia sicut instrumenta, ita etiam Scripturae quacunque in parte inueniuntur falsae, in totum reprobantur vel saltem suspectae redduntur. Unde & de Scripturis sacris, vt habetur distinct. 9. cap. si ad Scripturas sacras, asserit Augustin. quod si ad eas admissa fuerint vel officiosa mendacia, nihil auctoritatis remanebit in eis, dic ergo, quomodo isti respondent ad illud, quod (de approbatione opusculorum sacrorum, inter quae etiam opuscula Cypriani & Augustini & Hieronymi numerantur) distinct. 15. legitur manifeste. Magist. Dicunt isti, quod non omnia opuscula sanctorum, quantum ad omnia contenta in eis, sunt per ecclesiam approbata. Constat enim, quod in libris beati Augustini multa inueniuntur contraria veritati, quae etiam ipse postmodum reuocauit, & ita illa minime approbantur. Et sicut est de libris beati Augustini, ita est de libris multorum aliorum sanctorum, qui nequaquam quo ad omnia approbantur, omnes tamen libri sanctorum, de quibus in distinct. praedicta fit mentio, approbantur quo ad omnia, quae nec per auctoritatem, nec per alios sunt correcta. Discipul. Isto modo libros haereticorum approbates, quoad omnia, quae per catholicos minime sunt correcta, omnium enim veritatem est licitum approbare. Mag. Dicunt isti, quod non est simile de libris haereticorum, & de libris sanctorum, quia in libris haereticorum falsa principaliter tractantur & asseruntur: pauca autem vera inueniuntur inserta. In libris vero sanctorum vera principaliter intenduntur, & pauca reperiuntur contraria veritati, & ideo propter pauca inutilia non sunt tanta vtilia respuenda. Discipul. Explica mihi, an isti putant omnes veritates in libris sanctorum inuentas catholicas esse censendas. Magist. Nullatenus arbitrantur omnes veritates tractatas in libris sanctorum esse catholicas. Vnde dicunt, quod sancti aliqua tanquam catholica, quaedam autem tanquam necessaria non ad fidem spectantia, nonnulla vero tanquam probata tradiderunt, hoc vlterius ex auctoritatibus Augustini, quae distinct. 9. ponuntur, scilicet cap. noli, & cap. negare, & cap. neque, probatur etiam aperte, cui etiam concordat Anselmus lib. 1. Cur Deus homo, dicens de peccato, quod omnia quae dico, sic volo accipi, vt si quid dixero, quod maior non confirmat auctoritas, quamuis illud ratione probare videar, non alia certitudine accipiatur, nisi quod interim mihi videtur, donec Deus mihi melius reuelet. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Anselmus nonnulla tanquam probabilia solummodo dicere intendebat, &c.
units.tr: For an error that does not carry obstinacy with it does not detract from holiness. But it happens that someone errs against catholic truth without obstinacy. Therefore it is not absurd to affirm that the saints, while remaining saints, can err against catholic truth without obstinacy, and so it is not necessary to adhere firmly to everything the saints say. The second conclusion is proved thus: no one ought to assent to contraries. But the saints, in their writings already published by the Church, are found to be at odds with one another, even on matters known to pertain to the faith and the apostolic doctrine. For, as is held at distinct. 26., concerning the teaching of blessed Paul, who says that a bishop must be the husband of one wife and not of several, Jerome and Augustine put forward contrary opinions. Hence the Gloss at the said distinct. c. 1. says: "Jerome thinks wrongly here, whence Augustine corrects him soon after." Many of these same saints, as is clear from their letters, and as the Gloss recites at Gal. 2, concerning the rebuke by which blessed Paul said that blessed Peter was worthy of blame, held contrary views. Blessed Cyprian also wrote about the baptism of heretics differently from blessed Augustine, whence blessed Augustine also refuted that most holy Cyprian. For speaking of the holy Cyprian and others, as is held at de consec. dist. 4. c. quomodo, he says: "It has seemed otherwise to some outstanding men and bishops of Christ, among whom blessed Cyprian especially stood out, that the baptism of Christ cannot be among heretics or schismatics. There, because he did not distinguish the sacrament from its effect or use, and did not find the sacrament and its use among heretics in liberation from sins and in rectitude of heart, he also thought that the sacrament itself was not there." This indeed is Cyprian's opinion about the sacraments of heretics, and Augustine in the same place says and asserts the contrary. Clearly, then, the saints teach contrary things about the sacraments of the Church. Hence dist. 33. c. adhuc sciendum reads: "It must be known that the canons of the Apostles, by the authority of all of whom the Eastern Church and in part the Roman Church make use, and the distinguished martyr Cyprian, and all the bishops with him, call the baptism of heretics a laver of the devil. But Stephen and Cornelius, martyrs and Roman pontiffs, and the venerable Augustine in his book on baptism, vehemently refuted that same Cyprian and the aforesaid bishops for this reason, affirming that baptism, whether given or celebrated by a heretic or by a schismatic, in the manner of the Church, is valid." From these things it is gathered how Cyprian and Augustine handed down contrary things concerning the sacrament of the Church. These are also found in their writings. As is clear from what has been said, and from the chapter of the same Cyprian that is held at 1. q. c. si quis, it is plainly so. Therefore a Catholic ought not to adhere to all the assertions found in the works of the saints. Student. You have proved so plainly that the books of the saints are not to be approved in all things that I cannot dissent. From this it follows that nothing of authority remains in them, because, just as with documents, so also Scriptures, wherever they are found to be false in any part, are rejected entirely or at least rendered suspect. Hence also concerning the Holy Scriptures, as is held at distinct. 9. cap. si ad Scripturas sacras, Augustine asserts: "If even officious lies have been admitted into them, nothing of authority will remain in them." Tell me, then, how these men answer what is read plainly at distinct. 15. concerning the approval of the sacred writings, among which the writings of Cyprian, Augustine and Jerome are also counted. Master. These men say that not all the writings of the saints are approved by the Church as to everything contained in them. For it is established that in the books of blessed Augustine many things are found contrary to truth, which he himself afterwards retracted, and so those things are by no means approved. And as it is with the books of blessed Augustine, so it is with the books of many other saints, who are by no means approved in every respect. Nevertheless, all the books of the saints mentioned in the aforesaid distinct. are approved in everything that has not been corrected either by authority or by others. Student. In this way you approve the books of heretics, in everything that has not been corrected by Catholics, for it is lawful to approve the truths of all men. Master. These men say that the books of heretics and the books of saints are not alike, because in the books of heretics falsehoods are principally treated and asserted, while only a few truths are inserted. But in the books of the saints truths are principally intended, and few things are found contrary to truth; therefore, on account of a few useless things, things so useful should not be rejected. Student. Explain to me whether these men think that all the truths found in the books of the saints are to be regarded as catholic. Master. They by no means think that all the truths treated in the books of the saints are catholic. Hence they say that the saints handed down some things as catholic, some things as necessary but not pertaining to faith, and some things as merely probable. This is further shown plainly from the authorities of Augustine that are set out at distinct. 9., namely cap. noli, cap. negare, and cap. neque. It also agrees with Anselm in book 1 of Cur Deus homo, where, speaking of sin, he says: "I want everything I say to be taken in such a way that, if I say anything which a greater authority does not confirm, although I seem to prove it by reason, it is to be received with no other certainty than that it seems so to me for the time being, until God reveals something better to me." From these words it is gathered that Anselm intended to say some things only as probable, etc.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: In quo recitantur quinque genera veritatum, quibus non licet Christianum aliqualiter dissentire.
units.tr: In which are set out five kinds of truth, from which a Christian may in no way dissent.

units.la: Discipul. Ex verbis istis quae narrasti, magnam occasionem cogitandi mihi dedisti, de ipsis tamen plura quaerere nequaquam nunc intendo, sed quot generibus veritatis oportet Christianos catholicos assentire secundum sententiam praedictorum, absque omni probatione tibi placeat indicare. Magist. Tenent isti, quod quinque sunt genera veritatum, quibus non licet Christianis aliter dissentire. Primum est earum, quae in Scriptura sacra dicuntur, vel ex eis argumento necessario possunt inferri. Secundum est earum, quæ ab Apostolis ad nos per succedentium relationem vel Scripturas fidelium peruenerunt, licet in Scripturis sacris non inueniantur insertæ, nec ex solis eis possunt necessario argumento concludi. Tertium est earum, quas in fide dignis cronicis & historiis, relationibus fidelium inuenimus: Quartum est earum, quæ ex veritatibus primi generis & secundi tantummodo, vel quę ex eis vel alterius earum vna cum veritatibus tertii generis possunt manifeste concludi. Quintum est earum, quas Deus præter veritates reuelatas Apostolis; aliis reuelauit, vel etiam inspirauit, ac nouiter reuelaret, vel etiam inspiraret: quæ reuelatio vel inspiratio ad vniuersalem ecclesiam absque dubitatione peruenit, vel etiam peruenire. Discipul. Quamuis nō intenderim de istis te amplius molestare: quia tamen vnum genus veritatis, de quo nullus dubitat catholicus omisisti edicere, quare isti inter aliquas veritates illas, quæ in determinationibus & diffinitionibus ecclesiæ reperiuntur, nequaquam enumerant? Magist. De illis veritatibus mentionem non faciunt specialem, quia putant quod ecclesia rite procedens nullam veritatem determinat aut diffinit, nisi in Scriptura sacra aut traditionibus Apostolorum aut cronicis historiis vel reuelationibus indubitabilibus fidelium, vel his quæ sequuntur ex prædictis aut aliquo prædictorum, vel in reuelatione seu inspiratione diuina modo debito manifesta valeant se fundare, & ideo omnes veritates, quas determinat vel diffinit ecclesia, sub aliquo quinque generum præfatorum comprehendi noscuntur. Discipul. Illa quæ refers, vrgent me contra propositum præconceptum interrogare, quid de approbatione canonis Bibliæ & aliorum librorum postea conscriptorum ac omnium aliorum, quæ ecclesia noscitur approbare, assertores sentiunt memorati. Magist. Hoc pro certissimo tenent, quod non est in potestate ecclesiæ, quæcunque ad placitum approbare vel etiam reprobare: sed ecclesia rite approbando quæcunque in aliquo prædictorum generum quinque veritatum se fundauit. Vnde ad probationem, quantum ad rem, licet quantum ad nomen a determinatione vel diffinitione in proposito non discernuntur.
units.tr: Disciple. From the words you have just recited you have given me much to think about. I do not now intend to ask you more about them. Rather, please tell me, without any proof, which kinds of truth Catholic Christians must assent to according to the opinion of those I have mentioned. Master. These men hold that there are five kinds of truth to which Christians may not dissent in any way. The first kind is that which is stated in Holy Scripture, or which can be necessarily inferred from it by argument. The second kind is that which has come down to us from the Apostles through the handing down of successors or through the writings of the faithful, although it is not found inserted in the Holy Scriptures and cannot be necessarily concluded from Scripture alone. The third kind is that which we find in trustworthy chronicles and histories and in the accounts of the faithful. The fourth kind is that which can be plainly concluded from the truths of the first and second kinds alone, or from them, or from one of them together with truths of the third kind. The fifth kind is that which God has revealed or inspired to others, beyond the truths revealed to the Apostles, or which he newly reveals or inspires; and this revelation or inspiration has come, or will come, to the universal Church without doubt. Disciple. Although I did not intend to trouble you further about these, you have left out one kind of truth, about which no Catholic doubts. Why do they not list among these truths those that are found in the determinations and definitions of the Church? Master. They make no special mention of those truths, because they think that the Church, proceeding rightly, never determines or defines any truth except what can rest on Holy Scripture, the traditions of the Apostles, trustworthy chronicles or the indubitable revelations of the faithful, or on what follows from these, or from one of them, or on a divine revelation or inspiration made manifest in the due manner. So all the truths that the Church determines or defines are known to be included under one of the five kinds mentioned. Disciple. What you say urges me, against my settled purpose, to ask what the aforementioned writers think about the approval of the canon of the Bible, and of other books written afterwards, and of all the other things that the Church is known to approve. Master. They hold as most certain that it is not in the power of the Church to approve or even reject whatever it pleases. Rather, in approving rightly, the Church bases whatever it approves on one of the aforesaid five kinds of truth. Hence, as to the matter itself, the approval is a proof, although in name it is not distinguished from determination or definition in the present question.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: In quo ponitur descriptio hæresis, contra quam etiam obiicitur capitu- lo sequenti.
units.tr: In which a description of heresy is set out, against which an objection is also raised in the following chapter.

units.la: Discipulus. De veritatibus theologicis seu catholicis nonnulla quæsiui. Nunc vero ad hæreses eis contrarias transeamus. In primis autem affecto scire, si diffinitionem hæresis datam ab aliquo inueniisti. Magist. Quidam diffiniunt seu describunt hæresim dicentes, quod hæresis est dogma falsum fidei contrarium orthodoxa. In qua descriptione loco generis ponitur dogma falsum, quia omnis hæresis est dogma falsum: sed non omne dogma falsum debet hæresis reputari, quod autem omnis hæresis sit dogma falsum, beatus Hieronymus vt habetur 24. quaest. 3. cap. inter hæresim, testatur aperte dicens: hæresis peruersum dogma habet, dogma autem peruersum est falsum dogma, hæresis ergo est falsum dogma, sed non omne dogma falsum est hæresis, nam secundum Augustin. in Encher. in multis rebus errare, nullum aut minimum est peccatum, sed hæresis sicut infidelitas grauissimum est peccatum, ergo non omnis error est hæresis. Ex quo concluditur, quod non omne dogma falsum est hæresis, cum omnis error dogma falsum sit censendus, dogma ergo falsum in descriptione hæresis pro genere ponitur secundum istos, fidei autem contrarium orthodoxa ponitur loco differentiæ, per hoc enim ab aliis falsis, quæ non sunt hæreses, conuenienter hæresis est distincta, nam aliqua dogmata falsa non sunt contraria fidei catholicæ, & ideo hæreses minime nuncupantur. Discipul. Ex verbis beati Hieronymi allegatis moueor ad quærendum, an beatus Hieronym. cum dicit, hæresis peruersum dogma habet: intenderet diffinitionem aut descriptionem assignare. Magist. Dicunt illi, quorum ad præcedentem interrogationem sententiam recitaui; quod large accipiendo peruersum pro qualicunque perniciosō seu nociuo, beatus Hieronymus non intendit ibi hæresim diffinire, multa enim sunt dogmata perniciosa, quæ hæreses nullatenus sunt censenda. Si autem peruersum accipiatur magis stricte pro illo, quod est perniciosum in doctrina religionis, quemadmodum secundum beatum Augustinum vnum genus mendacii est, quod inuenitur in doctrina religionis: sicpotest concedi, quod beatus Hieronymus ibidem intendit descriptionem hæresis assignare, & sic dogma peruersum accipitur pro dogmate falso fidei catholicæ contraria orthodoxæ.
units.tr: Student. I have asked some questions about theological or catholic truths. Now let us turn to the heresies contrary to them. First, however, I want to know whether you have found a definition of heresy given by anyone. Master. Some define or describe heresy by saying that heresy is a false doctrine contrary to orthodox faith. In this description false doctrine is put in the place of the genus, because every heresy is a false doctrine; but not every false doctrine should be regarded as a heresy. That every heresy is a false doctrine blessed Jerome plainly testifies, as is found in 24 q. 3, c. "inter haeresim", saying: heresy has a perverse doctrine. A perverse doctrine, however, is a false doctrine, so heresy is a false doctrine. But not every false doctrine is a heresy, for according to Augustine in the Enchiridion, to err in many matters is no sin or the smallest sin, whereas heresy, like unbelief, is the gravest sin. Therefore not every error is a heresy. From this it follows that not every false doctrine is a heresy, since every error must be counted a false doctrine. So, according to these men, false doctrine in the description of heresy is put for the genus, while contrary to orthodox faith is put in the place of the difference; for by this heresy is suitably distinguished from other false doctrines that are not heresies, since some false doctrines are not contrary to the catholic faith and so are not called heresies at all. Discipul. Moved by the words of blessed Jerome cited, I ask whether blessed Jerome, when he says heresy has a perverse doctrine, intended to give a definition or description. Magist. Those whose opinion I recited in reply to the previous question say: taking perverse broadly for anything pernicious or harmful, blessed Jerome did not intend there to define heresy, for many doctrines are pernicious yet are in no way to be counted heresies. But if perverse is taken more strictly for what is pernicious in the doctrine of religion, just as according to blessed Augustine one kind of lie is that which is found in the doctrine of religion, then it can be conceded that blessed Jerome there intended to assign a description of heresy, and thus a perverse doctrine is taken for a false doctrine contrary to orthodox catholic faith.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: In quo obiicitur contra diffinitionem datam de hæresi, ad quam respondetur capitulo sequenti.
units.tr: In which an objection is raised against the definition of heresy given above, to which the following chapter replies.

units.la: Discipulus. Libenter scirem an omnes concorditer reputant hæresim prædicto modo describi debere. Magist. Sunt quidam qui non putant hæresim taliter describendam: qui tali rationi inniti videntur, multa dogmata falsa fidei contraria orthodoxæ fiunt nouiter hæreses, quamuis non de nouo incipiant esse falsa fidei contraria orthodoxæ, ergo priusquam hæreses debeant reputari, sunt dogmata falsa fidei orthodoxæ contraria. Ex quo euidenter concluditur, quod non omnia dogmata falsa fidei contraria orthodoxæ deberent hæreses reputari, antecedens videtur euidens, quia multæ sunt nouæ hæreses, quamuis prius falsa dogmata fuerint fidei orthodoxæ contraria. Vrbanus enim Papa, vt habetur 24. quæstion. 3. cap. notandum, ait: sanctus Augustinus cum legatis sanctæ Romanæ ecclesiæ, & cum sanctis episcopis suis Pelagium & Cælestinum nouam hæresim in sanctam Dei ecclesiam introducentes excommunicauit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Pelagius & Cælestinus opinionem, quæ tunc erat nova hæresis, in ecclesiam introduxerunt: & tamen illa opinio fuit prius contraria fidei orthodoxæ, ergo illa opinio seu assertio, priusquam esset hæresis, fuit dogma falsum fidei contrarium orthodoxæ, & ita illa non est descriptio conuertibilis cum hæresi, hinc Gratianus 24. quæst. 1. cap. 1. §. omni enim, ait: Omnis hereticus aut iam damnatam haeresim sequitur, aut nouam confingit. Et Glossa ibidem dicit: sed tu dic indistincte seu veterem (scilicet haeresim) siue nouam sequatur, excommunicatus est, licet sit occultus. Glossa etiam dicit: Si scirem prælatum meum esse hereticum, quia nouam haeresim fingit, nec tamen predicaret, si me excommunicaret, celebrarem in occulto. Ex his habetur aperte, quod fuerunt & possunt esse hæreses nouæ, quæ tamen non sunt noua falsa fidei contraria orthodoxæ: & per consequens non omne falsum fidei contrarium orthodoxæ debet inter hæreses computari.
units.tr: Discipulus. I would gladly know whether everyone agrees that heresy ought to be described in the way mentioned above. Magister. There are some who do not think heresy should be described in that way. They seem to rest on this argument: many false dogmas contrary to the orthodox faith become new heresies, although they did not begin only now to be false and contrary to the orthodox faith. Therefore, before they can be regarded as heresies, they are already false dogmas contrary to the orthodox faith. From this it is clearly concluded that not every false dogma contrary to the orthodox faith ought to be regarded as a heresy. The premise seems evident, because there are many new heresies, although they were earlier false dogmas contrary to the orthodox faith. For Pope Urban, as is found in 24. quaestion. 3. cap. notandum, says: Saint Augustine, together with the legates of the holy Roman church and with his holy bishops, excommunicated Pelagius and Celestius, who were introducing a new heresy into the holy church of God. From these words it is gathered that Pelagius and Celestius introduced into the church an opinion which was then a new heresy, and yet that opinion had earlier been contrary to the orthodox faith. Therefore that opinion or assertion, before it was a heresy, was a false dogma contrary to the orthodox faith, and so this description is not convertible with heresy. Hence Gratian, 24. quaest. 1. cap. 1. §. omni enim, says: Every heretic either follows a heresy already condemned, or fashions a new one. And the Gloss there says: But you, say without distinction whether he follows an old heresy (namely) or a new one, he is excommunicated, even if he is hidden. The Gloss also says: If I knew that my prelate was a heretic, because he fashions a new heresy, and yet did not preach it, and he excommunicated me, I would celebrate in secret. From these things it is plainly evident that there have been, and can be, new heresies which are nevertheless not new false dogmas contrary to the orthodox faith; and consequently not every falsehood contrary to the orthodox faith ought to be counted among the heresies.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: In quo dupliciter respondetur ad obiectionem factam capitulo precedenti.
units.tr: In which the objection raised in the preceding chapter is answered in two ways.

units.la: Discipul. His non obstantibus, diffinitio seu descriptio hæresis supra dicta congrua mihi videtur, qualiter igitur prædictis obiectionibus respondetur, indicare digneris. Magist. Qui prædictam diffinitionem vel descriptionem assignant, dupliciter tespondere conatur. Primo enim dicunt, quod aliqua hæresis dicitur nouiter esse noua, non quia in rei veritate incipiat hæresis esse nouiter: sed quia nouiter est asserta. Primo modo loquendi, quibus aliquæ veritates necesse dicuntur esse nouæ, non quando prius fuerint veritates, sed dicuntur nouæ, quia sunt nouiter publicatæ & dogmatizatæ. Etiam tali modo aliqui errores dicuntur esse noui, non quia prius fuerint in rei veritate errores, sed dicuntur noui, quia nouiter sunt asserti, & ille modus loquendi ex verbis Gelasii Papæ, vt habetur 24. q. 1. c. 1. colligitur euidenter, ait enim: Achatius non est factus inuentor noui erroris, sed veteris imitator, cui concordat Felix Papa in eisdem t. & c. & 9. c. Achatius, dicens: Achatius non fuit noui vel proprii inuentor erroris. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod si Achatius fuisset erroris assertor, fuisset reputatus noui erroris inuentor, & tamen idem error fuit antea error censendus. Multi enim errores, antequam asseratur ab aliquo, ab aliis non errantibus reprobantur, & per consequens antequam habeant assertorem vel defensorem, sunt errores censendi: & tamen secundum istum modum loquendi, si aliquis inciperet eos defendere, dicerentur noui errores, & simili modo loquendi, quidam Athenienses, vt habetur Act. 17. dicebant de beato Paulo: nouorum demoniorum videtur annunciator esse, appellantes nova demonia, non quia putabant, quod antea non fuissent dæmonia, sed quia putabant antiqua dæmonia à Paulo nouiter prædicari, & ita dicunt aliqui aliquas hæreses vocari nouas, propter nouitatem assertionis vel defensionis, qua aliquis eas nouiter asserit, vel defendit; quæ tamen prius in rei veritate fuerunt hæreses reputandæ. Aliter respondent prædictis (vt dicunt) minime obuiando, quod quemadmodum notatur in Glos. extra, de sum. trin. & fid. c. c. 1. fides aliter dicitur credulitas, secundum quam credimus, quod non videmus, & alio modo dicitur collectio articulorum fidei, licet etiam dicatur aliis sex modis, vt habetur ibidem, sic tam error, quam hæresis potest dupliciter dici, potest enim vno modo error dici actus vel habitus, quo quis errat, alio modo ipsum obiectum talis habitus vel actus primo modo errandi vocatur error, hæresis etiam potest accipi vno modo pro habitu vel pro actu hæresis, alio modo dicitur obiectum talis habitus vel actus primo modo accipiendo hæresim, & consimiliter errorem, multæ possunt esse nouæ hæreses & noui errores, quæ vel qui antea hæreses vel errores non fuerunt. Secundo modo accipiendo hæresim non dicuntur nouæ hæreses, nisi quia nouiter sunt assertæ, sicut dictum est in responsione priori: & consimiliter de multis erroribus potest dici, &c.
units.tr: Student. Notwithstanding these things, the definition or description of heresy given above seems suitable to me. Please deign to show how the aforesaid objections are answered. Master. Those who assign the aforesaid definition or description try to answer in two ways. For first they say that a heresy is called newly new, not because heresy in the reality of the matter begins to exist newly, but because it has newly been asserted. In the first way of speaking, some truths are necessarily called new, not when they were previously truths, but they are called new because they have newly been published and taught as doctrine. In this same way some errors are also called new, not because they were previously errors in the reality of the matter, but they are called new because they have newly been asserted. This way of speaking is clearly gathered from the words of Pope Gelasius, as found in 24 q. 1 c. 1: "Achatius was not made the inventor of a new error, but an imitator of an old one." Pope Felix agrees with this in the same title and in c. 9, Achatius, saying: "Achatius was not the inventor of a new or his own error." From these words it is given to understand that if Achatius had been an asserter of the error, he would have been regarded as the inventor of a new error, and yet the same error would previously have been considered an error. For many errors, before they are asserted by someone, are rejected by others who are not in error, and consequently, before they have an asserter or defender, they are to be considered errors. And yet, according to this way of speaking, if someone began to defend them, they would be called new errors.
