In the same way of speaking, certain Athenians, as is found in Acts 17, said of the blessed Paul: "He seems to be a proclaimer of new demons," calling them "new demons," not because they thought that demons had not existed before, but because they thought that Paul was newly preaching ancient demons. And so some say that certain heresies are called new on account of the novelty of the assertion or defence by which someone newly asserts or defends them, though in the reality of the matter they were previously to be reckoned heresies. Others answer the aforesaid objections (as they say) by a different means, namely, that just as it is noted in the Gloss on Extra, De summa Trinitate et fide, c. 1, that faith is called in one way credulity, by which we believe what we do not see, and in another way the collection of the articles of faith (and it is also called in six other ways, as is found there), so both error and heresy can be called in two ways. For error can be called in one way the act or habit by which someone errs, and in another way the very object of such a habit or act. Taking error in the first way is called error; heresy also can be taken in one way for the habit or act of heresy, and in another way it is called the object of such a habit or act. Taking heresy in the first way, and likewise error, many new heresies and new errors can exist which previously were not heresies or errors. Taking heresy in the second way, they are not called new heresies, except because they have newly been asserted, as was said in the earlier answer. And likewise it can be said of many errors, etc.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: In quo iterum obiicitur contra descriptionem hæresis ex dicto Hieronymi.
units.tr: In which a further objection is raised against the description of heresy taken from the saying of Jerome.

units.la: Discipulus. Vt mihi videtur, pertractata difficultas de hæresibus nouis magis est vocalis quam realis & ideo circa ipsam non amplius immoreris: sed an aliter obiiciatur contra descriptionem hæresis supra dictam noli celare. Magist. Per verba beati Hieronymi, quæ pronuntur 24. q. 3. cap. hæresis, dicta hæresis descriptio improbari videtur, ait enim: hæresis autem Græce ab electione dicitur, quod scilicet eam vnusquisque eligat disciplinam, quam putat esse meliorem. Ex quibus verbis duo dantur intelligi, primum est, quod ex quo hæresis ab electione dicitur, nullum falsum (tanquam ipsum elegerit dogmatizare vel opinari aut asserere) debet inter hæreses computari, secundum est, quod cum non solum infideles, sed etiam catholici & fideles eligant disciplinam, quam putant meliorem non solum assertiones infidelium, sed etiam assertiones catholicorum & fidelium debent hæreses ses appellari, & ex utroque istorum concluditur, quod descriptio haeresis saepe dicta est incongrue assignata, &c.
units.tr: The Pupil. As it seems to me, the difficulty about new heresies, which has now been treated, is more a matter of words than of substance, and so you need not dwell on it any longer; but do not hide from me whether the description of heresy given above is open to objection in some other way. The Teacher. From the words of blessed Jerome, which are cited in 24. q. 3. cap. hæresis, the description of heresy just given seems to be disapproved. For he says: Heresy is called in Greek from choice, because each person chooses for himself the teaching which he thinks to be better. From these words two things seem to follow. The first is that, since heresy is so called from choice, no falsehood should be counted among heresies on the ground that someone has chosen to teach, hold or assert it. The second is that, since not only unbelievers but also Catholics and believers choose the teaching which they think better, not only the assertions of unbelievers but also the assertions of Catholics and believers ought to be called heresies. From both of these it follows that the description of heresy often given has been assigned improperly, etc.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad dictum Hieronymi, ubi etiam ostenditur, quod non omnis electio doctrinae falsae, & ecclesia catholica contrariae debet haeresis reputari, & quod assertiones infidelium non sunt haereses.
units.tr: In which an answer is given to the saying of Jerome, where it is also shown that not every choice of a false doctrine contrary to the Catholic Church must be counted as heresy, and that the assertions of unbelievers are not heresies.

units.la: Discipul. Ista obiectio mihi fortis videtur, sed qualiter respondeatur ad ipsam, non differas explicare. Magist. Dicunt illi, quod verba sanctorum sane intelligenda sunt, quorum intellectus saepe ex diversis eorum dictis accipi debent, & ideo non semper intelligenda sunt sicut in superficie sonant, & ideo dicunt, quod licet praedicta verba B. Hieron. prima facie videantur praetendere, quod ante electionem actualem nullum falsum debeat haeresis appellari, & quod omnis disciplina, quam quis putat meliorem, sive sit vera sive falsa, possit ad haeresim pertinere, non tamen sic intelligit Hieronymus. Nam Hieronymus scribens praedicta verba super epist. ad Galat. inter schisma & haeresim hoc interesse arbitratur, quod haeresis peruersum dogma habet: schisma post principalem dissensionem ab ecclesia pariter separat, & parum post: caeterum nullum est schisma, nisi sibi aliquam haeresim confingat, ut recte ab ecclesia recessisse videatur. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod secundum B. Hieronymum haeresis sine peruerso dogmate contrario ecclesiae doctrinae minime invenitur. Quare verba Hieron. cum dicitur, haeresis autem Graece ab electione dicitur, &c. de electione non cuiuscunque; disciplinae falsae, sed contrariae ecclesiae disciplinae debet intelligi, & non debet intelligi de electione actuali, sed etiam magis potentiali, qua aliquis potest disciplinam falsam contrariam disciplinae ecclesiae eligere, quam putat meliorem.
units.tr: Student. That objection seems strong to me, but do not delay in explaining how it is to be answered. Teacher. They say that the words of the saints must be understood soundly, and that their meaning must often be gathered from their various statements, so that they are not always to be taken as they sound on the surface. They therefore say that although the words of St. Jerome seem at first sight to maintain that before an actual choice no false teaching should be called heresy, and that any discipline which someone thinks better, whether true or false, can belong to heresy, Jerome does not mean it in that way. For Jerome, writing those words on the Epistle to the Galatians, judges that the difference between schism and heresy is this: heresy has a perverse dogma; schism, after a principal dissension, separates equally from the Church; and shortly after: but there is no schism unless it fashions for itself some heresy, so that it may seem rightly to have withdrawn from the Church. From these words it is clear that, according to St. Jerome, heresy is hardly found without a perverse dogma contrary to the teaching of the Church. Therefore, when Jerome says now heresy is so called from choosing, etc., the choice must be understood not of any false discipline whatever, but of a discipline contrary to the discipline of the Church; and it must be understood not of actual choice only, but even more of potential choice, by which someone can choose a false discipline contrary to the discipline of the Church, which he thinks better.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: In quo inquiritur, utrum omnes assertiones, quae quomodolibet sacrae Scripturae adversantur, sint inter haereses computanda, & respondetur secundum unam opinionem, qua- e etiam probatur duabus rationibus, ad quas respondetur cap. 13.
units.tr: In which it is inquired whether all assertions that in any way oppose holy Scripture are to be counted among heresies, and it is answered according to one opinion, which is also supported by two arguments, to which an answer is given in chapter 13.

units.la: Discipul. Video quod verba Hieronymi sic intellecta praedictae descriptioni haeresis non repugnant. Ex qua sequi videtur, quod omnes assertiones, quae Scripturae sacrae quomodolibet adversantur, sunt inter haereses computandae, sed an omnes Christiani hoc sentiant & affirmer ignoro, quare si aliqui hoc non sentiunt, enarra. Magist. Fuerunt Manichaei, qui Vetus Testam. minime receperunt: aliqui etiam haeretici multa in Novo Testamento respuerunt. Discipul. Illi, de quibus nunc loqueris, fuerunt ab ecclesia haeretici condemnati, de quibus non curo: sed libenter cognoscerem, an sint aliqui catholici vel alii ab ecclesia nullatenus condemnati, qui non reputent omnes assertiones haereticas, quae sacrae Scripturae quomodolibet adversantur. Magist. Sunt quidam moderni dicentes, quod multae assertiones sunt, qui in rei veritate adversantur divinae Scripturae, quae tamen ab ecclesia minime sunt damnandae, nec sunt inter haereses numerandae, quemadmodum multae sunt veritates consonae Scripturae divinae (quae tamen non sunt per ecclesiam definitae vel determinatae) non sunt inter veritates catholicas computandae, sed postquam assertiones divinae Scripturae contrariae sunt & fuerunt per summum Pontificem condemnatae, pro haeresibus sunt habendae: & veritates consonae sacrae Scripturae, postquam fuerunt per summum Pontificem definitae seu determinatae catholicae sunt censendae, propter quod dicunt, quod Papa potest facere novum articulum fidei, & eadem ratione potest facere, quod eadem assertio quae prius non erat haeretica, postea per condemnationem esse haeretica incipiat. Discip. Haec opinio multis prioribus assertionibus, quae videbatur mihi probabiles, apparet omnino repugnans, ideo si rationibus vel auctoritatib. satagat se defendere declara. Magist. Ut audio in duobus praedictis se fundant. Primo in cap. Alexandri Tertii, extra, de haereticis, cum Christus, videlicet, ut dicunt facit novum articulum, scil. Christus est Deus & homo, quia ante tempora Alexandri praedicti licebat (ut dicunt) non credere Christum esse Deum & hominem. Secundo fundant se in constitutione Domini Innoc. cum inter nonnullos, in qua definitur deinceps, esse haereticum dicere, Christum & eius Apostolos non habuisse aliquid nec in speciali, nec in communi & per consequens antea non fuit haereticum. Ex quibus sequitur, quod Papa potest novos articulos fidei facere, & potest facere quod assertiones quae non fuerunt haereticae, esse haereticae de novo incipiant. Discip. Exemplum adductum de constitutione Patris sanctissimi domini Innoc. XXII. Papae peto quod nullatenus hic pertractes, quia ut dixi, postea de tota doctrina eiusdem summi Patris tibi quaestiones moebo: sed si, quaestione praedicta vel opinione aliquas rationes cogitasti, profer easdem. Mag. Opinio memorata potest aliter muniri. Primo sic, pro assertione haeresis est quis tanquam haereticus condemnandus, sed multae fuerunt assertiones falsae, de quibus assertores earum (tanquam fuerint ab ecclesia condemnatae) non fuerunt tanquam haeretici condemnandi, sed postquam dictae assertiones fuerunt ab ecclesia condemnatae, fuerunt assertores earum tanquam haeretici condemnandi, ergo tales assertiones ante condemnationem ecclesiae non fuerunt inter haereses computandae; qui tamen post condemnationem pro haerehæresibus fuerunt habendæ: & per consequens eadem assertio, quæ primo non est hæresis, per damnationem ecclesiæ cum hæresibus numeratur: quare eadem ratione, eadem assertio quæ primo non est catholica, postea per approbationem ecclesiæ fit catholica. Huiusmodi autem approbatio & damnatio spectat ad summum Pontificem, ergo summus Pontifex de assertione non catholica potest facere catholicam, de assertione non hæretica potest facere hæreticam: & ita novum articulum fidei facere potest, maior huius rationis est manifesta. Minor exemplis probatur aperte, nam Græci negantes Spiritum sanctum procedere à Filio, ante damnationem assertionis eorum non fuerunt hæretici reputati: qui tamen post damnationem eiusdem inter hæreticos deputantur, assertores etiam opinionis Ioachim à concilio generali damnatæ post damnationé hæretici iudicátur: ipse tamen Abbas Ioachim, quamuis ante damnationem & assertionem eandem tenuerit, non tamen fuit hæreticus, ut habetur ext. de sum. tri. & fid. c. cath. damnamus. Similiter quæ post constitutionem Alexandri III. quę habetur extra de hære. cum Christus, tenuerunt, quod Christus non est aliquid secundum quod homo, sunt hæretici iudicandi, secundum quod Glossa notat ibidem, qui tamen antea pro hæreticis minime habebātur. Patet ergo, quod pro nonnullis assertionibus non sunt assertores ante damnationem hæretici reputandi, qui tamen post damnationem inter hæreticos computantur. Secundo sic. Ille, ad quem pertinet authentice diffinire, quę assertio catholica, & quæ hæretica est censenda; de assertione non catholica, catholicam; & de assertione non hæretica, hæreticam facere potest, quia aliter diffinitio sua nihil videretur penitus operari, plus quam diffinitio vel determinatio doctorum, qui per auctoritates vel rationes declarant & probant, quæ assertio in rei veritate est catholica, & quæ hæretica æstimanda: sed ad summum Pontificem non solum per modum docentis vel doctrinæ: sed etiam auctoritate pertinet diffinire, quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica est censenda, ergo summus Pontifex de non catholica catholicam, & de assertione non hæretica hæreticam facere potest, &c.
units.tr: Pupil. I see that Jerome's words, understood in this way, do not conflict with the description of heresy given above. From this it seems to follow that all assertions that in any way oppose holy Scripture are to be counted among heresies. But I do not know whether all Christians think so and maintain it. So if some do not, please tell me. Master. There were the Manichaeans, who did not accept the Old Testament at all, and some other heretics who rejected much of the New Testament. Pupil. I am not concerned with those you now speak of, since they were condemned as heretics by the Church. I would gladly learn whether there are some Catholics, or others not condemned by the Church in any way, who do not regard all assertions that in any way oppose holy Scripture as heretical. Master. There are some modern writers who say that there are many assertions which in truth do oppose divine Scripture, yet are by no means to be condemned by the Church nor numbered among heresies. Just as there are many truths consonant with divine Scripture (which nonetheless have not been defined or determined by the Church) that are not counted among Catholic truths, so, once assertions contrary to divine Scripture have been condemned by the supreme Pontiff, they are to be held as heresies; and truths consonant with holy Scripture, once they have been defined or determined by the supreme Pontiff, are to be regarded as Catholic. For this reason they say that the Pope can make a new article of faith, and by the same reasoning he can make it so that an assertion which was not heretical before begins, through condemnation, to be heretical. Pupil. This opinion appears altogether to conflict with many earlier assertions which seemed to me probable. So, if you are going to defend it by reasons or authorities, explain them. Master. As I hear, they rest on two points. First, on the chapter of Alexander III, Extra, De haereticis, Cum Christus, namely that, as they say, he makes a new article: that Christ is God and man, because before the time of that Alexander it was (as they say) lawful not to believe that Christ is God and man. Second, they rely on the constitution of our lord Innocent, Cum inter nonnullos, in which it is defined from then on that it is heretical to say that Christ and his Apostles had nothing, neither individually nor in common; and consequently it was not heretical before. From these it follows that the Pope can make new articles of faith, and can make it so that assertions which were not heretical begin to be heretical anew. Pupil. I ask that you do not deal with the example adduced from the constitution of the most holy Father, our lord Innocent XXII, here, because, as I said, I will afterwards put questions to you about the whole teaching of that same supreme Father. But if you have thought of any reasons for the question or the opinion just mentioned, set them out. Master. The opinion mentioned can be supported in another way. First thus: a person who is to be condemned as a heretic on account of an assertion of heresy; yet many false assertions have existed, of which their asserters (even though those assertions had been condemned by the Church) were not to be condemned as heretics; but once those assertions were condemned by the Church, their asserters were to be condemned as heretics. Therefore such assertions were not counted among heresies before the condemnation of the Church; yet after the condemnation they were to be held as heresies, and consequently the same assertion, which at first is not a heresy, is by the condemnation of the Church numbered among heresies. Wherefore, by the same reasoning, the same assertion which at first is not Catholic becomes Catholic afterwards through the approval of the Church. Now such approval and condemnation belong to the supreme Pontiff. Therefore the supreme Pontiff can make a Catholic assertion out of a non-Catholic one, and a heretical one out of a non-heretical one; and so he can make a new article of faith. The major premise of this argument is manifest. The minor is clearly proved by examples. For the Greeks who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son were not regarded as heretics before their assertion was condemned; yet after its condemnation they are reckoned among heretics. The asserters of the opinion of Joachim, condemned by a general council, are likewise judged heretics after the condemnation; yet Abbot Joachim himself, although he held the same assertion before its condemnation, was not a heretic, as is found in Extra, De summa Trinitate et fide catholica, Damnamus. Similarly, those who after the constitution of Alexander III, found in Extra, De haereticis, Cum Christus, held that Christ is not something in so far as he is man, are to be judged heretics, as the Gloss notes in that place; yet before this they were by no means regarded as heretics. It is therefore plain that for some assertions the asserters are not to be condemned as heretics before the condemnation, yet after the condemnation they are counted among heretics. Secondly thus: he to whom it belongs authoritatively to define which assertion is to be held Catholic and which heretical, can make a Catholic assertion out of a non-Catholic one, and a heretical one out of a non-heretical one; for otherwise his definition would seem to accomplish nothing at all beyond the definition or determination of teachers, who by authorities or reasons declare and prove which assertion is in truth Catholic and which is to be judged heretical. But it belongs to the supreme Pontiff not only by way of teaching or doctrine, but also by authority, to define which assertion is to be considered Catholic and which heretical. Therefore the supreme Pontiff can make a Catholic assertion out of a non-Catholic one, and a heretical one out of a non-heretical one, etc.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: In quo ponitur opinio contraria opinioni precedenti, quæ probatur quatuor rationibus, vbi ostendit, quod veritates fidei sunt immutabiles & immutabiliter catholicæ.
units.tr: In which the opinion contrary to the preceding one is set out and proved by four arguments, showing that the truths of faith are unchangeable and unchangeably catholic.

units.la: Discip. Iste duæ rationes apparentiam habere videtur: tñ conclusio est mihi difficilis ad tenendum, unde si aliqui asserant contrarium, tibi placeat explicare. Mag. Sunt multi dicentes, quod sicut quantum ad ea, quę spectant ad fidem nostram, & nequaquam ex voluntate humana dependent, non potest summus Pontifex, nec etiam tota ecclesia Dei de assertione non vera facere veram: nec de assertione non falsa facere falsam, ita non potest de assertione non catholica facere catholicam: nec de assertione non hæretica facere hæreticam, & ideo non potest novum articulum fidei facere, nec de hæresi potest facere hæresim quocunq; modo, quia sicut veritates catholicæ absq; omni approbatione ecclesiæ ex natura sunt immutabiles & immutabiliter verę: ita immutabiliter sunt catholicæ reputandæ, & consimiliter sicut hæreses absque omni damnatione ecclesiæ sunt falsæ: ita absq; omni damnatione ecclesiæ sunt hæreses. Discip. Cum ista sententia magis me alliciat, ideo si potest rationibus confirmari, eas non differas allegare. Mag. Ista sententia rationibus paucis ostenditur, quarū prima est hæc, Si aliqua veritas est catholica: aut est dicēda catholica, quia à Deo revelata: vel quia in scripturis diuinis contenta: vel quia ab vniuersali ecclesia recepta, vel sequitur ex illis vel aliquo illorum, quæ sunt diuinitus reuelata, & in scripturis diuinis inuenta; & ab ecclesia vniuersali recepta, vel quia à summo Pontifice approbata. Si aliqua veritas ideo est catholica, quia est à Deo revelata: & revelatio diuina nullatenus dependet à summo Pontifice approbatiue, nec ex approbatione totius ecclesiæ, ergo approbatio summi Pontificis nihil facit ad hoc, quod talis veritas sit vere catholica. Si detur secundū sc. quod aliqua veritas est catholica: quia in scripturis diuinis inserta, & constat quod talem veritatem inseri in scripturis diuinis ex nulla approbatione ecclesiæ vel Papæ dependet, ergo talis veritas absq; omni approbatione tali est inter veritates catholicas numeranda. Si detur tertium, sc. quod aliqua veritas est catholica, quia in scripturis diuinis inserta, & ab ecclesia vniuersali acceptata vel recepta, quęrendum est, quare ecclesia vniuersalis talem recepit veritatem? vel quia sic diuinitus approbatur, revelatur vel inspiratur, & tūc absq; tali receptione ecclesiæ vere est catholica, quia diuinitus inspiratur, vel etiam revelatur, aut eā recipit vniuersalis ecclesia: quia eam in diuinis scripturis inuenit, & tūc absq; tali receptione adhuc est catholica iudicanda, aut eā recipit vniuersalis ecclesia, quia per experientiā vel rationem naturalē eam cognoscit, quod de multis veritatib. catholicis nullatenus dici potest: & tunc ecclesia in faciendo etiā veritatem aliam catholicā rationi vel experientię innitur vel niteretur, q dici non potest, sequeretur n. quod ecclesia vniuersalis omnem veritatē geometricam, & oēs alias quarumcunq; scientiarū demōstrationes probatas posset veritatib. catholicis aggregare. Ex quib. sequeretur, q omnes assertiones falsas huiusmodi veritatib. naturaliter notis contrarias posset ecclesia vniuersalis inter hæreses cōputare, & omnē assertorē cuiuscūq; assertionis falsæ & veritati naturaliter notæ contrariæ tanq; hæreticum condemnare: q est inconueniens reputandū, aut talem veritatem recepit vniuersalis ecclesia, quia sibi placet, quod dici non potest, quia tunc ecclesia vniuersalis in recipiendo aliquā veritate & faciendo ipsā catholicā inniteretur solūmodo humanæ volūtati; & ita fides nostra esset in voluntate hominum. Cum tamen asserat Apostolus, q; fides nostra non est in sapientia hominū 1.ad Cor. 2. & multo fortius non est in voluntate hominū. Ecclesia ergo vniuersalis nullā recipit veritatem tanq; catholicā, nisi quia diuinitus reuelatur, & quia in sacris literis inuenitur talis veritas: etiam si nulla esset ecclesia, vere esset catholica. Si detur quartum, sc. quod aliqua veritas catholica, quia sequitur ex illis vel aliquo illorum, quæ sunt diuinitus reuelata & in scripturis diuinis inserta, & ab ecclesia vniuersali recepta, palam est quod propter approbationē ecclesiæ nō magis potest ab eis inferri, ergo per talem approbationem non sit catholica. Si detur quintum sc. quod ideo aliqua veritas est catholica, quia à summo Pontifice est approbata, tunc quærendum est, an summus Pontifex approbando aliq; veritatem innititur alicui reuelationi vel etiam Scripturis sacris aut doctrinæ ecclesiæ vniuersalis, quodcunq; istorum detur, sequitur, q; summus Pontifex p approbationem suam non facit talem veritatem fuisse & esse catholicam, q; determinat & diffinit, vel summus Pontifex approbando aliquā veritatem propriæ prudentiæ vel voluntati innititur, & si hoc datur, sequitur quod propter talem approbationem summi Pontificis non est aliqua veritas pro catholica accipiēda, quia fides nostra nec in sapientia, nec in voluntate hominis potest consistere, patet ergo, quod nulla veritas est catholica, nisi quia diuinitus reuelata, vel quia in scripturis diuinis inserta, vel quia p certitudinem ecclesiæ vniuersali, innotuit, vel ex aliquo illorum necessario argumento concluditur. Nihil autem prædictorum ex approbatione summi Pontificis vel etiam ecclesiæ noscitur dependere. Ergo per approbationem talem nulla veritas catholica potest fieri: sed per talem approbationem aliquā veritate fuisse & esse catholicam dinoscitur & diffinitur. Et ita summus Pontifex non facit aliquam veritatem esse catholicam vel assertionem: sed p approbationem suam determinat & diffinit veritates & assertiones, quas approbat, esse & fuisse catholicas: per condemnationem suam determinat & diffinit assertiones, quas reprobat, fuisse & esse hæreticas, & ita non facit nouum articulum fidei: sed nouiter diffinit aliquem articulum pertinere & non pertinuisse ad catholicam veritatem, & ita quamuis talis veritas nouiter diffiniatur esse catholica, ea prius tamen fuit catholica. Secunda ratio est hæc, si aliqua veritas est catholica, quia est à Romano Pontifice solummodo approbata: aut ergo est catholica, quia est à Romano Pontifice implicite, siue explicite approbata: aut est tantummodo catholica, quia est à Romano Pontifice explicite approbata. Si detur primum, sequitur quod Romanus Pontifex non potest facere nouum articulum fidei de aliqua veritate, quæ ante necessaria existebat, quia omnes veritates diuinitus reuelatæ in Scripturis sacris insertæ, & quas ecclesia vniuersalis recipit, & quæ sequuntur ex aliqua vel ex aliquibus prædictarum, fuerunt ante implicite vel explicite per Romanos Pontifices approbatæ. Ipsi enim totam fidem ecclesiæ approbauerunt, & per consequens approbauerunt ea, quæ sequuntur; quia sicut qui vnum dicit, dicit & ea quæ sequuntur ex illo: ita qui vnum approbat, approbat omnia quæ sequuntur ex illo. Si autem detur secundum, scilicet quod omnino aliqua veritas solummodo dicitur catholica, quia est à Romano Pontifice explicite approbata: ergo tales veritates, Christus mortuos suscitauit, Christus fuit Deus & homo, Deus omnia præsciuit, & huiusmodi, non essent catholicæ reputandæ, nisi essent à Romano Pontifice explicite approbatæ, quod pro inconuenienti videtur hic habendum. Per illas itaq; rationes ostenditur, quod summus Pontifex non potest facere nouum articulum fidei, nec de veritate non catholica potest facere catholicam. Ex quo concludunt isti, q; de assertione non hæretica Romanus Pontifex non potest facere hæreticam: quia omni assertioni catholicæ contradicit assertio hæretica, & econuerso, quia sicut si vna condicionariarum est falsa, & econuerso, ita si vna condicionariarum est catholica, altera est hæretica, sed, sicut probatum est, Romanus Pontifex non potest de veritate non catholica facere catholicam, igitur nec de assertione hæretica potest facere non hæreticam. Tertia ratio est ista si ideo solummodo aliqua assertio est inter hæreses computanda, quia est à Romano Pontifice vel ab ecclesia condemnata: aut ergo quia condemnata siue explicite siue implicite, aut solummodo, quia damnata explicite. Si detur primum, sequitur quod omnis assertio, quæ potest licite damnari, est modo hæresis: quia omnis talis est iam per ecclesiā & Romanos Pontifices (qui totam fidem approbando omnem infidelitatem contrariam damnauerunt) explicite vel implicite condemnata. Si detur secundum, id est quod aliqua assertio non ideo solummodo est hæretica; quia explicite condemnata: ergo ista assertio, Christus non est homo, non erat hæretica, tanquam esset per ecclesiam reprobata: quod isti pro maximo inconuenienti habent. Quarta ratio, quæ eis demonstratiua videtur, est hæc: omnis assertio, cuius pertinax defensator est vere hæreticus, est vere hæresis: sed oēs pertinaces defensores assertionum, quæ possunt per ecclesiā rite & legitime tanquam hæreses condemnari, sunt vere hæretici, licet eorum assertiones non sint de facto explicite & sub propria forma ab ecclesia condemnatæ, ergo tales assertiones vel damnationes huiusmodi vere sunt inter hæreses numerandæ. Maior est manifesta: quia nemo est hæreticus, nisi propter hæresim, cui adhæret, minor auctoritate August. probatur, qui vt habetur 24. q.3.c. dixit Apostolus. & c.q.in ecclesia, asserit manifeste: quod qui suam sententiam falsam atque peruersam, & qui morbidum aliquid & prauum sapiunt & corrigi nolunt, sunt haeretici, sed omnis assertio, quæ potest per ecclesiam rite damnari, est falsa, morbida, peruersa, & praua, ergo omnis pertinax defensor talis assertionis, licet non sit de facto explicite per ecclesiam condemnata, est vere haereticus. Ex his concludunt isti, quod ecclesia non potest de assertione non haeretica facere haereticam: sed ecclesia aliquam haeresim condemnando determinat ac diffinit eam fuisse & esse haereticam.
units.tr: Disciple. These two arguments seem to have some force, but the conclusion is hard for me to accept, so if some people maintain the contrary, please explain it to me. Master. There are many who say that, just as the Supreme Pontiff, and indeed the whole Church of God, cannot make an assertion that is not true into a true one, or an assertion that is not false into a false one, with respect to the things that concern our faith and do not depend in any way on human will, so too he cannot make an assertion that is not catholic into a catholic one, or an assertion that is not heretical into a heretical one. For this reason he cannot make a new article of faith, nor can he make a heresy out of what is not a heresy in any way at all. For just as catholic truths are unchangeable by nature and unchangeably true without any approval of the Church, so they must be reckoned unchangeably catholic; and likewise, just as heresies are false without any condemnation by the Church, so they are heresies without any condemnation by the Church. Disciple. Since this view appeals to me more, if it can be confirmed by reasons, please do not delay in setting them out. Master. This view is shown by a few reasons, of which the first is this. If some truth is catholic, it must be said to be catholic either because it has been revealed by God, or because it is contained in the divine Scriptures, or because it has been received by the universal Church, or because it follows from those things, or from one of them, which have been divinely revealed and found in the divine Scriptures and received by the universal Church, or because it has been approved by the Supreme Pontiff. Now, if some truth is catholic because it has been revealed by God, and divine revelation in no way depends on the Supreme Pontiff's approval or on the approval of the whole Church, then the approval of the Supreme Pontiff contributes nothing to making such a truth truly catholic. Suppose, secondly, that some truth is catholic because it is inserted in the divine Scriptures; it is plain that the insertion of such a truth in the divine Scriptures depends on no approval of the Church or of the Pope; therefore such a truth, without any such approval, must be counted among the catholic truths. Suppose, thirdly, that some truth is catholic because it is inserted in the divine Scriptures and has been accepted or received by the universal Church. Then we must ask why the universal Church received that truth. Either it is because it has been thus divinely approved, revealed or inspired, and then it is truly catholic without that reception by the Church, since it is divinely inspired or revealed; or the universal Church receives it because it finds it in the divine Scriptures, and then it must still be judged catholic without such reception; or the universal Church receives it because it knows it through experience or natural reason, which cannot be said of many catholic truths at all; and then the Church, in making some other truth catholic, would rest, or would have to rest, on reason or experience, which cannot be said. For it would follow that the universal Church could add to the catholic truths every geometrical truth and all the proven demonstrations of any other sciences. From this it would follow that the universal Church could reckon among the heresies all false assertions contrary to truths naturally known, and condemn as a heretic every author of any false assertion contrary to a truth naturally known; which is to be regarded as absurd. Or else the universal Church received that truth because it pleased her, which cannot be said, since then the universal Church, in receiving some truth and making it catholic, would rest merely on human will, and so our faith would lie in the will of men. Yet the Apostle affirms that our faith does not rest in the wisdom of men (1 Cor. 2.), and much less in the will of men. Therefore the universal Church receives no truth as catholic except because it is divinely revealed and because such a truth is found in the sacred writings; even if there were no Church, it would truly be catholic. Suppose, fourthly, that some catholic truth follows from those things, or from one of them, which are divinely revealed, inserted in the divine Scriptures and received by the universal Church. It is plain that it cannot be inferred from them any the more because of the Church's approval; therefore it is not made catholic by such approval. Suppose, fifthly, that some truth is catholic because it has been approved by the Supreme Pontiff. Then we must ask whether the Supreme Pontiff, in approving some truth, rests on some revelation, or on the holy Scriptures, or on the teaching of the universal Church. Whichever of these is granted, it follows that the Supreme Pontiff by his approval does not make such a truth to have been and to be catholic, since he determines and defines it. Or else the Supreme Pontiff, in approving some truth, rests on his own prudence or will; and if this is granted, it follows that because of such approval of the Supreme Pontiff no truth is to be taken as catholic, since our faith can rest neither in the wisdom nor in the will of man. It is therefore evident that no truth is catholic except because it is divinely revealed, or because it is inserted in the divine Scriptures, or because it has become known to the universal Church by its certainty, or because it is concluded by necessary argument from one of these. But none of the things mentioned is known to depend on the approval of the Supreme Pontiff or even of the Church. Therefore no catholic truth can be made by such approval; but by such approval a truth is known and defined to have been and to be catholic. And so the Supreme Pontiff does not make any truth or assertion to be catholic; rather, by his approval he determines and defines that the truths and assertions he approves are and have been catholic, and by his condemnation he determines and defines that the assertions he rejects have been and are heretical. Thus he does not make a new article of faith; he newly defines that some article belongs, or did not belong, to catholic truth; and so, although such a truth is newly defined to be catholic, it nevertheless was catholic before. The second reason is this. If some truth is catholic because it has been approved only by the Roman Pontiff, then either it is catholic because it has been approved by the Roman Pontiff implicitly or explicitly, or it is catholic only because it has been approved by the Roman Pontiff explicitly. Suppose the first: it follows that the Roman Pontiff cannot make a new article of faith out of some truth which previously was necessary, since all the truths divinely revealed, inserted in the holy Scriptures, received by the universal Church, and following from any or all of the aforesaid, were previously approved implicitly or explicitly by the Roman Pontiffs. For they approved the whole faith of the Church, and consequently they approved the things that follow from it; for just as whoever says one thing also says what follows from it, so whoever approves one thing approves all that follows from it. But suppose the second, namely that some truth is called catholic solely because it has been explicitly approved by the Roman Pontiff. Then such truths as "Christ raised the dead," "Christ was God and man," "God foreknew all things," and the like, would not have to be reckoned catholic unless they had been explicitly approved by the Roman Pontiff; which seems to be an absurdity that must be avoided here. By these reasons, then, it is shown that the Supreme Pontiff cannot make a new article of faith, nor can he make a non-catholic truth into a catholic one. From this these men conclude that the Roman Pontiff cannot make a non-heretical assertion into a heretical one. For every catholic assertion is contradicted by a heretical assertion, and conversely; just as if one of two contradictory propositions is false, the other is true, so if one of two contradictory propositions is catholic, the other is heretical. But, as has been proved, the Roman Pontiff cannot make a non-catholic truth into a catholic one; therefore he cannot make a heretical assertion into a non-heretical one. The third reason is this. If an assertion is to be reckoned among the heresies only because it has been condemned by the Roman Pontiff or by the Church, then either it is because it has been condemned either explicitly or implicitly, or only because it has been condemned explicitly. Suppose the first: it follows that every assertion that can lawfully be condemned is now a heresy, since every such assertion has already been condemned explicitly or implicitly by the Church and the Roman Pontiffs, who, by approving the whole faith, condemned every contrary unbelief. Suppose the second, that some assertion is not heretical solely because it has been explicitly condemned; then the assertion "Christ is not man" was not heretical as if it had been rejected by the Church; which these men regard as a very great absurdity. The fourth reason, which seems to them demonstrative, is this. Every assertion whose stubborn defender is truly a heretic is truly a heresy. But all the stubborn defenders of assertions that can be rightly and lawfully condemned by the Church as heresies are truly heretics, even though their assertions have not in fact been explicitly condemned by the Church under their own form. Therefore such assertions, or such condemnations, are truly to be numbered among the heresies. The major premise is manifest, since no one is a heretic except on account of the heresy to which he adheres. The minor is proved by the authority of Augustine, who, as is found in the Decretum (24, q. 3, c. "dixit Apostolus," and c. q. "in ecclesia"), clearly asserts that those who hold their false and perverse opinion, who think something morbid and depraved and are unwilling to be corrected, are heretics. But every assertion that can be rightly condemned by the Church is false, morbid, perverse and depraved. Therefore every stubborn defender of such an assertion, even if it has not in fact been explicitly condemned by the Church, is truly a heretic. From these things these men conclude that the Church cannot make a non-heretical assertion into a heretical one; but by condemning a heresy the Church determines and defines that it has been and is heretical.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: In quo ponuntur solutiones rationum capitulo undecimo adductarum.
units.tr: In which are set out the solutions to the arguments adduced in chapter eleven.

units.la: Discipulus. Istæ assertiones ultimæ apparent mihi fortes: & tamen rationes pro prima sententia videtur difficiles, & ideo refer quomodo respondetur ad ipsas. Magist. Ad primam illarum respondent istius secundæ sententiæ assertores, dicentes, quod sicut sæpe aliquis est hæreticus, & tamen quia est tantummodo occultus hæreticus, non debet tanquam hæreticus iudicari, ita sæpe est aliquis hæreticus, quia hæresi pertinaciter adhæret: & tamen quia non est certum explicite, quod assertio sua est & fuit hæretica, tanquam explicite innotuerit ecclesiæ, quod assertio sua fuerit & est hæretica, nō debet tanquam hæreticus condemnari. Postquam autem aliquis per diligentem considerationem innotuerit ecclesiæ, quod assertio sua est hæretica, si talis pertinax inuenitur, debet tanquam hæreticus condemnari. Disc. Ista responsio videtur mihi apparēs; nisi quod dubito, de qua ecclesia isti loquuntur. Mag. Ipsi loquuntur de ecclesia, quæ est concilium generale vel Papa: quia non sufficit in hoc casu ad damnationem alicuius, quod innotescat alicui alteri, quam concilio generali vel Papæ, quod talis assertio fuerit hæretica. Disc. Dic quomodo respondet ad exempla de Græcis, Ioachim, & illorum qui dixerunt Christum non esse aliquid secundum quod homo. Magist. Dicunt quod assertiones istæ antea fuerint hæreticæ; pertinaces etiam assertores earum fuerunt hæretici: quia tamen antea nō innotuerat ecclesiæ, quod eorum assertiones fuerunt hæreticæ, non debuerunt tanquam hæretici condemnari, sed postea debuerunt damnari sicut hæretici. Disc. Intelligo responsionem eorū ad rationem illam, dicas ergo, quomodo respondent ad secundā. Mag. Respondent quod licet ad summum Pontificem non solum per modum doctrinæ, sed etiam autentice pertineat diffinire, quæ assertio catholica, quæ hæretica est censenda: non tamen potest facere de veritate non catholica veritatem catholicam, nec de assertione non hæretica hæreticam valet efficere, quo tamen non obstante diffinitio sua plus operatur, quam determinatio Doctoris: quia post determinationem Doctoris licet cuiuslibet (sicut prius) contrarium opinari, publice opinando tenere: hoc autem non licet post determinationē summi Pontificis. Aliud etiam operatur: quia post diffinitionem rectam summi Pontificis licet cuilibet episcopo & inquisitori prauitatis hæreticæ contra tenentes contrarium illius, quod rite per summum Pontificem diffinitum existit, procedere iuxta sanctiones canonicas: nisi tales offerrent se ad probandum, summum Pontificem errorem diffinisse: in quo casu esset ad concilium generale recurrendum, post determinationem autem cuiuslibet Doctoris non licet episcopis inquisitoribus prauitatis hæreticæ contra tenentes contrarium, magis procedere quam ante.
units.tr: Disciple. These last assertions seem strong to me, and yet the arguments for the first opinion appear difficult; so tell me how they are answered. Master. The advocates of this second opinion answer the first of those arguments by saying that, just as someone is often a heretic and yet, because he is only a hidden heretic, ought not to be judged as a heretic, so someone is often a heretic because he clings stubbornly to heresy, and yet, because it is not certain explicitly that his assertion is and was heretical, as if it had become explicitly known to the Church that his assertion was and is heretical, he ought not to be condemned as a heretic. Yet once someone, through careful consideration, has made it known to the Church that his assertion is heretical, if such a man is found to be stubborn, he ought to be condemned as a heretic. Disc. This answer seems to me plausible, except that I doubt which Church they mean. Mag. They mean the Church which is a general council or the Pope: for in this case it is not enough for the condemnation of anyone that it should become known to some other party, besides a general council or the Pope, that such an assertion is heretical. Disc. Tell me how they answer the examples of the Greeks, Joachim, and those who said that Christ is not anything according as he is man. Master. They say that these assertions were heretical beforehand, and that their stubborn advocates were heretics; yet because it had not previously become known to the Church that their assertions were heretical, they ought not to have been condemned as heretics, but afterwards they ought to have been condemned as heretics. Disc. I understand their answer to that argument; now tell me how they answer the second. Mag. They answer that although it belongs to the supreme Pontiff not only by way of teaching but also authoritatively to define which assertion is to be deemed catholic and which heretical, he cannot make a non-catholic truth into a catholic truth, nor can he make a non-heretical assertion into a heretical one. Nevertheless, his definition achieves more than a determination by a Doctor: for after a Doctor's determination it is still lawful for anyone (as before) to hold the contrary opinion and to maintain it publicly; but this is not lawful after a determination by the supreme Pontiff. It has also a further effect: for after a right definition by the supreme Pontiff, it is lawful for any bishop or inquisitor of heretical depravity to proceed, according to the canonical sanctions, against those who hold the contrary of what has been rightly defined by the supreme Pontiff; unless such persons offer to prove that the supreme Pontiff has defined an error, in which case recourse must be had to a general council. After a determination by any Doctor, however, it is not lawful for bishops or inquisitors of heretical depravity to proceed against those who hold the contrary any more than they could before.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: In quo invehitur contra Canonistas, asserentes quod Papa possit facere novum articulum, ubi etiam distinguitur de duplici acceptione articuli.
units.tr: In which he attacks the canonists who assert that the Pope can make a new article, and where a twofold sense of "article" is distinguished.

units.la: Discipulus. Licet quidam retulissent (de quibus miror) unde & de his postea interrogare reservo: tamen conclusio principalis secundæ sententiæ videtur mihi probabilis, & miror quod aliquis tenet, quod Papa possit facere novum articulum fidei: tamen qualiter respondetur ad ca.ext.de haret. cum Christus, indica mihi. Mag. Volo te scire, quod ista allegatio est quorundā canonistarum, de quibus nonnulli Theologi scandalizantur, quando vident eos de Theologicis difficultatibus se intromittere vltra verba Theologorum, quæ in scripturis suis inueniunt, aliquid ex suo ingenio proserendo, quia enim in Theologia sunt minime eruditi, ideo auctoritates Theologiæ (quas in suis libris recipiunt) non debent exponere vltra sensum grammaticalem: nec ex eisdem aliquas conclusiones inferre; nisi sequantur tam patenter, quod quilibet illiteratus vtens ratione posset aduertere, quia cum sæpe talium auctoritatum Theologiæ non habeant intellectum: si ex eis voluerint aliquas conclusiones inferre, facile incident in errores, quod in istis canonistis accidit; qui ex prædicto capitulo Alexandri Tertii, cum Christus, volebant inferre, quod Papa potest facere nouum articulum fidei, nam ex illo capitulo, credebant posse concludi, quod ante istam constitutionem licebat dicere, Christum non esse Deum & hominem; cum tamen non dicat, necibi etiam inhibeat dicere Christum non esse Deum & hominem, licet non prohiberet dicere, Christum non esse aliquid secundum quod homo. Cuius causam assignat, quia Christus est verus Deus & verus homo. Istæ autē sunt assertiones distinctæ: Christus est verus Deus & verus homo; &, Christus est aliquid secundū quod homo, vna tamen sequitur ex alia. Disc. Clare video, quod prædicti canonistæ capitulū prædictū, cum Christus, male allegabant ad probandum, quod ante tempora Alexandri licebat dicere, Christum non esse Deum & hominē. Sed videtur quod bene allegauerunt ad probandum, Papam posse facere nouum articulū fidei: quia quod Christus est aliquid secundum quod homo, ante tempora Alexandri III. non fuit articulus fidei: imo licebat contrariū opinari, ipse aūt fecit, vt esset articulus fidei: & quod non licet dicere contrarium, ergo ipse fecit nouum articulum fidei. Mag. Ad illam tuam obiectionē respondent secūdæ sententiæ assertores, dicentes: quod articulus fidei accipitur strictē pro veritate catholica in symbolo autenti-
units.tr: Disciple. Although some have reported this (which surprises me, and I reserve asking about it later), the main conclusion of the second opinion seems probable to me, and I am surprised that anyone holds that the Pope can make a new article of faith. But how is ca.ext.de haret. cum Christus to be answered? Tell me. Master. I want you to know that this citation belongs to certain canonists, at whom some theologians take offence when they see them meddling with theological difficulties beyond the words of the theologians found in their writings, and putting forward something of their own invention. Since they are very unlearned in theology, they should not expound the authorities of theology (which they take into their books) beyond the grammatical sense, nor draw conclusions from them, unless these follow so plainly that any unlettered man using reason could notice it. Since they often do not grasp the meaning of such theological authorities, if they wish to draw some conclusions from them they easily fall into error, which happened to these canonists. From the aforesaid chapter of Alexander III, cum Christus, they wanted to infer that the Pope can make a new article of faith. For they believed it could be concluded from that chapter that before this decree it was lawful to say that Christ is not God and man. Yet it does not say this, nor does it even forbid saying that Christ is not God and man, though it would not forbid saying that Christ is not something insofar as he is man. It gives the cause: because Christ is true God and true man. These, however, are distinct assertions: Christ is true God and true man; and Christ is something insofar as he is man. Yet one follows from the other. Disciple. I clearly see that the said canonists were wrong to cite that chapter, cum Christus, to prove that before the time of Alexander it was lawful to say that Christ is not God and man. But it seems they cited it well to prove that the Pope can make a new article of faith, because that Christ is something insofar as he is man was not an article of faith before the time of Alexander III. Rather, it was lawful to hold the contrary opinion. He, however, made it an article of faith, and it is not lawful to say the contrary; therefore he made a new article of faith. Master. The advocates of the second opinion answer your objection, saying that "article of faith" is taken strictly for a Catholic truth contained in the authentic creed

units.la: Nn co sub propria forma inserta: & sic non loquimur nunc de articulo fidei. Aliter potest accipi articulus fidei large pro omni veritate catholica, & isto modo est nunc sermo de articulo fidei. Et sic non potest Papa facere nouum articulum fidei, nec Papa Alexander fecit talem articulum: quia tunc non fecit nouam catholicam veritatem: sed fecit quod nec asserendo nec opinando diceretur contrarium illius, quod ante fuit catholica veritas: & quod dicentes contrarium, excommunicationis sententiae subderentur, & ita ista, Christus secundum quod hoc est & fuit aliquid, ante Alexandrum III. fuit vera catholica veritas. Sed ante tempora Alexandri non innotuit ecclesiae, quod esset catholica. Ex illis enim, quae in scripturis diuinis habentur, veritates multae sequuntur, quae tamen latent ecclesiam: & ideo catholicae sunt, licet ecclesia nondum diffinierit, an catholicam sapiant veritatem.
units.tr: inserted in its own proper form; and so we are not now speaking of an article of faith in that sense. It can be taken otherwise, loosely, for any Catholic truth, and in this sense we are now speaking of an article of faith. And so the Pope cannot make a new article of faith, nor did Pope Alexander make such an article, because he did not make a new Catholic truth. Rather, he made it so that no one, either by asserting or by holding an opinion, could say the contrary of what before was a Catholic truth, and that those saying the contrary would be subject to the sentence of excommunication. Thus this statement, that Christ insofar as he is something, was before Alexander III a true Catholic truth. But before the time of Alexander it had not become known to the Church that it was Catholic. For many truths follow from those contained in the divine Scriptures, which nonetheless lie hidden from the Church; and so they are Catholic, although the Church has not yet defined whether they carry a Catholic truth.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: In quo mouetur dubitatio, vtrum haeresis sit species specialissima, an alias adhuc sub se habeat species, ad quam respondetur sub distinctione conformiter ad opiniones supra recitatas de veritatibus.
units.tr: In which the question is raised whether heresy is a most specific species or has further species under it, and the answer is given with a distinction, in line with the opinions about truths recited above.

units.la: Discipul. Quia diffinitio haeresis (de qua disseruisti plura) inconueniens mihi videtur: nec tamen ex ea intelligo, an haeresis sit species specialissima, vel sub se species plures habens, de hoc quid sentiant literati, non postponas exprimere. Mag. De diffinitione specifica sunt plures opiniones. Quidam enim dicunt, quod eadem res sub diuersis speciebus collocari non potest: quidam autem dicunt contrarium. Discip. De talibus difficultatibus nullatenus te intromittas. Nam ad Philosophicas sententias spectat: quarum difficultates proprias quantum potes euita. Sed dic tamen nunc, quid tenetur de haeresibus: an omnes sub vno modo, vel nomine, vel genere, aut specie continentur: aut sub pluribus? Mag. Intentionem tuam aduerto: & ideo ad mentem tuam volo tibi opiniones contrarias recitare. Si recolis, de veritatibus catholicis opiniones narraui, quia quidam dicunt, quod illae solae veritates sunt catholicae reputandae, quae explicite vel implicite in scripturis diuinis habentur. Alii autem asserunt, quod praeter illas veritates sunt nonnullae aliae inter veritates catholicas numerandae, iuxta illas opiniones sunt etiam de haeresibus opiniones contrariae. Quidam enim tradunt, quod haeresis solummodo habet tres species siue tres modos haeresum diuersarum: propter quas debet solummodo quis puniri. Prima species vel primus modus haeresum est, earum videlicet, quae veritatib. sub forma propria in scriptura diuina repertis non solum quomodolibet aduersantur, sed etiam in eisdem terminis contradicunt, tales enim sunt illae: verbum non est caro factum: Deus non creauit in Principio coelum & terram: Christus non est assumptus in coelum, & huiusmodi. Aliae sunt haereses, quae patenter omni intelligenti & etiam illiterato, etiam his quae in scripturis diuinis habentur, aduersantur & repugnant; quales sunt tales: Christus non fuit natus pro salute nostra: nulla est vita beata, & consimiles. Aliae sunt haereses, quae non patent omnibus sed solummodo literatis & sapientibus eruditis in scripturis diuinis per magnam & subtilem consideratio-nem possunt sacris literis aduersari, cuiusmodi sunt tales: Christus non est aliquid secundum quod homo: duae personae sunt in Christo, & huiusmodi, multae aliae autem sunt, quae praedictos modos haeresum asserentes dicunt, videl. quod praeter haereses iam dictas sunt aliae duae: videl. quod doctrinae, quae absque scripturis Apostolicis per reuelationem fidelium sibi succedentium vel per scripturas fidelium ad nos peruenit, quomodolibet aduersantur, sed etiam illi errores, qui alicui veritati post tempora Apostolorum reuelatae repugnant: omnes illi sunt inter haereses computandi.
units.tr: Disciple: Since the definition of heresy (about which you have said a good deal) seems to me faulty, and I cannot tell from it whether heresy is a most specific species or contains several species under it, do not hesitate to tell me what learned men think about this. Master: There are several opinions about specific definition. Some say that the same thing cannot be placed under different species; others say the contrary. Disciple: Do not concern yourself at all with such difficulties. They belong to the philosophical opinions, and you should avoid their particular problems as far as you can. But tell me now what is held about heresies: are they all contained under one mode, name, genus or species, or under several? Master: I see what you are after, so I want to recite to you, to suit your purpose, the opposing opinions. If you recall, I described opinions about catholic truths, since some hold that only those truths are to be regarded as catholic which are contained in divine Scripture, either explicitly or implicitly. Others assert that besides those truths there are some others to be counted among the catholic truths; and in line with those opinions there are also opposing opinions about heresies. For some teach that heresy has only three species, or three modes of different heresies, on account of which someone ought alone to be punished. The first species, or first mode, of heresies is that of those which not only oppose in some way the truths found in divine Scripture in their proper form, but actually contradict them in the very same terms. Such are these: "The Word was not made flesh"; "God did not create heaven and earth in the beginning"; "Christ was not taken up into heaven"; and the like. Others are heresies which clearly oppose and contradict what is contained in divine Scripture, evident to every intelligent person, even the unlearned; such are these: "Christ was not born for our salvation"; "there is no blessed life"; and similar ones. Others are heresies which are not evident to everyone, but only to the learned and wise, who by great and subtle consideration of divine Scripture can set themselves against the sacred letters; of this kind are these: "Christ is not something according to his humanity"; "there are two persons in Christ"; and the like. There are, however, many others who, while asserting the aforesaid modes of heresies, say that besides the heresies already mentioned there are two more: namely, doctrines which, apart from the Apostolic Scriptures, come to us through the revelation given to faithful successors, or through the writings of the faithful, and which in any way oppose the truth; and also those errors which contradict some truth revealed after the times of the Apostles. All of these are to be counted among heresies.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: In quo ostenditur, quod praeter haereses praedictas sunt quidam errores mortiferi & haeresim sapientes, qui tamen stricte non debent haereses appellari.
units.tr: In which it is shown that, besides the heresies mentioned, there are certain deadly errors that savour of heresy but should not strictly be called heresies.

units.la: Discip. Ista secunda sententia magis mihi apparet consona veritati: sed dic mihi, an isti assertores omnes errores pestiferos, quos nulli licet Christiano fideli asserere, sub istis modis haeresum comprehendant. Magist. Praeter haereses supra dictas asserunt esse quosdam alios errores mortiferos: qui tamen non debent stricte haereses appellari, tales errores dicunt esse illos, qui cronicis & historiis ecclesiasticis fide dignis ac probatis gestis fidelium, quae rationabiliter negari non possunt, obuiari noscuntur. Alii adhuc sunt errores, qui veritatibus catholicis & cronicis vel historiis ecclesiasticis fide dignis ac gestis, quae rationabiliter negari non possunt, incompossibiles demonstrantur, cuiusmodi sunt tales Regulae religiosorum non sunt catholicae: fides B. Augustini non fuit vera nec fidelis: & huiusmodi, & istos errores quamuis stricte accipiendo vocabulum haeresis non reputant inter haereses computandos: dicunt tamen quod sapiunt haeresim manifestam; quod non est aliud quam dicere, quod ex eis & aliis veris, quae negari non possunt, sequatur haereses proprie dictae, & ideo dicunt, quod isti errores possunt large haereses appellari. Di. Enarra generales modos pestiferorum errorum, quos secundum sniam illa nulli licet catholico & fideli pertinaciter defensare. Magist. Tales modi generales (quorum aliqui sub se plures modos continent speciales) sunt quinque. Quorum primus est error, qui solis contentis in Scriptura divina repugnat, & ille plures modos continet speciales: sicut ex prædictis apparet, & omnes isti errores deberent hæreses appellari. Secundus est error eorum, qui doctrinæ Apostolicæ extra scripta eorum quoquo modo repugnant, & ille etiam continet plures modos. Tertius est eorum, qui revelatur vel inspiratur ecclesiæ post Apostolos quomodolibet obuiant. Quartus est eorum, qui chronicis & historiis & gestis ab ecclesia approbatis contrariantur. Quintus est eorum, qui scripturæ divinæ vel doctrinæ Apostolicæ extra scripturam eorum, vel inspiratis, vel revelatis ecclesiæ & aliis veris, quæ negari non possunt, incompossibiles demonstrantur, licet ex forma propositionum solis contentis in scriptura divina & doctrina Apostolica, & revelatis seu inspiratis ecclesiæ incompossibiles nequaquam appareant, & isti errores possunt proprie dici, sapere hæresim manifestam: licet stricte sumendo nomen hæresis; non sunt hæreses nuncupandæ. Talis est iste error: castitas monachorum castitati non præeminet coniugali, nam ille error ex forma propositionis non repugnat alicui contento in scriptura divina vel doctrina Apostolica, nec etiam repugnat alicui revelato vel inspirato ecclesiæ (ut videtur) contentis tamen in scriptura divina, & isti vero (quod nulla potest tergiversatione negari stricte sumpto vocabulo hæresis) monachi seruant & vouent perpetuam continentiam propter Deum, incompossibilis esse dinoscitur, & ideo iste error licet non videatur (stricte vocabulo sumpto) hæresis appellanda: sapit tamen hæresim manifestam, quia ex ipso & quodam vero aperte sequitur hæresis manifesta.
units.tr: Student. This second opinion seems to me more consistent with the truth. But tell me, do its advocates include all pestilent errors, which no Christian believer may assert, under these modes of heresy? Master. Besides the heresies mentioned above, they assert that there are certain other deadly errors which should not strictly be called heresies. They say these are the errors that are known to be opposed by chronicles and ecclesiastical histories worthy of belief, and by approved deeds of the faithful, which cannot reasonably be denied. There are yet other errors which are shown to be incompatible with catholic truths and with chronicles, ecclesiastical histories worthy of belief, and deeds which cannot reasonably be denied. Such are: "The rules of the religious orders are not catholic"; "The faith of St Augustine was neither true nor faithful"; and the like. Although, taking the word heresy strictly, they do not count these errors among the heresies, they nevertheless say that they savour of manifest heresy. This is no other than to say that from them and from other truths, which cannot be denied, proper heresies follow; and so they say these errors may be called heresies in a broad sense. Student. Set out the general modes of pestilent errors which, according to that opinion, no catholic and faithful man may stubbornly defend. Master. Such general modes, some of which contain several special modes under them, are five. The first is the error that contradicts only the contents of divine Scripture; this contains several special modes, as appears from what was said above, and all these errors ought to be called heresies. The second is the error of those who in any way contradict the doctrine of the Apostles outside their writings; this too contains several modes. The third is the error of those who in any way oppose what has been revealed or inspired to the Church after the Apostles. The fourth is the error of those who contradict chronicles, histories and deeds approved by the Church. The fifth is the error of those which are shown to be incompatible with divine Scripture, or with the Apostles' doctrine outside Scripture, or with what has been inspired or revealed to the Church, or with other truths which cannot be denied. Although, by the form of their propositions, they do not at all appear incompatible with the contents of divine Scripture and Apostolic doctrine alone, or with what has been revealed or inspired to the Church, these errors can properly be said to savour of manifest heresy; yet, taking the name heresy strictly, they are not to be called heresies. Such is this error: "The chastity of monks is not superior to marital chastity." By its form this error does not contradict any content of divine Scripture or Apostolic doctrine, nor (as it seems) anything revealed or inspired to the Church. Yet the monks, who keep and vow perpetual continence for God's sake, are known to be incompatible with it, which no evasion can deny when the word heresy is taken strictly. Therefore, although this error, taking the word strictly, does not seem to be called a heresy, it nevertheless savours of manifest heresy, because from it and from some truth, manifest heresy plainly follows.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: In quo requiritur, utrum omnis hæresis sit per ecclesiam condemnata, ad quod respondetur secundum unam opinionem, dicentem, quod sic. Vbi etiam ponuntur quatuor modi hæresum explicite damnatarum, & ibidem tractatur etiam de hæresibus damnatis implicite.
units.tr: In which it is asked whether every heresy has been condemned by the Church, and it is answered, according to one opinion which says that it has, that it has. Here are also set out four modes of heresies explicitly condemned, and heresies condemned implicitly are also discussed there.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunc quam vtile fuit inquirere, quæ veritates debeant catholicæ iudicari: quia ex solutione quæstionis ipsius potest intelligenti patere, qui errores debeant hæreses reputari. Ex inuestigatis etiam circa catholicas veritates sequi videtur, quod omnis hæresis sit damnata: quia cum omnis veritas catholica sit per ecclesiam approbata, videtur quod per eandem ecclesiam omnis hæresis est damnata: cum omnis hæresis alicui veritati catholicæ aduersetur, approbato autem vno contrariorum constat aliud reprobari & damnari, an ergo aliqui literati tenent, omnem hæresim esse damnatam, nequaquam occultes. Magist. Multi tenent (quod probare conantur) quod omnis hæresis est damnata, hoc enim concilium generale sub Innocent. Tertio, celebratum, de quo habetur extra, de hæret. excommunicamus, sentire videtur, ait enim: excommunicamus & anathematisamus omnem hæresim extollentem se aduersus hanc sanctam catholicam & orthodoxam fidem, quam superius exposuimus. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod omnis hæresis est excommunicata & anathematisata, & per consequens omnis hæresis est damnata. Disc. Ex hac auctoritate non videtur, quod omnis hæresis sit damnata: sed solummodo quod omnis hæresis extollens se aduersus fidem, quam supra generale concilium exposuit in ca. quod habetur extra, de sum. tri. & fid. cath. c. firmiter, sit damnata. Mag. Dicunt isti, per prædictum c. excommunicamus, omnis hæresis sit simpliciter damnata ex hoc ipso, quod omnis hæresis extollens se aduersus fidem catholicam in dicto capitulo firmiter, est damnata. Nam in dicto capitulo firmiter, tota fides catholica approbatur, ergo omnis hæresis simpliciter per capitulum excommunicamus, quod damnat omnem hæresim extollentem se aduersus fidem, quam expositi & approbauit in ca. firmiter, reprobatione damnatur. Quod autem ca. firmiter, approbet simpliciter totam fidem catholicam, patet expresse, cum asseredo & probando dicat, hæc sancta Trinitas secundum communem essentiam individua, & secundum personales proprietates distincta per Moysen & sanctos prophetas aliosque famulos suos iuxta ordinatissimam dispositionem temporum humano generi doctrinam tribuit salutarem, & tandem vnicus Dei filius Christus à tota Trinitate conuenienter incarnatus ex Maria semper virgine Spiritu sancto cooperante conceptus, verus homo factus ex humana anima rationali & humana carne compositus, vna in duabus naturis persona, viam vitæ manifestius demonstrauit. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod totam doctrinam Christi & famulorum suorum, qui veritates catholicas humano generi tradiderunt, prædictum concilium approbat manifeste, ergo & per capitulum, excommunicamus, simpliciter omnis hæresis est damnata, & per hoc Gloss. 24. q. 1. §. 1. notat apertte, dicens: omnis hæresis damnata, & omnis hereticus est excommunicatus quantumcunque fit occultus. Disc. Apparenter ostenditur, quod omnis hæresis damnata est, de quo tamen miror, eo quod sæpe audiui literatos distinguere inter illos fideles, qui incidunt in hæresim iam damnatam, & inter illos, qui incidunt in hæresim iam non damnatam. Unde & Gratian. vt habetur 24. q. 1. c. 1. eandem distinctionem approbare videtur dicens: omnis enim hereticus aut iam damnatam hæresim sequitur, aut nouam confingit. Cuius distinctionis primum membrum statim prosequitur eisdem c. & q. §. Si autem ex corde suo nouam hæresim confingit, &c. dicantes asserentes prædicti eandem distinctionem simpliciter negent. Mag. Non omnino negant dictam distinctionem, sed cum distinctione concedant dicentes, quod quædam hæreses sunt damnatæ explicite: quædam vero solum sunt damnatæ implicite, & ideo concedunt dictam distinctionem sub isto intellectu : quædam hæreses sunt damnatæ explicite, quædam non sunt damnatæ explicite. Disc. Quas vocant hæreses damnatas explicite? Magist. Hæresum damnatarum explicite ponunt quatuor modos. Primus est earum, quæ damnantur in speciali, in qua damnatione de ipsis hæresibus sub forma propria fit mentio specialis, isto modo hæreses Arrii, Nestorii, Euticii, & Macedonii, & Dioscori damnatæ fuerunt: sicut ex distinctione 15. cap. 1. & cap. sicut sunt & cap. sancta Rom. patenter habetur, sicut etiam damnatus est error Ioachim. extra, de summ. Trin. & fid. cap. damnatus. & error dicentium, Christum non esse aliquid secundum quod homo, extra, de hær. cum Christus. Secundus modus hæresum damnatarum explicite est earum, quarum contrariæ sub forma propria asseruntur seu approbantur: quia ex una contradictoriarum approbata explicite altera explicite intelligitur reprobata, tales sunt omnes hæreses, quæ contradicunt veritatibus catholicis, quæ in conciliis generalibus, symbolis ac decretis & decretalibus opusculis summorum etiam Pontificum tanquam catholicæ approbantur. Unde ista etiam hæresis, Deus non est factor omnium visibilium & invisibilium, est hæresis explicite condemnata pro eo, quod explicite per symbolum condemnatur. Tertius est earum, quarum contradictoriæ in aliquo volumine vel libro aut tractatu specialiter approbato tanquam catholico sub forma propria continentur. Et isto modo omnes hæreses, quarum contradictoriæ in canone Bibliæ confirmato sub propria forma continentur, hæreses damnatæ explicite sunt censendæ: quia eo ipso, quod canon Bibliæ explicite approbatur, omnes veritates in ipso assertæ approbantur, & per consequens earum contradictoriæ explicite reprobantur & damnantur. Quartus est earum, ex quibus patet cer etiam omnibus laicis visum habentibus rationis sequitur aliqua hæresis sub aliquo trium modorum priorum comprehensa. Disc.ip. Contra aliqua prædictorum possem dubia multa movere, & forsan non essent multum ad rem: quia voces sunt ad placitum, & ideo possunt vocare hæreses damnatas explicite stricte & large, sicut placet eis: dummodo in auctoritatibus non inveniatur expresse contrarium. Idcirco dicas, quas hæreses vocant damnatas solum implicite. Magister. Hæreses implicite damnatæ dicuntur illæ, de quibus viris literatis solummodo in literis sacris eruditis per subtilem considerationem patet, quomodo veritati catholicæ, contentæ in sacris Scripturis, vel doctrinæ expressæ universalis ecclesiæ adversantur: & quod ex eis sequitur aliqua hæresis aliquo prædictorum modorum damnata explicite, dicunt esse damnatas implicite & non explicite, talis hæresis fuit hæresis Græcorum dicentium, Spiritum sanctum non procedere a Filio, antequam damnaretur explicite. Multæ etiam hæreses, de quibus habetur in decretis, aliquando fuerunt huiusmodi, quæ postea explicite damnatæ fuerunt, tales sunt hæreses nonnullorum Doctorum modernorum. Est enim notorium, quod moderni Theologi circa divina opiniones tenent contrarias, quas putant in divinis scripturis fundari, quarum altera in rei veritate scripturæ divinæ repugnat, sicut & tenent contrarium opinantes. Unde & eam per scripturam divinam improbare nituntur, sicut in scripturis eorum patet aperte, & ita in rei veritate altera earum est damnata implicite: cum veritas contraria sit implicite approbata ex hoc, quod doctrina ecclesiæ, ex qua infertur, noscitur approbata.
units.tr: Student. It is now useful to inquire which truths ought to be judged catholic, for from the solution of this question an intelligent reader can see which errors ought to be counted as heresies. From the matters investigated concerning catholic truths, it seems to follow that every heresy has been condemned, for since every catholic truth has been approved by the Church, it seems that every heresy has been condemned by the same Church, since every heresy opposes some catholic truth; and since the approval of one of two contraries shows that the other is rejected and condemned. Do some learned men hold that every heresy has been condemned? This is not unknown. Master. Many hold this (and try to prove it), for the general council held under Innocent III, which is cited in Extra, de haeret., Excommunicamus, seems to say so, for it says: We excommunicate and anathematize every heresy that raises itself against this holy, catholic and orthodox faith, which we have set out above. From these words it is plainly clear that every heresy is excommunicated and anathematized, and consequently every heresy is condemned. Student. From this authority it does not seem that every heresy has been condemned, but only that every heresy which raises itself against the faith which the general council set out in the chapter cited in Extra, de summa Trinitate et fide catholica, c. Firmiter, has been condemned. Master. Those men say that by the aforesaid chapter Excommunicamus, every heresy is simply condemned, from the very fact that every heresy raising itself against the catholic faith is condemned in the said chapter Firmiter. For in that chapter Firmiter the whole catholic faith is approved, therefore every heresy is simply condemned by the chapter Excommunicamus, which condemns every heresy raising itself against the faith which it has set out and approved in the chapter Firmiter. That the chapter Firmiter simply approves the whole catholic faith is plain, since in asserting and proving it, it says: This holy Trinity, one in common essence, yet distinct in personal properties, gave saving doctrine to the human race through Moses and the holy prophets and its other servants, according to the most orderly arrangement of the times; and at last the only Son of God, Christ, fittingly incarnate by the whole Trinity, conceived of the Virgin Mary, ever a virgin, by the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, made true man, composed of a rational human soul and human flesh, one person in two natures, has more plainly shown the way of life. From these words it is to be understood that the aforesaid council plainly approves the whole doctrine of Christ and of his servants who handed down catholic truths to the human race. Therefore, by the chapter Excommunicamus, every heresy is simply condemned, and the Gloss on 24. q. 1. §. 1. clearly notes this, saying: Every heresy is condemned, and every heretic is excommunicated, however hidden he may be. Student. It is clearly shown that every heresy is condemned. Yet I wonder at this, for I have often heard learned men distinguish between those faithful who fall into an already condemned heresy and those who fall into a heresy not yet condemned. Hence Gratian also seems to approve the same distinction, as found in 24. q. 1. c. 1, saying: Every heretic either follows an already condemned heresy or invents a new one. The first member of this distinction he follows immediately in the same chapter and question, §. But if from his own heart he invents a new heresy, etc. The aforesaid objectors simply deny the same distinction. Master. They do not altogether deny the said distinction, but grant it with a qualification, saying that some heresies are explicitly condemned, while others are only implicitly condemned; and so they grant the said distinction in this sense: some heresies are explicitly condemned, some are not explicitly condemned. Student. What do they call heresies explicitly condemned? Master. They set out four modes of explicitly condemned heresies. The first is of those condemned by name, in which condemnation the heresies are mentioned specifically in their own form; in this way the heresies of Arius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Macedonius and Dioscorus were condemned, as is plainly seen from distinction 15, cap. 1, cap. Sicut sunt, and cap. Sancta Romana; just as the error of Joachim was condemned, Extra, de summa Trinitate et fide catholica, cap. Damnatus, and the error of those saying that Christ is not something according to the manner of man, Extra, de haeret., Cum Christus. The second mode of explicitly condemned heresies is of those whose contraries are asserted or approved in their own form; for from the explicit approval of one of two contradictories, the other is explicitly understood to be rejected. Such are all heresies which contradict catholic truths approved as catholic in general councils, creeds and decrees, and in the decretal writings even of the highest pontiffs. Hence this heresy also, that God is not the maker of all things visible and invisible, is an explicitly condemned heresy, because it is explicitly condemned by the creed. The third is of those whose contradictories are contained in their own form in some volume, book or treatise specially approved as catholic. In this way all heresies whose contradictories are contained in their own form in the canon of the Bible, once it has been confirmed, are to be judged explicitly condemned; for by the very fact that the canon of the Bible is explicitly approved, all truths asserted in it are approved, and consequently their contradictories are explicitly rejected and condemned. The fourth is of those from which it plainly follows, even to all laymen who have the use of reason, that some heresy is comprised under one of the three former modes. Student. I could raise many doubts against some of these, and perhaps they would not be much to the point, for words are by convention, and so they may call heresies explicitly condemned, strictly or broadly, as they please, provided nothing expressly to the contrary is found in the authorities. Therefore tell me which heresies they call condemned only implicitly. Master. Those are called implicitly condemned heresies, of which only learned men, learned in the sacred letters, see by subtle consideration how they oppose the catholic truth contained in Holy Scripture, or the expressly stated doctrine of the universal Church; and from them there follows some heresy condemned explicitly in one of the aforesaid modes, and these they say are condemned implicitly and not explicitly. Such was the heresy of the Greeks who said that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, before it was explicitly condemned.
