Many heresies also, mentioned in the decrees, were once of this kind, and were afterwards explicitly condemned. Such are the heresies of some modern doctors. For it is notorious that modern theologians hold contrary opinions about divine matters, which they think are founded in the divine Scriptures; of which one, in truth, contradicts the Scriptures of God, just as they who hold the contrary opinion also do. Hence they strive to refute it by the divine Scripture, as is plainly evident in their writings; and so in truth one of them is implicitly condemned, since the contrary truth is implicitly approved by the fact that the doctrine of the Church, from which it is inferred, is known to be approved.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: In quo notatur utilitas distinctionis capituli præmissi inquisitoribus hæreticæ pravitatis, quos scil. hæreses tenentes possunt condemnare.
units.tr: In which the usefulness of the preceding chapter's distinction is noted for the inquisitors of heretical depravity, namely, which holders of heresy they can condemn.

units.la: Discipulus. Sine isti deviant a proprio modo loquendi, sive non, video quod inter hæreses, quas dicunt esse damnatas explicite, & quas dicunt esse damnatas implicite, solum est aperta distinctio: sed ad quam utilitatem istam distinctionem assignent ignoro; & tamen desidero scire. Magister. Putant istam distinctionem esse summe necessariam episcopis & inquisitoribus hæreticæ pravitatis, ut sciant contra quos accusatos de hæresi debeant procedere, & contra quos potestatem procedendi non habent, nam omnes tenentes pertinaciter hæresim aliquo prædictorum modorum explicite damnatorum possunt legitime iudicare. Tenentes vero hæreses damnatas implicite tantummodo, iudicare non possunt, nec de talibus causam ventilare valent, nec inquisitionem discutere, nec de eisdem sententiam diffinitivam proferre. Sed huiusmodi hæresim asserens vel defendens summi Pontificis vel generalis concilii est reservandus examini. Discip. Si isti suam sententiam auctoritate vel ratione valeant confirmare, non tardes ostendere. Magister. Possunt se fundare in una ratione, quæ talis est. Ad illum solum spectat assertionem damnatam vel hæresim damnatam implicite, de qua nunquam innotuit ecclesiæ, an debeat hæresis reputari, tanquam hæreticam condemnare, ad quem spectat huiusmodi hæreses condemnare solenniter: quia videtur maxime veritati inhærere, quando inter catholicos literatos & in sacra pagina eruditos in tali assertione an debeat censeri hæretica, opiniones habentur contrariæ. Sed assertio, quæ in rei veritate est hæretica: de qua tamen an sit hæretica, inter doctores opiniones reperiuntur contrariæ, solenniter & explicite condemnare, pertinet ad summum Pontificem vel concilium generale, vel ad universalem ecclesiam, igitur ad nullum inferiorem summo Pontifice, nec ad collegium inferius summo concilio generali, vel universali ecclesiæ, spectat assertionem huiusmodi tanquam hæreticam explicite condemnare. Maiorstius rationis videtur esse certa: quia qui iudicialiter pronunciat aliquem hæreticum, potest pronunciare solenniter assertionem, pro qua iudicat eum esse hæreticam & inter hæreses computandam. Minorem ostendunt auctoritate & ratione. Primo auctoritate Innocentii Papæ, qui vt habetur vigesim.quart. quæst. 1. tap. quoties, ait: Quotiens fidei ratio ventilatur, arbitror omnes fratres episcopos non nisi ad Petrum sua rationis auctoritatem referre debere. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod quæstio fidei ad inferiorem summo Pontifice referri non debet. hinc est quod Glossa dicit ibidem: A'iud est quæstionem de fide motam terminare, quod non præterquam rationè fidei permittitur. Aliud est ipsam sine dissinitione ventilare, quod inferiores facere possunt. Et infra obiiciens ait: videtur contra extra, de hære. ad abolendam. Nam ibi innuitur, quod illi iudicandi sunt tanquam hæretici, quos ipsi iudicandos dixerunt, & respondens ait: Sed dic, quod illud intelligendum est, quando talè quid dicunt, quod certum est dictum eorum esse hæresim: nec vlli est dubium. Item ad idem videtur concordare Glossa prædicti capituli, super verbo in fide, quæ ait: In fide, id est fideliter agitare causam fidei, & non procedere ad sententiam vel determinationem, qui sint qui dubitant. Nam aliquibus videtur, quod episcopi possunt determinare, extra, de hereticis, ad abolendam. & de iudiciis, ac si clerici, & aliquando Papa, extra, de hære. cum Christus. Ex istis colligitur, quod nullus inferior summo Pontifice potest determinare quæstionem motam de fide, præcipue quando literati dubitant & contrarie opinantur. Hoc etiam Innocentius Tertius, extra de baptism. & eius effectu. cap. maiores, sentire videtur, ait enim: Maiores ecclesiæ causas, præsertim articulos fidei contingentes, ad Petri sedem referentes intelligi, qui cum quærenti Domino, quem discipuli dicebant, ipsum esse, respondisse notatur, Tu es Christus filius Dei viui. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod ad sedem beati Petri est quæstio fidei referenda: & ita nec collegium inferius collegio generalis concilii: nec aliquis episcopus inferior Papa potest aliquam hæresim, de qua est dubium an sit hæresis, condemnare; & per consequens nullum talem hæresim asserentem valet, tanquam hæreticum condemnare, irrationabile enim omnino videtur, quod episcopus vel inquisitor hæreticæ prauitatis, qui sæpe sacræ Scripturæ imperitus existit, opiniones Doctorum Theologiæ posset tanquam hæreticas condemnare.
units.tr: Disciple. Whether or not these men depart from their own manner of speaking, I see that the only clear difference between heresies they say are condemned explicitly and those they say are condemned implicitly lies in this distinction. But I do not know what use they assign to it, and yet I want to learn. Master. They think this distinction is absolutely necessary for bishops and inquisitors of heretical depravity, so that they know against whom, accused of heresy, they should proceed, and against whom they have no power to proceed. For they can lawfully judge all who obstinately hold a heresy condemned explicitly in one of the aforementioned ways. But they cannot judge those who hold only heresies condemned implicitly, nor can they take up such a case, examine the inquiry, or pronounce a final sentence concerning them. Rather, one who asserts or defends such a heresy is to be reserved for the examination of the supreme Pontiff or of a general council. Disciple. If these men can confirm their opinion by authority or by reason, do not delay in showing it. Master. They can rest it on one argument, which runs as follows. Only the one to whom it belongs to condemn solemnly a heresy or an assertion condemned implicitly, about which it has never been made known to the Church whether it ought to be regarded as heretical, is the one to whom it belongs to condemn such heresies solemnly, because he seems most to adhere to the truth when, among Catholic scholars and those learned in Sacred Scripture, opposing opinions are held on whether such an assertion ought to be judged heretical. But to condemn solemnly and explicitly an assertion which in the reality of the matter is heretical, though it is uncertain whether it is heretical, since teachers hold opposing opinions about it, belongs to the supreme Pontiff or a general council, or to the universal Church. Therefore it belongs to no one inferior to the supreme Pontiff, nor to any college inferior to a general council or the universal Church, to condemn explicitly an assertion of this kind as heretical. The major premise of the argument seems certain, because whoever judicially pronounces someone a heretic can solemnly pronounce the assertion for which he judges him to be a heretic and to be counted among heresies. They show the minor premise by authority and by reason. First, by the authority of Pope Innocent, who, as is found in the twenty-fourth case, question 1, chapter quoties, says: Whenever a matter of faith is debated, I think all the brother bishops ought to refer the authority of their judgment only to Peter. From these words it is to be understood that a question of faith ought not to be referred to someone inferior to the supreme Pontiff. Hence the Gloss says in the same place: It is one thing to bring to an end a question of faith that has been raised, which is permitted only by the reason of faith; it is another to debate it without a decision, which inferiors can do. And below, raising an objection, it says: It seems contrary to the decretal, on heretics, ad abolendam. For there it is implied that those are to be judged as heretics, whom they said should be judged, and answering, it says: But say that this must be understood when they say something of such a kind that their statement is certainly a heresy, and there is no doubt about it. Likewise, the Gloss on the same chapter seems to agree on the words in fide, which says: In fide, that is, to handle the cause of faith faithfully, and not to proceed to a sentence or determination, among those who doubt. For to some it seems that bishops can determine, in the decretal on heretics, ad abolendam, and on judgments, as if clerics can, and sometimes the Pope, in the decretal on heretics, cum Christus. From these things it is gathered that no one inferior to the supreme Pontiff can determine a question raised about faith, especially when learned men doubt and hold contrary opinions. Innocent III seems also to feel this, in the decretal on baptism and its effect, chapter maiores, for he says: The greater causes of the Church, especially those concerning articles of faith, are to be understood as referred to the seat of Peter, to whom, when the Lord asked whom the disciples said he was, it is noted that he answered, You are Christ, the Son of the living God. From these words it is plainly held that a question of faith is to be referred to the seat of blessed Peter; and so neither a college inferior to the college of a general council, nor any bishop inferior to the Pope, can condemn any heresy about which it is doubtful whether it is a heresy, and consequently cannot condemn as a heretic anyone who asserts such a heresy. For it seems entirely unreasonable that a bishop or an inquisitor of heretical depravity, who is often unskilled in Sacred Scripture, should be able to condemn as heretical the opinions of the doctors of theology.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: In quo fiunt tres instantiæ contra dicta in capitulo præcedenti de hæresum conde- mnatione, vbi etiam tractatur de articulis condemnatis Parisiis, ad quas respondetur capitulo 21. 22. & 23.
units.tr: In which three objections are raised against what was said in the preceding chapter about the condemnation of heresies. The articles condemned at Paris are also discussed here, and replies to them are given in chapters 21, 22 and 23.

units.la: Discipulus. Quamuis ista sententia videatur fortiter esse probata, tamen contra ipsam negantes in mente instantias reuoluo. Quarum prima est de Vniuersitate Parisiensi, quæ multas opiniones multorum, & etiam Thomæ ipso viuente, tanquam errores excommunicauit & damnauit. Secunda est de duobus archiepiscopis Cantuariensibus, quorum vnus erat Doctor Theologiæ de ordine Fratrum Prædicatorum, qui fuit postea Cardinalis. Secundus erat Doctor Theologiæ Fratrum Minorum, qui doctrinam Fratris Petri Iohannis damnauit, & ita videtur, quod tam ad collegium inferius concilio generali, quam ad alias personas inferiores summo Pontifice spectat opinates errores theologorum condemnare, quamobrem qualiter ad ista respondetur manifesta. Magist. Ad primam instantiam de Vniuersitate Parisiensi, respondetur multipliciter. Vno modo, quod multas assertiones temerarie damnauit damnando veritatem. Nullo modo enim potest solenniter absque temeritate veritas damnari: licet quis possit & valeat absque temeritate damnabili veritatis contrarium opinari & de veritate dubitare. Nunquam tamen veritas solenniter & publice absque temeritate damnabili damnatur. Cum igitur multorum iudicio inter articulos damnatos Parisiis contineantur complures veritates, sequitur quod eadem Vniuersitas plures assertiones temerarie condemnauit, & istius sententiæ fuerunt illi, qui post reuocationem dictæ sententiæ, quoad opinionem Thomæ easdem opiniones Thomæ prius damnatas nunc Parisiis tenent & approbant publice & occulte. Discipulus. Miror quod dicunt, vt refers, aliquos ante reuocationem sententiæ sancti Thomæ assertiones damnatas Parisiis tenuisse, forte, quod hoc fecerunt ignoranter, nescientes tales assertiones ibidem fuisse damnatas. Magister. Volo te scire, quod multi scienter nonnullas assertiones damnatas Parisiis occulte & publice docuerunt. Vnde scio quendam Doctorem de ordine Prædicatorum assertionem damnatam Parisiis ante dictam reuocationem determinasse, & cum contra se obiiceretur, quod dicta assertio, quam tenuit, esse damnata Parisiis: Respondit, damnationem illam nequaquam mare transisse. Istius etiam sententiæ fuit Magister Godfridus de Fontibus: & hoc determinasse videtur, vt in scripturis suis reliquit, quod articuli damnati erant corrigendi.
units.tr: Disciple: Although this opinion seems to have been strongly proved, I turn over in my mind some objections to those who deny it. The first concerns the University of Paris, which, while Thomas himself was still alive, excommunicated and condemned many opinions of many people as errors. The second concerns the two Archbishops of Canterbury. One of them was a Doctor of Theology of the Order of Preachers (the Dominicans), who was later made a Cardinal. The other was a Doctor of Theology of the Friars Minor (the Franciscans), who condemned the teaching of Brother Peter John. So it seems that it belongs both to a college inferior to a general council and to other persons inferior to the supreme Pontiff to condemn the errors of theologians that are held as opinions. For this reason I would like to see clearly how these objections are answered. Master: As to the first objection, concerning the University of Paris, the answer is manifold. In one way, it rashly condemned many assertions by condemning truth. For truth can in no way be solemnly condemned without rashness, although a person may, without damnable rashness, hold the contrary opinion and doubt the truth. Yet truth is never solemnly and publicly condemned without damnable rashness. Since, then, in the judgement of many, several truths are contained among the articles condemned at Paris, it follows that the same University rashly condemned several assertions. Those who held this view were the ones who, after the revocation of that sentence concerning the opinion of Thomas, now openly and secretly hold and approve at Paris the same opinions of Thomas that were earlier condemned. Disciple: I am surprised that, as you report, some people held the assertions condemned at Paris before the revocation of the sentence on St Thomas. Perhaps they did this in ignorance, not knowing that such assertions had been condemned there. Master: I want you to know that many knowingly taught some of the assertions condemned at Paris, both secretly and publicly. For this reason I know that a certain Doctor of the Order of Preachers maintained, before the said revocation, an assertion that had been condemned at Paris. When it was objected to him that the assertion he held had been condemned at Paris, he replied that that condemnation had by no means crossed the sea. Master Godfrey of Fontaines also held this view, and he seems to have maintained it, as he left it in his writings, that the condemned articles were to be corrected.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: In quo inquiritur de sententia excommunicationis lata à condemnantibus huiusmodi articulos, utrum liget tenentes huiusmodi articulos.
units.tr: In which it is inquired whether the sentence of excommunication pronounced by those who condemn such articles binds those who hold them.

units.la: Discipulus. Verba, quæ facis, me cogunt incidentaliter interrogare, si aliqui tenentes huiusmodi veritates eum assertionibus earundem excommunicationem incurrerint, cum sententia lata ex causa iniqua neminem videatur inuoluere. Magister. Nonnulli putant, quod si dicta sententia excommunicationis fuerit iniqua, ipsa nullum tenentem veritatem damnatam de facto potuit quo quomodo ligare, nec talis debuit se reputare ligatu, licet alii credentes sententiam dictam non esse iniquam, ipsum tanquam excommunicatum vitare debuerunt. Hanc assertionem triplici ratione probare nituntur: quarum prima est hæc, secundum Innocentium Tertium, ut habetur extra, de sentent. excommunicat. cap. per tuas: sententia excommunicationis continens intolerabilem errorem non ligat, sed excommunicare assertionem catholicam est intolerabilis error, ergo talis sententia nullum ligat. Secunda ratio est hæc, nullus potest cogi ad malum, negare autem assertionem catholicam, est de se malum, ergo ad hoc per nullam sententiam potest quis cogi, & per consequens sententia ad hoc coges est nulla. Sententia aut excommunicationis, qua excommunicatur catholica veritas, quantum est ex forma sententiæ, cogit negare catholicam veritatem, ergo talis sententia nulla est, & per consequens sententia ad hoc cogens est nulla, igitur non meretur dici sententia excommunicationis, qua excommunicatur catholica veritas, quantum est ex forma sententiæ: quia cogit negare catholicam veritatem, igitur talis sententia nulla est, & per consequens neminem ligat. Tertia ratio est hæc, sententia hæretici neminem ligat, ut habetur 24. quæst. 1. cap. audiamus, sed si dicta sententia excommunicationis se extendat ad catholicas veritates ferentes eandem sententiam fuerunt hæretici: quia dubius in fidem est infidelis & hæreticus, ergo multo fortius damnans sententialiter catholicam veritatem hæreticus est censendus, si autem ferentes dictam sententiam fuerunt hæretici, ipsa omnino nullum ligavit.
units.tr: Disciple. Your words compel me to ask, in passing, whether those who hold such truths and have incurred excommunication for their assertions are in fact bound, since a sentence pronounced on an unjust ground seems to bind no one. Master. Some think that if the said sentence of excommunication was unjust, it could not in any way bind anyone who in fact held the condemned truth, nor ought such a person to regard himself as bound, although others who believed the sentence was not unjust ought to have avoided him as excommunicated. They strive to prove this assertion by three arguments. The first is this: according to Innocent III, as found in extra, de sentent. excommunicat. cap. per tuas, a sentence of excommunication containing intolerable error does not bind. But to excommunicate a Catholic assertion is an intolerable error. Therefore such a sentence binds no one. The second argument is this: no one can be compelled to evil, and to deny a Catholic assertion is evil in itself. Therefore no one can be compelled to this by any sentence, and consequently a sentence that compels to this is void. A sentence of excommunication by which a Catholic truth is excommunicated, judged by the very form of the sentence, compels the denial of a Catholic truth. Therefore such a sentence is void, and consequently a sentence that compels this is void; hence a sentence by which a Catholic truth is excommunicated, judged by the very form of the sentence, does not deserve to be called a sentence of excommunication, because it compels the denial of a Catholic truth; therefore such a sentence is void and binds no one. The third argument is this: the sentence of a heretic binds no one, as found in 24. quæst. 1. cap. audiamus. But if the said sentence of excommunication extends to Catholic truths, those who pronounce that sentence were heretics, for one who doubts the faith is an unbeliever and a heretic. Therefore one who condemns a Catholic truth by sentence is to be judged all the more a heretic. If, then, those who pronounced the said sentence were heretics, the sentence bound no one at all.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXI.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad primam instantiam, de vniuersitate Parisiensi factam supra capitulo decimo huius.
units.tr: In which the first objection is answered, concerning the University of Paris, raised above in chapter ten of this book.

units.la: Discipul. An excommunicantes ignorantes assertionem catholicam sint censendi hæretici, postea diligenter inquiram, & ideo ad propositum reuertar, & modo ad præfatam sententiam seu instantiam de vniuersitate Parisiensi, qualiter respondetur enarra. Magist. Sunt quidam dicentes, quod Vniuersitas Parisiensis multas assertiones temerarie excommunicauit, & ideo non, quia illas assertiones putant sapere orthodoxam veritatem: sed quia quo quomodo repugnant fidei orthodoxæ, non apparet. Alii dicunt, quod ideo dicta excommunicatio fuit temeraria reputanda, quia excommunicantes potestatem, quam non habebant, indebite vsurpauerunt, & ideo iuste fuit sententia postea eadem reuocata. Adhuc est quarta responsio, quod episcopus Parisiensis auctoritate Apostolicæ sedis rite eandem tulit sententiam, damnare autem assertionem hæreticam auctoritate Apostolicæ sedis ad inferiorem summo Pontifice potest licite pertinere. Discipulus Sitam damnans solenniter assertionem catholicam, quam reuocans ritam & iustam damnationem hæreticæ prauitatis sit iudicandus hæreticus, de quo inferius interrogationes tibi proponentur, necessario concedendum est, quod ferentes dictam sententiam excommunicationis contra opiniones Theologiæ, vel postea reuocantes eandem, sint inter hæreticos computandi. Magister. Quibusdam videtur, quod ferentes aliique reuocantes sunt hæretici reputandi, sed qui verius dicant sciri non potest, nisi præcognoscendo an assertiones damnatæ & postea reuocatæ, hæreticæ vel catholicæ sint censendæ.
units.tr: Disciple. I will examine later whether those who excommunicate while ignorant of a catholic assertion are to be counted heretics; for now I will return to my purpose. Tell me how the aforementioned sentence or objection about the University of Paris is answered. Master. Some say that the University of Paris rashly excommunicated many assertions, and not because they think those assertions savour of orthodox truth, but because it does not appear how they conflict with the orthodox faith. Others say that the said excommunication must be regarded as rash because those who excommunicated usurped a power they did not have, and so the sentence was rightly revoked afterwards. There is a fourth answer: the bishop of Paris, by the authority of the Apostolic See, duly pronounced the same sentence, and it may lawfully belong to an inferior to condemn a heretical assertion by the authority of the Apostolic See, the supreme Pontiff being above him. Disciple. If one who solemnly condemns a catholic assertion, which afterwards he revokes, must be judged a heretic, as the just and rightful condemnation of heretical depravity, about which questions will be put to you below, then it must necessarily be conceded that those who pronounce that sentence of excommunication against the opinions of theology, or who afterwards revoke it, are to be counted among the heretics. Master. Some think that those who pronounce it and those who revoke it are to be regarded as heretics, but those who speak more truly say that it cannot be known unless one first learns whether the assertions condemned and afterwards revoked are to be judged heretical or catholic.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad instantiam secundam supra cap. 19. factam.
units.tr: In which an answer is given to the second objection raised above in chapter 19.

units.la: Discipulus. De illa instantia non amplius te intromittas: sed dic, quomodo ad secundam instantiam respondetur. Magister. Illa instantia comprehendit duas, quarum prima est de primo archiepiscopo, qui fuit de ordine Prædicatorum. Secunda est de secundo archiepiscopo, qui fuit ordinis minorum. De primo diuersis modis dicitur à diuersis. Dicunt enim quidam, quod damnatio sua temeraria existebat, eo quod veritates, ut dicunt, condemnauit. Unde quidam alius archiepiscopus ipsum de dicta damnatione acriter reprehendit, scribens ei epistolam, in qua manifeste asseruit, quod veritates damnauerat. Multi enim putantes ipsum veritates damnasse, quod fuerit hæreticus, neque quam affirmant: quia (ut dicunt) nullam catholicam veritatem, sed plures veritates philosophicas cas condemnauit, de assertionibus autem grammaticalibus, logicalibus & pure philosophicis in eadem damnatione se (vt asserunt) temere intromisit. Discipul. An ille propter illam damnationem fuerit haereticus reputandus, sciri non potest, nisi assertiones discuterentur, quas damnauit, quod ad praesens non intendo, sed posito quod damnasset aliquam assertionem, quae in rei veritate est praecipue physica, tanquam haereticam, nunquid fuisset haereticus? Magist. Quidam dicunt quod sic: quia pertinaciter dicens aliquid esse de veritate fidei, quod ad fidem non pertinet, est haereticus iudicandus. Discipul. De hoc postea perscrutabor: ideo ad propositum redeundum principale, & dic an aliqui alii praeter archiepiscopos, de quibus dixisti, senserunt fuisse temerariam damnationem praedictam. Magist. Plures alii ipsam fuisse temerariam reputarunt, plures enim Parisienses Doctores & Scholares assertiones damnatas a dicto archiepiscopo publice tenuerunt, nam opinionem Thomae de vnitate formae in homine inter alias condemnauit: & tamen tu scis, quod plures Parisiis ipsam publice tenent, & defendunt & docent: & ita est de multis aliis. Discipul. Dic aliam responsionem ad instantiam supradictam. Magist. Alii dicunt, quod dictus archiepiscopus dictos articulos temere condemnauit: non quia inter illas veritates aliquae sint damnatae: sed quia sibi potestatem, quam non habuit, vsurpauit. Discip. Isti reprehendendo dictam damnationem primo fundamento solummodo, quod scilicet nullus inferior summo pontifice habet potestatem aliquam assertionem tanquam haereticam condemnandi, inniti videntur. Magist. Non est, vt dicis, quia isti non solum innituntur fundamento praefato, sed etiam asserunt, quod assertiones praecipue physicae, quae ad Theologiam non pertinent, non sunt ab aliquo solenniter condemnandae seu interdicendae, quia in talibus quilibet debet esse liber vt libere dicat quod sibi placet, & ideo quia dictus archiepiscopus damnauit & interdixit opiniones grammaticales, logicales & pure physicas, sua sententia fuit temeraria reputanda. Discip. An liceat alicui tales assertiones damnare, nolo ad praesens inquirere: sed indica, si ad saepe dictam instantiam aliter respondetur. Magist. Sunt quidam tenentes, quod quilibet episcopus habet potestatem damnandi haereses, ex quo sibi patenter in notescit, quod fidei obuiant orthodoxe. Discipul. Isti negant, quod prius probasti, scilicet quod sola apostolica sedes potest terminare quaestionem motam de fide, unde non curo, quod plus loquaris de illo archiepiscopo: sed dic, quid dicitur etiam de secundo. Magist. Quidam putant ipsum temerarie condemnasse opiniones Thomae, quia continent veritatem, quidam autem, quia ad eum quamcunq; assertionem damnare minime pertinebat. Quidam vero dicunt, quod rite damnauit; quod illae opiniones fidei obuiant orthodoxae. Et quod illa opinio de vnitate formae in homine doctrinae ecclesiae manifeste repugnat, quae docet quod idem fuit corpus Christi viuum & mortuum. Et quilibet episcopus habet potestatem damnandi assertiones doctrinae ecclesiae repugnantes.
units.tr: Disciple. Do not pursue that objection any further, but tell me how the second objection is answered. Master. That objection contains two parts. The first concerns the first archbishop, who was of the Order of Preachers. The second concerns the second archbishop, who was of the Order of Friars Minor. Different people speak in different ways about the first. Some say that his condemnation was rash, because (they say) he condemned truths. For this reason another archbishop reproached him sharply for that condemnation, writing him a letter in which he clearly asserted that he had condemned truths. Many people, thinking that he condemned truths, do not deny that he was a heretic, but they assert that he condemned no Catholic truth; rather, he condemned several philosophical truths, and in that condemnation he (they claim) rashly meddled with grammatical, logical and purely philosophical assertions. Disciple. Whether he should be regarded as a heretic on account of that condemnation cannot be known unless the assertions he condemned are examined. I do not intend to do that for now. But suppose he condemned as heretical some assertion which in the truth of the matter is chiefly physical. Would he then have been a heretic? Master. Some say yes, because someone who obstinately asserts that something belongs to the truth of the faith when it does not belong to the faith is to be judged a heretic. Disciple. I will look into this later. Therefore let us return to our main point, and tell me whether any others besides the archbishops you mentioned have judged that condemnation to be rash. Master. Many others have judged it rash. Indeed, many teachers and scholars at Paris openly held the assertions condemned by that archbishop. For among other things he condemned the opinion of Thomas on the unity of form in man, and yet you know that many in Paris publicly hold, defend and teach it, and it is the same with many other opinions. Disciple. Give me another answer to the objection above. Master. Others say that the said archbishop rashly condemned those articles, not because any of those truths were condemned, but because he usurped a power he did not have. Disciple. Those who object to that condemnation seem to rest only on the first foundation, namely that no one below the supreme pontiff has any power to condemn an assertion as heretical. Master. That is not so, as you say, because these people not only rest on the foundation just mentioned, but also assert that assertions which are chiefly physical and do not belong to theology are not to be solemnly condemned or forbidden by anyone, because in such matters everyone ought to be free to say freely what pleases him. Therefore, because the said archbishop condemned and forbade grammatical, logical and purely physical opinions, his sentence is to be regarded as rash. Disciple. I do not wish to inquire for now whether it is lawful for anyone to condemn such assertions. But tell me whether the objection I mentioned so often is answered in some other way. Master. There are some who hold that every bishop has the power to condemn heresies, since it is plainly evident to him that they oppose the orthodox faith. Disciple. Those people deny what you proved earlier, namely that only the apostolic see can settle a question raised concerning the faith. So I do not care that you say more about that archbishop; tell me what is said about the second one. Master. Some think that he rashly condemned the opinions of Thomas because they contain the truth, while others think so because it did not belong to him at all to condemn any assertion. Still others say that he rightly condemned them, because those opinions oppose the orthodox faith. They also say that the opinion on the unity of form in man manifestly contradicts the teaching of the Church, which teaches that the same body of Christ was living and dead. And any bishop has the power to condemn assertions that contradict the teaching of the Church.

units.la: CAP. XXIII. In quo respondetur ad instantiam tertiam supra capitulo 19. factam.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII. In which an answer is given to the third objection raised above in chapter 19.

units.la: Discipulus. Narra quomodo respondetur ad tertiam instantiam de ordine Minorum, qui damnauit doctrinam Petri Iohannis. Magist. Ad illam multipliciter respondetur. Ad cuius euidentiam debes scire, quod de doctrina Petri Iohannis diversi diversimode sentiunt. Quidam enim putant totam doctrinam suam esse catholicam. Quidam aestimant quod nihil in ea inuenitur, quod haeresim sapiat manifestam, multa tamen falsa & fantastica continet: & praecipue cum futura praedicit. Alii reputant, quod haereses continet manifestas.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how one answers the third objection concerning the order of Minorites, who condemned the teaching of Peter John. Master. That objection is answered in several ways. To make this clear, you must know that people judge the teaching of Peter John in different ways. Some think that all his teaching is catholic. Others judge that nothing in it savours of manifest heresy, though it contains many false and fanciful things, especially when it foretells the future. Others hold that it contains manifest heresies.

units.la: Primi & secundi tenent, quod ordo Minorum dictam doctrinam temerarie condemnauit: imo nonnulli putant quod damnantes incurrerunt haereticam pravitatem: quia damnare sententialiter catholicam veritatem efficit damnantem haereticum pertinacem. Tertii variant, quidam enim licet reputent doctrinam Petri Iohannis esse haereticam, tamen Ordo antedictus temere condemnauit eandem potestatem, quam non habuit, vsurpando. Alii dicunt quod condemnantes nequaquam temere processerunt: quia processerunt auctoritate papae, & dicunt quod Nicolaus quartus eandem doctrinam mandauit condemnari. Tertii dicunt specialiter de illo capitulo Massiliensi, quod non temere condemnauit praedictam doctrinam; quia solum damnauit vel potius damnata declarauit vel pronunciauit ea, quae prius per concilium generale vel per aliquem Romanum pontificem damnata fuerunt vel quae aperte contradicebant scripturae diuinae. Discip. Illa vltima sententia magis mihi placet, pro eo praecipue, quod nec Ordini antedicto attribuit vsurpasse potestatem antedictam, quam non habuit, nec damnationi sanctissimi patris Domini Innocent. papae 22. noscitur obuiare: & ideo ipsam, quantum poteris, fulcire nitere. Magist. Istam sententiam declarare non possem, nisi articulos damnatos & acta Ordinis saepe dicti, ac etiam doctrinam fratris Petri praefati, de qua dicti articuli sunt accepti haberem, tu autem scis, quod nullum habeo praedictorum, & forte illi de Ordine nolunt mihi communicare praedicta.
units.tr: The first and second groups hold that the aforesaid Order condemned that teaching rashly. Some even think that those who condemned it fell into heretical depravity, because to condemn catholic truth by a formal sentence makes the one who condemns it a stubborn heretic. The third group differ among themselves. Some, though they consider Peter John's teaching heretical, hold that the said Order condemned it rashly, by usurping a power it did not have. Others say that the condemners did not proceed rashly at all, because they acted by the authority of the pope, and they say that Nicholas IV ordered this same teaching to be condemned. Others say, with respect to that chapter of Marseille in particular, that it did not condemn the said teaching rashly, since it only condemned, or rather declared and pronounced condemned, those things which had previously been condemned by a general council or by some Roman pontiff, or which openly contradicted divine Scripture. Disciple. I like that last opinion better, chiefly because it does not attribute to the aforesaid Order the usurpation of a power it did not have, nor is it seen to oppose the condemnation of the most holy father, our Lord Pope Innocent XXII. So I urge you to support it as far as you can. Master. I could not set out that opinion unless I had the condemned articles, the acts of the Order often mentioned, and also the teaching of the aforesaid Brother Peter from which those articles were taken. But you know that I have none of these, and perhaps the men of that Order are unwilling to share them with me.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: Vbi inquiritur, si quis inferior Papa possit licite quamcunq; assertionem non damna- tam explicite, tanquam hæreticam excommunicare vel damnare, vbi speciali- ter assignatur causa de opinione Thomæ, quare fuerit condemnata.
units.tr: Where it is inquired whether any inferior to the Pope may lawfully excommunicate or condemn any assertion not explicitly condemned, as heretical, where the cause for the condemnation of Thomas's opinion is specifically stated.

units.la: Discipulus. Ex quo illam sententiam vltimam declarare non potes, declarationem eiusdem vsq; ad aliud tempus (si forte prædicta ab eodem Ordine habere potueris) differamus: sed dic an aliqui sint, qui teneant quod aliquis inferior summo pontifice valeat licite quamcunque assertionem non damnatam explicite tanquam hæreticam excommunicare vel damnare. Magist. Ad hoc respondent quidam dicentes: quod quamuis non liceat alicui inferiori papa damnare &c. Licet tamen collegiis aliis & prælatis inferioribus papa assertiones erroneas ex causa rationabili interdicere, & præcipere, quod nullatenus publice defendantur. Et ideo dicunt, quod si Vniuersitas Parisiens & Cantuariens archiepiscopi sæpe fati ex causa rationabili opiniones Thomæ interdixissent, tantummodo præcipiendo quod publice eas non defenderent ac docerent Parisiis & ad sententiam excommunicationis & damnationis opinionum earundem nullatenus processissent, nil temerarie commississent. Discipul. An potest esse causa rationabilis præcipiendi opiniones aliquas publice non teneri. Magist. Dicunt quod pro scandalo & schismate aliisq; malis & periculis euitandis possunt opiniones aliquæ & quæstiones veræ rationabiliter interdici. Discip. Nunquid fuit vnquam aliquod scandalum de opinionibus Thomæ? Magist. Sæpe audiui à multis Anglis & Britonibus enarrare, quod de opinione Thomæ de vnitate formæ, quando conclusiones, quæ ex ipsa sequuntur, explicabantur, scandalum fuit in Anglia prope infinitum. Discipul. Quæ fuerunt illæ conclusiones sequentes ex opinione Thomæ de vnitate formæ, quæ expresse scandalizabant populum. Magist. Secundum istos subscriptæ sunt. Quod corpus Christi non fuit idem numero vnum & mortuum: & quod corpus Christi, quod iacuit in sepulchro, in ipso triduo nunquam fuit corpus Christi dum viueret: quod corpus & reliquiæ, quæ à fidelibus pro corporibus sanctorum & reliquiis venerantur, nunquam fuerunt corpora nec partes sanctorum dum viuerent: nec corpora mortua vnquam fuerunt corpora viuentium, quod caro mortua nunquam fuit viua. Discipul. Satis certificasti de conclusionibus sequentibus ex opinione de vnitate formæ substantialis, & ideo ad propositum redeundo explica rationes (si quæ sunt) pro assertione supradicta. Magist. Assertionem suam probant tali ratione. Omne illud, quod potest licite præterminiti à subditis, potest ex causa rationabili à prælatis & iurisdictionem habentibus super subditos interdici, nam qui potest & debet omnibus vtilitatibus omnium intendere & prouidere; potest & periculis obuiare, & in talibus licitis & honestis omnes subditos obedire, vt colligitur ex sacris canonibus 9. q. 4. c. si autem & c. si quis & c. absit. Sed opiniones aliquas non defendere, non docere, est licitum: imo quandoque expediens & necessarium, ergo potest à prælatis & collegiis iurisdictionem habentibus ex causa rationabili interdici. Discipul. Secundum hanc rationem liceret quandoque prælatis interdicere veritates, nam quandoque tacere veritatem est expediens. Magist. Interdicere veritatem omnibus & pro omni tempore non licet secundum istos: sed aliquibus tantum & pro aliquo tempore impedire, ne veritates aliquas docere præsumant, licet, sicut dicit Apostolus, mulieri docere non permitto, & Dominus in Euang. ait: nolite sanctum dare canibus, neque mittatis margaritas ante porcos. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod nec omnibus nec omni tempore veritatem expedit vel prædicare aut docere vel defendere. Discipul. Ex hoc videtur, quod nulli licet opiniones seu assertiones aliquas damnare: neque omnibus & pro omni tempore interdicere, licet aliquibus & pro aliquo tempore licite ipsas interdicere possint. Magist. Hanc conclusionem ipsi concedunt, & ideo signanter dicunt, quod ex causa rationabili, licet inferioribus aliquas assertiones interdicere per hoc insinuantes, quod cessante causa cessat interdictum.
units.tr: Student. Since you cannot explain that last opinion, let us postpone its explanation until another time (if perhaps you are able to obtain the aforesaid materials from the same Order). But tell me whether there are some who hold that any inferior to the supreme pontiff may lawfully excommunicate or condemn any assertion not explicitly condemned, as heretical. Master. Some answer this, saying that although it is not lawful for any inferior to the Pope to condemn, etc., nevertheless it is permitted to other colleges and inferior prelates of the Pope, for a reasonable cause, to forbid erroneous assertions and to command that they not be publicly defended in any way. And so they say that if the University of Paris and the archbishop of Canterbury, often mentioned, had for a reasonable cause forbidden the opinions of Thomas, merely commanding that they should not publicly defend or teach them at Paris, and had not proceeded to the sentence of excommunication and condemnation of those opinions, they would have committed nothing rashly. Student. Can there be a reasonable cause for commanding that certain opinions not be publicly held? Master. They say that for avoiding scandal, schism, and other evils and dangers, certain opinions and true questions can reasonably be forbidden. Student. Has there ever been any scandal about the opinions of Thomas? Master. I have often heard many Englishmen and Britons relate that, when the conclusions which follow from Thomas's opinion on the unity of form were explained, there was an almost infinite scandal in England. Student. What were those conclusions following from Thomas's opinion on the unity of form which expressly scandalized the people? Master. According to them, the following were set out: that the body of Christ was not the same numerically, one and dead; and that the body of Christ which lay in the sepulchre was never the body of Christ during those very three days while he lived; that the bodies and relics which the faithful venerate as the bodies of saints and as relics were never the bodies or parts of saints while they lived; nor were dead bodies ever the bodies of living persons, and that dead flesh was never living flesh. Student. You have sufficiently explained the conclusions following from the opinion on the unity of substantial form; so, returning to our subject, explain the reasons (if any there are) for the aforesaid assertion. Master. They prove their assertion by this reasoning: Whatever may lawfully be neglected by subjects may, for a reasonable cause, be forbidden by prelates who have jurisdiction over subjects. For whoever can and ought to attend to and provide for the advantage of all may also meet dangers, and in such lawful and honest matters all subjects are bound to obey, as is gathered from the sacred canons, 9 q. 4, c. si autem, c. si quis, and c. absit. But not to defend or teach certain opinions is lawful, indeed sometimes expedient and necessary; therefore it can, for a reasonable cause, be forbidden by prelates and colleges having jurisdiction. Student. According to this reasoning it would sometimes be lawful for prelates to forbid truths, for sometimes it is expedient to keep silent about a truth. Master. According to them, it is not lawful to forbid truth to everyone and at all times; but it is lawful to hinder some persons, and for some time, from presuming to teach certain truths, as the Apostle says, I do not permit a woman to teach, and the Lord in the Gospel says, Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine. From these words it is gathered that it is not expedient to preach, teach, or defend the truth either to all persons or at all times. Student. From this it seems that no one may condemn any opinions or assertions, nor forbid them to everyone and at all times, although they may lawfully forbid them to some and for some time. Master. They concede this conclusion, and therefore expressly say that, for a reasonable cause, it is permitted to inferiors to forbid certain assertions, thereby implying that when the cause ceases, the prohibition ceases.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Notat, quo fundamento debeat inniti Papa, vel concilium generale damnando aliquam assertionem explicite prius non damnatam, tanquam hæreticam, & ponuntur tres modi dicendi circa illud.
units.tr: Shows on what foundation the Pope, or a general council, must rest when condemning as heretical an assertion not previously condemned explicitly, and sets out three ways of speaking about it.

units.la: Discipulus. Licet circa prædicta mihi multæ dubitationes occurrant, illis tamen prætermissis ad intentum principale reuertor, mihi autem videtur probabile, quod nullus inferior papa potest aliquam assertionem non damnatam explicite tanquam hæreticam excommunicare vel damnare explicite: sed adhuc ignoro quo fundamento papa vel concilium generale indamnando explicite aliquam assertionem non damnatam tanquam hæreticam debet inniti. Vnde de hoc quid sentiunt tiantliterati dicere non postponas. Magist. Circa interrogationem tuam opiniones contrarias recitabo Dicunt enim quidam tenentes, quod tantæ auctoritatis est papa, quod ad placitum potest quamcunque assertionem tanquam hæreticam damnare, & isti dicuntur esse imitatores papæ Sergii persecutoris papæ Formosi: qui, vt in quodam libro de antiquissima litera legi in tantum volebant papam extollere, quod asserebant papam non posse damnari: sed quod quicquid faceret, salvaretur, ita isti dicunt, quod quicquid papa diffinit esse tenendum, omnes tenere & credere, hinc dicit Gloss. distinct. 9. c. si Romanorum: Illud quod papa approbat vel reprobat, nos approbare vel reprobare debemus. Discipul. Ista assertio sonat, quod papa hæreticari non potest, de quo postea interrogationem specialem habebo. Ideo de hoc pro nunc transeamus, & monstra vt promisisti assertionem contrariam. Magist. Alii asserunt manifeste, quod papa & concilium generale ac etiam vniversalis ecclesia, si recte damnat aliquam assertionem tanquam hæreticam, stricte loquendo de assertione hæretica, vni vel pluribus de tribus fundamentis debet inniti & se patenter fundare. Primum est super sacram scripturam, & isti fundamento innitebantur concilia generalia principalia, hæreses Arri, Macedonii, Nestorii, Eutichis & Dioscori condemnando, sicut enim aliqua istorum conciliorum condendo symbola in auctoritate sacræ scripturæ se fundabant, teste Isidoro, qui, vt habetur dist. 15. c. 1. ait: Sancti patres in concilio Niceno de omni orbe terrarum convenientes iuxta fidem catholicam & apostolicam post Apostolos symbolum tradiderunt: isti hæreses condemnando pro fundamento sacras literas posuerunt. Sic etiam Alex. tertius damnando assertionem dicentem, quod Christus non est aliquid secundum quod homo, in hac veritate à diuina scriptura accepta, Christus est verus Deus & homo, se fundauit. Sic etiam sancti Doctores reprobando ipsas per scripturas conuincere conabantur, sicut in libris eorum patenter habetur, vnde & Isidorus, vt habetur 24. q. 3. c. notandum, plures hæreses per scripturas sacras arguit euidenter. Secundum fundamentum est, doctrina Apostolica in scripturis Apostolicis non redacta, sed relatione succedentium fidelium vel scripturis fide dignis ad nos peruenit, & isti fundamento innititur Nicolaus papa, qui, vt habetur c. omnes, in decretis, dist. 22. vbi patenter colligitur diffiniens, hæreticum fore censendum, dicere ecclesiam Romanam non esse caput omnium ecclesiarum, cum tamen de hoc in scripturis sacris mentio minime habeatur: sed hoc Apostoli tradiderunt & docuerunt fideles, quæ doctrinæ relatione fidelium sibi succedentium & scripturis sanctorum patrum ad nos peruenerunt. Pro hoc faciunt rationes & auctoritates, quas supra (cum tractarem interrogationem tuam, quæ veritates sunt catholicæ reputandæ) adduxi. Tertium fundamentum est, reuelatio vel inspiratio noua diuina. Si enim aliqua veritas æterna, quæ pertinet ad salutem, de nouo reuelaretur ecclesiæ: ista esset tanquam catholica approbanda & omnem falsitatem ei contrariam posset ecclesia & etiam papa tanquam hæreticam condemnare. Et quamuis isti exemplum nesciant inuenire (quod vnquam ecclesia aliquam hæresim condemnando se in tali reuelatione vel inspiratione fundauerit) tamen dicunt, quod hoc non est impossibile: quia posset Deus, si sibi placeret, multas veritates catholicas nouiter reuelare vel inspirare. Discipul. Quid si papa, vel etiam concilium generale dicat, sibi aliquam veritatem esse reuelatam à Deo, vel etiam inspiratam: nunquid alii fideles credere astringuntur? Magist. Dicunt isti, quod absque miraculo manifesto non est eis credendum: quia non sufficit nude asserere, quod eis est veritas reuelata vel etiam inspirata: sed oportet quod talem reuelationem seu inspirationem miraculi operatione confirment apta. Discip. Quid dicerent isti, si omnes Christiani nullo excepto aliquam assertionem tanquam hæreticam firmiter acceptarent, quam tamen nec ex scripturis diuinis, nec ex aliqua doctrina ab ecclesia procedente possent ostendere. Magist. Dicunt quod talis veritas esset tanquam catholica acceptanda: quia talis concors adhæsio omnium Christianorum nullo excepto alicui assertioni huiusmodi sine miraculo non potest contingere, cum enim omnes fideles firmissime teneant, quod iuxta promissionem Saluatoris, Matthæi vltimo, vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem seculi, ecclesia vniversalis nunquam errabit, constat quod sine speciali inspiratione diuina nunquam ecclesia vniuersalis assertioni, quæ non dependet ex doctrina ecclesiæ præcedenti, firmiter adhærebit, & ideo tunc miraculum fieri esset credendum. Discipul. Quid sentiunt, si omnes Christiani propter paucos vel vnum assertioni tali (quæ ex doctrina ecclesiæ præcedenti probari non posset) adhærerent? Magist. Dicunt, quod si vnus solus dissentiret, non esset talis veritas acceptanda: quia in vno solo potest stare tota fides ecclesiæ, quemadmodum tempore mortis Christi tota fides ecclesiæ in sola beata virgine remanebat, nec est etiam credendum, quod omni tempore post tempora Apostolorum fuerint aliqui magis accepti Deo, quam fuerint Apostoli ante mortem Christi. Si ergo Christus post crucifixionem suam permisit cunctos Apostolos à fide catholica deuiare, & solam beatam virginem firmiter permanere in fide: temerarium est asserere, quod nunquam ante finem mundi Deus permittat totam multitudinem Christianorum præter vnum à fide recedere orthodoxa. Discipul. Ista nescio improbare: sed videtur quod ad hoc, vt omnes catholici teneantur alicui veritati nouiter reuelatæ firmiter adhærere: non sufficit eam operatione miraculi confirmare: cum per malos & infideles fiant mirabilia, sicut ex verbis euangelii Matt. 7. colligitur, & apparet Christo dicente: multi dicent mihi in illa die, Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetauimus, & in nomine tuo Daemonia eiecimus, & in nomine tuo multas virtutes fecimus, confitebor illis quia nunquam noui vos: hoc est, nunquam approbaui vos, huic etiam concordat Glo. ext. de haer. cum ex iniuncto, vbi habet, quod Quandoque, mirabilia fiunt per malos. Mag. Ad istam obiectionem respondent, dicentes, quod licet per malos fiant mirabilia: nunquam tamen fit verum miraculum ad confirmationem falsitatis assertæ p malos, & ideo quia docent aliquem errorem ad confirmationem illius erroris, nunquam fit verum miraculum, sed si praedicant veritatem, quamuis sint mali, fiunt aliquando mirabilia ad confirmationem veritatis, sicut Iudas proditor, quamuis fuerit malus, quia tamen docuit veritatem, miracula faciebat, quando ergo fit verum miraculum ad assertionem aliquam confirmandam, tenendum est indubie, quod talis assertio pro vera debet haberi, & hoc siue illi quibus revelata fuerint inter bonos, siue inter mafos computentur. Discipul. Ista responsio est apparens, unde quae dixisti de illa secunda sententia sufficiant: sed si nosti aliquos aliter dicere, non differas indicare. Magist. Nonnulli putant, quod tam concilium generale, quam etiam papa in damnando aliquam assertionem tanquam haereticam in sacra scriptura diuina sola debet se fundare: quia solae veritates in scriptura sacra contentae & quae sequuntur ex eis catholicae sunt censendae. De hac sententia tractatus praecedens te poterit informare.
units.tr: Disciple. Although many doubts occur to me about what has been said, I will set them aside and return to the main question. It seems probable to me that no inferior pope can excommunicate or explicitly condemn as heretical an assertion that has not been explicitly condemned. But I still do not know on what foundation the Pope or a general council must rest when explicitly condemning as heretical an assertion not previously condemned. So do not delay in telling me what the learned think about this. Master. In answer to your question I will recite the opposing opinions. Some hold that the Pope has such authority that he may at will condemn any assertion as heretical. These are said to imitate Pope Sergius, the persecutor of Pope Formosus. As I have read in a certain book on the most ancient letter, they wished to exalt the Pope so far that they asserted that the Pope cannot be condemned, but whatever he does, he is saved. So these men say that whatever the Pope defines is to be held, and that everyone must hold and believe it. Hence the Gloss says on distinction 9, chapter si Romanorum: What the Pope approves or rejects, we must approve or reject. Disciple. That statement implies that the Pope cannot be declared a heretic, about which I will later ask a separate question. So let us pass over this for now, and, as you promised, show me the opposing assertion. Master. Others plainly assert that the Pope and a general council, and also the universal Church, if they rightly condemn an assertion as heretical (speaking strictly of a heretical assertion), must rest and plainly base themselves on one or more of three foundations. The first is Holy Scripture. The chief general councils relied on this foundation when they condemned the heresies of Arius, Macedonius, Nestorius, Eutyches and Dioscorus. For when some of these councils drew up creeds, they based them on the authority of Holy Scripture, as Isidore attests, who says in distinction 15, chapter 1: The holy fathers, gathered at the Council of Nicaea from the whole world, handed down a creed after the Apostles, in accordance with the catholic and apostolic faith. In condemning these heresies, they took the sacred letters as their foundation. So too Alexander III, in condemning the assertion that Christ is not something according to his manhood, based himself on this truth received from divine Scripture, that Christ is true God and man. So too the holy Doctors, in refuting such errors, tried to convict them by Scriptures, as is plainly found in their books. Hence Isidore also, as is found in 24 q. 3, chapter notandum, clearly refutes many heresies by sacred Scriptures. The second foundation is apostolic doctrine that was not committed to the Apostles' writings, but has come down to us through the report of faithful successors or through trustworthy writings. Pope Nicholas relied on this foundation, as found in chapter omnes, in the Decretum, distinction 22, where he plainly defines that it must be judged heretical to say that the Roman Church is not the head of all churches, although there is hardly any mention of this in the sacred Scriptures. But the Apostles handed this down and taught it to the faithful, and this doctrine has come to us through the report of the faithful who succeeded them and through the writings of the holy Fathers. The reasons and authorities that I adduced above, when I was dealing with your question about which truths are to be regarded as catholic, favour this view. The third foundation is a new divine revelation or inspiration. For if some eternal truth pertaining to salvation were newly revealed to the Church, it would have to be approved as catholic, and the Church, and even the Pope, could condemn as heretical every falsehood contrary to it. And although these men cannot find an example of the Church ever having based its condemnation of some heresy on such a revelation or inspiration, they say that this is not impossible, since God could, if it pleased him, newly reveal or inspire many catholic truths. Disciple. What if the Pope, or even a general council, were to say that some truth had been revealed or inspired to them by God? Are other believers bound to believe it? Master. These men say that it must not be believed without a manifest miracle, because it is not enough merely to assert that a truth has been revealed or inspired to them. They must confirm such a revelation or inspiration by the working of a miracle that is suited to it. Disciple. What would these men say if all Christians, without exception, firmly accepted some assertion as not heretical, although they could show it neither from divine Scriptures nor from any doctrine proceeding from the Church? Master. They say that such a truth would have to be accepted as catholic, because such a united adherence of all Christians, without exception, to an assertion of this kind cannot come about without a miracle. For since all the faithful hold most firmly, according to the promise of the Saviour in the last chapter of Matthew, I am with you always, to the end of the age, that the universal Church will never err, it is clear that without special divine inspiration the universal Church would never firmly cling to an assertion that does not depend on the preceding doctrine of the Church. Therefore a miracle would then have to be believed to have occurred. Disciple. What do they think if all Christians adhered to such an assertion on the authority of a few, or of one, when it could not be proved from the preceding doctrine of the Church? Master. They say that if only one person dissented, such a truth would not have to be accepted. For the whole faith of the Church can rest in a single person, just as at the time of Christ's death the whole faith of the Church remained in the blessed Virgin alone. Nor is it to be believed that at any time after the Apostles there have been anyone more acceptable to God than the Apostles were before the death of Christ. If, then, after his crucifixion Christ allowed all the Apostles to turn aside from the catholic faith, and only the blessed Virgin to remain firm in the faith, it is rash to assert that God never before the end of the world will allow the whole multitude of Christians, except one, to fall away from the orthodox faith. Disciple. I do not know how to refute these points. But it seems that, for all Catholics to be bound to cling firmly to some newly revealed truth, it is not enough to confirm it by the working of a miracle, since wonders are also worked through evil and unfaithful men. This is gathered from the words of the Gospel, Matthew 7, where Christ says: Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and done many mighty works in your name? Then I will declare to them, I never knew you; that is, I never approved of you. The Gloss on ext. de haer., cum ex iniuncto agrees with this, where it says that sometimes wonders are wrought through evil men. Master. To this objection they reply that although wonders may be wrought through evil men, a true miracle is never wrought to confirm a falsehood asserted by evil men. And so, when they teach some error in order to confirm that error, no true miracle occurs. But if they preach the truth, then, although they are evil, wonders sometimes occur to confirm the truth, as Judas the traitor, although he was evil, nevertheless worked miracles because he taught the truth. Therefore, when a true miracle occurs to confirm some assertion, it must without doubt be held that this assertion is to be regarded as true, whether those to whom it was revealed are counted among the good or among the wicked. Disciple. That answer seems plausible, so what you have said about that second opinion will suffice. But if you know of others who say otherwise, do not hesitate to point them out. Master. Some think that both a general council and the Pope, in condemning some assertion as heretical, must base themselves on divine Scripture alone, because only the truths contained in Holy Scripture, and those that follow from them, are to be regarded as catholic. The preceding treatise can inform you about this opinion.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: Chapter XXVI.

units.la: Quaerit de illa modificatione sc. damnamus, si necessario, requiratur ad hoc, ut ponatur explicite, quatenus catholici talem assertionem habeant reprobare ut haereticam.
units.tr: He asks about that qualification, namely "we condemn", whether it is necessarily required, so that it must be stated explicitly, insofar as Catholics are to reject such an assertion as heretical.

units.la: Discipulus. Satis aduerto ex praecedentibus, quomodo illa sententia fulciri potest, & quomodo etiam poterit improbari: & ideo ad quaestionem aliam me converto, adhuc enim nescio an ad hoc quod catholici aliquam assertionem habere debeant pro damnata explicite, oporteat in damnationem talem vel aequipollentem modificationE vel specificationE vel determinationE tanquam haereticam vel veritati catholicae inimicam adiungere taliter vel aequipollenter proferendo sententiam talem assertionem tanquam haereticam vel veritati catholicae inimicam damnamus, unde circa hoc unam vel plures monstra sententias. Magist. Ad hoc dicunt, seu respondent dupliciter, quidam enim dicunt, quod talis modificatio seu determinatio in sententia est ponenda ad hoc, ut assertio improbata pro haeresi damnata explicite habeatur, quia dicunt quod assertio, quae non est damnata, tanquam haeretica haberi non debet. Alii dicunt quod ad hoc quod assertio, quae non est damnata tanquam pro haeretica habeatur, sufficit (absque determinatione tali) quod ipsa falsa assertio reprobetur vel veritas contraria explicite approbetur, & quod talis approbatio vel reprobatio fundetur in catholica veritate. Sic Alexand. Tertius interdicens & reprobans, ne aliquis dicat Christum non esse aliquid secundum quod homo: suam reprobationem fundauit in catholica veritate, ista videlicet: Christus est verus Deus & verus homo. Et ideo voluit, quod dicta assertio pro haeretica haberetur, licet talem determinationem (tanquam haereticam) condemnare vocaliter in sua probatione nequaquam expresserit.
units.tr: Disciple. I am sufficiently aware from what has gone before how that opinion can be supported, and how it can also be refuted. So I turn to another question. For I still do not know whether, in order that Catholics should hold some assertion as condemned explicitly, it is necessary to add to the condemnation such a qualification, specification or determination, as "as heretical" or "hostile to Catholic truth", by stating in such words or their equivalent: "we condemn this assertion as heretical or hostile to Catholic truth"; and on this point I ask you to show one or more opinions. Master. To this they answer in two ways. For some say that such a qualification or determination must be placed in the sentence, so that an assertion rejected is held as explicitly condemned for heresy, because they hold that an assertion which has not been condemned as heretical ought not to be regarded as heretical. Others say that, in order that an assertion which has not been condemned may be regarded as heretical, it is enough (without such a determination) that the false assertion itself be rejected, or the contrary truth be explicitly approved, and that such approval or rejection be grounded in Catholic truth. Thus Alexander III, forbidding and rejecting that anyone should say that Christ is not something according to his humanity, founded his rejection on Catholic truth, namely this: Christ is true God and true man. And so he wished that the said assertion be held as heretical, although he did not in his judgment expressly state in words that such a determination (as heretical) was condemned.

units.la: Hac etiam ratione probatur, nam veritas explicite approbata & in veritate catholica fundata pro catholica debet haberi, ergo & falsitas contraria debet haereticA iudicari, sed siue approbetur veritas, siue damnetur contraria falsitas, veritas approbatur: quia reprobatio vnius contradictoriorum est alterius approbatio: & econtrario, ergo talis assertio contraria veritati in fide fundata catholica haeretica est censenda & pro damnata explicite.
units.tr: This is also proved by this reasoning: for a truth explicitly approved and grounded in Catholic truth must be held as Catholic, therefore the contrary falsehood must also be judged heretical. But whether the truth is approved or the contrary falsehood condemned, the truth is approved, because the rejection of one of two contradictories is the approval of the other, and conversely. Therefore such an assertion contrary to a truth grounded in the Catholic faith is to be regarded as heretical and as explicitly condemned.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: Chapter XXVII.

units.la: In quo agitur de opinionibus Theologorum inter se diuersa sententium, in his etiam quae sunt fidei, & utrum hoc eis liceat, & Papa licite illos taliter opinari sinat, & ibi ponuntur duae opiniones circa praedicta.
units.tr: In which the opinions of theologians who differ from one another are discussed, including those on matters of faith, and whether this is permitted to them and whether the Pope lawfully allows them to hold such opinions. Two opinions on these matters are set out here.

units.la: Discipulus. Adhuc habeo quod de haeresum damnatione interrogem, mihi enim apparet, quod omnis error qualitercunque sic patenter, siue latenter scripturae diuinae obuians & repugnans, numero haeresum aggregatur, constat autem quod Theologi de his, quae spectant ad scripturam sacram, contraria opinantur: qui tamen omnes opiniones suas scriptura sacra fulcire nituntur; & per eandem scripturam sacram opiniones contrarias reprobare moliuntur, ergo aliquae dictarum opinionum contrariarum numero haeresum aggregantur, nunquid ergo papa damnabiliter peccat negligendo haereses huiusmodi condemnare? Magist. Quidam dicunt, quod papa in nullo peccat permittendo Theologos huiusmodi assertiones (quae sunt in rei veritate haereticae) opinando tenere, quod tali ratione videtur posse probari. Permittere licita non est peccatum: cum etiam quandoq; absq; peccato illicita permittantur, sed huiusmodi errores, qui non sunt damnati explicite, opinando tenere est illicitum, quia talis opinio, quando opinans paratus est corrigi, opinantem non reddit haereticum, ergo absque peccato permittit huiusmodi, quae in veritate sunt haereses, opinando teneri. Alii sentiunt, quod plures Romani pontifices damnabiliter in hoc peccauerunt. Quod probant per hoc, quod non solum haeretici, sed etiam haereses de ecclesia exstirpandae sunt, testante concilio generali, quod (prout habetur extra de haer. excommunicamus) episcopos indicat deponendos, q super exstirpando de suis dioecesibus haereticae pravitatis fermento negligentes fuerunt siue remissi. Ille ergo, ad quem spectat de officio sibi iniuncto haereses exstirpare, si negligens fuerit vel remissus, de damnabili negligentia vel regimine excusari non potest, sed ad summum pontificem spectat totam ecclesiam de haeresibus non solum iam damnatis explicite, sed etiam aliis quibuscunq; expurgare, ergo qui tales haereses sustinent teneri vel doceri, damnabiliter peccauerunt. Discip. Non videtur quod papa teneatur de omnibus haeresibus (quae non sunt damnatae explicite) purgare ecclesiam: sed sufficit sibi quod eam purget vel purgatam coleruet ab omni pravitate haeretica explicite iam damnata. Magist. Hoc improbant isti dicentes, quod papa qui haereses insurgentes de novo negligit improbare & damnare, Apostolos & sanctos patres, qui haereses pullulantes celerrime damnauerunt, nullatenus imitatur: quorum vestigiis tamen inhaerere oportet Romanum Pontificem, si eis vult in coelesti patri aggregari. Peccauerunt ergo summi pontifices, qui damnare haereses neglexerunt. Discip. Apostoli & sancti patres ideo haereses damnauerunt, quia inuenerunt pertinaces huiusmodi haeresum assertores, cum ergo Theologi haeresum, quas putant veritati catholicae minime obuiare, pertinaces non fuerint assertores, non fuerunt haereses (quas opinando solummodo docuerunt) per Romanos pontifices condemnandae. Magist. Istam excusationem Romanorum pontificum isti dupliciter nituntur impugnare. Primo quia nescierunt an Theologi suis opinionibus haereticis pertinaciter adhaeserunt, ex quo de hoc nullam inquisitionem omnino fecerunt, ergo inquirendo veritatem (ut periculis fidei obuiarent) negligentes & remissi fuerunt. Secundo sic: maiori periculo est fortius diligentius & celerius obuiandum, sed ex haeresibus publice opinatis & dogmatizatis maius imminet periculum religioni Christianae, quam ex consuetudinibus onerosis & prauis, quia esto quod dogmatizantes suis opinionibus minime pertinaciter adhaerent: tamen timendum est ne simplices Discipuli audientes assertiones huiusmodi a magnis doctoribus edoceri, & pro eis allegari fortiter, & a catholicis nullatenus condemnari, ex apparentia rationum, quas nesciunt soluere, in adhaesione pertinacem eisdem haeresibus inducantur, & ne haeresis pestiferae pro veritatibus catholicis incipiant venerari, & pertinaciter defensari sed consuetudines onerosae & prauae sunt celerrime comprimendae, ne in priuilegiorum ius ab ipsis assumantur, ut asserit Nicolaus papa, ut habetur dist. 8. c. male, ergo multo fortius haereses qualitercunque pullulauerint sunt euellendae radicitus & damnandae: ne a simplicibus & seducibilib. pro veritatibus catholicis approbentur. Discip. Ista ratio ultima est apparens: sed prima opinio apparentia carere videtur: quia secundum sacros canones non est aliqua inquisitio facienda, nisi prius fuerit diffamatus, ut habetur extra de accu. c. qualiter & quando, & in multis aliis locis, sed Theologi de haeresibus nullatenus diffamati fuerunt, ergo de eis summi pontificis non debuerunt inquirere. Magist. Dicunt illi, quod illa excusatio non est sufficiens, quia licet Theologi non fuerunt diffamati, quod essent haereticî, diffamabantur tamen: quia haereses docuerunt, unde etiam multi Theologi nunc putant, quod alii Theologi dogmatizant haereses, quamuis nolint asserere quod sint inter haereticos computandi. Multi etiam cum assertione forte putant, quod omnes opiniones Thomae, qui quondam fuerunt damnatae Parisiis, sint haereticae iudicandae. Item nonnulli etiam credunt, omnes opiniones, quas Cantuarienses archiepiscopi damnauerunt, inter haereses computandas, quidam enim firmissime credunt, quod dicere voluntatem nihil posse velle contra actuale iudicium rationis, sapiat haeresim manifestam: quia (ut dicunt) hoc omne meritum tollit & demerirum. Quidam etiam certitudinaliter credunt, quod dicere in homine non esse nisi unam formam substantialem, veritati obuiat orthodoxae. Quidam etiam putant, quod multae opiniones Scoti sunt inter haereses numerandae, dicere enim, quod sapientia Dei ab essentia Dei ex natura rei quomodolibet distinguatur, contradicere putant simplicitati diuinae: & per consequens veritati catholicae repugnare. Idem sentiunt de unitate minori, unitate numerali, & prioritatibus, quas ponunt in Deo, & de aliis quae opinantur quasi innumeris. Hoc idem de multis opinionibus Egidii multi aestimant, & ergo notorium est, quod Theologi haereses dogmatizare notantur, quamuis haretici minime reputantur, propter talem ergo famam debuerunt summi pontifices pro inquisitione facienda moneri. Discipul. Forte talis fama ad summos pontifices non peruenit. Magist. Dicunt illi, quod hoc omni probabilitate caret, nec verisimilitudinem habet, quod damnationes opinionum Thomae & aliorum, quae solenniter & publice plures factae fuerunt Parisiis & in Anglia, summos pontifices latuissent, praesertim cum quidam de ordine praedicatorum contra damnationem latam in Anglia ab archiepiscopo Cantuariensi contra quasdam opiniones Thomae ad curiam Romanam appellauerint: Et illa de causa accesserint ad eandem. Dicunt ergo, quamuis fama (quae opinantes essent haeretici) non peruenerit ad Romanos Pontifices, ipsos tamen non latuit quod opiniones eorum damnatæ fuerint Parisiis & in Anglia, quare ad inquisitionem faciendam procedere debuerunt exemplo sanctorum patrum, qui antequam Arrius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Nestorius, & alii multi pertinaces convincerentur hæresum defensores, de eis & eorum dogmatibus inquisitionem fecere solertem: exemplo etiam Innocent. tertii, qui vt extra de sum. tri. & fi. catb. c. damnamus, quamuis Ioachimus sui erroris nunquam fuit pertinax defensor; & licet eidem errori solemnis tunc temporis Doctor Ricardus de sancto Victore adhaeserit, quamuis non pertinaciter, tamen ad inquisitionem & damnationem faciendas processit.{5}
units.tr: Disciple. I still have a question about the condemnation of heresies. It seems to me that every error, however it arises, whether openly or secretly, that meets and contradicts Holy Scripture, is counted among the heresies. But it is clear that theologians hold contrary opinions on matters that concern Holy Scripture, and yet all of them strive to support their opinions from Holy Scripture, and by the same Holy Scripture they labour to refute the opposing opinions. So some of these contrary opinions are counted among the heresies. Does the Pope, then, sin damnably by neglecting to condemn heresies of this kind? Master. Some say that the Pope sins in no way by allowing theologians to hold such assertions as opinions, though in truth they are heretical. This can seem to be proved by the following reasoning. To permit what is lawful is not a sin, since even unlawful things are sometimes permitted without sin. But to hold as an opinion such errors as have not been explicitly condemned is unlawful, because such an opinion does not make the one holding it a heretic when he is ready to be corrected. Therefore the Pope permits, without sin, that things which are in truth heresies be held as opinions. Others hold that several Roman pontiffs have sinned damnably in this. They prove it thus: not only heretics but also heresies must be rooted out of the Church, as a general council testifies, which (as is found in extra de haer. excommunicamus) orders that bishops who were negligent or remiss in rooting out the leaven of heretical depravity from their dioceses be deposed. Therefore, he whose duty, laid upon him by his office, is to root out heresies, if he is negligent or remiss, cannot be excused of damnable negligence or poor government. But it belongs to the supreme pontiff to cleanse the whole Church of heresies, not only those already explicitly condemned but also all others whatever. Therefore those who sustain such heresies to be held or taught have sinned damnably. Disciple. It does not seem that the Pope is bound to purge the Church of all heresies that have not been explicitly condemned. It is enough for him that he purges it, or, having purged it, keeps it free from every heretical depravity already explicitly condemned. Master. Those who hold this view are refuted by the following: a Pope who neglects to reprove and condemn heresies newly arising does not imitate at all the Apostles and holy Fathers, who condemned swiftly the heresies that sprang up. Yet the Roman Pontiff must follow in their footsteps if he wishes to be numbered with them in the heavenly Father. Therefore the supreme pontiffs who neglected to condemn heresies have sinned. Disciple. The Apostles and holy Fathers condemned heresies because they found pertinacious asserters of them. Therefore, since theologians have not been pertinacious asserters of heresies which they think by no means oppose catholic truth, those heresies which they taught merely as opinions were not to be condemned by the Roman pontiffs. Master. Those men try to refute this excuse of the Roman pontiffs in two ways. First, because the pontiffs did not know whether the theologians clung pertinaciously to their heretical opinions, since they made no inquiry at all into it. Therefore, by not inquiring into the truth in order to meet the dangers to the faith, they were negligent and remiss. Second, thus: greater danger must be met more strongly, diligently and swiftly. But heresies publicly held and taught threaten the Christian religion with a greater danger than burdensome and depraved customs do. For even if those who teach them do not cling pertinaciously to their opinions, it must still be feared that simple disciples, hearing such assertions taught by great teachers, strongly argued for, and never condemned by Catholics, will be induced, by the appearance of arguments they cannot answer, into a pertinacious adherence to those very heresies. And pestilential heresies may begin to be venerated as Catholic truths and stubbornly defended. But burdensome and depraved customs must be suppressed very quickly, lest they assume the force of privileges, as Pope Nicholas asserts, as is found in dist. 8. c. male. Therefore, much more strongly must heresies, however they have sprung up, be torn out by the roots and condemned, lest they be approved by simple and seducible people as Catholic truths. Disciple. That last argument is plausible, but the first opinion seems to lack plausibility. According to the sacred canons, no inquiry is to be made unless the person has first been defamed, as is found in extra de accu. c. qualiter & quando, and in many other places. But the theologians were in no way defamed as heretics; therefore the supreme pontiffs ought not to have inquired about them. Master. Those men say that this excuse is not sufficient. Although the theologians were not defamed as being heretics, they were nevertheless defamed, since they taught heresies. Hence many theologians now think that other theologians teach heresies, although they are unwilling to assert that these should be counted among the heretics. Many, too, with some assertion, think that all the opinions of Thomas, which were once condemned at Paris, are to be judged heretical. Likewise some believe that all the opinions which the archbishops of Canterbury condemned are to be counted among the heresies. For some firmly believe that to say the will can will nothing against the actual judgment of reason savours of manifest heresy, because (as they say) this takes away all merit and demerit. Some also are certain that to say there is only one substantial form in man is opposed to orthodox truth. Some think that many opinions of Scotus are to be numbered among the heresies. For to say that the wisdom of God is in some way distinguished from the essence of God by the nature of the thing, they think contradicts the divine simplicity, and consequently opposes catholic truth. They feel the same about the lesser unity, numerical unity, and the priorities which they posit in God, and about other things which they hold almost without number. Many judge the same of many opinions of Giles. So it is notorious that theologians are noted for teaching heresies, although they are by no means considered heretics. Therefore, on account of such a reputation, the supreme pontiffs ought to have been urged to make an inquiry. Disciple. Perhaps such a reputation did not reach the supreme pontiffs. Master.
