Those men say that this lacks all probability and has no likelihood: that the condemnations of the opinions of Thomas and others, which were many times solemnly and publicly pronounced at Paris and in England, should have remained hidden from the supreme pontiffs. This is especially so since some of the Order of Preachers appealed to the Roman court against the condemnation pronounced in England by the archbishop of Canterbury against certain opinions of Thomas, and for that reason came to the same court. They say, therefore, that although the report that the holders would be heretics did not reach the Roman pontiffs, it was nonetheless not hidden from them that their opinions had been condemned at Paris and in England. Wherefore they ought to have proceeded to make an inquiry, following the example of the holy Fathers, who, before Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Nestorius and many other pertinacious defenders of heresies were convicted, made a diligent inquiry into them and their doctrines. They should also follow the example of Innocent III, who (as in extra de sum. tri. & fi. cath. c. damnamus), although Joachim was never a pertinacious defender of his error, and although the then renowned doctor Richard of Saint Victor adhered to the same error, though not pertinaciously, nevertheless proceeded to make an inquiry and a condemnation.{5}

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: Ponit excusationem summorum Pontificum in sacris literis minus peritorum.
units.tr: He sets out the excuse offered for the supreme Pontiffs, who are said to have been less skilled in the sacred letters.

units.la: Discipulus. Ista exempla animum meum fortiter angunt, unde cupio scire, si aliqui alter dictos summos pontifices excusare nitantur. Magist. Quidam per simplicitatem & imperitiam scripturarum eos excusant, dicentes quod a tempore Innocent. tertii non fuerunt aliqui summi pontifices in sacrarum literarum peritia excellentes, & ideo de intrinsecis & difficilibus quaestionibus se intromittere nullatenus debuerunt, sed talia discutienda Theologis reliquerunt, contenti his quae explicite approbata noscuntur, de opinionibus vero novis magis voluerunt iuxta consilium beati Hieronym. pie dubitare, quam aliquid temere diffinire. Discipul. Ista sententia correspondere videtur cum illis, qui dicunt, quod non ad Canonistas, sed ad Theologos principaliter pertinet inter veritates catholicas & haereses iudicare, plures enim post tempora Innocent. tertii fuerunt summi pontifices, qui peritissimi in iure canonico extiterunt, licet in Theologia non fuerunt excellentes, quare si ad Canonistas principaliter pertinet inter veritates catholicas & haereses iudicare, ipsi non damnando haereses inter Theologos damnatas (modo praedicto) excusari nequirent: sed nunquam, si fuissent magistri in Theologia, excusare valerent. Magist. Dicunt isti quod sic, quia multi, vt asserunt, sunt in Theologia doctoris nomen habentes, per fauores humanos & procurationes, indebitas aut ambitiones diabolicas ad magisterium exaltati, qui sacrarum litterarum sunt penitus imperiti.{10}
units.tr: Disciple. These examples greatly trouble my mind, and so I wish to know whether some others try to excuse those supreme pontiffs. Master. Some excuse them on the ground of simplicity and inexperience in the Scriptures, saying that from the time of Innocent III there were no supreme pontiffs excelling in knowledge of the sacred letters, and therefore they ought in no way to have meddled with intricate and difficult questions, but left such matters to the theologians, content with those things which are known to have been explicitly approved; and in regard to new opinions they preferred, following the counsel of the blessed Jerome, to doubt piously rather than rashly to define anything. Disciple. This view seems to agree with those who say that it belongs chiefly not to the canonists but to the theologians to judge between Catholic truths and heresies. For after the time of Innocent III there were many supreme pontiffs who were most skilled in canon law, although they were not outstanding in theology; so if it belongs chiefly to the canonists to judge between Catholic truths and heresies, they could not be excused for failing to condemn (in the aforesaid manner) heresies condemned among the theologians; but they could never be excused if they had been masters in theology. Master. Those men say that it is so, because many, as they assert, who bear the title of doctor in theology, have been raised to the teaching office through human favours and dealings, undue canvassing, or diabolical ambition, and yet are wholly unskilled in the sacred letters.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXIX.

units.la: Vbi inquiritur, si Pontifex minus peritus in litteris sacris, consilio tamen peritorum aliquam assertionem, tanquam haereticam valeat condemnare, & ponuntur duae opiniones.
units.tr: Where it is inquired whether a Pope who is less skilled in the sacred letters may nevertheless condemn an assertion as heretical with the counsel of learned men, and two opinions are set out.

units.la: Discipulus. Licet summi pontifices scripturae notitiam non habuerunt excellentem, tamen per hoc non videntur aliqualiter excusandi, quia poterant doctos consulere & peritos, qui autem potest habere copiam peritorum, non potest per ignorantiam excusari, talis ergo ignorantia scripturae diuinae eos nequaquam excusat: nisi forte dicant, quod quia in Theologia & in Philosophia (antequam ad papatum essent assumpti) nequaquam exercitati fuerunt, non poterant ad intelligendum tam subtiles difficultates Theologiae, etiam per informationem peritorum attingere. Sed etiam hoc sufficere non videtur: quia quamuis non potuissent intelligere informationes circa huiusmodi; debebant credere informationibus aliorum, vt appareret, & per consequens iuxta informationem peritorum (quamuis eas per intellectum non saperent) ad condemnationem haeresum procedere debuerunt. Vnde & de hoc vltimo, an scilicet si summus pontifex sacrarum literarum ignarus aliquam haeresim promulgatam (quamuis videre nequiret, quomodo veritati catholicae aduersatur) de consilio peritorum valeat condemnare, quid de hoc teneant homines docti manifesta. Magist. Quidam dicunt, quod summus pontifex in hoc casu debet credere eruditis in scriptura sacra, & iuxta eorum consilium (quamuis non videat, quomodo haeresis dogmatizata veritati repugnat) ad condemnationem eiusdem procedere. Alii vero assumpserunt manifeste, quod a quibuscunque & cuicunque dicatur aliquam assertionem haereticam esse censendam: ipse ad damnationem eius solennem nullo modo debet procedere: nisi ipsemet aperte consideraret vel diuina inspiratione, vel propria meditatione, vel librorum inspectione, aut aliorum informatione, aut aliquo alio modo, quod talis assertio veritati obuiat orthodoxae.{45} Dicunt etiam, quod si omnes in generali concilio congregati praeter ipsum assererent tale assertionem esse haereticam, nisi suam sententiam miraculo confirmarent, vel per informationes suas facerent ipsum aduertere, quod catholicae obuiat veritati, non deberet eam quantumcunq; omnes instarent solenniter condemnare: sed expectare teneretur, quousq; vel per reuelationem diuinam vel per mirabilem operationem facti ad talem haeresim reprobandam, vel propria meditatione vel aliena informatione aut quouis modo sibi innotesceret manifeste, quod talis assertio catholicae veritati repugnat. Discip. Miror quomodo isti dogmatisare praesumunt, quod vnus homo mortalis quacunq; praeditus dignitate magis debet adhaerere propriae fantasiae, quam omnibus viris literatis & sanctis ad generale concilium conuocatis. Magist. Sententiam praedictam non capis, vt video. Non enim dicunt, quod Papa debet fantasiae suae adhaerere, sed dicunt quod propter verba hominum nullam debet assertionem contra conscientiam vel praeter conscientiam propriam damnare. Discip. Videtur quod Papa hoc casu tenetur se conscientiis tot & tantorum virorum conformare. Magist. Dicunt quod in his quae fidei sunt, non debet Papa inniti conscientiis hominum, sed soli auctoritati diuinae.
units.tr: Disciple. Although the supreme pontiffs did not have an excellent knowledge of Scripture, they do not seem to be excused on that account in any way, because they were able to consult learned and skilled men; and whoever can have access to skilled men cannot be excused by ignorance. Such ignorance of divine Scripture therefore does not excuse them at all. Unless perhaps they say that, since they had never been trained in theology or philosophy (before they were raised to the papacy), they could not, even with the help of experts, grasp such subtle difficulties of theology. But even this does not seem sufficient, because although they could not understand the explanations of such matters, they ought to have believed the explanations of others, as seemed right, and consequently ought to have proceeded to the condemnation of heresies in accordance with the information of the experts (even though they did not grasp them by their own understanding). Hence, concerning this last point, namely whether a supreme pontiff ignorant of the sacred letters may condemn with the counsel of experts some heresy put forward (even though he could not see how it opposes Catholic truth), what learned men hold on this is plain. Master. Some say that in this case the supreme pontiff ought to believe those who are learned in sacred Scripture, and, according to their counsel, proceed to the condemnation of that heresy (even though he does not see how the heretical doctrine conflicts with the truth). Others, however, have clearly maintained that whoever and by whomever some assertion is said to be heretical, he ought by no means to proceed to its solemn condemnation unless he himself plainly perceives, either by divine inspiration, or by his own meditation, or by inspecting books, or by the information of others, or in some other way, that such an assertion opposes orthodox truth. They also say that if all those gathered in a general council, apart from him, were to declare such an assertion to be heretical, then unless they confirmed their opinion by a miracle, or by their information made him aware that it opposes Catholic truth, he should not condemn it solemnly even if all urged him; rather he is bound to wait until it becomes clear to him, either by divine revelation or by a marvellous work, or by his own meditation or another's information, or in whatever way, that such an assertion conflicts with Catholic truth in order to reject such a heresy. Disciple. I marvel how these men presume to lay down that a single mortal man, however endowed with dignity, ought rather to cling to his own fancy than to all learned and holy men summoned to a general council. Master. You do not grasp the aforesaid opinion, as I see. For they do not say that the Pope ought to cling to his own fancy, but they say that on account of the words of men he ought not to condemn any assertion against his conscience or apart from his own conscience. Disciple. It seems that in this case the Pope is bound to conform himself to the consciences of so many and such great men. Master. They say that in matters which belong to faith the Pope ought not to lean upon the consciences of men, but on divine authority alone.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Declarat quod Papa condemnando aliquam assertionem, tanquam haereticam, non debeat inniti sapientiae, vel scientiae hominum, sed tantum auctoritati diuinae vel miraculo manifesto.
units.tr: He declares that when the Pope condemns some assertion as heretical, he ought not to rely on the wisdom or knowledge of men, but only on the divine authority or on a manifest miracle.

units.la: Discip. Incipio magis aduertere sententiam memoratam. Unde ipsam auctoritatibus vel rationibus munire coneris. Magist. Pro illa sententia plures rationes auctoritatibus communitae possunt adduci. Quarum prima est haec. Omnes praeter Papam in Concilio generali congregati non sunt maioris auctoritatis, quam Christus: nec omnibus illis magis est credendum, quam Christo. Sed si Christus venisset & catholicam veritatem inauditam praedicasset, & ad confirmandum doctrinam suam nullum fecisset miraculum, Iudaei praedicatione suae minime credendo peccatum nullatenus habuissent. Ergo multo fortius potest Papa absq; peccato suae sententiae & omnium aliorum in generali concilio existentium (si per eos nullum fiat miraculum ad suam sententiam confirmandam, nec ipsi faciunt eum intelligere, quomodo sua sententia in veritate catholica est fundata) minime adhaerere, & per consequens non tenetur eos in eadem sententia sequi. Maior istius rationis est omni catholico manifesta. Minor auctoritate ipsius Christi probatur. Quia, vt legitur, Iohan. 15. loquens Iudaeis ait: Si opera non fecissem in eis, quae nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent, (scil. non credendo:) nunc autem & viderunt, (scil mirabilia manifesta quae feci) & oderunt me & patrem meum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod si Christus non fecisset miracula, Iudaei non credendo peccatum minime habuissent. Discip. Si illa ratio concluderet, sequeretur quod toti ecclesiae vniuersali fides minime esset adhibenda. Imo posset aliquis assertionem absque peccato (quam hactenus praedicauit vniuersalis ecclesia, si non videret quomodo esset consona scripturae diuinae) negare: cum tota congregatio quorumcunq; mortalium, nō sit tantae auctoritatis, quantae solus Christus. Et ita si Christo non fuisset credendum absq; miraculo, nec toti ecclesiae est credendum, nisi sententia ecclesiae aperto miraculo confirmetur. Magist. Ad illam obiectionem tuam dicerent illi, qui praedictam tenent sententiam, quod adhaerendo sententiae vniuersalis ecclesiae (nemine discrepante) quando eadem sententia alequo miraculo minime confirmatur, principaliter creditur Christo, cuius doctrina tota est miraculis innumeris confirmata. Ex quo sequitur, quod nunquam ecclesia vniuersalis (nemine discrepante) docet aliquid esse tenendum, nisi propter auctoritatem ecclesiae. Licet quodammodo etiam propter auctoritatem ecclesiae sit tenendum, in quantum firma fide tenetur, quod Christus docuit ecclesiam nunquam a fide catholica recessuram. Discip. Possem multa quaerere de ecclesia, quae errare non potest, & de concilio generali: sed omnia illaduxi ad aliud tempus differenda. Et ideo ad principale propositum reuertaris, & rationes complas in quibus potest praedicta sententia se fundare. Magist. Secunda ratio pro praedicta opinione est haec. Quia si Papa non propter miraculum aliquod, nec propter auctoritatem scripturae diuinae, nec propter aliquam auctoritatem quam videat, sed propter instantiam hominum aliquam assertionem damnat solenniter, eandem damnationem in sapientia aut voluntate hominum vel instantia fundare videretur. Si autem damnatio praui-tatis haereticae & approbatio catholicae veritatis eidem fundamento deberent inniti: ideo liceret Papae approbando aliquam catholicam veritatem in sapientia hominum vel voluntate & instantia se fundare; quod doctrinae Apostolicae manifeste repugnat. Ait enim Apostolus 1.ad Cor.3. Praedicatio mea non est in persuasibilibus humanae sapientiae verbis: sed in ostensione spiritus & veritatis vt fides nostra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in veritate Dei. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod fides Papae non in sapientia hominum, & per consequens multo magis nec in voluntate hominum aut instantia debet fundari & consistere. Quare nec approbatio catholicae veritatis in sapientia hominum vel voluntate aut instantia debet fundari. Et eadem ratione damnatio haereticae praui-tatis non debet fundari in aliquo praedictorum. Papa ergo ad hoc, vt rite damnet haereticam praui-tatem vel falsitatem, debet ad hoc vel per miraculum apertum induci, vel oportet eum manifeste cognoscere, quomodo talis falsitas veritati catholicae aduersatur, ne fides sua in sapientia hominum vel voluntate consistat. Tertia ratio est haec. Propter illos, qui possunt contra fidem errare, non est aliqua assertio neq; tanquam catholica approbanda, neque tanquam haeretica condemnanda. Sed omnes Magistri in Theologia & etiam omnes alii à Papa in generali concilio non sunt tota illa ecclesia, pro qua Christus rogavit, ne fides eius deficeret; licet (si sint catholici) sint pars illius ecclesiæ. Ergo propter illos omnes non debet Papa aliquam assertionem neq; tanquam nō catholicam neq; tanquā haereticam condemnare; nisi aperte ostendatur Papæ vel per operationem miraculi, vel per testimonium catholicæ veritatis, q à veritate nequaquam exorbitet. Quarta ratio est hæc. Papa non debet aliquam assertionem tanquam haereticam solenniter condemnare: nisi quam demonstratiue, vel firmissime credit esse haereticam. Qui autem scit demonstrare aliquam assertionem tanquam haereticam, rationi innititur. Qui autem credit, innititur auctoritati Papæ. Papa ergo in damnando aliquam assertionem tanquam haereticā vel innititur rationi vel auctoritati. Sed Papa qui nō videt quo modo dānanda assertio fidei obuiat orthodoxæ, rationi inniti non potest, sicut omni intelligenti constat. Ergo oportet quod innitatur auctoritati. Aut ergo innititur auctoritati diuinæ aut humanæ. Non diuinæ: quia non videt, quomodo talis assertio auctoritati diuinæ repugnat. Ergo Papa, si damnaret aliquam assertionem prædicto modo tanquam haereticam, inniteretur auctoritati humanæ. Sed auctoritati humanæ in his, quæ fidei sunt, est minime innitendum, quia fides nostra est supra intellectum humanum. Ergo intellectui humano in his quæ fidei sunt est nullatenus inhærendum. Quinta ratio est hæc. Omnes alii à Papa in generali concilio congregati non sunt maioris auctoritatis, quam fuerunt Apostoli & Moyses in veteri lege: sed Apostoli & Moyses doctrinam suam miraculis & testimoniis authenticis ab auditoribus iam receptis (ut reddatur credibilis) confirmauerunt: nec aliter populus eis credidisset. Ergo Papa non tenetur eis adhibere fidem, qui nec miraculo nec testimonio catholicæ veritatis sibi notæ, faciunt eum de sua scientia certum. Si ergo omnes alii in generali concilio nec miraculo nec auctoritate catholica ostenderent Papæ assertionem haereticam esse damnandam, non deberet Papa ipsam tanquam haereticam condemnare. Maior istius rationis videtur aperta. Minor ostenditur manifeste per exemplum de beato Paulo, qui doctrinam suam tam miraculis quam scripturarum testimoniis confirmauit. Unde ad Rom. 15. ait: Non enim audeo aliquid loqui eorum, quæ per me non efficit Christus in obedientiam gentium verbo & factu in virtute signorum & prodigiorum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod beatus Paulus doctrinam suam signis & prodigiis confirmauit de scripturarum testimoniis, & quæ adduxit beatus Paulus, patet ad Rom. 9. 10. 11. 1. Cor. 1. & 3. ad Heb. 1. & 3. & in multis aliis locis epistolarum suarum. Et quod etiam Apostoli doctrinam suam confirmauerunt, testatur Marcus in Euangelio suo, c. vlt. dicens: illi autem profecti praedicauerunt vbiq; Domino cooperante, sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis. Beatus etiam Petrus, vt patet Act. 1. auctoritatibus scripturarum receptarum à Iudaeis coram ipsis doctrinam suam confirmauit. Moysi quoq; dixit Dominus, vt legitur Exod. 4. quod si nec duobus quidem his signis crediderunt, nec audierunt vocem tuam: sume aquam fluminis, funde eam super aridam: & quicquid hauseris de fluuio, vertetur in sanguinem. Ex his aliisq; quamplurimis patet aperte, quod illi, per quos Deus docuit populū catholicam veritatem ad confirmationem suæ doctrinæ vel scripturarum testimonia adduxerunt, vel operatione miraculi veritatem ostenderunt, nec eis aliter populi credere artabantur. Discip. Ista responsio videtur probare tantum modo, quod Papa non tenetur sequi alios in damnando haeresim, quando nec miraculum faciunt, nec per se scripturam adducunt: sed si probant assertionem, quam petunt, damnari esse haereticam, videtur quod Papa damnare debet eandem: nec per hoc (quod non intelligit) valet aliqualiter excusari. Sic enim possunt multi haeretici excusari, quod videre non possunt, quomodo haereses suæ fidei obuiarent orthodoxæ. Magist. Ad haec alii responderent, quod si Papa informationi catholicorum per scripturam probantium manifeste aliquam assertionem veritati obuiare catholicæ, pertinaci animositate (quia scilicet alicui errori irrationabiliter adhaereret) nollet acquiescere: esset haereticus vel fautor prauitatis haereticæ iudicandus: sed si ex sola simplicitate (quia nō esset capax informationis, quæ ostendit assertionem esse haereticam) minime consentiret, non esset reprehensibilis iudicandus, nisi recusaret de veritate informari. Discip. Quomodo sit censendus haereticus, postea indagabo. Ideo alias rationes, si quas cogitasti, pro proposito principali adducas. Magist. Sexta ratio pro praedicta sententia est haec. Non minus debet intelligere sententiam suam seu diffinitionē summus pontifex, qua dānat haereticā prauitatē, quam debet iudex intelligere sententiā, qua dānat aliquē de crimine qualicunq; sed iudici dānanti quecunq; de crimine, nō sufficit credere consiliis suis, sed debet videre & considerare per seipsum, quomodo sententia sua iusticiā & æquitate contineat. E. similiter Papa in dānanda haereticā prauitatē nō solūmodo debet credere aliis, sed etiā oportet eū intelligere, quomodo dānanda assertio repugnat catholicæ veritati. Et maior patet: quia in maioribus causis maior est adhibenda cautela. Minor patet: quia nisi iudex deberet intelligere sententiā, quā dat, non requireretur sapientia in iudice, sed sufficeret q esset bonæ fidei sapientū acquiescens consiliis. Sed hoc est contra illud apostoli 1. ad Cor. 6. Non est inter vos sapiens quisquam qui possit iudicare inter fratrē & fratrē? Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, q nullus nisi sapiens debet iudicare inter fratrē & fratrē. Et ita qui iudicat, debet habere saltē iudicandi peritiā, vt sententiā, quam iudicat, intelligat. Aliter n. posset simplex & fatuus quicunq; iudex esse. Septima ratio est haec. Qui potest contradicere congregatis in generali concilio, nō tenetur acquiescere eorū sententiæ. Sed vnus etiam inferior Papa potest contradicere omnibus aliis in generali concilio congregatis. Ergo non tenetur acquiescere eorum sententiae. Ergo multo magis Papa si omnium aliorum in concilio generali existentium videret erroneam esse sententiam, vel non intelligeret ipsam esse catholicam vel sanam, cosequi non deberet. Maior patet. Minor ostenditur exemplo Pannucii, qui aliis in Nicena synodo contradixit, & ad partem suam traxit, vt habetur dist. 31. cap. Nicenam synodum. Vbi Gloss. super verbo sententiam: Vnus ergo potest contradicere toti vniuersitati, si habeat causam rationabilem. Et sequitur: nam vnus potest trahere alios ad partem suam. Vnus igitur potest omnibus illis in Concilio generali existentibus contradicere, & eos trahere ad partem suam. Ergo Papa non debet alios sequi, nisi cognouerit eos à iustitia & veritate nullatenus aberrare. Ex prædictis concludunt isti, quod si Papa omnes alios in generali concilio congregatos sequi non debet, vt aliquam assertionem condemnet tanquam haereticam, nisi videret quomodo dicta assertio catholicae obuiet veritati: multo magis si Papa cognouerit aliquos theologos aliquam assertionem reputare haereticam, non debet Papa informationem vel instantiam hominum omnium aliorum talem assertionem tanquam haereticam condemnare, nisi aperte cognouerit, quomodo fidei obuiat orthodoxę. Discip. Rationes prædictae videntur esse difficiles ad soluendum: quas tamen nolo nunc amplius pertractare: quia postquam totum opus praesens compleueris: & ego cum summo studio cogitauero, volo tecum illas rationes & omnia alia recitare, & mentem tuam de omnibus perscrutari. Sed dic an isti censeant, quod liceat Papae aliquam assertionem, de qua non constat sibi, an catholica vel haeretica sit censenda, interdicere & praecipere, quod minime publice dogmatisetur? Magist. Dicunt quod in casu si ex dogmatisatione alicuius assertionis magnum scandalum esset vel timeretur, quod multitudo pertinaciter adhaereret: liceret Papae praecipere à tali assertione cessare, quousque innotesceret an inter veritates, vel haereses computari debeat.
units.tr: Disciple. I am beginning to grasp the view you mentioned. So try to support it with authorities or reasons. Master. Several reasons for that view can be brought forward, each supported by authorities. The first is this. All who are gathered in a general council apart from the Pope have no greater authority than Christ, nor are they to be believed more than Christ. But if Christ had come and preached a catholic truth never heard before, and had worked no miracle to confirm his teaching, the Jews would not have sinned at all by refusing to believe his preaching. Therefore, much more strongly, the Pope, without sin, can refrain from adhering to his own opinion and to that of all others present in a general council (if no miracle is worked through them to confirm their opinion, and they do not make him understand how their opinion is grounded in catholic truth), and consequently he is not bound to follow them in that opinion. The major premise of this argument is plain to every catholic. The minor is proved by the authority of Christ himself. For, as we read in John 15, speaking to the Jews he said: If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin (that is, by not believing); but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father (that is, the manifest wonders which I did). From these words it is gathered that if Christ had not worked miracles, the Jews would not have sinned by not believing. Disciple. If that reasoning held, it would follow that the faith of the whole universal Church should not be given any credit at all. Indeed, someone could deny an assertion without sin, which the universal Church has hitherto preached, if he did not see how it agreed with divine Scripture, since the whole assembly of any mortals whatever is not of such authority as Christ alone. And so, if Christ was not to be believed without a miracle, neither is the whole Church to be believed, unless the Church's assertion is confirmed by an open miracle. Master. To that objection of yours, those who hold the aforesaid opinion would reply that by adhering to the assertion of the universal Church (with no one dissenting), when that same assertion is not confirmed by any miracle, we believe principally in Christ, whose whole doctrine has been confirmed by countless miracles. From this it follows that the universal Church (with no one dissenting) never teaches that anything is to be held except on account of the Church's authority. Yet in some measure it is also to be held on account of the Church's authority, insofar as it is held with firm faith that Christ taught that the Church would never fall away from the catholic faith. Disciple. I could ask many questions about the Church, which cannot err, and about a general council; but I have postponed all those matters to another time. So return to the main point and set out in full the reasons on which the aforesaid opinion can rest. Master. The second reason for the aforesaid opinion is this. If the Pope, not on account of any miracle, nor on account of the authority of divine Scripture, nor on account of any authority that he sees, but on account of the urging of men, solemnly condemns some assertion, that condemnation would seem to be grounded in the wisdom or will of men or in their urging. But if the condemnation of heretical perversity and the approval of catholic truth were to rest on the same foundation, then it would be lawful for the Pope, in approving some catholic truth, to ground it on the wisdom, will, and urging of men; and this plainly contradicts the doctrine of the Apostles. For the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 2: My preaching was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power; that your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. From these words it is plainly evident that the Pope's faith ought not to be grounded and to rest in the wisdom of men, and consequently much less in the will or urging of men. Therefore the approval of catholic truth also ought not to be grounded in the wisdom, will, or urging of men. And by the same reasoning, the condemnation of heretical perversity ought not to be grounded in any of these. Therefore, for the Pope to condemn heretical perversity or falsehood rightly, he must either be led to it by an open miracle, or it is necessary that he clearly know how such falsehood opposes catholic truth, so that his faith does not rest on the wisdom or will of men. The third reason is this. On account of those who may err against the faith, no assertion is to be approved as catholic, nor condemned as heretical. But all the teachers of theology and all others apart from the Pope gathered in a general council are not that whole Church for which Christ prayed that its faith should not fail; although (if they are catholics) they are a part of that Church. Therefore, on account of all of them, the Pope ought not to condemn any assertion either as non-catholic or as heretical, unless it is shown plainly to the Pope either by the working of a miracle or by the testimony of catholic truth, which in no way departs from the truth. The fourth reason is this. The Pope ought not to condemn any assertion solemnly as heretical unless he firmly believes, or believes by demonstration, that it is heretical. But he who knows how to demonstrate that an assertion is heretical relies on reason; he who believes relies on the authority of the Pope. Therefore the Pope, in condemning some assertion as heretical, relies either on reason or on authority. But the Pope who does not see how the assertion to be condemned opposes orthodox faith cannot rely on reason, as is evident to everyone who understands. Therefore he must rely on authority. He relies therefore either on divine or on human authority. Not on divine, because he does not see how such an assertion conflicts with divine authority. Therefore, if the Pope were to condemn some assertion in the aforesaid way as heretical, he would be relying on human authority. But in matters of faith one must by no means rely on human authority, because our faith is above human understanding. Therefore one must in no way adhere to human understanding in matters of faith. The fifth reason is this. All others gathered apart from the Pope in a general council are not of greater authority than were the Apostles and Moses under the old law; but the Apostles and Moses confirmed their teaching by miracles and by authentic testimonies, already accepted by their hearers, so that it might be made credible; nor otherwise would the people have believed them. Therefore the Pope is not bound to give faith to those who, by neither miracle nor testimony of catholic truth known to him, make him certain of their knowledge. If, then, all the others in a general council were to show the Pope neither by miracle nor by catholic authority that the assertion ought to be condemned as heretical, the Pope ought not to condemn it as heretical. The major premise of this reasoning seems plain. The minor is clearly shown by the example of the blessed Paul, who confirmed his teaching both by miracles and by the testimonies of the Scriptures. Hence he says in Rom. 15: For I will not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ has not wrought by me, to make the Gentiles obedient, by word and deed, through mighty signs and wonders. From these words it is gathered that the blessed Paul confirmed his teaching by signs and wonders and by the testimonies of the Scriptures; and the passages the blessed Paul adduced are evident in Rom. 9, 10, 11; 1 Cor. 1 and 3; Heb. 1 and 3, and in many other places of his epistles. That the Apostles also confirmed their teaching, Mark testifies in his Gospel, last chapter, saying: And they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word with signs following. The blessed Peter also, as is evident in Acts 1, confirmed his teaching before the Jews by the authorities of the Scriptures which they received. The Lord also said to Moses, as we read in Exod. 4: And it shall come to pass, if they will not believe even these two signs, neither hearken unto thy voice, that thou shalt take of the water of the river, and pour it upon the dry land; and the water which thou takest out of the river shall become blood upon the dry land. From these and very many other examples it is plainly clear that those through whom God taught the people catholic truth either adduced the testimonies of Scripture to confirm their teaching, or showed the truth by working a miracle, and the people were not compelled to believe them otherwise. Disciple. This answer seems to prove only that the Pope is not bound to follow others in condemning a heresy when they neither work a miracle nor themselves adduce Scripture; but if they prove that the assertion they seek to have condemned is heretical, it seems that the Pope ought to condemn it, and he cannot be excused in any way by the fact that he does not understand it. For in this way many heretics could be excused, since they cannot see how their heresies oppose orthodox faith. Master. To this others would reply that if the Pope, though manifestly informed by Catholics through Scripture that some assertion opposes catholic truth, were unwilling to yield, through obstinate animosity (namely because he adhered irrationally to some error), he would have to be judged a heretic or a supporter of heretical perversity; but if out of simple-mindedness (because he was not capable of the instruction which shows that the assertion is heretical) he did not consent, he should not be judged blameworthy, unless he refused to be informed about the truth. Disciple. I will look into later how he should be judged a heretic. So bring forward other reasons, if you have thought of any, in support of the main point. Master. The sixth reason for the aforesaid opinion is this. The supreme pontiff ought to understand his own sentence or definition, by which he condemns a heretical perversity, no less than a judge ought to understand the sentence by which he condemns anyone of whatever crime. But a judge who condemns anyone for any crime is not enough if he merely believes his advisers; he must himself see and consider how his sentence accords with justice and equity. Likewise, then, the Pope in condemning heretical perversity must not only believe others, but it is also necessary that he understand how the assertion to be condemned is opposed to catholic truth. The major premise is plain, because greater caution must be used in greater causes. The minor is plain, because unless a judge ought to understand the sentence he gives, no wisdom would be required of a judge, and it would be enough for him to be a man of good faith who yields to the advice of the wise. But this is contrary to that saying of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 6: Is there not a wise man among you, not one that shall be able to judge between his brethren? From these words it is given to understand that no one except a wise man ought to judge between brother and brother. And so whoever judges ought at least to have the skill of judging, so that he understands the sentence he pronounces; otherwise any simple and foolish man could be a judge. The seventh reason is this. He who can contradict those gathered in a general council is not bound to yield to their sentence. But even one inferior Pope can contradict all the others gathered in a general council. Therefore he is not bound to yield to their sentence. Therefore much more, if the Pope saw that the opinion of all the others present in a general council was erroneous, or did not understand it to be catholic or sound, he ought not to follow it. The major premise is plain. The minor is shown by the example of Pamphilus, who contradicted the others in the Synod of Nicaea and drew them to his side, as is found in dist. 31, chapter Nicenam synodum. There the Gloss, on the word sententiam, says: Therefore one man can contradict the whole universality, if he has a reasonable cause. And it follows: for one man can draw the others to his side. Therefore one man can contradict all those present in a general council and draw them to his side. Therefore the Pope ought not to follow the others unless he has recognized that they do not in any way stray from justice and truth. From the foregoing, these men conclude that if the Pope need not follow all the others gathered in a general council in condemning some assertion as heretical, unless he sees how the said assertion opposes catholic truth, then much more, if the Pope has recognized that some theologians consider an assertion heretical, he ought not to condemn such an assertion as heretical on the information or urging of all other men, unless he clearly recognizes how it opposes orthodox faith. Disciple. The foregoing reasons seem difficult to answer; yet I do not wish to treat them further now, because when you have completed the whole present work, and I have thought about them with the greatest care, I want to recite those reasons and all the others with you, and to examine your mind on all of them. But tell me: do these men hold that the Pope may forbid and command that some assertion, about which it is not established to him whether it is to be regarded as catholic or heretical, should not be publicly taught? Master. They say that in a case where, from the teaching of some assertion, great scandal were to arise or were feared, and the multitude would obstinately cling to it, the Pope may order that such an assertion cease until it becomes known whether it should be counted among the truths or among the heresies.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXI.

units.la: Inquirit an liceat Papa alios errores, quam haereses condemnare, & huiusmodi errores distinguuntur ibidem in tres differentias.
units.tr: Asks whether the Pope may condemn errors other than heresies, and distinguishes such errors into three kinds.

units.la: Discipulus. Multa de damnatione haeresium retulisti. Nunc peto, quod de damnatione aliorum errorum aliqua narrare digneris. Cupio enim scire, an literati putant, quod liceat papae errores alios quam haereses condemnare. Magist. Errores alii sunt in triplici differentia. Quidam enim nec contrariantur his, quae pertinet ad bonam fidem & ad bonos mores: nec eos tenere aliquod animae affert periculum. Tales sunt errores in puris Philosophicis, & etiam errores aliqui circa aliqua dicta diuina, de quibus inueniri non potest, quid indubie sit tenendum. De talibus loquitur Aug. in Enchirid. dicens. In rebus in quibus nihil interest ad capescendum Dei regnum errare, aut nullum, aut minimum est peccatum. De his etiam intelligit Anselm. lib. 1. Cur Deus homo. c. 18. dicens: In illis rebus de quibus diuersa sentiri possunt sine periculo (sicuti est istud, unde nunc agimus) si enim nescimus, vtrum plures homines eligendi sunt quam sint angeli perditi: an non alterum horum aestimamus plusquam alterum nullum puto animae esse periculum. Sic inquantum in huiusmodi rebus si exposuerimus diuina dicta, vt diuersis sententiis fauere videantur, nec alicubi inuenitur nec quid indubitanter tenendum sit determinatum, non arbitror reprehendi debere. Tales errores, secundum multos, non licet Papae damnare. Quia damnando animas illaqueaeret obligando fideles ad credendum aliquid forte contra conscientiam, vel negandum quod non tenere vel negare nullum parit periculum. Alii sunt errores repugnantes his, quae in gestis fidelium cronicis vel historiis fide dignis habentur. Et de istis dicunt nonnulli, quod ipsos potest Papa damnare, non tanquam haereticos, sed tanquam periculosos & ecclesiae perniciosos. Damna enim permaxima & pericula tam corporalia quam spiritualia possunt fideles incurrere, si quaecunque contenta in gestis, historiis & cronicis cuiilibet negare liceret. Cum ergo Papa damnis & periculis fidelium debeat obuiare, potest tales errores damnare & errantes debitae subdere vltioni. Alii sunt errores, de quibus dictum est prius. Ex quibus & aliis veris, quae negare non possunt, conuenit aliquam haereticam prauitatem inferre etiam quae proprie dicuntur sapere haeresim manifestam, & large possunt haereses appellari. Et tales errores non tanquam haereticos, (stricte loquendo) sed tanquam sapientes haeresim manifestam, licet proprie damnare. Si aliquis diceret castitatem, quam moniales vouerint, non esse altiorem castitate coniugii, deberet Papa tam asserentem pertinaciter quam assertionem damnare. Sic quidam errores negantes Fratres Praedicatores & Minores posse audire confessiones, sunt damnati: sicut summi pontifices Alex. tertius, Inno. 4. quosdam Magistros Parisienses & errores eorum contra statum & vitam Praedicatorum & Minorum solenniter damnauerunt.
units.tr: Disciple. You have told me much about the condemnation of heresies. Now I ask you to be good enough to tell me something about the condemnation of other errors. For I want to know whether learned men think that the Pope may condemn errors other than heresies. Master. Errors are of three kinds. Some neither conflict with what belongs to sound faith and good morals, nor does holding them endanger the soul. Such are errors in purely philosophical matters, and also certain errors concerning some divine sayings, about which it cannot be found what must indubitably be held. Augustine speaks of such in the Enchiridion, saying: In matters in which it makes no difference to attaining the kingdom of God whether one errs, either no sin or a very small one is committed. Anselm also understands these in Book 1 of Cur Deus homo, chapter 18, saying: In those matters about which different views can be held without danger (such as the one we are now discussing): for if we do not know whether more men are to be saved than there are fallen angels, or the reverse, I think there is no danger to the soul in holding either view rather than the other. Thus, so far as in such matters I expound divine sayings in a way that seems to favour various opinions, and nowhere is it found or determined what must be indubitably held, I do not think I ought to be blamed. According to many, the Pope may not condemn such errors, since by condemning them he would ensnare souls, binding the faithful to believe something perhaps contrary to conscience, or to deny what not holding or denying brings no danger. Others are errors that conflict with what is held in the deeds of the faithful, in chronicles or in trustworthy histories. And of these some say that the Pope can condemn them, not as heretical, but as dangerous and pernicious to the Church. For very great losses and dangers, both bodily and spiritual, could befall the faithful if it were permitted to deny whatever is contained in deeds, histories and chronicles. Since, therefore, the Pope ought to meet the losses and dangers of the faithful, he can condemn such errors and subject those who err to due punishment. Others are errors of the kind mentioned earlier. From these and other truths, which they cannot deny, it follows that some heretical depravity is introduced, including things that properly savour of manifest heresy, and which can broadly be called heresies. Such errors the Pope may properly condemn, not as heretical (strictly speaking), but as savouring of manifest heresy. If someone said that the chastity which nuns have vowed is not higher than the chastity of marriage, the Pope ought to condemn both the man who stubbornly asserts it and the assertion itself. So certain errors denying that the Friars Preachers and Friars Minor may hear confessions have been condemned; just as the supreme pontiffs Alexander III and Innocent IV solemnly condemned certain Parisian masters and their errors against the state and life of the Preachers and Minors.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXII.

units.la: In quo queritur, an liceat alicui inferiori Papa praedictos errores condemnare, & circa hoc ponuntur sententiae contrariae.
units.tr: In which it is asked whether it is lawful for any inferior to the Pope to condemn the aforesaid errors, and opposing opinions on this are set out.

units.la: Discipulus. Haec probabilia mihi videntur: sed videtur ne aliquibus, quod liceat alicui alii inferiori Papa errores huiusmodi condemnare? Magist. Sunt quidam dicentes, quod hoc inferiori Papa non licet, ex quo non licet ei condemnare haereses, quae magis quam quicunque alii errores religioni aduersantur & nocent Christianae, multo fortius non licet ei errores alios condemnare. Et hoc ratio videtur confirmare. Nam maiori periculo est fortius resistendum: sed haereses sunt magis periculosae fidei Christianae, quam alii errores. Cui igitur non licet condemnare haereses, dealiis erroribus se intromittere minime debet. Alii autem dicunt, quod inferioribus praelatis licet errores huiusmodi condemnare. Pro hac assertione sic arguitur. Quod aliquando licuit praelatis inferioribus, & non est per summum pontificem, nec per generale concilium revocatum, adhuc licet eisdem. Sed damnare errores huiusmodi licuit aliquando praelatis aliis, & non est revocatum. Ergo. Maior patet. Minor probatur. Nam cui licet veritates aliquas approbare, eidem licet assertiones salsas contrarias reprobare. Sed quondam licuit praelatis inferioribus veritatem asserentem aliquem esse sanctum & tanquam sanctum esse venerandum a fidelibus approbare. Quia licuit eis sanctos novos catalogo sanctorum ascribere. Ergo licuit eis assertionem falsam, quod tales non essent sancti vel venerandi a fidelibus, reprobare, & solenniter condemnare. Ergo adhuc licet eis errores aliquos condemnare. Discip. Ista ratio videtur concludere contra istos, qui probant tantummodo, quod aliquando licuit eis errorem dicentem, talem non esse sanctum, condemnare. Sed modo non licet eis talem errorem condemnare: sicut nec modo licet eis aliquem catalogo sanctorum ascribere. Magist. Non plene intelligis rationem eorum. Non enim intendunt probare, quomodo liceat inferioribus Papa asserentem vel assertionem eius, quod aliquis, pro quo Deus dicitur facere miraculum, non est sanctus, damnare: sed intendunt arguere, quod qua ratione licuit eis talem errorem damnare, licet etiam eis alios errores. Ex quibus & aliis veris & manifestis potest concludi, quod possunt haereses manifestas damnare. Potestas autem super alios errores non est revocata. Ergo adhuc possunt errores alios condemnare. Licet modo asserentem aliquem pro quo dicunt miraculum fieri non esse sanctum nequeant condemnare. Discip. Dictam rationem magis aduerto. Et ideo quomodo ad motiva aliorum respondetur, expone. Magist. Dicitur quod licet non valeant haereses condemnare, possunt tamen aliquos errores multo minores haeresibus condemnare: quia inferiores possunt multa minora, quibus tamen maiora negocia interdicta noscuntur, quia, ut ex lege divina Deut. 1. legitur seu colligitur, maiora negocia ad maiores oportet referre: nec tamen est dicendum, quod praelati haeresibus resistere non teneantur: sed non debent eis resistere damnando, sed eas summo pontifici vel generali concilio nunciando.
units.tr: Disciple. These things seem probable to me, but does it seem to some that it is lawful for some other inferior to the Pope to condemn errors of this kind? Master. There are some who say that this is not lawful for an inferior to the Pope, since it is not lawful for him to condemn heresies, which oppose the Christian religion and harm it more than any other errors; much more, then, is it not lawful for him to condemn other errors. Reason seems to confirm this. For what must be resisted with greater force is the greater danger; but heresies are more dangerous to the Christian faith than other errors. Therefore one who is not permitted to condemn heresies ought by no means to meddle with other errors. Others, however, say that inferior prelates may lawfully condemn errors of this kind. For this assertion the argument runs thus. What at some time was lawful for inferior prelates, and has not been revoked by the Pope or by a general council, is still lawful for them. But at some time it was lawful for other prelates to condemn errors of this kind, and it has not been revoked. Therefore it is still lawful. The major is plain. The minor is proved thus. For whoever may approve some truths may also reprobate contrary false assertions. But at one time it was lawful for inferior prelates to approve the truth that someone is a saint and is to be venerated by the faithful as a saint; for it was lawful for them to enrol new saints in the catalogue of saints. Therefore it was lawful for them to reprobate and solemnly condemn the false assertion that such men are not saints or worthy of veneration by the faithful. Therefore it is still lawful for them to condemn some errors. Disc. This argument seems to conclude against those who prove only that it was at one time lawful for them to condemn an error saying that such a man is not a saint. But now it is not lawful for them to condemn such an error, just as it is not now lawful for them to enrol anyone in the catalogue of saints. Mag. You do not fully understand their reasoning. For they do not intend to prove how it may be lawful for inferiors to the Pope to condemn one who asserts, or the assertion, that a man for whom God is said to work a miracle is not a saint; but they intend to argue that, by the same reasoning by which it was lawful for them to condemn such an error, it is lawful for them to condemn other errors as well. From these and other true and manifest points it can be concluded that they may condemn manifest heresies. Now the power over other errors has not been revoked. Therefore they can still condemn other errors. It is only that they cannot now condemn one who asserts that a man for whom they say a miracle is done is not a saint. Disc. I take the aforesaid argument more clearly. Therefore explain how the arguments of the others are answered. Mag. It is said that although they cannot condemn heresies, they can nonetheless condemn some errors far less grave than heresies; for inferiors may deal with many lesser matters, by which greater matters are known to be forbidden, since, as is read or gathered from the divine law in Deut. 1, greater matters must be referred to the greater. Yet it must not be said that prelates are not bound to resist heresies; but they ought not to resist them by condemning them, but by reporting them to the Pope or to a general council.

units.la: EXPLICIT LIBER SECVNDVS PRIMAE PARTIS Dialogorum. INCIPIT LIBER TERTIVS PRIMAE PARTIS, QVI SVNT catholici & qui haeretici, pertractans. CAP. I.
units.tr: Here ends the second book of the first part of the Dialogues. Here begins the third book of the first part, which treats of who are Catholics and who are heretics. Chapter I.

units.la: In quo primum proponitur, quomodo scilicet quis debeat catholicus reputari, & ibidem declaratur quid sit credere implicite.
units.tr: In which it is first set out who ought to be regarded as a Catholic, and it is also explained what it is to believe implicitly.

units.la: Discipulus. De veritatibus catholicis sufficiat praedicta quaesivisse. Nunc vero de catholicis & haereticis conabor nonnulla inquirere. Primo autem quaero, quis debet catholicus reputari. Magist. Ille est censendus catholicus, qui integram & inviolatam servat catholicam fidem. Discip. Quomodo potest simplex laicus integram fidem servare, qui de multis, quae ad fidem catholicam spectant, nunquam cogitavit. Talis ergo laicus catholicus non potest esse, si omnis catholicus integram tenet catholicam veritatem vel fidem. Magist. Respondent Theologi, quod servare vel tenere catholicam & integram fidem, continet omnia, quae ad fidem pertinent orthodoxam explicite vel implicite fideliter & absque ulla dubitatione credere. Discip. Quid est credere aliquid implicite? Magist. Respondent quod credere implicite est credere alicui vniuersali, ex quo multa sequuntur firmiter assentire, & nulli contrario pertinaciter adhaerere. Et imo qui firmiter tenent omnia tradita in scriptura & vniuersalis ecclesiae doctrina, esse vera & sana: & non adhaerent pertinaciter alicui assertioni contrariae veritati orthodoxae, fidem catholicam inviolatam tenent & integram, sunt catholici censendi. Discip. Videtur quod sufficiat credere omnia, quae credit vniuersalis ecclesia esse vera, ad hoc quod aliquis sit catholicus reputandus. Magist. Dicunt literati nonnulli, quod non sufficit credere omnia esse vera, quae vniuersalis credit ecclesia, nisi simul cum hoc nulli contrario particulari pertinaciter adhaereat. Multi etiam sunt haeretici damnati per concilia generalia, qui tamen firmiter tenuerunt tradita in scriptura sacra esse vera: quia tamen pertinaciter alicui assertioni in rei veritate contrariae assertioni scripturae divinae adhaeserunt, quamvis hoc eis non videretur, nihilominus non fuerunt catholici, sed haeretici iudicandi. Discip. Apparet mihi, quod non potest perfecte cognosci, quis sit reputandus catholicus, nisi sciatur quis sit haereticus iudicandus. Et ideo ad quaerendum de haereticis me converterem. Dic tamen prius, qualiter declaratur, quod aliquis potest credere, quod omnia quae continet scriptura divina vel vniuersalis ecclesia, sint vera: & tamen pertinaciter adhaeret alicui assertioni, quae contrariatur alicui veritati, quae in scriptura sacra vel in doctrina vniuersalis ecclesiae continetur? Magist. Hoc declarant sic. Sicut contingit aliquid scire in vniversali, & ignorare in particulari, secundum sententiam philosophi, quod non est aliud quam scire propositionem vniversalem & ignorare aliquam eius singularem: Sicut possum scire quod omnis homo est rationalis, ignorans hanc singularem; iste homo est rationalis, demonstrando aliquem, quem video a remotis, de quo ignoro an sit homo vel animal brutum: ita etiam contingit scire aliquam vniversalem, & reputare aliquam eius singularem esse falsam: sicut possum scire, quod omnis homo est risibilis, & tamen demonstrato aliquo homine, quem video à remotis quem puto esse asinum vel aliud animal (vt saepe contingit) possum credere quod ille non est risibilis: quia puto quod ille non est homo. Et sic possibile est, quod aliquis credat hanc vniuersale, omnia contenta in scriptura diuina sunt catholica & vera; & tamen credat hanc esse falsam, beatus Andreas fuit Apostolus Christi. Quia ignorat hanc veritatem; beatus Andreas fuit Apostolus Christi, contineri vel posse inferri ex scriptura diuina, quo posito si pertinaciter adhaereret quacunque ex causa huic; beatus Andreas non fuit Apostolus Christi, non Catholicus, sed haereticus esset iudicandus, quantumcunq; firmiter hanc vniuersalem, omnia quaecunque docet scriptura diuina, sunt catholica & vera, crederet.
units.tr: Disciple. It is enough to have asked about the Catholic truths mentioned above. Now I will try to inquire into some matters concerning Catholics and heretics. First, however, I ask: who ought to be regarded as a Catholic? Master. The one to be considered a Catholic is the one who keeps the whole and inviolate Catholic faith. Disciple. How can a simple layman keep the whole faith, when he has never given thought to many of the things that belong to the Catholic faith? So such a layman cannot be a Catholic, if every Catholic holds the whole Catholic truth or faith. Master. The theologians answer that to keep or hold the whole Catholic faith means to believe faithfully and without any doubt all the things that pertain to the orthodox faith, either explicitly or implicitly. Disciple. What is it to believe something implicitly? Master. They answer that to believe implicitly is to believe some universal proposition, from which many things follow, to assent firmly to it, and not to cling obstinately to anything contrary to it. Indeed, those who firmly hold all the things handed down in Scripture and the teaching of the universal Church to be true and sound, and do not obstinately cling to any assertion contrary to orthodox truth, hold the Catholic faith inviolate and entire, and are to be considered Catholics. Disciple. It seems that it is enough, for someone to be reckoned a Catholic, that he believe everything the universal Church believes to be true. Master. Some learned men say that it is not enough to believe all the things the universal Church believes to be true, unless at the same time one does not obstinately cling to any particular contrary opinion. Also, there are many heretics condemned by general councils who nevertheless firmly held that the things handed down in Holy Scripture are true; yet because they obstinately adhered to some assertion contrary in fact to an assertion of divine Scripture, although this did not seem so to them, they were nevertheless not Catholics but must be judged heretics. Disciple. It appears to me that one cannot fully know who is to be reckoned a Catholic unless it is known who is to be judged a heretic. And so I would turn to inquire about heretics. Yet tell me first, how is it explained that someone can believe that everything contained in divine Scripture or the universal Church is true, and yet obstinately adhere to some assertion which contradicts some truth contained in Holy Scripture or in the teaching of the universal Church? Master. They explain it thus. Just as it happens that one knows something in universal and is ignorant of it in particular, according to the opinion of the Philosopher, which is nothing other than knowing a universal proposition while being ignorant of one of its singular instances. As I can know that every man is rational, without knowing this singular proposition: this man is rational, pointing to someone whom I see from afar, about whom I do not know whether he is a man or a brute animal. So too it happens that one knows some universal and takes some singular instance of it to be false. As I can know that every man is risible, and yet, when some man whom I see from afar, and whom I think to be a donkey or some other animal (as often happens), is pointed out, I can believe that he is not risible, because I think he is not a man. And so it is possible that someone believes this universal, that all things contained in divine Scripture are Catholic and true, and yet believes this to be false: Saint Andrew was an Apostle of Christ. Because he does not know this truth, that Saint Andrew was an Apostle of Christ is contained in, or can be inferred from, divine Scripture. If, this being so, he obstinately adhered to the denial, for whatever cause, that Saint Andrew was an Apostle of Christ, he would be judged not a Catholic but a heretic, however firmly he believed the universal proposition that all things whatsoever divine Scripture teaches are Catholic and true.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Ponit distinctiones huius nominis haeretici, & ponuntur quinq.
units.tr: Sets out the distinctions of the word heretic, and there are five.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunc magis, quam ante, perpendo, quid ad cognoscendum, quis sit censendus catholicus, oportet scire, quis sit haereticus reputandus. Et imo de haereticis volo aliqua pertractari: ne tamen per aequiuocationem decipiar, dic primo, si hoc nomen haereticus habeat significationem vnam vel plures. Magist. Huius nominis haereticus plures significationes assignantur. Vno modo enim omnis excommunicatus, haereticus vocatur. Vnde 4. q. 1. c. 2. dicit Nicolaus Papa: haereticos autem dicimus tam eos qui ab ecclesia vniuersali sunt proiecti, quia qui post hac a nobis anathematizati sunt. Et in eodem capitulo notat Glossa dicens: Nota, quod omnis excommunicatus dicitur haereticus. Et hoc idem notat Glossa 24. q. 1. quia vero. Secundo modo dicitur haereticus, peruersor sacramentorum. Et sic simoniacus dicitur haereticus. Vnde Glossa, vt habetur 1. q. 1. Quisquis, ait: Quisquis per pecuniam ordinatur ad hoc quod fiat haereticus promouetur. Tertio modo dicitur haereticus, quicunque dubitat vel putat fidem Christianam esse falsam vel fictam. Et sic omnes Iudaei, Saraceni & Pagani sunt censendi haeretici. Hinc dicit Glossa 24. q. 3. quando large: Dicitur haereticus omnis, qui non tenet articulos fidei: & per hoc Iudaei & Gentiles sunt haeretici, & secundum hoc non omnis haereticus est excommunicatus. Isto etiam modo dubii in fide sunt haeretici, quia sunt infideles, extr. de haer. c. 1. Sic etiam qui primo sunt catholici, & postea reputant fidem catholicam esse falsam, sunt haeretici: & sic qui apostatant ore & mente a fide, haeretici sunt censendi. Si quis autem ipsorum tantummodo ore apostataret, non esset apud Deum haereticus, quamuis ecclesia ipsum deberet haereticum reputare, nisi constaret ipsum timore mortis apostatare. Quarto modo dicitur haereticus omnis Christianus, vel qui putat, aut qui putauerit se Christianum, errans pertinaciter contra veritatem. Discip. Quare dicitur, qui putat vel putauerit se Christianum fuisse. Magist. Dicitur propter illos, qui extra formam ecclesiae baptizantur, qui Christiani non sunt, sed putauerunt aut putant se Christianos esse; & tamen sunt haeretici: aliter tamen, quam Iudaei, vel Pagani, & aliter sunt puniendi. Discip. Dic, si alias habet significationes hoc nomen haereticus. Magist. Quinto modo dicitur haereticus, omnis pertinaciter adhaerens errori, qui sapit haereticam prauitatem.
units.tr: Disciple. Now, more than before, I see that to recognise who is to be judged a Catholic, one must know who is to be counted a heretic. I want some points about heretics to be discussed, but so that I am not deceived by an ambiguity, tell me first whether the word heretic has one meaning or several. Master. Several meanings are assigned to the word heretic. In one sense, every excommunicated person is called a heretic. Hence Pope Nicholas says in 4 q. 1 c. 2: We call heretics both those who have been cast out of the universal Church and those who are afterwards anathematized by us. In the same chapter the Gloss notes, saying: Note that every excommunicated person is called a heretic. The Gloss on 24 q. 1 (Quia vero) makes the same point. In the second sense, a heretic is a perverter of the sacraments. Thus a simoniac is called a heretic. Hence the Gloss, as found in 1 q. 1 (Quisquis), says: Whoever is ordained through money is promoted so that he becomes a heretic. In the third sense, anyone who doubts or thinks that the Christian faith is false or feigned is called a heretic. In this sense all Jews, Saracens and pagans are to be counted heretics. Hence the Gloss on 24 q. 3 (quando large) says: Everyone who does not hold the articles of faith is called a heretic, and in this way Jews and Gentiles are heretics, and in this sense not every heretic is excommunicated. In this same way, those who are doubtful in the faith are heretics, because they are unbelievers (Extra, de haereticis, c. 1). Likewise, those who were first Catholics and afterwards think the Catholic faith false are heretics; and so those who apostatise from the faith in word and mind are to be counted heretics. If, however, someone apostatised only in word, he would not be a heretic before God, although the Church ought to regard him as a heretic, unless it were certain that he apostatised out of fear of death. In the fourth sense, every Christian is called a heretic who is, or thinks himself, or once thought himself a Christian, and who errs obstinately against the truth. Disciple. Why is it said, who thinks or once thought himself to have been a Christian? Master. It is said for the sake of those who are baptized outside the form of the Church, who are not Christians, but who thought or think themselves to be Christians; and yet they are heretics, though they are to be punished differently from Jews or pagans. Disciple. Tell me whether this word heretic has other meanings. Master. In the fifth sense, a heretic is anyone who obstinately clings to an error that savours of heretical depravity.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Quaerit quis sit haereticus, secundum illam significationem, qua haereticus propter errorem in fide dicitur excommunicatus.
units.tr: He asks who is a heretic, in that sense in which a heretic is called excommunicate on account of error in the faith.

units.la: Discipulus. Clare intueor plures significationes huius nominis haereticus: quibusdam tamen earum notificatis licet saepe de haereticis mentio fiat. Dic ergo, si vidisti vel audisti descriptionem huius nominis haereticus in illa significatione, in qua communius accipitur. Magist. Tu forte intendis loqui de haeretico, qui est excommunicatus & conuictus legitime, & non se correxerit secundum formam ecclesiae, & est tradendus iudici seculari. Discip. Illud describe si potes. Magist. Quidam describunt eum dicentes: Haereticus est vere baptizatus vel pro baptizato se gerens, pertinaciter dubitans vel errans contra catholicam veritatem. Discip. Particulas declara, & quas personas intendunt includere. Magist. Per primam particulam, cum dicunt, vere baptizatus, excludunt baptizatos iocose, qui non pro baptizatis censentur. Comprehendunt autem per illam eandem particulam non solum Christianos a catholicis, sed etiam baptizatos ab haereticis in forma ecclesiae, & etiam illos, qui extra formam ecclesiae, quae scil. extra formam ecclesiae, puta sacramentum baptismi, nec quo ad gratiam, nec quo ad characterem quoquomodo suscipiunt, & pro baptizatis se gerunt. Per eandem etiam particulam excludunt Iudaeos, Saracenos & Paganos, qui nunquam baptizati fuerunt, nec pro baptizatis se gerunt; qui poena haereticorum, de quibus loqueris, minime sunt feriendi. Per secunda autem particulam, cum dicitur pro baptizato se gerens, comprehendunt illos, qui putant vel fingunt se baptizatos, & tanquam baptizati inter Christianos conuersantur. Qui si a fide recesserint, ac si fuissent vere baptizati, sunt plectendi. Per tertiam vero particulam, cum dicitur, pertinaciter dubitans vel errans contra catholicam veritatem: excluduntur omnes, qui ex simplicitate vel ignorantia sola absque omni pertinacia dubitarunt, vel dubitant, vel errant contra fidem. Tales enim non sunt censendi haeretici: sed sunt de fide cum diligentia informandi: qui si postea pertinaciter dubitauerint, vel errauerint, sunt haeretici iudicandi.
units.tr: Disciple. I clearly see several meanings of this word heretic, although a few of them have been explained, and people often speak of heretics. Tell me, then, whether you have seen or heard a description of the word heretic in that sense in which it is more commonly understood. Master. Perhaps you mean a heretic who has been excommunicated and lawfully convicted, who has not corrected himself according to the form of the Church, and is to be handed over to the secular judge. Disciple. Describe that, if you can. Master. Some describe him by saying: A heretic is one who has truly been baptized, or who presents himself as baptized, and who obstinately doubts or errs against catholic truth. Disciple. Explain the particles, and say which persons they intend to include. Master. By the first particle, when they say truly baptized, they exclude those who are baptized in jest and are not regarded as baptized. Yet by this same particle they comprehend not only Christians who are catholics, but also those baptized by heretics within the form of the Church, and also those who receive the sacrament of baptism outside the form of the Church (that is, the sacrament of baptism, as it were) in no way, either as to grace or as to the character, and yet present themselves as baptized. By this same particle they also exclude Jews, Saracens and pagans, who were never baptized and do not present themselves as baptized; these are by no means to be punished with the penalty of the heretics you are speaking of. By the second particle, when it is said presenting himself as baptized, they comprehend those who think or pretend that they are baptized and live among Christians as if they were baptized. If these fall away from the faith, they are to be punished just as if they had truly been baptized. By the third particle, when it is said, obstinately doubting or erring against catholic truth, all are excluded who have doubted, or doubt, or err against the faith from simplicity or ignorance alone, without any obstinacy. Such people are not to be regarded as heretics; they are to be instructed in the faith with care, and if afterwards they doubt or err obstinately, they are to be judged heretics.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: In quo obiicitur contra dicta in praecedenti capitulo de seriose baptizato extra formam ecclesiae, & ibidem declaratur, quomodo vario modo aliqui di- cuntur extra ecclesiam.
units.tr: In which objections are raised against what was said in the previous chapter about the seriously baptized outside the form of the Church, and it is explained how people are said to be outside the Church in various ways.

units.la: Discipulus. Ut materiam de haereticis magis intelligam, contra praedictam descriptionem multis modis obiiciam. Prima enim particula, quae ponitur loco generis, cum dicitur seriose baptizatus, non videtur convenienter poni: quia multi sunt seriose baptizati extra formam ecclesiae, qui quantumcunque erraverint pertinaciter, non sunt haeretici iudicandi, secundum quod nunc loquimur de haereticis, quia nunc solum loquimur de haereticis, qui sunt de foro ecclesiae, & per ecclesiam iudicandi. Illi autem, qui sunt extra ecclesiam, & nunquam fuerunt Christiani, non sunt per ecclesiam iudicandi teste, Apostolo, qui 1. ad Corinth. 5. cap. ait; Quid mihi de his qui foris sunt iudicare? sed baptizati extra formam ecclesiae semper fuerunt foris, & nunquam fuerunt Christiani. Igitur non sunt per ecclesiam iudicandi: & per consequens non sunt haeretici reputandi. Magist. Obiectio tua in aequivocatione fundatur. Nam variis modis aliqua dicuntur esse foris. Quidam enim sunt, qui nunquam nec vero, nec falso baptismo baptizati fuerunt, nec pro baptizatis qualitercunque se gesserunt. Et de his intelligit Apostolus: quia isti quantumcunque pertinaciter erraverunt contra catholicam veritatem, non sunt per ecclesiam (sicut haeretici baptizati) plectendi. Alii sunt foris, qui nunquam verum baptismum acceperunt, habuerunt tamen falsum baptismum vel pro baptizatis se gesserunt. Et isti (sicut qui fuerunt intra) iudicio ecclesiae sunt subiecti. Alii sunt foris, qui aliquando intus fuerunt, sed per censuram ecclesiasticam sunt ab ecclesia separati: & tamen aliquando manent intus. Et sic omnes excommunicati dicuntur foris. Hinc Hieron. ut habetur 24. q. 3. c. Si quis, ait: sicut interdum, ut ille, qui foris mittitur, intus sit, & iste foris, qui intus videtur retineri. Isti etiam quantumcunque sint foris, a iudicio ecclesiae minime sunt exempti.
units.tr: Student. So that I may understand the matter of heretics better, I will raise several objections against the above description. The first part, which is placed in the position of the genus, namely seriously baptized, does not seem to be fittingly placed. Many who are seriously baptized outside the form of the Church, however obstinately they have erred, are not to be judged heretics, since we are now speaking of heretics, that is, only of those who belong to the forum of the Church and are to be judged by the Church. But those who are outside the Church and were never Christians are not to be judged by the Church, as the Apostle witnesses in 1 Cor. 5, where he says: What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Those baptized outside the form of the Church, however, have always been outside and were never Christians. Therefore they are not to be judged by the Church, and consequently they are not to be regarded as heretics. Master. Your objection rests on an equivocation, for things are said to be outside in various ways. Some have never been baptized, either truly or falsely, nor have they conducted themselves as baptized persons in any way. It is of these that the Apostle speaks, since they, however obstinately they have erred against the Catholic truth, are not to be punished by the Church as baptized heretics are. Others are outside who never received true baptism, but either had false baptism or conducted themselves as baptized persons. These, like those who are inside, are subject to the judgment of the Church. Others are outside who were once inside but have been separated from the Church by ecclesiastical censure, and yet sometimes they remain inside. In this way all the excommunicated are said to be outside. Hence Jerome, as found in 24 q. 3 c. Si quis, says: Sometimes he who is sent outside is inside, and he who seems to be retained inside is outside. These people too, however much they are outside, are by no means exempt from the judgment of the Church.

units.la: Discip. Ista obiectio probabiliter soluta videtur; sed adhuc alia mihi occurrunt: quia amentes, dementes & penitus contradicentes, quamvis baptizentur, si postea pertinaciter erraverint, & in errore pertinaciter permanserint, non videntur haeretici reputandi: immo nec ad iurisdictionem ecclesiasticam pertinebunt. Magist. Dicunt isti describentes praedicto modo haereticum, quod taliter baptizati, si in contradictione persistant, nec vero baptismo nec falso intelliguntur baptizati. Non falso, ut constat: nec vero, quia quicunque baptizatur vero baptismo, characterem suscipit sacramenti. Discip. Quid dicunt de catechumenis experimentibus se habere propositum baptizandi; si, antequam baptizaretur, inciderent in haereticam pravitatem, vel ad ritum priorem redierint haeretici puniendi, pro eo quod se pro catholicis habuerunt. Quare si postea pertinaciter erraverint, pro haereticis sunt habendi. Item omnes adulti catholici & asserentes se habere propositum baptizandi, vel pro baptizatis baptismo flaminis se gerunt (tanquam baptizati) iudicio ecclesiae sunt subiecti, & per consequens si ad vomitum redierint, vel in errorem pertinacem inciderint, sunt per ecclesiam poena debita plectendi. Alii dicunt, quod tales, antequam baptizarentur, ad ecclesiasticam iurisdictionem non pertinent. Quare absque metu poenae ecclesiae & ad priorem possunt reuerti ritum, & in aliis pertinaciter errare.
units.tr: Student. This objection seems to have been answered in a plausible way, but other difficulties occur to me. Those who are mentally deficient, insane, or wholly lacking the use of reason, even if they are baptized, do not seem to be counted as heretics if afterwards they err obstinately and persist in their error; indeed they will not even fall under ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Master. Those who describe a heretic in the aforesaid way say that such persons, baptized in this manner, if they persist in contradiction, are understood to be baptized neither with true baptism nor with false. Not with false, as is clear; nor with true, because whoever is baptized with true baptism receives the character of the sacrament. Student. What do they say about catechumens who profess to have the intention of being baptized? If, before they were baptized, they fell into heretical perversity or returned to their former rite, they are to be punished as heretics, because they had presented themselves as Catholics. Therefore, if afterwards they err obstinately, they are to be held as heretics. Likewise all adult Catholics who assert that they have the intention of being baptized, or who conduct themselves as baptized persons by baptism of desire (as if they were baptized), are subject to the judgment of the Church. Consequently, if they return to their vomit or fall into obstinate error, they are to be punished by the Church with the penalty due. Others say that such persons, before they were baptized, did not belong to ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Therefore they may return to their former rite and err obstinately in other matters without fear of ecclesiastical punishment.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: In quo obiicitur contra ultimam particulam diffinitionis haeretici, scilicet pertinaciter, arguendo, quod ad hoc quod aliquis sit haereticus, sufficit quod sit dubius, vel errans in fide, & hoc pluribus auctoritatibus, ad quas respondetur responsioni generali capitulo nono, capitulo vero 10. specialiter ad singulas.
units.tr: In this chapter an objection is raised against the last part of the definition of heretic, namely "obstinately." The argument is that to be a heretic it is enough to be doubtful or erring in the faith. This is supported by several authorities, to which a general reply is made in chapter nine, and to each one specifically in chapter ten.

units.la: Discipulus. Licet de ista materia possem quaerere plura: quia tamen modo pauci vel nulli inveniuntur catechumi & non baptizati se pro baptizatis gerentes: & praesens opus volui fieri principaliter, ut melius controversias inter Christianos nostris temporibus ventilatas intelligerem: ad ultimam particulam descriptionis praemissae me transfero. Videtur enim, quod superflue sit positum pertinaciter: eo quod omnis Christianus, si simpliciter dubitat vel errat contra catholicam veritatem, est haereticorum numero aggregandus. Quod primo videtur posse probari auctoritate Innocent. 3. quae ut habetur, extr. de verb. sig. c. 1. super quibusdam scribens Comiti Tholosano ait: Tua devotio postulavit a nobis, qui sunt dicendi manifesti haeretici: super quo tibi duximus respondendum, illos esse intelligendos haereticos manifestos, qui contra catholicam fidem publice praedicant aut confitentur, seu defendunt errorem: vel qui coram praelatis suis convicti sunt, vel confessi, vel ab eis sententialiter damnati super haeretica pravitate. In quibus verbis de pertinacia nulla fit mentio. Quicunque ergo praedicat publice contra catholicam fidem, licet non pertinaciter erret, est dicendus haereticus. Hoc idem Caelestinus Papa, ut recitat Nicol. Papa, sentire videtur, qui, ut habetur 24. q. 1. c. ait Caelestinus, dicunt: si aliquis ab episcopo Nestorio aut ab aliis qui eum sequantur, (ex quo talia praedicare caperunt) vel excommunicatus vel exutus est seu antistitis seu clerici dignitate in nostra communione & durasse & durare manifestum est: nec iudicamus eum esse remotum: quia non poterat quenquam eius remouere sententia, qui in se prabuerat ipse remouendum.
units.tr: Disciple: I could raise many more points on this subject, but since few or no catechumens or unbaptized persons who pass themselves off as baptized are found nowadays, and since I wanted this work to be done chiefly so that I might better understand the controversies stirred up among Christians in our times, I turn to the last part of the definition given above. For it seems that "obstinately" has been added to no purpose, since every Christian who simply doubts or errs against catholic truth should be counted among the heretics. This could first seem to be proved by the authority of Innocent III, who, as is found in Extra, De verborum significatione, chapter 1, writing to the Count of Toulouse about certain people, says: "Your devotion has asked us who are to be called manifest heretics. On this we have thought fit to answer that those are to be understood as manifest heretics who publicly preach, confess or defend an error against the catholic faith, or who have been convicted or have confessed before their prelates, or have been sentenced by them as heretics." In these words no mention is made of obstinacy. Therefore whoever publicly preaches against the catholic faith, even if he does not err obstinately, is to be called a heretic. Pope Celestine seems to hold the same view, as Pope Nicholas quotes him in 24 q. 1 c.
