"Ait Caelestinus": "If anyone has been excommunicated, or stripped of the dignity of bishop or cleric, by Bishop Nestorius or by others who follow him, from the time when they began to preach such things, and it is clear that he has remained and still remains in this state, we do not judge him to be removed, because no sentence could remove anyone who had himself been prepared to be removed."

units.la: Ee Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod quam cito quis intendit prædicare contra catholicam veritatem, tacite excludendi alios potestatem amittit. Ex quo sequitur, quod talis est hæreticus reputandus. Et tamen ablq; pertinacia potest aliqua prædicare contraria catholicæ veritati. Ergo ad hoc, quod aliquis sit censendus hæreticus, non requiritur quod erret pertinaciter aut dubitet. Hoc etiam Beatus Hieronym. vt habetur 24. q. 1. c. hæc est fides, testari videtur, cum ait scribens Papæ: si autem hæc nostra confessio Apostolatus tui iudicio comprobatur, quicunq; me culpare voluerit, se imperitum aut malevolum vel etiam non catholicum, sed hæreticū comprobabit. Hic etiam de pertinacia nulla fit mentio. Ergo superflue ponitur pertinaciter in diffinitione prædicta. Item: Nullus nisi hæreticus damnatione hæreticorum involvitur teste Gelasio 24. quæst. 1. c. 1. Quicunq; in hæresim semel damnatam labitur, in eius damnatione seipsum involvit, vbi Papa inter labentem pertinaciter, vel non pertinaciter in hæresim semel damnatam non distinguit: & per consequens nos non debemus distinguere. Ergo quicunq; sive pertinaciter sive non pertinaciter labitur in hæresim semel damnatam, hæreticus est censendus. Hoci dem Gelasius, vt habetur in eisdem c. q. c. maiores, apte videtur asserere, dicens, auctore cuiuslibet infamia aut pariter errore damnato sufficere iudicauerunt, vt quisquis huiusmodi errorum communicator existeret, principali sententiæ damnationis eius effet astrictus. Cui Felix Papa, vt habetur eisdem c. 2. quæst. 6 Achatius secundus, concordare dicitur, dicens: itaque necesse est vt in illam iusta lance sententiam recideret, quam cum suis successoribus per conuenientiam synodalem susceperat auctor erroris. In his authoritatibus inter incidentem in hæresim pertinaciter & non pertinaciter isti summi pontifices non distinguunt: & tamen cum indiffinite & vniuersaliter dicant, sectatores hæreticorum similli sententiæ subiacere. Ergo superflue ponitur in diffinitione prædicta pertinaciter.
units.tr: From these words it is understood that as soon as someone intends to preach against catholic truth, he loses the power of tacitly excluding others. From this it follows that such a person must be regarded as a heretic. Yet someone may preach things contrary to catholic truth without obstinacy. Therefore, for someone to be judged a heretic, it is not required that he err obstinately or doubt. Blessed Jerome also seems to bear witness to this, as found in 24 q. 1 c. "Haec est fides," when he writes to the Pope: "If, however, this our confession is approved by your Apostleship's judgment, whoever wishes to blame me will show himself to be unskilled, or malicious, or even not a Catholic but a heretic." Here too no mention is made of obstinacy. Therefore "obstinately" is added to the above definition to no purpose. Again: according to Gelasius, as witnessed in 24 q. 1 c. 1, no one is involved in the condemnation of heretics except a heretic: "Whoever slips into a heresy once condemned involves himself in its condemnation." Here the Pope makes no distinction between one who slips into a condemned heresy obstinately and one who does not; and consequently neither should we. Therefore whoever slips into a heresy once condemned, whether obstinately or not, is to be counted a heretic. Gelasius likewise seems to assert the same aptly in the same chapter, "Maiores," saying: "They have judged that it is enough for the infamy of anyone, or for the error of anyone, to be condemned, so that whoever should be a communicant of such errors shall be bound by the principal sentence of his condemnation." Pope Felix II, in the same place (c. 2, q. 6, "Achatius secundus"), is said to agree with this, saying: "Therefore it is necessary that he fall back under that just sentence which the author of the error had accepted, together with his successors, through the synodal agreement." In these authorities the popes do not distinguish between one who falls into heresy obstinately and one who does not; and yet, since they speak without qualification and universally, they say that followers of heretics are subject to the same sentence. Therefore "obstinately" is added to the above definition to no purpose.

units.la: Item, Hieronym. super Epistolam ad Galat. 2. & ponitur 24. q. 3. c. hæresis, ait: quicunque ergo aliter scripturam intelligit, quam sensus Spiritus sancti flagitat, a quo scripta est, licet ab Ecclesia non recesserit, tamen hereticus appellari potest, & de carnis operibus est eligens quæ peiora sunt.
units.tr: Again, Jerome, on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2, and quoted in 24 q. 3 c. "Haeresis," says: "Whoever therefore understands Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit requires, by whom it was written, although he has not departed from the Church, may nevertheless be called a heretic, and he chooses from the works of the flesh the worse things."

units.la: Ad sectionem Dialogi pertinet; textus ut impressus est.
units.tr: This belongs to the section of the Dialogue; the text is as printed.

units.la: CAP. VI. Ostendit auctoritate Augustini, quod ad hoc, quod aliquis sit hæreticus, requiritur quod sit pertinax. Vbi etiam ponuntur quatuor conditiones, quarum vna ad minus, velomnes simul requiruntur, ad hoc, quod quis hæreticus sit censendus.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. He shows from the authority of Augustine that, for someone to be a heretic, it is required that he be obstinate. Here also four conditions are laid down, one of which at least, or all of them together, are required before someone is to be judged a heretic.

units.la: Magist. Si tibi exponerem, quomodo prædictam particulam probare niguntur, eorum rationes ad prædicta melius fortassis intelligeres. Discip. Expone. Magist. Quod pertinacia requiratur tam in dubitante vel errante ad hoc quod aliquis sit iudicandus hæreticus, multipliciter probare conantur. Primo auctoritate August. quæ ponitur 24. q. 3. c. dicit Apostolus, qui ait: nam qui sententiam suam quamvis falsam atq; perversam nulla pertinacia animo fixa defendunt, præsertim quam non audacia sua præsumptione pepererunt, sed a seductis atq; in errorem lapsis parentibus acceperunt: quærunt autem tanta sollicitudine veritatem, corrigi parati cum inuenerint, nequaquam sunt inter hæreticos deputandi. Ex quibus verbis, vt isti dicunt, colligitur euidenter, quod potest quis falsam & perversam tenere sententiam, & inter hæreticos minime computari. Discip. Clare mihi videtur probatum, quod non omnis dubitans vel errans contra fidem est hæreticus reputandus. Sed non est probatum, quod omnis hæreticus pertinaciter dubitat vel errat contra fidem. Et ideo illam particulam vltimam diffinitionis prædictæ, isti per præmissa verba Aug. minime probare possunt: quia omnis particula diffinitionis vel descriptionis cuiuscunq; datæ conuenienter, probari debet de descripto vel sumpto. Quod autem non probent omnem hæreticum pertinaciter dubitare vel errare contra fidem, ex verbis Beat. Aug. pa-tenter
units.tr: Teacher: If I were to explain to you how they try to prove that particular point, you would perhaps understand the reasons for what was said better. Student: Explain. Teacher: They try to prove in many ways that obstinacy is required both in one who doubts or errs, for him to be judged a heretic. First, by the authority of Augustine, which is cited in 24 q. 3 c. "The Apostle says," who writes: "For those who defend their opinion, however false and perverse, with no obstinacy fixed in their mind, especially one which they did not beget by their own presumptuous boldness, but received from parents who were led astray and had fallen into error, and who seek the truth with such eagerness that they are ready to be corrected when they have found it, are by no means to be counted among the heretics." From these words, as they say, it is clearly inferred that a person may hold a false and perverse opinion and yet not be reckoned a heretic at all. Student: It seems clear to me that it has been proved that not every one who doubts or errs against the faith is to be regarded as a heretic. But it has not been proved that every heretic doubts or errs obstinately against the faith. And so those men cannot prove that last clause of the aforesaid definition by the words of Augustine just cited, because every clause of a definition or description of anything whatever ought properly to be proved of the thing described or taken up. That they do not prove that every heretic doubts or errs obstinately against the faith clearly appears from the words of Blessed Augustine

units.la: {1} quo modo ad prædicta respondeat hæreticum taliter describentes. {·}enterapparet. Nam secundum beatum Augustinum ad hoc, quod aliquis tenens sententiam falsam atque peruersam, non debeat reputari haereticus, quatuor requiruntur. Primo quod sententiam falsam atque peruersam nulla pertinaci animositate defendat. Secundo quod talem sententiam non audacia suae praesumptionis inuenerit: sed a seductis parentibus atque in errorem lapsis acceperit. Tertio quod quaerat cauta sollicitudine veritatem. Quarto quod paratus sit corrigi cum inuenerit. Cuicunque ergo deficit aliquid istorum, est inter haereticos reputandus. Quamuis ergo quis non sit pertinax: sed cum audacia suae praesumptionis aliquam falsam & peruersam sententiam inuenerit: vel non quaerat cauta sollicitudine veritatem: aut si non sit paratus corrigi cum inuenerit: est inter haereticos computandus, iuxta sententiam Augustini. Magist. Ad illam obiectionem facile respondetur. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt isti esse sciendum, quod inter dubitantem & errantem pertinacem & interet erorem pertinaciter defendentem, differentia inuenitur. Quia multi haeretici dubitant vel errant pertinaciter, eo quod intus in mente sua dubitatione vel errore persistunt pertinaciter: qui tamen errorem susi vel dubitationem neque pertinaciter, neque aliquo modo defendunt: imo aliquando vel timore vel ambitione aut cupiditate vel aliqua de causa negant exterius, quod irreuocabiliter in mente tenent. Multi etiam econuerso falsam sententiam atque peruersam exterius pertinaci animositate defendunt vel defendere possunt, cui tamen nec pertinaciter nec aliquo modo in corde adhaerent. Nam contingit aliquando scientem defendere falsum. Quemadmodum saepe falsi & pessimi aduocati cupiditate ducti falsas causas & iniquas pertinacissima animositate defendunt. Et ita non omnis pertinaciter dubitans, vel errans falsam sententiam pertinaci animositate defendit, nec econuerso. Disc. Hoc quod nunc declaratum est, probabile puto, & ideo ad propositum applica. Dimittamus tamen loqui de dubitante, solummodo de errante loquendo. Quia forte dicunt isti, quod illa, quae de errante dicuntur, etiam de dubitante debent intelligi, prout dubitates de fide, sicut errantes contra fidem, inter haereticos computantur, vel ab haereticorum numero minime excluduntur. Magist. Sicut tibi placet solummodo de errante faciam mentionem, & qualiter saepe dicto modo describentes haereticum ad obiectionem tuam per praemissum notabile, quod tu approbare videris, respondeant, declarabo. Dicunt itaque, quod beatus Augustinus quatuor conditiones enumerat, quae requiruntur ad hoc, ut aliquis tenens falsam sententiam atque peruersam contra catholicam veritatem, non sit per Ecclesiam inter haereticos computandus: volens quod cuicunque defuerit aliqua conditionum praedictarum, est haereticus & etiam pertinax per Ecclesiam iudicandus: quamuis non omnis sit reputandus pertinax defensor praui tatis. Prima est, quod taliter errans errorem suum nulla pertinaci animositate defendat. Si enim errorem suum pertinaci animositate defenderet, catholici, qui de exterioribus non de interioribus motibus animae iudicant, debent eum inter haereticos computare, saltem praesumptione violenta, contra quam nulla est probatio in contrarium admittenda. Esto enim quod aliquis scienter contra conscientiam haeresim pertinaciter defenderet, ut ita in rei veritate apud Deum non esset haereticus, quamuis mortalissime peccaret, hoc tamen probare non posset: & ideo Ecclesia debet eum inter haereticos computare. Disc. Magis & magis intelligo differentiam inter haereticum & pertinacem; & inter pertinaci animositate haeresis defensorem. Unde videtur, quod potest aliquis etiam aliquam haeresim pertinaci animositate defendere, licet non debeant catholici ipsum haereticum reputare. Sicut si quis metu mortis coactus ab infidelibus errores eorum contra fideles pertinaci animositate defenderet, haeresim defenderet, & tamen non esset haereticus iudicandus. Quemadmodum beatus Marcellinus, qui metu mortis actum haereticalem commisit, fuit haereticus minime iudicandus. Magist. Dicunt isti, quod non bene intelligis, quis debeat reputari errorem pertinaci animositate defendere: quia ille solus, qui absq; metu mortis sponte & voluntarie errorem pertinaci animositate defendit. Et ideo ille, de quo tu ponis exemplum, quamdiu illum errorem defendit (& non nisi metu mortis) nullum errorem pertinaci animositate defendit. Disc. Illud non videtur bene dictum. Nam pertinax dicitur quasi impudenter tenax; & qui in sententia sua nimis persistit. Aliter enim nequaquam peccaret mortaliter errorem contra conscientiam defendendo. Ergo talis est erroris pertinax defensator: licet propter talem defensionem pertinacem non sit haereticus iudicandus, si constat fidelibus, & solummodo pro morte vitanda defendit errorem. Magist. Argumentum forte facis contra ipsos: & ideo forte dicerent, quod talis esset pertinax reputandus. Sed tamen non esset dicendum, quod errorem pertinaci animositate defenderet: quia voluntas animositatem spontaneam nullo metu coactam significare videtur. Et ita talis esset pertinax haeresis defensor: sed tamen non esset haereticus, nec haeresim etiam pertinaci animositate defenderet propter metum mortis illatum. Aliter dicerent, quod sicut animositas, ita etiam pertinacia voluntatem spontaneam nullo metu mortis coactam importat. Et ideo talis minime pertinax est dicendus. Disc. Nunc dicas, quid sentiunt isti de secundo, quod ponit Augustinus. Magist. Dicunt secundum Augustinum, quod qui audacia suae praesumptionis sententiam falsam inuenerint atque peruersam (licet quandoque talem sententiam nulla pertinaci animositate defendant) sunt pertinaces & haeretici iudicandi. Si autem non audacia suae praesumptionis, sed ex simplicitate vel ignorantia aliquam haeresim inuenirent, & factum eorum nihil aliud aggrauaret, neque per aliquod aliud possent conuinci: ita non essent pertinaces neque haeretici iudicandi. Qualiter autem innotescere possit, quod quis non ex audacia suae praesumptionis, sed ex simplicitate & ignorantia errorem inuenerit, seu peperit, non potest breuiter explicari. Disc. De hoc postea diligenter inquiram. Nunc autem isti ab intentione Augustini deuiare videntur. Nam in illa particula Augustinus duo simul iungit, ut aliquos errantes a numero haereticorum excludat, videvidelicet quod sententiam suam falsam non audacia suæ præsumptionis pepererint: & quod eam à parentibus seductis atq; in errorem lapsis acceperint. Ergo quicunq; sententiam suam peruersam à seductis & in errorem lapsis parentibus non accepit, est hæreticus iudicandus: sicut quicunq; sententiam peruersam audacia suæ præsumptionis peperit: est secundum istos hæreticus iudicandus. Confirmatur hæc conclusio, quia omnis, qui non accipit sententiam suam peruersam ab aliquo, & ipsam ex audacia suæ præsumptionis parit, quia aut habet à se aut ab alio. Sed secundum istos quicunq; hæresim de audacia suæ præsumptionis peperit, est hæreticus censendus. Ergo omnis errans contra fidem, qui errorem ab alio non acceperit, est inter hæreticos computandus. Et ita videtur, quod Augustin. ponit quinq; differentias, vt errantes à numero hæreticorum excludat. Magist. Dicunt quod Augu. illa duo simul iungit, non quod secundum eorum (scilicet quod à seductis atq; in errorem lapsis parentibus errantes suam sententiam peruersam acceperint) necessario requiritur ad hoc, quod errantes de numero hæreticorum sint censendi minime: sed illud secundum etiam ponit volens per ipsam assignare vnum modum probandi aliquos sententiam suam falsam ex audacia suæ præsumptionis minime peperisse: quia si à parentibus suis vel aliis quibuscunq; sententiam suam falsam acceperint, constat quod eam ex audacia suæ præsumptionis minime pepererint. Addit etiā illud secundum volens innuere, quod pluribus modis possunt errantes (errorem à suis accipientes parentibus) se excusare quam alii. Et ideo Augustin. non ponit ibi quinq;, sed quatuor, per quorum quodlibet potest quis probari & convinci hæreticus. Et quod quatuor eis contraria requirantur ad hoc quod aliquis errans non sit inter hæreticos computandus. Cum autem dicit, quod omnis, qui non accipit sententiam suam peruersam ab alio ipsam ex audacia suæ præsumptionis peperit & inuenit: Respondent, quod hoc non continet veritatem. Quidam enim absq; præsumptionis audacia ex ignorantia sola errores à seipsis inueniunt: quia tamen non sunt pertinaces, inter hæreticos minime numerantur. Discip. Expone quomodo declarant tertium, quod ponit August. Magist. Secundum eos Augu. intendit, quod ad hoc, quod aliquis errans contra fidem non sit hæreticus, requiritur quod quærat cauta sollicitudine veritatem. Non est autem intelligendum, oportere errantem omni tempore cauta sollicitudine quærere veritatem, si velit catholicus reputari: sed tunc oportet eum cauta sollicitudine quærere veritatem, si cupit à numero hæreticorum excludi, quando sibi à catholicis cum debitis circumstantiis monstratur, quod errat contra catholicam veritatem, & ipse non habet impedimentum legitimum, quare tunc non possit vel non debeat quærere veritatem. Alias enim haberetur contra ipsum præsumptio violenta, quod non ex simplicitate vel ignorantia, sed ex pertinacia sua adhæret errori. Discip. Dic de quarto. Magist. Quartum, quod etiam sufficit ad hoc, quod errans non sit numero hæreticorum aggregandus, est, quod paratus sit corrigi cum inuenerit veritatem: & sic nec pertinax, & per consequens nec hæreticus est censendus. Discip. Ista sola particula quarta reddit errantem pertinacem & hæreticum. Aliæ ergo superfluæ videntur. Magist. Licet secundum istos ista vltima particula reddat errantem pertinacem & hæreticum, & non alię: tamen ex aliis habetur violenta præsumptio, quod errans pertinaciter suo adhæreat errori: quia ex eo habetur præsumptio (cuius contrarium probari non potest) quod talis errans non est paratus corrigi: & per consequens inter pertinaces & hæreticos habendus.
units.tr: how they answer the foregoing objections, those who define a heretic in this way. This is plainly evident. For according to blessed Augustine, four things are required before someone who holds a false and perverse opinion ought not to be regarded as a heretic. First, that he defend the false and perverse opinion with no stubborn obstinacy. Second, that he did not discover such an opinion through the boldness of his own presumption, but received it from parents who had been led astray and had fallen into error. Third, that he seek the truth with careful diligence. Fourth, that he be ready to be corrected when he has found it. So whoever lacks any one of these is to be counted among the heretics. Therefore, although a man is not stubborn, yet if with the boldness of his presumption he has discovered some false and perverse opinion, or does not seek the truth with careful diligence, or is not ready to be corrected when he finds it, he is to be counted among the heretics, according to Augustine's judgment. Master. That objection is easily answered. To make this clear, you should know, they say, that there is a difference between one who doubts or errs stubbornly and one who stubbornly defends an error. For many heretics doubt or err stubbornly, because they persist stubbornly in their doubt or error inwardly in their minds, yet they neither stubbornly defend that error or doubt nor defend it in any way. Indeed, sometimes out of fear, or ambition, or greed, or some other cause, they deny outwardly what they hold unchangeably in their minds. Conversely, many defend, or are able to defend, a false and perverse opinion outwardly with stubborn zeal, though they do not cling to it stubbornly or in any way in their heart. For it sometimes happens that a man knowingly defends what is false, just as often skilled and very wicked advocates, driven by greed, defend false and unjust causes with the most stubborn zeal. And so not everyone who doubts or errs stubbornly defends a false opinion with stubborn zeal, nor conversely. Disciple. What has now been explained I think probable, and so apply it to the matter at hand. Yet let us drop speaking of the doubter, and speak only of the one who errs. For perhaps they will say that what is said of one who errs must also be understood of one who doubts about the faith, since those who doubt the faith, just like those who err against the faith, are counted among the heretics or are by no means excluded from the number of heretics. Master. As it pleases you, I will mention only the one who errs, and I will explain how those who often define a heretic in the said manner answer your objection, by means of the notable point just stated, which you seem to approve. They say, then, that blessed Augustine lists four conditions which are required so that one who holds a false and perverse opinion against the Catholic truth should not be counted among the heretics by the Church. He wishes that whoever lacks any one of the aforesaid conditions is to be judged by the Church a heretic and also stubborn, although not everyone is to be regarded as a stubborn defender of wickedness. The first is that one who thus errs does not defend his error with any stubborn zeal. For if he defended his error with stubborn zeal, Catholics, who judge by outward and not by inward movements of the soul, ought to count him among the heretics, at least on a violent presumption, against which no proof to the contrary is to be admitted. For even if someone knowingly defended heresy stubbornly against his conscience, so that in the truth of the matter before God he would not be a heretic, though he would sin most gravely, yet he could not prove this, and therefore the Church ought to count him among the heretics. Disciple. More and more I understand the difference between a heretic and one who defends a heresy with stubborn zeal. Hence it seems that someone may defend some heresy with stubborn zeal, and yet Catholics ought not to regard him as a heretic. For example, if someone, compelled by fear of death by unbelievers, defended their errors against the faithful with stubborn zeal, he would be defending a heresy, and yet he would not be judged a heretic. Just as blessed Marcellinus, who committed a heretical act from fear of death, was by no means to be judged a heretic. Master. They say that you do not rightly understand who ought to be regarded as one who defends an error with stubborn zeal, since only the one who, without fear of death, freely and willingly defends an error with stubborn zeal is such. And so he of whom you give the example, as long as he defends that error (and only from fear of death), defends no error with stubborn zeal. Disciple. That does not seem well said. For "stubborn" (pertinax) is said as if to mean impudently tenacious, and one who persists too much in his opinion. Otherwise he would not sin mortally by defending an error against his conscience. Therefore such a man is a stubborn defender of error, although, because of such a stubborn defence, he is not to be judged a heretic, if it is evident to the faithful and he defends the error only to avoid death. Master. Perhaps you are making an argument against them, and so perhaps they would say that such a man should be regarded as stubborn. But it should not be said that he defends the error with stubborn zeal, since the will seems to signify a zeal that is spontaneous and not compelled by any fear. And so such a man would be a stubborn defender of heresy, but he would not be a heretic, nor would he be defending the heresy with stubborn zeal, because of the fear of death imposed on him. They would put it another way: just as zeal, so also stubbornness implies a spontaneous will not compelled by any fear of death. And so such a man is by no means to be called stubborn. Disciple. Now tell me what they think about the second condition that Augustine lays down. Master. They say, following Augustine, that those who discovered a false and perverse opinion through the boldness of their presumption (although sometimes they defend such an opinion with no stubborn zeal) are to be judged stubborn and heretics. But if they discovered some heresy not through the boldness of their presumption, but from simplicity or ignorance, and their deed were aggravated by nothing else, nor could they be convicted by any other means, then they are not to be judged stubborn or heretics. However, how it can become known that someone discovered or produced an error not through the boldness of his presumption, but from simplicity and ignorance, cannot be briefly explained. Disciple. I will inquire about this carefully later. But now these men seem to depart from Augustine's intention. For in that clause Augustine joins two things together, so as to exclude from the number of heretics certain who err: namely, that they did not produce their false opinion through the boldness of their presumption, and that they received it from parents who had been led astray and had fallen into error. Therefore, whoever did not receive his perverse opinion from parents who had been led astray and had fallen into error is to be judged a heretic, just as whoever produced a perverse opinion through the boldness of his presumption is, according to them, to be judged a heretic. This conclusion is confirmed, because everyone who does not receive his opinion from anyone else, and produces it from the boldness of his presumption, has it either from himself or from another. But according to them, whoever produced a heresy from the boldness of his presumption is to be reckoned a heretic. Therefore everyone who errs against the faith and has not received the error from another is to be counted among the heretics. And so it seems that Augustine lays down five differences so as to exclude erring persons from the number of heretics. Master. They say that Augustine joins those two things together, not because, according to them, it is necessarily required (namely, that those who err have received their perverse opinion from parents who had been led astray and had fallen into error) in order that those who err should by no means be counted among the heretics. Rather, he also lays down that second point, wishing by it to indicate one way of proving that some people did not produce their false opinion through the boldness of their presumption: for if they received their false opinion from their parents or from anyone else whatever, it is clear that they did not produce it through the boldness of their presumption. He adds that second point also wishing to suggest that those who err may excuse themselves in more ways than others, when they have received the error from their parents. And so Augustine does not list five there, but four, any one of which can be used to prove and convict someone as a heretic. And that the four opposite things are required so that a person who errs is not to be counted among the heretics. As for his saying that everyone who does not receive his perverse opinion from another has produced and discovered it through the boldness of his presumption, they answer that this does not contain the truth. For some discover errors from ignorance alone, without any boldness of presumption, and because they are not stubborn, they are by no means numbered among the heretics. Disciple. Explain how they interpret the third thing that Augustine lays down. Master. According to them, Augustine means that for one who errs against the faith not to be a heretic, it is required that he seek the truth with careful diligence. However, it is not to be understood that one who errs must seek the truth with careful diligence at all times if he wishes to be regarded as a Catholic. Rather, he must seek the truth with careful diligence if he wishes to be excluded from the number of heretics, when it is shown to him by Catholics, with the due circumstances, that he errs against the Catholic truth, and he has no lawful hindrance why he could not or should not seek the truth at that time. For otherwise a violent presumption would be held against him, that he clings to the error not from simplicity or ignorance, but from his own obstinacy. Disciple. Tell me about the fourth. Master. The fourth, which is also sufficient so that one who errs is not to be numbered among the heretics, is that he be ready to be corrected when he has discovered the truth; and so he is judged neither stubborn, nor consequently a heretic. Disciple. That fourth clause alone makes the one who errs stubborn and a heretic. The others therefore seem superfluous. Master. Although according to them this last clause alone makes the one who errs stubborn and a heretic, and not the others, nevertheless from the others a violent presumption arises that the one who errs clings stubbornly to his error. For from this there arises a presumption (the contrary of which cannot be proved) that such a person who errs is not ready to be corrected, and consequently he must be held among the stubborn and the heretics.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Probat idem quod sextum alia auctoritate Augusti.
units.tr: He proves the same thing as the sixth, by another authority of Augustine.

units.la: Discipulus. Ad probandum, nullum errantem contra fidem esse hæreticum (nisi pertinaciter suo errori adhæreat) verba prædicta beati August. latis prolixe tractasti. Nunc ad eandem conclusionem aliquas probationes adducas, si quas cogitasti alias. Magist. Hæc eadem conclusio auctoritate August. contra Manicheos, qua recitatur 24. q. 3. c. qui in Ecclesia Christi, probatur, ait enim: qui in Ecclesia Christi morbidum aliquid prauumq; sapuerint, si correcti vt sanum rectumq; aliquid sapiant resistunt contumaciter: suaq; pestifera & mortifera dogmata emendare noluerint, sed defendere perfistunt, hæretici sunt. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, non omnes, qui in Ecclesia Christi morbidum prauumq; quid sapiunt, esse statim hæreticos iudicandos: sed ante ea sunt de pertinacia conuincendi, secundum quod in verbis scriptis innuit August. Discip. In verbis prædictis August. innuere videtur, quod non omnes errantes in Ecclesia Christi pertinaciter hæretici sunt censendi, cum videatur innuere, quod tria requirantur ad hoc, quod illi, qui in Ecclesia Christi morbidum aliquid prauumq; sapiunt, sint hæretici. Primum est, quod correcti vt sanum rectumq; quid sapiant, resistat contumaciter. Secundum est, quod si suos errores emendare noluerint. Tertium est, quod eosdem errores perfistant defendere. Si autem illa tria requirantur ad hoc, quod aliquis sit hæreticus (vt August. insinuare videtur) & multi suis erroribus adhærent pertinaciter, qui tamen eos non defendunt, imo quandoq; negant, sequitur quod non omnes suis erroribus pertinaciter adhærentes hæreticorum numero aggregantur. Magist. Dicunt isti, quod Augustinum male intelligis. Non enim vult August. quod illa tria requiratur ad hoc, quod aliquis sit hæreticus: imo vult, quod quodlibet istorum hæreticum facit errantem. Illa autem tria sic distinguuntur. Primum est quasi commune, & duo sunt quasi minus communia, exponentia quodammodo primum. Nam quod correpti vt sanum rectumq; quid sapiant, contumaciter resistant, dupliciter potest contingere: vel quia emendare (id est reuocare) nolunt vel defendere perfistunt. Et ita quodlibet istorum trium errantem reddit hæreticum & etiam pertinacem. Quare omnis pertinax hæreticus est censendus.
units.tr: Disciple. To prove that no one who errs against the faith is a heretic (unless he obstinately clings to his error), you have already treated the aforementioned words of blessed Augustine at considerable length. Now bring forward some other proofs for the same conclusion, if you have thought of any. Master. This same conclusion is proved by the authority of Augustine against the Manichaeans, which is quoted in 24. q. 3. c. qui in Ecclesia Christi. For he says: those who in the Church of Christ have tasted something diseased and perverse, if, when corrected, they stubbornly resist so that they taste something sound and right, and are unwilling to amend their pestilent and deadly dogmas but persist in defending them, are heretics. From these words it is given to understand that not all who taste something diseased and perverse in the Church of Christ are to be judged heretics at once; rather, before that they must be convicted of obstinacy, as Augustine hints in the words written. Disciple. In the aforementioned words Augustine seems to hint that not all who err in the Church of Christ are to be judged obstinate heretics, since he seems to hint that three things are required for those who in the Church of Christ taste something diseased and perverse to be heretics. The first is that, when corrected so that they may taste something sound and right, they stubbornly resist. The second is that they are unwilling to amend their errors. The third is that they persist in defending the same errors. If, then, those three things are required for someone to be a heretic (as Augustine seems to suggest), and many adhere obstinately to their errors yet do not defend them, but sometimes even deny them, it follows that not all who adhere obstinately to their errors are counted among the number of heretics. Master. Those men say that you misunderstand Augustine. For Augustine does not wish that those three things be required for someone to be a heretic; rather, he wishes that each one of them makes the erring person a heretic. Those three things, however, are distinguished thus: the first is, as it were, common, and the two are, as it were, less common, explaining the first in some way. For that, when corrected so that they may taste something sound and right, they stubbornly resist, can happen in two ways: either because they are unwilling to amend (that is, to retract) or because they persist in defending. And so each one of these three makes the erring person a heretic and also obstinate. Therefore every obstinate person is to be judged a heretic.

units.la: CAP.
CAP: VIII.
units.tr: CAP: VIII.

units.la: Probat idem quatuor rationibus.
units.tr: He proves the same by four arguments.

units.la: DIscipulus. Si adhuc sunt aliquæ auctoritates, vel rationes ad probandum, quod nullus errans nisi pertinax est hæreticus censendus, libenter auscultabo. Magist. Adhuc rationes aliquæ allegantur: quarum prima est hæc. Illi, qui non sunt à Catholicis repellendi, non sunt inter hæreticos computandi. Sed errantes & non pertinaciter non sunt à Catholicis repellendi. Ergo illi qui non sunt pertinaces, non sunt inter hæreticos computandi. Maior posset per Sacros Canones aperte probari: cum omnes hæretici sunt sententia excommunicationis innodati. Minor etiam clare probatur. Quia errantes, qui quærunt veritatem, non sunt à Catholicis repellendi, teste Pelagio Papa, qui vt habetur 24. q. 1. c. schisma, loquens de abundantibus in suo sensu, & per consequens errantibus, ait: si etiam ipsi (licet in suo sensu abundantes intra materna tamen positi viscera) quærerent veritatem, à nobis repellendi non essent. Ex quibus datur intelligi, quod quamdiu errantes etiam suo sensu abundantes quærerent veritatem prætendentes se velle corrigi, si veritatem invenerint, non sunt à catholicis repellendi. Et per consequens, quicunque non sunt pertinaces, non sunt à catholicis repellendi. Quicunque non est pertinax quærit veritatem pro loco & tempore, & à quibus tenetur quærere veritatem. Aliter enim pertinax esset censendus. Secunda ratio est hæc. Quicunque paratus est corrigi, non est censendus hæreticus. Sed quicunq; non est pertinax, paratus est corrigi. Ergo quicunq; non est pertinax, non est censendus hæreticus. Minor est evidens de se. Maior probatur per Gloss. 24. q. 3. c. dixit Apostolus, quæ ait: licet ergo tenet aliquis ea quæ sunt contra fidem (dum paratus sit corrigi) non est habendus hereticus. Et Gloss. e. c. & q. 1. c. a re certa, ait: licet quis erret (si tamen paratus est corrigi) non est hereticus. Tertia ratio est hæc. Qui firmiter credit omnia, quæ dicit vniversalis Ecclesia, esse catholica sana & vera, & nulli errori adhæret pertinaciter, est catholicus reputandus. Et per consequens non est habendus hæreticus. Sed qui errat (& non est pertinax) credit firmiter omnia, quæ dicit vniversalis Ecclesia, esse catholica, vera & sana, & nulli errori adhæret pertinaciter. Ergo talis non est hæreticus iudicandus. Quarta ratio est hæc. Non est maior ratio, quod vnus errans contra fidem non pertinaciter sit hæreticus, quam alius: quia de similibus simile est iudicium. Sed multi contra fidem errauerunt, qui tamen (quia nequaquam pertinaciter erraverunt) non fuerunt hæretici reputati. Ergo nec aliquis errans contra fidem (si non est pertinax) debet inter hæreticos computari. Maior est manifesta. Minor multis probatur exemplis. Augustinus enim in multis errauit, quæ postea retractauit: & per hoc se non fuisse pertinacem ostendit patenter. Et ideo non fuit hæreticus iudicatus. Idem patet de Hieronymo, de beato Cypriano, de quibus constat, quod pertinaces nullatenus extiterunt. Et propter hoc (quamuis errauerunt) hæretici non fuerunt.
units.tr: THE STUDENT. If there are still any authorities or arguments to prove that no one who errs should be judged a heretic unless he is obstinate, I shall gladly listen. THE MASTER. Some arguments are still put forward, the first of which is this. Those who are not to be rejected by Catholics are not to be counted among heretics. But those who err and not obstinately are not to be rejected by Catholics. Therefore those who are not obstinate are not to be counted among heretics. The major premise could be clearly proved from the Sacred Canons, since all heretics are bound by the sentence of excommunication. The minor premise is also clearly proved: because those who err and seek the truth are not to be rejected by Catholics, as Pope Pelagius testifies, who, as is found in 24. q. 1. c. schisma, speaking of those who abound in their own opinion, and consequently err, says: if even they (although abounding in their own sense and placed within the maternal bosom) were seeking the truth, they would not be rejected by us. From which it is to be understood that, as long as those who err, even those abounding in their own sense, seek the truth, professing that they wish to be corrected, if they find the truth they are not to be rejected by Catholics. And consequently, whoever is not obstinate is not to be rejected by Catholics. Whoever is not obstinate seeks the truth according to the place and time, and from those from whom he is bound to seek the truth. Otherwise he would be judged obstinate. The second argument is this. Whoever is ready to be corrected is not to be judged a heretic. But whoever is not obstinate is ready to be corrected. Therefore whoever is not obstinate is not to be judged a heretic. The minor is evident in itself. The major is proved by the Gloss on 24. q. 3. c. dixit Apostolus, which says: although someone holds those things which are contrary to the faith (provided he is ready to be corrected), he is not to be regarded as a heretic. And the Gloss on the same chapter and on q. 1, c. a re certa, says: although someone errs (if nevertheless he is ready to be corrected), he is not a heretic. The third argument is this. Whoever firmly believes all that the universal Church says to be catholic, sound and true, and does not cling obstinately to any error, is to be regarded as catholic. And consequently he is not to be regarded as a heretic. But whoever errs (and is not obstinate) firmly believes all that the universal Church says to be catholic, true and sound, and clings obstinately to no error. Therefore such a one is not to be judged a heretic. The fourth argument is this. There is no greater reason why one who errs against the faith, without obstinacy, should be a heretic than another, since like judgment is to be given in like cases. But many have erred against the faith who, because they did not err obstinately at all, were not regarded as heretics. Therefore neither should anyone who errs against the faith (if he is not obstinate) be counted among heretics. The major is manifest. The minor is proved by many examples. For Augustine erred in many things, which he afterwards retracted, and by this he plainly showed that he was not obstinate. And therefore he was not judged a heretic. The same is clear of Jerome and of blessed Cyprian, of whom it is established that they were in no way obstinate. And for this reason, although they erred, they were not heretics.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: In quo respondetur responsione generali ad auctoritates inductas capitulo quinto huius, & principaliter ad primam, distinguendo sex genera hereticorum.
units.tr: In which a general reply is made to the authorities cited in chapter five, chiefly the first, by distinguishing six kinds of heretics.

units.la: DIscipulus. Ad probandum, quod solus errans pertinaciter est hæreticus censendus, nolo ad præsens plures rationes audire: quia tecum post opus præsens omnia iterum perscrutabor. Et ideo quomodo respond eas ad illa, quæ adduxi in contrarium manifesta. Magist. Prima auctoritas, quam in contrarium allegasti, est Innoc. tertii, extra, de verbor. signif. super quibusdam verbis. Innoc. enumerat sex genera hominum, quos asserit esse hæreticos manifestos: Videlicet contra fidem publice prædicantes, profitentes, & errorem defendentes, coram prælatis convictos, confessos, & ab eis condemnatos de hæretica prauitate. Verba autem Innoc. deberent sane intelligi: quia aliter ex eis laberetur quis facile in errores. De prædicatoribus ergo publice contra fidem, debes distinguere: quia quod aliquis prædicet publice contra fidem quadrupliciter potest contingere. Vno modo, quod publice prædicet fidem Christianam esse falsam, dubiam, vanam & insanam. Et talis indubitanter est hæreticus manifestus: quia talis sine pertinacia inveniri non potest. Nam talis non est paratus corrigi per fidem Christianam, si non reputat eam veram, certam & sanam. Ergo pertinax & manifestus hæreticus est censendus. Secundo contingit aliquem prædicare contra fidem prædicando aliquem errorem, qui fidei obuiat Christianæ protestando, quod nunquam ab assertione sua desistet. Et talis est pertinax: quia non est paratus corrigi. Et ideo est hæreticus censendus. Tertio contingit aliquem prædicare publice contra fidem protestando, quod nihil intendit contra fidem orthodoxam tenere aut defendere temere. Et quia talis non ostendit se esse manifestum pertinacem: & quia non errat ex malitia & pertinacia: sed ex simplicitate vel ignorantia, non est hæreticus manifestus, nec ex sola tali publica prædicatione debet hæreticus reputari. Et propter hoc tales protestationes faciunt his temporibus (quibus quamplurimi ex odio, rancore, inuidia, malitia moliuntur meliores & sapientores sic de hæresi diffamare) complures docentes, prædicantes, & scribentes, vt coram omnibus se ostendant nullatenus pertinaces. Quarto contingit aliquem publice contra fidem prædicare simpliciter & absq; omni protestatione, quod non intendat vel intendit aliquid contra fidem temere defendere vel tenere. Et talis non est hæreticus censendus manifestus: sed examinandus est diligenter, an pertinaciter adhæreat errori, quem publice prædicauerit. Et si inuentus fuerit pertinax, debet
units.tr: DISCIPLE. To prove that only one who errs obstinately is to be counted a heretic, I do not want to hear many arguments at present, because I will go over everything again with you after the present work. So tell me how you answer those clear objections I brought against you. MASTER. The first authority you cited against us is that of Innocent III, extra, de verbor. signif. on certain words. Innocent lists six kinds of people whom he declares to be manifest heretics: namely, those who publicly preach against the faith, those who profess and defend error, those convicted before prelates, those who confess, and those condemned by them for heretical depravity. Innocent's words ought to be understood with care, since otherwise one could easily slip into error from them. So concerning those who publicly preach against the faith, you must make a distinction, because someone publicly preaching against the faith can happen in four ways. In one way, someone publicly preaches that the Christian faith is false, doubtful, vain and mad. Such a person is without doubt a manifest heretic, because such a person cannot be found without obstinacy. For he is not ready to be corrected by the Christian faith if he does not regard it as true, certain and sound. Therefore he is to be considered obstinate and a manifest heretic. Second, someone may preach against the faith by preaching some error that opposes the Christian faith, while protesting that he will never abandon his assertion. Such a person is obstinate, because he is not ready to be corrected, and so he is to be counted a heretic. Third, someone may publicly preach against the faith while protesting that he intends nothing against the orthodox faith and does not rashly hold or defend anything contrary to it. Since such a person does not show himself to be a manifest obstinate, and since he errs not from malice and obstinacy but from simplicity or ignorance, he is not a manifest heretic, and he ought not to be reckoned a heretic on the basis of such public preaching alone. For this reason, in these times, when very many people out of hatred, spite, envy and malice attack better and wiser men by slandering them as heretics, many teachers, preachers and writers make such protestations, so that before everyone they show themselves in no way obstinate. Fourth, someone may publicly preach against the faith simply and without any protestation, neither saying nor intending that he will rashly defend or hold anything against the faith. Such a person is not to be counted a manifest heretic, but must be carefully examined to see whether he obstinately adheres to the error he has publicly preached. And if he is found obstinate, he ought to be judged a heretic.

units.la: {mark} Numbers 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60 in the right margin are line numbers. debet haereticus iudicari. Ante examinationem autem est catholicus reputandus: quia quilibet reputandus est bonus, antequam contrarium sit aperte probatum, Et ideo talis praedicans, cum de assertione eius mentali constare non possit, non est haereticus iudicandus, quousque probetur contrarium. Sicut enim facta, quae dubium est quo animo fiant, in meliorem partem interpretari debemus, ut habetur extra, de Reg. Iur. c. Ssiore, ita cum nescimus quo animo praedicat quis aliquid contra fidem, animo scilicet pertinaciter adhaerendi, vel animo corrigendi se (si erraverit) in meliorem partem interpretari debemus, suspicando videlicet quod paratus est corrigi, cum veritas sibi fuerit manifesta. De secundo genere hominum, scilicet de profitentibus errorem, dicunt quod pertinaces sunt censendi haeretici manifesti. Professio enim a voluntate firmata solet procedere. Et ideo qui profitentur errore contrarium catholicae veritati, sunt reputandi firmati in errore. Quare pro pertinacibus sunt habendi. Et ex hoc sequitur, quod omnes iurantes se errorem aliquem fidei Christianae contrarium servaturos, & abiurantes quamcunque veritate catholicam, inter pertinaces & manifestos haereticos sunt censendi. Sicut enim professio & iuramentum, ita iuratio & abiuratio voluntate supponunt firmatam. De tertio genere hominum, scilicet qui defendunt errorem, distinguunt dicentes: Quod defendere errorem contingit dupliciter. Uno modo absque assertione temeraria, eo quod tuncita apparet. Et tales defendentes errorem suum verbo sive scripto, non sunt haeretici manifesti: quia parati sunt corrigi, cum inuenerint veritatem. Alio modo defendit quis errorem cum assertione temeraria, & talis est pertinax & haereticus manifestus. De quarto & quinto generibus, scilicet de convictis & confessis coram praelatis de haeretica pravitate, distinguunt. Quia illa pravitas potest attendi vel ex parte ipsorum convictorum, vel confessorum, aut solummodo ex parte erroris, de quo sunt convicti vel confessi. Si autem sit pravitas solummodo ex parte erroris, non ex parte confessorum vel convictorum, sic non sunt haeretici manifesti. Errores enim, quos tenuerunt Augustinus, Hieronymus, & Cyprianus, de quibus tactum est supra, & de quibus poterant convinci, pravi fuerunt: ipsi tamen non fuerunt pravi. Et ideo quamvis de illis erroribus coram praelatis convicti fuissent vel confessi, nullatenus haeretici extitissent. De sexto genere, scilicet de condemnatis de haeretica pravitate, absque distinctione dicunt, quod sunt haeretici manifesti, si rite & iuste fuerint condemnati. Quia nullus est sententialiter condemnandus de haeretica pravitate, nisi inveniatur pravitas non solum in errore, sed etiam in errante. Ista autem pravitas in errante est pertinacia. Et ideo soli pertinaces sunt de haeretica pravitate condemnandi. Discip. Ista probabilia mihi videntur: sed miror, quare Innoc. praedicto modo non distinxit. Magist. Respondetur, quod ideo, quia causae brevitas hoc non distinxit: sed quod taliter oporteat distinguere, ex aliis sacris canonibus evidenter apparet.
units.tr: Before examination, however, he is to be regarded as a Catholic, because everyone is to be regarded as good until the contrary has been clearly proved. So such a preacher, since his inner assertion cannot be known, is not to be judged a heretic until the contrary is proved. For just as we ought to interpret in the better sense deeds whose intention is doubtful, as is held in extra, de Reg. Iur. c. Ssiore, so when we do not know with what intention someone preaches something against the faith, namely whether with intention of obstinately adhering or of correcting himself if he has erred, we ought to interpret it in the better sense, supposing, that is, that he is ready to be corrected once the truth has been made plain to him. Concerning the second kind of people, namely those who profess error, they say that those who profess are to be counted manifest obstinate heretics. For a profession usually proceeds from a firm will. So those who profess an error contrary to Catholic truth are to be regarded as confirmed in error, and therefore are to be held obstinate. From this it follows that all who swear that they will keep some error contrary to the Christian faith, and who abjure any Catholic truth, are to be counted among the obstinate and manifest heretics. For just as profession presupposes a firm will, so do oath, swearing and abjuration. Concerning the third kind of people, namely those who defend error, they make a distinction, saying that defending error can happen in two ways. In one way, without rash assertion, when it is then evident. Those who defend their error by word or writing in this way are not manifest heretics, because they are ready to be corrected when they find the truth. In another way, someone defends error with rash assertion, and such a person is obstinate and a manifest heretic. Concerning the fourth and fifth kinds, namely those convicted and those confessing before prelates of heretical depravity, they make a distinction. For that depravity can be considered either on the part of the convicted or confessing persons themselves, or only on the part of the error of which they have been convicted or have confessed. If the depravity lies only on the part of the error, and not on the part of those who confessed or were convicted, then they are not manifest heretics. For the errors which Augustine, Jerome and Cyprian held, mentioned above, and of which they could have been convicted, were depraved, yet they themselves were not depraved. Therefore, although they had been convicted of or had confessed those errors before prelates, they would in no way have become heretics. Concerning the sixth kind, namely those condemned for heretical depravity, they say without distinction that they are manifest heretics, if they have been condemned duly and justly. For no one is to be condemned in judgment for heretical depravity unless depravity is found not only in the error but also in the one who errs. This depravity in the one who errs is obstinacy. Therefore only the obstinate are to be condemned for heretical depravity. DISCIPLE. These points seem plausible to me, but I wonder why Innocent did not make the distinction in the way you describe. MASTER. The answer is that the brevity of his purpose did not allow him to make this distinction; but that it ought to be made in this way clearly appears from other sacred canons.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Singulis respondet auctoritatibus in speciali.
units.tr: He answers each authority in particular.

units.la: Discipulus. Quamvis ex praedictis colligi possit, quomodo ad plures auctoritates, quas adduxi isto modo saepe tacto describentes haereticum responderent, volo tamen ut discurras per singulas. Magist. Ad auctoritatem Nicolai Papae recitantis verba Caelestini respondent, quod illa verba intelligenda sunt de publice praedicantibus scienter contra determinata a concilio generali, & de publice praedicantibus errores ipsos, eosdem temere asserendo, vel protestando se nunquam revocare eosdem, vel pertinaces se quomodolibet monstrando. Auctoritas vero Hieron. in oppositum allegatur: quia idem Hieron. in verbis adductis insinuare videtur, quod reprobans confessionem ab Apostolo approbatam non est ex hoc ipso haereticus reputandus, quia poterit esse imperitus. Et ita si ex sola imperitia dixerit contra veritatem, non est haereticus reputandus. Ad auctoritatem Gelasii dicunt, quod Gelasius intelligit de eo, qui scienter labitur in haeresim condemnatam. Talis enim est haereticus iudicandus. Et cum dicitur, Gelasius inter labentem in haeresim pertinaciter & non pertinaciter non distinguit: ergo neq; nos debemus distinguere: Isti respondent, quod ubi Papa vel canon non distinguit, neq; aliqua distinctio ex aliis canonibus, nec ex sacra scriptura, nec ex dictis autenticis, nec ex ratione evidenti patenter colligi potest, non debemus distinguere. Ubi autem ex aliquo vel aliquibus praedictorum distinctio manifeste accipitur, & non debemus distinguere. Sic enim est in proposito: quia ex aliis sacris canonibus & ratione aperte colligitur luculenter, quod inter labentem in haeresim damnatam pertinaciter & non pertinaciter, est distinctio manifesta. Dicunt etiam, quod Gelasius in cap. maiores, loquitur de scita communicatione erroris damnati, & etiam de pertinaci, sive sciat errorem esse damnatum sive ignoret. Ad auctoritatem Felicis Papae respondent, quod loquitur de Achatio, qui scienter damnato communicavit facinori. Et ideo fuit pertinax iudicandus: quia non erat paratus corrigi per doctrinam Ecclesiae. Ad auctoritatem Hier. quae ponitur 24. q.3.c. haeresis, respondetur: quod sicut recessus a malis duplex est, scilicet corporalis & spiritualis, prout asserit Aug. prout legitur 23. q.4.c. 1. sic recessus ab Ecclesia duplex est, scilicet corporalis & spiritualis. Corporalis autem recessus ex multis causis potest fieri. Potest enim aliquis recedere corporaliter ab Ecclesia, & ad haereticos corporaliter accedere: quia doctrinae suae vel opinioni Ecclesia non consentit aut reprobat. Et de isto recessu corporali ad praesens loquitur, non de aliquo recessu corporali, qui ex bona causa possit fieri. Alius est recessus ab Ecclesia spiritualis, & ille est duplex, scilicet manifestus & occultus, secundum quod haereticus est duplex scilicet manifestus & occultus. Similiter aliter intelligere scriptura, quae sensus Spiritus sancti flagitat, contingit dupliciter, scilicet cum pertinaci adhaesione & absque hac. QuiQuicunq; ergo cum pertinaci adhæsione aliter scripturam intelligit, quam sensus sancti Spiritus İntelligit, licet ab Ecclesia non recesserit, propter hoc neq; corporaliter Ecclesiæ suo sensui non consentit vel reprobat eundem vel spiritualiter manifeste, quia se esse pertinacem nequaquam ostendit apte: tamen hæreticus appellari potest, imo vere est hæreticus: quia ab Ecclesia recessit spiritualiter, licet occulte. Ad auctoritatem Stephani Papæ respondent dicentes, quod Stephanus Papa vocat illum dubium in fide, qui dubitat fidem Christianam esse veram vel sanam: non illum, qui dubitat de aliqua veritate catholica in speciali. Talis autem dubius in fide est pertinax seu pertinaciter dubitans: quia talis non est paratus corrigi per doctrinam, quam dubitat esse veram, cum nullus nisi per veritatem corrigi velit. Ille autem qui dubitat de aliquo articulo in speciali potest esse paratus corrigi per fidem Christianam, (quia per scripturam sacram) quam totam credit esse veram, licet dubitet de aliquo in speciali nesciens illud in sacris literis inveniri. Et ideo non est statim pertinax reputandus. Aliter est de illo, qui in genere vel universaliter dubitat fidem Christianam esse veram. Et de tali dubio in fide loquuntur Glossæ, quarum una 24. q. 1. super §. qui vero, ait: Vno modo dicitur hereticus, quicunq; dubius est in fide. Et alia Glossa eidem cap. & q. super. c. apte, ait: nota hæreticum esse titubantem in fide. Et post: nam & hæretici vocabulo continentur qui levi etiam argumento à fide deviant. Omnes enim loquuntur de illo qui dubitat fidem Christianam esse veram. Discip. Miror quod plus oportet dubitantem in fide esse pertinacem, quam dubitantem de aliquo articulo in speciali. Præsertim cum ita possit quis absq; pertinacia dubitari de universali, sicut de singulari. Magist. De hoc non reputant isti mirandum. Sicut enim inter propositiones est ordo, quia una est prior & alia posterior; una etiam fit nota per aliam: & sæpe nō econverso. Et ideo qui de propositione simpliciter prima in aliquo ordine, quæ nullo modo potest fieri nota per aliam, dubitaret, non esset præsumendum, quod vnquam ad illius notitiam esset venturus: licet si dubitaret de propositione posteriori, esset præsumendum, quod ad eius notitiam per propositiones priores posset attingere. Sic quia primum, quod oportet fidelem credere, est quod fides Christiana est vera: si de hoc quis dubitat, nihil remanet per quod ad aliquid firmiter credendum valeat revocari. Et ideo taliter dubitans tanquam pertinax & nolens corrigi est censendus. Si autem nullatenus dubitat fidem Christianam esse veram (licet dubitet de aliquo articulo speciali) præsumendum (nisi contrarium manifeste appareat) quod si sibi ostensus fuerit articulus, de quo dubitat, ad fidem pertinere catholicam, absq; mora se corriget. Discip. Quid si nullus potest sibi patenter ostendere, quod talis articulus ad fidem pertinet Christianam. Magist. Dicunt quod quousq; sibi fuerit evidenter ostensum dictum articulum ad fidem pertinere catholicam, sufficit sibi credere eum implicite, paratus credere explicite, cum sibi manifestum fuerit quod ad fidem pertinet Christianam. Discip. Procede ad alias auctoritates. Magist. Ad capitulum aperte, respondent quod loquitur de prædicante & titubante in fide: quia dubitant fidem Christianam esse veram. Ad verba Gratiani eodem modo respondent, quod loquitur de prædicante fidé esse falsam vel incertam, vel de pertinaci docente aliqua contra fidem. Non autem loquitur de illo, qui ex simplicitate vel ignorantia docet aliqua, quæ fidei obviant orthodoxæ. Ad rationem, qua innuitur, dicunt quod fides debet esse firma in universali, ut cuilibet veritati catholicæ firmiter, hoc est per fidem firmam vel implicite fidelis adhæreat: sed non est necesse, quod cuilibet adhæreat firmiter explicite. Et sic intelligendæ sunt auctoritates adductæ de concilio generali, & de Symbolo Athanasii. Dubitans autem in fide esse veram, non habet fidem firmam. Et sic loquitur Bernhardus. Et ideo non catholicus, sed hæreticus est censendus. Dubitans de aliquo articulo speciali habet firmam fidem, quod tota fides Christiana est vera & recta. Habet etiam fidem firmam implicite de eodem articulo, de quo dubitat. Et ideo est catholicus, licet de tali articulo non habeat firmam & explicitam fidem.
units.tr: Student. Although it may be gathered from what has been said how they would reply to the many authorities I have cited, describing the heretic in the way I have often touched on, I want you nonetheless to go through them one by one. Master. To the authority of Pope Nicholas, who recites the words of Celestine, they reply that those words are to be understood of those who publicly preach, knowingly, against what has been determined by a general council, and of those who publicly assert the same errors rashly, or protest that they will never retract them, or show themselves obstinate in any way. The authority of Jerome is cited against this, but Jerome in the words cited seems to suggest that one who rejects a confession approved by the Apostle is not on that account to be regarded as a heretic, since he may be unlearned. And so, if he has spoken against the truth from mere ignorance alone, he is not to be regarded as a heretic. To the authority of Gelasius they say that Gelasius means one who knowingly falls into a condemned heresy; such a person is to be judged a heretic. And when it is objected, Gelasius does not distinguish between one who falls into heresy obstinately and one who does not: therefore neither should we make a distinction, they answer that where the Pope or a canon makes no distinction, and no distinction can be plainly gathered from other canons, from Holy Scripture, from authentic sayings, or from clear reason, we ought not to make one. But where a distinction is plainly drawn from one or more of these sources, we ought to make it. This is the case in the present matter, for it is clearly and brightly gathered from other sacred canons and from reason that there is a manifest distinction between one who falls into a condemned heresy obstinately and one who does not. They also say that Gelasius, in cap. maiores, speaks of knowing communion with a condemned error, and of obstinate communion too, whether the person knows the error to be condemned or is ignorant of it. To the authority of Pope Felix they reply that he speaks of Achatius, who knowingly communicated in a deed already condemned; and so he was to be judged obstinate, because he was not prepared to be corrected by the teaching of the Church. To the authority of Jerome that is cited in 24. q.3.c. haeresis, the reply is this: just as withdrawal from evils is twofold, namely bodily and spiritual, as Augustine asserts and as is read in 23. q.4.c. 1., so withdrawal from the Church is twofold, namely bodily and spiritual. Bodily withdrawal can happen for many reasons. For a person may withdraw bodily from the Church and go over bodily to the heretics, because the Church does not agree with or condemns his teaching or opinion. It is of this bodily withdrawal that he speaks for the present, not of any bodily withdrawal that may be made for a good cause. The other kind is spiritual withdrawal from the Church, and this is twofold, namely manifest and hidden, just as heresy is twofold, namely manifest and hidden. Likewise, to understand Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit requires happens in two ways, namely with obstinate adherence and without it. Whoever therefore understands Scripture otherwise than the Holy Spirit's sense with obstinate adherence, although he has not withdrawn from the Church, is not on that account bodily withdrawn from the Church, nor does he dissent from or condemn its sense either bodily or manifestly in spirit, because he does not clearly show himself to be obstinate. Yet he may be called a heretic, and indeed truly is a heretic, because he has withdrawn from the Church spiritually, though secretly. To the authority of Pope Stephen they reply, saying that Stephen calls doubtful in the faith the one who doubts that the Christian faith is true or sound, not the one who doubts some particular Catholic truth. Such a person, doubtful in the faith, is obstinate, or doubts obstinately, because he is not prepared to be corrected by the teaching which he doubts to be true, since no one wishes to be corrected except by the truth. But one who doubts some particular article can be prepared to be corrected by the Christian faith (since it is through Holy Scripture), which he believes to be wholly true, even though he doubts some particular point, not knowing that it is found in the sacred letters. And so he is not at once to be regarded as obstinate. It is otherwise with one who doubts in general, or universally, that the Christian faith is true. It is of such doubt in the faith that the Glosses speak. One of them, on 24. q.1 on the §. qui vero, says: In one way he is called a heretic who is doubtful in the faith. And another Gloss on the same chapter and question, on the chapter apte, says: note that a heretic is one who wavers in the faith. And afterwards: for under the name of heretic are included also those who deviate from the faith even on a slight argument. For they all speak of one who doubts that the Christian faith is true. Student. I wonder why one doubting in the faith must be more obstinate than one doubting some particular article, especially since one may be doubtful in the universal just as without obstinacy as in the particular. Master. These men do not think this is to be wondered at. For just as there is an order among propositions, since one is prior and another posterior, and one is made known by another, and often not the reverse, so one who doubted a proposition that is simply first in some order, which cannot be made known by another, would not be presumed ever to come to know it; whereas if he doubted a later proposition, it would be presumed that he could attain knowledge of it through the earlier propositions. Thus, since the first thing a believer must believe is that the Christian faith is true, if someone doubts this, nothing remains by which he can be recalled to firmly believing anything. Therefore one who doubts in this way is to be judged obstinate and unwilling to be corrected. But if he does not doubt at all that the Christian faith is true (although he doubts some particular article), it is to be presumed (unless the contrary clearly appears) that if the article about which he doubts is shown to him to belong to the Catholic faith, he will correct himself without delay. Student. What if no one can plainly show him that such an article belongs to the Christian faith? Master. They say that until it has been clearly shown to him that the said article belongs to the Catholic faith, it is enough that he believes it implicitly, being prepared to believe it explicitly once it has become plain to him that it belongs to the Christian faith. Student. Proceed to the other authorities. Master. To the chapter aperte, they reply that it speaks of one who preaches and wavers in the faith, because such people doubt that the Christian faith is true. To the words of Gratian they reply in the same way, that he speaks of one who preaches that the faith is false or uncertain, or of an obstinate teacher of something against the faith. It does not speak of one who, from simplicity or ignorance, teaches things that run counter to the orthodox faith. To the argument by which a point is hinted at, they say that the faith must be firm in general, so that the faithful adhere firmly, that is, through firm faith or implicitly, to every Catholic truth; but it is not necessary that one adhere to each explicitly and firmly. And in this way the authorities cited from the general council and from the Athanasian Creed are to be understood. But one who doubts that the faith is true does not have firm faith. And this is how Bernard speaks. And therefore he is to be regarded not as a Catholic but as a heretic. One who doubts some particular article has firm faith that the whole Christian faith is true and right. He also has firm faith implicitly in the very article about which he doubts. And therefore he is a Catholic, although he does not have firm and explicit faith in that article.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Ponit tres instantias alias contra diffinitionem hæretici supra cap. 3. huius datam, quæ etiam soluuntur.
units.tr: He puts forward three other objections against the definition of the heretic given above in chapter 3 of this book, and these are also answered.

units.la: Discipulus: Adhuc ad vnam instantiam, quæ totam descriptionem hæretici memoratam videtur elidere, cupio responderi. Beatus enim Augustus vt habetur 24. q. 3. cap. hereticus, diffinit hæreticum in hunc modum: hereticus est, qui alicuius temporalis commodi & maxime vanæ gloriæ principatusq; sui gratia, falsas ac nouas opiniones gignit vel sequitur. Et qua diffinitione colligitur, quod qui tantummodo veteres hæreses imitatur, licet sint pertinaces, non sunt hæretici reputandi. Et ideo prior descriptio hæretici non est congrue assignata: quia competit multis (scilicet illis qui tantummodo veteres hæreses imitantur) qui tamen non sunt hæretici iudicandi, secundum diffinitionem Augusti, eo quod nouas opiniones neq; gignunt neq; sequuntur. Item, multi baptizati pertinaciter errant ex sola credulitate vel deceptione, non gratia alicuius temporalis commodi, nec vanæ gloriæ; nec principatus, nec gratia sua. Et per consequens secundum Augustum non sunt hæretici iudicandi. Et tamen illis competit descriptio sæpe fata. Ergo non est vera descriptio. Item, aliquis certus de fide & in nullo dubitans, alicuius temporalis commodi & vanæ gloriæ maxime, principatusq; sui gratia, contra conscientiam, potest nouas & falsas opiniones gignere atq; sequi. Ergo certus de fide & in nullo dubitans potest esse hæreticus secundum intentionem Augusti. male ergo describitur hæreticus, cum asseritur quod omnis hæreticus est pertinaciter dubitans vel errans contra catholicam veritatem. Magist. Ad illa isti dicunt, quod Augustus non intendit in verbis præscriptis hæreticum definire. finire: sed intendit assignare vnum modum cognoscendi haereticum; vt scilicet quicunque aliquius temporalis commodi & maxime vanae gloriae principatusq; sui gratia falsas ac nouas opiniones gignit vel sequitur, censeatur haereticus. Unde licet in propositione, quā ponit Aug. intelligatur vel primo ponatur vocaliter haereticus ante copulam, & ex hoc posset quis opinari, quod haereticus sit subiectum: secundum tamen rei veritatem, vt isti dicunt, haereticus debet esse praedicatum, & id quod sequitur, debet esse subiectum. Et isto modo sub bono intellectu concedenda est vniuersalis formata ex verbis August. ita videlicet: Quicunq; alicuius temporalis commodi & maxime vanae gloriae principatusq; sui gratia non pertinaciter defendendi nouas opiniones, vel falsas contra fidem gignit vel sequitur, est reputandus haereticus. Sed si contra conscientiam & in corde de aliquo pertinente ad fidem nullatenus dubitans praedicto modo haereses gigneret vel sequeretur, non esset apud Deum, qui cor intuetur, haereticus, quamuis mortalissime coram Deo peccaret. Discip. Quomodo debet quis haereticus reputari, si non est coram Deo haereticus? Magist. Ad hoc respondetur faciliter, quod de exterioribus habemus tantum modo iudicare: occulta autem ad iudicium spectant diuinum. Et ideo talis a nobis est censendus haereticus propter illa, quae nobis apparent exterius, licet apud Deum non sit haereticus. Quamuis saepe multos bonos arbitrari debemus, quia nullum malum in ipsis apparet nobis, qui tamen apud Deum sunt pessimi. Discip. Discurre per obiectiones, quas feci. Magist. Ad primam earum respondetur, quod qui veteres haereses imitantur pertinaciter sunt haeretici censendi. Et ideo non soli, qui quacunq; ex causa nouas & falsas opiniones gignunt vel sequuntur, sunt haeretici: sed etiam alii multi. Nam qui modo haeresim Arrii ab antiquo damnatam pertinaciter defensaret, esset haereticus iudicandus. Nec obstant verba August. quia (vt dictum est) non intendit per illa verba neq; diffinitionem neq; descriptionem haeretici assignare. Unde dicunt, quod saepe multi falluntur de enunciationibus sanctorum & auctorum, putantes velle diffinitiones vel descriptiones aliquarum rerum vel nominum assignare, cum tamen nunquam hoc intendant, sed solumodo proponentes particulares veras asserere. Ad secundam respondetur, quod pertinaciter errantes ex sola credulitate vel deceptione sunt haeretici iudicandi: quia non soli illi, de quibus loquitur August. in verbis praemissis, sed etiam alii sunt censendi haeretici. Ad tertiam dicunt illi, qui in corde non dubitant, tamen alicuius temporalis commodi gratia, vel forte pro temporali periculo (citra mortem) vitando, assertiones haereticales sequuntur, quales dicunt esse multos his diebus & maxime de ordine Fratrum Minorum, qui opiniones nouas de paupertate Christi & Apostolorum, ac etiam de animabus damnatorum & sanctorum, quas in cordibus suis putant haereticas, & tamen ipsas pertinaci animositate sequuntur, non sunt in veritate haeretici, & tamen a fidelibus (qui non habent de occultis motibus animae iudicare) sunt haeretici reputandi: & tamen in omnibus tanquam haeretici fugiendi: & si postea dicerent se dictas haereses in mente minime tenuisse, sed pro assequendo aliquo commodo temporali vel pro vitando periculo se finxisse tenere, non esset eis fides aliqua adhibenda, sed essent abomini assertione & testimonio tanquam falsi & duplices repellendi. Discip. De illis, quae isti adducunt in exemplum, alias interrogabo sollicite, & ad probandum quod isti, qui sunt sectatores sanctissimi patris Domini Innoc. Papae 22. non sunt haeretici nec errantes, sed catholici & fideles, fortiter allegabo. Magist. Vis ergo istius operis hic sit finis.
units.tr: Student: I would like a reply to one more objection, which seems to overturn the whole description of the heretic given above. Blessed Augustine, as found in 24. q. 3, cap. hereticus, defines the heretic in this way: a heretic is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage and especially of vain glory and his own preeminence, begets or follows false and new opinions. From this definition it follows that whoever merely imitates old heresies, however obstinate he may be, is not to be counted a heretic. So the earlier description of the heretic is not properly framed, because it applies to many (namely, those who only imitate old heresies) who nevertheless, by Augustine's definition, are not to be judged heretics, since they neither beget nor follow new opinions. Again, many baptized persons err obstinately out of mere credulity or deception, not for the sake of any temporal advantage, vain glory, preeminence, or favour of their own. Consequently, according to Augustine, they are not to be judged heretics, and yet the description mentioned above applies to them. Therefore it is not a true description. Again, someone who is certain of the faith and doubts nothing may, for the sake of some temporal advantage, and especially of vain glory, preeminence, or his own favour, and against his conscience, beget and follow new and false opinions. Therefore a man certain of the faith and doubting nothing can be a heretic in Augustine's sense. The heretic is therefore badly described when it is asserted that every heretic is one who obstinately doubts or errs against Catholic truth. Master: To these objections, those people reply that Augustine did not intend, in the words quoted, to define the heretic. He intended to give one way of recognizing a heretic, namely that whoever for the sake of some temporal advantage, and especially of vain glory, preeminence or his own favour, begets or follows false and new opinions, is to be judged a heretic. Hence, although in the proposition Augustine gives, the word heretic is set down first and stands before the copula, so that someone might suppose it to be the subject, nevertheless, they say, in the true sense of the matter the heretic must be the predicate, and what follows must be the subject. In this way a universal proposition formed from Augustine's words can be granted in a good sense, namely: whoever, for the sake of some temporal advantage and especially of vain glory, preeminence, or his own favour, begets or follows false opinions or new ones against the faith, defending them obstinately, is to be reckoned a heretic. But if someone, against his conscience and without any doubt in his heart about anything pertaining to the faith, begot or followed heresies in the manner described, he would not be a heretic before God, who looks upon the heart, even though he would sin most grievously before God. Student: How ought a man to be reckoned a heretic if he is not a heretic before God? Master: To this it is easily answered that we are able to judge only from outward things, but hidden things belong to the judgment of God. Therefore such a man is to be counted a heretic by us, on account of those things which appear to us outwardly, although before God he is not a heretic. Indeed, we ought often to think many men good, because no evil appears in them to us, though they are most wicked before God. Student: Go through the objections I have raised. Master: To the first of them it is answered that those who obstinately imitate old heresies are to be counted heretics. Therefore it is not only those who, for whatever reason, beget or follow new and false opinions who are heretics, but many others as well. For whoever in our time obstinately defended the heresy of Arius, long ago condemned, would have to be judged a heretic. Nor do Augustine's words stand in the way, because (as has been said) he did not intend by those words to assign either a definition or a description of the heretic. So they say that people often go wrong about the statements of saints and authors, supposing that they wish to set out definitions or descriptions of certain things or names, when in fact they never intend this, but only propose particular truths to assert. To the second objection it is answered that those who err obstinately out of mere credulity or deception are to be judged heretics, because not only those of whom Augustine speaks in the words quoted, but also others, are to be counted heretics. To the third, those people say that those who do not doubt in their hearts, yet for the sake of some temporal advantage, or perhaps to avoid some temporal danger short of death, follow heretical assertions, such as, they say, many in these days do, especially of the Order of Friars Minor, who put forward new opinions about the poverty of Christ and the apostles, and also about the souls of the damned and of the saints, which in their hearts they think heretical, and yet follow them with obstinate boldness, are not in truth heretics. Nevertheless they are to be counted heretics by the faithful (who cannot judge the hidden movements of the soul), and must be avoided in everything as heretics.
