And if afterwards they said that they had never really held those heresies in mind, but had only pretended to hold them in order to obtain some temporal advantage or to avoid danger, they should not be given any credence, but should be rejected as liars and double-dealers, their assertions and testimony being abominable. Student: About those examples which they bring forward, I shall question them carefully in another place, and I shall argue vigorously to prove that those who are followers of the most holy father, the lord Pope Innocent 22, are not heretics or erring, but Catholic and faithful. Master: Let this, then, be the end of this work.

units.la: Explicit Liber tertius Dialogorum.
units.tr: The End of the Third Book of the Dialogues.

units.la: Incipit Quartus Liber eiusdem primae partis, docens qualiter de pertinacia praesumitur haeretica quis debeat conuinci.
units.tr: Here begins the Fourth Book of the same first part, teaching how a person may be convicted of heretical pertinacity.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: In quo quaeritur & ponitur diffinitio pertinacis, secundum vnam opinionem.
units.tr: In which the question is raised and a definition of the pertinacious person is given, according to one opinion.

units.la: Discipulus. Volo hic istum librum finiri: & ad quartum me transferam. Intendo enim inquirere, quomodo de pertinacia debeat quis conuinci ante omnia. Cupio tamen scire, quomodo pertinacia diffinitione exprimente quid nominis diffinitur. Ex tali namq; diffinitione (vt puto) multae difficultates debent solui: nec sine ipsius notitia poterit sciri qualiter de pertinacia debeat quis conuinci. Magist. Pertinax a quibusdam diffinitur sic: pertinax est qui persistit in eo, quod debet dimittere. Istam diffinitionem declarant dupliciter. Primo modo auctoritate Isidori dicentis, quod pertinax dicitur quasi impudenter tenax. Ille autem est impudenter tenax, qui tenet quod debet dimittere. Ergo pertinax est ille, qui tenet & persistit in illo, quod debet dimittere. Secundo sic: Perseuerantia & pertinacia opponuntur, & contrarias debent diffinitiones habere. Sed perseuerans est ille, qui persistit in illo quod debet. Ergo pertinax est ille, qui persistit in illo quod debet dimittere. Disc. Miror, quia isti volunt probare diffinitione pertinacitatis de pertinace, cum diffinitio de diffinito probari non possit. Magist. Non intendunt probare proprie loquendo diffinitionem pertinacis de pertinacitate: sed volunt declarare, & per declarationes manifestare quodammodo diffinitionem pertinacis. Discip. De talibus diffinitionibus nolo me intromittere multum ad praesens: sed aliud mouet me contra diffinitionem praedictam: quia secundum eam omnis errans est pertinax. Omnis enim errans, quam diu est in errore, est pertinax. Sed nullus vnquam debet esse in errore: imo omnis errans debet errorem dimittere. Ergo omnis errans est pertinax. Magist. Dicunt per aequiuocationem te decipi. Est enim debitor necessitatis & debitor congruitatis. In prædicta autem diffinitione accipi debet secundum quod importat debitum necessitatis, vt iste sit sensus: pertinax est ille: qui persistit in aliquo quod de necessitate debet dimittere. Esto ergo quod omnis errans (debito, quod congruitatis dicunt) oportet errorem dimittere (quod non est verum :) non tamen omnis errans de necessitate salutis omni tempore debet errorem suum dimittere. Discip. Video quod isti diffinium pertinacem communius, quam competat erranti in fide. Et ideo appropria diffinitionem prædictam in fide erranti. Magist. Appropriatur sic. Pertinaciter dubitans contra fidem est, qui persistit in dubitatione circa ea quæ sunt fidei, quam debet de necessitate salutis dimittere. Discip. Secundum prædicta omnes Iudæi & Gentiles essent pertinaces, quia omnes tenentur errorem suum dimittere. Ista est difficultas, quæ longum tractatum requireret propter illos, qui nunquam de fide vera informati fuerunt, nec est desectus istorum qui informationem minime habuerunt, si qui sunt tales. De aliis autem Gentilibus & Iudæis isti dicunt aperte, quod debent in numero pertinacium reputari.
units.tr: Student. I wish this book to be finished here, and I will move on to the fourth. For I intend to inquire, above all, how someone ought to be convicted of pertinacity. I want to know, however, how pertinacity is defined by name, through a definition that expresses what it is. For many difficulties ought (I think) to be resolved from such a definition, and without knowing it one cannot know how someone ought to be convicted of pertinacity. Master. Some define the pertinacious person as follows: the pertinacious person is one who persists in that which he ought to give up. They explain this definition in two ways. First, on the authority of Isidore, who says that the pertinacious man is so called as if he were impudently tenacious. Now he is impudently tenacious who holds on to what he ought to give up. Therefore the pertinacious man is one who holds on to and persists in what he ought to give up. Second, thus: perseverance and pertinacity are opposites, and they ought to have contrary definitions. But the persevering man is one who persists in what he ought to do. Therefore the pertinacious man is one who persists in what he ought to give up. Student. I am surprised, because these men want to prove the pertinacious person by a definition of pertinacity, when a definition of the defined thing cannot be proved. Master. They do not intend to prove, strictly speaking, the definition of the pertinacious person from pertinacity; they wish to explain, and in some measure to make clear through their explanations, the definition of the pertinacious person. Student. I do not want to meddle much with such definitions for the present; but something else troubles me about the definition I mentioned, because according to it every person who errs is pertinacious. For everyone who errs, as long as he is in error, is pertinacious. But no one should ever be in error; rather, everyone who errs ought to give up his error. Therefore everyone who errs is pertinacious. Master. They say you are deceived by an ambiguity. For there is a debt of necessity and a debt of fitness. In the definition given, the word must be taken in the sense of a debt of necessity, so that the meaning is: the pertinacious person is one who persists in something that he must of necessity give up. Grant then that every person who errs ought (in the sense of fitness, as they call it) to give up his error, which is not true; still, not every person who errs must of necessity, for the sake of salvation, give up his error at every moment. Student. I see that these men define the pertinacious person too broadly, so that it fits anyone who errs in the faith. Therefore fit the aforesaid definition more narrowly to one who errs in the faith. Master. It is fitted thus: he is pertinaciously doubting against the faith who persists in doubt about the things of the faith, which he must of necessity give up for the sake of salvation. Student. According to what has been said, all Jews and Gentiles would be pertinacious, because all are bound to give up their error. This is a difficulty that would require a long treatment on account of those who were never instructed in the true faith, nor is there any lack of instruction in those who have had no instruction at all, if there are any such. But concerning the other Gentiles and Jews, these men openly say that they must be counted among the pertinacious.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: In quo quaeritur, quomodo valeat quis de pertinacia convinci. Et distinguitur de pertinacia interiori & exteriori: de pertinacia interiori tractatur capitulo tertio & quarto: d- e exteriore incipit tractare capitulo quinto.
units.tr: In which it is asked how someone may be convicted of obstinacy. A distinction is drawn between inward and outward obstinacy: inward obstinacy is treated in chapters three and four, and outward obstinacy begins to be treated in chapter five.

units.la: Discipulus. De illa difficultate ad præsens nolo tecum collocutione habere, sed volo te interrogare de proposito principali, scilicet quomodo de pertinacia valeat quis convinci. Magist. Circa illa quæ fidei sunt, duplex potest pertinacitas inveniri. Vna mentalis, quando quis scilicet pertinaciter corde adhæret prauitati hæreticæ vel pertinaciter dubitat de catholica veritate. Alia est pertinacitas exterior, quæ in facto vel in voce exteriori consistit. Prima pertinacia aliter quam per præsumptionem probabilem vel violentam convinci non potest a nobis: quia in talibus non necessario interioribus exteriora correspondent, imo tenetur vnum sæpe interius, & aliud exterius similatur. Discip. Quamuis intentio mea fuerit interrogare de pertinacia exteriori solummodo: causa tamen exercitii dicas aliqua de pertinacia interiori & mentali, quis videlicet pertinaciter erret in mente. Magist. Sunt quidam dicentes quod tripliciter potest quis pertinaciter errare in mente. Et primo quidem, Si quis non obstantibus miraculis, quæ audiuntur fuisse facta pro fide firmanda, putat fidem esse falsam vel incertam. Secundo si in generali credit totam fidem esse veram, alicui tamen errori in speciali (quam nescit ad fidem explicite pertinere) adhæret tam fortiter, quod quantumcunque sibi ostenderetur ad fidem pertinere, errorem nullo modo dimitteret huiusmodi, sed ante putaret fidem esse falsam. Sicut si in Veteri Testamento (quando fideles credere Trinitatem personarum cum vnitate Diuinitatis explicite minime tenebantur) aliquis credens totam doctrinam Moysi & fidelium esse veram in speciali, putasset quod tres personæ non sunt vnus Deus, & suo errori tam fortiter adhæsisset, quod ante doctrinam Moysi & Prophetarum credidisset esse falsam, quæ tenuisset tres personas esse vnum Deum. Iste (licet in genere credidisset totam fidem Moysi & Prophetarum esse veram) pertinax exstitisset. Tertio potest quis mentaliter esse pertinax in errore, si alicui errori inhæret & negligit, quomodo & quando debet quærere veritatem. Quia talis non est paratus corrigi, si persistit in errore, quem debet de necessitate salutis dimittere. Discip. Inter negligentiam & pertinaciam differentia invenitur. Sed ille vltimus est negligens. Ergo non est pertinax. Magist. Respondetur, quod quamuis negligentia & pertinacia distinguantur, tamen aliquis negligens est pertinax: nec est inconueniens, quod aliqua negligentia est pertinacia reputanda. Discip. Potest ne aliquis pertinaciter dubitare contra fidem. Mag. Dicitur, quot modis potest quis pertinaciter dubitare contra fidem, quot modis potest pertinaciter errare contra fidem. Disc. Nunquid aliquo modo potest distingui de pertinacia, propter pertinaciam interiorem. Mag. Aliter distinguitur de tali pertinacia, saltem quantum ad verba. Quia licut secundum Aug. quidam est hæreticus scienter, quidam vero inscienter: ita quidam est pertinax scienter, ille scilicet qui putat fidem Christianam pro aliqua sui parte esse falsam: & quidam est pertinax nescienter, qui scilicet credit in genere totam fidem Christianam esse veram in speciali, tamen alicui errori pertinaciter contra fidem adhæret. Discip. Quomodo potest quis scienter esse pertinax? Videtur enim, quod hoc contradictionem includat. Quia qui errat, putat esse verum circa quod errat, eo quod errare est approbare falsum pro vero. Nullus ergo scit se errare. Et ita scienter nullus est pertinax: quia nullus scit se esse pertinacem in errore. Magist. Ista clausula pertinacis, cum dicitur scienter, non debet referri ad pertinaciam errantis, vt scilicet aliquis sciat se pertinaciter errare: sed debet referri ad contrarietatem suæ pertinaciæ vel erroris ad fidem Christianam, vt dicatur scienter pertinax, qui scit assertionem, circa quam errat, esse contrariam fidei Christianæ. Quemadmodum quis dicitur hæreticus scienter, non quia scit se esse hæreticum, sed quia scit assertionem suam esse contrariam fidei Christianæ. Sic ille igitur vocatur scienter hæreticus, qui scit assertionem suam, quia in rei veritate est pertinax hæresis, esse contrariam fidei Christianæ. Sic ille dicitur scienter pertinax in errore hæretica li, qui scit assertionem, quam putat verum, esse contrariam fidei Christianæ. Ille autem dicitur ignoranter siue nescienter pertinax in errore hæretica li, qui assertionem suam nescit esse contrariam fidei Christianæ.
units.tr: Student. I do not wish to take up that difficulty with you at present, but I want to ask you about the main question, namely how someone may be convicted of obstinacy. Teacher. In matters of faith, obstinacy can be of two kinds. One is mental, when someone clings stubbornly in his heart to heretical perversity, or stubbornly doubts the Catholic truth. The other is outward obstinacy, which consists in deed or in outward speech. We cannot convict anyone of the first kind except by a probable or compelling presumption, because in such cases the outward does not necessarily correspond to the inward; indeed, a person often holds one thing inwardly and pretends another outwardly. Student. Although I meant to ask only about outward obstinacy, please tell me something about inward and mental obstinacy as well, that is, how someone may be obstinate in mind, for the sake of practice. Teacher. Some people say that a person can err obstinately in the mind in three ways. First, if someone, despite the miracles which are reported to have been done to confirm the faith, thinks the faith is false or uncertain. Second, if he believes in general that the whole faith is true, but clings so strongly to some error in particular (which he does not know belongs to the faith explicitly) that, however much it is shown to him that it belongs to the faith, he will in no way give up that error, but would rather think the faith false. For example, suppose that in the Old Testament (when the faithful were not explicitly required to believe the Trinity of persons together with the unity of the Godhead), someone who believed in general that the whole teaching of Moses and the faithful was true, but in particular thought that the three persons are not one God, and clung so strongly to his error that he would sooner have believed the teaching of Moses and the Prophets to be false than admit that the three persons are one God. Such a man, although he believed in general the whole faith of Moses and the Prophets to be true, would have been obstinate. Third, someone may be mentally obstinate in error if he clings to some error and neglects to seek the truth when and as he ought. For such a person is not ready to be corrected, if he persists in an error which he must of necessity give up for salvation. Student. There is a difference between negligence and obstinacy. But the last man is negligent. Therefore he is not obstinate. Teacher. The answer is that although negligence and obstinacy are distinguished, nevertheless someone who is negligent may be obstinate, and there is no absurdity in holding that some negligence should be counted as obstinacy. Student. Can someone obstinately doubt against the faith? Teacher. It is said that in as many ways as someone can obstinately doubt against the faith, in so many ways can he obstinately err against the faith. Student. Can obstinacy be distinguished in some way with respect to inward obstinacy? Teacher. Such obstinacy is distinguished in another way, at least as far as the words go. For just as, according to Augustine, one man is a heretic knowingly and another unknowingly, so one man is obstinate knowingly, namely he who thinks that some part of the Christian faith is false, and another is obstinate unknowingly, namely he who believes in general that the whole Christian faith is true, yet in particular clings stubbornly to some error against the faith. Student. How can someone be obstinate knowingly? For this seems to involve a contradiction, since whoever errs thinks that what he errs about is true, because to err is to approve what is false as true. No one therefore knows that he errs, and so no one is knowingly obstinate, since no one knows that he is obstinate in error. Teacher. The phrase "knowingly" in the expression "knowingly obstinate" should not be referred to the obstinacy of the one who errs, as if someone knew that he errs obstinately. It should be referred to the contrariety of his obstinacy or error to the Christian faith, so that he is called knowingly obstinate who knows that the assertion about which he errs is contrary to the Christian faith. Just as someone is called a heretic knowingly not because he knows himself to be a heretic, but because he knows that his assertion is contrary to the Christian faith, so he is called a knowing heretic who knows that his assertion, which in the truth of the matter is a heretical obstinacy, is contrary to the Christian faith. Thus he is said to be knowingly obstinate in heretical error who knows that the assertion which he takes to be true is contrary to the Christian faith. But he is said to be obstinate in heretical error ignorantly or unknowingly who does not know that his assertion is contrary to the Christian faith.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: In quo obiicitur contra dicta in capitulo precedenti, arguendo, quod nullus sit pertinax, vel haereticus nisi scienter: ubi etiam distinguitur de nescienter haeretico.
units.tr: In which objections are raised against what was said in the preceding chapter, arguing that no one is obstinate or a heretic except knowingly; and where a distinction is also drawn concerning the unknowing heretic.

units.la: Discipulus. Distinctionem inter scienter pertinacem & nescienter pertinacem: & similiter inter scienter haereticum & nescienter haereticum, modo aliter quam prius intelligo: & ideo quamvis putauerim prius nullum esse scienter pertinacem aut scienter haereticum, nunc mihi videtur quod omnis haereticus, qui scit assertionem suam (quae in rei veritate est pertinax haeresis) esse contrariam fidei Christianae. Et ita dicitur ignoranter siue nescienter haereticus, qui assertionem suam nescit esse contrariam fidei Christianae, sed putat esse consonam fidei Christianae: sic ille dicitur esse scienter pertinax in errore haereticali, qui scit assertionem (quam putat veram) esse contrariam fidei Christianae. Ille autem dicitur ignoranter siue nescienter pertinax in errore haereticali, qui assertionem, quam putat esse veram, nescit siue ignorat contrariam esse fidei. Et sic quilibet talis esset fidelis & catholicus, quia omnis haereticus est scienter pertinax & scienter haereticus, & nullus penitus nescienter. Quod potest tali ratione probari. Nam ad hoc, quod aliquis catholicus sit & fidelis, sufficit fides implicita. Hoc patet per exemplum de Cornelio centurione, de quo habetur Actor. 10. qui antequam de Christo fidem haberet explicitam, fuit fidelis, quia iustus & timens Deum, & per consequens fidem habuit saltem implicitam. Et ita fides implicita sufficit, quod quis sit catholicus & fidelis. Sed quicunque non est scienter pertinax, neque scienter haereticus (modo prius expositio) habet fidem implicitam: quia ex hoc ipso, quod non putat se errare contra fidem Christianam, credit totam fidem Christianam esse veram, licet in aliquo speciali erret. Qui autem credit tota Christianam fidem esse veram, habet fidem implicitam. Ergo est catholicus & fidelis, & per consequens non est pertinax neque haereticus. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia qui credit totam fidem Christianam esse veram, & habet fidem de omni veritate pertinente ad fidem Christianam, non est haereticus, & per consequens non est pertinax. Sed quicunque non est scienter pertinax, neque scienter haereticus, credit totam fidem Christianam esse veram: ergo habet fidem de omni veritate pertinente ad fidem Christianam, & per consequens nullo modo est pertinax nec haereticus. Magist. Istae obiectiones principaliter inducuntur ad probandum, quod nullus est scienter haereticus. Discip. Ita est. Magist. Dimittamus ergo loqui de pertinacitate, & sufficiat de haeretico facere mentionem. Discip. Placet, qui potest videre, quomodo potest quis esse haereticus nescienter, non dubitabit quin valeat quis esse haereticus nescienter. Magist. De nescienti haeretico distinguitur. Quidam enim sunt vel esse possunt nescienter haeretici, quia scienter & explicite arbitrantur aliquas assertiones sub forma propria scriptas in scriptura diuina ad fidem Christianam nullatenus pertinere. Tales fuerunt Manichei, qui secundum Isidorum, prout legitur 24. q. 3. c. quidam autem, Testamentum Vetus respuerunt, & nouum tantummodo ex parte receperunt, & ita putabant se catholicos & fideles Christianos: & ideo fuerunt nescienter haeretici, quia assertionem contentam in Veteri Testamento asseruerunt ad fidem Christianam minime pertinere. Quidam autem sunt nescienter haeretici, qui assertionem nullam pertinentem ad fidem Christianam sub propria forma scriptam in scriptura diuina repertam dubitant esse veram, quia totam scripturam diuinam recipiunt: sed tamen aliquas assertiones sequentes ex illis (propter hoc, quod aliter intelligunt scripturas diuinas, quam sensus Spiritus Sancti flagitat, a quo sumptae sunt) non credunt esse veras, quia non putant, quod sequantur ex illis. Quia autem credunt irreuocabiliter contrarias assertiones esse veras, ideo haeretici sunt censendi, qui tamen in genere credunt totam fidem Christianam esse veram.
units.tr: Disciple. I understand the distinction between the knowingly obstinate and the unknowingly obstinate, and likewise between the knowingly heretical and the unknowingly heretical, differently from before. So although I had previously thought there was no one knowingly obstinate or knowingly heretical, it now seems to me that every heretic who knows that his assertion (which in truth is an obstinate heresy) is contrary to the Christian faith is knowingly heretical. And so he is called unknowingly or ignorantly a heretic who does not know that his assertion is contrary to the Christian faith but thinks it agrees with the Christian faith. Thus he is said to be knowingly obstinate in heretical error who knows that the assertion he thinks true is contrary to the Christian faith. But he is said to be unknowingly or ignorantly obstinate in heretical error who does not know, or is ignorant, that the assertion he thinks true is contrary to the faith. And so every such person would be faithful and catholic, since every heretic is knowingly obstinate and knowingly heretical, and nobody at all is unknowingly so. This can be proved by the following argument. To be a catholic and a faithful person, implicit faith is enough. This is shown by the example of Cornelius the centurion, of whom we read in Acts 10, who, before he had explicit faith in Christ, was faithful, because he was just and fearing God, and so he had at least implicit faith. Therefore implicit faith suffices for someone to be catholic and faithful. But whoever is not knowingly obstinate, nor knowingly heretical (in the sense explained earlier), has implicit faith, because by the very fact that he does not think he errs against the Christian faith, he believes the whole Christian faith to be true, although he errs in some particular point. But whoever believes the whole Christian faith to be true has implicit faith. Therefore he is catholic and faithful, and consequently is neither obstinate nor heretical. This argument is confirmed thus: whoever believes the whole Christian faith to be true, and holds the faith concerning every truth pertaining to the Christian faith, is not a heretic, and consequently is not obstinate. But whoever is not knowingly obstinate, nor knowingly heretical, believes the whole Christian faith to be true. Therefore he holds the faith concerning every truth pertaining to the Christian faith, and consequently is in no way obstinate or heretical. Master. These objections are brought forward chiefly to prove that no one is knowingly a heretic. Disciple. That is so. Master. Let us then drop the discussion of obstinacy, and let it suffice to have mentioned the heretic. Disciple. Agreed. Whoever can see how a person can be a heretic unknowingly will not doubt that someone can be a heretic unknowingly. Master. A distinction is drawn concerning the unknowing heretic. For some are, or can be, unknowingly heretics, because they knowingly and explicitly judge that certain assertions, written in their proper form in divine Scripture, do not pertain at all to the Christian faith. Such were the Manichaeans, who, according to Isidore, as read in 24 q. 3 c. quidam autem, rejected the Old Testament and received only the New in part; and so they thought themselves catholic and faithful Christians. They were therefore unknowing heretics, because they asserted that the assertion contained in the Old Testament did not pertain at all to the Christian faith. Others are unknowing heretics who doubt that any assertion pertaining to the Christian faith, written in its proper form in divine Scripture, is true, because they receive all of divine Scripture; yet they do not believe certain assertions that follow from those passages (because they understand the divine Scriptures otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit, from whom they were taken demands), since they do not think these follow from them. But because they believe irrevocably that contrary assertions are true, such persons are to be judged heretics, although they generally believe the whole Christian faith to be true.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: In quo ponitur responsio ad probata capitulo precedenti: & ibi notatur distinctio de fide implicita.
units.tr: In which the answer is given to the arguments proved in the preceding chapter, and the distinction concerning implicit faith is noted.

units.la: Discipulus. Ad quid valet ista distinctio? Magist. Per istam distinctionem putant nonnulli demonstratiue probare, quod rationes tuae non concludunt. Discip. Quomodo? Magist. Ex primo membro probant, quod aliqui possunt esse nescienter haeretici, sic: Qui credunt in genere, quod tota fides Christiana est vera; & tamen credunt Vetus Testamentum vel Euangelium Lucae multa continere erronea, eo quod Vetus Testamentum vel Euangelium Lucae putant multa continere, quae ad fidem Christiana nullatenus pertinent, vere sunt haeretici, praesertim si sint pertinaces. Aliter enim posset quis absq; haeretica prauitate dicere, q; non omnia Euangelia ad fidem pertinent Christianam. Sed talis non est scienter haereticus, quia non credit se contrariari in aliquo fidei Christianae. Ergo aliquis potest esse haereticus nescienter, quemadmodum Manichei fuerunt haeretici nescienter, quia putauerunt se esse veraciter Christianos, & omnes alios Christianos, qui Vetus Testamentum receperunt, arbitrabantur haereticos contra fidem Christianam errantes. Discip. Dic quomodo ad obiectiones tactas superius respondeatur. Magist. Dicunt enim, quod obiectiones illae fundantur in aequiuocatione de fide implicita, est enim una fides implicita vera, omnem assertionem pertinentem, respectu cuiuscunq; haereticae prauitatis, excludens. Et illa fides implicita sufficit ad hoc, quod habens eam sit catholicus & fidelis. Alia est fides implicita falsa, qua scilicet creditur hæc est vera: fides Christiana est vera. Sed alia fides, quam illa, quæ est vera Christiana pro Christiana habetur. Et talem fidem habuerunt Manichei; quia credebant fidem Christianam esse veram. Sed illam fidem vocaverunt Christianam, quæ in rei veritate non est Christiana; imo est contraria fidei Christianæ. Et ita est de omnibus hæreticis nescienter: quia licet credant hanc esse veram: fides Christiana vel fides Ecclesiæ est vera: tamen fidem reputant Christianam, quæ in rei veritate non est Christiana, licet credant eam esse Christianam. Et ideo (quamvis nescienter) tamen hæretici sunt (Item patet de Bohemis.) Disc. Nunquid aliqui credentes fidem Christianā esse veram, habent falsam fidem? Magist. Nullus propter hoc, quod credit fidem Christianam esse veram, habet falsam fidem: sed credens quandam fidem esse Christianam, quæ in rei veritate non est Christiana, habet falsam fidem. Sicut Arrius in eo, quod credit quod fides Christiana est vera & Euangelium continet veritatem, non habet falsam fidem: sed credendo quod Filius Dei non est æqualis Patri, & quod hoc pertinet ad catholicam fidem, habuit falsam fidem. Disc. Adhuc non sunt illa argumenta soluta, quæ fundantur in hac propositione: omnis fides implicita vera sufficit ad hoc, quod habens eam sit catholicus & fidelis. Magist. De fide distinguitur. Quod quædam ponitur fides infusa, quam etiam parvuli baptizati habere dicuntur. Et de hac posset concedi propositio, quam assumis: sed illam habet nullus hæreticus nescienter. Alia est fides acquisita, quæ est incredulitas quædam, qua quis absque dubitatione alicui assertioni adhæret. Sicut est propositio falsa: quia non omnis fides talis implicita vera sufficit ad hoc, quod habens eam sit catholicus & fidelis. Quamvis enim nullus sit infidelis propter quamcunque fidem veram, tamen potest habere unam fidem veram esse infidelis propter aliam fidem falsam. Disc. Nihil modo quantum ad illam materiam: sed indica mihi, quid dicitur ad aliam propositionem: Qui credit totam fidem Christianam esse veram, habet fidem de omni veritate pertinente ad fidem Christianam? Magist. Hoc negatur de fide, quæ reddit aliquem catholicum, nisi credens totam fidem Christianam, nullam reputet fidem Christianam, nisi quæ vere Christiana est.
units.tr: Disciple. What is the use of this distinction? Master. By means of this distinction some people think they demonstrate that your arguments do not follow. Disciple. How so? Master. From the first member they prove that some people can be heretics without knowing it, in this way: those who believe in general that the whole Christian faith is true, and yet believe that the Old Testament or the Gospel of Luke contains many errors, because they think the Old Testament or the Gospel of Luke contains many things that have nothing to do with the Christian faith, are truly heretics, especially if they are obstinate. For otherwise someone could say, without heretical perversity, that not all the Gospels pertain to the Christian faith. But such a person is not a knowing heretic, because he does not believe that he contradicts the Christian faith in any point. Therefore someone can be a heretic without knowing it, just as the Manichaeans were heretics without knowing it: they thought they were truly Christians, and they judged all the other Christians who received the Old Testament to be heretics erring against the Christian faith. Disciple. Tell me how the objections raised above are answered. Master. They say that those objections rest on an ambiguity about implicit faith. There is one true implicit faith, which excludes every assertion that pertains to any heretical perversity whatever, and this implicit faith is enough for the one who has it to be catholic and faithful. There is another, false implicit faith, namely the belief that this is true: the Christian faith is true. But another faith, other than the true one, is taken for the Christian faith. The Manichaeans had such a faith, for they believed the Christian faith to be true; but they called Christian that faith which in reality is not Christian, indeed which is contrary to the Christian faith. And so it is with all heretics who are such without knowing it: although they believe this to be true, that the Christian faith or the faith of the Church is true, yet they regard as Christian a faith which in reality is not Christian, though they believe it to be Christian. And therefore (although without knowing it) they are nevertheless heretics. (The same is evident in the case of the Bohemians.) Disciple. Do some who believe the Christian faith to be true have a false faith? Master. No one, merely because he believes the Christian faith to be true, has a false faith; but one who believes some faith to be Christian which in reality is not Christian, has a false faith. Thus Arius, in that he believes the Christian faith to be true and the Gospel to contain truth, does not have a false faith; but by believing that the Son of God is not equal to the Father, and that this pertains to the catholic faith, he had a false faith. Disciple. The arguments founded on this proposition are still not resolved: every true implicit faith is sufficient for the one who has it to be catholic and faithful. Master. Faith is distinguished. There is a faith called infused, which even baptized infants are said to have. Of this faith the proposition you assume could be granted; but no heretic without knowing it has this. Another is acquired faith, which is a certain unbelief by which someone adheres to some assertion without doubt. The proposition is false as applied to this: not every such true implicit faith is sufficient for the one who has it to be catholic and faithful. For although no one is unfaithful on account of any true faith whatever, yet one can hold one true faith and be unfaithful on account of another, false faith. Disciple. Nothing more for now on that matter; but tell me what is said about the other proposition: he who believes the whole Christian faith to be true has faith concerning every truth pertaining to the Christian faith? Master. This is denied of the faith which makes someone catholic, unless the one who believes the whole Christian faith regards as Christian faith nothing but what is truly Christian.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: In quo tractatur de pertinacia exteriori secundum quam quis potest convinci iudicio exteriori, ponendo primum modum de eo, qui abjurat facto vel verbo fidem Christianam.
units.tr: In which is treated outward obstinacy, by which someone can be convicted by outward judgement; setting out the first way, concerning one who by deed or word abjures the Christian faith.

units.la: Discipulus. Postquam tecum collationem habui de pertinacia interiori: volo aliquam recipere de pertinacia exteriori, quando scilicet præter ea, quæ apparent exterius, debent catholici aliquem errantem contra fidem tanquam pertinacem habere: & quomodo de pertinacia in iudicio debeat quis convinci. In primis autem cupio scire, an uno modo tantum vel pluribus possit constare errantem aliquem contra fidem esse pertinacem. Magist. Plures modi ponuntur, quibus possunt catholici præsumptionem accipere volentiam de aliquo, quod est pertinax in errore. Disc. Primo tractemus unum modum, postea alium modum. Magist. Primus modus, quo potest quis de pertinacia deprehendi, est, cum in facto vel in verbo monstrat quis se non firmiter credere fidem Christianam esse veram & sanam: puta si dicit fidem esse falsam vel dubiam, vel ad sectam aliam se converrit, ut puta si facit se circumcidi, vel Mahometum adorat. De tali enim licet cuilibet iudicare, quod pertinaciter errat vel dubitat veritatem, & quod est scienter hæreticus manifestus. Et si convictus fuerit vel confessus in iudicio, quod tale aliquid dixerit vel fecerit, sine ulteriori examine est tanquam pertinax & hæreticus condemnandus. Disc. Potest ne inveniri casus, in quo possit hæreticus de tali hæresi excusari? Magist. Unus solus casus, quantum ad fidei abnegationem, excipitur, scilicet si metu mortis sit idem negavit, dicendo, fidem Christianam esse falsam vel dubiam. Duo vero excipiuntur, quantum ad factum hæreticale. Primus est, si quis metu mortis actum hæreticalem commiserit: puta si pro morte vitanda quis adoraverit Mahometum. Et isto modo excusabatur Beatus Marcellinus, qui sacrificando idolis non fuit factus hæreticus, licet peccatum mortale commiserit. Secundus casus est si absoluta coactione quis coactus fuerit actum hæreticalem committere: in quo casu etiam ab omni peccato excusatur. Disc. Vellem scire rationem, quare talis debet statim hæreticus & pertinax reputari: cum ita quis possit ambitione & cupiditate tractus facto vel verbo ostendere, se non tenere firmiter fidem Christianam esse veram, quam tamen in mente tenet esse veram, sicut quis potest hoc simulare metu mortis. Magist. Ratio assignatur: quia cum quis extra metum mortis aliquid dicit & facit, magis de voluntario habet, quam quando dicit aut facit aliquid metu mortis inductus. Et ideo nulla cupiditas vel ambitio excusat de pertinacia in licito iudicio hominem, quantumcunque facto vel verbo monstraret se fidem Christianam firmiter tenere. Et eodem modo dicitur, quod nec amor, nec odium, nec aliquid præter timorem mortis potest quemcunque in hoc casu excusare, quin sit hæreticus reputandus, nisi dicatur quod per gravia illata tormenta vel metum eorum in hoc casu valeat quis excusari. Disc. Nunquid modo prædicto est dicendum de omni scienter hæretico. Magist. De omni scienter hæretico sunt intelligenda prædicta.
units.tr: Student. After I have had our discussion about inward obstinacy, I want to take up outward obstinacy: namely, when Catholics ought to hold someone who errs against the faith as obstinate, over and above what appears outwardly, and how someone ought to be convicted of obstinacy in judgement. First, however, I wish to know whether it can be established that someone who errs against the faith is obstinate in only one way or in several. Master. Several ways are laid down by which Catholics may form a presumption about someone who is obstinate in error. Student. Let us first treat one way, and afterwards another. Master. The first way by which someone may be detected as obstinate is when, by deed or word, he shows that he does not firmly believe the Christian faith to be true and sound: for instance, if he says the faith is false or doubtful, or if he turns to another sect, as when he has himself circumcised or worships Mahomet. For concerning such a person anyone may judge that he obstinately errs or doubts the truth, and that he is a manifest heretic knowingly. And if he is convicted, or confesses in court, that he has said or done such a thing, he is to be condemned as obstinate and a heretic without further examination. Student. Can any case be found in which a heretic may be excused for such heresy? Master. Only one case is excepted as regards the denial of the faith: namely, if he has denied it out of fear of death, saying that the Christian faith is false or doubtful. Two cases, however, are excepted as regards a heretical deed. The first is if someone has committed a heretical act out of fear of death: for instance, if to avoid death he has worshipped Mahomet. In this way Blessed Marcellinus was excused, who, by sacrificing to idols, was not made a heretic, although he committed a mortal sin. The second case is if someone has been compelled by absolute coercion to commit a heretical act; in this case he is excused even from all sin. Student. I should like to know the reason why such a person must at once be reckoned a heretic and obstinate, since someone who is drawn by ambition and greed may by deed or word show that he does not firmly hold the Christian faith to be true, though in his mind he holds it to be true, just as someone may feign this out of fear of death. Master. The reason is given: because when someone says and does something apart from fear of death, he acts more voluntarily than when he says or does something induced by fear of death. And therefore no greed or ambition excuses a man from obstinacy in a lawful judgement, however much he might show by deed or word that he firmly holds the Christian faith. And in the same way it is said that neither love, nor hatred, nor anything other than fear of death can excuse anyone in this case from being reckoned a heretic, unless it is said that one may be excused in this case on account of the grievous torments inflicted, or the fear of them. Student. Is what has just been said to be said of every heretic who knowingly errs? Master. What has been said above is to be understood of every heretic who knowingly errs.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: In quo ponitur secundus modus, quo quis potest de pertinacia convinci: scilicet de eo, qui negat aliquam partem veteris, aut Noui Testamenti.
units.tr: In which the second way is laid down by which someone can be convicted of obstinacy: namely, of one who denies some part of the Old or New Testament.

units.la: Discipulus. Sufficiat dixisse praedicta de primo modo: dic nunc secundum, quo valeat de pertinacia quis convinci. Magist. Qui dicit aliquam partem Noui vel Veteri Testamenti aliquod salsum asserere, aut non esse recipiendam a catholicis, est haereticus & pertinax reputandus. Unde & propter hoc fuerunt Manichei haeretici & iudicati, quia Vetus Testamentum respuerunt, & Nouum Testamentum pro parte solummodo receperunt. Discip. Nunquid si aliquis laicus, qui de libro Iosue forte nunquam audiuit fieri mentionem, diceret eundem librum Iosue ad Testamentum Vetus minime pertinere, esset censendus haereticus? Magist. Differentia est inter dicentem aliquam scripturam ad Vetus vel ad Nouum Testamentum minime pertinere: & dicere aliquam partem Veteris Testamenti vel Noui non esse tenendam. Primus sit esset laicus vel illiteratus, non esset statim censendus haereticus, sed esset diligenter examinandus & etiam informandus. Et si post informationem conueniente non se corrigeret, esset pertinax reputandus. Si vero est literatus, sciens quos libros Ecclesia reputat esse de integritate Noui & Veteris Testamenti, & tamen hoc non obstante diceret librum Iosue vel alium ad Vetus Testamentum minime pertinere, esset statim haereticus iudicandus & pertinax, nec esset expectandus, ut se corrigeret, sed statim pro incorrigibili esset habendus. Secundus autem, qui scilicet dicit aliquâ parte Veteris vel Noui Testamenti non esse recipiendam, vel aliquid falsum asserere, siue literatus siue illiteratus exsisteret, esset statim iudicandus pertinax, nisi forte fuerit adeo simplex, quod nesciat quid per Nouum & Vetus Testamentum importetur, & seductus ab aliis dicat Nouum vel Vetus Testamentum aut aliam partem recipi non debere: firmiter tamen credens totam fidem esse Ecclesiae recipiendam. Talis enim non est inter haereticos computandus, sed per simplicitatem & ignorantiam excusandus. Et de talibus simplicibus ait August. ut habetur 24. q. 3. c. haereticus: Ille autem qui huiusmodi hominibus (scilicet haereticus) credit, imaginatione veritatis quadam est illusus. Et ideo non videtur, quod debeat pertinax iudicari, nisi credat fidem Ecclesiae esse falsam, vel alio modo pertinax convincatur.
units.tr: Disciple. Let it suffice to have said the above about the first way; now tell me the second, by which someone may be convicted of obstinacy. Master. Whoever says that some part of the New or Old Testament asserts something false, or that some part is not to be received by Catholics, is to be regarded as a heretic and obstinate. For this reason the Manichaeans also were condemned as heretics, because they rejected the Old Testament and received only a part of the New. Disciple. If some layman, who perhaps has never heard mention of the book of Joshua, were to say that this same book of Joshua does not belong to the Old Testament at all, would he be deemed a heretic? Master. There is a difference between one who says that some writing does not belong to the Old or New Testament, and one who says that some part of the Old or New Testament is not to be held. If the first were a layman or unlettered, he would not at once be deemed a heretic, but would be carefully examined and also instructed. And if after suitable instruction he did not correct himself, he would be regarded as obstinate. But if he is learned, knowing which books the Church holds to belong to the integrity of the New and Old Testament, and yet nevertheless said that the book of Joshua or another does not belong to the Old Testament at all, he would at once be judged a heretic and obstinate; nor would he be waited upon to correct himself, but would at once be held incorrigible. The second, however, who says that some part of the Old or New Testament is not to be received, or asserts something false, whether he is learned or unlearned, would at once be judged obstinate, unless perhaps he is so simple that he does not know what is meant by the New and Old Testament, and, led astray by others, says that the New or Old Testament or some other part ought not to be received, while firmly believing that the whole faith is to be received from the Church. For such a person is not to be counted among heretics, but is to be excused on account of his simplicity and ignorance. And concerning such simple people Augustine says, as it is found in 24 q. 3 c. Haereticus: But he who believes such men (namely heretics) has been deceived by a certain semblance of truth. And so it does not seem that he ought to be judged obstinate, unless he believes the faith of the Church to be false, or is otherwise convicted of obstinacy.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Mouet dubitationem incidentem circa secundum modum praecedenti capitulo positum, ad quam etiam respondetur. Vbi etiam notatur distinctio de impoenitenti & incorrigibili.
units.tr: The author raises a doubt arising from the second method laid down in the preceding chapter, and this doubt is also answered. Here too the distinction between the impenitent and the incorrigible is noted.

units.la: Discipulus. Circa illum modum de pertinacia conuincendi nolo multum insistere, quia non audeo, ne illi, inter quos modo controuersia vertitur, aliquid tale mutuo sibi imponant, nec aliquis alteri. Vnum tamen retulisti, quod peto declarari: quia forte utile erit, & ad multa genera haereticorum applicari poterit, vt videtur. Dixisti namq; quod si aliquis sciret, quos libros Ecclesia reputat de integritate Noui & Veteris Testamenti, & tamen hoc non obstante diceret, quod aliquis eorum ad Nouum vel Vetus Testamentum minime pertineret, esset statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus: nec esset expectandus, an correptus paratus esset se corrigere, sed statim pro incorrigibili esset habendus. De hoc enim ultimo miror, quomodo talis sit statim incorrigibilis reputandus. Qui enim corrigi potest, non est incorrigibilis. Talis autem corrigi potest. Ergo non est incorrigibilis reputandus. Magist. Multorum iudicio bene dixisti hoc, quod petis, utile esse ad multa: quia nonnulli ex declaratione ipsius multa probare conantur. Dicitur iraq; quod sicut impoenitens dupliciter accipitur. Vno modo pro illo, qui poenitere non potest, alio modo pro illo, qui est in proposito minime poenitendi: sic incorrigibilis dicitur dupliciter. Vno modo ille, qui non potest corrigi. Et talis non est in hac vita, praesertim si non est alienatus a sensu. Aliter dicitur ille incorrigibilis, qui est in proposito se nullatenus corrigendi, licet posset corrigi. Et omnis etiam talis incorrigibilis debet pertinax reputari. Unde talis incorrigibilis vocari potest pertinax, contumax, obstinatus, induratus. Non ergo (sicut accipis) qui corrigi potest, non est incorrigibilis: imo multi sunt incorrigibiles, qui sunt in proposito corrigendi se nullatenus, qui tamen corrigi possunt, & saepe incorrigibiles corriguntur. Quia de nullo incorrigibili in vita praesenti est penitus desperandum: sicut nec de aliquo impoenitente, quamdiu vixerit, est desperandum.
units.tr: Disciple. I do not wish to dwell much on that method of convicting someone of obstinacy, because I do not dare to do so, lest those between whom the controversy is now being waged should impose something of that kind on one another, or anyone on another. Yet you have mentioned one point which I ask to have explained, since perhaps it will be useful and can, as it seems, be applied to many kinds of heretics. For you said that if anyone knew which books the Church regards as belonging to the integrity of the New and Old Testaments, and yet, notwithstanding this, said that one of them did not belong to the New or Old Testament at all, he must at once be judged obstinate and a heretic; nor was one to wait to see whether, once corrected, he was ready to amend himself, but he was to be held at once as incorrigible. On this last point I am surprised how such a person can be reckoned incorrigible at once. For one who can be corrected is not incorrigible. Yet such a person can be corrected. Therefore he is not to be reckoned incorrigible. Teacher. In the judgement of many you have rightly said that what you ask is useful for many purposes, since some people try to prove many things from its explanation. Here, then, is the account. Just as impenitent is taken in two ways, in one sense for one who cannot repent, and in another for one who is strongly set on not repenting at all, so incorrigible is also used in two ways. In one sense it means one who cannot be corrected; such a person does not exist in this life, especially if he has not lost his mind. In another sense he is called incorrigible who is resolved never to amend himself, although he could be corrected. And every such incorrigible person must also be regarded as obstinate. Hence such an incorrigible person may be called obstinate, stubborn, contumacious, hardened. Therefore it is not the case (as you take it) that one who can be corrected is not incorrigible: indeed many are incorrigible who are resolved never to correct themselves, and yet who can be corrected, and often those who are incorrigible are corrected. For no incorrigible person in the present life is to be utterly despaired of, just as no impenitent person is to be despaired of as long as he lives.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Ponit tertium modum pertinacie de eo, qui credit, seu asserit totam Ecclesiam errare, & ponuntur duae contrariae opiniones, quae probantur capitulo sequenti immediate.
units.tr: He gives a third mode of pertinacity, concerning one who believes or asserts that the whole Church errs; two contrary opinions are set out, which are tested immediately in the following chapter.

units.la: Discipulus. Dic alium modum, quo de pertinacia debeat quis convinci. Magist. Dicunt nonnulli, quod ille debet pertinax iudicari, qui tenet vniuersalem Ecclesiam errare vel errasse, ex quo coepit Ecclesia Christiana congregari: licet credat fidem Christianam traditam a Christo & ab A postolis in nulla sui parte mendacium continere. Talis enim, vt dicunt, non est examinandus, an paratus sit corrigi, sed eo ipso, quod dicit, est pertinax reputandus. Discip. Nunquid omnes Literati sic sentiunt? Magist. Quidam tenent contrarium dicentes, quod absq; pertinacia & haeretica prauitate potest quis ex simplicitate & ignorantia dicere, Ecclesiam errare vel errasse. Et ideo dicunt, quod sic est examinandus solicite, an paratus sit corrigi an non. Et si quidem sit paratus corrigi, non est pertinax nec haereticus iudicandus: si autem corrigi nolit, est inter pertinaces & haereticos numerandus
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me another way by which someone ought to be convicted of pertinacity. Master. Some say that he ought to be judged pertinacious who holds that the universal Church errs, or has erred, since the Christian Church began to be gathered, even while he believes that the Christian faith handed down by Christ and the Apostles contains no falsehood in any part. Such a man, they say, is not to be examined as to whether he is ready to be corrected; by the very fact that he says this, he is to be regarded as pertinacious. Disciple. Do all the learned think so? Master. Some hold the contrary, saying that one may say, out of simplicity and ignorance, and without pertinacity or heretical depravity, that the Church errs or has erred. And therefore they say that such a man must be carefully examined as to whether he is ready to be corrected or not. If he is ready to be corrected, he is not to be judged pertinacious or heretical; but if he is unwilling to be corrected, he is to be counted among the pertinacious and heretics.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Ponit duas opiniones sibi inuicem contrarias in precedenti capitulo recitatas, & pro illis arguit.
units.tr: He sets out two opinions, recited in the preceding chapter, which are contrary to each other, and argues for them.

units.la: Discipulus. Quia nonnulli imponunt sanctissimo patri D. Ioann. Pa. 22. quod ipse habet dicere & afferere Ecclesiam errasse (de quo tamen aliquando collocutionem habebo) pro assertionibus contrariis supra dictis allegationes aliquas adducas. Magist. Pro prima assertione potest taliter allegari, fides Christiana est fides vniuersalis Ecclesiae, nec inter fidem Christianam & fidem vniuersalis Ecclesiae potest aliqua differentia reperiri. Qui ergo dicit, Ecclesiam vniuersalem errare vel errasse, dicit fidem Christianam esse erroneam, & est statim absq; vlteriori examinatione pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Igitur qui dicit, vniuersalem Ecclesiam errare vel errasse, est statim absq; aliqua examinatione pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Pro assertione contraria taliter allegatur. Qui dicit vel tenet aliquam assertionem, cuius contrarium non tenetur explicite credere, non est statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus: quia qua ratione potest quis tenere vnam assertionem haereticalem, cuius contrarium non tenetur explicite credere, absq; hoc, quod pertinax & haereticus iudicetur, eadem ratione, aliam quamcunq; assertionem haereticalem, cuius contrarium non tenetur explicite credere, potest dicere & tenere, absq; hoc quod statim debeat pertinax & haereticus iudicari. Sed non quilibet Christianus tenetur explicite credere, quod vniuersalis Ecclesia non errat vel errauit. Ergo quamuis aliquis dixerit, quod Ecclesia vniuersalis errat vel errauit, non est statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus, sed examinandus est an paratus sit corrigi. Maior istius rationis videtur esse manifesta. Minor probatur, quia nullus tenetur explicite credere conclusionem, qui non tenetur explicite credere antecedens, vel praemissas, propter quas tenetur conclusio. Sed quod vniuersalis Ecclesia non errat vel errauit, est conclusio, quae ideo credenda est, quia Christus dicit Matth. vlt. Vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsq; ad consummationem seculi: & quia rogauit pro Petro ne deficeret fides eius. Ista autem, ex quibus infertur, quod vniuersalis Ecclesia non erravit nec errat, multi non tenentur explicite credere: quia multi sunt illiterati, qui verba praedicta nunquam audierunt. Ergo nec tenentur explicite credere, quod Ecclesia vniuersalis non errat nec errauit. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia si quilibet Christianus tenetur explicite credere Ecclesiam vniuersalem non errare nec errasse: aut ergo tenetur hoc credere, quia in scriptura diuina asseritur; aut quia ad doctrinam pertinet vniuersalis Ecclesiae; aut quia in doctrina vniuersalis Ecclesiae vel scriptura diuina continetur; vel quia est ab Ecclesia vniuersali explicite approbatum; vel quia apud omnes catholicos tanquam catholicum diuulgatum extitit. Non propter primum, quia multa in sacra Scriptura asseruntur, quae non quilibet Christianus tenetur explicite credere: nec propter secundum, per eandem rationem: nec propter tertium vel quartum propter idem: nec propter quintum, quia haec veritas: Ecclesia vniuersalis non potest errare, non est apud omnes Christianos simplices & alios diuulgata. Multi enim sunt, qui de ea loqui non audierunt omnino. Discip. Si haec ratio procederet, videretur quod diuulgatio apud Christianos esset maioris auctoritatis, quam diuina scriptura: quia propter diuulgationem huiusmodi tenerentur omnes Christiani alicui veritati explicite assentire, cui tamen non tenerentur propter scripturam diuinam explicite adhaerere. Magist. Ad hoc dicitur, quod diuulgatio apud omnes Christianos non est maioris auctoritatis, quam scriptura diuina: sed est pluribus nota quam scriptura Diuina. Et ideo quod omnes Christiani tenentur credere explicite veritatem apud omnes Christianos & simplices diuulgatam, & non tenentur omnes explicite credere omnes veritates contentas in scriptura Diuina, non est propter maiorem auctoritatem talis diuulgationis, quam scripturae Diuinae. Sed quia talis diuulgatio ad notitiam plurium iam peruenit, & per hoc assignatur ratio, quare quisq; tenetur explicite credere fidem Christianam explicite esse veram: quia illa veritas apud omnes diuulgata existit, sicut & illa: fides quam Christus docuit vera est & sana. Discip. Dic quomodo respondetur ad rationem pro assertione contraria. Magist. Respondetur, quod peccat per fallaciam figurae dictionis: quia licet eadem sit fides Christiana & fides vniuersalis Ecclesiae, quando Ecclesia non errat, tamen secundum istos vniuersalis Ecclesia consignat vel significat Christianos in recto, quos taliter non signat fides Christiana. Et ideo, vt dicunt, non sequitur: quilibet Christianus tenetur explicite credere fidem Christianam esse veram: ergo tenetur credere explicite Ecclesiam vniuersalem non errare nec errasse. Discip. Non diffundas te ad illa quae ad rationalem spectat scientiam: sed dic, quomodo ad rationem in contrarium respondetur. Magist. Ad rationem illa dicitur, quod quandoq; magis tenetur quis credere explicite conclusionem, quam praemissas ex quibus infertur: propter hoc, quod conclusio magis quam praemissae apud Catholicos diuulgatur. Ita est de illa: Ecclesia vniuersalis non errat nec errauit. Haec enim sub istis verbis vel aequipollentibus apud omnes catholicos diuulgatur. Quilibet enim Christianus putat illa esse vniuersale Ecclesia, quae secu in fide concordat
units.tr: Disciple. Since some impute to the most holy father, Lord John, Pope XXII (about whom I will speak with you at some point), that he has said and asserted that the Church has erred, I will bring forward some arguments for the contrary assertions stated above. Master. For the first assertion the argument may be put thus: the Christian faith is the faith of the universal Church, and no difference can be found between the Christian faith and the faith of the universal Church. Therefore whoever says that the universal Church errs or has erred, says that the Christian faith is erroneous, and is at once to be reckoned a obstinate heretic without any further examination. Therefore whoever says that the universal Church errs or has erred is at once to be judged an obstinate heretic without any examination. For the contrary assertion the argument runs thus: whoever says or holds some assertion, the contrary of which he is not bound to believe explicitly, is not at once to be judged obstinate and a heretic. For by the same reasoning by which someone may hold one heretical assertion, the contrary of which he is not bound to believe explicitly, without being judged obstinate and a heretic, by the same reasoning he may say and hold any other heretical assertion, the contrary of which he is not bound to believe explicitly, without being at once judged obstinate and a heretic. But not every Christian is bound to believe explicitly that the universal Church does not err or has not erred. Therefore, although someone has said that the universal Church errs or has erred, he is not at once to be judged obstinate and a heretic, but must be examined as to whether he is ready to be corrected. The major premise of this argument seems plain. The minor is proved thus: no one is bound to believe explicitly a conclusion who is not bound to believe explicitly the antecedent or the premises on which the conclusion rests. But that the universal Church does not err or has not erred is a conclusion, which is to be believed because Christ says in Matt. ult.: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world," and because he prayed for Peter that his faith should not fail. But many people are not bound to believe explicitly the premises from which it follows that the universal Church has not erred nor does err, because many are unlettered and have never heard those words. Therefore they are not bound to believe explicitly that the universal Church does not err nor has erred. This argument is confirmed thus: if every Christian is bound to believe explicitly that the universal Church neither errs nor has erred, then either he is bound to believe this because it is asserted in divine Scripture; or because it pertains to the doctrine of the universal Church; or because it is contained in the doctrine of the universal Church or in divine Scripture; or because it has been explicitly approved by the universal Church; or because it has been published among all Catholics as Catholic. Not because of the first, since many things are asserted in holy Scripture which not every Christian is bound to believe explicitly; nor because of the second, for the same reason; nor because of the third or fourth, for the same reason; nor because of the fifth, since this truth, that the universal Church cannot err, has not been published among all Christians, simple and otherwise. For there are many who have never heard anything at all about it. Disciple. If this argument held, it would seem that publication among Christians had greater authority than divine Scripture, since because of such publication all Christians would be bound to assent explicitly to a truth to which they would not be bound to adhere explicitly on account of divine Scripture. Master. To this it is answered that publication among all Christians does not have greater authority than divine Scripture, but it is better known to more people than divine Scripture is. And so the fact that all Christians are bound to believe explicitly the truth published among all Christians and simple folk, and not all are bound to believe explicitly every truth contained in divine Scripture, is not because such publication has greater authority than divine Scripture, but because it has by now come to the knowledge of more people. And this is the reason given why each person is bound to believe explicitly that the Christian faith is explicitly true: that truth is published among all, just as this is: the faith which Christ taught is true and sound. Disciple. Tell me how the argument for the contrary assertion is answered. Master. It is answered that it commits the fallacy of figure of speech, since although the Christian faith and the faith of the universal Church are the same when the Church does not err, nevertheless, according to these men, the universal Church signifies or denotes Christians in the nominative, whom the Christian faith does not so denote. And therefore, as they say, it does not follow: every Christian is bound to believe explicitly that the Christian faith is true; therefore he is bound to believe explicitly that the universal Church does not err nor has erred. Disciple. Do not spread yourself on those matters which belong to the science of reasoning, but tell me how the argument to the contrary is answered. Master. To that argument it is said that sometimes a person is bound to believe a conclusion explicitly more than the premises from which it is inferred, because the conclusion is published among Catholics more than the premises are. So it is with this: the universal Church does not err nor has erred. For this is published among all Catholics in these words or equivalent ones. Every Christian thinks that the universal Church is that which agrees with him in faith.

units.la: Et Ideo sicut quilibet credit explicite se tenere veram fidem & non falsam: ita quilibet credit explicite vniuersalem Ecclesiam seruare veram & catholicam fidem & non falsam fidem. Quare sicut illa fides Christianorum est vera fides, est apud Christianos diuulgata, (& ideo tenetur ea quilibet explicite credere) ita, fides vniuersalis ecclesiae est vera fides, est apud Christianos diuulgata. Quare quilibet Christianus tenetur eam explicite credere. Et ideo quicunque illam negat, est statim sine maiori examinatione pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Discip. Isti videntur distinguere inter vniuersalem ecclesiam & multitudinem Christianorum. Nunquid ergo concedunt, quod quilibet tenetur explicite credere, quod multitudo vel maior pars Christianorum non errat, nec errauit in fide? Magist. Respondetur, quod non est necessarium credere implicite nec explicite multitudinem Christianorum non errare nec erasse in fide, nec maiorem partem, pro eo quod fides catholica in paucis potest seruari: imo nonnulli dicunt, quod in uno solo posset consistere, quia propter unum solum posset saluari, etiam quicquid Christus promisit Apostolis de fide catholica usque ad finem seculi datura.
units.tr: And so, just as each person explicitly believes that he holds the true faith and not a false one, so each person explicitly believes that the universal Church keeps the true and Catholic faith and not a false faith. Therefore, just as the faith of Christians is the true faith, and is published among Christians (and so each person is bound to believe it explicitly), so the faith of the universal Church is the true faith and is published among Christians. Therefore every Christian is bound to believe it explicitly. And so whoever denies it is at once, without further examination, to be reckoned an obstinate heretic. Disciple. These men seem to distinguish between the universal Church and the multitude of Christians. Do they therefore concede that every person is bound to believe explicitly that the multitude or the greater part of Christians does not err, nor has erred, in the faith? Master. It is answered that it is not necessary to believe, either implicitly or explicitly, that the multitude of Christians does not err nor has erred in the faith, nor the greater part of them, because the Catholic faith can be preserved in a few. Indeed some say that it could subsist in a single man, since for the sake of one alone it could be saved, even whatever Christ promised the Apostles to give concerning the Catholic faith until the end of the world.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Ponit quartum modum pertinacia de eo, qui assertionem catholicam apud eos, cum quibus moratur, diuulgatam, compos quidem rationis illam negat, aut oppo- sitam asserit, & quod talis sit pertinax probatur tri- bus rationibus.
units.tr: He sets out a fourth mode of obstinacy: when someone who is in his right mind denies a Catholic assertion that is commonly publicised among those with whom he lives, or asserts the opposite; and it is proved that such a person is obstinate by three arguments.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunquid est adhuc alius modus, quo de pertinacia valet quis conuinci? Magist. Quartus modus secundum nonnullos, quo statim aliquis pertinax & haereticus iudicatur, est. Si quis Christianus capax rationis & maxime intelligens, neget quamcunque assertionem catholicam, quae apud omnes catholicos & fideles, cum quibus conuersatur, tanquam catholica diuulgatur & a praedicantibus verba Dei publice praedicatur. Sicut apud omnes catholicos publice diuulgatur, quod Christus fuit crucifixus. Unde in omni ecclesia ostenditur crucifixus, & praedicantes verbum Dei hoc publice nuntiant & affirmant. Et ideo si quis inter Christianos nutritus negaret Christum esse crucifixum, esset statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Et quanto magis esset inter Christianos conuersatus, & plures intrasset ecclesias, & verbum Dei a pluribus audiuisset, & maiorem literaturam in sacra pagina & iure canonico haberet, tanto fortius esset statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Discip. Quia quidam (ut scis) putant ista de causa sanctissimum patrem do. I. Papam esse haereticum, pro eo, videlicet quod negat animas reproborum esse in inferno, & animas sanctorum in coelo non videre Deum, & Daemones non puniri, quas dicunt esse veritates catholicas apud omnes catholicos diuulgatas. Unde etiam dicunt, quod quamuis sermones suos nequaquam bullauerit, tamen est haereticus & pertinax iudicandus, peto quod praedictum modum de pertinacia conuincendi fortioribus allegationibus munire coneris, ut materiam habeam cogitandi, quomodo ad illas & alias pro defensionem Domini nostri summi pontificis valeam respondere. Magist. Quia negans aliquam assertionem catholicam apud omnes catholicos diuulgatam, ut statim absque examinatione vel discussione inter pertinaces & haereticos sit computandus, ostenditur primo sic. Sicut nulli licet ignorare ea, quae publice fiunt, secundum quod ex sacris canonibus colligitur euidenter. dist. 16. quod dictis & 12. q. 3. qui habuistis: sic non licet ignorare ea quae publice diuulgantur, nuntiantur & tanquam catholica praedicantur. Qui autem negat assertionem catholicam, quam sibi ignorare non licet, est pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Ergo qui negat assertionem catholicam tam publice scilicet apud omnes catholicos diuulgatam, statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus est. Secundo sic negans assertionem catholicam apud omnes catholicos diuulgatam non poterit per simplicitatem, & ignorantiam excusari, quod non per simplicitatem patet: quia ponitur, quod talis negans est capax rationis & intelligens. Si enim careret usu rationis, vel esset alienatus a sensu, bene excusaretur. Sed intelligens & instructus per simplicitatem excusari non potest. Nec potest per ignorantiam excusari: quia ignorantia iuris diuini apud omnes promulgati non excusat: sicut nec ignorantia iuris naturalis non excusat, secundum quod legitur in decretis 1. q. § 4. & notandum. Si ergo assertio negata sit apud omnes catholicos promulgata, negans eam nequit de pertinacia & pravitate haeretica excusari. Discip. Quid si in rei veritate ignoratalem assertionem ad fidem catholicam pertinere: numquid apud Deum excusaretur, si absque pertinacia eam negaret? Magist. Respondetur quod apud Deum excusaretur, & etiam apud ecclesiam, si probare valeret se ignorasse assertionem negatam apud catholicos esse tanquam catholicam diuulgatam. Sicut si quis inter aliquos Christianos in aliqua una domo semper fuisset a pueritia nutritus, licet postea diceret ex ignorantia Christum non fuisse crucifixum, & non pertinaciter adhaereat, eum non deberet ecclesia pertinacem & haereticum reputare, si omnes, cum quibus fuerat conuersatus, testimonium perhibent, quod nunquam aliquis eorum de crucifixione Christi sibi fuisset locutus. Discip. Circa tales casus, qui forte nunquam euenerunt, minime te dilates. Sed loquamur de illis Christianis, qui cum Christianis communiter conuersantur, ecclesias intrant, & de his quae ad fidem pertinent Christiana saepe audiunt conferentes. Et de talibus adhuc proba, si valeas, quod negantes assertionem catholicam apud omnes catholicos diuulgata statim sunt pertinaces & haeretici iudicandi. Magist. Tertio hoc probatur sic. Qui negat assertionem catholicam, quam debet & tenetur simpliciter & explicite credere, est pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Sed quilibet Christianus tenetur explicite credere omnem assertionem catholicam apud omnes catholicos diuulgatam. Ergo quicunq; negat talem assertionem, est tanquam pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Maior ex descriptione pertinacis patet. Quia pertinax est, qui persistit in eo quod debet dimittere. Talis est autem, qui negat assertionem catholicam, quam tenetur explicite credere: quia ex quo tenetur eam explicite credere, tenetur negationem eius dimittere: Ergo si negat, est pertinax. Minor probatur. Quia si aliquis tenetur aliquam assertionem catholicam explicite credere, aut ad hoc tenetur quod talis assertio est apud omnes catholicos tanquam catholica diuulgata: aut quia sic patenter ostenditur per scripturam diuinam, vel doctrinam seu determinationem vniuersalis ecclesiae, quod catholica est censenda. Si detur primum, habetur intentum. Quia quilibet Christianus tenetur explicite credere omnem assertionem catholicam, quam scit apud catholicos pro catholica diuulgatam. Quod si dicat se ignorare, oportet eum, si debet apud ecclesiam excusari, hoc probare. Secundum non potest dari: quia tunc nullus teneretur explicite Christum natum de virgine vel crucifixum credere, nec aliquem alium articulum fidei, antequam sibi per scripturam diuinam probaretur. Et ita quilibet laicus posset impune negare omnem articulum fidei, quousque sibi per librum ostenderetur, talem articulum fidei in Biblia contineri. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia qui negat fidem Christianam esse veram, vel sectam Sarracenorum non esse falsam & malam, est statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Sed hoc non est, nisi quia apud omnes catholicos diuulgatur, tanquam catholicum, quod fides Christiana est vera fides, & quod fides Sarracenorum est falsa fides. Ergo per eandem rationem, qui negat quamcunque assertionem catholicam apud omnes catholicos diuulgatam, est statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus: nec potest apud ecclesiam aliter excusari, nisi probet se ignorasse assertionem negatam esse taliter diuulgatam.
units.tr: Student. Is there yet another way by which someone may be convicted of pertinacity? Master. According to some, there is a fourth way, by which a person is at once judged pertinacious and heretical. If a Christian who is capable of reason, and especially one who understands, denies any catholic assertion that is published as catholic among all the catholics and faithful with whom he lives, and that is publicly preached by those who proclaim the word of God, then he is judged at once pertinacious and heretical. For example, it is publicly known among all catholics that Christ was crucified. Hence a crucified Christ is shown in every church, and those who preach the word of God announce and affirm this publicly. So if someone brought up among Christians were to deny that Christ was crucified, he would at once be judged pertinacious and heretical. And the more he had lived among Christians, the more churches he had entered, the more often he had heard the word of God, and the more learning he had in sacred page and canon law, so much the more strongly would he at once be judged pertinacious and heretical. Student. Because some people (as you know) think that for this very reason the most holy father, Lord Pope John, is a heretic, namely because he denies that the souls of the reprobate are in hell, that the souls of the saints do not see God in heaven, and that demons are not punished; these they say are catholic truths published among all catholics. Hence they also say that, although he never sealed his sermons with a bull, he is nonetheless to be judged a pertinacious heretic. I ask you to strengthen the aforesaid way of convicting of pertinacity with stronger arguments, so that I may have material to consider how I might answer those and other objections in defence of our lord the supreme pontiff. Master. That someone who denies an assertion published among all catholics as catholic should be counted at once as pertinacious and heretical, without examination or discussion, is shown first thus. Just as no one is allowed to be ignorant of what is done publicly, as is clearly gathered from the sacred canons (dist. 16. quod dictis & 12. q. 3. qui habuistis:), so one is not allowed to be ignorant of what is publicly published, announced and preached as catholic. But whoever denies a catholic assertion, which he is not allowed to be ignorant of, is to be judged pertinacious and heretical. Therefore whoever denies a catholic assertion published so publicly among all catholics is at once to be judged pertinacious and heretical. Secondly, thus: someone who denies a catholic assertion published among all catholics cannot be excused by simplicity and ignorance. That he cannot be excused by simplicity is evident, because it is assumed that such a denier is capable of reason and understanding. For if he lacked the use of reason, or were out of his mind, he could well be excused. But one who understands and has been instructed cannot be excused by simplicity. Nor can he be excused by ignorance, because ignorance of divine law that has been promulgated among all does not excuse, just as ignorance of natural law does not excuse, as is read in the decretals (1. q. § 4. & notandum). If, then, the denied assertion has been promulgated among all catholics, the one who denies it cannot be excused from pertinacity and heretical depravity. Student. What if, in the truth of the matter, he is ignorant that such an assertion belongs to the catholic faith? Would he be excused before God if he denied it without pertinacity? Master. The answer is that he would be excused before God, and also before the Church, if he could prove that he was ignorant that the assertion he denied was published among catholics as catholic. For example, if someone had always been brought up from childhood in one house among some Christians, and afterwards said that through ignorance Christ had not been crucified, and did not cling to this obstinately, the Church ought not to regard him as pertinacious and heretical, provided that all those with whom he had lived bear witness that none of them had ever spoken to him about the crucifixion of Christ. Student. Do not dwell on such cases, which perhaps never happen. But let us speak of those Christians who live in common with Christians, enter churches, and often hear and discuss Christian matters that pertain to the faith. And concerning such people, prove further, if you can, that those who deny an assertion published among all catholics are at once to be judged pertinacious and heretical. Master. Thirdly, this is proved thus. He who denies a catholic assertion, which he ought and is bound to believe simply and explicitly, is to be counted pertinacious and heretical. But every Christian is bound to believe explicitly every catholic assertion published among all catholics. Therefore whoever denies such an assertion is to be judged as pertinacious and heretical. The major premise is clear from the description of the pertinacious person: Because a pertinacious person is one who persists in what he ought to give up. Now the one who denies a catholic assertion which he is bound to believe explicitly is such a person, because since he is bound to believe it explicitly, he is bound to give up denying it; therefore if he denies it, he is pertinacious. The minor premise is proved thus. If someone is bound to believe some catholic assertion explicitly, then either he is bound to this because such an assertion is published among all catholics as catholic, or because it is plainly shown by divine Scripture, or by the teaching or determination of the universal Church, that it is to be regarded as catholic. If the first is granted, the point is established: every Christian is bound to believe explicitly every catholic assertion that he knows to be published as catholic among catholics. And if he says he is ignorant of it, he must prove this if he is to be excused before the Church. The second cannot be granted, because then no one would be bound to believe explicitly that Christ was born of a virgin or crucified, nor any other article of faith, until it had been proved to him from divine Scripture. And so any layman could with impunity deny every article of faith until it was shown to him from a book that such an article is contained in the Bible. This argument is confirmed thus: whoever denies that the Christian faith is true, or that the sect of the Saracens is not false and evil, is at once to be judged pertinacious and heretical. But this is so only because it is publicly taught among all catholics as catholic that the Christian faith is the true faith, and that the faith of the Saracens is false. Therefore by the same reasoning, whoever denies any catholic assertion published among all catholics is at once to be judged pertinacious and heretical, and cannot be excused before the Church unless he proves that he was ignorant that the assertion he denied had been published in this way.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Arguit contra modum quartum pertinacia precedentis cap. assignatum, excusando Papam Iohannem XXII.
