units.tr: He argues against the fourth mode of pertinacity assigned in the preceding chapter, excusing Pope John XXII.

units.la: Discipulus. Allega in contrarium. Magist. Negans veritatem catholicam, de qua nescitur, an per regulam fidei, scil. per scripturam, paratus sit corrigi, non est pertinax iudicandus. Hoc patet auctoritate Aug. superius allegata, quae ponitur 24. q. 3. dixit Apostolus. Hoc dicit Gloss. 17. dist. 1. c. nec licuit: Eo ipso, quo quis errat, non dicitur haereticus, si paratus est corrigi. Sed possibile est aliquem negare assertionem catholicam apud catholicos diuulgatam, quamuis nesciatur, an paratus sit corrigi per regulam fidei, scilicet per scripturam sacram. Potest enim quis talem assertionem negare, & tamen offerre se paratum corrigi, si sibi ostendatur, quod dicta assertio in sacra pagina vel in determinatione ecclesiae continetur. Ergo talis non est statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus; Sed examinandus est an paratus sit corrigi. Discip. Ista allegatio videtur fortis, & sufficienter Dominum Papam excusat, etiam esto quod erret. Magist. Alii reputant dictam allegationem nullam, quia ex ipsa sequeretur, sicut tactum est prius, quod cuilibet Christiano negare liceret Christum esse verum hominem, vel fuisse crucifixum. Posset enim dicere absque pertinacia per assertionem istam, nego Christum fuisse crucifixum, tamen paratus sum corrigi, si mihi per scripturam sacram vel determinationem ecclesiae ostendatur Christum fuisse crucifixum. Discip. Quare non potest talis excusari, ex quo paratus est corrigi? Magist. Ideo secundum multos talis excusatio non debet, quia esto quod esset possibile, quod aliquis talis esset paratus corrigi, tamen contra talem (quantumcunque dicat se paratum corrigi) est de pertinacia tam violenta praesumptio, ex quo non ignorat assertionem negatam esse tam publice praedicatam & asserit tam per ecclesiam, quod non est sibi credendum, cum dicit se paratum corrigi. Dictis enim talium est fides nullatenus adhibenda. Hinc de tali negante assertionem catholicam publice praedicatam, dicit Stephanus Papa, ut habetur extra, de haeret. cap. 1. Nec eis omnino credendum est qui sibi ipsis veritatis ignorant. Talibus cum contra Christianos testificari nituntur, nec (cum testimonium perhibent de seipsis) est omnino credendum. Quare quamuis se dicant paratos corrigi, sunt pertinaces & haeretici reputandi.
units.tr: Disciple. Allege something to the contrary. Master. One who denies a Catholic truth, when it is not known whether he is ready to be corrected by the rule of faith, namely by Scripture, is not to be judged pertinacious. This is clear from the authority of Augustine cited above, which is found in 24 q. 3, "dixit Apostolus." The Gloss says the same in 17 dist. 1, c. "nec licuit": by the very fact that someone errs, he is not called a heretic if he is ready to be corrected. But it is possible that someone denies a Catholic assertion widely held among Catholics, although it is not known whether he is ready to be corrected by the rule of faith, that is, by holy Scripture. For someone can deny such an assertion and yet offer himself as ready to be corrected, if it is shown to him that the said assertion is contained in holy Scripture or in the determination of the Church. Therefore such a person is not to be judged at once pertinacious and heretical; rather he is to be examined as to whether he is ready to be corrected. Disciple. This argument seems strong and sufficiently excuses the Lord Pope, even if he errs. Master. Others consider the said argument worthless, because it would follow from it, as was touched on before, that any Christian might be allowed to deny that Christ is true man, or that he was crucified. For he could say, without pertinacity, "I deny that Christ was crucified; yet I am ready to be corrected if it is shown to me by holy Scripture or the determination of the Church that Christ was crucified." Disciple. Why then can such a person not be excused, since he is ready to be corrected? Master. According to many, such an excuse ought not to hold, because although it might be possible that someone of this kind is ready to be corrected, nevertheless against such a person (however much he says he is ready to be corrected) there is a very strong presumption of pertinacity, since he is not ignorant that the assertion he denies is preached so publicly and affirmed so firmly by the Church that he is not to be believed when he says he is ready to be corrected. For the words of such people are in no way to be trusted. Hence, concerning such a person who denies a Catholic assertion publicly preached, Pope Stephen says, as found in Extra, De haereticis, chapter 1: "Nor are they at all to be believed who are ignorant of the truth themselves. When they strive to bear witness against Christians, nor (when they bear testimony about themselves) are they to be believed at all." Wherefore, although they say they are ready to be corrected, they are to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Quo ponitur quintus modus pertinacia, de eo, in quo praesumitur, quod neget aliquod contentum in sacra scriptura, quod scit ibi contineri, ubi etiam notatur quod violenta praesumptio sufficit ad sententiam definitivam.
units.tr: Here is set out the fifth mode of pertinacity, concerning the case in which a person is presumed to deny something contained in holy Scripture that he knows to be there, and where it is also noted that a strong presumption is sufficient for a definitive sentence.

units.la: Discipulus. Si est alius modus errantem contra fidem de pertinacia convincendi paratus sum audire. Magist. Dicunt nonnulli, quod ille est statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus, de quo est violenta praesumptio, quod negat aliquam assertionem, quam scit in scriptura diuina vel determinatione ecclesiae contineri. Puta si probari posset, quod prius assertionem, quam negat, legerit cum intellectu in scriptura diuina vel determinatione ecclesiae, probari posset quod prius eandem assertionem, quam negat, ex intentione docuerat vel etiam asseruerat publice vel occulte. De tali enim si non est probabile, quod oblitus fuerit illius quod didicerat, est praesumptio violenta, ꝓ scienter negat catholicam veritatem. Et per consequens pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Discip. De illo modo ponamus exemplum. Magist. Sunt nonnulli, qui de multis modernis pönunt exemplum, de omnibus videlicet illis, qui prius docuerunt Christum & Apostolos nullius rei proprietatem habuisse, dicentes quod haec veritas ex scriptura divina & determinatione ecclesiae manifeste accipitur, & postea veritatem negauerunt eandem. Cum non sit probabile, quod scripturae divinae & eiusdem determinationis Ecclesiae sint obliti, propter quod dicunt pertinaces illos & haereticos esse censendos. Discip. Istud exemplum tangit doctrinam sanctissimi patris Domini Iohan. 22. de quo alias tecum exquisite tractabo: ideo illo exemplo dimisso, proba si potes, quod negantes catholicam veritatem, quam prius reputauerunt catholicam, statim absque maiori examinatione pertinaces & haeretici sunt censendi. Magist. Hoc probatur primo sic. Qui scienter negat catholicam veritatem, est pertinax haereticus reputandus. Sed talis scienter negat catholicam veritatem. Non enim potest se per ignorantiam excusare, cum prius didicerit eandem veritatem ad fidem catholicam pertinere, si non est oblitus eorum quae didicit. Ergo ex quo negat veritatem, quam prius didicerat & tenuerat, est pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Secundo sic. Omnis apostata in catholica veritate, est pertinax & haereticus reputandus: quia talis est apostata a fide. Apostata autem a fide inter haereticos computatur: sed negans catholicam veritatem, quam prius catholicam reputauit, est apostata a catholica veritate: quia talis abiicit catholicam veritatem. Ergo est pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Maior videtur certa. Minor probatur: quia qui negat catholicam veritatem, quam prius agnouit esse catholicam, est peior infideli, qui nunquam novit veritatem catholicam, teste Innoc. tertio, qui, ut habetur extra, de Apostatis. c. quidam, ait: cum minus malum existat viam Domini non agnoscere quam post agnitionem retroire. Hinc beatus Petrus canonica sive 2. cap. 2. melius enim est (vel, erat) eis non cognoscere viam iustitiae, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti. Veritas autem catholica est via illa iustitiae. Ergo maius malum est post agnitam veritatem catholicam retroire, quam nunquam ipsam agnouisse. Sed hoc non esset maius malum, nisi ratione deterioris infidelitatis. Ergo qui negat catholicam veritatem, quam prius novit esse catholicam, infidelis est: & per consequens pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Discip. Videtur quod illae rationes non concludant. Tum quia potest quis negare veritatem catholicam, quam prius putauit catholicam, quamvis non noverit eam esse catholicam. Rationes autem praedictae videntur procedere de eo, qui negat veritatem catholicam, quamvis non solum putauit, sed etiam agnovit eam esse catholicam. Secundo, quia talis potest esse paratus corrigi: immo potest offerre se paratum corrigi. Ergo licet erret, non est inter haereticos computandus. Magist. Istae duae instantiae per idem videntur excludi, per hoc scilicet quod non est tali in hoc casu credendum, sive dicat quod hoc prius putauerit, non tamen agnouit veritatem, quam modo negat esse catholicam sive dicat se paratum corrigi. Quod enim in primo dicto sibi non credatur, ostenditur, quia illi, qui inuenitur sibiipsi esse contrarius, non est credendum, saltem secundo dicto ipsius, teste Innocent. tertio, qui, ut habetur extra de probationibus cap. per tuas, ait: Cum nimis indignum sit iuxta legitimas sanctiones, ut quod suo quisque voto dilucidum protestatus est, eundem casum proprio testimonio valeat infirmare. Gloss. extra de praesumptionibus, cap. literas, notat, dicens, hoc est, notabile, quod semper standum est pro dicto alicuius, si postea contrarium dicat, etiam in alio iudicio. supr. de testi. cum in tua, & etiam extra iudicium supr. de probationibus, per tuas. Ex his aliisque quamplurimis patet, quod qui inuenitur sibiipsi contrarius, non est credendum secundo dicto eius. Sed qui negat catholicam veritatem, inuenitur sibiipsi contrarius: quia dum putauerit dictam veritatem esse catholicam, dixit aut verbo, vel facto innuit se agnoscere illam veritatem esse catholicam. Ergo si postea dicat se non agnouisse dictam veritatem esse catholiccam, non est sibi credendum. Et per consequens per hoc excusari non potest, quin sit modo pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Secunda vero instantia, quod etiam non valeat, si dicat se paratum corrigi, ostenditur sic. Nulli erranti est credendum, quod sit paratus corrigi, nisi quando putatur ignoranter a veritate catholica deuiare. Sed ille non praesumitur ignoranter a veritate aliqua, quae est catholica, deuiare; sed praesumendum est, quod a fundamento, propter quod assertioni priori adhaeserit, omnino recessit. Fundamentum autem, propter quod tali assertioni adhaesit, est sacra scriptura vel doctrina ecclesiae. Ergo praesumendum, quod nunc reputat scripturam sacram vel doctrinam ecclesiae esse falsam. Sicut illi, qui postponunt doctrinam traditam in decretali Nicolai tertii, quae incipit: exiit qui seminat, putauerunt, tenuerunt ac docuerunt, quod Christus & Apostoli omnem proprietatem temporalium abdicarunt: & modo tenent assertionem contrariam, reputant doctrinam traditam in decretali praedicta, exiit, esse falsam. Et si dicerent, se putare eandem doctrinam esse veram, non esset eis credendum: quia sibiipsis contrarii probarentur. Praesumendum est ergo, quod negans catholicam veritatem, quam primo asseruit esse catholicam, non reputat sacram scripturam vel doctrinam ecclesiae esse veram. Tali autem non est credendum, quantumcunque dicat se paratum corrigi. Ergo & neganti veritatem catholicam, quam primo habuit pro catholica, non est credendum, quamuis dicat se paratum corrigi: & per consequens inter pertinaces & haereticos est censendus. Et ita stant insolutae rationes priores. Discip. Ista tantummodo probant, quod talis praesumitur pertinax & haereticus. Propter praesumptionem autem non est aliquis damnandus, nec graviter puniendus. Magist. Saepe propter sola praesumptione violentam sententiam etiam diffinitiua perfertur. Vnde & Salomon legitur 3.Reg.3. contendentibus duabus mulieribus coram eo pro puero, ex sola praesumptione diffinitiuam dedisse sententiam. Sic dicunt quidam in proposito, quod ex praesumptione violenta negans veritatem catholicam, quam prius asseruerat esse catholicam, est damnandus, & tanquam haereticus puniendus.
units.tr: Disciple. If there is another mode of convicting an erring person of pertinacity against the faith, I am ready to hear it. Master. Some say that a person must be judged at once pertinacious and heretical when there is a strong presumption that he denies some assertion which he knows to be contained in divine Scripture or in the determination of the Church. For example, if it could be shown that he had earlier read with understanding the assertion he now denies, either in divine Scripture or in the determination of the Church, it could be shown that he had earlier taught that same assertion, which he now denies, deliberately, or even asserted it publicly or privately. For regarding such a man, if it is not probable that he has forgotten what he had learned, there is a strong presumption that he knowingly denies a catholic truth, and consequently he is to be counted pertinacious and heretical. Disciple. Let us take an example of that mode. Master. There are some who give as an example many moderns, namely all those who once taught that Christ and the Apostles had no ownership of any thing, saying that this truth is plainly drawn from divine Scripture and the determination of the Church, and afterwards denied the same truth. Since it is not probable that they have forgotten the divine Scripture and the same determination of the Church, they say those men are to be counted pertinacious and heretical. Disciple. That example touches on the doctrine of the most holy father, Lord John XXII, about which I shall treat with you at length on another occasion. So, setting that example aside, prove if you can that those who deny a catholic truth, which they previously held to be catholic, are to be counted at once pertinacious and heretical without a fuller examination. Master. This is first proved thus. Whoever knowingly denies a catholic truth is to be counted a pertinacious heretic. But such a person knowingly denies a catholic truth. For he cannot excuse himself by ignorance, since he had earlier learned that this same truth belongs to the catholic faith, if he has not forgotten what he learned. Therefore, since he denies a truth which he had previously learned and held, he is to be counted pertinacious and heretical. Secondly, thus. Every apostate from catholic truth is to be counted pertinacious and heretical, because such a person is an apostate from the faith. But an apostate from the faith is reckoned among the heretics. Now one who denies a catholic truth, which he had previously regarded as catholic, is an apostate from catholic truth, because such a person casts off catholic truth. Therefore he is to be judged pertinacious and heretical. The major premise seems certain. The minor is proved thus: one who denies a catholic truth, which he had earlier recognized as catholic, is worse than an unbeliever who never knew the catholic truth, as Innocent III says, who, as is found in extra, de Apostatis. c. quidam, says: since it is a lesser evil not to know the way of the Lord than, after knowing it, to turn back. Hence the blessed Peter in his canonical Epistle, chapter 2: for it were better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. Now the catholic truth is that way of righteousness. Therefore it is a greater evil, after recognizing the catholic truth, to turn back than never to have recognized it. But this would not be a greater evil, except by reason of a worse unbelief. Therefore one who denies a catholic truth which he previously knew to be catholic is an unbeliever, and consequently is to be counted pertinacious and heretical. Disciple. It seems that those arguments do not conclude. For someone may deny a catholic truth which he previously thought catholic, although he did not know it to be catholic. The arguments just given seem to apply to one who denies a catholic truth although he not only thought but also recognized it to be catholic. Secondly, such a person may be ready to be corrected; indeed he may offer himself as ready to be corrected. Therefore, even if he errs, he is not to be counted among the heretics. Master. These two objections seem to be answered by the same point, namely that such a person is not to be believed in this case, whether he says that he previously thought so but did not truly recognize the truth he now denies to be catholic, or whether he says that he is ready to be corrected. For that he is not to be believed in the first statement is shown by the fact that one who is found to be contrary to himself is not to be believed, at least in his second statement, as Innocent III says, as is found in extra de probationibus, cap. per tuas: since it is most unworthy, according to lawful sanctions, that a man should be able to weaken by his own testimony the case which he has openly declared by his own vow. The Gloss on extra de praesumptionibus, cap. literas, notes, saying: this is notable, that one must always stand by the statement of someone if he afterwards says the contrary, even in another trial; see above de testibus, cum in tua, and also outside a trial, above de probationibus, per tuas. From these and very many other sources it is clear that one who is found to be contrary to himself is not to be believed in his second statement. But one who denies a catholic truth is found to be contrary to himself, because, while he had thought that truth to be catholic, he said either in words or by deed that he recognized that truth to be catholic. Therefore if he later says that he did not recognize that truth to be catholic, he is not to be believed. And consequently he cannot be excused by this from being counted pertinacious and heretical now. The second objection, that it also has no force if he says he is ready to be corrected, is shown thus. No erring person is to be believed when he says he is ready to be corrected, unless he is thought to have strayed from catholic truth in ignorance. But such a person is not presumed to have strayed in ignorance from some truth which is catholic; rather it must be presumed that he has wholly withdrawn from the foundation on which he adhered to the former assertion. The foundation on which he adhered to that assertion is holy Scripture or the doctrine of the Church. Therefore it must be presumed that he now considers holy Scripture or the doctrine of the Church to be false. Just as those who rejected the doctrine handed down in the decretal of Nicholas III which begins exiit qui seminat, thought, held and taught that Christ and the Apostles renounced all ownership of temporal goods, and now hold the contrary assertion, they regard the doctrine handed down in the aforesaid decretal, exiit, as false. And if they said that they thought the same doctrine was true, they would not be believed, because they would be proved contrary to themselves. Therefore it must be presumed that one who denies a catholic truth which he first asserted to be catholic does not regard holy Scripture or the doctrine of the Church as true. And such a person is not to be believed, however much he says that he is ready to be corrected. Therefore one who denies a catholic truth which he first held to be catholic is not to be believed, although he says he is ready to be corrected, and consequently he is to be counted among the pertinacious and heretical. And so the earlier arguments stand unanswered. Disciple. These things only prove that such a person is presumed to be pertinacious and heretical. But no one is to be condemned on a presumption, nor severely punished. Master. Often a definitive sentence is pronounced on a strong presumption alone. Hence we read that Solomon, in 3 Kings 3, when two women contended before him over a child, gave a definitive sentence on presumption alone. So some men say in this matter that one who, on a strong presumption, denies a catholic truth which he had earlier asserted to be catholic, is to be condemned and punished as a heretic.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Ponit duos alios modos pertinacia, de eo scilicet, qui scienter negat doctrinam sanctorum: & de eo qui legitime correptus suum errorem revocare negligit.
units.tr: He sets out two other modes of obstinacy: that of the man who knowingly denies the doctrine of the saints, and that of the man who, being lawfully corrected, neglects to retract his error.

units.la: DIscipulus. Ad alios modos conuincendi errantes de pertinacia & haeretica prauitate procede. Magist. Alius modus de pertinacia conuincendi dicitur esse, cum quis scienter negat doctrinam sanctorum. Quidam enim affirmant, quod talis est statim pertinax & haereticus iudicandus. Aliis dicentibus, quod talis, licet corrigi nolit, non est pertinax nec haereticus reputandus. Discip. Haec difficultas dependet ex alia, quam supra tractauimus, an scil. tenere assertiones sanctorum sit necessarium ad salutem. Ideo circa illam hic noli insistere, sed ad alium modum (de pertinacia quempiam conuincendi) festina. Magist. Ille de pertinacia conuincitur, qui correptus legitime se non corrigit, nec emendat, suam scilicet haeresim reuocando. Hoc scil. ex verbis Augustin. superius allegatis quae ponuntur, 28. quaest. 3. c. qui in ecclesia, colligitur euidenter. Quod etiam talis sit pertinax iudicandus, probatur aperte, quia qui non est paratus corrigi, debet pertinax iudicari. Qui autem correptus legitime haeresim suam non reuocat, non est paratus corrigi. Ergo talis est pertinax reputandus. Discip. Quia illum modum de pertinacia conuincendi super audiui; & alii sunt mihi omnino noui, cupio illum modum exquisitius pertractari. Duo autem peto circa hunc modum discutias; ad quem videlicet spectat errantem corrigere. Et qualis debet esse illa correctio, quae est legitima & sufficiens reputanda. Magist. Videndum primo de correctione: secundo de corripiente. Discip. Tene ordinem in procedendo, quem vis. Magist. Quantum ad correctorem, dicitur, quod illa sola correctio censenda est sufficiens & legitima reputanda, qua aperte erranti ostenditur, quod assertio sua catholicae obuiat veritati, ita quod iudicio intelligentium nulla posset tergiuersatione negare, quin sibi sit sufficienter & aperte ostensum, quod error suus catholicae veritati repugnat. Verbi gratia: si quis ex ignorantia Euangelii textum ignorans diceret, sicut quidam in Auinione publice praedicauit (ut fertur) quod milites fregerunt crura Christi. Et sibi per textum Euangelii Iohan. 19. vbi sic legitur: Venerunt ergo milites & primi quidem fregerunt crura & alterus qui crucifixus est cum eo. Ad Iesum autem cum venissent, ut viderunt eum iam mortuum, non fregerunt eius crura. ostenderetur contrarium. Ista correctio deberet sufficiens reputari: quia iudicio cuiuslibet intelligentis talis nulla posset euadendo tergiuersatione negare, quin esset sibi aperte probatum, quod assertio sua euangelicae obuiat veritati. Si quis etiam ex ignorantia dogmatizaret duas personas, sicut duas substantias, fuisse in Christo, sibi per textum synodi Ephesinę ostenderetur, quod hoc est haeresis Nestorii per eandem synodum condemnata, nulla posset tergiuersatione negare, quod non esset sibi aperte probatum, quod assertio sua esset haeresis condemnata: & per consequens, quod veritati catholicae aduersatur. Et ideo talis correctio esset sufficiens & legitima reputanda. Secundo videndum de corripiente: de quo distinguitur. Quidam corripiunt increpando, & poena debita puniendo, quidam charitatiue monendo, & errorem tantummodo reprobando. Primus modus pertinet ad praelatos & iurisdictionem habentes: Secundus modus pertinet ad quemlibet Christianum.
units.tr: STUDENT. Proceed to the other ways of convicting erring men of obstinacy and heretical perversity. TEACHER. The other way of convicting someone of obstinacy is said to be when a person knowingly denies the doctrine of the saints. Some affirm that such a person is at once to be judged obstinate and heretical; others say that such a person, even if he is unwilling to be corrected, is not to be regarded as obstinate or heretical. STUDENT. This difficulty depends on another which we treated above, namely whether it is necessary for salvation to hold the assertions of the saints. So do not dwell on that here, but hasten on to the other way of convicting someone of obstinacy. TEACHER. A man is convicted of obstinacy who, when lawfully corrected, does not correct or amend himself, that is, by retracting his heresy. This is clearly gathered from the words of Augustine cited above, which are found in 28 q. 3 c. Qui in ecclesia. That such a person is also to be judged obstinate is plainly proved, because whoever is not prepared to be corrected must be judged obstinate. But whoever, when lawfully corrected, does not retract his heresy, is not prepared to be corrected. Therefore such a person is to be regarded as obstinate. STUDENT. Since I have heard about that mode of convicting of obstinacy, and the others are entirely new to me, I wish this mode to be treated more exactly. I ask you to discuss two things about it: first, to whom it belongs to correct an erring man; and second, what kind of correction ought to be regarded as lawful and sufficient. TEACHER. We must first consider the correction, and second the one who corrects. STUDENT. Keep to whatever order of treatment you wish. TEACHER. As regards the one who corrects, it is said that only that correction is to be counted sufficient and lawful which openly shows the erring man that his assertion stands against Catholic truth, so that, by the judgment of anyone who understands, he could deny by no evasion that it has been sufficiently and openly shown to him that his error contradicts Catholic truth. For example: if someone, through ignorance of the Gospel and not knowing the text, were to say, as a certain man at Avignon is reported to have preached publicly, that the soldiers broke the legs of Christ, and he were shown the contrary by the text of the Gospel of John 19, where it is read thus: "The soldiers therefore came, and brake the legs of the first, and of the other which was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they brake not his legs." This correction ought to be regarded as sufficient, because by the judgment of anyone who understands, such a man could by no evasion deny that it had been plainly proved to him that his assertion opposes the Gospel truth. Likewise, if someone through ignorance were to teach that there were two persons, as two substances, in Christ, and it were shown to him from the text of the Council of Ephesus that this is the heresy of Nestorius condemned by that same council, he could deny by no evasion that it had not been plainly proved to him that his assertion was a condemned heresy, and consequently that it opposes Catholic truth. And therefore such a correction would be regarded as sufficient and lawful. Second, we must consider the one who corrects, and here a distinction is drawn. Some correct by rebuking and by punishing with the due penalty; others by admonishing in charity and only rebuking the error. The first mode belongs to prelates and those who hold jurisdiction; the second mode belongs to every Christian.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: In quo tractatur specialiter de eo qui correptus a suo praelato de errore, an teneatur illum immediate revocare, quamquam sibi non fuerit patenter ostensum, quod suus error contradicat catholicae veritati. Et respondetur, quod non, secundum vnam opinionem, & probatur duabus rationibus.
units.tr: In which it is treated specifically of the one who, corrected by his prelate for an error, is bound to retract it at once, even though it has not been clearly shown to him that his error contradicts Catholic truth. And it is answered that he is not, according to one opinion, and this is proved by two arguments.

units.la: DIscipulus. Ex quo intelligo quae est correptio sufficiens & legitima reputanda secundum multos, & distinctionem de corripiente errantem considero. Cupio scire an omnes sciant literati, quod errans correptus a praelato suo vel habente iurisdictionem super ipsum teneatur errorem suum revocare, licet non fuerit sibi patenter ostensum per eundem, quod error suus catholicae obuiat veritati, vtrum scilicet ad solam monitionem vel increpationem praelati sui errorem suum debeat revocare. Magist. De hoc diuersimode opinantur Doctores. Dicunt enim nonnulli, quod nullus correptus a praelato iurisdictionem habente tenetur errorem revocare, antequam fuerit sibi patenter ostensum modo praedicto, quod error suus est contrarius veritati. Hoc probant primo sic. Illi, qui in expositione scripturae diuinae, & per consequens in traditione eorum, quae ad fidem pertinent orthodoxam, praefertur praelatis & iurisdictionem habentibus, non tenentur nec debent, si erraverint ignoranter, opiniones suas tanquam haereticas (licet sint in rei veritate erroneae) revocare, quamuis correpti fuerint a praelatis vel aliis; nisi eis patenter fuerit ostensum, quod opiniones suae veritati obuiant orthodoxae. Quia qui maioris auctoritatis est in aliquo, nequaquam in hoc minori subiicitur. Ergo qui præferuntur prælatis in expositione scripturæ diuinæ, non subiiciuntur eis in hoc: sed Doctores & tractatores scripturæ diuinæ præferuntur prælatis & iurisdictionem habentibus in expositione scripturæ diuinæ: & per consequens in traditione illorum ad fidem pertinent orthodoxam. Ergo doctores non tenentur opiniones suas, licet sint erroneæ, reuocare, si fuerint à prælatis correpti, nisi probatum fuerit eis euidenter, quod eorum opiniones obuiant veritati. Maior est certa. Et minor probatur primo auctoritate Gratiani in decretis dist. 20. c. 1. quæ ait: aliud est causis terminum imponere, aliud scripturas sanctas diligenter exponere, & ita patet, quod diuinarum scripturarum tractatores, si scientia pontificibus præmineant, licet dignitatis eorum apicem non sunt adepti, in sacrarum literarum expositionibus eis præponuntur, in causis vero diffiniendis secundum post eos locum merentur. Ex his patenter habetur, quod doctores in expositionibus scripturæ pontificibus præferuntur. Quod etiam ratione eiusdem Gratiani ostenditur, quam ponit sub his verbis: quia quicunque maiori ratione vtitur, eo maioris auctoritatis eius verba esse videntur. Plurimi autem tractatores (quia sunt plenori gratia spiritus sancti & ampliori scientia alijs præcellentes) rationi magis adhæsisse probantur. Vnde nonnullorum pontificum constitutis Augustini, Hieronymi, atque aliorum tractatorum dicta videntur esse præferenda. His verbis ostenditur, quod in his, quæ ad fidem pertinent, Doctores sunt pontificibus præferendi. Et ita, nisi fuerint ab eis correpti legitime modo præexposito, non tenentur opiniones suas, si fuerint erroneæ, reuocare. Discip. Ista ratio videtur dupliciter deficere. Primo, quia Grat. loquitur de doctoribus ab ecclesia approbatis: sic de Augustino, Hieronymo, & aliis non modernis similibus doctoribus. Et ideo licet illi sancti sint in expositionibus scripturarum, pontificibus præponendi: Doctores tamen moderni temporis episcopis & inquisitoribus hæreticæ prauitatis præferri non debent. Secundo videtur deficere: quia non sequitur, Doctores non debent suas opiniones ad correptionem iurisdictionem habentibus reuocare, nisi modo prædicto fuerunt correpti legitime. Ergo alii simplices correcti à prælatis, non debent reuocare suos errores, nisi fuerint sæpe dicto modo correcti legitime. Magist. Ad illas instantias, vt apparet ex prædictis, est facile respondere. Ad primam dicunt, quod Grat. non loquitur solummodo de doctoribus ab ecclesia approbatis, sed etiam loquitur de aliis, sicut etiam loquitur de aliis pontificibus quam de illis, qui fuerunt temporibus doctorum, qui nunc sunt ab ecclesia approbati. Comparat enim in genere statum doctorum ad statum pontificum. Et ideo sicut antiquitus Doctores in traditione eorum, quæ spectant ad fidem, fuerunt pontificibus præferendi: ita & nunc sunt Doctores modernis pontificibus præferendi, dum modo sint Doctores propter scientiam excellentem & vitam laudabilem, & non propter munera & preces violentas vel fauores humanos ad magisterium sublimati. Vnde, vt suam intentionem aperte declarent, dicunt, quod Gratianus non loquitur de Doctoribus, prout his diebus nomen Doctoris accipitur, sed loquitur de intelligentibus scripturæ diuinæ tractatoribus, siue Magistri, siue Discipuli appellentur. Multi enim, qui vocantur Discipuli, in expositione scripturæ diuinæ sunt præferendi Magistris: & ideo sunt etiam pontificibus in huiusmodi præferendi. Vnde & ratio Gratiani ita concludit de eruditis modernis: sicut de antiquis tractatoribus scripturarum. Quia eruditi his temporibus scientia ampliori præcellunt. Ergo in huiusmodi sunt episcopis & inquisitoribus illiteratis & simplicibus præferendi. Ad secundam tuam instantiam dicunt: quod qua ratione periti correpti à prælatis vel iurisdictionem habentibus non tenentur suas opiniones reuocare, nisi legitime fuerint ab eis modo memorato correpti: eadem ratione nec simplices peritorum sequaces tenentur opiniones, quas de peritioribus acceperunt, aliqualiter reuocare, nisi fuerint correpti legitime. Ex quo sequitur, quod etiam alii simplices non tenentur (nisi correpti legitime) suas opiniones erroneas reuocare: quia omnes simplices consilii iure censeri videntur.
units.tr: Disciple. From this I understand what kind of correction is considered sufficient and legitimate according to many, and I am considering the distinction concerning the one who corrects an erring person. I wish to know whether all learned people know that an erring person who has been corrected by his prelate, or by one who has jurisdiction over him, is bound to retract his error, even though it has not been clearly shown to him by that same person that his error opposes Catholic truth; that is, whether he ought to retract his error on the mere admonition or rebuke of his prelate. Master. Doctors hold differing opinions on this. For some say that no one corrected by a prelate who has jurisdiction is bound to retract his error until it has been clearly shown to him, in the manner described, that his error is contrary to the truth. They prove this first thus. Those who are preferred to prelates and those with jurisdiction in the exposition of divine Scripture, and consequently in the handing down of those things that pertain to orthodox faith, are not bound, and ought not, if they have erred in ignorance, to retract their opinions as heretical (although in truth they are erroneous), even if they have been corrected by prelates or others, unless it has been clearly shown to them that their opinions oppose orthodox truth. For he who has greater authority in some matter is in no way subject to another in that lesser matter. Therefore those who are preferred to prelates in the exposition of divine Scripture are not subject to them in this; but doctors and interpreters of divine Scripture are preferred to prelates and those with jurisdiction in the exposition of divine Scripture, and consequently in the handing down of those things that pertain to orthodox faith. Therefore doctors are not bound to retract their opinions, even if they are erroneous, when they have been corrected by prelates, unless it has been clearly proved to them that their opinions oppose the truth. The major premise is certain. The minor is proved first by the authority of Gratian in the Decretum, dist. 20, c. 1, which says: It is one thing to set limits to lawsuits, another to expound the holy Scriptures diligently; and thus it is plain that the interpreters of divine Scriptures, if they surpass the pontiffs in knowledge, although they have not attained the summit of the pontiffs' dignity, are placed before them in the exposition of the sacred letters, but in defining causes they deserve a place second after them. From these words it is plainly held that doctors are preferred to pontiffs in the exposition of Scripture. This is also shown by the reasoning of the same Gratian, which he sets out in these words: because whoever uses the greater reason, his words seem to have the greater authority. Now most interpreters (because they excel others in a fuller grace of the Holy Spirit and greater learning) are shown to have clung more to reason. Hence the sayings of Augustine, Jerome and other interpreters seem to be preferred to the constitutions of some pontiffs. By these words it is shown that in those things which pertain to faith, doctors are to be preferred to pontiffs. And so, unless they have been lawfully corrected by them in the manner set out above, they are not bound to retract their opinions, if these are erroneous. Disciple. This argument seems to fail in two ways. First, because Gratian speaks of doctors approved by the Church: thus of Augustine, Jerome and other similar doctors who are not modern. And so, although those saints are to be placed before pontiffs in the exposition of Scriptures, modern doctors ought not to be preferred to bishops and inquisitors of heretical depravity. Secondly, it seems to fail because it does not follow that doctors ought not to retract their opinions when corrected by those with jurisdiction, unless they were lawfully corrected in the manner described. Therefore other simple people corrected by prelates are not bound to retract their errors unless they have been lawfully corrected in the aforesaid manner. Master. These objections, as appears from what has been said, are easy to answer. To the first they say that Gratian does not speak only of doctors approved by the Church, but also speaks of others, just as he also speaks of other pontiffs than those who lived in the times of the doctors who are now approved by the Church. For he compares in general the state of doctors with the state of pontiffs. And so, just as in ancient times doctors were to be preferred to pontiffs in the handing down of those things that concern faith, so now too doctors are to be preferred to modern pontiffs, provided they are doctors on account of excellent learning and a praiseworthy life, and not raised to teaching by gifts, violent entreaties or human favours. Hence, to make their meaning plain, they say that Gratian does not speak of doctors in the sense in which the name Doctor is used in these days, but speaks of interpreters of divine Scripture who understand it, whether they are called masters or disciples. For many who are called disciples are to be preferred to masters in the exposition of divine Scripture, and so they are also to be preferred to pontiffs in such matters. Hence also Gratian's reasoning concludes of learned moderns just as of ancient interpreters of Scripture, because learned men of these times surpass others in greater learning. Therefore in such matters they are to be preferred to bishops and inquisitors who are unlearned and simple. To your second objection they say: by the same reason that skilled men corrected by prelates or those with jurisdiction are not bound to retract their opinions unless they have been lawfully corrected by them in the aforesaid manner, by the same reason neither are the simple followers of the skilled bound in any way to retract the opinions they have received from the more skilled, unless they have been lawfully corrected. From this it follows that other simple people too are not bound (unless lawfully corrected) to retract their erroneous opinions, because all simple people are deemed to be under the law of counsel.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: In quo ponuntur tres aliæ rationes, probantes eandem positionem, c. 14. assignatam.
units.tr: In which three other reasons are set out, proving the same position assigned in ch. 14.

units.la: Discipulus. Si habes rationes plures pro conclusione præfata, illas adducas. Magist. Eadem conclusio sic probatur. Quin in his, quæ fidei sunt, non tenetur alteri fidem indubiam exhibere, non tenetur ad solam assertionem eius vel monitionem, aut increpationem, opinionem erroneam reuocare: quia qui opinionem erroneam reuocat, debet assertionem contrariam firma fide tenere: & eadem ratione veritati catholicæ firmiter adhærere, & falsitati contrariæ dissentire. Sed subditi in his, quæ fidei sunt, non tenentur prælatis suis fidem indubiam adhibere: Tum quia tunc fides subditorum in sapientia hominum consisteret: Tum quia prælati tam ex simplicitate vel ignorantia, quam ex pertinacia possunt contra fidem errare. Ergo ad solam assertionem eorum vel monitionem vel increpationem non tenentur subditi suas opiniones erroneas reuocare: Sed si reuocanitionem vel increpationem non tenentur subditi suas opiniones erroneas reuocare: Sed si reuocare tenentur, oportet quod prælati per regulam fidei eis patenter ostendant, quod opiniones suæ fidei obuiant orthodoxæ. Tertio sic. Ad correptionem illius, quod debet esse paratus ad satisfactionem poscenti rationem de fide, non tenetur quis opinionem suam erroneam reuocare, nisi idem rationem reddiderit, quod talis opinio est tanquam erronea reuocanda. Quia si aliquis absque reddita ratione tenetur opinionem suam tanquam erroneam reuocare, alius non tenetur de opinione reuocanda reddere rationem. Sed prælati corripientes subditos de erroribus contra fidem debent esse parati ad satisfactionem poscenti rationem de fide, & per consequens, debent esse parat ad satisfactionem poscenti rationem de his reuocandis quae dicuntur fidei aduersari, teste beato Petro, qui canonica sua prima cap. 3. scribens praelatis singulariter ait: Dominum autem Christum sentite in cordibus vestris parati semper ad satisfactionem omni poscenti vos rationem, de ea quae in vobis est fide. Ergo subditi non tenentur opiniones suas erroneas contra veritatem catholicam reuocare propter correptionem praelatorum quamcunque, nisi fuerit legitima correptio modo supradicto. Quarto sic: Subditi non tenentur in illo casu ad correptionem praelatorum opiniones, quas ignorant esse erroneas, reuocare: in quo casu licitum est eis a praelatorum sententia appellare: quia cui licet licite ab aliqua sententia appellare, non tenetur eidem sententiae obedire. Sed a praelato corripiente aliquem de errore, & non monstrante per regulam fidei, quod dictus error veritati repugnat, licet appellare. Ergo propter talem correptionem non tenetur quis opinionem, quam nescit esse erroneam, reuocare. Maior per sacros canones aperte probatur. Ait enim Victor, ut habetur 2. q. 6. c. si quis putauerit se a proprio metropolitano grauari, apud primatem dioceseos aut penes vniuersalis ecclesiae apostolicae sedem iudicetur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod si quis putauerit se a praelato de errore inique correptum, sibi licet appellare. Quod etiam multis aliis sacris canonibus posset copiose probari sed causa breuitatis pertranseo. Discip. Per illam rationem probatur, quod correptus legitime de errore, non tenetur suum errorem reuocare, quia licet sibi appellare. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur, quod correptus legitime a praelato de errore, si appellat frustratorie aut friuole, puniri debet per ecclesiam: quinetiam apud Deum peccat, qui videlicet quoquomodo maliciose (ex quo est legitime correptus) appellat. Discip. Vna obiectio, quae totum processum praedictum videtur infringere, mihi occurrit. Nam cum dicunt isti, quod correptus legitime a praelato tenetur errorem reuocare, & aliter non quaeritur ab eis, quia aut errans tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, aut tenet errorem damnatum duntaxat implicite. Si tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, eam statim reuocare tenetur, alioquin poterit cum suus praelatus debitae subdere vltioni. Si autem tenet haeresim damnatam implicite duntaxat, non tenetur eam pro quacunque correctione praelati inferioris summo pontifice reuocare. Magist. Ad hoc respondet, quod non tenetur aliquis statim reuocare haeresim damnatam explicite, quando ignorat eam damnatam esse explicite. Sed si sibi ostenditur, quod est damnata explicite, statim eam reuocare tenetur. Cum vero dicis, quod praelatus potest talem errantem debitae subdere vltioni, verum est ordinem debitum conseruando: puta vt primo per regulam fidei ostendat erranti, quod error suus catholicae obuiat veritati. Et si tunc errorem nequaquam reuocauerit, ipsum poena digna compellat.
units.tr: Disciple. If you have several reasons for the proposition stated above, please bring them forward. Master. The same conclusion is proved in this way. In matters of faith, a person is not bound to give another person undoubted faith, and so is not bound to retract an erroneous opinion merely on that person's assertion, admonition or rebuke. For whoever retracts an erroneous opinion must hold the contrary assertion with firm faith, and by the same reasoning must cling firmly to Catholic truth and dissent from the contrary falsehood. But subjects, in matters of faith, are not bound to give their prelates undoubted faith, partly because the faith of subjects would then rest on the wisdom of men, and partly because prelates can err against the faith through simplicity or ignorance as well as through obstinacy. Therefore subjects are not bound to retract their erroneous opinions on the bare assertion, admonition or rebuke of their prelates. But if they are bound to retract them, it is necessary that the prelates openly show them, by the rule of faith, that their opinions oppose orthodox faith. Third, thus. A person is not bound to retract his erroneous opinion in response to a rebuke from someone who ought to be ready to give an account of the faith to anyone who asks for one, unless that person also gives a reason why such an opinion must be retracted as erroneous. For if someone is bound to retract his opinion as erroneous without a reason being given, then another person is not bound to give a reason for the opinion to be retracted. But prelates who rebuke their subjects for errors against the faith ought to be ready to give an account of the faith to anyone who asks for one, and consequently ought to be ready to give an account of why those things which are said to oppose the faith must be retracted. Blessed Peter, writing specially to prelates in his first canonical epistle, chapter 3, says: "But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts, being ready always to give an answer to every one that asketh you a reason of the faith that is in you." Therefore subjects are not bound to retract their erroneous opinions against Catholic truth on account of any rebuke whatever from their prelates, unless the rebuke is lawful in the manner described above. Fourth, thus. In that case, subjects are not bound by the rebuke of their prelates to retract opinions which they do not know to be erroneous; in such a case it is lawful for them to appeal from the prelate's sentence. For whoever may lawfully appeal from a sentence is not bound to obey that sentence. But when a prelate rebukes someone for an error, and does not show by the rule of faith that the said error is contrary to the truth, it is lawful to appeal. Therefore a person is not bound to retract, on account of such a rebuke, an opinion which he does not know to be erroneous. The major premise is plainly proved by the sacred canons. For Victor says, as is found in 2 q. 6 c.: "If anyone thinks that he has been wronged by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the apostolic see of the universal Church." From these words it is gathered that if anyone thinks that he has been unjustly rebuked for error by a prelate, he may appeal. This could also be proved at length from many other sacred canons, but for the sake of brevity I pass over them. Disciple. By that reasoning it is proved that a person lawfully rebuked for error is not bound to retract his error, because he may appeal. Master. To this it is answered that a person lawfully rebuked by a prelate for error, if he appeals frivolously or in order to delay, ought to be punished by the Church; indeed he also sins before God, namely whoever appeals maliciously in any way after he has been lawfully rebuked. Disciple. One objection occurs to me which seems to overturn the whole preceding argument. For when those men say that a person lawfully rebuked by a prelate is bound to retract his error, and that nothing else is asked of them, then either the erring person holds a condemned heresy explicitly, or he holds an error condemned only implicitly. If he holds a heresy explicitly condemned, he is bound to retract it at once, or else his prelate may hand him over to due punishment. But if he holds a heresy condemned only implicitly, he is not bound to retract it, for any correction by an inferior prelate, before the supreme pontiff. Master. To this he answers that a person is not bound to retract at once a heresy explicitly condemned when he does not know that it has been explicitly condemned. But if it is shown to him that it has been explicitly condemned, he is bound to retract it at once. As for your saying that a prelate can hand such an erring person over to due punishment, that is true, provided the due order is observed: that is, first the prelate shows the one in error, by the rule of faith, that his error opposes Catholic truth; and if he then does not retract the error at all, the prelate compels him by a punishment he deserves.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: In quo ponitur opinio contraria, seu arguitur contra dictum opinionis cap. 14. positam, & hoc tribus rationibus, ad quas respondetur cap. 18. huius.
units.tr: In which the contrary opinion is set out, or an argument is made against the opinion stated in chapter 14, and this with three reasons, to which an answer is given in chapter 18 of this book.

units.la: Discipulus. Miror quosdam dicunt, tenentem haeresim damnatam explicite non debere statim (quamuis correptus fuerit a praelato) eandem haeresim reuocare. Hoc enim scripturae diuinae sacris canonibus, consuetudini ecclesiae, & rationi repugnare videtur. Quod enim scripturae diuinae repugnet probatur. Nam omnis haereticus tenetur haeresim suam reuocare. Qui autem tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, est haereticus. Ergo talis statim tenetur de necessitate salutis haeresim reuocare. Maior est manifesta: quia qui non tenetur haeresim suam reuocare, non tenetur eam dimittere: & per consequens non peccat mortaliter, saltem tali haeresi adhaerendo: ex quo sequitur, quod non est haereticus. Minor probatur, quia magis est haereticus reputandus, qui tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, quam qui non tenet doctrinam catholicam. Sed qui non tenet doctrinam catholicam, est haereticus, quia vitandus, teste beato Iohanne, qui in canonica sua ita ait: si quis venit ad vos & doctrinam suam non affert, nolite recipere eum in domum, nec aue ei dicatis. Qui enim dicit illi aue, communicat operibus illius malignis. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod qui non tenet doctrinam catholicam, est a fidelibus vitandus. Ergo & qui tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, est vitandus. Sed nullus propter haeresim, antequam sit haereticus, est vitandus. Ergo qui tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, est haereticus. Item quod dicta assertio sacris canonibus aduersetur, ostenditur. Ait enim Gelasius Papa, vt habetur 24. q. 1. c. 1. Quicunque in haeresim semel damnatam labitur, eius damnationem seipsum inuoluit. Ex quibus verbis clare colligitur, quod qui lapsus fuerit in haeresim damnatam, explicite, est damnatus. Quod etiam idem Gelasius eisdem cap. & q. c. maiores, & Felix Papa c. Achatius, attestantur aperte, sed damnatus propter haeresim est haereticus. Ergo lapsus in haeresim damnatam explicite, est haereticus. Haereticus autem tenetur statim haeresim suam reuocare. Ergo tenens haeresim damnatam explicite, tenetur eam statim reuocare. Hoc etiam per consuetudinem ecclesiae declaratur. Nam inquisitores haereticae prauitatis conuictum quecunque, qui tenuerit haeresim damnatam explicite, statim contra ipsum, sicut contra haereticum manifestum procedunt, & reputant haereticum, quamuis paratus sit corrigi. Si autem haereticus sit, tenetur suam haeresim reuocare. Ergo &c. Hoc etiam ratione probatur. Nam si tenens haeresim damnatam explicite, non tenetur statim suam haeresim reuocare, hoc non est, nisi quia se valet per ignorantiam excusare dicendo, quod talem assertionem esse explicite condemnatam nescit. Sed talis ignorantia non excusat. Tum quia ignorantia iuris non excusat, vt habetur 1. q. 4. §. & notandum: Tum quia constitutio apostolicae sedis omnes astringit, postquam publicata est, nec aliquis post duos menses valeret se per ignorantiam excusare. fare, vt habetur extra de constitut. cap. vltimo, & notat Gloss. 4. e. t. super cap. cognoscentes. Ergo consimiliter damnatio explicita omnes astringit, saltem post dos menses. Tum quia in his, quae publice fiunt, non potest quis ignorantiam allegare, vt ex sacris canonibus colligitur euidenter. Cum ergo explicita damnatio cuiuscunq; publice facta sit non potest quis haeresim tenens damnatam explicite se per ignorantiam excusare. Et per consequens statim reuocare tenetur, & nullo modo tenetur excusari, quin haereticus sit censendus. Haec sunt, quae mihi admirationem ingerunt quod viri literati dicunt, quod aliquis potest tenere haeresim damnatam explicite, quamuis non sit haereticus: & ideo non statim tenetur talem haeresim reuocare. Vnde qualiter respondeant ad illa, non differas referare.
units.tr: Student. I am surprised that some say that a person who holds a heresy explicitly condemned need not immediately renounce that heresy, even if he has been rebuked by his prelate. For this seems to conflict with the divine Scriptures, the holy canons, the custom of the Church, and reason. That it conflicts with the divine Scriptures is proved as follows. Every heretic is bound to renounce his heresy. Whoever holds a heresy explicitly condemned is a heretic. Therefore such a person is bound, by necessity of salvation, to renounce the heresy at once. The major premise is plain: for whoever is not bound to renounce his heresy is not bound to give it up, and consequently does not sin mortally, at least by clinging to such a heresy; from which it follows that he is not a heretic. The minor is proved, because a person who holds a heresy explicitly condemned is to be regarded as more of a heretic than one who does not hold catholic doctrine. But one who does not hold catholic doctrine is a heretic, because he is to be avoided, as the blessed John testifies in his epistle, where he says: If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say to him, Hail. For whoever says Hail to him shares in his evil works. From these words it is clear that whoever does not hold catholic doctrine is to be avoided by the faithful. Therefore whoever holds a heresy explicitly condemned is also to be avoided. But no one is to be avoided on account of heresy before he is a heretic. Therefore whoever holds a heresy explicitly condemned is a heretic. Likewise, that the said assertion runs counter to the holy canons is shown as follows. Pope Gelasius says, as found in 24. q. 1. c. 1: Whoever once slips into a heresy already condemned involves himself in its condemnation. From these words it is clearly gathered that whoever has fallen into a heresy explicitly condemned is condemned. Gelasius himself attests this plainly in the same chapter and question, in maiores, and Pope Felix in chapter Achatius. But a person condemned on account of heresy is a heretic. Therefore one who has fallen into a heresy explicitly condemned is a heretic. A heretic, however, is bound to renounce his heresy at once. Therefore one who holds a heresy explicitly condemned is bound to renounce it at once. This is also declared by the custom of the Church. For the inquisitors of heretical depravity, against whomever is convicted of holding a heresy explicitly condemned, at once proceed as against a manifest heretic, and regard him as a heretic, even though he is ready to be corrected. But if he is a heretic, he is bound to renounce his heresy. Therefore etc. This is also proved by reason. For if one who holds a heresy explicitly condemned is not bound to renounce his heresy at once, this can only be because he may excuse himself through ignorance, saying that he does not know that such an assertion has been explicitly condemned. But such ignorance does not excuse. Both because ignorance of the law does not excuse, as found in 1. q. 4. §. et notandum; and because a constitution of the apostolic see binds all once it has been published, and no one could excuse himself through ignorance after two months, as found in extra de constitut. cap. ultimo, and as the Gloss notes on 4. e. t. super cap. cognoscentes. Therefore, similarly, an explicit condemnation binds all, at least after two months. Again, in matters that are done publicly, one cannot plead ignorance, as is evidently gathered from the holy canons. Since, then, the explicit condemnation of anyone is made publicly, a person holding a heresy explicitly condemned cannot excuse himself through ignorance. And consequently he is bound to renounce it at once, and in no way can he be excused from being regarded as a heretic. These are the points that move me to wonder why learned men say that someone may hold a heresy explicitly condemned without being a heretic, and therefore is not at once bound to renounce such a heresy. Please do not delay in telling me how they answer these arguments.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Probat duabus rationibus, quod tenens haeresim damnatam explicite non sit statim inter haereticos computandus.
units.tr: He proves by two arguments that one who holds a heresy condemned explicitly is not to be counted at once among the heretics.

units.la: Discipulus. Pro assertione praedicta argutum est supra libro 3. quo probatum est ibidem, Quod non omnis errans contra fidem, est haereticus censendus. Illa autem argumenta ibidem adducta concludunt, quod etiam tenens haeresim damnatam explicite non statim est haereticus iudicandus. Ex quo sequitur quod non tenetur statim suam haeresim reuocare. Discip. Si fundant se in aliqua ratione speciali ad probandum, quod tenens haeresim damnatam explicite non sit statim inter haereticos computandus istam libenter audirem. Magist. Vna earum ratio talis est. Nullus est reputandus magis haereticus propter haeresim damnatam ab ecclesia explicite, quam propter haeresim explicite, cuius contradictoria in scriptura diuina sententialiter & vocaliter continetur, nisi talis damnatio sit magis diuulgata inter Christianos quam veritas scripturae diuinae. Sed multae sunt haeresES damnatae explicite in conciliis generalibus quae non sunt magis diuulgatae quam scriptura diuina, & non semper est aliquis statim reputandus haereticus, si tenet aliquam haeresim, cuius contradictoria in sacris literis continetur, sed examinandus est, an scienter vel ignoranter. Et si scienter, an pertinaciter vel absque pertinacia teneat haeresim. Igitur similiter licet quis teneat haeresim damnatam explicite, non est semper statim haereticus reputandus, sed inuestigandum est primo, an de pertinacia possit conuinci per testes vel alia similia documenta. Et si non potest probari, quod sit pertinax, examinandus est, an sit paratus se corrigere, si ostenderetur sibi aperte, quod haeresis sua sit explicite condemnata. Secunda ratio eorum est haec. Nullus statim est reputandus haereticus, si tenet haeresim, cuius contradictionem non tenetur explicite credere. Haec n. est causa, quare si aliquis neget aliquam veritatem contentam explicite in scriptura diuina, non est propter hoc statim reputandus haereticus. Sed nullus vel pauci tenentur explicite credere omnes veritates contradictorias haeresibus damnatis explicite: quia multi non habent libros, nec habere possunt, in quibus damnationes explicite continentur. Ergo licet ignoranter teneat quis haeresim damnatam explicite, non est statim pertinax haereticus iudicandus. Discip. Quomodo potest quis negare veritatem expresse contentam in scriptura sacra, nisi sit haereticus. Magist. Sufficit credere omnem veritatem scripturae diuinae implicite. Sicut enim beatus Augustinus aliquas veritates contentas in scriptura nescienter negauit: & ideo non fuit haereticus iudicandus. Et sic etiam beatus Hieron. veritatem euangelii negare videtur, cum loquens de Redemptore nostro in quadam homelia dicit: & interrogabat discipulos suos sic dicens: quem dicunt homines esse filium hominis: non dicit, quem me dicunt esse homines, ne iactanter de se quaerere videatur. Et tamen Lucas in euangelio cap 9. expresse refert, quod Iesus interrogauit discipulos suos dicens: quem me dicunt esse turba. Vbi inter Hieron. & beatum Lucam aperta contrarietas inuenitur: & tamen Hieron. non est reputandus haereticus, quia non pertinaciter, sed quia de textu euangelii Lucae tunc non recordabatur, negauit veritatem euangelii.
units.tr: Disciple. In support of the aforesaid assertion, a subtle point was raised above in book 3, where it was proved that not every one who errs against the faith is to be judged a heretic. Those arguments adduced there conclude that even one who holds a heresy explicitly condemned is not at once to be judged a heretic. From this it follows that he is not bound to retract his heresy at once. Disciple. If they rest on some special reason to prove that one who holds a heresy explicitly condemned is not at once to be counted among the heretics, I would gladly hear it. Master. One of their reasons is this. No one is to be regarded as more of a heretic on account of a heresy explicitly condemned by the Church than on account of a heresy whose contradictory is contained in divine Scripture expressly and in words, unless such condemnation is more widely known among Christians than the truth of divine Scripture. But there are many heresies explicitly condemned in general councils which are not more widely known than divine Scripture; and one who holds some heresy whose contradictory is contained in the sacred letters is not always to be regarded at once as a heretic, but it must be examined whether he holds it knowingly or ignorantly, and if knowingly, whether he holds it obstinately or without obstinacy. Therefore, likewise, although someone holds a heresy explicitly condemned, he is not always to be regarded at once as a heretic; rather, it must first be investigated whether his obstinacy can be proved by witnesses or other similar evidence. And if it cannot be proved that he is obstinate, it must be examined whether he is ready to correct himself, if it were shown to him plainly that his heresy has been explicitly condemned. Their second reason is this. No one is at once to be regarded as a heretic if he holds a heresy whose contradiction he is not bound to believe explicitly. For this is the reason why, if someone denies some truth expressly contained in divine Scripture, he is not on that account at once to be regarded as a heretic. But no one, or few, are bound to believe explicitly all the truths contradictory to heresies explicitly condemned, because many do not have books, nor can they have them, in which the condemnations are explicitly contained. Therefore, although someone holds a heresy explicitly condemned in ignorance, he is not to be judged an obstinate heretic at once. Disciple. How can anyone deny a truth expressly contained in sacred Scripture without being a heretic? Master. It is enough to believe every truth of divine Scripture implicitly. For just as blessed Augustine, unknowingly, denied some truths contained in Scripture, and therefore was not to be judged a heretic; so also blessed Jerome seems to deny a truth of the Gospel, when, speaking of our Redeemer in a certain homily, he says: and he asked his disciples, saying: whom do men say that the Son of man is; he does not say, whom do men say that I am, lest he seem to seek boastfully about himself. And yet Luke in the Gospel, chapter 9, expressly relates that Jesus asked his disciples, saying: whom do the crowds say that I am. Here a plain contradiction is found between Jerome and blessed Luke; and yet Jerome is not to be regarded as a heretic, because he did not deny the truth of the Gospel obstinately, but because at that time he did not remember the text of Luke's Gospel.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: In quo ponuntur responsiones ad rationes in contrarium opinionis capitulo 14. huius superius posita, facta as. cap. 16.
units.tr: In which replies are given to the arguments against the opinion set out above in chapter 14 of this work, made in chapter 16.

units.la: Discipulus. Per instantias, quas feci, discurre. Magist. Ad primam tuam respondetur, quod non omnis tenens haeresim damnatam explicite, est haereticus reputandus, licet multi tenentes haereses damnatas explicite per aliqua documenta valeant probari haeretici. Videlicet si possint conuinci quod pertinaciter tenuerunt haeresim damnatam explicite. Cum vero dicis, quod magis est reputandus haereticus, qui tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, quam qui non tenet doctrinam catholicam: hoc si debet concedi, verum est de illo, qui pertinaciter tenet haeresim damnatam explicite. Si autem nescienter absque omni pertinacia tenet haeresim damnatam explicite, non continet veritatem: loquendi scil. de illo, qui non reputat doctrinam Christianam esse veram, de quo loquitur beatus Hieron. in verbis adductis. Non enim loquitur beatus Hieron. de illo, qui ignoranter aliquam specialem catholicam veritatem non teneret: quia talis, nisi alias de pertinacia conuincetur, non esset a catholicis euitandus. Ad decreta, quae adducis, breuiter respondetur, quod omnes loquuntur de illis, qui scienter labuntur in haeresim iam damnatam. Ad consuetudinem inquisitorum, quam allegas, dicunt quidam, quod inquisitores nonnulli quae praelati saepe inique procedunt & iniuste. Multi, vt dicunt, sunt illiterati & simplices, cupiditate & auaritia excæcati: qui ideo de hæresi accusatos satagunt condemnare, vt bona eorum acquirant. Et ideo in eorum consuetudine nulla assertio est fundata. Ad rationem tertiam, quæ magis vigere videtur, dicunt quod aliqui tenentes hæreses condemnatas explicite possunt se per ignorantiam excusare; aliqui vero non possunt, quia quidam diuersis modis (sicut ex prædictis patet, & inferius, si interrogationes de hac materia fueris prosecutus, amplius apparebit) cõuinci poterint de pertinacia manifesta, illi videlicet qui prius eandē hæresim asseruerunt esse damnatam. Et qui alios ad tenendū eandē quomodolibet coegerūt, & qui protestabantur eandem se velle irrationabiliter defensare, & multi alii, de quibus dictū est supra, & si voluerit dicetur inferius. Illi autē qui nullo modo de pertinacia possunt cõuinci, & parati sunt corrigi, potuerunt se per ignorantiam excusare dicentes: nos ignoramus tales hæreses esse damnatas: imo ignoramus eas catholicæ veritati quomodolibet aduersari. Discip. Antequam procedas vlterius, dicas an in sacra pagina & in iure canonico eruditi valeant, si tenent, hæreses damnatas explicite se per ignorantiam excusare. Magist. Dicitur quod sic: quia eruditi non tenentur habere noticiam de omnibus hæresibus, quæ explicite sunt damnatæ, & ideo si ignoranter tenentur eas parati corrigi, non sunt hæretici reputandi. Discip. Quomodo respondetur ad illa, per quæ probaui, quod ignorantia non excusat. Magist. Ad primum dicitur, quod ignorantia iuris duplex est, Quædam est ignorantia iuris, quod oportet scire: & illa non excusat, alia est ignorantia iuris quod non oportet scire: & illa excusat à peccato, licet forte in quibusdam aliis non excusat. Ille ergo, qui tenet hæreses, quarum contradictorias oportet eum explicite credere, non potest per ignorantiam excusari. Et ideo quicunq; inter Christianos conuenienter enutritus tenet fidem Christianam esse falsam, vel Christum non fuisse crucifixum, vel non fuisse incarnatum, vel aliquid huiusmodi, cuius nullus Christianus debet esse ignarus, non potest per ignorantiam excusari: quia explicite tenetur credere quod fides Christiana est vera, & quod Christus fuit crucifixus, & huiusmodi: quæ facile est scire, & inter Christianos diuulgantur. Qui autem tenet hæreses, quarum contradictorias non tenetur credere explicite, posset per ignorantiam excusari, dummodo nullam pertinaciam adiungeret. Ad secundum de constitutione sedis Apostolicæ dicitur, quod omnes astringit, postquam est ita publice diuulgata, quod nullus potest ignorantiam allegare. Si autem non fuerit ita publice diuulgata, non astringit ignorantes, qui non laborant ignorantia crassa & supina. Quod ergo dicitur, quod omnes astringit post duos menses, verum est omnes scientes & omnes ignorantes damnabili ignorantia laborantes. Alios autem non astringit, licet facientes contrarium peccent contra Deum, licet forte astringat eos ad pœnam per ecclesiam infligendam. Durum enim videtur nonnullis dicere, quod omnes Christiani tenentur scire omnes determinationes summorum pontificum: cum nonnulli studentes in eis aliquando per duos annos & amplius multas earum ignorant. Multi enim ad earum copiam nullatenus possunt attingere. Ad tertium dicunt, quod etiam in his, quæ publice fiunt, contingit quandoq; ignorantiam allegare, prout ex sacris canonibus colligitur. Et nonnunquam talem ignorantiam sufficit solo iuramento probare. Et ita dicunt in proposito, quod quamuis quondam fuerunt aliquæ hæreses publice condemnatæ; tamen possunt etiam literati ignorantiam allegare dicentes, se nescire tales hæreses fuisse damnatas. Et si petatur ab eis probatio, quod ignorent, sufficit quod iurent se ignorare. Et sic à prauitate hæretica per ignorantiam excusantur.
units.tr: Student. Run through the objections I have raised, one by one. Master. To your first objection the answer is this: not everyone who holds a heresy condemned explicitly must be reckoned a heretic, although many who hold condemned heresies explicitly can be proved heretics by some evidence, namely if it can be shown that they held the condemned heresy explicitly and obstinately. When you say that whoever holds a condemned heresy explicitly is to be reckoned a heretic more than whoever does not hold Christian doctrine, this may be conceded, and it is true of the man who holds the condemned heresy explicitly and obstinately. But if someone holds a condemned heresy explicitly through ignorance, without any obstinacy, the claim does not hold: I mean concerning the man who does not consider Christian doctrine to be true, of whom Saint Jerome speaks in the words you cite. For Saint Jerome is not speaking of a man who, through ignorance, did not hold some particular Catholic truth, since such a man, unless he were otherwise convicted of obstinacy, would not have to be avoided by Catholics. To the decrees you cite, the brief answer is that they all speak of those who knowingly fall into a heresy already condemned. As for the custom of the inquisitors which you allege, some say that certain inquisitors often act unjustly and wrongly, as prelates do. Many of them, they say, are unlettered and simple, blinded by greed and avarice, and so they are eager to condemn accused persons of heresy in order to acquire their goods. Therefore no assertion founded on their custom has any weight. To the third objection, which seems to have more force, they say that some who hold condemned heresies explicitly can excuse themselves by ignorance, but others cannot, because some of them can be convicted of manifest obstinacy in various ways (as is clear from what has been said above, and will appear more fully below if you pursue your questions on this matter): namely those who earlier asserted that this same heresy was condemned, those who compelled others in any way to hold it, those who protested that they wished to defend it unreasonably, and many others of whom it has been said above, and of whom more will be said below if you wish. But those who cannot be convicted of obstinacy in any way, and are ready to be corrected, may excuse themselves by ignorance, saying: we do not know that such heresies are condemned; indeed, we do not know that they in any way oppose Catholic truth. Student. Before you proceed further, tell me whether learned men in sacred Scripture and canon law can, if they hold explicitly condemned heresies, excuse themselves by ignorance. Master. It is said that they can, because learned men are not bound to know all the heresies that have been explicitly condemned, and so if they hold them through ignorance and are ready to be corrected, they are not to be reckoned heretics. Student. How do you answer the arguments by which I proved that ignorance does not excuse? Master. To the first, it is said that ignorance of law is twofold. There is ignorance of law which one must know, and this does not excuse; and there is ignorance of law which one need not know, and this excuses from sin, though perhaps in some other matters it does not excuse. Therefore whoever holds heresies whose contradictories he must explicitly believe cannot be excused by ignorance. And so whoever, properly brought up among Christians, holds that the Christian faith is false, or that Christ was not crucified, or was not incarnate, or anything of this kind, of which no Christian ought to be ignorant, cannot be excused by ignorance, because he is bound to believe explicitly that the Christian faith is true, and that Christ was crucified, and so on: things which are easy to know and are widely spread among Christians. But whoever holds heresies whose contradictories he is not bound to believe explicitly could be excused by ignorance, provided he adds no obstinacy. To the second objection, concerning the constitution of the Apostolic See, it is said that it binds all men once it has been so publicly promulgated that no one can plead ignorance. But if it has not been so publicly promulgated, it does not bind those who are ignorant and do not labour under gross and culpable ignorance. Therefore what is said, that it binds everyone after two months, is true of all who know it and of all who are ignorant through culpable ignorance. But it does not bind others, although those who act contrary to it sin against God, and although perhaps it binds them to the punishment inflicted by the Church. For it seems hard to some to say that all Christians are bound to know all the determinations of the supreme pontiffs, since some who study them for two years or more still do not know many of them. For many cannot possibly reach their multitude. To the third objection they say that even in matters which are done publicly it is sometimes possible to plead ignorance, as is gathered from the sacred canons. And such ignorance can sometimes be proved by oath alone. And so they say, in the present case, that although some heresies were at one time publicly condemned, even learned men may plead ignorance, saying that they did not know such heresies had been condemned. And if they are asked to prove that they are ignorant, it is enough that they swear that they are ignorant. And so they are excused from heretical depravity through ignorance.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: Chapter XIX.

units.la: In quo inuestigatur de propositione, seu assertione duos sensus habente, vnum hæreticum & alium catholicum, vtrum tenens eam in sensu damnato, seu hæretico, nesciens tamen ipsam esse damnatam, sit hæreticus censendus, & respondetur sub distinctione.
units.tr: In which it is investigated whether one who holds a proposition or assertion with two senses, one heretical and one Catholic, in the condemned or heretical sense, without knowing that it has been condemned, is to be regarded as a heretic. The answer is given with a distinction.

units.la: Discipulus. Adhuc de illa materia vnam difficultatem discutias, an videlicet sciens hæresim esse damnatam, quam putat esse ambiguam duos sensus habentem, si teneat sensum damnatum, quem non putat esse damnatum, valeat de prauitate hæretica per ignorantiam excusari. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur, quod si sciens hæresim esse damnatam, non tenetur scire sub quo sensu sit damnata, licet tenuerit sensum damnatum, non est statim hæreticus iudicandus. Si autem tenetur scire sub quo sensu est damnata, non potest per ignorantiam excusari. Primum sic probatur. Damnata aliqua assertione nullus per illam damnationem astringitur ad negandum aliam assertionem, quæ ex sola assertione damnata inferri non potest, sed ex assertione ambigua diuersos sensus habente, sensus determinatus non potest inferri. Ergo damnata assertione ambigua non astringitur quis negare determinatum sensum: quia potest probabiliter dubitare in quo sensu sit condemnata. Ergo si quis ex ignorantia absq; pertinacia tenet hæresim ambiguam condemnatam in illo sensu, in quo secundum intentionem condemnantium est damnata: si etiam illum sensum minime expresserunt, non est statim pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus, sed antea ostendendum est sibi aperte, quod non solum assertio ambigua est damnata, sed etiam quod talis sensus determinatæ veritati obuiat orthodoxæ. Discip. Illi videntur errare, cum dicunt assertionem ambiguam esse damnatum. Cum assertio ambigua damnari non debeat, praesertim si habeat aliquem sensum catholicum. Magist. Respondetur tibi; quod tu erras aperte dicens, quod nunquam assertio ambigua habens aliquem sensum catholicum est damnata. Unde & aliquando assertiones contradictoriae secundum vocem sunt damnatae, ex quo tamen contradictoriae sunt secundum vocem altera istarum vel utraq; habet sensum verum. Discip. De ista ponas exemplum, si potes. Magist. Isidorus, ut habetur 24. q. 3. c. quidam autem, ad hoc videtur exemplum adducere manifestum; aperte insinuans, quod utraque istarum, Deus creat mala, Deus non creat mala, est haeresis condemnata. Und & assertores utriusq; haereticos reputat manifestos, dicens, Colluciani a quodam Collucione nuncupati: qui dicunt Deum non facere mala contra illud quod scriptum est: ego sum Deus creans malum. Floriani a Floriano: qui contrario dicunt Deum creasse malum, contra hoc quod scriptum est: fecit Deus omnia bona. Ex his verbis colligitur, quod utraque istarum, Deus creat mala: Deus non creat mala & haeresis explicite condemnata. Et tamen ista Deus creat mala, est assertio ambigua habens aliquem sensum catholicum, scilicet istum, Deus creat malum poenae. Et similiter ista, Deus non creat mala, habet sensum catholicum, scilicet istum, Deus non creat mala culpae. Discip. Secundum ista videtur, quod isti concedunt, quod aliquis absque haeretica pravitate potest tenere, Deum creare mala culpae: quia dicunt, quod aliquis potest tenere assertionem ambiguam damnatam in eo sensu, in quo est damnata absque haeretica pravitate. Magist. Male arguis secundum istos: quia arguis a particulari seu indefinita aequipollente particulari ad singularem determinatam.
