Non enim dicunt, quod semper potest quis tenere assertionem ambiguam damnatam in eo sensu, in quo est damnata absq; haeretica pravitate: sed quandoq;, quia, ut dicunt, si tenetur quis scire sensum, in quo est damnata assertio esse haeretica, si tenet talem assertionem in tali sensu statim est haereticus iudicandus: si vero non tenetur hoc scire, non est haereticus reputandus. Discip. Quomodo ergo est procedendum contra talem? Magist. Respondetur supra: quia, ut dicunt, non sufficit ostendere tali, quod assertio ambigua est damnata sed etiam oportet sibi aperte ostendere, quod talis sensus catholicae veritati repugnat.
units.tr: Student. Let us discuss one more difficulty on this matter. Suppose someone knows that a heresy has been condemned, and he thinks it is ambiguous and has two senses. If he holds the condemned sense, which he does not think has been condemned, can he be excused from heretical depravity through ignorance? Master. To this it is answered that if someone knows that a heresy has been condemned, but is not bound to know under which sense it was condemned, then even though he holds the condemned sense, he is not to be judged a heretic at once. But if he is bound to know under which sense it was condemned, he cannot be excused through ignorance. The first point is proved as follows. No one is bound by a condemned assertion to deny another assertion that cannot be inferred from the condemned assertion alone. From an ambiguous assertion with several senses, however, no determinate sense can be inferred. Therefore, by the condemnation of an ambiguous assertion, no one is bound to deny a determinate sense, because he can reasonably doubt in what sense it was condemned. So if someone, through ignorance and without obstinacy, holds an ambiguous condemned heresy in the sense in which, according to the intention of those who condemned it, it was condemned, and if they did not expressly state that sense, he is not to be judged obstinate and heretical at once. Instead, it must first be shown to him plainly that not only is the ambiguous assertion condemned, but also that such a sense conflicts with the determinate, orthodox truth. Student. Those men seem to be wrong who say that an ambiguous assertion is condemned. An ambiguous assertion ought not to be condemned, especially if it has some Catholic sense. Master. You are told in reply that you are plainly wrong to say that an ambiguous assertion having some Catholic sense is never condemned. Hence it also happens that contradictory assertions are sometimes condemned according to their wording, although, since they are contradictory in wording, one or both of them has a true sense. Student. Give an example of this, if you can. Master. Isidore, as found in 24 q. 3 c. Quidam autem, seems to offer a clear example here. He plainly implies that each of the two statements, God creates evils and God does not create evils, is a condemned heresy. He also judges the proponents of each to be manifest heretics, saying: "The Collucianists, named after a certain Collucio, who say that God does not make evil, against what is written: I am God, creating evil. The Florianists, named after Florianus, who on the contrary say that God created evil, against what is written: God made all things good." From these words it follows that each of the two statements, God creates evils and God does not create evils, is explicitly condemned as heresy. Yet God creates evils is an ambiguous assertion with a Catholic sense, namely that God creates the evil of punishment. Likewise God does not create evils has a Catholic sense, namely that God does not create the evil of guilt. Student. According to this, it seems these men grant that someone can, without heretical depravity, hold that God creates the evil of guilt, since they say that someone can hold an ambiguous assertion condemned in the sense in which it is condemned without heretical depravity. Master. You argue badly by their standard, because you argue from a particular or indefinite proposition, equivalent to a particular one, to a single determinate case. They do not say that one can always hold an ambiguous assertion condemned in the sense in which it is condemned without heretical depravity. They say it is sometimes possible, because, as they hold, if someone is bound to know the sense in which the assertion is condemned as heretical, and holds that assertion in that sense, he is to be judged a heretic at once. If he is not bound to know this, he is not to be reckoned a heretic. Student. How, then, ought one to proceed against such a person? Master. It was answered above: as they say, it is not enough to show such a person that the ambiguous assertion is condemned. It is also necessary to show him plainly that such a sense conflicts with Catholic truth.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Quaerit de simplici correctione non quidem legitima, qua quis admonetur a Papa, quatenus assertionem, quam quis nesciens profert, tenetur corrigere.
units.tr: Asks about a simple correction, not the legitimate kind, by which someone is admonished by the Pope to correct an assertion that he has uttered without knowing it.

units.la: Discipulus. Ut cerno, secundum istos episcopi & inquisitores in vanum errantes corrigunt, nisi probauerint ea patenter doctrinae catholicae aduersari. Sed adhuc ignoro, quid putant de Papa, an scilicet ad simplicem correptionem Papae absque tali correptione, quam vocant legitimam, teneantur nescienter errantes suas haereses revocare. Magist. Dicunt quod non. Tum quia Papa de fide tenetur reddere rationem: quia, sicut narrat Glossa extra de rescriptis, si quando de omnibus reddi ratio debet si potest. Tum quia in causa fidei a Papa licet appellare. Tum quia fides nostra non consistit in sapientia Papae. Nullus ergo in his, quae fidei sunt, tenetur credere Papae, nisi per regulam fidei dicti sui rationem ostendat. Discip. Illud videtur consuetudini ecclesiae repugnare. Nam Papa aliquando damnat haereses, cuius damnationis suae nullam reddit rationem; & concilia generalia, symbola condiderunt articulos distinguentia. Quos tamen per regulam minime probaverunt. Ergo non videtur quod Papa semper teneatur reddere rationem damnationis haereticae pravitatis. Magist. Respondetur, quod nunquam invenitur, quod Papa aliquam haeresim damnaverit, & damnationis suae non reddiderit rationem: sed aliquando ex damnatione, aliquando cum eadem damnatione. Sic n. fecit Alexand. tertius, sicut patet de haeret. c. cum Christus. Sic n. Innoc. tertius, ext. de sum. tri. c. damnamus. Siaute non reddat rationem in damnatione ipsa, debet in aliis assertionibus suis eiusdem damnationis suae reddere rationem de generalibus conciliis condentibus symbola, respondetur, quod licet in ipsis symbolis non probent per regulam fidei articulos symbolorum, tamen extra simbola manifeste probantur: quia vel condentes symbola ipsos articulos probant, vel probationes approbant aliorum tacite vel expresse. Discip. Quid si quis defenderet coram Papa haeresim, quam dicere se putare consonam fidei orthodoxae? Magist. Dicunt, quod si milliesies defenderet haeresim nescienter, cum protestatione expressa veritatis, quod paratus est corrigi, cum agnoverit opiniones suas catholicae fidei obviare, etiam coram Papa non esset haereticus iudicandus, nisi per alia legitima documenta haereticus probaretur, quia sicut prima vice licet sibi nescienter tali modo opinionem erroneam defendere, ita licet secunda vice & tertia & semper quousque fuerit sibi probatum aperte, quod sua opinio est inter haereticas computanda. Discip. Forte diceret aliquis opinionem suam defendens, etiam postquam opinio sua fuerit probata haeretica, quod non est sibi ostensum, quod opinio sua fidei obviat orthodoxae: & ita nunquam posset convinci. Magist. Non sufficit sibi negare opinionem suam esse probatam haereticam, sed cogitur stare iudicio peritorum; qui si reputauerint sufficienter esse probatum, quod opinio est haeretica, tenetur eam revocare, alioquin inter pertinaces & haereticos est censendus. Discip. Quid si errent periti & omnes theologiae Magistri una cum Papa? Magist. Si de facto damnauerint innocentem, poterit scil. iura suam causam per appellationis remedium subleuare. Si autem appellationi suae legitimae non defertur, non restat nisi ut gratiae divinae se committat, & non timeat de hominum societate (iudicio iniquo) deleri: quia de libro viventium conscientia non delet iniqua. Discip. Quid si in scriptis haeresim manifestam defendefenderet? Magist. Quidam dicunt, quod propter hoc non est pertinax nec haereticus iudicandus, quia quantum ad hoc non refert an verbo vel scripto opinionem erroneam teneat vel defendat: Nam beatus Cyprianus opinionem haereticam in scriptis reliquit: quia tamen eam pertinaciter non defendit, non fuit haereticus iudicandus. Sic etiam abbas Ioachim. opinionem haereticam scripsit, sicut testatur Innoc. 3. de sum. tri. & fi. ca. c. damnamus, & tamen non fuit haereticus iudicandus, Gloss. super dicto c. damnamus, dicente de eodem Ioachim, quia paratus fuit corrigi & correxit se, ut sequitur, non debet dici haereticus, licet quandoque erraverit in fide. Sic etiam Petrus Iohannis, licet opiniones suae quas in scriptis reliquit, fuerunt tanquam haereticae condemnatae, ipse tamen nec pertinax nec haereticus fuit iudicandus. Sic etiam beatus Hieron. licet opiniones erroneas scripserit, quas non legitur revocasse, non est haereticus reputandus. Discip. Secundum illa videtur, quod nullus post mortem posset de haeresi accusari: cuius tamen contrarium asserunt sacri canones manifeste. Magist. Respondetur, quod propter hoc solum modo, quod quis haeresim tenuerit verbo vel scripto, non esset post mortem accusandus de haeresi. Sed si quomodocunque poterit probari, quod haeresim verbo vel facto tenuerit pertinaciter, post mortem poterit de haeresi accusari, quia si per alium modum quam per verba vel scripta solam haeresim exprimentia, puta verba vel scripta vel facta declarauit, per quae pertinacia valuerit ostendi pertinax fuisse, est damnandus. Discip. De hoc ponas exemplum, ut quod dicitur magis intelligam. Magist. Si de aliquo post mortem probatum extiterit, quod verbo vel scripto tenuerit, duas personas fuisse in Christo, non est propter hoc solum haereticus reputandus, sed per simplicem ignorantiam poterit excusari. Si autem probatum fuerit, quod sciuerit dictam assertionem esse damnatam, & quod postea eam vel verbo vel scripto tenuerit, est de pertinacia & de prauitate haeretica condemnandus. Discip. Ut concipio, secundum istos eodem modo contra vivum & mortuum de haeresi accusatum oportet procedere: inquisitoribus tamen sufficit tantummodo, quod probetur aliquo modo, verbo vel scripto ipsum haeresim tenuisse. Magist. De inquisitoribus dicunt isti, quod saepe inique procedunt: & quod sunt ecclesiae Dei valde nocui, tanquam lucris temporalibus totaliter inhiantes.
units.tr: Disciple. As I see it, according to these men, bishops and inquisitors correct in vain those who err, unless they have proved that the errors plainly oppose Catholic doctrine. But I still do not know what they think about the Pope: whether those who err unknowingly are bound to retract their heresies at a simple correction from the Pope, without the kind of correction they call legitimate. Master. They say they are not. First, because the Pope is bound to give a reason for what he believes, since, as the Gloss narrates on the decretal On Rescripts, a reason ought to be given for everything, if it can be. Second, because in a matter of faith one may appeal from the Pope. Third, because our faith does not rest on the wisdom of the Pope. No one, therefore, is bound to believe the Pope in matters of faith unless he shows the reason for his saying by the rule of faith. Disciple. This seems to contradict the custom of the Church. For the Pope sometimes condemns heresies and gives no reason for his condemnation; and general councils have drawn up creeds that distinguish the articles, which nevertheless they have in no way proved by the rule of faith. Therefore it does not seem that the Pope is always bound to give a reason for condemning a heresy. Master. The answer is that it is never found that a Pope condemned some heresy and gave no reason for his condemnation; but sometimes he gives the reason in the condemnation itself, and sometimes alongside it. Thus Alexander III did so, as is clear from the decretal On Heretics, Christ. Thus also Innocent III, in the decretal On the Trinity, we condemn. But if he does not give a reason in the condemnation itself, he ought to give the reason in his other assertions of the same condemnation. As for the objection about the general councils that drew up creeds, the answer is that although in the creeds themselves they do not prove the articles of the creeds by the rule of faith, nevertheless they are plainly proved outside the creeds, because either those who drew up the creeds prove the articles themselves, or the proofs are approved, tacitly or expressly, by others. Disciple. What if someone defended a heresy before the Pope, which he thinks agrees with orthodox faith? Master. They say that even if he defended a heresy a thousand times without knowing it, with an express declaration of the truth, that he is ready to be corrected once he has recognised that his opinions oppose the Catholic faith, he should not be judged a heretic even before the Pope, unless he is proved a heretic by other lawful evidence. For just as it is permitted to him to defend an erroneous opinion in this way the first time without knowing it, so it is permitted the second time, and the third, and always, until it has been clearly proved to him that his opinion is to be counted among the heretical ones. Disciple. Perhaps someone defending his opinion would say, even after his opinion has been proved heretical, that it has not been shown to him that his opinion opposes orthodox faith, and so he could never be convicted. Master. It is not enough for him to deny that his opinion has been proved heretical; he is compelled to abide by the judgment of experts. If they judge that it has been sufficiently proved that the opinion is heretical, he is bound to retract it; otherwise he is to be counted among the obstinate and heretical. Disciple. What if the experts err, and all the teachers of theology along with the Pope? Master. If they have in fact condemned an innocent man, he may, of course, by right relieve his cause by the remedy of appeal. But if his lawful appeal is not granted, nothing remains except that he commit himself to the grace of God, and not fear to be blotted out from the fellowship of men by an unjust judgment, because conscience does not blot out from the book of the living the things that are unjust. Disciple. What if he defended a manifest heresy in writing? Master. Some say that for this reason he is not to be judged obstinate or heretical, because in this respect it makes no difference whether someone holds or defends an erroneous opinion by word or in writing. For blessed Cyprian left a heretical opinion in writing, yet because he did not obstinately defend it, he was not to be judged a heretic. Likewise Abbot Joachim wrote a heretical opinion, as Innocent III attests in the decretal On the Trinity, we condemn, and yet he was not judged a heretic. The Gloss on that decretal, speaking of the same Joachim, says that because he was ready to be corrected and corrected himself, as follows, he ought not to be called a heretic, although he sometimes erred in the faith. Likewise Peter John, although the opinions he left in writing were condemned as heretical, was nevertheless to be judged neither obstinate nor heretical. Likewise blessed Jerome, although he wrote erroneous opinions which we do not read that he retracted, is not to be counted a heretic. Disciple. According to these examples it seems that no one could be accused of heresy after his death, yet the sacred canons plainly assert the contrary. Master. The answer is that the mere fact that someone held a heresy by word or in writing would not make him liable to accusation of heresy after death. But if it can somehow be proved that he held the heresy obstinately, by word or deed, he can be accused of heresy after death, because if he declared it by some means other than by words or writings that express only the heresy itself, such as words, writings or deeds by which his obstinacy can be shown, he is to be condemned. Disciple. Give me an example of this, so that I may understand what is said better. Master. If it has been proved of someone after his death that he held by word or in writing that there were two persons in Christ, he is not therefore to be counted a heretic for this alone, but he may be excused on the ground of simple ignorance. If, however, it has been proved that he knew that the said assertion had been condemned, and that afterwards he held it by word or in writing, he is to be condemned for obstinacy and heretical depravity. Disciple. As I understand it, according to these men, one must proceed in the same way against the living and the dead when accused of heresy; but for the inquisitors it is enough that it be proved in some way that he held the heresy, by word or in writing. Master. Concerning the inquisitors, these men say that they often proceed unjustly, and that they are very harmful to the Church of God, as men who wholly covet temporal gains.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI.

units.la: In quo consequenter agitur de correptione, qua quis a socio sive a quocunque, sibi non superiore, corripitur, utrum suum errorem teneatur deponere. Et respondetur quod sic, si scilicet correptio fuerit legitima, & hoc probatur tribus rationibus.
units.tr: On what follows: whether a person corrected by a companion, or by anyone else who is not his superior, is bound to give up his error. The answer is yes, provided the correction is lawful, and this is proved by three arguments.

units.la: Discipulus. Dicas nunc de correcto a socio vel alio, qui super ipsum nullam iurisdictionem penitus noscitur obtinere. Magist. Dicunt praedicti, quod correptus legitime de haeresi a socio vel a subdito, vel a quocunque, tenetur statim absque mora haeresim suam dimittere: ita quod si continuatur post talem correptionem eandem haeresim scripto vel verbo tenere, aut vera quomodolibet reputare, est pertinax reputandus. Quod probant primo sic. Fides nostra non est in sapientia hominum secundum Apostolum 1. ad Corinth. 2. ergo ad hoc quod quis teneatur haeresim suam deponere, non refert a quo homine sibi per regulam fidei ostendatur, quod opinio sua obviat fidei orthodoxae. Sed si alicui a praelato suo patenter ostenditur, quod opinio sua fidei obviat orthodoxae, eam statim tenetur dimittere, alioquin pertinax est censendus. Ergo tenetur ad id, a quocunque est hoc patenter sibi demonstratum. Secundo sic. Qui non est paratus corrigi, si errat est pertina. Sed ille, qui correptus legitime a quocunque hoc est si sibi patenter est ostensum (scilicet opinio sua fidei obviat orthodoxae) non statim opinionem suam dimittit, non est paratus corrigi. Ergo talis est haereticus & pertinax iudicandus. Tertio sic: non minus tenetur quis errorem dimittere, si veritatem inuenerit per instructionem cuiuscunque alterius, quam si veritatem inuenerit per se ipsum. Qui autem per seipsum inuenerit veritatem, statim tenetur errorem dimittere, exemplo venerabilis Anselmi. lib. 1. Cur Deus homo. c. 18. dicentis: certum sum, si quid dico (quod sacrae scripturae absque dubio contradicat) quod falsum est: nec illud tenere volo, si cognoscero. Ergo si veritatem inuenerit consonam scripturae sacrae per informationem cuiuscunque alterius sive socii, sive subditi, errorem contrarium debet absque mora dimittere. Discip. Secundum illud nulla videtur differentia inter correptum a praelato, & ab alio non praelato, etiam subdito. Magist. Respondetur: quod quantum ad hoc, quod error dimittatur, non est differentia; sed quantum ad alia multa, magna differentia reperitur. Praelatus enim & iurisdictionem habens super alium potest ipsum citare ad rationem ponere, & ut suam informationem audiat coartare, & ad publicam revocationem compellere ipsum, & si in praedictis & aliis ad sua pertinentibus officium inventus fuerit pertinax & rebellis, cum animadversione condigna punire. Qui autem super errantem iurisdictionem non habet, in eo praedicta non poterit exercere. Discip. Ponunt ne aliquam aliam differentiam inter Papam corripientem & alios praelatos corripientes errantes? Magist. Quantum ad haereses damnatas explicite, conformiter dicunt de Papa, & aliis prælatis, sed quantum ad hæreses damnatas solummodo implicite, magna differentia inuenitur: quia super tenentes hæreses damnatas solummodo implicite, prælati inferiores nullam iurisdictionem habere noscuntur, vt eos punire possint vel ad aliquid coartare. Sed si in suis conscientiis eos putauerint pertinaces, debent eos apostolico accusare vel denunciare. Apostolicus autem poterit eos examinare, & si pertinaces inuenerit, condemnare.
units.tr: Student. Now tell me about the person corrected by a companion or another who has no jurisdiction at all over him. Master. The aforementioned say that a person lawfully corrected for heresy by a companion, a subordinate, or anyone at all is bound to abandon his heresy at once, without delay. So if after such correction he continues to hold the same heresy in writing or speech, or to regard it as true in any way, he is to be counted obstinate. They prove this first as follows. Our faith does not rest on the wisdom of men, according to the Apostle, 1. ad Corinth. 2. Therefore, to be bound to give up his heresy, it does not matter by whom a man is shown by the rule of faith that his opinion conflicts with sound faith. But if someone is plainly shown by his superior that his opinion conflicts with sound faith, he is bound to abandon it at once, or else he is to be judged obstinate. Therefore he is bound to do so by whoever has plainly demonstrated it to him. Secondly, whoever is not ready to be corrected, if he errs, is obstinate. But the one who, lawfully corrected by anyone at all (that is, if it has been plainly shown to him that his opinion conflicts with sound faith), does not at once give up his opinion, is not ready to be corrected. Therefore such a man is to be judged heretical and obstinate. Thirdly: a person is no less bound to give up an error if he finds the truth through the instruction of someone else than if he finds it through himself. Yet whoever finds the truth by himself is at once bound to give up error, after the example of the venerable Anselm, lib. 1. Cur Deus homo, c. 18, who says: I am certain that if I say anything which without doubt contradicts holy Scripture, it is false, and I do not wish to hold it once I recognise it. Therefore, if he finds the truth agreeing with holy Scripture through the information of any other person, whether a companion or a subordinate, he must give up the contrary error without delay. Student. By that reasoning there seems to be no difference between one corrected by a superior and one corrected by a non-superior, even a subordinate. Master. The answer is that as far as giving up the error goes there is no difference, but in many other respects there is a great difference. For a superior who has jurisdiction over another can summon him to give an account, can compel him to hear his information, can force him to a public retraction, and, if he is found obstinate and rebellious in these matters or in others that pertain to his office, can punish him with fitting penalty. But one who has no jurisdiction over the erring person cannot exercise these powers over him. Student. Do they hold any other difference between the Pope correcting and other prelates correcting erring persons? Master. As regards heresies condemned explicitly, they hold the same about the Pope and other prelates. But as regards heresies condemned only implicitly, there is a great difference. For lower prelates are known to have no jurisdiction over those who hold heresies condemned only implicitly, so that they could punish them or compel them to anything. But if they judge them obstinate in their consciences, they ought to accuse or denounce them to the Apostolic See. The Apostolic See, however, may examine them and, if it finds them obstinate, condemn them.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: In quo ponitur septimus modus pertinacia, eius scilicet, qui per potestatem iuam donis, minis, seu quouis alio modo aliòs cogit, seu allicit ad suum errorem defendendum.
units.tr: In which the seventh mode of pertinacity is set out, namely of the one who, by his power, compels or entices others to defend his error by gifts, threats, or any other means.

units.la: Discipulus. Cupio scire, si modus alius assignatur errantem de pertinacia conuincendi. Magist. Septimo modo nonnullorum iudicio est quis de pertinacia iudicandus, puta si alios ad suum pertinacem defendendum errorem præceptis, comminationibus, pœnis, præmiis, promissionibus iuratis, vel alio quouis modo artare molitur. Quod n. talis pertinax & hæreticus sit censendus, multis rationibus probare conantur. Quarum prima est hæc. Non minus delinquit, qui alios cogit ad hæresim pertinacem defendendam, quam qui erranti consentit vel non resistit cum possit. Sed talis est non solum modo consentiens & non resistens, sed etiam cogens & impellens. Qui autem erranti & hæresim pertinacem defendenti consentit vel non resistit, cum potest, simili crimine irretitur: & per consequens pertinax & hæreticus est censendus. Ergo & cogens seu compellens alios hæresim pertinaciter defendere est pertinax & hæreticus reputandus. Maior est manifesta. Minor sacris canonibus manifeste probatur. Ait enim Isidorus, vt habetur 21. q. 1. c. Qui peccantibus consentit: Si quis alterius errori consentit, sciat se cum illo simili modo culpabilem iudicandum, Et Leo Papa vt habetur extra de hæret. qui alios, ait: qui alios cum potest non revocat ab errore, seipsum errare demonstrat. Et Innoc. Papa, vt habetur in cano. dist. 83. c. Error, ait: Error cui non resistitur approbatur, & veritas cum minime defensatur, opprimitur. Ex his aliisque pluribus aperte colligitur, quod qui consentit hæreticæ prauitati, inter hæreticos computatur. Ergo multo magis qui compellit alios hæresim pertinaciter defendere, vel hæresi pertinaciter adhærere, est pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus. Secunda ratio est hæc. Non minus peccant, qui alios cogunt minis, terroribus, iuramentis vel præceptis aut comminationibus ad peccandum, quam qui mandant aliis aliquod crimen committere. Sed qui hoc faciunt, consimili crimine inuoluuntur. Ergo qui cogunt alios ad peccatum quodcunque, consimili modo tenentur: & per consequens qui cogunt ad prauitatem hæreticam pertinaciter defensare, sunt similii pertinacia irretiti. Maior huius rationis est nota de se. Minor probatur auctoritate Alexand. tertii, qui, vt habetur extra. de sen. ex cap. mulieres, ait: cum is vere communicat, cuius auctoritate vel mandato delicta committuntur. Patet ergo, quod qui mandant aliis, vt crimen committant, consimili crimine inuoluntur. Tertio ratio est hæc. Ille dicitur facere qui per alium facit. Unde & ille dicitur vere occidere, qui per alium occidit, teste Clemente tertio, qui, vt habetur extra, de clericis pugnantibus in duello. cap. hæreticus, ait: homicidium tam facto quam præcepto, siue consilio, aut defensione, non est dubium perpetrari. Ergo consimiliter ille dicitur hæresim pertinaciter defensare, qui per alium hæresim pertinacem defendit. Sed qui cogit alios hæresim pertinacem defendere, pertinaciter hæresim defendit per alios. Ergo & ipse debet dici pertinax defensator. Quarta ratio est hæc. Magis dicitur agere agens quam consulens. Sed iste de consilio, cuius aliquod crimen committitur, dicitur illud crimen committere, teste Aug. qui, vt habetur de pœnitentia dist. 1. c. periculose, ait: periculose decipiunt qui existimant eos tantum homicidas esse, qui manibus hominem occidunt, & non potius eos per quorum consilium, fraudem & exhortationes homines extinguuntur. Nam Iudæi nequaquam Dominum proprio manibus interfecerunt, sicut scriptum est: nobis non licet interficere quenquam, sed tamen illius mors Domini imputatur, quia ipsum cum lingua intersecerunt, dicentes, crucifige, crucifige eum. Ergo multo magis, qui cogit alium, vt crimen committat, ille crimen committit, & ita qui cogit alium hæresim pertinaciter defensare, ipse noscitur hæresim pertinaciter tenere. Quinta ratio est hæc. Participantes criminosis in crimine, eodem crimine inoluuntur: sed qui cogit alios hæresim pertinaciter defensare, participat in crimine hæresim pertinaciter defensantis: quia impendit ei auxilium & fauorem. Ergo talis pertinax est reputandus. Sed qui cogit alios ad suam hæresim pertinaciter defendendam, non est paratus corrigi. Ergo est pertinax censendus. Sexta ratio est hæc. Qui cogit alios ad hæresim irrevocabiliter defensare & tenere. Talis autem est pertinax. Ergo &c. Discip. Istæ rationes procedunt tantummodo de cogente alios hæresim suam pertinaciter defensare absque pertinacia. Ergo licet aliquis cogat alios pœnis, minis, præceptis & iuramentis hæresim defensare, dummodo non cogat eos pertinaciter defensare, non est pertinax nec hæreticus reputandus. Quod videtur posse probari tali ratione. Qui cogit alium, & non ad peccatum mortale, non committit peccatum. Et per consequens non est propter talem coactionem pertinax & hæreticus reputandus: Cum omnis hæreticus in peccato mortali existat. Sed defensare hæresim non est semper peccatum mortale. Ergo propter talem coactionem non est pertinax & hæreticus reputandus. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur, quod licet possit quis hæresim absque pertinacia defensare, tamen cogens alium absolute hæresim defensare, quantum in se est, cogit ipsam hæresim pertinaciter defensare, sicut qui cogit alium iurare ad aliquam assertionem, quæ est hæretica, quod eam irrevocabiliter & in perpetuum defensabit: quantum in eo est cogit ipsam eandem assertionem pertinaciter defensare, licet in potestate ipsius tali modo coacti sit postea eandem hæresim minime defensare. Et imo talis cogens debet reputari pertinax hæresis defensator, licet coacti iurare velint postea eandem hæresim minime defensare, sed volunt venire contra illicitum iuramentum. Cum vero dicis, quod qui cogit alium, & non ad peccatum mortale, non committit peccatum mortale. Hoc tibi negatur, quia potest aliquis peccare mortaliter, etiam alium cogendo ad bonum. Nam qui cogit vouere castitatem vel paupertatem vel aliquid aliud supererogationis, potest peccare mortaliter: quia talia suaderi possunt, imperari non possunt. De talibus enim loquens dicit Aug. quod nemo cogitur legibus bene facere, sed male facere prohibetur.
units.tr: Student. I want to know whether another mode is given for convicting an erring person of pertinacity. Master. By the judgment of some, a seventh mode is that someone is to be judged pertinacious if he endeavours to bind others to defend his pertinacious error by commands, threats, penalties, rewards, sworn promises, or any other means. Some try to prove by many arguments that such a person is to be regarded as pertinacious and heretical. The first is this. He who compels others to defend a pertinacious heresy is no less at fault than he who consents to an erring person, or does not resist him when he can. But such a man not only consents and does not resist, but also compels and drives. Now he who consents to an erring person defending a pertinacious heresy, or does not resist him when he can, is involved in a like crime, and consequently is to be regarded as pertinacious and heretical. Therefore he who compels or forces others to defend a pertinacious heresy is also to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical. The major premise is plain. The minor is clearly proved by the sacred canons. For Isidore says, as it is found in 21, q. 1, c. Qui peccantibus consentit: "If anyone consents to another's error, he should know that he is to be judged guilty in the same way as that man." And Pope Leo, as it is found in extra, de haeret., Qui alios, says: "He who does not call back others from error, when he can, shows that he himself is in error." And Pope Innocent, as it is found in the canon, dist. 83, c. Error, says: "An error that is not resisted is approved, and when the truth is not defended at all, it is crushed." From these and many other sources it is plainly gathered that he who consents to heretical depravity is counted among the heretics. Therefore, much more so, he who compels others to defend a heresy pertinaciously, or to cling to a heresy pertinaciously, is to be judged pertinacious and heretical. The second argument is this. Those who compel others by threats, terrors, oaths, or commands to sin are no less at fault than those who order others to commit a crime. But those who do this are involved in a like crime. Therefore those who compel others to any sin are bound in a like manner, and consequently those who compel others to defend a heretical depravity pertinaciously are entangled in a like pertinacity. The major premise of this argument is known in itself. The minor is proved by the authority of Alexander III, who, as it is found in extra, de sent. ex., cap. Mulieres, says: "He truly shares in the communion of the crime by whose authority or command the offences are committed." It is plain, therefore, that those who order others to commit a crime are involved in a like crime. The third argument is this. He is said to act who acts through another. Hence also he is truly said to kill who kills through another, as Clement III testifies, who, as it is found in extra, de clericis pugnantibus in duello, cap. Haereticus, says: "There is no doubt that homicide is perpetrated as much by a deed as by a command, or by counsel or defence." Therefore, in the same way, he is said to defend a heresy pertinaciously who defends a pertinacious heresy through another. But he who compels others to defend a pertinacious heresy pertinaciously defends the heresy through others. Therefore he himself must also be called a pertinacious defender. The fourth argument is this. He who acts is said to act more than he who advises. But one whose counsel leads to a crime being committed is said to commit that crime, as Augustine testifies, who, as it is found in de poenitentia, dist. 1, c. Periculose, says: "They deceive dangerously who think that only those are murderers who kill a man with their own hands, and not rather those through whose counsel, fraud and exhortations men are destroyed. For the Jews never killed the Lord with their own hands, as it is written: 'It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death'; yet the death of the Lord is imputed to them, because they slew him with their tongue, saying, 'Crucify, crucify him.'" Therefore, much more, he who compels another to commit a crime commits that crime himself, and so he who compels another to defend a heresy pertinaciously is himself known to hold that heresy pertinaciously. The fifth argument is this. Those who take part with criminals in a crime are involved in the same crime. But he who compels others to defend a heresy pertinaciously takes part in the crime of one who defends a heresy pertinaciously, because he gives him aid and favour. Therefore such a man is to be regarded as pertinacious. But he who compels others to defend his heresy pertinaciously is not ready to be corrected. Therefore he is to be counted pertinacious. The sixth argument is this. He who compels others to defend and hold a heresy irrevocably is pertinacious. But such a man is pertinacious. Therefore etc. Student. These arguments proceed only from one who compels others to defend his heresy pertinaciously, without pertinacity of his own. Therefore, although someone compels others by penalties, threats, commands and oaths to defend a heresy, provided he does not compel them to defend it pertinaciously, he is not to be regarded as pertinacious or heretical. This seems to be provable by the following reasoning. He who compels another, and not to a mortal sin, does not commit sin. And consequently he is not to be regarded as pertinacious and heretical on account of such compulsion, since every heretic exists in mortal sin. But to defend a heresy is not always a mortal sin. Therefore he is not to be regarded as pertinacious and heretical on account of such compulsion. Master. To this it is answered that, although a person can defend a heresy without pertinacity, yet one who compels another to defend a heresy absolutely, so far as it lies in him, compels that heresy itself to be defended pertinaciously, just as one who compels another to swear to some assertion that is heretical, that he will defend it irrevocably and forever: so far as lies in him, he compels that very assertion to be defended pertinaciously, although it lies in the power of the man so compelled afterwards not to defend that same heresy at all. Indeed such a compeller ought to be reckoned a pertinacious defender of heresy, even though those who were compelled to swear afterwards wish not to defend the same heresy at all, but want to go back on the unlawful oath. As for your saying that he who compels another, and not to a mortal sin, does not commit a mortal sin: this is denied to you, because a person can sin mortally even by compelling another to good. For he who compels someone to vow chastity or poverty, or anything else of supererogation, can sin mortally, because such things can be urged but cannot be enjoined. For Augustine, speaking of such things, says that no one is compelled by laws to do well, but is forbidden to do ill.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: In quo tractatur 8. modus pertinacia, scilicet eius qui alium veritatem catholicam vi aut metu abiurare cogit, ubi etiam probatur, quod talis per ignorantiam nequaquam excusari potest. Et probatur unica ratione.
units.tr: In which the eighth mode of pertinacity is treated, namely of one who compels another by force or fear to abjure a Catholic truth; where it is also proved that such a person cannot in any way be excused by ignorance. And this is proved by a single argument.

units.la: Discipulus. Est ne alius modus aliquem de pertinacia convincendi? Magist. Potest octauo de pertinacia & prauitate hæretica quis convinci, si cogat aliquem veritatem catholicam abiurare, aut poenis vel præceptis catholicam veritatem negare compellit, quod enim cogens alios veritatem quamcunque catholicam abiurare, pertinax & hæreticus sit censendus, ostenditur. Nam qui cogit aliquem veritatem catholicam abiurare, cogit eundem hæresi contrariæ irrevocabiliter adhærere. Talis autem, sicut ex capitulo præcedenti apparet, est pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus. Ergo &c. Et per eandem rationem ostenditur, quod qui cogit alios minis, poenis vel præceptis aliquam negare veritatem catholicam, est pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus. Discip. Potest ne talis compellens per aliquam ignorantiam excusari, puta si credit, quod assertio, quam cogit alium abiurare vel negare, sit hæreticalis. Magist. Dicitur quod talis per nullam potest ignorantiam excusari: quia nullus valet absque temeritate quomodolibet attentare cogere alium iuramento, poenis, minis, vel præceptis aliquam assertionem abiurare vel negare, nisi sit certus certitudine sufficienti, quod non est consona catholicæ veritati. Ergo temerarie cogit alium abiurare vel negare eandem. Temeritas autem in hoc casu pertinaciæ æquipollet. Ergo talis est pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus.
units.tr: Disciple. Is there another way of convicting someone of pertinacity? Master. A person can be convicted of pertinacity and heretical depravity in the eighth way, if he compels someone to abjure a Catholic truth, or by penalties or commands forces him to deny a Catholic truth. That whoever compels others to abjure any Catholic truth is to be judged pertinacious and a heretic is shown as follows. For whoever compels someone to abjure a Catholic truth compels that same person to cling irrevocably to the contrary heresy. Such a person, as appears from the preceding chapter, is to be judged pertinacious and a heretic. Therefore &c. By the same reasoning it is shown that whoever compels others by threats, penalties or commands to deny any Catholic truth is to be judged pertinacious and a heretic. Disciple. Can such a compeller be excused by some ignorance, say if he believes that the assertion which he compels another to abjure or deny is heretical? Master. It is said that such a person cannot be excused by any ignorance, because no one can, without rashness, undertake in any way to compel another by oath, penalties, threats or commands to abjure or deny any assertion, unless he is certain with sufficient certainty that it is not consonant with Catholic truth. Therefore he rashly compels another to abjure or deny the same. But rashness in this case is equivalent to pertinacity. Therefore such a person is to be judged pertinacious and a heretic.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: Ponit 9. modum pertinacia de eo, qui assertionem hæreticam, tanquam catholicam se iurat seruaturum, & quod neq; talis per ignorantiam excusatur, & probatur duabus rationibus.
units.tr: Gives the ninth mode of convicting someone of pertinacity: one who swears that he will keep a heretical assertion as if it were Catholic; and that such a person is not excused by ignorance; this is proved by two arguments.

units.la: Discipulus. Sunt plures modi aliquem de pertinacia convincendi? Magist. De pertinacia & prauitate hæretica ille convincitur necessario, qui abiurat catholicam veritatem, vel iurat se quamcunque assertionem, quæ est in rei veritate hæretica, tanquam catholicam, in perpetuum seruaturum. Quod omnis talis sit pertinax & hæreticus reputandus tali ratione ostenditur. Qui firmat se propositio negandi assertionem, quæ est catholica, vel tenendi assertionem quæ est hæretica, pertinax est censendus. Talis autem est ille, qui abiurat veritatem, quæ est catholica, vel iurat se seruaturum assertionem, quæ est hæretica. Ergo pertinax est censendus. Item errans contra fidem catholicam, qui non est paratus corrigi, pertinax & hæreticus est censendus. Huiusmodi est abiurans catholicam veritatem, & qui iurat se hæresim defensurum, vel quod assertioni quæ est hæretica adhærebit, nec est paratus corrigi. Igitur pertinax & hæreticus est censendus. Discip. Nonne potest talis aliquo modo de pertinacia excusari? Magist. Respondetur, quod metu mortis vel gravium tormentorum potest a pertinacia & prauitate hæretica excusari, sed non a peccato mortali. Discip. Videtur quod ignorantia talem poterit excusare. Ignorantia enim excusat a mendacio istum, qui dicit falsum, quod putat esse verum ut asserit Augustin. ut habetur 22.c.18. Is autem. Ergo similiter ignorantia poterit excusare illum, qui abiurat catholicam veritatem quam putat hæreticam, & illum, qui iurat se tenere assertionem hæreticam, quam putat catholicam. Magist. Respondeo tibi, quod aliquis potest excusari a mendacio, qui tamen a temeritate nullatenus excusatur, teste Aug. vbi allegas, qui ait: Nemo mentiens iudicandus est, qui dicit falsum, quod putat verum: quia quantum est in ipso, non fallit ipse, sed fallitur. Non ita mendacii, sed aliquando temeritatis arguendus est, qui falsa incaute credit aut pro veris habet. Sic abiurans similiter iurans modo prædicto a mendacio poterit excusari, sed a temeritate minime excusatur. Et ideo nec a pertinacia poterit excusari. Potest enim pertinacia absque mendacio reperiri: sicut in his, qui sunt nescienter hæretici, reperiuntur. Tales enim cum putant esse vera, quæ dicunt, minime mentiuntur: & tamen pertinaces dicuntur seu censentur, quia nequaquam corrigi sunt parati.
units.tr: Pupil. Are there several ways of convicting someone of pertinacity? Master. A person is necessarily convicted of pertinacity and heretical depravity who abjures Catholic truth, or who swears that he will keep forever, as Catholic, any assertion which is in fact heretical. That every such person is to be judged pertinacious and heretical is shown by this argument. Whoever resolves to deny an assertion which is Catholic, or to hold an assertion which is heretical, is to be considered pertinacious. Now such a person is one who abjures a truth which is Catholic, or who swears that he will keep an assertion which is heretical. Therefore he is to be considered pertinacious. Again, one who errs against the Catholic faith and is not prepared to be corrected is to be considered pertinacious and heretical. Of this kind is the one who abjures Catholic truth, and who swears that he will defend heresy, or that he will adhere to an assertion which is heretical, and is not prepared to be corrected. Therefore he is to be considered pertinacious and heretical. Pupil. Can such a person not be excused from pertinacity in some way? Master. The answer is that through fear of death or of severe torments he can be excused from pertinacity and heretical depravity, but not from mortal sin. Pupil. It seems that ignorance could excuse such a person. For ignorance excuses from lying the one who says what is false, which he thinks to be true, as Augustine asserts, as is found in 22 c. 18 "Is autem." Therefore in the same way ignorance could excuse the one who abjures Catholic truth which he thinks heretical, and the one who swears that he holds a heretical assertion which he thinks Catholic. Master. I answer you that someone can be excused from lying who yet is in no way excused from rashness, as Augustine witnesses, the passage you cite, where he says: "No one who says what is false, which he thinks true, is to be judged a liar, since so far as lies in him he does not deceive, but is deceived. He is to be charged not with lying, but sometimes with rashness, who incautiously believes or holds as true what is false." So one who abjures, or swears in the aforesaid manner, may be excused from lying, but is by no means excused from rashness. And therefore he cannot be excused from pertinacity either. For pertinacity can be found without lying, as it is found in those who are heretics without knowing it. For such people, since they think the things they say to be true, do not lie at all; and yet they are called or considered pertinacious, because they are in no way prepared to be corrected.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: In quo ponitur decimus modus pertinacia, videlicet qui veritatem catholicam defendentes impedit aut molestat: & probatur tribus rationibus, ubi etiam notatur, quod non est minor confirmatio catholica veritatis per Scripturam sacram, quam per miraculum.
units.tr: In this part the tenth mode of pertinacity is laid down, namely of those who hinder or harass those who defend Catholic truth. It is proved by three arguments, and it is also noted that the confirmation of Catholic truth by holy Scripture is no less than its confirmation by miracle.

units.la: Discipulus. Ad alium modum errantem de pertinacia convincendi procedo. Magist. Decimo est quis de pertinacia convincendus, si errans contra fidem prosequitur vel molestat aut impedit catholicam veritatem defendentes aut prauitatem haereticam impugnantes. Quod enim tales sint pertinaces & haeretici reputandi, tali ratione probatur. Qui declarationem veritatis catholicae & damnationem prauitatis haereticae latagit impedire, non est paratus corrigi, nec quaerit canta sollicitudine veritatem: & per consequens pertinax est censendus. Sed errans, qui prosequitur aut molestat aut impedit catholicam veritatem defensantes, & prauitatem haereticam impugnantes, declarationem veritatis catholicae & damnationem prauitatis haereticae satagit impedire. Ergo talis est pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Item errantes contra fidem, qui damnabiliter veritati resistunt, sunt pertinaces & haeretici iudicandi: quia reprobi contra fidem sunt; & inter pertinaces & haereticos computandi. Huiusmodi tunt errantes, qui damnabiliter veritati resistunt, teste Apostolo 2. ad Tim. 3. qui de talibus ait: quemadmodum Iambres & Mambres resistiuerunt Moysi, ita & hi resistunt veritati, homines corrupti, mente reprobi circa fidem. Sed qui persequuntur aut molestant vel impediunt catholicae veritatem defendentes, & prauitatem haereticam impugnantes, damnabiliter veritati resistunt. Ergo si errant, pertinaces & haeretici sunt censendi. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia magis delinquunt, qui catholicae veritati resistunt, quam qui resistunt publicae potestati. Sed secundum Apostolum ad Rom. 13. qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit. Qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi damna acquirunt. Ergo multo magis, qui catholicae veritati resistunt, sibi damnationem acquirunt: sed non nisi propter pertinaciam. Quia non pertinaciter resistere veritati, damnabile non videtur. Ergo tales pertinaces & haeretici sunt censendi. Item, eadem ratio confirmatur, quia non minus peccat, qui catholicae veritati resistit, & acquiescit haereticae prauitati, quam qui non acquiescit veritati & credit iniquitati. Qui autem non acquiescit veritati & credit iniquitati, peccat mortaliter, teste Apostolo ad Rom. 2. qui ait: Iis autem qui ex contentione & qui non acquiescunt veritati, credunt iniquitati, ira, tribulatio, indignatio & angustia. Ergo qui catholicae veritati resistit, & credit haereticae prauitati, peccat mortaliter: sed non est sine pertinacia. Ergo talis pertinax & haereticus est censendus.
units.tr: Student. I now proceed to the other kind of erring person to be convicted of pertinacity. Master. The tenth kind is someone to be convicted of pertinacity if, erring against the faith, he pursues, harasses or hinders those who defend Catholic truth or attack heretical depravity. That such people are to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical is proved by this reasoning. Whoever strives to hinder the declaration of Catholic truth and the condemnation of heretical depravity is not ready to be corrected and does not seek the truth with due care, and consequently is to be judged pertinacious. But the erring man who pursues, harasses or hinders those who defend Catholic truth and attack heretical depravity strives to hinder the declaration of Catholic truth and the condemnation of heretical depravity. Therefore such a man is to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical. Likewise, those who erring against the faith resist the truth in a damnable way are to be judged pertinacious and heretical, because they are reprobate with regard to the faith and are to be counted among the pertinacious and heretical. Such are the erring who resist the truth in a damnable way, as the Apostle witnesses in 2 Tim. 3, who says of such people: "As Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so also do these resist the truth, men corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith." But those who persecute, harass or hinder those who defend Catholic truth and attack heretical depravity resist the truth in a damnable way. Therefore, if they err, they are to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical. This argument is confirmed as follows: those who resist Catholic truth sin more than those who resist the public authority. But according to the Apostle in Rom. 13, "he who resists the power resists the ordinance of God; and those who resist bring damnation upon themselves." Therefore much more do those who resist Catholic truth bring damnation upon themselves, and this only on account of pertinacity, since to resist the truth non-pertinaciously does not seem damnable. Therefore such people are to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical. Likewise the same argument is confirmed, because whoever resists Catholic truth and gives assent to heretical depravity sins no less than whoever does not assent to the truth and believes iniquity. But whoever does not assent to the truth and believes iniquity sins mortally, as the Apostle says in Rom. 2: "To those who are contentious and do not obey the truth but obey iniquity, there will be wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish." Therefore whoever resists Catholic truth and believes heretical depravity sins mortally, and this is not without pertinacity. Therefore such a person is to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical.

units.la: Amplius, Christiani qui propter persecutionem, quam inferunt defendentibus catholicam veritatem, & impugnantibus haereticam prauitatem, sunt peiores his, qui carnali immunditia sunt infecti. Illa patet: quia non sunt minus mali, quam illi qui praedicatores veritatis audire recusant, qui tamen recusantes veritatis praedicatores audire, peiores sunt illis, qui peccatis carnis sunt infecti: veritate ipsa testante, quae ait praedicatoribus Euangelicae veritatis Matth. 10. Quicunque non receperit vos nec audierit sermones vestros, exeuntes foras de domo vel de civitate, excutite pulverem de pedibus vestru. Amen dico vobis, tolerabilius erit terra Sodomorum & Gomorreorum in die iudicii quam illi civitati. Ergo qui declarationem veritatis & defectionem haereticae prauitatis impediunt pertinaces & haeretici sunt censendi: quia prauitas peccati eorum ad aliud genus peccati, quam infidelitatis, haeresis vel pertinacia non poterit reduci. Discip. Ista ratio non videtur habere apparentiam, nisi de Apostolis & praedicatoribus miracula facientibus: quia veritas ipsa Apostolis facturis miracula loquebatur. Et ideo qui impugnaret veritatem catholicam defendentes & prauitatem haereticam impugnantes, quorum sermones & operationes Deus miraculis confirmaret, esset peior enormibus peccatoribus iudicandus: non autem qui impugnat alios miracula minime facientes. Magist. Istam obiectionem sive responsionem alii evacuare conantur, dicentes, quod non minoris auctoritatis est confirmatio veritatis catholicae per Scripturam sacram, quam per operationem miraculi: ita ut qui non credit scripturae Divinae, nec operationi miraculi per fidem firmiter adhaeret, ipso Abraham testante, qui diviti epulonii petenti operationem miraculi, scilicet mortui resurrectionem propter fratres ad poenitentiam inducendos, sic Lucae 16. ait: Si Moysen & Prophetas non audiunt, neque si quis ex mortuis resurexit, credent. Hinc Innoc. tertius hoc sentire videtur, ut habetur extra, de haeret. cum ex iniuncto, affirmat quod sic ad probandum invisibilem visionem a Deo sufficit operatio miraculi, & ita etiam sufficit testimonium dicens in haec verba: oportet affirmet illam invisibilem operationem miraculo vel per testimonium scripturae speciale. Ergo consimiliter, ut veritatis catholicae defendentes & impugnantes haereticae prauitatis nullatenus molestentur, sufficit eis suas assertiones testimoniis confirmare absque operatione miraculi. Unde & tempore Antichristi, electi miracula minime sunt facturi, sed loco miraculi scripturae testimonis fulcientur. Discip. Alio modo videntur omnes rationes praedictae posse infringi. Nam veritatem catholicam defendere, & prauitatem haereticam impugnare, ad Doctorum spectat officium, ut habetur extra, de haer. cum ex iniuncto. Sed ut habetur ibidem, cum doctorum ordo sit precipuus in Ecclesia, non debet sibi quisquam indifferenter praedicatoris officium vsurpare. Ergo licite conuenit veritatem catholicam defendentes & prauitatem hæreticam impugnantes impedire: & per consequens tales impedientes non sunt propter hoc pertinaces, nec hæretici iudicandi. Magist. Prædictis videtur assertoribus, quod rationes eorum nequaquam intelligis. Non enim intendunt, vt asserunt, quod quilibet sibi posset indifferenter officium Doctoris assumere: sed affirmant, quod nullus propter hoc, quod veritatem confitetur catholicam, & hæreticam reprobat prauitatem, est quomodo libet molestandus: licet posset quis merito molestari, scilicet vbi non debet, aut quando non debet, aut quouis alio modo, quam debet catholicam veritatem confiteri vel prauitatem hæreticam impugnare. De illis ergo persequentibus intendit principaliter. Et ideo sequitur, & suis falsis assertionibus aduersantur: quia debitis circumstantiis obseruatis quilibet Christianus debet habere libenter veritatem defensare, id est confiteri catholicā, & prauitatem hæreticam detestari. Nec propter hoc debet persecutionem aliquam à catholicis sustinere. Qui propter hoc alicui persecutionem inferret, esset inter hæreticos computandus.
units.tr: Further, Christians who, on account of the persecution they inflict on those defending Catholic truth and attacking heretical depravity, are worse than those infected with carnal impurity. The first point is clear: they are no less wicked than those who refuse to hear the preachers of the truth; yet those who refuse to hear the preachers of the truth are worse than those infected with the sins of the flesh, the truth itself bearing witness, which says to the preachers of the Gospel truth, Matt. 10: "Whoever does not receive you nor hear your words, when you go out of that house or city, shake off the dust from your feet. Amen I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city." Therefore those who hinder the declaration of the truth and the rejection of heretical depravity are to be reckoned pertinacious and heretical, because the depravity of their sin cannot be reduced to any kind of sin other than unbelief, heresy or pertinacity. Student. This argument does not seem to have force unless it concerns the Apostles and preachers who worked miracles, since the truth itself spoke to the Apostles who were to work miracles. And so whoever attacked those defending Catholic truth and opposing heretical depravity, whose words and works God confirmed by miracles, would be judged worse than the grossest sinners; but not someone who attacks others who work no miracles. Master. Some try to overturn this objection or reply, saying that the confirmation of Catholic truth by holy Scripture is of no less authority than its confirmation by the working of a miracle, so that whoever does not believe the divine Scripture, nor firmly cleaves to the working of a miracle through faith, is refuted by Abraham himself, who, in Luke 16, answers the rich man who asked for a miracle, namely the raising of the dead to lead his brothers to repentance: "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead." Hence Innocent III seems to hold this view, as is found in Extra, De haeret., Cum ex iniuncto, where he affirms that for proving an invisible vision from God the working of a miracle suffices, and likewise the testimony suffices, speaking in these words: "it must be affirmed that invisible operation either by a miracle or by a special testimony of Scripture." Therefore, similarly, so that those defending Catholic truth and attacking heretical depravity are in no way harassed, it is enough for them to confirm their assertions by testimonies, without the working of a miracle. Hence also in the time of Antichrist the elect will by no means work miracles, but instead will be supported by the testimony of Scripture. Student. In another way all the above arguments seem to be capable of being overturned. For to defend Catholic truth and to attack heretical depravity belongs to the office of the teachers, as is found in Extra, De haeret., Cum ex iniuncto. But as is found in the same place, since the order of teachers is pre-eminent in the Church, no one should indiscriminately usurp to himself the office of preacher. Therefore it is lawful to hinder those who defend Catholic truth and attack heretical depravity, and consequently such hinderers are not on that account to be judged pertinacious or heretical. Master. Those asserters seem to me not to understand their own arguments. For they do not intend, as they assert, that anyone at all may indiscriminately assume the office of teacher; but they affirm that no one, for the reason that he confesses Catholic truth and rejects heretical depravity, is in any way to be harassed, although someone might deservedly be harassed, namely where he ought not to be, or when he ought not, or in any way other than he ought to confess Catholic truth or attack heretical depravity. So it is at those persecutors that they chiefly aim. And therefore it follows, "and oppose their false assertions," because, with the due circumstances observed, every Christian ought willingly to defend the truth, that is, to confess Catholic truth and to detest heretical depravity. Nor on that account ought he to suffer any persecution from Catholics. Whoever inflicted persecution on someone for this reason would be counted among the heretics.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: In quo ponitur 11. modus pertinacia, scilicet eius qui errat, nolens tamen se submittere correctioni eius, seu eorum, quorum interest corrigere errantes: vbi etiam notatur de Papa qui concilium impedit, ne forte eius assertio condemnetur.
units.tr: In which the eleventh mode of obstinacy is set out, namely that of one who errs but refuses to submit himself to the correction of those whose business it is to correct erring persons. Here it is also noted that the Pope hinders a council, lest perhaps his assertion be condemned.

units.la: Discipulus. Satis audiui de isto modo errantem de pertinacia conuincendi: & ideo alium modum expone. Magist. Vndecimo est quis de pertinacia conuincendus, si errans contra fidem catholicam correptioni & emendationi illius vel illorum, cuius vel quorum interest, subiicere se recusat. Hoc tali ratione probatur. Ille, qui iudicium subterfugit, pro nocenti debet haberi, teste Bonifacio Papa, qui, vt habetur extra, de præsumpt. c. nullus dubitat, ait: nullus dubitat, quod ita nocens iudicium subterfugit, quemadmodum vt absoluatur, qui est innocens, quærit. cui concordat Pelagius Papa, qui, vt habetur II. q. 1. Christianus, ait: qui iudicium refugit, apparet eum de iustitia diuisum. Hoc etiam ex auctoritate Bonif. Papæ, qui ponitur 3. q. 9. c. deteminamus: & ex verbis Greg. quæ ponuntur 74. dist. c. honoramus, colligitur euidenter. Errans ergo contra fidem, qui iudicium subterfugit, pertinax & hæreticus est censendus.
units.tr: Pupil. I have heard enough about that mode of convicting the erring person of obstinacy, so explain another. Teacher. The eleventh way is that a person is to be convicted of obstinacy if, while erring against the Catholic faith, he refuses to submit himself to the correction and emendation of the person or persons whose business it is. This is proved by the following argument. One who evades judgment must be held to be guilty, as Pope Boniface attests, who says (as it is found in extra, de praesumpt. c. nullus dubitat): nobody doubts that a guilty person who evades judgment seeks acquittal in the same way as an innocent person does. Pope Pelagius agrees with this, who says (as it is found in II, q. 1, Christianus): one who shrinks from judgment appears to be divided from justice. This is also clearly gathered from the authority of Pope Boniface, which is cited in III, q. 9, c. determinamus, and from the words of Gregory cited in dist. 74, c. honoramus. Therefore one who errs against the faith and evades judgment is to be judged obstinate and heretical.

units.la: Qui autē correptioni & emendationi illius vel illorum, cuius, vel quorum interest, subiicere se recusat, iudicium subterfugit. Ergo pertinax & hæreticus est censendus. Discip Ista ratio videtur procedere de vocato ad iudicium, & le per contumaciam absentante, & de aliis nihil probare videtur. Magist. Non solum de vocato ad iudicium, & se per contumaciam absentante: sed etiam de impediente, ne fiat iudicium, vt dicunt isti, conuincit ratio supra dicta. Quia sicut ille non est immunis à crimine, qui iustitiam fieri nititur impedire, quamuis ad iudicium minime sit vocatus (vt habetur extra, de officio & potestate iudicis delegati. c. 1.) ita errans contra fidem, & ne de errore suo fiat iudicium impediens, non potest à crimine excusari. Sed illud crimen non videtur tibi aliud, quam pertinacia. Ergo talis est merito pertinax iudicandus. Item errans contra fidem, qui non est paratus corrigi, nec quærit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, est pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus, vt ex verbis August. quæ ponuntur 24. q. 3. c. dixit Apostolus, colligitur euidenter, quod qui correctioni & emendationi illius vel illorum, cuius vel quorum interest, subdere se recusat, impediens quoquo modo ne error suus rite & legitime examinetur, quamuis non sit vocatus ad iudicium, non est paratus corrigi, nec quærit cauta sollicitudine veritatem. Ergo pertinax hæreticus est censendus. Amplius veritate testante, vt habetur Ioh. 3. Qui male agit odit lucem & non venit ad lucem, vt non arguantur opera eius. Ex quibus colligitur, quod qui non venit ad lucem, vt non arguantur opera eius, male agit. Nam si non male ageret, faceret veritatem. Si autem faceret veritatem, veniret ad lucem, ibidem veritate dicente: qui autem facit veritatem venit ad lucem. Errans ergo contra fidem, si non venit ad lucem distincti & clari examinis illorum, quorum interest illuminare errantem: male agit. Ista autem malicia non est nisi pertinacia. Ergo talis pertinax & hæreticus est censendus. Discip. Per istam rationem apparet, quod omnis errans, nisi statim veniat ad lucem, petens suam assertionem per illos, quorum interest, examinari & discuti, est pertinax & hæreticus reputandus. Quod nimis videtur durum, quia multos Theologos crimine pertinaciæ implicaret. Magist. Sicut scis, præcepta affirmatiua obligant semper, sed non pro semper. Et ideo errans, quamuis teneatur venire ad lucem iusti iudicii, tamen non pro omni tempore ad hoc tenetur. Sed non impedire iudicium fieri, cum sit præceptum negatiuum, pro omni tempore obligat. Non differendum autem est venire ad lucem, quando expedit & oportet. Et ideo (licet non omni tempore veniat ad lucem petendo suam assertionem discuti diligenter) non est pertinax reputandus: sed quandocunq;, ne sua assertio arguatur, nititur impedire, ne ad examen debitum deducatur, est habendus odiré lucem. Ex prædictis isti inferre conantur, quod vbi Papa aliquam hæresim dogmatisat; vel impedit generale concilium celebrari, ne sua assertio discutiatur, pertinax & hæreticus est censendus.
units.tr: But whoever refuses to submit himself to the correction and emendation of the person or persons whose business it is, evades judgment. Therefore he is to be judged obstinate and heretical. Pupil. This argument seems to apply to one who has been summoned to judgment and stays away out of contumacy, and it seems to prove nothing about others. Teacher. The argument given above convicts not only one who has been summoned to judgment and stays away out of contumacy, but also one who hinders judgment from taking place, as these men say. For just as one is not free from crime who tries to prevent justice from being done, even though he has not been summoned to judgment (as is found in extra, de officio et potestate iudicis delegati, c. 1), so one who errs against the faith, and by hindering judgment on his error, cannot be excused from crime. But that crime seems to you to be nothing other than obstinacy. Therefore such a person is rightly to be judged obstinate. Likewise, one who errs against the faith, who is not prepared to be corrected and does not seek the truth with careful diligence, is to be judged obstinate and heretical, as is clearly gathered from the words of Augustine cited in XXIV, q. 3, c. dixit Apostolus. So whoever refuses to submit himself to the correction and emendation of the person or persons whose business it is, and in any way hinders his error from being properly and lawfully examined, even though he has not been summoned to judgment, is not prepared to be corrected and does not seek the truth with careful diligence. Therefore he is to be held an obstinate heretic. Further, with the truth bearing witness, as is found in John 3: Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved. From this it is gathered that one who does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved, does evil. For if he did not do evil, he would do the truth. But if he did the truth, he would come to the light, the truth itself saying there: but he who does the truth comes to the light. Therefore one who errs against the faith, if he does not come to the light of a distinct and clear examination by those whose business it is to enlighten the erring person, does evil. But this wickedness is nothing other than obstinacy. Therefore such a person is to be judged obstinate and heretical. Pupil. By this argument it appears that every erring person, unless he immediately comes to the light, seeking that his assertion be examined and discussed by those whose business it is, is to be reckoned obstinate and heretical. This seems too harsh, since it would implicate many theologians in the crime of obstinacy. Teacher. As you know, affirmative precepts always oblige, but not for all times. Therefore the erring person, although he is bound to come to the light of a just judgment, is not bound to do so at all times. But not to hinder judgment from being made, since this is a negative precept, obliges at all times. Yet coming to the light should not be postponed when it is fitting and necessary. Therefore, although he does not at all times come to the light, seeking that his assertion be carefully discussed, he is not to be reckoned obstinate; but whenever he strives to prevent his assertion from being refuted, and to prevent it from being brought to due examination, he is to be held to hate the light. From the foregoing, these men try to infer that where the Pope teaches some heresy, or prevents a general council from being held, lest his assertion be discussed, he is to be reckoned obstinate and heretical.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: In quo ponitur modus 12. pertinacia eius, scilicet, qui de suo errore reprehenditur à peritis, & nihilominus de veritate renuit informari, & de eius doctrina scandalizatur fides, & probatur 4. rationibus.
units.tr: In which the twelfth mode of pertinacity is set out: namely, when a man who is rebuked for his error by learned people, and yet refuses to be instructed in the truth, and whose teaching gives offence to the faith. This is proved by four arguments.

units.la: Discipulus. Si aliter potest errans de pertinacia conuinci, non differas declarare. Magist. Duodecimo potest quis conuinci pertinax (vt nonnulli dicunt) si de veritate damnabiliter renuit informari. Ad cuius euidentiam distinguunt dicentes, quod aut errantis assertio tanquam haeretica lis reprehenditur à peritis, & cuius dogmatisatione scandalisentur fideles, aut nequaquam reprehenditur à peritis, nec de eius dogmatisatione aliquod scandalum est exortum. In secundo casu quamuis de veritate interdum apud Deum pertinax habeatur, tamen in foro Ecclesiae non videtur, quod sit haereticus iudicandus, licet postea tanquam haeresis eadem assertio damnaretur. In primo casu dicunt, quod renuens de veritate informari etiam in foro Ecclesiae est pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Quod multis rationibus probare niTuntur. Quarum prima est haec. Errans contra fidem, qui non est paratus corrigi, nec quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, est pertinax & haereticus iudicandus 23. q. 1. cap. dixit Apostolus. Qui autem de veritate renuit informari, si eius error deprehenditur à peritis, & non est paratus corrigi, nec quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Discip. Ista ratio videtur concludere etiam de illo, qui de veritate renuit informari, cuius opinio non reprehenderetur à peritis, & de qua opinione nullum scandalum est exortum: quia talis non quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur, quod ratio praedicta de tali non concludit: quia iste praesumitur esse paratus corrigi, & etiam cauta sollicitudine quaerere veritatem, quando non apparet, quod damnabiliter nolit corrigi, vel negligat corrigi: nec apparet ex sui erroris amore, quod omittat quaerere veritatem. Talis autem est ille, de cuius opinione nullum est scandalum: nec eius opinio tanquam haereticalis reprehenditur à peritis. Ille autem, qui à peritis reprehenditur, & de cuius dogmatizatione scandalum est exortum, si quando oportet, & quomodo oportet, & vbi oportet, non quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, est violenta praesumptio, quod nollet veritatem suae opinioni contrariam declarari; sed magis vellet opprimi veritatem. Quia si (teste Iuno. Papa, vt habetur dist. 83. §. 3.) veritas cum minime defensatur, opprimitur, multo magis cum minime veritas quaeritur, quando quaeri debet, opprimitur. Oppressor autem veritatis catholicae pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Secunda ratio est haec. Magis vel non minus delinquit, qui seipsum, cum potest & debet, ab errore non reuocat, quam qui alios, cum potest & debet, ab errore non reuocat. Sed qui alios cum potest, ab errore non reuocat, inter errantes damnabiliter numeratur, vt sacri canones testantur aperte. Ergo qui seipsum cum potest & debet, ab errore non reuocat, inter errantes damnabiliter numeratur. Sed errans, de cuius errore scandalum est exortum, & qui tanquam haereticus reprehenditur à peritis, si de veritate renuit informari, seipsum, cum potest & debet, ab errore non reuocat. Ergo inter errantes damnabiliter est censendus. Talis autem est pertinax errans: quia errare absq; pertinacia errantem non reddit damnabilem. Talis ergo pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Tertia ratio est haec. Qui inique opiniones haereticales sapit & impias, pertinax est reputandus: quia absq; pertinacia nemo opiniones impias inique sapit. Qui enim absq; pertinacia sapit opiniones impias, quamuis sapiat impie, non tamen inique impie sapit. Sed errans contra catholicam fidem, qui de veritate renuit informari, inique & impie sapit, teste Leone Papa, qui, vt habetur 24. q. 3. 6. quid autem iniquius, ait: quid autem iniquius quam impia sapere & doctoribus sapientibus non credere. Sed in hanc insipientiam cadunt, qui nec ad veritatem agnoscendam aliquo impediuntur obstaculo, nec ad Prophetic as voces, nec ad Apostolicas Literas, nec ad Euangelicas auctoritates, sed ad semetipsos recurrunt. Ex his verbis colligitur euidenter, quod qui impia sapit, & non credit sapientibus, nec ad scripturas recurrit authenticas, nequissimus est censendus. Sed qui de veritate renuit informari, non credit sapientibus, nec ad scripturas recurrit authenticas. Ergo talis nequissimus, & per consequens pertinax est censendus. Quarta ratio est haec. Qui ideo magister erroris existit, quia non vult esse discipulus veritatis: per consequens est pertinax reputandus. In tali enim (vltra ignorantiam intellectus) in voluntate malitia inuenitur. Ista autem malitia voluntatis, vel est pertinacia, vel non est sine pertinacia. Sed errans, qui cum potest & debet de veritate renuit informari, ideo magister existit erroris: quia non vult esse discipulus veritatis. Qui enim non vult audire veritatem, non vult esse discipulus veritatis. Ergo pertinax est reputandus.
units.tr: Disciple. If a person in error can be convicted of pertinacity in some other way, please do not delay in explaining it. Master. A twelfth way, as some say, is that a man may be convicted of pertinacity if he refuses, to his condemnation, to be instructed in the truth. To make this clear, they distinguish: either the assertion of the one in error is rebuked by learned men as heretical, and its teaching causes offence to the faithful, or it is not rebuked by learned men at all, and no offence has arisen from its teaching. In the second case, although he may sometimes be regarded as pertinacious before God for the truth, he does not seem in the forum of the Church to be judged a heretic, even if that same assertion is later condemned as heresy. In the first case they say that the man who refuses to be instructed in the truth is to be reckoned pertinacious and a heretic even in the forum of the Church. They try to prove this by many arguments. The first is this. One who errs against the faith, who is not ready to be corrected, and does not seek the truth with careful diligence, is to be judged pertinacious and a heretic (23 q. 1, c. Dixit Apostolus). But one who refuses to be instructed in the truth, if his error is detected by learned men, and he is not ready to be corrected, and does not seek the truth with careful diligence, is to be reckoned pertinacious and a heretic. Disciple. This argument seems to conclude also about the man who refuses to be instructed in the truth, whose opinion is not rebuked by learned men, and from whose opinion no offence has arisen, because such a man does not seek the truth with careful diligence. Master. To this it is answered that the argument above does not conclude about such a man, because he is presumed to be ready to be corrected and to seek the truth with careful diligence, since it does not appear that he wilfully refuses or neglects to be corrected, and it does not appear, from love of his error, that he omits to seek the truth. But such a man is one whose opinion gives no offence, and whose opinion is not rebuked by learned men as heretical. However, the man who is rebuked by learned men, and whose teaching has caused offence, if, when and as and where it is required, he does not seek the truth with careful diligence, there is a strong presumption that he would not want the truth contrary to his opinion to be made clear, but would rather wish the truth to be suppressed. For if (as Pope Iuno says, as is found in dist. 83, §3) truth is suppressed when it is not defended at all, much more is it suppressed when the truth is not sought at all, when it ought to be sought. But the suppressor of catholic truth is to be reckoned pertinacious and a heretic. The second argument is this. He who does not recall himself from error, when he can and ought to, sins no less, or more, than he who does not recall others from error, when he can and ought to. But he who does not recall others from error when he can, is numbered among the damnably erring, as the sacred canons plainly testify. Therefore he who does not recall himself from error when he can and ought to, is numbered among the damnably erring. But the one in error, whose error has caused offence, and who is rebuked by learned men as a heretic, if he refuses to be instructed in the truth, does not recall himself from error when he can and ought to. Therefore he is to be reckoned damnably among the erring. Such a man, moreover, is a pertinacious error-holder, because error without pertinacity does not make the one in error damnable. Therefore such a man is to be reckoned pertinacious and a heretic. The third argument is this. He who wickedly holds heretical and impious opinions is to be reckoned pertinacious, because no one wickedly holds impious opinions without pertinacity. For he who holds impious opinions without pertinacity, though he holds them impiously, does not hold them wickedly and impiously. But the one who errs against the catholic faith, and who refuses to be instructed in the truth, holds opinions wickedly and impiously, as Pope Leo testifies, who, as is found in 24 q. 3, c. 6, says: "What is more wicked than to hold impious views and not to believe wise teachers?" But into this folly fall those who are not hindered by any obstacle from recognising the truth, neither from the prophetic voices, nor from the apostolic letters, nor from the evangelical authorities, but who have recourse to themselves. From these words it is clearly gathered that he who holds impious views, and does not believe the wise, and does not have recourse to the authentic Scriptures, is to be reckoned most wicked.
