But he who refuses to be instructed in the truth does not believe the wise, and does not have recourse to the authentic Scriptures. Therefore such a man is to be reckoned most wicked, and consequently pertinacious. The fourth argument is this. He who is a teacher of error because he does not wish to be a disciple of the truth, is consequently to be reckoned pertinacious. For in such a man (beyond the ignorance of the intellect) malice is found in the will. But this malice of the will is either pertinacity or is not without pertinacity. But the one in error, who, when he can and ought, refuses to be instructed in the truth, is a teacher of error because he does not wish to be a disciple of the truth. For he who does not wish to hear the truth does not wish to be a disciple of the truth. Therefore he is to be reckoned pertinacious.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII.

units.la: Ponit tres alios modos pertinacia.
units.tr: Sets out three other modes of pertinacity.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunquid est alius modus conuincendi errantem de pertinacia? Magist. Tredecimo potest quis de pertinacia conuinci, si verbis vel factis protestatur se assertionem suam (quae est haereticalis) minime revocaturum; quia talis non est paratus corrigi. Et per consequens pertinax est censendus. Discip. Dic alium modum. Magist. Quartodecimo conuincitur quis errans de pertinacia & haeretica pravitate, si in haereticae pravitatis fautorem prohibeeret legi scripturas catholicas, vel prohiberet praedicari, aut publicari catholicas veritates: quia talis est defensor haereticae prauitatis, & oppressor catholicae veritatis. Discip. Est ne alius modus concuincendi aliquem errantem de pertinacia? Discip. Quintodecimo quis conuincitur de pertinacia, qui in defensione haereticae prauitatis nouos errores fingit: quia talis non est paratus corrigi, nec quaerit cauta solicitudine veritatem. Ergo est pertinax censendus.
units.tr: Student. Is there any other way of convicting an erring person of pertinacity? Teacher. Thirteenthly, a person can be convicted of pertinacity if he declares by word or deed that he will by no means retract his assertion, which is heretical, because such a person is not ready to be corrected. And consequently he is to be judged pertinacious. Student. Name another way. Teacher. Fourteenthly, an erring person is convicted of pertinacity and heretical depravity if he forbids the reading of Catholic Scriptures to a supporter of heretical depravity, or forbids the preaching or publishing of Catholic truths, because such a person is a defender of heretical depravity and an oppressor of Catholic truth. Student. Is there another way of convicting an erring person of pertinacity? Teacher. Fifteenthly, a person is convicted of pertinacity who, in defending heretical depravity, invents new errors, because such a person is not ready to be corrected, nor does he seek the truth with careful diligence. Therefore he is to be judged pertinacious.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIX.

units.la: Ponit 16. modum specialiter de Papa conuincendo de pertinacia, si scilicet errorem contra fidem solenniter afferendo, tanquam catholicum illum praecipit a Chris- tianis teneri. Et probatur quinque rationibus.
units.tr: He gives the sixteenth way of convicting the Pope specifically of obstinacy, namely, if he solemnly asserts an error against the faith and commands that it be held by Christians as Catholic. This is proved by five arguments.

units.la: Discipulus: Alium modum vellem audire. Magist. Dicunt nonnulli, quod decimosexto potest Papa specialiter conuinci, scilicet de pertinacia & haeretica prauitate, si errorem, quem contra fidem diffinit solenniter, a Christianis asserit tanquam catholicum esse tenendum. Quod enim talis Papa sit haereticus reputandus, probatur primo sic. Quia, qui artat alios ad errorem pertinaciter defendendum, est pertinax. Hoc ex superioribus colligitur euidenter. Sed Papa solenniter aliquem errorem diffiniens esse catholicum artat catholicos ad errorem, quantum in eo est, pertinaciter defendendum & seruandum. Quia sicut constitutio Sedis Apostolicae legitime facta omnes astringit, ut habetur extra, de constitut. cap. vlt. ita Papa vel gerens se pro Papa diffinitiue pronuntians assertionem haereticam esse tenendam, quantum in ipso est, omnes astringit ad candem assertionem haereticam irreuocabiliter defendendam & tenendam. Ergo pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Secundo sic: ille, qui per se vel per alios prosequitur, punit vel molestat catholicam veritatem confitentes & prauitatem haereticam detestantes, est pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Haec in superioribus est fundata. Papa autem, qui solenniter diffinit aliquam assertionem, quae est haeretica, esse tenendam per se vel per alios, quantum in ipso est, per suam constitutionem omnes contradicentes reddit anathematizari dignos. Nicolao Papa in vniuersali Synodo praesidente, qui, vt habetur 25. q. 2. c. si quis, ait: si quis dogmata, mandata, interdicta, sanctiones vel decreta pro catholica fide vel Ecclesiastica doctrina, pro correctione imminentium vel futurorum malorum a Sedis Apostolicae praesule salubriter promulgata contempserit, anathema sit. Catholicos etiam contradicentes suae diffinitioni, quantum in ipso est, subiicit multis aliis poenis. Quia praeceptis & diffinitionibus Apostolicis resistentes poenis variis puniuntur, secundum q; ex verbis Gregor. quae ponuntur dist. 12. c. praeceptis. & dist. 9. c. nulli. & ex verbis Adriani Papae, quae recitantur 25. q. 1. c. generali, & aliis sacris canonibus colligitur euidenter, per alios etiam contradicentes catholicos, quantum in se est, punitur, persequitur & molestat: quia quantum in ipso est, inferiores praelatos astringit, vt contradicentes suae assertioni poenis omnibus, quas praelati debent inobedientibus, Apostolicis mandatis infligere, plectant. Ergo talis se gerens pro Papa, pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Tertio sic. Errans contra fidem est pertinax & haereticus reputandus: qui facto vel verbo protestatur se nolle corrigi per illos, quorum interest: quia talis non est paratus corrigi, & per consequens pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Sed Papa potest esse huiusmodi. Igitur &c. minor aperte probatur. Qui autem gerit se pro Papa & solenniter haeresim diffinit esse tenendam facto protestatur & verbis se nolle corrigi per illos, quorum interest, puta per concilium generale, ad quod spectat etiam Papam emendare. Ergo pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Maior pater, & minor aperte probatur. Quia ex quo (quantum in ipso est) per constitutionem suam omnes Christianos: & per consequens concilium generale (cum soli Christiani in generali concilio debeant interesse) artat ad suam assertionem tenendam, facto protestatur & ostendit, quod per generale concilium non vult suam assertionem reuocare. Hoc etiam verbo protestatur, cum in fine Bullae nulli liceat contraire. Etiam diffinitur per eum: qui talia verba vel aequipollentia in constitutionum Papalium Literis consueuerunt poni & subintelliguntur, licet non ponantur. Ergo talis est haereticus & pertinax censendus. Quarto sic, qui in aliqua assertione haeresi se firmauit vltimate pertinax & haereticus est censendus: quia talis irreuocabiliter assertionem affirmat haereticam. Sed diffiniens eam esse tenendam in eandem assertionem per vltimatam deliberationem se firmat. Ergo pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Quinto, qui nimis in errore persistit: quia ad diffiniendum errorem esset tenendum nullus potest absq; temeritate procedere. Ergo talis pertinax & haereticus est censendus.
units.tr: Disciple: I would like to hear another way. Master: Some say that the Pope can be convicted specifically, in the sixteenth way, of obstinacy and heretical depravity, if he solemnly defines an error against the faith and declares to Christians that it is to be held as Catholic. That such a Pope must be regarded as a heretic is proved first thus. He who forces others to defend an error obstinately is obstinate. This is clearly gathered from what was said above. But the Pope, when he solemnly defines some error as Catholic, forces Catholics, so far as he is able, to defend and keep that error obstinately. For just as a constitution of the Apostolic See, lawfully made, binds everyone (as is found in extra, de constitut. cap. vlt.), so the Pope, or one who presents himself as Pope and pronounces authoritatively that a heretical assertion is to be held, binds all, so far as he can, to defend and hold that same heretical assertion irrevocably. Therefore he must be judged obstinate and a heretic. Second, thus: he who, either himself or through others, pursues, punishes or harasses those who confess the Catholic truth and detest heretical depravity, must be regarded as obstinate and a heretic. This has been established above. But the Pope, who solemnly defines that some heretical assertion is to be held, either himself or through others, by his constitution makes all who contradict it worthy of anathema, so far as he is concerned. Pope Nicholas, presiding over a universal Synod, who (as is found in 25. q. 2. c. si quis) said: if anyone shall despise the decrees, commands, prohibitions, sanctions or decisions, promulgated salutarily for the correction of present or future evils by the prelate of the Apostolic See, concerning the Catholic faith or ecclesiastical doctrine, let him be anathema. He also subjects Catholics who contradict his definition, so far as he is concerned, to many other penalties. For those who resist Apostolic precepts and definitions are punished with various penalties, according to what is clearly gathered from the words of Gregory, which are set down in dist. 12. c. praeceptis. and dist. 9. c. nulli., from the words of Pope Adrian, which are recited in 25. q. 1. c. generali, and from other sacred canons. Thus he also punishes, persecutes and harasses, through others, Catholics who contradict him, so far as he is concerned, because, so far as he is able, he binds lower prelates to punish those who contradict his assertion with all the penalties which prelates ought to inflict on the disobedient, in accordance with Apostolic commands. Therefore one who presents himself as Pope in this way must be judged obstinate and a heretic. Third, thus: one who errs against the faith must be regarded as obstinate and a heretic if by deed or word he declares that he is unwilling to be corrected by those whom it concerns, because such a person is not prepared to be corrected and consequently must be judged obstinate and a heretic. But the Pope can be of this kind. Therefore etc. The minor premise is clearly proved. Now he who presents himself as Pope and solemnly defines heresy to be held, by his deed and word declares that he is unwilling to be corrected by those whom it concerns, namely by a general council, to which it also belongs to correct the Pope. Therefore he must be judged obstinate and a heretic. The major premise is evident, and the minor is clearly proved, because, since he binds all Christians by his constitution (so far as he is concerned), and consequently a general council (since only Christians ought to take part in a general council), to hold his assertion, he by deed declares and shows that he does not wish to revoke his assertion through a general council. He also declares this by word, since at the end of the Bull it is forbidden to anyone to contradict it. Moreover, it is defined by him who is accustomed to have such words, or equivalent ones, placed and understood in the letters of Papal constitutions, even when they are not written. Therefore such a man must be judged a heretic and obstinate. Fourth, thus: he who has firmly held to some heretical assertion is ultimately to be regarded as obstinate and a heretic, because such a person affirms the heretical assertion irrevocably. But one who defines it to be held as the same assertion firmly settles on it by ultimate deliberation. Therefore he must be judged obstinate and a heretic. Fifth, he who persists too much in error: for no one can proceed to define an error to be held without temerity. Therefore such a person must be judged obstinate and a heretic.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: In quo ponitur 17. modus de Papa specialiter, si quis eius tali diffinitioni consentit aliquo modo, & ibidem ponitur modus 18. de Episcopis etiam taliter diffinientibus tali assertioni esse assentiendum.
units.tr: In which the seventeenth mode is laid down concerning the Pope in particular: whether anyone assents to his such definition in any way; and there too the eighteenth mode is laid down, concerning bishops who likewise define that such an assertion is to be assented to.

units.la: Discipulus. Tracta alium modum, errantem de pertinacia conuincendi. Magist. Decimoseptimo de pertinacia & prauitate haeretica potest quis conuinci, si tali diffinitioni Papae consentit consulendo, cooperando, inducendo, vel diffiniendo esse taliter asserendo. Hoc tali ratione probatur, facientes & consentientes consimili crimine inuoluuntur, sicut & eos par poena constringit, secundum quod sacri canones asserunt manifeste. Sed Papa taliter diffiniens assertionem haereticam pro catholica esse tenendam, pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Ergo omnes consentientes eidem sunt inter pertinaces & haereticos computandi. Discip. Ista ratio pro isto modo sufficiat. Ideo dicalium modum de pertinacia convincendi. Magist. Decimooctavo est quis pertinax reputandus, si inferior Episcopus summo Pontifice aliquam assertionem haereticam per sententiam diffinitivam determinat esse tenendam, iniungens aliis & imponens, quod ipsi sentiant ipsam, & reputrent eam esse catholicam. Quicunq; etiam tali determinationi consentit, pertinax & haereticus est censendus. Hoc ex praecedentibus satis apparet; quia si Papa taliter determinans & sibi consentientes sunt pertinaces & haeretici reputandi: multo magis inferior Papa taliter determinans, officium vsurpando Papale, & sibi consentientes, sunt pertinaces & haeretici iudicandi.
units.tr: Disciple. Propose another mode of convicting one who errs of obstinacy. Master. In the seventeenth place, a person may be convicted of obstinacy and heretical perversity if he consents to such a definition of the Pope, by consulting, co-operating, inducing, or himself defining and asserting it in the same way. This is proved by the following reasoning: those who act and those who consent are involved in the same crime, and the same penalty binds them, as the sacred canons plainly declare. But the Pope, defining in this way that a heretical assertion is to be held as catholic, is to be judged obstinate and heretical. Therefore all who consent to him are to be counted among the obstinate and heretical. Disciple. Let this reasoning suffice for this mode. Now tell me another mode of convicting of obstinacy. Master. In the eighteenth place, a person is to be reckoned obstinate if an inferior bishop, by a definitive sentence, determines that some heretical assertion is to be held, enjoining and imposing on others that they should think it and regard it as catholic. Whoever also consents to such a determination is to be judged obstinate and heretical. This is sufficiently clear from what has gone before: for if the Pope, determining thus, and those consenting to him are to be reckoned obstinate and heretical, much more is an inferior bishop who so determines, usurping the Papal office, and those consenting to him, to be judged obstinate and heretical.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXI.

units.la: Ponit 19. modum, scilicet eius qui potestatem habens haeretica prauitati non resistit, qui magis fautores, quam haeretici sunt censendi.
units.tr: Gives the nineteenth way: of one who has power but does not resist heretical depravity, who are to be judged rather supporters than heretics.

units.la: Discipulus. Describe alium modum de pertinacia conuincendi errantem. Magist. Decimonono potest de pertinacia quis conuinci, si potestatem habens prauitati haereticae non resistit. Hoc per sacros canones multipliciter videtur posse probari. Ait enim Innoc. Papa, ut habetur dist. 83. c. error: Error cui non resistitur, approbatur. Qui autem errorem approbat, videtur pertinax iudicandus. Ergo qui errori non resistit, si potest, pertinax est censendus. Item, Leo Papa, ut habetur extra, de haeret. qui alios, ait: qui alios cum potest ab errore non reuocat seipsum errare demonstrat. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod qui potest haereticos ab errore reuocare, & non reuocat, est inter haereticos computandus: & per consequens pertinax est censendus. Item, Iohan. Papa dist. 80. c. faciliter, ait: Faciliter praesumit dubio culpam habet qui potest corrigere & negligit emendare. Qui itaq; pertinaces haereticos, quos potest corrigere, negligit emendare, pertinaciae & haereticorum culpam habet: & per consequens inter pertinaces & haereticos est habendus. Discip. Vellem scire, an omnes literati sentiant tales esse haereticos. Magist. Quidam dicunt, quod magis proprie debent vocari fautores haereticorum & haereticae prauitatis quam haeretici: tamen pertinaces, etiam secundum eos, poterunt appellari, quia pertinacia ad plura vitia quam ad haeresim se extendit.
units.tr: Disciple. Describe another way of convicting a man who errs of pertinacity. Master. Nineteenthly, a man may be convicted of pertinacity if, having power, he does not resist heretical depravity. This seems to be provable in many ways from the sacred canons. For Pope Innocent says, as is found in dist. 83, c. Error: An error that is not resisted is approved. But he who approves an error seems to be judged pertinacious. Therefore he who does not resist an error, if he can, is to be considered pertinacious. Likewise Pope Leo, as is found in Extra, de haeret., says of others: He who does not recall others from error, when he can, shows that he himself is in error. From these words it is understood that he who can recall heretics from error and does not, is to be counted among the heretics, and consequently is to be considered pertinacious. Likewise Pope John, dist. 80, c. Faciliter, says: He who easily presumes is at fault in doubt; he who can correct and neglects to amend has the fault. Therefore he who neglects to amend pertinacious heretics whom he can correct, has the guilt of pertinacity and of heretics, and consequently is to be held among the pertinacious and the heretics. Disciple. I would like to know whether all learned men think such men are heretics. Master. Some say that they ought more properly to be called supporters of heretics and of heretical depravity than heretics; yet, even according to them, they may be called pertinacious, because pertinacity extends to more vices than heresy does.

units.la: Explicit Liber Quartus primae partis.
units.tr: Here ends the Fourth Book of the First Part.

units.la: INCIPIT LIBER QVINTVS EIVSDEM PARTIS, DOCENS QVI POSSVNT PRAVITATE haeretica maculari. CAP. I.
units.tr: BOOK FIVE OF THE SAME PART, TEACHING WHO CAN BE STAINED WITH HERETICAL DEPRAVITY. CHAPTER I.

units.la: Capitulum primum quarit, vtrum Papa canonice electus haereticari possit. Quod sic: primo auctoritatibus, deinde exemplis ostenditur. Et hoc capitulo secundo.
units.tr: The first chapter asks whether a canonically elected Pope can be made a heretic. That he can is shown first by authorities and then by examples. This is done in the second part of the chapter.

units.la: Discipulus. Quia mihi videtur, quod qui non resistunt prauitati haereticae, cum possunt, sunt potius fautores quam haeretici nuncupandi, de ipsis hic nolo plus inquirere: sed postea, quando defautoribus receptoribus & defensoribus haereticorum interrogabo, quam plurima de ipsis etiam inuestigare curabo. Nunc autem postquam quaesiui, quomodo potest quis conuinci esse haereticus, indagare propono, qui possint prauitate haeretica maculari. Et quia omnes Christiani sentire videntur, quod tota multitudo Christianorum haereticari non potest: Quidam autem secundo, quod nec concilium generale: Aliqui vero tertio quod Romana Ecclesia: Nonnulli autem quarto quod nec collegium Cardinalium: Aliqui vero quinto quod nec etiam Papa potest haeretica pollui prauitate. Ideo de istis quinq; quid sentiant Christiani, cupio vt mihi reueles. Primo autem dicas: An omnes putent Papam intrantem canonice haereticari non posse. Magist. De hoc sunt opiniones contrariae. Sunt enim quidam dicentes, quod Papa intrans canonice errare potest contra catholicam veritatem, & prauitati haereticae pertinaciter adhaerere. Alii autem dicunt, quod Papa intrans canonice contra fidem errare non potest. Discip. Quomodo primi opinantes se muniunt, non differas explicare. Magist. Assertionem praedicta auctoritatibus & exemplis ac etiam rationibus fulcire nituntur. Primo autem hoc authoritate Beati Pauli conantur ostendere, quia Hebr. 7. sic legitur: Omnis pontisex ex hominibus assumptus pro omnibus constituitur in his quae sunt ad Deum, vt offerat Deo sacrificia pro peccatis, & qui condolere possit his qui ignorant & errant, quoniam & ipse circumdatus est infirmitate. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnis pontifex ex hominibus assumptus, qualis est summus pontifex, sicut condolere potest his qui ignorant & errant, ita & infirmitate, id est, potentia ignorandi & errandi circumdatus dignoscitur. Item, prim. Corinth. decim. Apostolus generaliter admonet omnes in gratia minime confirmatos dicens: qui se existimat stare, videat ne cadat. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod omnis homo in gratia minime confirmatus potest cadere in peccatum: & per consequens potest errare contra fidem. Item, Apostolus ad Gal. 6. vniuersitatem erudiens praelatorum, quoquomodo debent subditos instruere suos, ait: si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, instruite huiusmodi in spiritu lenitatis considerans teipsum ne & tu tenteris. Ex quibus datur intelligi, quod de omni delicto, de quo præoccupatus fuerit subditus homo, potest prælatus tentari, & consimile delictum committere. Cum ergo à prædicta admonitione Apostoli Papa minime sit exceptus, & subditi possunt errare contra fidem, considerare debet etiam summus Pontifex, ne de errore contra fidem tentatus in hæreticam incidat prauitatem. Item hoc probatur auctoritate Bonifacii, qui legitur dist. 40. c. si Papa, qui loquens de Papa ait: huiusmodi culpas redarguere præsumit nullus mortalium: quia cunctos ipse iudicaturus à nemine est iudicandus, nisi deprehendatur à fide deviius. Ex quib. verbis evidenter colligitur, quod Papa à fide deviare potest catholica, & hæreticam incurrere prauitatem. Quod Glossa ibidem asserit manifeste, di. super verbo à fide, quod intelligit Hug. cum Papa non vult corrigi. Si enim paratus esset corrigi, non posset accusari. Et infra: fit specialiter mentio de hæresi, ideo quia etsi occulta esset hæresis, de illa posset accusari. Et infra quærit dicens: Nunquid posset Papa statuere, quod non posset accusari de hæresi. Et respondet dicens: Respondeo quod non: quia ex hoc periclitaretur tota Ecclesia. Ex his verbis patenter habetur, quod Papa potest de hæresi accusari, & per consequens potest prauitate hæretica irretiri. Item, eandem assertionem auctoritate Vrbani Papæ, quæ ponitur 25. q. 1. c. sunt quidam, nituntur astruere. Ait enim Vrbanus Papa: Sciendum summopere est, quod inde novas leges potest condere, unde Evangelista aliquid nequaquam dixerint. Ubi vero aperte Dominus, vel eius Apostoli, aut eos sequentes sancti Patres sententialiter aliquid dixerunt, ibi non novam legem Romanus pontifex dare potest, sed potius quod prædicatum est ut ad animam & sanguinem confirmare debet. Si enim quod docuerunt Apostoli & Prophetæ, destruere (quod absit) niteretur, non sententiam dare, sed magis errare convinceretur. Ex his insinuatur, quod quamuis Romanus pontifex non debeat, tamen potest errare contra Apostolos & Prophetas: & ita potest hæretica infici prauitate. Quod Glossæ multæ super decreta sententialiter & vocaliter asserunt & affirmant. Glossa enim 24. q. 1. c. fi. quando quis incidit in hæresim iam damnatam, est casus, in quo Papa iam Papam ligare potest: & in quo Papa canonem latæ sententiæ incidit. Nec obstat illa regula, par parem soluere vel ligare non potest. Quia si Papa hæreticus est, in eo quod hæreticus, est minor quocunque catholico. Item eadem cap. 2. q. 1. c. recta: & dicit Glossa: quæro de qua Ecclesia intelligas, quod dicitur quod non possit errare? non de ipso Papa: quia Ecclesia dicitur, ut supra eodem. Quicunque 27. q. 1. scire debes quod certum est, quod Papa potest errare, sicut 19. dist. c. Anastasius & 40. dist. si Papa. Item, 24. q. 1. qua ad perpetuam. dicit Glossa quod Papa contra generale Ecclesiæ statutum dispensare non potest, nec contra articulos fidei. Nam & si omnes assentiant ei, non valet statutum, sed omnes hæretici essent 15. dist. sicut.
units.tr: Disciple. Since it seems to me that those who do not resist heretical depravity when they can are rather to be called favourers than heretics, I do not want to inquire further about them here. Later, when I question about the favourers, receivers and defenders of heretics, I will take care to investigate a great deal about them as well. Now, however, having asked how a man can be convicted of being a heretic, I propose to inquire which people can be stained with heretical depravity. Since all Christians seem to think that the whole multitude of Christians cannot be made heretical; others, secondly, that not even a general council can; some, thirdly, that the Roman Church can; some, fourthly, that not even the college of Cardinals can; and others, fifthly, that not even the Pope himself can be polluted with heretical depravity. So I want you to tell me what Christians think about these five. First, however, tell me: do all think that a Pope who enters office canonically cannot be made a heretic? Master. On this there are contrary opinions. Some say that a Pope who enters office canonically can err against Catholic truth and cling pertinaciously to heretical depravity. Others say that a Pope who enters office canonically cannot err against the faith. Disciple. Do not delay in explaining how the first group fortifies its position. Master. They strive to support their assertion with the aforementioned authorities, examples and also reasons. First, they try to show by the authority of blessed Paul, since Hebr. 7. reads thus: Every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in those things which pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, and who can have compassion on those who are ignorant and go astray, since he himself also is compassed with infirmity. From these words it is gathered that every high priest taken from among men, such as the supreme pontiff, can have compassion on those who are ignorant and err, and is likewise recognised as encompassed by infirmity, that is, by the power of ignorance and error. Likewise, 1 Cor. 10: the Apostle generally admonishes all who are not at all confirmed in grace, saying: let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. From these words it is made clear that every man not at all confirmed in grace can fall into sin, and consequently can err against the faith. Likewise the Apostle, to Gal. 6, teaching the whole body of prelates how they ought to instruct their subjects, says: if a man be overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you too be tempted. From these words it is made clear that a prelate can be tempted by any fault into which a subject has been overtaken, and commit a like fault. Since therefore the Pope is in no way excepted from this admonition of the Apostle, and subjects can err against the faith, the supreme Pontiff too ought to consider, lest, tempted to error against the faith, he fall into heretical depravity. Likewise this is proved by the authority of Boniface, who is read in dist. 40. c. si Papa, and who, speaking of the Pope, says: no mortal presumes to rebuke such faults, because he himself who is about to judge all is to be judged by no one, unless he is found to have deviated from the faith. From these words it is clearly gathered that the Pope can deviate from the Catholic faith and incur heretical depravity. The Gloss there asserts this plainly, on the words "from the faith": Hugo understands it of when the Pope does not wish to be corrected. For if he were ready to be corrected, he could not be accused. And further: mention is made specifically of heresy, because even if the heresy were hidden, one could be accused of it. And further it asks: Could the Pope decree that he could not be accused of heresy? And it answers: I answer no, because by this the whole Church would be endangered. From these words it is plainly held that the Pope can be accused of heresy, and consequently can be ensnared by heretical depravity. Likewise they try to establish the same assertion by the authority of Pope Urban, which is found in 25. q. 1. c. sunt quidam. For Pope Urban says: It must be borne in mind above all that the Roman pontiff can make new laws only where the Evangelists have said nothing at all. But where the Lord, or his Apostles, or the holy Fathers following them, have clearly stated something by way of judgment, there the Roman pontiff cannot give a new law, but ought rather to confirm what has been preached, even to the soul and the blood. For if he were to strive (which God forbid) to destroy what the Apostles and Prophets taught, he would not be giving a judgment but would be convicted of error. From this it is hinted that although the Roman pontiff ought not, yet he can err against the Apostles and Prophets, and so can be infected with heretical depravity. Many Glosses on the decretals assert and affirm this both in sentence and in words. For the Gloss on 24. q. 1. c. fi. when someone falls into a heresy already condemned, this is a case in which a Pope can bind a Pope, and in which a Pope incurs the canon of latae sententiae. Nor does that rule stand in the way, that an equal cannot loose or bind an equal. For if the Pope is a heretic, in that he is a heretic he is lesser than any Catholic whatever. Likewise the same cap. 2. q. 1. c. recta: and the Gloss says: I ask of which Church you understand what is said, that it cannot err? Not of the Pope himself, because the Church is spoken of as above, in the same place. Whoever 27. q. 1. You ought to know that it is certain that the Pope can err, as in 19 dist. c. Anastasius and 40 dist. si Papa. Likewise, 24. q. 1. qua ad perpetuam. The Gloss says that the Pope cannot dispense against a general statute of the Church, nor against the articles of faith. For even if all assent to him, the statute is not valid, but all would be heretics, 15 dist. sicut.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod Papa canonice electus hæreticare potest, exemplis.
units.tr: In which it is proved, by examples, that a canonically elected Pope can be made a heretic.

units.la: Discipulus. Istæ auctoritates sufficiant pro assertione prædicta: ideo adducas exempla. Magist. Quod Papa intrans canonice potest errare contra catholicam veritatem multis exemplis ostenditur. Apertum autem exemplum est de Apostolorum principe Beato Petro, quem ideo (ut videtur) divina prouidentia, postquam ipsum ad Papatum assumpsit, errare permisit, ne successores eius (ipso fide, constantia & sanctitate longe inferiores) se non posse errare putarent. Quod autem Beatus Petrus contra veritatem Euangelii erraverit, Beatus Paulus Gal. 2. asserit manifeste, dicens: cum autem venisset Cephas Antiochiam, in faciem ei restitit, quia reprehensibilis erat. Et quod reprehensibilis erat, apparet: quia errauit contra Euangelicam veritatem. Et quod errauit contra Euangelicam veritatem, ostendit subdens: Cum vidissem quod non recte ambulabat ad veritatem Euangelii, dixi Cephæ coram omnibus: si tu (cum Iudæus sis) gentiliter vivis & non Iudaice, quomodo cogis gentes Iudaizare? Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod Beatus Petrus à veritate deviavit. Unde quod à fide Christi exorbitaverit, habetur in decretis 2. q. 7. cap. 7. testes, ecce: Vbi Gratia. allegat, quod subditi valeant reprehendere prælatos per exemplum de Paulo qui reprehendit Beatum Petrum. Cui allegationi respondet dicens, quod hoc licet, quando prælati à fide exorbitant, quemadmodum exorbitavit Beatus Petrus. Unde dicit ibidem in hæc verba: Paulus Petrum reprehendit, qui princeps Apostolorum erat. Unde datur intelligi quod subditi possunt reprehendere prælatos, si fuerint reprehensibiles. Et isti allegationi respondet dicens: sed hoc facile refellitur, si unde fit reprehensus, aduertitur. Petrus cogebat gentes Iudaizare & à veritate Euangelii recedere cum Iudæis gremiaciens: & à cibis gentilium latenter se subtrahens. Par autem est in se à fide exorbitare & alios exemplo vel verbo à fide deducere. Ergo hoc exemplo non probantur prælati accusandi à subditis, nisi forte à fide exorbitauerint, vel exorbitare coegerint. Ex his verbis patet, quod Beatus Petrus errauit non recedendo ad veritatem Euangelii ambulando. Disc.ip. Nunquid Doctores moderni tenent, quod Beatus Petrus errauit contra fidem. Magist. Thomas de Aquino hoc tenet manifeste. Nam 2. 2. q. 33. art. 4. dicit in hæc verba: in faciem resistere coram omnibus excedit modum fraternæ correctionis. Et ideo Paulus Petrum non reprehendisset, nisi aliquo modo esset ei par quantum ad fidei defensionem. Et subdit: Sciendum tamen est, quod vbi imminet periculum fidei, etiam publice essent prælati à subditis arguendi. Unde & Paulus, qui erat subditus Petro, propter imminens periculum scandali circa fidem Petrum publice arguit. Discipulus. Miror, quomodo isti præsumunt Beatum Petrum inter hæreticos numerare. Magist. Erras ipsis imponendo falsum, quod minime dicunt. Non enim sentiunt, quod Beatus Petrus fuerit hæreticus, lic et errauerit; quia suo errori pertinaciter aequaq; adhæsit, nā ad correctionē B. Pauli statim se corre xit, & reprehensionem eiusdem libenter audiuit: nec B. Paulum prædicantem veritatem in aliquo m olestauit. Disc. Vt video secundum istos, si B. Petrus suo errori pertinaciter adhæsisset, fuisset inter h æreticos computandus, ideo ad alia exempla te conuerte. Mag. Secundum exemplum de B. Marcello Papa, qui contra fidem errauit idola adorando, de quo Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur distil. 21. nunc autem, ait: tempore Diocletiani & Maximiani Augustorum Marcellinus episcopus vrbis Romanæ, qui postea insignis martyr effectus est, adeo compulsus est à paganis vt templum eorum ingressus grana thuris super prunas imponeret. Et in Legenda eiusdem sic legitur: Marcellinus ad sacrificandum ductus est, vt thurificaret, quod etiam fecit. Et in cronicis sic habetur: qui compulsus à Diocletiano incensum idolis dedit. Et infra; ad scelus, inquit, idololatriæ iudico me deponendum, & anathematizo, quicunque corpus meum tradiderit sepulturæ, & flens dixit: heu me anathematizari, & non possum in sacerdotio remanere. Ex his colligitur, quod beatus Marcellinus Papa contra fidem errauit, scelus idololatriæ committendo. Disc. Per illa non probatur, quod B. Marcellinus tunc errauit in mente prauitati hæreticæ adherendo, sed quia actum idolatriæ commisit. Magist. Verum est, quod B. Marcellinus non errauit in mente prauitati hæreticæ adhærendo, ex hoc tamen, quod facto negauit Christum, dum renuit confiteri se esse Christianum, infertur quod potuit errare in mente, & quod potuit effici hæreticus, sicut idolatra fuit effectus. Discip. Dic alia exempla. Magister. Tertium exemplum ponitur de Liberio Papa, qui consensit perfidiæ Arrianæ, sicut in Cronicis legitur manifeste. Discip. Non dicitur, quod Liberius existens verus Papa Arrianis consenserit, sed solummodo postquam renunciauit Papatui. Mag. Dicunt isti, quod nullus Papa manens Papa potest errare pertinaciter contra fidem, quia eo ipso, quo pertinaciter contra fidem errauerit, est extra Papatu priuatus de iure, licet de facto gereret se pro Papa, ideo non intendunt isti, quod Papa posset fieri hæreticus, cum manet Papa: sed quod verus Papa postea potest hæreticari, quod contigit de Liberio supradicto, qui primo verus Papa & postea hæreticus est effectus. Quod autem primo renunciauerit Papatui, hoc accidit, poterat enim hæreticari, licet nunq; renunciasset Papatui. Disc. Sunt ne plures exempla? Mag. Quartum exemplum ponitur de Anastasio II. qui propter hæreticam prauitatem fuit à Romana repudiatus ecclesia. De quo in decre. dist. 19. sic legitur: Anastasius secundus natione Romanus, fuit temporibus Theoderici regis, eodem tempore multi clerici se à communione ipsius abegerunt, eo quod communicas-set sine consilio episcoporum vel presbyterorum ecclesiæ cuncta catholica, decano Thessalonicensi nomine Fotino, qui infelicre communicauerat Achatio, & quia voluit occulte reuocare Achatium, & non potuit, nutu Dei percussus est. Quia, vt dicit Gloss. & accepit à Cronicis, dum assellaret, emisit viscera. Ex his patet, quod iste Anastasius prauitate hæretica extitit maculatus: propter quam clerici catholici se ab eius communione laudabiliter abegerunt. Disc. Ex his non habetur, quod Anastasius fuerit hæreticus: sed quod communicauit hæretico, sc. Fotino, multi enim communicant hæreticis, qui hæretici minime sunt censendi. Magist. Iste communicauit pertinaciter hæreticis in crimine. Vnde dicit Gloss. hic communicauit in maleficio, sc. in hæresi, & ideo fuit hæreticus: quia scienter communicauit in hæresi per ecclesiam condemnata, vt patet ex hoc, quod Achatium, quem sciuit propter hæresim iam damnatam ab ecclesia condemnatum, voluit reuocare, & ideo ille Anastasius incidit scienter in assertionem, quam sciuit esse damnatam, quare fuit hæreticus reputandus. Disc. Ex Cronicis & glossis super decretis satis apparet Anastasium fuisse hæreticum, ideo aliud pone exemplum. Mag. Quintum exemplum adducitur non ad probandum, quod Papa de facto errauit: sed ad verificandum, quod potuit hæreticari, & de prauitate hæretica accusari. Nam sic legitur in decretis 2. q. 7. c. non incompetenter §. cum Balaam, Romana synodus ordinauit, quod Simachus Papa accusatus accusantium propositionibus responderet. Vnde sicut legitur ibidem: Simachus Papa in Romana synodo dignitate sua expoliatus prius statui pristino reddi deberetur, vt tunc expoliatus veniret ad causam, & si ita recte videretur, accusantium propositionibus responderet, digna res visa est maximo numero sacerdotum atque meretur effectum, & cum postmodum ordinarent, quomodo esset accusandus prefatus Papa, vt causam diceret, occurrebat, sed ab æmulis est impeditus. Ex his verbis colligitur, quod Simachus Papa extitit accusatus, & quod iudicio synodali poterat accusari, de quo autem crimine fuerit accusatus, explicat Gloss. dist. 17. §. hinc etiam, dicens quod Simachus Papa prius fuerat accusatus de hæresi: sed cum appareret calumnia accusantis, fuit postea absolutus, patet ergo quod ex his, quod synodus reputauit Simachum Papam posse de hæresi accusari: & per consequens Papa potest hæreticari. Sextum exemplum ponitur de Leone, quem conuicit B. Hilarius episcopus Pictauiensis. de illo tamen sunt opiniones: quibusdam dicentibus, quod non fuit verus Papa, antequam in hæresim laberetur. Septimum exemplum ad probandum, quod Papa potest hæreticari: probatur de Syluestro II. de quo legitur, quod diabolo fecit homagium, quem etiam in Papatu exercens consuluit, ex quo arguunt, quod potuit hæreticari: quia omnis dæmonum inuocator & cultor, habensque cum dæmoniis societatem pestiferam, potest hæreticam incurrere prauitatem. Octauum exemplum est de pluribus summis Pontificibus tenentibus contra ea, quæ fidei sunt, assertiones contrarias, videl. de Iohanne 22. ex vna parte, & de Nicolao III. aliisque quampluribus ex altera: qui de paupertate Christi & Apostolorum eius contrariam sententiam diffinierunt vel approbauerunt ab aliis diffinitam, quam sententiam prædictus Ioh. 22. reprobat manifeste. Ex quo infertur, quod vel Ioh. 22. vel Nico. III. ex quo alter eorum errauit in fide, fuit hæreticus reputandus. Nam ille eorum, qui errauit solenniter diffiniendo aliosq; ad tenendum artando pertinaciter suo errori adhæsit, alter eorum erraui-t in fide, & fuit hæreticus iudicandus. Item ponitur exemplum de Innocentio III. & eodem Ioh. 22. quod alter eorum errauit. Nam Innocentius III. sicut legitur ext. de celebratione missarum. cap. cum Martha, ponit & asserit manifeste, quod sancti in coelo sunt perfecte beati, & quod omnia eis ad votum succedunt: & per consequens vident Deum. Iterum in li. de contemptu mundi, idem Inno. dogmatizat, quod animae reproborum sunt nunc in inferno, ubi graviter puniuntur. Iohan. 22. docet & probat, quod animae sanctorum non vident Deum, & quod animae reproborum non sunt in inferno, nec ante diem generalis iudicii puniuntur, cum ergo contradictoriae simul verae esse non possunt, constat quod alter istorum erravit, & ita liquet aperte, quod Papa potest errare. Item ponitur de Ioh. 2 2. & de B. Gregorio, nam sicut ex li. Dialogorum B. Gregorii clare patet, ipse sensit, quod animae sanctorum in coelo vident Deum, & quod animae reproborum puniuntur in inferno. Ioh. 22. negat utrunque, ergo alter eorum erravit. Item ponitur exemplum de eodem Ioh. 22. & multis aliis summis Pontificibus, qui sibi circa rerum contingentiam contradicunt, nam Ioh 22. dogmatizat & probat, quod omnia de necessitate eveniunt, quia omnia praeordinata sunt a Deo, ordinatio aut Dei impediri non potest. Unde & propter hoc in constitutione sua, quia vir reprobus, tenet expresse, quod Christus inquantum homo, regno temporali & dominio universali rerum renunciare non potuit, quia contra ordinationem Patris fecisset. Propter hoc etiam distinctionem Theologorum de potentia Dei absoluta & ordinata impugnat. Propter hoc etiam dicit, quod Deus necessario praedestinavit electis vitam aeternam, & minime contingenter, & ita plane putat, quod omnia de necessitate eveniunt, cui tamen plures summi Pontifices contradicunt, ait n. Iohan. Papa VIII. ut habetur di. 8. c. facientis quoque, proculdubio culpam habet, qui potest corrigere & negligit emendare. Ex quib. verbis colligitur evidenter, quod quandoque quis non corrigit, quod potest corrigere, & ita potest corrigere & non corrigere, quare non omnia de necessitate eveniunt. Item Greg. Papa, ut dicitur di. 83. c. consentire videtur, ait: consentire videtur erranti, qui dum ad resecanda quae corrigi debent, non occurrit. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod potest aliquis corrigere & non corrigere, quae tamen debet, & per consequens potest corrigere & potest non corrigere. Item Leo Papa, ut habetur ext. de haret. c. qui alios, ait: qui alios cum potest ab errore, non revocat. Item Eleutherius Papa, ut habetur 2. q. 7. c. negligere, ait: negligere quippe cum possit perturbare peruersos nihil aliud quam foues. Item Innoc. III. ut habetur ext. de sent. excom. c. quanto, ait: Facientes & consentientes pari poena plectendos catholica damnat auctoritas: eos delinquentibus favere interpretans, qui cum possint manifesto facinori desunt obviare. Item Innoc. Papa, ut habetur 83. di. c. error, ponit eadem verba cum Eleutherio, dicens: Neglige quippe cum possis peruersos perturbare, &c. Item Simachus Papa, ut habetur ead. di. c. 1. ait: mortem enim languentibus probatur infligere, qui hanc cum possit non excludit. Ecce summi Pontifices sententialiter & vocaliter asserunt manifeste, quod potest quis facere, quod non facit, quod etiam sententialiter multi alii Papae in scripturis suis affirmant, & per consequens secundum eos non omnia de necessitate eveniunt, sicut asserit Ioh. 22. ergo vel ille erravit, vel alii erraverunt: & constat quod hoc tangit fidem, ergo aliquis summus Pontifex contra fidem erravit.
units.tr: Disciple. These authorities are enough to support the assertion made above, so please give examples. Master. That a Pope who has been canonically installed can err against Catholic truth is shown by many examples. The clearest example is that of the prince of the Apostles, Blessed Peter. After Divine Providence had raised him to the papacy, it allowed him, as I suppose, to err, so that his successors, who were far below him in faith, constancy and holiness, would not think they could not err. That Blessed Peter erred against the truth of the Gospel, Blessed Paul plainly asserts in Gal. 2., saying: But when Cephas had come to Antioch, I withstood him to his face, because he was to be blamed. That he was to be blamed appears from the fact that he erred against the Gospel truth. And that he erred against the Gospel truth Paul shows by adding: When I saw that they did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: if you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do and not as the Jews, how can you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews? From these words we are given to understand that Blessed Peter had turned aside from the truth. That he had strayed from the faith of Christ is found in the decrees, 2. q. 7. cap. 7 testes, ecce, where the Gratian allows that subjects may rebuke their prelates, by the example of Paul who rebuked Blessed Peter. To this allegation he replies, saying that this is lawful when prelates stray from the faith, as Blessed Peter strayed. So he says in the same place, in these words: Paul rebuked Peter, who was the prince of the Apostles. From this we are given to understand that subjects may rebuke their prelates if they deserve rebuke. And to this allegation he replies: but this is easily refuted if one notes why Peter was rebuked. Peter compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, and by joining the Jews at table he departed secretly from the truth of the Gospel, withdrawing himself from the food of the Gentiles. But it is one thing to stray from the faith oneself, and another to lead others away from the faith by example or word. Therefore prelates are not proved to be liable to accusation by their subjects by this example, unless perhaps they have strayed from the faith or compelled others to stray. From these words it is plain that Blessed Peter erred by not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel. Disciple. Do the modern teachers hold that Blessed Peter erred against the faith? Master. Thomas Aquinas plainly holds this. For in 2. 2. q. 33. art. 4. he says in these words: To resist someone to his face in front of everyone goes beyond the measure of fraternal correction. And so Paul would not have rebuked Peter unless he was in some way his equal in the defence of the faith. And he adds: It must be known, however, that where danger threatens the faith, even prelates may be publicly rebuked by their subjects. Hence Paul, who was a subject of Peter, publicly rebuked Peter because of the danger of scandal threatening the faith. Disciple. I marvel how these men presume to count Blessed Peter among the heretics. Master. You are wrongly attributing to them something they do not say at all. They do not hold that Blessed Peter was a heretic, though he erred; for he clung to his error in no way stubbornly, since at Paul's correction he at once amended himself and gladly heard Paul's rebuke, nor did he trouble Paul in any way while Paul preached the truth. Disc. As I see it, according to these men, if Blessed Peter had stubbornly clung to his error, he would have been reckoned among the heretics. So turn to other examples. Mag. The second example is of Blessed Marcellus the Pope, who erred against the faith by worshipping idols. Pope Nicholas speaks of him, as is found in dist. 21. nunc autem: In the time of the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian, Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, who afterwards became a famous martyr, was so compelled by the pagans that he entered their temple and placed grains of incense on the coals. And in the Legend of the same man it is read thus: Marcellinus was led to sacrifice, that he might burn incense, which he also did. And in the chronicles it is found thus: who, compelled by Diocletian, gave incense to the idols. And below: I judge myself to be deposed for the crime of idolatry, he says, and I anathematize whoever shall commit my body to burial, and weeping he said: Alas, that I am anathematized, and I cannot remain in the priesthood. From these things it is gathered that Blessed Marcellinus, the Pope, erred against the faith by committing the crime of idolatry. Disc. These things do not prove that Blessed Marcellinus then erred by clinging to the heretical perversity in his mind, but only that he committed an act of idolatry. Mag. It is true that Blessed Marcellinus did not err by clinging in mind to heretical perversity. Yet from the fact that by his deed he denied Christ, when he refused to confess that he was a Christian, it follows that he could err in mind, and that he could be made a heretic, just as he was made an idolater. Disciple. Give other examples. Master. The third example is given of Pope Liberius, who consented to the Arian perfidy, as is plainly read in the chronicles. Disciple. It is not said that Liberius, while he was the true Pope, consented to the Arians, but only after he had renounced the papacy. Master. These men say that no Pope who remains Pope can stubbornly err against the faith, because by the very fact that he stubbornly errs against the faith, he is deprived of the papacy by law, even if in fact he continues to act as Pope. So these men do not mean that a Pope could become a heretic while he remains Pope; they mean that a true Pope can afterwards be made a heretic, which happened to Liberius mentioned above, who was first a true Pope and afterwards became a heretic. That he first renounced the papacy happened because he could be made a heretic even though he had never renounced the papacy. Disc. Are there more examples? Mag. The fourth example is of Anastasius II, who on account of heretical perversity was rejected by the Roman Church. Of him the decree reads thus in dist. 19.: Anastasius II, a Roman by birth, lived in the time of King Theodoric. At that time many clergy withdrew from his communion, because he had communicated without the counsel of the bishops or elders with the whole Catholic Church, with the deacon of Thessalonica named Photinus, who had communicated unhappily with Acacius, and because he wished secretly to recall Acacius and could not, he was struck down by the will of God. For, as the Gloss says, taken from the chronicles, while he was going to stool he discharged his bowels. From this it is plain that this Anastasius was stained with heretical perversity, on account of which the Catholic clergy rightly withdrew from his communion. Disc. From these things it does not follow that Anastasius was a heretic, but only that he communicated with a heretic, namely Photinus; for many communicate with heretics who are by no means to be judged heretics. Master. He communicated stubbornly with heretics in a crime. Hence the Gloss says: here he communicated in wickedness, that is, in heresy, and therefore he was a heretic, because he knowingly communicated in a heresy condemned by the Church, as is clear from the fact that he wished to recall Acacius, whom he knew to be condemned by the Church on account of an already condemned heresy; and so that Anastasius knowingly fell into an assertion which he knew to have been condemned, and therefore he must be reckoned a heretic. Disc. From the chronicles and the glosses on the decrees it is sufficiently clear that Anastasius was a heretic, so give another example. Mag. The fifth example is brought forward not to prove that a Pope actually erred, but to show that he could be made a heretic and accused of heretical perversity. For it is read thus in the decrees, 2. q. 7. c. non incompetenter §. cum Balaam: the Roman synod ordained that Pope Symmachus, when accused, should answer the charges of his accusers. Accordingly, as is read in the same place: Pope Symmachus, having been stripped of his dignity in the Roman synod, ought first to be restored to his former state, so that he might then come to the cause stripped of dignity, and if it seemed right, answer the charges of his accusers. This matter seemed worthy to the greatest number of priests and deserves to be carried out; and when they afterwards ordained how the aforesaid Pope should be accused, so that he might state his case, it came about, but he was prevented by his rivals. From these words it is gathered that Pope Symmachus was accused, and that by synodal judgement he could be accused. Of what crime he was accused the Gloss explains in dist. 17. §. hinc etiam, saying that Pope Symmachus had earlier been accused of heresy, but when the calumny of the accuser appeared, he was afterwards acquitted. It is therefore plain that from the fact that the synod judged Pope Symmachus could be accused of heresy, it follows that a Pope can be made a heretic. The sixth example is of Leo, whom Blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, convicted. Yet there are differing opinions about him, some saying that he was not a true Pope before he fell into heresy. The seventh example, to prove that a Pope can be made a heretic, concerns Sylvester II, of whom it is read that he did homage to the devil, and who, while he was exercising the papacy, consulted him. From this they argue that he could be made a heretic, because every invoker and worshipper of demons, who has a pestilent fellowship with demons, can fall into heretical perversity. The eighth example is of several supreme Pontiffs who held assertions contrary to what belongs to the faith, namely John XXII on the one hand, and Nicholas III and many others on the other, who defined or approved concerning the poverty of Christ and his Apostles the opposite opinion, which had been defined by others; and this opinion the aforesaid John XXII plainly rejects. From this it follows that either John XXII or Nicholas III, since one of them erred in the faith, must be reckoned a heretic. For whichever of them erred by solemnly defining and compelling others to hold it, and clung stubbornly to his error, the other of them erred in the faith and must be judged a heretic. Likewise an example is given of Innocent III and the same John XXII, that one of them erred. For Innocent III, as is read in the Extravagants, de celebratione missarum, cap. cum Martha, states and plainly asserts that the saints in heaven are perfectly blessed, and that everything succeeds for them as they wish, and consequently that they see God. Again, in the book on the contempt of the world, the same Innocent teaches that the souls of the reprobate are now in hell, where they are grievously punished. John XXII teaches and proves that the souls of the saints do not see God, and that the souls of the reprobate are not in hell, nor are they punished before the day of the general judgement. Since contradictories cannot both be true at the same time, it is certain that one of them erred, and so it is clear that a Pope can err. Likewise an example is given of John XXII and Blessed Gregory; for, as is plainly clear from the Dialogues of Blessed Gregory, he held that the souls of the saints in heaven see God, and that the souls of the reprobate are punished in hell. John XXII denies both, so one of them erred. Likewise an example is given of the same John XXII and many other supreme Pontiffs, who contradict him concerning the contingency of things. For John XXII teaches and proves that all things happen of necessity, because all things have been predestined by God, and the ordination of God cannot be hindered. Hence also in his constitution Quia vir reprobus he expressly holds that Christ, as man, could not renounce temporal kingdom and universal dominion over things, because he would have acted against the ordination of the Father. For this reason he also attacks the distinction of the theologians between God's absolute and ordained power. For this reason too he says that God necessarily predestined the elect to eternal life, and not contingently; and so he plainly thinks that all things happen of necessity. Yet many supreme Pontiffs contradict this. For Pope John VIII says, as is found in dist. 8. c. facientis quoque: without doubt he is at fault who can correct and neglects to amend. From these words it is evidently gathered that sometimes a man does not correct what he could correct, and so he can correct and can not correct; therefore not all things happen of necessity. Likewise Pope Gregory, as it is said in dist. 83. c. consentire videtur, says: He seems to consent to the one who is in error, who, when he has the opportunity to cut away what ought to be corrected, does not do so. From these words it is given to understand that a man can correct and not correct what he nevertheless ought to correct, and consequently he can correct and he can not correct. Likewise Pope Leo, as is found in the Extravagants, de haeresi, c. qui alios, says: He who, when he can, does not call others back from error. Likewise Pope Eleutherius, as is found in 2. q. 7. c. negligere, says: For he who, when he can, neglects to disturb the perverse, does nothing but foster them. Likewise Innocent III, as is found in the Extravagants, de sententia excommunicationis, c. quanto, says: The Catholic authority condemns those who do and those who consent to be punished with equal penalty, interpreting as favourers of wrongdoers those who, when they could, fail to oppose a manifest crime. Likewise Pope Innocent, as is found in dist. 83. c. error, gives the same words as Eleutherius, saying: For you neglect to disturb the perverse when you could, etc. Likewise Pope Symmachus, as is found in the same dist. c. 1, says: For he who, when he can, does not prevent it is judged to inflict death on the sick. Behold, the supreme Pontiffs plainly assert both in their judgements and in their words that a man can do what he does not do; and many other Popes also affirm this in their writings. Consequently, according to them, not all things happen of necessity, as John XXII asserts. Therefore either he erred, or the others erred; and it is certain that this touches the faith. Therefore some supreme Pontiff has erred against the faith.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: In quo eadem conclusio, scil. quod Papa canonice electus potest manens Papa errare a fide, & haereticari, hoc probatur 15. rationibus.
units.tr: In which the same conclusion, namely that a canonically elected Pope, while remaining Pope, can err from the faith and become a heretic, is proved by fifteen arguments.

units.la: Discip. Illa, quae tangunt sanctissimum Patrem dominum Iohan. 22. volo usque ad tractatum de dogmatib. ipsius differre: nunc vero rationes & assertione praedicta producas in medium. Mag. Quod Papa intrans canonice potest ante omne renunciationem spontaneam non solum errare, sed etiam pravitate haeretica foedari, multis rationib. in scripturis authenticis fundatis assertores praefati probare conatur. Prima talis est. Quis purus viator habens usum rationis non confirmatus in gratia potest contra fidem errare, & eidem errori pertinaciter adhaerere, quia talis potest a veritate, quae non est nota, nec per experientiam certa accepta, nec est sibi demonstrative probata, si voluerit, diuertere, & eius contrarium opinari, quia secundum B. August. credere nullus potest, nisi voles, sed Papa est purus viator & non comprehensor, si non esset comprehensor, errare non posset. Papa etiam est habens usum rationis (ut communiter) si enim per infirmitatem aut senectutem, vel per aliquam aliam causam perderet usum rationis; & tunc quidiu usu rationis careret, haereticari non potest, quemadmodum pueri amentes & dormientes, statu isto durante haereticari non possunt. Papa insuper non est confirmatus in gratia, cum possit peccare & damnari, ergo talis Papa potest veritati, quae non est per se nota, nec per experientiam certam accepta, nec est sibi demonstrative probata, si voluerit, dissentire. Multae autem sunt catholicae veritates, quae nec per se sunt notae, nec per experientiam certam acceptae, nec sunt Papae demonstrative probatae: cum dicat beatus Gregorius, fides non habet meritum, cui ratio humana praebet experimentum, ergo huiusmodi veritatibus Papa potest, si voluerit, dissentire: & per consequens pravitate haeretica poterit irretiri. Secunda ratio est haec. Constitutus in officio, per quod non necessario neque confirmatur, nec necessario augentur gratia & virtutes, potest labi in haereticam pravitatem, si ante susceptum officium potuit haeretica pravitate foedari, haec est nota, quod sine gratia vel virtute non potest aliquis viator a pravitate haeretica praeservari, qui prius poterat eandem pravitatem incurrere, nisi perderet usum rationis, nec in susceptione Papalis officii non necessario conferuntur gratia & virtutes, nec etiam necessario tunc augentur, ergo cum Papa ante susceptum Papale officium potuit haeretica pravitate inuolui, sequitur etiam, quod post susceptum officium, si non perdiderit usum rationis, possit eadem labe foedari, maior patet, minor ratione & auctoritatib. probatur. Ratione quidem: quia suscipiens Papatus officium poterit esse in peccato mortali, existeti aut in peccato mortali gratiae virtutes minime conferuntur, neque etiam stante in peccato mortali augentur virtutes in ipso, ergo potest contingere, quod in assumpto ad Papatum neq; virtutes & gratiæ augeantur, neq; tunc consecratur eidem. Quod etiam multis testimoniis sanctorum videtur aperte probari. B. enim Gregor. vt habetur dist. 40. ca. non loca, ait: non loca vel ordines creatori nostro nos proximos faciunt: sed nos aut merita nostra bona ei coniungunt, aut mala disiungunt. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod nulla dignitas ecclesiastica absque bonis meritis facit Deo proximos ad idem officium vel dignitatem assumptos. Ex quo manifeste concluditur, quod in susceptione Papalis officii gratia & virtutes non necessario conferuntur, neque de necessitate augentur: cum absq; bonis meritis & cum demeritis possit ambitiosus vel aliquo alio crimine irretitus ad officium Papatus assumi. Hinc etiam idem Greg. vt habetur dist. prædicta, ca. Nos, ait, nos, qui præsumus, non ex locorum vel generis dignitate, sed morum nobilitate innotescere debemus, nec vrbium claritate, sed fidei puritate, & B. Ambrof. vt habetur ea dist. c. illud, ait: illud autem aduerte, quod extra Paradisum vir factus est, mulier intra Paradisum; vt aduertas, quod non loci, non generis nobilitate, sed virtute vnusquisque gratiam comparat sibi. Et B. Hieron. vt habetur dist. præfata, c. non est facile, ait: non est facile stare in loco Petri & Pauli, sed tenere cathedram cum Christo regnantium: quia hinc dicitur non sanctorum filii sunt, qui tenent loca sanctorum, sed qui exercent opera eorum. Et idem Chrysost. ead. dist. c. multi, ait: non facit cathedra sacerdotem, sed sacerdos cathedram: non locus sanctificat hominem, sed homo locum. Et idem prout recitatur eadem di. c. vlt. ait: non qui maior fuerit in honore, ille est maior, sed qui fuerit iustior, ille maior est. Ex his aperte patet, quod in susceptione ecclesiasticæ dignitatis neq; gratia & virtutes necessario conferuntur, neq; ipsas necesse est augeri. Quod etiam per scripturam diuinam probari videtur, vt habetur 2. Mach. s non propter locum gentem, sed propter gentem Dominus locum elegit. Ex quo sequitur, q; propter dignitate prælatorum, sed propter merita prælatorum Deus approbauit dignitatem, & ideo susceptione dignitatis non est necesse gratia vel virtutem infundi vel augeri. Disc. Ex illa ratione sequitur, q; in susceptione ordinū, nec in alicuius dignitatis ecclesiasticæ susceptione gratia cōfertur vel augetur. Mag. Ex illa ratione nō sequitur, quia ex collatione ordinū gratia non confertur nec augetur: sed sequitur, sicut in collatione baptismi & aliorū sacramentorum propter indispositionē baptizati, puta si in peccato mortali præexistit, potest cōtingere q; gratia nō cōferatur nec augeatur, & ita potest hoc accidere & in ordinum, & cuiuscunq; dignitatis ecclesiæ susceptione. Disc. Alias rationes adducas. Mag. Tertia ratio est hæc, qui nō est cōfirmatus in fide, si vsū habeat rationis, potest errare contra fidē, sed Papa nō est confirmatus in fide, quia si esset cōfirmatus in fide, p aliquod donū supnaturale cōfirmaretur in fide, sed nullū donum supernaturale apparet collatū Papæ, p quod cōfirmetur in fide. Inter omnia n. dona supnaturalia, quæ de lege cōi puris viatoribus conferentur, præcipua & maxime stabilientia recipiente in fide, sunt gratia & virtutes Theologicæ sc. fides, spes & caritas, & dona Spiritus sancti. Sed p illa purus viator minime cōfirmatur in fide, cum illa pfectiora & maiora sæpe inueniātur in aliis, q; in Papa, qui tn p ipsa minime cōfirmatur in fide, ergo Papa minime cōfirmatur in fide, & ita nullū donū supernaturale collatum ipsum cōfirmat in fide, quare contra fidē potest errare. Disc. Ista ratio non concludit, quia probaretur per ipsam, q; concilium generale, imo tota cōgregatio fidelium, potest errare contra fidē: quia nullū donū supernaturale apparet collatū cōcilio generali, nec congregationi fidelium, per q; confirmetur in fide, cū gratia & virtutes, & dona Spiritus S. viatores nō confirmēt in fide: quæ tn inter oia dona supnaturaliter collata cōcilio generali & cōgregationi fideliū noscuntur esse præcipua. Mag. Assertores prædicti cōcedunt, q; ratio illa sic vniuersaliter sumpta non cōcludit: quia possibile est apud Deum non solū congregatione fideliū, sed & Papā & quelibet aliū viatorē absq; dono supernaturali animā informante ab errore & hæresi præseruare, per q; congregatio fideliū vsq; ad consummationē seculi pmanebit immunis: hoc tn non debet de psona, nec de collegio affirmari, nisi de quo vel qua Deus reuelauit, q; nunq; errabit contra fidē. Deus aūt hoc reuelauit de congregatione fidelium, non de Papa, & ideo temerarium est dicere; q; Papa intrans canonice nunq; errabit contra fidē. Disc. Alias rationes allega. Mag. Quarta ratio eorū est hæc, non minoris efficaciæ & virtutis respectu actus fidei sunt ecclesiastica sacramēta, q; quecunq; dignitas ecclesiastica, sed p suscēptionē actus fidei (qui vocatur sacramentū, ext. de baptismo & eius effectu) nullus cōfirmatur in fide, quin postea possit errare contra fidē, ergo p suscepti-onem dignitatis ecclesiasticæ, etiam Papalis nullus cōfirmatur in fide.
units.tr: Disciple: Those matters which touch the most holy Father, Lord John XXII, I would like to postpone until the treatise on his doctrines. For now, put forward your arguments and the assertion stated above. Master: The aforesaid advocates try to prove by many arguments founded on authentic writings that a Pope who has been canonically elected can err, and can even be defiled by heretical depravity, before any voluntary renunciation. The first argument is this. Any mere wayfarer who has the use of reason and is not confirmed in grace can err against the faith and cling obstinately to that error, because such a person can, if he wishes, turn away from a truth that is not known, nor accepted through certain experience, nor demonstratively proved to him, and hold the contrary opinion, since, according to Blessed Augustine, no one can believe unless willing. But the Pope is a mere wayfarer and not one who has attained the goal; if he had attained it, he could not err. The Pope also has the use of reason (as is usual). For if through infirmity, old age, or some other cause he lost the use of reason, then, as long as he lacked it, he could not become a heretic, just as insane children and sleepers cannot become heretics while in that state. Moreover, the Pope is not confirmed in grace, since he can sin and be damned. Therefore such a Pope can, if he wishes, dissent from a truth that is not known in itself, nor accepted through certain experience, nor demonstratively proved to him. Now there are many Catholic truths which are neither known in themselves, nor accepted through certain experience, nor demonstratively proved to the Pope; since Blessed Gregory says, faith has no merit where human reason supplies the proof. Therefore the Pope can, if he wishes, dissent from such truths, and consequently he can be ensnared by heretical depravity. The second argument is this. One who is placed in an office, through which he is not necessarily confirmed, nor necessarily increased in grace and virtues, can fall into heretical depravity, if before taking up the office he could have been defiled by heretical depravity. This is a known principle: no wayfarer who could previously fall into the same depravity can be preserved from heretical depravity without grace or virtue, unless he lost the use of reason. Nor are grace and virtues necessarily conferred upon taking up the Papal office, nor are they then necessarily increased. Therefore, since the Pope, before taking up the Papal office, could have been involved in heretical depravity, it follows that after taking up the office, if he has not lost the use of reason, he can be stained by the same fall. The major premise is plain; the minor is proved by reason and by authorities. By reason indeed: because one who takes up the Papal office may be in mortal sin, and while he is in mortal sin, grace and virtues are not conferred, nor are virtues increased in him while he remains in mortal sin. Therefore it can happen that in the one assumed to the Papacy neither virtues nor graces are increased, nor is he then consecrated to it. This also seems clearly proved by many testimonies of the saints. For Blessed Gregory, as found in dist. 40, c. non loca, says: Places or orders do not make us near to our Creator; our good merits join us to him, or our evils separate us. From these words it is understood that no ecclesiastical dignity makes anyone near to God, to be assumed to the same office or dignity, without good merits. From this it is clearly concluded that in the assumption of the Papal office grace and virtues are not necessarily conferred, nor are they of necessity increased, since a man who is ambitious or entangled in some other crime can be assumed to the Papal office without good merits and with demerits. Hence also the same Gregory, as found in the aforesaid distinction, c. Nos, says: We who preside ought to become known not by the dignity of places or of birth, but by the nobility of our morals, nor by the splendour of cities, but by the purity of faith. And Blessed Ambrose, as found in the same distinction, c. illud, says: Notice, moreover, that man was made outside Paradise, woman inside Paradise, so that you may notice that each one acquires grace for himself not by the nobility of place or of birth, but by virtue. And Blessed Jerome, as found in the aforesaid distinction, c. non est facile, says: It is not easy to stand in the place of Peter and Paul, but to hold the chair of those reigning with Christ; for it is said that they are not the children of the saints who hold the places of the saints, but those who perform their works. And the same Chrysostom, in the same distinction, c. multi, says: The chair does not make the priest, but the priest the chair; the place does not sanctify the man, but the man the place. And the same, as cited in the same distinction, c. ult., says: He who is greater in honour is not greater, but he who is more righteous is greater. From these things it is plainly evident that in the assumption of ecclesiastical dignity grace and virtues are neither necessarily conferred, nor is it necessary that they be increased. This also seems to be proved by Divine Scripture, as found in 2. Mach.: The Lord chose the place not on account of the people, but the people on account of the place. From this it follows that God approved the dignity of prelates not on account of their dignity, but on account of the merits of the prelates; and therefore, on the assumption of dignity, it is not necessary that grace or virtue be infused or increased. Disciple: From that argument it follows that neither in the reception of orders nor in the assumption of any ecclesiastical dignity is grace conferred or increased. Master: From that argument it does not follow that grace is not conferred or increased by the conferral of orders; rather, it follows that, just as in the conferral of baptism and of the other sacraments, because of the unfitness of the one baptized (for instance, if he was already in mortal sin), it can happen that grace is not conferred nor increased, so this too can happen in the reception of orders and of any dignity of the Church. Disciple: Bring forward the other arguments. Master: The third argument is this. One who is not confirmed in the faith, if he has the use of reason, can err against the faith. But the Pope is not confirmed in the faith, because if he were confirmed in the faith, he would be confirmed in the faith by some supernatural gift; yet no supernatural gift appears to have been conferred on the Pope by which he is confirmed in the faith. For among all the supernatural gifts which are ordinarily conferred on mere wayfarers, the chief and most steadying gifts for one who receives them in the faith are grace and the theological virtues, namely faith, hope and charity, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But a mere wayfarer is by these not at all confirmed in the faith, since these more perfect and greater gifts are often found in others than in the Pope; yet the Pope is by these in no way confirmed in the faith. Therefore the Pope is in no way confirmed in the faith, and thus no supernatural gift conferred on him confirms him in the faith, so that he can err against the faith. Disciple: This argument does not conclude, because by it it would be proved that a general council, indeed the whole congregation of the faithful, can err against the faith; for no supernatural gift appears to have been conferred on a general council or on the congregation of the faithful by which it is confirmed in the faith, since grace, the virtues, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit do not confirm wayfarers in the faith; yet these are known to be the chief of all the gifts supernaturally conferred on a general council and on the congregation of the faithful. Master: The aforesaid advocates concede that this argument, taken so universally, does not conclude; for it is possible with God that not only the congregation of the faithful, but also the Pope and any other wayfarer, without a supernatural gift informing the soul, may be preserved from error and heresy, so that the congregation of the faithful may remain immune until the end of the age. Yet this ought not to be affirmed of a person or of a college, except of one to whom or to which God has revealed that it will never err against the faith. But God has revealed this of the congregation of the faithful, not of the Pope; and therefore it is rash to say that a Pope who has been canonically elected will never err against the faith. Disciple: Bring forward the other arguments. Master: Their fourth argument is this, of no less force and power with respect to the act of faith than any ecclesiastical dignity are the ecclesiastical sacraments; but through the reception of the act of faith (which is called a sacrament, ext. de baptismo et eius effectu) no one is confirmed in the faith, so that he cannot afterwards err against the faith. Therefore, through the reception of an ecclesiastical dignity, even the Papal one, no one is confirmed in the faith.

units.la: Quinta ratio est talis, nō minus repugnat errori fidei & gratia, q; quecunq; dignitas ecclesiastica, ergo non magis cōfirmatur, quis per dignitatē ecclesiasticā contra errorē & hæresim, q; per fidē & gratiam sed nullus purus viator cōfirmatur in fide p fidem & gratiā, q; n possit errare & infici prauitate hæretica, ergo nullus per dignitatē ecclesiasticam etiā Papalem cōfirmatur in fide, q; n postea possit hæretica prauitate fœdari. Sexta ratio est hæc, tā Papa iuste depositus, q; Papa, qui sponte renunciauit Papatui, potest errare contra fidē, ergo Papa ante depositionem vel renunciationē spontaneam potest errare contra fidē. Antecedens patet: quia si Papa depositus, & qui renunciauit Papatui, nō potest errare contra fidē, sequeretur quod aliquis purus viator multis inuolutus peccatis alius à Papa non posset contra fidē errare, consequētia probatur: quia per actum meritorium non acquiritur potestas viatori errandi contra fidē: sed tā depositio Papæ q; renunciatio spontanea potest esse meritoria, cum n. Papa dignus depositione suā depositionē acceptat, vel propter Deū sustinet patienter, in hoc meretur, unde si Ioh. 22. qū deponebatur de Papatu, amore Dei patienter toleraßet, apud Deum meritū habuisset, probabile est etiā, q; tam Symachus Papa, qui renuncians Papatui ad hæsit vndecim milib. quam Cœlestinus V. renunciando Papatui merebatur corā Deo. Ergo nec per depositionē, nec p renunciationē huiusmodi acquiritur potestas errandi contra fidē, & ita Papa ante depositionē vel renunciationem habet potestatē errandi contra fidem. Disc. Ista ratio videtur vnā affirmationem falsam accipere, qp Papa sc. possit ante depositionē contra fidem errare. Nā videtur secundū iura, qp quamcito Papa errat contra fidē, tamcito esset depositus. Mag. Ad illam instantiā nonnulli respondent dicentes: qp duplex est depositio, sc. ab homine & à iure, ante depositionem ab homine potest Papa errare contra fidē, & haereticā incurrere prauitatē, & de illa depositione procedit ratio supradicta, qa primo effectus haereticus, & postea cōuersus & sacrificans Deo potest deponi ab homine, & depositionem meritorie acceptare, ante depositionē aut à iure potest Papa ex simplicitate vel ignorantia contra fidem errare, sed non haereticorum numero aggregari, quare licet à fide ex ignorantia vel simplicitate deuiauerit (si tamen paratus est corrigi) non est Papatu priuatus, sed si pertinaciter errori contra fidem adhaeserit, est ipso facto depositus, & de iure omni auctoritate nudatus; sed nō ab homine, sed à iure. Disc. Addealias rationes. Mag. Septima eorum ratio est haec, nullus per dignitatem acceptam indigne, illegitime & inique confirmatur in fide, sed contingit aliquem indignum ad Papatum ascendere illicite & iniique: quia per ambitionem & simoniam, & per vias alias impias & iniquas, ergo talis per Papatum in fide nullatenus confirmatur. Octaua ratio eorum est haec. Ille status, per quem assumens ipsum confirmatur in fide; & in quo nullus potest errare, non est fugiendus à viro perfecto, sed toto desiderio appetendus, quia talis status vel est omnino ab omni periculo spirituali securus, vel est minus periculosus statu, in quo nō est quis cōfirmatus in fide: eo qp propter defectum fidei & imperfectior sit & ad peccandū procliuior, sed Papatus non est appetendus, sed est fugiendus, nec minus periculosus qā alii status, in quib. conuenit errare contra fidē, propter quod & B. Clemens recusauit fieri Papa, ergo per Papatum nemo confirmatur in fide. Nona ratio eorum est. Ille, qui contra fidem errare nō potest, ad diffiniendū & determinandum dubia, quę contra fidem emergunt, non indiget aliorum constitutorū in hac vita mortali peritia; sicut qui in geometria vel alia facultate errare nō potest, ad diffiniendum dubia in eadem aliorum consilio minime indigeret, sicut etiam quia congregatio fidelium contra fidem errare non potest, aliorum qā Christianorum sapientiam non requirit ad diffiniendum illa, quae sunt consona catholicae veritati, sed Papa ad multa dubia, quę circa fidē emergunt catholicam, declaranda & diffinienda indiget aliorum peritia, aliter enim pro dubiis declarandis & haeresib. extirpandis frustra fuissent generalia concilia congregata: frustra etiam vocaret in sacra pagina eruditos, ergo Papa potest contra fidem errare.
