From these words it is understood that Christ gave the power of correcting in the forum of the Church to the Church, and not to any apostle in particular. Disciple. In these words it is a matter of fraternal correction, not of judicial correction in the forum of the Church. Master. These men reply that at the beginning of the passage Christ speaks of fraternal correction, which must precede at least a judicial correction; but at the end he speaks of judicial correction in the forum of the Church, when he said: And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the Church; but if he neglect to hear the Church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican. Disciple. How can it stand that Christ committed the power of correcting in the forum of the Church solely to the Church, when the Apostle Paul excommunicated the Corinthians and, in his first epistle to Timothy, asserts that he had delivered certain persons to Satan? Master. To this it is answered that by the commission of Christ the community of the faithful alone had the power of correcting in the forum of the Church; yet Christ did not bind the community of the faithful to one fixed manner of correcting, namely when the whole community could correct the offenders, as when it was expedient, or through some single person who would stand in the place of the community. And so they say that Saint Paul received his power of correcting from the community of the faithful of one province or of several provinces. Disciple. It follows from this that Christ did not leave any head of the Church. Master. These men concede that Christ did not leave a head of the Church who, by the ordinance of Christ, would have the power of restraining offenders in the forum of the Church; nor did he provide insufficiently for the Church. For in ordaining that the Church should have the power of correcting, he arranged that the Church should choose for itself one head or several, according to the diversity of provinces. Indeed they say that it is for the good of the community of the Church that it be in the power of the Church to choose for itself one head or several, and also to depose them whenever it seems expedient to the Church. Therefore, since Christ provided most excellently for the Church, he placed in the power of the Church the choice of one head or several for itself. For just as it is often expedient for a community to have one head, so at other times it may be expedient for a community to be ruled by several. For just as it is sometimes expedient to have a perpetual ruler, so at other times it is expedient to have a ruler who is not perpetual but holds office for a time. And so in certain secular communities it is not imprudently ordained that rulers resign their office every year, or after three months, or some other number of months, years or days, or are altogether deposed; and in some communities not one ruler alone but several are set over the government. The reason for these arrangements is this: in providing for the government of any community, one must consider not only the condition and manners of the subjects but also the manners and condition of those who are to be set over them. And so, because it can happen that no one suitable can be found in a community to take the government upon himself alone, in such a case not one but several will govern the community profitably.

units.la: Quando autem in communitate inuenitur idoneus, vt solus regat, & subditi sponte vnius regnum patiuntur, tunc melius est vnum quam plures communitati præesse, ergo propter multiplicem varietatem personarum, locorum & temporum non potest in his certa regula dari. Cum ergo Christus, vbi certa regula dari non potest conuenienter, nequaquam ecclesiæ certam regulam tradiderit, relinquitur quod Christus minime ordinauit semper vnum caput ecclesiæ præficiendum, cum hoc sæpe possit in præiudicium ecclesiæ redundare. Discip. Isti omnino nituntur potestatem summi pontificis annullare: sed de hoc transeamus ad præsens, & si aliter assertores præfari suam opinionem, quod beatus Petrus non accepit à Christo super alios Apostolos potestatem seu primatum, fulcire nituntur enarra. Magist. Eandem assertionem auctoritatibus sanctorum munire conantur. Et primo auctoritate beati Anacleti, qui fuit vicinus temporibus Apostolorum, & ideo gesta Apostolica sibi cognita fuerunt, ait enim idem Anacletus, vt recitatur di. 21. cap. in nouo: In nono testamento post Christum Dominum à Petro cœpit sacerdotalis ordo: quia ipsi primo pontificatus in ecclesia Christi datus est, dicente Domino: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram edificabo ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferi non prævalebunt aduersus eam: & tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum. Hinc ergo ligandi & soluendi potestatem accepit, primus autem à Domino, primum q; ad fidele populum virtute sua prædicationis adduxit: cæteri vero Apostoli cum eodem pari consortio honore & potestatem acceperunt. Ex quibus verbis colligunt isti, quod beatus Petrus nullam super alios Apostolos ex ordinatione Christi habuit potestatem: tum quia asserit Anacletus, ipsos pares in potestate fuisse: tum quia asserit pontificatum ecclesiæ datum beato Petro in potestate ligandi & soluendi constitere, omnes autem Apostoli in hac potestate pares fuerunt, ergo quantum ad pontificatum erant pares. Discip. Ista auctoritas non facit pro eis: quia, vt dicit ibi Glo. cum omnis episcopus est par Apostolico quantum ad ordinem & rationem consecrationis, Petrus tamen fuit maior aliis in administratione. Mag. Nonnulli prædictorum assertorum dicunt hic Glossam errare, quia textum aperte corrumpit: quia textus affirmat omnes Apostolos cum beato Petro pares in potestate fuisse, administratio autem est potestas quædam vel potestatis actus. Ego Petrus alios Apostolos nullatenus in administratione præcellebat.
units.tr: When, however, a man fit to rule alone is found in a community, and the subjects willingly submit to the rule of one, then it is better for one rather than several to preside over the community. Therefore, because of the manifold variety of persons, places and times, no fixed rule can be given in these matters. Since Christ, where no fixed rule can suitably be given, has not handed down a fixed rule to the Church at all, it follows that Christ did not ordain that one head should always be set over the Church, since this could often turn out to the Church's prejudice. Disciple. These men strive altogether to annul the power of the supreme pontiff. But let us pass over this for now; tell me, if the asserters, having stated their opinion, strive to support it, that blessed Peter did not receive from Christ any power or primacy over the other apostles. Master. They try to confirm the same assertion by the authority of the saints. First, by the authority of blessed Anacletus, who lived close to the times of the apostles, and so the apostolic deeds were known to him. For Anacletus says, as is quoted in Dist. 21, chapter "In nono": In the ninth testament, after Christ the Lord, the priestly order began with Peter, because the pontificate in the Church of Christ was first given to him, the Lord saying: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." He therefore received the power of binding and loosing, and he was the first appointed by the Lord, and the first to bring the faithful people to faith by the power of his preaching; the other apostles, indeed, received power and honour with the same equal partnership. From these words they gather that blessed Peter had no power over the other apostles by Christ's ordinance, both because Anacletus asserts that they were equal in power, and because he asserts that the pontificate given to blessed Peter consists in the power of binding and loosing, and all the apostles were equal in this power; therefore they were equal as to the pontificate. Disciple. This authority does not support them, because, as the Gloss says there, since every bishop is equal to the apostolic one as to the order and manner of consecration, Peter nevertheless was greater than the others in administration. Master. Some of the aforesaid asserters say that the Gloss here errs, because it plainly corrupts the text: for the text affirms that all the apostles were equal to blessed Peter in power, but administration is a kind of power, or an act of power. I hold that Peter did not in any way surpass the other apostles in administration.

units.la: Item prædictam assertionem, quod beatus Petrus alios Apostolos minime præcellebat, probant auctoritate beati Cypriani, qui, vt habetur 28. q. 1. c. loquitur, ait: loquitur Dominus ad Petrum, Ego dico tibi quia tu es Petrus & super hanc Petram ædificabo ecclesiam meam, super vnum ædificat ecclesiam, & quamuis Apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam parem potestatem tribuat, & dicat: sicut misit me pater & ego mitto vos; accipite Spiritum sanctum: tamen vt vnitatem manifestaret, vnitatis eiusdem originem ab vno incipientem sua auctoritate disposuit hoc: erant vtiq; Apostoli cæteri, quod Petrus fuit, pari consortio praediti honorum & potestatis. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod licet Petrus prius tempore habuerit potestatem à Christo, postea tamen Apostoli parem potestatem acceperunt, & ita Petrus extunc eos ex ordinatione Christi in potestate (& per consequens nec in administratione) nullatenus præcellebat. Item hoc probant auctoritate beati Aug. quæ ponitur 24. q. 9. c. Paulus, ait: Paulus enim Petrum reprehendit: quod non auderet, nisi se non imparem esse sciret. Discip. Ad hoc respondet Glo. ibi dicens, quod sciuit se non imparem meritis, non tamen administratione. Mag. Hanc rationem reputant falsam & friuolam, falsa est enim, vt dicunt, quod licet Paulus sciuisset se esse in charitate & multa merita habuisse, non tamen sciuit se esse parem beato Petro in meritis: imo probabile est, quod tanquam vere humilis reputauit beatum Petrum se præcellere sanctitate, etiam non nisi per reuelationem valuit scire, se non imparem meritis beato Petro, non autem legitur, quod Deus reuelauerit beato Paulo, quod meritis fuerit par beato Petro: quia quod de scripturis authenticis nou profertur, temere affirmatur. Est etiam friuola: quia ad hoc, quod aliquis reprehendat alterum, non requiritur paritas meritorum, tunc enim nunquam vnus homo potest licite reprehendere meliorem. Intendit enim Aug. quod Paulus par fuit beato Petro potestate, & ei non erat subiectus, nec in administratione, nec in aliis quibuscunque, quæ ad superioritatem & potestatem spectant.
units.tr: Likewise, to prove the aforesaid assertion, that blessed Peter by no means surpassed the other apostles, they rely on the authority of blessed Cyprian, who, as is found in Caus. 24, q. 1, c. loquitur, says: The Lord speaks to Peter: "I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." He builds the church upon one; and although after his resurrection he gives equal power to all the apostles and says, "As the Father sent me, so I send you; receive the Holy Spirit," yet in order to show the unity, he arranged by his own authority that the origin of that unity should start from one. The other apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership of honour and power. From these words it is implied that although Peter first had power from Christ in time, yet afterwards the apostles received equal power, and so from that time Peter, by Christ's ordinance, did not surpass them in power (and consequently not in administration either). Likewise they prove this by the authority of blessed Augustine, which is cited in Caus. 24, q. 9, c. Paulus, where he says: For Paul rebuked Peter, which he would not have dared to do unless he knew he was not unequal to him. Disciple. To this the Gloss there replies, saying that he knew he was not unequal in merits, but not in administration. Master. They consider this reason false and frivolous. It is false, they say, because even if Paul knew that he was in charity and had many merits, he did not know that he was equal to blessed Peter in merits. Indeed it is probable that, being truly humble, he considered blessed Peter to surpass him in holiness; and he could know that he was not unequal to blessed Peter in merits only by revelation, yet we do not read that God revealed to blessed Paul that he was equal to blessed Peter in merits, because what is not brought forward from the authentic Scriptures is rashly asserted. It is also frivolous, because for one man to rebuke another it is not required that their merits be equal; otherwise no man could lawfully rebuke a better man. Augustine means that Paul was equal to blessed Peter in power, and was not subject to him, either in administration or in any other matters that pertain to superiority and power.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: In quo ponitur opinio contraria, quare ad oppositum arguitur probando, quod beatus Petrus habuit ex ordinatione Christi super alios Apostolos principatum, & hoc quinq; rationibus.
units.tr: In which the contrary opinion is set out, and it is argued against the opposite view, proving by five reasons that the blessed Peter received a primacy over the other Apostles by the ordinance of Christ.

units.la: Discip. Non putabam pro illa opinione hæretica, quod tot auctoritates vocales sonarent, ipsa tamen nolo nunc plures allegationes audire, quamuis velim eam magis diligenter discutere. Sed vt veritatem catholicam contrariam molius intelligam, quomodo eadem veritas maiori auctoritate muniatur, ostende mihi, nullatenus manifestans quam assertionem reputes veriorem. Magist. Quod beatus Petrus super Apostolos habuit potestatem & primatum à Christo, multis modis ostenditur. Primo sic: ille, cuius curae & regimini tempore Apostolorum fuit totus grex Dominicus commissus à Christo, etiam super Apostolos, qui tunc erant de grege Dominico, quam & regimen accepit à Christo. Sed curae & regimini beati Petri totus grex Dominicus commissus fuit à Christo, dicente eidem Ioh. vltim. Pasce oves meas, inter illas oves & has non distinguens: ergo & Apostoli, qui extra numerum ovium nequaquam censendi fuerunt, curae & regimini beati Petri subiecti fuerunt. Secundo sic: illi, cui terreni simul & coelestis imperii iura commissa fuerunt tempore Apostolorum, ipsi Apostoli subiecti fuerunt: Sed B. Petro tempore Apostolorum praedita iura commissa fuerunt, teste Nicolao papa, qui, vt habetur 22. distin. ca. 1. omnes supra Petram fidei mox nascentis erigit, qui beato Petro claviger terreni imperii iura commisit, ergo Apostoli, qui tunc fuerunt, beato Petro subiecti exiterunt. Tertio sic: Caput super alia membra principatum habere dignoscitur, beatus autem Petrus caput fuit Apostolorum, teste Leone papa, qui, vt habetur 19. dist. ca. ista Beatus, ait; Ita Dominus noster Iesus Christus humani generis Salvator instituit, vt veritas, quae ante legis & Prophetarum praeconio continebatur, per Apostolicam tubam in salutem vniuersitatis exiret, sicut scriptum est: In omnem terram exiit sonus eorum, & in fines orbis terrae verba eorum, sed huiusmodi muneris sacramentum ita Dominus ad omnium Apostolorum officium pertinere voluit, vt in beatissimo Petro Apostolorum omnium summo principaliter collocaret, vt ab ipso quasi quodam capite dona sua velut in corpus omne diffunderet. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod beatus Petrus institutus fuit caput Apostolorum à Christo, & super ipsos habuit primatum à Christo. Quarto sic: Ille, qui tempore Apostolorum omnium ecclesiarum constituit sacerdotes, super ipsos Apostolos habuit principatum. Sed temporibus Apostolorum beatus Petrus omnium ecclesiarum constituit sacerdotes, iuxta tenorem Innocen. papae, qui, vt legitur di. 11. c. quis nesciat, ait: cum sit manifestatum, omnem Italiam, Galliam & Hispaniam & Africam atque Siciliam, Insulas interiacentes, nullum instituisse super ecclesias, nisi eos, quos venerabilis Apostolus Petrus & successores eius constituerunt sacerdotes. Ergo beatus Petrus super alios Apostolos habuit principatum. Quinto sic: beatus Petrus acceperat potestatem regendi omnes Apostolos, teste Gregor. qui, vt recitatur 11. q. 7. c. Petrus, ait: Petrus potestatem regendi acceperat, & tamen idem Apostolus Apostolorum primus querimonia contra eum &c. Ergo beatus Petrus super Apostolos potestatem habuit & principatum. Discip. Non curo, quod pro veritate praedicta multas rationes adducas, cum auctoritas debeat ad eam tenendam sufficere. Canit enim ecclesia vniversalis de beato Petro, Tu es pastor ovium princeps Apostolorum. Ideo ad alias quatuor assertiones, de quibus fecisti mentionem procede, & motiva earum compendiose declara.
units.tr: Disciple. I did not think that opinion heretical, since so many authorities seem to speak in its favour. Still, I do not now want to hear more arguments for it, although I would gladly examine it more carefully. But so that I may better understand the contrary Catholic truth, and how that truth is supported by greater authority, show me this, and do not yet reveal which assertion you consider truer. Master. That the blessed Peter had power and primacy over the Apostles from Christ is shown in many ways. First, thus: the one to whose care and rule the whole Lord's flock was committed by Christ in the time of the Apostles, that flock including the Apostles themselves, who then belonged to the Lord's flock, also received that rule from Christ. But the whole Lord's flock was committed by Christ to the care and rule of blessed Peter, when he said to him in John, last chapter, Feed my sheep, without distinguishing between those sheep and these. Therefore the Apostles too, who certainly cannot be counted outside the number of the sheep, were subject to the care and rule of blessed Peter. Second, thus: those to whom the rights of both earthly and heavenly rule were committed in the time of the Apostles were themselves subject to the Apostles. But the rights of that power were committed to blessed Peter in the time of the Apostles, as Pope Nicholas testifies, who, as it is found in Dist. 22, c. 1, says: He raises up all upon Peter, the foundation of the faith just beginning, who committed to blessed Peter, as keeper of the keys, the rights of earthly rule. Therefore the Apostles who were then living were made subject to blessed Peter. Third, thus: it is recognised that the head has primacy over the other members, and blessed Peter was the head of the Apostles, as Pope Leo testifies, who, as it is found in Dist. 19, c. Ista beatus, says: Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race, so arranged that the truth, which was proclaimed before by the law and the Prophets, should go out for the salvation of the whole world through the Apostolic trumpet, as it is written: Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. But the Lord willed that the sacrament of this office, pertaining to the duty of all the Apostles, should be placed chiefly in blessed Peter, the highest of all the Apostles, so that from him, as from a kind of head, he might pour out his gifts over the whole body. From these words it is plainly evident that blessed Peter was appointed head of the Apostles by Christ, and had primacy over them from Christ. Fourth, thus: he who in the time of the Apostles appointed the elders of all the churches had primacy over the Apostles themselves. But in the time of the Apostles blessed Peter appointed the elders of all the churches, according to the words of Pope Innocent, who, as is read in Dist. 11, c. Quis nesciat, says: Since it has been made manifest that no one in all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa and Sicily, and the islands lying between, appointed any to churches except those whom the venerable Apostle Peter and his successors had appointed as elders. Therefore blessed Peter had primacy over the other Apostles. Fifth, thus: blessed Peter had received power to rule all the Apostles, as Gregory testifies, who, as is quoted in C. 11, q. 7, c. Petrus, says: Peter had received power to rule, and yet the same Apostle, first among the Apostles, was complained of against him, etc. Therefore blessed Peter had power and primacy over the Apostles. Disciple. I do not mind your bringing many arguments for the truth you have stated, since authority should be enough to hold it. The universal Church sings of blessed Peter: You are the shepherd of the sheep, the prince of the Apostles. So go on to the other four assertions you mentioned, and briefly explain the reasons for them.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: In quo probatur secunda, tertia & quarta assertionibus praeditis arguitur: & praecipue pro quarta.
units.tr: In which the second, third and fourth assertions are proved, and the fourth in particular is argued against.

units.la: Magist. Secunda assertio praedictorum est propositia sc. supra c. 14. quod beatus Petrus non fuit Romanus episcopus. Ad quod ponendum mouentur ex hoc, quod in tota scriptura divina actus Apostolicos describente minime reperitur, quod beatus Petrus fuerit Romae, & non videtur verisimile, quod beatus Petrus rexisset Romanam ecclesiam: & tamen beatus Lucas de ipso nullam omnino fecisset mentionem. Tertia assertio est: quod beatus Petrus ex ordinatione Apostolorum super eos habuit principatum. Et auctoritate beati Anacleti, quae ponitur 21. dist. in nono, ostenditur, ait enim loquens de beato Petro: caeteri vero Apostoli cum eodem pari consortio honorem & potestatem acceperunt, ipsumque principem eorum esse voluerunt. Ergo ex electione Apostolorum beatus Petrus factus est princeps eorum. Quarta assertio eorum est, quod ex ordinatione Christi nullus sacerdos super alios habet potestatem aliquam. Nec vnus habet maiorem potestatem super gregem sibi commissum, quam alius, ex constitutione Christi. Sed omnis superioritas vnius sacerdotis super alium in remedium schismatis est propter bonum commune ab ipsis etiam sacerdotibus instituta. Haec autem auctoritate Hieronym. (quae ponitur di. 93. c. legimus) probare nituntur, ait enim: Cum Apostolus perspicue docet eosdem esse episcopos, quos presbyteros, quid patitur mensarum & viduarum minister &c. Et infra: audi aliud testimonium, in quo etiam manifestissime declaratur vel comprobatur eundem esse episcopum & presbyterum, propter hoc reliqui te Creta, vt ea quae deerant corriperes & constitueres presbyteros per civitates, sicut ego tibi mandavi, si quis sine crimine, vnius vxoris vir, filios habens fideles, & non in accusatione luxuriae, aut non subditos, oportet enim episcopum esse sine crimine quasi Dei dispensatorem, 1. ad Tim. 4. Noli negligere gratiam, quae data est tibi per prophetiam & per impositionem manus mei presbyterii. Sed & Petrus in prima epistola: presbyteros, qui in nobis sunt precor ego compresbyter, & infra. Parua tibi videntur tantorum virorum testimonia, clangat tuba euangelica filius tonitrui quem Deus amauit plurimum, qui de pectore Saluatoris doctrinarum fluenta potauit, presbyter electa Domina & filiis eius quos ego diligo in veritate. Et in alia Epistola presbyter Caio carissimo quem ego in veritate diligo. Quod autem postea vnus electus est, qui, vt praeponeretur caeteris in schismatis remedium factum est, ne vnusquisque, ad se trahens ecclesiam Christi rumperet, nam & Alexandria à Marco Euangelista vsque ad Heradam & Dionysium episcopos presbyteri semper ex se vnum eligebant, & in excelsiori gradu collocabant, quem episcopum nominabant, quomodo si exercitus imperatorem faciat. Ex his verbis colligunt isti, quod inter presbyteros, de qb. exemplificat beatus Hieron. nulla erat superioritas ex ordinatione Christi, cum post exempla omnia supra dicta dicat Hiero. quod autem unus electus est, qui ceteris praponeretur, in schismatis remedium factus est. Ex quibus datur intelligi, quod praelatio unius presbyteri super alios post ordinationem Christi ab ipsis presbyteris existit instituta. Beatus autem Hiero. exemplificat de B. Petro & de B. Iohanne Evangelista, & de aliis presbyteris per Timotheum constituendis. Ergo B. Petrus super alios presbyteros qualescunq; ex ordinatione Christi nullam habuit superioritatem. Ex quo concludunt, quod nullus presbyter ex ordinatione Christi est superior alio, sed ex ordinatione humana tantum modo. Item specialiter, quod episcopi super presbyteros superioritatem non habeant ex ordinatione Christi, auctoritate Hiero. super epistolam ad Thimo. quae ponitur di. 95. ca. olim, ostendunt, ait enim: olim idem presbyter & episcopus, & antequam diaboli instinctu studia in religione vel schismata fierent, & diceretur in populis: ego sum Pauli, ego sum Apollo, ego Cephae, communi presbyterorum concilio gubernabatur: postquam unusquisque eos, quos baptizaverat suos esse putabat, non Christi, in toto orbe decretum est, ut unus de presbyteris superponeretur & schismatis semina tollerentur. Et paulo post: sicut ergo presbyteri sciunt se ex ecclesiae consuetudine ei, qui sibi praepositus fuerat esse subiectos, ita episcopi ipsi noverunt se magis consuetudine, quam dispensatione Dominica veritate presbyteris esse maiores, & in communi debere ecclesiam regere. His verbis, ut videtur, aptissime affirmatur, quod ex institutione divina inter presbyteros & episcopos nulla est distinctio. Unde isti dicunt, quod olim quilibet episcopus erat presbyter, & quilibet presbyter erat episcopus, & ideo tota distinctio inter Papam & patriarcham, archiepiscopos & episcopos, & inter episcopos & presbyteros solummodo ex ordinatione humana est, & non ex ordinatione Christi.
units.tr: Master. The second of the aforesaid assertions is the proposition (see above, chapter 14) that St Peter was not bishop of Rome. They are moved to hold this because nowhere in the whole of divine Scripture, in the Acts of the Apostles, is it found that St Peter was at Rome, and it does not seem likely that St Peter governed the Roman Church; and yet St Luke would have made no mention of him at all. The third assertion is that St Peter had pre-eminence over the others by the appointment of the Apostles. This is shown by the authority of St Anacletus, which is cited in dist. 21, in the ninth, for he says, speaking of St Peter: The other Apostles, however, received honour and power with him on equal terms, and they wished him to be their prince. Therefore, by the election of the Apostles, St Peter was made their prince. The fourth assertion of theirs is that by the ordinance of Christ no priest has any power at all over others, and that one does not have greater power over the flock committed to him than another by the constitution of Christ. Any superiority of one priest over another, as a remedy for schism, is for the common good and was instituted by the priests themselves. They try to prove this by the authority of Jerome (which is cited in dist. 93, c. legimus), for he says: Since the Apostle clearly teaches that the bishops and the presbyters are the same, what becomes of the minister of tables and of widows? etc. And below: Hear another testimony, in which it is also very plainly declared and proved that the bishop and the presbyter are the same: "For this cause I left you in Crete, that you should set in order the things that were wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed you: if any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of riot or unruly. For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God" (1 Tim. 4). "Neglect not the gift that is in you, which was given you by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery" (1 Tim. 4). And Peter in his first epistle: "The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder" (1 Pet. 5). And further on: Do the testimonies of such great men seem small to you? Let the Gospel trumpet sound, the son of thunder whom God loved most, who drank the streams of doctrine from the breast of the Saviour: "The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth." And in another epistle: "The elder to the most beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth" (3 John 1). But that afterwards one was chosen, who was set over the others as a remedy for schism, was done so that no one, drawing the Church of Christ to himself, might tear it apart. For at Alexandria, from the Evangelist Mark down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always chose one of their own and placed him in a higher rank, calling him bishop, just as an army makes a general. From these words those people conclude that among the presbyters, of whom St Jerome gives examples, there was no superiority by the ordinance of Christ, since Jerome, after all the examples cited above, says that the one who was chosen to be set over the others was made so as a remedy for schism. From this it is understood that the preeminence of one presbyter over the others after the ordinance of Christ was instituted by the presbyters themselves. St Jerome gives examples of St Peter, of St John the Evangelist, and of other presbyters to be appointed by Timothy. Therefore St Peter had no superiority over the other presbyters, whatever they were, by the ordinance of Christ. From this they conclude that no presbyter is superior to another by the ordinance of Christ, but only by human ordinance. Likewise, that bishops do not have superiority over presbyters by the ordinance of Christ, they show by the authority of Jerome on the epistle to Timothy, which is cited in dist. 95, c. olim; for he says: Formerly the presbyter and the bishop were the same, and before, at the instigation of the devil, parties arose in religion and schisms, and it was said among the peoples, "I am of Paul, I am of Apollos, I am of Cephas," they were governed by the common council of the presbyters. After each one began to think that those whom he had baptized were his own and not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be set over the others, so that the seeds of schism might be removed. And a little later: Just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one who was set over them, so bishops also know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the Lord's disposition, and that they ought to rule the Church in common. From these words it is very clearly affirmed, as it seems, that by divine institution there is no distinction between presbyters and bishops. Hence these men say that formerly every bishop was a presbyter and every presbyter was a bishop, and therefore the whole distinction between the Pope and the patriarch, between archbishops and bishops, and between bishops and presbyters, is by human ordinance only and not by the ordinance of Christ.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XVIII.

units.la: In quo arguitur pro quinta & sexta assertionibus.
units.tr: In which the fifth and sixth assertions are argued for.

units.la: Disc. Quinta assertio praedictorum est: Quod Romana ecclesia ante tempora Constantini super alias ecclesias non habuit principatum. Sexta vero assertio eorum est: Quod Romana ecclesia a Constantino Imperatore super alias ecclesias primatum & principatum accepit. Istas autem duas assertiones simul quidam sic niktuntur probare. Constantinus Imperator constituit, ut Romanus Pontifex esset caput omnium ecclesiarum. Ergo Romana ecclesia a Constantino & non aliter super alias ecclesias habuit principatum. Antecedens probatur per illud in decre. di. 96. & accipitur de gestis B. Silvestri, ubi sic habetur: Constantinus Imperator quarto die sui baptismatis privilegium Romanae ecclesiae Pontificis contulit, ut in toto orbe Romae Pontifices vel sacerdotes ita caput suum habeant, sicut iudices regem. Et infra: Et sicut nostra est terrena imperialis potentia, ita & eius sacrosanctam ecclesiam Romanam decernimus venerantes honorare & amplius, quam nostrum imperium terrenumque thronum sedem sacrosanctam B. Petri gloriose exaltari, tribuentes ei potestatem & gloriam & dignitatem atque vigorem, & honorificentiam, imperialem atque decernentes sancimus, ut principatum teneat tam super quatuor sedes Alexandrinam, Antiochenam, Hierosolymitanam & Constantinopolitanam, quam etiam super omnes in universo orbe terrarum Dei ecclesias. Et Pontifex qui pro tempore ipsius sacrosanctae Romanae ecclesiae extiterit, celsior & princeps cunctis sacerdotibus & totius mundi existat, & eius iudicio, qua ad cultum vel fidem Christianorum & stabilitatem procreanda fuerint, firmiter disponantur. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, ut videtur, quod Romana ecclesia non nisi a Constantino super alias ecclesias obtinuit principatum.
units.tr: Disc. The fifth assertion of the aforesaid is this: that the Roman church had no pre-eminence over the other churches before the time of Constantine. The sixth assertion of theirs is this: that the Roman church received the primacy and pre-eminence over the other churches from the Emperor Constantine. Some people try to prove these two assertions together in this way. Emperor Constantine ordained that the Roman Pontiff should be the head of all the churches. Therefore the Roman church had pre-eminence over the other churches from Constantine and from no other source. The antecedent is proved by the passage in Decretum, dist. 96, which is taken from the Acts of St. Silvester, where it reads as follows: "On the fourth day after his baptism, the Emperor Constantine conferred on the Pontiff of the Roman church the privilege that, throughout the whole world, the Pontiffs or priests of Rome should have their head just as judges have a king." And further on: "And just as our earthly imperial power is ours, so we decree that the most holy church of Rome be honoured and exalted above our imperial power and earthly throne, with reverence, and that the most holy see of the blessed Peter be gloriously raised up, giving it power, glory, dignity, vigour and imperial honour; and we decree and sanction that it hold the primacy both over the four sees of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople, and also over all the churches of God in the whole world. And the Pontiff who shall be in office for the time being in that most holy Roman church shall be higher and the prince of all priests and of the whole world, and by his judgement shall be firmly settled whatever is to be ordained for the worship and faith of Christians and for their stability." From these words it is given to understand, as it seems, that the Roman church obtained pre-eminence over the other churches only from Constantine.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Ubi ponitur contraria super principatu Romanae ecclesiae assertio, sive opinio, scil. quod Romana ecclesia non accepit a Constantino Imperatore super alias ecclesias principatum, sed hanc habuit a conciliis generalibus.
units.tr: Where the contrary assertion is set out concerning the primacy of the Roman church, or opinion, namely that the Roman church did not receive primacy over the other churches from the Emperor Constantine, but held it from the general councils.

units.la: Disc. Ista assertio de principatu Romanae ecclesiae mihi non placet, ideo assertionem contrariam allegationibus fulcire conaris. Mag. Pluribus modis ponitur, quod Romana ecclesia ante temporā Constantini super omnes alias habuit principatum, sed unus modus est, quod habuit principatum auctoritate conciliorum generalium. Unde in decre. sic legitur 1. di. 17. §. hinc etiam scientes, quod eius sedi primam Petri Apostoli meritis, deinde secunda iussione Domini conciliorum venerandorum auctoritas singularem in ecclesiis tradidit potestatem. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod veneranda concilia tradiderunt sedi B. Petri singularem super ecclesias potestatem.
units.tr: Student: This assertion about the primacy of the Roman church does not please me, so you are trying to support the contrary assertion with arguments. Master: It is put forward in several ways that the Roman church had primacy over all the others before the time of Constantine, but one way is that it had primacy by the authority of the general councils. Hence in the Decretum it is read thus (Dist. 17, §. Hinc etiam scientes): "Knowing that to this see the authority of the venerable councils, first by the merits of the Apostle Peter and then by the second command of the Lord, gave a singular power over the churches." From these words it is held that the venerable councils gave to the see of Blessed Peter a singular power over the churches.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: Ubi deducitur auctoritatibus, quod ecclesia Romana super alias ecclesias habuit princi- patum immediate a Christo per evangelium, & ante ascensionem.
units.tr: Where it is shown from authorities that the Roman Church had primacy over the other churches immediately from Christ, through the Gospel, and before the ascension.

units.la: Disc. Aliter dicit, quod Romana ecclesia a Christo immediate, qui ordinavit B. Petrum in summum Pontificem, dicens: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam, super omnes ecclesias primatum & principatum accepit. Hoc Pelagius Papa in decr. di. 21. c. quanquam, aperte sentire videtur, cum dicit: Sancta Romana ecclesia catholica & Apostolica nullis synodicis constitutionibus caeteris ecclesiis praelata est, sed evangelica voce Domini & Salvatoris. toris nostri primatum obtinuit tu es (inquiens Deus) Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Hoc etiam Nicolaus Papa videtur asserere, qui, ut legitur 22.di.c.1. ait: omnes siue Patriarchae in cuiuslibet apicem, siue metropoleos primatus, ac episcopatus cathedras, vel ecclesiarum cuiuslibet ordinis instituit Romana ecclesia: illam vero solus ipse fundauit, & supra Petram fidei mox nascentis erexit, & parum post: non ergo qualiber terrena sententia, sed illud verbum, per quod constitutum est coelum & terra, per quod dicitur, quia condita sunt omnia elementa, ecclesiam fundauit Romanam. His etiam verbis Anacletus consentire videtur, qui, ut habetur 22.dist.ca. sacrosancta, ait: sacrosancta ecclesia & Apostolica non ab Apostolis: sed ab ipso Domino nostro saluatore primatum obtinuit: sicut beato Petro Apostolo dixit: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Hoc etiam Gelasius Papa, ut legitur 9.q.3.c. cuncta, comprobare videtur. Ait enim: Apostolica sedes sine vlla synodo precedente & soluendi quod synodus iniquè damnauerat, nulla synodo exercente, quos oportuit habuit facultatem, & hoc nimirum pro suo principatu, quem beatus Petrus Domini voce & tenuit semper & tenebit. Item Leo Papa, ut habetur 24.q.1.c. cum beatissimus, ait: cum beatissimus Petrus Apostolus a Domino acceperit principatum, & Romana ecclesia in eius remaneat institutis. Ex his omnibus datur intelligi, quod Romana ecclesia ab ipso Christo ante ascensionem eius in coelum recepit & habuit super omnes alias ecclesias principatum.
units.tr: Disc. Another view holds that the Roman Church received from Christ directly, who appointed blessed Peter as supreme Pontiff, saying: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church," primacy and sovereignty over all churches. Pope Pelagius seems clearly to hold this in the Decretum, dist. 21, c. "quanquam," when he says: "The holy Roman Church, catholic and apostolic, has been placed above other churches by no synodal decrees, but by the evangelical voice of the Lord and our Saviour it obtained primacy, when (God says) 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.'" Pope Nicholas also seems to assert this, who, as is read in dist. 22, c. 1, says: "The Roman Church established all patriarchs, whether at the summit of any metropolitan primacy or episcopal sees, or churches of any rank; but it alone founded that church and raised it upon the rock of the faith just then coming into being." And a little later: "It was therefore not by any earthly sentence, but by that word through which heaven and earth were established, and through which all the elements are said to have been created, that he founded the Roman Church." Anacletus also seems to agree with these words, who, as is held in dist. 22, c. "sacrosancta," says: "The holy and apostolic Church obtained primacy not from the apostles, but from our Lord and Saviour himself, who said to blessed Peter the apostle: 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.'" Pope Gelasius likewise seems to confirm this, as is read in C. 9, q. 3, c. "cuncta." For he says: "The apostolic see, without any preceding synod, and with no synod exercising authority, had the power to loose what a synod had unjustly condemned, and to hold accountable those it ought to; and this indeed by its primacy, which blessed Peter held and will always hold by the voice of the Lord." Likewise Pope Leo, as is found in C. 24, q. 1, c. "cum beatissimus," says: "Since blessed Peter the apostle received primacy from the Lord, the Roman Church remains in his institutions." From all these things it is understood that the Roman Church received and held primacy over all other churches from Christ himself, before his ascension into heaven.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod ecclesia Romana super omnes alias ecclesias habuit principatum immediate a Petro se transferente in ecclesiam Romanam, quo probato deducuntur corollarie tres conclusiones, vbi postea notatur, si tamen possit transferre sedem a Roma ad aliam ciuitatem, vbi respondetur secundam opinionem, quod sic, opinio secunda.
units.tr: In which it is proved that the Roman Church had supremacy over all other churches immediately, by Peter transferring his see to the Roman Church. Once this is proved, three corollary conclusions follow, and it is then asked whether the Pope could transfer his see from Rome to another city. The answer is given according to the second opinion, that he can. Second opinion.

units.la: Mag. Tertius modus dicendi est, quod Romana ecclesia non habuit immediate a Christo super alias ecclesias principatum: imo per plures annos Domini post ascensionem alii ecclesiae fuit subiecta, nec etiam habuit primo principatum a conciliis, vel etiam a collegio Apostolorum. Sed primo immediate habuit principatum a B. Petro transferente sedem suam in Romanam ecclesiam, eam omnibus ecclesiis aliis praeferente, & ideo a Christo habuit immediate principatum. B. enim Petrus electus in Papam & praelatum totius ecclesiae a saluatore ante ascensionem pro se & pro suis successoribus, ac etiam pro ecclesia, vbi sedem suam disponeret collocare, primatum habuit. Et ideo quia transtulit sedem suam de Antiochia, extunc Romana ecclesia super alias ecclesias obtinuit principatum. Hoc Marcellinus scribens omnibus episcopis per Antiochiam constitutis, vt habetur 24.q.1.c. rogamus, ait enim: Rogamus vos fratres dilectissimi, vt non aliud doceatis neque sentiatis, quam a B. Petro Apostolo & reliquis Apostolis & patribus accepistis, ipse est caput totius ecclesiae: cui Dominus ait: Tu es Petrus, & super & c. Eius sedes primitus fuit apud vos, quae postea iubente Domino Roma translata est, cui adminiculante gratia diuina hodierna die ipsi praesidemus. Si vero vestra Antiochia, quae olim prima erat, Romana cessit sedi, nulla est quae non sit subiecta eius ditioni. Ex his plures assertiones ad suum propositum pertinentes isti niti untur colligere. Quarum prima est, quod Dominus ante ascensionem suam B. Petrum caput constituit totius ecclesiae. Et hoc etiam Anacletus Papa, vt habetur di.22 c, sacrosanctam, asserit manifeste dicens, inter B. Apostolos quaedam fuit dissensio, & licet oes Apostoli essent cum B. Petro, tamen a Domino concessum est (& ipsi inter se idipsum voluerunt) vt reliquis omnib. praeesset Apostolis, & Cephas, id est caput & principatum teneret Apostolatus, quod Christus promisit dicens: tu vocaberis Cephas. Secunda assertio, quam isti colligunt ex praedictis est, quod ecclesia Antiochena super alias ecclesias habuit principatum. Quia sicut B. Petrus fuit praelatus & princeps Christianorum omnium, ita eius sedes prima fuit inter oes ecclesias. B. aut Petrus prius Romae habuit sedem Antiochiae, sicut hic dicitur. Quod etiam asserit Anacletus di. vbi prius: tertia vero sedes Antiochiae eiusdem B. Petri Apostoli habetur honorabilis, quam illic prius quam Romam veniret habuit. Et his concordat Anteros Papa, vt scribitur 7.q.1.c. mutationes, dicens, Petrus factus magister meus, tibi princeps Apostolorum de Antiochia ciuitate vtilitatis causa est translatus Romam, vt ibidem potius proficere posset. Ex his habet, quod sedes Petri primo fuit Antiochiae: vbi (sicut in Cronicis reperitur) sedit annis septem, & ista ecclesia Antiochena septem annis super oes ecclesias & super Romanam sedem ante quam aliqui Romani conuersi fuissent, obtinuit principatum. Tertia assertio, quam colligunt ex praedictis est, quod Romana ecclesia post Antiochiam obtinuit principatum, & sic post passionem Domini duxerunt undecim anni, antequam ecclesia Romana haberet super alias ecclesias principatum. Ex quo concludunt, quod ante ascensionem Domini nequaquam habuit principatum. Dist. Si praedicta vera essent, ecclesia Hierosolymitana super alias ecclesias quatuor annis haberet principatum: quia sicut habetur in Cronicis B. Petrus post passionem Domini ante quam Antiochiae sibi sedem eligeret, cathedram quatuor annis tenuit, nec legitur vbi sederit nisi Hierosolymis, ergo Hierosolymitana ecclesia super alias ecclesias tunc obtinuit principatum: quod tamen veritatem non videtur habere. Mag. Ad hoc respondetur, quod B. Petrus quatuor annis tenuit cathedram, nullam sibi ecclesiam eligendo, sed tanquam praelatus & princeps omnium sedebat vbicumque volebat. Sed post quatuor annos sibi in Antiochia sedem elegit, volens alium (dum esset ibidem) praefficere ipsum, & ideo non Hierosolymitana ecclesia fuit prima: quia, sicut legitur in Legenda B. Iacobi, idem Iacobus statim post passionem Domini ab Apostolis Hierosolymitanorum fuit episcopus ordinatus, & ita Petrus illam ecclesiam sibi non appropriauit: sed illi, sicut caeteris omnibus, praefuit, & ita non Petrum episcoepiscopum habuit speciale, aliter fuisset de ecclesia Antiochena. Disc. Adhuc cupio scire, an secundum istos Papa potest transferre sedem Papalem de Roma in aliam ciuitatem. Mag. Ad hoc quidam eorum dicunt, q; bene potest fieri auctoritate summi Pontificis, quorum ratio est, quia Papa respectu sedis Apostolicae est tantae potestatis, quantae fuit B. Petrus, sicut ergo B. Petrus utilitatis causa transtulit sedem suam de una ciuitate ad aliam: ita potest Papa sedem Papalem de Roma transferre ad aliam ciuitatem. Disc. Nunquid secundum istos esset concedendum, si Papa transferret sedem Parisios, q; ecclesia Parisiensis voce euangelica Domini obtinuit principatum? Mag. Diceretur quod sic: quia illo modo dicitur de Romana ecclesia, quod voce euangelica Domini obtinuit principatum, propter hoc quod Deus ante ascensionem suam (ut Euangelia testantur) B. Petro contulit principatum, cui dedit potestatem praeficiendi quamcunq; ecclesiam, in qua sibi sedem eligeret in ecclesiis vniuersis, ita ecclesia Parisiensis diceretur obtinere super alias ecclesias voce Euangelica Domini principatum, quia Dominus ante ascensionem suam cuilibet successori B. Petri in ipso Petro dedit potestatem quamcunq; ecclesiam praeficiendi aliis ecclesiis vniuersis. Disc. Tenerent omnes isti, quod Papa posset sedem transferre de Roma. Mag. Multi eorum affirmant, quod Papa non potest: quia B. Petrus non auctoritate propria, sed iubente Domino de Antiochia sedem transtulit Romam, & ideo non posset transferre eandem sedem de Roma, nisi Dominus ipse iuberet. Disc. Dic aliam rationem, qua ostenditur, quod ecclesia Hierosolymitana super omnes alias ecclesias quatuor annis habuit principatum. Mag. Alia ratio est, quod verum est; etiam ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam tanto tempore habuisse super alias omnes ecclesias principatum, eo quod tot annis ibi sedit beatus Petrus.
units.tr: Mag. The third way of speaking is this: the Roman Church did not have supremacy over other churches immediately from Christ. Indeed, for several years after the Lord's ascension it was subject to other churches, and it did not first receive its supremacy from councils or even from the college of the Apostles. Rather, it first had supremacy from the Blessed Peter, who transferred his see to the Roman Church and set it above all other churches. Therefore it had supremacy immediately from Christ. For the Blessed Peter, chosen by the Saviour before the ascension to be Pope and prelate of the whole Church, held the primacy for himself, for his successors, and also for the church in which he would decide to establish his see. And so, because he transferred his see from Antioch, the Roman Church from that time obtained supremacy over the other churches. Marcellinus, writing to all the bishops established in Antioch, says this, as found in 24 q. 1 c. Rogamus: "We ask you, most beloved brothers, that you teach and hold nothing other than what you received from the Blessed Peter the Apostle, the other Apostles and the Fathers. He is the head of the whole Church, to whom the Lord said: 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church' [Matth. 16.]. His see was first among you, but afterwards, at the Lord's command, it was transferred to Rome, where, by divine grace, we preside today. If your Antioch, which was once first, has yielded to the Roman see, then there is no church that is not subject to its authority." From these statements, those who labour to gather them draw several assertions relevant to their purpose. The first is that before his ascension the Lord appointed the Blessed Peter head of the whole Church. Pope Anacletus also asserts this plainly, as found in dist. 22 c. Sacrosanctam, saying: "There was a certain disagreement among the Blessed Apostles. Although all the Apostles were with the Blessed Peter, it was nevertheless granted by the Lord (and they themselves wished the same among themselves) that he should preside over all the other Apostles, and that Cephas, that is, the head, should hold the principate of the Apostleship, as Christ promised when he said: 'You shall be called Cephas' [John 1.]." The second assertion that they draw from the foregoing is that the Church of Antioch had supremacy over the other churches. For just as the Blessed Peter was the prelate and prince of all Christians, so his see was first among all churches. But the Blessed Peter had his see at Antioch before Rome, as is said here. Anacletus also asserts this in the passage cited above: "The third see, that of Antioch, is held to be honourable, which the same Blessed Peter the Apostle held there before he came to Rome." Pope Anteros agrees with these words, as written in 7 q. 1 c. Mutationes, saying: "Peter, made my master, was transferred from the city of Antioch to Rome, the prince of the Apostles, for the sake of usefulness, so that he might be able to make greater progress there." From this it follows that the see of Peter was first at Antioch, where (as is found in the chronicles) he sat for seven years, and this Church of Antioch held the supremacy over all churches and over the Roman see for seven years, before any Romans had been converted. The third assertion that they draw from the foregoing is that the Roman Church obtained supremacy after Antioch, and so eleven years passed after the Lord's passion before the Roman Church had supremacy over the other churches. From this they conclude that it had no supremacy at all before the Lord's ascension. Disc. If the foregoing were true, the Church of Jerusalem would have held supremacy over the other churches for four years. For, as the chronicles record, after the Lord's passion and before he chose his see at Antioch, the Blessed Peter held the chair for four years, and it is read that he sat nowhere but at Jerusalem. Therefore the Church of Jerusalem then obtained supremacy over the other churches, which nevertheless does not seem to be true. Mag. To this it is answered that the Blessed Peter held the chair for four years without choosing any church for himself, but sat wherever he wished as prelate and prince of all. But after four years he chose Antioch for his see, wishing (while he was there) to set another over it. Therefore the Church of Jerusalem was not the first, because, as is read in the Legend of the Blessed James, that same James was ordained bishop of the Jerusalem churches by the Apostles immediately after the Lord's passion. Thus Peter did not appropriate that church to himself, but presided over it, as over all the others, and so he did not have a special bishopric there, otherwise it would have been the Church of Antioch. Disc. I still want to know whether, according to these men, the Pope can transfer the papal see from Rome to another city. Mag. To this, some of them say that it can well be done by the authority of the supreme Pontiff. Their reason is that the Pope, with respect to the Apostolic see, has as much power as the Blessed Peter had. Therefore, just as the Blessed Peter, for the sake of usefulness, transferred his see from one city to another, so the Pope can transfer the papal see from Rome to another city. Disc. Would these men therefore have to concede, if the Pope transferred the see to Paris, that the Church of Paris would obtain supremacy by the evangelical voice of the Lord? Mag. It would be said that it would, because in that way it is said of the Roman Church that it obtained supremacy by the evangelical voice of the Lord, on account of the fact that God, before his ascension (as the Gospels testify), conferred supremacy on Peter, to whom he gave the power of setting over the universal Church whatever church he chose as his see. In the same way the Church of Paris would be said to obtain supremacy over the other churches by the evangelical voice of the Lord, because the Lord, before his ascension, gave to any successor of Peter, in Peter himself, the power of setting over all the other churches whatever church he chose. Disc. Would all of these men hold that the Pope could transfer the see from Rome? Mag. Many of them affirm that the Pope cannot, because the Blessed Peter did not transfer the see from Antioch to Rome by his own authority, but at the Lord's command. Therefore he could not transfer the same see from Rome unless the Lord himself commanded it. Disc. Give another reason which shows that the Church of Jerusalem had supremacy over all other churches for four years. Mag. Another reason is true: the Church of Jerusalem had supremacy over all other churches for so long because the Blessed Peter sat there for so many years.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: In quo reuertitur ad praecedentis tertiae quaestionis principalis decisionem, ponendo probandoque contrariam priori assertionem, scilicet quod Romana ecclesia, quae est a totali congregatione fidelium distincta, potest contra fidem errare, & hoc quidem probat hic vnica tantum ratione.
units.tr: In which he returns to the decision of the principal question of the third question, setting out and proving the opposite of the earlier assertion, namely that the Roman Church, which is distinct from the whole congregation of the faithful, can err against the faith. He proves this with only one argument.

units.la: Disc. Omissa ista materia de principatu Romanae ecclesiae, ad propositum principale reuertere, & motiua tenentiu, q; Romana ecclesia, quae est distincta a congregatione fidelium (sicut caput a corpore) possit contra fidem errare, adducas in medium. Mag. Ad probandum ecclesiam Romanam contra fidem posse errare, nonnulli plures rationes adducunt. Quorundam autem ratio fundamentalis est quaedam ratio saepe tacta superius ad illas assertiones ostendendas, quae talis est. Illud, q; promittitur toti & nulli parti, non debuit alicui parti attribui, etiam principaliori. Sed nunquam errare contra fidem toti congregationi fidelium promissum fuit a Christo, & nulli parti fuit hoc promissum a Christo, ergo non debet hoc alicui particulari ecclesiae catholicorum attribui, cum ergo Romana ecclesia sit pars ecclesiae, & non sit tota ecclesia, non posse errare contra fidem, non est attribuendum Romanae ecclesiae. Disc. Nonne qu Christus dixit Petro: ego pro te rogaui, Petre, vt non deficiat fides tua, promisit ecclesiae, cuius Petrus erat futurum caput, quod nunq; fides sua deficeret? Mag. Dicunt q; hoc dixit Christus Petro non in persona alicuius ecclesiae particularis, sed pro vniuersali ecclesia. Cuius rationem assignant dicentes: quia qu Christus dixit verba praedicta Petro, Petrus non magis fuit caput ecclesiae Romanae, q; Antiochiae: quia tunc habiturus erat primo sedem in Antiochia, & postea in Roma. Cum ergo in verbis praedictis non plus fiat mentio de Roma quam de Antiochia, non plus debet intelligi de Roma q; de Antiochia: Quia verba generalia ad omnia particularia aequaliter se habent, sed praedicta verba no debet intelligi de Antiochia: quia fides illius ecclesiae iam defecit, ergo nec de Romana ecclesia debent intelligi. Disc. Quomodo dicunt, q; fides ecclesiae Antiochiae defecit, cum adhuc sit patriarcha Antiochenus, qui potest vocari ecclesia Antiochena? Mag. Quod sit aliquis patriarcha Antiochenus, non est ex promissione Christi, sed ex voluntaria summi Pontificis ordinatione, qui creat patriarcha talem, licet ecclesia Antiochena defecerit & saepe accidit, q; nullus est patriarcha Antiochenus. Disc. Licet moriatur patriarcha Antiochenus, non tn moritur ecclesia Antiochena, quia adhuc remanet aliquis, qui potest creari in patriarcham Antiochenum. Mag. Per talem modum potest dici, quod nunquam potest deficere fides ecclesiae Massiliensis, quia semper est aliquis, qui posset creari in episcopum Massilien. Dicunt ergo isti, cum ex solis scripturis diuinis teneatur, q; ecclesia Christiana nunq; errauit contra fidem: quia semper erunt in ecclesia Christi fideles & verba scripturae diuinae intelligentes. Ex his colligitur, q; ecclesia nunquam errabit contra fidem. Et cum nulla de Romana ecclesia faciat penitus mentionem, no plus quam de ecclesia Antiochena, sicut temerarium fuit asserere q; ecclesia Antiochena no errabit contra fidem, ita & nunc temerarium est asserere, quod Romana ecclesia nunquam errabit contra fidem. Disc. Licet scriptura diuina, quae insinuat quod ecclesia nunquam errabit contra fidem, de Romana ecclesia non vocalem faciat mentionem: tn de Romana ecclesia verba illa scripturae debent intelligi: quia scriptura diuina est intelligenda, sicut a sanctis patribus est exposita, sancti autem intelligunt verba de Romana ecclesia. Unde & asserunt, quod Romana ecclesia nunquam errabit contra fidem. Mag. Ad hoc tripliciter respondetur, q; sancti non exponunt verba ista scripturae de Romana ecclesia prout Romana ecclesia est pars distincta contra ecclesias: sed exponunt verba scripturae de materia illa loquentia de ecclesia catholica & Apostolica, quae comprehendit omnem ecclesiam tenentem fidem Apostolorum, siue Romae, siue in Hispania, siue in Anglia, siue in Gallia, siue in Alemania. Nec dicunt, quod Romana ecclesia, quæ est Romæ vel de facto gerit se pro Romana ecclesia, non posset errare vel nunquam errabit contra fidem. Licet aliquando affirment, q; non inueniatur errasse secundum se totā, q̄uis aliquando pro maiori parte errauerit. Tempore n. Liberii, postquam consensit fidei Arrianæ, maior pars Christianorum Romę hæreticæ prauitati cōsensit, tunc n. pauci Romani Imperatori Liberio resistebāt: & illi pauci clerici, qui erant contrarii Liberio, occidebantur. Licet etiam sancti asseruerint, quod ecclesia Romana secundum se totam in tempore præterito non errauerit contra fidē, nunquam tn affirmant q; non errabit in futuro. Disc. Hi errant aperte: quia sicut allegasti prius, B. Hiero. loquitur de futuro dicens, B. Petro opem ferenti in futuro seculo permanebit sine vlla hereticorum insultatione. Mag. Dicunt te decipi per sermonem ambiguum, cuius sensus nescis distinguere. Verba B. Hiero. secundum vnum sensum æquipollent conditionali tali: si B. Petrus opem tulerit, in futuro seculo permanebit, &c. & ille sensus est verus, licet temerarium sit asserere, quod B. Petrus opem feret, quia nescitur an Deus & similiter B. Petrus deseret Romanam ecclesiam, quemadmodum iam multis temporibus deseruit ecclesiam Antiochenam. Alius sensus æquipollet causali tali: quia B. Petrus opem feret, in futuro seculo permanebit &c. & sic non intelligit Hieron. Tertius sensus est temporalis talis: dum B. Petrus opem feret &c. & ille sensus etiam est verus. Sed nescitur, quanto tempore B. Petrus opem feret Romanæ ecclesiæ contra insultationem hæreticorum. Et ideo temerarium est asserere, quod vsque ad finem seculi opem feret ecclesiæ Romanæ, quæ est pars ecclesiæ vniuersalis, contra hæreticos.
units.tr: Objector. Set aside that matter about the primacy of the Roman Church and return to the main question. Bring forward the arguments by which you hold that the Roman Church, which is distinct from the congregation of the faithful (as the head is from the body), can err against the faith. Teacher. Several people offer many arguments to prove that the Roman Church can err against the faith. The basic argument of some of them is a certain argument, often touched on above, used to demonstrate those assertions, and it runs like this. What is promised to the whole and to no part ought not to be attributed to any part, even a more important one. But Christ promised the whole congregation of the faithful that it would never err against the faith, and he made no such promise to any part. Therefore this should not be attributed to any particular church of Catholics. Since, then, the Roman Church is a part of the church and not the whole church, it should not be attributed to the Roman Church that it cannot err against the faith. Objector. Did not Christ, when he said to Peter, I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail, promise the church of which Peter was to be the head that his faith would never fail? Teacher. They say that Christ said this to Peter not in the person of any particular church but on behalf of the universal church. They give this reason: when Christ spoke those words to Peter, Peter was no more the head of the Roman Church than of the Antiochene Church, since he was going to have his see first in Antioch and afterwards in Rome. Since, then, no more mention is made of Rome than of Antioch in those words, they should be understood no more of Rome than of Antioch, because general words stand equally toward all particulars. But those words cannot be understood of Antioch, because the faith of that church has already failed. Therefore they cannot be understood of the Roman Church either. Objector. How can they say that the faith of the Antiochene Church has failed, when there is still an Antiochene patriarch, who can be called the Antiochene Church? Teacher. That there should be some Antiochene patriarch is not due to a promise of Christ but to the voluntary appointment of the supreme Pontiff, who creates such a patriarch. Yet the Antiochene Church has failed, and it often happens that there is no Antiochene patriarch at all. Objector. Even if the Antiochene patriarch dies, the Antiochene Church does not die, because someone remains who can be created Antiochene patriarch. Teacher. In that way one could say that the faith of the Church of Marseilles can never fail, because there is always someone who could be created bishop of Marseilles. They say, therefore, since it is held from Scripture alone that the Christian Church has never erred against the faith, that there will always be faithful people in the Church of Christ who understand the words of divine Scripture. From this it follows that the Church will never err against the faith. And since Scripture makes no mention at all of the Roman Church, any more than of the Antiochene Church, just as it was rash to assert that the Antiochene Church would not err against the faith, so it is now rash to assert that the Roman Church will never err against the faith. Objector. Although the divine Scripture, which implies that the Church will never err against the faith, makes no explicit mention of the Roman Church, nevertheless those words of Scripture must be understood of the Roman Church, because divine Scripture is to be understood as the holy Fathers have expounded it, and the holy Fathers understand those words of the Roman Church. Hence they also assert that the Roman Church will never err against the faith. Teacher. To this one replies in three ways. The holy Fathers do not expound those words of Scripture of the Roman Church as the Roman Church is a part distinct from the other churches. Rather, they expound the words of Scripture, which speak of that matter, as referring to the catholic and apostolic Church, which comprises every church holding the faith of the Apostles, whether at Rome, in Spain, in England, in Gaul, or in Germany. Nor do they say that the Roman Church, which is at Rome or acts in fact as the Roman Church, could not err or will never err against the faith. Although they sometimes affirm that it is not found to have erred in its entirety, even though at times it erred for the greater part. For in the time of Liberius, after he consented to the Arian faith, the greater part of the Christians at Rome consented to the heretical depravity; only a few Romans then resisted the Emperor Liberius, and those few clergy who were opposed to Liberius were put to death. Even if the holy Fathers have asserted that the Roman Church in its entirety did not err against the faith in past time, they never affirm that it will not err in future. Objector. Those people are plainly wrong, because, as you cited earlier, St Jerome speaks of the future when he says: To St Peter, bringing aid, it will remain in the future age without any insult from heretics. Teacher. You are deceived by an ambiguous statement whose sense you do not know how to distinguish. The words of St Jerome, in one sense, are equivalent to a conditional such as: if St Peter brings aid, it will remain in the future age, and so on. That sense is true, although it is rash to assert that St Peter will bring aid, since it is not known whether God and St Peter will abandon the Roman Church, just as for many ages he has already abandoned the Antiochene Church. Another sense is equivalent to a causal clause: because St Peter will bring aid, it will remain in the future age, and so on. But Jerome does not mean it in that sense. The third sense is temporal: while St Peter brings aid, and so on. That sense too is true. But it is not known for how long St Peter will bring aid to the Roman Church against the insults of heretics. Therefore it is rash to assert that he will bring aid to the Roman Church, which is a part of the universal church, against heretics until the end of the age.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: In quo præcedentis capituli assertionem aliis nouem difficilibus rationibus probat, sc. quod Romana ecclesia specialiter partialiterve sumpta potest contra fidem errare.
units.tr: In which he proves the assertion of the preceding chapter by nine other difficult arguments, namely that the Roman Church, taken specifically or partially, can err against the faith.

units.la: Disc. Vellem scire, an isti aliis rationib. satagunt munire suam assertionem. Mag. Pluribus aliis rationibus suam assertionem fulcire nituntur. Vnde ratio eorum talis est. Omnis ecclesia, quæ incipit post passionē Christi, potest contra fidem errare: quia illa ecclesia, q̄ dixit Christus vsq; in finem seculi in fide p manşuram, fuit etiam in sui parte ante ascensionē Christi. Christus n. prædicens ecclesiā suam vsq; ad finem seculi p manşuram in fide cum dixit Matt. vlt. Vobiscum sum omnib. diebus vsq; ad consummationem seculi, nō solum intelligebat de ecclesia futura post suam ascensionē, sed etiam intelligebat, q; pro nullo tempore nec ante ascensionem, nec post erat tota ecclesia Christianorum à fide catholica recessura. Non ergo intellexit de ecclesia, quæ incipit post ascensionem, sed ecclesia Romana incepit post ascensionē Domini: quia Apostoli & alii discipuli Christi post ascensionem Christi prius prædicauerunt in aliis locis q; Romæ. Ergo verba Christi de ecclesia in fide vsq; in finē seculi p manşura, non debent de ecclesia Romana intelligi determinate, sed sub disiunctione & in communi de Roma & aliis debet intelligi. Quia fides catholica in ecclesia Romana, vel in ecclesia Pisana, vel in aliqua alia vsq; in finem seculi permanebit, semper n. erit aliquis catholicus & fidelis. Tertia ratio eorum est hæc: Ecclesia Romana postquam inchoata fuit, potuit contra fidem errare, ergo adhuc potest errare contra fidem. Antecedens patet, quia ante aduentum B. Petri Romana ecclesia, inchoata ibidem, errare potuit contra fidem, non n. tunc magis erat ecclesia Romana confirmata in fide, quam aliæ ecclesiæ. Cōsequentia patet: quia non legitur, q; in fide postea fuerit cōfirmata, ergo temerarium est asserere quod errare non poterit. Disc. Videtur quod ex quo Apostoli Petrus & Paulus consecrarunt & fundarunt Romanam ecclesiā errare non potuit. Mag. Hoc non videtur secundum istos veritatē habere: quia Apostoli Petrus & Paulus non aliter fundarunt ecclesiam Romanam, nisi Romanos in fide sollicite instruendo, & eos ad fidem & bona opera, doctrina & exemplo, hortando, doctrinā miraculis confirmando, & tandem ciuitatē Romanam suo martyrio consecrando. Sed prædicta omnia fecit Christus Hierosolymitanæ ecclesiæ, quia ipsam diligenter in fide instruxit, ipsamq; ad fidem & bona opera doctrina & exemplis & miraculis hortabatur: pro qua etiam, sicut pro cæteris, mortem accepit, & sic Hierosolyma sua passione & morte cōsecrata fuit. Et tamen per omnia illa ecclesia Hierosolymitana in fide minime extitit confirmata, cum tamen opera, vita & doctrina & mors Christi multo maioris efficaciæ fuerint, quam doctrina, opera & vita & martyrium Apostolorū Petri & Pauli. Etiam alii Apostoli fundauerunt ecclesiam Antiochenam. B. enim Paulus plures fundauerat ecclesias, alii etiam Apostoli alias ecclesias suo martyrio consecrarunt, & tamen nulla earum erat in fide confirmata. Ergo consimiliter non apparet aliud fuisse factum in ecclesia Romana, vnde in fide debeat reputari confirmata. Multa enim maiora & ad stabilitatem fidei facta fuerunt Hierosolymis & in Iudæa, quam in Romana ecclesia. Si ergo nec Hierosolyma nec Iudæa confirmata fuit in fide, temerarium est dicere, quod ecclesia Romana confirmata sit in fide. Vnde etiam ex hoc quarta ratio sic formatur: non magis electa fuit à Deo ecclesia Romana, quam ecclesia Hierosolymitana, sed Deus permisit ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam totam à fide recedere, ergo est temerarium dicere, quod Deus nunquam permittet omnes Romanos à fide recedere. Et ita Romana ecclesia errare poterit contra fidem. Disc. Quāuis omnes Romani, qui conuersantur Romæ, contra fidem errarent, Romana tamen ecclesia non erraret: quia tunc Romana ecclesia non esset Romæ, sed alibi; sicut Romana ecclesia est apud Auinionem. Mag Dicunt isti, quod in hoc cauillose per æquiuocationem conaris pcedere. Quia quærunt, quam ecclesiam vocas Romanam ecclesiam. Aut enim vocas Romanam ecclesiam, Papam, seu multitudinem, siue clericorum siue aliorum in partibus Romanis degentium, vel domicilia ibidem habentium. Aut vocas Romanam ecclesiam, clericos, titulos habentes in Roma. Aut vocas Romanam ecclesiam, Papam cum cardinalibus, vel Papam solum, vel collegium cardinalium. Aut vocas ecclesiam Romanam illos, qui tenent fidem, quam Apostoli fundauerunt & prædicauerunt Romæ. Si primo modo vocas ecclesiam Romanam, stat argumentum: quia omnes Romani habentes domicilia Romæ possent contra fidem errare: sicut & omnes Hierosolymitani aliquando errauerunt. Si secundo modo, adhuc stat argumentum: quia non sunt magis electi clerici à Deo habentes titulos in Roma, quam fuerunt clerici habentes titulos Hierosolymis, illi autem sunt errantes, ergo & omnes habentes titulos in Roma possunt errare. Item temerarium est dicere, quod non possunt omnes habentes titulos in Roma à paganis vel aliis malis occidi, ergo tunc non esset fides in clericis habentib. titulos Romæ. Et (cum tunc deficeret fides) de illis non sunt intelligenda verba Christi, quib. promisit fidem usq; in finem seculi duraturã. Si vocas ecclesiam Romanam, Papa cum cardinalibus, vel Papam solum, vel collegium cardinalium solum: adhuc potest errare, quia temerarium est dicere, Papam cum cardinalibus, si non essent plures, non posse contra fidem errare. Si autem vocas ecclesiam Romanã, quæ tenet fidem, quam Apostoli prædicauerunt & fundauerunt Romæ, sic concedunt, q Romana ecclesia errare non potest, sed illa Romana ecclesia vniuersalis est, vbicunq; fuerint catholici & fideles. Et hæc ecclesia est, quæ vocatur ecclesia catholica & Apostolica, quæ errare non potest, ita comprehendit Pisanos & Lombardos, & Hispanos, sicut Romanos, & de illa sola concedunt isti, q errare non potest. Quinta ratio eorum est hæc: Ecclesia Romana, quæ est una ecclesia particularis, siue comprehendat omnes Romanos, siue clerum Romanum tantummodo, siue Papam cũ cardinalibus, non est magis electa à Deo, q fuerit gens Iudæorum, de qua Christus fuit suscepturus carnê humanam, quos principaliter ipse saluare venerat, ipso dicente Matt. 15. Non sum missus nisi ad oues quæ perierant domus Israel, sed gens illa non fuit confirmata in fide, quin potuerit errare, ergo nec ecclesia Romana est confirmata in fide, quin possit errare. Discipul. Per istam rationé probaretur, quod tota multitudo Christianorum posset cõtra fidem errare: sicut tota multitudo gentis Iudæorum potuit errare contra fidem. Mag. Respondetur, quod argumentum non procedit de tota multitudine Christianorum, sicut de Romana ecclesia: quia extra vniuersalem ecclesiam non est salus eo q Christus nunquã aliam legem præter Christianam est daturus: quemadmodum daturus fuit aliam legem præter legem Iudæorum, extra aũt ecclesiam Romanã, quæ est ecclesia particularis, potest esse salus, multi n. præter Romanos saluantur, & ideo licet argumentum prædictũ concludat de ecclesia Romana, quæ potest errare, sicut potuit errare multitudo Iudæorũ, non tñ concludit de ecclesia vniuersali. Sexta ratio eorum accipitur ex prædictis: quia omnis ecclesia, extra q potest esse salus, potest cõtra fidem errare, extra ecclesiã aût Romanam potest esse salus, quemadmodũ post ascẽsionem Christi fuit salus, antequã Romana ecclesia inchoaretur, ergo Romana ecclesia poterit contra fidẽ errare. Septima eorum ratio est hæc, illa ecclesia, quæ contra fidem errare non potest, non indiget aliorum consilio pro quæstionib fidei terminandis, ecclesia aût Romana indiget aliorum consilio in quæstionibus fidei terminandis, aliter n. ad determinandas & diffiniendas quæstiones motas de fide congregarentur inutiliter cõcilia generalia, ergo ecclesia Romana potest errare contra fidẽ. Octaua ratio eorũ est hæc: Illa ecclesia, quæ potest fieri auctoritate papæ aliis ecclesiis inferior, potest contra fidẽ errare, illa n. ecclesia, quæ nõ potest contra fidẽ errare, non habet aliam ecclesiã superiorem, ecclesia aût Romana auctoritate papæ potest fieri inferior aliis ecclesiis, posset n. papa sedem transferre papalem de Roma ad aliam ciuitatem: quo facto, Romana ecclesia alteri esset subiecta, ergo Romana ecclesia potest contra fidem errare. Nona ratio eorum est hæc, temerarium est dicere, illam gentem non posse cõtra fidem errare, quæ est ante diem iudicii peritura, sed gens Romanorum ante diem extremam peribit, sicut enim legitur Num. 24. Venient in triremibus de Italia, superabunt Assyrios, vastabuntque Hebræos, & ad extremum etiam ipsi peribunt. Ista verba de solis Romanis possunt intelligi, Romani ergo peribunt, & per consequens temerarium est dicere, quod inter Romanos fides vsque ad finem seculi remanebit. Discipulus. Verba prædicta possunt intelligi de Romanorum imperio temporali, quia illud peribit: sed non oportet dicere, quod intelligantur de ecclesia Romanorum. Magister. Isti non intelligunt verba prædicta de ecclesia Romana, quod nunquam errabit contra fidem: quia, sicut reputant temerarium dicere, quod ecclesia Romana errabit contra fidem: quia neutra pars istius contradictionis ex scripturis authenticis potest inferri, & ideo verba prædicta de potentia Romanorum temporali intelligunt, ex his arguentes, quod temerarium est asserere, ecclesiam in Roma nullatenus defecturam: quia licet Deus possit sua sola potentia contra infidelium potentiam conseruare loca fidelium, tamen temerarium est dicere, quod Dominus de facto aliquem vel ciuitatem fidelium miraculose contra irruentes potentias infidelium cõseruabit, maxime tempore Antichristi, quia pseudochristi & pseudoprophetæ Antichristi dabunt signa magna & prodigia, & electi non habebunt gratiam faciendi mirabilia, sicut habuerunt Apostoli & alii martyres Christi. Temerarium est ergo asserere, quod Deus ciuitatem Romanam à iugo infidelium præseruabit, quare cum potentia Romanorum temporalis inceperit dudum deficere, & continue magis ac magis deficiat, & potentia infidelium & malorum præualeat, non apparet quin ciuitas Romana possit ab infidelibus subiugari, quemadmodum antiquitus Romana ciuitas sibi alias prouincias subiugauit, quia sicut sine temeritate nequaquam asseritur, quod ciuitas Romana ad dominium veniet paganorum, ita temerarium (dicitdiuinando de futuris nobis incognitis) asseritur, quod nunquam infideles sunt ciuitatem occupaturi Romanam, & cunctos de eadem ciuitate fideles expulsuri, & ita temerarium est dicere, quod nunc de Roma omnes catholici expellentur. Et sicut temerarium est dicere, quod nunquam omnes Christiani expellerentur de ciuitate Romana nequaquam amplius reuersuri: ita temerarium est dicere, q; si potentia infidelium omnes Christiani Romani praeter decem vel duodecim essent expulsi de Roma nunquam in perpetuo reuersuri: quod illi decem vel duodecim remanentes non possunt contra fidem errare. Disc. Si modo omnes Christiani de ciuitate Romana per potentiam infidelium expellerentur, non propter hoc ecclesia Romana desineret: sicut nec expulsi desinerent esse Romani. Magist. Concedunt quod propter hoc non desineret Romana ecclesia, expulsis tamen mortuis sine prole (quod non est impossibile) desineret Romana ecclesia, & amplius nō essent aliqui Christiani Romani. Disc. Mortuis omnibus illis sine prole adhuc possunt ordinari clerici loco priorum, & illud collegium clericorum posset vocari Romana ecclesia. Magist. Hoc impugnatur dupliciter, primo, quia per talem modum posset dici, quod ecclesia Pisana non posset contra fidem errare: quia siue Pisani occ expellerentur de Pisis, siue omnes fierent haeretici, siue vniuersi morerentur, possent clerici ordinari, & vocaliter titulus priorum Pisanorum deputari. Secundo quia dicunt nonnulli, quod fides ecclesiae posset in puris laicis remanere: imo dicunt quidam posse saluari in mulieribus, quemadmodum tempore passionis Christi saluata fuit in sola matre Christi. Disc. Dic rationem illorum decimam, quā habent pro assertione sua principali. Mag. Decima ratio eorum est haec: Ecclesia militans non magis est accepta Deo, quam fuerit tota multitudo angelorum ante confirmationem bonorum & casum malorum, sed nulla pars totius multitudinis angelorum ante confirmationem bonorum & casum malorum, sic à Deo extiterit accepta, quin pars illius totius multitudinis labi potuerit in peccatum & aeternaliter condemnari: licet Deus ordinauerit, quod tota multitudo angelorum nullatenus laberetur, ergo consimiliter nulla pars multitudinis ecclesiae sic praeseruatur à Deo, quin possit contra fidem errare, Romana autem ecclesia est pars multitudinis ecclesiae, ergo Romana ecclesia, quae est pars ecclesiae, potest contra fidem errare.
