units.tr: Disciple. I should like to know whether these men labour to support their assertion with other arguments. Master. They strive to bolster their assertion with many other arguments. Their reasoning runs as follows. Every church that began after the passion of Christ can err against the faith, because that church which Christ said would remain in the faith until the end of the age was also present in a part of itself before Christ's ascension. For when Christ, foretelling that his Church would remain in the faith until the end of the age, said in Matthew at the end, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age, he meant not only the Church that would exist after his ascension, but he also understood that at no time, either before or after the ascension, would the whole Christian Church fall away from the Catholic faith. Therefore he did not speak of the Church that begins after the ascension. But the Roman Church began after the Lord's ascension, because the apostles and the other disciples of Christ preached in other places before they preached at Rome. Therefore the words of Christ about the Church remaining in the faith until the end of the age ought not to be understood specifically of the Roman Church, but disjunctively and in general, of Rome and the other places as well. For the Catholic faith will remain until the end of the age either in the Roman Church, or in the Church of Pisa, or in some other; for there will always be some Catholic and faithful people. Their third argument is this: the Roman Church, after it was founded, was able to err against the faith; therefore it can still err against the faith. The antecedent is clear, because before the coming of blessed Peter the Roman Church, then only begun there, was able to err against the faith; for the Roman Church was then no more confirmed in the faith than the other churches. The consequence is clear, because it is not read that it was afterwards confirmed in the faith; therefore it is rash to assert that it will not be able to err. Disciple. It seems that, since the apostles Peter and Paul consecrated and founded the Roman Church, it could not err. Master. This does not seem to them to be true, because the apostles Peter and Paul founded the Roman Church in no other way than by carefully instructing the Romans in the faith, exhorting them to faith and good works by doctrine and example, confirming their teaching by miracles, and at last consecrating the city of Rome by their martyrdom. But Christ did all these things for the Church of Jerusalem: he diligently instructed it in the faith, exhorted it to faith and good works by teaching, example and miracles, and for it, as for the others, he accepted death, and so Jerusalem was consecrated by his passion and death. Yet that Church of Jerusalem was by no means confirmed in the faith by all these things, although the works, life, teaching and death of Christ were of far greater efficacy than the teaching, works, life and martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul. The other apostles also founded the Church of Antioch. Blessed Paul had founded several churches, and other apostles consecrated other churches by their martyrdom, and yet none of them was confirmed in the faith. Therefore, in the same way, it does not appear that anything else was done in the Roman Church by which it should be regarded as confirmed in the faith. For greater things, and things more conducive to the stability of the faith, were done at Jerusalem and in Judea than in the Roman Church. If, then, neither Jerusalem nor Judea was confirmed in the faith, it is rash to say that the Roman Church is confirmed in the faith. Hence from this comes their fourth argument, formed thus: the Roman Church was not more chosen by God than the Church of Jerusalem; but God permitted the whole Church of Jerusalem to fall away from the faith; therefore it is rash to say that God will never permit all the Romans to fall away from the faith. And so the Roman Church can err against the faith. Disciple. Although all the Romans who live at Rome were to err against the faith, the Roman Church would nevertheless not err, because then the Roman Church would not be at Rome but elsewhere, just as the Roman Church is at Avignon. Master. These men say that you are trying to proceed in this sophistical way by equivocation. For they ask which church you call the Roman Church. Do you call the Roman Church the Pope, or the multitude, whether of clergy or of others dwelling in the Roman region or having homes there? Or do you call the Roman Church the clergy who hold titles in Rome? Or do you call the Roman Church the Pope with the cardinals, or the Pope alone, or the college of cardinals? Or do you call the Roman Church those who hold the faith which the apostles founded and preached at Rome? If you call the Roman Church in the first sense, the argument stands, because all the Romans who have homes at Rome could err against the faith, just as all the people of Jerusalem have at some time erred. If in the second sense, the argument still stands, because the clergy who hold titles in Rome are no more chosen by God than were the clergy who held titles at Jerusalem, and those were in error; therefore all who hold titles in Rome can err too. Likewise it is rash to say that all who hold titles in Rome cannot be killed by pagans or other wicked men; then there would be no faith among the clergy who hold titles at Rome; and (since faith would then fail) the words of Christ, in which he promised that faith would endure until the end of the age, cannot be understood of them. If you call the Roman Church the Pope with the cardinals, or the Pope alone, or the college of cardinals alone, it can still err, because it is rash to say that the Pope with the cardinals, if there were not several of them, could not err against the faith. But if you call the Roman Church that which holds the faith the apostles preached and founded at Rome, then they concede that the Roman Church cannot err; but that Roman Church is universal, wherever Catholics and faithful people are. This is the church which is called the Catholic and Apostolic Church, which cannot err; it thus includes the people of Pisa, the Lombards and the Spaniards as well as the Romans, and it is of this alone that these men concede that it cannot err. Their fifth argument is this: the Roman Church, which is one particular church, whether it comprises all the Romans or only the Roman clergy, or the Pope with the cardinals, was not more chosen by God than the nation of the Jews, from which Christ was to take human flesh, and whom he had principally come to save, as he himself said in Matthew 15: I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Yet that nation was not so confirmed in the faith that it could not err; therefore neither is the Roman Church so confirmed in the faith that it cannot err. Disciple. By this reasoning it would be proved that the whole multitude of Christians could err against the faith, just as the whole multitude of the Jewish nation could err against the faith. Master. It is answered that the argument does not proceed of the whole multitude of Christians as it does of the Roman Church, because outside the universal Church there is no salvation, since Christ will never give any law other than the Christian law, just as he was going to give another law besides the law of the Jews. But outside the Roman Church, which is a particular church, there can be salvation, for many are saved besides the Romans. Therefore, although the aforesaid argument concludes of the Roman Church, which can err, just as the multitude of the Jews could err, it does not conclude of the universal Church. Their sixth argument is drawn from what has been said: every church outside which there can be salvation can err against the faith; but outside the Roman Church there can be salvation, just as after Christ's ascension there was salvation before the Roman Church began; therefore the Roman Church can err against the faith. Their seventh argument is this: that church which cannot err against the faith does not need the counsel of others in settling questions of faith; but the Roman Church does need the counsel of others in settling questions of faith, for otherwise general councils would be gathered in vain to determine and define questions raised about the faith; therefore the Roman Church can err against the faith. Their eighth argument is this: that church which can by the authority of the Pope be made inferior to other churches can err against the faith; for that church which cannot err against the faith has no superior church. But the Roman Church can by the authority of the Pope be made inferior to other churches; for the Pope could transfer the papal see from Rome to another city, and once this was done the Roman Church would be subject to another; therefore the Roman Church can err against the faith. Their ninth argument is this: it is rash to say that a nation which is destined to perish before the day of judgement cannot err against the faith; but the nation of the Romans will perish before the last day, as it is read in Numbers 24: They shall come in galleys from Italy, they shall subdue the Assyrians and afflict the Hebrews, and at last they too shall perish. These words can be understood of the Romans alone; therefore the Romans will perish, and consequently it is rash to say that faith will remain among the Romans until the end of the age. Disciple. The aforesaid words can be understood of the temporal empire of the Romans, because that will perish; but it is not necessary to say that they are to be understood of the Church of the Romans. Master. These men do not understand the aforesaid words of the Roman Church as meaning that it will never err against the faith; for, just as they consider it rash to say that the Roman Church will err against the faith, since neither part of this contradiction can be inferred from authentic Scriptures, so they understand the words above of the temporal power of the Romans. From this they argue that it is rash to assert that the Church in Rome will in no way fail; for although God could by his power alone preserve the places of the faithful against the power of the unbelievers, yet it is rash to say that the Lord will in fact miraculously preserve some faithful person or city against the attacking powers of unbelievers, especially in the time of Antichrist, when the false christs and false prophets of Antichrist will give great signs and wonders, and the elect will not have the grace of working miracles, as the apostles and other martyrs of Christ had it. It is therefore rash to assert that God will protect the city of Rome from the yoke of unbelievers. Wherefore, since the temporal power of the Romans began long ago to fail and continually fails more and more, while the power of unbelievers and wicked men prevails, it does not appear why the city of Rome could not be subjugated by unbelievers, just as in ancient times the city of Rome subjugated other provinces to itself. For just as it is not asserted without rashness that the city of Rome will come under the dominion of pagans, so it is rash (since we are divining about future things unknown to us) to assert that unbelievers will never occupy the city of Rome and drive out all the faithful from that city; and thus it is rash to say that all Catholics will now be expelled from Rome. And just as it is rash to say that all Christians will never be expelled from the city of Rome and will never return, so it is rash to say that if by the power of unbelievers all the Christians of Rome except ten or twelve were expelled from Rome, they would never return for ever, and that those ten or twelve who remained could not err against the faith. Disciple. If now all the Christians were expelled from the city of Rome by the power of unbelievers, the Roman Church would not for that reason cease to exist, just as the expelled would not cease to be Romans. Master. They concede that for this reason the Roman Church would not cease, but if those expelled died without offspring (which is not impossible), the Roman Church would cease, and there would be no more Christian Romans. Disciple. When all those without offspring were dead, clergy could still be ordained in place of their predecessors, and that college of clergy could be called the Roman Church. Master. This is attacked in two ways. First, because in this way it could be said that the Church of Pisa could not err against the faith; for whether the Pisans were either driven out of Pisa, or all became heretics, or all died, clergy could be ordained and, by name, the title of the former Pisans assigned to them. Second, because some say that the faith of the Church could remain in mere laypeople; indeed some say that it could be saved in women, just as at the time of Christ's passion it was saved in the mother of Christ alone. Disciple. Tell me their tenth argument, which they hold for their principal assertion. Master. Their tenth argument is this: the militant Church is not more acceptable to God than was the whole multitude of angels before the confirmation of the good and the fall of the wicked; but no part of the whole multitude of angels before the confirmation of the good and the fall of the wicked was so accepted by God that part of that whole multitude could not slip into sin and be eternally condemned; although God ordained that the whole multitude of angels should in no way fall. Therefore likewise no part of the multitude of the Church is so preserved by God that it cannot err against the faith. But the Roman Church is a part of the multitude of the Church; therefore the Roman Church, which is a part of the Church, can err against the faith.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationes 13. cap. probantes, quod ecclesia Romana partialiter sumpta contra fidem errare non potest.
units.tr: In which the reasons of chapter 13 are answered, which prove that the Roman Church, taken in part, cannot err against the faith.

units.la: Disc. Licet firmiter teneatur, quod ecclesia Romana contra fidem errare non possit, secundum q; rationes & auctoritates prius inductae, probant aperte, tn quomodo asserentes Romanam ecclesiam posse errare contra fidē, respondent ad eas, velis exponere. Cum n. omnes responsiones eorū ad ipsas irrationabiles esse cognouero, magis veritatē earum intelligam. Mag. Ad primā earum respondent dicentes, istam esse falsam: Illa ecclesia, quae voce euangelica Domini & Saluatoris nostri caeteris ecclesiis est praelata, contra fidem errare non potest, nam ecclesia Antiochena ita fuit ecclesiis à voce euangelica Dei & saluatoris nostri praelata, sicut ecclesia Romana. Quia non inuenitur, quod aliter ecclesia Romana voce Saluatoris fuerit praelata aliis ecclesiis, nisi quia beatus Petrus à Deo nostro cunctis praelatus fidelibus sedem tenebat in Roma. Sed beatus Petrus primo sedem tenebat Antiochiae. Ergo pro illo tempore, quo Petrus sedit Antiochiae, ecclesia Antiochena voce euangelica Domini Saluatoris nostri fuit cunctis praelata ecclesiis. Sed ecclesia Antiochena non fuit confirmata in fide, sed errare potuit contra fidem. Ergo non obstante, quod ecclesia Romana voce euangelica Domini nostri & saluatoris sit praelata vniuersis ecclesiis, ipsa tamen non est confirmata in fide, sed contra fidem posset errare. Et ideo dicunt, quod temerarium est dicere, quod nunquam errabit contra fidem: & etiā temerarium est dicere, quod errabit: quia vtrunq; est nobis ignotum, quia nec vnū necalterum illorū reuelatum est à Deo. Cum vero dicitur, quod opus Dei ab hominib. dissolui non potest: Respondent, quod multa opera Dei ab hominibus possunt dissolui, charitas enim & aliae virtutes infusae viatori, sunt opera Dei, & tamen per liberum arbitrium dissolui possunt, quia habens primo charitatem & virtutes potest peccare mortaliter, per peccatum autem mortale caritas expellitur. Sic dicunt de Romana ecclesia, quod licet in beato Petro receperit principatum, tota tamen Romana ecclesia potest ab infidelibus vsque ad finem seculi occupari. Nec scitur an infideles totam Romam vnquam sint capturi, & vsque in finem seculi rerenturi. Posset etiam tota Romana ecclesia & omnes Christiani in ipsa ad aliam sectam conuerti, nec scit aliquis nisi Deus aut cui reuelasset, an tota Romana ecclesia tempore Antichristi conuertetur ad ipsum: imo nescitur vtrum aliquando tota Roma & omnes habitantes in ipsa conuertentur ad sectam Machometi, vel ad aliquam prauitatem. Cum autem in eadem ratione accipitur, q; si illa ecclesia, quae voce diuina caeteris ecclesiis est praelata, contra fidem erraret, desineret esse praelata & caput aliarum ecclesiarum, respondent: q; si tota Roma ad sectam Sarracenorum vel ad aliquam aliam prauitatem haereticam, & Papa & omnes cardinales & omnes clerici titulos Romae habentes in prauitatem haereticam laberentur: adhuc posset dici, q; Romana ecclesia aliquo modo desineret esse caput aliarū ecclesiarum, nō quod tūc de facto esset aliquis Papa, vel aliquod collegiū, vel aliqua persona extra Romam, vel aliquā ecclesiā particularem, qui vel quę vel quod esset caput ecclesiarum aliarum: sed quia eligendus est summus Pontifex per catholicos, qn posset conuenienter, qui caput esset omniū catholicorū, & de iure, licet nō de facto,
units.tr: Student. Although it is firmly held that the Roman Church cannot err against the faith, the reasons and authorities brought forward earlier prove this clearly. Yet you wish to explain how those who assert that the Roman Church can err against the faith answer them. For once I know that all their replies to these arguments are unreasonable, I shall understand their truth better. Master. They answer the first of them by saying that it is false: "The church which, by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Saviour, has been placed above the other churches cannot err against the faith." For the church of Antioch was placed above the churches by the evangelical voice of God and our Saviour just as the Roman church was. It is not found that the Roman church was placed above the other churches by the voice of the Saviour, except that blessed Peter, set above all the faithful by our God, held his see in Rome. But blessed Peter first held his see at Antioch. Therefore, for the time when Peter sat at Antioch, the church of Antioch was placed by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Saviour above all the churches. But the church of Antioch was not confirmed in the faith; it could err against the faith. Therefore, although the Roman church is placed by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Saviour above all the churches, it is nonetheless not confirmed in the faith, and could err against the faith. And so they say that it is rash to say that it will never err against the faith, and rash also to say that it will err, because both are unknown to us, since neither the one nor the other has been revealed to us by God. When it is said that the work of God cannot be dissolved by men, they reply that many works of God can be dissolved by men. For charity and the other virtues infused into a wayfarer are works of God, and yet they can be lost through free will, since one who has charity and the virtues can sin mortally, and through mortal sin charity is driven out. So they say of the Roman church that, although it received its primacy in blessed Peter, the whole Roman church can nevertheless be occupied by infidels until the end of the age. Nor is it known whether the infidels will ever capture all of Rome and hold it until the end of the age. The whole Roman church and all the Christians in it could also be converted to another sect, and no one knows, except God or whomever he has revealed it to, whether the whole Roman church will be converted to Antichrist in his time. Indeed, it is not known whether at some time all of Rome and all its inhabitants will be converted to the sect of Mahomet, or to some other depravity. When, moreover, the same argument is put forward, that if the church which has been placed above the other churches by divine voice erred against the faith, it would cease to be placed above them and to be the head of the other churches, they reply: even if all Rome were to fall into the sect of the Saracens, or into some other heretical depravity, and the Pope, all the cardinals, and all the clergy holding titles in Rome were to fall into heretical depravity, it could still be said that the Roman church would in some sense cease to be the head of the other churches, not because at that time there would in fact be some Pope, or some college, or some person outside Rome, or some particular church, which would be the head of the other churches; but because the supreme Pontiff is to be chosen by Catholics, when it can be done fittingly, who would be the head of all Catholics, and by right, although not in fact,

units.la: &c. ato, sedem Romæ tenere deberet, quemadmodum nunc creantur patriarchæ Antiochenus, Alexand. & Hierosolymitanus, qui de iure in prædictis ciuitatib. sedere debent. & ideo quemadmodum nunc dicitur, quod ecclesia Constantinopolitana est secunda post Romanam; & Alexandrina, tertia; & Antiochena, quarta; & Hierosolymitana, quinta. quia si ciuitates prædictæ essent à fidelib. occupatæ, præfatæ ecclesiæ ordinem talem haberent. & de facto patriarchæ à prædictis ciuitatibus appellati, quando creantur, talem ordinem tenent inter se. Ita si omnes Romani essent auersi à fide, adhuc summus pontifex esset caput fidelium. & si Romana ciuitas iterum conuerteretur ad fidem, deberet primitatem respectu aliarum ecclesiarum habere. DIS. Si tota Roma esset ab infidelib. occupata, vel ad aliam sectam conuersa: nunquid secundum istos oportet creare clericos loco priorum qui fuerunt Romæ, sicut oporteret creare summum pontificem, qui de iure deberet Romæ sedem habere. M A G. Respondeat, quod sufficeret solummodo summum pontificem eligere: quia alii tituli Romæ præter papatum possunt variari, & voluntarie minui, & augeri. unde & modo sunt plures, quam fuerunt temporibus Apostolorum. nec forte, aliquis istorum fuit tempore Beati Petri, & ideo si Romana ecclesia esset auersa à fide, sufficeret catholicis eligere Papam Romanum: quemadmodum nunc creatur patriarcha Antiochenus, nec titulos aliquos Romæ oporteret aliquibus clericis assignare. sicut nec modo clericis, qui quondam fuerunt in ciuitatibus patriarchalibus, deputantur. Concedunt ergo isti, quod verba Pelagii continent veritatem, quod Romana ecclesia & apostolica ecclesia nullis synodicis constitutis subiicitur principaliter: sed euangelica voce domini & saluatoris nostri primatum obtinuit in Petro, quando dominus præfecit B. Petrum fidelibus vniuersis. nec per alium modum obtinuit primatum super alias ecclesias, nisi quia dominus beatum Petrum prætulit omnibus, nullam tunc de Romana ecclesia faciens mentionem. sed B. Petrus postea ibidem elegit sedem. & ideo ex tunc auctoritate Dei, qui voluit illam sedem quam Petrus eligeret, esse primam, Romana ecclesia primatum obtinuit. Ad secundam rationem multipliciter respondetur. Vno modo dicitur, quod Romana ecclesia super alias ecclesias priuilegium posset amittere: quia Papa potest transferre sedem papalem de Roma ad aliam ciuitatem, sicut B. Petrus transtulit de Antiochia sedem in Romam. Aliter dicitur, quod licet Romana ecclesia possit ad tempus de facto amittere priuilegium super alias ecclesias, non tamen simpliciter: quia si Romana ecclesia rediret ad fidem, recuperaret idem priuilegium, quod habuit ante. Tertio dicitur, quod si Romana ecclesia rediret ad fidem, distinguendo ipsam contra Papam, qui gubernat ipsam, amittere potest simpliciter priuilegium absque translatione sedis, quia illud priuilegium consistit principaliter in potestate eligendi summum pontificem & ordinandi apostolicam sedem. sed hoc priuilegium potest amittere absque translatione sedis; sicut quondam amisit. nã sicut habetur di. 64. c. Adrian. hoc ius habuit Carolus magnus, & postea obtinuit Otho primus rex Theutonicorum, sicut legitur 8. dist. in synodo. ergo ecclesia Romana priuilegiu suu pot amittere. Ad auctoritatem autem Nicolai Papæ dicitur, quod Nicolaus papa loquitur de ecclesia Romana, quæ est Papa: quia illi soli ecclesiæ Romanæ, quæ est Papa, in B. Petro immediate fuit traditum priuilegium. Illa autem ecclesia Romana, quæ est subiecta Papæ, nullum priuilegium habet, nisi à Papa: quod Papa potest, quando sibi placet, auferre. Unde ergo Nicolaus Papa vult asserere, quod qui Romanæ ecclesiæ, quæ est Papa, priuilegium conatur auferre, asserendo videlicet ipsum non esse prælatum omnium Christianorum, hæreticus est; quia incidit in assertionem erroneam, quæ sapit hæresim manifestam: quia ex ipsa & quibusdam veris, quæ nulla possunt tergiuersatione negari, sequitur hæresis manifesta, quod B. Petrus videlicet non fuit à Christo omnibus prælatus fidelibus. & ideo illi qui dicunt, quod Papa non potest transferre sedem papalem de Roma, dicunt quod talis sic nitens auferre priuilegium ecclesiæ Romanæ (quæ est Papa) est hæreticus, stricte sumpto hæretico. qui autem dicunt, quod Papa potest auferre sedem, dicunt quod est hæreticus large sumpto hæretico, secundum quod aliquis dicitur hæreticus qui pertinaciter tenet assertionem, quæ non est hæresis stricte sumpta hæresi: sed est hæresis, secundum quod omnis assertio sapiens hæresim manifestam hæresis appellatur. qualiter autem tales assertiones distinguantur, ex superioribus, vbi actum est de hæresibus, patere potest. Ad tertiam respondetur, quod sine ecclesia Romana, quæ est Papæ subiecta, & quæ non est Papa, posset regi vniuersalis ecclesia. Ad Auctoritatem B. Anacleti respondetur, quod apostolica sedem vocat summum pontificem: & summus pontifex, siue fit Romæ Papatus siue sit alibi, est caput & cardo, quo omnes ecclesiæ domino disponente reguntur, quando est verus Papa. hæc tamen ecclesia contra fidem errare potest: quia Papa potest hæretica incurrere prauitatem. sed tunc substituendus est ei alius à catholicis catholicus, qui ecclesiam regat catholicam, siue fuerit in Italia, siue fuerit in Hispania. Ad quartam rationem dicitur, quod hæc est falsa; illa ecclesia errare non potest contra fidem, à qua quicunque dissentit, non est inter catholicos episcopos computandus. Sed illa de inesse est vera: illa ecclesia non errat contra fidem, à qua quicunque dissentit ab ea &c. Et ideo quamdiu Romana ecclesia non errat contra fidem: quicunque dissentit ab ea in fide, non est inter catholicos computandus. Sed si erraret contra fidem, non haberet veritatem. Beatus autem Hieron. loquebatur pro tempore suo, quando ecclesia Romana firma mansit in fide. Si autem erraret contra fidem, dissentientes ab ea in fide essent inter catholicos numerandi. Ad quintam rationem dicitur, quod aliquem esse extra Romanam ecclesiam dupliciter potest intelligi, telligi, vel quia est contrarius pertinaciter quantum ad ea quae fidei sunt, vel quia non est Romanus, sed est de aliqua ecclesia particulari. Qui primo modo est extra ecclesiam Romanam, quamdiu ecclesia Romana non errat, salvari non potest, nisi redierit. & sic loquitur Hieron. Qui secundo modo est extra Romanam ecclesiam, salvari potest. Hiero. autem principaliter loquitur de Papa successore B. Petri, & de illo habet veritatem: quicunque est sibi contrarius pertinaciter in his quae fidei sunt salvari non potest. Ad sextam rationem dicitur, quod B. Cyprianus loquitur de cathedra Petri, qui est summus pontifex catholicus tenens sedem B. Petri, sive fuerit Romae sive Lugduni. Innocentius enim tertius, ut de se patet, loquitur de successoribus beati Petri catholicis. Ad septimam dicitur, quod licet quantum ad multa sit similitudo inter corpus Christi mysticum, quod est ecclesia, & corpus materiale hominis; non tamen est quantum ad omnia simile. Corpus ergo hominis nec ad tempus manet vivum sine capite. corpus autem Christi mysticum sine capite ad tempus vivum manere potest: saepe caret capite in terris, quamvis tunc habeat caput in coelis, scilicet Christum, qui est caput ecclesiae, ut habetur ad Ephes. 1. Crebro enim caret summo pontifice, qui est caput ecclesiae nec tamen tunc desinit esse spiritualiter viva; imo vivit vita gratiae. Debet tamen, quando convenienter poterit, sibi constituere caput. Corpus ergo Christi mysticum potest esse sine multis membris. quaelibet enim ecclesia particularis est membrum ecclesiae. Unde ecclesia Parisiensis, Lugdunensis, Lingoniensis, Lucensis, Ianuensis, Constantiensis, &c. sunt membra ecclesiae; & tamen sine istis posset esse corpus Christi mysticum, quamvis enim praedictae ecclesiae a fide discederent, non propter hoc corpus Christi mysticum deperiret. Et ideo quamvis Romana ecclesia post Papam sit membrum principale ecclesiae, sive ipsa tamen posset ecclesia esse. Ad octavam dicitur, quod Romanam ecclesiam potest malitia extinguere. cum vero dixit Pelagius Papa, quod nulla alia ecclesia, nisi quae in apostolica est radice fundata, est catholica; haec concedunt, quia omnis catholica, sive sit Parisiana, sive Neapolitana, in apostolica radice est fundata; quia in doctrina apostolorum. Cum vero allegat Augustinum, respondetur per idem, quod ecclesiam constitutam in radice apostolicae sedis per successores episcoporum, hoc est ecclesiam tenentem doctrinam apostolicam, quam rexerunt successores episcopi (quamvis aliquando tale regimen fuerit interruptum) & regent in futurum (licet forte cum magna interruptione regiminis) nulla malitia hominis valebit extinguere. Et illa ecclesia sive fuerit Romae, sive Eugubii, sive in Hispania, sive in Britannia, non poterit esse nulla. quamvis omnes Romani & tota Italia ac Francia & Hispania & Alemannia a catholica fide recederent. Quia si non fuerit in regionibus supradictis omnibus, erit in Syria vel in Aegypto, vel Aethiopia, vel India, vel alibi, ubi Deo placuerit. Ad auctoritatem primam Hiero. respondetur, quod B. Hiero. loquitur pro tempore praeterito ante sua tempora: & non loquitur pro futuris temporibus. Et si loqueretur pro temporibus futuris, posset intelligi sine, quod loqueretur de ecclesia apostolica, quae fidem sequitur apostolorum. Ad aliam auctoritatem Hiero. responsum est supra, quod verba Hieron. intelligenda sunt sub conditione; si B. Petrus opem ferret.
units.tr: &c. ato, ought to hold the see at Rome, just as the patriarchs of Antioch, Alexandria and Jerusalem are now created, and who by right ought to sit in those cities. So, just as it is now said that the Church of Constantinople is second after the Roman, Alexandria third, Antioch fourth and Jerusalem fifth, the churches would hold this same order among themselves if those cities were occupied by the faithful. And in fact the patriarchs, when they are created, are named after those cities and keep this order among themselves. So too, if all the Romans had turned away from the faith, the supreme pontiff would still be the head of the faithful; and if the city of Rome were converted to the faith again, it ought to have the primacy over the other churches. OBJ. If the whole of Rome were occupied by unbelievers, or turned to another sect, then according to your view, must clergy be created to replace those who were in Rome, just as the supreme pontiff would have to be created, since he ought by right to have his seat at Rome? MAG. The answer is that it would be enough merely to elect a supreme pontiff, since the other titles at Rome apart from the papacy can be changed, and voluntarily diminished or increased. For this reason there are now more of them than there were in the time of the Apostles, and perhaps some of them did not exist in the time of Blessed Peter. So if the Roman church turned away from the faith, it would be enough for Catholics to elect a Roman Pope, just as the Patriarch of Antioch is now created, and there would be no need to assign any of those titles at Rome to any clerics, just as now no clerics are appointed to those titles that once belonged to the patriarchal cities. These men therefore concede that the words of Pelagius contain the truth: that the Roman church and the apostolic church is not subject principally to any synodal constitutions, but by the gospel voice of the Lord and our Saviour it obtained the primacy in Peter, when the Lord set Blessed Peter over all the faithful. Nor did it obtain the primacy over the other churches in any other way, except that the Lord placed Blessed Peter above all, making no mention at that time of the Roman church. But Blessed Peter afterwards chose his see there, and from that time, by the authority of God, who willed that the see which Peter chose should be the first, the Roman church obtained the primacy. To the second argument there are several answers. In one way it is said that the Roman church could lose its privilege over the other churches, because the Pope can transfer the papal see from Rome to another city, just as Blessed Peter transferred his see from Antioch to Rome. In another way it is said that although the Roman church may de facto lose its privilege over the other churches for a time, it does not lose it absolutely, because if the Roman church returned to the faith it would recover the same privilege which it had before. Thirdly, it is said that if the Roman church returned to the faith, distinguishing it from the Pope who governs it, it could lose the privilege absolutely without any transfer of the see, because that privilege consists principally in the power of electing the supreme pontiff and ordaining the apostolic see. This privilege can be lost without transfer of the see, as it once was. For, as is found in Dist. 64, c. Adrian, Charlemagne had this right, and afterwards Otto the First, king of the Germans, obtained it, as is read in Dist. 8, in the synod. Therefore the Roman church can lose its privilege. As for the authority of Pope Nicholas, it is said that Pope Nicholas speaks of the Roman church which is the Pope, because the privilege was delivered immediately in Blessed Peter to that Roman church alone which is the Pope. But the Roman church which is subject to the Pope has no privilege except from the Pope, which the Pope can take away whenever he pleases. Hence, when Pope Nicholas wishes to assert that whoever tries to take away the privilege of the Roman church, which is the Pope, by asserting that he is not set over all Christians, is a heretic, he is asserting this because such a person falls into an erroneous assertion which savours of manifest heresy. For from that assertion, together with certain truths which cannot be denied by any evasion, there follows a manifest heresy: namely, that Blessed Peter was not set over all the faithful by Christ. And therefore those who say that the Pope cannot transfer the papal see from Rome say that such a person, who strives to take away the privilege of the Roman church (which is the Pope), is a heretic in the strict sense of the word "heretic". Those who say that the Pope can take away the see say that he is a heretic in the broad sense of the word, according to which someone is called a heretic who stubbornly holds an assertion that is not heresy in the strict sense, but is heresy in the sense that every assertion savouring of manifest heresy is called heresy. How such assertions are to be distinguished can be seen from what was said above, where heresies were discussed. To the third argument it is answered that the universal church could be governed without the Roman church, which is subject to the Pope and which is not the Pope. To the authority of Blessed Anacletus it is answered that he calls the supreme pontiff the apostolic see; and the supreme pontiff, whether the papacy is at Rome or elsewhere, is the head and hinge by which all churches are governed, under the Lord's disposition, when he is a true Pope. Yet this church can err against the faith, because the Pope can fall into heretical depravity. But then another Catholic must be substituted for him by Catholics, to govern the Catholic church, whether he be in Italy or in Spain. To the fourth argument it is said that this is false: a church from which whoever dissents is not to be counted among Catholic bishops cannot err against the faith. But this in the sense of inherence is true: the church from which whoever dissents from it, etc., does not err against the faith. And therefore, as long as the Roman church does not err against the faith, whoever dissents from it in faith is not to be counted among Catholics. But if it erred against the faith, it would not have the truth. Blessed Jerome, however, was speaking for his own time, when the Roman church remained firm in the faith. If, however, it erred against the faith, those who dissented from it in faith would have to be numbered among Catholics. To the fifth argument it is said that to be outside the Roman church can be understood in two ways: either because one is stubbornly opposed in the matters of faith, or because one is not a Roman but belongs to some particular church. Whoever is outside the Roman church in the first sense cannot be saved, as long as the Roman church does not err, unless he returns. And so Jerome speaks. Whoever is outside the Roman church in the second sense can be saved. Jerome, however, speaks principally of the Pope, the successor of Blessed Peter, and of him it is true that whoever is stubbornly opposed to him in the matters of faith cannot be saved. To the sixth argument it is said that Blessed Cyprian speaks of the chair of Peter, which is the catholic supreme pontiff holding the see of Blessed Peter, whether he be at Rome or at Lyons. For Innocent the Third, as is clear from himself, speaks of the catholic successors of Blessed Peter. To the seventh it is said that although there is in many respects a likeness between the mystical body of Christ, which is the church, and the material body of man, it is not like in every respect. Therefore the body of a man cannot remain alive even for a time without a head. But the mystical body of Christ can remain alive for a time without a head: it often lacks a head on earth, although it then has a head in heaven, namely Christ, who is the head of the church, as is found in Ephesians 1. For it often lacks the supreme pontiff, who is the head of the church, and yet it does not then cease to be spiritually alive; indeed it lives the life of grace. Nevertheless, when it can conveniently do so, it ought to appoint a head for itself. The mystical body of Christ therefore can exist without many members, for every particular church is a member of the church. Hence the churches of Paris, Lyons, Langres, Lucca, Genoa, Constance, etc., are members of the church; and yet without them the mystical body of Christ could exist, for even if the aforesaid churches fell away from the faith, the mystical body of Christ would not perish on that account. And so, although the Roman church after the Pope is the principal member of the church, nevertheless the church itself could still exist. To the eighth it is said that malice can extinguish the Roman church. When Pope Pelagius said that no church except the one founded on the apostolic root is catholic, they concede this, because every catholic church, whether it be Parisian or Neapolitan, is founded on the apostolic root, namely in the doctrine of the apostles. When he cites Augustine, the same answer is given: the church established on the root of the apostolic see through the successors of the bishops, that is, the church holding the apostolic doctrine which the successors of the bishops have ruled (although such government has sometimes been interrupted), and will rule in the future (perhaps with a great interruption of government), no malice of man will be able to extinguish. And that church, whether it be at Rome, at Gubbio, in Spain or in Britain, cannot cease to exist, even if all the Romans and all Italy, France, Spain and Germany fell away from the Catholic faith. For if it were not in all the aforesaid regions, it would be in Syria or Egypt, or Ethiopia, or India, or elsewhere, wherever God pleases. To the first authority of Jerome it is answered that Blessed Jerome speaks of the past time before his own times, and does not speak of future times. And if he spoke of future times, it could be understood that he spoke of the apostolic church, which follows the faith of the apostles. To the other authority of Jerome, it was answered above that the words of Jerome are to be understood under the condition: if Blessed Peter should bring aid.

units.la: CAP. XXV. In quo ponitur quarta quaestio principalis, scilicet utrum generale concilium ecclesiae in haereticam pravitatem labi possit; quod sic quinque rationibus hic arguitur &c. sequenti quatuor exemplis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV. In which the fourth principal question is set out, namely whether a general council of the Church can fall into heretical depravity; this is argued here with five reasons, and then with four examples that follow.

units.la: DISCIP. Satis, quantum desidero ex opere isto, disseruimus de Romana ecclesia, an valeat haereticari. Ideo nunc de generali concilio conferamus: an queat labi in haereticam pravitatem.
units.tr: DISCIP. We have discussed enough, as far as I wish from this work, whether the Roman Church can become heretical. So now let us take up the general council: whether it can fall into heretical depravity.

units.la: MAG. De generali concilio sunt assertiones contrariae. Una est, quod haereticari non potest; alia est, quod haeretica potest labe respergi.
units.tr: MAG. There are contrary assertions about a general council. One is that it cannot become heretical; the other is that it can be stained with heretical corruption.

units.la: DIS. Quamvis sit missim, e putem, quod concilium generale haereticari non potest, tamen rationes pro assertione contraria libenti animo auscultabo.
units.tr: DIS. Although I think it is already fairly clear that a general council cannot become heretical, I will nevertheless gladly listen to the reasons for the opposite assertion.

units.la: MAG. Quod concilium generale possit errare contra fidem, rationibus & exemplis videtur posse probari. Prima autem ratio, quae etiam ad alias assertiones superius est inducta, talis est: Una est sola ecclesia militans, quae contra fidem errare non potest: quia de sola universali ecclesia militante invenitur in scripturis authenticis, quod errare non potest. Concilium autem generale, licet sit pars ecclesiae militantis universalis, tamen non est ecclesia universalis. Igitur temerarium est dicere, quod concilium generale contra fidem errare non potest.
units.tr: MAG. That a general council can err against the faith seems capable of being proved by reasons and examples. The first reason, which was also brought forward above for the other assertions, goes like this: there is only one Church militant that cannot err against the faith, because the authentic Scriptures teach that only the universal Church militant cannot err. A general council, although it is part of the universal Church militant, is not the universal Church itself. It is therefore rash to say that a general council cannot err against the faith.

units.la: DIS. Licet concilium generale non sit ecclesia universalis, tamen repraesentat ecclesiam universalem, & eius vices gerit. Et ideo sicut ecclesia universalis contra fidem errare non potest, ita etiam concilium generale contra fidem errare non potest.
units.tr: DIS. Although a general council is not the universal Church, it represents the universal Church and acts in its place. And so, just as the universal Church cannot err against the faith, so too a general council cannot err against the faith.

units.la: MAG. Haec responsio impugnatur primo, quia sicut concilium generale repraesentat ecclesiam universalem, & eius vices gerit; ita etiam Papa repraesentat ecclesiam universalem & eius vices gerit: quia est persona publica totius collegii gerens vices & curam. Sed Papa, hoc non obstante, potest contra fidem errare. Igitur & generale concilium, hoc non obstante, poterit contra fidem errare.
units.tr: MAG. This answer is attacked first of all in this way: just as a general council represents the universal Church and acts in its place, so too the Pope represents the universal Church and acts in its place, since he is the public person of the whole body, bearing its office and care. But the Pope, notwithstanding this, can err against the faith. Therefore a general council, notwithstanding this too, can err against the faith.

units.la: Secundo: quia non omni praerogativa gaudet persona vel collegium, quae vel quae gerit vices alterius, qua gaudet communitas, cuius vices gerit. Ergo ex hoc quod ecclesia universalis non potest contra fidem errare, inferri non potest quod concilium generale non potest contra fidem errare; licet gerat vices universalis ecclesiae.
units.tr: Second, because a person or body that acts in the place of another does not enjoy every privilege that the community enjoys, whose place it takes. Therefore from the fact that the universal Church cannot err against the faith it cannot be inferred that a general council cannot err against the faith, even though it acts in the place of the universal Church.

units.la: Secunda ratio est haec: Illa congregatio quae potest voluntate humana dissolvi, potest contra fidem errare: quia illa ecclesia, quae contra fidem errare non potest, usque ad finem saeculi permanebit, iuxta promissionem Christi Matth. ult. Sed concilium generale potest humana voluntate dissolvi, sicut & dissolvitur. Ergo generale concilium potest contra fidem errare. Tertia tia ratio est hæc. Illæ personæ, quæ in diuersis locis existentes possunt contra fidem errare, etiam si ad eundem locum conueniunt, poterunt contra fidem errare. quia concursus ad eundem locum non reddit aliquos inobliquabiles à fide: quia sicut locus non sanctificat homines, ita & locus nullos confirmat in fide. sed omnes ad generale concilium conuenientes, antequam conuenirent, poterant contra fidem errare. quia si conteneant ceteri vel ducenti episcopi, constat omnes ex arbitrio voluntatis poterant in hæreticam incidere prauitatem. ergo etiam postquam conueniunt, poterunt labi in hæreticam prauitatem. DIS. Ista ratio non procedit, quia Deus specialiter congregatis in vnum assistit, ipsa veritate testante, quæ ait Matth. 18. vbi sunt duo vel tres congregati in nomine meo; ibi sum ego in medio eorum. & ideo licet conuenientes ad concilium generale ante poterunt contra fidem errare: postquam tamen conuenerint in nomine Christi, errare non poterunt.
units.tr: The second reason is this: that assembly which can be dissolved by human will can err against the faith, because the Church which cannot err against the faith will remain until the end of the age, according to Christ's promise in the last chapter of Matthew. But a general council can be dissolved by human will, as indeed it is dissolved. Therefore a general council can err against the faith. The third reason is this: those persons who, existing in different places, can err against the faith, will also be able to err against the faith even if they come together in one place, because coming together in one place does not render anyone immovable in the faith; for just as a place does not sanctify men, so a place confirms no one in the faith. But all who come together to a general council, before they came together, could err against the faith, since, if there were a hundred or two hundred bishops, it is clear that all of them, by the choice of their will, could fall into heretical depravity. Therefore even after they have come together, they will be able to slip into heretical depravity. DIS. This reason does not hold, because God specially assists those gathered into one, as the Truth itself testifies in Matthew 18: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." And so, although those who come to a general council could err before, once they have come together in the name of Christ they cannot err.

units.la: MAG. Ista responsio impugnatur: quia licet Deus assistat specialiter congregatis in vnum in nomine Christi: ipsi tñ in gratia & fide minime confirmantur, etiam dum simul localiter remanserint, quin possint per liberum voluntatis arbitrium à gratia Dei & fide recedere. & ideo quamuis Deus specialiter assistat ad generale concilium congregatum in nomine Christi, tamen per talem assistentiam diuinam in fide nullatenus confirmantur, quin possint labi in errorem. Vnde per istam responsionem haberetur, quod nullum prouinciale concilium posset errare contra fidem; quia si in vnum conuenerint in nomine Christi in prouinciali concilio congregati, Deus specialiter assistit eisdem; sequeretur etiam per illud medium, quod nullum generale ac prouinciale capitulum clericorum vel religiosorum Mendicantium posset contra fidem errare: quia nonnunquam in Christi nomine congregantur.
units.tr: MAG. This answer is attacked: although God specially assists those gathered into one in the name of Christ, they themselves are by no means confirmed in grace and faith, even while they remain together in the same place, so that they can still turn away from the grace of God and the faith by the free choice of the will. And so, although God specially assists a general council gathered in the name of Christ, they are in no way confirmed in the faith by such divine assistance, so that they cannot fall into error. Hence by this answer it would follow that no provincial council could err against the faith; for if those gathered in one in the name of Christ in a provincial council are specially assisted by God, it would also follow by the same means that no general or provincial chapter of clerics or Mendicant religious could err against the faith, since they sometimes gather in the name of Christ.

units.la: Quarta ratio eorum est hæc: nulla vocatio humana certarum personarum, nec etiam aliqua humana commissio facta specialibus personis potest eas in fide confirmare, vel ab errore præseruare: quia sola potentia Dei ecclesia catholica ab erroribus præseruatur. sed certæ personæ in generali concilio congregatæ non vocantur nisi vocatione humana, nec aliquam auctoritatem, nec potestatem accipiunt, nisi ex commissione humana igitur per hoc, quod in generali concilio conueniunt, non confirmantur in fide, nec necessario ab erroribus præseruantur. ergo ita potuerunt, postquam fuerunt ad generale concilium congregati, incidere in hæreticam prauitatem, sicut ante poterant.
units.tr: Their fourth reason is this: no human calling of certain persons, nor any human commission given to particular persons, can confirm them in the faith or preserve them from error, because the Catholic Church is preserved from errors by the power of God alone. But certain persons gathered in a general council are called only by human calling, and they receive no authority or power except by human commission. Therefore by the fact that they come together in a general council they are not confirmed in the faith, nor are they necessarily preserved from errors. Therefore, after they have been gathered to a general council, they could fall into heretical depravity just as they could before.

units.la: Quinta ratio est hæc: Si in generali concilio congregati contra fidem errare non possunt: aut hoc est ratione sapientiæ, qua præfulgent; aut ratione sanctitatis, qua pollent; aut ratione auctoritatis seu potestatis, qua habent; aut ratione promissionis Christi, qua promisit apostolis fidem vsque in finem seculi duraturam. non propter primum: tum quia sæpe multi sapientes catholici inueniuntur extra concilium generale, qui possunt defendere fidem, licet omnes errarent in generali concilio congregati. Tum quia Deus sæpe reuelat paruulis, quæ à sapientibus & prudentibus abscondantur. licet ergo omnes in generali concilio errarent, & solum paruuli & illiterati ad concilium minime conuenirent, non esset adhuc desperandum, quin Deus veritatem catholicam paruulis reuelaret, vel eisdem veritatem notam defendere inspiraret.
units.tr: The fifth reason is this: if those gathered in a general council cannot err against the faith, this is either by reason of the wisdom in which they excel, or by reason of the holiness in which they are strong, or by reason of the authority or power they hold, or by reason of Christ's promise, by which he promised the apostles that the faith would endure until the end of the age. Not because of the first: partly because many wise Catholics are often found outside a general council who can defend the faith, even if all were to err in a gathered general council; and partly because God often reveals to little ones what is hidden from the wise and prudent. So even if all in a general council were to err, and only the little ones and the unlearned did not come to the council, it would still not be hopeless that God might reveal the Catholic truth to the little ones, or inspire them to defend the truth they know.

units.la: Hoc enim esset ad gloriam Dei: qui in hoc ostenderet, fidem nostram non esse in sapientia hominum ad concilium generale vocatorum, sed in virtute Dei, qui nonnunquam quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit, vt confundat sapientes. Nec propter sanctitatem ad concilium generale vocatorum, est dicendum, quod non possunt contra fidem errare: tum quia interdum ad generale concilium sanctiores nequaquam conueniunt: tū quia scitas in ecclesia militate nullos confirmat in fide.
units.tr: For this would be to the glory of God, who would thereby show that our faith rests not in the wisdom of men called to a general council, but in the power of God, who sometimes chooses what is foolish in the world in order to confound the wise. Nor is it to be said, because of holiness, that those called to a general council cannot err against the faith: partly because sometimes holier men by no means come to a general council; and partly because learning in the Church confirms no one in the faith.

units.la: Nec propter tertium est dicendum, quod non sint contra fidem errare; quia auctoritas vel potestas in hac vita nullos confirmant in fide, sicut per auctoritates inductas supius (vbi ingsitu fuit, an Papa possit contra fidem errare) sufficienter videtur ostensum. Nec propter quartum: quia Christus promittendo apostolis fidem vsque ad finem seculi duraturam, de generali concilio nullā fecit penitus mentionem.
units.tr: Nor is it to be said, because of the third, that they cannot err against the faith, since authority or power in this life confirms no one in the faith, as has been sufficiently shown by the authorities cited above (where it was asked whether the Pope can err against the faith). Nor is it to be said, because of the fourth: for in promising the apostles that the faith would endure until the end of the age, Christ made no mention at all of a general council.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: In quo probatur eadem conclusio, scilicet quod generale concilium errare potest contra fidem, quatuor exemplis ostenditur.
units.tr: In which the same conclusion is proved, namely that a general council can err against the faith, is shown by four examples.

units.la: MAG. Secundo ostenditur exemplis, quod generale concilium potest contra fidem errare. Primum exemplum est de synodo Stephani Papæ septimi, qui erroneas ordinationes factas per Formosum Papam irritas esse decreuit. Vnde & postea synodo celebrata Rauennæ per Iohan. Papam nonum extitit reprobata. Igitur concilium generale poterit errare: quia constat, quod altera istarum synodorum, quarum vna alteram reprobauit, errauit. DIS. Altera istarum synodorum errauit, sed non contra fidem; quia errauit tantum contra ordinationes Formosi Papæ. MAG. Haec responsio impugnatur; quia ois congregatio, quæ potest errare contra bonos mores, potest errare contra fidem. Qua mali mores excæcant intellectum: & ita potest peccare, potest incidere in errorem et contra fidem. Si ergo altera istarum synodorum errauit contra mores impie & iniq; approbado vel reprobado ordinationes factas p Formosum Papam, sequitur quod et poterat contra fidem errare.
units.tr: MAG. Secondly, it is shown by examples that a general council can err against the faith. The first example is the synod of Pope Stephen VII, who decreed that the ordinations made by Pope Formosus were void. And afterwards, by a synod celebrated at Ravenna under Pope John IX, that decree was reprobated. Therefore a general council can err, because it is certain that one of those two synods, of which the one reprobated the other, erred. DIS. One of those synods erred, but not against the faith; for it erred only against the ordinations of Pope Formosus. MAG. This answer is challenged, because every congregation that can err against good morals can err against the faith. For evil morals blind the understanding, and so it can sin, and can fall into error even against the faith. If therefore one of those synods erred against morals, impiously and unjustly approving or reprobating the ordinations made by Pope Formosus, it follows that it could also err against the faith.

units.la: DIS. Aliter potest respondi ad exemplum promissum: quod synodus celebrata p Stephanum septimum non fuit concilium generale, sed fuit quædam synodus particularis quorundam episcoporum ad synodum particularem per eundem Stephanum vocatorum.
units.tr: DIS. The example put forward can be answered otherwise: the synod celebrated under Stephen VII was not a general council, but a certain particular synod of some bishops, summoned by the same Stephen to a particular synod.

units.la: MAG. Hoc nō videtur aliis stare posse: quia omnis synodus auctoritate Papæ congregata concilium generale vocatur, vt notat Glo. di. 17. c. 1. quod conciliorum quadā sunt generalia, quædam particularia sive prouincialia, quædam epalia. Vnde est, quod a Papa vel eius legato cum cuibus episcopis statuitur. Nunquam ei legitur ad aliquod concilium generale ces epos conuenisse. cum igitur synodus Stephani auctoritate Papæ fuerit celebrata; sequitur quod concilium generale debuit appellari. DIS. Adducunt nec plura exempla, quod concilium generale potest errare? MAG. Adducunt et in exemplum synodum Ephesinam secunsecundam: quæ errauit. & ideo reprobata fuit, secundum quod notat Glo. di. 15. c. 1. Tertium exemplum eorum est de generali concilio Lugdunensi sub Greg. 10. celebrata: quod contra bonos mores errauit approbando ordines prædicatorum & Minorum, vt habetur extra de regularib. c. religiosum. Quod n. errauit, probant ex hoc, quod status Fratrum Minorum est illicitus, secundum q; ex constitutionib. Iohan. 22. (Ad conditorem. &, quia quorundam: & quia vir reprobus) constat aperte. 5 Quartum exemplum est de concilio Viennensi, quod errauit, constitutionem Nico. 3. quæ incipit: Exiit qui seminat approbando, quod per constitutionem Io. 22. probare nituntur.
units.tr: MAG. This does not seem able to stand with the others, because every synod convened by the authority of the Pope is called a general council, as the Gloss notes on Dist. 17, c. 1, where it says that some councils are general, some particular or provincial, and some ... Hence it is that they are decreed by the Pope or his legate with certain bishops. Nowhere is it read that bishops gathered for any general council without him. Since therefore the synod of Stephen was celebrated by the authority of the Pope, it follows that it ought to have been called a general council. DIS. Do they adduce further examples that a general council can err? MAG. They also adduce as an example the second Synod of Ephesus, which erred, and therefore was reprobated, as the Gloss notes on Dist. 15, c. 1. Their third example is the general council of Lyons celebrated under Gregory X, which erred against good morals in approving the orders of the Preachers and the Minors, as is found in Extra, De regularibus, c. Religiosum. For they prove that it erred from this: that the state of the Friars Minor is unlawful, which clearly follows from the constitutions of John XXII (Ad conditorem, and Quia quorundam, and Quia vir reprobus). Their fourth example is the council of Vienne, which erred in approving the constitution of Nicholas III that begins "Exiit qui seminat," which they seek to prove by the constitution of John XXII.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Vbi ad oppositam assertionem, scilicet quod generale concilium non potest contra fidem errare, arguitur septem rationibus, ad quas respondetur capitulo sequenti. 10
units.tr: Here, against the opposite assertion, namely that a general council cannot err against the faith, an argument is made by seven reasons, to which the following chapter replies.

units.la: DE istis duobus exemplis vltimis, quæ tangunt constitutionem domini Ioh. Papæ tecum, quando te interrogabo de tota doctrina eiusdem domini nostri Papæ, collationem habebo. Et ideo de istis ad præsens supersedeas, & p assertione contraria, quod concilium gen. generale contra fidem errare non possit, allegare nitaris. M A G. Quod concilium generale contra fidem errare non possit, multis viis videtur posse probari; quarum prima est: Illa congregatio, cuius iudicio in 15 causa fidei Romanus pontifex est subiectus, contra fidem errare non potest; quia Papa non tenetur parere mandatis alicuius congregationis, quæ potest contra fidem errare. Si eni o posset errare contra fidem, posset Papa illud iudicium merito recusare. Sed Papa in causa fidei iudicio generalis concilii est subiectus, vt notatur di. 19. c. Anastasius, quod synodus in causa fidei sit maior Papa. ergo synodus generalis contra fidem errare non potest. Secunda ratio est hæc. In ecclesia 20 militante est certum iudicium de difficilibus & obscuris, quæ circa fidem emergunt. aliter enim tota ecclesia militans posset contra fidem errare. sed vltimum iudicium circa difficilia & obscura circa fidem emergentia penes concilium residet generale. ergo concilium generale contra fidem errare non potest. Tertia ratio est. Illa congregatio, à qua in causa fidei non est licitum appellare, contra fidem errare non potest. Omnis vero causa vitiata est per appellationis remedium subleuanda, 2. q. 6. liceat. Causa autem fidei tractata coram illa congregatione, quæ contra fidem valet errare, potest vitiari. ergo licet causam fidei tractatam coram tali congregatione (si fuerit vitiata) per appellationis remedium subleuare, & ita licet ab eis appellare. sed à concilio generali in causa fidei appellare non licet. Si enim appellare liceret, aut appellandum esset ad aliud concilium, aut ad Papam, aut ad vniuersalem ecclesiam. non ad aliud concilium generale; qui eadem ratione ab illo alio concilio generali appellare liceret; & ita finis tali causæ imponi non posset. nec esset appellandum ad Papam: quia Papa in facto fidei est inferior concilio generali. ergo à generali concilio ad ipsum appellare non licet. nec est appellandum ad ecclesiam vniversalem; quia frustra esset talis appellatio, cum vniversalis ecclesia simul in vnum conuenire non possit. Quarta ratio est hæc: Congregatio quæ non potest de hæresi accusari non potest errare contra fidem. concilium autem generale non potest de hæresi accusari. non enim inuenitur persona vel collegium, cui in causa fidei generale concilium sit subiectum. ergo generale concilium contra fidem errare non potest. Quinta ratio est hæc: Illa congregatio, cuius opera omni manent stabilita vigore, contra fidem errare non potest: quia error contra fidem nullo pœstali latis manere vigore. Sed opera generalis concilii omni manent stabilita vigore, teste Isidoro, qui vt recitatur di. 15. c. 1. ait: hæ sunt quatuor synodi principales fidem nostram plenissime continentes. sed si qua sunt similia alia, quæ sancti patres spiritu Dei plensanxerunt, omni manent stabilita vigore. ergo concilium generale contra fidem errare non potest. Sexta ratio est hæc. Illa congregatio contra fidem errare non potest, cuius diffinitiones & determinationes tanquam vniuersali consensu constitutæ sunt censendæ. vniuersalis autem congregatio est concilium generale, teste Greg. qui vt habetur di. 15. c. siue. ait: Hi vero, quas prefata veneranda concilia personas recipiunt, respuo: quæ venerantur, amplector, quia cum vniuersali sunt consensu constituta, se & non illa destruit, quisquis præsumpserit absoluere, quos ligant: aut ligare, quos absoluunt. ergo concilium generale contra fidem errare non potest. D I S. Ista auctoritas Gregorii non videtur ad propositum; quia B. Greg. loquitur ibi solummodo de quatuor conciliis principalibus, non de omnibus. M A G. Ad hoc respondetur, quod licet Greg. loquatur de quatuor principalibus conciliis, tamen assignat rationem, quare sunt recipienda, quia scilicet sunt vniuersali consensu constituta. sed vnum concilium generale non est magis vniuersali consensu constitutum quam aliud: imo vnum non esset generale. Eadem autem ratio & causa eundem habet effectum. Si autem æquatuor principalia concilia sint recipienda omnino, quia sunt vniuersali consensu constituta, ergo omnia generalia concilia sunt recipienda, quia sunt vniuersali consensu instituta. Concilium autem quod est omnino recipiendum & amplectendum, contra fidem errare non potest. igitur nullum concilium generale potest contra fidem errare. Septima ratio est hæc: Illa congregatio, cuius institutiones & opera conseruanda & constituenda discernuntur, non potest contra fidem errare. opera autem & constitutiones omnium generalium conciliorum obseruanda & constituenda discernuntur, teste Gelasio, vt habetur dist. 15. c. sanctissimi. o. ait: si qua sunt consimilia à s. patribus, hactenus instituta, post istorum quatuor auctoritates & obseruanda & custodiela determinamus. Ergo concilium generale contra fidem errare non pot. Octaua ratio est hæc: Illa congregatio contra fidem errare non pot. qua errare vniuersalis erraret ecclesia: sed errare generali concilio vniuersalis erraret ecclesia, qua ista errare nullus inueniretur, quæ aut esset vel posset eadem defendere orthodoxa. ergo generale concilium contra fidem errare non potest.
units.tr: ON these last two examples, which touch on the constitution of Lord Pope John, I will have a discussion with you when I question you about the whole teaching of that lord our Pope. So for now set these aside, and try to argue for the contrary assertion, that a general council cannot err against the faith. MAG. That a general council cannot err against the faith seems capable of being proved in many ways. The first is this: that congregation to whose judgment the Roman pontiff is subject in a matter of faith cannot err against the faith, since the Pope is not bound to obey the commands of any congregation that can err against the faith. For if it could err against the faith, the Pope could rightly refuse that judgment. But in a matter of faith the Pope is subject to the judgment of a general council, as is noted in dist. 19, c. Anastasius, which says that a synod is greater than the Pope in a matter of faith. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith. The second reason is this. In the militant Church there is a certain judgment on the difficult and obscure matters that arise concerning the faith; otherwise the whole militant Church could err against the faith. But the final judgment on difficult and obscure matters arising concerning the faith rests with a general council. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith. The third reason is this. That congregation from which it is not lawful to appeal in a matter of faith cannot err against the faith. But every case that has been vitiated can be relieved by the remedy of appeal, 2 q. 6, Liceat. A matter of faith treated before a congregation that can err against the faith may be vitiated. Therefore it is lawful to relieve a matter of faith treated before such a congregation (if it has been vitiated) by the remedy of appeal, and so it is lawful to appeal from them. But it is not lawful to appeal from a general council in a matter of faith. For if appeal were lawful, it would have to be made either to another council, or to the Pope, or to the universal Church. Not to another general council, since by the same reasoning it would be lawful to appeal from that other general council too, and so an end could never be put to such a case. Nor is it to be made to the Pope, since in a matter of faith the Pope is inferior to a general council. Therefore it is not lawful to appeal from a general council to him. Nor is it to be made to the universal Church, since such an appeal would be pointless, because the universal Church cannot assemble together in one place. The fourth reason is this: a congregation that cannot be accused of heresy cannot err against the faith. But a general council cannot be accused of heresy. For no person or college is found to whom a general council is subject in a matter of faith. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith. The fifth reason is this: that congregation whose works remain established with full force cannot err against the faith, because an error against the faith cannot remain in force. But the works of a general council remain established with full force, as witnessed by Isidore, who, as is cited in dist. 15, c. 1, says: these are the four principal synods most fully containing our faith; but if there are any other similar ones, which the holy Fathers have sanctioned by the Spirit of God, they remain established with full force. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith. The sixth reason is this. That congregation cannot err against the faith whose definitions and determinations are to be regarded as established by universal consent. But a universal congregation is a general council, as witnessed by Gregory, who, as is found in dist. 15, c. Sive, says: those persons whom these venerable councils receive I reject; those which they venerate I embrace, because, since they were established by universal consent, whoever presumes to absolve those whom they bind, or to bind those whom they absolve, destroys himself and not them. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith. DIS. This authority of Gregory does not seem to bear on the point, because Blessed Gregory there speaks only of the four principal councils, not of all of them. MAG. To this it is answered that although Gregory speaks of the four principal councils, nevertheless he assigns the reason why they are to be received, namely that they were established by universal consent. But one general council is not established by universal consent any more than another; indeed, one would not be general at all. The same reason and cause, however, has the same effect. If the four principal councils are to be received absolutely because they were established by universal consent, then all general councils are to be received, because they were established by universal consent. But a council that is to be wholly received and embraced cannot err against the faith. Therefore no general council can err against the faith. The seventh reason is this: that congregation whose institutions and works are discerned to be preserved and established cannot err against the faith. But the works and constitutions of all general councils are discerned to be preserved and established, as witnessed by Gelasius, who, as is found in dist. 15, c. Sanctissimi, says: whatever similar things the holy Fathers have hitherto instituted, we determine that they are to be observed and kept after the authority of these four. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith. The eighth reason is this: that congregation cannot err against the faith by which the universal Church would err. But if a general council erred, the universal Church would err, since no one would be found who could either defend these errors as orthodox or who could be defended as orthodox. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: In quo ad rationes precedentis capituli probantis, quod generale concilium errare non potest contra fidem, respondent tenentes contrarium.
units.tr: In which those who hold the contrary answer the arguments of the preceding chapter, which prove that a general council cannot err against the faith.

units.la: DISCIP. Quamuis indubitanter existimem, concilium generale contra fidem errare non posse; qualiter tamen tenentes assertionem contrariam ad rationes inductas pro veritate respondeant, non differas propalare.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Although I firmly believe that a general council cannot err against the faith, please do not delay in explaining how those who hold the opposite view answer the arguments brought forward for the truth.

units.la: MAG. Ad primam rationem respondetur, quod haec est falsa: Illa congregatio, cuius iudicio in causa fidei Romanus pontifex est subiectus, contra fidem errare non potest, quia licet Papa non sit subiectus alicuius congregationis iudicio, quae errat contra fidem: quia episcopo, quod contra fidem pertinaciter erraret, nullus catholicus in causa fidei esset eius subiectus iudicio; illius tamen congregationis recto iudicio non falso parere tenetur, quae potest errare contra fidem licet non erret. Quemadmodum quilibet Christianus in causa fidei subiectus est Papae, quando non errat contra fidem, licet possit contra fidem errare. Sic etiam sub diri episcoporum, quantum ad ea, quae certa sunt esse fidei consona orthodoxae, subsunt episcopis: qui tamen episcopi, quantum ad illa, de quibus certum est, quod sunt haereses damnatae explicite, possunt contra fidem errare. Cum vero accipitur, quod Papa non tenetur stare mandatis alicuius congregationis, qui potest contra fidem errare, hoc negatur: licet parere non debeat mandatis alicuius congregationis, quae errat contra fidem, sicut nec aliquis alius Christianus. Nec Papa potest recusare iudicium illius congregationis, quae potest contra fidem errare; licet posset recusare illius iudicium, quae errat contra fidem. DIS. Quid si de facto concilium generale erraverit condemnando Papam de haeretica pravitate inique & falso? MAG. Dicunt quod in tali casu nihil restaret eidem, nisi aliud concilium generale vocare, vel per potentiam se tueri, vel omni humano deficiente consilio & auxilio se divinae gratiae committere, & patienter illam iniuriam tolerare.
units.tr: MASTER. To the first argument the reply is that this is false: "That assembly, by whose judgment the Roman pontiff is subject in a matter of faith, cannot err against the faith." For although the Pope is not subject to the judgment of any assembly that errs against the faith, since if the Pope himself were to err obstinately against the faith, no Catholic would be subject to his judgment in a matter of faith, nevertheless he is bound to obey the sound judgment of that assembly which can err against the faith, even though it does not err. Just as every Christian is subject to the Pope in matters of faith when the Pope does not err against the faith, although he could err against the faith. So also under the bishops, as far as those things are concerned which are certainly consonant with the orthodox faith, the faithful are subject to the bishops; yet those bishops, as far as those matters are concerned which are certainly condemned as heresies, can err against the faith. But when it is taken to mean that the Pope is not bound to abide by the commands of any assembly that can err against the faith, this is denied: just as any other Christian, he ought not to obey the commands of an assembly that errs against the faith. Nor can the Pope refuse the judgment of an assembly that can err against the faith, although he could refuse the judgment of one that errs against the faith. DISCIPLE. What if a general council has in fact erred, condemning the Pope of heretical depravity unjustly and falsely? MASTER. They say that in such a case nothing would remain for him except to summon another general council, or to defend himself by force, or, when all human counsel and help fail, to commit himself to the divine grace and patiently bear that injury.

units.la: Ad secundam rationem dicitur quod licet iudicium multis modis accipiatur, ad praesens tamen sufficit duos modos exponere. Est itaque iudicium certae & veridicae cognitionis, quo vnusquisque bene iudicat, de quo quis noscit, & illud iudicium pertinet ad quemlibet in qualibet arte peritum. Est aliud iudicium auctoritatis sive iudicialis sententiae. Primo modo loquendo de iudicio. In ecclesia militante est certum iudicium, quantum ad ea, quae necesse est credere explicite ad salutem aeternam consequendam: quia semper vsq; ad finem mundi erunt aliqui catholici, qui tali modo in vera fide explicite permanebunt. Sed circa illa, quae non sunt necessaria explicite credere, non est necesse, quod semper in ecclesia militante sit tale iudicium. Quia multa sunt, de quibus melius est pie dubitare, quam vnam partem contradictionis vel aliam temere affirmare: nunquam tamen circa quaecunq; talia catholica omnes Christiani neq; pertinaciter errabunt, neq; pertinaciter dubitabunt: sed supererunt aliqui in ecclesia, qui circa huiusmodi loco & tempore oportunis quaerent cauta sollicitudine veritatem, parati etiam tenere explicite, si eam inueniunt sive per propriam meditationem, sive per occasionem acceptam a scripturis, sive aliis hominibus quibuscunque, sive per diuinam reuelationem. & ideo nunquam omnes incident in haereticam pravitatem. Iudicium vero auctoritatis sive iudicialis sententiae non oportet, quod sit semper certum in ecclesia militante; imo potest deficere aliquando, ut videtur, etiam aliquando defecit. Tempore enim Liberii Papae, qui postquam consenserat perfidiae Arianae, tenuit Papatum sex annis. verum iudicium auctoritatis & iudicialis sententiae nullum fuit de his, quae pertinebant ad fidem. Ante etiam tempora Constantini tute iudicium de his, quae fidei sunt, defecisse videtur: quia teste Isid. ut habetur di. 1 f. c. 1. illis temporibus Christianitas in diuersas haereses scissa fuit: quia non erat catholicis facultas conueniendi in vnum. DIS. Isid. dicit ibi, quod episcopis non erat facultas conueniendi in vnum. & ideo Christianitas in diuersas haereses scissa fuit. Ex quo datur intelligi, quod si tunc fuisset facultas conuenendi ad concilium generale, Christian. tas in diuersas haereses scissa non fuisset. Et ita videtur, quod concilium generale contra fidem errare non potest. MAG. Ad hoc respondetur, quod Isid. loquitur pro illo tempore, pro quo episcopi fuerunt catholici. & verum est, quod concilium generale episcoporum catholicorum, quamdiu permanserint in catholica veritate, errare non potest. omnes tamen illi episcopi possunt contra fidem errare, etiam cum omnibus clericis suis. DIS. Die quomodo respondetur ad tertiam rationem. MAG. Ad tertiam rationem respondent isti, quod si concilium generale contra fidem erraret, ab ipso appellare liceret. Et cum dicitur, quod ad aliud concilium generale appellare non liceret: Dicunt, quod ad aliud concilium generale, si daretur facultas concilium congregandi, appellare liceret. Et si iterum illud concilium erraret, liceret ad aliud appellare. & sic semper quousque catholici conuenirent. Iterum si Papa non esset praesens in concilio generali; si concilium errareret contra fidem, ad ipsum Papam appellare liceret, vel ad Papam cum alio concilio congregando. Ad ecclesiam etiam vniuersalem, si conuenire posset, esset principaliter appellandum.
