Si vero Christianitas tantum esset pravitate infecta haeretica, quod Papa & cardinales & praelati & clerici, & principes & potentes essent haeretici: & soli pauci simplices & pauperes in fide manerent catholici; & concilium reputatum generale contra fidem erraret, aliud non restaret fidelibus quam dolor & gemitus: consiliumq; tenere B. Hieron. quod dat viro ecclesiastico & prudenti, quando in ecclesia, quae domus Dei vocatur, inualescit iniquitas, iustitia omnino deprimitur. qui vt recitatur. 11.q.3.c. quando ergo vir, ait. Quando ergo vir ecclesiasticus & prudens atq; intelligens multas impietates in ea quae vocatur domus Dei, esse cognouerit, & non solum multas, sed etiam fortes, & quae opprimere possunt iustitiam: & in tantu doctorum rabiem processisse, vt accipiant pratium in iudicio, & omnia pro muneribus faciant, pauperes deuitent in portis & audire contemnant, taceat in illo tempore, ne det sanctum canibus, & ne mittat margaritas inter porcos, qui onuerfi conculcent eas, & imitetur Ieremiam dicentem: solus sedebam, quia amaritudine repletus eram. sic vt catholicus & fidelis, quando multas haereses esse in Christianitate cognouit: & corruisse veritatem catholicam in plateis. & iterum praelatorum, doctorum, clericorum, potentium & principum rabiem processisse vt fidem tonentur destruere orthodoxam, doctrinam patrum sanctorum audire contemnicant, veritatis catholicae doctores occidant, tnbulent, persequantur & infestent: taceat in illo tempore nec publice coram eis appellet, ne det sanctum canibus, & mittat margaritas ante porcos, qui conuersi conculcent eas, scripturas sanctas perperam exponendo, & ipsas interpretantes ad falsitatem haereticam distorquendo. & imitetur Ieremiam dicentem: solus sedebam, quia amaritudine repletus eram. Ad quartam rationem respondetur, quod concilium generale de iure potest de haeresi accusari. Si enim concilium generale conuocatum primo fidele ante corporalem dissolutionem eiusdem in haeresim laberetur, posset de iure coram Papa catholico (si non esset praesens) de haeresi accusari; & iuxta sanctiones canonicas iudicari. Si vero Papa tali concilio interesset, & vna cum illa congregatione in haereticam prauitatem inciderer, potestas iudicandi omnes esset ad catholicos devoluta. Sicut si omnes praelati & clerici mundi prauitate inficerentur haeretica, potestas iudicandi omnes devolueretur ad catholicos laicos & fideles. Concilium ergo generale, dum manet fidele, nulli personae vel particulari collegio in causa fidei est subiectum, licet ipsum manens infidele vniuersali ecclesiae sit subiectum. Sed si ante recessum conuenientium adinuicem corporaliter, talis congregatio in haeresim laberetur, statim tota ista congregatio ipso iure esset alii personae vel collegio aut congregationi subiecta. Ad quintam rationem respondetur, quod Isidorus loquitur de conciliis generalibus rite congregatis & rite celebratis absque omni errore in bonis & in catholica veritate. Ad sextam rationem respondetur similiter, quod Greg. loquitur de conciliis generalibus rite a catholicis celebratis. Ad septimam dicitur eodem modo, quod Gelasius loquitur de conciliis rite a sanctis patribus celebratis, qui si fuissent haeretici, nequaquam fuissent sancti. Ad octauam respondetur, quod si concilium in haeresim laberetur, remanerent alii catholici, qui occulte vel publice prout expediret, auderent fidem defendere orthodoxam. Ille autem, qui reprobatis filiis carnalibus Abrahae potest de lapidibus suscitare filios Abrahae spirituales, iuxta Baptistae sententiam, potens est & omnibus ad generale concilium conuenientibus in haeresim lapsis, imo omnibus clericis mundi & potentibus secularibus falsitate damnatis haeretica, de lapidibus, id est, laicis rudibus & abiectis pauperibus & despectis catholicis, Dei filios suscitare. Sicut enim in idiotis (sacerdotibus & religiosis ac magistratibus repudiatis) fidem primitus fundauit catholicam: ita omnibus literatis & potentibus datis in reprobum sensum, potest dare pauperes, simplices illiteratos & rusticos in aedificationem ecclesiae orthodoxae.
units.tr: To the second argument it is said that, although judgment is understood in many ways, it is enough for the present to explain two senses. There is the judgment of certain and true knowledge, by which each person judges well concerning what he knows, and this judgment belongs to anyone skilled in any art. There is another judgment, that of authority or of a judicial sentence. Speaking in the first sense of judgment: in the militant Church there is certain judgment as regards those things which it is necessary to believe explicitly in order to obtain eternal salvation, because until the end of the world there will always be some Catholics who will remain explicitly in the true faith in this way. But concerning those things which need not be believed explicitly, it is not necessary that such judgment should always exist in the militant Church. For there are many matters on which it is better to doubt piously than rashly to affirm one part of a contradiction or the other; yet concerning any such Catholic matters, not all Christians will ever err obstinately or doubt obstinately. Rather, there will remain in the Church some who, in a place and time suitable for such matters, will seek the truth with cautious diligence, ready also to hold it explicitly if they find it, whether through their own meditation, or through an occasion received from the Scriptures, or from any other men, or through divine revelation. And therefore never will all fall into heretical depravity. But judgment of authority, or judicial sentence, need not always be certain in the militant Church; indeed it can fail at times, as it seems, and at times it has in fact failed. For in the time of Pope Liberius, who, after he had consented to the Arian perfidy, held the papacy for six years, there was no true judgment of authority or judicial sentence concerning the matters pertaining to the faith. Likewise, before the times of Constantine, judgment on matters of faith seems to have failed altogether, because, as Isidore testifies, as is found in Dist. 1, c. 1, in those times Christianity was split into various heresies, since Catholics had no opportunity of meeting together as one. DISCIPLE. Isidore says there that the bishops had no opportunity of meeting together, and therefore Christianity was split into various heresies. From this it is to be understood that if at that time there had been an opportunity of gathering in a general council, Christianity would not have been split into various heresies. And so it seems that a general council cannot err against the faith. MASTER. To this it is replied that Isidore speaks of that time, when the bishops were Catholics. And it is true that a general council of Catholic bishops, as long as they remain in the Catholic truth, cannot err. Yet all those bishops can err against the faith, even together with all their clergy. DISCIPLE. Tell me how you answer the third argument. MASTER. To the third argument these men reply that if a general council erred against the faith, it would be lawful to appeal from it. And when it is said that one could not appeal to another general council, they say that one could appeal to another general council, if an opportunity were given to convene a council; and if that council also erred, it would be lawful to appeal to yet another, and so always until Catholics could meet together. Again, if the Pope were not present at the general council, and the council erred against the faith, it would be lawful to appeal to the Pope himself, or to the Pope with another council summoned. The appeal should also be made principally to the universal Church, if it could assemble. But if Christianity were so infected with heretical depravity that the Pope, the cardinals, the prelates, the clergy, the princes and the powerful were all heretics, and only a few simple and poor people remained Catholic in the faith, and a council regarded as general erred against the faith, nothing would remain for the faithful except grief and lamentation. And they hold the counsel that St Jerome gives to an ecclesiastical and prudent man, when iniquity grows strong in the Church, which is called the house of God, and justice is wholly suppressed; which, as it is cited in C. 11, q. 3, c. "Quando ergo vir," reads: "When therefore an ecclesiastical and prudent and intelligent man has perceived many impieties in that which is called the house of God, and not only many but also strong ones, which can oppress justice; and when the rage of the teachers has advanced so far that they accept bribes in judgment, and do everything for gifts, and avoid the poor at the gates and despise hearing them; let him keep silent in that time, lest he give what is holy to dogs, and lest he cast pearls before swine, who, turned round, trample them underfoot, and let him imitate Jeremiah saying: 'I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness.'" Thus the Catholic and faithful man, when he has perceived that many heresies exist in Christianity, and that Catholic truth has fallen in the streets, and again that the rage of prelates, teachers, clergy, the powerful and princes has advanced so far that they strive to destroy the orthodox faith, despise hearing the doctrine of the holy Fathers, kill, harass, persecute and attack the teachers of Catholic truth; let him keep silent in that time, nor appeal publicly before them, lest he give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine, who, turned round, trample them underfoot, by expounding the holy Scriptures perversely and twisting them into heretical falsehood; and let him imitate Jeremiah saying: "I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness." To the fourth argument it is replied that a general council can rightly be accused of heresy. For if a general council, lawfully convened, should first fall into heresy before its bodily dissolution, it could rightly be accused of heresy before the Catholic Pope (if he were not present), and be judged according to the canonical sanctions. But if the Pope were present at such a council and fell into heretical depravity together with that assembly, the power of judging all would pass to the Catholics. Just as if all prelates and clergy of the world were infected with heretical depravity, the power of judging all would pass to the Catholic laity and the faithful. Therefore a general council, while it remains faithful, is subject in a matter of faith to no person or particular college, although if it remains unfaithful it is subject to the universal Church. But if, before those assembled have separated bodily from one another, such an assembly should fall into heresy, then at once that whole assembly would by law itself be subject to another person, college or assembly. To the fifth argument it is replied that Isidore speaks of general councils lawfully gathered and lawfully celebrated, free from all error in good things and in the Catholic truth. Likewise to the sixth argument it is replied that Gregory speaks of general councils lawfully celebrated by Catholics. To the seventh it is said in the same way that Gelasius speaks of councils lawfully celebrated by the holy Fathers, who, if they had been heretics, would by no means have been holy. To the eighth it is replied that if a council fell into heresy, there would remain other Catholics who, openly or secretly as circumstances required, would dare to defend the orthodox faith. But He who, having rejected the carnal sons of Abraham, is able, according to the saying of the Baptist, to raise up spiritual sons of Abraham from stones, is able also, when all those who come to a general council have fallen into heresy, and indeed when all the clergy of the world and the secular powerful have been condemned by heretical falsehood, to raise up the sons of God from stones, that is, from rude laymen, poor and despised, and from those scorned as Catholics. For just as at the beginning He founded the Catholic faith on uneducated men (having rejected priests, religious and magistrates), so, to all the learned and powerful who have been given over to a reprobate mind, He can give the poor, simple, unlettered and rustic for the building up of the orthodox Church.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: Vbi ad tractationem quinta assertionis superius primo capitulo huius libri allegata accedit ur, super qua formari potest quinta quaestio principalis, haec scilicet, vtrum tota multitudo fidelium haereticari possit. Pro cuius decisione prius hanc quaestionem tractat: Vtrum totus clerus possit haeretica falsitate irretiri: pro qua ponitur talis conclusio: Quod tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem catholicam errare. & per consequens totus clerus non est illa ecclesia, quae contra fidem errare non potest. quod probat decem rationibus.
units.tr: Here we come to the discussion of the fifth assertion, cited above in the first chapter of this book, from which the fifth principal question can be formed: namely, whether the whole multitude of the faithful can be made heretical. To decide it, he first takes up this question: whether the whole clergy can be ensnared in heretical falsehood. For this he puts forward the following conclusion: the whole multitude of clergy can err against the Catholic faith, and consequently the whole clergy is not that church which cannot err against the faith. He proves this by ten arguments.

units.la: DISCIP. Admiratione permouentur, quod isti praesumunt asserere, totum clerum posse falsitate haeretica irretiri. Et quia vix vnquam aliquis sine motiuo assentit errori, aperias vnde isti mouentur pro opinione praedicta. MAG. Principale motiuum eorum est hoc (quod saepe pro multis assertionibus est inductum) quod vna sola est videlicet ecclesia militans, quae contra fidem errare non potest. constat autem, quod congregatio fidelium, quae clericos & laicos comprehendit de facto, vel comprehendere potest, nequit contra fidem errare. Multitudo autem tota clericorum non est illa congregatio, licet sit pars eius, quemadmodum & multitudo laicorum est pars eius. ergo tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. They are amazed that these men dare to assert that the whole clergy can be ensnared in heretical falsehood. And since hardly anyone assents to an error without some motive, explain to me what moves them to hold this opinion. TEACHER. Their main motive is this, which has often been brought up in support of many assertions: there is only one church militant, and it cannot err against the faith. Now it is certain that the assembly of the faithful, which in fact includes or can include both clergy and laity, cannot err against the faith. But the whole multitude of clergy is not that assembly, although it is a part of it, just as the multitude of laity is a part of it. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith.

units.la: DISCIP. Habent ne alia fundamenta minus principalia pro assertione praedicta. MAGIST. Aliis rationibus se munire nituntur. Vnde secundum motiuum eorum est hoc: tota illa particularis multitudo Christianorum, qui in omnibus locis ponunt scandalum fidei orthodoxae: & qui soli secundum ecclesiam, & populos de domo Dei seducunt, potest contra fidem errare. Huiusmodi est multitudo clericorum, teste B. Hieron. qui vt recitatur, 24. q. 3. transferunt, ait; Veteres scrutans historias inuenire non possum fidisse ecclesiam & de domo Dei populos seduxisse, praeter eos, qui sacerdotes a Deo positi fuerant & prophetae, id est, speculatores. isti autem recurruint in laqueum tortuosum in omnibus locis ponentes scandalum. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod sacerdotes & speculatores, id est, doctores, consueuerunt ecclesiam Dei scindere, & populos de domo Dei seducere, scandalu fidei orthodoxæ ponendo vbique. ergo omnes sacerdotes possunt contra fidem errare. Nomine autem sacerdotis intelliguntur inferiores clerici; quod notat Gloss. ext. de cohabitatione clericorum & mulierum. ca. 2. quisque sacerdotum. ergo tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Do they have other, less principal foundations for the aforesaid assertion? TEACHER. They strive to fortify themselves with other arguments. So their second motive is this: that whole particular multitude of Christians who set a stumbling-block to the orthodox faith in all places, and who alone among the church and the peoples seduce them from the house of God, can err against the faith. Such a multitude is the clergy, as blessed Jerome testifies, who, as it is recited in 24 q. 3, Transferunt, says: "Searching the ancient histories, I cannot find that the church ever trusted, or led the peoples away from the house of God, except those who had been appointed priests and prophets by God, that is, watchmen. These fell back into the twisting snare, setting up stumbling-blocks in all places." From these words it is to be understood that priests and watchmen, that is, teachers, have been accustomed to divide the church of God and to seduce the peoples from the house of God, setting up a stumbling-block to the orthodox faith everywhere. Therefore all priests can err against the faith. By the name priests are understood the lower clergy, as the Gloss notes on Extra, de cohabitatione clericorum et mulierum, c. 2, Quisque sacerdotum. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith.

units.la: Tertium motiuum est tale: tota multitudo illorum, qui sunt deteriores laicis, potest contra fidem errare. quia nulla apparet ratio, quare Deus talem multitudinem ab errore contra fidem specialiter præseruaret. Sed clerici sunt deteriores laicis, secundum quod notat Gloss. depœ. di. 1. c. quis aliquando, dicens: habes ex hoc ca. quod clerici sunt deteriores laicis. 24. quæst. 3. transferunt. ergo tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare.
units.tr: Their third motive is this: the whole multitude of those who are worse than the laity can err against the faith, because no reason appears why God would especially preserve such a multitude from error against the faith. But the clergy are worse than the laity, as the Gloss notes on De paen. dist. 1, c. Quis aliquando, saying: "You have from this chapter that the clergy are worse than the laity; 24 q. 3, Transferunt." Therefore the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith.

units.la: Quartum motiuum eorum est: tota multitudo illorum, à quibus omnia mala procedunt, potest contra fidem errare: quia ab illis præcipue hæretica prauitas noscitur prouenire. Sed omnia mala à sacerdotibus processerunt, vt notat Gloss. dist. ca. purgabit. ergo tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare.
units.tr: Their fourth motive is this: the whole multitude of those from whom all evils proceed can err against the faith, because heretical depravity is known to arise chiefly from them. But all evils have proceeded from priests, as the Gloss notes on dist. c. Purgabit. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith.

units.la: Quintum motiuum eorum est hoc: tota multitudo illorum potest contra fidem errare, quos valent laici iudicare. Sed malos clericos valent laici iudicare, teste Hiero. qui, vt habetur dist. 8. q. 1. c. vereor, ait: Vereor quomodo regina Austri veniens à finibus terræ audire sapientiam Salomonis, iudicatura est homines temporis sui: & viri Niniuitæ actu pœnitentiæ ad prædicationem Ionæ condemnabunt eos, qui maiorem etiam Ionæ saluatorem contempserunt: sic plurimi in populo episcopos iudicabunt. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod temerarium est asserere, quod nunquam laici episcopos in comparatione vitæ iudicabunt, sicut ergo laici possunt in moribus & fide errare, ita etiam episcopi. & etiam eadem ratione alii clerici contra bonos mores & fidem possunt errare. Ergo temerarium est asserere, quod nunquam tota multitudo clericorum errabit.
units.tr: Their fifth motive is this: the whole multitude of those whom the laity are able to judge can err against the faith. But the laity are able to judge bad clergy, as blessed Jerome testifies, who, as it is found in dist. 8 q. 1, c. Vereor, says: "I fear how the queen of the south, coming from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, will judge the men of her own time; and the men of Nineveh, by their repentance at the preaching of Jonah, will condemn those who despised even a greater Saviour than Jonah. So many among the people will judge the bishops." From these words it is to be understood that it is rash to assert that the laity will never judge bishops in comparison of life. Therefore, just as the laity can err in morals and faith, so can bishops; and by the same reasoning other clergy too can err against good morals and the faith. Therefore it is rash to assert that the whole multitude of clergy will never err.

units.la: Sextum motiuum eorum est hoc: multitudo illorum potest contra fidem errare, quibus laici possunt esse meliores. sed laici possunt esse meliores clericis, teste beato Hier., qui, vt habetur: 8. quæst. 1. c. qualis, ait. Qualis erit edificatio discipuli, si intelligat magistro se esse maiorem. & infra; Vehementer ecclesiam Dei destruit hoc. scil. meliores esse laicos quam clericos. Ex quibus verbis insinuatur aperte, quod laici possunt esse clericis meliores. sicut ergo tota multitudo laicorum potest contra fidem errare: ita tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare.
units.tr: Their sixth motive is this: the multitude of those whom the laity can surpass in goodness can err against the faith. But the laity can be better than the clergy, as blessed Jerome testifies, who, as it is found in 8 q. 1, c. Qualis, says: "What kind of edification will a disciple be, if he understands himself to be greater than his master?" And further on: "This greatly destroys the church of God," namely, that the laity be better than the clergy. From these words it is plainly suggested that the laity can be better than the clergy. Therefore, just as the whole multitude of laity can err against the faith, so the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith.

units.la: Septimum motiuum est tale: multitudo illorum potest contra fidem errare, qui possunt peccare, & de quibus vix aliquis inuenitur vere pœnitens post peccatum, quia peccatum excæcat intellectum: & ita tandem poterit, si per pœnitentiam minime deleatur, ad errorem contra fidem deducere. Sed clerici omnes possunt peccare, & de clericis vix inuenitur aliquis vere pœnitens post peccatum, teste Iohann. Chrysost. qui, vt habetur de pœnitentia dist. 1. c. quis aliquando vidit clericum cito pœnitentiam agentem: & si deprehensus humiliauerit se, non ideo dolet quod peccauit: sed confunditur, quia per dilapsu gloriam suam. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod clerici raro inueniuntur vere pœnitentes. Ergo est temerarium asserere, quod multitudo tota clericorum nunquam contra fidem errabit.
units.tr: Their seventh motive is this: the multitude of those who can sin, and among whom scarcely anyone is found truly repentant after sin (because sin blinds the understanding, and so at last, if it is not wiped out by repentance, it can lead one into error against the faith), can err against the faith. But all clergy can sin, and among the clergy scarcely anyone is found truly repentant after sin, as John Chrysostom testifies, who, as it is found in De paen. dist. 1, c. Quis aliquando, says: "Have you ever seen a cleric quickly doing penance? And if, when caught, he humbles himself, it is not that he grieves for having sinned, but he is ashamed because by his fall he has lost his glory." From these words it is to be understood that clergy are rarely found truly repentant. Therefore it is rash to assert that the whole multitude of clergy will never err against the faith.

units.la: Octauum motiuum est tale: multitudo illorum potest contra fidem errare, qui sola dignitate ecclesiastica virtutes & gratiam minime conferente nec augente alios catholicos & fideles noscuntur præcellere. Quia ex quo per talem dignitatem gratia & virtutes nec conferuntur neque augentur necessario, nihil habent. Quare non possunt (sicut prius) contra fidem errare. Sed clerici vltra laicos fideles & catholicos nihil necessario obtinent, nisi clericatum, quæ dignitas ecclesiastica appellatur. Nulla autem dignitas ecclesiastica in ecclesia militante confert necessario gratiam & virtutes, nec necessario auget, sicut in superioribus per auctoritates plurimas est ostensum. Ergo tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare, sicut poterant omnes contra fidem errare quando laici exiterunt.
units.tr: Their eighth motive is this: the multitude of those who are known to surpass other Catholic and faithful people merely by ecclesiastical dignity, which does not confer or increase virtues and grace, can err against the faith. For since by such a dignity grace and virtues are neither conferred nor increased of necessity, they have nothing of the kind, and therefore they cannot (as before) err against the faith. But the clergy obtain nothing necessarily beyond the faithful and Catholic laity except clerical status, which is called an ecclesiastical dignity. But no ecclesiastical dignity in the church militant necessarily confers grace and virtues, nor necessarily increases them, as has been shown above by very many authorities. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith, just as all could err against the faith when there were no laity.

units.la: Nonum eorum motiuum est tale: si multitudo tota clericorum non potest contra fidem errare, sicut tota multitudo laicorum potest contra fidem errare; aut hoc est ratione regiminis & auctoritatis, quam habent clerici super laicos; aut ratione maioris sanctitatis, qua clerici pollent; aut ratione maioris sapientiæ & literaturæ, quam habent clerici vltra laicos; aut quia tota multitudine clericorum errante tota fides periclitaretur catholica. Non propter primum; tum quia, sicut prædictum est, dignitas aut regimen ecclesiasticum non necessario confert habenti, nec necessario auget in eo gratiam & virtutem. Tum quia summus pontifex, quantum ad regimen & potestatem ecclesiasticam, plenitudinem obtinet potestatis: & tamen Papa potest hæretica prauitate fœdari. ergo & tota multitudo clericorum, non obstante tali regimine, prauitate poterit hæretica maculari.
units.tr: Their ninth motive is this: if the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith, while the whole multitude of laity can, then this is either because of the rule and authority which the clergy have over the laity, or because of the greater holiness in which the clergy excel, or because of the greater wisdom and learning which the clergy have beyond the laity, or because if the whole multitude of clergy erred, the whole Catholic faith would be endangered. Not on account of the first: first, because, as has been said, ecclesiastical dignity or government does not of necessity confer grace and virtue on the one who holds it, nor necessarily increase them in him; second, because the supreme pontiff, as far as ecclesiastical rule and power go, holds the fullness of power, and yet the Pope can be defiled by heretical depravity. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy, despite such rule, can also be stained by heretical depravity.

units.la: Secundum etiam non obstat: quia multi inueniuntur laici clericis sanctiores & in fide stabiliores, teste Ambrosio, qui, vt habetur. 8. quæst. 1. c. quid autem, ait: quid autem ego vos arguo, cum possitis me uno sermone convincere? convincor enim, cum in hac parte clericos vobis video magis negligentes. quomodo enim possum corrigere filios, cum fratres emendare non possim? aut qua fiducia succensear laicis, cum à consortibus (pudoris verecundia) contice[sc]am? Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod laici possunt esse clericis sanctiores. Ergo propter maiorem sanctitatem non dicitur, quod tota multitudo clericorum non potest contra fidem errare. Nec propter maiorem sapientiam seu literaturam, quam clerici pollent, debet dici, quod tota multitudo clericorum errare non potest contra fidem: quia sicut sapientia vel literatura est saepe occasio stabilitatis in fide, ita est saepe occasio haereticae pravitatis. Unde communiter inventores haeresum sunt viri literati, scripturarum noticiam divinarum habentes, suos errores ex ipsis sacris literis assumentes, ipsosque errores per sacras scripturas fulcire conantes, secundum quod testatur beatus Clemens, & legitur di. 28. ca. relatum. Et beatus Hieron. insinuat in prologo Bibliae asserens nonnullos ad voluntatem suam sacram scripturam trahere repugnantem. Propter maiorem ergo noticiam scripturarum non est dicendum, quod si tota multitudo clericorum erraret, periclitaretur fides. Quia, sicut testificatur beatus Paulus. 1. Corinth. 8. Fides nostra non est in sapientia hominum, sed est in virtute Dei. Sed virtute Dei potest fides catholica sustentari in laicis, sicut in literatis & clericis. Praesertim cum saepe simplices laici & pauperes stabiliores in fide inveniantur, quam clerici: maxime cum Christus fidem per idiotas & illiteratos fundaverit. Ergo quamvis omnes clerici deviarent a fide, non periclitaretur fides. Decimum motivum eorum est tale: tota multitudo clericorum non est sanctior nec fide stabilior, quam fuit collegium apostolorum. Collegium autem apostolorum tempore passionis Christi erravit in fide. ergo & multitudo clericorum potest in fide errare. Dicunt ergo isti, quod sicut temerarium est dicere, quod tota multitudo clericorum non errabit contra fidem; ita temerarie dicitur, quod multitudo clericorum nec tempore Antichristi, nec alio tempore contra fidem errabit. De nulla enim congregatione multitudinis vel collegio firmiter est tenendum, quod nunquam contra fidem errabit, nisi inquantum hoc potest colligi ex verbis Christi promittentis apostolis, quod fides catholica est usque ad finem seculi permansura. In promissione autem licet Christus locutus fuerit apostolis, qui erant episcopi, non tamen loquebatur practise pro ipsis, sed locutus est pro futuris. Inter illos autem futuros nullam de clericis specialem fecit mentionem. Nec verba sua intelligenda sunt de aliqua multitudine speciali Christianorum, sed de tota multitudine: quia haec nunquam erit vera: tota multitudo Christianorum errat in fide; sed an haec erit vera: tota multitudo clericorum errat in fide, nescitur a nobis, sed a Deo, qui omnia futura novit. Praedictae assertioni concordat Gloss. 28. quaest. 1. ca. a recta: Quaero de qua ecclesia intelligitur, quod dicitur, quod non possit errare. Et respondens ait: Respondeo quod ipsa congregatio fidelium hic dicitur ecclesia. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod congregatio fidelium est illa ecclesia, de qua dicitur, quod errare non potest. Ad congregationem autem fidelium ita pertinent laici fideles, sicut clerici. Igitur de multitudine clericorum non debet intelligi, quod errare non possit.
units.tr: The second objection does not hold either, because many laymen are found who are holier than clergy and more steadfast in the faith. Ambrose, as it is found in 8. quæst. 1. c. quid autem, says: "But why do I accuse you, when you could convict me with a single word? I am convicted, for I see that in this matter the clergy are more negligent than you. For how can I correct sons when I cannot amend brothers? Or with what confidence can I rebuke the laity, when I must blush before my own companions out of shame?" From these words it is clear that laymen can be holier than clergy. Therefore, because of greater holiness, it is not said that the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith. Nor, because of the greater wisdom or learning which the clergy possess, should it be said that the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith, since learning is often an occasion of steadfastness in the faith, but it is also often an occasion of heretical depravity. Hence those who invent heresies are commonly learned men, who have knowledge of the divine Scriptures, who take up their errors from the sacred letters themselves and try to prop up those very errors by the holy Scriptures, as the blessed Clement testifies, and as is read in dist. 28 c. relatum. And the blessed Jerome hints at this in the prologue to the Bible, asserting that some drag the holy Scripture to their own will, although it resists. Therefore, because of greater knowledge of the Scriptures, it is not to be said that if the whole multitude of clergy erred, the faith would be in danger. For, as the blessed Paul testifies, 1 Cor. 8: "Our faith is not in the wisdom of men, but is in the power of God." But by the power of God the Catholic faith can be sustained in laymen just as in the learned and the clergy. Especially since simple and poor laymen are often found more steadfast in the faith than clergy, most of all since Christ founded the faith through unlearned and illiterate men. Therefore, although all the clergy were to turn aside from the faith, the faith would not be in danger. The tenth argument of these men is this: the whole multitude of clergy is not holier, nor more steadfast in the faith, than the college of the apostles was. But the college of the apostles erred in the faith at the time of Christ's passion. Therefore the multitude of clergy too can err in the faith. These men therefore say that just as it is rash to say that the whole multitude of clergy will not err against the faith, so it is rashly said that the multitude of clergy will never err against the faith, either in the time of Antichrist or at any other time. For concerning no gathering of a multitude or college is it to be firmly held that it will never err against the faith, except insofar as this can be gathered from the words of Christ promising the apostles that the Catholic faith would remain until the end of the age. But in that promise, although Christ spoke to the apostles, who were bishops, he did not speak properly for them, but spoke for those who would come. Among those future people, however, he made no special mention of the clergy. Nor are his words to be understood of some particular multitude of Christians, but of the whole multitude, because this would never be true: the whole multitude of Christians errs in the faith. But whether this will be true, that the whole multitude of clergy errs in the faith, is not known to us, but to God, who knows all future things. The aforesaid assertion agrees with the Gloss on 28 q. 1 c. a recta: "I ask of what church it is understood that it cannot err." And answering, it says: "I answer that the very congregation of the faithful is here called the church." From these words it is gathered that the congregation of the faithful is that church of which it is said that it cannot err. Now the faithful laity belong to the congregation of the faithful just as the clergy do. Therefore it should not be understood of the multitude of clergy that it cannot err.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Ponit opinionem contrariam, scil. quod totus clerus contra fidem errare non potest. Ubi etiam ponitur haec conclusio, scil. quod soli clerici sunt ecclesia. Qua probatur septem rationibus, ad quas respondetur capitulo sequenti.
units.tr: He sets out the opposing opinion, namely that the whole clergy cannot err against the faith. Here also this conclusion is laid down, that the clergy alone are the Church. It is proved by seven reasons, to which the next chapter replies.

units.la: DISCIP. Pro ista assertione, quam existimo falsam, satis allegasti. Ideo quaeso quod pro assertione contraria alias allegationes adducas. MAGIST. Duo sunt fundamenta principalia assertionis contrariae: ex quibus sequitur, quod multitudo clericorum contra fidem errare non potest. Primum est, quod ecclesia contra fidem errare non potest. Secundum est quod multitudo clericorum est ecclesia. DISCIP. Quod ecclesia non possit errare contra fidem, concedunt adversarii. Ideo solum proba, quod soli clerici sunt ecclesia. MAGIST. Quod soli clerici sunt ecclesia, ex verbis sanctorum patrum colligitur manifeste. Ait enim Adrianus Papa, ut legitur di. 63. c. 1. quisquis saecularium principum vel potentum, vel alterius dignitatis laicus adversus communem vel consonantem atque catholicam electionem ecclesiastici ordinis agere tempaverit, anathema sit, donec obediat & consentiat quicquid ecclesia de electione aut ordinatione praesulis se velle monstraverit. Ex quibus patet, quod ecclesia contra laicos est distincta; ergo soli clerici sunt ecclesia. Item Inno. tertius, ut habetur ext. de constit. c. Ecclesia, ait: non attemptantes quod laicis super ecclesias, & personas ecclesiasticas nulla sit attributa facultas. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod laici super ecclesiam vel personas ecclesiasticas nullam habent penitus facultatem. Constat autem, quod nonnulli laici super alios laicos obtinent potestatem. Igitur laici non sunt personae ecclesiasticae nec sunt de ecclesia: & ita soli clerici dicuntur ecclesia. DISCIP. Notum est, quod soli clerici vocantur ecclesia & ecclesiastici viri. Quare, cum constet, quod ecclesia non potest contra fidem errare, sequitur quod tota multitudo clericorum nunquam deviabit a fide. Ideo circa istud medium amplius non insistas, sed alia media coneris adducere. MAGIST. Secundum medium pro assertione praedicta est: tota multitudo illorum non potest errare contra fidem, ad quos & non ad alios spectat quaestiones fidei terminare, & contra fidem errantes corrigere: qua multitudine totali errante, tota fides periret. Sed ad solos clericos & non ad laicos spectat quaestiones fidei terminare, & errantes contra fidem corrigere. Ergo tota multitudo clericorum nequit contra fidem errare, cum fides perire non possit. Maior videtur certa, quia nunquam erit ecclesia Dei vsq; ad finem seculi absq; auctoritate quæstiones terminandi & hæreticos corrigendi. Minor quo ad vtramq; partem probatur. Quod enim ad solos clericos spectat quæstiones fidei terminare, patet quia ad solam sedem apostolicam, cui soli clerici præsident, spectat quæstiones fidei terminare. 24. q. 1. c. quotiens. & ext. de baptismo & eius effectu, maiores. Secunda pars etiam probatur, quod hæresis est crimen hæreticum. ergo ad solos clericos spectat de crimine illo cognoscere. DISC. De hac materia quæram postea multa. ideo de illa pertranseas: & aliud motiuum pro assertione prædicta inducas. MAGIST. Tertium motiuum eorum est tale. Tota multitudo illorum non potest contra fidem errare, qui nullius iudicio extra illam multitudinem sunt subiecti. quia si tota illa multitudo contra fidem erraret, nullus esset, qui hæreticos punire valeret. sed clerici nullius alterius, quam clericorum sunt subiecti iudicio, vt sacri canones attestantur. ergo tota multitudo clericorum contra fidem errare non potest. Quartum medium eorum est tale. Tota multitudo eorum non potest contra fidem errare, qui soli & non alii potestatem habent eligendi caput ecclesiæ: quia nunquam ecclesia ad statum illum peruenire, quin possit sibi caput eligere: cum quælibet congregatio possit sibi statuere caput. (sed soli clerici & non laici habent potestatem eligendi caput ecclesiæ. scil. summum pontificem, iuxta canonicas sanctiones. ergo tota multitudo clericorum nunquam errabit contra fidem. Quintum motiuum eorum est tale: domus Dei, quæ est ecclesia militans, non potest esse nulla, sicut nec ecclesia potest esse nulla, 24. q. 91. c. petenda, teste Hieron. vt legitur 24. q. 1. c. omnibus, qui ait: omnibus consideratū puto me temere non dicere, alios esse ita in domo Dei vt ipsi sint eadem domus Dei quæ dicitur ædificari super petram, quæ vnica & columba appellatur. Et paruum post: quæ domus etiam claues accepit ac potestatem ligandi & soluendi. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod domus Dei, quæ vnica columba vocatur, quam constat esse ecclesiam catholicam, claues habet ac potestatem ligandi & soluendi. claues autem & prædicta potestas in solis sacerdotibus inueniuntur. ergo vsque ad finem seculi erunt in ecclesia catholica aliqui sacerdotes. & per consequens nunquam tota multitudo clericorum contra fidem errabit. Sextum motiuum est tale: Christus vsque ad finem seculi in ecclesia militante permanebit non solum per fidem & dilectionem, sed etiam per suam præsentiam sacramentalem. ergo semper erunt in ecclesia aliqui sacerdotes, qui potestatem habebunt conficiendi corpus Christi. sed si tota multitudo clericorum hæreticaretur, non esset in ecclesiis, qui potestatem haberet conficiendi corpus Christi, quod nunquam accidet. ergo nunquam tota multitudo clericorum exorbitabit à fide. Septimum eorum motiuum est tale: ecclesiastica hierarchia vsque in finem seculi permanebit. sed in solis prælatis & sacerdotibus & cæteris clericis consistit ecclesiastica hierarchia. ergo vsque ad finem seculi aliqui prælati & sacerdotes & alii clerici fideles & catholici permanebunt. Tria vltima motiua confirmantur vna ratione tali: si tota multitudo clericorum posset hæreticari, eadem ratione tota multitudo clericorum posset per mortem extingui, immo occidi. Sed nunquam ante finem mundi tota multitudo clericorum erit extincta: quia si tota multitudo clericorum esset extincta, non solum ecclesia esset actu priuata clauibus regni cœlorum, & potentia ligandi & soluendi, ac etiam sacramento corporis Christi & ecclesiastica hierarchia; sed etiam priuata esset potestate habendi prædicta. Quamuis etiam si tota multitudo clericorum hæreticaretur, vel ecclesia careat prædictis, de facto tamen si remanserint alii clerici hæretici, possent aliqui catholici ordinari ab eis, quod, vt videtur, aliquibus esset licitum in illo casu, sicut in articulo necessitatis licet ab hæreticis baptismum accipere. quibus ordinatis possunt omnia prædicta reparari. sed si nulli clerici nec catholici nec hæretici remaneant, nunquam posset aliquis in ecclesia habere claues, neque potestatem ligandi atque soluendi, nec conficere corpus Christi: & cessaret omnis ecclesiastica hierarchia. & ita inconueniens est dicere, quod tota multitudo clericorum posset per mortem extingui: quare inconueniens est asserere totam multitudinem clericorum posse in hæreticam incidere prauitatem. Octauum motiuum est tale: tota multitudo eorum nequit contra fidem errare, à qua quicunque separatur, pacem cum ecclesia Dei habere non potest. sed qui separatur à tota multitudine clericorum, pacem cum ecclesia Dei habere non potest, teste Cypriano, qui, vt recitatur 7. quæst. 1. c. nunciamus, ait, qui ergo nec coniunctionem pacis, nec vnitatem spiritus obseruat & se ab ecclesiæ vinculo & sacerdotum collegio separat, episcopi nec potestatem potest habere nec honorem, qui episcopatus nec vnitatem habere voluit, nec pacem. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod qui separat se à collegio sacerdotum, nec honorem nec pacem nec vnitatem cum ecclesia Dei potest habere. Ergo tota multitudo clericorum, quæ intelligitur nomine sacerdotum, contra fidem errare non potest.
units.tr: STUDENT. You have said enough in support of this assertion, which I think is false. So I ask you to bring forward other arguments for the contrary assertion. MASTER. The contrary assertion has two chief foundations, from which it follows that the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith. The first is that the Church cannot err against the faith. The second is that the multitude of clergy is the Church. STUDENT. Our opponents grant that the Church cannot err against the faith. So prove only that the clergy alone are the Church. MASTER. That the clergy alone are the Church is plainly gathered from the words of the holy Fathers. For Pope Adrian says, as it is read in Dist. 63, c. 1: "Whoever among secular princes or powers, or any other lay person of whatever dignity, shall presume to act against the common and harmonious and catholic election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema, until he obeys and consents to whatever the Church shows it wishes concerning the election or ordination of the prelate." From these words it is clear that the Church is distinguished from the laity; therefore the clergy alone are the Church. Likewise Innocent III, as it is held in Extra, De constitutionibus, c. Ecclesia, says: "Not presuming that laymen have any authority over churches and ecclesiastical persons." From these words it is understood that laymen have no authority at all over the Church or ecclesiastical persons. Yet it is certain that some laymen have power over other laymen. Therefore laymen are not ecclesiastical persons, nor are they of the Church; and so the clergy alone are called the Church. STUDENT. It is well known that the clergy alone are called the Church and ecclesiastical men. Hence, since it is agreed that the Church cannot err against the faith, it follows that the whole multitude of clergy will never depart from the faith. So do not dwell further on this middle term, but try to bring forward other means. MASTER. The second means for the aforesaid assertion is this: the whole multitude of those who alone, and not others, have the right to settle questions of faith and to correct those who err against the faith, cannot err against the faith; for if that whole multitude erred, the faith itself would perish. But questions of faith are settled, and those who err against the faith are corrected, by the clergy alone and not by the laity. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith, since the faith cannot perish. The major premise seems certain, because there will never be a Church of God until the end of the world without the authority to settle questions and to correct heretics. The minor is proved on both counts. That the settling of questions of faith belongs to the clergy alone is evident, because it belongs to the apostolic see alone, over which the clergy alone preside, to settle questions of faith (24 q. 1, c. Quotiens; and Extra, De baptismo et eius effectu, Maiores). The second part is also proved, because heresy is a heretical crime; therefore it belongs to the clergy alone to take cognizance of that crime. STUDENT. I shall ask many things about this subject later; so pass over it now and bring forward another motive for the aforesaid assertion. MASTER. Their third motive is this. The whole multitude of those who are subject to no judgment outside that multitude cannot err against the faith; for if that whole multitude erred against the faith, there would be no one able to punish heretics. But the clergy are subject to the judgment of none other than clergy, as the sacred canons attest. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith. Their fourth means is this. The whole multitude of those who alone, and not others, have the power to elect the head of the Church cannot err against the faith; for the Church never reaches that state without being able to choose a head for itself, since any congregation can set up a head for itself. But the clergy alone, and not the laity, have the power to elect the head of the Church, namely the supreme pontiff, according to the canonical sanctions. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy will never err against the faith. Their fifth motive is this: the house of God, which is the militant Church, cannot be empty, just as the Church cannot be empty (24 q. 1, c. Petenda), as Jerome testifies, as it is read in 24 q. 1, c. Omnibus, where he says: "I think that, having considered everything, I do not say rashly that there are others in the house of God who are themselves the same house of God, which is said to be built upon the rock, which is called the one dove." And a little later: "This house also received the keys and the power of binding and loosing." From these words it is gathered that the house of God, which is called the one dove, and which is plainly the catholic Church, has the keys and the power of binding and loosing. But the keys and that said power are found only in priests. Therefore there will be some priests in the catholic Church until the end of the world, and consequently the whole multitude of clergy will never err against the faith. The sixth motive is this: Christ will remain in the militant Church until the end of the world, not only through faith and love but also through his sacramental presence. Therefore there will always be in the Church some priests who have the power of consecrating the body of Christ. But if the whole multitude of clergy became heretical, there would be no one in the churches with the power of consecrating the body of Christ; which will never happen. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy will never stray from the faith. Their seventh motive is this: the ecclesiastical hierarchy will remain until the end of the world. But the ecclesiastical hierarchy consists only in prelates, priests and the other clergy. Therefore until the end of the world there will remain some prelates, priests and other faithful and catholic clergy. These last three motives are confirmed by one argument: if the whole multitude of clergy could become heretical, then by the same reasoning the whole multitude of clergy could be extinguished by death, indeed be killed. But before the end of the world the whole multitude of clergy will never be extinguished; for if the whole multitude of clergy were extinct, the Church would not only be actually deprived of the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing, and of the sacrament of the body of Christ and the ecclesiastical hierarchy, but would also be deprived of the power of having those things. Moreover, even if the whole multitude of clergy became heretical, or the Church lacked the aforesaid things, yet in fact, if other heretical clergy remained, some catholics could be ordained by them, which, as it seems, would be lawful for some in that case, just as in a case of necessity it is lawful to receive baptism from heretics. Once they are ordained, all the aforesaid things can be restored. But if no clergy remained, neither catholic nor heretical, no one in the Church could ever have the keys, or the power of binding and loosing, or consecrate the body of Christ, and the whole ecclesiastical hierarchy would cease. And so it is absurd to say that the whole multitude of clergy could be extinguished by death; therefore it is absurd to assert that the whole multitude of clergy could fall into heretical depravity. The eighth motive is this: the whole multitude of them cannot err against the faith, and whoever is separated from it cannot have peace with the Church of God. But whoever is separated from the whole multitude of clergy cannot have peace with the Church of God, as Cyprian testifies, who, as it is quoted in 7 q. 1, c. Nunciamus, says: "Therefore whoever does not observe the bond of peace or the unity of the Spirit, and separates himself from the bond of the Church and the college of priests, can have neither the power nor the honour of a bishop, since he who did not wish to have the unity of the episcopate nor its peace." From these words it is understood that whoever separates himself from the college of priests can have neither honour nor peace nor unity with the Church of God. Therefore the whole multitude of clergy, which is understood by the name of priests, cannot err against the faith.

units.tr: CAP. XXXI.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad præcedentis capituli rationes, probantes quod totus clerus sit ecclesia, quæ contra fidem errare non potest.
units.tr: In which the reasons of the preceding chapter are answered, which prove that the whole clergy is the Church, and that the Church cannot err against the faith.

units.la: DISCIP. Ista media pro assertione, quam reputo esse veram, mihi sufficiunt. nec puto, quod aduersarii ad ipsas responsiones inuenire poterint apparentes. Tamen, vt melius veritatem eorum intelligam, dic quomodo ad ipsas aduersarii respondere nituntur.
units.tr: STUDENT. These arguments are enough for me in support of the position I hold to be true, and I do not think the opponents will be able to find any plausible replies to them. Still, so that I may better understand their view of the truth, tell me how the opponents try to answer them.

units.la: MAG. Primum omnino friuolum arbitrantur: quia per æquiuocationem procedere videtur. Nam hoc nomen, ecclesia, habet varias significationes. quandoq; accipitur pro domo materiali, sic accipitur ecclesia. 1. ad Corinth. 3. cum dicit apostolus: Numquid domos non habetis ad manducandum & bibendum, aut etiam ecclesiam Dei contemnitis. Secundo modo accipitur hoc nomen, ecclesia, pro congregatione Christianorum fidelium generali vel particulari, quae tam viros quam mulieres comprehendere potest. & sic accipitur ecclesia Act. 2. cum dicit apostolus: Maioribus natu attendite vobis & universo gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus posuit episcopos regere ecclesiam Dei. vbi nomine ecclesia comprehendit tam viros quam mulieres. Sicut etiam accipit apostolus nomen ecclesiae in epistola ad Philemonem, cum dicit ecclesia quae in domo tua est. quia in domo Philemonis erant tam viri quam mulieres: & forte nullus clericus erat in ea, nisi episcopus. fortasse quia nec ipse Philemon praeditus erat ecclesiastica dignitate. Sic etiam ipse apostolus accipit in aliis epistolis suis ecclesiam. Et isto modo accipitur ecclesia Prouerb. 5. cum dicitur: Penes fui in omni malo in medio ecclesiae & synagoga. Sicut etiam in canone accipitur ecclesia, de consec. dist. 1. c. ecclesia, vbi dicit Nicolaus Papa: Ecclesia i. catholicorum collectio, quomodo sine apostolica sedis initialetur nutu, quando iuxta sacra decreta, nec ipsa debet abque praeceptione Papae basilica noviter construi, quae & ipsam catholicorum intra semet amplecti caeterum dignoscitur. vbi ecclesia accipitur pro collectione catholicorum, quae mulieres & laicos nequaquam excludit. In duabus significationibus praedictis dicunt isti, nomen ecclesia accipi in scriptura divina. & ideo dicunt quod ad ecclesiam, secundum quod in scriptura divina (quae est totius fidei catholicae fundamentum) accipitur, ita laici & mulieres fideles pertinent, & sunt personae ecclesiasticae, sicut clerici. In iure autem canonico hoc nomen ecclesia significationes habet alias a praedictis: quia clerici nomen ecclesiae ad clericos restrinxerunt, clericos solummodo vocantes ecclesiam: cum tamen, sicut dictum est, secundum quod scriptura divina vtitur nomine ecclesia, ita sunt personae ecclesiasticae laici & mulieres, sicut clerici. Quia ita sunt de ecclesia, sicut clerici. Et sic accipiendo ecclesiam solummodo pro clericis, adhuc plures habet significationes, secundum quod notatur ext. de vet. sig. ca. clerici. Quia quandoque significat tantum episcopum. 7. q. 1. c. scire. Quandoque ponitur pro maiori parte capituli. 56. di. c. apostata. Quandoque restringitur ad canonicos ministros ecclesiae. 6. di. ca. vlt. & 10. q. 1. c. antiquos. Quandoque designat quamlibet ecclesiam prouinciae. ext. de vsu pallii, cum super. Per hoc respondent ad rationem primam dicentes, quod aliqua ecclesia potest contra fidem errare: & aliqua ecclesia non potest contra fidem errare. Clerici autem sunt illa ecclesia, quae potest contra fidem errare, sed non sunt illa ecclesia, quae non potest errare, licet sint catholici. sicut pars illius ecclesiae quae non potest errare. Quod vero sit aliqua ecclesia, quae potest haereticari auctore beati Ambrosii, probare nituntur. aut enim Ambrosius vt recitatur 24. q. 1. c. quae dignit: si qua est ecclesia, quae fidem respuat, neq; apostolica praedicationis fundamenta possideat, neque quicquam labe perfidiae possit aspergere, deserenda est. Quod apostolus quoque apparenter sine euidenter asserit, dicens: Haereticum hominem post vnam & alium correptionem devita. Ex quibus verbis euidenter apparet, quod aliqua ecclesia potest infici haeretica pravitate. & illam ecclesiam dicunt esse clericorum, quae tunc non esset vera ecclesia, sed esset ecclesia malignantium nutriendanda. Cum vero dixisti, notum esse, quod soli clerici vocantur ecclesiastici viri, dicunt quod contrarium per scripturam divinam, & etiam per decreta sanctorum patrum est notum: sicut ostensum est. DISCIP. Ista ratio non est ita fortis; sicut videbatur: quia clare probatum est, quod saepe vocabulum ecclesiae laicos & mulieres etiam comprehendit. ideo indica, quomodo ad secundum membrum respondetur. MAGIST. Ad secundam respondent arguendo maiorem dicentes, quod quamuis (quando clerici sunt catholici & in sacra pagina periti, & laici sunt illustrati diuinarum scripturarum ignari) laici de quaestionibus fidei se non debeant principaliter intromittere, sed a clero addiscere, quae fidei sunt: nec debeant errantes contra fidem principaliter corrigere, sed exequi ea, quae ad correctionem haereticorum ordinantur prouide a praelatis: tamen si clerici omnes in haereticam inciderent pravitatem, omnia praedicta, quantum suppetit notitia laicorum, pertinent ad eosdem. DISCIP. De ista materia interrogabo postea plura. ideo transi ad rationem tertiam. MAGIST. Ad rationem tertiam respondetur, quod clerici non sunt exempti a iudicio laicorum, nisi ex voluntate laicorum. & ideo si omnes clerici essent effecti haeretici, omnes essent iudicio laicorum subiecti. quia nunquam fuit intentio laicorum concedere clericis immunitatem, quando omnes fidem catholicam impugnarent. DISCIP. De hoc conferam postea tecum. ideo dic, quomodo respondent ad quartum motivum. MAGIST. Respondetur quod si omnes clerici haeretricarentur, potestas eligendi summum pontificem deuoluta esset ad laicos: sicut etiam laici habuerunt potestatem summum pontificem eligendi.
units.tr: MASTER. First, they consider the argument altogether trivial, because it seems to proceed by equivocation. For the word "church" (ecclesia) has various meanings. Sometimes it is taken for a material building, as in 1 Corinthians 3, where the Apostle says: "Have you not houses to eat and drink in, or do you despise the church of God?" In a second sense, the word "church" is taken for the general or particular assembly of faithful Christians, which can include both men and women. In this sense the church is taken in Acts 20, where the Apostle says: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to rule the church of God," where by the name church he includes both men and women. The Apostle also uses the name church in this way in his letter to Philemon, where he says: "the church that is in your house." For in Philemon's house there were both men and women, and perhaps there was no cleric in it except the bishop, or perhaps not even Philemon himself held ecclesiastical office. The Apostle uses "church" in the same way in his other letters. It is also used in this sense in Proverbs 5, where it is said: "I was almost in all evil, in the midst of the church and the synagogue." Likewise the canons use the word "church" in Decretum, dist. 1 de consecr., c. "Ecclesia," where Pope Nicholas says: "The church, that is, the gathering of Catholics, may not be started without the assent of the apostolic see; and according to the holy decrees, a basilica may not be newly built without the Pope's command, since it is recognised that it embraces within itself the Catholics." Here "church" is taken for the gathering of Catholics, which by no means excludes women and laymen. These people say that in the two senses just mentioned the word "church" is used in divine Scripture, which is the foundation of the whole Catholic faith. Therefore, they say, in the sense in which it is used in divine Scripture, laymen and faithful women belong to the church and are ecclesiastical persons, just as clerics are. In canon law, however, the word "church" has meanings other than those mentioned, because clerics have restricted the name church to clerics, calling only clerics "the church." Yet, as has been said, in the sense in which divine Scripture uses the name church, laymen and women are ecclesiastical persons just as clerics are, since they are of the church just as clerics are. And when "church" is taken only for clerics, it still has several meanings, as is noted in Extra, De veteri signif., c. "Clerici." Sometimes it signifies only the bishop (Decretum 7 q. 1, c. "Scire"). Sometimes it is used for the greater part of a chapter (Decretum 56, c. "Apostata"). Sometimes it is restricted to the canonical ministers of the church (Decretum 6 dist., last c., and 10 q. 1, c. "Antiquos"). Sometimes it designates any church of a province (Extra, De usu pallii, c. "Cum super"). By this they answer the first argument, saying that some church can err against the faith, and some church cannot err against the faith. The clergy, however, are that church which can err against the faith, but they are not that church which cannot err, even though they are Catholics, just as a part of that church which cannot err is not the whole. As to whether there is some church which can be made heretical, they try to prove this on the authority of the blessed Ambrose. For either Ambrose (as is quoted in Decretum 24 q. 1, c. "Quae dignitas") says: "If there is any church which rejects the faith and holds neither the foundations of apostolic preaching nor can be cleansed of the stain of perfidy, it must be abandoned." The Apostle also asserts this, though apparently not so clearly, when he says: "Avoid a heretical man after one or two admonitions." From these words it is quite evident that some church can be infected with heretical depravity. And they say that this church is the clergy, which would then no longer be the true church but a church of evildoers to be shunned. When you said that it is well known that only clerics are called ecclesiastical men, they reply that the contrary is known from divine Scripture and also from the decrees of the holy Fathers, as has been shown. STUDENT. That argument does not seem as strong as it appeared, since it has been clearly proved that the word "church" often includes laymen and women too. So tell me how they answer the second point. MASTER. In answer to the second argument they deny the major premise, saying that although laymen should not principally meddle in questions of faith (when the clergy are Catholic and skilled in Holy Scripture and the laymen are ignorant of the divine Scriptures), but should learn from the clergy what belongs to the faith; and although they should not principally correct those who err against the faith, but carry out what has been wisely ordained by the prelates for correcting heretics; nevertheless, if all the clergy fell into heretical depravity, all the things mentioned pertain to the same laymen, so far as the knowledge of laymen extends. STUDENT. I shall ask more about this matter later. So pass on to the third argument. MASTER. To the third argument it is answered that clerics are not exempt from the judgement of laymen except by the laymen's will. Therefore, if all clerics became heretics, they would all be subject to the judgement of laymen, because it was never the laymen's intention to grant clerics immunity when they all attacked the Catholic faith. STUDENT. I shall discuss this with you later. So tell me how they answer the fourth argument. MASTER. They answer that if all the clergy were made heretics, the power of electing the supreme pontiff would pass to the laity, just as the laity once had the power of electing the supreme pontiff.

units.la: DISCIP. De hoc etiam specialiter indagabo. ideo qualiter respondetur ad quintum motivum, responde. MAGIST. Tria motiva sequentia eandem difficultatem continere videntur, propter quam dicunt nonnulli: quod quamuis maior pars, immo fere tota multitudo clericorum possit contra fidem errare, & fidem catholicam pertinaciter impugnare, tamen semper permanebit saltem vnus episcopus sacerdos catholicus, qui illa, quae ordinis sunt, licite valeat exercere. Et ideo concludunt illi, quod omnes magistri theologiae & inferiores clerici episcopo sacerdote possunt contra fidem errare. Deus tamen semper conseruabit aliquem sacerdotem episcopum orthodoxum, ne ecclesia potestatem habendi claves regni coelorum, & auctoritate ligandi & soluendi, ac potestatem conficiendi corpus Christi, & habendi ecclesiasticam hierarchiam, amittat. Sed tenentes, quod tota multitudo clericorum potest haereticari, dicunt quod quamuis omnes clerici haereticarentur, propter hoc ecclesia potestatem habendi praedicta nequaquam amitteret, licet illa nunquam posset habere per humanam potentiam, sed per miraculosam operationem diuinam. Deus enim posset (si omnes clerici essent facti haeretici) diuersis modis de aliquibus laicis catholicis sacerdotes & episcopos ordinare. Sola enim voluntate posset hoc facere: quod etiam posset suae ecclesiae reuelare. Qua reuelatione facta & per miraculu confirmata, omnes catholici deberent taliter ordinatos a Deo, sicut veros episcopos & sacerdotes habere. DISCIP. Istud non est probabile, quod Deus taliter sacerdotes & episcopos ordinaret. MAGIST. Dicunt isti, quod sicut temerarium est asserere, quod Deus taliter sacerdotes & episcopos ordinaret: ita est temerarium est hoc negare: quia hoc est de futuris temere diuinare. Dicere vero, quod Deus hoc non possit facere, reputant haeresim manifestam: quia articulum fidei de omnipotentia Dei impudenter impugnat. DISCIP. Dic responsionem istorum ad ultimum motiuum. MAGIST. Ad ultimum motiuum respondetur, quod qui separat se a tota multitudine clericorum, quando sunt catholici, non potest cum ecclesia Dei pacem habere. Et in hoc casu debent intelligi verba Cypriani. Cum autem omnes clerici essent haeretici, qui non separarent se ab eorum collegio saltem spiritualiter, & ignorantia probabili minime laborarent, cum ecclesia Dei pace nequaquam haberent.
units.tr: STUDENT. I shall also inquire into this point specifically. So answer how they reply to the fifth argument. MASTER. The following three arguments seem to involve the same difficulty, on account of which some maintain that although the greater part, indeed almost the whole multitude of clergy, can err against the faith and stubbornly attack the Catholic faith, still at least one bishop or Catholic priest will always remain, who may lawfully exercise those things that belong to the order. And so they conclude that all teachers of theology and lower clergy, with a bishop or priest, can err against the faith. God, however, will always preserve some orthodox priest or bishop, lest the church lose the power of holding the keys of the kingdom of heaven, the authority of binding and loosing, the power of consecrating the body of Christ, and of having the ecclesiastical hierarchy. But those who hold that the whole multitude of clergy can be made heretical say that even if all the clergy were made heretics, the church would by no means lose the aforesaid powers, although it could never have them through human power, but only through a miraculous operation of God. For God could (if all the clergy had become heretics) ordain priests and bishops from some Catholic laymen in various ways. He could do this by his will alone, and he could also reveal this to his church. Once this revelation had been made and confirmed by a miracle, all Catholics ought to hold such men, ordained by God, as true bishops and priests. STUDENT. It is not credible that God would ordain priests and bishops in such a way. MASTER. These people say that just as it is rash to assert that God would ordain priests and bishops in such a way, so it is rash to deny it, because that would be rashly divining about future events. But to say that God cannot do this they regard as manifest heresy, because it impudently attacks the article of faith concerning the omnipotence of God. STUDENT. Tell me their answer to the last argument. MASTER. To the last argument it is answered that whoever separates himself from the whole multitude of clergy, while they are Catholic, cannot have peace with the church of God. In this case the words of Cyprian must be understood. But if all the clergy were heretics, those who did not separate themselves from their assembly, at least in spirit, and who were not labouring under a plausible ignorance, could by no means have peace with the church of God.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: In quo probatur tribus rationibus, quod tota multitudo virorum, tam clericorum quam laicorum, potest contra fidem errare, & fides catholica in mulieribus conseruari.
units.tr: In which it is proved by three arguments that the whole multitude of men, both clergy and laity, can err against the faith, and that the Catholic faith is preserved in women.

units.la: DISCIP. Licet teneam, quod tota multitudo clericorum non possit contra fidem errare, tamen ad rationes in contrarium respondere: Quia conabor per meditationem propriam responsiones ad ipsas rationabiles inuenire, de quibus post praesentis operis completionem inde tecum collocutionem habere. Nunc autem quia in superioribus videbaris innuere aliquos affirmantes, quod tota multitudo virorum & clericorum & laicorum potest contra fidem errare: peto ut aliqua motiua pro praedicta assertione inuenire nitaris. MAGIST. Verum est, quosdam tenere, quod tota multitudo virorum potest contra fidem errare, & quod fides catholica in mulieribus catholicis conseruari. Pro quibus principale motiuum est in promptu. Est tale (sicut saepe tactum est prius) Vnica est ecclesia militans, quae contra fidem errare non potest, quia nunquam inuenitur, quod sint plures ecclesiae militantes, quae contra fidem errare non possunt. Multitudo autem virorum non est illa ecclesia vnica, quae contra fidem errare non potest; sed solummodo pars illius ecclesiae, quando viri sunt catholici. Si enim viri non essent pars illius ecclesiae, sed tota illa vnica ecclesia, quae errare non potest, nulla mulier saluaretur: quia nulla persona viatrix saluatur, nisi sit de illa ecclesia militante, quae errare non potest. Si autem multitudo virorum non est illa vnica ecclesia, quae errare non potest, sequitur quod tota multitudo virorum potest contra fidem errare. Secundum motiuum eorum est tale: tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare. ergo tota multitudo virorum potest contra fidem errare. Consequentia probatur: quia tota multitudo virorum, & tota multitudo clericorum non differunt, nisi sicut duae partes ecclesiae militantis; quarum vna est maior, & alia minor. Sed non apparet ratio, quare non ita pars maior possit errare, sicut minor. Quia quod tota multitudo virorum non possit errare, non potest alia ratio cogitari, nisi propter maiorem sapientiam virorum quam mulierum, vel propter maiorem sanctitatem, vel propter maiorem capacitatem ecclesiasticae potestatis, scilicet ordinandi, & claudendi ecclesiae, & potestatis conficiendi corpus Christi, & dispensandi ecclesiastica sacramenta. Sed ex omnibus istis non potest concludi, quod tota multitudo clericorum non potest contra fidem errare: sicut quod tota multitudo virorum, sicut ex praecedentibus patere videtur. Si ergo tota multitudo clericorum potest contra fidem errare, etiam tota multitudo virorum poterit haereticari, sed tota multitudo clericorum potest haereticari, sicut dicunt superius esse probatum. igitur &c. Tertium motiuum est tale: Istud quod semel accidit, & non est reuelatum a Deo, quod nunquam de caetero euenit, nec per rationem naturalem potest probari quod non sit venturum, temerarium est asserere quod nunquam eueniet. Sed aliquando tota multitudo virorum contra fidem erravit: scilicet tempore passionis Christi. Tunc enim tota fides Christianae ecclesiae in matre Christi remansit. non est autem iam reuelatum a Deo, quod hoc nunquam postea fiat. & constat quod per rationem naturalem probari non potest. Ergo absque temeritate minime affirmatur, quod nunquam tota multitudo virorum contra fidem errabit. DISCIP. Christus reuelauit apostolis, quod nunquam tota multitudo virorum errabit, cum dicit Mat. vlt. Ecce vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsq; ad consummationem seculi. non enim dixit hoc eis pro ipsis apostolis, quia ipsi erant ante finem seculi morituri: ergo dixit eis pro successoribus eorundem. MAGIST. Hoc non reputant isti concludere: quia Christus, cum dixit verba praedicta apostolis pro fidelibus credentibus & crediturs in eum, ita enim erant mulieres crediturae in ipsum, sicut viri: quia verba Christi ad viros restringi non debent. propter idem dicunt, quod verba Christi, cum dixit Petro: Ego pro te rogaui, Petre, vt non deficiat fides tua: ad viros sunt minime coarctanda.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Although I hold that the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith, I will still try to answer the arguments to the contrary. By my own reflection I will endeavour to find answers to them that are reasonable, and afterwards I will discuss them with you when this work is finished. But since in the earlier part you seemed to hint at some who affirm that the whole multitude of men, both clergy and laity, can err against the faith, I ask you to find some reasons for that assertion. TEACHER. It is true that some hold that the whole multitude of men can err against the faith, and that the Catholic faith is preserved in Catholic women. Their chief argument is ready to hand, and it runs as follows (as has often been said before). There is one Church militant, which cannot err against the faith, because it is never found that there are several militant churches which cannot err against the faith. But the multitude of men is not that one Church which cannot err against the faith; it is only a part of that Church, when the men are Catholic. For if men were not a part of that Church, but the whole of that one Church which cannot err, no woman would be saved, since no person on pilgrimage is saved unless he belongs to that militant Church which cannot err. If, then, the multitude of men is not that one Church which cannot err, it follows that the whole multitude of men can err against the faith. Their second argument is this: the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith; therefore the whole multitude of men can err against the faith. The consequence is proved thus: the whole multitude of men and the whole multitude of clergy differ only as two parts of the militant Church, one of which is larger and the other smaller. But there appears to be no reason why the larger part should not be able to err just as the smaller can. For no other reason can be thought of why the whole multitude of men cannot err, except because men have greater wisdom than women, or greater holiness, or greater capacity for ecclesiastical power, namely of ordaining and shutting the churches, of consecrating the body of Christ, and of dispensing the ecclesiastical sacraments. But from all these it cannot be concluded that the whole multitude of clergy cannot err against the faith, just as it cannot be concluded that the whole multitude of men cannot, as appears from what has gone before. If therefore the whole multitude of clergy can err against the faith, the whole multitude of men will also be able to become heretical; but the whole multitude of clergy can become heretical, as they say was proved above. Therefore, etc. Their third argument is this: what has once happened, and has not been revealed by God as never to happen again, and cannot be proved by natural reason not to be going to happen, it is rash to assert will never happen. But at one time the whole multitude of men did err against the faith, namely at the time of the Passion of Christ. For then the whole faith of the Christian Church remained only in the mother of Christ. Now it has not been revealed by God that this will never happen again, and it is plain that it cannot be proved by natural reason. Therefore it is not affirmed without rashness that the whole multitude of men will never err against the faith. DISCIPLE. Christ revealed to the apostles that the whole multitude of men will never err, when he says in Matthew's last chapter: "Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world." For he did not say this to them for the apostles themselves, since they were going to die before the end of the world; therefore he said it to them for their successors. TEACHER. Those people do not think this conclusion follows, because Christ, when he spoke those words to the apostles, spoke them for the faithful who believe and will believe in him; for women were to believe in him just as men were, since the words of Christ ought not to be restricted to men. For the same reason they say that the words of Christ, when he said to Peter: "I have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith fail not," ought by no means to be confined to men.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXIII.

units.la: In quo ad oppositum arguitur duabus rationibus, quod tota multitudo virorum & clericorum & laicorum contra fidem errare non possit.
units.tr: In which the opposing view is argued on two grounds: that the whole multitude of men, both clergy and laity, cannot err against the faith.

units.la: MAGIST. Non est autem modo credendum, quod tota multitudo virorum contra fidem errabit: sicut non est credendum, quod infideles unquam totam Christianitatem occupabunt. Hoc enim scripturae divinae & verbis Christi videtur apertissime obviare. Christus enim, ut legitur Matth. 24. praedicans destructionem Iudaici populi, quae facta postea fuit per Titum & Vespasianum, dixit: Erit enim tunc tribulatio magna, qualis nunquam fuit ab initio mundi usque modo, nec fiet, & nisi breviati fuissent dies illi, non fieret salva omnis caro. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod nunquam futura est tanta tribulatio, quanta fuit facta per Romanos. Si autem tota Christianitas, quantum ad vivos, destrueretur, multo maior esset tribulatio Christianorum, quam illa, quam fecerunt Romani. Ergo nunquam tota multitudo virorum Christianorum destruetur. & per consequens nunquam errabit contra fidem. Item, futura maxima Christianorum auersio a fide erit tempore Antichristi, sed tempore eius remanebunt plures viri fideles Christiani, ipsa veritate testante, quae, ut habetur Matth. 24. loquens de persecutione futura tempore Antichristi, ait: Surgent pseudo Christi & pseudo prophetae, & dabunt signa magna & prodigia, ita ut in errorem ducantur (si fieri possit) etiam electi. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod tempore Antichristi aliqui erunt sancti viri electi, qui in errorem minime inducentur. quod beatus Iohann. in apocal. in diversis locis testari videtur. haec sunt inter alia, quae assertionem praefatam de improbabilitate conuincunt aperte. DISCIP. Licet de conclusione non dubitem, tamen quomodo potest ad ista respondeni, ut clarius veritatem intelligam, ac de multis quae ad istam spectant materiam occasionem cogitandi habeam, pandere velis.
units.tr: MASTER. Now it must not be believed that the whole multitude of men will err against the faith, just as it must not be believed that unbelievers will ever occupy the whole of Christendom. For this seems most clearly to contradict the divine Scriptures and the words of Christ. For Christ, as we read in Matthew 24, foretelling the destruction of the Jewish people, which was afterwards carried out by Titus and Vespasian, said: "For then there shall be great tribulation, such as was not from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved." From these words it is gathered that a tribulation as great as the one brought about by the Romans will never come again. If, however, the whole of Christendom, so far as the living are concerned, were destroyed, the tribulation of Christians would be far greater than that which the Romans inflicted. Therefore the whole multitude of Christian men will never be destroyed, and consequently will never err against the faith.
