Si autem Christus per testes, qui secundum leges repelli non possunt, fuisset de crimine damnationis dignissimus ordine iudiciario servato convictus, Pilatus Christum condemnando non peccasset, quia fuisset per falsos testes deceptus. iudex autem iudicans secundum allegata amore iustitiae non peccat, licet condemnet innocentem.
units.tr: For in that case it would not be lawful to resist even a usurper of the papacy or any tyrant. So the Apostle speaks of ordained power, not usurped. Therefore Christ too spoke of power in this way, and so he concedes that Pilate had ordained power over him. Yet he hints that Pilate abused this ordained power when he says: "He who delivered me to you has the greater sin," as if to say: you have sin enough in handing over to death one not confessed nor lawfully convicted of a crime worthy of death; yet because you do this out of fear, while others delivered me to you out of malice and envy, they have the greater sin. And so Pilate had ordinary power over Christ, insofar as he was mortal. Theophylact seems to hold this too, on John 8, "Do you say this of yourself, or did others tell you about me?", saying: as if Christ said, namely, if you speak this from yourself, show the signs of my rebellion; or if you have heard it from others, make an ordinary inquiry. From these words it is gathered that Pilate had the power of an ordinary inquiry into the crimes imputed to Christ, and whoever has the power of ordinary inquiry into a man of ill repute has coercive jurisdiction over him. Therefore Pilate had coercive jurisdiction over Christ. Likewise Bernard, writing to the bishop and archbishop of Sens, says: "Since Christ himself acknowledges that the power of the Roman governor was ordained from heaven over him as well," etc. From these words it is gathered that Pilate's power was not usurped but ordained from heaven, and therefore he had coercive jurisdiction over Christ. Yet he could not justly have exercised it against Christ, unless Christ had been lawfully convicted before him, as far as the judge could ascertain, of a crime. But if Christ had been convicted, by witnesses who cannot be rejected under the laws, of a crime deserving condemnation, with the judicial order observed, Pilate would not have sinned in condemning Christ, since he would have been deceived by false witnesses. A judge who, out of love of justice, judges according to the allegations made does not sin, even if he condemns an innocent man.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: In quo ponitur tertia ratio principalis ad probandum, quod aliquis secularis & specialiter Imperator sit iudex ordinarius Papae, & similiter quarta.
units.tr: In which is set out the third principal argument for proving that a secular ruler, and especially the Emperor, is the ordinary judge of the Pope, and likewise the fourth.

units.la: DISCIP. Pro ista assertione quae adduxisti, ad praesens sufficiat. & ideo aliam rationem adducas.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. For the present, what you have adduced in support of this assertion is enough. So bring forward another argument.

units.la: MAG. Ad probandum, quod imperator est iudex ordinarius Papae. Tertia ratio talis est. Ille est iudex ordinarius Papae, a quo Papa habet super alias ecclesias principatum. sed huc habet Papa ab imperatore. Probatur privilegium Constantini imperatoris concessum Romano pontifici, quod est superius allegatum. ergo imperator est ordinarius iudex summi pontificis. Quarta ratio est talis: imperator fuit iudex ordinarius beati Petri. ergo est iudex ordinarius Papae. consequentia est euidens; quia Papa non est magis exemptus quam fuit B. Petrus. antecedens probatur: quia omnes apostoli, quantum ad hoc, quod essent subiecti vel non subiecti iurisdictioni imperatoris, fuerunt pares. sed beatus Paulus fuit subiectus iurisdictioni imperatoris, quia ad Caesarem tanquam ad superiorem appellauit. ergo beatus Petrus fuit subiectus. DIS. Dicetur istis, quod Paulus appellauit, non quia esset subiectus iurisdictioni imperatoris, sed quia volebat caute nolidias Iudaeorum euadere. MAG. Hoc impugnatur sic secundum B. Ambr. vt habetur. 22. q. vlt. 6. Mentiri, non solum in falsis verbis sed etiam in simulatis operibus mendacium est. vbi no. Glo. quod facti mentimur, sicut & verbis. Beatus igitur Paulus si non erat vere subiectus imperatori, facto mentiebatur, cum simulauerit se subiectum iudicio Caesaris appellando. Tale autem crimen non est B. Paulo imponendum. igitur beatus Paulus vere fuit subiectus imperatori. Hanc etiam conclusionem per exemplum ostendunt. nam sicut legitur in Chronicis Iohan. 12. erat venator & totus lubricus, adeo quod foeminas publice tenebat. propter quod quidam cardinalium & Romanorum scripserunt occulte & cito Imperatori Saxonum, vt scandalo compatiens ecclesiae sine mora Romam properaret, hoc Papa percipiens Iohanni diacono cardinali, tanquam huius facti consiliario, nasum, & alteri Iohanni subdiacono, qui literas scripserat, manum amputari fecit. Hucum frequenter per imperatorem & clerum de sua correctione fuisset monitus, non correctus, praesente imperatore, de Papatu destitutus communi voto Leo Papa eligitur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod imperator iudex est ordinarius Papae. aliter enim imperator praedictum Papam nullatenus deposuisset. DIS. Dicerent aliqui, quod imperator iniuste processit; nec dictus Papa fuit vere depositus, sed de facto fuit tantummodo a Papatu spoliatus. MAG. Haec responsio impugnatur: quia si Papa Iohan. remansisset verus Papa, ille, qui ibi successit, ipso viuente non fuisset verus Papa, sed Papatus innatus. ex quo sequitur, quod omnia, quae egit, nullius fuissent roborationis vel momenti, sed debeant omnia irrita revocari: quod tamen minime fuit factum, imo quod successor ipsius Iohan. ipso viuente fuit verus Papa, tota tenet ecclesia. ergo Papa Ioh. fuit vere depositus.
units.tr: MASTER. To prove that the Emperor is the ordinary judge of the Pope, the third argument runs as follows. He is the ordinary judge of the Pope from whom the Pope holds primacy over other churches. But the Pope holds this from the Emperor. This is proved by the privilege of the Emperor Constantine granted to the Roman bishop, which was cited above. Therefore the Emperor is the ordinary judge of the supreme pontiff. The fourth argument is this: the Emperor was the ordinary judge of the blessed Peter. Therefore he is the ordinary judge of the Pope. The consequence is evident, since the Pope is no more exempt than blessed Peter was. The antecedent is proved as follows: all the apostles were equal in respect of whether they were subject or not subject to the jurisdiction of the Emperor. But blessed Paul was subject to the jurisdiction of the Emperor, since he appealed to Caesar as to a superior. Therefore blessed Peter was subject too. DISCIPLE. To this it will be said that Paul appealed not because he was subject to the Emperor's jurisdiction, but because he wished to escape the snares of the Jews warily. MASTER. This is refuted thus, according to blessed Ambrose, as it is found in 22 q. last, c. 6: "To lie is not only to speak falsely but also to do a false thing in pretence." Where the Gloss notes that we lie by deeds as well as by words. Therefore blessed Paul, if he was not truly subject to the Emperor, was lying by his deed, since he pretended to be subject to Caesar's judgment by appealing. But such a crime is not to be imputed to blessed Paul. Therefore blessed Paul was truly subject to the Emperor. They also show this conclusion by example. For as we read in the chronicles of John XII, he was a hunter and utterly lewd, so that he kept women openly. On account of this, some of the cardinals and Romans secretly and quickly wrote to the Emperor of the Saxons, that he, taking pity on the scandal to the Church, should hasten to Rome without delay. The Pope, perceiving this, had the nose of John the deacon, a cardinal, as the counsellor of this deed, cut off, and the hand of another John, a subdeacon who had written the letters. When he had often been admonished by the Emperor and the clergy about his amendment and had not amended, then, with the Emperor present, he was deposed from the papacy, and by the common vote Pope Leo was elected. From these words it is gathered that the Emperor is the ordinary judge of the Pope. For otherwise the Emperor would in no way have deposed the said Pope. DISCIPLE. Some would say that the Emperor proceeded unjustly, and that the said Pope was not truly deposed, but was only de facto stripped of the papacy. MASTER. This reply is refuted, because if John XII had remained the true Pope, the one who succeeded there, while he was still alive, would not have been the true Pope but an illegitimate papacy. From this it follows that all that he did would have been of no validity or weight, but all of it ought to be revoked as void. Yet this was by no means done; on the contrary, the whole Church holds that the successor of this John, while John was still alive, was the true Pope. Therefore Pope John was truly deposed.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: Chapter VI.

units.la: In quo arguitur in contrarium, scilicet quod nullus secularis etiam imperator est iudex ordinarius Papae, & hoc probatur auctoritatibus & quinque rationibus ca. isto & sequenti: ad quas respondetur in confuso c. 8. & 9. c. specialiter ad singulas.
units.tr: In which the contrary is argued, namely that no secular ruler, not even the emperor, is the ordinary judge of the Pope. This is proved by authorities and by five reasons in this chapter and the next. Answers are given in general in chapters 8 and 9, and to each reason in particular.

units.la: DISCIP. Puto quod fortiores rationes pro opinione praedicta fecisti. ideo ad assertionem contrariam te conuerte. & quod nec imperator nec aliquis secularis sit iudex ordinarius Papae nitaris ostendere. hanc enim assertionem puto consonam veritati. MAGIST. Quod nec imperator nec aliquis secularis sit iudex ordinarius Papae, auctoritatibus & rationibus nonnulli probare nituntur. Est autem prima ratio talis, Imperator non est iudex ordinarius illius, qui non habet superiorem in terra. sed Papa non habet superiorem in terra. ergo &c. maior probatione non indiget: quia iudex est superior illo, cuius est iudex. minor est, probata superius per plures auctoritates & rationes. DIS. Prius ostensum est generaliter, quod Papa non habet superiorem in terris: nunc autem specialiter probatur, quod imperator vel aliquis laicus vel populus non est iudex ordinarius ipsius. MAG. Quod specialiter imperator non sit iudex Papae, ostenditur primo sic. inferior non est iudex ordinarius sui superioris. sed imperator est inferior Papae, & eius iurisdictioni subiectus. ergo &c. maior est manifesta. unde dicit Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur dist. 22. c. superior: Sole clarius exhibuimus, non posse quicquam, qui minoris auctoritatis est, in eum, qui maioris est potestatis, iudiciis suis addicere, aut propriis diffinitionibus subiugare. Minor vero sanctorum auctoritatibus comprobatur. ait enim Greg. Nazianzen. vt habetur dist. 10. c. suscipitis, scribens imperatoribus Constantinopolitanis: suscipitis ne libertatem, verbi libertatem accipitis, quod lex Christi sacerdotali vos subiecit potestati, atque istis tribunalibus subdidit. dedit enim nobis potestatem: dedit principatum multo perfectiorem principatibus vestris. Item Felix Papa, vt habetur eadem dist. c. certum, ait: Certum est hic rebus vestris ac salutare est, vt cum de causis Dei agitur iuxta ipsius constitutionem, regiam voluntatem sacerdotibus Christi studeatis subdere, non praeferre. & infra: neque eius sanctionibus velle dominari, cuius Deus voluit clementia tua pia devotionis collā submittere. hoc idem habetur dist. 96. c. duo sunt, & c. si imperator. Ex quibus verbis & multis aliis habetur, quod imperator est inferior Papa.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I think you have made the stronger arguments for the opposing opinion. So turn to the contrary assertion, and try to show that neither the emperor nor any secular ruler is the ordinary judge of the Pope. I think this assertion agrees with the truth. MASTER. Some try to prove, by authorities and reasons, that neither the emperor nor any secular ruler is the ordinary judge of the Pope. The first reason is this: the emperor is not the ordinary judge of one who has no superior on earth. But the Pope has no superior on earth. Therefore, etc. The major needs no proof, since a judge is superior to the one whose judge he is. The minor has been proved above by several authorities and reasons. DISCIPLE. It was shown in general before that the Pope has no superior on earth. Now it is proved in particular that the emperor, or any layman, or the people, is not his ordinary judge. MASTER. That the emperor in particular is not the Pope's judge is shown first as follows. An inferior is not the ordinary judge of his superior. But the emperor is inferior to the Pope and subject to his jurisdiction. Therefore, etc. The major is plain. So Pope Nicholas says, as found in dist. 22, c. superior: "We have shown more clearly than the sun that one who has less authority cannot subject to his judgments, or bring under his own decisions, one who has greater power." The minor is confirmed by the authority of the saints. For Gregory Nazianzen, writing to the emperors of Constantinople, says (as found in dist. 10, c. suscipitis): "You receive freedom, I mean the freedom of speech, that the law of Christ has made you subject to the priestly power and placed you under these tribunals. For it has given us power; it has given a principate far more perfect than your principates." Likewise Pope Felix, as found in the same distinction, c. certum, says: "It is certain and wholesome for you that, when the affairs of God are handled according to his own institution, you should be careful to subject the royal will to the priests of Christ, not to set it above them." And below: "nor wish to rule over those by whose decrees God willed that your merciful piety should bow its neck." The same is found in dist. 96, c. duo sunt, and c. si imperator. From these words and many others it is held that the emperor is inferior to the Pope.

units.la: Quod etiam multis rationibus nonnulli probare nituntur. Primo quia, qui iurat alii fidelitatem, est inferior illo cui iurat. imperator praestat iuramentum fidelitatis Papae dist. 63. tibi domino Io. &c. Secundo imperator est inferior illo, qui habet potestatem transferendi imperium de gente in gentem. hanc potestatem habet Papa, extra de elec. ergo &c. Tertio qui habet potestatem alium excommunicandi, est superior. sed Papa potest excommunicare imperatorem. igitur maior patet, & minor probatur dist. 96. duo sunt. Quarto, qui potest deponi ab alio, est inferior
units.tr: Some also try to prove this by many reasons. First, one who swears fealty to another is inferior to the one to whom he swears. The emperor swears fealty to the Pope, dist. 63, tibi domino Io., etc. Second, the emperor is inferior to one who has the power to transfer the empire from nation to nation. The Pope has this power, extra de elect. Therefore, etc. Third, one who has the power to excommunicate another is superior. But the Pope can excommunicate the emperor. The major is clear, and the minor is proved in dist. 96, duo sunt. Fourth, one who can be deposed by another is inferior

units.la: co. eo. imperator autem potest deponi à Papa. 25. q. 1. alius, &c. Quinto, imperator est inferior illo, qui temporalibus & spiritualibus potest subditos imperatorum & regum legitimare. hoc potest Papa, extra qui filii sint legitimi, per venerabilem, ergo, &c.
units.tr: (c. eo.) The emperor, however, can be deposed by the Pope, 25 q. 1, alius, etc. Fifth, the emperor is inferior to one who can legitimate the subjects of emperors and kings, both in temporal and in spiritual matters. The Pope can do this, extra qui filii sint legitimi, per venerabilem. Therefore, etc.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: Chapter VII.

units.la: In quo probatur idem, quod capitulo praecedenti.
units.tr: In which the same thing is proved as in the preceding chapter.

units.la: DISCIP. Omittas istam materiam, & alias rationes adducas ad probandum, quod imperator non est iudex ordinarius Papae. MAG. Secunda ratio ad hoc principalis talis est. Imperator non est iudex ordinarius illius, qui imperialibus legibus est solutus: quia leges superioris subiectos astringunt: nisi specialiter per superiorem sint exempti. Papa autem a legibus imperialibus minime est astrictus, di. 18. c. 1. & c. quoniam. ergo imperator non est iudex ordinarius Papae.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Leave aside that material, and bring forward other reasons to prove that the emperor is not the ordinary judge of the Pope. MASTER. The second main reason for this is as follows. The emperor is not the ordinary judge of one who is released from the imperial laws, because laws bind the subjects of a superior, unless they are specially exempted by the superior. But the Pope is not bound at all by imperial laws, di. 18. c. 1. & c. quoniam. Therefore the emperor is not the ordinary judge of the Pope.

units.la: Tertia ratio est ista. Imperator non est iudex ordinarius aliquorum clericorum inferiorum Papa. ergo multo magis non est iudex ordinarius Papae. consequentia est evidens, antecedens vero per innumeros canones sacros posset ostendi. Unde in concilio Carthaginensi, ut habetur 12. q. 1. c. placuit, sicut legitur: placuit ne quis unquam clericus ab imperatore cognitionem publicarum iudiciorum petierit, honore proprio privatur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod imperator non est iudex ordinarius clericorum, &c. Quarta ratio est haec. Ille iudex non est ordinarius Papae, ad quem a Papa appellare non licet, sed non licet appellare a Papa ad imperatorem. 9. q. 3. ita ipse & c. cuncta. ergo imperator non est iudex ordinarius Papae. Quinta ratio est haec. Imperator non est iudex illius cui Christus iura imperii commisit. sed iura imperii B. Petro & eius successoribus Christus commisit, di. 22. c. 1. ergo imperator non est iudex ordinarius Papae.
units.tr: The third reason is this. The emperor is not the ordinary judge of some lower clergy, so much less is he the ordinary judge of the Pope. The consequence is evident, and the antecedent could be shown by countless sacred canons. Hence at the Council of Carthage, as read in 12 q. 1, c. placuit: "It has been decided that no cleric shall ever seek from the emperor a hearing of public judgments; he is deprived of his own honour." From these words it is gathered that the emperor is not the ordinary judge of clerics, etc. The fourth reason is this. That judge is not the ordinary judge of the Pope to whom one may not appeal from the Pope; but one may not appeal from the Pope to the emperor, 9 q. 3, ita ipse & c. cuncta. Therefore the emperor is not the ordinary judge of the Pope. The fifth reason is this. The emperor is not the judge of one to whom Christ entrusted the rights of empire. But Christ entrusted the rights of empire to St. Peter and his successors, di. 22, c. 1. Therefore the emperor is not the ordinary judge of the Pope.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Respondet in generali sub duplici opinione adrationes & auctoritates, c. 6. & 7. adductas, in hoc capitulo incipit respondere ad primam.
units.tr: He answers in general the reasons and authorities adduced in chapters 6 and 7 under two opinions; in this chapter he begins to answer the first.

units.la: DISCIP. Licet non dubitem nullum mortalium esse superiorem summo pontifice; tamen cupio scire quomodo ad rationes hoc probantes adversarii respondere conantur. MAG. Non omnes, qui tenent imperatorem esse superiorem & iudicem ordinarium Papae, in modo ponendi concordat. & ideo non eodem modo ad rationes praescriptas respondent. DISC. Dic illos diversos modos ponendi. MAG. Sunt quidam dicentes, quod Papa in spiritualibus imperatori minime est subiectus; sed quantum ad iurisdictionem temporalem est sibi subiectus, & quantum est ex ordinatione Christi: quia nec Christus quantum ad iurisdictionem temporalem, nullum at itolum a iurisdictione temporali imperatorum exemit; sed omnes in huiusmodi voluit principatibus saecularibus esse subiectos, in cuius signum ipse soluit pro propria persona tributum. Alii dicunt, quod imperator in quantum gerit personam populi Christiani, in omnibus tam spiritualibus quam temporalibus est superior Papa & iudex ordinarius, sed non. DIS. De iurisdictione temporali Papae & imperatoris pertranseas, quia in tractatu de opinabilibus. Iob. 22. de hoc tibi plures quaestiones moveho. MAG. Tu forsitan aliter accipis iurisdictionem temporalem, quam isti. DIS. Accipio iurisdictionem temporalem pro illa, cui aliquis est subiectus ratione praediorum, quae de imperatore tenet. MAG. Aliter accipiunt ipsi. DIS. Quomodo? MAG. Dicunt quod iurisdictio temporalis non solum respicit praedia & temporales divitias, sed etiam personas: quia omnes personae in dominio alicuius principis commorantes, sive sint divites, sive pauperes, iurisdictioni principis sunt subiectae: a quo (si deliquerint) condigna debent animadversione puniri, nisi per principem vel superiorem alium sint exemptae. DIS. Video quid per iurisdictionem temporalem intendunt: sed ignoro quae spiritualia vocant. MAG. Spiritualia vocant illa, quae religioni Christianae sunt propria; quae in nulla secta alia sunt reperta, nec ad legem naturae sunt spectantia: sicut quae pertinent ad sacramenta ecclesiastica dispendenda, & ad causas fidei terminandas, quae directe in criminibus, quae contra Christi religionem committuntur. de huiusmodi enim imperator (nisi sicut caeteri Christiani) se intromittere non debet: quia imperator Christianus ratione suae dignitatis maiorem potestatem vel iurisdictionem nullatenus habet, quam habuerunt imperatores pagani. illis enim imperatores Christiani successerunt; & ideo idem ius cum illis, & non aliud ratione imperii possidere noscuntur. quia ergo de huiusmodi spiritualibus se intromittere ad imperatores paganos minime pertinebat; nec ad imperatorem Christianum, in quantum imperatorem, spectant talia. DISCIP. Ergo secundum istos, si Papa homicidium, furtum, adulterium, & consimilia crimina quae imperatores & reges palam punire solebant committeret, imperator ipsum punire valeret.
units.tr: STUDENT. Although I do not doubt that no mortal is superior to the supreme pontiff, I still want to know how the opponents try to answer the reasons that prove this. TEACHER. Not all who hold that the emperor is superior to the Pope and his ordinary judge agree on the way of putting it, and so they do not all answer the stated reasons in the same way. STUD. Tell me those different ways of putting it. TEACH. Some say that the Pope is in no way subject to the emperor in spiritual matters, but in temporal jurisdiction he is subject to him, and this by the ordinance of Christ. For Christ did not exempt any single person from the temporal jurisdiction of the emperors; rather he willed that all, in such secular principalities, should be subject, and as a sign of this he himself paid tribute in his own person. Others say that the emperor, insofar as he bears the person of the Christian people, is superior to the Pope and his ordinary judge in all things, spiritual as well as temporal. STUD. You may pass over the temporal jurisdiction of the Pope and the emperor, since I shall raise many questions about this with you in my treatise on matters of opinion. Job 22. TEACH. Perhaps you understand temporal jurisdiction differently from them. STUD. I take temporal jurisdiction to be that to which someone is subject by reason of the estates he holds from the emperor. TEACH. They understand it otherwise. STUD. How? TEACH. They say that temporal jurisdiction concerns not only estates and temporal wealth but also persons, because all persons dwelling under the dominion of some prince, whether rich or poor, are subject to the prince's jurisdiction; if they offend, they ought to be punished with due penalty, unless they are exempted by the prince or some other superior. STUD. I see what they mean by temporal jurisdiction, but I do not know what they call spiritual things. TEACH. They call spiritual those things which are proper to the Christian religion, which are not found in any other sect and do not belong to the law of nature: such as those things that pertain to the administering of the ecclesiastical sacraments and to the settling of questions of faith, and crimes committed directly against the religion of Christ. For in such matters the emperor ought not to meddle, except as any other Christian would. For a Christian emperor, by reason of his dignity, has in no way greater power or jurisdiction than the pagan emperors had. For the Christian emperors succeeded them, and so they are known to hold the same right as those, and no other, by reason of the empire. Since it did not belong to pagan emperors to meddle in such spiritual matters, neither do such things belong to a Christian emperor as emperor. STUD. Then according to them, if the Pope were to commit murder, theft, adultery and similar crimes, which emperors and kings were accustomed to punish openly, the emperor would be able to punish him?

units.la: MAG. Hoc nonnulli concedunt, licet dicant quidam eorum, quod non deberet eum deponere, nisi
units.tr: TEACH. Some concede this, although some of them say that he ought not to depose him unless he is shown to be incorrigible.

units.la: {1} Tomus caput. nisi incorrigibilis probaretur. DIS. Modo opinionem istorum intelligo. & quamuis eam inter haereses reputem numerandam; de illa tamen tecum in tractatu de dogmatibus Iohan. 22. prolixius disputabo. nunc autem dic qualiter ad rationes per auctoritates pro assertione contraria factas respondent. De secundo modo probandi nihil dicas ad praesens, sed infra c. 10. MAG. Ad primam negant minorem, cum accipitur, quod imperator est inferior Papa, & eius iurisdictioni subiectus quantum ad iurisdictionem temporalem ex ordinatione Christi. & ideo in hoc Papa non est iudex imperatoris, in quantum commissarius vel delegatus populi Romani. DIS. Ista sunt verba mirabilia & inaudita, nec ego ea intelligo: sed si potes, fac ut intelligam illa, & tunc de eis citius iudicabo. MAG. Ut ea intelligas, scire debes, quod secundum istos imperator & quilibet rex temporalis habet a Deo quodammodo mediate iurisdictionem suam temporalem: quia secundum apostolum ad Rom. 13. non est potestas, nisi a Deo; cum immediate iurisdictionem suam habet Imperator a populo Romano; Rex Franciae a populo suo; rex Angliae a populo suo, rex Castellae a populo suo. & sic quilibet a populo suo habet iurisdictionem suam, nisi sit aliquis rex, cuius populus alicui alteri sit subiectus, qui possit populo suo dare regem: quemadmodum imperatores quondam diversi populis Reges dederunt, quia illi populi imperatori & populo Romano subiecti fuerunt. imperator suam iurisdictionem a populo Romano obtinuit. populus autem Romanus ex causa rationabili, sicut imperatorem instituit, ita eum potuit destituere, eiusque iurisdictionem minuere & augere. Ex quo sequitur, quod populus Romanus ex causa rationabili potuit imperatorem in aliquo casu alterius, cuius committeretur iurisdictioni, subiicere. quare potuit Papa causam imperatoris delegare. in quo casu Papa tanquam delegatus seu commissarius auctoritate populi Romani super imperatorem iurisdictionem potuit obtinere. quam iurisdictionem beatus Petrus a Christo non suscepit. & ideo Papa in quantum successor beati Petri eam minime habet. DIS. Nunc verba praedicta intelligo, quamvis ea reputem verbosa. & ideo ad rationes factas accedo. MAGIST. Propter diversas opiniones antequam narrem, quomodo ad rationes explicite respondeatur, oportet illas opiniones exprimere. DIS. Dic quae sunt illae opiniones. MAGIST. Sicut tactum est prius; sunt quidam dicentes, quod Romanus Pontifex nullam iurisdictionem vel potestatem ex ordinatione Christi habuit ultra alios quoscunque presbyteros: sed omnem dignitatem suam & potestatem ultra alios habuit ab imperatore vel ab ecclesia, scilicet ex concilio generali. Alii dicunt quod beatus Petrus pro se & suis successoribus dignitatem Papalem & primatum super omnes alios fideles recepit a Christo. Sed ista dignitas & primatus, ut dicunt, consistit in ordinando & praeficiendo episcopos, presbyteros & doctores populo Christiano nullam habens ex ordinatione Christi iurisdictionem coactivam annexam; sicut nec habet res temporales annexas. sed sicut Papa temporalia a fidelibus orthodoxis accepit, ita a communitate fidelium solummodo habuit iurisdictionem coactivam. Omnis enim communitas potest sibi aliquem praeficere, qui habeat potestatem maleficos coercendi. Ecclesia autem fidelium ad hoc officium Papatus sibi praefecit, in nullo tamen iurisdictionem imperatorum disrumpendo vel diminuendo, etiam paganorum: quia hoc non potuit, eo quod omnes catholici tunc temporis imperatoribus infidelibus subiecti fuerunt. DIS. Ego omnino vellem exire istam materiam de iurisdictione imperatorum; & ad alium differre tractatum, & tu me semper plus & plus trahis ad ipsum. unde istis omnibus omissis breviter narra, quomodo ad rationes & auctoritates inductas respondetur. MAG. Sunt quidam unam rationem dantes generalem ad omnes auctoritates, asserentes quod Papa habet iurisdictionem super imperatores & reges, & quantum ad iurisdictionem est superior: dicentes, quod tales auctoritates non continent veritatem, & ideo sunt nullatenus admittendae. Alii autem intellectum sanctorum patrum reputant consonum veritati: sed dicunt, quod nonnulli clerici in ambitione & avaritia excaecati verba eorum nimis large contra mentem eorum sumunt. DIS. Istorum responsiones volo audire MAG. Isti ad evidentiam rationum suarum dicunt esse sciendum: quod poenitentia unum est de ecclesiasticis sacramentis; & ideo pertinet ad praelatos, qualiter ad ipsos spectat in foro conscientiae poenitentium peccata cognoscere, & ipsis debitam poenitentiam iniungere, & propter istam poenitentiam & potestatem, quam sacerdotes in foro conscientiae habere noscuntur, omnes Christiani eis sunt subiecti. extra autem forum conscientiae nullam habent iurisdictionem a Christo immediate: sed illam habent a communitate fidelium, vel ab illo in quem communitas fidelium suam transtulit potestatem.
units.tr: {1} Tome, chapter. Unless he is shown to be incorrigible. STUD. Now I understand the opinion of these men, and although I think it should be counted among the heresies, I will dispute it with you at more length in my treatise on dogmas, John 22. But now tell me how they answer the reasons and the authorities brought forward for the contrary assertion. As for the second way of proving it, say nothing for the present; it will come below, in chapter 10. TEACH. To the first they deny the minor premise, when it is taken that the emperor is inferior to the Pope and subject to his jurisdiction in temporal jurisdiction by the ordinance of Christ. And so in this respect the Pope is not the judge of the emperor insofar as he is a commissioner or delegate of the Roman people. STUD. These are strange and unheard-of words, and I do not understand them. But if you can, make me understand them, and then I shall judge them more quickly. TEACH. To understand them, you must know that according to these men the emperor and every temporal king has his temporal jurisdiction from God in a certain mediate way, because according to the apostle, in Romans 13, there is no power but of God. But the emperor has his jurisdiction immediately from the Roman people; the king of France from his people; the king of England from his people; the king of Castile from his people. And so each has his jurisdiction from his own people, unless there is some king whose people is subject to some other, who could give his people a king. Just as the emperors of old gave kings to various peoples, because those peoples were subject to the emperor and the Roman people. The emperor obtained his jurisdiction from the Roman people; and the Roman people, for a reasonable cause, could appoint him and in the same way depose him, and diminish or enlarge his jurisdiction. From this it follows that the Roman people, for a reasonable cause, could subject the emperor in some case to the jurisdiction of another to whom the matter was committed. Therefore the Pope could delegate the emperor's case, and in that case the Pope, as delegate or commissioner, could obtain jurisdiction over the emperor by the authority of the Roman people. Blessed Peter did not receive this jurisdiction from Christ, and so the Pope, insofar as he is the successor of blessed Peter, does not have it at all. STUD. Now I understand the words above, although I consider them wordy. So I come to the reasons advanced. TEACH. Before I relate how the reasons are answered explicitly, it is necessary, because of the different opinions, to set out those opinions. STUD. Tell me what those opinions are. TEACH. As was touched on before: some say that the Roman Pontiff had no jurisdiction or power by the ordinance of Christ beyond any other presbyters whatever, but he had all his dignity and power over the others from the emperor or from the Church, namely from a general council. Others say that blessed Peter received for himself and his successors the Papal dignity and primacy over all other faithful from Christ. But this dignity and primacy, they say, consists in ordaining and setting over the people of Christ bishops, presbyters and teachers, having no coercive jurisdiction annexed to it by the ordinance of Christ, just as it has no temporal goods annexed. But just as the Pope received temporal goods from the orthodox faithful, so he has coercive jurisdiction only from the community of the faithful. For every community can set over itself someone who has the power to restrain wrongdoers. The Church of the faithful set him over this office of the Papacy, yet without in any way breaking up or diminishing the jurisdiction of the emperors, even pagan ones; for this it could not do, since all Catholics at that time were subject to unbelieving emperors. STUD. I would very much like to leave this matter of the jurisdiction of emperors altogether and defer it to another treatise, and you keep dragging me more and more into it. So, leaving all these things aside, briefly tell me how the reasons and authorities brought forward are answered. TEACH. Some give one general reason against all the authorities, asserting that the Pope has jurisdiction over emperors and kings and is superior to them in jurisdiction; they say such authorities do not contain the truth and so must by no means be admitted. Others, however, think the sense of the holy Fathers is consistent with the truth, but they say that some clergy, blinded by ambition and avarice, take their words far too broadly, contrary to their meaning. STUD. I want to hear their answers. TEACH. These men, to make clear their reasons, say that one must know this: penance is one of the ecclesiastical sacraments; and therefore it belongs to the prelates, just as it belongs to them in the forum of conscience to know the sins of penitents and to impose on them the due penance. And because of this penance and the power which priests are known to have in the forum of conscience, all Christians are subject to them. But outside the forum of conscience they have no jurisdiction immediately from Christ; they have it from the community of the faithful, or from him to whom the community of the faithful has transferred its power.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: In quo specialiter respondetur ad singulas auctoritates & rationes inductas ca. 6. & 7. probantes, quod nullus secularis etiam imperator: sit index ordinarius Papae.
units.tr: In which each of the authorities and arguments adduced in chapters 6 and 7, to prove that no secular ruler, not even the emperor, is the ordinary judge of the Pope, is answered individually.

units.la: DISCIP. Adhuc tu trahis me ad materiam, quam nollem hic tractare: & ideo quomodo ad rationes & auctoritates inductas respondetur: narra succincte. Ad primam auctoritatem Gregorii Nazianzeni respondetur, quod per tribunal & principatum praelatorum intelligit potestatem testatem, quam in foro conscientiæ super pœnitentes noscuntur habere. Ista vero potestas quia spiritualis est, & ordinatur ad vitam consequendam æternam, multo perfectior est illa iurisdictione temporali coactiva regum & principum, quæ principaliter instituta est ad temporalia disponenda. Ad auctoritatem Felicis Papæ respondetur, quod illa voluntas in fide catholica addiscenda, & sacramentis ecclesiasticis suscipienda, debet esse subiecta sacerdotibus, si sacerdotes idem retinent orthodoxam, nihil contra fidem seu iustitiam imperantes. Si vero a catholica deccommon auerint veritate, vel sibi quam de iure non habent vsurpauerint potestatem, reges in huiusmodi nullatenus sunt subiecti. Verba ergo Felicis Papæ sane intelligenda sunt, & non sunt ex ambitione clericorum cupientium in populis & in clero propter doctrinam beati Petri apostoli dominari in præiudicium regum & principum exponenda. Consimiliter respondetur ad c. Hoc sunt, & ad c. si imperator. nam dicunt isti, Papam a concilio generali & universali ecclesia aliquam potestatem habere super principes vltra illam, quam habet a Christo, & in quantum est successor B. Petri. Ad primam vero rationem inducatam ad probandum, quod imperator est inferior Papa: Respondetur primo, quod maior non est vniuersaliter vera, sed capit instantiam, quando aliquis sponte iurat alij fidelitatem, talis enim ante iuramentum non est inferior illo semper, cui iurat, quamuis per iuramentum quodammodo seipsum inferiorem illo efficit. Ad minorem vero dicitur dupliciter. vno modo, quod imperator nunquam iuravit fidelitatem Papæ, nisi sponte nea voluntate. & ideo sibi successoribus legem consimilem per tale iuramentum nequaquam imposuit. Aliter respondetur, quod ex ordinatione Romanorum, a quibus Imperator suam habuit iurisdictionem, potuit Imperator Papæ iurare, & in hoc tenuisset Papa non vicem beati Petri, hec in hoc fuit vicarius Christi, sed in hoc fuisset commissarius Romanorum. Ad secundam respondetur similiter, quod Papa non transtulit imperium a Græcis in Germanos in quantum vicarius Christi & successor beati Petri; quia ratione vicariatus illius & successionis huius non habet maiorem auctoritatem super imperium, quam super regnum Francorum vel Anglorum. sicut ergo in quantum vicarius Christi & successor beati Petri non potest transferre regnum Francorum ue vna domo in aliam, ita ratione vicariatus & successionis non potuit de gente in gentem transferre imperium Romanorum, qui sibi ex causa rationabili potestatem huius contulerunt. Ad tertiam respondetur tripliciter. Sunt enim quidam dicentes, quod cum excommunicatio sit potius iurisdictionis, quam ordinis: idcirco Papa in quantum vicarius Christi & successor beati Petri neminem excommunicare potest, sed potestatem excommunicandi habet ab ecclesia vniuersali, quæ in eum transtulit talem potestatem. Alii autem dicunt, quod non Papa, sed Imperator in imperio, & rex in regno suo potestatem habet excommunicandi. DIS. Istas opiniones puto erroneas: sed tamen secundam magis abhorreo. de ipsis tamen in alio tractatu collocutionem habebo; nunc autem dic tertiam responsionem. MAG. Tertia responsio est, quod Papa in quantum vicarius Christi habet potestatem excommunicandi, sed pœnam maiorem nullatenus insertendi. Dicunt enim quidam, quod est vltima pœna, quam possunt ecclesiastici exercere. isti dicunt ergo quod Papa in hoc est imperatore superior: sed tamen in aliis est inferior ipso scilicet in omni iurisdictione temporali. Ad quartam rationem respondetur, quod Papa non potest imperatorem deponere ratione Papatus: sicut nec ratione Papatus potest deponere regem Franciæ, sicut Zacharias Papa regem Francorum auctoritate populi regni illius depos uit: & ita illi principalitet deposuerunt, & vt testatur Glo. 15. q. 6. c. alius dicitur depositus, quia de omnibus consensit. ita Papa auctoritate Romanorum posset imperatorem deponere. Ad quintam rationem respondetur, quod Papa ratione Papatus non potest illegitimos in temporalibus legitimare: si autem hoc fecit de facto, ratione alicuius alterius potestatis quæ non est annexa Papatui, hoc fecit. DIS Respondeo ad secundam principalem rationem. MAG. Ad secundam rationem respondetur, quod Papa ratione Papatus non est solutus legibus imperialibus, quæ diuinis legibus minime repugnant: licet aliunde forsitan sit solutus. Ad tertiam rationem principalem respondetur, quod clerici, nisi sint exempti auctoritate regum vel concilii generalis, pertinent ad forum secularium potestatum. Ad quartam rationem respondetur, quod in temporalibus licet appellare a Papa ad imperatorem, nisi per vniuersalem ecclesiam sit exemptus. Ad quintam dicitur, quod Christus commisit Petro iura imperii terreni, hoc est, potestatem super malos in spiritualibus, non in temporalibus.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. You are still drawing me into a subject I would rather not treat here. So tell me briefly how the arguments and authorities adduced are answered. MASTER. To the first authority, that of Gregory Nazianzen, the answer is that by "tribunal" and "principate" he means the power of binding and loosing which the prelates are known to have over penitents in the forum of conscience. This power, since it is spiritual and is directed to attaining eternal life, is far more excellent than the temporal and coercive jurisdiction of kings and princes, which was established chiefly for ordering temporal affairs. To the authority of Pope Felix the answer is that the willingness to learn the Catholic faith and to receive the ecclesiastical sacraments ought to be subject to the priests, provided that the priests keep to sound doctrine and command nothing contrary to faith or justice. But if they have departed from the Catholic truth, or have usurped a power which they do not hold by right, kings are in no way subject to them in such matters. The words of Pope Felix must therefore be understood soundly, and are not to be expounded, out of the ambition of clerics who wish to lord it over peoples and the clergy, to the prejudice of kings and princes, on the strength of the teaching of the blessed apostle Peter. The same answer applies to c. Hoc sunt and c. si imperator; for those men say that the Pope has, from a general and universal council and from the Church, some power over princes beyond that which he has from Christ and as successor of St Peter. To the first argument brought forward to prove that the emperor is inferior to the Pope, the answer is first that the major premise is not universally true, but admits of an exception, namely when someone freely swears fidelity to another. Such a person before the oath is not always inferior to the one to whom he swears, although by the oath he in some measure makes himself inferior to him. To the minor premise there are two answers. In one way: the emperor never swore fidelity to the Pope except of his own free will, and so he never imposed a similar law on his successors by such an oath. Otherwise: by the appointment of the Romans, from whom the emperor had his jurisdiction, the emperor could swear to the Pope; and in doing so the Pope would not have held the place of St Peter, nor would he have been Christ's vicar in that matter, but he would have been a commissioner of the Romans. To the second argument the answer is likewise that the Pope did not transfer the empire from the Greeks to the Germans as Christ's vicar and successor of St Peter; for by virtue of that vicariate and that succession he has no greater authority over the empire than over the kingdom of the Franks or of the English. Just as, as Christ's vicar and successor of St Peter, he cannot transfer the kingdom of the Franks from one house to another, so by virtue of his vicariate and succession he could not transfer the Roman empire from nation to nation; those who conferred that power on him did so for a reasonable cause. To the third argument the answer is threefold. For there are some who say that, since excommunication belongs rather to jurisdiction than to orders, the Pope, as Christ's vicar and successor of St Peter, cannot excommunicate anyone; rather he has the power of excommunicating from the universal Church, which has transferred such power to him. Others say that it is not the Pope but the emperor in his empire, and the king in his kingdom, who has the power of excommunicating. DIS. I think these opinions are erroneous, though I abhor the second more. I will hold a discussion about them in another treatise; now tell me the third answer. MAG. The third answer is that the Pope, as Christ's vicar, has the power of excommunicating, but in no way of inflicting a greater penalty. For some say that excommunication is the last penalty that churchmen can exercise. These men therefore say that in this the Pope is superior to the emperor, but in other matters he is inferior to him, namely in all temporal jurisdiction. To the fourth argument the answer is that the Pope cannot depose the emperor by virtue of his papacy, just as by virtue of his papacy he cannot depose the king of France. Pope Zacharias deposed the king of the Franks by the authority of the people of that kingdom; and so they principally deposed him, as the Gloss attests on 15 q. 6 c. alius dicitur depositus, because he consented in all things. Thus the Pope, by the authority of the Romans, could depose the emperor. To the fifth argument the answer is that the Pope, by virtue of his papacy, cannot legitimate illegitimate persons in temporal matters; if he did so in fact, he did it by virtue of some other power which is not attached to the papacy. DIS. I respond to the second principal argument. MAG. To the second argument the answer is that the Pope, by virtue of his papacy, is not released from imperial laws, which in no way conflict with divine laws, although perhaps he is released from them on some other ground. To the third principal argument the answer is that clerics, unless they are exempted by the authority of kings or of a general council, belong to the jurisdiction of the secular powers. To the fourth argument the answer is that in temporal matters one may appeal from the Pope to the emperor, unless one has been exempted by the universal Church. To the fifth it is said that Christ committed to Peter the rights of the earthly empire; that is, power over the wicked in spiritual matters, not in temporal ones.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Vbi probatur rationibus, auctoritatibus & exemplis, quod Papa de crimine hæresis falsa accusa- tus seu diffamatus non sit iudicio vniuersalis ecclesiæ subiectus, ad quas etiam respondetur capitulo 63. huius.
units.tr: Where it is proved by reasons, authorities and examples that the Pope, falsely accused or defamed of the crime of heresy, is not subject to the judgment of the universal Church; to which objections are also answered in chapter 63 of this work.

units.la: DIS. Mihi placet, quod expediuisti te breuiter de rationibus supradictis: tum quia in alio tractatu super ipsos redibo: tum quia non audiui quod frater MAG. de Zelena & sequaces sui, quorum dicta contra dominum Papam principaliter examinare propono, dogmatizat, vel sentiat, quod Papa non habeat iurisdictionem coactiuam, vel quod imperatori subiectus sit. Ideo ad secundam assertionem, quæ recitasti in secundo ca. huius sexti, te conuerte, & motiua illius enarra. MAG. Illa assertio continet duas, quarum prima est: quod si Papa esset de hæresi grauiter diffamatus, ecclesia vniuersalis, & ec concilium generale, & etiam aliqua alia congregatio vel persona potestate inquirendi & coercendi ipsum haberet. DIS. Circa hanc partem peto, vt disseras primo, an ecclesia vniuersalis, si Papa esset de haeresi graviter diffamatus, super ipsum potestatem haberet. MAG. Circa hoc, ut dixi, est una assertio, quod sic aliorum autem est assertio, quod non, dicentium quod licet Papa effectus haereticus ecclesiae sit subiectus, quia eo ipso quod sit haereticus fiet non Papa. si tamen falso fuerit de haeresi diffamatus, non est subiectus ecclesiae, nec ecclesia in hoc casu habet potestatem aliquam super ipsum. DIS. Motiva utriusque assertionis auscultabo libenter. primo autem allega motivum secundae assertionis. MAG. Primum motivum est tale. nulla falsa infamia potest personae vel collegio vel congregationi iurisdictionem aut potestatem conferre. sed Papa de haeresi minime diffamatus non est de iurisdictione ecclesiae, nec subest ei. ergo nec Papa falso de haeresi diffamatus est ecclesiae subiectus. Secundum motivum est tale. Ille qui in aliqua causa est aliis superior, non est in eadem causa inferior illis: quia in eadem causa idem respectu eiusdem vel eorundem non potest esse superior & inferior. manens vero Papa in causa fidei est omnibus aliis superior; quia si omnes Christiani sibi in causa fidei erronee dissentirent, omnes de iure (licet de facto non potest) coercere deberet. ergo Papa propter nullam falsam infamiam fit subiectus ecclesiae in causa haeresis. Tertium motivum est tale. si Papa de haeresi diffamatus iudicio ecclesiae esset subiectus, ecclesia posset iudicare de ipso. hoc autem non potest fieri; quia cum ecclesia universalis simul convenire non potest, oportet generale concilium convocare ad diffiniendum de causa Papae. sed nullus potest absque Papa generale concilium vocare, nec ipse potest compelli per aliquem concilium generale congregare. quia si aliquis posset eum compellere generale concilium congregare, ille esset superior Papa. & ita aliqua persona esset superior Papa. quod non est verum, ut dicunt. ecclesia ergo universalis de Papa iudicare non potest. & ita Papa quantumcunque fuerit de haeresi diffamatus, ecclesiae minime est subiectus. Praedicta assertio auctoritatibus & exemplis videtur posse probari. plures namque auctoritates hoc expresse sonantes, sup. primo capitulo huius sexti sunt inductae. Hoc etiam alia auctoritate simul & exemplo probatur. nam (prout recitatum est sup. ubi inquisitum est, an Papa posset haereticari) Nicolaus Papa, ut legitur di. 21. c. nunc autem ait: Tempore Diocletiani & Maximiani Augustorum Marcellinus episcopus urbis Romanae, qui postea insignis martyr effectus est, adeo compulsus fuit a paganis, ut templum eorum ingressus thuris grana super prunas imponeret. cuius rei gratia collecto universorum concilio episcoporum, & inquisitione facta, hoc idem pontifex se egisse confessus est. nullus tamen illorum in eum proferre sententiam ausus est, dum ei sepissime omnes dicerent, tuo ore iudica causam tuam, non nostro iudicio: sed collige in sinu tuo causam tuam. & rursus, quomodo ex te (inquiunt) iustificaberis, aut ex ore tuo damnaberis. Item dicunt: Prima sedes non iudicabitur a quoquam. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod beatus Marcellinus fuit de haeresi diffamatus: nec mirum, cum actum haereticum commiserit. Ex quo enim idolis immolavit, fuit de apostasia perfidiae vehementer suspectus: quia potuit de haeresi graviter diffamari. hoc tamen non obstante, nemo episcoporum fuit ausus in ipsum proferre sententiam. ergo quandocunque Papa fuerit diffamatus de haeresi, nullius subiectus est iudicio.
units.tr: DIS. I am pleased that you have dealt briefly with the reasons above: partly because I shall return to them in another treatise, and partly because I have not heard that Brother MAG. of Zelena and his followers, whose statements I propose to examine chiefly against the lord Pope, teach or hold that the Pope has no coercive jurisdiction, or that he is subject to the emperor. So turn to the second assertion, which you recited in the second chapter of this sixth part, and set out its grounds. MAG. That assertion contains two parts, the first of which is this: if the Pope were gravely defamed of heresy, the universal Church, and also a general council, and indeed some other assembly or person, would have power to inquire into him and restrain him. DIS. On this part I ask you first to discuss whether the universal Church, if the Pope were gravely defamed of heresy, would have any power over him. MAG. On this, as I have said, there is one assertion that it would, while others hold the contrary assertion, saying that although a Pope who has become a heretic is subject to the Church (because by the very fact that he is a heretic he ceases to be Pope), yet if he has been falsely defamed of heresy, he is not subject to the Church, and the Church in this case has no power at all over him. DIS. I will gladly hear the grounds of both assertions. But first give the ground of the second assertion. MAG. The first ground is this: no false infamy can confer jurisdiction or power on a person, a college or an assembly. But a Pope who has not been defamed of heresy is not under the jurisdiction of the Church, nor subject to it. Therefore neither is a Pope falsely defamed of heresy subject to the Church. The second ground is this: he who is superior to others in some matter is not inferior to them in the same matter, because in the same matter the same person cannot be both superior and inferior with respect to the same or the same persons. But the Pope, remaining Pope, is superior to all others in matters of faith; for if all Christians dissented from him in a matter of faith, wrongly, he ought by right (although not in fact, which is not possible) to restrain them all. Therefore the Pope, on account of no false infamy, becomes subject to the Church in a matter of heresy. The third ground is this: if the Pope, defamed of heresy, were subject to the judgment of the Church, the Church could pass judgment on him. But this cannot be done, since the universal Church cannot assemble together at once, so a general council must be summoned to decide the Pope's cause. But no one can summon a general council without the Pope, nor can the Pope himself be compelled by anyone to convene a general council. For if anyone could compel him to convene a general council, that person would be superior to the Pope; and so some person would be superior to the Pope, which, as they say, is not true. Therefore the universal Church cannot judge the Pope; and so, however much the Pope may be defamed of heresy, he is in no way subject to the Church. This assertion seems capable of proof by authorities and examples. For several authorities plainly saying this were cited above in the first chapter of this sixth part. This is also proved by one authority together with an example. For Pope Nicholas (as was recited above, where it was inquired whether a Pope could be made a heretic) says, in Dist. 21, chapter Nunc autem: In the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, who afterwards became a famous martyr, was so compelled by the pagans that he entered their temple and placed grains of incense on the coals. For this reason a council of all the bishops was gathered, an inquiry was made, and the pontiff confessed that he had done this same thing. Yet none of them dared pronounce sentence against him, since all of them repeatedly said to him: judge your own cause by your own mouth, not by our judgment; but gather your cause in your own bosom. And again: how will you be justified by yourself, or be condemned by your own mouth? They also say: The first see shall not be judged by anyone. From these words it is understood that the blessed Marcellinus was defamed of heresy; nor is this surprising, since he had committed a heretical act. For from the time he sacrificed to idols he was gravely suspected of apostasy from the faith, and so he could well have been gravely defamed of heresy. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, none of the bishops dared pronounce sentence against him. Therefore, whenever a Pope has been defamed of heresy, he is subject to no one's judgment.

units.la: DISCIP. Ista ratio non videtur concludere, quod Papa de haeresi diffamatus non sit subiectus ecclesiae universali & concilio generali: quia auctoritas Nicolai non loquitur de ecclesia universali & concilio generali, sed de quibusdam episcopis, qui convenerunt ad inquirendum de causa Papae Marcellini.
units.tr: DISCIP. This argument does not seem to conclude that a Pope defamed of heresy is not subject to the universal Church and a general council, because the authority of Nicholas does not speak of the universal Church or a general council, but of certain bishops who met to inquire into the cause of Pope Marcellinus.

units.la: MAG. Dicunt alii, quod auctoritas praedicta Nicolai manifeste declarat, quod Papa de haeresi diffamatus est ecclesiae universali vel collegio generali minime subiectus: quia secundum B. Hilarium, intelligentia dictorum ex causis est assumenda dicendi, ad intelligendum verba praedicta, quae Nicolaus Papa recitat, recurrendum est ad causam dicendi. causam autem quare episcopi, qui convenerant ad inquirendum de facto Papae, cum dixerunt, tuo ore iudica causam tuam, non nostro iudicio, ipsimet assignant dicentes: prima sedes non iudicabitur a quoquam. in verbis istis insinuant aperte, quod summus pontifex etiam in casu illo, in quo fuerunt, scilicet, si summus pontifex fuerit de haeresi diffamatus, a nullo est penitus iudicandus. & ita nec ab ecclesia universali, nec a concilio generali est Papa diffamatus de haeresi iudicandus, quia ex quo ipsi, quorum verba approbantur, a canone minime distinxerunt, nec debemus distinguere. Secundo probatur eadem assertio de Simacho Papa, de quo legitur. di. 17. §. hinc, in haec verba: episcopi in synodo residentes congregata auctoritate eiusdem Simachi dixerunt. Simachus Papa sedis apostolicae praesul ab huiusmodi opinionibus impeditus, quantum ad homines respicit, sit immunis & liber, cuius causam totam Dei iudicio servamus.
units.tr: MAG. Others say that the aforesaid authority of Nicholas plainly declares that a Pope defamed of heresy is in no way subject to the universal Church or to a general college: because, according to blessed Hilary, the understanding of sayings is to be drawn from the causes of their saying; to understand the words above, which Pope Nicholas recites, we must have recourse to the occasion of their utterance. Now the reason why the bishops, who had met to inquire into the deed of the Pope, said judge your own cause by your own mouth, not by our judgment, they themselves assign when they say: the first see shall not be judged by anyone. In these words they openly imply that the supreme pontiff, even in that case in which they were, namely if the supreme pontiff were defamed of heresy, is to be judged by no one at all. And so the Pope defamed of heresy is to be judged neither by the universal Church nor by a general council, since those whose words are approved did not distinguish in the canon, and we ought not to distinguish either. Second, the same assertion is proved concerning Pope Symmachus, of whom it is read in Dist. 17, §. hinc, in these words: the bishops sitting in synod, gathered by the authority of that same Symmachus, said: Symmachus, Pope, the prelate of the apostolic see, being hindered by such opinions, is, so far as men are concerned, free and immune; his whole cause we leave to the judgment of God.

units.la: Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Simachus Papa iudicio synodi non erat subiectus, licet fuerit haeresi diffamatus. Praeterea quia ut Glo. notat ibidem, istae opiniones, quibus fuerat Simachus impeditus, causam haeresis contingebant. ait enim: primo fuit (scilicet Simachus) accusatus de haeresi. sed cum appareret calumnia accusantis, fuit postea absolutus, ut ibidem dicitur.
units.tr: From these words it is gathered that Symmachus, Pope, was not subject to the judgment of the synod, although he had been defamed of heresy. Moreover, as the Gloss notes in the same place, those opinions by which Symmachus had been hindered concerned the charge of heresy. For it says: first Symmachus was accused of heresy; but when the calumny of the accuser appeared, he was afterwards absolved, as is said there.

units.la: CAP. 60.
units.tr: CHAPTER 60.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Vbi arguitur ad oppositum, quod Papa de haeresi diffamatus sit iudicio vniuersalis ecclesiae subiectus: & hoc 5. rationibus.
units.tr: Where the opposite is argued, that the Pope, if defamed of heresy, is subject to the judgment of the universal Church, and this by five reasons.

units.la: DISCIP. Ad praesens sufficiant istae allegationes pro assertione praedicta, & ideo motiua assertionis contrariae non differas allegare. MAG. Quod Papa sic de haeresi diffamatus sit subiectus iudicio ecclesiae vniuersalis, nonnulli conantur ostendere. Primo sic. Ille, qui potest accusari & iudicari de haeresi, est subiectus iudicio vniuersalis ecclesiae, si fuerit de haeresi diffamatus. Papa autem potest de haeresi accusari & iudicari. di. 4. si Papa. ergo, &c. Secundo sic: Qui potest ab aliquo reprehendi pro haeresi, est subiectus in eadem causa iudicio vniuersalis ecclesiae. sed Papa potest pro haeresi ab aliquo reprehendi. hoc probatur per exemplum de B. Petro, quem B. Paulus (quia non ambulabat ad veritatem euangelii) reprehendit ad Gal. 2. ergo Papa, si fuerit de haeresi diffamatus, iudicio vniuersalis ecclesiae est subiectus. Tertio sic: Minor iudicio superioris est subiectus. sed Papa est minor ecclesia vniuersali, sicut orbis maior est vibe. ergo, &c. Quarto sic: Nulli corpori sufficienter est prouisum, nisi membra putrida, quae totum corpus valent inficere, possint abscindi. sed tota ecclesia militans vnum corpus est, teste apostolo qui Ro. 12. ait: vnum corpus sumus in Christo. istius autem corporis Papa est membrum. ergo non est sufficienter prouisum ecclesiae, nisi Papa posset abscindi per ecclesiam, si haereticam prauitatem incurrat. cum ergo Christus non defecerit in necessariis ecclesiae militantis, sequitur quod per ecclesiam militantem Papa, si efficiatur haereticus, post abscindi: & per consequens si fuerit de haeresi diffamatus, iudicio vniuersalis ecclesiae est subiectus. Quinto sic: Ille, qui est de aliquo crimine denunciandus ecclesiae, iudicio vniuersalis ecclesiae est subiectus, si fuerit diffamatus. sed Papa potest pro crimine haeresis denunciari ecclesiae, Christo dicente Math. 18. Si peccauerit in te frater tuus. & post: si non audierit te, dic ecclesiae. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod cum Papa censendus sit frater, ipse potest pro crimine potissime haeresis denunciari ecclesiae. ergo si fuerit de crimine haeresis diffamatus, iudicio ecclesiae est subiectus.
units.tr: STUDENT. For the present these allegations are enough for the aforesaid assertion, so do not delay in setting out the arguments for the contrary view. MASTER. Some try to show that the Pope, if defamed of heresy, is thus subject to the judgment of the universal Church. (1) First, thus: whoever can be accused and judged of heresy is subject to the judgment of the universal Church, if he has been defamed of heresy. But the Pope can be accused and judged of heresy (dist. 4, "si Papa"). Therefore, etc. (2) Second, thus: whoever can be rebuked by someone for heresy is subject to the judgment of the universal Church in the same matter. But the Pope can be rebuked for heresy by someone. This is proved by the example of St Peter, whom St Paul rebuked because he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the gospel (Gal. 2). Therefore the Pope, if he has been defamed of heresy, is subject to the judgment of the universal Church. (3) Third, thus: a lesser person is subject to the judgment of his superior. But the Pope is less than the universal Church, just as the world is greater than the city. Therefore, etc. (4) Fourth, thus: no body is sufficiently provided for unless its putrid members, which could infect the whole body, can be cut off. But the whole militant Church is one body, as the apostle witnesses when he says in Rom. 12: we are one body in Christ. The Pope is a member of this body. Therefore the Church is not sufficiently provided for unless the Pope can be cut off by the Church, should he fall into heretical depravity. Since therefore Christ has not failed in what is necessary for the militant Church, it follows that the Pope, if he becomes a heretic, can afterwards be cut off by the militant Church; and consequently, if he has been defamed of heresy, he is subject to the judgment of the universal Church. (5) Fifth, thus: whoever is to be denounced to the Church for some crime is subject to the judgment of the universal Church, if he has been defamed. But the Pope can be denounced to the Church for the crime of heresy, Christ saying in Matt. 18: If thy brother shall trespass against thee ... and if he shall neglect to hear thee, tell it unto the Church. From these words it is gathered that, since the Pope is to be counted a brother, he can be denounced to the Church above all for the crime of heresy. Therefore, if he has been defamed of the crime of heresy, he is subject to the judgment of the Church.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: In quo agitur de concilio generali, utrum habeat potestatem super Papam de haeresi diffamatum, & probatur quinque rationibus, quod non: ad quas respondetur infra capitulo 64. huius.
units.tr: In which it is discussed whether a general council has power over the Pope when he is defamed of heresy. It is proved by five arguments that it does not, and replies to these are given below in chapter 64 of this work.

units.la: DISCIP. De Ecclesia vniuersali, an sibi summus pontifex sit subiectus; quae dixisti sufficiant. Nunc autem sententias peritorum de concilio generali, an super Papam de haeresi diffamatum iurisdictionem vel potestatem obtineat, aperire digneris. MAG. Sunt nonnulli dicentes, quod concilium generale super Papam de haeresi infamatum nullam habet iurisdictionem omnino. quod pluribus rationibus nituntur ostendere. Est autem prima ratio talis: ecclesia vniuersalis nullam habet iurisdictionem super Papam de haeresi diffamatum. quod nituntur per rationes post adductas ostendere. ergo multo fortius concilium generale non habet iurisdictionem super Papam de haeresi diffamatum. Secundo: nulla congregatio specialis in quacunque causa habet iurisdictionem super Papam, cum in omni causa quaelibet congregatio particularis Papa inferior sit censenda. concilium autem generale est quaedam congregatio particularis seu specialis: quia omnes Christianos minime comprehendit. ergo concilium generale non habet iurisdictionem super Papam. Tertio sic: illa congregatio, quae potest contra fidem errare, non habet iurisdictionem super Papam de haeresi mendaciter diffamatum. generale autem concilium potest contra fidem errare, sicut nonnulli per plures rationes probare nituntur. ergo, &c. Quarto sic: illa congregatio, quae in causa haeresis est inferior Papa etiam de haeresi diffamato, non est in eadem causa Papa superior. sed totum concilium generale praeter Papam est in causa haeresis Papa inferius. quia si totum concilium generale praeter Papam etiam de haeresi mendaciter diffamatum contra fidem erraret, ipse omnes de iure punire deberet. Ergo in causa haeresis Papa concilio generali est superior. DIS. totum concilium generale praeter Papam non potest contra fidem errare: quia Deus, qui promisit fidem catholicam usq; ad finem seculi duraturam, non permitteret. MA. Ista responsio impugnatur. tum quia esto, quod totum concilium generale praeter Papam erraret, nequaquam fides Christiana deficeret, quia saluaretur in Papa, & in multis aliis. fides autem in solo Papa potest seruari; quemadmodum tempore passionis Christi in vnica muliere remansit. tum quia vnus potest ad se trahere totum concilium generale, & vnus potest toti residuo concilii generalis contradicere, sicut notatur di. 15. c. Nicaena. ergo multo fortius Papa, qui est principalis & caput concilii generalis, potest toti residuo contradicere. & per consequens residuo minime est subiectus. Quinto sic: illa congregatio, quae nullam auctoritatem habet, nisi a Papa, & quae absque Papa congregari non potest, nullam habet iurisdictionem super Papam, nisi Papa sponte eius iudicio se submittat. sed concilium generale nullam habet iurisdictionem seu potestatem aut auctoritatem nisi a Papa; nec potest absque eius mandato aliqualiter celebrari. ergo si Papa non voluntarie se submittat iudicio generalis concilii, minime ei est subiectus.
units.tr: STUDENT. Concerning the universal Church, and whether the supreme pontiff is subject to it, what you have said is enough. Now please explain the opinions of the learned on whether a general council holds jurisdiction or power over the Pope when he is defamed of heresy. MASTER. Some say that a general council has no jurisdiction at all over a Pope who is infamed of heresy, and they try to show this by several arguments. The first argument is this: the universal Church has no jurisdiction over a Pope defamed of heresy. They try to show this by the arguments set out above. Therefore, much more strongly, a general council has no jurisdiction over a Pope defamed of heresy. Second: no particular assembly, in any cause whatever, has jurisdiction over the Pope, since in every matter any particular assembly must be judged inferior to the Pope. A general council, however, is a certain particular or special assembly, because it does not embrace all Christians. Therefore a general council has no jurisdiction over the Pope. Third, thus: that assembly which can err against the faith has no jurisdiction over a Pope falsely defamed of heresy. A general council can err against the faith, as some try to prove by many arguments. Therefore, etc. Fourth, thus: that assembly which, in a cause of heresy, is inferior to the Pope even when he is defamed of heresy, is not superior to the Pope in the same cause. But the whole general council apart from the Pope is inferior to the Pope in a cause of heresy, because if the whole general council apart from the Pope, even when falsely defamed of heresy, erred against the faith, he himself ought by right to punish them all. Therefore, in a cause of heresy, a general council is inferior to the Pope. STUDENT. The whole general council apart from the Pope cannot err against the faith, because God, who promised that the Catholic faith would last until the end of the age, would not permit it. MASTER. This reply is attacked. First, because even if the whole general council apart from the Pope were to err, the Christian faith would by no means fail, since it would be preserved in the Pope and in many others. Yet the faith can be preserved in the Pope alone, just as at the time of Christ's passion it remained in one woman. Second, because one man can draw the whole general council to himself, and one man can contradict the whole remainder of a general council, as is noted in dist. 15, c. Nicaena. Therefore, much more strongly, the Pope, who is the principal and head of a general council, can contradict the whole remainder, and consequently is not subject to the remainder at all. Fifth, thus: that assembly which has no authority except from the Pope, and which cannot be gathered without the Pope, has no jurisdiction over the Pope unless the Pope of his own accord submits himself to its judgment. But a general council has no jurisdiction, power or authority except from the Pope, nor can it in any way be held without his command. Therefore, if the Pope does not voluntarily submit himself to the judgment of a general council, he is in no way subject to it.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: In quo probatur duabus rationibus & aliquibus auctoritatibus, quod Papa de haeresi diffamatus subiicitur concilio generali.
units.tr: In which it is proved by two arguments and some authorities that the Pope, when defamed of heresy, is subject to a general council.

units.la: DISCIP. Quomodo allegatur in contrarium, manifesta. MAG. Quod Papa iudicio generalis concilii sit subiectus, quidam moliuntur ostendere. Primo sic: Ecclesia vniuersalis iurisdictionem obtinet super Papam de haeresi diffamatum. igitur & ista congregatio, quae vicem gerit vniuersalis ecclesiae, habet iurisdictionem super Papam de haeresi diffamatum. concilium autem generale tenet vicem ecclesiae vniuersalis. ergo, &c. Secundo sic: diffamatus de aliquo crimine est iudicio concilii generalis subiectus, & eidem concilio super obiecto crimine respondere tenetur. Papa autem diffamatus de haeresi generali concilio respondere tenetur. Vnde & in decre. 2. q. 7. c. nos, sic legitur; Simachus Papa in Romana synodo dignitate sua expoliatus prius statui pristino reddi praecipitur, vt tunc veniret ad causam, & si ita rectum videtur, accu saztum propositionibus responderet. digna res visa est maxime numero sacerdotum, atque meretur effectum. Cum postmodum ordinaretur, quomodo esset accusandus praefatus Papa, vt causam diceret occurrebat, sed ab amulis est impeditus. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod Simachus Papa, qui fuit de haeresi accusatus, sicut notatur in Glo. di. 17. §. hinc, coram synodo respondere debebat. ergo in causa haeresis concilium generale est super Papam de haeresi diffamatum. Tertio per glossas super decretis hoc probatur. ait enim Glo. di. 19. c. Anastasius: Papa tenetur requirere concilium episcoporum. quod verum est, vbi agitur de fide: & tunc synodus maior est Papa. his verbis patenter asseritur, quod in causa fidei synodus maior est Papa. Item Glo. di. 15. c. sicut, dicit in haec verba; videtur quod Papa non possit destruere statuta concilii: quia orbis maior est vrbe. vnde requirit Papa consensum concilii 19. di. Anastasius. 71. ar. 19. di. 1. §. hinc, & extra de electione signati, vbi dicitur: concilium non potest Papae legem imponere, & 15. q. 9. veniam. sed intelligi quod hoc dicitur circa articulos fidei. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod circa articulos fidei maior synodus est Papa, & sibi legem potest imponere: & per consequens in causa fidei synodus iurisdictionem habet super Papam. Item Glo. 20. di. 31 c. nunc autem, ait: quare isti non deposuerunt Papam, cum esset confessus de haeresi, vt 60. di. si Papa, dicens quod paratus erat corrigi. Licet enim sit Papa haereticus vel alius, si tamen paratus est corrigi, non deponitur, vt & 24. q. 3. dixit apostolus. vel ideo non debebat ipsum deponere, quia coactus fecit. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod episcopi potestatem habent deponendi Papam de haeresi accusatum; licet non debeant ipsum semper deponere, quia aliquando non est dignus deponi. causam tamen Papae habent audire, & ita potestatem obtinent super ipsum.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. How the contrary is alleged is plain. MASTER. Some people labour to show that the Pope is subject to the judgment of a general council. First, thus: the universal Church has jurisdiction over a Pope defamed of heresy. Therefore this congregation, which takes the place of the universal Church, also has jurisdiction over a Pope defamed of heresy. But a general council holds the place of the universal Church. Therefore, etc. Second, thus: one defamed of any crime is subject to the judgment of a general council and is bound to answer to that council on the crime alleged. But a Pope defamed of heresy is bound to answer to a general council. Hence also in Decretum 2, q. 7, c. nos, we read thus: Pope Symmachus, stripped of his dignity in the Roman synod, was first ordered to be restored to his former state, so that he might then come to the case and, if it seemed right, answer the accusations put to him. The matter seemed worthy above all to the number of priests, and it deserves to take effect. When afterwards it was arranged how the said Pope should be accused, so that he might state his case, it came about that he was prevented by his rivals. From these words it is to be understood that Pope Symmachus, who had been accused of heresy, as is noted in the Gloss on d. 17, §. hinc, ought to have answered before the synod. Therefore in a cause of heresy a general council has jurisdiction over a Pope defamed of heresy. Third, this is proved by the glosses on the decrees. For the Gloss on d. 19, c. Anastasius, says: The Pope is bound to seek the council of bishops. This is true where the matter concerns the faith, and then the synod is greater than the Pope. By these words it is plainly asserted that in a matter of faith the synod is greater than the Pope. Likewise the Gloss on d. 15, c. sicut, says in these words: It seems that the Pope cannot overturn the statutes of a council, because the world is greater than the city. Hence the Pope requires the consent of the council, d. 19, Anastasius; 71, ar. 19, d. 1, §. hinc; and Extra, de electione, signati, where it is said: A council cannot impose a law on the Pope, and 15, q. 9, veniam. But it is understood that this is said with reference to the articles of faith. From these words it is gathered that with respect to the articles of faith the greater synod is above the Pope and can impose a law on him, and consequently in a cause of faith the synod has jurisdiction over the Pope. Also the Gloss on 20, d. 31, c. nunc autem, says: why did those not depose the Pope, since he had confessed to heresy, as in 60, d. si Papa, saying that he was ready to be corrected? For even if a Pope or anyone else is a heretic, if he is ready to be corrected he is not deposed, as the Apostle also said in 24, q. 3. Or else they ought not to have deposed him, because he was compelled to act. From these words it is to be understood that bishops have the power to depose a Pope accused of heresy, although they ought not always to depose him, because sometimes he is not worthy to be deposed. Nevertheless they have to hear the Pope's case, and so they hold power over him.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: Ponit vnum modum dicendi de Papa taliter diffamato, quod non solum concilium generale sed etiam episcopi in tali casu habent potestatem inquirendi de ipso, & causam huius & modum assignat.
units.tr: It sets out one way of speaking about a Pope who is so publicly defamed that not only a general council but also the bishops, in such a case, have power to inquire into him; and it assigns the reason for this and the manner of doing so.

units.la: DISCIP. Allegationes praescriptae me fere ad perplexitatem inducunt. Durum enim mihi videtur asserere, quod omnes super pastorem, membra super caput, filii super patrem, discipuli super magistrum, subditi super praelatum iurisdictionem aut potestatem aut auctoritatem obtineant: praesertim cum iniqua & falsa infamia iurisdictionem non debeat nec possit tribuere. & ideo graue apparet dicere, quod Papa de haeresi mendacicer diffamatus propter talem infamiam cuiuscunque vel quorumcunque subdatur iudicio; maxime cum impossibile minime videtur, quod tota fides catholica in solo Papa remaneat, saltem pro aliquo tempore breui. Ex alia parte zelus fidei Christianae me subtiliter angit; ne dicam nullam debere fieri inquisitionem aut iudicium de Papa super haeresis crimine diffamato. quare cum probabiliter teneam, Papam posse haereticam prauitatem incurrere, si de ipso nulla possit inquisitio fieri, tota fides posset periclitari. vnde si aliqui istam perplexitatem nituntur dissoluere, mihi reuelat. MAGIST. Est quaedam assertio, quod propter nullam infamiam falsam habet ecclesia iurisdictionem super Papam. si tamen Papa fuerit de haeresi taliter diffamatus, quod sine scandalo ecclesiae vel periculo fidei toleran non posset, non solum vniuersalis ecclesia aut concilium generale, sed etiam episcopi habent potestatem inquirendi de ipso. Quem si deprehenderint manifeste haereticum ipsum debent coercere, vel aliis denunciare prauitatem eiusdem. DIS.
