Since, then, a Pope who definitively pronounces that Christ was a false prophet is manifestly a blasphemer of Christ, it clearly follows that just as Jews, because they are blasphemers of Christ, ought not to exercise the force of power over Christians, so a Pope who definitively pronounces Christ to have been a false prophet, because he is a blasphemer of Christ, ought not to exercise the force of power over Christians. The tenth reason: one may lawfully appeal in a case of heresy from one who acts as judge and pronounces an unjust sentence against the faith, and to whom one may not lawfully appeal in a case of faith. For one may lawfully appeal to a man acting as judge only where it is not lawful to appeal from someone. But one may not lawfully appeal to a Pope who definitively pronounces the law of Christ false and the law of the Saracens to be held, since they are of a different faith from Catholics. Yet Catholics may not appeal to the judgement of a man of another faith, as the Council of Carthage testifies, cited in 2 q. 6, c. "Catholicus": a Catholic who appeals his cause, whether just or unjust, to the judgement of another judge, let him be excommunicated. Therefore one may not lawfully appeal to a Pope who definitively pronounces the law of the Saracens to be held, and consequently one may lawfully appeal from him. The eleventh reason: one may lawfully appeal from an excommunicate who acts as judge. But a Pope who definitively pronounces the Christian faith false is excommunicate, like one who falls into a heresy already condemned, as the gloss on 24 q. 1, c. "Qui" says: this is a case in which the Pope falls under the canon of sentence already pronounced. Therefore one may lawfully appeal from him. The twelfth reason: one may lawfully appeal against a sentence which is neither to be held, nor to be observed, nor to be feared; for a sentence from which one may not appeal is one to be feared. But the definitive sentence by which the Pope pronounces the Christian law false is neither to be observed, nor to be feared, nor to be held, since a sentence pronounced against the divine law is not to be feared, just as no agreement against the laws of God is to be kept. Therefore one may lawfully appeal from such a sentence. The thirteenth reason: one may lawfully appeal from one who may lawfully be challenged. But a man who pronounces the law of Christians false may lawfully be challenged in every case of faith. Such a Pope would be a manifest enemy of all Christians and of the whole Christian law. Therefore one may lawfully appeal from such a man in a case of faith.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Adducit instantiam contra conclusionem & casum positum capitulo praecedenti, ad quam datur duplex responsio. prima ponitur in hoc capitulo. secunda vero habetur infra capitulo 28. vbi etiam nota inter respondendum, quod quandoq; in casu licet in causa fidei ad infidelem appellare.
units.tr: It raises an objection against the conclusion and the case stated in the preceding chapter, to which a twofold answer is given. The first is set out in this chapter; the second is found below in chapter 28, where it is also noted, in answering, that in some cases it is lawful to appeal to an unbeliever in a matter of faith.

units.la: DISCIP. Videtur quod hic argumentis abundas pro assertione praedicta. ideo non multiplices amplius argumenta: sed quomodo ad quandam instantiam, quam faciam contra praedicta secundum assertionem praescriptam, debeat responderi, indicare digneris. Videtur namque quod omnia argumenta nihil concludunt: quia papa pronuncians diffinitiue legem Christianam esse falsam, est inter infideles indubie numerandus. ab infideli autem fideles appellare non debet. Nusquam enim legitur, quod sancti martyres, cum cogerentur negare fidem, ab infidelibus iudicibus appellassent: nec etiam apostoli contra principes sacerdotum, cum protulissent contra fidem sententiam, appellaverunt. ergo a papa pronunciante diffinitiue legem Christianam esse falsam, non debent catholici appellare. MAGIST. Ad istam instantiam potest dari duplex responsio. prima est, quod non est necessarium absolute appellare a papa iniquam contra fidem proferente sententiam: propter quod multi fideles contra infideles & haereticos minime inveniuntur appellasse. Sed sufficit in multis casibus sententia papae vel alterius contra fidem simpliciter impugnare, detestari & horrere. Quemadmodum sancti patres absque appellatione haereticorum assertiones iniquas per sacras literas impugnarunt. Verumtamen aliquando expedit appellare exemplo beati Pauli, qui ad Caesarem appellavit. DISCIP. Non videtur, quod beatus Paulus appellavit pro causa fidei, sed pro aliis criminibus, quae sibi imponebantur mendaciter a Iudaeis. ergo per exempla beati Pauli probari non potest, quod expediat pro causa fidei a papa haeretico appellare.
units.tr: STUDENT. It seems that you have an abundance of arguments for the aforesaid assertion. So do not multiply arguments any further, but please indicate how one should answer a certain objection that I will raise against the aforesaid assertion. For it seems that all the arguments conclude nothing, because the pope, who pronounces definitively that the Christian law is false, must undoubtedly be counted among the unbelievers. But the faithful ought not to appeal from an unbeliever. For nowhere is it read that the holy martyrs, when they were compelled to deny the faith, appealed from unbelieving judges; nor did the apostles appeal against the chief priests when they had pronounced sentence against the faith. Therefore Catholics ought not to appeal from a pope who pronounces definitively that the Christian law is false. TEACHER. To this objection a twofold answer can be given. The first is that it is not absolutely necessary to appeal from a pope who pronounces an unjust sentence against the faith; for which reason many of the faithful are found to have never appealed against unbelievers and heretics. But in many cases it is enough simply to attack, detest and abhor the sentence of the pope, or of anyone else, against the faith, just as the holy Fathers, without any appeal, attacked the unjust assertions of heretics by means of the Sacred Letters. Nevertheless, sometimes it is expedient to appeal, following the example of blessed Paul, who appealed to Caesar. STUDENT. It does not seem that blessed Paul appealed for a cause of faith, but for other charges which the Jews falsely laid against him. Therefore it cannot be proved by the examples of blessed Paul that it is expedient to appeal from a heretical pope in a cause of faith.

units.la: MAGIST. Nonnullis apparet, quod beatus Paulus pro causa fidei appellavit, quod ex serie actuum apostolorum videtur posse probari. nam 23. c. act. apostolorum sic legitur scripsisse tribunus Claudius praesidi Felici de Paulo: virum hunc comprehensum a Iudaeis & incipientem interfici ab eis superveniens cum exercitu eripui, cognito quia Romanus est. volensque scire causam, quam obiiciebant illi, deduxi eum in concilium eorum, quem inveni accusari de quaestionibus legis eorum, nihil vero dignum morte, aut vinculis habentem crimen. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod super causa fidei inter Iudaeos & Paulum quaestio vertebatur. pro ista autem causa Paulus postea appellavit. ergo super causa fidei appellavit ad Caesarem. Rursus 24. c. habetur expresse, quod Paulus de causa fidei accusabatur a Iudaeis. unde & orator eorum accusans Paulum dicit: inuenimus hunc hominem pestiferum & concitantem seditionem omnibus Iudaeis in vniuerso orbe, & actorem seditionis sectae Nazarenorum, qui etiam templum violare conatus est. Ex quibus verbis apparet, quod Paulus accusabatur de fide. Et quod pro illa causa appellavit, patet. 25. c. sic legatur: Paulo autem omnibus reddente rationem, quoniam neque in legem Iudaeorum, neque in templum, neque in Caesarem quicquam peccavi. Festus autem volens praestare Iudaeis gratiam, respondens Paulo dicit: vis Hierosolymam ascendere, & ibi de his iudicari apud me? dixit autem Paulus, ad tribunal Caesaris sto, ubi me oportet iudicari. Iudaeis non nocui, sicut tu melius nosti. si enim nocui, aut dignum morte aliquid feci, non recuso mori: si vero nihil est horum, de quibus hi accusant me, nemo potest illis me donare. Caesarem appello. & post Festus loquens de Iudaeis accusantibus Paulum, ait: Cum ergo huc convenissent sine ulla dilatione, sequenti die sedens pro tribunali iussit adduci virum, de quo cum stetissent accusatores, nullam causam deferebant, de quibus ego suspicabar malum. quaestiones vero quasdam de sua superstitione habebant adversus eum, & de quodam Iesu defuncto, quem affirmabat Paulus viuere. haesitans autem ego de huiusmodi quaestione dicebam, si vellet ire Hierosolymam, & ibi iudicari de isto. Paulo autem appellante, ut seruaretur Augusti cognitioni, iussi seruari eum, donec mittam eum ad Caesarem. Ex quibus verbis colliguntur duo. primum, quod pro illa quaestione, quae vertebatur inter Iudaeos & Paulum, Paulus Caesarem appellavit. Secundum est, quod super fide Christi inter ipsos quaestio vertebatur. Ex quibus sequitur, quod pro causa fidei Paulus Caesarem appellavit.
units.tr: TEACHER. Some think it apparent that blessed Paul appealed for a cause of faith, which can be proved from the sequence of the Acts of the Apostles. For in chapter 23 of Acts it is written that the tribune Claudius wrote to the governor Felix about Paul: "This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them; coming upon them with soldiers, I rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman. Wishing to know the charge they brought against him, I brought him before their council, and I found that he was accused concerning questions of their law, but had nothing worthy of death or of bonds." From these words it is gathered that the dispute between the Jews and Paul was concerning a matter of faith. And Paul afterwards appealed on this very ground. Therefore he appealed to Caesar concerning a matter of faith. Again, in chapter 24 it is stated expressly that Paul was accused by the Jews concerning the faith. Hence their orator, accusing Paul, says: "We have found this man to be a pestilent fellow, stirring up sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, who also tried to profane the temple." From these words it appears that Paul was accused concerning the faith, and it is plain that he appealed on that charge. Chapter 25 reads thus: "Paul, answering for himself, said: Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I offended in anything." But Festus, wishing to show favour to the Jews, answering Paul, says: "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me?" Paul said: "I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. For if I have done wrong, or committed anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die; but if none of those things are true of which these men accuse me, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar." And afterwards Festus, speaking of the Jews who accused Paul, says: "When therefore they had come together here without any delay, on the next day, sitting on the judgment seat, I ordered the man to be brought. When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge against him of such evils as I suspected; but they had certain questions against him about their own superstition, and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. Being at a loss how to inquire into such a matter, I asked whether he would go to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning these things. But when Paul appealed to be reserved for the judgment of Augustus, I ordered him to be kept until I might send him to Caesar." From these words two things are gathered. First, that Paul appealed to Caesar concerning that question which was in dispute between the Jews and Paul. Second, that the dispute between them was concerning faith in Christ. From these it follows that Paul appealed to Caesar for a cause of faith.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Dat instantiam ex dictis in ca. 20. vbi potest inferri, quod ad papam haereticum possit appellari, ac per consequens ab eo, nemini licet appellare, quod videtur contrarium dictis capitulo 18. huius.
units.tr: He raises an objection from what was said in chapter 20, where it can be inferred that one may appeal to a heretical pope, and consequently that one may not appeal from him, which seems contrary to what was said in chapter 18 of this book.

units.la: DISCIP. Stuporem mihi praedicta ingerunt vehementem, quia penè incredibile mihi videtur, quod pro causa fidei in quocunque casu ad hominem contrariae sectae liceat appellare. & tamen apparenter ostenditur, quod Paulus pro causa fidei Caesarem, qui erat sectae contrariae, appellavit. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod non est inconueniens ad papam haereticum appellare. & per consequens ab eo appellare non licet; quia pro eadem causa non est ab eodem & ad eundem appellandum. & ita praedictae assertioni, quae dicit, quod licet a papa haeretico appellare contrariari videtur. Unde quomodo ad istam contrarietatem respondere contingat, enarra. MAG. Pro dissoluenda contrarietate praefata, dicunt quidam esse notandum, quod implicitè contingit ad aliquem pro aliqua causa fidei appellare. Vno quidem modo, vt ad eum, qui habet quaestiones motas de fide iuxta sanam doctrinam ex officio terminare. & isto modo ad nullum hominem alterius sectae, sive fuerit paganus, sive haereticus, est pro causa fidei appellandum, quia ad solos summos pontifices catholicos & fideles ac generale concilium catholicorum spectat quaestiones fidei terminare, sicut in sacris canonibus patenter apparet. Aliter contingit aliquem ad alium pro causa fidei appellare, non quidem sicut ad illum, qui habet causas fidei terminare, sed tanquam ad illum, qui ex officio, vel electione appellantis, aut alio quovis modo potest cognoscere, ab appellans debeat pro causa huiusmodi ab aemulis accusari vel in iudicio aliquo appellatus conueniri. Sic dicitur, q si aliquis super aliquo dubio fidei (q non est certum esse haeresis, nec est haeresis damnata explicite, licet sit haeresis damnata implicite) accusaretur coram episcopo, talis pro quaestione huiusmodi posset ad metropolitanum appellare. Non quidem tanq ad illum, qui habet tale dubium diffinire, sed tanquam ad illum, ad quem spectat scire & iudicare, q talis quaestio non per episcopum, nec per metropolitanum debet determinari: sed q est summo pontifici, vel generali concilio reseruanda. Per praedicta supradicta contrarietas dissoluitur, quia p causa fidei in nullo casu est ad hominem sectae contrariae appellandum, tanquam ad illum, qui quaestionem fidei habeat diffinire. nec isto modo Paulus Caesarem appellauit, sciebat q Caesar fidem Pauli salsissimam reputabat.
units.tr: STUDENT. The things said above fill me with great astonishment, since it seems to me almost incredible that one may appeal, in any case whatsoever, to a man of a contrary sect for a cause of faith. Yet it is clearly shown that Paul appealed for a cause of faith to Caesar, who belonged to a contrary sect. From this it seems to follow that it is not inappropriate to appeal to a heretical pope, and consequently that one may not appeal from him, since one must not appeal from and to the same person for the same cause. So the assertion mentioned above, that one may appeal from a heretical pope, seems to be contradicted. Explain, therefore, how this contradiction may be answered. MASTER. To resolve the aforesaid contradiction, some say that it must be noted that one may appeal to someone for a cause of faith in an implicit way. In one way, namely, as to one who has by his office the duty of settling questions of faith according to sound doctrine. In this way, one must not appeal for a cause of faith to any man of another sect, whether he is a pagan or a heretic, because it belongs only to the supreme catholic pontiffs and faithful, and to a general council of catholics, to settle questions of faith, as is plainly evident in the sacred canons. In another way, a person may appeal to another for a cause of faith, not indeed as to one who has the duty of settling matters of faith, but as to one who, by his office, or by the choice of the appellant, or in some other way, can take cognizance of the matter, when the appellant must be accused of such a cause by his rivals or summoned to some court. Thus it is said that if someone were accused before a bishop concerning some doubtful point of faith (which is not certainly heresy, nor explicitly condemned as heresy, although it is implicitly condemned as heresy), such a person could appeal to the metropolitan for a question of this kind. Not indeed as to one who has the power to define such a doubt, but as to one to whom it belongs to know and judge that such a question must be determined not by the bishop, nor by the metropolitan, but is to be reserved to the supreme pontiff or a general council. By what has been said, the aforesaid contradiction is resolved, because for a cause of faith one must in no case appeal to a man of a contrary sect as to one who is able to define the question of faith. Nor did Paul appeal to Caesar in this way, for he knew that Caesar regarded Paul's faith as thoroughly sound.

units.la: Aliquando tamen licuit pro causa fidei ad hominem sectae alterius appellare, tanquam ad illum, qui ex officio vel electione appellantis, vel alio quovis modo cognoscere potuit, quod iudices sui de quaestione fidei se intromittere minime debuerunt. & hoc modo Paulus ad Caesarem appellauit. Sciebat enim Paulus, quod nulla persecutio adhuc per Romanos aut Caesarem fuerat contra Christianos excitata. & ideo sciebat, quod iudices Caesaris de tali quaestione secundum leges Caesaris se intromittere non debebant, propter q, vt habetur Act. 18. Galio proconsul Achayae, cum Paulus sibi accusaretur a Iudaeis, quod contra legem persuaderet colere Deum, accusationem eius audite nolebat, dicens: siquidem iniquum aliquid aut facinus pessimum, o viri Iudaei, recte vos sustinerem. si vero quaestiones sunt de verbo & nominib. legis vestrae, vosipsi videritis. iudex horum verborum nolo esse, & minuit eos a tribunali. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod iudices missi ad Caesarem de his, quae pertinebant ad legem, iudicandi potestatem minime habuerunt. vnde & Pilatus, sicut euangelica patefacit historia, propter nullam accusationem, quae de lege deferebatur contra ipsum, reputauit se iudicare debere Christum. sicut etiam ex actib. apostolorum c. 23. 25. & 26 tribunus Lysias, Felix praeses, Festus praeses, & rex Agrippa, propter illa, quae obiiciebantur contra Paulum de lege & de doctrina Pauli iudicabant illum minime puniendum. Paulus ergo sciens, quod talis quaestio etiam secundum leges & consuetudines Romanorum ad iudices & publicas potestates inferiores Caesaris nullatenus pertinebat, Caesarem appellauit, tanquam ad illum, qui iudicaret talem quaestionem ad iudices, coram quibus Paulus fuerat accusatus, minime pertinere.
units.tr: Yet at times it has been lawful to appeal for a cause of faith to a man of another sect, as to one who, by his office or by the choice of the appellant, or in some other way, could recognise that his own judges ought in no way to meddle with a question of faith. And in this way Paul appealed to Caesar. For Paul knew that no persecution had yet been stirred up against the Christians by the Romans or by Caesar. Therefore he knew that Caesar's judges ought not to meddle with such a question according to Caesar's laws. For this reason, as is recorded in Acts 18, when Paul was accused by the Jews before Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, of persuading men to worship God contrary to the law, Gallio refused to hear the accusation, saying: "If indeed it were some wrong or wicked crime, O Jews, I would reasonably bear with you; but if the questions concern a word and names of your law, look to it yourselves; I refuse to be a judge of such matters," and he drove them from the tribunal. From these words it is gathered that judges sent by Caesar had no power to judge matters that pertained to the law. Hence also Pilate, as the Gospel history makes clear, thought he ought not to judge Christ on account of any accusation concerning the law brought against him. Likewise, as Acts, chapters 23, 25 and 26 show, the tribune Lysias, the governor Felix, the governor Festus and King Agrippa judged that Paul was in no way to be punished for the things alleged against him concerning the law and the teaching of Paul. Paul therefore, knowing that such a question, even according to the laws and customs of the Romans, did not pertain at all to the inferior judges and public powers of Caesar, appealed to Caesar, as to one who would judge that such a question did not belong to the judges before whom Paul had been accused.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXII.

units.la: In quo ponuntur quatuor obiectiones sive instantiae contra ea, quae dicta sunt in responsione capituli praecedentis ad obiectionem ibi factam.
units.tr: In which four objections, or challenges, are set out against what was said in the reply in the preceding chapter to the objection raised there.

units.la: DISCIP. Contra praedicta quatuor mihi obiectiones occurrunt. Primo, quibusdam videtur, quod ex quo praeses Festus sciebat, quod talis quaestio ad illum non spectabat, non oportuit propter hoc Paulum appellare ab ipso; quia appellatio vel est a grauamine, vel est a sententia. Paulus autem non appellauit a sententia Festi, quia nullam tulit: nec a grauamine, quia nullum volebat inferre. nam si Paulus non appellasset, volebat ipsum dimittere. Secundo videtur, quod Paulus non debuit Caesarem appellare; quia sciebat ipsum inimicum fidei suae, & q sententiam daret contra Paulum. Tertio apparet, quod Paulus facto mentiebatur recognoscendo Caesarem iudicem suum; cum tamen praesertim in causa fidei non fuerit iudex suus, nec superior. Quarto videtur, q a I hominem alterius sectae liceat appellare, tanquam ad illum qui possit quaestionem fidei terminare, & distinguere, vel diffinire. Nam ad illum licet pro causa fidei illo modo appellare, qui potest esse iudex in causa fidei habens potestatem diffiniendi, quod pertinet ad veritatem fidei orthodoxae. sed hoc potest homo alterius sectae. nam sicut patet in li. de alteriatione Athanasii contra Arrium, Athanasius & aemuli sui paganum in iudicem pro causa fidei elegerunt. ergo & ad hominem alterius sectae est licitum pro causa fidei appellare. haec sunt, quae mouent me contra praedicta. tu autem aperi, quomodo respondetur ad illa.
units.tr: DISCIP. Four objections occur to me against what has been said. First, some think that since Governor Festus knew this question did not belong to him, there was no need for Paul to appeal to Caesar on that account, because an appeal is either from a grievance or from a sentence. Paul did not appeal from a sentence of Festus, since Festus pronounced none, and not from a grievance, since Festus intended to inflict none; for if Paul had not appealed, Festus meant to dismiss him. Second, it seems that Paul ought not to have appealed to Caesar, since he knew that Caesar was an enemy of his faith and would pass sentence against Paul. Third, it appears that Paul lied in fact when he acknowledged Caesar as his judge, although, especially in a matter of faith, Caesar was neither his judge nor his superior. Fourth, it seems that a man may appeal to a man of another sect, as to one who can settle and define a question of faith. For in a matter of faith one may appeal in this way to someone who can be a judge in a matter of faith and who has the power to define what pertains to the truth of the orthodox faith; but a man of another sect can be such a person. For, as appears in the book of Athanasius against Arius concerning the alteration, Athanasius and his rivals chose a pagan as judge in a matter of faith. Therefore it is also lawful to appeal in a matter of faith to a man of another sect. These are the things that move me against what has been said. Do you explain how these are answered.

units.la: MAG. Ad primam obiectionem respondetur, quod Paulus appellauit a Festo ad Caesarem propter grauamina, quae timebat. timuit enim, quod quemadmodum Pilatus quamuis nullam causam mortis reputaret in Christo, tamen tradidit Iudaeis crucifigendum, ita Festus traderet Paulum Iudaeis accusantibus occidendum; quamuis putaret ipsum Paulum crimen dignum morte nullatenus commisisse. quod Paulus aperte insinuat dicens Festo: si vero nihil est eorum, de quibus hi accusant me, nemo potest me illis dare: Caesarem appello.
units.tr: MAGIST. To the first objection the answer is that Paul appealed from Festus to Caesar because of the grievances he feared. For he feared that, just as Pilate, although he found no cause of death in Christ, nevertheless handed him over to the Jews to be crucified, so Festus would hand Paul over to the Jews, who were accusing him, to be put to death, although Festus thought Paul himself had committed no crime deserving death. Paul openly hints at this when he says to Festus: "But if there is nothing in the things of which these men accuse me, no one can hand me over to them: I appeal to Caesar."

units.la: DISCIP. Vnde timuit Paulus, quod Festus volebat eum tradere Iudaeis.
units.tr: DISCIP. So Paul feared that Festus wanted to hand him over to the Jews.

units.la: MAGIST. Ex hoc, quod interrogauit Paulum, an vellet ascendere Hierosolymam, & iudicium subire apud ipsum de impositis, & ex hoc quod fauorabilis esset Iudæis accusantibus Paulum. ex hoc enim ipso, quod volebat Festus se intromittere de quæstione, quæ ad ipsum etiam secundum leges & consuetudines Romanorum minime pertinebat, ipsum suspectum habebat. & ideo appellauit: quamuis etiam aliud motiuum habuit appellandi, vt scil. per appellationem liberatus a persecutione Iudæorum in Iudæa, deduceretur Romam, vt ibi euangelium prædicaret iuxta præceptum Christi, vt apparet act. 23. demandatis & dicentis: constans esto Paule, sicut enim testificatus es de me in Hierusalem, sic oportet etiam te Romæ testificari. Ad secundam obiectionem dicitur, quod Paulus nesciuit Cæsarem manifestum inimicum doctrinæ suæ, quia nondum Cæsar persecutus fuerat Christianos. esto etiam, quod sciuisset eum inimicum, potuisset Cæsarem appellare: quia ex causa rationabili licet ad inimicum appellare. sicut etiam licet alicui ex causa se iudicio inimici submittere. Paulus ergo volens a Iudæis liberari, & Romam ad euangelium prædicandum adduci, appellauit. & licet sciuisset Cæsarem fidei inimicum, appellasset. Ad tertiam respondetur dupliciter. uno modo, quod Paulus erat inferior Cæsare, & Cæsar erat iudex suus ordinarius. Aliter dicitur, quod licet Cæsar non fuerit iudex ordinarius Pauli, tamen Paulus potuit se submittere iudicio Cæsaris, quemadmodum papa potest se submittere iudicio subditi sui. x.q.7.mo. & ideo Paulus appellando Cæsarem, submittit se iudicio Cæsaris, quod sibi licitum erat ex causa rationabili. DISCIP. Quomodo licuit Paulo se submittere iudicio Cæsaris infidelis, cum non liceat clericos se submittere iudicio secularium potestatum fidelium. MAGIST. Respondetur, quod quamuis hoc non liceat clericis in multis causis se submittere iudicio secularium potestatum, non tamen est ex lege diuina, nec ex ordinatione Christi, neque ex lege naturæ: sed ex iure positivo humano, ad quod ius Paulus minime tenebatur respondere: quia nec tunc extitit introductum, & ideo sibi licuit se iudicio Cæsaris submittere. quod fecit de facto, Cæsarem appellando. Ad quartam respondetur, quod dupliciter aliquis potest esse iudex in causa fidei. uno modo est aliquis ordinarius iudex in causa fidei habens ex officio potestatem quæstiones fidei terminandi. & ad talem iudicem licet pro causa fidei appellare. sed talis iudex in causa fidei non potest esse alterius sectæ. Alio modo potest esse alius iudex quasi arbiter electus. & hoc contingit dupliciter: quia dupliciter contingit committere in aliquem super causa fidei: vel scilicet promittendo, quod illud tenebitur, quod ipse secundum conscientiam suam reputauit firmiter esse tenendum: vel quod illud tenebitur, quod ipse iudicauit consonum esse fidei Christianæ. primo modo liceret compromittere in aliquem infidelem, si nulla humana constitutio obuiaret. Secundo modo licuit compromittere aliquando in aliquem infidelem: sicut Athanasius & hæretici sui æmuli in quendam paganum industrem & literatum promiserunt, promittendo scilicet quod illud tenerent, quod ipse iudicaret esse consonum fidei Christianæ. qui auditis allegationibus vtriusque partis pro Athanasio tulit sententiam, diffiniendo videlicet quod assertio Athanasii erat consona, & necessario sequebatur ex libris Christianorum, quos tam Athanasius quam sui aduersarii receperunt, quamuis ipse iudex ipsos nullo modo suscipieret. DISCIP. Videtur quod Athanasius compromittendo in paganum peccauit mortaliter, se videlicet obligando ad hæresim sustinendam, si ipse paganus dedisset sententiam, quod assertio hæreticorum erat consona fidei Christianæ. MAGIST. Respondetur quod Athanasius non peccauit: quia licet promitteret stare sententiæ pagani prædicti, non tamen promisit stare iniquæ sententiæ eius. & ideo non se obligauit ad hæresim sustinendam, si diffiniisset assertionem hæreticorum fuisse consonam fidei Christianæ. quia iniquum arbitrium nullatenus est seruandum, ext. de arbi. c. non sum. & c. ex posita. in tali enim promisso subintelligenda est talis ordinatio, licet non exprimatur, nisi arbiter fuerit arbitratus inique. DISCIP. Videtur quod Athanasius non debuit compromittere in paganum super quæstione fidei, cum secundum iura canonica etiam super rebus spiritualibus non liceat compromittere in laicum ext. de arbi. c. contingit. MAG. Respondetur, quod de rebus spiritualibus non potest compromitti in laicum ex ordinatione ecclesiæ, & non ex lege diuina. & Athanasius licite in paganum compromisit, quia tunc non erat prohibitum. DISC. Miror quod Athanasius voluit compromittere in paganum, cum pagani nequeant esse testes contra Christianos. MAG. Respondetur quod ecclesia, postquam habuit fauorem imperatorum & regum, multa statuit contra paganos, quæ nec ex lege diuina nec ex ordinatione Christi erant antea constituta. & ideo multa sunt modo illicita, quæ tunc licita erant. tunc nam licitum erat sub imperatore apostata militare. unde & multi sancti martyres & alii Christiani sub Iuliano apostata militabant, & sibi in his, quæ non erant contra legem diuinam, obedierunt sine peccato. nunc tamen nulli Christiano licet sub imperatore apostata militare. sic nunc esset illicitum de fide, compromittere in paganum: tempore autem Athanasii non erat illicitum. DISC. Quæ utilitas fuit, quod Athanasius compromisit in paganum. MAG. Respondetur quod multiplex fuit utilitas: quia catholici post sententiam pagani per Athanasio fide poterat liberius pdicare; & hæretici multorum amiserunt fauorem. unde a. hoc accidit, gesta illorum temporum te poterunt edocere. DISC. Videtur quod Athanasius compromittendo se in paganum, fidem catholicam magno periculo exponebat: quin debuit euitare. MAG. Respond. quod Athanasius periculo probabili se minime exponebat. sciebat n. paganum illum virum esse magnæ fidelitatis & constantiæ, ac eximiæ intelligetiæ contra ordinem assertionum, quarum vna sequitur ex alia; & et repugnantia assertionum, quarum vna alteri aduersabatur, sciebat aduertere. & ideo Athanasius sciens prædictum paganum virtutib. politicis & rationali scientia illustratum, ipsius iudicio modo prædicto absque periculo probabiliter committi; licet non absque omni periculo qualitercunque possibili. periculum autem qualitercunque possibile, nullus vitare tenetur, quia per hoc à bonis impediretur permaximis. esset enim similis illi; de quo dicit Sapi. Eccles. Iiast. primo, Qui observat ventum, non seminat; & qui considerat nubes, nunquam metet, &c.
units.tr: MAGIST. This is clear from the fact that Festus asked Paul whether he would go up to Jerusalem and submit to judgment there on the charges laid against him, and from the fact that Festus was inclined to favour the Jews who accused Paul. For from this very fact, that Festus wanted to meddle in a question which, even by the laws and customs of the Romans, did not belong to him, Paul held him under suspicion. And so he appealed. Yet he had also another motive for appealing: that, once freed by the appeal from the persecution of the Jews in Judaea, he might be taken to Rome and there preach the gospel according to Christ's command, as appears in Acts 23, where the Lord says to him: "Be of good courage, Paul, for as you have testified of me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify at Rome." To the second objection it is said that Paul did not know that Caesar was a manifest enemy of his teaching, since Caesar had not yet persecuted the Christians. Even granting that he had known Caesar to be an enemy, Paul could still have appealed to him, because for a reasonable cause it is lawful to appeal to an enemy, just as it is lawful for someone, for a reasonable cause, to submit himself to the judgment of an enemy. So Paul, wishing to be freed from the Jews and to be taken to Rome to preach the gospel, appealed; and although he knew Caesar to be an enemy of the faith, he appealed. To the third, the answer is twofold. In one way: Paul was inferior to Caesar, and Caesar was his ordinary judge. In another way: although Caesar was not Paul's ordinary judge, Paul could still submit himself to Caesar's judgment, just as the pope can submit himself to the judgment of his subject (x.q.7.mo.). And so Paul, by appealing to Caesar, submitted himself to Caesar's judgment, which was lawful for him for a reasonable cause. STUDENT. How was it lawful for Paul to submit himself to the judgment of an unbelieving Caesar, when it is not lawful for clergy to submit themselves to the judgment of believing secular powers? MAGIST. The answer is that although it is not lawful for clergy in many cases to submit themselves to the judgment of secular powers, this prohibition does not come from divine law, nor from the ordinance of Christ, nor from the law of nature, but from human positive law, which Paul was in no way bound to obey, since that law had not yet been introduced; and so it was lawful for him to submit himself to Caesar's judgment, which in fact he did by appealing to Caesar. To the fourth, the answer is that a person can be a judge in a matter of faith in two ways. In one way, someone is an ordinary judge in a matter of faith, having by his office the power to settle questions of faith; and it is lawful to appeal in a matter of faith to such a judge. But such a judge in a matter of faith cannot belong to another sect. In another way, someone can be a judge as a chosen arbiter. This happens in two ways, since a matter of faith can be committed to someone in two ways: either by promising that he will be held to whatever he himself, in his conscience, judges to be firmly to be held; or that one will be held to whatever he judges to be in agreement with the Christian faith. In the first way it would be lawful to submit the matter to an unbelieving arbiter, if no human constitution stood in the way. In the second way, it was at times lawful to submit the matter to an unbelieving arbiter, as Athanasius and his heretical rivals promised to a certain pagan, learned and skilled, namely that they would hold to whatever he judged to be in agreement with the Christian faith. He, having heard the arguments of both parties, pronounced sentence in favour of Athanasius, defining that Athanasius's assertion was consistent with, and necessarily followed from, the books of the Christians, which both Athanasius and his adversaries accepted, although the judge himself would in no way accept them. STUDENT. It seems that Athanasius, by submitting the matter to a pagan, sinned mortally, binding himself to uphold heresy, if the pagan had given the judgment that the assertion of the heretics was consistent with the Christian faith. MAGIST. The answer is that Athanasius did not sin, because although he promised to abide by the sentence of the said pagan, he did not promise to abide by an unjust sentence. And so he did not bind himself to uphold heresy, even if the arbiter had defined the assertion of the heretics to be consistent with the Christian faith; for an unjust judgment is in no way to be kept (ext. de arbi. c. non sum. & c. ex posita.). For in such a promise there must be understood this condition, though it is not expressed: that the arbiter has not judged unjustly. STUDENT. It seems that Athanasius ought not to have submitted a question of faith to a pagan, since according to the canon law it is not lawful to submit even spiritual matters to a layman (ext. de arbi. c. contingit.). MAG. The answer is that spiritual matters cannot be submitted to a layman by the ordinance of the Church, not by divine law; and Athanasius lawfully submitted the matter to a pagan, because at that time it was not forbidden. STUD. I am surprised that Athanasius wished to submit the matter to a pagan, since pagans cannot be witnesses against Christians. MAG. The answer is that the Church, after it gained the favour of emperors and kings, enacted many things against pagans which had not been established before, either by divine law or by the ordinance of Christ. And so many things are now unlawful which were then lawful. For then it was lawful to serve as a soldier under an apostate emperor; hence many holy martyrs and other Christians served as soldiers under the apostate Julian, and obeyed him without sin in those things which were not contrary to divine law. Now, however, it is unlawful for any Christian to serve as a soldier under an apostate emperor. So now it would be unlawful to submit a matter of faith to a pagan; but in the time of Athanasius it was not unlawful. STUD. What advantage was there in Athanasius submitting the matter to a pagan? MAG. The answer is that the advantages were many: after the pagan's sentence, the Catholics could preach the faith more freely through Athanasius, and the heretics lost the favour of many. From this, the deeds of those times can teach you more. STUD. It seems that by submitting himself to a pagan, Athanasius exposed the Catholic faith to great danger, which he ought to have avoided. MAG. The answer is that Athanasius did not expose himself to any probable danger. For he knew that this pagan was a man of great fidelity and constancy, and of outstanding understanding, and he knew how to notice the order of assertions, one following from another, and the contradiction of assertions, one opposing another. And so Athanasius, knowing that the said pagan was distinguished by political virtues and rational learning, judged that the matter could be probably committed to his judgment in the way described, without danger, although not without every danger that could possibly arise. But no one is bound to avoid a danger that could in any way possibly arise, for by that he would be hindered from the greatest good. For he would be like the man of whom Ecclesiastes says in Sirach (Sapi. Eccles. Iiast. primo): "He who watches the wind will not sow; and he who considers the clouds will never reap," etc.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Vbi queritur, quare potius dicatur in positione eorum, qui ponunt quod à Papa causa hereseos interiecta liceat seu expediat appellare; cuius assignantur tres rationes.
units.tr: Where it is asked why it is said, in the position of those who hold that it is lawful or expedient for a heretic to appeal from a judgment of the Pope, when an intervening cause of heresy is involved, that there are three reasons assigned for this.

units.la: DISCIP. Ad principalem responsionem, quam dedisti ad instantiam meam, quod non est appellandum à Papa pronunciante diffinitive legem Christianam esse falsam, nolo redire, nec eam magis discutere. Cupio ergo audire, quare assertores prædicti asserunt expedire, quod a tali sententia Papæ hæretici appelletur. MAG. Huius dicti inter alias rationes tres assignantur: Prima est: ut contra sententiam iniquam in causa fidei adhibeatur remedium; quod consueuit contra iniquas alias sententias adhiberi. Secunda est: ut cum manifesta solennitate iniqua sententia contra fidem prolata catholicam impugnetur. Tertia est: ut satisfaciat simplicibus & iuristis, qui forte non crederent aliquem posse licite impugnare sententiam iniquam contra fidem, & huius impugnantem esse a catholicis defendendam, nisi contra eadem appellaret.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Regarding the main answer you gave to my objection, namely that one must not appeal from a Pope who pronounces definitively that the Christian law is false, I do not wish to return to it or discuss it further. I would therefore like to hear why the proponents of that position assert that it is expedient for heretics to appeal from such a sentence of the Pope. TEACHER. Among other reasons, three are assigned for this statement. The first is that a remedy may be applied against an unjust sentence in a matter of faith, as is customarily applied against other unjust sentences. The second is that an unjust sentence pronounced against the faith is opposed by the Catholic side with clear and public solemnity. The third is that it satisfies simple folk and jurists, who might perhaps not believe that anyone may lawfully oppose an unjust sentence against the faith, and that one who opposes it must be defended by Catholics, unless he appeals against it.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: In quo inuestigatur, quare dicatur in conclusione, quod licet seu expedit, quia posita est c.18. vbi probatur quod non sit necessarium à tali sententia in qua appellare, & probantur quinque rationibus, ad quas respondetur infra capitulo 29.
units.tr: In which it is investigated why it is said in the conclusion that it is lawful or expedient, since it is laid down in chapter 18 that it is not necessary to appeal from such a sentence, and this is proved by five reasons, to which replies are given below in chapter 29.

units.la: DISCIP. Intelligo rationes, quas isti dicunt, quod nonnunquam expedita tali sententia appellare: sed nescio motiua eorum, quare dicunt quod non est absolute necessarium a tali sententia appellare. ideo qua ratione mouentur, enarra. MAG. Quod non sit absolute necessarium a tali sententia iniqua appellare, seruando scilicet formam & puncta, quæ in appellationibus secundum iura humana oportet obseruare, sic ostendunt: non magis est necessarium appellare a sententia prolata contra legem Dei & fidem Christianam; quam a sententia prolata contra canones & leges humanas. sed a sententia prolata contra canones & leges humanas non est necessarium appellare, teste Gregorio nono; qui, ut habetur extra de sent. & re iudic. c. 1. ait: sententia contra canones legesve prolata (licet non sit appellatione suspensa) non potest subsistere ipso iure. Vbi dicit Glos. sententia lata contra leges, i.e. ius constitutionis, ita quod sententia exprimatur, nulla est ipso iure, & citra appellationem rescinditur. ergo multo magis sententia lata contra fidem nulla est ipso iure absque omni appellatione. ergo non est necesse absolute appellare a sententia lata contra fidem catholicam. Secundo sic: a sententia, quæ non potest transire in rem iudicatam, nec valet firmitatem sententiæ obtinere; non est absolute necessarium appellare. hæc enim ratio assignatur in decretis. 2. quæst. 6. c. si quis. §. diffinitiuas; quare a pluribus sententiis non est necesse appellare, vbi sic habet. Si sententia lata fuerit contra res prius inductas, à quibus provocatum non est, sententiæ auctoritatem non obtinebit. & ideo appellare non est necesse. & ita si plures iudices dati fuerunt, & vnus tantum ex eis pronunciasse proponitur, non videtur appellandi necessitas fuisse, cum sententia firmitatem iuris non contineat. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod à sententia, quæ non potest transire in rem iudicatam, nec valet firmitatem sententiæ obtinere; non est necesse appellare. sed sententia lata contra fidem non potest transire in rem iudicatam, nec valet auctoritatem seu firmitatem sententiæ obtinere. ergo ab illa non est necessarium appellare. Tertio sic: In nulla causa, contra quam nulla præscriptio currere potest, est necesse appellare ab iniqua sententia. sed contra fidem nulla præscriptio currere potest, quin sententia lata contra fidem catholicam reuocetur, quandocunque veritas fuerit manifestata: quia omne, quod est fidei contrarium orthodoxæ, vanum & irritum est habendum. ergo à sententia lata contra fidem non est necesse appellare.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. I understand the reasons which these men give for saying that it is sometimes expedient to appeal from such a sentence. But I do not know their grounds for saying that it is not absolutely necessary to appeal from such a sentence. So explain by what reasoning they are moved. MAGISTER. That it is not absolutely necessary to appeal from such an unjust sentence, provided one observes the form and the points which must be observed in appeals under human law, they show as follows. (1) It is no more necessary to appeal from a sentence passed against the law of God and the Christian faith than from a sentence passed against the canons and human laws. But it is not necessary to appeal from a sentence passed against the canons and human laws, as Gregory IX witnesses, who says, as is found in Extra, De sententia et re iudicata, c. 1: a sentence passed against the canons or the laws (although it is not suspended by appeal) cannot subsist by law itself. Where the Gloss says: a sentence passed against the laws, that is, against the right of the constitution, so that the sentence is expressed, is void by law itself and is rescinded without appeal. Therefore much more a sentence passed against the faith is void by law itself, without any appeal. Therefore it is not absolutely necessary to appeal from a sentence passed against the Catholic faith. (2) From a sentence which cannot pass into a judgment that has the force of res iudicata, and cannot obtain the validity of a sentence, it is not absolutely necessary to appeal. This reason is given in the Decretum, 2 q. 6, c. Si quis, §. Diffinitivas, which is why it is not necessary to appeal from several sentences. There it reads: If a sentence is passed against matters previously introduced, from which no appeal has been made, it will not obtain the authority of a sentence. And so, if several judges were appointed and only one of them is said to have pronounced, there seems to have been no need to appeal, since the sentence does not contain the force of law. From these words it is gathered that from a sentence which cannot pass into res iudicata and cannot obtain the force of a sentence, it is not necessary to appeal. But a sentence passed against the faith cannot pass into res iudicata, nor can it obtain the authority or force of a sentence. Therefore there is no need to appeal from it. (3) In no cause against which no prescription can run is it necessary to appeal from an unjust sentence. But against the faith no prescription can run, so that a sentence passed against the Catholic faith is not revoked whenever the truth has been made manifest, because whatever is contrary to orthodox faith must be held vain and void. Therefore it is not necessary to appeal from a sentence passed against the faith.

units.la: Quarto sic: Iniqua sententia lata contra fidem non potest esse magis priuilegiata, quam sententia lata contra matrimonium. sed sententia lata contra matrimonium, tale priuilegium obtinet, ut ab ea appellare non sit necesse: quia à sententia lata contra matrimonium, licet non sit appellatum, ipsa tamen reuocanda est, quandocunque ostensum fuerit fuisse iniquam, secundum quod colligitur manifeste ex canonibus sacris, extra de sent. & re iudic. c. lator. & c. consanguinei, & quamplurimis aliis. hic Glos. c. prædicto lator, notat dicens: contra matrimonium non currit præscriptio. 3. q. 3. quando patri; etiam si ab illa sententia non fuerit appellatum, quia sententia lata contra matrimonium non transit in rem iudicatam, quin reuocetur quandocunque fuerit error deprehensus. ergo multo magis à sententia lata contra catholicam fidem non est necesse appellare.
units.tr: (4) An unjust sentence passed against the faith cannot be more privileged than a sentence passed against marriage. But a sentence passed against marriage enjoys such a privilege that it is not necessary to appeal from it, because a sentence passed against marriage must be revoked whenever it is shown to have been unjust, even if no appeal has been made from it. This is plainly gathered from the sacred canons, Extra, De sententia et re iudicata, c. Lator, and c. Consanguinei, and very many others. Here the Gloss on the aforesaid c. Lator notes, saying: prescription does not run against marriage, 3 q. 3, Quando patri; even if no appeal was made from that sentence, because a sentence passed against marriage does not pass into res iudicata but is revoked whenever an error is detected. Therefore much more it is not necessary to appeal from a sentence passed against the Catholic faith.

units.la: Quinto sic: causa fidei est magis fauorabilis: & per consequens priuilegiis debet gaudere maioribus. bus, quam causæ matrimonii & nonnullæ ciuiles. sed nonnullæ causæ ciuiles tali priuilegio gaudent; quod non est necesse ab iniqua sententia appellare. ergo multo magis causa fidei tali debet gaudere priuilegio, vt ab iniqua sententia contra fidem non sit appellare necesse.
units.tr: (5) A cause of faith is more favourable and consequently ought to enjoy greater privileges than the causes of marriage and some civil causes. But some civil causes enjoy such a privilege that it is not necessary to appeal from an unjust sentence in them. Therefore much more a cause of faith ought to enjoy such a privilege, that it is not necessary to appeal from an unjust sentence against the faith.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Inquirit circa supradicta in modo dicendi de appellatione, scil. quare modificatur conclusio, quod non sit necesse appellare secundum formam iuris. vbi etiam distinguitur de appellatione lata contra fidem. ad formam vero quaestionis respondetur infra capitulo 27. huius.
units.tr: He inquires about the foregoing remarks on appeal, namely why the conclusion is qualified, that it is not necessary to appeal according to the form of law. Here too a distinction is drawn concerning an appeal against what is pronounced against the faith. The answer to the question's form is given below, in chapter 27 of this book.

units.la: DISCIP. Rationes aduerto, quare dicitur, quod non est absolute necessarium appellare à sententia lata contra fidem. Sed ignoro, quare ista assertio taliter modificatur; non est necesse appellare seruando formam & puncta, quæ in appellationibus secundum iura humana oportet seruare. vnde rationem istius modificationis assigna. MAG. Ad intelligendum illud, quod quaeris, distinguitur, quia appellatio lata contra fidem quadrupliciter accipitur. Primo accipitur pro libello continente formam appellationis, quæ communiter consueuit in aliis appellationibus obseruari, notante videlicet personam appellantem, & contra quam appellat, & causam pro qua appellatur, vel sententiam à qua appellatur, & tempus quo appellatur, etiam alias circumstantias, quæ ad appellationis formam debitam requiruntur.
units.tr: STUDENT. I take note of the reasons why it is said that it is not absolutely necessary to appeal from a sentence pronounced against the faith. But I do not know why this assertion is qualified in this way: that it is not necessary to appeal while keeping the form and the points that must be observed in appeals under human law. So give the reason for this qualification. TEACHER. To understand what you ask, a distinction is needed, because an appeal against the faith is taken in four ways. First, it is taken for the written document containing the form of appeal, which is usually observed in other appeals: that is, naming the appellant, the party against whom he appeals, the cause for which he appeals or the sentence from which he appeals, the time at which he appeals, and the other circumstances required for a proper form of appeal.

units.la: Secundo modo accipitur appellatio pro voce, qua quis absolute in præsentia iudicis dicit, appello. vnde Gloss. 2. quæst. 6. cap. potest appellatione, §. formam appellationis, dicens: si coram iudice appellat, sufficit si dicat, appello.
units.tr: Second, an appeal is taken for the spoken word by which someone, in the presence of the judge, simply says, "I appeal." Hence the Gloss on 2. q. 6, chapter potest, in the section formam appellationis, says: if he appeals before the judge, it is enough that he say, "I appeal."

units.la: Tertio modo accipitur appellatio pro impugnatione iniquæ sententiæ latæ contra fidem. & sic quicunque impugnaret sententiam Papæ latam contra fidem, intelligitur appellare ab eodem, licet non diceretur, appello. Quarto modo potest dici appellatio à sententia Papæ lata contra fidem, omne factum, quo patiens se ostendit Papæ sententiam reprobare, detestari, seu horrere. & illo modo clerici Romani, qui se à communione Anastasii, etiam de quo habetur dist. 19. Anastasius, abegerunt, dici poterant appellatores, quia facto ipsum tanquam haereticum reprobauerunt.
units.tr: Third, an appeal is taken for the challenging of an unjust sentence pronounced against the faith. In this sense, anyone who impugns a sentence of the Pope pronounced against the faith is understood to appeal from it, even if he does not say, "I appeal." Fourth, an appeal from a sentence of the Pope pronounced against the faith can mean any act by which the person affected shows that he rejects, detests, or abhors the Pope's sentence. In this sense the Roman clergy, who withdrew from communion with Anastasius (of whom we read in dist. 19, Anastasius), could be called appellants, because by their deed they rejected him as a heretic.

units.la: DISCIP. Duo prima membra istius distinctionis intelligo. Sed alia duo non videntur connexienter assignari: quia secundum tertium membrum omnis impugnans verbo alicuius iudicis sententiam diceretur appellare ab eodem, quod nullam verisimilitudinem habet. Secundum quartum vero membrum inobediens sententiæ iudicis absque omni verbo appellandi diceretur appellans. MAG. Ad hoc soluendum dicitur esse notandum: quod secundum iura dupliciter appellare contingit; scilicet verbo & facto. Quod verbo appellare contingit, tu concedis. quod etiam facto valeat quis appellare, asserit Innoc. tertius manifeste, qui, vt habetur extra, de appell. c. dilecti, ait: cum autem plus sit ad sedem apostolicam facto prouocare, quam verbo, &c. vbi dicit Gloss. plus est factis demonstrare, quam verbis dicere. & Gloss. 5. q. 3. c. æstimant, ait: ipso facto appellam. ex quibus verbis patet, quod quartum membrum est congrue assignatum, quia scil. facto contingit appellare à sententia Papæ lata contra fidem. non autem aliter contingit appellare à sententia Papæ lata contra fidem, nisi facto ostendendo, quod talis sententia est tanquam haeretica computanda. ergo ille quartus modus appellandi congrue assignatur. ex isto modo patet etiam, quod tertius modus etiam congrue assignatur. quia vel plus vel non minus est manifeste & constanter asserere viua voce vel scripto sententiam Papæ esse haereticam. sed, sicut ostensum est, qui facto insinuat sententiam esse haereticam, facto intelligitur appellare. ergo & qui verbo vel scripto sententiam Papæ tanquam haereticam constanter impugnat, intelligitur appellare, licet verba non scribat vel proferat appellandi. DISCIP. Dic quomodo ad ista inconuenientia (quæ intuli) respondetur.
units.tr: STUDENT. I understand the first two parts of this distinction. But the other two do not seem to be properly connected. For according to the third part, every person who impugns the sentence of any judge by word would be said to appeal from that judge, which has no plausibility at all. And according to the fourth part, a person who disobeys a judge's sentence without any word of appealing would be called an appellant. TEACHER. To answer this, it must be noted that under law there are two ways of appealing, namely by word and by deed. That one may appeal by word you concede. That one may also appeal by deed is clearly asserted by Innocent III, who, as we find outside the decretals, de appellationibus, chapter dilecti, says: "Since it is more to appeal to the apostolic see by deed than by word," and so on. There the Gloss says that it is more to show by deeds than to say by words. And the Gloss on 5. q. 3, chapter aestimant, says: "I appeal by the very deed." From these words it is evident that the fourth part is properly assigned, because one can appeal by deed from a sentence of the Pope pronounced against the faith, and one cannot appeal from such a sentence in any other way than by deed, showing that such a sentence must be regarded as heretical. Therefore that fourth way of appealing is properly assigned. From this way it is also clear that the third way is properly assigned too. For it is either more or not less to assert clearly and constantly, by living voice or in writing, that the Pope's sentence is heretical. But, as has been shown, whoever by deed signifies that a sentence is heretical is understood to appeal by deed. Therefore whoever constantly impugns, by word or in writing, a Pope's sentence as heretical is also understood to appeal, even if he does not write or utter the words of appeal. STUDENT. Tell me how these absurdities which I have raised are answered.

units.la: MAG. Vt responsiones ad illa percipias, duo dicuntur esse notanda. Primum est, quod sicut cuilibet Christiano interest sententiam Papæ latam contra fidem catholicam detestari, impugnare, reprobare & horrere: ita & cuilibet Christiano licet (si voluerit) ab iniqua sententia Papæ contra fidem catholicam lata appellare, primo & secundo modo accepta appellatione: quia ab iniqua sententia Papæ quilibet potest (cuius interest) appellare. Secundo dicitur esse notandum, quod quia papale officium dicitur esse supremum in ecclesia, nec est aliquis qui ex officio sit vero Papa superior in spiritualibus, ideo quando Papa profert sententiam contra fidem, subtilitates iuris, quæ contra prælatos inferiores proferentes sententiam contra fidem seruant, non sunt stricte seruandæ: nec et litera legum ciuilium & canonicorum in hoc casu est omnino seruanda. sed oportet ad legem diuinam & rationem naturalem, ac intentionem legislatoris, & ad legem q. instituisset (si legem specialem de Papa proferente sententiam contra fidem constituisset) recurrere. Propter hoc respondendum ad primum inconueniens: quia non omnis impugnans verbo alicuius iudicis sententiam dicere debet appello: tum quia non cuiuslibet interest appellare à sententia iudicis vel etiam reprobare: quia de modo appellandi à sententiis iudicis inferioris, sunt positæ leges expressæ. & ideo qui in talibus non seruat huiusmodi leges, non intelligitur appellare: secus est de omni Christiano impugnante absque verbo appellandi sententiam Papæ contra fidem. tum quia cuilibet Christiano licet nolicet (si voluerit) à tali sententia appellare, quia talis sententia est praeiudicialis omni catholico & ideo sua interest sententiam talem impugnare & per consequens sibi licet, si voluerit, à tali sententia appellare, exprimendo vocabulum appellandi. tum quia de modo appellandi à sententia Papae contra fidem non sunt leges speciales institutae: imo secundum leges à tali sententia, cum in rem iudicatam transire non valeat, non est necesse appellare. & ideo quicunque sententiam Papae contra fidem latam verbo vel scripto constanter impugnat absque verbo appellandi, intelligitur appellare tertio modo: & tantum valet secundum rem, ac si verbum appellandi proferret. Per praedicta etiam patet ad secundum inconveniens, quod intulisti, quia inobediens sententiae iudicis inferioris verbum appellandi nequaquam omittens non intelligitur facto appellare, quia cautum est in iure, quod in hoc casu ad hoc, quod aliquis intelligitur appellans, oportet quod infra certum tempus viva voce, vel scripto cum debitis circumstantiis vocem appellationis adhibeat. sed de modo appellandi à sententia haereticali Papae, nihil est in iure statutum. Et ideo eo ipso, quod quis facto ostendit se reprobare sententiam Papae tanquam haereticam, facto intelligitur appellare.
units.tr: TEACHER. So that you may grasp the answers to them, two points are to be noted. The first is this: just as it is in the interest of every Christian to detest, impugn, reject, and abhor a sentence of the Pope pronounced against the Catholic faith, so every Christian is also permitted, if he wishes, to appeal from an unjust sentence of the Pope pronounced against the Catholic faith, taking appeal in the first and second senses; for any person who has an interest may appeal from an unjust sentence of the Pope. The second point to be noted is that, since the papal office is said to be supreme in the Church, and there is no one who by office is truly superior to the Pope in spiritual matters, therefore when the Pope pronounces a sentence against the faith, the legal subtleties that are observed against inferior prelates who pronounce sentences against the faith are not to be strictly observed; nor is the letter of civil and canon laws to be wholly observed in this case. Rather, one must have recourse to the divine law, to natural reason, to the intention of the lawgiver, and to the law which he would have enacted, had he set down a special law concerning a Pope who pronounces a sentence against the faith. For this reason the first absurdity should be answered thus: not every person who impugns by word the sentence of some judge must say, "I appeal." This is so, first, because it is not in everyone's interest to appeal from a judge's sentence, or even to reject it; for express laws have been laid down concerning the manner of appealing from the sentences of inferior judges, and therefore a person who does not observe such laws in these matters is not understood to appeal. It is otherwise with every Christian who impugns, without the word of appeal, the Pope's sentence against the faith. Second, every Christian is permitted, whether he wills it or not, to appeal from such a sentence if he wishes, since such a sentence is prejudicial to every Catholic, and therefore it is in his interest to impugn such a sentence, and consequently he may, if he wishes, appeal from such a sentence by expressing the word of appealing. Third, because no special laws have been instituted concerning the manner of appealing from a Pope's sentence against the faith, indeed under the laws, since such a sentence cannot pass into a thing adjudged, it is not necessary to appeal. Therefore whoever constantly impugns by word or in writing a Pope's sentence pronounced against the faith, without the word of appealing, is understood to appeal in the third way, and this has the same force in substance as if he had uttered the word of appealing. From what has been said it is also clear how to answer the second absurdity you raised: a person who disobeys the sentence of an inferior judge, but does not omit the word of appealing, is not understood to appeal by deed. For the law has provided that, in that case, for someone to be understood as appealing, he must, within a certain time, employ the word of appeal, by living voice or in writing, with the due circumstances. But nothing has been laid down by law concerning the manner of appealing from a heretical sentence of the Pope. Therefore, by the very fact that someone shows by deed that he rejects the Pope's sentence as heretical, he is understood to appeal by deed.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: Assignat duas rationes, quare non sit assignatum aliquod speciale statutum in iure de modo appellandi à sententia Papae haereticali, & assignantur duae causae.
units.tr: He gives two reasons why no special statute in law has been laid down on the manner of appealing from a heretical sentence of the Pope, and the reasons are set out.

units.la: DISCIP. Quare non est aliquod speciale statutum in iure de modo appellandi à sententia Papae haereticali. MAG. Huius duae assignantur causae. Prima est: quia non est necesse à tali sententia appellare, primo modo vel secundo accepto vocabulo appellationis, eo quod talis sententia in rem iudicatam transire non potest. Secunda, quia leges fiunt ex his, quae saepius accidunt, raro autem accidit Papam ferre sententiam haereticalem. ideo non est necesse de hoc legem statuere.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Why is there no special statute in law about the manner of appealing from a heretical sentence of the Pope? MASTER. Two reasons are given for this. The first is that there is no need to appeal from such a sentence, by the first or second manner of taking the word "appeal", because such a sentence cannot pass into a judgment that has become final. The second is that laws are made from those things which happen more often, whereas it rarely happens that the Pope pronounces a heretical sentence. Therefore there is no need to make a law about this.

units.la: DISCIP. Leges generaliter factae sunt de modo appellandi. quare ergo non sunt illae leges seruandae, cum quis vult à sententia Papae haretici appellare.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Laws have been made in general about the manner of appealing. Why, then, are those laws not to be observed when someone wishes to appeal from the sentence of a heretical Pope?

units.la: MAG. Ad hoc respondsum est prius. dictum enim est, quod quia verus Papa non habet superiorem in terris: ideo cum sententiat contra fidem, non est necesse regulas generales de appellationibus datas seruare. hoc enim posset in periculum fidei redundare.
units.tr: MASTER. To this the answer has been given before. For it has been said that, since the true Pope has no superior on earth, therefore when he pronounces sentence against the faith, it is not necessary to observe the general rules on appeals given in law. For this could tend to the peril of the faith.

units.la: DISCIP. Videtur quod regulae datae de appellationibus strictius sunt seruandae, cum quis vult à Papa appellare, quam si vult ab alio appellare. quia maior reverentia adhibenda est Papae, quam aliis inferioribus. ergo regulae quae possunt derogari honori Papae, strictissime sunt seruandae, eo quod nullus debet gaudere maiori priuilegio, quam Papa.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. It seems that the rules laid down on appeals are to be observed more strictly when someone wishes to appeal from the Pope than when he wishes to appeal from another. For greater reverence is to be shown to the Pope than to other inferiors. Therefore the rules which can detract from the honour of the Pope are to be observed most strictly, since no one ought to enjoy a greater privilege than the Pope.

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quod leges canonicae & ciuiles secundum diuersitatem causarum, personarum, temporum & periculi quod imminet, ac etiam circa alias circumstantias sunt magis strictae vel minus strictae seruandae, vel penitus non seruandae. & ideo quia Papa ferens sententiam contra fidem, grauius peccat quam alius: quia peccatum ex dignitate augetur. facilius est etiam habere iusticiam de inferiori, quam de Papa, si tulerit contra fidem sententiam. maius etiam periculum imminet omnibus Christianis ex sententia haereticali Papae. ideo si quis voluerit in communi forma à tali Papae sententia appellare in fauorem fidei, cui magis fauendum est quam Papae, minus artandus est ad formam appellationis, quam si à sententia iudicis inferioris duxerit appellandum. unde in hoc casu in fauorem fidei, quantum ad multa, minor reuerentia est exhibenda Papae, & minori priuilegio debet gaudere. quemadmodum si accusetur, minori priuilegio gaudet, quam nonnulli alii praesules, quia, ut habetur. 2. quaest. 4. c. praesul, praesul nonnisi. 72. testibus debet damnari. Papa autem tali priuilegio minime gaudet, teste Glossa ibidem, quaeait: nunquid contra Papam duplicabuntur testes: quinimo duo sufficiunt, & in hoc est deteriores conditionis: quia ipse sine comparatione aliorum creatus est. & ideo sine spe veniae damnandus est, ut diabolus. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod nonnunquam Papa propter crimen ipsius minori priuilegio gaudet, quam inseriores Episcopi. quod praecipue seruandum est, quando ex crimine Papae maius periculum imminet Christianitati: quod accidit, quando Papa contra fidem profert sententiam.
units.tr: MASTER. It is answered that the canon and civil laws are to be observed more strictly or less strictly, or not at all, according to the diversity of causes, persons, times and the danger that threatens, and also according to other circumstances. And so, because a Pope who pronounces sentence against the faith sins more gravely than another (since sin is increased by dignity), and because it is also easier to obtain justice from an inferior than from the Pope if he has pronounced a sentence against the faith, and because a greater danger threatens all Christians from a heretical sentence of the Pope, therefore, if anyone wishes to appeal in the common form from such a sentence of the Pope in favour of the faith, which must be favoured more than the Pope, he is to be bound less strictly to the form of appeal than if he had to appeal from the sentence of an inferior judge. Hence in this case, in favour of the faith, in many respects less reverence is to be shown to the Pope, and he ought to enjoy a lesser privilege. Just as, if he is accused, he enjoys a lesser privilege than some other prelates, because, as is held in 2. quaest. 4, c. "Praesul" and "Praesul nonnisi", he ought to be condemned by 72 witnesses. But the Pope does not enjoy that privilege at all, as the Gloss there witnesses, which asks: will the witnesses be doubled against the Pope? Rather, two suffice, and in this he is in a worse condition, because he was created without comparison with others, and therefore he is to be condemned without hope of pardon, like the devil. From these words it is plain that sometimes the Pope, on account of his crime, enjoys a lesser privilege than the inferior bishops. This is especially to be observed when a greater danger threatens Christendom from the Pope's crime, which happens when the Pope pronounces a sentence against the faith.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVII.

units.la: In quo ponitur ad longum responsio ad formam quaesiti in 25. capitulo positi.
units.tr: In which a lengthy response is given to the form of the question posed in chapter 25.

units.la: DISCIP. Applica supradicta ad interrogationem meam, quare supra dicitur, quod à sententia Papae haretici non est necesse appellare, seruando formam & puncta, &c. MAG. Ad interrogationem praepositam taliter applicantur: quod videlicet non est necesse appellare à tali sententia Papae, primo modo & secundo modo accepto vocabulo appellationis. & propter hoc in assertione praedicta est addita modificatio memorata. necesse tamen est appellare, tertio modo vel quarto modo, à sententia Papæ hæretica, quando scitur esse hæretica: quia talis sententia est impugnanda, & qui scit eam esse hæreticam, facto debet ostendere, quod reputat eam esse hæreticam.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Apply what has been said above to my question: why was it said above that one need not appeal from the sentence of a heretical Pope, provided the form and points are observed, etc.? MASTER. The application to the question put forward is as follows: namely, that one need not appeal from such a sentence of the Pope in the first and second senses of the word "appeal" as accepted. For this reason the aforementioned qualification was added to the said assertion. Yet one must appeal, in the third or fourth sense, from a heretical sentence of the Pope when it is known to be heretical, because such a sentence must be opposed, and whoever knows it to be heretical must, by the very act, show that he judges it to be heretical.

units.la: Discip. Nunquid solus ille, contra quem lata est talis sententia, tenetur appellare taliter ab eodem. Magist. Respondetur, quod non solus ille, sed quilibet catholicus sciens talem sententiam esse hæreticam, appellare debet: quia aliter esset fautor Papæ hæretici. Discip. Nunquid tenetur infra certum tempus taliter appellare, ne sententia transeat in rem iudicatam? Mag. Respondetur, quod non est tempus sibi determinatum: quia non oportet taliter appellare, ne sententia transeat in rem iudicatam, sed ne appellans favere hæretico videatur.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Is only the man against whom such a sentence is pronounced bound to appeal from it in this way? MASTER. The answer is that not only he, but every Catholic who knows such a sentence to be heretical ought to appeal, for otherwise he would be a supporter of a heretical Pope. DISCIPLE. Is he bound to appeal in this way within a certain time, lest the sentence pass into a judgment that cannot be reversed? MASTER. The answer is that no time is fixed for him, because one ought to appeal not to prevent the sentence from passing into a judgment that cannot be reversed, but to prevent the appellant from seeming to favour the heretic.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: In quo datur secunda responsio ad instantiam factam in cap. 20. contra argumenta facta in cap. 19. ubi notatur quod necessaria sit appellatio à sententia Papæ hæretici sub forma communi, etiam infra tempus à iure statutum, quod probatur tribus rationibus, ad quas respondetur cap. 30. huius.
units.tr: In which a second answer is given to the objection raised in chapter 20 against the arguments put forward in chapter 19. Here it is noted that appeal from a sentence of a heretical Pope must be made in the common form, even within the time fixed by law. This is proved by three reasons, to which an answer is given in chapter 30 of this work.

units.la: Discip. Ex his cogito, quod talis modus appellandi tractari habet, cum de fautoribus hæreticorum exquisite inquiretur. ideo de hoc supersedeas. Et indica, quomodo aliter respondetur ad instantiam, qua probaui, quod à Papa pronunciante fidem catholicam esse falsam, non est aliquatenus appellandum. dixisti enim, quod ad illam instantiam duplex datur responsio. cum ergo tractauerimus vnam, dic aliam. Mag. Dicitur quod à tali sententia necesse est appellare in forma communi appellandi insuper & infra tempus statutum à iure. quia aliter non audiretur quis contra sententiam Papæ, si ipsam postea satageret impugnare. Pro hac autem assertione potest taliter allegari, qui à sententia iniqua infra tempus statutum à iure negligit appellare, per interpretationem iuris latæ sententiæ parere videtur, extra de sen. & re iudic. qui ad consultationem, qui autem sententiæ paret, impugnare ipsam non potest, quia quod semel approbatum est, postea reprobari non potest, dist. 4. in istis, & 8. quæst. 2. dilectissimi. ergo qui non appellat infra tempus assignatum à iure, postea non auditur. & ita appellare est necesse, si quis unquam voluerit sententiam Papæ hæreticam impugnare.
units.tr: Student. From these things I gather that this manner of appealing ought to be treated when the supporters of heretics are examined exactly; so you may set that aside for now. And show me how else one answers the objection by which I proved that when the Pope declares the Catholic faith to be false, one must not appeal from it in any way. For you said that a twofold answer is given to that objection. Since we have dealt with one, tell me the other. Master. It is said that from such a sentence one must appeal in the common form of appealing, and moreover within the time fixed by law. For otherwise no one would be heard against the Pope's sentence if he tried to impugn it afterwards. In support of this assertion the following may be alleged: whoever neglects to appeal within the time fixed by law from an unjust sentence seems, by the interpretation of law, to have obeyed the sentence passed, Extra, On Sentence and Res Judicata, "who to consultation"; but whoever obeys a sentence cannot impugn it, because what has once been approved cannot afterwards be reproved, Dist. 4, "in istis," and C. 8, q. 2, "dilectissimi." Therefore whoever does not appeal within the time assigned by law is afterwards not heard. And so one must appeal, if anyone ever wishes to impugn a heretical sentence of the Pope.

units.la: Secundo sic: appellationis remedium est ad præsidium innocentiæ institutum, extra de appellationibus, cum speciali. ergo quanto magis innocentia impugnat, tanto magis est necessarium remedium appellationis. sed quando Papa pronunciat diffinitiue contra fidem catholicam, ipsam esse falsam, maxime innocentia impugnatur. ergo tunc maxime necessarium est ad appellationis remedium convolare: & ita à tali sententia est appellare necesse.
units.tr: Secondly, thus: the remedy of appeal was instituted as a protection of innocence, Extra, On Appeals, "cum speciali." Therefore the more innocence is attacked, the more necessary the remedy of appeal becomes. But when the Pope pronounces definitively against the Catholic faith, declaring it to be false, innocence is attacked most of all. Therefore it is then most necessary to fly to the remedy of appeal, and so from such a sentence one must necessarily appeal.

units.la: Tertio sic: unoquoque utendum est ad usum, ad quem noscitur institutum. appellatio autem est instituta, ut oppressi releuentur, 21. quæst. 6. cum omnis oppressus, & c. ideo: & multis aliis canonibus sacris hoc idem habetur. ergo appellatione est utendum ad releuandum oppressos. sed catholici maxime opprimuntur, si Papa sententiat fidem catholicam sive Christianam esse falsam. ergo in hoc casu est præcipue utendum appellationis remedio. ergo à tali sententia est necessarium appellare, &c.
units.tr: Thirdly, thus: everything must be used for the purpose for which it is known to have been instituted. Appeal, however, was instituted so that the oppressed might be relieved, C. 21, q. 6, "cum omnis oppressus," etc.; and the same is held in many other sacred canons. Therefore appeal must be used to relieve the oppressed. But Catholics are especially oppressed if the Pope pronounces the Catholic or Christian faith to be false. Therefore in this case above all the remedy of appeal must be used. Therefore from such a sentence it is necessary to appeal, etc.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXIX.

units.la: In quo ponuntur responsiones ad rationes capituli 24. probantes quod non sit necessarium à sententia iniqua Papa hæretici appellare.
units.tr: In which are set out the replies to the arguments of chapter 24, which prove that it is not necessary to appeal from the unjust sentence of a heretical Pope.

units.la: Discip. Tam rationes, quibus ostenditur, quod non est necesse appellare à sententia Papæ diffinitiue pronunciantis, fidem Christianam esse falsam, quam rationes pro assertione contraria allegatæ apparentes mihi videntur. ideo peto, ut referas, quomodo respondetur ad utrasque. primo tamen respondeas ad rationes probantes, quod non est necesse appellare. Magist. Ad primam istarum dicitur, quod non est necesse appellare à sententia lata contra leges & canones, quia hoc cautum est in iure. non est autem cautum in iure, quod non est necesse appellare à sententia Papæ pronunciantis legem Christi esse falsam.
