And so I understand the aforesaid assertion better than before. Still I should like to know whether the assertion, often repeated, is explained more fully than before.

units.la: MAGIST. Videtur quod vltimate sic valeat explicari: quilibet catholicus & fidelis impugnantes zelo fidei orthodoxæ Papam haereticum, cum euidenter indiget, & necessario vel periculum immineret fidei Christianæ, tenetur necessitate salutis modo sibi possibili & congruenti defendere, si alius non apparet in promptu, quem probabiliter credat velle vel posse taliter impugnantes Papam haereticum defensare.
units.tr: MASTER. It seems that it may ultimately be explained thus: every Catholic and faithful person, who out of zeal for the orthodox faith attacks a heretical Pope, when there is manifest need and when danger threatens the Christian faith, is bound of necessity to salvation to defend such a person in a manner that is possible and fitting for him, if no other is readily at hand whom he reasonably believes willing or able to defend those who thus attack a heretical Pope.

units.la: DISCIP. Quid si quis credat tales ex rancore & odio, aut aliis ex mala radice Papam haereticum mala intentione impugnare, nunquid tenetur eos praedicto modo defendere? MAG. nullus debet praesumere talem Papam haereticum mala intentione impugnare, nisi sibi constet legitimo & non ex leui iudicio. Sitamen constaret sibi, quod ex mala intentione hæreticus Papam impugnarent, eos deberet defendere, ne propter impugnationem prauitatis hæreticæ paterentur: maxime si ex omissione defensionis ipsorum periculum fidei videtur imminere. quia in hoc magis veritas defenditur catholica, quam prauitatem hæreticam impugnantes. ad veritatem autem catholicam defendendam vniuersi catholici sunt astricti.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. What if someone believes that such men attack a heretical Pope out of spite and hatred, or from some other bad root, with an evil intention? Is he nonetheless bound to defend them in the aforesaid way? MASTER. No one ought to presume that a Pope is attacked as a heretic with an evil intention unless it is clear to him on lawful grounds and not on a light judgment. But if it were clear to him that heretics were attacking the Pope from an evil intention, he ought to defend them, lest they suffer for attacking the perversity of heresy; especially if danger to the faith seems to threaten from the omission of their defence. For in this way the Catholic truth is defended more than the heretical perversity is opposed by those who attack it. And all Catholics are bound to defend the Catholic truth.

units.la: DISCIP. De quo periculo fidei imminenti intelligitur dicta assertio, cum dicit, quod taliter impugnantes Papam hæreticum sunt tuendi, quando periculum fidei imminet.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. To what imminent danger to the faith does the aforesaid assertion refer, when it says that those who attack a heretical Pope in this way are to be protected when danger to the faith threatens?

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur quod intelligitur de periculo fidei in vna regione vel regno: imo etiam vni soli homini imminenti, quia si aliquis probabiliter æstimaret, quod vnum regnum vel regio aut ciuitas, vel etiam vnus homo auerteretur à fide, vel fauéret hæreticæ prauitati, nisi taliter impugnantes Papam hæreticum defenderet, ipsos non tuendo (si posset) mortaliter peccaret.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer is that it refers to danger to the faith in one region or kingdom, or even to danger threatening only one man; for if someone reasonably judged that one kingdom, region or city, or even one man, would be turned away from the faith or would favour heretical perversity unless he defended those who attack a heretical Pope in this way, then he would sin mortally if he did not protect them (if he were able to).

units.la: CAP. XXXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXXI.

units.la: In quo assignantur tres aliæ rationes idem quod prius probantes: & sic in numero habentur rationes 14. probantes quod impugnantes Papam hæreticum, etiam si non appellent, catholici tales defendere tenentur.
units.tr: In which three further reasons are given proving the same thing as before. In this way there are fourteen reasons proving that Catholics are bound to defend those who attack a heretical Pope, even if they do not appeal to him.

units.la: DISCIP. Assertionem prædictam (vt æstimo) clare intelligo: quamuis non sit mihi demonstratum, quod contineat veritatem, pro qua adhuc allegare conaris, vt sciam fundamenta, quibus frater Michael & sui sequaces probare niituntur, quod sunt à catholicis contra summum Pontificem defendendi. MAG. Assertio memorata vndecimo tali ratione videtur posse probari. Illud, sine quo periclitaretur tam fides catholica quam humana societas, magis est à catholicis impendendum pro fide catholica conseruanda, quam pro societate humana conseruanda: eo quod quilibet catholicus magis zelare tenetur pro fide, quam pro societate humana. absque mutua autem defensione periclitatur tam catholica fides, quam humana societas. pro humana autem societate conseruanda Christiani auxilium mutuum sibi debent impendere: quia quemadmodum, veritate testante, vt habetur Matth. 12. omne regnum diuisum desolabitur: & omnis ciuitas vel domus diuisa contra se non stabit: sic omnis societas per mutuam defensionem minime colligata non stabit, quod veritas ipsa prius insinuare videtur aperte, cum dicit: qui autem non est mecum, contra me est: & qui non congregat mecum, dispergit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod qui non est cum aliquo, ipsum modo conuenienti & possibili defendendo contra ipsum esse dignoscitur. Ex quo sequitur, quod talis societas minime stabit. & ita pro humana societate seruanda debet vnus alteri defensionem impendere: ergo multo magis pro seruanda fide catholica debet vnusquisque alteri defensionem & tuitionem (cum potest) impendere. Ex quo infertur, quod impugnantibus Papam hæreticum est defensio adhibenda.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I think I clearly understand the assertion just made, although it has not been shown to me that it contains the truth for which you are still trying to argue. I want to know the foundations on which Brother Michael and his followers try to prove that such men are to be defended by Catholics against the Supreme Pontiff. MASTER. The assertion mentioned above can be proved by an eleventh argument. That without which both the Catholic faith and human society would be endangered must be defended by Catholics more for the preservation of the Catholic faith than for the preservation of human society, since every Catholic is bound to be more zealous for the faith than for human society. But both the Catholic faith and human society are endangered without mutual defence. Christians ought to give one another mutual help for the preservation of human society, because, as the truth itself testifies in Matthew 12, "every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand." So every society that is not held together by mutual defence will not stand. The truth itself seems to have stated this plainly beforehand when it says: "He that is not with me is against me, and he that gathereth not with me scattereth." From these words it follows that whoever is not with someone is recognised as being against him, if he does not defend him in a suitable and possible way. From this it follows that such a society will by no means stand. So, if one must give defence to another in order to preserve human society, then much more must each one give defence and protection to another (when he can) in order to preserve the Catholic faith. From this it is inferred that those who attack a heretical Pope are to be given defence.

units.la: Duodecima ratio talis est: qui debet alteri auxilium & consilium in aliqua causa impendere, debet eidem defensionem congruam exhibere. catholicus autem debet impugnantibus Papam hæreticum auxilium & consilium impendere. aliter enim zelator fidei catholicæ nequaquam existeret. ergo debet eis defensionem etiam impendere.
units.tr: The twelfth reason is this: whoever must give help and counsel to another in some matter must also give him suitable defence. But a Catholic must give help and counsel to those who attack a heretical Pope; otherwise he would by no means be a zealot for the Catholic faith. Therefore he must also give them defence.

units.la: Tredecima ratio talis est: quilibet tenetur defendere, si potest, patientem quamcunque iniuriam. ergo multo magis quilibet tenetur defendere, si potest, patientem iniuriam propter iustitiam: quia defendendo fidem catholicam Papa hæreticus nititur impugnare. consequentia est manifesta & euidens: quia patiens iniuriam est maxime defendendus; si propter iustitiam & fidem catholicam iniuriam non situr suscipere. Antecedens autem auctoribus sanctorum patrum videtur aperte probari. ait enim Simachus Papa, vt habetur di. 83. c. presbyter: mortem enim languentib' probatur infligere, qui hanc (cum possit) non excludit. & per consequens iniuriam videtur inferre, qui hanc (cum possit) non excludit. nullus autem debet iniuriam inferre. ergo quilibet tenetur iniuriam patientem (cum possit) defendere. Item Ambros. in lib. de officiis, & ponitur di. 86. c. Pasce, ait: qui enim pascendo hominem potes seruare: si non paueris, fame occidisti. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ille dicitur occidere alium, qui sustentationem (cum possit) non exhibet corporalem. ergo similiter ille intelligitur iniuriam irrogare, qui cum potest iniuriam non excludit. & ita quilibet, si potest, debet defendere iniuriam patientem. Item Innoc. tertius, vt habetur extra, de sent. excom. quanta, asserit manifeste, quod facientes & consentientes pari poena plectendos catholicta condemnat auctoritas, eos delinquentibus fauere interpretans, qui cum possunt, manifesto facinori desinunt obuiare. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod qui primum ab inferenda iniuria non defendit, cum potest, est pari poena cum iniuriante plectendus. & ita quilibet, cum potest, patienti iniuriam debet defensionem impendere.
units.tr: The thirteenth reason is this: everyone is bound to defend, if he can, anyone who suffers any injury. Therefore much more is everyone bound to defend, if he can, one who suffers injury for justice' sake, because a heretical Pope strives to attack him for defending the Catholic faith. The consequence is plain and evident: the one suffering injury is most of all to be defended if he is suffering it for justice and the Catholic faith. The antecedent is clearly proved by the authority of the holy Fathers. For Pope Symmachus says, as is found in dist. 83, c. Presbyter: "For he is held to inflict death on the sick who does not prevent it when he can." And consequently he who does not prevent an injury when he can seems to inflict it. But no one ought to inflict injury. Therefore everyone is bound to defend, when he can, one who suffers injury. Likewise Ambrose, in his book On Duties, and it is cited in dist. 86, c. Pasce, says: "For if you can save a man by feeding him and you do not feed him, you have killed him by hunger." From these words it is gathered that the one who does not give bodily sustenance when he can is said to kill another. So likewise he is understood to inflict injury who does not prevent an injury when he can. And thus everyone, if he can, ought to give defence to one who suffers injury. Likewise Innocent III, as is found in Extra, De sententia excommunicationis, Quanta, plainly asserts that the authority of the Catholic Church condemns those who do and those who consent to be punished with the same penalty, interpreting as favourers of wrongdoers those who, when they can, cease to oppose a manifest crime. From these words it is made clear that whoever does not defend first against the infliction of injury, when he can, is to be punished with the same penalty as the one inflicting it. And thus everyone, when he can, ought to give defence to one who suffers injury.

units.la: CAP. XLII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLII.

units.la: Ponit vnam euasionem, videlicet quod talis defensio non spectat nisi ad illos, qui habent iurisdictionem super iniuriantes. & hoc probatur auctoritatibus & rationibus. vbi etiam probatur, quod socius socium defendere non debet, & per consequens non tenetur. cuius oppositum probatur capitulo immediate sequenti. & ad has auctoritates & rationes respondetur infra, 44. huius.
units.tr: He raises one way of escape, namely that such a defence belongs only to those who have jurisdiction over the wrongdoers. This is proved by authorities and reasons, and it is also shown that one companion ought not to defend another, and therefore is not bound to. The opposite is proved in the chapter immediately following. The answers to these authorities and reasons are given below, in chapter 44 of this work.

units.la: DISCIP. Auctoritates praedictae de solis iudicibus vel praelatis habentibus super alios potestatem intelligi debent: non autem de illis, qui potestatem vel iurisdictionem super iniuriantes nullam habent. Quod pluribus modis videtur posse probari. Primo autem auctoritate beati Augustin. quae ponitur 23. quaest. 4. cap. forte, ostenditur. ait enim: Forte in populo Dei stat iuxta te auarus, raptor, inhians rebus alienis, quem nosti talem, & fidelis est, vel fidelis potius vocatur. non eum potes de Ecclesia pellere: non habes aliquem aditum castigando vel corrigendo ipsum corrigere. accessurus est tecum ad altare, noli timere. & infra eodem: c. si iudex es, si iudicandi potestatem accepisti, ecclesiastica regula si apud te accusatur, si veris documentis testibusque convincitur, coherce, corripe, excommunica, & degrada. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod non ad socios, sed ad praelatos spectat corrigere delinquentes: & per consequens non ad socios, sed ad praelatos spectat defendere passos iniurias. quia cuius est defendere patientem iniuriam, eius est reprimere: & per consequens plectere iniuriam inferentem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. The authorities cited above must be understood of judges alone, or of prelates who have power over others, and not of those who have no power or jurisdiction over the wrongdoers. This can be proved in several ways. First, by the authority of blessed Augustine, which is cited in 23. quaest. 4, chapter "Forte", where he says: "Perhaps there stands beside you in the people of God a covetous man, a robber, greedy for other people's goods, whom you know to be such, yet he is a believer, or rather is called a believer. You cannot drive him out of the Church; you have no means of correcting him by rebuke or admonition. He will come with you to the altar; do not be afraid." And further on, in the same chapter: "If you are a judge, if you have received the power of judging, and if by ecclesiastical rule he is accused before you and is convicted by clear proofs and witnesses, restrain him, rebuke him, excommunicate him, and depose him." From these words it is understood that it belongs not to companions but to prelates to correct offenders, and therefore it belongs not to companions but to prelates to defend those who suffer wrongs, because whoever is bound to defend the one suffering wrong is also bound to restrain him, and therefore to punish the one who inflicts the wrong.

units.la: Secundo probatur idem sic: si socius tenetur defendere socium, videns aliquem verberare clericum, & non defendens ipsum, sententiam excommunicationis incurrit, iuxta auctoritatem Innocentii tertii allegatam superius. sed hoc est inconveniens, sicut Glossa ibidem ratione tali probat: nullus excommunicatur ex facto alterius, nisi participando in locutione, vel oratione, aut in crimine fuerit ei comparus, vel eius mandato obediendo, vel auctoritate praedicando. supra cap. mulieres. sed hic nullo tali modo participat. ergo non est excommunicatus. & per consequens socius non tenetur defendere socium.
units.tr: Second, the same is proved thus: if a companion is bound to defend a companion, and a man who sees another beating a cleric and does not defend him incurs the sentence of excommunication, according to the authority of Innocent III cited above, then this is absurd, as the Gloss on that passage proves by this reasoning: no one is excommunicated for another's deed unless he takes part by speaking or praying, or is his accomplice in the crime, or obeys his command, or supports him by authority, as stated above in the chapter "Mulieres". But here he takes part in none of these ways. Therefore he is not excommunicated, and therefore a companion is not bound to defend a companion.

units.la: Tertio probatur idem ratione, quam innuit Glossa vbi supra. & eandem tangit Glossa 23. quaest. 3. cap. non inferenda. quae potest sic formari, nullus tenetur ad id, pro quo potest exp acto recipere pecuniam: quia illud, ad quod quis de necessitate absque omni pacto tenetur, debet gratis impendere. sed pro defensione socii socius licite recipit pecuniam: nec recepram pecuniam tenetur restituere. ergo socius non tenetur de necessitate socium absque pacto defendere.
units.tr: Third, the same is proved by the reasoning which the Gloss hints at in the passage above, and which it also touches on in 23. quaest. 3, chapter "Non inferenda". It can be framed thus: no one is bound to do that for which he may lawfully receive payment, because what a man is bound to do of necessity, without any agreement, he ought to render freely. But a companion lawfully receives payment for defending a companion, and he is not bound to restore the money received. Therefore a companion is not bound of necessity to defend a companion without an agreement.

units.la: Quarto probatur idem sic: non magis tenetur socius socium de necessitate defendere, quam tenetur medicus periclitantem infirmum gratis curare. sed medicus non tenetur gratis infirmum curare, quia de suo non tenetur quis ferre beneficium. 10. quaest. 1. precarie. ergo nec socius tenetur gratis socium defendere.
units.tr: Fourth, the same is proved thus: a companion is no more bound of necessity to defend a companion than a physician is bound to treat a sick man in danger without payment. But a physician is not bound to treat the sick man for nothing, because no one is required to bear a benefit at his own expense (10. quaest. 1, "Precarie"). Therefore neither is a companion bound to defend a companion for nothing.

units.la: Quinto sic: defensio socii est quaedam militia vel aliquid simile militiae. sed nemo tenetur suis stipendiis militare, teste Apostolo 1. ad Corinth. 9. qui ait: quis militat suis stipendiis? quasi diceret, nullus. ergo nemo tenetur alium gratis defendere.
units.tr: Fifth: the defence of a companion is a kind of soldiering, or something similar to soldiering. But no one is bound to serve as a soldier at his own expense, as the Apostle witnesses in 1 Cor. 9, where he says: "Who serves as a soldier at his own charges?" as if he were saying, no one. Therefore no one is bound to defend another for nothing.

units.la: Sexto sic: defendere socium est benefacere. sed nemo tenetur alii benefacere gratis: quia per leges nemo cogitur benefacere, sed malefacere prohibetur, vt testatur Augustinus contra Pelagium, & ponitur 22. quaest. 5. ad fidem. ergo nemo tenetur socium gratis defendere. Ex quo sequitur, quod non tenentur omnes catholici impugnantes Papam haereticum defendere. DISCIP. Porro quia, vt aestimo, Frater. MAGIST. Et adhaerentes sibi illos, qui ipsos contra summum Pontificem non defendunt, reprehensibiles arbitrantur, putantes quod non solum pro causa fidei patientes, sed etiam alii pro leuioribus causis sustinentes persecutiones & iniurias non tantum a praelatis, sed etiam a sociis & aliis sunt pro viribus defendendi: peto quod assertionem praedictam, quod socius videlicet tenetur defendere socium, allegationibus quantum potes fortioribus munire coneris, & quomodo ad rationes in contrarium, quas adduxisti, frater.
units.tr: Sixth: to defend a companion is to do good. But no one is bound to do good to another for nothing, because by the laws no one is compelled to do good, but is forbidden to do evil, as Augustine testifies against Pelagius, and as is cited in 22. quaest. 5, "Ad fidem". Therefore no one is bound to defend a companion for nothing. From this it follows that not all Catholics who attack the heretical Pope are bound to defend those who are attacking him. MASTER. And those who cling to them think that those who do not defend them against the Supreme Pontiff are blameworthy, supposing that not only those who suffer for the cause of faith, but also others who bear persecutions and injuries for lighter causes, are to be defended as far as they can be, not only by prelates but also by companions and others. I ask you, brother, to fortify the assertion just stated, namely that a companion is bound to defend a companion, with the strongest arguments you can, and to show how you answer the reasons to the contrary which you have brought forward.

units.la: MAG. Et sui respondeant, studeas propalare, vt per huiusmodi impugnationes, quibus praedicti frater. MAG. Et sui, dominum summum Pontificem & sibi adhaerentes impugnare conantur, magis profunde intelligam, & quomodo debent reprobari & refelli, euidentius aduertam.
units.tr: MASTER. And let your followers answer; take care to make known how such attacks, by which the aforesaid brother and his followers try to assail the Supreme Pontiff and those who cling to him, should be rejected and refuted, so that I may understand them more deeply and notice more clearly how they ought to be refuted.

units.la: CAP. XLIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIII.

units.la: In quo probatur oppositum, quod socius socium defendere debet auctoritatibus plurimis & sex rationibus & exemplis quinque.
units.tr: In which the opposite is proved: that one fellow member must defend another, by very many authorities, six arguments and five examples.

units.la: MAGIST. Nequaquam deciperis existimando, quod frater MAG. & adhaerentes sui valde reprehensibiles nonnullos reputant Christianos, & a peccato mortali nullatenus excusandos: pro eo quod eis defensionem contra dominum Innoc. non impendunt, dicentes, quod quilibet (cum potest) modo congruenti & sibi compossibili tenetur socium iniuriam patientem defendere & à periculo liberare. Ex quo moliuntur inferre, quod cum ipsi propter iusticiam & fidem catholicam persecutiones grauissimas patiantur, sunt à catholicis defendendi, & à periculis liberandi.
units.tr: TEACHER. You are quite wrong to suppose that my brother MAG. and his adherents consider some Christians very blameworthy, and not to be excused from mortal sin in any way, because they do not give them a defence against Lord Innocent. They say that everyone, when he can, is bound, by a suitable and compatible means, to defend a fellow sufferer of injury and to free him from danger. From this they try to infer that, since they suffer the gravest persecutions for justice and the Catholic faith, they must be defended by Catholics and freed from their dangers.

units.la: Quod autem socius socium iniuriam patientem (cum potest) modo sibi congruenti & possibili teneatur etiam gratis defendere, auctoritatibus, rationib. & exemplis videtur posse probari. Hoc enim Ambrosius, vt allegatum est superius, notabiliter & sententialiter videtur asserere, dicens: qui enim non repellit à socio iniuriam (si potest) tantum est in vitio quantum ille, qui facit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod qui non defendit socium, culpam incurrit.
units.tr: That a fellow member must also defend a fellow sufferer of injury (when he can) by a means suitable and possible to him, even without reward, seems capable of being proved by authorities, reasons and examples. Ambrose, as was cited above, appears to assert this plainly and as a maxim, saying: "Whoever does not repel injury from a fellow (if he can) is as much at fault as the one who does it." From these words it is gathered that whoever does not defend a fellow incurs blame.

units.la: MAG. Istam Gloss. exponam, quia repellere iniuriam est defendere reputandum.
units.tr: TEACHER. I will explain that Gloss, because to repel injury is to be considered a defence.

units.la: DISCIP. Ad hoc respondet Gloss. ibidem dicens: si potest, id est, si est in potestate positus, ex quibus verbis Gloss. datur intelligi, quod Ambrosius loquitur de praelatis.
units.tr: STUDENT. The Gloss answers this in the same place, saying: "if he can," that is, if he is placed in a position of power. From these words the Gloss gives us to understand that Ambrose is speaking of prelates.

units.la: MAG. Glossa super illam expositionem hoc non asserit; sed tantummodo recitat, quod in fine illius notulae reprobare videtur, dicens: sed istis asserentibus expositione praedicta obuiat infra eodem.cap.vlt. ex quo capitulo colligitur euidenter, quod turba Iudaeorum, quae non defendit Christum contra principes ipsum volentes occidere, nequaquam fuit immunis à scelere. ex quo sequitur, quod non solum praelati, sed etiam plebeii tenentur defendere Christum contra Praelatos eorum: & ita socius etiam tenetur defendere socium. Quod etiam illa expositio corrumpat textum, patet aperte, cum loquitur expresse de illo, qui à socio iniuriam non repellit. DISCIP. Ad idem plures auctoritates adducas. MAG. Hoc idem Ambrosius, vt superius est adductum, asserit manifeste: quia dicit, quod tueri à latronibus socios plena iusticia est. opus autem iusticiae tenetur quilibet exercere. ergo de necessitate iusticiae sunt socii defendendi. Item, idem habetur dist. 86.c. non satis, loquens qualiter opus misericordiae tenetur proximo impendere, qualis est non solum praelatus, sed etiam subditus, ait: si tempore periculi, quo rapitur ad mortem, plus apud te pecunia tua valeat quam vita morituri, non est leue peccatum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod debet quis socium à morte redimere: & per consequens eadem ratione tenetur eum, si potest, defendere. Item ista videtur esse Salomonis, qui in proverbiis secundum Hier. & in prologo paruulum carissimum docens: & per consequens non ad praelatum, sed ad alium sermonem dirigens, ait: erue eos qui ducuntur ad mortem, & qui trahuntur ad interitum liberare non cesses. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod non solum praelati, sed etiam alii persecutiones & iniurias patientes defendere tenentur. DISCIP. Sufficiunt ad praesens auctoritates istae pro assertione praedicta: ideo rationes induxas.
units.tr: TEACHER. The Gloss does not assert this in its explanation; it merely reports it, and seems to reject it at the end of that note, saying: "but those who maintain the aforesaid explanation are opposed below in the same chapter, at the last chapter." From that chapter it is clearly gathered that the crowd of Jews who did not defend Christ against the rulers who wished to kill him was by no means free from crime. From this it follows that not only prelates but also common people are bound to defend Christ against their prelates, and so a fellow member too is bound to defend a fellow member. That this explanation also corrupts the text is plain, since it speaks expressly of one who does not repel injury from a fellow. STUDENT. Adduce more authorities on the same point. TEACHER. Ambrose himself, as was cited above, plainly asserts the same thing, since he says that to protect fellows from robbers is full justice. But everyone is bound to exercise the work of justice. Therefore fellows must of necessity be defended as a matter of justice. Again, the same is found in Dist. 86, chapter "Non satis," where it speaks of how the work of mercy is bound to be rendered to a neighbour, and of what sort, not only a prelate but also a subject: "If at a time of danger, when a man is being dragged to death, your money counts for more with you than the life of the one about to die, it is no slight sin." From these words it is gathered that a man ought to redeem a fellow from death, and consequently, by the same reasoning, is bound to defend him, if he can. Again, this seems to be the saying of Solomon, who in the Proverbs, according to Jerome and in the prologue, teaching his dearest little son, and consequently directing his speech not to a prelate but to another, says: "Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to deliver those who are being dragged to destruction." From these words it is gathered that not only prelates but also others are bound to defend those who suffer persecutions and injuries. STUDENT. These authorities are enough for the present to support the assertion I made; so I have brought forward the reasons.

units.la: MAG. Prima ratio talis est: Qui debent sibi mutuum auxilium & fauorem impendere, & sibi mutuam defensionem tenentur impendere. omnes autem Christiani siue catholici sibi debent mutuum auxilium, consilium & fauorem impendere. Tum, quia omnes catholici sunt membra vnius corporis, membra autem pro se inuicem sollicita sunt. 1. Corinth. 12. Tum quia Episcopi, quorum vnus est praelatus alterius, auxilium mutuum sibi debent impendere, teste Innocent. secundo, qui, vt dicitur. &c. di. c. praecipimus, ait: Praecipimus vt Episcopi ad solum Deum & salutem populi habentes respectum illum omni tepiditate remota ad pacem firmiter tenendam mutuum consilium sibi & auxilium praebeant: nec hoc alicuius amore vel odio permittant. quod si quis in hoc opere Dei tepidus inuentus fuerit, damnum propriae dignitatis incurrat. Cui etiam concordat Alexand. Papa, qui, vt legitur 3. quaest. 1. c. nulli, ait: Qui autem ex nostro fuerit collegio & ab auxilio vestro se subtraxerit, magis schismaticus quam sacerdos esse probatur. Ecce, inquit, Propheta, ecce quam bonum & quam iocundum habitare fratres in vnum. illi vero non habitant in vnum, qui à fratrum se solatio subtrahunt. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod Episcopi & sacerdotes, quorum etiam vnus alteri minime est subiectus, auxilium sibi mutuum debent impendere & per consequens sibi debent defensionem mutuam congruentem praestare. Ex quo sequitur, quod socius socium debet defendere. Secunda ratio talis est: Magis tenetur socius socium (à suo non inferiori patientem iniuste) defendere, quam viri ecclesiastici teneantur defendere sceleratos, qui eis minime sunt subiecti. sed viri ecclesiastici sceleratos & impios ad ecclesiam fugientes, licet eis nullatenus sint subiecti, defendere tenentur. ergo multo magis socius socium innocentem debet defendere. minor probatur auctoritate Gregor. qui vt habetur 23. quaest. 5. cap. reos, ait: Reos sanguinis defendat ecclesia. vbi dicit Gloss. omnes fugientes ad ecclesiam tenetur defendere, vt 17. quaest. 4. reum. & hoc est verum, siue sint rei siue non.
units.tr: TEACHER: The first reason is this. Those who ought to give one another mutual help and favour are bound to offer one another mutual defence. All Christians, or Catholics, ought to give one another mutual help, counsel and favour. This is so because all Catholics are members of one body, and members are mutually concerned for one another (1 Cor. 12.). It is also so because bishops, of whom one is the superior of another, ought to give each other mutual help. Innocent the Second teaches this, as it is said in dist. (c. Praecipimus), when he says: "We command that bishops, looking solely to God and to the salvation of the people, and putting aside all lukewarmness, offer each other mutual counsel and help in firmly maintaining peace, and that they not permit this to be swayed by love or hatred. If anyone is found lukewarm in this work of God, let him incur the loss of his own dignity." Pope Alexander agrees, as is read in 3 quaest. 1 (c. Nulli): "Whoever belongs to our college and withdraws himself from your help is shown to be more a schismatic than a priest. Behold," he says, quoting the Prophet, "behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. But those do not dwell together in unity who withdraw from the comfort of their brothers." From these words it is evident that bishops and priests, not one of whom is subject to another, ought to give each other mutual help, and consequently ought to render one another fitting mutual defence. From this it follows that a companion ought to defend his companion. The second reason is this: a companion is more bound to defend his companion (who is unjustly suffering injury from one who is not his inferior) than churchmen are bound to defend wicked men who are not subject to them. But churchmen are bound to defend wicked and impious men who flee to the Church, even though they are in no way subject to them. Therefore, much more, a companion ought to defend an innocent companion. The minor premise is proved by the authority of Gregory, who, as is found in 23 quaest. 5 (c. Reos), says: "Let the Church defend those guilty of bloodshed." Where the Gloss says that all who flee to the Church are to be defended, as in 17 quaest. 4 (Reum), and this holds true whether they are guilty or not.

units.la: DISCIP. Hoc dicit Greg. quia viri ecclesiastici ecclesiam defendere tenentur, & ideo tenentur prohibere ne fugientibus ad ecclesiam violentia fiat. MAGIST. Tu aliam causam assignas, quam Gregorius, quare rei sunt ab Ecclesia defendendi. Nam Gregorius causam assignat sui dicti, cum immediate post verba praedicta subiungit, ne effusionis sanguinis fiat particeps. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ideo viri ecclesiastici debent defendere reos ad Ecclesiam fugientes, ne homicidii fiant participes. Quia qui non resistit, cum potest, consentit, iuxta sanctorum patrum sententias. ergo consimiliter qui non defendit socium iniuriam patientem, cum possit, iniuriae crimen incurrit. Vnde ex hoc tertia ratio formatur. Quilibet catholicus ad hoc tenetur, fine quo etiam in crimine participat criminoso. sed qui non defendit (cum potest) socium iniuriam patientem, participat in crimine iniuriam inferenti. ergo socius socium (cum potest) tenetur defendere. maior est manifesta. minor auctoritatibus sanctorum patrum patrum ostendi videtur. ait enim Euleutherius Papa, vt habetur 2. quaest. 7. cap. negligentia: Negligentia cum possis perturbare peruersos, nihil est aliud quam fauere. nec caret scrupulo societatis occultae, qui manifesto facinori desinit obuiare. eadem sententia verbaliter ponitur dist. 83. cap. error. & 23. quaest. tertia, cap. qui potest, ponitur sub his verbis: qui potest obuiare & perturbare peruersos, & non facit, nihil est aliud quam fauere impietati eorum. nec caret scrupulo societatis occultae, qui manifesto facinori desinit obuiare. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod qui non resistit iniuriam facienti, eidem communicat in crimine atq; fauet.
units.tr: STUDENT: Gregory says this because churchmen are bound to defend the Church, and therefore are bound to prevent violence being done to those who flee to the Church. TEACHER: You assign a different reason from the one Gregory gives for why the guilty are to be defended by the Church. For Gregory gives the reason for his statement when, immediately after the words just cited, he adds: "lest they become partakers in the shedding of blood." From these words it is gathered that churchmen ought to defend the guilty who flee to the Church for this reason: lest they become partakers in manslaughter. For he who does not resist when he can, consents, according to the opinions of the holy Fathers. Therefore, similarly, he who does not defend a companion suffering injury, when he is able to, incurs the guilt of injury. Hence a third reason is formed from this. Every Catholic is bound to do whatever, if left undone, would make him a participant in the crime of the criminal. But he who does not defend (when he can) a companion suffering injury becomes a participant in the crime of the one inflicting the injury. Therefore a companion is bound to defend a companion (when he can). The major premise is manifest. The minor premise seems to be shown by the authority of the holy Fathers. For Pope Eleutherius says, as is found in 2 quaest. 7 (c. Negligentia): "Negligence, when you are able to restrain the perverse, is nothing other than favouring them. Nor is he free from the stain of secret fellowship who ceases to stand in the way of an open crime." The same opinion is stated almost word for word in dist. 83 (c. Error), and in 23 quaest. 3 (c. Qui potest) it is put in these words: "He who is able to stand in the way of and restrain the perverse, and does not do so, is nothing other than favouring their impiety. Nor is he free from the stain of secret fellowship who ceases to stand in the way of an open crime." From these words it is gathered that he who does not resist one doing injury thereby shares in the crime and favours it.

units.la: DISCIP. Verba quae allegasti, de praelatis tantummodo debent intelligi, secundum quod notat Gloss. 2. quaest. 7. negligentia.
units.tr: STUDENT: The words you have quoted ought to be understood only of prelates, as the Gloss notes on 2 quaest. 7 (Negligentia).

units.la: MAGIST. Haec responsio dupliciter impugnatur. Primo quia Gloss. hoc non asserit, sed tantummodo dicit, quod ista videtur de praelatis tantum loqui. Secundo quia perturbare peruersos contingit dupliciter. Vno modo ipsos pro sua peruersitate poena congrua puniendo, & sic perturbare peruersos regulariter solummodo pertinet ad iudices vel praelatos. Alio modo exhortatione malum reprobando, & illo modo saltem eis expedit verbis monitoriis resistendo, & istud spectat ad omnes, Gloss. ibidem aperte insinuante, quod quilibet tenetur perturbare, id est, prohibere & removere a malo: & hoc cum commode illud facere potest, aliter enim peccat, qui sic non prohibet. & subdit, secundum hoc quilibet tenetur prohibere iniuriam a proximo. & per consequens proximum saltem verbis (si potest) defendere debet, licet non sit praelatus ipsius.
units.tr: MAGISTER. This response is attacked in two ways. First, because the Gloss does not assert it but merely says that these words seem to speak only of prelates. Second, because disturbing the perverse happens in two ways. In one way, by punishing them with a fitting penalty for their perversity; and in that way, disturbing the perverse regularly pertains only to judges or prelates. In the other way, by reproving evil through exhortation; and in that way at least it is fitting for them to be resisted with words of admonition, and this concerns everyone, as the Gloss there plainly insinuates, that anyone is bound to disturb, that is, to restrain and remove from evil, and this when he can do so conveniently, for otherwise he who does not restrain in this way sins. And it adds: according to this, anyone is bound to prevent injury to his neighbour. And consequently he ought to defend his neighbour, at least with words (if he can), even though he is not that neighbour's prelate.

units.la: Quarta ratio est haec. ille tenetur (si potest) defendere socium iniuriam patientem, qui tenetur corrigere & corripere iniuriam inferentem. nam corrigendo iniuriari volentem defendit, quantum in se est, ipsum qui esset passurus iniuriam. sed alii, quam iudices vel praelati (si possunt) tenentur corrigere iniuriari volentem. ergo si commode possunt, debent defendere alium, qui est passurus iniuriam. maior euidens esse videtur primo auctoritate beati Augustin. qui li. de verbis domini, & ponitur 23. quaest. 4. cap. primo tolerandi quidam sunt mali; nec corporaliter ab eis recedatur, sed spiritualiter; spiritualiter autem exire est facere quod pertinet ad correptionem malorum, quantum licet pro gradu cuiuslibet salua pace. vbi dicit Gloss. super verbo pro gradu, id est pro dignitate & officio cuiuscunque. alio tantum modo debent praelati corrigere delinquentes: alio modo socii praelatus corrigit increpando, verberando, vt infra c. quaest. c. forte. socius vero monendo & reprobando factum. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod non solum praelati, sed etiam alii tenentur corrigere delinquentes & iniurias aliis facientes: quod etiam idem August. vt habetur 23. quaest. 5. cap. non putes, sentire videtur: ait enim: non putes te tunc amare seruum tuum, quando eum non caedis: & infra: aut tunc amare vicinum tuum, quando non corrigis eum; non est ista charitas, sed languor. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod vicinum vicinus tenetur corrigere. Item Anacletus, vt habetur 24. quaest. 3. c. tam sacerdotes, ait: tam sacerdotes quam reliqui fideles omnes summam debent habere curam de his qui pereunt. ergo ad omnes spectat corrigere iniuriam inferentes.
units.tr: The fourth reason is this. He who is bound (if he can) to defend a companion suffering injury is also bound to correct and rebuke the one inflicting injury. For by correcting the one who wishes to do injury, he defends, as far as in him lies, the one who would be about to suffer it. But others besides judges or prelates (if they are able) are bound to correct the one wishing to do injury. Therefore, if they can conveniently do so, they ought to defend the other who is about to suffer injury. The major premise seems clearly true, first by the authority of blessed Augustine, who in his book on the words of the Lord, and it is placed in 23. quaest. 4. chap. "Primo tolerandi quidam sunt mali": "nor are we to withdraw from them bodily, but spiritually; and to withdraw spiritually is to do what pertains to the correction of evil men, as far as is allowed according to each one's rank, saving peace." Where the Gloss says on the words "according to rank" that this means according to the dignity and office of each person. In one way only are prelates bound to correct offenders; in another way the companions of prelates correct by rebuking and beating, as below in the chapter of quaest. "forte"; but a companion corrects by admonishing and reproving the deed. From these words it is to be understood that not only prelates but also others are bound to correct offenders and those who do injury to others. Augustine himself seems to think the same, as is found in 23. quaest. 5. chap. "non putes": for he says: do not think that you love your servant when you do not beat him; and below: or that you love your neighbour when you do not correct him; that is not charity but lethargy. From these words it is held that a neighbour is bound to correct his neighbour. Likewise Anacletus, as is found in 24. quaest. 3. chap. "tam sacerdotes," says: both priests and all the other faithful ought to have the greatest care for those who perish. Therefore it pertains to everyone to correct those who inflict injury.

units.la: DISCIP. Scis quia multi istis diebus tenent doctrinam Thomae de Aquino. quare dic, quid ipse sentit de hac re, an scilicet ad omnes spectat corrigere delinquentes.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. You know that many in these days hold the doctrine of Thomas Aquinas. Therefore tell me what he himself thinks about this matter, namely whether it pertains to everyone to correct offenders.

units.la: MAGIST. Ipse tenet quod sic. nam secunda secundae, quaest. 33. art. 3. dicit sic: Duplex est correctio. vna quidem quae est actus charitatis, quae specialiter tendit ad emendationem fratris delinquentis per simplicem admonitionem. Et talis correctio pertinet ad quemlibet charitatem habentem, siue sit subditus, siue praelatus. Et articulo quarto dicit sic: correctio fraterna, quae est actus charitatis, pertinet ad vnumquemque respectu personae, ad quam charitatem debet habere; si in eo aliquid corrigibile inueniat.
units.tr: MAGISTER. He himself holds that it does. For in the second part of the second part, question 33, article 3, he says thus: "Correction is twofold. One indeed is an act of charity, which tends specially to the amendment of the erring brother by simple admonition; and such correction pertains to everyone who has charity, whether he be a subject or a prelate." And in article 4 he says thus: "Fraternal correction, which is an act of charity, pertains to each one with respect to the person whom he ought to love, if he finds in him anything correctable."

units.la: DISCIP. Non adducas plura ad probandum, quod omnes tenentur corrigere iniuriari volentem: sed adhuc proba, quod socius tenetur socium iniuriam patientem defendere.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. Do not bring more to prove that all are bound to correct one wishing to do injury; but still prove that a companion is bound to defend a companion suffering injury.

units.la: MAG. Quinta ratio pro assertione praedicta est haec. ad eundem spectat malum proximi removere (si potest) ad quem spectat bonum eiusdem (si potuerit) procurare: sed quilibet tenetur proximi bonum procurare, quia aliter charitatem ad ipsum minime habet. ergo quilibet tenetur malum alterius removere, si potest. & ita tenetur remouere malum iniuriam patientis. sed saepe hoc non fit, nisi ipsum defendendo. ergo quilibet tenetur alium defendere, si potest.
units.tr: MAGISTER. The fifth reason for the aforesaid assertion is this. The one to whom it belongs to remove his neighbour's evil (if he can) is also the one to whom it belongs to procure his neighbour's good (if he is able); but everyone is bound to procure his neighbour's good, because otherwise he does not have charity toward him at all. Therefore everyone is bound to remove another's evil, if he can. And so he is bound to remove the evil of one suffering injury. But this is often not done unless by defending him. Therefore everyone is bound to defend another, if he can.

units.la: Sexta ratio est haec: non minus indiget in periculo constitutus contra volentem iniuriari defendi, quam esuriens cibari & sitiens potari. sed quilibet, qui potest, tenetur esurientes cibare & sitientes potare, si per aliunm illis minime subuenitur. ergo quilibet tenetur alium defendere, si potest, si non appareat aliquis, qui velit & possit eum defendere.
units.tr: The sixth reason is this: one placed in danger needs to be defended against one wishing to do injury no less than the hungry need to be fed and the thirsty to be given drink. But anyone who is able is bound to feed the hungry and give drink to the thirsty, if they are not at all helped by another. Therefore anyone who is able is bound to defend another, if no one appears who is willing and able to defend him.

units.la: DISCIP. Adducas exempla pro eadem assertione.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. Bring examples for the same assertion.

units.la: MAGIST. Primum exemplum est de Abraham, qui, vt legitur Genes. 14. quamuis non haberet iurisdictionem super capientes Loth fratrem suum, & alios, tamen non solum Loth defendit; sed etiam irruit super capientes, eosque percussit & reduxit Loth cum substantia eius.
units.tr: MAGISTER. The first example is of Abraham, who, as we read in Genesis 14, although he had no jurisdiction over those who took his brother Lot and others, not only defended Lot, but also fell upon those who took him, struck them down, and led back Lot with his possessions.

units.la: Secundum est de Moyse, qui Hebraeum percussum ab Aegyptio defendit, & occidit Aegyptium, vt legitur Exod. 2. de quo scribit Ambrosius, vt habetur 23. quaest. 3. cap. non inferenda, dicens: cum vidisset Hebraeum ab Aegyptio recipiente iniuriam, defendit vt Aegyptium prosterneret. & tamen super Aegyptios, aut Hebraeos tunc Moyses nullam iurisdictionem habuit potestatem de quo etiam, vbi prius, Exod. 7. scribitur, quod filias sacerdotis Madian à pastoribus defensauit: cum tamen neque super puellas, neque super pastores iurisdictionem habuit.
units.tr: The second is of Moses, who defended a Hebrew struck by an Egyptian, and killed the Egyptian, as we read in Exodus 2; of which Ambrose writes, as is found in 23. quaest. 3. chap. "non inferenda," saying: when he had seen the Hebrew suffering injury from the Egyptian, he defended him so that he struck down the Egyptian. And yet Moses at that time had no jurisdiction or power over the Egyptians or the Hebrews. Concerning this also, earlier, in Exodus 7, it is written that he defended the daughters of the priest of Midian from the shepherds, although he had no jurisdiction either over the girls or over the shepherds.

units.la: Tertium exemplum de Raab meretrice, quæ, vt habetur Iosue 2. exploratores filiorum Israel abscondendo defendit.
units.tr: The third example is of Rahab the harlot, who, as is found in Joshua 2, defended the spies of the sons of Israel by hiding them.

units.la: Quartum exemplum est de beato Petro, qui etiam arma mouendo Christum defensare cupiebat, Matth. 26. & non videtur de voluntate defendendi reprehensus à Christo, sed quia hæsitare videbatur, an Christus aliter quam per arma poterat defensari. propter quod Christus ipsum acriter increpando, dixit: an putas quia non possum rogare patrem meum & exhibebit mihi plusquam duodecim legiones angelorum?
units.tr: The fourth example is of blessed Peter, who, moving his weapons, also wished to defend Christ, Matthew 26; and he was not rebuked by Christ for the will to defend, but because he seemed to hesitate whether Christ could be defended in any other way than by arms. On account of which Christ, sharply rebuking him, said: "Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would send me more than twelve legions of angels?"

units.la: Quintum exemplum est de discipulis Damasci, qui, vt legitur Act. 9. beatum Paulum submittendo illum in sporta contra Iudæorum insidias defendebant. Alia complura exempla, quod alii quam prælati in periculo positos defendebant, tam in scriptura diuina quam in aliis scriptis authenticis, scribuntur aperte.
units.tr: The fifth example is of the disciples at Damascus, who, as we read in Acts 9, defended blessed Paul by letting him down in a basket against the snares of the Jews. Many other examples, that persons other than prelates defended those placed in danger, are plainly written both in divine Scripture and in other authentic writings.

units.la: CAP. XLIV.
units.tr: CAP. XLIV.

units.la: Ponit responsiones ad auctoritates & rationes capituli 42. probantes huius oppositum, scilicet quod socius socium defendere non tenetur.
units.tr: Gives replies to the authorities and arguments of chapter 42, which prove the opposite, namely that a companion is not bound to defend a companion.

units.la: DISCIP. Volo plures allegationes audire pro assertione prædicta. & ideo dic, quomodo possunt obiectiones, quas feci, dissolui.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I want to hear more arguments in support of the aforesaid assertion. So tell me how the objections I raised can be resolved.

units.la: MAGIST. Prima auctoritas Augustini quam allegas, non loquitur specialiter de iniuriantibus aliis, sed de delinquentibus in communi. quia tamen assertores prædicti consimiliter dicunt de omnibus peccantibus corrigendis & de passis iniuriam defendendis. ideo ad auctoritatem Augustin. prædictam respondent dicentes, quod in prima parte loquitur Augustinus de his, qui auctoritatem iudiciariam non habent, corrigendo secrete apud delinquentes nequaquam proficerent, sed eos deteriores efficerent. in hoc enim casu non debet aliquis (iurisdictionem nullatenus habens) corrigere delinquentes. consimiliter vbi aliquis intendendo defendere patientes iniuriam ipsos defendere non posset, & ad deteriora inferentes iniuriam provocaret, deberet defensionem subtrahere. sed sicut subditi peccant mortaliter, si timore temporalium aut humanum fauorem perdendi, aut personale periculum euitandi, vel ob aliquod terrenum habendum socios vel prælatos, cum probabiliter putant, quod possunt eos à peccato retrahere, negligunt secreto corrigere. ita peccant mortaliter, qui, cum conuenienter possunt, ex timore vel cupiditate defensionem in periculis constitutis vel patientibus iniuriam non impendunt.
units.tr: MASTER. The first authority of Augustine that you cite does not speak specifically of those who wrong others, but of wrongdoers in general. Yet since the advocates of this view say the same about all sinners who should be corrected and about those suffering injury who should be defended, they answer the aforesaid authority of Augustine by saying that in the first part Augustine speaks of those who have no judicial authority, and that by correcting wrongdoers in private they would in no way succeed, but would make them worse. In this case, anyone who has no jurisdiction at all ought not to correct wrongdoers. Likewise, where someone who intends to defend those suffering injury could not defend them and would provoke those inflicting injury to worse deeds, he ought to withhold his defence. But just as subjects sin mortally if, from fear of temporal losses, or from fear of losing human favour, or of avoiding personal danger, or for some earthly gain, they neglect to correct their companions or prelates in private, when they probably think they could turn them from sin, so those sin mortally who, when they conveniently can, out of fear or greed do not render defence to those placed in danger or suffering injury.

units.la: DISCIP. Est ne aliquis doctor modernus, qui teneat, quod non corrigentes in casu prædicto peccantes peccant mortaliter?
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Is there any modern teacher who holds that those who do not correct sinners in the aforesaid case sin mortally?

units.la: MAG. Thomas de Aquino hoc sentit expresse. dicit enim 2. 2. quæst. 33. art. 2. quod prætermittitur fraterna correctio cum peccato mortali, quando scilicet formidatur iudicium vulgi & carnis excruciatio, vel peremptio: dum tamen hæc ita dominentur, quod fraternæ charitati præponantur. & hoc videtur contingere, quando aliquis præsumit de aliquo delinquente probabiliter, quod posset eum à peccato retrahere: & tamen propter timorem vel cupiditatem præter-mittat. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod etiam pro morte vitanda non debet quis dimittere corrigere delinquentem, si probabiliter credit, quod potest eum per secretam correctionem retrahere à peccato. Ex quo concluditur, quod quilibet catholicus debet (si potest) corrigere inferentem iniuriam & per consequens defendere iniuriam patientem. DISCIP. Quid dicitur ad hoc, quod accipitur in illa obiectione, quod videlicet, cuius est defendere patientem iniuriam, eius est reptimere: & per consequens plectere iniuriam inferentem.
units.tr: MASTER. Thomas Aquinas holds this expressly. For he says in 2.2, q. 33, art. 2, that fraternal correction is omitted with mortal sin, namely when the judgment of the crowd or the torment or death of the flesh is feared, provided these things so dominate that they are put before fraternal charity. And this seems to happen when someone presumes, with probability, about some wrongdoer that he could turn him from sin, and yet out of fear or greed passes it over. From these words it is gathered that one ought not to omit correcting a wrongdoer even to avoid death, if one probably believes that one can turn him from sin by private correction. From this it follows that every Catholic ought (if he can) to correct the one inflicting injury and, consequently, to defend the one suffering injury. DISCIPLE. What is to be said in reply to what is taken from that objection, namely that whoever has the duty of defending one suffering injury has the duty of restraining, and consequently of punishing, the one inflicting it?

units.la: MAG. Ista negatur tanquam falsa: quia ad plures pertinet defensio patientium & in periculis positorum, ad quos tamen quamuis pertineat reprimere iniuriantes cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ, ad eos tamen non spectat plectere iniuriam facientes. quemadmodum cuilibet licet vim vi repellere cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ. dist. 1. c. tutelæ. & c. ius naturale, ad quem tamen non semper pertinet illatam iniuriam vindicare.
units.tr: MASTER. That is denied as false, because the defence of those suffering injury and placed in danger belongs to many. Although it belongs to them to restrain those who wrong, with the moderation of blameless protection, it does not belong to them to punish those who inflict injury. Just as anyone may repel force with force within the moderation of blameless protection (dist. 1, c. tutelae; c. ius naturale), yet it does not always belong to him to avenge the injury done.

units.la: DISCIP. Dicad secundam obiectionem. MAGIST. Ad illam potest dici, quod quamuis videns clericum verberari non incurrat excommunicationis sententiam, si ipsum (quamuis possit) non defendat, tamen peccat mortaliter, si ipsum non defendit cum possit. quod non habet tantum veritatem de clerico verberato, sed & de laico verberato iniuste. quia ex charitate fraterna quilibet, cum conuenienter potest, tenetur in omni periculo subuenire. & hæc responsio ex Glossa super prælegato capitulo quanto colligitur, quæ ait: videtur peccare omnis, qui non defendit alium (si potest) 23. q. 3. non inferenda. & cap. vlt. & si non possit aliter defendere, saltem defendat clamore. & infra: si ergo non habeam aliquam potestatem, video quod aliquis voluit verberare clericum, siue percutere sine meo consilio vel auxilio: non credo quod sim excommunicatus, si non prohibeo, licet alias forte peccem, quia ipsum non defendo, cum possum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur primo, quod sunt diuersi modi defendendi; cum aperte dicatur, quod potest quis defendere clamore. & eadem ratione contingit quis defendere verbis monitoriis monendo inferentem rentem iniuriam, quod desistat. quod etiam Gloss. ibidem asserit manifeste dicens: alia est prohibitio sociorum & aliorum: quia solummodo verbis & non factis vindicando iniuriam illatam licet facere, si possint, teneantur defendere, saltem exposito periculo occultando. sicut enim secundum Augustin. ut habetur 23. quaest. 4. cap. ipsa pietas, quilibet tenetur alium se volentem occidere liberare, & de periculo, si potest, etiam violenter extrahere; ita tenetur quilibet alium quaesitum occidi de periculo liberare, si potest, saltem si non potest aliter occultando. sunt ergo diversi modi defendendi alium in periculo constitutum. Secundo ex verbis Glossae colligitur, quod videns clericum verberari, & non defendens, si potest, licet peccet, tamen excommunicationis non incurrit sententiam. & per hoc respondetur ad rationem Glossae superius allegatam: quia per illam rationem non concluditur, quod non defendens clericum, si potest, non peccat: sed quod non incidit in excommunicationis sententiam.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Tell me the second objection. MASTER. To it one can say that although someone who sees a cleric being beaten does not incur the sentence of excommunication if he does not defend him (though he could), yet he sins mortally if he does not defend him when he can. This holds not only of a beaten cleric but also of a layman unjustly beaten. For out of fraternal charity anyone, when he conveniently can, is bound to come to aid in every danger. This answer is drawn from the Gloss on the aforesaid chapter Quanto, which says: "Everyone who does not defend another (if he can) seems to sin," 23, q. 3, non inferenda, and in the last chapter. "And if he cannot defend him in any other way, at least let him defend him by shouting." And further on: "So if I have no power, and I see that someone wishes to beat a cleric, or strike him, without my counsel or help, I do not think I am excommunicated if I do not forbid it, although perhaps I sin in other respects, because I do not defend him when I can." From these words it is gathered, first, that there are different ways of defending, since it is plainly said that one may defend by shouting. And by the same reasoning one may defend by admonishing the one inflicting injury with words of warning, that he desist. The Gloss itself also asserts this clearly, saying: "It is one thing to forbid companions and others, because it is permitted to avenge an injury inflicted only by words and not by deeds; if they can, they are bound to defend, at least by disclosing the danger in secret." For just as, according to Augustine (as found in 23, q. 4, c. ipsa pietas), anyone is bound to rescue another who wishes to kill himself, and, if he can, even to drag him forcibly from danger, so anyone is bound to rescue from danger another who is sought to be killed, if he can, or at least, if he cannot otherwise, by disclosing it secretly. There are therefore different ways of defending another placed in danger. Second, from the words of the Gloss it is gathered that someone who sees a cleric being beaten and does not defend him, if he can, although he sins, does not incur the sentence of excommunication. And by this one answers the reasoning of the Gloss cited above: for by that reasoning it is not concluded that one who does not defend a cleric, when he can, does not sin, but that he does not incur the sentence of excommunication.

units.la: DISCIP. Videtur quod ista ratio non concludit, quod non incidit in excommunicationis sententiam: quia iudex vel iurisdictionem habens non defendendo clericum, cum potest, incidit in excommunicationis sententiam: & tamen nullo praedictorum modorum participat clericum verberanti: quia nec locutione, nec oratione, nec in crimine, nec eius mandato clericus verberatur, nec auctoritatem praestat: quia plus est auctoritatem praestare, quam non defendere. MAG. Potest dici (ut innuit Glossa) quod iudex & superior non defendendo, auctoritatem praestat. & ideo incidit in sententiam excommunicationis. DISCIP. Haec sententia non videtur sufficiens: quia si iudex non defendendo auctoritatem praestat, eadem ratione socius non defendendo causam vel occasionem praestat. qui autem causam praestat vel occasionem, ita punitur sicut faciens: sicut qui occasionem damni dat, damnum dedisse videtur, extra, de iniuriis & damno dato, si culpa. ergo si iudex, qui non defendit clericum verberatum (cum potest) sententiam excommunicationis incurrat, & quilibet alius, qui non defendit clericum, excommunicationis sententia innodatur.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. It seems that this reasoning does not conclude that he does not incur the sentence of excommunication. For a judge or one having jurisdiction who does not defend a cleric when he can does incur the sentence of excommunication, and yet he takes part in none of the aforesaid ways in the act of the one beating the cleric: the cleric is not beaten by his speech, prayer, crime, or command, nor does he give authority, for giving authority is more than not defending. MASTER. It can be said (as the Gloss hints) that a judge or superior, by not defending, gives authority, and so incurs the sentence of excommunication. DISCIPLE. This answer does not seem sufficient. For if a judge, by not defending, gives authority, then by the same reasoning a companion, by not defending, gives cause or occasion. But whoever gives cause or occasion is punished just as the doer is: as one who gives occasion for loss seems to have caused the loss (extra, de iniuriis et damno dato, si culpa). Therefore if a judge who does not defend a beaten cleric (when he can) incurs the sentence of excommunication, then any other person who does not defend a cleric is bound by the sentence of excommunication.

units.la: MAGIST. Tu tangis unum motivum fundamentale quorundam dicentium, quod quilibet, qui potest, debet defendere impugnantes Papam haereticum, quamvis nesciat Papam esse haereticum.
units.tr: MASTER. You touch on one fundamental motive of certain people who say that anyone who can ought to defend those who attack a heretical Pope, even though he does not know that the Pope is a heretic.

units.la: DISCIP. Ex quo est istud unum de motivis illorum, maiorem tractatum de isto usque ad illam materiam censeo differendum: tamen nunc dicam breviter, quomodo per Glossam praedictam ad hoc respondere contingat. MAG. Potest dici, quod quamvis iudex sive alius, qui clericum non defendit, si potest, mortaliter peccat: ex lege tamen naturae neuter sententiam excommunicationis incurrit: quia poena excommunicationis solummodo ex iure positivo infligitur. poenae autem iuris positivi sunt restringendae, & nullatenus ampliandae. & ideo salva lege positiva sententia excommunicationis lata per canonem contra non defendentes clericum, ad pauciores (quantum permittit canon) debet extendi. cum ergo canon praedictus aperte salvari possit, intelligendo ipsum tantummodo de potestatem & iurisdictionem habentibus, quod gravius peccant non defendendo, quam alii: de aliis non debet intelligi, licet alii non defendentes clericum, cum possunt, peccent mortaliter.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Since this is one of their motives, I think a fuller treatment of it should be deferred until we reach that matter. Nevertheless, I will say briefly now how it may be answered through the aforesaid Gloss. MASTER. It can be said that although a judge, or anyone else, who does not defend a cleric, when he can, sins mortally, yet by the law of nature neither incurs the sentence of excommunication, because the penalty of excommunication is inflicted only by positive law. But the penalties of positive law are to be restricted and in no way extended. And therefore, with positive law preserved, the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the canon against those who do not defend a cleric ought to be extended to fewer people (as far as the canon permits). Since, therefore, the said canon can clearly be preserved by understanding it only of those who have power and jurisdiction, who sin more gravely by not defending than others do, it should not be understood of others; although others who do not defend a cleric, when they can, sin mortally.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic ad tertiam rationem. MAGIST. Ad tertiam respondetur quod haec non est vera: nullus tenetur ad illud, pro quo potest ex pacto pecuniam recipere. si quis enim indigeret alium in articulo extremae necessitatis ex fame posset licite sibi vendere panem: & tamen si alius non haberet unde emeret vel etiam nollet, teneretur sibi gratis dare panem pro vita sustentanda; si tamen in necessitate constitutus extrema haberet, unde sibi necessaria vitae ab aliis emere posset, essentque praesentes qui vendere vellent necessaria: iste non tenetur gratis sibi necessaria exhibere. sic in proposito licet recipere pecuniam pro defensione socii; si socius potest & vult dare pecuniam, vel aliquis alius, qui potest & vult eum defendere, vel ipse potest defendere semetipsum. si autem non potest semetipsum defendere, vel non potest aut non vult dare pecuniam, pro defensione sua, alius tenetur eum defendere absque pecunia. poterit tamen postea ab eo petere pecuniam, & alius sibi dare tenebitur.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. Tell me how to answer the third argument. MAGISTER. To the third it is answered that this is not true: no one is bound to do that for which he can lawfully receive money by agreement. For if someone were in extreme need of food, and in the very article of death from hunger, another could lawfully sell him bread; and yet if the other had no means of buying, or were unwilling, he would be bound to give him bread gratis to sustain his life. But if the man in extreme need had the means to buy the necessities of life from others, and sellers who wished to sell those necessities were present, the other is not bound to supply them to him gratis. So in the present case it is lawful to receive money for the defence of a companion: if the companion can and will pay, or someone else who can and will defend him, or he himself can defend himself, then no more is needed. But if he cannot defend himself, or cannot or will not pay money for his defence, another is bound to defend him without payment. He may, however, afterwards ask payment from him, and the other will be bound to give it.

units.la: Ad quartam respondet Gloss. dist. 83. cap. primo, dicens: patet hoc quod medicus debet curare pauperem infirmum; quia plus debet valere apud eum vita illius, quam propria pecunia. sed si infirmus dives est, & nihil vult dare medico, nunquid gratis eum tenetur curare? cum nemo de suo cogatur facere beneficium; ut 10. quaest. 2. praecariae, cum etiam licite potest recipere mercedem, ut 14. quaest. 5. non sane, dico quod tenetur eum curare suis expensis. & si convaluerit, repetat expensas, quia utiliter gessit negocium eius.
units.tr: To the fourth the Gloss answers on Dist. 83, chapter 1, saying: It is clear that a physician ought to treat a poor sick man, because his life ought to count for more with him than his own money. But if the sick man is rich and wishes to give the physician nothing, is he bound to treat him gratis? Since no one is compelled to do a kindness out of his own resources (as in 10 q. 2, Praecariae), and since he may also lawfully receive a fee (as in 14 q. 5, Non sane), I say that he is bound to treat him at the sick man's expense. And if the sick man recovers, he shall repay the expenses, because he has managed the man's business to good effect.

units.la: DISCIP. Ista videtur mihi fortis allegatio pro assertione praefata, quod scil. quilibet tenetur in periculo constitutum defendere & iuvare. cui repugnare videtur, quod Gloss. asserit dicens: nemo de suo cogitur facere beneficium. 10. q. 2. praecariae. Vide quomodo ad hoc respondetur, expone.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. This seems to me a strong argument for the assertion stated above, namely that everyone who is placed in danger is bound to defend and help. The Gloss, which says that no one is compelled to do a kindness out of his own resources (10 q. 2, Praecariae), seems to oppose it. See how this is answered, and explain it.

units.la: MAG. Dicitur quod illa auctoritas truncate allegatur: quia verba illius capituli 10. q. 2. praecariae, sunt haec: Cum ratio & usus obtineant neminem cui non vult contra utilitatem & rationem cogi de proprio facere beneficium. quae longe aliam sententiam continent, quam dicere quod nemo de proprio cogitur facere beneficium: saepe enim lege divina pariter & naturae ac lege humana cogitur quis de suo beneficium facere. aliter ei nemo eleemosynam de suo facere aliis teneretur; quod legi divinae & naturae ac humanae noscitur obviare. nemo tamen contra utilitatem suam & contra rationem cogitur de proprio beneficium facere: non enim eleemosynam dare de proprio est contra rationem nec contra vtilitatem spiritualem eleemosynam facientis, licet quandoq; sic contra vtilitatem temporalem. sicut etiam defendere socium gratis absq; mercede temporali non est contra vtilitatem saltem spiritualem defendentis, nec contra rationem. & ideo saepe cogitur aliquis lege naturae & diuina tale beneficium aliis gratis impendere.
units.tr: MAGISTER. It is said that this authority is cited in a truncated form, for the words of that chapter, 10 q. 2, Praecariae, are these: "Since reason and custom hold that no one may be compelled to do a kindness out of his own resources against his advantage and against reason." These words contain a quite different sense from saying that no one is compelled to do a kindness out of his own resources. For often by divine law, and equally by natural and human law, a man is compelled to do a kindness from his own resources; otherwise no one would be bound to give alms from his own means, which is known to be contrary to divine, natural and human law. Yet no one is compelled against his own advantage and against reason to do a kindness from his own resources: for to give alms from one's own means is neither against reason nor against the spiritual advantage of the giver, although at times it may be against his temporal advantage. Likewise, to defend a companion gratis, without temporal reward, is not against the advantage of the defender, at least the spiritual advantage, nor against reason. And therefore a man is often compelled by natural and divine law to bestow such a kindness gratis upon others.

units.la: DISCIP. Ista responsio videtur apparens. ideo dic, qualiter ad quintam rationem respondetur.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. That answer seems plausible. Therefore tell me how the fifth argument is answered.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur, quod regulare est neminem teneri suis stipendiis militare pro persona priuata. fallit tamen in casu, quia si aliquis militando potest saluare vitam alterius, qui non potest sibi reddere stipendium, debet pro eo stipendiis propriis militare saluando vitam eiusdem. Si enim miles viderit socium in bello ab aduersariis fortiter impugnatum, & in mortis periculo constitutum, debet, si potest, non sperando ab ipso stipendium ipsum de periculo liberare.
units.tr: MAGISTER. It is answered that the general rule is that no one is bound to serve as a soldier at his own expense on behalf of a private person. This rule admits an exception, however: if someone by fighting can save the life of another who cannot repay him his wages, he ought to fight at his own expense for him, saving that man's life. For if a soldier sees a companion in battle hard pressed by the enemy and placed in peril of death, he ought, if he can, to free him from danger without hoping for payment from him.

units.la: DISCIP. Miles recipit stipendium a principe pro principe & aliis fidelibus defendendis, quando potest. quare debet absque stipendio recipiendo a socio ipsum, quando expedierit, defendere.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. A soldier receives pay from the prince for defending the prince and other faithful men, when he can. Therefore he ought, without pay from his companion, to defend him when it is expedient.

units.la: MAG. Sicut miles recipit stipendium a principe etiam pro aliis commilitonib. quando expedierit, defendendis: ita quilibet recipit praeceptum a Deo & a lege naturae pro sociis, quando necesse fuerit, defendendis. non minus autem obligatur quis ex praecepto diuino & lege naturae, quam ex stipendio recepto a principe. quare sicut milites tenetur commilitones defendere, quando conuenienter potest: ita socius socium, quando conuenienter potest, tenetur defendere.
units.tr: MAGISTER. Just as a soldier receives pay from the prince also for defending his fellow soldiers when it is expedient, so everyone receives a command from God and from the law of nature to defend his companions when it is necessary. Yet a man is bound by divine command and the law of nature no less than by pay received from a prince. Therefore, just as soldiers are bound to defend their fellow soldiers when they conveniently can, so a companion is bound to defend a companion when he conveniently can.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic qualiter ad obiectionem vltimam respondetur. MAG. Respondetur, quod quamuis per leges nemo cogatur benefacere, tamen saepe per leges cogitur quis bonum facere. lex enim neque diuina neque humana cogit benefacere. quia dicit Augustin. post verba, quae allegastis, benefacere nemo potest, nisi elegerit, nisi amauerit; quod est in libera voluntate. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod sicut voluntas non potest cogi: ita nemo potest cogi benefacere. & quandoque quidem absolute, quandoque autem conditionaliter. & sic per leges diuinas & humanas cogitur quis conditionaliter benefacere, scilicet si voluerit vitare poenam temporalem vel aeternam, tenetur socium, cum potest, defendere.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. Tell me how the last objection is answered. MAGISTER. It is answered that although no one is compelled by laws to do good, yet often a man is compelled by laws to do good. For neither divine nor human law compels a man to do good. Augustine says, after the words you have cited: "No one can do good unless he has chosen to, unless he has loved to, which lies in free will." From these words it is gathered that just as the will cannot be compelled, so no one can be compelled to do good; and this is sometimes absolutely, sometimes conditionally. Thus by divine and human laws a man is compelled conditionally to do good, namely, if he wishes to avoid temporal or eternal punishment; he is bound, when he can, to defend his companion.

units.la: DISCIP. Istam responsionem rationabilem arbitror: cui tamen Gloss. super illo verbo, cogitaui, repugnare videtur, cum dicit: qui ex timore benefacit, reputatur non facere. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod aliquis potest benefacere ex timore. & ita saltem aliquis timore conditionaliter cogitur benefacere, quemadmodum cogitur bonum facere.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. I judge this a reasonable answer, yet the Gloss on that word "cogitavi" seems to oppose it, when it says: "He who does good from fear is reckoned not to do it." From these words it is gathered that someone can do good from fear, and so at least someone is conditionally compelled by fear to do good, just as he is compelled to do good.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur, quod Glossa intentionem textus August. expressius habuisset, si dixisset, qui ex timore bonum facit, reputatur non facere, sicut dicit August. vt habetur extra de reg. iur. qui ex timore facit praeceptum aliter quam debeat facit, & ideo non iam facit. potest tamen dici, quod Gloss. posuit benefacere pro bonum facere. non est autem dubium, quin leges cogant saepe bona facere. & ideo saepe metu legum & timore nonnulli benefaciunt accipiendo benefacere pro bonum facere. Sed August. aliter accipit, quia pro meritorie & ex bona voluntate facere.
units.tr: MAGISTER. It is answered that the Gloss would have expressed Augustine's meaning more clearly had it said: "He who does good from fear is reckoned not to do it," as Augustine says, as is found in the Extra, De regulis iuris: "He who acts from fear does the command otherwise than he ought, and therefore does not act at all." It may however be said that the Gloss put benefacere for bonum facere. There is no doubt that laws often compel men to do good; and so often, through fear of laws and dread, some men do good, taking benefacere to mean bonum facere. But Augustine understands it differently, namely as doing good meritoriously and from a good will.

units.la: CAP. XLV.
units.tr: CHAP. XLV.

units.la: In quo pertractatur tertia conclusio cap. 17. posita scilicet quod deferendum sit appellationi a Papa catholico pro causa haeresis interiecta, antequam constet ipsam non esse legitimam. & probatur sex rationibus. Oppositum vero huius probatur capitulo immediate sequenti, scilicet quod non sit deferendum tali appellationi. in principio tamen capituli proponitur, quomodo quaedam de nescientibus Papam esse haereticum, vtrum tales teneantur defendere impugnantes ipsum, ad quam respondetur infra cap. 50. huius.
units.tr: In this chapter the third conclusion of chapter 17 is examined, namely that an appeal lodged against a Catholic Pope on the ground of heresy must be granted a hearing, before it is established that the appeal is not lawful. This is proved by six arguments. The opposite is proved in the chapter immediately following, namely that such an appeal must not be granted a hearing. At the beginning of the chapter, however, it is raised how some people who do not know that the Pope is a heretic ask whether such people are bound to defend those who attack him. This is answered below, in chapter 50 of this work.

units.la: DISCIP. Allegationes, quas supra in diuersis capitulis adduxisti ad probandum, quod catholici, qui possunt, de necessitate tenentur Papam haereticum impugnantes defendere, tantummodo de scientibus & credentibus Papam esse haereticum videtur concludere, quod illi soli scilicet qui credunt aut sciunt Papam esse haereticum, tenentur de necessitate salutis ipsum impugnantes, si possunt, defendere: non autem videntur ostendere, quod nescientes Papam esse haereticum, teneantur defendere ipsum de prauitate haeretica impugnantes. ideo quid de hoc sentiunt literati propalam.
units.tr: STUDENT: The arguments you have adduced in various chapters above, to prove that Catholics who are able are of necessity bound to defend a heretical Pope against those who attack him, seem to conclude only about those who know and believe that the Pope is a heretic. That is, only those who believe or know the Pope to be a heretic are of necessity bound, for the salvation of their souls, to defend him, if they can, against his attackers.
