Ad secundam dicitur: quod non est semper præsumendum, quod impugnans Papam de hæretica prauitate, siue appellando siue accusando, siue testificando causa inuidiæ moueatur; nec est semper præsumendum, quod accusatio ex inuidia nõ ex charitate procedat: imo nisi apparuerit aliquod indicium inuidiæ speciale, præsumendum est quod accusatio ex charitate fiat, cum accusare prælatū etiam (circumstantiis debitis obseruatis) ad rectitudinem & Dei timorem pertineat, teste Greg. qui, vt legitur 2.q.7.c.sicut, ait: sicut laudabile & discretum est reuerentiam & honorem exhibere primoribus, ita rectitudinis & Dei timoris est, si que in eis sunt, qua indigent correctione nulla dissimulatione postponere, ne totum (quod absit) corpus morbus inuadat, si langour non fuerit curatus in capite. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod non est præsumendum statim accusationem prælati fieri ex inuidia, sed ex zelo charitatis. Ad allegationes tuas respondet Gloss. 2.q.7. si quis Episcopus, super illo verbo illaudabile, dicens: vel dic illaudabilem, quo ad vulgippinionem. Nam aliter præsumitur quis bono zelo accusare, vt extra, de do. & contum. veritatis est verbum. ex charitate enim debet prouenire accusatio; extra, de accusationibus. si quis Episcopus, & qui accusat, publica salutis custodiam gerit, vt Cod. de famosis libellis, lege vna. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod non est semper præsumendum ex inuidia accusationem fieri: imo si accusans sit hactenus bonæ famæ, nec apparet quod fuerit inimicus accusati, nec facile litigans, nec vilis aut leuis persona, sed omni suspitione carens, præsumendum est quod bono zelo accusare proponat. Et consimiliter est dicendum de impugnantibus Papam de hæretica prauitate. Non autem est verisimile, quod aliquis bonæ famæ & opinionis, mansuetus & humilis, litigia minime quærens, discretus & prouidus, se velit periculis infinitis exponere Papam de hæretica prauitate impugnando, nisi conscientia vrgeatur. Quare præsumendum est, antequam contrarium appareat, quod impugnans Papam de hæretica prauitate, & per consequens confusioni perpetuæ: imo pluripluribus mortis periculis se exponens, zelo fidei orthodoxæ (quam vitæ corporali videtur facto proponere) moueatur. Et ideo omnes impugnantes Papam de hæretica prauitate, antequam constiterit legitimis documentis, quod zelo malo moueantur, sunt à catholicis, qui possunt, defendendi: qui etiam eius zelo fidei orthodoxæ (prout statim ex officio cuiuslibet congruit) tenentur impendere auxilium, consilium & fauorem. Et consimiliter si taliter impugnantes fuerint deprehensi malo zelo moueri, quia de falsitate conuincuntur, vel in probatione eorum quæ imponunt Papæ deficiunt, sunt acerrime puniendi: & videtur quod essent curiæ seculari tradendi. Patet ergo secundum istos, quod si impugnantes Papam de hæretica prauitate quæruntur ad mortem, sunt à catholicis defendendi. Ex quo infertur, quod etiam ab omni sunt persecutione & periculo liberandi, quia consimiliter & eadem ratio videtur, quod & sint liberandi à maiori periculo & minori.
units.tr: Master. Taking the words "attack" and "defence" in this sense, it is first shown by a certain argument, which was touched on earlier in chapter 44, that all Catholics are bound to defend those who unjustly attack the Pope, even a Catholic Pope, against the charge of heretical depravity (before it is established by legitimate proofs that they are acting maliciously). The argument runs as follows. Whoever gives occasion for loss is held to have caused the loss (extra, de iniuriis & damno dato, si culpa). Likewise, whoever gives occasion for persecuting, harassing or wronging someone is held to have inflicted the persecution, harassment or wrong. But a man who does not defend those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, when he is able to do so, gives occasion for persecuting, harassing or wronging them. For if he defended them, as he could, he would prevent the persecution, harassment or wrong that has been or will be inflicted. Therefore such a man who does not defend them is seen, and is judged, to have inflicted these things. But no one ought to inflict persecution, harassment or wrong on those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity before it is established that they are acting maliciously. Therefore everyone who is able is bound to defend them. Disciple. Giving occasion for loss, persecution, injury or harm happens in two ways: either by doing or saying something positively, or by leaving something undone negatively. Whoever gives occasion for loss by the first means is held to have caused the loss and is considered blameworthy. But whoever gives occasion for loss, persecution, harm or injury by leaving something undone does not seem to have caused the loss or harassment, and is not to be held guilty. For then anyone who failed to help another, or failed to enrich him, and as a result another suffered loss, would be seen to have caused the loss and would have to be judged blameworthy, which is too harsh. Master. This answer seems to conflict with the assertions of the holy Fathers, for they understand that not only does he cause loss who gives occasion for loss by doing or saying something, but also he who gives occasion for loss by leaving something undone, and who is bound to answer for it, at least in the sight of God. This seems to be provable by many authorities. Gregory IX, as we read in extra, de iniuriis & damno dato, si culpa, says: "If loss has been caused or injury inflicted through your fault, or you have delayed bringing help to others who are being wronged, or this has happened through your inexperience or negligence, you must make amends for these things by law. Nor does ignorance excuse you, if you ought to have known that injury or loss could reasonably result from your act." From these words it is clearly gathered that one is understood to cause loss not only when he gives occasion for loss by word or deed, but also when, by negligence, he gives occasion for loss by leaving something undone, and is for this judged guilty. Likewise, whoever gives occasion for death merely by leaving something undone is judged guilty of homicide, as Ambrose attests, who says, as it stands in 86. dist. pasce: "Whoever, by not feeding a man, could have saved him, (unless he was poor), has killed him." Therefore, similarly, whoever gives occasion for loss or harm merely by leaving something undone is seen to cause the loss or harm, and must be held accountable and guilty. Disciple. Although these arguments seem to have great weight, I see nonetheless that, generally, whoever gives occasion for loss by leaving something undone must be judged guilty, since someone may also give occasion for loss by doing something without fault: 23. q. 5. c. de occidendis. And so, from the fact that someone does not defend those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, although it follows from his not defending them that they suffer loss or harm, it cannot be inferred that such a non-defender should be considered blameworthy. Master. Some strive to exclude this answer or objection. To make clear the meaning of the rule stated above, namely that whoever gives occasion for loss, etc., they explain it in two cases. First, when someone gives occasion for loss merely by leaving something undone. Second, when someone gives occasion for loss by doing or saying something. As to the first, they say: if someone gives occasion for loss merely by leaving something undone, either he was bound to do that thing, and then he incurs guilt by such an omission. Hence in Exodus we read, and it is recited in extra, de iniuriis & damno dato: "If another man's ox was a known gorer yesterday and the day before, and its owner did not keep it in, he shall restore ox for ox." Where the Gloss on the words "did not keep it in" adds: "that is, and it has killed another's ox, so he is liable, because loss was caused by fault and negligence, since he ought to have shown diligence." From these words it is to be understood that the owner of the ox is liable for not keeping it in, if his ox causes damage, because he ought to have taken care, since he knew his ox was a gorer. But if someone gives occasion for loss merely by leaving undone something he was not bound to do, then whatever loss results from the occasion given, he who gave the occasion is free from fault. The divine law seems to suggest this in Exodus 21, where it is read thus: "If a goring ox kills a man or a woman, and they die, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be innocent. But if the ox was a known gorer yesterday and the day before, and its owner was warned, and he did not shut it up, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner shall also be put to death." From these words it is to be understood that if the death of a man or woman happens through not shutting in an ox, when the owner was not bound to shut it in, it is not imputed to the owner who did not shut it in. And so, one who gives occasion for loss by leaving undone something he was not bound to do is not judged guilty. Second, they say that if someone gives occasion for loss by doing something, he either undertakes a lawful or an unlawful act. If unlawful, all the loss that follows is imputed to him. If he undertakes a lawful act, and applies the diligence he ought, no loss that follows is imputed to him. But if he does not apply due diligence, then the loss that follows is imputed to him. Disciple. These points seem to me very reasonable, but I do not see how they ought to be applied to our purpose. Master. It appears to some that it can be demonstrated that those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity are to be defended by Catholics. In order to make their reasoning clearer, they first prove this conclusion: that those who attack the Pope for depravity in this way, if they are sought out or led to death, are to be freed from bodily death by Catholics, if they are able. And from this conclusion they infer that they are to be rescued by Catholics from every persecution and danger. Disciple. Prove first that such men are to be freed from bodily death. Master. This is shown by the authority of Solomon, cited above, who says: "Rescue those who are led to death, etc." Augustine, as we read in 23. q. 4. c. ipsa pietas, seems to assert this plainly, saying: "that if two were in a house about to collapse, we are bound, if we can, to free both." For, as he says in the same place, "if we did not, we would be judged cruel." If two were in some house about to collapse, and neither wished to leave, and one wished to kill himself, if the other were freed, we ought to free that one from death. Likewise, if many were in a house about to collapse, and if only one were freed, while all the others wished to throw themselves down and kill themselves, we ought to rescue that one. Therefore everyone is bound, if he can, to free another from death even if he is unwilling and does not consent, even if others would kill themselves because of the rescue of that one. Therefore, much more strongly, if someone is unjustly and against his will led to death, others who can free him from death are bound to do so. From this it follows that those who can ought to defend those sought for death. And so, if anyone wishes to seek out for death those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, the Catholics who can, either by resisting with arms, if it lies within their power, or by warning or entreating those seeking them to death, or by other means by which they can restrain such wickedness, or by hiding those sought for death or not handing them over, ought to defend them. Disciple. By this reasoning, whoever saw robbers, murderers and other malefactors condemned by a judge and led to death, ought to free them if he could. Master. To this it is answered that it is otherwise with those who are condemned to death by the due order of judgment, and with those who, without any examination of the cause, are exposed to danger of death because they wish to attack a superior. For the former are not to be freed from death, since it is always presumed that what is done by a judge and in accordance with his sentence is right, unless it has been legitimately overturned, either by appeal or by some other suitable means. And so such condemned men are not to be freed from death, unless the sentence of the judge had been appealed. For then they would have to be freed by whoever was able. But the latter are to be freed by those who can do so fittingly. And so, if the Pope were to order some men to be seized and led to death because they attacked him for heretical depravity, for a cause on account of which they strive to attack a superior, they would have to be freed. For in this case the presumption would have to be in favour of those attacking the Pope, and not in favour of the Pope. That the presumption ought to be in favour of those attacking the Pope is shown as follows. Just as everyone is presumed good unless the contrary is proved, so of everyone it must be presumed that he acts rightly unless the contrary is established by legitimate proofs. And so if someone does what can be done rightly, it must be presumed that he acts rightly, until the contrary is established. For things that can be done rightly or wrongly are to be interpreted in the better sense. Since, therefore, it is possible that someone attacks the Pope for heretical depravity rightly, justly and truthfully, it must be presumed of anyone who attacks the Pope for heretical depravity that he acts rightly and justly, until the contrary is shown against those attacking. Therefore, those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity must be presumed, before it is established by legitimate proofs, not to attack maliciously or unjustly. That the presumption is not in favour of the Pope, who, before judgment, would order those attacking him in this way to be handed over to death, or even thrown into prison, or otherwise harshly treated, is proved as follows. For nothing is to be presumed in favour of one who evades judgment; rather the contrary is to be presumed: extra, de praesumptionibus, nullum, and ii. q. i. Christianum, and 3. q. 9. decreuimus, and dist. 74. honorati. But a Pope who ordered those attacking him to be handed over to death or harshly treated would be evading judgment. Therefore the presumption would not be in his favour, but against him. Disciple. These arguments seem to fail in two ways. For nothing is to be presumed in favour of one who evades judgment when he is bound to stand trial. But the Pope is not bound to stand trial. Therefore, if he evades judgment, it is not on that account to be presumed against him. Secondly, they fail because nothing is to be presumed in favour of one who is presumed to act from envy and not from charity. But whoever attacks the Pope for heretical depravity would have to be presumed to act from envy and not from charity, just as an accusation is presumed to be made from envy rather than from charity: 6. q. 1. c. si omnia, in the text and the Gloss, and 2. q. 7. si quis Episcopus, where the canon calls accusation an unpraiseworthy action. Therefore nothing at all is to be presumed in favour of those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, but rather it is to be presumed against them, as against detractors. Master. To the first of these objections some strive to reply, saying that the Pope is bound to stand trial if some men appear (who cannot be repelled by a legitimate exception) who wish to accuse him of heretical depravity. For since, as they say, it is plain that he can be accused of heresy, it is clearly inferred that there are some who are able to accuse the Pope of heresy. From this it follows plainly that the Pope in such a case is bound to stand trial. And so, if he evades judgment, he makes himself suspect, and it is rightly to be presumed against him. To the second objection it is said: it is not always to be presumed that one who attacks the Pope for heretical depravity, whether by appealing, accusing or testifying, is moved by envy; nor is it always to be presumed that an accusation proceeds from envy and not from charity. Indeed, unless some special sign of envy appears, it must be presumed that an accusation is made from charity, since to accuse a prelate, even with the due circumstances observed, belongs to righteousness and the fear of God, as Gregory attests, who, as we read in 2. q. 7. c. sicut, says: "Just as it is praiseworthy and wise to show reverence and honour to the chief men, so it belongs to righteousness and the fear of God not to pass over in silence, through any dissimulation, whatever in them needs correction, lest (which God forbid) disease attack the whole body, if the sickness is not cured in the head." From these words it is to be understood that it must not be presumed at once that an accusation of a prelate is made from envy, but from the zeal of charity. The Gloss on 2. q. 7. si quis Episcopus, on the words "unpraiseworthy," replies to your objections, saying: "Or say 'unpraiseworthy' with regard to the common opinion. For otherwise one is presumed to accuse from good zeal, as in extra, de dolo et contumacia: 'Truth is a word.' For accusation ought to arise from charity; extra, de accusationibus, si quis Episcopus; and the accuser keeps watch over public safety, as in Cod. de famosis libellis, lege una." From these words it is gathered that it is not always to be presumed that an accusation is made from envy; indeed, if the accuser has hitherto been of good repute, and it does not appear that he was an enemy of the accused, nor a quarrelsome litigant, nor a base or light person, but free of all suspicion, it must be presumed that he proposes to accuse from good zeal. And the same must be said of those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity. It is not, however, probable that a man of good name and reputation, gentle and humble, who seeks no lawsuits, prudent and provident, would wish to expose himself to infinite dangers by attacking the Pope for heretical depravity, unless his conscience compelled him. Wherefore it must be presumed, until the contrary appears, that one who attacks the Pope for heretical depravity, and consequently exposes himself to perpetual confusion, and indeed to many dangers of death, is moved by zeal for the orthodox faith, which he appears to prefer, by his deed, to his bodily life. And so all who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, before it is established by legitimate proofs that they are moved by evil zeal, are to be defended by those Catholics who can; and these are also bound to give help, counsel and favour out of zeal for the orthodox faith (as is fitting for everyone's office at once). And likewise, if such attackers are caught being moved by evil zeal, because they are convicted of falsehood, or fail in proving what they charge against the Pope, they are to be most severely punished, and it seems they would have to be handed over to the secular court. It is plain, then, according to these men, that if those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity are sought for death, they are to be defended by Catholics. From this it is inferred that they are also to be freed from every persecution and danger, since by the same reasoning it seems that they are to be freed from greater danger and from lesser alike.

units.la: CAP. LI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LI.

units.la: In quo ponuntur aliæ rationes 10. probantes conclusionem positam capitulo immediate precedenti, scilicet quinquagesimo, & sic in toto sunt 11. rationes probantes, quod nescientes tenentur defendere impugnantes Papam de hæretica prauitate, antequam eis constiterit, quod malo zelo prouocati.
units.tr: In which are set out ten further arguments proving the conclusion laid down in the immediately preceding chapter, the fiftieth. In all, then, there are eleven arguments proving that those who are ignorant are bound to defend those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, before it is established to them that these men are provoked by a bad zeal.

units.la: Discipulus. Puto, quod si omnes rationes pro assertione prædicta, quantum possemus, profundius discutere moliremur, librum maximum faceremus, & forte omnes difficultates tactas à iuristis de appellationibus, recusationibus, denuntiationibus, inquisitionibus & testibus, exceptionibus, accusationibus, diffamationibus, calumniis, prouocationibus, præsumptionibus & purgationibus, disserere cogeremur. Ideo absq; perscrutatione subtili aliqua media brevissime tange, quibus videatur ostendi assertio memorata. Nam illis omnibus intellectis melius sciam Dominum summum pontificem ab opinionibus æmulorum defendere. Secunda ratio ad probandum, quod omnes catholici, qui congrue possunt, tenentur defendere impugnantes Papam de hæretica prauitate, antequam constiterit, quod malo zelo procedunt, si fuerint in periculo constituti, talis est. Vnusquisq; tenetur alii facere, quod sibi vult fieri, teste veritate, quæ Matth. 7. ait: Omnia ergo quaecunq; vultis ut faciant vobis homines & vos facite eis similiter. Hoc est enim lex & Prophetæ. Luc. 6. ait: Prout vultis ut faciant vobis homines & vos facite illis similiter. Sed vnusquisq; propter zelum bonum periculis mortis vel aliis quibuscunq; malis expositus rationabiliter vellet ab aliis defendi, foueri & iuuari. Ergo quicunq; videt alium in mortis periculo vel aliis constitutum propter impugnationem Papæ de hæretica prauitate, quam præsumit vel præsumere debet ex bono zelo procedere, tenetur eum, si potest, defendere, fouere & iuuare. Tertia ratio est hæc: Qui sunt audiendi in aliqua causa, sunt etiam si quærantur ad mortem pro tali causa, defendendi. Sed volentes Papam impugnare de hæretica prauitate, sunt in fauorem fidei audiendi: ergo sunt etiam defendendi. Quarta ratio est hæc. Sicut ad legislatorem pertinet prouidere subiectis, ne criminentur iniuste: ita ad ipsum cauere spectat, ne delinquere valeant insolenter. Sed Deus est perfectissimus legislator, cuius subiecti sunt summus pontifex & vniuersi catholici. Ergo sicut ad legem Diuinam omnibus datam catholicis spectat prouidere summo pontifici, ne à subditis suis criminetur iniuste, ita ad legem Diuinam spectat cauere ne summus pontifex in suorum subditorum perniciem & fidei periculum Christianæ delinquere valeat insolenter. Sed si impugnantes Papam de hæretica prauitate non essent à catholicis defendendi, Papa libere absq; metu legis cuiuscunq; potest prædicare, docere & tenere hæreticam prauitatem insolenter in catholicorum perniciem & periculum fidei orthodoxæ &c. Ergo taliter impugnantes Papam sunt à catholicis defendendi. Quinta ratio est hæc: Ad charitatem fraternam spectat proximis in cunctis suis necessitatibus subuenire, iuxta illud Beati Iohan. in canonica 1. c. 3. qui habuerit substantiam mundi huius, & viderit fratrem suum necessitatem habere, & clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in eo? Quasi diceret nullo modo. Et ideo subdit: Non diligamus verbo nec lingua, sed opere & veritate. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnes tenemur proximis, cum indigent, si possumus non solum verbo aut lingua, sed etiam veritate & opere subuenire. Quod maxime continet veritatem, quando præsumimus vel præsumere debemus proximos nostros absq; culpa sua & ex bonitate sua necessitatem vel indigentiam, quam sustinent, incidisse. Sed si videmus impugnantes Papam de hæretica prauitate in grauibus periculis constitutos: si non constet nobis legitime, quod ex malo zelo procedunt, oportet præsumere ipsos ex bono zelo & bonitate sua in talia pericula incidisse. Ergo tunc eis maxime subuenire tenemur. Et p consequens eos, si possumus, defendere & liberare tenemur. Sexta ratio est hæc: Magis tenetur catholicus catholicū desedere, ne pro fide catholica patiatur iniuste, quam teneatur seruus defendere Dominum suum, ne sibi pro causa temporali iniuria inferatur. Sed seruus quamuis iurisdictionem non habeat, debet defendere Dominum suum, ne sibi pro causa temporali iniuria inferatur. Ergo multo magis catholicus non prælatus catholicum debet defendere, ne pro fide catholica contra iustitiam patiatur. Septima ratio est hæc: illum debet vnusquisq;, si potest, defendere, qui patitur pro causa, quam quilibet tenetur vitæ corporali præponere. Ergo pro fide patientem catholica quilibet debet, si potest, defendere. Sed qui cernit impugnantes Papam de hæretica prauitate (antequam conuincantur de zelo malo) periculis propter huiusmodi impugnationem expositos, praesumere debet, quod pro fide catholica patiantur. Ergo tunc eos, si potest, tenentur defendere. Octava ratio est haec: Qui tenetur alterius bonum procurare, debet malum eius, si potuerit, removere. Sed quilibet catholicus tenetur bonum impugnantium Papam de haeretica pravitate procurare. Aliter enim non diligeret ipsos, sicut seipsum. Ergo si viderit in periculo constitutos, debet eos, si potest, a periculo liberare. Nona ratio est haec: Quilibet catholicus magis tenetur diligere personam proximi propter impugnationem Papae haeretici de pravitate haeretica in periculo constitutam, quam teneatur asinum vel iumentum inimici, si prostratum viderit, subleuare. Sed quilibet tenetur asinum inimici sui, si prostratum viderit, subleuare, teste lege divina, quae vt habetur Exod. 23. air: Si videris asinum odientis te iacere sub onere, non pertransibis, sed subleuabis cum. Ergo multo fortius si viderit catholicum, quem nescit errare, pati iniuriam vel in periculo constitutum propter zelum fidei orthodoxae, ipsum liberare tenetur si potest. Decima ratio est haec: vnusquisque proximum suum, sicut seipsum, debet diligere, Matth. 22. ergo quilibet debet facere alii in extremo periculo constituto, quod vult facere pro seipso. Sed quilibet vult seipsum defendere: Ergo quilibet tenetur defendere proximum suum in periculo constitutum, maxime si propter iustitiam periculum sustinere videtur. Quilibet ergo si viderit proximum suum in periculo constitutum, propter hoc quod impugnat Papam de haeretica pravitate, non constat sibi quod malo zelo mouetur, ipsum defendere tenetur. Vndecima ratio est haec: Id quod extra necessitatis tempus est licitum, tempore necessitatis extremae est debitum: cum videamus multa, quae extra tempus necessitatis extremae sunt illicita, tempore necessitatis extremae esse non solum licita, sed etiam debita. Dare enim rem alienam pauperi pro sustentatione sua extra tempus necessitatis est illicitum, secundum quod sacri canones testantur aperte & ratio manifestat. Dare tamen rem alienam pauperi pro sustentatione naturae tempore necessitatis extremae, quando, scilicet aliter ille pro tempore sustentari non potest, est debitum. Qui enim videret pauperem mori fame, & non posset sustentare ipsum, nisi dando sibi panem alienum, si non appareret alius, qui vellet aut posset pauperi subuenire, peccaret mortaliter, nisi panem alterius praeberet. Id ergo quod extra tempus extremae necessitatis est licitum, pro tempore necessitatis est debitum. Sed defendere impugnantes Papam de haeretica pravitate extra tempus necessitatis extremae est licitum, saltem si Papa non praecipit contrarium. Ergo tempore necessitatis extremae defendere taliter impugnantes Papam, siue Papa praecipiat siue non, est debitum. Papa enim non potest praecipere contra id, quod homo debet alii tempore necessitatis extremae, nisi ipse per se vel per alium necessitatem extremam patienti voluerit ministrare. Non enim Papa posset praecipere cuicunque non pascere de alieno pauperem constitutum in necessitate extrema, si aliter non posset pascere eum; nec Papa per se vel per alium vellet pascere, nec appareret alius, qui posset eius indigentiae subuenire. Nihil enim Papa potest praecipere, quod obuiat charitati fraternae. Ergo consimiliter non potest Papa praecipere alicui, quod non defendat (modo sibi congruente) impugnantem Papam de pravitate haeretica, si est in extremo periculo constitutus, & non constat sibi, quod talis impugnans malo zelo mouetur. Et si Papa daret tale praeceptum, sibi non esset obediendum quoquo modo, quia praeciperet contra legem Diuinam.
units.tr: Pupil. I think that if we tried to discuss all the arguments for the aforesaid assertion as thoroughly as we could, we would be making a very large book, and we would perhaps be obliged to dispute all the difficulties raised by the lawyers concerning appeals, recusations, denunciations, inquisitions and witnesses, exceptions, accusations, defamations, calumnies, provocations, presumptions and purgations. So, without any subtle investigation, touch briefly on some means by which the said assertion may seem to be shown. For once I have understood all of those, I shall know better how to defend the lord Pope from the opinions of his rivals. The second argument, to prove that all Catholics who are able to do so are bound to defend those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, before it is established that they act from a bad zeal, if they have been placed in danger, goes like this. Everyone is bound to do to another what he wishes to be done to himself, as the truth witnesses, which says in Matthew 7: "Therefore whatever you wish that men should do to you, do so to them likewise; for this is the law and the Prophets." Luke 6 says: "As you wish that men should do to you, do likewise to them." But everyone, exposed to the danger of death or to any other evils on account of a good zeal, would reasonably wish to be defended, cherished and helped by others. Therefore whoever sees another placed in danger of death or some other peril on account of attacking the Pope for heretical depravity, which he presumes, or ought to presume, arises from a good zeal, is bound, if he can, to defend, cherish and help him. The third argument is this: those who ought to be heard in any cause are also to be defended, even if they are sought for death on account of that cause. But those who wish to attack the Pope for heretical depravity ought to be heard in favour of the faith; therefore they are also to be defended. The fourth argument is this. Just as it belongs to the lawgiver to provide that his subjects are not unjustly accused, so it is his concern to take care that they may not be able to sin insolently. But God is the most perfect lawgiver, whose subjects are the supreme pontiff and all Catholics. Therefore, just as it belongs to all Catholics, under the divine law given to them, to provide that the supreme pontiff is not unjustly accused by his subjects, so it belongs to the divine law to take care that the supreme pontiff may not be able to sin insolently to the ruin of his subjects and the peril of the orthodox faith of Christians. But if those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity were not to be defended by Catholics, the Pope could freely, without fear of any law, preach, teach and hold heretical depravity insolently, to the ruin of Catholics and the peril of the orthodox faith, and so on. Therefore those who attack the Pope in such a way are to be defended by Catholics. The fifth argument is this: it belongs to fraternal charity to come to the aid of neighbours in all their needs, according to that saying of the blessed John in his first canonical epistle, chapter 3: "Whoever has this world's goods, and sees his brother have need, and shuts up his bowels of compassion from him, how does the love of God abide in him?" As if he said, in no way. And therefore he adds: "Let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and truth." From these words it is gathered that we are all bound to help our neighbours, when they are in need, if we can, not only by word or tongue, but also in truth and deed. This especially holds when we presume, or ought to presume, that our neighbours have fallen into the need or want they suffer without any fault of their own, and from their goodness. But if we see those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity placed in grave dangers, and it is not lawfully established to us that they act from a bad zeal, we must presume that they, from a good zeal and their own goodness, have fallen into such dangers. Therefore we are especially bound to help them then, and consequently, if we can, we are bound to defend and free them. The sixth argument is this: a Catholic is more bound to defend another Catholic from suffering unjustly for the Catholic faith than a servant is bound to defend his lord from being wronged for a temporal cause. But a servant, although he has no jurisdiction, ought to defend his lord from being wronged for a temporal cause. Therefore much more ought a Catholic who is not a prelate to defend a Catholic from suffering against justice for the Catholic faith. The seventh argument is this: anyone ought, if he can, to defend the one who suffers for a cause which everyone is bound to put before his bodily life. Therefore any Catholic ought, if he can, to defend one who suffers for the Catholic faith. But whoever sees those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity (before they are convicted of a bad zeal) exposed to dangers on account of such an attack, ought to presume that they suffer for the Catholic faith. Therefore, then, they are bound to defend them, if they can. The eighth argument is this: whoever is bound to procure another's good ought, if he can, to remove that person's evil. But every Catholic is bound to procure the good of those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity. For otherwise he would not love them as himself. Therefore, if he sees them placed in danger, he ought, if he can, to free them from danger. The ninth argument is this: every Catholic is more bound to love the person of his neighbour, placed in danger on account of attacking a heretical Pope for heretical depravity, than he is bound to raise up the ass or beast of burden of his enemy, if he sees it fallen. But everyone is bound to raise up the ass of his enemy, if he sees it fallen, the divine law witnessing, which, as is found in Exodus 23, says: "If you see the ass of him who hates you lying under its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall surely help him with it." Therefore much more strongly, if he sees a Catholic, whom he does not know to be in error, suffering wrong or placed in danger for the zeal of the orthodox faith, he is bound to free him if he can. The tenth argument is this: everyone ought to love his neighbour as himself (Matthew 22). Therefore everyone ought to do for another placed in extreme danger what he wishes to do for himself. But everyone wishes to defend himself. Therefore everyone is bound to defend his neighbour placed in danger, especially if he seems to suffer that danger for the sake of justice. Therefore, if anyone sees his neighbour placed in danger because he attacks the Pope for heretical depravity, and it is not established to him that he is moved by a bad zeal, he is bound to defend him. The eleventh argument is this: what is lawful outside a time of necessity is owed in a time of extreme necessity; since we see that many things which are unlawful outside a time of extreme necessity are not only lawful but even owed in a time of extreme necessity. For to give another's property to a poor man for his support outside a time of necessity is unlawful, as the sacred canons plainly attest and reason makes manifest. Yet to give another's property to a poor man for the sustenance of nature in a time of extreme necessity, that is, when he cannot otherwise be sustained for the time being, is owed. For whoever saw a poor man dying of hunger, and could not sustain him except by giving him another's bread, would sin mortally if, when no other appeared who wished or was able to help the poor man, he did not offer the bread of another. Therefore what is lawful outside a time of extreme necessity is owed in a time of necessity. But to defend those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity is lawful outside a time of extreme necessity, at least if the Pope does not command the contrary. Therefore in a time of extreme necessity to defend such attackers of the Pope is owed, whether the Pope commands it or not. For the Pope cannot command against what a man ought to give another in a time of extreme necessity, unless he himself, either personally or through another, has wished to minister to the one suffering extreme necessity. For the Pope could not command anyone not to feed a poor man placed in extreme necessity from another's goods, if otherwise he could not feed him; nor, if the Pope himself, personally or through another, were unwilling to feed him, and no other appeared who could relieve his need. For the Pope can command nothing which stands in the way of fraternal charity. Therefore likewise the Pope cannot command anyone not to defend (in a manner fitting to him) one who attacks the Pope for heretical depravity, if he is placed in extreme danger and it is not established to him that such an attacker is moved by a bad zeal. And if the Pope were to give such a command, it would by no means be to be obeyed, because he would be commanding against the divine law.

units.la: CAP. LII.
units.tr: CHAP. LII.

units.la: Ponit quaestionem de prælatis, qui habent subditos impugnantes Papam de haeretica pravitate, si eos defendere teneantur. Et respondetur quod sic, quod probatur tetiam 4. rationibus.
units.tr: He raises the question whether prelates who have subjects attacking the Pope for heretical depravity are bound to defend them. He answers that they are, and proves this also by four reasons.

units.la: DIscipulus. Desine allegare pro assertione praedicta, & dic quomodo potest ostendi, quod praelatii iurisdictione habentes debent defendere sibi subiectos, si Papa de pravitate haeretica per eos noluerint impugnari. Mag. Nonnullis videtur, quod tales praelati teneantur suos subditos taliter Papa impugnantes defendere. Et hoc videtur posse probari, primo sic: Qui oues luae curae commissas, quas reputat innocentes, vel reputare debet, non defendit, cum potest, mercenario comparatur, de quo dicit Christus Ioh. 14. Videt lupum venientem & dimittit oues & fugit, & lupus rapit & dispergit oues: mercenarius autem fugit, quia mercenarius est. &c. Sed praelati debent esse pastores, non mercenarii. Ergo tenentur oues suas, praecipue quas reputant innocentes vel reputare debent, ab inuasoribus defensare. Disc. Praelati debent defendere oues contra lupos, non contra Papam. Ideo si Papa mandauerit impugnantes ipsum de pravitate haeretica captiuari, vel incarcerari, aut poena alia plecti, eos non debent defendere. Magist. Ex ista responsione tua putant nonnulli demonstratiue probare assertionem praedictam: quia praelati debent defendere oues suas contra lupos, si possint. Sed si Papa mandauerit captiuari, & male tractari ipsum de haeretica pravitate impugnare volentes absque causae cognitione, vel antequam de malo zelo fuerint aperte conuicti, inter lupos gregem Dominicum crudeliter inuadentes est merito computandus. Quia propter opus, quod licitum inuenitur, nullus debet puniri, priusquam conuincatur, tale opus non bene, sed impie perpetrasse. Constat autem, quod impugnare Papam de pravitate haeretica potest esse licitum: quia Papa potest esse haereticus, & de haeresi licite impugnari. Si igitur appareat, quod talis impugnatio ex malitia & ex iniquitate non procedit, puniri non debet. Ergo Papa puniens & male tractans ipsum taliter impugnare volentes, antequam ostenderit, quod male mouentur contra, ipsos potestatem tyrannicam exercere dignoscitur. Et per consequens est inter lupos merito numerandus. Ex quo sequitur, quod prælati contra ipsum tenentur omnes suos in hoc casu defendere. Discip. Prælati inferiores supponere debent, quod Papa iuste facit, quicquid facit, & ideo præsumere debent, quod iuste mandat ipsum impugnare volentes pœna debita plecti. Magist. Sunt autem nonnulli dicentes, quod hic incidis in hæresim manifestam, in quam, (vt dicunt) plurimi modernis temporibus sunt prolapsi: quemadmodum fertur de multis, qui asserunt, Papam Deum reputandum in terris. Et ideo nulli licet iudicare, quod vnquam aliquod peccatum committat. Dicunt ergo quod hæc est manifesta hæresis, scilicet quod prælati inferiores debent supponere, quod Papa iuste facit, quicquid facit. Ex hoc enim sequeretur, quod si prælati viderent Papam Dæmones invocare, Christum blasphemare, fidem negare, adulterium committere, innocentem occidere, pejorare Ecclesias, beneficia vendere, ad vsuras dare pecuniam, deberent ipsum excusare, & quod bene faceret iudicare, quod est hæresis manifesta. Dicunt ergo, quod iuxta sententiam Bedæ, de criminibus manifestis quotumcunq; Papæ & aliorum permittitur iudicare. Quod etiam exemplo Beati Pauli constat aperte, qui de facto Beati Petri iudicauit aperte. Et ideo ipsum male fecisse publice reprehendit. Si ergo Papa mandaret ipsum impugnare volentes male tractari, antequam eos indebite impugnare monstraret: liceret cuilibet iudicare Papam impie & iniuste procedere. Imo de principali impositio, scilicet de prauitate hæretica suspectum habere deberent: & prælati suas oues ab eo tanquam à lupo crudeli defendere tenerentur. Discip. Mirum est quod isti dicunt, cum asserunt, cuilibet liceret iudicare Papam in hoc impie & iniuste procedere: & quod prælati debent taliter impugnantes contra Papam defendere, cum Papa sit magis immediatus prælatus taliter impugnantium, quam quicunq; alius prælatus inferior. Quare qui eos defendit contra Papam, iniuriam Papæ noscitur irrogare à iurisdictione Papæ suos subiectos subtrahendo. Magist. Respondetur ad hoc, quod taliter impugnantes sunt pars contra Papam. Quare in hoc Papa iudex eorum esse non debet: cum nullus esse debet iudex in propria causa. Discip. Hoc non videtur verum de Papa: quia potest esse iudex in propria causa, teste Innoc. tertio, qui, vt habetur, extra, de iudic. cum venisset, ait: cum super privilegiis Sedis Apostolicæ causa vertitur, volumus de ipsa per alios iudicari. Ergo Papa potest esse iudex in propria causa. Et per consequens si aliqui volunt impugnare Papam, ipse Papa potest esse iudex. Et ita si dat sententiam contra eos mandando, quod detineantur vel incarcerentur, vel alias puniantur, standum est sententiæ eius. Magist. Hoc quibusdam apparet contra rationem omnino. Nam licet Papa debeat iudicare inter litigantes super interpretandis priuilegiis, quia eius est interpretari, cuius est condere: licet etiam posset esse iudex in propria causa, quæ de rebus temporalibus verteretur: non tamen cum de crimine impugnatur. Et ita Papa nullo modo debet esse iudex, quando apparet ipsum de hæresi impugnare volentes. Quare si ipsos Papa ex hoc punit, licet cuilibet iudicare, quod iniuste & impie agit, & quod iudicium subterfugere quærit. Quare etiam de hæresi esset merito suspectus habendus. Discip. Alias rationes allega. Magist. Secunda ratio pro eadem assertione talis est: magis tenentur prælati defendere impugnantes ipsum de hæretica prauitate, antequam constiterit sibi ipsos ex malo zelo procedere, quam tenentur defendere viduas & pupillos. Sed prælati viduas & pupillos tenentur defendere, dist. 87. c. 1. & ca. defensionis. Ergo multo magis tenentur defendere Papam de hæresi impugnantes, antequam sibi constiterit quod sint nocentes. Tertia ratio est hæc. Prælati tenentur defendere sibi subiectos (etiam contra Papam) contra quos nulla causa iniquitatis obiicitur. Si enim Papa aliquos vellet confundere absq; omni causa, prælati eorum si possint, eos defendere tenentur. Ergo multo magis tenentur prælati defendere sibi subiectos, si pro causa, quæ præsumenda est iusta, à Papa ad mortem vel ad aliam confusionem quæruntur iniuste. Sed qui impugnare desiderant Papam de hæretica prauitate, antequam constiterit, quod malo zelo moueantur, præsumendi sunt causam iustam habere. Ergo tunc à prælatis sunt potissime defendendi. Quarta ratio est hæc. Illi, qui tenentur Papam de hæretico crimine corrigere, tenentur volentes ipsum de eodem crimine impugnare defendere: nisi constiterit eis, quod malo zelo moueantur. Sed prælati tenentur Papam de hæresi corrigere, si eum sciuerint hæreticam prauitatem incurrisse: quia aliter Papa de hæresi accusari non posset. Ergo tenentur cum volentes de hæresi impugnare defendere.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Stop citing authorities for the assertion above, and tell me how it can be shown that prelates who hold jurisdiction ought to defend their subjects if they are unwilling, on the Pope's account, to be attacked for heretical depravity. MASTER. Some think that such prelates are bound to defend their subjects who attack the Pope in this way. This can seem provable first as follows. Whoever does not defend, when he can, the sheep committed to his care, which he regards or ought to regard as innocent, is compared to a hireling, of whom Christ says in John 14: The wolf comes and the hireling sees it and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep; but the hireling flees because he is a hireling, etc. But prelates ought to be shepherds, not hirelings. Therefore they are bound to defend their sheep from invaders, especially those whom they regard or ought to regard as innocent. DISCIPLE. Prelates ought to defend the sheep against wolves, not against the Pope. So if the Pope orders that those who attack him for heretical depravity be taken, imprisoned, or punished in some other way, they ought not to defend them. MASTER. On the basis of your answer some think the assertion above is proved demonstratively, because prelates ought to defend their sheep against wolves if they can. But if the Pope orders that those who wish to attack him for heretical depravity be seized and cruelly treated without any hearing of the case, or before they have been clearly convicted of bad zeal, he deserves to be counted among the wolves who savagely attack the Lord's flock. For no one ought to be punished for an act that is found to be lawful until he is convicted of having committed that act not rightly but impiously. Now it is clear that to attack the Pope for heretical depravity can be lawful, since the Pope can be a heretic and can lawfully be attacked for heresy. If it therefore appears that such an attack does not proceed from malice and iniquity, it ought not to be punished. Therefore a Pope who punishes and mistreats those who wish to attack him in this way, before he has shown that they are moved wrongly against him, is known to exercise tyrannical power. And consequently he is rightly to be numbered among the wolves. From this it follows that prelates are bound in this case to defend all their people against him. DISCIPLE. Lower prelates ought to presume that whatever the Pope does, he does justly, and so they ought to presume that he justly orders those who attack him to be punished as they deserve. MASTER. Yet some say that here you fall into manifest heresy, into which, as they say, very many in modern times have fallen, as is reported of many who assert that the Pope is to be regarded as God on earth, and that therefore no one may judge that he ever commits any sin. They say, then, that it is manifest heresy that lower prelates ought to presume that whatever the Pope does, he does justly. For it would follow from this that if prelates saw the Pope invoking demons, blaspheming Christ, denying the faith, committing adultery, killing the innocent, defiling churches, selling benefices, and lending money at usury, they ought to excuse him and judge that he acts well, which is manifest heresy. They say, therefore, that according to the opinion of Bede, judgment is permitted of the manifest crimes of the Pope and of others, however many they be. This also is clearly established by the example of blessed Paul, who openly judged the deed of blessed Peter, and therefore publicly rebuked him for having acted badly. So if the Pope ordered those who wish to attack him to be mistreated before he showed that they attacked him wrongly, it would be lawful for anyone to judge that the Pope acts impiously and unjustly. Indeed, they ought to be suspicious of the principal charge itself, namely of heretical depravity, and prelates would be bound to defend their sheep from him as from a cruel wolf. DISCIPLE. It is strange what these men say, when they assert that anyone may judge that the Pope acts impiously and unjustly in this, and that prelates ought to defend against the Pope those who attack him in this way, since the Pope is the more immediate prelate of those who attack him than any lower prelate. Therefore whoever defends them against the Pope is known to do injury to the Pope by withdrawing his subjects from the Pope's jurisdiction. MASTER. To this it is answered that those who attack him in this way are a party against the Pope. Therefore the Pope ought not to be their judge in this matter, since no one ought to be judge in his own cause. DISCIPLE. This does not seem true of the Pope, because he can be judge in his own cause, as witnessed by Innocent III, who, as is held in the Extravagants, De iudiciis, Cum venisset, says: when the case concerns the privileges of the Apostolic See, we wish it to be judged by others. Therefore the Pope can be judge in his own cause. And consequently, if some wish to attack the Pope, the Pope himself can be judge, and so if he gives sentence against them, ordering that they be detained, imprisoned, or otherwise punished, his sentence must be upheld. MASTER. To some this appears wholly contrary to reason. For although the Pope ought to judge between litigants concerning the interpretation of privileges, because it belongs to the one who makes a law to interpret it, and although he could also be judge in his own cause when the matter concerns temporal things, yet he may not be judge when he is attacked for a crime. And so the Pope ought in no way to be judge when it is clear that he is being attacked for heresy by those who wish to attack him. Therefore, if the Pope punishes them for this, anyone may judge that he acts unjustly and impiously, and seeks to escape judgment. Hence he would also rightly be held suspect of heresy. DISCIPLE. Give other reasons. MASTER. The second reason for the same assertion is this. Prelates are more bound to defend those who attack the Pope for heretical depravity, before it is established to them that these men act from bad zeal, than they are bound to defend widows and orphans. But prelates are bound to defend widows and orphans (Dist. 87, c. 1, and the chapter Defensionis). Therefore much more are they bound to defend those who attack the Pope for heresy, before it is established to them that these are guilty. The third reason is this. Prelates are bound to defend their subjects (even against the Pope) against whom no cause of wrongdoing is alleged. For if the Pope wished to ruin some without any cause, prelates, if they can, are bound to defend them. Therefore much more are prelates bound to defend their subjects if they are unjustly sought by the Pope for death or some other ruin, on account of a cause which is to be presumed just. But those who desire to attack the Pope for heretical depravity, before it is established that they are moved by bad zeal, are to be presumed to have a just cause. Therefore they are above all to be defended by the prelates. The fourth reason is this. Those who are bound to correct the Pope for the crime of heresy are bound to defend those who wish to attack him for the same crime, unless it is established to them that these are moved by bad zeal. But prelates are bound to correct the Pope for heresy if they know that he has incurred heretical depravity, because otherwise the Pope could not be accused of heresy. Therefore they are bound to defend those who wish to attack him for heresy.

units.la: CAP. LIII.
units.tr: CAP. LIII.

units.la: In quo probatur quod etiam ad idem tenentur Reges & alterae potestates, & hoc vnica ratione.
units.tr: In which it is proved that kings and other powers are bound to the same duty, and this for one reason alone.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunquid reges & principes & aliæ publicæ potestates tenentur, volentes Papam de hæresi impugnare defendere? Magist. Dicunt quidam quod sic: fundantes se in hoc, quod causa fidei per sacros canones est causa vniuersorum fidelium. Et ideo omnes fideles tenentur causam fidei defendere, & fouere. Quare etiam debent defendere causam fidei prosequentes si non constat, quod eandem causam false prosequuntur & inique. Qui autem impugnant Papam de hæretica prauitate, causam fidei ostendunt se prosequi. Ergo reges & aliæ publicæ potestates eos tenentur defendere, si non constiterit eis, quod fouent causam iniustam. Hoc etiam probant plures rationes supra adductas.
units.tr: Disciple. Are kings and princes and other public powers bound, if they are willing to attack or defend the Pope on the charge of heresy? Master. Some say they are, resting on this: that the cause of the faith, according to the sacred canons, is the cause of all the faithful. Therefore all the faithful are bound to defend and foster the cause of the faith. Hence they ought also to defend those who pursue the cause of the faith, unless it is established that they pursue the same cause falsely and unjustly. Those who attack the Pope for heretical wickedness show that they are pursuing the cause of the faith. Therefore kings and other public powers are bound to defend them, unless it has become clear to them that they are supporting an unjust cause. This is also proved by the several reasons adduced above.

units.la: CAP. LIIII. Vbi inquiritur, utrum reges & principes pro tali defensione debeant arma movere? & quod sic, respondetur, & probatur tribus rationibus.
units.tr: CHAP. 54. Where it is asked whether kings and princes ought to take up arms for such a defence, and it is answered that they ought, and this is proved by three arguments.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunquid reges & principes debent arma movere pro defensione illorum, qui volunt Papam de haeresi impugnare? Magist. Respondent quidam sic, dicentes, quod si appareant dicentes se velle Papam de haeresi legitime impugnare: qui sunt tales, quod ab actione seu impugnatione Papae sunt nullatenus repellendi: reges & principes ac aliae publicae potestates, in quorum dominio seu iurisdictione morantur, pro eorum defensione res & personas, si oportuerit, tenentur exponere. Quod tali ratione nituntur ostendere. Pro defensione illorum debent reges & principes arma movere, si oportuerit, & etiam res & personas suas exponere, qui cum sint a regibus & principibus defendendi, prosequuntur causam pro qua reges & principes debent, si oportuerit, arma movere, ac etiam res & personas suas exponere. Quia cum tales ex tali causa defenduntur, magis defenditur causa quam ipsi. Sed reges & principes debent arma movere, ac res & personas suas exponere pro causa, quam taliter impugnantes Papam prosequuntur: quia pro causa fidei ad talia facienda tenentur. Ergo pro defensione eorum consimilia facere astringuntur. Item, reges pro iustitia usque ad mortem certare tenentur, iuxta illud Eccles. 4. usque ad mortem certa pro iustitia. Sed sicut iustum est reges & principes defendere fidem catholicam, ita iustum est eos defendere illos, qui causam fidei prosequuntur: cuiusmodi sunt inter alios illi, qui Papam de haeresi impugnare volunt. Ergo pro defensione eorum reges & principes usque ad mortem certare tenentur: & per consequens pro eis arma movere, ac res & personas suas exponere, si oportuerit, de necessitate iuste compelluntur. Amplius: non minus tenentur reges & principes repellere a subditis suis violentiam inferendam, quam tenentur vindicare illatam iniuriam. Sed reges & principes ad vindicandam iniuriam illatam volentibus Papam de pravitate haeretica impugnare, arma movere tenentur. Ergo etiam ad repellendam violentiam inferendam taliter impugnantibus Papam deberent arma movere. Et ita pro eorum defensione arma movere tenentur. Maior videtur aperta. Minor ostenditur sic. Non minus tenentur reges & principes arma movere pro vindicanda iniuria subditis illata in contemptum fidei Christianae, quam pro iniuria illata subditis in contemptum regiae maiestatis. Sed pro secundo reges arma movere tenentur, exemplo Dauid regis, qui, ut legitur 2. Reg. 10. Amonitas potenter invasit propter iniuriam factam nuntiis eius. Ergo reges & principes pro vindicanda iniuria illata in contemptum fidei Christianae arma movere tenentur.
units.tr: Disciple. Are kings and princes bound to take up arms in defence of those who wish to attack the Pope for heresy? Master. Some answer yes, saying that if there appear people who declare that they wish to attack the Pope for heresy lawfully (and who are such that they must in no way be driven back from the action or attack upon the Pope), then kings and princes, and the other public powers in whose dominion or jurisdiction they dwell, are bound, if necessary, to expose their goods and persons in their defence. They try to show this by the following reasoning. Kings and princes ought to take up arms, if necessary, and also to expose their goods and persons, in defence of those who, since they are to be defended by kings and princes, pursue the cause for which kings and princes ought, if necessary, to take up arms and expose their goods and persons. For when such people are defended on account of such a cause, the cause is defended more than the persons themselves. But kings and princes ought to take up arms and expose their goods and persons for the cause which those who attack the Pope in this way pursue, because they are bound to do such things for the cause of the faith. Therefore they are bound to do like things in defending them. Again, kings are bound to contend even unto death for justice, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus 4: "Contend even unto death for justice." But just as it is right for kings and princes to defend the Catholic faith, so it is right for them to defend those who pursue the cause of the faith, such as, among others, those who wish to attack the Pope for heresy. Therefore kings and princes are bound to contend even unto death in their defence, and consequently they are justly compelled, of necessity, to take up arms for them and to expose their goods and persons, if necessary. Furthermore: kings and princes are no less bound to repel violence being inflicted on their subjects than they are bound to avenge an injury done. But kings and princes are bound to take up arms to avenge an injury done to those who wish to attack the Pope for heretical depravity. Therefore they ought also to take up arms to repel violence being inflicted on those who attack the Pope in this way. And so they are bound to take up arms in their defence. The major premise is evident. The minor is shown thus: kings and princes are no less bound to take up arms to avenge an injury done to their subjects in contempt of the Christian faith than to avenge an injury done to their subjects in contempt of royal majesty. But kings are bound to take up arms for the second case, by the example of King David, who, as we read in 2 Kings 10, "powerfully invaded the Ammonites on account of the injury done to his messengers." Therefore kings and princes are bound to take up arms to avenge an injury done in contempt of the Christian faith.

units.la: CAP. LV. In quo respondetur ad auctoritates & rationes, quibus probatur, quod a Papa appellare non licet, c. 16. positas.
units.tr: CAP. LV. In which answer is given to the authorities and arguments, set out in chapter 16, by which it is proved that one may not appeal from the Pope.

units.la: Discipulus. Multa scrutati sumus de appellationibus a summo pontifice, & de impugnantibus ipsum, motiuaq; quaedam illorum, qui asserunt, quod saepe expedit a Papa haeretico appellare, licet (quantum est de iure divino & humano) non oporteat appellare, sed sufficit impugnare: & quod impugnantes Papam de haeretica pravitate, antequam constiterit eos malo zelo moveri, sunt a catholicis defendendi, iuvandi & fovendi. Quae omnia & eis annexa tecum post completionem operis iterum pertractabo: & quid tu de omnibus sentias, indagabo. Ideo finem istius materiae faciendo, dic quomodo ad allegationes, quibus ostenditur, quod a Papa appellare non licet, respondetur. Magist. Illae allegationes positae sunt supra c. 16. ubi per rationes & auctoritates ostenditur, quod in nullo casu licet a summo pontifice appellare. Ad intelligentiam autem auctoritatum dicunt quidam esse notandum, quod non semper verbum generale est generaliter intelligendum: quod per infinita exempla scripturae divinae dicunt posse probari, de quibus adducam pauca. Legitur enim 4. Reg. 7. Iuit ergo Azael in occursum eius (scilicet Helisei) habens secum munera, & omnia bona Damasci. De quo tamen constat, quod in Damasco etiam multa bona reliquit. Nec etiam de omni genere bonorum Damasci habuit secum. Non enim portavit aliqua secum de omni specie lapidum, vasorum, instrumentorum, lignorum, animalium, ciborum, metallorum, & caeterarum rerum, quae erant in Damasco. Etiam Marc. 1. de Ioh. legitur: Egrediebatur ad illum (scilicet Iohannem Baptistam) omnis iudaea regio, & Hierosolymitae universi, ut baptizarentur ab illo. Et tamen Hierosolymitae multi a Iohanne minime baptizati fuerunt: & patet, quod nulli sacerdotum & seniorum, qui erant Hierosolymis, ab ipso baptisari volebat, quia sibi nullatenus credebant, teste Salvatore, qui ut habetur Matt. 11. dicit: Venit ad vos Iohannes in via iustitiae, & non credidistis ei. Et ita verba praedicta non sunt generaliter intelligenda. Sic etiam saepe mandata generali iussione nonnulla intelliguntur, extra, de officio legati, quod translationem. Verba ergo generalia non semper debent generaliter intelligi. Per hoc ad auctoritatem Gelasii respondent quidam dicentes, quod ab Apostolica Sede, hoc est a Papa, nunquam prorsus est appellandum, nisi inveniatur contra fidem errare, vel in aliquo crimine, de quo scandalizetur Ecclesia, incorrigibilem se ostendat. Aliter dicunt aliqui, quod Gelasius loquitur de appellationibus, absque quibus sententia iudicis transit in rem iudicatam. Tali enim appellatione non est appellandum a Papa, licet contra fidem errauerit orthodoxam: quia talis sententia contra fidem, sive appellatur, sive non, non potest trasire in rem iudicatam, & ideo dicunt, quamuis liceat, tamen non est necesse a talia sententia appellare. Et quamuis à tali sententia aliquis non appellaret; in quodcunq; tempus transierit, licebit tamen sententiam impugnare. Aliter dicunt nonnulli, quod Gelasius loquitur de appellationibus pro causis particularibus, non pro causis, quae tangunt totam Christianitatem interiectis. Non enim licet appellare (vt dicunt) nisi Papa errauerit contra fidem, vel nisi sit incorrigibilis de aliquo crimine, de quo omnes Christiani laeduntur. Pro aliis autem causis appellare non licet: quamuis quidam dicant, quod si Ecclesia vniuersalis conueniret in vnum, ipsa haberet Papam de omni crimine iudicare. Discip. Quamuis non audierim, quod frater M. & adhaerentes sui istud vltimum opinentur, tamen alias super isto volo tecum diligentius disputare, & motiua eorum ad reprobandum sollicite perscrutari. Nunc vero dic, quomodo ad aliam auctoritatem Gelasii respondetur. Magist. Ad illam auctoritatem Gelasii respondetur, sicut ad praecedentem, quod loquitur in aliis causis, quam in causis fidei, vel de appellationibus, sine quibus sententia transit in rem iudicatam. Sunt enim nonnulli, qui horrent audire, quod quamuis Papa assereret legem Christianam esse falsam, & Christum fuisse pseudo Prophetam, modo liceret appellare ab ipso. Discip. Illae sunt haereles tam patentes, & totam fidem catholicam eneruantes, quod non est negandum, quin pro talibus à summo pontifice appellare liceat: tamen, vt videtur, pro aliis appellare non licet. Magist. Dicunt nonnulli, quod hic erras aperte; quia si licet pro maxima haeresi appellare à summo pontifice, & pro minima haeresi appellare licebit. Quia idem iuris est in parvis, sicut in magnis. Quod Alexander tertius, vt habetur extr. de appel. c. de appel. aperte testari videtur dicens: De appellationibus pro causis minimis interpositis volumus te tenere, quod eis pro quacunque tenuis causa fiant, non minus est quam siperent pro maioribus deferendum. Vbi dicit Glossa: Pro quocunque appellante ita potest quis gravari in parvo, sicut in magno. Quantitas causae non facit, quare introducta sit appellatio, sed magnum gravamen supra cap. 4. ad nostram. Et infra eodem cum speciali cap. perpe. Sicut etiam in minima re furtum committitur. 14. quaest. v. cap. vltimo. Ex his colligitur, quod si licet à summo pontifice appellum committitur, puta si pronunciaret vel assereret legem Christianam esse falsam & malare pro maxima haeresi: puta si pronunciaret vel assereret legem Christianam esse falsam & malam; vel Christum fuisse pseudoprophetā: licebit pro minima haeresi appellare ab ipso. Et consimili ratione licet impugnare & accusare Papam, si minimam haeresim qualitercunque sacris literis obuiantem praesumpserit affirmare. Per eandem rationem dicunt, quod si impugnantes etiam & accusantes Papam asserentem, quod fides Christiana est mala & falsa, sunt à catholicis defendendi: impugnantes etiā & accusantes de minima haeresi quantumcunq; latente sunt à catholicis defendendi.
units.tr: Disciple. We have examined at length the appeals from the supreme pontiff, and those who attack him, and some of the motives of those who assert that it is often expedient to appeal from a heretical Pope, although (so far as divine and human law go) one ought not to appeal, but it is enough to oppose him; and that those who oppose the Pope on account of heretical depravity, before it is established that they are moved by an evil zeal, are to be defended, aided and cherished by Catholics. I will go over all these points again with you, with what is connected to them, after the completion of the work, and I will inquire what you think of them all. So, to bring this subject to an end, tell me how the arguments by which it is shown that one may not appeal from the Pope are answered. Master. Those arguments were set out above in chapter 16, where by reasons and authorities it is shown that in no case is it lawful to appeal from the supreme pontiff. To understand the authorities, however, some say that it must be noted that a general word is not always to be understood generally. They say this can be proved by countless examples from Divine Scripture, of which I will give a few. For we read in 4. Reg. 7.: "Azael went to meet him (namely Elisha), taking with him gifts and all the good things of Damascus." Yet it is clear that he left many good things in Damascus as well, and he did not take with him every kind of good thing from Damascus. For he did not carry with him some of every kind of stone, vessel, implement, wood, animal, food, metal and other things that were in Damascus. Likewise we read in Mark 1. about John: "All the region of Judea went out to him (namely John the Baptist), and all the people of Jerusalem, to be baptized by him." And yet many of the Jerusalemites were not baptized by John at all; and it is plain that he did not wish to baptize any of the priests and elders who were in Jerusalem, because they did not believe him at all, as the Saviour testifies, who says in Matt. 11.: "John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him." So the words quoted are not to be understood generally. Likewise general commands are often understood in a limited sense, as in the Extra, on the office of the legate, concerning translation. General words, therefore, must not always be understood generally. In reply to the authority of Gelasius, some answer by saying that one must never at all appeal from the Apostolic See, that is from the Pope, unless he is found to err against the faith, or shows himself incorrigible in some crime which scandalizes the Church. Others say differently, that Gelasius speaks of appeals without which the sentence of a judge passes into a thing adjudged. With such an appeal one may not appeal from the Pope, even if he has erred against the orthodox faith; because such a sentence against the faith, whether it is appealed or not, cannot pass into a thing adjudged. Therefore, they say, although one may do so, it is not necessary to appeal from such a sentence. And even if someone does not appeal from such a sentence, it will nevertheless be lawful to oppose the sentence at whatever time. Some others say differently, that Gelasius speaks of appeals in particular causes, not in causes which touch the whole of Christendom. For it is not lawful to appeal (as they say) unless the Pope has erred against the faith, or unless he is incorrigible in some crime by which all Christians are injured. As for other causes, it is not lawful to appeal; although some maintain that if the universal Church came together into one, it would itself have the right to judge the Pope in every crime. Disciple. Although I have not heard that brother M. and his adherents hold this last view, I still wish to dispute this with you more carefully on another occasion, and to examine diligently their motives for rejecting it. But now tell me how the other authority of Gelasius is answered. Master. The other authority of Gelasius is answered as the preceding one was: that he speaks of causes other than causes of faith, or of appeals without which the sentence passes into a thing adjudged. For there are some who shrink from hearing that, even if the Pope should assert that the Christian law is false and that Christ was a pseudo-prophet, it would nevertheless be lawful to appeal from him. Disciple. Those are heresies so manifest, and so enervating of the whole Catholic faith, that it cannot be denied that for such things it is lawful to appeal from the supreme pontiff; yet, it seems, it is not lawful to appeal for other things. Master. Some say that you are plainly in error here; for if it is lawful to appeal from the supreme pontiff for the greatest heresy, it will be lawful to appeal for the smallest heresy too. For the law is the same in small matters as in great. Alexander III seems plainly to bear witness to this, as is found in the Extra, on appeals, chapter "On appeals," where he says: "We wish you to hold that appeals lodged in the smallest causes must be treated, whatever the trivial cause for which they are made, no less than if they were brought in greater matters." Where the Gloss says: "For any appellant, one may be aggrieved in a small matter just as in a great one. It is not the size of the cause that is the reason why appeal was introduced, but a serious grievance," see above chapter 4, "ad nostram." And below in the same title, in the special chapter "Perpe." Just as theft is committed even in a very small thing, 14. quaest. 5, last chapter. From these things it is gathered that if an appeal from the supreme pontiff is lawful, for instance if he should pronounce or assert that the Christian law is false and bad, and that Christ was a pseudo-prophet, then for the smallest heresy it will also be lawful to appeal from him. And by a like reasoning it is lawful to oppose and accuse the Pope if he presumes to assert any heresy, however small, that somehow opposes the sacred letters. By the same reasoning, they say, if those who oppose and accuse the Pope for asserting that the Christian faith is bad and false are to be defended by Catholics, then those who oppose and accuse him of even the smallest heresy, however hidden, are likewise to be defended by Catholics.

units.la: Discip. Ista nimis me vrgent, de quibus post opus istud mentem tuam exequiram. Nunc vero dic, quomodo ad rationes, quibus ostenditur, quod à Papa appellare non licet, respondetur. Magist. Ad primam respondetur, q; si Papa fieret haereticus, superiorem habet in terris. Et ideo ab eo appellare licet. Et ita licet impugnare & accusare ipsum. Ad secundā respondetur, q; à iurisdictione Papae haeretici sunt omnes catholici absoluti. Et ideo à Papa haeretico licet cuilibet appellare, non vt eximeretur à iurisdictione Papae haeretici: qui non per appellationem, sed per apostasiam Papae quilibet à iurisdictione sua est exemptus. Licet tamen appellare à Papa haeretico, quia forte videt, quod per appellationem vtilius & efficacius Papam haereticum poterit impugnare. Si autem Papa non errat contra fidem, appellans ab ipso false & iniquē non est à iurisdictione Papae simpliciter & absolute exemptus, sed ad tempus, vt Papae innocentia declaratur, & calumniator euidentius conuincatur, & à crimine puniatur. Nec est habendus pro exempto. Alii autem nescientes illum inique procedere, in fauorem fidei Christianae & vt vel Papae innocentia declaratur, vel eius malitia confundatur, debent tamen appellantem defendere, qui vt postquam fuerit de iniquitate conuictus, vt aceibe puniatur, fideliter laborare. Discip. Quid si Papa tenuerit aliquam assertionem contrariam veritati, quam non tenetur explicite credere: & alius ipsum de tali errore impugnauerit: catholicae, quam non tenetur explicite credere, nunquid talis impugnans à iurisdictione Papae est exemptus? Magist. Respondetur quod in hoc casu talis impugnans non est à tota iurisdictione Papae exemptus etiam ad tempus: quia in omnibus, quae non sunt in derogationem impugnationis suae, sicut prius obedire tenetur. Quantum vero ad illa, quae suam impugnationem impedire valerent, Papae deberet minime obedire: quia fi des catholica est summo pontifici praeferenda. Imo etiam quaelibet minima veritas catholica est summo pontifici etiam catholico praeponenda. Et ideo impugnantes assertionem Papae haereticam contrariam veritati, quam Papam explicite credere non tenetur (& propter hoc Papa in tali casu non esset haereticus, sed catholicus reputandus) in nullo debet obedire Papae in praeiudicium impugnationis suae legitimae: licet sibi in aliis teneatur obedire. Discip. Dic qualiter ad tertiam rationem respondetur. Magist. Dicitur quod ab obedientia Papae haeretici licet recedere, exemplo illorum, qui ab obedientia Anastasii secundi laudabiliter recesserunt. Ab obedientia autem Papae catholicorum, qui ab obedientia Anastasii secundi laudabiliter recesserunt, contra fidem, quo ad aliquid, quod non tenetur credere explicite, non licet absolute, licet errantis contra fidem, quo ad aliquid, quod non tenetur credere explicite, non licet absolute, licet assertionem suam licear impugnare. Et si aliquid praeciperet, quod esset in praeiudicium impugnationis suae, quantum ad hoc, non esset obediendum eidem. Capitulū autem dist. 2. assumptum loquitur de Papa haeretico super hoc praecipiente, q; fit in derogationem diuini honoris & fidei orthodoxae. Ad quartā rationem respondetur, quod non licet eidē, p eadē causa eodē tempore absolute appellare ab aliquo & ad ipsum. Et ideo qui appellaret à Papa, p haeresi, modo liceret sibi tūc, p haeresi appellare ad ipsum. Et si de facto appellaret, esset tanquā sibimet contrarius repellēdus. Pro diuerso autē tempore licet eidē, p eadē causa appellare ab aliquo & ad ipsum: & ecōuerso. Vnde saepe quis appellat ad episcopum suum vel metropolitanū, qui tamen postea, si senserit se grauatū indebite, vel reputauerit sententiam datam iniquam, appellat ab illo. Sic aliquis reputans Papam catholicum, poterit ad ipsum pro causa haeresis appellare: a quo tamen si aliquid diffinerit & asseruerit fidei contrarium orthodoxae, sibi appellare licebit. Ad quintam rationem respondetur, quod pro aliqua causa temporali appellare ab imperatore liceret: sicut etiam de aliqua posset coram Papa appellare. Nam & populus posset ex causa Imperatorem deponere; quemadmodum diversa regna suos reges deposuisse leguntur. Ad sextam respondetur, quod ab illo, ad quem sunt omnes causae fidei deferendae, non est appellandum, si non contra fidem errauerit orthodoxam. Si autem errauerit, licet appellare ab ipso, & etiam licet ipsum fortiter impugnare. Et tali impugnationi est ab omnibus catholicis deferendum. Et tales impugnantes sunt ab omnibus catholicis (quantum congruerit cuilibet) defendendi. Discip. Nunquid secundum illos tenentur catholici talibus impugnationibus summi pontificis adhaerere? Magist. Respondetur, quod multi tenentur taliter impugnantes Papam defendere, & eorum impugnationibus adhaerere. Quia ad hoc, quod aliquis teneatur taliter impugnantes Papam haereticum defendere, & impugnationibus eorum deferre, sufficit quod nesciat eos malo zelo Papam de haeresi impugnare. Cum etiam iudex quandoque sciens appellationem iniquam & falsam debeat eidem deferre. Ad hoc autem, quod teneatur quis impugnationibus adhaerere, requiritur quod sciat, quod talis impugnatio continet aequitatem & veritatem. Et ideo qui sciunt aliquos Papam de haeresi impugnare, quamuis non debeant impugnationibus eorum adhaerere, debent tamen eos defendere, quousque causa fuerit terminata, & iterum quaerere sollicite veritatem, iuxta legem divinam, quae ut habetur Deut. 13. sic praecepit: Si audieris in una urbium tuarum, quas Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi ad habitandum, dicentes aliquos, egressi sunt filii Belial, & euerterunt habitatores urbis, atque dixerunt: Eamus & seruiamus diis alienis, quos ignoratis. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod si aliqui asserunt Papam vel alium velle fidem corrumpere orthodoxam, non sunt statim repellendi, nec in continuo cruciandi, vel alias male tractandi: sed prius est veritas sollicite inquiranda; & per consequens ipsi interea sunt defendendi.
units.tr: Discip. These matters press on me hard, and after this work I will examine your view of them. But now tell me how the reasons by which it is shown that one may not appeal from the Pope are answered. Magist. To the first, it is answered that if the Pope became a heretic, he would have a superior on earth. Therefore one may appeal from him, and so one may also oppose and accuse him. To the second, it is answered that all Catholics are absolved from the jurisdiction of a heretical Pope. Therefore one may appeal from a heretical Pope to anyone, not in order to be exempted from the jurisdiction of a heretical Pope, since anyone is freed from his jurisdiction not by appeal but by the Pope's apostasy. Yet one may appeal from a heretical Pope, because perhaps by appeal he can oppose the heretical Pope more usefully and effectively. But if the Pope is not erring against the faith, one who appeals from him falsely and unjustly is not simply and absolutely exempted from the Pope's jurisdiction, but only for a time, so that the Pope's innocence may be declared, the slanderer may be more clearly convicted, and he may be punished for his crime. Nor is he to be regarded as exempt. Others, however, not knowing that he is proceeding unjustly, ought nevertheless to defend the appellant, in favour of the Christian faith and so that either the Pope's innocence may be declared or his malice confounded, and they should labour faithfully so that, once he has been convicted of injustice, he may be punished quickly. Discip. What if the Pope has held some assertion contrary to the truth, which one is not bound to believe explicitly, and another has opposed him over such an error? Is such an opponent not exempt from the Pope's jurisdiction? Magist. It is answered that in this case such an opponent is not exempt from the Pope's whole jurisdiction, even for a time, because in all matters that do not tend to undermine his opposition he is still bound to obey, as before. But as regards those things which could hinder his opposition, he ought by no means to obey the Pope, because the Catholic faith is to be preferred to the supreme pontiff. Indeed, even the smallest Catholic truth is to be placed before the supreme pontiff, even a Catholic one.
