Therefore those who oppose the Pope's heretical assertion, contrary to the truth, which the Pope is not bound to believe explicitly (and on account of this, in such a case the Pope would not be regarded as a heretic but as a Catholic), ought in no way to obey the Pope to the prejudice of their lawful opposition, although they are bound to obey him in other matters. Discip. Tell me how the third reason is answered. Magist. It is said that one may withdraw from the obedience of a heretical Pope, following the example of those who laudably withdrew from the obedience of Anastasius II. But from the obedience of a Catholic Pope, those who withdrew laudably from the obedience of Anastasius II did not withdraw absolutely, even if his assertion is opposed; and if he commanded anything that would be to the prejudice of their opposition, in that respect he should not be obeyed. The chapter assumed at dist. 2. speaks of a heretical Pope who commands this, namely something done to the dishonour of divine majesty and of the orthodox faith. To the fourth reason it is answered that it is not lawful for the same person, for the same cause, at the same time, to appeal absolutely from someone and to him. Therefore, one who appealed from the Pope for heresy could not at that time appeal to him for heresy; and if he did so in fact, he would be rejected as one contradicting himself. At a different time, however, it is lawful for the same person, for the same cause, to appeal from someone and to him, and conversely. Hence one often appeals to one's bishop or metropolitan, but afterwards, if he feels he has been unduly burdened, or thinks the sentence given was unjust, he appeals from him. So someone who regards the Pope as Catholic may appeal to him for a cause of heresy, yet if afterwards he should define and assert something contrary to the orthodox faith, it will be lawful for him to appeal from him. To the fifth reason it is answered that one could appeal from the emperor for some temporal cause, just as one could also appeal before the Pope in some matter. For the people too could depose an emperor for a cause; just as we read that various kingdoms have deposed their kings. To the sixth it is answered that one must not appeal from him to whom all causes of faith are to be referred, unless he has erred against the orthodox faith. But if he has erred, it is lawful to appeal from him and also to oppose him vigorously. And such opposition is to be supported by all Catholics (as far as it befits each one). And such opponents are to be defended by all Catholics (as far as is fitting for each). Discip. According to them, are Catholics bound to adhere to such oppositions to the supreme pontiff? Magist. It is answered that many are bound to defend those who oppose the Pope in this way, and to adhere to their opposition. For it suffices, for one to be bound to defend those who oppose a heretical Pope in this way and to yield to their opposition, that one does not know that they oppose the Pope on account of heresy out of a bad zeal. Since also a judge, who knows that an appeal is unjust and false, must sometimes yield to it. But to be bound to adhere to someone's opposition, it is required that one knows that such opposition contains equity and truth. Therefore those who know that some men oppose the Pope on a charge of heresy, although they ought not to adhere to their opposition, nevertheless ought to defend them until the case is decided, and again to seek the truth carefully, according to the divine law, which, as we have it in Deut. 13., commands thus: If you hear in one of your cities, which the Lord your God will give you to dwell in, that certain men, sons of Belial, have gone out and have overthrown the inhabitants of the city, and have said: Let us go and serve other gods, whom you do not know. From these words it is made clear that if some assert that the Pope or another wishes to corrupt the orthodox faith, they are not to be rejected at once, nor immediately tortured or otherwise ill-treated; but the truth must first be carefully sought, and consequently in the meantime they are to be defended.

units.la: CAP. LVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER 56.

units.la: Quaeritur, si Papa praevitate haeretica diffamatus impedierit inquisitionem de ipso fiendam, quid agendum sit catholicis, ubi nota de iniectione manuum violentarum in Papam, seu clericum, quomodo & quando fieri possit.
units.tr: It is asked: if the Pope, defamed for heretical depravity, hinders an inquiry into himself from being made, what the Catholics ought to do, and where the note of laying violent hands on the Pope, or on a cleric, may be incurred, and how and when it may be done.

units.la: Discipulus. Non modicam apparentiam habere videtur ex auctoritate Deuteron. 13. scripta videtur trahere falcimentum, quod si aliqui maxime viri literati & hactenus bonae opinionis & famae constanter affirmant & se offerant se probaturos Papam esse pravitate haeretica vitiatum vel irreticum: alii catholici debent in favorem fidei sollicite quaerere veritatem. Ideo ad primam materiam, a qua (ex quo de appellationibus a summo pontifice & impugnantibus ipsam tractavimus) aliqualiter disgressi videmur: volo reverti & diligenter discutere, qualiter si Papa fuerit diffamatus debent catholici inquirendo veritatem procedere: quia sic limpidius inspiciam veritatem. Inprimis autem cupio scire, quid secundum istas assertiones catholicis sit agendum, si postquam catholici zelo fidei Christianae accensi, inquirere coeperint de Papa super crimine haeresis diffamato, Papa taliter diffamatus eos totis viribus molitus fuerit impedire. Magist. Respondent aliqui, quod eo ipso quod Papa in hoc casu niteretur catholicos impedire, ne de ipso inquirerent veritatem, deberent ipsum magis suspectum habere; eo quod ostenderet se lucem odire, & quod nollet ad lucem distrahi iudicii venire, ne arguerentur ipsius errores. Et propter hoc debebent magis sollicite quaerere veritatem, & auxilium brachii secularis requirere pro inquisitione securius facienda. Discip. Quid si Papa nullo modo vellet desistere ab impediendo, ne ad inquisitionem procederent? Magist. Respondetur, quod si non possent catholici aliter ad inquisitionem procedere, nisi prius summum pontificem captivarent, ipsum deberent capere & tenere, si potentiam talem possent habere, invocato auxilio brachii secularis. Discip. Hic isti videntur contradicere assertioni priori. Nam prius dixerunt, quod nulla persona aut collegium habet iurisdictionem de haeresi super Papam mendaciter diffamatum, licet debeant catholici dubitare, an habeant iurisdictionem super ipsum. Et ideo teneantur ad inquisitionem procedere faciendam. Nunc autem dicunt, quod habent potestatem ipsum capiendi. Potestas autem capiendi nunquam est sine iurisdictione. Ergo sibi ipsis contradicunt aperte. Magist. Dicunt quod hic ostendis te scripturarum & rationis naturalis intellectum nequaquam habere. Nam potestas detinendi capiendi & ligandi freneticum & Dominum suum se praecipitare volentem, vel in aqua submergere, vel alio modo occidere semetipsum, secundum quod ex verbis beati Augustini, quae ponuntur 5. q. 5. non omnis, & 23. q. 4. c. ipsa pietas & c. minimum, colligitur evidenter, ad omnes in charitate existentes pertinet. Discip. Istud exemplum non est ad propositum: quia secus est de aliquo subdito se volente occidere, quia perdidit usum rationis: & de Papa, qui est omnium caput, in quem in nullo casu licet manus inicere violentas. Magist. Male dicis, ut dicunt, cum asseris, quod in nullo casu licet in Papam manus iniicere violentas: quamvis non licet in ipsum manus iniuriosas inicere, si Papa sive effectus freneticus, aut aliter alienatus a sensu non habens usum rationis ex desperatione vel tristitia vel alia causa quacunque, vellet seipsum occidere semetipsum de muro praecipitando, vel aliter, violenter esset tenendus. Si etiam esset in aliqua domo, quam quis sciret certissime ruituram, & ille sibi praenunciaret domum ruituram; si Papa nollet credere, nec exire, Papa in hoc casu esset extrahendus invitus, & ita manus violenta inicienda esset in Papam. In pluribus etiam casibus aliis licite posset quicunque servus manus iniicere violentas in Papam, ipsumque ligare, & fortiter detinere. Exita manifeste potestas capiendi & detinendi ab omni iurisdictione poterit separari. Non enim per phrenesim Papae vel alterius volentis occidi seipsum, tribuitur alicui iurisdictio supra volentem se occidere, & tamen tunc habet etiam servus potestatem capiendi, ligandi & etiam detinendi Papam. Discip. Cogor concedere, potestas capiendi, ligandi & detinendi ab omni iurisdictione poterit separari. Sed hoc non accidit, nisi quis velit seipsum occidere. Magist. Quid si Papa vellet absque necessitate in seipsum manus iniicere, oculos eruere, aut manus vel pedes abscindere? Discip. Etiam tunc posset licite ab alio absque iurisdictione ligari. Magist. Si Papa vellet alium occidere sine causa, nunquid illi liceret vim vi repellere absque iurisdictione? Discip. De hoc vellem scire, quid praedicti assertores dicant. Magist. Dicunt, quod liceret regi saltem vel laico vim vi repellere; & tamen per talem repulsam inrisdictionem super Papam repellendi vim ut minime obtineret. Discip. Non adducunt exempla, nisi ubi ipsi immineret mors corporalis, vel saltem laesio gravis. Magist. Si licet pro morte corporali, imo pro gravi iniuria corporali propria & aliena fidelium euitanda manus iniicere violentas in Papam absque iurisdictione speciali multitudinis fidelium: multo magis pro morte spirituali euitanda licebit in casu manus iniicere violentas in Papam. Consimili enim modo arguendi arguit beatus Augustinus ad probandum, quod licet in haereticos exercere vindictam, ut habetur 23. q. 4. c. ipsa pietas, fundans se in isto medio: omne quod debemus impendere hominibus pro morte eorum temporali vitanda, debemus eisdem dependere pro morte aeterna vitanda, dicit in haec verba: quid igitur de opere misericordiae pro vita aeterna adipiscenda & poena aeterna vitanda hominibus impendere iudicandum est, si pro salute ista non solum temporali, sed etiam brevi & ad tempus exiguum liberanda, sic nos subvenire hominibus ratio vera & benigna compellit? Ex quibus verbis & Augustino, processu ibidem, vbi per multa probat exempla, quod debemus etiam illos, qui minime sunt de iurisdictione nostra, liberare a morte invitos, & in eos iniicere manus violentas pro morte vitanda, colligunt isti, quod si pro vitanda morte Papae & alterius licet manus iniicere violentas in Papam, ipsumque capti uare, tenere & ligare; multo fortius licebit in casu pro morte spirituali vitanda ipsius Papae & alterorum pro vita aeterna adipiscenda, saluandoque grege dominico manus iniicere violentas in Papam ipsumq; fortiter ligare & tenere. Discip. Istud videtur apparens, si constaret Papam velle spiritualiter corrumpere orthodoxos, quod capi posset & teneri: sed propter infamiam fallam, de qua non constaret, quod non esset falsa, non esset hoc agendum. Magist. Non dicunt isti, quod propter insamiam Papa capiuari deberet: sed asserunt, quod si patenter impediret inquisitionem debitam fieri de ipso pro salute totius Christianitatis, deberet detineri per illos, qui tantam haberent potestatem temporalem: nec detinentes essent excommunicati. Sicut nec illi sententiam excommunicationis incurrerent, qui Papam volentem seipsum, vel alium innocentem absque causa occiderent, detinerent. Absque n. temeritate vel dolo non incidit quis in canonem propter iniectionem manuum in Papam vel alium clericum. Discip. Violentia non videtur esse sine temeritate vel dolo. Magist. Respondent, quod aequivocas de vocabulo violentia, & aliter vis vti vocabulo, quam ipsi accipiant. Episcopi enim accipiunt iniectionem manuum violentam pro omni iniectione manuum in inuitum, & sic constat, quod iniecto manuum violenta in aliquem potest esse charitativa absque omni temeritate & dolo.
units.tr: Disciple. It seems to carry no small plausibility, and the passage from Deuteronomy 13 that has been written seems to carry a sickle-like force, that if some men, most learned and hitherto of good opinion and reputation, constantly affirm and offer themselves to prove that the Pope is tainted with heretical depravity or is a heretic, then other Catholics ought to seek the truth diligently in favour of the faith. Therefore I wish to return to the first subject, from which we seem to have somewhat digressed (since we have treated of appeals from the supreme pontiff and of those who assail them), and to discuss carefully how the Catholics ought to proceed in seeking the truth if the Pope has been defamed; for in this way I shall look at the truth more clearly. But first I wish to know what, according to these assertions, is to be done by Catholics, if, after Catholics, kindled with zeal for the Christian faith, have begun to inquire into the Pope on a charge of heresy that has been spread abroad, the Pope, so defamed, has striven with all his strength to hinder them. Master. Some answer that, by the very fact that in this case the Pope tries to hinder Catholics from inquiring into the truth about him, they ought to hold him all the more under suspicion, because he shows that he hates the light and does not wish to be dragged into the light of judgment, lest his errors be exposed. And for this reason they ought all the more diligently to seek the truth, and to ask for the help of the secular arm in order to make the inquiry more securely. Disciple. What if the Pope were in no way willing to desist from hindering them from proceeding to the inquiry? Master. The answer is that if the Catholics could not otherwise proceed to the inquiry unless they first seized the supreme pontiff, they ought to seize and hold him, if they could have such power, calling upon the aid of the secular arm. Disciple. Here these men seem to contradict their earlier assertion. For they said before that no person or college has jurisdiction over the Pope when he has been falsely defamed of heresy, although Catholics ought to doubt whether they have jurisdiction over him, and therefore are bound to proceed to the inquiry. But now they say that they have the power of seizing him. Yet the power of seizing is never without jurisdiction. Therefore they plainly contradict themselves. Master. They say that here you show that you have no understanding of Scripture or of natural reason. For the power to restrain, seize and bind a madman who wishes to throw himself down, or to drown himself in water, or otherwise to kill himself, is, as is clearly gathered from the words of blessed Augustine quoted in 5 q. 5 non omnis and 23 q. 4 c. ipsa pietas and c. minimum, pertaining to all who are existing in charity. Disciple. That example is not to the purpose: for it is otherwise with a subject who wishes to kill himself, because he has lost the use of reason; and with the Pope, who is the head of all, against whom in no case is it lawful to lay violent hands. Master. They say you speak wrongly when you assert that in no case is it lawful to lay violent hands on the Pope: although it is not lawful to lay injurious hands on him, if the Pope, being a frenzied man, or otherwise deprived of his senses and without the use of reason, through despair or sadness or any other cause whatever, should wish to kill himself by throwing himself from a wall, or otherwise, he would have to be restrained by force. Likewise, if he were in some house which someone knew for certain was about to collapse, and that man warned him that the house was going to fall, and the Pope would not believe nor leave, then the Pope in this case would have to be drawn out against his will, and so violent hands would have to be laid on the Pope. In many other cases also, any servant might lawfully lay violent hands on the Pope, bind him and hold him fast. Thus it is plain that the power of seizing and restraining can be separated from all jurisdiction. For it is not through the frenzy of the Pope, or of another who wishes to kill himself, that jurisdiction over one who wishes to kill himself is given to anyone; and yet even then the servant has the power of seizing, binding and even restraining the Pope. Disciple. I am compelled to concede that the power of seizing, binding and restraining can be separated from all jurisdiction. But this does not happen unless someone wishes to kill himself. Master. What if the Pope wished, without necessity, to lay hands on himself, to tear out his eyes, or to cut off his hands or feet? Disciple. Even then he could lawfully be bound by another without jurisdiction. Master. If the Pope wished to kill another without cause, would it not be lawful for that man to repel force with force without jurisdiction? Disciple. On this I should like to know what the aforesaid asserters say. Master. They say that it would be lawful at least for a king, or a layman, to repel force with force; and yet by such repulsion he would not obtain any jurisdiction over the Pope for repelling force. Disciple. They do not adduce examples except where bodily death, or at least grave injury, threatens. Master. If it is lawful to lay violent hands on the Pope without special jurisdiction of the multitude of the faithful in order to avoid bodily death, or indeed grave bodily injury to oneself or to others among the faithful, then much more will it be lawful, in such a case, to lay violent hands on the Pope in order to avoid spiritual death. For blessed Augustine argues in a like manner to prove that it is lawful to exercise vengeance against heretics, as is found in 23 q. 4 c. ipsa pietas, founding himself on this principle: whatever we ought to bestow on men to avoid their temporal death, we ought to bestow on them to avoid eternal death. He says in these words: What then is to be judged of the work of mercy to be bestowed on men in order to obtain eternal life and to avoid eternal punishment, if true and kindly reason compels us to help men in this way for a salvation that is not only temporal but also brief and to be delivered for a very short time? From these words, and from Augustine's argument in the same place, where he proves by many examples that we ought also to deliver from death those who are in no way under our jurisdiction, even against their will, and to lay violent hands on them to avert death, these men conclude that if it is lawful to lay violent hands on the Pope, and to seize, hold and bind him, in order to avert the death of the Pope and of others, much more will it be lawful, in such a case, to lay violent hands on the Pope and to hold him fast and bind him firmly, in order to avert the spiritual death of the Pope himself and of others, and to obtain eternal life, and to save the Lord's flock. Disciple. That seems plausible, if it were established that the Pope wished to corrupt the orthodox spiritually, so that he could be seized and held; but on account of a false infamy, of which it was not established that it was not false, this ought not to be done. Master. These men do not say that on account of infamy the Pope ought to be seized; but they assert that if he openly hindered the due inquiry being made into him for the salvation of the whole of Christendom, he ought to be detained by those who had such temporal power, and those detaining him would not be excommunicated. Just as those who might detain a Pope who wished to kill himself, or another innocent man, without cause, would not incur the sentence of excommunication. For without rashness or deceit no one falls under the canon on account of laying hands on the Pope or on another cleric. Disciple. Violence does not seem to be without rashness or deceit. Master. They answer that you are equivocating about the word violence, and you wish to use the word in a different sense from what they understand by it. For the Bishops understand by laying violent hands any laying of hands on an unwilling person; and so it is plain that the laying of violent hands on someone can be charitable, without any rashness or deceit.

units.la: CAP. LVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 57.

units.la: Docet, ad quos spectat inquirere veritatem de eo, scilicet summo pontifice, si haeretica pravitate fuerit maculatus, seu graviter diffamatus.
units.tr: It teaches to whom it belongs to inquire into the truth about the Pope himself, namely whether he has been stained by heretical depravity or seriously defamed.

units.la: Discipulus. Ex quo secundum istos super Papa de crimine haeresis diffamato catholici habent inquirere, & ipsum etiam captiuare, si propter resistentiam eius aliter non possunt procedere ad inquisitionem faciendam, peto ut dicas, ad quos secundum istos assertores spectat inquisitio supradicta. Magist. Dicunt quod spectat ad illos catholicos, ad quos Papae spectaret punitio, si esset manifeste in haeresi deprehensus. Unde, ut dicunt, praedicta inquisitio primo & principaliter spectaret ad vniuersalem ecclesiam, si essent ita pauci catholici, quod omnes conuenirent in vnum, vel possent leuiter conuenire. Secundo pertineret ad concilium generale, quod vicem tenet vniuersalis ecclesiae. Tertio si nec vniuersalis ecclesia conuenire ret in vnum, nec generale conuocaretur concilium, spectaret ad dioecesanum, in cuius dioecesi moraretur Papa cum consilio vicinorum episcoporum, si esset necesse. Si autem Dioecesanus negligeret, pertineret ad sedem, vel clerum, vbi Papa moraretur. Si vero clerici omnes essent damnabiliter negligentes, talis inquisitio spectaret ad laicos.
units.tr: Disciple. Since, according to these men, Catholics must inquire into the Pope when he has been defamed of the crime of heresy, and even take him captive, if they cannot otherwise proceed to make the inquiry because of his resistance, I ask you to tell me to whom, according to these advocates, the aforesaid inquiry belongs. Master. They say it belongs to those Catholics to whom punishment of the Pope would belong if he were manifestly caught in heresy. Hence, as they say, the aforesaid inquiry would belong first and principally to the universal Church, if the Catholics were so few that they could all come together into one place, or could easily come together. Secondly, it would pertain to a general council, which holds the place of the universal Church. Thirdly, if neither the universal Church could come together into one place nor a general council be convoked, it would belong to the diocesan of the diocese in which the Pope was staying, together with the counsel of the neighbouring bishops, if it were necessary. But if the diocesan were negligent, it would pertain to the see or the clergy where the Pope was staying. If indeed all the clergy were damnably negligent, such an inquiry would belong to the laity.

units.la: CAP. LVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 58.

units.la: Vbi ostenditur, quæ & qualis debeat esse infamia, propter quam de Papa sit inquisitio facienda. Vbi nota de ortu fama alicuius, secundum distinctionem personarum, & qualis debeat fieri per iudicem processus in primo genere fame.
units.tr: Where it is shown what kind of infamy ought to be, and on account of which infamy an inquiry concerning the Pope is to be made. Here note the origin of the reputation of anyone, according to the distinction of persons, and how the judge ought to conduct the process in the first kind of reputation.

units.la: Discipulus. Video, quod isti proportionabiliter dicunt de inquisitione facienda de Papa super hæresi diffamato, sicut dicunt de punitione Papæ in manifesta hæresi deprehensi. Ideo istam materiam censeo differendam, quousque inuestigauero, quis debet punire Papam, qui manifeste deprehenditur de hæresi. Nunc autem dicas, propter quam infamiam secundum istos est de Papa inquisitio facienda. Magist. Vt ad tuam interrogationem perfecte respondeant, distinguunt: quod aut fama est orta a certis personis prouidis & discretis, integræ opinionis & famæ, ante infamiam Papæ volentibus Papam accusare de hæresi: aut orta est ab incerto auctore volente contra Papam inscribere, seu denunciare volente. Si primo modo, dicunt quod omnino procedendum est ad inquisitionem, nisi Papa sponte se velit iudicio bonorum virorum submittere, si autem orta est fama ab incerto auctore, vel certo denunciare volente, & non est tanta infamia, quin absque scandalo ecclesiæ & periculo fidei valeat tolerari, vel etiam dissimulari, non videtur quod sit ad inquisitionem procedendum: aliter de necessitate salutis tenetur ille, cuius interest, & potest, diligenter inquirere veritatem. Discipul. Dic quomodo secundum istos procedere debet iudex iuxta primum membrum. Magist. Dicunt, quod cum aliquis Papam vult de hæresi accusare, tunc ille, qui esset iudex Papæ in hæresi deprehensi, debet suam intentionem exprimere: quam iudex, quæcunque sit ille, siue ecclesiasticus, siue laicus, debet diligenter examinare. Et si inuenit ipsum ad accusandum idoneum, denunciet Papæ quod de hæretica prauitate impetitur, rogando eum quod iudicio eligendorum se submittat exemplo sanctorum patrum, qui pro minoribus criminibus se aliorum iudicio subiecerunt. Quod si Papa de sua confidens innocentia pro omni scandalo amouendo consenserit facere, eligantur iudices a Papa & accusare volente, qui secundum iustitiam sine personarum acceptione procedant. Si autem papa noluerit quoquomodo se submittere iudicio, ille, qui esset iudex manifeste Papæ in hæresi deprehensi, si habeat tantam potestatem temporalem, vel habere potuerit ratione dubii: quia dubitatur an sit de iurisdictione iudicis supradicti, citet eundem, & tandem, si potuerit, compellat Papam sibi respondere. Discip. Ista narratio multos videtur includere errores. Talis enim processus non est circa aliquem alium a Papa habendus. Ergo nec circa Papam. Item quomodo potest aliquis citare Papam, qui non est iudex Papæ? Amplius, non videtur, quod Papa teneatur iudicio cuiuscunque se submittere. Rursus: talis processus non videtur in legibus præfinitus. Quare temere isti talem modum procedendi præfigunt. Magist. Istas obiectiones & multas alias isti assertores faciunt contra seipsos. Respondentq; ad ipsas dicentes, primo ad vltimam, quod non intendunt aliquam formam procedendi circa Papam præfigere: sed quia Papa superiorem in causa hæresis, quamdiu manet Papa, non habet. Et qualiter sic, procederitur circa Papam, contra quem apparet legitimus accusator de hæresi in legibus minime inuenitur, ne Papa contra fidem errare possit insolenter, & catholicos secum trahere in errorem, oportet modum aliquem specialem rationi consonum, non verbis lecitis inuenire. Quemadmodum si regnum aliquod ex causa rationabili regem suum vellet compellere in iudicio coram populo respondere: quia in legibus regnorum de hoc casu nihil penitus habetur, oporteret modum aliquem specialem excogitare, qui esset in tali casu seruandus. Modus autem superius recitatus de Papa, quem cupit aliquis idoneus accusare, rationabilis istis apparet. Quare videtur illis, quod modus prædictus circa Papam congrue poterit obseruari. Nec tamen inuident cuicunq;, qui modum magis rationabilem excogitare valebit. Et forte in aliquo casu propter statem vel auctoritatem Papæ poterit dari modus certus in omni casu seruandus: nec forte propter potestatem, quod male arguis: talis processus non est tenendus circa alium a Papa: Ergo nec circa Papam, quia non constat, quod non habet superiorem in hac causa; eo quod non constat ipsum esse hæreticum, necesse est aliquid speciale seruare, & modo speciali procedere. Cum vero dicis, quod nullus potest citare Papam, qui non est iudex Papæ: Respondent, quia non solum qui est in rei veritate iudex alicuius, sed etiam qui dubitatur esse iudex, potest ipsum citare. Ideo potest quis citare Papam, quando dubitatur probabiliter, an sit iudex eius. Discip. Nemo debet dubitare se esse iudicem Papæ: quia debet esse certus, quod non est iudex Papæ antequam conuincatur. Magist. Videtur quod quamdiu non apparet quis idoneus, qui vellet accusare Papam, nec est graviter diffamatus, debet quilibet esse certus, se non esse iudicem Papæ. Quam cito autem apparet accusator idoneus, de quo præsumitur quod bono zelo Papam accusare proponitur; vel Papa est de hæresi graviter diffamatus, ita quod talis diffamatio conuenienter dissimulari non potest, quicunq; esset iudex Papæ, si Papa esset manifeste in hæresi deprehensus, posset probabiliter dubitare, se esse iudicem Papæ. Postquam autem Papa esset aperte in hæresi deprehensus, talis non debet dubitare, sed debet esse certus, quod est iudex Papæ. Non ergo in hoc casu quilibet debet esse certus, se non esse iudicem Papæ. Imo potest probabiliter dubitare, Papam ex suo delicto esse effectum de iurisdictione sua. lm, & propter dubitationem probabilem habet potestatem in iure citandi ipsum. Discip. Quid si non audet citare ipsum id est Papam. Magist. Respondent, quod si principes & potestates ac clerici & laici causam Dei negligerent; & favor Papae indebitus ita multitudinem occuparet, quod Papa nec ad submittendum se iudicio, nec ad respondendum quomodolibet induci vel cogi posset: non restaret illis, qui eum de iure citare deberent, nisi dolor & gemitus, & esset eis seruandum consilium beati August. quod dat catholicis, quando potestas habet multitudinem sociorum, qui lib. 2. contra Episcopum Parmenianum vt recitatur 23. q. 4. c. non potest, ait: non potest esse a multis salubris correctio, nisi cum ipse corripitur, qui non habet socium multitudinem. Cum veruidem morbus plurimos occupauerit, nihil aliud boni restat, quam dolor & gemitus. Et infra: venerun cum contagio peccandi multitudinem inuaserit divina disciplina vera misericordia necessaria est. Nam consilia separationis & inania sunt isti & perniciosa, atque sacrilega, quia impia & superba, & plus perturbant bonos infirmos, quam corrigant animosos malos. Et infra: turba autem iniquorum, cum facultas est in populu promendi sermonem, generali obiurgatione ferienda est, & maxime si occasionem atq; opportunitatem prebuerit Deo, qua eos appareat pro suis meritis vapulare. Sic si contra Papam appareat idoneus accusator, vel ipse fuerit de haeresi graviter diffamatus, si multitudo sibi faueret, vt nec induci vel cogi posset in iudicio parere, nihil aliud accusatori illius, qui esset iudex suus, si esset manifeste in haeresi deprehensus, & aliis catholicis bonis restaret quam dolor & gemitus. Tunc enim citatio & accusatio essent inanes: & tamen non solum occulte, sed etiam publice, cum facultas haberetur, absq; perturbatione bonorum essent fautores Papae graviter increpandi, & modis omnibus inducendi, vt laborarent fideliter, quantum liceret pro officio cuiuslibet, quatenus in fauorem fidei Christianae Papa iudicio se submitteret illius, qui esset iudex suus, si esset manifeste in haeresi deprehensus, responderet rogaretur. Cum autem dicis, quod Papa non tenetur se submittere iudicio cuiuscunque: respondent, quod in casu pro scandalo evitando, & veritate catholica declaranda & exaltanda, ac pro communi utilitate procuranda, tenetur Papa de necessitate salutis se iudicio inferiorum submittere.
units.tr: Student. I see that these men say, in a parallel way, about an inquiry to be made into the Pope when he is defamed of heresy, just as they say about the punishment of the Pope when he is caught in manifest heresy. So I think this matter should be postponed until I have investigated who ought to punish the Pope who is manifestly caught in heresy. For now, however, tell me on account of what infamy, according to them, an inquiry concerning the Pope is to be made. Master. So that they may answer your question fully, they make a distinction: either the reputation has arisen from certain prudent and discerning persons of unblemished opinion and reputation, who, before the Pope's infamy, were willing to accuse the Pope of heresy; or it has arisen from an unknown author who wishes to post or denounce something against the Pope. If it is the first way, they say that proceeding to an inquiry is entirely necessary, unless the Pope himself is willing to submit to the judgment of good men. But if the reputation has arisen from an unknown author, or from a known one who wishes to denounce, and the infamy is not so great that it can be tolerated, or even overlooked, without scandal to the Church and danger to the faith, it does not seem that one should proceed to an inquiry; otherwise, by the necessity of salvation, whoever is concerned and able is bound to diligently inquire into the truth. Student. Tell me how, according to them, the judge ought to proceed under the first member. Master. They say that when someone wishes to accuse the Pope of heresy, then he who would be the judge of the Pope caught in heresy ought to state his intention; and the judge, whoever he may be, whether ecclesiastical or lay, ought to examine it diligently. And if he finds the accuser suitable, he should announce to the Pope that he is being attacked for heretical depravity, asking him to submit himself to a judgment of elected men, after the example of the holy fathers, who submitted themselves to the judgment of others even for lesser crimes. But if the Pope, confident of his innocence, consents to do this in order to remove all scandal, judges are to be chosen by the Pope and by the accuser who is willing, and they are to proceed according to justice, without respect of persons. If, however, the Pope is unwilling in any way to submit himself to judgment, then he who would be the manifest judge of the Pope caught in heresy, if he has such temporal power, or could have had it on account of doubt (since it is doubted whether he falls under the jurisdiction of the aforesaid judge), let him cite the same, and at length, if he can, compel the Pope to answer to him. Student. This account seems to contain many errors. For such a process is not to be held against anyone other than the Pope; therefore neither against the Pope. Again, how can anyone cite the Pope who is not his judge? Further, it does not seem that the Pope is bound to submit to the judgment of anyone whatever. Again: such a process does not seem to be prescribed in the laws. Why, then, do these men rashly prescribe such a mode of proceeding? Master. These assertors raise these objections and many others against themselves. And they answer them, first to the last, saying that they do not intend to prescribe any form of proceeding against the Pope; but because the Pope, as long as he remains Pope, has no superior in a cause of heresy. And as to how a proceeding is to be conducted against the Pope, against whom a lawful accuser of heresy appears, this is by no means found in the laws; so that the Pope may not be able to err insolently against the faith and draw Catholics with him into error, it is necessary to find some special mode consonant with reason, not one by lawful words. Just as if some kingdom, for a reasonable cause, wished to compel its king to answer in judgment before the people: since nothing at all is found in the laws of kingdoms about this case, one would have to devise some special mode to be observed in such a case. But the mode recited above concerning the Pope, whom someone suitable wishes to accuse, appears reasonable to them. Therefore it seems to them that the aforesaid mode can fittingly be observed with regard to the Pope. Nor do they begrudge anyone who will be able to devise a more reasonable mode. And perhaps in some case, on account of the status or authority of the Pope, a certain mode may be given to be observed in every case; nor, perhaps, on account of his power, as you argue wrongly: such a process is not to be held against anyone other than the Pope; therefore neither against the Pope, because it is not established that he has no superior in this cause. Since it is not established that he is a heretic, it is necessary to observe something special and to proceed in a special mode. As for your saying that no one can cite the Pope who is not his judge, they answer that not only he who is in truth the judge of someone, but also he who is doubted to be the judge, can cite him. Therefore anyone can cite the Pope when it is probably doubted whether he is his judge. Student. No one ought to doubt that he is the judge of the Pope, because he ought to be certain that he is not the Pope's judge until he is convicted. Master. It seems that as long as no suitable person appears who would wish to accuse the Pope, and he is not gravely defamed, anyone ought to be certain that he is not the judge of the Pope. But as soon as a suitable accuser appears, of whom it is presumed that he is proposed to accuse the Pope with good zeal, or the Pope is gravely defamed of heresy, so that such defamation cannot fittingly be overlooked, whoever would be the judge of the Pope, if the Pope were manifestly caught in heresy, could probably doubt that he is the Pope's judge. But after the Pope has been openly caught in heresy, such a person ought not to doubt, but ought to be certain that he is the judge of the Pope. In this case, therefore, not everyone ought to be certain that he is not the Pope's judge. Indeed, he can probably doubt that the Pope has, by his own crime, been made subject to his jurisdiction. Indeed, on account of a probable doubt he has the power in law to cite him. Student. What if he does not dare to cite him, that is, the Pope? Master. They answer that if princes and powers, as well as clergy and laity, neglected the cause of God, and an undue favour toward the Pope so occupied the multitude that the Pope could not be induced or compelled in any way either to submit to judgment or to answer, then there would remain for those who ought to cite him by right nothing but grief and groaning; and they should observe the counsel of blessed Augustine, which he gives to Catholics when a power has a multitude of allies. He says, in the second book against Parmenian the bishop, as is recited in 23 q. 4 c. non potest: There cannot be salutary correction by many, except when he who is not accompanied by a multitude is himself corrected. But when the same disease has taken hold of very many, nothing else of good remains but grief and groaning. And below: when the contagion of sinning has invaded the multitude, divine discipline and true mercy are necessary. For the counsels of separation are vain, pernicious, and sacrilegious, since they are impious and proud, and they disturb the good weak ones more than they correct the proud bad ones. And below: but the crowd of the wicked, when there is opportunity to speak to the people, must be struck with a general rebuke, especially if it has offered God an occasion and opportunity by which it may appear that they are being beaten for their merits. Thus, if a suitable accuser appears against the Pope, or he himself has been gravely defamed of heresy, and the multitude favoured him so that he could not be induced or compelled to appear in judgment, nothing else would remain for his accuser, for him who would be his judge if he were manifestly caught in heresy, and for the other good Catholics, than grief and groaning. For then citation and accusation would be in vain. And yet, not only secretly but also publicly, when the opportunity were had and without disturbance of the good, the partisans of the Pope were to be severely rebuked, and by all means induced to labour faithfully, as far as it is lawful for the office of each, so that for the favour of the Christian faith the Pope might be asked to submit himself to judgment, and to answer before him who would be his judge if he were manifestly caught in heresy. But when you say that the Pope is not bound to submit to the judgment of anyone whatever, they answer that in a case, for the avoiding of scandal and for declaring and exalting Catholic truth, and for procuring the common good, the Pope is bound by the necessity of salvation to submit himself to the judgment of inferiors.

units.la: CAP. LIX.
units.tr: CAP. LIX.

units.la: Ostendit, quod Papa in casu illo de necessitate salutis tenetur se submittere iudicio suorum inferiorum, si accusator appareat idoneus. Et probatur unica ratione.
units.tr: Shows that in that case the Pope is bound, as a matter of necessity for salvation, to submit to the judgment of his inferiors, if the accuser appears to be a fit one. And this is proved by a single argument.

units.la: Discipulus. Ostende rationem eorum, quare si appareat accusator idoneus, Papa de necessitate salutis se iudicio inferiorum suorum submittere tenetur. Magist. Non putes, quod ipsi intendant dicere, Papam in omni casu ad voluntatem cuiuslibet se debere submittere iudicio aliorum: sed volunt, quod absq; causa rationabili Papa non debet iudicium recusare, quando ex submissione sua declaretur veritas & iustitia. Et talis submissio nulli speciale praeiudicium generaret, & accusantis zelus vel malitia pandieretur. Ad hoc autem dicendum tali ratione moventur. Utilitas propria & communis sunt praeferendae malitiae propriae & alienae, omniq; utilitati Papae temporali. Nam multorum utilitas praeferenda est utilitati vnius, vt habetur 7. q. 1. Scias, & 2. quaest. 1. in scripturis, & 23. q. 3. quia ad perpetuum. Ergo multo fortius utilitas propria & communis praeferendae sunt utilitati propriae: & multo fortius praeferendae sunt malitiae propriae & alienae. Sed Papa, quem accusator idoneus vult de haeresi accusare, submittendo se iudicio catholicorum procurat utilitatem propriam & communem: quia procurat declarationem veritatis & iustitiae, quae est utilitas propria & communis. Et haec utilitas propriam utilitatem non impedit. Ergo Papa ad hoc tenetur in casu hoc de necessitate salutis. Hoc autem faciendo, si est innocens, ab omni impetitione super crimine falso liberat semetipsum, accusantisq; malitiam vel innocentiam manifestat, & veritatem exaltat; ac bono exemplo sibi subditos aedificat vniuersos, dum ex zelo veritatis & iustitiae suorum inferiorum iudicium non recusat. Si ergo Papa est reus, multo magis tenetur se submittere aliorum iudicio, vel sponte renunciare papatui: quia absque periculo animae non potest papatui praesidere: eo quod omnis haereticus publicus & occultus est omni ecclesiastica dignitate priuatus. Discip. Ista assertio videtur probabilitate carere, quia per praedictam rationem Papa pro omni iniuria, quam faceret alicui, & pro omni excessu tenetur se subdere aliorum iudicio. Si enim pro crimine falso teneretur se subdere iudicio aliorum: multo fortius pro vera iniuria & vero excessu se subdere iudicio teneretur. Sed hoc constat esse falsum, & per verba Aug. euidenter conuincitur, qui in libro De vita clericorum, vt recitatur dist. 86. vbi asserit manifeste, quod cum praelatus corrigendo subditos suos modum excedit, ab eis nequaquam exigitur, vt veniam a subditis expostulet. Ergo multo magis si Papa de crimine falso impetitur, non est necesse, quod inferiorum iudicio se submittat. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur, quod non est simile de iniuriis & non nullis aliis criminibus, & de haeresi: quia iniuriae & alia crimina multa, Papam reum non deponunt, potestq; Papa aliter satisfacere pass is iniuriam, & de suis scandalizatis excessibus, quam se alicuius iudicio submittendo. Et ideo quando potest, non tenetur se submittere iudicio alicuius. Sed crimen haeresis Papam de papatu deponit ipso facto. Et ideo si non potest aliter satisfacere accusare volenti, & scandalizatis de ipso, nisi se submittat iudicio, ad hoc de necessitate salutis astringitur. Et consimiliter dicunt, quod si Papa de aliqua iniuria vel aliquo excessu non aliter posset satisfacere illi vel illis, cui vel quibus tenetur, quam se submittendo iudicio, ad hoc esset de necessitate salutis astrictus. Si vero Papa se nullius subdendo iudicio potest satisfacere ipsum de haeresi accusare volenti, & aliis scandalizatis de ipso poterit alium modum tenere. Ad Augustin. dicunt, quod praelatus, qui in corrigendo modum excedit, aliter potest potest satisfacere subditis, quam ab eis veniam postulando. Et ideo non exigitur de ipso, ut veniam postulet ab eis. Discip. Quomodo secundum istos posset Papa satisfacere accusare violenti, nisi subderet se alicuius iudicio? Magist. Respondetur, quod saepe potest negativa probari: Et ideo si esset talis casus, quod contrarium illius, quod accusare volens intendit, posset Papa probare, sufficeret Papae talem negativam probare, nec tunc tenetur se subdere alicuius iudicio.
units.tr: The Pupil: Show me the reasoning by which they hold that, if a fit accuser appears, the Pope is bound, as a matter of necessity for salvation, to submit to the judgment of his inferiors. The Master: Do not suppose that they mean the Pope must in every case submit to the will of anyone whatever in judgment. Rather, they hold that without a reasonable cause the Pope ought not to refuse judgment when, by his submission, truth and justice are made manifest, and the zeal or malice of the accuser is laid bare. Their reason for this is as follows. Our own advantage and the common advantage are to be preferred to our own malice and that of others, and to every temporal advantage of the Pope. For the advantage of many is to be preferred to the advantage of one, as is held in 7 q. 1 "Scias", and 2 q. 1 "In scripturis", and 23 q. 3 "Quia ad perpetuum". Therefore much more strongly are our own and the common advantage to be preferred to one another's advantage, and much more strongly are they to be preferred to our own malice and that of others. But the Pope, whom a fit accuser wishes to accuse of heresy, by submitting himself to the judgment of Catholics, secures his own and the common advantage, because he secures the declaration of truth and justice, which is an advantage both proper and common. And this advantage does not hinder his own advantage. Therefore in this case the Pope is bound to do so as a matter of necessity for salvation. Moreover, by doing this, if he is innocent he frees himself from every charge of a false crime, and makes manifest the malice or the innocence of the accuser, and exalts the truth; and by a good example he edifies all his subjects, while from zeal for truth and justice he does not refuse the judgment of his inferiors. If therefore the Pope is guilty, he is much more bound to submit himself to the judgment of others, or to renounce the papacy of his own accord, since without danger to his soul he cannot preside over the papacy, because every heretic, whether open or secret, is deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity. The Pupil: This assertion seems to lack probability, because by the aforesaid reasoning the Pope would be bound to submit himself to the judgment of others for every injury he did to anyone and for every excess. For if he were bound to submit to the judgment of others for a false crime, much more strongly would he be bound to submit to their judgment for a true injury and a true excess. But this is plainly false, and it is clearly refuted by the words of Augustine, who in his book On the Life of Clerics, as it is quoted in dist. 86, asserts plainly that when a prelate in correcting his subjects exceeds the measure, they by no means require of him that he beg pardon from them. Therefore much more, if the Pope is charged with a false crime, it is not necessary that he submit himself to the judgment of his inferiors. The Master: To this it is answered that the case of injuries and certain other crimes is not like that of heresy. For injuries and many other crimes do not depose the Pope as guilty, and the Pope can make satisfaction for the injury done and for the excesses that have given scandal in another way than by submitting himself to someone's judgment. And therefore, when he can, he is not bound to submit himself to anyone's judgment. But the crime of heresy deposes the Pope from the papacy by the very fact. And therefore, if he cannot otherwise make satisfaction to one who wishes to accuse him, and to those scandalized by him, unless he submits himself to judgment, he is bound to this as a matter of necessity for salvation. And they likewise say that if the Pope could not otherwise make satisfaction for some injury or excess to the person or persons to whom he is bound than by submitting to judgment, he would be bound to this as a matter of necessity for salvation. But if the Pope, by submitting himself to no one's judgment, can satisfy the one who wishes to accuse him of heresy, and the others scandalized by him, he may adopt another course. To Augustine they reply that a prelate who exceeds the measure in correcting can satisfy his subjects in another way than by begging pardon from them. And therefore it is not required of him that he beg their pardon. The Pupil: How, according to these men, could the Pope satisfy an accuser who wishes to accuse him, unless he submitted himself to someone's judgment? The Master: It is answered that a negative can often be proved. And therefore, if there were such a case that the Pope could prove the contrary of what the accuser intends, it would suffice for the Pope to prove such a negative, and then he is not bound to submit himself to anyone's judgment.

units.la: CAP. LX.
units.tr: CHAPTER LX.

units.la: In quo declaratur, quomodo se debeat habere summus pontifex, si se sponte arbitrorum iudicio submiserit, si accusans ipsum in probatione defecerit. Et ponuntur duae conclusiones, & prima, scil. quod de necessitate salutis se teneatur purgare, si grave scandalum apud catholicos generaretur, probatur octo rationibus.
units.tr: In which it is explained how the supreme pontiff ought to conduct himself if he has voluntarily submitted himself to the judgment of arbitrators, and his accuser fails to prove the charge. Two conclusions are laid down, and the first, namely that he is bound by necessity of salvation to clear himself if grave scandal would arise among Catholics, is proved by eight arguments.

units.la: Discipulus. Puto quod intelligam istorum in hac parte sententiam. Sed quaeso indica mihi, quid isti iudicant agendum, si Papa se sponte iudicio arbitrorum submiserit, & accusator in probatione defecerit: an scil. Papa teneatur se purgare. Magist. Dicunt, quod si Papa apud bonos & graves est enormiter de haeresi diffamatus, ita quod grave scandalum apud catholicos est exortum, ipse de necessitate salutis se purgare tenetur, si aliter famam suam recuperare non potest. Si autem taliter non est diffamatus, ad purgationem minime obligatur. Discip. Pro primo membro si habes aliqua motiva, profer in medium. Magist. Dicta assertio pluribus rationibus videtur posse probari. Quarum prima talis est: qui famam suam integram & illaesam servare tenetur, si potest, etiam ipsam si absque culpa sua vel etiam ex negligentia laesa est vel perdita de necessitate salutis reparare & restaurare, si potest, astringitur. Sed Papa de necessitate salutis (si absque crimine potest) tenetur famam suam illaesam & integram custodire. Ergo si fama Papae est ex aliquo casu laesa vel perdita, & ipse est immunis, de necessitate salutis si potest famam suam recuperare vel restaurare & reintegrare tenetur. Et per consequens si non potest aliter, quam se purgando hoc facere, se purgare legitime de necessitate tenetur. Maior videtur evidens. Minor probatur auctoritate Augustini, qui, ut legitur 12. q. 1. cap. nolo, ait: nolo ut aliquis de nobis inveniat occasionem male viuendi. Providemus enim bona, ut ait Apostolus, non solum coram Deo, sed etiam coram omnibus hominibus, propter nos conscientia nostra necessaria est: propter vos fama nostra non pollui, sed pollere debet in nobis. Duae res sunt, conscientia & fama bona. Conscientia necessaria est tibi, fama proximo tuo. Qui confidens conscientia sua negligit famam suam, crudelis est. Item Greg. ut habetur 11. q. 3. cap. Non sunt audiendi sive viri sive foeminae, qui quando reprehenduntur in aliqua negligentia, per quam sit, ut in malam veniant suspitionem (unde vitam suam longe abesse sciunt) dicunt coram Deo sufficere sibi conscientiam puram, existimationem hominum non solum impudenter, verumetiam crudeliter contemnentes, cum occidant animas aliorum. Et infra: Provide quisquis a criminibus flagitiorum atque facinorum vitam suam custodit, sibi benefacit: quisquis etiam famam, aliis miscricors est. Nobis enim est necessaria vita nostra, aliis fama. Ex his aliisque quamplurimis colligitur evidenter, quod quilibet Christianus, quantum in ipso est, famam suam servare debet illaesam. Ergo potissime ad hoc summus pontifex obligatur. Quia ad illa, quae sunt de iure naturae & ad utilitatem proficiunt aliorum non minus quam alii, est astrictus. Et ex hoc evidenter infertur, quod famam suam, si laesa est vel perdita (si non potest aliter) per purgationem restaurare debet.
units.tr: Student. I think I understand their opinion on this point. But please tell me what they judge should be done if the Pope has voluntarily submitted himself to the judgment of arbitrators, and the accuser has failed to prove his case: namely, whether the Pope is bound to clear himself. Master. They say that if the Pope has been grievously defamed of heresy among good and serious men, so that grave scandal has arisen among Catholics, he is bound by necessity of salvation to clear himself, if he cannot otherwise recover his reputation. If, however, he has not been defamed in this way, he is by no means obliged to purge himself. Student. If you have any arguments for the first part, bring them forward. Master. This assertion can be proved by several arguments. The first is this: whoever is bound to keep his reputation whole and unharmed, if he can, is also bound, by necessity of salvation, to repair and restore it, if he can, even when it has been damaged or lost without his own fault or through someone else's negligence. But the Pope is bound by necessity of salvation (if he can do so without sin) to keep his reputation unharmed and whole. Therefore, if the Pope's reputation has been damaged or lost through some occurrence, and he is himself blameless, he is bound by necessity of salvation to recover or restore his reputation and make it whole again, if he can. And consequently, if he cannot do this otherwise than by clearing himself, he is lawfully bound by necessity to clear himself. The major premise seems evident. The minor is proved by the authority of Augustine, who, as is read in 12. q. 1, c. nolo, says: I do not want anyone to find an occasion for living badly among us. For we provide good things, as the Apostle says, not only before God but also before all men. Our conscience is necessary for us; our good name must not be polluted, but must shine among you. There are two things, conscience and a good name. Conscience is necessary for you, a good name for your neighbour. He who trusts in his conscience and neglects his good name is cruel. Likewise Gregory, as is found in 11. q. 3, c. Non sunt audiendi: Men or women who, when they are rebuked for some negligence through which they fall into bad suspicion (though they know their life is far from it), say that a clear conscience is enough for them before God, despise the esteem of men not only shamelessly but also cruelly, since they destroy the souls of others. And below: Whoever guards his life from the crimes of shameful and wicked deeds does good to himself; whoever is also merciful to others in guarding his good name does good to them. For our life is necessary for us, our good name for others. From these and very many other passages it is clearly gathered that every Christian, so far as in him lies, ought to keep his reputation unharmed. Therefore the supreme pontiff is bound to this above all. For he is bound to those things which belong to the law of nature and profit others no less than they profit anyone else. And from this it is plainly inferred that if his reputation has been damaged or lost, he ought to restore it by purgation, if he cannot do so otherwise.

units.la: Secunda ratio est haec, non minus debet Papa bonis satisfacere & modestis, apud quos de haeresi graviter infamatur, quam detractoribus malevolis & malignis, teste Gregor. ut habetur 11. q. 3. cinter verba: Quid enim si homines nos non laudant, & conscientia nostra liberos nos esse demonstraret. Et infra: quid enim aliud detrahentes faciunt, nisi in pulverem sufflant, ut in oculos suos terram excitent: ut unde plus detractationis perflant, inde magis nihil veritatis videant. Vocandi tamen sunt etiam ipsi, & tranquille admonendi, cui satisfieri modis omnibus debet, scientes quod de iudaeis veritas dicit, ne forte scandalizemus eos. Ex quibus verbis patet ergo habetur, quod innocens a detractoribus malevolis & malignis mendaciter diffamatus ipsis modis omnibus satisfacere debet. Ergo multo magis sive fortius, si Papa apud bonos & honestos est de haeresi graviter vel mendaciter diffamatus. Et per consequens, si non potest aliter excusare, purgando satisfacere debet.
units.tr: The second argument is this: the Pope ought to satisfy good and modest men, among whom he is gravely defamed of heresy, no less than malevolent and malignant detractors, as Gregory teaches, as is found in 11. q. 3, among the words: For what if men do not praise us, and our conscience shows that we are free? And below: For what else do detractors do but blow dust into the air, so as to stir earth into their own eyes, so that the more they blow up detraction, the less they see any truth? Yet they too must be called, and gently admonished, and satisfied in every way, knowing that the truth speaks of the Jews, lest perhaps we scandalize them. From these words it is therefore plain that an innocent man, who has been falsely defamed by malevolent and malignant detractors, ought to give them satisfaction in every way. Much more, then, and more strongly, if the Pope has been gravely or falsely defamed of heresy among good and honest men. And consequently, if he cannot otherwise excuse himself, he ought to satisfy them by clearing himself.

units.la: Tertia ratio est haec. Papa non minus quam alii peccatum mortale vitare tenetur. Sed cum diffamatus de crimine recusat se purgare (cum non potest sua innocentiam aliter declarare) est peccatum mortale; cum hoc sit scandalizare pusillos & infirmos; & etiam magnis & perfectis occasionem scandali dare. Tale autem scandalum est peccatum mortale. Quod ex gravitate poenae (quae sibi debetur) constat aperte, cum Salvator dicat Matth. 6. Qui autem scandalizaverit unum de pusillis, qui in me credunt, expedit ei, ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo eius, & demergatur in profundum maris. Ergo Papa tale scandalum de necessitate salutis vitare tenetur. Et ita debet se purgare, si non potest aliter suam innocentiam declarare, & infamiam exortam sedare. Discip. Dicerent forte aliqui, quod si Papa diffamatus nolit se purgare, & alii scandalizantur ex hoc: scandalum tale non est datum, sed acceptum. Et ideo propter tale scandalum non tenetur Papa se purgare. Magist. Hanc responsionem alii impugnare nituntur probantes, quod tale scandalum est datum non acceptum: quia ille, qui ex forma facti reddit se suspectum de crimine, scandalizat infirmos actione, quantum in se est. Qui autem renuit se purgare, quando est graviter diffamatus, de crimine reddit se suspectum. Immo videtur, quod de facto fatetur se convictum: quia non minus se reddit conuictum de crimine, qui diffamatus renuit se purgare, quam qui vocatus in iudicium nititur subterfugere, cum gravius & periculosius sit subire iudicium, quam purgationem praestare, sed qui iudicium subterfugit, ostendit se conuictum, extra de praesump. nullus, & 11. q. 1. Christianus, & 3. q. 9 decreuimus, & di. 74. c. honoratus, ergo multo fortius qui diffamatus est, & se purgare recusat, ostendit se conuictum, & per consequens scandalum generat manifestum.
units.tr: The third argument is this. The Pope, no less than others, is bound to avoid mortal sin. But when a man who is defamed of a crime refuses to clear himself (when he cannot otherwise declare his innocence), it is a mortal sin, since this means scandalizing the little ones and the weak, and also giving occasion of scandal to the great and perfect. Such scandal is a mortal sin, which is plain from the severity of the punishment due to it, since the Saviour says in Matth. 6: But whoever shall scandalize one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea. Therefore the Pope is bound by necessity of salvation to avoid such scandal. And so he ought to clear himself, if he cannot otherwise declare his innocence and allay the infamy that has arisen. Student. Some might perhaps say that if a defamed Pope is unwilling to clear himself, and others are scandalized by this, the scandal is not given but taken. And therefore the Pope is not bound to clear himself on account of such scandal. Master. Others strive to refute this answer, proving that such scandal is given, not taken: for he who by the appearance of his conduct makes himself suspected of a crime gives scandal to the weak by his action, so far as in him lies. Now he who refuses to clear himself when he is gravely defamed makes himself suspected of a crime. Indeed, it seems that he in fact confesses himself guilty, because a man who, though defamed, refuses to clear himself shows himself guilty of the crime no less than one who, summoned to judgment, tries to escape it. For it is more grievous and more dangerous to undergo judgment than to make purgation, and he who evades judgment shows himself guilty: Extra de praesumptionibus, nullus, and 11. q. 1, Christianus, and 3. q. 9, decrevimus, and dist. 74, c. honoratus. Therefore much more strongly, he who is defamed and refuses to clear himself shows himself guilty, and consequently gives manifest scandal.

units.la: Quarta ratio est haec. Illa oportet papam facere, quae sunt facilia ad agendum: & sibi nec temporaliter nec spiritualiter obsunt; sed spiritualiter prosunt; & quorum omissio est periculosa subditis & nociua, sed quod papa diffamatus de haeretica pravitate se purget, saltem per proprium iuramentum, est facile, & si est innocens, sibi nec temporaliter, nec spiritualiter obest: imo spiritualiter prodest, talis autem purgationis omissio est subditis periculosa pariter & nociua, ergo talem purgationem papa exhibere tenetur. Maior videtur manifesta: quia qui talia subditis negligit exhibere, ostendit aperte se vtilitatem subditorum non amare: cum sine damno proprio temporali & spirituali & labore graui vtilitatem propriam despiciat procurare. Maior quantum ad omnes suas partes veritatem continere videtur, nam purgatio, praesertim per proprium iuramentum, nulli debet videri difficilis, talis autem purgatio exhibenti nec temporaliter nec spiritualiter nocet: sed spiritualiter prodest, cum sit actus meritorius subiectos aedificans, & ab infamia liberans exhibentem. Quod autem talis purgationis omissio sit subditis periculosa, patet de se, quoniam offendiculum praebet infirmis, & conscientias percutit subditorum.
units.tr: The fourth argument is this. The Pope ought to do those things which are easy to do, and which harm him neither temporally nor spiritually, but profit him spiritually; and whose omission is dangerous and harmful to his subjects. But for the Pope, defamed of heretical depravity, to clear himself, at least by his own oath, is easy, and if he is innocent, it harms him neither temporally nor spiritually; indeed it profits him spiritually. The omission of such purgation, however, is equally dangerous and harmful to his subjects. Therefore the Pope is bound to offer such purgation. The major premise seems manifest: for whoever neglects to offer such things to his subjects plainly shows that he does not love the good of his subjects, since he despises to seek his own good without loss to himself, temporal or spiritual, and without heavy labour. The major premise seems to hold true in all its parts: for purgation, especially by one's own oath, ought to seem difficult to no one, and such purgation harms the one who offers it neither temporally nor spiritually; indeed it profits him spiritually, since it is a meritorious act that builds up his subjects and frees the one who offers it from infamy. That the omission of such purgation is dangerous to subjects is plain in itself, since it presents a stumbling block to the weak and wounds the consciences of the subjects.

units.la: Quinta ratio est haec, qui ex debito charitatis tenetur proximo exhibere illud, quod minus est vtile sibi, tenetur etiam illud, quod magis est vtile, exhibere proximo, si est aeque facile, nec sibi, necalicui praeiudiciale in aliquo magis quam illud, quod est minus vtile, vbi enim ex debito charitatis tenetur aliquis proximum suum vestire, & ex eiusdem debito caritatis tenetur eundem pascere & potum dare, si aeque faciliter potest, & non maius damnum aut periculum sibi vel alii imminet ex vno quam ex alio, sed magis vtile est fidelibus, quod papa de haeresi diffamatus suam innocentiam se purgando declararet, quam sit vestiri ab ipso, pasci & potari, sed papa tenetur ad opera misericordiae corporalia & spiritualia, si habet: ergo magis tenetur ad purgationem, quae non immerito spiritualis misericordia est censenda, si aeque faciliter absque damno & periculo aliorum & proprio eam valeat exhibere.
units.tr: The fifth reason is this. Whoever is bound by the debt of charity to give his neighbour what is less useful to him is also bound to give him what is more useful, if it is equally easy and does not harm himself or anyone else more than the lesser thing would. Where someone is bound by charity to clothe his neighbour, and by the same charity to feed him and give him drink, if he can do so equally easily, and no greater loss or danger threatens himself or another from one act than from the other, then he is bound to the one as much as to the other. But it is more useful to the faithful that the pope, defamed as a heretic, should declare his innocence by clearing himself than that he should be clothed, fed and given drink by the pope. Yet the pope is bound to the works of mercy, both bodily and spiritual, if he has them to give. Therefore he is bound all the more to the purgation, which is rightly judged a spiritual mercy, if he can perform it equally easily, without loss or danger to others or to himself.

units.la: Sexta ratio est haec, qui tenetur scandala euitare & minime sustinere, tenetur suscitata tollere & sedare si potest, sed papa tenetur scandala euitare & minime sustinere: quia non erit aliter imitator Christi dicentis: vt autem non scandalizemus eos &c. Matth. 17. neque Apostoli Pauli dicentis, 1. ad Corinth. 8. si esca mea scandalizat fratrem meum, non manducabo carnem in aeternum, ne fratrem scandalizem, neque illud Apostoli ad Rom. 14. hoc iudicate, iudicate magis ne ponatis offendiculum fratri vel scandalum, ergo papa tenetur scandala suscitata a subditis remouere, si potest, & maxime quae de persona sua sunt exorta, sed si est de haeresi diffamatus, graue scandalum de ipso est exortum, ergo hoc scandalum remouere debet, si potest: & si non potest aliter remouere, nisi seipsum purgauerit, se purgare tenetur.
units.tr: The sixth reason is this. Whoever is bound to avoid giving scandal and not to bear it is bound to remove and calm the scandals that have arisen, if he can. But the pope is bound to avoid giving scandal and not to bear it, for otherwise he would not be an imitator of Christ, who said: "Lest we should offend them" (Matt. 17). Nor would he be an imitator of the Apostle Paul, who said: "If meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend" (1 Cor. 8), nor of that saying of the Apostle to the Romans: "Judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way" (Rom. 14). Therefore the pope is bound to remove the scandals raised by his subjects, if he can, and especially those that have arisen concerning his own person. But if he has been defamed as a heretic, a grave scandal has arisen concerning him, and so he must remove this scandal if he can. And if he cannot remove it in any other way than by clearing himself, he is bound to clear himself.

units.la: Septima ratio est haec. Ille qui propter scandala euitanda debet bona spiritualia dimittere, multo magis propter idem debet spiritualia bona perficere, papa autem propter scandala euitanda debet nonnulla spiritualia bona omittere, saltem ad tempus, sicut praedicatione verbi Dei, punitione malorum, & nonnulla alia, ergo multo magis propter scandala euitanda debet spiritualia bona pficere, sed qui diffamatus se purget, est bonum spirituale, ergo propter scandala euitanda pariter & sedanda debet papa, si est diffamatus, se purgare. Diss. Ista ratio duplyciter videtur peccare, primo quia si concluderet, sequeretur quod propter scandalum euitandum aliquis tenetur religionem intrare, & proprietatem omnium temporalium in perpetuum abdicare: quod non videtur verum. Secundo deficit: quia quod papa purget se, non videtur bonum spirituale: quia talis purgatio posset esse sibi nociua, nullum autem bonum spirituale est alicui nociuum. Magist. Primam tuam instantiam isti niituntur excludere dicentes, quod ratio illa concludit de bonis spiritualibus, quae non sunt supererogationis, huiusmodi autem est purgatio canonica, quando aliquis est de crimine diffamatus, & ideo quando papa est de haeresi diffamatus, debet se purgare propter scandalum euitandum: non tamen tenetur proprietatem omnium abdicare, quia hoc est supererogationis: & ideo ad hoc non tenetur. Secundam instantiam excludunt dicentes, quod purgatio non debet esse nociua papae, nisi propter malam voluntatem papae, quemadmodum & omnia bona spiritualia propter caritatem possunt esse occasio nocumenti, sunt tamen inter bona spiritualia computanda.
units.tr: The seventh reason is this. Whoever must give up spiritual goods for the sake of avoiding scandal must all the more, for the same reason, pursue spiritual goods. But the pope, for the sake of avoiding scandal, must omit some spiritual goods, at least for a time, such as the preaching of God's Word, the punishment of evil-doers, and several others. Therefore, all the more, for the sake of avoiding and calming scandal, he must pursue spiritual goods. But to clear oneself when defamed is a spiritual good. Therefore, to avoid and calm scandal, the pope, if he is defamed, must likewise clear himself. Objection. This argument seems to err in two ways. First, if it were conclusive, it would follow that to avoid scandal a man is bound to enter religious life and renounce for ever the ownership of all temporal goods, which does not seem true. Second, it fails, because that the pope clear himself does not seem to be a spiritual good, since such a purgation could be harmful to him, and no spiritual good is harmful to anyone. Answer. Your first objection they try to exclude by saying that the argument concludes only about spiritual goods that are not works of supererogation. Canonical purgation, when someone is defamed of a crime, is of this kind, and so when the pope is defamed as a heretic he must clear himself to avoid scandal. He is not, however, bound to renounce all his property, since that is a work of supererogation, and so he is not bound to it. To your second objection they reply that purgation can be harmful to the pope only through the pope's own bad will, just as all spiritual goods can occasionally become a cause of harm when pursued out of charity. They are nevertheless counted among the spiritual goods.

units.la: Octaua ratio est haec, praelatus, qui tenetur subditos suos a minori damno vel periculo liberare, debet eos a maiori damno vel periculo eripere, sed papa subditos suos tenetur a damno & periculo corporali & temporali, si potuerit, liberare, sicut & quilibet Christianus, iuxta illud Exo. 23. Si videris asinum odientis te iacere sub onere, non pertransibis, sed leuabis cum eo, & iuxta illud Prou. 24. Erue eos qui ducuntur ad mortem, & qui trahuntur ad interitum liberare non cessos, & iuxta illud Psal. Eripite pauperem, & egenum de manu peccatorum liberate, ergo multo magis debet papa suos subditos scandalizatos de ipso a damno & periculo spirituali, si potuerit, liberare. Hoc autem potest se purgando, ergo tenetur seipsum purgare. Dicunt ergo isti propter istas rationes & alias, quarum multiplicitate te nolo grauare: quod papa de haeresi grauiter diffamatus propter famam propriam restaurandam & propter scandalum candalum euitandum pariter & sedandum, & propter exaltationem & dilatationem fidei Christianæ, ac etiam propter subditos ab omni periculo spirituali præseruandos debet se purgare, quomodo enim, vt dicunt, papa pro fide catholica dilatanda, & pro quibus suis animam suam morti exponeret, si non curat pro eis se à crimine purgare? aut quomodo cum Apostolo carnem non manducaret in æternum, ne fratrem suum scandalizaret, si non curat famam propriam declarare? aut quomodo turam debitam subditorum suorum censendus est habere, si negligendo se purgare animas occidit eorum.
units.tr: The eighth reason is this. A prelate who is bound to free his subjects from a lesser loss or danger must rescue them from a greater loss or danger. But the pope is bound, if he can, to free his subjects from bodily and temporal loss and danger, as is any Christian, according to Exodus 23: "If thou seest the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, thou shalt not pass by, but shalt surely help with him"; and according to Proverbs 24: "Deliver them that are drawn unto death, and forbear not to deliver those that are ready to be slain"; and according to the Psalm: "Defend the poor and fatherless; do justice to the afflicted and needy. Rid them out of the hand of the wicked" (Psalm 82). Therefore the pope must all the more free his subjects, who are scandalized by him, from spiritual loss and danger, if he can. He can do this by clearing himself, and therefore he is bound to clear himself. These men, then, on these and other reasons, which I do not wish to burden you with by their multitude, say that a pope who is gravely defamed as a heretic must clear himself: to restore his own good name, to remove and calm the scandal, and to advance and spread the Christian faith, and also to keep his subjects safe from every spiritual danger. For how, as they say, would the pope expose his soul to death for the spreading of the Catholic faith, and for those for whose sake he would do so, if he does not care to clear himself of a crime? Or how would he not eat flesh for ever, lest he offend his brother, as the Apostle says, if he does not care to make his own reputation plain? Or how is he to be thought to have due care of his subjects if, by neglecting to clear himself, he destroys their souls?

units.la: CAP. LXI.
units.tr: CAP. LXI.

units.la: Facit vnam instantiam contra dicta cap. 60. eam deducendo in duplici exemplo, ad quam tripliciter respondetur, vbi etiam contra responsiones instatur, quæ etiam soluuntur.
units.tr: He raises one objection against the points of chapter 60, drawing it out in a twofold example. It is answered in three ways, and where the answers are themselves opposed, the opposition is pressed; these too are resolved.

units.la: Dicit: Ista sententia decretis sanctorum priorum summorum pontificum obuiare videtur, nam Sixtus papa & Leo papa licet se purgauerint, ad hoc tamen minime tenebatur. Vnde Sixtus papa scribens omnibus episcopis, vt recitatur 2. q. 4. c. mandastis, ait: mandastis vt scriberem vobis, qualiter instans iurgium contra me instigatum sit, vel à quo, vt vestro adminiculo pelleretur, & causa mea firmaretur, scitote me criminari à quodam Basso, & iniuste me persequi, quod audiens Valentinianus Augustus nostra auctoritate Synodum congregari iussit; & facto consilio cum magna examinatione satisfaciens omnibus (licet euadere aliter satis potuissem) suspitionem tamen fugiens coram omnibus me purgari scilicet me à suspitione & æmulatione liberans: sed non aliis, qui noluerint aut sponte hoc non elegerint faciendi formam dans. Item Leo papa, vt habetur eisdem ca. & q. c. auditum, ait: auditum est fratres charissimi, qualiter mali homines in me gratia crimina confinxerunt, quamobrem ego Leo pontifex sancta Romana ecclesia purifico me in conspectu vestro coram Deo & Angelis eius, quia istas criminosas & sceleratas res, quas mihi obiciunt illi, nec perpetraui, nec perpetrari feci vel iussi, hoc autem faciès non legem prescribo cæteris quia ad facere cogantur. Ex quibus auctoritatibus videtur manifeste probare, quod summus pontifex diffamatus ad purgationem nequaquam astringitur, licet sponte, si voluerit, valeat se purgare, qualiter tamen ad ista prædicti assertores respondeant, manifesta. Mag. Prædictas instantias multis modis refellere moliuntur, primo dicentes: quod prædicti summi pontifices Sixtus & Leo sponte non de necessitate se purgare volebant, & ideo in tali casu, in quo Sixtus & Leo erant, formam faciendi consimilem aliis minime præfixerunt. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod, sicut notat Glos. 11. q. 3. c. in cunctis, infamia orta ab inimicis non inducit purgationem, extra de purgatione c. in immunitate & 2. q. 5. c. omnibus. Nec ab omnibus etiam personis, nec ab illis qui de facili credunt. Quod etiam Innoc. tertius, vt habetur extra de accusatione c. qualiter & quando, testari videtur dicens, quod cum prælatus excedit, si per clamorem & famam ad aures superiorum peruenerit, non quidem à maleuolis & maledicis, sed à prouidis & honestis: nec semel tantum, sed sæpe (quod clamor innuit & diffamatio manifestat) debet coram ecclesia superioribus veritatem diligentius perscrutari. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod propter infamiam ortam ab inimicis maledicis & leuibus personis non est necesse purgationem præstare. Ex quo isti respondent ad prædictas instantias dicentes, quod si prædicti pontifices Sixtus & Leo diffamati fuerint, illa infamia orta fuit ab inimicis & maledicis detractoribus. Quod euidenter Sixtus de se insinuat dicens, scitote me criminari à quodam Basso iniuste & persequi. Hoc etiam Leo de se aperte demonstrat dicens: mali homines, qui in me gratia crimina confinxerunt. Ex quibus verbis apparet, quod si isti pontifices diffamati fuerint, illa infamia à malis procedit, quare propter talem infamiam non fuit necesse vt se purgauerint. Secundo dicunt, quod sæpe diti pontifices non erant diffamati, sed solum modo accusati, & ideo non fuit necesse, quod purgationem præstarent, quia accusatore deficiente, non cogitur reus se purgare, nisi fuerit diffamatus. Tertio dicunt, quod prædicti summi pontifices se purgando legem similem faciendi aliis summis pontificibus minime præbuerunt: quia nec potuerunt eis legem imponere, cum non habet imperium par in parem, præbuerunt eis tamen exemplum simile faciendi, & summi pontifices in tali casu ad hoc ex lege diuina & iure naturæ, ac debito charitatis necessario sunt adstricti. Disc. Nulla istarum responsionum videtur satisfacere, prima non: quia videtur, quod vndecunque illius infamia sit exorta, debet diffamatus purgationem exhibere, vnde & rationes, quas adduxisti de laborante infamia vndecunque exorta æque videntur concludere, quod etiam Glos. de accusationibus, qualiter & quando, insinuare videtur, dicens: Satis potest dici, quod indicenda est purgatio, vndecunque procedat infamia, saltem propter scandalum, ar. primum de purgatione c. accedens. Secunda autem responsio videtur deficere: quia secundum Greg. sicut supius allegasti, de detractoribus modis omnibus satisfieri debet, ergo papæ prefati suis detractoribus & criminatoribus satisfacere debuerunt: & per consequens saltem propter eos debuerunt se purgare.
