Tertia responsio non procedit: qa Sixtus non solum asserit, se aliis simile faciendi formam minime dare, sed etiā dicit, q aliter euadere potuisset. Mag. Ista & plura alia allegant contra seipsos; quæ etiam conantur dissoluere. Ad euidentiam primæ obiectionis dicunt esse notandum, quod infamia aliquando vsque ad bonos & honestos procedit. Interdum vero prouidi & discreti ex infamia suscitata nihil mali suspicantur, contra taliter diffamatum in primo casu, siue infamia exorta sit ab in certo auctore, siue à certo auctore prouido & honesto, siue à certo auctore store maleuolo, inuido, maledico, vili persona vel à personis suspiciosis & quæ facile credunt, sicut vndecunq; purgatio est præstanda, & de taliter diffamato apud prouidos & honestos, vndecunq; fama mala procedat, loquitur Glossa inducta, & de tali ratione inductæ superius videntur concludere. In secundo autem casu, quando solummodo apud inimicos detractores, maleuolos & suspectos, & qui facile credunt, aliquis diffamatus existit, purgationem præstare non oportet, & in hoc casu loquitur Innoc. tertius, & Glos. 11. q. 3. in cunctis. Ad secundam obiectionem respondetur, quod detractoribus inimicis & maleuolis satisfieri debet absque onere satisfacientis & periculo, quando de eorum correctione spes habetur, si vero de eorum correctione nequaquam spes habetur, non debet satisfacere ipsis. Et ideo prædicti summi pontifices suis detractoribus debuerunt satisfacere absque onere purgationis eis veritatem indicando & monendo, ne ipsi mendaciter diffamarent, si habeatur spes de correctione ipsorum. Ad tertiam respondetur, quod Sixtus aliter potuisset euadere, quam se purgando, quia apud prouidos & honestos non extitit diffamatus, & criminator ipsius incorrigibilis putabatur. Discip. Quid est agendum secundum istos, si papa de hæresi grauiter diffamatus nullo modo voluerit se purgare? Mag. Dicunt quod pro conuicto debet haberi: & ideo patu est priuandus. Discip. Quomodo probant quod pro conuicto debet haberi? Mag. Hoc probant sic: magis debet haberi pro conuicto papa diffamatus, qui se purgare recusat, quam ille qui cupit se purgare, cum purgatores habere non potest, iste enim prætendit, quod paratus est corrigi, nec in hoc peccat quod desiderat se purgare, præsertim si est innocens, licet ex aliquo casu purgatores habere non possit, ille vero incorrigibilem se ostendit, & nouum scandalum & peccatum committit, nam se purgare recusat, sed qui cupit se purgare, cum purgatores habere non possit, pro conuicto haberi non debet, extra de purgatione canonica, cum per & c. interreit, etiam extra de Symo. insinuatum & c. de hoc, ergo multo fortius si papa de hæresi diffamatus est grauiter, & se nullatenus vult purgare, pro conuicto debet haberi. Per hoc enim est contra ipsum præsumptio violenta, propter quam poterit merito condemnari. Discip. Quis secundum istos debet papam se purgare nolentem damnare? Mag. De hoc sunt diuersæ opiniones, vna est, quod papa eo ipso, quod diffamatus esset de hæresi & requisitus nollet se purgare, esset ipso facto papatu priuatus, tanquam hæreticus. Alia est, quod non esset ipso facto depositus, sed esset per iudicem deponendus. Discip. Per quem? Mag. Vna est opinio, quod per concilium generale. Alia est, quod per diœcesanum, vel per illum qui est iudex papæ, si esset per euidentiam rei in hæresi deprehensus, vnde quidam dicunt, quod esset deponendus à Romanis.
units.tr: He says: This opinion seems to stand against the decrees of the holy earlier Supreme Pontiffs. For Pope Sixtus and Pope Leo, although they cleared themselves, were by no means bound to do so. Hence Pope Sixtus, writing to all the bishops, as it is quoted in 2 q. 4 c. mandastis, says: "You commanded me to write to you how a troublesome quarrel has been stirred up against me, and by whom, so that by your help it might be driven away and my cause be confirmed. Know that I am accused by a certain Bassus and unjustly persecuted. When the Emperor Valentinian heard this, by our authority he ordered a synod to be assembled; and after counsel was taken and a thorough examination made, I satisfied everyone (although I could well have escaped otherwise), yet to avoid suspicion I cleared myself before them all, freeing myself from suspicion and rivalry. But I did this without giving a form to others who would not or did not willingly choose to do the same." Likewise Pope Leo, as it is found in the same chapter and question, c. auditum, says: "It has been heard, dearest brothers, how wicked men have invented crimes against me out of hatred. Therefore I, Leo, bishop of the holy Roman Church, purify myself in your sight, before God and his Angels, because the criminal and wicked things which they lay to my charge I neither committed, nor caused to be committed, nor ordered. Yet I do not prescribe a law to the rest by doing this, since they are not compelled to do the same." From these authorities it seems clearly to prove that a Supreme Pontiff who is defamed is in no way bound to clear himself, although, if he wishes, he may do so willingly. How the aforesaid assertors answer these objections, however, is plain. Teacher: They labour to refute the aforesaid objections in many ways. First, they say that the said Supreme Pontiffs, Sixtus and Leo, wished to clear themselves willingly and not of necessity, and therefore in such a case, in which Sixtus and Leo stood, they did not lay down a similar form of action for others. To make this plain, they say it must be noted that, as the gloss on 11 q. 3 c. in cunctis observes, infamy arising from enemies does not require purgation (extra de purgatione c. in immunitate, and 2 q. 5 c. omnibus); nor does it arise from all persons, nor from those who readily believe. Innocent III also seems to testify to this, as is found in extra de accusatione c. qualiter et quando, saying that when a prelate has gone astray, if this reaches the ears of his superiors through outcry and report, it must come not from the malevolent and slanderers but from the prudent and honest; and not once only but often (as the outcry suggests and the defamation makes manifest) the truth must be more carefully searched out before the Church by his superiors. From these words it is understood that, on account of infamy arising from enemies, malicious and light persons, it is not necessary to make purgation. On this basis they answer the aforesaid objections, saying that if the said Pontiffs Sixtus and Leo were defamed, that infamy arose from enemies and malicious detractors. Sixtus indicates this clearly about himself, saying: "Know that I am unjustly accused by a certain Bassus and persecuted." Leo also shows this plainly about himself, saying: "wicked men, who invented crimes against me out of hatred." From these words it appears that if these Pontiffs were defamed, that infamy came from wicked men, and so on account of such infamy it was not necessary for them to clear themselves. Secondly, they say that those Pontiffs were often not defamed but only accused, and therefore it was not necessary for them to make purgation, because when the accuser is lacking, the accused is not compelled to clear himself unless he has been defamed. Thirdly, they say that the said Supreme Pontiffs, by clearing themselves, did not lay down a similar law for other Supreme Pontiffs: for they could not impose a law on them, since an equal has no power over an equal; yet they did give them an example of acting similarly, and Supreme Pontiffs in such a case are necessarily bound to do so by divine law, by the law of nature, and by the debt of charity. Disciple: None of these answers seems to satisfy. The first does not: for it seems that, from whatever source the infamy has arisen, the defamed person ought to make purgation; whence also the reasons you adduced, concerning infamy arising from whatever source, seem equally to conclude this; and the gloss on the chapter qualiter et quando also seems to suggest it, saying: "It can well be said that purgation must be ordered, from whatever source the infamy proceeds, at least on account of scandal, argument from the first in de purgatione c. accedens." The second answer also seems to fail: for according to Gregory, as you cited above, one must make satisfaction to detractors in every way; therefore the aforesaid Popes ought to have made satisfaction to their detractors and accusers, and consequently at least on their account they ought to have cleared themselves. The third answer does not hold: for Sixtus not only asserts that he gave no form for others to act similarly, but also says that he could have escaped otherwise. Teacher: They allege these and many other things against themselves, and they also try to dissolve them. To make the first objection plain, they say it must be noted that infamy sometimes reaches even good and honest people. But sometimes prudent and discreet people, on hearing the infamy raised, suspect no evil against the person so defamed; in the first case, whether the infamy arose from an uncertain author, or from a certain author who is prudent and honest, or from a certain author who is malicious, envious, slanderous, of base character, or from suspicious persons who readily believe, purgation is to be made in any case; and the gloss cited speaks of a person so defamed among the prudent and honest, whatever the source of the bad report, and the reasons adduced above seem to conclude in this way. In the second case, when someone is defamed only among enemies, detractors, malicious and suspicious persons who readily believe, it is not necessary to make purgation; and in this case Innocent III speaks, and the gloss 11 q. 3 in cunctis. To the second objection it is answered that satisfaction must be made to enemies and malicious detractors without the burden and danger of the one who satisfies, when hope exists of their correction; but if there is by no means hope of their correction, one ought not to satisfy them. Therefore the aforesaid Supreme Pontiffs ought to have satisfied their detractors without the burden of purgation, by showing them the truth and warning them, lest they defame falsely, if there is hope of their correction. To the third it is answered that Sixtus could have escaped otherwise than by clearing himself, because among the prudent and honest he had not been defamed, and his accuser was thought to be incorrigible. Disciple: What is to be done, according to these men, if a Pope, gravely defamed of heresy, will in no way clear himself? Teacher: They say that he must be held as convicted, and therefore he is to be deprived of the papacy. Disciple: How do they prove that he must be held as convicted? Teacher: They prove it thus: a Pope who is defamed and refuses to clear himself must be held as convicted more than one who desires to clear himself but cannot find compurgators; for the latter claims that he is ready to be corrected, and he does not sin in desiring to clear himself, especially if he is innocent, even though for some chance reason he cannot obtain compurgators; but the former shows himself incorrigible, and commits a fresh scandal and sin, for he refuses to clear himself. But one who desires to clear himself, when he cannot obtain compurgators, ought not to be held as convicted (extra de purgatione canonica, cum per et c. interreit; also extra de simonia insinuatum and c. de hoc). Therefore much more strongly, if a Pope is gravely defamed of heresy and in no way wishes to clear himself, he must be held as convicted. For by this there is a violent presumption against him, on account of which he may rightly be condemned. Disciple: According to these men, who ought to condemn a Pope who refuses to clear himself? Teacher: On this there are diverse opinions. One is that the Pope, by the very fact that he is defamed of heresy and, being asked, refuses to clear himself, is ipso facto deprived of the papacy as a heretic. Another is that he is not deprived ipso facto, but must be deposed by a judge. Disciple: By whom? Teacher: One opinion is that it is by a general council. Another is that it is by the diocesan, or by one who is the judge of the Pope, if he has been caught in heresy by the plain evidence of the fact; whence some say that he should be deposed by the Romans.

units.la: CAP. LXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXII.

units.la: In quo ponitur responsio ad auctoritates & rationes primi capituli huius, vbi probatum fuit, quod Papa non habeat superiorem in terris.
units.tr: In which the answer is given to the authorities and arguments of the first chapter of this book, where it was proved that the Pope has no superior on earth.

units.la: Discip. Dic quomodo ad auctoritates in contrarium primo capitulo huius sexti adductas præfati respondent assertores. Mag. Ad omnes auctoritates, quæ contra præfatam assertionem sonare videntur, vnicam dant responsionem generalem, dicentes quod intelligi debent, quando papa non est diffamatus de hæresi, nec in aliquo crimine, de quo scandalizaretur ecclesia, incorrigibilis notorie reperitur. Discip. Ista generali responsione non obstante, dic quomodo ad singulas auctoritates responsiones dant speciales: & quomodo eas pertractare conantur. Mag. Dicunt, quod prima auctoritas sumpta ex illo cap. 9. & c. nemo, soluit seipsam, cum dicit expresse: nemo iudicabit primam sedem iustitiam temperare desiderantem. Ex quibus verbis intelligitur, quod illud capitulum loquitur de papa, quando desiderat iustitiam temperare, tunc autem non est incorrigibilis, nec hæreticus, licet enim papa etiam notorie deliquerit, si tamen desiderat iustitiam temperare, non est ideo incorrigibilis reputandus. Discip. Secunda auctoritas eiusdem expresse insinuat, quod papa in nullo casu est iudicandus, cum dicit, à quoquam, neque enim ab Augusto, &c. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod papa in nullo casu est iudicandus à quoquam. Mag. Isti respondent dicentes, quod sane debes intelligere verba præfata, vt intelligas ea, quæ in casu, in quo loquuntur præcedentia verba, quando sc. papa desiderat iustitiam temperare, vnde quod non sic generaliter nullo casu excepto debeant intelligi, Glos. ibidem asserit manifeste dicens: nemo iudicabitur, nisi se alicuius iudicio submittat, vt 2. q. 7. nos. si etiam in causa hæresis 40. di. si papa, & cum submittit se confessori suo, tenetur ei parere, hic exprimunt tres casus, in quibus potest papa ab alio iudicari. Quartum casum exprimit Glos. dist. 40. si papa, sicut est dictum; quando scilicet de crimine notorio papæ scandalizatur ecclesia, & ipse est incorrigibilis, & ita patet, quod verba prædicta non debent sine exceptione intelligi, quando tamen ipsemet papa vult & potest facere iustitiam, non esset ab aliquo iudicandus. Discipul. Quid si papa esset hæreticus, & vellet se corrigere iustitiam temperando, esset ne ab alio iudicandus? Magist. Respondent dicentes, quod papa, si efficiatur hæreticus, eo ipso non est papa, & ideo quantumcunque tunc cupieret facere iustitiam, esset ab alio iudicandus, sed si manet verus papa, & vult facere iustitiam, non debet ab aliquo iudicari. Discipul. Si papa manens papa quocunque crimine inuolutus (volens facere iustitiam) non est ab aliquo iudicandus, ergo nullus alius habet super ipsum iurisdictionem coactiuam: quia incorrigibilitas papæ non tribuit alicui iurisdictionem. Magist. Dicunt quod sicut ratione delicti fit aliquis prius non subditus alicuius de iurisdictione eius, ita papa ratione incorrigibilitatis & criminis, de quo scandalizatur ecclesia, fit de iurisdictione illorum, qui prius fuerunt sibi subiecti. Disc. Quid si papa primo incorrigibilis appareret, & postea cum causa sua inciperet ventilari, correctionem promitteret, & corrigi vellet: nunquid qui inceperunt discutere causam papæ, ipsum iudicare deberent? Magist. Circa hoc sunt assertiones diversæ, una est, quod ex quo isti, qui inciperent ventilare causam papæ, habuissent iurisdictionem super papam (propter promissionem papæ) nequaquam dictam iurisdictionem amitterent: & ideo ipsum iudicare valerent. Alia est: quod sicut per incorrigibilitatem papæ acquiritur iurisdictio super ipsum, ita per corrigibilitatem amittitur. Disc. Quomodo secundum istam assertionem est nota incorrigibilitas papæ? Mag. Respondetur, quod erit nota cum per præsumptionem violentam constat, quod habet propositum se nullatenus corrigendi: puta quod asserit, quod non vult se corrigere: vel quia sæpe monitus non se corrigit. Sic enim Imperator & Romani Papa Iohanne 12. incorrigibilem indicaverunt, quia sæpe monitus nullatenus se correxit.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how the defenders of that view answer the authorities cited against it in the first chapter of this sixth part. Master. To all the authorities that seem to speak against that assertion they give one general answer: they say that they must be understood as applying when the Pope has not been defamed of heresy, nor is found to be notoriously incorrigible in some crime which scandalises the Church. Disciple. Setting aside that general answer, tell me how they give special answers to the individual authorities, and how they try to deal with them. Master. They say that the first authority, taken from chapter 9 and the canon Nemo, resolves itself, since it says expressly: No one shall judge the first see, which desires to temper justice. From these words it is understood that the chapter speaks of the Pope when he desires to temper justice. Then he is not incorrigible or a heretic. For although the Pope may have sinned notoriously, if he desires to temper justice he is not on that account to be regarded as incorrigible. Disciple. The second authority of the same chapter expressly suggests that the Pope is to be judged in no case, since it says: by no one, for not even by Augustus, and so on. From these words it seems to be given to understand that the Pope is to be judged by no one in any case. Master. These men answer, saying that you must properly understand the words cited, so that you understand them of the case in which the preceding words speak, namely when the Pope desires to temper justice. Hence they should not be understood so generally, with no case excepted. The Gloss on the same passage clearly asserts this, saying: No one will be judged unless he submits himself to someone's judgment, as in 2 q. 7, Nos, and Si etiam in causa haeresis, 40 dist., Si papa. And when he submits himself to his confessor, he is bound to obey him. Here they set out three cases in which the Pope can be judged by another. The Gloss on dist. 40, Si papa, sets out a fourth case, as has been said: namely when the Church is scandalised by the Pope's notorious crime and he is incorrigible. And so it is plain that the words cited ought not to be understood without exception. When, however, the Pope himself wishes and is able to do justice, he is not to be judged by anyone. Disciple. What if the Pope were a heretic, and wished to correct himself by tempering justice? Would he then be judged by another? Master. They answer, saying that if the Pope becomes a heretic, he by that very fact ceases to be Pope. Therefore, however much he then desired to do justice, he would be judged by another. But if he remains a true Pope and wishes to do justice, he ought not to be judged by anyone. Disciple. If the Pope, remaining Pope and entangled in whatever crime, is not judged by anyone when he wishes to do justice, then no one else has coercive jurisdiction over him. For the Pope's incorrigibility does not give jurisdiction to anyone. Master. They say that just as through a crime someone who was previously not subject to another's jurisdiction becomes so, so the Pope, by reason of incorrigibility and of the crime which scandalises the Church, comes under the jurisdiction of those who were previously subject to him. Disciple. What if the Pope at first appeared incorrigible, but afterwards, when his case began to be debated, promised correction and wished to be corrected? Should those who began to examine the Pope's case judge him? Master. On this point there are differing assertions. One is that since those who began to examine the Pope's case had jurisdiction over him (by the Pope's promise), they would never lose that jurisdiction, and so they would be able to judge him. The other is that just as jurisdiction over the Pope is acquired through his incorrigibility, so it is lost through his correctability. Disciple. According to this assertion, how is the Pope's incorrigibility recognised? Master. The answer is that it will be recognised when it is established by a violent presumption that he has a purpose of not correcting himself in any way: for example, if he declares that he does not wish to correct himself, or because, though often admonished, he does not correct himself. For so the Emperor and the Romans judged Pope John XII incorrigible, because, though often admonished, he never corrected himself.

units.la: Discip. Dic quomodo respondetur ad auctoritatem Symachi papæ. Mag. Dicitur quod intelligenda est: quando papa non est de hæresi graviter diffamatus, nec in aliquo crimine, de quo scandalizetur ecclesia, incorrigibilis invenitur, cum vero dicitur, quod ubi canon non excipit, nec nos debemus excipere: Respondetur, quod illa regula est regulariter vera: fallit tamen, ubi alius casus non excipit, & ubi scriptura divina excipit, vel etiam ubi ius naturale, vel ratio evidens naturalis dictat excipiendum. Sic autem est in proposito: quia ratio naturalis & ius naturale dictant, quod ubi papa esset notorie hæreticus, vel criminosus, & scandalizaret ecclesiam, & se nollet corrigere, abiiciendus esset, quæ ratio scripturæ divinæ concordat approbanti assertionem Sophæ principis sacerdotum dicentis: Expedit ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, ne tota gens pereat. Ex quibus veribis colligitur, quod sicut fuit expediens, quod Christus innocens pro populo moreretur, ne tota gens periret, ita etiam expedit, quod papa hæreticus & criminosus & incorrigibilis moriatur, similiter sit de papatu proiectus, & non tota gens pereat. Discipul. Quæ est illa ratio naturalis, quæ dictat papam criminosum & incorrigibilem abiiciendum? Mag. Dicitur quod ratio est illa, videlicet quod membrum incurabile totius corporis infectiuum est pro salute corporis amputandum. Disc. Salus Christianorum a Deo dependet, Deus autem potest conservare salutem eorum absque amputatione membri incurabilis. Magist. Respondetur, quod ubi fideles possunt humanum auxilium invenire, non debent ad potentiam divinam recurrere, hoc enim esset Deum tentare, quare si aliquod membrum apparet incurabile, debet humanitus amputari.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how the authority of Pope Symmachus is answered. Master. It is said that it must be understood of the case in which the Pope has not been gravely defamed of heresy, nor is found incorrigible in some crime which scandalises the Church. As for the saying that where the canon makes no exception, we too ought to make none, the answer is that this rule is generally true, but it has exceptions: where another case is excepted, where Divine Scripture makes an exception, or where natural law or evident natural reason dictates that an exception be made. Now this is the case in the matter at hand. For natural reason and natural law dictate that where the Pope would be notoriously a heretic or criminal, scandalise the Church, and be unwilling to correct himself, he should be cast off. This reason agrees with Holy Scripture, which approves the saying of Caiaphas, the high priest: It is expedient that one man should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish (John 11:50). From these words it is gathered that just as it was expedient for the innocent Christ to die for the people, lest the whole nation perish, so it is expedient that a Pope who is heretical, criminal and incorrigible should die, that is, be cast out of the papacy, so that the whole nation does not perish. Disciple. What is that natural reason which dictates that a criminal and incorrigible Pope should be cast off? Master. The reason is this: an incurable member which infects the whole body must be amputated for the good of the body. Disciple. The welfare of Christians depends on God, and God can preserve their welfare without amputating an incurable member. Master. The answer is that where the faithful can find human help, they ought not to have recourse to divine power, for this would be to tempt God. Therefore, if a member appears incurable, it must be amputated by human means.

units.la: Discipul. Dic quomodo respondetur ad tertiam auctoritatem Antheri papæ. Magist. Respondetur, quod Antherus papa loquitur, quando papa vult seipsum corrigere. Unde hæc est differentia inter papam & alios corrigendos; quia alii licet non sint incorrigibiles, iudicantur a papa, papa autem, qui non est incorrigibilis, a Domino solo iudicatur. Discipul. Dic quomodo dicunt, quod papa in causa hæresis, licet non probetur incorrigibilis, ab alio iudicatur. Magist. Videtur quod male intelligas assertionem prædictam, tenet enim assertio sæpe dicta, quod nunquam est papa iudicandus ab homine, nisi submittat se iudicio, vel nisi incorrigibilis ostendatur, & ideo papa existens papa non est pro causa hæresis alicuius subiectus iudicio, licet si papa de hæresi fuerit diffamatus, & recusaverit se subdere iudicio aut purgare, alii potestatem habeant inquirendi de ipso, imo etiam citandi ipsum, sed antequam apparuerit incorrigibilis, vel hæreticus, ipsum corrigere non possunt. Discipul. Istud omnino est irrationabile reputandum, quod aliquis habeat potestatem inquirendi de aliquo & citandi ipsum; & tamen non habet potestatem iudicandi eundem: cum inquirere & citare non pertineant, nisi ad iurisdictionem habentem, qui autem habet iurisdictionem super aliquem ratione alicuius criminis, habet potestatem iudicandi & coercendi eundem, aliter enim talis iurisdictio esset omnino inutilis iudicanda &c. Magist. Ad hanc obiectionem responsum est prius, ubi ostensum est, quod quando dubitatur de iurisdictione, ratione illius dubitationis potest quis habere potestatem inquirendi & citandi alium, licet in rei veritate iurisdictionem non habeat super ipsum. Discipul. Ista responsio videtur contraria veritati: quia quando dubitatur de iurisdictione alicuius, eo ipso non est iudex: sicut quando dubitatur de tutela duorum, neuter est tutor. Magist. Dicunt te aperte errare contra iura: quia sæpe ratione dubitationis fit, quod alias non fieret: & præcipue ratione dubitationis de iurisdictione alicuius, dum enim aliquis, qui in rei veritate non est subiectus alicuius episcopi, graviter (licet mendaciter) diffamatur de liquisse in diœcesi episcopi non fuit; talis episcopus sup diffamatum iurisdictionem minime habet, quia falsa infamia; & tum episcopus propter infamiam habet potestatem inquirendi & citandi diffamatum, si fuerit in diœcesi sua. Disc. Istud exemplum est ad oppositum, quia talis episcopus habet iurisdictionem sup taliter diffamatum: eo quod si crimen fuerit probatum contra ipsum, poterit de hoc eum condemnare, si autem non fuerit probatum legitime, poterit eum absolvere, non solum aut sententia condemnationis, sed etiam sententia absolutionis spectat ad iurisdictionem habentem. Mag. Respondetur tibi, quod in hoc casu episcopus diffamato non prefert sententiam absolutionis tantum habens iurisdictionem super ipsum: sed pronunciabit diffamatum, eo quod nullum crimen est probatum contra ipsum ad suam iurisdictionem minime pertinere. Disc. Hæc responsio non videtur sufficiens, quod talis episcopus potest indicere purgationem taliter diffamato, indicere autem purgationem pertinet ad iurisdictionem habentem, ergo &c. Mag. Ad hoc dupliciter respondetur, uno modo, quod episcopus non potest tantum iurisdictionem habens super diffamatum eidem purgationem indicere, sed potest eum rogare, quod propter scandalum vitandum vel sedandum se purgare.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how the third authority, that of Pope Anterus, is answered. Master. The answer is that Pope Anterus speaks when the Pope wishes to correct himself. Hence the difference between the Pope and other persons to be corrected is this: others, although they are not incorrigible, are judged by the Pope; but the Pope, who is not incorrigible, is judged by the Lord alone. Disciple. Tell me how they say that the Pope, in a case of heresy, although it is not proved that he is incorrigible, is judged by another. Master. It seems that you misunderstand the assertion mentioned. For the assertion often mentioned holds that the Pope is never to be judged by a man unless he submits himself to judgment, or unless he is shown to be incorrigible. Therefore, while he is Pope, the Pope is not subject to judgment in a case of heresy. Nevertheless, if the Pope has been defamed of heresy and refuses to submit himself to judgment or to purge himself, others have the power to inquire into him, and even to summon him. But before he has appeared incorrigible or a heretic, they cannot correct him. Disciple. It must be regarded as altogether unreasonable that someone should have the power to inquire into another and to summon him, and yet not have the power to judge him. For inquiring and summoning belong only to one who has jurisdiction. And whoever has jurisdiction over someone by reason of some crime has the power to judge and to coerce him. Otherwise such jurisdiction would be wholly useless... Master. This objection has already been answered earlier, where it was shown that when jurisdiction is in doubt, one may, by reason of that doubt, have the power to inquire into and to summon another, although in truth he has no jurisdiction over him. Disciple. That answer seems contrary to the truth. For when someone's jurisdiction is in doubt, he is by that very fact not a judge, just as when the guardianship of two persons is in doubt, neither is guardian. Master. They say you are plainly mistaken and contrary to the law. For often, by reason of a doubt, something happens which otherwise would not happen; and especially by reason of a doubt about someone's jurisdiction. For when a man who is in truth not subject to any bishop is gravely, though falsely, defamed of having committed some crime in the bishop's diocese, that bishop has no jurisdiction over the defamed man, because the infamy is false. Yet on account of the infamy the bishop has the power to inquire into and to summon the defamed man, if he is in his diocese. Disciple. That example tells against you, for such a bishop has jurisdiction over the defamed man. For if the crime is proved against him, he can condemn him for it; and if it is not legitimately proved, he can absolve him. Not only a sentence of condemnation but also a sentence of absolution belongs to the one who has jurisdiction. Master. The answer to you is that in this case the bishop, who does not have jurisdiction over the defamed man, does not pronounce a sentence of absolution. Rather he declares the defamed man innocent, since no crime has been proved against him, and that falls outside his jurisdiction. Disciple. This answer does not seem sufficient, for such a bishop can order a purgation for the defamed man, and ordering a purgation belongs to the one who has jurisdiction. Therefore... Master. To this there are two answers. In one way: the bishop, who does not have jurisdiction over the defamed man, cannot order him to purge himself, but he can ask him to purge himself in order to avoid or calm the scandal. If he refuses to purge himself, then on account of the scandal which his refusal causes, the matter falls under the bishop's jurisdiction, because that scandal is not without fault. In another way it is said: the defamed man ought to be referred to his superior, and that superior ought to order the purgation for him.

units.la: put purget, quod si ipse noluerit, ratione scandali, quod praestat nolendo se purgare, sit de iurisdictione episcopi: quia illud scandalum non est sine delicto. Aliter dicitur, quod debet diffamatum ad suum superiorem remittere, & ille sibi debet purgationem indicere. Discip. Satis tractauimus istud exemplum, & ideo pone aliud, quod ratione dubitationis de iurisdictione potest quis inquirere vel citare aliquem, super quem tamen iurisdictionem minime habet. Magist. Aliud exemplum ponitur extra de rescript. c. pastoralis: vbi asseritur, quod quando de reuocatione literarum ambigitur, tam priores iudices quam posteriores, si neuter voluerit differre, de huiusmodi reuocatione cognoscere possunt: & tamen alteri nullam iurisdictionem habent omnino. Aliud exemplum est de legatis, ad quos litere tacita veritate vel suggesta falsitate per fraudem & malitiam impetrantur, qui antequam de hoc eis fuerit facta fides per tales literas, possunt citare partem aduersam, eo quod dubitant an littere sint legitime impetrate: qui tamen postq; sciuerint, quod non sunt impetrate legitime, eis vt non debet, extra de rescriptis. super literis, sic dicunt esse de papa, quod propter nullam infamiam de haeresi est aliquius iudicio subiectus: de quo tamen catholici, eo quod dubitatur, an sit haereticus, & per consequens an sit subiectus eorum iurisdictioni, possunt & debent inquirere, possuntque citare ipsum, quod si nec vult se iudicio submittere, nec purgare, cum pro conuicto interpretatione iuris debent habere: & ideo tunc poterunt eum legitime coercere.
units.tr: ...put that he purges himself; if he is unwilling, then because of the scandal he causes by refusing to purge himself, the matter falls within the bishop's jurisdiction, since that scandal is not without fault. Otherwise it is said that the bishop ought to refer the man who is defamed to his superior, and that superior ought to appoint the purgation for him. Disciple: We have treated that example sufficiently, so put another one, in which through doubt about jurisdiction someone may inquire into or summon a person over whom he in fact has no jurisdiction at all. Master: Another example is given in the Extra, On Rescripts, chapter "Pastoralis", where it is asserted that when there is doubt about the revocation of letters, both the earlier judges and the later ones, if neither is willing to defer, may take cognizance of such a revocation, although the one has no jurisdiction at all over the other. Another example concerns the legates, against whom letters are obtained by fraud and malice, by concealing the truth or suggesting falsehood; before it has been established to them by such letters, they may summon the opposing party, because they doubt whether the letters were lawfully obtained. But once they know that they were not lawfully obtained, they should no longer do so, as the Extra, On Rescripts, chapter "Super literis" says. They likewise say of the pope that, since he is not subject to anyone's judgment on account of any infamy of heresy, Catholics may and ought to inquire, because it is doubtful whether he is a heretic and consequently whether he is subject to their jurisdiction, and they may summon him. If he is willing neither to submit himself to judgment nor to purge himself, they ought to hold him as convicted by the interpretation of the law, and then they may lawfully coerce him.

units.la: Discip. Sufficiunt ad praesens ista de auctoritate Antheri: & dicad illam de Constantino. Magist. Respondetur, quod Constantinus non loquitur specialiter de summo pontifice, sed generaliter de omnibus clericis, qui tamen possunt ab homine iudicari.
units.tr: Disciple: For the present, what you have said about the authority of Anterus is enough; now tell me about the one from Constantine. Master: It is answered that Constantine does not speak specifically of the supreme pontiff, but generally of all clerics, who nevertheless may be judged by a man.

units.la: Discip. De illa materia, an scilicet clerici debeant a laicis iudicari, alias disputabo: ideo dic quomodo respondetur ad auctoritatem Gelasii papae. Mag. Respondetur, quod illa verba Gelasii papae intellecta de summo pontifice non possunt generaliter absq; omni exceptione intelligi. Tunc enim papa non posset alterius iudicio subiectus submittere. Tunc etiam, si papa iudicaret fidem Christianam esse falsam & ficta, & publice idolis immolaret, nulli liceret iudicare de ipso. Debent ergo intelligi, si manens papa incorrigibilis minime reperitur. Et eodem modo respondetur ad auctoritatem Nicolai papae, & similiter respondetur ad alias auctoritates, quae idem sonare videntur. Discipul. Dic quomodo respondetur ad rationes, quae eodem capitulo primo huius sexti sunt adductae. Magist. Ad primam diciturr, quod in casu haeresis licet appellare a summo pontifice, iura autem adducta loquuntur in alio casu, quam in casu haeresis. Discip. De hac materia transi: quia dudum contuli tecum de ipsa, ideo ad secundam rationem te conuerte. Magist. Ad secundam rationem respondetur, quod idem respectu eiusdem & eorundem potest esse superior & inferior in diuersis causis, sic enim delegatus est inferior ordinario iudice in multis causis, & in aliqua causa est eo superior. Sic papa de haeresi diffamatus & notorie criminosus, de quo scandalizatur ecclesia, si incorrigibilis fuerit, in causa sua est inferior catholicis aliis: in aliis tamen causis & ante pronunciationem sententiae in causa sua omnibus est superior. Ad tertiam rationem dicitur, quod papa potest accusari, nec obstat quod quaedam decreta dicunt, quod omnes pastorem accusare non possunt: quia illa capitula sane intelligenda sunt, & in multis casibus capiunt iustantias, sicut per sacros canones declaratur aperte.
units.tr: Disciple: I shall dispute that question, whether clerics ought to be judged by laymen, at another time; so tell me how the authority of Pope Gelasius is answered. Master: It is answered that those words of Pope Gelasius, if understood of the supreme pontiff, cannot be understood generally without any exception. For then the pope could not submit himself to the judgment of another. Likewise, if the pope were to judge the Christian faith to be false and feigned, and publicly sacrifice to idols, no one would be permitted to judge him. They must therefore be understood to apply if the pope is found to remain incorrigible. The same answer is given to the authority of Pope Nicholas, and likewise to the other authorities which seem to sound the same. Disciple: Tell me how the arguments adduced in the first chapter of this Sixth Book are answered. Master: To the first it is said that in the case of heresy it is lawful to appeal from the supreme pontiff, but the laws cited speak of a case other than heresy. Disciple: Pass over this matter, since I discussed it with you some time ago; so turn to the second argument. Master: To the second argument it is answered that the same person, with respect to the same people, can be both superior and inferior in different causes. Thus a delegate is inferior to the ordinary judge in many cases, and in some cause is superior to him. So the pope, defamed of heresy and notoriously criminal, by whom the Church is scandalized, if he is incorrigible, is inferior to other Catholics in his own cause; but in other causes, and before the pronouncement of sentence in his own cause, he is superior to all. To the third argument it is said that the pope can be accused, and it is no obstacle that certain decrees say that not all pastors can be accused; for those chapters are rightly to be understood, and in many cases they admit exceptions, as is clearly declared by the sacred canons.

units.la: CAP. LXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 63.

units.la: In quo ad rationes probantes, quod Papa de haeresi falso diffamatus non sit iudicio ecclesiae subiectus, respondetur, quae tacta sunt supra 10. c. huius.
units.tr: In which, as to the arguments proving that the Pope, though falsely defamed of heresy, is not subject to the judgment of the Church, the answer is what was touched upon above in chapter 10 of this book.

units.la: Discipul. Quomodo secundum praedictam assertionem ad rationes adductas in contrarium in decimo huius sexti respondetur, non differas explicare. Magist. Ad primam illarum rationum respondetur, quod falsa infamia non tribuit alicui super alium iurisdictionem coactiuam, nonnunquam tamen mouet rationabiliter iurisdictionem habentem ad inquirendum de aliquo, an ad eius iurisdictionem pertineat, sicut si aliquis exemptus a iurisdictione episcopi falso fuerit accusatus de crimine, ratione cuius esset de iurisdictione huius episcopi: talis infamia non tribuit iurisdictionem episcopo super exemptum, & tamen rationabiliter mouebit episcopum ad inquirendum de talite diffamato. Sic dicunt in proposito, quod nulla infamia falsa tribuit alicui iurisdictionem super papa, tamen debet mouere catholicos fidei zelatores ad inquirendum, an talis infamia contineat veritate. Non enim videtur eis, quod aliquis Christianitatis amator debeat asserere, quod (si papa esset publice & graviter diffamatus, quod vellet Sarracenos super Christianos inducere, & per eos Christianos vniuersos cogere ad recipiendam sectam Sarracenorum, & negandum Christum) non debeat Christiani veritatem inquirere, nec periculo futuro occurrere. Discipul. Propter solam infamiam non deberent catholici procedere ad talem inquisitionem de summo pontifice faciendam, nisi apparerent praesumptiones violentae, quod papa vellet praedicto modo, vel alio consimili Christianitatem destruere. Magist. Si concedas, quod propter infamias & praesumptiones violentas in quocunque casu sit de summo pontifice inquirendum, putant istu habere propositum: quod licet in casu de summo pontifice inquisitionem facere diligentem, antequam sit ipso iure papatu priuatus, ergo propter infamiam & propter praesumptiones violentas non est ipso facto papatu priuatus, nec a sacerdotio dotio summo distinguendus, ergo adhuc manet verus papa, & tamen concedis, quod propter infamiam & præsumptiones huiusmodi de ipso licet inquirere veritatem, ergo in casu licet de papa inquirere, licet in rei veritate non sit alicuius iurisdictioni subiectus, in quibus autem casibus specialibus, & propter quam infamiam, & propter cuiusmodi præsumptiones hoc liceat, isti nequaquam specificant, nisi duos casus generaliter assignando: si scilicet est de hæresi graviter diffamatus, & si incorrigibilem de aliquo crimine se ostendit.
units.tr: Disciple. Explain how, according to the aforesaid assertion, the arguments adduced to the contrary are answered in the tenth chapter of this sixth part; do not delay. Master. To the first of those arguments it is answered that a false infamy does not confer coercive jurisdiction over another; nevertheless it may reasonably move one who has jurisdiction to inquire into a person, whether the person falls under his jurisdiction. For example, if someone exempt from a bishop's jurisdiction were falsely accused of a crime, by reason of which he would fall under this bishop's jurisdiction, such an infamy does not confer jurisdiction over the exempt man upon the bishop, and yet it will reasonably move the bishop to inquire into the man so defamed. So they say in the present case: no false infamy confers jurisdiction over the Pope upon anyone, yet it ought to move Catholics, zealous for the faith, to inquire whether such an infamy contains the truth. For it does not seem to them that any lover of Christianity ought to assert that, if the Pope were publicly and gravely defamed of wishing to bring the Saracens against the Christians and, through them, to compel all Christians to accept the sect of the Saracens and to deny Christ, Christians should not inquire into the truth nor meet the coming danger. Disciple. Catholics ought not to proceed to such an inquiry into the supreme pontiff on the infamy alone, unless violent presumptions appeared that the Pope wished to destroy Christianity in the aforesaid manner or some similar one. Master. If you grant that on account of infamies and violent presumptions in any case inquiry must be made concerning the supreme pontiff, they think they have their point: that although in a case concerning the supreme pontiff a diligent inquiry may be made before he is by law deprived of the papacy, therefore on account of infamy and violent presumptions he is not ipso facto deprived of the papacy, nor is he to be distinguished from the supreme priesthood; therefore he remains the true Pope still; and yet you concede that on account of such infamy and presumptions it is lawful to inquire into the truth about him. Therefore in a case it is lawful to inquire about the Pope, although in the truth of the matter he is subject to no one's jurisdiction. In what special cases, and on account of what infamy, and what kind of presumptions, this is permitted, these men by no means specify, except that they assign two cases in general: namely, if he is gravely defamed of heresy, and if he shows himself incorrigible in some crime.

units.la: Discip. Dic quomodo respondetur ad secundam rationem. Magist. Respondetur, quod in una & eadem causa numero & eodem tempore idem respectu eiusdem vel eorundem non est superior & inferior: idem tamen respectu alicuius vel aliquorum in una causa vel in uno tempore est superior & in alia causa eiusdem speciei & in alio tempore respectu eiusdem vel eorundem est inferior. Rex enim alicuius regni, quod alteri quam regi non est subiectum, licet non habet superiorem personam, potest tamen in aliqua causa esse inferior regno, unde & regnum in casu iuste posset regem incorrigibilem deponere: & tamen quando Rex inveniretur immunis a tali delicto, & omnes de regno suo culpabiles in delicto, consimiliter probaretur quod Rex esset superior omnibus, & omnes posset de iure iuste punire, si tantam haberet potentiam temporalem. Sic etiam dicitur esse in ordinibus Mendicantium, quod capitulum generale pro aliquo delicto potest prælatum suum supremum deponere: & tamen si ipse immunis esset a delicto tali, & omnes in generali capitulo congregati essent culpabiles, ipse in omnes & singulos iustitiam posset exercere. Discip. Istud exemplum non videtur conveniens: quia quod generalia capitula Ordinum Mendicantium possint pro aliquo delicto prælatos suos supremos deponere, habent ex privilegio speciali Romani pontificis. Mag. Hoc (dicut isti) non impedit dictum eorum: quia undecunque habeat, concedendum est, quod idem respectu eiusdem vel eorundem est in una causa & in uno tempore superior: & in alia causa eiusdem speciei est inferior alio tempore. Ex quo concludunt, quod non est inconveniens, quod idem respectu eorundem in una causa sit superior, & tamen alias in causa alia eiusdem speciei illi, qui sunt inferiores, habeant potestatem inquirendi de superiori suo. Ex ita dicunt esse de papa: quod si omnes Christiani errarent in fide præter papam, ipse omnes de iure punire deberet: & tamen in alio casu si Christiani in fide persuaderent catholica, & papa esset de hæresi graviter diffamatus, catholici haberent potestatem inquirendi de ipso, si tamen ipsum invenirent innoxium, nullam iurisdictionem super ipsum haberent.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how the second argument is answered. Master. It is answered that in one and the same cause, in number and at the same time, the same person is not superior and inferior with respect to the same person or persons; yet the same person, with respect to someone or some persons, may be superior in one cause or at one time, and in another cause of the same kind and at another time be inferior with respect to the same person or persons. For the king of a realm, which is subject to no one other than the king, though he has no superior person, can nevertheless in some cause be inferior to the realm; whence in such a case the realm could justly depose an incorrigible king. And yet, when the king was found free of such a crime, and all in the realm were guilty of the crime, it would similarly be proved that the king was superior to all, and could justly punish all by right, if he had so much temporal power. So too it is said to be among the orders of the Mendicants that the general chapter may depose their supreme prelate for some crime; and yet if he himself were free of such a crime, and all gathered in the general chapter were guilty, he could exercise justice over all and each. Disciple. That example does not seem fitting, because that the general chapters of the Mendicant Orders may depose their supreme prelates for some crime they have from a special privilege of the Roman pontiff. Master. This (they say) does not hinder their statement: for whencesoever they have it, it must be granted that the same person with respect to the same or the same persons is superior in one cause and at one time, and in another cause of the same kind is inferior at another time. From this they conclude that it is not inconsistent that the same person with respect to the same persons should be superior in one cause, and yet in another cause of the same kind those who are inferior should have power to inquire into their superior. They say the same is true of the Pope: that if all Christians erred in the faith except the Pope, he ought by right to punish them all; and yet in another case, if Christians held the Catholic faith and the Pope were gravely defamed of heresy, the Catholics would have power to inquire into him, but if they found him innocent, they would have no jurisdiction over him.

units.la: Discip. Video intentionem istorum ad secundam rationem. Dic quomodo respondetur ad tertiam. Mag. Ad tertiam dicitur, quod non solum ecclesia universalis habet potestatem inquirendi de papa super crimine hæresis graviter diffamato, sed etiam alii, qui haberent iudicare papam, si esset manifeste in hæresi deprehensus, habent potestatem inquirendi de ipso, quemadmodum absque universali ecclesia & concilio generali episcopi convenerunt ad inquirendum de facto beati Marcellini, qui idololatriam commiserat. Discip. Istud peccatum fuit ita horrendum, quod dissimulari non poterat. Mag. Si concedas, quod pro quocunque peccato sit inquirendum de papa, totam istam assertionem everuas, quæ dicit, quod papa in nullo casu habet superiorem in terris: quia si concedatur, quod papa pro publica idololatria, vel si publice & manifeste prædicaret Christum fuisse mendacem & falsum prophetam, aut fidem Christianam esse falsam, aut sectam Sarracenorum esse tenendam, aut se circumcideret & Iudæum efficeret, vel corpus Christi in lacum proiiceret, vel resurrectionem futuram negaret, aut aliquid tale omnibus fidelibus detestandum præsumeret perpetrare, esset catholicorum subiectus iudicio: oportet consequenter concedere, quod papa potest in casu habere superiorem in terris. Ex quo sequitur, quod posset accidere casus, quod de papa diffamato haberent fideles inquirere veritatem. Discipul. Nunquid secundum istos est concedendum, quod aliqua persona habet potestatem inquirendi de papa super crimine hæresis diffamato? Mag. Isti concedunt quod sic: sicut concedunt, quod si papa esset in hæresi notorie deprehensus, aliqua persona haberet iurisdictionem super ipsum. Discip. Dic, quomodo respondetur ad exempla de Marcellino & Symacho. Magist. Respondetur, quod per utrumque exemplum habent isti propositum, nam de beato Marcellino de hæresi diffamato inquisitionem fecerunt episcopi, & ipsi propter talem infamiam reputaverunt se potestatem habere inquirendi de papa, sed postquam inquisierunt & invenerunt veritatem, scilicet quod beatus Marcellinus non erat hæreticus, & quod idololatraverat timore mortis, tantummodo constabat eis, quod licet antea haberent potestatem inquirendi veritatem de papa propter dubitationem in cordibus exortam, & ex infamia precedenti, tamen post inquisitionem non habuerunt potestatem iudicandi ipsum, nec sibi de iure debebant aliquam pœnitentiam pro commisso infligere. Consimiliter dicunt de Symacho papa, quod (quia in generali in concilio congregati non invenerunt ipsum hæreticum) non habuerunt potestatem iudicandi ipsum, prius tamen propter infamiam suscitatam de ipso habuerunt potestatem inquirendi & etiam cogendi ipsum oppositionibus respondere, quod ex verbis superius allegatis (ut videtur istis) evidenter apparet.
units.tr: Disciple. I see the intention of these men regarding the second argument. Tell me how the third is answered. Master. To the third it is said that not only the universal Church has power to inquire into the Pope on a gravely defamed charge of heresy, but also others who would have power to judge the Pope, if he were manifestly caught in heresy, have power to inquire into him, just as, without the universal Church and a general council, bishops met to inquire into the deed of blessed Marcellinus, who had committed idolatry. Disciple. That sin was so horrible that it could not be overlooked. Master. If you grant that concerning any sin whatever the Pope must be inquired into, you overturn that whole assertion which says that the Pope in no case has a superior on earth. For if it is granted that the Pope, for public idolatry, or if he publicly and openly preached that Christ was a liar and a false prophet, or that the Christian faith was false, or that the sect of the Saracens was to be held, or if he circumcised himself and made himself a Jew, or cast the body of Christ into a pit, or denied the future resurrection, or presumed to perpetrate anything of this kind to be detested by all the faithful, he would be subject to the judgment of Catholics; it must consequently be granted that the Pope can in such a case have a superior on earth. From this it follows that a case could arise in which the faithful should inquire into the truth about a Pope who had been defamed. Disciple. Is it therefore to be granted, according to these men, that some person has power to inquire into a Pope defamed of the crime of heresy? Master. These men grant that it is so, just as they grant that if the Pope were notoriously caught in heresy, some person would have jurisdiction over him. Disciple. Tell me how the examples of Marcellinus and Symmachus are answered. Master. It is answered that by each example these men make their point: for the bishops made an inquiry into blessed Marcellinus, who was defamed of heresy, and on account of such infamy they judged that they had power to inquire into the Pope; but after they had inquired and found the truth, namely that blessed Marcellinus was not a heretic, and that he had sacrificed to idols out of fear of death, it was clear to them only that, although before they had power to inquire into the truth about the Pope on account of the doubt arisen in their hearts and the preceding infamy, yet after the inquiry they had no power to judge him, nor ought they by right to impose any penance on him for what he had committed. They say similarly of Pope Symmachus that, since the men gathered in a general council did not find him a heretic, they had no power to judge him; yet before, on account of the infamy raised against him, they had power to inquire and even to compel him to answer the objections, which clearly appears (as it seems to these men) from the words cited above.

units.la: CAP. LXIV.
units.tr: CAP. LXIV.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationes probantes, quod concilium generale non habet iurisdictionem supra Papam de cri- mine haeresis diffamatum, superius c. 12. huius adductas.
units.tr: In which the arguments are answered that prove a general council does not have jurisdiction over the Pope in the case of a defamed crime of heresy, adduced above in chapter 12 of this work.

units.la: DISC. De istis responsionibus sollicite cogitabo, & post istud opus de ipsis tecum conferam diligenter. Nunc autem quaeso vt dicas, quomodo isti assertores respondent ad rationes adductas supra 12. huius sexti, quibus ostenditur, quod concilium generale non habet iurisdictionem super Papam de crimine haeresis diffamatu. MAG. Ad primam illarum respondent, quod ecclesia vniuersalis si esset simul congregata, sicut aliqui potuit simul congregari (& nescitur an ad tantam paucitatem deuenient, quod posset insimul convenire) potestatem haberet inquirendi de Papa super crimine haeresis diffamato: & si probaretur haereticus, ipsum punire deberet. Ad rationes autem in contrarium responsum est prius. Ad secundam dicitur, quod in casu non solum congregatio particularis, sed etiam aliqua persona potestate haberet super Papam, si n. (vt dicunt) Papa publice praedicaret & assereret fidem Christianam vanam esse & falsam, & fictam, & iniquam, Dioecesanus catholicus, cui hoc constaret, haberet potestate de iure capiendi & detinendi ipsum. Si etiam Papa esset Iudaeus vel Sarracenus, deficientibus praelatis ecclesiasticis ipsum potestas secularis captiuare deberet, si aut Papa de tali flagitio esset grauiter diffamatus, non solum concilium generale, sed etiam praelatus specialis haberet potestatem inquirendi de Papa, non captiuandi vel puniendi. Ad tertiam respondetur, quod etiam persona, quae potest contra fidem errare, dum tamen non errat de facto, posset in casu supra Papam habere iurisdictionem. Ad quartam respondetur, vt patet per illa, quae sunt dicta in capitulo praecedenti, quia sicut, si Papa esset in haeresi notorie deprehensus, concilium generale haberet iurisdictionem super ipsum, & tamen si Papa esset fortis in fide, & omnes alii de concilio generali errarent, essent sibi subiecti: ita si Papa esset in haeresi diffamatus, concilium generale haberet potestatem inquirendi de ipso: & tamen si Papa non erraret, & omnes alii errarent, Papa ipsos de iure iudicare deberet, & hoc quia (sicut dictum est) in diuersis causis eiusdem speciei diuersis temporib. idem respectu eiusdem & eorundem potest esse superior & inferior. Ad quintum dicitur, quod concilium generale habet potestatem principaliter ab ecclesia vniuersali, cuius vicem gerit, & cuius auctoritate principaliter conuocatur; sed immediate per Papam, si est catholicus, & desiderat sequi iustitiam, congregetur, vnde & absque Papa congregari posset in casu.
units.tr: DISC. I will think carefully about these answers, and after this work I will go over them with you thoroughly. Now, please tell me how these defenders respond to the arguments adduced above in the twelfth chapter of this sixth part, which show that a general council does not have jurisdiction over the Pope in the case of a defamed crime of heresy. MAG. To the first of those arguments they reply that the universal Church, if it were gathered together at one time, as some council could be gathered together (and it is not known whether it could ever come down to so small a number that it could assemble as one), would have authority to inquire into the Pope regarding the defamed crime of heresy, and if he were proved a heretic, it ought to punish him. The arguments to the contrary have been answered above. To the second it is said that in such a case not only a particular council but even a single person would have authority over the Pope: for if (as they say) the Pope were to preach publicly and assert that the Christian faith is vain, false, feigned and wicked, a Catholic diocesan to whom this was known would have the right to seize and detain him. Likewise, if the Pope were a Jew or a Saracen, then, with ecclesiastical prelates failing, the secular power ought to take him captive. But if the Pope were gravely defamed of such a disgrace, not only a general council but even a special prelate would have authority to inquire into the Pope, though not to take him captive or punish him. To the third it is answered that even a person who can err against the faith, provided he does not in fact err, could in such a case have jurisdiction over the Pope. To the fourth it is answered, as is plain from what was said in the preceding chapter: just as, if the Pope were notoriously caught in heresy, a general council would have jurisdiction over him, and yet if the Pope were strong in the faith and all the others in the general council erred, they would be subject to him; so, if the Pope were defamed of heresy, a general council would have authority to inquire into him, and yet if the Pope did not err and all the others did, the Pope ought to judge them by right. This is because (as has been said) in different cases of the same kind, at different times, the same person may be superior and inferior with respect to the same and the same persons. To the fifth it is said that a general council has its authority principally from the universal Church, whose place it holds and by whose authority it is principally convoked; but it is convoked immediately by the Pope, if he is Catholic and desires to follow justice; hence, in such a case, it could also be gathered without the Pope.

units.la: CAP. LXV.
units.tr: CHAP. LXV.

units.la: In quo assignantur modi, in quibus fideles habent iurisdictionem, seu potestatem super Papam, vbi ponuntur 4. casus, vbi notatur, quae sit potestas simpliciter & secundum quid.
units.tr: In which the modes are set out by which the faithful have jurisdiction, or power, over the Pope. Four cases are laid down, and it is noted what power is absolute and what power is in a certain respect only.

units.la: DISC. Recitasti nonnulla, de quibus inuestigationem specialem habebo, veruntamen antequam proponam, numera modos, in quibus catholici & fideles habent potestatem super Papam. MAG. Intendis solummodo loqui de Papa, qui est verus; vel generaliter de illo, qui postquam fuit Papa verus, gerit se pro Papa, siue de iure fuerit siue non? DISC. Loquor de omni illo, qui postquam fuisset verus Papa, gereret vel niteretur se gerere pro Papa. MAG. Adhuc volo scire, de qua potestate intelligis, an de potestate, quae est iurisdictio, an de omni alia, quam potest quis licite in alium exercere? Minister enim iudicis potest exercere potestatem in damnatum per iudicem; & tamen iurisdictionem habet minime super eum, potest etiam quis licite insidiantem occidere: & tamen ex hoc iurisdictionem super insidiantem minime habet, contingit etiam quandoque, licite absque iudicis auctoritate latrones occidere, super quos occidens iurisdictionem minime habet, licet enim non habenti iurisdictionem vim vi repellere. DISC. Aperte conspicio, quod contingit non habentem iurisdictionem licite potestatem in aliquem exercere, & ideo loquor de potestate iuridica communiter dicta. MAG. Nunc video intentionem tuam; & ideo ad mentem tuam respondebo. Dico, quod assertores praedicti asserunt manifeste, quod contingit licite exercere potestate simpliciter, vel secundum quid in Papam. DISC. Expone, quid potestatem vocant potestate simpliciter, & quid secundum quid. MAG. Potestatem simpliciter vocat, qua quis vel ordinarie vel aliquo casu pro aliquo tempore determinato contingit in alium exercere ipso nolente, & a principio renitente. Potestatem secundum quid vocant, qua potest quis in alium exercere ipso volente. DISC. Intelligo distinctionem eorum: & ideo explica, in quibus casibus contingit fideles licite exercere potestatem in Papam verum, vel in eum, qui fuit vel gerit se pro Papa. Magister. Dicunt quod potestatem secundum quid possunt catholici exercere in Papam, si eorum iudicio vel potestati inquirendi se submittat, sicut enim Leo Papa iudicio Imperatoris & suorum se submisit. Vnde etiam, vt legitur 2. quaestion. 7. cap. nos, scribens Ludouico Imperatori ait: Nos si incompetenter aliquid egimus in subditis, iuste legu tramitem non obseruauimus, vestro ac Missorum vestrorum cuncta volumus emendare iudicio. Etiam Gregorius cupiebat se subdere aliorum iudicio, qui, vt habetur causa, & quae praedictis, cap. si quis, ait: Si quis super his nos redarguere voluerit, vel extra auctoritatem nos facere contenderit, veniat ad sedem Apostolicam, vt ibi ante confessionem beati Petri mecum iuste decertet, quatenus ibi vnus ex nobis sententiam suscipiat suam. Ex his datur intelligi, quod cum Papa iudicio se submittit, alius in ipsum suscipisuscipit potestatem, sicut autem Papa potest submittere se iudicio aliorum, ita valet committere aliis potestatem inquirendi de ipso. Discip. Refer casus, in quibus haberet simpliciter aliquis potestatem in Papam. Magister. Ponunt quatuor casus, nec tamen alios negant. Primus est, si Papa in se vel alium manus crudeles cupit mittere: puta, si seipsum vult occidere, aut graviter vulnerare, vel mutilare, vel alium sine omni causa vult occidere. In hoc enim casu licet Papam, sive fuerit alienatus a sensu sive non, compescere & modo debito coercere. Secundus casus est, si Papa, hoc est, qui fuit verus Papa, & cupit se gerere pro Papa, in haeresi manifeste deprehenditur, tunc enim licet eum detinere, & de sede deicere violenter, & debitae subdere ultioni. Tertius est, si Papa in aliquo crimine fuerit deprehensus, de quo scandalizatur ecclesia, & ipse incorrigibilem se ostendit. Quartus, si fuerit de haeresi diffamatus, & mendaciter, tunc enim catholici habent potestatem inquirendi de ipso, licet non habeant potestatem iudicandi ipsum, nisi cum scandalo ecclesiae irrevocabiliter sive pertinaciter se submittere vel purgare renuit. Praeter istos casus forte ponerent alios, sed ad istos, vel ad aliquem istorum poterunt forte reduci.
units.tr: STUDENT. You have recited several points that I shall want to examine in particular, but before you propose them, tell me the modes in which Catholics and the faithful have power over the Pope. MASTER. Do you mean only the Pope who is genuinely Pope, or in general anyone who, after having been Pope, acts as Pope, whether rightly or not? STUDENT. I mean anyone who, after being a true Pope, would act, or try to act, as Pope. MASTER. I want to know further what kind of power you mean: power of jurisdiction, or any other power that one may lawfully exercise over another? A minister of a judge may exercise power over a man condemned by the judge, and yet he has no jurisdiction over him. One may also lawfully kill a would-be assassin, and yet by doing so one does not thereby gain jurisdiction over the assassin. It also sometimes happens that robbers may lawfully be killed without the authority of a judge, and the one who kills them has no jurisdiction over them, for even a man without jurisdiction may repel force by force. STUDENT. I clearly see that a person without jurisdiction may lawfully exercise power over someone, and so I am speaking of power in the juridical sense, as it is commonly understood. MASTER. Now I see what you intend, and so I shall answer in line with your meaning. I say that the aforementioned champions openly assert that one may lawfully exercise power over the Pope, either absolute power or power in a certain respect. STUDENT. Explain what they call absolute power and what they call power in a certain respect. MASTER. They call absolute power that by which someone may exercise power over another, either ordinarily or in some particular case for a determined time, even against that other's will and from the outset in spite of his resistance. They call power in a certain respect that by which one may exercise power over another with that other's consent. STUDENT. I understand their distinction. So explain in what cases Catholics may lawfully exercise power over a true Pope, or over one who has been Pope or who acts as Pope. MASTER. They say that Catholics may exercise power in a certain respect over the Pope if he submits himself to their judgment or to their power of inquiry, just as Pope Leo submitted himself to the judgment of the Emperor and of his own people. Hence also, as we read in 2 Quaest. 7, c. Nos, writing to the Emperor Louis, he says: If we have acted improperly toward our subjects, and have not kept to the path of just law, we wish to amend all things by your judgment and that of your envoys. Gregory too was willing to subject himself to the judgment of others; as is found in the cause and the matters mentioned above, in c. Si quis, he says: If anyone wishes to rebuke us in these matters, or strives to act against us beyond authority, let him come to the Apostolic See, so that there, before the confession of blessed Peter, he may contend justly with me, and there one of us may receive his sentence. From these things it is to be understood that when the Pope submits himself to judgment, another takes up power over him; and just as the Pope can submit himself to the judgment of others, so he can commit to others the power of inquiring into him. STUDENT. Tell me the cases in which someone would have absolute power over the Pope. MASTER. They lay down four cases, though they do not deny that there may be others. The first is if the Pope desires to lay cruel hands upon himself or upon another: for example, if he wishes to kill himself, or gravely wound or maim himself, or to kill another without any cause. In this case it is lawful to restrain the Pope, whether or not he has lost his reason, and to coerce him in a fitting manner. The second case is if the Pope, that is, one who has been a true Pope and desires to act as Pope, is manifestly caught in heresy; for then it is lawful to detain him, to depose him from the see by force, and to hand him over to due punishment. The third is if the Pope has been caught in some crime, on account of which the Church is scandalized, and he shows himself incorrigible. The fourth is if he has been publicly defamed of heresy, and falsely; for then Catholics have the power of inquiring into him, although they have no power of judging him, unless he refuses, to the scandal of the Church, to submit or to clear himself irrevocably or obstinately. Apart from these cases they might perhaps lay down others, but these, or some of them, may perhaps be reduced to these.

units.la: CAP. LXVI.
units.tr: Chapter 66.

units.la: Vbi incipit secunda pars principalis huius libri sexti, in qua inuestigare intendit de punitione Papae haretici. Et primo de poena depositionis eius a Papatu & omni ecclesiastica dignitate. Qualiter Papa vel alius si efficiatur vere haereticus, & non solum sit falso diffamatus, feriendus sit canonice & puniendus. Pro cuius determinatione primo quaeritur, utrum Papa, si efficiatur vere haereticus, sit ipso facto omni auctoritate & ecclesiastica dignitate privatus? Quod sic: primo ostenditur, quia ex iure divino deduci potest praedicta quaestionis prima assertio seu conclusio, scilicet quod Papa si vere efficiatur haereticus, eo facto non est verus Papa, sed iure divino & Christi sententia est eo facto a Papatu privatus, quod ratione ostenditur.
units.tr: Here begins the second principal part of this sixth book, in which the author intends to inquire into the punishment of a Pope who is a heretic. First, concerning the penalty of his deposition from the papacy and from every ecclesiastical dignity: how a Pope, or anyone else, who truly becomes a heretic, and is not merely falsely accused, is to be struck down and punished according to the canons. To determine this, it is first asked whether a Pope who truly becomes a heretic is, by that very fact, stripped of all authority and ecclesiastical dignity. The answer is yes. First, it is shown that from divine law the first assertion or conclusion of this question can be deduced, namely that if a Pope truly becomes a heretic, he by that very fact is no longer a true Pope, but by divine law and the sentence of Christ he is by that fact deprived of the papacy. This is shown by reason.

units.la: Discipulus. Postquam de Papa super crimine haeresis mendaciter diffamato plura quaesivi, & quaedam interserui de Papa effecto haeretico; volo nunc plura de Papa vere haeretico indagare. In primis autem exordiis disseras, an Papa, si efficiatur haereticus, ipso facto sit omni auctoritate & ecclesiastica dignitate nudatus. Magist. De hoc videntur esse diversae sententiae. Una est, quod Papa, si efficiatur haereticus sive manifestus, sive occultus, ipso facto est Papatu privatus, quamvis ab ecclesia toleretur. Discipu. Quo iure dicunt Papam Papatu esse privatum si haereticam incurrerit pravitatem? Mag. Dicunt quod iure divino est privatus. Discip. Quomodo possunt hoc dicere, cum in tota scriptura divina nulla mentio de Papa haeretico penitus habeatur? Mag. Respondent, quod licet in scriptura divina nulla mentio de Papa haeretico specialis & vocalis inveniatur, plura tamen universalia in Scriptura sacra reperiuntur, quae possunt ad Papam haereticum applicari. Ex quibus & ista vel consimili (Papa est haereticus) concluditur evidenter, quod Papa haereticus non est Papa verus: & per consequens quod est Papatu privatus. Disc. Hoc scire desidero, quomodo ex contentis in scriptura divina probare nituntur, quod Papa, si efficiatur haereticus, non est verus Papa. Mag. Hoc per plures rationes probare conantur. Quarum prima est haec, verus Papa quantumcunque sceleratus & impius a catholicis est sequendus: quia licet eius opera imitanda non sint, eius tamen doctrina est servanda. Ipsa veritate testante, quae Matth. 23. ait: super cathedram Moysi sederunt scribae & Pharisaei, omnia ergo quaecunque dixerint vobis, servate & facite: secundum vero opera eorum nolite facere. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod sacerdotes veteris legis sequendi fuerunt, quantum ad doctrinam & praecepta, ergo multo magis sequendus est, quamdiu manet Papa. Sed si Papa efficeretur haereticus, nullatenus est sequendus: praecipiente Christo, qui vt habetur Luc. 21. ait: multi venient in nomine meo dicentes, ego sum: & tempus appropinquabit: nolite ergo ire post illos. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod qui venerit in nomine Christi, & tamen est adversarius Christi, non est eundum post eum. Sed qui dicit se esse vicarium Christi, venit in nomine Christi, & si errat contra fidem, est adversarius Christi: ergo non est eundum post illum, nec est aliquo modo sequendus, & per consequens non est verus vicarius Christi, quia verus vicarius Christi est sequendus, & ita Papa, quam cito fit haereticus, sententia Christi Papatu est privatus. Disc. Ista ratio videtur tripliciter deficere, primo, quia male intelliguntur verba Christi, cum dicit: Multi venient in nomine meo dicentes, ego sum. Non enim loquitur de illis Christus, qui venturi erant in nomine Christi, asserentes se esse vicarios Christi, quales sunt summi Pontifices: sed loquitur de illis, qui venturi erant in nomine Christi, dicturi se habere potestatem & dignitatem ac sublimitatem Christi, & illi nullo modo sunt sequendi. Si enim aliquis Papa primo catholicus, postea diceret se esse Christum, & quod honor divinus esset ei impendendus, nullo modo esset eundum post ipsum. Secundo videtur deficere praedicta ratio: quia ire post Papam contingit dupliciter, vel sequendo doctrinam, vel praeceptum eius, quamvis ergo Papa efficeretur haereticus, non esset eundum post ipsum sequendo eius doctrinam: quia doctrina haeretica est omnimodo vitanda: esset tamen eundum post ipsum, eius obediendo praeceptis; & ita maneret verus Papa. Tertio deficit ratio supra dicta: quia si ipsa concluderet, probaret aperte, quod si Papa absque omni pertinacia erraret contra
units.tr: Disciple. After I have asked many things about a Pope falsely accused of the crime of heresy, and have inserted some remarks about a Pope who has become a heretic, I now want to investigate further about a Pope who is truly a heretic. At the very outset, please explain whether a Pope, if he becomes a heretic, is by that very fact stripped of all authority and ecclesiastical dignity. Master. On this there seem to be differing opinions. One view is that a Pope who becomes a heretic, whether manifest or hidden, is by that very fact deprived of the papacy, although the Church tolerates him. Disciple. By what right do they say that a Pope is deprived of the papacy if he falls into heretical depravity? Master. They say that he is deprived by divine right. Disciple. How can they say this, since in the whole of divine Scripture there is no mention at all of a heretical Pope? Master. They answer that although no special and explicit mention of a heretical Pope is found in divine Scripture, yet many universal statements are found in Holy Scripture which can be applied to a heretical Pope. From these, together with this or a similar premise (the Pope is a heretic), it is evidently concluded that a heretical Pope is not a true Pope, and consequently that he is deprived of the papacy. Disc. I would like to know how they try to prove from what is contained in divine Scripture that a Pope, if he becomes a heretic, is not a true Pope. Mag. They try to prove this by several arguments. The first is this: a true Pope, however wicked and impious he may be, must be followed by Catholics, because although his works are not to be imitated, his teaching is to be kept. The truth itself bears witness, saying in Matthew 23: The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works. From these words it is gathered that the priests of the old law were to be followed in doctrine and precepts; therefore much more is a Pope to be followed as long as he remains Pope. But if a Pope became a heretic, he is in no way to be followed, Christ commanding it, who, as is related in Luke 21, says: Many will come in my name, saying, I am he, and the time is near; do not therefore go after them. From these words it is gathered that one who comes in the name of Christ, and yet is an adversary of Christ, is not to be followed. But one who says he is the vicar of Christ comes in the name of Christ, and if he errs against the faith, he is an adversary of Christ; therefore one must not go after him, nor is he to be followed in any way, and consequently he is not a true vicar of Christ, because the true vicar of Christ is to be followed. Thus a Pope, as soon as he becomes a heretic, is deprived of the papacy by the sentence of Christ. Disc. This argument seems to fail in three ways. First, because the words of Christ are wrongly understood when he says: Many will come in my name, saying, I am he. Christ is not speaking of those who would come in the name of Christ, asserting that they are vicars of Christ, as the supreme Pontiffs are; he is speaking of those who would come in the name of Christ, claiming to have the power, dignity and exaltedness of Christ; and such men are in no way to be followed. For if some Pope who was at first Catholic afterwards said that he was Christ, and that divine honour was to be paid to him, one would in no way go after him. Second, the said argument seems to fail because going after a Pope happens in two ways, either by following his doctrine or by obeying his precept. Although, then, a Pope became a heretic, one would not be going after him by following his doctrine, because heretical doctrine is to be avoided in every way; yet one would be going after him by obeying his precepts, and so he would remain a true Pope. Third, the argument above is defective, because if it were conclusive, it would clearly prove that if a Pope, without any obstinacy, erred against the faith, he would be deprived of the papacy.

units.la: Ioan. 3. contra fidem, esset Papatu priuatus. Nam qui docet falsam doctrinam siue pertinaciter, siue non pertinaciter, non est in hoc sequendus, & ita qui veniret in nomine Christi, dicens: ego sum Papa & vicarius Christi, & teneret quomodocunq; doctrinam contra fidē, non est eundum post illum, & per consequens esset Papatu priuatus, quod est omnino contrarium veritati. Mag. Istas instantias tuas quidam friuolas arbitrantur putantes per ipsas demonstratiue probare coclusionem intentam. Per primam enim ostenduntur (vt eis videtur aperte) quod Papa, si efficiatur haereticus, voce Christi est Papatu priuatus, talem namq; faciunt rationem.
