Verum inter ipsum & summum Pontificem nouae legis talis fuit differentia, quod summus sacerdos veteris legis effectus haereticus, si postea conuertebatur ad fidem veram, sacerdotium recuperabat amissum, quemadmodum excommunicatus & executione priuatus officii, quando absoluitur, officii recuperat executionem, sed si summus Pontifex nouae legis efficitur haereticus, quomodocunq; occultus, sic Papatum amittit, quod quantumcunq; postea conuertatur ad fidem, Papatum nequaquam recuperabit. Istud videtur ratione carere, cum nequeat neq; auctoritate scripturae diuinae, neq; ratione muniri. Quod non ratione, de se patet: quia talia, quae sunt positiua, per rationem probari non possunt, neque auctoritate scripturae diuinae; quia talis differentia inter summum Pontificem veteris legis & Papam in tota scriptura non poterit inueniri. Magister. Respondetur, quod talis differentia ex Scripturis sacris accipit fulcimentum. Constat enim secundum scripturam diuinam, quod summum sacerdotium veteris legis certae cognationi & generi debebatur, nullus enim praeter filios Aaron debuit esse summus Pontifex, Papatus autem certae cognationi aut generi non debetur. Petrus enim nequaquam pro se & filiis suis Papatum recepit a Christo: Ex quo ergo iure successionis, qui erat summus sacerdos in veteri lege sacerdotium summum obtinuit, & non erat statutum in veteri lege, quod summus sacerdos effectus haereticus (ipso ab haeresi desistente) non recuperaret illud, quod sibi debebatur iure successionis hereditariae, conueniens fuit, vt videtur, quod ipse ad fidem reuersus recuperaret sacerdotium, quod per haereticam prauitatem amiserat. Papa autem iure successionis hereditariae Papatum minime habet, & ideo si propter perfidiam haeresis Papatu priuatur, nequaquam Papatum recuperat, nisi eligeretur de nouo. Aliter dicitur, quod quia summus sacerdos antiquae legis sacerdotium habuit iure successionis: ideo executionem officii amittere potuit propter haereticam prauitatem. Officium autem, quamdiu vixit, non amisit. Sed Papa non habet officium Papatus iure successionis, ideo amittendo executionem Papalis officii, ipsum officium Papale amittit. Et ista differentia est inter Papam haereticum & summum sacerdotem haereticum in veteri lege.
units.tr: Disciple. That assertion is purely negative, and so when it says that Scripture nowhere finds a heretical Pope to be deprived of the papacy by the very fact of his heresy, it seems that this could not be proved against a stubborn opponent except by going through each passage of Holy Scripture, especially those dealing with heretics or unbelievers. I do not want you to do that. So, since you have offered what seem to me the stronger arguments for this side, I ask you to show how it is possible to answer them. I will discuss the arguments given for the other side with you after we finish this dialogue. Master. There are two ways of answering the first of these arguments. The first says that the high priest of the old law, by the very fact of becoming a heretic, was deprived of the high priesthood, and that he was then not the true high priest in the reality of the matter, although he remained high priest in men's opinion. But there was this difference between him and the Pope of the new law: if a high priest of the old law became a heretic and afterwards turned back to the true faith, he recovered the priesthood he had lost, just as an excommunicated person, or one deprived of the exercise of his office, recovers the exercise of it when he is absolved. But if the Pope of the new law becomes a heretic, however secretly, he thereby loses the papacy, and however much he turns back to the faith afterwards, he will never recover the papacy. This seems to lack reason, since it can be supported neither by the authority of Holy Scripture nor by argument. That it lacks reason is plain in itself, because positive matters of this kind cannot be proved by reason, nor by the authority of Holy Scripture, since such a difference between the Pope and the high priest of the old law cannot be found anywhere in all of Scripture. Master. The answer is that such a difference does have support from Holy Scripture. For according to divine Scripture, the high priesthood of the old law was owed to a certain kinship and lineage: no one but the sons of Aaron was to be high priest. The papacy, however, is not owed to any particular kinship or lineage. For Peter did not receive the papacy from Christ for himself and his sons. Therefore, since the high priest of the old law held the high priesthood by right of succession, and since the old law did not provide that a high priest who became a heretic (if he gave up his heresy) would not recover what was owed to him by right of hereditary succession, it seems fitting that he, returning to the faith, would recover the priesthood which he had lost through heretical depravity. But the Pope does not hold the papacy by hereditary right of succession. Therefore, if he is deprived of the papacy on account of the perfidy of heresy, he never recovers it, unless he is elected anew. The other answer is that, because the high priest of the old law held the priesthood by right of succession, he could lose the exercise of his office on account of heretical depravity, but he did not lose the office itself as long as he lived. The Pope, however, does not hold the office of the papacy by right of succession. Therefore, by losing the exercise of the papal office, he loses the papal office itself. This is the difference between a heretical Pope and a heretical high priest under the old law.

units.la: Discipulus. Intelligo responsionem istorum ad primam rationem, ideo indica qualiter respondetur ad secundam rationem. Mag. Ad secundam rationem dicitur, quod omnes episcopi & praelati ecclesiastici incurrentes haereticam prauitatem, siue publice, siue occulte iure diuino suis dignitatibus sunt priuati. Quia in his, quae sunt propria religioni Christianae, nulla potest esse communicatio haeretici ad fidelem. Et ideo quantum ad illa quae spiritualia sunt, haereticus fidelibus praesse non potest. Distinctio enim fidelis & infidelis non est ex iure humano, siue canonico & ciuili, sed est ex iure diuino. Et ideo quod infideles (qualis est omnis haereticus) fidelibus in spiritualibus praesse non debeant, est ex iure diuino. Quare iure diuino omnis haereticus omni praelatione ecclesiastica est priuatus, quod Apostolus secund. Corinth. sext. insinuare videtur, ait enim: Nolite iugum ducere cum infidelibus, quae enim participatio iustitiae cum iniquitate? aut quae societas lucis ad tenebras? quae autem concordia Christi ad Belial? aut quae pars fidelis cum infideli? quis autem consensus templo Dei cum idolis? In quibus verbis Apostolus videtur insinuare & praecipere fidelibus vniuersis, ne subsint infidelibus, & ne communicent eis. Quod potissime veritatem habet quantum ad spiritualia & ea, quae propria sunt religioni Christianae, quamuis enim in temporalibus possint fideles subesse infidelibus, & communicare in spiritualibus: tamen ipsis subesse non debent. Et ita omnis haereticus, cum sit infidelis, iure diuino omni praelatione ecclesiastica est priuatus, & ita maior illius rationis est falsa secundum assertionem illam. Ad probationem eius respondetur, quod licet episcopi inferiores summo Pontifice & alii praelati (si haereticam incurrerint prauitatem) sint iure diuino omni ecclesiastica praelatione priuati: tamen ex causa rationabili per ordinationem concilii generalis vel summi Pontificis possunt, (si conuersi fuerint) ad suas restitui dignitates, quamuis enim iure diuino haeretici sunt omni ecclesiastica praelatione priuati; restitutio tamen eorum ad pristinam dignitatem (si conuersi fuerint) ex iure diuino nullatenus est interdicta, & ideo per ecclesiam restitui possunt, & talis restitutio vel est noua electio, vel aequipollet electioni noui. Disc. Illa responsio sacris canonibus obuiare videtur. Nam videtur quod episcopus factus haereticus, iure diuino non sit episcopatu priuatus. Quia qui iure diuino est episcopatu priuatus, statim absq; licentia quacunq; episcopatui renunciare teneretur. Qui enim auctoritate superioris est dignitate priuatus, non debet petere ab inferiori cedendi licentiam. Sed episcopus factus haereticus, non potest renunciare sine licentia Papae, qui est inferior lege diuina, ext. de renunciat. cap. nisi & ca. post translationem, ergo episcopus factus haereticus, non est per legem diuinam episcopatu priuatus. Item, si episcopus haereticus esset iure diuino episcopatu priuatus; quilibet, qui fuit subditus eius, sciens ipsum esse haereticum, ipsum vitare deberet; nec deberet sibi quomodolibet obedire. Sed hoc canoni Symachi Papae, qui ponitur 8. q 4. c. nonne, aperte repugnat, qui iubet nullum clericum ante tempus sententiae ab episcopo suo discedere, dicens: nonne directa sunt verba canonum? Si quis clericorum ab episcopo suo ante tempus sententia pro dubia suspitione discesserit, manifestam in eum manere censuram, lex enim ecclesiastica Pontificem ab aliis accusatum priusquam sub luce obiecta constituerint, exigit non relinqui. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod ante tempus sententiae non est ab obedientia episcopi haeretici recedendum, & per consequens non est iure diuino episcopatu priuatus. Mag. Ad euidentia primae obiectionis rationis, quae fundatur in hoc, quod pro nullo crimine potest episcopus renunciare episcopatui sine licentia Papae, dicitur esse sciendum, q; sicut recitat Gloss. in c. praeallegato, ext. de renunciatione c. nisi, de hoc sunt opiniones contrariae: quibusdam dicentibus, quod nullus criminosus, nullus irregularis potest renunciare sine licentia Papae: etiam si titulum non habeat, vt simoniacus & intrusus, & secundum istos videtur, quod episcopus factus haereticus non potest renunciare sine licentia Papae. Alii dicunt, quod quidam renunciare possunt sine licentia Papae. Unde dicunt, quod symoniacus & intrusus non habent titulum, sed fures & invasores sunt 1. q. 1. c. ordinationes, & ideo quanto plus tenent, tanto plus peccant, quia fur est semper in mora. Unde dicunt, quod isti renunciare tenentur auctoritate canonis 1. q. 1. si quis, etiam absque licentia Papae, sed in illis, qui titulum habent, secus est, ibi enim necessaria est licentia Papae, patet ergo quod de petenda cedendi licentia sunt opiniones diuersae. Hoc viso dicitur distinguendo, vt videtur concordando cum Gloss. quae opiniones recitat, supradictas, quia episcopus criminosus, aut habet titulum secundum veritatem, aut secundum hominum opinionem, sicut Symoniacus saltem non notorius, sed occultus vel non notorius haereticus: aut non habet titulum neque secundum veritatem, neque secundum opinionem hominum; sicut publice intrusus. In secundo casu videtur, quod talis statim cum habet conscientiam & propositum renunciandi, statim renunciare debet, nec videtur quod vnq; teneatur petere cedendi licentiam, si autem criminosus habeat titulum secundum veritatem, nullo modo potest cedere absq; licentia petita & obtenta, si autem habeat titulum non secundum veritatem, sed secundum opinionem hominum ab omni administratione & executione officii statim cessare tenetur, & nihilominus in manu superioris, sc. papae renunciare debet, & ita quodammodo petere cedendi licentia vel verius renunciare, quare non potest retinere officium explicite allegando, & hoc debet non quia sit dignitate priuatus, sed quia debet satisfacere illis, qui ipsum reputant verum titulum habuisse, praesertim cum possit esse occultum, quod non habuit titulum verum: & nullus debet diffamare seipsum, quare non diffamet seipsum debet petere cedendi licentiam & auctoritate superiorum renunciare solenniter. His Gloss. concordare videtur, quae ait: licet titulum non habeat symoniacus, tamen videtur habere titulum, cum enim per electionem habuit ecclesiam, quo ad communem opinionem habet titulum, si occulta fuerit symonia. Unde propter hoc saltem tenetur licentiam petere, & causa potest subesse: quia si bene administraverit, Papa de facili dispensabit cum eo, & per hoc posset dici, quod intrusus omnino cedere debet: quia nec quantum ad opinionem, nec quantum ad veritatem titulum habet. Ex his patet, quod quandoq; occupans dignitatem debet statim cedere: quandoq; non debet statim cedere publice sc. renunciando, licet nunq; ante tale renunciationem cessare debet ab omni administratione & officii executione, p hoc ad tuam obiectionem taliter respondetur, q; interdum episcopus iure diuino episcopatu priuatus licet statim debet cessare ab administratione officii, potest tu & debet publice ex causa petere cedendi licentia a superiori iure diuino: no quia no est priuatus iure diuino, sed ex alia rationabili causa, sic est de episcopo prauitate haeretica incurrente, q; debet petere licentia cedendi. Non quia no sit de iure diuino priuatus, sed quia ante perfidia haeresis habuit verum titulum; & post habuit secundum hominum opinionem, & ideo debet statim cessare ab omni administratione & executione episcopalis officii. Sed no debet statim publice & solenniter renunciare; praesertim si est occultus haereticus, ne prodat & diffamet seipsum: sed debet a Papa petere licentia renuntiandi, vt sic auctoritate Papae publice & solenniter renuntiet, ne credatur quod renuntiet propter haeretica prauitatem. Disc. Propter hanc rationem non deberet cessare ab executione episcopalis officii: quia si sic procederet, diffamaret seipsum. Magist. Dicitur quod absque diffamatione sui ipsius de haeretica prauitate potest cessare ab executione episcopalis officii. Et ideo debet cessare: quia sibi non licet quantumcunque sit poenitens exequi officium episcopale, ex quo fuit haereticus & p superiorem vel potestate habentem est minime restitutus. Sed petere licentiam renunciandi vel renunciare in manu Papae, licet sibi quantumcunq; fuerit haeretica prauitate foedatus, & ideo hoc debet facere, tum propter statutum ecclesiae, tum propter scandala euitanda. Ad secundam obiectionem dicitur, quod quicunque scit episcopum suum esse haereticum, ipsum debet non episcopum reputare & sibi minime obedire, sicut notat Gloss. 2. quaestion. 7. cap. sacerdotes, & Glossa 24. quaest. 1. cap. 1. quae ait: si scirem praelatum meum esse haereticum, quia nouam haeresim fingit, nec tamen praedicaret, si me excommunicaret, celebrarem in occulto, sed non in aperto. Ex quibus verbis clare apparet, quod episcopo haeretico non debet sciens ipsum esse haereticum obedire: sed licet ab ipso discedere, quare iam sententia legis diuinae & etiam constitutionis ecclesiae est damnatus. Nec huic obuiat canon Simachi Papae, si quis subtiliter verba eius inspexerit. Nam, sicut expresse patet, ipse loquitur de illis, qui pro dubia suspitione ab episcopo accusato antequam obiecta constiterint, praesumunt recedere, quod est minime faciendum. Quia quantumcunque episcopus aliquis fuerit effectus haereticus, nullus subditus eius dubia suspitione debet ab eo recedere ante tempus sententiae. Secus est de illo, qui non dubitat, sed scit episcopum suum in prauitatem haereticam incidisse.
units.tr: Student. I understand their reply to the first argument; now tell me how the second argument is answered. Master. To the second argument it is said that all bishops and ecclesiastical prelates who fall into heretical depravity, whether openly or secretly, are deprived of their dignities by divine right. For in those matters that belong to the Christian religion there can be no communion between a heretic and a faithful person. Therefore, as far as spiritual things are concerned, a heretic cannot preside over the faithful. The distinction between faithful and unfaithful does not rest on human law, whether canon or civil, but on divine law. So the rule that unbelievers (and every heretic is such) ought not to preside over the faithful in spiritual matters comes from divine law. Hence by divine right every heretic is deprived of all ecclesiastical prelacy. The Apostle seems to hint at this in 2 Cor. 6, where he says: Be not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship have righteousness and unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? and what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel? And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? In these words the Apostle seems to hint at, and to command all the faithful, that they should not be subject to unbelievers and should not have communion with them. This holds especially as regards spiritual matters and those that belong to the Christian religion. For although the faithful may be subject to unbelievers in temporal affairs and have communion with them in spiritual ones, yet they ought not to be subject to them in spiritual things. And so every heretic, being an unbeliever, is by divine right deprived of all ecclesiastical prelacy; and therefore the major premise of that argument is false, according to that assertion. To its proof it is answered that although lower bishops, the supreme Pontiff, and other prelates, if they fall into heretical depravity, are by divine right deprived of all ecclesiastical prelacy, yet for a reasonable cause, by the ordinance of a general council or of the supreme Pontiff, they can (if they are converted) be restored to their former dignities. For although heretics are by divine right deprived of all ecclesiastical prelacy, their restoration to their former dignity, if they are converted, is nowhere forbidden by divine right; and therefore they can be restored by the Church, and such a restoration is either a new election or is equivalent to a new election. Student. That answer seems to conflict with the sacred canons. For it seems that a bishop who has become a heretic is not deprived of his episcopate by divine right. For whoever is deprived of the episcopate by divine right would be bound to resign at once, without any permission at all. For one who has been removed from his dignity by the authority of a superior ought not to ask a lower authority for permission to resign. But a bishop who has become a heretic cannot resign without the permission of the Pope, who is inferior to divine law (Ext., De renunciatione, cap. Nisi, and cap. Post translationem). Therefore a bishop who has become a heretic is not deprived of his episcopate by divine law. Again, if a heretical bishop were deprived of his episcopate by divine right, then anyone who had been his subject, knowing him to be a heretic, ought to shun him and should in no way obey him. But this openly contradicts the canon of Pope Symmachus, which is found in 8 q. 4, c. Nonne, which orders that no cleric shall leave his bishop before the time of sentence. It says: Do not the words of the canons plainly say: If any of the clergy has departed from his bishop before the time of sentence, on account of a doubtful suspicion, the censure shall remain manifest against him; for ecclesiastical law requires that a Pontiff accused by others shall not be left before they have established the charges in the light. From these words it is to be understood that, before the time of sentence, one must not withdraw from the obedience of a heretical bishop, and consequently he is not deprived of the episcopate by divine right. Master. To make clear the first objection, which rests on the point that a bishop cannot resign his episcopate for any crime without the Pope's permission, it must be known that, as the Gloss cited in the aforementioned chapter, Ext., De renunciatione, cap. Nisi, reports, there are contrary opinions on this. Some say that no criminal and no irregular person can resign without the Pope's permission, even if he has no title, like a simoniac or an intruder; and according to them it seems that a bishop who has become a heretic cannot resign without the Pope's permission. Others say that some can resign without the Pope's permission. They say that simoniacs and intruders have no title, but are thieves and usurpers (1 q. 1, c. Ordinationes); and so the more they hold on, the more they sin, because a thief is always in the wrong. Hence they say that such men are bound by the authority of the canon (1 q. 1, Si quis) to resign even without the Pope's permission; but it is otherwise with those who have a title, for in their case the Pope's permission is necessary. It is clear, then, that opinions differ about seeking leave to resign. Having considered this, the answer is given by making a distinction, which seems to agree with the Gloss that reports the aforementioned opinions. A criminal bishop either has a title in truth, or has one in the opinion of men, like a simoniac who is at least not notorious but hidden; or he has no title either in truth or in the opinion of men, like one who is an openly intruded bishop. In the second case it seems that such a man, as soon as he is aware of it and intends to resign, ought to resign at once, nor does it seem that he is ever bound to ask leave to resign. But if the criminal has a title in truth, he can in no way resign without asking for and obtaining leave. If, however, he has a title not in truth but in the opinion of men, he is bound at once to cease from all administration and performance of the office, and nevertheless he ought to resign into the hands of his superior, that is, the Pope; and so, in a sense, he asks leave to resign, or rather resigns. Therefore he cannot keep the office by openly alleging something; and he ought to do this not because he is deprived of the dignity, but because he must satisfy those who think he had a true title, especially since it may be hidden that he had no true title. And no one ought to defame himself; therefore, lest he defame himself, he ought to ask leave to resign and resign solemnly by the authority of his superiors. The Gloss seems to agree with this, which says: Although a simoniac has no title, yet he seems to have one, since by election he has obtained the church; so far as common opinion goes he has a title, if the simony is hidden. Therefore for this reason at least he is bound to ask leave, and there may be a cause for it, since if he has administered well, the Pope will easily dispense with him; and by this one could say that an intruder must altogether resign, because he has a title neither as to opinion nor as to truth. From these things it is clear that sometimes one who holds a dignity ought to resign at once, and sometimes he ought not to resign publicly at once, that is, by resigning, although he must never, before such resignation, cease from all administration and performance of his office. Accordingly, to your objection the answer is given in this way: sometimes a bishop who is deprived of the episcopate by divine right must at once cease from the administration of his office, yet he can and ought publicly, for a cause, to ask leave to resign from his superior, by divine right; not because he is not deprived by divine right, but because of another reasonable cause. So it is with a bishop who falls into heretical depravity: he ought to ask leave to resign. Not because he is not deprived by divine right, but because before the perfidy of heresy he had a true title, and after it he has one only in the opinion of men; and so he ought at once to cease from all administration and performance of the episcopal office. But he ought not at once to resign publicly and solemnly, especially if he is a secret heretic, lest he betray and defame himself; but he ought to ask the Pope for leave to resign, so that by the Pope's authority he may resign publicly and solemnly, lest it be believed that he resigns because of heretical depravity. Student. For this reason he ought not to cease from performing the episcopal office, since if he did so he would defame himself. Master. It is said that he can cease from performing the episcopal office without defaming himself as a heretic. And so he ought to cease; for it is not lawful for him, however penitent he may be, to perform the episcopal office, since he has been a heretic and has not been restored by a superior or by one who has power to do so. But to ask leave to resign, or to resign into the Pope's hands, is lawful for him, however much he has been defiled by heretical depravity; and therefore he ought to do this, both because of the statute of the Church and in order to avoid scandals. To the second objection it is said that whoever knows his bishop to be a heretic ought to regard him as no bishop and by no means obey him, as the Gloss notes on 2 q. 7, cap. Sacerdotes, and the Gloss on 24 q. 1, cap. 1, which says: If I knew my prelate to be a heretic, because he invents a new heresy, and yet did not preach it, and if he excommunicated me, I would celebrate in secret, but not in the open. From these words it is clearly apparent that one who knows a heretical bishop to be a heretic ought not to obey him, but may withdraw from him; for he has already been condemned by the sentence of divine law and also by the constitution of the Church. Nor does the canon of Pope Symmachus stand in the way of this, if one looks closely at his words. For, as is plainly evident, he speaks of those who, on a doubtful suspicion, presume to withdraw from a bishop accused by them before the charges have been established; and this is by no means to be done. For however much a bishop may have become a heretic, no subject of his ought to withdraw from him on a doubtful suspicion before the time of sentence. It is otherwise with one who does not doubt but knows that his bishop has fallen into heretical depravity.

units.la: Disc. Dic quomodo ad rationem tertiam respondetur. Mag. Ad tertiam respondetur sic: quod secus est de praelatione ecclesiastica & seculari. Nam praelatio ecclesiastica introducta est a iure diuino: quia ex ordinatione diuina est, quod vnus fidelis aliis fidelibus in spiritualibus praesse debet: praelatio vero secularis introducta est a iure humano. Et ideo quia distinctio debet esse inter fideles & infideles quoad spiritualia, nec in spiritualibus communicant vel concordant, sed dissentiunt, possunt autem in temporalibus concordare, ideo licet principes seculares, quamuis efficiantur haeretici, non sint iure diuino principatu seculari priuati, praelati tamen ecclesiae si efficiantur haeretici iure diuino, ipso facto principatu ecclesiastico sunt priuati. Discipulus. Ista responsio tripliciter videtur deficere. Primo, quia aliquorum regum principatus secularis fuit a iure diuino: & tamen quamuis fuissent effecti haeretici, non fuissent principatu seculari iure diuino priuati, ergo non est haec causa, quare principes ecclesiastici, si efficiuntur haeretici, iure diuino sunt priuati: quia eorum scilicet principatus est a iure diuino. Secundo videtur etiam, quod principes seculares, si efficiantur haeretici, iure diuino suis principatibus sunt priuati, quia illi sunt iure diuino priuati principatu suo, quibus ex praecepto iuris diuini fideles communicare non debent. Sed ex praecepto iuris diuini fideles infidelibus communicare non debent, teste Apostolo, qui sicut allegatum est prius, ait: nolite iugum ducere cum infidelibus: ergo principes seculares, si efficiantur haeretici, iure diuino suis principatibus sunt priuati. Tertio videtur, quod propter hoc, quod fideles & infideles, quoad spiritualia dissentiunt & discordant, non est dicendum, quod infideles quoad spiritualia fidelibus praesse non possint. Nam boni & mali, quo ad spiritualia dissentiunt & discordant, & tamen mali bonis, quo ad spiritualia praesse possunt, ergo consimiliter licet fideles & infideles, quo ad spiritualia dissentiant & discordent, tamen quoad spiritualia infideles fidelibus praesse valebunt. Magister. Ad primam respondetur, quod non ideo praelati ecclesiastici, cum efficiuntur haeretici, omni praelatione ecclesiastica sunt iure diuino priuati, quia sint praelati a iure diuino. Sed quia praelatio ecclesiastica a iure diuino solummodo sumpsit originem, nec humanitus est inuenta, quamuis quod aliqui sint praelati ecclesiastici habeant a iure humano. Quod enim vnus sit episcopus & non alius, est a voluntate humana eligentium & consentientium. Praelatio autem secularis est inuenta, vel potuit humanitus ordinari, licet quidam fuerint principes seculares ex speciali ordinatione diuina. Et ideo idem dicendum est de illis principibus secularibus, qui ex ordinatione praefuerunt diuina, sicut & de aliis regibus siue principibus, qui ex ordinatione praefuerunt humana, qui non aliud ius vel praelationem habuerunt aliam, licet consimile ius vel praelationem habuerunt ab alio isti, quam alii. Praelati autem ecclesiastici aliud ius & aliam praelationem habent, quam principes seculares: quia praelationem habent inuentam diuinitus, quam infideles super fideles habere non debent. Et causa apparentior assignatur: quia fideles & infideles in spiritualibus, quae respicit praelatio ecclesiastica, non communicant, sed discordant. Et ideo sicut infideles nolunt in ritibus suis doceri & regi ab aliquo ritus contrarii: ita non debent fideles, quoad spiritualia & ritus religionis suae aliquo modo infideli subesse. Ad aliam obiectionem respondetur, quod principes seculares infideles, siue nunquam fidem susceperint, siue fidem susceptam reliquerint, vel pertinaciter contra fidem errauerint, non sint principatibus iure diuino priuati, nec regulariter ex praecepto iuris diuini fideles vitare eos tenentur, quia in temporalibus eos vitare non necessario astringuntur regulariter ex iure diuino: licet ex iure diuino aliqui infideles fuerint specialiter deuitandi, sed in spiritualibus & in his, quae contra religionem faciunt Christianam eos vitare tenentur. Quod enim infideles ex iure diuino non sunt in omnibus equitandi, aperte insinuat Paulus, cum dicit prima ad Corinth. septim. Si quis frater vxorem habeat infidelem, & hac consentit habitare cum illo; non dimittat illam, & si qua mulier habet virum infidelem & hic consentit habitare cum illa, non dimittat virum. Ex quibus datur intelligi, quod licet fidelibus communicare cum infidelibus, quod etiam in plerisque locis epistolarum suarum innuit manifeste praecipiens fidelibus Dominis & etiam infidelibus obedire, veruntamen in his, quae erant contra legem diuinam nec eis communicare, nec eis obedire debebant, teste beato Augustino, qui vt habetur ii. quaestion. 3. cap. imperatores, ait: Iulianus extitit Imperator infidelis: nonne extitit apostata iniquus & idolatra: milites Christiani seruierunt Imperatori infideli, vbi veniebant ad causam Christi non agnoscebant, nisi illum qui in caelo erat, quando volebat vt idola colerent & thurificarent praeponebant illi Deum, quando autem dicebat, producite aciem: ite contra illam gentem: statim obtemperabant & distinguebant Deum aeternum a Domino temporali. Ex quibus verbis colligitur: quod infidelibus etiam haereticis in noua lege licebat fidelibus in temporalibus obedire, sed non in spiritualibus, & ideo quantum est ex iure diuino, non sunt infideles & haeretici regulariter deuitandi. Et per hoc patet responsio ad obiectionem tertiam. Disc. Hoc videtur contradicere supradictis, & etiam B. Cypriano, qui (vt allegasti ratione 13. p assertione illa) ex iure diuino accepit fundamentum, quod infidelibus etiam in temporalibus non debet communicare fideles, cum probat quod cum infidelibus nec terrestribus nec secularis potus debet esse communis per hoc, quod legitur in libro Regū, propheta qui iuit ad exprobrandum Ieroboam prohibitus fuit a Deo comedere panem & bibere vinum in loco illo. Mag. Ad hoc dicitur, quod hoc fuit speciale in exprobrationem & aggravationem ac detestationem peccati Ieroboam, qui apostatavit a fide & alios apostatare fecit, ex hoc tamen exemplo accipit Cyprianus argumentū, quod haereticis cupientibus alios ad suam trahere prauitatem (si comode vitare possunt) nullatenus communicare debemus, & ita quod hoc regulare est, quod infidelibus quibuscunq; absq; causa rationabili & necessitate vrgente ex praecepto iuris diuini communionem negare non debemus, nec tenentur, hoc autem generale est, quod eis in spiritualibus & in his, quae religioni Christianae sunt propria, neque obedire, neque subesse valemus, nisi praeceptis legis diuinae contraire velimus.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how the third reason is answered. Master. The third is answered thus: it is otherwise with ecclesiastical and secular authority. For ecclesiastical authority was instituted by divine right, since it is by divine ordinance that one believer should preside over other believers in spiritual matters. Secular authority, however, was instituted by human right. Because there must be a distinction between believers and unbelievers in spiritual matters, and they do not share or agree in them but disagree, whereas they can agree in temporal matters, it follows that secular princes, even if they become heretics, are not deprived of their secular principality by divine right. Ecclesiastical prelates, however, if they become heretics, are by divine right deprived of their ecclesiastical principality by that very fact. Disciple. This answer seems to fail in three ways. First, the secular principality of some kings was by divine right, and yet, even if they had become heretics, they would not have been deprived of their secular principality by divine right. So this is not the reason why ecclesiastical princes, if they become heretics, are deprived by divine right, namely because their principality is by divine right. Second, it also seems that secular princes, if they become heretics, are deprived of their principalities by divine right, because those are deprived by divine right of their principality with whom believers ought not to communicate by a precept of divine right. But by a precept of divine right believers ought not to communicate with unbelievers, as the Apostle, whom we cited earlier, says: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Therefore secular princes, if they become heretics, are deprived of their principalities by divine right. Third, it seems that because believers and unbelievers disagree and conflict in spiritual matters, it cannot be said that unbelievers are unable to preside over believers in spiritual matters. For good and bad men disagree and conflict in spiritual matters, and yet bad men can preside over good men in spiritual matters. Therefore, in the same way, although believers and unbelievers disagree and conflict in spiritual matters, unbelievers will nevertheless be able to preside over believers in spiritual matters. Master. To the first, it is answered that ecclesiastical prelates, when they become heretics, are not deprived of all ecclesiastical authority by divine right because they were prelates by divine right. Rather, ecclesiastical authority took its origin from divine right alone and was not devised by men, although the fact that certain men are ecclesiastical prelates has its basis in human right. For that one man is a bishop and another is not comes from the will of those who elect and consent. Secular authority, however, was devised, or could have been ordained, by men, although some were secular princes by a special divine ordinance. And therefore the same must be said of those secular princes who presided by divine ordinance as of other kings or princes who presided by human ordinance. These did not have any other right or authority, although those princes had a right or authority similar to others, though received from a different source. But ecclesiastical prelates have a different right and a different authority from secular princes, because they hold an authority divinely established, which unbelievers ought not to hold over believers. And a more obvious cause is given: believers and unbelievers do not communicate in spiritual matters, which ecclesiastical authority concerns, but disagree. Therefore, just as unbelievers do not want to be taught or ruled in their rites by anyone of a contrary rite, so believers ought not in any way to be subject to an unbeliever in spiritual matters and in the rites of their religion. To the other objection it is answered that unbelieving secular princes, whether they have never received the faith, or have abandoned the faith they received, or have stubbornly erred against the faith, are not deprived of their principalities by divine right, nor are believers as a rule bound by a precept of divine right to shun them. For they are not necessarily bound by divine right, as a general rule, to shun them in temporal matters, although by divine right some unbelievers were to be shunned in particular. But in spiritual matters, and in those things which are contrary to the Christian religion, they are bound to shun them. That unbelievers are not by divine right to be avoided in everything, the Apostle plainly indicates when he says in 1 Cor. 7: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away; and if a woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not put away her husband. From these words it is understood that, even in the New Law, believers were permitted to communicate with unbelievers, which he also clearly suggests in many places of his letters, when he directs believers to obey their masters, even unbelieving ones. Yet in those things which were against the divine law they were neither to communicate with them nor obey them, as blessed Augustine testifies, who, as is found in 2 Q. 3, c. Imperatores, says: Julian was an unbelieving emperor; was he not a wicked apostate and idolater? Christian soldiers served the unbelieving emperor, and when it came to the cause of Christ, they acknowledged no one but the one who was in heaven. When he wanted them to worship and burn incense to idols, they put God before him; but when he said, "Draw up your battle line, go against that nation," they at once obeyed, and distinguished the eternal God from the temporal lord. From these words it is gathered that believers, even in the New Law, were allowed to obey unbelievers and heretics in temporal matters, but not in spiritual ones; and therefore, as far as divine right goes, unbelievers and heretics are not to be shunned as a general rule. And by this the answer to the third objection is made clear. Disciple. This seems to contradict what was said above, and also blessed Cyprian, who (as you cited in reason 13, in that assertion) took the foundation from divine right, that believers ought not to communicate even in temporal matters with unbelievers, when he proves that neither earthly nor secular drink ought to be shared with unbelievers, from what is read in the Book of Kings: the prophet who went to rebuke Jeroboam was forbidden by God to eat bread or drink wine in that place. Master. To this it is said that this was a special case, for the rebuke, aggravation and detestation of the sin of Jeroboam, who apostatized from the faith and made others apostatize. Yet from this example Cyprian takes an argument that we ought by no means to communicate with heretics who desire to draw others to their wickedness (if we can conveniently avoid them). So the general rule is that we ought not, and are not bound by a precept of divine right, to deny communion to any unbelievers without a reasonable cause and a pressing necessity. This, moreover, is the general principle: that in spiritual matters, and in those things proper to the Christian religion, we can neither obey nor be subject to them, unless we wish to act contrary to the precepts of the divine law.

units.la: Disc. Explana, quomodo ad alias rationes respondetur. Mag. Ad quartam rationē patet responsio per praedicta, quod non est contra legem diuinam haereticos & alios infideles in temporalibus praesidere fidelibus, ideo Ioseph & Daniel & alii catholici & fideles, tam in Nouo Testamento quam in veteri constituti absq; transgressione legis diuinae infidelibus in temporalibus seruierunt. Ad quintam rationem dicitur, quod hoc non est generaliter verum: ad quem spectat institutio alicuius, ad eundē spectat destitutio eiusdē. Nam metropolitanus potest confirmare, consecrare & constituere clericum in episcopum, & tamen eundē destituere minime valet & esto, quod haec esset vera generaliter; haec tamen est omnino falsa: ad illum pertinet destitutio alicuius, ad quem institutio spectat eiusdē: quia institutio sacerdotis spectat ad episcopū, & tamē superior episcopo potest destituere ipsum, ita esto quod eligentes Papam possent destituere ipsum; ex hoc non sequitur, quod non potest destitui a iure diuino, quod est super omne ius humanum & omnium eligentiū potestatem. Ad sextam dicitur, quod ecclesia vniuersalis regitur a Spiritu S. & ideo ecclesia vniuersalis nunq; deficiet in his, quae necessaria sunt ad salutē, licet in aliis deficere possit pariter & errare, & ideo si Papa esset haereticus occultus: & per consequens Papatu priuatus, & ideo illa quae iurisdictionis sunt exercere non posset, quamuis posset facere ea, quae ordinis sunt, Deus ecclesiae prouideret; vel reuelando ecclesiae perfidiam Papae, & quod non valuerunt quantum ad ea, quae iurisdictionis sunt illa quae fecit; vel consecrando alios episcopos; vel per alium modum sibi possibilē, licet nobis ignotū, & ideo nullus ordo ecclesiasticus necessarius ad salutē vniuersalis ecclesiae confunderetur, licet multa, sine quib. poterit esse salus, possent esse confusa. Praeseruaret n. Deus ne confunderetur illa, quae in vniuersali ecclesia sunt necessaria ad salutē. Vnde illa ratio cōcludit aequaliter, quod mulier nō potest putari Papa & haberi pro Papa, quod paganus & infidelis (reputatus tn Christianus fidelis) nō potest haberi pro Papa. Quia si mulier vel paganus infidelis haberetur pro Papa, & de facto cōsecraret episcopos, & ordinaret Christianos & dignitates ecclesiasticas promoueret, nō minus confunderetur ecclesiastica Hierarchia, quam si Papa haereticus iure diuino Papatu priuatus putaretur Papa, & Papale officium in omnibus exerceret, imo magis confunderetur ecclesiastica Hierarchia, quā si haereticus iure diuino Papatu priuatus putaretur a catholicis esse Papa: licet ordinando de facto & consecrando nulli tribueret executionem officii, verumtamen ordinem conferret, dummodo seruaret ordinem ecclesiae, mulier autem ac paganus vel Iudaeus, qui nunquam fuit Christianus, nec executionem nec aliquem ordinem verum conferret, licet seruaret formam ecclesiae, cum ergo constat, quod aliquando mulier a catholicis putabatur Papa, & eadem ratione aliquis paganus vel Iudaeus retinens in corde infidelitatis perfidiam posset putari Christianus & in Papa assumi, non est incredibile, quin aliquando haereticus habeatur pro Papa, licet verus Papa non sit, eo quod iure diuino est Papatu priuatus. Sic ergo constat, quod maior difficultas est, si mulier habeatur pro Papa, quam si Papa fiat haereticus, sed iure diuino ipse sit Papatu priuatus. Ad vltimam rationem respondetur, quod licet in sacra Scriptura de priuatione officii & beneficii sub his verbis mentio nullatenus habeatur: sub aliis tamen verbis de hac poena mentio in diuinis scripturis habetur. Quare ex hoc ipso, quod Papa haereticus non est sequendus, sed vitandus: & ex hoc, quod non est ei in spiritualibus communicandum; habetur hoc, quod Papa haereticus officio & beneficio est priuatus. Quia Papa verus, qui non est officio priuatus, est non solum in temporalibus, sed etiam in spiritualibus sequendus, & est ei nedum in temporalibus, sed & in spiritualibus communicandum, & est obediendum eidem. Constat autem per scripturam sacram, quod Papa haereticus, quando scitur esse haereticus, non est sequendus, nec est ei in spiritualibus communicandum, ergo per Scripturam sacram officio & beneficio est priuatus.
units.tr: Disc. Explain how the other arguments are answered. Mag. The reply to the fourth argument follows from what has been said: it is not against the divine law for heretics and other unbelievers to rule over the faithful in temporal matters. Thus Joseph, Daniel and other catholic and faithful men, both under the New Testament and under the Old, served unbelievers in temporal affairs without transgressing the divine law. To the fifth argument it is said that this is not generally true: the one to whom the institution of something belongs is also the one to whom its removal belongs. For the metropolitan can confirm, consecrate and appoint a cleric as bishop, and yet he by no means has the power to depose him. And even if this were generally true, it is wholly false that the removal of anything belongs to the one to whom its institution belongs. For the institution of a priest belongs to the bishop, and yet a superior of the bishop can depose him. So, even if those who elect the Pope could depose him, it does not follow that he cannot be deprived by divine law, which stands above all human law and the power of all electors. To the sixth argument it is said that the universal Church is governed by the Holy Spirit, and therefore the universal Church will never fail in those things that are necessary for salvation, although it may fail and err in other things. So if the Pope were a hidden heretic, and consequently deprived of the papacy, and therefore unable to exercise those things that belong to jurisdiction, though he could still do those things that belong to orders, God would provide for the Church. He would either reveal to the Church the Pope's treachery, so that his acts concerning jurisdiction would have no force; or he would consecrate other bishops; or he would do so by some other means possible to him, though unknown to us. Thus no ecclesiastical order necessary for the salvation of the universal Church would be thrown into confusion, although many things without which salvation could still be had might be thrown into disorder. For God would preserve the universal Church from confusion in those things that are necessary to salvation. Hence that argument equally concludes that a woman cannot be thought of as Pope and regarded as Pope, and that a pagan or unbeliever (though reputed a faithful Christian) cannot be regarded as Pope. For if a woman or a pagan unbeliever were regarded as Pope, and in fact consecrated bishops, ordained Christians and promoted men to ecclesiastical dignities, the ecclesiastical hierarchy would be thrown into no less confusion than if a heretic, deprived of the papacy by divine law, were thought to be Pope and exercised the papal office in every respect. Indeed the hierarchy would be thrown into greater confusion than if a heretic, deprived of the papacy by divine law, were held by catholics to be Pope. For although such a heretic, ordaining and consecrating in fact, would not confer the exercise of his office on anyone, he would still confer orders, provided he kept the form of the Church. But a woman, or a pagan or Jew who had never been a Christian, would confer neither the exercise of office nor any true order, even if they kept the form of the Church. Since, then, it is established that at some time a woman was thought by catholics to be Pope, and by the same reasoning some pagan or Jew who keeps the unbelief of his heart could be thought a Christian and be taken up as Pope, it is not incredible that at some time a heretic may be regarded as Pope, although he is not the true Pope, because by divine law he has been deprived of the papacy. So it is clear that there is a greater difficulty if a woman is regarded as Pope than if the Pope becomes a heretic but by divine law is deprived of the papacy. To the last argument it is answered that although Holy Scripture nowhere mentions the deprivation of office and benefice under these words, mention of this penalty is nevertheless found in the divine Scriptures under other words. Therefore, from the very fact that a heretical Pope is not to be followed but avoided, and from the fact that he is not to be communicated with in spiritual matters, it follows that a heretical Pope is deprived of office and benefice. For a true Pope, who is not deprived of office, is to be followed not only in temporal but also in spiritual matters; he is to be communicated with not only in temporal but also in spiritual matters, and he is to be obeyed. But it is established by Holy Scripture that a heretical Pope, when it is known that he is a heretic, is not to be followed, nor is he to be communicated with in spiritual matters. Therefore by Holy Scripture he is deprived of office and benefice.

units.la: CAP. LXIX.
units.tr: CAP. LXIX.

units.la: In quo ponitur secunda quaestio praambula huius secundae partis, sc. quam potestatem habet ecclesia vniuersalis supra Papam haereticum. Quae quidem quaestio consequenter conformiterque ad precedentem varios habet opinantes, & sunt 4 in numero, quorum quilibet ponit vnam conclusionem responsiuam, primam prosequitur in hoc c. secundam 70. tertiam 71. & quartam 72.
units.tr: In which the second preliminary question of this second part is set out, namely what power the universal Church has over a heretical Pope. This question, following and corresponding to the previous one, has four differing opinions, each of which puts forward one responding conclusion. The first is pursued in this chapter, the second in chapter 70, the third in chapter 71, and the fourth in chapter 72.

units.la: Disc. Allegasti multa ad probandū & defendendum assertionem, quae dicit, quod Papa haereticus factus est de iure diuino Papatu priuatus. Nunc aut peto, vt referas, quā potestatē secundū litera-tostos habet ecclesia super papam labem haereticam incurrentem. Magist. Circa interrogationem illam opiniones reperiuntur contrariae. Quarum una est dicentium papam haereticum esse iure diuino priuatum papatu, qui tenent quod papa haereticus non maiori priuilegio gaudet, quam alius episcopus, si prauitate haeretica fuerit maculatus. Et ideo nec ecclesia vniuersalis, nec concilium generale, & quaelibet persona catholica habet eandem potestatem super papam haereticum, q; super alium episcopum haereticum habere dignoscitur. Et pro illa assertione arguitur sic. Si papa effectus haereticus haberet priuilegium speciale, quod alii episcopi haeretici minime habent: aut habet illud priuilegium iure diuino, aut a iure humano. Non a iure diuino: quia in tota scriptura diuina non poterit inueniri, quod inter papam haereticum & episcopum & alium haereticum fiat distinctio. Nec habet aliquod speciale a iure humano: quia etiam ius humanum inter papam haereticum & alium episcopum haereticum non distinguit. Nullo ergo priuilegio gaudet papa haereticus speciali. Discipul. Dicetur forte, quod ex recto dictamine rationis papa haereticus gaudet priuilegio speciali. Quia sicut secundum rectam rationem nobiles minus puniuntur, quam ignobiles 24. q. i. c. qui contra, ita videtur quod secundum rectam rationem minus sunt puniendi maiores in ecclesia quam minores. Cum ergo papa in ecclesia sit maximus, videtur quod secundum rectam rationem minus puniendus est (si efficiatur haereticus) quam alius episcopus haereticus inferior. Et ita gaudet aliquo priuilegio speciali. Magist. Nonnullis apparet, quod ratio tua non concludit propositum sed magis oppositum, nam crimini grauiori maior debetur vindicta, extra de haeret. excommunicamus, vbi sic scribitur: in quo maior est culpa, maior exerceatur vindicta. Sed labes haeretica grauior est in papa, quam in alio inferiori episcopo, ergo secundum rectam rationem grauius puniri debet: Quia, vt notat Glos. 2. q. 5. c. praesul, papa quantum ad aliquid deterioris conditionis est, quia ipse sine cooperatione aliorum creatus est, & ideo sine ipse veniae condemnandus est, vt Diabolus. Ad rationem ergo tuam respondetur, quod quantum ad aliquid est simile de nobili & ignobili, & de papa haeretico & alio episcopo haeretico, & quantum ad aliquid est dissimile. Est enim simile quantum ad hoc, quod sicut nonnulla peccata grauiora sunt in nobili quam in ignobili, ita perfidia haeresis grauior est in illo qui fuit papa, quam in aliquo alio episcopo, & ideo sicut nobilis quantum ad poenam aliquam grauius punitur quam ignobilis (vt notat Glo. super praeallegatum capitulum, qui contra pacem) sic papa haereticus grauius est puniendus quam alius episcopus haereticus. Est autem quantum ad hoc dissimile, quia nobilis per peccatum suum nobilitatem non amittit, sed retinet, & ideo aliqua poena minus punitur quam ignobilis, nimirum quia si poena aliqua speciali (puta verberibus vel consimili puniretur, sicut ignobilis) alii innocentes de genere suo vituperandi forent. Sed si papa fiat haereticus, dignitatem papalem non retinet, sed amittit, & ideo propter dignitatem, quam non retinet, debet minui poena: & ideo similiter grauius puniendus est papa haereticus, quam alius episcopus haereticus, nec aliquo gaudet priuilegio speciali.
units.tr: Disciple. You have adduced many arguments to prove and defend the assertion that a heretical Pope has been deprived of the papacy by divine right. Now I ask you to explain what power, according to the learned, the Church has over a Pope who falls into the stain of heresy. Master. Concerning that question, there are conflicting opinions. One of them is held by those who say that a heretical Pope is deprived of the papacy by divine right. They hold that a Pope who has been stained by heretical depravity enjoys no greater privilege than any other bishop. Therefore neither the universal Church, nor a general council, nor any Catholic person has over a heretical Pope the same power that is recognised as existing over any other heretical bishop. And for this assertion the argument runs as follows. If a Pope who has become heretical had a special privilege that other heretical bishops do not have, then he has that privilege either by divine right or by human right. Not by divine right, because nowhere in the whole of divine Scripture can it be found that a distinction is made between a heretical Pope and another heretical bishop. Nor does he have any special privilege by human right, because human law too makes no distinction between a heretical Pope and another heretical bishop. Therefore a heretical Pope enjoys no special privilege. Disciple. Perhaps it will be said that by the right dictate of reason a heretical Pope enjoys a special privilege. For just as according to right reason nobles are punished less than commoners 24. q. 1. c. qui contra, so it seems that according to right reason those greater in the Church are to be punished less than those lesser. Since, then, the Pope is the greatest in the Church, it seems that, if he becomes a heretic, he is by right reason to be punished less than another, inferior heretical bishop. And so he enjoys some special privilege. Master. It seems to some that your reasoning does not prove the proposition but rather the opposite. For a greater punishment is owed to a graver crime extra de haeret. excommunicamus, where it is written thus: where the fault is greater, the vengeance should be greater. But the stain of heresy is graver in the Pope than in any inferior bishop. Therefore, according to right reason, he ought to be punished more severely. For, as the Gloss notes 2. q. 5. c. praesul, the Pope is in a worse condition in some respects, because he was created without the cooperation of others, and therefore he is to be condemned without pardon, like the Devil. To your argument, then, it is answered that in some respects the noble and the commoner, and the heretical Pope and another heretical bishop, are alike, and in some respects they are unlike. They are alike in this: just as some sins are graver in a noble than in a commoner, so the treachery of heresy is graver in one who was Pope than in any other bishop; and therefore, just as a noble is punished more severely than a commoner in respect of some penalty (as the Gloss notes on the aforementioned chapter qui contra pacem), so a heretical Pope is to be punished more severely than another heretical bishop. They are unlike in this: a noble does not lose his nobility through his sin but keeps it, and so he is punished less than a commoner by some penalty, namely because if he were punished by some special penalty (say by beating or something similar, as a commoner would be), other innocent men of his kind would be disgraced. But if a Pope becomes a heretic, he does not keep the papal dignity but loses it, and so, on account of the dignity he no longer keeps, the penalty ought to be lessened. Therefore, similarly, a heretical Pope is to be punished more severely than another heretical bishop, and he enjoys no special privilege.

units.la: CAP. LXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 70.

units.la: Ponit secundam opinionem, & responsionem suam ad quaesitum capitulo praecedenti, & respondet sub tribus conclusionibus, qua etiam probantur secundum ordinem.
units.tr: He sets out the second opinion and his answer to the question in the preceding chapter, and he answers under three conclusions, which are also proved in order.

units.la: Discipul. Dixisti circa interrogationem meam esse opiniones contrarias, recitasti vnam, dic ergo aliam. Mag. Alia opinio est dicentium, quod papa haereticus non est iure diuino papatu priuatus, qui tenent, quod nullas super papam obtinet potestatem, nisi ecclesia vniuersalis vel concilium generale, ecclesia autem vniuersalis, si conueniret in vnum, & etiam concilium generale, habet potestatem deponendi papam, & sibi poenas alias infligendi. Aliae autem congregationes & personae antequam papa haereticus per vniuersalem ecclesiam aut concilium generale fuerit papatu priuatus, super papam haereticum nullam obtinent potestatem: sed postquam fuerit depositus iurisdictioni inferiorum summo pontifice (sicut caeteri haeretici) est subiectus: nisi ecclesia vniuersalis vel concilium generale post depositionem vlteriorem punitionem papae haeresi sibi specialiter reseruaret. Discipul. Mihi videtur, quod tenentes illam opinionem tria probare deberent, quorum primum est, quod papa haereticus non est iure diuino papatu priuatus. Secundum quod ecclesia vniuersalis & etiam concilium generale habeat potestatem deponendi papam haereticum. Tertium est, quod nulla congregatio vel persona inferior ecclesia vniuersali & concilio generali potestatem habet supra papam haereticum deponendum. Si enim ista essent vera, caetera essent plana. De primo autem tractatum est supra, vbi adducta sunt rationes ad probandum, quod papa haereticus non est iure diuino papatu priuatus. Ideo pro secundo ad probandum scilicet, quod ecclesia vniuersalis & concilium generale potestatem habet papam haereticum deponendi alias rationes excogita. Mag. Ad satisfaciendum petitioni tuae oportet duo probare, quorum primum est, quod ecclesia vniuersalis habet potestatem deponendi papam haereticum. Secundum, quod concilium generale talem obtinet potestatem. Primum autem probatur primo sic. Illa congregatio, quae potestatem habet super papam de haeresi mendaciter diffamatum, multo magis potestatem habet super papam veraciter haeresi irretitum, sed ecclesia vniuersalis habet potestatem, scilicet inquirendi de papa super crimine haeresis diffamato, licet mendaciter, vt probatum est supra in hoc extra 6. 2. Ergo multo magis vniuersalis ecclesia habet ptatem deponendi papam de haeretica prauitate conuictum. Discipul. Cerno, quod rationes illae cap. 2. huius sexti adductae magis concludunt de papa haeretico, quam de crimine haeresis mendaciter diffamato. Ideo ad praesens nolo pro assertione hac alias rationes audire, quare transi ad secundum. Magist. Secundum scilicet quod concilium generale habet potestatem deponendi papam haereticum, sic probatur. Concilium generale est supra papam de haeresi diffamatum, sicut ostensum est supra c. 13. ergo multo fortius habet potestatem vere haereticum deponendi. Discip. Illae etiam assertiones in capitulo illo adductae, sunt, ut arbitror, fortiores, quae potuerunt cogitari ad probandum, quod concilium generale habet potestatem super papam haereticum. Ideo accede ad tertium probandum: scilicet quod nulla congregatio vel persona ecclesiastica ecclesia vniuersali & concilio generali inferior: habet potestatem papam haereticum deponendi. Mag. Hoc probatur primo sic, inferior iudicare non potest superiorem, distin. 21. ca. inferiar & c. denique, & c. submittitur & c. in tantum. Sed papa etiam haereticus, si non est iure diuino papatu priuatus, est superior omni congregatione inferior vniuersali ecclesia & concilio generali: est etiam superior omni persona alia ecclesiastica, ergo a nulla illarum poterit iudicari. Secundo sic: Non minor auctoritas requiritur in iudicante papa haereticum quam in iudicante alium episcopum haereticum. Sed episcopus haereticus iudicari non potest ab aliqua persona vel congregatione inferiori se, si non esset haereticus. Quia episcopus haereticus non potest deponi ab aliquo sacerdote vel congregatione suae dioecesis. Igitur nec papa potest deponi ab aliqua persona vel congregatione inferiori concilio generali. Tertio sic: Quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus debet approbari: ita causa, quae omnes tangit, ab omnibus tractari debet: sed causa papae haeretici omnes tangit Christianos. Ergo per omnes Christianos vel congregationem, quae gerit vice omnium Christianorum, cuiusmodi est concilium generale, tractari debet: & per consequens nulla persona vel congregatio inferior concilio generali, potest deponere papam haereticum.
units.tr: Student. You said that there are opposing opinions on my question. You have recited one; now tell me the other. Master. The other opinion is held by those who say that a heretical pope is not deprived of the papacy by divine right. They hold that no one has power over the pope except the universal Church or a general council. The universal Church, if it were gathered together, and also a general council, has the power to depose the pope and to inflict other penalties on him. Other assemblies and persons, however, before a heretical pope has been deprived of the papacy by the universal Church or a general council, have no power over a heretical pope. But once he has been deposed, he is subject to the jurisdiction of the superior, as the other heretics are, the supreme pontiff. The exception is that the universal Church or a general council may reserve to itself the specific further punishment of the pope for heresy after his deposition. Student. It seems to me that those who hold that opinion ought to prove three things. The first is that a heretical pope is not deprived of the papacy by divine right. The second is that the universal Church and also a general council have the power to depose a heretical pope. The third is that no assembly or person inferior to the universal Church and a general council has power to depose a heretical pope. If these things were true, the rest would be plain. Now, the first point has been treated above, where arguments were brought to prove that a heretical pope is not deprived of the papacy by divine right. So for the second point, namely that the universal Church and a general council have power to depose a heretical pope, devise other arguments. Master. To satisfy your request, it is necessary to prove two things. The first is that the universal Church has power to depose a heretical pope. The second is that a general council holds such power. The first is proved in the following way. That assembly which has power over a pope falsely defamed of heresy has much more power over a pope truly entangled in heresy. But the universal Church has power, namely to inquire into a pope defamed of the crime of heresy, even if falsely, as was proved above in extra 6. 2. Therefore the universal Church has even more power to depose a pope convicted of heretical depravity. Student. I see that those arguments adduced in chapter 2 of this sixth book conclude more about a heretical pope than about the crime of heresy falsely imputed. So for the present I do not wish to hear other arguments for this assertion; pass on to the second. Master. The second, namely that a general council has power to depose a heretical pope, is proved thus. A general council is above a pope defamed of heresy, as was shown above in c. 13. Therefore it has much more power to depose one who is truly heretical. Student. Those assertions too, adduced in that chapter, are, I think, the strongest that could be devised to prove that a general council has power over a heretical pope. So proceed to the third thing to be proved: namely that no ecclesiastical assembly or person inferior to the universal Church and a general council has power to depose a heretical pope. Master. This is proved first thus. An inferior cannot judge a superior, distin. 21. ca. inferiar & c. denique, & c. submittitur & c. in tantum. But the pope, even if heretical, if he is not deprived of the papacy by divine right, is superior to every assembly inferior to the universal Church and a general council; he is also superior to every other ecclesiastical person. Therefore he cannot be judged by any of them. Second, thus: no less authority is required in one who judges a heretical pope than in one who judges another heretical bishop. But a heretical bishop cannot be judged by any person or assembly inferior to himself, unless he were a heretic. For a heretical bishop cannot be deposed by any priest or assembly of his diocese. Therefore neither can the pope be deposed by any person or assembly inferior to a general council. Third, thus: what touches all must be approved by all; so a matter which touches all must be dealt with by all. But the cause of a heretical pope touches all Christians. Therefore it must be dealt with by all Christians, or by an assembly which acts on behalf of all Christians, such as a general council. And consequently no person or assembly inferior to a general council can depose a heretical pope.

units.la: CAP. LXXI.
units.tr: CAP. LXXI.

units.la: Ponit tertiam opinionem, quae respondet sub vnica conclusione duas continentes particulas, quas etiam probat exemplo & duabus rationibus.
units.tr: Sets out the third opinion, which answers with a single conclusion containing two parts, and proves it by an example and by two arguments.

units.la: Discipul. Sunt ne plures opiniones circa interrogationem meam, quam tibi proposui. Magist. Tertia est opinio, quod non solum vniuersalis ecclesia & concilium generale, sed dioecesis Romana collegium Cardinalium & Imperator & etiam episcopus, in cuius dioecesi moraretur papa haereticus, posset eundem deponere. Haec opinio quantum ad Romanos probatur per exemplum de Ioan. 12. quem priuauerunt Romani papatu, & alium elegerunt. Quantum autem ad episcopum, in cuius dioecesi moraretur, probatur primo sic. Ex iure diuino ad quemlibet spectat episcopum suam dioecesim de pravitate haeretica expurgare, ergo quilibet haereticus trahens moram in episcopatu cuiuscunq; episcopi est subiectus iudicio illius episcopi. Aliter enim non haberet episcopus potestatem suam dioecesim de omni haeretica pravitate purgandi. Ergo papa haereticus est subiectus iudicio episcopi, in cuius dioecesi commoratur, ergo episcopus ille potest deponere papam haereticum. Secundo sic: Episcopi vicini dioecesi, in qua papa haereticus moraretur, haberent potestatem papam haereticum deponendi. Ergo multo magis episcopus, in cuius dioecesi moratur papa haereticus, saltem cum vicinorum episcoporum consilio, haberet potestatem deponendi papam haereticum. Antecedens patet per exemplum de episcopis tempore beati Marcellini, qui, ut legitur dist. 21. c. nunc autem, & allegatum est supra, cum venerunt ad inquirendum de beato Marcellino, qui idolatraverat, quem deposuissent, si eum in perfidia haeresis inuenissent.
units.tr: Disciple. Are there several opinions on the question I have put to you? Master. The third opinion is that not only the universal Church and a general council, but also the Roman diocese, the college of Cardinals, the Emperor, and even the bishop in whose diocese the heretical pope happens to be staying, can depose him. As far as the Romans are concerned, this opinion is supported by the example in John 12, whom the Romans deprived of the papacy and replaced with another. As for the bishop in whose diocese he is staying, it is proved first as follows. By divine right it belongs to every bishop to purge his own diocese of heretical corruption; therefore every heretic who tarries in the diocese of any bishop is subject to that bishop's judgment. Otherwise the bishop would not have the power to purge his diocese of all heretical corruption. Therefore the heretical pope is subject to the judgment of the bishop in whose diocese he stays, and so that bishop can depose the heretical pope. Secondly, as follows: the bishops neighbouring the diocese in which a heretical pope was staying would have the power to depose him. Therefore much more the bishop in whose diocese the heretical pope stays, at least with the counsel of the neighbouring bishops, would have the power to depose him. The antecedent is clear from the example of the bishops in the time of blessed Marcellinus, who, as we read in dist. 21, c. nunc autem, and as was cited above, when they came to inquire into blessed Marcellinus, who had committed idolatry, would have deposed him had they found him in the obstinacy of heresy.

units.la: CAP. LXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 72.

units.la: In quo ponitur quarta opinio, quae respondendo ad quaesitum talem ponit conclusionem, sci- licet quod Papa haereticus, nisi sponte renunciare voluerit, a quacunque congregatione vel persona deponi non potest, quae probatur duabus rationibus fundamentalibus opinantium.
units.tr: In which the fourth opinion is set out, which, in answer to the question, puts forward this conclusion: that a heretical Pope, unless he is willing to resign of his own accord, cannot be deposed by any congregation or person whatever. This is proved by two foundational arguments of those who hold it.

units.la: Discipul. Si sunt plures opiniones circa interrogationem meam, enarra. Magist. Est vna opinio, quod papa haereticus nisi sponte renunciare voluerit, a quacunque congregatione vel persona deponi non potest. Fundamentum autem istius opinionis est hoc: quia inferior suum superiorem deponere non potest, papa autem haereticus cum non sit de iure diuino papatu priuatus, secundum istam opinionem est superior omni congregatione & persona Christiana, tota enim ecclesia distincta a papa est inferior papa, ergo tota ecclesia distincta a papa non potest deponere papam, qui non est iure diuino depositus. Secundum fundamentum dictæ opinionis est tale. Omnes subditi simul alicuius Patriarchæ vel Metropolitani non possunt deponere talem Patriarcham vel Metropolitanum hæreticum, si non est de iure depositus, ergo omnes subditi papæ non possunt papam hæreticum deponere, si non est de iure diuino depositus.
units.tr: Student. If there are several opinions on my question, please set them out. Master. There is one opinion, that a heretical Pope, unless he is willing to resign of his own accord, cannot be deposed by any congregation or person whatever. The foundation of this opinion is this: an inferior cannot depose his superior; but a heretical Pope, since he has not been deprived of the papacy by divine law, is according to this opinion superior to every congregation and every Christian person; for the whole Church, considered apart from the Pope, is inferior to the Pope. Therefore the whole Church, considered apart from the Pope, cannot depose the Pope, who has not been deposed by divine law. The second foundation of this opinion is as follows: all the subjects together of some Patriarch or Metropolitan cannot depose such a heretical Patriarch or Metropolitan, if he has not been deposed by law; therefore all the subjects of the Pope cannot depose a heretical Pope, if he has not been deposed by divine law.

units.la: CAP. LXXIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXIII.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod Papa hæreticus est iure humano à papatu & omni ecclesiastica dignitate priuatus.
units.tr: In which it is shown that a heretical Pope is deprived of the papacy and of every ecclesiastical dignity by human law.

units.la: Discipul. Prima istarum opinionum, scilicet quod papa hæreticus est iure diuino papatu & ecclesiastica dignitate priuatus (vt videtur) fortiter est fundata. Secunda etiam opinio & tertia tolerati videntur. Quarta autem (in præiudicium fidei orthodoxæ) ad fauorem papæ hæretici videtur induEta, quia si papa hæreticus non esset iure diuino papatu priuatus, nec ab aliqua congregatione vel persona deponi valeret, posset papa hæreticus libere absque timore pœnæ temporalis vel coercionis humanæ fidem abnegare catholicam, & cogere Christianos ad sectam Saracenorum vel Iudæorum vel aliorum infidelium acceptandam, quod horrerent audire catholici & fideles, ideo illa opinione quarta pro nunc dimissa, volo opiniones alias quantum ad aliud pertractari. Videtur enim quod omnes illæ in hoc conueniunt, quod si in his diebus quis papa efficeretur hæreticus, ipso facto esset de iure papatu priuatus. Vnde quid de hoc sentiant literati non differas iudicare.
units.tr: Disciple. The first of these opinions, namely that a heretical pope is deprived of the papacy and of ecclesiastical dignity by divine law, appears (so it seems) to be firmly founded. The second and third opinions also seem tolerable. The fourth, however, seems to have been introduced to the prejudice of the orthodox faith and in favour of a heretical pope. For if a heretical pope were not deprived of the papacy by divine law, and could not be deposed by any assembly or person, then a heretical pope could freely, without fear of temporal punishment or human coercion, renounce the Catholic faith and compel Christians to accept the sect of the Saracens, the Jews, or other unbelievers, which Catholics and the faithful would shudder to hear. So I set aside that fourth opinion for now, and I want the other opinions to be treated in another respect. For all of them seem to agree on this: that if anyone were to become a heretic while pope in these days, he would by that very fact be deprived of the papacy by right. Therefore, do not delay in judging what the learned think about this.

units.la: Magist. Verum dicis, quod tres opiniones prædictæ tenent pro firmo: quod si papa nunc incurreret hæreticam prauitatem, esset de iure papatu & omni ecclesiastica dignitate priuatus. Prima enim tenet, quod esset de iure diuino papatu priuatus. Secunda & tertia tenent, quod esset iure humano priuatus. Pro primo istorum argumentatum est multipliciter supra cap. 68. Secundum probatur sic: Concilium generale habet potestatem deponendi & damnandi papam hæreticum, sicut probatum est supra, ergo si sententia vel damnatio generalis concilii indistincte lata fuerit contra hæreticos, est ad papam hæreticum extendenda. Vbi enim canon generalis concilii non distinguit, nec nos debemus distinguere. Sed omnes hæretici, nullo excepto, sunt per generale concilium condemnati, teste generali concilio sub Innocentio tertio celebrato, qui, vt habetur extra de hereticis, excommunicamus, ait: Excommunicamus itaque & anathematizamus omnem hæresim extollentem se aduersus hanc orthodoxam & catholicam fidem, condemnantes vniuersos hæreticos quibuscunque nominibus censeantur.
units.tr: Master. You speak truly, that the three aforementioned opinions firmly hold that if the pope were now to fall into heretical depravity, he would be deprived of the papacy and of every ecclesiastical dignity by right. The first holds that he would be deprived by divine right. The second and third hold that he would be deprived by human right. For the first of these, arguments have been advanced in many ways above, in chapter 68. The second is proved thus: a general council has the power to depose and condemn a heretical pope, as has been proved above; therefore, if the sentence or condemnation of a general council has been pronounced indiscriminately against heretics, it must be extended to a heretical pope. For where the canon of a general council makes no distinction, neither should we make one. But all heretics, none excepted, have been condemned by a general council, as witnessed by the general council celebrated under Innocent III, which, as is found in Extra, On Heretics, says: "We therefore excommunicate and anathematize every heresy that raises itself against this orthodox and Catholic faith, condemning all heretics, by whatever names they are called."

units.la: Sententiam etiam huiusmodi contra omnes hæreticos indistincte tulit concilium Carthaginense quartum, quod, vt legitur 24 q. 3. c. clericus, ait: Clericus hæreticorum ac schismaticorum tam communia quam sodalitates euitet, æqualiter eorum conuenticula non ecclesia, sed concilia sunt appellanda, cum eis neque orandum est neque psallendum. His etiam concordat concilium Martini papæ, vt habetur 7. quaest. 1. cap. non liceat, ait: Non liceat clericis vel laicis ab hæreticis eulogia (id est benedictiones) accipere: quia maledictiones sunt magis quam benedictiones, neque liceat aut cum hæreticis aut cum schismaticis orare. Item concilium Africanum, vt habetur extra de hæreticis, ait: Si quis episcopus heredes instituerit extraneos a consanguinitate sua vel hæreticos, vel consanguineos aut paganos prætulerit, saltem post mortem eius anathema dicatur: Item in eodem concilio, vt habetur 2. c. in eos, sic loquitur: In eos, qui catholici non sunt, etiam si consanguinei episcopi fuerint, prælati vel presbyteri nihil conferant. Item in concilio Laodecensi, vt habetur 1. quaest. 1. c. non oportet, sic scribitur: non oportet hereticorum benedictiones accipere, quoniam maledictiones sunt magis quam benedictiones. Ex quibus aliisque quampluribus colligitur, quod in omnes hæreticos indistincte per generalia concilia sententiæ plures lunt prolatæ. Ergo omnia illa concilia generalia & alia sunt ad papam hæreticum extendenda. Quod Gloss. super prælegatum capitulum, si quis episcopus, videtur asserere manifeste dicens: Idem iuris est de paganis & de hereticis, idem de omnibus qui catholici non sunt. Cum ergo paganus non sit verus papa, nec hæreticus est verus papa. Et ita papa hæreticus est papatu priuatus, & per consequens sententia diuina vel humana lata est contra ipsum. Secundo probatur eadem conclusio sic: Quicunque in hæresim damnatam semel labitur, eius damnatione seipsum inuoluit, 4. q. Achatium. Sed papa hæreticus incidit in antiquam hæresim per generale concilium damnatam explicite vel implicite, quia omnis hæresis est explicite per generalia concilia iam condemnata. Ergo papa hæreticus incidit in hæresim iam damnatam. Ergo si eius damnatione inuoluitur per generalia concilia papa hæreticus est damnatus.
units.tr: A sentence of this kind against all heretics, without distinction, was also pronounced by the Fourth Council of Carthage, which, as is read in 24 q. 3, c. Clericus, says: "A cleric shall avoid the communities and fellowships of heretics and schismatics alike; their gatherings are to be called not churches but conventicles; neither must one pray with them nor sing psalms with them." The council of Pope Martin also agrees with this, as is found in 7 q. 1, c. Non liceat, which says: "It is not lawful for clerics or laymen to receive eulogies (that is, blessings) from heretics, because they are curses rather than blessings, nor is it lawful to pray either with heretics or with schismatics." Likewise the African council, as is found in Extra, On Heretics, says: "If any bishop has appointed as heirs strangers unrelated to him by blood, or heretics, or has preferred relatives or pagans, let anathema be pronounced against him at least after his death." Again, in the same council, as is found in c. 2, In eos, it speaks thus: "Toward those who are not Catholic, even if they are relatives of a bishop, prelates or presbyters shall confer nothing."
