Again, in the Council of Laodicea, as is found in 1 q. 1, c. Non oportet, it is written: "It is not fitting to receive the blessings of heretics, since they are curses rather than blessings." From these and many other sources it is gathered that sentences have been pronounced by general councils indiscriminately against all heretics. Therefore all those general councils and others must be extended to a heretical pope. The Gloss on the aforementioned chapter, Si quis episcopus, seems to assert this plainly, saying: "The law is the same concerning pagans and heretics, the same concerning all who are not Catholic." Since, then, a pagan is not a true pope, neither is a heretic a true pope. And so a heretical pope is deprived of the papacy, and consequently a sentence, divine or human, has been pronounced against him. Second, the same conclusion is proved thus: whoever once slips into a condemned heresy involves himself in its condemnation (4 q. Achatium). But a heretical pope falls into an ancient heresy condemned by a general council, either explicitly or implicitly, since every heresy has already been explicitly condemned by general councils. Therefore a heretical pope falls into a heresy already condemned. Therefore, if he is involved in its condemnation through the general councils, a heretical pope has been condemned.

units.la: Discip. Secundum ista ad damnandum papam hæreticum, non oporteret generale concilium conuocari: quia ad damnandum hæresim iam damnatam non est necesse generale concilium conuocari: imo nulla est conuocanda congregatio, ex quo iam damnatus est papa hæreticus: cuius tamen oppositum videtur veritatem habere. Nam ad inquirendum de papa super crimine hæresis diffamato, oportet aliqp concilium generale vel aliud conuocari: exemplo istorum, qui ad inquirendum de beato Marcellino quondam idololatra conuenerunt. Ergo etiā ad deponendum papam hæreticum oportet concilium conuocari. Mag. Ad hoc respondetur sic, q papa hæreticus vel iure diuino, secundum primam opinionem, vel iure humano, concilii videlicet generalis, (secundum alias opiniones) est damnatus. & papatu priuatus, quia omni ecclesiastica dignitate est nudatus. Et ideo ad deponendum papam de iure non est necesse concilium congregari. Oportet tamen in casu concilium conuocari ad potenter pellendum papam haereticum de Apostolica sede ad ecclesiam Dei salubriter disponendam, vel ad audiendam causam & accusationem papae haeretici, & ad probandum ipsum esse haereticum. Sicut enim episcopi conuenerunt ad inquirendum de beato Marcellino, non quia fuisset damnatus, si fuisset haereticus: sed quia volebant inquirere veritatem, quem si iniue nissent esse haereticum, pronunciassent ipsum esse damnatum. Discip. Est ne aliquod exemplum de aliquo papa haeretico, qui absque conuocatione noui concilii generalis fuerit ab ecclesia haereticus condemnatus? Magist. Exemplum ponitur de Anastasio, quem clerici Romani absque congregatione noui concilii generalis reputabant condemnatum; & se ab eius communione laudabiliter abegerunt, vt habetur dist. 19. Anastasius, vt notat Glos. quod clerici illi non recesserunt ante sententiam, quia inciderat (scilicet Anastasius) in haeresim iam damnatam. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod ad damnandum papam haereticum non est necesse concilium generale nouiter congregari. Quia quemadmodum verberans clericum ipso facto nulla denunciatione noua vel sententia expectata, imo si ipse solus esset conscius facti sui, excommunicationis sententia est ligatus, quia incidit in canonem latae sententiae: ita papa haereticus ipso facto nulla alia expectata sententia vel conuocatione est iure diuino vel humano damnatus. Discip. Exemplum istud non videtur esse ad propositum: quia Anastasius inciderat in haeresim iam damnatam, posset autem papa effici haereticus, licet non incideret in haeresim iam damnatam. Magist. Respondetur, quod ista instantia dictum exemplum non impedit: quia omnis haeresis est damnata, vt supra 2. huius est ostensum. Et ideo quicunque papa efficeretur haereticus, inciderit in haeresim iam damnatam, licet posset incidere in haeresim damnatam implicite. Inter haeresim autem damnatam implicite & damnata explicite non est differentia: ad hoc quod incidens in haeresim damnata solummodo implicite sit damnatus. Sed quantum ad hoc potest esse differentia, quod incidens in haeresim explicite non solum est damnatus, sed etiam pro damnato est habendus. Incidens autem pertinaciter in haeresim damnatam solummodo implicite, quamuis esset damnatus, non tamen esset pro damnato habendus: sed ad habendum ipsum pro damnato oporteret concilium generale congregari. Anastasius autem secundus incidit in haeresim iam damnatam explicite, & ideo non solum fuit damnatus, sed etiam pro damnato fuit habendus. Est ergo exemplum ad propositum quantum ad hoc, quod papa quantumcunque efficeretur haereticus, esset damnatus: non est tamen ad propositum quantum ad hoc, quod sit pro damnato habendus, nisi incidat in haeresim damnatam explicite, cuiusmodi est omnis haeresis, quae in eisdem terminis alicui veritati scripturae diuinae contradicit aut quae contradicit alicui veritati, quae patenter omnibus iudicio rationis ytentibus sequitur ex contento vel contentis in scriptura diuina, vel contradicit veritati, quae est apud omnes catholicos tanquam catholica diuulgata.
units.tr: Disciple. According to these arguments, it would not be necessary to convene a general council to condemn a heretical pope, since for condemning a heresy already condemned there is no need to convene a general council; indeed, no assembly ought to be convened at all, since the heretical pope has already been condemned. Yet the opposite seems to be true. For to inquire into a pope on a charge of heresy that has been spread abroad, a general council or some other assembly must be convened, as in the example of those who gathered to inquire into the blessed Marcellinus, once guilty of idolatry. Therefore it is also necessary to convene a council to depose a heretical pope. Master. To this it is answered thus: a heretical pope has been condemned and deprived of the papacy, either by divine right, according to the first opinion, or by human right, namely of a general council (according to the other opinions), because he has been stripped of every ecclesiastical dignity. And therefore, to depose a pope by right, it is not necessary to convene a council. Yet in such a case a council must be convened to effectively drive the heretical pope from the apostolic see, so that the church of God may be wholesomely ordered, or to hear the case and accusation against the heretical pope and to prove that he is a heretic. For just as the bishops gathered to inquire into the blessed Marcellinus, not because he would have been condemned had he been a heretic, but because they wished to inquire into the truth, which, if they had found him to be a heretic, they would have pronounced him condemned. Disciple. Is there any example of a heretical pope who was condemned by the Church as a heretic without the convening of a new general council? Master. An example is given of Anastasius, whom the Roman clergy, without the gathering of a new general council, regarded as condemned, and whom they laudably withdrew from communion with, as is found in dist. 19, Anastasius, as the Gloss notes: "those clergy did not withdraw before the sentence, because he (namely Anastasius) had fallen into a heresy already condemned." From these words it is plainly evident that to condemn a heretical pope it is not necessary to convene a newly gathered general council. For just as a man who strikes a cleric is bound by the sentence of excommunication by that very fact, without any new denunciation or awaited sentence, and even if he alone were aware of his deed, since he has fallen under the canon of a sentence already pronounced; so a heretical pope is, by that very fact, condemned by divine or human right, without any other sentence or convocation being awaited. Disciple. That example does not seem to fit the point, because Anastasius had fallen into a heresy already condemned, whereas a pope could become a heretic without falling into a heresy already condemned. Master. It is answered that this objection does not undermine the example, because every heresy is condemned, as was shown above in book 2. And therefore whoever as pope became a heretic would fall into a condemned heresy, although he could fall into a heresy condemned only implicitly. Yet between a heresy condemned implicitly and one condemned explicitly there is no difference in this respect: that one who falls into a heresy condemned only implicitly is condemned. But there can be a difference in this respect: one who falls into a heresy condemned explicitly is not only condemned but must also be held as condemned. Yet one who obstinately falls into a heresy condemned only implicitly, although he would be condemned, would not thereby be held as condemned; to have him held as condemned, a general council would have to be convened. But Anastasius the Second fell into a heresy already condemned explicitly, and therefore he was not only condemned but was also to be held as condemned. So the example fits the point in this respect: that however much a pope became a heretic, he would be condemned. It does not, however, fit in this respect: that he must be held as condemned, unless he falls into a heresy condemned explicitly. Such is every heresy which, in these very terms, contradicts some truth of Holy Scripture, or which contradicts some truth that clearly follows, to all who use reason, from what is contained in, or from the contents of, the divine Scripture, or which contradicts a truth that is accepted among all Catholics as commonly held Catholic doctrine.

units.la: CAP. LXXIV.
units.tr: CAP. LXXIV.

units.la: In quo quaeritur in generali, quae poena Papa haereticus sit plectendus.
units.tr: In which it is asked in general what penalty a heretical Pope is to be punished with.

units.la: Discipul. Postquam disseruimus de papa haeretico, an sit papatu priuatus; peto vt secundum opiniones praedictas exponas, qua poena papa haereticus est plectendus. Mag. Respondetur quod papa haereticus omnibus poenis est subditus & subdendus, quibus alii haeretici saltem episcopi inuoluuntur vel sunt inuoluendi. Quia, sicut dictum est, papa haereticus non gaudet priuilegio speciali nec in taxatione poenarum haereticorum papa prauitate haeretica irretitus excipitur. Quare cum sit damnatus siue iure diuino, siue iure humano, omnibus poenis haereticis indistincte per ius diuinum & ius naturale per generalia concilia & canones summorum pontificum inflictis noscitur subiacere. Discip. Aperte video, quod si papa haereticus est damnatus siue a iure diuino & a statutis generalium conciliorum, quod poenis inflictis haereticis a iure diuino & a statutis generalium conciliorum inuoluitur. Sed dic, quomodo subiacet poenis illatis haereticis per summos pontifices? Mag. Sic probatur, si papa haereticus est damnatus, siue per ius diuinum, siue per canonem conciliorum generalium, factus est inferior summo pontifice, si alius papa catholicus eligatur. Ex quo sequitur, quod omnibus poenis, quas idem summus pontifex de nouo electus diceret indistincte haereticis imponendas, papa haereticus est plectendus. Praedecessores noui summi pontificis fuerunt eiusdem auctoritatis, cuius est iste, ergo si papa haereticus subiaceret poenis per suum successorem impositis, ita subiaceret omnibus poenis praedecessorum suorum haereticis indistincte inflictis.
units.tr: Disciple. Having discussed whether a heretical pope is deprived of the papacy, I ask that you explain, according to the opinions mentioned above, with what penalty a heretical pope is to be punished. Master. The answer is that a heretical pope is, and ought to be, subject to all the penalties to which other heretics, at least bishops, are or ought to be liable. For, as has been said, a heretical pope does not enjoy any special privilege, and in the assessment of penalties for heretics the pope, caught in the snare of heretical depravity, is not exempted. Therefore, since he has been condemned either by divine law or by human law, he is known to be subject, without distinction, to all the penalties imposed on heretics by divine law and natural law, through general councils and the canons of the supreme pontiffs. Disciple. I see clearly that if the pope, being a heretic, has been condemned either by divine law or by the decrees of general councils, he is caught up in the penalties imposed on heretics by divine law and the decrees of general councils. But tell me, how is he subject to the penalties imposed on heretics by the supreme pontiffs? Master. It is proved thus: if a heretical pope has been condemned, either by divine law or by a canon of general councils, he has become inferior to the supreme pontiff if another, catholic pope is elected. From this it follows that a heretical pope is to be punished with all the penalties which the newly elected supreme pontiff would say are to be imposed on heretics without distinction. The predecessors of a new supreme pontiff have the same authority as he has; therefore, if a heretical pope were subject to penalties imposed by his successor, he would likewise be subject to all the penalties imposed without distinction on the heretics of his predecessors.

units.la: CAP. LXXV.
units.tr: Chapter 75.

units.la: Quærit in speciali qua scilicet pœna talis Papa hæreticus debeat plecti.
units.tr: Inquires in particular what punishment such a heretical pope ought to suffer.

units.la: DIscipul. Ex quo modum prædictum ponendi intelligo, discurramus per pœnas, quibus papa hæreticus est plectendus. Mag. Vt ordinatius procedatur, duæ distinctiones secundum primam opinionem dicuntur esse notandæ. Quarum prima est, quod pœnarum hæreticis debitarum, quædam taxantur & determinantur in iure diuino vel naturali, quædam in iure humano. Secunda distinctio est quod hæretici aliquas pœnas incurrunt ipso facto, sed sunt eis etiam per catholicos vel per catholicum infligendæ. Discipul. Incipias ergo à pœnis hæreticorum, quæ taxantur in iure diuino vel in iure naturali secundum primam opinionem. Magist. Pœna hæreticorum, quam incurrit omnis hæreticus, siue papa siue alius, est priuatio omnis ecclesiasticæ prælationis. Quia omnis hæreticus licet non sit priuatus charactere, qui conseritur in ordinibus, est tamen omni ecclesiastica prælatione priuatus. Si enim secundum iura humana in iure diuino & naturali fundata qui præest, & alii quibus præest debent esse eiusdem professionis spiritualis, propter quod abbas Monachorum debet esse Monachus, & Canonicorum Canonicus, vt ex sacris Canonibus colligitur, extra de elect. c. cum causam & c. cum in magistrum, & 16. q. 7. & extra de institutis in ecclesia: multo magis secundum ius diuinum qui præest in spiritualibus, & illi quibus præest, debent esse eiusdem professionis saltem generalis, hæreticus autem & catholicus non sunt eiusdem professionis etiam generalis, hæretici enim & catholici in nulla una professione conueniunt, sed discrepant & discordant, ergo hæreticus catholicis præesse non potest. Quod etiam aperte in lege veteri figuratum est Deuter. 22. vbi dicitur non arabis in boue & asino: non induéris vestimento quod ex lana linoque contextum est. In quibus verbis innuitur, quod in vna eademque congregatione non debet esse dispar professio, quare hæreticus præesse catholicis non potest. Discipul. Per istam rationem probaretur, quod catholicus hæreticis præesse non potest, cuius tamen videtur oppositum, cum Iudæi sint serui Christianorum, extra de Iudæis. Et per eandem rationem infideles fidelibus in temporalibus præesse non possent, nec vnquam poterunt: cum fideles & infideles diuersæ professionis existant. Magist. Ad primam instantiam respondetur, quod catholicus præesse non debet hæreticis ad informandum & regendum in sua superstitione eosdem: licet possit eisdem præesse ad puniendum eos, si contra Deum vel bonos mores deliquerint, ergo consimiliter hæreticus præesse non debet catholicis ipsos instruendo & regendo in obseruantia religionis Christianæ. Cum ergo prælatus fidelium in religionis obseruantia Christianæ fidem catholicam docere debeat & regere Christianos, nullo modo secundum legem diuinam & rationem naturalem in diuina lege & in propositionibus naturaliter notis simul fundatam hæreticus præesse poterit catholicis orthodoxis: quia omnis hæreticus etiam secundum legem diuinam omni prælatione est priuatus. Ad secundam instantiam respondetur, quod licet fideles & infideles diuersæ professionis existerent, & ideo nec fidelis infidelium nec infidelis fidelium debet esse doctor & rector, quoad illa, quæ ad suam professionem spectare noscuntur: tamen in temporalibus, quæ omnia communia sunt Christianis fidelibus & infidelibus, & quæ nullam sibi professionem certam determinant, & infidelis fidelibus & fidelis infidelibus, quod est ex lege diuina, præesse valebit. Et ita per vtramque instantiam tuam, vt videtur, poterit patenter inferri, quod quemadmodum legi diuinæ repugnat, quod fidelis sit doctor & rector infidelium quantum ad illa, quæ ad professionem infidelium spectant, tuncenim in talibus communicaret eisdem: Ita legi diuinæ repugnat quod infidelis sit doctor & rector fidelium, quantum ad illa quæ ad religionem pertinent Christianam. Quare per legem diuinam omnis hæreticus omni prælatione ecclesiastica est priuatus. Et est hæc pœna ad papam hæreticum extendenda: tum quia maius periculum imminet fidei orthodoxæ, si esset verus papa, quam si esset verus episcopus: tum quia si hæreticus non poterit esse in minori officio propter repugnantiam, quam habet ad religionem Christianam, multo magis non poterit fungi officio maiori. Et ita non poterit esse verus papa.
units.tr: Disciple. Since I understand the method you have set out, let us go through the punishments by which a heretical pope is to be punished. Master. To proceed in an orderly way, two distinctions are to be noted, according to the first opinion. The first is that some of the punishments due to heretics are fixed and determined by divine or natural law, and others by human law. The second distinction is that heretics incur some punishments by the very fact of their heresy, but these must also be inflicted on them by Catholics or by a Catholic. Disciple. Begin, then, with the punishments of heretics that are fixed by divine or natural law, according to the first opinion. Master. The punishment that every heretic incurs, whether pope or another, is deprivation of all ecclesiastical preferment. For every heretic, although he is not deprived of the character conferred in ordination, is nevertheless deprived of every ecclesiastical preferment. For if, according to human laws founded in divine and natural law, the one who presides and those over whom he presides must belong to the same spiritual profession (for which reason the abbot of the monks must be a monk, and the canon a canon, as is gathered from the sacred canons, Extra, De electione, c. Cum causam and c. Cum in magistrum; 16 q. 7; and Extra, De institutis in ecclesia), then much more according to divine law the one who presides in spiritual matters and those over whom he presides must belong to the same profession, at least a general one. But a heretic and a Catholic do not belong to the same profession, not even a general one, for heretics and Catholics agree in no single profession but differ and disagree. Therefore a heretic cannot preside over Catholics. This was also foreshadowed in the law of Moses, Deut. 22., where it is said: You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together; you shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen. In these words it is implied that in one and the same congregation there must not be a diverse profession; therefore a heretic cannot preside over Catholics. Disciple. By this reasoning it would be proved that a Catholic cannot preside over heretics, yet the opposite seems to be the case, since Jews are the servants of Christians, Extra, De Iudaeis. And by the same reasoning infidels could not preside over the faithful in temporal matters, nor ever will be able to, since the faithful and the infidels are of different professions. Master. To the first objection it is answered that a Catholic ought not to preside over heretics in order to instruct and govern them in their superstition, although he may preside over them to punish them if they have sinned against God or good morals. Likewise, therefore, a heretic ought not to preside over Catholics by instructing and governing them in the observance of the Christian religion. Since, then, the prelate of the faithful, in the observance of the Christian religion, ought to teach and govern Christians in the Catholic faith, a heretic can in no way preside over orthodox Catholics according to divine law and natural reason, which are founded together in divine law and in propositions naturally known; for every heretic, even according to divine law, is deprived of all preferment. To the second objection it is answered that although the faithful and the infidels are of different professions, and therefore neither an infidel should be a teacher and ruler of the faithful, nor a faithful man of the infidels, in those matters which are known to belong to their profession, nevertheless in temporal matters, which are all common to faithful and infidels alike and which do not assign to them any fixed profession, an infidel can preside over the faithful and a faithful man over infidels, as divine law allows. And so, by both of your objections, it can apparently be clearly inferred that just as it is contrary to divine law for a faithful man to be a teacher and ruler of infidels in those matters which belong to the profession of infidels (for then he would have fellowship with them in such matters), so it is contrary to divine law for an infidel to be a teacher and ruler of the faithful in those matters which pertain to the Christian religion. Therefore, by divine law, every heretic is deprived of all ecclesiastical preferment. And this punishment is to be extended to a heretical pope: both because a greater danger threatens orthodox faith if he were a true pope than if he were a true bishop, and because if a heretic cannot hold a lesser office on account of the incompatibility he has with the Christian religion, much less can he discharge a greater office. And so he cannot be a true pope.

units.la: CAP. LXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXVI.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod omnes hæretici incurrunt pœnam infamiæ.
units.tr: In which it is proved that all heretics incur the penalty of infamy.

units.la: DIscipulus. De ista pœna satis dixisti: ideo dic aliam pœnam, quam iure diuino vel iure naturali papa hæreticus & generaliter omnes hæretici ipso facto incurrunt. Magist. Vna assertio est, quod omnes hæretici incurrunt pœnam infamiæ. Dicitur enim esse sciendum, quod, sicut notat Glossa 3. quæst. 7. porro, alia est infamia iuris, alia facti. Infamia facti est, quando quis infamatur apud bonos & graues viros. Infamia iuris est diminutio status alicuius. Primam infamiam hæretici, præsertim occulti, non semper incurrunt: quia nonnulli hæretici non semper apud bonos & graues diffamantur. Apud quos tamen interdum catholici grauissime infamantur. Secundam autem infamiam, papa hæreticus & generaliter omnes hæretici incurrunt. Ad euidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod infamia iuris quandoque irrogatur ipso facto, quandoque per sententiam. Et vtroque modo incurrunt infamiam vniuersi: quia ex hoc ipso, quod efficiuntur hæreticis, hæretici, committunt peccatum dignum infamia. Etiam per sententiam eis infamia irrogatur, dum per legem diuinam de crimine maximo condemnatur, & illæsæ dignitatis statu priuatur. Discip. Videtur secundum istos, quod infamia iuris est duplex, igitur vt intentionem eorum melius aduertam, expone istos duos modos infamiæ iuris. Magi. Vt clarius eorum habeas intellectum, scire debes, quod infamia per sententiam irrogata duplex est, quædam est, quæ est irrogata per sententiam latam à iure, quædam per sententiam latam ab homine. Primam infamiam incurrunt semper hæretici. Secundam infamiam non incurrunt semper, quamtamen non in quantum viri catholici & ab omni crimine innocentes non incurrunt: quia sæpe catholici condemnantur ab homine, & hæretici exaltantur & honorantur. Ex his enim dicunt, quod infamia sit læsæ dignitatis status moribus ac legibus comprobatus. Infamia iuris est duplex, secundum quod status hominis dupliciter lædi potest: quia aut læditur per actum infamiæ, committendo videlicet actum infamiæ, quemadmodum de iniquis dicunt Salomon Prouerb. 2. Querum via peruersa & infames gressus eorum. Et 8. & cap. dicit: Ambulans recto itinere & timens Deum despicitur ab eo, qui infami graditur via, patenter insinuans, quod omnes gressus & viæ prauorum sunt infames. Et hæc est infamia quamuis non semper habeant annexam infamiam facti, quia omnes actus malorum in quantum mali sunt, iure diuino aut iure naturali vel humano damnantur. Et hæc infamia iuris potest vocari infamia irrogata per sententiam latam à iure. Aliter læditur status hominis per superiorem suum ipsum de crimine condemnantem & dignitate famæ illæsæ priuantem, licet interdum nihil commiserit, propter quod infamia lædi debeat. Et hæc infamia potest vocari infamia iuris irrogata per sententiam iudicis. Discip. Intelligo distinctionem eorum de duplici infamia iuris, per quam patenter aduerto, quod papa hæreticus & omnes hæretici infamia iuris primo modo dicta sunt infames: quia eorum viæ & pertinaciæ sunt infames: sicut & alii actus praui malorum sunt infames secundum sententiam Salomonis. Sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod sint infames infamia iuris secundo modo dicta. Et ideo quomodo hoc probare nituntur, ostende. Magist. Videris velle transire ad pœnas, quæ irrogantur à iure humano.
units.tr: Disciple. You have said enough about that penalty, so now tell me another penalty which heretics, and above all a heretical pope, and in general all heretics incur by divine law or natural law, by the very fact of being heretics. Master. One assertion is that all heretics incur the penalty of infamy. It should be understood, as the Gloss notes on 3. quæst. 7. porro, that there is one infamy of law and another of fact. Infamy of fact is when someone is defamed among good and serious men. Infamy of law is a diminution of someone's status. Heretics, especially secret ones, do not always incur the first infamy, because some heretics are not always spoken ill of by good and serious men, although Catholics are sometimes most gravely defamed among them. But a heretical pope and all heretics in general incur the second infamy. To make this clear, it should be understood that infamy of law is sometimes imposed by the very fact, and sometimes by sentence. In both ways all of them incur infamy, because by the very fact that they become heretics, they commit a sin worthy of infamy. Infamy is also imposed on them by sentence, when they are condemned by divine law for the greatest crime and deprived of the status of undiminished dignity. Disciple. According to these men, it seems that infamy of law is twofold. So that I may grasp their meaning better, explain these two modes of infamy of law. Master. So that you may have a clearer understanding of them, you must know that infamy imposed by sentence is twofold. One kind is imposed by a sentence passed by law, another by a sentence passed by a man. Heretics always incur the first. They do not always incur the second, though they do not incur it insofar as they are Catholic men innocent of every crime, since Catholics are often condemned by men while heretics are exalted and honoured. From these things they say that infamy is a damage to the status of dignity, approved by customs and laws. Infamy of law is twofold, according to the two ways in which a man's status can be damaged. It is damaged either by an act of infamy, namely by committing an infamous act, as Solomon says of the wicked in Proverbs 2: Whose way is perverse and whose steps are infamous. And in chapter 8 he says: He who walks in the straight path and fears God is despised by him who walks in an infamous way, clearly suggesting that all the steps and ways of the wicked are infamous. This is infamy even though they do not always have infamy of fact attached, because all the acts of evil men, insofar as they are evil, are condemned by divine law, natural law, or human law. This infamy of law may be called infamy imposed by a sentence passed by law. Otherwise, a man's status is damaged when his superior condemns him for a crime and deprives him of the dignity of an unblemished reputation, even though sometimes he has committed nothing for which his infamy ought to be damaged. This infamy may be called infamy of law imposed by the sentence of a judge. Disciple. I understand your distinction between the twofold infamy of law, and I clearly see that a heretical pope and all heretics are infamous in the first sense, because their ways and obstinacy are infamous, just as other evil acts of the wicked are infamous according to Solomon's judgment. But it does not follow from this that they are infamous in the second sense. So show me how they try to prove this. Master. You seem to want to pass on to the penalties imposed by human law.

units.la: Discipul. Quia aliquoties eadem pœna iure diuino, naturali & humano infertur: ideo vndecunque infamia hæreticis irrogetur, dic qualiter probetur quod omnes hæretici sunt infames. Magist. Hoc multis auctoritatibus & rationibus videtur posse probari. Dyonysius enim papa, vt legitur 2. q. 7. alieni, hoc videtur asserere manifeste, ait enim: infames esse omnes censemus, qui suam fidem aut Christianam legem prænaricantur, omnes autem hæretici legem Christianam præuaricantur, ergo omnes sunt infames. His etiam concordat Stephanus papa, qui, vt habetur 9. q. 2. c. infames, ait: infames omnes personas etiam dicimus, quæ pro aliqua culpa notantur infamia, id est omnes qui Christiana legis normam abiiciunt. Omnes ergo hæretici sunt infames. Quod etiam rationibus videtur posse probari. Quarum prima est hæc. Omnes iniqui qui regnum Dei minime possidebunt, sunt infames, teste Fabiano papa, qui, vt habetur 6. q. 1. c. illi, ait: Illi, qui illa peccata perpetrant, de quibus Apostolus ait, Quoniam qui talia agunt regnum Dei non consequuntur, valde cauendi sunt, & ad emendationem si venire noluerint, compellendi sunt, quia infamiæ macula sunt aspersi & in baratrum dilabuntur. Sed hæretici sunt iniqui, qui regnum Dei non consequuntur, ergo hæretici sunt infames. Secunda ratio est hæc. Minoris culpæ est peccatum luxuriæ quam peccatum hæresis, sed incontinenter viuentes sunt infames, quia non sunt bonæ famæ, dicente Hely sacerdote ad filios suos, qui dormiebant cum mulieribus quæ obseruabant ad hostium tabernaculi, vt legitur r. Reg. 2. Et quare facitis res huiusce modi, quas ego audio pessimas ab omni populo, nolite filii mei, non enim est bona fama, quam audio, ergo multo magis hæretici sunt infames.
units.tr: Disciple. Since the same penalty is sometimes imposed by divine, natural and human law, whatever the source from which infamy is imposed on heretics, tell me how it is proved that all heretics are infamous. Master. This seems capable of being proved by many authorities and reasons. Pope Dionysius, as we read in 2. q. 7. alieni, seems to assert this plainly, for he says: We judge all to be infamous who prevaricate against their faith or the Christian law. But all heretics prevaricate against the Christian law; therefore all are infamous. Pope Stephen agrees with this, who, as found in 9. q. 2. c. infames, says: We also call infamous all persons who are marked with infamy for some fault, that is, all who cast off the rule of Christian law. Therefore all heretics are infamous. This also seems capable of being proved by reasons. The first is this. All the wicked who do not possess the kingdom of God are infamous, as Pope Fabian witnesses, who, as found in 6. q. 1. c. illi, says: Those who commit those sins of which the Apostle says, "Those who do such things do not inherit the kingdom of God," are to be greatly guarded against, and if they are unwilling to come to amendment, they are to be compelled, because they are stained with the blot of infamy and slip into the abyss. But heretics are wicked people who do not inherit the kingdom of God; therefore heretics are infamous. The second reason is this. The sin of lust is of lesser guilt than the sin of heresy, but those who live incontinently are infamous, because they do not have a good reputation, as the priest Eli said to his sons, who slept with the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle, as we read in 1 Kings 2: Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil deeds from all the people. Do not, my sons, for the report that I hear is not good. Therefore much more so heretics are infamous.

units.la: CAP. LXXVII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXVII.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod omnes hæretici sunt ab omni testimonio repellendi.
units.tr: In which it is proved that all heretics are to be excluded from every testimony.

units.la: Discipulus. Dic, si papa hæreticus & alii hæretici alia pœna plectuntur secundum ius diuinum, vel ius naturale, vel etiam humanum. Mag. Sunt nonnulli dicentes, quod papa hæreticus & generaliter omnes hæretici hac pœna plectuntur ipso iure, quod sunt ab omni testimonio repellendi, nec cis in quocunq; negocio est credendum. Discip. Moliuntur ne hanc assertionem aliquibus rationibus vel auctoritatibus munire? Mag. Hanc assertionem pluribus rationibus in scripturis fundatis authenticis & auctoritatibus multis probare nituntur. Est autem prima ratio talis. Nullus criminosus est ad testimonium admittendus, nec ei in quocunq; negocio est credendum, omnes autem hæretici sunt & criminosi, ergo nullus hæreticus est ad testimonium admittendus: sed est ab omni testimonio repellendus: & ei in nullo negocio est credendum. Disc. Sola maior istius rationis probatione indigere videtur. Nam saepe in scripturis legi authenticis (nec tamen vade habeat firmitatem inuenire) verum scilicet ex iure diuino vel naturali aut solummodo ex constitutione humana habeatur: quod tamen scire a multis temporibus affectaui. Et ideo circa istam maiorem primo eam auctoritatibus munire nitaris. Secundo, an ex sola constitutione humana dependeat, vel ex iure diuino aut naturali capiat fulcimentum, velis differere. Sic enim fortassis ad veritatem perueniam. Magist. Fateor quod quia multos noui scelestos igne vel perpetuo carcere notorie dignos, qui de personis innocentibus grauia confinxerunt & mendaciter imposuerunt ex odio vel rancore, istam materiam libenter secundum opiniones hominum discutiam. Et quid ego sentiam, toti mundo alias explicabo. De hac enim materia librum intendo facere specialem. Discip. Et ego huiusmodi criminatores & detractores agnoui. De quibus in tertia parte huius operis, scilicet tractatu de gestis circa fidem altercantium orthodoxam, in speciali tibi plures quaestiones proponam. Quia impositores & relatores falsorum criminum in tantum odio habeo, quod mihi videtur eos esse dignos poena maiori, quam illi qui essent impositis criminibus irretiti. Nunc vero circa maiorem praestriptam, sicut dixi, procede. Magist. Quod omnes criminosi sunt a testimonio repellendi, multis auctoritatibus videtur posse probari. Ait enim Damasus Papa, vt habetur 2. q. 7. cap. testes: Testes absq; vlla infamia aut suspitione vel manifesta macula, cum vera fidei plenitudine instructi esse debent. Item Caelestinus Papa tertius, vt legitur extr. de exceptionibus c. 1. ait: Cum sicut canonica instituta declarant, testes absq; vlla infamia vel suspitione vel manifesta macula inferendo testimonium requirantur. Item Pontianus Papa, vt habetur 3. q. v. c. suspectos, ait: suspectos aut inimicos aut facile litigantes & eos qui non sunt bonae conuersationis, aut quorum vita est accusabilis, & qui rectam non tenent aut docent fidem, accusatores esse & testes, antecessores nostri Apostoli prohibuerunt, & nos eorum auctoritate submonemus, atq; temporibus futuris prohibemus. Ex quibus verbis patet aperte, quod criminosi sunt a testimonio repellendi. Discip. Scio quod saepe inuenitur in iure, quod criminosi sunt a testimonio repellendi, & quod etiam sunt ab accusatione penitus submouendi: ad quod tamen probandum alias auctoritates adducas. Et alias signa; vbi debeant reperiri. Magist. Quod criminosi sunt ab accusatione penitus repellendi, testatur Iulianus Papa, qui, vt legitur 3. q. v. c. similiter, ait: Similiter in praefixa synodo est decretum, ne suspecti aut infames aut criminosi, aut gratiosi, aut calumniatores vel affines aut scelerati aut facile litigantes suscipiantur accusatores: sed tales qui omni carent vitio aut suspitione. Item Eusebius Papa, vt habetur eadem causa & q. c. constituimus, ait: constitutimus cum omnibus qui nobiscum sunt episcopis, vt homicida, malefici & fures, sacrilegi, raptores, adulteri, incestuosi, venefici, suspecti, criminosi, domestici, periuri, & qui raptum fecerunt, vel qui falsum testimonium dixerunt, seu qui ad sortilegos diuinos concurrunt, similesq; eorum, ad nullatenus accusandum vel ad testimonium sunt admittendi, quia infames sunt & iuste repellendi, quia funesta est in talibus vox eorum. Ex quibus patet expresse, quod criminosi tam ab accusatione quam a testimonio sunt penitus repellendi. Quod etiam asseritur manifeste 3. q. 4. c. nulli & cap. si quis & c. sanguinei, & 3. q. 4. canonica & 6. q. 1. omnes & c. quiescite, & extr. de desponsatione impuberum, cum in tua, & 22. q. 1. prohibentur, & extr. de accusationibus, cum oporteat, in textu & Glos. & extr. de testibus, veniens. Quod etiam criminosi non sunt in testimonium admittendi; probatur ratione. Minus sunt admittendi, criminis conuicii, quam quibus crimina opponuntur. Sed illi, quibus crimina opponuntur, siue in modum exceptionis siue in modum accusationis non sunt in testimonium admittendi; extr. de testibus c. super eos & ca. testimonium; & c. ultimo & extr. de exceptione, c. deniq. Ergo multo magis notorie criminosi & victi vel confessi de crimine, non sunt in testimonium admittendi. Discip. Istae allegationes pro assertione sufficiant. Ideo ad secundum te conuerte. Et unde accipitur, quod criminoso in nullo negocio fides debeat adhiberi secundum beatorum sententias manifesta. Magist. Circa hoc contigit diuersimode opinari. Est enim vna opinio, quod non ex constitutione humana, sed ex recta ratione & iure diuino nulli criminoso est credendum. Quia de nullo criminoso est firmiter praesumendum, quod sit verax, & quod nolit mentiri vel etiam periurare. Illi autem in praeiudicium alterius nullatenus est credendum, de quo non est praesumendum, quod sit verax, & quod nolit mentiri. Igitur nulli criminoso in quocunque negotio praecipue in alterius praeiudicium est credendum. Discip. Ista opinio duo probare debet: quorum primum est, quod de nullo criminoso est firmiter credendum, quod sit verax, & quod nolit mentiri vel periurare. Secundum est, quod illi non est credendum, de quo non est firmiter praesumendum, quod verax est, & quod nolit mentiri. Magist. Primum declaratur sic. Ille, de quo constat, quod careat aliqua vera virtute, non est praesumendum, quod careat vitio oppositio saltem secundum praeparationem cordis, licet constare posset quod careat contrario vitio, quantum ad opus exterius. Multi enim sunt, de quibus constat, quod non sunt vere iusti: quia constat quod exercent opera iusta ex timore vel cupiditate. De quibus tamen per consequens constat, quod non sunt iniusti, quo ad opus exterius, quia nullum faciunt iniustum: sed non constat quod non sunt iniusti secundum praeparationem cordis. Criminosus autem caret illa virtute, scil. veritate, quae est vera virtus. Ergo de criminoso est nullatenus praesumendum, quod non sit falsus & mendax & quod nolit mentiri. Discip. Ista ratio videtur mihi mirabilis. Nam sequitur ex ipla, quod nunquam de aliquo pagano vel infideli constat, quod habuerit veram virtutem, quae est veritas seu veracitas: quia nulla est virtus sine sana fide. Ideo sicut nec iustitia est sine sana fide, teste Aug. vt habetur 3. q. 1. c. vbi, ait: Vbi sana fides non est, ibi non potest esse sana iustitia. Ergo consimiliter vbi sana fides non est, veritas seu veracitas esse non potest. Constat autem quod pagani veram fidem minime habuerunt. Ergo de nullo illorum praesumendum fuit, quod vnquam esset ad testimonium admittendas, quod constat esse falsum. Magist. Ad istam instantiam respondetur distinguendo de vera virtute. Ad cuius evidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod bonum actum exteriorem, sicut dicere veritatem recte iudicare, pascere pauperem, & actus alios bonos exercere, contingit tripliciter, vel propter Deum, vel quia dictatur a ratione recta, vel quia neque propter hoc quod Deo placet, neq; quia dictatur a ratione recta, sed propter aliquod bonum vtile aut delectabile consequendum, vel propter aliquod malum ac periculum euitandum. Actibus bonis primo modo elicitis correspondent virtutes perfectae. Qui enim ex habitu veritatem loquitur propter Deum, habet veritatem seu veracitatem, quae est virtus perfecta, quam habent soli fideles; quia illi soli propter Deum verum ex caritate veritatem loquuntur. Et ista virtus nullum vitium secum compatitur. Quia habeas talem virtutem secundum praeparationem cordis habet omnes virtutes & actus eorum omni vitio caret. Quemadmodum habens charitatem secundum praeparationem cordis habet omnes virtutes & omni vitio caret. Actibus bonis secundo modo elicitis correspondent virtutes verae, sed imperfectae respectu virtutum primarum. Qui enim ex habitu veritatem dicit propter hoc, quod ratio recta dictat veritatem esse dicendam (licet de Deo non cogitet) habet veritatem seu veracitatem, quae est vera virtus. Habens taliter veritatem secundum praeparationem cordis, habet omnes virtutes morales & omni vitio caret. Et ideo talis veritas omne vitium excludit, & potest vera virtus vocari; sed est imperfecta, sicut actus in tali dicente est imperfectus. Velle enim dicere veritatem propter Deum est multo perfectior actio, quam tantummodo velle dicere, quia recta ratio dictat veritatem esse dicendam: quemadmodum Deus est perfectior quam ratio recta, & ideo ista veritas est imperfectior alia. Virtutes autem isto modo dictae fuerunt secundum alios in Philosophia multis & paganis quampluribus, quia plures eorum ideo fecerunt actus bonos ex genere, quia secundum rationem rectam viuere voluerunt. Actibus autem bonis exterioribus tertio modo elicitis correspondent verae virtutes neque perfectae neque imperfectae: quia nec virtutes generantur ex eis, necipsi ex virtutibus generantur. Qui enim loquitur veritatem, vel vt honoretur, vel ditetur, vel vt infamiam aut aliquod malum euitet; non ideo verax & virtuosus est. Quemadmodum ambitiosi, hypocritae, auari & alii multis criminibus inuoluti veritatem dicunt, & actus bonos aliquos operantur: non autem habent veritatem, quae est virtus vera nec persecta neque imperfecta. Tales enim non sunt virtuosi, sed ambitiosi, timidi vel auari. Omnamque opera sua faciunt vel vt videantur ab hominibus & honorentur laudentur & exaltentur ab eis, vel vt acquirant pecuniam, aut vt infamiam & confusionem temporalem euadant. Discip. Antequam ista ad propositum applicentur, ad istam instantiam respondeas: an scil. sic dicentes tenent virtutes perfectas & imperfectas esse distinctas specie, vel solo numero propter maiorem & minorem gradum eiusdem perfectionis secundum speciem. Magist. Circa istam opinionem habentur assertiones contrariae, quibusdam asserentibus quod non distinguuntur specie: aliis opinantibus quod specie distinguuntur. Quemadmodum actus voluntatis quo elicitur vel imperatur bonus actus exterior, quia a recta ratione dictatur. Illi enim ponunt omnes veras virtutes esse in voluntate: & quod quibuslibet distinctis actibus bonis voluntatis distinguuntur habitus correspondent.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me, if the Pope and other heretics are punished in some other way, whether by divine law, natural law, or even human law. Master. Some say that the Pope, when he is a heretic, and all heretics in general, are by law itself punished in this way: they are to be excluded from all testimony, and no one is to believe them in any matter. Disciple. Do they try to support this assertion with any reasons or authorities? Master. They try to prove this assertion by many reasons founded on genuine Scripture and by many authorities. The first reason runs as follows. No criminal is to be admitted as a witness, nor is he to be believed in any matter. All heretics are criminals. Therefore no heretic is to be admitted as a witness, but is to be excluded from all testimony, and is not to be believed in any matter. Disc. The major premise seems to need proof by itself. For I have often read in genuine Scripture (though I have not yet been able to find where it has firmness) whether this is held by divine or natural law, or only by human enactment. I have long tried to know this. So, concerning this major premise, first try to support it by authorities; second, tell me whether it depends on human enactment alone, or draws its support from divine or natural law. In that way I may perhaps come to the truth. Master. I confess that, since I know many wicked men who deserve fire or perpetual prison for having invented serious charges against innocent persons and falsely imputed them out of hatred or spite, I will gladly discuss this matter according to the opinions of men. What I myself think I will explain to the whole world elsewhere, for I intend to write a special book on this subject. Disciple. I too know such accusers and slanderers. About them I will put many questions to you in particular in the third part of this work, namely the treatise on those who dispute over the orthodox faith. I hold the inventors and reporters of false charges in such hatred that it seems to me they deserve a greater punishment than those who are entangled in the charges imposed on them. But now, as I said, proceed with the major premise. Master. That all criminals are to be excluded from testimony can, it seems, be proved by many authorities. Pope Damasus says, as found in 2 q. 7, c. testes: Witnesses ought to be instructed in the full truth of the faith, without any infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain. Likewise Pope Celestine III, as read in extr. de exceptionibus, c. 1, says: Since, as the canonical institutions declare, witnesses are to be sought for giving testimony without any infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain. Likewise Pope Pontian, as found in 3 q. 5, c. suspectos, says: Our forefathers the Apostles forbade that the suspected, enemies, the quarrelsome, those who are not of good conduct, or whose life is open to accusation, and who do not hold or teach the right faith, be accusers and witnesses; and we, on their authority, admonish and forbid it for future times. From these words it is clear that criminals are to be excluded from testimony. Disciple. I know that it is often found in the law that criminals are to be excluded from testimony, and that they are also to be entirely removed from accusation. But for that you should bring other authorities, and show where they ought to be found. Master. That criminals are to be entirely excluded from accusation is attested by Pope Julius, who, as read in 3 q. 5, c. similiter, says: Likewise it was decreed in the synod before us that the suspected, infamous, criminal, the favourites, the slanderers, the relatives, the wicked, or the quarrelsome are not to be received as accusers, but only such as are free from every fault or suspicion. Likewise Pope Eusebius, as found in the same cause and question, c. constituimus, says: We lay down, together with all the bishops who are with us, that murderers, sorcerers and thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, adulterers, incestuous persons, poisoners, the suspected, criminals, domestics, perjurers, those who have carried off women, or who have given false witness, or who run to diviners and such like, are in no way to be admitted to accuse or to give testimony, because they are infamous and rightly rejected, since their voice is deadly in such matters. From these words it is plainly evident that criminals are entirely to be excluded both from accusation and from testimony. This is also clearly asserted in 3 q. 4, c. nulli and c. si quis, c. sanguinei, and 3 q. 4, canonica, and 6 q. 1, omnes, c. quiescite, and extr. de desponsatione impuberum, c. cum in tua, and 22 q. 1 they are forbidden; and extr. de accusationibus, c. cum oporteat, in the text and gloss, and extr. de testibus, c. veniens. That criminals are also not to be admitted as witnesses is proved by reason. Those against whom crimes are alleged are less to be admitted than those whom the crimes are alleged against. But those against whom crimes are alleged, whether by way of exception or by way of accusation, are not to be admitted as witnesses (extr. de testibus, c. super eos and c. testimonium; and c. ultimo, and extr. de exceptione, c. denique). Therefore much more so those who are notoriously criminal, and who have been convicted or confessed of a crime, are not to be admitted as witnesses. Disciple. Let these allegations suffice for the assertion. Therefore turn to the second point. And from where is it gathered, according to the clear judgment of the blessed ones, that no faith is to be given to a criminal in any matter? Master. On this point opinions have differed. For one opinion holds that no criminal is to be believed, not by human enactment, but by right reason and divine law. For no criminal can firmly be presumed to be truthful, or unwilling to lie or even to commit perjury. But no one is to be believed to the prejudice of another if it cannot be presumed of him that he is truthful and unwilling to lie. Therefore no criminal is to be believed in any matter whatsoever, especially to another's prejudice. Disciple. That opinion must prove two things: first, that no criminal can firmly be believed to be truthful and unwilling to lie or to perjure himself; second, that no one is to be believed of whom it cannot firmly be presumed that he is truthful and unwilling to lie. Master. The first is made clear thus. Someone who is known to lack some true virtue cannot be presumed to lack the opposing vice, at least as far as the disposition of the heart goes, even though it may be known that he lacks the contrary vice as far as outward action is concerned. For there are many of whom it is known that they are not truly just, because it is known that they perform just deeds out of fear or greed. Of these, however, it is consequently known that they are not unjust in outward action, since they do no unjust deed; but it is not known that they are not unjust in the disposition of the heart. A criminal, however, lacks that virtue, namely truthfulness, which is a true virtue. Therefore of a criminal it cannot in any way be presumed that he is not false and lying, and that he is not unwilling to lie. Disciple. This reasoning seems to me remarkable. For it follows from it that it is never known of any pagan or unbeliever that he had true virtue, which is truth or truthfulness, since there is no virtue without sound faith. Therefore, just as justice is not without sound faith, as Augustine attests, as found in 3 q. 1, c. ubi, he says: Where there is not sound faith, there cannot be sound justice. Therefore similarly, where there is not sound faith, truth or truthfulness cannot exist. But it is clear that the pagans had no true faith at all. Therefore of none of them could it be presumed that he was ever fit to be admitted as a witness, since it is known to be false. Master. To this objection the answer is given by making a distinction concerning true virtue. To make this clear, it must be understood that a good outward act, such as telling the truth, judging rightly, feeding the poor, and performing other good acts, happens in three ways: either on account of God, or because it is dictated by right reason, or neither on account of what pleases God nor because it is dictated by right reason, but in order to obtain some useful or pleasant good, or to avoid some evil and danger. To good acts elicited in the first way correspond perfect virtues. For one who speaks the truth from habit for God's sake has truth or truthfulness, which is a perfect virtue, possessed only by the faithful; for only they speak the truth for God's sake out of charity. And this virtue is not compatible with any vice. For whoever has such a virtue in the disposition of his heart has all the virtues, and his acts are free from every vice; just as one who has charity in the disposition of his heart has all the virtues and is free from every vice. To good acts elicited in the second way correspond true but imperfect virtues, imperfect in comparison with the first virtues. For one who speaks the truth from habit, because right reason dictates that the truth is to be spoken (even if he does not think of God), has truth or truthfulness, which is a true virtue. One who has truth in this way in the disposition of his heart has all the moral virtues and is free from every vice. And therefore such truth excludes every vice, and can be called a true virtue; but it is imperfect, just as the act of one who speaks in this way is imperfect. For to wish to speak the truth for God's sake is a much more perfect action than merely wishing to speak it because right reason dictates that it should be spoken; just as God is more perfect than right reason, and so this truth is more imperfect than the other. Moreover, according to some philosophers, such virtues were attributed to many pagans, since many of them did good deeds of this kind because they wished to live according to right reason. To good outward acts elicited in the third way correspond true virtues that are neither perfect nor imperfect, because virtues are neither generated from such acts, nor do such acts arise from virtues. For one who speaks the truth in order to be honoured, or enriched, or to avoid infamy or some other evil, is not on that account truthful and virtuous. Just as ambitious men, hypocrites, the greedy and others entangled in many crimes speak the truth and perform some good acts, yet they do not have truthfulness, which is a true virtue, neither perfect nor imperfect. For such men are not virtuous, but ambitious, timid, or greedy. And they do all their works either so that they may be seen by men and be honoured, praised and exalted by them, or so that they may acquire money, or so that they may escape temporal infamy and shame. Disciple. Before these things are applied to the matter at hand, answer this objection: whether those who speak in this way hold that perfect and imperfect virtues are distinct in kind, or only in number, on account of a greater and lesser degree of the same perfection in kind. Master. On this opinion there are contrary assertions: some maintain that they are not distinguished in kind, others that they are distinguished in kind. Just as the act of the will by which a good outward act is elicited or commanded is good, because it is dictated by right reason. For those men hold that all true virtues are in the will, and that the habits corresponding to them are distinguished by the distinct good acts of the will.

units.la: Discip. Opiniones praedictas intelligo, quarum discussionem curiosis reputo relinquendam: quia parum vtilitatis habent. In hoc autem opere vtilia tantum reputo pertractanda. Ideo dic, quomodo perilla, quae de virtute perfecta & imperfecta dicta sunt, ad instantiam factam respondetur. Magist. Respondetur, quod non solum qui habet virtutem perfectam (quae sine fide & caritate minime reperitur) sed etiam qui habet virtutem quamcunque moralem veram (licet imperfectam respectu virtutis, quae est in fidem & caritatem habentibus) habet secundum praeparationem cordis omnes virtutes morales & omni morali vitio caret. Et ideo talis virtuosus secundum praeparationem cordis est verax, neque est falsus neque mendax. Tales autem virtutes morales, vt quidam putant, in multis fuere paganis. Multi enim eorum secundum rationem rectam viuere nitebantur & vixerunt. Quare veraces fuerunt: & ideo in testimonium admittendi fuerunt. Quia ergo quilibet etiam paganus praesumendus est virtuosus virtute morali imperfecta, nisi constet contrarium, Pagani, qui non fuerunt aliquo crimine morali inuoluti, ad testimonium admittendi fuerunt. Quando autem dicit Augustin. Vbi fides sana non est, noh potest esse iustitia: ipse loquitur de iustitia perfecta, cui correspondent actus iusti ex charitate Dei elicíti. Talis enim iustitia in paganis & in quibuscunque carentibus sana fide non fuit. Tamen iustitia, quae vocatur iustitia politica vel ciuilis, fuit in pluribus. Multi enim corum multa fecerunt, non propter aliquod lucrum vel commodum vel honorem, vel propter aliquod exterius malum vel periculum euitandum, sed quia rectam rationem sequi volebant.
units.tr: Disciple. I understand the opinions mentioned above, though I think their discussion should be left to the curious, since they are of little use. In this work I think only what is useful should be treated. So tell me how the things said about perfect and imperfect virtue answer the objection raised. Master. The answer is this: not only the one who has perfect virtue (which is never found without faith and charity) but also the one who has any true moral virtue (although imperfect compared with the virtue of those who have faith and charity) has, according to the disposition of the heart, all the moral virtues and is free from every moral vice. Such a virtuous person, according to the disposition of his heart, is truthful, and is neither false nor a liar. Some think that such moral virtues were found in many pagans. For many of them strove to live according to right reason, and did so. Therefore they were truthful, and so should have been admitted as witnesses. Since, then, every pagan too must be presumed virtuous with an imperfect moral virtue unless the contrary is established, those pagans who were not entangled in any moral crime should have been admitted as witnesses. When Augustine says, "Where there is no sound faith, there cannot be justice," he is speaking of perfect justice, to which correspond the righteous acts elicited from the love of God. Such justice was not present in pagans, or in anyone lacking sound faith. Yet what is called political or civil justice was found in many. For many of them did many things not for any gain, advantage or honour, nor to avoid some external evil or danger, but because they wished to follow right reason.

units.la: Discip. Licet praescripta apparentia & subtilia videantur, contra ipsa tamen aliquae mihi obiectiones occurrunt. Quarum prima est haec: quod secundum assertiones sanctorum patrum pagani non sunt ad testimonium admittendi 2. q. 7. pagani. Secunda ratio est, quia omnes pagani sunt & fuerunt criminosi: quia infidelitas species criminis dignoscitur esse. Et tamen secundum praedicta aliqui pagani fuerunt in testimonium admittendi. Ergo criminosus est ad testimonium admittadmittendus. Tertia ratio est: quod si ideo pagani aliqui fuerunt reputandi veraces & non falsi neq; mendaces, quia secundum rationem rectam viuere nitebantur. Et constat q; multi criminosi secundum rationem viuere moliuntur. Qui enim ex sola ignorantia peccant secundum rationem viuere conari videntur. Multi autem criminosi ex sola ignorantia peccant. Ergo multi criminosi, omnes scilicet ex ignorantia delinquentes, sunt in testimonium admittendi. Magist. Ad primam istarum respondetur, quod pagani, quos a testimonio decreta sanctorum patrum excludunt, fuerunt ex maliria Christianis infesti. Et ideo tanquam inimici suspecti non fuerunt contra Christianos in testimonium admittendi coram iudice Christiano. Ad secundam dicitur, quod nonnulli fuerunt pagani, qui nequaquam criminosi fuerunt. Nam & Iob paganus fuit: & multi alii boni, qui ad legem Mosaicam nequaquam astricti fuerunt. Et ideo eis adhibenda fides fuit. Si etiam aliqui essent in puris naturalibus constituti secundum rationem viuere saragentes, non essent criminosi censendi. Et ideo esset credendum eisdem: quia virtutes morales haberent imperfectae. Illi autem pagani, qui crimine infidelitatis irretiti fuerunt, de stricto iure non fuerunt in testimonium a fidelibus admittendi: sed tamen infideles, qui infidelitatem crimen esse minime putauerunt, eos recipere debuerunt. Discip. Nunquid secundum ista opinione aliqui philosophi vel Imperatores & alii pagani, qui idola coluerunt, habuerunt aliquam virtutem, licet imperfectam? Magist. Respondetur quod nullus idolatra siue paganus siue alius dum erat idolatra, habuit veram virtutem etiam imperfectam. Nam omnes tales criminosi fuerunt, & nullum damnabile vitium stat cum vera virtute. Quia sicut dictum est, quicunq; habet vnam veram virtutem, habet secundum praeparationem cordis omnem aliam virtutem. Et ideo omni vitio caret. Discip. Contra hoc est obiectio tertia, quam feci: & ideo indica, quomodo respondetur ad ipsam. Magist. Ad ipsam dicitur, quod nulli criminoso viuere secundum rationem donatur. Cum vero dicitur, quod qui ex sola ignorantia peccat, secundum rationem viuere conari videtur: Respondetur, quod quaedam ignorantia excusat, vt actum, qui communiter est peccatum, reddat ab omni peccato immunem; vel saltem faciat veniale peccatum. Et qui ex tali ignorantia peccat, vel facit actum qui communiter est peccatum, non est criminosus. Alia est ignorantia, quae non excusat, vel saltem non excusat a peccato mortali. Et ex tali ignorantia multi criminosi peccant. Sed nullus peccans ex ignorantia tali nititur viuere secundum rationem. Si enim secundum rationem viuere conaretur: quomodo esset viuendum, inquireret diligenter. Si autem inquireret, inueniret. Si inuenire non posset; ipsum ignorantia inuincibilis excusaret. Et propterea Philosophi & alii idolatrantes non fuerunt a crimine excusati. Quia aut sciuerunt idola non esse colenda, quemadmodum Philosophi plures docuerunt in scholis, nihil diuinitatis esse in Idolis; & quod eis non esset honor diuinus aliqualiter exhibendus; & tamen cum aliis idola coluerunt. Et de illis constat, quod criminosi fuerunt, & secundum rationem viuere nullatenus conabantur. Aut huiusmodi idolatrantes ignoraverunt huiusmodi idola non esse colenda. Et constat quod ignorantia inuincibili minime laborabant: quia per rationem naturalem poterant inuenire, quod nihil diuinitatis erat in idolis manus factis: & quod eis honor diuinus non debuit exhiberi. Ergo laborabant ignorantia affectata & crassa & supina. Talis autem ignorantia non excusat, imo talis ignorantia est damnabilis. Et ideo criminosi fuerunt. Et ideo secundum rationem nullatenus viuere nitebantur. Quare nullam veram virtutem etiam imperfectam, quae potest esse sine fide & charitate, penitus habuerunt. Et ideo districto iure in nullo negotio debuerunt fideles & virtuosi eis indubitatam credulitatem aliqualiter adhibere. Discip. Ista ultima dicta prioribus repugnare videntur. Dictum est enim prius, quod multi Philosophi habuerunt veras virtutes, licet imperfectas. Nunc autem asseritur, q; nullus Idolatra habuit veram virtutem. Constat autem quod omnes Philosophi fuerunt idolatrae. Ergo secundum ultimo dicta nullam habuerunt veram virtutem: & sic ultima prioribus contradicunt. Magist. Respondetur, quod non constat omnes Philosophos fuisse Idolatras. Ideo probabile est, quod aliqui non fuerunt Idolatrae. Quicunq; enim secundum rationem viuere nitebantur, idolatriam euitauerunt. Si ergo aliqui Philosophi vel alii secundum rationem viuere conabantur, Idolatrae non fuerunt.
units.tr: Disciple. Although what has been prescribed seems plausible and subtle, several objections nevertheless occur to me against it. The first is this: according to the assertions of the holy Fathers, pagans are not to be admitted as witnesses (2. q. 7, Pagani). The second reason is that all pagans are, and have been, criminals, since unbelief is recognised as a species of crime. Yet according to what has been said, some pagans were to be admitted as witnesses. Therefore a criminal is to be admitted as a witness. The third reason is this: if some pagans were to be regarded as truthful and not false or lying, because they strove to live according to reason, and it is evident that many criminals also strive to live according to reason (for those who sin from ignorance alone seem to try to live according to reason), and many criminals sin from ignorance alone, then many criminals, namely all those who offend from ignorance, are to be admitted as witnesses. Master. To the first of these, the answer is that the pagans whom the decrees of the holy Fathers exclude from testimony were hostile to Christians out of malice, and so, being suspect as enemies, they were not to be admitted as witnesses against Christians before a Christian judge. To the second, it is said that some pagans were not criminal at all. For Job was a pagan, and so were many other good men who were not bound to the Mosaic law at all, and so they were to be given credence. Even if some were placed in pure nature and strove to live according to reason, they should not be considered criminals, and so they were to be believed, since their moral virtues would be imperfect. But those pagans who were entangled in the crime of unbelief were not, strictly speaking, to be admitted as witnesses by the faithful; yet unbelievers who did not judge unbelief to be a crime ought to have received them. Disciple. According to this opinion, did some philosophers or emperors and other pagans who worshipped idols have some virtue, though imperfect? Master. The answer is that no idolater, whether pagan or otherwise, while he was an idolater, had true virtue, even imperfect. For all such people were criminals, and no damnable vice is compatible with true virtue. Because, as has been said, whoever has one true virtue has, according to the disposition of his heart, every other virtue, and so is free from every vice. Disciple. Against this is the third objection I raised, so tell me how it is answered. Master. To it the answer is that living according to reason is not granted to any criminal. When it is said that one who sins from ignorance alone seems to try to live according to reason, the answer is that some ignorance excuses, so as to render an act which is commonly sin free from all sin, or at least make it a venial sin; and one who sins from such ignorance, or does an act which is commonly sin, is not a criminal. There is another ignorance which does not excuse, or at least does not excuse from mortal sin. From such ignorance many criminals sin. But no one who sins from such ignorance strives to live according to reason. For if he were striving to live according to reason, he would diligently inquire how he ought to live; and if he inquired, he would find out. If he could not find out, invincible ignorance would excuse him. And for this reason the philosophers and the other idolaters were not excused from crime. For either they knew that idols were not to be worshipped, as many philosophers taught in their schools, that there was nothing divine in idols, and that divine honour was not to be paid to them in any way; and yet they worshipped idols along with others. And of these it is evident that they were criminals, and in no way strove to live according to reason. Or such idolaters did not know that such idols were not to be worshipped. And it is evident that they did not labour under invincible ignorance, since by natural reason they could discover that there was nothing divine in idols made by hands, and that divine honour should not be paid to them. Therefore they laboured under affected, gross and supine ignorance. Such ignorance does not excuse; indeed, such ignorance is damnable. And so they were criminals, and so in no way strove to live according to reason. Therefore they had entirely no true virtue, even imperfect, which can exist without faith and charity. And so, by strict right, the faithful and virtuous ought in no matter to give them any unquestioning credence. Disciple. These last statements seem to contradict the earlier ones. For it was said earlier that many philosophers had true virtues, though imperfect. But now it is asserted that no idolater had true virtue. It is certain, however, that all philosophers were idolaters. Therefore, by what was said last, they had no true virtue, and so the last contradicts the earlier. Master. The answer is that it is not certain that all philosophers were idolaters. It is therefore probable that some were not idolaters. For whoever strove to live according to reason avoided idolatry. So if some philosophers or others strove to live according to reason, they were not idolaters.

units.la: CAP. LXXVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXVIII.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod omnis criminosus secundum praeparationem cordis omni vitio irretitur.
units.tr: In which it is proved that every criminal, according to the disposition of the heart, is ensnared in every vice.

units.la: Discipulus. Istam rationem, per quam probatur, quod de nullo criminoso est firmiter praesumendum, quod sit verax, intelligo. Quae in hoc mihi fundari videtur, quod omnis criminosus secundum praeparationem cordis omni crimine irretitur: quemadmodum habens charitatem vel quamcunque veram virtutem secundum praeparationem cordis habet omnem actum virtutis sibi possibilem. Hoc autem tam mirabile mihi apparet, quod nullus intellectus hoc debeat opinari, cum quaedam vitia sint omnino contraria. Qui autem habet vnum contrariorum, non habet etiam secundum praeparationem cordis reliquum contrariorum. Propterea quaedam sunt vitia penitus disparata. Qui autem habet vnum disparatorum, non propter hoc dignoscitur habere reliquum, etiam secundum cordis praeparationem. Ergo non omnis criminosus habet secundum praeparationem cordis omnia vitia. Item saepe videmus aliquos vno crimine irretitos, qui alia crimina in se & in aliis detestantur in tantum, quod ante se morti exponerent, quam crimina talia committerent quoquo modo. Ergo sunt etiam secundum praeparationem cordis omni crimine irretiti. Ista sunt pet quae patenter ostenditur, ut videtur, quod non omnis criminosus secundum praeparationem cordis omni crimine irretitur. Quae quamuis evidentia & insolubilia mihi appareant, peto tamen ut gratia exercitii, quomodo ad ipsa respondeatur, enarres. Magist. Responsiones ad ista melius intelliges, si tibi fuerit declaratum, quid est secundum opinionem contrariam, secundum praeparationem cordis aliquo vitio irretiri. Disc. Rogo quod declares. Magist. Dicunt quod irretiri aliquo vitio secundu praeparationem cordis non est aliud, quam habere aliquam dispositionem vel principium inclinans naturaliter ad vitium, & per nullam veram virtutem a tali vitio refrenari: sicut habere actus virtutum secundum praeparationem cordis non est aliud, quam habere dispositionem vel principium inclinans ad actus virtutum. Propter quod qui habet charitatem habet secundum praeparationem cordis omnes actus virtutum sibi possibiles. Intantum quod qui habet charitatem exit in omnem actum virtutis, quando tenetur. Quod si dimitteret quemcunque actum virtutis, quando tenetur, caritatem amittit. Sic homo iracundus habet secundum praeparationem cordis actus omnium vitiorum, quae dicuntur filii esse irae: quia habet dispositionem inclinantem ad actus omnium vitiorum illorum, licet per passionem aliquam parumper & pro tempore retrahatur. Disc. Intelligo, quid isti vocant secundum praeparationem cordis aliquo vitio irretiri. Ideo quomodo ad praedictas instantias respondetur expone. Magist. Ad praedictas instantias repellendas dicunt isti esse notandum, quod quemadmodum in speculabilibus quaedam sunt principia universalia, ex quibus conclusiones plurimae demonstrantur (propter quod dicitur, quod principia sunt minima in quantitate & maxima in virtute: quia ex uno principio cum aliis propositionibus assumptis immediate aut mediate conclusiones innumerabiles inferuntur) Et sicut in naturalibus quaedam sunt causae universales & quodammodo illimitatae, ex quibus diversi & innumeri causantur effectus, quandoque quidem ex illis solis quandoque, ex illis & aliis particularibus causis concurrentibus: ita ut eadem causa universalis vel propter diversitatem passivorum, vel propter diversitatem particularium agentium sit causa contrariorum. Ita in moralibus sunt quaedam dispositiones ad plures actus virtutum vel vitiorum naturaliter inclinantes. Quemadmodum charitas imperat & inclinat ad omnes actus virtutum omnium, & ira ad contumelias, rixas, contentiones; detractiones; percussiones; homicidia, & plures alios vitiosos actus inclinat. Et per hoc ad tuas instantias respondetur. Ad primam dicitur, quod quamuis quaedam vitia sint contraria, & ideo actus eorum simul esse non possunt: tamen habens unum vitium, habet unam malam dispositionem inclinantem ad actum vitii contrarii, nisi impediatur vel deficiat aliquid ad actum vitii contrarii requisitum. Verbi gratia: Prodigalitas & tenacitas sunt vitia contraria: & tunc tenax potest habere actum prodigalitatis secundum praeparationem cordis: quia in tenace propter ipsam tenacitatem est desiderium pecuniam acquirendi. Et ideo si tenax videt, quod per actum prodigalitatis potest multa acquirere, ex desiderio acquirendi plura, exit in actum prodigalitatis. Sic etiam videmus, quod vitia & virtutes contrariantur: & tamen saepe vitiosus habet actus virtutis secundum praeparationem cordis. Saepe enim mendax, ut sibi credatur, loquitur veritatem: & ambitiosus, ut magnos honores acquirat, paruos honores spernit & respuit. Disc. Clare video, quod licet aliqua vitia sint contraria: tamen habens unum vitium potest omnes actus vitii contrarii habere secundum praeparationem cordis. Imo etiam videtur secundum praedicta, quod qui habet unam virtutem, habet actum vitii contrarii secundum praeparationem cordis, sic habens vitium, habet actum virtutis, secundum praeparationem cordis. Magist. Respondetur quia non est simile de actibus vitiorum exterioribus, & de actibus virtutum interioribus. Nam multi sunt actus vitiorum exteriores, qui nullo modo bene fieri possunt. Sicut mentiri nullo modo potest fieri bene. Actus fornicandi & multi alii nequaquam bene fieri possunt. Nullus autem est actus virtutis exterior, quin male fieri possit. Nam orationes, eleemosynae, male fieri possunt, imo actus martyrii male suscipi potest. Propter quod criminosus habet actus virtutum exteriores, sed non interiores secundum praeparationem cordis. Unde hypocritae, ambitiosi, avari, superbi, & alii criminosi, nonnunquam mirabiles actus virtutum exteriores exercent. Unde de hypocritis dicit Christus Matth. 5, Exterminant enim facies suas, ut appareant hominibus ieiunantes. Et de ambitioso dicit Innocentius tertius: Humanitatem simulat & benignitatem mentitur; affabilem se exhibet, benignitatem ostendit. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod vitiosi possunt actus virtutis exteriores secundum praeparationem cordis exercere. Sed virtuosus actus vitiorum non habet secundum praeparationem cordis, quia illi a virtuoso nequaquam fieri possunt. Disc. Ista instantia non est ita fortis, sicut ante putaui: ideo dic, quomodo respondetur ad secundam. Magist. Respondetur ad secundam, quod nulli actus vitiorum sunt taliter disparati, quin quocunque crimine irretitus habeat aliquam dispositionem malam inclinantem naturaliter (nisi impediatur) saltem alia causa concurrente ad quemlibet actum vitiosum. Et ideo quilibet criminosus habet actus cuiuslibet vitii secundum praeparationem cordis. Disc. Quae est illa dispositio mala, quae inclinat ad omnem actum vitiosum? Magist. Respondetur quod tales dispositiones malae sunt plures, scilicet contemptus rationis, amor sui, auersio a Deo, & huiusmodi, quae a nullo vitio separantur, quemadmodum plures conditiones bonae omni virtuti sunt annexae. Propter quas quicunque habet unam veram virtutem, habet actum omnis virtutis sibi possibilis secundum praeparationem cordis. Qui enim est castus, quia vult viuere secundum rectam rationem, ipse etiam vult facere omnem actum virtutis cuiuslibet: quando recta ratio dictat quod actum virtutis facere debet. Et sine tali voluntate & dispositione inclinante ad omnem actum cuiuslibet virtutis secundum dictamen rectæ rationis non habet castitatem; quæ est virtus vera, quantumcunq; ab omni actu venereo impudico abstineat. Et ita qui habet veram castitatem, quæ est virtus, quantumcunq; non exerceat actum cuiuslibet virtutis, tamen secundum præparationem habet omnem actum cuiuslibet virtutis sibi possibilem.
units.tr: Student. I understand the argument by which it is proved that no criminal can firmly be presumed to be truthful. It seems to me to rest on this: every criminal, according to the disposition of his heart, is ensnared in every crime, just as a person who has charity, or any true virtue, has, according to the disposition of his heart, every act of virtue possible to him. Yet this seems so remarkable to me that no intellect should hold it, since some vices are wholly contrary to one another. Someone who has one of two contraries does not also have, according to the disposition of his heart, the other contrary. Therefore some vices are entirely disparate. And someone who has one of two disparate vices is not thereby known to have the other, even according to the disposition of the heart. So not every criminal has all vices according to the disposition of his heart. Again, we often see people ensnared in one crime who so detest other crimes, in themselves and in others, that they would expose themselves to death rather than commit such crimes in any way. So they too are ensnared in every crime according to the disposition of the heart. These are the points by which it seems plainly shown that not every criminal is ensnared in every crime according to the disposition of the heart. Although these points seem to me evident and insoluble, I ask you, as an exercise, to explain how one answers them. Master. You will understand the answers to these better if it has first been explained to you what the opposing view holds: to be ensnared in some vice according to the disposition of the heart. Student. Please explain it. Master. They say that to be ensnared in some vice according to the disposition of the heart is nothing other than to have some disposition or principle that naturally inclines one to vice, and is not restrained from that vice by any true virtue. Likewise, to have acts of virtue according to the disposition of the heart is nothing other than to have a disposition or principle inclining one to acts of virtue. For this reason, whoever has charity has, according to the disposition of the heart, all the acts of virtue possible to him, so much so that whoever has charity breaks out into every act of virtue when he is bound to it. If he were to omit any act of virtue when he is bound to it, he would lose his charity. So an angry man has, according to the disposition of the heart, the acts of all those vices which are called the children of wrath, because he has a disposition inclining him to the acts of all those vices, although by some passion he is held back for a little while and for the time being. Student. I understand what these people mean by being ensnared in some vice according to the disposition of the heart. So explain how one answers the instances mentioned. Master.
