To repel the instances mentioned, these people say that it must be noted that, just as in speculative matters there are certain universal principles from which very many conclusions are demonstrated (which is why it is said that principles are smallest in quantity and greatest in power, since countless conclusions follow from one principle together with other propositions assumed immediately or mediately), and just as in natural things there are certain universal causes, in some way unlimited, from which diverse and countless effects are caused, sometimes from those causes alone and sometimes from those together with other particular causes concurring, so that the same universal cause is the cause of contraries, either because of the diversity of the things acted upon or because of the diversity of the particular agents; so too in moral matters there are certain dispositions which naturally incline to many acts of virtue or of vice. Thus charity commands and inclines to all the acts of all the virtues, and anger inclines to insults, quarrels, contentions, detractions, blows, homicides, and many other vicious acts. And by this the instances are answered. To the first we say that although some vices are contrary, and so their acts cannot be present together, nevertheless someone who has one vice has one bad disposition inclining him to an act of the contrary vice, unless something required for an act of the contrary vice is hindered or lacking. For example, prodigality and tightfistedness are contrary vices, and so the tightfisted man can have an act of prodigality according to the disposition of the heart, because in the tightfisted man, from the very tightfistedness, there is a desire to acquire money. Therefore, if the tightfisted man sees that through an act of prodigality he can acquire much, he goes out into the act of prodigality from his desire to acquire more. In the same way we see that vices and virtues are contrary, and yet a vicious person often has acts of virtue according to the disposition of the heart. For the liar often speaks the truth so that he may be believed, and the ambitious man, in order to gain great honours, scorns and rejects small honours. Student. I clearly see that although some vices are contrary, someone who has one vice can have, according to the disposition of the heart, all the acts of the contrary vice. Indeed, it even seems from what has been said that whoever has one virtue has an act of the contrary vice according to the disposition of the heart, and so whoever has a vice has an act of virtue according to the disposition of the heart. Master. The answer is that the case of outward acts of vice is not like that of inward acts of virtue. For there are many outward acts of vice which can in no way be done well: to lie can in no way be done well; the acts of fornication and many others can by no means be done well. But there is no outward act of virtue which cannot be done badly: prayers and almsgiving can be done badly, and even the act of martyrdom can be undertaken badly. Hence the criminal has outward acts of virtue, but not inward ones, according to the disposition of the heart. So hypocrites, the ambitious, the greedy, the proud, and other criminals sometimes perform admirable outward acts of virtue. Of hypocrites Christ says in Matt. 5, For they disfigure their faces, that they may appear to men to be fasting. And of the ambitious man Innocent III says: He feigns humanity and lies about kindness; he presents himself as affable and shows kindness. From these words it is plain that vicious people can perform outward acts of virtue according to the disposition of the heart. But the virtuous person does not have acts of vice according to the disposition of the heart, because such acts can by no means be done by a virtuous person. Student. That instance is not as strong as I had thought before. So tell me how one answers the second. Master. To the second we answer that no acts of vice are so disparate that whoever is ensnared in any crime does not have some bad disposition naturally inclining him (unless it is hindered) to every vicious act, at least with some other cause concurring. And so every criminal has the acts of every vice according to the disposition of the heart. Student. What is that bad disposition which inclines to every vicious act? Master. The answer is that there are several such bad dispositions, namely contempt of reason, self-love, aversion from God, and the like, which are not separated from any vice, just as several good conditions are attached to every virtue. Because of these, whoever has one true virtue has, according to the disposition of the heart, the act of every virtue possible to him. For whoever is chaste, because he wishes to live according to right reason, also wishes to perform every act of any virtue whenever right reason dictates that he ought to perform that act of virtue. Without such a will and a disposition inclining him to every act of any virtue according to the dictate of right reason, he does not have chastity, which is a true virtue, however far he abstains from every impure venereal act. And so whoever has true chastity, which is a virtue, although he does not exercise the act of every virtue, nevertheless has, according to the disposition, every act of any virtue possible to him.

units.la: Discip. Dic quomodo respondetur ad instantiam tertiam, quam feci. Magist. Respondetur quod non ideo dicitur quis habere actum vitiosum secundum præparationem cordis, quia semper est paratus in omnem eventum actum huiusmodi exercere. Sic enim mendax non haberet secundum Papam rationem cordis actum mendacii. Nequaquam enim vult semper mentiri. Neque aliquis criminosus haberet secundum propriam rationem cordis actus vitii, quo noscitur irretiri. Neq; enim luxuriosus, neq; gulosus, neq; iracundus, neque invidus, neque superbus semper vult actus vitiosos exteriores elicere: & tamen quilibet vitiosus habet secundum præparationem cordis actus vitii, quibus noscitur irretiri. Dicitur ergo (sicut dictum est) quis habere actus vitiosos secundum præparationem cordis: quia habet dispositionem malam inclinantem naturaliter ad actus vitiosos exteriores: & per nullam veram virtutem ab actu huiusmodi cohibetur. Non tamen semper exercet huiusmodi actus; quia sæpe ab actibus exercendis huiusmodi prohibetur, vel propter absentiam causæ particularis, quæ ad actum talem requiritur: vel propter aliquam aliam causam prædominantem & impedientem talem actum. Verbi gratia: Luxuriosus quærens delectationem in actibus venereis, in nullo propter rationem rectam à libidine se refrenans, habet dispositionem malam ad omnes actus venereos inclinantem, s. desiderium delectandi in actu venereo qui tamen sæpe ab actu venereo restringitur, vel quia deficit sibi obiectu, vel concupiscit, vel quia timet confusionem. Propter timorem pœnæ vel confusionis aut inhonorationis vel damni temporalis multi abstinent à peccato luxuriæ, qui alias nunquam abstinerent. Sicut etiam multi mendaces sæpe minime mentiuntur, vel non indignantur contra aliquem, cui nocere desiderant, vel quia timent in mendacio deprehendi. Sicut etiam furesæpe non furantur, quia nihil inueniunt quod furentur, vel quia pœnam furti formidant. Omnes tamen prædicti habent actus huiusmodi vitiosos secundum præparationem cordis. Sic est de multis criminosis, qui antea moterentur quam crimina quædam committerent, nou ex amore virtutis, sed quia habent aliquas passiones, vel dispositiones malas vel non virtuosas ad actum contrarium inclinantes: utpote vel quia timent inhonorationem, vel confusionem, aut aliquid aliud, quod antequam illud incurrerent, mortem susciperent. Et tamen cum hoc stat, quod habeant huiusmodi actus secundum præparationem cordis modo prædicto, quemadmodum hypocritæ & occulte luxuriosi & mendaces, antequam deprehenderentur in actu luxuriæ vel mendacii, mortis se exponerent; & tamen habent huiusmodi actus secundum præparationem cordis, à quibus sæpe se strictissime restringunt, quia timor confusionis & verecundiæ in eis dominantur passioni & vitio ad actum luxuriæ vel etiam mendacii inclinanti. Discip. Ista opinio intellecta modo præscripto maiorem apparentiam habere videtur, quam antea arbitrabar. Ideo pro ipsa sic intellecta allegare coneris. Magist. Ista opinio multis rationibus munitur. Quarum prima est hæc. Omnis superbus habet secundum præparationem cordis omnes actus vitiosos. Sed omnis criminosus est superbus. Igitur omnis criminosus habet secundum præparationem cordis actus omnium vitiorum. Maior probatur sic. Qui habet initium omnis peccati, habet secundum præparationem cordis actum vitiosum. Habere autem secundum præparationem cordis actum vitiosum est habere dispositionem inclinantem ad omnia peccata, & per nihil virtuosum retrahitur à peccato. Igitur qui habet initium omnis peccati, habet omnia peccata secundum præparationem cordis. Omnis autem superbus habet initium omnis peccati, teste Sapiente, qui Eccles. 18. ait Initium omnis peccati est superbia. Igitur omnis superbus habet omnem actum peccati secundum præparationem cordis. Item, qui habet matrem omnium vitiorum habet omnem actum vitiosum secundum præparationem cordis: quia ex matre omnium vitiorum omnes actus vicios oriuntur vel oriri possunt. Omnis autem superbus habet matrem omnium vitiorum; quia secundum beatum Greg. superbia est mater omnium vitiorum. Igitur omnis superbus habet omnem actum vitiosum secundum præparationem cordis. Minor vero, quod omnis criminosus est superbus, probatur primo sic, ex precedentibus. Quia omnis criminosus habet initium omnis peccati. Quia sine initio neq; est medium, neq; finis, superbia autem est initium omnis peccati. Igitur omnis criminosus habet superbiam. Secundo probatur auctoritate Innocentii, qui loquens de superbia ait: Importabilis superbia omnibus odiosa, inter alia vitia tu semper es prima; tu semper es ultima. Nam omne peccatum te accedente committitur, te recedente dimittitur. Scriptum est enim: initium omnis peccati superbia primogenita mors. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod nullum peccatum absq; superbia reperitur; & ita omnis criminosus est superbus. Quod etiam tertio sic probatur: Omnis criminosus avertitur à Deo. Quicunq; autem à Deo avertitur, eo quod Deum contemnit & contra Deum erigitur, superbia elevatur. Igitur omnis criminosus est inter superbos merito computandus. Quod veritatem habet secundum quosdam, prout omnis aversio à Deo vocatur superbia, non prout solus appetitus propriæ excellentiæ superbia appellatur. Discip. Pauco quod ad probandum tam maiorem quam minorem huius rationis multas scires tam rationes quam auctoritates adducere. Sed nolo eos pro nunc audire: cupio tamen scire, an aliquis doctorum, qui sequelam habuit, & tamen à pluribus improbatur, sentiat quod omnis superbus secundum præparationem cordis omni crimine irretitur. Magist. Nonnullis apparet quod hoc est de intentione Thomæ de Aquino. Nam secunda secundæ q. 16. art. 2. 2. ait: Superbia potest considerari secundum redundantiam, quemadmodum & alia peccata. Et secundum hoc habet quandam generalitatem, quantum scilicet ex superbia oriri possunt omnia alia peccata duplici ratione. Uno modo per se, inquantum scilicet omnia alia peccata ordinantur ad finem superbiæ, quæ est propria excellentia, ad quam potest ordinari illud, quod quis inordinate appetit. Alio modo indirecte, & quasi per accidens, scilicet removendo prohibens inquantum scilicet per superbiam homo contemnit divinam legem, per quam prohibetur à peccando, secundum illud: Confregisti iugum, rupisti vincula, dixisti non serviam. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ex superbia possunt oriri omnia peccata. Ex quo sequitur quod omnis superbus secundum præparationem cordis omnibus criminibus irretitur; licet à quibusdam criminibus aliquando per aliquas passiones non per virtutes veras prohibeatur. Discip. Sufficiant ista pro assertione prædicta, & si aliæ tibi rationes occurrunt, de illis breviter te expedias. Magist. Secunda ratio ad probandum, quod omnis criminosus secundum præparationem cordis omni crimine irretitur, talis est. Non est maior ratio de uno crimine, quam de alio quo criminosus aliquo speciali crimine irretitus sit secundum præparationem cordis omni alio crimine involutus. Sed criminosus cupiditate, quæ est speciale peccatum implicitum omni alio peccato involvitur secundum præparationem cordis, teste Apostolo, qui ait, ut legitur Thim. 6. Radix omnium malorum est cupiditas. Ubi Glossa obiiciens ait: alibi dicit sic scriptura: quod superbia est initium omnis peccati. Hic vero dicitur, quod avaritia sive cupiditas radix est omnium malorum, quæ non videntur convenire. Et respondens ait: Sciendum nobis est utrumque vere dictum esse si peccatorum genera attendantur. Nullum enim genus peccati est, quod aliquando non proveniat ex cupiditate. Et est vice aliquis homo qui ex cupiditate fit superbus, & aliquis est qui ex superbia fit cupidus. Est enim aliquis homo qui non esset amator pecuniæ, nisi per hoc putaret se excellentiorem esse. Et est qui non amaret excellentiam, nisi putaret per hoc maiores divitias habere. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnia peccata ex cupiditate seu avaritia oriri possunt. Quare omnis cupidus seu avarus secundum præparationem cordis est omni crimine irretitus. Hoc est dictum, nullum crimen est quod avarus seu cupidus propter habendam pecuniam non committeret, si nulla eum passio timoris seu erubescentiæ aut aliqua alia nequaquam rationis iudicio regulata eum à committendo crimine prohiberet, ita quod per nullam veram virtutem à quocunque committendo crimine retrahitur. Tertia ratio est hæc. Homo iracundus secundum præparationem cordis est omni crimine irretitus. Igitur per rationem consimilem omnis criminosus secundum præparationem cordis est omni crimine irretitus. Antecedens probatur: quia qui est in ianua omnium vitiorum omnibus criminibus secundum præparationem cordis involvitur. Homo autem iracundus est in ianua omnium vitiorum, teste Glossa super illo verbo Proverb. 29. Vir iracundus provocat rixas. Ubi ait: Ianua omnium vitiorum iracundia, quæ clausa virtutibus intrinsecus dabitur quies, quæ aperta ad omne facinus armabitur animus. Igitur homo iracundus in ianua vitiorum existens ad omnia genera peccatorum armatur. Et per consequens secundum præparationem cordis omni crimine irretitur. Discip. Mirum est quod dicit Glossa, scilicet quod clausa iracundia intrinsecus virtutibus dabitur quies, cum multos videamus mansuetos, qui tamen multis aliis criminibus involvuntur. Magist. Respondetur, quod nunquam iracundia, quæ est ianua omnium vitiorum, vere est clausa, nisi per mansuetudinem, quæ est vera virtus, quæ nullum vitium secum patitur, quia nullus est vere mansuetus, nisi mansuetudinem propter Deum vel propter rationem rectam conservet. Qui autem est mansuetus propter Deum, omni vitio carnali caret: & secundus similiter, scil. qui est mansuetus, ut rationi rectæ se conformet, nulli vitio subiacet criminali. Multi autem videntur mansueti, qui ab omni iracundia exteriori se cohibent, ut aliquod malum aut periculum euitent, vel ut honorem aut aliquod bonum utile vel delectabile consequantur. Sermones tales non sunt mansueti mansuetudine, quæ est virtus vera. Quemadmodum multi actum fortitudinis exteriorem perficiunt, vel quia magnitudinem periculi non perpendunt, vel propter aliquius passionis impulsum, vel propter aliquod temporale commodum acquirendum aut incommodum euitandum, qui in rei veritate fortitudine, quæ est virtus, carent, licet fortes plerumque putentur. Discipul. Per istam rationem de nullo potest sciri, quod habeat virtutem, & quod non sit criminosus. Itaque si nulli criminoso est credendum, nulli hominum certa fides est adhibenda. Magist. Dicitur quod absque operatione miraculi facti in testimonium sanctitatis alicuius de nullo potest per certitudinem sciri, quod non sit criminosus; quia tamen ea, quæ fieri possunt bene & male in meliorem partem interpretari debemus, extr. de reiu. eslote: Ideo multi sunt virtuosi censendi, quia omnes, qui nullum actum faciunt, qui non possit bono animo fieri, & quo animo illos faciant ignoramus, illos virtuosos censere debemus. Et ideo tales sunt ad testimonium admittendi. Discip. Compleas alias rationes. Magist. Quarta ratio pro prædicta assertione est hæc. Ille qui in minori crimine involutus est, eo ipso secundum præparationem cordis maiori crimine irretitur. Igitur & omnibus criminibus secundum cordis præparationem noscitur irretitus: quia omnia crimina vel sunt maiora, vel sunt minora, vel sunt æqualia. Si igitur minori crimine inuoluitur, criminibus maioribus secundum præparationem cordis noscitur involutus: multo magis secundum præparationem cordis minoribus & æqualibus esse involutus est putandus: & ita secundum præparationem cordis omnibus criminibus irretitur, secundum minori crimine irretitur eoipso secundum præparationem cordis maiori crimine irretitur, ipsa veritate testante, quæ Luc. 18. ait: Qui in modico iniquus est, & in maiori iniquus est. Quæ verba secundum actum nequaquam possunt intelligi: quia multi crimina minora committunt, qui tamen non faciunt actu maiora. Ergo illa verba quantum ad præparationem parationem cordis debent intelligi. Vt iste sit sensus: Quii in modico iniquus est, secundum praeparationem cordis etiam in maiori iniquus est: hoc est, per nullam veram virtutem a maiori crimine coercetur. Et quicunq; minori crimine irretitur, si possit & tentatus fuerit & non timeat confundi, nec aliquod vtile delectabile amittere, a crimine maximo & enormissimo se nullatenus continebit. Quia si criminosus a crimine quocunque de quo tentatur se cohibet propter aliquem finem: vel aliquod motiuum se cohibet ab eodem, & non propter finem virtutis, nec propter motiuum dictatum ratione recta. Ergo propter aliquem alium finem vel aliud motiuum se cohibet. Illo ergo fine vel motiuo remoto se minime cohibebit. Et ita criminosus secundum praeparationem cordis omni crimine alio irretitur: licet quandoque ab actu pro tempore refrenetur. Quia tamen non refrenatur propter Deum, nec propter bonum virtutis siue propter rationem rectam, siue aliunde, dicitur habere talem actum secundum praeparationem cordis. Quemadmodum (sicut dictum est prius) luxuriosus habet actum luxuriae secundum praeparationem cordis, licet interdum ex aliqua alia causa quam ex ratione recta ab actu luxuriae se refrenet. Quinta ratio est haec: Qui habet radicem omnium criminum, habet omnia crimina secundum praeparationem cordis. Omnis criminosus habet radicem omnium criminum, quia amorem sui, non Dei, qui est radix omnium criminum. Quod expresse insinuat Beatus Paulus 2. Thim. 3. dicens: Erunt homines seipsos amantes cupidi, elati, superbi, blasphemi, parentibus non obedientes, ingrati, scelesti, sine affectione, sine pace, criminatores, incontinentes, immites sine benignitate, proditores, protervi, timidi, caeci, voluptatum amatores magis quam Dei. Vbi Gloss. Ex eo enim quod seipsos & non Deum amant, ex qua radice haec quae sequuntur mala oriuntur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnia mala, quae Apostolus enumerat, ex amore sui oriuntur. Cum ergo omnia peccata spiritualia & corporalia valeant ad illam reduci; sequitur quod ex amore sui omnia peccata oriri possunt. Ergo amans seipsum, non Deum, habet omnia peccata secundum praeparationem cordis, licet aliquando ab aliquibus non propter bonum virtutis se abstineat. Sexta ratio est haec: Qui est reus omnium criminum, habet omnia crimina secundum praeparationem cordis vel secundum actum. Sed omnis criminosus est reus omnium criminum, teste Beato Iacobo, qui ait: qui offenderit etiam in vno, factus est omnium reus. Ergo omnis criminosus habet omnia crimina secundum actum. Ergo habet omnia crimina secundum cordis praeparationem. Discip. Cessa allegare pro ista assertione, quae tenet quod omnis criminosus est secundum praeparationem cordis omni actu criminis irretitus. Ex quo sequitur primum, quod assumptum est circa rationem, quae probatur in principio huius capituli, quod non ex constitutione sola humana, sed ex ratione recta & iure Diuino accipitur, quod nulli criminoso in quocunq; negotio est credendum. Quia ex illa assertione sequitur, quod de nullo criminoso est firmiter praesumendum, quod sit verax, & quod nolit mentiri. Ideo nunc pro secundum istam opinionem, scilicet quod illi non est credendum, de quo non est firmiter praesumendum, quod sit verax & quod nolit mentiri. Magist. Hoc probatur sic: nulli nisi qui reputatur verax est credendum. Illi ergo de quo non est firmiter praesumendum, quod sit verax, non est credendum.
units.tr: Discip. Tell me how you answer the third objection that I raised. Magist. The answer is that a person is not said to have a sinful act in the disposition of the heart merely because he is always ready to perform such an act in any circumstance. On that reasoning, a liar would not, according to the Papist, have the act of lying in the disposition of his heart, for he by no means wishes always to lie. Nor would a criminal have in his heart the acts of the sin by which he is known to be ensnared. A man who is lustful, gluttonous, angry, envious or proud does not always want to perform the outward sinful acts, and yet every sinner has in the disposition of his heart the sins by which he is known to be ensnared. So it is said (as has been said) that a person has sinful acts in the disposition of his heart because he has a bad disposition which naturally inclines him to outward sinful acts, and no true virtue restrains him from such acts. Yet he does not always perform such acts, because he is often kept from performing them, either by the absence of some particular cause required for such an act, or by some other cause that prevails over and hinders such an act. For example, a lustful man who seeks pleasure in sexual acts, and who in no way restrains himself from lust by right reason, has a bad disposition which inclines him to all sexual acts, namely a desire to take pleasure in the sexual act. Yet he is often restrained from the sexual act, either because the object is lacking to him, or because he is satiated, or because he fears disgrace. Through fear of punishment, or of shame, dishonour or temporal loss, many abstain from the sin of lust who would otherwise never abstain. Likewise many liars often do not lie at all, or do not become angry with someone whom they desire to harm, either because they fear to be caught in a lie. Thieves, too, often do not steal because they find nothing to steal, or because they dread the punishment for theft. Yet all those mentioned have such sinful acts in the disposition of their hearts. It is the same with many criminals, who would sooner die than commit certain crimes, not out of love of virtue, but because they have some passions or bad or non-virtuous dispositions inclining them to the contrary act: for instance, because they fear dishonour, or shame, or something else, for which they would accept death before incurring it. And yet it stands that they have such acts in the disposition of the heart in the manner described, just as hypocrites, secret lechers and liars would expose themselves to death before being caught in an act of lust or lying; and yet they have such acts in the disposition of the heart, from which they often restrain themselves most strictly, because the fear of shame and modesty prevails over the passion and vice that inclines them to the act of lust or even of lying. Discip. This opinion, understood in the way prescribed, seems to have more plausibility than I previously thought. So try to argue for it as thus understood. Magist. This opinion is supported by many arguments. The first of these is this. Everyone proud has in the disposition of his heart all sinful acts. But every criminal is proud. Therefore every criminal has in the disposition of his heart the acts of all sins. The major premise is proved thus. Whoever has the beginning of every sin has in the disposition of his heart a sinful act. But to have a sinful act in the disposition of the heart is to have a disposition inclining one to all sins, and to be held back from sin by nothing virtuous. Therefore whoever has the beginning of every sin has all sins in the disposition of his heart. But every proud man has the beginning of every sin, as the wise man attests, who says in Ecclesiasticus 18: "The beginning of all sin is pride." Therefore every proud man has every sinful act in the disposition of his heart. Likewise, whoever has the mother of all vices has every sinful act in the disposition of his heart, because from the mother of all vices all sinful acts arise, or can arise. But every proud man has the mother of all vices, because according to Blessed Gregory pride is the mother of all vices. Therefore every proud man has every sinful act in the disposition of his heart. As for the minor premise, that every criminal is proud, it is proved first in this way, from what has gone before. Every criminal has the beginning of every sin. Since without a beginning there is neither middle nor end, and pride is the beginning of every sin, therefore every criminal has pride. Secondly, it is proved by the authority of Innocent, who, speaking of pride, says: "Unbearable pride, hateful to all, among the other vices you are always first; you are always last. For every sin is committed with you present, and is put away when you withdraw. For it is written: 'The beginning of all sin is pride, the firstborn of death.'" From these words it is gathered that no sin is found without pride, and so every criminal is proud. This is also proved thirdly in this way: every criminal turns away from God. But whoever turns away from God, because he despises God and rises up against God, is lifted up in pride. Therefore every criminal rightly ranks among the proud. This holds true according to some, inasmuch as every turning away from God is called pride, not inasmuch as only the desire for one's own excellence is called pride. Discip. You could bring forward many reasons and authorities for proving both the major and the minor premise of this argument. But for now I do not want to hear them. I would still like to know whether any of the teachers who had a following, yet is disapproved by many, holds that every proud man is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart. Magist. To some it seems that this is the intention of Thomas Aquinas. For in the second part of the second part, question 162, article 2, he says: "Pride can be considered in terms of its overflow, just as other sins can. And in this sense it has a certain generality, namely insofar as all other sins can arise from pride in two ways. In one way directly, namely insofar as all other sins are ordered to the end of pride, which is one's own excellence, to which anything that a man inordinately desires can be ordered. In another way indirectly and as it were by accident, namely by removing an obstacle, insofar as through pride a man despises the divine law, by which he is restrained from sinning, according to the words: 'You have broken the yoke, you have burst the bonds, you said: I will not serve.'" From these words it is gathered that all sins can arise from pride. From this it follows that every proud man is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart, although from certain crimes he is sometimes restrained by some passions, not by true virtues. Discip. These things are enough to support the aforesaid assertion. And if other arguments occur to you, dispatch them briefly. Magist. The second argument for proving that every criminal is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart is this. There is no greater reason for one crime than for another, so that a criminal ensnared in some particular crime is involved in every other crime in the disposition of his heart. But a criminal, through greed, which is a special sin entangled with every other sin, is involved in every other sin in the disposition of his heart, as the Apostle attests, who says, as is read in 1 Timothy 6: "The root of all evils is the love of money." Here the Gloss, raising an objection, says: "Scripture says elsewhere that pride is the beginning of every sin. But here it is said that avarice or greed is the root of all evils, which do not seem to agree." And answering, it says: "We must recognise that both are truly said, if the kinds of sin are considered. For there is no kind of sin that does not sometimes arise from greed. And it is sometimes the case that a man becomes proud out of greed, and some become greedy out of pride. For there is a man who would not love money unless he thought that by it he was more excellent. And there is one who would not love excellence unless he thought that by it he had greater riches." From these words it is gathered that all sins can arise from greed or avarice. Therefore every greedy or avaricious man is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart. That is to say, there is no crime which the avaricious or greedy man would not commit for the sake of getting money, if no passion of fear or shame, or some other thing not regulated by the judgement of reason, restrained him from committing the crime; so that he is held back from committing any crime by no true virtue. The third argument is this. A wrathful man is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart. Therefore, by similar reasoning, every criminal is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart. The antecedent is proved thus: whoever stands at the door of all vices is involved in every crime in the disposition of his heart. But a wrathful man stands at the door of all vices, as the Gloss attests on the verse of Proverbs 29: "A wrathful man stirs up strife." There it says: "Anger is the door of all vices; when it is shut, rest will be given to the virtues within; when it is open, the mind will be armed for every wickedness." Therefore a wrathful man, standing at the door of vices, is armed for all kinds of sin. And consequently he is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart. Discip. It is strange what the Gloss says, namely that when anger is shut, rest is given to the virtues within, since we see many meek men who are nonetheless involved in many other crimes. Magist. The answer is that anger, which is the door of all vices, is never truly shut except by meekness, which is a true virtue and suffers no vice along with it, since no one is truly meek unless he keeps his meekness for God's sake or for the sake of right reason. And whoever is meek for God's sake is free from every carnal vice; and likewise the one who is meek so as to conform himself to right reason is subject to no criminal vice. But many appear meek who restrain themselves from all outward anger in order to avoid some evil or danger, or to obtain honour or some useful or pleasant good. Such people are not meek with the meekness that is a true virtue. Just as many perform the outward act of courage either because they do not weigh the greatness of the danger, or because of the impulse of some passion, or to gain some temporal advantage or avoid some disadvantage; these lack in very truth the courage that is a virtue, although they are commonly thought brave. Discipul. By this reasoning, one cannot know of anyone that he has virtue and is not a criminal. So if no criminal is to be believed, no certain trust is to be placed in any man. Magist. It is said that without a miracle performed as a testimony to someone's holiness, one cannot know with certainty of anyone that he is not a criminal. Yet because we ought to interpret for the better those things that can be done well or badly, extr. de reiu. eslote: therefore many are to be judged virtuous: since we ought to judge virtuous all who do no act which cannot be done with a good mind, and whose mind in doing such acts we do not know. And therefore such people are to be admitted as witnesses. Discip. Complete the other arguments. Magist. The fourth argument for the aforesaid assertion is this. He who is involved in a lesser crime is by that very fact ensnared in a greater crime in the disposition of his heart. Therefore he is also known to be ensnared in all crimes in the disposition of his heart, since all crimes are either greater, or lesser, or equal. If, then, he is involved in a lesser crime, he is known to be involved in greater crimes in the disposition of his heart; much more, then, is he to be thought involved in lesser and equal crimes in the disposition of his heart; and thus he is ensnared in every crime in the disposition of his heart. He who is ensnared in a lesser crime is by that very fact ensnared in a greater crime in the disposition of the heart, the truth itself bearing witness, which says in Luke 18: "He who is unjust in the least is also unjust in the greater." These words cannot be understood with regard to the act, because many commit lesser crimes who yet do not actually commit greater ones. Therefore those words must be understood with regard to the disposition of the heart. The sense is this: he who is unjust in the least is also, in the disposition of his heart, unjust in the greater; that is, he is restrained from the greater crime by no true virtue. And whoever is ensnared in a lesser crime, if he is able, and is tempted, and does not fear disgrace, and would lose no useful or pleasant thing, will by no means restrain himself from the greatest and most heinous crime. For if a criminal restrains himself from whatever crime he is tempted to, he does so for some end, or from some motive, and not for the end of virtue, nor for a motive dictated by right reason. Therefore he restrains himself for some other end or motive. If that end or motive is removed, he will by no means restrain himself. And so the criminal is ensnared in every other crime in the disposition of his heart, although at times he is restrained from the act for the time being. Yet because he is not restrained for God's sake, nor for the good of virtue, whether that be right reason or something else, he is said to have such an act in the disposition of his heart. Just as (as was said before) a lustful man has the act of lust in the disposition of his heart, although at times for some cause other than right reason he restrains himself from the act of lust. The fifth argument is this. Whoever has the root of all crimes has all crimes in the disposition of his heart. Every criminal has the root of all crimes, namely love of himself, not of God, which is the root of all crimes. This the Blessed Paul expressly hints at in 2 Timothy 3, saying: "Men will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without goodness, traitors, headstrong, fearful, blind, lovers of pleasures rather than of God." Here the Gloss says: "For from the fact that they love themselves and not God, from that root these evils which follow arise." From these words it is gathered that all the evils which the Apostle lists arise from self-love. Since therefore all spiritual and bodily sins can be reduced to it, it follows that all sins can arise from love of oneself. Therefore one who loves himself, not God, has all sins in the disposition of his heart, although at times he abstains from some of them not for the good of virtue. The sixth argument is this. Whoever is guilty of all crimes has all crimes in the disposition of his heart or in act. But every criminal is guilty of all crimes, as the Blessed James attests, who says: "Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all." Therefore every criminal has all crimes in act. Therefore he has all crimes in the disposition of his heart. Discip. Stop arguing for this assertion, which holds that every criminal is ensnared in every act of crime in the disposition of his heart. From it there follows first what was assumed concerning the reasoning proved at the beginning of this chapter: that it is not taken from human constitution alone, but from right reason and divine law, that no criminal is to be believed in any business whatever. For from that assertion it follows that no criminal is to be firmly presumed to be truthful, and to be unwilling to lie. So now, according to this opinion, namely that a person is not to be believed of whom it cannot firmly be presumed that he is truthful and unwilling to lie. Magist. This is proved thus: no one is to be believed except one who is reckoned truthful. Therefore one of whom it cannot firmly be presumed that he is truthful is not to be believed.

units.la: CAP. LXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 79.

units.la: In quo probatur secunda pars, scilicet maioris primae rationis huius capituli in principio posita, scilicet an hoc accipiatur ex iure Diuino, seu humano, quod nulli criminoso sit credendum. Et ponuntur duae opiniones contrariae praecedentibus capitulo 78. positis.
units.tr: In which the second part is proved, namely the second part of the first major premise of this chapter, set out at the beginning: whether it is received from divine law or from human law that no criminal is to be believed. And two opinions contrary to those set out in the preceding chapter 78 are put forward.

units.la: Discipulus. Ista assertio euidens mihi videtur. Ideo pertractata assertione dicente, quod ex ratione recta & iure Diuino accipitur, quod nulli criminoso est credendum, dissere opinionem contrariam. Magist. Circa opinionem contrariam sunt duo modi ponendi. Vnus modus ponendi est, quod ex ratione recta & iure Diuino absq; omni constitutione humana accipitur, quod aliquibus criminosis in nullo negotio est credendum. Ex constitutione autem humana sola habetur, quod quibusdam criminosis non est credendum. Discip. Opinionem istam expone. Magist. Opinio ista ponit, quod ex recta ratione accipitur absq; omni constitutione humana, quod illis criminosis, qui inuoluuntur criminibus, quae ad falsitatem vel mendacium, quod committitur factis vel verbis, pertinent quoquomodo, non est credendum in quocunq; negotio. Huiusmodi sunt periuri, mendaces, hypocritae, simulatores, ficti, qui libellos famosos componunt, retinent, diuulgant, & qui falsum testimonium dixerunt, vel ad dandum falsum testimonium alios induxerunt, & qui sic aliis iunt subiecti, vt probabile sit quod de facili possunt induci vt falsum testimonium dicant, & omnes qui cupiunt placere hominibus, quales sunt ambitiosi, dolosi, bilingues, proditores, criminatores, diffamatores, falsorum criminum impositores, detractores, libenter audientes susurratores, murmuratores, adulteri, conspiratores, contentiosi & contumeliosi, suspitiosi, temere iudicantes, interpretantes in peiorem partem, quae bono animo fieri possunt, qui secreta reuelant, & consimiles. Isti sunt ab omni testimonio repellendi. Et quaecunq; constitutio humana constitueret, quod aliqui istorum essent ad testimonium admittendi, esset constitutio iniqua, nec esset seruanda. Alii criminosi a ferendo testimonio per rationem rectam vel per ius diuinum nullatenus prohibentur: licet prohibeantur per constitutionem humanam. Tales sunt gulosi & luxuriosi & alii pauci. Ista opinio fundatur in hoc, quod propter illa crimina, quae veritati repugnant, & non propter alia, est q per ius naturale & diuinum à testimonio repellendus. Sed sola crimina quae ad mendacium (quod verbis vel factis committitur) spectant, veritati repugnant. Ergo de iure naturae & Diuino propter solam huiusmodi crimina est quis à testimonio repellendus. Discip. Ob prolixitatem vitandam dimitto opinionem istam, & transeo ad aliam. Mag. Alia opinio est, quod propter nullum crimen ex iure naturae, vel Diuino est quis à testimonio repellendus. Sed quod aliquis criminosus repellitur, est solummodo ex iure humano. Discip. Pro ista assertione nitere allegare. Magist. Pro ista assertione arguitur. Nihil à principe aut à praelato rite statui potest, quod iuri naturali vel Diuino repugnat. Sed in legibus ciuilibus & canonicis inuenitur, quod in aliquo casu quicunque criminosi etiam & haeretici & alii ad accusandum & testificandum debent admitti. Ergo non est contra ius naturale nec contra Diuinum, quod criminosi ad accusationem & testimonium admittantur. Maior videtur certa. Minor per plura iura probatur. Nam Papa ius dedit, vt habetur extra, de symonia c. tanta, ait: Tanta est labes huius criminis (scilicet symoniae) quod etiam serui aduersus Dominum & quilibet criminosi ad accusationem admittantur. Et infra: quem quilibet (scilicet symoniacum) vt ab ordine male accepto remoueatur accusare potest, vel etiam meretrix. Ex quibus colligitur, quod interdum criminosi debent ad accusandum admitti. Item, Iulius Papa, vt habetur 15. q. 3. c. nemini: Nemini praeterquam de crimine maiestatis laesa confesso super alienum crimen credi oportet. Vbi dicit Glos. & praeterquam in crimine symonia. Et infra: Item, falsarius auditur contra socium. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod nonnunquam criminosis est credendum. Et per consequens sunt ad testimonium admittendi: quia illi recipiendi sunt, quibus est credendum. Item, 2. q. 7. si haereticus, sic legitur: Si haereticus contra haereticum litiget, liceat cuicunque eorum haereticum testem adducere. Si autem orthodoxus litiget contra haereticum, pro orthodoxo quidem haeretici valeat testimonium, contra orthodoxum autem solius orthodoxi testimonium valeat. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod testimonium haeretici non solum valet pro haeretico contra haereticum: imo etiam pro orthodoxo valet. Ergo interdum admittendum est testimonium criminosi. Item, socii criminis quandoque ad testimonium admittuntur, extra, de testibus, quoniam aliqua. & 6. q. 1. c. quaero, scilicet si quis cum militibus, & extra de testi. cogendi. c. vlt. dicitur. Quod sicut notat Glos. extra, de actionibus. c. cum, quod in exceptis criminibus, scilicet in crimine laesae maiestatis, symonia & haeresis, viles personae recipiantur. Quod etiam extra, de symonia. t. litet haeresis. & c. per tuas, innuitur, vt videtur. Et ita habetur, quod non est ex iure naturali vel Diuino quod criminosis fides non debet adhiberi.
units.tr: Disciple. This assertion seems self-evident to me. Therefore, having examined the assertion which says that it is received from right reason and divine law that no criminal is to be believed, set out the opposing opinion. Master. There are two ways of putting the opposing opinion. The first way is that it is received from right reason and divine law, apart from any human enactment, that criminals are not to be believed in any matter whatever; while from human enactment alone it is held that certain criminals are not to be believed. Disciple. Explain this opinion. Master. This opinion holds that it is received from right reason, apart from any human enactment, that those criminals who are involved in crimes which in any way pertain to falsehood or lying, committed by deeds or words, are not to be believed in any matter whatever. Such are perjurers, liars, hypocrites, dissemblers, deceivers, those who compose, keep or spread defamatory pamphlets, and those who have given false testimony or induced others to give it, and those who are so subject to others that it is probable they can easily be induced to give false testimony; and all who seek to please men, such as the ambitious, the crafty, the double-tongued, traitors, accusers, slanderers, fabricators of false charges, detractors, those who gladly listen to whisperers, murmurers, adulterers, conspirators, the quarrelsome and abusive, the suspicious, those who judge rashly and interpret in the worse part things that can be done in good faith, those who reveal secrets, and the like. These are to be repelled from every testimony. And any human enactment which established that any of these should be admitted to testify would be an unjust enactment and not to be observed. Other criminals are in no way forbidden by right reason or by divine law to bear witness, although they are forbidden by human enactment. Such are the gluttonous, the lustful, and a few others. This opinion rests on the ground that a person is to be repelled from testimony by natural and divine law on account of those crimes which are opposed to truth, and not on account of others. But only those crimes which pertain to lying (which is committed by words or deeds) are opposed to truth. Therefore by natural and divine law a person is to be repelled from testimony on account of such crimes alone. Disciple. For the sake of brevity I drop this opinion and pass to the other. Master. The other opinion is that by no crime is a person to be repelled from testimony by natural or divine law; rather, that a criminal is repelled only by human law. Disciple. Make some effort to allege arguments for this assertion. Master. The argument for this assertion runs as follows. Nothing can be rightly enacted by a prince or a prelate which is contrary to natural or divine law. But in the civil and canon laws it is found that in certain cases all criminals, even heretics and others, ought to be admitted to accuse and to testify. Therefore it is not contrary to natural law nor to divine law that criminals be admitted to accusation and testimony. The major premise seems certain. The minor is proved by several laws. For the Pope gave a law, as is found in the Extra, On Simony, chapter Tanta, which says: "So great is the stain of this crime (namely simony) that even slaves against their master and any criminals are admitted to accusation." And below: "whom anyone (namely a simoniac) may accuse so that he be removed from an order badly received, even a prostitute." From these it is gathered that at times criminals ought to be admitted to accuse. Likewise Pope Julius, as is found in 15 q. 3 c. Nemini: "To no one, except one who has confessed to the crime of treason, must credit be given when he accuses another of a crime." Where the Gloss says: "and except in the crime of simony." And below: "Likewise, a forger is heard against an accomplice." From these words it is made clear that sometimes credit is to be given to criminals. And consequently they are to be admitted to testify, since those are to be received to whom credit is given. Likewise, 2 q. 7 Si haereticus, thus it is read: "If a heretic goes to law against a heretic, it is permitted to either of them to bring forward a heretic as witness. But if an orthodox man goes to law against a heretic, the testimony of a heretic is valid for the orthodox man, but against the orthodox man only the testimony of an orthodox man is valid." From these words it is held that the testimony of a heretic is valid not only for a heretic against a heretic, but even for an orthodox man. Therefore sometimes the testimony of a criminal must be admitted. Likewise, accomplices in crime are at times admitted to testify, Extra On Witnesses, Quoniam aliqua, and 6 q. 1 c. Quaero, namely if anyone (is) with soldiers, and Extra On Compelling Witnesses c. last, it is said; which, as the Gloss notes Extra On Actions c. Cum, that "in the excepted crimes, namely the crime of treason, simony and heresy, base persons are received." Which also seems to be hinted at in Extra On Simony, title Litet haeresis, and c. Per tuas. And so it is held that it is not by natural or divine law that faith should not be given to criminals.

units.la: Discip. Quamuis ista appareant mihi consona veritati: peto tamen indices, quomodo ad ista secundum opinionem in contrariam respondetur. Magist. Ad intelligentiam praedictorum aliquae dicuntur distinctiones esse notandae. Quarum prima est, quod aliqui admittuntur ad accusandum vel denunciandum, aut ad inquisitionem aliquam prosequendum: aliqui autem tantum audiuntur ad testificandum. Secunda distinctio est, quod criminosi aut emendati sunt a crimine, aut non sunt emendati de crimine. Tertia est, quod ille, contra quem debet aliquis audiri, aut est bonae famae, aut est apud viros probos & honestos grauiter diffamatus. Quarta est, quod aliquis auditur vel de rigore iuris, vel de temperantia aequitatis. Per praedictas distinctiones respondetur ad rationes pro ista secunda opinione adductas. Ad primam enim dicitur, quod propter immanitatem quorundam criminum, scilicet haeresis, laesae maiestatis, symoniae, & etiam aliorum, ex quibus periculum imminet, congrue criminosi etiam de crimine minime emendati, quantum est de iure naturali & Diuino, possunt audiri, praecipue contra grauiter infamatum ad accusandum & denunciandum & etiam inquisitionem prosequendum, sed non ad testimonium. Et huius ratio assignatur: quia qui ad accusandum admittitur, non ideo admittitur, vt sibi credatur, sed vt per informationem ipsius ad veritatem perueniatur. Saepe enim per informationes malorum veritatem inuenire contingit. Et ideo nonnunquam sunt criminosi propter bonum commune & periculum & malum bonis communis vitandum ad accusandum admittendi. Sed aliter dicitur de teste: quia semper fides adhibetur testi admisso. Criminoso autem nunquam est credendum. Et ideo criminosus admitti non debet. Et huic concordare videtur Glos. 6. q. 1. c. quare, quae ait: Tota vis negotii pendet in testimonio, sed non in accusatione: quia scilicet testi adhibetur fides. Fides autem accusatori minime adhibetur. Discip. Si accusatori fides nullatenus adhibetur, quare non indifferenter criminosus accusator admittitur contra quemcunque de crimine qualicunque? Magist. Ideo non est criminosus ad accusandum admittendus, quia omnis accusatus multipliciter fatigatur ac grauatur ac impeditur, dum oportet ipsum coram iudice comparere, & accusanti respondere. Non debet autem quis absque causa antequam de crimine conuincatur propter verbum illius, cui non est credendum, taliter fatigari. Et ideo criminosus non est indifferenter ad accusandum admittendus. Discip. Per istam responsionem probaretur, quod in nullo casu criminosus erit admittendus, quia nunquam debet aliquis puniri vel aliqualiter fatigari propter verbum illius, cui non est credendum. Imo per istam rationem videtur posse probari, quod nullus esset ad accusandum admittendus: quia nullus puniri debet aut grauari antequam constet ipsum esse dignum poena. Sed omnis accusatus punitur & grauatur multis laboribus eundo ad iudicem, respondendo accusanti. Ergo secundum praedicta (cum fides accusanti non adhibeatur) non est propter verbum ipsius accusatus quoquo modo vexandus. Et ideo nullus esset ad accusandum admittendus. Magist. Ad ista respondetur, quod saepe ex iusta causa & ratione recta: imo ex iure naturae & pro statu naturae corruptae aliqui fatigantur & vexantur absque omni culpa. Quia aliter respublica & bonum commune conseruari non posset. Propter quod rationabile est, quod interdum propter verbum illius, cui non est credendum, fatigetur aliquis, vt per talem modum praecaueatur periculo comcommunis boni. Propter hoc dicitur, quod rationabile est, quod propter solum verbum ipsius, cui non est credendum, aliquis, qui nescitur esse innocens, fatigetur. Et ille cui non est credendum, ad accusandum debet admitti. Quia aliter pax communis conseruari non posset. Discip. Istud ultimum videtur prioribus repugnare. Nam prius dictum est, quod accusantibus minime fides adhibetur. Hic autem dicitur, quod ille cui credendum non est, ad accusandum debet admitti. Ergo aliquando accusatoribus est credendum. Magist. Respondetur, quod multi sunt fide digni, in quibus est credendum: quibus tamen non debet fides in omni casu, maxime in praeiudicium alterius adhiberi. Nullus enim ad testimonium est admittendus, nisi fuerit fide dignus. Et tamen si vnus solus quantumcunq; fuerit fide dignus contra aliquem testificetur, non sibi credendum est in praeiudicium alterius, vt propter testimonium eius reus culpabilis reputetur. Sicut quantumcunq; accusator fuerit fide dignus, non est sibi credendum, vt propter accusationem ipsius accusatus culpabilis iudicetur. Discip. Dic quomodo ad secundam instantiam respondetur. Magist. Respondetur, quod Iulius Papa in illo decreto non accipit stricte tredi, sed communiter pro audiri. Quia etiam in crimine laesae maiestatis, quando accusatur socius a socio, non est accusanti credendum, vt propter accusationem tale debeat pro convicto haberi: cum tamen etiam quantumcunq; accusans esset bonae famae & immunis a crimine laesae maiestatis auditur: non vt sibi credatur, sed vt vias ostendat, per quas posset veritas inveniri.
units.tr: Disciple. Although these seem to me consonant with truth, I ask you to show how, according to the opposing opinion, these arguments are answered. Master. For the understanding of the foregoing, some distinctions are said to be worth noting. The first is that some are admitted to accuse or denounce, or to pursue some inquiry, while others are heard only to bear witness. The second distinction is that criminals either have been amended of their crime or have not been amended of it. The third is that the person against whom someone is to be heard either is of good repute or is gravely defamed among upright and honest men. The fourth is that someone is heard either by the strictness of law or by the moderation of equity. By these distinctions the arguments adduced for this second opinion are answered. For to the first it is said that, on account of the enormity of certain crimes, namely heresy, treason, simony, and also of others from which danger threatens, criminals, even those not at all amended of their crime, may fittingly be heard, so far as natural and divine law is concerned, especially against one gravely infamed, to accuse and denounce and also to pursue an inquiry, but not to testify. And the reason for this is assigned: because one who is admitted to accuse is not admitted so that credit may be given to him, but so that through his information the truth may be reached. For it often happens that the truth is found through the information of bad men. And therefore criminals are sometimes to be admitted to accuse, on account of the common good and in order to avoid the danger and harm to the common good. But it is otherwise said of a witness: for faith is always given to an admitted witness, whereas credit is never to be given to a criminal. And therefore a criminal ought not to be admitted. And the Gloss on 6 q. 1 c. Quare seems to agree with this, which says: "The whole force of a case depends on testimony, but not on accusation," namely because faith is given to a witness, whereas faith is by no means given to an accuser. Disciple. If no faith is at all given to an accuser, why is a criminal accuser not admitted indifferently against anyone whatever, of whatever crime? Master. A criminal is not to be admitted to accuse indifferently because every accused person is wearied, burdened and hindered in many ways, since he must appear before the judge and answer the accuser. But no one ought, without cause and before he is convicted of a crime, to be so wearied on account of the word of one who is not to be believed. And therefore a criminal is not to be admitted indifferently to accuse. Disciple. By this answer it would be proved that in no case will a criminal be admitted, since no one ought ever to be punished or in any way wearied on account of the word of one who is not to be believed. Indeed by this reasoning it seems it could be proved that no one would be admitted to accuse, since no one ought to be punished or burdened until it is established that he deserves punishment. But every accused person is punished and burdened with many labours in going to the judge and answering the accuser. Therefore, according to what has been said (since faith is not given to the accuser), the accused is by no means to be harassed on account of his word. And so no one would be admitted to accuse. Master. To these it is answered that often, for a just cause and by right reason, indeed by natural law and for the state of corrupted nature, some are wearied and vexed without any fault. For otherwise the commonwealth and the common good could not be preserved. Wherefore it is reasonable that at times someone should be wearied on account of the word of one who is not to be believed, so that in this way the danger to the common good may be forestalled. On this account it is said that it is reasonable that someone who is not known to be innocent be wearied merely on account of the word of one who is not to be believed. And that one who is not to be believed ought to be admitted to accuse. For otherwise the common peace could not be preserved. Disciple. This last point seems to contradict what was said before. For earlier it was said that faith is by no means given to accusers. Here, however, it is said that one who is not to be believed ought to be admitted to accuse. Therefore at times credit is given to accusers. Master. It is answered that many are worthy of belief, and credit is given to them; yet faith ought not to be applied to them in every case, and especially not to the prejudice of another. For no one is to be admitted to testify unless he is worthy of belief. And yet if one alone, however worthy of belief, testifies against someone, credit is not to be given to him to the prejudice of another, so that on account of his testimony the defendant is held guilty. Just as, however worthy of belief the accuser may be, credit is not to be given to him so that the accused is judged guilty on account of his accusation. Disciple. Tell me how the second objection is answered. Master. It is answered that Pope Julius in that decree does not take "to be believed" strictly, but commonly for "to be heard." For also in the crime of treason, when one accomplice accuses another, credit is not given to the accuser so that on account of the accusation the other must be held convicted; yet although the accuser, however well reputed and free from the crime of treason, is heard, this is not so that credit may be given to him, but so that he may show the ways by which the truth could be found.

units.la: Socii enim criminis scientes secreta sociorum suorum saepe sciunt ostendere, quomodo socii per evidentiam rei poterant deprehendi in facto: vel quomodo aliter eorum nequitia posset probari legitimis documentis. Disci. Per hoc videtur, quodlibet criminosus esset audiendus contra quemcunq;: quia crimina propter bonum commune sunt sollicite indaganda. Ergo quilibet (vt corrigantur) debet audiri. Mag. Respondetur, quod dupliciter potest quis audiri. Vno modo in iudicio: & tali modo non est quilibet criminosus audiendus contra omne, quem accusare voluerit. Quia talis audientia nunquam est sine fatigatione ac grauatione alicuius quali infamia illius, contra quem datur. Nunquam autem sine manifesta & patente causa est aliquis bonae famae grauandus, propter verbum cuiuscunq;, cui non est credendum. Cuiusmodi est omnis criminosus. Aliter quis posset audiri extra iudicium in secreto. Et sic potest omnis criminosus audiri contra quemcunq;: quia per talem auditionem nec opinio generatur, nec infamia aggravatur, vt in aliquo fatigetur: quia nec est titandus, nec ad rationem ponendus: sed ideo praelatus audire potest tales, vt sit magis sollicitus ad informandum illum & instruendum, cuius crimen sibi refertur. Discip. Videtur quod si audiretur extra iudicium in secreto, quod opinio alterius est grauata saltem apud illum qui audit. Magist. Respondetur, quod sicut apud audientem alicuius confessionem non debet opinio confitentis esse grauata: ita etiam multo fortius apud audientem in secreto narrationem alicuius criminosi de aliquo crimine, non debet opinio eius esse grauata, licet posset esse magis cautus observando secrete vias eius, maxime si narrans sibi crimen aliquam apparentiam veritatis videatur habere.
units.tr: Men who share in a crime often know their associates' secrets, and so they can show how those associates might have been caught in the act, or how their wickedness might otherwise be proved by lawful evidence. Disciple. It seems to follow that a criminal should be heard against anyone at all, since crimes must be diligently investigated for the common good. Therefore anyone (so that wrongs may be corrected) ought to be heard. Master. The answer is that a person can be heard in two ways. In one way, in court, and in that way a criminal should not be heard against everyone he wishes to accuse. Such a hearing always wears down and burdens the reputation of the person it is brought against, some kind of infamy. Yet a person of good reputation should never be burdened without a clear and evident cause, on the word of someone who is not to be believed, and every criminal is such a person. In another way, a person can be heard outside court, in private. In that way any criminal may be heard against anyone at all, because such a hearing creates no opinion and aggravates no infamy, so that the accused is not harassed in any way. He is not summoned or called to account. Rather, the prelate may hear such people so that he will be more careful to inform and instruct the one whose crime has been reported to him. Disciple. It seems that if he were heard privately, outside court, the reputation of the other man would at least be burdened in the eyes of the one who hears him. Master. The answer is that just as a penitent's reputation ought not to be burdened in the eyes of the one who hears his confession, so much more strongly the reputation of an accused person ought not to be burdened in the eyes of someone who privately hears a criminal's report of another's crime. He may be more cautious, quietly watching the other's ways, especially if the accusation seems to him to have some appearance of truth, but the reputation of the accused should not be damaged.

units.la: Discip. Nunquid debet scribere talem accusationem secretam? Magist. Dicitur quod non, quia talis scriptura posset in aliquo casu ad aliorum notitiam etiam aemulorum & ad accusati infamiam devenire. Disc. Dic quomodo respondetur ad illa, quae dicit Glos. super praeallegato capitulo Iulii Papae. Mag. Respondetur, quod in crimine simoniae auditur socius criminis ad accusandum, si socius fugerit diffamatus: sed non auditur ad testificandum. Similiter confessio vnius latronis auditur contra alios, non vt sibi credatur sicut testi, sed vt detegatur quomodo possunt alii deprehendi. Similiter familiaris contra Dominum auditur non ad testificandum, sed accusandum secrete vel publice. Similiter falsarius contra socium auditur, non ad testificandum, sed ad accusandum secrete vel publice. Cum autem dicitur, quod illi recipiendi sunt, quibus est credendum: verum est, sed non illi soli sunt recipiendi ad accusandum. Quia in quibusdam criminibus recipi possunt ad accusandum illi, quibus non est credendum. Quia interdum tales manifestant vias, quibus veritas reperitur.
units.tr: Disciple. Should he write down such a secret accusation? Master. It is said that he should not, because such a writing might in some case come to the knowledge of others, even rivals, and bring infamy upon the accused. Disciple. Tell me how the things the Gloss says on the chapter of Pope Julius cited above are answered. Master. The answer is that in the crime of simony an accomplice in the crime is heard as an accuser if the accomplice has fled after being defamed, but he is not heard as a witness. Likewise the confession of one robber is heard against the others, not so that he is believed as a witness, but so that it may be disclosed how the others can be caught. Likewise a household servant is heard against his lord, not as a witness, but as an accuser, privately or publicly. Likewise a forger is heard against his accomplice, not as a witness, but as an accuser, privately or publicly. When it is said that those should be received who are believed, that is true, but they are not the only ones who may be received as accusers. For in certain crimes people may be received as accusers even though they are not believed, because sometimes such people reveal the ways by which the truth can be found.

units.la: Discip. Dic quomodo ad tertiam respondetur. Mag. Respondetur secundum Glos. ibidem, quod illa auctoritas est falsa: quia haereticus nunquam admittitur ad accusandum. Aliter potest dici, quod in casu criminosus potest admitti, quando scilicet aduersarius non potest eum repellere. Et ideo haereticus contra haereticum potest admitti: quia haereticus propter crimen haeresis non potest contra ipsum excipere: sed contra orthodoxum nequaquam recipi debet. Quia orthodoxus propter crimen haeresis contra ipsum excipere potest. Aliter dicitur, quod lex illa iniqua est simpliciter; cum haeretici pro nullo testimonium ferre valeant in praeiudicium cuiuscunq;. Licet posset valere, per aliquod liberando, vbi nulli neq; bono neq; malo per testimonium eius posset praeiudicium generari. Ad quartam respondetur, quod socii criminis, qui non sunt de crimine emendati, contra socium, qui non est apud bonos & prouidos diffamatus, non sunt vnquam ad testimonium admittendi: licet in quibusdam criminibus debeant ad accusandum admitti. Socii autem criminis qui sunt de crimine emendati, de rigore iuris non sunt ad testimonium recipiendi: licet de temperantia aequitatis possint admitti, praesertim si accusatus per modum exceptionis contra eos nequaquam crimen opponit. Ad, autem extra, De testibus, respondetur, quod mulieres cum quibus dicitur quis peccasse, non sunt ad testimonium admittendae: nec hoc in illo capitulo habetur: sed insinuatur quod mulieres tales sunt audiendae, vt scilicet dicant aliqua indicia, quibus possit veritas declarari. Et ideo assertionibus mulierum huiusmodi non est adhibenda fides: licet quandoque viam aperire valeant veritatis. Ad illud 6. q. 1. c. si quis communicationibus: respondetur, quod talis socius criminis audiri debet, sed ad testificandum admitti non debet. Et per hoc respondetur ad rationem ultimam extra, De testibus cogendis. Discip. Si nec socius criminis, nec quicunque alius criminosus criminosi essent ad testimonium admittendi, nullus criminosus posset convinci de crimine. Hoc autem in communis boni periculum redundaret. Ergo & socii criminis & etiam criminosi sunt ad testimonium admittendi: aliter multi criminosi evaderent impuniti. Hoc etiam scilicet quod socii criminis & etiam criminosi in testimonium admittuntur, quaedam religiones nunc observant, nec est praesumendum quod religiones aliquid observent iniquum. Ergo &c. Magist. Ad primum eorum respondetur, quod melius est multos criminosos occultos absque poena transire, quam unum innocentem iniuste condemnari. Et ideo cum constet multos saepe dicere testimonium falsum, cum magna diligentia examinari testes oportet, ut quantum possibile est, sit omnino probabile, quod nullomodo vellent asserere falsitatem. De criminoso autem talis probabilitas haberi non potest: quod videlicet nullo modo velit asserere falsitatem. Cuius ratio inter alias assignatur talis. Tanta est nequitia & superbia criminosi, quod cum semel confusus fuerit & infamis, omnes alios vellet in reeclationem suę confusionis & infamiae similiter confusione & infamiae subiacere. Quare non solum propter hoc, quod criminosus secundum praeparationem cordis est omnibus vitiis irretitus, & per consequens pnus est ad testificandum falsum: sed etiam propter hoc quod (ut communiter) socios in confusione & infamia cupit habere: non est probabile, quod criminosus nullo modo velit asserere falsitatem. Criminosus autem ad testimonium dicendum nullo modo debet admitti, quod maxime veritate habet: quando criminosus contra aliquem vel habet causam aliquam, vel qualemcunque discordiam. Si enim ut communiter criminosus socios in confusione & infamia cupit habere, non est dubium quin desideret illos, quibus inimicatur, socios habere. Aliquibus enim inimicatur in speculabilibus solis confusioni similiter subiacere. Quare contra tales ad testificandum nullo modo debet admitti. Discip. Non videtur quod criminosi communiter desiderent eos, contra quos causam vel iniuriam habent, notari de crimine: cum multos criminosos cernamus, qui alios etiam quibus inimicantur non diffamant. Magist. Respondetur, licet communiter criminosi vellent alios notari infamia: tamen ab infamatione & detractione ac mendaciis saepe retrahuntur: vel quia timent in mendaciis deprehendi, vel quia timent illos vel amicos eorum quos infamare desiderant; vel quia dubitant quod eis non credatur, vel propter aliam causam quae ad timorem vel amorem sui noscitur pertinere: qui etiam propter aliquam causam malam unum diffamant & de alio modo mala loquuntur: quare non est eis adhibenda fides. Nec posset quicunque Imperator vel rex, aut Papa statuere, quod criminosus ad testimonium praecipue contra illum cuius est amicus vel contra quem causam habet, vel rancorem, reciperetur quoquo modo. Quod adhuc tali ratione probatur. Maxime debet esse sollicitudo in superioribus, ne succumbant per fallum testimonium innocentes. Cuius ratio est: quia nemo neq; per voluntatem aut sanctitatem vitae, neq; per honestam conversationem, neq; per sapientiam, neq; per testimonium multorum laudabile, neq; quocunque alio modo praeter Divinum miraculum potest contra infamationes, criminationes, criminum impositores & detractores, mendacia & falsa testimonia se munire, testante Sapiente, qui ait:
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how the third objection is answered. Master. It is answered, following the Gloss on the same passage, that the authority in question is false, because a heretic is never admitted as an accuser. But it may be said otherwise, that in some case a criminal may be admitted when his adversary cannot exclude him. Thus a heretic may be admitted against a heretic, because a heretic cannot object to him on the ground of heresy, but he must never be admitted against an orthodox man, since an orthodox man can object to him on the ground of heresy. It may also be said that the law in question is simply unjust, since heretics are not capable of bearing witness to the prejudice of anyone at all. Yet it might hold good in some case where, by freeing someone, their testimony could prejudice neither good nor bad people. To the fourth objection the answer is that accomplices in a crime who have not been reformed of it must never be admitted as witnesses against an accomplice who has not been defamed among good and prudent people, although in certain crimes they ought to be admitted as accusers. Accomplices who have been reformed of their crime, by the strict rule of law, are not to be received as witnesses, although by the moderation of equity they may be admitted, especially if the accused does not in turn bring the crime against them by way of exception. As for the chapter in Extra, De testibus, the answer is that women with whom someone is said to have sinned are not to be admitted as witnesses, nor does that chapter say so. It suggests only that such women should be heard, so that they may state some signs by which the truth can be made clear. Therefore no trust is to be placed in the assertions of such women, although at times they may open a way to the truth. To the passage at 6 q. 1, c. Si quis communicationibus, the answer is that such an accomplice in a crime should be heard, but he ought not to be admitted to give testimony. By this the final objection in Extra, De testibus cogendis, is answered. Disciple. If neither an accomplice in a crime nor any other criminal were to be admitted as a witness against a criminal, no criminal could be convicted of a crime. But this would bring danger to the common good. Therefore both accomplices and criminals are to be admitted as witnesses, or else many criminals would escape unpunished. That accomplices and even criminals are admitted as witnesses is also observed today by certain religious orders, and it is not to be presumed that religious orders observe anything unjust. Therefore etc. Master. To the first of these the answer is that it is better that many hidden criminals pass without punishment than that one innocent person be unjustly condemned. Therefore, since it is established that many people often give false testimony, witnesses must be examined with great diligence, so that, as far as possible, it is wholly probable that they would in no way wish to assert falsehood. But no such probability can be had concerning a criminal, namely that he would in no way wish to assert falsehood. One reason for this is assigned among others, as follows. The wickedness and pride of a criminal are so great that, once he has been put to shame and made infamous, he wants all others to be subject to the same shame and infamy, in order to restore his own confusion and infamy. Hence, not only because the criminal, by the disposition of his heart, is caught in every vice and is therefore prone to bear false witness, but also because (as is common) he desires to have companions in shame and infamy, it is not probable that a criminal would in no way wish to assert falsehood. A criminal, however, must in no way be admitted to give testimony, above all when he has some cause against someone, or any kind of quarrel with him. For if, as is common, a criminal desires to have companions in shame and infamy, there is no doubt that he wants those with whom he is at enmity to be companions in it. For he is at enmity with some people only so that they too may be subject to the same shame in his speculations. Therefore against such people he must in no way be admitted to give testimony. Disciple. It does not seem that criminals commonly desire those against whom they have a cause or a grievance to be branded with a crime, since we see many criminals who do not defame even those with whom they are at enmity. Master. The answer is that although criminals commonly wish others to be marked with infamy, they are often restrained from defamation, slander and lies, either because they fear being caught in their lies, or because they fear those people or their friends whom they wish to defame, or because they doubt that they will be believed, or for some other reason that is known to pertain to fear or love of themselves. Some of them, for some bad reason, defame one person and speak ill of another in a different way, and so no trust is to be placed in them. Nor could any emperor, king or Pope decree that a criminal should be received in any way at all as a witness, especially against one of whose friendship he is a part, or against whom he has a cause or a grudge. This is further proved by the following reason. The greatest care must be taken by superiors that innocent people do not succumb through false testimony. The reason is this: no one, neither by his goodwill nor by the holiness of his life, nor by honest conduct, nor by wisdom, nor by the praise of many witnesses, nor in any other way apart from a divine miracle, can protect himself against infamies, accusations, those who impose crimes, detractors, lies and false testimony, as the Wise Man testifies, who says:

units.la: Non est arbitrii nostri quod quisque loquatur:
units.tr: It is not in our power what anyone says:

units.la: Imo sanctitas, bonitas, sapientia, iustitia & veritas, sicut summae ad invidiam provocant criminosos, ita ex eis scelerati viri ad mentiendum de virtuosis & innocentibus incitantur. Et ita sancti viri per virtutes contra criminosorum diffamationes & mendacia minime muniuntur. De quo tam in veteri lege quam in scripturis sanctorum authenticis manifesta habemus exempla: Ioseph enim sanctus ab infamia & a falso testimonio non potuit custodiri. Nec Susanna per castitatem contra infamiam & falsa testimonia valuit se munire. Sanctus etiam Athanasius neq; per sanctitatem neq; per fidei sinceritatem haereticos refrenavit, nec mulierem inducere potuit quae eum de fornicatione publice accusaret, & se ab eo praegnantem asseveret. Nullo ergo modo humanae fragilitati possibile est, ut possit se quis contra mendacia & falsa testimonia communire. Quia secundum iudicium sapientis: honor est in potestate honorantis & non in potestate honorati, ita vituperium est in potestate vituperantis & non in potestate vituperati. Et ideo in nullius potestate est, ut non crimine infametur vel contra ipsum falsum testimonium proferatur. Quare superiores, qui debent innocentiam defendere & tueri, summe cauere tenentur, ne innocentia per infamiam aut falsum testimonium maculetur. Hoc autem non facerent, nisi omnes criminosos, & praecipue de iniuria aut discordia vel contrarietate suspectos repellerent. Igitur tales ad testimonium non debent admittere. Quod adhuc auctoritate confirmatur. Constantinus Imperator, ut legitur 2. q. 1. c. Iudex, ait: Iudex criminosum discordiam, non ante sententiam diffinitivam proferat, quam aut reum ipse se confiteatur, aut per innocentes testes convincatur. Ex quibus verbis patenter colligitur, quod nunquam debet quis per criminosos testes convinci. Huic concordat Felix Papa: qui, ut habetur causa 6. q. 6. c. supradictis, primates, ait: Primates accusatum iudicientes Episcopum non ante sententiam damnationis proferant, quam aut reum ipse se confiteatur, aut per innocentes canonice examinatos regulariter testes convincatur. Ex quibus aliisque quampluribus patet aperte, quod testes debent esse innocentes omni infamia & suspitione carentes. Cum autem dicis, quod nisi socii criminis aut alii criminosi essent ad testimonium admittendi, raro possent convinci de crimine criminosi. Respondetur, quod hoc non continet veritatem: quia multi criminosi per testes idoneos, multi etiam per indicia & documenta legitima convinci possunt de crimine. Nec aliter sunt quicunque de crimine publice accusandi, secundum quod extra. l. 2. de probatio, & recitatur 4. q. 3. c. sciant, ubi sic dicitur: sciant cuncti accusatores, rem se debere deferre per publicam vocationem, qua munita sit testibus idoneis vel instructa apertissimis documentis vel indiciis ad probationem indubitatam & luce clarioribus expedita. Nullus ergo criminosus ad testificandum est idoneus reputandus. Quod etiam tali ratione probatur. Crimen magis repugnat idoneitati quam conditio, consanguinei tas & familiaritas, quae possunt in viris optimis & verissimis inveniri. Sed conditio, puta servitus, famulatio & consanguinei tas, obviant idoneitati testium & repugnant: Quia servi & cognati, familiares ac domestici accusantis ad testificandum contra accusatum admitti non debent, 3. q. 2. c. 1. & c. de accusationibus. & c. nullus. & s. accusatores. Ergo multo magis criminosi ad testificandum non debent admitti. Admittuntur tamen saepe, quia de facto multoties debitus ordo iuris contra innocentes & criminosos non servatur. Cum vero dicis, quod quaedam religiones criminosos & socios criminis ad testificandum admittunt. Respondetur a nonnullis, quod tales consuetudines & statuta sunt iniqua ex zelo indiscreto vel hypocrisi ortum habentia. Multi enim religiosi scelerratissimi & alii criminosi, non servato recto ordine iudiciario, prosequuntur, detestantur & execrantur, ut sancti & zelatores sanctitatis & honestatis ab omnibus reputentur. Et ideo facta vel statuta eorum ad exemplum minime sunt trahenda: quia non exemplis, sed legibus consonis rectae rationi iudicare oportet. Ratio enim recta (maxime in scriptura Divina fundata) omnibus exemplis, legibus & statutis humanis omnimode est praeferenda. Cum igitur ratio dicet, quod criminoso in nullo negotio est credendum, propter nulla exempla debet quis in praeiudicium alterius credere criminoso maxime periuro, mendaci, detractori, falsorum criminum impositori, calumniatori, compositori falsorum libellorum, & similibus, qui factis vel verbis mentiri noscuntur. Novi enim nonnullos, qui hac arte utuntur, quod quando contra aliquem offenderunt, statim ipsum de aliquo crimine per infamiam maculare nituntur.
