Et si non audent in publico, ad detractiones occultas se converterunt. Discip. Nunquid tales postquam de crimine sunt emendati ad testificandum debent admitti & eis in aliquo negotio est credendum? Magist. Vna est assertio quod talibus & vniuersaliter illis, qui in quocunque periurio vel mendacio perniciosò semel fuerint legitime deprehensi, nunquam in perpetuum est credendum, nisi per apertam operationem miraculi facti vel testimonium sanctitatis eorum ostensi fuerint de tali crimine emendati. Cuius assertionis ratio tacta est supra, quia scilicet nullus potest se contra adversarios custodire: maxime qui habet inimicos, aemulos, contrarios & adversarios, etiam in opinionibus, vel qui alios quomodocunque offendit. Et ideo vix aut nunquam potest sufficiens adhiberi cautela, ne mendaciis occulte vel publice diffametur. Propter quod videmus, quod fere omnes magnae personae & in quacunque gratia excellentes, quae malos offendunt, infamia facti de aliquo crimine infamantur: licet saepe talis infamia nihil aut parum nocere queat. Alia est assertio, quod mendaces & periuri, detractores, falsorum criminum impositores, libellorum famosorum compositores, & alii qui factis vel verbis in mendaciis fuerint deprehensi, postquam diu viis exquisitis fuerint de veritate probati, possunt ad testimonium assumi. Alia assertio est, quod omnes huiusmodi possunt ad famam & ad testimonium auctoritate principis admitti: & extunc eis sicut aliis est credendum.
units.tr: Indeed, holiness, goodness, wisdom, justice and truth, just as they provoke envy in the wicked, so also they incite wicked men to lie about the virtuous and the innocent. Thus holy men are by no means protected against the slanders and lies of criminals by their virtues. We have clear examples of this both in the Old Law and in the authentic writings of the saints. Holy Joseph could not be guarded from infamy and false witness. Nor could Susanna protect herself against infamy and false witness by her chastity. Holy Athanasius likewise did not restrain heretics by his holiness or by the sincerity of his faith, nor could he prevent a woman from publicly accusing him of fornication and declaring that she was pregnant by him. Therefore it is in no way possible for human frailty to fortify itself against lies and false witness. For according to the judgment of the wise man: honour is in the power of the one who honours, and not in the power of the one who is honoured, so dishonour is in the power of the one who dishonours, and not in the power of the one who is dishonoured. And so it is not in anyone's power to avoid being defamed by a crime, or to avoid having false testimony brought against him. Hence superiors, who are bound to defend and protect innocence, are under the strictest obligation to take care that innocence is not stained by infamy or false witness. Yet they would not do this unless they repelled all criminals, and especially those suspected of injury, discord or opposition. Therefore they ought not to admit such persons as witnesses. This is further confirmed by authority. The Emperor Constantine, as is read in 2. q. 1. c. Iudex, says: A judge shall not pronounce a definitive sentence against an accused criminal in matters of discord, unless either the accused himself confesses, or he is convicted by innocent witnesses. From these words it is plainly gathered that no one ought ever to be convicted by criminal witnesses. Pope Felix agrees with this, who, as is found in causa 6. q. 6. c. cited above, Primates, says: Primates judging a bishop who has been accused shall not pronounce a sentence of condemnation, unless either the accused himself confesses, or he is convicted by witnesses who have been canonically examined and who are, as a rule, innocent. From these and many other passages it is clearly evident that witnesses must be innocent, free of all infamy and suspicion. But when you say that, unless accomplices in crime or other criminals were admitted as witnesses, a criminal could rarely be convicted of crime, the answer is that this is not true: for many criminals can be convicted of crime by suitable witnesses, and many also by lawful indications and documents. Nor are those who are to be publicly accused of crime any different, according to l. 2. de probat., and 4. q. 3. c. sciant, where it is said: Let all accusers know that they must bring the matter forward by public summons, fortified by suitable witnesses or furnished with most evident documents or indications, sufficient for an indubitable proof and clearer than light. Therefore no criminal is to be regarded as a fit witness. This is also proved by the following reasoning. Crime is more incompatible with fitness to testify than status, kinship or familiarity, which may be found in the best and most truthful men. But status, such as servitude, service and kinship, stands in the way of and opposes the fitness of witnesses: for servants, relatives, intimates and household members of an accuser ought not to be admitted to testify against the accused, 3. q. 2. c. 1. and c. de accusationibus, and c. nullus, and s. accusatores. Therefore much more ought criminals not to be admitted to testify. Yet they are often admitted, because in fact the proper order of law is frequently not observed against both innocent and criminal persons. As for your point that certain religious orders admit criminals and accomplices in crime as witnesses, some answer that such customs and statutes are unjust, arising from indiscreet zeal or hypocrisy. For many most wicked religious men and other criminals, without observing the right judicial order, pursue, denounce and curse others, so that they may be regarded by all as saints and zealots of holiness and honesty. Therefore their deeds or statutes are by no means to be taken as examples, for one must judge not by examples but by laws consonant with right reason. Indeed, right reason (especially when founded on Divine Scripture) is in every way to be preferred to all examples, laws and human statutes. Therefore, since reason declares that a criminal is not to be believed in any matter, no one ought, to the prejudice of another, to believe a criminal on the strength of any examples, especially a perjurer, a liar, a slanderer, a fabricator of false charges, a calumniator, a composer of false libels, and the like, who are known to lie by deeds or words. For I know some who use this art: when they have offended someone, they immediately strive to stain him with some crime by defamation, and if they do not dare to do so in public, they turn to secret slanders. Student. Ought such persons, once they have been corrected of their crime, to be admitted as witnesses, and is their word to be believed in any matter? Master. One assertion is that such persons, and in general all those who have once been lawfully caught in any pernicious perjury or lie, are never to be believed again in perpetuity, unless they have been shown to be corrected of such a crime by a clear working of a miracle or by evidence of their holiness. The reason for this assertion has been touched on above, namely that no one can guard himself against his adversaries, especially one who has enemies, rivals, opponents and adversaries, even in matters of opinion, or who has in any way offended others. And so it is scarcely or never possible to employ sufficient caution, so that one is not defamed by lies, secretly or publicly. Because of this we see that almost all great persons, and those who excel in any kind of grace, who offend wicked men, are defamed by some factual crime, although such infamy can often do little or no harm. Another assertion is that liars and perjurers, slanderers, fabricators of false charges, composers of defamatory libels, and others who have been caught in lies by deeds or words, after they have been proved truthful for a long time by sought-after means, may be admitted to testify. Another assertion is that all such persons may be admitted to reputation and to testimony by the authority of the prince, and that thereafter they are to be believed just like others.

units.la: CAP. LXXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXX.

units.la: In quo ponuntur sex aliae rationes ad probandum idem, quod in capitulo 77. in principio praeponebatur, scilicet quod Papa haeretico in nullo est credendum. Probatur etiam auctoritatibus.
units.tr: In which six further arguments are set out to prove the same point that was put forward at the beginning of chapter 77, namely that the Pope, being a heretic, is not to be believed in any matter. It is also proved by authorities.

units.la: Discipulus. Aperte conspicio, quod ista assertio, criminoso in nullo negotio est credendum: difficultates habet quamplurimas, quas nolo amplius pertractare: sed ad librum, quem de hac materia & ei connexis es facturus, censo differendas. Ideo praedictam assertionem aliis assertionibus & auctoritatibus fulcire nitaris, non specificando an ex iure naturali & Divino aut humano procedant, quod Papae haeretico in nullo negotio est credendum. Magist. Secunda ratio, qua specialiter ostenditur, quod Papae haeretico in nullo negotio est credendum, in praeiudicium catholici est. Inimico in nullo negotio est credendum contra aliquem. 3. q. 5. c. accusatores. & c. suspectos. & c. canonica. & extra, de accusationibus. c. cum pro. & c. meminimus. Papa autem haereticus omnium catholicorum est inimicus: quoniam haeretici catholicos graviter persequuntur. Ideo Papae haeretico in nullo negotio est credendum. Tertia ratio talis est: mendacibus in nullo est credendum negotio. Papa haereticus, sicut quilibet alius haereticus, periculo pessimo & pessimo genere mendacii noscitur laborare. Mendacio videlicet in doctrina religionis, de quo Augustinus in li. de mendac. & ponitur 22. quaest. 3. cap. primum, ait: Primum capitale est mendacium & longe fugiendum, quod fit in doctrina religionis & ad quod mendacium nulla conditione quis debeat adduci. Ergo Papae haeretico in nullo negotio est credendum. Quarta ratio est haec: Apostatis minime est credendum. 3. quaest. 4. c. beatus. Papa autem haereticus est apostata a fide. Igitur sibi minime est credendum. Quinta ratio est haec: Nulli excommunicato est credendum, teste Stephano, qui, ut legitur 3. quaest. 4. c. nullus, ait: nullus anathematizatorum suscipiatur, nec a quoquam credantur quae ab eis dicuntur vel scribuntur. Papa autem haereticus est excommunicatus. Igitur ei in nullo negotio est credendum. Sexta ratio est haec: Nulli in nullo negotio est credendum, qui non est ad accusandum admittendus; quia minus est recipere aliquem ad accusandum quam credere ei. In plerisque enim negotiis multi non fide digni accuaccusare possunt: sed sóli fide digno est credendum. Illi enim qui non est fide dignus, credi non debet. Papa autem haereticus ad accusandum nullatenus debet admitti: quia nullus haereticus aut ii fide suspectus debet ad accusandum admitti. 3. q. 4. c. si quis. & 2. q. 6. c. suspectos. & ca. nullus. Ergo Papae haeretico in nullo negotio est credendum. Septima ratio est haec: Non magis est credendum haereticis quam fautoribus & defensoribus haereticorum. Sed fautoribus & defensoribus eorum minime est credendum, nec sunt ad testimonium admittendi. extra, de haereticis. c. excommunicamus. Igitur multo fortius haereticis minime est credendum. Ex quo sequitur, quod Papae haeretico fides nullatenus debet adhiberi. Quod etiam auctoritatibus videtur sic posse probari. Ait enim Papa Stephanus ut habetur extra, de haereticis, c.1. Nec eis omnino credendum est, qui fidem veritatis ignorant. Papa autem haereticus fidem veritatis ignorat: imo fidem veritatis impugnat. Ergo ei in nullo negotio est credendum. Item, Aug. ad Bonifacium scribens, ut habetur 23. q. 4. c. ipsa pietas, ait: qui Divina testimonia non sequuntur, pondus humani testimonii perdiderunt. Papa autem haereticus Divina testimonia non sequitur; cum Divina testimonia destruere & impugnare nititur. Igitur ad testimonium perhibendum non debet admitti. Et per consequens sibi credi non debet. Item, in concilio Toletano, ut habetur 2. q. 7. c. non potest, sic legitur: Non potest erga homines esse fideles, qui Deo extiterit infideles. Sed Papa haereticus Deo infidelis extitit. Igitur erga homines fidelis esse non potest. Illi autem non est credendum, qui erga homines fidelis esse non potest. Igitur Papae haeretico in nullo negotio, maxime contra catholicum est credendum. Item, ibidem subiungitur: sicut in fide suspecti Christi sunt, ita in testimonio humano dubii habentur. Igitur multo magis de quibus certum est per experientiam, quod contra fidem errant, certi in humano testimonio non debent haberi. Et per consequens Papae haeretico minime est credendum. Item, vbi prius subditur: infirmari oportet eorum testimonium, qui in fide falsi habentur. Papa autem haereticus est falsus in fide. Igitur infirmari oportet testimonium eius. Et per consequens nullatenus ei est credendum. Item, vbi prius legitur: nec est eis credendum, qui veritatis a se fidem abiecerint. Papa autem haereticus a se fidem abiecit. Igitur Papae haeretico nullo modo est credendum.
units.tr: Disciple. I clearly see that this proposition, that a criminal is not to be believed in any business, raises very many difficulties, which I do not want to take up again. But I think they should be deferred to the book you are going to write on this subject and related matters. So try to support the aforesaid proposition with other propositions and authorities, without specifying whether they proceed from natural and divine law or from human law, that the Pope, being a heretic, is not to be believed in any business. Master. The second argument, by which it is especially shown that the Pope, being a heretic, is not to be believed in any business, is to the prejudice of Catholics. One is not to be believed in any business against someone, if he is that person's enemy. 3. q. 5. c. accusatores. & c. suspectos. & c. canonica. & extra, de accusationibus. c. cum pro. & c. meminimus. Now the heretical Pope is the enemy of all Catholics, since heretics persecute Catholics severely. Therefore the heretical Pope is not to be believed in any business. The third argument runs thus: one is not to be believed in any business if he is a liar. A heretic, like any other heretic, is known to suffer from a most dangerous and most serious kind of lying. Namely the lie told in the teaching of religion, of which Augustine, in the book On Lying, and as is set down in 22. quaest. 3. cap. primum, says: The first and chief lie, and one to be shunned far away, is that which is told in the teaching of religion, and to which no one ought to be drawn by any condition. Therefore the heretical Pope is not to be believed in any business. The fourth argument is this: one is by no means to be believed who is an apostate. 3. quaest. 4. c. beatus. Now the heretical Pope is an apostate from the faith. Therefore he is by no means to be believed. The fifth argument is this: no excommunicated person is to be believed, on the testimony of Stephen, who, as we read in 3. quaest. 4. c. nullus, says: Let none of those who are anathematized be received, nor let anything be believed from them that is said or written by them. Now the heretical Pope is excommunicated. Therefore he is not to be believed in any business. The sixth argument is this: one is not to be believed in any business who is not to be admitted as an accuser, since it is a lesser matter to admit someone as an accuser than to believe him. For in most matters many untrustworthy people can accuse, but only a trustworthy person is to be believed, since one who is not trustworthy ought not to be believed. Now the heretical Pope ought by no means to be admitted as an accuser, since no heretic, or one suspected of the faith, ought to be admitted as an accuser. 3. q. 4. c. si quis. & 2. q. 6. c. suspectos. & ca. nullus. Therefore the heretical Pope is not to be believed in any business. The seventh argument is this: heretics are not to be believed more than the supporters and defenders of heretics. But their supporters and defenders are by no means to be believed, nor are they to be admitted as witnesses. extra, de haereticis. c. excommunicamus. Therefore much more certainly heretics are by no means to be believed. From this it follows that faith ought in no way to be given to the heretical Pope. This also seems to be provable by authorities in this way. For Pope Stephen says, as it is found in extra, de haereticis, c.1. Nor is credence at all to be given to those who are ignorant of the faith of the truth. Now the heretical Pope is ignorant of the faith of the truth; indeed he attacks the faith of the truth. Therefore he is not to be believed in any business. Likewise Augustine, writing to Boniface, as it is found in 23. q. 4. c. ipsa pietas, says: Those who do not follow the divine testimonies have lost the weight of human testimony. Now the heretical Pope does not follow the divine testimonies, since he strives to destroy and attack the divine testimonies. Therefore he ought not to be admitted to give testimony, and consequently he is not to be believed. Likewise, in the Council of Toledo, as it is found in 2. q. 7. c. non potest, it reads thus: He cannot be faithful toward men who has been unfaithful toward God. But the heretical Pope has been unfaithful toward God. Therefore he cannot be faithful toward men. Yet no credence is to be given to one who cannot be faithful toward men. Therefore, least of all against a Catholic, is credence to be given to the heretical Pope in any business. Likewise, in the same place it is added: Just as those suspected in the faith are doubtful in Christ, so they are held doubtful in human testimony. Therefore, much more, those whom experience has shown for certain to err against the faith must not be held certain in human testimony. Consequently the heretical Pope is by no means to be believed. Likewise, where it is said before: the testimony of those who are held false in the faith ought to be weakened. Now the heretical Pope is false in the faith. Therefore his testimony ought to be weakened, and consequently he is in no way to be believed. Likewise, where it is read before: nor is credence to be given to those who have cast off the faith of the truth from themselves. Now the heretical Pope has cast off the faith from himself. Therefore the heretical Pope is in no way to be believed.

units.la: CAP. LXXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXI.

units.la: Quaerit quomodo Papa haereticus sit excommunicatus & a quo, scilicet sive a iure Divino vel humano, & quot sint excommunicationes.
units.tr: He asks how a heretical Pope is excommunicated, and by whom, that is, whether by divine or human law, and how many kinds of excommunication there are.

units.la: DISCIP. De ista materia, quae allegasti, ad praesens sufficiant. Ideo dic, si Papa haereticus aliqua poena alia est puniendus. MAGIST. Una est assertio, quod Papa haereticus de facto sententiam excommunicationis incurrat, quemadmodum verberans clericum. Licet nequaquam nominatim excommunicetur de novo, vel etiam denuncietur, ipse de facto excommunicationis sententia est ligatus. DISC. Videtur secundum istam assertionem, quod Papa haereticus sententia excommunicationis lata a iure inuoluitur: sed minime explicatur a quo iure, scilicet Divino vel humano sit lata ista sententia. Ideo dic, quo iure secundum istam assertionem Papa haereticus excommunicationis sententia innodatur.
units.tr: STUDENT. Let what you have cited on this subject suffice for now. So tell me whether a heretical Pope is to be punished with some other penalty. TEACHER. One view is that a heretical Pope incurs the sentence of excommunication de facto, just as one who strikes a cleric does. Although he is by no means excommunicated again by name, or even publicly declared so, he is bound by the sentence of excommunication de facto. STUDENT. According to this view, it seems that a heretical Pope is caught up in a sentence of excommunication pronounced by law, but it is not explained by which law, whether divine or human, this sentence was pronounced. So tell me, according to this view, by which law a heretical Pope is bound by the sentence of excommunication.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur distinguendo, quod excommunicatio sit separatio ab actu legitimo. Quot sunt actus legitimi, tot potuerunt esse excommunicationes. Est autem unus actus legitimus inter Christianos, qui est participatio sacramentorum. Alius autem instructio seu informatio in fide & moribus publica vel occulta. Alius est communio fidelium in comedendo & bibendo & conversatione. Alius est testimonium perhibere. Plures sunt alii actus legitimi: sed de praedictis ad praesens loqui sufficiat. Dicitur ergo quod quaedam est separatio seu excommunicatio a participatione sacramentorum Ecclesiae. Quaedam ab instructione Christianorum in fide & in moribus publica vel occulta. Quaedam a testimonio perhibendo. Quaedam a communione fidelium. Primam & secundam incurrit excommunicationem Papam haereticus a iure Divino: quia Papa haereticus est extra Ecclesiam & a corpore Ecclesiae separatus tanquam destructor Ecclesiae & lubuerfor. Et ideo nec suscipere nec administrare debet Ecclesiastica sacra, nisi in necessitate sacramentu baptismi, nec Christianos docere debet publice vel occulte. De tertia separatione sunt opiniones, de quibus dictum est prius, quibusdam dicentibus quod Papa haereticus ex iure Divino & naturali a testimonio perhibendo excluditur, aliis asserentibus quod solummodo ex iure humano repellitur. Quartam separationem incurrit Papa haereticus solummodo ex iure humano, quo omnes haeretici a communione fidelium separantur.
units.tr: TEACHER. The answer is given by a distinction: excommunication is separation from a lawful act. There could be as many excommunications as there are lawful acts. Now there is one lawful act among Christians, which is participation in the sacraments. Another is public or private instruction in faith and morals. Another is the fellowship of the faithful in eating, drinking and conversation. Another is bearing witness. There are several other lawful acts, but it is enough to speak of those named for the present. So it is said that one separation or excommunication is from participation in the sacraments of the Church; another is from the instruction of Christians in faith and morals, public or private; another is from bearing witness; another is from the fellowship of the faithful. A heretical Pope incurs the first and second excommunications by divine law, because a heretical Pope is outside the Church and cut off from the body of the Church, as a destroyer and subverter of the Church. Therefore he ought neither to receive nor to administer the holy things of the Church, except in necessity, in the sacrament of baptism, nor ought he to teach Christians, publicly or privately. Concerning the third separation there are opinions, as was said earlier: some hold that a heretical Pope is excluded from bearing witness by divine and natural law, while others assert that he is repelled only by human law. A heretical Pope incurs the fourth separation solely by human law, by which all heretics are separated from the fellowship of the faithful.

units.la: DISCIP. Istam sententiam plane intelligo, circa quam duo tantummodo probare nitaris. Primum quod excommunicatio, quae est separatio a communione omnium fidelium iure Divino nequaquam infligitur. Secundo quod haereticus hanc excommunicationem de facto incurrit. MAGIST. Primum huius multis modis posset probari. Primo modo exemplis sanctorum, qui in infidelibus & haereticis in temporalibus communicaverunt: sicut multi viri sancti cum Iuliano haeretico, postquam fuit Imperator, communicaverunt. DISCIP. Istud exemplum sufficit mihi pro nunc: ideo pro secundo allegare coneris. MAGIST. Secundum probatur. Omnes haeretici, qui sententiis generalium conciliorum & summorum pontificum sunt subiecti, ipso facto sententiam talis excommunicationis incurrunt. Quia ipso facto incidunt in canonem late sententiae contra omnes haereticos indistincte prolatae, extra, de haereticis, c. ad abolendam, & c. excommunicamus. 1. & 2. & c. sicut, & extra de sententia excom. c. noverit. Sed Papa haereticus est subiectus sententiis generalium conciliorum & summorum pontificum: quemadmodum (ipso viuente) si esset generale concilium aggregatum. Et si summus Pontifex nouus erit creatus iurisdi-
units.tr: STUDENT. I understand this view clearly, and you are trying to prove only two points about it. First, that excommunication, which is separation from the fellowship of all the faithful, is by no means imposed by divine law. Second, that a heretic incurs this excommunication de facto. TEACHER. The first point could be proved in many ways. The first way is by the examples of the saints, who had dealings with unbelievers and heretics in temporal matters, just as many holy men communed with the heretic Julian after he became emperor. STUDENT. That example is enough for me for now, so try to allege a second one. TEACHER. The second point is proved thus. All heretics who are subject to the sentences of general councils and of the supreme pontiffs incur the sentence of such excommunication by that very fact, because by that very fact they fall under the canon of the sentence pronounced in general against all heretics without distinction: Extra, De haereticis, c. Ad abolendam, and c. Excommunicamus; 1 and 2; c. Sicut; and Extra, De sententia excommunicationis, c. Noverit. But a heretical Pope is subject to the sentences of general councils and of the supreme pontiffs, just as he would be, while living, if a general council were assembled; and if a new supreme pontiff were created, he would be subject to the jurisdiction of the council as well as of the supreme pontiff.

units.la: Gio otioni tam concilii quam summi pontificis esset subiectus. Igitur Papa haereticus ipso facto sententiam excommunicationis incurrit. Quod Gloss. (24.q.1. c. super illo verbo: quicunq; in haeresim semel damnatam labitur, eius damnatione seipsum involuit) insinuare videtur dicens: hic est casus in quo Papam ligare potest; & canonem latae sententiae incidit. Nec obuiat regula illa, quia par parem soluere aut ligare non potest: quia si Papa est haereticus (in eo quod haereticus) minor est quocunq; catholico. Ex quibus colligitur, quod Papa effectus haereticus sententia praedecessoris sui contra haereticos indistincte prolata ligatur. Et ideo non est maior ratio, quod ligetur una sententia sui praedecessoris contra haereticos indistincte prolata quam alia. Ergo Papa haereticus omni sententia Romanorum Pontificum contra haereticos indistincte prolata subiacet, vt probatum est supra. Igitur Papa haereticus ipso facto sententiam excommunicationis incurrit. Ex quo concluditur, quod omnes, qui scirent ipsum esse haereticum, ipsum tanquam excommunicatum excommunicatione maiori vitare deberent, nec licet sibi aliqualiter obedire.
units.tr: ...of both the council and the supreme pontiff. Therefore a heretical Pope incurs the sentence of excommunication by that very fact. The Gloss seems to hint at this, when it says (24, q. 1, c. on the words "whoever falls back into a heresy once condemned, by that condemnation involves himself"): "This is a case in which the Pope can be bound, and he falls under the canon of sentence pronounced." Nor does that rule stand in the way, that an equal cannot absolve or bind an equal, because if the Pope is a heretic (insofar as he is a heretic) he is inferior to any Catholic whatever. From these things it is gathered that a Pope who has become a heretic is bound by the sentence of his predecessor pronounced without distinction against heretics. And therefore there is no greater reason for his being bound by one sentence of his predecessor pronounced without distinction against heretics than by another. Therefore a heretical Pope is subject to every sentence of the Roman Pontiffs pronounced without distinction against heretics, as has been proved above. Therefore a heretical Pope incurs the sentence of excommunication by that very fact. From this it follows that all who knew him to be a heretic ought to avoid him as one excommunicated with the greater excommunication, and it is not lawful for them to obey him in any way.

units.la: CAP. LXXXII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXII.

units.la: De tribus aliis poenis Papa haeretico infligendis.
units.tr: Concerning three other penalties to be inflicted on a heretical Pope.

units.la: Discipulus. Dic an secundum dicentes Papam haereticum ipso facto esse Papatu priuatum, Papa haereticus aliqua poena sit plectendus. Magist. Dicunt, quod multiplici poena (quam de facto incurrit) per iudicem competentem puniri debet secundum canonicas sanctiones. Discip. Numera poenas aliquas graviores, quibus est Papa haereticus feriendus secundum assertores praedictos. Magist. Dicunt quod de Sede Apostolica est repellendus per potentiam temporalem: quia magis repugnat catholicae sedi & dignitati Papali labes haeretica, quam intrusio; cui haeretica prauitas minime est annexa: sed huiusmodi intrusus de eadem Sede Apostolica est pellendus, dist. 79. Si quis pecunia. Ergo multo magis Papa haereticus de Sede Apostolica per temporalem potentiam est repellendus. Secundo dicunt, quod est ab omni ordine Ecclesiastico degradandus: & nisi ad fidei vnitatem redierit, tradendus est curiae seculari. Si autem redierit, est perpetuo carceri mancipandus. Probantur haec extra, de haereticis, ad abolendam. & c. excommunicamus. Tertio dicunt, quod bona eius, si habuerit quaedam propria, sunt penitus confiscanda, extra, de haereticis. Omnia ista vna ratione, quae tacta est prius, fulcire niituntur: quae haec est. Papa haereticus non gaudet beneficio vel priuilegio speciali vltra alios Episcopos labem haereticam incurrentes: Quia in nulla sententia canonis generalis concilii vel summi pontificis contra haereticos lata specialiter excipitur Papa haereticus magis quam alii Episcopi. Cum igitur Papa haereticus sit subiectus sententiis omnium generalium conciliorum ac summorum pontificum, sequitur quod quaecunq; poena Episcopis haereticis debet infligi, infligenda est Papae haeretico. Sed poenae praedictae Episcopis haereticis debent infligi. Igitur eisdem poenis est Papa haereticus feriendus. Et ita licet Papa haereticus ipso facto de Apostolica Sede non sit expulsus, nec omni praerogatiua ordinis Ecclesiastici degradatus, nec sit traditus curiae seculari, nec sit perpetuo carceri mancipatus, nec bona ipsius propria confiscentur: tamen omnes poenae praedictae per iudicem competentem sibi debent infligi. Discip. Nunquid secundum istos Papa haereticus aliquas alias poenas praeter poenas haereticis infligendas debet sustinere? Magist. Respondetur, quod si Papa de nullo alio crimine, quam de crimine prauitatis haereticae potest conuinci, poenis est haereticorum solummodo complectendus. Si autem de aliquo alio crimine, puta de homicidio facto consilio, praecepto vel defensione commisso, aut crimine laesae maiestatis, aut simonia, vel rapina, aut depraedatione, seu guerrarum concitatione, aut innocentium damnatione, vel persecutione, vel quocunq; alio crimine potest legitime conuinci, poenis huiusmodi criminum est plectendus.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me: according to those who say that a heretical Pope is deprived of the Papacy by the very fact (ipso facto), is a heretical Pope to be punished with some penalty? Master. They say that he is to be punished by the competent judge with the manifold penalty which he has in fact incurred, according to the canonical sanctions. Disciple. Name some of the more severe penalties with which a heretical Pope is to be struck, according to the aforesaid advocates. Master. They say that he is to be driven out of the Apostolic See by temporal power, because a heretical stain is more contrary to the Catholic See and the Papal dignity than intrusion, with which heretical depravity is by no means connected; but an intruder of this kind is to be expelled from that same Apostolic See (dist. 79, Si quis pecunia). Therefore, much more, a heretical Pope is to be removed from the Apostolic See by temporal power. Secondly, they say that he is to be degraded from every ecclesiastical order, and, unless he returns to unity of the faith, he is to be handed over to the secular court; but if he returns, he is to be consigned to perpetual prison (see extra, De haereticis, Ad abolendam, and c. Excommunicamus). Thirdly, they say that his goods, if he has any property of his own, are to be utterly confiscated (extra, De haereticis). They strive to support all these things by one reason, which was touched on earlier, and which is this: a heretical Pope does not enjoy any special benefit or privilege beyond other bishops who incur the heretical stain, because in no sentence of a general council or of the supreme pontiff issued against heretics is the heretical Pope specially excepted more than other bishops. Since, therefore, the heretical Pope is subject to the sentences of all general councils and supreme pontiffs, it follows that whatever penalty ought to be inflicted on heretical bishops is to be inflicted on the heretical Pope. But the aforesaid penalties ought to be inflicted on heretical bishops. Therefore the heretical Pope is to be struck with the same penalties. And so, although the heretical Pope is not expelled from the Apostolic See by the very fact, nor degraded from every prerogative of the ecclesiastical order, nor handed over to the secular court, nor consigned to perpetual prison, nor are his own goods confiscated, nevertheless all the aforesaid penalties ought to be inflicted on him by the competent judge. Disciple. According to these men, does a heretical Pope have to undergo any penalties other than those to be inflicted on heretics? Master. The answer is that if the Pope can be convicted of no other crime than the crime of heretical depravity, he is to be punished with the penalties of heretics only. But if he can be lawfully convicted of some other crime, for example of homicide committed by counsel, command or defence, or of the crime of treason, or of simony, or of rapine or plunder, or of stirring up wars, or of the condemnation or persecution of the innocent, or of any other crime whatsoever, he is to be punished with the penalties of such crimes.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXIII.

units.la: De competenti iudice Papa haretici.
units.tr: On the competent judge of a heretical Pope.

units.la: Discipulus. Aduerto, quod isti assertores inter Papam haereticum puniendum & Episcopos haereticos puniendos paruam aut nullam differentiam arbitrantur, quantum ad poenas haereticis & criminosis aliis infligendas. Ideo post praedicta ad interrogandum de iudice competenti Papae haeretici, per quem scilicet poenae praedictae sibi imponi debeant, me conuertam. Quamuis in principio huius sexti multa disseruisti de iudice veri Papae super crimine haeresis mendaciter diffamati: & supra c. 72. 73. 74. & 75. aliqua dixeris de habente potestatem haereticum Papam deponendi: volo tamen nunc de iudice, qui poenis haereticorum Papam haereticum debet exponere, magis exquisite inquirere. Dicigitur inprimis, an ad vnam vel plures iudices de iure pertineat Papae haeretico praedictas poenas, scilicet expulsionem de Apostolica Sede, degradationem, incarcerationem vel traditionem curiae seculari, & bonorum proprionum confiscationem infligere. Vna opinio tenet, quod praedictas poenas infligere Papae haeretico de iure spectat ad generale concilium, si fuerit congregatum: & ad Papam catholicum, si fuerit electus canonice. Si autem nec concilium generale fuerit congregatum, nec electus fuerit Papa catholicus, praefatis poenis ferire Papam haereticum spectat ad collegium cardinalium. Et si illi fuerint negligentes, pertinet ad Episcopum, in cuius dioecesi Papa haereticus commoratur. Si autem praelati & clerici damnabiliter Papam neglexerint coercere, per principes seculares & laicos
units.tr: Disciple. I notice that these defenders of the view judge that there is little or no difference between a heretical Pope to be punished and heretical bishops to be punished, as far as the penalties to be inflicted on heretics and other criminals are concerned. So after what has been said, I turn to ask about the competent judge of a heretical Pope, by whom the aforementioned penalties ought to be imposed on him. Although at the beginning of this sixth part you discussed at length the judge of a true Pope who has been falsely accused of the crime of heresy, and in chapters 72, 73, 74 and 75 you said something about the one who has the power to depose a heretical Pope, I now wish to inquire more carefully into the judge who ought to subject a heretical Pope to the penalties of heretics. First, then: does it belong by law to one judge or to several to inflict on a heretical Pope the said penalties, namely expulsion from the Apostolic See, degradation, imprisonment or surrender to the secular court, and confiscation of his own goods? One opinion holds that it belongs by law to a general council, if one has been convened, and to the catholic Pope, if he has been canonically elected, to inflict the aforesaid penalties on a heretical Pope. But if neither a general council has been convened nor a catholic Pope elected, it belongs to the college of cardinals to strike a heretical Pope with the aforesaid penalties. And if they are negligent, it belongs to the bishop in whose diocese the heretical Pope dwells. But if the prelates and clergy culpably neglect to restrain the Pope, then by secular princes and laymen he is to be duly expelled.

units.la: Lce & laicos est debite expellendus. Ista assertio habet multas particulas, de quibus singulis te interrogare propono. Primo autem disleramus de concilio generali, ad quem scilicet (si Papa fuerit effectus haereticus) spectat generale concilium congregare. Magist. Quod Papa fiat haereticus multis modis potest contingere: quia aut est occultus haereticus, aut manifestus & notorius. Si est occultus haereticus, ita quod de haeresi convinci non potest, dicunt quidam, quod si Papa est de haeresi diffamatus, exemplo Simachi Papae, ipse & non alius debet concilium generale congregare ad semetipsum purgandum. Et si noluerit se purgare, & de sua infamia intolerabile scandalum generatur, per alios debet generale concilium congregari. Si autem Papa est haereticus manifestus, ita quod probari potest per testes idoneos & legitima documenta, non tamen est haereticus notorius, quia pauci sciunt ipsum haereticum, tot tamen sciunt, quod possunt ipsum convincere: dicunt quidam, quod Papa haereticus debet concilium convocare, quod si noluerit, est per alios congregandum. Si vero Papa est notorius haereticus per evidentiam rei vel confessionem: puta quia publice aliquam assertionem, quae est haeresis manifesta, cuius contrarium tenetur credere explicite, tenet vel tenere fatetur: ut puta si publice & notorie praedicaret Christum non fuisse natum de virgine, aut legem Christianorum esse falsam, vel fateretur publice se hoc tenere vel tenuisse, vel etiam de tali aliquo dubitasse. Dicunt nonnulli quod Papa haereticus in hoc casu non debet concilium generale convocare: sed illi, qui sciunt ipsum esse notorium haereticum, debent aliis catholicis intimare, ut ipsi ad concilium generale conveniant: nisi prius electores summi pontificis alium in Papam elegerint orthodoxum. Tunc enim ille electus in Papam debet generale concilium (si necesse fuerit) convocare. Si autem electores pravitate haeretica una cum Papa fuerint involuti, vel sibi favorem praestiterint; alii fideles debent ad generale concilium pro faciendo iustitia convenire, si propter maliciam hominum alio modo de ipso iustitia fieri nequit.
units.tr: ...and laymen is to be duly expelled. This assertion has many parts, and I propose to question you about each of them individually. First, then, let us discuss the general council, namely to whom it belongs (if the Pope has become a heretic) to convene a general council. Master. That a Pope becomes a heretic can happen in many ways, since he is either a hidden heretic or a manifest and notorious one. If he is a hidden heretic, so that he cannot be convicted of heresy, some say that if the Pope has been defamed of heresy, following the example of Pope Symmachus, he himself, and no one else, ought to convene a general council to clear himself. And if he refuses to clear himself, and an intolerable scandal arises from his infamy, the general council ought to be convened by others. But if the Pope is a manifest heretic, so that he can be proved by competent witnesses and lawful documents, yet is not a notorious heretic, because few know him to be a heretic (though enough know him that they can convict him), some say that the heretical Pope ought to convene a council, and that if he refuses, it is to be convened by others. But if the Pope is a notorious heretic, by the evidence of the fact or by his own confession, for instance because he publicly holds or confesses that he holds some manifest heretical assertion, the contrary of which he is bound to believe explicitly, as for instance if he publicly and notoriously preached that Christ was not born of a virgin, or that the law of the Christians is false, or publicly confessed that he holds this, or has held it, or even has doubted some such thing: some maintain that in this case a heretical Pope ought not to convene a general council, but that those who know him to be a notorious heretic ought to notify other catholics that they should assemble for a general council, unless first the electors of the supreme pontiff have chosen another orthodox man as Pope. For then that elected Pope ought to convene a general council (if it is necessary). But if the electors have been involved along with the Pope in heretical wickedness, or have given him their favour, other faithful people ought to gather for a general council to do justice, if on account of men's malice justice cannot otherwise be done concerning him.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIV.
units.tr: Chapter 84.

units.la: In quo inquiritur per quem concilium generale possit congregari, si Papa fuerit haereticus, & electores Papae sibi adhaereant. Ubi etiam probatur, quod concilium generale possit absque Papa congregari.
units.tr: In which it is asked by whom a general council can be convened if the Pope is a heretic and the electors of the Pope side with him; and where it is also shown that a general council can be convened without the Pope.

units.la: Discipulus. Quia a manifestioribus expedit inchoare: ideo primo dicas de concilio, quomodo si Papa est notorie haereticus, & electores summi pontificis in haeretica pravitate sibi consentiant, vel eidem indebite faveant: nec patet alia via, per quam possit Papa haereticus coerceri, per quem scilicet generale concilium debeat congregari. Mag. Dicunt, quod hoc in casu quilibet catholicus, qui scit Papam haereticum esse notorium, vel audit publice divulgari, quod Papa est notorie haereticus, debet esse paratus, si expedit, ad generale concilium convenire, debetque quilibet in quantum sibi competit pro gradu suo alios exhortari catholicos, ut ad concilium generale conveniant. Veruntamen spectat principaliter ad praelatos & in divina lege peritos. Secundo spectat ad reges & principes & alias publicas potestates. Tertio autem spectat ad omnes catholicos viros & mulieres. Unde etiam mulieres catholicae scientes Papam esse haereticum, & electores circa electionem summi pontificis negligentes, debent si expedit catholicos exhortari, ut ad generale concilium pro Ecclesia ordinanda concurrant: imo & ipsemet ire debent, si potuerint bono communi prodesse. Discip. Ista assertio mirabilis mihi videtur. Tria enim absurda continet, ut apparet: quorum primum est, quod generale concilium absque auctoritate Papae debeat congregari. Secundum est quod reges & principes & alii laici ad generale concilium debeant convenire. Tertium quod mulieres debeant ac valeant generali concilio interesse. Quod enim primum sit absurdum, per sacros canones probatur aperte. Nam sicut habetur di. 17. per totum, Concilium generale absque auctoritate summi pontificis congregari non potest. Ait enim Pelagius Papa: multi denuo Apostolici & catholici atque Ecclesiastici instituuntur regulis, non debere absque licentia Romani pontificis concilia celebrari. In quibus verbis clare patet, quod generale concilium absque Papa congregari non debet. Quare cum puto quod assertores praedicti sine motivo non dicunt contrarium, dic motiva eorum. Ipsis namque argumentis intelliga clarius veritatem. Mag. Quod absque auctoritate Papae possit generale concilium congregari nonnullis rationibus videtur posse probari. Quarum prima est haec: Concilium particulare potest licite congregari absque auctoritate Papae ad iudicandum de eodem vero Papa. Ergo multo magis generale concilium poterit congregari ad iudicandum de pseudo Papa haeretico absque eius auctoritate. Antecedens duobus manifestis exemplis videtur probari. Primum est de Episcopis, qui convenerunt ad inquirendum de facto & idolatria beati Marcellini, quorum congregatio fuit particulare concilium congregatum absque auctoritate eiusdem Papae Marcellini. Secundum est de illorum congregatione, qui convenerunt ad iudicandum & deponendum Papam Iohannem 12. quae congregatio non fuit concilium generale, sed particulare solummodo. Ergo multo magis posset ficri concilium generale ad iudicandum de Papa haeretico in haeresi notorie deprehenso. Discip. Ista ratio videtur aperte probare, quod absque auctoritate pseudo Papae haeretici possit generale concilium congregari: sed non probat quod valeat congregari absque auctoritate veri Papae. Unde & videtur, quod si Papa fuerit haereticus, eligendus est Papa catholicus, antequam generale concilium convocetur. Magist. Nonnullis apparet, quod ratio (secundum supra dicta) ostendit parenter, quod absque auctoritate cuiuscunque Papae veri & falsi potest generale concilium convocari. Nam [illegible, ~12 letters] licitum est concilium particulare fieri absq; auctoritate Papæ ad inquirendum vel iudicandum de vero Papa: multo magis licitum est generale concilium celebrari tempore vacationis Apo-stolicæ Sedis absq; auctoritate Papæ ad pseudo Papam debite coercendum: præsertim si pseudo Pa-pa uiolenter contendere potest. Sed primum licitum est, sicut per duo exempla probatum existit. Ergo & secundum licitum debet reputari. Secunda ratio est hæc. Omnis populus & omnis communitas & om-ne corpus, qui absq; consensu vel auctoritate cuiuscunq;, q nō est de corpore, potest sibi ius statuere, potest aliquos eligere, q vicem gerant totius communitatis aut corporis absq; alterius auctoritate. Sed omnes fideles sunt vnum corpus, Paulo dicente ad Ro.12. Multi vnū corpus sumus in Christo: & sunt vnus populus & vna communitas. Ergo possunt eligere aliquos, qui vice gerant totius corporis. Tales autem electi simul conuenerint, concilium generale constituent: quia concilium generale nō videtur esse aliud q congregatio aliquorū, qui vicem gerant totius Christianitatis. Potest ergo concilium generale congregari absq; auctoritate cuiuslibet, q non est catholicus & fidelis. Et p consequens absq; auctoritate Papæ hæretici. Tertia ratio est hæc: Vniuersalis Ecclesia in vnū conueniens ad aliquid ordinandū potest ad concilium generale conuocari. Sed vniuersalis Ecclesia posset ad tā paruum numerū deuenire, quod posset in simul conuocati. Nam in tam paruo numero fuit aliquando post ascensionē Christi. Igitur non est impossibile, q ad tale numerū iterum pueniat. Et p consequens nō est impossibile, q vniuersalis Ecclesia ad concilium generale conueniat, etiā si nullus esset verus Papa. Sicut nō est impossibile, q sede vacante vniuersalis Ecclesia simul conueniat. Non minoris autē potestatis seu auctoritatis vniuersalis est Ecclesia, quando nō posset insimul conuenire, propter magna multitudinē q quando po-test simul conuenire. Igitur quicquid posset vniuersalis Ecclesia p se, si posset insimul conuenire, po-test per aliquos electos à diuersis partibus Ecclesiæ. Igitur posito q diuersæ partes vniuersalis Ecclesiæ eligerent aliquos, qui conuenirent in vnū ad ordinandum de Ecclesia Dei: Illi sic electi conuenientes in vnū (non obstante q nullus esset verus Papa) possent concilium generale appellari. Et ita potest concilium generale, quando non esset verus Papa, absq; auctoritate Papæ congregari. Discip. Aliqualiter modum ponendi prædictum intelligo, vt tamen eum magis intelligam, & sic clarius peneniam ad veritatem, declara per quem modum secundum assertionem prædictam debeat concilium generale conuocari. Magist. Dicitur, quod rationabile esset de qualibet parrochia vel aliqua cō-munitate (quæ posset faciliter in vnum conuenire) mitti aliquem vel aliquos ad concilium Episcopale vel ad Parlamentum regis ac principis, aut alterius publicæ potestatis, quæ eligeret vel eligerent aliquos mittendos ad concilium generale: qui taliter electi à conciliis Episcopalibus vel Parlamentis secularium potestatum in vnum locum conuenientes possunt generale concilium appellari. Disc. Quid si aliqua parrochia vel etiam diœcesis nollet aliquos mittere ad concilium generale? Magist. Respondetur, quod propter contradictionem ipsorum non esset communis vtilitas omittenda: imo est assertio dicens, quod si multæ diœceses, vel regna contradicunt generali concilio congregando, potestas congregandi concilium generale esset de iure ad alia regna vel diœceses deuoluta: quia impedientes communē vtilitatem fidei Christianæ potestatem conueniendi ad generale concilium merito priuarentur. Discip. Istam opinionem intelligo, licet eam non reputem consonam veritati. Tamen qualiter respondetur secundum eam ad auctoritates, quibus asseritur manifeste, quod absq; auctoritate summi pontificis non debeat concilium generale congregari, aperias. Magist. Respondetur, quod regulariter concilium generale nequaquam congregari debet absq; auctoritate summi pontificis. Fallit tamen in casu, qui accidit, quando scilicet Papa efficeretur hæreticus; & electores summi pontificis negligerent Papam eligere; nec posset aliter quam per generale concilium Ecclesiæ prouideri. Propter quod, vt dicitur, auctoritates summorum pontificum asserentium quod concilium generale absq; auctoritate Papæ congregari non debet, nequaquam sunt hegandæ: sed sunt sane intelligendæ, vt nullo modo interpretentur in præiudicium fidei Christianæ, quę summo pontifici, etiam catholico, est modis omnibus præferenda.
units.tr: Disciple. Since it is useful to begin with the more evident matters, first tell me about the council: how, if the Pope is notoriously a heretic and the electors of the supreme pontiff agree with him in his heretical depravity or improperly favour him, and no other way is open by which a heretical Pope could be restrained, namely by whom a general council ought to be convened. Master. They say that in this case any Catholic who knows that the Pope is notoriously a heretic, or hears it publicly proclaimed that the Pope is notoriously a heretic, ought to be ready, if it is expedient, to come together in a general council, and each person, as far as his rank allows, ought to exhort other Catholics to assemble in a general council. Yet this belongs chiefly to the prelates and those skilled in the divine law. Second, it belongs to kings, princes and other public powers. Third, it belongs to all Catholic men and women. Hence Catholic women too, who know that the Pope is a heretic and who neglect the election of the supreme pontiff, ought, if it is expedient, to exhort Catholics to gather for the ordering of the Church in a general council; indeed they themselves ought to go, if they can be of benefit to the common good. Disciple. This assertion seems to me astonishing. For it plainly contains three absurdities: the first is that a general council ought to be convened without the authority of the Pope; the second is that kings, princes and other laymen ought to come to a general council; the third is that women ought and may take part in a general council. That the first is absurd is clearly proved by the sacred canons. For, as is found throughout Dist. 17, a general council cannot be convened without the authority of the supreme pontiff. Pope Pelagius says: many new rules of the apostolic, Catholic and ecclesiastical kind have been established, that councils must not be held without the permission of the Roman pontiff. In these words it is clear that a general council ought not to be convened without the Pope. Therefore, since I think the aforesaid advocates do not say the contrary without reason, tell me their reasons. By their very arguments you will understand the truth more clearly. Master. That a general council can be convened without the authority of the Pope seems capable of proof by several arguments. The first is this: a particular council can lawfully be convened without the authority of the Pope to judge even a true Pope. Therefore much more a general council can be convened, without his authority, to judge a false heretical Pope. The antecedent seems proved by two clear examples. The first concerns the bishops who met to inquire into the crime and idolatry of blessed Marcellinus; their gathering was a particular council convened without the authority of that same Pope Marcellinus. The second concerns those who met to judge and depose Pope John XII; that gathering was not a general council but only a particular one. Therefore much more could a general council be held to judge a heretical Pope caught in manifest heresy. Disciple. This argument clearly seems to prove that a general council can be convened without the authority of a false heretical Pope, but it does not prove that it can be convened without the authority of a true Pope. Hence it also seems that if the Pope is a heretic, a Catholic Pope must be elected before a general council is summoned. Master. It appears to some that the argument (according to what has been said above) shows plainly that a general council can be convened without the authority of any Pope, true or false. For [illegible, about twelve letters] it is lawful for a particular council to be held without the authority of the Pope to inquire into or judge a true Pope; much more is it lawful for a general council to be celebrated, in a time when the Apostolic See is vacant, without the authority of the Pope, to restrain a false Pope duly, especially if the false Pope can contend by force. But the first is lawful, as has been proved by two examples. Therefore the second too ought to be regarded as lawful. The second argument is this: every people, every community and every body which, without the consent or authority of anyone who is not of that body, can establish law for itself and choose some persons to act on behalf of the whole community or body without another's authority. But all the faithful are one body, as Paul says in Romans 12: we, being many, are one body in Christ; and they are one people and one community. Therefore they can choose some persons who act on behalf of the whole body. Such chosen persons, meeting together, will constitute a general council, because a general council seems to be nothing other than a gathering of some persons who act on behalf of the whole of Christendom. Therefore a general council can be convened without the authority of anyone who is not Catholic and faithful, and consequently without the authority of a heretical Pope. The third argument is this: the universal Church, coming together into one to order something, can be summoned to a general council. But the universal Church could come down to so small a number that it could be gathered together at once. For at one time after the ascension of Christ it was in such a small number. Therefore it is not impossible that it should again come to such a number. And consequently it is not impossible that the universal Church should come together in a general council even if there were no true Pope, just as it is not impossible that the universal Church should come together while the see is vacant. The universal Church has no less power or authority when it cannot come together at once because of its great multitude than when it can come together at once. Therefore whatever the universal Church could do of itself, if it could come together at once, it can do through some persons chosen from its different parts. Supposing, then, that different parts of the universal Church chose some persons who came together into one to order matters concerning the Church of God, those persons so chosen and meeting together (even though there were no true Pope) could be called a general council. And so, when there was no true Pope, a general council could be convened without the authority of the Pope. Disciple. I understand the aforesaid method of positing it in some way, but so that I may understand it better and so reach the truth more clearly, explain by what method, according to the aforesaid assertion, a general council ought to be convened. Master. It is said that it would be reasonable for someone or some persons to be sent from each parish or any community (which can easily come together into one) to an episcopal council or to the parliament of a king, prince or other public power, and that these would choose one or more persons to be sent to a general council; persons so chosen by episcopal councils or by the parliaments of secular powers, and meeting together in one place, can be called a general council. Disciple. What if some parish, or even a diocese, were unwilling to send anyone to a general council? Master. The answer is that the common advantage ought not to be abandoned because of their refusal. Indeed there is an assertion that if many dioceses or kingdoms oppose the convening of a general council, the power of convening a general council would by right pass to other kingdoms or dioceses, because those who hinder the common good of the Christian faith would deservedly be deprived of the power of assembling for a general council. Disciple. I understand this opinion, although I do not think it agrees with the truth. Nevertheless, explain how, according to it, one answers the authorities which plainly assert that a general council ought not to be convened without the authority of the supreme pontiff. Master. The answer is that as a rule a general council ought by no means to be convened without the authority of the supreme pontiff. Yet there is an exception in the case that arises when the Pope becomes a heretic and the electors of the supreme pontiff neglect to elect a Pope, and the matter cannot be provided for except by a general council of the Church. Because of this, as it is said, the authorities of the supreme pontiffs who assert that a general council must not be convened without the authority of the Pope are by no means to be rejected; they are rather to be understood soundly, so that they are in no way interpreted to the prejudice of the Christian faith, which is to be preferred in every way to the supreme pontiff, even a Catholic one.

units.la: CAP. LXXXV.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXV.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod reges & principes & alii laici ad generale concilium debeant, si voluerint, conuenire.
units.tr: In which it is proved that kings, princes and other laymen may, if they wish, come together to a general council.

units.la: Discip. Aduerto, quomodo probari potest primum, quod circa assertionem in præcedenti capitu-lo recitatam irrationabile videbatur. Ideo dic, an secundum hoc possit aliquo modo probari, scilicet quod reges & principes & alii laici ad generale concilium debeant, si voluerint, conuenire. Magist. Antequam motiua dictæ assertionis adducam, ostendam tibi, quare secundum quosdam vna congregatio dicatur & non alia concilium generale, quo declarato motiua quæ proferam magis intelliges. Dicitur autem quod congregatio quæcunq; non ideo solum modo vocatur concilium generale, quia auctoritate summi pontificis conuocatur. Tunc enim omne consistorium cum Papa esset concilium generale. Illa igitur congregatio esset concilium generale reputanda, in qua diuersæ personæ gerentes auctoritatem & vicem vniuersarum partium totius sanitatis ad tractandum de communi bono rite conueniunt, nisi aliqui noluerint vel non potuerint conuenire. Vnde si aliquæ prouinciæ nollent vel non possent personas habentes auctoritates & vicem earum transmittere, non minus esset concilium generale censendum. Ilio viso videtur posse probari, quod reges & principes ac nonnulli laici possunt si voluerint ad generale concilium conuenire: & eiusdem concilii tractatibus interesse. Quod probatur primo auctoritate Nicolai Papæ, quæ ponitur di. 96. c. vbi nam, qui ait: Vbinam legistis Imperatores antecessores vestros synodalibus conuentibus interfuisse, nisi forsitan in quibus de fide tractatum est, qua vniuersalis est, quæ omnibus communis est, qua non solum ad clericos, verum etiam ad laicos & omnes pertinet Christianos. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod conciliis, in quibus de fide tractatur, possunt laici interesse. Quod etiam auctoritatibus simul & exemplis ostenditur. Gelasius enim Papa, vt habetur dist. 15. c. Sancta Romana Ecclesia post illas Noui & Veteris Testamenti scripturas, quas regulariter suscipimus, etiam has suscipi non prohibet: synodum sanctam Nicenam 318. patrum, mediante maximo Constantino Augusto, in qua Arrius haereticus condemnatus est: sanctam synodum Constantinopolitanam, mediante Theodosio seniore Augusto, in qua Macedonius haereticus debitam damnationem excepit. Et infra: Sanctam synodum Chalcedonensem, mediante Martiano Augusto, Anastasio Constantinopolitano Episcopo, in qua Nestoriana & Eutychiana haereses simul cum Dioscoro eiusdem complicibus damnata sunt. Item, Isidorus 6. li. Ethimo. c. 19. & habetur dist. prædicta c. 1. ait: Tertia synodus Ephesina 70. Episcoporum sub minore Theodosio Augusto edita est. Et infra: Quarta synodus Chalcedonensis 63. sacerdotum sub Martiano principe est habita. Item, vt habetur dist. 96. in alia actione Chalcedonensis synodi Martianus Imperator dixit: nos ad confirmandam fidem, non ad potentiam ostendendam exemplo religiosissimi principis Constantini synodo interesse volumus, vt vnitate inuenta non vltra multitudo prauis attractata doctrinis discordet. Item, vt habetur 12. quæst. 1. cap. futuram, de Constantino sic legitur: Idem vero præsidens sancta synodo, quæ apud Niceam congregata est, cum querelam quorundam conspiceret coram se deferendam, ait: vos à nemine diiudicari potestis & c. Item, Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur dist. vigesim. prim. ca. nunc autem, ait: cum tempore quodam contra Sixtum Papam tentassent quosdam malirumoris obiicere, & in concilio, cui Valentinianus intererat, dictum fuisset, non licere aduersus pontificem dare sententiam, surrexit protinus idem Imperator, & in arbitrio præfati pontificis tribuit iudicare iudicium suum. Ex quibus omnibus tam auctoritatibus quam exemplis ostensum videtur, quod Imperatores licite interfuerunt conciliis generalibus: & per consequens licite possunt laici (si voluerint) conciliis generalibus interesse. Quod etiam ratione videtur posse probari, quæ talis est. Quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus tractari & approbari debet, vt notatur in Glos. di. 96. c. vbi nam. Et extra de maior. & obedientia. c. inter quatuor, notat Glos. quod omnes, quos negotium tangit, vocandi sunt. Sed ea quæ tractantur in concilio generali omnes tangunt: quia in concilio generali tractari debet de fide & de aliis quæ ad omnes pertinent Christianos. Igitur laici quos tangunt generalia concilia licite si voluerint poterunt interesse.
units.tr: Disciple. I notice how this first point might be proved, since the assertion recited in the previous chapter seemed unreasonable. So tell me whether it can in any way be proved that kings, princes and other laymen may, if they wish, come to a general council. Master. Before I give the arguments for that assertion, I will show you why, according to some, one gathering is called a general council and another is not. Once that is settled, you will understand better the arguments I put forward. It is said that not every gathering is called a general council merely because it is convened by the authority of the pope. If that were so, every consistory with the Pope would be a general council. A gathering should therefore be regarded as a general council when persons who hold the authority and place of all the parts of the whole body meet in due form to deal with the common good, unless some are unwilling or unable to come. So if some provinces were unwilling or unable to send persons holding authority and standing in their place, it would still be counted a general council. With this in view, it seems it can be shown that kings, princes and some laymen may, if they wish, come to a general council and take part in its deliberations. This is first proved by the authority of Pope Nicholas, cited in Dist. 96, c. "Ubinam", who says: "Where have you read that your predecessor emperors took part in synodal assemblies, except perhaps those in which matters of faith were treated, which is universal, which is common to all, which pertains not only to clerics but also to laymen and to all Christians?" From these words it is clear that laymen may take part in councils in which matters of faith are treated. This is also shown both by authorities and by examples. Pope Gelasius, as is found in Dist. 15, c. "Sancta Romana Ecclesia", after those Scriptures of the New and Old Testament which we regularly accept, does not forbid that these also be accepted: the holy Nicene synod of 318 Fathers, under the great Emperor Constantine, in which the heretic Arius was condemned; the holy Constantinopolitan synod, under the elder Emperor Theodosius, in which the heretic Macedonius received his due condemnation. And below: the holy Council of Chalcedon, under the Emperor Marcian, with Anastasius, Bishop of Constantinople, in which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies were condemned together with Dioscorus, their accomplice. Likewise Isidore, in book 6 of the Etymologies, c. 19, and in the same distinction, c. 1, says: "The third synod of Ephesus of 70 bishops was held under the younger Emperor Theodosius." And below: "The fourth synod of Chalcedon of 63 priests was held under the Emperor Marcian." Likewise, as is found in Dist. 96, in another session of the Council of Chalcedon, the Emperor Marcian said: "We wish to take part in the synod to confirm the faith, not to display power, following the example of the most pious Emperor Constantine, so that, once unity is found, the multitude, led astray by depraved teachings, may no longer be at odds." Likewise, as is found in 12 Qu. 1, c. "Futuram", of Constantine it is read thus: "The same man, presiding over the holy synod gathered at Nicaea, when he saw that complaints of certain men were to be laid before him, said: you cannot be judged by anyone, etc." Likewise, Pope Nicholas, as is found in Dist. 21, c. "Nunc autem", says: "When at one time certain men had tried to bring evil rumours against Pope Sixtus, and in a council which Valentinian attended it had been said that it was not lawful to pass sentence against a bishop, the same Emperor at once rose and left it to the judgement of the said bishop to decide his own judgement." From all these authorities and examples it seems shown that emperors lawfully took part in general councils, and consequently laymen too may lawfully, if they wish, take part in general councils. This can also be shown by reason, which is as follows. What touches all must be dealt with and approved by all, as is noted in the Gloss on Dist. 96, c. "Ubinam". And the Gloss on Extra, "De maioritate et obedientia", c. "Inter quatuor", notes that all whom the business concerns must be summoned. But the matters treated in a general council touch all, since in a general council there must be treatment of faith and of other things which pertain to all Christians. Therefore laymen whom general councils concern may lawfully take part, if they wish.

units.la: Discip. Per rationem istam quilibet laicus posset interesse concilio generali, si vellet: si illa quæ tractantur in generali concilio ab omnibus tractari debent. Magist. Ad istam instantiam respondetur, quod hæc regula, quod omnes tangit ab omnibus tractari debet, intelligenda est, si ab omnibus potest & non apparet ratio manifesta, quare aliquis debeat ab huiusmodi tractatu repelli. Nunc autem non possunt omnes neq; laici neq; clerici ad generale concilium conuenire. Et ideo non omnes debent interesse per seipsos. Debent tamen omnes, qui voluerunt; nisi appareat ratio manifesta repellendi eos per procuratores & alios gerentes mediate vel immediate in speciali, vel cum aliis vices eorum concilio interesse. Et ideo cum dicitur de regibus & principibus & aliis magnis personis laicis, nisi appareat ratio quare debeant repelli, poterint per seipsos si voluerint conciliis generalibus interesse. Unde si reges voluerint poterunt per seipsos conciliis generalibus interesse, nec est necesse quod procuratores vel alios habentes potestatem eorum mittant ad concilium generale. Regnum autem & aliæ communitates, quæ regibus non subsunt, quæ interesse per se non possunt, debent mittere, si volunt procuratores aut subditos vel alios quocunq; nomine censeantur, qui eorum habeant potestatem quantum ad ea quæ tractanda sunt in concilio generali. Discip. Ista opinio seipsam impugnat. Nam si ipsi non debent concilio interesse, de quibus apparet ratio manifesta, quare debent repelli: sequitur quod laici interesse non debent. Nam de illis est ratio euidens, quare sunt a concilio generali excludendi: quia videlicet causa Dei ad laicos nequaquam spectat. Unde Felix Papa, vt legitur dist. 10. c. certum est, ait: Certum est huiusmodi rebus nostris esse salubre, vt cum de causis Dei agitur iuxta ipsius constitutum regiam voluntatem sacerdotibus Christi studeatis subdere, non præferre. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod laici de causis Dei se intromittere non debent. Et per consequens à generali concilio tenentur excludi. Item, ex consuetudine hactenus obseruata hoc constat aperte. Nam ad generalia concilia soli clerici consueuerunt venire: & soli clerici sola concilia celebrauerunt, sicut & ipsi soli vocantur. Magist. Ad primam istarum respondent, quod causæ fidei non solum ad clericos, sed etiam spectant ad laicos. Sicut etiam Deus non solum est Deus clericorum: sed etiam & laicorum. Verumtamen causæ Dei principalius spectant ad clericos, quam ad laicos, si clerici in causis Dei non errent pro eo quod clerici Diuinis sint specialiter deputati. Et sic intelligenda sunt verba Felicis Papæ. Si autem clerici in causis Dei & præcipue contra fidem errent catholicam: causa Dei etiam spectat ad laicos & non ad clericos contra fidem errantes. Discip. De hoc postea interrogabo per plura. Ideo dic quomodo ad secundam rationem respondere contingat. Magist. Dicitur quod circa celebrationem generalium conciliorum multa fuerunt seruanda temporibus retroactis, quæ non sunt nunc de necessitate seruanda, quamuis antea rationabiliter fuerint obseruata: & adhuc talia poterunt venire tempora, quod congruum esset quod seruentur. Et ideo conceditur, quod temporibus præteritis, quibus prælati & clerici sanctitate vitæ doctrinæ & zelo boni communis, & etiam circa temporalia magna industria {a}ductia & experientia clarueunt: congruum fuit vt ipsi soli generalia concilia celebrarent, & vt laici (nisi in casibus specialibus) subtraherentur à tractatoribus concilii generalis. Et tamen in potestate extitit laicorum generalibus conciliis interesse. Sed si vices suas tacite vel expresse clericis committerunt, arctari minime debuerunt. Et ideo quantumcunq; placeret rectoribus & communitatibus laicorum generalibus conciliis interesse, clerici eos excludere de iure non possunt. Discip. Quomodo potest ostendi, quod laici vnquam committerunt potestatem & vices suas clericis ad generale concilium conuocatis. Magist. Videtur quod ex hoc clare potest ostendi, quod in multis conciliis generalibus ordinata fuerint, quae absq; consensu laicorum tacito vel expresso non poterant ordinari. Cum igitur non sit aliqualiter praesumendum, quod generalia concilia praesumpserint ordinare ea, quae potestatem exercebant eorum: videtur dicendum, quod in generalibus conciliis congregati commissionem aliquam & potestatem à laicis habuerint. Discip. Pone aliqua exempla de ordinatis in conciliis generalibus, quae absq; consensu expresso vel tacito laicorum minime statui debuerunt. Magist. Ponitur exemplum de pluribus libertatibus Ecclesiasticis, quibus clerici absq; consensu laicorum gaudere non debent: cum sit in manifestum praeiudicium laicorum. Clerici autem absq; consensu laicorum nihil in praeiudicium eorum possunt statuere; quia, teste Innocentio tertio, vt habetur extra, de iudiciis. c. nouit, sicut laici iurisdictionem clericorum perturbare; ita clerici iurisdictionem laicorum non debent minuere. Quare clerici in praeiudicium laicorum absq; eorum consensu nihil possunt de rebus temporalibus & libertatibus eorum disponere. Discip. Quo iure clerici gaudeant libertatibus Ecclesiasticis, an scilicet iure Diuino vel humano, & an iure solum modo canonico, vel iure regum & principum secularium. Secundo tractatu istius operis diligenter inquiram. Ideo materiam istam dimitte. Et dic breuiter, quare dicitur, quod mulieres non sunt simpliciter contra voluntatem eorum à generalibus conciliis excludendae. Magist. Dicitur quod hoc est propter vnitatem fidei virorum & mulierum, quae omnes tangit: & in qua non masculus nec foemina, secundum Apostolum ad Collo. 3. In nouo homine non est masculus & foemina. Et ideo vbi sapientia, bonitas, vel potentia mulierum esset tractatui fidei (de qua potissime est tractandum in concilio generali) necessaria, non est mulier à generali concilio excludenda.
units.tr: Disciple. By this argument any layman could take part in a general council if he wished, if what is treated in a general council must be dealt with by all. Master. To this objection the reply is that this rule, "what touches all must be dealt with by all", is to be understood as applying if it can be done by all and there is no clear reason why someone should be kept away from such deliberations. Now, however, not all can come to a general council, neither laymen nor clerics. And so not all ought to take part in person. Yet all who wish should do so, unless there is a clear reason to exclude them, by proxies and others who act for them, either directly or indirectly, in particular cases, or with others who take their place at the council. And so, when it is said of kings, princes and other great lay persons, unless there appears a reason why they should be excluded, they may, if they wish, take part in general councils in person. Hence, if kings wish, they may take part in general councils in person, and it is not necessary that they send proxies or others who have their authority to the general council. But kingdoms and other communities which are not subject to kings, and which cannot take part in person, ought to send, if they wish, proxies or subjects or others, by whatever name they are called, who hold their authority in regard to the matters to be treated in the general council. Disciple. This opinion refutes itself. For if those ought not to take part in the council against whom there is a clear reason for exclusion, it follows that laymen ought not to take part at all. For there is a plain reason why they must be excluded from a general council, namely that the cause of God in no way concerns laymen. Hence Pope Felix, as is read in Dist. 10, c. "Certum est", says: "It is certain that it is salutary for matters like ours that, when the cause of God is dealt with, you should subject yourselves to the priests of Christ according to his own constitution, and not put yourselves before them." From these words it is clear that laymen ought not to meddle in the causes of God, and consequently they must be excluded from a general council. Again, it is plainly established by the custom observed until now. For only clerics have been accustomed to come to general councils, and only clerics have held councils, just as only they are summoned. Master. To the first of these, the answer is that matters of faith pertain not only to clerics but also to laymen, just as God is not only the God of clerics but also of laymen. Yet the causes of God pertain more principally to clerics than to laymen, provided that clerics do not err in the causes of God, because clerics are specially set apart for divine things. And the words of Pope Felix are to be understood in this way. But if clerics err in the causes of God, and especially against the Catholic faith, then the cause of God pertains also to laymen, and not to clerics, when they err against the faith. Disciple. I will question you more about this later. Now tell me how it may be answered to the second argument. Master. It is said that in the holding of general councils many things were to be observed in earlier times which are not now of necessity to be observed, although they were reasonably observed before; and still other times may come in which it would be fitting that they be observed. And so it is granted that in past times, when prelates and clerics shone with holiness of life, teaching and zeal for the common good, and also with great skill and experience in temporal affairs, it was fitting that they alone should hold general councils, and that laymen (except in special cases) should be kept away from the deliberators of a general council. Yet it was within the power of laymen to take part in general councils. But if they had committed their authority to the clerics, tacitly or expressly, they ought not to have been restricted at all. And so, however much it might please the rulers and communities of laymen to take part in general councils, clerics cannot by right exclude them. Disciple. How can it be shown that laymen ever committed their power and authority to the clerics called to a general council? Master. It seems that this can clearly be shown from the fact that many things were decreed in many general councils which could not be decreed without the tacit or express consent of laymen. Since, then, it is in no way to be presumed that general councils presumed to decree those things which concerned the exercise of laymen's power, it seems we must say that those gathered in general councils had some commission and power from laymen. Disciple. Give some examples of things decreed in general councils which ought not to have been settled without the express or tacit consent of laymen. Master. An example is given of the many ecclesiastical liberties which clerics ought not to enjoy without the consent of laymen, since they would be a plain prejudice to laymen. Clerics, moreover, cannot decide anything to the prejudice of laymen without their consent; because, as Innocent III testifies, in Extra, "De iudiciis", c. "Nouit", just as laymen disturb the jurisdiction of clerics, so clerics ought not to diminish the jurisdiction of laymen. Therefore clerics cannot, to the prejudice of laymen, dispose of their temporal affairs and liberties without their consent. Disciple. By what right do clerics enjoy ecclesiastical liberties: whether by divine or human right, and whether by canon law alone, or by the right of kings and secular princes? I will examine this carefully in the second treatise of this work. So set this matter aside, and briefly tell me why it is said that women are not to be excluded from general councils absolutely against their will. Master.
