It is said that this is on account of the unity of faith of men and women, which touches all, and in which, according to the Apostle to the Colossians 3, "there is neither male nor female in the new man". And so, where the wisdom, goodness or power of women would be necessary for the treatment of faith (which above all must be dealt with in a general council), a woman is not to be excluded from a general council.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVI.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXVI.

units.la: In quo quaeritur, quam potestatem habeat concilium generale supra Papam in haeresi deprehensum.
units.tr: In which it is asked what power a general council has over a Pope caught in heresy.

units.la: Discipulus. Istam assertionem de mulieribus (quae secundum Apostolum docere non debent) tam irrationabilem aestimo, quod nolo eam amplius pertractari. Ideo ipsa dimissa: dic quam potestatem habeat concilium generale super Papam in haeresi deprehensum. Magist. Ad hoc respondeo: est primus, quod concilium generale debet Papam haereticum de Apostolica Sede expellere (si aliter non poterit) per potentiam temporalem. Et illam poenam sibi non potest remittere; licet secundum quosdam, si Papa haereticus rediret ad catholicam vnitatem, concilium generale, si non esset Papa ipsum de facto nouiter in Papam eligere, & in Sedem Apostolicam collocare posset. Aliis dicentibus, quod ad concilium generale electio summi pontificis minime spectat, sed specialiter ad Romanos. Secundo potest concilium generale Papam haereticum expulsum de Apostolica Sede ab omni Ecclesiastico ordine degradare; sed istam poenam potest absolute sibi retinere. Sicut & potest ipsum curiae tradere seculari vel perpetuo carceri mancipare, & omnia bona eius propria confiscare. Quibus tamen poenis non de necessitate tenetur haereticum Papam percellere: quia istae sunt poenae non à iure Diuino, sed à iure positiuo taxatae. Istud autem continet veritatem, si Papa interfuerit generali concilio, sed si sede vacante fuerit celebratum concilium generale videtur; quod concilium generale praedictas poenas Papae haeretico non potest remittere. Quia in huiusmodi poenis (haereticis infligendis) concilium generale minime Papam comprehendens, est inferius & minoris iurisdictionis quam sit Papa. Et ideo cum huiusmodi poenae à Papa vel à conciliis generalibus praesente Papa sint taxatae, per generale concilium sede vacante remitti non possunt. Discip. Secundum ista vnum concilium generale maiorem potestatem haberet, quam aliud. Et per consequens aliud non esset generale. Magist. Respondetur quod non est inconueniens, vnum concilium habere maiorem potestatem quam aliud: & tamen vtrumq; esse generale. Quemadmodum vsq; ad finem seculi Ecclesia vniuersalis vno tempore habet maiorem potestatem & maiorem auctoritatem quam in alio. Nam Ecclesia vniuersalis maiorem potestatem habet & auctoritatem Apostolica Sede vacante, quam quando non vacat.
units.tr: Disciple. I think this assertion about women (who, according to the Apostle, ought not to teach) is so unreasonable that I do not wish to discuss it any further. So let it be set aside, and tell me what power a general council has over a Pope caught in heresy. Master. To this I answer: first, a general council ought to expel a heretical Pope from the Apostolic See (if it cannot do so otherwise) by temporal power. And it cannot remit that penalty to him; although, according to some, if the heretical Pope returned to Catholic unity, the general council could, if the Pope were not already in office, elect him anew and set him in the Apostolic See. Others say that the election of the supreme pontiff does not belong to a general council at all, but specially to the Romans. Secondly, a general council can, once the heretical Pope has been expelled from the Apostolic See, degrade him from every ecclesiastical order; but it can keep this penalty for itself absolutely. Just as it can also hand him over to the secular court or consign him to perpetual imprisonment, and confiscate all his private goods. Yet the heretical Pope is not necessarily bound to be struck with these penalties, because these are penalties fixed not by divine law but by positive law. This is true, however, if the Pope was present at the general council; but if a general council was celebrated while the see was vacant, it seems that the general council cannot remit the aforesaid penalties to a heretical Pope. For in imposing such penalties on heretics, a general council that does not include the Pope is inferior and of lesser jurisdiction than the Pope is. And therefore, since penalties of this kind have been fixed by the Pope or by general councils with the Pope present, they cannot be remitted by a general council while the see is vacant. Disciple. According to this, one general council would have greater power than another, and consequently the other would not be general. Master. It is answered that there is no inconvenience in one council having greater power than another, and yet both being general. Just as, until the end of the world, the universal Church at one time has greater power and greater authority than at another. For the universal Church has greater power and authority when the Apostolic See is vacant than when it is not vacant.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXVII.

units.la: Quod Papa nouiter electus canonice potest alium Papam haereticum punire. Et quas poenas potest ei remittere & quas non.
units.tr: That a Pope newly and canonically elected can punish another Pope who is a heretic, and which penalties he can remit to him and which he cannot.

units.la: Discip. Dic de summo pontifice, si fuit nouiter electus, quam poenam potest Papae haretico infligere? Magist. Tenent nonnulli pro certissimo, quod Papa electus canonice quamuis in Sede Apostolica intronisatus non fuerit, potest Papae haeretico omnes poenas praedictas & alias imponere.
units.tr: Discip. Tell me about the supreme pontiff: if he has been newly elected, what penalty can he inflict on a Pope who is a heretic? Magist. Some hold as quite certain that a Pope canonically elected, even if he has not yet been enthroned in the Apostolic See, can impose on a heretical Pope all the aforesaid penalties and others besides.

units.la: {a} ductia] doctrina, sic in editione. re, quas tamen omnes praeter primam, scilicet expulsionem de Sede Apostolica, valet sibi remittere de plenitudine potestatis. Quomodo etiam Papam haereticum, si ad fidei unitatem redierit absq; degradatione, licet non absq; poenitentia & abnegatione prauitatis absq; incarnatione & bonorum suorum confiscatione, imo etiam absq; abiuratione prauitatis haereticae potest recipere. Discip. De summo pontifice si esset electus canonice dubium non videtur, quin posset Papam haereticum debita poena punire: sed non videtur, quod ante iustitiam factam de Papa haeretico vel ante mortem eius posset alius Papa rite substitui. Magist. Nonnulli habent quod non est dubitatio apud intelligentes, quin posset eligi verus Papa pro haeretico Sedem Apostolicam occupanti: quia sede vacante notorie potest eligi verus Papa. Sed quam cito Papa sit notorie haereticus, Sedes Apostolica notorie vacat. Igitur quantumcunq; haereticus Papa de facto occuparet Sedem Apostolicam, est Papa catholicus eligendus.
units.tr: {a} ductia] doctrina, thus in the edition. ...re, all of which, except the first, namely expulsion from the Apostolic See, he may remit to him by the fullness of power. In the same way he can receive a heretical Pope back, if he returns to unity of the faith, without degradation, though not without penance and renunciation of his depravity, and without imprisonment and confiscation of his goods; indeed even without abjuration of the heretical depravity. Discip. If the Pope was canonically elected, there seems to be no doubt that he could punish a heretical Pope with the due penalty; but it does not seem that another Pope could be rightly substituted before justice has been done on the heretical Pope, or before his death. Magist. Some hold that among the learned there is no doubt that a true Pope could be elected in place of a Pope who occupies the Apostolic See as a heretic, since a true Pope can be elected notoriously when the see is vacant. But as soon as a Pope is notoriously a heretic, the Apostolic See is notoriously vacant. Therefore, however heretical the Pope who de facto occupies the Apostolic See, a Catholic Pope is to be elected.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXVIII.

units.la: In quo ostenditur, quam potestatem habet collegium Cardinalium supra Papam.
units.tr: In which it is shown what power the college of cardinals has over the Pope.

units.la: Discipulus. Haec materia locum habet in tractatu De gestis circa fidem altercantium orthodoxam. Ideo ad collegium cardinalium te converte: & quam potestatem habeat super Papam haereticum manifestum expone. Magist. De hoc sunt assertiones contrariae. Una est, quod collegium cardinalium super Papam haereticum nulla potestatem habet specialem, nisi sicut caeteri Episcopi, Presbyteri & Diaconi. Cuius ratio assignatur talis. Collegiū cardinalium nullā potestatem aut iurisdictionē habet ex ordinatione Diuina vel ex iure Diuino: cum ex iure Diuino sit nullatenus institutum: imo nec in toto iure Diuino de ipso sit mentio. Omnē igitur potestatem aut iurisdictionem habet collegiū cardinalium à summo pontifice. Sed non legitur quod summus pontifex aliquam potestatem vel iurisdictionem specialem dederit collegio cardinalium super Papam haereticum. Igitur nullam iurisdictionem habet super Papam haereticum. Item, consiliarii alicuius praelati vel principis ex hoc, quod consiliarii sunt, non habent iurisdictionem specialem super praelatum vel principem delinquentē. Sed cardinales sunt tantummodo consiliarii Papae: & in hoc solùmodo praecellunt alios clericos & praelatos saltē Romanos. Igitur collegiū cardinalium non habet specialiter corrigere vel punire Papā, si haeretica incurrerit prauitate. Disc. Ista ratio accipit manifeste falsum, scil. q; cardinales solùmodo praecellunt alios clericos in hoc, q; sunt consiliarii Papae: qa constat, q; in hoc praecellunt, quod habent ius eligendi summū pontificē. Multa etiā alia priuilegia habent vltra clericos alios & praelatos. Mag. Respondetur, quod per accidens est, q; collegiū cardinalium habet ius eligendi summū pontificē. Unde & aliquando ius illud nequaq; habuit: & adhuc posset illo iure priuari. Posset enim ius eligendi summū pontificē concedi Imperatori vel aliis Episcopis aut clericis quam cardinalibus. Et ita est p accidens, quod collegiū cardinaliū habet ius eligendi summū pontificem. Et sic est p accidens, quod cardinales multa priuilegia habent, quibus alii plati & clerici minime gaudent. Quare per hoc, quod cardinales habent ius eligendi summū pontificē & alia priuilegia multa concludi nō potest, quod habent iurisdictionē speciale super Papam haereticū. Et ideo cum non habeatur in iure, quod cardinales super Papā haereticum specialem obtineant iurisdictionē, non est eis talis iurisdictio tribuenda. Disc. Prima ratio fortis mihi videtur: nec scio respondere ad ipsam. Quid autē sentis de ipsa, post hoc opus ingram. Nunc autem dic, q d haberet facere collegium cardinaliū secundum istam assertionem, si Papa efficeretur haereticus. Mag. Secundū istā assertionem, si Papa efficeretur haereticus, vltra illa quae alii clerici & plati eorundē ordinū & graduum deberent facere circa Papam haereticū cardinales nihil haberent facere, nisi ea quae eis cōpetunt, quando Sedes Apostolica vacat p mortem naturale summi pontificis. Et ideo sicut moriente Papa cardinales habent eligere summū pontificem, ita si constiterit collegio cardinaliū Papam esse haereticū manifestum, ad electionē veri summi pontificis deberent procedere. Disc. Ista opinio apparentia videtur habere. Et prima ratio est tam fortis, q ad ipsam nescio respondere. De qua q d sentias, post completionē huius operis indagabo. Nunc autem enarra assertionē contrariam. Mag. Alia assertio est, q si Papa efficeretur haereticus, collegiū cardinalium deberet specialiter ipsum debita poena punire. Cuius ratio assignatur talis. Ad quē spectat institutio alicuius, ad eundē pertinet destitutio eiusdē, si ille nō habeat superiorem. Primas enim habet instituere Episcopū, quē tamen nō potest destituere: quia tā primas quam constitutus ab eo habent superiorē, q reseruat sibi destitutionē taliter instituti. Sed si primas non haberet superiorē, qui instituit Episcopū, posset ex causa destituere. Institutio autē summi pontificis spectat ad collegiū cardinalium, q non habet superiorem, qui sibi reseruet destitutionē summi pontificis, si efficeretur haereticus. Igitur ad collegium cardinalium specialiter spectat destitutio, si haereticam incurrat prauitatem. Et per consequens punitio Papae haeretici ad collegium cardinalium spectat. Item, non minoris iurisdictionis est capitulum cardinalium, quam capitulum alicuius Ecclesiae cathedralis. Sed capitulum (sede vacante) potest punire haereticos, qui in eadem dioecesi iunt reperti, extra, de haereticis. c. ad abolendam: vbi habetur, quod clerici sede vacante possunt haereticos iudicare. Ergo multo magis collegium cardinalium sede vacante potest Papam haereticum iudicare. Discip. Per istam rationem probaretur (sede vacante) per hoc quod Episcopus haereticam incurreret prauitatem, posset capitulum suum Episcopum iudicare. Magist. Respondetur, quod Episcopi habent priuilegium speciale, quod scilicet non possunt iudicari, nisi per Episcopos vel Papam: cum inquisitores haereticae prauitatis non habeant potestatem inquirendi de episcopis. Et ideo capitulum non habet potestatem iudicandi episcopum suum haereticum, sed in collegio cardinalium sunt plures episcopi. Et ideo poterit Papam haereticum iudicare. Discip. Nunquid capitulum (si episcopus efficeretur haereticus) obediet ei, ex quo eum iudicare non potest? Magist. Respondetur, quod capitulum, si constet ei episcopum in labem haereticam incidisse, ei obedire non debet: nec tamen iudicabit ipsum, sed insinuabit & accusabit eum superiori, qui habet potestatem iudicandi ipsum.
units.tr: Disciple. This matter belongs in the treatise on the acts of those who dispute over the orthodox faith. So turn to the college of cardinals, and explain clearly what power it has over a heretical Pope. Master. On this point there are opposing assertions. One is that the college of cardinals has no special power over a heretical Pope, beyond that of other bishops, presbyters and deacons. The reason given for this runs as follows. The college of cardinals has no power or jurisdiction from divine ordinance or from divine law, since it was never instituted by divine law; indeed, the whole of divine law makes no mention of it. Therefore the college of cardinals has all its power and jurisdiction from the supreme pontiff. But we do not read that the supreme pontiff gave the college of cardinals any special power or jurisdiction over a heretical Pope. Therefore it has no jurisdiction over a heretical Pope. Likewise, the counsellors of any prelate or prince do not, simply because they are counsellors, have special jurisdiction over the prelate or prince who offends. But cardinals are only counsellors of the Pope, and in this they surpass other clergy and prelates, at least Roman ones. Therefore the college of cardinals has no special right to correct or punish the Pope if he falls into heretical depravity. Disciple. This argument plainly assumes something false, namely that cardinals surpass other clergy only in being counsellors of the Pope. For it is clear that they surpass others in having the right to elect the supreme pontiff. They also have many other privileges beyond other clergy and prelates. Master. The answer is that it is by accident that the college of cardinals has the right to elect the supreme pontiff. Hence at some times it has not had that right at all, and it could still be deprived of it. For the right to elect the supreme pontiff could be granted to the Emperor, or to other bishops or clergy other than cardinals. So it is by accident that the college of cardinals has the right to elect the supreme pontiff. And in the same way it is by accident that cardinals have many privileges which other prelates and clergy do not enjoy. Therefore from the fact that cardinals have the right to elect the supreme pontiff and many other privileges, it cannot be concluded that they have special jurisdiction over a heretical Pope. And so, since the law does not hold that cardinals have special jurisdiction over a heretical Pope, such jurisdiction is not to be attributed to them. Disciple. The first argument seems strong to me, and I do not know how to answer it. Afterwards, when this work is finished, I will look into what you think of it. But now tell me what the college of cardinals would have to do, according to this assertion, if the Pope became a heretic. Master. According to this assertion, if the Pope became a heretic, the cardinals would have nothing to do beyond what other clergy and prelates of the same order and rank ought to do concerning a heretical Pope, except what belongs to them when the Apostolic See is vacant through the natural death of the supreme pontiff. And so, just as on the death of the Pope the cardinals have to elect a supreme pontiff, so if it were established to the college of cardinals that the Pope was manifestly a heretic, they ought to proceed to the election of a true supreme pontiff. Disciple. This opinion seems to have some plausibility. And its first argument is so strong that I do not know how to answer it. I will examine what I think of it after this work is completed. But now set out the opposing assertion. Master. The other assertion is that if the Pope became a heretic, the college of cardinals ought to punish him specially with the appropriate penalty. The reason given for this runs as follows. Whoever has the power to institute something also has the power to depose it, if he has no superior. For the primate has the power to institute a bishop, yet he cannot depose him, because both the primate and the one appointed by him have a superior, who reserves to himself the deposition of one so appointed. But if the primate who institutes a bishop had no superior, he could depose him for cause. Now the institution of the supreme pontiff belongs to the college of cardinals, and it has no superior who reserves to himself the deposition of the supreme pontiff should he become a heretic. Therefore deposition, should he fall into heretical depravity, belongs specially to the college of cardinals. And consequently the punishment of a heretical Pope belongs to the college of cardinals. Likewise, the chapter of cardinals has no less jurisdiction than the chapter of any cathedral church. But the chapter, when the see is vacant, can punish heretics found within the same diocese, extra, de haereticis. c. ad abolendam, where it is held that clergy, while the see is vacant, may judge heretics. Therefore much more so the college of cardinals, while the Apostolic See is vacant, can judge a heretical Pope. Disciple. By this reasoning it would follow that, while the see is vacant, if a bishop fell into heretical depravity, his chapter could judge the bishop. Master. The answer is that bishops have a special privilege, namely that they cannot be judged except by bishops or the Pope, since inquisitors of heretical depravity have no power to inquire into bishops. Therefore the chapter has no power to judge its heretical bishop; but there are several bishops in the college of cardinals. Therefore it can judge a heretical Pope. Disciple. Will the chapter, if the bishop became a heretic, obey him, since it cannot judge him? Master. The answer is that if it is established to the chapter that the bishop has fallen into heretical stain, it ought not to obey him; yet it will not judge him, but will report and accuse him to the superior who has the power to judge him.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXIX.

units.la: In quo quaeritur, qualiter Romani possunt Papam haereticum punire. Et quod similiter est dicendum de eis, sicut de collegio cardinalium, ut in precedenti capitulo.
units.tr: In which it is asked how the Romans can punish a heretical Pope; and that concerning them the same must be said as concerning the college of cardinals, as in the preceding chapter.

units.la: Disciplus. Nunquid Romani, si Papa fiat haereticus, possunt eum poenis praedictis punire? Magist. De hoc possunt esse diversi modi dicendi. Unus, quod si Papa efficitur haereticus, Romani possunt & debent Papam haereticum expellere de apostolica sede, eumque vitare tenentur, & alium Papam sibi possunt eligere, illi scil. Romani, quibus ius competit eligendi. Sed alias poenas, scil. degradationem, incarcerationem, & bonorum suorum confiscationem sibi non possunt infligere. Alius modus dicendi potest esse, quod Romani omnibus praedictis modis & poenis possunt Papam haereticum coercere. Isti modi dicendi fulciuntur similibus rationibus, quibus assertiones contrariae de collegio cardinalium recitatae in priori cap.
units.tr: Disciple. Can the Romans, if the Pope becomes a heretic, punish him with the aforesaid penalties? Master. On this question there can be different ways of speaking. One is that if the Pope becomes a heretic, the Romans can and ought to expel the heretical Pope from the apostolic see, and they are bound to avoid him, and they can choose another Pope for themselves, namely those Romans to whom the right of electing belongs. But they cannot inflict on him other penalties, namely deposition, imprisonment, and confiscation of his goods. Another way of speaking can be that the Romans can restrain a heretical Pope by all the aforesaid means and penalties. These ways of speaking are supported by similar arguments to those by which the contrary assertions about the college of cardinals, recited in the former chapter, are supported.

units.la: CAP. XC.
units.tr: CHAPTER XC.

units.la: Vbi inquiritur, utrum episcopus Diaecesanus posset Papam haereticum punire. Quod sic, tribus rationibus probatur. Et ibidem ponitur opin. contraria, & probatur unica ratione, ad quam etiam respondetur.
units.tr: Where it is inquired whether a diocesan bishop could punish a heretical Pope. That this is so is proven by three reasons. The contrary opinion is set out there and proven by a single reason, to which an answer is also given.

units.la: Disciplus. Istam materiam duxi ad alia tempora reseruandam. Ideo tracta de Diaecesano, in cuius Diaecesi haereticus Papa moraretur, scil. si Papa haereticus de facto teneret curiam in Parisiis, vel in Florentia, vel alia civitate episcopum habente: an episcopus civitatis posset de iure Papam haereticum coercere poenis praefatis. Magist. Sunt nonnulli dicentes, quod Diaecesanus episcopus, in cuius Diaecesi Papa haereticus notorie moraretur, de iure valeret, & deberet invocato auxilio brachii secularis, si tantam posset habere potentiam, Papam haereticum captiuare, ipsumque denunciare ab omnibus catholicis detinendum. Probatur hoc primo sic: Haereticus, qui nullo modo gaudet privilegio speciali ultra haereticos episcopos, quantum ad praedicta, est subiectus Diaecesani iudicio: quia alii episcopi in his subiecti sunt iudicio Diaecesani. Sed Papa haereticus nullo modo gaudet privilegio speciali ultra alios episcopos, sicut ostensum est supra c. 71. Igitur Papa haereticus quantum ad praedicta subditur iudicio Diaecesani. Item quantum ad praedicta est Papa subiectus iudicio illius, qui tenetur terram ad sui iurisdictionem spectantem de omni prauitate haeretica expurgare: quia sine praedictis terra de haeretica prauitate purgari non potest. Ad episcopum autem spectat totam suam diaecesim de omni haeretica prauitate expurgare, extr. de haereticis cap. excommunicamus. in fine, ubi sic legitur: si quis autem episcopus super expurgando de sua diaecesi haeretica prauitatis fermento negligens fuerit vel remissus, cum id certis inditiis apparuerit & ab episcopali officio deponatur: & in locum ipsius alter substituatur, qui velit & possit haereticam confundere prauitatem. Igitur Papa haereticus quantum ad praedicta iudicio episcopi est subiectus. Tertio probatur idem sic: Ratione delicti fit aliquis de foro alterius, extr. de raptoribus, c. 1. & 13. q. 6. c. 1. & extr. de foro competenti, postulasti & 6. q. 3. c. placuit. Igitur si Papa haereticus in Diaecesi alicuius episcopi male docendo vel parochianos episcopi ad prauitatem inducendo delinquit, fit de foro eiusdem episcopi & eidem est subiectus. Episcopus autem potest sibi subiectos haereticos captiuare. Igitur de iure potest episcopus captiuare Papam haereticum in sua diaecesi commorantem. Discip. Licet sit regula generalis, quod ratione delicti fit quis de foro alterius: tamen, sicut dicit Glossa extr. de raptoribus cap. 1. ab hac generalitate excipitur quilibet superior, qui vbicunque crimen committat non potest iudicari nisi a Papa, si agatur ad depositionem. Cum ergo nullus sit superior Papa, nullus inferior poterit iudicare ipsum quantumcunque in diaecesi delinquat alterius. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur, quod licet de intellectu Glossae (quantum prima facie sonat) inter Iuristas fuerint opiniones diversae, secundum quod innuit Glossa 3. q. 3. cap. 1. Unde & Glossa vbi prius, scil. extr. de raptoribus c. 1. dicit, opinionem huiusmodi fuisse, quod si archiepiscopus committit crimen aliquod in parochia alterius archiepiscopi, vel episcopi suffraganei alterius archiepiscopi, iudicari potest ab allo archiepiscopo vel episcopo archiepiscopi. Ad hoc enim 96. dist. cap. duo, vbi Ambrosius ratione criminis commissi in sua parrochia excommunicauit Imperatorem: quod alias non auderet. Tamen de illo, qui non est maior, imo minor omni episcopo, videtur tenendum, quod ratione delicti fit de foro episcopi illius, in cuius dioecesi probatur delinquere. Cum igitur Papa haereticus non sit maior, sed minor omni episcopo, quia omnis haereticus minor est omni catholico 24. quaest. 1. cap. Si autem, sequitur quod Papa haereticus ratione delicti fit de foro dioecesani, in cuius dioecesi commoratur. Glossa igitur, quae dicit, quod a generalitate istius regulae excipitur quilibet superior &c. intelligeda est de superioribus, qui non obstante delicto permanet superior. De illo autem, qui fuit superior, & per consequens delictum ipso facto fit inferior, & omni superioritate spirituali priuatur ipso iure: non debet intelligi, vt videtur. Quare cum Papa haereticus ipso facto factus est inferior omni catholico, in Papa haeretico non habet dictum Glossae locum. Et ideo episcopus, in cuius dioecesi Papa haereticus moraretur, posset ipsum detinere, non tamen solenniter degradare, sicut nec eum deponere posset. Quod ex hoc probatur, quod depositiones episcoporum solummodo pontifici reseruantur: extra de translationibus 23. q. 7. c. quaevis & c. dudum & c. discutere. Et propter hoc etiam episcopus non posset Papam haereticum seculari curiae tradere: quia nullus episcopus, antequam fuerit ab omni ordine ecclesiastico degradatus, curiae seculari est tradendus. Discip. Narra assertionem contrariam. Magist. Assertio contraria tenet, quod nullus potest Papam haereticum detinere, nec aliquam in eum dictare sententiam. Quae tali ratione probatur. Ille non est iudex alterius, nec aliquam potestatem habet super ipsum, cuius sententia lata contra ipsum (sine examinatione, vtrum sit iusta vel iniusta) est penitus reprobanda, & nullo modo seruanda. Sed sententia cuiuslibet episcopi lata contra ipsum, qui habetur pro Papa, siue sit haereticus siue catholicus, absq; examinatione vtrum sit iusta est penitus reprobanda. Igitur nullus episcopus est iudex Papae haeretici. Maior videtur esse manifesta: quia de sententia illius, qui se asserit iudicem alicuius alterius, & allegat causam possibilem, ex qua esset iudex eius, est inquisitio facienda, an causa, quam allegat, sit vera. Et per consequens est inquisitio facienda, an sententia eius sit iusta vel iniusta. Minor vero exemplo probatur. Nam Dioscorus sententiam excommunicationis in Papam Leonem dictauit: & videtur probabile, quod contra eum allegauit haereticam prauitatem: & tamen absq; omni examinatione vel inquisitione, an sententia Dioscori esset iusta vel iniusta, fuit eadem sententia reprobanda, teste Nicolao Papa, qui, vt habetur dist. 21. c. in tantum, referens verba concilii Chalcedonensis, ait: quoniam secundum excessibus priorem iniquitatem valde transcendit, praesumpsit enim excommunicationem dictare etiam aduersus archiepiscopum magnae Romae Leonem &c. Nunquam ibi legis inquisitionem fuisse factam, vtrum iuste vel iniuste Dioscorus ipsam excommunicationem dictasset: non plane, sed absq; controuersia hoc in eo vlti sunt, quia cum esset inferior, potiorem quibuslibet conatus est lacessere iniuriis. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod si aliquis episcopus ex quacunq; causa Papam praesumpserit captiuare, vel excommunicare, vel lacessere qualicunq; iniuria, non est inquirendum, an Papa sit catholicus vel haereticus: quia de sententia talis episcopi vel alia iniuria seu molestia illata Papae, nulla est inquisitio certe penitus facienda. Ergo siue Papa sit haereticus, siue catholicus, nullus episcopus debet ei molestiam inferre qualemcunq;. Et per consequens eum detinere non debet. Discip. Ista ratio non videtur concludere. Et tamen dic, quomodo respondetur ad ipsam. Magist. Respondetur, quod notorium fuit Dioscorum esse haereticum. Et ideo nullam penitus habuit iurisdictionem super Papam, etiam si fuisset haereticus. Quare de sententia eius non fuit inquisitio facienda, an esset iniusta, hoc est an esset ex causa iusta, quamuis notorium fuerit quod non fuit iusta ex origine. Secus autem esset de episcopo catholico: quia si esset episcopus catholicus, vel episcopus de quo non esset manifestum, quod esset haereticus: si Papam captiuaret vel denunciaret tanquam haereticum excommunicatum & excommunicationis sententiam incurrisse, esset inquisitio facienda, an iuste vel indebite processisset. Et si inueniretur, quod Papa esset manifeste haereticus, factum episcopi esset a catholicis approbandum. Discip. Nunquid Papa haereticus posset appellare ab episcopo taliter ipsum detinente. Magist. Respondetur quod de iure non posset, nisi allegaret causam probabilem, quae si esset probata, deberet sufficiens reputari.
units.tr: Disciplus. I have thought this matter should be reserved for another time. So treat of the diocesan bishop in whose diocese a heretical Pope might stay, that is, if a heretical Pope were in fact holding his court in Paris, or in Florence, or in another city that has a bishop: whether the bishop of that city could by right coerce the heretical Pope with the aforesaid penalties. Magist. Some say that the diocesan bishop in whose diocese a heretical Pope notoriously stays would by right, and ought, having invoked the aid of the secular arm, if he could have so great a power, to take the heretical Pope captive and to proclaim that he be held by all Catholics. This is proved first thus: a heretic who in no way enjoys a special privilege beyond other heretical bishops, as far as the aforesaid matters go, is subject to the judgment of the diocesan, because other bishops are subject in these matters to the judgment of the diocesan. But a heretical Pope in no way enjoys a special privilege beyond other bishops, as has been shown above ch. 71. Therefore the heretical Pope, as far as the aforesaid matters go, is subject to the judgment of the diocesan. Likewise, as far as the aforesaid matters go, the Pope is subject to the judgment of him who is bound to cleanse of all heretical depravity the land belonging to his jurisdiction, because without these things the land cannot be purged of heretical depravity. It belongs to the bishop to cleanse his whole diocese of all heretical depravity, extr. de haereticis cap. excommunicamus at the end, where it reads: "if any bishop is negligent or remiss in cleansing his diocese of the leaven of heretical depravity, and this appears by certain signs, he shall be deposed from the episcopal office, and another shall be substituted in his place who is willing and able to confound heretical depravity." Therefore the heretical Pope, as far as the aforesaid matters go, is subject to the judgment of the bishop. Thirdly, the same is proved thus: by reason of a crime someone becomes subject to another's forum, extr. de raptoribus, c. 1. & 13. q. 6. c. 1. & extr. de foro competenti, postulasti & 6. q. 3. c. placuit. Therefore if the heretical Pope sins in the diocese of some bishop, by teaching badly or by leading the bishop's parishioners into depravity, he becomes of that bishop's forum and is subject to him. But a bishop can take captive heretics subject to him. Therefore by right a bishop can take captive a heretical Pope dwelling in his diocese. Discip. It is a general rule that by reason of a crime someone becomes subject to another's forum; yet, as the Gloss says in extr. de raptoribus cap. 1. any superior is excepted from this generality, who, wherever he commits a crime, cannot be judged except by the Pope, if the matter concerns deposition. Since there is no superior above the Pope, no inferior can judge him, however much he sins in another's diocese. Magist. To this it is answered that although among the jurists there have been differing opinions about the meaning of the Gloss (as it sounds at first sight), as the Gloss in 3. q. 3. cap. 1. hints, the Gloss in the place just cited, namely extr. de raptoribus c. 1. says that the opinion of this kind was that if an archbishop commits some crime in the parish of another archbishop, or of a suffragan bishop of another archbishop, he can be judged by that other archbishop or bishop. For to this end 96. dist. cap. duo, where Ambrose, by reason of a crime committed in his parish, excommunicated the Emperor, which otherwise he would not have dared. Yet concerning one who is not greater but rather less than every bishop, it seems to be held that by reason of a crime he becomes subject to the forum of that bishop in whose diocese he is proved to sin. Since therefore a heretical Pope is not greater but less than every bishop, because every heretic is less than every Catholic 24. quaest. 1. cap. it follows that the heretical Pope by reason of his crime becomes subject to the forum of the diocesan in whose diocese he dwells. The Gloss, therefore, which says that "any superior is excepted from the generality of this rule," etc., is to be understood of superiors who remain superior notwithstanding the crime. But of one who was a superior, and who through the crime becomes inferior by the very fact and is deprived of all spiritual superiority by law itself, it ought not, as it seems, to be understood. Wherefore, since the heretical Pope has by the very fact become inferior to every Catholic, the Gloss's saying has no place in the case of a heretical Pope. And therefore a bishop in whose diocese a heretical Pope dwelt could detain him, but could not solemnly degrade him, just as he could not depose him. This is proved from the fact that depositions of bishops are reserved solely to the pontiff: extra de translationibus 23. q. 7. c. quaevis & c. dudum & c. discutere. And for this reason a bishop also could not hand a heretical Pope over to the secular court, because no bishop may be handed over to the secular court before he has been degraded from every ecclesiastical order. Discip. Relate the contrary assertion. Magist. The contrary assertion holds that no one can detain a heretical Pope, or pronounce any sentence against him. This is proved by the following reason. He who is not another's judge and has no power over him, whose sentence passed against him (without examining whether it is just or unjust), is wholly to be rejected and in no way observed. But the sentence of any bishop passed against him who is held to be Pope, whether he is heretical or Catholic, without examining whether it is just, is wholly to be rejected. Therefore no bishop is the judge of a heretical Pope. The major premise seems plainly true, because when someone asserts that he is the judge of another and alleges a possible cause by which he would be that person's judge, an inquiry must be made whether the cause he alleges is true, and consequently whether his sentence is just or unjust. The minor premise is proved by example. For Dioscorus pronounced a sentence of excommunication against Pope Leo, and it seems probable that he alleged heretical depravity against him; yet without any examination or inquiry whether Dioscorus's sentence was just or unjust, that same sentence was rejected, as Pope Nicholas testifies, who, as is found in dist. 21. c. in tantum, quoting the words of the Council of Chalcedon, says: "because he greatly exceeded his earlier iniquity by the excesses, for he presumed to pronounce excommunication even against Leo, archbishop of Great Rome, etc." Nowhere is it read that any inquiry was made whether Dioscorus had pronounced that excommunication justly or unjustly. Indeed not; but without dispute they punished him for this, because, being an inferior, he attempted to assail the greater with insults of every kind. From these words it may be understood that if any bishop, for whatever cause, presumes to take the Pope captive, or to excommunicate him, or to harass him with any injury, there is no need to inquire whether the Pope is Catholic or heretical; for certainly no inquiry is to be made into the sentence of such a bishop, or into any other injury or annoyance inflicted on the Pope. Therefore whether the Pope is heretical or Catholic, no bishop ought to inflict any annoyance on him whatever, and consequently ought not to detain him. Discip. This argument does not seem to conclude. Yet tell me how it is answered. Magist. It is answered that it was notorious that Dioscorus was a heretic, and therefore he had no jurisdiction at all over the Pope, even if the Pope had been a heretic. Hence no inquiry was to be made into his sentence, whether it was unjust, that is, whether it was pronounced for a just cause, although it was notorious that it was not just from its origin. It would be otherwise with a Catholic bishop, because if he were a Catholic bishop, or a bishop about whom it was not manifest that he was a heretic, and if he took the Pope captive, or denounced him as a heretic and as having incurred the sentence of excommunication, an inquiry would have to be made whether he had proceeded justly or unduly. And if it were found that the Pope was manifestly a heretic, the bishop's deed would have to be approved by Catholics. Discip. Could a heretical Pope appeal from a bishop who so detained him? Magist. It is answered that by right he could not, unless he alleged a probable cause, which, if it were proved, ought to be considered sufficient.

units.la: CAP. XCI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCI.

units.la: In quo inquiritur vtrum principes seculares & laici habeant potestatem coercendi Papam haereticum & puniendi. Prima opinio est quod non: quae probatur octo rationibus. Ad quas respondetur capitulo 100.
units.tr: In which it is inquired whether secular princes and laypeople have power to restrain and punish a heretical Pope. The first opinion is that they do not, and this is supported by eight arguments. These are answered in chapter 100.

units.la: DIscipulus. Haec de potestate Dioecesani super Papam haereticum manifestum ad praesens sufficiant. Et ideo ad principes seculares & laicos me conuerto: de quibus festina differre, an potestatem habeant Papam coercendi. Magist. De hoc opiniones reperiuntur contrariae. Vna est, quod coercio papae haeretici ad principes seculares & laicos minime spectat. Quod multis modis ostenditur. Primo sic: Coercio Papae haeretici non spectat ad illos, de quorum foro non est Papa haereticus. Sed Papa haereticus non est de foro secularium potestatum. Ergo coercio eius ad principes seculares & laicos minime spectat. Maior videtur nota. Minor probatur. Clerici non sunt de foro iudicis secularis 2. q. 1. fere per totum. Et Coelestinus Papa, vt habetur extr. de iudiciis c. cum non ab homine, ait: Si clericus in quacunque ordine constitutus in furto vel homicidio vel periurio seu aliquo crimine fuerit deprehensus legitime & convictus, ab ecclesiastico iudice deponendus est. Et per consequens clericus pro nullo crimine apud secularem iudicem est iudicandus. Papa autem haereticus est clericus. Ergo non est de foro iudicis secularis. Secundo: Papa haereticus non est de foro illius iudicis, ad quem non spectat de causa prauitatis haereticae cognoscere. Sed ad iudicem secularem non spectat cognoscere de causa haereticae prauitatis: sicut ad ipsum non pertinet causa fidei. Ergo Papa haereticus non est de foro iudicis secularis: Maior est nota. Minor auctoritatibus sanctorum patrum probatur aperte. Ait enim Felix Papa, vt allegatum est supra, prout legitur distinct. 10. certum est, ait: Certum est hoc nostris rebus esse salutare, vt cum de causis Dei agitur, iuxta ipsius constitutum, regiam voluntatem sacerdotibus Christi studeatis subdere, non praeferre. Et Nicolaus Papa, vt legitur distinct. 96. cap. denique, ait: Hi quibus tantum humanis rebus & non diuinis praeesse permissum est, quo modo de his per quos diuina ministrantur, iudicare praesumant penitus ignorantes. Item distinct. 98. cap. satis evidenter, sic legitur: Deputatus est Candidianus magnificentissimus Comes stretiorum domesticorum transfire usque ad sanctissimam synodum nostram, & in nullo quidem quae facienda sunt de piis dogmatibus quaestiones seu potius expositiones communicare. Iniquum namque est cum qui non sit in ordine sanctissimorum episcoporum ecclesiastica intermiscere tractatibus. Item Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur distinct. 10. imperium, ait: Imperium nostrum suis publicis rei quotidianae administrationibus debet esse contentum, non usurpare quae sacerdotibus Domini solummodo competunt.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Let what has been said about the power of the diocesan over a heretical Pope suffice for now. I therefore turn to secular princes and laypeople, and I want to settle quickly whether they have power to restrain the Pope. MASTER. On this question there are opposing opinions. One is that the restraint of a heretical Pope does not belong at all to secular princes and laypeople. This is shown in many ways. First, thus: the restraint of a heretical Pope does not belong to those whose jurisdiction the Pope does not fall under. But a heretical Pope is not under the jurisdiction of secular powers. Therefore his restraint does not belong to secular princes and laypeople at all. The major premise is well known. The minor is proved as follows. Clerics are not under the jurisdiction of a secular judge, as 2. q. 1. shows almost throughout. Pope Celestine also says, as is held in extr. de iudiciis c. cum non ab homine, If a cleric, in whatever order he is placed, is lawfully caught and convicted of theft, homicide, perjury or any other crime, he is to be deposed by an ecclesiastical judge. And consequently a cleric is to be judged for no crime before a secular judge. But the Pope is a cleric. Therefore he is not under the jurisdiction of a secular judge. Second: a Pope who is a heretic is not under the jurisdiction of the judge to whom it does not belong to take cognizance of the cause of heretical depravity. But it does not belong to a secular judge to take cognizance of the cause of heretical depravity, just as the cause of faith does not belong to him. Therefore a heretical Pope is not under the jurisdiction of a secular judge. The major is well known. The minor is plainly proved by the authority of the holy Fathers. For Pope Felix says, as cited above and as read in dist. 10: It is certain that this is salutary for our affairs, that when the causes of God are handled, according to his own ordinance, you should take care to subject the royal will to the priests of Christ, not to set it above them. And Pope Nicholas, as read in dist. 96, chapter denique, says: Those to whom only human and not divine affairs have been permitted to be placed in charge should not presume to judge those through whom divine things are ministered, being wholly ignorant of them. Likewise, in dist. 98, chapter satis evidenter, it is read thus: Candidianus, the most magnificent Count of the domestic guards, was assigned to cross over to our most holy synod, and by no means to share in the questions or rather expositions of what is to be done concerning pious dogmas. For it is unjust for one who is not in the order of the most holy bishops to intrude into ecclesiastical discussions. Likewise Pope Nicholas, as is held in dist. 10, imperium, says: Our empire ought to be content with the public administration of everyday affairs, and not to usurp what belongs to the priests of the Lord alone.

units.la: Item Iohannes Papa, vt legitur distinctione 96. cap. si Imperator ait: Si Imperator catholicus est, quod salua pace ipsius dicimus, filius est non praesul ecclesiae. Quod ad religionem competit, discere et conuenit non docere. Habet privilegia potestatis suae, quae administrandi legibus publicis diuinitus est consecratus, vt eius beneficiis non ingratus circa dispositionem caelestis ordinis nihil usurpet. Ad sacerdotes enim Deus voluit, quae ecclesiae disponenda sunt, pertinere, non ad seculi potestates. Et infra: non a legibus publicis, non a potestatibus saecularibus, sed a pontificibus & sacerdotibus omnipotens Deus religionis Christianae clericos & sacerdotes voluit ordinari, & discuti, & recipi de erroreremeantes. Item beatus Cyprianus, vt legitur dist. 10. cap. quoniam, scribens Iuliano sic ait: quoniam idem mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus sic actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis officia potestatis utriusque distinxit, propria volens medicinali humilitate corda sursum efferri, non humana superbia rursus in inferna demergi, vt etiam Christiani Imperatores pro aeterna vita pontificibus indigerent, & pontifices pro cursu temporalium tantummodo rerum imperialibus legibus vterentur, quatenus spiritualis actio a carnalibus incursibus distaret, & Dei militans minime se negotiis saecularibus implicaret: ac vicissim non illi rebus diuinis praeesse viderentur, qui esset saecularibus negotiis implicitus. Ex quibus aliisque pluribus videtur aperte probari, quod principes seculares & laici de causis Dei rebus diuinis piis dogmatibus & religione Christiana se intromittere minime debent. Ex quibus verbis patenter infertur, quod causa fidei & haereticae prauitatis ad ipsos non spectat. Quare Papa haereticus necalius haereticus est de foro iudicis secularis. Tertio sic: crimen ecclesiasticum non pertinet ad iudicem secularem. Sed prauitas haeretica est crimen ecclesiasticum. Et per consequens nec Papa haereticus est de foro iudicis secularis. Minor huius rationis est tam nota, quod probatione non indiget. Maior autoritate & ratione probatur. Auctoritate quidem patet, quia 11. quaest. 1. cap. si quis cum clerico, sic legitur: Si autem crimen ecclesiasticum est secundum canones ab episcopo sua causa examinatio & poena procedat, nullam communionem aliis iudicibus in huiusmodi causis habentibus. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod crimen ecclesiasticum ad iudicem secularem non spectat. Quod etiam ratione probatur. Quia causa quae tantum modo ad iudicem peritum & exercitatum in ea pertinere dignoscitur. Unde secundum Alexandrum tertium, vt habetur extr. de consan. cap. 1. non sunt causae matrimonii tractandae per quoslibet, sed per iudices discretos. Vbi Glossa notat, quod duo exiguntur ad cognoscendum & videndum de causa matrimoniali, scilicet scientia canonum & quod habeat iurisdictionem. Et infra dicitur, quod causa non est delegandae nisi perito & exercitato, vt habetur 2. quaest. 2. cap. vltim. de poenitentia distinct. 6. cap. 1. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod causa non debet committi nisi perito. Unde & Glossa distinct. 20. cap. 1. notat, quod nullus potest esse iudex maxime ecclesiasticus, nisi sit peritus. Sed iudex secularis in causa criminis ecclesiastici minime est peritus, cum noticiam scripturarum (per quam cognoscitur crimen ecclesiasticum) constet eum non habere. Igitur crimen ecclesiasticum ad iudicem secularem minime spectat. Et per consequens crimen haeresis (quod per solam diuinam scripturam cognoscitur) cuius non habet noticiam secularis iudex, ad ipsum non spectat. Quarto sic: Maiores causae sunt ad maius iudicium deferendae: quod tam ex scripturis diuinis, quam ex sacris canonibus colligitur euidenter.
units.tr: Again Pope John, as read in dist. 96, chapter "si Imperator," says: "If the emperor is Catholic, which we say with due respect to his peace, he is a son, not a prelate, of the Church. What belongs to religion is for him to learn and to agree to, not to teach. He has the privileges of his power, which he has been consecrated by God to administer by public laws; so that, not ungrateful for his benefits, he should usurp nothing in the arrangement of the heavenly order. For God willed that the things to be arranged in the Church belong to the priests, not to the secular powers." And further: "Not by public laws, not by secular powers, but by pontiffs and priests did Almighty God will that the clergy and priests of the Christian religion be ordained, examined, and received back from error." Again blessed Cyprian, as read in dist. 10, chapter "quoniam," writing to Julian, says: "Since the same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, has so distinguished the offices of each power by their own acts and distinct dignities, wishing to raise hearts upward by his healing humility and not to sink them again into hell by human pride; so that even Christian emperors should need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs should use imperial laws only for the course of temporal things; so that the spiritual action might stand apart from carnal assaults, and the soldier of God might not entangle himself in secular business; and conversely, that those should not seem to preside over divine things who are caught up in secular business." From these and many other passages it seems clearly proved that secular princes and laymen ought in no way to meddle in the causes of God, in divine things, in pious doctrines, and in the Christian religion. From these words it is plainly inferred that the cause of faith and of heretical depravity does not belong to them. Therefore a heretical Pope is not under the court of a secular judge, nor is any other heretic. Third: an ecclesiastical crime does not belong to a secular judge. But heretical depravity is an ecclesiastical crime. Consequently a heretical Pope is not under the court of a secular judge either. The minor of this argument is so well known that it needs no proof. The major is proved by authority and by reason. By authority it is plain, for in 11. q. 1, chapter "si quis cum clerico," it is read thus: "If, however, it is an ecclesiastical crime according to the canons, let the examination and punishment of the case proceed from the bishop, with no fellowship given to other judges who have a claim in such cases." From these words it is evidently gathered that an ecclesiastical crime does not belong to a secular judge. This is also proved by reason, because a cause is recognised as belonging only to a judge skilled and practised in it. Hence, according to Alexander III, as found in extr. de consan. chapter 1, causes of marriage are not to be handled by just anyone, but by discreet judges. There the Gloss notes that two things are required to know and judge a matrimonial cause, namely knowledge of the canons and jurisdiction. And further it is said that a cause ought not to be entrusted except to one skilled and practised, as in 2. q. 2, chapter "ultim.," and de poenitentia dist. 6, chapter 1. From these words it is gathered that a cause ought not to be committed except to one skilled. Hence the Gloss on dist. 20, chapter 1, also notes that no one can be a judge, especially an ecclesiastical one, unless he is skilled. But a secular judge is by no means skilled in a case of an ecclesiastical crime, since it is agreed that he does not have knowledge of the Scriptures, by which an ecclesiastical crime is recognised. Therefore an ecclesiastical crime does not belong to a secular judge. And consequently the crime of heresy, which is known only through the divine Scripture, of which the secular judge has no knowledge, does not belong to him. Fourth: greater causes are to be referred to a greater court; this is plainly gathered from both the divine Scriptures and the holy canons.

units.la: Nam, vt legitur Exod. 18. Ietro cognatus Moysi dedit eidem consilium dicens: esto tu populo in his quae ad Deum pertinent vt referas quae dicuntur ad eum. Et post: provideas de omni plebe viros potentes ac timentes Deum in quibus sit veritas, & qui oderint auaritiam & constitue ex eis tribunos. Et post: quicquid autem maius fuerit referant ad te, & ipsi minora tantummodo iudicent: Cuius consilio Moyses acquieuit, dum sic legitur ibidem: quibus auditis fecit Moyses omnia quae ille suggesserat: & electis viris strenuis de cunctis Israel constituit eos principes populi, tribunos, centurionies, quinquagenarios & decanos, qui iudicabant plebem omni tempore. Quicquid autem grauius erat, referebant ad eum faciliora tantummodo iudicantes & Deuter. 1. dixit Moyses iudicibus constitutis ab ipso, parum audietis sicut magnum: nec accipietis cuiusquam personam: quia Dei iudicium est. Quod si difficile vobis videbitur aliquid fuerit visum, referte ad me, & ego audiam. Et cap. 17. sic scribitur: si difficile & ambiguum apud te iudicium esse perspexeris inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, lepram & non lepram, & iudicium intra portas tuas videris verba variari, surge & ascende ad locum quem elegerit DOMINVS DEVS tuus: veniesque ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & ad iudicem qui fuerit illo tempore, quaeresque ab eo, qui iudicabat tibi iudicii veritatem. Ex quibus aliisque auctoritatibus scripturae diuinae patenter colligitur, quod maiores causae sunt ad superiores iudices deferendae. Quod etiam sacri canones protestantur. Anacletus enim Papa, vt legitur 2.q.6.c. omnis oppressus, ait: Si autem difficiles causae aut maiora negotia orta fuerint, ad maiorem sedem referantur. Item Pelagius Papa, vt habetur dist. 17. c. multis, ait: Si vero in qualibet prouincia orta fuerint quaestiones, & ipsius intra prouinciam episcopos discrepare coeperit ratio, atque intra ipsos dissidentes non conueniant, ad maiorem sedem referantur. Et infra: maiores vero & difficiliores quaestiones (vt sancta synodus statuit, & vt beata consuetudo exigit) ad sedem Apostolicam semper referantur. Ex quibus aliisque quam pluribus patet aperte, quod maiores causae sunt ad maius iudicium deferendae. Sed causa haeresis est inter maximas computanda. Ergo causa haeresis est ad maius iudicium deferenda. Iudicium autem ecclesiasticum est maius iudicio seculari, teste Gregorio Nazianzeno, qui, vt habetur extr. dist. c. suscipitis, scribens Imperatoribus Constantinopolitanis ait: Libenter accipitis quod lex Christi sacerdotali vos subiecit potestati, atque ipsius tribunalibus subdit. Dedit enim nobis potestatem; dedit principatum multo perfectiorem principatibus vestris. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod iudicium ecclesiasticum est maius iudicio seculari. Ergo causa haeresis non ad iudicem secularem, sed ad iudicem ecclesiasticum debet deferri.
units.tr: For, as is read in Exod. 18, Jethro, the kinsman of Moses, gave him counsel, saying: "Be you for the people in those things which pertain to God, that you may bring the matters that are said to him. And further: provide out of all the people able men who fear God, in whom there is truth, and who hate covetousness, and appoint them as tribunes over them." And further: "But whatever is greater, let them refer to you, and let them judge only the smaller matters." Moses assented to this counsel, as is read in the same place: "When these things were heard, Moses did all that he had suggested; and having chosen strong men from all Israel, he appointed them as leaders of the people, tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifties and of tens, who judged the people at all times. But whatever was more serious they referred to him, judging only the easier matters." And in Deut. 1 Moses said to the judges appointed by him: "You shall hear the small as well as the great; you shall not accept anyone's person, for the judgement is God's. If anything seems difficult to you, refer it to me, and I will hear it." And in chapter 17 it is written: "If you perceive that a judgement is difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and not leprosy, and you see the words varying within your gates, arise and go up to the place which the LORD your God shall choose; and you shall come to the priests of the Levitical race, and to the judge who shall be in that time; and you shall ask him, who shall judge you, for the truth of the judgement." From these and other passages of divine Scripture it is plainly gathered that greater causes are to be referred to higher judges. The holy canons also declare this. For Pope Anacletus, as read in 2. q. 6, c. omnis oppressus, says: But if difficult causes or greater matters arise, let them be referred to the greater see. Likewise Pope Pelagius, as found in dist. 17, c. multis, says: But if questions arise in any province, and the bishops within that province begin to disagree, and those who dissent cannot agree among themselves, let them be referred to the greater see. And further: But the greater and more difficult questions (as the holy synod has decreed, and as blessed custom requires) are always to be referred to the Apostolic See. From these and many more it is plainly evident that greater causes are to be referred to a greater court. But the cause of heresy is to be counted among the greatest. Therefore the cause of heresy is to be referred to a greater court. But the ecclesiastical court is greater than the secular court, as Gregory Nazianzen bears witness, who, as found in extr. dist. c. suscipitis, writing to the emperors of Constantinople, says: You gladly accept that the law of Christ has subjected you to the priestly power and placed you under its tribunals. For it has given us authority; it has given us a principate far more perfect than your principates. From these words it is given to understand that the ecclesiastical court is greater than the secular court. Therefore the cause of heresy is to be brought not to the secular judge but to the ecclesiastical judge.

units.la: Quinto sic: Potestas iudiciaria seu secularis & potestas iudiciaria sacerdotalis sunt potestates distinctae, secundum quod testatur beatus Cyprianus, vt habetur dist. 10. c. quoniam, prout allegatum extitit. Ad potestates autem iudiciarias distinctas spectant causae distinctae. Ad iudiciariam autem potestatem sacerdotalem pertinet causa haeresis. Ergo causa haeresis non pertinet ad potestatem iudiciariam secularem. Et per consequens Papa haereticus non est de foro iudicis secularis. Sexto sic: non aliam potestatem iudiciariam habent seculares iudices Christiani, quam habent seculares iudices pagani. Nam Imperatores Christiani successerunt paganis, & reges Christiani successerunt regibus paganis. Successores autem eodem iure & potestate gaudent, qua praedecessores. Ergo iudices seculares Christiani non habent aliam iudiciariam potestatem, quam pagani habuerunt. Cum igitur causa haeresis ad iudices paganos minime pertineat: Igitur nec causa haeresis spectat ad seculares Christianos. Et per consequens Papa haereticus non est de foro iudicis secularis. Septimo sic: hu illa causa, quae spectat ad Imperatores, reges & iudices, Imperialibus & secularibus legibus est tenendum. Quia vnaquaeque causa terminanda est per leges huiusmodi fori, ad quod dicitur pertinere. Sed in causa haeresis non est Imperialibus seu secularibus vtendum legibus, teste Nicolao Papa, qui, vt habetur dist. 10. c. 1. ait: Lege Imperatoris non in omnibus, ecclesiasticis controuersiis vtendum est. Et infra: Imperiali iudicio non possunt iura ecclesiastica dissolui. Ergo causa haeresis ad iudicem secularem minime spectat. Et per consequens Papa haereticus non est de foro iudicis secularis. Octauo sic: Ad eundem spectat causa haeresis, ad quem pertinet causa fidei; quemadmodum eadem scientia est contrariorum. Sed causa fidei ad iudicem secularem minime spectat, cum videatur ad solum summum pontificem pertinere 34.q.1. quoniam. Et extr. de baptismo & eius effectu c. maiores. Ergo ad iudicem secularem causa haeresis minime spectat. Et per consequens Papa haereticus non est de foro iudicis secularis.
units.tr: Fifthly, thus: the judicial power of the secular sphere and the judicial power of the priesthood are distinct powers, as the blessed Cyprian testifies, as found in dist. 10, c. Quoniam, as has been cited above. Causes that are distinct belong to distinct judicial powers. But the cause of heresy belongs to the judicial power of the priesthood. Therefore the cause of heresy does not belong to the secular judicial power. And consequently a heretical Pope is not within the jurisdiction of a secular judge. Sixthly, thus: Christian secular judges have no other judicial power than that which pagan secular judges had. For Christian emperors succeeded pagan emperors, and Christian kings succeeded pagan kings. Successors enjoy the same right and power as their predecessors. Therefore Christian secular judges do not have any other judicial power than the pagans had. Since, then, the cause of heresy did not belong at all to pagan judges, neither does the cause of heresy pertain to Christian secular judges. And consequently a heretical Pope is not within the jurisdiction of a secular judge. Seventhly, thus: that cause which belongs to emperors, kings and judges must be decided by imperial and secular laws, because every cause must be ended by the laws of the court to which it is said to belong. But in the cause of heresy imperial or secular laws are not to be used, as Pope Nicholas testifies, who, as is found in dist. 10, c. 1, says: "The law of the emperor is not to be used in all ecclesiastical controversies." And below: "Ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment." Therefore the cause of heresy by no means belongs to a secular judge. And consequently a heretical Pope is not within the jurisdiction of a secular judge. Eighthly, thus: the cause of heresy belongs to the same authority to which the cause of faith belongs, just as there is one science of contraries. But the cause of faith by no means belongs to a secular judge, since it seems to pertain to the supreme pontiff alone, 34 q. 1, Quoniam; and Extra, de baptismo et eius effectu, c. Maiores. Therefore the cause of heresy by no means belongs to a secular judge. And consequently a heretical Pope is not within the jurisdiction of a secular judge.

units.la: CAP. XCII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 92.

units.la: Opinionem contrariam ponit, cuius duos modos dicendi recitat. Et primum prosequitur, scil. Quod coercio Papae haeretici & punitio principaliter spectat ad laicos, in hoc capitulo. Secundum vero capitulo sequenti.
units.tr: He sets out the contrary opinion, and recites its two ways of putting it. He first pursues the one, namely that the restraint and punishment of a heretical Pope belongs principally to laymen, in this chapter. The second he takes up in the following chapter.

units.la: Discipulus. Dixisti, quod de potestate principum secularium & aliorum laicorum super Papam sunt opiniones contrariae. Recisti autem vnam: ideo recita aliam contrariam. Magist. Circa opinionem contrariam sunt modi ponendi contrarii: quibusdam dicentibus, quod coercio principaliter spectat ad laicos, qui communitatum causas gerunt, cuiusmodi sunt principes seculares & publicae potestates. Aliis dicentibus, quod coercio Papae haeretici & aliorum haereticorum principaliter spectat ad summum pontificem & praelatos: secundario autem spectat ad seculares principes & laicos. Et hoc in duobus casibus. Vno quidem, si principes seculares & laici super hoc a praelatis ecclesiae fuerint requisiti. Et etiam in alio casu, si videlicet fuerint haeretica pravitate maculari, vel haereticorum fautores aut in corrigendo Papam haereticum damnabiliter negligentes. Discip. Secundus modus videtur apparens. Primum autem haereticalem aestimo: & tamen motiua illius modi dicendi audire desidero. Magist. Motiua huius modi dicendi virtualiter continentur supra in rationibus in principio huius sexti, c. 3. 4. & 5. contentis, quibus ostenditur, quod Imperator est iudex ordinarius Papae. Et quod Papa ex ordinatione Christi nullam iurisdictionem coactiuam habet. Ad hoc etiam posset adduci ratio fundamentalis quorundam, quae tacta est supra lib. quinto cap. 15. per quam probatur, quod ecclesia Romana no habet ex institutione Christi super alias ecclesias principatum. Discip. Ex quo illa ratio fundamentalis quorundam est plana, applica eam ad quaestionem hic propositam. Magist. Ratio illa ad conclusionem propositam taliter applicatur. In tota scriptura non inuenitur aliquid ordinatum de potestate coercendi delinquentes, nisi Matt. 18. cum Christus dicit: si peccauerit in te frater tuus vade & corripe ipsum inter te & ipsum solum. Si te audierit, dierit, lucrati es fratrem tuum: si autem non audierit, accipe adhuc vnum tecum vel duos: quia in ore duorum vel trium testium stat omne verbum. Quod si non audierit eos, dic ecclesiæ. Si autem non audierit ecclesiam, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. In quibus verbis Christus potestatem coercendi delinquentes commisit ecclesiæ. In ecclesia autem in scriptura diuina vbique comprehenduntur clerici & laici, nec vnquam in scriptura laici à nomine ecclesiæ excluduntur. Si ergo potestas coercendi hæreticos commissa est ecclesiæ: nec est commissa clericis in speciali: ergo communitas fidelium habet primo & principaliter potestatem coercendi hæreticos, sicut & alios delinquentes. Illa autem, quæ competunt communitati principaliter & primo, non deriuantur nisi in eum, qui gerit vicem & causam communitatis. Talis autem est princeps secularis. Ergo principi seculari, non clericis, competit principaliter potestas coercendi hæreticos. Et ad ipsum pertinet principaliter potestas coercendi hæreticos: & ita ad ipsum pertinet principaliter Papa hæreticum coercere. Disc. Ista ratio est omnino irrationabilis, & militat contra seipsam: quia si potestas coercendi hæreticos & alios delinquentes tradita est primo à Christo communitati ecclesiæ, & communitas potest transferre potestatem suam in quem voluerit: ergo communitas ecclesiæ ita poterit transferre illam potestatem in clericum vel clericos, sicut in laicum vel laicos. Cum ergo non legatur, quod communitas fidelium talem potestatem coercendi hæreticos transtulit in laicos, non est dicendum, quod talem potestatem habeant laici à communitate fidelium, cum quia per Christi verba prædicta non est commissa ecclesiæ potestas coercendi delinquentes, sed tantummodo videtur iniungi, quod delinquentes, qui incorrigibiles apparuerint, euitentur. Quod patet per illud, quod vltimo dicitur: Si autem ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. Per quæ verba intelligitur, quod delinquentes incorrigibiles, sicut ethnici & publicani sunt habendi. Communitas autem fidelium per verba præfata non recipit potestatem coercendi ethnicos & publicanos à Christo. Igitur per eadem verba non recipit potestatem coercendi delinquentes credentes. Sed videtur per illa imponi fidelibus, quod sicut ethnici & publicani sunt ab eis vitandi, quantum ad hoc, quod non sunt eis secreta fidei communicanda, iuxta illud Matt. 7. Nolite sanctum dare canibus: ita etiam credulis incorrigibilibus secreta fidei communicari non debent. Magist. Istis non obstantibus nonnulli putant, quod ratio prædicta concludat si perficiatur. Nam sicut percipimus, secundum eos sic perfici debet: contra rationem & veritatem rei publicæ est, quod diuersæ personæ habentes potestates omnino distinctas, quæ nec integrant vnam potestatem, nec vna dependet ab alia, habeant iurisdictionem coactiuam super eandem communitatem etiam pro diuersis criminibus. Quia posset concurrere, quod se mutuo impedirent, & quod pax & concordia communitatis per tales distinctas potestates tolleretur. Posset enim accidere, quod eadem persona esset inuoluta criminibus ita diuersis, quorum vnum pertineret ad vnam potestatem, & aliud ad aliam. Quo posito si vtraque potestas vellet exercere iustitiam circa delinquentem eandem personam, oporteret quod vna potestas raperet vel defenderet delinquentem contra aliam potestatem: & ita pax & concordia in communitate dissiparetur. Si enim idem sit fur & hæreticus, & ratione hæresis pertinet ad iudicem ecclesiasticum, & ratione furti ad iudicem secularem: si neuter iudex voluerit alteri deferre, sed vterque vult trahere reum ad ius suum: vnus propter hæresim, alius propter furtum: inter ipsos oriretur seditio. Cum ergo communitas seditionis occasiones & schismatum tollere teneatur, non licet eidem communitati concedere taliter clericis potestatem coercendi hæreticos & in principem secularem transferre potestatem malefactores alios castigandi. Sed constat quod principes seculares habent iurisdictionem coactiuam super quamplurimos criminosos. Ergo clerici pro illo crimine habent iurisdictionem coactiuam super eosdem. Et ita si subditi alicuius regis vel principis fiant hæretici, ab eodem rege vel principe puniri debent, pro hæresi sicut pro criminibus aliis. Disc. Per plures leges habetur, quod hæretici non per reges & principes, sed per clericos iudicare debent. Magist. Dicunt quidam, quod tales leges sunt iniquæ iuri naturali & recto dictamini rationis obuiantes manifeste: & ideo pro legibus non sunt habendæ.
units.tr: Disciple. You said that there are opposing opinions about the power of secular princes and other laymen over the Pope. You recited one, so now recite the other opposing view. Master. Concerning the opposing opinion there are different ways of putting it. Some say that coercion belongs chiefly to the laity, who manage the affairs of communities, such as secular princes and public authorities. Others say that the coercion of a heretical Pope and of other heretics belongs chiefly to the supreme pontiff and the prelates, but secondarily to secular princes and laymen. And this holds in two cases. In one, if the secular princes and laymen have been asked to do so by the prelates of the Church. The other case is if they have been stained with heretical depravity, or are supporters of heretics, or have culpably neglected to correct a heretical Pope. Disciple. The second form seems plausible. I judge the first to be heretical, yet I want to hear the arguments for that way of speaking. Master. The arguments for this way of speaking are implicitly contained in the reasons set out above at the beginning of this sixth book, chapters 3, 4 and 5, which show that the Emperor is the ordinary judge of the Pope, and that the Pope, by the ordinance of Christ, has no coercive jurisdiction. To this might also be added a fundamental argument of certain people, touched on above in book 5, chapter 15, by which it is proved that the Roman Church does not, by the institution of Christ, have primacy over the other churches. Disciple. Since that fundamental argument of certain people is clear, apply it to the question proposed here. Master. That argument is applied to the proposed conclusion as follows. In the whole of Scripture nothing is ordained concerning the power to restrain offenders, except Matthew 18, where Christ says: "If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone. If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother. But if he will not hear thee, take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." In these words Christ committed to the church the power to restrain offenders. In divine Scripture, however, clergy and laity are everywhere included in the church, and in Scripture laymen are never excluded from the name of church. If therefore the power to restrain heretics was committed to the church, and was not committed to the clergy in particular, then the community of the faithful has first and chiefly the power to restrain heretics, just as it does other offenders. But what belongs to a community first and chiefly is passed on only to the person who carries out the role and cause of the community. Such a person is a secular prince. Therefore the power to restrain heretics belongs chiefly to the secular prince, not to the clergy. And the power to restrain heretics belongs chiefly to him, and so it belongs chiefly to him to restrain a heretical Pope. Disciple. That argument is wholly unreasonable and works against itself. For if the power to restrain heretics and other offenders was first handed on by Christ to the community of the church, and the community can transfer its power to whomever it wishes, then the community of the church could transfer that power to a cleric or clerics just as much as to a layman or laymen. Since, then, we do not read that the community of the faithful transferred such a power to restrain heretics to laymen, we must not say that laymen have such a power from the community of the faithful. Moreover, by the words of Christ quoted above, the power to restrain offenders was not committed to the church, but it seems only to be enjoined that offenders who prove incorrigible be avoided. This is clear from the last words: "If he will not hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." By these words it is understood that incorrigible offenders are to be held as heathens and publicans. But by the words cited the community of the faithful does not receive from Christ the power to restrain heathens and publicans. Therefore by the same words it does not receive the power to restrain offenders who are believers. Rather, it seems that by these words the faithful are charged that, just as heathens and publicans are to be avoided by them, in that the secrets of the faith are not to be communicated to them (according to Matthew 7: "Give not that which is holy unto the dogs"), so likewise the secrets of the faith ought not to be communicated to incorrigible believers. Master. Notwithstanding these objections, some think that the argument stated above is conclusive if it is carried through. For, as we understand, it must be carried through as follows: it is contrary to the reason and truth of the commonwealth that different persons holding wholly distinct powers, which neither make up one power nor depend one upon another, should have coercive jurisdiction over the same community, even for different crimes. For it could happen that they hinder each other, and that the peace and concord of the community would be destroyed by such distinct powers. For it could happen that the same person was involved in crimes so different that one belonged to one power and another to the other. Given this, if each power wished to exercise justice against the same offender, one power would have to snatch the offender away from the other power or defend him against it, and so peace and concord in the community would be dissolved. For if the same man is both a thief and a heretic, and by reason of heresy he belongs to the ecclesiastical judge, but by reason of theft to the secular judge, and if neither judge is willing to yield to the other, but each wants to draw the accused to his own law, the one on account of heresy and the other on account of theft, then sedition would arise between them. Since, therefore, the community is bound to remove the occasions of sedition and schisms, it is not lawful for that same community to grant to the clergy such a power to restrain heretics in such a way, and to transfer to the secular prince the power to punish other evildoers. But it is certain that secular princes have coercive jurisdiction over very many criminals. Therefore the clergy have coercive jurisdiction over the same persons for that crime. And so, if the subjects of some king or prince become heretics, they ought to be punished by that same king or prince for heresy, just as for other crimes. Disciple. Many laws hold that heretics ought to be judged not by kings and princes but by clerics. Master. Some say that such laws are unjust, and that they plainly oppose natural law and the right dictate of reason, and therefore they are not to be held as laws.

units.la: CAP. XCIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCIII.

units.la: In quo ponitur secundum modum, siue secunda opinio & veritas, quod coercitio Papæ hæretici & punitio spectat principaliter ad clericos & ordinarie: Secundario vero & in casu ad laicos. Et ponuntur tria probanda. Secundum probatur capitulo 94. & sequentibus duobus, tertium vero capitulo 97.
units.tr: In which is set out, according to the second way of stating the matter and the truth, that the restraint and punishment of a heretical Pope belong principally and ordinarily to the clergy, but secondarily and in a particular case to laymen. Three things are to be proved: the second is proved in chapter 94 and the two following, and the third in chapter 97.

units.la: Discipulus. Quia de isto modo ponendi, quem puto omnino erroneum, in aliis tractatibus saepe occasionem habeo loquendi, & ideo isto modo dimisso nitere declarare secundum modum ponendi, qui minus veritati repugnare videtur. Magist. Dicunt quidam, quod si Papa manifeste & publice incurreret in haereticam pravitatem, puta si publice prædicaret & doceret contra veritatem catholicam apud catholicos diuulgatam (vt pote determinaret aut prædicaret vel teneret verum corpus Christi in sacramento altaris minime contineri, aut resurrectionem non esse futuram, vel animas reproborum non affligi aut cruciari, vel non esse in inferno, aut aliquid huiusmodi, cuius contrarium tenetur explicite credere, vel quia apud catholicos publice tanquam catholicum diuulgaret vel diffinitiue terminaret quemcunque errorem quantumcunq; paruum diuinae scripturae ac doctrinae vniuersalis ecclesiae obuiantem: si clerici crederent vel fauerent eidem, ac circa correctionem aut cohibitionem ipsius essent damnabiliter negligentes, principes seculares, in quorum dominio moratur, & etiam populus, qui sciret ipsum haereticum, coercere debent, si possent, inuocato auxilio (si oportet) vicinarum regionum. Si autem princeps, in cuius dominio Papa moraretur, crederet vel faueret eidem aut ipsum damnabiliter negligeret coercere, alii principes & laici, qui scirent Papam esse haereticum, inquantum eis potentia & vires superpeterent, ad coercendum ipsum essent astricti. Unde circa istum modum tria probare & declarare nituntur. Primo enim nituntur ostendere, quod causa fidei aliquo modo spectat ad laicos. Secundo satagunt explanare, quomodo causa fidei spectat ad laicos. Tertio moliuntur ostendere, quod coertio Papae haeretici in aliquo casu spectat ad laicos, etiam a praelatis ecclesiae minime requisitos.
units.tr: Disciple. Since I often have occasion in other treatises to speak of this way of putting the matter, which I think wholly mistaken, I will set it aside and try to explain the way of putting it that seems less opposed to the truth. Master.
