Some say that if the Pope should openly and publicly fall into heretical depravity, for example if he publicly preached and taught against the Catholic truth made known among Catholics (such as by determining, preaching or holding that the true body of Christ is not contained in the sacrament of the altar, or that there will be no resurrection, or that the souls of the reprobate are not afflicted or tormented, or that there is no hell, or anything of this kind whose contrary we are explicitly bound to believe); or if he, publicly among Catholics and as a Catholic, spread abroad or definitively settled any error, however small, opposing divine Scripture and the doctrine of the universal Church: then, if the clergy believed or favoured him, or were culpably negligent about correcting or restraining him, the secular princes in whose dominion he lives, and also the people who knew him to be a heretic, ought to restrain him if they could, calling in (if need be) the help of neighbouring regions. If, however, the prince in whose dominion the Pope dwelt believed or favoured him, or culpably neglected to restrain him, the other princes and laymen who knew the Pope to be a heretic were bound to restrain him, insofar as their power and strength extended. Hence, concerning this way of putting the matter, they strive to prove and explain three things. First, they try to show that the cause of faith somehow pertains to laymen. Second, they labour to explain how the cause of faith pertains to laymen. Third, they undertake to show that the restraint of a heretical Pope, in some case, pertains to laymen, even when it has not been sought from the prelates of the Church.

units.la: Primum probatur primo sic: Ad illum quodammodo spectat quaestio fidei vel causa, qui potest concilio generali, in quo tractatur de fide, interesse. Imperatores autem (& per rationem consimilem reges & laici) aliquo modo possunt generali concilio (in quo tractatur de fide) interesse, sicut ostensum est prius c. 85. Ergo ad imperatores, reges & laicos aliquo modo causa fidei noscitur pertinere. Secundo ad illum aliquo modo pertinet quaestio causae fidei, qui fidem defendere tenetur. Quia nullus rem ad ipsum impertinentem omnino tenetur defendere, teste Sapiente, qui Eccles. 2. ait: De eo re, quae te non molestat, ne certaueris: qualis est omnis res, quae ad te omnino non pertinet.
units.tr: The first is proved first in this way. The question or cause of faith belongs in some sense to the one who can take part in a general council, at which matters of faith are treated. Emperors (and by similar reasoning kings and laymen) can in some sense take part in a general council (at which matters of faith are treated), as was shown earlier in chapter 85. Therefore the cause of faith is known in some sense to pertain to emperors, kings and laymen. Second, the question of the cause of faith in some sense pertains to the one who is bound to defend the faith. For no one is wholly bound to defend a matter that does not concern him at all, as the Wise Man says in Ecclesiasticus 2: "Do not strive about a matter that does not trouble you, such as every matter that does not pertain to you at all."

units.la: Sed laici fidem suam defendere tenentur: alioquin proditores veritatis & haeretici sunt censendi 1. q. 3. c. nolite, vbi Iohannes Chrysostomus ait: sicut sacerdos debitor est vt veritatem, quam audiuit a Deo, legitime praedicet: sic laicus debitor est vt veritatem, quam audiuit a sacerdotibus probatam quidem scripturae defendat. Quod si non fecerit, prodidit veritatem. Ergo quaestio fidei quandoq; spectat ad laicos. Tertio sic: ad ipsum spectat aliquo modo quaestio fidei, qui pro veritate fidei defendenda leges potest statuere.
units.tr: But laymen are bound to defend their faith, otherwise they are to be judged betrayers of the truth and heretics, as in 1 q. 3, chapter Nolite, where John Chrysostom says: "Just as a priest is bound to preach lawfully the truth that he has heard from God, so a layman is bound to defend the truth that he has heard from the priests, approved indeed by Scripture. If he does not do so, he has betrayed the truth." Therefore the question of faith sometimes pertains to laymen. Third, in this way: the question of faith in some sense pertains to the one who can enact laws for the defence of the truth of the faith.

units.la: Sed Imperator & laici possunt statuere leges pro veritate fidei defendenda. Ad populum & laicos aliquo modo quaestio fidei noscitur pertinere. Maior videtur euidens, s. q nemo de re, quae ad cum omnino non pertinet, valet legem statuere. Maior authoritatibus & exemplis & rationibus videtur posse probari.
units.tr: But the Emperor and laymen can enact laws for the defence of the truth of the faith. Therefore the question of faith is known in some sense to pertain to the people and to laymen. The major premise seems evident, namely that no one can enact a law about a matter that does not pertain to him at all. The major premise seems capable of being proved by authorities, examples and reasons.

units.la: Augustinus enim, vt habetur 11. q. 3. cap. Imperatores, ait: Imperatores si in errore essent (quod absit) & pro errore suo contra veritatem legem darent, per quae iusti probarentur & coronarentur: non tamen faciendum est, quod illi iubent. Et infra: quando autem Imperatores veritatem tenent, & pro ea contra errorem iubent, quod quisquis contempserit ipse sibi iudicium acquirit. Item Idem ad Vincen. ait, vt habetur 23. q. 4. cap. non inuenitur, ait: Quis enim vestrum non laudat leges Imperatorum datas ab eis aduersus sacrificia paganorum, quae per conuenientiam pro fide data videntur? Item Idem ad Bonifacium, vt habetur dist. 9. c. 1. loquens de Imperatoribus, ait: quando autem pro veritate contra falsitatem constituunt bonas leges, terrentur seruientes & corrigantur intelligentes. Et alibi: quicunque vero legibus Imperatorum, quae pro veritate feruntur obtemperare non vult, grande acquirit supplicium. Et, vt habetur 23. q. 4. c. ecclesia, ait: quod autem dicunt (scilicet haeretici, qui contra suas impietates leges iustas institui nolunt) non petisse a regibus terra Apostolos talia, non considerant aliud fuisse tunc temporis, & omnia suis temporibus conuenire. Quis enim in Christum crediderat tunc Imperator? quis enim propietate contra impietatem leges ferendo fauiret? tunc enim adhuc propheticum complebatur: quare fremuerunt gentes & populi meditati sunt inania. Assiterunt reges terrae & principes conuenerunt in vnum. Et nondum illud agebatur, quod paulo post in eodem Psalmo dicebatur: & nunc reges intelligite: erudimini qui iudicatis terram: seruite Domino in timore, & exultate ei cum tremore: quomodo ergo reges Domino seruiant in timore, nisi ea quae contra Deum iussa sunt religiosa seueritate prohibendo atque plectendo. Aliter n. seruit, quia est rex, & aliter quia est homo. Quia est homo seruit Deo fideliter viuendo: Quia est rex, seruit leges iusta praecipientes & contraria prohibentes conuenienti vigore sancienda. Ex quibus patet aperte, quod imperatores & publicae potestates licite pro fide possunt leges statuere. Quod etiam exemplis ostenditur. Nam reges infideles qua fideles leges pro fide laudabiliter ediderunt. Na Nabuchodonosor legem edidit pro fidei veritate, qui vt legitur Danielis 3. ait: A me ergo positum est hoc decretum, vt omnis populus, tribus & lingua quicunque locutus fuerit blasphemiam contra Deum Sydrach, Misach & Abednago, dispereat & domus eius vastetur. Neque enim est alius qui possit ita saluare. Rex etiam magnus Artaxerxes, vt legitur Hester vltim. legem edidit dicens: Hoc autem est edictum, quod emittimus in cunctis urbibus, vt liceat Iudaeis vti legibus suis. Reges etiam fideles leges pro fidei veritate condiderunt. Quod testatur Augustinus aperte in Epistola ad Vincentium, vt habetur 23. quaest. 6. cap. vides, ait: Ciuitas mea, quae cum tota esset in partes Donati, ad vnitatem catholicam legum imperialium timore conuersa est. Igitur Imperatores leges pro fide catholica ediderunt. Quod etiam ratione videtur posse probari. Nam ille potest leges pro fide constituere, qui non solum contemplatione hominum, sed contemplatione Dei potest iura statuere. Sed Imperator & populus contemplatione Dei possunt leges statuere, dist. 1. cap. ius ciuile, vbi sic dicitur: Ius ciuile est quod quicunque populus vel quaecunque ciuitas sibi proprium humana diuinaque causa constituit, id est, contemplatione Dei & hominum, secundum Glossam ibidem. Ergo laici in fauorem fidei leges condere valent. Discip. Ista sententia, quod laici possunt aliquas leges pro fide statuere, quae aliquam habeant firmitatem (nisi a summo pontifice vel praelatis ecclesiae fuerint confirmatae) sacris canonibus obuiare videtur. Quia Innocent. tertius, vt habetur extr. de constitutionibus cap. ecclesia, ait: nos attendentes quod laicis & religiosis super ecclesiis & personis ecclesiasticis nulla est attributa facultas, apud quos obsequendi manet necessitas, non auctoritas imperandi: a quibus si quid motu proprio statutum fuerit, quod ecclesiarum respiciat commodum & favorem, nullius firmitatis esse constat, nisi ab ecclesia fuerit approbatum. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod super his, quae ad ecclesiam spectant statutum laicorum nullam obtinet firmitatem, nisi ab ecclesia fuerit approbatum, quaestio autem fidei ad ecclesiam spectat, ergo statutum laicorum in favorem etiam Dei editum nullius est momenti, nisi ab ecclesia fuerit confirmatum. Item in synodo Simachi Papae, ut habetur 16. quaestion. ultim. cap. non placuit, sic legitur: non placuit laicum statuendi in ecclesia habere aliquam potestatem, cui obsequendi manet necessitas, non auctoritas imperandi. Ex quibus verbis potest intelligi, quod laicus nihil potest statuere de his, quae ad ecclesiam spectant, quaestio autem fidei ad ecclesiam spectat, ergo laicus in favorem fidei nihil potest statuere. Item in synodo Eugenii Papae, ut legitur extra de iudiciis, cap. decreuimus, sic habetur: Decreuimus ut clerici tractare ecclesiastica negocia non praesumant, & ut episcopi, abbates, & archiepiscopi & alii ecclesiarum praelati de negociis ecclesiasticis, maxime de illis quae spiritualia esse noscuntur, laicorum iudicio non dispenent. Ex quibus colligitur, quod nec etiam laicorum iudicio sunt spiritualia disponenda, ergo cum inter negocia spiritualia sit quaestio fidei potissime computanda, videtur quod laici de his, quae ad fidem spectant, se intromittere minime debent, & per consequens pro fide nihil statuere possunt. Item minus est disponere de ecclesiasticis dignitatibus, & rebus ecclesiarum, quam de fide, qui autem non potest minus, neque maius potest. Quod autem laici de dignitatibus ecclesiasticis & rebus ecclesiarum nihil disponere valeant, sacris canonibus affirmatur. Nam 16. quaestion. ultim. ca. laici, sic legitur: Laicis quamuis religiosis nulla de dignitatibus ecclesiasticis aliquid disponendi legitur attributa facultas. Item Innocentius Tertius, ut habetur extra, de arbitris. cap. decim. ait: Adhuc generaliter prohibemus, ne super rebus spiritualibus compromittatur in laicum: quia non decet, ut laicus in talibus arbitretur, ergo multo magis non decet, ut laicus de fide & dignitatibus ecclesiasticis & rebus ecclesiarum aliquid legem statuendo decernat. Item sexta distinctio. de statuto Basilii in favorem ecclesiae edito sic legitur: Scripturam, quae in sacerdotali concilio recitata est, euidentissimis documentis constat esse inualidam, primum quidem, quia contra patrum regulas a laicis quamuis religiosis, quibus nulla de ecclesiasticis facultatibus aliquid disponendi legitur vnquam attributa facultas, facta videatur. Item Innocentius Tertius, ut legitur extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, ait: Nulla fuit laicis attributa potestas de rebus ecclesiasticis disponendi, apud quos subsequendi manet necessitas, non auctoritas imperandi.
units.tr: For Augustine, as found in 11 q. 3, chapter Imperatores, says: "If emperors were in error (which God forbid), and by their error issued laws against the truth, by which the just would be tested and crowned, yet what they command is not to be done." And below: "But when emperors hold the truth, and for it command against error, whoever scorns it acquires judgment for himself." Likewise the same writer to Vincentius, as found in 23 q. 4, chapter Non inuenitur, says: "For which of you does not praise the laws of the emperors given against the sacrifices of the pagans, which through agreement seem to be given for the faith?" Likewise the same writer to Boniface, as found in dist. 9, c. 1, speaking of emperors, says: "When they establish good laws for the truth against falsehood, those who serve are terrified and those who understand are corrected." And elsewhere: "Whoever is unwilling to obey the laws of the emperors which are enacted for the truth acquires a great punishment." And, as found in 23 q. 4, chapter Ecclesia, he says: "As for what they say (namely the heretics, who are unwilling that just laws be instituted against their impieties), that the Apostles did not ask for such things from the kings of the earth, they do not consider that the times were otherwise, and that all things agree with their own times. For who among the emperors had believed in Christ at that time? Who, enacting laws against impiety for piety's sake, would have favoured it? For then the prophecy was still being fulfilled: 'Why have the nations raged and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood up and the princes gathered together.' And that was not yet being done which was said a little later in the same Psalm: 'And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth; serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.' How then do kings serve the Lord in fear, unless by forbidding and punishing with religious severity the things that are commanded against God? For a king serves in one way because he is a king, and in another because he is a man. As a man he serves God by living faithfully; as a king he serves by enacting, with fitting vigour, laws that command what is just and forbid what is contrary." From these things it is plainly evident that emperors and public powers may lawfully enact laws for the faith. This is also shown by examples. For unbelieving kings have issued laws for the faith commendably, as believers would. King Nebuchadnezzar issued a law for the truth of the faith, who, as we read in Daniel 3, said: "Therefore a decree has been issued by me, that every people, tribe and tongue that speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego shall perish, and his house shall be laid waste. For there is no other who can save in this way." King Artaxerxes the Great also, as we read in the last chapter of Esther, issued a law saying: "This is the edict which we send out in all the cities, that the Jews may be permitted to use their own laws." Believing kings also enacted laws for the truth of the faith. Augustine testifies to this plainly in his Epistle to Vincentius, as found in 23 q. 6, chapter Vides: "My city, which was wholly divided into the parties of Donatus, has been converted to Catholic unity through fear of imperial laws." Therefore emperors enacted laws for the Catholic faith. This too can be shown by reason. For he can enact laws for the faith who can establish rights not only out of regard for men but out of regard for God. But an emperor and the people can enact laws out of regard for God, as dist. 1, chapter Ius ciuile, says: "Civil law is that which any people or any city establishes for itself, both human and divine, that is, out of regard for God and men," according to the Gloss there. Therefore laymen are able to enact laws in favour of the faith. Disciple. This opinion, that laymen can enact some laws for the faith which have some binding force (unless they have been confirmed by the supreme Pontiff or the prelates of the Church), seems to conflict with the sacred canons. For Innocent III, as found in the Extra, De constitutionibus, chapter Ecclesia, says: "We, considering that no authority has been granted to laymen and religious over churches and ecclesiastical persons, among whom remains the necessity of obeying but not the authority of commanding, and that whatever has been enacted by them of their own accord, which concerns the advantage and favour of the churches, is plainly of no force unless it has been approved by the Church." From these words it is to be understood that a layman's enactment concerning the things that pertain to the Church has no force unless it has been approved by the Church. But the question of faith pertains to the Church. Therefore a layman's enactment, made even in favour of God, is of no moment unless it has been confirmed by the Church. Likewise, in the synod of Pope Symmachus, as found in 16 q. ult., chapter Non placuit, it is read thus: "It has not pleased that laymen should have any power of enacting in the Church, among whom remains the necessity of obeying but not the authority of commanding." From these words it can be understood that a layman can decide nothing about the things that pertain to the Church. But the question of faith pertains to the Church. Therefore a layman can enact nothing in favour of the faith. Likewise, in the synod of Pope Eugenius, as read in the Extra, De iudiciis, chapter Decreuimus, it is held thus: "We have decreed that clerics not presume to handle ecclesiastical business, and that bishops, abbots, archbishops and other prelates of the churches not dispose of ecclesiastical business, especially those things which are known to be spiritual, by the judgment of laymen." From these it is gathered that even spiritual matters are not to be arranged by the judgment of laymen. Therefore, since the question of faith is especially to be counted among spiritual business, it seems that laymen ought in no way to meddle with the things that pertain to faith, and consequently cannot enact anything for the faith. Likewise, it is a smaller matter to dispose of ecclesiastical dignities and the goods of the churches than to dispose of faith; but whoever cannot do the lesser thing cannot do the greater. That laymen can dispose of nothing concerning ecclesiastical dignities and the goods of the churches is affirmed by the sacred canons. For in 16 q. ult., chapter Laici, it is read thus: "To laymen, however religious, no power is read as having been granted to dispose of anything concerning ecclesiastical dignities." Likewise Innocent III, as found in the Extra, De arbitris, chapter 10, says: "Further, we generally prohibit that matters spiritual be submitted to a layman, because it is not fitting that a layman should arbitrate in such matters." Therefore much more is it not fitting that a layman should decree, by enacting a law, anything concerning faith, ecclesiastical dignities and the goods of the churches. Likewise, in dist. 6, concerning the statute of Basil issued in favour of the Church, it is read thus: "The writing which was recited in the sacerdotal council is shown by the clearest evidence to be invalid, first because it seems to have been made by laymen, however religious, to whom no power of disposing of ecclesiastical goods has ever been read as granted, contrary to the rules of the Fathers." Likewise Innocent III, as read in the Extra, De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, says: "No power has been granted to laymen to dispose of ecclesiastical goods, among whom remains the necessity of obeying, not the authority of commanding."

units.la: Ex quibus aliisque quampluribus colligitur euidenter, quod non solum de fide, sed etiam de dignitate & rebus ecclesiae laici leges condendi nullam habent penitus potestatem. Et quamuis haec conclusio mihi videtur certa secundam canonicas sanctiones, tamen quomodo ad allegationes praescriptas respondere contingat, non differas recitare. Magister. Allegationes tuae praedictae a nonnullis pueriles & friuolae reputantur, quia videtur eis, quod sacrorum canonum non habeas intellectum. Ad cuius euidentiam est sciendum, quod rem aliquam ad alium pertinere dupliciter potest contingere, res enim aliqua ad aliquem pertinet tanquam in potestate illius aliquo modo existens, vt scilicet de ea sicut sibi placuerit, dum modo non contra Deum vel rationem rectam, aut leges iustas seu consuetudines rationales valeat ordinare, & isto modo dignitates ecclesiasticae, & res ecclesiarum pertinent ad praelatos ecclesiae. Alio modo pertinet res aliqua ad alium tanquam ab eo defendenda, & sic res ecclesiarum pertinent ad laicos: quia laici debent defendere res ecclesiarum, sic fides pertinet ad laicos: quia eam diligenter & potenter defendere astringuntur. Ex his respondetur ad omnes allegationes tuas, quod laici possunt statuere leges suos subditos artius obligando, ne personas ecclesiasticas, vel res earum offendant, vel molestent iniuste: quos in contrarium facientes poenis possunt debitis coercere: quamuis huiusmodi poenis personas ab eorum exceptas potestate nequeant castigare, sic principes & reges, ac publicae potestates & communitates leges possunt statuere pro fide salubrius defendenda: possuntque punire suos subditos fidem nequiter impugnantes, quamuis punire non valeant eos, qui a sua iurisdictione sunt exempti. Discipulus. Nitere allegare pro assertione praedicta. Magister. Quia reges & principes & publicae potestates ciuitates aliaeque communitates, quae potestatem habent condere leges de temporalibus statuere leges queant pro veritate fidei tenenda & defendenda & nullatenus impugnanda vel reiicienda; eisdemque legibus suos subditos obligare, sic videtur posse probari. Omnis persona & vniuersitas iurisdictionem habens coactiuam de his, ad quae pet se & subditos faciendo obligatur, legem potest statuere, & ad ea facienda subditos subpoena rationabili obligare, sed omnis persona fidelis & etiam vniuersitas iurisdictionem habens coactiuam per se & subditos tenetur fidem catholicam defendere, igitur de fide defendenda potest legem statuere & subditos ad fidem defendendam sub poena rationabili obligare. Secundo probatur idem sic: Quilibet habens iurisdictionem coactiuam ad ea per leges suas potest subditos suos obligare, quae pacem & tranquillitatem procurant & conseruant & quorum contraria pacem & tranquillitatem omnimodam dissipant & conturbant, sed fidem negare & impugnare & abiicere, pacem & tranquillitatem ciuium dissipat & conturbat: quia homines diuersarum sectarum minime pacifice inter se viuunt, ergo omnis persona & communitas habens iurisdictionem coactiuam potest per leges subditos obligare, ne fidem catholicam impugnare aut abiicere quoquo modo praesumant. Tertio sic: non minorem potestatem habet rex vel princeps super subditos suos in his, quae sunt contra fidem & bonos mores, quam ha-beat
units.tr: From these and many other arguments it is clearly gathered that laymen have no power whatsoever to enact laws not only concerning faith but also concerning the dignity and property of the Church. And although this conclusion seems certain to me according to the canonical sanctions, do not delay in reciting how it is possible to answer the allegations set out above. Master. Your allegations mentioned above are regarded by some as childish and frivolous, because they seem not to understand the sacred canons. To make this plain, it must be known that a thing can belong to someone in two ways. A thing belongs to a person in one way as existing in some sense under his power, so that he may dispose of it as he pleases, provided he does not thereby act against God, right reason, just laws or rational customs. In this way ecclesiastical dignities and the property of churches belong to the prelates of the Church. In another way a thing belongs to someone as something he is to defend, and in this way the property of the churches belongs to laymen, because laymen ought to defend the property of the churches, just as the faith belongs to laymen, because they are bound to defend it diligently and vigorously. From this, an answer is given to all your allegations: laymen can enact laws binding their subjects more tightly, so that they do not offend or unjustly harass ecclesiastical persons or their property; and those who act to the contrary they can restrain with due penalties. Although they cannot, by such penalties, punish persons who are exempt from their power, so princes and kings, and public authorities and communities, can enact laws for defending the faith more wholesomely, and can punish their subjects who wickedly assail or cast off the faith, although they cannot punish those who are exempt from their jurisdiction. Disciple. Try to give arguments for the assertion above. Master. That kings and princes and public authorities, cities and other communities which have the power to make laws concerning temporal matters, can enact laws for holding and defending the truth of the faith, and by no means for assailing or rejecting it, and can bind their subjects by these same laws, can be proved thus. Every person and body that has coercive jurisdiction may enact a law concerning those things to which it binds itself and its subjects, and may bind subjects under a reasonable penalty to do them. But every faithful person, and also every body that has coercive jurisdiction, is bound by itself and its subjects to defend the Catholic faith; therefore it can enact a law concerning the defence of the faith and bind its subjects under a reasonable penalty to defend it. Secondly, the same is proved thus: whoever has coercive jurisdiction can by his laws bind his subjects to those things which promote and preserve peace and tranquillity, and whose contraries utterly dissolve and disturb peace and tranquillity. But to deny, assail and cast off the faith dissolves and disturbs the peace and tranquillity of the citizens, because men of different sects do not live peacefully among themselves. Therefore every person and community having coercive jurisdiction can by law bind its subjects not to presume in any way to assail or cast off the Catholic faith. Thirdly, thus: a king or prince has no less power over his subjects in those things which are against the faith and good morals than a husband has over his wife, or a father over his offspring; but a husband can and ought to correct his wife when she errs against the faith and good morals, and a father has to correct his offspring when they err against the faith and good morals. Therefore a king and a prince can correct his subjects when they err against the faith and good morals. But a king or even a prince has power to enact a law concerning those matters on account of which he can correct his subjects. Therefore kings and princes can impose laws on their subjects for holding the faith.

units.la: Fff beat maritus super vxorem, vel pater super prolem suam, sed maritus coniugem suam errantem contra fidem & bonos mores potest & debet corrigere: & pater prolem suam errantem contra fidem & bonos mores habet corrigere, ergo rex & princeps subditos suos errantes contra fidem & bonos mores potest corrigere, sed rex aut etiam princeps de his, propter quae subditos potest corrigere, valet legem statuere, ergo rex & princeps pro fide tenenda a subditis suis legem possunt eis imponere.
units.tr: over his wife, or a father over his offspring, but a husband ought to correct his wife who errs against the faith and good morals, and a father has to correct his child who errs against the faith and good morals. Therefore a king and a prince can correct his subjects who err against the faith and good morals; but a king, or even a prince, has the power to enact laws about those matters for which he can correct his subjects. Therefore kings and princes can impose laws on their subjects for keeping the faith.

units.la: Discipulus. Praedicta assertio non ita mihi videtur irrationabilis, sicut antea videbatur: & ideo cupio ipsius intellectum pleniorem habere: quia per hoc manifestius animaduertam, an sit consona vel dissona veritati, magis autem explicabis eam, si indicaueris, quomodo ad singulas allegationes contra eam adductas responderi contingat, ideo per omnes discurre. Magister. Ad auctoritatem Innocentii Tertii respondetur, quod ecclesiae & personae ecclesiasticae a iurisdictione laicorum sunt exemptae, & ideo super ecclesiis ordinandis vel conferendis, vel aliqua commutatione circa ecclesias facienda, seu etiam super personis ecclesiasticis puniendis, vel quomodolibet gubernandis, aut ad aliquid faciendum vel non faciendum artandis: laici nihil in earum commodum respicientes & fauorem possunt statuere, quod firmitatem obtineat, nisi ab ecclesia fuerit approbatum: quin tamen aliqua possint statuere in ecclesiarum & personarum ecclesiasticarum commodum & fauorem sub certis poenis suos subditos prohibendo, ne ecclesiis & personis ecclesiasticis molestiam inferant vel grauamen, Innocentius minime negat, nonne potest rex absque inquisitione cuiuscunque praelati ecclesiae statuere, quod quicunque clericum occidit, poena capitali plectatur? Nunquid potest statuere absque inquisitione ecclesiae, quod qui res ecclesiasticas furatus fuerit; poena mortis vel alia puniatur? Si ergo laici possunt statuere leges pro rebus temporalibus ecclesiae & personis ecclesiasticis a suis subditis nullatenus molestandis: multo fortius pro fide catholica, quam magis defendere & tueri tenentur, quam res ecclesiarum & personas ecclesiasticas quascunque, possunt leges statuere, ne quis subditus eorum fidem negare vel impugnare audeat quoquomodo.
units.tr: Disciple. The aforesaid assertion does not seem to me as unreasonable as it did before, and so I wish to have a fuller understanding of it, because through this I shall more clearly perceive whether it is consonant or dissonant with the truth. You will explain it more fully if you indicate how an answer may be given to each of the allegations brought against it, so please go through them all. Master. To the authority of Innocent III it is answered that churches and ecclesiastical persons are exempt from the jurisdiction of laymen; and therefore, concerning churches to be ordained or conferred, or any exchange to be made regarding churches, or even concerning ecclesiastical persons to be punished, or in any way governed, or constrained to do or not to do something, laymen, having no regard for their advantage or favour, cannot enact anything that has validity unless it has been approved by the Church. Yet Innocent by no means denies that they may enact some things for the advantage and favour of churches and ecclesiastical persons, prohibiting their subjects under certain penalties from causing harm or burden to churches and ecclesiastical persons. Can not a king, without inquiry by any prelate of the Church, enact that whoever kills a cleric shall be punished by capital penalty? Can he not enact, without inquiry by the Church, that whoever has stolen church property shall be punished by death or otherwise? If therefore laymen can enact laws for the temporal goods of the Church and for ecclesiastical persons, that their subjects shall in no way harass them, then much more, for the Catholic faith, which they are more bound to defend and protect than any church property or ecclesiastical persons whatever, they can enact laws that no subject of theirs shall dare in any way to deny or assail the faith.

units.la: Quod etiam tali ratione probatur, magis spectat ad principem constitutum a Deo (qualis est princeps vtens legitima potestate) vlcisci iniuriam Dei quam ciuium suorum, vt habetur vi- gesim. tert. quaestion. tert. cap. fi ea , sed rex & princeps possunt & debent legem statuere, ne vnus subditorum peccet in alterum, ergo multo magis potest condere leges, ne quisquam subditorum suorum fidem impugnet, exemplo Nabuchodonosor regis, qui legem dedit, ne quisquis Deum verum praesumeret blasphemare. Ad auctoritatem sumptam ex synodo Simachi Papae respondetur etiam per idem, quod laici non habent potestatem aliquid in ecclesia statuendi, quod immutationem circa ecclesias inducat; habent tamen statuere, ne quis eis subditus fidem catholicam impugnet, neget aut blasphemet, vel fidem quoquomodo subuertat. Ad auctoritatem ex synodo Eugenii Papae similiter respondetur, quod laici ecclesiastica negocia de rebus ac personis ecclesiasticis vel regendis, vel aliter immutandis se intromittere vel tractare non debent, nec clerici talia negocia laicorum iudicio, hoc est eorum auctoritate disponere debent, possunt tamen laici ordinare, vt clerici in ecclesiasticis disponendis negociis minime infestentur: possuntque eis aliquas libertates conferre exemplo principum antiquorum, qui, vt testatur Innocentius Tertius, extr. de rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis, cum laicis, ecclesiasticam libertatem multis priuilegiis muniuerunt, sic etiam possunt laici in fauorem fidei Christianae plura ordinare, ad quae seruanda suos subditos possunt legibus coartare. Si enim laici extra deuotionem, quam habent ad fidem catholicam, possunt in fauorem clericorum nonnulla statuere; & eis libertates plures tribuere: multo fortius possunt in fauorem fidei quamplurima statuere, & ad ea restringere sibi subditos. Ad auctoritatem, quae ponitur 16. quaestion. vltim. cap. laicus, respondetur: quod laici non possunt aliquid statuere circa dignitates immutandas: possunt tamen statuere plura pro dignitatibus ecclesiasticis defendendis, ad quae subditos (& non alios a potestate eorum exemptos) possunt constringere, nisi in casu. Cum vero dicitur: qui non potest minus, nec maius potest, dicitur quod ista fallit, quia saepe aliqua maiora spectant ad iurisdictionem vel potestatem aliquorum, ad quorum iurisdictionem vel potestatem quaedam minora non pertinent. In proposito tamen non fallit: quia sicut possunt laici quaedam statuere pro defensione ecclesiasticarum dignitatum, ita possunt nonnulla statuere pro defensione fidei orthodoxae. Ad auctoritatem Innoc. III. ext. de arbitris, respondetur, quod arbiter recipit potestatem ordinandi aliquid esse faciendum, & ideo in rebus spiritualibus laicus arbiter esse non potest: tamen cuilibet, cum hoc constat, quod laicus valeat ordinare, ne subditi sui res spirituales inuadant vel impugnent. Ad auctoritatem 6. dist. de statuto Basilii respondetur 16. quaestion. vltim. cap. laicis, vbi dicitur quod ideo statutum extitit reprobatum, quia plura agenda circa electionem summi Pontificis & res ecclesiasticas ordinauit, si autem solum statuisset, quod nullus sibi subditus de rebus ecclesiae se intromittere, vel electionem summi Pontificis impedire praesumeret, statutum suum non fuisset vltra reprobatum. Ad vltimam auctoritatem Innocentii Tertii consimiliter dicitur, quod laici de rebus ecclesiae distribuendis vel exponendis non possunt penitus ordinare, non tamen negat, quin potestatem habeant statuendi, ne res ecclesiae a suis subditis inuadantur.
units.tr: This is also proved by such a reason: it belongs more to a prince appointed by God (such as a prince exercising lawful power) to avenge the injury done to God than to avenge the injury done to his citizens, as is held in Dist. 23, quaest. 3, cap. fin. But a king and a prince can and ought to enact a law that one of his subjects shall not sin against another; therefore much more can he enact laws that none of his subjects shall assail the faith, following the example of King Nebuchadnezzar, who gave a law that whoever presumed to blaspheme the true God should be punished. To the authority taken from the synod of Pope Symmachus, the same answer is given: laymen have no power to enact anything in the Church that would bring about a change concerning churches; yet they may enact that none of their subjects assail, deny or blaspheme the Catholic faith, or in any way overthrow the faith. To the authority from the synod of Pope Eugenius, a similar answer is given: laymen ought not to meddle with or treat ecclesiastical affairs concerning churches and ecclesiastical persons, either to govern them or to alter them otherwise, nor ought clerics to arrange such affairs by the judgement of laymen, that is, by their authority. Nevertheless, laymen can ordain that clerics shall in no way be molested in arranging ecclesiastical business; and they can grant them certain liberties, following the example of the ancient princes who, as Innocent III testifies, Extra, De rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis, cum laicis, fortified ecclesiastical liberty with many privileges. So also laymen can, for the favour of the Christian faith, ordain many things which they can bind their subjects by laws to observe. For if laymen, apart from the devotion they have to the Catholic faith, can enact some things in favour of clerics and grant them many liberties, much more can they enact very many things in favour of the faith and bind their subjects to them. To the authority cited in 16, quaest. ult., cap. laicus, it is answered that laymen cannot enact anything to alter ecclesiastical dignities; yet they can enact many things for defending ecclesiastical dignities, to which they can bind their subjects (and not others who are exempt from their power), except in a case of necessity. When it is said, "He who cannot do less cannot do more," it is answered that this does not hold, because often some greater matters belong to the jurisdiction or power of certain persons, to whose jurisdiction or power certain lesser matters do not belong. In the present case, however, it does not fail, because just as laymen can enact some things for defending ecclesiastical dignities, so they can enact some things for defending the orthodox faith. To the authority of Innocent III, Extra, De arbitris, it is answered that an arbiter receives the power of ordaining that something is to be done, and therefore a layman cannot be an arbiter in spiritual matters; yet it is granted to anyone that a layman may ordain, so that his subjects do not seize or assail spiritual matters. To the authority of Dist. 6, the statute of Basil, it is answered from 16, quaest. ult., cap. laicis, where it is said that the statute was therefore rejected because it ordained many things concerning the election of the supreme Pontiff and ecclesiastical affairs; but if it had merely enacted that no subject of his should presume to meddle in ecclesiastical affairs or to impede the election of the supreme Pontiff, his statute would not have been rejected further. To the last authority of Innocent III, it is likewise said that laymen cannot wholly ordain concerning the distribution or disposal of church property; yet he does not deny that they have power to enact that church property shall not be seized by their subjects.

units.la: CAP. XCIV.
units.tr: CAP. XCIV.

units.la: In quo tractatur secundum probandum, scilicet quomodo quaestio sine causa fidei spectet ad laicos, & nota ibidem, quot modis quaestio fidei ventilari potest.
units.tr: In which the second point to be proved is treated, namely how a question of faith, without a cause of faith, concerns the laity, and it is noted there in how many ways a question of faith can be debated.

units.la: DIscip. Satis disseruisti, an quaestio fidei spectat ad laicos an non: nunc dic (secundum quod promisisti) per quem modum vidisti fidei quaestio ventilari potest seu spectat ad laicos. Per hoc autem de praedictis magis advertam, an aliquid contineant veritatis. Mag. Dicitur quod quaestionem ventilari multis modis potest accipere. Aut enim ventilatur quaestio de aliquo pertinente ad fidem, quod apud omnes catholicos tanquam catholicum exitit hactenus divulgatum, puta si aliqui incipiant vertere in quaestionem, an Christus sit verus Deus & verus homo; vel an Christus fuerit natus de virgine, vel beata vita sit futura: vel aliud consimile, de quo notum sit apud omnes catholicos literatos & illiteratos, quod ad fidem pertinet orthodoxam. Aut ventilatur de aliquo, quod est ab aliqua ecclesia explicite approbatum, licet talis approbatio non sit apud omnes catholicos divulgata. Puta si aliqui incipiant vertere in quaestionem, an Salomon fuerit filius Bersabeae, vel vir eius, audiui enim a quodam fide digno, quod asseruit se fuisse praesentem, quando quidam Magister in Theologia Parisiis tenuit in scholis, quod Bersabeae erat uxor Salomonis, dicens, quod illud quod dicitur in genealogia Salvatoris: David autem rex genuit Salomonem, &c. debet sic punctuari: David autem rex genuit Salomonem, ut ibi sit finis versus, & alius versus sic incipiat; ex ea quae fuit Vriae, Salomon genuit Roboam, quamuis igitur haec veritas; Salomon fuit filius Bersabeae, sit ab ecclesia explicite approbata, quemadmodum scriptura divina est explicite approbata: tamen potest ab insipientibus nonnunquam verti in quaestionem, sicut posset verti in quaestionem veritas Scripturae divinae, quae non est apud catholicos omnes tanquam catholica divulgata, sicut etiam potest verti, an in Christo fuerunt duae voluntates, quamuis in Christo non esse duas voluntates sit explicite pro haeresi condemnata. Aut ventilatur quaestio de aliquo, quod non est implicite approbatum, nec est haeresis explicite condemnata, sicut quaestio fidei inter Theologos saepissime ventilatur, sicut ante determinationem ecclesiae de processione Spiritus sancti a Filio inter Graecos & Latinos quaestio vertebatur. Loquendo de quaestione fidei primo modo dicta dicitur, quod talis quaestio multipliciter spectat ad laicos, uno modo, ut laici eandem assertionem apud catholicos divulgatam pro loco & tempore fateantur: quia secundum Apostolum ad Romanos decimo. Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem. & veritas ipsa Lucae undecimo ait: Qui erubuerit meos sermones, hunc filius hominis erubescet cum venerit in maiestate sua & Patris & sanctorum angelorum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod quilibet fidelis astringitur veritatem fidei sibi notam solenniter confiteri, quare laici in quaestione tali fidei veritatem sibi notam confiteri tenentur. Discipulus. Dic in quibus casibus laici tenentur veritatem fidei, de tali quaestione simplici confiteri. Magister. Respondetur, quod in duobus casibus laici, sicut & omnes Christiani, ad talem quaestionem de necessitate salutis sunt astricti.
units.tr: Disciple. You have discussed sufficiently whether a question of faith concerns the laity or not. Now tell me, as you promised, in what way you have seen that a question of faith can be debated or concerns the laity. I will then judge better whether what you have said contains any truth. Master. It is said that a question can be debated in many ways. A question may be raised about something that pertains to faith and that has so far been made known among all Catholics as Catholic, for example if some people begin to dispute whether Christ is true God and true man, or whether Christ was born of a virgin, or whether there will be a blessed life, or some other similar matter that is known among all Catholics, learned and unlearned, to belong to orthodox faith. Or a question may be raised about something that a church has explicitly approved, although such approval is not made known among all Catholics. For example, if some people begin to dispute whether Solomon was the son of Bathsheba or her husband. For I once heard from a trustworthy man, who said he was present when a certain Master of Theology taught in the schools at Paris, that Bathsheba was Solomon's wife. He said that what is said in the genealogy of the Saviour, And David the king begat Solomon, etc., should be pointed thus: And David the king begat Solomon, so that the verse ends there, and the next verse begins: of her that had been the wife of Urias, Solomon begat Roboam. Although this truth, that Solomon was the son of Bathsheba, has been explicitly approved by the Church, just as divine Scripture has been explicitly approved, nevertheless it can sometimes be called into question by the unwise, just as the truth of divine Scripture, which is not made known among all Catholics as Catholic, could be called into question. Likewise it can be asked whether there were two wills in Christ, although that there are not two wills in Christ has been explicitly condemned as heresy. Or a question may be raised about something that has not been implicitly approved and is not explicitly condemned as heresy, as a question of faith is very often debated among theologians. Thus before the Church's determination, the question was debated between Greeks and Latins about the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. Speaking of a question of faith in the first sense just mentioned, it is said that such a question concerns the laity in several ways. In one way, so that the laity confess the same assertion that is made known among Catholics, according to place and time. For, according to the Apostle in Romans chapter ten, With the heart man believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. And the Truth itself says in Luke chapter eleven: Whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he shall come in his own glory, and in his Father's, and of the holy angels. From these words it is gathered that every believer is bound to confess solemnly the truth of the faith known to him, so that the laity too, in such a question, are bound to confess the truth of the faith known to them. Disciple. Tell me in what cases the laity are bound to confess the truth of the faith in such a simple question. Master. It is answered that in two cases the laity, like all Christians, are bound by necessity of salvation to such a question.

units.la: Primus est, quando per omissionem huiusmodi confessionis subtraheretur honor fidei, quando videlicet per omissionem huiusmodi confessionis auerterentur alii a fide, vel converterentur ad haereticam pravitatem. Secundo sunt laici ad confessionem talem astricti, quando per omissionem confessionis huiusmodi fideles aliquod detrimentum incurrerent, aut subtraheretur a fidelibus aliquod subsidium impendendum, utpote si defendentes aliquam veritatem catholicam in tali quaestione mota per confessionem principis sui provocarentur ad defendendum, iuuandum, & favendum confitentibus catholicis veritatem & impugnantibus haereticam pravitatem, per omissionem autem talis confessionis, seu per taciturnitatem subditi principis provocarentur ad impugnandum defendentes catholicam veritatem, & ad subtrahendum eis favorem, auxilium & consilium oportunum, in hoc casu de necessitate salutis deberet princeps catholicam veritatem circa talem quaestionem publice confiteri: & consimiliter de aliis laicis est dicendum. Discipulus. Vellem scire, an aliquis Doctor modernus praeter Doctores autenticos concordat cum ista sententia. Magister. Ista sententia videtur esse Thomae secunda secundae quaestion. tertio, articulo secundo, qui ait: confiteri fidem non semper, nec in quolibet loco est de necessitate salutis: sed aliquo loco & tempore, quando scilicet per omissionem huiusmodi confessionis subtraheretur honor Dei & utilitas proximi impendenda: puta si aliquis interrogatus de fide taceret, & ex hoc crederetur, vel quod non habet fidem, vel quod fides non est vera, vel alii per taciturnitatem auerterentur a fide, in huiusmodi casibus confessio fidei est de necessitate salutis: & post dicit, quod quando honor Dei & utilitas proximi hoc exposcit, non debet esse contentus homo, ut per fidem suam ipse divinae veritati coniungatur: sed debet fidem exterius confiteri: & post: dicendum est, quod in casu necessitatis vbi fides periclitatur, quilibet tenetur fidem suam aliis propalare, vel ad instructionem aliorum fidelium, sive confirmationem, vel ad reprimendum infidelium insultationem: & post: si aliqua utilitas fidei praepararetur, aut necessitas adsit (contempta turbatione infidelium) debet homo publice fidem confiteri. Vnde Matth. decimo quinto dicitur, quod cum discipuli dixissent Domino, quod Pharisei audito eius verbo scandalizati sunt, Dominus respondit: sinite eos, scilicet turbari: caeci sunt & duces caecorum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod principes & alii laici siue interrogenterrogentur siue non interrogentur (si per omissionem confessionis veritatis eis notæ circa quæstionem motam de fide, alii à fide vel à defensione necessaria fidei auertantur, vel fideles aliqua dispendia patiantur) de necessitate salutis veritatem notam publice confiteri tenentur, & non solum viri ad confessionem publicam veritatis eis notæ, sed etiam mulieres in supradictis obligantur casibus. Discipulus. Quid si prælati ecclesiæ mandarent laicis, quod à tali confessione cessarent? Magister. Respondere deberent verbum Petri dicentis Actorum quinto, Obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus. Discipulus. Nonne laici debent sequi doctrinam prælatorum ecclesiæ, cum dicat Cælestinus Papa, distinct. 62. cap. docendus: Docendus est populus non sequendus? Magister. Respondetur, quod docendus est populus in his quæ ignorat, ab eis autem quæ didicit à fideli ecclesia, non est auertendus. Discipulus. Et quibus credet populus, nisi prælatis ecclesiæ? Magister. Respondetur, quod populus magis credet scripturæ diuinæ, quam omnibus clericis: quia scriptura diuina est omnibus mortalibus præferenda. Item magis credet populus toti communitati fidelium præcedentium, quam multitudini existentium in vita præsenti, & ideo si multitudo clericorum recedat ab illis, quæ priores nunc regnantes cum Christo concorditer tenuerunt, non essent vllatenus audiendi, sed essent pœnis debitis coercendi. Disc. Dixisti vnum modum, per quem quæstio fidei mota de aliquo apud omnes orthodoxos, tanquam catholica diuulgata spectat ad laicos, ideo nunc dic alium modum secundum opinionem prius recitatam. Mag. Dicitur quod quæstio talis sic secundo spectat ad laicos, ideo consequenter dicitur quod laici omnes constringantur, tenentes, prædicantes, docentes, seu etiam dubitantes assertionem, quæ est contraria veritati, esse veram; & omnes negantes vel dubitantes catholicam veritatem taliter diuulgatam esse de substantia fidei, tanquam excommunicatos & hæreticos vitare & pro non prælatis habere: & eis nullatenus obedire tenentur. Verbi gratia: si aliqui prædicarent, docerent, vel assererent quoquomodo, vel etiam dubitarent Christum non fuisse natum de virgine, vel non fuisse passum, aut non resurrexisse à mortuis, laici autem omnes tales (etiam si aliquis eorum Papali fuisset præditus dignitate) tanquam hæreticos & excommunicatos vitare, & eis nullatenus obedire tenentur. Quod enim tales sunt reputandi hæretici, ex his quæ dicta sunt libro 4. cap. 2. colligitur euidenter. Quod autem sint excommunicati, ex cap. 6i. huius sexti apparet. Ex quibus sequitur luculenter, quod laici scientes Papam vel alios clericos prædicare, docere, vel qualitercunque tenere aliquam assertionem, quæ catholicæ veritati apud omnes orthodoxos vulgatæ contradicit, non debent aliqualiter obedire. Discipulus. Dic, quid si principes & alii laici nesciunt per scientiam certam Papam tenere vel docere contra talem veritatem catholicam: sciunt tamen Papam esse de tali doctrina pestifera publice diffamatum, nunquid ipsum vitare tenentur? Magister. Respondetur, quod non propter verba paucorum, sed propter publicam famam laicorum, ad quos talis fama peruenerit, Papam talia prædicantem vitare tenentur, quia ad hoc, quod aliquis excommunicatus vitetur, sufficit publica fama, extra, de sententia excommunicat. cum desideres, libro quinto, vbi Clemens Tertius dicit in hæc verba: Tua quæstioni hunc finem duximus imponendum, quod si publica fama est aliquem verberasse clericum, nec episcopus nec alius communicare sibi debet, nisi ad arbitrium episcopi de hoc se purgauerit, vel ad cautelam absolutionis beneficium consequatur, ergo à simili, si fama publica est, Papam vel alium prædicare, docere, vel tenere contra veritatem apud omnes catholicos diuulgatam, nec laici nec clerici sibi communicare debent, nisi se purgauerit, vel absolutionis beneficium rite & debite consequatur. Discipulus. Mirum videtur, quod propter famam Papa debeat euitari, præsertim cum fama probationem non faciat: & per consequens nec certitudinem faciat, antequam igitur aliquis sit certus, Papam ab homine vel à iure esse depositum, eum vitare non debet. Præterea in dubiis via tutior est tenenda, tutius enim est obedire, quam non obedire, quando dubitatur an aliquis sit verus Papa, licet ergo propter famam de Papa, quod prædicet contra talem veritatem catholicam, possit quis dubitare, an sit verus Papa, tamen propter talem dubium non debet ab obedientia eius recedere. Mag. Dicitur ad primum, quod quamuis per solam famam, quantumcunq; publicam nemo de crimine conuincatur, tamen sunt propter famam nonnunquam quædam agenda, & aliqua omittenda. Nam fama impedit matrimonium contrahendum, ext. de consanguin. & affinitate, super eo, & propter famam est diffamato purgatio indicenda, 2. qu. 3. si mala fama, sic etiam propter famam est obedientia deneganda. Cum autem dicitur, quod in dubiis via tutior est tenenda, respondetur, quod ex hoc aperte concluditur, quod Papa hæreticus propter solam famam publicam est vitandus, & ei est nullatenus obediendum. Nam si in dubiis via tutio est tenenda, illa autem via, qua est minus periculum, est tutior reputanda, igitur via, quæ maiori careret periculo, est tenenda, obedire autem hæretico Papæ & communicare eidem maius habet periculum, quam eum vitare, & ei minime obedire: quia ex obedientia & communione cum Papa hæretico immineret periculum fidei orthodoxæ, tale autem periculum est maius omni periculo, quod potest personæ (Papæ etiam catholici) imminere, igitur periculum fidei orthodoxæ est summe vitandum, igitur cum propter famam publicam dubitatur, an Papa inciderit in prauitatem hæreticam, vitandus est, ne ex communione eius periculum immineat fidei orthodoxæ. Discip. Nunquid propter omnem famam publicam laici tenentur Papam hæreticum denitare? Magister. Videtur nonnullis probabile, quod quia Papa tanquam signum est positus ad sagittam, & multos habet offendere, ideo est cautela diligens adhibenda, ne criminetur inique; ita tamen vt caueatur ne delinquere valeat infolenter, igitur apparet, quod propter famam ab incerto auctore vel certis auctoribus maledicis & maledictis ortam, non est Papa hæreticus à nescientibus eum esse hæreticum, euitandus. [illegible, ~6 letters] per famam ortam ex certis authoribus bonae famae hactenus (praesertim qui sunt in sacris paginis eruditi) valentibus Papam de pravitate haeretica accusare; seipsos ad poenam talionis (si in probatione defecerint) obligare, est Papa haereticus deuitandus, etiam antequam in iudicio de haeresi conuincatur. Discipulus. Dic secundum priorem assertionem, an quaestio fidei de qua est sermo, alio modo spectat ad laicos. Magist. Dicitur quod quaestio fidei, de qua sermo habitus est prius, sic spectat ad laicos, quod & principes seculares & alii laici debent defendere catholicos prauitatem haereticam impugnantes, in tantum quod scientes Papam haereticum, vel ad quos peruenit fama publica (modo praefato) quod Papa est haereticus, tenentur de necessitate salutis in fauorem fidei Christianae omnes accusantes Papam haereticum, & pro ipsa causa haeresis appellantes, ac ipsum de haeresi impugnantes, si possunt, ab omni molestia eis per Papam haereticum, vel eius complices inferenda & illata defendere. Discipulus. Illa quae tractauimus supra in isto sexto a capite decimo vsque ad capitulum vigesimum quintum, ad istum modum poterunt applicari, vt videtur, ideo dic alium modum, quomodo quaestio fidei spectat ad laicos. Magister. Dicitur, quod quaestio fidei talis, de qua sermo habitus est prius, sic spectat ad laicos, quod tractantibus de tali quaestione (maxime si clerico suspectos habuerint) possunt si voluerint interesse, quia, sicut tactum est prius, quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus debet tractari, talis autem quaestio fidei tangit omnes laicos, ergo laici (maxime curam aliorum gerentes) possunt tractatoribus de tali quaestione fidei interesse. Discipulus. Quamuis de hoc videatur esse dictum, supra, cum de concilio generali ageretur, vbi allegationes adduxisti, quod laici, si voluerint, possunt generali concilio, in quo tractatur de fide catholica, interesse: tamen adhuc ad assertionem praedictam allegare conare. Magister. Quod laici tractantibus de huiusmodi quaestione fidei valeant interesse, nititur posse probari tali ratione. Illi possunt tractantibus de quaestione fidei interesse, qui loqui de his, quae spectant ad quaestionem fidei sunt minime prohibendi, quia tales si non sunt prohibendi, sunt audiendi, si loqui voluerint, sed laici non sunt prohibendi loqui quaestiones fidei, teste Glossa quae super illud Ad Thessalonicenses vl-tim. Spiritum nolite extinguere, ait: Si cui Spiritus sanctus ad horam quid revelauit, nolite prohibere loqui: quia Deus qui est alias aperuit, saepe revelat minori quod melius est. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ille in quaestione fidei loqui prohiberi non debet, cui Deus quandoque meliora revelat, sed Deus revelat quandoque laicis meliora. Vnde & Dauid regi quamuis non esset sacerdos, Spiritus sanctus quamplurima reuelauit, laicis etiam aliis tam in Veteri, quam in Nouo Testamento plura ad fidem spectantia, & ad catholicam fidem reuelata fuerunt. Vnde & Christus dicit Matthaei vndecimo. Confiteor tibi pater Domine caeli & terrae: quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus & prudentibus, & revelasti ea parvulis. Igitur laici in sacra pagina maxime eruditi a tractantibus de quaestione fidei, quae ad omnes pertinet Christianos, excludi non debent. Discipulus. Ista assertio consuetudini ecclesiae maxime repugnare videtur. Tum, quia secundum assertionem praecedentem etiam mulieres a tractatibus fidei non sunt excludendae. Tum, quia quandoque quaedam abscondunter a viris, quae mulieribus reuelantur: & tamen mulieres ad tractatus fidei sunt nullatenus admittendae, cum etiam mulieres in ecclesia loqui non debeant, sed solum domi interrogare viros suos de ignotis, teste Apostolo, qui primo ad Corinth. 14. ait: Mulieres in ecclesiis taceant, non enim permittitur eis loqui, sed subditae esse sicut lex dicit: Si quid autem volunt discere, domi viros suos interrogent, turpe autem est mulieri in ecclesia loqui, igitur mulieres tractatibus de quaestionibus fidei interesse non debent. Magister. Ad primum istorum respondetur, quod non est ex consuetudine ecclesiae, quod ad tractatus fidei vnquam laici recipiantur: quia, sicut probatum est prius, saepe conciliis generalibus, in quibus tractabatur de quaestionibus fidei, Imperatores fuerunt praesentes, saepe tamen quaestiones fidei per solos clericos tractabantur: quia tunc temporis clerici de fide non fuerunt suspecti, qui vita, scientia, & zelo fidei catholicae praefulserunt: & laici interesse non curabant, scientes quod quaestiones fidei sufficienter per clericos ad honorem Dei & exaltationem fidei tractabantur. Si enim principes ex zelo fidei se tractarib. huiusmodi ingessissent, clerici tunc temporis fidei zelatores eos nullatenus repulissent, sed libenti animo audiuissent. Ad secundum respondetur, quod mulieres non sunt passim ad tractatus fidei admittendae, si tamen sunt aliquae mulieres sapientia, sanctitate, potentia & virtutibus praecellentes, petentes ex zelo fidei audientiam, cum fides pertractatur, non sunt repellendae, si enim Iudith vidua petens audientiam a presbyteris, cum de liberatione patriae tractaretur, non fuit repulsa, sed audita: multo magis in casu nostro, quia maior debet esse sollicitudo de salutatione fidei, quam de liberatione patriae. Si mulier sapientia, potentia & sanctitate praecellens ex zelo fidei petierit audientiam cum de quaestione fidei tractatur, repelli non debet, sed audiri, imo nonnunquam cum quaestio fidei agitatur pro consilio & auxilio obtinendo, ad mulieres sapientia, sanctitate & potentia praecellentes expedit recursum habere pro quaestione fidei laudabiliter terminanda, exemplo Mardochaei, qui pro salutatione populi Dei auxilium ab Hestel regina supplicitor postulauit. Quamuis igitur mulieres non sint passim ad tractatus fidei admittendae, non sunt tamen omni tempore repellendae: cum quaestio fidei ad eas pertinere noscatur, in tantum quod si omnes viri diffinirent & assererent esse tenendum, quod Christus non fuit natus de virgine, aut quod animae damnatorum non cruciantur in inferno, aliquid huiusmodi, mulieres deberent resistere, & illa tenere quae ab orthodoxis didicerant. Cum vero dicit Apostolus, quod mulieres in ecclesiis taceant, &c. Respondetur, quod Apostolus loquitur, cum ad audiendum verbum Dei conuenerint, volens quod mulieres sic in ecclesiis taceant, quod officium docendi non habeant, & ideo vbi verbum Dei proponeretur à catholico & fideli, licet mulieres ignorent aliqua, quae proponuntur à praedicante, non debent in ecclesiis interrogare, quae ignorant: sed domi viros suos & aliquos Doctores vel doctos interrogent, aliter est vbi tractatur, quomodo fides est seruanda & defendenda, tunc enim possunt nonnullae mulieres esse vtiles & causam fidei multipliciter promouere, & ideo à talibus tractatibus non sunt omnes & omni tempore excludendae. Disc. Spectat ne quaestio fidei alio modo ad laicos? Mag. Quaestio fidei cum aliquid apud oēs catholicos tanquam catholicum diuulgatū in quaestione vertitur, sic spectat ad laicos, quod prohibere possunt & statuere leges, ne aliquis in terris eorum subiectis dominiis contra veritatē taliter diuulgatam praedicare aut docere praesumat, exemplo Nabuchodonosor regis, qui quis non esset clericus nec praelatus ecclesiae, legē statuit, ne quis Dei Sydrach, Mysach, & Abdenago praesumeret blasphemare, hoc ex his, quae dicta sunt prius, vbi ostensum est, quod laici possunt pro fide leges statuere, colligitur euidenter. Disc. Nunquid possunt laici coercere transgressores praeceptorum & legum suarum huiusmodi? Mag. Respondetur, quod transgressores huiusmodi, qui à iurisdictione laicorum sunt exempti, puta clerici, non possunt regulariter coercere; in casu tamen possunt.
units.tr: The first case is when, by omitting such a confession, the honour of the faith would be diminished, namely when others would be turned away from the faith or drawn into heretical wickedness by its omission. Second, laymen are bound to such a confession when, by omitting it, the faithful would suffer some loss, or some help due to the faithful would be withheld. For example, if men defending some Catholic truth on a question of this kind, raised by the confession of their prince, were provoked to attack them, and if, by the omission of that confession or by the silence of a subject prince, they were provoked to oppose those defending Catholic truth and to withhold from them favour, aid and fitting counsel, then in such a case the prince would be bound, for the sake of salvation, to confess the Catholic truth publicly on that question. The same is to be said of other laymen. Student. I should like to know whether any modern teacher, apart from the authentic doctors, agrees with this opinion. Master. This opinion seems to be that of Thomas, in the second part of the second part, question 3, article 2, who says: to confess the faith is not always, nor in every place, necessary for salvation, but at a certain place and time, namely when by the omission of such a confession the honour of God and the good of one's neighbour would be lost: for example, if someone, questioned about the faith, kept silent, and from this it were believed either that he has no faith, or that the faith is not true, or others were turned away from the faith by his silence. In such cases, confession of the faith is necessary for salvation. And afterwards he says that when the honour of God and the good of one's neighbour demand it, a man should not be content to be joined to the divine truth by his faith alone, but ought to confess his faith outwardly. And again: it must be said that in a case of necessity, where the faith is in danger, everyone is bound to make his faith known to others, either for the instruction and strengthening of other faithful people, or to restrain the insolence of unbelievers. And again: if some advantage to the faith is to be gained, or if necessity is at hand, then (disregarding the disturbance of unbelievers) a man ought to confess the faith publicly. Hence it is said in Matthew 15 that when the disciples told the Lord that the Pharisees were offended on hearing his word, the Lord answered: let them alone, that is, let them be troubled; they are blind and leaders of the blind. From these words it is clearly gathered that princes and other laymen, whether they are questioned or not, if by the omission of the confession of the truth known to them, on a question raised concerning the faith, others are turned away from the faith or from the necessary defence of the faith, or the faithful suffer some loss, are bound, for the sake of salvation, to confess publicly the truth known to them. Not only men, but women too, are bound to public confession of the truth known to them in the cases mentioned above. Student. What if the prelates of the Church commanded laymen to cease from such a confession? Master. They ought to answer with the words of Peter, who says in Acts 5: We ought to obey God rather than men. Student. Ought not laymen to follow the teaching of the prelates of the Church, since Pope Celestine says, Distinction 62, chapter Docendus: The people are to be taught, not to be followed? Master. The answer is that the people are to be taught in those things which they do not know, but they are not to be turned away from what they have learned from the faithful Church. Student. And whom will the people believe, if not the prelates of the Church? Master. The answer is that the people will believe the divine Scripture more than all the clergy, because divine Scripture is to be preferred to all mortals. Likewise the people will believe the whole community of the faithful who went before more than the multitude now living in the present life. Therefore, if the multitude of clergy departs from those things which the former, who now reign with Christ, held in harmony, they are by no means to be heard, but are to be restrained by the punishments due to them. Stud. You have stated one way by which a question of faith raised about something, as commonly published among all the orthodox as Catholic, belongs to laymen. Now state another way according to the opinion recited earlier. Mast. It is said that a question of this kind belongs to laymen in a second way. Consequently it is said that all laymen are bound, whether holding, preaching, teaching, or even doubting, to hold the assertion contrary to the truth to be true, and all who deny or doubt that the Catholic truth so published is of the substance of the faith, they are bound to avoid as excommunicated and heretics, to regard as non-prelates, and by no means to obey. For example: if some men preached, taught, or asserted in any way, or even doubted, that Christ was not born of a virgin, or did not suffer, or did not rise from the dead, then all laymen are bound to avoid such men as heretics and excommunicates, and by no means to obey them, even if one of them were endowed with papal dignity. That such men are to be regarded as heretics is clearly gathered from what was said in book 4, chapter 2. That they are excommunicated appears from chapter 61 of this sixth book. From these things it clearly follows that laymen who know that the Pope or other clerics preach, teach, or hold in any way an assertion that contradicts the Catholic truth published among all the orthodox, ought in no way to obey them. Student. Tell me: what if princes and other laymen do not know for certain that the Pope holds or teaches against such Catholic truth, but they know that the Pope is publicly reported to be of such a pestilent doctrine? Are they bound to avoid him? Master. The answer is that laymen are bound to avoid the Pope when he preaches such things, not because of the words of a few, but because of the public report that reaches the laymen; for to make an excommunicate man to be avoided, public report is enough. See extra, de sententia excommunicationis, cum desideres, book 5, where Clement III says in these words: We have decided to put this end to your question: that if it is public report that someone has struck a cleric, neither the bishop nor anyone else ought to hold communion with him, unless he has cleared himself of this at the bishop's judgment, or has obtained the benefit of absolution as a precaution. Therefore, by like reasoning, if it is public report that the Pope or another preaches, teaches, or holds against a truth published among all Catholics, neither laymen nor clerics ought to hold communion with him, unless he has cleared himself, or has rightly and duly obtained the benefit of absolution. Student. It seems strange that the Pope should be avoided on account of report, especially since report proves nothing, and therefore does not even produce certainty. So until someone is certain that the Pope has been deposed by man or by law, he ought not to avoid him. Moreover, in doubtful matters the safer way is to be followed, for it is safer to obey than not to obey, when it is doubtful whether someone is the true Pope. So although, on account of report that the Pope preaches against such Catholic truth, one may doubt whether he is the true Pope, yet on account of such doubt one ought not withdraw from his obedience. Master. To the first point it is answered that although no one is convicted of a crime by report alone, however public, nevertheless on account of report some things are sometimes to be done and some omitted. For report prevents a marriage from being contracted (see extra, de consanguinitate et affinitate, super eo), and on account of report purgation is imposed on the person defamed (2, qu. 3, si mala fama). So also on account of report obedience is to be refused. But when it is said that in doubtful matters the safer way is to be followed, the answer is that from this it is plainly concluded that a heretical Pope is to be avoided on the strength of public report alone, and is in no way to be obeyed. For if in doubtful matters the safer way is to be followed, and the way with less danger is to be regarded as safer, then the way that lacks the greater danger is to be followed. But to obey a heretical Pope and to communicate with him carries a greater danger than to avoid him and not obey him at all: for from obedience to and communion with a heretical Pope there would threaten danger to the orthodox faith, and such danger is greater than any danger that can threaten a person, even a Catholic Pope. Therefore the danger to the orthodox faith is to be avoided above all. Therefore, when on account of public report it is doubtful whether the Pope has fallen into heretical wickedness, he is to be avoided, lest danger to the orthodox faith threaten from communion with him. Student. Are laymen bound to avoid a heretical Pope on account of every public report? Master. It seems probable to some that, since the Pope is set as a mark for the arrow and has many to offend him, careful caution must be used lest he be accused unjustly; yet so that care is taken lest he be able to offend insolently. Therefore it appears that a Pope is not to be avoided as a heretic by those who do not know him to be a heretic, on account of report arising from an uncertain author, or from certain malicious authors and men maligned. [illegible] on account of report arising from certain authors of good repute hitherto (especially those learned in the sacred pages) who are able to accuse the Pope of heretical wickedness; if they bind themselves to the penalty of retaliation (should they fail in the proof), the heretical Pope is to be avoided, even before he is convicted of heresy in judgment. Student. Tell me, according to the earlier assertion, whether the question of faith we are discussing belongs to laymen in another way. Master. It is said that the question of faith, of which we spoke earlier, belongs to laymen in such a way that princes and other laymen ought to defend those who oppose heretical wickedness, to such an extent that those who know the Pope to be a heretic, or to whom public report (in the manner mentioned) has come that the Pope is a heretic, are bound, for the sake of salvation and in favour of the Christian faith, to accuse the heretical Pope, all who appeal on the very cause of heresy, and all who oppose him in matters of heresy, if they can, and to defend them from every annoyance inflicted or to be inflicted on them by the heretical Pope or his accomplices. Student. The things we treated above in this sixth book, from chapter 10 to chapter 25, seem to be applicable in this way. So tell me another way in which the question of faith belongs to laymen. Master. It is said that a question of faith such as we have discussed earlier belongs to laymen in such a way that those who treat of such a question (especially if they regard a cleric as suspect) may, if they wish, take part in it. For, as was said before, what touches all ought to be treated by all; and such a question of faith touches all laymen; therefore laymen (especially those who care for others) may take part in those who treat of such a question of faith. Student. Although this seems to have been said above, when we were discussing a general council, where you brought forward arguments that laymen, if they wish, may take part in a general council in which the Catholic faith is treated, nevertheless I still try to bring forward the assertion mentioned. Master. That laymen may take part in those treating of such a question of faith is sought to be proved by the following argument. Those may take part in those treating of a question of faith who are in no way to be forbidden to speak of things that concern the question of faith; for such persons, if they are not to be forbidden, are to be heard if they wish to speak. But laymen are not to be forbidden to speak on questions of faith, as the Gloss on the last chapter of the first letter to the Thessalonians, Spiritum nolite extinguere, says: If the Holy Spirit has revealed something to anyone for a while, do not forbid him to speak, for God, who has opened other things, often reveals to the lesser what is better. From these words it is gathered that one who may at some time have better things revealed by God is not to be forbidden to speak on a question of faith; but God sometimes reveals better things to laymen. Hence, although David was not a priest, the Holy Spirit revealed very many things to him; and in both the Old and the New Testament many things pertaining to the faith were revealed to other laymen, and things revealed for the Catholic faith. Hence Christ also says in Matthew 11: I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones. Therefore laymen, especially those most learned in the sacred page, ought not to be excluded from those treating of a question of faith, which pertains to all Christians. Student. This assertion seems to be very much opposed to the custom of the Church. First, because according to the preceding assertion even women should not be excluded from treatments of the faith. Second, because sometimes things are hidden from men that are revealed to women; yet women are by no means to be admitted to treatments of the faith, since women ought not to speak in the Church, but only at home to ask their husbands about things they do not know, as the Apostle witnesses, who says in 1 Corinthians 14: Let women keep silence in the churches, for it is not permitted them to speak, but to be subject, as the law says. If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the church. Therefore women ought not to take part in treatments of questions of faith. Master. To the first of these it is answered that it is not by custom of the Church that laymen are ever admitted to treatments of the faith. For, as was proved before, Emperors were often present at general councils, in which questions of faith were treated; yet questions of faith were often treated by clerics alone, because at that time the clergy were not suspected in matters of faith; they shone in life, learning and zeal for the Catholic faith, and laymen did not care to take part, knowing that questions of faith were sufficiently treated by the clergy to the honour of God and the exaltation of the faith. For if princes, out of zeal for the faith, had thrust themselves into such treatments, the clergy, then the zealots of the faith, would by no means have repelled them, but would have heard them with a willing mind. To the second it is answered that women are not to be admitted to treatments of the faith indiscriminately; yet if there are some women who excel in wisdom, holiness, power and virtues, and who, out of zeal for the faith, ask for a hearing when the faith is being discussed, they are not to be repelled but heard. For when the widow Judith asked a hearing from the elders when the deliverance of the homeland was being discussed, she was not repelled but heard; much more so in our case, since concern for the salvation of the faith ought to be greater than for the deliverance of the homeland. If a woman who excels in wisdom, power and holiness, out of zeal for the faith, asks for a hearing when a question of faith is being treated, she ought not to be repelled but heard. Indeed, sometimes, when a question of faith is being debated in order to obtain counsel and help, it is useful to have recourse to women who excel in wisdom, holiness and power, for the praiseworthy settling of a question of faith, after the example of Mordecai, who humbly asked Queen Esther for help for the salvation of the people of God. Although, therefore, women are not to be admitted to treatments of the faith indiscriminately, they are nevertheless not to be repelled at all times, since a question of faith is known to pertain to them, to such an extent that if all men were to define and assert that something must be held, such as that Christ was not born of a virgin, or that the souls of the damned are not tormented in hell, or anything of that kind, women ought to resist and hold to what they had learned from the orthodox. As for the Apostle's saying that women keep silence in the churches, etc., the answer is that the Apostle speaks of when they have gathered to hear the word of God, wishing that women so keep silence in the churches that they have no office of teaching; and therefore, where the word of God is set forth by a Catholic and faithful man, although women may not understand some things that are set forth by the preacher, they ought not to question in the churches about what they do not understand, but at home they should ask their husbands and some teachers or learned men. It is otherwise where it is being treated how the faith is to be kept and defended; for then some women can be useful and promote the cause of the faith in many ways, and therefore they are not to be excluded from such treatments in every way and at all times. Stud. Does a question of faith belong to laymen in another way? Mast. When a question is being raised about something published among all Catholics as Catholic truth, it belongs to laymen in such a way that they may forbid and enact laws, so that no one in lands subject to their dominion presumes to preach or teach against the truth so published.
