Contra crimen, quod est gravius in se & toti communitati fidelium periculosius & perniciosius oportet catholicos & fideles cum maiori vigore & sollicitudine & cautela resistere, sed crimen haeresis in papa gravius est & toti communitati fidelium perniciosius & periculosius, si circa eius correctionem ecclesiastica potestas deficit, sive per malitiam sive impotentiam sive per damnabilem negligentiam sive per ignorantiam, quam sit crimen apostasiae ab ordine etiam post trinam monitionem, ergo cum maiori vigore, sollicitudine & cautela debent catholici universi rescindere crimen haeresis in papa; quam crimen apostasiae in clerico etiam post trinam admonitionem, sed publicae potestates punire possunt clericos apostatas ab ordine post trinam admonitionem, ergo multo fortius deficiente ecclesiastica potestate publicae potestates papam haereticum compescere possunt, maior primi Syllogismi patet aperte, nam saepe videmus crimina leviora in se graviusque puniri propter hoc quod sunt communitati periculosiora, & ita magis resistitur crimini leviori propter hoc solum, quod est communitati periculosius, unde & in multis regionibus, regnis & terris furtum gravius punitur quam adulterium: quoniam furtum punitur poena capitali, quia est periculosius: adulterium vero non sic punitur, furtum autem licet sit periculosius communitati, tamen est levius, teste Salomone, qui Proverbio 6. ait: non grandis est culpa cum quis furatur, furatur enim ut esurientem impleat animam: deprehensus quoque reddet septuplum, & omnem substantiam domus suae tradet & liberabitur, qui autem adulter est, propter cordis inopiam perdet animam suam, turpitudinem & ignorantiam congregabit sibi, & opprobrium eius non delebitur. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod crimen furti est minus grave, quam adulterium. Sic etiam licet detractio levius puniatur, quam furtum vel rapina: tamen gravius crimen est censendum, teste Anacleto papa, qui ait ut habetur 6. quaest. 1. c. deteriores, ait: deteriores sunt qui doctorum vitam moresque corrumpunt, qui substantias aliorum pradiaque diripiunt, ipsi enim ea quae extra nos sunt (licet nostra sint) auferunt: nostri quoque detractores & morum corruptores nostrorum, sive qui aduersus nos armantur, proprie nos ipsos diripiunt, & ita constat, quod minora saepe (quae magis nocent rei publicae) gravius puniuntur, quod Glossa extra, de immunitate ecclesiarum cap. ultimo, insinuare videtur, quae tamen enim dicens: quare publicus latro & depopulator agrorum potius extrahuntur ab ecclesia, quam alius malefactor, qui forte deterior est? Et respondens ait: Quoniam plerumque interest illos puniri, quam alios malefactores: cum pluribus exitia cogitent, quam alii, 23. quaest. 4. c. est iniusta, quod est capitulum Ambrosii, vbi ait: Si quis latronem filium deprecantibus motus & lachrymis coniugis eius inflexus absoluendum putat: cui adhuc latrocinandi aspirat affectus, nonne innocentes tradet exitio, qui liberat exitia multorum cogitantem?
units.tr: Disciple: If you have thought of some reasons for this assertion, bring them forward. Master: The above assertion can be proved by many reasons, of which the first is this. Catholics and the faithful must resist a crime with greater vigour, care and caution if it is graver in itself and more dangerous and pernicious to the whole community of the faithful. But the crime of heresy in the pope is graver and more pernicious and more dangerous to the whole community of the faithful, if ecclesiastical power fails to correct him, whether through malice, impotence, damnable negligence or ignorance, than the crime of apostasy from holy orders, even after threefold admonition. Therefore all Catholics must cut out the crime of heresy in the pope with greater vigour, care and caution than the crime of a cleric's apostasy after threefold admonition. But public powers can punish clergy who apostatize from their order after threefold admonition. Therefore, much more strongly, when ecclesiastical power fails, public powers can restrain a heretical pope. The major premise of the first syllogism is plain, for we often see lesser crimes, lesser in themselves, punished more severely because they are more dangerous to the community. So a lesser crime is resisted more only because it is more dangerous to the community. Hence in many regions, kingdoms and lands theft is punished more severely than adultery, since theft is punished by capital penalty because it is more dangerous, whereas adultery is not so punished. Yet theft, though more dangerous to the community, is the lighter crime, as Solomon testifies in Proverbs 6, where he says: "A man is not greatly to blame when he steals, for he steals to satisfy his hunger; yet if he is caught he shall restore sevenfold, and give up all the substance of his house. But he who commits adultery, for lack of heart, destroys his own soul; he shall gather to himself dishonour and shame, and his reproach shall not be wiped out." From these words it is understood that theft is a less grave crime than adultery. So too, although slander is punished more lightly than theft or robbery, it is still to be judged the graver crime, as Pope Anacletus testifies, as found in 6 q. 1 c. deteriores: "Worse are those who corrupt the lives and morals of teachers, and who tear away the goods and estates of others. For they take away those things which are outside us, though they are ours. Our slanderers and corrupters of our morals, and those who arm themselves against us, tear us apart in the most proper sense." And so it is established that lesser things, which harm the commonwealth more, are often punished more severely. The Gloss, extra, de immunitate ecclesiarum, last chapter, seems to hint at this, for asking, "Why is a public robber and plunderer of fields dragged from the church rather than another evildoer, who perhaps is worse?", it answers: "Because it is generally more important that they be punished than other evildoers, since they plan destruction for many more than others," as in 23 q. 4 c. est iniusta. That is a chapter of Ambrose, where he says: "If someone, moved by the prayers and tears of his robber son, and yielding to the entreaties of his wife, thinks he should be acquitted, will he not hand over the innocent to destruction, while freeing a man who still has the desire to rob and plans destruction for many?"

units.la: Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ideo aliqua crimina grauius vindicantur, quia sunt grauius communitati nociua, & ita patet maior Syllogismi primi. Minor (scilicet quod crimen haeresis in papa non solum est in se grauius, sed etiam periculosius & perniciosius communitati) est de se manifesta & ex verbis Augustin. quae ponuntur distinct. 83. capitulo nemo, patenter habetur. Ait enim: Nemo quippe in ecclesia amplius nocet, quam si peruerse agens, nomen & ordinem sanctitatis & sacerdotis habet, delinquentem namque hunc redarguere nullus praesumit, & in exemplum culpa vehementer extenditur, quando pro reuerentia peccatoris honoratur. Ex quibus inferri potest, quod nemo amplius in ecclesia nocet, quam qui peruerse docens nomen papae habet, quia doctrina eius pestifera vehementer diffunditur, si pro reuerentia summi pontificis haereticus honoratur.
units.tr: From these words it is gathered that some crimes are punished more severely because they are more harmful to the community, and so the major premise of the first syllogism is plain. The minor premise (namely that the crime of heresy in the pope is not only graver in itself, but also more dangerous and pernicious to the community) is evident in itself, and it is plainly had from the words of Augustine set down in dist. 83, chapter Nemo. For he says: "Indeed no one does more harm in the Church than one who, acting perversely, has the name and order of holiness and of priest. For no one presumes to rebuke such a sinner, and the fault is spread widely as an example when the sinner is honoured out of reverence for him." From these words it can be inferred that no one does more harm in the Church than one who, teaching perversely, has the name of pope, because his pestilent doctrine spreads widely if a heretic is honoured out of reverence for the supreme pontiff.

units.la: Quod autem publicae potestates punire debeant apostatantem ab ordine clericum post trinam monitionem (quae est minus periculosa & minus nociua quam crimen haereticae prauitatis in papa) patet aperte ex eo, quod extra de sententia excommunicationis, capitulo in audientia, sic legitur: huiusmodi clerici si a prelatis suis tertio moniti militaria arma nolunt deponere, de priuilegio clericorum subsidium aliquod habere non debent, igitur multo fortius si papa a fide catholica apostataverit, prauitatem haereticam incurrendo, & docendo si praelati ecclesiae eum noluerint vel non potuerint coercere, compesci debet per publicas potestates.
units.tr: That the civil authorities ought to punish a cleric who apostatises from his order after a third warning (which is less dangerous and less harmful than the crime of heretical depravity in a pope) is plainly shown by the chapter in audientia in the decretal extra, de sententia excommunicationis, which reads: If such clerics, after a third warning from their prelates, are unwilling to lay down the weapons of war, they ought to have no help from the privilege of clerics. Therefore, much more strongly, if a pope has fallen away from the Catholic faith, incurring heretical depravity and teaching it, and if the prelates of the Church have been unwilling or unable to restrain him, he must be restrained by the civil authorities.

units.tr: {5} What is in the margin at 'Disciput' ...

units.la: Discipul. Ista ratio falsum videtur accipere, cum innuit, quod peccatum leuius aliquotiens grauius vindicatur: & quod peccatum periculosius est grauius puniendum, utrumque enim istorum scripturis autenticis repugnare videtur. Ait enim Hieronymus, ut legitur 24. q. 1. c. non affer amus: quis iam dubitet hoc esse sceleratius commissum, quod est grauius vindicatum? Ex quibus verbis patenter videtur haberi, quod grauius peccatum grauius vindicatur. Quod etiam secundum, scilicet quod peccatum magis nociuum grauius debeat vindicari, scripturae diuinae repugnat, patet, nam furtum est peccatum magis nociuum communitati quam adulterium: & tamen adulterium poena capitis punitur, non autem furtum. Magist. Ad primum istorum respondetur, quod regulare est illud, quod est sceleratius commissum, esse grauius vindicandum, fallit tamen in casu secundum quod notat Glos. 1. quaest. 1. c. cito, nam interfector proprie uxoris punitur grauius quam matricida 33. q. 2. admonere, etiam in multis aliis casibus fallere inuenitur. Ad secundum autem dicitur, quod accidit furto quod sit magis nociuum communitati quam adulterium, aliquando est magis nociuum & aliquando minus nociuum, & ideo aliquando minus punitur in aliquibus regionibus, & quandoque grauius vindicatur, sed crimen haeresis in papa est periculosissimum: ideo contra crimen haeresis papae est vigilantissime occurrendum & ideo nullum crimen clericorum minus haeresi in nullo casu debet magis spectare ad laicos, quam crimen haeresis in papa, quando clerici nolunt aut non possunt papam haereticum coercere.
units.tr: Student. This argument seems to take a false premise, since it implies that a lesser sin is sometimes punished more severely, and that a more dangerous sin must be punished more severely. Both of these seem to contradict the authentic Scriptures. For Jerome says, as is read in 24. q. 1. c. non afferamus: who could doubt that this is the more wickedly committed thing, which is more severely punished? From these words it seems clearly to follow that a more grievous sin is more grievously punished. The second point, namely that a sin more harmful should be punished more severely, is contrary to the divine Scripture, as is plain: theft is more harmful to the community than adultery, and yet adultery is punished by death, but theft is not. Master. To the first of these we reply that the rule is that what is committed more wickedly should be punished more severely, but it fails in a case, as the Gloss notes on 1. quaest. 1. c. cito, for the killer of his own wife is punished more severely than the matricide, 33. q. 2. admonere; and it is found to fail in many other cases too. To the second we say that it happens that theft is sometimes more harmful to the community than adultery and sometimes less harmful, and therefore it is sometimes punished less in some regions, and sometimes more severely. But the crime of heresy in a pope is most dangerous, and therefore one must be most vigilant against the crime of heresy in a pope; and so, in no case should any crime of clerics concern the laity more than heresy in a pope, when clerics are unwilling or unable to restrain a heretical pope.

units.la: Secunda ratio est haec: Qui ecclesiam Dei a Deo recipiunt defendendam, nec propter clericorum impotentiam nec propter eorum malitiam nec propter eorum ignorantiam nec propter eorum negligentiam debet circa defensionem negligentes existere vel remissi esse, principes autem seculi a Deo suscipiunt ecclesiam defendendam, teste Isidoro, qui, ut legitur 23. q. 5. c. principes, ait: Cognoscant principes seculi Deo se debere rationem esse redituros propter ecclesiam, quam Christo tuendam suscipiunt, nam siue augeatur pax & disciplina ecclesiae per fideles principes siue soluatur: ille ab eis rationem exigit, qui eorum potestati suam ecclesiam credidit committendam, igitur principes populi deficiente ecclesiastica potestate siue per impotentiam siue per malitiam siue per ignorantiam vel negligentiam, defensionem ecclesiae negligere minime debent, non autem defendunt ecclesiam nisi papam haereticum cupientem fidem & veritatem ecclesiae dissipare a conatu maligno curauerint prohibere, ergo deficiente ecclesiastica potestate aliquo praedictorum modorum principes seculi papam haereticum, ne fidem corrumpat ecclesiae, prohibere tenentur.
units.tr: The second reason is this: those who receive the Church of God from God to defend must not be negligent or remiss in its defence, whether through the impotence of the clergy, their wickedness, their ignorance or their negligence. But the princes of the world receive the Church from God to defend, as Isidore testifies, who says, as is read in 23. q. 5. c. principes: Let the princes of the world recognise that they must render an account to God for the Church, which they take up to protect for Christ; for whether the peace and discipline of the Church is increased or undone through faithful princes, he demands an account from them who has entrusted his Church to their power to be committed. Therefore, when ecclesiastical power is lacking, whether through impotence, wickedness, ignorance or negligence, the princes of the people ought by no means to neglect the defence of the Church. But they do not defend the Church unless they take care to prohibit a heretical pope who desires to scatter the faith and truth of the Church from a malicious attempt. Therefore, when ecclesiastical power is lacking in any of the aforesaid ways, the secular princes are bound to prohibit a heretical pope from corrupting the faith of the Church.

units.la: Tertia ratio est haec: Non minorem potestatem habent laici super papam haereticum sedem Apostolicam occupantem inique, quam super papam intrusum sedem Apostolicam inuadentem, nam vterque sedem Apostolicam occupat inique, sed papa haereticus vltra occupationem sedis iniustam catholicos nititur trahere ad haereticam prauitatem, ad quod intrusus papa non conatur.
units.tr: The third reason is this: the lay powers have no less authority over a heretical pope who unjustly occupies the Apostolic See than over a pope who has been intruded and invades the Apostolic See, for both occupy the Apostolic See unjustly. But a heretical pope, beyond his unjust occupation of the see, strives to draw Catholics into heretical depravity, which an intruded pope does not attempt.

units.la: Laici autem potestatem habent papam intrusum de Apostolica sede pellendi, teste Nicolao papa, qui, ut legitur distin. 70. c. Si quis pecunia, ait: Si quis pecunia vel gratia humana, aut populari seu militari tumultu: sine concordi & Canonica electione Cardinalium & sequentium religiosorum clericorum fuerit Apostolica sedi intronizatus, non Apostolicus sed Apostaticus habeatur. Licet itaque Cardinalibus, & aliis clericis Deum timentibus & laicis inuasorem illum anathematizare: & humano auxilio a sede Apostolica pellere, ergo multo magis laici potestatem habent pellendi a sede Apostolica papam haereticum eandem sedem indignius occupantem: quam si solummodo absque haeretica prauitate esset sedis inuasor, praesertim si praelati ecclesiae noluerint vel non potuerint papam haereticum debite coercere.
units.tr: Moreover, laymen have power to drive an intruded pope from the Apostolic See, as Pope Nicholas testifies, who says, as is read in distin. 70. c. Si quis pecunia: If anyone has been enthroned on the Apostolic See by money or human favour, or by a popular or military tumult, without the united and canonical election of the cardinals and the religious clerics who follow them, let him be regarded not as an apostolic but as an apostate. It is therefore lawful for the cardinals, and other clerics who fear God, and for laymen, to anathematise that invader and, with human help, to drive him from the Apostolic See. Therefore, much more do laymen have power to drive from the Apostolic See a heretical pope who occupies the same see more unworthily, than one who was merely an invader of the see without heretical depravity, especially if the prelates of the Church have been unwilling or unable to restrain the heretical pope properly.

units.la: Quarta ratio est haec: Gregorius in concilio generali Lugdunensi, ut habetur extra, de electio-nibus nibus: Vbi periculum intenditur in periculo est plenius agendum & consulendum, led maius periculum immineret Christianitati, si papa haeretica prauitate fuerit maculatus, & clerici ipsum noluerint vel non potuerint coercere, quam si sacerdos enormitatibus se miscuerit. Sacerdos enim se enormitatibus immiscendo potest licite per principes seculi coerceri, extra, de sentent. excommunicationis, perpendimus, vbi sic dicitur: perpendimus ex literis tuis, quod quidam sacerdos pro eo, quod filium regis se nominari praesumpsit, & armis acceptis seditionem fecit & guerram, ab Comite iussu est fustigari, qui postea de eius mandato tractus patibulo expiravit. Et ideo sic duximus respondendum, quod si memoratus sacerdos talimodo processit, & non propulsando sed inferendo iniuriam fuerit occisus, non videtur nobis quod interfectores eius propter hoc ad obtinendam absolutionem apostolicam sedem adire cogantur, vbi dicit Glos. quod clericus immiscendo se enormitatibus privilegium amittit, igitur multo magis si papa est haereticus, & si ipsum clerici noluerint, vel non potuerint coercere, est per principes seculi coercendus.
units.tr: The fourth reason is this: Gregory, in the General Council of Lyons, as is held in the decretal extra, de electionibus: Where danger is greatest, there must be more full action and consultation. But greater danger would threaten Christendom if a pope were stained with heretical depravity and the clerics were unwilling or unable to restrain him, than if a priest had involved himself in outrages. For a priest who involves himself in outrages may lawfully be restrained by secular princes, extra, de sententia excommunicationis, perpendimus, where it is said: We have weighed from your letters that a certain priest, because he presumed to call himself the son of a king, and took up arms and made sedition and war, was ordered by a count to be whipped, and afterwards, by his command, was dragged to the gallows and expired. And so we have thought that this answer must be given: if the said priest so proceeded, and was killed not by repelling but by inflicting injury, it does not seem to us that his killers are on that account to be compelled to seek apostolic absolution. Where the Gloss says that a cleric, by involving himself in outrages, loses his privilege. Therefore, much more so if the pope is a heretic, and if the clerics have been unwilling or unable to restrain him, he must be restrained by the secular princes.

units.la: Quinta ratio est haec: Publicę vtilitatis interest ne crimina remaneant impunita, extra, de sent. excommunicationis, vt fama, quod potissime de illis criminibus potest intelligi, quae in dispendium salutis omnium vergere dignoscuntur, crimen autem haeresis in papa praecipue noscitur vergere in dispendium omnium Christianorum: cum fides catholica, quam papa haereticus satagit extirpare, sit fundamentum salutis ominium Christianorum, igitur crimen haeresis in papa impunitum nullatenus debet remanere, & per consequens si clerici non potuerint vel noluerint papam haereticum coercere, per fideles laicos comprimi debet.
units.tr: The fifth reason is this: it is of public benefit that crimes should not remain unpunished, extra, de sententia excommunicationis, ut fama, which can be understood most of all of those crimes which are known to tend to the ruin of the salvation of all. But the crime of heresy in a pope is especially known to tend to the ruin of all Christians, since the Catholic faith, which a heretical pope labours to uproot, is the foundation of the salvation of all Christians. Therefore the crime of heresy in a pope must by no means remain unpunished, and consequently, if the clerics have been unable or unwilling to restrain a heretical pope, he must be checked by the faithful laity.

units.la: Sexta ratio est haec: Sicut secundum canonicas sanctiones potius consideranda est causa facti quam ipsum factum: ita in legibus statuendis, interpretandis & intelligendis causa statuendi considerari debet, teste Isidoro, qui, vt allegatum est superius, distinct. 19. capitulo primo, ait: sciendum est quod pleraque capitula ex causa, ex persona, ex loco & tempore consideranda sunt, in pluribus autem decretis generalium conciliorum & summorum pontificum habetur, quod Domini temporales terras sibi subiectas ab haeretica prauitate studeant expurgare, extra, de haereticis, c. ad abolendam, & c. excommunicamus, talia autem statuta non sunt in fauorem alicuius personae: sed in fauorem vel in defensionem aut saluationem fidei catholicae ordinata, igitur quandocunque imminet periculum fidei orthodoxae, Domini temporales siue requirantur per praelatos, siue non, terras suas purgare tenentur ab haeretica prauitate. Ex quo patenter infertur: quod si clerici noluerint, vel non potuerint papam haereticum coercere: principes seculares & laici in fauorem & saluationem fidei Christianae papam haereticum debent coercere. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia posita causa ponitur effectus. Et vbi est ratio eadem, debet esse idem ius, scilicet causa & ratio quare principes seculi & publicae potestates, cum fuerint requisiti a praelatis ecclesiae, debent terras suas ab haeretica prauitate purgare, est ne fides periclitetur ecclesiae, sed si papa fuerit haereticus & clerici noluerint vel non potuerint ipsum coercere, periclitabitur fides ecclesiae, nisi papa haereticus prohibitus fuerit alios haeretica prauitate inficere per potentiam laicalem, ergo in hoc casu cum clerici noluerint, vel non potuerint papam haereticum coercere, ipsum comprimere debet potentia laicalis.
units.tr: The sixth reason is this: just as, according to the canonical sanctions, the cause of a deed is to be considered rather than the deed itself, so in enacting, interpreting and understanding laws the reason for enacting them ought to be considered. Isidore testifies to this, who, as was cited above, distinct. 19, chapter one, says: It must be known that most chapters are to be considered in view of the cause, the person, the place and the time. In many decrees of general councils and of the supreme pontiffs it is held that temporal lords should take care to purge the lands subject to them of heretical depravity, extra, de haereticis, c. ad abolendam, and c. excommunicamus. But such statutes are not enacted in favour of any person, but are ordained in favour of, or in defence or salvation of, the Catholic faith. Therefore, whenever danger threatens the orthodox faith, temporal lords, whether they are required by the prelates or not, are bound to purge their lands of heretical depravity. From this it is plainly inferred that if the clerics have been unwilling or unable to restrain a heretical pope, the secular princes and the laity ought to restrain a heretical pope in favour of and for the salvation of the Christian faith. This reason is confirmed thus: because when the cause is posited, the effect is posited; and where the reason is the same, the law must be the same. The cause and reason why secular princes and civil authorities, when they are required by the prelates of the Church, ought to purge their lands of heretical depravity, is so that the faith of the Church may not be endangered. But if the pope is a heretic and the clerics have been unwilling or unable to restrain him, the faith of the Church will be endangered, unless the heretical pope is prevented by lay power from infecting others with heretical depravity. Therefore, in this case, when the clerics have been unwilling or unable to restrain a heretical pope, lay power ought to restrain him.

units.la: Septima ratio est haec: Magis defendenda est catholica fides, si eiusdem fidei periculum immineat, quam propria persona, hoc patet: quia catholici in multis casibus pro defensione fidei orthodoxae propriας personas tenentur morti exponere, sed laicis catholicis licet clericos attentantes eos occidere potenter repellere & detinere eosdem, si alio modo eorum violentiam non possunt euadere, quia licitum est vim vi repellere, dist. 1. ius naturale, igitur multo magis si papa haereticus fidem conatur subuertere: & clerici nolunt vel non possunt ipsum comprimere, est per laicos comprimendus, ac in firma custodia detinendus, si alter nequit pro sua insania prohiberi.
units.tr: The seventh reason is this: the Catholic faith is to be defended more than one's own person when danger threatens the faith itself. This is clear, because in many cases Catholics are bound to expose their own persons to death in defence of the orthodox faith. Yet Catholic laymen may lawfully repel by force clerics who attempt to kill them, and may restrain those clerics if they cannot otherwise escape their violence, because it is lawful to repel force with force, dist. 1. ius naturale. Much more, then, if the heretical pope tries to subvert the faith, and the clerics are unwilling or unable to restrain him, he is to be restrained by the laity and held in close custody, if he cannot otherwise be prevented from his madness.

units.la: Octaua ratio est: Sicut (iuxta promissionem Christi) fides catholica vsque ad finem seculi permanebit: ita in ecclesia Dei potestas de iure coercendi haereticos vsque ad finem seculi remanebit, sed si papa cum omnibus clericis esset haereticus, potestas coercendi de iure haereticos non esset in papa & in clericis: quia illi omni potestate spirituali essent priuati, igitur in isto casu potestas coercendi haereticos de iure esset ad laicos deuoluta, & ita laici in hoc casu haberent de iure potestatem papam haereticum coercendi, & clericos sibi credentes.
units.tr: The eighth reason is this: just as the Catholic faith will remain until the end of the age, according to the promise of Christ, so the power of rightfully restraining heretics will remain in the Church of God until the end of the age. But if the pope together with all the clergy were heretical, the power of rightly restraining heretics would not reside in the pope or in the clergy, because they would be deprived of all spiritual power. Therefore in that case the power of restraining heretics would pass by right to the laity, and so in this case the laity would have the right to restrain the heretical pope and the clerics who follow him.

units.la: Nona ratio est haec. Principes seculares & laici arctius astringuntur fidem defendere orthodoxam, quam propriam patriam. Hoc probatione non indiget, sed principes seculares propriam patriam, cum periculum imminet, tenentur defendere, ergo multo magis cum periculum imminet fidei propter impotentiam vel malitiam, aut damnabilem negligentiam vel ignorantiam clericorum ex perfidia & potentia papae haeretici fidem subuertere molientis, principes seculares & laici quamuis non fuerint per clericos requisiti debent resistere viriliter & eum potenter a sua velania prohibere.
units.tr: The ninth reason is this. Secular princes and laymen are more strictly bound to defend the orthodox faith than their own country. This needs no proof. But secular princes are bound to defend their own country when danger threatens. Much more, then, when danger threatens the faith, through the incapacity, wickedness, or damnable negligence or ignorance of the clergy, and through the perfidy and power of a heretical pope who is trying to overthrow the faith, secular princes and laymen, even though they have not been asked by the clergy, ought to resist vigorously and forcibly restrain him from his madness.

units.la: Decima ratio est haec: Qui debitor est, vt catholicam veritatem defendat, debitor est vt potenter resistat catholicam veritatem impugnanti. Laicus autem debitor est, vt catholicam veritatem sibi notam defendat, igitur debitor est vt resistat viriliter & potenter catholicam veritatem impugnanti, & per consequens laici (licet fuerint per clericos nullatenus requisiti) si ipsi clerici papam haereticum noluerint vel non potuerint coercere, ipsum debent comprimere. Maior apparet aperte: quia secundum Innocent. vt habetur distinctio. 83. error. Veritas cum minime defensatur, opprimitur, negligere quippe, cum possit perturbare peruersos, nihil aliud est quam fouere, nec caret scrupulo societatis occulta, qui manifesto facinori definit obuiare, & per consequens eis, qui debent veritatem defendere, licet impugnanti veritatem pro viribus obuiare. Minor probatur auctoritate Iohannis Chrysost. qui, vt legitur 11. q. 3. c. nolite, ait, sicut superius allegatum existit: nam sicut sacerdos debitor est vt veritatem, quam audiuit a Deo, libere praedicet, sic laicus debitor est vt veritatem quam audiuit a sacerdotibus (probatam quidem in scripturis) defendat fiducialiter, quod si non fecerit, prodidit veritatem. Ex quibus verbis patet aperte, quod laicus debitor est vt defendat catholicam veritatem.
units.tr: The tenth reason is this. Whoever is bound to defend Catholic truth is bound to resist forcefully those who attack it. The layman is bound to defend the Catholic truth known to him; therefore he is bound to resist vigorously and forcefully those who attack Catholic truth. Consequently the laity (even though they have in no way been asked by the clergy), if the clergy themselves are unwilling or unable to restrain the heretical pope, ought to restrain him. The major premise is plain, because according to Innocent, as found in distinctio. 83. error.: "When truth is not defended, it is oppressed; for to neglect to disturb the perverse, when one can, is nothing other than to foster them; nor is he free from the guilt of secret complicity who fails to oppose a manifest crime. Consequently, those who ought to defend the truth may also, as far as their strength allows, oppose one who attacks the truth." The minor premise is proved by the authority of John Chrysostom, who says, as is read in 11. q. 3. c. nolite, as cited above: "For just as the priest is bound to preach freely the truth he has heard from God, so the layman is bound to defend boldly the truth he has heard from the priests (indeed proved from the Scriptures); and if he does not do so, he has betrayed the truth." From these words it is clear that the layman is bound to defend Catholic truth.

units.la: Discip. Ista ratio non probat, quod laicus sit debitor vt defendat veritatem, nisi fuerit a sacerdotibus requisitus, quod innuit Chrysost. cum dicit: Laicus debitor est vt defendat veritatem, quam audiuit a sacerdotibus probatam quidem in scripturis, ergo solum debet veritatem defendere, quando sacerdotes probant sibi veritatem per scripturas: & ipsum vt defendat requirunt. Magist. Nonnullis apparet quod friuola est instantia seu responsio, tum quia si laicus est debitor vt defendat veritatem, quam audiuit a sacerdotibus, multo fortius debitor est vt defendat veritatem quam legit in scripturis sacris. Tum quia laicus potuit audire veritatem a sacerdotibus ante omnem impugnationem veritatis. Igitur etiam mortuis sacerdotibus laicus debitor est vt veritatem quam audiuit ab eis in scripturis probatam, defendat. Ad defendendum enim veritatem non debet mouere laicum auctoritas sacerdotum, sed auctoritas & veritas scripturarum, & ita debet veritatem defendere, quamuis minime a sacerdotibus requiratur. Discipul. Alias rationes ad assertionem praedictam adducas. Magist. Undecima ratio est haec: ad illos spectat papam coercere haereticum, qui ipsum minime coercendo a scelere nullatenus sunt immunes, sed laici non sunt immunes a scelere, si papam haereticum cum eum clerici noluerint vel non potuerint coercere, non coercent, ergo in hoc casu debent papam haereticum coercere. Maior probatione non indiget. Minor probatur sic, qui habent auctoritatem coercendi summos sacerdotes occisores Christi, habent & auctoritatem coercendi haereticos negantes fidem Christi. Populus autem habuit auctoritatem coercendi summos sacerdotes occisores Christi, aliter non coercendo a scelere fuissent immunes, cuius contrarium dicit Augustin. Psalmo 60. & ponitur 23. q. 3. c. vltim. ait: ostendit propheta nec illos immunes a scelere esse, qui permiserunt principibus Christum crucifigere & interficere, cum pro multitudine timentur: & possent illos a facto & se a consensu liberare. Qui enim definit obuiare cum potest peruersis & non facit: consentire videtur, ergo consimiliter populus habet auctoritatem coercendi papam haereticum, & alios haereticos fidem catholicam destruentes, si clerici noluerint, vel non potuerint eos coercere, nec est immunis a scelere si permittit papae haeretico fidem corrumpere orthodoxam. Duodecima ratio est haec: Non minus tenentur principes seculi fidem catholicam contra papam haereticum defendere, quam tenentur socii socios, & infirmos contra latrones defendere, sed socii tenentur socios infirmos contra latrones defendere, teste Ambros. qui, vt legitur 22. q. 3. cap. fortitudo, ait: fortitudo quae bello tuetur a barbaris patriam vel domi defendit infirmos vel a latronibus socios, plena iustitia est, igitur multo magis principes fidem catholicam contra papam haereticum, quem nolunt vel non possunt clerici comprimere, tenentur coercere. Tertiadecima ratio est haec: qui alium tanquam excommunicatum vitare tenentur, ipsum a se in firma custodia sequestrare deberent, si aliter eius communionem euitare non possunt, sed principes seculares laici scientes papam esse haereticum, ipsum tanquam excommunicatum vitare tenentur, quia omnis haereticus sententia excommunicationis inuoluitur, igitur principes seculares & laici scientes papam esse haereticum, ipsum sub firma custodia sequestrare tenentur, si eius communionem aliter vitare non possunt, quantumcunque non fuerint a clericis requisiti.
units.tr: Discip. This argument does not prove that the layman is bound to defend the truth unless he has been asked by the priests, which Chrysostom implies when he says: "The layman is bound to defend the truth which he heard from the priests, indeed proved from the Scriptures." Therefore he ought to defend the truth only when the priests prove the truth to him from the Scriptures and ask him to defend it. Magist. It seems to some that this objection or reply is frivolous, both because if the layman is bound to defend the truth he heard from the priests, he is much more bound to defend the truth he reads in the holy Scriptures; and because the layman could have heard the truth from the priests before any attack on the truth. Therefore, even when the priests are dead, the layman is bound to defend the truth he heard from them and found proved in the Scriptures. For it is not the authority of the priests but the authority and truth of the Scriptures that ought to move the layman to defend the truth, and so he ought to defend the truth even if no priest asks him. Discipul. Bring forward the other reasons you adduce for the aforesaid assertion. Magist. The eleventh reason is this: it belongs to those who cannot be free from guilt if they fail to restrain a heretic to restrain the heretical pope. Laymen are not free from guilt if, when the clergy are unwilling or unable to restrain the heretical pope, they do not restrain him. Therefore in this case they ought to restrain the heretical pope. The major premise needs no proof. The minor is proved thus: those who have authority to restrain the chief priests who were murderers of Christ also have authority to restrain heretics who deny the faith of Christ. But the people had authority to restrain the chief priests who were murderers of Christ; otherwise, by not restraining them, they would not have been free from guilt. The contrary of this Augustine says in Psalm 60, and it is placed in 23. q. 3. c. ultim.: "The prophet shows that those are not free from guilt who allowed the princes to crucify and kill Christ, though they feared the multitude, and who could have freed themselves from the deed and from consent. For he who fails to oppose the perverse when he can, and does not do so, seems to consent." Therefore, similarly, the people have authority to restrain the heretical pope and other heretics who destroy the Catholic faith, if the clergy are unwilling or unable to restrain them; nor is he free from guilt who permits the heretical pope to corrupt the orthodox faith. The twelfth reason is this: secular princes are no less bound to defend the Catholic faith against a heretical pope than companions are bound to defend their companions and the weak against robbers. But companions are bound to defend their weak companions against robbers, as Ambrose attests, who, as is read in 22. q. 3. cap. fortitudo, says: "The courage which by war protects the homeland from barbarians, or at home defends the weak or companions from robbers, is full justice." Therefore much more are princes bound to restrain a heretical pope who attacks the Catholic faith, when the clergy are unwilling or unable to restrain him. The thirteenth reason is this: those who are bound to avoid another as excommunicate ought to keep him apart in close custody if they cannot otherwise avoid his communion. But secular princes and laymen who know that the pope is a heretic are bound to avoid him as excommunicate, because every heretic is involved in the sentence of excommunication. Therefore secular princes and laymen who know that the pope is a heretic are bound to keep him under close custody, if they cannot otherwise avoid his communion, however much they have not been asked by the clergy.

units.la: CAP. C.
units.tr: CHAPTER C.

units.la: In quo respondetur primo ad auctoritates capitulo 98. & conseque- nter ad rationes & auctoritates capitulo 91. in con- trarium adductas.
units.tr: In which the authorities of chapter 98, and consequently the reasons and authorities adduced to the contrary in chapter 91, are answered first.

units.la: Discipulus. De istis rationibus post completionem huius operis collationem habebo, nunc autem peto, vt indices quomodo in contrarium respondere contingat, & primo dic ad illa, quae allegantur superius capitul. 98. Magist. Ad illa vnica ratione respondetur: quod illae auctoritates ibidem adductae sunt purae affirmatiuae, & ideo ista negatiua: haeretici non sunt puniendi per laicos, nisi fuerint a prelatis ecclesiae requisiti, inferri non potest. Discipul. Ista est breuis responsio, de qua alias tecum conferam diligenter, ideo ostende, quomodo respondetur ad allegationes supra capitulo 91. adductas. Magist. Ad primam dicitur, quod papa haereticus in casu praescripto, scilicet quando clerici nollent vel non possent eum corrigere, est de foro iudicis secularis, quantum ad hoc, quod potest ipsum in firma custodia detinere & prohibere ne in alios virus prauitatis haereticae effundat: potest etiam de ipso inquirere, ipsumque sollicite examinare & audire, sed non potest degradare, neque diffinitivam contra ipsum profertre sententiam, & in hoc deferretur futuris praelatis catholicis zelum ex fidei charitate habituris, quia secundum nonnullos degradatio papae haeretici, & prolatio diffinitivae sententiae contra ipsum esse a praelatis ecclesiae (quibus Spiritus sanctus infunditur) reservatae. Cum vero accipitur, quod clerici non sunt de foro iudicis secularis: Respondetur, quod hoc fallit in multis casibus, extra de sentent. excommunic. cum vero ab homine, & c. perpendimus, & extra, de appell. capitul. 1. & extra, de vita & honesta. cleric. capitul. ultimo. unde sicut allegatum est prius, Glossa 23. quaestion. 5. cap. principes, plures casus notat, in quibus laici habent iurisdictionem super clericos, inter quos est unus, cum clerici volunt fidem subvertere, ad forum pertinent iudicis secularis, potissime papa haereticus, quem clerici nolunt, vel non possunt corrigere, ad forum spectabit iudicis secularis, quia si periculis minoribus oportet occurrere, multo fortius necesse est maioribus periculis obviare, ut colligi potest ex verbis beati Gregorii in generali concilio Lugdunensi extra de electionibus, ubi periculum, libro 6. Sed minus periculum immineret fidei, si clerici inferiores fuerint prauitate haeretica irretiti, quam si papa conatus fuerit totam ecclesiam labe haeretica maculare, igitur si quicunque clerici inferiores in quocunque casu spectant ad forum iudicis secularis: potissime debent iudices seculares & laici resistere papae haeretico, quando eum clerici nolunt vel non possunt coercere.
units.tr: Pupil. I will compare these arguments with you carefully after the whole work is finished. For now I ask you to show how it is possible to answer the arguments on the other side, and first tell me how to answer those cited above in chapter 98, Master. To those authorities one argument suffices: those authorities cited there are purely affirmative, so the negative proposition heretics are not to be punished by laymen unless they have been required by the prelates of the Church cannot be inferred from them. Pupil. That is a brief answer, and I will examine it with you thoroughly at another time. So show me how the arguments cited above in chapter 91 are answered. Master. To the first, it is said that a heretical pope, in the case described, namely when the clergy are unwilling or unable to correct him, falls under the jurisdiction of the secular judge insofar as the secular judge may keep him in close custody and prevent him from pouring the poison of heretical depravity into others. He may also inquire into the pope's case, examine him carefully and hear him, but he may not depose him or pronounce a definitive sentence against him. This is reserved for the future Catholic prelates who will have zeal from the love of the faith, because, according to some, the deposition of a heretical pope and the pronouncing of a definitive sentence against him belong to the prelates of the Church, on whom the Holy Spirit is poured out. As for the objection that clerics are not under the jurisdiction of the secular judge, the answer is that this fails in many cases: Extra, de sententia excommunicationis, cum vero ab homine, etc., perpendimus; and extra, de appellationibus, cap. 1; and extra, de vita et honestate clericorum, cap. ultimo. Hence, as was said earlier, the Gloss on 23 q. 5, cap. principes notes several cases in which laymen have jurisdiction over clerics. Among them is this: when clerics wish to subvert the faith, they fall under the jurisdiction of the secular judge. Above all, a heretical pope, whom the clergy are unwilling or unable to correct, will fall under the jurisdiction of the secular judge. For if lesser dangers must be met, much more must greater dangers be resisted, as can be gathered from the words of blessed Gregory, cited at the general Council of Lyons in extra, de electionibus, Ubi periculum, liber 6. But a lesser danger threatens the faith if inferior clerics are entangled in heretical depravity than if the pope attempts to stain the whole Church with heretical corruption. Therefore, if any inferior clerics in any case fall under the jurisdiction of the secular judge, then above all the secular judges and laymen ought to resist a heretical pope when the clergy are unwilling or unable to restrain him.

units.la: Discipul. Per istam rationem laici in hoc casu possent papam haereticum neci tradere corporali: quia in nonnullis casibus laici clericos haereticos licite possent occidere. Magist. Respondetur, quod in omnibus causa est consideranda, causa autem quare clerici haeretici in nonnullis casibus fiant de foro iudicis secularis, est ut ad terrorem aliorum debite comprimantur. Similiter causa, quare papa haereticus, quem clerici nolunt vel non possunt coercere, est per laicos comprimendus, est, ne fides catholica per papam haereticum comprimatur, & ideo ubi fides saluaretur catholica per solam vinculationem, vel captiuationem papae haeretici, laici ad aliam poenam procedere non deberent, ubi autem a papa haeretico in sola captiuitate detento periculum fidei probabiliter timeretur, & per eius mortem fides saluaretur, ad mortem corporalem papae haeretici possent procedere laici zelo fidei orthodoxae.
units.tr: Pupil. By this argument, in this case, laymen could put a heretical pope to bodily death, since in some cases laymen may lawfully kill heretical clerics. Master. It is answered that in all cases the cause must be considered. The cause why heretical clerics in some cases pass under the jurisdiction of the secular judge is that they may be duly restrained, to the terror of others. Similarly, the cause why a heretical pope, whom the clergy are unwilling or unable to restrain, must be restrained by laymen is that the Catholic faith may not be suppressed by a heretical pope. Therefore, where the Catholic faith could be saved by binding or imprisoning a heretical pope alone, laymen ought not to proceed to any other punishment. But where the faith is probably in danger from a heretical pope kept only in captivity, and the faith would be saved by his death, laymen may, out of zeal for the orthodox faith, proceed to the bodily death of the heretical pope.

units.la: Discipul. Licet saepe reperiatur cautum in iure, quod clerici non spectant ad forum iudicis secularis, tamen in multis casibus hoc fallit, qui per conditores legum, quibus cauetur, quod clerici non pertinent ad forum iudicis secularis, plures casus excipiuntur, inter quos non inuenitur casus de papa haeretico, quia de illo casu in iure nunquam fit mentio, ideo casus de papa haeretico non debet inter alios casus computari, & ita papa haereticus nunquam spectabit ad forum iudicis secularis, nisi per praelatos ecclesiae fuerit traditus curiae seculari. Confirmatur haec ratio: quia eius est interpretari legem, cuius est condere, cum igitur conditor legum, quibus cauetur, quod clerici non spectant ad forum iudicis secularis, nunquam dictas leges taliter interpretetur, ut casum de papa haeretico excipiat, in nullo casu papa haereticus spectabit ad forum iudicis secularis, nisi in quo secundum exceptiones sacrorum canonum aliquando clerici haeretici fiunt de foro iudicis secularis. Illi autem non fiunt de foro iudicis secularis, quin scilicet primo fuerint degradati: & postea traditi curiae seculari, extra, de haereticis, ad abolendam, & capit. excommunicamus, igitur similiter papa haereticus non spectabit ad forum iudicis secularis, nisi antea fuerit degradatus, & curiae seculari traditus.
units.tr: Pupil. Although the law often provides that clerics do not fall under the jurisdiction of the secular judge, nevertheless in many cases this does not hold. The makers of the laws that state that clerics do not fall under the secular judge's jurisdiction make several exceptions, and among them there is no case of a heretical pope. The law never mentions that case, so the case of a heretical pope should not be counted among the other cases. Thus a heretical pope will never fall under the jurisdiction of the secular judge unless he has been handed over to the secular court by the prelates of the Church. This argument is confirmed as follows: the power to interpret a law belongs to the one whose power it is to enact it. Therefore, since the maker of the laws providing that clerics do not fall under the secular judge never interprets those laws so as to except the case of a heretical pope, a heretical pope will in no case fall under the secular judge's jurisdiction, except in the cases in which, according to the exceptions of the sacred canons, heretical clerics sometimes come under the secular judge. But those clerics do not come under the secular judge unless they were first deposed and then handed over to the secular court: extra, de haereticis, ad abolendam, and cap. excommunicamus. Likewise, then, a heretical pope will not fall under the secular judge's jurisdiction unless he was first deposed and handed over to the secular court.

units.la: Magist. Respondetur, quod non illius solius est interpretari legem, cuius est condere, quod Glossa extra, de apostatis capitul. primo, insinuat manifeste, nam diversas interpretationes legum enumerans, quarum prima est principis legem condentis, alia consuetudinis, alia iudicis, subiungit: alia est quae non est generalis, nec redigenda in scriptis magistrorum. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod non solius condentis legem est interpretari eandem. Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod interpretatio legis non videtur esse, nisi quaedam declaratio intellectus legis seu expositio apertior, unde tunc solum videtur interpretatio legum, quando ignoratur intellectus legis. Ex tribus autem causis potest ignorari intellectus legis. Quandoque enim verba legis propter aliqua verba aequiuoca vel multiplicia in ipsa contenta, possunt habere diversos sensus, quorum nullus repugnat iuri diuino, nec iuri naturali, nec iuri positiuo minime abrogato, & in hoc casu interpretatio legis solummodo spectat ad conditorem legis vel superiorem, qui eandem legem condere posset. Quia sicut aliorum non est condere legem ambiguam, sic non est aliorum condere eandem sub determinato sensu, & per consequens non est aliorum asserere talem sub tali sensu debere intelligi, quandoque autem ignoratur ultimus intellectus legis per ignorantiam iurium positiuorum: quando scilicet nesciuntur exceptiones legum, quae ex iure positiuo dependent, & ideo necesse est declarare, & exponere siue interpretari quomodo lex debet intelligi. Et talis interpretatio, expositio siue declaratio intellectus legis spectat ad consuetudinem, quae est optima legum interpres: Et ad iudicem, cuius est legum & consuetudinum habere peritiam: Et ad magistros, hoc est Iurisperitos, ad quos spectat notitiam legum habere. Interdum autem ignoratur intellectus legum propter ignorantiam iuris diuini, vel iuris naturalis, siue rationis naturalis, aut rationis acceptae simul a iure
units.tr: Magist. I answer that it does not belong only to the one who makes a law to interpret it. The Gloss on extra, de apostatis, capitul. primo, makes this plain: listing the various kinds of interpretation of laws, its first is that of the prince who makes the law, another is that of custom, another that of the judge, and it adds: another is that which is not general and is not to be reduced to writing by the teachers. From these words it follows that interpreting a law does not belong only to the one who enacts it. To make this clear, it should be noted that an interpretation of a law seems to be nothing other than some declaration of its meaning, or a fuller explanation, so that interpretation of laws seems to be needed only when the meaning of the law is not known. The meaning of a law may be unknown for three reasons. Sometimes the words of the law, because of some ambiguous or multiple-meaning terms contained in it, can bear different senses, none of which conflicts with divine law, natural law, or positive law not at all repealed; in this case the interpretation of the law belongs only to its maker or to a superior who could make the same law. For just as it is not for others to make an ambiguous law, so it is not for others to enact the same law under a definite sense, and consequently it is not for others to assert that it must be understood in such and such a sense. Sometimes, however, the ultimate meaning of a law is unknown through ignorance of positive laws, namely when the exceptions to laws that depend on positive law are not known; and so it is necessary to declare, expound, or interpret how the law ought to be understood. Such interpretation, exposition, or declaration of the meaning of a law belongs to custom, which is the best interpreter of laws; to the judge, whose duty it is to have skill in laws and customs; and to the teachers, that is, the jurists, whose business it is to know the laws. At other times the meaning of laws is unknown through ignorance of divine law, or of natural law, or of natural reason, or of reason taken together with

units.la: [Marginal line numbers 5–60 in the right margin, as printed.] àiure diuino & naturali dictamine rationis, verbi gratia, vt habetur extra de sponsalibus c. veniens, papa mandat statuendo legem: quod si quis inueniatur cognouisse mulierem, cui fidem dedit de matrimonio contrahendo, debet remanere in eadem. Si quis autem attendat verba legis, & nescierit ius diuinum, quo conceditur, quod licet causa fornicationis dimittere vxorem, intellectum legis verum nequaquam habebit. Item vt habetur extra de depositi c. 2. depositori licet pro voluntate sua depositum reuocare: tamen ignarus iuris naturalis (quo cauetur ne ad patriam expugnandam depositum reposcatur) nequaquam vltimate intelligit. Cum igitur ex ignorantia iuris diuini & iuris naturalis ignoratur intellectus legis: & ob hoc necessaria est interpretatio siue expositio & declaratio intellectus legum: principalissime spectat ad peritos in iure diuino & philosophia morali in tantum, quod si institutor legis non sufficienter fuerit instructus in scriptura diuina & philosophia morali, interpretatio talis ab eo conditę legis principalius spectat ad aliquos eruditos quam ad ipsum, imo ipse posset & deberet in casu interpretationem legis suae ab eis recipere. Quemadmodum secundum mundi sapientem ad immunia spectat dicere, quo casu verba legis non sunt seruanda, quod fit per agnitionem aequitatis naturalis. Vnde si illitteratus experientia rerum & negociorum peritia carens, statuit legem, solum considerans ea quae communiter accidunt, philosophus eruditus & expertus melius dicet, in quibus casibus verba legis non sunt seruanda, & profundiorem intellectum legis habebit, quam rex qui statuit eam. Discipul. Narratio supra dicta plura dubia, imo falsa continere videtur, quorum duo tantum ad praesens reprobare conabor, quorum primum est. Quod dicit aliquam legem esse ambiguam duos sensus habentem, quod Isidorus reputare videtur fallum. Isidorus enim (vt habetur distinct. 4. c. erit) asserit, quod lex debet esse manifesta, ne aliquid per obscuritatem in captiuatione contineat, lex enim ambigua diuersos sensus habens est obscura, igitur lex non debet esse ambigua. Secundum est, quod dicit interpretationem legis ad peritos spectare.
units.tr: with divine law and the dictate of natural reason. For example, as is found in extra de sponsalibus c. veniens, the pope, in enacting a law, orders that if anyone is found to have known a woman to whom he gave his promise of marriage to be contracted, he must remain bound to her. But if someone attends only to the words of the law, and does not know the divine law by which it is permitted to put away a wife on account of fornication, he will by no means have the true meaning of the law. Likewise, as is found in extra de depositi c. 2., it is lawful for a depositor to reclaim a deposit at his own pleasure; yet one ignorant of natural law (by which it is provided that a deposit is not to be demanded back for the purpose of attacking one's country) will by no means understand it fully. Since, therefore, the meaning of a law is unknown through ignorance of divine and natural law, and for this reason the interpretation, exposition, or declaration of the meaning of laws is necessary, it belongs chiefly to those skilled in divine law and moral philosophy; so much so that if the maker of a law has not been sufficiently instructed in divine Scripture and moral philosophy, an interpretation of the law he has made belongs more chiefly to some learned men than to himself, and indeed he could and should receive an interpretation of his law from them in a case. Just as, according to the wise men of the world, it belongs to immunia to say in what case the words of a law are not to be kept, which is done by recognizing natural equity. Hence, if an unlettered man, lacking experience of affairs and skill in business, enacts a law, considering only what commonly happens, a learned and experienced philosopher will say better in what cases the words of the law are not to be kept, and will have a deeper understanding of the law than the king who enacted it. Discipul. The aforesaid account seems to contain several doubtful, indeed false, points, of which I will undertake to refute for now only two. The first is that it says a law may be ambiguous, having two senses, which Isidore seems to consider false. For Isidore (as is found in distinct. 4. c. erit) asserts that a law ought to be clear, lest anything be contained in it obscurely in the matter of captivity; for an ambiguous law having different senses is obscure; therefore a law ought not to be ambiguous. The second is that it says the interpretation of a law belongs to experts.

units.la: Hoc enim Augustin. cuius verba ponuntur di. supradicta c. in istis temporalibus, ait enim: In istis temporalibus legibus quamquam de his homines iudicent, cum eas instituunt, tamen cum fuerint instituta ac firmata, non licebit iudici de ipsis iudicare, sed secundum ipsas. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod de legibus temporalibus iudicare non licet: & per consequens eas interpretari non licet. Magist. Ad primum istorum respondetur, quod quamuis quantum conuenienter fieri potest lex debeat esse manifesta, ne aliquid per obscuritatem in captionem contineat: tamen non est dicendum, quia leges multae sic sint ambiguae quod in eis verba multiplicia diuersos habentia sensus ponantur, cum etiam in lege diuina talis diuersitas & multiplicitas reperiatur, teste Gloss. ad Gal. 6. super illud Apostoli, vnusquisque onus suum portabit, ait: quod dicitur, videtur contrarium precedentibus, vbi ait: alter alterius onera portate, & declarans, quod non est contrarium dicit: quod non est hoc contrarium precedentibus: quia nomen oneris multis modu accipitur. Multa enim sunt verba quae in diuersis locis posita varie intelliguntur: sicut hoc nomen oneris, quod nisi sub diuersis significationibus acceperis, proculdubio putabis eundem sibi in loquendo esse contrarium. Et hac est causa, quare cum Paulus ante diceret: alter alterius onera portate: hic dicit, vnusquisque onus suum portabit. Ex quibus verbis patet aperte, quod verba ambigua & multiplicia reperiuntur in lege diuina, igitur nec ab humanis legibus hoc est negandum, & non est inconueniens, quod lex humana possit diuersis modis intelligi.
units.tr: For this is what Augustine says, whose words are cited in the distinction above, in the chapter in istis temporalibus. He says: In these temporal laws, although men judge about them when they enact them, nevertheless once they have been enacted and confirmed, it is not lawful for a judge to pass judgment on them, but he must judge according to them. From these words it is plainly clear that it is not lawful to judge temporal laws, and consequently not lawful to interpret them. Master. To the first of these objections the answer is that, although a law ought to be as clear as can reasonably be managed, so that nothing in it is open to misuse through obscurity, it does not follow that many laws are not so ambiguous that words with several meanings are used in them. Such variety and multiplicity is found even in divine law, as the Gloss shows on Galatians 6, on the Apostle's words Each one shall bear his own burden. It says: What is said seems contrary to what went before, where he says: Bear one another's burdens. But explaining that it is not contrary, it says: this is not contrary to what went before, because the word "burden" is taken in many ways. For there are many words which, used in different places, are understood in various senses, like this word "burden", which, unless you take it under different meanings, you will certainly think to be contradictory in what he says. And this is the reason why, when Paul had said before, "Bear one another's burdens", here he says, "Each one shall bear his own burden". From these words it is clear that ambiguous and multiple-meaning words are found in divine law, so this cannot be denied of human laws either, and there is nothing absurd in a human law being capable of being understood in different ways.

units.la: Ad secundum dicitur, quod quamuis secundum sententiam beati Augustin. de temporalibus legibus, quae sunt purae positiuae, postquam fuerunt institutae & firmatae, nec iudex nec alius debeat iudicare, an sunt seruandae vel non seruandae: quia constat quod seruandae sunt, licebit tamen non solum iudici & eruditis & doctis iudicare & indagare secundum quem intellectum seruandae sunt, & secundum quem intellectum seruandae non sunt, sicut secundum mundi sapientum immunia iudicat, in quo casu verba legis non sunt seruanda, vtens naturali dictamine rationis, hoc est vtens iure naturali: quia ex quo nulla lex positiua iusta potest esse contraria iure naturali, lex quaecunque humana in nullo casu, in quo si seruaretur, sicut verba sonant, esset contraria, minime est seruanda, sicut dictum est supra, similiter lex humana, imo & lex naturae, vt innuit Isidorus, prout recitatur dist. 1. ius naturale, statuit quod res deposita, quando deponitur, restituatur: & tamen si quis gladium depositum reposceret ad occidendum seipsum vel alium innocentem iniuste, gladius depositus sibi restitui non deberet. Quia qui in hoc casu restitueret depositum, ageret contra ius naturale, quo quilibet obligatur flagitium & dispendium proximi prohibere, si potest.
units.tr: To the second objection it is said that, although according to the opinion of the blessed Augustine concerning temporal laws, which are purely positive, once they have been enacted and confirmed, neither a judge nor anyone else ought to judge whether they are to be kept or not kept (since it is agreed that they are to be kept), nevertheless it is permitted not only to the judge but also to the learned and the wise to judge and inquire in what sense they are to be kept and in what sense they are not to be kept. For example, by the judgment of the wise of the world, in a case where the words of the law are not to be kept, one uses the natural dictate of reason, that is, one uses natural law. For since no just positive law can be contrary to natural law, any human law which, in some case where it would be kept as the words sound, would be contrary to natural law, is by no means to be kept, as was said above. Similarly, human law, indeed even the law of nature, as Isidore suggests (as it is recited in distinction 1, ius naturale), lays down that a deposited thing, when it is deposited, is to be restored. Yet if someone unjustly demanded back a deposited sword in order to kill himself or another innocent person, the deposited sword ought not to be returned to him. For whoever restored the deposit in this case would act against natural law, by which everyone is bound to prevent a crime and a loss to his neighbour, if he can.

units.la: Discipul. Dic quomodo per praedicta contingat repellere rationem, quam feci. Magist. Respondetur, quod licet in iure contra regulam, qua dicitur quod clerici non spectant ad forum iudicis secularis excipiantur casus, in quibus regula illa fallit, non fiat mentio de papa haeretico, debet tamen inter alios computari. Cuius ratio est: quia sicut licet de multis quae spectant ad ius naturae, non fiat mentio in iure scripto, tamen facienda sunt, cum occurrerit necessitas faciendi: ita licet in iure scripto non fiat mentio de casu, in quo papa esset haereticus: tamen casus ille excipi debet, quando papa incurrit haereticam prauitatem, & clerici nollent vel non possent eum coercere. Disc. Quare non excipitur casus de papa haeretico, si clerici nollent vel non possent eum coercere: quando cum conditoribus canonum, glossatoribus & doctoribus excipiuntur casus, in quibus illa regula fallit, quod clerici non sunt de foro iudicis secularis? Magist. Respondetur quod sicut leges non feruntur nisi de his quae saepe accidunt: & non de illis quae accidunt raro vel nunquam: ita sæpe à conditoribus legum & glossatoribus eorundem ac doctoribus non excipiuntur casus, in quibus regulæ generales fallunt, nisi illi qui sæpe accidunt: & non illi qui raro, vel nunquam accidunt. Casus autem de papa hæretico, quem clerici nolunt vel non possunt corrigere raro accidit. De nullo enim papa hæretico ante tempora nostra vnquam legitur, quod clerici saltem omnes in coercendo papam hæreticum fuerint negligentes. Nam & Liberio papæ hæretico multi viriliter restiterunt, & Anastasium hæreticum multi clerici fortiter impugnauerunt, & à communione eius laudabiliter abegerunt, & ita iste casus ante tempora nostra non videtur accidisse, & propter hoc conditores legum & glossatores earundem aliique doctores excipiendo casus, in quibus regula fallit, qua dicitur, quod clerici non sunt de foro iudicis secularis, de papa hæretico, quem clerici nolent vel non possent corrigere, non fecerunt mentionem, & ideo iste casus multo magis excipiendus est, quam alii casus, quos conditores canonum & glossatores excipiunt. Discipul. Quare debet excipi iste casus? Magist. Respondetur quod ideo debet excipi, quia exceptio casus ex ratione euidenti (cui nulla lex humana praeiudicare potest) quoquomodo patenter infertur. Discipul. Quæ est illa ratio? Magist. Ratio est haec. Ille casus à regula generali excipi debet: quo non excepto detrahitur honori diuino, fides periclitatur catholica, ac detrimentum & periculum & dispendium spirituale omnium fidelium procuratur. Haec est manifesta: quia contra honorem diuinum nulla regula est obseruanda. Iterum: nulla lex humana, quæ cedit seu vergit in periculum fidei, & dispendium salutis æternæ, ab homine statui potest. Si enim pacta, promissiones, vota & iuramenta, quæ vergunt in interitum salutis æternæ, seruanda non sunt secundum Canonicas sanctiones: ratione consimili leges quæcunque in illo casu, in quo vergerent in periculum fidei catholicæ, & dispendium spirituale fidelium, non sunt seruandæ. Sed in casu prædicto de papa hæretico, quem clerici nolunt vel non possunt coercere, non excepto à regula illa: clerici non sunt de foro iudicis secularis: honori diuino detrahitur, quia inferiores cum facile sequantur exempla maiorum à vero cultu (papam hæreticum imitando) se subtraherent. Fides etiam periclitatur catholica: quia sicut teste beato Hieronymo, vt legitur 24. quæst. 3. c. resecande, Arrius, qui in Alexandria vna scintilla fuit, sed quoniam non statim oppressus est; per totum orbem eius flamma populata est: multo magis papa haereticus, si non fuerit statim extinctus, eius flamma haereticæ prauitatis totum depopulabitur orbem inficiendo labe haeretica Christianos, & ita si casus ille non excipitur à regula memorata, fides periclitatur ecclesiæ, & per consequens periculum & detrimentum ac dispendium spirituale omnium fidelium procuratur. Quare ille casus est excipiendus omnino: nec papa de plenitudine potestatis posset facere, quod casus ille non exciperetur, vt notat Glossa distinct. 40. si papa, dicens: nunquid posset papa statuere, quod non posset accusari de haeresi? Respondetur quod non posset statuere quod non posset accusari: quia ex hoc fides periclitaretur ecclesia. Iterum quod casus ille debeat excipi, probatur ex hoc: quia teste Isidoro, vt habetur dist. 3. ca. erit, nullo priuato commodo, sed pro communi vtilitate ciuium lex debet conscribi. Lex igitur quæ esset contra vtilitatem ciuium, non esset lex, sed si casus ille de papa haeretico, quem nollent vel non possent clerici corrigere, ab ipsa lege qua cauetur quod clerici non sunt de foro iudicis secularis, non exciperetur, esset contra vtilitatem Christianorum, igitur non esset vera lex, sed falsa, iniqua & iniusta, quare non esset seruanda, quia secundum Esaiam 10. c. scribitur: ve qui condunt leges iniquas.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how, by what has been said, it is possible to refute the argument I have made. Master. The answer is that, although in law, against the rule that clerics are not subject to the secular judge's jurisdiction, exceptions are made in cases where that rule fails, no mention is made of a heretical pope; yet he ought to be counted among the others. The reason is this: just as many things which belong to natural law are not mentioned in written law, yet they are to be done whenever the need to do them arises, so although no mention is made in written law of the case in which a pope would be a heretic, that case nevertheless ought to be excepted, when a pope falls into heretical depravity and the clerics are unwilling or unable to restrain him. Disciple. Why is the case of a heretical pope not excepted, if the clerics are unwilling or unable to restrain him, when the framers of the canons, the glossators and the teachers do except the cases in which that rule, that clerics are not under the secular judge, fails? Master. The answer is that just as laws are not enacted except concerning those things which happen often, and not concerning those which happen rarely or never, so the framers of laws, their glossators and teachers often do not except cases in which general rules fail, except those which happen often, and not those which happen rarely or never. Now the case of a heretical pope, whom clerics are unwilling or unable to correct, rarely happens. For we read of no heretical pope before our own times in whom all the clerics, at least, were negligent in restraining him. For many men bravely resisted the heretical pope Liberius, and many clerics stoutly attacked the heretic Anastasius and laudably cut him off from communion; so this case does not seem to have occurred before our times. For this reason the framers of laws, their glossators and other teachers, in excepting the cases in which the rule fails, by which it is said that clerics are not under the secular judge's jurisdiction, did not mention a heretical pope whom clerics would be unwilling or unable to correct. Therefore this case ought to be excepted much more than the other cases which the framers of canons and the glossators except. Disciple. Why ought this case to be excepted? Master. The answer is that it ought to be excepted because the exception of the case follows plainly, in some way, from a clear reason, which no human law can prejudice. Disciple. What is that reason? Master. The reason is this. A case must be excepted from the general rule if, unless it is excepted, honour is taken from God, the Catholic faith is endangered, and harm, danger and spiritual loss are brought upon all the faithful. This is evident, because no rule is to be observed against the honour of God. Again: no human law which tends towards danger to the faith and loss of eternal salvation can be enacted by a man. For if pacts, promises, vows and oaths which tend to the ruin of eternal salvation are not to be kept according to the canonical sanctions, then by a similar reasoning, any laws whatever, in a case where they would tend towards danger to the Catholic faith and spiritual loss to the faithful, are not to be kept. But in the aforesaid case of a heretical pope, whom clerics are unwilling or unable to restrain, not excepted from that rule, "clerics are not under the secular judge", honour is taken from God, because inferiors, easily following the examples of their superiors, would withdraw from true worship by imitating a heretical pope. The Catholic faith is also endangered, because, as the blessed Jerome testifies (as we read in 24 q. 3, c. resecande), Arius, who in Alexandria was one spark, but because he was not put out at once, the flame spread through the whole world. Much more would a heretical pope, if he were not put out at once, lay waste the whole world with the flame of his heretical depravity, infecting Christians with the heretical taint. So if that case is not excepted from the aforesaid rule, the faith of the Church is endangered, and consequently danger, detriment and spiritual loss are brought upon all the faithful. Therefore that case must certainly be excepted. Nor could the pope, by the fullness of power, make it so that the case was not excepted, as the Gloss notes on distinction 40, si papa, saying: Could the pope decree that he could not be accused of heresy? The answer is that he could not decree that he could not be accused, because by this the Church's faith would be endangered. Again, that this case ought to be excepted is proved from this: since, as Isidore testifies (as it is found in distinction 3, erit), a law ought to be written not for any private advantage but for the common benefit of the citizens. A law, therefore, which was against the benefit of the citizens would not be a law. But if the case of a heretical pope, whom clerics would be unwilling or unable to correct, were not excepted from that very law which provides that clerics are not under the secular judge's jurisdiction, it would be against the benefit of Christians. So it would not be a true law but a false, iniquitous and unjust one, and therefore it would not be binding, because, according to Isaiah 10, it is written: Woe to those who make iniquitous laws.

units.la: Discipul. Contra prædicta impugnatio fortis occurrit, quia si verba legum in quibusdam casibus, qui non sunt excepti in legibus, non essent seruanda, posset ad libitum quilibet excipere casus à lege, quos vellet, & dicere: in istis casibus verba legis sicut sonant non sunt seruanda, & ita ex lege nulla haberetur certitudo, quando verba legis non essent seruanda, & quando essent seruanda. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur, quod non licet excipere cuilibet casum ad libitum & dicere; verba legis in tali casu non sunt seruanda, sed si dicit in tali casu verba legum non sunt seruanda, oportet quod hoc ostendat per legem superiorem vel per rationem euidentem, & si altero illorum modorum patenter ostendit verba legum in tali casu non esse seruanda, standum est dicto suo: non quia ipse dicit, sed quia hoc lex superior vel ratio euidens ostendit. Et ratio huius est: quia nulla potest esse lex, quæ legi superiori, vel apertæ rationi repugnet, vnde quæcunque lex ciuilis repugnat legi diuinæ vel rationi apertæ, non est lex, eodem modo verba legis canonicæ vel ciuilis, in illo casu quo repugnarent legi diuinæ, scilicet scripturæ sacræ vel rationi rectæ, non essent seruanda. Discipul. Ad quem pertinet iudicare verba legis canonicæ vel ciuilis scripturæ diuinæ repugnare vel rationi rectæ? Magist. Respondetur quod hoc iudicare per modum doctrinæ & simplicis assertionis spectat ad eruditum in scriptura diuina & ratione naturali ac philosophia morali pollentem, hoc autem iudicare ex auctoritate officii obligando ad hoc seruandum & tenendum spectat ad conditorem legis cum consilio peritorum in scripturis sacris & naturali ratione pollentium.
units.tr: Disciple. A strong objection arises against what has been said. If the words of laws were not to be kept in certain cases that the laws do not except, then anyone could pick out whatever cases he liked from the law and say: in these cases the words of the law, as they sound, are not to be kept. In that case there would be no certainty from the law about when its words are to be kept and when not. Master. To this it is answered that it is not permitted for anyone to except a case at will and say that the words of the law are not to be kept in it. If someone says that the words of the laws are not to be kept in such a case, he must show this either through a higher law or through evident reason. If he clearly shows by one of these two means that the words of the laws are not to be kept in such a case, one must abide by his statement: not because he says so, but because a higher law or evident reason shows it. The reason is this: no law can stand against a higher law or plain reason. Hence any civil law that contradicts divine law or plain reason is not a law. In the same way, the words of canon or civil law are not to be kept in that case where they would conflict with divine law, that is, with Holy Scripture or right reason. Disciple. Who is to judge whether the words of canon or civil law conflict with divine Scripture or right reason? Master. It is answered that to judge this by way of teaching and simple assertion belongs to one who is learned in divine Scripture and strong in natural reason and moral philosophy. But to judge this with the authority of office, obliging people to observe and hold it, belongs to the maker of the law, together with the counsel of those skilled in holy Scripture and natural reason.

units.la: Discipul. Igitur secundum prædicta Theologi & Philosophi haberent iudicare de intellectu legum ciuilium & canonum. Magist. Conceditur quod ultimum iudicium de intellectu legum ciuilium & canonum est seruandum Theologis & Philosophis, quemadmodum ultimum iudicium de aliquo dubio in scientia inferiori reseruandum est scientiae superiori eo modo, quo per principia iudicandum est de conclusione, quae sequitur ex principiis.
units.tr: Disciple. Then, according to what has been said, theologians and philosophers would have to judge the meaning of civil laws and canons. Master. It is granted that the final judgment on the meaning of civil laws and canons belongs to theologians and philosophers, just as the final judgment on some doubt in a lower science is reserved to a higher science. A conclusion that follows from principles is judged by those principles.

units.la: Discipulus. De hac materia dictum est supra libro primo, ideo transi & monstra, quomodo respondetur ad secundam rationem, supra adductam cap. 91. Magister. Respondetur, quod nonnunquam ad iudicem secularem spectat cognoscere de causa haereticae pravitatis: & hoc dupliciter, uno modo per seipsum, quia & ipse tenetur multa scire, per quem potest in causa pravitatis haereticae in casibus multis iudicare, etiam absque aliorum consilio peritorum. Si enim aliquis Christianus dixerit fidem Christianam falsam & malam: Iudex secularis non debet indigere consilio, ut sciat, an talis sit tanquam haereticus condemnandus: sed ipse tenetur scire, quod talis est haereticus reputandus & de haeresi condemnandus.
