Respondetur, quod hoc non obstat, quia sicut est prudenter futuris talibus occurrendum distinct. 23. in nomine, & ad cautelam futurorum est aliquid faciendum, extra de electionibus, licet: ita ex causa aliqua statuuntur & etiam praecipiuntur, quae non in tempore, quo statuuntur & etiam praecipiuntur, sed in tempore futuro locum valebunt habere, & ideo talia statuta non pro tempore, quo fiunt, sed pro tempore futuro debent intelligi, & ideo licet aliquis praelatus, quando Papa esset haereticus, statueret sub graui poena, quod nullus subditorum ditorum suorum diffinitiones Papae audeat reprobare, tale statutum, quantum est ex forma verborum, non deberet intelligi pro tempore, quo fit; nec etiam pro tempore, quo Papa esset haereticus: sed pro tempore, quo erat summus Pontifex catholicus, & catholice de diffinitionibus circa fidem diffiniret, tale enim statutum, quantum est ex forma verborum, taliter debet intelligi, qualiter intelligeretur, si non solum secundum veritatem, sed etiam secundum opinionem omnium fidelium vacaret Apostolica sedes; & qualiter intelligeretur, si non solum secundum veritatem, sed etiam secundum opinionem omnium catholicorum Papa, qui est haereticus, esset omni auctoritate & dignitate priuatus, & ideo sicut tunc non intelligeretur de diffinitionibus Papae haeretici: ita nec nunc debet intelligi de diffinitionibus Papae haeretici, quantumcunque a multitudine Christianorum minime crederetur, quod vacaret Apostolica sedes, aut quod Papa esset haereticus. Disc. Ex qua causa licet concedere tale statutum tali intentione, quod statutum illud non debet intelligi de diffinitionibus Papae qui est haereticus: sed de diffinitionibus futuri Papae catholici? Magist. Respondetur, quod hoc liceret in casu ad dilucidandum sententiam Papae haeretici, si enim aliquis praelatus sciens diffi-nitiones Papae esse haereticas, vel etiam dubitans eas esse haereticales, probabiliter ex certis coniecturis & causis aestimaret, quod Papa eum & sibi subiectos male tractaret, nisi tale quid statueret, posset idem praelatus condere tale statutum, non intelligens statutum de illo, qui habetur pro Papa, nec de diffinitionibus suis; sed de futuro Papa catholico, & de diffinitionibus eius orthodoxis, verbis enim generalibus & figuratiis locutionibus, atque ambiguis etiam verbis aequivocis ac multiplicibus licet deludere sententiam perfidorum. Magister. Licet videatur, quod talis praelatus suam intentionem occultando deludens Papam (etiam haereticum) graviter peccet, quia non videtur a vitio simulationis immunis: tamen motiua dicentium, quod taliter liceat aliquos deludere, non differas inducere.
units.tr: Student. Suppose the Pope were to define some heretical assertion as to be held as Catholic, and another prelate (say an archbishop or a bishop, or any other who knows the Pope's definition to be heretical) were to ordain, decree, command or order under grave penalty that none of his subjects should dare in any way to condemn the Pope's definition, but that each of his subjects should speak of it, and also of the Pope's person, in a wholly reverent manner, without expressly naming the Pope in such an ordinance, statute, precept or mandate. Is such a prelate to be regarded as believing the Pope's error and as a heretic? Master. On this there are different opinions. One is that such a prelate is to be regarded as believing the Pope's error and as a heretic. That he is to be counted among those who believe the Pope's error is proved as follows: he decrees that the Pope's definition must in no way be condemned, but that one must speak of it with reverence, whereas error must be condemned and one must not speak of error with reverence. Therefore whoever ordains, decrees or commands this believes the Pope's definition is to be held, and consequently he is rightly counted among those who believe the Pope's error. That such a prelate is to be regarded as a heretic is proved by this reasoning: whoever believes an error against the faith and by statutes and precepts compels others to hold the same error is to be counted a heretic, as can apparently be proved from what was said in the fourth book. But such a prelate believes the Pope's error, and by statutes and precepts compels others to hold the same error. Therefore he is not merely one who believes the Pope's error, but is to be judged a heretic. There is another opinion: that if an inferior prelate, say an archbishop or some other prelate, uses precisely these words or their equivalents, I decree, I command, or I order, under pain of excommunication or even imprisonment, that none subject to me dare to condemn the definitions of the lord supreme Pontiff, or on that account speak ill in any way of the Pope's person, but that all speak of them with complete reverence, such a prelate, without further examination, is not to be counted among those who believe the Pope's error, nor among heretics. The reason assigned is this: because of such general words, which can be understood of the definitions of a Catholic Pope just as well as of the definitions of a heretical Pope, no one is to be counted among those who believe the Pope's errors or among heretics on account of such general words. But the aforesaid words can be understood of the definitions of a Catholic Pope just as well as of the definitions of a heretical Pope. Therefore on account of such general words no one is to be counted among those who believe or among heretics. Student. This rule would seem plausible if, when such a statute is made, there were a Catholic Pope, just as there is a heretical Pope. Master. It is answered that this is no objection, because just as future situations of this kind must be prudently provided against (dist. 23, in nomine), and something must be done as a precaution against future events (extra, de electionibus, licet), so also statutes are sometimes enacted and commands given for some cause, which will have their force not at the time when they are enacted and commanded, but in the future. Therefore such statutes must be understood not with reference to the time when they are made, but with reference to the future. So, although a prelate, when the Pope was a heretic, might decree under grave penalty that none of his subjects dare to condemn the Pope's definitions, such a statute, as far as the form of its words goes, ought not to be understood with reference to the time when it is made, nor to the time when the Pope was a heretic, but to the time when he was the Catholic supreme Pontiff and defined Catholically concerning matters of faith. For such a statute, as far as the form of its words goes, must be understood in the way it would be understood if the Apostolic See were vacant not only in truth but also in the opinion of all the faithful; and in the way it would be understood if the Pope who is a heretic were deprived of all authority and dignity not only in truth but also in the opinion of all Catholics. Therefore, just as it would not then be understood of the definitions of a heretical Pope, so now too it ought not to be understood of the definitions of a heretical Pope, however little the multitude of Christians might believe that the Apostolic See was vacant or that the Pope was a heretic. Student. For this reason, may it be conceded that such a statute, with such an intention, is not to be understood of the definitions of a Pope who is a heretic, but of the definitions of a future Catholic Pope? Master. It is answered that this would be permissible, in order to clarify the sentence of a heretical Pope, if a prelate who knew the Pope's definitions to be heretical, or who even doubted that they were heretical, judged with probability from certain conjectures and causes that the Pope would treat him and his subjects badly unless he enacted something of this kind. The same prelate could then frame such a statute, not understanding it as referring to the one who is held to be Pope, nor to his definitions, but to a future Catholic Pope and his orthodox definitions. For by general words, figurative expressions and ambiguous and equivocal words, which are many-sided, one may elude the sentence of the faithless. Master. Although it may seem that such a prelate, by concealing his intention and deceiving the Pope (even a heretical one), sins gravely, since he does not seem to be free from the vice of dissimulation, nevertheless I shall not delay to bring forward the arguments of those who say that it is lawful thus to deceive certain people.

units.la: Magister. Quod liceat taliter deludere tales ad eorum sententiam declinandam, sic videtur posse probari. Cui licet uti insidiis ad hostes seu aemulos expugnandos: eidem licet uti verbis generalibus ac aequivocis, & multiplicibus, atque sermonibus figuratiis ad malignorum sententiam declinandam; sed omni iusto, & sancto licet uti insidiis ad hostes seu aemulos expugnandos 24. quaestion. 3. Dominus noster, ergo homini iusto & sancto licet uti verbis generalibus & aequiuocis, ac multiplicibus, & etiam sermonibus figuratiis ad malorum sententiam declinandam. Secundo sic, dolus qui potest esse absque mendacio, verbo & facto est licitus contra ho-stem, sed delusio, quae fit verbis generalibus, aequiuocis, multiplicibus & figuratiuis, est dolus quidam: & potest esse absque mendacio, verbo & facto, ergo huiusmodi delusio hostis est licita. Maior dictis maiorum ostenditur, ait enim beatus Hieronymus, ut habetur 23. quaestion. 2. cap. vtilem: Vtilem simulationem & in tempore assumendam Hiehu regis Israel nos docet exemplum, qui cum non potuisset interficere sacerdotes Baal, nisi finxisset se idolum velle colere, finxit dicens: congregate mihi omnes sacerdotes Baal, &c. Et infra: Achab seruiuit sibi in pauci, & ego seruiam sibi in multis, & Dauid quando mutauit faciem suam coram Abimelech, & dimisit eum & abiit, nec mirum, si licet iu-stos homines sibi aliqua simulare pro tempore ad suam & aliorum salutem, cum & ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus non habens peccatum nec peccati carnem, simulationem carnis peccatricis assumpsit, condemnans in carne peccatum. Unde Glossa super Psalmum secundum articulum dicit, quod dolus contra hostem bonus est. Ita Origenes, ut legitur distinctione 43. cap. in mandatis, loquens de viro malis moribus inuoluto se ingerente ad scrutandum secreta fidei, ait: Si ingesserit se & provocauerit nos dicere, qua eum minus agentem recte non oporteat audire, prudenter eum debemus eludere, vbi dicit Glossa: nota dolum esse bonum contra hostem. Item Glossa 22. quaestion. 2. cap. Dominus noster, ait sic: Igitur per insidias & per dolum possumus licite vincere hostes nostros: dum tamen fidem non rumpamus hosti. Ex quibus patet, quod dolus, qui potest esse absque peccato, facto vel verbo est licitus contra hostem. Minor, sc. quod delusio quae fit generalibus verbis, etiam est dolus, qui potest esse absque mendacio, verbo & facto, patet. Quia verba, in quibus potest veritas reperiri, possunt omni carere mendacio, sed in verbis aequiuocis & multiplicibus atque ambiguis, ac etiam figuratiuis potest veritas reperiri: aliter vir iustus nunquam eis uti deberet, ergo talia verba omni possunt carere mendacio, ergo ad hostis malitiam declinandam licitum est uti talibus, quae bonum intellectum possunt habere.
units.tr: Master. That it is lawful thus to deceive such people, in order to turn aside their sentence, may be proved as follows. Whoever may use ambushes to overcome enemies or rivals may also use general, equivocal and many-sided words, and figurative speech, to turn aside the sentence of evil men. But every just and holy man may use ambushes to overcome enemies or rivals (24, quaest. 3, Dominus noster). Therefore a just and holy man may use general and equivocal words, many-sided words, and also figurative speech, to turn aside the sentence of evil men. Secondly, thus: a deceit which can be carried out without lying in word and deed is lawful against an enemy. But the deception which is effected by general, equivocal, many-sided and figurative words is a kind of deceit, and it can be carried out without lying in word and deed. Therefore such deception of an enemy is lawful. The major premise is shown by the sayings of the greatest authorities. For the blessed Jerome says, as is found in 23, quaest. 2, cap. utilem: "The example of Hiehu, king of Israel, teaches us that a useful pretence may be adopted at the right time. When he could not kill the priests of Baal unless he pretended that he wished to worship the idol, he pretended, saying: Gather to me all the priests of Baal," etc. And below: "Ahab served him in a few things, and I shall serve him in many; and David, when he changed his face before Abimelech, sent him away and went off." Nor is it surprising if just men may for a time pretend certain things for their own and others' safety, since our Lord Jesus Christ himself, though having no sin nor the flesh of sin, assumed the pretence of sinful flesh, condemning sin in the flesh. Hence the Gloss on the second article of the Psalm says that a deceit against an enemy is good. Thus Origen, as is read in distinction 43, cap. in mandatis, speaking of a man of evil morals who insinuates himself in order to search out the secrets of the faith, says: "If he thrusts himself upon us and provokes us to speak, when we ought not to listen to him since he is not acting rightly, we must prudently elude him." Where the Gloss says: "Note that a deceit against an enemy is good." Likewise the Gloss on 22, quaest. 2, cap. Dominus noster, says thus: "Therefore by ambushes and by deceit we may lawfully conquer our enemies, provided that we do not break faith with the enemy." From these passages it is plain that a deceit which can be carried out without sin in word or deed is lawful against an enemy. The minor premise, namely that deception effected by general words is also a deceit which can be carried out without lying in word and deed, is plain. For words in which truth can be found can be free of all lying. But in equivocal, many-sided and ambiguous words, and also in figurative ones, truth can be found; otherwise a just man would never be obliged to use them. Therefore such words can be free of all lying, and so it is lawful to use those words which can have a good meaning in order to turn aside the malice of an enemy.

units.la: Discipulus. Non ex opinionibus singulorum, sed ex communi usu nomina sunt intelligenda, ergo si talia verba communiter intellecta habeant malum sensum, sub malo sensu deberent intelligi. Item, non licet eum decipere, cui fidelitas est seruanda, sed hosti cuicunque seruanda est fidelitas, sicut etiam fides sibi promissa est ei seruanda, ergo nulli licet hostem quemcunque per verba generalia, aequiuoca, multiplicia, seu ambigua, vel figuratiua decipere. Item, verba cuiuscunque intelligenda sunt, sicut ea Deus accipit, Deus autem accipit verba alicuius, sicut intelligit ille cui dicuntur, sed subditi, quibus dicerentur verba talis statuti, intelligerent ea de Papa, qui a multitudine Christianorum haberetur pro Papa, ergo sic deberent intelligi. Quod autem Dominus Deus accipiat verba hominis, sicut ille intelligit, cui dicuntur, patet. Nam Deus non facit differentiam inter verba iuramenti & simplicis loquelae, teste Chrysostom. qui (vt habetur 22. quaestion. quint. cap. iuramenti) ait: Dominus noster inter iuramentum & loquelam nullam vult esse distinctionem, quia sicut in iuramento nullam conuenit esse perfidiam, ita quoque in verbis nostris nullum debet esse mendacium, sed Deus accipit verba iuramenti, sicut ille intelligit cui iuratur, teste Isidor. qui (vt legitur 22. quæstion. quint. cap. quacunque) ait: quacunque arte verborum quis iuret, Deus tamen, qui conscientia testis est, ita hac accipit, sicut ille cui iuratur intelligit, ergo etiam Deus sic accipit verba talis statuti, sicut illi, qui illo astringuntur, intelligunt. Et confirmatur hæc ratio, quia statutum non debet esse captiosum, vt scilicet aliter intelligatur, quam illi quibus dicitur intelligunt distinctione quarta. erit; sed subditi talis prælati, nescientes Papam esse hæreticum, neque scientes diffinitionem eius esse hæreticam, intelligerent tale statutum de illo qui habetur pro Papa, & de diffinitionibus eius, ergo sic deberet intelligi. Et hæc sunt, quæ mouent animum meum ad tenendum, quod sermonibus ambiguis, & generalibus nullius est deludenda malitia, ad quæ gratia exercitii satagas respondere. Magister. Sunt nonnulli, qui ista friuola putant: quorum tibi responsiones breuiter recitabo. Ad primum itaque dicitur, quod ambiguitas, & similiter generalitas verborum quandoque incidit in iudiciis, quandoque in contractibus, quandoque in legibus constitutis, quandoque in doctrina alicuius scribentis aut docentis, quandoque in simplici assertione, seu narratione alicuius verbi. Quando igitur ambiguitas, vel generalitas verborum incidit in iudiciis vel contractibus, non est semper recurrendum ad mentem loquentis: quem scilicet ex virtute verborum potest habere sensum, secundum quod ex verbis Glossæ, extra de sponsalibus, cap. ex literis, colligitur euidenter. Quando vero ambiguitas vel generalitas verborum in statutis vel legibus reperitur: si fuerit talis ambiguitas, vel generalitas verborum, quod sensus qui ex virtute verborum huiusmodi potest haberi, neque legi naturæ, nec legi humanæ (minime abrogatæ) repugnat: neque potest vergere in nocumentum iustum alterius: recurrendum est ad intentionem legem statuentis, & sic intelligenda est lex, quemadmodum ipse intelligit, & si quis aliter intelligit, talis intellectus in damnum vel periculum, aut infamiam statuentis redundare non debet, quia in talibus, in quibus ambiguitas vel generalitas verborum incidit, vbi virtus verborum permittit verum sensum, qui neque iuri diuino, neque iuri naturali, nec humano (nullatenus abrogato) repugnat: neque potest vergere in nocumentum iniustum alterius: quia cuius est condere, eius est interpretari, & quem in condendo habeat sensum exprimere. Discipulus. Quid si conditor legis talis est mortuus, antequam sensum, quem habeat in condendo legem, expresserit. Magister. Respondetur, quod sicut facta quæ possunt fieri bene vel male, in meliorem partem interpretanda sunt: ita peritus in arte distinguendi diuersos sensus legum talia verba generalia & ambigua, in meliorem partem interpretari debet, vt scilicet lex condita talis magis valeat & putetur iusta & licita, quam illicita vel iniusta. Similiter dicitur, quod vbi incidit ambiguitas vel generalitas verborum in doctrina alicuius scribentis aut docentis, recurrendum est ad intentionem loquentis, vt ipse seipsum exponat, & si quidem exprimit sensum verum, quem permittit virtus verborum, est nullatenus reprobandus, nisi conuinci posset, quod talis sensus verus aliis dictis eius esset contrarius vel impertinens: & quod talibus verbis generalibus vel ambiguis vsus fuisset ad aliquem introducendum errorem, tunc enim putandum esset, quod talem sensum verum contra conscientiam exprimeret, vel taceret alium sensum ad aliquod incommodum vel periculum euitandum, vel ad aliquod commodum consequendum. Deambiguitate etiam verborum, quæ incidit in simplici loquela vel narratione, recurrendum est ad intentionem loquentis, vt stetur interpretationi & intellectui suo, nisi probetur aperte, vel violenter aut probabiliter præsumatur, quod tali modo loquendi generali & ambiguo vsus est ad aliquem decipiendum iniuste, vel ad aliquem alium malum finem. Per hoc respondetur ad primam tuam instantiam, quia cum dicis, non ex opinionibus singulorum, sed ex communi vsu nomina sunt intelligenda, dici potest, quod hæc regula fallit in multis casibus: secundum quod ex Glossa prædicta extra de sponsalib. ca. ex literis potest haberi patenter, & ideo quando quis legem statuit, vel etiam loquitur, vt iuste & licite hostem suum deludat, non est recurrendum ad communem intelligentiam verborum: sed recurrendum est ad intentionem loquentis siue legem statuentis, & siquidem exprimit sensum, quem permittit sensus verborum, quantumcunque non sit sensus, quem homines conuenienter de talibus verbis concipiunt, sed sensus valde extraneus & inusitatus, ita tamen quod virtus verborum ita permittat: standum est conditioni statuentis & sensui loquentis, si talis sensus solummodo sit ad sensum loquentis, & non vergat in nocumentum, vel præiudicium illicitum aut iniquum alterius: & quantumcunque esset in nocumentum seu præiudicium aliorum iustum & licitum. Discipulus. Si posset probari, quod in verbis ambiguis recurrendum esset ad intentionem loquentis: & non ad communem intelligentiam verborum, prædicta ratio apparentiam videretur habere, ideo quæ ad hoc allegare contingat, ostende. Magister. Quod recurrendum sit ad intentionem loquentis, & non ad communem intelligentiam loquentis, dicta maiorum sonare videntur, ait enim Glossa extra de verborum significationibus, cap. intelligentia, Non statim debemus intelligere verba, vt prima facie sonare videntur; maxime vbi ambigua sunt, sed debemus recurrere ad intentionem loquentis, & hoc dat argumentum bonum supra de prebendis, c. vltim. & cap. cum tamen, & in fine dicit sic: argumentum quod verba ad extraneum sensum sunt trahenda, vbi res aliter salua esse non potest. Et consimiliter verba sunt trahenda ad sensum extraneum, quando aliter veritas verborum, vel æquitas saluari non potest, quod intelligendum est, quod talis sensus extraneus nulli nocet iniuste: & verba ad introducendum errorem minime sunt adiecta, ideo in hoc standum est interpretationi seu expositioni loquentis. Item Glossa, extra, de procura. cap. petitio, ait: quando verba generalia siue dubia ponuntur in huiusmodi instrumentis procuratorum recurrendum est ad ad intentionem constituentis, sicut & in priuilegiis, infra de decimis, cap. ex multiplici, cap. cum tamen. Item Glossa extra, de prebendis, cap. cum tamen, ait: recurrendum esse ad intentionem loquentis, mandantis, & scribentis. Discipulus. Scio Glossas in multis locis asserere, recurrendum esse ad intentionem loquentis, mandantis & scribentis: sed vellem scire, in quibus auctoritatibus se fundare nituntur. Magister. Fundant se in diuersis auctoritatibus sanctorum, quae in decretis & decretalibus inseruntur. Prima est Gregor. quae ponitur 22. quaestion. 5. cap. humana, qui ait: certe nouerit ille, qui intentionem & voluntatem alterius variis verbis explicat, quia non debet aliquis verba considerare, sed voluntatem & intentionem: quia non debet intentio verbis deseruire, sed verba intentioni. Secunda est beati Hieronymi, qui, vt legitur 1. quaestion. 1. cap. Marcion, ait: nec putemus in verbis scripturarum esse euangelium, sed in sensu; non in superficie, sed in medulla; non in sermonum foliis, sed in radice rationis. Tertia est beati Clementis, quae ponitur distinction. 37. cap. relatum, qui ait: Sunt multa verba in scripturis diuinis, qua possunt retrahi ad eum sensum, quem sibi ipsonte vnusquisque praesumpserit, sed non oportet. Quarta est Hilarii, quae ponitur extra, de verborum significatione cap. intelligentia, qui ait: Intelligentia dictorum ex causis est assumenda dicendi, quia non sermoni res, sed rei subiectus est sermo. Discipulus. Define plures auctoritates adducere, quia in tractatu De gestis circa fidem altercantium orthodoxam super materiam hanc reuertar, vbi in speciali de peruertentibus scripturam, & dicta aliorum inquiram. Magister. Si interrogaueris me de hoc in illo tractatu: narrabo tibi opinionem aliquorum de quibusdam magistris & praelatis in particulari, quos probare nituntur: imo videtur eis, quod probant eos propter tale vitium esse peiores & grauioribus inuolutos criminibus, quam sint fures, latrones, praedones, fornicatores, & adulteri, & maiori poena & confusione plectendos. Discipulus. Isti grandia respondent, quae nunquam valebunt persoluere, & tamen quomodo persoluere conabuntur (cum ad illum tractatum veniemus) gratia exercitii, libenter auscultabo, nunc autem qualiter ad instantias alias supra inductas respondetur, expone. Magister. Ad secundam dici potest, quod decipere aliquem contingit duplicater, vel falsum dicendo, quod nullum sensum potest habere verum: aut aliquid illicitum committendo, & sic nulli est licitum decipere alium, cui fidelitas est seruanda: vel veritatem & mentem, ac intentionem & consilium occultando, aut aliquid licitum faciendo, per quem modum in publicis bellis decipiuntur hostes: quia & eis consilia occultantur, & bellatores vbi hostes non aestimant, collocantur: multisque aliis modis licitis decipiuntur hostes. Et isto modo condens statutum vtens verbis generalibus & ambiguis, quae ita possunt intelligi ex forma verborum de Papa catholico futuro, sicut de Papa haeretico: si Papa superstes esset haereticus, deludit Papam haereticum non falsum dicendo, nec iniustum ius aliquod statuendo, sed mentem suam & intentionem & sensum, quem habet de verbis sui statuti celando: ideo nullum committit illicitum, sed pro salute sua caute deludit hostis nequiriam. Ad tertiam respondetur, quod non semper Deus accipit verba iuramenti, sicut ille cui iuratur intelligit, teste Gratiano, qui (22. quaestion. quint. cap. qui perirare) ait: ex his omnibus colligitur, quod iuramenta secundum intentionem praestantis non recipientis a Deo iudicantur. Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod sicut iurans, ita conditor legis, doctor & simpliciter loquens aliquando vtitur calliditate iniqua ad alium malitiose & iniuste decipiendum, & in isto casu verba iurantis, legem condentis, scribentis & loquentis sic intelligenda sunt, sicut & ille, qui simplici intentione & pura recipit verba & intelligit, & in isto casu loquitur Isidorus, cum dicit: quacunque arte verborum (scilicet iniqua & callida ad iniuste & impie decipiendum alios) quis iuret; Deus tamen, qui conscientia (scilicet tam callide iniqua iurantis, quam simplici intentione recipientis) testis est, ita hac accipit, sicut ille cui iuratur, intelligit, sic etiam quando quis calliditate iniqua ad decipiendum alios aliquid statuit, docet vel loquitur, Deus sic accipit verba, sicut illi quibus dicuntur, intelligunt, aliquando autem sicut iurans, ita conditor legis, docens, scribens, & loquens vtitur calliditate bona, non ad alium decipiendum iniuste, sed ad salutem suam vel aliorum, absque hoc, quod cuicunque iniuste officiat, & in isto casu intelligenda sunt verba, sicut iurans, legem condens, Doctor aut scribens, vel loquens intelligit: quando scil. forma verborum talem sensum permittit, quantumcunque sit extraneus & communi intelligentiae verborum non correspondet. Ad confirmationem quae difficilior esse videtur, potest dici, quod quando subditi alicuius praelati vel omnes, vel multi sunt pestilentes, insidiantes suo praelato, & ad insidiandum & impugnandum eundem dispositi & parati: in quo casu sicut liceret praelato inferiori Papam si esset haereticus licita cautela deludere, ita si essent sui subditi pestilentes, liceret sibi per tale statutum eosdem deludere, aliquando autem subditi sunt benevoli, rationabiles, praeoculis diuinum timorem habentes, & in hoc casu praelatus tale statutum ambiguum absque declaratione & interpretatione conuenienti apud subditos suos nequaquam publicare deberet. Vnde si vellet statutum condere ad deludendam malitiam persequentis sensum rectum, deberet subditis explicare. Discipulus. Recitasti diuersas sententias de statuto inferioris praelati sub verbis generalibus: quae de omni Papa praesente vel futuro, ac etiam diffinitionibus eorundem possunt intelligi, obligare sibi subiectos ad reuerenter loquendum de Papae persona: nullum tamen nominando & diffinitionibus eius nullatenus reprobandis. Nunc autem dic, quid est tenendum de tali statuto, si de nullo alio, quam de Papa haeretico posset intelligi, quia nomen Papae haeretici expresse exprimitur in eodem. Magister. Ad hoc secundum aliquos respondetur, quod talis praelatus credens & haereticus est censendus. Quod autem inter credentes debeat computari, videtur tali ratione posse probari. Ille, qui expresse asserit, mandat, aut praecipit errores alicuius haeretici esse tenendos. nendos inter credentes eius errorib. est censendus, sed talis prælatus per tale statutum assereret, præciperet & mandaret errores Papæ hæretici esse tenendos, ergo inter credentes computari deberet. Quod etiam esset hæreticus reputandus probatur ex hoc: quod qui cogit aliquos pœnis, præceptis, statutis ad pertinaciter errores contra fidem tenendos, est inter hæreticos computandus, talis esset prælatus, qui conderet statutum, de quo est sermo, ergo esset inter hæreticos computandus.
units.tr: Discipulus. Names must be understood according to common usage, not according to the opinions of individuals. So if such words, understood in the common way, carry a bad sense, they ought to be understood in that bad sense. Likewise, it is not lawful to deceive someone to whom faithfulness is owed. Faithfulness is owed to any enemy whatever, just as a promise made to him must be kept. Therefore no one may deceive any enemy by general, equivocal, manifold, ambiguous, or figurative words. Again, a person's words must be understood as God takes them, and God takes a person's words as the one to whom they are addressed understands them. The subjects to whom the words of such a statute would be addressed would understand them of the Pope, whom the multitude of Christians regarded as Pope; therefore they ought to be understood in that way. That the Lord God takes a person's words as the one to whom they are spoken understands them is plain. For God makes no difference between the words of an oath and of ordinary speech, as Chrysostom says (as it is found in 22 Quaest. 5, c. Iuramenti): Our Lord wills that there be no distinction between an oath and ordinary speech. For just as there ought to be no perfidy in an oath, so there ought to be no lie in our words. But God takes the words of an oath as the one to whom the oath is sworn understands them, as Isidore says (as it is read in 22 Quaest. 5, c. Quacunque): By whatever art of words a man swears, God, who is witness to the conscience, takes it just as the one to whom the oath is sworn understands it. Therefore God also takes the words of such a statute as those who are bound by it understand them. This argument is confirmed by the fact that a statute ought not to be captious, so that it is understood otherwise than those to whom it is addressed understand it (Dist. 4, c. Erit). But the subjects of such a prelate, not knowing that the Pope is a heretic and not knowing that his definition is heretical, would understand such a statute of the one who is held to be Pope, and of his definitions. Therefore it ought to be understood in this way. These are the considerations that move my mind to hold that by ambiguous and general words no one's malice is to be eluded, which you, out of a wish to exercise your wits, will try to answer. Magister. There are some who think these arguments trifling. I shall briefly recite their replies to you. To the first, then, it is said that ambiguity, and likewise the generality of words, sometimes arises in judgments, sometimes in contracts, sometimes in established laws, sometimes in the teaching of some writer or teacher, and sometimes in a simple assertion or narration of some matter. When, therefore, the ambiguity or generality of words arises in judgments or contracts, one does not always have to have recourse to the mind of the speaker, whose sense may be gathered from the force of the words, as is plainly gathered from the words of the Gloss (Extra, De sponsalibus, c. Ex literis). But when the ambiguity or generality of words is found in statutes or laws: if the ambiguity or generality of the words is such that the sense which can be had from the force of those words conflicts neither with the law of nature nor with human law (not abrogated in any way), and cannot turn to the unjust hurt of another, then one must have recourse to the intention of the lawgiver, and the law is to be understood as he himself understands it. And if someone understands it otherwise, that understanding ought not to redound to the damage, danger, or infamy of the lawgiver. For in such cases, where ambiguity or generality of words arises, and the force of the words allows a true sense which conflicts neither with divine law, nor with natural law, nor with human law (in no way abrogated), and cannot turn to the unjust hurt of another, the reason is that whoever has the power to enact a law has the power to interpret it, and to express the sense he had in enacting it. Discipulus. What if the author of such a law has died before he expressed the sense he had in enacting the law? Magister. The answer is that just as deeds that can be done well or badly are to be interpreted in the better part, so one skilled in the art of distinguishing the various senses of laws ought to interpret such general and ambiguous words in the better part, so that the law so enacted may be held rather valid, just and lawful, than unlawful or unjust. Similarly, it is said that where the ambiguity or generality of words arises in the teaching of some writer or teacher, one must have recourse to the intention of the speaker, so that he may explain himself. And if he does express the true sense which the force of the words allows, he is by no means to be condemned, unless it could be shown that this true sense is contrary to or foreign to his other statements, or that he used such general or ambiguous words to introduce some error. For then it would have to be thought that he expressed that true sense against his conscience, or was silent about another sense in order to avoid some inconvenience or danger, or to gain some advantage. As for ambiguity of words that arises in a simple speech or narration, one must have recourse to the intention of the speaker, so that his own interpretation and understanding stand, unless it is clearly proved, or violently or probably presumed, that he used such a general and ambiguous manner of speaking to deceive someone unjustly or for some other evil end. By this, the first objection of yours is answered: when you say that names must be understood not according to the opinions of individuals but according to common usage, it can be said that this rule fails in many cases, as can be plainly had from the aforesaid Gloss (Extra, De sponsalibus, c. Ex literis). Therefore, when someone enacts a law, or even speaks, in order to deceive his enemy justly and lawfully, one must not have recourse to the common understanding of the words, but to the intention of the speaker or lawgiver. And if he expresses a sense which the sense of the words permits, however much it is not the sense which men ordinarily conceive from such words, but a very strange and unusual sense, provided the force of the words so allows it, then one must abide by the condition of the lawgiver and the sense of the speaker, if that sense is only a sense in the speaker's mind and does not turn to the unlawful or unjust hurt or prejudice of another. And this holds however much it might be a just and lawful hurt or prejudice to others. Discipulus. If it could be proved that in ambiguous words one must have recourse to the intention of the speaker and not to the common understanding of the words, the aforesaid argument would seem to have some plausibility. So point out what authorities one might cite for this. Magister. That one must have recourse to the intention of the speaker, and not to the common understanding, seems to be the sense of the greater authorities. For the Gloss says (Extra, De verborum significatione, c. Intelligentia): We ought not to understand words at once as they seem to sound at first sight, especially where they are ambiguous, but we ought to have recourse to the intention of the speaker. And this gives a good argument in De praebendis, c. ultimum, and c. Cum tamen. And at the end it says: the argument is that words are to be drawn to a strange sense where the matter cannot otherwise be saved. And similarly words are to be drawn to a strange sense when the truth or equity of the words cannot otherwise be saved, which is to be understood to mean that such a strange sense harms no one unjustly, and that the words were not added at all to introduce error. Therefore in this matter one must abide by the interpretation or exposition of the speaker. Likewise the Gloss (Extra, De procuratoribus, c. Petitio) says: when general or doubtful words are placed in instruments of this kind of procurators, one must have recourse to the intention of the one who appoints, as also in privileges (Infra, De decimis, c. Ex multiplici, c. Cum tamen). Likewise the Gloss (Extra, De praebendis, c. Cum tamen) says: one must have recourse to the intention of the speaker, the one who commands, and the writer. Discipulus. I know that the Glosses in many places assert that one must have recourse to the intention of the speaker, the commander, and the writer. But I should like to know on what authorities they rest this. Magister. They rest it on various authorities of the saints, which are inserted in the Decrees and Decretals. The first is Gregory, which is given in 22 Quaest. 5, c. Humana, who says: Surely he will know, who explains the intention and will of another in various words, that one ought not to consider the words but the will and intention. For intention ought not to serve words, but words ought to serve intention. The second is that of blessed Jerome, who, as is read in 1 Quaest. 1, c. Marcion, says: Let us not think that the gospel is in the words of the Scriptures, but in the sense; not in the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of the discourse, but in the root of reason. The third is that of blessed Clement, which is given in Dist. 37, c. Relatum, who says: There are many words in the divine Scriptures which can be drawn back to the sense that each one may presume for himself, but it is not right. The fourth is that of Hilary, which is given in Extra, De verborum significatione, c. Intelligentia, who says: The understanding of what is said is to be taken from the causes of speaking, because speech is subject not to the thing, but the thing to speech. Discipulus. Define more authorities, since I shall return to this matter in the treatise On the Deeds of Those Who Dispute Concerning the Orthodox Faith, where I shall inquire in particular about those who pervert Scripture and the sayings of others. Magister. If you ask me about this in that treatise, I shall tell you the opinion of some concerning certain teachers and prelates in particular, whom they try to prove guilty. Indeed, they seem to think that, on account of this vice, those whom they prove guilty are worse and more entangled in graver crimes than thieves, robbers, plunderers, fornicators, and adulterers, and deserve a greater punishment and disgrace. Discipulus. Those men answer with grand things which they will never be able to make good. Yet how they will try to make them good (when we come to that treatise) I shall gladly hear, for the sake of exercise. But now, explain how the other objections brought forward above are answered. Magister. To the second it can be said that to deceive someone happens in two ways: either by saying a falsehood that cannot have any true sense, or by committing something unlawful. In this sense it is not lawful to deceive another to whom faithfulness is owed. Or else by concealing the truth, the mind, the intention, and the counsel, or by doing something lawful, as enemies are deceived in public wars. For counsels are concealed from them, and soldiers are stationed where the enemy does not expect them, and enemies are deceived by many other lawful means. And in this way, one who enacts a statute using general and ambiguous words, which can be understood from the form of the words of a future Catholic Pope as well as of a heretical Pope, if the Pope in office were a heretic, deceives the heretical Pope not by speaking falsely, nor by enacting any unjust right, but by concealing his mind, intention, and the sense he has of the words of his statute. Therefore he commits nothing unlawful, but for his own safety he cautiously eludes the wickedness of his enemy. To the third it is answered that God does not always take the words of an oath as the one to whom the oath is sworn understands them, as Gratian says (22 Quaest. 5, c. Qui perierat): From all these things it is gathered that oaths are judged by God according to the intention of the one who swears, not of the one who receives them. For the clearer understanding of this, it must be known that just as the one who swears, so also the author of a law, the teacher, and one who speaks simply sometimes uses wicked cunning to deceive another maliciously and unjustly. In such a case, the words of the one swearing, of the one enacting the law, the writer, and the speaker are to be understood as he who receives the words with simple and pure intention understands them. In this case Isidore speaks when he says: By whatever art of words (namely, wicked and crafty, to deceive others unjustly and impiously) a man swears, God, however, who is witness to the conscience (namely, of the one swearing with such crafty wickedness, and of the one receiving with simple intention), takes it just as the one to whom the oath is sworn understands it. So also, when someone by wicked cunning enacts, teaches, or speaks something to deceive others, God takes the words as those to whom they are addressed understand them. Sometimes, however, like the one swearing, the author of the law, the teacher, the writer, and the speaker uses good cunning, not to deceive another unjustly, but for his own salvation or that of others, without harming anyone unjustly. In this case the words are to be understood as the one swearing, enacting the law, the teacher, the writer, or the speaker understands them, namely when the form of the words permits such a sense, however strange it may be and however little it corresponds to the common understanding of the words. To the confirmation, which seems more difficult, it can be said that when all or many of the subjects of some prelate are pestilent, plotting against their prelate and disposed and ready to plot and to attack him, in such a case, just as a lower prelate would be permitted to elude the Pope, if he were a heretic, by lawful caution, so if his subjects were pestilent, it would be lawful for him by such a statute to elude them. But at other times the subjects are benevolent, reasonable, and have the fear of God before their eyes, and in this case the prelate ought by no means to publish such an ambiguous statute among his subjects without a suitable declaration and interpretation. Hence, if he wishes to enact a statute to elude the malice of a persecutor, he ought to explain the right sense to his subjects. Discipulus. You have recited various opinions about the statute of an inferior prelate under general words, which can be understood of every Pope present or future, and also of their definitions, and which can bind his subjects to speak reverently of the person of the Pope, naming no one, and not in any way condemning his definitions. But now say what is to be held about such a statute if it could be understood of no one but a heretical Pope, since the name of a heretical Pope is expressly stated in it. Magister. To this, some answer that such a prelate is to be considered a believer and a heretic. That he ought to be counted among the believers can seem to be proved by this reasoning. One who expressly asserts, commands, or orders that the errors of some heretic are to be held is to be considered among the believers of those errors. But such a prelate would by such a statute assert, order, and command that the errors of a heretical Pope are to be held. Therefore he ought to be counted among the believers. That he is also to be reputed a heretic is proved from this: whoever compels some by penalties, precepts, and statutes to hold errors obstinately against the faith is to be counted among the heretics. Such a prelate would be one who enacted the statute of which we are speaking. Therefore he is to be counted among the heretics.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: In quo inquiritur, quid sit sentiendum de eo, qui tantummodo ex mandato Papæ hæretici eius assertiones hæreticas inter sibi subiectos divulgat, tanquam tenendas.
units.tr: In which it is inquired what is to be thought of one who, only by the command of the Pope, publishes the Pope's heretical assertions among his subordinates as things to be held.

units.la: Disc. Dic de prælato inferiori, qui sciens diffinitiones Papæ esse hæreticas ipsas de mandato eiusdem Papæ hæretici tanquam tenendas solummodo divulgaret inter sibi subiectos. Mag. Diversimode respondetur. Dicitur enim vno modo, quod quantumcunq; talis coram Deo non esset hæreticus, nec credens erroribus Papæ hæretici: tamen apud fideles, qui de occultis iudicare non possunt, esset credens erroribus Papæ hæretici iudicandus. Quod enim esset credes censendus ex hoc probatur. Quia qui divulgat aliquem errorem tanquam tenendum asserit verbo vel facto talem errorem esse tenendum, sed qui asserit aliquem errorem esse tenendum, debet reputari credens tali errori, ergo qui divulgat talem errorem tanquam credendum est hæreticus censendus: & inter credentes merito computatur. Quod vero talis hæreticus sit censendus ostenditur, quia qui verbo vel facto cogit alios ad pertinaciter errores tenendos, quibus credit, est hæreticus reputandus, talis autem prælatus, quantum in se est cogit alios ad pertinaciter tenendos errores contentos in diffinitionibus Papæ hæretici: quibus dicit se credere, ergo hæreticus est censendus. Disc. Talis prælatus nullum cogeret ad tenendos errores Papæ, quia si solum divulgat illos errores, non cogit alios ad tenendum eosdem. Magi. Respondetur, quod qui solum divulgat errores & non divulgaret præceptu, quo mandatur sub grani pœna, quod certi teneantur errores, quodammodo cogit audientes tenere errorem, hoc autem faceret, qui tales diffinitiones Papæ hæretici divulgaret, quia in eisdem diffinitionibus præciperetur sub grani pœna, quod tenerentur illi errores contenti, ergo talis divulgans cogeret alios ad pertinaciter tenendos errores, & per consequens esset hæreticus reputandus. Aliter dicitur, quod talis prælatus divulgans diffinitiones Papæ, quas scit esse hæreticas, mortaliter peccat & inter credentes apud catholicos est reputandus: sed non est inter hæreticos computandus. Quod autem mortalissime peccat, probatur. Nam qui sciéter alios inducit inquantum in se est ad negandum catholicā fidem, mortaliter peccat, sed qui divulgat diffinitiones Papæ hæretici, quas scit hæreticas, quantū in se est, scienter inducit alios ad negandum catholicam veritatem: quia quantum est ex forma divulgationis per divulgationem huiusmodi audientes ad tenendas diffinitiones Papæ hæretici inducuntur, ergo talis divulgans mortalissime peccat. Item secundum Apostolum ad Rom. 1. non solum peccant, qui mala faciunt, sed etiam qui consentiunt facientibus, sed talis divulgans diffinitiones Papæ hæretici consentit Papæ hæretico, & inducit catholicos ad tenendos errores. Igitur talis divulgans gravissime peccat. Quod vero talis divulgans debeat à catholicis inter credentes erroribus Papæ hæretici computari, licet in rei veritate non sit credens, patet, quia licet corde non credat, tamen diffinitiones Papæ hæretici exterius confitetur, catholici autem non de corde, sed de exteriori confessione iudicare debent, ergo talis inter credentes est à catholicis numerandus. Quod autem non sit hæreticus iudicandus, probatur per hoc, quia talis qui solummodo diffinitiones Papæ hæreticales divulgat, licet possit probari errans, non tamen de pertinacia: & quod non sit corrigi paratus potest convinci, ergo hæreticus non est iudicandus. Disc. Aduerto quod ad sciendum, an talis divulgans diffinitiones Papæ hæreticales sit pertinax & hæreticus iudicandus, oportet ad illa quæ tractauimus superius libro quarto recurrere: quæ hic non reputo replicanda: sed pero scire an idem sentiendum sit de prælato divulgante diffinitiones Papæ hæreticas, quas scit esse hæreticas; & de alio divulgante diffinitiones easdem, quas nescit esse hæreticas. Magister. Quantum ad ecclesiam, idem est tenendum de vno & alio, quia inter vnum & alium in actibus exterioribus nulla appparet distantia: sed apud Deum magna est inter eos distantia, sicut coram Deo magna differentia reperitur inter corde credentem & confitentem eundem; & non credentem corde, tamen expressius confitentem.
units.tr: Objection: Tell me about a lower prelate who, knowing the definitions of the Pope to be heretical, merely publishes them among his subordinates as things to be held, on the command of that same heretical Pope. Master: The answer is given in different ways. One way says that, however such a man may not be a heretic before God, nor a believer in the errors of the heretical Pope, yet before the faithful, who cannot judge hidden things, he is to be judged a believer in the errors of the heretical Pope. That he is to be counted a believer is proved thus: whoever by word or deed states that some error is to be held, asserts that the error is to be held; but whoever asserts that some error is to be held must be considered a believer in that error; therefore whoever publishes such an error as to be believed is to be deemed a heretic, and is rightly counted among the believers. That such a man is to be deemed a heretic is shown because whoever by word or deed compels others to hold errors pertinaciously, which he himself believes, is to be reckoned a heretic; but such a prelate, so far as in him lies, compels others to hold pertinaciously the errors contained in the definitions of the heretical Pope, which he says he believes; therefore he is to be deemed a heretic. Objection: Such a prelate would compel no one to hold the Pope's errors, because if he only publishes those errors, he does not compel others to hold them. Master: It is answered that whoever merely publishes errors, without publishing a precept by which it is commanded under penalty of grave punishment that certain errors be held, does in some measure compel the hearers to hold the error; but he who publishes such definitions of the heretical Pope does this, because in those same definitions it is commanded under penalty of grave punishment that the errors contained in them be held; therefore such a publisher compels others to hold errors pertinaciously, and consequently is to be reckoned a heretic. Another view says that such a prelate, publishing the Pope's definitions which he knows to be heretical, sins mortally and is to be reckoned among the believers by the Catholics; but he is not to be counted among the heretics. That he sins most grievously is proved: whoever knowingly leads others, so far as in him lies, to deny the Catholic faith sins mortally; but whoever publishes the definitions of the heretical Pope, which he knows to be heretical, so far as in him lies knowingly leads others to deny Catholic truth, because by the very form of such publication the hearers are led to hold the definitions of the heretical Pope; therefore such a publisher sins most grievously. Likewise, according to the Apostle to the Romans 1, not only do those who do evil sin, but also those who consent to those who do it; but such a publisher of the definitions of the heretical Pope consents to the heretical Pope and leads Catholics to hold errors. Therefore such a publisher sins very gravely. That such a publisher ought by Catholics to be counted among the believers in the errors of the heretical Pope, although in truth he is not a believer, is evident, because although he does not believe in his heart, yet he outwardly confesses the definitions of the heretical Pope, and Catholics ought to judge not by the heart but by outward confession; therefore such a man is to be numbered among the believers by Catholics. That he is not to be judged a heretic is proved by this: that such a man who only publishes the heretical definitions of the Pope, although he may be proved to be in error, is not proved to be pertinacious; and that he is not ready to be corrected can be convicted; therefore he is not to be judged a heretic. Objection: I note that to know whether such a publisher of heretical definitions of the Pope is to be judged pertinacious and a heretic, it is necessary to return to those things we treated above in the fourth book, which I do not think should be repeated here; but I wish to know whether the same is to be thought of a prelate who publishes the heretical definitions of the Pope, which he knows to be heretical, and of another who publishes the same definitions, which he does not know to be heretical. Master: As regards the Church, the same is to be held of the one and of the other, because between the one and the other no difference appears in outward acts; but before God there is a great distance between them, just as before God there is a great difference between one who believes in his heart and confesses the same, and one who does not believe in his heart yet confesses more expressly.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: In quo specialiter inquiritur de eis, qui credunt corde errori explicite damnato, aut qui non corde credunt, nihilominus tamen extrinsecus publice confitentur, talem errorem timore seu minis coacti aut ambitione allecti, qui scilicet inter eos graviùs peccent, pro eius responsione ponuntur duae opiniones.
units.tr: In this chapter it is inquired specifically about those who believe with the heart an error that has been explicitly condemned, or who do not believe it in their hearts but nonetheless publicly confess such an error outwardly, being compelled by fear or threats, or lured by ambition. Two opinions are put forward in answer to which of these sins more gravely.

units.la: Disc. Parum disgrediendo à proposito principali te interrogare studebo de comparatione credentis corde errori damnato explicite Papæ hæretici, vel aliorum hæreticorum, quem scit esse damnatum: & non credentis corde tali errori, quem scit esse damnatum explicite: tamen timore vel ambitione, aut ex aliqua causa tracti, talem errorem occulte, vel publice confitentis, docentis, praedicantis, vel laudantis tanquam catholicum & consonum veritati. Primo enim quaero, quis eorum gravius peccat coram Deo? Magister. Circa hoc sunt diversi modi dicendi. Vnus est, quod gravius peccat ille, qui corde credit errori tali damnato Papae haeretici vel alterius haeretici: quam ille, qui non credit corde, & tamen exterius confitetur. Cuius ratio assignatur talis, tale peccatum infidelitatis est gravissimum peccatorum, quod Augustin. sentire videtur, qui (super illud Iohan. 15. si non venissem & locutus eis non fuissem peccatum non haberent) ait: magnum quidem peccatum sub generali nomine vult intelligi. Hoc est peccatum infidelitatis, quo tenentur cuncta peccata, qui credit in corde errori, quem sciuit esse damnatum, peccat peccato infidelitatis, ergo gravius peccat, quam ille qui non credit corde: & tamen solum modo talem errorem exterius confitetur, praedicat, docet vel laudat. Secundo sic. Gravius peccatum poena graviori punitur, secundum illud Deuteronom. 20. promensura peccati erit & plagarum modus, sed qui timore mortis inter Sarracenos vel alios infideles constitutus negaret Christum, & Machometum laudaret, & veneraretur, minus punitur, quam si solum corde hoc faceret. Primus enim non esset excommunicatus, nec omni gradu ecclesiastico privaretur, quemadmodum beatus Marcellinus, licet negasset Christum & sacrificasset idolis timore mortis, non fuit excommunicatus, nec omni gradu & ecclesiastica dignitate privatus, ergo qui corde credit errori damnato gravius peccat, quam qui in corde non credit, & exterius tantum confitetur & tenet.
units.tr: Student. Digressing a little from the main question, I shall try to ask you about the comparison between one who believes with the heart an error explicitly condemned, whether of the heretical Pope or of other heretics, which he knows to be condemned, and one who does not believe such an error in his heart, which he knows to be explicitly condemned, but who, drawn by fear or ambition or some other cause, secretly or publicly confesses, teaches, preaches or praises that error as Catholic and agreeing with the truth. First, I ask: which of these sins more gravely before God? Master. On this point there are different ways of speaking. One is that the one who believes such an error in his heart, condemned in the Pope or in another heretic, sins more gravely than the one who does not believe it in his heart but outwardly confesses it. The reason given is this: such a sin of unbelief is the gravest of sins, which Augustine seems to hold, when he says (on that passage of John 15, If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin): It is indeed a great sin, which is meant under the general name. This is the sin of unbelief, by which all sins are held. One who believes in his heart an error he knows to be condemned commits the sin of unbelief; therefore he sins more gravely than one who does not believe in his heart but only confesses, preaches, teaches or praises that error outwardly. Second, thus: a more grievous sin is punished with a heavier penalty, according to Deuteronomy 20, The measure of the sin shall be the measure of the stripes. But one who, out of fear of death among the Saracens or other unbelievers, denied Christ and praised and worshipped Mohammed, is punished less than one who did this only in his heart. For the former would not be excommunicated, nor deprived of every ecclesiastical rank, just as the blessed Marcellinus, although he denied Christ and sacrificed to idols out of fear of death, was not excommunicated, nor deprived of every rank and ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore one who believes a condemned error in his heart sins more gravely than one who does not believe it in his heart and only outwardly confesses and holds it.

units.la: Alius modus dicendi circa propositam interrogationem est: quod ille peccat gravius, qui non credit corde tali errori: & tamen talem errorem exterius confitetur, docet, praedicat, aut laudat: & maxime si promittit aut iurat, quod talem assertionem, quam putat corde erroneam, in perpetuum tenere proponit. Cuius ratio assignatur, quia scienter peccans gravius peccat, quam peccans ignoranter. Vnde Augustinus dicit (vt habetur 6. quaestion. 1. cap. quaero) regulam esse, quare peccata scientium peccatis ignorantium praeponuntur, sed qui corde non credit errori & exterius confitetur, scienter peccat, aliusautem peccat ignoranter credens verum esse quod tenet, ergo gravius peccat, qui non credit corde, & tamen exterius tenet talem errorem: quam ille qui credit corde eundem. Secundo sic. Gravius peccat, qui mentitur, quam ille, qui solummodo dicit salsum credens esse verum quod dicit, secundum quod ex verbis beati Augustin. in Ench. quae ponuntur 22. quaest. 2. c. hic autem, colligitur euidenter, nam qui mentitur, vult fallere: qui autem dicit falsum, quod putat esse verum, non vult fallere, gravius autem est velle fallere, quam non velle fallere, ergo mentiens gravius peccat: quam proferens falsum quod putat esse verum. Ille autem qui non credit erroribus haereticorum sive Papae, sive aliorum: & tamen exterius tenet tales errores, mentitur; quia contra id, quod in animo sentit, loquitur voluntate fallendi. Ille autem, qui credit tali errori confitendo tamen exterius, non mentitur: quia contra id quod in animo sentit non loquitur, ergo gravius peccat, quam qui corde non credit haereticorum erroribus. Disc. Rationes pro utroque modo ponendi praedicto apparentes mihi videntur, & ideo dic quomodo ad utrasque potest responderi. Magister. Ad primam pro primo modo dicendi, dicerent forte alii, quod infidelitas non esset gravissimum peccatorum, nam odium Dei videtur multo gravius. Ad Augustum autem dicitur quod ipse non dicit infidelitatem esse gravissimum peccatorum: sed dicit esse magnum peccatum, quo tenentur cuncta peccata causaliter vel dispositive aut occasionaliter, saepe autem peccatum minus est causa, dispositio vel occasio gravioris. Ad secundum potest dici, quod multum refert ex qua causa vel occasione quis negat Christum. Qui enim timore mortis negaret Christum, minus peccaret quam negans absque tali timore, quia talis negatio parum haberet de voluntario, & ideo diminueretur peccatum: & esset minus peccato infidelitatis seu haeresis: & minus putari deberet, & ideo beatus Marcellinus negando Christum & sacrificando idolis timore mortis nec fuit excommunicatus, nec dignitate Papali privatus, sed non ita diminuit voluntarium peccatum, quando quis negat amore precationis, honoris, vel dignitatis, aut status, aut cupiditate commodi temporalis, vel honoris adipiscendi, & ideo qui negat Christum in tali casu, vel etiam scienter, tenet errorem damnatum & sententiam excommunicationis incurrit, & omni dignitate ecclesiastica & auctoritate privatur, nec talis minus peccat, quam qui credit mente errori damnato: imo magis peccaret, licet qui timore mortis ore non corde diceret se credere tali errori damnato, minus peccaret quam mente credens. Discipulus. Dic quomodo potest ad rationes in oppositum responderi. Magister. Ad primam illorum dicitur, quod regula illa quandoque fallit, interdum enim peccata scientium peccatis ignorantium praeponuntur. Crucifixores enim Christi licet se praestare obsequium Deo crediderunt gravius tamen peccauerunt, quam fures vel latrones & ebriosi scienter, quia, vt videtur innuere Augustin. hoc facit in quibusdam criminibus scelerum magnitudo, quod facit in quibusdam aliis, quantum ad actu exteriorem scienter commissio. Ad secundam potest dici, quod licet quantum ad crimen mendacii exterioris gravius peccat, qui mentitur, quam qui loquitur falsum, quod putat esse verum, tamen quantum ad aliquem modum peccandi interius potest gravius peccare ille, qui loquitur falsum, quod putat esse verum, quam ille qui mentitur. Vnde qui dicit se credere erroribus alicuius haeretici, vt talis haeretici gratiam consequatur vel indignationem euitet: & tamen mente non credit eisdem erroribus: gravius peccat quantum ad crimen mendacii, quam ille qui credit & dicit se credere eisdem erroribus, quantum tamen ad credulitatem interiorem minus peccat quam alius, quia primus non habet credulitatem mentalem erroneam, secundus autem habet credulitatem mentalem damnabilem. & ita quantum ad hoc, minus peccat. Discipul. Hic restaret eadem quæstio quæ prius: vtrum scilicet crimen mendacii in mentiente huiusmodi sit grauius, quam error mentalis in illo qui loquitur falsum quod putat esse verum, quam tamen quæstionem ad præsens noli tractare: quia eam ad aliud opus censeo differendam, nunc autem dicas, qua pœna feriendus est vterque prædictorum, scilicet ille qui mentiendo dicit se assertionibus alicuius hæretici adhærere: & ille qui mente huiusmodi credit erroribus. Magist. Respondetur quod vterque puniendus est pœna hæreticorum, quia vnus est hæreticus apud Deum & ecclesiam, alius autem licet non sit hæreticus coram Deo: est tamen apud catholicos hæreticus reputandus: & ideo sicut hæreticus condemnandus. Discipul. Nunquid sunt æqualiter puniendi: vel vnus est grauius feriendus quam alius? Magist. Respondetur quod si ille qui non credit erroribus alicuius hæretici, & tamen (vt eius gratiam consequatur vel indignationem euitet) dicit se tenere assertiones easdem, postea resilit volens se forsitan excusare, quod non credidit erroribus eisdem, grauius est plectendus quam ille qui credit & fatetur se eisdem erroribus credidisse, si vterque redit ad fidei veritatem. Cuius ratio assignatur, quia qui fatetur se non credere erroribus, nec credidisse, si vtique cedit erroribus, quibus prius se dixerat adhærere: puniendus est tam pro peccato in fide, quam pro peccato in moribus, quia prius exterius tenebat pertinaciter hæreticam prauitatem, & ideo catholici, qui de manifestis & non de occultis iudicare debent: ipsum punient pro hæretica prauitate, est etiam puniendus pro crimine in moribus: quia pro crimine mendacii, alius autem crimine mendacii non irretitur asserens se tenuisse mente q; corde dedebat, primus autem mentiebatur aperte de seipso dicens se tenere quod nequaquam corde credebat, & ideo non solum tanquam hæreticus: sed tanquam falsus & mendax, bilinguis & duplex, est grauius puniendus, putandusque est omni dolositate, proditione, falsitate, periurio & similibus (saltem secundum præparationem cordis) iniquitatibus inuolutus, quare nunquam in quocunque negotio est sibi credendum: sed pro infami & ignominioso est in perpetuum habendus.
units.tr: The other way of speaking on the question proposed is that one sins more gravely who does not believe such an error in his heart, yet outwardly confesses, teaches, preaches or praises that error, and especially if he promises or swears that he intends to hold for ever the assertion which he thinks erroneous in his heart. The reason given is that one who sins knowingly sins more gravely than one who sins in ignorance. Hence Augustine says (as is found in 6. quaestion. 1. cap. quaero) that it is a rule that the sins of those who know are placed above the sins of the ignorant. But one who does not believe the error in his heart and yet outwardly confesses it sins knowingly, while the other sins in ignorance, believing that what he holds is true. Therefore one who does not believe in his heart but yet outwardly holds such an error sins more gravely than one who believes it in his heart. Second, thus: one who lies sins more gravely than one who merely says what is false while believing it to be true. This is plainly evident from the words of the blessed Augustine in the Enchiridion, cited in 22. quaest. 2. c. hic autem, for he who lies wishes to deceive, whereas he who says what he thinks true does not wish to deceive; and to wish to deceive is more grave than not to wish to deceive. Therefore the one who lies sins more gravely than the one who asserts what he thinks true. Now one who does not believe the errors of heretics, whether of the Pope or of others, yet outwardly holds those errors, lies, because he speaks against what he feels in his mind, with the will to deceive. But one who believes such an error in his heart yet confesses it outwardly does not lie, because he does not speak against what he feels in his mind. Therefore one who does not believe the errors of heretics in his heart sins more gravely. Student. The reasons put forward for each of these ways of speaking seem convincing to me, so tell me how each of them may be answered. Master. To the first reason for the first way of speaking, some others might perhaps reply that unbelief is not the gravest of sins, for hatred of God seems much graver. But it is said of Augustine that he does not claim unbelief to be the gravest of sins; he says it is a great sin, by which all sins are held causally, or dispositively, or occasionally; and often a sin is less a cause, disposition or occasion of a graver one. To the second reason it may be said that it matters much from what cause or occasion someone denies Christ. For one who denied Christ out of fear of death would sin less than one who denied him without such fear, because such a denial would have little of the voluntary in it, and so the sin would be diminished, and would be less than the sin of unbelief or heresy, and should be thought less serious. That is why the blessed Marcellinus, denying Christ and sacrificing to idols out of fear of death, was neither excommunicated nor deprived of his Papal dignity. But a voluntary sin is not diminished in this way when someone denies Christ out of love of gain, of honour or dignity, or of status, or out of desire for temporal advantage or for the attainment of honour. So one who in such a case denies Christ, or even does so knowingly, holds a condemned error, incurs the sentence of excommunication, and is deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity and authority; nor does he sin less than one who believes the condemned error in his mind. Indeed he would sin more; although one who, out of fear of death, says with his mouth, not his heart, that he believes such a condemned error, sins less than one who believes it in his mind. Student. Tell me how the reasons on the other side may be answered. Master. To the first of them it is said that this rule sometimes fails, for the sins of those who know are sometimes placed below the sins of the ignorant. The crucifiers of Christ, though they believed they were rendering obedience to God, nevertheless sinned more gravely than thieves, robbers and drunkards who sin knowingly, because, as Augustine seems to suggest, the greatness of the crime makes in some offences what, in others, the knowing commission of the outward act does. To the second it may be said that although one who lies sins more gravely in respect of the outward crime of lying than one who speaks what is false but believes it true, yet in some respect of inward sinning, one who speaks what he believes to be false may sin more gravely than one who lies. Hence one who says he believes the errors of some heretic, in order to obtain that heretic's favour or avoid his anger, yet in his mind does not believe those errors, sins more gravely in respect of the crime of lying than one who believes and says he believes those errors. Yet in respect of inward belief he sins less than the other, because the first has no erroneous mental belief, whereas the second has a damnable mental belief; and so in this respect he sins less. Student. Here the same question as before remains: namely, whether the crime of lying in one who lies is graver than the inward error of one who speaks what is false, believing it to be true. But do not treat that question now, for I think it should be deferred to another work. Now tell me what penalty each of the two just mentioned ought to suffer: the one who by lying says he adheres to the assertions of some heretic, and the one who in his mind believes the errors of such a heretic. Master. The answer is that each ought to be punished with the penalty of heretics, for the one is a heretic before God and the Church, and the other, although he is not a heretic before God, is nevertheless to be regarded as a heretic among Catholics, and so must be condemned as a heretic. Student. Are they to be punished equally, or is one to be struck more severely than the other? Master. The answer is that if one who does not believe the errors of some heretic, yet (in order to obtain his favour or avoid his anger) says he holds the same assertions, and afterwards retracts, perhaps claiming to excuse himself by saying he never believed those errors, he is to be punished more severely than one who believed and confessed that he had believed those errors, provided both return to the truth of the faith. The reason given is this: one who confesses that he does not believe the errors and never believed them, yet surely yields to the errors to which he had earlier said he adhered, must be punished both for his sin against the faith and for his sin in conduct. For previously he held stubbornly outwardly to the heretical depravity, and so Catholics, who ought to judge what is manifest and not what is hidden, will punish him for heretical depravity, and he is also to be punished for a crime of conduct, namely the crime of lying. The other is not entangled in the crime of lying, since he says he held in his mind what he did not believe in his heart. The first, however, was openly lying about himself, saying he held what he did not at all believe in his heart. Therefore he is to be punished more severely, not only as a heretic but as a false and lying, double-tongued and duplicitous person; and he is to be considered involved in every deceit, betrayal, falsehood, perjury and similar iniquities (at least in the preparation of his heart); so that he is never to be believed in any business, but is to be held for ever as infamous and disgraced.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Inquirit de ignorantibus huiusmodi errores esse damnatos, neque eis pertinaciter adhærent: vtrum tales sint hæretici censendi.
units.tr: He inquires whether those who hold such errors in ignorance, and do not cling to them stubbornly, are to be regarded as heretics, since the errors have been condemned.

units.la: Discipul. Audiui diuersas sententias de credentibus hæreticorum erroribus, quos sciunt ab ecclesia condemnatos, nunc autem discutias de credentibus, qui non sciunt hæreticorum errores esse damnatos, nec pertinaciter adhærent eisdem: an scilicet tales hæretici sint censendi, cum Gregor. 9. vbi prius de credentibus hæreticorum erroribus non distinguit. Magist. Si loquaris de erroribus, qui obuiant veritatibus catholicis, quas credens non tenetur explicite credere, sed solum implicite. Dicunt quidam quod credentes huiusmodi erroribus non sunt hæretici reputandi, tales enim credentes videntur esse illi, de quibus loquitur Augustin. vt habetur 24. q. 3. c. hæreticus: ille autem, qui huiusmodi hominibus credit, imaginatione quadam veritatis est illusus, & ideo deceptus, non hæreticus videtur esse putandus. Si autem loquaris de erroribus, qui opponuntur catholicis veritatibus, quas quis tenetur explicite credere, videtur quibusdam quod tales credentes quamuis non pertinaciter adhæreant, sunt hæretici reputandi, aliis dicentibus quod nullus potest credere errori contrario veritati catholicæ, quam tenetur explicite credere, nisi pertinaciter eidem errori adhæreat, quia eo ipso quod quis credit errori contrario veritati catholicæ, quam tenetur explicite credere, non est paratus corrigi, & per consequens pertinax est censendus. Discip. Sunt ne credentes eisdem erroribus reputandi hæretici: vel omnes pro hæreticis nequaquam habendi? Magist. Respondetur quod non: quia aliqui credentes aliquibus erroribus sunt hæretici reputandi, & alii credentes eisdem erroribus non sunt hæretici reputandi, & hoc potest contingere dupliciter, primo quia aliqui tenentur credere explicite veritates contrarias illis erroribus: alii non tenentur explicite credere veritates illas. Secundo potest hoc contingere, quod aliqui pertinaciter adhærent, aliqui non pertinaciter adhærent. Discipul. Quia, vt æstimo, ad sciendum quis credens hæreticorum erroribus censendus hæreticus: & quis non est censendus: oportet scire, quis credens est pertinax: & quis credens non est pertinax, eo quod pertinax credens est hæreticus. Ille autem qui non credit pertinaciter credens non est hæreticus reputandus, quis autem sit pertinax: & quomodo de pertinacia debeat quis conuinci, tractatum superius est lib. 4. ideo circa hanc materiam hic nolo insistere, propter quod dic breuiter, quomodo debet intelligi auctoritas Gregorii 9. ca. 1. huius libri allegata. Magist. Breuiter respondetur, quod debet intelligi de credentibus hæreticorum erroribus, quos sciunt esse damnatos, vel quibus pertinaciter credunt, quo etiam modo dicitur, quod debet intelligi auctoritas Gelasii papæ posita 24. q. 1. c. 1. quicunque in hæresim damnatam semel labitur, eius damnatione seipsum innodat.
units.tr: Disciple. I have heard various opinions about believers in the errors of heretics that the Church has condemned and whose condemnation they know. Now, however, please discuss believers who do not know that the errors of heretics have been condemned and do not obstinately cling to them. Are such people to be counted as heretics, given that Gregory 9, in the passage cited earlier, makes no distinction about believers in the errors of heretics? Master. If you are speaking of errors that run counter to Catholic truths, which the believer is not bound to believe explicitly but only implicitly, some hold that believers in such errors are not to be reckoned heretics. Such believers seem to be those of whom Augustine speaks, as found in 24 q. 3 c. Hereticus: but whoever believes such men has been deceived by a certain semblance of truth, and so he is to be considered deceived rather than a heretic. If, however, you are speaking of errors that are opposed to Catholic truths which a person is bound to believe explicitly, some think that such believers, even if they do not cling to the error obstinately, are to be reckoned heretics. Others reply that no one can believe an error contrary to a Catholic truth that he is bound to believe explicitly without clinging obstinately to that error. For by the very fact that someone believes an error contrary to a Catholic truth he is bound to believe explicitly, he is not ready to be corrected, and consequently he is to be considered obstinate. Disciple. Are believers in these errors to be counted heretics, or are they not to be regarded as heretics at all? Master. The answer is that they are not all the same. Some believers in certain errors are to be reckoned heretics, and others who believe the same errors are not to be reckoned heretics. This can happen in two ways. First, some are bound to believe explicitly the truths contrary to those errors, while others are not bound to believe those truths explicitly. Second, it can happen that some cling to the error obstinately, while others do not. Disciple. As I understand it, to know which believers in the errors of heretics are to be counted heretics and which are not, one must know who is an obstinate believer and who is not, since an obstinate believer is a heretic. Whoever does not believe obstinately is not to be reckoned a heretic. But how one is to be convicted of obstinacy has been treated above in book 4, so I do not wish to dwell on that matter here. Therefore, briefly tell me how the authority of Gregory 9, c. 1 of this book, cited above, is to be understood. Master. Briefly, the answer is that it must be understood of believers in the errors of heretics whose condemnation they know, or whom they believe obstinately. In the same way, the authority of Pope Gelasius, given in 24 q. 1 c. 1, must be understood: whoever has once fallen into a condemned heresy binds himself by that condemnation.

units.la: Hhh 4 CAP.
units.tr: Hhh 4 CHAP.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: In quo quaritur de credentibus ipsis haereticis, eos reputantes catholicos, ignorantes tamen in quo discrepant à doctrina catholica, an scilicet tales sint haeretici, aut qua debeant plecti poena, & respondetur sub duplici opinione.
units.tr: Here it is asked about the heretics themselves who believe, who think themselves Catholic while being ignorant of where they differ from Catholic doctrine: whether such people are heretics, or what punishment they ought to suffer; and the answer is given under a twofold opinion.

units.la: Discip. Postquam vidimus de credentibus explicite haereticorum erroribus: consideremus de credentibus ipsis haereticis, qui scilicet reputarent ipsos catholicos: licet ignorarent, in quo discrepant à doctrina catholica atque sana, an scilicet tales sint haeretici reputandi: & qua poena debeant plecti. Magist. Circa hoc possunt esse diversi modi dicendi, unus est, quod tales, si nullum errorem haereticorum explicite credunt, qui nesciunt in speciali, qui sint errores eorum, non sunt inter haereticos computandi stricte loquendo de haereticis: large tamen accipiendo haereticos pro implicite pertinaciter tenentibus errores, qui sapiunt haeresim manifestam, haeretici sunt censendi.
