units.la: Discip. Dixisti secundum vnam assertionem, quod reputantes damnabiliter Papam esse catholicum (qui in rei veritate est hæreticus) debent censeri credentes. Ideo nunc dic secundum assertionem eandem, qua pœna tales sunt plectendi. Magist. Pœna eorum secundum assertionem præscriptam taxatur, extra de hereticis cap. excommunicamus primo, cum dicitur: credentes praeterea, receptatores, defensores & fautores haereticorum excommunicationi decernimus subiacere: statuentes si mitter, postquam quilibet talium fuerit excommunicatione notatus, si satisfacere contempserit infra annum, ex tunc ipso iure sit factus infamis, nec ad publica officia, seu consilia, nec ad eligendos aliquos huiusmodi, nec ad testimonium admittatur: sit etiam intestabilis, vt nec testandi liberam habeat facultatem, nec ad hereditatis successionem accedat: nullus nullum praeterea ipsi super quocunque negotio, sed ipse alii respondere cogatur. Quod si forte iudex extiterit, eius sententia nullam obtineat firmitatem, nec causa aliqua ad eius audientiam perferantur. Si fuerit advocatus, nullatenus eius patrocinium admittatur, si tabellio, instrumenta confecta per ipsum nullius sint momenti, sed cum actore damnato damnentur. Et in similibus idem praecipimus observari. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod credentes, de quibus hic fit mentio, poena haereticorum sunt minime puniendi. Ex quo videtur patenter inferri, quod credentes, quorum poena hic taxatur, non sunt haeretici iudicandi: quia si essent haeretici, poena haereticorum essent merito percellendi. Et ita videtur aperte ostendi, quod aliter accipitur nomen credentium in isto c. 1. & 2. cap. eiusdem c. excommunicamus 2. ubi credentes haeretici iudicantur. Hic autem non reputantur haeretici. Patet ergo hic qua poena credentes, qui damnabiliter reputant Papam esse catholicum (qui tamen est haereticus) sint plectendi. Verumtamen circa poenas credentium & aliorum in scripturis taxatas sunt diversae opiniones. Una est quod credentes, receptatores, defensores & fautores haereticorum ipso facto sunt solummodo excommunicationis sententia involuti, & si nunquam nominatim a praelatis ecclesiae fuerint denunciati excommunicati: alias poenas non incurrunt, si satisfacere contempserint infra annum. Alia est opinio, quod omnes praedicti omnes alias poenas ab excommunicatione post annum incurrunt, si satisfacere infra annum contempserint, sive fuerint denunciati, sive non; excommunicati.
units.tr: Discip. You said, according to one assertion, that those who culpably regard the Pope as Catholic (who in truth is a heretic) ought to be counted as believers. Now therefore tell me, according to the same assertion, what punishment such persons are to suffer. Magist. Their punishment is laid down according to the aforesaid assertion, extra de hereticis, chapter excommunicamus primo, where it is said: "Moreover we decree that believers, harbourers, defenders and supporters of heretics are subject to the sentence of excommunication, decreeing that if any one of them has been marked with excommunication and has scorned to make satisfaction within a year, then from that time he is by law made infamous, and is not admitted to public offices or councils, nor to the choosing of any such persons, nor to give testimony; he is also to be intestable, so that he has no free power of making a will, nor may he succeed to an inheritance; no one is to answer him in any matter, but he is compelled to answer others. If he happens to be a judge, his sentence is to have no firmness, nor are any causes to be brought before his hearing. If he is an advocate, his patronage is in no way to be admitted; if a notary, the instruments drawn up by him are of no moment, but are to be condemned together with the condemned plaintiff. And we command the same to be observed in similar cases." From these words it is gathered that the believers spoken of here are by no means to be punished as heretics. From this it seems plainly to follow that the believers whose punishment is laid down here are not to be judged heretics, for if they were heretics they would rightly be struck with the penalties of heretics. And so it seems clearly shown that the name of believers is taken otherwise in this chapter 1 and 2, and in the same chapter excommunicamus 2, where believers are judged heretics. Here, however, they are not regarded as heretics. It is therefore plain here what punishment those believers are to suffer who culpably regard the Pope as Catholic (who nevertheless is a heretic). Yet there are diverse opinions about the punishments of believers and of others laid down in the Scriptures. One is that believers, harbourers, defenders and supporters of heretics are by the very fact involved only in the sentence of excommunication, and if they have not been named and denounced as excommunicate by the prelates of the Church, they incur no other penalties, if they have scorned to make satisfaction within a year. Another opinion is that all the aforesaid incur all other penalties after a year, from excommunication, if they have scorned to make satisfaction within the year, whether they have been denounced or not, as excommunicate.

units.la: Discip. Dixisti secundum unam opinionem de illis, qui reputant Papam haereticum esse catholicum: quia nolunt scire vel non curant scire eum esse haereticum: nunc dic de illis, qui putant Papam esse haereticum, qui tamen non contemnunt scire. Magist. Respondetur, quod si sint aliqui, qui nesciunt Papam esse haereticum, & ignorantia eorum non est affectata, neque crassa & supina: quia in nullo resisterent illis, qui eos vellent de perfidia Papae haeretici informare, sed parati essent eos audire, non sunt poena aliqua feriendi, propter hoc, nisi in aliquo alio delinquere conuincantur. Ignorantia enim talis eos excusat.
units.tr: Discip. You have told me about one opinion concerning those who regard the Pope, who is a heretic, as Catholic, because they are unwilling or do not care to know that he is a heretic. Now tell me about those who think the Pope is a heretic, but who nevertheless do not despise knowing it. Magist. It is answered that if there are some who do not know that the Pope is a heretic, and whose ignorance is not affected, nor gross and supine, because they would in no way resist those who wished to inform them of the perfidy of the heretical Pope, but would be ready to hear them, such persons are not to be struck with any punishment on this account, unless they are convicted of offending in some other respect. For such ignorance excuses them.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: In quo ponuntur tres rationes probantes, quod talibus impugnantibus Papam haereticum non est credendum. Quarum prima infra c. 24. huius solvitur. Secunda & tertia c. 26. solvuntur.
units.tr: In which three arguments are set out to show that such people, who attack the Pope as a heretic, are not to be believed. The first of these is answered below in chapter 24 of this work; the second and third are answered in chapter 26.

units.la: Discip. Supra recitasti opinionem dicentem, quod volentes perfidiam Papae haeretici declarare debent audiri. Et quod nolentes eos audire credentes Papam haereticum esse catholicum, sunt sententia excommunicationis involuti. Nunc autem dic, an talibus volentibus perfidiam Papae haeretici declarare, fides debeat adhiberi. Magist. Una assertio est, quod talibus minime est credendum. Quod probatur primo sic. Illud non debet quis facere, quod sacra pagina reprehendit. Sed fidem adhibere narrantibus aliquid sinistrum de aliquo sacra pagina reprehendit. Eccl. 19. vbi sic scribitur: Qui cito credit, levis est corde & minorabitur. Ergo homo non debet credere referentibus & narrantibus Papam esse haereticum. Item, minus credenda sunt mala quae referuntur de aliquo, quam bona: quia unusquisque promptior esse debet ad iudicandum bene de proximo quam male. Sed bona relata de aliquo non sunt statim credenda. Unde & regina Saba cum multa excellentia audiuisset de Salomone, laudabiliter dicit ad Salomonem, ut legitur 3. Reg. 10. Verus est sermo quem audiui in terra mea super sermonibus tuis & super sapientia tua: & non credebam narrantibus mihi donec ipsa veni & vidi oculis meis: & probaui quod media pars mihi nunciata non fuerat. Ergo multo magis non debet quis credere narrantibus mala de aliquo. Et ita referentibus Papam esse haereticum, minime est credendum. Secundo sic. Illud quod dissuadetur in scriptura diuina, minime est agendum. Sed credere narrantibus sive bona fide sive mala dissuadetur in scriptura diuina. Ergo non debet quilibet narrantibus fidem adhibere: & per consequens referentibus Papam esse haereticum, fides est nullatenus adhibenda. Maior est manifesta: quia nihil dissuadetur in scriptura diuina, nisi peccatum, quod catholicus minime facere debet. Minor diuersis auctoritatibus scripturae diuinae aperte videtur posse probari. Eccl. 19. sic scribitur: Non omni verbo credas. Et Ierem. 12. legitur: Ne credas eis, cum locuti fuerint tibi bona. Et Mich. 7. Nolite credere amico. Et Iohan. 4. Nolite enim omni spiritui credere. Ex quibus aliisque quam pluribus colligitur, quod credere narrantibus dissuadet scriptura diuina. Quare sicut aliqui narrent, quod Papa est haereticus, eis nullatenus est credendum. Tertio sic. Nullum crimen est credendum de aliquo, antequam ordine iudiciario obseruato probatum exiterit. Sed per solam narrationem illorum, qui asserunt Papam secundum ordinem iuris minime est probatum. Igitur talibus referentibus Papam esse haereticum fides debet nullatenus adhiberi. Minor, ut videtur, probatione non indiget: quia absque iudice vel non secundum ordinem iuris nullus debet condemnari. Maior per sanctos canones videtur aperte posse probari. Nam, ut legitur 30. quaest. 5. cap. 1. §. in certa, Papa ait: Quamuis enim vera sint non tamen credenda sunt: nisi quae manifesto indicio comprobantur: nisi quae manifesto iudicio conuincuntur: nisi quae iudiciario ordine publicantur. Idem narrat Sixtus Papa, qui (vt legitur c. & q. praedictis c. nullum) ait: mala itaque audita nullum moueant: nec passim dicta absque certa probatione quisquam vnquam credat, sed ante audita diligenter inquirat: nec precipitando quicquam aliquis agat. agat. Item Augustinus (vt habetur 2, q. 3. c. in cunctis) Constantino Mediolanensi episcopo, ait: De vestra igitur sanctitate absit à Christianorum iudicio ea quae maledicorum hominum rationibus confícta creditur in qualicunque modulo suspitionis adduci & sacri eloquii testimonium tenemus, vt mala malorum cum forsitan dicuntur nisi probata credi non debeant, sed citius probata vtcunque vt nimia lenitas esse ostenderem, si qui mala graui-a credere studeant, quae probari non possunt. Item Gregorius (vt legitur dist. 96. cap. si quid vero de quocunque clerico ad aures tuas peruenerit, quod te iuste posit offendere, facile non credas, nec te ad vindictam res accendat incognita: sed praesentibus ecclesiae tuae senioribus diligenter est veritas perscrutanda. Et eadem sententia sub eisdem verbis habetur extr. de symonia, licet Holi. Item Augustinus in epistola ad Vicentium (vt habetur 23. q. 4. quam magnum) ait: Facta nocentium quae innocentibus demonstrari vel ab innocentibus credi non possunt, non coinquinant quenquam. Ex quibus aliisque quam pluribus videtur aperte probari: quod mala de aliquo credi non debent, antequam secundum ordinem iuris manifeste probentur: & per consequens referentibus extra iudicium Papam esse haereticum minime est credendum. Discip. Videtur quod istae ultimae auctoritates non faciunt ad propositum: quia loquuntur solum de iudicibus & praelatis: qui non debent credere ea, quae deferuntur ad ipsos, antequam probentur aperte: cum hoc tamen stat, quod alii debeant credere his, quae de perfidia Papae haeretici nuntiantur. Magist. Hoc videtur irrationabiliter dictum: quia illi qui leuius decipi possunt, non debent esse promptiores ad credendum narranti quam alii. Sed alii quam iudices & praelati leuius decipi possunt: quia minorem peritiam & experientiam rerum habent, quam iudices & praelati. Ergo minus debent credere huiusmodi relationibus, antequam clare secundum iudiciarium ordinem sint probatae.
units.tr: Student. Earlier you recited the opinion that those who wish to declare the treachery of a heretical Pope ought to be heard, and that those who refuse to hear them, while believing the Pope to be a heretic yet Catholic, are caught up in the sentence of excommunication. Now tell me whether faith ought to be given to such people who wish to declare the treachery of a heretical Pope. Teacher. One view is that such people are by no means to be believed. This is proved first as follows. A man ought not to do what Holy Scripture rebukes. But Holy Scripture rebukes giving credit to those who tell something harmful about someone. Ecclesiasticus 19, where it is written thus: He that believeth lightly is light of heart, and shall be diminished. Therefore a man ought not to believe those who report and relate that the Pope is a heretic. Likewise, reports of evil about someone are less to be believed than reports of good, since everyone ought to be readier to judge well of his neighbour than ill. But good reports about someone are not to be believed at once. Hence also the queen of Sheba, when she had heard of Solomon's great excellence, said to Solomon, praising him, as we read in 3 Kings 10: It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thine acts and of thy wisdom: howbeit I believed not their words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me. Therefore much more ought a man not to believe those who relate evil about someone. And so, to those who report that the Pope is a heretic, no belief is to be given. Second, as follows. What Holy Scripture dissuades from is by no means to be done. But giving credit to those who report, whether in good faith or in bad, is dissuaded in Holy Scripture. Therefore no one ought to give credit to whoever reports something, and consequently to those who say the Pope is a heretic, belief is by no means to be given. The major premise is plain, since nothing is dissuaded in Holy Scripture except sin, which a Catholic ought by no means to commit. The minor premise seems clearly provable from various authorities of Holy Scripture. Ecclesiasticus 19 is written thus: Believe not every word. And Jeremiah 12 reads: Believe them not, though they speak fair words unto thee. And Micah 7: Trust ye not in a friend. And John 4: Believe not every spirit. From these and many other passages it is gathered that Holy Scripture dissuades from believing those who report. Therefore, just as some relate that the Pope is a heretic, they are by no means to be believed. Third, as follows. No crime is to be believed of anyone before it has been proved by the observance of the judicial order. But by the mere report of those who assert that the Pope is a heretic, it has not been proved according to the order of law. Therefore to those who report that the Pope is a heretic, belief ought by no means to be given. The minor premise, as it seems, needs no proof, since no one ought to be condemned without a judge or not according to the order of law. The major premise seems clearly provable from the sacred canons. For, as we read in 30 q. 5 c. 1 §. in certa, the Pope says: For although they are true, yet they are not to be believed, unless they are confirmed by manifest evidence; unless they are convicted by manifest judgment; unless they are published by the judicial order. Pope Sixtus says the same, who (as we read in the chapter and question cited above, c. nullum) says: Evil things that are heard should therefore move no one, nor should anyone ever believe things said everywhere without certain proof, but should first inquire diligently into what has been heard, nor should anyone act precipitately. Likewise Augustine (as found in 2 q. 3 c. in cunctis), writing to Constantius, bishop of Milan, says: Far be it, therefore, from the judgment of Christians, out of your holiness, that anything which is invented from the arguments of evil-speaking men should be brought into any slightest suspicion; and we hold the testimony of sacred speech, that the evil things of evil men, when perhaps they are spoken, ought not to be believed unless proved; but rather, when proved in whatever way, they should be believed. It would show excessive leniency if men were eager to believe grave evils which cannot be proved. Likewise Gregory (as we read in dist. 96 c. si quid vero): if anything about any cleric reaches your ears which could justly offend you, do not easily believe it, nor let an unknown matter kindle you to vengeance; but the truth should be carefully examined in the presence of the elders of your church. The same sentence, under the same words, is also found in extra de simonia, though Holy (?) has it differently. Likewise Augustine in his letter to Vincentius (as found in 23 q. 4 quam magnum) says: The deeds of the guilty, which cannot be shown to the innocent, nor believed by the innocent, do not defile anyone. From these and many other passages it seems clearly proved that evil things about anyone ought not to be believed before they are manifestly proved according to the order of law; and consequently, to those who report that the Pope is a heretic outside of judgment, belief is by no means to be given. Student. It seems that these last authorities do not bear on the point, because they speak only of judges and prelates, who ought not to believe what is laid before them until it is clearly proved; yet it remains consistent that others ought to believe what is announced about the treachery of a heretical Pope. Teacher. This seems to be said without reason, because those who can be deceived more easily ought not to be readier to believe a narrator than others. But others than judges and prelates can be deceived more easily, since they have less skill and experience of affairs than judges and prelates. Therefore they ought to believe such reports less, until they have been clearly proved according to the judicial order.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Ponitur pro conclusione seu assertione c. 11. quinq; distinctiones & septem conclusiones. Prima probatur hic, secunda & tertia, c. 14. quarta c. 15. quinta c. 16. sexta c. 17. septima probatur c. 21.
units.tr: This is put forward as the conclusion or assertion of chapter 11, which contains five distinctions and seven conclusions. The first is proved here, the second and third in chapter 14, the fourth in chapter 15, the fifth in chapter 16, the sixth in chapter 17, and the seventh is proved in chapter 21.

units.la: Discipulus. Quamuis praescripta assertio videtur bene fundata, tamen peto vt assertionem contrariam recitare digneris: & eam aeque fulcire nitaris. Magist. Tenentes assertionem contrariam variis modis reputant distinguendum. Quorum prima distinctio sumitur ex Glossa dist. 65. c. si quis, quod duplex est credulitas: vna quae spectat ad iudicem: alia quae spectat ad socios. Credulitas quae spectat ad iudicem est illa, secundum quam iudex debet proferre sententiam. Credulitas quae spectat ad socios est illa, qua quis extra iudicium credit socio. Secunda distinctio est: quia aut referentes perfidiam Papae haeretici vel quodcunque crimen alterius fuerunt ante prouidi & discreti & bonae famae: aut fures, criminosi & malae famae: Tertia distinctio est: quia aut narrant tantum secundum famam, aut secundum certam scientiam. Quarta distinctio est, quia si referentes sunt criminosi & malae famae: aut ad assertionem relationis suae adducunt alia legitima documenta, aut nulla. Quinta distinctio est: quia aut referunt notoria, aut illa quae non sunt notoria, quae tamen probari possunt. Iuxta has distinctiones tenent isti septem conclusiones.
units.tr: Discipulus. Although the assertion just stated seems well founded, I ask you kindly to recite the contrary assertion and to labour equally to support it. Magist. Those who hold the contrary assertion make various distinctions. The first distinction is taken from the Gloss on Dist. 65, c. si quis, which says that there are two kinds of credulity: one that concerns the judge, and one that concerns associates. The credulity that concerns the judge is that on which the judge must pronounce sentence. The credulity that concerns associates is that by which someone believes an associate outside a judicial proceeding. The second distinction is this: those who report the perfidy of a heretical Pope, or any other crime, were either previously prudent, discreet and of good repute, or else thieves, criminals and of bad repute. The third distinction is this: they either report only what is common talk, or they report from certain knowledge. The fourth distinction is this: if the reporters are criminals and of bad repute, they either bring other lawful proofs to support their report, or none. The fifth distinction is this: they report either notorious matters, or matters that are not notorious but can be proved. In accordance with these distinctions they hold the following seven conclusions.

units.la: Quarum prima est, quod loquendo de credulitate, quae spectat ad iudicem, nullus debet credere referentibus Papam esse haereticum: nisi sit notorium, aut iudiciario ordine obseruato probatum.
units.tr: The first of these is that, speaking of the credulity that concerns the judge, no one ought to believe those who report that the Pope is a heretic, unless it is notorious or has been proved in the proper judicial order.

units.la: Secunda conclusio est, quod loquendo de credulitate, quae est inter socios (secundum quod vnus socius extra iudicium credit alteri) nullus tenetur credere vni soli cuiuscunque famae vel opinionis existat, asserens Papam esse haereticum. Tertia conclusio, quod vni soli bonae famae & opinionis referenti per certam scientiam Papam esse haereticum: potest quis credere absque peccato, licet ei credere minime teneatur. Quarta conclusio est, quod pluribus honestis & discretis referentibus per certam scientiam Papam esse haereticum, tenetur quis credere. Quinta conclusio est: quod referentibus prouidis, & honestis, per famam publicam Papam esse haereticum, debet quis credere. Sexta conclusio est: quod quibuscunque criminosis adducentibus legitima documenta, quod Papa est haereticus, credendum est. Septima conclusio est: quod quibuscunque criminosis vel malae famae, si non declauerint per legitima documenta Papam esse haereticum, non est credendum.
units.tr: The second conclusion is that, speaking of the credulity that exists between associates (in so far as one associate believes another outside a judicial proceeding), no one is bound to believe any single person, of whatever reputation or standing, who asserts that the Pope is a heretic. The third conclusion is that a person may believe, without sin, a single reporter of good repute and standing who reports from certain knowledge that the Pope is a heretic, although he is by no means bound to believe him. The fourth conclusion is that one is bound to believe several honest and discreet persons who report from certain knowledge that the Pope is a heretic. The fifth conclusion is that one ought to believe prudent and honest persons who report, by public fame, that the Pope is a heretic. The sixth conclusion is that whatever criminals bring lawful proofs that the Pope is a heretic must be believed. The seventh conclusion is that criminals, or persons of bad repute, who do not demonstrate by lawful proofs that the Pope is a heretic, are not to be believed.

units.la: Discip. Si prolixe istas conclusiones septem nitaris ostendere, librum nimis prolixum efficeres. Ideo eas succincte probes. Magist. Prima conclusio per auctoritates allegatas in capitulo praecedenti pro assertione contraria, sufficienter videtur esse probata. Nam auctoritates ultimae asserunt manifeste, quod iudex non debet credere his quae dicuntur, nisi probentur. Hoc est, non debet reputare sententiam super his quae subiiciuntur esse ferendam, antequam sint aperte probata. Quod intelligendum est de illis quae non sunt notoria: similiter aliis. Et ideo quicunque esset iudex Papae haeretici, non deberet contra eum diffinitionem diffinitiuam sententiam ferre, antequam conuinceretur legitime, vel esset confessus: nisi esset no‐torium, ipsum esse haereticum. In notoriis enim non est necesse ordinem iudiciarium obseruare. Discip. Nunquid ille qui esset iudex Papae haeretici, poterit absque manifesta probatione in iudicio Papam haereticum detinere: vel aliter circa diffinitiuam coartare. Magist. Respondetur quod tanta & talis posset fieri iudici fides extra iudicium de perfidia Papae haeretici & de imminente periculo: quod iudex ante sententiam iudicialiter captam posset Papam haereticum detinere. Quod probatur sic. Aeque vel magis potest iudex detinere illum, de quo est facta sibi fides extra iudicium, qui maiori & periculosiori & perniciosiori crimine alligatur; quam alium de maiori solum suspectum. Quia fides de maiori crimine magis debet movere iudicem ad detinendum criminosum quam sola suspitio de minori. Sed iudex potest detinere illum qui de minori crimine & minus periculosiori, quam sit crimen haeresis, est ei suspectus. Ergo multo magis potest detinere Papam haereticum, de quo est sibi facta fides certa extra iudicium, quod est haereticus, quod intendit fideles auertere a fide orthodoxa. Maior probatur auctoritate Alexandri tertii, qui (vt habetur extra, de depositio c. 1.) mandauit, vt furem suspectum iudices vel legati sub quaestione ad rationem ponerent, etiam si oporteret vinculis alligatum, donec reddere compelleretur pecuniam. Vbi dicit Glossa super verbo quaestione: Nota quod suspecti torquendi sunt & in vinculis detinendi. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod Alexander loquitur in casu, in quo non fuit conuictus, sed suspectus tantummodo. Et ita suspecti solummodo possunt in vinculis detineri. Item ex c. Caroli Imperatoris, vt distinct. 19. cap. in memoriam, sic habetur: si vero (quod non decet) quilibet siue sit presbyter siue diaconus aliquam perturbationem machinando, & nostro ministerio insidiando redarguatur falsam ab Apostolica sede detulisse epistolam, vel aliud quod inde non venerit salua fide & integra apud Apostolicum humilitate, penes ipsum sit potestas, vt eum in carcerem aut in aliam detrudat custodiam: vsque quo per episcopum vel per idoneos suae partis legatos apostolicam interpellet sublimitatem, vt potissimum sua sancta legatione dignetur discernere, & quid de talibus Romana lex statuit diffinire. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod ante sententiam, & antequam sit certum, aliquem esse falsarium, licite in carcere detinetur. Quod Glossa super verbo carcerem, aperte insinuat dicens: si certum eum falsarium, deponitur so. distinct. si episcopus, extra, de crimine falsi, ad falsarium. Sed vbi dubium est, fit, quod hic dicitur, in casu qui tantum sunt suspecti licite detinentur. Quod etiam extra, de rescriptis, ex literis, innituntur manifeste. Et hoc obtinuit consuetudo iudicum fidelium ecclesiasticorum & secularium, Igitur multo fortius si Papa est haereticus: & suo iudici facta est fides de eius perfidia, etiam extra iudicium licebit eidem iudici praecipere (si periculum viderit imminere) Papam haereticum etiam in vinculis detineri.
units.tr: Discip. If you labour to show these seven conclusions at length, you will make a book far too long. So prove them briefly. Magist. The first conclusion seems sufficiently proved by the authorities cited in the preceding chapter for the contrary assertion. For the last of those authorities plainly state that a judge ought not to believe what is said unless it is proved. That is, he ought not to regard himself as able to pass sentence on the matters put before him until they have been openly proved. This must be understood of matters that are not notorious; likewise of other matters. And so whoever was judge of a heretical Pope ought not to pass a definitive sentence against him until he had been convicted lawfully or had confessed, unless it were notorious that he was a heretic. For in notorious cases there is no need to observe the judicial order. Discip. Can the man who was judge of a heretical Pope hold the Pope in judgement, or otherwise restrain him from a definitive ruling, without a manifest proof? Magist. The answer is that the judge may come to such a firm and definite belief about the perfidy of a heretical Pope, and about the imminent danger, outside the judicial proceeding, that before a sentence has been judicially passed he may hold the heretical Pope in custody. This is proved thus. A judge may detain with equal or greater right the man against whom he has formed a belief outside the proceeding, who is bound by a greater, more dangerous and more pernicious crime, than another who is merely suspected of a lesser crime. For belief about a greater crime ought to move a judge to detain a criminal more than mere suspicion of a lesser one. But a judge may detain one who is suspected of a lesser and less dangerous crime than heresy. Therefore much more may he detain a heretical Pope, about whom he has a certain belief outside the proceeding that he is a heretic, which means that he intends to turn the faithful away from the orthodox faith. The major premise is proved by the authority of Alexander III, who (as is found in extra, de depositio c. 1.) ordered that a suspected thief should be brought to account under interrogation by judges or legates, even if he had to be bound in chains, until he was compelled to repay the money. Here the Gloss on the word quaestione says: Note that the suspected are to be tortured and kept in chains. From these words it is plain that Alexander is speaking of a case in which the man was not convicted but only suspected. And so the suspected alone may be kept in chains. Likewise from the chapter of the Emperor Charles, as found in distinct. 19. cap. in memoriam, the following is laid down: If indeed (which is not fitting) anyone, whether he be a presbyter or a deacon, stirring up some disturbance and plotting against our ministry, is convicted of having falsely brought a letter from the Apostolic See, or of some other matter that has not come from there, with his faith and his standing with the Apostolic See unimpaired, it shall be in the power of the one who holds him to put him in prison or some other custody, until he appeals to the Apostolic majesty through a bishop or through suitable legates of his own party, so that, by his holy legation, it may deign chiefly to discern and to define what Roman law has decreed concerning such persons. From these words it is given to understand that, before sentence, and before it is certain that someone is a forger, he may lawfully be held in prison. The Gloss on the word carcerem plainly hints at this, saying: if he is certainly a forger, he is deposed; see Dist. 50, si episcopus; extra, de crimine falsi, ad falsarium. But where there is doubt, what is said here is done, and those who are only suspected may lawfully be detained. The decretals extra, de rescriptis, ex literis also plainly support this. And this has been the established custom of faithful judges, both ecclesiastical and secular. Therefore, much more strongly, if the Pope is a heretic, and his judge has come to a belief about his perfidy, even outside the proceeding, that judge may, if he sees danger impending, order the heretical Pope to be held even in chains.

units.la: Discip. Contra hoc duae occurrunt instantiae. Prima est, quod aliter tractandus est Papa (quamuis efficiatur haereticus) quam alii in ecclesiastica dignitate constituti. Ergo licet aliquando criminosi crimine haeresis irretiti valeant detineri: tamen Papa est nullatenus detinendus. Secunda est instantia, quod licet Papa efficitur haereticus, tamen antequam degradetur, & traditus fuerit curiae seculari, gaudet priuilegio clericali. Et per consequens absque excommunicationis vinculo nullus eum detinere valebit. Magist. Istae instantiae friuolae reputantur. Vnde ad primam dicitur, quod quia Papa (si efficiatur haereticus) ipso facto tam iure diuino quam iure humano est omni dignitate & auctoritate priuatus: & nullo gaudet priuilegio vltra alios episcopos effectos haereticos: imo videtur, quod si non sit alius Papa, quando Papa est haereticus, non potest recursus haberi ad Papam verum: quando autem Papa manente catholico, si alii episcopi efficiantur haeretici, potest haberi recursus ad Papam verum: oportet in hoc casu speciali aliquid obseruare circa Papam haereticum, vt scilicet contra eum strictius & rigidius, quam contra episcopos, quando Papa est catholicus per inferiores iudices procedatur. Quia tunc non possunt habere recursum ad Papam verum.
units.tr: Discip. Two objections arise against this. The first is that the Pope must be treated differently (even though he has become a heretic) from others placed in ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore, although criminals entangled in the crime of heresy may sometimes be detained, the Pope must by no means be detained. The second objection is that, although the Pope becomes a heretic, yet before he is deposed and handed over to the secular court he enjoys clerical privilege. And consequently no one will be able to detain him without the bond of excommunication. Magist. These objections are regarded as trifling. To the first it is said that, since the Pope (if he becomes a heretic) is by that very fact stripped of all dignity and authority, both by divine right and by human law, and enjoys no privilege beyond other bishops who have become heretics; indeed it seems that, if there is no other Pope while the Pope is a heretic, no appeal can be made to a true Pope. But when the Pope remains Catholic and other bishops become heretics, an appeal can be made to the true Pope. In this special case something must be observed concerning a heretical Pope, namely that proceedings against him by inferior judges must be stricter and more rigorous than against bishops, when the Pope is Catholic. For in that case the others cannot have recourse to a true Pope.

units.la: Si vero Papa labente in haeresim manifestam electores alium Papam nouum elegerint catholicum, videtur eodem modo procedendum per iudices inferiores Papa circa Papam haereticum & circa alios episcopos haereticos labe respersos: nisi Papa haereticus maiori vteretur potentia temporali. Tunc enim animosius & efficacius esset procedendum contra ipsum. Quia vbi instat maius periculum, ibi est fortius & plenius consulendum. Ad secundam instantiam respondetur, quod licet Papa haereticus non careret omni priuilegio clericali, non propter hoc tamen iudex eius vel alius auctoritate iudicis detinens ipsum sententiam excommunicationis incurreret: quia licet iudici & aliis auctoritate eius violenter clericos detinere, extr. de sen. excommunicationis, vt fama.
units.tr: If, however, while the Pope has fallen into manifest heresy, the electors choose another new Pope who is Catholic, it seems that the same procedure should be followed through lower judges against the heretical Pope, and against other bishops stained by the taint of heresy—unless the heretical Pope were to use greater temporal power. For then it would have to be proceeded against more boldly and more effectively, since where the greater danger threatens, there the more vigorous and complete remedy must be applied. To the second objection it is answered that, although a heretical Pope would not lack every clerical privilege, nevertheless his judge, or another acting on the judge's authority, who detains him, does not thereby incur the sentence of excommunication: because, although it is forbidden to detain clerics violently by the authority of a judge or of others acting under him, see extr. de sent. excommunicationis, ut fama.

units.la: Discip. Illa decretalis non loquitur, nisi de laicis, qui auctoritate praelatorum possunt capere clericos violenter. Ergo saltem nullus laicus siue sit rex siue princeps, vel alius valet capere Papam haereticum absque sententia excommunicationis. Magist. Respondetur quod hoc generale est, quod omnis superior habens iurisdictionem coactiuam potest subditum detinere & capere absque sententia excommunicationis. Et ideo quia reputant se sufficienter probare, quod in casu laici habent iurisdictionem coactiuam super Papam haereticum: de qua probatione visum est libr. 6. ideo dicunt, quod in casu possunt laici etiam absque auctoritate clericorum violenter Papam haereticum detinere & in vinculis custodire. Cum vero dicis, quod decretalis allegata non loquitur, nisi de laicis, qui auctoritate superiorum possunt absque excommunicationis sententia clericos detinere, respondetur quod in illa decretali vnus solummodo casus excipitur, in quo licet laicis in clericos manus iniicere violentas. Cum quo stat, quod multi alii casus excipiantur. Et ita potest aliquis laicus in casu in Papam hæreticum absque excommunicationis causa vel sententia manus iniicere violentas.
units.tr: Disciple. That decretal speaks only of laymen, who by the authority of prelates may seize clerics violently. Therefore at least no layman, whether he be king or prince or anyone else, may seize a heretical Pope without a sentence of excommunication. Master. The answer is that this is a general rule: every superior who has coercive jurisdiction may detain and seize a subject without a sentence of excommunication. And since they think they have sufficiently proved that in this case laymen have coercive jurisdiction over a heretical Pope—a proof which it seemed right to set out in lib. 6, ideo—they say that in this case laymen may also, even without the authority of clerics, violently detain a heretical Pope and keep him in chains. As for your claim that the decretal cited speaks only of laymen who by the authority of superiors may detain clerics without a sentence of excommunication, the answer is that in that decretal only one case is excepted, in which laymen are permitted to lay violent hands on clerics; and this does not rule out that many other cases are excepted too. And so in such a case any layman may lay violent hands on a heretical Pope without any cause or sentence of excommunication.

units.la: Disc. Miror quod cum nulla lex loquitur de Papa hæretico, isti ita turpiter de punitione Papæ hæretici loqui præsumunt, cum vbi leges deficiunt, oportet ad conditorem legum recurrere. Aliter enim liceret cuilibet in tali casu, vbi leges deficiunt, ad sensum suum recurrere, & propriæ inniti prudentiæ, contra illud Prouerb. 3. ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ. Magist. Respondetur quod vbi est aliquid necessario agendum, si leges potissime deficiunt: quia in tali casu generali & singulari nulla lex specialis est edita: nec potest conuenienter absque periculo haberi recursus ad conditorem legum in scripturis diuinis ratione & industria naturali ac rationabili scientia præcellentem: recurrendum est ad peritos in prædictis & in legibus, si possunt haberi. Si autem iudex est omnibus prædictis instructus, ipse suo sensu vti potest in tali casu. Et ideo quia de Papa hæretico leges non sunt editæ speciales, quando Papa esset hereticus & ex perfidia eius periculum immineret: & non esset Papa catholicus, ad quem conuenienter posset haberi recursus: alii iudices inferiores scriptis diuinis & iuri naturali innitendo ipsum debite debent corrigere. Discip. Secundum ista magis esset innitendum in casu isto Theologis & in philosophia & scientia morali peritis quam Iuristis. Magist. Hoc nonnulli concedunt, sicut tactum est prius, quod vbicunq; emergit dubitatio inter Iuristas, quæ per aliquam legem expressam solui non potest, ad Theologos & Philosophos est vltimo recurrendum: ad quos spectat, si fuerint præcellentes, ( licet nullum gradum in theologia & philosophia habuerint ) de legibus quibuscunque profundius & certius (licet non promptius) iudicare, quam ad Iuristas, nisi Iuristæ in aliis scientiis fuerint excellentes.
units.tr: Disciple. I wonder that, although no law speaks of a heretical Pope, these men presume so shamefully to speak of punishing a heretical Pope, since where the laws fail, one must have recourse to the author of the laws. Otherwise anyone at all would be free in such a case, where the laws fail, to resort to his own opinion and rely on his own prudence, against the saying of Prov. 3, Do not lean on your own prudence. Master. The answer is that where something must necessarily be done, if the laws are wholly lacking—because in such a general and singular case no special law has been issued—and recourse cannot suitably be had, without danger, to the author of the laws, who in the divine Scriptures surpasses in reason, natural ingenuity and rational learning, then recourse must be had to those skilled in these matters and in the laws, if they can be found. If, however, the judge is instructed in all the aforesaid things, he may himself use his own judgement in such a case. And so, since no special laws have been enacted concerning a heretical Pope, when the Pope would be heretical and danger threatened from his perfidy, and there would be no Catholic Pope to whom recourse could suitably be had, the other lower judges ought to correct him duly, relying on the divine Scriptures and on the natural law. Disciple. In that case one should rely more on theologians and those skilled in philosophy and moral science than on jurists. Master. Some concede this, as was said before: that wherever a doubt arises among jurists which cannot be resolved by some express law, recourse must finally be had to theologians and philosophers, whose office it is, if they are outstanding (although they have held no degree in theology or philosophy), to judge of any laws more deeply and more certainly (though not more readily) than jurists can, unless the jurists are also excellent in other sciences.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Probat secundam & tertiam conclusiones positas capitulo precedenti: quæ etiam immediate in principio capituli ponuntur.
units.tr: It proves the second and third conclusions laid down in the preceding chapter, which are also stated at the very beginning of this chapter.

units.la: Discipulus. De hoc disputatum est libro primo. Ideo conuertas te ad conclusionem in principio cap. precedenti propositam. Magist. Secunda conclusio in proposito est hæc, loquendo de credulitate extra iudicium, secundum quod vnus socius credit alteri, nullus tenetur credere vni soli cuiuscunque famæ aut opinionis existat narranti Papam esse hæreticum. Hoc videtur posse sic probari. Nullus tenetur credere alium esse malum, antequam probetur. Ergo nullus tenetur credere Papam esse hæreticum, antequam probetur. Sed relatio vnius nihil probat. Ergo propter relationem vnius nullus tenetur credere Papam esse hæreticum. Discip. Istam conclusionem nolo discutiamplius, quia satis apparet mihi certa. Ideo tertiam conclusionem probare nitaris. Magist. Tertia conclusio est, quod vni soli bonæ famæ & opinionis asserenti Papam esse hæreticum potest quis credere absque peccato: licet sibi credere minime teneatur: quæ videtur sic posse probari. Si duo æqualis famæ & opinionis sibi contrariantur circa idem, licet alicui credere, cui vult illorum. Sed possibile est, quod Papa & aliquis alius apud eundem eiusdem famæ & opinionis, quo ad veritatem & bonitatem vitæ existunt. Ergo si vnus se gerit pro Papa catholico & alius dicit eum esse hæreticum, licet ei apud quem æqualis famæ & opinionis existunt credere, cui illorum voluerit. Et ita licet sibi credere asserenti Papam esse hæreticum. Item frustra alicuius peccatum alteri reuelatur, nisi liceat illi cui reuelatur credere reuelanti. Sed peccatum alicuius etiam occultum licite in secreto alteri qui potest prodesse & non obesse, reuelatur: imo nonnunquam reuelare debet. Ergo licet cui reuelatur credere reuelanti: & per consequens si aliquis etiam in secreto reuelet alii perfidiam Papæ hæretici licet credere reuelanti.
units.tr: Student. This was discussed in book one. So turn back to the conclusion set out at the beginning of the previous chapter. Master. The second conclusion in our present question is this: speaking of belief outside judgement, in the way one companion believes another, no one is bound to believe any single person, of whatever reputation or standing, who tells him that the Pope is a heretic. This seems to be provable as follows. No one is bound to believe that another is wicked before it is proved. Therefore no one is bound to believe that the Pope is a heretic before it is proved. But the report of one man proves nothing. Therefore, on the strength of one man's report, no one is bound to believe that the Pope is a heretic. Student. I do not wish to examine that conclusion further, since it seems certain to me. So try to prove the third conclusion. Master. The third conclusion is that a person may believe, without sin, a single man of good reputation and standing who asserts that the Pope is a heretic, although he is not at all bound to believe him. This seems provable as follows. If two men of equal reputation and standing contradict each other about the same matter, one may believe whichever of them he wishes. But it is possible that the Pope and someone else, equal in reputation and standing with the same people, both exist, as regards truth and the goodness of their lives. Therefore, if one man acts as a Catholic Pope and another says he is a heretic, and those among whom they have equal reputation and standing exist, one may believe whichever of them he wishes. And so it is lawful to believe the man who asserts that the Pope is a heretic. Likewise, a sin of someone is revealed to another in vain unless the one to whom it is revealed may believe the one who reveals it. But the hidden sin of someone may lawfully be revealed in secret to another who can benefit and not harm; indeed, sometimes he ought to reveal it. Therefore it is lawful for the one to whom it is revealed to believe the one who reveals it; and consequently, if anyone reveals to another, even in secret, the treachery of a heretical Pope, it is lawful to believe the one who reveals it.

units.la: Discip. Hæc ratio in vno falso fundari videtur, quod videlicet licet alicui reuelare peccatum alterius occultum. Quod tamen esse illicitum multis modis videtur posse probari. Primo quidem, quia proditionem facere nulli est licitum. Sed reuelare crimen occultum est proditionem facere, teste Augustin, qui, vt legitur 2. quæst. 1. cap. si peccauerit, ait: Quia enim secretum fuit, quando in te peccauit: secretum quoque sit quando tu corrigis, quia peccauit in te. Nam si solum nosti, quia peccauit in te, eum vt coram omnibus arguere, non eris corrector, sed proditor. Ergo non licet peccatum occultum alicuius alteri reuelare: quia sicut contigit aliquem prodere multis: ita conuenit prodere aliquem vni soli. Si igitur ille est proditor peccati occulti, qui multis reuelat: ita est proditor, qui vni soli reuelat. Item, quod fidelitati repugnat, nulli est licitum. Sed reuelare peccatum alicuius occultum, fidelitati repugnat, teste Salomone, qui Prou. 2. ait: Qui ambulat fraudulenter reuelat arcana. Qui autem fidelis est, celat amici commissum. Ergo non licet peccatum proximi alteri reuelare. Item, non solum est detractor, qui falsum dicit, sed etiam qui peccatum occultum reuelat. Sed non licet verba detractoria loqui. Ergo nulli licet crimen occultum alicuius alterius.
units.tr: Student. This argument seems to be founded on one falsehood, namely that it is lawful to reveal to someone another's hidden sin. That this is unlawful, however, seems provable in many ways. First, indeed, because it is lawful for no one to commit betrayal. But to reveal a hidden crime is to commit betrayal, as Augustine testifies, who, as we read in 2 Quaest. 1, chapter si peccaverit, says: For since it was a secret when he sinned against you, let it also be secret when you correct him, because he sinned against you. For if you know only that he sinned against you, to rebuke him before everyone is not to be a corrector but a traitor. Therefore it is not lawful to reveal another's hidden sin to someone else, because just as it is wrong to betray someone to many, so it is wrong to betray someone to one alone. So if he is a betrayer of a hidden sin who reveals it to many, then he is a betrayer who reveals it to one alone. Likewise, what is opposed to faithfulness is lawful for no one. But to reveal someone's hidden sin is opposed to faithfulness, as Solomon testifies, who says in Prov. 2: He who walks deceitfully reveals secrets; but he who is faithful conceals what has been entrusted by a friend. Therefore it is not lawful to reveal a neighbour's sin to another. Likewise, not only is he a slanderer who tells a falsehood, but also he who reveals a hidden sin. But it is not lawful to speak slanderous words. Therefore it is lawful for no one to reveal further any hidden crime of another. From this it is plainly inferred that it is lawful for no one to reveal to another the treachery of a heretical Pope, if it is hidden. For if anyone presumes to reveal the hidden treachery of a heretical Pope, he sins mortally; and the one to whom he reveals it in secret ought to regard him as sinning mortally. Wherefore he ought to hold him in his heart as a criminal. And consequently he ought not to believe him at all, because a criminal is never to be believed. These are the reasons which move me to hold that no one ought to believe one who asserts in secret that the Pope is a heretic. Moreover, since we ought to hear not only true assertions but also false ones (for through them our minds are stirred up, according to the saying of the Wise Man), I am therefore eager to allege arguments for the contrary assertion.

units.la: Marginal numerals 30–60 are section numbers, not printed text. ulterius reuelare. Ex quo patenter infertur, quod nulli licet perfidiam Papæ hereticI alteri reuelare, si est occulta. Quia si quis perfidiam Papæ hæretici occultam reuelare præsumit, peccat mortaliter, Et ille, cui reuelat secreto, debet ipsum reputare peccare mortaliter. Quare ipsum pro criminoso debet habere in corde suo. Et per consequens ipsi nullatenus credere debet. Quia criminoso nunquam est credendum. Hæc sunt, quæ mouent me ad tenendum, quod nullus debet credere asserenti secrete esse Papam hereticum. Porro quia non solum assertiones veras, sed etiam falsas debeam audire, Per ipsas enim nostra excitantur ingenia, iuxta sententiam Sapientis. Ideo pro assertione contraria satage allegare. Magist. Sunt quidam dicentes, quod licet non debeat quis passim crimen alicuius occultū alteri reuelare: tamen in casu, quando qs per certitudinem, non solum modo per famam scit aliquē aliquod crimen cōmisisse, vel etiā velle committere: licet sibi nō omnibus, sed alicui reuelare secrete. Et ideo si Papa perfidia hæresis est respersus, & incedit Christianos à fide auertere orthodoxā, licet vnus solet sciret, sibi liceret alicui principi aut regi vel alteri qui posset prodesse & non obesse crimen & intentione Papæ maleuolam reuelare. Quod enim licet crimen alicuius occultum alteri reuelare, Aug. videtur asserere, qui in Regula sua docet, quod peccatum fratris prius præposito debet ostendi, q; testibus. Ergo licet alteri crimen fratris occultum præposito reuelare. Item, verus Christianus Christum debet in suis operibus imitari. Sed Christus crimen & intentione puersam Iudæ occultam non solū vni, sed etiam pluribus reuelauit, cū dixit de ipso Mar.14. Vnus ex duodecim qui intingit mecum manum in catino me tradet. Et Iohan. 12. sic legitur Christus dixisse Apostolis: Amen amen dico vobis quod vnus ex vobis me tradet. Et sequitur: Ille est cui intinctum panem porrexero. Et tamen intinxit panem, & dedit Iudæ Simonis Scariotis. Igitur licet peccatum alterius occultum aliis reuelare. Discip. Per istam rationem probaretur, quod liceret non vni soli, sed etiam omnibus reuelare peccatum alicuius occultum. Quia Christus non vni solum, sed omnibus aliis Apostolis peccatum Iudæ reuelauit. Magist. Respondetur, quod peccatum alicuius occultum non solum vni, sed etiam multis reuelare licet: quia omnibus illis qui possunt prodesse & non obesse. Hinc est quod quia omnes Apostoli præter Iudam erant tales, quod poterant prodesse & non obesse. Ideo omnibus reuelauit peccatū Iudæ. Hanc rationem videtur innuere Gloss. 2. q. 1. ca. si peccauerit. Quæ super verbo promptior obiiciens ait: sed nunquid Dominus prodidit crimen Iudæ cum dixit: qui intingit mecum manum? &c. post respondens ait: respondetur; poterant prodesse. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod illis licet reuelare crimen alicuius occultum, qui possunt prodesse. Et ideo si multi sunt, qui prodesse possunt, multis crimen occultum licite reuelarur. Sed quia nonnunquam inuenitur, quod omnes possunt prodesse & non obesse: imo multi obessent: ideo omnibus nunquam debet reuelari crimen occultum, quod probari non potest. Quare cum magna cautela est crimen alicuius occultum alteri reuelandum. Quia nulli criminoso quantumcunq; sit prælatus, nulli de quo sciens peccatum occultum suspicatur, quod non sit constans in amore ad omnem proximum amicum & inimicum est pandendum peccatum occultum alterius. Quia de omni tali dubitandum est, an velit tantum prodesse & non obesse. Discip. Ergo secundum ista discipulus non tenetur reuelare peccatum occultum prælato suo in secreto. Magist. Conceditur quando sciens peccatum occultum alterius cognoscit prælatum suum aliquando peccasse mortaliter & etiam in secreto: vel dubitat eum nolle etiam pro morte vitanda peccare mortaliter. Si autem subditus in conscientia sua reputat prælatum suum esse talem, quod nec pro aliquo temporali commodo consequendo, nec pro morte corporali vitanda vellet peccare mortaliter: tunc crimen occultum fratris non posset prælato suo reuelare secrete, & omni alii, quem talem putat, si non decipitur, potest peccatum occultum reuelare: Quia talis est ille, qui potest prodesse & non obesse. Si autem alicui alteri crimen reuelat occultum, proditor & detractor est censendus: nec debet de peccato mortaliter aliter excusari, nisi probabiliter credat, quod reuelando bono tommuni aut peccatori proficiat.
units.tr: Master. Some say that although a man ought not to reveal anyone's hidden crime to another at random, nevertheless in a case where someone knows for certain, and not merely by report, that a certain person has committed some crime or even wishes to commit one, it is lawful for him to reveal it in secret, not to everyone but to one person. And so, if the Pope is tainted with the treachery of heresy and sets out to turn Christians away from the orthodox faith, then even if only one man knows it, it would be lawful for him to reveal the crime and the Pope's malevolent intention to some prince or king, or to another who could benefit and not harm. For Augustine seems to assert that it is lawful to reveal to another a hidden crime of someone, since in his Rule he teaches that a brother's sin ought to be shown first to the superior, and then to witnesses. Therefore it is lawful to reveal a brother's hidden crime to a superior. Likewise, a true Christian ought to imitate Christ in his works. But Christ revealed the hidden crime and wicked intention of Judas not only to one person but to several, when he said of him in Mark 14: One of the twelve, who dips with me in the dish, will betray me. And in John 12 Christ is thus read to have said to the Apostles: Verily, verily, I say to you that one of you will betray me. And it follows: He is the one to whom I shall give the bread after I have dipped it. And yet he dipped the bread and gave it to Judas Iscariot, son of Simon. Therefore it is lawful to reveal another's hidden sin to others. Student. By this argument it would be proved that it is lawful to reveal someone's hidden sin not only to one person but to everyone. For Christ revealed Judas's sin not only to one but to all the other Apostles. Master. The answer is that it is lawful to reveal someone's hidden sin not only to one but also to several, namely to all those who can benefit and not harm. Hence, because all the Apostles except Judas were such men, as could benefit and not harm, therefore he revealed Judas's sin to all of them. The Gloss on 2 Quaest. 1, chapter si peccaverit, seems to hint at this argument, which, objecting on the word promptior, says: But did the Lord betray Judas's crime when he said: "He who dips with me in the dish," etc.? and afterwards, answering, says: The answer is: they could benefit. From these words it is gathered that it is lawful to reveal someone's hidden crime to those who can benefit. And so, if there are many who can benefit, a hidden crime may lawfully be revealed to many. But since it is sometimes found that not all can benefit and not harm, indeed that many would harm, therefore a hidden crime which cannot be proved should never be revealed to all. Wherefore a hidden crime of someone is to be revealed to another with great caution. For the hidden sin of another is not to be disclosed to anyone, however much he may be set above others, and to no friend or enemy about whom one knowingly suspects a hidden sin, unless he is constant in love towards every neighbour. For concerning every such person one must doubt whether he wishes only to benefit and not harm. Student. Therefore, according to these things, a disciple is not bound to reveal a hidden sin in secret to his superior. Master. That is granted when one who knows another's hidden sin recognises that his superior has at some time sinned mortally, even in secret; or doubts that he would be unwilling to sin mortally even to avoid death. But if a subordinate in his conscience judges his superior to be such that he would be unwilling to sin mortally either to gain some temporal advantage or to avoid bodily death, then he could not reveal a brother's hidden crime to his superior in secret; and he can reveal a hidden sin to anyone else whom he thinks to be such, if he is not deceived, because such a man is one who can benefit and not harm. But if he reveals a hidden crime to any other person, he is to be considered a betrayer and a slanderer, and he ought not to be excused of mortal sin in any other way, unless he credibly believes that by revealing it he will benefit the common good or the sinner.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Vbi ponitur quarta conclusio supra c. 13. posita, & probatur 4. rationibus, scilicet, Quod pluribus honestis & discretis referentibus per scientiam certam Papam esse hereticum, tenetur aliquis credere extra iudicium, & nota ibidem de testibus adducendis.
units.tr: Where the fourth conclusion, set out above in chapter 13, is stated and proved by four reasons, namely, that when many honest and discreet people report, from certain knowledge, that the Pope is a heretic, one is bound to believe it outside a judicial process; and note there concerning the witnesses to be brought forward.

units.la: Discipulus. Puto, quod ista materia multas habet difficultates annexas, quæ succincte dilucidari non possunt. Ideo ipsam usque ad tractatum Degestu circa fidem altercantium orthodoxam (in quo de detractoribus, impositoribus falsorum criminum, calumniantibus & proximorum diffamatibus seu diffamatoribus in particulari sollicite indagabo) sentio differendam. Nunc vero ad quartam conclusionem assertionis cap. decim. tertio. recitatæ accede. Magist. Quarta conclusio ibi posita est, quod pluribus honestis & discretis referentibus per scientiam certam Papam esse hereticum tenetur aliquis credere extra iudicium. Quod videtur sic posse probari, In actibus humanis illud, quod habet maiorem probabilitatem, magis credendum est. Sed maiorem probabilitatem habet, quod dictum multorum sit verum, quam quod dictum unius. Cum ergo Papa sit unus, licet ipse negaret se esse haereticum, si multi asserrent ipsum esse haereticum, magis esset credendum multis, quam Papae haeretico. Et ita credendum est Papam haereticum esse. Disc. Ista ratio nihil probat. Quia nonnunquam plus credendum est uni, quam multis. Mag. Si hoc esset verum, rationem pfatam minime impediret. Nam si plus credetur uni quam pluribus, hoc non est praecipue propter maiorem dignitatem. Quia quilibet in dignitate constitutus plurium testimonio potest convinci. Quod non esset verum, si ex hoc ipso, q aliquis est in dignitate maiori constitutus, plus esset sibi soli credendum quam aliis multis. Ergo si est plus credendum uni quam multis: hoc est vel quia melioris rationem habet a se, vel quia melioris vitae, vel quia de causa est magis instructus, vel propter aliquam rationem consimilem. Si ergo Papa non est melioris vitae, quam multi, q dicunt eum esse haereticum, nec magis literatus in scripturis Diuinis, nec in aliquo alio excellit: nisi in sola dignitate Papali & annexis dignitati: non est magis sibi credendum quam multis. Igitur si multi asserunt, quod Papa est haereticus, est eis credendum. Item, non minus est credendum aliquibus extra iudicium, quam in iudicio. Sed multis in iudicio asserentibus Papam esse haereticum esset credendum. Aliter enim Papa nunquam posset convinci de haeretica pravitate. Ergo multis asserentibus extra iudicium Papam esse haereticum, est credendum. Disc. Ista ratio videtur peccare dupliciter. Primo, quia testes in iudicio sunt iurati. Extra vero iudicium non iurant. Magis autem credendum est iuratis, quam non iuratis. Ergo magis credendum est multis in iudicio, q extra iudicium. Secundo, ad condemnandum Papam non sufficeret duos testes adducere: cum praesul non debeat condemnari nisi cum 72. testibus 2. q. 5. praesul. Ergo nec duobus asserentibus extra iudicium Papam esse haereticum, est credendum. Mag. Non habes mentem asserentium conclusionem supra scriptam. Non enim intendunt, quod quilibet audiens aliquos asserentes Papam esse haereticum, statim fidem eis debeat adhibere. Sed volunt quod huiusmodi asserentes Papam esse haereticum: antequam credatur eis, sunt cum maxima diligentia examinandi: utrum scilicet sint parati iurare illa, quae asserunt de Papa esse vera: vel utrum possunt ea apertis ostendere documentis, pro qua haeresi dicunt Papam esse haereticum: quomodo sciunt Papam huiusmodi haeresim affirmare: quomodo sciunt eum esse in sua haeresi pertinacem. Et tandem videtur expediens, quod talibus asserentibus Papam esse haereticum, antequam credatur eis, examinentur extra iudicium, & exigant iuramentum quod circa ipsum Papa haereticum manifestam dicant veritatem, ut forte non minus tales asserentes Papam esse haereticum, antequam credatur eis examinentur extra iudicium, quam essent examinandi in iudicio. Quamvis ad iurandum & alia facienda non debeant compelli extra iudicium, sicut in iudicio compelli valerent. Quibus rite factis credendum est eis extra iudicium, sicut in iudicio creditur. Licet credulitas in iudicio aliquem alium effectum possit & debeat habere, quam credulitas sola extra iudicium. Haec maxime seruanda sunt circa extraneos ignotos, circa quos est sollicite inquirendum, cuius vitae & opinionis extiterint. An etiam pro alia causa quam pro causa fidei habuerint occasionem male volendi Papae. Per hoc respondetur ad primam instantiam, quam fecisti: quia ab asserentibus extra iudicium Papam esse haereticum, videtur ad maiorem cautelam debere exigi iuramentum. Ad secundam videtur respondere Glossa super praeallegatum c. praesul. quae quaerens ibidem: Nunquid contra Papam duplicantur testes? Et infra respondetur dicens: non, imo duo sufficiunt, & in hoc est deterior conditio, quia ipse sine comparatione alium creatus est: & ideo sine spe veniae damnandus est, ut Diabolus. Dicunt tamen quod si duo tantum testes apparent Papam de haeretica pravitate accusantes, examinandi essent multum stricte, propter hoc quod Papa, qui est positus quasi signum ad sagittam, habet multos offendere. Et sic etiam dicunt, quod si quis audit duos viros sibi notos, bonos, sanctos & veraces, qui necamore nec odio alicuius, nec timore nec cupiditate vellent alicui crimen imponere; asserentes se scire Papam haeresim manifestam & determinatam pertinaciter tenuisse, declarantes modum haeresis & pertinaciae, debet credere eis & reputare Papam esse haereticum. Disc. Quare dicunt isti, quod asserentes Papam esse haereticum, examinandi sunt, an ea quae dicunt de Papa possunt aperte ostendere documentis? Magist. Hoc dicunt propter hoc, quod asserunt dupliciter posse aliquos perfidiam Papae haereticiI declarare. Vno modo per testimonium proprium, si videlicet affirmant se audisse Papam asserentem pertinaciter haeresim determinatam & apertam; vel etiam docentem haeresim contrariam veritati catholicae, quam credere tenetur explicite. Puta si dicunt se audiuisse Papam asserere, quod fides Christiana est falsa: vel quod Christus non est verus Deus. Vel quod Christus non fuit passus: vel aliquid huiusmodi. Vel etiam si affirmant se audiisse Papam pertinaciter asserere vel defendere quantamcunque haeresim scripturae sanctae aduersantem. Aliter possunt aliqui perfidiam Papae haereticI declarare per testimonium proprium, seu per legitima documenta: puta si ostenderent Bullam Papae in qua diffiniretur haeresis manifeste: vel si ostenderet copiam Bullae per regiones fidelium publicatam: etiam si ostenderent instrumentum vel scripturam authenticam modum quo Papa fuerit convictus de pravitate haeretica continentem. Disc. Si habes alias rationes ad conclusionem praedictam adducas. Magist. Adhuc tertia ratio est haec: Ad illa quae innocentiae sunt, quilibet obligatur. Sed credere vitiis bonae famae & opinionis, cum aliqua asserunt & affirmant, ad innocentiam spectat, teste Ambrosio, qui, ut habetur 22. q. 4. c. innocens, ait: innocens credit omni verbo. Non vituperanda facilitas, sed laudanda bonitas. Cum ergo viri boni & veraces asserunt & affirmant modo praedicto Papam esse haereticum, eis audiens fidem adhibere tenetur. Quarta ratio est haec: Illud non est omittentendum, sine quo societas humana & conuersatio mutua hominum rite non posset conseruari. Sed nisi vnus alteri credat, nec humana societas, nec mutua conuersatio hominum rite potest conseruari. Igitur tenetur vnus alteri credere: nisi sit aliquo crimine irretitus, propter quod de falsitate debeat haberi suspectus. Cum autem credendum est in vno, & in omnibus: quia si aliquibus in vno credendum est, hoc non est, nisi quia praesumerentur veraces. Si enim non praesumerentur veraces, non esset eis credendum. Qui autem praesumitur verax, in omnibus dictis suis praesumitur verax. Ergo veracibus asserentibus Papam esse haereticum est credendum. Disc. Per istam rationem probaretur, quod vni soli asserenti modo praeexposito Papam esse haereticum esset credendum. Quia praesumitur verax. Ergo in omnibus est sibi credendum. Magist. Respondetur quod secus est de vno & de pluribus. Quia plus est credendum pluribus quam vni. Et ideo propter assertionem multorum potest quis credere licite malum de alio quem plures asserunt esse malum. Sed quando vnus profert malum de aliquo, propter talem relationem non est magis praesumendum de illo, de quo malum narratur, eum esse malum, quam illum esse veracem, qui narrat. Et ideo nullus tenetur credere vni soli referenti Papam esse haereticum. Disc. Non adducas plures rationes pro ista assertione seu conclusione: sed dic quem effectum debet habere ista credulitas. Magist. Respondetur distinguendo: quia aut illa credulitas fit iudici Papae haeretici, aut alii qui non est iudex eius. Si fit iudici Papae haeretici, & qui faciunt talem credulitatem iudici sunt parati in iudicio eadem asserere, iudex ad condemnationem Papae haeretici debet procedere. Si autem ista credulitas fit alii quam iudici, & sit talis credulitas quod Papa potest convinci legitime: illi, qui taliter credunt Papam esse haereticum, ipsum tanquam excommunicatum vitare tenentur. Et ideo ei nullatenus obedire debent: sed pro defensione fidei in quantum possunt modis sibi convenientibus laborare tenentur: ne videlicet Papa haereticus inficere valeat orthodoxos.
units.tr: Student. I think this subject has many difficulties attached to it, which cannot be cleared up briefly. So I judge that it should be postponed until the treatise Degestum on the Faith of Orthodox Disputants, in which I shall carefully inquire into detractors, fabricators of false charges, slanderers and defamers of neighbours in particular. For now, let us come to the fourth conclusion of the assertion recited in chapter thirteen. Master. The fourth conclusion posited there is that, when many honest and discreet people report from certain knowledge that the Pope is a heretic, one is bound to believe it outside a judicial process. This can seemingly be proved as follows: in human acts, that which has greater probability is to be believed more. But it is more probable that what many say is true than what one says. Therefore, since the Pope is one man, even if he himself denied being a heretic, if many affirmed that he is a heretic, they would be more to be believed than the heretical Pope. And so it must be believed that the Pope is a heretic. Student. That argument proves nothing, because sometimes one is to be believed more than many. Master. If that were true, it would not in the least hinder the argument stated. For if one is believed more than many, this is not chiefly because of greater dignity. Since anyone placed in a dignity can be convicted by the testimony of many. That would not be true if, by the very fact that someone has been placed in a greater dignity, he alone were to be believed more than many others. Therefore, if one is to be believed more than many, this is either because he has a better reputation in himself, or because of a better life, or because he is better informed about the matter, or for some similar reason. If, then, the Pope is not of a better life than the many who say he is a heretic, nor more learned in Holy Scripture, nor excels in anything else, except in papal dignity and what is attached to that dignity, then he is not to be believed more than many. Therefore, if many assert that the Pope is a heretic, they are to be believed. Likewise, one is no less to be believed outside a judicial process than within one. But if many in a judicial process asserted that the Pope is a heretic, they would be believed. Otherwise the Pope could never be convicted of heretical depravity. Therefore, when many assert outside a judicial process that the Pope is a heretic, they are to be believed. Student. This argument seems to err in two ways. First, because witnesses in a judicial process are sworn, whereas outside it they do not swear. But sworn witnesses are to be believed more than unsworn ones. Therefore many in a judicial process are to be believed more than those outside it. Second, to condemn the Pope it would not suffice to bring forward two witnesses, since a prelate ought not to be condemned except with seventy-two witnesses, 2. q. 5, praesul. Therefore not even two asserting outside a judicial process that the Pope is a heretic are to be believed. Master. You do not grasp the intention of those who assert the conclusion written above. For they do not mean that anyone who hears some asserting the Pope to be a heretic must straightway give them credence. Rather they hold that such assertors, before they are believed, must be examined with the greatest diligence: whether, namely, they are ready to swear to what they assert about the Pope as true; or whether they can show by plain documents for what heresy they say the Pope is a heretic; how they know that the Pope affirms a heresy of this kind; how they know that he is obstinate in his heresy. And finally it seems expedient that, before such assertors that the Pope is a heretic are believed, they should be examined outside a judicial process, and should be required to swear that they speak the manifest truth about the Pope as a heretic; so that perhaps such assertors are not examined any less outside a judicial process than they would be examined in one. Although, for swearing and doing other things, they ought not to be compelled outside a judicial process as they could be compelled within one. When these things have been duly done, they are to be believed outside a judicial process just as they are believed within one. Although belief within a judicial process can and should have another effect than belief alone outside it. These things are above all to be observed concerning unknown foreigners, about whom careful inquiry must be made as to what their life and reputation have been, and whether they had some occasion, for a cause other than the cause of faith, to wish ill to the Pope. By this I answer your first objection: since, in the case of those asserting outside a judicial process that the Pope is a heretic, an oath seems to be required as a greater safeguard. To the second, the Gloss on the aforementioned chapter praesul seems to reply, which asks there: Are two witnesses doubled against the Pope? And further on it answers, saying: No; indeed two suffice, and in this his condition is worse, because he was created without comparison with any other, and therefore he is to be condemned without hope of pardon, like the Devil. Yet they say that if only two witnesses appear accusing the Pope of heretical depravity, they would have to be examined very strictly, because the Pope, who is placed as it were as a mark for the arrow, has many who would be offended by him. And so they also say that if anyone hears two men known to him, good, holy and truthful, who out of neither love nor hatred of anyone, nor out of fear or greed, would wish to impute a crime to anyone; asserting that they know the Pope to have obstinately held a manifest and determined heresy, declaring the manner of the heresy and the obstinacy, he ought to believe them and to hold the Pope to be a heretic. Student. Why do these men say that those asserting the Pope to be a heretic must be examined as to whether what they say about the Pope can be plainly shown by documents? Master. They say this because they assert that there are two ways in which one can declare the perfidy of a heretical Pope. In one way, through one's own testimony, if namely they affirm that they heard the Pope obstinately asserting a determined and manifest heresy; or even teaching a heresy contrary to the Catholic truth, which one is bound to believe explicitly. Suppose they say they heard the Pope assert that the Christian faith is false, or that Christ is not true God, or that Christ did not suffer, or something of that kind. Or even if they affirm that they heard the Pope obstinately assert or defend any heresy whatever that opposes Holy Scripture. Otherwise some can declare the perfidy of a heretical Pope through another's testimony, or through lawful documents: for example, if they showed a papal bull in which a heresy was plainly defined; or if they showed a copy of the bull published throughout the regions of the faithful; or even if they showed an instrument or an authentic writing containing the manner in which the Pope was convicted of heretical depravity. Student. If you have other reasons for the aforesaid conclusion, bring them forward. Master. A third reason is this: everyone is bound to those things which concern innocence. But to believe those who assert and affirm, with good report and opinion, certain things, pertains to innocence, as Ambrose witnesses, who, as is found at 22. q. 4. c. innocens, says: The innocent man believes every word. It is not a fault to be easy-going, but a virtue to be kind. Therefore, when good and truthful men assert and affirm in the aforesaid manner that the Pope is a heretic, the hearer is bound to give them credence. The fourth reason is this: that must not be omitted without which human society and mutual intercourse among men cannot properly be preserved. But unless one believes another, neither human society nor mutual intercourse among men can properly be preserved. Therefore one is bound to believe another, unless he is entangled in some crime on account of which he should be held suspect of falsehood. Since, however, one is to be believed in one matter, one is to be believed in all: for if one is to be believed in one matter, this is only because they would be presumed truthful. For if they were not presumed truthful, they would not be believed. But he who is presumed truthful is presumed truthful in all his statements. Therefore, when truthful men assert that the Pope is a heretic, they are to be believed. Student. By this argument it would be proved that even a single person asserting the Pope to be a heretic in the manner just set out would be believed, since he is presumed truthful, and therefore is to be believed in all he says. Master. It is answered that the case of one and of many is otherwise. For more is to be believed to many than to one. And therefore on account of the assertion of many one may lawfully believe evil of another whom many assert to be evil. But when one man brings forward evil about someone, on the strength of such a report one should not presume more that the person of whom the evil is told is evil than that the one who tells it is truthful. And therefore no one is bound to believe one man alone who reports that the Pope is a heretic. Student. You are not to adduce several reasons for this assertion or conclusion; instead, say what effect this belief ought to have. Master. The answer is made by distinction: for that belief is either given to the judge of the heretical Pope, or to someone else who is not his judge. If it is given to the judge of the heretical Pope, and those who give such belief to the judge are ready to assert the same things in a judicial process, the judge ought to proceed to the condemnation of the heretical Pope. But if this belief is given to someone other than a judge, and it is such a belief that the Pope can be lawfully convicted, those who believe in this way that the Pope is a heretic are bound to avoid him as excommunicated. And therefore they must by no means obey him; but for the defence of the faith they are bound to labour, by whatever means are suitable to them so far as they can, lest the heretical Pope should be able to infect the orthodox.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Probat quintam conclusionem, c. 13. huius positam, scilicet quod viris prouidis & honestis referentibus per famam honestam Papam esse haereticum, est credendum.
units.tr: He proves the fifth conclusion, stated above in chapter 13, namely that when prudent and honest men report, on the strength of an honest reputation, that the Pope is a heretic, they are to be believed.

units.la: Disciplus. Conclusionem quintam supra c. 13. praemissam discutias. Magist. Quinta conclusio est haec. Viris prouidis & honestis referentibus per famam honestam Papam esse haereticum, est credendum. Quae sic probatur. Illis est credendum Papam esse haereticum, propter quorum relationem Papa tanquam haereticus est vitandus, extra, de sententia excommunicationis, cum desideres. Papa autem haereticus est excommunicatus. Ergo propter solam famam publicam est vitandus. Et per consequens videtur quod referentibus Papam esse haereticum per publicam famam est credendum. Disc. De hoc tactum est libro sexto c. 6. vbi recitasti virtualiter opinionem eandem, quae videtur mihi falsa. Nam quia constat quod saepe publica fama est falsa, & saepe ita diffamantur de crimine innocentes sicut nocentes, nullo modo videtur quod propter relationem publicae famae debeat Papa haereticus censeri.
