Quia ita potest diffamari Papa catholicus, sicut haereticus. Magist. Licet argumentum tuum non videatur habere colorem: tamen conclusio supradicta clarius, quam prius, ab aliquibus explicatur. Disc. Dic primo, quomodo argumentum meum non videatur habere colorem. Magist. Dicitur quod non obstante, quod ita diffamentur innocentes sicut nocentes, est tamen aliquis propter famam publicam euitandus, quemadmodum non obstante quod ita conuincuntur saepe innocentes per testes, qui veraces credantur sicut rei: tamen priusquam aliquis conuictus & damnatus fuit, siue innocens fuit siue reus, sententia est seruanda. Et si est sententia, quae sequestratione a fidelium coetu includat, est vitandus. Disc. De hac responsione in alio tractatu faciam mentionem. Ideo dic, quomodo praedicta conclusio explicatur. Magist. Distinguitur de referentibus per famam publicam, Papam esse haereticum. Quia aut narrant famam publicam, quam sciunt a quibus orta fuit: aut quam nesciunt a quibus orta fuit, nec an aliae aliquae personae possunt veritatem famae probare. In primo casu videtur quod propter talem narrationem sit Papa haereticus ab audientibus euitandus. In secundo casu non videtur quod debet euitari.
units.tr: Student. Let us examine the fifth conclusion laid down above in chapter 13. Master. The fifth conclusion is this: when prudent and honest men report, on the strength of an honest reputation, that the Pope is a heretic, they are to be believed. It is proved as follows. Those are to be believed that the Pope is a heretic on whose report the Pope is to be avoided as a heretic (Extra, On the Sentence of Excommunication, Cum desideres). But the Pope, being a heretic, is excommunicated. Therefore he is to be avoided on public report alone. And consequently it seems that those who report that the Pope is a heretic on public report are to be believed. Student. This was touched on in book six, chapter 6, where you virtually recited the same opinion, which seems to me false. For since it is certain that public report is often false, and innocent men are often defamed of crime just as the guilty are, it seems in no way that the Pope should be judged a heretic on the report of public rumour. For a Catholic Pope can be defamed just as a heretic can. Master. Although your argument does not seem to have any plausibility, the aforesaid conclusion is explained more clearly by some than before. Student. Tell me first how my argument can be said to lack plausibility. Master. It is said that, notwithstanding that innocent men are defamed just as the guilty are, still someone is to be avoided on account of public report, just as, notwithstanding that innocent men are often convicted by witnesses who are believed to be truthful just as the accused are, nevertheless, before anyone has been convicted and condemned, whether innocent or guilty, the sentence must be observed; and if it is a sentence which excludes a person from the assembly of the faithful, he is to be avoided. Student. I shall make mention of this response in another treatise. So tell me how the aforesaid conclusion is explained. Master. A distinction is drawn concerning those who report, on public rumour, that the Pope is a heretic. For either they relate a public rumour whose origin they know, or a rumour whose origin they do not know, nor whether any other persons are able to prove the truth of the rumour. In the first case it seems that, on account of such a report, the Pope is to be avoided as a heretic by those who hear it. In the second case it does not seem that he ought to be avoided.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Probat conclusionem sextam supra c. 13. positam, scilicet quod quibuscunque criminosis adducentibus legitima documenta, vel indicia manifesta, quod Papa est haereticus, est credendum, & quomodo & qualiter, exponitur ibidem. Et etiam notatur distinctio inter legitima documenta & indicia manifesta. De legitimis documentis tractatur in 15. c. & 18. de indiciis manifestis c. 20.
units.tr: He proves the sixth conclusion laid down above in chapter 13, namely that whoever is a criminal bringing forward legitimate documents or manifest indications that the Pope is a heretic is to be believed; how and in what manner this is to be understood is explained there. There is also a note on the distinction between legitimate documents and manifest indications. Legitimate documents are treated in chapter 15 and chapter 18; manifest indications in chapter 20.

units.la: Disciplus. Illa conclusione dimissa, de qua te alias diligenter interrogabo seu interrogare intendo, dissere conclusionem sextam supra cap. decimo tertio recitatam. Magist. Conclusio sexta est, quod quibuscunque criminosis adducentibus legitima documenta vel indicia manifesta, quod Papa est haereticus, est credendum. Non quidem quod propter assertionem criminosorum, sed propter ipsa documenta legitima & indicia manifesta credatur Papa esse haereticus. Discip. Quae sunt illa documenta legitima & indicia manifesta, propter quae credendum est Papam esse haereticum? Magist. De hoc tactum est supra c. 15. vbi dictum est, quomodo possunt aliqui perfidiam Papae haeretici declarare per legitima documenta. Disc. Si illis aliquid est addendum secundum taliter opinantes, non differas explanare. Magist. Inter legitima documenta & indicia manifesta distinguunt. Nam legitima documenta vocant scripturas perfidiam Papae haeretici absq; pallio comprobantes. Indicia manifesta vocant suspiciones seu praesumptiones, probabiliter perfidiam Papae haeretici comprobantes. Discip. Pone exempla de praedictis. Magist. De legitimis documentis supra c. 15. posita sunt exempla. Quorum primum est de Bulla Papae haeretici, in qua aliquis error contra doctrinam Ecclesiae affirmatur. Secundum est de copia Bullae eius. Tertium est de aliquo instrumento vel scriptura autentica modum, quo fuit Papa haereticus coniectus de haeresi, continente. Et quartum potest esse vel scriptura autentica alicuius praelati vel principis transumptum Bullae, vel illius particulae in qua error haereticalis asseritur, continens. Discip. Antequam exemplifices de indiciis manifestis, peto vt tractes duo exempla prima de legitimis documentis: & primo primum. Magist. Quod propter talem Bullam Papae haeresim asserentem sit credendum Papam esse haereticum, sic videtur posse probari. Quia quod non esset credendum Papam esse haereticum propter huiusmodi Bullam, aut hoc est quia Papa posset sub Bulla haeresim asserere absq; haeretica prauitate: aut quia taliter Bullae fides minime esset adhibenda. Non propter primum, quia supra lib. 4. vides probatum aperte, quod Papa sub Bulla asserens haeresim est pertinax. Et per consequens haereticus reputandus: quia non est paratus corrigi, & vltimata deliberatione haeresim diffinuit. Nec propter secundum: quia Bullae Papali fides debet adhiberi. Discip. Videtur quod isti sint sibiipsis contrarii. Nam asserere videntur, quod Papae haeretico in nullo negotio est credendum. Ergo nec Bullae suae fides debet aliqualiter adhiberi. Et ita Papa propter suam Bullam minime est haereticus reputandus. Discip. Dicunt quod ipsos nequaquam intelligis. Cum enim dicunt, quod Papae haeretico nullo modo est credendum, intelligendum est pro se vel contra alium. Ei tamen sicut cuilibet criminoso credendum est contra se. Vnde si criminosus confiteatur factum suum, creditur sibi, quia aliter propter confessionem propriam minime damnaretur. Si tamen criminosus confiteatur vel asserat crimen alterius, sibi nullatenus est credendum. Similiter dicunt, quod diffinitioni haereticali Papae haeretici bene credendum est contra Papam, vt propter eam haereticus iudicetur: sed Bullae huiusmodi in aliis non est credendum. Si enim in eadem Bulla vel alia Papae haeretici aliquid asseratur contra fidem, vel etiam in praeiudicium cuiuscunq; catholici, sibi nullatenus est credendum: quia nullo negotio supra alium Papae haeretico est credendum.
units.tr: Disciple. Setting aside that question, about which I shall or intend to question you carefully at another time, explain the sixth conclusion recited above in chapter thirteen. Master. The sixth conclusion is that whoever is a criminal bringing forward legitimate documents or manifest indications that the Pope is a heretic is to be believed. Not indeed that the Pope is believed to be a heretic on the strength of the criminals' assertion, but on the strength of the legitimate documents and manifest indications themselves. Disciple. What are those legitimate documents and manifest indications on account of which we must believe the Pope to be a heretic? Master. This was touched on above in chapter 15, where it was said how some can declare the Pope's heretical perfidy by legitimate documents. Disciple. If anything must be added to these for those who think in this way, do not delay in explaining it. Master. They distinguish between legitimate documents and manifest indications. For they call legitimate documents writings that prove the Pope's heretical perfidy without a cloak. They call manifest indications suspicions or presumptions that prove the Pope's heretical perfidy with probability. Disciple. Give examples of the aforesaid. Master. Examples of legitimate documents were given above in chapter 15. The first of these concerns a Bull of a heretical Pope in which some error against the doctrine of the Church is affirmed. The second concerns a copy of his Bull. The third concerns some authentic instrument or writing containing the manner in which the Pope was convicted of heresy. And the fourth may be an authentic writing of some prelate or prince containing a transcript of the Bull, or of that part of it in which the heretical error is asserted. Disciple. Before you give examples of manifest indications, I ask you to treat the first two examples of legitimate documents, and first the first. Master. That on account of such a Bull asserting heresy the Pope must be believed to be a heretic can be proved thus. Because whatever would make us not believe the Pope to be a heretic on account of such a Bull is either that the Pope could assert heresy in a Bull without heretical depravity, or that faith should in no way be given to the Bull in such a case. Not the first, because above in book 4 you clearly see it proved that a Pope asserting heresy under a Bull is obstinate, and consequently is to be regarded as a heretic, because he is not ready to be corrected and, by his final deliberate decision, defines heresy. Nor the second, because faith must be given to a papal Bull. Disciple. These people seem to be contrary to themselves. For they seem to assert that nothing in any business is to be believed of a heretical Pope. Therefore faith should not in any way be given to his Bull either, and so the Pope should not be regarded as a heretic on account of his Bull. Disciple. They say that you by no means understand them. For when they say that in no way is a heretical Pope to be believed, it must be understood as said in his own favour or against another. Yet as to himself, he is to be believed against himself, as any criminal is. Hence if a criminal confesses his own deed, he is believed, since otherwise he would by no means be condemned on his own confession. If, however, a criminal confesses or asserts the crime of another, he is by no means to be believed. Similarly they say that the heretical definition of a heretical Pope is rightly to be believed against the Pope, so that on account of it he may be judged a heretic; but Bulls of this kind are not to be believed in other matters. For if in the same Bull, or in another Bull of a heretical Pope, something is asserted against the faith, or even to the prejudice of any Catholic, he is by no means to be believed in that, since a heretical Pope is in no business to be believed over another.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: In quo ponitur secundum documentum legitimum, scilicet de copia Bullae Papae haeretici, in qua haeresis affirmatur. Vbi etiam ponuntur duae conclusiones, prima scilicet, quod de constitutione haereticali Papae solenniter & publice promulgata nullus tenetur se per ignorantiam excusare. Vbi notantur sex casus, in quibus ignorantia non excusat. Secunda vero conclusio probatur c. 19.
units.tr: This chapter sets out the second legitimate piece of evidence, namely a copy of a bull of a heretical Pope in which heresy is asserted. It also lays down two conclusions. The first is that no one is excused by ignorance of a heretical constitution of the Pope that has been solemnly and publicly promulgated. Six cases in which ignorance does not excuse are noted. The second conclusion is proved in chapter 19.

units.la: Discipulus. Dicas secundum exemplum de copia Bullae Papae haeretici, in qua haeresis affirmatur: quod propter talem copiam siue transumptum Papa debeat haereticus iudicari. Magist. Hoc videtur posse probari sic. In omnibus credendum est copiae siue transumpto Bullae Papae catholici. Ergo credendum est copiae siue transumpto Bullae Papae haeretici, in his quae sunt contra ipsum. Antecedens videtur probatione minime indigere. Consequentia probatur propter hoc, quod tantum valet copia siue transumptum Bullae Papae catholici (quantum ad omnia quae continet) quantum valet ipsa Bulla haeretici Papae contra se. Sed ipsa Bulla Papae catholici valet quantum ad omnia quae continet & includit. Ergo sicut in omnibus credendum est Bullae Papae catholici, ita quantum ad illa quae sunt contra Papam haereticum credendum est Bullae Papae haeretici. Discip. Videtur quod nec transumptum Bullae Papae catholici, nec transumptum Bullae Papae haeretici à criminosis vel infamibus diuulgatum fidem facere debeat cuicunque: quia sicut vita criminosorum debet esse suspecta, ita etiam tales transumptiones statutorum vel ostensiones transumptorum Papalium debent esse suspectae, vt nullus talibus ostensionibus statutorum Papalium fidem debeat adhibere. Quia non debet quis propter criminosos credere illa esse vera transumpta. Magist. Ad hoc respondetur distinguendo de diffinitionibus Papae siue haeretici, siue catholici: quia aut sunt publice & solenniter promulgatae, aut non. De primis dicitur, quod ignorantia talium non excusat post duos menses. De secundis dicitur: quod de eis potest per ignorantiam excusari. Et per hoc dicitur ad argumentum, quod fecisti concedendo quod propter criminosos siue ostensionem transumptorum Papalium à criminosis factam, nullus teneatur credere vnquam. voquâm Papam esse haereticum. Tamen propter huiusmodi ostensionem transumptorum Papalium continentium prauitatem haereticam a criminosis factam, si aliquis in rei veritate ignorat Papam talem definitionem dedisse, debet inquirere veritatem. Discip. Hic deberent isti duo probare. Quorum primum est, quod de constitutione haereticali Papae publice & solenniter promulgata nullus tenetur se per ignorantiam excusare. Secundum est, quod propter verba criminosorum ignorantes talem constitutionem haereticalem Papae deberent quaerere veritatem. Unde de istis duobus velis differere: & non solum referas circa ipsa sententiam praedictorum, sed etiam aliorum: Magist. Circa primum sunt diuersae sententiae. Una est, quod nullus de constitutione haereticali Papae post duos menses potest per ignorantiam se excusare. Nec potest in hoc casu ignorantiam allegare. Si allegat non est sibi credendum, nisi ignorantiam probauerit: quemadmodum nullus potest ignorantiam allegare de constitutione Papae catholici post duos menses: quia eam omnes scire tenentur, & omnes ad eius obseruantiam obligantur. Et ista videtur sententia fuisse Glossatorum decretalium & decretorum. Unde de sententia publice promulgata cardinalium infra legationem suam, de qua minus videtur, dicit Gloss. extra, de postulationibus, ca. prim. Cum publice sententia illa fuerit publicata, eam ignorare non potest nec debet: & praesumitur eam scire 13. q 2. qui & humanis. 16. dist. quod dicitur. Et infra: vbi enim allegatur ignorantia circa ea quae plurimi sciunt & publice sunt, non creditur nisi hoc fieri probet. Item, Gloss. extra, de constitutionibus. c. cognoscentes, loquens de constitutione Papae ait: ex quo publice publicata est, tenetur ad ipsius obseruantiam. Et omnes obligat post duos menses à tempore publicationis elapsos. Item, Gloss. 19. dist. ca. vltim. ait: nulli licet ignorare ea, quae publice facta sunt. Item, Gloss. 8. quaest. prim. cap. licet, ait: In his quae publice facta sunt, non potest contradici. Item, Gloss. dist. 54. vbi, ait: vbi aliqua sunt publice facta, nemo auditur contradicitor. Ex quibus aliisque quamplurimis colligitur (vt habetur) quod non tolum non auditur, qui allegat se ignorare constitutionem Papae publice promulgatam, sed etiam qui allegat se ignorare alia quaecunque, quae tamen publice facta sunt. Quia quamuis dicat se nescire Papam edidisse constitutionem, in qua assertio quae est haeretica definitur, non est sibi credendum: quia ex quo talis constitutio haereticalis est publice promulgata, quilibet praesumitur scire ipsam, Discip. In quo fundant se Glossae praedictae. Magist. In legibus ciuilibus & canonicis quamplurimus se fundant: de quibus suffi-ciat adducere Epistolam Innocentii tertii ad Decanum & Capitulum Senonense, quae ponitur extra de postulationibus, cap. prim. in qua ponens allegationes procurationi Episcopi Altisiodorensis, volentis eundem Episcopum per ignorantiam excusare, & eam excludens sic ait: Quoniam antequam idem Magister ad Sedem Apostolicam accessisset (nobis quasi pro certo constabat) quod Episcopus interdicti sententiam non seruasset: quod & idem Magister non negauit in fratrum nostrorum praesentia requisitus à nobis in ipsius Episcopi excusationibus allegans, quod sententiam latam nullatenus contra nos ser-uare tenebatur, quod ad eius notitiam nec per cardinalem tunc Apostolicae Sedis legatum, qui eandem sententiam promulgauit, nec per deputati ad hoc executoris mandatum vel literas peruenisset. Et infra: quod nec sufficit, imo nec proficit ad excusationem praedicti Episcopi, cum cardinalis idem sententiam interdicti prae-sentibus multis solenniter ac publice promulgauit, & eadem interdicti sententia in regno Franciae iam à multis publice coeperit obseruari: nec sit necessarium, cum constitutio solenniter editur ac publice promulgatur, ipsius notitiam singulorum auribus per speciale mandatum vel literas inculcare: sed illud solum sufficit, vt ad eius obseruantiam teneantur, qui nouerint eam solenniter editam ac publice promulgatam, & effet con-tra quosdam, qui Sardicense concilium non seruabant, tanquam illud non habuerunt aut perceperunt canoni-ca auctoritate, in quo eis non facile facultas credendi tribuitur, cum idem penes illos in suis regionibus actum fuit & receptum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod constitutione aliqua publice ac solenniter promulgata, nulli eam ignorare licet: ita quod si fuit constitutio Papae omnes ligat & omnes eam scire tenentur. Si autem fuit praelati inferioris omnes de sua iurisdictione debent scire ipsam. Ex eisdem etiam infertur, quod illa quae publice fiunt nemini commoranti in loco vbi publice fiunt, licet ignorare. Ex quibus concluditur, quod si Papa constitutionem haereticalem publice & solenniter promulgat, nemini licet ignorare ipsam.
units.tr: Disciple. Give me an example, from a copy of a bull of a heretical Pope in which heresy is asserted, showing that because of such a copy or transcript the Pope ought to be judged a heretic. Master. This seems capable of proof as follows. Whatever is in a copy or transcript of a bull of a catholic Pope must be believed. Therefore a copy or transcript of a bull of a heretical Pope must be believed in those matters that are against him. The antecedent hardly seems to need proof. The consequence is proved because a copy or transcript of a bull of a catholic Pope has exactly as much weight (in respect of everything it contains) as the bull of a heretical Pope has against himself. But the bull of a catholic Pope has full weight in everything that it contains and includes. Therefore, just as everything in a bull of a catholic Pope is to be believed, so in what runs against the heretical Pope the bull of the heretical Pope is to be believed. Disciple. It seems that neither a transcript of a bull of a catholic Pope nor a transcript of a bull of a heretical Pope, when published by criminals or men of ill repute, ought to carry credit with anyone. For just as the lives of criminals must be regarded with suspicion, so too such transcripts of statutes, or displays of Papal transcripts, must be regarded with suspicion, so that no one should give credit to such displays of Papal statutes. For no one ought to believe, on the word of criminals, that these are true transcripts. Master. To this it is answered by distinguishing the Pope's definitions, whether of a heretical or of a catholic Pope, since they are either publicly and solemnly promulgated or not. Of the first kind it is said that ignorance of them is no excuse after two months. Of the second kind it is said that ignorance of them can be an excuse. And so the reply to your argument is this: you have conceded that, because of criminals or the display of Papal transcripts made by criminals, no one is ever bound to believe that the Pope is a heretic. Nevertheless, because of such a display by criminals of Papal transcripts containing heretical perversity, if anyone in actual fact is ignorant that the Pope has given such a definition, he ought to inquire into the truth. Disciple. Here you should prove these two points. The first is that no one is excused by ignorance of a heretical constitution of the Pope that has been publicly and solemnly promulgated. The second is that, on the word of criminals, those ignorant of such a heretical constitution of the Pope ought to seek the truth. So, on these two points, I want you to speak at length, and to report not only the opinions of the men just mentioned but also those of others. Master. On the first point there are differing opinions. One is that no one can, after two months, excuse himself on the ground of ignorance of a heretical constitution of the Pope. Nor in such a case can he plead ignorance. If he does plead it, he is not to be believed unless he proves the ignorance he pleads, just as no one can plead ignorance of a constitution of a catholic Pope after two months, because everyone is bound to know it and everyone is obliged to observe it. This seems to have been the opinion of the glossators of the Decretals and the Decretum. Hence, concerning a sentence publicly promulgated by cardinals within their legation, of which less seems to be known, the Gloss on Extra, de postulationibus, cap. 1 says: "Since that sentence has been published publicly, it cannot and ought not to be ignored, and it is presumed to be known" (C. 13 q. 2, Qui et humanis; D. 16, Quod dicitur). And further on: "Where ignorance is pleaded concerning things that most people know and that are public, it is not believed unless the one pleading it proves that it is so." Likewise the Gloss on Extra, de constitutionibus, c. Cognoscentes, speaking of a constitution of the Pope, says: "Since it has been published publicly, he is bound to observe it; and it binds all after two months have passed from the time of publication." Likewise the Gloss on D. 19, the last chapter, says: "It is not lawful for anyone to be ignorant of what has been done publicly." Likewise the Gloss on C. 8 q. 1, cap. Licet, says: "Against things that have been done publicly, nothing can be objected." Likewise the Gloss on D. 54, Ubi, says: "Where things have been done publicly, no one is heard as a contradicter." From these and very many other passages it is gathered (as is said) that not only is he not heard who pleads that he was ignorant of a publicly promulgated constitution of the Pope, but also he who pleads that he was ignorant of any other thing that has nonetheless been done publicly. For although he says that he did not know that the Pope had issued a constitution in which the heretical assertion is defined, he is not to be believed, because once such a heretical constitution has been publicly promulgated, everyone is presumed to know it. Disciple. On what grounds do the aforesaid Glosses rest? Master. Very many authorities in civil and canon law rest on them. Of these it is enough to cite the letter of Innocent III to the Dean and Chapter of Sens, which is found in Extra, de postulationibus, cap. 1. In it, in answering the pleas offered on behalf of the Bishop of Auxerre, who wished to excuse that bishop on grounds of ignorance, and in rejecting them, he says: "Since, before the same master came to the Apostolic See, it was quite certain to us that the bishop had not observed the sentence of interdict; and the same master did not deny this when, in the presence of our brethren, he was questioned by us. In defence of the bishop he alleged that he was in no way bound to observe the sentence pronounced against us, because it had reached his knowledge neither through the cardinal, at that time Legate of the Apostolic See, who promulgated the same sentence, nor through the mandate or letters of the executor deputed for this purpose." And further on: "This is not enough, nor does it even help to excuse the said bishop, since the same cardinal solemnly and publicly promulgated the sentence of interdict in the presence of many people, and the same sentence of interdict had already begun to be observed publicly by many in the kingdom of France. Nor is it necessary, when a constitution has been solemnly issued and publicly promulgated, to impress its knowledge on the ears of each individual by special mandate or letters. It is enough that those who know it to have been solemnly issued and publicly promulgated are bound to observe it. This would be against certain people who did not keep the Council of Sardica, as if they had not received it or had not had it by canonical authority, a council in which it is not easy for them to be granted credence, since it was enacted and accepted in their own regions." From these words it is gathered that, once any constitution has been publicly and solemnly promulgated, no one is allowed to be ignorant of it: so that if it is a constitution of the Pope, it binds all, and all are bound to know it. If it is a constitution of a lower prelate, all within his jurisdiction ought to know it. It is also inferred from the same that things done publicly cannot be ignored by anyone who lives in the place where they are done publicly. From these it is concluded that, if the Pope publicly and solemnly promulgates a heretical constitution, no one is allowed to be ignorant of it.

units.la: Discip. Non apparet, quod omnes debeant scire constitutiones Papae haereticas: cum non sit verus praelatus omnium. Ad nullius autem constitutiones constringuntur Christiani, nisi veri Papae. Quia constitutio solius veri Papae omnes astringit. Magist. Respondetur, quod ad sciendum constitutiones Papae haeretici quilibet, qui nescit eum esse haereticum, & reputat eum verum Papam, est astrictus. Sed postquam scit Papam esse haereticum, non tenetur scire constitutiones eius posteriores, nisi sicut caeterorum haereticorum scripta & dicta. In casu autem catholicus obligatur ad sciendum constitutiones & dicta haereticorum: non ad probandum, sed ad improbandum. Ex quibus infertur, quod quilibet tenetur scire constitutionem haereticalem Papae nisi sint aliqui, qui peralium modum quam per constitutionem haereticalem sciant ipsum esse haereticum. Quod enim quilibet aliis tenetur scire constitutionem haereticalem Papae probatur: quia aut antequam scit constitutionem haereticalem ipsius reputat eum verum Papam, aut non reputat eum verum Papam. Si reputat eum verum Papam: ergo tenetur scire constitutionem eius. Si non reputat eum verum Papam: hoc non est, nisi quia scit vel tenetur scire constitutionem haereticalem eius. Et ita vel scit & tenetur scire constitutionem haereticalem eius, si nescit eum esse haereticum per alium modum.
units.tr: Disciple. It does not appear that everyone ought to know the heretical constitutions of the Pope, since he is not the true prelate of all. Christians are bound only by the constitutions of the true Pope, for the constitution of the true Pope alone binds all. Master. The answer is that anyone who does not know that the Pope is a heretic, and regards him as the true Pope, is bound to know his constitutions. But once one knows that the Pope is a heretic, one is not bound to know his later constitutions, except as the writings and sayings of other heretics. Yet a catholic is bound to know the constitutions and sayings of heretics, not in order to prove them but in order to refute them. From these points it follows that everyone is bound to know a heretical constitution of the Pope, except for those who know by some other means than through the heretical constitution that he is a heretic. That everyone else is bound to know the heretical constitution of the Pope is proved as follows: either before he knows his heretical constitution he regards him as the true Pope, or he does not regard him as the true Pope. If he regards him as the true Pope, then he is bound to know his constitution. If he does not regard him as the true Pope, this is only because he knows, or is bound to know, his heretical constitution. And so either he knows, and is bound to know, his heretical constitution, if he does not know by some other means that he is a heretic.

units.la: Discip.
units.tr: Disciple.

units.la: Disc. Nunquid secundum Glossam in nullo casu potest quis allegare se ignorare constitutiones Papæ, vel ea quæ publice fiunt. Magist. Respondetur quod secundum Glos. aliquando contingit talem ignorantiam allegare. Sed taliter alleganti minime est credendum, nisi ignorantiam probauerit, quam allegauit. Quam quidem aliquando potest probare iuramento: aliquando autem iuramentum non sufficit. De hoc tamen Gloss. di. 83. diuersas recitat opiniones, dicens: cum constitutio fit publice promulgata, quilibet tenetur eam scire usq; ad duos menses, vt in autent. & noua constit. §. 1. secundum canones vero ad sextum mensem, vt 18. di. decreuimus. Quia ergo præsumebatur peruenisse ad ipsos, tenebantur ipsi probare ignorantiam, vt hic, & extra de electione, innotuit, & 1. q. 1. si quis autem si nouerit. Et infra: Sed qualiter probatur aliquis se ignorasse dicto suo sacramento, vt 34. q. 2. in literis, vt no. 4. q. 5. quisquis. in fine. c. vlti. etiam alio modo si potest probando se fuisse in alio loco: & forte si præsumptio est contra eum, non crederetur suo iuramento. Disc. Si conuentus aliquis vel collegium diceret se ignorasse, nunquid omnes iurabunt? Magist. Dico quod sufficit, quod Episcopus cum maioribus de capitulo iuret, vt ff. de di. q. & de renunciatione. Alii dicunt, quod eo ipso probatur ignorantia, quod non probatur scientia. Disc. Durum mihi videtur asserere, quod omnes teneantur scire constitutiones Papæ: quia tunc tenerentur omnes scire omnia decreta & omnes decretales summorum pontificum: quod rationabile non videtur: quia cum multis annis sciri non possunt. Ideo circa prædicta aliam narra sententiam. Mag. Quorundam aliorum est sententia, quod Episcopi inferiores non tenentur scire quicunq; constitutionem Papæ, neq; hæreticale neq; aliam, nisi fuerit per Episcopum publicata. Dicunt enim quod prælati immediate subditi Episcopo constituti non tenentur scire constitutionem Papæ, nisi prælati sui indicauerint eis: & sic vsq; ad laicos & alios curam animarum non habentes, qui non tenentur scire constitutionem Papæ nisi plebani seu rectores eorum, aut alii prælati superiores publicant eandem constitutionem Papæ inter ipsos. Sic etiam dicunt de religiosis, quod religiosi subditi nullam constitutionem Papæ scire tenentur, antequam prælati eorum publicauerunt ea inter ipsos, hæc sententia videtur posse probari. Primo sic: si quilibet teneretur scire constitutionem Papæ post duos menses vel post sex: frustra Episcopi tenerentur ea publicare. Sed Episcopi tenentur publicare constitutionem Papæ. Ergo ante publicationem non omnes tenentur scire constitutionem Papæ. Maior videtur manifesta. Minor ostenditur sic. Nō minus tenentur Episcopi publicare constitutionem Papæ & ea quæ in conciliis provincialibus singulis annis aguntur. Sed illa debent Episcopi publicare, sicut in concilio tali decernitur, vt habetur di. 18 determinimus. Ergo constitutiones Papæ nouiter editas publicare tenentur. Itē, nō transitur ab extremo in extremū, nisi per medium. Sed Episcopi sunt medii inter Papā & suos subiectos. Ergo non tenentur subiecti scire constitutiones Papæ, nisi eis per Episcopos tanquam per medium intimentur. Tertio sic. Nullus potest ad impossibile obligari. Sed impossibile est illiteratos intelligere constitutiones Papæ: nisi prælati expositerint eis. Ergo non tenentur eas scire, antequam per prælatos eorum fuerint eis expositæ. Disc. Ista sententia decreto Innocentii tertii superius allegato aduersari videtur, cum dicitur: nec sit necessarium, cum constitutio solenniter editur & publice promulgatur, ipsius notitiam singulorum auribus per speciale mandatum vel literas inculcare. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod nonnulli tenentur scire constitutionem solenniter editam & publice promulgatam, licet eorum auribus neq; ab ipso, neq; ab aliquo inferiori per speciale mandatum, vel literis fuerit intimata. Et ita ad hoc, quod teneatur scire constitutionē Papæ, illa publicatio præter primam quæ fit in curia Papæ requiritur. Item, non est consuetudo Ecclesiæ, quod omnes constitutiones Papæ nouiter editæ priusquam obligent per Episcopos dimulgentur. Ergo prima solennis dimulgatio sufficit ad hoc, quod constitutio Papæ obliget vniuersos. Hoc etiam Glos. super dicto capitulo Innoc. tertii videtur asserere, quæ dicit, quod videtur sufficere quod per solam famam ad ipsum peruenit. Item, præceptum superioris non minus obligat, quam præceptum inferioris. Ergo simpliciter dimulgatio facta per superiorem non minus obligat, quod dimulgatio facta per inferiorem. Sed dimulgatio constitutionis Papæ facta per Episcopum ligat inferiores Episcopo. Ergo non minus ligat omnes dimulgatio facta per Papam. Itē, sicut Episcopi sunt superiores Abbatibus, Decanis, Archidiaconis & huiusmodi inferioribus plebis, ita Archiepiscopi sunt superiores Episcopis. Sed constitutio Papæ ligat inferiores Episcopos, licet ad eos per Archiepiscopos nequaquam peruenat, extra, de postul. c. 1. Ergo & constitutio Papæ ligat inferiores Episcopis, licet Episcopi non publicauerint constitutionē eandē. Hac inter alia mouent me contra prædictam sententiā. Ideo alia sententiam libenter audire. Mag. Sunt quidam Glossæ de ista materia negare nolunt. Sed eas, vt affirmant, explanant de constitutione Papæ dupliciter distinguentes, aut enim publice feruntur non solū in curia Papæ, sed in vniuersis regionibus Christianorum Papa de aliqua determinata materia constitutionē nouiter edidisse: aut talis rumor ad omnes regiones Christianorum vel aliquas non peruenit. Item, aut constitutio Papæ noua omnes tangit, aut aliquas determinatas personas vel aliqua collegia certa. Si itaque aliqua constitutio noua Papæ in eius curia solenniter & publice promulgatur, quæ omnes tangit, & publicus rumor, aut firmo de tali constitutione ad omnes regiones Christianorum peruenit: omnes conclusiones constitutionis huiusmodi scire tenentur, præcipue illi qui de facili per se vel per alios eam scire possunt. Ab hac tamen regula secundum quosdam excipiuntur milites, rustici, iuniores, & mulieres, qui constitutionem tale scire non tenentur. Et secundum quosdam vero, si eam de facili possunt scire, eam ignorare non debent: præcipue si fit constitutio, quæ bonum commune respiciat. Huius ratio assignatur talis. Ignorantia crassa & supina & peior nullum excusat. Sed ignorantia iuris quantum libet tangat quod per se potest de facili scire, est ignorantia crassa & supina vel peior. Ergo talis ignorantia nullum excusat. Maior probatur auctoritate Alexandri tertii: qui, vt habetur extra, de ordinato ab eo qui renunciauit episcopatui, c.1. ait: Si ab eodem sacros ordines scienter quis acceperit, qui indignum se facit, excusationem officii non habebit. vbi autem non scienter, poterit, nisi crassa & supina fuerit ignorantia, discretus pontifex dispensare. Ex quibus colligitur, quod ignorantia crassa & supina dispensationem licitam impedit: & per consequens ignorantia crassa & supina non excusat. quod Gloss. extra de electione. cap. innotuit, asserit manifeste dicens: ignorantia crassa & supina vel peior non excusat. minor, scilicet quod ignorantia iuris quantumlibet tangeret quod potest de facili scire, est ignorantia crassa & supina vel peior. & talis ignorantia est damnabilis. teste Augustin. qui, vt habetur distinct. 37. cap. vlti. ait: non omnis ignorans immunis est a poena. ille enim potest excusari a poena, qui quod discere non inuenit. illis autem ignosci non potest, qui habentes a quo addiscerent, operam non dederunt. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod ignorantia illa, quae spectat ad ipsos, qui possunt facilitep scire, minime excusatur. quod etiam Apostolus 2. ad Corinth. 15. aperte insinuat, cum dicit: vt etiam recitatur dist. 37. §. vt itaque. qui ignorat ignorabitur. quod Gratianus ibidem dicit intelligendum de eo, qui noluit intelligere, vt bene ageret. vbi dicit Gloss. qui ignorat & qui negligit scire, vel qui contemnit scire. & infra: nec etiam excusatur quis per ignorantiam, qui potest habere copiam peritorum. ff. de iur. & fac. igno. regula, vel si sua prudentia facilitep potest id scire. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnes illos ignorantia non excusat, qui noluunt scire, qui ideo ignorant, quia non dant operam ad sciendum, qui negligunt scire, qui contemnunt scire, qui habent copiam peritorum, qui sua prudentia possunt scire. & ita omnis talis ignorantia est damnabilis: & per consequens est crassa & supina vel peior. Ex quo infertur, quod constitutio Papae quantum ad subiectum constitutionis contentae in ipsa omnes tenentur scire, si omnes tangit & rumor de tali constitutione ad omnes regiones Christianorum peruenit: & nemini licet ignorare ea, de quibus in regione vbi moratur ignorare est publicus rumor. si autem rumor de tali constitutione non ad omnes regiones Christianorum peruenit, commorantes in regionibus in quibus nullus est rumor de constitutione talis Papae eam scire non tenentur: quia ignorantia probabilis eos excusat. ignorans enim sicut errans quemadmodum insinuat Gloss. 1. q. 4. §. notandum, non est necesse quod sit nimis scrupulosus & diligens & curiosus in inquirendo: nec quod sit nimium negligens & dissolutus in inquirendo. ille autem, qui in regione moratur, vbi de constitutione Papae noua nulla fit mentio, non est nimium negligens & dissolutus. ergo in inquirendo, ignorantia probabili laborat: & per consequens est merito excusandus, licet constitutione Papae non sciat. Si vero constitutio Papae non tangit omnes, sed aliquas determinatas personas, puta tantummodo Episcopos, vel tantummodo monachos, vel tantummodo presbyteros, seu rectores, vel aliquas alias certas personas, vel collegia, non omnes tenentur scire constitutionem eius: sed tantummodo illi quos constitutio tangit: & illorum subiecti solummodo, qui in regionib. manent, vbi inter tales personas de constitutione huiusmodi est publicus rumor. Per hoc dicitur ad propositum de constitutione haereticali, propter quod cum talis constitutio Papae omnes tangit, quia fidem omnium quantum in se est destruit & eneruat, omnes illi qui in regionibus commorantur in quibus est rumor publicus de constitutione tali scire tenentur non ad seruandum, sed ad resistendum pro posse. Illi autem qui morarentur in regionibus, vbi non est rumor de tali constitutione, eam scire non tenentur. & ideo si eam non impugnant, per ignorantiam probabilem excusantur. Discip. Nunquid secundum istos ad hoc quod aliqui teneantur scire constitutionem haereticalem Papae, requiritur quod in omnibus ciuitatibus illius regionis fiat talis rumor? Mag. Respondetur distinguendo, quod manentium in aliqua regione quidam ex consuetudine in vna ciuitate morantur continue non transeundo de ciuitate in ciuitatem, quidam vero ad ciuitates diuersas proficiscuntur. primi non tenentur scire constitutionem haereticam Papae, antequam rumor de tali constitutione Papae haereticali ad ciuitatem peruenit. alii vero tenentur scire si in aliquam ciuitatem sunt soliti proficisci vbi rumor talis fuerit dimulgatus. Discip. Ista non videntur bene dicta, quia subditi & simplices non tenentur habere explicitam fidem de multis, quae credit Ecclesia. ergo multo fortius non tenentur habere notitiam explicitam de constitutionibus Papae haereticalibus, quantumcunq; fuerit rumor, quod de fide constitutiones haereticales edidit. Mag. Respondetur distinguendo de constitutionibus Papae haereticalibus: quia aut continent haeresim contrariam veritati catholicae quam quilibet tenetur scire explicite, puta si diffiniret, quod fides Christiana est falsa, vel quod Christus non fuit mortuus, aut quod animae reproborum minime cruciantur, aut quod non est alia vita futura, etiam talem constitutionem omnes manentes in ciuitatibus, ad quas rumor vel fama de constitutione tali peruenit, scire tenentur. quemadmodum veritatem contrariam tenentur explicite credere veritatem catholicam & pro illo loco & tempore eam exterius confiteri: ita haeresim contrariam debent discredere & mente & pro loco & tempore exterius reprobare & horrere. si vero non contineat talem haeresim contrariam veritati catholicae, quam omnes tenentur credere explicite, est haeresis quae contrariatur veritati quam aliqui credere tenentur explicite, & aliqui ad hoc non tenentur. illi qui non tenentur explicite credere veritatem contrariam haeresi distincte in constitutione Papae non tenentur scire constitutionem Papae haereticalem: nisi in casu. illi vero qui tenentur credere explicite veritatem, tenentur etiam scire constitutionem Papae haereticalem, si fama de tali constitutione ad ciuitatem vbi morantur peruenit.
units.tr: Student. Does the Gloss hold that in no case may anyone plead ignorance of the Pope's constitutions or of what is done publicly? Master. The answer is that, according to the Gloss, such ignorance can sometimes be pleaded. But a person pleading it is not to be believed unless he proves the ignorance he alleges. He can sometimes prove it by oath, but sometimes an oath is not enough. On this point the Gloss on di. 83. sets out various opinions: when a constitution is published publicly, everyone is bound to know it within two months, as in the Authentic, Novae constitutiones, §1; but by the canons, within six months, as in D. 18, Decrevimus. Since it is presumed to have reached them, they are bound to prove their ignorance, as here, and in the title on elections, Innotuit, and in C. 1, q. 1, Si quis autem, and Si noverit. And further: But how a person proves that he was ignorant may be shown by his oath, as in C. 34, q. 2, In literis; as noted in C. 4, q. 5, Quisquis, at the end, and in the last chapter. It may also be shown in another way, if he can prove that he was in another place. And perhaps, if there is a presumption against him, his oath will not be believed. Student. If some chapter or college says that it was ignorant, will all of its members have to swear? Master. I say that it is enough for the bishop to swear together with the senior members of the chapter, as in D. (de diversis) and in the title on renunciation. Others say that ignorance is proved simply by the fact that knowledge is not proved. Student. It seems harsh to me to assert that everyone is bound to know the Pope's constitutions, for then everyone would be bound to know all the decrees and all the decretals of the supreme pontiffs. That does not seem reasonable, since they cannot be known even in many years. So please give me another opinion on these matters. Master. There is an opinion of certain others that the lower bishops are not bound to know every constitution of the Pope, whether heretical or other, unless it has been published by the bishop. For they say that prelates who are subordinate immediately to a bishop are not bound to know a papal constitution unless their own prelates have made it known to them. And so on down to the laity and others who have no care of souls, who are not bound to know a papal constitution unless their parish priests or rectors, or other superior prelates, publish that constitution among them. They say the same of religious: subordinate religious are bound to know no papal constitution until their prelates have published it among them. This opinion seems capable of proof. First, thus: if everyone were bound to know a papal constitution after two months or after six, bishops would be bound to publish it in vain. But bishops are bound to publish papal constitutions. Therefore, before publication, not everyone is bound to know the papal constitution. The major premise is plain. The minor is shown thus: bishops are no less bound to publish the papal constitutions than the things decided each year in provincial councils. But they must publish those as the council decrees in that place, as is found in D. 18, Determinimus. Therefore they are bound to publish newly issued papal constitutions. Again, one does not pass from one extreme to the other except through the middle. But bishops are the middle between the Pope and their subjects. Therefore subjects are not bound to know papal constitutions unless these are notified to them through the bishops as through a middle. Third, thus: no one can be obliged to the impossible. But it is impossible for the unlettered to understand papal constitutions unless their prelates explain them. Therefore they are not bound to know them before their prelates have explained them. Student. This opinion seems opposed to the decree of Innocent III cited above, where it says: nor is it necessary, when a constitution is solemnly issued and publicly promulgated, to impress knowledge of it on the ears of each person by a special mandate or letters. From these words it is gathered that some are bound to know a constitution solemnly issued and publicly promulgated, even though it has not been made known to their ears either by the Pope himself or by any inferior by special mandate or letters. And so, for a person to be bound to know a papal constitution, publication beyond the first, which takes place at the papal court, is not required. Again, it is not the custom of the Church that all newly issued papal constitutions be disseminated through the bishops before they bind. Therefore the first solemn dissemination is enough for a papal constitution to bind everyone. The Gloss on Innocent III's chapter seems to assert this too, when it says that it seems sufficient that it reached him through rumour alone. Again, a command of a superior binds no less than a command of an inferior. Therefore a dissemination made simply by a superior binds no less than one made by an inferior. But the dissemination of a papal constitution made by a bishop binds the bishop's inferiors. Therefore a dissemination made by the Pope binds everyone no less. Again, just as bishops are superior to abbots, deans, archdeacons and such lesser clergy of the parish, so archbishops are superior to bishops. But a papal constitution binds inferior bishops, even though it by no means reaches them through the archbishops, Extra, De postulatione, c. 1. Therefore a papal constitution also binds the inferiors of bishops even if the bishops have not published that same constitution. These and other considerations move me against that opinion. So I should gladly hear another opinion. Master. Certain Glosses on this matter are unwilling to deny it, but they explain it, as they affirm, concerning a papal constitution, making a twofold distinction. For either the Pope has newly issued a constitution on some particular matter, and it is publicly circulated not only at the papal court but throughout all the regions of Christians, or such a rumour does not reach all or some regions of Christians. Again, either a new papal constitution touches everyone, or certain determined persons or particular colleges. Therefore, if some new constitution of the Pope is solemnly and publicly promulgated at his court, which touches everyone, and public report, or certain fame of such a constitution, reaches all the regions of Christians, then everyone is bound to know the provisions of such a constitution, especially those who can easily know it, either themselves or through others. From this rule, however, according to some, soldiers, country people, the young and women are excepted, since they are not bound to know such a constitution. But according to others, if they can easily know it, they ought not to be ignorant of it, especially if the constitution concerns the common good. The reason for this is assigned as follows: crass, supine and worse ignorance excuses no one. But ignorance of law, however much it concerns what a person can easily know, is crass and supine ignorance or worse. Therefore such ignorance excuses no one. The major premise is proved by the authority of Alexander III, who, as is found in the title De ordinato ab eo qui renunciavit episcopatui, c. 1, says: If anyone has knowingly received holy orders from the same man, he who makes himself unworthy will have no excuse from office. But where it was not knowingly done, the discreet pontiff may dispense, unless the ignorance was crass and supine. From this it is gathered that crass and supine ignorance prevents lawful dispensation, and consequently that crass and supine ignorance does not excuse. The Gloss on the title on elections, chapter Innotuit, plainly asserts this, saying: crass and supine ignorance, or worse, does not excuse. The minor premise, namely that ignorance of law, however much it concerns what can easily be known, is crass and supine ignorance or worse, and such ignorance is damnable, is attested by Augustine, who, as is found in D. 37, last chapter, says: not every ignorant person is free from punishment. For he can be excused from punishment who did not find a way to learn; but those who had someone from whom to learn and did not take the trouble cannot be pardoned. From these words it is evidently gathered that the ignorance which pertains to those who could easily know is in no way excused. The Apostle also clearly suggests this in 2 Corinthians 15, when he says: he who is ignorant will be ignored; which Gratian in the same place says must be understood of the person who was unwilling to understand so as to act well. Here the Gloss says: he who is ignorant, and he who neglects to know, or who despises knowing. And further: nor is a person excused by ignorance who can have access to skilled people, Digest, De iuris et facti ignorantia, rule, or if by his own prudence he could easily know it. From these words it is gathered that ignorance does not excuse all those who are unwilling to know, who are ignorant because they do not take pains to know, who neglect to know, who despise knowing, who have access to skilled people, or who could know by their own prudence. And so every such ignorance is damnable, and consequently is crass and supine or worse. From this it follows that, as regards the subject matter of a papal constitution, everyone is bound to know its contents if it touches everyone and the rumour of such a constitution has reached all the regions of Christians; and no one may be permitted to be ignorant of what is publicly rumoured in the region where he dwells. But if rumour of such a constitution has not reached all the regions of Christians, those living in regions where there is no rumour of such a papal constitution are not bound to know it, because a probable ignorance excuses them. For an ignorant person, like one who errs, as the Gloss on C. 1, q. 4, §Notandum points out, need not be overly scrupulous, diligent and curious in inquiring; nor need he be excessively negligent and lax in inquiring. But one who dwells in a region where no mention at all is made of a new papal constitution is not excessively negligent and lax. Therefore, in inquiring, he suffers from a probable ignorance, and consequently he is rightly excused, even though he does not know the papal constitution. But if a papal constitution does not touch everyone, but certain determined persons, for example only bishops, or only monks, or only priests, or rectors, or certain other particular persons or colleges, not everyone is bound to know it, but only those whom the constitution touches, and only their subjects who dwell in regions where there is public rumour of such a constitution among those persons. By this, a reply is given to the point about a heretical constitution: since such a papal constitution touches everyone, because as far as it lies in itself it destroys and weakens the faith of all, all those who dwell in regions where there is public rumour of such a constitution are bound to know it, not in order to observe it, but in order to resist it as far as they can. Those who dwell in regions where there is no rumour of such a constitution are not bound to know it; and so, if they do not oppose it, they are excused by probable ignorance. Student. According to these authors, does it follow that for some to be bound to know a heretical papal constitution, such rumour must arise in all the cities of that region? Master. The answer is given by distinguishing: of those dwelling in a region, some by custom live continually in one city, without travelling from city to city, while others set out for different cities. The first are not bound to know a heretical papal constitution until rumour of such a heretical papal constitution has reached their city. The others, however, are bound to know it if they are accustomed to set out for some city where such rumour has been spread. Student. These things do not seem well said, because subjects and simple people are not bound to have explicit faith in many things that the Church believes. Therefore much less are they bound to have explicit knowledge of heretical papal constitutions, however much rumour there may be that the Pope has issued heretical constitutions concerning the faith. Master. The answer is given by distinguishing among heretical papal constitutions. For either they contain a heresy contrary to Catholic truth, which everyone is bound to know explicitly, as if he were to define that the Christian faith is false, or that Christ did not die, or that the souls of the reprobate are not tormented at all, or that there is no other future life. In such a case, everyone dwelling in cities to which rumour or report of such a constitution has come is bound to know it, just as they are bound to believe explicitly the Catholic truth opposed to that error, and to confess it outwardly in that place and at that time; so they ought to reject that contrary heresy in mind, and to condemn and abhor it outwardly according to place and time. But if the constitution does not contain such a heresy contrary to Catholic truth, which everyone is bound to believe explicitly, but a heresy opposed to a truth that some are bound to believe explicitly and others are not, then those who are not bound to believe explicitly the truth opposed to the heresy as distinctly stated in the papal constitution are not bound to know the heretical papal constitution, unless in a particular case. But those who are bound to believe explicitly the truth are also bound to know the heretical papal constitution if the report of such a constitution has reached the city where they dwell.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: In quo probatur duabus rationibus conclusio secunda posita cap. 18. immediate praecedenti, scil. quod propter verba criminosorum ignorantes talem constitutionem haereticalem Papae debent quaerere veritatem.
units.tr: In which the second conclusion, laid down in the immediately preceding chapter 18, is proved by two arguments: namely, that on account of the words of criminals, those who are ignorant of such a heretical constitution of the Pope ought to seek out the truth.

units.la: DISCIP. Nunc tracta secundum praemissa secundum quaestum praecedentis capituli: an scilicet propter verba criminosorum asserentium constitutionem haereticalem Papae esse nouiter editam debeant ignorantes inquirere veritatem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Now treat, according to the premises and the question of the preceding chapter: whether, on account of the words of criminals asserting that a heretical constitution of the Pope has been newly issued, the ignorant ought to inquire after the truth.

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quod si aliqui criminosi diffamant Papam in genere dicentes: quod in constitutione sua haeresim diffinit, neque constitutionem neq; haeresim specificando, non est necesse propter verba eorum inquirere veritatem. Si autem in speciali tam haeresim quam constitutionem specificant dicendo, in tali constitutione Papa talem haeresim diffinit: videtur quod illi, qui veritatem contrariam credere tenentur explicite, licet non debeant credere criminosis, debent tamen cauta sollicitudine quaerere veritatem, legendo scilicet in statuto constitutionem eandem. Hoc probatur primo sic. In dubiis via tutior est tenenda, extra de spon. iuuenis. & de paen. dist. 7. c. si quis posit um. & extra de homicidio, significasti. & c. ad audientiam. Sed quaerere veritatem de constitutione Papae, cum nuntiatur haeresim continere, est via tutior: quia omni caret periculo. Non quaerere aurem veritatem, magnum habet periculum: propter hoc nisi quaereretur veritas posset in nonnullis periclitari fides. Ergo propter huiusmodi famam veritas sollicite est quaerenda. Secundo sic. Propter assertionem de constitutione haereticali Papae est quaerenda veritas extra iudicium, propter quorum denuntiationem coram iudice esset veritas iudiciaria inquirenda. Sed propter denunciationem criminosorum debet iudex Papae haeretici inquirere veritatem. Nam criminosi in exceptis criminib9, inter quae est haeresis, ad denunciandum debent admitti. Ergo etiam extra iudicium propter assertionem talem criminosorum veritas est quaerenda.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer is that if certain criminals defame the Pope in general terms, saying that in his constitution he defines heresy, without specifying either the constitution or the heresy, it is not necessary to inquire into the truth on account of their words. But if they specify in particular both the heresy and the constitution, saying in such a constitution the Pope defines such a heresy, it seems that those who are bound to believe the contrary truth explicitly, although they ought not to believe the criminals, ought nevertheless with careful diligence to seek out the truth, namely by reading that same constitution in the statute book. This is proved first thus. In doubtful matters the safer way is to be taken (Extra, de sponsalibus, Iuvenis; and de paenitentia, dist. 7, c. Si quis positum; and Extra, de homicidio, Significasti; and c. Ad audientiam). But to seek the truth about a constitution of the Pope, when it is reported to contain heresy, is the safer way, since it is free of all danger. Not to seek the truth, however, carries great danger: for unless the truth were sought, faith could in some people be imperilled. Therefore, on account of such a report, the truth is to be sought with care. Secondly, thus. On account of an assertion about a heretical constitution of the Pope the truth is to be sought outside a court of law, just as, on account of their accusation before a judge, the judicial truth would have to be inquired into. But on account of the accusation of criminals the judge ought to inquire into the truth about a heretical Pope; for criminals, in cases excepted from the crimes, among which is heresy, ought to be admitted to make accusations. Therefore, even outside a court of law, on account of such an assertion of criminals, the truth is to be sought.

units.la: DISCIP. Secundum canonicas sanctiones de nullo est inquisitio facienda, nisi fuerit graviter diffamatus. Ergo propter verba criminosorum non est de Papa inquisitio facienda, nisi taliter fuerit diffamat9: quod absq; scandalo tolerari non posset.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. According to the canonical sanctions, no inquiry is to be made concerning anyone unless he has been gravely defamed. Therefore, on account of the words of criminals, no inquiry is to be made concerning the Pope unless he has been so defamed, which could not be tolerated without scandal.

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quam iudicialis inquisitio, quae absq; grauatione & nota illius, de quo inquiritur, nequaquam fieri potest, non erit aliter facienda, nisi fuerit diffamatus. & de illa inquisitione loquuntur canonicae sanctiones: quia inquisitio veritatis quae fit extra iudicium quae in casu proposito solum per inspectionem scandalum & studium constitutionis haereticalis Papae fieri potest, facienda est etiam absq; praecedente infamia Papae: quia per talem inquisitionem veritatis nullum grauamen vel non infertur illi de quo inquiritur, licet postea inuenientes veritatem debeant Papam haereticum euitare.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer is that a judicial inquiry, which cannot in any way be carried out without burden and mark upon the person inquired into, is not to be undertaken unless he has been defamed; and it is of that inquiry that the canonical sanctions speak. But an inquiry into the truth which is made outside a court of law, which in the case proposed can be carried out only by inspecting the scandal and studying the heretical constitution of the Pope, is to be undertaken even without a prior infamy of the Pope; for by such an inquiry into the truth no burden is laid upon the person inquired into, although, having discovered the truth, they ought afterwards to avoid the heretical Pope.

units.la: DISCIP. Ista responsio non videtur sufficere, quia propter verba criminosorum non est credendum, quod transsumpta ostensa sint vera transsumpta. Ergo licet in illis transsumptis per criminosos ostensis inueniatur aliqua haeresis diffinita, non est credendum Papa esse haereticum.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. This answer does not seem sufficient, because on account of the words of criminals it is not to be believed that the transcripts shown are true transcripts. Therefore, even if some defined heresy is found in those transcripts shown by criminals, it is not to be believed that the Pope is a heretic.

units.la: MAG. Ad hoc respondetur, quod in hoc casu non solum audiens relationem ostendentium transsumpta huiusmodi debet illa transsumpta legere & studere, sed etiam diligenter inquirere, an sint vera vel falsa transsumpta: quod quia potest fieri absq; nota & grauamine Papae, & si est innocens ex abundanti cautela tenetur audiens huius criminosi huiusmodi inquirere veritatem huius.
units.tr: MASTER. To this it is answered that in this case the hearer of those who show such transcripts ought not only to read and study those transcripts, but also diligently to inquire whether they are true or false transcripts; and since this can be done without mark and burden upon the Pope, and if he is innocent, the hearer of such a criminal is bound, out of abundant caution, to inquire into the truth of the matter.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: Vbi ponuntur indicia manifesta, quae narrata & etiam visa causant vehementem suspicionem de assertione haereticali Papae & quod reuelantibus illa est credendum.
units.tr: Where the manifest indications are set out, which, whether told or seen, cause a strong suspicion of the Pope's heretical assertion, and where it must be believed that those who report them are right.

units.la: DISCIP. Quia rato aut nunquam inuenitur criminosus, qui publice se auderet offerre ad conuincendum Papam catholicum statuta haereticalia edidisse: & propter hoc ex hoc ipso, quod criminosi, si publice & manifeste etiam extra iudicium de Papa talia affirmarent, esset quaedam praesumptio, quod eorum assertio esset a veritate extranea. Quapropter circa istam materiam nolo amplius immorari. Ideo de indiciis manifestis, de quibus dictum est supra 17. velis dicere.
units.tr: DISCIP. Because a criminal is rarely or never found who would dare to present himself publicly to convict a Catholic Pope of having issued heretical decrees. For this very reason, if criminals were to affirm such things about the Pope publicly and openly, even outside a trial, there would be a certain presumption that their assertion was foreign to the truth. So I do not wish to dwell any longer on this matter. Please tell me about the manifest indications, which were mentioned above in chapter 17.

units.la: MAG. Sententia praedictorum, quod asserentibus extra iudicium indicia manifesta declarantia perfidiam Papae haeretici est credendum. Cuius ratio assignatur talis. Magis credendum est asserentibus indicia manifesta ad aliquod comprobandum, quam assertioni simplici aliquorum fide dignorum, cum et nunquam credatur uni, de con. di. 4. parvulos. & c. cum itaq. ergo multo fortius asserentibus Papam esse haereticum, & similiter cum hoc afferentib. indicia manifesta, hoc est suspiciones & praesumptiones probabiles, quibus eius perfidia declaratur, est credendum. DISCIP. Pone exemplum, ut melius praedicta intelligam. MAG. Exempla multa possent poni, secundum quas suspiciones seu praesumptiones possunt esse quamplurime, imo innumerae. Vnus autem potest esse tale. Ponatur quod Papa publice praedicet, quod Christus non fuerit verus Deus, aut quod non fuerit passus aut aliquid tale, quod est haereticum manifeste. Insuper omnes tenentes contrarium persequatur, destruat & confundat omnes et suam doctrinam pestiferam defendentes, praedicantes & docentes diligat, promoveat & exaltet. Sint et alii, qui ignorent Papam talem haeresim praedicare, tenere & docere: & tamen sciunt sciant quosdam alios de eadem doctrina inter se altercationem habere: quorum quidam tenent catholicam veritatem & alii eam impugnant. hoc posito: si taliter ignorantes Papam haereticã doctrinam pdicare, asserere vel tenere audierint post aliquos referentes, q talis est doctrina Papae, & ad hoc confirmandum inducentes, quod defensores veritatis catholicae Papa deprimit & confundit, docentes vero contrariam haereticam prauitatem promouet & exaltat. sicut ipsi ignorantes et Papa esse haereticus manifeste conspiciunt taliter adducentib. indicia manifesta ad probandum Papa esse haereticum est credendum: quia p dicto eorum est psumptio violenta. Ex quo Papa talem doctrinam haereticam defendentes diligit, iuuat & exaltat: & tenentes veritatem catholicam odit, psequitur & molestat. q psumptio magis ostenditur violenta, si nulla ratio appareat, quare istos deprimit & illos exaltat: nihilominus isti doctrinam talem negat, & alii tenent eandem. quo et nimis vrgeri videntur, si Papa alios, quos ante diligebat, odit vel psequit, ex quo doctrina sua haeretica impugnare coeperunt: & ecce nueiso eos, quib. fauorabiliter videbat, cariores habet, ex quo doctrinam suam haereticam defenderunt, docuerunt, diuulgauerunt, asseruerunt vel tenuerunt. qa per talem psumptionem credendum est Papam esse haereticum. Item, si Papa de haeresi diffamatur, maxime p viros literatos & in sacra pagina eruditos, petentes instanter & totus virib. laborantes, vt generale concilium celebretur ad discutiendum & examinandum illa, q Papae tanquam haereticalia imponuntur, se subiicere generalis concilii iudicio idem generale concilium ne celebretur impedire recusat: est contra ipsum praesumptio violenta, quod est haeretica labe respersus. Item si de haeresi manifesta publice diffamatur, & ipse de tali haeresi se non purget, sed etiam praedicat, tenet & docet, est contra eum praesumptio violenta, quod est haereticus manifestus, & ita asserentib. tales praesumptiones apertas ad probandum Papam esse haereticum, videtur esse credendum.
units.tr: MAG. The view of the people mentioned is that those who assert, outside a trial, that manifest indications show the Pope's perfidy to be heretical are to be believed. The reason given is this. More credit is to be given to those who assert manifest indications in proof of something than to a bare assertion by some trustworthy men, since one witness is never believed alone (de con. di. 4. parvulos. & c. cum itaq.). Therefore, much more strongly, those who assert that the Pope is a heretic are to be believed, and likewise those who bring with this assertion manifest indications, that is, suspicions and probable presumptions, by which his perfidy is declared. DISCIP. Give an example, so that I may understand these matters better. MAG. Many examples could be given, by which the suspicions or presumptions could be very numerous, indeed countless. One could be this. Suppose the Pope publicly preaches that Christ was not true God, or that he did not suffer, or something of that kind, which is manifestly heretical. Suppose further that he persecutes all who hold the contrary, destroys and crushes all who defend and teach his pestilent doctrine, and loves, promotes and exalts them. Suppose there are others who do not know that the Pope preaches, holds and teaches such a heresy, yet they know that some others quarrel among themselves over this same doctrine: some hold the Catholic truth and others attack it. Granted this, if such ignorant people hear, after some reporters, that this is the Pope's doctrine, and these reporters add in confirmation that the Pope depresses and crushes the defenders of Catholic truth, but promotes and exalts those who teach the contrary heretical depravity, then, just as the ignorant themselves plainly see, when manifest indications are brought forward in this way to prove that the Pope is a heretic, one must believe them, because their statement carries a violent presumption. For the Pope loves, helps and exalts those who defend such heretical doctrine, and hates, pursues and harasses those who hold the Catholic truth. The presumption appears all the more violent if no reason appears why he depresses these men and exalts those; yet these men deny such a doctrine while others hold the same. Things seem to press even harder if the Pope hates or pursues others whom he had loved before, from the time they began to attack his heretical doctrine; and see, he now holds dearer those whom he had favoured, since they defended, taught, spread, asserted or held his heretical doctrine. By such a presumption, therefore, the Pope must be believed to be a heretic. Likewise, if the Pope is publicly defamed of heresy, especially by learned men versed in Holy Scripture, who urgently beg and labour with all their strength that a general council be held to discuss and examine the charges laid against the Pope as heretical, and he refuses to submit himself to the judgment of a general council or to allow it to be held, there is a violent presumption against him that he is stained with heresy. Likewise, if he is publicly defamed of manifest heresy and does not clear himself of it, but even preaches, holds and teaches it, there is a violent presumption against him that he is a manifest heretic. And so, to those who assert such open presumptions in proof that the Pope is a heretic, it seems one must give belief.

units.la: DISCIP. Videtur quod ista dicta inter se repugnant. nam suspicio sine praesumptio non est credulitas, nec est causa credulitatis. cum ergo indicia manifesta non sint nisi quaedam suspiciones seu praesumptiones, propter indicia manifesta non debet quis credere Papam esse haereticum.
units.tr: DISCIP. These statements seem to contradict one another. For suspicion without presumption is not belief, nor is it a cause of belief. Since manifest indications are nothing but certain suspicions or presumptions, no one ought to believe the Pope to be a heretic on account of manifest indications.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur quod differentia est inter scientiam & credulitatem. quia scientia est ex evidentia rei: credulitas autem non est ex evidentia rei. & ideo licet indicia manifesta, quae sunt suspiciones seu probationes probabiles vel violentae nunquam causant scientiam: causant saepe tamen credulitatem: saepe tamen non causant tam certam credulitatem, quod credens a sua credulitate neq; debeat nec possit recedere.
units.tr: MAGIST. The answer is that there is a difference between knowledge and belief. Knowledge comes from the evidence of the thing, but belief does not. And so, although manifest indications, which are suspicions or probable or violent presumptions, never produce knowledge, they often do produce belief; yet often they do not produce so certain a belief that the believer ought not, or cannot, withdraw from it.

units.la: DISCIP. Quomodo posset probari, quod praesumptio probabilis vel violenta causet aliquam credulitatem? MAG. Hoc videtur aperte posse probari. Primo per hoc, quod index absque credulitate, quod reus sit damnandus, non debet ad sententiam condemnationis procedere: sed saepe etiam diffinitiua sententia condemnationis de aliquo fertur propter solam praesumptionem, extra de praesump. cap. afferte. vbi dicit Gloss. super verbo data: haec enim fuit sententia diffinitiua lata per solam praesumptionem. & c. quanto. & infra Glossa: violenta praesumptio quandoque sufficit ad condemnationem: ergo ad credulitatem nonnunquam sufficit violenta praesumptio.
units.tr: DISCIP. How could it be proved that a probable or violent presumption causes some belief? MAG. This seems clearly provable. First, a judge ought not to proceed to a sentence of condemnation against anyone without some belief that the accused should be condemned; yet often a definitive sentence of condemnation is pronounced on someone on the strength of presumption alone (extra de praesump. cap. afferte), where the Gloss says on the word data: for this was a definitive sentence pronounced on presumption alone, etc. (cap. quanto). And below, the Gloss says: a violent presumption is sometimes sufficient for condemnation. Therefore a violent presumption is sometimes sufficient for belief.

units.la: Secundo probatur idem sic: Compurgatores alicuius se purgantis licite, iurant se credere, quod purgans se dicit veritatem, extra, de purgationibus vel de purgatione canonica: cap. de testibus. & cap. quotiens. & cap. ultim. sed talem credulitatem non habent, nisi ex sola praesumptione, qua praesumunt quod purgatus noluit periurare. ergo sola praesumptio sufficit ad credulitatem.
units.tr: Second, the same is proved thus. The compurgators of someone who lawfully clears himself swear that they believe the one clearing himself is speaking the truth (extra, de purgationibus vel de purgatione canonica: cap. de testibus, cap. quotiens, cap. ultim.). But they have no such belief except from presumption alone, by which they presume that the man who clears himself would not wish to perjure himself. Therefore presumption alone is sufficient for belief.

units.la: DISCIP. Videtur quod hic possit fieri difficultas de differentia inter praesumptionem & credulitatem. quia tamen non reputo eam multum vtilem ad propositum, quod intendo, nolo vt eam discutias: sed dic quem effectum habebit ista credulitas de perfidia Papae haeretici, quae solis praesumptionibus probabilibus vel violentis seu indiciis manifestis habetur. MAG. Respondetur; quod talis credulitas talem effectum debet habere. respectu personae Papae haeretici duplicem potest habere effectum, secundum quod varia potest esse praesumptio de perfidia Papae haeretici; quia aut est talis praesumptio, quod non sufficit ad condemnationem; etiam si esset ordine iudiciario seruato probata: aut est praesumptio violenta, quod sufficit ad condemnandum Papam haereticum, si probata extitit. propter primam praesumptionem & credulitatem Papa secreto est vitandus, sed non in publico. Quod enim sit in secreto vitandus, patet per hoc, quod quilibet qui creditur esse excommunicatus, est vitandus saltem in secreto. sed Papa propter credulitatem creditur esse excommunicatus. igitur a tali credulitate saltem in secreto est vitandus. Quod autem non sit vitandus in publico propter talem credulitatem, videtur sic posse probari: nullus debet alium in publico tanquam haereticum & excommunicatum vitare, nisi possit probari excommunicatus: vel nisi publica fama de excommunicatione eius possit probari excommunicatus. sed Papa propter talem praesumptionem solum neq; potest probari excommunicatus: neq; potest probari fama quod est excommunicatus. ergo propter talem praesumptionem non est in publico vitandus. DISCIP. Potest esse, quod talis praesumptio sit publica vel etiam notoria. ergo fama est quod Papa est haereticus: & per consequens fama est quod est excommunicatus. propter famam autem est aliquis tanquam excommunicatus, &c. etiam in publico deuitandus, extra de sent. excom. cum consideres. ergo propter talem praesumptionem debet Papa etiam in publico deuitari.
units.tr: DISCIP. A difficulty could arise here about the difference between presumption and belief. Since I do not consider that very useful to my purpose, I do not want you to discuss it. Rather, say what effect this belief about the Pope's heretical perfidy will have, a belief held from probable or violent presumptions or manifest indications alone. MAG. The answer is that such belief ought to have such an effect. With respect to the person of the heretical Pope, it can have a twofold effect, since the presumption about the Pope's heretical perfidy can be of different kinds. For either it is a presumption that is not sufficient for condemnation even if it were proved with the judicial order observed, or it is a violent presumption which suffices to condemn the heretical Pope, if it has been proved. On account of the first presumption and belief, the Pope is to be avoided in secret, but not in public. That he is to be avoided in secret is clear, because whoever is believed to be excommunicate is to be avoided at least in secret. But the Pope, on account of belief, is believed to be excommunicate; therefore, because of such belief, he is to be avoided at least in secret. That he is not to be avoided in public on account of such belief seems provable thus. No one ought to avoid another in public as a heretic and excommunicate unless the excommunication can be proved, or unless public report of his excommunication can be proved. But the Pope, on account of such presumption alone, can neither be proved excommunicate nor can it be proved by report that he is excommunicate. Therefore, on account of such presumption, he is not to be avoided in public. DISCIP. It may be that such a presumption is public, or even notorious. Then it is common report that the Pope is a heretic, and consequently common report that he is excommunicate. On account of report, a man is to be avoided even in public as excommunicate (extra de sent. excom. cum consideres). Therefore, on account of such a presumption, the Pope ought to be avoided even in public.

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quod non propter solam praesumptionem talem, quae non sufficit ad condemnacondemnationem Papæ hæretici, quantumcunque publica sit, notoria poterit haberi, quod Papa sit tanquam hæreticus publice diffamatus. aliter enim ex præsumptione nulla consurget infamia. & ideo propter tales præsumptiones solas non est Papa reputandus hæreticus vel excommunicatus.
units.tr: MAG. The answer is that a presumption of this kind alone, however public it may be, is not enough to condemn the Pope as a heretic. Such a presumption cannot give rise to a notorious reputation that the Pope is publicly defamed as a heretic. Otherwise no infamy would arise from presumption at all.
