Therefore, on such presumptions alone, the Pope is not to be regarded as a heretic or as excommunicate.

units.la: DISCIP. Nonne lex dicit, ex levi causa probatur quis hæreticus? ergo propter præsumptionem probabilem est Papa reputandus hæreticus.
units.tr: DISCIP. Does not the law say that a person is proved a heretic on slight grounds? Therefore, on a probable presumption, the Pope is to be regarded as a heretic.

units.la: MAG. Ad hoc respondet Glos. extra de præsump. c. literas, quod lex debet intelligi, quantum ad hoc, quod suspectus de hæresi habeatur: sed non ut condemnetur de hæresi. quod Innocent. tertius cap. literas, satis aperte insinuare videtur: propter solam suspicionem quamvis vehementem nolumus eum de tam graui crimine (scilicet hæresis) condemnare. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod non propter omnem præsumptionem est quis hæreticus reputandus, licet propter eam suspectus de hæresi habeatur.
units.tr: MAG. To this the gloss on extra de praesumptionibus, c. literas replies that the law must be understood to mean that a man is held suspect of heresy, but not that he is condemned for heresy. Innocent III seems to hint at this quite plainly in cap. literas: on account of suspicion alone, however strong, we are unwilling to condemn him of so grave a crime (namely heresy). From these words it is clear that a person is not to be regarded as a heretic on account of every presumption, although he may be held suspect of heresy on account of it.

units.la: DISCIP. Dixisti de præsumptione, quod non sufficit ad condemnandum eum de hæretica pravitate: nunc dic de alia. MAG. Dicitur, quod si est præsumptio tam violenta contra Papam, quod sufficeret ad condemnandum eum de hæretica pravitate, si fuerit in iudicio comprobata, credens propter talem præsumptionem Papam esse hæreticum, si poterit eam probare in iudicio, tenetur Papam in publico tanquam hæreticum & excommunicatum vitare. DISCIP. Hoc videtur repugnare assertioni concilii generalis sub Innocent. tertio celebrati, quod, ut legitur extra de hæreticis cap. excommunicato ait: qui autem inventi fuerint sola suspicione notabiles, nisi iuxta considerationem suspicionis qualitatem personæ propriam innocentiam congrua purgatione monstraverint, anathematis gladio feriantur & usque ad satisfactionem condignam ab omnibus euitentur: ita quod si per annum in excommunicatione perstiterint, ex tunc velut hæretici condemnentur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod propter nullam præsumptionem seu suspicionem de hæretica pravitate est aliquis excommunicatus, licet sit excommunicandus. MAG. Ad hoc respondetur, quod verba præmissa concilii generalis intelligenda sunt de suspicione probabili, quæ non est adeo violenta, quod ad condemnationem sufficiat, non de illa quæ sufficit ad condemnationem. Quod non sit aliqua suspicio seu præsumptio, quæ ad condemnandum aliquem tanquam hæreticum sufficiat, & propter quam debeat hæreticus reputari, patet per verba, quæ immediate sequuntur verba præscripta, cum dicit concilium generale: ita quod si per annum in excommunicatione perstiterit, ex tunc velut hæreticus condemnetur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur evidenter, quod est aliqua præsumptio, quæ sufficit ad condemnandum hæreticos: quia scilicet ex hoc, quod aliquis in excommunicatione perfistit per annum, propter suspicionem autem præcedentem de hæretica pravitate non habetur per certam scientiam, quod est hæreticus, sed solummodo præsumptiue.
units.tr: DISCIP. You have spoken of presumption, saying that it is not enough to condemn him of heretical pravity; now tell me about another kind. MAG. It is said that if there is a presumption against the Pope so violent that it would suffice to condemn him of heretical pravity, if it were proved in judgment, then one who believes the Pope to be a heretic on account of such a presumption, if he can prove it in judgment, is bound to avoid the Pope publicly as a heretic and excommunicate. DISCIP. This seems to contradict the declaration of the general council held under Innocent III, which, as we read in extra de haereticis, cap. excommunicato, says: Those who are found to be marked by suspicion alone, unless, according to the consideration of the suspicion and the quality of the person, they show their innocence by a fitting purgation, are to be struck with the sword of anathema and avoided by all until they make due satisfaction; so that if they persist in excommunication for a year, they are then to be condemned as heretics. From these words it is gathered that no one is excommunicate on account of any presumption or suspicion of heretical pravity, although he ought to be excommunicated. MAG. To this it is answered that the foregoing words of the general council are to be understood of a probable suspicion which is not so violent that it suffices for condemnation, and not of that which suffices for condemnation. That there is some suspicion or presumption which suffices to condemn a man as a heretic, and on account of which he ought to be reckoned a heretic, is plain from the words which immediately follow the words quoted, where the council says: so that if he persists in excommunication for a year, he is then to be condemned as a heretic. From these words it is evidently gathered that there is some presumption which suffices to condemn heretics: namely because, from the fact that a man persists in excommunication for a year, and because of the earlier suspicion of heretical pravity, it is not known with certain knowledge that he is a heretic, but only presumptively.

units.la: CAP. XXI. Vbi probatur septima conclusio supra c. 13. posita, scil. Quod quibuscunque criminosis & existentibus malæ famæ, si non declararent per legitima documenta aut manifesta indicia, Papam esse hæreticum, minime est credendum.
units.tr: CAP. XXI. Where the seventh conclusion, laid down above in chapter 13, is proved, namely: that to any persons who are criminal and of bad repute, if they do not make it clear by legitimate documents or manifest indications that the Pope is a heretic, no credence is to be given.

units.la: DISCIP. Postquam recitasti quem effectum debet habere credulitas hæretica per solam præsumptionem respectu Papæ: dic quem effectum debet habere respectu aliorum. MAG. Dicitur quod credentes propter solam præsumptionem Papam esse hæreticum, debent illis, qui Papam impugnant de pravitate hæretica, nisi constiterit eis legitimis documentis, quod calumniose vel maliciose procedunt, præbere defensionem, quam possunt, ac etiam consilium, auxilium & favorem, & eos in nullo molestare. DISCIP. Hæc assertio mihi dependere videtur ex his, quæ dicta sunt lib. 6. c. 33. vsq; ad c. 35. vbi allegasti quod impugnantes Papam hæreticum de hæretica pravitate sunt a catholicis defendendi. Ideo circa primam noli insistere: sed circa septimam conclusionem c. 13. istius septimi recitatam. MAG. Septima conclusio est, quod quibuscunque criminosis & existentibus malæ famæ, si non declararent per legitima documenta aut manifesta indicia Papam esse hæreticum, minime est credendum. Hoc videtur posse probari sic. Nulli criminoso in quocunque negotio est credendum. Igitur nec criminosis contra Papam est credendum de hæretica pravitate, si dictum suum nec per legitima documenta, nec per indicia manifesta probauerit, antecedes probari poterit, vt videtur, per illa quæ dicta sunt lib. 6. c. 79. consequentia nullatenus probatione videtur indigere.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. After you have recited what effect heretical credulity ought to have, on the strength of presumption alone, with respect to the Pope, tell me what effect it ought to have with respect to others. MAGISTER. It is said that those who believe the Pope to be a heretic on presumption alone ought, unless it has been established to them by legitimate documents that those who attack the Pope proceed in a calumnious or malicious way, to offer to those who impugn the Pope on the charge of heretical depravity whatever defence they can, and also counsel, aid and favour, and not to trouble them in any way. DISCIPULUS. This assertion seems to me to depend on what was said in book 6, chapters 33 to 35, where you argued that those who impugn a Pope as a heretic on the charge of heretical depravity are to be defended by Catholics. So do not dwell on the first point, but on the seventh conclusion, recited in chapter 13 of this seventh book. MAGISTER. The seventh conclusion is that to any persons who are criminal and of bad repute, if they do not make it clear by legitimate documents or manifest indications that the Pope is a heretic, no credence is to be given. This seems capable of being proved thus. No criminal is to be believed in any matter whatever. Therefore neither are criminals to be believed against the Pope on the charge of heretical depravity, if they have not proved their assertion either by legitimate documents or by manifest indications. The antecedent can, it seems, be proved by what was said in book 6, chapter 79; the consequence seems not to need any proof at all.

units.la: CAP. XXII. In quo correspondenter etiam agitur de scriptis eorum, qui Papa hæreticum impugnant, & eum hæreticum esse nitantur convincere, utrum scil. talia sint videnda & prælegenda, & quod sic, probatur tribus rationibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII. In which, in the same way, it is discussed whether writings of those who attack the Pope as a heretic and try to prove him a heretic ought to be read and studied beforehand. It is shown that they should, by three arguments.

units.la: DISCIP. Quantum ad opus istud mihi sufficiunt ea, quæ dicta sunt in genere, prædicto c. 19. huius. Ideo ad materiam aliam annexam præcedentib. me conuerto. Inquisiuimus enim supra, an imponentes Papæ hæretico perfidiam hæresis sint audiendi, & an eis fides debeat adhiberi. Nunc autem interrogo, an scripta eorum, quæ perfidiam Papæ hæretici declarare niituntur, sint videnda, si in scripturis personam Papæ hæretici & doctrinam eius conati fuerint reprobare. MAGIST. Respondetur, quod scripta talium cum diligentia & studio sunt videnda. quia eisdem rationibus, quibus ostenditur, quod imponentes Papæ hæretico prauitatem hæreticam, debent audiri, videtur posse probari.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. For this work, what has been said in general in chapter 19 above is enough for me. So I turn to the related matter that follows the earlier ones. We have inquired above whether those who charge the Pope with heretical perfidy are to be heard, and whether they should be believed. Now I ask whether the writings of those who try to declare the perfidy of a heretical Pope should be read, if they have tried in their books to refute the person of the heretical Pope and his teaching. TEACHER. The answer is that the writings of such men should be read with care and diligence, since it seems that the same arguments by which it is shown that those who charge the heretical Pope with heretical depravity must be heard can be used to prove this.

units.la: DISCIP. Allega rationes speciales, si quas habes.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Give the special arguments, if you have any.

units.la: MAG. Hoc videtur posse probari sic. magis legenda & videnda sunt scripta catholicorum hæreticam impugnantium prauitatem, quam scripta paganorum infidelium & hæreticorum, quæ catholicam reprobant veritatem. sed scripta paganorum & hæreticorum sunt legenda & videnda, non ad approbandum vel tenendum, sed ad reprobandum vel ad cóuincendum. ergo multo magis scripta perfidiam Papæ hæretici impugnantium & reprobantium sunt legenda & videnda. Maior probatione non indiget. Minor auctoritatibus manifestis videtur posse probari. Hieronymus enim, vt legitur dist. 37. cap. qui de mensa, ait: qui de mensa & vino regis nolunt comedere ne polluantur, vtique si sapientiam atque doctrinam Babyloniorum sirent peccatum esse, nunquam acquiescerent discere, quod non licebat. discimus autem, non vt sequantur: sed vt iudicent & conuincant. quomodo si quispiam aduersus mathematicos velit describere imperitus mathesis risui patebat: & aduersus philosophos disputans, si ignorat documenta philosophorum. discant ergo ea mente documenta & doctrinam Chaldaicam, qua etiam Moyses omnem sapientiam Aegyptiorum didicerat. Item Ambrosius, vt habetur dist. predicta, legimus, ait: legimus aliqua ne negligamur, legimus ne ignoremus, legimus non vt teneamus, sed vt repudiemus. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod scripta philosophorum, paganorum & hæreticorum, & sunt legenda & videnda, non vt probentur, sed vt reprobentur. ergo multo magis scripta catholicorum declarantium perfidiam Papæ hæretici sunt legenda & videnda.
units.tr: TEACHER. This seems to be provable as follows. The writings of Catholics who attack heretical depravity ought to be read and studied more than the writings of pagan unbelievers and heretics who attack Catholic truth. But the writings of pagans and heretics are to be read and studied not to be approved or held, but to be refuted and convicted. Therefore all the more the writings of those who attack and refute the perfidy of a heretical Pope are to be read and studied. The major premise needs no proof. The minor seems provable from clear authorities. Jerome says, as is read in dist. 37, chapter "Qui de mensa": Those who refuse to eat of the king's table and wine, lest they be defiled, would certainly never have agreed to learn what was not allowed, if the wisdom and learning of the Babylonians were a sin. We learn, however, not so that we may follow them, but so that we may judge and convict them. Thus, if someone wished to write against the mathematicians, while ignorant of mathematics he would lay himself open to ridicule; and if he disputed against the philosophers while ignorant of their teachings. Let them therefore learn the teachings and doctrine of the Chaldeans in that spirit, just as Moses too had learned all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Likewise Ambrose, as is found in the same distinction: We read some things so that we are not neglected, we read so that we are not ignorant, we read not so that we may hold them, but so that we may reject them. From these words it is plain that the writings of philosophers, pagans and heretics are to be read and studied, not to be approved, but to be refuted. Therefore all the more are the writings of Catholics declaring the perfidy of a heretical Pope to be read and studied.

units.la: DISCIP. Hæc ratio non procederet, nisi constaret scribentes esse catholicos. quando autem non constaret eos esse catholicos, scripta eorum videnda non essent.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. This argument would not hold unless it were certain that the writers are Catholics. But when it is not certain that they are Catholics, their writings should not be read.

units.la: MAG. Nonnullis apparet, quod omnino hic deciperis. quia arguentes alios contra posuisse libros aduersus Papam & doctrinam eius aut reputant eos catholicos, aut hæreticos: aut dubitant nescientes an sint catholici vel hæretici. Si reputant eos catholicos, libros eorum non debent respuere, sed videre. si reputant eos hæreticos, libros eorum videre debent ad reprobandum errorem, & ad respondendum sophisticis argumentis eorum. exemplo sanctorum & Moysi & Danielis, qui libros infidelium perlegerunt. quomodo enim hæreticorum fallaciæ dissoluantur, nisi legantur? Si autem dubitant nescientes eos esse neque catholicos neque hæreticos, debent libros eorundem legere & videre, vt approbent, si sint catholici, vel reprobent, si fuerint hæretica labe respersi. DISCIP. Facias alias rationes.
units.tr: TEACHER. To some it appears that you are altogether mistaken here. For those who accuse others of having written books against the Pope and his teaching either regard them as Catholics or as heretics, or they doubt, not knowing whether they are Catholic or heretical. If they regard them as Catholics, they ought not to reject their books but to read them. If they regard them as heretics, they ought to read their books in order to refute the error and to answer their sophistical arguments, following the example of the saints, of Moses and of Daniel, who read through the books of unbelievers. For how can the deceptions of heretics be dissolved unless they are read? But if they doubt, not knowing whether these men are Catholic or heretical, they ought to read and examine their books, so that they may approve them if they are Catholic, or reject them if they are stained with heretical taint. DISCIPLE. Give other arguments.

units.la: MAG. Secunda ratio specialiter probat, quod ignorantes Papam esse hæreticum, scripta aliorum contra ipsum debent legere & videre. nam dubia de his maxime, quæ sunt necessaria ad salutem, sunt diligenter discutienda, teste apostolo primo ad Thessalon. omnia autem probate, quod bonum est tenete. vbi dicit, probate. Glossa: ratione discutite, omnia probando incerta. certa ei non indigent discussione. & quod bonum est, id est, quod bonum inuenitur, tenete. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod dubia, præsertim, si fidem & salutem tangant, sunt discutienda diligenter. sed illa quæ scribuntur contra Papam hæreticum, sunt necessaria ad salutem, quia spectant ad fidem, quæ est necessaria ad salutem. ergo nescientes an tales scribentes sint catholici vel hæretici, debent eorum scripta diligenter discutere & examinare. Tertia ratio est hęc. Illorum scripta sunt videnda, cum quibus est licitum disputare, quia per eandem rationem ore quis profert & scribit. quod autem debet audiri, debet etiam legi, si scribitur. Sed cum illis, qui dicunt & scribunt Papam esse hæreticum, licitum est disputare ad veritatem inueniendam. ergo & eorum scripta debent legi & videri.
units.tr: TEACHER. The second argument proves specifically that those who do not know whether the Pope is a heretic ought to read and examine the writings of others against him. For doubtful matters, especially those that are necessary for salvation, must be carefully investigated, as the Apostle witnesses in 1 Thess.: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Here he says prove. The Gloss: Examine by reason, testing all things that are uncertain; things that are certain need no investigation. And that which is good, that is, that which is found good, hold fast. From these words it is gathered that doubtful matters, especially if they touch faith and salvation, are to be carefully investigated. But those things written against a heretical Pope are necessary for salvation, because they concern the faith, which is necessary for salvation. Therefore those who do not know whether such writers are Catholic or heretical ought to examine and test their writings carefully. The third argument is this. Those writings are to be read whose authors it is lawful to dispute with, for by the same reasoning a person speaks and also writes. But what ought to be heard ought also to be read, if it is written. But it is lawful to dispute with those who say and write that the Pope is a heretic, in order to find the truth. Therefore their writings also ought to be read and examined.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: Vbi consequenter agitur de illis, qui talidicto vel scripto Papam, qui vere est hæreticus, impugnantibus minime credere vellent, aut certe eosdem audire recusarent; vtrum tales credentes Papæ hæretico sint censendi, & qua pratera plectendi.
units.tr: Where it is treated in order whether those who are unwilling to believe anyone who attacks the heretical Pope by word or in writing, or who refuse to hear such attackers, are to be counted as believers in the heretical Pope, and by what penalty they are to be punished.

units.la: DISCIP. Quia istæ rationes videntur mihi apparentiam aliqualem habere, reputo probabile, quod scripta catholicorum contra Papam hæreticum sunt nullatenus condemnanda, sed contra prædicta aliquæ obuiationes mihi occurrunt. nolo tamen hic eas tractare: sed inferius dabo tibi occasionem discutiendi eas. Ideo dic nunc breuiter, an illi, qui nolunt credere referentibus Papam esse hæreticum, quando in rei veritate esset hæreticus, & qui nolunt scripta catholicorum contra Papam hæreticum legere, nec videre, sunt inter damnabiliter credentes Papæ hæretico numerandi, & qua pœna sunt plectendi. MAG. Iuxta pertractata duas interrogationes proponis. ad quarum primam distinguendo respondetur, quod nolentium credere Papam esse hæreticum, quandoesset hæreticus, quidam sunt qui damnabiliter nolunt hoc credere: vel quia nolunt de eius perfidia informari, vel quia licet sint informati, nolunt informationib. sufficientibus & fidem facientibus de perfidia Papæ hæretici adhibere fidem. quidam autem sunt vel esse possunt, qui absq; crimine nolunt credere Papam esse hæreticum; vtpote illi, per quos non stat, quin de perfidia Papæ hæretici informentur, & eisdem informationibus fidem facientibus de perfidia Papæ hæretici credant & fidem adhibeant. Item damnabiliter recusantium credere Papam esse haereticum, quidam sunt qui quamuis credant Papam esse haereticum, in nullo possunt ei vel eius erroribus obuiare publice vel occulte: aliqui vero possent eius erroribus publice vel occulte obuiare. Dicitur ergo, quod nolentes credere informationibus rationabilibus facientibus fidem de perfidia Papae haeretici, si possunt sibi vel eius erroribus obuiare, non solum credentes damnabiliter Papae haeretico, sed etiam fautores eiusdem sunt censendi. Si vero in nullo possunt Papae haeretico, nec eius erroribus obuiare, credentes & non fautores reputari debent. Si vero aliqui sint, qui nolunt credere Papam esse haereticum, quia non sunt de eius perfidia informati, nec per eos fiat quod non informentur: nec fautores nec damnabiliter credentes Papae haeretico sunt censendi.
units.tr: DISCIP. Since those arguments seem to me to have some plausibility, I judge it probable that the writings of Catholics against the heretical Pope ought in no way to be condemned. But several objections against what has been said occur to me. I do not wish to deal with them here, but later I will give you the opportunity to examine them. So now tell me briefly whether those who are unwilling to believe those who report that the Pope is a heretic, when in truth he is a heretic, and those who are unwilling to read or even look at Catholic writings against the heretical Pope, are to be counted among those who believe the heretical Pope to their damnation, and by what penalty they are to be punished. MAG. You propose two questions, arising from what we have already discussed. To the first, the answer is made by distinction. Of those who are unwilling to believe that the Pope is a heretic, when he is one, some refuse to believe it to their damnation: either because they do not wish to be informed of his perfidy, or because, although they have been informed, they refuse to give credit to information that is sufficient and trustworthy concerning the perfidy of the heretical Pope. But there are, or may be, others who refuse without sin to believe that the Pope is a heretic: namely, those through whom it is not the case that they are not informed of the perfidy of the heretical Pope, and who believe and give credit to that information, which is trustworthy concerning his perfidy. Again, among those who refuse to believe the Pope is a heretic to their damnation, some believe him to be a heretic, yet are in no position to oppose him or his errors, either publicly or in secret; but others could oppose his errors publicly or in secret. It is said, therefore, that those who refuse to believe reasonable information which gives trustworthy grounds for believing the perfidy of the heretical Pope are to be counted not only as believing the heretical Pope to their damnation, but also as his supporters, if they are able to oppose him or his errors. If, however, they can in no way oppose the heretical Pope or his errors, they ought to be regarded as believers but not as supporters. If there are some who refuse to believe that the Pope is a heretic because they have not been informed of his perfidy, and it is not through them that they are kept uninformed, then they are to be counted neither as supporters nor as believing the heretical Pope to their damnation.

units.la: DISCIP. Intelligo responsionem istorum quantum ad hoc: ideo dic, qua poena illi qui damnabiliter renuunt credere Papam esse haereticum sunt plectendi.
units.tr: DISCIP. I understand the answer of those men as far as this goes. So tell me what penalty those who refuse to believe to their damnation that the Pope is a heretic are to suffer.

units.la: MAG. Ad hoc patet responsio per illa, quae dicta sunt hic & superius. cap. 2. quia, ut dictum est ibi, tales sunt damnabiliter credentes. ibi autem dictum est, quod credentes sunt excommunicationis sententia innodati. Igitur qui damnabiliter renuunt credere Papam esse haereticum, sunt excommunicationis sententia & vinculo allegati.
units.tr: MAG. The answer to this is plain from what has been said here and above, in chapter 2. For, as was said there, such persons are believers to their damnation, and it was said there that believers are bound by the sentence of excommunication. Therefore those who refuse to believe to their damnation that the Pope is a heretic are bound by the sentence of excommunication and by its chain.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic ad secundam interrogationem.
units.tr: DISCIP. Now tell me the answer to the second question.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad ipsam respondetur, quod illi qui damnabiliter renuunt legere vel videre aut audire scripta catholicorum contra Papam haereticum, si possunt obuiare Papae haeretico vel eius erroribus, non solum credentes, sed etiam fautores eiusdem sunt habendi. Si autem obuiare non possunt, solummodo credentes sunt putandi. & tam illi quam hi excommunicationis sententia sunt ligati. DISCIP. Nunquid quae dicta sunt prius secundum ista debent intelligi? MAG. Liquet quod grauius peccent illi qui credunt Papae haeretico, quam aliis, eo quod Papa haereticus est magis nocinus & magis periculosus quam alii haeretici.
units.tr: MAG. To that question the answer is that those who refuse to read, look at, or hear the writings of Catholics against the heretical Pope to their damnation, if they are able to oppose the heretical Pope or his errors, are to be held not only as believers but also as his supporters. If, however, they cannot oppose him, they are to be thought merely believers; and both the one sort and the other are bound by the sentence of excommunication. DISCIP. Ought what was said earlier to be understood in accordance with this? MAG. It is clear that those who believe the heretical Pope sin more gravely than others, because the heretical Pope is more harmful and more dangerous than other heretics.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: Soluit rationem primam factam supra c. 12. probantem quod impugnantibus Papam haereticum non sit credendum, notatur etiam ibidem de detractoribus: & quomodo vel quando malum de aliquo dictum sit credendum vel non credendum.
units.tr: It solves the first argument made above in chapter 12, which proves that one should not believe those who attack the heretical Pope. It is also noted there concerning detractors, and how and when evil spoken of someone is to be believed or not believed.

units.la: DISCIP. Propter illa, quae in hoc loco dicta sunt, hic esset locus quaerendi de fautoribus haereticorum, sed antequam inquiram de his peto ut respondeas ad rationes supra c. 12. allegatas, quibus ostenditur, quod volentibus declarare perfidiam Papae haeretici minime est credendum. Puto enim, quod per responsiones, quas narrabis, siue aliquae earum sint rationabiles siue irrationabiles, totam materiam de credentibus haereticis clarius & magis profunde intelligam.
units.tr: DISCIP. Because of what has been said in this place, this would be the place to inquire about the supporters of heretics. But before I inquire about them, I ask you to respond to the arguments alleged above in chapter 12, by which it is shown that one should in no way believe those who wish to declare the perfidy of the heretical Pope. For I think that through the answers you will give, whether some of them are reasonable or unreasonable, I shall understand the whole matter of believers in heretics more clearly and more deeply.

units.la: MAG. Ad primam dicitur, quod sacra pagina minime reprehendit omnes adhibentes fidem narrantibus aliquid sinistrum de aliquo, sed eum qui cito credit narrantib. mala de alio sacra pagina reprehendit, propter quod scribitur, quod qui cito credit, leuis est corde. Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur esse sciendum: quod non ideo dicitur aliquis damnabiliter cito credere, quia statim credit, quando aliquid siue bonum siue malum narratur de alio. nam & Dauid, ut legitur 2. Reg. 3: ut audiuit, Ioab interfecisse Abner, credidit, nec tamen in hoc peccauit. Sed qui credit cito malum de proximo, leuis corde est & si malum quod cito credit de proximo est peccatum mortale, credendo cito mortaliter peccat. Est ergo videndum, quis credit cito malum de proximo, & quis non credit cito. Dicitur igitur quod aliquis potest credere malum de aliquo dupliciter, quia vel credit malum de aliquo, quod ipsemet percipit de ipso, vel solummodo ex relatione seu narratione aliorum. Si autem aliquis credit malum de aliquo ex aliquo, quod ipsemet percipit de ipso, hoc potest esse dupliciter. Aut illud potest fieri bene & male, aut tantummodo male. Si potest fieri bene & male: ergo ut communiter illud non fit, nisi male (licet in casu singulari & speciali & raro posset fieri bene.) Aut frequenter fit bene & frequenter fit male, sicut frequenter homines cum mulieribus bona intentione loquuntur: saepe etiam bona intentione visitant eas, & dant munera ipsis, ac diuersa solacia habent cum eis: & saepe cum eis mala intentione talia fiunt. Si in hoc casu vel consimili aliquis credat peccatum mortale de alio, peccat mortaliter, quod est iudicium temerarium contra charitatem, quam habere debet ad proximum, quia illa quae possunt fieri bene & male, in meliorem partem interpretari debemus, sicut dicit Beda, ut habetur extra de regulis iuris, eslote. Si autem illud, ex quo quis credit malum de alio, est tale quod ut communiter fit male: raro autem vel nunquam fit bene, licet posset fieri bene, sic non peccat quis suspicando malum de alio. peccat tamen firmiter credendo malum de ipso. & multo magis peccat credendo malum grauius, quam sit illud, quod videt de alio: maxime si illud malum, quod credit de alio, est aliquod enorme excedens peccata, quae ab hominibus communiter fiunt. Sicut si quis videns aliquem multum iratum contra alium, crederet quod ille iratus intenderet eundem occidere, multo magis peccaret, quam solummodo credendo iram, quam videt esse peccatum mortale. & tamen credendo ipsum ex hoc solo, quod irascitur, peccare mortaliter (si iratus ultra non procedat) peccat mortaliter. Potest enim quis irasci multum & interesse contra alium zelo iustitiae & intentione bona absque peccato mortali, & quandoque venialiter solum. Verumtamen suspicando vel dubitando talem iram esse peccatum mortale in ipso non est peccatum mortale. Si etiam ex illis quae habent aliquam speciem mali, quae tamen possunt in casu fieri absque peccato mortali, quis credat aliud peccatum graue committere, peccat grauiter. & de hoc videtur poni exemplum. 34. dist. c. 1. vbi Nico. Papa scribens Aldino Archiepiscopo de immoderata familiaritate, quam habuit quidam Episcopus cum filia sua, noluit credere, quod idem Episcopus carnaliter peccauerat cum filia sua eadem, licet illa immoderata familiaritas habuit speciem mali, sed vult propter scandalum, quod eadem familiaritatem dimittat, scribens in haec verba: Nicolaus, &c. relatum est apostolatui nostro de hoc Episcopo, quod cum quadam filia sua immoderatam tenuit familiaritatem. & ob illud mala fama orta sit ei: pro quare a sanctitate tua caeteris quae coepiscopis tuis ammonitus correctusque est: sed nullatenus emendatus, quae res in hoc maxime displicet, & magis ac magis de se reddit opinionem deteriore, quo beatitudini tuae & coepiscoporum tuorum rationibus non obedit, & per inobedientiam in culpam prothoplausti relabitur. oportet igitur fraternitatem tuam synodale cum Episcopis & suffraganeis tuis convocare consilium, & salutarib. eloquiis Episcopum convenire, atque illi pastorali auctoritate praecipere, quatenus ab omnium bestiarum vel volucrum venatione penitus alienus existat, atque ab immoderata filiae suae familiaritate se omnino cohibeat. quod si parere contempserit, & tam pro venationis inclinatione quam pro immoderata filiae suae conversatione vitanda vobis ammonentib. obedire distulerit, a vestro collegio excommunicatus abscedat. quod si in hoc contumax apparuerit, a ministerio cessare debebit. Ex his verbis colligitur, quod Episcopus immoderatam familiaritatem habuit cum filia sua. & qualis fuit illa immoderata familiaritas, Glossa super verbo fama exprimit dicens: coram omnib. eam deosculabatur & ponebat manum in gremio eius. quod ipsem mali videtur habere, quia ut communiter osculum mulieris nimium iteratum & positio manus in gremium siue sinum ex immundo corde procedit, & cor impudicum praetendit, & tamen ex tali specie mali noluit nihilominus Nicol. Papa non solum credere, sed nec etiam suspicari, quod idem Episcopus in lapsum carnis inciderit, & etiam noluit quod ei indiceretur purgatio, non obstante mala fama ex hoc orta de ipso, testante Glossa, quae ibidem ait: non quod aliquid in ipso existimaretur propter foedus naturale, sed quia coram omnibus eam nimis osculabatur & ponebat manum in gremium eius, & ideo non fuit ei indicta purgatio.
units.tr: MAG. To the first, it is said that Holy Scripture does not at all rebuke all who give credence to those who report something unfavourable about someone; rather, it rebukes him who readily believes those who report evil about another, for it is written that he who readily believes is light of heart. To make this clear, it must be understood that a person is not said to believe too readily to his damnation merely because he believes at once when something, whether good or bad, is reported about another. For David too, as we read in 2 Sam. 3, when he heard that Joab had killed Abner, believed it, and yet he did not sin in this. But he who readily believes evil of his neighbour is light of heart; and if the evil that he readily believes of his neighbour is a mortal sin, then by believing readily he sins mortally. We must therefore consider who readily believes evil of his neighbour, and who does not readily believe it. It is said, then, that one can believe evil of someone in two ways: either he believes evil of someone on the basis of what he himself perceives of that person, or only on the report or narration of others. If someone believes evil of another on the basis of what he himself perceives of him, this can happen in two ways. Either the act can be done well and badly, or only badly. If it can be done well and badly, then, as a rule, it is not done except badly (although in a single, special and rare case it could be done well). Or it is frequently done well and frequently done badly, as men frequently speak with women with good intentions, often also visit them with good intentions, give them gifts, and have various comforts with them; and often such things are done with them with bad intentions. In this case, or in a similar one, if someone believes a mortal sin of another, he sins mortally, because it is a rash judgement contrary to the charity which he ought to have toward his neighbour; for those things which can be done well and badly we ought to interpret in the better part, as Bede says, and as is found in extra de regulis iuris, eslote. If, however, that on the basis of which someone believes evil of another is of such a kind that, as a rule, it is done badly, and rarely or never done well, although it could be done well, then one does not sin by suspecting evil of another; yet he sins by firmly believing evil of him. And he sins much more when he believes an evil that is graver than what he sees of the other, especially if the evil he believes of another is something enormous and exceeding the sins that are commonly committed by men. Thus, if someone seeing another very angry with a third person should believe that the angry man intended to kill him, he would sin much more than if he believed only the anger, which he sees to be a mortal sin. And yet, if he believes on this alone, that the man is angry, that he sins mortally (if the angry man does not proceed further), he sins mortally. For a man may be very angry with another and take a stand against him from zeal for justice and with good intention, without mortal sin, and sometimes only venially. Yet to suspect or doubt that such anger in him is a mortal sin is not itself a mortal sin. Likewise, if someone believes that another has committed some other grave sin on the basis of things which have some appearance of evil, but which in a given case can be done without mortal sin, he sins gravely. And an example of this seems to be given in Dist. 34, c. 1, where Pope Nicholas, writing to Aldinus, Archbishop, about the immoderate familiarity which a certain bishop had with his own daughter, did not wish to believe that the same bishop had sinned carnally with that daughter, although that immoderate familiarity had an appearance of evil. But because of the scandal, he wished that the familiarity be given up, writing in these words: "Nicholas, etc. It has been reported to our apostolate about this bishop that he kept an immoderate familiarity with a certain daughter of his, and that from this an evil reputation has arisen for him. For this reason he has been admonished and corrected by your holiness and by your fellow bishops, but in no way amended. This thing displeases most of all, and makes his reputation worse and worse, since he does not obey the reasons of your blessedness and of your fellow bishops, and through disobedience he relapses into the guilt of the first transgressor. It is necessary, therefore, that your brotherhood convene a synodal council with your bishops and suffragans, and address the bishop with wholesome words, and command him with pastoral authority, that he keep himself wholly free from the hunting of all beasts and birds, and that he restrain himself entirely from the immoderate familiarity with his daughter. If he scorns to obey, and delays to obey you admonishing him, both on account of his inclination to hunting and for the avoiding of his immoderate association with his daughter, let him be excommunicated by your college and depart. If he shows himself stubborn in this, he shall be obliged to cease from the ministry." From these words it is gathered that the bishop had an immoderate familiarity with his daughter. And what sort of immoderate familiarity it was, the Gloss on the word "fama" declares, saying: "he kissed her in front of everyone and placed his hand in her lap." This in itself seems to have an appearance of evil, because, as a rule, a kiss repeated too often on a woman and the placing of a hand in her lap or bosom proceeds from an impure heart and shows an unchaste mind. Yet, despite such an appearance of evil, Pope Nicholas nevertheless was unwilling not only to believe, but even to suspect, that the same bishop had fallen into carnal sin; and he was also unwilling that a purgation be ordered for him, although an evil reputation had arisen concerning him from this, as the Gloss attests, which says there: not that anything was thought of him on account of natural kinship, but because he kissed her too much in front of everyone and placed his hand in her lap, and therefore a purgation was not ordered for him.

units.la: DISCIP. Quare non fuit ei indicta purgatio, ex quo extitit diffamatus; teste Nicolao, qui in verbis praemissis dicit, ob illud mala fama orta est ei?
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Why was no purgation imposed on him, since he was defamed, as Nicholas testifies in the words quoted above, which say that a bad reputation arose for him because of that?

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quod purgatio non debet diffamato indici, nisi quando de crimine diffamatur. Iste autem Episcopus de crimine, puta de lapsu criminis, minime extitit diffamatus: sed erat tantummodo diffamatus de immoderata familiaritate filiae suae, quae quamuis fuerit immoderata, & ut communiter immoderata familiaris mulieris sit cum peccato mortali: tamen talis immoderatio potest carere peccato mortali: quia non omnis immoderatio est peccatum mortale. Ideo iste Episcopus non fuit de crimine diffamatus. quare sibi non debuit indici purgatio: sed debuit ammoneri, quia etiam de venialibus ammonitio fieri potest.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer is that purgation ought not to be imposed on a defamed person unless he is defamed of a crime. This bishop, however, was not defamed of a crime, such as a sin of the flesh. He was only defamed of an immoderate familiarity with his daughter. Although such familiarity was immoderate, and immoderate familiarity with a woman is usually a mortal sin, such immoderation can be free of mortal sin, because not every immoderation is a mortal sin. So this bishop was not defamed of a crime, and purgation should not have been imposed on him. He should have been admonished instead, since admonition can be given even for venial sins.

units.la: DISCIP. Unde accidit, quod aliquis credit malum de alio, ex illo quod frequenter fit bene & male, & ex illo quod habet spem mali & frequenter fit male, & nunquam vel raro bene.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. How does it happen that someone thinks ill of another because that other often does good and evil, and because he has a hope of evil and often does evil, and never or rarely does good?

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quod ut communiter hoc provenit ex duobus, ex hoc videl. quod taliter credentes malum de alio consimilibus criminib. publice vel occulte aut voluntate sunt infecti: & ideo iudicant de aliis, sicut sentiunt de seipsis. & quia credunt alios esse tales in actibus exterioribus etiam indifferentibus, quales sciunt esse seipsos publice vel occulte, aut secundum voluntatem & desiderium cordis. unde sunt quidam, qui omnes suspiciosos & cito credentes crimina quecunque de proximo repurant actu vel voluntate eisdem criminibus irretitos. provenit etiam talis credulitas mala ex inimicitia vel odio, aut ira, quam habent sic credentes ad illos, quos credunt esse malos: quia vnusquisque malus cito credit malum de illo, quem odit.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer is that this usually arises from two things. First, those who think ill of another in this way are themselves tainted with the same crimes, publicly or secretly, or in their will; so they judge others as they feel about themselves. And since they believe others to be such in outward actions, even indifferent ones, as they know themselves to be, publicly or secretly, or in the desire and longing of their heart, there are some who suspect and quickly believe every crime of their neighbour, because they judge him by their own act or will ensnared in those same crimes. Second, such bad credulity also arises from enmity, hatred or anger which those who believe in this way bear toward those whom they think to be evil, since every wicked man readily believes evil of the one he hates.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic de credente aliquem esse malum ex aliquo, quod non potest fieri nisi male.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Tell me whether someone believes another to be evil because of something that can be done only in an evil way.

units.la: MAGIST. Dicitur quod qui credit aliquem esse malum, quia percipit per seipsum aliquid de eo, quod non potest fieri nisi tantummodo male: non peccat ex hoc quod credit malum de ipso. quia propter illa, quae non possunt fieri bene, licitum est cuilibet iudicare & reputare malum illum qui facit. haec est sententia Bedae, ut habetur extra de regulis iur. estote. qui ait: quod scriptum est; Ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos, de manifestis dictum est, quae non possunt bono animo fieri, ut stuprum, blasphemia, furtu, haeresis, & similia, de quibus nobis permittitur iudicare. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod propter illa, quae non possunt fieri bene, licet credere aliquem esse malum.
units.tr: MASTER. It is said that one who believes another to be evil, because he perceives in himself something of that person that cannot be done except in an evil way, does not sin by believing evil of him. For on account of those things which cannot be done well, anyone may lawfully judge and reckon him who does them to be evil. This is the opinion of Bede, as found in the Extra, in the title on the rules of law, "Estote", who says: what is written, "By their fruits you shall know them", has been said of manifest things which cannot be done with a good mind, such as fornication, blasphemy, theft, heresy and the like, concerning which we are permitted to judge. From these words it is gathered that, on account of those things which cannot be done well, it is lawful to believe someone to be evil.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic de isto, qui credit malum de alio solummodo propter relationem vel narrationem alicuius vel aliquorum.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Tell me about one who believes evil of another solely on the report or narration of some one person or of several.

units.la: MAG. De hoc, scilicet quando quis debeat credere malum de aliquo propter relationem vel narrationem alicuius vel aliquorum, & quando non debet, difficile vel impossibile est dare regulam generalem, quae in nullo casu deficiat. quia aliquando credendum est extra iudicium dicto vnius: aliquando non est credendum dicto vnius etiam extra iudicium: aliquando credendum est dicto multorum, & aliquando non: quandoque etiam credendum est famae, & quandoque non est credendum famae: interdum etiam credendum est praesumptionibus, quae narrantur interdum illis minime est credendum, ista omnia, ut nonnullis apparet, per rationes apertas, exempla & iura possent copiose probari: sed propter prolixitatem vitandam videtur non esse insistendum. dicitur igitur, quod quemadmodum, ut habetur extra de testibus c. praeterea, iudex circumspectus & discretus debet formare motum animi sui ex argumentis & testimoniis, quae rei aptiora esse compererit, ita etiam vnusquisq; audiens extra iudicium referentes malum de aliquo ad hoc, quod credat vel non credat, saepe ex multis conscientiam suam formare tenetur: quia saepe extra iudicium sicut in iudicio ad faciendum fidem de malo alterius, & si non possunt singula, tamen multa collecta simul iuvant.
units.tr: MASTER. Concerning this, namely when a person ought to believe evil of someone on the report or narration of one or more people, and when he ought not, it is difficult or impossible to give a general rule which fails in no case. Sometimes one must believe the word of one person even outside judgment; sometimes one must not believe the word of one person even outside judgment; sometimes one must believe the word of many, and sometimes not; sometimes one must believe rumour, and sometimes not; at times one must believe presumptions, and at times they are by no means to be believed. All these things, as seems clear to some, could be copiously proved by open reasons, examples and laws; but to avoid prolixity it seems we should not dwell on them. We say, therefore, that just as, as is found in the Extra, in the title on witnesses, chapter "Praeterea", a wise and discerning judge ought to form the motion of his mind from the arguments and testimonies which he finds most fitting to the matter, so also everyone hearing reports of evil about someone outside judgment is often bound to form his conscience, in order to believe or not believe, from many things together. For outside judgment, as in judgment, often serves to establish belief about another's evil; and if the individual items cannot do so, yet many gathered together help.

units.la: Discip. Applica praedicta ad propositum.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Apply what has been said to our purpose.

units.la: Magist. Secundum ista dicitur aliquis cito credere malum de proximo, qui ex his solum modo, quae possunt fieri bene & male, credunt ipsum esse malum. qui autem credunt ipsum esse malum ex his, quae nunquam bono animo fieri possunt, non cito credunt. Iterum qui ex his, quae possunt fieri bene & male & aliis multis concurrentibus simul, ex quibus simul potest quis licite informare conscientiam suam de malo proximi, non cito credit eum esse malum. Item si ex sola relatione malorum inimicorum aduersariorum causam habentium contra aliquem abs q; aliis ami- niculis quis ipsum credit esse malum, cito credit. qui autem credit ex relatione virorum fidelium, praesertim sub iuramento afferentium per certam scientiam malum de proximo etiam extra iudicium, non cito credit. Iterum qui ex relatione malorum vel inimicorum aliis concurrentib. indiciis & amminiculis, quae simul iuncta faciunt fidem credit, non cito credit. Discip. Satis apparet, quod non est facile dare regulam generalem, qua cognoscatur, quando quis credit cito vel non credit cito extra iudicium, quia alio modo dicitur vnus credere ito in vno casu, & alio modo idem vel alter in alio casu. hoc generali omisso, dicalias vias secundum istos, quib. in speciali cognoscitur, quod credens Papam esse haereticum credit cito vel non cito.
units.tr: MASTER. According to these principles, someone is said to believe evil of his neighbour quickly if he believes him to be evil only from those things which can be done both well and badly. But those who believe him to be evil from things which can never be done with a good mind do not believe quickly. Again, one who believes from things that can be done well and badly, together with many other concurring circumstances from which one may lawfully inform his conscience about his neighbour's evil, does not believe him to be evil quickly. Likewise, if someone believes another to be evil solely on the report of evil enemies or adversaries who have a cause against him, without other supports, he believes quickly. But one who believes on the report of faithful men, especially those who assert with certain knowledge and under oath evil about a neighbour, even outside judgment, does not believe quickly. Again, one who believes on the report of evil men or enemies, together with other concurring indications and supports which together make belief, does not believe quickly. DISCIPLE. It is clear enough that it is not easy to give a general rule by which one may recognise when someone believes quickly or not quickly outside judgment, since one person is said to believe quickly in one case and in another way the same or another person in a different case. Setting this general point aside, tell me the other ways, according to these authorities, by which it is recognised in particular whether one who believes the Pope to be a heretic believes quickly or not.

units.la: Magist. De hoc dicitur, quod videns Bullam haereticalem Papae & videns Papam esse haereticum, non credit cito, nec peccat in aliquo, imo peccaret, si haereticum eum non credit, quia scire tenetur, quod quamuis non omnis errans contra fidem sit haereticus, tamen errans contra fidem & suum errorem solenniter vltimata deliberatione diffiniens, haereticus est. Item videns transsumptum bullae haereticalis, & cognoscens quod est transsumptum bullae, ac credens in ipso haeresim diffiniri; & ex hoc credens Papam esse haereticum, non cito credit, imo credere tenetur de necessitate salutis: sicut credere tenetur, si videret bullam talis Papae haeretici. Iterum si quis audit alios, qui hactenus bonae famae sunt, publice & constanter asserere, & paratos iurare, Papam haeresim manifestam, quam in speciali exponunt & exprimunt, solenniter diffinisse, quamuis neque bullam haereticalem neq; transsumptum ostenderent, & ex hoc credens Papam esse haereticum, non cito credit nec peccat credendo. Item audiens Papam publice ex determinata haeresi diffamari: nec Papa negat se illam docere, nec purgat in aliquo famam suam, non cito credit, si credit ipsum esse haereticum. Item audiens a fide dignis Papam publice praedicare haereses manifestas, & quod tenentibus, docentibus, praedicantibus & divulgantibus ipsas fovet & eos diligit, promovet & honorat: tenentes autem contrarias veritates odit, persequitur & molestat, non credit cito, si credit ipsum Papam esse haereticum. Item sciens quod Papae a viris literatis hactenus prouidis & discretis reputatis haereses manifestae imponuntur, qui etiam petunt cum instantia fieri concilium generale: si Papa impedit celebrari concilium generale, nec suam declarat innocentiam de impositis criminibus manifestis, non cito credit, si ipsum credit esse haereticum. qui autem videns in bulla Papae assertionem aliam continet, quae sensum haereticum potest habere: & nec ex antecedentibus, nec ex sequentibus, nec ex aliis dictis vel scriptis talis Papae potest patenter inferri, quod sensus haereticus de mente Papae est, cito credit & peccat mortaliter, si sic credit eum esse haereticum, quia maliciose peruertit assertionem Papae. & idem est tenendum de assertionibus & opinionibus aliorum. Item qui videt aliquod scriptum Papae, in quo nihil diffinitiue tanquam Papa determinat, sed tanquam priuata persona de diuersis tractandis docet & inquirit. & in eodem scripto haeresim reperit manifestam, cuius contrarium veritatem non tenetur Papa explicite credere; si propter talem haeresim credit Papam esse haereticum, cito credit, licet non cito credat credendo ipsum errare. Si autem in scripto Papae quae reperiat haeresim manifestam, cuius contrarium tenetur credere explicite, & non solummodo recitatam, sed assertam aut opinatam vel etiam dubitatam, non credit cito, si credit Papam haereticum ante dictum. unde si quis legeret in libro, sermone seu scripto Papae quocunque, quod Christus non fuit mortuus: quod non ascendit in coelum: aut quod mortui non resurgent: quod non est infernus, vel aliquod tale, cuius contrarium Papa tenetur explicite credere, non crederet cito, qui statim crederet Papam esse haereticum, postquam sibi constaret tale scriptum esse Papae. Item, qui videns solummodo aliquas reportationes sermonum vel determinationum aut assertionum Papae, in quibus haeresis, de qua non est mentio principalis, asseritur, si credit Papam esse haereticum, cito credit & peccat mortaliter. si vero audit a fide dignis talem haeresim esse de mente Papae, & quod est veraciter reportata & non ex errore, non credit cito, si credit Papam esse haereticum. Item, qui audit aliquos criminosos, pestilentes, inimicos Papae, leues, vel detractores conspirantes malum de aliis credentes faciliter referentes Papam esse haereticum, cito credit, licet in rei veritate esset haereticus. talibus enim nunquam in praeiudicium alterius est credendum. DISCIP. Videtur quod credendum sit eis, quia non est verisimile, quod aliquis sit immemor tantae senitatis corporalis, quam spiritualis, sed tales si mendaciter Papam de haeresi diffamarent, essent in periculo tam corporis quam animae, quia & damnabiliter mentirentur, & Papa de eis grauissimam sumeret vltionem.
units.tr: MASTER. On this point it is said that one who sees a heretical bull of the Pope, and sees that the Pope is a heretic, does not believe quickly, nor does he sin in anything; indeed he would sin if he did not believe him a heretic, because he is bound to know that, although not every person erring against the faith is a heretic, yet one who solemnly defines his error against the faith, after final deliberation, is a heretic. Likewise, one who sees a copy of a heretical bull, and knows that it is a copy of a bull, and believes that heresy is defined in it, and from this believes the Pope to be a heretic, does not believe quickly; indeed he is bound to believe it for the necessity of salvation, just as he would be bound to believe if he saw the bull of such a heretical Pope. Again, if someone hears others, who until now have had a good reputation, publicly and constantly assert, and are ready to swear, that the Pope has solemnly defined a manifest heresy, which they set out and express in particular, even though they do not show the heretical bull or a copy of it, and from this believes the Pope to be a heretic, he does not believe quickly, nor does he sin in believing. Likewise, one who hears that the Pope is publicly defamed for a definite heresy, and the Pope neither denies that he teaches it nor in any way clears his reputation, does not believe quickly if he believes him to be a heretic. Likewise, one who hears from trustworthy people that the Pope publicly preaches manifest heresies, and that he favours, loves, promotes and honours those who hold, teach, preach and spread them, while he hates, persecutes and harasses those who hold contrary truths, does not believe quickly if he believes the Pope to be a heretic. Likewise, one who knows that manifest heresies are imposed on the Pope by learned men, until now regarded as wise and discerning, who also insistently ask that a general council be held, and the Pope prevents a general council from being convened and does not declare his innocence of the manifest crimes charged against him, does not believe quickly if he believes him to be a heretic. But one who, seeing in a bull of the Pope an assertion which can bear a heretical sense, and from which neither the preceding nor the following words, nor other sayings or writings of that Pope, can plainly show that a heretical sense is in the Pope's mind, believes quickly and sins mortally if he thus believes him to be a heretic, because he maliciously perverts the Pope's assertion. And the same must be held concerning the assertions and opinions of others. Likewise, one who sees some writing of the Pope, in which he does not determine anything definitively as Pope, but teaches and inquires about various matters as a private person, and in the same writing finds a manifest heresy, the contrary of which the Pope is not bound to believe explicitly; if he believes the Pope to be a heretic because of such heresy, he believes quickly, although he does not believe quickly that the Pope is in error by believing it. But if in a writing of the Pope he finds a manifest heresy, the contrary of which one is bound to believe explicitly, and it is not merely recited but asserted, or held as an opinion, or even doubted, he does not believe quickly if he believes the aforesaid Pope to be a heretic. Hence, if someone should read in any book, sermon or writing of any Pope that Christ did not die, that he did not ascend into heaven, that the dead will not rise, that there is no hell, or anything of that kind, the contrary of which the Pope is bound to believe explicitly, he would not believe quickly who immediately believed the Pope to be a heretic, once it was established to him that such a writing was the Pope's. Likewise, one who sees only some reports of sermons, determinations or assertions of the Pope, in which a heresy that is not the main subject is asserted, believes quickly and sins mortally if he believes the Pope to be a heretic. But if he hears from trustworthy people that such a heresy is in the Pope's mind, and that it is truly reported and not a mistake, he does not believe quickly if he believes the Pope to be a heretic. Likewise, one who hears some criminal, pestilent or hostile persons, enemies of the Pope, or light and slanderous people, conspiring to think evil of others, and easily reporting the Pope to be a heretic, believes quickly, even if in the truth of the matter the Pope were a heretic; for such people must never be believed to the prejudice of another. DISCIPLE. It seems that they should be believed, since it is not likely that anyone would be so forgetful of his bodily safety as of his spiritual safety; but such people, if they defamed the Pope of heresy falsely, would be in danger both of body and of soul, since they would lie damnably, and the Pope would take the most severe vengeance on them.

units.la: MAGIST. Distinguitur de hoc: quia aut tales criminosi, pestilentes & huiusmodi solum modo in occulto diffamant Papam de haeretica prauitate, aut publice in speciali sibi imponunt haereses manifestas, offerentes se probaturos Papam esse haereticum, & tamen petentes iustitiam in primo casu non esset eis credendum. & qui eis credit, cito credit: nec etiam propter eorum verba in occulto est aliquo modo suspicandum vel praesumendum Papam esse haereticum, quia verba in tali occulto non debent facere fidem, sed debent esse suspecta, vt nequaquam in praeiudicium cuiuscunque credatur eisdem. In secundo vero casu, licet talibus minime sit credendum, propter eos tamen licet suspicari Papam esse haereticum, & dubitare de fidelitate eius in tantum quod quilibet quantum sibi licet pro gradu suo & officio tenetur de hoc quaerere sollicite veritatem.
units.tr: MASTER: A distinction must be made here. Such men, criminals, pests and the like, either slander the Pope for heretical depravity only in secret, or they openly and publicly charge him with manifest heresies, offering to prove that the Pope is a heretic and at the same time demanding justice. In the first case they are not to be believed; and whoever believes them believes rashly. Nor, on account of their words spoken in secret, is anyone to suspect or presume in any way that the Pope is a heretic, for words spoken in such secrecy ought not to carry credibility but ought to be regarded with suspicion, so that they are never believed to the prejudice of anyone. In the second case, although such men are by no means to be believed, nevertheless on their account it is permissible to suspect that the Pope is a heretic and to doubt his faithfulness to such an extent that everyone, so far as his rank and office allow, is bound to inquire diligently into the truth of the matter.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Pertractat vnam difficultatem, scilicet an propter relationem detrahentium maior sit suspicio de aliquo habenda, vbi etiam notantur quaedam valde necessaria de mendacio.
units.tr: Treats of one difficulty, namely whether greater suspicion ought to be had of someone on account of the report of detractors. Certain very necessary points about lying are also noted here.

units.la: DISCIP. Aliqualiter distinguendo interrogo, an propter verba criminosorum & detractorum & huiusmodi pestilentium publice haeresim siue aliud crimen de aliquo asserentium maior suspicio sit habenda de Papa siue de alio praelato vel subdito diuite & potente vel paupere.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I ask, making a distinction, whether greater suspicion ought to be had of the Pope, or of any other prelate or subject, rich and powerful or poor, because of the words of criminals, detractors, and such pestilent men who publicly assert heresy or some other crime about him.

units.la: MAG. Ad hoc dicitur distinguendo, quod aut imponentes vel referentes crimen de alio sunt laesi, turbati vel provocati qualitercunque ab eo, cui crimen imponunt, sive etiam sunt aemuli, inimici, aduersarii vel quocunque modo sive in agibilibus sive in speculabilibus notabiliter contrariantes eidem, sive in causa amici sui subditi praelati vel quomodolibet talibus, adhaerentes aut imponentes vel etiam referentes crimen de alio non sunt laesi. nec per aliquod factum aut dictum eius vel amicorum eius sunt provocati contra ipsum, nec aliquam intentionem notabilem sive contrarietatem neque in speculabilibus neque in agibilibus habent contra ipsum. Si itaque aliqui diffamant vel imponunt sive referunt crimen de paupere amico secundum veritatem secundum opinionem ipsorum laesi vel quomodolibet perturbati contra ipsum: vel sunt inimici aemuli, aduersarii, perturbati vel aliquo modo contrariantes eidem, minus credendum est eis, quam si imponerent vel referrent crimen de Papa etiam dictis modis Papae aemuli existentes, sive non similiter si referentes crimen de Papa & de paupere nec ab vno nec ab alio sunt offensi: nec aliquam rationem contrarietatis vel inimicitiae plus habent supra vnum quam supra alium, magis praesumendum est de referentibus crimen Papae quam pauperis quod minime mentiantur. Si vero referentes crimen de paupere contra ipsum nullam rationem contrarietatis vel inimicitiae habet contra Papam, quem simpliciter infamant, habent rationem contrarietatis praedictae; magis praesumedum est tunc de crimine pauperis quam de crimine Papae, quod a veritate nequaquam aberrant, nec eidem proportionabiliter esse credendum, dicitur de omnibus supradictis, scilicet praelato & subdito & paupere.
units.tr: MASTER. To this I answer by distinguishing. Either those who impute or report a crime about another are wronged, troubled, or provoked in some way by the man they accuse, or they are his rivals, enemies, or opponents, or in some way notably opposed to him, whether in matters of action or of speculation; or, in the cause of a friend, subject, prelate, or anyone of that kind, they cling to such people, or impute or report a crime about another, and yet are not wronged. They have not been provoked against him by any deed or word of his or of his friends, and they hold no notable intention or opposition against him, either in speculation or in action. So if some men defame, impute, or report a crime, truly or as they believe, about a poor friend, while they are wronged or somehow troubled by him, or are his enemies, rivals, opponents, troubled, or in some way opposed to him, they are to be believed less than if they imputed or reported a crime about the Pope while being rivals of the Pope in the aforesaid ways. It is not the same if those who report a crime about the Pope and about a poor man are offended by neither one nor the other, and have no ground of opposition or enmity greater against one than against the other. Then we ought rather to presume that those reporting a crime about the Pope do not lie, rather than those reporting one about the poor man. But if those who report a crime about the poor man against him have no ground of opposition or enmity against the Pope, whom they simply defame, but do have that ground against the poor man, then we ought to presume more readily that the crime of the poor man is true, rather than the crime of the Pope, because they by no means stray from the truth. And what is said of these things, namely that one is not to be believed in proportion, is said of all the aforesaid: prelate, subject, and poor man alike.

units.la: DISCIP. Primum probare breuiter conteris.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Briefly prove the first point.

units.la: MAG. Primum sit, quod minus credendum est aduersariis, qui erga pauperem sunt offensi vel turbati, quam aduersariis Papae. Probatur primo sic. Tanto minus credendum est aduersariis alicuius imponentibus siue referentibus crimen de eo, quanto habent pauciora ipsos retrahentia a talibus diffamationib. & relationib. de ipso. sed aduersarii pauperis sunt huiusmodi, quia quicquid retraheret aduersarium pauperis a talibus, etiam retraheret aduersarium Papae. Si enim ex conscientia dimitterit aduersarius pauperis referre talia de paupere: hoc etiam dimitteret aduersarius Papae de Papa. Si etiam dimittit ne inueniatur mendax, eadem ratione ne mendax inueniatur de Papa. Si etiam dimittit ne scandalisetur vel offendat multo magis ex hoc silebit de Papa. & sic consimiliter quicquid tales retraheret a referendo malum de paupere, retraheret aduersarium Papae ad referendum malum de Papa. multa vero retrahunt aduersarium Papae a referendo malum de Papa quae non retrahunt aduersarium pauperis a referendo de paupere: puta timor potentiae Papae. Vnde per experientiam quotidianam videtur, quod nonnulli aduersarii Papae timore potentiae Papae a relatione criminum eius se compescunt: quamen contra pauperes eis crimen imponendo vel imponitra referendo linguas suas laxare impudenter non desinunt. Similiter spes obtinendi beneficium vel honorem a Papa potest retrahere aduersarium eius a praedictis relationibus: non autem aduersarium pauperis, a quo beneficium vel honorem magnum sperare non potest. plura etiam alia retraherent & retrahunt aduersarium Papae, quae nequaquam aduersarium pauperis retrahere dinoscuntur. ergo minus credendum est aduersariis pauperis imponentibus sibi crimen vel impositum referentibus, quam aduersario Papae sibi eadem facientibus.
units.tr: MASTER. Let the first point be this: those adversaries who are offended or troubled toward a poor man are to be believed less than the adversaries of the Pope. It is proved first thus. The adversaries of anyone who impute or report a crime about him are to be believed less in proportion as fewer things restrain them from such defamations and reports about him. But the adversaries of a poor man are of this kind, because whatever would restrain the adversary of a poor man from such things would also restrain the adversary of the Pope. For if from conscience the adversary of a poor man would refrain from reporting such things about the poor man, the adversary of the Pope would likewise refrain from reporting them about the Pope. If he refrains lest he be found a liar, then by the same reasoning he refrains lest he be found a liar about the Pope. If he refrains lest he cause scandal or offence, much more will he be silent about the Pope for this reason. And so, in the same way, whatever would restrain such men from reporting evil about a poor man would restrain the adversary of the Pope from reporting evil about the Pope. Yet many things restrain the adversary of the Pope from reporting evil about the Pope which do not restrain the adversary of a poor man from reporting about the poor man, for example, fear of the Pope's power. Hence daily experience shows that some adversaries of the Pope restrain themselves from reporting his crimes for fear of his power, yet against poor men, by imputing crimes to them or by reporting what has been imputed, they never stop shamelessly loosing their tongues. Likewise, the hope of obtaining a benefice or honour from the Pope can restrain his adversary from the aforesaid reports, but not the adversary of a poor man, from whom he cannot hope for any great benefice or honour. Many other things would restrain, and do restrain, the adversary of the Pope, which are known not to restrain the adversary of a poor man. Therefore the adversaries of a poor man who impute a crime to him, or who report what has been imputed, are to be believed less than the adversary of the Pope who does the same to the Pope.

units.la: Secundo sic. minus credendum est aduersariis eorum, qui citius & facilius & communius calumniam lumniam luminiam, odium, persecutionem & infestationem aliorum incurrunt, quantum ad opus exterius, quam aduersarius illius, qui non ita cito, nec ita faciliter calumniam, odium & cætera incurrit. Sed huiusmodi est pauper respectu Papæ. Ergo minus aduersariis eius in talibus est credendum. Maior est manifesta: quia homines facilius maxime loquuntur de illis, quos calumniantur, persequuntur & odiunt, quam de aliis. Propter quod secundum iura testimonium inimici nullatenus est admittendum. Minor autem per scripturas diuinas probatur aperte. Unde Prouerb. c. 14. dicitur: etiam proximo suo pauper odiosus erit, amici vero diuitum multi. quod præcipue verum est de odio exteriori: quia licet sæpe diuites odium interius plurimum incurrant, quam pauperes, pro eo quod plures offenduntur, sæpe tamen odientes diuites odium in exteriori opere minime manifestant. Item Salomon ibidem c. 4. Diuitia addunt amicos plurimos: a paupere autem & hi quos habuit separantur. & post: multi conluntur personam diuitis & amici sunt donum tribuentis: fratres hominis pauperis oderunt eum, insuper & amici longe recesserunt ab eo. Ex quibus patet, quod pauperes citius quam diuites odium incurrunt. Item Ecclesiastici 13. scribitur: diues locutus est & omnes tacuerunt, & verbum illius usque ad nubes perducent: pauper locutus est, & dicunt, quis est hic? & si offenderit, subuertunt illum. Item ibidem: Diues commotus conformatur ab amicis suis, humilis autem cum ceciderit expelletur & a notis. Diuiti decepto multi recuperatores, locutus est superba, & iustificauerunt illum; humilis deceptus est, insuper & arguitur, locutus est sensate & non est ei datus locus. Et Amos 4. sic scribitur: Vaccæ pingues, qui estis in monte Samariæ, qui calumniam facitis egenis, & confunditis pauperes. Ex quibus aliisque verbis quamplurimis aperte colligitur, quod pauperes communius persecutionem, infestationem & calumniam patiuntur, quam diuites & potentes: & ideo minus credendum est aduersariis eorum, quam diuitum de ipsis siniistra narrantibus. Magis igitur præsumendum de aduersariis Papæ, cum publice crimen hæresis vel aliquid sibi imponunt, quod dictum eorum non est a veritate totaliter alienum, quamuis si sint criminosi, eis sit fides nullatenus adhibenda, & multo minus crederet pauperibus crimen imponentibus, aut ab aliis impositum narrantibus vel diuulgantibus quoquomodo, quod maxime continet veritatem, quando pauper multos offendit & plurimos habet aduersarios diuites & potentes. In hoc enim casu celeratior homo mundi unico verbo potest de paupere infamiam salsissimam absque diuino miraculo indelibilem sustinere. Si enim mendacissimus crimen quodcunque de paupere odioso confinxerit, & uni soli asserendo retulit, ille aliis dimulgabit, dicens, tale crimen tali imponitur, quod postea alii certissime narrabunt: & sic tale mendacium tanquam verum & certum ad omnes eius inimicos deveniet, & amicos tandem non latebit: & sic erit apud omnes (quamuis mendaciter) diffamatus, quare causa pauperis odiosi est diligentissime & strictissime perscrutanda, ne per potentiam & mendacia opprimatur.
units.tr: Secondly, thus. The adversaries of those who more quickly, more easily, and more commonly incur calumny, hatred, persecution, and molestation from others, as far as outward action goes, are to be believed less than the adversary of one who does not so quickly or so easily incur calumny, hatred, and the rest. But a poor man, compared with the Pope, is of this kind. Therefore his adversaries are to be believed less in such matters. The major premise is plain, because men especially speak more about those whom they slander, persecute, and hate than about others. On account of this, by the laws, the testimony of an enemy is by no means to be admitted. The minor premise is clearly proved by the divine Scriptures. Thus Prov. ch. 14 says: Even to his neighbour the poor man is hateful, but the friends of the rich are many. This is especially true of outward hatred, because although the rich often incur more inward hatred than the poor, since more people are offended by them, yet the rich who hate often do not show their hatred in outward action. Likewise Solomon in the same place, ch. 4: Riches add many friends, but from the poor even those whom he has are separated. And afterwards: Many flatter the person of the rich, and are friends of the giver of gifts; the brothers of the poor man hate him, and moreover his friends have gone far away from him. From these things it is plain that the poor incur hatred more quickly than the rich. Also in Ecclesiasticus 13 it is written: When the rich man speaks, all are silent, and they raise his word up to the clouds; when the poor man speaks, they say, who is this? And if he stumbles, they overthrow him. Likewise in the same place: When the rich man is moved, he is supported by his friends; but the humble, when he has fallen, is cast out even by acquaintances. When the rich man is deceived, there are many to restore him; he spoke proudly, and they justified him; the humble man is deceived, and moreover he is rebuked; he spoke sensibly, and no place was given him. And Amos 4 is written thus: You fat cows who are on the mountain of Samaria, who do violence to the needy, and crush the poor. From these and very many other passages it is openly gathered that the poor more commonly suffer persecution, molestation, and calumny than the rich and powerful. Therefore their adversaries are to be believed less than the rich who speak ill of them. Rather, one should more readily presume concerning the adversaries of the Pope, when they publicly impute to him the crime of heresy or something else, that their saying is not wholly alien to the truth, although if they are criminals, no faith is in any way to be given to them. And much less would one believe those who impute a crime to a poor man, or who report or spread in any way what has been imputed by others, which is most often true, when the poor man has offended many and has many rich and powerful adversaries. For in this case the most wicked man of the world can, with a single word, bring upon a poor man a most bitter infamy which is indelible without a divine miracle. For if the most lying man has invented some crime about a hated poor man, and has reported it while asserting it to a single person, that person will publish it to others, saying that such a crime has been imputed to such a man; afterwards others will report it as most certain; and so this lie, as true and certain, will come to all his enemies, and will not in the end escape his friends; and thus he will be defamed before everyone, though falsely. Wherefore the cause of a hated poor man is to be searched out most diligently and most strictly, lest he be oppressed by power and lies.

units.la: DISCIP. Nunquid peccant mortaliter, qui conficta mendacia absque assertione solummodo recitando publicant & diuulgant.
units.tr: DISCIP. Do those who publish and spread invented lies, merely repeating them without asserting them, sin mortally?

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quod peccant omnes tales mortaliter.
units.tr: MAG. The answer is that all such people sin mortally.

units.la: DISCIP. Istud videtur durum, cum videamus fere omnes relata crimina etiam non probata aliis narrare. Quod etiam hoc non sit peccatum mortale, videtur posse probari: quia relatio criminis, pro qua nullum damnum neq; in persona neq; in bonis temporalibus neq; in fama incurritur, non videtur peccatum mortale. Sed sæpe crimina referuntur absque prædictis damnis illius de quo referuntur. Ergo talis relatio non est semper peccatum mortale.
units.tr: DISCIP. This seems harsh, since we see almost everyone also relate charges that have not been proved. It also seems that this is not a mortal sin: the relating of a charge, from which no harm is incurred to the person, to temporal goods, or to reputation, does not seem to be a mortal sin. But crimes are often reported without any such harm to the person they are reported about. Therefore such a report is not always a mortal sin.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad primum istorum concedo, quod fere omnes adulti detractionis vitio quod est peccatum mortale sunt impliciti. quod Glos. super illud Prouerb. 24. (cum detractoribus non commiscearis) testari videtur dicens: Hoc sæpe vitio periclitatur pene genus humanum. Unde quamplurimi reperiuntur qui reputant se sanctos & sine peccato mortali: & tamen decies aliquando vnà die alii detrahendo & relata crimina enarrando, peccant mortaliter.
units.tr: MAGIST. To the first of these points I grant that almost all adults are entangled in the vice of detraction, which is a mortal sin. The Gloss on Proverbs 24 ("do not associate with detractors") seems to bear witness to this, saying: This vice endangers almost the whole human race. Hence very many are found who think themselves holy and free of mortal sin; yet sometimes ten times in a single day, by detracting others and recounting crimes, they sin mortally.

units.la: DISCIP. Et quo ignorant gravitatem relationis criminum, quæ minime sunt probata, excusari videntur.
units.tr: DISCIP. And since they do not know how grave it is to relate crimes that have not been proved at all, they seem to be excused.

units.la: MAG.
