Respondetur quod ignorantia iuris, præcipue naturalis, non excusat: & ideo quamuis ignorent gravitatem criminis huius, non sunt excusati: quia de iure naturali est, quod nemo debet referre crimen de alio, nisi notorium vel confessum vel manifeste probatum, nisi constaret certitudinaliter, vel saltem probabiliter, quod ex tali relatione criminis ille, de quo refertur, nunquam imperpetuum iacturam in honore vel aliquo alio esset passurus. Ignorantia ergo huius non excusat, quæ tamen in multis minime reperitur: quia multi legunt in scripturis gravitatem detractionis & a prædicantibus & docentibus verbum Dei: & tamen se ab huiusmodi vitio non compescunt. Et ideo conceditur, quod sæpe omnes adulti hoc vitio damnabiliter sunt infecti. & sæpe magis ac gravius isto vitio laborant, qui sanctiores cupiunt reputari, ut de multis qui raro vel nunquam reputant se peccare mortaliter vel volunt absque peccato mortali censeri, & pro sanctis haberi, ita ut liceat viris sanctis & discretis iudicare, asserere & sentire, quod sepissime peccant mortaliter & quod sunt homines malæ & reprobæ vitæ. Sicut enim licet ei, qui videt alium furari vel percutere innocentem aut etiam fornicari, aut audiuit alium blasphemare & fidem negare: licet absque vitio iudicare, quod furans, percutiens, fornicans, blasphemans, & fidem negans peccat mortaliter: ita ei qui audierit alium crimen falsum vel occultum, quod non est notorium neq; confessum, neq; potest aperte probari de proximo referetem, licet absque vitio iudicare, quod peccat mortaliter cuiuscunque dignitatis, præeminentiæ, conditionis, status, opinionis aut famæ est. Sic referens antedictus, etiam si putaretur quod Deus nulla miracula fecisset pro eo, nisi tali modo referret crimen alterius falsum vel occultum, quod certitudinaliter vel saltem probabiliter crederetur, quod talis relatio nunquam deberet obesse, neque in fama neque in alio modo ei, de quo tale crimen refertur.
units.tr: MAG. The answer is that ignorance of the law, especially of natural law, does not excuse. Therefore, although they are ignorant of the gravity of this crime, they are not excused, because it is a matter of natural law that no one should report a crime about another unless it is notorious, confessed, or clearly proved, unless it is certain, or at least probable, that from such a report the person about whom it is told would never suffer lasting loss of honour or of anything else. Ignorance of this therefore does not excuse, although it is found in very few, for many read in the Scriptures how grave detraction is, and hear it from preachers and teachers of the Word of God, and yet do not restrain themselves from this vice. And so it is granted that very often all adults are damnably infected with this vice, and often those who most wish to be thought holier labour under it more and more gravely. Many of them rarely or never think they sin mortally, or want to be judged free of mortal sin and held to be holy. Thus it is lawful for holy and discerning men to judge, assert and think that such people very often sin mortally and are men of wicked and reprobate life. For just as one who sees another steal, or strike an innocent man, or even commit fornication, or who hears another blaspheme and deny the faith, may judge without fault that the thief, striker, fornicator, blasphemer and denier of the faith sins mortally, so one who has heard another report a false or hidden crime about a neighbour, one that is neither notorious nor confessed, nor can be openly proved, may judge without fault that the reporter sins mortally, whatever the dignity, eminence, condition, status, reputation or fame of the person. The reporter just described, even if it were thought that God had worked no miracles for him, ought never to be harmed in reputation or in any other way by such a report about another person's crime, unless the crime was certainly, or at least probably, believed to be true.

units.la: Discip. Si ista essent vera, pauci his diebus salvarentur.
units.tr: DISCIP. If these things were true, few would be saved in these days.

units.la: Mag. Respondetur, quod his diebus verificata est auctoritas Salomonis, qui Ecclesiastici primo ait: Stultorum infinitus est numerus; quanquam principalissime intelligendam nonnulli putant de illis, qui dicentes se esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt, quales praecipue arbitrantur illos, qui iuxta testimonium Salvatoris colantes culicem, camelum deglutiunt, qui similes sunt sepulchris dealbatis, qui a foris quidem apparent hominibus iusti, intus autem pleni sunt hypocrisi & iniquitate. quia foris & in incessu, veste, ieiuniis, orationibus & caeremoniis diversa exempla sanctitatis ostendunt: intus autem pleni sunt invidia, odio, ira, rancore, superbia, inani gloria & ambitione, ex quibus in persecutionem innocentium, detractiones, susurrationes, adulationes, simulationes, schismata, contentiones, & discordias, dolos, praeditiones, variaque crimina spiritualia deteriora furto & fornicatione prorumpunt, qui tamen sancti volunt omnino putari.
units.tr: MAG. The answer is that in these days the authority of Solomon has been borne out, who says in Ecclesiasticus 1: "The number of fools is infinite." Although some think this is chiefly to be understood of those who, claiming to be wise, have become fools, such as those who, according to the testimony of the Saviour, strain out the gnat and swallow the camel, who are like whitened sepulchres, appearing outwardly righteous to men but within full of hypocrisy and iniquity. For outwardly, in their bearing, dress, fasts, prayers and ceremonies, they display various examples of holiness; but within they are full of envy, hatred, anger, rancour, pride, vainglory and ambition, out of which break forth persecution of the innocent, detractions, whisperings, flatteries, pretences, schisms, contentions and discords, deceits, betrayals, and various spiritual crimes worse than theft and fornication. Yet these people want to be thought wholly holy.

units.la: Discip. De hac materia in speciali interrogabo te plura in tractatu De gestis circa fidem alterCantium orthodoxam. ideo dic breviter, quomodo respondetur ad secundum, quod tetigi.
units.tr: DISCIP. I will question you at more length on this matter in particular in the treatise On the Deeds Concerning the Orthodox Faith of the Altercantians. So tell me briefly how the second point I touched on is answered.

units.la: Mag. Respondetur quod sicut extra de iniuriis & damno. c. vlt. qui occasionem damni dat, damnum dedisse videtur: sic qui aliquid facit, ex quo potest verisimiliter damnum contingere vel iactura, non est immunis a culpa, quia quilibet de necessitate salutis cavere tenetur, ne aliquid faciat maxime absque commodo proposito, ex quo potest damnum vel iactura proximo provenire. propter hoc enim in lege divina praecipiebatur, quod fodiens cisternam operiret eam, sicut habetur Exod. 21. quia ipsa operta non poterat bos vel asinus in eam cadere. propter hoc etiam, ut habetur ibidem, praecipitur, ut dominus bovis quem sciret cornupetam recluderet eum, quia ipso non reclusó poterat hominem vel mulierem occidere. unde & in hoc casu dominus non recludens ipsum, si aliquem occidebat, praecipitur occidi, cum sic legitur ibidem: si bos cornupeta fuerit ab heri & nudius tertius, & contestati sunt dominum eius, nec reclauserit eum dominus: occideritque virum, aut mulierem, & bos lapidibus obruetur, & dominum eius occident. & ob eandem rationem cavebatur in lege, ut faciens novam domum faceret murum tecti per circuitum. unde Deut. 22. sic legitur: Cum aedificaveris domum novam, facies murum tecti per circuitum, ne effundatur sanguis in domo tua, & si ruens labens alio & in praeceps ruente. Ex quibus apertè colligitur, quod quilibet de necessitate salutis ea tenetur facere, quibus omissis potest damnum verisimiliter vel iactura proximo provenire. ergo per eandem rationem quilibet de necessitate salutis tenetur ea omittere, quibus non omissis, sed factis, potest verisimiliter proximus damnum vel notabilem laesionem incurrere. sed ex relatione falsi criminis vel occulti maxime publica, potest verisimiliter damnum in fama vel honore sive aliis proximo provenire, si licet forte tunc, quando refertur, nullum tale inferatur. quia aliquis eorum, qui audierit a primo referente, potest postea idem crimen in notabile detrimentum alterius enarrare. quare a remotione criminis talis de necessitate salutis quilibet abstinere tenetur, nisi forte ex levibus & probabilibus coniecturis & urgentibus arbitretur, quod nunquam in posterum nec ex ipso nec ex aliquo audientium ex occasione talis relationis aliquod eveniet detrimentum.
units.tr: MAG. The answer is that just as, by Extra, de iniuriis et damno, c. vlt., one who gives the occasion of a loss is held to have caused the loss, so one who does something from which damage or loss may probably befall another is not free from blame. Everyone is bound, by necessity of salvation, to take care not to do anything, especially without a good purpose, from which damage or loss may come to a neighbour. For this reason the divine law commanded that one who digs a cistern should cover it, as is found in Exodus 21, because an ox or ass could not fall into it once covered. For this reason too, as is stated there, the owner of an ox known to gore must shut it up, since if it was not shut up it could kill a man or woman. Hence in such a case, if the owner did not shut it up and it killed someone, he was commanded to be put to death, as is read there: "If an ox is a gorer from yesterday and the day before, and its owner has been warned, and he does not shut it up, and it kills a man or woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be put to death." For the same reason the law required that one who builds a new house should make a parapet around the roof. Thus Deuteronomy 22 reads: "When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet around the roof, so that blood is not shed in your house if anyone falls from it." From these things it is clearly gathered that everyone is bound by necessity of salvation to do those things the omission of which could probably cause damage or loss to a neighbour. By the same reasoning, everyone is bound by necessity of salvation to omit those things which, if done, could probably cause a neighbour damage or serious injury. But from the report of a false or hidden crime, especially a public one, damage to a neighbour's reputation, honour or other interests may probably follow, even if no such harm is done at the time it is reported, because one of those who heard it from the first reporter may afterwards relate the same crime to another's serious detriment. Wherefore everyone is bound, by necessity of salvation, to refrain from spreading such a crime, unless he judges, from slight, probable and pressing conjectures, that no harm will ever follow in future, either from himself or from any of those who hear it on the occasion of such a report.

units.la: Discip. Circa hanc materiam magis quam proposuerim evagari sumus. ideo caeteris praetermissis unam solummodo obiectionem contra primam conclusionem principalem peto secundum opinionem praedictam dissolui. Est autem obiectio talis: minus credendum est referentibus crimen de illo ad cuius condemnationem est cum cautela & diligentia procedendum; quam referentibus crimen de illo ad cuius condemnationem non oportet cum tanta cautela procedere: sed cum maiori cautela procedendum est ad condemnationem Papae & Praelatorum ac divitum & potentum, quam subditorum & pauperum. ergo minus credendum est referentibus crimen de Papa potentibus & divitibus & praelatis, quam referentibus de pauperibus & subditis, sive referentes fuerint criminosi & infames, sive fuerint bonae famae. Maior videtur aperta. Minor auctoritate Innocentii tertii probatur, quae ponitur extra de accusationibus. cap. qualiter, secundo ait: licet autem hoc fit observandum in subiectis, diligentius tamen observandum est in praelatis, qui quasi signum sunt positi ad sagittam, & quia non possunt omnibus complacere, cum ex officio teneantur non solum arguere, sed etiam increpare, quin etiam interdum suspendere, nonnunquam ligare, frequenter odium multorum incurrunt & insidias patiuntur. & ideo sancti patres providere statuerunt, ut ne accusatio praelatorum facile admittatur, ne concussis columnis corruat aedificium, nisi diligens adhibeatur cautela. propter quam non solum false, sed maligne criminum impositioni ianua percludatur. Ex quibus colligitur, ut videtur, quod in procedendo contra praelatos, maior est adhibenda cautela, quam contra alios procedendo. quare minus credendum est, pro referentibus crimen de Papa, quam referentibus crimen de aliis quibuscunque.
units.tr: DISCIP. We have wandered further in this matter than I intended. So, setting the rest aside, I ask that one objection against the first principal conclusion be resolved according to the opinion stated above. The objection is this: charges reported against one for whose condemnation one must proceed with caution and diligence are to be believed less than charges reported against one for whose condemnation there is no need to proceed with such caution. But one must proceed with greater caution to condemn the Pope, prelates, the rich and the powerful than subjects and the poor. Therefore charges against the Pope, the powerful, the rich and prelates are to be believed less than charges against the poor and subjects, whether the reporters are criminal and infamous or of good reputation. The major premise is clear. The minor is proved by the authority of Innocent III, which is given in Extra, de accusationibus, c. qualiter, where in the second place he says: "Although this must be observed in subjects, it must be observed more diligently in prelates, who are set up as a mark for the arrow. Since they cannot please everyone, and since by their office they are bound not only to rebuke but also to reprove, and even at times to suspend and sometimes to bind, they often incur the hatred of many and suffer snares. Therefore the holy Fathers decided to provide that the accusation of prelates should not be readily admitted, lest the building fall when its pillars are shaken, unless diligent caution is applied, for which reason the door is shut not only to false but also to malicious imposition of crimes." From these things it seems to follow that greater caution must be applied in proceeding against prelates than in proceeding against others. Therefore less credence should be given to those reporting a crime about the Pope than to those reporting a crime about anyone else whatever.

units.la: Mag. Ad hoc respondetur, quod Innocentius in decretali praedicta considerauit ea, quae frequentius accidunt, non ea quae raro. & ideo quia saepius accidit quod praelati multos offendunt, pauperes autem quia timent sibi, cavent ab offensis: & ideo tot nec tam potentes offendunt, sicut praelati. hinc ut frequenter de facto maior cautela adhibenda est, cum praelatus accusatur, defertur, denunciatur vel diffamatur, quam cum pauper. si tamen de facto pauper abiec-tus {u}us & oppressus offenderet, tot & tam potentes & tam graviter, sicut praelatus, maior cautela adhibenda esset, quando talis pauper diffamaretur vel etiam accusaretur ab aemulis vel provocatis contra ipsum aut ab inimicis eorum, quam si praelatus dives & potens accusaretur vel diffamaretur a talibus. quemadmodum si aliquis omni auxilio destitutus impugnaretur iniuste ab aemulis aeque potentibus, magis iuvandus esset quam dives & potens, quia per potentiam posset ab impugnantibus se tueri. si enim rex vel princeps tam pauperem rusticum quam Comitem diuitem potentem contra adversarios aeque potentes debeat defensare: necesse est quod maius auxilium pauperi quam Comiti potenti exhibeat. sic si pauper tot & tantos vel plures vel potentes habeat aemulos ipsum graviter diffamantes vel quantumlibet impedientes, quapropter maiori auxilio indiget quam Papa. & ideo minus credendum est talibus aemulis pauperis, quam aequalibus vel minoribus aemulis Papae.
units.tr: MASTER. To this it is answered that Innocent, in the decretal mentioned, considered what happens more often, not what happens rarely. Because it happens more often that prelates offend many people, while the poor, fearing for themselves, take care to avoid giving offence, they do not offend so many or such powerful people as prelates do. Hence, as a matter of fact, greater caution is usually to be exercised when a prelate is accused, reported, denounced or defamed than when a poor man is. Yet if a poor man, cast down and oppressed, were to give offence to as many and as powerful people, and as seriously, as a prelate does, then greater caution would have to be exercised when such a poor man was defamed, or even accused, by rivals or by those provoked against him, or by their enemies, than if a rich and powerful prelate were accused or defamed by such people. It is like this: if someone stripped of all help were unjustly attacked by rivals equally powerful, he would need more help than a rich and powerful man, because the rich man could defend himself against his assailants by his power. For if a king or prince ought to protect a poor peasant as well as a rich and powerful count against equally powerful adversaries, he must necessarily give more help to the poor man than to the powerful count. So if a poor man has as many great rivals, or more, or more powerful ones, who defame him gravely or hinder him in whatever way, he needs more help than the Pope does. And therefore less credence is to be given to such rivals of the poor man than to rivals of the Pope who are equal or inferior.

units.la: CAP. XXVI. Ubi solvuntur duae aliae rationes supra cap. 12. posita, probantes quod talibus impugnantibus non sit credendum, ubi etiam notatur, quomodo & quando mala sive bona de aliquo narrata sint credenda.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI. Where two other arguments set out above in chapter 12 are answered, which argue that no credence is to be given to such attackers; where it is also noted how and when good or bad reports about someone are to be believed.

units.la: DISCIP. De ista materia & annexis eidem puto quod scires quamplurima recitare, quae ad tractatum De gestis circa fidem altercantium orthodoxam volo differri. ideo dic, quomodo respondetur ad rationes alias, quibus supra cap. 12. videtur ostendi, quod volentibus perfidiam Papae haeretici declarare fides non debeat adhiberi.
units.tr: STUDENT. On this matter and its related questions, I think you know a great many things to recite, which I want to be deferred to the treatise On the Acts of Those Disputing about the Orthodox Faith. So tell me how the other arguments are answered, by which, as set out above in chapter 12, it seems to be shown that credence ought not to be given to those who wish to declare the Pope a heretic in his faithlessness.

units.la: MAG. Ad secundam rationem adductam ibidem respondetur, quod saepe neque bona narrata de aliquo neque mala sunt credenda. quando enim nescitur, unde vel a quibus fama sive bona sive mala habeat ortum, non est famae credendum, neque bonae neque malae. similiter quando scitur, quod fama bona vel mala orta est ab inimicis, criminosis, maliuolis, maledicis, vel ab his qui faciliter credunt, vel rumores incertos libenter narrant & asserunt, vel a mendacibus & falsis hominibus, aut adulatoribus, ambitiosis vel avaris, histrionibus vel aliis quibuscunque, qui hominibus placere desiderant, non est tali famae credendum. quando autem quis scit vel per se vel per alios fide dignos, quod fama bona vel mala ortum habet a fide dignis personis, nec sunt amici speciales nec inimici eius cuius famam divulgant bonam vel malam, nec sunt ambitiosi nec hominibus placere desiderant, nec sunt mendaces nec detractores nec maledici, credere tali famae bonae vel malae non videtur illicitum, ita tamen quod propter famam, malam de aliquo absque certitudine sufficienti nullus ad actum praeiudicialem illi, de quo est mala fama, prorumpat. & ideo personis fide dignis quae non odio nec rancore asserunt & cupiunt declarare perfidiam Papae haeretici est credendum, nisi aliquid eis contingat obiicere, quare eis minime est credendum. ad illud autem quod dicitur de regina Sabba, respondetur, quod quaedam fama vaga de excellentia Salomonis saltem quantum ad ipsam pervenerat, de qua nesciebat, unde vel a quibus ortum habuerit: & ideo eis tanquam prudens & sagax fidem adhibere nolebat. secus est de fama Papae haeretici, quando bullam haereticalem vel transumptum per universum orbem promulgatum ostendit. & ideo in hoc casu credere Papam esse haereticum est licitum, debitum atque iustum.
units.tr: MASTER. To the second argument adduced in the same place, it is answered that often neither good nor bad reports about someone are to be believed. For when it is not known whence or from whom a report, whether good or bad, has arisen, no credence is to be given to the report, neither good nor bad. Likewise, when it is known that a good or bad report has arisen from enemies, criminals, the malicious, slanderers, or from those who believe readily and eagerly repeat and assert uncertain rumours, or from liars and false men, or flatterers, the ambitious or the greedy, actors or any others who desire to please men, such a report is not to be believed. But when someone knows, either himself or through other trustworthy persons, that a good or bad report has arisen from trustworthy persons, and that those who spread it are neither his special friends nor enemies of the man whose good or bad report it is, nor ambitious, nor desirous of pleasing men, nor liars, detractors or slanderers, then it does not seem unlawful to believe such a good or bad report, provided that, on account of a bad report about someone without sufficient certainty, no one proceeds to a prejudicial act against the man of whom the report is bad. And so persons worthy of trust, who do not assert and wish to declare the Pope's heretical faithlessness out of hatred or rancour, are to be believed, unless something can be objected to them, in which case they are by no means to be believed. As for what is said about the Queen of Sheba, it is answered that some vague report of Solomon's excellence had indeed reached her, though she did not know whence or from whom it had arisen; and so she, as a prudent and shrewd woman, was unwilling to give credence to them. It is otherwise with the report of a heretical Pope, when someone shows a heretical bull or a transcript of it published throughout the whole world. And therefore in this case it is lawful, proper and just to believe that the Pope is a heretic.

units.la: Ad tertiam rationem breviter respondetur: quod credere narrantibus sive bona sive mala non universaliter dissuadetur in scriptura divina. sed omnibus & semper credere dissuadetur, propter quod signanter dicitur Ecclesiastici decimoquinto, non omni verbo credas, quia alicui credendum est & alicui verbo minime est credendum. ad aliud autem, quod adducitur de Hieremia 12. patet ex serie textus, quod loquitur de inimicis. nam ibidem praemittitur: fratres tui & domus patris tui etiam ipsi pugnaverunt adversus te, & clamaverunt post te plena voce. & tunc immediate subiungitur, ne credas eis cum locuti fuerint tibi bona. & ita patet, quod loquitur de inimicis, quod nunquam eis est credendum iuxta illud Sapientis Ecclesiastici 12. non credas inimico tuo in aeternum: sicut autem tu non debes credere inimico tuo in aeternum: ita nec in aeternum credere debes inimico alterius contra ipsum. Ad illud Mich. 7. Nolite credere amico: respondetur, quod loquitur de amico trahente ad infidelitatem vel peccatum. ad dictum Iohan. 4. Nolite omni spiritui credere. patet quia signanter dicit, omni spiritui credere: quia alicui spiritui nullatenus est credendum. propter quod subdit ibidem cui est credendum: sed probate spiritum si ex Deo sit. quamvis si qui dixerint Papam esse haereticum, non statim credendum est eis, sed quia nunciant periculum esse oppositum orthodoxorum, probandi sunt, hoc est examinandi sunt sollicite, si legitima documenta attulerit ad probandum Papam esse haereticum: puta si bullam ostenderint haereticalem vel transumptum ipsius publice & solenniter promulgatum, est credendum & dicendum Papam esse haereticum.
units.tr: To the third argument it is answered briefly: that believing those who report either good or bad things is not universally discouraged in Holy Scripture. But believing everyone, and always, is discouraged; for this reason it is said pointedly in Ecclesiasticus 15, "Do not believe every word, for one ought to believe some things and not to believe any word at all." As for the other passage, adduced from Jeremiah 12, it is clear from the sequence of the text that it speaks of enemies. For the verse just before reads: "Your brethren and your father's house, even they have fought against you, and have cried out after you with a full voice." And then immediately follows: "Do not believe them, when they speak good things to you." And so it is clear that it speaks of enemies, to whom one must never give credence, in line with the saying of the wise man in Ecclesiasticus 12, "Do not trust your enemy for ever." But just as you ought not to trust your enemy for ever, so you ought not to believe for ever the enemy of another against him. To the passage in Micah 7, "Do not believe a friend," it is answered that it speaks of a friend who leads one into unfaithfulness or sin. To the saying in John 4, "Do not believe every spirit," it is clear, because it says pointedly "believe every spirit"; for no spirit whatever is to be believed. On this account the same passage adds whom one should believe: "but test the spirits whether they are of God." Although, if some have said that the Pope is a heretic, they are not to be believed at once; but because they announce a danger to the orthodox, they are to be tested, that is, they are to be carefully examined, to see whether they have brought legitimate proofs that the Pope is a heretic. For instance, if they show a heretical bull or a transcript of it published publicly and solemnly, then it is to be believed and said that the Pope is a heretic.

units.la: Ad quartam rationem respondetur, quod maior falsa est, propter tres instantias, tum quia notorium est credendum, licet secundum ordinem iudiciarium minime sit probatum: tum quia confesso de crimine absque omni ordine est credendum: tum quia extra iudicium & in multis est credendum absque ordine iudiciario observato. ad omnes igitur auctoritates unico verbo respondetur. detur, quod omnes intelligendæ sunt de credulitate iudicis in iudicio, quando crimen impositum non est notorium, nec reus confitetur crimen impositum. & ideo si crimen hæresis Papæ imponitur, de quo coram iudice accusatur, iudex, nisi sit notoria hæresis Papæ, vel ipse confiteatur, non debet credere illa credulitate, quæ habenda est in iudicio, antequam ordine iudiciario observato probetur, licet credulitate quæ spectat ad aliquem non tanquam ad iudicem credere possit in casu Papam esse hæreticum. si enim aliqui fide digni, de quorum fidelitate iudex non dubitat, referunt assertione iudicii se audivisse Papam negare fidem vel resurrectionem mortuorum, iudex potest credere eis illa credulitate, quæ inter socios habenda est, sed non debet habere illam credulitatem quæ ad iudicem spectat, antequam in iudicio probatum legitime extitit, nisi sit notorium iudici & aliis, vel nisi Papa in iudicio hæresim confiteatur.
units.tr: To the fourth argument it is answered that the major premise is false, on three counts: first, because what is notorious is to be believed, even if it has not been proved according to the judicial order; second, because a man who confesses a crime is to be believed without any order whatever; third, because outside a court and in many matters one is to be believed without the judicial order being observed. To all the authorities, therefore, one answer suffices: grant that they are all to be understood of the credence of a judge in court, when the crime charged is not notorious and the accused does not confess the crime charged. And so, if the crime of heresy is charged against the Pope, of which he is accused before a judge, the judge, unless the Pope's heresy is notorious or he himself confesses it, ought not to believe with that credence which is to be had in court, before it has been proved according to the judicial order; although with the kind of credence that pertains to someone not as a judge, he may believe in this case that the Pope is a heretic. For if some trustworthy persons, whose fidelity the judge does not doubt, report by their own assertion that they heard the Pope deny the faith or the resurrection of the dead, the judge may believe them with the credence that is to be had among companions; but he ought not to have that credence which pertains to a judge, before it has been lawfully proved in court, unless it is notorious to the judge and to others, or unless the Pope in court confesses the heresy.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVII.

units.la: Quæritur, qui sint probandi inter hæreticorum fautores, de quibus etiam distinguitur.
units.tr: Whom should we count as proven supporters of heretics? This question also has its distinctions.

units.la: DISCIP. Quamvis cogitaverim per singula quæ allegata sunt pro sententia supra cap. 13. recitata discurrere: quia tamen prolixitatem magnam volo vitare, illis usque post completionem huius operis remanentibus indiscussis, ad fautores hæreticorum & præcipue Papæ hæretici me converto, de quibus in primis peto ut dicas secundum unam sententiam vel plures, qui fautores hæreticorum debent reputari.
units.tr: STUDENT. Although I had meant to go through one by one the arguments that were brought forward for the opinion recited above in chapter 13, I want to avoid great prolixity. Those points will remain undiscussed until this work is finished. I turn instead to the supporters of heretics, and especially to a heretical Pope. On these matters I first ask you to tell me, according to one opinion or several, who ought to be reckoned supporters of heretics.

units.la: MAGIST. De fautoribus hæreticorum distinguitur, quia aut fauent tantummodo personis hæreticorum, eis scilicet præbendo consilium & auxilium qualecunque, nihil de eorum erroribus penitus intromittendo, quomodo sæpe Christiani Iudæis, Sarracenis & aliis infidelibus fauent, quamvis eorum erroribus penitus non faveant, nec adhæreant. Sæpe enim reges & principes fauendo Iudæis & infidelibus eos in officiis publicis præfecerunt: quamvis eorum errores minime approbarent. Christiani etiam qui, ut habetur extra, de Iudæis & Sarracenis. c. ad liberandam, Sarracenis consilium vel auxilium ad terræ sanctæ stipendium impendere arma, ferrum & galearum ligamina deferentes eisdem: illi etiam, qui eis galeas vel naves vendebant, poterant fautores Sarracenorum non immerito approbari: & tamen erroribus contra fidem non favebant: nec fuerunt per Ecclesiam fautores prauitatis hæreticæ vel infidelitatis iudicati. aut fautores hæreticorum favent eorum erroribus ipsos approbando, docendo, divulgando, animo alliciendi vel attrahendi aliquos ad probationem eorum: & hi non solum fautores hæreticorum, sed etiam sunt fautores hæreticæ prauitatis. primi autem sunt fautores hæreticorum duntaxat: sed non sunt censendi fautores hæreticæ prauitatis.
units.tr: MASTER. Supporters of heretics are distinguished, because they either favour only the persons of heretics, by offering them whatever counsel and help they can without in any way taking up their errors. So Christians often favour Jews, Saracens and other unbelievers, though they do not favour or adhere to their errors at all. Kings and princes, out of favour to Jews and unbelievers, have often placed them in public offices, though they did not approve of their errors in the least. Likewise, Christians who, as is found in Extra, de Judaeis et Saracenis, c. Ad liberandam, gave the Saracens counsel or aid for the support of the Holy Land, by bringing them weapons, iron and helmet straps, or who sold them helmets or ships, could not unreasonably be approved as supporters of the Saracens. Yet they did not favour errors against the faith, and the Church did not judge them supporters of heretical depravity or of unbelief. Or else supporters of heretics favour their errors by approving them, teaching them, and spreading them, intending to win over or draw some people to adopt them. These are not only supporters of heretics but also supporters of heretical depravity. The first kind are supporters of heretics only; they are not to be counted supporters of heretical depravity.

units.la: DISCIP. Mihi apparet secundum prædicta, quod aliqui sunt vel possunt esse fautores hæreticorum, quamvis non sint fautores hæreticæ prauitatis. sed nunquid econverso aliqui sunt vel possunt esse fautores hæreticæ prauitatis, quamvis non sint fautores hæreticorum?
units.tr: STUDENT. From what you have said it seems to me that some are, or can be, supporters of heretics without being supporters of heretical depravity. But conversely, is it not possible that some are, or can be, supporters of heretical depravity without being supporters of heretics?

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur quod sic. sicut enim potest quis tenere doctrinam alicuius non propter eum, sed quia reputat eam veram: & tamen in nullo est fautor & amicus eius: imo potest esse æmulus & inimicus eius mortalis. ita potest quis favere erroribus aliquorum, licet personis eorum non faveat, sed penitus adversetur.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer is yes. Just as someone may hold a teaching of another, not because of that man, but because he thinks it true, and yet be in no way his supporter or friend, indeed may be his mortal rival and enemy, so someone may favour the errors of some people, even though he does not favour their persons but is wholly opposed to them.

units.la: DISCIP. Ex his mihi videtur, quod isti habent de fautoribus ponere distinctionem trimembrem: quia aliqui sunt fautores hæreticorum tantummodo & non hæreticæ prauitatis: aliqui hæreticæ prauitatis & non hæreticorum: aliqui vero sunt fautores hæreticorum & hæreticæ prauitatis.
units.tr: STUDENT. From this it seems to me that these writers must make a threefold distinction among supporters: some are supporters of heretics only and not of heretical depravity; some of heretical depravity and not of heretics; and some are supporters both of heretics and of heretical depravity.

units.la: MAG. De hoc ita dicunt, ut eis imponis. DISCIP. Dic ergo secundum istos, quomodo fautores à criminibus, de quibus supra inquisivimus, distinguuntur. MAG. De quibus fautoribus interrogas? DISCIP. Primo dic de fautoribus hæreticorum. MAG. De fautoribus hæreticorum adhuc distinguitur: quia quidam (scienter fauent hæreticis, hoc est sciétes eos esse hæreticos. quomodo multi Christiani fauent scienter Iudæis & Sarracenis, quos sciunt esse Iudæos & Sarracenos: sicut etiam sæpe parentes fauent filiis & filii parentibus, quamvis sciunt eos esse hæreticos. Alii ignoranter fauent, quia ignorant esse hæreticos. primi scilicet, si qui fauent (scienter & non fauent hæreticæ prauitati: non sunt credentes nec hæreticis nec eorum erroribus: quia non approbant ipsos errores, nec ipsos reputant inter catholicos numerandos. qui autem ignoranter fauent hæreticis, hoc est nescientes eos esse hæreticos, sunt aliquo modo censendi credentes: quia ipsos, qui sunt hæretici, credunt inter catholicos computandos. & sic laborant ignorantia damnabili affectata, videl. aut crassa aut supina damnabiliter sunt credentes hæretici & excommunicationis sententia sunt ligati. si autem laborant ignorantia probabili aut invincibili, quæ non est damnabilis, sunt aliquo modo credentes, sed non damnabiliter censendi credentes. nec sunt de numero illorum credentium qui extra de hæreticis c. excommunicamus, primo, excommunicationis sententia innodantur.
units.tr: MASTER. They speak about this just as you put it. STUDENT. Tell me then, according to them, how supporters are distinguished in respect of the crimes we have investigated above. MASTER. Which supporters do you ask about? STUDENT. First tell me about supporters of heretics. MASTER. The supporters of heretics are distinguished further. Some favour heretics knowingly, that is, knowing them to be heretics, as many Christians knowingly favour Jews and Saracens whom they know to be Jews and Saracens; likewise parents often favour their children, and children their parents, though they know them to be heretics. Others favour them unknowingly, because they do not know they are heretics. Those who favour them knowingly, but do not favour heretical depravity, are not believers, either in the heretics or in their errors, because they do not approve the errors themselves nor reckon the heretics among Catholics. But those who favour heretics unknowingly, that is, not knowing them to be heretics, are in some sense to be counted believers, because they believe that the heretics ought to be counted among Catholics. Thus they labour under an ignorance that is damnable and affected, namely either gross or supine; they are damnably believers of heretics and are bound by the sentence of excommunication. If, however, they labour under a probable or invincible ignorance, which is not damnable, they are in some sense believers, but are not to be considered damnable believers. Nor are they among those believers who, as Extra, de Haereticis, c. Excommunicamus, are first bound by the sentence of excommunication.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic quomodo fautores hæreticæ prauitatis à credentibus distinguuntur. MAG. Fautores hæreticæ prauitatis sunt censendi credentes hæreticorum erroribus, de quibus legitur extra de hæreticis c. excommunicamus. Secundi sunt credentes hæreticis, de quibus etiam fit mentio extra de hæreticis hæretici. cap. excommunicamus, primo, quia fautores hæreticæ prauitatis & prauitatem hæreticam reputant catholicam veritatem, & ipsos auctores reputant catholicos vel saltem recte tenentes.
units.tr: STUDENT. Tell me how supporters of heretical depravity are distinguished from believers. MASTER. Supporters of heretical depravity are to be counted believers in the errors of heretics, as is read in Extra, de Haereticis, c. Excommunicamus. The second kind are believers in heretics, which is also mentioned in Extra, de Haereticis, c. Excommunicamus, first of all, because supporters of heretical depravity regard heretical depravity as Catholic truth, and they regard its authors as Catholics, or at least as holding the truth rightly.

units.la: Discip. Dic de fautoribus tam hæreticorum quam hæreticæ prauitatis quomodo à credentibus distinguuntur.
units.tr: STUDENT. Tell me how supporters both of heretics and of heretical depravity are distinguished from believers.

units.la: Magist. Respondetur ad hoc, sicut dictum est de fautoribus hæreticæ prauitatis.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer to this is the same as what was said about supporters of heretical depravity.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: In quo agitur de fautoribus hæreticæ prauitatis, vbi etiam datur distinctio inter credentes & fautores.
units.tr: In which the favourers of heretical depravity are treated of, and a distinction is also drawn between believers and favourers.

units.la: Discip. Iuxta distinctionem prædictam de fautoribus hæreticorum & hæreticæ prauitatis, de omnibus interrogabo diuersa. incipiam autem primo à fautoribus hæreticæ prauitatis iudicandis.
units.tr: Disciple. In keeping with the distinction just made between the favourers of heretics and of heretical depravity, I will ask about each kind separately. I shall begin with the favourers of heretical depravity who are to be judged.

units.la: Magist. Omnes modos fauendi hæreticæ prauitati non est facile numerare. & ideo videtur difficile dare regulam generalem, qua de omnibus cognoscitur an faueant vel non faueant hæreticæ prauitati.
units.tr: Master. It is not easy to enumerate all the ways of favouring heretical depravity. So it seems hard to give a general rule by which one may know, in every case, whether a person favours heretical depravity or does not.

units.la: Discip. Dic aliquos modos fauendi hæreticæ prauitati, ex quibus alii facilius agnoscantur.
units.tr: Disciple. Name some of the ways of favouring heretical depravity, so that some of them may be recognised more easily.

units.la: Magist. Quamuis fauere hæreticæ prauitati aliquomodo distinguatur à credere hæreticæ prauitati, quia fauor videtur actum exteriorem respicere; credere autem actum interiorem: tamen in omnibus modis exterioribus quibus aliquis ostendit aut declarat se credere hæreticorum erroribus, eisdem modis videtur fauere eisdem erroribus. & ideo quicunque dicit se erroribus adhærere, aut laudat eos tanquam catholicos, vel diuulgat tanquam consonantes veritati, vel legit, docet aut prædicat tanquam tenendo, vel scribit animo adhærendi, vel suadet, præcipit, cõsulit, aut quouis modo inducit alios ad tenendum eos, videtur hæreticæ prauitati adhærere. qui etiam quoquomodo prosequitur impugnantes errores eosdem, aut propter impugnationem huiusmodi quomodolibet aduersatur vel etiam infestat docentes, tenentes, & prædicantes contrariam veritatem, fautor prauitatis hæreticæ est tenendus.
units.tr: Master. Although favouring heretical depravity is in some respects distinct from believing it, since favour seems to concern an outward act while belief is an inward act, yet by whatever outward means a person shows or declares that he believes the errors of heretics, by those same means he seems to favour those errors. Therefore whoever says that he adheres to the errors, or praises them as Catholic, or spreads them as agreeing with the truth, or reads, teaches or preaches them as things to be held, or writes with the intention of adhering to them, or urges, orders, advises, or in any way leads others to hold them, is seen to adhere to heretical depravity. Whoever also in any way pursues those who attack these same errors, or on account of such an attack opposes or even harasses in any way those who teach, hold and preach the contrary truth, is to be regarded as a favourer of heretical depravity.

units.la: Discip. Sunt aliqui modi speciales, quibus sit quis dicendus fautor prauitatis hæreticæ à Papa hæretico si essent hærétici ad inuicem?
units.tr: Disciple. Are there some special ways by which a person is to be called a favourer of heretical depravity, if the Pope were a heretic and they were heretics among themselves?

units.la: Mag. Difficile vel fere impossibile est secundum quosdam, quod aliquis fauear aliquo modo errori Papæ, quin possit eodem modo fauere errori alterius, quamuis si Papa esset hæreticus de facto aliquibus modis, aliqui fauerent erroribus eius, qui non fauerent de facto erroribus aliorum.
units.tr: Master. According to some, it is difficult or almost impossible for anyone to favour the Pope's error in some way without being able to favour the error of another in the same way. Yet if the Pope were in fact a heretic in certain respects, some would favour his errors who would not in fact favour the errors of others.

units.la: Discip. Qui sunt isti modi? Mag. Vnus modus est consentiendo affirmationi diffinitioni erroneæ Papæ hæretici contra fidem. si enim Papa esset hæreticus & contra fidem aliquid diffiniret: quicunq; diffinitioni suæ erroneæ consentiret, esset fautor hæreticæ prauitatis. Quicunque etiam consuleret vel induceret, aut hortaretur eum ad diffiniendum aliquid contra fidem esset fautor hæreticæ prauitatis. Quicunq; etiam solenniter in scholis diffinitionem suam hæreticalem legeret, & tanquam tenendam, vel super ipsam non approbando, vel approbando, Glossas, apparatus, literam, vel scripta quæcunq; componeret, esset fautor hæreticæ prauitatis. Quicunq; etiam (cum posset conuenienter) eandem diffinitionem hæreticalem minime impugnaret, esset inter fautores prauitatis hæreticæ numerandus, qui etiam impugnantes, detestantes & reprobantes diffinitionem prædictam, propter hoc quomodolibet infestaret, diffamaret, reprobaret, vitaret vel vitandos aut quocunq; modo molestandos putaret, non esset à fautoria prauitatis hæreticæ alienus. Qui etiam scripturas catholicas contrarias prædictæ diffinitioni, eo quod contrariæ essent eidem, tenen-ti, legi, prædicari vel doceri præsumeret prohibere, inter fautores prauitatis hæreticæ esset non immerito computandus. Qui iuraret vel promitteret, quoquomodo diffinitionem talem Papæ se esse in perpetuum seruaturum, esset fautor hæreticæ prauitatis. qui etiam catholicas scripturas ad reprobandum diffinitionem hæreticalem Papæ positas in detestationem earum combureret tanquam erroneas, aut aliquod circa eas lubricum exerceret, à fautoria prauitatis hæreticæ nequaquam esset immunis. qui etiam in fauorem Papæ hæretici nouos errores confingeret, quemadmodum Sergiani in fauorem Sergii Papæ Episcopi secundum multos finxerunt errelores, dicentes Papa non posse damnari, sicut in quodam antiquissimo opere edito contra Sergianos legi, esset inter fautores prauitatis hæreticæ numerandus.
units.tr: Disciple. What are those ways? Master. One way is by consenting to a heretical and erroneous definition of the Pope against the faith. For if the Pope were a heretic and defined something against the faith, whoever consented to his erroneous definition would be a favourer of heretical depravity. Whoever also advised, induced or urged him to define something against the faith would be a favourer of heretical depravity. Whoever also solemnly read out his heretical definition in the schools as something to be held, and either approved or disapproved of it, and composed glosses, commentaries, a text, or any writings whatever upon it, would be a favourer of heretical depravity. Whoever also, although he could properly do so, did not oppose that heretical definition at all, is rightly to be counted among the favourers of heretical depravity. Whoever, too, opposed, detested and condemned that definition, yet on that account harassed, defamed, condemned, shunned, or thought that those who opposed it should be shunned or troubled in any way, is not free from the favouring of heretical depravity. Whoever also presumed to forbid the holding, reading, preaching or teaching of Catholic writings that were contrary to that definition, because they were contrary to it, may not undeservedly be reckoned among the favourers of heretical depravity. Whoever swore or promised in any way that he would keep such a definition of the Pope for ever, would be a favourer of heretical depravity. Whoever also burned Catholic writings set against the Pope's heretical definition, in order to condemn that definition, detesting them as erroneous, or who carried on any wanton behaviour towards them, is by no means free from the favouring of heretical depravity. Whoever also, in order to favour a heretical Pope, invented new errors, as the Sergians, according to many, invented errors in favour of Sergius, a Pope and bishop, saying that the Pope cannot be condemned, as is read in a very ancient published work against the Sergians, would be counted among the favourers of heretical depravity.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXIX.

units.la: In quo specialiter agitur de fautoribus consentientibus diffinitioni Papæ hæretica li, vbi etiam de quadruplici distinguitur consensu.
units.tr: In which it is treated specifically of those supporters who consent to the heretical definition of a Pope, where also a fourfold distinction of consent is drawn.

units.la: Discip. Quoniam iuxta canonicas sanctiones ad cautelam futurum est aliquid faciendum: quia vt leges imperiales insinuant, & recta ratio dictat, prouidere quis debet, quod contingi potest. unde & viri prudentes & providi & discreti pacis in tempore munitiones parant, fortes ædificant, civitates fabricant, divitias congregant, & thesauros, propinquos & amicos confœderant, ut si eis rabies bellorum ingereret, hostilis aggressio facilius reprimatur. Idcirco quamvis his temporibus à Papa catholico fides catholica defendatur virilius, & hæretica pravitas animosius expurgetur, quia tamen potest contingere, ut si nostris diebus vel futuris Papa surgat hæreticus, sequaces & fautores quam plures habebit vel habiturus, qui veritatem catholicam reprobare & destruere aut extirpare, aut ad hæreticam pravitatem inducere satageret toto posse contra huiusmodi causam possibilem cupio me & alios præmunire, ut si vnquam talis casus acciderit, ego & alii orthodoxi sciamus, quos debeamus fautores hæreticæ pravitatis & Papæ hæretici reputare: propter quod de fautoribus hæreticę pravitatis discurrere: & in speciali te interrogare propono. Dic ergo primo de consentientibus diffinitioni hæreticali Papæ hæretici, an aliquis absque peccato mortali diffinitioni valeat consentire.
units.tr: Disciple. Since, according to the canonical sanctions, something must be done in advance as a precaution: for, as the imperial laws instruct and right reason dictates, one ought to provide for what may happen. Hence wise, provident and discreet men also prepare defences in time of peace, build strongholds, found cities, gather riches, and form alliances with kinsmen and friends, so that if the fury of war should come upon them, a hostile attack may be more easily repelled. Therefore, although in these times the Catholic faith is defended more vigorously by the Catholic Pope, and heretical depravity is purged more boldly, yet because it can happen that in our own days or in the future a Pope may arise who is a heretic, and who will have or would have very many followers and supporters, who would strive with all their power to reprove and destroy or extirpate the Catholic truth, or to lead people into heretical depravity, I wish to forearm myself and others against such a possible case, so that if ever such a case should occur, I and other orthodox persons may know whom we ought to reckon as supporters of heretical depravity and as supporters of a heretical Pope. On account of this I propose to discuss the supporters of heretical depravity and to question you in particular. Tell me therefore first, concerning those who consent to the heretical definition of a heretical Pope, whether anyone can consent to the definition without mortal sin.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad euidentiam interrogationis tuæ nonnulli dupliciter distinguunt de consensu. Contingit enim dupliciter consentire diffinitioni hæreticali Papæ, scil. vel consentiendo quod Papa diffiniat assertionem, quæ est hæretica; vel consentiendo assertioni quæ per Papam hæreticum diffinitur. Si enim volens hæresim diffinire requirat aliorum consensum, posset vnus dicere; consentio assertioni, quia reputat eam veram: Et, consentio cum diffiniatis eam. & iste proprie consentiret diffinitioni Papæ hæretici. Alius vero posset respondere tali assertioni: quia reputo eam veram, sed non consentio quod diffiniatis eam. & iste non assentiret proprie diffinitioni, quæ est actus diffiniendi, consentiret tamen diffinitioni quæ potest vocari assertio diffinitiua. Quemadmodum fides aliquando vocatur actus credendi: & aliquando ipsum obiectum creditum. vnde & collectio articulorum, quos credimus, aliquando vocatur Fides, vt notat Gloss. extra de sum. trin. & fid. cathol. cap. firmiter. Alia distinctio ponitur de consensu, quam ponit Glossa extra de officio dele. c. 1. dicitur: Nota quod quadruplex est consensus, scil. negligentia, consilii, cooperationis, & auctoritatis siue defensionis.
units.tr: Master. To make clear the sense of your question, some distinguish consent in two ways. For one may consent to the heretical definition of a Pope in two ways: either by consenting that the Pope define an assertion which is heretical, or by consenting to an assertion which is defined by a heretical Pope. For if a Pope who wishes to define a heresy asks for the consent of others, one might say: "I consent to the assertion, because I judge it true," and "I consent that you define it." This person would properly consent to the definition of a heretical Pope. Another, however, might answer such an assertion thus: "I judge it true, but I do not consent that you define it." This person would not properly assent to the definition, which is the act of defining, yet he would consent to what may be called the defining assertion. Just as faith is sometimes called the act of believing, and sometimes the object believed; whence also the collection of articles which we believe is sometimes called Faith, as the Gloss notes on Extra, de summa Trinitate et fide catholica, chapter "Firmiter." Another distinction of consent is drawn, which the Gloss sets down on Extra, de officio delegati, chapter 1, "Dicitur": "Note that consent is fourfold, namely negligent, of counsel, of cooperation, and of authority or defence."

units.la: DISCIP. Puto quod istas distinctiones, & diffinitiones intelligo. ideo iuxta membrum earum te interrogare studebo. dic ergo primo, an solummodo consentientes assertioni hæreticali Papæ non consentiendo quod diffiniat eam semper peccat mortaliter.
units.tr: Disciple. I think I understand these distinctions and definitions. I shall therefore try to question you according to their parts. Tell me first, whether one who merely consents to a heretical assertion of a Pope, without consenting that he define it, always sins mortally.

units.la: MAGIST. De assertione Papæ hæretici distinguitur. quia aut est talis assertio, quod consentiens tenetur credere explicite contrariam veritatem. & in hoc casu consentiens peccat mortaliter, & est hæreticus reputandus, secundum quod colligi potest quarto huius c. 11. & 72. aut assertio Papæ hæreticalis est talis; quod assentiens non tenetur credere explicite contrariam veritatem. & tunc aut in consensu est pertinax, aut non est pertinax. si est pertinax; peccat mortaliter & est hæreticus reputandus, & poena hæreticorum plectendus. si vero non est pertinax, sed paratus est corrigi: & solummodo est deceptus, & quærit cauta sollicitudine veritatem; non peccat mortaliter, nec per consequens est hæreticus reputandus, nec Papæ fautor hæreticæ pravitatis.
units.tr: Master. A distinction is made concerning the heretical assertion of a Pope. For either the assertion is such that the consenting person is bound to believe explicitly the contrary truth; and in this case the consenting person sins mortally and is to be reckoned a heretic, as can be gathered from book four of this work, chapters 11 and 72. Or the heretical assertion of the Pope is such that the assenting person is not bound to believe the contrary truth explicitly; and then either he is stubborn in his consent or he is not stubborn. If he is stubborn, he sins mortally, is to be reckoned a heretic, and is to be punished with the penalty of heretics. But if he is not stubborn, but is ready to be corrected, and is only deceived, and seeks the truth with cautious diligence, he does not sin mortally, nor consequently is he to be reckoned a heretic, nor a supporter of heretical depravity.

units.la: DISCIP. Quid de illo qui exterius consentit assertioni Papæ, vel vt placeat vel vt saltem non displiceat, & corde dissentiat?
units.tr: Disciple. What of the one who outwardly consents to the Pope's assertion, either to please or at least not to displease, while dissenting in his heart?

units.la: MAG. Respondetur, quod peccat mortaliter, quia in doctrina relationis aperte mentitur. & ideo magis peccat quam ille, qui ore & mente consentit. quia ille licet dicat falsum; tamen non mentitur: & ideo non peccat nisi venialiter: vel minus peccat quam ille qui ore consentit; & dissentiret corde. iste enim est falsus duplex, mendax & proditor agnitæ veritatis. & ideo merito est infamis omni spoliandus honore, & in perpetuum ab omni testimonio repellendus.
units.tr: Master. The answer is that he sins mortally, because in the report of his doctrine he openly lies. And therefore he sins more than one who consents with mouth and mind, since that one, although he says what is false, does not lie; so he sins only venially. Or he sins less than one who consents with his mouth while dissenting in heart. For this man is doubly false, a liar and a betrayer of the truth he knows. And therefore he is rightly infamous, to be stripped of every honour, and to be debarred from every testimony for ever.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: In quo declarantur 4. modi consensus capitulo præcedenti positi, & in c. 31. agitur de consensu negligentiæ etiam in 32. de consensu consilii & cooperationis.
units.tr: In which the four modes of consent set out in the preceding chapter are explained. In chapter 31 the consent of negligence is discussed, and in chapter 32 the consent of counsel and of cooperation.

units.la: DISCIP. Hæc quæ dicta sunt de consentientibus assertioni Papæ tantummodo ex his quæ dicta sunt prius de credentib. & ex illis quæ tractata sunt lib. 4. dependere videntur: ideo transeas ad consentientes, quod Papa hæreticam diffiniat pravitatem, qui scilicet requisiti à Papa cósentiunt, quod assertio, quæ in rei veritate est hæreticalis, diffiniatur solenniter tanquam catholica. & quod illis omnibus iniungatur, vt eam sicut catholicam teneant, sentiant & accipeant.
units.tr: STUDENT. What has been said about those who consent to the Pope's assertion seems to depend only on what was said earlier about believers and on what was treated in book 4. So pass on to those who consent to the Pope's defining a heretical error: namely, those who, when asked by the Pope, agree that an assertion which is in truth heretical be solemnly defined as catholic, and that all be commanded to hold, feel and accept it as catholic.

units.la: MAGIST. Dixi prius, quod quadrupliciter quis potest consentire, de quo igitur consentiente niteris?
units.tr: TEACHER. I said earlier that one can consent in four ways. Which of these consents are you asking about?

units.la: DISCIP. Licet istam distinctionem quadrimembrem in genere aliquo modo intelligam: tamen ad consentientem diffinitionem hæreticalem Papæ hæretici ipsam nescio declarare. ideo in primis declara quomodo contingit quadrupliciter diffinitioni hæreticali Papæ hæretici consentire. MAGIST. Quod quadrupliciter consentire contingat diffinitioni hæreticali Papæ hæretici, nonnulli declarant dicentes, quod ille consentit consensu negligentiæ diffinitioni prædictæ, qui sciens eam esse hæreticalem non resistit.
units.tr: STUDENT. I understand this fourfold distinction in a general way, but I do not know how to apply it to the consent given to a heretical definition of a Pope who is a heretic. So first explain how it happens that one consents in four ways to a heretical definition of a heretical Pope. TEACHER. That one can consent in these four ways to a heretical definition of a heretical Pope is explained by some, who say that he consents to the aforesaid definition by consent of negligence who, knowing it to be heretical, does not resist it.

units.la: Disc. Quomodo potest ostendi, quod non resistens ei consentit? Mag. Hoc pluribus sanctorum patrum auctoritatibus videtur posse probari. Ait enim Innocentius Papa, ut dicitur dist.83. c. error: Error cui non resistitur, approbatur. Ex quibus verbis sic arguitur. Error cui non resistitur approbatur. ergo diffinitio haereticalis Papae, cui non resistitur, approbatur. qui autem ipsum approbat, consentit eidem. ergo qui non resistit, consentit eidem. Item ibidem dicit Innocentius: Veritas cum minime defensatur, opprimitur. Ex quibus verbis infertur, quod veritas contraria diffinitioni haereticali Papae, cum minime defensatur, opprimitur. qui autem veritatem opprimit catholicam, consentit contrariae haereticae pravitati. qui vero non resistit, non defendit. ergo qui non resistit diffinitioni haereticali Papae, consentit eidem. Item ibidem subditur: nec caret scrupulo societatis occultae, qui manifesto facinori desinit obviare. & eandem sententiam sub eisdem verbis asserit Eleuterius Papa, ut habetur 2. q. 7. c. negligere, & Anastasius ad Damasum Papam, ut legitur 23. q. 3. c. qui potest, sic ait: Qui potest obviare & perturbare peruersos & non facit: nihil est aliud quam favere impietati eorum, nec caret scrupulo, &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod qui potest resistere diffinitioni Papae & non resistit, consentit eidem. & idem, ut legitur 23. quaest. 3. cap. ostendit, videtur asserere sicens: Qui definit obviare cum potest, consentit ergo qui non resistit diffinitioni haereticali Papae, consentit. Item Gregorius ut habetur dist.83. cap. consentire, ait: Consentire videtur erranti qui ad resecanda quae corrigi debent non occurrit. ergo qui non resistit diffinitioni haereticali Papae, consentit eidem. quod intelligendum est, quando quis scit diffinitionem Papae esse haereticalem, & potest resistere & non resistit.
units.tr: STUDENT. How can it be shown that one who does not resist consents? TEACHER. This seems to be provable by the authority of many Fathers. For Pope Innocent says, as is cited in dist. 83, c. Error: "An error that is not resisted is approved." From these words the argument runs thus: an error that is not resisted is approved; therefore a heretical definition of the Pope that is not resisted is approved; and whoever approves it consents to it; therefore whoever does not resist consents to it. Again, in the same place Innocent says: "Truth, when it is not at all defended, is overwhelmed." From these words it follows that the truth opposed to a heretical definition of the Pope, when it is not at all defended, is overwhelmed; but whoever overwhelms the catholic truth consents to the contrary heretical error; and whoever does not resist does not defend; therefore whoever does not resist a heretical definition of the Pope consents to it. Again in the same place it is added: "Nor is he free from the stain of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime." Pope Eleutherius asserts the same opinion in the same words, as is found in 2 q. 7, c. Negligere, and Anastasius to Pope Damasus, as is read in 23 q. 3, c. Qui potest, says: "He who can oppose and rebuke the perverse and does not do so is nothing other than favouring their impiety, nor is he free from the stain," etc. From these words it is gathered that whoever can resist a definition of the Pope and does not resist consents to it. And the same, as is read in 23 q. 3, c. (as cited), seems to assert, saying: "He who is able to oppose and does not, consents." Therefore whoever does not resist a heretical definition of the Pope consents. Again Gregory, as is found in dist. 83, c. Consentire, says: "He seems to consent to one who errs who does not come forward to cut away what ought to be corrected." Therefore whoever does not resist a heretical definition of the Pope consents to it. This must be understood to apply when someone knows the Pope's definition to be heretical and is able to resist, yet does not resist.

units.la: Disc. Dic de consensu consilii. Mag. Ille dicitur consentire consulendo, qui suadet & inducit Papam vel hortatur, quod assertionem quae est haereticalis, solenniter diffiniat & determinet esse tenendum. Disc. De consensu cooperationis.
units.tr: Disc. Tell me about the consent of counsel. Mag. He is said to consent by counsel who persuades and urges the Pope, or exhorts him, to solemnly define and determine that an assertion which is heretical must be held.

units.la: Mag. Ille dicitur consentire cooperando diffinitioni haereticali Papae, qui assertionem Papae haereticalem solenniter diffiniendo dictat, scribit, & rationibus aut auctoritatibus quod sit tenenda & solenniter diffinienda probare molitur.
units.tr: Disc. Tell me about the consent of cooperation. Mag. He is said to consent by cooperating in a heretical definition of the Pope who dictates, writes, and labours to prove by arguments or authorities that a heretical assertion of the Pope is to be held and solemnly defined.

units.la: Disc. Ergo secundum ista quicunque scriberet talem diffinitionem, consentiret cooperando eidem.
units.tr: Disc. Then, according to this, anyone who wrote such a definition would consent by cooperating in it.

units.la: Mag. Si quis scribit talem diffinitionem haereticalem Papae postquam existit promulgata, non intelligitur consentire cooperando actum diffiniendi siue determinandi, qui iam praecessit. qui autem scriberet eam ante actum diffiniendi, si intelligeret & adverteret, quod assertio diffiniendi fidei repugnaret, intelligeretur consentire cooperando. si autem hoc non adverteret, esset per ignorantiam excusatus.
units.tr: Mag. If someone writes such a heretical definition of the Pope after it has been promulgated, he is not understood to consent by cooperating in the act of defining or determining, which has already taken place. But if he wrote it before the act of defining, and understood and noticed that the assertion conflicted with the defining of the faith, he would be understood to consent by cooperating. If, however, he did not notice this, he would be excused by ignorance.

units.la: Disc. De consensu auctoritatis siue defensionis.
units.tr: Disc. Tell me about the consent of authority or of defence.

units.la: Mag. Consensus auctoritatis & consensus defensionis distinguui videntur, sicut auctoritas & defensio distinguuntur. auctoritas enim ad superiorem spectare videtur: defensio tam ad maiorem quam ad minorem potest pertinere. nam & superior potest inferiorem defendere: & inferior potest defendere superiorem. imo quamuis unus habeat auctoritatem supra seipsum: potest tamen quis defendere seipsum, iuxta illud Roman. 2. Vosmetipsos defendentes, charissimi. Et Act. 12. dixi, cum sim defensurus hodie me. consensus ergo auctoritatis respectu diffinitionis papalis locum non videtur habere: cum Papa nullius auctoritate vel mandato possit aliquid diffinire. sed consensus defensionis potest habere locum respectu Papae. potest enim aliquis consentire diffinitioni haereticali offerens se diffinitionem defensurum eandem.
units.tr: Mag. The consent of authority and the consent of defence seem to be distinguished just as authority and defence are distinguished. For authority seems to belong to a superior; defence can pertain both to a greater and to a lesser person. For a superior may defend an inferior, and an inferior may defend a superior. Indeed, although one may have authority over himself, yet he can defend himself, according to that passage of Romans 2: "Defending yourselves, dearly beloved." And Acts 12: "I am about to defend myself today." Therefore the consent of authority does not seem to have a place with respect to a papal definition, since the Pope cannot define anything by the authority or command of anyone. But the consent of defence can have a place with respect to the Pope. For someone can consent to a heretical definition by offering himself to defend that same definition.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXI.

units.la: In quo agitur de consensu negligentiae.
units.tr: In which the consent of negligence is discussed.

units.la: Disc. Omisso consensu defensionis, quousque tractaverimus de defensionibus haereticorum: & omisso consensu auctoritatis, qui, ut videtur, respectu Papae locum habere non potest, interrogabo te. Primo de consensu negligentiae, si omnino talis per consensum peccet mortaliter.
units.tr: Disc. Leaving aside the consent of defence, until we have treated of the defences of heretics, and leaving aside the consent of authority, which, as it seems, cannot apply with respect to the Pope, I will question you. First, about the consent of negligence: whether any such consent sins mortally.

units.la: Mag. Ista negligentia qua quis negligit resistere Papae, quando assertionem haereticalem diffinire solenniter sive determinare conatur (& ideo intelligitur consentire) videtur esse quaedam taciturnitas. quamobrem videndum est, an omnis taciturnitas in hoc casu sit peccatum mortale: & an pro consensu sit habenda. Circa quam sunt diversae sententiae. Una est, quod aliqua taciturnitas in hoc casu est peccatum mortale, & aliqua minime. quia aliqua est habenda pro consensu, & aliqua pro consensu minime est habenda. taciturnitas enim illius, qui reclamando posset praedictam diffinitionem impedire, esset peccatum mortale: & pro consensu esset habenda. unde si Papa requirendo concilium cardinalium aut aliorum super aliqua assertione haeretica diffinienda, unus posset reclamando impedire Papam a diffinitione huiusmodi: quia forte esset tantae opinionis & famae in populo: vel tantae potentiae quod Papa ipso reclamante talem diffinitionem minime attentaret. si ille taceret, peccaret mortaliter: & eius taciturnitas esset pro consensu habenda. Si vero esset aliquis qui reclamando eam impedire non posset, tacendo non peccaret mortaliter: nec eius taciturnitas esset pro consensu habenda. Huic sententiae Glossa extra de praesumptionibus c. nonne, concordare videtur. ait enim: melius dicam, ubi prohibitionis mea possum prohibere quod fit, & tacco tunc taciturnitas sitar pro consensu habetur. Si vero per prohibitionem meam non possum prohibere, quod sit: tunc non obest mihi taciturnitas. & hanc eandem diffinitionem ponit Gloss. dist. 27. cap. disco, hoc etiam Glossa 2. quaest. 7. cap. plerique insinuare videtur, distinguens tres casus, in quibus taciturnitas minime nocet. taciturnitas non nocet ei qui non potest probare. Item non nocet ei qui non potest impedire vel etiam erubescit loqui. Item non nocet ei qui scit suum ius dubitare & post sequitur, alias semper obstat taciturnitas, ut extra, de his quae fiunt a praelat. sine consensu, cap. continebatur. & 54. dist. si servus. Ex quibus patet, quod si requisitus a Papa super aliqua assertione haereticali diffiniendá prohibere non potest, huiusmodi taciturnitas non nocet. Si vero potest prohibere, taciturnitas nocet & est habenda pro consensu.
units.tr: Mag. That negligence by which someone neglects to resist the Pope, when he tries solemnly to define or determine a heretical assertion (and so is understood to consent), seems to be a kind of silence. Therefore we must consider whether every silence in this case is a mortal sin, and whether it is to be held as consent. On this there are differing opinions. One is that some silence in this case is a mortal sin and some is not at all: for some is to be held as consent, and some is not to be held as consent at all. For the silence of one who, by protesting, could prevent the said definition would be a mortal sin and would be held as consent. Hence, if the Pope, asking the council of the cardinals or others to define some heretical assertion, one of them could by protesting prevent the Pope from such a definition, perhaps because he has such great reputation and fame among the people, or such great power, that the Pope, with him protesting, would not dare to make such a definition: if he were silent, he would sin mortally, and his silence would be held as consent. But if there were someone who could not prevent it by protesting, he would not sin mortally by keeping silent, nor would his silence be held as consent. The Gloss on Extra, de praesumptionibus, c. nonne, seems to agree with this opinion. For it says: "I shall speak more plainly: where I can by my prohibition stop what is done, and I keep silent, then my silence is held as consent. But if I cannot stop it by my prohibition, then my silence does not harm me." And the Gloss on dist. 27, c. disco, sets down this same distinction; the Gloss on 2 q. 7, c. plerique also seems to suggest it, distinguishing three cases in which silence does no harm: silence does not harm one who cannot prove; likewise it does not harm one who cannot prevent, or who is ashamed to speak; likewise it does not harm one who knows his right is in doubt and afterwards follows it; otherwise silence always stands in the way, as in Extra, de his quae fiunt a praelat. sine consensu, c. continebatur, and 54 dist., si servus. From these things it is plain that if, when asked by the Pope to define some heretical assertion, one cannot prohibit it, such silence does no harm. But if one can prohibit it, silence does harm and is to be held as consent.

units.la: DISCIP. Ista sententia probabilis mihi videtur. Ideo ad intelligendam ea aliqualiter volo insistere, quare secundum istam sententiam dicas quid tenendum est de taciturnitate alicuius collegii: puta si Papa requireret collegium super huiusmodi diffinitione: nunquid, si taceret, peccaret mortaliter, & pro consentiente debeat haberi?
units.tr: DISCIP. This opinion seems probable to me. Therefore, to understand it somewhat more, I want you to tell me, according to this opinion, what must be held about the silence of a whole body: suppose the Pope were to ask the college about such a definition; if they kept silent, would they sin mortally, and ought they to be held as consenting?

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur, quod si totum collegium posset prohibere diffinitionem huiusmodi, collegium tacendo peccaret mortaliter, & pro consentiente deberet haberi. Si autem impedire non posset, taciturnitas non noceret.
units.tr: MAGIST. It is answered that if the whole college could prohibit such a definition, the college by keeping silent would sin mortally and ought to be held as consenting. But if it could not prevent it, the silence would not harm.

units.la: DISCIP. Si collegium potens prohibere tacendo peccat mortaliter: quis ergo primo de omnibus peccat, non videtur, quia primus non peccat tacendo: quia ille prohibere non posset. & eadem ratione nec secundus requisitus peccat, nec tertius. & sic videtur quod nullus tacendo peccat. ergo nec totum collegium tacendo peccat.
units.tr: DISCIP. If a college able to prohibit sins mortally by keeping silent, then who sins first of all does not seem clear: the first does not sin by keeping silent, because he could not prohibit it. And by the same reasoning neither the second questioned nor the third sins. And so it seems that no one sins by keeping silent. Therefore neither does the whole college sin by keeping silent.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur, quod primus tacendo peccat. Tum quia debet probabiliter suspicari, quia si ipse diffinitioni iniquae resistit, alii etiam resistent eidem. Tum quia ex quo nescit quod alii non concordabunt cum eo, potest probabiliter dubitare, an ipse reclamando una cum aliis posset diffinitionem haereticam impedire. In dubiis autem via tutior est tenenda sine sequenda. via autem tutior est quod reclamet. ergo tunc reclamare tenetur. Tum quia tacendo scandalisat alios praebens eis occasionem tacendi in causa fidei. ergo tacendo peccat mortaliter. ita secundus & tertius, & deinceps usque ad minorem partem collegii. postquam autem maior pars collegii consenserit tacendo: ille qui postea fuit requisitus; si cernens quod maior pars collegii tacendo consenserit, & Papa propter minorem partem suam diffinitionem haereticalem nequaquam dimittet: non peccat tacendo, ex quo per suam contradictionem prohibere non posset. & ideo respondetur, quod licet solus prohibere non posset, tamen posset cum aliis prohibere; & ideo quia non constat sibi, quod alii resistent, peccat tacendo.
units.tr: MAGIST. It is answered that the first sins by keeping silent. Both because he ought to suspect with probability that if he himself resists the unjust definition, others also will resist it; and because, since he does not know that the others will agree with him, he can reasonably doubt whether by protesting together with the others he could prevent the heretical definition. In doubtful matters, however, the safer course is to be followed, and the safer course is to protest. Therefore he is then bound to protest. And again, because by keeping silent he gives scandal to others, offering them an occasion of keeping silent in a matter of faith. Therefore he sins mortally by keeping silent. So too the second and third, and onward to the lesser part of the college. But after the greater part of the college has consented by keeping silent, the one who was asked afterwards, perceiving that the greater part has consented by silence and that the Pope, on account of his lesser part, will by no means give up the heretical definition, does not sin by keeping silent, since by his contradiction he could not prohibit it. And so the answer is that although he alone could not prohibit it, yet he could prohibit it together with the others; and therefore, because it is not certain to him that the others will resist, he sins by keeping silent.

units.la: DISCIP. Quid si Papa simul requirit omnes Cardinales, & non vnum ante alium, quis peccat, si omnes tacent? MAG. Dicitur quod in hoc casu peccant tacendo mortaliter, quia in hoc casu quilibet tenetur respondere, ac si esset primus requisitus. DISCIP. Dic aliam sententiam.
units.tr: DISCIP. What if the Pope asks all the cardinals at once, and not one before another: who sins if all keep silent? MAG. It is said that in this case they sin mortally by keeping silent, because in this case each is bound to answer as if he were the first asked. DISCIP. Tell me another opinion.

units.la: MAGIST. Alia sententia est, quod requisitus a Papa super aliqua assertione haereticali diffiniendá, si scit Papam obviare doctrinae ecclesiae & tacet; sive etiam reclamando possit prohibere huiusmodi diffinitionem sive non, peccat mortaliter, nisi ex conditione tali, quod periculum fidei vel fidelium sequeretur. Primum probatur: quia ad exteriorem confessionem fidei quilibet est astrictus, quando requiritur, si ex omissione confessionis alii scandalizantur: quia quilibet tenetur vitare scandalum fratris sui. Sed Cardinalis sive possit prohibere diffinitionem haereticalem Papae sive non possit, si tacet requisitus de veritate fidei proximos scandalizat, quia per eius taciturnitatem alii possunt praesumere, quod haereticae consentiat pravitati. ergo sive reclamando possit diffinitionem impedire haereticalem Papae sive non, tenetur in hoc casu ne infirmos & simplices scandalizet ad exteriorem confessionem catholicae veritatis.
units.tr: MAGIST. The other opinion is that one asked by the Pope to define some heretical assertion, if he knows that the Pope opposes the doctrine of the Church and keeps silent, whether or not by protesting he could prevent such a definition, sins mortally, unless the condition is such that danger to the faith or to the faithful would follow. The first is proved thus: every person is bound to outward confession of the faith when it is required, if others are scandalised by the omission of the confession, since everyone is bound to avoid giving scandal to his brother. But a cardinal, whether or not he could prevent the heretical definition of the Pope, if he keeps silent when asked about the truth of the faith, scandalises his neighbours, because by his silence others may presume that he consents to the heretical perversity. Therefore, whether or not by protesting he could prevent the heretical definition of the Pope, in this case he is bound, lest he scandalise the weak and simple, to outward confession of the Catholic truth.

units.la: Secundum, scilicet quod si ex conditione tali sequeretur periculum fidei vel fidelium; quia Papa haereticus & complices sui ad exteriorem fidelium persecutionem vel ad magis divulgandum errorem cum multorum periculo inflammarentur, tacens non peccaret mortaliter. probatur per illud Matth. 12. Nolite sanctum dare canibus.
