At least from the form of the words it appears that Jerome conditionally submitted the faith he had learned in the Church to the Pope's correction, since first he says: "This is the faith, most blessed Pope, which we learned in the Catholic Church," and afterwards adds: "in which if less skilfully," and so on. Master. The answer is that although Jerome could conditionally submit his faith to the Pope's correction without danger, since a conditional asserts nothing (and so this conditional is true: if something false is asserted in the Gospel, it must be corrected), nevertheless blessed Jerome in the words quoted did not intend to submit his faith to the Pope's correction. He intended to submit conditionally to the Pope's correction his exposition concerning the faith, so that the sense of his words is this: concerning which faith, to be expounded and explained, if anything has been stated rather unskilfully or without enough care, we wish to be corrected by you, and so on. Just as if someone who wrote a commentary on the Gospel were to say: "This is the Gospel; in which, if I have said anything less than well, I am ready to be corrected."

units.la: CAP. LXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXII.

units.la: In quo enumerantur alia praerogativa, in quibus debent praeminere tales impugnatores idonei.
units.tr: In which other prerogatives are listed that such fit opponents ought to excel in.

units.la: Discipulus. Si te praedicto modo circa alias praerogativas, quibus praeminere debet impugnator idoneus Papae haeretici dilatares, multis lectoribus operis huius fastidium generares. Ideo alias succincte percurras. Magist. Aliae praerogativae impugnatorum Papae haeretici assignantur. Quarum aliquae sunt communes impugnantibus corporaliter & spiritualiter Papam haereticum: aliquae vero sunt propriae impugnantibus spiritualiter Papam haereticum. Unde oportet eos, qui corporaliter vel spiritualiter Papam haereticum magnam sequelam habentem satagunt impugnare, tanquam directores & capita aliarum nouarum viarum existere inuentores. Quia sicut (teste beato August. ad Bonifacium) ut legitur dist. 50. cap. ut constitueretur, infirmitates nouae & extraneae emergentes cogunt multas inuenire medicinas multorum experimenta morborum: ita casus noui & extranei emergentes cogunt industrias ad occurrendum vias nouas & extraneas inuenire. Cum ergo sit valde extraneum atque rarum, quod Papa sit prauitate infectus haeretica: ad Papam viriliter impugnandum oportet vias extraneas cogitare, praesertim si potentum fuerit fauore munitus. Quicunque vero contra Papam haereticum voluerit solummodo uti rationibus, erit forsitan similis medico imperito, qui vult uno collyrio oculos curare. Non sufficit autem impugnatori idoneo Papae haeretici contra ipsum vias extraneas inuenire, nisi cum fuerit expediens ipsas curauerit effectui mancipare, ut videlicet non timeat aggredi nouitates. Quamuis enim nouitates inutiles, perniciosae & periculosae sint omnino vitandae: nouitates tamen utiles & necessariae & salubres sunt cariius amplectendae. Non est aptus ad quaecunque ardua peragenda, qui omnes hortet nouitates. Si Alexander Macedo aggredi nouitates timuisset, maiorem partem mundi sibi nullatenus subdidisset. Si ciuitas Romana nouitates minime accepisset, nunquam pacem in vniuerso orbe fecisset. Quid loquar de sanctis hominibus & Apostolis? si nouitates inducere formidassent, ad nouam legem gentes nullatenus convertissent. Non sunt ergo nouitates penitus respuendae: sed sicut vetusta, cum apparuerint onerosa, sunt omnimode abolenda: ita nouitates cum utiles, fructuosae, necessariae, expedientes secundum rectum iudicium videbuntur, sunt animosius amplectendae. Non autem sufficit impugnatori idoneo Papae haeretici nouitates cum opportunum fuerit, attentare, nisi etiam cum expediens fuerit periculis & laboribus & etiam mortis si oportuerit se exponat. Qui enim omnia pericula expauescit, similis est illi, de quo dicitur Eccles. 11. Qui obseruat ventum, non seminat: & qui considerat nubes, nunquam metet. Rursus, si habet diuitias, debet esse paratus expensas effundere: quia nulla eleemosyna corporalis extra articulum necessitatis extremae est ita necessaria. Neque enim monasteriorum constructio, neque pauperum dubrumcunque sustentatio, neque ecclesiarum aedificatio, neque miserabilium personarum defensio, neque captiuorum redemptio, neque pro tetra sanctae recuperatione largitio, potest aequiparari expensis, quae fiunt ad impugnandum Papam haereticum & fidem catholicam defendendam & exaltandam: eo quod exaltatio & defensio fidei catholicae est omnibus temporalibus praeferenda. Amplius, impugnator idoneus Papae haeretici perditionem rerum bonorum & famae nullatenus expauescat. Haec enim omnia sunt inter bona minima computanda. Nec propter ista est defensio fidei aliquatenus omittenda. Quamuis enim vnusquisque, si conuenienter potest famam suam, quae inter omnia bona temporalia videtur praeminere, ad aedificationem proximi & propter scandalum cuitandum seruare teneatur: propter ipsam tamen seruandam non est defensio fidei derelinquenda. Quia absq; fama est salus: & saepe fama est causa perditionis aeternae. Et ideo qui de perditione famae nimium contristatur, vt aliquid spectans ad honorem Dei vel salutem suam vel proximorum omittat, non est dignus regno Dei. Talis enim cum Apostolo nequaquam propter proximum omnia velut stercora arbitratur, sed gloria vexatur inani, omnia opera sua faciens vt ab hominibus videatur. Iterum, impugnator idoneus Papae haeretici omnem duplicitatem euitet, ne scilicet facto, verbo vel scripto patenter ostendat, quod ipsum habet pro vero summo pontifice. Quamuis enim nonnunquam licitis & utilibus simulationibus vti expediens censeatur: tamen vti duplicitate, quae falsitatem includit, semper est illicitum reputandum. Teste sapiente, qui Eccles. 2. ait: Va duplici corde & peccatori terram ingredienti duabus viis. Sit insuper in prosequendo negocio fidei contra Papam haereticum calidus, non tepidus. Tepidus enim in hoc negocio, praesertim si est magnus & potens, non solummodo de ore Dei euometur, sed etiam pauperibus & simplicibus sibi adhaerentibus erit causa & occasio confusionis & destructionis, non tantum modo temporalis, sed etiam forsitan spiritualis. Quia si non ferventer defendit eos, Papa haereticus & complices sui tanquam belluae crudelissimae ipsos tam spiritualiter quam corporaliter satagerent trucidare. Oportet etiam impugnatores idoneos Papae haeretici amore & concordia fortius adiuuari: ne se dissensionibus & contentionibus odiosis, & aemulationibus, & schismatibus disiungentes facilius desolentur. Quia teste Saluatore: Omne regnum diuisum contra se desolabitur, & omnis ciuitas vel domus contra se diuisa non stabit. Quare impugnatores Papae haeretici quantumcunq; iustam causam habuerint, non sperent, quod per ipsos tam laudabilem finem accipiant si inter se discordes et diuturne ...
units.tr: Disciple. If you had gone on at length about the other prerogatives in which a fit opponent of the heretical Pope must excel, you would have caused many readers of this work to grow weary. So please go through the rest briefly. Master. Other prerogatives of opponents of the heretical Pope are set down. Some are common to those who oppose the heretical Pope either bodily or spiritually; others belong only to those who oppose him spiritually. Hence those who strive to oppose, either bodily or spiritually, a heretical Pope who has a large following must be like leaders and founders who open other new ways. For, as blessed Augustine teaches in his letter to Boniface (as is read in dist. 50, chap. ut constitueretur), just as new and unfamiliar diseases force people to discover many remedies through the experience of many illnesses, so new and unfamiliar crises force people to devise new and unfamiliar ways of meeting them. Since it is therefore very unusual and rare for a Pope to be tainted with heretical depravity, bravely opposing the Pope requires devising unusual methods, especially if one is protected by the favour of the powerful. Whoever wishes to use only the ordinary arguments against a heretical Pope will perhaps be like an unskilled doctor who wants to cure eyes with a single eye-salve. Yet a fit opponent of the heretical Pope does not suffice merely by discovering unusual methods against him; he must also put them into effect when it is expedient, so that he does not fear to undertake novelties. For although useless, harmful and dangerous novelties must be avoided altogether, useful, necessary and wholesome novelties are to be embraced all the more eagerly. A man who urges every novelty is not fit for carrying out any difficult task; but one who fears all novelties is not fit either. If Alexander the Macedonian had feared to undertake novelties, he would never have subjected most of the world to himself. If the Roman state had never accepted novelties, it would never have made peace throughout the whole world. Why speak of holy men and the Apostles? If they had feared to introduce novelties, they would never have converted the nations to the new law. Novelties, therefore, are not to be utterly rejected; but just as old institutions, when they have proved burdensome, must be abolished in every way, so novelties, when they appear useful, fruitful, necessary and expedient by sound judgement, are to be embraced with courage. Nor does it suffice for a fit opponent of the heretical Pope to attempt novelties when it is fitting; he must also expose himself to dangers, labours, and even death if necessary, when this is expedient. For whoever dreads every danger is like the man of whom Ecclesiastes 11 says: "He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap." Again, if he has riches, he ought to be ready to spend them freely, since no bodily alms is so necessary outside the moment of extreme need. Indeed, the building of monasteries, the support of the poor of whatever kind, the building of churches, the defence of wretched persons, the ransoming of captives, or the giving of money for the recovery of the Holy Land cannot be compared with the expense incurred in opposing the heretical Pope and in defending and exalting the Catholic faith, since the exaltation and defence of the Catholic faith is to be preferred to all temporal things. Moreover, a fit opponent of the heretical Pope must by no means fear the loss of goods and reputation. For all these are to be counted among the least of goods. Nor on account of them is the defence of the faith in any way to be neglected. For although each person is bound, if he can do so properly, to preserve his reputation, which seems to stand out among all temporal goods, for the edification of his neighbour and to avoid scandal, yet the defence of the faith is not to be abandoned for the sake of preserving it. For "safety is not in reputation," and often reputation is the cause of eternal ruin. Therefore whoever is too much saddened by the loss of reputation, so that he omits anything pertaining to the honour of God or to his own salvation or that of his neighbours, is not worthy of the kingdom of God. For such a person, unlike the Apostle, does not count all things as dung for the sake of his neighbour, but is "vexed by empty glory," doing all his works that he may be seen by men. Again, a fit opponent of the heretical Pope must avoid all duplicity, so that he does not openly show by deed, word or writing that he regards him as the true supreme pontiff. For although it is sometimes judged expedient to use lawful and useful dissimulations, nevertheless to use a duplicity which involves falsehood must always be regarded as unlawful. The wise man, who says in Ecclesiastes 2, bears witness: Woe to the double-hearted, and to the sinner who goes into the land by two ways. Moreover, in carrying on the cause of the faith against the heretical Pope, let him be fervent, not lukewarm. For a lukewarm man in this business, especially if he is great and powerful, will not only be spewed out of the mouth of God, but will also be the cause and occasion of confusion and destruction for the poor and simple who cling to him, not only temporal but perhaps also spiritual. For if he does not defend them ardently, the heretical Pope and his accomplices would seek to slaughter them, both spiritually and bodily, like most cruel beasts. Fit opponents of the heretical Pope must also be strengthened all the more by love and concord, lest, divided by dissensions, hateful quarrels, rivalries and schisms, they be more easily laid waste. For, as the Saviour testifies: Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. Therefore, however just their cause, let opponents of the heretical Pope not hope that they will bring such a praiseworthy end about if they are discordant and divided among themselves in a damnable way over a long period.

units.la: Quia absq; fama est salus. Quare impugnatores Papae haeretici quantumcunq; iustam causam habuerint, non sperent, quod per ipsos tam laudabilem finem accipiant si inter se discordes exititerint damnabiliter & diuisi. Tales enim non sunt de semine illorum per quos fides orthodoxa exaltabitur: sed per aliam occasionem Deus causam fidei feliciter terminabit. Impugnator igitur idoneus Papae haeretici gloriam propriam minime quaerat, quasi velit, quod per ipsam solummodo victoria habeatur, sed gaudeat per quemcunq; causa fidei licite adiuuatur: nec facta nec consilia minorum despiciat: quia saepe paruulis reuelantur, quae a sapientibus & prudentibus abscond��ntur. Sit consiliarius assiduè inquisitiuus & interrogatiuus viarum & modorum, quibus est contra Papam haereticum procedendum. Quia teste Salomone: Erit salus, vbi erunt multa consilia. Et quamuis minorum consilia saepe minime sint spernenda: tamen a sapientibus est maxime in hoc casu consilium requirendum: ne aliquis de sapientia propria, tanquam sit sufficiens, quoquo modo confidat. Si enim mille carentes potentia temporali, quorum quilibet sapientia Salomonem excederet, Papam haereticum regum & principum fauore fulcitum satagerent impugnare, aliorum consilio indigerent: nec tamen propter hoc pauciores & minus sapientes aliqualiter debent formidare contra Papam haereticum bellum accipere. Quia quamuis nihil de contingentibus omittere debeant, in sua tamen sapientia vel virtute sperare non debent: sed in virtute Dei, quae, si certauerit usque ad mortem, expugnabit pro eis inimicos eorum. Quamobrem nullam multitudinem eorum adhaerentium Papae haeretico expauescant. Quia, sicut allegatum est supra, teste Iuda Machabeo, non est differentia in conspectu Dei caeli liberare in multis aut in paucis. Et Exodi 23. vnicuique fideli in haec verba mandatur: non sequeris turbam ad faciendum malum: nec in iudicio plurimorum acquiesces sententiae, vt a vero deuies.
units.tr: For safety is not in reputation. Therefore, however just their cause, opponents of the heretical Pope should not hope that they will bring about so praiseworthy an end if they are discordant and divided in a damnable way among themselves. For such men are not of the seed of those through whom the orthodox faith will be exalted; God will bring the cause of the faith to a happy conclusion by some other means. Let the fit opponent of the heretical Pope therefore not seek his own glory, as if victory were to be had only through himself, but let him rejoice that the cause of the faith is helped by anyone whatsoever in a lawful way; let him not despise the deeds and counsels of the lesser people, since often what is hidden from the wise and prudent is revealed to little ones. Let him be a counsellor who constantly inquires and asks about the ways and methods by which one must proceed against the heretical Pope. For, as Solomon says: There will be safety where there are many counsels. And although the counsels of lesser people should often not be despised, nevertheless in this case counsel is to be sought above all from the wise, lest anyone trust in his own wisdom, as if it were sufficient in any way. For if a thousand men lacking temporal power, each of whom surpassed Solomon in wisdom, were to strive to oppose a heretical Pope supported by the favour of kings and princes, they would still need the counsel of others; and yet for that reason fewer and less wise men ought not in any way to be afraid to take up war against the heretical Pope. For although they must omit nothing that is within their power, they must not place their hope in their own wisdom or strength, but in the power of God, who, if they fight even unto death, will overcome their enemies for them. Therefore let them not fear the great number of those who cling to the heretical Pope. For, as has been said above, on the testimony of Judas Maccabeus, there is no difference in the sight of the God of heaven to deliver by many or by few. And Exodus 23 commands every faithful person in these words: You shall not follow a crowd to do evil, nor shall you agree with the judgement of the many so as to turn aside from the truth.

units.la: Cuius rationem assignat Psalmista dicens: defecit sanctus, diminutae sunt veritates a filiis hominum, vana locuti sunt vnusquisq; ad proximum suum. Et alibi ait: Omnes declinauerunt, simul inutiles facti sunt: non est qui faciat bonum, non est vsque ad vnum. Rationem etiam eiusdem assignat Salomon Eccles. 1. dicens: Stultorum infinitus est numerus. Nec Esaias rationem eius tacuit, cum dicit: Omne caput languidum & omne cor moerens a planta pedis vsque ad verticem non est in eo sanitas. Imo etiam Saluator ipse rationem dicti prioris expressit, cum dicit Matth. 7. Lata porta & spaciosa via est, quae ducit ad perditionem: & multi sunt qui intrant per eam. Quam angusta & arta via, quae ducit ad vitam: & pauci sunt qui inueniunt eam. Et alibi ait: multi enim sunt vocati, pauci vero electi. Ex quibus verbis aliisque innumeris nonnulli accipiunt argumenta ad probandum, quod propter quantamcunq; multitudinem adhaerentium Papae haeretico non debent pauere paucissimi contra Papam haereticum patenter insurgere. Ante omnia tamen ab omni peccato mortali se seruare tenentur: quia, sicut non est speciosa laus in ore peccatorum, ita defensio vel impugnatio haereticae prauitatis pars caelestium coram Deo est minime pretiosa, licet vtilis aliis esse possit. Oportet igitur impugnatorem idoneum Papae haeretici, non solum peccata carnalia, sed etiam spiritualia declinare. Propter quod nonnulli putant, quod his diebus essent paucissimi impugnatores idonei Papae haeretici: quia fere totum mundum, tam clericos quam laicos, tam religiosos quam seculares dubitant peccatis mortalibus spiritualibus, fornicatione & furto peioribus, enormiter irretitos, vt ambigant non minus modo quam tempore Noe, verificari illud Gen. 6. Corrupta est autem terra coram Deo, & repleta est iniquitate.
units.tr: The Psalmist gives the reason for this, saying: "The holy man has failed, the truths are diminished among the sons of men; they have each spoken vain things to his neighbour." And elsewhere he says: "They have all gone aside, together they have become unprofitable: there is none who does good, there is not even one." Solomon too gives the reason for the same thing in Ecclesiastes 1, saying: "The number of fools is infinite." Nor does Isaiah pass over its reason, when he says: "The whole head is sick and the whole heart is faint; from the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no soundness in it." Indeed the Saviour himself expressed the reason for the former saying, when he says in Matthew 7: "Wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it. How narrow and strait is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it." And elsewhere he says: "For many are called, but few chosen." From these words and from countless others some people draw arguments to prove that, because of however great a multitude adhering to the heretical Pope, the very few should not be afraid to rise up openly against the heretical Pope. Above all, however, they are bound to keep themselves free from every mortal sin: for just as praise is not becoming in the mouth of sinners, so the defence or assault upon heretical depravity, though it may be useful to others, is by no means a precious thing before God as a heavenly act performed by those who are themselves unclean. It is therefore necessary that a suitable assailant of the heretical Pope avoid not only carnal sins but also spiritual ones. For this reason some think that in these days there are very few suitable assailants of the heretical Pope: because almost the whole world, clergy and laity alike, religious and secular alike, is so enormously entangled in spiritual mortal sins, worse than fornication and theft, that they doubt, no less now than in the time of Noah, that what is said in Genesis 6 is fulfilled: "Now the earth was corrupt before God, and filled with iniquity."

units.la: DIALOGVS. CAP. LXXIII.
units.tr: DIALOGUE. CHAPTER 73.

units.la: In quo enumerantur quaedam speciales prærogatiuæ, tantummodo spiritualiter impugnantibus Papam hereticum competentes.
units.tr: In which certain special prerogatives are enumerated, which belong only to those who oppose the heretical Pope spiritually.

units.la: Discipulus. De isto vltimo dicto vehementer admiror: cuius tamen motiua in tractatu De gestis circa fidem altercantium orthodoxam sollicite indagabo: nunc autem cum plures prærogatiuas tergeris, quibus secundum quorundam sententiam oportet impugnatores idoneos Papæ hæretici præeminere, quæ omnes communes impugnatoribus corporaliter & spiritualiter Papam hæreticum mihi videntur: numera aliquas prærogatiuas speciales, quibus expedit præeminere impugnatores Papæ hæretici per testimonia scripturarum præcipue, si Papa hæreticus errore coloratos & latentes conatus fuerit diffinitiue populis Christianis tradere. Magist. Dicitur quod huiusmodi impugnatores idoneos Papæ hæretici oportet sanctarum habere intelligentiam scripturarum, vt scilicet non solum memoriam verborum retineant, sed intellectum capiant veritatis. Quia, teste Hier. vt legitur 1.q.1. ca. Marcion: non in verbis scripturarum est Euangelium, sed in sensu, non in superficie, sed in medulla, non in sermonum foliis, sed in radice rationis. Multi enim quamuis memoria vigeant, vt literas multas retineant, & prompte quæ voluerint recitent & allegent, carent tamen iudicio & acumine rationis, ita vt ad verum intellectum aliquando per seipsos nesciant peruenire. Et de istis potest verificari illud Apostoli 2. Thim. 3. semper addiscentes & nunquam ad scientiam veritatis peruenientes. Tales autem non sunt idonei ad impugnandum errores occultos & latentes. Alii sunt vigentes rationis iudicio, quamuis in memoria deficere videantur; & illi, quamuis interdum cum magno labore & tarde, sunt idonei errores occultos & latentes ac coloratos Papæ hæretici impugnare.
units.tr: Disciple. I am greatly surprised by that last saying, though I will diligently search out its grounds in the treatise On the acts of those disputing about the orthodox faith. Now, since you list several prerogatives which, according to some opinion, the suitable opponents of a heretical Pope ought to excel in, and which all seem to me to be common to those who oppose a heretical Pope both bodily and spiritually, name some special prerogatives in which opponents of a heretical Pope ought especially to excel, chiefly through the testimonies of Scripture, if the Pope should attempt to hand down to Christian peoples, authoritatively, errors that are coloured and hidden. Master. It is said that such suitable opponents of a heretical Pope must have an understanding of the holy Scriptures, so that they not only retain the words in memory but grasp the truth in its sense. For, as Jerome witnesses, as is read in D.1 c. Marcion: "The Gospel is not in the words of Scripture but in the sense, not on the surface but in the marrow, not in the leaves of speech but in the root of reason." For many, although their memory flourishes so that they retain many letters and readily recite and cite whatever they wish, nevertheless lack judgement and keenness of reason, so that by themselves they sometimes cannot arrive at the true sense. Of these may be verified that saying of the Apostle, 2 Tim. 3: "always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth." Such people are not fit to oppose hidden and concealed errors. Others are vigorous in the judgement of reason, although they seem to fail in memory; and these, though sometimes with great labour and slowly, are fit to oppose the hidden, concealed and coloured errors of a heretical Pope.

units.la: Quamuis enim sæpe sint imperiti sermone & eloquentia carent & ornatu verborum, non tamen scientia; quia illi sciunt ex paucis multa elicere. Et illi perspicue vident, quæ veritati sunt contraria, quæ consona, quæ antecedentia, quæ consequentia, quæ impertinentia sunt censenda, qui etiam rationes sophisticas & auctoritates male intellectas non de facili seducuntur. Per quam autem scientiam rationis iudicium ad prædicta potissime adiuuetur, libro 9. De optimo genere addiscendi poteris inuenire.
units.tr: For although they are often unlearned, and lack fluency of speech, eloquence and ornament of words, they do not lack knowledge, since they can draw much out of few things. They clearly see what is contrary to the truth, what agrees with it, what goes before, what follows, and what is to be judged irrelevant; and they are not easily led astray even by sophistical arguments and authorities badly understood. Through what knowledge of reason the judgement is especially helped toward these things, you may find in book 9, On the best way of learning.

units.la: Qui autem memoria & iudicio præpollent, quod raro accidit, vt quidam æstimant, qui essent in facultatibus literis eruditi, essent maxime idonei impugnatores errorum Papæ infecti prauitate hæretica. Oportet autem impugnatores idoneos Papæ hæretici summe cauere, ne assertiones ipsius ambiguas contra mentem eius vel etiam præter mentem ipsius ad peruersum nitantur trahere intellectum: & multo fortius assertiones eius veras in omni sensu peruertere minime debent.
units.tr: But those who excel both in memory and in judgement, which rarely happens, as some think, and who would be learned in the faculties of letters, would be the most fit opponents of errors infected with heretical depravity by the Pope. Yet suitable opponents of a heretical Pope must take the greatest care not to strive to twist his ambiguous assertions against his mind, or even beyond his mind, into a perverse sense; and much more strongly they must by no means distort his true assertions in any sense.

units.la: Si enim aliquod fecerint prædictorum, præsertim scienter, vel etiam ex ignorantia crassa & supina, non solum coram Domino peccare mortaliter iudicabuntur, sed etiam apud intelligentes maligni & inuidi aut iniusti apparebunt. Inprimis igitur mentem ipsius ex omnibus dictis eius, quando assertio non est ambigua, inuestigent.
units.tr: For if they do any of the aforesaid things, especially knowingly, or even from gross and careless ignorance, they will be judged not only to sin mortally before the Lord, but will also appear malicious, envious or unjust to intelligent people. First, therefore, let them investigate his mind from all his sayings, when the assertion is not ambiguous.

units.la: Si enim assertio eius non est ambigua, sed sensum habens tantum modo falsum, non est necesse ad alia dicta eius recurrere. Cum vero patuerit manifeste sensum eius esse erroneum, non cauillose, non per auctoritates male intellectas, non per assertiones dubias, de quibus est licitum disputare; non per rationes fantasticas non intelligibiles & intricatas, non per dicta illorum, quos licitum est negare: sed per scripturas authenticas bene & sane intellectas, aut per rationes apertas, euidentes, irrefragabiles, studeant reprobare & fundare solidissime contrariam veritatem.
units.tr: For if his assertion is not ambiguous, but has only a false sense, it is not necessary to have recourse to his other sayings. But when his sense has clearly been shown to be erroneous, let them strive to refute it and to establish the contrary truth most solidly: not captiously, not through badly understood authorities, not through doubtful assertions about which it is lawful to dispute, not through fanciful, unintelligible and intricate arguments, not through the sayings of those whom it is lawful to deny; but through authentic Scriptures rightly and soundly understood, or through clear, evident and irrefutable reasons.

units.la: Hæc autem omnia amore faciant veritatis & odio falsitatis, vt ira, rancore vel odio personæ Papæ hæretici nulla moueantur. Disc. Cum instarem, quod hoc opus inciperes, arbitrabar breuem tractatulum De hereticis nos facturos: qui præter æstimationem mdam in longum aliquantulum est protensus, quem si omnes difficultates nunc mihi de Papa hæretico eiusque complicibus occurrentes tibi differendas exponerem, oporteret extendere in immensum.
units.tr: Let them do all these things out of love of truth and hatred of falsehood, so that they are moved by no anger, rancour or hatred toward the person of the heretical Pope. Disciple. When I pressed you to begin this work, I thought we would produce a brief little treatise On heretics; which, beyond my estimate, has stretched out to some length. If I were now to set out for you, to be deferred, all the difficulties that occur to me concerning the heretical Pope and his accomplices, it would be necessary to extend it immeasurably.

units.la: Sane cum opera prolixa pluribus dignoscantur ingrata modernis, sit hic primus summo noster de hereticis consumptus. Nunc autem benevolentiæ tuæ gratias ago, quod personam indulgens recitantis votis meis, nunc abbreuiando, nunc falsas sententias recitando, & pro eis fortiter allegando: nunc ad rationes probabiles respondendo: nunc argumentationes sophisticas soluendo: nunc veritates absque probationibus referendo, & quantum ad omnia alia descendere studuisti. Istum autem modum vtilem reputaui: quia sic nec ad probandum, nec ad reprobandum aliquid præscriptorum amor & odium tuæ personæ quemcunque mouebit: sed omnibus legentibus materia datur cogitandi.
units.tr: Indeed, since long works are known to be unwelcome to moderns, this first of our works on heretics has been completed in summary form. Now I give thanks for your kindness, because, indulging the wishes of the one reciting, you have sometimes abbreviated, sometimes recited false opinions and argued strongly for them, sometimes responded to probable reasons, sometimes solved sophistical arguments, sometimes related truths without proofs, and have striven to go through all the other points as far as possible. I have judged this method useful, for thus neither love nor hatred of your person will move anyone either to prove or to refute any of the things written; but material for thought is given to all readers.

units.la: Puto enim, quod cum ista fuerint diuulgata, tum propter raritatem, tum propter vtilitatem viri literati & intelligentes (zelum veritatis & boni communis habentes, quæ vera iunt rationibus manifestis & testimoniis scripturarum apertis) satagent confirmare: & quæ falsa sunt, reprobare studebunt. Tum etiam (vt æstimo) cum mentem tuam cœperis aperire de prædictis operatis facies manifesta & præclara, plana veritate referta, ad omnium vtilitatem fidelium & Dei omnipotentis honorem. Cui gloria, laus & imperium in secula seculorum, Amen.
units.tr: For I think that once these things have been published, both because of their rarity and their usefulness, learned and intelligent men, who have zeal for truth and the common good, will labour to confirm what is true by manifest reasons and clear testimonies of Scripture, and will strive to refute what is false. Then also, as I judge, when you have begun to open your mind about the aforesaid works, you will make them plain and illustrious, filled with clear truth, for the benefit of all the faithful and the honour of almighty God. To whom be glory, praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: EXPLICIT LIBER SEPTIMVS PRIMÆ PARTIS PRINCIPALIS DIALOGORUM.
units.tr: Here ends the seventh book of the first principal part of the Dialogues.

units.la: SECVNDA PARS PRINCIPALIS DIALOGORVM EST DE DOGMATIBVS PAPAE IOHANNIS 22. QVAE DIVIDITVR IN DVOS TRACTATVS. IN PRIMO PONVNTVR ERRO- RES eiusdem, ac probantur rationibus suis propriis per eundem factis. In secundo vero rationes soluuntur, reprobantur atq; destruuntur rationibus & auctoritatibus sanctorum, probantes animas purgatas ante diem iudicii non videre facialiter Deum.
units.tr: THE SECOND PRINCIPAL PART OF THE DIALOGUES CONCERNS THE DOCTRINES OF POPE JOHN XXII. IT IS DIVIDED INTO TWO TREATISES. IN THE FIRST, HIS ERRORS ARE SET OUT AND PROVED BY HIS OWN ARGUMENTS, MADE BY HIM. IN THE SECOND, THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED, REFUTED AND OVERTHROWN BY ARGUMENTS AND AUTHORITIES OF THE SAINTS, PROVING THAT THE SOULS OF THE PURGED DO NOT SEE GOD FACE TO FACE BEFORE THE DAY OF JUDGMENT.

units.la: PROOEMIVM,
units.tr: PREFACE

units.la: In quo ponitur prima ratio pro assertione, seu haresi prima Papae Iohannis 22. scilicet quod animae purgatae non vident facialiter Deum ante diem iudicii, quae probatur ratione & auctoritatibus, ad quas respondetur & veritas opposita probatur.
units.tr: In which the first argument is set out in support of the assertion, or first heresy, of Pope John XXII, namely that the purged souls do not see God face to face before the day of judgment. This is proved by reason and authorities, to which an answer is given, and the opposing truth is proved.

units.la: VErba oris eius iniquitas & dolus: ait Psalmista, per spiritum praeuidens Prophetice protestationem seu reuocationem verbalem facta, siue retractatione friuolam, Ioannis, vicesimi secundi superstitiosam iniquitatem haereticam, imo & dolum mortiferum, continentem. Et in eadem protestatione, retractione, seu reuocatione (vt in sequentibus apparebit) per rationes haereticales haeresim manifestam probare conatur, & vulpinam malitiam ad simplices seducendos verbis ambiguis & dolosis nititur palliare. Sane vt hoc euidentius ostendatur, ipsam protestationem vel reuocationem (vt reportata a quibusdam extitit) ponemus per particulas, impugnationes propriας submittendo.
units.tr: "The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit": the Psalmist, foreseeing by the Spirit, spoke prophetically of this verbal protestation, or recantation, or frivolous retraction of John XXII, which contains a superstitious and heretical iniquity, indeed a deadly deceit. And in this same protestation, retraction or recantation (as will appear in what follows), he tries to prove by heretical arguments a manifest heresy, and he strives to cloak his foxlike malice with ambiguous and deceitful words, in order to seduce simple people. Indeed, so that this may be shown more clearly, we shall set out the protestation or recantation itself (as it was reported by certain persons) in sections, adding our refutations of each.

units.la: Reportationes igitur supradicta in hac verba incipiunt.
units.tr: The reports cited above begin with these words.

units.la: ANno Domini millesimo trecentesimo 33. legi die Lunae tertio Ianuarii: Dominus Iohannes 22. tenuit consistorium publicum: in quo primo fecit legi allegationes & rationes aliquorum (vt dixi) qui tenent, quod animae sanctorum purgatae non vident clare, & facialiter Deum. Quibus allegationibus & rationibus lectis, per clericos suos, sicut ipsemet ordinauit & voluit, in eodem consistorio ipsemet verbo & cum magno feruore probare est nisus, quod animae sanctorum purgatae non vident facialiter Deum vsque post diem iudicii, rationes suas breuiter repetendo: quae fundantur in quinque viis, seu fundamentis. Haec sunt verba reportantium illa quae audiuerunt & viderunt narrantium.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1333, on Monday 3 January, I read that Lord John XXII held a public consistory. In it he first had read the allegations and arguments of certain persons (as I have said) who hold that the souls of the saints, once purged, do not see God clearly and face to face. After these allegations and arguments had been read by his clerks, as he himself had ordered and wished, he himself, in the same consistory, with great fervour, undertook to prove by word of mouth that the souls of the saints, once purged, do not see God face to face until after the day of judgment, briefly repeating his arguments, which are based on five ways, or foundations. These are the words of those who report what they heard and saw being related.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: In quo ponitur prima ratio Iohannis 22. probans haeresim principalem.
units.tr: In which the first argument of John 22 is set out, proving the principal heresy.

units.la: SVa prima ratio fuit, quod cum visione clara sanctorum non stat spes. Sed animae sanctorum sperant corporum resurrectionem vsque ad diem iudicii. Igitur vsque tunc non habent claram Dei visionem. Maior (vt dicit) patet per beatum Thomam prima secunda. Minor patet per sacram scripturam. Tunc quia Iob dicit, & in nouissimo die de terra surrecturus sum. Tum quia in Apoc. animae sanctorum martyrum postulant, & murmurando implorant vindictam de sanguine proprio. Haec ratio praeter haeresim principalem, aliam haeresim manifestam includit: quae est, quod omnis sperans aliquod futurum, non videt clare diuinam essentiam. Quia per hoc, quod animae sanctorum sperant corporum resurrectionem, probare cogitur, quod non habent claram Dei visionem. Quę probatio nulla esset, nisi teneret, quod omnis sperans aliquod futurum non habet claram Dei visionem. Quod autem hoc sit haereticum liquet aperte. Constat enim, quod Christus ante passionem suam gloriam impassibilitatis & immortalitatis speravit. Si igitur, qui sperat aliquod futurum, non videt diuinam essentiam: sequitur quod Christus ante passionem, & resurrectionem, diuinam essentiam minime viderat. Haec ratio confirmatur. Quia ex persona Christi Psalmista: In te Domine speraui, non confundar in aeternum, dum scilicet insultabitur mihi habenti similitudinem corporis peccati. Igitur Christus aliquando sperauit: & tamen Christus ab instanti suae conceptionis vidit diuinam essentiam. Igitur non omnis, qui sperat aliquod futurum, caret visione diuina. Hoc idem patet de angelis, qui hominum resurrectionem futuram sperant; qui tamen vident Deum, iuxta illud Matt. 8. Angeli eorum semper vident faciem patris. Igitur non omnes, qui sperant aliquid futurum &c. Haeresi igitur supradicta faciliter reprobata: respondendum est ad rationem sophisticam, quam in fulcimentum principalis erroris adducit. Ad cuius euidentiam est sciendum: q quamuis visio facialis Diuinae essentiae, & actus sperandi visionem eandem, simul stare non possunt: visio tamen facialis, & actus sperandi aliqd aliud, quam illa visione facialem, simul stant in eodem. Anima enim Christi (quia ab instanti suae conceptionis vidit diuinam essentiam) visionem illam non speravit: sed speravit resurrectionem corporum, quae futura est. Porro quia ille in dictis Thomae se fundare videtur: ideo, ut pateat euidenter, quod ipse Thomam neququam intelligit, etiam propter illos, qui doctrinam Thomae recipiunt, ostendendum est, q praedictus Thomas asserit manifeste in secunda secunda q.18. art.2. in solutione primae rationis dicit in haec verba: Christus & si esset comprehensor, & per consequens beatus, quantum ad diuinam fruitionem: erat tamen similiter viator, quantum ad passibilitatem naturae, quam adhuc gerebat. Et ideo gloriam impassibilitatis & immortalitatis sperare poterat. Et infra in solutione tertiae rationis: non tamen ita quod haberet virtutem spei: sed magu ex virtute charitatis, sicut etiam qui charitatem habet Dei, eadem charitate diligit proximum. Infra ait: cum spes sit virtus Theologica, habens Deum pro obiecto: principale obiectum spei est gloria animae, quae in fruitione Dei, ut consistit, non autem gloria corporis. Ex his patet aperte, quod iste doctor tenet, quod habens talem actum sperandi, non habet spem, quae virtus Theologica est. Si autem spes accipiatur pro actu sperandi, quemadmodum fides quandoq; accipitur pro actu credendi: de qua Aug. dicit: Fides seu undam quam credimus quod non videmus: quod notatur in Glo. extra de summa Trinitate & fide catholica, firmiter. Sic dicendum est, quod cum visione clara non stat actus sperandi respectu visionis diuinae: sed cum visione clara stat actus sperandi quaedam alia futura non habita. Cum tamen dicit, quod hoc patet per Thomam prima secunda. Respondetur, quod Thomas ibidem intendit, quod cum clara visione non stat spes, quae est virtus Theologica: cum ipsa tamen stat actus sperandi aliquid adhuc futurum, quemadmodum (prout adductum est) exemplificabat de Christo, in quo fuerunt simul visio clara & actus sperandi gloriam impassibilitatis & immortalitatis. Quod enim dicit, quod anima sanctorum sperant corporum resurrectionem usq; ad diem iudicii: hoc conceditur, quia sperant non per spem, quae est virtus theologica, quae primo est respectu gloriae animae: sed per actum sperandi, qui secundum quosdam a charitate Dei procedit, secundum quosdam a Deo & Diuina essentia, secundum quosdam ab habitu spei acquisito, quae non est virtus Theologica, secundum quosdam a desiderio corporis reuniendi. Et istae opiniones non sunt discutiendae ad praesens. Sed hic tenendum est, quod absq; habitu spei, quae est virtus Theologica, sanctorum animae per actus sperandi sperant corporum resurrectionem, non visionem diuinae essentiae. Quando minor probatur auctoritate Iob, in nouissimo die &c. dicendum est, quod per illa verba probatur, quod animae sanctorum sperant corporum resurrectionem. Sed non probatur per eam, quod animae sanctorum habent spem, quae est virtus theologica: vel actum sperandi, qui non stat cum visione clara. Cum autem eandem minorem probare conatur per hoc, quod in Apoc. legitur, ut dicit, quod anima sanctorum postulant & murmurando implorant vindictam de sanguine, dicendum, quod auctoritatem Apoc. non bene allegat. Quamuis enim in Apoc. dicitur, quod clamant voce magna dicentes, usquequo Domine sanctus & verus non iudicas & vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui habitant in terra? Ex quibus verbis sequitur, quod desiderant, implorant & sperant vindictam de sanguine proprio. Et ideo habent actum sperandi & etiam visionem claram & perfectam: non tamen habetur in Apoc. quod animae sanctorum murmurando implorent vindictam praedictam. Nomen enim murmurandi in scriptura Diuina vel semper vel frequentius in mala significatione accipitur, & aliquam speciem tristitiae videtur annexam habere. Sanctorum autem animae nullum actum eliciunt, necaliquam tristitiam habent. Et ideo non est concedendum, quod murmurant de dilatione vindictae. Videtur igitur in verbis praedictis, cum dicit, murmurando implorant, etiam nouam haeresim manifestam innuere: quod scilicet sancti in caelo non sunt ab omni malo culpae & poenae penitus liberati.
units.tr: Their first argument was this: hope does not stand together with the clear vision of the saints. But the souls of the saints hope for the resurrection of their bodies until the day of judgement. Therefore until then they do not have the clear vision of God. The major premise, as he says, is shown by blessed Thomas, prima secunda. The minor premise is shown by Holy Scripture: first, because Job says, "And in the last day I shall rise from the earth"; second, because in the Apocalypse the souls of the martyrs ask for, and with murmuring implore, vengeance for their own blood. Besides the principal heresy, this argument contains another, plain heresy: that everyone who hopes for something future does not see the divine essence clearly. For by the fact that the souls of the saints hope for the resurrection of their bodies, he is forced to prove that they do not have the clear vision of God. This proof would be no proof unless it held that everyone who hopes for something future does not have the clear vision of God. That this is heretical is plain. For it is certain that Christ, before his passion, hoped for the glory of impassibility and immortality. If, then, whoever hopes for something future does not see the divine essence, it follows that Christ, before his passion and resurrection, had not seen the divine essence at all. This argument is confirmed. For the Psalmist, speaking in the person of Christ, says: "In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded," namely while they insult me, having the likeness of sinful flesh. Therefore Christ at some time hoped, and yet Christ from the moment of his conception saw the divine essence. Therefore not everyone who hopes for something future lacks the divine vision. The same is evident of the angels, who hope for the future resurrection of men, and yet see God, according to that saying of Matthew 18: "Their angels always see the face of my Father." Therefore not all who hope for something future etc. Having thus easily refuted the aforesaid heresy, we must answer the sophistical argument which he brings forward in support of the principal error. To make this clear, it must be known that although the face-to-face vision of the divine essence and the act of hoping for that same vision cannot stand together, the face-to-face vision and the act of hoping for something other than that vision can stand together in the same person. For the soul of Christ (since from the moment of his conception it saw the divine essence) did not hope for that vision, but hoped for the resurrection of bodies, which is yet to come. Moreover, because he seems to rest his case on the words of Thomas, therefore, so that it may plainly appear that he has not understood Thomas at all, and also for the sake of those who accept the teaching of Thomas, it must be shown that the said Thomas clearly asserts in secunda secunda, q. 18, art. 2, in the solution of the first objection, these words: Christ, although he was a comprehensor, and consequently blessed as to divine enjoyment, was nevertheless likewise a wayfarer as to the passibility of the nature which he still bore. And therefore he could hope for the glory of impassibility and immortality. And below, in the solution of the third objection: not, however, in such a way that he had the virtue of hope, but rather from the virtue of charity, just as one who has the love of God also loves his neighbour with the same charity. Further on he says: since hope is a theological virtue, having God as its object, the principal object of hope is the glory of the soul, which consists in the enjoyment of God, and not the glory of the body. From these things it is clear that this teacher holds that one who has such an act of hoping does not have hope, which is a theological virtue. But if hope is taken for the act of hoping, just as faith is sometimes taken for the act of believing (of which Augustine says: faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, as is noted in the Gloss on Extra, de summa Trinitate et fide catholica, firmiter), then it must be said that with the clear vision the act of hoping does not stand with respect to the divine vision; but with the clear vision there stands an act of hoping for some other future thing not yet possessed. When he says, however, that this is shown by Thomas in prima secunda, the answer is that Thomas there means that with the clear vision there does not stand hope, which is a theological virtue; yet with the same vision there does stand an act of hoping for something still future, just as (as has been adduced) he exemplified in Christ, in whom there were together the clear vision and the act of hoping for the glory of impassibility and immortality. As for the statement that the souls of the saints hope for the resurrection of their bodies until the day of judgement, this is granted, because they hope not through hope, which is a theological virtue and is primarily directed to the glory of the soul, but through an act of hoping, which according to some proceeds from the charity of God, according to some from God and the divine essence, according to some from an acquired habit of hope (which is not a theological virtue), and according to some from a desire for the reunion of the body. These opinions need not be discussed at present. But here it must be held that, without the habit of hope, which is a theological virtue, the souls of the saints by acts of hoping hope for the resurrection of their bodies, not for the vision of the divine essence. When the minor premise is proved by the authority of Job, "in the last day" etc., it must be said that by those words it is proved that the souls of the saints hope for the resurrection of their bodies. But it is not proved by that passage that the souls of the saints have the hope which is a theological virtue, or an act of hoping which does not stand with the clear vision. When he tries to prove the same minor premise by what he says is read in the Apocalypse, that the souls of the saints ask for and with murmuring implore vengeance for blood, it must be said that he does not cite the authority of the Apocalypse rightly. For although in the Apocalypse it is said that they "cry with a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" it follows from these words that they desire, implore and hope for vengeance for their own blood. And therefore they have an act of hoping and also the clear and perfect vision; but it is not found in the Apocalypse that the souls of the saints implore the aforesaid vengeance with murmuring. For the word murmuring in Divine Scripture is always, or more often, taken in a bad sense, and seems to carry with it some kind of sadness. But the souls of the saints elicit no such act, nor have any sadness. And therefore it must not be conceded that they murmur at the delay of vengeance. It seems, then, that in the aforesaid words, when he says they implore with murmuring, he also hints at a new and manifest heresy: namely, that the saints in heaven are not wholly freed from every evil of guilt and punishment.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: In quo ponitur secunda ratio pro errore capituli praecedentis, quatuor haereticas assumit, & duo ambigua, quae ordine suo perscrutantur, & errores confutantur.
units.tr: In which the second argument for the error of the preceding chapter is set out. It assumes four heretical positions and two ambiguous ones, which are examined in their order, and the errors are refuted.

units.la: SEquitur in reuocatione facta & friuola, secunda ratio, quam fecit, quae fuit talis. Vltra visionem claram Diuinae essentiae anima non possunt exaltari, quia vltra summam nihil altius est. Et certum est, quod illa visio clara est summa exaltatio animarum. Sed in die iudicii Deus sanctos & illorum animas exaltabit. Igitur usque tunc non vident facialiter Deum alias tunc non exaltarentur. Minorem huius rationis probat: quia usque ad diem iudicii supplicamus & petimus, ut mos exaltet in salutem paratam. Quoniam animae sanctorum, ut habetur in Apocalypsi, usque ad diem iudicii erunt sub altari, & post diem iudicii super altare videbunt Deum facie ad faciem, ut exponit Beatus Bernhardus. Probatur etiam auctoritate Beati Petri dicentis 1. Petr. 5. Vt nos exaltet in salutem &c. Haec verba huius protestationis seu reuocationis intellecta, sicut ipse ea intelligit, plura haeretica alia ambigua disputabilia continent manifeste. Primum haereticale est, quod anima videns Diuinam essentiam ad maiorem gradum perfectionis exaltari non potest. Secundum haereticale est, quod si anima alicuius videt Diuinam essentiam, totus homo compositus ex anima illa vidente diuinam essentiam & carne exaltari non potest. Quod isti duo contineant verba praedicta, patet aperte, quia in eis asseritur manifeste, quod si animæ sanctorum nunc videant facialiter Deum, nec animæ sanctorum, nec ipsi sancti exaltarentur in die iudicii. Tertium haereticale, quod animæ sanctorum usq; ad finem iudicii non vident facialiter Deum. Primum ambiguum siue multiplex & disputabile est, quod vltra visionem claram diuinæ essentiæ non possunt exaltari. Secundum quod visio clara est summa exaltatio animarum. Quod autem primum, scilicet quod anima videns diuinam essentiam ad maiorem gradum perfectionis exaltari non potest, sit erroneum, probatur primo. Si anima Beati Pauli adepta est beatitudinem, & secundum veritatem & secundum istum adipiscetur maiorem & perfectionem gradum visionis diuinæ, quam in raptu habuit. Igitur videns diuinam essentiam ad maiorem gradum perfectionis, scilicet visionis diuinæ potuit exaltari. Minor est manifesta secundum omnes. Maior probatur primo auctoritate Aug. ad Orosium, qui ait: Taliter raptus fuerat Paulus in tertium cœlum, ad intellectualem visionem in Deum: non per corpus, nec per similitudinem corporis, sed sicut est ipsa veritas cerneret. Ex his verbis habetur, quod anima Pauli in rapta vidit Deum. Secundo probatur idem auctoritate eiusdem Aug. li. 22. super Genesi ad literam, qui ait, quod mente conspicitur ita secreta & remota, & omnino arrepta à sensibus carnis atq; mundata, vt illa quae in cœlo sunt & ipsam substantiam verbum q; Domini, per quod facta sunt omnia in charitate Spiritus sancti ineffabiliter valent videre Deum & audire, non incongruenter arbitramur & illuc esse Apostolum raptum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Beatus Paulus raptus fuit ad visionem substantiæ Dei: & tamen anima Pauli post mortem eius ad clariorem visionem extitit exaltata. Quod etiam Paulus in raptu viderit diuinam essentiam habetur in Glo. 2. Cor. 12. qua dicit sic: tertium (supple cœlum) spirituale, vbi angeli & sancta animæ fruuntur Dei contemplatione. Ad quod cum dicit se raptum sanctus Paulus, significat quod Deus ostendit ei vitam, in qua videndus est in aeternum. Et post: scio hominem huiusmodi raptum, id est contra naturam eleuatum, vsq; ad tertium cœlum, id est cognitionem diuinitatis. Et post: tertium cœlum est intellectualis visio, quando nec corpora nec imagines eius videntur, sed in incorporeis substantiis intuitus mentis mira Dei potentia figitur. Ad hanc raptus est Apostolus, vt ipsum Deum in se, non in aliqua figura videret. Et post: hoc est tertium cœlum, scilicet visio, qua Deus videtur facie ad faciem. Et iste est Paradysus (si dici potest) etiam Paradysorum. Et post: ad tertium cœlum se raptum dicit, quasi diceret, non humano sensu vidi (& si in corpore anima existente videret) ne sit contra illud, quod Deus dicit Moysi: non videbit me homo & viuet. Tunc enim Apostolus non fuit homo, id est secundum vsum sensuum corporis: sed ablatus est ei omnis sensus hominis: quia necesse est abstrahi ab hac vita mente, quando in illius ineffabilis visionis lucem assumitur. Et post: non sic incredibile est quibusdam sanctis nondum ita defunctis, vt sepelienda cadavera remanerent, etiam istam excellentiam reuelationis fuisse concessam. Sic igitur non credimus pro tanto Apostolo doctori gentium raptor vsq; ad istam excellentissimam visionem. Voluit enim Deus demonstrare vitam, in qua post hanc videndus est in aeternum. Et cur non dicatur ista Paradysus regio, vbi anima, vbi ipse Deus est, vbi scilicet ipsam Dei substantiam verbum Dei & Spiritum sanctum ineffabiliter videt? Post. Hoc est tertium cœlum, ad quod se raptum dicit Apostolus, vbi illi (scilicet angeli) Deum vident. Et post tertium cognitio etiam diuinitatis, ad quam raptus est Apostolus. Et post: raptus est in Paradysum: id est in eam tranquillitatem, qua fruuntur illi, qui sunt in cœlis Hierusalem: & sic videre potuit, quod nunquam corporeis sensibus impeditus videre poterat. Et post: audiuit arcana verba, id est percepit intimationem de secreta Dei scientia. Ex his tria colliguntur aperte. Primum est, quod Beatus Paulus vidit diuinam essentiam in raptu, & in hoc verbis praedictis pluries sententialiter & verbabiliter replicatur, secundum quod sanctæ animæ nunc vident Deum, cum dicatur, tertium cœlum esse spirituale, vbi angeli & etiam anima sancta, vbi scilicet ipsum Dei verbum ac Spiritum sanctum ineffabiliter vident. Ex quibus sequitur secundum quod anima videns Deum potest exaltari ad clariorem visionem. Quia anima Beati Pauli nunc clarius videt Deum, & videbit post iudicium, quam vidit in raptu, & animæ sanctæ clarius videbunt eum post iudicium qua modo videant. Tertium quod sequitur ex praedictis est, quod inuentor haeresum praedicatarum frustra & inaniter iactat se studuisse originalia sanctorum, ex quo in communissimis Glossis ex originalibus sanctorum acceptis ista tam patentet expressa non vidit. Secundo sic: quando aliqua forma eadem secundum speciem participatur ab vno, & ab alio minus perfecte, non est dicendum quin Deus de potentia absoluta posset aliquem participantem talem formam minus perfecte ad eundem gradum eiusdem formæ si sibi complacuerit exaltare. Talis enim forma potest augeri. Igitur non est impossibile eam de minori gradu ad maiorem transire. Sed visio Diuinæ essentiæ ab vno participatur perfectius, & ab alio minus perfecte. Vnus enim clarius videt diuinam essentiam, quam alius. Sicut enim distat stella à stella secundum Apostolum I. ad Cor. 15. sic vna anima clarius videt quam alia. Quod manifeste asserit Augustinus in libro de correctione, & recitatur de poenitentia, dist. 4. cap. in domo, qui ait sic: Parat nos sibi & se nobis, vt maneat in nobis & nos in eo, quantum quisque erit particeps eius plus vel minus, pro diuersitate meritorum. Et hæc est multitudo mansionum. Igitur non est dicendum, quod Deus non possit animam videntem Deum ad clariorem gradum visionis, si voluerit, exaltare.
units.tr: Next comes the second argument of his retraction, which is both empty and trifling, and which he made in this form: Beyond the clear vision of the divine essence, souls cannot be exalted, because nothing is higher than the highest. It is certain that this clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls. But on the day of judgment God will exalt the saints and their souls. Therefore until then they do not see God face to face; otherwise they would not then be exalted. He proves the minor premise of this argument: because until the day of judgment we beg and ask that he may exalt us into the salvation prepared. For the souls of the saints, as we read in the Apocalypse, will be under the altar until the day of judgment, and after the day of judgment they will see God face to face upon the altar, as Blessed Bernard explains. He also proves it by the authority of Blessed Peter, who says in 1 Pet. 5: that he may exalt us in salvation, and so on. These words of this protestation or retraction, understood as he himself understands them, plainly contain several other heretical and ambiguous, disputable points. The first heretical point is that a soul seeing the divine essence cannot be exalted to a greater degree of perfection. The second heretical point is that if the soul of anyone sees the divine essence, the whole man, composed of that seeing soul and of flesh, cannot be exalted. That these two propositions are contained in the words cited is plain, since they clearly assert that if the souls of the saints now see God face to face, neither the souls of the saints nor the saints themselves would be exalted on the day of judgment. The third heretical point is that the souls of the saints do not see God face to face until the end of judgment. The first ambiguous and disputable point is that beyond the clear vision of the divine essence they cannot be exalted. The second is that the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls. That the first point, namely that a soul seeing the divine essence cannot be exalted to a greater degree of perfection, is false, is proved first as follows. If the soul of Blessed Paul has obtained blessedness, and in truth and according to his own view will attain a greater and more perfect degree of the vision of God than he had in his rapture, then a soul seeing the divine essence can be exalted to a greater degree of perfection, namely of the vision of God. The minor premise is plain to all. The major premise is proved first by the authority of Augustine to Orosius, who says: Paul was thus caught up into the third heaven, to an intellectual vision of God, not through the body nor through any likeness of a body, but he beheld the truth itself as it is. From these words it is clear that the soul of Paul in his rapture saw God. Secondly, the same is proved by the authority of the same Augustine in book 22 on Genesis according to the letter, who says that the mind is so withdrawn and remote, and wholly seized and cleansed from the senses of the flesh, that it can ineffably see God and hear those things which are in heaven, and the very substance of the Word of the Lord, through whom all things were made, in the charity of the Holy Spirit; and we judge not unfittingly that the Apostle was caught up there. From these words it is clearly gathered that Blessed Paul was caught up to the vision of the substance of God; and yet the soul of Paul, after his death, was exalted to a clearer vision. That Paul in his rapture also saw the divine essence is found in the Gloss on 2 Cor. 12, which says: the third heaven (supply: heaven) is spiritual, where angels and holy souls enjoy the contemplation of God. When the holy Paul says that he was caught up, it signifies that God showed him the life in which he is to be seen for ever. And again: I know a man of this kind, that is, lifted above nature, up to the third heaven, that is, the knowledge of the divinity. And again: the third heaven is intellectual vision, when neither bodies nor their images are seen, but the gaze of the mind is fixed on incorporeal substances by the wonderful power of God. To this the Apostle was caught up, so that he might see God himself in himself, not in any figure. And again: this is the third heaven, namely the vision by which God is seen face to face. And this is Paradise (if it may be so called), even the Paradise of paradises. And again: he says that he was caught up to the third heaven, as if he meant, I saw not with human sense (although, while the soul was in the body, he saw), lest this be against what God says to Moses: no man shall see me and live. For then the Apostle was not a man, that is, not according to the use of the bodily senses; rather every human sense was taken from him, because the mind must be drawn away from this life when it is taken up into the light of that ineffable vision. And again: it is not so incredible that some saints, not yet so departed that their corpses remained to be buried, were granted even this excellence of revelation. Thus we do not believe that the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, was caught up only to that most excellent vision. For God wished to show the life in which, after this one, he is to be seen for ever. And why should this not be called the Paradise, the region where the soul is, where God himself is, where it sees ineffably the very substance of God, the Word of God and the Holy Spirit? And afterwards: this is the third heaven, to which the Apostle says he was caught up, where the angels see God. And afterwards: the third heaven is also the knowledge of the divinity, to which the Apostle was caught up. And afterwards: he was caught up into Paradise, that is, into that tranquillity which those enjoy who are in the heavenly Jerusalem; and so he could see what he could never see while impeded by bodily senses. And afterwards: he heard secret words, that is, he perceived the intimation of the secret knowledge of God. From these things three points are openly gathered. The first is that Blessed Paul saw the divine essence in his rapture; and in this the words cited are repeated several times in sense and in wording, so that holy souls now see God, since the third heaven is said to be spiritual, where the angels and also the holy soul see the very Word of God and the Holy Spirit ineffably. From these it follows, secondly, that a soul seeing God can be exalted to a clearer vision. For the soul of Blessed Paul now sees God more clearly, and will see him after the judgment more clearly than he saw him in his rapture; and the holy souls will see him more clearly after the judgment than they now see him. The third point that follows from what has been said is that the inventor of the aforesaid heresies vainly and emptily boasts that he has studied the originals of the saints, since in the most common Glosses, drawn from the originals of the saints, he did not see these things so plainly expressed. Secondly, thus: when some form is shared in the same species by one and by another in a less perfect way, it must not be denied that God, by his absolute power, could, if it pleased him, exalt a participant in such a form, less perfectly, to the same degree of that form. For such a form can be increased. Therefore it is not impossible for it to pass from a lesser degree to a greater. But the vision of the divine essence is shared more perfectly by one and less perfectly by another. For one sees the divine essence more clearly than another. For as star differs from star, according to the Apostle in 1 Cor. 15, so one soul sees more clearly than another. This Augustine clearly asserts in his book On Correction, and it is cited in the Decretum on repentance, dist. 4, in the chapter In domo, where he says: He prepares us for himself and himself for us, so that he may abide in us and we in him, in proportion as each shall be more or less a partaker of him, according to the diversity of merits. And this is the multitude of mansions. Therefore it must not be said that God cannot, if he wills, exalt a soul that sees God to a clearer degree of vision.

units.la: Secundum haereticale, quod continet verba praedicta, est, quod si anima alicuius videt Diuinam essentiam, totus homo compositus ex anima illa vidente essentiam Diuinam & corpore exaltari non potest. Hoc enim verbo Apostoli ad Philippenses c. 2. apertissime obuiat & repugnat. Dicit enim Apostolus, loquens de Christo: humiliauit semetipsum factus obediens vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Propter quod & Deus exaltauit illum. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod Christus post mortem, quando corpus gloriosum assumpsit, à Deo exititit exaltatus: & tamen ante mortem & tempore mortis anima Christi vidit diuinā essentiā. Igitur homo compositus ex corpore & anima poterit exaltari, licet anima eius viderit diuinā essentiam. Haereticalis etiam assertio supradicta verbis Beati Petri repugnat. Loquens enim Beatus Petrus, vt habetur Act. 2. de Christo post passionem suam ait: Hunc Iesum resuscitauit Deus, cuius nos testes sumus. Dextera igitur Dei exaltatus, & promissione Spiritus sancti acceptā à patre, effudit &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod Christus in resurrectione sua fuit exaltatus, licet antea viderit Diuinam essentiam. Igitur consimiliter licet animae sanctorum videant ante diem iudicii Diuinam essentiam, tamen cum corpora gloriosa in resurrectione sument, poterunt sancti ex corpore & anima constituti per Diuinam potentiam exaltari. Et ita assertio supradicta sapit haeresim manifestam. Amplius assertio memorata sancto Euangelio contradicit. Glorificatio enim poterit exaltatio nuncupari. Sed Christus postquam anima sua vidit Diuinam essentiam, fuit glorificatus. Quod Beatus Iohan. Euangelista 7. cap. aperte insinuat dicens: In nouissimo autem die magno festivitatis stabat Iesus & clamabat: Si quis sitit veniat ad me & bibat, qui credit in me, sicut dicit scriptura, flumina de ventre eius fluent aquae viuae. Hoc autem dixit de Spiritu sancto, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum. Nondum enim erat Spiritus datus: quia ille nondum erat glorificatus. Ex quibus verbis innuitur, quod ille post praedicationem suam & passionem: & per consequens postquam anima eius vidit Diuinam essentiam, fuit glorificatus. Igitur etiam postea fuit exaltatus. Ex quo sequitur euidenter, quod anima alicuius poterit primo videre facialiter Deum, & ipse compositus ex corpore & anima poterit postea exaltari: & ita licet animae sanctorum facialiter nunc videant Deum, tamen ipsi sancti in iudicio constituti ex anima & corpore poterunt exaltari.
units.tr: The second heretical point contained in the words quoted above is that if the soul of anyone sees the divine essence, the whole man, composed of that seeing soul and of the body, cannot be exalted. This plainly contradicts and opposes the words of the Apostle in Philippians 2, where he says, speaking of Christ: "He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him." From these words it is clearly evident that Christ was exalted by God after death, when he took up his glorified body; yet before death, and at the time of death, the soul of Christ saw the divine essence. Therefore a man composed of body and soul can be exalted, even though his soul has seen the divine essence. The assertion quoted above also contradicts the words of Saint Peter. For Saint Peter, speaking of Christ after his passion, as we read in Acts 2, says: "This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses. Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth" etc. From these words it is plainly gathered that Christ was exalted in his resurrection, although he had earlier seen the divine essence. Therefore, in the same way, although the souls of the saints see the divine essence before the day of judgment, yet when they take up glorified bodies at the resurrection, the saints, made up of body and soul, can be exalted by divine power. And so the assertion above smells of manifest heresy. Furthermore, the said assertion contradicts the holy Gospel. For glorification may be called exaltation. But Christ, after his soul had seen the divine essence, was glorified. The Evangelist John plainly hints at this in chapter 7, saying: "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying: If any man thirst, let him come unto me and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given, because that Jesus was not yet glorified." From these words it is implied that he was glorified after his preaching and passion, and consequently after his soul had seen the divine essence. Therefore he was also afterwards exalted. From this it follows plainly that the soul of anyone may first see God face to face, and that the man himself, composed of body and soul, may afterwards be exalted; and so, although the souls of the saints now see God face to face, the saints themselves, constituted of soul and body in judgment, can nevertheless be exalted.

units.la: Tertium haereticale contentum in verbis praedictis est, quod animae sanctorum vsque ad diem iudicii non vident facialiter Deum. Hoc autem in diuersis operibus est multipliciter improbatum. Ideo hoc pro nunc breuissime improbabo, & per vnicam auctoritatem Apostoli demonstrabo, quod animae sanctorum in coelo facialiter vident Deum. Ait enim 2. Corinth. 5. Dum sumus in corpore, peregrinamur à Domino. Per fidem enim ambulamus & non per speciem. Ex quibus verbis liquide constat, quod Apostolus probat, quod dum sumus in corpore, à Domino peregrinamur, per hoc quod ambulamus per fidem & non per spem. Ex qua argumentatione Apostoli ista propositio patenter accipitur: quicunque ambulat per fidem & non per spem, peregrinatur à Domino. Sed Apostolus desiderabat ante diem iudicii esse praesens apud Deum, & non peregrinari à Domino, ipso testante, qui post verba praedicta subiungit: Audemus autem & bonam voluntatem habemus magis peregrinari à corpore, & praesentes esse ad Deum. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod Apostolus desiderabat non peregrinari à Domino, sed esse praesens apud Deum ante diem iudicii: quia hoc desiderabat, dum esset peregrinus in corpore diu ante diem iudicii. Igitur desiderabat non peregrinari Deo, sed esse apud Deum ante diem iudicii. Sed, sicut acceptum est ab Apostolo: quicunque ambulat per spem & non per fidem, non peregrinatur à Deo. Et per consequens, quilibet qui non peregrinatur à Deo, ambula per spem & non per fidem. Igitur Apostolus desiderabat ambulare per spem, & non per fidem ante diem iudicii. Quod minime desideraret, si sciuisset animas sanctorum ante diem iudicii Diuinam essentiam non visuras.
units.tr: The third heretical point contained in the words quoted above is that the souls of the saints do not see God face to face until the day of judgment. This has been refuted in many ways in various works. Therefore I will refute it very briefly for now, and show by the single authority of the Apostle that the souls of the saints in heaven see God face to face. For he says in 2 Corinthians 5: "While we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight." From these words it is clear that the Apostle proves that, while we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord, because we walk by faith and not by sight. From this argument of the Apostle the following proposition is plainly drawn: whoever walks by faith and not by sight is absent from the Lord. But the Apostle desired, before the day of judgment, to be present with God and not to be absent from the Lord, as he himself testifies, who after the words quoted adds: "We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord." From these words it is plainly held that the Apostle desired not to be absent from the Lord, but to be present with God before the day of judgment; for he desired this while he was still absent in the body, long before the day of judgment. Therefore he desired not to be absent from God, but to be with God before the day of judgment. But, as has been received from the Apostle: whoever walks by sight and not by faith is not absent from God. And consequently, whoever is not absent from God walks by sight and not by faith. Therefore the Apostle desired to walk by sight, and not by faith, before the day of judgment. He would certainly not have desired this, if he had known that the souls of the saints would not see the divine essence before the day of judgment.

units.la: Primum ambiguum siue multiplex & disputabile contentum in verbis praedictis est: quod vltra visionem claram Diuinae essentiae animae non possunt exaltari. Hoc enim potest habere multiplicem intellectum. Vnus est, quod vltra claram visionem Diuinae essentiae animae non possunt exaltari ad quemcunque gradum clarioris visionis, nec ad aliquam perfectionem vel gaudium vel honorem, quod vel quem nunc minime habent. Et iste sensus est erroneus: quia vltra claram visionem, quam nunc habent animae sanctorum, exaltabuntur ad aliquod gaudium actuale, quod tunc minime habent. Tunc enim gaudebunt de completione ciuitatis coelestis, & de vnione sua cum corporibus gloriosis. Et ideo tunc exaltabuntur ad aliquam perfectionem, quam modo non habent. Sic enim anima Christi post resurrectionem quodammodo exitit exaltata: quia tunc recepit gaudium de impassibilitate & immortalitate corporis Christi. Tunc enim ipsa anima Christi ab omni dolore & tristitia fuit penitus aliena: & ita exaltata ad statum, quem non habuit ante resurrectionem Christi, teste Christo, qui dixit, anima mea tristis est vsque ad mortem. Alius intellectus verborum praedictorum est iste: vltra claram visionem Diuinae essentiae non possunt animae exaltari ad aliquam perfectionem distinctam specie à clara visione Dei maiorem & perfectiorem clara visione & fruitione Dei. Et ideo animae post iudicium, licet exaltabuntur ad clariorem visionem, non tamen visione distincta specie à visione praecedente. Gaudium etiam, quod habebunt de completione ciuitatis coelestis & assumptione corporum gloriosorum, non erit maius, neque perfectius visione clara & fruitione quam nunc habent. Et ita iste sensus in nihilo concludit intentum istius protestantis, seu renouantis. Sed primus sensus, si esset verus, euidenter inferret intentum eius. Et ideo assertionem praedictam accipit in sensu primo, propter quod errat aperte.
units.tr: The first ambiguous or manifold and disputable point contained in the words quoted above is that souls cannot be exalted beyond the clear vision of the divine essence. For this may have more than one meaning. One is that souls cannot be exalted beyond the clear vision of the divine essence to any degree of clearer vision, nor to any perfection, joy or honour which they do not now have, or do not have at all. And this sense is erroneous, because beyond the clear vision which the souls of the saints now have, they will be exalted to some actual joy which they then do not have at all. For then they will rejoice in the completion of the heavenly city, and in their union with glorified bodies. And so then they will be exalted to some perfection which they do not now have. For in this way the soul of Christ, after the resurrection, was in a certain manner exalted, because then it received joy from the impassibility and immortality of Christ's body. For then the soul of Christ itself was utterly free from all pain and sadness; and so it was exalted to a state which it did not have before the resurrection of Christ, as Christ himself bears witness, who said, "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death." Another meaning of the words above is this: souls cannot be exalted beyond the clear vision of the divine essence to any perfection distinct in kind from the clear vision of God, greater and more perfect than the clear vision and enjoyment of God. And therefore souls after judgment, although they will be exalted to a clearer vision, will not, however, have a vision distinct in kind from the preceding vision. Nor will the joy which they will have in the completion of the heavenly city and the assumption of glorified bodies be greater or more perfect than the clear vision and enjoyment which they now have. And so this sense does nothing to establish the aim of this protester, or renewer. But the first sense, if it were true, would plainly infer his aim. And therefore he takes the assertion above in the first sense, on account of which he plainly errs.

units.la: Sed diceret aliquis, quod ille non accipit verba praedicta secundum intellectum primum. Quia tunc haberet concedere, quod tunc videns Diuinam essentiam nihil posset aliud recipere nec desiderare quod non diceret. Quia tunc anima Christi non potuisset desiderare resumptionem seu assumptionem corporis gloriosi. Ad hoc dicendum est: quod ipse concedit, inquiens quod infertur. Nam alibi dicit haec verba: Visia facialis praedicta non compatitur secum desiderium alicuius alterius rei.
units.tr: But someone might say that he does not take the words above in the first sense. For then he would have to concede that someone who sees the divine essence could receive or desire nothing else that he would not speak of. For then the soul of Christ could not have desired the resumption or assumption of a glorified body. To this it must be replied: he concedes it, saying what is inferred. For elsewhere he says these words: "The aforesaid face-to-face vision does not admit with it the desire of any other thing."
