units.la: Quæ apertissime sunt hæreticalia reputanda: quia Euangelio contrariantur. Cum Christus, qui vidit diuinam essentiam, dicat Lucæ 22. Desiderio desideraui hoc Pascha manducare vobiscum. Ex quibus verbis patenter infertur, quod visio facialis compatitur secum desiderium alicuius rei. Secundum ambiguum & disputabile contentum in verbis prædictis est, quod visio clara est summa exaltatio animarum. Hoc enim potest habere multiplicem intellectum. Quorum vnus est iste: inter omnes exaltationes animarum distinctas specie clara visio est summa. Et inter modernos de hoc sunt diuersæ opiniones: quibusdam dicentibus, quod visio clara Dei est summa perfectio animæ quia perfectior est fruitione diuina. Aliis dicentibus, quod ideo est summa, quia est fruitio diuina. Non enim ponunt quod visio Dei, fruitio aut dilectio patriæ, realiter distinguantur. Aliis asserentibus, quod clara visio Dei non est summa: sed fruitio aut dilectio patriæ est altior & perfectior visione. Et ideo negant visionem claram esse summam exaltationem animarum, dicentes quod fruitio, seu dilectio Dei est altior.
units.tr: These statements are to be regarded as most plainly heretical, because they are contrary to the Gospel. For Christ, who saw the divine essence, says in Luke 22: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you." From these words it is plainly inferred that the face-to-face vision admits with it the desire of some thing. The second ambiguous and disputable point contained in the words above is that the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls. For this may have more than one meaning. One of these is this: among all the distinct kinds of exaltation of souls, the clear vision is the highest. And among the moderns there are various opinions on this: some saying that the clear vision of God is the highest perfection of the soul because it is more perfect than the enjoyment of God; others saying that it is the highest because it is the enjoyment of God. For they do not hold that the vision of God, the enjoyment or the love of the homeland, are really distinct. Others maintaining that the clear vision of God is not the highest, but that the enjoyment or love of the homeland is higher and more perfect than the vision; and therefore they deny that the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls, saying that the enjoyment or love of God is higher.

units.la: Aliis intellectus verborum prædictorum est iste. Visio clara est sic summa exaltatio animarum, quod animæ videntes clare Deum ad nullam perfectionem specie distinctam maiorem illa quam habent potuerunt exaltari. Et iste sensus verus est, siue visio sit perfectior, siue fruitio. Quia nunquam habebunt animæ in se formaliter aliquam perfectionem distinctam specie à visione Dei perfectiorem visione & dilectione seu fruitione Dei. Tertius sensus est iste. Visio clara sic est summa exaltatio animarum, quod anima videns Deum nullo modo neque ad vlteriorem gradum visionis Diuinæ, neque ad quodcunque aliud perfectius, vel imperfectius visione Dei poterit exaltari. Et iste est sensus istius protestantis vel æquiuocantis. Quia aliter prædicta verba nullo modo possunt inferre conclusionem intentam. Sed iste sensus est erroneus, vt ex prædictis patet aperte. Nam ex his verbis sequitur euidenter, quod anima Christi non vidit Deum ante resurrectionem vel ante mortem Christi, quia potuit contristari. Postea autem ad statum omnis impassibilitatis extitit exaltata. Sensus enim prædictus Magistro Sententiarum aperte repugnat, qui libro 2. dist. vndecim. dicit, angelos videntes Deum in congregationem & beatitudinem proficere dicens, in hæc verba: Illa vero quod alii superius dicunt, probabilius videtur, quod angeli vsque ad iudicium in scientia & in alia possunt proficere. Et ita anima videns Deum, potest ad aliud exaltari. Nec est hoc negandum, cum omnis exaltatio sit de minori secundum speciem ad maius secundum speciem. Cum etiam sæpe in humanis exaltationibus videmus tales retentis maioribus dignitatibus ad minores compossibiles maioribus exaltari. Unde & nonnunquam cardinalis ad officium summi pœnitentiarii postea exaltabitur, cardinalatu retento: sic animæ sanctæ videntes Deum retenta Dei visione, ad aliquid aliud minus visione diuina poterunt exaltari & etiam ad clariorem visionem Dei.
units.tr: Another interpretation of the foregoing words is this: the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls in such a way that souls seeing God clearly could not be exalted to any perfection distinct in species and greater than the one they have. This sense is true, whether the vision or the enjoyment is the more perfect. For souls will never possess formally in themselves any perfection, distinct in species from the vision of God, more perfect than the vision and the love or enjoyment of God. A third sense is this: the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls in such a way that a soul seeing God can in no way be exalted either to a higher degree of divine vision or to anything else more or less perfect than the vision of God. This is the sense of this protester or equivocator, since otherwise the foregoing words could in no way yield the conclusion intended. But this sense is erroneous, as is plain from what has been said. For from these words it clearly follows that the soul of Christ did not see God before the resurrection or before the death of Christ, because it could be saddened, and afterwards was exalted to the state of complete impassibility. This sense clearly contradicts the Sentences of the Master, who in book 2, distinction eleven says that angels seeing God advance in glory and blessedness, in these words: Those things indeed which others say above seem more probable, that the angels can advance in knowledge and in other things until the judgment. So a soul seeing God can be exalted to something else. Nor is this to be denied, since every exaltation is from the lesser in species to the greater in species. Also in human exaltations we often see such men, while keeping their greater dignities, being raised to lesser offices compatible with the greater; hence sometimes a cardinal is afterwards promoted to the office of chief penitentiary while retaining the cardinalate. So holy souls, while retaining the vision of God, can be exalted to something else less than the divine vision, and also to a clearer vision of God.

units.la: His visis ad rationem istius est facile respondere. Cum enim primo dicit, vltra visionem claram Diuinæ essentiæ non possunt exaltari. Patet ex prædictis, quod hoc in hoc sensu, quem habet iste de ipsa & ex quo sequitur conclusio quam intendi, est erronea: quia vltra visionem claram, non clarissimam Diuinæ essentiæ, est visio clarior, ad quam possunt animæ exaltari. Unde vltra albedinem non intensissimam, est intensior: & vltra charitatem non perfectissimam, est charitas persectior.
units.tr: To what has been said, it is easy to answer the argument of this man. When he first says, beyond the clear vision of the divine essence they cannot be exalted, it is plain from what has been said that in the sense he gives it, and from which the conclusion I am aiming at follows, it is erroneous: for beyond the clear vision, though not the clearest vision, of the divine essence there is a clearer vision to which souls can be exalted. Thus beyond a whiteness that is not the most intense, there is a more intense whiteness, and beyond a charity that is not the most perfect, there is a more perfect charity.

units.la: Cum secundo dicit (vltra summum nihil est) dicendum, quod hoc etiam potest habere multiplicem intellectum: quia aliquid dicitur summum multipliciter. Aliquid enim est simpliciter summum, & eo nihil est altius. Aliud autem dicitur summum secundum speciem, sicut inter omnes species coloris albedo potest esse summa, & inter omnia genera visionum visio intellectualis dicitur summa. Aliter potest aliquid summum esse quadam aggregatione: quia scilicet omnia possibilia ad perfectionem alicuius spectantia comprehendit. Secundum quem modum beatitudo, quæ est status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectus, potest dici summa. Aliter dicitur aliquid summum in vna specie, per quem modum intensissima albedo potest dici summa. Et visio animæ Christi est summa inter omnes charitates charitas. Sic etiam inter reges vnus potest dici summus, & maximus. Accipiendo igitur summum primo modo, sic summo nihil est altius. Accipiendo summum secundo modo, sic summo nihil distinctum specie, est altius. Nam in genere virtutum nulla virtus distincta à charitate est altior charitate: vna tamen charitas est altior alia. Sic in genere cognitionum Dei nulla cognitio distincta à visione clara Dei, est altior visione clara Dei, vna tamen visio clara Diuinæ essentiæ est altior alia. Visio enim, qua videt Deum anima Christi, est clarior visione qua angelus videt Deum. Et ideo quamuis visio clara Dei sit summa inter cognitiones, quibus Deus cognoscitur: non est tamen inconueniens, quod animæ primo videant Deum minus clare, & postea exaltentur ad clariorem visionem. Sic summo nihil est inter illa, quæ possunt eidem rei competere altius, licet Deus sit altior tali summo. Accipiendo autem summum tertio modo, sic summo nihil est altius in tali specie. Unde intensissima nigredine nullus color niger est altior ipsa, tamen est aliquis alius color altior. Sic enim patet, quod summum potest capi multipliciter. Et ideo ista: summo nihil est altius, habet varios sensus: quorum vnus est verus, & alius falsus. Cum vero accipit tertio, quod visio clara est summa exaltatio animarum, patet per prædicta, quod ista varios habet sensus falsos. Quia ista falsa est accipiendo summum tertio modo. Accipiendo etiam summum quarto modo est falsa: quia visio clara, quâ hunc habent animæ sanctæ, non est summa exaltatio animarum, propter quod non est clarissima visio, quam habebunt. Habiturę enim sunt post iudicium clariorem. Accipiendo autem summum primo modo, sic non est ad propositum, accipiendo autem secundo modo, sic diuersæ sunt opiniones, sicut dictum est: quibusdam dicentibus, quod clara visio est perfectior dilectione seu fruitione Dei, & illi dicerent quod visio clara est summa exaltatio animarum sic accipiendo summum. Aliis dicentibus, quod dilectio seu fruitio est perfectior & altior visione, & illi dicerent, quod visio non est summa exaltatio animarum, sed fruitio.
units.tr: When he says secondly (beyond the highest there is nothing), it must be said that this too can have several meanings, because something is called highest in several ways. Something is highest absolutely, and nothing is higher than it. Something else is called highest in its kind, as among all the species of colour whiteness can be the highest, and among all the kinds of vision intellectual vision is called the highest. Again, something can be highest by aggregation, namely because it comprises all possible things pertaining to the perfection of something; in this way blessedness, which is the state of all good things made perfect in aggregate, can be called the highest. In another way something is called highest within one species; in this way the most intense whiteness can be called the highest. And the vision of the soul of Christ is the highest charity among all charities. So too among kings one can be called the highest and greatest. Taking the highest in the first way, then, nothing is higher than the highest. Taking it in the second way, nothing distinct in species from the highest is higher than it; for in the genus of virtues no virtue distinct from charity is higher than charity, yet one charity is higher than another. So in the genus of knowledge of God no knowledge distinct from the clear vision of God is higher than the clear vision of God, yet one clear vision of the divine essence is higher than another. For the vision by which the soul of Christ sees God is clearer than the vision by which an angel sees God. And so, although the clear vision of God is the highest among the knowledges by which God is known, it is not inconsistent that souls should first see God less clearly and afterwards be exalted to a clearer vision. Thus nothing is higher than the highest among those things which can belong to the same thing, although God is higher than any such highest. Taking the highest in the third way, nothing is higher than the highest in that kind. Hence, though no black is higher than the most intense blackness, there is some other colour higher than it. In this way it is plain that the highest can be taken in several senses. Therefore the statement nothing is higher than the highest has various senses, of which one is true and another false. When he takes it in the third way, that the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls, it is plain from what has been said that this statement has various false senses, because it is false when the highest is taken in the third way. It is also false when the highest is taken in the fourth way, because the clear vision which holy souls now have is not the highest exaltation of souls, for the clearest vision which they will have is not yet. For after the judgment they will have a clearer one. Taking the highest in the first way, the matter is not to the point; taking it in the second way, the opinions differ, as has been said: some hold that the clear vision is more perfect than the love or enjoyment of God, and these would say that the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls, taking the highest in that way. Others hold that the love or enjoyment is more perfect and higher than the vision, and these would say that it is not the vision but the enjoyment that is the highest exaltation of souls.

units.la: Cum vero quarto dicit, quod in die iudicii cum Deus sanctos & illorum animas exaltabit: ista continetur sub isto intellectu, quod animæ sanctorum tunc habebunt clariorem visionem Dei: & etiam gaudium de visione corporum gloriosorum, & de completione ciuitatis Hierusalem & aliis multis, & ista erit exaltatio animarum, sanctos vero, id est personas integras compositas ex corpore & anima, exaltabit, quod tunc dabit eis beatitudinem perfectam, quam ipsi prius non habuerunt: imo nec ipsi videbunt prius Deum, licet animæ sanctorum & non ipsi modo vident Deum. Dicendum est, quod male infert, si proportiones præcedentes sane intelligantur. Si autem intelligantur, sicut isti intelligunt, secundum quod dictum est, sic ex propositionibus hæreticalibus infert conclusionem hæreticam. Intelligit enim: quod visio clara sic est summa exaltatio animarum, quod anima videns Deum nihil potest acquirere, nec aliquo modo proficere, nec aliquid non habitum desiderare. Et iste sensus est erroneus: quia sequeretur, quod anima Christi non vidisset Deum ab instanti conceptionis Christi.
units.tr: When he fourthly says that at the day of judgment, when God will exalt the saints and their souls, this is covered by the meaning that the souls of the saints will then have a clearer vision of God, and also joy in the vision of the glorified bodies, and in the completion of the city of Jerusalem and many other things; this will be the exaltation of souls, while God will exalt the saints, that is, the whole persons composed of body and soul, in that he will then give them perfect blessedness, which they did not previously have. Indeed they themselves will not see God before, although the souls of the saints, and not they themselves, now see God. It must be said that he draws a wrong inference, if the premises are understood correctly. But if they are understood as these men understand them, according to what has been said, then he infers a heretical conclusion from heretical premises. For he means that the clear vision is the highest exaltation of souls in such a way that a soul seeing God can acquire nothing, nor advance in any way, nor desire anything it does not have. And this sense is erroneous, for it would follow that the soul of Christ had not seen God from the moment of Christ's conception.

units.la: Cum autem sexto dicit, alias tunc non exaltarentur: hoc non sequitur ex præcedentibus, sicut ostensum est, quia, sicut dictum est, quamuis sanctorum animæ videant Deum, tamen animæ ad clariorem visionem poterunt exaltari, & ipsi sancti, quando resurgent in corpore ad visionem diuinæ essentiæ, & impassibilitatem & alias dotes corporis & animæ poterunt exaltari. Cum sic conatur probare minorem, scilicet quod Deus in die iudicii sanctos, & illorum animas exaltabit, per hoc quod usque ad diem iudicii sunt sub altari, & post diem iudicii videbunt Deum facie ad faciem. Dicendum est, quod iste textum libri Apocalypsis male intelligit, non enim ideo animæ martyrum dicuntur sub altari usq; ad diem iudicii, quia non vident deitatem Christi, sed tantum humanitatem, sicut iste textus false exponitur: sed dicuntur sub altari, quia absconsæ nobis & existentibus in inferno, & in purgatorio, saltem multæ ab omni malo protectæ clare Deum vident & ipso fruuntur. Porro quia quantum ad hoc motiuum in beato Bernardo nititur se fundare, verba eiusdem beati Bernardi non intelligit, quia non intendit, nisi quod sancti secundum animas collocantur sub Christo, & Deum vident, donec ipsi sancti integri & perfecti secundum corpus & animam procedant, completo numero fratrum, & participent regnum. Sed forte diceret aliquis: si sancti tunc participant regnum, & regnū est visio Dei: igitur antea non habebunt visionem Dei. Ad hoc dicendum, quod licet quandoque regnum vocatur clara visio Dei, sicut etiam regnum Dei nonnunquam vocatur ecclesia præsens: tamen interdum regnum Dei appellatur beatitudo consummata comprehendens animæ & corporis beatitudinem & istud regnum Dei de communi lege sancti ante diem iudicii nequaquam participabunt: imo ipsi ex anima & corpore constituti non habebunt de communi lege prius visionem Dei, sed animæ ipsorum tantummodo, & de isto regno & gloria animæ & corporis loquitur ibi. Sed adhuc quæreret aliquis, quomodo sancti erunt super altare post iudicium secundum beatum Bernardum, cum nunquam erunt super Christum? Ad hoc potest responderi dupliciter, uno modo, quod in scriptura diuina non legitur, quod animæ sanctorum post iudicium erunt super altare, nec meminime legisse, quod hoc Bernardus dicat. Aliter potest dici, quod ideo possunt dici animæ super altare post iudicium, quia tunc non erunt post iudicium quibusdam electis absconditæ: tunc autem dicuntur sub altari: quia videntes Deum quasi absconsæ consolantur & gaudent in Deo: gloria enim earum latet plures electos, & plures existentes in inferno, & ideo possunt dici sub altari, quia ibidem absconditæ. Cum vero vltimo allegat beatum Petrum dicentem: prout nos exaltet in salutem &c. Dicendum est, quod auctoritas Petri non facit pro isto, quia beatus Petrus loquebatur hominibus integris ex anima & corpore constitutis, & verum est, quod illi exaltabuntur ad visionem claram in die iudicii, & non ante, de communi lege, quia licet animæ multorum antea clare vident Deum, tamen homines compositi ex corpore & anima, de communi lege antea non videbunt Deum, & per istum modum omnes fere auctoritates, quas pro hæresi supradicta in duobus maximis tractatibus & prolixis adducit, soluuntur: quia loquuntur de electis compositis ex corpore & anima, qui de communi lege Deum ante diem iudicii non videbunt.
units.tr: When he sixthly says, otherwise they would not then be exalted, this does not follow from what precedes, as has been shown, because, as has been said, although the souls of the saints see God, yet souls can be exalted to a clearer vision, and the saints themselves, when they rise in the body, can be exalted to the vision of the divine essence, and to impassibility and the other gifts of body and soul. He tries to prove the minor premise in this way, namely that God at the day of judgment will exalt the saints and their souls, because until the day of judgment they are under the altar, and after the day of judgment they will see God face to face. It must be said that he misunderstands this text of the book of Revelation. For the souls of the martyrs are not said to be under the altar until the day of judgment because they do not see the deity of Christ but only his humanity, as this text is falsely explained; rather they are said to be under the altar because they are hidden from us and existing in hell and in purgatory, or at least many of them, sheltered from all evil, see God clearly and enjoy him. Moreover, since he tries to found his argument on the blessed Bernard, he does not understand the words of the same blessed Bernard, for he means only that the saints according to their souls are placed under Christ and see God, until the saints themselves, whole and perfect according to body and soul, advance when the number of brethren is complete and share in the kingdom. But perhaps someone would say: if the saints then share in the kingdom, and the kingdom is the vision of God, then they will not have the vision of God before. To this it must be said that although sometimes the kingdom is called the clear vision of God, just as the kingdom of God is sometimes called the present church, yet at other times the kingdom of God is called consummated blessedness, comprising the blessedness of soul and body; and by the common law the saints will by no means share in that kingdom before the day of judgment. Indeed they, composed of soul and body, will not by the common law have the vision of God before, but only their souls; and it is of that kingdom and of the glory of soul and body that he speaks there. But someone would still ask: how, according to the blessed Bernard, will the saints be above the altar after the judgment, since they will never be above Christ? To this one may answer in two ways. In one way, that in divine Scripture it is not read that the souls of the saints will be above the altar after the judgment, nor do I recall ever reading that Bernard says this. Otherwise it can be said that the souls can be called above the altar after the judgment because then they will no longer be hidden from some of the elect; but they are said to be under the altar then, because, seeing God, they are as it were hidden and console themselves and rejoice in God, for their glory is hidden from many of the elect and from many existing in hell, and so they can be called under the altar, since they are hidden there. But when he at last cites the blessed Peter saying, as he may exalt us to salvation, etc., it must be said that the authority of Peter does not support this, because the blessed Peter was speaking to men whole and composed of soul and body, and it is true that they will be exalted to the clear vision at the day of judgment and not before, by the common law; for although the souls of many see God clearly before, yet men composed of body and soul will not, by the common law, see God before the day of judgment. In this way almost all the authorities which he brings forward for the aforesaid heresy in his two very large and lengthy treatises are answered, because they speak of the elect composed of body and soul, who by the common law will not see God before the day of judgment.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Ponit tertiam rationem pro hæresi principali, quæ innititur huic fundamento, scilicet quod cum clara visione non stat doctrina, seu notitia alicuius de nouo.
units.tr: He sets out the third argument for the principal heresy, which rests on this foundation: that clear vision does not stand together with teaching, or with knowledge of anything new.

units.la: Tertia via, super quam se fundauit, est: quia, prout dicit, visio beata non stat cum doctrina: quia quicunque clare videt Deum, videt & omnia, secundum Gregorium dicentem: quid est quod non videt qui videntem omnia videt? sed secundum beatum Augustin. De cura pro mortuis agenda, anima sanctorum illa quæ fiunt hic apud viuentes, ex se non cognoscunt, sed eis innotescunt, aut per animas nouiter decedentes. cedentium seu morientium, aut per revelationes angelorum, qui curam habent nem immediatam a Deo, cum igitur non videant omnia, per consequens nec faci ratio eius tertia in una haeresi manifesta est fundata: quod scilicet clar esse non potest, vel saltem non est sine omniscientia, quia asserit manife la ignorant: igitur omnia sciunt, sed haec haeresis scripturae divinae ape stolus ad Ephes. 3. Mihi enim omnium sanctorum minimo data est gratia haec: gabiles divitias Christi, & illuminare omnes quae sit dispensatio sacramenti abscon creavit, ut innotescat principibus & potestatibus in caelestibus per ecclesiam mul bus verbis ultimate colligitur, quod angeli sancti ante incarnationem la secreta de incarnatione Christi ignorabant, angeli tunc viderunt D dentes Deum omnia sciunt: imo multa ignorant. Quod vero secun Angeli sancti videntes Deum aliqua de incarnationis mysterio ignora missa asserit manifeste, dicens in persona beati Pauli & exponens verb est mihi evangelizare, & illuminare, & videre, quid hoc est? quia per hoc aliqu hoc didicerunt, & hoc, quod ait evangelizare: dico ita, ut multiformis sapientia notescat per ecclesiam, quae dona Dei recipit: id est per Apostolos in ecclesia pradi id est pro diversis ordinibus angelorum, qui sunt in caelestibus, id est in caelo, v que beatus Hieronymus angelicas dignitates supra memoratum mysterium aliq impleta est passio Christi, & Apostolorum praedicatio per gentes dilatata. Und xerunt: Quis est iste, qui venit de Edom? & in Psal. Quis est iste rex gloriae. Non phetis: sed etiam potestatibus caelestibus multiformis sapientia Dei per ecclesiam mis igitur dicitur Dei sapientia: quia multipliciter multas species, & forma testates per ecclesiam agnoverunt. Ex his omnibus colligitur evidente Deum aliquid accreuit per ecclesiam, & quod aliquid didicerunt per asterium redemptionis humanae, quod ante redemptionem & passio stolorum non intellexerunt ad purum seu plenum: & quod multiform Angelis Deum videntibus revelata, & quod Angeli multitudinem sap quibus omnibus patenter concluditur: quod visio beata stat cum de qui clare vident Deum, vident omnia, & quod aliqui qui faciliter vid atque aliqua eis docentur, & quod eis aliquid revelatur, & quod non s cialiter clare Deum, quae omnia iste negat aperte in verbis praemissis.
units.tr: The third path on which he bases himself is this: as he says, the blessed vision does not stand together with teaching, because whoever clearly sees God sees all things as well, following Gregory, who says: "What is it that he does not see who sees the one who sees all things?" But according to the blessed Augustine, in his book On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead, the souls of the saints do not know by themselves the things that happen here among the living, but these become known to them either through the souls of those newly departing or dying, or through the revelations of angels, who have immediate care from God. Since therefore they do not see all things, consequently they do not clearly see God face to face. The third argument of this heresy is therefore founded on one manifest error: namely, that clear vision cannot exist, or at least cannot exist without omniscience. He asserts plainly that the angels are ignorant of some things, and therefore they know all things; but this heresy is contrary to the divine Scripture. The Apostle says in Ephesians 3: "To me, the least of all the saints, is this grace given, to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to make all men see what is the dispensation of the mystery which from the beginning of the world has been hidden in God, who created all things; to the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God." From these words it is finally gathered that the holy angels, before the incarnation of Christ, were ignorant of the secrets of the incarnation of Christ. The angels, who then saw God, therefore know all things? Nay, they are ignorant of many things. That the holy angels, who see God, are ignorant of some things of the mystery of the incarnation, he asserts plainly, speaking in the person of the blessed Paul and explaining the words "to me it is given to evangelize, and to enlighten, and to see": what is this? Because by this they learned some things, and by what he says, "to evangelize," I mean: that the manifold wisdom might be made known through the church, which receives the gifts of God, that is, through the Apostles preached in the church, for the various orders of angels which are in heavenly places, that is, in heaven. Blessed Jerome, on this mystery, explains the angelic dignities as follows: the passion of Christ was accomplished, and the preaching of the Apostles spread among the nations. And the angels say: "Who is this who comes from Edom?" And in the Psalm: "Who is this King of glory?" Not only to men, but also to the heavenly powers, the manifold wisdom of God is made known through the church. The wisdom of God is therefore called manifold, because it knows many species and forms in many ways, and the heavenly powers came to know these through the church. From all these things it is gathered clearly that God has increased something through the church, and that the angels learned something through the mystery of human redemption, which before the redemption and the passion of Christ and the preaching of the Apostles they did not understand fully or completely; and that a manifold wisdom was revealed to the angels who see God, and that the angels are taught some things, and that something is revealed to them. All these things are concluded plainly from these words: that the blessed vision stands together with knowledge; that those who clearly see God see all things; and that some who see God face to face are ignorant of some things, and that some things are taught to them, and that something is revealed to them. This he openly denies in the words cited above.

units.la: Sed dicet aliquis, Augustinus praemissis obviare videtur, qui sup Angelis: non latuit eis mysterium regni caelorum, quod tempore opportuno quo ex hac peregrinatione liberati, eorum coetu coniungamur. Sed ad hoc re Magister Sententiarum libro 2. dist. 11. ad eandem obiectionem respondet dicit enim Glossa: ne videantur sibi contradicere in praedictu sacra pagina Augustinus, ita potest declarari, quod factum est, & ut illu qui maioris dignitatis illa nunciata sunt, cognita fuerunt experta vt pote familiaribus nunciis, illi vero cognita essent. Ex quibus verbis liquet aperte: quod licet Angeli see dem cognoverunt, quidam tamen Angeli videntes Deum minoris d uerunt, & ita non omnes videntes Deum omnia vident.
units.tr: But someone will say that Augustine seems to contradict what has been said, since he writes of the angels: "The mystery of the kingdom of heaven was not hidden from them, which at the appointed time, when we are freed from this pilgrimage, we shall be joined to their company." But the Master of the Sentences, Book 2, distinction 11, answers this same objection. For the Gloss says: "Lest Augustine seem to contradict himself in the said sacred page, it can be explained that it happened, and that those things were announced to those of greater dignity, and were known and experienced by them, as to familiar messengers; but they were known to the others." From these words it is clear that, although the angels all knew these things, some angels who see God are of lesser dignity, and so not all who see God see all things.

units.la: Item, quod non omnes videntes omnia sciant, sed ignorant aliqu tur dicens, Matth. 24. De die autem illa & hora nemo novit, neque Angeli c Deum, licet non omnia sciant.
units.tr: Likewise, not all who see God know all things, but some things are unknown to them, as the Lord says in Matthew 24: "But of that day and hour knows no one, no, not the angels of heaven"; so some who see God do not know all things.

units.la: Amplius, Apostolus Paulus in raptu viderat divinam essentiam, f men Paulus non omnia novit, & ita non omnis videns Deum scit omn
units.tr: Furthermore, the Apostle Paul had seen the divine essence in his rapture, yet Paul did not know all things. And so not every one who sees God knows all things.

units.la: Rursus, de Christo singulare dicit Apostolus ad Colloss. 2. In qu scientia absconditi. Igitur istud nulli alii videnti Deum debet attribui, he lare animae Christi, quod ipsa sola inter spiritus videntes Deum habe bis euangelicis Iohan. 3. posse probati videtur. Soli enim Chr mensuram, igitur solus Christus habuit omnem scientiam, & ita rare.
units.tr: Again, the Apostle says something singular about Christ, Colossians 2: "In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." Therefore this must not be attributed to any other who sees God, but belongs to the soul of Christ alone, which alone among the spirits that see God has it. This also seems to be proved by the Gospel of John 3: "For God gives not the Spirit by measure to him." Christ alone, therefore, had all knowledge, and so not every one who sees God has all knowledge.

units.la: His visis distinguendo, facile est rationem praedictam refellere. visio beata non stat cum doctrina: dicendum est, quod haec est erronea, f vero secundo dicit probando per hoc minorem: quia quicunque clare vi Gregor. dicentem: quid est quod non videt qui videntem omnia videt? D dicit Magister Sententiarum libro 2. distinct. 11. dicens in haec verba: Gre Angelis: quid est, quod ibi nesciant, ubi scientem omnia sciunt? videtur dicere q sit quod nesciant, sed accipiendum est hoc de his, quorum cognitio beatum facit cog sterium trinitatis & unitatis pertinent, haec sunt verba Magistri sentent li videntes Deum non omnia sciunt, & quod Gregorius non loc rarum, sed de his quae spectant ad mysterium trinitatis & unitati infert dicens: & per consequens secundum beatum Gregorium, qui vi rant aliquas quae apud viventes fiunt: nec docentur de aliquo: nec revelatur eis aliquid quod prius non viderunt. Dicendum est, quod ex verbis Gregorii male intellectis (ut ostensum est per Magistrum sententiarum) infert tres conclusiones erroneas. Prima est, quod qui facialiter vident Deum, non ignorant aliqua. Secunda est, quod non docentur ab aliquo. Tertia est, quod non revelatur eis aliquid, quod prius non viderint, quas esse erroneas superius per Apostolum Paulum & Glossam est probatum. Auctoritas Augustini, quam adducit, secundum bonum intellectum est concedenda, quia sive dictum Augustini intelligitur de mortuis videntibus Deum, sive de aliis: concedendum est, quod non omnia sciunt omnes mortui, quae hic aguntur, quia, sicut ostensum est, etiam videntes Deum non omnia vident. Et ideo cum ultimo concludit dicens: cum igitur non vident omnia: & per consequens non facialiter clare vident Deum. Dicendum est, quod non sequitur, sicut nec sequitur, angeli boni non viderunt omnia, puta incarnationem: igitur non viderunt clare Deum.
units.tr: Having seen these things, it is easy to refute the aforesaid argument by a distinction. As to the claim that the blessed vision does not stand together with teaching: it must be said that this is erroneous. As to the minor premise, which he proves in the second place, because "whoever clearly sees God sees all things," and he cites Gregory, "What is it that he does not see who sees the one who sees all things?": the Master of the Sentences, Book 2, distinction 11, says in these words: "Gregory, speaking of the angels: what is it that they do not know there, where the one who knows all things knows? It seems to say that there is something they do not know; but this must be understood of those things whose knowledge makes one blessed, which pertain to the mystery of the Trinity and the Unity." These are the words of the Master of the Sentences. From this it is evident that those who see God do not know all things, and that Gregory is not speaking here of all things, but of those which concern the mystery of the Trinity and Unity. He infers, saying: "And consequently, according to the blessed Gregory, those who see God do not see the things that take place among the living, nor are they taught anything by anyone, nor is anything revealed to them that they did not see before." It must be said that from the words of Gregory, badly understood (as has been shown by the Master of the Sentences), he draws three erroneous conclusions. The first is that those who see God face to face do not ignore anything. The second is that they are not taught by anyone. The third is that nothing is revealed to them which they had not seen before. These have been shown above to be erroneous, by the Apostle Paul and by the Gloss. The authority of Augustine which he cites is to be granted in its good sense, because whether the saying of Augustine is understood of the dead who see God, or of others, it must be granted that not all the dead know the things that are done here, since, as has been shown, even those who see God do not see all things. And so when he concludes at the end, saying: "Since therefore they do not see all things, and consequently do not clearly see God face to face," it must be said that this does not follow, just as it does not follow that the good angels did not see all things, for example the incarnation, and therefore did not clearly see God.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: Ponit tres vias, sive tres suppositiones. Quibus suppositis secundum singulas rationes procedit, conclusionem principalem probando. Ex prima via, sive suppositione format tres rationes, quae etiam confutantur, secunda via ponitur capitulo 5. & tertia capitulo 6.
units.tr: He sets out three ways, or three suppositions. Having laid these down, he proceeds according to each argument, proving the principal conclusion. From the first way, or supposition, he forms three arguments, which are also refuted. The second way is set out in chapter 5, and the third in chapter 6.

units.la: Sequitur in potestatione friuola memorata, quia dicit, quod ad videndam & inuestigandam veritatem istius conclusionis debet attendere tria. Primum est, cui merces clarae visionis promittitur. Secundus est tempus, pro quo merces promittitur. Tertium ad quid futurum iudicium generale ordinatur. His praemissis, in quibus tres ultimas vias fundat, statim subiunxit de eo, cui promittitur, in quo consistit prima via suae probationis sic. Si attendamus, cui illa merces in sacra pagina promittitur, certum est quod toti suppositio. Probatur primo: quia Iacobus ait: beatus vir qui sustinet tentationem &c. & certum est, quod anima non est vir. Secundo ad idem. Quia Christus dicit: omnis qui reliquit patrem &c. vitam aeternam habebit &c. certum est: quod illi, quibus loquebatur, erant suppositi, & non anima separata. Ad idem est, quod Christus ducit: vos qui reliquistis omnia &c. certum est, quod illi qui erant hic, erant beatus Petrus & alia suppositi, & non eorum anima separata. Item merces illa reddetur pro operibus misericordiae. Unde Christus dicet in iudicio: esuriui & mihi dedistis &c. sed certum est, quod suppositum, & non anima separata, dedit eleemosynam: igitur suppositio, & non anima separata reddetur merces. Post tres rationes praedictas ponit alias tres sumptas ex tribus notabilibus, quae dicit esse attendenda. Prima autem ratio eius, quae hic ponitur, est haec. Visio beata est reddenda toti supposito, & non anima separata, igitur anima sanctorum in caelo non vident Deum. Ista ratio est quasi principalius motiuum ipsius pro haeresi supradicta, propter quod ipsam saepe replicat, & reputat ipsam irrefragabilem, ponens enim ipsam in sermone, qui incipit, Gaudete in Domino, & in tractatu, qui incipit. Quaere verum anime sanctorum &c. Antecedens ipse probat sic, visio illa, quae est merces, reddetur illi, cui promittitur, sed merces promittitur supposito & non anima separata, igitur &c. Minor probatur tribus auctoritatibus, & una ratione. Sed ista fundamento haereticali innititur: quod scilicet merces non nisi supposito & non animae promittitur. Ad euidentiam eius est veritas elucidanda. Secundo, haeresis fundamento haereticali praefato contraria est probanda. Tertio discurrendo per auctoritates, quas adducit, sunt illa quae apparent in contrarium repellenda. Circa primum est sciendum, quod ista est catholica veritas, quod merces quae includit gloriam animae & corporis, soli supposito seu homini integro ex corpore & anima constituto promittitur, & illa de communi lege non dabitur ante diem iudicii generalis, merces autem, quae non includit gloriam animae & corporis, sed solum gloriam animae: scilicet visionem Dei, & fruitionem, promittitur animae antequam corpus resumpserit, & ideo ista merces dabitur multis animabus a corpore separatis. Est tamen aduertendum, quod gloria animae datur: & dabitur multis animabus ante iudicium, respectu quarum non dicitur proprie merces, quia non dicitur merces propter meritum illarum, sed potest dici merces earum propter meritum Christi, quod promittitur. Secundum est, quod visio diuinae essentiae animabus ante vniuersale iudicium est promissa. Primum sic ostenditur: animabus decedentium nihil purgandum habentibus requies promittitur. Hanc non oportet probare, quia nota est, & inuentor haeresis memoratae eam non negat, cum concedat expresse in multis locis animas separatas esse in quiete, sed ista quies est quaedam merces, quae datur multis animabus propter meritum earum, igitur animabus aliqua merces promittitur.
units.tr: He goes on in the aforementioned frivolous treatise, where he says that to see and investigate the truth of this conclusion one must attend to three things. The first is to whom the reward of clear vision is promised. The second is the time for which the reward is promised. The third is the purpose for which the general judgment is ordained. With these premises laid down, on which he founds his last three ways, he at once turns to the one to whom it is promised, and on this rests his first way of proof: If we consider to whom that reward is promised in holy scripture, it is certain that it is promised to the whole suppositum. He proves it first: because James says, blessed is the man who endures temptation, etc., and it is certain that the soul is not a man. Second, to the same point: because Christ says, everyone who has left father, etc., shall have eternal life, etc. It is certain that those to whom he was speaking were the supposita, and not the separated soul. To the same point is what Christ says: you who have left all things, etc. It is certain that those who were present there were blessed Peter and the others, as supposita, and not their separated souls. Likewise, that reward will be rendered for works of mercy. Hence Christ will say at the judgment: I was hungry and you gave me food, etc. But it is certain that the suppositum, and not the separated soul, gave alms. Therefore the suppositum, and not the separated soul, will receive the reward. After these three arguments, he gives three others, drawn from three points which he says must be considered. His first argument here is this: The blessed vision is to be rendered to the whole suppositum, and not to the separated soul; therefore the souls of the saints in heaven do not see God. This argument is, as it were, his chief motive for the aforesaid heresy, and for that reason he repeats it often and regards it as irrefutable, placing it in the sermon that begins Rejoice in the Lord, and in the treatise that begins Seek the truth about the souls of the saints, etc. He proves the antecedent thus: That vision, which is the reward, will be given to the one to whom it is promised; but the reward is promised to the suppositum and not to the separated soul; therefore etc. The minor premise is proved by three authorities and one argument. But this rests on a heretical foundation, namely that the reward is promised only to the suppositum and not to the soul. To make this evident, the truth must be explained. Second, the heresy must be proved contrary to the aforesaid heretical foundation. Third, by running through the authorities he adduces, those which seem to point the other way must be rejected. On the first point it must be known that this is the Catholic truth: the reward which includes the glory of soul and body is promised only to the suppositum, that is, to the whole man made up of body and soul, and by the common law it will not be given before the day of the general judgment. But the reward which does not include the glory of soul and body, only the glory of the soul, namely the vision and enjoyment of God, is promised to the soul before it resumes its body; and so this reward will be given to many souls separated from the body. It must, however, be noted that the glory of the soul is given, and will be given to many souls before the judgment; with respect to these it is not properly called a reward, because it is not a reward for their merit, but it can be called their reward on account of the merit of Christ, which is promised. The second point is that the vision of the divine essence has been promised to souls before the universal judgment. The first is shown thus: rest is promised to the souls of the departed who have nothing to be purged. There is no need to prove this, because it is well known, and the author of the aforesaid heresy does not deny it, since he expressly concedes in many places that the separated souls are at rest. But this rest is a certain reward, which is given to many souls on account of their merit; therefore some reward is promised to souls.

units.la: Iterum, esse in caelo, videre & gaudere de humanitate Christi est merces, ista enim dabuntur omnibus electis propter meritum Christi, & aliquibus propter meritum proprium simul, & meritum Christi, sed ista animabus sanctis promittitur, igitur animabus separatis aliqua merces promittitur. Quod vero visio Dei aliquibus animabus promittitur, Saluator noster Iohan. 7. innuit manifeste dicens: pater quos dedisti mihi volo ut ubi ego sum, & sint illi mecum, ut videant claritatem meam quam dedisti &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Christus praedicando promisit, quod omnes qui erunt ibi vident, & videbunt claritatem deitatis Christi, & ita illis visio Dei promittitur. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod Christus loquitur de claritate sua secundum humanitatem, quam vident animae separatae in caelo. Sed hæc euasio est nulla: quia Christus loquitur de claritate, quam habuit antequam mundus esset, ipso ibidem dicente ad patrem: clarifica me tu pater apud temetipsum claritate quam habuit prius quam mundus esset apud te, illa autem claritas, quam habuit Christus antequam mundus esset, est claritas deitatis: igitur qui sunt in cœlo cum Christo, vident claritatem deitatis eius.
units.tr: Again, to be in heaven, to see and rejoice in the humanity of Christ, is a reward. These things will be given to all the elect on account of the merit of Christ, and to some also on account of their own merit together with the merit of Christ. But these things are promised to the holy souls; therefore some reward is promised to the separated souls. That the vision of God is promised to some souls our Saviour clearly intimates in John 7, saying: Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am they also may be with me, that they may behold my glory, which you have given me, etc. From these words it is gathered that Christ, in speaking, promised that all who are there see, and will see, the glory of Christ's deity, and so the vision of God is promised to them. But perhaps someone would say that Christ speaks of his glory according to his humanity, which the separated souls see in heaven. But this evasion is worthless, because Christ speaks of the glory which he had before the world was, he himself saying there to the Father: Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was. That glory which Christ had before the world was is the glory of his deity. Therefore those who are in heaven with Christ see the glory of his deity.

units.la: Hæc de ista materia ad præsens sufficiant, quoniam non est intentionis meæ in hoc opere principalem hæresim, per exquisita media improbare: sed motiva hic adducta repellere, & tertio per illa quæ adducit discurram. Cum itaque dicit: si attendamus cui merces illa in sacra pagina promittitur: certum est quod toti suppposito, verum est, quod aliqua merces promittitur toti suppposito: quia illa quæ gloriam animæ & corporis comprehendit, aliqua autem promittitur in communi, suppposito & animæ separatæ, & illæ sunt multæ, esse enim cum Christo in cœlo, similiter gaudere, & videri humanitatem Christi est merces quædam, quæ tamen promittitur & toti suppposito, & animæ separatæ. Consortium Dei & Angelorum est quædam merces, quæ toti suppposito & animæ separatæ promittitur. Quia, teste Ambrosio, animæ separatæ ad gaudium transeunt Angelorum. Etiam suppposita post iudicium ad Angelorum consortium perducentur, sic etiam visio Dei est merces: & tamen promittitur, & toti suppposito, & animæ separatæ purgatæ. Et ideo licet mille millia auctoritatum adduceret ad probandum quod merces, quæ est visio promittitur toti suppposito: eadem facilitate diceretur, quod non posset per eas probare, quod merces quæ est visio non promittitur animabus purgatis: imo habitatio cœlestis & promittitur toti suppposito & promittitur animæ separatæ. Cum igitur dicit beatus Iacobus: beatus vir qui sustinet temptationem: concedendum est, quod hic promittitur corona vitæ toti suppposito, sed ista propositio est tota affirmativa, ideo ex ipsa non sequitur negativa ista: scilicet, corona vitæ non promittitur animæ separatæ. Esto etiam quod in his verbis non promitteretur corona vitæ animæ separatæ: ex hoc non posset inferri, nisi Sophistice, quod alibi non promittitur corona vitæ animæ separatæ, sæpe enim in scriptura sacra aliquid, quod in uno loco non promittitur, in alio loco promittitur, veruntamen potest dici, quod in his verbis promittitur corona vitæ & toti suppposito & animæ separatæ. Ex hoc enim, quod promittitur toti suppposito post iudicium, promittitur & animæ postquam fuerit corporaliter expurgata.
units.tr: Let these things about this matter suffice for the present, since it is not my intention in this work to refute the principal heresy by elaborate means, but to repel the arguments adduced here, and to run through the authorities he cites in the third place. When he says: If we consider to whom that reward is promised in holy scripture, it is certain that it is promised to the whole suppositum: it is true that some reward is promised to the whole suppositum, for that which includes the glory of soul and body is promised to the suppositum; but some is promised in common to the suppositum and to the separated soul, and these are many. To be with Christ in heaven, likewise to rejoice in and to behold the humanity of Christ, is a certain reward which is promised both to the whole suppositum and to the separated soul. The fellowship of God and the angels is a certain reward which is promised both to the whole suppositum and to the separated soul, because, as Ambrose testifies, the separated souls pass to the joy of the angels. Likewise the supposita, after the judgment, will be brought to the fellowship of the angels. So too the vision of God is a reward, and yet it is promised both to the whole suppositum and to the purged separated soul. Therefore, even if he were to adduce a thousand thousand authorities to prove that the reward which is the vision is promised to the whole suppositum, one could with equal ease say that they could not prove that the reward which is the vision is not promised to purged souls. Indeed, the heavenly habitation is both promised to the whole suppositum and promised to the separated soul. Therefore, when blessed James says, blessed is the man who endures temptation, it must be conceded that here the crown of life is promised to the whole suppositum; but that proposition is wholly affirmative, and so the negative proposition does not follow from it, namely that the crown of life is not promised to the separated soul. Even granting that in these words the crown of life were not promised to the separated soul, it could not be inferred from this, except sophistically, that the crown of life is nowhere promised to the separated soul; for often in holy scripture something which is not promised in one place is promised in another. Indeed it can be said that in these words the crown of life is promised both to the whole suppositum and to the separated soul. For from the fact that it is promised to the whole suppositum after the judgment, it is also promised to the soul once it has been cleansed in body.

units.la: Cum vero dicit, certum est quod anima non est vir. Ista est cavillosa & puerilis deductio, si enim omnino probaret, quod animæ separatæ non promittitur corona vitæ quia anima non est vir: probabitur sibi, quod nulli mulieri promittitur corona vitæ, quia certum est quod nulla mulier est vir, promittitur autem in auctoritate Iacobi corona vitæ & viris & mulieribus, quia per nomen viri subintelligitur & mulieris, quia in multis quod dicitur de viris, intelligendum est etiam de mulieribus, sic etiam quamvis beatus Iacobus non exprimat nomen animæ: tamen intelligendum est, quod ex hoc ipso, quod corona vitæ promittitur viris, intelligitur etiam promissa animabus sanctis purgatis. Cum autem dicit, quod Christus dicit: omnis qui reliquit patrem &c. vitam æternam habebit &c. certum est, quod illi quibus loquebatur erant suppposita & non anima separata: totum hoc est concedendum, sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod animæ non promittitur visio Dei, quia ex affirmativa tali non sequitur negativa, Christus enim loquebatur suppositis, & aliqua dixit illis non tantum pro suppositis, sed etiam pro animabus suis, ideo cum dixit hoc etiam, vitam æternam habebit, hoc non tantum dixit pro suppositis, sed etiam pro animabus, postquam fuerint purgatæ, cum autem dicit ad idem, quod Christus ait: vos qui reliquistis omnia &c. & certum est quod illi erunt Petrus & alia suppposita & non eorum anima separata, dicendum est, quod ista verba possunt intelligi de suppositis tantum, quia suppposita & non animæ separatæ sedebunt super sedem iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel, sed non sequitur, quod iste honor promittitur suppositis & non animabus separatis. Cum vero ultimo dicit, quod merces illa reddetur pro operibus misericordiæ, unde Christus dicet in iudicio, esurivi & dedistis mihi &c. sed certum est quod suppposi-tum & non anima separata dedit eleemosynam, igitur suppposito & non anima separata reddetur. Dicendum, quod merces illa multis reddetur non pro operibus misericordiæ, multi enim saluabuntur, qui nullum opus omnino misericordiæ fecerunt, & licet illa merces sit multis reddenda pro operibus misericordiæ: non tamen reddetur illis suppositis tantummodo pro operibus misericordiæ: scilicet quæ suppposita fecerunt opera misericordiæ: sed etiam pro operibus misericordiæ reddetur animabus illorum ante diem iudicii generalis, patet igitur, quod ratio ista & aliæ allegationis præscriptæ non plus concludunt de visione Dei, quam de habitatione cœlesti, quia ita promittitur habitatio cœlestis toti suppposito, sicut visio Dei.
units.tr: When he says, it is certain that the soul is not a man, this is a captious and childish inference. If it proved completely that the separated soul is not promised the crown of life because the soul is not a man, it would also prove that no woman is promised the crown of life, because it is certain that no woman is a man. Yet in the words of James the crown of life is promised to men and to women alike, because the name of man is understood to include woman, as in many places what is said of men must also be understood of women. So too, although blessed James does not name the soul, it must be understood that, from the very fact that the crown of life is promised to men, it is also promised to the holy souls once they have been purged. When he says that Christ said, whoever has left father, etc., shall have eternal life, etc., and that it is certain that those whom he was addressing were persons and not separated souls, all this must be granted, but it does not follow that the vision of God is not promised to the soul, because a negative does not follow from such an affirmative. Christ was speaking to persons, but he said some things to them not only as persons but also on behalf of their souls. Therefore, when he said this as well, shall have eternal life, he said it not only on behalf of the persons but also on behalf of the souls, once they have been purged. When he says, to the same effect, what Christ said: you who have left all things, etc., and that it is certain those men were Peter and the other persons and not their separated souls, it must be said that these words can be understood of persons only, because persons, and not separated souls, will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel; but it does not follow that this honour is promised to persons and not to separated souls. Finally, when he says that that reward will be paid for works of mercy, whence Christ will say at the judgement, I was hungry and you gave me, etc., and that it is certain that the person and not the separated soul gave alms, therefore the reward will be paid to the person and not to the separated soul, it must be said that this reward will be paid to many who are not saved for works of mercy, for many will be saved who have done no work of mercy at all; and although that reward is to be paid to many for works of mercy, it will not be paid only to those persons who did works of mercy; it will also be paid for works of mercy to the souls of those persons before the day of the general judgement. It is plain, then, that this argument and the others of the aforesaid allegation conclude no more about the vision of God than about the heavenly habitation, since the heavenly habitation is promised to the whole person just as the vision of God is.

units.la: Item, si ratio illa concluderet hæresim memoratam: sequeretur per eandem rationem, quod ante iudicium nulla anima separata saluabitur: & nulla anima separata damnabitur, nam sicut toti suppposito clara visio Dei promittitur & toti suppposito Christus damnationem si non crediderit comminatur dicens, ut legitur Matt. vlt. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit: qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. In quibus verbis constat aperte, quod Christus loquitur de suppositis: quia totus homo credit & baptisatur. Si igitur propter hoc quod visio clara Dei toti suppposito promittitur, sequiretur quod animæ separatæ non viderent Deum, eadem ratione per hoc quod Christus comminatur damnationem toti suppposito, contingeret inferri quod animæ separatæ ante diem iudicii nec erunt salvæ nec damnatæ, quod catholicus nullus ignorat esse hæreticum.
units.tr: Likewise, if that argument proved the aforesaid heresy, it would follow by the same reasoning that no separated soul will be saved before the judgement, and no separated soul will be condemned. For just as the clear vision of God is promised to the whole person, so Christ threatens damnation to the whole person if he does not believe, saying, as we read in Matt. vlt., He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned. In these words it is plain that Christ speaks of persons, because the whole man believes and is baptized. If therefore it followed, because the clear vision of God is promised to the whole person, that separated souls do not see God, then by the same reasoning, because Christ threatens damnation to the whole person, it could be inferred that separated souls before the day of judgement will be neither saved nor damned. No Catholic is ignorant that this is heretical.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: In quo ponitur ratio precedens secunda via: scilicet de tempore, quae soluitur.
units.tr: In which the second argument from time is set out and answered.

units.la: SEquitur nunc alia via de tempore: pro quo merces prædicta promittitur, vbi dicit, quod si attendatur sacra scriptura, inuenitur solum post iudicium, primo, quia post iudicium dicetur: venite benedicti patris mei, percipite regnum, & illud: cum sederit filius hominis in sede maiestatis suæ, sedebitis & vos &c. & hoc: gaudete quia merces vestra multa est in coelo. Hic ponit tertiam rationem ex tempore, quo reddetur merces, & potest sic formari. Merces prædicta, scilicet visio Dei, reddetur solum post diem iudicii, igitur animæ sanctæ ante diem iudicii non videbunt Deum, consequentia videtur manifesta, antecedens probatur per illud Matthæi 15. Venite benedicti patris mei, percipite regnum &c. Sed hæc ratio accipit hæresim, quam probare deberet, quia accipit, quod merces, quæ est visio, non promittitur, nisi pro tempore post iudicium, quod deberet probare. Et ideo non restat hic, nisi respondere ad probationem suam, quæ propter sæpe dicta est exclusa, quia, sicut dictum est, visio Dei promittitur toti suppositio, & illa promissio, quæ de communi lege est facta, non implebitur ante iudicium, promittitur etiam animæ visio nihil purgandum habenti, & illa promissio fit pro tempore etiam ante iudicium generale, cum hoc tamen stat, quod promissio quæ fit animæ nihil purgandum habenti ante dictum iudicium impleatur, & ita patet, quod ex illa auctoritate: venite benedicti &c. non potest inferri, quod animæ sanctæ antea non videbunt Deum, sed potest inferri, quod homines integri ex corpore & anima de communi lege antea non videbunt Deum. Sed si quæratur, vbi promittitur dicta merces animæ nihil purgandum habenti? dicendum, quod Christus, vt legitur Lucæ 13. mercedem promisit omni animæ purgatæ, cum dixit latroni, hodie mecum eris in paradiso, hoc enim non dixit latroni suppositο, sed pro anima eius, & non solum pro anima eius, sed pro anima purgata, quæ vadit ad paradisum p paradisum autem, de quo fit mentio, intelligitur beatitudo regni coelestis, quæ non est sine visione. Et quod de tali intellexerit Christus, ostenditur ex serie euangelici textus, nam dicente latrone ad Iesum: Domine memento mei, dum veneris in regnum tuum, respondit Dominus: amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in paradiso. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi: quod idem intelligebat Christus per paradisum, quod intelligebat latro per regnum Christi, sed latro per regnum Christi intelligebat gloriam Christi, quæ non est sine visione clara Dei. Igitur Christus per paradisum intellexit visionem Dei, vt iste sit sensus: hodie mecum eris in paradiso, id est, sicut ego video & videbo deitatem, ita tu mecum hodie videbis clare deitatem eandem. Ex his aliisque pluribus, quæ causa brevitatis omittuntur, patenter habetur: quod falsum asserit, cum dicit, quod in scriptura sacra inuenitur quod visio Dei promittitur solum pro tempore post iudicium: quia promittitur animabus purgatis pro tempore ante iudicium ibi, sicut dictum est: hodie mecum eris in paradiso, & Ioh. 17. vbi Christus dixit: volo vt vbi ego sum & ipsi sint mecum vt videant claritatem meam, & primæ ad Cor. 13. Cum dicit Apostolus, videmus nunc per speculum in enigmate, tunc autem quando prophetiæ euacuabuntur facie ad faciem, prophetiæ autem, de quibus loquitur Apostolus, non sunt in coelo. Igitur animæ quæ sunt in coelo, vident facie ad faciem. Quod etiam dicta visio iam sit data, asserit manifeste scriptura diuina, quia Apoc. 6. dicit beatus Ioh. data sunt illis sanctis (secundum animam) singulæ stolæ albæ, quæ sunt visiones Dei. Quando vero dicit, post iudicium dicetur, venite benedicti patris mei percipite regnum &c. verum est, quod tunc dicetur suppositis integris, & ideo istud ante iudicium non implebitur, quia supposita integra de communi lege antea non percipient regnum Dei, cum hoc tamen stat, quod animæ multorum antea videbunt Deum. Cum autem allegat illud Christi, cum sederit filius hominis in sede maiestatis suæ: sedebitis & vos, dicendum est, quod istud non implebitur ante iudicium generale, cum hoc tamen stat quod animæ Apostolorum nunc vident Deum. Multa enim, & diuersa sunt promissa Apostolis: quorum aliqua sunt modo impleta, aliqua vero implebuntur in die iudicii, sed post diem iudicii cessabunt, sicuti sedebitis super sedes iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel, nam post diem iudicii minime iudicabunt, aliqua vero implebuntur in die iudicii, & sine fine manebunt, sicut quod erunt in anima & corpore gloriosi. Igitur per hoc, quod in die iudicii sedebunt Apostoli super sedem iudicantes &c. non poterit probari, quod ante diem iudicii animæ eorum non videant essentiam diuinam, cum constet ipsum esse hæresim manifestam. Cum vero vltimo dixit hoc: gaudete, quia merces vestra multa est in coelo, hoc non est ad propositum: quia constat secundum istum, quod merces animarum multa est in coelo, quia secundum eum vident & gaudent de humanitate Christi, gaudium enim est secundum istum multum. Manifestum est igitur, quod non tantum merces suppositorum post iudicium erit in coelo, sed etiam mercesanimarum nunc in coelo est multa, & ideo per verba prædicta probari nullo modo potest, quod animæ sanctæ nunc non vident Deum: sicut per ipsa probari non potest, quod nunc vident humanitatem Christi.
units.tr: Next comes another argument from time, for which the aforesaid reward is promised. He says that if one attends to Holy Scripture, one finds that it is given only after judgement; first, because after judgement it will be said: "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom," and that: "When the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit," etc., and this: "Rejoice, because your reward is great in heaven." Here he gives a third argument from the time when the reward will be rendered, and it can be formed thus: the aforesaid reward, namely the vision of God, will be rendered only after the day of judgement; therefore holy souls will not see God before the day of judgement. The consequence seems plain. The antecedent is proved by Matthew 15: "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom", etc. But this argument assumes the very heresy it ought to prove, for it assumes that the reward, which is the vision, is promised only for the time after judgement, and that is what it ought to prove. So there remains only to answer its proof, which has been set aside often enough already. For, as has been said, the vision of God is promised to the whole supposit, and that promise, made under the common law, will not be fulfilled before judgement. The vision is also promised to the soul that has nothing to be purged, and that promise is made for the time even before the general judgement. Yet it stands with this that the promise made to the soul having nothing to be purged is fulfilled before the said judgement. And so it is plain that from that text, "Come, you blessed", etc., it cannot be inferred that holy souls did not see God before; what can be inferred is that whole men, body and soul together, under the common law, did not see God before. But if it is asked where the said reward is promised to the soul that has nothing to be purged, the answer is that Christ, as we read in Luke 13, promised the reward to every purged soul when he said to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise." For he did not say this to the supposit of the thief, but to his soul; and not only to his soul, but to the purged soul, which goes to paradise. By paradise, which is mentioned here, is understood the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom, which is not without vision. And that Christ meant such a thing is shown by the sequence of the gospel text. For when the thief said to Jesus, "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom," the Lord replied: "Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." From these words it is made clear that Christ meant by paradise the same thing the thief meant by the kingdom of Christ. But the thief by the kingdom of Christ meant the glory of Christ, which is not without the clear vision of God. Therefore Christ by paradise meant the vision of God, so that the sense is: "Today you will be with me in paradise," that is, just as I see and shall see the Deity, so today you too will see that same Deity clearly with me. From these and many other points, which are omitted for the sake of brevity, it is evident that he asserts falsely when he says that Holy Scripture finds the vision of God promised only for the time after judgement. For it is promised to purged souls for the time before judgement, as was said there: "Today you will be with me in paradise"; and John 17, where Christ said: "I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory"; and 1 Corinthians 13, where the Apostle says: "Now we see through a glass in a riddle, but then face to face," and the prophecies, of which the Apostle speaks, will be done away; but the prophecies of which the Apostle speaks are not in heaven. Therefore souls that are in heaven see face to face. That this vision has already been given is clearly asserted by divine Scripture as well, for in Revelation 6 the blessed John says: "There were given to those holy ones (according to the soul) each a white robe," which are visions of God. But when he says, "After judgement it will be said, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom,'" etc., it is true that it will then be said to the whole supposits, and therefore this will not be fulfilled before judgement, because whole supposits under the common law do not receive the kingdom of God before; yet it stands that the souls of many see God before. As for his citing that saying of Christ, "When the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you shall sit," it must be said that this will not be fulfilled before the general judgement, yet it stands that the souls of the Apostles now see God. For many and diverse promises were made to the Apostles; some of these have now been fulfilled, some will be fulfilled on the day of judgement but will cease after the day of judgement, such as "you shall sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel," for after the day of judgement they will in no way judge; and others will be fulfilled on the day of judgement and will remain without end, such as that they will be glorious in soul and body. Therefore, from the fact that on the day of judgement the Apostles will sit on thrones judging, etc., it cannot be proved that before the day of judgement their souls do not see the divine essence, since it is plain that this very claim is manifest heresy. When at last he said this: "Rejoice, because your reward is great in heaven," this has nothing to do with the point at issue, for by his own account it is plain that the reward of souls is great in heaven, since according to him they see and rejoice in the humanity of Christ, and joy, in his view, is great. It is therefore evident that the reward of supposits will not be in heaven only after judgement, but the reward of souls is now great in heaven. Therefore by the aforesaid words it cannot in any way be proved that holy souls do not now see God, just as it cannot be proved by them that they now see the humanity of Christ.

units.la: CAP. VI. Ponit rationem procedentem ex tertia suppositione seu via supra c. 4. proposita, quae etiam impugnatur & soluitur.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. He sets out an argument that follows from the third supposition, or way, proposed above in chapter 4, which is also refuted and resolved.

units.la: SEquitur: Si etiam attendatur tertium, scilicet ad quid generale iudicium Dei ordinatur, videtur quod frustra fiat iudicium, si merces illa ante iudicium animabus reddatur. Hic ponitur ultima ratio eius pro haeresi memorata, quae ex his quae dicta sunt contra priores convincitur manifeste, per ipsam enim probaretur, quod animae sanctorum nec sunt in coelo nec aliquod gaudium habent, quia secundum illam rationem frustra fieret iudicium generale, si animae sanctorum nunc gauderent. Si enim dicat iste, quod quamuis animae sanctae aliquod gaudium nunc habeant, tamen illud iudicium tunc non fiet frustra, quia animae sanctae tunc visionem Dei percipient, & tota supposita suscitabuntur, & in regnum Dei intrabunt. Eadem facilitate diceretur, quod quamuis animae sanctae nunc videant Deum: tamen illud iudicium tunc non fiet frustra: quia tunc animae clariorem visionem habebunt, & toti homines integri ex corpore & anima constituti tunc gloriam corporis & animae obtinebunt. Ad rationem itaque breviter est dicendum, quod iudicium generale non fiet frustra: licet animae sanctorum nunc videant divinam essentiam: quia illud generale iudicium ad multa alia ordinatur, ordinatur enim, ut supposita integra ex corpore & anima constituta gloriam corporis & animae tunc percipiant: quamuis animae quorundam prius perceperunt, ordinatur etiam, ut gloria omni animae, quae prius vidit divinam essentiam, augeatur, fiet etiam ut multae animae, quae prius non viderunt divinam essentiam, quia purgatae non fuerunt, tunc corporibus unitae percipient visionem Dei. Fiet etiam, ut mali extunc non solum in anima, sed etiam in corpore crucientur, ordinatur etiam ad hoc, quod extunc cessat omnis status merendi & demerendi, propter ista igitur erronee dicitur, quod frustra fieret iudicium generale, si animabus separatis visio clara antea redderetur. Cum infertur: igitur videtur, quod frustra fiat iudicium, si merces illa ante iudicium animabus reddatur, de mercede, quae gloriam animae & corporis comprehendit, posset concedi, sed illa merces non redditur animabus separatis: quia glorificatio corporis ante iudicium de communi lege non reddetur.
units.tr: It follows: "If we also consider the third point, namely what end God's general judgment is ordained to, it seems that the judgment would be made in vain if that reward were given to the souls before the judgment." Here he gives his last argument for the heresy mentioned above. It is plainly refuted by what has been said against the earlier arguments, since by this reasoning it would be proved that the souls of the saints are neither in heaven nor have any joy, because on that reasoning the general judgment would be in vain if the souls of the saints now rejoiced. For if he replies that although the souls of the saints now have some joy, the judgment will not be in vain then, because the souls of the saints will then perceive the vision of God, and the whole supposita will be raised and will enter into the kingdom of God, then with the same ease it could be said that although the souls of the saints now see God, that judgment will still not be in vain then, because then the souls will have a clearer vision, and all men, made whole from body and soul, will then obtain the glory of body and soul. So, to answer the argument briefly: the general judgment will not be made in vain, even though the souls of the saints now see the divine essence, because that general judgment is ordained to many other ends. For it is ordained so that the supposita, made whole of body and soul, may then receive the glory of body and soul, although the souls of some have received it earlier; it is also ordained so that glory is increased for every soul that earlier saw the divine essence; and it will also come about that many souls which earlier did not see the divine essence, because they were not yet purged, will then, united to their bodies, receive the vision of God. It will also come about that the wicked will then be tormented not only in soul but also in body; and it is ordained also to this end, that from then on every state of meriting and demeriting ceases. Therefore it is wrongly said, on these grounds, that the general judgment would be made in vain if a clear vision were given to the separated souls beforehand. When he concludes: "therefore it seems that the judgment is made in vain if that reward is given to the souls before the judgment," this could be conceded of a reward that includes the glory of soul and body; but that reward is not given to separated souls, because by the common law the glorification of the body will not be given before the judgment.

units.la: CAP. VII. In quo recitatur causa talis positionis & modus revocationis, & sunt circa ista sex consideranda, primum deducitur in hoc capitulo, secundum in sequenti, & sic consequenter.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. In which the cause of such a position and the manner of its retraction are set out; and there are six points to be considered about these, the first being drawn out in this chapter, the second in the next, and so on in order.

units.la: SEquitur: Et quia non est dicendum, quod illud iudicium est solum verbale, inane & fictum, idcirco super ista quaestione vigilemus positis motivis pro haeresi saepe fata. Hic inventor istius atque defensor verbalem, fictam & friuolam ponit detestationem seu revocationem, & in hac parte sunt sex, quia primo iste ponit motivum, quare praedictam materiam indagavit. Secundo dicit, quod conclusioni suae amore veritatis adhaesit. Tertio manifestat, quare ipse praedictam assertionem suam voluit promulgare, & publice praedicare. Quarto dicit, quod non fuit intentionis suae aliquid dicere contra fidem, & ideo quandam fecit protestationem seu revocationem, ut ne de haeresi condemnetur. Quinto verbis dolosis & ambiguis se non pertinaciter referre pro assertione praedicta praetendit. Ultimo narratur, quod de revocatione sua petiuit fieri publicum instrumentum.
units.tr: It follows: "And because it is not to be said that that judgment is merely verbal, empty and fictitious, let us therefore be watchful on this question, the motives for the heresy having been set forth, which have often been spoken of." This inventor and defender of that position puts forward a verbal, fictitious and frivolous detestation or retraction, and in this part there are six points. For first he sets out the motive by which he investigated the matter. Second, he says that he adhered to his conclusion out of love of truth. Third, he explains why he wished to publish and openly preach that assertion of his. Fourth, he says that it was not his intention to say anything against the faith, and so he made a certain protestation or retraction, so that he might not be condemned for heresy. Fifth, he pretends by deceitful and ambiguous words that he does not stubbornly stand by the aforesaid assertion. Last, it is related that he asked for a public instrument to be drawn up concerning his retraction.

units.la: Dicit igitur, quod ideo super ista quaestione voluit vigilare, quia iudicium generale non est solum verbale, inane & fictum. In his verbis cum assertiones & motiva pro assertione saepe dicta referit, aperte insinuat, quod iudicium generale est frustra, inane & fictum, si animae sanctorum ante iudicium videant Deum, sed hoc in praecedentibus evidentius est manifestum.
units.tr: He says, therefore, that he wished to be watchful on this question because the general judgment is not merely verbal, empty and fictitious. In these words, when he repeats the assertions and the motives for the assertion often mentioned, he clearly insinuates that the general judgment is vain, empty and fictitious if the souls of the saints see God before the judgment; but this is made more evident in what has gone before.

units.la: CAP. VIII. Deducit & narrat secundum, quare scilicet sua conclusioni adhaesit, cuius motivum nullum esse convincitur.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. He draws out and sets out the second point: why he clung to his conclusion, the motive for which is shown to be none.
