units.la: SEquitur: Et in conscientia mea dico, quod libenter essemus pro alia conclusione & libentius quam pro ista conclusione negativa: si vera ostenderetur & necessaria, & si clarum esset in fide, quod animae sanctorum nunc viderent faciem Dei, nullus haberet tamen defendere istam fidem, nec defendere plusquam nos, sum enim Christi vicarius licet indignus, & vicarius generalis plus habet defendere honores principaliter, quam quicunque particularis vicarius.
units.tr: It follows: "And in my conscience I say that we would gladly hold to another conclusion, and more gladly than to this negative conclusion, if it were shown to be true and necessary, and if it were clear in the faith that the souls of the saints now see the face of God. Yet no one would be more bound to defend that faith than we are, for I am Christ's vicar, though unworthy, and a general vicar has more duty to defend the honours of his lord chiefly than any particular vicar."

units.la: Item, Quomodo posset aliquis credere, quod si anima patris mei vel matris mea videret clare faciem Dei, quod ego vellem negare: absit. Unde ubi veritas probaretur clarius, ita libenter & amplius staremus pro conclusione. fione affirmatiua. Hic dicit, quod suæ assertioni amore veritatis adhæsit. Quod ostendit per hoc, quod libentius esset pro conclusione alia, si sibi probaretur esse vera. Si per hoc credit de hæresi excusari, turpiter est deceptus. Nam quilibet hæreticus amore veritatis, quam credit, suæ hæresi pertinaciter noscitur adhærere, & tamen hoc non obstante, hæretici de sua prauitate hæretica nullatenus excusantur. Igitur quantumcunque amore veritatis, sicut credit, adhæret conclusioni nephariæ prædictæ: scilicet quod anima sanctorum in cœlo non vident Deum: tamen per hoc de hæresi nullatenus excusatur. Quod autem omnis hæreticus, imo Iudæi & pagani amore veritatis, quam credunt, suis adhæreant erroribus, auctoritatibus manifestis ostenditur. Hieronymus enim, vt habetur 24. quæstion. 3. cap. hæresis, dicit in hæc verba: hæresis ab electione dicitur, quod scilicet eam vnusquisque sibi eligat disciplinam, quam putat esse meliorem. Ex quibus verbis manifeste colligitur, quod hæretici illas tenent & eligunt assertiones, quas reputant veriores, & ita suis hæresibus amore veritatis, quam credunt, adhærent libentius, quamuis multi eorum tenerent contrarias, si eis probarentur esse verae: & tamen per hoc de hæresi nullatenus excusantur, igitur nec iste per hoc poterit de hæresi excusari. De Iudæis etiam idem probatur auctoritate Christi dicentis Iohan. decimosexto. Venit hora vt omnis, qui interficit vos, arbitretur obsequium se præstare Deo. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod Iudæi quodam veritatis amore persequebantur Apostolos: nec tamen propter hoc fuerunt excusandi, igitur nec iste est de hæresi excusandus propter hoc, quod libentius teneret contrarium sui erroris, si sibi ostenderetur esse verum. Item Apostolus de Iudæis ad Roman. 4. dicit: Testimonium perhibebo illis, quod æmulationem quidem Dei habent, sed non secundum scientiam, vbi dicit Glossa, pro dilectione Dei putant se facere: sed veram dilectionem Dei non habent. Ex quibus verbis potest patenter inferri, quod potest quis hæreses impie defensare, putans se hoc facere veritatis amore: licet verum veritatis amorem non habeat, & ideo de erroris defensione non est excusatus, & ita per hoc, quod iste credit assertionem suam esse veram, & libentius teneret sibi contrariam, si crederet eam esse veram: non potest de hæresi excusari, licet per hoc possit haberi, quod hoc facit falso veritatis amore. Paulus ante conuersionem suam persequebatur ecclesiam Dei: & negabat incarnationem Christi: pro qua libentius laborasset, si fuisset sibi probata, & tamen hoc non obstante de errore damnabiliter non potuit excusari. Igitur licet iste credat assertionem suam esse veram: & libentius teneret contrariam, si sibi esse vera & necessaria probaretur: non poterit per hoc de prauitate hæretica excusari, sed per hoc haberi potest, quod quodam falso veritatis amore assentit errori, rursum per verba prædicta non potest plus haberi, nisi quod iste ignoranter errat, sed ignorantia non semper excusat in casu isto: sicut inferius ostendetur, igitur per verba prædicta non potest de prauitate hæretica excusari. Quod ignorantia non semper excusat, patet manifeste per illud Actuum tertio, quod dicit Petrus perfidis Iudæis: fratres scio, quod per ignorantiam fecistis, sicut & principes vestri. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod Iudæi ignoranter suis erroribus adhærebant, & tamen per talem ignorantiam non poterant excusari, sic licet iste ignoranter teneat & defendat hæresim prædictam, & libentius vellet assertionem contrariam credere si sibi probaretur esse vera: Tamen per hoc non poterit de prauitate hæretica excusari, per talem enim modum omnes Iudæi, Sarraceni & pagani, idolatræ, & hæretici, imo vniuersaliter omnes errantes possunt se de suis erroribus excusare. Vix enim posset aliquis inueniri, qui non diceret, quod libentius teneret assertionem contrariam, si sibi probaretur aperte esse vera. Quis enim diceret, quod libentius diceret falsum quam verum? Patet igitur ex prædictis, quod iste inuentor hæresis memoratæ per verba prædicta, & similia non poterit excusari. Est tamen aduertendum, quod licet præcise per talia verba non possit errans contra fidem de prauitate hæretica excusari: non tamen est dicendum, quod omnis errans contra fidem nitens se per verba talia excusare, est hæreticus reputandus, quia potest quis errans contra fidem in casu aliquo satagens se per verba talia excusare de prauitate hæretica, immunis existere, sed iste inuentor hæresis sæpe dictæ nullo modo valet de prauitate hæretica excusari, sicut inferius ostendetur. Cum igitur dicit: libenter essemus pro alia conclusione & libentius, quam pro ista negatiua conclusione, dicit, non afferendo nec opinando, sed tantummodo recitando, si vera & necessaria ostenderetur, quare per prædicta verba non potest de hæresi excusari, sicut ostensum est prius. Cum autem dicit: si clarum esset in fide, quod anima vident nunc faciem Dei, nullum haberet tantum defendere istam fidem, nec defenderet plusquam nos. Ex quibus verbis colligitur euidenter, quod ipse non credit animas sanctorum nunc videre faciem Dei, quia dicit: quod si esset clarum, nullum defenderet plusquam ipse: sed ipse non defendit, imo impugnat. Igitur non credit hoc esse clarum in fide. Sum enim Christi vicarius: etiam ista verba sonant, quod sic deberet defendere, quia tamen sæpe vicarius generalis defendere honorem domini principalis, quam particularis, plus debet. Item, quomodo posset aliquis credere, quod si anima patris mei vel matris mea videret clare faciem Dei, quod ego vellem negare, absit. Ex his etiam verbis notatur, quod non credit animam cuiuscunque separatam clare videre faciem Dei. Vnde vbi veritas probaretur clarius, libenter & amplius flaremus pro conclusione affirmatiua quam negatiua: hic insinuat, quod non tenet conclusionem negatiuam, nisi amore veritatis, sed per talia verba de prauitate hæretica minime excusatur.
units.tr: Likewise: "How could anyone believe that if the soul of my father or my mother clearly saw the face of God, I would wish to deny it? Far be it. Hence, where the truth was proved more clearly, we would stand for the affirmative conclusion more gladly and more fully." Here he says that he clung to his assertion out of love of truth. He shows this by saying he would more willingly hold the other conclusion if it were proved to him to be true. If he thinks he can be excused from heresy by this, he is shamefully deceived. For every heretic is known to cling stubbornly to his heresy out of love of the truth he believes, and yet heretics are in no way excused from their heretical perversity on that account. So, however much, as he believes, he clings out of love of truth to the wicked conclusion mentioned above, namely that the souls of the saints in heaven do not see God, he is by this in no way excused from heresy. That every heretic, indeed Jews and pagans, cling to their errors out of love of the truth they believe, is shown by plain authorities. For Jerome, as is found in 24. quaest. 3, cap. haeresis, says in these words: heresy is so called from choice, because each person chooses for himself the teaching that he thinks is better. From these words it is clearly gathered that heretics hold and choose those assertions which they judge truer, and so they cling to their heresies more willingly out of love of the truth they believe, although many of them would hold the contrary if it were proved to them to be true. And yet by this they are in no way excused from heresy. Therefore neither can this man be excused from heresy by this. The same is also proved about the Jews by the authority of Christ, who says in John 16: The hour comes when everyone who kills you will think he is offering service to God. From these words it is plainly evident that the Jews persecuted the apostles out of a certain love of truth, and yet they were not for that reason excused. Therefore neither is this man to be excused from heresy because he would more willingly hold the contrary of his error, if it were shown to him to be true. Likewise the Apostle, speaking of the Jews in Rom. 4, says: I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, where the Gloss says: they think they do it for the love of God, but they do not have the true love of God. From these words it can plainly be inferred that a person may impiously defend heresies, thinking he does so out of love of truth, although he does not have true love of truth; and so he is not excused for defending error. Thus, because this man believes his assertion to be true, and would more willingly hold the contrary if he believed it to be true and necessary, he cannot be excused from heretical depravity by this. Yet it can be concluded from this that he assents to error out of a certain false love of truth. Further, from the words above nothing more can be gathered than that this man errs in ignorance; but ignorance does not always excuse in this case, as will be shown below. Therefore from the words above he cannot be excused from heretical depravity. That ignorance does not always excuse is plainly shown by Acts 3, where Peter says to the faithless Jews: Brethren, I know that you did it in ignorance, as did also your rulers. From these words it is plainly established that the Jews clung to their errors in ignorance, and yet they could not be excused by such ignorance. So, although this man holds and defends the aforesaid heresy in ignorance, and would more willingly believe the contrary assertion if it were proved to him to be true, nevertheless he cannot on this account be excused from heretical depravity. For in this way all Jews, Saracens and pagans, idolaters and heretics, indeed all who err in general, could excuse themselves for their errors. For scarcely anyone could be found who would not say that he would more willingly hold the contrary assertion if it were plainly shown to him to be true. For who would say that he would more willingly say what is false than what is true? It is therefore clear from what has been said that this inventor of the heresy mentioned, by the words above and similar ones, cannot be excused. It must nevertheless be noted that although a person who errs against the faith cannot be excused from heretical depravity by such words alone, it should not be said that every person who errs against the faith and strives to excuse himself by such words is to be counted a heretic. For a person who errs against the faith may in some case, striving to excuse himself by such words, be free from heretical depravity. But this inventor of the heresy often mentioned can in no way be excused from heretical depravity, as will be shown below. When he therefore says: we would gladly be for another conclusion, and more gladly than for this negative conclusion, he says, not affirming nor holding an opinion, but merely reciting, if it were shown to be true and necessary, that by these words he cannot be excused from heresy, as was shown before. When he says: if it were clear in the faith that the souls now see the face of God, no one would defend that faith more than we, from these words it is plainly gathered that he himself does not believe that the souls of the saints now see the face of God, since he says that if it were clear, he would defend it more than anyone; but he does not defend it, rather he attacks it. Therefore he does not believe this to be clear in the faith. For I am Christ's vicar: these words also imply that he ought to defend it in this way, since nevertheless a general vicar ought more to defend the honour of his principal lord than a particular one. Likewise, how could anyone believe that if the soul of my father or my mother clearly saw the face of God, I would wish to deny it? Far be it. From these words too it is noted that he does not believe that the soul of anyone separated [from the body] clearly sees the face of God. Hence, where the truth was proved more clearly, we would stand more gladly and more fully for the affirmative conclusion than for the negative one: here he hints that he does not hold the negative conclusion except out of love of truth, but by such words he is in no way excused from heretical depravity.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Ostendit tertium: scil. quae ratio induxit Ioh. 22. ad hanc haeresim promulgandam & praedicandam: & hanc assignat fuisse studium in originalibus sanctorum.
units.tr: He shows the third point: namely, what reason led John 22 to proclaim and preach this heresy, and he states that it came from his study of the originals of the saints.

units.la: SEquitur: licet nos, postquam fuimus in isto statu, studuimus singulariter sanctorum originalia & acceptauimus quaestiones, quas faciunt in ista materia, & frequenter in sermonibus fecimus mentionem, & maxime vtile fuit: quia alii vel non habent originalia, vel non curant studere in eis. Sunt enim hodie studentes & alii applicati quibusdam scripturis, & illas habent pro euangeliis & epistolis: & amplius parum quarunt, & ideo quia ista studuimus in originalibus: ista proposuimus, ista inquisiuimus. Hic assignat rationes, quare assertionem praedictam voluit promulgare & publice praedicare, quia scilicet propter hoc ipse habuit & studuit originalia sanctorum, vt dicit: & alii vel non habent vel non studeant, & propter hoc istam assertionem tanquam ignotam aliis voluit tanquam catholicam diuulgare, sed istis verbis aperte insinuat, vnde sibi acciderit, quod inter haereses est prolapsus, quia enim in originalibus sanctorum & in scripturis diuinis absque doctore & sine scholastico exercitio, aliisque scientiis, quae lacrae Theologiae famulari noscuntur, nequaquam prius acquisitis, studere praesumpsit, non recte intelligens ex auctoritatibus male intellectis, quamplures assertiones haereticales nisus est inferre, & ideo magister erroris extitit, & nunquam fuit discipulus veritatis, non attendens illud Hieronymi ad Paulinum: hac a me praescripta sunt breuiter, neque enim epistolares agnitiones euagare longius patiebantur, vt intelligeres te in Scripturis sacris sine praemio monstrante semitam non posse ingredi, nec mirum, cum secundum eundem ibidem, quia qui variam supellectilem & vilia opuscula fabricant, absque doctore esse non possunt, quod cupiunt, quomodo igitur iste inscius primitus, minus etiam peritus, in senectute sua studere incipiens originalia sanctorum, ipsa sine doctore intelligat: cum vix aut nunquam valeat vnicus reperiri viuens, qui metaphysicam sine doctore addiscat? reuera iste videtur delirus senex, quem beatus Hieronymus inter alios temere praesumentes Scripturas sacras docere, antequam discant, acriter reprehendit dicens ibidem: sola scripturarum ars est, quam sibi passim omnis vendicat. Et parum post: hanc garrula anus: hanc delirus senex: hanc sophista verbosus: hanc vniuersi praesumunt, lacerant, docent antequam discant. Cum igitur dicit (postquam fuimus in isto statu: studuimus singulariter originalia sanctorum) ostendit vnde sibi contigit, quod tot haereses dogmatizauit, quod scilicet studuit originalia sanctorum, quae nequaquam intelligit: & tamen se intelligere putat, & ideo ad suas haereses ipsa repugnantia molitur pertrahere. Cum vero dicit (& attendimus quaestiones suas, quas faciunt in materia ista) quia & si a pueritia sanctorum originalia studuisset, ad multorum contentorum in eis verum intellectum nullatenus peruenisset: quanto magis senex, qui a pueritia fluctibus seculi insistebat: & postquam fuit ad istum statum assumptus, occupationibus extitit infinitis implicitus: ad verum intellectum profundarum & subtilium veritatum, quae in sanctorum auctoritatibus inseruntur, nequaquam attinget. (Et frequenter in sermonibus fecimus mentionem) verba sanctorum erronee peruertendo. (Et maxime vtile fuit) imo pernitiosum extitit, & nociuum. Quia per sermones suos ambitiosos, quam plurimos ad negandam fidei agnitae veritatem, & ad probandam, tenendam, docendam & defendendam haereticam prauitatem induxit, ac inter Christianos dissensiones, aemulationes, & schismata seminauit (Quia alii vel non habent originalia, vel non curant studere in eis. Sunt enim hodie studentes & alii applicati quibusdam scripturis, & illas habent pro euangeliis & epistolis, & amplius parum quarunt) hoc putant nonnulli veritatem de multis habere, qui sunt magistri antequam discipuli, sed propter aliorum imperitiam & ignorantiam ista determinatio nullatenus excusatur. (Et ideo quia ista studuimus in originalibus, ista proposuimus, ista inquisiuimus) male studuit originalia, & ideo haereticalia multa proposuit & defendit.
units.tr: It follows: although we, since we have been in this state, have made a special study of the originals of the saints, and have taken up the questions they raise on this subject, and have often made mention of them in sermons, and this has been most useful, because others either do not have the originals or do not care to study them. For nowadays there are students and others devoted to certain writings, who hold them as gospels and epistles, and seek little beyond them; and so, because we have studied these things in the originals, we have put these things forward and inquired into these things. Here he gives the reasons why he wished to publish and publicly preach the aforesaid assertion: namely, because for this very reason he had and studied the originals of the saints, as he says, and others either lack them or do not study them. For this reason he wished to spread abroad this assertion as catholic, though it was unknown to others. But in these words he clearly reveals how he came to fall into heresy. For, presuming to study the originals of the saints and the divine Scriptures without a teacher and without scholastic training, and without the other sciences which are known to serve sacred theology and which he had not acquired beforehand, he did not understand rightly, and from badly understood authorities he undertook to draw many heretical assertions. So he became a teacher of error, and never was a disciple of the truth, not heeding that saying of Jerome to Paulinus: I have set these things down briefly for you, for the limits of a letter did not allow me to wander further, so that you may understand that without a guide who shows the path, one cannot enter upon the sacred Scriptures. Nor is this surprising, since, according to the same Jerome in the same place, those who fashion various household goods and cheap little works cannot achieve what they desire without a teacher. How, then, can this man, ignorant from the start and even less skilled, beginning in his old age to study the originals of the saints, understand them without a teacher, when scarcely or never can one living man be found who learns metaphysics without a teacher? Indeed this man seems a doting old man, whom blessed Jerome sharply rebukes among others who rashly presume to teach the sacred Scriptures before they have learned them, saying in the same place: the art of the Scriptures alone is one which everyone claims for himself everywhere. And shortly after: this the chattering old woman, this the doting old man, this the wordy sophist; all presume to tear it apart and teach it before they have learned it. When, therefore, he says (since we have been in this state, we have made a special study of the originals of the saints), he shows how it came about that he taught so many heresies: namely, that he studied the originals of the saints, which he does not in the least understand; and yet he thinks he understands them, and so he strives to drag into his heresies the very things that contradict them. When he says (and we have considered their questions, which they raise on this subject), even if he had studied the originals of the saints from boyhood, he would never have reached a true understanding of the many matters contained in them; how much less so an old man who from boyhood was engaged in the waves of the world, and who, once raised to this state, was entangled in endless occupations, will he attain the true understanding of the deep and subtle truths that are inserted in the authorities of the saints. (And we have often made mention of them in sermons): by perverting the words of the saints. (And this has been most useful): nay, it was rather pernicious and harmful. For through his ambitious sermons he led very many to deny the truth of the faith once acknowledged, and to prove, hold, teach and defend heretical depravity, and he sowed dissensions, rivalries and schisms among Christians. (Because others either do not have the originals or do not care to study them. For nowadays there are students and others devoted to certain writings, and hold them as gospels and epistles, and seek little beyond them): some think they have the truth about many things who are teachers before they are disciples; but on account of the inexperience and ignorance of others, this determination is in no way excused. (And so, because we have studied these things in the originals, we have put these things forward, we have inquired into these things): he studied the originals badly, and therefore proposed and defended many heretical things.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Ostendit quartum, scilicet quod facta est Iohannis XXII. reuocatio, seu retractatio, quae sub verbis cuiusdam friuola protestationis est facta.
units.tr: He shows the fourth point: that a retraction or recantation of John XXII was made, under the cover of a frivolous protestation.

units.la: SEquitur: Nunquam tamen mea intentionis fuit dicere aliquid contra fidem, & si aliquid diximus, tutum ex tunc reuocamus. Hic ponitur protestatio, seu retractatio, vel reuocatio ficta & friuola inuentoris haeresis saepe dictae. Circa istam partem facienda sunt tria. Primo enim probandum est, quod verba praedicta ipsum non excusant, quin fuerit & adhuc sit haereticus. Secundo ostendendum est, quod assertor haeresis ante dictae, licet posset conuerti ad catholicam veritatem, tamen nullo modo poterit excusari, quin sit haereticus. Tertio dicendum est, qualiter reuocationem oportet ipsum facere, si velit inter catholicos reputari: quae scilicet declararet ipsum non esse haereticum: licet per nullam reuocationem poterit declarare, se non fuisse haereticum.
units.tr: It follows: Yet it was never my intention to say anything against the faith, and if I have said anything, from now on I retract it as false. Here is set out the protestation, or retraction, or recantation, feigned and frivolous, of the author of the heresy often mentioned. Three things must be dealt with regarding this part. First, it must be proved that the words quoted do not excuse him, so that he was and still is a heretic. Second, it must be shown that the asserter of the heresy mentioned above, although he could be converted to Catholic truth, nevertheless cannot in any way be excused from being a heretic. Third, it must be said how he ought to make a recantation if he wishes to be counted among Catholics, namely one that would declare him not to be a heretic, although by no recantation can he show that he was never a heretic.

units.la: Ad euidentiam istorum sunt aliqua notanda, quorum primum est: quod duae sunt differentiae credendorum. Quaedam enim sunt credenda explicite, & quaedam sunt credenda implicite, patet aperte: quia nullus Christianus debet totam fidem Christianam ignorare, igitur sibi non sufficit solummodo credere fidem Christianam esse veram: sed oportet quod aliquid explicite credat, quod ad fidem pertinet Christianam, & ita quilibet catholicus aliquid credere tenetur explicite. Quod Augustinus super Iohan. prout recitatur de consecr. distinctio. 4. cap. 1. aperte insinuat, dicens: Necessarium est visibile sacramentum aquae ad ablutionem visibilis corporis, sicut necessaria est doctrina invisibilis fidei ad sanctificationem invisibilis animae. Ex his aperte colligitur, quod quilibet Christianus debet aliqua addiscere de fide Christiana, quae credat explicite. Item idem Augustinus, ut habetur distinctione praedicta, cap. ante baptismum catechizandi debet hominem praevenire officium, ut fidei primum catechuminus accipiat rudimentum, & cap. sequenti sic legitur: Ante vigesim. dies baptismi ad purgationem exercismi catechumini currant, in quibus vigesim. diebus omnino symbolum, quod est, Credo in Deum patrem omnipotentem, spiritualiter doceantur. Ex his patet, quod baptisati fidem suam antequam ad alia se transferant, debent addiscere, quod etiam ex tractatu de eo distinctione quart. cap. symbolum, & cap. catechismi, & cap. non licet, & cap. postquam, patenter habetur. Ex quo patenter infertur, quod quisquam catholicus aliqua credere tenetur explicite. Quod vero aliqua sunt credenda implicite, est manifestum. Nam quilibet catholicus tenetur credere totam scripturam divinam, quam tamen ignorat, & ita non possunt eam credere explicite, sufficit igitur eis, quod credant eam implicite. Porro, quia multi doctrinam Thomae recipiunt: pro illis adducenda sunt verba ipsius, quibus ostenditur distinctio supra dicta, ait itaque secunda secundae quaestio. 2. cap. quint. articul. quint. Quantum igitur ad primum prima credibilia, qua sunt articuli fidei non solum tenetur homo implicite credere: sed etiam explicite, quantum ad alia credibilia non tenetur homo explicite credere: sed solummodo implicite vel in praeparatione animi, inquantum paratus est credere quicquid in scriptura divina continetur. Ex his patenter habetur, quod aliqua sunt credenda explicite, & aliqua implicite. Secundo notandum, quae sunt illa, quae sunt credenda explicite. Circa quod notandum, quod aliqua sunt credenda ab omnibus Christianis de communi lege: quia omnes Christiani de communi lege ea credere tenentur explicite. Alia vero credenda non sunt ab omnibus explicite de necessitate: sed ab aliquibus tantum. Prima credenda explicite sunt illa, quae sunt apud omnes catholicos, tanquam catholica divulgata, cuiusmodi sunt articuli fidei contenti in Credo in Deum patrem omnipotentem creatorem. Illos enim articulos fidei omnes Christiani tenentur credere & addiscere, praeter quos etiam sunt nonnulla alia, quae omnes tenentur credere explicite, licet in dictis articulis non contineantur: sicut quod animae reprobórum infernum descendunt, ubi graviter puniuntur: quod animae electorum, qui sunt in purgatorio, erunt in coelo, quod daemones in inferno torquentur: quod sunt aliqui alii sancti in coelo & boni & similia, quae ideo ecclesia catholica credere tenetur explicite, quia sunt veritates explicitae catholicae apud omnes catholicos tanquam catholicae divulgatae. Aliqua vero sunt credenda explicite non ab omnibus, quia non omnes catholici tenentur credere ea explicite: sed illi scilicet, qui sciunt ipsa in scriptura divina, aut in doctrina ecclesiae contineri, quia illi, qui tenentur scire scripturam divinam & doctrinam ecclesiae, multa tenentur credere explicite: ad quorum fidem explicitam alii tenentur. Propter quod praelati & maxime praelatus praelatorum, id est summus Pontifex, multa tenentur credere explicite, quae alii non tenentur explicite credere. Propter illos autem, quae doctrinae Thomae adhaerent, sunt verba eiusdem de hac materia recitanda, ait itaque secunda secundae quaestio. 2. articul. 6. Explicatio fidei ad inferiores homines, oportet quod perveniat per maiores, & ideo sicut superiores angeli, qui inferiores illuminant, habent pleniorem notitiam de rebus divinis quam inferiores, ut Dionysius dicit 12. cap. coelestis Hierarchiae: ita superiores homines, ad quos pertinet aliis erudire, tenentur habere pleniorem notitiam de credendis & magis explicite credere. Ex his patet, quod de intentione istius doctoris est, quod aliqui tenentur aliqua credere explicite, ad quorum fidem explicitam alii non tenentur. Sed quaeretur forte aliquis, quae sunt illa credenda explicite ab aliquibus, & non ab omnibus? Ad quod potest responderi, quod illa sunt in duplici differentia, quaedam enim sunt, quae de necessitate spectant ad officium aliquorum, sicut qui habent officium praedicationis aliqua tenentur credere explicite, ad quae alii non tenentur, quaedam vero sunt ab aliquibus credenda explicite, & non ab omnibus, quia ad aliquorum perveniat notitiam, quod in scriptura divina, aut in doctrina vniuersalis ecclesiae explicite continentur: licet hoc ad notitiam omnium nequaquam pervenerit. Sicut aliqui sciunt in literis sacris contineri, quod Abraham habuit plures uxores, & quod Helisaeus prophetauit post Heliam, & quod Christus fugit in Aegyptum: & ideo illi tenentur explicite credere supradicta. Aliqui autem ignorant haec in sacris literis reperiri, & illi non tenentur illa credere explicite, sed implicite solum, & sic loquendo de credere explicite, poterit contingere, quod laicus tenetur aliquid explicite credere, ad quod credendum explicite episcopus aliquis etiam in Theologia Magister minime tenetur, si enim laicus sciret in scriptura divina reperiri, quod Amasias fuit filius Ioas, ipse teneretur hoc credere explicite, episcopus autem in Theologia Magister, si non teneret in memoria, quod hoc reperitur in scriptura divina, non teneretur pro tunc hoc credere explicite. Isto igitur modo accipiendo credere explicite ab aliquo, omne credibile potest esse credendum explicite ab aliquo, quia nullum est credibile, quia aliquis possit scire in scriptura divina vel doctrina ecclesiae explicite vel implicite contineri. tineri, qui autem scit illud in scriptura divina siue explicite, siue implicite contineri, tenetur illud credere explicite, ideo &c. & ex hoc sequitur, quod aliquis tenetur uno tempore solum aliquid credere implicite, & alio tempore tenetur illud credere implicite, ideo &c. Et hoc quidem Thomas aperte insinuat dicens: quantum ad aliqua credibilia non tenetur homo explicite credere: sed solum implicite vel in praeparatione animi, inquantum paratus est credere, quicquid in scriptura divina continetur, sed tunc hoc solum tenetur credere explicite, quando hoc ei constiterit in doctrina fidei contineri. Haec allegatio fit pro illis, qui tenent doctrinam Thomae.
units.tr: To make these points clear, some things must be noted. The first is that there are two kinds of things to be believed. Some must be believed explicitly, and some must be believed implicitly. This is plain: no Christian ought to be ignorant of the whole Christian faith, so it is not enough for him merely to believe that the Christian faith is true; he must explicitly believe something that pertains to the Christian faith, and so every Catholic is bound to believe something explicitly. Augustine, on John, as quoted in de consecr. distinctio 4, cap. 1., plainly hints at this when he says: The visible sacrament of water is necessary for the washing of the visible body, just as the teaching of the invisible faith is necessary for the sanctifying of the invisible soul. From this it is plainly gathered that every Christian ought to learn some things of the Christian faith which he believes explicitly. Again, the same Augustine, as found in the aforesaid distinction, chapter Before baptism, the office of catechizing ought to precede the man, so that the catechumen may receive the first rudiments of the faith, and in the following chapter it reads thus: Within the twenty days before baptism, the catechumens should run through the purifying exorcisms, and during those twenty days they should be taught wholly spiritually the creed, which is, I believe in God the Father almighty. From this it is clear that the baptized, before they turn to other matters, ought to learn their faith; this is also plainly found in the treatment de eo, distinctio 4, chapters symbolum, catechismi, non licet, and postquam. From which it is plainly inferred that any Catholic is bound to believe some things explicitly. That some things must be believed implicitly is obvious. For every Catholic is bound to believe the whole divine Scripture, which yet he does not know, and so they cannot believe it explicitly; it suffices for them, then, that they believe it implicitly. Moreover, since many accept the doctrine of Thomas, the words of Thomas himself must be cited on this point, by which the distinction stated above is shown. He says thus, in the second part of the second part, question 2, chapter 5, article 5: As to the first things to be believed, which are the articles of faith, a man is bound not only to believe them implicitly but also explicitly; as to other things to be believed, a man is not bound to believe them explicitly, but only implicitly, or in a preparation of mind, insofar as he is ready to believe whatever is contained in divine Scripture. From these words it is plainly established that some things must be believed explicitly and some implicitly. Second, it must be noted which things are those to be believed explicitly. On this point it must be noted that some things are to be believed by all Christians by common law, because all Christians by common law are bound to believe them explicitly. Other things are not necessarily to be believed explicitly by all, but only by some. The first things to be believed explicitly are those which are known to all Catholics as commonly received Catholic teaching, such as the articles of faith contained in I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator. All Christians are bound to believe and learn those articles of faith, besides which there are also some other things which all are bound to believe explicitly, although they are not contained in the said articles: for example, that the souls of the reprobate descend into hell, where they are severely punished; that the souls of the elect who are in purgatory will be in heaven; that the devils are tormented in hell; that there are other saints in heaven, both good, and similar things. The Catholic Church is bound to believe these explicitly, because they are explicit Catholic truths known to all Catholics as commonly received Catholic teaching. Other things are to be believed explicitly not by all, because not all Catholics are bound to believe them explicitly, but only those who know that these things are contained in divine Scripture or in the doctrine of the Church. For those who are bound to know divine Scripture and the doctrine of the Church are bound to believe many things explicitly, and others are bound to their explicit faith. On this account prelates, and especially the prelate of prelates, that is the supreme Pontiff, are bound to believe explicitly many things which others are not bound to believe explicitly. Regarding those who adhere to the doctrine of Thomas, the words of the same author on this matter must be cited; he says thus, in the second part of the second part, question 2, article 6: The explanation of the faith must reach the lower people through the greater; and so, just as the higher angels, who enlighten the lower, have fuller knowledge of divine things than the lower, as Dionysius says in chapter 12 of the Celestial Hierarchy, so the higher men, to whom it belongs to teach others, are bound to have fuller knowledge of what is to be believed and to believe more explicitly. From this it is clear that it is the intention of this doctor that some are bound to believe some things explicitly, for whose explicit faith others are not bound. But perhaps someone will ask: which are those things to be believed explicitly by some and not by all? To this it can be answered that these are of two kinds. For some are such that by necessity they belong to the office of certain persons; thus those who hold the office of preaching are bound to believe some things explicitly which others are not bound to believe. Other things are to be believed explicitly by some and not by all, because it comes to the knowledge of some that what is explicitly contained in divine Scripture or in the universal doctrine of the Church, although this has by no means come to the knowledge of all. Thus some know that it is contained in the sacred letters that Abraham had several wives, that Elisha prophesied after Elijah, and that Christ fled into Egypt; and therefore they are bound to believe these things explicitly. Others are ignorant that these things are found in the sacred letters, and these are not bound to believe them explicitly, but only implicitly. And speaking in this way of believing explicitly, it may happen that a layman is bound to believe something explicitly, which some bishop, even a master in theology, is by no means bound to believe explicitly. For if a layman knew that it is found in divine Scripture that Amaziah was the son of Joash, he would be bound to believe this explicitly; but a bishop who is a master in theology, if he did not keep in memory that this is found in divine Scripture, would not for that time be bound to believe this explicitly. In this sense, then, of believing explicitly by someone, every thing that can be believed can be believed explicitly by someone, because there is no thing believable that someone may not know to be contained in divine Scripture or in the doctrine of the Church, either explicitly or implicitly; and whoever knows that a thing is contained in divine Scripture, whether explicitly or implicitly, is bound to believe it explicitly, and so on. And from this it follows that someone is bound at one time to believe something only implicitly, and at another time he is bound to believe it explicitly, and so on. Thomas indeed hints at this plainly when he says: as to some things to be believed, a man is not bound to believe them explicitly, but only implicitly, or in a preparation of mind, insofar as he is ready to believe whatever is contained in divine Scripture; but then he is bound to believe this explicitly only when it has been established for him that this is contained in the doctrine of faith. This citation is made for those who hold the doctrine of Thomas.

units.la: Tertio notandum, quod haeretici sunt in duplici differentia, quidam enim sunt scientes haeretici: & quidam sunt haeretici non scientes. Illi sunt scientes haeretici, qui sciunt se Christianae fidei obuiare, sicut apostatae a fide, qui fidem Christianam arbitrantur falsam. Illi sunt haeretici nescientes, qui putant se tenere fidem Christianam: sed reputant & tenent pertinaciter quandam fidem esse Christianam, quae in rei veritate non est. Multi enim fuerunt haeretici, qui putabant se solos catholicos, & omnes alios eis contrarios a veritate catholica deuiare. Haec distinctio ex verbis beati Augustini, quae ponuntur 6. quaestion. 1. cap. quaero, patenter accipitur, ait enim: quaero enim quis peccet gravius, qui nesciens haeresim incurrit, an qui scienter ab auaritia, id est ab idolatria non recessit? secundum illam regulam, qua peccata scientium peccatis ignorantium praeponuntur, auarum conscientia vincit in scelere, sed si forte hunc faciat in haeresi ipsius scelerius magnitudo, quod facit in auaritia scientis admissio, haereticus nesciens auaro scienti coaequatur, vbi dicit Glossa super verbo nesciens: Iste est ignorans haereticus, qui sequitur opinionem, quam putat veriorem, & 24. quaestion. 3. cap. haeresis. Ex his patenter habetur, quod aliqui sunt scientes haeretici, & aliqui nescientes. Quod etiam probatur, quia Arrianus Sabellius & alii plures damnati fuerunt haeretici: sed non fuerunt scientes haeretici, quia scripturae diuinae & doctrinae Apostolicae & ecclesiae vniuersalis putabant se firmiter adhaerere, & in illa doctrina se fundare putauerunt, igitur non fuerunt scientes haeretici, quemadmodum apostatae a fide decedentes negant Christianam fidem, & Scripturam sacram, dicentes eam esse falsam & fictam. Fuerunt igitur praedicti haeretici nescientes, & nonnulli scientes.
units.tr: Thirdly, it must be noted that heretics are of two kinds: some are knowing heretics, and some are unknowing heretics. Those are knowing heretics who know that they oppose the Christian faith, like apostates from the faith, who consider the Christian faith false. Those are unknowing heretics who think they hold the Christian faith, but who regard as Christian, and hold stubbornly, some faith which in the truth of the matter is not Christian. For there were many heretics who thought that they alone were catholic and that all others who opposed them had strayed from catholic truth. This distinction is plainly taken from the words of blessed Augustine, which are set down in 6. quaestion. 1. cap. quaero, for he says: "For I ask, who sins more gravely: he who unknowingly falls into heresy, or he who knowingly does not withdraw from covetousness, that is, from idolatry? According to that rule, by which the sins of those who know are placed before the sins of those who are ignorant, the covetous conscience surpasses in wickedness; but if perhaps the greatness of the heresy's wickedness makes him, the unknowing heretic is equated with the knowing covetous man, as the commission of the knowing man does in covetousness." Where the Gloss on the word "unknowing" says: "This is the ignorant heretic, who follows the opinion which he thinks truer," and 24. quaestion. 3. cap. haeresis. From these things it is plainly held that some are knowing heretics and some unknowing. This is also proved, because Arius, Sabellius and many others were condemned as heretics, yet they were not knowing heretics, since they thought that they firmly adhered to the Scriptures, the apostolic doctrine and the universal Church, and believed that they were grounded in that doctrine. Therefore they were not knowing heretics, just as apostates who fall away from the faith deny the Christian faith and the holy Scripture, saying that it is false and feigned. Therefore the aforesaid heretics were unknowing, and some were knowing.

units.la: Quarto sciendum, quod errantes contra fidem Christianam aberrant ipso facto, & hoc contingit dupliciter: quia aut errant contra veritatem, quam tenentur explicite tenere vel credere: sicut si quis assentiret Christum non fuisse mortuum, putans hoc ad fidem Christianam minime pertinere. Quidam autem errant contra veritatem, quam non tenentur credere explicite: sicut si aliquis putat Christum non fugisse in Aegyptum. Et quidem adhuc contingit dupliciter, quia quidam errant pertinaciter, nec parati sunt corrigi. Quidam vero errant, sed parati sunt corrigi. Ista quatuor praedicta possunt per exempla aperta probari: sed videtur, quod probatione non egent. Primi autem errantes sunt haeretici manifesti, & similiter secundi, & tertii, sed non quarti, quod per multas rationes & auctoritates aperte vel apertas posset ostendi, sed causa breuitatis vnica auctoritas adducetur, qua quatuor praedicta probantur. Est autem auctoritas Augustini, quae ponitur 24. quaestion. 3. cap. dicit Apostolus, qui ait: qui sententiam suam, quamuis peruersam aut falsam nulla pertinacia animositate defendunt, praesertim quam non audacia suae praesumptionis popererunt: sed a seductis & in errorem lapsis parentibus acceperunt, quaerunt autem cauta sollicitudine veritatem, corrigi parati, cum inuenerint: nequaquam sunt inter haereticos computandi. Ex his verbis patenter infertur, quod scientes errantes contra Christianam veritatem sunt haeretici reputandi, quia secundam verba praemissa errans contra fidem, qui non est paratus corrigi, est haereticus; sed haereticans scienter contra fidem non est paratus corrigi: quia errans contra fidem debet corrigi per regulam fidei Christianae, qui ergo regulam fidei putat falsam, non est paratus corrigi, igitur est inter haereticos praedictis concluditur, quod errans contra veritatem catholicam, est haereticus reputandus: quia talis non quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, nec paratus est corrigi. Constat enim quod iste, qui non credit hoc, quod credere tenetur de necessitate salutis, non quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, nec paratus est corrigi. Igitur est inter haereticos numerandus secundum auctoritatem Augustini praedictam. Tertio ex auctoritate praescripta euidenter ostenditur, quod errans pertinaciter contra veritatem catholicam, quam non tenetur explicite credere, est haereticorum numero aggregandus. Nam errans pertinaciter contra fidem catholicam, quam non tenetur explicite credere, defendens enim pertinaci animositate falsam & iniquam sententiam comprobatur, quia defendens pertinaciter sententiam falsam contrariam veritati, quam non tenetur explicite credere propter solam pertinaciam, & non solum propter defensionem inter haereticos numeratur, sed defendens pertinaci animositate falsam & iniquam sententiam, secundum Augustin. inter haereticos computatur, igitur errans pertinaciter contra fidem catholicam, quam non explicite tenetur credere, haereticus est censendus. Quarto ex auctoritate supra dicta infertur, quod errans pertinaciter contra catholicam veritatem, quam non tenetur credere, non est inter haereticos computandus, quia talem dicit Augustin. inter haereticos minime computandum, talis enim paratus est corrigi per regulam fidei Christianae, & ideo non errat scienter contra fidem, quaerit etiam cauta sollicitudine veritatem, & ideo non contra aliquid, quod tenetur credere explicite, errat, quia etiam paratus est corrigi, non errat pertinaciter: sed ex sola simplicitate, vel ignorantia errat, & ideo non est inter haereticos computandus.
units.tr: Fourthly, it must be known that those who err against the Christian faith go astray by the very fact, and this happens in two ways: either they err against a truth which they are bound to hold or believe explicitly, as if someone should assent that Christ was not dead, thinking that this does not pertain at all to the Christian faith; or some err against a truth which they are not bound to believe explicitly, as if someone thinks that Christ did not flee into Egypt. And indeed this again happens in two ways, because some err obstinately and are not prepared to be corrected, while others err but are prepared to be corrected. The first of the aforesaid four can be proved by clear examples, but it seems that they need no proof. Now those who err in the first and second ways are manifest heretics, and likewise those in the third, but not those in the fourth, which could be shown clearly by many reasons and authorities; but for the sake of brevity a single authority will be adduced, by which the aforesaid four are proved. It is the authority of Augustine, which is set down in 24. quaestion. 3. cap. The Apostle speaks, who says: "Those who defend their opinion, however perverse or false, without any obstinate animosity, especially one which they have not fallen into through the audacity of their presumption, but have received from parents who were seduced and had fallen into error, and who seek the truth with cautious diligence, being ready to be corrected when they have found it, are by no means to be counted among the heretics." From these words it is plainly inferred that knowing errors against Christian truth are to be considered heresy, because, according to the words premised, one who errs against the faith and is not prepared to be corrected is a heretic; but one who knowingly errs against the faith is not prepared to be corrected, because one who errs against the faith ought to be corrected by the rule of the Christian faith; he who therefore thinks the rule of the faith false is not prepared to be corrected, and therefore is to be numbered among the heretics. From the aforesaid it is concluded that one who errs against catholic truth is to be reckoned a heretic, because such a person does not seek the truth with cautious diligence, nor is he prepared to be corrected. For it is certain that he who does not believe what he is bound to believe of necessity for salvation does not seek the truth with cautious diligence, nor is he prepared to be corrected. Therefore he is to be numbered among the heretics according to the aforesaid authority of Augustine. Thirdly, from the authority written above it is evidently shown that one who obstinately errs against catholic truth, which he is not bound to believe explicitly, is to be added to the number of heretics. For one who obstinately errs against the catholic faith, which he is not bound to believe explicitly, is proved to defend with obstinate animosity a false and iniquitous opinion; for one who stubbornly defends an opinion false and contrary to a truth which he is not bound to believe explicitly, on account of obstinacy alone, is numbered among the heretics not only for the defence; and one who defends with obstinate animosity a false and iniquitous opinion is, according to Augustine, counted among the heretics. Therefore one who obstinately errs against the catholic faith, which he is not bound to believe explicitly, is to be judged a heretic. Fourthly, from the authority cited above it follows that one who obstinately errs against catholic truth, which he is not bound to believe, is not to be counted among the heretics, because Augustine says that such a person is by no means to be counted among the heretics. For such a person is prepared to be corrected by the rule of the Christian faith, and therefore he does not err knowingly against the faith; he also seeks the truth with cautious diligence, and therefore, since he errs against nothing which he is bound to believe explicitly, and since he is prepared to be corrected, he does not err obstinately, but errs only from simplicity or ignorance, and therefore is not to be counted among the heretics.

units.la: Quinto notandum est, quod non solum per verba praedicationis dogmatizantes seu per determinatiominationes, diffinitiones, assertiones verbales errantes contra veritatem de pertinacia conuincuntur, verumetiam per facta & opera sæpe pertinaces probantur. Ille enim, qui præsumptione violenta potest cōuinci negare aliquam veritatem catholicam, quam prius agnouit esse catholicam, est pertinax reputandus. Item iste qui correctus legitime se non emendat. Item ille, qui molestat aut persequitur catholicam veritatem contrariam defendentes & prauitatem hæreticam impugnantes. Item ille qui recusat se subiicere correctioni & emendationi illius vel illorum, cuius vel quorum interest. Item ille qui de veritate pœnituit informari. Item ille qui ad suum tenendum errorem, alios pœnis vel præceptis vel iuramentis commouit & coegit. Item qui coegit alium veritatem catholicam abiurare, est pertinax reputandus. His enim in numeris aliisque quampluribus est errans de pertinacia conuincendus, & inter hæreticos computandus.
units.tr: Fifthly, it must be noted that those who err against the truth are convicted of obstinacy not only by the words of their preaching, by their determinations, definitions and verbal assertions, but also by deeds and works, and they are often proved obstinate. For he who by violent presumption can be convicted of denying some catholic truth which he had previously acknowledged to be catholic is to be considered obstinate. Likewise, he who, when lawfully corrected, does not amend himself. Likewise, he who harasses or persecutes those who defend catholic truth and attacks heretical perversity. Likewise, he who refuses to submit himself to the correction and amendment of him or those whose concern it is. Likewise, he who is sorry to be instructed in the truth. Likewise, he who by punishments, precepts or oaths has moved and compelled others to hold his error. Likewise, he who has compelled another to abjure catholic truth is to be considered obstinate. By these and many other instances the one who errs is to be convicted of obstinacy and counted among the heretics.

units.la: Sexto notandum est, quod differentia est inter protestationem & reuocationem, protestationem enim quantum ad propositum spectat, potest facere tam ille, qui errat, quam ille qui non errat contra fidem, errans enim contra fidem protestatur, quod non intendit aliquid dicere contra fidem, & talis protestatio si est vera, declarat protestantem non errare vel non dicere aliquid scienter contra fidem, & in hoc ostendit, quod non est scienter hæreticus, sed non suffragatur sibi, quin possit esse nesciens hæreticus, non errans etiam contra fidem protestatur per hoc ostendens, quod si erraret, non erraret nisi ex simplicitate vel ignorantia, non ex pertinacia, revocatio autem non pertinet nisi ad errantem tantummodo, qui enim non errat, non debet aliquid revocare, sed qui errat contra fidem, cum cognouerit se errasse, tunc debet facere tam reuocationem quam protestationem, quod debet fateri se errasse, & debet promittere, quod de cætero contra fidem nequaquam errabit.
units.tr: Sixthly, it must be noted that there is a difference between a protestation and a retraction. For as far as the purpose is concerned, a protestation may be made both by one who errs and by one who does not err against the faith. For one who errs against the faith protests that he does not intend to say anything against the faith; and if such a protestation is true, it shows that the one protesting does not err, or does not say anything knowingly against the faith, and in this it shows that he is not a knowing heretic; but it does not follow that he cannot be an unknowing heretic. One who does not err against the faith also protests, showing by this that, if he were in error, he would err only from simplicity or ignorance, not from obstinacy. A retraction, however, pertains only to the one who errs; for one who does not err ought to retract nothing. But one who errs against the faith, when he has recognised that he has erred, must then make both a retraction and a protestation: he must confess that he has erred, and must promise that henceforth he will by no means err against the faith.

units.la: Septimo notandum est: quod reuocatio, quam facit errans contra fidem, non debet esse conditionalis, sed debet esse pura & absque omni conditione. Sicut enim pœnitentia de peccato commisso non debet esse conditionalis, sed sine conditione: ita non debet quis errans reuocare errorem suum sub conditione, sed absolute. Unde quod aliqui errantes contra fidem, & etiam aliqui non errantes ex consuetudine reuocant aliqua sine conditione dicentes: si aliquid dixi vel dixero contra fidem, reuoco totum: talis revocatio magis dicenda est protestatio, quam reuocatio, talis enim non fatetur se errasse, sed fatetur, quod non dixit vel dicet scienter contra veritatem, & quod si sciuerit se dixisse aliquid contra fidem, paratus est reuocare. Magna autem est differentia inter reuocationem & protestationem. Si sciret aliquid dicere contra fidem, talis enim non reuocat, sed protestatur se paratum reuocare, si se cognouerit contra fidem errasse vel errare.
units.tr: Seventhly, it must be noted that the retraction which one who errs against the faith makes ought not to be conditional, but must be pure and without any condition. For just as repentance for a sin committed ought not to be conditional but unconditional, so one who errs ought not to retract his error under a condition, but absolutely. Hence, when some who err against the faith, and even some who do not err, out of habit retract certain things without condition, saying: if I have said or shall say anything against the faith, I retract all of it, such a retraction ought rather to be called a protestation than a retraction. For such a person does not confess that he has erred, but confesses that he has not said, and will not knowingly say, anything against the truth, and that if he should learn that he has said anything against the faith, he is ready to retract it. Yet there is a great difference between a retraction and a protestation. If someone knew he was saying something against the faith, he would not retract, but would protest that he is ready to retract if he recognised that he had erred or was erring against the faith.

units.la: His visis probanda sunt tria, quæ in principio istius capituli præmissa sunt: Quorum primum est intentio hæresis sæpe dictæ (scilicet quod anima sanctorum in cœlo non videbunt clare Deum ante diem iudicii) non potest per verba, quæ hic dixit, aliqualiter excusari, quin fuerit & adhuc sit hæreticus. Quod probatur sic: per verba communia catholicis & hæreticis obduratis & perfidis non potest tenens hæresim contrariam veritati catholicæ, quam tenetur credere explicite excusari, quin fuerit & adhuc sit hæreticus. Quia hæretici verba talia communia catholicis & hæreticis proferentes, morem simiæ imitantur: quæ cum sit expers penitus rationis, in quibusdam gestibus & actibus sequi animal rationale conatur, licet non sit 1. quæstion. 1. sic qui sunt hæretici cum sunt à fide catholica alieni, in quibusdam verbis catholicos imitantur, sed frustra, quia per talia minime excusantur. Sed verba prædicta, quæ iste profert, sunt communia catholicis & hæreticis obduratis & perfidis, dicunt enim catholici: dicunt & omnes nescientes hæretici, quantumcunque obdurati & perfidi: quod non est intentionis eorum aliquid dicere contra fidem, & si aliquid dixerint, reuocant totum, talem enim protestationem & reuocationem, quæ magis dicenda est protestatio quam reuocatio, omnes Sabelliani, omnes Arriani, omnes Donatistæ, omnes Græci & cæteri hæretici vniuersi (quia alios sibi contrarios reputabant hæreticos & se catholicos) saltem protestati fuissent: qui tamen per talem protestationem nullatenus excusati fuissent. Igitur cum iste teneat hæresim contrariam veritati, quam tenetur credere explicite, per verba huiusmodi minime excusatur, quin fuerit & adhuc sit hæreticus. Et si dicatur, quod per illam rationem nullus errans contra fidem per talem protestationem excusaretur, quin esset hæreticus, cum talis protestatio sit sic communis catholicis & multis hæreticis: quia omnibus hæreticis, qui sunt nescientes hæretici, secundum quod tenens, aut prædicans hæresim contrariam veritati catholicæ. Probabiliter potest dici: quod nullus errans pertinaciter apud Deum per talem protestationem poterit excusari: licet apud ecclesiam, quæ decipi potest, possit errans contra veritatem catholicam (quam non tenetur credere explicite) excusari; si per alium modum de pertinacia conuinci non possit, & tunc quidem eum non excusat solummodo protestatio huius, sed simul per huiusmodi protestationem & defectum probationis per alium modum de pertinacia conuincendi.
units.tr: Having seen this, the three things set out at the beginning of this chapter must be proved. The first of them is that the intention of the heresy mentioned above (namely that the souls of the saints in heaven do not see God clearly before the day of judgement) cannot in any way be excused by the words he has used here, so that he has been and still is a heretic. This is proved as follows: a person who holds a heresy contrary to Catholic truth, which he is bound to believe explicitly, cannot be excused by words common to Catholics and to obstinate and faithless heretics, so as to cease to be and to be a heretic. For heretics who utter such words, common to Catholics and heretics, imitate the manner of the ape: which, though wholly devoid of reason, tries to copy a rational animal in certain gestures and actions, although it is not 1. quaest. 1. So heretics, being estranged from the Catholic faith, imitate Catholics in certain words, but in vain, since they are in no way excused by them. But the words quoted above, which this man utters, are common to Catholics and to obstinate and faithless heretics: for Catholics say them, and all heretics who know nothing say them, however obstinate and faithless they are, that it is not their intention to say anything against the faith, and that if they have said anything, they retract all of it. All the Sabellians, all the Arians, all the Donatists, all the Greeks, and all other heretics without exception (since they regarded others as heretics opposed to themselves and themselves as Catholics) would have made at least such a protestation, and yet they were in no way excused by such a protestation. Therefore, since this man holds a heresy contrary to the truth which he is bound to believe explicitly, he is not excused by words of this kind from having been and still being a heretic. And if it be objected that by that reasoning no one erring against the faith would be excused by such a protestation from being a heretic, since such a protestation is so common to Catholics and to many heretics, because all heretics who know nothing are heretics according to whether they hold or preach a heresy contrary to Catholic truth: it may be answered probably that no one who errs obstinately can be excused before God by such a protestation; although before the Church, which can be deceived, a person erring against Catholic truth (which he is not bound to believe explicitly) may be excused, if he cannot be convicted of obstinacy by any other means; and then indeed the protestation of this man does not excuse him alone, but together with such a protestation and the lack of proof of obstinacy by any other way of convicting him.

units.la: Sed qui tenet, docet, aut prædicat hæresim contrariam veritati catholicæ, quam tenetur credere explicite, & hoc ipse scit: constat posse de hæretica prauitate conuinci, & ideo talis per protestationem huiusmodi nullo modo poterit excusari. Octauo igitur ista duo sunt probanda. Primum est, quod iste, qui prædicat, & tenet hæresim contrariam veritati, quam tenetur credere explicite, statim absque maiori inquisitione, est hæreticus iudicandus. Secundum quod licet talis possit converti ad catholicam veritatem, tamen nullo modo nec per protestationem prædictam, necalio modo quocunque poterit excusari, quin fuerit hæreticus. Primum aperte probatur sic. Illa veritas quæ est apud omnes catholicos, tanquam catholica diuulgata, est ab omnibus credenda explicite. Hoc ex notabili tertio supra scripto colligitur euidenter, sed quod animæ sanctorum in cœlo clare vident Deum, postquam iste ad Papatum fuit assumptus, & ante fuit apud omnes catholicos, tanquam catholica diuulgata, & quamdiu postquam iste Papatui præsidebat, nullus casus eam in dubium reuocauit, igitur tenebatur & tenetur etiam eam credere explicite, sicut illam, Christus fuit passus. Ex quo sequitur, quod iste tenet & prædicat hæresim contrariam veritati, quam tenetur credere explicite. Quare statim sine maiori inquisitione vel examinatione hæreticus est iudicandus. Hoc enim ex quarto notabili suprascripto colligitur euidenter, ibi enim probatum est, quod omnis talis errans est hæreticus manifestus, & ideo quando constat, quod talis errat, est hæreticus reputandus. Hoc etiam aliter consimiliter probatur. Qui teneret & doceret Christum non fuisse passum, & mortuum: ideo esset statim hæreticus reputandus, quia apud omnes catholicos tanquam catholicum diuulgatur, quia Christus fuit passus & mortuus, igitur quicunque negat veritatem, quæ apud omnes tanquam catholica diuulgatur, est hæreticus reputandus. Nec est de tali quærendum, an paratus sit corrigi, vel non paratus sit corrigi: an protestetur, vel non protestetur: sed statim est hæreticus reputandus. Aliter enim inter errantes contra illa, quæ tenetur credere explicite: & inter errantes contra illa, quæ non tenentur credere explicite: differentia assignari nequiret. Item errans contra fidem (si debet de hæretica prauitate excusari) oportet quod per ignorantiam excusetur, errans igitur contra fidem, qui laborat ignorantia (quæ non excusat nisi probetur) antequam probet, non debet per ignorantiam excusari. Similiter qui errat contra veritatem (quæ apud omnes catholicos est tanquam catholica diuulgata) nec ignorat talem veritatem esse apud omnes tanquam catholicam diuulgatam: non laborat ignorantia, quæ ipsum apud ecclesiam excusat, nisi ignorantiam talem probauerit. Quia secundum sanctos canones, illa quæ publice fiunt, nemini licet ignorare. Et si talem ignorantiam allegauerit, ipsam probabit 9. quæstion. 1. ordinationes, in textu, & in glossa, igitur qui negat catholicam veritatem communiter apud catholicos diuulgatam, si protestando qualitercunque se voluerit per ignorantiam de prauitate hæretica excusare: oportet quod ignorantiam huiusmodi probet. Unde si iste posset probare legitime, quod nunquam audiuit aliquem catholicum prædicare, tenere, docere, vel afferere animas sanctorum in cœlo videre Deum; posset de prauitate hæretica excusari: sed aliter non. Sicut etiam si quis negans Christum fuisse passum, per protestationem huiusmodi, scilicet quod non intenderet aliquid dicere contra fidem: & si diceret, totum reuocaret, de prauitate hæretica excusaretur, nisi per alium modum de pertinacia conuinceretur. Sic ergo pro prolixitate vitanda probatum est unica ratione: quod per sacros canones asserentes, quod nulli licet ignorare ea quæ publice fiunt, geruntur & tenentur, posset multipliciter confirmari: quod inuentor hæresis supradictæ, per illam protestationem quam fecit, nullo modo possit excusari, quin fuit, & adhuc sit hæreticus.
units.tr: But whoever holds, teaches or preaches a heresy contrary to Catholic truth, which he is bound to believe explicitly, and knows this himself, it is clear that he can be convicted of heretical depravity, and therefore such a person can in no way be excused by a protestation of this kind. Eighthly, therefore, these two things must be proved. The first is that this man, who preaches and holds a heresy contrary to the truth which he is bound to believe explicitly, is to be judged a heretic at once, without further inquiry. The second is that although such a person can be converted to Catholic truth, yet he can in no way be excused, neither by the aforesaid protestation nor in any other manner whatever, from having been a heretic. The first is clearly proved as follows. That truth which is among all Catholics, as commonly published as Catholic, must be believed explicitly by all. This is clearly gathered from the notable third point written above. But that the souls of the saints in heaven see God clearly, since this man was raised to the Papacy and before, was among all Catholics as a commonly published Catholic truth, and as long as this man has presided over the Papacy no case has called it into doubt; therefore he was bound, and is bound, to believe it explicitly as well, just as he believes that Christ suffered. From this it follows that this man holds and preaches a heresy contrary to the truth which he is bound to believe explicitly. Wherefore he is to be judged a heretic at once, without further inquiry or examination. For this is clearly gathered from the fourth notable point written above, since it was there proved that every such person who errs is a manifest heretic, and therefore when it is established that such a person errs, he is to be regarded as a heretic. This is also proved in a similar way another manner. Whoever held and taught that Christ had not suffered and died would at once be regarded as a heretic, because it is commonly published among all Catholics as Catholic that Christ suffered and died; therefore whoever denies a truth which is commonly published among all as Catholic is to be regarded as a heretic. Nor is it to be asked of such a person whether he is ready to be corrected or not ready to be corrected, whether he makes a protestation or does not: he is at once to be regarded as a heretic. For otherwise no difference could be assigned between those who err against what they are bound to believe explicitly and those who err against what they are not bound to believe explicitly. Likewise, one who errs against the faith, if he is to be excused of heretical depravity, must be excused on the ground of ignorance; therefore one who errs against the faith and pleads ignorance, which does not excuse unless it is proved, must not be excused by ignorance before he proves it. Similarly, one who errs against a truth which is commonly published among all Catholics as Catholic, and does not claim to be ignorant that such a truth is among all as commonly published Catholic, does not plead the ignorance which excuses him before the Church, unless he proves such ignorance. For according to the holy canons, things that are done publicly may not be ignored by anyone. And if he alleges such ignorance, he will prove it, 9. quaest. 1, ordinationes, in the text and in the gloss; therefore one who denies a Catholic truth commonly published among Catholics, if by protesting in whatever way he wishes to excuse himself of heretical depravity through ignorance, must prove such ignorance. Hence, if this man could legitimately prove that he had never heard any Catholic preach, hold, teach or assert that the souls of the saints in heaven see God, he could be excused of heretical depravity; but otherwise not. Likewise, if someone denying that Christ suffered, by a protestation of this kind, namely that he did not intend to say anything against the faith, and if he did say anything, retracts all of it, he would be excused of heretical depravity, unless he were convicted of obstinacy by some other means. So, to avoid prolixity, it has been proved by a single argument: since the holy canons assert that no one may be ignorant of what is done, performed and held publicly, this could be confirmed in many ways: that the inventor of the aforesaid heresy cannot in any way, by that protestation which he made, be excused from having been, and still being, a heretic.

units.la: Secundum autem probandum est: quod licet posset conuerti ad catholicam veritatem, tamen nullo modo, nec per protestationem prædictam, nec alio modo quocunque poterit excusari, quin fuerit hæreticus. Quod breuiter sic probatur. Qui in rei veritate est hæreticus, licet posset conuerti: tamen nullo modo poterit excusari, quin fuerit malus, sed iste fuit hæreticus, igitur licet posset conuerti ad catholicam fidem: tamen non poterit excusari, quin fuerit hæreticus. Maior est manifesta. Minor probatur. Primo per prædicta, quia prædicauit, & docuit hæresim contrariam veritati catholicæ, quam tenetur credere explicite, igitur fuit hæreticus. Secundo probatur sic, sicut patet ex quinto notabili, errans contra catholicam veritatem non solum vincitur per verba, quæ asserit: sed etiam per facta & opera, & ideo ad conuincendum istum de pertinacia & prauitate hæretica, non solum attendenda sunt verba ipsius, sed simul cum verbis consideranda sunt opera eius, per quæ aliquis de pertinacia conuincitur manifeste. Præterea sic. Errans contra fidem, qui prædicantes, docentes, vel defendentes, aut tenentes catholicam veritatem, & impugnantes hæreticam prauitatem persequitur, & molestat, est hæreticus iudicandus, sicut tactum est in quinto notabili suprascripto. Sed iste prædicantes & tenentes catholicam veritatem, scilicet quod animæ sanctorum in cœlo vident Deum: & impugnantes contrariam hæreticam prauitatem, persequitur & molestat, igitur hæreticus est censendus. Maior istius rationis est manifesta: Quæ tamen multis modis ostenditur. Primo modo sic, reprobi circa fidem sunt hæretici reputandi, qui autem prædicantes veritatem catholicam & prauitatem hæreticam impugnantes persequitur & molestat, est reprobus circa fidem: quia damnabiliter veritati resistit, qui sunt autem damnabiliter veritati resistunt, reprobi circa fidem, teste Apostolo, qui 2. ad Tim. 2. ait: Quemadmodum autem Iannes & Mambres restiterunt Moysi, ita & hi resistunt veritati, homines corrupti mente, reprobi circa fidem: & per eonsequens sunt hæretici iudicandi. Secundo sic, errans contra fidem, qui persequitur & molestat veritatem catholicam confitentes, & prauitatem hæreticam impugnantes: non quærit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, nec paratus est corrigi, talis autem hæreticus est manifestus, secundum Augustinum, ut habetur 24. quæstion. 3. dicit Apostolus, igitur tales persequentes veritatem catholicam confitentes, sunt hæretici manifesti. Item sic: Grauius peccat & delinquit, qui catholicam veritatem impugnat, quam qui non recipiunt prædicatores catholicæ veritatis: & tamen peccant mortaliter, testante ipsa veritate, Matthæi decimo quæ ait: quicunque non receperit vos, neque audierit sermones vestros, exeuntes foras de domo vel civitate excutite pulverem de pedibus vestris, amen dico vobis, tolerabilius erit terræ Sodomorum & Gomorrhæorum in die iudicii, quam illi civitati. Igitur grauius vel non minus peccant: qui ideo alios persequuntur vel molestant, quia catholicam tenent vel prædicant veritatem, & prauitatem impugnant hæreticam. Sed peccatum tale & tam graue non est sine pertinacia. Igitur tales sunt pertinaces, & per consequens hæretici censendi. Sic igitur probata est maior: quod errans contra fidem, qui prædicantes & afferentes catholicam veritatem, aut impugnantes hæreticam prauitatem persequitur & molestat, est hæreticus iudicandus. Minor autem, quod isti prædicantes & tenentes animas sanctorum in cœlo videre Deum, & impugnantes contrariam hæreticam prauitatem persequitur & molestat, per opera eius aperte probatur. Primo: quia ideo, vt fertur, quendam prædicatorem Magistrum in Theologia carceri mancipauit. Secundo, quia, vt dicitur, volentes prædicare veritatem catholicam priuauit sermonibus consuetis. Tertio quia, vt narratur, quondam amicos suos suadentes sibi veritatem prædictam, male portauit. Quarto, quia (sicut fertur) scripta defendentium veritatem prædictam, conatur peruertere, & arripere eos in verbis, vt sic eos cogat à veritate consona cessare. Ista & alia multa, quæ dicitur fecisse in defensores veritatis catholicæ consistunt in facto, & ideo non per rationem, vel auctoritatem, sed per testes & alia documenta legitima sunt probanda.
units.tr: The second point to prove is that, although he could be converted to the Catholic truth, he cannot be excused from having been a heretic in any way, neither by the aforesaid protestation nor by any other means. This is proved briefly as follows. Whoever is in fact a heretic, even if he could be converted, can in no way be excused from having been a wicked man. But this man was a heretic. Therefore, even if he could return to the Catholic faith, he cannot be excused from having been a heretic. The major premise is plain. The minor is proved as follows. First, from what was said above: he preached and taught a heresy contrary to the Catholic truth, which people are bound to believe explicitly. Therefore he was a heretic. Second, it is proved thus. As is clear from the fifth notable point, a person who errs against the Catholic truth is refuted not only by the words he asserts but also by his deeds and works. So, to convict this man of obstinacy and heretical wickedness, not only his words but also his works must be considered together with them, since a person is manifestly convicted of obstinacy by these. Moreover, thus: whoever errs against the faith and persecutes and harasses those who preach, teach or defend or hold the Catholic truth, and who attack heretical wickedness, is to be judged a heretic, as was touched on in the fifth notable point above. But this man persecutes and harasses those who preach and hold the Catholic truth, namely that the souls of the saints see God in heaven, and who attack the contrary heretical wickedness. Therefore he is to be counted a heretic. The major premise of this argument is plain, and it is shown in many ways. In the first way: those who are reprobate concerning the faith are to be reckoned heretics. Whoever persecutes and harasses those who preach the Catholic truth and attack heretical wickedness is reprobate concerning the faith, because he resists the truth to his damnation. Those who resist the truth to their damnation are reprobate concerning the faith, as the Apostle testifies in 2 Tim. 2., where he says: "Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith." Consequently they are to be judged heretics. Second, thus: a person who errs against the faith, and who persecutes and harasses those who confess the Catholic truth and attack heretical wickedness, does not seek the truth with careful diligence, nor is he ready to be corrected. Such a heretic is manifest, according to Augustine, as is found in 24. q. 3, "The Apostle says". Therefore those who persecute those who confess the Catholic truth are manifest heretics. Likewise: he who attacks the Catholic truth sins more gravely and offends more than he who does not receive the preachers of the Catholic truth. Yet both sin mortally, as the truth itself testifies in Matt. 10., which says: "Whoever does not receive you, nor hear your words, when you leave that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Truly I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city." Therefore those who persecute or harass others, because they hold or preach the Catholic truth and attack heresy, sin no less, or more gravely. But such a sin, so grave, is not without obstinacy. Therefore such people are obstinate, and consequently are to be counted heretics. Thus the major premise has been proved: whoever errs against the faith, and persecutes and harasses those who preach and affirm the Catholic truth or attack heretical wickedness, is to be judged a heretic. The minor, that this man persecutes and harasses those who preach and hold that the souls of the saints see God in heaven, and who attack the contrary heretical wickedness, is clearly proved by his deeds. First, because, as it is reported, he handed over a certain preacher, a master in theology, to prison for this reason. Second, because, as it is said, he deprived those wishing to preach the Catholic truth of their customary sermons. Third, because, as it is related, he treated badly certain of his friends who urged him toward the aforesaid truth. Fourth, because (as is reported) he tries to pervert the writings of those who defend the aforesaid truth, and to catch them out in their words, so as to force them to cease from the harmonious truth. These and many other things which he is said to have done against the defenders of the Catholic truth consist in fact, and therefore they are to be proved not by argument or authority, but by witnesses and other lawful documents.

units.la: Secundo, per opera eius ostenditur, quod est hæreticus manifestus, nam errans contra fidem, qui in fauorem sui erroris reprobos & malignos promouet & exaltat: hæreticus est censendus: quia talis non est paratus corrigi, & per consequens est hæreticus reputandus. Sed inuentor hæresis sæpedictæ in fauorem erroris sui reprobos, vt refertur, promouet & exaltat, igitur est hæreticus censendus. Maior est manifesta. Minor in facto consistit, & ideo per legitima documenta est probanda.
