Ex dictis aperte colligitur, quod duo promittebantur probanda in principio istius capituli: quod scilicet assertor hæresis antedictæ possit conuerti ad catholicam veritatem: tamen nullo modo poterit excusari, quin fuerit hæreticus.
units.tr: Second, it is shown by his works that he is a manifest heretic. For whoever errs against the faith, and who promotes and exalts the reprobate and malicious in favour of his error, is to be counted a heretic, because such a person is not ready to be corrected, and consequently is to be regarded as a heretic. But the author of the aforesaid heresy, as is reported, promotes and exalts the reprobate in favour of his error. Therefore he is to be counted a heretic. The major premise is plain. The minor consists in fact, and therefore is to be proved by lawful documents. From what has been said it is clearly gathered that two things were promised to be proved at the beginning of this chapter: namely, that the author of the aforesaid heresy can be converted to the Catholic truth, yet he can in no way be excused from having been a heretic.

units.la: Tertio principaliter est dicendum, quale reuocationem ipsum oportet facere: si velit inter catholicos reputari, qui scilicet declaret ipsum non esse hæreticum: licet per nullam reuocationem poterit declarare se non fuisse hæreticum. Ad <?>us euidentiam est sciendum, quod errantes primo modo, secundo & tertio, de quibus dictum est in tertio notabili, ad hoc quod debeant catholici reputari, necesse est quod simpliciter & absolute sine omni conditione (sicut dictum est in quinto notabili) reuocent suum errorem, & fateantur se errasse. Errantes autem quarto modo, de quo dictum est in quinto notabili supra scripto, si cognouerint se errasse primam reuocationem absque omni conditione ad hoc, quod pro catholicis habeantur satisfacere restringuntur. Si autem aliquis errauerit quarto modo, non tenetur aliquid reuocare proprie loquendo: sicut ante dictum est in sexto notabili: sed sufficit sibi facere protestationem, nisi per alia verba eius, aut opera posset de pertinaci animositate conuinci. Ex istis duo liquide constant. Primum est, quod omnes hæretici, siue scientes sint hæretici, siue nescientes hæretici (de quorum differentia dictum est in tertio notabili supra scripto) & omnes catholici, qui sciunt se ex ignorantia vel ex simplicitate contra fidem errasse: ad hoc quod pro catholicis habeantur, tenentur errorem suum pure & absolute & simpliciter sine omni conditione, notificatione, & palliatione reuocare, & se erraße confiteri. Secundum est, quod catholicus errans ex sola simplicitate non tenetur aliquem errorem reuocare, sed si nihil habetur contra ipsum, nisi quod talem errorem tenuit absque omni pertinacia opinando, antequam sibi constiterit quod errauit: sufficit quod protestetur se ex intentione nihil dixisse: etiam quod paratus est reuocare, si cognouerit se errasse.
units.tr: Third, it must be said chiefly what kind of retraction he must make if he wishes to be counted among Catholics, that is, to declare that he is not a heretic. Yet by no retraction can he show that he was not a heretic. For the clearer understanding of this, it must be known that those who err in the first, second and third ways, of whom we spoke in the third notable point, must, if they are to be regarded as Catholics, simply and absolutely, without any condition (as was said in the fifth notable point), retract their error and confess that they have erred. But those who err in the fourth way, of which we spoke in the fifth notable point above, if they have recognised that they erred, are bound to make the first retraction without any condition in order to be held as Catholics and to make satisfaction. If, however, someone has erred in the fourth way, he is not, strictly speaking, bound to retract anything, as was said before in the sixth notable point, but it is enough for him to make a protestation, unless by his other words or deeds he could be convicted of obstinate animosity. From these two things it is clearly established. The first is that all heretics, whether they knowingly are heretics or unknowingly are heretics (concerning whose difference we spoke in the third notable point above), and all Catholics who know that they have erred against the faith through ignorance or simplicity, are bound, in order to be held as Catholics, to retract their error purely, absolutely and simply, without any condition, qualification or evasion, and to confess that they have erred. The second is that a Catholic who errs from simplicity alone is not bound to retract any error; but if nothing is held against him except that he held such an error without any obstinacy, in opinion, before it was established to him that he had erred, it is enough that he protests that he said nothing from intention, and even that he is ready to retract if he recognises that he has erred.

units.la: Primum istorum auctoritate, exemplis, & ratione probatur, auctoritate quidem: Primo Leonis Papæ prim. quæstion. septim. cap. saluberrimum, euidenter ostenditur. Ait enim: Saluberrimum, & spirituali medicinæ utilitate plenissimum est, vt siue presbyteri, siue diaconi, siue subdiaconi, aut cuiuscunque ordinis clerici, qui se videri correctos volunt, atque ad fidem catholicam, quam quidem amiserant, rursum reuerti ambiunt, prius errores suos, & ipsos auctores erroris à se damnatos sine ambiguitate fateantur, & sensibus prauis etiam peremptis, nulla desperandi superfit occasio, nec vllum membrum talium possit societate violentari: cum per omnia professio propria coeperit illis obuiare. Ex quibus euidenter colligitur, quod omnes errantes contra fidem, qui volunt videri correcti, suos errores reuocare tenentur. Sed dices forte, ex hac auctoritate videtur posse inferri, quod qualitercunque errantes teneantur errorem suum reuocare, si voluerint videri correcti: cuius tamen oppositum assumitur in secundo, quod sequitur ex dictis. Ad hoc est facile respondere: quod errantes primo modo, secundo, tertio & quarto, si errasse cognouerint, tenentur velle videri correcti, & ideo pure & sine omni conditione suos errores reuocare tenentur. Errantes autem quarto modo, si se errasse nequaquam cognouerunt, non tenentur de hoc velle videri correcti pro tunc: sed nec tenentur tunc scire se errasse. Ad prædictam conclusionem est concilium Martini Papæ: in quo, vt legitur prim. quæstion. septim. cap. si quis episcopus vel aliquis episcopi presbyter aut diaconus vel accolitus opinionem offenderit: & ob hanc causam fuerit excommunicatus, nullus episcopus in communione cum recipiat, nisi prius in communi concilio, porrecto fidei suae libello, satisfaciat omnibus, ita liberam suam teneat purgationem, hoc idem & de fidelibus laicis fit decretum, si in aliqua haeresis opinione fuerint nodati. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi: quod omnes errantes contra fidem, qui errores suos revocare tenentur, pure suam debent confiteri fidem, & per consequens pure & absque conditione suos errores revocare. Hoc etiam ex decret. Papae Lucii, quod ponitur extra, de haereticis, ad abolendam, potest intelligi, vel colligi evidenter. Verum quia auctoritates praedictae, & alia de ista materia, ad intellectum peruersum possunt trahi, sunt duo notanda. Quorum primum est, quod in auctoritatibus praedictis quaedam ponuntur, quae sunt de iure humano & positivo. Aliquid autem continent, quod est de iure divino, quod omnes summi Pontifices, & omnia generalia concilia mutare non possunt. Asserunt autem auctoritates praefatae, quod errantes contra fidem errorem suum revocare pure tenentur, quod verum est secundum legem divinam, quantum ad simplicitatem revocationis, praesertim si aliqui scandalizati fuerint de errore, debent enim errorem dimittere, & propter scandalum eruendum fateri se erasse, & veritatem catholicam fateri, iuxta illud Matthaei decimo. Omnis igitur qui confitetur me coram hominibus: confitebor & ego eum coram Patre meo qui in caelis est, & ad Romanos 4. corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem fit consessio ad salutem. Quod autem secundum concilium Martini Papae errantes debeant libellum fidei suae in concilio communi porrigere: & secundum Lucium Papam, haeretici debent suam haeresim abiurare: & ex iure humano & ex iure positivo (quod ex causa iusta instituitur) potest ex rationabili causa mutari.
units.tr: This first point is proved by authority, by examples, and by reason. The authority comes first. The First Question, Distinction Seven, chapter Saluberrimum, of Pope Leo clearly shows it. For he says: It is most wholesome, and full of spiritual medicine, that whether presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any other order, who wish to be seen as corrected and eagerly desire to return to the Catholic faith, which they had indeed abandoned, first confess without ambiguity their errors and the authors of those errors, whom they have condemned, and that, even when their perverse opinions have been removed, no occasion for despair remains, and no member of such persons may be cut off from fellowship, since their own profession of faith will meet them at every turn. From these words it is plainly gathered that all who err against the faith and wish to be seen as corrected are bound to retract their errors. But perhaps you will say that from this authority it seems to follow that persons who err in any way are bound to retract their error if they wish to be seen as corrected; yet the opposite is assumed in the second point, which follows from what has been said. The answer to this is easy: those who err in the first, second, third, and fourth ways, if they have recognised that they erred, are bound to wish to be seen as corrected, and therefore they are bound to retract their errors simply and without any condition. Those who err in the fourth way, however, if they have by no means recognised that they erred, are not bound at that time to wish to be seen as corrected, nor are they then bound to know that they erred. The council of Pope Martin also supports the aforementioned conclusion, in which, as is read in the First Question, Distinction Seven, chapter If any bishop, or any presbyter or deacon or acolyte of a bishop, has given offence in opinion, and for this cause has been excommunicated, let no bishop receive him into communion unless first, in a general council, having presented a written statement of his faith, he has satisfied all, and so holds his own purgation free; the same decree is made also concerning lay believers, if they have been entangled in some opinion of heresy. From these words it is made clear that all who err against the faith, and are bound to retract their errors, ought to confess their faith purely, and consequently to retract their errors purely and without condition. This can also be understood or plainly gathered from the decretal of Pope Lucius, which is placed in the Extra, De haereticis, Ad abolendam. But since the aforementioned authorities, and others on this subject, can be drawn into a perverse sense, two things must be noted. The first is that the aforementioned authorities contain some things which belong to human and positive law, while they also contain something which belongs to divine law, and which all the supreme Pontiffs and all general councils cannot change. The aforementioned authorities assert that those who err against the faith are bound to retract their error purely; this is true according to divine law as regards the simplicity of the retraction, especially if some have been scandalised by the error. For they ought to abandon the error, and, to remove the scandal, to confess that they have erred and to confess the Catholic truth, in accordance with Matthew 10: Everyone therefore who confesses me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven; and Romans 4: with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. But that, according to the council of Pope Martin, those who err must present a written statement of their faith in a general council, and that, according to Pope Lucius, heretics must abjure their heresy, may be changed for a reasonable cause, since human and positive law, which is instituted for a just cause, may be altered by a reasonable cause.

units.la: Secundo sciendum est, quod haeretici sic tenentur suum errorem revocare, quod debent simpliciter & pure fateri graviter se deliquisse, & ideo secundum canonicas sanctiones, sunt graviter puniendi, sed ignorantes contra fidem ex sola simplicitate & ignorantia absque omni pertinacia, licet pure & sine omni conditione debeant revocare suum errorem, non tamen tenentur fateri se errando peccasse, saltem mortaliter. Nec post revocationem huiusmodi est eis poenitentia imponenda: nisi forte sponte vel ad cautelam, vel ex humilitate voluerint poenitentiam sustinere. Nec propter talem errorem sunt infamia aliqua notandi. Et sic auctoritatibus patet, quod omnes haeretici sive scientes, sive nescientes, si voluerint corrigi videri, & etiam omnes catholici errantes, postquam cognoverunt se erasse, pure & sine omni conditione & sine palliatione suum debent revocare errorem, fatendo se erasse, & protestando, quod de caetero scienter contra catholicam veritatem nequaquam intendant errare.
units.tr: Secondly, it must be understood that heretics are bound to retract their error in such a way that they must simply and purely confess that they have grievously sinned. Therefore, according to the canonical sanctions, they are to be severely punished. But those who err against the faith through simplicity and ignorance alone, without any obstinacy, although they must retract their error purely and without any condition, are not bound to confess that they sinned by erring, at least not mortally. Nor, after such a retraction, is penance to be imposed on them, unless perhaps they choose of their own accord, as a precaution or out of humility, to undergo penance. Nor are they to be marked with any infamy on account of such an error. And so the authorities make it plain that all heretics, whether knowing or unknowing, if they wish to be seen as corrected, and also all Catholics who err, once they have recognised that they have gone astray, must retract their error purely, without any condition and without evasion, confessing that they have erred and declaring that from now on they will by no means knowingly intend to err against Catholic truth.

units.la: Haec eadem assertio aperte probatur exemplis. Primum exemplum habetur in decretis 1. quaestion. septim. cap. maximum, ubi de quodam haeretico dicit Leo Papa: Maximum quoque ex laico reprehensibili licet ordinatum, tamen si Donatista iam non est, & a spiritu schismatica prauitatis alienus est, ab episcopali (quam quoquo modo adeptus est) non repellimus dignitate. Itaque ipse libello ad nos directo catholicum se esse manifestet. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod iste quondam Donatista pure & sine omni conditione debuit manifestare se esse catholicum. Quod facere nequaquam potuit, nisi pure, & sine omni conditione haeresim abnegando. Secundum exemplum ponitur, ca. Donatum, de quodam alio, de quo idem Leo Papa sic ait: Donatum autem Sciatensem ex Nouatiano (ut comperimus) cum sua plebe conuersum, ita Dominico gregi volumus praesidere, ut libellum fidei suae ad nos meminerit dirigendum, quo & Nouatiani dogmatis damnet errorem, & plenissime confiteatur catholicam veritatem. Ex his colligitur, quod iste Donatus debuit plenissime catholicam veritatem confiteri, igitur & debuit pure & sine omni conditione prauitatem haereticam abnegare. Tertium exemplum ponitur de consecratione, distinctione, secund. cap. ego Berengarius, ubi clare habetur, quod Berengarius pure, & sine omni conditione & palliatione sane revocavit errorem, imo anathematizavit dicens: Ego Berengarius, indignus ecclesiae sancti Mauritii Andegauensis diaconus, cognoscens veram catholicam & Apostolicam fidem anathematizo omnem haeresim: praecipue eam, de qua hactenus infamatus sum, qua astruere conatur panem & vinum, &c. Ex his verbis patenter habetur, quod iste pure, & sine omni conditione ac palliatione revocavit errorem. Quartum exemplum de beato Augustino, qui quandoque praedicavit errorem, absolute, pure & sine omni conditione revocavit eundem. Unde in epistola ad Vincentium, & ponitur vigesim. tert. quaestion. sext. cap. vides, sic dicit: mea primitus erat sententia, neminem ad Christi veritatem cogendum, verbo esse agendum, disputatione pugnandum, ratione vincendum, ne fictos catholicos haberem, quos apertos haereticos noveram. Sed hac opinio mea non contradicentium verbis tantum, sed demonstrantium superabatur exemplis. Ex quibus verbis patenter habetur, quod beatus Augustinus pure & sine conditione fatebatur opinionem suam superatam a veritate fuisse, & ita opinionem suam pure sine omni conditione revocavit. Non enim in revocatione necesse est uti verbo revocandi: sed sufficit verbis aequipollentibus uti. Si enim dicit quis: reprehendo hanc opinionem meam, vel sententiam: vel, dico esse falsam, aut contra veritatem: imo si dicit, fateor assertionem contrariam esse veram: vel verba aequipollentia profert: in rei veritate, pure, & sine omni conditione, errorem suum praetendit revocare: Et isto modo Augustinus errores suos revocavit quamplures, ipsomet testante: qui in principio libri Retractationum ait: iamdiu id facere cogitabam, atque disponebam, quod nunc adiuuante Domino aggredior, quia differendum esse non arbitror, ut opuscula mea sive in libris, sive in epistolis, sive in tractatibus, cum quadam severitate iudiciaria recensean, & quod me offenderit velut centesimo stylo denotem. Neque enim quisquam nisi imprudens, ideo quia mea errata reprehendo, me reprehendere audebit. Sed si dicit, non es debuisse à me dici, qua postea etiam mihi displicerent, verum dicit, & mecum facit, eo‐rum quippe reprehensor est, quorum & ego sum. Et postea ait: quicunque ista lecturi sunt, non me imi‐tentur errantem, sed in melius proficientem. Ex his aliisque quamplurimis verbis beati Augustini con‐ cluditur aperte, quod beatus Augustinus errores suos pure & sine conditione voluit revocare. Unde & in libro Retractationum de se, & de suis opinionibus loquens sepe vtitur talibus verbis: temere dictum est, minus considerate dictum est; hoc improbo: & non approbo: nec illud mihi placet. Ex quibus modis loquendi colligitur evidenter, quod Augustinus plures errores pure & sine omni con‐ ditione ac palliatione revocavit: licet plura dicta sua non revocaverit in libro Retractationum, sed retractavit exponendo, quem de ipsis habuit intellectum. Sed forte quaereret aliquis, an Augustinus fuerit haereticus, ex quo plures errores contra fidem docuerat. Ad quod dicendum est, quod Augustinus post conversionem suam, propter nullum errorem fuit haereticus reputan‐ dus, quia nullum errorem contrarium veritati catholicae: quae apud omnes catholicos tanquam catholica exstitit divulgata: nec aliquem errorem contra veritatem catholicam, quam tenebatur credere explicite: tenuit, etiam opinando, sed ex sola ignorantia aut simplicitate errauit, quae‐siutque cauta sollicitudine veritatem: quam postquam invenit, statim correxit se, ac loco & tem‐ pore opportunis pure, & sine omni conditione revocavit errorem, & confitebatur plenissime ca‐ tholicam veritatem.
units.tr: This same assertion is clearly proved by examples. The first example is found in the decrees, 1. quaest. 7, cap. Maximum, where Pope Leo says of a certain heretic: Although Maximum was ordained as a layman, which is blameworthy, nevertheless, if he is no longer a Donatist and is free from the spirit of schismatic perversity, we do not remove him from the episcopal dignity, which he has obtained in whatever way. Let him therefore make himself known as a Catholic by a written statement addressed to us. From these words it is clear that this former Donatist ought to have shown himself to be a Catholic purely and without any condition. He could not have done so unless he renounced the heresy purely and without any condition. The second example is given in cap. Donatum, concerning another man, of whom the same Pope Leo says: We have learned that Donatus of Sciatis has been converted with his flock from Novatianism. We wish him to preside over the Lord's flock on this condition: that he remember to send us a written statement of his faith, in which he both condemns the error of the Novatian teaching and most fully confesses the Catholic truth. From this it is gathered that this Donatus ought to have confessed the Catholic truth most fully, and therefore also ought to have renounced the heretical perversity purely and without any condition. The third example is given in de consecratione, distinctione 2, cap. Ego Berengarius, where it is clearly stated that Berengarius retracted his error purely, without any condition or evasion, and indeed anathematised it, saying: I, Berengarius, unworthy deacon of the church of St Maurice of Angers, knowing the true Catholic and Apostolic faith, anathematise every heresy, especially that by which I have hitherto been defamed, which tries to assert that the bread and wine, etc. From these words it is plainly evident that he retracted his error purely, without any condition or evasion. The fourth example is of blessed Augustine, who, when he had at some time taught an error, retracted it absolutely, purely and without any condition. Hence, in the letter to Vincent, which is cited in 23. quaest. 6, cap. Vides, he says: My view at first was that no one should be compelled to the truth of Christ, that we should act by words, fight by disputation, and conquer by reason, lest I should have as Catholics those whom I knew to be open heretics. But this opinion of mine was overcome not only by the words of those who contradicted me, but by the examples of those who demonstrated the point. From these words it is plainly evident that blessed Augustine confessed without condition that his opinion had been overcome by the truth, and so he retracted his opinion purely and without any condition. For in a retraction it is not necessary to use the word "retract"; it is enough to use equivalent words. If someone says: "I rebuke this opinion of mine or this view," or "I say it is false or contrary to the truth," or even, "I confess that the contrary assertion is true," or uses words of equivalent meaning, he in fact intends to retract his error purely and without any condition. In this way Augustine retracted very many of his errors, as he himself testifies in the beginning of the book of Retractations, where he says: I had long been thinking of and planning to do what I now undertake with the help of the Lord, because I do not think it should be put off: to review my little works, whether in books, letters or treatises, with a certain judicial severity, and to mark with a sort of hundredth stroke of the pen whatever has displeased me. For no one, unless imprudent, will dare to rebuke me because I rebuke my own errors. But if someone says that I ought not to have said things which later displeased even me, he speaks the truth and agrees with me; for he is the rebuker of those things of which I too am a rebuker. And afterwards he says: Whoever is going to read these things, let them not imitate me in my error, but in my progress towards the better. From these and very many other words of blessed Augustine it is clearly concluded that blessed Augustine wished to retract his errors purely and without condition. Hence also, in the book of Retractations, speaking of himself and of his opinions, he often uses such words as: This was said rashly; this was said without sufficient consideration. I disapprove of this, I do not approve of it, and that does not please me. From these modes of speaking it is evidently gathered that Augustine retracted many errors purely and without any condition or evasion, although in the book of Retractations he did not retract many of his statements, but reviewed them by explaining the sense in which he had understood them. But perhaps someone might ask whether Augustine was a heretic, since he had taught many errors against the faith. To this it must be replied that Augustine, after his conversion, was not to be regarded as a heretic on account of any error, because he held no error contrary to Catholic truth, which had been made known among all Catholics as Catholic; nor did he hold, even by opinion, any error against the Catholic truth which he was bound to believe explicitly. He erred only through ignorance or simplicity, while seeking the truth with careful diligence. As soon as he found it, he immediately corrected himself, and at a suitable place and time retracted his error purely and without any condition, and he most fully confessed the Catholic truth.

units.la: Sic igitur manifeste est ostensum, quod tam omnes haeretici, quam catholici ex ignorantia contra fidem errantes, postquam cognoverint se erraße, pure & sine omni conditione errores suos revocare tenentur, & haec eadem assertio ratione probatur. Nam quilibet catholicus lo‐co & tempore opportunis, aliis circumstantiis necessariis debitis observatis, pure, & sine omni conditione confiteri tenetur catholicam veritatem. Confessio autem catholicae veritatis est re‐ probatio contraria haereticae prauitatis antea tentae, & pure & sine conditione revocatio haere‐ticae prauitatis.
units.tr: Thus it has been clearly shown that both all heretics and all Catholics who err against the faith through ignorance are bound, once they have recognised that they have gone astray, to retract their errors purely and without any condition. This same assertion is also proved by reason. For every Catholic, at a suitable place and time, with the other necessary circumstances duly observed, is bound to confess the Catholic truth purely and without any condition. Now the confession of Catholic truth is the rejection of the contrary heretical perversity previously held, and the retraction of the heretical perversity purely and without condition.

units.la: Sic igitur quilibet loco & tempore opportunis, aliis circumstantiis debitis & necessariis ob‐ servatis, pure & sine conditione, postquam novit se errasse, errorem revocare tenetur. Am‐ plius secundum Augustinum in epistola ad Vincentium, & ponitur 23. quaestion. 7. cap. ultimo, quod quasi nemo potest gaudere se esse correctum, nisi doleat se fuisse peruersum, & secundum Gelasium, vt 24. quaestion. 2. cap. legitur, nulli nisi corrigenti se est venia concedenda. Igitur consimiliter, nemo potest gaudere se ad catholicam veritatem esse reuersum, nisi doleat se a veritate catholica deuiasse, & per consequens qui contra fidem erravit (& si vere & non ficte reuertitur) omnem dimittit haereticam prauitatem & errorem contrarium, nec potest ante errorem perfecte, meritorie & virtuose dimittere, nisi satisfaciat illis, quos prius scandalizauerit: vel quibus dedit occasionem errandi, quod nequaquam facere potest, nisi pure & sine omni conditione revocando errorem. Igitur talem revocationem eum facere oportet, si idem catholicis satisfacere cupit. Istae autem rationes non procedunt de haereticis errantibus non manifestis, sed occultis: quia illis sufficit ad veritatem redire catholicam, & qui damnabiliter erraverunt, confiteri debent secundum formam ecclesiae sacerdoti, licet rationes procedant de haereticis, & errantibus manifestis & publicis, qui alios scandalizauerunt, vel saltem aliis occasionem errandi dederunt, & quod debent isti pure, & sine omni conditione revocare errores.
units.tr: Thus, anyone, at a suitable place and time, with the other due and necessary circumstances observed, is bound, once he knows that he has erred, to retract his error purely and without condition. Furthermore, according to Augustine in the letter to Vincent, which is cited in 23. quaest. 7, cap. ultimo, almost no one can rejoice that he has been corrected unless he grieves that he has been perverse; and according to Gelasius, as is read in 24. quaest. 2, cap., pardon is to be granted to no one except one who corrects himself. Therefore, similarly, no one can rejoice that he has returned to Catholic truth unless he grieves that he has strayed from Catholic truth. Consequently, whoever has erred against the faith (if he truly and not feignedly returns) puts off all heretical perversity and the contrary error. Nor can he perfectly, meritoriously and virtuously put off the error before he makes satisfaction to those whom he has previously scandalised, or to whom he has given an occasion of erring. This he cannot do unless he retracts the error purely and without any condition. Therefore he must make such a retraction if he wishes to satisfy the Catholics also. But these arguments do not apply to heretics who err in a hidden way and are not manifest; for it is enough for them to return to Catholic truth, and those who have erred culpably ought to confess to the priest according to the form of the Church. The arguments do apply, however, to heretics and to those who err in a manifest and public way, who have scandalised others or at least given others an occasion of erring; and these must retract their errors purely and without any condition.

units.la: Tertio idem probatur ratione, sicut peccata sunt purganda, sic revocandi sunt errores, sed secundum Calixtum Papam, vt habetur extra de poenitentiis & remissionibus, cap. prim. manifesta peccata non sunt occulta correctione purganda, nec sunt sub conditione expurganda. Igitur errores manifesti, & divulgati non sunt secrete nec sub conditione: sed pure & simpliciter revocandi. Sic ergo patet, quod omnes haeretici & omnes revocantes, postquam cognoverint se errare, pure & sine omni conditione suos errores revocare tenentur: vel occulte saltem coram Deo, si sint occulti, & non publici, & errores suos non publicauerunt, quia illis quos scandalizauerunt, vel quibus saltem occasionem errandi dederunt, satisfacere obligantur: Secundo probandum est, quod errans contra catholicam veritatem, quam non tenetur explicite credere; ex sola simplicitate vel ignorantia absque omni pertinacia: antequam cognoverit se errasse, non tenetur errorem aliquem revocare: sed sufficit protestari, quod paratus est revocare, si se errare cognoverit. Quod probatur sic, nullus tenetur mentiri. Igitur talis non tenetur recognoscere se errare: quamdiu sibi non constat quod erraverit, & sic errorem revocare non debet. Sed diceret aliquis: quod per hanc rationem nullus haereticus nescienter teneretur suam haeresim revocare: quia mentiri non dicit se errasse, ex quo credit se nunquam errasse. Ad hoc potest dici, quod per rationem praedictam bene probatur, quod haereticus nescienter stante conscientia, qua putat se veritatem tenere, non debet revocare errorem: sed illam conscientiam tenetur dimittere: & non tenetur haeresim tenere. Sed qui errat contra veritatem, quam non tenetur explicite credere, non tenetur de necessitate salutis conscientiam talem dimittere, nec mortaliter peccat conscientiam talem habendo, antequam cognoverit se errare, & ideo non est simile de haeretico, & de tali errante.
units.tr: Thirdly, the same point is proved by reason. Just as sins must be purged, so errors must be revoked. But according to Pope Callistus, as found in extra de poenitentiis & remissionibus, cap. prim., manifest sins are not to be purged by secret correction, nor are they to be purged under a condition. Therefore manifest and publicly spread errors are not to be revoked in secret or under a condition, but purely and simply. So it is plain that all heretics, and all who revoke, once they have recognised that they are in error, are bound to revoke their errors purely and without any condition. Or at least, if their error is hidden and not public, and they have not published it, they must do so secretly before God; but they are obliged to make satisfaction to those whom they have scandalised, or to whom they have at least given occasion of error. Secondly, it must be proved that one who errs against a Catholic truth, which he is not bound to believe explicitly, through mere simplicity or ignorance and without any obstinacy, is not bound to revoke any error before he has recognised that he has erred. It is enough for him to protest that he is ready to revoke it if he comes to recognise that he is in error. This is proved thus: no one is bound to lie. Therefore such a person is not bound to acknowledge that he is in error, so long as it is not evident to him that he has erred, and so he ought not to revoke the error. But someone might say: by this reasoning no heretic who errs unknowingly would be bound to revoke his heresy, since he would not be lying in saying that he has not erred, given that he believes he has never erred. To this it can be answered that the foregoing argument rightly proves that a heretic who errs unknowingly, while his conscience tells him that he holds the truth, ought not to revoke the error; but he is bound to give up that conscience, and he is not bound to hold the heresy. But one who errs against a truth which he is not bound to believe explicitly is not bound, by necessity of salvation, to give up such a conscience, nor does he sin mortally by having that conscience before he has recognised his error. Therefore the case of the heretic is not like the case of such an erring person.

units.la: Ex praedictis concluditur manifeste, qualem revocationem debet facere inventor haeresis praedictae, si velit inter catholicos reputari, quae scilicet declaret ipsum non esse haereticum pro haeresi memorata: licet per nullam declarationem poterit declarare se non fuisse haereticum: quia ipse pure & sine omni conditione, ac palliatione dictam haeresim revocare tenetur, his verbis vel aequipollentibus : Abnego haeresim quam probavi & docui, quia asserui quod anima sanctorum in caelo non clare vident Deum, consentio autem fidei orthodoxa, ac corde & ore confiteor, quod anime sanctorum purgate in caelo sunt Deum facialiter, clare videntes. Quod autem talem revocationem facere teneatur, ex praemissis ostenditur. Nam ostensum est, quod omnes errantes contra veritatem catholicam, quam credere tenentur explicite, suum errorem, pure & sine omni conditione revocare tenentur. Sed iste errat contra veritatem catholicam, quam credere tenetur explicite. Igitur dictam haeresim pure, & sine omni conditione revocare tenetur. Et ideo cum dicit: nunquam tamen nostra intentionis fuit dicere aliquid contra fidem: per haec verba minime excusatur, sicut nec Graeci, Iacobitae, Georgiani, Arriani, Sabelliani, Donatistae, & alii haeretici quamplurimi minime excusantur: licet non fuerit intentionis eorum aliquid dicere contra fidem, licet enim excusetur per hoc, quod non fuerit scienter, vel sciens haereticus: non tamen poterit excusari, quin fuerit saltem nesciens, vel nescienter haereticus. Duobus autem modis debet convinci. Primo, quia non credit veritatem, quam debet credere explicite, & ideo posito hoc: quamuis per solas probationes convinci non posset: tamen convincitur per opera sua, cum ostendunt pertinaciam manifestam: & quod non quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem: & quod non est paratus corrigi. Cum autem dicit: quod si aliquid dixerimus, &c. ex nunc revocamus: quamuis hic utatur verbo revocandi, tamen ista non est revocatio proprie loquendo, sed est magis protestatio. Et ideo hic probanda sunt duo. Primo, quod hic non ponitur revocatio proprie dicta, secundo, quod ista protestatio sibi non prodest. Quod vero non sit hic revocatio, patet: quia conditionalis nihil ponit, haec autem est conditionalis, igitur non est revocatio alicuius erroris. Secundo, quia revocatio est erroris confessio, qui autem dicit aliquid conditionaliter, nihil prositetur, igitur &c. Tertio, quia catholicus, qui nunquam erravit, nullum debet revocare errorem, praedicta autem verba potest & debet dicere omnis catholicus, igitur haec nulla est revocatio. Quarto, talia verba etiam diceret omnis nesciens sive nescienter haereticus, qui errori suo pertinaciter adhaereret, putans cum esse catholicam veritatem: & tamen talis per talia verba nullum intendit revocare errorem, igitur talia verba revocationem non continent. Secundo probatur: quod dicta protestatio sibi minime prodest. Primo, quia protestatio tunc non prodest, cum quis facit in contrarium, extra de sensibus, cap. olim, & de constitutionibus tantum, sed iste facit multa contra protestationem praedictam: quia per multa facta & opera ostendit se ad revocandum nullatenus esse paratum, sicut ostensum est prius, igitur talis protestatio tali minime prodest. Secundo: quia protestatio conditionalis minime prodest protestanti, quare ignorantia vel simplicitas non excusat, quia in diffinitionibus & obiectis fidei taliter protestantur catholici, ut insinuent se errare (si errant) non ex pertinacia aliqua, sed ex ignorantia vel simplicitate solta. Et ideo talis protestatio in diffinitionibus valet solummodo, quando protestans potest per simplicitatem vel ignorantiam excusari. Sed quod iste istis modis excusari non valeat, constat aperte. Primo non simplicitate, quia ex multa deliberatione, meditatione & studio dicit, & cum hoc praedicat haeresim saepe dictam. Nec valet per ignorantiam excusari: quia ignorantia illorum, quae quis scire tenetur, nequaquam excusat, ipse autem tenetur scire, quod haec est veritas catholica, scilicet quod animae sanctorum in caelo clare vident Deum: Quia hoc tenetur ipse scire explicite; cum sit veritas apud omnes catholicos diuulgata, igitur per ignorantiam excusari non potest. Tertio probatur sic: per protestationem communem catholicis & haereticis non potest errans contra catholicam veritatem, quam tenetur credere explicite, excusari, hoc ex praecedentibus satis apparet, sed talis protestatio est communis catholicis, & haereticis nescienter, omnes enim tam isti, quam alii protestantur, vel protestari possunt esse parati, quodsi aliquid dixerint contra fidem, totum revocant, & iste in hoc casu errat contra veritatem catholicam, quam tenetur credere explicite, igitur per talem protestationem minime excusatur, nec talis protestatio sibi prodest. Quarto sic: si talis protestatio sibi prodesset, eadem ratione prodesset neganti quantamcunque veritatem catholicam, sed hoc est manifeste falsum: quia tunc liceret cuicunque praedicare publice, quod Christus non est passus, nec mortuus, nec natus de virgine, & quod non est alia vita perpetua post istam vitam: & quod bona opera non prosunt post mortem: & quod Deus non est diligendus: & quod non est obediendum Deo: & alia consimilia praedicare liceret, absque metu haereticae prauitatis, si praedicans protestaretur dicens: ista dico & teneo, tamen non est intentionis mea aliquid dicere contra fidem, & si aliquid dixi, totum ex nunc revoco, sed hoc est inconueniens manifestum. Igitur sicut nec illis, ita nec isti talis protestatio prodest.
units.tr: From what has been said it is clearly shown what kind of revocation the author of the aforesaid heresy must make if he wishes to be counted among Catholics: namely, a declaration that he is not a heretic for the heresy mentioned. Yet by no declaration will he be able to show that he was not a heretic, because he is bound to revoke that heresy purely and without any condition or pretext, in these words or their equivalent: I renounce the heresy which I have defended and taught, because I asserted that the souls of the saints in heaven do not see God clearly; but I assent to the orthodox faith, and with heart and mouth I confess that the souls of the saints purged in heaven see God face to face, clearly. That he is bound to make such a revocation is shown from what has been premised. For it has been shown that all who err against a Catholic truth which they are bound to believe explicitly are bound to revoke their error purely and without any condition. But he errs against a Catholic truth which he is bound to believe explicitly. Therefore he is bound to revoke that heresy purely and without any condition. And so when he says: nevertheless it was never our intention to say anything against the faith, he is by these words in no way excused, just as the Greeks, Jacobites, Georgians, Arians, Sabellians, Donatists and very many other heretics are not excused. Although it was not their intention to say anything against the faith, yet a heretic who knows what he is doing can be excused only by the fact that he did not act knowingly; he cannot be excused from being at least an unknowing heretic. Moreover, he must be convicted in two ways. First, because he does not believe a truth which he ought to believe explicitly; so, granting this, although he could not be convicted by proofs alone, he is convicted by his own works, since they show manifest obstinacy, that he does not seek the truth with careful diligence, and that he is not ready to be corrected. As for his saying: if we have said anything, etc., we now revoke it: although he here uses the word revoke, this is not a revocation properly speaking, but rather a protestation. Therefore two things must be proved here: first, that no revocation properly so called is set down here; second, that this protestation does him no good. That there is no revocation here is plain: because a conditional statement asserts nothing, and this is a conditional statement, so it is not a revocation of any error. Second, because a revocation is a confession of error, but one who says something conditionally confesses nothing; therefore etc. Third, because a Catholic who has never erred has no error to revoke, yet any Catholic can and should say the aforesaid words; therefore these are no revocation. Fourth, every unknowing heretic who stubbornly clings to his error, thinking it to be Catholic truth, would also say such words, and yet such a person by such words intends to revoke no error; therefore such words do not contain a revocation. Second, it is proved that the said protestation does him no good at all. First, because a protestation does no good when someone acts to the contrary (extra de sensibus, cap. olim, & de constitutionibus tantum); but he does many things against the said protestation, since by many deeds and works he shows that he is in no way ready to revoke, as was shown earlier. Therefore such a protestation does him no good. Second, because a conditional protestation does not help the one who makes it, for ignorance or simplicity excuses only where it is the protestation that is made by Catholics in definitions and objects of faith, so that they may hint that they are in error (if they are in error), not through any obstinacy but through ignorance or mere simplicity. And so such a protestation in definitions holds good only when the protester can be excused by simplicity or ignorance. But that this man cannot be excused in either of these ways is perfectly clear. Not by simplicity, because he says it after much deliberation, meditation and study, and besides he preaches the aforesaid heresy often. Nor can he be excused by ignorance, for ignorance of those things which a man is bound to know never excuses; and he is bound to know that this is the Catholic truth, namely that the souls of the saints in heaven see God clearly, because he is bound to know this explicitly, since it is a truth made known among all Catholics. Therefore he cannot be excused by ignorance. Third, it is proved thus: by a protestation common to Catholics and heretics who err unknowingly, one who errs against a Catholic truth which he is bound to believe explicitly cannot be excused. This is sufficiently clear from what precedes. But such a protestation is common to Catholics and to unknowing heretics, for all of them, both these and others, protest, or can protest, that they are ready, if they have said anything against the faith, to revoke all of it. And this man in this case errs against a Catholic truth which he is bound to believe explicitly. Therefore he is not excused by such a protestation, nor does such a protestation do him any good. Fourth, thus: if such a protestation did him good, it would do good by the same reasoning to one who denies any Catholic truth whatever. But this is manifestly false, for then anyone would be allowed to preach publicly that Christ did not suffer, nor die, nor was born of a virgin; that there is no eternal life after this life; that good works do not profit after death; that God is not to be loved; that God is not to be obeyed; and it would be allowed to preach other things of the same kind without fear of heretical depravity, provided the preacher protested, saying: I say and hold these things, yet it is not my intention to say anything against the faith, and if I have said anything, I revoke all of it from now on. But this is manifestly absurd. Therefore, just as such a protestation does not help those others, so it does not help this man either.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Vbi ponitur quintum recitatum supra capitulo septimo, scilicet dolosa revocatio, qua confutatur.
units.tr: Where the fifth recitation cited above in chapter seven is set out, namely the deceitful retraction, and is refuted.

units.la: SEquitur: Si quis magnus aut paruus aliquid habet pro conclusione affirmativa, secure det mihi & libenter recipiemus. Hic narratur, quo inuentor erroris praedicti verbis dolosis & ambiguis se non pertinaciter zelare pro assertione prædicta prætendit. Sed dolus eius, cum dicit: si quis magnus, aut parum aliquid habet pro conclusione affirmativa, securè det mihi. Et hoc ex eius operibus perpenditur euidenter. Nam ex persecutione, quam infert zelatoribus catholicæ veritatis, constat aperte, quod qui daret sibi aliquid pro veritate, suo errori contraria, se periculo & confusioni exponeret, eo quod zelatores & defensores catholicæ veritatis, eius gratiam perdunt, & indignationem incurrunt: licet interdum forte ergo aliquos callide suam indignationem occultet. Hoc in facto consistit, ideo non per rationem, vel auctoritatem, sed per facta eius aut opera debet ostendi. Cum vero dicit: libenter recipiemus: suam dolositatem & malitiam per verba ambigua molitur abscondere. Nam potest quis allegationes suas contra opinionem suam libenter recipere, vel ad reprobandum, vel ad respondendum, vel ad inuestigandum, quæ suæ opinioni dissentiunt, vel ad discutiendum, vel ad probandum. Primis tribus modis videtur probabile: quod ipse libenter reciperet allegationes pro parte affirmativa, ut scilicet eas reprobet, vel eis respondeat, vel quæ suo errori dissentiunt, inuestiget, & eas (si viderit tempus) destruat, & confundat. Sed ad discutiendum & probandum, facta eius ostendunt, quod non libenter recipiat allegationes contra suum errorem.
units.tr: It follows: If anyone, great or small, has something to put forward as an affirmative conclusion, let him give it to me securely, and we will gladly receive it. Here it is related by what means the author of the aforesaid error, with deceitful and ambiguous words, pretends that he does not stubbornly defend his assertion. But his deceit is evident from the words, when he says: if anyone, great or small, has something to put forward as an affirmative conclusion, let him give it to me securely. And this is plainly weighed from his own works. For from the persecution which he brings upon the defenders of Catholic truth, it is clear that whoever should give him anything in support of a truth contrary to his error would expose himself to danger and confusion, because the defenders and champions of Catholic truth lose his favour and incur his displeasure, although he may sometimes cunningly conceal his displeasure from some. This consists in fact, and therefore it must be shown not by reason or authority but by his deeds and works. When he says: and we will gladly receive it, he labours to hide his duplicity and malice behind ambiguous words. For a person may gladly receive arguments against his own opinion, either to reject them, or to answer them, or to investigate those which dissent from his opinion, or to discuss them, or to prove them. Of the first three ways, it seems probable that he would gladly receive arguments on the affirmative side, namely so that he may reject them, or answer them, or investigate those which dissent from his error, and destroy and confound them (if he sees the time). But as to discussing and proving, his deeds show that he does not gladly receive arguments against his error.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Deducit sextum capitulo 7. assignatum.
units.tr: He deduces the sixth point assigned in chapter 7.

units.la: Equitur: Et super hoc statim petiuit fieri publicum instrumentum: & solutum est consistorium. Hic ultimo narratur, quod de revocatione sua, vel protestatione petiuit fieri publicum instrumentum: sed per præcedentia patet, quod iuxta processum præcedentem, tale instrumentum sibi non poterit suffragari. Eo quod prædicta protestatio sibi minime prodest. Omnia suprascripta, quæ de meo protuli: sicut & dicta mea & opuscula vniuersa correctioni, & emendationi illius vel illorum, cuius vel quorum interest, submitto: paratus, si cognouero, quod aliquid dixerim contrarium veritati, omnimode revocare. Si vero assertiones istius, vel opera aliter recitauerim, quam veritas habeat, reportatoribus imputetur.
units.tr: It follows: "And upon this he at once asked that a public instrument be made, and the consistory was dissolved." Here at last it is related that he asked for a public instrument concerning his revocation or protestation. But from what has gone before it is clear that, according to the preceding procedure, such an instrument cannot avail him, since the aforesaid protestation does him no good at all. All the things written above, which I have put forward, together with my sayings and all my little works, I submit to the correction and emendation of that person or those persons whom it concerns; and I am ready, if I come to know that I have said anything contrary to the truth, to revoke it altogether. But if I have related the assertions of this man, or his works, otherwise than the truth has them, let the blame be laid on the reporters.

units.la: Explicit primus tractatus.
units.tr: Here ends the first treatise.

units.la: SECVNDVS TRACTATVS
units.tr: THE SECOND TREATISE

units.la: IN QVO RATIONES IOHANNITARVM CONFVTAT, PROBANTES quod anima purgatæ, vel sanctorum in cœlo non vident Deum facialiter.
units.tr: IN WHICH HE REFUTES THE ARGUMENTS OF THE JOHANNITES, PROVING that the souls of the purged, or of the saints in heaven, do not see God face to face.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CAP. I.

units.la: Ostendit modum procedendi huius tractatus.
units.tr: Shows the method of proceeding in this treatise.

units.la: QValis est rector ciuitatis, tales sunt inhabitantes in ea. Quia subiectis existit quodammodo naturale (vel vt placeant, vel vt displiceant) suis se rectoribus conformare. Affectant autem rectores præcipue, vt lectæ suæ (quantum ad ea quæ fidei, & religionis existimant) subiecti seruentius acquiescant. Et ideo cum rector infectus fuerit hæretica prauitate, quia ei placere desiderant, prauitate consimili imuoluuntur, quia exemplum erroris vehementer ostenditur, quando errans timore potentiæ honoratur. Cum igitur rector in Aviniónica ciuitate circa visionem animarum sanctarum in cœlo, damnabiliter (vt fertur) noscitur errare: consequens est, quod qui ei cupiunt placere, errorem istius non metuant publicare: & rationibus & auctoritatibus quauis scriptura communitas. Sane licet plures in sacris literis eruditi prædicti rectoris errorem de visione animarum sanctarum in cœlo, in diuersis operibus reprobauerunt luculenter, fundamentaque suorum sequacium eliserunt euidenter: assertiones tamen & motiua quorundam, qui in fauorem rectoris prædicti, quod animæ sanctæ in cœlo non vident Deum, publice prædicare, asserere, & docere præsumunt, in præsenti opusculo confutare conabor. Non tamen principalem errorem improbare studebo. Quia in aliis operibus in quisitius eius poterit improbatio reperiri: sed ad quasdam rationes sophisticas, quas ad muniendum prædictum errorem adducunt, satagam respondere. Et quorundam errores, quos incidentaliter dogmatizant, breuiter reprobabo.
units.tr: As the ruler of a city is, so are its inhabitants. For subjects naturally tend, in some measure, to conform themselves to their rulers, whether to please them or to avoid displeasing them. Rulers, moreover, especially desire that their subjects, in matters they regard as belonging to faith and religion, should acquiesce more eagerly in their chosen opinions. So when a ruler has been tainted with heretical depravity, those who want to please him become entangled in a like depravity, since the example of error is powerfully displayed when the one who errs is honoured out of fear of his power. Since, then, the ruler in the city of Avignon is known (so it is reported) to err damnably concerning the vision of the souls of the saints in heaven, it follows that those who wish to please him do not fear to publish his error, backing it with arguments and authorities drawn from every kind of writing. Indeed, although many scholars learned in the sacred writings have clearly refuted the error of the said ruler concerning the vision of the souls of the saints in heaven in various works, and have plainly overthrown the foundations of his followers, nevertheless in the present little work I will try to confute the assertions and arguments of certain men who presume to proclaim, assert and teach publicly, in favour of the said ruler, that the holy souls in heaven do not see God. I shall not, however, make it my aim to disprove the principal error itself, since a refutation of it can be found in his other works in more detail. Rather, I will take care to answer certain sophistical arguments which they bring forward to fortify the said error. And I will briefly refute the errors of some men which they teach incidentally.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Primam rationem soluit, quæ ex eo procedit, quod tempus credendi, quod vsque ad diem iudicii durabit, non patitur secum tempus Deum beatifice videndi.
units.tr: He answers the first argument, which runs from the fact that the time of believing, lasting until the day of judgment, does not allow the time of beatifically seeing God to exist alongside it.

units.la: QVod igitur animæ sanctæ in cœlo non vident Deum, quidam sic probare niuntur. Tempus credendi & tempus beatifice Deum videndi non compatiuntur se inuicem: secundum doctrinam Apostoli in multis locis, quia fidei succedit visio. Sed tempus credendi (secundum omnes sanctos) durabit vsq; ad diem iudicii. Igitur animæ sanctorum Deum non vident, nec videbunt. Quamuis istius rationis solutio exquisita in tractatu contra tractatum predicti Rectoris, in quo probare conatur, quod animæ sanctæ in cœlo non vident Deum, potuerit inueniri, ipsam tamen volo hic aliter pertractare. Maior itaque rationis præscriptæ sensum habet falsum, nam si intelligatur, quod tempus credendi & tempus Deum beatifice videndi, nullo modo sunt simul, pro diuersis falsa est: quia constat, quod quantum ad angelos, est nunc tempus Deum beatifice videndi, & pro Christo est etiam nunc tempus Deum beatifice videndi: quia Christus & angeli nunc beatifice vident Deum, & tamen pro viatoribus tempus est nunc credendi. Si autem intelligitur, quod in eodem tempus credendi, & tempus Deum beatifice videndi non stant simul, conceditur. Cum autem dicitur, quod tempus credendi durabit vsque ad diem iudicii, verum est in viatoribus: quoniam in cœlo non est tempus nunc Deum credendi esse trinum & vnum. Sed quod fides sit in omnibus viuis & mortuis, probatur per illud Apostoli ad Ephes. 4. Dedit quosdam quidem Apostolos, quosdam vero prophetas, alios vero euangelistas, alios autem pastores & doctores ad societatem sanctorum in opus mysterii & ædificationem corporis Christi, donec occurramus omnes in vnitatem fidei & agnitionis filii Dei, in virum perfectum, in mensuram ætatis plenitudinis Christi, iste autem occursus non erit ante diem iudicii, igitur fides durabit in omnibus tam viuis quam defunctis vsque ad diem iudicii. Ad hanc probationem est facile respondere, quia Apostolus in verbis prædictis intendit ostendere: quod vsque 'ad diem iudicii stabit prælatio, Glossa teste, quæ super verbo donec, ait: quod tamdiu durabit hæc prælatio etiam ordinata: donec & in die iudicii nos omnes, qui sumus in vnitate fidei, &c. Prælatio autem illa, de qua Apostolus loquitur, non est nunc in cœlo quantum ad alias sectas, igitur per verba Apostoli non potest probari, quod fides sit nunc in cœlo: sed fides est & erit vsque ad iudicium in vita mortali, & hoc est verum: quod in mortali durabit spes vsq; ad diem iudicii. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod Glossa asserit ibi, quod fides remanebit in omnibus quousque omnes occurramus in vnitate fidei, quia dicit: quæ prælatio durabit donec in diem iudicii, omnes in vnitate fidei, id est in vna & non discrepante fide, igitur vsque ad illam occurramus. Ex quibus colligitur, quod omnes saluandi occurrent in die iudicii in vna & non discrepante fide, igitur vsque ad illum occursum omnes tenebunt fidem, igitur vsque ante illum occursum nullus saluandus erit sine fide, & per consequens non videbit Deum. Sed ad hoc respondetur, quod male allegatur Glossa, quia non est intentio Glossæ, quod durabit prælatio donec omnes occurramus in vnitate fidei: quia multi in fine prælationis occurrent non in fide, sed in clara visione: sed est intentio quod prælatio durabit donec omnes qui sumus, quamdiu sumus in vita præsenti in vna, & non discrepanti fide occurremus. Aliqui tamen occurrent in clara visione: & aliqui occurrent in fide. Et quod sic debeat intelligi Glossa, patet, quia dicit: donec in die iudicii omnes, qui sumus in vnitate fidei: & in vna & non discrepante fide, quamdiu scilicet sumus in vita præsenti: non autem pro vita post mortem. Nec vnquam dixit Apostolus, quod fides in omnibus defunctis saluandis remanebit.
units.tr: Some men try to prove, therefore, that the holy souls in heaven do not see God. The time of believing and the time of beatifically seeing God, they say, are not compatible with each other, according to the Apostle's teaching in many places, since sight succeeds faith. But the time of believing (according to all the saints) will last until the day of judgment. Therefore the souls of the saints do not see God, nor will they see him. Although a full solution of this argument could have been found in the treatise against the treatise of the aforementioned Rector, in which he tries to prove that the holy souls in heaven do not see God, I want to handle it here in a different way. The major premise of the stated argument therefore has a false sense. If it is understood that the time of believing and the time of beatifically seeing God are in no way simultaneous, it is false, because it is clear that, as far as the angels are concerned, it is now the time of beatifically seeing God, and for Christ too it is now the time of beatifically seeing God, since Christ and the angels now see God beatifically, and yet for wayfarers it is now the time of believing. If, however, it is understood that in the same person the time of believing and the time of beatifically seeing God do not stand together, that is granted. But when it is said that the time of believing will last until the day of judgment, this is true of wayfarers, since in heaven it is not now the time to believe that God is three and one. That faith remains in all the living and the dead is proved by that passage of the Apostle to the Ephesians, chapter 4: He gave some apostles, and some prophets, and some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, until we all come in the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ. But that coming together will not happen before the day of judgment; therefore faith will last in all, both living and departed, until the day of judgment. This proof is easy to answer, because the Apostle in the words cited intends to show that the arrangement will remain until the day of judgment, as the Gloss attests, which, on the word until, says: this arrangement, though ordained, will last as long as, until the day of judgment, we all who are in the unity of faith, and so on. But that arrangement of which the Apostle speaks does not now exist in heaven with respect to the other sects. Therefore it cannot be proved from the words of the Apostle that faith is now in heaven; but faith is and will be until the judgment in mortal life, and this is true: that hope will last in mortal life until the day of judgment. Perhaps someone would say that the Gloss there asserts that faith will remain in all until we all come together in the unity of faith, because it says: this arrangement will last until the day of judgment, all in the unity of faith, that is, in one and non-discordant faith, therefore until we come together. From this it is gathered that all who are to be saved will come together on the day of judgment in one and non-discordant faith; therefore until that coming together all will hold the faith, and therefore until before that coming together no one who is to be saved will be without faith, and consequently will not see God. But to this it is answered that the Gloss is wrongly cited, because the Gloss does not intend that the arrangement will last until we all come together in the unity of faith; for many at the end of the arrangement will come together not in faith but in clear vision. Its intention is rather that the arrangement will last until we all who are, in one and non-discordant faith, come together, as long as we are in the present life. Some, however, will come together in clear vision, and some in faith. That the Gloss ought to be understood in this way is plain, because it says: until on the day of judgment all of us who are in the unity of faith: and in one and non-discordant faith, namely as long as we are in the present life, and not for life after death. Nor did the Apostle ever say that faith will remain in all who are to be saved after death.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAP. III.

units.la: Addücit aliam rationem probantem idem, quæ fundatur super oratione ecclesiæ in canone, vbi dicitur, qui nos præcesserunt & dormiunt, &c.
units.tr: He brings forward another argument proving the same thing, based on the prayer of the Church in the Canon, where it is said: "who have gone before us and sleep," etc.

units.la: Rursus pro errore prædicto taliter allegatur. Ad hoc scil. quod animæ sanctæ in cœlo Deum minime sunt visuræ, est oratio ecclesiæ, quæ dicit pro defunctis: Qui nos præcesserunt & dormiunt in somno pacis: pro quibus orat ecclesia, vt lucem viuendi Deus eis concedat in futurum, scilicet post diem iudicii. Et si dicatur eis, quod hæc oratio est pro defunctis, quorum animæ sunt in purgatorio: Hoc improbare conantur dicentes: quod hoc non est verum, quia in oratione ecclesiæ præmittitur, quod dormiunt in somno pacis, & non pœnæ & afflictionis. Ex quibus clare patet, quod oratio illa non fit pro animabus in purgatorio existentibus: sed pro illis animabus, quæ sunt in pace & quiete, & exspectant post vltimum iudicium, & non ante, Dei visionem & suam beatificationem. Vt istius allegationis peruersitas clarius demonstretur, est primo sciendum, quod pacis vocabulum accipitur multipliciter in scripturis. Vno modo importat concordiam vnius ad alterum, teste Glossa quæ super illud ad Romanos decimo quinto. Deus autem spei repleat vos omni gaudio & pace in credendo, qui, vt repleat vos pace habita in credendo, id est concordia adinuicem. Et super illud ad Romanos decimo quarto, non est enim regnum Dei esca & potus, sed iustitia & pax: dicit Glossa: pax, id est concordia, quæ est effectus iustitiæ. Aliter accipitur pax pro reconciliatione ad Deum, quæ est per charitatem, sicut accipitur pax, cum dicit Apostolus ad Romanos 1. Gratia vobis & pax à Deo Patre, etiam teste Glossa, quæ ait ibidem: sicut gratia Dei est, qua donantur nobis peccata: ita pax est, qua ex inimicis reconciliamur Deo. Sic enim accipit pacem Apostolus in ead. epist. c. 5. dicens: Iustificati igitur ex fide pacem habeamus, teste Glossa quæ ad idem: habeamus pacem ad Deum, quia ibidem ei reconciliati sumus, sic etiam accipitur pax ad Col. 3. cum dicit Apostolus: pax Christi exultet in cordibus vestris, teste Glossa quæ dicit ibidem: pax Christi, id est quam Christus habuit in se & haberi præcepit: vel quam inter Deum & hominem fecit: exultet in cordibus vestris, causa exultationis, quia virtum. utrumque erit, si habeatur charitas, quae veram habet pacem, quae puro corde custoditur, pax enim dici non potest, quae non habet charitatem, charitas vero semper secum habet pacem.
units.tr: Again, the aforesaid error is supported in the following way. For the claim that holy souls in heaven are by no means going to see God, there is the prayer of the Church for the dead: "who have gone before us and sleep in the sleep of peace," for whom the Church prays that God may grant them the light of life in the future, namely after the day of judgment. If it is objected that this prayer is for the dead whose souls are in purgatory, they try to refute this by saying that it is not true, because the prayer of the Church first states that they "sleep in the sleep of peace," and not of punishment and affliction. From this it is clear that the prayer is not made for souls existing in purgatory, but for those souls which are in peace and rest, and which await God's vision and their own beatification only after the last judgment, and not before. To show more clearly how perverse this argument is, we must first know that the word "peace" is used in many ways in Scripture. In one sense it signifies the concord of one person with another, as the Gloss shows on Romans 15: "Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing," where "that he may fill you with peace" means having been brought to concord with one another. And on Romans 14, "For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace," the Gloss says: "peace, that is, concord, which is the effect of righteousness." In another sense peace is taken for reconciliation with God, which comes through charity, as when the Apostle says in Romans 1, "Grace to you and peace from God the Father," which the Gloss also explains: "as the grace of God is that by which sins are given to us, so peace is that by which we are reconciled to God from being enemies." The Apostle takes peace in this way in the same epistle, chapter 5, saying: "Therefore, being justified by faith, let us have peace," and the Gloss on this says: "let us have peace with God, because we have been reconciled to him there." Peace is also taken in this sense in Colossians 3, where the Apostle says: "let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts." The Gloss there says: "the peace of Christ, that is, which Christ had in himself and commanded to be had, or which he made between God and man; let it rejoice in your hearts, as the cause of rejoicing, because both will be a virtue if charity is had, which has true peace and is kept in a pure heart. For peace cannot be called peace if it does not have charity; charity always has peace with it."

units.la: Tertio accipitur pax pro tranquillitate mentis, & iste modus accipiendi pacem praedictis modis minime contrariatur: quamvis inter ipsum & alios aliqua distinctio valeat assignari, & ideo tam isto modo quam secundo modo accipitur pax. Cum dicit Apostolus ad Romanos primo: gratia vobis & pax, teste Glossa, quae ibidem ait: & pax, id est reconciliatio ad Deum & tranquillitas mentis: sic etiam accipitur in aliis salutationibus epistolarum beati Pauli, sicut Glossa asserit manifeste. Sed sicut mentis tranquillitas est duplex, una scilicet perfecta quae omnem anxietatem & afflictionem excludit: alia imperfecta quae aliquam afflictionem secum compatitur: ita pax est duplex, una quae omnem afflictionem excludit, de qua dicitur in Psal. mansueti autem hereditabunt terram, & delectabuntur multitudine pacis. Alia est pax quae non omnem anxietatem & afflictionem excludit: quam optabat Apostolus discipulo suo Timotheo dicens: gratia (supple, sit tibi) & misericordia & pax: id est tranquillitas mentis & praelibatio vitae aeternae, sit tibi secundum vitam aeternam pax, quae tranquillitas mentis potest haberi, unde & tranquillitatem mentis sanctae Apostoli habuerunt in hac vita: & tamen omni afflictione minime caruerunt. Unde & Christus dixit Apostolis: pacem meam do vobis, quibus tamen dixit, in mundo pressuram habebitis, quibus ante dixit: Haec locutus sum vobis ut in me pacem habeatis, sic igitur praedictis modis accipitur pacis vocabulum in scripturis, licet etiam aliter accipi possit. Ex praedictis aliisque quam pluribus, quae causa abbreviationis omitto, liquide constat, quod non omnis pax omnem poenam, afflictionem & anxietatem excludit, sed aliquam secum compatitur.
units.tr: In the third sense, peace is taken for tranquillity of mind, and this way of taking peace is by no means contrary to the aforesaid ways, although some distinction can be drawn between this sense and the others; so peace is taken both in this way and in the second way. When the Apostle says in Romans 1, "Grace to you and peace," the Gloss there says: "and peace, that is, reconciliation with God and tranquillity of mind." It is also taken so in the other salutations of the epistles of the blessed Paul, as the Gloss clearly asserts. But just as tranquillity of mind is twofold, one perfect, which excludes all anxiety and affliction, the other imperfect, which is accompanied by some affliction, so peace is twofold. One excludes all affliction, of which it is said in Psalm 37: "the meek shall inherit the land, and shall delight themselves in the multitude of peace." The other is peace which does not exclude all anxiety and affliction. This the Apostle desired for his disciple Timothy, saying: "grace (understand, be with you) and mercy and peace," that is, tranquillity of mind and a foretaste of eternal life: may peace be yours according to eternal life. This tranquillity of mind can be had, and so the holy Apostles had tranquillity of mind in this life, and yet by no means lacked all affliction. Hence Christ also said to the Apostles, "My peace I give to you," and yet to the same he said, "in the world you will have tribulation," and before this he had said: "I have spoken these things to you, that in me you may have peace." Thus the word peace is used in Scripture in the aforesaid senses, although it may also be taken in other ways. From the aforesaid and from many others, which I omit for the sake of brevity, it is clearly established that not every peace excludes every punishment, affliction and anxiety, but some peace is accompanied by them.

units.la: Ad allegationem igitur per suprascripta contingit dupliciter respondere. Uno modo, quod in illa oratione, memento Domine famulorum famularumque tuarum, qui nos praecesserunt cum signo fidei & dormiunt in somno pacis, orat ecclesia pro illis, qui in purgatorio puniuntur, quia licet graviter affligantur, pacem tamen quae est reconciliatio ad Deum, noscuntur habere. Qui enim in charitate cum venialibus decesserunt, reconciliationem, quam ad Deum habuerunt in hac vita, minime perdiderunt. Et ideo in purgatorio existentes, pacem habent ad Deum, licet graviter affligantur. Quemadmodum Apostoli & Prophetae & Martyres & alii sancti, quando etiam affligebantur gravissime, pacem & reconciliationem habuerunt ad Deum. Et ideo concedendum est, quod animae in purgatorio existentes dormiunt in somno pacis, licet non dormiant in somno illius pacis, quae omnem poenam & afflictionem excludit. Quare pro illis ecclesia conuenienter orat, ut scilicet post unam pacem divina clementia aliam eis largiatur, unde & istam duplicem pacem, quarum una est post aliam, quam tamen non excludit oratio praedicta ecclesiae, aperte insinuat, cum dicit: cum signo fidei, & dormiunt in somno pacis, ipsis Domine & omnibus in Christo quiescentibus locum refrigerii, lucis & pacis, ut indulgeas deprecamur. His liquide constat, quod ecclesia pro illis, qui dormiunt in somno pacis, tantum exorat ut eis locum pacis indulgeat, dormiunt etiam in somno pacis: & tamen orat ecclesia, ut ad locum pacis perveniant: quia licet dormiant in somno pacis, quae est reconciliatio ad Deum, ad locum tamen pacis, quae omnem anxietatem & afflictionem excludit, nullatenus intraverunt. Et ita patet aperte, quod dicta allegatio ex ignorantia multiplicis nominis pacis procedit, si enim isti inter pacem & pacem sciuissent distinguere, siluissent. Sicut autem est distinguendum inter pacem & pa-cem: sic etiam distinguendum est inter quietem & quietem, de multiplici enim quiete legitur in scriptura divina, sed de duplici quiete solummodo ad praesens loqui sufficiat. Est enim quaedam quies ab actibus vitiorum, de qua dicitur Esaiae primo: quiescite agere perverse, & ista quies non omnem afflictionem & poenam excludit, cum ista quies in praesenti (saltem ad tempus) possit haberi. Alia est quies, quae erit in vita aeterna, quae omnem poenam & afflictionem excludit, animae igitur in purgatorio existentes in Christo quiescunt ab omnibus actibus vitiorum: quia nullum actum vitiosum committunt, sed quietem aeternam, quae omnem poenam & afflictionem excludit, minime sunt adeptae, orat igitur ecclesia, ut animae quiescentes in Christo ab omnibus actibus vitiorum ad locum refrigerii, qui caret omni afflictione, ducantur. Cum igitur dicunt isti, quod animae in purgatorio non dormiunt in somno pacis, si intelligant (ut series dictorum suorum insinuat) quod nullo modo dormiunt in somno pacis, errant aperte, quia hoc non est aliud, quam dicere, quod non essent reconciliatae ad Deum, sed animae illae dormiunt in somno pacis, quamvis in afflictione & poena: quia non omnis pax poenam & afflictionem excludit. Aliter ad allegationem praedictam potest dici: quod ecclesia in oratione praedicta non solum orat pro animabus in purgatorio existentibus, sed etiam orat pro animabus sanctis in coelo, ut scilicet animae sanctae quae dormiunt in somno pacis, resumptis corporibus ad locum refrigerii, lucis & pacis, quae ultimum gradum essentialem & accidentalem pacis aeternae, quem quandoque habituae sunt, includit, perveniant, quam pacem animae in coelo ante diem iudicii non habebunt. Quamvis enim nunc videant Deum, & sint beatae: beatitudo tamen earum, & per consequens pax earum aeterna erit post iudicium augmentata, quia tunc clarius videbunt Deum, & de resumptione corporum & completione civitatis aeternae & aliis pluribus tunc post gaudebunt.
units.tr: To the argument based on the aforesaid, one can therefore reply in two ways. In one way: in that prayer, "remember, Lord, your servants, men and women, who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace," the Church prays for those who are punished in purgatory, because although they are severely afflicted, they are known to have the peace which is reconciliation with God. For those who have died in charity with venial sins have by no means lost the reconciliation with God which they had in this life. And so those existing in purgatory have peace with God, although they are severely afflicted, just as the Apostles and Prophets and Martyrs and other saints had peace and reconciliation with God even when they were most grievously afflicted. Therefore it must be conceded that the souls existing in purgatory sleep in the sleep of peace, although they do not sleep in that sleep of peace which excludes all punishment and affliction. So the Church rightly prays for them, namely that after one peace the divine mercy may grant them another. This twofold peace, one after the other, the aforesaid prayer of the Church also clearly suggests, when it says: "with the sign of faith, and who sleep in the sleep of peace, we beseech you, Lord, to grant to them and to all who rest in Christ a place of refreshment, light and peace." From this it is clearly established that the Church prays for those who sleep in the sleep of peace only that they may be granted a place of peace; they do sleep in the sleep of peace, and yet the Church prays that they may come to the place of peace, because although they sleep in the sleep of peace, which is reconciliation with God, they have by no means entered the place of peace, which excludes all anxiety and affliction. And so it is plainly evident that the said argument arises from ignorance of the many meanings of the word "peace"; if these people had known how to distinguish between peace and peace, they would have kept silent. Just as one must distinguish between peace and peace, so one must also distinguish between rest and rest, for we read of many kinds of rest in divine Scripture, but for now it is enough to speak of two kinds of rest. There is a rest from the acts of vices, of which it is said in Isaiah 1: "cease to do evil." This rest does not exclude all affliction and punishment, since it can be had in the present life (at least for a time). The other is the rest which will be in eternal life, which excludes all punishment and affliction. The souls existing in purgatory therefore rest in Christ from all acts of vice, because they commit no sinful act, but they have not yet attained the eternal rest which excludes all punishment and affliction. The Church therefore prays that the souls resting in Christ from all acts of vice may be led to the place of refreshment, which is free from all affliction. Therefore, when these people say that the souls in purgatory do not sleep in the sleep of peace, if they mean (as the sequence of their words suggests) that in no way do they sleep in the sleep of peace, they are plainly wrong, for this is nothing other than saying that they would not be reconciled to God; but those souls do sleep in the sleep of peace, although they are in affliction and punishment, because not every peace excludes punishment and affliction. The aforesaid argument can also be answered in another way: the Church in the aforesaid prayer prays not only for souls existing in purgatory, but also for the holy souls in heaven, that the holy souls who sleep in the sleep of peace, having taken up their bodies again, may come to the place of refreshment, light and peace, which includes the last essential and accidental degree of eternal peace, which they will possess at some time; the souls in heaven will not have this peace before the day of judgment. For although they now see God and are blessed, their blessedness, and consequently their eternal peace, will be increased after the judgment, because then they will see God more clearly, and will rejoice then in the resurrection of the body, the completion of the eternal city and many other things.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Ponit tertiam rationem probantem idem quod prius.
units.tr: He gives a third argument proving the same thing as the previous one.

units.la: AMplius quidam prædictum errorem, quod animæ in cœlo non vident Deum, sic probare nituntur. Ambrosius enim in lib. de Pomo mortis dicit, quod anima purgata post claustrum corporum, visione spirituali, qua est per speciem, videt Deum, & certum est, quod nulla species est ita medium efficax, sicut humanitas Christi hominis &c. Sed ista allegatio prædictum errorem aperte convincit.
