Nam qui videt Deum per speciem, clare videt Deum, videre enim per speciem distinguitur contra videre per speculum & in ænigmate, & per consequens distinguitur contra noritiam illam, quæ est per fidem, quod Apostol. 2. ad Cor. 5. aperte insinuat dicens: Per fidem enim ambulamus & non per speciem, ubi dicit Glo. & est illuminatio per speciem: modo per speciem tantum illuminamur non per speculum: homini enim mortalem vitam adhuc agenti non potest contingere, ut dimisso atque discusso omni nubilo fantasiarum corporalium serenissima & incommutabili tanta veritatis luce potiatur: & mente penitus à consuetudine vitæ humanæ alienata, constanter & indeclinabiliter illi adhaereat. Ex his verbis aperte colligitur, quod visio Dei per speciem à cognitione distinguitur, & quod visio Dei per speciem cum fide non manet, quare si secundum beatum Ambrosium (ut iste allegat) animæ purgatæ post claustrum corporum visione, quæ est per speciem, vident Deum: sequitur quod non ambulant tunc per fidem, si autem per fidem tunc non ambulant, clare vident Deum.
units.tr: Moreover, some try to prove the aforementioned error, that souls in heaven do not see God, in this way. Ambrose, in the book On the Death of Man, says that the soul, purified after it leaves the prison of the body, sees God by a spiritual vision, which is through a species; and it is certain that no species is as effective a means as the humanity of Christ the man, etc. But this citation clearly refutes the aforementioned error. For whoever sees God through a species sees God clearly. To see through a species is distinguished from seeing through a mirror and in an enigma, and consequently it is distinguished from that knowledge which is through faith. The Apostle clearly hints at this in 2 Cor. 5, saying: For we walk by faith, not by sight, where the Gloss says: and there is illumination through a species; now we are illuminated only through a species and not through a mirror. For it cannot happen to a man still living a mortal life that, with every cloud of bodily fantasies dismissed and dispelled, he should attain such a most serene and unchangeable light of truth, and, with his mind wholly estranged from the habits of human life, should cling to it steadfastly and unswervingly. From these words it is clearly gathered that the vision of God through a species is distinguished from knowledge, and that the vision of God through a species does not remain together with faith. Therefore, if, according to Blessed Ambrose (as this man cites him), souls purified after they leave the prison of the body see God by the vision that is through a species, it follows that they do not then walk by faith; and if they do not then walk by faith, they clearly see God.

units.la: Cum autem iste dicit, quod nulla species est tam medium efficax, sicut est humanitas Christi hominis, multipliciter errat. Primo in hoc, quod adducit in probatione, quod visio Dei per speciem, de qua loquuntur sancti, fit per creaturam mediam repræsentantem divinam essentiam, quod falsum est: quia species illa per quam debent sancti sanctos in cœlo videre & Deum: non est aliqua creatura, sed est ipsa divina essentia, teste Glossa, quæ super illud Apostoli 2. ad Corinth. 5. per fidem enim ambulamus, non per speciem, dicit primo, non per præsentiam eorum ambulare, igitur per speciem est ambulare per præsentiam divinæ essentiæ, ut scilicet ipsa divina essentia per seipsam & non per creaturam aliam videatur.
units.tr: But when this man says that no species is as effective a means as the humanity of Christ the man, he errs in many ways. First, in this, that he adduces in proof that the vision of God through a species, of which the saints speak, takes place through a created intermediary representing the divine essence. This is false, because that species through which the saints are to see the saints and God in heaven is not any created thing, but is the divine essence itself, as the Gloss testifies. On that saying of the Apostle in 2 Cor. 5, for we walk by faith, not by sight, the Gloss first says: not to walk through their presence. Therefore to walk by species is to walk through the presence of the divine essence, namely, so that the divine essence itself is seen through itself and not through another creature.

units.la: Glo. 2. ad Corinth. 12. super illud Apostoli: Scio hominem in Christo ante annos 14. in corpore &c.
units.tr: Gloss on 2 Cor. 12, on the Apostle's words: I know a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, in the body, etc.

units.la: hoc etiam Glos. 2. ad Corinth. 12. super illud Apostoli: Scio hominem in Christo ante annos 14. in corpore &c. asserit manifeste, & loquens de visione intellectuali non per aliquam creaturam ait: ubi & Deus videtur non per corporalem visionem, ut in Synai Moyses: vel spiritualem, ut vidit Esaias & Iohannes in Apocalypsi, sed per speciem & non in ænigmate. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod visio, qua Deus videtur per speciem, non est per aliquam creaturam: sed per ipsam divinam essentiam.
units.tr: Also the Gloss on 2 Cor. 12, on the Apostle's words: I know a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, in the body, etc., clearly asserts, and speaking of intellectual vision not through any creature, says: where God is also seen not by bodily vision, as Moses on Sinai, or by spiritual vision, as Isaiah and John saw in the Apocalypse, but through a species and not in an enigma. From these words it is to be understood that the vision by which God is seen through a species is not through any creature, but through the divine essence itself.

units.la: Unde & Glo. ibidem subdit: Hoc modo visionem petiuit Moyses videre Deum in substantia, qua Deus est, quam in multis figuris viderat & facie ad faciem ei locutus fuerat, ut quia ibi illud est in illa specie, qua Deus est, certius videtur. Ecce quod aperte asseritur, quod quando videtur Deus in sua substantia, videtur in specie, qua Deus est: & per consequens visio Dei per speciem non est per mediam creaturam, sed est per ipsam divinam essentiam suam, unde & Glos. subdit ibidem, quod ubi idest in aliqua claritate speciei, nemo videns in isto sensibus Deum videt: hoc est tertium cœlum, scilicet visione qua Deus videtur facie ad faciem & iste est paradisus (si potest dici) paradisorum.
units.tr: Hence the same Gloss, in the same place, adds: In this way Moses sought to see God in the substance by which God is God, whom he had seen in many figures and to whom he had spoken face to face, so that, since there it is in that species by which God is God, it is seen more certainly. Behold, it is plainly asserted that when God is seen in his own substance, he is seen in the species by which he is God; and consequently the vision of God through a species is not through an intermediary creature, but through his own divine essence. Hence the Gloss also adds in the same place that where, that is, in some clarity of the species, no one who sees God in this life with the senses sees him; this is the third heaven, namely, the vision by which God is seen face to face, and this is paradise (if it can be called so) of paradises.

units.la: Ex quibus verbis patet, quod visio Dei non per mediam creaturam est visio, qua Deus in claritate speciei suæ videtur, & per consequens visio Dei per speciem est visio Dei non per mediam creaturam. Quod Glos. super illud 1. ad Corinth. 13. Videmus nunc per speculum & in ænigmate: tunc autem facie ad faciem, testatur aperte dicens: Tunc autem videbimus facie ad faciem, id est in similitudine a simili recto vultu se intuentium. Est enim quaedam visio huius temporis & altera futuri. Ista est per fidem: illa erit per speciem. Ex quibus verbis evidenter habetur, quod visio Dei per speciem distinguitur a visione per fidem, & visio Dei per speciem est illa, quam vocat ibi Apostolus facie ad faciem: non autem per mediam creaturam, igitur visio Dei per speciem de qua loquitur Apostolus, & alii sancti, non est per humanitatem Christi, nec per aliquam aliam creaturam.
units.tr: From these words it is evident that the vision of God not through an intermediary creature is the vision by which God is seen in the clarity of his own species, and consequently the vision of God through a species is the vision of God not through an intermediary creature. The Gloss on 1 Cor. 13, now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face, clearly bears witness to this, saying: But then we shall see face to face, that is, in a likeness, from a like-looking, straight face of those who gaze upon one another. For there is one vision of this time and another of the future. The former is through faith; the latter will be through a species. From these words it is evidently established that the vision of God through a species is distinguished from the vision through faith, and that the vision of God through a species is that which the Apostle there calls face to face, and not through an intermediary creature. Therefore the vision of God through a species, of which the Apostle and the other saints speak, is not through the humanity of Christ, nor through any other creature.

units.la: Errat igitur iste, cum dicit, visionem Dei per speciem esse per mediam creaturam, sic secundum alios errat & asserit, quod nulla species est ita medium efficax, sicut humanitas Christi hominis. Tum quia secundum eos natura aggregata medium est magis efficax, quam humanitas Christi hominis. Tum, quia secundum eosdem visio intuitiva Dei, qua anima Christi videntis Deum est medium ita efficax ad videndum Deum, sicut humanitas Christi. Qui enim videt humanitatem Christi, non necessario videt illam visionem, qua anima Christi videt divinam essentiam secundum ipsos. Ita visio Dei creata est medium efficax magis quam humanitas Christi.
units.tr: This man therefore errs when he says that the vision of God through a species is through an intermediary creature. Thus he errs also according to the others, who assert that no species is as effective a means as the humanity of Christ the man. This is so because, according to them, a created nature taken together is a more effective means than the humanity of Christ the man. And again, because according to the same men, the intuitive vision of God by which the soul of Christ sees God is as effective a means of seeing God as the humanity of Christ is. For whoever sees the humanity of Christ does not necessarily see that vision by which the soul of Christ sees the divine essence, according to them. Thus the created vision of God is a more effective means than the humanity of Christ.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: In quo ponitur quarta ratio ad idem probandum innitens auctoritati beati Bernardi.
units.tr: In which a fourth argument is set out to prove the same point, resting on the authority of blessed Bernard.

units.la: ITem pro conclusione prædicta taliter allegatur beatus Bernardus, fecit enim sermones specialiter, quod animæ sanctæ non vident Deum ante diem iudicii nec divinam essentiam immediate: sed bene vident Christi humanitatem, igitur non est dicendum, quod animæ sanctæ in cœlo nunc vident Deum. Sed istam allegationem repellere non est difficile, eo quod in manifesto falso fundatur, non enim sermonem fecit Bernardus, quod animæ sanctæ ante diem iudicii divinam essentiam non vident immediate, illam enim visionem nunquam negat a sanctis in cœlo: licet a sanctis ante diem iudicii negaret beatitudinem consummatam. Porro quia verba beati Bernardi, ex quibus huiusmodi ignari occasionem possunt sumere opinandi, quod beatus Bernard. senserit animas nunc in coelo non videre Deum vel diuinam essentiam immediate: in quodam opere sunt tractata & expositá diligenter: ipsa ordine tunc duxi praesentibus inserendum, sententiam tamen aliquorum verborum ipsius, quae praedictum errorem sonare videntur, censui recitandum, & quomodo debent intelligi breuissime declarabo, beatus igitur Bernar. in quodam sermone de omnibus sanctis loquens de animabus sanctis in coelo, docet & asserit, quod animae sanctae in coelo sunt in atriis, & non in domo Dei, habent gustum laetitiae, sed non habent satietatem gloriae: sunt securae, sed non sunt beatae, habent diuitias spiritus, sed non libertatem domus illius torrentis voluptatis. Ex quibus aliisque consimilibus apparet, quod beatus Bernardus in diversis operibus & sermonibus noscitur affirmare: posse inferri videtur, quod animae sanctae in coelo non vident Deum nunc, nec ante diem generalis iudicii sunt visurae.
units.tr: Likewise, for the aforesaid conclusion, Blessed Bernard is cited thus: he wrote a special sermon in which he says that the holy souls do not see God before the day of judgment, nor the divine essence immediately, but that they do see the humanity of Christ. Therefore, it is said, the holy souls in heaven now do not see God. But this allegation is not hard to refute, because it rests on a manifest falsehood. Bernard did not write in a sermon that the holy souls before the day of judgment do not immediately see the divine essence. He never denies that vision to the saints in heaven, though he does deny that the saints before the day of judgment have consummate blessedness. Since the words of Blessed Bernard, from which the ignorant may take occasion to suppose that he thought the souls now in heaven do not see God or the divine essence immediately, have been treated and explained carefully in a certain work, I have judged it right to insert that work here in its proper place. Still, I thought fit to recite the meaning of certain words of his that seem to sound the aforesaid error, and to declare very briefly how they ought to be understood. Blessed Bernard, speaking in a certain sermon on All Saints about the holy souls in heaven, teaches and asserts that the holy souls in heaven are in the courts, and not in the house of God; they have a taste of joy, but not the satiety of glory; they are secure, but not blessed; they have the riches of the spirit, but not the freedom of that house, the stream of pleasure. From these and similar passages it appears that Blessed Bernard is known to affirm in various works and sermons that the holy souls in heaven do not now see God, and it seems to follow that they are not going to see him before the day of the general judgment.

units.la: Sed si variae significationes vocabulorum, quibus vtitur Bernard. istis non essent ignotae, nullatenus aestimarent beatum Bernardum praedictum errorem sensisse. Ad cuius euidentiam est sciendum, quod sicut nomen beatitudinis in diuersis locis, multis modis accipitur: sic etiam plura vocabula & termini quibus beatus Bernardus vtitur, loquendo de ista materia, multipliciter accipi possunt: licet quaedam illorum non omnibus eisdem modis accipi debeant, quibus nomen beatitudinis accipi reperitur. Nomen autem beatitudinis aliquando operationem intellectualem vere optimam secundum speciem noscitur importare. Et illo modo quicunque videt Deum, est beatus, siue optima operatio intellectualis naturae secundum speciem sit visio Dei siue fruitio, quia nec visio de fruitione, nec fruitio talis a visione diuinae essentiae separatur. Aliter accipitur beatitudo pro statu huiusmodi operationis intellectualis naturae optimo secundum speciem & omne bonum tam essentiale quam accidentale (quod vnquam eiusdem naturae intellectualis conuenit) includente, sic dicitur beatitudo esse status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectus: cui scilicet nihil deest de omnibus bonis, quod vnquam habebit. Et istam beatitudinem vocat beatus Bernardus beatitudinem consummatam: a quibusdam integra beatitudo, tam primo modo quam secundo modo dicta est nuncupata. Dicitur etiam beatitudo status perfectorum & in gratia existentium, vt sunt iusti in hac vita, & animae purgandorum post mortem. Sic beatus Iacobus loquitur, cum dicit: beatus vir qui sustinet tentationem: quia cum probatus fuerit, accipiet coronam vitae, similiter etiam loquitur Psalmista, cum dicit: beati immaculati in via, beati qui scrutantur testimonia eius, sic dixit Christus Petro, beatus es Simon Bariona, quia sanguis & caro non reuelauit tibi. Et alibi: beati pauperes, beati qui lugent, beati mites &c. Quanquam autem propter prosperitatem mundanam dicuntur esse beati, teste Christo qui dicit: beatum dixerunt populum cui haec sunt. Sic etiam secundum vnum sensum potest intelligi illud Malachiae 4. nam beatos dicimus arrogantes. Prima beatitudo omnem molestiam, anxietatem, poenam, afflictionem excludit nunc de facto: licet desiderium maiorem perfectionem vel aliquod commodum acquirendi compatitur, & ideo interdum non vocatur beatitudo consummata: scilicet quae est status omnium bonorum essentialium & accidentalium aggregatione perfectus. Secunda beatitudo omnem molestiam, afflictionem, anxietatem, & etiam desiderium acquirendi maiorem perfectionem vel commodum futurum excludit, & ideo beatitudo consummata & integra potest merito appellari. Tertia beatitudo nec desiderium habendi maiorem gradum perfectionis vel commodum aliquod acquirendi vel anxietatem & poenam excludit. Quarta beatitudo falsa est, quamuis appareat beatitudo multis. Quemadmodum autem beatitudo diuersas significationes habet: sic etiam tales termini, domus Dei, & regnum coelorum, tenebrae autem Dei: & plures alii, quibus vtitur beatus Bernardus diuersimode accipi possunt. Quandoque enim important beatitudinem, quae est status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectus: quae omne desiderium commodum quodcunque vel maiorem gradum perfectionis habendi excludit. Alii termini tales important beatitudinem primo modo dictam: quae desiderium habendi maiorem gradum perfectionis beatitudinis essentialis & commodum futurum nequaquam excludit. Per istam distinctionem respondetur ad omnes auctoritates beati Bernardi quae sonare videntur, quod animae sanctae in coelo non vident Deum: quia nunquam eis negat visionem diuinae essentiae: licet neget eis esse in domo Dei: gloriae satietatem habere: esse beatas: habere torrentem voluptatis: & quaedam alia negat eis. Ex quibus tamen videtur inferri, quod animae sanctae in coelo non vident Deum, sed si verba bene intelligantur & sane, ex eis hoc inferri non potest, Bernard. enim huiusmodi terminos domus Dei, torrens voluptatis: & similes accipit primo modo: scilicet secundum quod beatitudinem consummatam, quae est status omnium bonorum accidentalium & essentialium importare noscuntur, non accipit huiusmodi terminos: sed secundum quod important praecise beatitudinem, quae est optima operatio intellectualis naturae: qualis est visio diuinae essentiae, vel fruitio quae sine visione minime repitur. Nihil aliud igitur beatus Bernar. intelligit, nisi quod animae sanctae in coelo ante diem iudicii, quamuis videant diuinam essentiam, non tamen carent omni desiderio habendi maiorem gradum visionis eiusdem: nec carent omni expectatione delectationis futurae non habitae, quia expectant resumptionem corporum & completionem ciuitatis aeternae: de quibus sunt delectationem modica habituras. Vnde quamuis habeant stolam animae: corporis tamen stolam non habent, beatus igitur Bernard. in verbis de hac materia a sanctis aliis in sententia discordare nolebat: sed eandem sententiam intendit, quam expressit beatus Gregor. cum dixit 4. libro Dialogorum loquens de animabus sanctis in coelo: Hec eis nimirum crescit in iudicio, quod nunc animarum stola, postmodum vero etiam corporum beatitudine perfruuntur, vnde ipsa in ipsa carne gaudebunt, in qua dolores pro Domino cruciatus, tulerunt. Pro hac quippe geminata stola eorum scriptum est: in terra sua duplicia possidebunt. Hoc etiam ante resurrectionis diem de sanctorum animabus scriptum est: sunt data illis singula stola alba, & dictum est eis, ut requiescerent tempus adhuc modicum, donec compleatur numerus servorum & fratrum eorum. Qui itaque multipliciter singuli binas in iudicio stolas habituri sunt: quia modo animarum tantummodo, tunc autem animarum & corporum simul gloria laetabuntur. Hanc inquam sententiam beatus Bernardus aliis verbis (licet quantum ad aliquid obscurioribus) volebat exprimere, cum dixit in quodam sermone de omnibus sanctis: Tres sunt sanctarum animarum status: Primus in corpore corruptibili. Secundus in requie. Tertius in beatitudine consummata. Hic est tertius status in requie, qui omnem poenam & afflictionem excludit, in quo stola animae est collocata, sed secundus status non est in beatitudine consummata: quia adhuc stola corporum non habetur. Vocat autem Bernar. beatitudinem consummatam, cui nihil deest unquam habendum. Et isto modo secundum beatum Gregor. & Bernar. secundus status animarum sanctarum non est in beatitudine consummata: quia adhuc deest stola corporis, quae postmodum est habenda. Tertius autem status est in beatitudine consummata: quia nihil unquam habendum tunc deerit, tunc enim habebuntur stolae binae.
units.tr: But if the various meanings of the words Bernard uses were not unknown to these people, they would by no means suppose that Blessed Bernard held the aforesaid error. To make this clear, it must be known that just as the name blessedness is taken in many ways in different places, so also the many words and terms that Blessed Bernard uses in speaking on this subject can be understood in several senses, although some of them ought not to be taken in all the same ways as the name blessedness is. The name blessedness sometimes signifies an intellectual operation that is truly the best of its kind. In this sense whoever sees God is blessed, whether the best intellectual operation of a rational nature is the vision of God or the enjoyment of it, since neither the vision is separated from the enjoyment nor the enjoyment from the vision of the divine essence. In another sense, blessedness is taken for the state of such an intellectual operation, the best of its kind, including every good, both essential and accidental, that can ever belong to that rational nature. In this sense blessedness is said to be the state made perfect by the aggregate of all goods, to which nothing is lacking of all the goods it will ever have. Blessed Bernard calls this blessedness consummate blessedness, and some have called it whole blessedness. Both the first and the second sense are so named. Blessedness is also said to be the state of those who are perfect and existing in grace, such as the righteous in this life and the souls of those being purged after death. So Blessed James speaks when he says: Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life. The Psalmist speaks similarly when he says: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, blessed are they that search his testimonies. So Christ said to Peter: Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee. And elsewhere: Blessed are the poor, blessed are they that mourn, blessed are the meek, etc. Although people are also called blessed on account of worldly prosperity, as Christ bears witness when he says: Blessed are the people that are in such a case. Thus also, in one sense, that saying of Malachi 4 can be understood: And we call the proud happy. The first blessedness excludes every trouble, anxiety, punishment and affliction in the present fact, although it admits a desire for greater perfection or for some advantage to be acquired; and therefore it is sometimes not called consummate blessedness, that is, the state made perfect by the aggregate of all essential and accidental goods. The second blessedness excludes every trouble, affliction, anxiety, and also the desire to acquire greater perfection or future advantage; and therefore it may rightly be called consummate and whole blessedness. The third blessedness excludes neither the desire to have a higher degree of perfection, nor the wish to acquire some advantage, nor anxiety and punishment. The fourth blessedness is false, although it appears to many to be blessedness. Just as blessedness has diverse meanings, so also such terms as the house of God, and the kingdom of heaven, but the darkness of God, and several others that Blessed Bernard uses, can be taken in different ways. For sometimes they signify the blessedness that is the state made perfect by the aggregate of all goods, which excludes every desire for any advantage or for a higher degree of perfection to be had. Other such terms signify the blessedness of the first sense, which by no means excludes the desire for a higher degree of perfection of essential blessedness and for future advantage. By this distinction a reply is given to all the passages of Blessed Bernard that seem to sound as if the holy souls in heaven do not see God: for he never denies them the vision of the divine essence, although he denies that they are in the house of God, that they have the satiety of glory, that they are blessed, that they have the stream of pleasure, and certain other things. From these things it seems to follow that the holy souls in heaven do not see God; but if the words are rightly and soundly understood, this cannot be inferred from them. For Bernard takes such terms as the house of God, the stream of pleasure, and similar ones, in the first sense; that is, as signifying the consummate blessedness which is known to be the state of all accidental and essential goods, he does not take such terms in that way, but as they signify precisely the blessedness which is the best intellectual operation of a rational nature, such as the vision of the divine essence, or the enjoyment which is found in no way without the vision. Therefore Blessed Bernard means nothing else than that the holy souls in heaven before the day of judgment, although they see the divine essence, nevertheless do not lack every desire to have a greater degree of that vision, nor do they lack every expectation of future delight not yet had, because they await the resumption of their bodies and the completion of the eternal city, in which they are going to have a modest delight. Hence, although they have the stole of the soul, they do not yet have the stole of the body. Blessed Bernard, therefore, in his words on this subject, did not wish to disagree in opinion with the other saints, but intended the same opinion that Blessed Gregory expressed when, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, speaking of the holy souls in heaven, he said: Surely this grows to them in the judgment: that now they enjoy the stole of souls, but afterwards also the blessedness of bodies; therefore they will rejoice in the very flesh in which they bore torments and sufferings for the Lord. For over this double stole it is written: In their land they shall possess the double. This was also written of the souls of the saints before the day of the resurrection: to each was given a white stole, and it was said to them that they should rest yet a little while, until the number of their fellow servants and brethren should be completed. Therefore each of them is going to have two stoles in the judgment, because now they rejoice in the glory of souls only, but then in the glory of souls and bodies together. This opinion, I say, Blessed Bernard wished to express in other words (though somewhat more obscurely in some respects) when he said in a certain sermon on All Saints: There are three states of holy souls: the first in a corruptible body; the second in rest; the third in consummate blessedness. This third state is in rest, which excludes all punishment and affliction, in which the stole of the soul is placed; but the second state is not in consummate blessedness, because the stole of the bodies is not yet had. Bernard calls consummate blessedness that to which nothing is lacking that is ever to be had. And in this way, according to Blessed Gregory and Bernard, the second state of the holy souls is not in consummate blessedness, because the stole of the body, which is to be had afterwards, is still lacking. The third state, however, is in consummate blessedness, because nothing will then be lacking that is ever to be had, since then the double stoles will be had.

units.la: Eandem etiam sententiam expressit beatus Bernar. cum post verba praedicta subiunxit: Primus denique in tabernaculis: secundus in atriis: tertius in domo Dei. Hic enim secundus status est in atriis: quia anima sancta ante diem iudicii ad ultimum gradum beatitudinis nequaquam pervenient, nec stolam corporis de communi lege sunt antea habituræ. Tertius autem status est in domo Dei, hoc est tunc ad tantam gloriam animæ & corporis, quod nunquam ulteriorem percipient. Et hanc sententiam ab aliis verbis voluit explicare, cum dicit: in tabernaculis gemitus poenitentiæ: in atriis gustus laetitiæ: in domo societas gloriæ. Hæ animæ sanctæ in secundo statu gustant laetitiam de visione essentiæ: sed adhuc desiderium habent amplius degustari, & ita satietatem, quæ omne desiderium firmiter excludit, minime sunt adeptæ in te, hoc est in Deo: sed quando conferet gloriam corporis & stolam animæ: præhabitam perficiet, & hæc est satietas gloriæ, illa scilicet satietas, quæ omne desiderium cuiuscunque futuræ delectationis excludit. Quam etiam satietatem vberem domus Dei torrentem voluptatis vocat. Necex verbis eiusdem contra catholicam veritatem iam diuulgatam praedictam iam à sanctis patribus explicatam, vlla calumnia colligatur: sed verba ipsius aliorum sanctorum patrum assertionibus & scripturæ divinæ sententiis concordant.
units.tr: The same opinion was also expressed by the blessed Bernard, when after the words quoted above he added: "The first, indeed, is in the tabernacles; the second in the courts; the third in the house of God. For this second state is in the courts, because holy souls before the day of judgment will by no means arrive at the last degree of blessedness, nor will they have the robe of the body before that, according to the common law. The third state, however, is in the house of God, that is, then the souls and bodies will come to such great glory that they will never receive anything further." And he wished to explain this opinion in other words, when he says: "In the tabernacles, groaning of repentance; in the courts, taste of joy; in the house, fellowship of glory." These holy souls in the second state taste the joy of the vision of the essence, but they still have a desire to be tasted more, and so they have not yet attained that satiety in you, that is, in God, which firmly shuts out every desire; that satiety will come when he bestows the glory of the body and perfects the robe previously held by the soul. This is the satiety of glory, that satiety which excludes every desire for any future delight. This same satiety he also calls the torrent of pleasure of the plenteous house of God. Nor can any calumny be drawn from the same words against the catholic truth already made known and previously explained by the holy Fathers; rather, the words of the same other holy Fathers agree with the assertions and the sentences of divine Scripture.

units.la: ADhuc pro eodem errore allegarur sic, ad Tim. 4. Scribit Apostolus: Repositia est mihi corona iustitiæ quam reddet mihi Dominus in illa die iustus iudex. Ex quibus nituntur isti concludere, quod Apostolo ante loante diem iudicii corona iustitiæ, quæ est visio essentiæ diuinæ, non reddetur: & ratione consimili nec aliis reddetur. Sed ista verba Apostoli recte intellecta, pro prædicto errore non faciunt. Nam dupliciter possunt intelligi, vno modo de die resolutionis beati Pauli: vt iste sit sensus: reposita est mihi corona iustitiæ, quantum ad stolam animæ, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illa die resolutionis meæ, de qua prius dixerat: ego enim iam delibor, & tempus resolutionis meæ instat. Et secundum istum intellectum pro eodem accipit tempus suæ resolutionis & illam diem in qua redditurus erat sibi Dominus coronam iustitiæ. Aliter possunt verba prædicta intelligi de vltima die iudicii; & tunc intendit Apostolus loqui de corona iustitiæ, quantum ad stolam corporis: quia stola corporis Apostolo & aliis de communi lege ante diem generalis iudicii non reddetur. Et hoc est, quod quidam dixere, quod Apostolus loquitur de supposito communi & integro & ex corpore & anima composito, cui corona iustitiæ ante diem iudicii generalis non reddetur. Quia licet anima sit prius coronam iustitiæ habitura: totus tamen homo integer, ex corpore & anima constitutus, non stolam animæ, nec stolam corporis ante diem generalis iudicii habebit. Vnde quamuis anima beati Pauli nunc videat Deum, & ita habeat stolam vnam: tamen beatus Paulus integer ex corpore & anima constitutus, nunc non videt Deum. Quia non est nunc ex corpore, & anima constitutus.
units.tr: Still in support of the same error, they argue from 2 Tim. 4: "The Apostle writes: There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me in that day." From these words they try to conclude that the crown of righteousness, which is the vision of the divine essence, is not given to the Apostle before the day of judgment, and by a similar argument not to anyone else. But these words of the Apostle, rightly understood, do not support the said error. They can be understood in two ways. In one way, they refer to the day of Paul's departure, so that the sense is: a crown of righteousness is laid up for me, as regards the stole of the soul, which the Lord will give me in that day of my departure, of which he had spoken earlier: For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. On this reading, the Apostle takes the time of his departure and the day on which the Lord would give him the crown of righteousness as the same. In the other way, the words may be understood of the last day of judgment, and then the Apostle intends to speak of the crown of righteousness as regards the stole of the body, because by the common law the stole of the body is not given to the Apostle or to others before the day of the general judgment. This is what some have said: that the Apostle speaks of a common and whole supposit, composed of body and soul, to which the crown of righteousness is not given before the day of the general judgment. For although the soul is to receive the crown of righteousness earlier, the whole man, made up of body and soul, will not have the stole of the soul or the stole of the body before the day of the general judgment. Hence, although the soul of the blessed Paul now sees God, and so has one stole, the blessed Paul himself, made up of body and soul, does not now see God, because he is not now made up of body and soul.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: In quo arguitur contra solutionem secundam in præcedenti capitulo ad authoritatem Apostoli datam, & hoc per authoritatem Iohannis in Apocalypsi.
units.tr: In which the second solution given in the preceding chapter, to the authority of the Apostle, is refuted, and this is done by the authority of John in the Apocalypse.

units.la: SEd contra illud vltimum de suppositis, & in fulcimentū erroris prædicti, taliter allegatur. Beatus Iohannes vidit animas interfectorū propter verbum Dei esse vsq; ad diem iudicii sub altari id est, sub altari humanitatis Christi. Et certum est, quod subiectione potestatis & dignitatis erunt sub humanitate Christi, etiam post diem iudicii, vel post iudicium. Quod ergo tunc ascendant super altare: ideo erit post diem iudicii per ascensum contemplationis, & ad videndum iudicium immediate.
units.tr: But against that last point about the supposed passages, and as a prop for the aforesaid error, the following is alleged. Blessed John saw that the souls of those slain for the word of God are under the altar until the day of judgment, that is, under the altar of the humanity of Christ. And it is certain that they will be under the humanity of Christ in subjection of power and dignity even after the day of judgment, or after the judgment. Therefore, when they then ascend above the altar, this will happen after the day of judgment, by an ascent of contemplation, and in order to see the judgment immediately.

units.la: Sed illa allegatio sic dicentes inuoluit dupliciter, primo: quia capitaneo suo obuiat, quod eos ipsi reddit obnoxios, secundo, quia agnitam veritatem impugnant: quod Deo reddit eos obnoxios.
units.tr: But that allegation, as those who say such things present it, is doubly involved. First, because it runs counter to their own captain, which makes them liable to him; second, because they attack a truth already acknowledged, which makes them liable to God.

units.la: Quid enim capitaneo suo reddat eos obnoxios, patet aperte, quia cuidam errori suo obuiant manifeste, ipsi enim tenet, dogmatizat, & prædicat: quod Christus post diem generalis iudicii non regnabit. Isti vero hoc docent aperte, quod animæ post diem iudicii generalis subiectione potestatis & dignitatis erunt sub humanitate Christi, & per consequens post iudicium generale erit potestatiue super animas regressurus. Secundo, ista allegatio dicta Deo & eius veritati, cui resistunt, reddit ipsos obnoxios, eo quod scripturam diuinam ad peruersum conantes trahere intellectum, dicunt animas sanctas in cœlo non videre Deum.
units.tr: That it makes them liable to their captain is plain enough, since they openly oppose one of his own errors. For he holds, teaches and preaches that Christ will not reign after the day of the general judgment. But these men openly teach that the souls, after the day of the general judgment, will be under the humanity of Christ in subjection of power and dignity, and consequently that after the general judgment Christ will return to rule over the souls with power. Second, this allegation makes them liable to God and to his truth, which they resist, inasmuch as, trying to bend the divine Scripture to a perverse sense, they say that the holy souls in heaven do not see God.

units.la: Vt autem appareat, quod prædictum errorem ex verbis scripturæ quam allegant elicere nequeant. Primo namque allegant non integre, sed truncate verborum seriem libri Apocalypsis, ex quibus præfatum errorem conantur concludere. Et quod errorem suum ex eis trahere nequeant est monstrandum. Secundo, quomodo verba illa intelligi debeant, est sciendum. Series igitur verborum, ex quibus isti probare niruntur, quod animæ sanctæ in cœlo nunc non vident Deum, est talis.
units.tr: In order to show that they cannot draw the aforesaid error from the words of Scripture which they allege, let us first note that they cite not the whole sequence of the words of the book of Revelation but a truncated one, from which they try to conclude the aforesaid error. And it must be shown that they cannot derive their error from them. Second, we must know how those words ought to be understood. The sequence of words from which these men labour to prove that the holy souls in heaven do not now see God is as follows.

units.la: Et cum aperuisset quintum sigillum: vidi sub altare animas interfectorum propter verbum Dei & propter testimonium quod habebant: & clamabant voce magna dicentes: vsque quo Domine sanctus & verus non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui habitant in terra? Et data sunt illis stolæ albæ: & dictum est illis vt requiescerent tempus adhuc modicum, donec compleantur eorum conserui & fratres eorum, qui interficiendi sunt sicut & illi. Ex quibus isti eliciunt, quod animæ in cœlo modo non vident Deum. Ex quibus beatus Gregor. & alii sancti patres volebant concludere oppositum, quod animæ sanctæ in cœlo beatitudinem animæ, quæ est visio Dei vel non sine visione Dei & non corporis sunt adeptæ.
units.tr: And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held. And they cried with a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth? And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled. From these words they infer that souls in heaven do not now see God. From the same words blessed Gregory and other holy Fathers wished to conclude the opposite: that the souls of the saints in heaven have obtained the blessedness of the soul, which is the vision of God, or at least not without the vision of God, and not that of the body.

units.la: Ex verbis etiam prædictis licet notum & apertum sit, quod animæ sanctæ sub altari Dei quiescunt, tamen quod erunt post iudicium iuxta altare Dei mentio non habetur, nec valet: modo sunt sub altari Dei: igitur post iudicium erunt iuxta altare Dei, quemadmodum non sequitur: nunc requiescunt (sicut ex verbis eisdem colligitur) igitur post iudicium minime requiescent. Quod enim nunc requiescant, patet, cum in verbis præscriptis sic legatur: dictum est illis vt requiescerent adhuc modicum tempus donec compleantur conserui eorum &c. Ex quibus tamen concludi non potest, quod completo numero conseruorum nullatenus requiescent, quemadmodum ex hoc quod dicitur Matth. 1. Et non cognoscebat eam donec peperit filium suum primogenitum: concludi non potest, quod primogenito nato cognoscebat eam, & ideo consimiliter ex hoc, quod beatus Iohannes vidit animas interfectorum nunc esse sub altari, concludi non potest, quod post iudicium non erunt sub altari Dei. Licet (sicut postea ostendetur) concedi possit sub sano intellectu, quod animæ sanctæ post iudicium generale erunt sub altari Dei. Ex his patenter habetur, quod per verba Apocalypsis supra scripta concludi non potest, quod animæ sanctæ in cœlo nunc non videant Deum, ex hoc q nunc sunt sub altari Dei, & quod clamant, & q respondetur eis q requiescant donec impleatur numerus conseruorum eorū & fratrum ipsorū. Ex quibus no sequitur, q nunc non vident Deū. Vt aut habeatur verus intellectus scriptorum verborum: est sciendum, quod illud, quod est sub aliquo, quodammodo videtur abscondito: sed quod est supra aliquid, altum & manifestum apparet. Quorum vtrumque ipse Saluator insinuat dicens, Matt. 5. Non potest abscondi ciuitas supra montem posita: neque accendunt lucernam: & ponunt eam sub modio: sed super candelabrum, vt luceat omnibus qui in domo sunt. Quia igitur animae nunc in coelo sunt multis electis, & etiam malis abscondite: ideo nunc dicuntur esse sub altari Dei. Quia licet Deum videant, sicut vt a ciuibus ciuitatis supernae minime abscondantur, nobis tamen, & illis qui sunt in purgatorio, & in inferno, nequaquam apparent. In die autem iudicii generalis electis omnibus apparebunt, reprobi etiam, tam homines quam daemones, aperte videbunt eas ascendere in coelum, & ita quodammodo erunt supra altare Dei, hoc est, non erunt illo modo abscondite, quomodo nunc constat eas abscondi, & iste est verus intellectus beati Bernardi, cum loquitur de ista materia. Ipse enim in quodam sermone de omnibus sanctis sic ait: In hunc igitur locum Saluator descendens contriuit portas aereas, & vectes ferreos confregit, eductosque vinctos de domo carceris sedentes in vmbra mortis (hoc est secundum aliquos, quiescentes, sed in tenebris & in vmbra mortis) iam tunc quidem sub altari Dei collocauit: assumens eos in tabernaculo suo in die malorum, & protegens eos in abscondito tabernaculi sui, donec veniat tempus quo procedant, vel completo numero fratrum, & percipiant regnum, quod eis paratum est ab origine mundi. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod secundum Bernardum, ideo animae sanctae sub altari Dei sunt: quia in tabernaculo Dei sunt abscondite, & non quidem Deo & ciuibus coelestis Hierusalem: sed nobis, & aliis qui sunt in purgatorio & in inferno. Si enim constet nobis, animas Apostolorum, & quorundam aliorum sanctorum esse in coelo: hoc tamen nunc constat in sola fide. In die autem iudicii omnes electi clare videbunt animas, quas nunc credunt esse in coelo. Et ita quodam modo sunt sub altari, sub intellectu isto, quod multis electis sunt nunc abscondite. Et ideo nunc possunt secundum alium intellectum dici sub altari Dei, eo quod tunc erunt, sicut modo sunt, sub domo & protectione. Quare si potest catholice dici, quod animae sanctae & sancti integri ex corporibus & animabus constituti, qui erunt sub altari, post iudicium generale videbunt clare Deum: sequitur euidenter ex hoc, quod animae sanctae in coelo nunc non vident Deum, cum aperte dicat, quod completo numero fratrum percipient regnum, quod eis paratum est ab origine mundi. Sed forte diceret: si nunc perciperent regnum eis paratum ab origine: sequitur quod tunc non percipient, & per oppositum: si nunc non possident, nunc non vident Deum. Ad hoc potest multipliciter responderi, vno modo, quod secundum beatum Bernardum sancti & integri ex anima & corpore constituti, imo percipient regnum eis paratum ab origine mundi, & ita beatus Bernardus non intendit negare animas sanctas percepisse regnum eis paratum ab origine mundi, & si hoc negaret, determinationi summi pontificis & doctrinae vniuersalis ecclesiae contradicere videretur, nam, vt legitur extra de haereticis c. maiores. Innocentius tertius ait: & si originali culpa remittebatur per circumcisionis mysterium, & damnationis periculum vitabatur: non tamen peruenisset ad regnum coelorum, quod vsque ad mortem Christi fuit omnibus obseratum, sed per sacramentum baptismi Christi sanguine inebriati culpa remittitur, vitatur periculum, & ad regnum coelorum etiam perducitur, cuius iamam Christi sanguis fidelibus suis misericorditer reseruauit. His verbis patenter habetur seu asseritur, quod animae sanctae iam peruenerunt ad regnum coelorum: & per consequens perceperunt regnum eis paratum ab origine mundi. Cui alludit doctrina vniuersalis ecclesiae, cum in laudem martyrum fideles cantare non cessent: Istorum autem est regnum coelorum, qui contempserunt vitam mundi, & peruenerunt ad praemia regni. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod sicut regnum coelorum, secundum beatum Gregor. aliquando praetiens ecclesia dicitur: ita & regnum coelorum locus coelestis & naturalis aliquando vocatur, & ideo quamuis animae sanctae non vident Deum: potest tamen concedi, quod sunt in regno coelorum. Sed istae assertiones sanctorum patrum peruerterent sententiam, quando enim sancti loquuntur de regno coelorum percipiendo post vitam praesentem accipiunt regnum coelorum, vt visionem Dei claram includit, & sic accipit Bernardus, cum dicit in auctoritate superius allegata, quod percipient regnum quod est eis paratum, sed non tunc primo percipient secundum animam: licet tunc primo percipiant regnum secundum corpus, & ideo totus homo integer non ante percipiet de communi lege regnum coelorum. Aliter potest dici, quod licet animae sanctae iam perceperint regnum, quod in visione Dei consistit: animae tamen sanctae non perceperunt illud regnum, quod omnem perfectionis gradum & delectationem habendam includit, per quod regnum Bernardus intelligit beatitudinem consummatam, quae scilicet omnem delectationem & perfectionem vnquam habendam includit, & ita Bernardus aliter accipit quodcunq; regnum coelorum, vt pro regno futuro accipiatur, quam communiter alii doctores & patres sancti: licet etiam in multis locis sic aliquando regnum coelorum vtatur, regnum itaque, quod est beatitudo cui nihil deest habendum, animae ante diem iudicii non habebunt: habent tamen visionem Dei nunc, quamuis quasi in abscondito, quod Glossa super illud Psalmi: abscondens eos in abscondito faciei tuae: insinuare videtur, cum dicitur: dum mali turbabuntur, ipsi (sancti scilicet) erunt in abscondito faciei tuae videntes te Domine, & ita nunc animae sanctae sunt occultae: ideo sub altari Dei, sed in die iudicii erunt manifestae. Quemadmodum Christus nunc est occultus: sed tunc erit manifestus, teste Glossa, quae super illud Psalmi: sede a dextris meis, ait: sede secundum quod homo in pectoribus misericordia, & iterum, sede occultus, donec regnes manifestus. Cum igitur (dicunt isti) certum est, quod subiectione potestatis & dignitatis eius sunt animae sanctae sub humanitate Christi, etiam post iudicium: concedit, quod in hoc non errant, licet in hoc suo Magistro (quamuis forsitan ignoranter) inueniantur aduersi. Si enim aduertissent, quod Magister eorum tenet, quod Christus post iudicium non regnabit, bit, vt creditur : tacuissent, quia ipsi cupiunt esse tales, qualis doctor eorum. Sed tamen quia dicunt, quod post diem iudicii ascendent super altare, vt videant Deum immediate, & non ante, aperte errant, sicut alibi est ostensum. Et auctoritas ex Apocalypsi sumpta, eis minime suffragatur, sicut ex praecedentibus liquide patet.
units.tr: From the words cited above, it is clear and evident that the holy souls rest under the altar of God. But the claim that they will be near the altar of God after the judgment has no basis in the text, and the inference does not follow: they are now under the altar of God, therefore after the judgment they will be near the altar of God; just as it does not follow that, since they now rest (as is gathered from the same words), they will by no means rest after the judgment. That they now rest is plain, since the passage reads: it was said to them that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow servants and their brethren should be fulfilled, &c. Yet from these words it cannot be concluded that, once the number of their fellow servants is complete, they will in no way rest. Compare Matt. 1: And he knew her not until she had brought forth her firstborn son. From this it cannot be concluded that he knew her after the firstborn was born. Likewise, from the fact that the blessed John saw the souls of the slain now under the altar, it cannot be concluded that after the judgment they will not be under the altar of God. (As will be shown later, it may be granted in a sound sense that the holy souls, after the general judgment, will be under the altar of God.) It is therefore plain that from the words of the Apocalypse quoted above it cannot be concluded that the holy souls in heaven do not now see God, merely because they are now under the altar of God, and cry out, and are answered that they should rest until the number of their fellow servants and brethren is complete. It does not follow from these things that they do not now see God. Now, to obtain the true sense of the words of Scripture, it must be known that what is under something seems in some way hidden, but what is above something appears high and manifest. The Saviour himself indicates both of these when he says, Matt. 5. A city set on a hill cannot be hid. Neither do men light a candle and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that it may give light to all that are in the house. Since, therefore, the souls are now in heaven and hidden from many of the elect and even from the wicked, they are now said to be under the altar of God. For although they see God, and are not hidden from the citizens of the heavenly city, yet they do not at all appear to us, nor to those who are in purgatory and in hell. But on the day of the general judgment they will appear to all the elect, and the reprobate also, both men and devils, will plainly see them ascending into heaven; and so in some way they will be above the altar of God, that is, they will not be hidden in the way they are now plainly hidden. This is the true sense of the blessed Bernard when he treats of this matter. For in a certain sermon on All Saints he says: Descending, therefore, into this place, the Saviour broke the brazen gates and shattered the iron bars, and led out the prisoners from the house of confinement, those sitting in the shadow of death (that is, according to some, resting, but in darkness and in the shadow of death); already then he placed them under the altar of God, taking them into his tabernacle in the day of evils, and protecting them in the hidden place of his tabernacle, until the time comes when they shall go forth, or when the number of their brethren is complete, and they receive the kingdom which has been prepared for them from the foundation of the world. From these words it is gathered that, according to Bernard, the holy souls are under the altar of God because they are hidden in the tabernacle of God, and this not from God or from the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, but from us and from others who are in purgatory and in hell. For if it is certain to us that the souls of the Apostles and of certain other saints are in heaven, yet this is now known only by faith. But on the day of judgment all the elect will clearly see the souls which they now believe to be in heaven. And so in a certain way they are under the altar, in the sense that they are now hidden from many of the elect. And therefore they can now be said, in another sense, to be under the altar of God, because then they will be, as they are now, under the house and protection. Wherefore, if it can be rightly said by the Catholic faith that the holy souls and the saints made whole, constituted of bodies and souls, who will be under the altar, will after the general judgment see God clearly, it plainly follows from this that the holy souls in heaven do not now see God, since he expressly says that when the number of the brethren is complete they will receive the kingdom which has been prepared for them from the foundation of the world. But perhaps someone would say: if they were now to receive the kingdom prepared for them from the beginning, it would follow that then they would not receive it, and conversely: if they do not now possess it, they do not now see God. To this it can be answered in several ways. In one way: according to the blessed Bernard, the saints made whole, constituted of soul and body, will indeed receive the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world; and so the blessed Bernard did not intend to deny that the holy souls have received the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world. If he denied this, he would seem to contradict the decision of the supreme pontiff and the teaching of the universal Church. For, as is read in the chapter Maiores, Extra, On Heretics, Innocent III says: And if by the mystery of circumcision original guilt was remitted and the danger of damnation was avoided, yet one would not have come to the kingdom of heaven, which until the death of Christ was closed to all; but through the sacrament of baptism, those made drunk with the blood of Christ have their guilt remitted, the danger is avoided, and they are even led to the kingdom of heaven, the gate of which the blood of Christ has now mercifully kept open for his faithful. By these words it is plainly held, or asserted, that the holy souls have now come to the kingdom of heaven, and consequently have received the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world. The teaching of the universal Church agrees with this, since the faithful never cease, in praise of the martyrs, to sing: Theirs is the kingdom of heaven, who have despised the life of the world and have come to the rewards of the kingdom. But perhaps someone would say that, just as the blessed Gregory sometimes says that the Church is called the kingdom of heaven in the present time, so the heavenly and natural place is sometimes called the kingdom of heaven; and therefore, although the holy souls do not see God, it may nevertheless be granted that they are in the kingdom of heaven. But these assertions of the holy Fathers would overturn the sentence; for when the saints speak of receiving the kingdom of heaven after the present life, they take the kingdom of heaven as including the clear vision of God, and so Bernard takes it when, in the authority cited above, he says that they will receive the kingdom which is prepared for them; but they do not receive it first in respect of the soul, although they will first receive it in respect of the body; and therefore the whole man, entire, will not receive the kingdom of heaven before, by the common law. Otherwise it may be said that, although the holy souls have already received the kingdom, which consists in the vision of God, yet they have not received that kingdom which includes every degree of perfection and delight to be had. By that kingdom Bernard understands consummated blessedness, which includes all delight and perfection ever to be had. And so Bernard takes the kingdom of heaven in a different sense, as meaning the future kingdom, from what other teachers and holy Fathers commonly do, although in many places he too sometimes uses the term kingdom of heaven in this way. Therefore the souls will not have that kingdom, which is blessedness lacking nothing, before the day of judgment; yet they now have the vision of God, although as it were in hiding, which the Gloss on the verse of the Psalm, hiding them in the secret place of your face, seems to suggest when it says: while the wicked are troubled, they (namely the saints) will be in the hidden place of your face, seeing you, Lord; and so now the holy souls are hidden, therefore under the altar of God, but on the day of judgment they will be made manifest. Just as Christ is now hidden but will then be manifest, as the Gloss attests, which on the verse of the Psalm, sit at my right hand, says: sit according to what he is as man, in the bosom of mercy; and again, sit hidden, until you reign manifest. Since, therefore (they say), it is certain that by the subjection of his power and dignity the holy souls are under the humanity of Christ, even after the judgment, I grant that in this they do not err, although in this they are found opposed to their own Master (perhaps through ignorance). For if they had noticed what their Master holds, that Christ will not reign after the judgment, as is believed, they would have kept silent, since they themselves wish to be such as their teacher is. But yet, because they say that after the day of judgment they will ascend above the altar to see God immediately, and not before, they plainly err, as has been shown elsewhere. And the authority taken from the Apocalypse gives them no support at all, as is clear from what has gone before.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Friuolam euasionem Iohannitarum elidit, & confutat ratione unica.
units.tr: He refutes the flimsy escape of the Johannites by a single argument.

units.la: NON solum autem pro errore praedicto friuolas allegationes adducunt: sed etiam ad euacuandas auctoritates, errores eorum apertissime convincentes, responsionem vanissimam dare conantur dicentes: quod auctoritates & scripturae sanctorum (si quae inveniuntur dicentes, quod animae nunc videant Deum facialiter) accipiendae sunt & intelligendae secundum locutionem devoti affectus, secundum quod sancti meditatione devota frequenter, ubi erat affectus eorum, & ubi secundum affectum loquebantur, accipiunt praeteritum pro praesenti, & praesens pro futuro. Sed ista responsio est friuola, quae improbatione non indiget, & eam unica ratione breviter improbabo. Quod enim sancti loquendo de visione animarum sanctarum non vtantur praeterito pro praesenti, & praesenti pro futuro, sic patenter ostenditur. Vbicunque sancti loquuntur de visione animarum sanctarum, non vtuntur praeterito pro praesenti ad monstrandum tantum suum affectum ad sanctos, sed ad monstrandum veritatem de visione earum pro praesenti. Sancti autem frequenter cum loquuntur de visione animarum sanctarum, solum loquuntur ad monstrandum veritatem de visione earum pro praesenti, igitur non vtuntur praesenti pro futuro, sed pro praesenti. Maior est manifesta: quia si vterentur praesenti pro futuro, in nullo monstrarent veritatem pro praesenti, sed pro futuro magis. Minor etiam legenti auctoritates sanctorum apparet indubia, nam beatus Gregorius in 4. libro Dialogorum, cum interrogaretur a Petro: quid est quod si anima sancta modo sunt in coelo, quod in die iudicii pro sua iustitia retributione recipient? Respondet in haec verba: hoc eis nimirum crescit in iudicio, quod nunc animarum stola: postmodum vero etiam corporum beatitudine perfruuntur, & tamen post asserit, quod animabus nunc datae sunt singulae stolae albae, & infra affirmatur, quod non scient omnia, tunc non loquebantur solummodo secundum affectum, sed veritatem de beatitudine & visione animarum sanctorum pro praesenti voluit declarare, igitur non vtebantur praesenti pro futuro, sed pro praesenti. Innocentius etiam Tertius sicut legitur extra, de celebratione missarum, cum Martha, dicit, quod sancti orationibus nostris non indigent pro eo, quod cum sint perfecte beati, omnia eis ad vota succedunt, non tamen voluit suum ad sanctos affectum monstrare: sed etiam de beatitudine earum pro praesenti declarare vult veritatem, igitur minime vsus est praesenti pro futuro, vel praeterito pro praesenti.
units.tr: Nor do they bring forward flimsy arguments only for the aforesaid error; they also try, in order to nullify the authorities that convict their error most plainly, to give a most empty answer, saying that the authorities and the writings of the saints (if any are found saying that souls now see God face to face) are to be taken and understood according to the manner of speaking of a devout affection: namely, that the saints, in their devout meditation, where their affection was and where they spoke according to their affection, frequently take the past for the present and the present for the future. But this answer is flimsy, and needs no refutation; I shall briefly refute it with a single argument. For that the saints, when speaking of the vision of holy souls, do not use the past for the present and the present for the future, is plainly shown thus. Wherever the saints speak of the vision of holy souls, they do not use the past for the present merely to show their affection towards the saints, but to show the truth about their vision as present. Now the saints, when they speak of the vision of holy souls, frequently speak only to show the truth of their vision as present; therefore they do not use the present for the future, but for the present. The major premise is manifest: for if they used the present for the future, they would show the truth as present in no way, but rather as future. The minor premise also appears beyond doubt to any reader of the authorities of the saints. For blessed Gregory in the fourth book of the Dialogues, when Peter asked him: what is it that holy souls now in heaven will receive on the day of judgment as the retribution of their righteousness? answers in these words: this, surely, is increased for them at the judgment, that they now enjoy the stole of souls, but afterwards also the blessedness of bodies; and yet afterwards he asserts that single white stoles have now been given to the souls, and below it is affirmed that they will not know all things. Then they were not speaking merely according to affection, but Gregory wished to declare the truth about the blessedness and vision of the holy souls as present; therefore they were not using the present for the future, but for the present. Innocent the Third also, as is read in the Extra, On the celebration of masses, with Martha, says that the saints do not need our prayers, because, since they are perfectly blessed, all things turn out according to their wishes; yet he did not wish merely to show his affection towards the saints, but also wishes to declare the truth about their blessedness as present; therefore he by no means used the present for the future, or the past for the present.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Confutat quoddam dictum Iohannitarum, dicentium scilicet, quod simplices non habeant de quaestione fidei se intromittere.
units.tr: He refutes a certain saying of the Johannites, namely that the simple should not meddle in questions of faith.

units.la: CAETERUM ad simplices seducendos dicunt praefati sequaces errorum, quod simplices inferiores de quaestione praedicta non debent se intromittere. Et si aliquis dicat, Christianus sum: volo scire fidem & veritatem, ideo moveor ad quaerendum de hoc, quia simplex sum. Isti respondent dicentes: Dico tibi, credere explicite, quod ecclesia explicavit: & alia implicite, donec ecclesia aliter declaret. Sed in ista assertione duos insinuant errores, quorum primus est: quod simplices non debent se intromittere de quaestione praedicta, & iste error in quodam alio Tractatu reprobatus existit. Secundus error est, quod simplices non debent explicite credere, nisi quod ecclesia explicavit, vocando ecclesiam, papam & Cardinales, quia de illa ecclesia isti loquuntur, sicut de pluribus assertionibus eorum patenter habetur. Sed quod hoc sit erroneum, probatur aperte, nam quilibet Christianus credere debet omne illud, de quo in speciali est certus, quod ex contentis in scriptura divina sequitur evidenter, sed alii, quam papa & Cardinales possunt esse certi de multis quae sequuntur evidenter ex contentis in scriptura divina: quae tamen papa & Cardinales nunquam declarauerunt, imo forte quae papa & Cardinales nunquam in speciali cognouerunt: sed tantum implicite crediderunt, igitur possunt Christiani & quandoque tenentur explicite credere aliqua, quae papa & Cardinales nunquam explicite declarauerunt. Maior est manifesta. Quia qui certus est de antecedente, & consequentia: certus est de consequente. Et ita qui credit explicite antecedens, & certus est de consequentia, quia consequens ex antecedente infertur, de consequente dubius esse non potest. Cui illud Philosophi alludit, simul inducit cognovit, quamvis enim aliquis possit esse de maiore certus, & tamen dubius vel contrariae opinionis de conclusione: tamen si certus est de maiore & de minore, quas applicat ad conclusionem: de conclusione dubius esse non potest. Qui igitur explicite credit aliqua, quae legit in scriptura divina: etiam de quocunque est certus, quod evidenter sequitur ex illis: de illa conclusione esse dubius non potest. Et per consequens, vel scit eam, vel explicite credit. Et ideo si est conclusio, quae per rationem demonstrari potest: sequitur quod explicite credit eam, & non potest non credere eam explicite, quamdiu adverterit, quod ex contentis in scriptura divina sequitur evidenter. Minor quamuis videatur probatione minime indigere, tamen auctoritatibus venerabilium patrum probatur aperte. Ait enim Augustinus, ut legitur 24. q. 3. cap. vltimo: Ideo diuina prouidentia multos diuersis erroribus haereticos esse permittit, ut cum interrogant nos ea quae nesciunt, possunt catholici per scripturas diuinas, quae nesciuerint prius, a discere, per consequens ipse est certus p solas scripturas diuinas de his, quae papa & Cardinales nullatenus declarabant. Ad hoc etiam est auctoritas accepta ab August. super illud Apostoli, 1. Cor. 11. oportet haereses esse, ut qui probati sunt in nobis manifesti fiant, quae potest adduci, ait enim Glossa: Omnes inimici ecclesiae vel errore caecati vel malitia depravati prosunt, quia si accipiunt potentiam corporaliter affligendi, exercent eius patientiam, si enim male sentiendo aduersantur, exercent eius sapientiam. Ab aduersario enim mota continue discendi existit occasio, multa quippe ad fidem pertinentia dum haereticorum inquietatione exagitantur, ut aduersus eas defendi possint, & considerantur diligentius, & interrogantur celerius, & probantur instantius. Et infra: prosunt igitur haeretici, non verum docendo, quod nesciunt, sed ad verum quaerendum & adipiscendum catholicos excitando. Ex quibus verbis patenter colligitur, quod catholici, & haeretici excitati, multas possunt ignotas veritates per scripturas sacras addiscere: licet eas papa & Cardinales hactenus non attentauerunt declarare. Unde & dicunt nonnulli, quod occasione haeresum, quas Magister istorum & rector solenniter diffinivit, & publice praedicauit, in nonnullis pullulant innumerae veritates, quarum sunt multae redargutae iam in scripturis, quae toti communitati Christianorum tam laicorum, quam clericorum fidelium inaestimabilem fidelitatem seu utilitatem inferent (ut putant firmissime) in futurum, quas tamen veritates etiam praecedentes summi pontifices & Cardinales catholici nullatenus declarant: quia occasionem declarandi ante tempora illius rectoris minime habuerunt. Sed forte diceret aliquis, quod simplices non debent credere, nisi ea quae papa & Cardinales tradunt credere explicite: nec debent inuestigare secreta scripturae, sed communibus debent esse contenti: imo etiam de intellectu proprio non debent praesumere ut aliquid credant explicite, nisi quod eis papa & Cardinales tradiderint. Sed qui ista assereret, nouorum esset inuentor errorum. Nam licet simplices non teneantur regulariter explicite credere, nisi illa quae iam nunc credenda sunt a clero explicite declarata, tamen simplices legendo scripturas diuinas rationis acumine (quod & simplices non omnino carent) aliquid (quod papa & Cardinales minime declarauerunt) aduertunt euidenter sequi ex scripturis diuinis: hoc possunt & debent in hoc casu explicite credere: nec tenentur papam & Cardinales consulere, quia papae & Cardinalibus scripturam sacram praeferre tenentur. Sed diceret forte aliquis, quod simplices saluantur in fide maiorum, igitur non debent habere fidem explicitam de aliquo, nisi de quo papa & Cardinales habent fidem explicitam, ideo videtur inconueniens dicere, quod aliquid sit spectans ad fidem catholicam, de quo papa & Cardinales non habent fidem explicitam. Sed respondetur, quod simplices saluantur in fide propria: quia si ipsi non habent fidem in se, non saluantur. Est tamen quidam modus saluandi, quia saluantur in fide maiorum, quia quantum ad multa sufficit eis credere implicite, quod maiores credunt explicite, quod verum est, si maiores explicite habent fidem eandem, quam minores: & minores non aduertunt aliquid sequi ex scriptura diuina, nisi quod maiores sequi percipiunt. Cum vero dicitur, papa & Cardinales habent fidem explicitam de omnibus quae spectant ad fidem catholicam. Dico quod hoc non est semper verum: cum saepe non habeant fidem explicitam de omnibus illis, qui necesse fuerit eos credere explicite. Cum vero praesumitur in ratione, quod simplices non debent inuestigare secreta scripturae diuinae, istud non est verum: quia tunc nullus simplex deberet praesumere vacare studio scripturae sacrae, & ita nullus deberet in scriptura sacra studere, antequam esset papa vel Cardinalis, quia omnis studens in scriptura sacra oportet quod aliquando incipiat, quando autem quicunque incipit studere in scriptura sacra, quoad notitiam scripturarum sacrarum est inter simplices computandus, igitur nullus antequam esset papa vel Cardinalis deberet incipere studere in sacris scripturis. Cum autem assumitur, quod simplices non debent de intellectu proprio praesumere, ut aliquid credant explicite, nisi quod papa & Cardinales crediderunt. Dicendum est, quod simplices non debent praesumere de proprio intellectu, sed scripturae sacrae firmiter adhaerere: ut quod euidenter conspexerint ex sacris scripturis inferri, hoc explicite credant, siue fuerit siue non fuerit a papa & Cardinalibus declaratum. Et ratio huius est, quia papa & Cardinales non sunt regula fidei nostrae: quia licet papa catholicus & Cardinales catholici deberent doctores esse fidei Christianae: ita quod quicquid secundum regulam fidei docuerint vel diffinierint, hoc sit a fidelibus firmiter sentiendum: tamen si aliquid contra regulam fidei, quam scriptura diuina docet, docuerint aut diffinire praesumpserint, non sunt sequendi, sed a catholicis arguendi, & tanquam haeretici deuitandi. Errantes igitur inebriati dicentes, quod homo Christianus nihil debet explicite credere, nisi quod papa & Cardinales declarant, qui volunt contra Apostolum, papam dominari fidei nostrae: & qui non quaerunt intelligere veritatem, sed ea quae suo rectori & magistro sunt placita: auribus simplicium nullatenus sunt audiendi, sed sunt tanquam euersores fidei repellendi. Haec autem contra dicta sufficiant. Si autem dicta eorum aliter, quam se habeat veritas, reprobaui, mihi nullatenus imputetur: quia sub illa forma mihi declarata suerunt, intentionis autem meae est solummodo falsam sententiam, & ipsius quicunque assertores fuerint, & non alios, improbare. Si autem dixi imperite, correctionem charitatiuam nullatenus recusabo.
units.tr: Moreover, to seduce the simple, the aforesaid followers of error say that lower, simple people ought not to meddle in the question mentioned. And if anyone says, I am a Christian: I want to know the faith and the truth, and so I am moved to inquire into this, because I am simple, they reply: I tell you, believe explicitly what the Church has explained, and believe the rest implicitly, until the Church declares otherwise. But in this assertion they insinuate two errors. The first is that the simple ought not to meddle in the question mentioned, and this error has been condemned in a certain other Treatise. The second error is that the simple ought not to believe explicitly anything except what the Church has explained, meaning by "the Church" the pope and the Cardinals, for it is of that church that these men speak, as is plainly evident from many of their assertions. But that this is erroneous is clearly proved. For every Christian ought to believe whatever he is specifically certain follows evidently from the contents of divine Scripture. Yet persons other than the pope and the Cardinals can be certain of many things that follow evidently from the contents of divine Scripture, things which the pope and the Cardinals have never declared, indeed which perhaps the pope and the Cardinals have never specifically known, but have believed only implicitly. Therefore Christians can, and sometimes are bound to, believe explicitly some things which the pope and the Cardinals have never explicitly declared. The major premise is manifest. For whoever is certain of the antecedent and of the consequence is certain of the consequent. And so whoever explicitly believes the antecedent, and is certain of the consequence, because the consequent is inferred from the antecedent, cannot be doubtful about the consequent. To this the saying of the Philosopher alludes: he who induces, knows at the same time. For although someone may be certain of the major premise and yet doubtful or of a contrary opinion about the conclusion, nevertheless, if he is certain of the major and of the minor, which he applies to the conclusion, he cannot be doubtful about the conclusion. Therefore whoever explicitly believes certain things that he reads in divine Scripture, and is certain of whatever follows evidently from them, cannot be doubtful about that conclusion. And consequently he either knows it or believes it explicitly. Therefore, if there is a conclusion that can be demonstrated by reason, it follows that he believes it explicitly, and cannot fail to believe it explicitly, so long as he notices that it follows evidently from the contents of divine Scripture. The minor, although it seems to need hardly any proof, is nonetheless clearly proved by the authorities of venerable Fathers. For Augustine says, as is read in 24 q. 3, last chapter: Therefore divine providence permits many heretics to exist in diverse errors, so that when they question us about things which they do not know, Catholics may, through the divine Scriptures, learn what they had not known before. Consequently he himself is certain, through the divine Scriptures alone, of those things which the pope and the Cardinals in no way declared. There is also to this purpose an authority taken from Augustine on that saying of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 11: there must be heresies, that those who are approved among you may be made manifest, which can be adduced, for the Gloss says: All enemies of the Church, whether blinded by error or depraved by malice, are useful, because if they receive the power of afflicting the body, they exercise its patience; for if they oppose it by thinking badly, they exercise its wisdom. For from the adversary's assault arises a continual occasion for learning, since many things pertaining to the faith, while they are stirred up by the harassment of heretics, are defended against them, are considered more carefully, are asked about more quickly, and are tested more urgently. And below: Heretics are therefore useful, not by teaching what they do not know to be true, but by stirring the Catholics to seek and attain the truth. From these words it is plainly gathered that Catholics, and heretics who are stirred up, can learn many unknown truths through the holy Scriptures, although the pope and the Cardinals have not hitherto attempted to declare them. Hence some also say that, on the occasion of the heresies which the master and ruler of these men has solemnly defined and publicly preached, countless truths spring up in many places, of which many have already been refuted in the Scriptures, and which will bring (as they firmly think) inestimable faith and usefulness in the future to the whole community of Christians, both laity and faithful clergy. Yet even the earlier supreme pontiffs and the Catholic Cardinals in no way declared these truths, because they had no occasion to declare them before the time of that ruler. But perhaps someone would say that the simple ought to believe explicitly only what the pope and the Cardinals hand down for belief, and ought not to search out the secrets of Scripture but be content with common things; indeed they should not presume, on their own understanding, to believe anything explicitly unless the pope and the Cardinals have handed it on to them. But whoever asserts this is the inventor of new errors. For although the simple are not ordinarily bound to believe explicitly anything except what has already been explicitly declared by the clergy as to be believed now, nevertheless the simple, reading the divine Scriptures with the keenness of reason (which the simple also do not wholly lack), notice that something (which the pope and the Cardinals have in no way declared) evidently follows from the divine Scriptures. In this case they can and ought to believe it explicitly, nor are they bound to consult the pope and the Cardinals, because they are bound to prefer holy Scripture to the pope and the Cardinals. But perhaps someone would say that the simple are saved in the faith of their betters; therefore they ought not to have explicit faith about anything except what the pope and the Cardinals hold explicitly, and so it seems wrong to say that something belongs to the Catholic faith about which the pope and the Cardinals do not have explicit faith. But it is answered that the simple are saved in their own faith, for if they do not have faith in themselves, they are not saved. Yet there is a certain mode of being saved in the faith of their betters, because for many things it is enough for them to believe implicitly what their betters believe explicitly. This is true if the betters have explicitly the same faith as the lesser, and the lesser do not notice that anything follows from divine Scripture except what the betters perceive to follow. When it is said that the pope and the Cardinals have explicit faith about all things that pertain to the Catholic faith, I say that this is not always true, since they often do not have explicit faith about all those things which it is necessary for them to believe explicitly. When it is assumed in argument that the simple ought not to search out the secrets of divine Scripture, this is not true, because then no simple person ought to presume to devote himself to the study of holy Scripture, and so no one ought to study holy Scripture before he became a pope or a Cardinal. For every student of holy Scripture must at some point begin, and whoever begins to study holy Scripture must, as regards knowledge of the Scriptures, be counted among the simple; therefore no one, before he became a pope or a Cardinal, ought to begin studying the holy Scriptures.
