When it is further assumed that the simple ought not to presume on their own understanding to believe anything explicitly unless the pope and the Cardinals have believed it, the answer must be that the simple ought not to presume on their own understanding, but should cling firmly to holy Scripture, so that whatever they plainly see to be inferred from the holy Scriptures, that they believe explicitly, whether or not it has been declared by the pope and the Cardinals. And the reason for this is that the pope and the Cardinals are not the rule of our faith. For although a Catholic pope and Catholic Cardinals ought to be teachers of the Christian faith, so that whatever they teach or define according to the rule of faith must be firmly held by the faithful, nevertheless, if they teach or presume to define anything contrary to the rule of faith which divine Scripture teaches, they are not to be followed, but are to be refuted by Catholics and shunned as heretics. Therefore those erring and intoxicated men who say that a Christian man ought to believe explicitly nothing except what the pope and the Cardinals declare, and who, against the Apostle, wish the pope to lord it over our faith, and who seek not to understand the truth but what is pleasing to their ruler and master, are by no means to be listened to by the ears of the simple, but are to be repelled as subverters of the faith. Let these things suffice against their sayings. If I have refuted their statements otherwise than the truth stands, this is in no way to be imputed to me, since they were declared to me under that form; my intention is only to refute the false opinion, and its asserters whoever they are, and not others. If I have spoken unskillfully, I will by no means refuse charitable correction.

units.la: EXPLICIT SECUNDUS TRACTATUS secunda partis.
units.tr: END OF THE SECOND TREATISE, OF THE SECOND PART.

units.la: TERTIA PARS PRINCIPALIS DIA- LOGORVM TRACTAT DE GE- STIS DIVERSORVM CHRISTIANO- RVM, ET DIVIDITVR IN NOVEM TRACTA- TVS, quorum quilibet subdiuiditur in diuersos libros.
units.tr: THE THIRD PART OF THE PRINCIPAL DIALOGUES, CONCERNING THE DEEDS OF VARIOUS CHRISTIANS, AND IT IS DIVIDED INTO NINE TREATISES, each of which is subdivided into various books.

units.la: Discipul. Salomonis vtcunq; sequendo vestigia proposui in animo meo, quaerere & investigare sapienter de omnibus quae fiunt sub sole, in ecclesia scilicet militante: de qua non omnes Christiani his diebus consimiliter opinantur. Quia enim quidam circa fidem catholicam altercantur se haereticos mutuo appellantes: quidam eorum apud quosdam, & alii apud alios veram existimant ecclesiam consistere militantem, pinde ad tertiam partem Dialogi nostri (quam ab initio de gestis circa fidem altercantium orthodoxam volui appellari) nostram intentionem vertamus, quantum nostrae occupationes & studia praesentis cogruat temporis qualitati, quia vt beatus asserit August. ad Bonifacium militem, & habetur 23. q. 4. c. si ecclesia: omnia debent suis temporibus convenire: quam in nouem tractatus volo secari, quorum vnumquemq; in diuersos libros censeo diuidendum, primi namq; duo erunt praeparatorii & praeambuli ad sequentes, in quibus de gestis diuersorum Christianorum scrutabimur.
units.tr: Disciple. I have resolved in my mind, following somewhat in the footsteps of Solomon, to inquire into and investigate wisely all the things that are done under the sun, namely in the militant Church, concerning which not all Christians in these days think alike. For since some of them dispute about the Catholic faith, calling each other heretics, and some of them think that the true militant Church exists among certain people and others think it exists among others, let us turn our intention to the third part of our Dialogue (which I at first wished to call concerning the deeds of those who dispute about the orthodox faith), as far as our occupations and studies and the character of the present time allow. For, as the blessed Augustine says in his letter to Boniface the soldier, and it is held in 23 q. 4 c. si ecclesia: all things ought to suit their times. I wish this to be cut into nine treatises, each of which I think should be divided into various books; for the first two will be preparatory and introductory to the following, in which we shall examine the deeds of various Christians.

units.la: Primus quidem disputando de potestate papae & cleri.
units.tr: The first, indeed, disputing concerning the power of the pope and the clergy.

units.la: Secundus de potestate & iuribus Romani Imperii, in quo quamplurima de iuribus regum ac principum ac etiam laicorum aliquorum tractabimus.
units.tr: The second concerning the power and rights of the Roman Empire, in which we shall treat very many matters concerning the rights of kings and princes and also of certain laymen.

units.la: Tertius de gestis Ioh. 22. quem nonnulli putant propter haereticam prauitatem diu antequam de hoc mundo migraret, omni dignitate ecclesiastica fuisse priuatum. Alii ipsum fuisse catholicum & in vero papatu finisse dies suos existimant.
units.tr: The third concerning the deeds of John 22, whom some think to have been deprived of all ecclesiastical dignity, because of his heretical perversity, long before he departed from this world. Others think that he was a Catholic and ended his days in true papacy.

units.la: Quartus de gestis Domini Lodoici de Bauaria: quem aliqui verum Imperatorem non reputant, alii contrarium arbitrantur.
units.tr: The fourth concerning the deeds of Lord Louis of Bavaria, whom some do not regard as the true Emperor, while others think the contrary.

units.la: Quintus de gestis Benedicti 12. quem multi, sed non omnes, tanquam summum pontificem venerantur.
units.tr: The fifth concerning the deeds of Benedict 12, whom many, but not all, venerate as the supreme pontiff.

units.la: Sextus de gestis fratris Michaelis de Celena.
units.tr: The sixth concerning the deeds of Brother Michael of Cesena.

units.la: Septimus de gestis & doctrina fratris Giraldi Odonis, quorum vnum quidam, alii alium verum Generalem ordinis Fratrum Minorum affirmant.
units.tr: The seventh concerning the deeds and teaching of Brother Geraldus Odonis, of whom some affirm one man and others another to be the true General of the Order of Friars Minor.

units.la: Octauus de gestis fratris Guilhelmi de Ockam.
units.tr: The eighth concerning the deeds of Brother William of Ockham.

units.la: Nonus de gestis aliorum Christianorum, regum, principum, & praelatorum ac subditorum laicorum ac clericorum secularium religiosorum Fratrum Minorum & aliorum, qui alicui & aliquibus de praenominatis personis adhaerent, obediunt, consentiunt, communicant, fauent vel quomodolibet praebere auxilium, aut consilium dignoscuntur, vel ipsos, aut eorum aliquem impugnant, molestant, vel reprehensibilem aut reprehensibiles arbitrantur. Magist. Tam tua instantia, quam desiderium perficiendi praedicta aggredi mihi suadet: sed timor calumniam incurrendi illorum, qui forsitan dicent me audere illicite disputare de potestate summi pontificis, dissuadet: praesertim cum leges etiam Canonicae & ciuiles videantur asserere, quod sacrilegium incurrit, qui praesumit de auctoritate principis disputare, ideo si tibi videtur de praefatis me nullatenus intromittā: maxime cum ad libros necessarios non valeam (vt aestimo) peruenire. Disc. Timor non te retrahat memoratus: quia sicut videmus catholicos de fide absq; periculo iustae calumniae ad exercitium disputare. Doctores enim sacrae Theologiae de fide in scholis publice disputant, & contra veritatem fidei quos sciunt acutius arguentes nullum crimen incurrunt: licet nec tunc nec vnquam postea veritatem quaestionis disputate determinent, baccalarii etiam & prudentes, quantum possunt fortius irreprehensibiliter, imo saepe laudabiliter contra veritatem arguunt & allegant, sic de potestate summi pontificis ad exercitium contingit laudabiliter disputare. Cum igitur contra potestatem papae neq; asserendo neque dubitando aliquid sis dicturus, sed solummodo recitando: sicut pro toto isto Dialogo peractum est inter nos a principio de potestate papae & omnibus aliis, quae commemorauì tractanda, nullatenus metuas indagare. Praesertim cum sciam te paratum omnem veritatem de potestate papae & aliam quam teneris explicite credere, opportunis loco & tempore, quando erit expedies, occulte & publice confiteri. Nec librorum carentia te retardet: quia licet non possis facere opus perfectum, aliquid tamen facere non erit inutile: quia occasionem faciendi opera perfecta copiam librorum habentibus ministrabis. Mag. Quod absq; assertione & dubitatione falsa liceat recitare, & in persona dicere aliorum: quodq; non sit necesse omni tempore ore veritatem, etiam catholicam confiteri (cū cadat sub praecepto affirmatiuo, quod semper obligat, sed non pro semper) multis modis possset ostendi. Ideoq; malignorum paruipendens calumnias, tuę instantiae acquiescam: & ad exercitanda studiosorum ingenia tā circa potestatem papae q; circa alia quae duxeris inquirenda: etiam sententias & opiniones quas reputo erroneas, imo haereticas recitabo: pro quibus quo voluero fortius allegabo: quod etiam tu poteris interdum facere, si tibi videbitur. Incipe igitur sine mora primum tractatum.
units.tr: The ninth concerning the deeds of other Christians: kings, princes, and prelates, and subjects, laymen and clergy, secular and religious, Friars Minor and others, who are known to adhere to, obey, consent to, communicate with, favour, or in any way give help or counsel to any or all of the aforementioned persons, or who attack, harass, or consider reprehensible either them or any of them. Master. Your insistence, as well as the desire to accomplish what has been said, urges me to undertake it; but fear of incurring the calumny of those who will perhaps say that I dare to dispute unlawfully about the power of the supreme pontiff dissuades me, especially since the canon and civil laws seem to assert that he incurs sacrilege who presumes to dispute about the authority of the prince. Therefore, if it seems right to you, I shall in no way concern myself with the aforementioned matters, especially since I cannot (as I judge) come to the necessary books. Disciple. Let not the aforementioned fear hold you back, for we see that Catholics dispute about the faith without danger of just calumny in exercise. For teachers of sacred theology dispute publicly about the faith in the schools, and those who argue most sharply against the truth of the faith incur no crime, although neither then nor ever afterwards do they settle the truth of the question disputed; bachelors too and prudent men, as strongly as they can, blamelessly, indeed often commendably, argue and allege against the truth; so it is possible to dispute commendably about the power of the supreme pontiff by way of exercise. Since therefore you are going to say nothing against the power of the pope, neither by asserting nor by doubting, but only by reciting, as throughout this whole Dialogue has been done between us from the beginning, concerning the power of the pope and all the other matters which I have mentioned for treatment, you should by no means fear to inquire. Especially since I know you are ready, at a fitting place and time, when it shall be expedient, to confess openly and privately all the truth about the power of the pope and whatever else you are bound to believe explicitly. Nor let the lack of books hold you back, for although you cannot produce a perfect work, to do something will not be useless, since you will furnish the occasion for those who have a supply of books to produce perfect works. Master. That it is lawful to recite, without assertion and without false doubt, and to speak in the person of others, and that it is not necessary at all times to confess the truth with the mouth, even the Catholic truth (since it falls under an affirmative precept, which always binds but not for always), could be shown in many ways. Therefore, making little account of the calumnies of the malicious, I shall yield to your insistence, and in order to exercise the minds of students both concerning the power of the pope and concerning the other matters you wish to be inquired into, I shall even recite opinions and views which I hold to be erroneous, indeed heretical, and for which I shall argue as strongly as I wish; which you too may sometimes do, if it seems good to you. Begin therefore without delay the first treatise.

units.la: TRACTATVS PRIMVS DE POTESTATE PAPAE ET CLERI. LIBER PRIMVS. CAP. I.
units.tr: TRACTATUS PRIMUS DE POTESTATE PAPAE ET CLERI. LIBER PRIMUS. CAP. I.

units.la: In quo recitantur quinq; opiniones de potestate summi Pontificis, prima & sibi contraria pertractantur à capitulo 2. vsq; ad cap. 9. secunda cap. 10. tertia cap. 11. & quarta cap. 13. quinta vero cap. 16.
units.tr: In which five opinions concerning the power of the supreme Pontiff are set out; the first, and those opposed to it, are treated from chapter 2 to chapter 9; the second in chapter 10; the third in chapter 11; the fourth in chapter 13; and the fifth in chapter 16.

units.la: DIscip. Claues regni cœlorum esse datas à Christo Romano pontifici, id est beato Petro, Christianorum non ambigit (vt æstimo) multitudo, quare non dubito, quin sibi à Christo aliqua potestas concessa. Plures etiam auctoritates sanctorum patrum videntur asserere q; aliquam ex humana ordinatione acceperit potestatem. Ad quarum vtramq; : si vtramq; habeat interrogabo quamplura. Quam videlicet & quo iure, diuino scilicet an humano, habeat potestatem super spiritualia & ecclesiasticas personas: quam & quo iure super laicos in spiritualibus, quam & quo iure super res & iura temporalia, quæ ad solam Romanam spectant ecclesiam: quam & quo iure super res & temporalia iura, quæ ad alios clericos pertinere noscuntur: quam & quo iure super personas, res & iura temporalia fidelium laicorum: & quam & quo iure super res infidelium & etiam personas ipsorum. Postea autem nonnulla similia de potestate cleri perscrutari propono, ante omnia autem interrogare decreui, an potestas papæ ad omnia, quæ non sunt contra legem diuinam, neque contra ius naturæ, se extendat. Hæc enim interrogatio videtur comprehendere omnia prædicta de potestate papæ, & forte ex sententia & opinionibus circa ipsam, quas recitare studebis, dabitur mihi occasio de singulis in speciali quærendi. Mag. Circa hanc interrogationem diuersæ & aduersæ inueniuntur sententiæ. Vna est, quod papa tam in spiritualibus quàm in temporalibus, talem ex ordinatione Christi habet plenitudinem potestatis, vt regulariter & in omni casu omnia possit, quæ non sunt expresse contra legem Dei neq; contra ius naturæ. Alia est, quod talem plenitudinem potestatis habet ex iure diuino in spiritualibus non in temporalibus. Tertia est, quod talem potestatis plenitudinem habet partim ex ordinatione Christi, partim ex ordinatione humana. Quarta est, quod talem plenitudinem potestatis non habet nec à iure diuino nec à iure humano: neque regulariter neque casualiter siue in casu, & circa hanc sunt modi diuersi ponendi. Quinta est quod talem plenitudinem potestatis simpliciter non regulariter neq; à iure diuino neq; à iure humano habet: sed casualiter siue in casu habet talem plenitudinem potestatis à iure diuino siue ex speciali ordinatione Christi.
units.tr: DIsciple. That the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given by Christ to the Roman pontiff, that is, to the blessed Peter, the multitude of Christians does not doubt (as I judge); therefore I do not doubt that some power was granted to him by Christ. Indeed, many authorities of the holy Fathers seem to assert that he received some power by human ordinance as well. To each of these, if he holds both, I shall put many questions. Namely, by what right, whether divine or human, he holds power over spiritual things and ecclesiastical persons; by what right over laymen in spiritual matters; by what right over goods and temporal rights which pertain to the Roman Church alone; by what right over goods and temporal rights which are known to pertain to other clergy; by what right over the persons, goods and temporal rights of the faithful laity; and by what right over the goods of unbelievers and also over their persons. Afterwards I propose to inquire into some similar matters concerning the power of the clergy; but above all I have decided to ask whether the power of the Pope extends to all things which are not against the divine law nor against the law of nature. For this question seems to comprehend all the aforesaid matters concerning the power of the Pope, and perhaps from the opinions and views about it which you are eager to recite, I shall be given occasion to inquire into each point in particular. Master. Concerning this question, diverse and opposing opinions are found. One is that the Pope, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, has by the ordinance of Christ such a fullness of power that, as a rule and in every case, he can do all things which are not expressly against the law of God nor against the law of nature. Another is that he has such a fullness of power from divine right in spiritual but not in temporal matters. A third is that he has such a fullness of power partly by the ordinance of Christ and partly by human ordinance. A fourth is that he has no such fullness of power, neither from divine right nor from human right, neither as a rule nor occasionally or in a particular case, and concerning this there are different ways of putting it. A fifth is that he simply does not have such a fullness of power as a rule, neither from divine right nor from human right; but in a particular case, or occasionally, he does have such fullness of power from divine right or from a special ordinance of Christ.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: In quo probatur prima opinio capitulo precedenti recitata.
units.tr: In which the first opinion recited in the preceding chapter is proved.

units.la: DIsf. Istas discutiamus sententias, vt acutius & profundius valeamus intelligere veritatem, pro prima igitur aliquas allegationes adducas. Mag. Prima sententia in verbis euangelii, imo ipsius Christi fundari videtur: qui, vt legitur Matt. 16. dixit Petro: Tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum: & quodcunq; ligaueris &c. & quodcunq; solueris &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur quod Christus dedit beato Petro, & per consequens successoribus eius, absq; exceptione plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit: quia verbo generali omnia debent comprehendi, di. 19. si Romanorum, & 1. q. 1. sunt nonnulli, & 24. q. 3. putat. Discip. Ista allegatio impugnari potest, vt videtur, nam sæpe verbum generale non est generaliter intelligendum, extr. de iureiur. ad nostram & 1. q. 1. iudices, unde & verbum generale sæpe restringitur, vt notat Glo. extr. de appel. sua nobis, cuius exempla quamplurima in scripturis diuinis habentur, Matt. enim 3. dicitur, quod exibat ad eum omnis regio trans Iordanem & baptizabantur in Iordane ab eo, & tamen multi non exibant nec baptizabantur à Iohanne. Et Luc. 3. dicitur, quod cogitantibus omnibus de Iohanne, ne forte ipse esset Christus, & tamen multi hoc minime cogitauerunt: quia nec illi qui non credebant in Christum: nec illi qui Iohanne non putauerunt apheram. Alia exempla innumera possunt adduci, in quibus verbum generale non debet generaliter intelligi, sed restringi. Dimittentur tamen ad præsens omnia, pter quædam pauca, q; de potestate & subiectione loquuntur: licut & verba Christi pmissa. Ait itaq; Apostolus ad Eph. 5. Vt ecclesia subiecta est Christo: ita & mulieres viris suis in omnibus, vbi verbum in omnibus non debet generaliter absq; omni exceptione, etiam quo ad licita, intelligi, qa vxores non sunt in omnibus licitis subiectæ viris: cum quoad multa licita vir & vxor ad paria iudicentur, extr. de diuortiis c. gaudemus. Apostolus etiam ad Colloss. 4. ait: Filii obedite parentibus p omnia, & post: Serui obedite p omnia Dominis carnalibus, & ad Eph. 9. ait: Serui obedite Domini carnalibus cum omni timore & tremore, & 1. ad Tim. 9. Quicunq; sunt subugo serui, Dominos suos omni honore dignos arbitrentur, & ad Titum: Seruos Dominus suos esse subditos in omnibus esse placentes, & Pet. 2. sic legitur: Subiecti estote omni humanæ creaturæ, propter Deum, & post: Serui subiecti estote in omni timore Domini, non tantum bonis & modestis, sed etiam discolis. Et 1. ad Tim. 2. ait Apostolus: Mulier in silentio discat cum omni subiectione. In quibus omnibus verba generalia nō debent generaliter absq; omni exceptione intelligi, qa in multis nec mulieres viris, nec filii parentibus, nec serui Dominis, nec fideles omniaomnibus hominibus sunt subiecti, igitur consimiliter per hoc, quod Christus dixit Petro: Quodcunq; ligaueris &c. non potest intelligi, quod omnes mortales in omnibus absque omni exceptione successoribus beati Petri sint subiecti, vt in omnes homines quoad omnia de se licita, plenitudinem tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus habeant potestatis. Magist. Ista obiectio duobus modis repellitur: Primo, quia si secundum canones sacros, vbi canon non excipit aut diffinit aut determinat, nec excipere nec diffinire nec determinare debemus, 31. quaest. 1. quod si dormierit, & q. 5. consuluisti, 55. si euangelica, multo fortius vbi Dominus non excipit, diffinit vel determinat, nec nos excipere, diffinire nec determinare debemus. Sed Christus concedendo Petro potestatem super omnes nihil excepit, nec diffiniuit, nec determinauit, sed indistincte & generaliter dixit: Quodcunque ligaueris &c. igitur nec nos aliquid debemus ab eius potestate excipere, aut eam aliquo modo diffinire vel determinare. Petrus igitur in omnibus temporalibus & spiritualibus accepit a Christo plenitudinem potestatis. Amplius, beneficium principis largissime interpretandum est, extra de Simonia. c. vltim. & extra de dict. ex parte, igitur & potestas collata Petro a principe principum Christo largissime interpretanda est, vt ab eius potestate nec in spiritualibus nec in temporalibus aliquid penitus subtrahatur. Secundo repellitur obiectio supradicta auctoritate Innoc. tertii, qui (vt legitur extra de maio. & obe. c. sane, ait: Dominus dixit ad Petrum, & etiam Petrus dixit ad successores: quodcunque ligaueris &c. nihil excipiens, qui dixit: quodcunque ligaueris &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod a potestate data a Christo beato Petro & successoribus eius neque in temporalibus neque in spiritualibus aliquid est excipiendum, habet igitur papa talem plenitudinem potestatis a Christo.
units.tr: Disciple. Let us examine these opinions so that we may understand the truth more sharply and deeply. For the first, then, bring forward some arguments. Master. The first opinion seems to be founded on the words of the Gospel, indeed on Christ himself, who, as we read in Matt. 16., said to Peter: To thee I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatsoever thou shalt bind etc., and whatsoever thou shalt loose etc. From these words it is gathered that Christ gave to the blessed Peter, and consequently to his successors, without exception, the fullness of power, so that he may do all things, because all things must be included under a general word (dist. 19, si Romanorum; 1 q. 1, sunt nonnulli; 24 q. 3, putat). Student. This argument can be attacked, as it seems, for a general word is often not to be understood generally (extra, de iureiur., ad nostram; 1 q. 1, iudices), whence a general word is often restricted too, as the gloss notes (extra, de appel., sua nobis). Very many examples of this are found in the divine Scriptures. For Matt. 3. says that all the region beyond the Jordan went out to him and were baptized by him in the Jordan, and yet many did not go out nor were baptized by John. And Luke 3. says that all were musing about John, whether perhaps he himself were the Christ, and yet many did not think this at all: neither those who did not believe in Christ, nor those who did not think John was the forerunner. Countless other examples can be adduced in which a general word ought not to be understood generally but restricted. Nevertheless, let all of these be set aside for now, except a few which speak of power and subjection, as also the words of Christ quoted above. Thus the Apostle says in Eph. 5.: As the Church is subject to Christ, so also wives to their husbands in all things, where the word in all things must not be understood generally and without any exception, even as to lawful matters, since wives are not subject to their husbands in all lawful things, when husband and wife are judged equal in many lawful matters (extra, de divortiis, c. gaudemus). The Apostle also says in Col. 4.: Children, obey your parents in all things, and afterwards: Servants, obey in all things your fleshly masters; and in Eph. 6.: Servants, obey your fleshly masters with all fear and trembling; and in 1 Tim. 6.: Whoever are servants under the yoke, let them count their masters worthy of all honour; and to Titus: Servants should be subject to their masters in all things, pleasing them; and 1 Pet. 2. reads thus: Be subject to every human creature for God's sake, and afterwards: Servants, be subject in all fear of the Lord, not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward. And the Apostle says in 1 Tim. 2.: Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection. In all these passages the general words ought not to be understood generally and without every exception, since wives are not subject to husbands, nor children to parents, nor servants to masters, nor believers to all men in many things. Therefore, in the same way, from the fact that Christ said to Peter: Whatsoever thou shalt bind etc., it cannot be understood that all mortals, without any exception, are subject in all things to the successors of the blessed Peter, so that they have over all men, in all things lawful in themselves, a fullness of power both in temporal and in spiritual matters. Master. This objection is refuted in two ways. First, because if, according to the sacred canons, where a canon does not except, define or determine, we ought not to except, define or determine either (31 q. 1, quod si dormierit; q. 5, consuluisti; 55, si evangelica), much more so where the Lord does not except, define or determine, we ought not to except, define or determine either. But Christ, in granting Peter power over all, excepted nothing, defined nothing, determined nothing, but spoke indistinctly and generally: Whatsoever thou shalt bind etc. Therefore neither ought we to except anything from his power, or define or determine it in any way. Peter therefore received from Christ a fullness of power in all temporal and spiritual matters. Furthermore, a prince's favour is to be interpreted most liberally (extra, de Simonia, c. ultim.; and extra, de dict. ex parte). Therefore the power conferred on Peter by Christ, the Prince of princes, is also to be interpreted most liberally, so that nothing at all is withdrawn from his power, either in spiritual or in temporal matters. Second, the above objection is refuted by the authority of Innocent III, who (as we read in extra, de maiorit. et obed., c. sane) says: The Lord said to Peter, and Peter also said to his successors: whatsoever thou shalt bind etc., excepting nothing, he who said: whatsoever thou shalt bind etc. From these words it is gathered that nothing is to be excepted from the power given by Christ to the blessed Peter and his successors, neither in temporal nor in spiritual matters. Therefore the Pope has such a fullness of power from Christ.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Vbi secundo probatur prima opinio, per hoc, quod Papae est in omnibus obediendum, quod probat auctoritatibus tribus & rationibus duabus.
units.tr: Where, secondly, the first opinion is proved, namely that the Pope must be obeyed in all things. This is proved by three authorities and two arguments.

units.la: Discip. Super praemissam auctoritatem Saluatoris postea reuertemur, ideo alias allegationes adducas. Magist. Quod papa habet in temporalibus & spiritualibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, probatur. Ille cui ex praecepto diuino est in omnibus obediendum & in nullo penitus resistendum, habet immediate a Deo huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis, papae autem ex praecepto diuino obediendum est in omnibus, & in nullo resistendum penitus, teste Grego. qui, vt habetur d. 12. c. praeceptis, ait: Praeceptis Apostolicis non dura superbia resistatur, & per obedientiam quae a sancta Romana ecclesia & Apostolica auctoritate iussa sunt salutifere impleantur, & infra: cuius auctoritate sanctionem omnes teneant sacerdotes, qui nolunt Apostolica Petra, super quam Christus vniuersalem fundauit ecclesiam, soliditate dimelli. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod propter auctoritatem concessam a Christo Romanae ecclesiae est in omnibus obediendum, & in nullo penitus resistendum. Hoc etiam Stephanus papa, vt habetur di. 19. c. enimuero, videtur asserere, cum ait: Enimuero in speculum & exemplum sancta Romana ecclesia, cui nos Christus praeesse voluit, ab omnibus quicquid ordinauit, perpetuo & irrefragabiliter obseruandum est &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod propter ordinationem Christi Romanae ecclesiae obediendum est in omnibus. Hinc Leo papa, vt habetur eadem di. c. ita Dominus, ait: huius muneris sacramentum ita Dominus ad omnium Apostolorum officium pertinere voluit, vt in beatissimo Petro Apostolorum omnium summe principaliter collocaret, &c. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod qui potestati Petri & successorum eius aliquo modo inobediens inuenitur, Dei ordinationem infringit, quare ex ordinatione Christi est, quod papae obediendum est in omnibus. Quod etiam ratione probatur, quia illi ex ordinatione obediendum est in omnibus, cuius omnia praecepta accipienda sunt tanquam diuina voce prolata, sed omnia praecepta papae sicut & sanctiones eius accipienda sunt tanquam diuina voce prolata, di. 19. sic omnes, igitur ex ordinatione Dei est ei obediendum in omnibus. Amplius illi ex praecepto Dei est in omnibus obediendum, qui absq; haeresi non potest esse schismaticus, & omnes alii possunt esse schismatici, tanquam ab illo diuisi. Sed papa non potest esse schismaticus, nisi fiat haereticus, omnes autem alii possunt esse schismatici, licet non statim sint haeretici, igitur papae est ex praecepto Dei in omnibus obediendum. Maior probatur per hoc, quod ille, cui non est obediendum ex praecepto Dei, in omnibus potest multa praecipere, in quibus alii sibi obedire non tenentur. Quare propter praecepta huiusmodi in quibus sibi non tenentur obedire, potest inter praecipientem & illos quibus fiunt praecepta huiusmodi oriri discordia, diuisio, dissensio, & scissura, & inde consequens schisma, quia schisma, quod Graecum nomen est, scissuram notat 24. q. 1. c. schisma. Illo igitur casu vel praecipiens vel illi quibus fiunt huiusmodi praecepta est schismaticus vel schismatici, sed illi, quibus fiunt praecepta, non sunt schismatici: cum non sint non obediendo aliquo crimine irretiti, ex quo nullatenus obedire tenentur. Quare praecipiens est schismaticus reputandus propter iniusta praecepta: licet non fiat haereticus. Minor, quod ad primam partem sc. quod papa absq; haeresi non possit esse schismaticus, probatur p hoc, quod schismaticus dicitur ille, qui ab ecclesiae vniuersalis vnitate recedit 24. q. 1. c. schisma & c. loquitur Dominus & c. alienus & c. quia ex sola, sed papa nisi fiat haereticus ab vniuersalis ecclesiae vnitate non recedit: cum ab ipso quamdiu manet in fide Petri vnitas vniuersalis ecclesiae incipiat, 24. q. 1. loquitur Dominus, igitur papa nisi fiat haereticus, schismaticus esse non potest. Secunda pars manifeste patet: quia omnis a papa absq; haeresi saltem in principio non obediendo vniuersali ecclesiae in his in quibus tenetur potest fieri schismaticus. Ex his colligitur quod ex præcepto Dei seu ex ordinatione Christi, Petro & successoribus eius est in omnibus obediendum: & in nullo penitus resistendum, igitur ex ordinatione Christi papa habet tam in spiritualibus quam in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit, quæ non sunt de se illicita, ita vt per solam humanam ordinationem, vel voluntatem non possunt fieri illicita. Disc. Priusquam ad alias allegationes procedas, refer quare dicitur quod papa ex ordinatione Christi omnia potest, quæ non sunt de illicita &c. Mag. Hoc dicitur propter vota, iuramenta, promissiones, pacta, & alia quæcunq; per quæ homines se obligant ad illa, ad quæ alias minime obligantur, quia per talia in nullo penitus derogatur potestati papæ, quin talibus quibuscunque non obstantibus omnia possit & in omnibus sit obediendum ei, eo quod in omnibus talibus potestas & auctoritas papæ intelligitur semper excepta, extra de iureiurando, veniens, & extra de electionibus, significasti.
units.tr: Disciple. Since we will return later to the Saviour's authority cited above, bring forward other allegations. Master. That the Pope has such a fullness of power in temporal and spiritual matters is proved as follows. He to whom obedience is due in all things and to whom no resistance at all may be offered, by divine precept, has this kind of fullness of power immediately from God. But the Pope is to be obeyed in all things, by divine precept, and no resistance at all is to be offered to him, as Gregory testifies, who, as it is found in d. 12. c. praeceptis, says: "Let no stubborn pride resist the Apostolic precepts, and let those things which are commanded by the holy Roman Church and by Apostolic authority be carried out for salvation through obedience," and further: "By his authority let all priests hold to the decree, who are unwilling to be dissolved from the solidity of the Apostolic rock, upon which Christ founded the universal Church." From these words it is gathered that, on account of the authority granted by Christ to the Roman Church, it must be obeyed in all things and no resistance at all may be offered to it. Pope Stephen also seems to assert this, as it is found in di. 19. c. enimuero, when he says: "Indeed, the holy Roman Church, over which Christ willed that we should preside, as a mirror and example, is to be observed by all, perpetually and without exception, in whatever it has ordained," etc. From these words it is gathered that, on account of Christ's ordination, the Roman Church must be obeyed in all things. Hence Pope Leo, as it is found in the same di. c. ita Dominus, says: "The Lord willed that the sacrament of this office should pertain to the duty of all the Apostles, yet placed it chiefly and principally in the most blessed Peter above all the Apostles," etc. From these words it is shown that whoever is found in any way disobedient to the power of Peter and his successors overturns God's ordinance. Therefore, by the ordinance of Christ, the Pope must be obeyed in all things. This is also proved by reason: he to whom obedience is due in all things by ordinance is one whose every precept must be received as though spoken by the divine voice; but every precept of the Pope, like his decrees, must be received as though spoken by the divine voice, di. 19. sic omnes. Therefore, by the ordinance of God, he is to be obeyed in all things. Furthermore, he to whom obedience is due in all things by precept of God is one who cannot be a schismatic without being a heretic, whereas all others can be schismatics, as those separated from him. But the Pope cannot be a schismatic unless he becomes a heretic, whereas all others can be schismatics even if they are not at once heretics. Therefore, by precept of God, the Pope must be obeyed in all things. The major premise is proved as follows: he to whom obedience is not due by precept of God can command many things in which others are not bound to obey him. Therefore, because of such precepts, in which they are not bound to obey, discord, division, dissension and rupture may arise between the one commanding and those to whom such precepts are given, and from this a consequent schism, since schisma, which is a Greek word, denotes a split, 24. q. 1. c. schisma. In that case, either the one commanding or those to whom such precepts are given is, or are, schismatic. But those to whom the precepts are given are not schismatics, since by not obeying they are not entangled in any crime, from which they are in no way bound to obey. Therefore the one commanding must be reckoned a schismatic on account of unjust precepts, even though he does not become a heretic. As for the minor premise, namely that the Pope cannot be a schismatic without being a heretic, the first part is proved as follows: he is called a schismatic who withdraws from the unity of the universal Church, 24. q. 1. c. schisma, c. loquitur Dominus, c. alienus, and c. quia ex sola. But the Pope, unless he becomes a heretic, does not withdraw from the unity of the universal Church, since, as long as he remains in the faith of Peter, the unity of the universal Church begins with him, 24. q. 1. loquitur Dominus. Therefore the Pope, unless he becomes a heretic, cannot be a schismatic. The second part is quite evident: for any man who, at least at the start, does not obey the universal Church in those matters in which he is bound, can become a schismatic, without being a heretic. From these points it is gathered that by precept of God, or by the ordinance of Christ, obedience is due in all things to Peter and his successors, and no resistance at all may be offered to them. Therefore, by the ordinance of Christ, the Pope has a fullness of power both in spiritual and in temporal matters, so that he can do all things which are not in themselves unlawful, such that they cannot be made unlawful by human ordinance or will alone. Disciple. Before you proceed to other allegations, explain why it is said that the Pope can do, by the ordinance of Christ, all things which are not unlawful, etc. Master. This is said on account of vows, oaths, promises, pacts and all other things by which men bind themselves to those things to which they are otherwise in no way bound, because through such things nothing at all is taken away from the power of the Pope; rather, whatever such things may be, the Pope's power and authority are understood to remain always excepted in all such things, and he may do all things and must be obeyed in all things, extra de iureiurando, veniens, and extra de electionibus, significasti.

units.la: CAP. IV. In quo tertio probatur duodecim rationibus prima opinio.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. In which the first opinion is proved, thirdly, by twelve arguments.

units.la: Discip. De ista materia in speciali tangemus in diuersis locis: ideo alias allegationes adducas. Mag. Quod papa habeat ex ordinatione Dei talem plenitudinem potestatis, probatur: quia qui omnibus legibus positiuis est solutus habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, quia qui non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, aliqua lege humana potest constringi: eo quod non habet potestatem supra omnes leges humanas, papa autem legibus est solutus, ita quod est supra omnes leges humanas: cum etiam leges impiales possit dissoluere, sicut plures canones videtur asserere, di. 19 quæcunq; igitur papa habet ex ordinatione Dei talem plenitudinem potestatis. Amplius, vicarius Christi habet plenitudinem potestatis ex ordinatione eiusdem Christi: cum Christus habuerit huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis & in committendo Petro vices suas nihil in talibus sibi interdixit, igitur papa habet talem ordinationem potestatis ex ordinatione Christi, cum sit Christi vicarius. Rursus papa habet plenitudinem potestatis, sed non habet aliquam potestatem ab homine, ergo ex sola ordinatione Dei habet plenitudinem potestatis. Minor colligitur & habetur ex diuersis canonibus sacris 2. q. 6. c. decreto & c. qui se scit, etiam diuersi canones sacri videntur asserere, vnde Innoc. tertius, vt habetur extra de iudiciis, nouit, ait: Cum enim non humanæ constitutioni, sed diuinæ potius innitamur, quia potestas nostra non est ex homine, sed ex Deo, nullus qui sit sanæ mentis ignorat, quin ad officium nostrum spectet de quocunq; mortali peccato corripere quemlibet Christianum. Et beatus Anacletus, vt habetur di. 22. c. sacrosancta, ait: Hæc vero Apostolica sedes caput & cardo, vt præfatum est, à Domino & non ab alio constituta &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod papa nullam potestatem habet ab homine. Quod etiam ratione videtur posse probari. Nā nullus est dicendus hæreticus, propter hoc, quod negat à quocunq; potestatem, quam à solo homine habere dignoscitur, quia talis licet erret, non tamen errat contra scripturam sacram, q non est ab homine, sed à Deo, sed q negat à papa potestatem suam, est hæreticus reputandus, vt testatur Nicolaus papa, secundum q habetur d. 22. c. 1. igitur papa à solo Deo recipit potestatem. Item quod papa habeat plenitudinem potestatis à Deo, ostenditur, nam ab eodem habet Romanus Pontifex plenitudinem potestatis & potestatem concedendi indulgentias, vt innuitur ext. de pæn. & re. cum ex eo, in fine, sed Romanus Pontifex habet à solo Deo & non ab homine potestatem concedendi indulgentias, igitur à solo Deo habet plenitudinem potestatis. Item, ille habet à Deo plenitudinem potestatis, de cuius iudicio & potestate non est licitum iudicare, nec etiā disputare in dubium reuocando potestatem eiusdem, q a de potestate eius, q non habet à Deo plenitudinem, de cuius etiā iudicio licet iudicare, si non secundū potestatem sibi concessam, sed vsurpatā præsumpserit iudicare, sed nemini licet iudicare vel etiā dubitando de iudicio & potestate summi pontificis disputare, ergo à Deo habet plenitudinē potestatis. Maior videtur esse eiusdē, minor per auctoritates diuersas ostenditur, ait enim Nicolaus papa, vt habetur 9 q. 3. patet, ipsecto sedu Apostolica, cuius auctoritate maius nō est iudicium, à nemine fore retractandū: nec cuiquā de eius liceat iudicare iudicio. Et Gelasius papa, vt habetur eisdē causa & q. c. ipsi, ait: nec de eius vnquam præceperunt iudicio iudicari, sententiāq; eius constituerunt non oportere dissolui, cuius potius sequenda decreta mandauerunt. Et 17. q. 4. si quis, sic scribitur: de iudicio summi pontificu alicui disputare non licet, & ibidem sic legitur: committunt etiā sacrilegium, qui contra legis sanctitatē diuinæ aut nesciendo committunt aut negligendo violāt & offendunt aut qui de principali iudicio certant & disputant. Et eisdē causa & q. c. nemini, vbi dicit Nicolaus papa: Nemini de sedis Apostolicæ iudicio iudicare aut illius sententiā retractare permissum est, videlicet propter ecclesiæ Romanæ primatū Christi munere in beato Petro Apostolo diuinitus collatū Ex his atq; aliis multis colligitur, q papa potestatem concessam à Christo Romanæ ecclesiæ nemini licet iudicare aut disputare de eius iudicio aut potestate, ergo habet à Christo plenitudinē potestatis. Quod adhuc tali ratione probetur. Ab eodem habet papa plenitudinem potestatis, à quo habet claues regni cœlorum, sed claues regni cœlorū habet à Christo, ergo & plenitudinē potestatis habet à Christo. Minor patet ex verbis Christi, quæ dixit Petro Matt. 16. Tibi dabo claues regni cælorum. Maior probatur: quia omnis potestas, quam habet papa, spectat ad claues, eo quod omnis potestas papæ aut est ordinis aut iurisdictionis. Potestas autem quam habet ratione ordinis spectat ad claues secundum omnes. Potestas etiam quam habet ratione iurisdictionis spectat ad claues, teste August. qui scribens ad Bonifacium, vt habetur dist. 50. c. vt constitueretur, ait: Vt constitueretur in ecclesia ne quisquam post alicuius criminis pœnitentiam clericatum accipiat: vel ad clericatum redeat: vel in clericatu maneat non desperatione indulgentia sed rigore factum est disciplinæ, alioquin contra claues datas ecclesiæ agitur, de quibus dictum est: quodcunque sol-
units.tr: Student. We will deal with this matter in particular at various points later, so please bring forward other proofs. Master. That the pope has by the ordinance of God such fullness of power is proved as follows. Whoever is released from all positive laws has such fullness of power. Whoever does not have such fullness of power can be bound by some human law, since he does not have power over all human laws. But the pope is released from laws, so that he is above all human laws; and he can also dissolve imperial laws, as several canons seem to assert (dist. 19, Quaecunque). Therefore the pope has by the ordinance of God such fullness of power. Furthermore, the vicar of Christ has fullness of power by the ordinance of Christ himself. Christ had this kind of fullness of power, and in committing his place to Peter he forbade him nothing in such matters. Therefore the pope has this ordinance of power by the ordinance of Christ, since he is Christ's vicar. Again, the pope has fullness of power, but he has no power from man. Therefore he has fullness of power by the sole ordinance of God. The minor premise is drawn from, and found in, various sacred canons (C. 2, q. 6, c. Decreto and c. Qui se scit). Various sacred canons also seem to assert it. Hence Innocent III, as found in Extra, de iudiciis, Novit, says: "For since we rely not on human constitution but rather on divine, because our power is not from man but from God, no one of sound mind is unaware that it belongs to our office to rebuke any Christian whatever for any mortal sin." And Blessed Anacletus, as found in dist. 22, c. Sacrosancta, says: "This Apostolic See, as has been said, is the head and hinge, constituted by the Lord and not by another," etc. From these words it is gathered that the pope has no power from man. This can also be shown by reason. For no one is to be called a heretic merely because he denies that power comes from someone whom he is known to have it from only a man. For such a person, although he may err, does not err against Holy Scripture, which says that power is not from man but from God. But whoever denies that he has his power from the pope is to be regarded as a heretic, as Pope Nicholas testifies, according to what is found in dist. 22, c. 1. Therefore the pope receives power from God alone. Likewise, that the pope has fullness of power from God is shown as follows. The Roman Pontiff has from the same God both fullness of power and the power of granting indulgences, as is hinted in Extra, de poenitentiis et remissionibus, Cum ex eo, at the end. But the Roman Pontiff has the power of granting indulgences from God alone and not from man. Therefore he has fullness of power from God alone. Again, he has fullness of power from God whose judgment and power it is not lawful to judge, nor even to call into doubt by disputing his power. For whoever presumes to judge the power of one who does not have fullness from God, whose judgment it is lawful to judge if he does so not according to power granted to him but according to usurped power, does so presumptuously. But it is lawful for no one to judge, or even to dispute with doubt, the judgment and power of the supreme pontiff. Therefore he has fullness of power from God. The major premise seems to be of this kind; the minor is shown by various authorities. For Pope Nicholas says, as found in 9, q. 3, Patet: "The Apostolic See itself, by whose authority there is no greater judgment, is to be retracted by no one, nor is it permitted for anyone to judge its judgment." And Pope Gelasius, as found in ibid. and q. c. Ipsi, says: "They never ordained that anyone should be judged by its judgment, and they decreed that its sentence ought not to be dissolved, whose decrees they commanded to be followed rather." And 17, q. 4, Si quis reads thus: "It is not lawful to dispute concerning the judgment of the supreme pontiff." And there it is read: "They also commit sacrilege who, against the holiness of divine law, either commit or violate and offend by ignorance or negligence, or who contend and dispute about the chief judgment." And in the same cause and question, c. Nemini, where Pope Nicholas says: "It is permitted to no one to judge the judgment of the Apostolic See or to retract its sentence," namely on account of the primacy of the Roman Church, conferred divinely by Christ's office upon the blessed Apostle Peter. From these and many other authorities it is gathered that the power granted by Christ to the Roman Church may not be judged, nor may its judgment or power be disputed by anyone. Therefore he has fullness of power from Christ. This is further proved by the following argument. The pope has fullness of power from the same source from which he has the keys of the kingdom of heaven. But he has the keys of the kingdom of heaven from Christ. Therefore he also has fullness of power from Christ. The minor is plain from the words of Christ which he spoke to Peter in Matthew 16: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." The major is proved thus: every power which the pope has pertains to the keys, since every power of the pope is either of order or of jurisdiction. The power he has by reason of order pertains to the keys according to all. The power he has by reason of jurisdiction also pertains to the keys, as Augustine testifies, who, writing to Boniface and as found in dist. 50, c. Ut constitueretur, says: "That it be established in the Church that no one who has received clerical orders after doing penance for some crime, or who returns to the clergy, or who remains in the clergy, shall be so treated not by despair of indulgence but by the rigour of discipline; otherwise action would be taken against the keys given to the Church, of which it has been said: whatever you shall loose"

units.la: aeris veris super terram, erit solutum & in cœlis. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod potestas puniendi criminosos, quæ competit ecclesiæ Romanæ, iurisdictionis, non ordinis, spectat ad claues ecclesiæ, igitur ratione consimili omnis talis potestas, quæ competit ecclesiæ ratione iurisdictionis spectat ad easdem claues. Quod Papa habeat à Christo immediate plenitudinem potestatis, probatur, quia cui ab aliquo concessum est maius, ab eodem & minus concessum videtur ext. de decimis ex parte 27. qu. 2. sunt qui dicunt, sed maius est dispensare contra Deum & contra Apostolum, quam posse ea, quæ nec sunt contra legem diuinam, nec contra ius naturæ. Et Papa autem habet à Christo potestatem dispensandi contra Deum & contra Apostolum, teste Glos. quæ 25.q.1. sup. c. sunt quidem, ait: satis potest sustineri, quod Papa contra Apostolum dispensat: non tamen in his quæ pertinent ad articulos fidei, & eodem modo dispensat in euangelio interpretando ipsum, & ext. de fo. compe, licet, in fine. Hoc etiam probatur exemplis. Nam Papa dispensat contra Deum in iuramento & in voto. Nam Dominus per prophetam: vouete & reddite, & Matt. 5. Redeant Domino iuramenta tua, & tamen in his dispensat Papa 15.q.6. iuratos, ext. de voto c. in multis, ergo multo fortius Papa potest omnia, quæ non sunt contra legem Dei nec contra ius naturæ. Præterea habet plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit, cuius sententia siue iusta, siue iniusta est timenda: & eiusdem præceptum siue iustum, siue iniustum est timendum & seruandum, sed sententia Papæ siue iusta, siue iniusta est timeda 2.q.3. sententia, ergo Papa omnia potest. Adhuc ille, qui à nemine reprehendi debet pro quocunq; facto, habet plenitudinem potestatis à Christo, vt omnia possit, quia si non haberet talem plenitudinem potestatis, posset excedere potestatem suam: & per consequens in talib. peccaret, quilibet autem peccator, etiā prælatus, potest & debet corripi & reprehendi de omni peccato: maxime si non timetur probabiliter, quod ex correctione fiet deterior, iuxta illud euangelii: Si peccauerit in te frater tuus vade, &c. quod ad omnes extenditur, vt ex sacris canonib. colligitur, Papa autem à nemine debet reprehendi seu corripi, dist. 40. si Papa, igitur Papa habet plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit, sed non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis ab homine, ergo habet eam à Christo. Amplius, qui non potest contra fidem errare, habet plenitudinem potestatis à Deo, vt omnia possit, quia qui non potest contra fidem errare, non potest errare contra bonos mores, & per consequens quicquid secerit, irreprehensibile est & licite factum, & ita omnia potest quæ vult. Papa autem non potest contra fidem errare. Ad quod probandum adducte sunt allegationes plures in prima parte huius Dialo. li.5.c.4. ergo Papa habet à Christo plenitudinem potestatis. Præterea qui habet à Christo plenitudinem potestatis super concilium generale: habet etiam multo fortius à Christo plenitudinem potestatis super alios. Papa autem habet à Christo plenitudinem potestatis sup concilio generale, talem autem potestatem non habet à concilio generali: cum vnum concilium non possit alii legem vel subiectionem imponere, quia non habet imperium par in pare, igitur si habet eam: habet ipsam ab aliquo superiori concilio generali, superior autem non est, nisi Christus, ergo si Papa habet talem plenitudinem potestatis super generale concilium, habet ipsam à Christo, restat ergo probare, quod Papa habeat talem plenitudinem potestatis, id est talem potestatem super concilium generale, quod per auctoritates manifestas videtur ostendi, ait n. Pascasius Papa, vt habetur ext. de elect. significasti: Cum omnia concilia per ecclesiam Romanam auctoritatem & facta sint & robur acceperint, & in eorum statu Romani Pontificis patenter excipiatur auctoritas, & Gratian. 25.q.1. si igitur, ait: Sacri canones ita aliquid constituunt vt sue interpretationis auctoritatem sancta Romana ecclesia conseruent, ipsi namque soli canones valent interpretari, qui im habent condendi eos, vnde in nonnullis capitulis conciliorum, cū aliquid obseruandum determinetur, statim subinfertur: nisi auctoritas Romana ecclesia obuiet: vel, salua tamen in omnib. Apostolica auctoritate. Ex quibus aliisq; quamplurimis colligitur, quod Papa habet super generale concilium plenitudinem potestatis, ergo multo fortius habet plenitudinem potestatis super omnes alios. Præterea qui habet potestatem à Christo super ista, quæ sunt super naturale æquitate, multo magis habet potestatem à Christo super omnia licita, quæ naturali æquitati non obuiant. Quia cui concessum est maius, & minus concessum esse videtur, sed Papa habet potestatem super illa, quæ naturali obuiat æquitati, ergo habet à Christo plenitudinem potestatis: vt omnia possit quæ sunt licita, & naturali æquitati non obuiant. Maior videtur probatione minime indigere. Minor probatur, nam pueros, qui seipsos nesciunt regere, habere curam & regimen animarum rationali obuiat æquitati, quæ ratio naturalis dictat, quod qui nescit se regere, non debet alios gubernare, imo & veritas euangelica hoc insinuat, cum Christus dicat Matt. 15. Cæcus autem si cæco ducatum præstet, ambo in foueam cadunt. Hoc etiā Alexander III. sequens dictamen rationis rectæ, vt habetur ext. de ætate & qualitate præficiendorum, c. indecoris, videtur innuere dicens: Indecoris est vt ii debeant ecclesias regere, qui non noverunt gubernare seipsos: cum ad ecclesiarum regimen tales persona sint admittenda, qui discretione præeminent & morum fulgent honestate, cui Gregor. IX. (vt habetur ext. de electio. cum in magistrum) concordare videtur dicens: cum in magistrum assumi non debet, qui formam discipuli non assumpsit: nec perficiendum qui subesse non nouit, &c. Ex quibus aliisque quamplurimis patet, quod æquitas naturalis exigit, quod pueri qui nec se, nec alios regere sciunt, ad regimen & curam animarum assumi non debent. Et tamen contra hanc naturalem æquitatem potest Papa præcipere, teste Glos. quæ vt habetur ext. de ætate & qualitate præficiendorum, super c. eam te, ait: si ex certa scientia scriberet Papa pro minori, eius mandato esset obediendum, quia sacrilegii instar obtinet dubitare an id sit dignum, quem princeps elegerit 17.q.4. §. qui autem, & cap. de crimine sacrilegii l.2. hoc etiam Alexander Tertius mandasse videtur, vt habetur ext. de ætate & qualitate præficiendorum, ex ratione, qui pueros infra decennium constitutos non remouet ab ecclesiis, quæ erant eis concessæ per episcopum Couuenirensem: sed scienter tolerat eos & mandat vt tolerentur.
units.tr: whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven. From these words it is gathered that the power of punishing criminals, which belongs to the Roman Church, pertains to the keys of the Church as a matter of jurisdiction, not of orders. Therefore, by similar reasoning, every such power that belongs to the Church by reason of jurisdiction pertains to the same keys. That the Pope has the fullness of power immediately from Christ is proved as follows: to whomever something greater has been granted by someone, the lesser is also seen to have been granted by the same person ext. de decimis ex parte 27. qu. 2. sunt qui dicunt. But it is a greater thing to dispense against God and against the Apostle than to be able to do those things which are neither contrary to the divine law nor contrary to the law of nature. And the Pope has from Christ the power to dispense against God and against the Apostle, according to the Gloss, which says, 25.q.1. sup. c. sunt quidem: it can well be maintained that the Pope dispenses against the Apostle; yet not in those matters which pertain to the articles of faith, and in the same way he dispenses in interpreting the Gospel itself, and ext. de fo. compe, licet, in fine. This is also proved by examples. For the Pope dispenses against God in oaths and in vows. For the Lord says through the prophet: vow and pay, and Matt. 5: Render to the Lord your oaths; and yet the Pope dispenses in these matters, 15.q.6. iuratos, ext. de voto c. in multis. Therefore, much more strongly, the Pope can do all those things which are not contrary to the law of God nor to the law of nature. Moreover, he has the fullness of power, so that he can do all things; his sentence, whether just or unjust, is to be feared; and his precept, whether just or unjust, is to be feared and observed. But the sentence of the Pope, whether just or unjust, is to be feared, 2.q.3. sententia. Therefore the Pope can do all things. Again, he who ought not to be rebuked by anyone for any deed whatever has from Christ the fullness of power, so that he can do all things; for if he did not have such fullness of power, he could exceed his power, and consequently would sin in such matters. But any sinner, even a prelate, can and ought to be corrected and rebuked for every sin, especially if it is not probable that he will become worse through correction, according to that word of the Gospel: If your brother sins against you, go, etc., which extends to all, as is gathered from the sacred canons. But the Pope ought to be rebuked or corrected by no one, dist. 40. si Papa. Therefore the Pope has the fullness of power, so that he can do all things. But he does not have such fullness of power from man; therefore he has it from Christ. Furthermore, he who cannot err against the faith has the fullness of power from God, so that he can do all things; for he who cannot err against the faith cannot err against good morals, and consequently whatever he does is beyond reproach and lawfully done, and so he can do all that he wills. But the Pope cannot err against the faith. Several allegations, to prove this, have been adduced in prima parte huius Dialo. li.5.c.4. Therefore the Pope has from Christ the fullness of power. Moreover, he who has from Christ the fullness of power over a general council has much more strongly from Christ the fullness of power over others. But the Pope has from Christ the fullness of power over a general council, and he does not have such power from a general council, since one council cannot impose law or subjection on another, for equal does not have authority over equal. Therefore, if he has it, he has it from some superior general council; but there is no superior except Christ. Therefore, if the Pope has such fullness of power over a general council, he has it from Christ. It remains, then, to prove that the Pope has such fullness of power, that is, such power over a general council, which seems to be shown by clear authorities. For Pope Paschal says, as is found ext. de elect. significasti: Since all councils have both been made and received their force through the authority of the Roman Church, and in their state the authority of the Roman Pontiff is openly excepted. And Gratian, 25.q.1. si igitur, says: The sacred canons so establish something that the holy Roman Church preserves the authority of their interpretation; for the canons alone have the power of interpreting, who have the power of enacting them. Hence in some chapters of councils, when something is determined to be observed, it is at once added: unless the authority of the Roman Church opposes; or, saving in all things the Apostolic authority. From these and very many other things it is gathered that the Pope has over a general council the fullness of power; therefore, much more strongly, he has the fullness of power over all others. Moreover, he who has from Christ power over those things which are above natural equity has much more from Christ power over all lawful things which do not oppose natural equity. For to whom something greater is granted, the lesser also seems to be granted; but the Pope has power over those things which oppose natural equity; therefore he has from Christ the fullness of power, so that he can do all lawful things which do not oppose natural equity. The major premise seems to need no proof. The minor is proved thus: that boys, who do not know how to govern themselves, should have the care and rule of souls, opposes rational equity, which natural reason dictates: that he who does not know how to govern himself ought not to govern others. Indeed, the evangelical truth also insinuates this, since Christ says in Matt. 15: If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the pit. Alexander III also, following the dictate of right reason, seems to hint at this, as is found ext. de ætate & qualitate præficiendorum, c. indecoris, saying: It is unseemly that those should rule churches who do not know how to govern themselves, since persons who excel in discretion and shine with the honesty of their morals ought to be admitted to the rule of churches. Gregory IX (as is found ext. de electio. cum in magistrum) seems to agree, saying: He who has not taken on the form of a disciple ought not to be assumed as a master, nor is one to be promoted who does not know how to be subject, etc. From these and very many other things it is plain that natural equity requires that boys, who know how to govern neither themselves nor others, ought not to be assumed to the rule and care of souls. And yet, against this natural equity, the Pope can command, according to the Gloss, which, as is found ext. de ætate & qualitate præficiendorum, super c. eam te, says: if the Pope were to write in favour of someone less worthy from certain knowledge, his command would have to be obeyed, because it amounts to sacrilege to doubt whether he is worthy whom the prince has chosen, 17.q.4. §. qui autem, & cap. de crimine sacrilegii l.2. Alexander III also seems to have commanded this, as is found ext. de ætate & qualitate præficiendorum, since he did not remove from the churches boys under ten years of age, which had been granted to them by the bishop of Coventry, but knowingly tolerated them and ordered that they be tolerated.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Vbi arguitur contra primam opinionem, scilicet quod sit falsa, periculosa, perniciosa, & haereticalis.
units.tr: Where the first opinion is argued against, namely that it is false, dangerous, pernicious, and heretical.

units.la: Dissip. Pro praedicta opinione allegationes retigisti: & aestimo fortiores: ideo pro ea ad praesens alias non adducas, quia istae soluuntur patenter: sed ad alias in contrarium posset forsitan leuiter respondéri. Magister. Sunt nonnulli, qui opinionem praescriptam falsam, periculosam, perniciosam ac haereticalem aestimant, quod multipliciter probare conantur. Lex enim Christiana ex institutione Christi est lex libertatis respectu veteris legis: quae respectu nouae legis fuit lex seruitutis. Sed si Papa haberet à Christo talem plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia posset, quae non sunt contra legem diuinam, nec contra legem naturae: lex Christiana ex institutione Christi esset lex intolerabilis seruitutis: & multo maioris seruitutis quam fuerit lex vetus, ergo Papa non habet à Christo talem plenitudinem potestatis, tam in spiritualibus quam in temporalibus. Maior auctoritatibus apertissimis scripturae diuinae videtur posse probari, beatus enim Iacobus in canonica sua ca. 1. eam vocat legem perfectae libertatis, dicens: Quicunque prospexerit in lege perfecta libertatis, & permanserit in ea non auditor obliuiosus factus, sed factor operis: hic beatus erit in facto suo. Et Apostolus ad Galat. ait: neque Titus qui mecum erat, cum esset gentilis, compulsus est circuncidi: sed propter introductos falsos fratres, qui introierant explorare libertatem nostram, quam habemus in Christo Iesu, vt nos in seruitutem redigerent, quibus nec ad horam cessimus subiectioni, vt veritas euangelica permaneat apud vos. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod lex euangelica est lex libertatis, per quam Christiani à seruitute sunt erepti vltra in seruitutem minime reducendi. Quod etiam Apostolus cap. quint. videtur asserere dicens: vtinam & abscindantur, qui vos conturbant, vos enim in libertatem vocati estis fratres, tantum ne libertatem in occasionem detis carnis, sed per charitatem seruite inuicem. Item beatus Petrus, vt habetur Actuum decimo quinto ait: Quid tentatis Deum imponere iugum super ceruices discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus? Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Christianis non est tam graue iugum seruitutis impositum, sicut fuit positum super Iudaeos. Vnde beatus Iacobus ibidem post verba Petri dixit: Ego iudico non inquietari eos, qui ex gentibus conuertuntur ad Deum: sed scribere ad eos vt abstineant se à contaminationibus simulachrorum, & fornicatione, & suffocato sanguine, & haec sententia Iacobi ab Apostolis & senioribus, imo à Spiritu sancto extitit approbata. Vnde & ibidem subiungitur: Tunc placuit Apostolis & senioribus cum omni ecclesia eligere viros ex eis, & mittere Antiochiam cum Paulo & Barnaba, Iudam qui cognominatur Barsabas, & viros primos in fratribus, scribentes per manus eorum epistolam continentem hac: Apostoli & seniores fratres. Et post: visum est Spiritui sancto & nobis, nihil vltra imponere vobis onerum, quam necessaria: vt abstineatis ab immolatione simulacrorum & sanguine suffocato & fornicatione: à quibus custodientes vos bene agetis. Ex quibus colligitur, quod Christiani per legem euangelicam sunt à seruitute multiplici liberati, & quod lex euangelica est lex minoris seruitutis, quam fuerit lex vetus. Quod Augustinus ad inquisitiones Ianuarii, vt habetur distinctione duodecim cap. omnia, videtur innuere manifeste, dicens de quibusdam, qui Christianam religionem seruitute nimia oppresserunt: quamuis enim neque hoc inueniri possit, quomodo contrafiedem sint: ipsam tamen religionem (quam paucissimis & manifestissimis celebrationum sacramentis misericordia Dei voluit esse liberam) seruilibus oneribus premunt, adeo vt tolerabilior fit conditio Iudaeorum: qui etsi iam tempus liberationis non agnouerunt, legalibus tamen sacramentis, non humanis praesumptionibus subiiciuntur. Item Apostolus ad Galatas quart. Non sumus ancilla filii, sed libera, qua libertate Christus nos liberauit, state, & nolite iterum iugo seruitutis contineri. Et Apostolus secund. ad Corinth. tert. Vbi autem Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. Ex quibus omnibus colligitur, quod maioris libertatis est lex noua quam vetus. Minor autem praedictae allegationis, quod scilicet lex noua siue euangelica esset intolerabilis seruitutis, & maioris quam fuerit lex vetus: si Papa haberet ex institutione Christi talem plenitudinem potestatis, tam in spiritualibus quam in temporalibus, videtur probatione nullatenus indigere.
units.tr: Dissip. You have advanced arguments for the aforesaid opinion, and I judge them stronger. So I will not put forward others for it at present, since these are plainly answered; but to the arguments on the other side one could perhaps reply lightly. Magister. There are some who judge the aforesaid opinion false, dangerous, pernicious, and heretical, and they try to prove this in many ways. The Christian law, by the institution of Christ, is a law of liberty in comparison with the old law, which in comparison with the new law was a law of bondage. But if the Pope had from Christ such a fullness of power that he could do everything that is not against the divine law or the law of nature, then the Christian law, by the institution of Christ, would be a law of intolerable bondage, and of far greater bondage than the old law was. Therefore the Pope does not have from Christ such a fullness of power, both in spiritual and in temporal matters. The major premise seems to be provable from the most manifest authorities of divine Scripture. For the blessed James, in his canonical epistle, chapter 1, calls it the law of perfect liberty, saying: Whoever looks into the perfect law of liberty, and continues in it, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in his doing. And the Apostle to the Galatians says: But neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised; and that because of false brethren secretly brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage; to whom we did not yield, no, not for an hour, that the truth of the gospel might continue with you. From these words it is clear that the gospel law is a law of liberty, by which Christians have been delivered from bondage, and are by no means to be led back into it. The Apostle seems to assert the same in chapter 5, saying: I would they were even cut off which trouble you. For you, brethren, have been called to liberty; only do not use liberty as an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another. Likewise the blessed Peter, as is found in Acts 15, says: Why do you tempt God by putting a yoke on the necks of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? From these words it is gathered that a yoke of bondage so heavy was not laid on Christians as was laid on the Jews. Hence the blessed James, in the same place, after Peter's words said: I judge that we should not trouble those among the Gentiles who turn to God, but write to them that they abstain from pollutions of idols, from fornication, from what is strangled, and from blood. And this opinion of James was approved by the Apostles and elders, indeed by the Holy Spirit. Hence it is added in the same place: Then it pleased the Apostles and elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas, called Barsabas, and Silas, leading men among the brethren; writing by them a letter in this form: The apostles and elders, brethren. And after: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication; if you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. From these it is gathered that Christians, through the gospel law, have been freed from many kinds of bondage, and that the gospel law is a law of less bondage than the old law was. Augustine, in his letters to Januarius, as found in Distinction 12, chapter Omnia, seems clearly to hint at this, speaking of certain people who oppressed the Christian religion with excessive bondage: For although it cannot be found how these things are consistent, they nevertheless burden that religion (which by the mercy of God was willed to be free, with very few and very plain celebrations of sacraments) with servile burdens, so that the condition of the Jews becomes more bearable; for they, though they have not recognized the time of liberation, are nevertheless subject to legal sacraments, not to human presumptions. Likewise the Apostle to the Galatians, chapter 4: We are not children of the bondwoman but of the free; with which liberty Christ has made us free. Stand fast, therefore, and do not be entangled again with a yoke of bondage. And the Apostle, 2 Corinthians, chapter 3: Now where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. From all these it is gathered that the new law is a law of greater liberty than the old. As to the minor premise of the argument, namely that the new or gospel law would be a law of intolerable bondage, and of greater bondage than the old law was, if the Pope had by the institution of Christ such a fullness of power, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, it seems in no way to need proof.

units.la: Si enim hoc esset, omnes Christiani essent serui: & nullus esset liberae conditionis, omnes enim essent serui summi Pontificis, & summus Pontifex tantam potestatem in temporalibus haberet super Imperatorem, & reges & principes, & laicos vniuersos, ac omnes omnino Christianos, & quantum ad personam, & quantum ad res ipsorum, quantam vnquam Dominus temporalis habuit, vel habere potuit super quemcunquem seruum. Ita quod Papa libere posset priuare reges & principes, ac omnes alios Christianos regnis & omnibus rebus: reges & principes quibuscunque aliis subdere, & constituere eos seruos ipsorum. Haec enim & similia non sunt contra legem diuinam nec contra legem naturae: quia si essent contra legem diuinam, vel legem naturae, ipsissimet regibus & aliis Christianis essent illicita: & per consequens nullis liceret res suas alteri dare, vel se alterius subiicere potestati. Et ita constat, quod lex Christiana esset maioris seruitutis, quo ad temporalia, quam lex vetus, si Papa in temporalibus haberet huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis, quia illi qui erant sub lege Mosaica, nulli mortali erant in temporalibus tali modo subiecti, quia tale dominium, nec rex nec summus Pontifex habebant. Vnde & Naboth Israelites laudabiliter denegauit dare & vendere vineam suam regi cupienti emere ipsam. Esset etiam lex moderna maioris seruitutis, uitutis, quoad spiritualia, siue quoad illa, quæ pertinent vel pertinere possunt ad exteriorem cultum diuinum, quam fuerit lex Mosaica, quia si Papa haberet talem plenitudinem potestatis, plures & graviores huiusmodi observantias corporales imponere regibus & principibus ac omnibus Christianis, quam fuerint in lege veteri ordinatæ, nec cuicunque Christiano liceret in huiusmodi non obedire, si Papa haberet talem plenitudinem potestatis. Ex istis concluditur, quod prædicta opinio de plenitudine potestatis summi Pontificis non solum falsa, sed etiam hæreticalis est habenda, cum sit manifeste contra Scripturam sacram, asserentem quod lex Christiana est lex libertatis: & per consequens Christiani non fiunt serui cuiuscunque mortalis per legem Christianam, sed liberi sunt, quantum est de ratione euangelicæ legis. Est etiam (vt dicunt) perniciosa & periculosa: quia si Papa vteretur tali potestate priuando reges & alios Christianos regnis & rebus suis pro suæ voluntatis arbitrio, & eos subiiciendo seruituti vel operibus seruilibus, orirentur schismata & dissensiones, bella, guerræ inter Christianos: etiam periculum & dispendium totius Christianitatis.
units.tr: For if this were so, all Christians would be slaves, and none would be of free condition; for all would be slaves of the supreme Pontiff, and the supreme Pontiff would have over the Emperor, kings and princes, all laymen, and absolutely all Christians, both as to their persons and as to their goods, as great a power as any temporal lord ever had or could have over any slave whatever. So the Pope could freely deprive kings and princes and all other Christians of their kingdoms and all their possessions, subject kings and princes to whomever he pleased, and make them his slaves. For these things and similar ones are not against the divine law nor against the law of nature; for if they were against the divine law or the law of nature, they would be unlawful even for the kings and other Christians themselves, and consequently no one would be allowed to give his goods to another, or to submit himself to another's power. And so it is clear that the Christian law would be a law of greater bondage, as to temporal matters, than the old law, if the Pope had such a fullness of power in temporal matters; because those who were under the Mosaic law were in temporal matters subject to no mortal in such a way, since neither king nor supreme Pontiff had such dominion. Hence also Naboth the Israelite rightly refused to give or sell his vineyard to the king who wished to buy it. The modern law would also be of greater bondage, as to spiritual matters, or as to those which pertain or can pertain to the external worship of God, than the Mosaic law was; for if the Pope had such a fullness of power, he could impose more and heavier bodily observances of this kind on kings, princes, and all Christians than were ordained in the old law; and no Christian would be permitted to disobey in such matters, if the Pope had such a fullness of power. From these things it is concluded that the aforesaid opinion about the fullness of power of the supreme Pontiff is to be held not only false but also heretical, since it is manifestly against holy Scripture, which asserts that the Christian law is a law of liberty; and consequently Christians do not become slaves of any mortal through the Christian law, but are free, as far as the nature of the gospel law is concerned. It is also (as they say) pernicious and dangerous: for if the Pope were to use such power, depriving kings and other Christians of their kingdoms and goods at the discretion of his own will, and subjecting them to servitude or servile works, there would arise schisms and dissensions, wars and battles among Christians, and danger and loss to all Christendom.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: In quo ponitur exposiio prædicta rationis de libertate euangelica, secundum primam opinionem, & probatur duabus rationibus, ad quas respondetur infra c. 7.
units.tr: In which the aforesaid explanation of the reason concerning evangelical liberty is set out according to the first opinion, and is proved by two arguments, to which an answer is given below in chapter 7.

units.la: DIscipulus. Quia, vt puto, istud est principalius vel de principalibus fundamentis & motiuis, quare quidam dicunt, quod Papa non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis. Ideo contra ipsum volo obiicere, vt responsionibus, quas recitabis ad obiectiones contra ipsum, quale sit magis apparet. Videtur itaque, quod lex Christiana non dicatur in Scripturis sacris lex libertatis: quia per eam Christiani fiant liberi, ne sint subiecti in omnibus summo Pontifici, quod innuit motiuum præcedens. Sed dicitur lex libertatis: quia per eam Christiani efficiuntur liberi à seruitute peccati vel legis Mosaicæ. Vnde & plures auctoritates adductæ expresse loquuntur de libertate à seruitute legis Mosaicæ: sicut illa ad Galat. 2. & 5. & illa Actum 15. & illa ad Galat. 4. Aliæ autem auctoritates intelligi possunt de libertate à seruitute peccati, igitur per ipsas probari non potest, quod Christiani per legem Christianam efficiuntur liberi à seruitute, qua tenentur summo Pontifici: ne sc. in omnibus temporalibus & spiritualibus sint sibi subiecti, quæ non sunt contra legem Dei, nec contra legem naturæ. Vnde & quod auctoritates scripturæ diuinæ non debeant intelligi de libertate & subiectione, qua subduntur Christiani summo Pontifici, ratione probatur.
