Nam si lex Christiana esset taliter lex libertatis, nulli liceret se subdere summo Pontifici vel alii cuicunque mortali. Et ita, vt quidam dicunt Fratres Minores, si per regulam suam tenentur in omnibus obedire summo Pontifici, eorum regula esset hæreticalis, quia esset contra legem Christianam, quæ est lex libertatis liberans Christianos ne homini sint subiecti. Amplius secundum beatum Iacobum, vt allegatum est, lex Christiana est lex perfectæ libertatis, perfecta autem libertas omni seruituti repugnat, ergo si lex Christiana est lex libertatis liberans Christianos, ne homini sint subiecti: sequitur quod nullus debet esse seruus hominis cuiuscunque. Et ita reges & principes & alii laici, & etiam ecclesia nullos seruos haberent, quod legibus ciuilibus & sacris canonibus obuiat manifeste. Propter ista videtur, quod motiuum præscriptum non probatur, quod Papa non habeat plenitudinem potestatis, tam in spiritualibus quam in temporalibus, tu autem narra, quomodo respondetur ad ista.
units.tr: THE DISCIPLE. Since, as I think, this is one of the principal foundations and motives why some say that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power, I want to object against it, so that it may become clearer what kind of answers you will give to the objections against it. It seems, then, that the Christian law is not called in the holy Scriptures a law of liberty because through it Christians become free so as not to be subject to the highest Pontiff in everything, which the preceding motive suggests. But it is called a law of liberty because through it Christians are made free from the bondage of sin or of the Mosaic law. Hence the many authorities cited expressly speak of liberty from the bondage of the Mosaic law, such as that in Galatians 2 and 5, that in Acts 15, and that in Galatians 4. Other authorities, however, can be understood of liberty from the bondage of sin; therefore it cannot be proved by them that Christians, through the Christian law, are made free from the servitude by which they are bound to the highest Pontiff, namely, that in all temporal and spiritual matters they are not subject to him, which are not contrary to the law of God or the law of nature. Hence, that the authorities of divine Scripture ought not to be understood of the liberty and subjection by which Christians are subject to the highest Pontiff, is proved by reason. For if the Christian law were in such a way a law of liberty, it would not be lawful for anyone to subject himself to the highest Pontiff or to any other mortal. And so, as some Friars Minor say, if by their rule they are bound to obey the highest Pontiff in all things, their rule would be heretical, because it would be contrary to the Christian law, which is the law of liberty freeing Christians from being subject to any man. Furthermore, according to the blessed James, as has been cited, the Christian law is the law of perfect liberty; but perfect liberty is incompatible with all servitude. Therefore, if the Christian law is the law of liberty freeing Christians from being subject to any man, it follows that no one ought to be the servant of any man whatever. And thus kings, princes and other laymen, and also the Church, would have no servants, which plainly conflicts with civil laws and sacred canons. For these reasons it seems that the stated motive, that the Pope does not have fullness of power both in spiritual and in temporal matters, is not proved. Now you, tell me how these points are answered.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Vbi ponitur confutatio prædictæ exusionis, expositionis & rationis contra primam opinionem, & ad rationes capituli præcedentis respondetur.
units.tr: Where the refutation of the aforesaid exposition, explanation and reasoning against the first opinion is set out, and the arguments of the preceding chapter are answered.

units.la: Magister. Ad primum istorum dicitur, quod quamuis auctoritates specialem faciant mentionem de libertate à seruitute Mosaicæ legis: tamen omnes intelligi debent ab omni seruitute tanta, quanta fuit seruitus Mosaicæ legis, & hoc saltem quo ad aliqua negatiue, vt scilicet nullus per euangelicam legem obligetur ad tantam seruitutem, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis, licet aliqui Christiani ratione delicti vel ex voluntate, seruitute quacunque occasione (non tamen per legem Christianam) tanta seruitute vel maiori teneantur astricti. Si enim Christiani quacunque seruitute, quo ad opera exteriora, tanta vel maiori, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis, per legem euangelicam tenerentur, non posset lex euangelica magis dici lex libertatis, quam lex Mosaica: quantumcunque liberari essent à seruitute Mosaicæ legis.
units.tr: Master. To the first of these it is said that although the authorities make specific mention of liberty from the bondage of the Mosaic law, they must nevertheless all be understood as referring to freedom from every bondage as great as the bondage of the Mosaic law. This holds at least negatively, namely that no one is bound by the gospel law to a bondage as great as that of the old law, although some Christians, by reason of a crime or of their own will, or on some other occasion, may be bound to a bondage equal or greater (though not by the Christian law). For if Christians were bound by the gospel law to an external bondage, in outward works, equal or greater than that of the old law, the gospel law could no more be called a law of liberty than the Mosaic law, however much they were freed from the bondage of the Mosaic law.

units.la: Qui enim liberatur ab vna seruitute, & premitur alia æquali vel maiori: non est magis liber, quam prius extiterat. Sicut qui liberatur ab vno vinculo corporali, & alio æquali vel forto ac confringitur, non est solutus, sed magis ligatus. Cum vero lex euangelica secundum veritatem scripturæ diuinæ sit lex magis libertatis, quam vetus lex: legem euangelicam Christiani neque seruituti legis Mosaicæ, neque cuicunque alii seruituti exteriori maiori vel tantæ, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis, subduntur. Quare etiam auctoritates illæ, quæ occasione seruitutis veteris legis de libertate Christianorum loquuntur, de libertate ab omni seruitute tanta, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis debent intelligi. Quare cum seruitus, qua aliquis alteri obligatur in omnibus obedire, quæ non sunt contra legem diuinam: nec contra legem naturæ, sit maior, quam fuerit seruitus veteris legis: etiam de libertate ab illa seruitute auctoritates præscriptæ debent intelligi. Et ita, vt dicunt isti, per ipsas probatur aperte, quod memorata opinio de plenitudine potestatis summi Pontificis est hæreticalis, tanquam contraria diuinæ scripturæ. Discipulus. Antequam procedatur contra ista obiicio, quia non videtur, quod quamuis Papa haberet huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis: Christiani essent pressi maiori seruitute, vel tanta, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis. Nam talem potestatem habent aliqui prælati religiosi super fratres suos, vel possent habere. Quia possunt aliqui religiosi promittere in omnibus obedientiam prælatis suis: & tamen illi religiosi non premerentur tanta seruitute, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis: quia nec tales religiosi essent serui, non enim religiosi sunt serui suorum prælatorum: nec prælati sunt Domini fratrum suorum. Magister. Huic respondetur, quod quamuis Papa possit habere talem potestatem supra illum, qui voluerit fieri seruus Papæ, & se in omnibus subdere potestati ipsius: tamen nec Papa, nec aliquis prælatus religiosus habet talem potestatem super quoscunque religiosos: qui scilicet vouent vel vouerunt obedientiam, paupertatem, & castitatem, quia religiosi tales quicunque regulam quam vouent seruare tenentur. Propter quod nec Papa, nec alius habet talem plenitudinem potestatis super ipsos, nec ipsi sunt serui Papæ, vel alterius prælati, secundum quod nomen seruorum in scientiis legalibus frequenter accipitur, quia nec Papa, nec alius potest eos occupare in seruilibus operibus, dimissis illis, quæ spectant ad substantiam regulæ suæ: nec potest eis præcipere vt habeant proprium vel contrahant matrimonium: quæ tamen sunt licita de se, licet facta sint illicita religiosis per votum sponte ab eis emissum. Discipulus. De potestate Papæ super rel giosos postea disputemus, ideo de hac materia amplius ad præsens non loquaris. Sed narra an secundum istos non solum per hoc, quod auctoritates introductæ affirmant legem Christianam esse legem libertatis, sed etiam per alia verba in auctoritatibus eisdem accepta possit probari, quod Christiani per legem euangelicam tanta seruitute minime constringuntur, quanta fuit veteris legis. Magister. Dicunt, quod per auctoritates prædictas posset hoc probari; non tamen æque patenter per omnes. Discipulus. Dic, per quas dicunt isti hoc patentius posse probari. Magister. Dicunt, quod per acceptam de Actibus 15. ca. patenter hoc probatur, nam Apostoli inspiratione Spiritus sancti nunciauerunt gentibus libertatem à iugo seruitutis ad consolationem ipsarum, & ne dolerent se per seruitutem onerosam inquietari. Vnde Iacobus (vt allegatum est) dixit: ego iudico non inquietari eos, qui ex gentibus conuertuntur ad Deum, & de ipsis gentibus conuersis ad Deum recepta epistola Apostolorum seniorum super prædicta libertate sic scribitur eodem cap. Quam cum legissent, gaudisi sunt super consolatione, sed si conuersi ex gentibus liberati fuissent à seruitute legis Dei, & maiori seruitute Petri & successorum eius fuissent subiecti: & de inquietatione maiorum non immerito doluissent, & materiam consolationis minime habuissent. Ab omni igitur seruitute maiori: & tanta, quanta fuit seruitus legis Mosaicæ, liberati fuerunt. Quod in verbis Apostolorum insinuatur, cum dicitur: Visum est Spiritui sancto, & nobis, nihil vltra imponere vobis oneris, quam hæc necessaria, vt abstineatis, &c. Si enim nihil vltra oneris voluerunt eis imponere: noluerunt eis imponere seruitutem neque maiorem, neque tantam, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis. Discipulus. Videtur quod ista verba nihil vltra imponere vobis oneris, non debeant tam generaliter intelligi. Nam licet Apostoli non imposuerint Christianis onera veteris legis: imposuerunt eis tamen multa præter illa, quæ nominantur in verbis præmissis. Multos enim canones condiderunt, in quibus præceperunt multa, præter illa quæ enumerantur in verbis prædictis, sicut patet in decretis distinctione decim. sext. cap. propter, & duodecim. quæst. prim. cap. dilectissimis, & cap. sint manifestæ, & cap. ex his, verba igitur præmissa Actuum decimo quinto, solum debent intelligi de onere legis Mosaicæ. Magister. Ad hoc respondetur, quod licet Apostoli plures canones condiderint & præceperint multa præter illa, quæ enumerantur Actuum decimo quinto, nihil tamen præceperunt subditis minime requisitis & non consentientibus, nisi quæ erant de lege diuina & iure naturali: & necessitas vel vtilitas publica postulabat: & quorum præceptio absque dispendio non poterat prætermitti: in quibus & qualibus nunc summus Pontifex obtinet potestatem.
units.tr: For one who is freed from one bondage but pressed by another equal or greater is no freer than he was before. Just as one who is released from one bodily chain, but is bound by another equal or stronger chain, is not loosed but more tightly bound. But since the gospel law, according to the truth of divine Scripture, is a law of greater liberty than the old law, Christians are subject neither to the bondage of the Mosaic law, nor to any other external bondage greater than or as great as that of the old law. Therefore those authorities which speak of the liberty of Christians on the occasion of the bondage of the old law must also be understood as speaking of liberty from every bondage as great as the bondage of the old law. Hence, since the bondage by which someone is obliged to another to obey in all things that are not contrary to divine law or the law of nature is greater than the bondage of the old law, the aforesaid authorities must also be understood as speaking of liberty from that bondage. And so, as these men say, it is clearly proved by them that the aforesaid opinion concerning the fullness of the power of the supreme Pontiff is heretical, as being contrary to divine Scripture. Disciple. Before we proceed against these points, I object, because it does not seem that, even if the Pope had such a fullness of power, Christians would be pressed by a greater bondage, or one as great as that of the old law. For some religious prelates have, or could have, such power over their brothers. For some religious can promise obedience to their prelates in all things, and yet those religious are not pressed by a bondage as great as that of the old law, because such religious are not slaves, since religious are not slaves of their prelates, nor are prelates lords of their brothers. Master. To this it is answered that although the Pope may have such power over one who wishes to become the Pope's servant and to submit himself to his power in all things, neither the Pope nor any religious prelate has such power over all religious who vow, or have vowed, obedience, poverty and chastity; for all such religious are bound to keep the rule which they vow. Therefore neither the Pope nor anyone else has such a fullness of power over them, nor are they slaves of the Pope or of any other prelate, in the sense in which the name of slaves is commonly used in legal writings. For neither the Pope nor anyone else can employ them in servile works, setting aside those things which pertain to the substance of their rule, nor can he order them to have property or to contract marriage. Yet these things are in themselves lawful, though they become unlawful for religious through the vow which they have freely made. Disciple. We shall dispute later about the power of the Pope over religious, so do not speak further of that matter for now. But tell me whether, according to these men, it can be proved not only by the fact that the introduced authorities affirm the Christian law to be a law of liberty, but also by other words taken from the same authorities, that Christians are by the gospel law not bound by a bondage as great as that of the old law. Master. They say that this could be proved by the aforesaid authorities, but not equally clearly by all of them. Disciple. Tell me which of them they say can be proved more clearly. Master. They say that this is clearly proved from the fifteenth chapter of Acts. For the Apostles, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, announced to the Gentiles liberty from the yoke of bondage, for their comfort, and so that they should not grieve at being troubled by a burdensome servitude. Hence James (as was alleged) said: "I judge that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who are converted to God." And concerning these Gentiles converted to God, the letter of the Apostles and elders concerning the aforesaid liberty is written thus in the same chapter: "When they had read it, they rejoiced at the consolation." But if the converts from the Gentiles had been freed from the bondage of the law of God, and had been subject to a greater bondage to Peter and his successors, they would have grieved, not undeservedly, at the trouble of greater burdens, and would not have had any matter for consolation. Therefore they were freed from every greater bondage, and from one as great as the bondage of the Mosaic law. This is hinted at in the words of the Apostles, when they say: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain," etc. For if they wished to lay no greater burden upon them, they did not wish to impose upon them a bondage either greater than, or as great as, that of the old law. Disciple. It seems that these words, "to lay upon you no greater burden," ought not to be understood so generally. For although the Apostles did not impose upon Christians the burdens of the old law, they nevertheless imposed many things besides those named in the words quoted. For they drew up many canons, in which they commanded many things beyond those enumerated in the aforesaid words, as is clear in the Decretum, distinction 16, chapter "Propter," and in cause 12, question 1, chapters "Dilectissimis," "Sint manifestae," and "Ex his." Therefore the aforesaid words of Acts 15 must be understood only of the burden of the Mosaic law. Master. To this it is answered that although the Apostles drew up many canons and commanded many things beyond those enumerated in Acts 15, they nevertheless commanded nothing to subjects who were not required and did not consent, except what was of divine law and the law of nature, or what public necessity or utility demanded, and what could not be omitted without loss. It is in these matters, and in such matters, that the supreme Pontiff now holds power.

units.la: Discipulus. Istud vltimum dictum (vt puto) non potest ad intentionem dicentium verbis breuibus explicari, ideo ipso dimisso ad sensus, quia de ipso post tractabimus: Dic an per aliquam aliam auctoritatem prius adductam, sicut isti patenter posse probari, quod Scriptura loquens de libertate legis euangelicæ dicit intelligi, etiam de libertate ab alia seruitute, quam à seruitute legis Mosaicæ. Magister. Hoc dicunt posse ostendi auctoritate Apostoli, cum dicit secundo ad Corinth. tertio. Vbi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas, ibi enim Apostolus non loquitur specialiter de libertate à seruitute legis veteris: sed magis generaliter, igitur intelligit Apostolus, quod vbi est Spiritus Domini: ibi non solum est libertas à seruitute veteris legis: sed etiam ibi libertas est ab omni seruitute, quoad opera exteriora: quæ est tanta, quanta fuit seruitus veteris legis.
units.tr: Disciple. That last statement (as I think) cannot be explained in brief words to the intention of those who say it. So, setting it aside, we turn to the meanings, since we shall treat it later. Tell me whether, by some other authority adduced earlier, as these men clearly say can be proved, Scripture, speaking of the liberty of the gospel law, is to be understood as also speaking of liberty from some other bondage than the bondage of the Mosaic law. Master. They say this can be shown by the authority of the Apostle when he says in 2 Corinthians 3: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." For there the Apostle does not speak specifically of liberty from the bondage of the old law, but rather in general. Therefore the Apostle understands that where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is not only liberty from the bondage of the old law, but there is liberty from every bondage in outward works, which is as great as the bondage of the old law.

units.la: Quod auctoritatibus sanctorum Patrum ostenditur, nam per illam auctoritatem Apostoli sancti Patres probant, quod licet clericis, inuitis episcopis, monasteria monachorum intrare. Nam enim Vrbanus Papa, vt legitur 19. quæstion. 2. cap. dua: Qui Spiritu Dei aguntur, lege Dei ducuntur, quis est, qui possit Spiritui sancto digne resistere? quisquis igitur hoc Spiritu ducitur, etiam episcopo suo contradicente, eat liber nostra auctoritate, iusto enim lex non est posita: sed ubi spiritus Dei est, ibi libertas, & si spiritu Dei deducimini, non estis sub lege. Innocentius Tertius ext. de regularibus, c. licet, ait: Licet quibusdam monachis. Et infra: quia tamen ubi spiritus Dei est, ibi libertas, & qui spiritu Dei aguntur non sunt sub lege, & quia lex non est posita iusto. Ea ratione hoc videtur illis concessum fuisse, ne quis ex temeritate vel levitate in iacturam, vel iniuriam sui ordinis sub praetextu maioris religionis ad alium ordinem transfuolaret. Ex quibus colligitur, quod per libertatem concessam Christianis probatur, quod licet clericis ad religionem, & religiosis ad arctiorem transire: quod tamen probari non posset, si per libertatem Christianorum Apostolus intelligeret tantummodo libertatem a servitute Mosaicae legis. Hoc etiam per auctoritatem Augustini superius allegatam videtur posse expresse probari. Nam Augustinus in verbis illis per libertatem, quam Christiana religio ex misericordia Dei consecuta est, illos iudicat arguendo, qui eandem religionem diversis oneribus opprimebant, adeo ut tolerabilior sit conditio Iudaeorum, quam Christianorum: qui tamen oneribus legis Mosaicae Christianos minime deprimebant. Igitur intendit Augustinus, ut Christiana religio non solum sit liberata ab oneribus veteris legis: sed etiam ab aliis oneribus, quae aequaliter vel magis premant, quam onera Mosaicae legis. Discipulus. Dic, quomodo respondetur ad rationes, quibus supra capitulo sexto visus fui probare: quod auctoritates adductae cap. quint. non debent intelligi de libertate a subiectione, qua Christiani secundum primam sententiam summo Pontifici sunt subiecti. Magister. Ad primam ipsarum respondetur secundum quosdam, quod auctoritates de libertate evangelicae legis non debent, quo ad omnes intelligi affirmatiue, sed quo ad multos negatiue: sicut factum est primo, quemadmodum illa verba Apostoli: Spiritus sit unus uxoris & viri, & illa Salvatoris: In ore duorum vel trium stat omne verbum, & multae aliae debent intelligi negatiue, non enim illi, qui erant servi ante conversionem ad fidem, per conversionem fiebant liberi: sed per legem evangelicam nullus ducebatur ad maiorem servitutem, quam erat servitus veteris legis. Et ideo licet per evangelicam legem non fiat servus Papae: absque transgressione eiusdem legis potest quis, si sponte voluerit se facere servum Papae, vel si ex alia iusta & licita causa fiat servus Papae: in nullo derogatur evangelicae legi, quia lex evangelica licet non inducat huiusmodi servitutem, non tamen prohibet. Quod autem ibidem accipitur, quod Fratres Minores tenentur in omnibus obedire Papae: dicunt isti falsum esse, licet quidam Fratres Minores (ut fertur) hoc non teneant dicentes, quod liceret eis & tenentur etiam accipere uxores, si sola voluntate Papae hoc praeciperetur, de quibus postea in hoc tractatu, & etiam in novo tractatu huius tertiae partis nostri Dialogi tractabimus. Fratres enim Minores non tenentur obedire Papae praecipienti aliquid contra substantiam regulae suae, & ideo regula eorum non haereticalis, sed catholica est censenda. Ad secundam rationem, quam fecisti, respondetur quod lex Christiana non dicitur lex libertatis, quia liberat Christianos ab omni servitute: sed quia non premit Christianos tanta servitute, quanta pressi fuere Iudaei, & ideo licet regibus & aliis Christianis servos habere, licet per legem Christianam nullus Christianus fiat servus cuiuscunque. Et ad beat. Iacobum dicitur, quod non intendit legem Christianam esse legem perfectae libertatis, ut nullus Christianus cuicunque homini sit subiectus, Christiani enim Papae sunt subiecti: & multis principibus & aliis Christianis subduntur. Sed ideo dicit eam esse legem perfectae libertatis: quia per eam religio Christiana paucis sacramentis & sacramentalibus, seu ceremonialibus ex institutione divina subiicitur: & per ipsam nullus Christianus servus cuiuscunque mortalis efficitur, nec etiam nisi in his, quae spectant ad necessitatem vel utilitatem ipsius aut reipublicae alicuius hominis subditur potestati. Quare pro se & omnibus populis universis & praelatis ecclesiae dicit Apostolus 2. ad Corinth. ultim. Non enim possumus aliquid adversus veritatem: sed pro veritate. Et post hoc: Absens scribo, non ut praesens durius agam secundum potestatem, quam Dominus dedit mihi in aedificationem & non in destructionem vestram. Ex quibus colligitur, quod Apostoli nullam potestatem habuerunt a Deo super fidelibus, nisi quae ad utilitatem subiecti vel communitatis cuiuscunque inducit. Etiam quia paucis divinis est suppositi sacramentis, merito debet dici lex perfectae libertatis, praesertim respectu legis Mosaicae, quae quamplurimus sacramentis & ceremoniis vix portabilibus subiectos involuit, non tamen dicitur lex perfectissimae libertatis, in perfectione enim sunt gradus, quare non omne perfectum est perfectissimum reputandum, perfectissima autem libertas in hac vita mortali nequaquam habebitur.
units.tr: This is shown by the authority of the holy Fathers. For by that saying of the Apostle, the holy Fathers prove that clerics may enter monasteries of monks even against the will of their bishops. For Pope Urban says, as we read in 19 Quaest. 2, c. Dua: Those who are led by the Spirit of God are guided by the law of God. Who is able to resist the Holy Spirit worthily? Whoever therefore is led by this Spirit, even if his bishop contradicts, let him go free by our authority, for the law is not laid down for the righteous; but where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty, and if you are led by the Spirit of God, you are not under the law. Innocent III, in Ext. de regularibus, c. Licet, says: It is permitted to some monks. And below: because where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty, and those who are led by the Spirit of God are not under the law, and because the law is not laid down for the righteous. For this reason it seems to have been granted to them, so that no one, out of rashness or fickleness, should fly over to another order under the pretext of greater holiness, to the loss or injury of his own order. From these things it is gathered that by the liberty granted to Christians it is proved that clerics may pass to a religious life, and religious to a stricter one. This could not be proved, however, if the Apostle meant by the liberty of Christians only liberty from the servitude of the Mosaic law. This also seems able to be proved expressly by the authority of Augustine cited above. For Augustine, in those words, by the liberty which the Christian religion has obtained through the mercy of God, judges those who oppressed the same religion with various burdens, so that the condition of the Jews was more tolerable than that of the Christians, who nevertheless did not at all oppress the Christians with the burdens of the Mosaic law. Therefore Augustine intends that the Christian religion be freed not only from the burdens of the old law, but also from other burdens which press equally or more heavily than the burdens of the Mosaic law. Disciple. Tell me, how is answer made to the arguments which I seemed, in the sixth chapter above, to prove: that the authorities cited in the fifth chapter ought not to be understood of liberty from the subjection by which Christians, according to the first opinion, are subject to the supreme Pontiff? Master. To the first of them it is answered, according to some, that the authorities about the liberty of the evangelical law ought not to be understood affirmatively for all, but negatively for many, as was done first with those words of the Apostle: Let the spirit be one of wife and husband, and with that saying of the Saviour: In the mouth of two or three every word stands, and many others ought to be understood negatively. For those who were slaves before conversion to the faith did not become free through conversion; but by the evangelical law no one was led into greater servitude than the servitude of the old law. And therefore, although through the evangelical law no one is made a slave of the Pope, yet without transgression of that same law someone may, if he voluntarily wishes to make himself a slave of the Pope, or if he becomes a slave of the Pope from some other just and lawful cause; nothing is taken away from the evangelical law, because the evangelical law, although it does not bring about such servitude, does not however forbid it. As for what is there taken up, that the Lesser Brothers are bound to obey the Pope in all things, these men say it is false, although some Lesser Brothers (as it is reported) do not hold this, saying that it would be lawful for them, and they are even bound to take wives, if this were commanded by the will of the Pope alone; about which we will treat later in this treatise, and also in the new treatise of this third part of our Dialogue. For the Lesser Brothers are not bound to obey the Pope commanding anything contrary to the substance of their rule, and therefore their rule is to be judged not heretical but catholic. To the second argument which you made, it is answered that the Christian law is not called the law of liberty because it frees Christians from every servitude, but because it does not press Christians with such servitude as the Jews were pressed with; and therefore it is lawful for kings and other Christians to have slaves, although through the Christian law no Christian is made a slave of anyone. And as to blessed James, it is said that he did not intend the Christian law to be the law of perfect liberty in the sense that no Christian is subject to any man, for Christians are subject to the Pope, and are subordinated to many princes and other Christians. But he calls it the law of perfect liberty for this reason: because through it the Christian religion is subjected to few sacraments and sacramentals, or ceremonial rites, by divine institution; and through it no Christian is made the slave of any mortal, nor is he subject to the power of any man except in those matters which concern the necessity or usefulness of himself or of some commonwealth. Wherefore the Apostle says, for himself and for all peoples and all prelates of the Church, in 2 Cor. last chapter: For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. And after this: Being absent, I write, lest being present I should act more sharply, according to the power which the Lord has given me for building up and not for destroying you. From these things it is gathered that the Apostles had no power from God over the faithful except that which leads to the usefulness of the subject or of any community. Also, because it is subjected to few divine sacraments, it ought rightly to be called the law of perfect liberty, especially in comparison with the Mosaic law, which enveloped its subjects in very many sacraments and ceremonies, hardly bearable; yet it is not called the law of most perfect liberty, for there are degrees of perfection, and so not everything perfect is to be reckoned most perfect; but most perfect liberty will by no means be had in this mortal life.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: In quo probantur duo, sc. quod non omnes Christiani sunt servi Papae: & quod multi Christiani habent proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium.
units.tr: In which two things are proved: first, that not all Christians are servants of the Pope; and second, that many Christians have ownership and dominion over temporal goods.

units.la: Discipulus. Adhuc ut intelligatur profundius, quale sit motivum praecedens, cupio audire aliquas allegationes praeter scriptas, ad probandum quod non omnes homines sunt servi summi Pontificis, ex quo isti opinantes inferre nituntur, quod Papa non habet ex institutione Christi talem plenitudinem potestatis. Mag. Quod non omnes Christiani sint servi summi Pontificis secundum strictissimam significationem huius nominis servus, quod tamen secundum istos sequeretur, si Papa haberet tam in temporalibus, quam in spiritualibus huiusmodi plenitudine potestatis, multis modis ostenditur. Servus enim nulla proprietatem seu dominium cuiuscunque rei temporalis, dum manet seruus, potest habere: quia quicquid acquirit seruus, Domino acquirit & ipsius Domini est, reges autem & principes, ac alii quamplurimi Christiani habent dominium & potestatem quamplurium rerum temporalium, ergo non omnes homines sunt serui Papæ: secundum illam significationem nominis serui, secundum quam Dominus potest vendere, dare, & alienare seruum suum, & ab eo omnem rem temporalem propria voluntate auferre, quod tamen sequeretur, si Papa haberet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis. Discipulus. Quomodo probatur, quod reges & principes & plures alii Christiani habent proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium ? Magister. Hoc multis modis ostenditur, nam illi habent dominium & proprietatem rerum temporalium, per quorum iura temporalia possidentur, distinction. 8. quo iure, ergo Imperatores & reges habent dominium & proprietatem rerum temporalium. Amplius: illi habent dominium & proprietatem rerum temporalium, quorum legibus etiam summi Pontifices pro cursu temporalium rerum legibus Imperatorum & regum vtuntur, sed summi Pontifices pro cursu temporalium rerum legibus Imperatorum & regum vtuntur, distinction. 10. quoniam idem, & distinctio. 96. cum ad virum, ergo imperatores & reges habent proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium. Rursus: episcopi interdum præter res ecclesiæ habent res proprias 12. quæst. 1. cap. episcopi, & cap. manifesta, & t. certe, & ca. sicut manifeste, ergo alii, quam Papa possunt proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium possidere. Adhuc: reges & principes ac alii fideles laici donant res temporales ecclesiis, ergo habent proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium. Item Iudæi & infideles habent proprietatem rerum temporalium, ergo multo fortius reges & principes Christiani habent huiusmodi rerum temporalium proprietatem. Discipulus. Istud est ita diuulgatum, tam in legibus ciuilibus & canonicis, quam in communi opinione hominum, quod non curo pro ipso plures allegationes adducere. De quo tamen possem quærere: an sit hæreticum dicere, nullum Christianum habere proprietatem temporalium rerum: quod vero ad tractatum de iuribus Romani Imperii reseruare propono. Ideo redeamus ad probandum, quod non omnes Christiani sunt serui Papæ. Magister. Hoc aliter probatur, seruus non potest habere alium seruum, sed plures laici habent seruos, distinction. 54. cap. 1. & 2. & cap. quicunque, & in multis aliis capitulis, ergo non omnes homines sunt serui Papæ. Amplius: multi ab ecclesia consequuntur libertatem, 12. quæstion. 2. si quos de seruis ecclesiæ, & cap. episcopus, & cap. libertati, & in multis aliis capitulis habetur, quod non omnes homines sunt serui summi Pontificis, multi ergo homines sunt liberi. Quod Saluator testari videtur dicens Matth. 17. filii sunt liberi, & Apostolus ad Gal. 4. ait: Quanto tempore heres paruulus est, nihil differt a seruo, cum sit Dominus omnium: sed sub tutoribus & actoribus est vnusquisque vsque ad præfinitum tempus a Patre. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod cum venerit tempus præfinitum a Patre, differt a seruo, & per consequens tunc nec Papæ, nec alterius est seruus.
units.tr: Student. So that I may understand the preceding argument more deeply, I would like to hear some arguments besides those already written, to prove that not all men are servants of the supreme Pontiff. From this, those who hold this view try to infer that the Pope does not have such fullness of power by the institution of Christ. Master. That not all Christians are servants of the supreme Pontiff, in the strictest sense of the word servant, can be shown in many ways. This is what they would have to concede if the Pope had such fullness of power over temporal matters as well as spiritual ones. For a servant, as long as he remains a servant, can hold no ownership or dominion over any temporal thing. Whatever a servant acquires, he acquires for his master and it belongs to his master. But kings, princes and many other Christians have dominion and power over many temporal things. Therefore not all men are servants of the Pope, at least in the sense of servant in which a master may sell, give and alienate his servant, and take from him any temporal thing at his own will. Yet this would follow if the Pope had such fullness of power over temporal matters. Student. How is it proved that kings, princes and many other Christians have ownership and dominion over temporal goods? Master. This is shown in many ways. Those have dominion and ownership of temporal goods by whose temporal laws such goods are possessed, distinction 8, quo iure. Therefore emperors and kings have dominion and ownership of temporal goods. Further, those have dominion and ownership of temporal goods by whose laws even the supreme Pontiffs use the laws of emperors and kings in the course of temporal affairs. But the supreme Pontiffs do use the laws of emperors and kings in the course of temporal affairs, distinction 10, quoniam idem, and distinction 96, cum ad virum. Therefore emperors and kings have ownership and dominion of temporal goods. Again: bishops sometimes have their own goods besides the goods of the Church, 12 q. 1, cap. episcopi, cap. manifesta, t. certe, and ca. sicut manifeste. Therefore others besides the Pope can possess ownership and dominion of temporal goods. Moreover: kings, princes and other faithful laymen give temporal goods to churches. Therefore they have ownership and dominion of temporal goods. Likewise, Jews and unbelievers have ownership of temporal goods. Therefore Christian kings and princes have much more strongly such ownership of temporal goods. Student. This is so widely accepted, both in civil and canon law and in the common opinion of men, that I do not care to bring forward many arguments for it. Yet I could ask whether it is heretical to say that no Christian has ownership of temporal goods. However, I propose to reserve this for the treatise On the rights of the Roman Empire. So let us return to proving that not all Christians are servants of the Pope. Master. This is proved in another way. A servant cannot have another servant. But many laymen have servants, distinction 54, cap. 1 and 2, and cap. quicunque, and in many other chapters. Therefore not all men are servants of the Pope. Further: many obtain liberty from the Church, 12 q. 2, si quos de servis ecclesiae, and cap. episcopus, and cap. libertati, and it is found in many other chapters. So not all men are servants of the supreme Pontiff, and many men are therefore free. The Saviour seems to bear witness to this when he says in Matthew 17, the sons are free. And the Apostle says in Galatians 4: "As long as the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a servant, though he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the Father." From these words it is gathered that when the time appointed by the Father has come, he differs from a servant, and consequently at that time he is the servant neither of the Pope nor of anyone else.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod Papa non habet plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus, octo ratio- nibus, & est secunda opinio primo capitulo posita.
units.tr: In which it is proved, by eight reasons, that the Pope does not have fullness of power in temporal matters, and this is the second opinion set out in the first chapter.

units.la: Discip. Puto me aduertere, quomodo isti per libertatem Christianorum probare nituntur, quod Papa non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, præsertim in temporalibus, ideo pro eadem opinione adhuc aliter allegare conaris. Mag. Hoc aliis modis videtur posse probari, nam vicarius non habet maiorem potestatem (in quantum vicarius) quam ille cuius est vicarius, ergo Papa in quantum vicarius Christi; non habet maiorem potestatem in temporalibus, quam habuerit Christus in quantum homo passibilis & mortalis. Sed Christus in quantum homo passibilis & mortalis non habuit huiusmodi potestatem in temporalibus: cum non habuerit dominium omnium temporalium: nec alii fuerint serui eius secundum strictam significationem nominis seruorum, ipso testante, qui, vt habetur Ioh. 15. dixit Apostolis: Iam non dicam vos seruos, quia seruus nescit quid facit Dominus eius, ergo Papa non habet huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis. Disc. De fundamento istius allegationis satis poterit inueniri in quarto tractatu tertiæ partis istius Dialogi, ad quam pertinet exquisite disserere de paupertate Christi, ideo hac dimissa adduc alias. Magister. Probatur idem sic. Qui non debet se secularibus negociis implicare, non debet habere in secularibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, Papa autem non debet se secularibus implicare, ergo non habet nec habere debet talem plenitudinem potestatis in secularibus. Maior probatur: Quia frustra datur alicui potestas, quam exercere non debet. Unde & reges accipientes a Deo potestatem iudicandi, ac iustitiam & iudicium faciendi, & non facientes sæpe in sacris litteris arguuntur. Sapientiæ sexto sic dicitur Regibus peruerse vel negligenter exercentibus officium regni: data est a Domino potestas vobis, & virtus ab altissimo, qui interrogabit opera vestra, & cogitationes scrutabitur, quoniam cum essetis ministri regni illius, non recte iudicastis, &c. vbi dicit Glossa: Nota quod quilibet debet facere ea, quæ sue conditioni conueniunt, & per consequens illa potissime debet quis facere, ad quæ facienda ex speciali ordinatione Dei accepit potestatem, qui igitur speciali ter ex institutione & ordinatione Christi accepit in secularibus plenitudinem potestatis: potissime etiam vltra alios debet se secularibus implicare negociis, ne in commissa sibi potestate negligetem & desidem se ostendat. Minor, quod Papa scilicet non debet se negociis secularibus implicare, patenter videtur ostendi per Apostolum 2. ad Corinth. 2. cap. dicentem: Nemo militans Deo implicat se negociis secularibus, vt ei placeat cui se probauit. Cum igitur Papa praecipue inter omnes Deo debeat militare, vt ei placeat: ipse minus quam alii debet se negociis secularibus implicare, hinc ex canone Apostolorum, vt legitur distinctione octuagesima, ca. cap. episcopus, sic habetur: Episcopus autem sacerdos aut diaconus nequaquam seculares curas assumant, sin aliter, deiiciantur, & cap. episcopus, sic scribitur: Episcopus nullam rei familiaris curam ad seipsum reuocet: sed lectioni & orationi & verbo praedicationis tantummodo vacet, & 21. quaestion. 5. cap. 1. sic legitur: Apostolorum statuta sunt quae dicunt: nemo militans Deo, implicat se negociis secularibus, proinde aut clerici sint sine actionibus dominorum, aut actores sine officio clericorum. Ex quibus aliisque quamplurimis canonibus sacris, quae habentur decim. sext. quaestion. septim. summen- nulli, & distinctione 88. per totum, & 21. quaestion. 3. cap. placuit, & cap. Cyprianus, & cap. mollitiis, & cap. sacerdotum, & extra, ne clerici vel monachi saecularibus se negociis immisceant, per totum, & aliis locis quam multis colligitur, quod clerici episcopi non debent se secularibus negociis implicare, & per consequens Papa praecipue debet a talibus abstinere. Tum quia inter episcopos & clericos est praecipuus atque primus, & maxime debet in spiritualibus occupari. Tum quia praecipue tenet locum Apostolorum, & specialiter principis Apostolorum, qui hoc docuerunt & fecerunt, quos debet potissime imitari.
units.tr: Disc. I think I see how these men try to prove from the liberty of Christians that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power, especially in temporal matters. So you are trying to argue for the same opinion in another way. Mag. This seems capable of being proved in other ways. A vicar does not have greater power (insofar as he is a vicar) than the one whose vicar he is. Therefore the Pope, insofar as he is Christ's vicar, does not have greater power in temporal matters than Christ had as a passible and mortal man. But Christ, as a passible and mortal man, did not have such power in temporal matters, since he did not have dominion over all temporal things, and others were not his servants in the strict sense of the word "servants," as he himself testifies. As we read in John 15, he said to the Apostles: Now I will not call you servants, because a servant does not know what his Lord is doing. Therefore the Pope does not have such a fullness of power. Disc. The foundation of this argument can be found sufficiently in the fourth treatise of the third part of this Dialogue, to which it belongs to discuss the poverty of Christ in detail. So, setting that aside, bring another. Mag. The same is proved thus. Whoever ought not to involve himself in secular business ought not to have such a fullness of power in secular matters. But the Pope ought not to involve himself in secular matters. Therefore he does not have, and ought not to have, such a fullness of power in secular matters. The major premise is proved as follows: power given to someone is given in vain if he ought not to exercise it. Hence kings also, who receive from God the power of judging and of doing justice and judgment, and who do not do so, are often rebuked in the sacred letters. In Wisdom 6 it is said to kings who exercise the office of the kingdom perversely or negligently: Power has been given you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will question your works and search your thoughts, since, when you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, etc. Here the Gloss says: Note that everyone ought to do those things which suit his condition, and consequently one ought above all to do those things for which he has received power by a special ordinance of God. Therefore whoever has received, by a special institution and ordination of Christ, a fullness of power in secular matters ought especially, beyond others, to involve himself in secular business, lest he show himself negligent and slothful in the power committed to him. The minor premise, that the Pope ought not to involve himself in secular business, is plainly shown by the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 2, who says: No one who serves God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please him to whom he has enlisted. Since therefore the Pope, above all others, ought to serve God so as to please him, he ought less than others to involve himself in secular business. Hence, from the canon of the Apostles, as we read in distinction 80, chapter Episcopus, it is held: A bishop, priest or deacon should by no means take up secular cares; otherwise let them be deposed. And in the chapter Episcopus it is written: A bishop should not take upon himself any care of household affairs, but should devote himself only to reading, prayer and the word of preaching. And in 21 question 5, chapter 1, it is read: The statutes of the Apostles say: no one who serves God involves himself in secular business; therefore let clerics be free of the business of lords, or those who do business be free of the office of clerics. From these and very many other sacred canons, found in dec. sext., question 7, "Summen nulli," and in distinction 88 throughout, and 21 question 3, chapter placuit, and chapter Cyprianus, and chapter mollitiis, and chapter sacerdotum, and extra, ne clerici vel monachi saecularibus se negociis immisceant, throughout, and from many other places, it is gathered that clerics and bishops ought not to involve themselves in secular business. Consequently the Pope in particular ought to abstain from such things. This is so, first, because among the bishops and clerics he is the chief and first, and ought most of all to be occupied with spiritual things. Second, because he especially holds the place of the Apostles, and especially of the chief of the Apostles, who taught and did these things, and whom he ought above all to imitate.

units.la: Discipulus. Non oportet summum Pontificem se in omnibus vitae Apostolicae conformare: quia Apostoli abdicarunt proprietatem temporalium rerum, extra, de ver. sig. lib. 6. cap. exiit, & tamen Papa potest habere proprium, ergo similiter Papa potest se implicare multis secularibus negociis, quibus se minime implicauerunt. Magister. Ad haec respondeat isti, quod licet Papa non teneatur in omnibus vitae Apostolicae conformare: tamen nihil est sibi specialiter iniunctum a Christo, quod Apostolicae vitae repugnet implicari saecularibus negociis repugnet vitae Apostolicae, inferunt isti, quod specialiter iniunctum Papae a Christo. Quare nec sibi data specialiter est a Christo plenitudo potestatis in saecularibus, cum teneatur exequi potestatem, quam specialiter habet ordinatione & constitutione Christi. Disc. Aliter nitaris allegare pro opinione praescripta. Magi. Papa non habet talem in spiritualibus & temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis ostenditur. Nam qui est minor & minister, & seruus aliorum, in quos non debet exercere potestatem, non habet super eos tam in spiritualibus, quam in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis. Nam qui habet super alios talem potestatis plenitudinem, est Dominus eorundem, nullus enim Dominus maiorem potestatem, quam plenitudinem potestatis potest habere super quoscunque, nullus autem respectu eiusdem est seruus & dominus: qui etiam habet plenitudinem potestatis super alios praecipue potest & debet exercere potestatem in eos. Papa autem est minor & minister, & seruus Christianorum, in quos non debet exercere potestatem, teste Christo, qui, vt legitur Matth. 22. dixit Apostolis: Scitis quod principes gentium dominantur eorum: & qui maiores sunt potestatem exercent in eos, non ita erit inter vos, sed quicunque voluerit inter vos maior fieri, sit vester minister: & qui voluerit inter vos primus esse, erit seruus vester, & Matthaei 24. dixit Christus: qui maior est vestrum, erit vester minister. Et Marc. 9. dixit: Si quis voluerit primus esse, erit quasi omnium nouissimus & omnium minister, & 10. cap. Scitis quod ii, qui videntur principari gentibus, dominantur eis, & principes eorum potestatem habent ipsorum, non ita autem est in vobis, sed quicunque voluerit fieri maior, erit vester minister: & quicunque voluerit primus esse, erit omnium seruus. Et vt habetur Lucae 20. Christus dixit Apostolis: Reges gentium dominantur eorum: & qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur, vos autem non sic: sed qui maior est in vobis, fiat sicut minor, & qui praecessor est, sicut ministrator. Ex quibus patet, quod primus spiritualis inter Christianos, scil. Papa, est minor & minister & seruus aliorum, in quos potestatem exercere non debet, igitur non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis. Discipulus. Ista allegatio in simili tractata est aliquantulum diffuse libro sexto prima partis istius dialogi cap. 3. ideo ipsa omissa, alias cure adducere. Magister. Quod Papa non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, sic probatur. Nam qui non est constitutus a Christo iudex secularis, non habet in secularibus talem plenitudinem potestatis a Christo, Papa non est constitutus a Christo iudex secularium, teste beato Petro, qui, sicut legitur in epistola Clementis, vt habetur vndec. quaestion. septim. te quidem, ait: Te quidem oportet irreprehensibiliter viuere, & summo studio niti, vt omnes vitae huius occupationes abiicias, ne fideiussor existas, ne aduocatus litium fias, ne ve in aliqua occupatione prorsus inueniaris mundialis negocii occasione perplexus, neque enim iudicem, neque cognitorem secularium negociorum te hodie vult ordinare Christus, igitur Papa non habet talem, praesertim in secularibus plenitudinem potestatis. Item, qui non est dominus clericorum, non habet super eos plenitudinem potestatis, Papa autem non est dominus clericorum, teste beato Petro, qui in canonica sua prima cap. 5. ait: neque vt dominantes in clero, ergo Papa non habet etiam super clerum talem plenitudinem potestatis. Amplius, cum eam potestatem habet Papa in terris suae temporali iurisdictioni subiectis, quam in aliis terris non sunt suae temporali iurisdictioni subiectae, ergo non habet in omnibus talem plenitudinem potestatis. Discipul. Dicerent primi opinantes, quod omnes terrae temporali iurisdictioni Papae subiectae sunt. Mag. Huic Innocentius Tertius obuiare videtur, qui, vt habetur extr. de haereticis, vergentis, terras suae temporali iurisdictioni subiectas distinguit ab aliis, dicens: In terris vero temporali nostra iurisdictioni subiectis bona haereticorum statuimus publicari: & in aliis idem praecipimus fieri per potentes & principes seculares. Discipulus. Adhuc adhuc allegationem adducas. Magister. Aliter probatur, quod Papa specialiter in temporalibus non habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, nam omnis potestas in temporalibus est ab illo, qui habet temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit in temporalibus, quae nec iuri diuino, nec iuri naturae repugnat, sed potestas imperialis & regalis aliorum quae principum laicorum non est a Papa. Unde & rex Franciæ superiorem in temporalibus non recognoscit, ext. qui filii sunt legitimi, per veram adilem, ergo Papa non habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis. Disc. De distinctione potestatum spiritualis & secularis, & an potestas sit à Papa, diffuse tractabimus in secundo tractatu ipsius tertia partis nostri dial. ideo allegationem aliam adducas. Mag. Quod Papa non habeat in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis, ostenditur. Nam contra illum, qui habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, nulla currit præscriptio, contra Papam autem currit præscriptio, saltem centenaria, ext. de præscript. si diligenti, igitur Papa non habet in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: Discipulus. The supreme Pontiff does not need to conform himself in all things to the Apostolic life, because the Apostles renounced ownership of temporal goods (extra, de ver. sig., lib. 6, cap. exiit), and yet the Pope may have property. Therefore, similarly, the Pope may involve himself in many secular affairs in which the Apostles did not involve themselves at all. Magister. To these points those men reply that although the Pope is not bound to conform himself in all things to the Apostolic life, nothing has been specifically enjoined on him by Christ that conflicts with the Apostolic life. Involvement in secular business conflicts with the Apostolic life. They therefore infer that nothing has been specifically enjoined on the Pope by Christ to involve himself in secular business. Hence neither has a fullness of power in secular matters been specifically given to him by Christ, since he is bound to exercise only the power which he has specifically by the ordinance and institution of Christ. Disc. You are trying to argue otherwise for the opinion set out above. Magi. It is shown that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power in spiritual and temporal matters. For he who is lesser, a minister, and a servant of others, over whom he ought not to exercise power, does not have over them a fullness of power either in spiritual or in temporal matters. He who has such a fullness of power over others is their lord, for no lord can have greater power than a fullness of power over whomever he rules. But no one is both servant and lord with respect to the same people. Moreover, he who has a fullness of power over others especially can and ought to exercise power over them. But the Pope is lesser, a minister, and a servant of Christians, over whom he ought not to exercise power, as Christ testifies. As we read in Matthew 22, he said to the Apostles: You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them. It shall not be so among you; but whoever wishes to become greater among you, let him be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant. In Matthew 24 Christ said: He who is greatest among you shall be your minister. In Mark 9 he said: If anyone wishes to be first, he shall be last of all and the minister of all. In chapter 10: You know that those who seem to rule over the nations lord it over them, and their princes have power over them. It is not so among you; but whoever wishes to become greater shall be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first shall be the servant of all. And as we read in Luke 20, Christ said to the Apostles: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. But you are not so; rather, let him who is greater among you become as the least, and he who leads as one who serves. From these passages it is plain that the first spiritual man among Christians, namely the Pope, is lesser, a minister, and a servant of others, over whom he ought not to exercise power. Therefore he does not have such a fullness of power. Discipulus. This argument was treated somewhat at length in a similar context in book six, first part of this dialogue, chapter 3. So, omitting it, bring another. Magister. That the Pope does not have such a fullness of power is proved thus. He who has not been appointed by Christ as secular judge does not have from Christ such a fullness of power in secular matters. The Pope has not been appointed by Christ as judge of secular affairs, as the blessed Peter testifies. As we read in the epistle of Clement, found in 11 question 7, "te quidem," Peter says: You indeed ought to live blamelessly and to strive with the utmost effort to cast off all the occupations of this life, lest you become a surety, lest you become an advocate in lawsuits, or lest you be found wholly entangled in any occupation through worldly business. For Christ does not wish to appoint you today either as judge or as arbiter of secular affairs. Therefore the Pope does not have such a fullness of power, especially in secular matters. Likewise, he who is not lord of the clergy does not have a fullness of power over them. The Pope is not lord of the clergy, as the blessed Peter testifies in his first canonical epistle, chapter 5, where he says: nor as lords over the clergy. Therefore the Pope does not have such a fullness of power even over the clergy. Moreover, the Pope has that power in lands subject to his temporal jurisdiction which he does not have in other lands that are not subject to his temporal jurisdiction. Therefore he does not have such a fullness of power in all things. Discipulus. The earlier proponents would say that all lands are subject to the temporal jurisdiction of the Pope. Mag. Innocent III seems to stand against this. As found in extra, de haereticis, vergentis, he distinguishes the lands subject to his temporal jurisdiction from the others, saying: In lands subject to our temporal jurisdiction we decree that the goods of heretics be confiscated; and in others we command the same to be done by powerful princes and secular rulers. Discipulus. Bring still another argument. Magister. It is proved in another way that the Pope does not have such a fullness of power specifically in temporal matters. For all power in temporal matters comes from him who has a fullness of temporal power, so that he can do everything in temporal matters that conflicts neither with divine law nor with natural law. But the imperial and royal power of the other lay princes is not from the Pope. Hence the king of France also recognizes no superior in temporal matters (extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, per veram adilem). Therefore the Pope does not have such a fullness of power in temporal matters. Disc. We shall treat at length the distinction between spiritual and secular power, and whether power is from the Pope, in the second treatise of the third part of our dialogue. So bring another argument. Mag. It is shown that the Pope does not have a fullness of power in temporal matters. For no prescription runs against him who has such a fullness of power in temporal matters, but prescription does run against the Pope, at least a centenary prescription (extra, de praescriptionibus, si diligenti). Therefore the Pope does not have such a fullness of power in temporal matters.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Vbi ponitur secunda opinio capitulo primo recitata, scilicet quod Papa habet plenitudinem potestatis in spiritualibus, & probatur quatuor rationibus & duabus auctoritatibus.
units.tr: Where the second opinion, recited in chapter one, is set out, namely that the Pope has fullness of power in spiritual matters, and it is proved by four arguments and two authorities.

units.la: Disc. Hæc ad præsens de prima sententia, quam supra c. 1. recitasti, sufficiat, ideo ad secundam sententiam eod. cap. recitatam te converte. Mag. Sententia illa duas partes includit, vnam sc. affirmatiuam, & aliam negatiuam. Prima est, quod Papa habet ex ordinatione Christi talem plenitudinem potestatis in spiritualibus. Secunda est, quod non habet ex ordinatione Christi talem plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus. Disc. Allega primo pro prima parte. Mag. Quod Papa in spiritualib. talem habeat plenitudinem potestatis ex ordinatione Christi probatur. Quia sicut ea, quæ sunt secularia debet disponi per principem secularem: ita quæ sunt spiritualia, sunt per summum Pontificem ordinanda & disponenda, sed princeps supremus secularis habet in secularibus plenitudinem potestatis. Amplius: Christus dedit Petro plenitudinem potestatis, cum dixit: Quodcunque ligaueris super terram, &c. sed non dedit plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus, ergo dedit sibi plenitudinem potestatis in spiritualibus. Rursus, qui potest omnem hominem de quocunque peccato corripere, & pœna debita coercere, habet in spiritualibus plenitudinem potestatis, Papa autem potest omnem hominem de peccato corripere, ext. de iudiciis, nouit, igitur Papa habet in spiritualibus plenitudinem potestatis. Iterum, omnia spiritualia possunt ad causas Dei reduci, sed omnes causæ Dei spectant ad summum Pontificem: quia spectant ad episcopos & clericos, dist. 96. si Imperator, inter episcopos autem Papa est primus, ergo omnes causæ Dei spectant ad ipsum, quare in spiritualibus habet plenitudinem potestatis. Hoc Iulius Papa sentire videtur: qui, vt habetur dist. 11. ca. nolite, ait: Satis enim indignum est, quimcunque vel Pontificum vel ordinum consequentium hanc regulam refutare, quam B. Petri sedem & sequi viderit & docere, multum enim conuenit, vt totum corpus ecclesiæ in hac sibi obseruatione concordet, quæ inde auctoritatem habet, vbi Dominus totius ecclesiæ posuit principatum. Et Nicolaus Papa eadem dist. c. consequens, ait: Consequens est, vt quid ab huius sedis rectoribus plena auctoritate sancitur, nullius consuetudinis præpediente occasione propriâs tantum sequendo voluntates remoueatur, vbi Glossa super hoc verbo plena, dicit: Papæ auctoritas plena est: aliorum episcoporum semiplena. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Papa habet à Christo, saltem in spiritualibus, plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: Student. Let this suffice for the present concerning the first opinion, which you recited above in chapter 1. Now turn to the second opinion, recited in the same chapter. Master. That opinion contains two parts, one affirmative and the other negative. The first is that the Pope, by the appointment of Christ, has such fullness of power in spiritual matters. The second is that he does not have such fullness of power in temporal matters by the appointment of Christ. Student. Offer your proofs first for the first part. Master. That the Pope has such fullness of power in spiritual matters by the appointment of Christ is proved as follows. Just as secular affairs ought to be arranged by the secular prince, so spiritual affairs are to be ordained and arranged by the chief Pontiff; but the supreme secular prince has fullness of power in secular matters. Furthermore, Christ gave Peter fullness of power when he said: Whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth, etc. But he did not give him fullness of power in temporal matters; therefore he gave him fullness of power in spiritual matters. Again, whoever can rebuke any man for any sin and restrain him with the punishment due is endowed with fullness of power in spiritual matters; the Pope can rebuke every man for sin (Extra, De iudiciis, Nouit); therefore the Pope has fullness of power in spiritual matters. Again, all spiritual things can be traced back to the causes of God, but all the causes of God belong to the chief Pontiff, because they belong to bishops and clerics (Dist. 96, Si imperator); and among bishops the Pope is first; therefore all the causes of God belong to him, and so he has fullness of power in spiritual matters. Pope Julius seems to think this, who, as is found in Dist. 11, c. Nolite, says: "It is indeed shameful that any of the Pontiffs or of the consequent orders should refute this rule, which he has seen the see of St. Peter both follow and teach; for it is very fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which derives its authority from the place where the Lord has set the principate of the whole Church." And Pope Nicholas, in the same Dist., c. Consequens, says: "It follows that what is ordained with full authority by the rulers of this see should be removed, with no hindrance from any custom, by those who follow only their own wills," where the Gloss on the word plena says: "The authority of the Pope is full; that of other bishops is half-full." From these words it is gathered that the Pope has fullness of power from Christ, at least in spiritual matters.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: Chapter XI.

units.la: In quo pertractatur tertia opinio primo cap. recitata, vbi etiam specialiter probatur, quod Papa accepit aliquam potestatem à conciliis generalibus.
units.tr: In which the third opinion, recited in chapter one, is discussed, and where it is also specifically proved that the Pope received some power from the general councils.

units.la: Discipulus. Si Papa habet talem plenitudinem potestatis à Christo, tam in temporalibus, quam in spiritualibus, non est dubium quin à Christo habeat in spiritualibus plenitudinem potestatis, quare allegationes, quæ supra capitulo primo pro prima sententia sunt adductæ, pro ista secunda parte secundæ sententiæ etiam possunt adduci, & ideo pro ista nolo ad præsens plures allegationes audire. Similiter pro secunda parte eiusdem secundæ sententiæ possunt allegari plura, quæ tacta sunt supra capitulo quinto, septimo, octauo & nono. Quare sententia ista dimissa, tertia quæ tacta est supra capitulo primo nitantur discutere. Circa quam primo modum ponendi audire desidero. Magister. Illa sententia ponit, quod Papa habet tam in spiritualibus, quam in temporalibus talem plenitudinem potestatis, partim ex ordinatione Christi, partim ex ordinatione humana: dicens, quod Papa habet immediate à Christo plenam potestatem in foro pœnitentiali, iuxta illud Matthæi decimo sexto. Quodcunque ligaueris super terram, &c. Habet etiam à Christo potestatem docendi totum populum Christianum, secundum illud Iohan vltim. pasce oues meas. Habet etiam à Christo potestatem distribuendi & conferendi ecclesiasticas dignitates, iuxta illud verbum Christi ad Petrum, Iohan. prim. Tu vocaberis Cephas, id est caput. Ex hoc enim quod caput est, habet in membra influere diuersa officia conferendo. Habet etiam à Christo, quod maiora negocia ecclesiæ sunt ad ipsum referenda, ex hoc ipso, quod constituit ipsum caput aliorum. A conciliis autem generalibus habet potestatem, quantum ad omnia quæ spectant ad regimen totius populi Christiani, quorum potestas non est sibi specialiter à Christo concessa. Discipul. Circa istam sententiam multa essent tractanda, quae vel plura eorum tacta sunt in his, quae dicta sunt circa primam sententiam, vel tangentur cum discutietur vltima sententia, quae supra cap. primo extitit recitata. Vnde vnum tantummodo, quod ista sententia ponit, volo vt aliquibus allegationibus fulcire conaris: quod videlicet Papa aliquam receperit à conciliis generalibus potestatem. Hoc enim illis auctoritatibus obviare videtur, quae dicunt, quod concilia generalia robur habent, & auctoritatem à Romana ecclesia. Magister. Quod Papa aliquam potestatem acceperit à conciliis generalibus, videtur posse tali modo probari. Papa habet potestatem aliquam à canonibus, & non nisi à canonibus generalium conciliorum, ergo à conciliis generalibus habet aliquam potestatem. Prima diuersis auctoritatibus sanctorum videtur posse probari, ait enim Iulius Papa scribendo Orientalibus episcopis, vt habetur distinct. 17. cap. regula: regula vestra nullas habet vires nec habere poterit, quoniam nec ab orthodoxis episcopis hoc concilium actum est, nec Romana ecclesia legatio interfuit, canonibus praecipientibus, sine eius auctoritate concilia fieri non debere. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod à canonibus est praeceptum, quod solus Papa habeat auctoritatem congregandi concilia. Item Gelasius Papa, vt habetur 9. quaestion. 3. cap. ipsi, ait: Ipsi sunt canones, qui appellationes totius voluerunt deferre: ab ipsa vero nusquam appellare debere sanxerunt, ac per hoc illam de tota ecclesia iudicare, ipsam ad nullius commeare iudicium, nec de eius vnquam praeceperunt iudicio iudicare: sententiamque eius constituerunt non oportere dissolui: cuius potius sequenda decreta mandauerunt. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod à canonibus non à Christo immediate habet Papa, vt liceat omnibus appellare ad ipsum, & quod ab ipso appellare non licet: & quod ipse potest de tota ecclesia iudicare: & quod ipse nullius subest iudicio: & quod eius sententia in omnibus est tenenda: & per consequens, quod eius praeceptis est in omnibus & ab omnibus obediendum. Ex quo infertur, quod Papa à conciliis generalibus habet plenitudinem potestatis, quantum ad omnia, quae non sunt sibi immediate concessa à Christo. Item Gregorius, vt habetur 2. quaestion. 7. cap. decreto, ait: Liceat post auditionem primatum dioecesos, si necesse fuerit nos appellare, & nostra auctoritate, aut ante ius, aut ante legatos de nostro latere missos, iuxta decreta Patrum, suas exercere atque diffinire actiones. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod à decretis Patrum habet Papa, vt liceat appellare ad ipsum. Item Pelagius Papa, vt habetur distinction. 17. cap. multis, ait: Maiores vero ac difficiliores quaestiones, vt sancta synodus statuit, & vt beata consuetudo exigit, ad sedem Apostolicam semper deferantur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod à synodo & consuetudine, & non immediate à Christo habet Papa, vt maiores causae deferantur ad ipsum. Item Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur 11. quaestion. 6. c. arguta, ait: Priuilegia tamen Apostolicae sedis vos obliuioni tradere nullatenus debuistis, quibus venerandi canones iudicia totius ecclesiae ad hanc deferri iubent. Ex quibus verbis videtur haberi, quod Papa à canonibus acceperit potestatem. Item beatus Petrus potestatem accepit à collegio, distinction. 11. in nouo. distinction. 17. huic & 3. quaestion. 6. dudum, ergo & Papa potestatem potest accipere à concilio generali. Discipulus. Probare nunc niteris, quod Papa habet plenitudinem potestatis, siue à Christo, siue ab humana ordinatione. Magister. Hoc videtur posse ostendi pluribus auctoritatibus sanctorum Patrum. Hoc enim Gregorius testari videtur secund. quaestion. 6. decreto. Et Iulius Papa eadem causa & quaestion. cap. qui se. Hoc etiam Innocentius Tertius in concilio generali, vt habetur extra, de paenitent. & remission. cap. cum ex eo, videtur asserere manifeste. Quod etiam ratione probatur, quia ille, cui obediendum est in omnibus, habet vel à Christi ordinatione, vel ab ordinatione humana, aut partim ab vna, & partim ab alia plenitudinem potestatis, sed Papae obediendum est in omnibus: teste Gregorio, qui (vt habetur distinction. decim. non. cap. nulli) ait: Nulli fas est vel nolle, vel posse transgredi Apostolicae sedis praecepta, nec nostra dispensationis ministerium, &c. Sitque alienus à diuinis & a pontificalibus officiis, qui noluerit praecepti obtemperare Apostolicis. Hoc etiam Stephanus Papa, vt habetur 4. distinction. quoniam vero, vt allegatum est prius, affirmare videtur. Et Iulius Papa, vt habetur vigesim. quint. quaestion. secund. cap. amputato, ait: Ea vero quae sunt ab Apostolis eorumque successoribus ad huiusmodi sancta sedis examen ab antecessoribus instituta, nulla desidia negligantur, nulla dissensione violentur, nulla contractatione turbentur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Papae est obediendum in omnibus, igitur habet plenitudinem potestatis, vel immediate ex institutione Christi, vel ab ordinatione humana, aut partim ab vna, & partim ab alia.
units.tr: Disciple. If the Pope has such fullness of power from Christ, both in temporal and in spiritual matters, there is no doubt that he has the fullness of spiritual power from Christ. So the arguments that were brought forward in chapter one for the first opinion can also be brought forward for this second part of the second opinion, and therefore I do not wish to hear many arguments for it at present. Likewise, many things that were touched on in chapters five, seven, eight and nine can be alleged for the second part of this same second opinion. So, setting that opinion aside, let us try to examine the third, which was touched on in chapter one. About this one, I first want to hear how it is stated. Master. That opinion holds that the Pope has such fullness of power, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, partly by the ordinance of Christ and partly by human ordinance. It says that the Pope has from Christ immediately full power in the penitential forum, according to that passage of Matthew 16: Whatsoever you shall bind upon earth, and so on. He also has from Christ the power to teach the whole Christian people, according to the words of John 21: Feed my sheep. He also has from Christ the power to distribute and confer ecclesiastical dignities, according to Christ's word to Peter in John 1: You shall be called Cephas, that is, head. For from the fact that he is the head, he has the power to flow diverse offices into the members by conferring them. He also has from Christ that the greater affairs of the Church are to be referred to him, from the very fact that Christ made him the head of the others. But from the general councils he has power in all those matters which concern the government of the whole Christian people, and the power over which was not specially granted to him by Christ. Disciple. Many things would need to be treated concerning this opinion, some of which have already been touched on in what was said about the first opinion, and others will be touched on when we examine the last opinion, which was recited in chapter one. Therefore I want you to try to support with some arguments the one point which this opinion asserts, namely that the Pope has received some power from the general councils. For this seems to conflict with those authorities which say that the general councils have their strength and authority from the Roman Church. Master. That the Pope has received some power from the general councils seems capable of being proved in the following way. The Pope has some power from the canons, and only from the canons of the general councils; therefore he has some power from the general councils. The first point seems capable of being proved by various authorities of the holy Fathers. For Pope Julius, writing to the Eastern bishops, says, as is found in distinct. 17, cap. regula: Your rule has no force, nor will it ever have, since this council was not held by orthodox bishops, nor was the Roman Church present by its legate, the canons commanding that councils must not be held without its authority. From these words it is gathered that it is commanded by the canons that the Pope alone has authority to convene councils. Likewise Pope Gelasius, as is found in 9. quaestion. 3. cap. ipsi, says: It is the canons themselves which have willed that appeals from the whole Church should be carried to him; and they have decreed that appeal must never be made from him; and so they have willed that he should judge concerning the whole Church, that he should not come under the judgment of anyone, and that no one should ever pass judgment on his judgment; and they have ordained that his sentence must not be dissolved, but rather that his decrees must be followed. From these words it is gathered that the Pope has from the canons, and not immediately from Christ, that it is lawful for all to appeal to him, that it is not lawful to appeal from him, that he can judge the whole Church, that he is subject to no one's judgment, that his sentence is to be upheld in all things, and consequently that his commands are to be obeyed in all things and by all. From this it follows that the Pope has from the general councils the fullness of power in all those matters which have not been granted to him immediately by Christ. Likewise Gregory, as is found in 2. quaestion. 7. cap. decreto, says: After hearing the primate of the diocese, let it be lawful, if it is necessary, for us to appeal, and by our authority, either before the law or before legates sent from our side, according to the decrees of the Fathers, to exercise and determine their actions. From these words it is intimated that the Pope has from the decrees of the Fathers that it is lawful to appeal to him. Likewise Pope Pelagius, as is found in distinct. 17, cap. multis, says: But the greater and more difficult questions, as the holy synod has decreed and as blessed custom demands, are always to be referred to the Apostolic See. From these words it is gathered that the Pope has from the synod and from custom, and not immediately from Christ, that the greater cases are to be referred to him. Likewise Pope Nicholas, as is found in 11. quaestion. 6. c. arguta, says: You must by no means have let slip from memory the privileges of the Apostolic See, by which the venerable canons order the judgments of the whole Church to be referred to this see. From these words it seems to be understood that the Pope has received his power from the canons. Likewise the blessed Peter received power from the college, distinct. 11, in novo; distinct. 17, huic; and 3. quaestion. 6, dudum; therefore the Pope too can receive power from a general council. Disciple. You are now trying to prove that the Pope has the fullness of power, whether from Christ or from human ordinance. Master. This seems capable of being shown by many authorities of the holy Fathers. For Gregory seems to bear witness to this in secund. quaestion. 6, decreto. And Pope Julius in eadem causa & quaestion, cap. qui se. Innocent III also seems clearly to assert this in the general council, as is found in extra, de paenitent. & remission., cap. cum ex eo. This is also proved by reason, because he to whom obedience is due in all things has his fullness of power either from the ordinance of Christ, or from human ordinance, or partly from the one and partly from the other; but obedience is due to the Pope in all things. Gregory bears witness to this, who (as is found in distinction 19, cap. nulli) says: It is not lawful for anyone either to be unwilling or to be able to transgress the precepts of the Apostolic See, or the ministry of our dispensation, etc. And let him be alien from divine and pontifical offices who is unwilling to obey the Apostolic precepts. Pope Stephen also seems to affirm this, as is found in 4. distinction, quoniam vero, as was alleged before. And Pope Julius, as is found in twenty-fifth quaestion 2, cap. amputato, says: Those things which have been instituted by the Apostles and their successors, by the predecessors, for the examination of this holy see, are not to be neglected through any sloth, nor violated through any dissension, nor disturbed through any mishandling. From these words it is gathered that obedience is due to the Pope in all things; therefore he has the fullness of power, either immediately from the institution of Christ, or from human ordinance, or partly from the one and partly from the other.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAP. XII.

units.la: In quo arguitur contra opinionem tertiam in precedenti capitulo recitatam, probando, quod neque auctoritate Christi Papa sit dominus omnium in temporalibus.
units.tr: In which the third opinion, recited in the preceding chapter, is argued against, proving that the Pope is not, by the authority of Christ, lord of all in temporal matters.

units.la: Discipulus. Contra istam sententiam nitaris allegare. Magister. Sunt quidam, qui istam sententiam non reputant haereticalem, sicut primam: tamen ipsam falsam & irrationabilem ac periculosam existimant.
