Falsam quidem existimant: Quia ex ipsa, sicut ex prima, sequitur, quod omnes Christiani sunt serui summi Pontificis, accipiendo nomen serui secundum significationem eius strictissimam, secundum quam in sententiis legalibus accipitur & vocatur. Qui enim habet siue ex ordinatione diuina, siue ex ordinatione humana, siue partim ex vna & partim ab alia, plenitudinem potestatis, tam in spiritualibus, quam in temporalibus super omnes Christianos (vt omnia possit, quae non sunt contra legem Dei, nec contra legem naturae, ita vt ab eius potestate per nullum actum humanam se posset, quicunque in quocunque, quod non est illicitum d[?] ris subtrahere) habet super omnes Christianos tantum dominium temp[?] habere potuit quicunq; Dominus super seruum suum. Si igitur Papa h[?] nos talem plenitudinem potestatis, Papa haberet plenissimum dominium reges & principes & alios universos: omnes etiam essent serui eius, & pos[?] sine omni culpa, & absq; omni causa priuare quemcunque regem regn[?] posset reg[?] subiicere cuicunq; rustico ad suae arbitrium voluntatis: & obed[?]: nec posset rex quicunque in talibus vel consimilibus sibi licit[?] reputant & absurdum. Discipulus. Dic, quare isti non reputant istam op[?] ponat omnes Christianos esse seruos, & scriptura diuina asserat legem e[?] tatis, & per consequens illa opinio scripturae diuinae repugnat, quare v[?] ut prima, secundum istos haereticalis debeat aestimari. Magister. Dicu[?] esse respondendum per aliqua, quae dicta sunt prius. Nam auctoritates tes legem Christianam esse legem libertatis, negatiue debent intelligi, & eos est haereticalis, quia ex ipsa sequitur, quod omnes Christiani per leg[?] ui summi Pontificis, & per consequens lex euangelica nec negatiue, n[?] libertatis: sed etiam lex horrendissimae seruitutis. Ista autem opinio te[?] Christiani sint effecti serui summi Pontificis per legem euangelicam: s[?] tur, quod omnes Christiani per voluntariam [?] facti sunt [?] enim, quod sponte & voluntarie omnes Christiani [?] se in o[?] non erat sibi concessa a Christo immediate. Et haec [?] tem in alic[?] stiani. Unde & rex aliquis posset se facere saltem in casu seruum summi subdendo se in omnibus potestati Papae. Si essent etiam solummodo d[?] ni, vel paulo plures, possent omnes se facere seruos Papae, hoc tamen s[?] factum, ideo haec opinio non est haereticalis, sed falsa. Quod enim hoc[?] quod haec opinio sit falsa, probatur per leges innumeras ciuiles & canon[?] sunt serui & quidam liberi. Disc. Quare dicunt isti praescriptam opinior[?] Hoc dicunt, quia si Papa haberet huiusmodi potestatem, posset imm[?] communitati Christianorum, posset enim Papa, si fieret occultus haer[?] secta paganorum vel aliqua alia infidelium, leuiter exponere totam [?] enim spoliare solo praecepto suo, omnes Christianos rebus suis, &c. arm[?] bus deberent contra inimicos defendi, quo facto infideles vocati per l[?] tem pro eis, & postea publice assentientem eis, possent leuiter omnen[?] tem pro eis, & postea publice assentientem eis, possent leuiter omnen[?]
units.tr: Discipulus. You are trying to bring arguments against this opinion. Magister. There are some who do not regard this opinion as heretical, as they do the first, yet they judge it false, irrational and dangerous. They judge it false because, as from the first, it follows from it that all Christians are servants of the supreme Pontiff, taking the word "servant" in its strictest sense, in which it is understood and used in legal writings. For whoever has the fullness of power, whether by divine ordination, by human ordination, or partly by the one and partly by the other, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, over all Christians (so that he may do anything that is not against the law of God or the law of nature, and so that no human act could withdraw anyone from his power, provided it is not unlawful), has over all Christians as much dominion as a lord has over his servant. If therefore the Pope had such fullness of power, the Pope would have the most complete dominion over kings, princes and all others; all of them would also be his servants, and he could, without any fault and without any cause, deprive any king of his kingdom, and subject any peasant to whomever he wished at his own will; and no king could regard as lawful for himself, in such or similar matters, obedience... and they consider this absurd. Discipulus. Tell me, why do these men not regard that opinion as heretical, since it asserts that all Christians are servants, and divine Scripture asserts the law of liberty, so that this opinion is repugnant to divine Scripture, and why should it not, like the first, be judged heretical by them? Magister. I say it must be answered by what has been said before. For the passages of Scripture which call the Christian law a law of liberty must be understood negatively; and this opinion is heretical, because it follows from it that all Christians are bound by the law of the supreme Pontiff, and consequently the gospel law is not only not free, negatively speaking, but is a law of the most horrible servitude. But this opinion holds that Christians have become servants of the supreme Pontiff through the gospel law; since it is asserted that all Christians, by a voluntary act, became subject to him, it is not that they spontaneously and voluntarily submit themselves, but that this power was not granted to him immediately by Christ. And this would be the case in other Christians as well. Whence also some king could make himself, at least in that case, a servant of the supreme Pontiff, by submitting himself in all things to the power of the Pope. Even if there were only a few, or a few more, who could all make themselves servants of the Pope, this has not been done; therefore this opinion is not heretical but false. That this opinion is false is proved by countless civil and canon laws, which show that some men are servants and some free. Disc. Why do they say the aforesaid opinion is dangerous? Magister. They say this because, if the Pope had such power, he could at once harm the whole community of Christians. For if some secret heretical sect of pagans or some other infidels arose, the Pope could easily expose the whole [Church] to them, and could despoil all Christians of their goods by his sole command, etc. All Christians would have to be defended with arms against the enemies, and once this was done, the infidels, called in through the [...] for them, and afterwards publicly assenting to them, could easily all...

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: In quo pertractatur quarta opinio, quae diuersos modos
units.tr: In which the fourth opinion is treated, which holds diverse modes...

units.la: Discipulus. Nunc videamus de quarta sententia, quae tacta est supra c. Papa talem plenitudinem potestatis non habet, neque ab institu[?] tione humana, neque regulariter, neque casualiter. Sed diuersimode p[?] nim dicunt, quod Papa nullam potestatem habet a Christo vltra alios [?] potestatem, sicut & alii sacerdotes, super alios. Nullam tn potestate[?] poenitentiae: sed habet potestatem docendi & informandi laicos, sicut [?] tem coactiuam aliqualem non plenam habet a communitate fidelium [?] mano Pontifici, & nulli sacerdoti, aliqualem tribuebant super totam [?] testatem. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod Papa a Christo immediate habe[?] omnes Christianos: non tamen plenam in omnibus, neque in spirit[?] bus. Ab hominibus vero fidelibus nullam recepit potestatem, neque
units.tr: Disciple. Now let us look at the fourth opinion, which was touched on above. Its holders say that the Pope does not have such fullness of power, neither from human institution, nor regularly, nor casually. Instead they say in different ways that the Pope has no power from Christ beyond that of other priests, who have power over others in the same way. He has no power of penance, but he has the power of teaching and instructing the laity, as other priests do. Some grant him a certain coercive power, though not a full one, from the community of the faithful, and they give it to the Pope alone and to no other priest; others grant him a certain power over the whole... Others, however, say that the Pope has immediately from Christ power over all Christians, but not full power in all things, nor in spiritual matters. He has received no power from the faithful men...

units.la: Nonnulli vero dicunt, quod Papa in spiritualibus habet potestatem, n[?] sto, in temporalibus vero nullam habet potestatem spiritualem a Christ[?] tamen plenam, sed limitatam, prout fideles limitare voluerunt. Disc. [?] tinent, quae si discuteremus prolixe, oportet [?] nos for sitan taedium leg[?] ter transeamus. Praesertim cum occasione [?] nda omnia tangemus inf[?] tur primo, unde mouentur primi dicentes, quod Papa nullam potestat[?] sacerdotes. Mag. Istud dicunt propter auctoritates, quae ponuntur dist. 93 recitaui supra prima parte istius dial. li. 5. 18. c. in quibus asserere videtur Hi[?] cerdos ex ordinatione seu institutione Christi est maior alio, neque in[?] tione. Hoc etiam videtur posse probari per hoc, quod Apostoli fueru[?] quantum fuit ex ordinatione Christi dist. 21. c. in nomo. 24. q. 1. c. loquitur
units.tr: Some, however, say that the Pope has power in spiritual matters, but in temporal matters he has no spiritual power from Christ. This power is not full but limited, as the faithful have wished to limit it. Disciple. These are the opinions which, if we discussed them at length, might perhaps weary the reader; so let us pass over them briefly. Especially since we will touch on everything below, in the place where it arises. Let us first take up those who say that the Pope has no power over other priests. Master. They say this on account of the authorities set out in dist. 93, which I recited above in the first part of this dialogue, book 5, chapter 18, where he seems to assert that a priest, by the ordination or institution of Christ, is not greater than another, neither in power nor in jurisdiction. This also seems to be proved by the fact that the Apostles were equal, as far as the ordination of Christ went, dist. 21, c. "in nomine", and 24 q. 1, c. "loquitur".

units.la: Christo super alios sacerdotes non habuerunt aliquam p[?]
units.tr: Christ did not give the Apostles any power over the other priests...

units.la: mnes sacerdotes, quantum est ex speciali ordinat[?]
units.tr: All priests, as far as comes from a special ordination of Christ...

units.la: sti, sunt pares successoribus beati Petri.
units.tr: ...are equal to the successors of blessed Peter.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: In quo arguitur contra opinionem quartam, in capitulo precedenti pertractatam, aliquibus auctoritatibus & duabus rationibus.
units.tr: In which the fourth opinion, treated in the preceding chapter, is argued against by several authorities and two reasons.

units.la: Discip. Dic breuiter, an aliqui nitantur istam assertionem repellere. Mag. Hoc quidam erroneum reputant, & sacris canonibus apertissime obuiare, qui ponuntur dist. 21. c. quamuis, & c. sacrosancta & 9. q. 3. c. cuncta, & 24. q. 1. cum beatissimus, quos etiam allegaui prima parte huius dialogi li. 3. ca. 10. Haec etiam assertio Innocentii III. refragari videtur, qui, vt habetur ext. de maioritate & obedientia, solita, sicut & allegatum est prius, dicit se non constitutioni humanae, sed potestati diuinae inniti, ergo Papa ex Deo immediate habet aliquam potestatem super omnes Christianos. Quod & ratione probatur, quia nulla communitas, praecipue magna, est bene & convenienter ordinata, quae nullum caput habet, quia teste Salomone Prou. 11. Vbi non est gubernator, populus corruet, sed communitas fidelium fuit optime & congruentissime ordinata a Christo, igitur Christus dedit caput communitati fidelium: sed non nisi Petrum, ergo Petrus fuit a Christo constitutus caput vniuersorum fidelium. Amplius, non minus congrue & vtiliter est ordinatus a Christo populus Christianus, qua fuerit populus Hebraeorum, sed ille populus ex ordinatione diuina habuit caput, saltem in spiritualibus, sc. summum sacerdotem, qui omnibus aliis sacerdotibus fuit superior, ergo & populus Christianus ex ordinatione Christi habet vnum caput, quod est superius omnibus aliis sacerdotibus Christianis. Quod etiam Marcellus Papa, vt habetur 2. quaestion. 1. cap. rogamus, & Innocentius Tertius extra de translatione, & omnes Patres sancti tenere videntur.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me briefly whether some people try to refute that assertion. Master. Some regard it as erroneous and as flatly contrary to the sacred canons, which are laid down in dist. 21, c. quamuis, c. sacrosancta, 9 q. 3, c. cuncta, and 24 q. 1, cum beatissimus, which I also cited in the first part of this dialogue, book 3, chapter 10. This assertion also seems to conflict with Innocent III, who, as is found in Extra, De maioritate et obedientia, Solita, and as was cited earlier, says that he relies not on human constitution but on divine power. Therefore the Pope has from God directly some power over all Christians. This is also proved by reason, because no community, especially a large one, is well and properly ordered if it has no head. For, as Solomon witnesses in Proverbs 11, "Where there is no governor, the people falls." But the community of the faithful was ordered very well and most fittingly by Christ. Therefore Christ gave a head to the community of the faithful. But he gave it to none except Peter. Therefore Peter was appointed by Christ as the head of all the faithful. Further, the Christian people was ordered by Christ no less fittingly and profitably than the people of the Hebrews was. That people, by divine ordinance, had a head, at least in spiritual matters, namely the high priest, who was superior to all the other priests. Therefore the Christian people also, by the ordinance of Christ, has one head, which is superior to all other Christian priests. Pope Marcellus also seems to hold this, as is found in 2 q. 1, c. rogamus, and Innocent III in Extra, De translatione, and all the holy Fathers seem to hold it too.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: In quo iterum probatur, quod Papa nullam potestatem plenariam coactiuam habet a Christo immediate, sed tantummodo limitatam, & hoc a fidelibus.
units.tr: In which it is again proved that the Pope has no full coercive power immediately from Christ, but only a limited power, and this from the faithful.

units.la: Discipulus. Dic nunc, quae praefati opinantes dicunt Papam nullam potestatem coactiuam accepisse a Christo. Magister. Hoc dicunt propter hoc, quod (secundum eos) tota communitas fidelium debet habere supremo, qui potestatem habeat coactiuam, subesse, a quo omnes alii iudices potestatem coactiuam accipiant, ille autem non esse debet Papa: quia tunc tota iurisdictio laicorum periret. Papa recepit potestatem coactiuam a Christo. Disc. Istam materiam conabor tecum discutere in tractatu de iuribus Romani imperii. Et ideo isto, & etiam quibusdam aliis praetermissis, nitaris allegare pro vltimo dicto: quod sc. Papa in temporalib. nullam potestatem specialem habet immediate a Christo, sed a suis fidelibus: non tamen plenam sed limitatam, prout fideles limitare volebant. Magister. Quod Papa in temporalibus nullam potestatem habuit immediate a Christo, videtur diuersimode posse probari. Nam sicut Imperator se habet ad temporalia, ita Papa se habet ad spiritualia, inquantum recipit immediate a Christo potestatem, sed Imperator nullam potestatem habet in spiritualibus, ergo Papa in temporalibus nullam potestatem habet immediate a Christo. Amplius, sicut allegatum est prius 9. c. secundum Scripturas sacras & canones: Papa non debet se secularibus negociis implicare, & per consequens non est sibi specialiter commissum a Christo, vt se implicet secularibus negociis, quare (vt videtur) a Christo immediate nullam recepit in temporalibus potestatem. Discipul. Quomodo probatur, quod Papa habet a fidelibus potestatem in temporalibus? Magi. Hoc ponitur propter canones sacros, per quos habetur, quod Papa in multis casibus se de temporalibus intromittit, ext. de foro competenti, c. licet, & ext. de iudiciis, c. nouit, & ext. qui filii sunt legitimi per venerabilem, & in multis aliis locis innumeris habetur, quod Papa iurisdictionem temporalem exercet: quam tamen non habet a Christo, sicut dicitur prius probatum, ergo habet eam a fidelibus. Quod tali ratione probatur. Nam Papa non habet immediate a Christo iurisdictionem maiorem in una regione quam in alia, sed de facto & de iure maiorem iurisdictionem exercet in temporalibus in una regione quam in alia, igitur illam potestatem non habet immediate a Christo, habet ergo eam ab aliquo alio, & non nisi a fidelibus, ergo ab ipsis fidelibus aliquam habet in temporalibus potestatem: non tamen plenam, sed limitatam. Quia fideles tradendo in temporalibus potestatem, nullatenus se constituerunt seruos eius, ergo plenitudinem potestatis minime conferebant.
units.tr: Student: Now tell me what the aforementioned opinion holders say, that the Pope received no coercive power from Christ. Master: They say this because, in their view, the whole community of the faithful must be subject to some supreme person who has coercive power, and from whom all other judges receive their coercive power. That person, they hold, must not be the Pope, because otherwise the whole jurisdiction of the laity would perish. The Pope received coercive power from Christ. Student: I will try to discuss this matter with you in a treatise on the rights of the Roman empire. So, setting that aside along with some other points, you should rest on your last claim: namely, that the Pope has no special power in temporal affairs immediately from Christ, but from his faithful people, and not full power but limited, to the extent that the faithful wished to limit it. Master: That the Pope had no power in temporal affairs immediately from Christ can be proved in several ways. For just as the Emperor stands in relation to temporal affairs, so the Pope stands in relation to spiritual affairs, insofar as he receives power immediately from Christ; but the Emperor has no power in spiritual affairs; therefore the Pope has no power in temporal affairs immediately from Christ. Furthermore, as was stated earlier in chapter 9, according to the sacred Scriptures and canons, the Pope ought not to involve himself in secular business, and consequently Christ has not specially committed to him the task of involving himself in secular business. Hence (as it seems) he received no power in temporal affairs immediately from Christ. Student: How is it proved that the Pope has power in temporal affairs from the faithful? Master: This is posited on account of the sacred canons, by which it is held that the Pope intrudes himself into temporal affairs in many cases (Extra, de foro competenti, c. licet; Extra, de iudiciis, c. nouit; Extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem), and in countless other places it is held that the Pope exercises temporal jurisdiction. Yet he does not have it from Christ, as was proved above; therefore he has it from the faithful. This is proved by the following reasoning. The Pope does not have from Christ immediately a greater jurisdiction in one region than in another, but in fact and in law he exercises greater jurisdiction in temporal affairs in one region than in another. Therefore he does not have that power immediately from Christ; he has it, then, from someone else, and only from the faithful. Therefore he has some power in temporal affairs from the faithful themselves, but not full power, only limited. For the faithful, in handing over power in temporal affairs, did not in any way make themselves his slaves, and so they did not confer fullness of power at all.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAP. XVI.

units.la: In quo ponitur opinio quinta, sc. quod Papa non habet a Christo potestatem disponendi regulariter de temporalibus, sed eam habet casualiter.
units.tr: In which the fifth opinion is set out, namely that the Pope does not have from Christ the power to dispose of temporal affairs as a rule, but has it only by chance.

units.la: Discipulus. Ad sententiam quintam tactam sup. c. 1. transeamus: quam primo satagas explicare: & inde qualiter intelligi debeat explana. Magister. Illa sententia (sicut dixi) tenet, quod Papa talem plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus & spiritualibus, vt omnia per potentiam ordinatam vel absolutam possit, quæ non sunt contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale & simpliciter neque à iure diuino, neque humano, sed ex ordinatione diuina habet casualiter, siue in casu & secundum quid huiusmodi plenitudinem debet intelligi. Papa à iure diuino, siue ex ordinatione disponendis se intromittere minime debet, quamdiu temporalia prout disponuntur, nisi accipiendo temporalia à laicis pro sua sustentatione ideo non habet potestatem à Christo regulariter disponendi & ordinandi reges & principes, & alios laicos spectare noscuntur. Casualiter tamen temporalia peralios in periculum communitatis Christianorum, vel aliam traderentur, vel in casu consimili conuerterentur ad malum, & posset & potest huiusmodi periculis viam præcludere, Papa à iure diuino de temporalibus, quicquid pro bono communi & salutione fidei & periculis necessario faciendum sibi recta ratio dictaret, & ita in tali casu quodammodo, & secundum quid plenitudine potestatis, non quia tota sua, quo ad dominium & proprietatem, nec quod posset ad libitum supra hil potest rex vel alius laicus facere de quacunque re temporali, quia ideo hoc fieri expediret, & non esset alius, per quem conuenienter fieri posset, haberet plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus simpliciter, sed tantum militer in spiritualibus non habet à iure diuino regulariter & simpliciter potestatis, quare sine culpa & absque causa non potest præcipere fidelibus: imo etiam multa alia, non enim absque culpa & sine causa potest contrahat matrimonium, neque vouceat virginitatem & castitatem: & tamen unum, neque ius naturale: sed utrumque licite fieri potest. Et sic de multis aliis spectant, super quæ Papa à iure diuino regulariter & simpliciter non obtinet: super quæ tamen casualiter obtinet plenitudinem potestatis secundum tionem deliciti, aut propter aliquam notabilem necessitatem vel utilitatem, cum imminet periculum, potest præcipere cuicunque quicquid in spiritualibus Dei vel naturæ. Et ita secundum istos Papa potest casualiter à iure diuino in temporalibus habere plenitudinem potestatis: non simpliciter, sed secundum quid plenissima potestas, est tamen gradus, singularis & quam magnificentia regna transferre, reges & principes, aliumque laicum quemcunque privare, aliisque conferre. In spiritualibus etiam omnia potest in casu. Et in particulari, in quibus prædicta potest vel aliquid prædictorum, non potest dari doctrina vniuersalis, per quam absque errore sciatur magnæ talia Papa & quando non; & qualia potest in vno casu & qualia in alio. In casu, quæ in alio casu minime potest.
units.tr: Disciple. Let us pass on to the fifth opinion, touched on above in chapter 1. First, please explain it, and then how it ought to be understood. Master. That opinion (as I have said) holds that the Pope has such a fullness of power over temporal and spiritual matters that, by ordained or absolute power, he can do anything that is not contrary to divine law or to natural law. He has this power neither simply from divine law nor from human law, but by divine ordination he has it casually, that is, in a particular case and in a qualified sense, and such fullness must be understood in that way. By divine law, or by ordinance, the Pope ought by no means to meddle in temporal affairs as they are ordered, except when he takes temporal goods from laymen for his own sustenance. Therefore he does not have from Christ the power to dispose and ordain regularly over kings, princes and the other laymen, whose concerns are known to belong to the secular sphere. Yet if temporal goods were handed over to others to the danger of the Christian community, or in a similar case were turned to evil, the Pope both could and can close off such dangers. By divine law he may decide, concerning temporal matters, whatever right reason dictates must be done for the common good, the salvation of the faith and the averting of dangers. Thus in such a case he has, in a certain manner and in a qualified sense, a fullness of power. This is not because the goods are wholly his in terms of ownership and property, nor because he may do at will anything he likes with any temporal thing, as a king or other layman may not, but because it would be expedient to do so and there is no other by whom it could fittingly be done. He does not have fullness of power over temporal matters absolutely, and likewise in spiritual matters he does not have from divine law a regular and absolute power, so that he cannot command the faithful without fault and without cause. There are many other things as well: one cannot contract marriage without fault and without cause, nor vow virginity and chastity. Yet neither of these is contrary to natural law, but each may be done lawfully. The same holds for many other matters over which the Pope does not hold power regularly and absolutely from divine law. Over these, however, he holds fullness of power casually, according to the circumstances of the offence, or on account of some notable necessity or utility when danger threatens; he can then command anyone whatever, in spiritual matters or in those of God or nature. According to these men, the Pope can therefore casually have from divine law a fullness of power in temporal matters: not absolutely, but in a qualified sense. This most complete power is nevertheless a single and distinct degree, by which he may transfer great kingdoms, depose kings, princes and any other layman, and confer them on others. In spiritual matters too he can do all things in a given case. But as to which matters the aforesaid powers, or any of them, may be exercised, no universal doctrine can be given by which one may know without error when the Pope may do such things and when not, and what he may do in one case and what in another, since in one case he can do what in another case he cannot.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Narrat, quam potestatem dederit Christus regulariter
units.tr: Narrates what power Christ gave generally

units.la: Discipul. Quamuis inter prædicta aliqua sint mihi obscura, quæ forsitan lucidabis, tamen pro nunc præscriptam opinionem, quo ad illa obscura explanare. Sed cum dixeris breuiter (secundum illam sententiam) quam potestatem dederit Petro regulariter & successoribus eius, & quā dederit ei casualiter in casu dum eandem opinionem, quam potestatem aut iurisdictionem Christus & in ipso successoribus eius. Mag. Dicitur quod Christus constituit B. Petrum aliorum Apostolorum & vniuersorum fidelium: dans ei regulariter in spiritualibus propter regimen communitatis fidelium quantum ad bonos mores, & quasi fidelium sunt de necessitate facienda vel omittenda, omnem potestatem sed prouide, & ad vtilitatem communem committerentur vni homini; a eam coactiua absque omni detrimento ac dispendio notabili & enormi principū & aliorum quorumcunque laicorum vel clericorum, quæ eis iure ante vel post institutionem legis euangelicæ competebant. In temporalibus solummodo ius petendi temporalia pro sua sustentatione & sui potestatem siue in spiritualibus, siue in temporalibus habent nunc successores beati Petri, scilicet Romani Pontifices. Omnem autem potestatem ter ultra istam habuerunt vel habent summi Pontifices ex humana condicione submissione, vel ex consensu expresso vel tacito, aut propter impotentiam hominum aliorum, vel ex consuetudine, vel quomodocunque runt & obtinent.
units.tr: Disciple. Although some of the aforesaid points are obscure to me, which perhaps you will clarify, nevertheless for the present I want you to explain the stated opinion with regard to those obscure points. But since you have said briefly (according to that opinion) what power Christ gave to Peter in general and to his successors, and what he gave him in a particular case, while holding the same opinion, what power or jurisdiction Christ gave, and in him to his successors. Master. It is said that Christ appointed Blessed Peter over the other Apostles and all the faithful, giving him, in spiritual matters, generally, for the government of the community of the faithful as regards good morals, and, as far as things that must of necessity be done or omitted by the faithful are concerned, all power, but provided, and to be committed for the common good to one man, and that coercive power, without any harm or notable and enormous loss to princes and to any other laymen or clergy, which by right they possessed before or after the institution of the evangelical law. In temporal matters only the right to ask for temporal things for his maintenance and for the exercise of his office. The successors of Blessed Peter, namely the Roman Pontiffs, now have power both in spiritual and in temporal matters. Moreover, the supreme Pontiffs have had or have, beyond that power, every other power which they have obtained from human submission or condition, or from express or tacit consent, or on account of the impotence of other men, or from custom, or however they have come to have and hold it.

units.la: Disc. Ista narratio continet multa mihi obscura: quæ vt melius intelligi hi studeas explicare: & qualiter distinguitur ab aliis opinionibus, declarare.
units.tr: Disciple. That account contains many things that are obscure to me, which you should try to explain, so that they may be better understood, and show how it is distinguished from other opinions.

units.la: Christum constituisse B. Petrum caput, principem & praelatum aliorum Apostolorum ac universorum fidelium, intendit elidere opinionem tenentem quod beatus Petrus non fuit caput ecclesiae ex institutione Christi: sed solummodo ex electione, seu institutione Apostolorum, seu aliorum fidelium. Per spiritualia autem, de quibus fecit mentionem, intelligit illa quae ex institutione evangelicae legis sunt propria evangelicae legi in nulla alia lege, saltem humana vel secta reperta, sicut sunt dispensatio sacramentorum novae legis, ordinatio sacerdotum, & clericorum institutio, vel promotio illorum, qui debent regere & instruere populum Christianum, etiam in his quae spectant ad fidem & cultum divinum, & similia. Per hoc autem quod dicit Christum dedisse beato Petro potestatem ... ad spiritualia, quae sunt de necessitate facienda, vel de necessitate emittenda, intendit excludere a regulari potestate Petri illa spiritualia, quae supererogationis sunt: quae scilicet sunt consilii & non praecepti. Et universaliter omnia, sine quibus conuenienter regi potest populus Christianus, & absque quibus quamuis fiant, vel omittantur, nec fides nec boni mores periclitantur. Et ideo non potest papa regulariter praecipere Christiano, quod seruet virginitatem, vel contrahat matrimonium, aut paupertatem assumat, vel divitias retineat, possideat, vel quando non tenetur ex praecepto Dei, eleemosynam faciat vel non faciat. Licet in casu plura talia praecipere posset, & si extra casum utilitatis vel multa talia praeceperit, praeceptum suum non tenet, sed est nullum: nec ille cui fit, tenetur ei obedire, etiam si propter hoc eum excommunicauerit, talis sententia tanquam continens intolerabilem errorem esset nulla & minime formidanda, nec de necessitate seruanda. Per hoc autem quod dicit, dans ei omnem potestatem in ... quae non periculose, sed provide & ad utilitatem communem committeretur uni homini, intendit excludere a regulari potestate papae omnem potestatem quae si uni homini committeretur regulariter, poterit faciliter periculum notabile toti communitati fidelium imminere: cui non posset absque miraculo, vel cum maxima difficultate via praecludi. Propter quod quamuis de necessitate sit aliquis successurus summo pontifici: tamen papa non habet potestatem ordinandi quis debeat sibi succedere. Propter hoc etiam est quaedam sententia tenens, quod quamuis ... electio summi pontificis sit de necessitate facienda: tamen papa non habet a Christo potestatem regulariter ordinandi, quomodo & a quibus debeat eligi summus pontifex. Quia si talem potestatem haberet regulariter papa immediate a Christo, cum papa, tanquam homo peccabilis (sicut caeteri erroribus, prauis affectionibus, negligentiis ac malitiis & nequitiis valeat irretiri) posset faciliter ex negligentia vel malitia relinquere totam Christianitatem absque noctore eligendi summum pontificem, per quod periclitaretur bonum com-mune.
units.tr: By saying that Christ appointed Blessed Peter head, prince and prelate over the other Apostles and all the faithful, the author intends to refute the opinion holding that Blessed Peter was not head of the Church by the institution of Christ, but only by the election or appointment of the Apostles or of other faithful. By spiritual matters, of which he made mention, he means those things which, by the institution of the evangelical law, belong peculiarly to the evangelical law and are found in no other law, or at least in no human law or sect, such as the dispensing of the sacraments of the new law, the ordination of priests, the institution of clergy, or the promotion of those who ought to rule and instruct the Christian people, including in those matters which concern the faith and divine worship, and the like. By the words that he says Christ gave to Blessed Peter power ... over spiritual things, which must of necessity be done or of necessity be omitted, he intends to exclude from Peter's general power those spiritual things which are of supererogation, that is, which belong to counsel and not to precept; and in general all those things without which the Christian people can be suitably governed, and without which, whether they are done or left undone, neither faith nor good morals are endangered. And therefore the Pope cannot generally command a Christian to keep virginity, or to contract marriage, or to take up poverty, or to keep and possess riches, or to give alms or not to give alms when he is not bound by a precept of God. Although in a particular case he could command many such things, and if outside such a case of usefulness he commands many such things, his precept does not hold but is null, and the one to whom it is given is not bound to obey him, even if on this account he has excommunicated him; such a sentence, as containing an intolerable error, would be null and in no way to be feared, nor of necessity to be observed. By the words, giving him all power in ... which would be committed to one man not dangerously but providently and for the common good, he intends to exclude from the Pope's general power every power which, if it were committed to one man generally, could easily bring a notable danger upon the whole community of the faithful, a danger which could not be averted without a miracle or with the greatest difficulty. For this reason, although it is of necessity that someone should succeed the supreme Pontiff, yet the Pope does not have the power to ordain who ought to succeed him. For this reason too there is a certain opinion holding that, although the election of the supreme Pontiff must of necessity be made, yet the Pope does not have from Christ the general power of ordaining how and by whom the supreme Pontiff ought to be elected. For if the Pope had such a power generally and immediately from Christ, since the Pope, as a fallible man (like others he can be ensnared by errors, depraved affections, negligences, and wickednesses and malice), could easily through negligence or malice leave the whole of Christianity without a head to elect a supreme Pontiff, by which the common good would be endangered.

units.la: Posset enim ex causa vel propter culpam priuare Cardinales potestate & iure eligendi summum pontificem, quo facto vel negligendo vel ex malitia differendo vel tempus sufficiens ordinandi non habendo, posset mori antequam de electoribus summi pontificis ordinaretur. Et ita periculum & detrimentum boni communis tota Christianitas sine potestate & iure eligendi summum pontificem remaneret. Et ideo secundum istam sententiam talis potestas non est regulariter concessa a Christo summo pontifici, nec etiam aliqua alia potestas, quae periculose concederetur uni personae, propter quod secundum eos nullo modo est Dominus omnium temporalium, quia tale Dominium esset nimis periculosum fidelibus. Per hoc autem quod tenet Christum dedisse papae libertatem absque omni notabili & enormi detrimento & dispendio iuriuim temporalium Imperatorum &c. intendit asserere, quod papa quicunque, quo ad personam suam, est liber, & nequaquam regulariter subiectus homini cuicunque, etiam si ante electionem suam fuisset seruilis conditionis, vel alio modo imperatori aut regi vel alii Christiano vel non Christiano: quia libertas vnius hominis quo ad personam suam non est notabiliter damnosa imperatori vel alii. Et ideo papa quantumcunque fuisset seruus, eo ipso quod est papa vel electus in papam, in libertatem eripitur. Casualiter tamen papa, puta si efficiatur haereticus vel in quocunque crimine appareat incorrigibilis, & de eo scandalizatur ecclesia, humano iudicio est subiectus: & debet per hominem iudicari, & poenam debitam sustinere de iure. Per hoc autem quod dicit, Christum dedisse regulariter beato Petro quo ad huiusmodi aliqualem iurisdictionem etiam coactiuam absque detrimento & dispendio notabili & enormi iurium temporalium &c. intendit dicere, quod papa habet a Christo regulariter potestatem puniendi crimina mere ecclesiastica, quae scilicet committuntur directe in legem Christianam quo ad illa quae sunt propria legi Christianae, & quae non ab aliis sectis minima immediate reputantur. Ita tamen, quod talis punitio non sit in notabile damnum & iudicium aliorum, qui minime peccauerunt. Et si seruus alienus committat crimen ecclesiasticum, papa potest ipsum punire: ita tamen, quod Dominus seruo absque culpa sua notabile damnum non incurrat. Per hoc quod dicit Christum dedisse beato Petro & successoribus eius libertatem & iurisdictionem & potestatem huiusmodi absque detrimento & dispendio notabili & enormi iurium temporalium imperatorum, regum & aliorum, quae eis iure naturali & civili ante vel post institutionem legis evangelicae competebant, intendit astruere quod per hoc, quod beatus Petrus & successores eius erunt ad summum sacerdotium sublimati, imperatores & reges & alii siue fideles, qui fuerunt ante vel post institutionem legis evangelicae, suis iuribus temporalibus minime priuabantur, sed ipsa retinebant, nec regulariter papae in temporalibus subiiciebantur. Sed veri imperatores & reges & Domini rerum suarum temporalium ac seruorum & subditorum sibi sicut antea remanebant, nec efficiebantur servi cuiuscunque, nec regulariter praeceptis papae tenebantur quo ad temporalia obedire. Nec sententia papæ excommunicationis, vel alia, si fuerit lata contra imperatorem vel alium, quia præceptis huiusmodi non obedit, aut iura sua defendit, regulariter tenet: Sed tanquam continens intolerabilem errorem est nulla penitus reputanda, & minime formidanda quantumcunque non seruetur. Per hoc autem quod dicit Christum dedisse beato Petro in temporalibus solummodo in petendi temporalia pro sua sustentatione & officii sui executione, vult excludere omnem opinionem tenentem, quod papa in temporalibus habet regulariter plenitudinem potestatis, vel etiam potestatem de temporalibus disponendi vel quamcunque iurisdictionem temporalem super imperium, vel quamcunque aliam regionem. Et etiam opinionem tenentem quod papa non habet aliquod ius exigendi quæcunque temporalia. Per hoc enim, quod dicit vltimo capitulo, quod omnem potestatem, quam regulariter vltra istam quam habuerunt vel habent summi pontifices ex humana ordinatione &c. intendit, quod successores beati Petri licet non excesserint in potestate aliqua beatum Petrum, quam haberent ex sola ordinatione Christi & ex iure diuino: tamen magnam tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus obtinuerunt ex iure humano, quæ non habuit beatus Petrus. Et quod potestas papæ ex iure humano potest augeri: & quod vnus summus Pontifex habet vel habere potest maiorem potestatem vel meliorem quam alius. Et hæc de primo libro dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: For he could, for some cause or on account of some fault, deprive the Cardinals of the power and right of electing the supreme Pontiff; and once this was done, either by neglecting it or by malice deferring it, or not having sufficient time to ordain it, he could die before the electors of the supreme Pontiff were ordained. And so, through the danger and detriment to the common good, all Christianity would remain without the power and right of electing a supreme Pontiff. And therefore according to this opinion such a power has not been generally granted by Christ to the supreme Pontiff, nor any other power which would be dangerously granted to one person; on account of which, according to them, he is in no way Lord of all temporal things, since such dominion would be too dangerous for the faithful. By the words in which he holds that Christ gave the Pope liberty without any notable and enormous detriment and loss to the rights of the temporal Emperors etc., he intends to assert that any Pope, as regards his own person, is free and in no way generally subject to any man, even if before his election he had been of servile condition, or in some other way to the Emperor or king or any other Christian or non-Christian; because the liberty of one man as regards his own person is not notably harmful to the Emperor or anyone else. And therefore the Pope, however much he may have been a slave, is by that very fact that he is Pope or elected Pope, rescued into liberty. Nevertheless, by accident, the Pope, for instance if he becomes a heretic or appears incorrigible in any crime, and the Church is scandalized by him, is subject to human judgment, and ought by right to be judged by a man and to undergo the due punishment. By the words in which he says that Christ gave to Blessed Peter generally, as regards such matters, some jurisdiction, even coercive, without any notable and enormous detriment and loss to temporal rights etc., he means to say that the Pope has from Christ, generally, the power of punishing crimes that are purely ecclesiastical, namely those committed directly against the Christian law, as regards those things which are proper to the Christian law and which are not immediately regarded as belonging to other sects. Yet in such a way that such punishment is not a notable loss and judgment against others who have not sinned at all. And if another's slave commits an ecclesiastical crime, the Pope can punish him; yet in such a way that the master does not incur a notable loss without fault of his own. By saying that Christ gave to Blessed Peter and his successors liberty, jurisdiction and power of this kind without notable and enormous detriment and loss to the temporal rights of Emperors, kings and others, which belonged to them by natural and civil right before or after the institution of the evangelical law, he intends to assert that, because Blessed Peter and his successors would be exalted to the supreme priesthood, Emperors, kings and others, whether faithful or not, who existed before or after the institution of the evangelical law, were in no way deprived of their temporal rights, but retained them, nor were they generally made subject to the Pope in temporal matters. But true Emperors and kings and lords of their own temporal things, and of their servants and subjects, remained as before, nor were they made slaves of anyone, nor were they generally bound to obey the Pope's precepts as regards temporal things. Nor does a sentence of excommunication by the Pope, or any other, if it has been pronounced against an Emperor or another because he does not obey such precepts or defends his rights, hold in general; but as containing an intolerable error it is to be regarded as wholly null and in no way to be feared, however much it is not observed. By saying that Christ gave to Blessed Peter, in temporal matters only, the right to ask for temporal things for his maintenance and the execution of his office, he wishes to exclude every opinion holding that the Pope has generally the fullness of power in temporal matters, or even the power of disposing of temporal things, or any temporal jurisdiction over the empire or over any other region; and also the opinion holding that the Pope has no right to demand any temporal things at all. For by saying in the last chapter that he has, generally, beyond that power which the supreme Pontiffs had or have from human ordinance etc., he intends that the successors of Blessed Peter, although they have not exceeded Blessed Peter in any power which they would have from Christ's ordinance alone and from divine right, have nevertheless obtained great power, both in temporal and in spiritual matters, from human right, which Blessed Peter did not have. And that the power of the Pope can be increased by human right; and that one supreme Pontiff has or can have a greater or better power than another. And let these things said about the first book suffice.

units.la: Explicit primus liber.
units.tr: The first book ends.

units.la: INCIPIT LIBER SECVNDVS PRIMI tractatus huius tertia partis. CAP. I.
units.tr: BOOK TWO OF THE FIRST TREATISE OF THIS THIRD PART. CHAPTER I.

units.la: In qua inquiritur, vtrum expediat toti communitati fidelium vni capiti principi & prælato fideli subesse.
units.tr: In which it is inquired whether it is expedient for the whole community of the faithful to be subject to one head, a faithful prince and prelate.

units.la: DISCIP. Quoniam ista quinta assertio via media inter alias quatuor incedendo cum qualibet illarum in quibusdam concordat, & in aliquibus discrepare dignoscitur, ipsam quo ad alias partes eius exquisite discutere, etiam alias quodammodo pertractare: ideo de ipsa aliquantulum inquiramus, incipientes a prima eius particula. An scilicet Christum constituerit beatum Petrum caput, principem & prælatum aliorum Apostolorum & vniuersorum fidelium. Ad cuius intelligentiam pleniorem ante omnia conferendo scrutemur: an expediat toti communitati fidelium vni capiti, principi & prælato fideli sub Christo subiici & subesse, primo autem pro parte affirmatiua nitaris allegare. Magister. Quod toti congregationi fidelium expediat vni capiti fideli sub Christo subesse videtur multis modis posse probari. Nam vni corpori expedit vnum caput habere, corpus enim sine capite imperfectum esse dignoscitur, cum principaliori membro sit orbatum. Corpus vero habens capita duo vel plura, monstruosum esse videtur, omnes autem fideles sunt vnum corpus: teste Apostolo ad Rom. 12. Multi, inquam, vnum corpus sumus in Christo, ergo cunctis fidelibus expedit vni capiti subesse, illud autem caput non debet esse infidele: quia omnia alia membra, præcipue in his quæ spectant ad salutem animæ, conaretur inficere, igitur debet esse fidele. Discipulus. Ista allegatio videtur deficere: eo quod non probat, quod illud caput debeat esse sub Christo: imo per ipsam ostendi videtur, quod vniuersi fideles non debent vni capiti sub Christo subesse: cum Christus sit caput totius ecclesiæ, vt Apostolus ait ad Ephes. 1. & in pluribus aliis locis asserit manifeste. Ex quo sequitur quod (cum corpus habens duo vel plura capita, monstruosum debeat reputari, vt innuit allegatio supra dicta) tota congregatio fidelium non debeat vni capiti sub Christo subesse: sed oportet ipsam solum Christum pro capite venerari. Magister. Nonnullis apparet, quod ista obiectio facile potest excludi, quia quamuis Christus sit caput ecclesiæ: tamen sub Christo oportet quod sit aliud caput eiusdem ecclesiæ, quod sub Christo curam eius gerat: eo quod ecclesiæ esse debet vicarius rector, qui corporaliter sit præsens eidem: qui eam visibiliter regat: ad quem fideles (cum necesse fuerit) pro variis necessitatibus corporaliter possint accedere: per quem modum Christus ecclesiam minime regit, quia solummodo inuisibiliter regit, nisi aliquando in casu. Licet ergo Christus sit caput: tamen homo mortalis fidelis debet esse caput, quamuis sub capite, nec tamen propter hoc monstruosum est putandum corpus. Constat enim, quod episcopus est caput respectu sibi subiectorum, & rex est caput sibi subditorum: & tamen omnes habent vnum caput Deum. Quamuis ergo corpus naturale esset monstruosum, si haberet duo capita naturalia vel plura, quorum vnum non est caput alterius: tamen vnum corpus mysticum potest habere plura capita spiritualia, quorum vnum sit sub alio: nec hoc est monstruosum, sed naturale & multis expediens & decorum. Discip. Alias allegationes ad eandem quæstionem adducas. Mag. Idem sic probatur, expedit vni ouili, vt ab vno pastore regatur & pascatur: quod Saluator ipse insinuare videtur, cum dicit (vt habetur Ioh. 10.) Fiet vnum ouile & vnus pastor, tota autem congregatio fidelium est vnum ouile, ipso pastore supremo testante: qui (vbi prius) dixit: alias oues habeo quæ non sunt ex hoc ouili: & illas me oportet adducere & vocem meam audient & fiet vnum ouile &c. Igitur expedit, quod tota congregatio fidelium vni subsit pastori, non solummodo Christo, qui inuisibiliter pascit ecclesiam, sed etiam visibili, qui sensibiliter pascat: imo etiam fideli, & non infideli, quia ille forte lupus & fur fit in dispergendo, mactando, & perdendo omnes Christi. Amplius, omni populo expedit vni rectori subesse, teste Salomone, qui Proverb. 11. ait: Vbi non est gubernator, populus corruet, dicens: vbi non est gubernator: non, vbi non sunt gubernatores, vbi etiam videtur innuere manifeste, quod vbi non est vnus gubernator, populus corruet, tota autem congregatio fidelium est vnus populus: licet plures populos partiales includat, teste beato Iohanne, qui Apocalyp. 21. c. ait: Ecce tabernaculum Dei cum hominibus & habitabit cum eis, & ipsi populus eius erunt, ergo expedit toti vniversitati fidelium vni capiti & gubernatori subesse. Rursus, communitas illa, quae optime regi non potest multitudine iudicum, qui possunt inter se circa causas & negotia contrariari, & etiam in totius communitatis periculum discordare, expedit vt vno supremo rectori & capiti subsit, qui possit omnibus indicare iudicii veritatem, quod Deus ipse in populo suo ordinare videtur, Deuter. 17. dicens: Si difficile & ambiguum apud te iudicium esse prospexeris inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, lepram & non lepram: & iudicium intra portas tuas videris variari, surge & ascende ad locum, quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, veniens ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis & ad iudicem qui fuerit illo tempore, quaeresque ab eis, qui indicabunt tibi iudicii veritatem. Sed communitas fidelium etiam ad ea quae sunt propria religioni Christianae, & quae ad fideles iudices & rectores minime spectant, multitudine iudicum, qui possunt circa causas & negotia huiusmodi in communitatis periculum discrepare, conuenienter regi non potest: cum in diuersis prouinciis, diocesibus & ciuitatibus necesse sit distinctos constituere iudices & doctores, igitur expedit toti communitati fidelium, vt pro huiusmodi casibus subsit vni capiti & rectori fideli & non infideli: quoniam infidelis in talibus iudicium omnino subuerteret, & nequaquam veritatem iudicii indicaret.
units.tr: Disciple. Since this fifth assertion takes a middle way between the other four, agreeing with each of them in some points and differing from them in others, let us examine it carefully as to its other parts, and in some measure treat the others as well. So let us inquire a little into it, beginning with its first part: whether Christ appointed blessed Peter as head, prince and prelate of the other Apostles and of all the faithful. For a fuller understanding of this, let us first examine by comparison whether it is expedient for the whole community of the faithful to be subject to one faithful head, prince and prelate under Christ. On the affirmative side, you should first set out your arguments. Master. That it is expedient for the whole congregation of the faithful to be subject to one faithful head under Christ seems capable of proof in many ways. For it is expedient for one body to have one head, since a body without a head is known to be imperfect, being deprived of its chief member. A body with two or more heads, however, seems monstrous. But all the faithful are one body, as the Apostle witnesses in Rom. 12: We, being many, are one body in Christ. Therefore it is expedient for all the faithful to be subject to one head, and that head must not be unbelieving, because an unbelieving head would try to infect all the other members, especially in those matters which concern the salvation of the soul. Therefore it must be faithful. Disciple. This argument seems to fall short, because it does not prove that this head must be under Christ. Indeed, through it there seems to be shown that all the faithful ought not to be subject to one head under Christ, since Christ is the head of the whole Church, as the Apostle says in Eph. 1 and clearly asserts in many other places. From this it follows that (since a body with two or more heads must be regarded as monstrous, as the argument above suggests) the whole congregation of the faithful ought not to be subject to one head under Christ, but must venerate Christ alone as head. Master. To some it appears that this objection can easily be answered. Although Christ is the head of the Church, there must nevertheless be under Christ another head of the same Church, who bears its care under Christ. For the Church ought to have a vicar and ruler who is bodily present to it, who rules it visibly, and to whom the faithful can have bodily access when need arises for various necessities. In this way Christ does not rule the Church at all, since he rules it only invisibly, except sometimes in an emergency. Therefore, although Christ is head, a mortal faithful man ought also to be head, though under the head, and the body is not on that account to be thought monstrous. For it is clear that a bishop is head with respect to those subject to him, and a king is head of his subjects, and yet all have one head, God. Therefore, although a natural body would be monstrous if it had two or more natural heads, of which one is not the head of another, nevertheless one mystical body can have several spiritual heads, one of which is under another. This is not monstrous, but natural, and useful and fitting for many. Disciple. Bring forward other arguments on the same question. Master. The same is proved thus. It is expedient for one flock to be ruled and fed by one shepherd, which the Saviour himself seems to hint at when he says (as in Ioh. 10): There shall be one fold and one shepherd. The whole congregation of the faithful is one fold, the supreme Shepherd himself bearing witness, who said above: I have other sheep which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold, and so on. Therefore it is expedient that the whole congregation of the faithful be subject to one shepherd, not only Christ, who feeds the Church invisibly, but also a visible one who feeds it perceptibly, and indeed a faithful one and not an unbelieving one, since the latter might perhaps be a wolf and a thief in scattering, slaughtering and destroying all of Christ's flock. Moreover, it is expedient for every people to be subject to one ruler, as Solomon witnesses, who says in Proverb. 11: Where there is no governor, the people falls, saying where there is no governor, not where there are no governors. Here he also seems plainly to hint that where there is not one governor, the people falls. The whole congregation of the faithful is one people, although it includes several partial peoples, as the blessed John witnesses in Apocalyp. 21: Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people. Therefore it is expedient for the whole universality of the faithful to be subject to one head and governor. Again, a community which cannot be well governed by a multitude of judges, who may disagree among themselves about causes and affairs, and even bring danger to the whole community by their discord, is expedient to be subject to one supreme ruler and head, who can declare to all the truth of judgment. God himself seems to ordain this among his people, in Deuter. 17, saying: If you see that judgment is difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and not leprosy, and you see judgment varying within your gates, arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose, coming to the priests of the Levitical race and to the judge who shall be in those days; and you shall ask them, and they shall declare to you the truth of judgment. But the community of the faithful cannot be suitably governed in matters which belong to the Christian religion, and which do not pertain to faithful judges and rulers at all, by a multitude of judges who could disagree about such causes and affairs to the peril of the whole community. For in different provinces, dioceses and cities it is necessary to appoint distinct judges and teachers. Therefore it is expedient for the whole community of the faithful, in such cases, to be subject to one head and ruler who is faithful and not unbelieving, since an unbeliever would utterly subvert judgment in such matters and would never declare the truth of judgment.

units.la: Disc. Videtur quod auctoritas in hac allegatione adducta contra opinionem militet: quia ex ipsa colligitur, quod in tali casu non est recurrendum ad vnum caput vel iudicem, sed ad plures, cum dicat expresse: veniesque ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis ad iudicem, igitur in veteri lege fuit recurrendum ad plures in huiusmodi casu. Quod ex verbis, quae sequuntur, probari videtur, cum dicitur: Facies quodcunque dixerint, qui praesunt loco quem elegerit Dominus, & post: Qui autem superbierit nolens obedire sacerdotis imperio, qui eo tempore ministrat Domino tuo, & decreto iudicis, morte morietur homo ille. Ex quibus verbis, vt videtur, datur intelligi, quod in huiusmodi casu vltima decisio causae pertinebat ad plures.
units.tr: Disciple. The authority adduced in this argument seems to tell against the opinion, for from it it is gathered that in such a case one must not have recourse to one head or judge, but to several, since it says expressly: and you shall come to the priests of the Levitical race and to the judge. Therefore in the old law, in such a case, one had to have recourse to several. This seems to be proved from the words that follow, where it says: You shall do whatever those who preside in the place which the Lord shall choose shall say; and after: But the man who acts proudly, unwilling to obey the command of the priest who then ministers to your Lord, and the decree of the judge, that man shall die the death. From these words, as it seems, it is given to understand that in such a case the final decision of the cause belonged to several.

units.la: Magister. Respondetur tibi, quod de praecepto Dei vnus debet esse in populo Iudaico iudex supremus, caput omnium atque rector siue sacerdos siue alius: qui tamen de consilio sacerdotum decidere debuit causas maiores: & ita recurrendum fuit tunc ad vnum tanquam ad caput & iudicem supremum, & ad plures tanquam ad consiliarios capitis & iudicis. Disc. Adhuc alias allegationes ad idem adducas. Magist. Alia allegatio potest esse talis. Illis, qui in vna fide & quibusdam eisdem ritibus & observantiis concordare tenentur, expedit vnum habere caput: quod saluo alio iure ad huiusmodi veritatem transgressores cogat vel saltem inducat, quia absque tali capite faciliter diuiderentur in diuersas sectas & haereses atq; in observantias & ritus illicitos. Sed tota communitas Christianorum in vna fide ac quibusdam eisdem ritibus & observantiis concordare videtur, quia, vt testatur Apostolus ad Eph. 4. Vna fides, vnum baptisma, ergo toti communitati fidelium expedit vnum caput habere fidele, non infidele: quoniam infidelis ad fidem contrariam ac observantias & ritus illicitos fideles induceret. Adhuc illis, qui subsunt diversis iudicibus potentibus errare circa maiora negotia, expedit vnum caput habere, ad quod eadem maiora negotia referantur, per quod iudicentur iuste & rite.
units.tr: Master. In reply to you: by God's precept there must be in the Jewish people one supreme judge, the head of all and ruler, whether priest or other, who yet ought to decide the greater causes with the counsel of the priests. And so one then had to have recourse to as head and supreme judge, and to several as counsellors of the head and judge. Disciple. Bring forward further arguments on the same point. Master. Another argument can be of this kind. It is expedient for those who are bound to agree in one faith and certain same rites and observances to have one head, who, apart from other right, compels or at least induces transgressors of this truth to it; for without such a head they would easily be divided into diverse sects and heresies, and into illicit observances and rites. But the whole community of Christians seems to agree in one faith and certain same rites and observances, since, as the Apostle testifies in Eph. 4: One faith, one baptism. Therefore it is expedient for the whole community of the faithful to have one faithful head, not an unbelieving one, since an unbeliever would induce the faithful to a contrary faith and to illicit observances and rites. Moreover, for those who are subject to different judges who may err about greater matters, it is expedient to have one head to whom those greater matters are referred, so that they may be judged justly and properly.

units.la: Quod Moyses de consilio Ietro cognati sui ex recta ratione moti sapienter fecisse in populo sibi commisso videtur, de quo Exod. 8. sic legitur: Quibus audictis Moyses fecit omnia quae ille (scilicet Ietro) suggesserat: & electis viris strenuis de cunctis Israelitico constituit eos principes populi, tribunos, & centuriones, quadragenarios, & decanos, qui iudicabant populum omni tempore, quicquid autem grauius erat, referebant ad eum: faciliora tantummodo iudicantes, qui etiam, vt habetur Deut. 1. dixit inferioribus iudicibus: Si difficile aliquid vobis visum fuerit, referte ad nos, & ego audiam. Fideles autem per latitudinem orbis dispersi subsunt in his quae ad religionem pertinent Christianam, diversis iudicibus & praelatis, quorum multi saepe sufficientem non habent maiorum negotiorum peritiam, ergo expedit toti communitati fidelium vnum caput habere, ad quod huiusmodi maiora negotia referantur. Disc. Ad istas duas rationes simul potest dupliciter responderi, vno modo, quod tam pro transgressoribus seu nolentibus compellendis ad vnitatem fidei & observantiarum ac ritvarious ecclesiasticorum, quam pro maioribus negotiis recurrendum est ad concilium generale, non ad aliquam vnam personam. Aliter, quod recurrendum est ad iudicem supremum secularem, qui habet tam de spiritualibus quam temporalibus iudicare.
units.tr: Moses seems to have acted wisely, moved by sound reason, in following the advice of his father-in-law Jethro concerning the people committed to him. Exodus 18 reads: When Moses heard this, he did all that Jethro had suggested. He chose strong men from all Israel and made them leaders of the people: tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten, who judged the people at all times. Whatever was more difficult they referred to him, and they judged only the easier cases. Likewise, as Deuteronomy 1 records, he said to the lower judges: If anything seems difficult to you, refer it to us, and I will hear it. The faithful, however, are scattered across the breadth of the world, and in matters pertaining to the Christian religion they are subject to many different judges and prelates, many of whom often lack sufficient skill in the greater matters. Therefore it is expedient for the whole community of the faithful to have one head, to which such greater matters may be referred. Disciple. To these two reasons one may reply in two ways at once. First, that for compelling transgressors, or those unwilling, to unity of faith and to the observances and ecclesiastical rites, as well as for greater matters, recourse must be had to a general council, and not to any single person. Second, that recourse must be had to a supreme secular judge, who has the authority to judge both spiritual and temporal matters.

units.la: Mag. Primam istarum quidam impugnant per hoc, quod cum fideles per prouinciarum quamplurium latitudinem sint diuisi, difficiliter & in longo tempore generale concilium congregatur: & non absque grauissimis laboribus & expensis, quare cum tales casus omni anno etiam pluries possunt contingere, non expedit communitati fidelium p omni tali casu generale concilium congregari, quare ad leuius in huiusmodi casibus praecauedum periculis expedit, vt communitas fidelium habeat vnum caput & praelatum, qui huiusmodi habeat potestatem, ad quam p supremis praelatis cum excesserint puniendis & aliis maioribus negotiis, ad quae sufficit vnius hominis pitia & potentia, terminandis recurratur. Secunda responsio p hoc repellitur, q: sicut ante ascensionem Christi & etiam aliquo tempore post nulla erat fidelis secularis & laicus, q potestate vel iurisdictione seculare habere: ita etiam posset adhuc contingere: & tamen pro huiusmodi casibus expediret communitati fideliū prouideri, ergo expedit communitati fidelium vt habeat vnum caput praeter potestates & iudices lailaicos, quod in huiusmodi habeat potestatem, quia imperator aut rex aut alius princeps secularis non habet ex officio suo super fideles potestatem: cum aliquando imperator ac omnes reges & principes seculares fuerint infideles & adhuc possent esse. Aliter autem infidelis in talibus posset habere potestatem super fideles, qui in omnibus perperam iudicaret. Discipulus. Adhuc aliquas allegationes adducas. Magister. Alia allegatio potest esse talis. Non expedit communitati fidelium ut multi inter eos & praecipue super alios potestatem habentes absque omni timore correctionis & poenae temporalis delinquere valeant insolentes, quia, ut habetur 6. q. 1. ex merito, capite languescente caetera membra inficiuntur, quare cum praelati fidelium, sicut & caeteri, proni sunt ad malum: pro eo quod, ut ait concilium Toletanum, ut habetur 12. q. 1. c. 1. omnis aetas ab adolescentia in malum prona est, summe expedit fidelibus, ut praelatos, quos divinus timor a malo non revocat, temporalis saltem poena cohibeat a peccato, extra, de vita & honestate clericorum c. ut clericorum, ergo expedit congregationi fidelium, ut habeat unum caput, quod etiam universos praelatos valeat corrigere, si in periculum religionis Christianae deliquerunt. Nec valeat dicere, ut quibusdam apparet, quod talis correctio spectet ad iudicem laicum: quia sicut tactum est prius, ante non fuit laicus fidelis, qui aliquam iurisdictionem haberet super quoscunque, & adhuc esset possibile, quod omnes laici fideles infidelium potestati subderentur. Igitur praeter iudicem laicum expedit, ut aliquis praelatus fidelis super alios praelatos habeat potestatem in huiusmodi.
units.tr: Master. Some oppose the first of these by arguing that, since the faithful are divided across the breadth of many provinces, a general council is assembled with difficulty and only after a long time, and not without very heavy labours and expense. Therefore, since such cases may arise every year, and even several times a year, it is not expedient for the community of the faithful to convene a general council for every such case. Rather, in order to guard more easily against dangers in such cases, it is expedient that the community of the faithful have one head and prelate who holds such authority, so that recourse may be had to him for the settling of such cases, both the punishment of those who have overstepped and other greater matters, for which the wisdom and power of one man suffice. The second reply is refuted in this way: just as before the ascension of Christ, and even for some time after, there was no faithful secular and lay person who could have power or jurisdiction in secular matters, so it could still happen now. Yet it would still be expedient for the community of the faithful to be provided for in such cases. Therefore it is expedient for the community of the faithful to have one head, besides the civil powers and lay judges, who may hold authority in such cases. For the emperor, or a king, or another secular prince does not, by virtue of his office, have power over the faithful, since emperors and all kings and secular princes have sometimes been, and still could be, unbelievers. Otherwise, an unbeliever might in such matters have power over the faithful and judge wrongly in everything. Disciple. Bring forward some further arguments. Master. Another argument may be this. It is not expedient for the community of the faithful that many among them, and especially those holding power over others, should be able to offend insolently without any fear of correction or temporal punishment. For, as is said in 6, q. 1, ex merito, when the head languishes, the other members are infected. Therefore, since the prelates of the faithful, like everyone else, are prone to evil (because, as the Council of Toledo says, as found in 12, q. 1, c. 1, every age is prone to evil from youth onward), it is most expedient for the faithful that temporal punishment at least restrain from sin those prelates whom the fear of God does not recall from evil (Extra, de vita et honestate clericorum, c. ut clericorum). Therefore it is expedient for the congregation of the faithful to have one head, who may also be able to correct all the prelates if they have offended to the danger of the Christian religion. Nor can it be said, as some think, that such correction belongs to a lay judge. For, as was said before, there was formerly no faithful layman who had any jurisdiction over anyone, and it would still be possible that all the faithful laity should be subject to the power of unbelievers. Therefore, besides a lay judge, it is expedient that some faithful prelate have power over the other prelates in such matters.

units.la: Item, idem est expediens toti & parti, paruis & magnis, sicut idem iuris est in toto & in parte, paruis & magnis, extra de appellationibus c. maioribus 14. q. ultima c. ultima sed cuilibet populo fideli partiali expedit ut habeat unum episcopum, qui sit caput in spiritualibus, & non plures, 7. quaestio. 1. in apibus, vbi dicit Hieronymus. Ecclesiarum singuli episcopi, singuli archiepiscopi, Diaconi & omnis ordo ecclesiasticus suis regoribus nititur, igitur toti communitati fidelium expedit unum caput habere. Praeterea expedit communitati fidelium ut in his quae ad religionem pertinent Christianam, illo regimine gubernetur, quod politiae optimae seculari maxime assimilatur, politia autem optima secularis est regnum, teste Aristotele, qui 8. Ethicorum, ait: Politiae autem sunt species tres, aequales autem transgressiones, puta corruptiones harum, sunt autem politiae quidem regnum & aristocratia, tertia autem, quae a preciis, quam Timocratiam dicere conueniens videtur. Politiam autem consueuerunt ipsam vocare plures, harum autem optima quidem regnum, & post loquens de tyrannide, ait: manifestum in hac quoniam pessima, pessimum autem contrarium optimo. Ex quibus verbis colligitur & patenter habetur, quod regnum inter omnes politias est optima, unius autem regni est unus rex, qui omnibus praeest. Igitur & toti multitudini fidelium expedit, ut unus omnibus praesit. Adhuc, non minor unitas capitis requiritur in tota communitate fidelium, quam in tota universitate mortalium, sed expedit toti universitati mortalium, ut unus omnibus principetur, igitur etiam expedit toti communitati fidelium, ut habeat unum caput quod praesit fidelibus universis.
units.tr: Likewise, the same thing that is expedient for the whole is expedient for the part, for small and great alike, just as the same law holds for the whole and the part, for small and great alike (Extra, de appellationibus, c. maioribus; 14, q. ultima, c. ultima). But it is expedient for every partial population of the faithful to have one bishop, who is the head in spiritual matters, and not more than one (7, quaestio 1, in apibus), where Jerome says: Each bishop of the churches, each archbishop, deacon, and every ecclesiastical order rests upon its rectors. Therefore it is expedient for the whole community of the faithful to have one head. Moreover, it is expedient for the community of the faithful to be governed, in matters pertaining to the Christian religion, by that form of rule which is most like the best secular polity. The best secular polity is the kingdom, according to Aristotle, who says in the eighth book of the Ethics: There are three kinds of polity, and their equal deviations, that is, their corruptions, are: the kingdom and aristocracy, and the third, which it is fitting to call timocracy, from honour. Many are accustomed to call polity by that name. Of these, the best is the kingdom. And afterwards, speaking of tyranny, he says: It is clear in this that it is the worst, and the worst is the contrary of the best. From these words it is gathered and plainly held that the kingdom is the best of all polities, and a single kingdom has a single king, who presides over all. Therefore it is also expedient for the whole multitude of the faithful that one should preside over all. Further, no less unity of head is required in the whole community of the faithful than in the whole universe of mortals. But it is expedient for the whole universe of mortals that one should rule over all. Therefore it is also expedient for the whole community of the faithful to have one head who presides over all the faithful.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: In quo arguitur in contrarium eius, quod in primo cap. dicebatur, & ad primam respondetur cap. 15. ad alias vero cap. 19. ad secundam vero respondetur cap. 29. inferius.
units.tr: In which the opposite of what was said in the first chapter is argued, the first objection is answered in chapter 15, the others in chapter 19, and the second is answered below in chapter 29.

units.la: Discipulus. Ex ista ratione coniicio, quod ex his quae potero inuenire in secundo tractatu tertiae partis Dialogi primi libri: vbi tractatur an expediat toti mundo, vni principi seculari subesse: potest perpendi faciliter, qualiter pro utraque parte hoc valeat allegari. Omnia enim illa vel plura possunt ad istam materiam applicari, ideo pro ista assertione praescripta noli amplius allegare: sed leuius ad assertionem contrariam studeas pertransfire, pro ipsa paucas allegationes & breues inducendo. Mag. Quod communitati fidelium non expediat vni capiti sub Christo subesse, videtur sic posse probari. Nullum iniustum est expediens communitati fidelium. Sed vnum esse caput & principari universis fidelibus est iniustum. Multi enim inter fideles sunt aequales vel nesciuntur esse inaequales & prudentia & virtute & omnibus conditionibus, quae ad bonum caput & principem requiruntur. Sed iniustum est, ut aliquis sibi similibus & aequalibus principetur. Quod Aristoteles tertio politicae, & c. 15. testari videtur, cum dicit: Similibus secundum naturam idem iustum necessarium & eandem dignitatem secundum naturam esse, quare siquidem inaequalibus aequale aliud tantum habere vel vestimentum nocivum corporibus, sic habent & quae circa honores sunt, similiter autem & inaequalem aequales, propter quod quidem vel magis principari quam subiici iustum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod iniustum est ut aliquis sibi similibus & aequalibus principetur, quorum enim est eadem virtus & sufficientia, eorum debet esse aequalis honor & dignitas, quemadmodum in naturalibus quae non habent virtutem digestivam aequalem, non debent recipere alimentum aequale. Ergo non expedit, ut unus sit caput totius communitatis fidelium. Amplius: Id quod est inutile, non expedit congregationi fidelium, sed unum caput praeesse congregationi fidelium est inutile, quia caput quod non potest in operatione debitam, est inutile reputandum. Operatio autem debita capitis quod membris caeteris principatur, est in iniquitates irrumpere, delinquentem poenis congruis coercendo, igitur qui non potest impios coercere, inutiliter principatur. Quod Sapiens Ecclesiast. 7. videtur innuere dicens: Noli Noli quaerere fieri iudex, nisi virtute valeas irrumpere iniquitates, ne forte extimescas faciem potentis & ponas scandalum in agilitate tua, qui autem praeesset congregationi fidelium, non posset delinquentes debite castigare: cum talis castigatio seu punitio praecipue multitudinis & potentum absque potentia temporali communiter sine diuitiis copiosis exerceri non possit. Hinc rex, ad quem spectat cohibere crimina, secundum quod testatur beatus Cyprianus, ut habetur 23. q. 5. c. rex debet, potentia debet & diuitiis abundare. Teste Aristotele, qui 8. Ethicorum ait: Non enim est rex qui non per se sufficiens & omnibus bonis superexcellens est, talis autem nullo modo indiget. Qui autem praest congregationi fidelium, non propter hoc diuitiis abundaret. Tum quia tempore Apostolorum, quando fuit congregatio fidelium optime gubernata, nullus fidelis praepositus aliis diuitiis abundabat. Tum quia Christus nullas diuitias pro quocunque praelato fidelium ordinauit, sed magis consuluisse videtur ut nunc fideles praecipui victu & vestitu essent contenti. Hinc Apostolus 1. ad Tim. 6. pro se & aliis qui fidelibus praerant, ait: Habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur hiis contenti sumus. Tum quia si caput fidelium diuitiis abundaret, cum imperatores & reges ac principes seculares diuitiis affluant inter ipsos & caput fidelium cum inuicem in multis communicent & insimul habitent, dissensiones & guerrae periculosissimae facilius orirentur: quia inter diuites, qui insimul commorantur, leuiter nascuntur lites & iurgia, ex quibus ad pugnas & guerras proceditur. Cuius exemplum habemus Gen. 13. vbi propter diuitias facta est rixa inter pastores Abraham & Loth, & Abraham timuit ne inter se & Loth quamuis essent sancti & propinqui propter copiam facultatum, si manerent simul, periculosa dissensio oriretur. Ibidem enim sic legitur: Erat quippe substantia eorum multa & nequibant habitare communiter. Unde & facta est rixa inter pastores gregum Abraham & Loth, & postea: dixit igitur Abraham ad Loth, ne quaeso sit iurgium inter me & te & inter pastores meos & pastores tuos: fratres enim sumus: ecce vniuersa terra coram te est: recede a me obsecro. Inter diuites igitur de facili discordiae suscitantur. Unde & nonnulli existimant dissensiones, guerras, pugnas & praelia, ac ciuitatum & regionum destructiones & vastationes, innumeraque alia mala, quae in Italia multis retroactis temporibus, & adhuc non desinant, acciderunt, ex diuitiis Romanae ecclesiae processisse: fuisset que expedients toti ecclesiae Dei, ut eadem Romana ecclesia paupertatem Apostolorum & modum eorum viuendi (omnibus pompis quo ad vasa, vestes & supellectilem vniuersam ac scutiferos & alios quomodolibet seruientes atque quae nunc alia procul motis) facto & opere imitata fuisset, nullatenus igitur, ut nonnullis apparet, expedit communitati fidelium vnum caput habere.
