Rursus: Expedit communitati fidelium, ut regatur a pluribus, ergo non expedit sibi ut subsit vni capiti & praelato, antecedens videtur posse probari per rationes consimiles illis, quas Aristoteles 3. politica allegat ad ostendendum, quod melius est ciuitatem regi optimis legibus quam optimis hominibus, & pluribus optimis, quam vno optimo viro. Quarum aliquae ad propositum possunt taliter applicari. Per illum vel illos expedit regi totam congregationem fidelium, cuius vel quorum iudicium est certius & melius in iudicando & discernendo, quae sint procuranda tanquam communia toti communitati fidelium, & quae tanquam inutilia & nociua sunt penitus repellenda, & cuius vel quorum est plura talia perpendere & videre. Absque enim plena talium certaque peritia nulla communitas potest commode gubernari: quia ipse Saluator Matth. 15. ait. Si caecus caecum ducat, & ambo in foueam cadunt. Sed plures melius & certius in talibus iudicant & discernunt, ac plura talia perpendunt & vident, quam vnus solus.
units.tr: Pupil. From the arguments I can find in the second treatise of the third part of the first book of the Dialogue, where it is discussed whether it is expedient for the whole world to be subject to one secular prince, I gather that it is easy to see how these can be alleged on either side. For all or most of those arguments can be applied to this question. So, for the thesis stated above, do not bring forward any more; rather, pass more lightly over the opposite thesis, offering a few short arguments in its support. Master. That it is not expedient for the community of the faithful to be subject to one head under Christ can be proved as follows. Nothing unjust is expedient for the community of the faithful. But it is unjust for there to be one head who rules over all the faithful. Among the faithful there are many who are equal, or who are not known to be unequal in prudence, virtue, or any of the qualities required in a good head and ruler. But it is unjust for someone to rule over those who are like him and equal to him. Aristotle seems to bear witness to this in the third book of the Politics, chapter 15, when he says: "For things that are alike by nature, the same justice and the same dignity are necessary by nature. Hence to give unequal things an equal share, or equal clothing to unequal bodies, is harmful; so it is also with honours. Likewise, to make the unequal equal is also unjust; hence it is just that the one should rule rather than be ruled." From these words it is gathered that it is unjust for someone to rule over those who are like him and equal to him. For those who have the same virtue and sufficiency ought to have equal honour and dignity, just as in natural things, those that do not have an equal digestive power ought not to receive equal nourishment. Therefore it is not expedient that there be one head of the whole community of the faithful. Furthermore: what is useless is not expedient for the congregation of the faithful. But for one head to rule over the congregation of the faithful is useless, because a head that cannot perform the duty required of it must be counted useless. The proper duty of a head who rules over the other members is to break into wickedness and restrain the offender with fitting punishments. Therefore one who cannot restrain the wicked rules to no purpose. The Wise Man seems to hint at this in Ecclesiasticus 7, saying: "Do not seek to become a judge, unless you have the strength to break into wickedness, lest perhaps you fear the face of the powerful and put a stumbling-block in your uprightness." But one who presided over the congregation of the faithful would not be able to punish offenders properly, since such correction or punishment, especially of the multitude and of the powerful, cannot generally be carried out without temporal power and abundant riches. Hence a king, whose task it is to check crimes, as Saint Cyprian testifies, as it is found in 23. q. 5. c. rex debet, must abound in power and riches. Aristotle bears witness, who says in the eighth book of the Ethics: "For he is not a king who is not self-sufficient and far superior to all good things; such a one needs nothing at all." But one who presides over the congregation of the faithful would not, for that reason, abound in riches. First, because in the time of the Apostles, when the congregation of the faithful was best governed, no faithful man set over others abounded in riches. Second, because Christ appointed no riches for any leader of the faithful, but seems rather to have wished that the faithful, even the chief among them, should be content with food and clothing. Hence the Apostle, in 1 Timothy 6, speaking for himself and for others who presided over the faithful, says: "Having food and covering, with these we are content." Third, because if the head of the faithful abounded in riches, then since emperors, kings, and secular princes are rich, and the head of the faithful and they share with one another in many things and dwell together, dangerous dissensions and wars would more easily arise. For among rich men who live together, quarrels and strife arise lightly, and from these they proceed to fights and wars. We have an example of this in Gen. 13., where, because of riches, a quarrel arose between the herdsmen of Abraham and Lot, and Abraham feared that if they remained together, a dangerous dissension would arise between himself and Lot, although they were holy and related, because of the abundance of their possessions. For there it is read thus: "Their substance was great, and they could not dwell together. So there arose a strife between the herdsmen of Abraham's flocks and the herdsmen of Lot." And afterwards: "Abraham therefore said to Lot: Let there, I pray you, be no strife between me and you, nor between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brethren. Behold, the whole land is before you; depart from me, I beg you." Among the rich, therefore, discords are easily stirred up. Hence some also think that the dissensions, wars, fights, and battles, and the destructions and devastations of cities and regions, and the countless other evils which happened in Italy in many past times and still do not cease, have arisen from the riches of the Roman Church. And it would have been expedient for the whole Church of God if the same Roman Church had imitated in deed the poverty of the Apostles and their manner of living, without all the pomps as to vessels, clothing, and all household furniture, and without shield-bearers and other servants of whatever kind, and without the other things that are now far removed from that. Therefore, as it seems to some, it is in no way expedient for the community of the faithful to have one head. Again: it is expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by many, therefore it is not expedient for it to be subject to one head and prelate. The antecedent seems capable of proof by reasons similar to those which Aristotle alleges in the third book of the Politics, to show that it is better for a city to be ruled by the best laws than by the best men, and by many best men rather than by one best man. Some of these can be applied to our purpose in this way. It is expedient for the whole congregation of the faithful to be ruled by the one or the few whose judgment is more certain and better in judging and discerning what things are to be pursued as common to the whole community of the faithful, and what things are to be utterly rejected as useless and harmful, and who are able to weigh and see many such matters. For without full and certain skill in such matters, no community can be governed well, because the Saviour himself says in Matthew 15: "If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the pit." But many judge and discern such matters better and more surely, and weigh and see many such things, than one alone.

units.la: Vnde & Aristoteles 3. politicor. c. 13. ait: Conuenientes disceptant & consiliantur & iudicant, haec autem sunt iudicia omnia de singularibus secundum vnumquodque igitur oportet quicunque fore deteriora, sed est aequitas ex multis: sicut concenatio comparata pulchrior vna & simplici, propter hoc iudicat melius turba vna, quam vnus quicunque & cap. 14. ait: Inconueniensque forte vtique esse videbitur, si melius perciperet quis duobus oculis & duabus auribus, & ageret duobus pedibus & manibus, quam multi multis. Hoc enim inconueniens est dicere quod vnus duobus oculis & duabus naribus melius aut plura percipiat: & quod vnus melius aut plura operetur duobus pedibus & duabus manibus, quam multi multis pedibus & multis manibus. Multi igitur certius & plura vident. Vnde & Act. 15. legitur, quod conuenerunt Apostoli & seniores videre de verbo hoc: scilicet de quaestione, quae super circumcisione seruanda inter beatos Paulum & Barnabam ac quosdam Christianos alios vertebatur. Apostolus etiam Paulus, ut ipse testatur ad Gal. contulit cum aliis Apostolis Euangelium ne forte in vacuum curreret ac cucurrisset. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod plura & certius vident plures quam vnus & optimus, teste Innoc. papa, qui, ut habetur distin. 20. cap. de quibus, ait: Facilius & eadem ratione certius inuenitur, quod & pluribus senioribus quaeritur. Hinc est quod pro difficilioribus & maioribus negotiis ecclesiasticis, quando imminerit, generale concilium congregatur, igitur expedit toti congregationi fidelium, ut pluribus quam ab vno regantur.
units.tr: Hence Aristotle also says in the third book of the Politics, chapter 13: "Those who come together deliberate, take counsel, and judge; and all these judgments concern particulars. Each individual may be worse, but the whole is better, for the many together are like a feast made by many contributions, which is finer than one simple dish. For this reason the crowd judges better than any single man." And in chapter 14 he says: "It would seem perhaps unfitting if someone perceived better with two eyes and two ears, and acted with two feet and two hands, than many with many." For it is unfitting to say that one man with two eyes and two nostrils perceives better or more things, and that one man with two feet and two hands works better or more than many with many feet and many hands. Therefore many see more and more certainly. Hence it is also read in Acts 15 that "the apostles and elders came together to see about this matter", namely the question which was being argued between the blessed Paul and Barnabas and certain other Christians concerning the keeping of circumcision. The Apostle Paul also, as he himself testifies in Galatians, communicated the gospel with the other apostles, lest perhaps he should run, or had run, in vain. From these words it is gathered that many see more and more certainly than one, even the best one, as Pope Innocent testifies, who, as it is found in distin. 20. cap. de quibus, says: "It is more easily and by the same reasoning more certainly found what is sought from several elders." Hence it is that for more difficult and greater ecclesiastical affairs, when the need arises, a general council is convened. Therefore it is expedient for the whole congregation of the faithful to be ruled by many rather than by one.

units.la: Amplius, ab illo vel illis expedit regi communitatem fidelium, cuius vel quorum appetitus siue voluntas est minus corruptibilis & peruertibilis a malitia, concupiscentiis, affectionibus & passionibus prauis, oportet enim principem esse virtuosum & bonum ac passionum minime sectatorem. Impii enim & qui sequuntur passiones & affectiones prauas, non sunt digni aliqualiter principari, teste Salomon: qui Prouerb. 28. ait: regnantibus impiis ruina homin. & 29. Cum impii sumpserint principatum, gemet populus. Hic Sapiens ille letro rationi rectae assentiens dedit consilium Moysi, ut solummodo bonos viros praficeret populo, dicens: Prouide tamen de omni plebe viros potentes & timentes Deum, in quibus sit veritas, & qui oderunt auari auaritiam, & constitutę ex eis tribunes &c. Et Aristoteles 3. politicor. c. 2. ait: ἀνδρεῖος, id est virtuosos principari oportet. Plures autem sunt minus peruertibiles & corruptibiles à malitiis, concupiscentiis, assectionibus & passionibus prauis, quam vnus. Igitur magis expedit communitati fidelium regi à pluribus, quam ab vno. Maior istius rationis etiam innumeris auctoritatibus tam Philosophorum quam fidelium posset ostendi: sed videtur tam nota, quod non oportet eam plus probare. Minor videtur posse probari multis modis. Ait enim Aristo. 3. poli. c. 8. Multos enim quorum vnusquisq; est non studiosus virtutis, tamen contingit, cum conuenerint, esse meliores illis (scilicet paucis & per consequens multo magis vno) non vt magis studiosi, sed simul omnes veluti comportare censum hu, qui vna expensa elargiti sunt, multis enim existentibus vnamquamque partem habere virtutis & prudentiae & fini congregatorum quasi vnum hominem multitudinem & multorum pedum & multarum manuum prorsus habentem, sic & sic, qua circa mores & circa intellectum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod melius est totam multitudinem principari, quam paucos etiam virtuosos. Ex quo infertur, quod melius est plures regere, quam vnum solum. Item, cap. 14. quaerit, vtrum vnus princeps difficilius poterit peruerti & corrumpi, quam plures etiam boni viri, dicens: Si plures sint boni viri & ciues, vtrum magis incorruptibiles sit princeps? & respondetur dicens: sed magis plures quidem numero: boni autem viri. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod plures sunt magis incorruptibiles & imperuertibiles à passionibus prauis, quam vnus, vnde & videtur concludere, quod melius est ciuitatem regi à pluribus, quam ab vno, dicens: aut palam quod plures scilicet melius regent quam vnus. Vnde & ibidem videtur concludere Aristot. quod aristocratia, quae est principatus plurium bonorum, est eligibilior & melior quam regnum, quod est vnius, dicens: Si itaque plurium principatum, bonorum autem virorum omnium quae aristocratiam ponendum, eum autem, qui vnius regnum & cum potentia & fine potentia existente principatu fit accipere plures. Ex praedictis omnibus concluditur, quod melius est communitatem fidelium regi pluribus, quam ab vno, qui sit omnium aliorum caput & princeps & praelatus.
units.tr: Furthermore, the community of the faithful is better ruled by one or those whose desire or will is least liable to corruption and perversion by wickedness, lusts, affections and evil passions. For a prince must be virtuous and good, and not a follower of the passions at all. Impious men, and those who follow evil passions and affections, are not fit to rule in any way, as Solomon says in Proverbs 28: When the impious rule, men are ruined, and again in 29: When the impious take up power, the people will groan. That wise man, agreeing with sound reason, also gave Moses the advice to set over the people only good men, saying: But provide out of all the people men of ability who fear God, men in whom there is truth, who hate covetousness, and appoint such over them as tribunes, etc. And Aristotle, Politics 3, chapter 2, says: Virtuous men ought to rule [ἀνδρεῖος]. Now there are fewer men who are corrupted and perverted by wicked desires, lusts, affections and evil passions than there is one man. Therefore it is more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by many than by one. The major premise could be shown by countless authorities, both of the philosophers and of the faithful, but it seems so well known that it need not be proved further. The minor premise seems capable of proof in many ways. For Aristotle says in Politics 3, chapter 8: For though each of the many is not devoted to virtue, yet when they have come together it may happen that they are better than those few (and consequently much more than one), not as individuals but all together, just as a feast provided by many contributors is better than one provided at one person's expense. For when there are many, each can have a share of virtue and prudence, and when they have come together the multitude becomes like one man with many feet, many hands and many senses, and so too in respect of character and intellect. From these words it is gathered that it is better for the whole multitude to rule than for a few, even virtuous ones. From this it follows that it is better to rule by many than by one alone. Likewise, in chapter 14, he asks whether a single prince can be more easily perverted and corrupted than many good men, saying: If there are many good men and citizens, is the prince more incorruptible? And the answer is given: rather the many, by number, are the good men. From these words it is made clear that many are more incorruptible and less liable to be overthrown by evil passions than one. Hence he seems to conclude that it is better for a state to be ruled by many than by one, saying: Clearly, then, the many will rule better than one. So too in the same place Aristotle seems to conclude that aristocracy, which is the rule of many good men, is more desirable and better than kingship, which is the rule of one, saying: If, then, the rule of many, and of all good men, is to be called aristocracy, while the rule of one man, whether with power or without power, is kingship, we must take the rule of many. From all that has been said it is concluded that it is better for the community of the faithful to be ruled by many than by one, who is the head, prince and chief of all the others.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Exponit aliqua, quae in praecedenti capitulo in arguendo fuerunt assumpta: & dividit communitates secundum intentionem Aristot. 1. politicorum & determinat principaliter de prima.
units.tr: Explains some points that were assumed in the preceding chapter in the argument, and divides the communities according to the intention of Aristotle, Politics book 1, and deals mainly with the first.

units.la: Discipul. Quia superius Aristotelem allegasti in Politicis & etiam Ethicis, & es inferius forsitan allegaturus compluries, qui pluribus vocabulis vtitur, quorum significationes puris Iurisdis & aliis qui in Philosophia morali minime studuerunt, sunt ignota. Ideo vt tractanda melius intelligantur ab illis, significationes aliquorum huiusmodi vocabulorum studeas explicare, vna cum hoc (sub breui compendio) quis & qualiter secundum intentionem Aristotelis in Politicis & Ethicis debeat aliis principari, prout alii qui ipsum intelligunt, exponunt. Cum enim ipse de hac materia dissuse tractauerit, & in multis rationabiliter processisse putetur, non modica occasio tribuetur studiosis intelligendi, quis & qualiter inter catholicos debeat alios tam in spiritualibus quam in temporalibus gubernare. Magister. Quamuis quod petis non reputem facile: tamen satisfacere voluntati tuae conabor, & tibi intentionem Aristotelis in hoc secundum opinionem quorundam, cum quibus tamen non omnes concordant, in omnibus recitabo. Dicitur igitur quod Aristoteles 1. Poli. ponit tres communitates, in quibus aliquis vel aliqui debet vel debent principari aliis. Quarum prima secundum eum est domus: quae tres combinationes, communitates seu coniugationes complectitur, scilicet eam quae est viri ad vxorem: & illam quae est patris ad filium: & illam quae est Domini ad seruos. Prima autem combinatio vocatur ab Aristotele nuptialis. Secunda potest vocari paterna, & eam Aristoteles vocat celmostinam, id est factiuam filiorum. Tertiam vero Aristoteles vocat despoticam, id est dominatiuam, despotes enim est idem quod Dominus, & principatus despoticus est principatus dominatiuus.
units.tr: Disciple. Since you cited Aristotle above in the Politics and also in the Ethics, and you will perhaps cite him often below, using many terms whose meanings are unknown to lawyers and others who have not studied moral philosophy, I ask you to explain the meanings of some such terms. Along with this, please set out briefly who and how, according to Aristotle's intention in the Politics and Ethics, one ought to govern others, as those who understand him explain it. For although he treated this subject in many places and is thought to have reasoned well in many of them, it will give students no small opportunity to understand who and how Catholics ought to govern others, both in spiritual and in temporal matters. Master. Although I do not regard what you ask as easy, I will try to satisfy your wish. I will recite for you, in full, Aristotle's intention on this point according to the opinion of certain writers, with whom, however, not all agree. Aristotle, then, in Politics book 1, Pol. 1, lays down three communities in which one person or several ought to rule over others. The first of these, according to him, is the household. It embraces three combinations, or communities and unions: that of husband and wife; that of father and son; and that of master and slaves. Aristotle calls the first combination nuptial. The second may be called paternal, and Aristotle calls it ktetic (celmostina), that is, the begetting of children. The third Aristotle calls despotic, that is, dominating, for despotes is the same as lord, and despotic rule is lordly rule.

units.la: Vt tamen haec melius intelligantur, dicitur esse sciendum, quod huiusmodi vocabula Dominus, Dominans, Dominator & consimilia non eadem significatione in diuersis scripturis & scientiis accipiuntur, sed aequiuoce: propter cuius aequiuocationis ignorantiam saepe ignoratur intellectus auctorum vtentium talibus vocabulis, secundum sensus contrarios. Omissis autem variis significationibus huiusmodi vocabulorum Dominus, Dominans, praedominans, Dominium, Dominantium, & consimilium, quibus diuersimode vtuntur interdum Philosophia naturalis & moralis, & legalis scientia, ac vulgaris locutio: illae, quibus saepe vtuntur scripturae diuinae, duae sunt tantummodo, quae videntur ad propositum exponendae. Est igitur sciendum secundum istos, quod Dominus vno modo dicitur respectu subiectorum liberorum quidem: quibus scilicet dominatur quis non principaliter propter vtilitatem propriam, sed principaliter propter vtilitatem subditorum, & talis Dominus non vocatur ab Aristotele despotes, nec principatus, quo talis principatur vocatur ab eo despoticus. Aliter dicitur Dominus respectu subiectorum non liberorum, sed seruorum, qui sunt possessio domini, quemadmodum aliae res temporales dicuntur possessio alicuius, & talis Dominus vocatur ab Aristotele despotes & principatus eius vocatur despoticus, qui despotes, sicut possidet res alias temporales propter vtilitatem propriam, & non propter vtilitatem earum, sic principatur seruis principaliter propter vtilitatem propriam, & non propter vtilitatem seruorum: licet saepe secundum Aristotelem idem sit expediens serseruis & Domino. Quare licet inueniatur ab Arist. in Politi. quod rex sit Dominus sibi subiectorum: tamen nusquam inuenitur, quod debet dici despotes, vel quod principatus regalis debeat despoticus appellari: licet quandoq; principatus tyrannicus, despoticus nominetur propter similitudinem magnam inter despoticum & tyrannicum principatum. Quia proprie loquendo principatus despoticus non est tyrannicus. Sicut enim aliqui iuste sunt serui secundum Aristotelem: tam illi scilicet qui à ratione deficiunt, vt nesciant regere seipsos; licet corpore sint robusti, vt aliis valeant deseruire, qui secundum Aristot. dicuntur naturaliter serui: quam illi qui sunt serui secundum legem, quia in bello iusto capiuntur, vel aliter fiunt serui aliorum. Sic principatus despoticus, qui est solum modo respectu talium seruorum, est iustus & licitus atque bonus. Principatus autem tyrannicus est iniustus, illicitus atq; malus, vnde & secundum Aristot. tyrannis est pessima politia.
units.tr: So that these points may be better understood, it should be known that such words as Dominus, Dominans, Dominator and the like are not taken in the same sense in different writings and sciences, but equivocally. Because of ignorance of this equivocation, the meaning of authors who use such words is often missed, since they carry opposite senses. Leaving aside the various meanings of such words as Dominus, Dominans, praedominans, Dominium, Dominantium and the like, which natural and moral philosophy, legal science and ordinary speech use in different ways, there are only two senses, often used in Holy Scripture, that seem to need explaining for our purpose. According to these authors, then, it should be known that Dominus is used in one way with respect to free subjects: those over whom someone rules not chiefly for his own advantage but chiefly for the advantage of his subjects. Such a lord is not called despotes by Aristotle, nor is the rule by which he rules called despotic by him. In another way Dominus is used with respect to subjects who are not free but slaves, who are the property of their master, just as other temporal things are said to be someone's possession. Such a lord is called by Aristotle despotes, and his rule is called despotic. As the despot holds other temporal things for his own advantage and not for theirs, so he rules his slaves chiefly for his own advantage and not for theirs, although according to Aristotle what is useful to the slaves is often also useful to the master. Therefore, although it is found in Aristotle's Politics that the king is lord of his subjects, nowhere is it found that he should be called a despot, or that royal rule should be called despotic. Sometimes, however, tyrannical rule is named despotic, because of the great likeness between despotic and tyrannical rule. For, properly speaking, despotic rule is not tyrannical. Just as some men are justly slaves according to Aristotle, namely those who fall short of reason so that they cannot govern themselves, though they are strong in body to serve others, and who by Aristotle are called slaves by nature; and as others are slaves by law, because they are taken in a just war or otherwise become the slaves of others; so despotic rule, which exists only with respect to such slaves, is just, lawful and good. Tyrannical rule, on the other hand, is unjust, unlawful and bad; hence also, according to Aristotle, tyranny is the worst form of government.

units.la: Præter principatum despoticum, quo paterfamilias principatur seruis in domo, est principatus paternus, quo filiis tanquam liberis principatur: quibus secundum Arist. regaliter & non despotice principatur. Non quod principatus paternus sit principatus regalis: quia principatus regalis non est nisi respectu ciuitatis vel regni: quod maius est ciuitate, & vt plurimum plures ciuitates complectitur. Sed pater dicitur filiis regaliter principari: non quidem quando domus, in qua principatur, est pars vici vel ciuitatis aut regni: sed in domo, quae non est pars communitatis perfectioris, qualiter Adam principabatur filiis suis, & Noe filiis suis, antequam filii illi diuersas domos haberent. Talis autem principatus paternus, licet non dicatur regalis stricte loquendo, potest tamen dici regalis propter magnam similitudinem ad principatum regalem stricte sumptum. Sicut enim in regno habetur regem, qui proprissime & autentice dicitur rex, vnus existens principatur omnibus liberis principaliter, propter vtilitatem subiectorum secundum voluntatem suam, non secundum legem, secundum Aristot. 3. poli. c. 15. Quod qualiter debeat intelligi, postea exponitur sic. In domo, quae non est pars communitatis perfectioris, quandocunq; est talis pater, principatur filiis principaliter propter vtilitatem ipsorum secundum voluntatem suam, non secundum legem, ita vt filios delinquentes omni poena, qua expedit, valeat castigare, possit de ipsis & ipsis facere quaecunq; redundant in vtilitatem ipsorum: quibus quia non principatur principaliter propter vtilitatem propriam, non despotice, sed quodammodo potest dici regaliter principari. In domo autem quae est pars vici vel ciuitatis pater non principatur filiis regaliter: quia non habet tantam potestatem super filios, vt principetur eis secundum voluntatem suam, non secundum legem. Etiam in multis quae pertinent ad vtilitatem ipsorum, nec pro multis delictis potest cos poena, qua expedit, coercere secundum quod talis vindicta est illi, qui principatur in vico vel in ciuitate aut in regno seruanda. Paterfamilias autem in domo principatur vxori neq; despotice neq; regaliter, non despotice, quia non est serua: nec regaliter, quia non debet principari ei secundum voluntatem suam, sed secundum legem matrimonii. Neq; enim tantam potestatem habet vir super vxorem, quantam habet pater super filios, quando non est pars perfectioris communitatis, principatur ergo vir vxori principatu politico.
units.tr: Besides despotic rule, by which the head of the household rules his slaves in the house, there is paternal rule, by which a father rules his children as free persons. According to Aristotle, children are ruled over in a royal, not a despotic, manner. This is not because paternal rule is royal rule, since royal rule exists only with respect to a city or kingdom, which is larger than a city and usually embraces several cities. Rather, a father is said to rule his children in a royal manner not when the household in which he rules is part of a village, city or kingdom, but in a household that is not part of a more perfect community, as Adam ruled his sons and Noah his sons before those sons had separate households. Such paternal rule, although strictly speaking it is not called royal, can nevertheless be called royal because of its great resemblance to royal rule strictly understood. For just as in a kingdom there is a king, who in the most proper and authentic sense is called king, and who, being one, rules all free persons chiefly for the advantage of his subjects, according to his own will and not according to law (according to Aristotle, Pol. 3, c. 15), so the matter should be understood as follows. In a household that is not part of a more perfect community, whenever there is such a father, he rules his children chiefly for their advantage, according to his own will and not according to law, so that he may punish his delinquent children with whatever penalty is expedient and may do with them whatever tends to their advantage. Since he does not rule them chiefly for his own advantage, his rule is not despotic, and it may be said in some sense to be royal. But in a household that is part of a village or city, the father does not rule his children in a royal manner, because he does not have such power over his children that he may rule them according to his own will and not according to law. Also, in many matters that concern their advantage, and for many offences, he cannot restrain them with whatever penalty is expedient, since such punishment belongs to the one who rules in the village, city or kingdom. The head of the household, however, rules his wife neither despotically nor royally: not despotically, because she is not a slave; nor royally, because he ought not to rule her according to his own will, but according to the law of marriage. For a husband does not have as much power over his wife as a father has over his children when the household is not part of a more perfect community. So the husband rules his wife with political rule.

units.la: Hic enim principatus viri super vxorem assimilatur principatui politico, in hoc scilicet, quod in principatu politico principantes secundum virtutem & sapientiam antecellunt sibi subiectos: sic naturaliter vir excedit vxorem secundum sapientiam & virtutem, nisi aliquid accidat praeter naturam, secundum Arist. 1. Poli. sicut contingit in masculis effoeminatis, per quem modum intelligenda sunt, quae dicta sunt superius de principatu despotico & paterno: quando scilicet natura non deficit in despote vel patre. Si enim natura ex aliqua causa deficeret in patre vel despote, non esset iustum naturale desipotem aut patrem, seruis vel filiis principari, quorum tamen principatus sunt naturales, id est ex ratione naturali, non ex institutione humana proueniëntes, quando natura non deficit in patre vel despote. Tres autem praedicti principatus ad oeconomiam, id est ad gubernationem domus spectant, & sic accipitur oeconomia ab Aristotele in Philosophia morali, licet oeconomus in iure vocetur ille, cui res ecclesiastica gubernanda mandatur, vt qui administrat res canonicorum, qui in quibusdam ecclesiis appellatur praepositus.
units.tr: For the husband's rule over his wife is compared to political rule in this respect: in political rule, those who rule surpass their subjects in virtue and wisdom. So, according to Aristotle, Pol. 1, by nature the man surpasses the woman in wisdom and virtue, unless something happens contrary to nature, as happens in effeminate men. In the same way, what has been said above about despotic and paternal rule must be understood, namely when nature is not lacking in the despot or father. For if nature were lacking in the father or despot for some cause, it would not be natural justice for the despot or father to rule over slaves or children. Yet these rules are natural, that is, they arise from natural reason and not from human institution, when nature is not lacking in the father or despot. These three kinds of rule belong to the economy, that is, to the government of the household, and in this sense Aristotle uses the term economy in moral philosophy. In law, however, the economus is the one to whom the management of ecclesiastical property is entrusted, as the administrator of the goods of canons, who in some churches is called the praepositus.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Determinatio de secunda communitate, quae dicitur vicus.
units.tr: Determination concerning the second community, which is called the village.

units.la: MAgister. Secunda communitas, quae est perfectior domo, vocatur vicus: quia ex multis domibus constat, tanquam ex partibus, nec tamen ad tantam perfectionem attigit, vt ciuitas sit & debeat appellari, ista autem communitas si non sit pars perfectioris communitatis (scilicet ciuitatis aut alterius comprehendentis multos vicos seu vicinias aut ciuitates) & in ipsa multitudo domorum processit ex vno parente superstite, rationabile est vt ab illo regatur secundum voluntatem, non secundum legem, quantum ad illos qui processerunt ab ipso, si in eo natura non deficit, quemadmodum filii reguntur à patre. Quantum ad vxores autem, quarum non est parens, rationabile est, vt politice principetur, quia ratio exigit vt leges matrimonii conseruet, secundum quam vir & vxor in multis ad paria iudicantur. Si autem multitudo domorum vici non processit ab vno parente superstite, rationabile est vt aliquo regimine simili regimini, quo regitur ciuitas, gubernetur.
units.tr: Master. The second community, which is more perfect than the household, is called the village, because it consists of many households as of parts, yet it has not reached such perfection that it is, or ought to be called, a city. If this community is not a part of a more perfect community (namely a city, or another community embracing many villages or neighbourhoods or cities), and if the multitude of households in it has proceeded from one surviving parent, it is reasonable that it be governed by him according to his will, not according to law, as far as concerns those who have proceeded from him, provided that nature does not fail in him, just as children are governed by their father. As for the wives, however, of whom he is not the parent, it is reasonable that he preside over them in a civil manner, because reason requires that he preserve the laws of marriage, according to which husband and wife are judged to be equal in many respects. If, however, the multitude of households in the village has not proceeded from one surviving parent, it is reasonable that it be governed by some form of rule similar to that by which a city is governed.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Determinat de tertia communitate, quae dicitur ciuitas.
units.tr: He treats of the third community, which is called the city.

units.la: MAgist. Tertia communitas est, quae ex pluribus vicis componitur, vocatur ciuitas, quam dicit Aristot. 1. poli. esse principalissimam omnium communitatum, quod dicitur veritatem habere de communitatibus simul habitantium, non de communitate habitantium in distantibus locis & in pluribus ciuitatibus, qualis communitas est Regnum vel Ducatus: quod etiam potest communitas appellari, quia est illorum qui simul communicant in multis & ab vno principante reguntur, & multa, quae dicuntur de ciuitate, proportionaliter intelligenda sunt de regno & quacunque communitate, quae plures complectitur ciuitates. Ciuitas autem est multitudo ciuium habitantium ciuitatem, quorum ordo vocatur politia, sine ordine enim nulla est ciuitas. Nisi enim habeat principantem vel principantes & subiectos, non est ciuitas appellanda, in qua diuersi & diuersimode sunt subiecti saltem saepe & in perfectissima ciuitate. Quidam enim reperiuntur subiecti tanquam serui vel mercenarii aut bannansi. Dicuntur autem bannansi, qui naturaliter seu corporaliter operantes opere suo maculant corpus, & isti in ciuitate, quae temperata & rationabili vitur politia, non sunt proprie ciues. Alii autem in ciuitate sic sunt subiecti, quod aliquo modo participant principatum, quia quamvis non principentur, tamen aliquo modo ad principatum attingunt: quia ad iudicium vocantur & consilium, vel eligunt principantem, aut electores principantis. Principans autem in ciuitate aliquando vocatur ab Aristotele policernia. Policernia autem secundum quosdam tres habet significationes. Primo autem significat impositionem ordinis politiae. Secundo impositorem ipsius. Tertio significat ipsum ordinem impositum, qui est politia, & ita policernia in vna significatione idem est, quod Dominus & principans in ciuitate.
units.tr: Master. The third community is the one composed of several villages, and it is called a city. Aristotle, in the 1. poli., says it is the most principal of all communities. That holds true of communities whose members live together in one place, not of a community whose members live in distant places and in several cities, such as a Kingdom or a Duchy. That too may be called a community, since it consists of people who share many things together and are ruled by one governor. Many things said of the city must be understood proportionally of a kingdom, and of any community that embraces several cities. A city, however, is a multitude of citizens living in one city, and their order is called the polity, for there is no city without order. For unless it has a governor or governors and subjects, a community cannot be called a city, even if in it persons are subject in various ways, and this is often so even in the most perfect city. Some are found to be subject as slaves, or as hired workers, or as bannansi. Those are called bannansi who work naturally or physically and by their labour stain the body. In a city that is well governed and follows a reasonable polity, such people are not properly citizens. Others, however, are so subject in the city that they share in the governing in some way: although they do not rule, they nevertheless reach towards rule in some measure, because they are called to judgement and counsel, or they elect the ruler, or they are electors of the ruler. The ruler in a city is sometimes called by Aristotle policernia. According to some, policernia has three meanings. First, it signifies the imposing of the order of the polity. Second, it signifies the one who imposes it. Third, it signifies the order itself that is imposed, which is the polity. Thus policernia, in one sense, is the same as lord and ruler in the city.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Diuidit politias in duas species principales.
units.tr: He divides polities into two principal species.

units.la: MAgister. Politiarum autem duae sunt species primae: sicut & duae sunt species propriae principatuum siue praelationum, & principantium siue praelatorum seu rectorum. Omnis enim principatus aut ordinatur principaliter ad bonum seu conferens commune bonum, scilicet principantis & principantium & etiam subiectorum: aut non ordinatur ad bonum commune. Si ordinetur ad bonum commune, sic est principatus temperatus & rectus. Si non ordinatur ad bonum commune, est principatus vitiatus & transgressio: quia est corruptio & transgressio principatus temperati & rectique iusti. Politia igitur omnis, aut est temperata & recta: vel est vitiata & transgressa. perfectionem importat. In principatu autem despotico est detrimentum multorum ex hoc ipso, quod despotes potest uti sibi subiectis & bonis eorum ad propriam utilitatem, & ideo talis potestas maiorem imperfectionem boni melioris, scilicet boni multorum includit. Propter quod principatus despoticus non solum qui est unius patrisfamilias in una domo, sed qui esset unius regis in uno regno: & per consequens qui est unius imperatoris in toto orbe, esset simpliciter imperfectior principatu tali regali. Praeterea principatum regalem sunt alii principatus regales diversimode deficientes ab isto: convenientes tamen in hoc, quod sunt Monarchiae quaedam. Quidam enim principatus unius Monarchiae deficit ab isto, quantum ad intentionem boni communis, quia scilicet non institutus totaliter propter bonum commune, sed etiam propter bonum proprium, & talis principatus regalis aliqd habet de principatu tyrannico vel despotico: & est quodammodo mixtus ex principatu despotico, tyrannico, & regali. In quantum enim quo ad aliqua intendit bonum commune: & in quantum solus principatur, habet aliquid de principatu regali. In quantum vero bonum proprium etiam intendit, habet aliqd de principatu tyrannico & despotico, & ideo est quodammodo mixtus ex principatibus illis, unde & aliquis principatus regalis & tyrannicus vocatur ab Aristo. Principatus autem unius interdum deficit a supra dicto principatu regali quantum ad potestatem, quod scilicet non habet illam plenitudinem potestatis, quam habet principatus regalis praefatus. Et talis principatus regalis dicitur secundum quod licet unus principetur, modo tamen principatur secundum voluntatem, sed quibusdam consuetudinibus humanitus introductis astringitur, quas tenetur servare, & ipsas se servaturum iurare vel promittere obligatur, & quanto plures tales leges & consuetudines servare tenetur, tanto magis recedit a memorato principatu regali: & ideo forte his diebus non est in universo orbe talis principatus scilicet primus regalis. Secundum Aristot. nullus est dignus tali regno, nisi sapientia & virtute & bonis omnibus tam corporis quam animae, quam etiam exterioribus bonis, scilicet amicis & divitiis, superexcellat. Aliter enim timendum est, ne ad tyrannidem se conuertat, unde & propria bona debet habere vel ex se vel ex assignatione illorum, quibus praeest, ut bona liberorum nequaquam sibi appropriet, nec etiam quoquomodo accipiat, nisi evidens utilitas vel manifesta necessitas hoc exposcat. Isti principatui regali etiam summae opponitur tyrannis, quae est transgressio & corruptio eius, quae est prima species & pessima politiae vitiatae, quia tyrannis non intendit bonum subiectorum, nisi per accidens, sed principaliter intendit bonum proprium, sive bonum proprium sit bonum etiam aliorum, sive sit malum ipsorum. Fiunt autem tyranni secundum Aristo. 5. Politi. c. 8. saepe ex Demagogis, sunt autem Demagogi, ducentes populum secundum voluntatem suam de beneplacito populi, non tanquam reges aut Domini vel Tyranni seu ius regendi populum aut imperandi habentes: sed quasi procuratores & concionatores seu monitores instigant populum ad illa, quae populo placent id est quibus populus credit, & ideo Arist. vocat eos 4. Politic. c. 3. adulatores, talis enim saepe, postquam sibi vnierint populum, incipiunt propter potentiam tyrannizare: & etiam involuntariis dominari. Fiunt etiam Tyranni nonnunquam ex regibus, quia, ut dicit Aristo. 8. Ethicorum, malus rex tyrannus fit, si enim secundum legem incipiat principari involuntariis propter bonum proprium, fit tyrannus, si incipiat principari voluntariis propter bonum proprium, fit proprie despotes. Cuius principatus nonnunquam Tyrannis ab Aristotele vocatur, propter similitudinem magnam ad despoticam: non tamen Tyrannis proprie est despotia, sicut ex supradictis patere potest. Ex praedictis colligi potest, quod principatui regali, praesertim potissimo, non solum Tyrannis proprie dicta, sed etiam principatus despoticus aliquo modo opponitur, vel est principatus ita disparatus, ut nullus vnus principatus possit esse regalis & despoticus respectu eorundem: quod tamen aliquis dominetur regaliter, & aliquis despotice, inconueniens non videtur.
units.tr: Master. There are two primary species of polities, just as there are two proper species of principates or governments, and of those who govern, that is, of prelates or rulers. Every principate is either ordered principally to the good, that is, to the common good of the ruler, the rulers and also the subjects, or it is not ordered to the common good. If it is ordered to the common good, it is a temperate and right principate. If it is not ordered to the common good, it is a corrupt principate and a transgression, because it is a corruption and transgression of a temperate and right, just principate. Every polity, therefore, is either temperate and right, or corrupt and transgressive. [...] In a despotic principate there is a loss to many for this very reason, that the despot can use his subjects and their goods for his own advantage. For this reason such a power includes a greater imperfection of the better good, namely the good of many. On account of this, a despotic principate, not only that of one father of a family in one household, but also that of one king in one kingdom, and consequently that of one emperor over the whole world, would be simply more imperfect than such a royal principate. Moreover, there are other royal principates, differing from this one in various ways, yet agreeing in this, that they are certain kinds of monarchy. For one principate of a single monarchy falls short of this one in regard to the aim of the common good, since it is instituted not entirely for the common good but also for its own good; such a royal principate has something of a tyrannical or despotic principate, and is in a way mixed from the despotic, tyrannical and royal. Insofar as it aims at the common good in some respects, and insofar as one alone rules, it has something of a royal principate. Insofar as it also aims at its own good, it has something of a tyrannical and despotic principate, and so it is in a way mixed from those principates; whence Aristotle also calls some royal principate tyrannical. A principate of one man sometimes falls short of the aforesaid royal principate in power, namely in that it does not have that fullness of power which the aforesaid royal principate has. And such a royal principate is said to be one in which, although one man rules, he nevertheless rules according to his own will, yet is bound by certain customs introduced by human agreement, which he is obliged to keep, and he is bound to swear or promise that he will keep them; and the more such laws and customs he is obliged to keep, the further he withdraws from the aforesaid royal principate. For this reason, perhaps in these days there is no such principate, namely the first royal kind, anywhere in the whole world. According to Aristotle, no one is worthy of such a kingdom unless he surpasses all others in wisdom and virtue and in all goods, both of body and of soul, and also in external goods, namely friends and riches. Otherwise there is reason to fear that he will turn to tyranny; hence he ought to have his own goods, either from himself or by assignment from those over whom he presides, so that he never appropriates to himself the goods of his children, nor takes them in any way, unless evident advantage or manifest necessity demands it. To this royal principate of the highest kind is opposed tyranny, which is the transgression and corruption of it, and which is the first and worst species of a corrupt polity; for tyranny does not aim at the good of the subjects except incidentally, but chiefly aims at its own good, whether its own good is also the good of others or is their harm. Now according to Aristotle, Politics 5, ch. 8, tyrants often arise out of Demagogues, who lead the people according to their own will and by the pleasure of the people, not as kings or lords or tyrants having a right to rule or command the people, but as procurators, preachers or advisers, they urge the people toward those things which please the people, that is, which the people believe in; and for this reason Aristotle calls them flatterers, Politics 4, ch. 3. For such men, after they have united the people to themselves, begin to tyrannize because of their power, and to rule even over the unwilling. Tyrants also sometimes arise from kings, because, as Aristotle says in Ethics 8, a bad king becomes a tyrant: if he begins to rule over the unwilling for his own good, though he rules according to law, he becomes a tyrant; if he begins to rule over the willing for his own good, he becomes properly a despot. The principate of this kind is sometimes called Tyranny by Aristotle, on account of its great similarity to the despotic; yet tyranny is not properly despotism, as can be seen from what has been said above. From what has been said it can be gathered that the royal principate, especially the most powerful, is opposed not only to tyranny properly so called but also in some way to despotic principate, or else that these principates are so distinct that no one principate can be both royal and despotic with respect to the same persons; yet that one man should rule royally and another despotically does not seem absurd.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: In quo tractatur de aristocratia, & sibi opposita oligarchia politia speciebus.
units.tr: In which aristocracy is treated, and oligarchy, the species of polity opposed to it.

units.la: Magist. Secunda species politiae temperatae & rectae atq; iustae vocatur aristocratia, in qua scilicet aliqui pauci viri & optimi principantur propter bonum commune multitudinis, & non propter bonum proprium. Quia licet habeat plures species, ut docet Aristo. 3. politicorum c. 1. tamen prima & optima species eius est, quando in sublimando aliquos in principatum aristocraticum potest haberi, & habetur respectus solummodo ad virtutes scilicet intellectuales & morales, non ad divitias, nec ad potentiam, nec ad amicos, nec ad quaecunq; quae possent absq; bonitate & sapientia reperiri. Politia autem intemperata & vitiata atq; transgressa, quae ad aristocratiae directe opponitur, vocatur oligarchia, quando aliqui scilicet divites vel potentes vel qualitercunq; insignes propter bonum proprium principantur, in tantum quod si etiam optimi viri principentur propter bonum proprium, & non principentur propter bonum multitudinis, dicentur esse oligarchice principari: & principatus eorum esset oligarchicus reputandus. Et ideo quicquid sit in electione principantium vel sublimatione seruando respectum ad alia praerogatiuam quam ad sapientia & virtutem (puta ad divitias vel potentiam vel genus vel amicos vel dignitatem vel superioritatem seu maioritatem vel sequelam, aut quamcunq; aliam excellentiam) obligarchicum est habendum. Nec tamen est hoc semper reputandum, quia ex causa propter bonum finem, licet in huiusmodi ad aliquam aliam praerogatiuam vel excellentiam habere respectum, tam aristocratiae quam oligarchiae sunt diversae species, de quibus non est tractandum ad praesens.
units.tr: Magist. The second species of a temperate, right and just polity is called aristocracy, in which a few men, namely the best, rule for the common good of the multitude and not for their own good. For although it has several species, as Aristotle teaches in Politics 3, chapter 1, its first and best species is when, in raising men to aristocratic rule, one can have regard and does have regard only to intellectual and moral virtues, and not to wealth, nor to power, nor to friends, nor to anything else that could be found without goodness and wisdom. But a polity that is intemperate, corrupted and perverted, which is directly opposed to aristocracy, is called oligarchy, when certain men who are wealthy or powerful or in some way distinguished rule for their own good; to such an extent that if even the best men ruled for their own good and not for the good of the multitude, they would be said to rule oligarchically, and their rule would be regarded as oligarchic. And therefore, whatever is done in choosing rulers or in raising men to office, if regard is paid to any preeminence other than wisdom and virtue (for example to wealth, power, birth, friends, dignity, superiority or majority, a following, or any other excellence), it must be held to be oligarchic. Yet this is not always to be judged so, because for some good end it is possible to have regard to some other preeminence or excellence in such matters; aristocracy and oligarchy are then different species, which need not be treated at present.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: In quo determinat de tertia specie politiae, quae Timocratia dicitur, & sibi opposita Democratia.
units.tr: In which he determines concerning the third species of polity, which is called timocracy, and its opposite, democracy.

units.la: Mag. Tertia species politiae temperatae & rectae ac iustae diversis nominibus appellatur, uno nomine vocatur communi nomine politia, quod in una significatione est commune ad omnem politiam rectam & non rectam. In alia significatione signat solummodo quandam speciem politiae, quae alio nomine timocratia nominatur, de qua sunt diversae opiniones, una est, quod timocratia sive politia communi nomine dicta est illa, in qua principantur multi propter bonum commune, sive sint optimi sive non optimi: sive sint divites sive pauperes, ita quod politia per se per multitudinem distinguitur ab aristocratia. Alia est, quod politia est illa, in qua principantur aliqui egeni virtuosi propter bonum commune. Alia est, quod politia est illa, in qua principantur aliqui neq; optimi neque mali, sed mediocres propter virtutem & bonum commune, ita quod per defectum virtutis & bonitatis distinguitur ab aristocratia. Sed quacunque politia debeat appellari timocratia vel politia tanquam nomine communi: politia vitiata & transgressa vocatur Democratia, quando scilicet populus principatur vel ordinat & constituit principantem, non propter bonum commune, quae species diversas complectitur. Sicut autem omnium politiarum temperatarum optima est regnum, & post eam aristocratia, & ultimo timocratia: sic politiarum intemperatarum sive vitiatarum pessima est tyrannis, & post ipsam oligarchia, sed in democratia minima perversitas reperitur, secundum Aristo. 8. Ethicorum.
units.tr: Master. The third species of polity, which is temperate, right and just, is called by various names. By one name it is called, in its common sense, polity, which in one meaning is common to every polity, right or not right. In another meaning it signifies only a certain species of polity, which by another name is called timocracy. Concerning this there are different opinions. One is that timocracy, or polity taken in the common sense, is that in which many rule for the common good, whether they are the best or not the best, whether rich or poor, so that polity is distinguished in itself from aristocracy by the multitude of rulers. Another is that polity is that in which some needy but virtuous men rule for the common good. Another is that polity is that in which some rule who are neither the best nor the wicked, but middling, for virtue and the common good, so that it is distinguished from aristocracy by a lack of virtue and goodness. But whatever polity ought to be called timocracy, or polity as a common name, the corrupted and transgressed polity is called democracy, when namely the people rule, or appoint and constitute a ruler, not for the common good; this embraces various species. Just as, among all temperate polities, the best is kingship, and after it aristocracy, and last timocracy, so among intemperate or corrupted polities the worst is tyranny, and after it oligarchy; but in democracy the least perversity is found, according to Aristotle, Ethics, book 8.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: In quo quibusdam aliis rationibus probatur, quod magis expedit communitatem re- gi ab uno, quam a pluribus.
units.tr: In which, by several other arguments, it is proved that it is more expedient for a community to be ruled by one than by many.

units.la: Disc. Expositi, ut aestimo, significationes vocabulorum extraneorum secundum quorundam opinionem, quae frequentius in auctoritatibus Aristotelis iam allegatis & allegandis ponuntur, ideo noli plura exponere, sed ad quaesitum principale revertere, & qualiter ad allegationes supra primo & secundo capitulo huius secundi pro opinionibus diversis & adversis inductas secundum ipsas respondere contingat, studeas recitare. Verumtamen antequam ipsas responsiones enarres, peto ut aliquas allegationes adducas ad probandum quod magis expediat toti communitati fidelium regi ab uno quam a pluribus. Mag. Quod petis, dupliciter intelligi potest, quia dupliciter contingit plures regere sibi subiectos, uno modo, ut plures diversos habeant sibi subiectos, itaq; regimen plurium ad eosdem minime se extendat, quemadmodum plures archiepiscopi regunt omnes in una regione diffusa existentes: & diversa regna a diversis regibus, quorum nullus est sub alio & quandoq; ipsis nullus praeest, reguntur. Aliter plures regunt sibi subiectos: sic scilicet, quod omnes eosdem habent subiectos, quibus communi consilio principantur, quemadmodum in aristocratia & politia stricte sumpta, ac in politiis vitiatis & transgressis eisdem oppositis, scilicet in oligarchia & democratia reperitur. Sive primo modo sive secundo modo intelligas, potes superius primo cap. huius secundi ad id quod petis allegationes aliquas invenire. Quia aliquae earum non solum probant, quod expedit communitati fidelium regi ab uno & non a pluribus primo modo, sed etiam videntur ostendere, quod expedit ei gubernari ab uno & non a pluribus secundo modo. Quare non videtur necesse ad id q; petis plures allegationes adducere. Disc. Quamvis ad id q; peto possunt allegationes aliquae supra inductae allegari, & etiam plura circa consimile materiam, ex quibus potero plura aduertere circa hoc petitum, q; dicentur in secundo tractatu huius Dialogi li.3. tamen volo ut aliquas speciales allegationes inducas ad probandum, q; magis expedit communitatem fidelium regi ab uno, q; a pluribus secundo modo. Mag. Hoc videtur posse sic probari. Illo regimine expedit magis regi communitate fidelium, quod magis assimilatur regimini & principatui naturali, quia sicut ars si est recta imitatur naturam, ita principatus, si est rectus, imitatur & assimilatur principatui naturali, & p consequens principatus, qui magis assimilatur principatui naturali, est rectior & perfectior, & p consequens magis expediens. Sed regimen sive principatus unius, quando scilicet unus solus regit multos & praesidet eis, magis assimilatur principatui naturali, quam regimen seu principatus plurium, quare tale regimen assimilatur principatui regali, qui est unius. Principatus autem regalis magis assimilatur principatui naturali, quam principatus aristocraticus vel politicus stricte sumptus, quia magis assimilatur communitati, quae est domus, in qua principatur unus paterfamilias. Unde & principatus patrisfamilias regalis quodammodo esse videtur, teste Arist. qui poli.i.e.10. ait: Paterfamilias principatur natus regaliter, & code c. dicit. Puerorum autem principatus regalis, & q; enim genuit & secundum amorem principans & secundum senectutem est: quod quidem regalis species principatus. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod principatus regalis assimilatur communitati, quae est domus, in qua principatur unus & non plures, neq; primo modo neque secundo modo. Communitas autem domus est naturalis secundum Aristotel. qui i. poli. in prologo ait: In omnem quidem igitur diem communitas constituta secundum naturam domus est, quibus verbis habetur; quod communitas illa, quae est domus, est secundum natura & naturalis principatus, ergo regalis magis assimilatur principatui naturali, quam aristocraticus & politicus stricte sumptus. Et per consequens principatus ille, qui magis assimilatur regali (scilicet in quo vnus regit & non plures, magis assimilatur principatui naturali: & per consequens est perfectior & melior atq; magis expedicns. Ex quo infertur, quod magis expedit communitatem fidelium ab vno regi quam a pluribus, etiam secundo modo. Discipul. Videtur quod ista allegatio non concludit, quare principatus regalis magis assimilatur communitati illi, quae est domus quam principatus politicus, in quo principantur plures. Quia secundum Aristot. 1. Politi. c. 2. & 10. communitatis illius, quae domus est, quae est communitas oeconomica, sunt tres partes, quarum una est despotica, alia nuptialis, & tertia paterna. Et ideo sunt ibi tres principatus specie differentes scilicet despoticus, quo paterfamilias principatur servis. Politicus, quo paterfamilias principatur vxori, & regalis, quo paterfamilias principatur liberis siue natis. Ait enim Aristot. Quoniam tres partes oeconomicae erant, vna quidem despotica, de qua dictum est prius, vna autem paterna, tertia autem nuptialis, etenim mulieri praest & natis tanquam liberis quidem, ambobus autem non eodem modo principatur, sed mulieri quidem politice: natis autem regaliter. Ex quibus verbis colligit, quae dicta sunt: & infertur, quod non magis assimilatur communitati domus principatus regalis quam politicus. Quia sicut vni parti assimilatur principatus regalis: ita alteri parti assimilatur principatus politicus. Quare, vt videtur, non magis assimilatur principatus regalis principatui naturali, quam principatus politicus: cum principatus, quo paterfamilias in domo principatur vxori, cui assimilatur principatus politicus, sit naturalis: sicut principatus, quo principatur natis cui assimilatur principatus regalis. Quia teste Aristot. eodem ca. dicente: Masculus natura foemella principalior, nisi aliqualiter constet praeter naturam & scimus & perfectum est, scilicet principalius minore & imperfecto. Ex quo concluditur, quod masculus naturaliter principatur vxori, & pater natis. Quod de masculo, respectu vxoris, patenter dicit Aristoteles 1. Poli. ca. 3. adhuc autem masculum ad foeminam natura, hoc quidem melius: hoc autem deterius, & hoc quidem principans: hoc autem principatum. Ex istis infertur, quod ex hoc quod principatus regalis assimilatur principatui naturali, probari non potest, quod sit melior & perfectior principatu aristocratico & politico stricte sumpto. Magister. Istam responsionem quidam negare niuntur dicentes, quod licet tam principatus regalis quam politicus & etiam aristocraticus, imo omnis principatus rectus assimiletur aliquo modo principatui naturali: tamen principatus regalis magis assimilatur principatui naturali perfectori & meliori, quam principatus politicus stricte sumptus. Principatus enim patrisfamilias respectu natorum principalior est & perfectior atque melior quam principatus quo principatur vxori. Tum quia principatus respectu liberorum est melior quam principatus respectu vxoris. Quia inter liberos sunt masculi, qui meliores sunt foeminis, sicut supra per Aristotelem est probatum, principatus autem meliorum subiectorum semper est melior, secundum eundem 1. Poli. cap. 3. Tum quia principatus, quo paterfamilias principatur vxori, est propter principatum quo principatur natis: quia propter prolem procreandam vxor principaliter est ducenda. Tum quia pater naturaliter plus diligit filios quam vxorem; quia naturaliter seu naturali coniunctione & perfectiori sunt sibi coiuncti quam vxor, & ita in communitate domus principalissimus & aptissimus & naturalissimus principatus est ille, quo paterfamilias principatur natis: cui assimilatur principatus regalis, ergo principatus regalis est perfectior aliis principatibus in communitate domus. Adhuc, principatus regalis similior est principatui naturali, quo paterfamilias principatur natis quam principatus politicus principatui quo paterfamilias principatur vxori. Na regalis principatus assimilatur principatui paterno tam quo ad vnitatem principantis, quam quo ad plenitudinem potestatis: quia in vtroq; principatu est vnus principans: & vterque habet plenitudinem potestatis, quia in vtroq; principatu est vnus principans super sibi subiectos. Principatus autem politicus licet assimiletur principatui, quo paterfamilias principatur vxori, in hoc quod neuter principans habet plenitudinem potestatis: tamen in hoc differt, quod in principatu politico principans non est vnus sed plures. In principatu autem naturali quo paterfamilias principatur vxori, principans est vnus, siue habeat plures vxores siue vnam, & ita principatus regalis magis assimilatur principatui naturali, quam principatus patrisfamilias respectu vxoris. Ex quo concluditur, quod magis expedit communitatem fidelium regi ab vno quam a pluribus.
units.tr: Disciple. I think the meanings of the foreign words have been explained, according to the opinion of certain writers, which are frequently found in the passages of Aristotle already cited and yet to be cited. So do not explain more, but return to the main question, and try to recite how the authorities brought forward above, in the first and second chapters of this second book, in support of diverse and opposing opinions, are to be answered. Before you give those answers, however, I ask you to bring forward some authorities to prove that it is more expedient for the whole community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many. Master. What you ask can be understood in two ways, because many can rule their subjects in two ways. In one way, many have different subjects, so that the rule of the many does not extend to the same people. Thus several archbishops rule all those living in one widely spread region, and different kingdoms are ruled by different kings, none of whom is under another and over whom sometimes no one presides. In the other way, many rule subjects who are the same for all of them, whom they govern by common counsel. This is found in aristocracy and in polity strictly so called, and in the corrupted and perverted forms opposed to them, namely oligarchy and democracy. Whichever way you understand it, you can find in the first chapter of this second book some authorities for what you ask. For some of them not only prove that it is expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one and not by many in the first way, but also seem to show that it is expedient for it to be governed by one and not by many in the second way. So it does not seem necessary to bring forward many more authorities for what you ask. Disciple. Although some of the authorities cited above can be applied to what I ask, and many more on similar matter can be adduced, from which I may notice more about this request, which will be stated in the second treatise of this Dialogue, book 3, nevertheless I want you to bring forward some special authorities to prove that it is more expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many in the second way. Master. This seems capable of being proved thus. That form of rule is more expedient for the community of the faithful which more closely resembles natural rule and natural principate. For just as art, if it is right, imitates nature, so a principate, if it is right, imitates and resembles the natural principate. Consequently, the principate which more closely resembles the natural principate is more correct and more perfect, and therefore more expedient. But the rule or principate of one, when one alone rules many and presides over them, more closely resembles the natural principate than the rule or principate of many does. Therefore such rule resembles the regal principate, which belongs to one. The regal principate resembles the natural principate more than the aristocratic principate or the polity principate strictly so called does, because it resembles the community that is the household, in which one father of the family rules. Hence the principate of the father of the family also seems in some way to be regal, as Aristotle attests, who says in Politics book 1, chapter 10: "The father of the family rules, being born to rule in a regal manner." In the same chapter he says: "The principate over children is regal, for the one who begot them rules by love and by age; this is indeed a species of regal principate." From these words it is gathered that the regal principate resembles the community that is the household, in which one rules and not many, in neither the first nor the second way. The community of the household is natural, according to Aristotle, who in the prologue of Politics book 1 says: "Indeed, every day the community established according to nature is the household." From these words it is held that the community that is the household is according to nature, and that its principate is natural. Therefore the regal principate resembles the natural principate more than the aristocratic and the polity principate strictly so called. And consequently that principate which more closely resembles the regal one (namely, the one in which one rules and not many) more closely resembles the natural principate, and is therefore more perfect, better and more expedient. From this it follows that it is more expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many, even in the second way. Disciple. It seems that this argument does not prove why the regal principate resembles that community which is the household more than the polity principate, in which many rule. For according to Aristotle, in Politics book 1, chapters 2 and 10, the parts of that community which is the household, the economic community, are three: one is despotic, another nuptial, and the third paternal. Therefore there are three principates differing in species: the despotic, by which the father of the family rules over slaves; the polity principate, by which the father of the family rules over his wife; and the regal principate, by which the father of the family rules over his free children, whether born or begotten. For Aristotle says: "Since the economic parts were three, one despotic, of which we have spoken before, one paternal, and the third nuptial; for he presides over the wife and the children as free, but he does not rule both in the same way: the wife in a political manner, and the children in a regal manner." From these words what has been said is gathered, and it is inferred that the regal principate does not resemble the community of the household more than the polity principate does. For as the regal principate resembles one part, so the polity principate resembles the other part. Hence, as it seems, the regal principate does not resemble the natural principate more than the polity principate does. The principate by which the father of the family rules his wife in the house, to which the polity principate corresponds, is natural, just as the principate by which he rules the children, to which the regal principate corresponds, is natural. For according to Aristotle in the same chapter, "the male is by nature more fitted to rule than the female, unless somehow it is contrary to nature; and the more perfect is more fitted to rule than the less perfect and the imperfect." From this it is concluded that the male naturally rules the wife and the father rules the children. Aristotle says this plainly of the male with respect to the female in Politics book 1, chapter 3: "Moreover, the male is by nature better than the female, and one is better, the other worse; one rules, the other is ruled." From these points it follows that from the fact that the regal principate resembles the natural principate, it cannot be proved that it is better and more perfect than the aristocratic and the polity principate strictly so called. Master. Some men strive to deny this answer, saying that although the regal principate, and likewise the polity principate, and even the aristocratic, indeed every right principate, resembles the natural principate in some way, nevertheless the regal principate resembles the more perfect and better natural principate more than the polity principate strictly so called does. For the principate of the father of the family over the children is more principal, more perfect and better than the principate by which he rules the wife. This is so, first, because the principate over children is better than the principate over the wife, since among the children there are males, who are better than females, as was proved above by Aristotle; and the principate over better subjects is always better, according to the same Politics book 1, chapter 3. Second, the principate by which the father of the family rules his wife exists for the sake of the principate by which he rules the children, since a wife is principally to be taken for the sake of procreating offspring. Third, the father naturally loves his sons more than his wife, since they are joined to him by a natural and more perfect bond than the wife is. So in the community of the household the most principal, most apt and most natural principate is that by which the father of the family rules the children, to which the regal principate corresponds. Therefore the regal principate is more perfect than the other principates in the community of the household. Further, the regal principate is more similar to the natural principate, by which the father of the family rules the children, than the polity principate is to the principate by which he rules the wife. For the regal principate resembles the paternal principate both in the unity of the one ruling and in the fullness of power. In each principate there is one ruler, and each has full power, because in each principate there is one ruler over his subjects. The polity principate, although it resembles the principate by which the father of the family rules the wife, in that neither ruler has full power, nevertheless differs in this: in the polity principate the ruler is not one but many. But in the natural principate by which the father of the family rules the wife, the ruler is one, whether he has several wives or only one. So the regal principate resembles the natural principate more than the principate of the father of the family with respect to the wife does. From this it is concluded that it is more expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: Vbi iterum vnica ratione probatur, quod magis expedit communitati fidelium regi ab vno, quam a pluribus.
units.tr: Where again it is proved by a single argument that it is more expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many.

units.la: Discipulus. Hic possemus multa scrutari de principatu regali & plenitudine potestatis: tam patris respectu natorum, quam regis respectu sibi subiectorum. Sed quia haec postea forte habebunt locum: ideo ipsis pertransitis aliam allegationem adducas ad probandum, quod magis expedit communitati fidelium regi ab vno quam a pluribus. Magist. Hoc iterum quidam sic probant. Illud regimen est maxime expediens communitati fidelium, quo amicitia & concordia maxime conseruatur; & seditio, quae est cuiuslibet communitatis corruptio, deuitatur, teste Arist. qui 2. poli. c. 3. ait: Amicitiam putamus maximum omnem bonorum communitatibus, sic enim vtique minime seditiones faciunt, & 8. eiusdem c.1. ait: Videtur autem & ciuitates continere amicitiam: & legis positores magis circa ipsam studeant, quam iustitiam, concordia enim simile animi quid amicitia videtur esse, hanc autem maxime appetunt, hoc etiam ipsa veritas Matt. 12. insinuare videtur, cum dicit: Omne regnum diuisum contra se desolabitur: & omnis ciuitas aut domus &c.
units.tr: Student. Here we could examine at length the kingly rule and the fullness of power, both that of a father over his children and that of a king over his subjects. But since these matters will perhaps have their place later, pass them by, and bring forward another argument to prove that it is more expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many. Teacher. Some people prove this again in the following way. That form of government is most expedient for the community of the faithful which best preserves friendship and concord, and avoids sedition, which is the corruption of any community. Aristotle, in the second book of the Politics, chapter 3, says: "We think friendship is the greatest good for communities, for it is in this way that they least of all stir up factions." And in the eighth book, chapter 1, of the same work, he says: "Friendship also seems to hold cities together, and lawgivers take more pains over it than over justice, for concord seems to be something like friendship, and this is what they most desire." This also seems to be what the truth itself suggests in Matthew 12, when it says: "Every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation, and every city or house etc."

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: In quo inuestigatur, quis debeat omnibus principari, & qualis debeat esse.
units.tr: In which it is investigated who ought to rule over all, and what sort of man he ought to be.

units.la: DIscipulus. Satis quidem modo allegationibus plurimis, quanquam multo plures adducere posses, probasti quod vnus in principatu ecclesiae esse debeat, quia maius bonum & maior vnitas & concordia ex hoc generatur & nutritur. Qualis tamen ille debeat esse, libenter scire vellem. Magister. Circa id, quod petis tibi explanari, duo sunt modi dicendi. Quidam enim dicunt, quod nullus debet caeteris omnibus principari, nisi reliquos omnes sapientia & virtute praecellat. Alii vero dicunt, quod aliquis potest reliquis omnibus principari, quamuis non praestet omnibus sapientia & virtute, & iste modus iterum diuersificatur. Quoniam quidam dicunt, quod si in populo Christiano nullus inueniatur excellentior caeteris, si tamen aliquis bonus inueniatur, talis erit eligendus in papam. Sed si nullus inueniatur bonus & idoneus, nullus est ad tantum beneficium sublimandus. Secundum alios vero, siue inueniatur aliquis bonus siue non, tamen aliquis est in summum pontificem eligendus, & ad hoc probandum tali innituntur rationi: Quoniam melius est qualecunque caput habere, quam capite omnino carere.
units.tr: Disciple. You have indeed proved well enough, by very many arguments (though you could bring forward far more), that there ought to be one ruler in the Church, because a greater good, greater unity and concord are generated and nourished by this. Still, I should gladly like to know what sort of man he ought to be. Master. Concerning what you ask to have explained, there are two ways of speaking. Some say that no one ought to rule over all the others unless he surpasses them all in wisdom and virtue. Others say that someone may rule over the rest even though he does not excel them all in wisdom and virtue; and this second view again divides. For some say that if no one in the Christian people is found to be more excellent than the rest, yet if some good man is found, he is to be chosen as pope; but if no one is found who is good and fit, no one is to be raised to so great an office.
