Others, however, say that whether or not a good man is found, someone must still be chosen as supreme pontiff; and to prove this they rely on this argument: it is better to have some head, whatever kind it is, than to have no head at all.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: In quo iterum arguitur pro primo modo dicendi, etiam superius c. 2. probato: & eadem argumenta possunt contra tertium modum induci, & argumenta soluuntur infra c. 16.
units.tr: In which the first way of speaking is again argued for, already proved above in chapter 2; and the same arguments can be brought against the third way. The arguments are answered below in chapter 16.

units.la: DIscip. Quoniam secundum modum dicentium, quod aliquando ecclesia deberet esse sine principe & pastore, satis irrationabilem reputem, cum hoc totam politiā destruat & hierarchicū, quare vt pro ipso aliquas alleges rationes non curo, ipsum tanquam vanum relinquamus. Alius vero modus eiusdem secundi modi dicentiū, quod qualitercunq; aliquis sit si alius inuenitur melior & dignior in summum pontificem possit eligi, primo modo dicendi omnino repugnat. Quare aliquas rationes & auctoritates in contrarium adducas, nam per eas primus modus magis confirmabitur. Magist. Contra illum modum dicendi & pro primi confirmatione arguitur primo ab aliis sic. Ille debet eligi in pastore respectu cuius caeteri possunt dici & appellari grex, sed respectu nullius dicuntur grex, nisi eius qui singulos praecellit scientia & sanctitate, igitur nullus tal s debet eligi in summum pontificē, qui sit aequalis caeteris. Maior videtur probatione non indigere, minor vero probatur. Quoniam pastor debet singulis praestare ducatum scientia, vt habetur di. 63. Ephesios, & 8. q. 1. audacter, in fi. Similiter & vitae sanctitate, vt scribitur 11. q. 3. praecipue, & per consequens in huiusmodi praecellere singulos debet. Item idem patet auctoritate Simachi papae, quae scribitur 1. q. 1. vbi sit, inquit: Vtilissimus computandus est nisi praecellat scientia & sanctitate, qui est honore praestantior. Praeterea praestantior & sanctior est ad sacerdotium eligendus & singulis praeferendus, vt inquit Hieron. Et Leo papa, qui, vt habetur dist. 63. si forte, sic inquit: Is metropolitani iudicio praeferatur qui maioribus iuuatur studiis & meritis. Et Ambrof. Diaconi & presbyteri cunctum populum vitam secularem in omnibus ducentem debent conuersatione & sermone praire, igitur & quantumcunq; sanctos debet vita & conuersatione praire, qui singulis debet praesse, plures aliae possent adduci rationes & auctoritates, quas gratia breuitatis transire oportet.
units.tr: Student. Since I regard the second way of speaking, that at times the Church ought to be without a prince and pastor, as quite unreasonable, because it destroys the whole polity and hierarchy, I do not care to allege reasons for it; let us leave it aside as empty. The other form of that second way, that whatever a man is, if someone else is found better and more worthy, he may be chosen as supreme pontiff, is entirely opposed to the first way. So bring forward some reasons and authorities to the contrary, for through them the first way will be confirmed more strongly. Master. Against that way of speaking, and in confirmation of the first, the argument is first made from others as follows. He who ought to be chosen as pastor, and with respect to whom the rest can be called and named a flock, but with respect to no one are they called a flock except him who surpasses each in learning and holiness; therefore no one who is equal to the rest ought to be chosen as supreme pontiff. The major premise seems not to need proof; the minor is proved thus. Because a pastor ought to lead each man by his learning, as is found in di. 63. Ephesios, & 8. q. 1. audacter, at the end. Likewise also by holiness of life, as is written in 11. q. 3. praecipue, and consequently he ought to excel each of them in such things. Likewise the same is clear from the authority of Pope Symmachus, which is written in 1. q. 1. vbi sit, where he says: He is to be counted most useful, unless he excels in learning and holiness, who is more eminent in honour. Moreover, the more eminent and holier man is to be chosen for the priesthood and preferred to each, as Jerome says. And Pope Leo, who, as is found in dist. 63. si forte, says thus: He is to be preferred to the judgment of the metropolitan who is aided by greater studies and merits. And Ambrose: Deacons and presbyters ought to surpass in conduct and speech all the people who lead a secular life in all things. Therefore, since the one who ought to preside over each must also surpass in holiness and conduct as much as possible, many other reasons and authorities could be adduced, which for the sake of brevity must be passed over.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: Chapter XIII.

units.la: Probat idem quod prius, scilicet quod nullus debet praesse semper cunctis fidelibus: nisi omnes alios superet virtute & sapientia, & hoc duabus rationibus, ad quas respondetur cap. 17.
units.tr: The author proves the same point as before, namely that no one should always preside over all the faithful unless he surpasses all others in virtue and wisdom. He gives two reasons for this, which are answered in chapter 17.

units.la: DIscipulus. Si aliquae aliae allegationes tibi occurrunt ad probandum, quod nullus debet praesse cunctis fidelibus, nisi omnes superet in sapientia & virtute, adducas. Magist. Hoc adhuc probatur sic. Non minor sapientia & virtus requiritur ad principantem in spiritualibus toti congregationi fidelium, quam ad regem, qui in temporalibus praesidet sibi subiectis, vt Arist. 7 politicorum ca. 13. velle videtur: cum secundum ipsum non est iustum aliquos semper principari (qualiter principantur reges, & etiam summi pontifices) & alios semper subiici; nisi differant a subiectis sibi, quantum dii & heroes differunt ab hominibus, qui sunt simpliciter secundum ipsum omnibus hominibus excellentes. Ait enim sic: Si igitur fuerint tantum differentes alteri ab alteris, quantum Deos & heroes aestimamus ab hominibus differre, vt confestim primo secundum corpus multam habentes excellentiam, demum secundum animam & indubitata sit & manifesta excellentia principantium respectu subiectorum palam: quia melius vitam suam &c. Illud enim quod est excellentius & perfectius, quamdiu manet tale, natum est principari illis, qui ab excellentia tanta deficiunt. Quando autem non inueniuntur tales, qui differant ab aliis, quemadmodum differunt dii & heroes ab hominibus: tunc non est iustum, vt aliqui eorum principentur aliis secundum totam vitam suam. Sed iustum est, vt omnes quodammodo communicent principatui, vt scilicet omnes qui sunt aequales in sapientia & virtute, vicissim principentur: primo aliqui, & postea alii, vt Arist. ibidem velle videtur dicens: Quoniam ante hac non facile accipere, neq; (sicut apud Indos ait Silax) esse reges tantum differentes a subiectis, manifestum quod propter multas causas intrari omnes communicare, eo quod est secundum partem principari & subiici, vt scilicet nullus principetur toto tempore vitae suae, sed illi aliquando subiiciuntur. Cuius rationem assignat dicens: Quod enim aequale, idem omnibus similibus. Ex quibus verbis ratio talis elicitur. Iniustum est vitaut aliquis semper principetur sibi aequalibus & similibus, ergo quando aliqui sunt similes, iniustum est, ut aliqui eorum semper principetur, & alii subiiciantur. Quare concluditur, quod si inter fideles sint multi similes inter se in sapientia & virtute, iniustum est ut unus eorum semper toto tempore vitae suae principetur: & alii semper subiiciantur. Quare cum Papa toto tempore vitae suae debeat praesse fidelib. universis, iniustum est ut aliquis efficiatur Papa, si alii inveniuntur sibi similes in sapientia & virtute. Iniustum est igitur, ut aliquis fiat Papa, nisi sapientia & virtute fideles superet universos. Amplius: principatus Papalis est perfectior principatu regali, teste Gregorio Nazianzeno, qui, ut legitur distinct. 10. c. suscipitis, ait scribens Imperatoribus Constantinopolitanis: dedit & nobis potestatem: dedit principatum multo perfectiorem principatibus vestris. Nullus autem est dignus principatu regali, nisi superet alios sapientia & virtute: imo omnibus bonis, ut Aristoteles videtur asserere 8. Ethicor. sicut allegatum est supra cap. 2. huius secundi. Quod etiam probatur ex hoc, quod regnum est secundum aristocratiam institutum, secundum Aristotelem lib. 5. politicorum cap. 8. in aristocratia autem principantur illi, qui sunt caeteris meliores, secundum eundem 4. politicorum c. 5. igitur & in regno nullus debet principari regaliter; nisi caeteros antecellat. Unde & Deus, quando primo regem populo suo praefecit, optimum totius populi elegit, testante Samuele, qui de ipso, scil. Saule pro tempore illo dixit 1. Regum 10. Certe videtis, quem elegit Dominus, quoniam non est similis ei in omni populo, ergo multo fortius, nullus est dignus principatu Papali, nisi omnes praecellat sapientia & virtute. Ergo quando non invenitur aliquis, cuius excellentia tanta sit indubitata & manifesta (cum excellentia principantium debeat esse indubitata & manifesta, secundum Aristotelem, ut dictum est prius in primo c.) tunc nullus est ad summum Pontificem eligendus: sed assumendi sunt plures excellentiores aliis, qui aristocratice vel politice omnes alios regant.
units.tr: Disciple. If any other arguments occur to you for proving that no one should preside over all the faithful unless he surpasses all of them in wisdom and virtue, bring them forward. Teacher. This is proved further as follows. In spiritual matters, the one who presides over the whole congregation of the faithful needs no less wisdom and virtue than a king, who presides in temporal affairs over his subjects, as Aristotle seems to hold in 7 Politics, ch. 13. For according to him it is not just that some should always rule (as kings and also the supreme pontiffs rule) and others always be subject, unless they differ from their subjects as much as gods and heroes differ from men, who are, by his account, simply superior to all other men. For he says: If, then, some are as different from others as we judge gods and heroes to differ from men, so that at once they have great superiority in body and then, in soul, an undoubted and manifest superiority of the rulers over the subjects, because they live better their life, etc. For that which is more excellent and more perfect, as long as it remains such, is by nature fitted to rule those who fall short of such excellence. But when no such men are found who differ from others as gods and heroes differ from men, then it is not just that some of them should rule the others for their whole lives. Rather, it is just that all should in some measure share in rule, so that all who are equal in wisdom and virtue take turns ruling: first some, and afterwards others. Aristotle seems to say the same in the same place, saying: Since, as the Indians say (according to Silax), it is not easy to find kings who differ from their subjects, it is clear that for many reasons all men should share, since to rule and to be ruled in turn is a matter of part-and-part, so that no one rules for the whole of his life, but those men are at times subject. He gives the reason for this, saying: For what is equal is the same for all who are alike. From these words the following argument is drawn. It is unjust that someone should always rule over those equal and similar to himself; therefore, when some are similar, it is unjust that one of them should always rule and the others be subject. Hence it follows that if among the faithful there are many who are similar to one another in wisdom and virtue, it is unjust that one of them should rule for the whole of his life, and the others always be subject. Therefore, since the Pope ought to preside over all the faithful for the whole of his life, it is unjust that anyone should become Pope if others are found who are similar to him in wisdom and virtue. It is unjust, then, that anyone should become Pope unless he surpasses all the faithful in wisdom and virtue. Furthermore: the papal rule is more perfect than royal rule, as Gregory Nazianzen testifies, who, as is read in Distinction 10, chapter "Suscipitis", writing to the Emperors of Constantinople, says: He has given us also power, a rule far more perfect than your rules. But no one is worthy of royal rule unless he surpasses others in wisdom and virtue; indeed, in all good qualities, as Aristotle seems to affirm in 8 Ethics, as was alleged above in chapter 2 of this second book. This is also proved from the fact that kingship is instituted on the aristocratic model, according to Aristotle in Politics 5, ch. 8; and in an aristocracy the rulers are those who are better than the rest, according to the same author in Politics 4, ch. 5. Therefore even in a kingdom no one should rule as king unless he excels the rest. Hence God, when he first set a king over his people, chose the best of the whole people, as Samuel bears witness, who said of Saul, for that time, in 1 Kings 10: Surely you see whom the Lord has chosen, for there is none like him among all the people. Therefore, much more strongly, no one is worthy of the papal rule unless he surpasses all in wisdom and virtue. Therefore, when there is found no one whose excellence is so great, undoubted and manifest (since the excellence of rulers ought to be undoubted and manifest, according to Aristotle, as was said before in the first chapter), then no one is to be chosen as supreme pontiff, but several more excellent than the rest must be taken up, who together rule all the others in an aristocratic or polity-like manner.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Ubi probatur secunda pars secundi modi dicendi, scilicet quod magis expedit populo Christiano regi ab uno, qui etiam non cunctos excellat sapientia & virtute, quam a pluribus. Quod probat exemplis veteris Testamenti & Novi.
units.tr: Where the second part of the second view is proved, namely that it is more expedient for the Christian people to be ruled by one man, even if he does not surpass all others in wisdom and virtue, than by many. This is proved by examples from the Old and New Testaments.

units.la: Discipulus. Ex rationibus istis mihi dedisti occasionem cogitandi quamplura, tam pro conclusione ad quam inducuntur, quam contra, necnon etiam circa totam materiam, quam in principio huius secundi coepimus pertractare. An scilicet expediat congregationi fidelium uni praelato subesse, ideo exquisitius quam proposuerim ipsam, & quae prius tacta sunt, intendo discutere, & quantam virtutem rationes pro una parte, & pro alia allegatae obtineant investigare. Inprimis autem aliquas allegationes inducas ad probandum; quod quamvis in omni populo Christiano nullus esset, qui omnes alios virtute & sapientia superaret; melius esset populum Christianum regi ab uno, quam a pluribus; secundum quod tenet secundus modus ponendi, qui recitatus est superius capitulo undecimo huius secundi. Magister. Hoc sic videtur posse probari. Tale regimen maxime expedit toti congregationi fidelium, quo Deus tam in Veteri Testamento, quam in Novo voluit populum suum gubernari, cum ipse omnis regiminis virtuosi & utilis sit optimus & sapientissimus instructor. Sed Deus tam in Veteri Testamento, quam in Novo voluit totum populum suum gubernari ab uno, qui per totam vitam suam esset omnium gubernator, quamvis non esset omnes alios in sapientia & virtute praecellens. Nec enim invenitur, quod aliquis iudex & rex in veteri Testamento omnes alios excelleret sapientia & virtute. Sanctus etiam Petrus non videtur fuisse sanctior universis Apostolis & aliis orthodoxis. Sanctus enim Iohannes Apostolus in amore Christi, & per consequens in sanctitate & virtute ipsum praecessisse videtur. Sancto etiam Paulo sapientia videtur fuisse inferior. Igitur non obstante, quod non inveniatur aliquis Christianus, qui excellat omnes alios sapientia & virtute, est tamen aliquis ad summum Pontificum eligendus, qui Christianorum omnium sit praelatus.
units.tr: Disciple. From these arguments you have given me occasion to think about many things, both in favour of the conclusion they are brought forward to support and against it, and also about the whole subject we began to treat at the start of this second part: namely, whether it is expedient for the congregation of the faithful to be subject to a single prelate. I intend therefore to discuss it more carefully than I had proposed, to revisit the points touched on earlier, and to examine how much force the arguments alleged on each side have. First, however, bring forward some arguments to prove that, although in no Christian people would there be anyone who surpassed all others in virtue and wisdom, it would still be better for the Christian people to be ruled by one than by many, as the second view holds, which was recited above in chapter eleven of this second book. Master. This can be proved as follows. That form of government is most expedient for the whole congregation of the faithful by which God wished his people to be governed, both in the Old Testament and in the New, since he himself is the best and wisest teacher of every virtuous and useful government. But God wished his whole people to be governed, in both the Old and New Testaments, by one man, who throughout his whole life would be the governor of all, even though he did not surpass all others in wisdom and virtue. For it is not found that any judge or king in the Old Testament surpassed all others in wisdom and virtue. Saint Peter also does not seem to have been holier than all the Apostles and other orthodox believers. For Saint John the Apostle seems to have surpassed him in love of Christ, and consequently in holiness and virtue. Saint Paul also seems to have been inferior to him in wisdom. Therefore, although it is not found that any Christian surpasses all others in wisdom and virtue, nevertheless someone is to be chosen as supreme Pontiff who is set over all Christians.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationem primam supra c. 2. huius factam pro primo modo dicendi.
units.tr: In which the first argument, made above in chapter 2 of this book for the first way of speaking, is answered.

units.la: Discipulus. Ut mihi & aliis detur occasio inveniendi circa praedicta clarius veritatem, ad omnia, quae pro assertionibus contrariis sunt adducta, responsiones aliquas studeas recitare. Primo autem narra, quomodo respondetur ad illa, quae contra secundum modum ponendi supra cap. 2. recitantur: & quae pro eo quod ultimo allegasti militare videntur, ille enim modus ponendi habere aliquam apparentiam mihi videtur. Magister. Ille modus ponendi est bipartitus, dicitur uno modo, quod si in populo Christiano non inveniatur aliquis excellentior omnibus aliis; & tamen inveniatur idoneus atque bonus aliquis; talis est eligendus in Papam. Sed si nullus inveniatur bonus & idoneus, nullus est ad tum beneficium sublimandus. Aliter dicitur, quod sive inveniatur idoneus sive non, aliquis est ad summum Pontificium eligendus: quia melius est qualemcunque in caput habere quam capite omnino mutilum. mnino catere. Discipulus. Primo narra, quomodo secundum primum istorum modorum respondetur. Magister. Ad primam allegationem, quae inducitur supra cap. 2. huius secundi, quae in auctoritate Aristotelis fundari videtur, qui videtur asserere iniustum esse, vt aliquis principetur sibi similibus & aequalibus: Respondetur, quod si in aliqua communitate omnes essent boni, & nullatenus peruertibiles per malitiam in actu vel potetia, iniustum esset vt aliquis principaretur sibi similibus & aequalibus in sapientia & virtute: quia tunc nulla ratio apparet, quare plus deberet vnus quam alius principari, sed quando in aliqua communitate sunt multi aut plures peruerti possunt: & cum maior pars & potentior voluntarie sustinet principatum vnius, vt a tali voluntate auerti non possint: tunc expedit vt vnus super omnes accipiat principatum, dummodo inueniatur talis, qui sit dignus principari deterioribus, eo quod aliter non esset bonus vel idoneus reputandus. Si autem est aliqua pars tam potens, quod possit seditionem periculosam toti communitati suscitare: quae compesci non posset; & principatum vnius vellet nullatenus sustinere: tunc non esset aliquis omnibus sibi similibus & aliis praeferendus: sed esset talis principantis institutio ad tempus aliud differenda, quemadmodum enim interdum propter malitiam subditorum episcopus licite deserit ipsos etiam penitus renunciando regimini, extra de renuncia, nisi cum pridem septim. quaestion. prim. hoc tamen seruandum: sic propter malitiam aliquorum quandoque licet institutionem principantis differre, & ideo quamuis regulariter expediat toti communitati fidelium, vt aliquis vnus, qui omnibus aliis praesit, ad summum sacerdotium eligatur: tamen si esset tanta malitia alicuius partis Christianorum, quae posset exponere totam Christianitatem periculo, & nullo modo vellet vni summo sacerdoti obedire: non esset tunc aliquis ad tale officium eligendus, sed esset eius electio differenda. Sicut enim saepe permittuntur minora mala, vt maiora vitentur, distinction. tert. cap. omnis: sic nonnunquam omittuntur bona quaedam, etiam magna, vt maxima pericula declinentur. Aristoteles intelligit, quod iniustum est, quod aliquis aliquibus similibus in virtute & aequalibus principetur, nisi ex aliqua vtilitate vel necessitate expediat ordinare, vt aliquis etiam sibi similibus & aequalibus & non solum aequalibus & dissimilibus principetur. Ad rationem vero Aristotelis, qua absolute & sine distinctione vel modificatione videtur probare, quod iniustum est, quod aliquis sibi similibus principetur: quia aequalibus secundum virtutem debetur aequalis honor & dignitas. Respondetur, quod quando conuenienter & vtiliter fieri potest, vt aequalibus aequalis honor & dignitas tribuatur, hoc faciendum est, in quo casu loquitur Aristoteles, tamen quando non est possibile, aut non est vtile, vel est minus vtile, praesertim communi bono, quod aequalis honor & dignitas aequalibus conferatur: tunc absque omni iustitia, imo iusta electione vel sorte, aut quouis alio licito modo aliquis, quo ad dignitatem & honores, potest similibus & aequalibus praeferri. Et si alii in hoc turbarentur, & ad seditionem faciendam prouocarentur: efficerentur dissimiles & inaequales secundum virtutem alteri, cui prius aequales & similes extiterant, tanquam ambitiosi & inuidi praeferentes honorem proprium bono communi: cum magis periclitari vellent bonum commune vel minime procurari, quam aliquem eis cum vtilitate communi praeferri. Exemplum autem Aristotelis de habentibus aequalem vel inaequalem virtutem digestiuam; & de habentibus aequale vel inaequale corpus (quia aequalibus secundum virtutem digestiuam, vel corpus expedit habere aequale alimentum vel vestitum, quod nocet inaequalibus secundum virtutem digestiuam & corpus) non concludit vniuersaliter absque omni exceptione, quod aequalibus & similibus secundum virtutem debeat dari idem honor & dignitas, quia in ministrando alimentum & vestitum aequalibus vel inaequalibus secundum virtutem digestiuam corporis solummodo attenditur propria virtus, & proprium vniuscuiusque ipsorum, quid scilicet expediat vel noceat vnicuique ipsorum diuisim. In distribuendo autem honores & dignitates quandoque solum attenditur meritum & dignitas illorum, quibus debent distribui, quia tunc iniustum est, vt aequalibus inaequalis honor seu dignitas tribuatur, & tunc bonum est exemplum Aristotelis. Quandoque autem non solum attenditur meritum & dignitas honorandorum, sed etiam attenditur vtilitas publica, quae melius procuratur principaliter per vnum quam per plures, & tunc quia maior respectus habendus est ad bonum commune, quam ad meritum & dignitatem honorandorum, iustum est vt aequalibus & similibus secundum virtutem non aequalis honor & virtus tribuatur.
units.tr: Student. So that I and others may have occasion to grasp the truth more clearly on these matters, please set out some answers to all the arguments that have been brought for the opposite positions. First, tell me how one answers those objections that are raised against the second way of stating the position, above in chapter 2, and against the arguments that you cited last, which seem to support that view, since it appears to me to have some plausibility. Master. That way of stating the position has two parts. In one form it says that if no one in the Christian people is found to excel all the others, yet someone suitable and good is found, such a man is to be chosen as Pope. But if no one good and suitable is found, no one is to be raised to that office. In the other form it says that whether or not a suitable man is found, someone must be chosen as supreme Pontiff, because it is better to have some sort of head than to be altogether without a head. Student. First tell me how one answers according to the first of these forms. Master. To the first argument, introduced above in chapter 2 of this second book, which seems to rest on the authority of Aristotle, who appears to assert that it is unjust for someone to rule over those who are like and equal to him: the answer is that if in some community all were good and in no way capable of being perverted by malice, either in act or in potential, it would be unjust for someone to rule over those who are like and equal to him in wisdom and virtue, since then no reason would appear why one should rule more than another. But when in some community there are many, or more, who can be perverted, and the greater and more powerful part freely submits to the rule of one, so that they cannot be turned away from that willing submission, then it is expedient that one man above all others receive the principate, provided that someone is found who is worthy to rule over the worse, since otherwise he would not be reckoned good or suitable. If, however, there is some part so powerful that it could stir up a dangerous sedition throughout the whole community, one that could not be checked, and that would in no way be willing to endure the rule of one, then no one should be preferred to all his like and to the others. Rather, the institution of a ruler must be deferred for a time. For just as sometimes, because of the wickedness of his subjects, a bishop lawfully abandons them, even renouncing the government altogether (Extra, de renuntiatione; cf. Quaestion. prim., hoc tamen servandum), so sometimes, because of the malice of certain people, it is lawful to defer the institution of a ruler. Therefore, although it is generally expedient for the whole community of the faithful that one man, who is to preside over all others, be chosen as supreme priest, yet if there were such malice in some part of the Christians that it could expose all Christendom to danger and would in no way be willing to obey one supreme priest, then no one should be chosen for that office, and the election should be deferred. For just as lesser evils are often tolerated so that greater ones may be avoided (Distinctio 3, cap. Omnis), so also certain goods, even great ones, are sometimes set aside so that the greatest dangers may be averted. Aristotle means that it is unjust for someone to rule over those who are equal and like him in virtue, unless for some advantage or necessity it is expedient to arrange that someone rule not only over his equals and likes, but also over those who are unequal and unlike. As for Aristotle's argument, which seems to prove without distinction or qualification that it is unjust for someone to rule over those who are like him, because equal honour and dignity are owed to those equal in virtue, the answer is this. When it can be done fittingly and advantageously to give equal honour and dignity to equals, this must be done, and this is the case Aristotle is speaking of. But when it is not possible, or not advantageous, or is less advantageous, especially for the common good, to confer equal honour and dignity on equals, then without any injustice, indeed by a just election or by lot, or by any other lawful means, someone may be preferred, in respect of dignity and honours, to his like and equals. And if others were disturbed by this and provoked to make sedition, they would thereby become unlike and unequal in virtue to the one who had previously been their equal and like, since they, being ambitious and envious, would be preferring their own honour to the common good, when they would rather endanger the common good or see it neglected than see someone preferred to them with advantage to the community. Aristotle's example, however, of those who have equal or unequal digestive power, and of those who have equal or unequal bodies (since it is expedient for those equal in digestive power to have equal food or clothing, while unequal food or clothing would harm those unequal in digestive power and body), does not conclude universally, without any exception, that equals and likes in virtue ought to be given the same honour and dignity. For in supplying food and clothing to those equal or unequal in the digestive power of the body, only their own virtue and what is each man's own is considered, namely what is expedient or harmful to each of them taken separately. But in distributing honours and dignities, sometimes only the merit and dignity of those to whom they are to be distributed is considered. In that case it is unjust that unequal honour or dignity be given to equals, and then Aristotle's example is apt. But sometimes not only the merit and dignity of those to be honoured is considered, but also public advantage, which is better secured principally through one than through many. Then, since greater regard must be had to the common good than to the merit and dignity of those to be honoured, it is just that unequal honour and virtue, rather than equal honour, be given to those who are equal and like in virtue.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Respondet rationibus cap. 12. adductis.
units.tr: Replies to the arguments adduced in chapter 12.

units.la: Discipulus. Quia contra istum modum videntur specialiter allegari ea, quae allegata sunt prius cap. 12. & 13. ibi enim ostenditur, quod nullus debet praeferri cunctis fidelibus, nisi praecellat virtute & sapientia vniuersos, cuius contrarium tenet praedictus modus ponendi, ideo narra, qualiter respondetur ad ipsa. Magister. Ad illa, quae 12. cap. inducuntur, respondetur quod regulariter, quando inuenitur aliquis, qui veritate & sapientia omnes alios superet & excellat, ille praeferendus est in summum Pontificem, & regulariter peccant, qui scienter talem dimittunt: & essent quasi merito potestate eligendi priuandi, & in hoc casu loquuntur auctoritates inductae, quando autem non inuenitur aliquis talis, sed multi sunt similes & aequales secundum virtutem, tunc non est eligendus talis, cum mallem sit talis, nec tamen propter hoc debet differri electio quousque inueniatur talis, sed suffi-cit tunc vnus æqualium vel similium in sapientia & virtute habendo respectu ad aliquid aliud, quod ... tur eidem, vt eligatur. Discip. Quamuis istam responsionem (vt puto) intelligum: tamen qualiter ista opinio auctoritates supra 12. cap. allegatas (quæ forte contra ipsam militare videntur) exponit, ignoro, ideo breviter discurre per ipsas: & dic quem intellectum habent de ipsis. Magister. Ad illam rationem, quæ dicit, quod talis debet eligi, respectu cuius cæteri grex dicantur. Respondetur, quod potest habere duplicem intellectum verum. Vnus est, quod quando aliquis eligitur talis, elegi debet respectu cuius cæteri boni & mali dici possint merito grex. Alius est, quod quia in ecclesia semper inueniuntur mali, debet eligi talis respectu cuius cæteri, id est mali, grex dicantur. Non tamen est possibile vt eligatur talis respectu, cuius eminentes in sapientia & virtute possint dici g... Ad aliam, quæ ponitur 1. quæstion. 1. cap. vilissimus, id est valde vilis est putandus, nisi præcellat malos & indignos tanto honore, scientia, & sanctitate: sed non est vilissimus reputandus, quamuis non præcellat scientia & sanctitate eminentes secundum sapientiam & virtutem. Ad tertiam ... est Hieronymi, respondetur quod quando est aliquis præstantior, sanctior, &c. ille ad sacerdotium eligendus est; quando autem non est talis, sufficit eligere præstantiorem, sanctiorem, doctiorem & in omni virtute eminentiorem omnib. malis & stultis in populo. Ad auctoritatem Leonis Papæ consimiliter dicitur, quod quando est aliquis optimus, ipse est eligendus: quando non est aliquis optimus, eligendus est bonus. Ad auctoritatem Ambrosii diaconi & presbyteri sanctum populum vitam ducentem in omnibus secularem, debent conuersatione & sermone præire, conceditur: sed non oportet, quod præeant illos ex populo, qui ducunt vitam singulariter sanctam. Discipulus. Puto me non ignorare, qualiter ista opinio intelligat omnes canones sacros, qui in hoc contra ipsam militare videntur. Sed dic an teneat electionem debere cassari, si non eligatur optimus, quando optimus & excellentior omnibus inueniatur. Magister. Tenet quod quia propter scandala, turbationes, seditiones etiam, sæpe tolerantur minora mala vt maiora vitentur: ita potest electio boni non optimi, quando inuenitur optimus, licita non cassari & sæpe periculosissime cassaretur. Discipulus. Nunquid non obstante, quod talis electio cassari non debeat, tenetur electus bonus non consentire electioni de se factæ, vel cedere, si iam consenserit, quando aliquis optimus est dimissus? Magister. Respondetur, quod talis quando optimus alius inuenitur, si absque periculo vel turbatione notabili valeat non consentire, vel cedere, si consenserit, de necessitate salutis tenetur non consentire vel cedere: maxime si cum bono exemplo & ædificatione totius communitatis fidelium hoc facere possit. Aliter enim damnabiliter bonum vel honorem proprium bono communi præferret.
units.tr: Disciple. Because the passages cited in chapters 12 and 13 seem to be specially brought against this way of thinking (for there it is shown that no one should be preferred to all the faithful unless he surpasses all in virtue and wisdom, whereas the aforesaid view holds the opposite), please tell me how the replies to those passages go. Master. To the arguments set out in chapter 12, the reply is this: as a rule, when someone is found who surpasses and excels all others in truth and wisdom, he is to be preferred as the supreme Pontiff, and those who knowingly pass over such a man as a rule sin, and would, as it were, deserve to be stripped of the power of electing. It is in this case that the cited authorities speak. But when no such man is found, and there are many who are equal and similar in virtue, then such a man should not be chosen, since it would be better that he were one; nor on that account should the election be deferred until such a man is found. Instead, it is enough then to choose one of the equals or similars in wisdom and virtue, having regard to something else which ... is given to the same man, that he may be elected. Disciple. Although I think I understand this reply, I do not know how this opinion explains the authorities cited above in chapter 12, which perhaps seem to militate against it. So, briefly run through them and tell me what sense they have. Master. To that argument which says that the one who should be chosen is the one with respect to whom the others are called the flock, the reply is that it can have a twofold true sense. One is that when someone is chosen, he ought to be chosen as the one with respect to whom the others, both good and bad, can rightly be called the flock. The other is that, because bad men are always to be found in the Church, he ought to be chosen as the one with respect to whom the others, that is, the bad, are called the flock. Yet it is not possible that he be chosen with respect to whom those who are eminent in wisdom and virtue can be called ... To the other argument, which is laid down in Distinction 1, chapter Vilissimus, namely that a man is to be regarded as very base (vilissimus) unless he surpasses the wicked and unworthy in such great honour, learning and holiness: the reply is that he is not to be regarded as most base, although he does not surpass in learning and holiness those who are eminent in wisdom and virtue. To the third ... of Jerome, the reply is that when there is someone more outstanding, holier, etc., he is the one who is to be chosen to the priesthood; but when there is no such man, it is enough to choose the more outstanding, holier, more learned, and the one who excels in every virtue, over all the wicked and foolish among the people. Likewise, to the authority of Pope Leo, the reply is that when there is someone best, he is to be chosen; when there is no one best, the good man is to be chosen. To the authority of Ambrose, that deacons and elders, who must lead the holy people living a life wholly secular, ought to go before them in conduct and speech, it is granted; but it is not necessary that they go before those of the people who lead a singularly holy life. Disciple. I think I do not fail to understand how this opinion interprets all the sacred canons which seem to militate against it. But tell me whether it holds that the election must be annulled if the best man is not chosen, when the best and most excellent of all is to be found. Master. It holds that, because for the sake of scandals, disturbances and even sedition, lesser evils are often tolerated so that greater ones may be avoided, so the election of a good man, though not the best, may, when the best is to be found, be lawfully left unannulled; and it would often be annulled to great peril. Disciple. Notwithstanding that such an election ought not to be annulled, is the good man who has been elected bound not to consent to the election made in his favour, or, if he has already consented, to yield, when a better man has been passed over? Master. The reply is that when another, the best, is found, if he can refuse to consent, or yield if he has consented, without danger or notable disturbance, he is bound of necessity for salvation to refuse or to yield; especially if he can do this with a good example and the edification of the whole community of the faithful. For otherwise he would damnably prefer his own good or honour to the common good.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationes & auctoritates cap. 13. adductas.
units.tr: In which an answer is given to the reasons and authorities adduced in chapter 13.

units.la: Discipulus. Dic nunc qualiter respondetur ad illa, quæ supra 13. capitulo sunt adducta. Magister. Omnia illa fundantur in hoc (vt videtur) quod nullus est dignus principatu regali, nisi superet omnes alios sapientia & virtute, secundum quod Aristoteles in politicis & etiam in Ethicis sentire videtur: vt nullus debeat esse rex, nisi sit optimus & melior secundum sapientiam & virtutem omnibus sibi subiectis. Ad quod non dicitur, quod est secundum Aristotelem vniuersaliter absque omni exceptione verum. Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod principatum regalem pluribus modis contigit adipisci, de quibus ad præsens sufficit enumerare duos. Quorum vnus est, quando aliquis à subditis voluntarie sublimatur in regem. Alius est, quando quis voluntarie de principatu despotico, quem iuste adeptus fuit, ad principatum regalem se transfert. Si primo modo debeat quis ad principatum regalem regulariter assumi, assumendus est optimus secundum sapientiam & virtutem, si inueniatur talis, & nullum iustum impedimentum impedit promotionem eius. Et si tale genus inueniatur, quod tali modo excedat omnes alios, iustum est regulariter vt tale genus regnet. Et sic intelligit Aristoteles 2. politicorum & 16. cum dicit: Cum igitur sic genus totum & alios vnum acciderit esse differenter secundum virtutem tantum, vt excedat quæ illius ea, quæ aliorum omnium: tunc iustum est genus hoc esse regale & dominans omnium: & regem vnum hunc, sicut & dictum est prius. Si autem non inueniatur; inueniuntur tamen multi boni: aliquis eorum assumendus est, cuius principatum alii ei similes & æquales in sapientia & virtute propter commune bonum patienter & libenter ferre tenentur. Qualiter autem assumi debeat, postea, si volueris, poteris inquirere. Si autem secundo modo peruenerit quis ad principatum regalem: puto quia primo obtinuit dominium regionis totius & omnium habitantium in ea, siue per occupationem, siue per donationem, siue peremptionem, siue per iustum bellum, siue quocunq; alio modo iusto: & postea renuens principatum despoticum contentus est solo principatu regali, vt sc. principaliter velit principari eis propter bonum & conferens subditorum, non propter bonum proprium (qualiter principatur despotes) poterit iuste potiri principatu regali, quamuis non sit optimus hominum, quia ex hoc quod partem iuris sui dimittit, & partem retinet, non est iniustus censendus, licet non sit optimus. Ad Aristotelem autem, qui innuit 7. politicorum, cap. 13. quod non est iustum aliquos semper principari, nisi tm differant à subditis, quantum dii & heroes differunt ab hominibus. Respondetur multis modis. Vno modo, quod hoc est verum, si attendatur solummodo meritum & dignitas principantis: non autem si attenditur vtilitas boni communis. Aliter dicitur, quod hoc est verum de iusto naturali in particulari, puta quod non est iustum naturale, vt isti principentur omnibus aliis, nisi tali modo differant ab omnibus illis, quibus principantur, per quem modum iustum est, vt ille vir principetur vxori suæ vel vxoribus, & pater filiis, & iste Dominus seruis, qui naturaliter sunt serui secundum Aristotelem prim. politicorum. Sed non est verum de iusto positiuo, nam sæpe fit iustum & naturale, vt aliquis dominetur multis sibi similibus & æqualibus in communitate perfecta: quia si sunt tot similes & æquales secundum virtutem, quod non possunt vtiliter omnes simul principari: & tamen talis communitas sine principante non potest consistere secundum Aristotelem. Et quia non est iustum naturale, vt magis isti principentur quam illi, necesse est quod per iustum positiuum determinetur, quod isti principentur, vel simpliciter secundum totam vitam suam vel ad tempus. Et sicut non obstante, quod non sit iustum naturale, vt iste principetur secundum totam vitam suam sibi similibus & æqualibus, qualiter intelligit Aristoteles: tamen ex causa fieri potest iustum positiuum, quod Aristoteles negare non intendit. Discipulus. Quomodo potest esse iustum naturale, quod aliquis principetur sibi similibus: & tamen non est iustum naturale, quod iste principetur similibus: & sic de singulis? Magister. Respondetur, quod ista interrogatio tua procedit ex ignorantia primiciuorum, scilicet logicalium, quæ nullus desudans cuicunque scientiæ ignorare debeter, aliter enim procederet sophistice, quando putabit se demonstratiue procedere. Dicitur igitur, quod sicut tam vniuersalis quam particularis est necessaria, cuius tamen quælibet singularis est contingens: ita possibile est, quod particularis sit secundum iustitiam naturalem, & tamen nulla singularis erit secundum iustitiam naturalem. Quare possibile est, quod aliquem debere principari sibi similibus, sit iustum naturale: & tamen non est iustum naturale istum debere principari sibi similibus, & sic de singulis, & sicut possibile est, quod propositio cathegorica de disiuncto extremo, in qua subiiciuntur termino discreto contento sub aliquo termino communi sit necessaria: & tamen quod disiuncta correspondens cum modo necessitatis sit falsa, & ideo nulla singularium illarum sit necessaria. Ita potest contingere, quod talis sit vera: istum vel illum, & sic de singulis principari sibi similibus est iustum naturale: si sit cathegorica de disiuncto subiecto: & tamen quod disiunctiua sit salsa, & per consequens quælibet singularis est falsa. Vt igitur secundum istos absque omni deceptione in talibus procedatur, diligentissime est cognoscenda differentia inter propositionem disiunctiuam & de disiuncto extremo: & inter propositionem de eisdem terminis acceptam in sensu compositionis & in sensu diuisionis secundum quosdam: vel inter diuersos sensus propositionum talium secundum amphibologiam, secundum nonnullos. Quod sæpe propter ignorantiam diuersitatis inter tales propositiones & sensus, intellectus auctorum in pluribus ignoratur, dum putantur vnum habuisse sensum, vt habent alium, imo quandoque habuerunt contrarium & variis modis sophismata fiunt in talibus (quamuis ignorantur à multis) dum vnus sensus vel propositio æquiualens sophistice infertur ex alio, aut econuerso ex propositione in vno sensu accepta, vel ex vno sensu inferuntur illa, quæ non ex ipso, sed ex alio sensu loquuntur. Vel econuerso, vnus sensus sophistice concluditur ex illis: Ex quibus alius sensus vero argumento potest inferri. Pluribus etiam aliis modis fiunt sophismata in talibus propter ignorantiam distinctionis huius sensus earundem propositionum secundum vocem.
units.tr: Disciple. Now tell me how the things adduced in chapter 13 above are answered. Master. All of those arguments, as it seems to me, rest on this: that no one is worthy of royal rule unless he surpasses all others in wisdom and virtue, as Aristotle appears to hold in the Politics and also in the Ethics, namely that no one ought to be king unless he is the best and superior to all those subject to him in wisdom and virtue. To this it is not answered that this is true of Aristotle universally, without any exception. To make this clear, it must be noted that royal rule can be acquired in several ways, of which for the present it is enough to list two. One is when someone is voluntarily raised up as king by his subjects. The other is when someone voluntarily passes from despotic rule, which he has justly acquired, to royal rule. If someone is to be regularly chosen for royal rule in the first way, he should be chosen as the best in wisdom and virtue, if such a man is found, and no just impediment stands in the way of his promotion. And if there is found a class which in this way surpasses all others, it is regularly just that this class should rule. Aristotle understands it so in Politics 2 and 16, when he says: Since, then, it happens that one whole class and the others differ in virtue only, so that the excellence of that class surpasses that of all the others, then it is just that this class should be royal and rule over all, and that one man be king, as was said before. But if such a man is not found, yet many good men are found, one of them is to be chosen, and the others, who are like him and equal to him in wisdom and virtue, are bound to bear his rule patiently and willingly for the common good. How he ought to be chosen you may afterwards inquire, if you wish. But if someone comes to royal rule in the second way, I suppose that he first obtained dominion over the whole region and all its inhabitants, whether by occupation, by gift, by destruction, by a just war, or by any other just means; and afterwards, refusing despotic rule, he is content with royal rule alone, so that he wishes to rule over them principally for their good and advantage, not for his own good (as a despot rules). Such a man may justly obtain royal rule, although he is not the best of men, because by giving up part of his right and keeping part, he is not to be considered unjust, even if he is not the best. As for Aristotle, who hints in Politics 7, chapter 13 that it is not just for some to rule always unless they differ from their subjects as much as gods and heroes differ from men, the answer is given in many ways. In one way, this is true if only the merit and dignity of the ruler are considered, but not if the usefulness of the common good is considered. Otherwise it is said that this holds true of natural right in particular: that it is not naturally just for these men to rule over all others unless they differ from those they rule over in such a way; in this way it is just that a husband rule his wife or wives, and a father his children, and a lord his slaves, who by nature are slaves according to Aristotle in the first book of the Politics. But this is not true of positive right, for it often becomes just and natural that someone should rule over many who are like him and equal to him in a perfect community. For if there are so many men alike and equal in virtue that they cannot all rule usefully at once, and yet such a community cannot exist without a ruler according to Aristotle, then, since it is not natural justice that these men rule rather than those, it must be determined by positive justice that these men should rule, either for their whole life or for a time. And just as, although it is not natural justice that this man should rule his equals for his whole life, as Aristotle understands it, yet by reason of some cause positive justice may come about, which Aristotle did not intend to deny. Disciple. How can it be natural justice that someone should rule over men like himself, and yet it is not natural justice that this particular man should rule over men like himself, and so with each individual? Master. The answer is that this question of yours arises from ignorance of the first principles, namely the logical ones, which anyone who labours at any science ought not to be ignorant of; otherwise he would reason sophistically when he thinks he is reasoning demonstratively. It is said, then, that just as a universal proposition is necessary and yet each singular instance of it is contingent, so it is possible that a particular proposition should be according to natural justice, and yet no singular instance will be according to natural justice. Hence it is possible that it is natural justice that someone ought to rule over men like himself, and yet it is not natural justice that this man ought to rule over men like himself, and so with each singular instance. And just as it is possible that a categorical proposition with a disjunctive extreme, in which a discrete term contained under some common term is the subject, is necessary, and yet the corresponding disjunctive proposition with the mode of necessity is false, and therefore none of those singular instances is necessary; so it can happen that such a proposition is true: "this man or that man, and so with each, to rule over his equals is natural justice," if it is a categorical proposition with a disjunctive subject; and yet the disjunctive proposition is false, and consequently each singular instance is false. Therefore, so that in such matters one may proceed without any deception, the difference must be most carefully known between a disjunctive proposition and one with a disjunctive extreme; and between a proposition taken with the same terms in the sense of composition and in the sense of division, according to some; or between the different senses of such propositions by way of amphibology, according to others. Because of ignorance of the difference between such propositions and senses, the meaning of the authors is often misunderstood in many places, while it is thought that they had one sense when they had another, indeed sometimes they had the contrary. And in such matters sophisms are made in various ways (though they are unknown to many), when one sense or an equivalent proposition is sophistically inferred from another, or conversely from a proposition taken in one sense, or from one sense are inferred things that speak not from it but from another sense; or conversely, one sense is sophistically concluded from those things from which another sense can be inferred by a true argument. Sophisms are also made in such matters in many other ways, through ignorance of the distinction of the senses of the same propositions according to their wording.

units.la: Discipulus. Recitasti duos modos respondendi ad Aristotelem: nunc recita alium, sic occurrerit. Magister. Aliter dicitur, quod non est iustum aliquos vel aliquem semper principari, nisi tantum differant, vel differat à subiectis, quantum differunt dii & heroes ab hominibus: si probabiliter timetur, quod æquales, si non æqualiter honorentur, periculosas dissensiones & seditiones procurabunt. Discipulus. Secundum ista discurre per auctoritates, quæ allegatæ sunt supra capit. quart. Magister. Primam auctoritatem Aristotelis concedit ista opinio, sicut sonat. Ad secundam dicitur, quod quando sunt plures æquales in aliqua communitate perfecta, vult Aristoteles, quod expedit omnes participare principatum secundum partem, id est quandoque principari, quandoq; subiici: quádo probabiliter timetur, aliter periculosæ seditiones orientur, nisi quilibet qui est æque dignus aliquando principetur. Si autem de huiusmodi seditione minime formidatur, expedit si aliquis inueniatur idoneus, vt vnus tanquam rex omnibus principetur, etiam secundum totam vitam suam: nisi præsumatur, quod velit principatum regalem in tyrannidem conuertere: vel timetur de aliquo alio modo, quod posset propter aliquam malitiam accidere. Ad aliam autem per Aristotelem: quod enim æquale, idem similibus, responsum est prius. Ad aliam cum accipitur ab Aristotele, quod nullus est dignus principari regulariter, nisi superet omnes alios omnibus bonis. Respondetur, quod hoc verum est, si solummodo attendantur meritum, & dignitas personæ illius, qui debet esse rex, non habendo respectum ad bonum commune. Ad aliam, cum accipitur, quod regnum est secundum aristocratiam institutum, in qua solummodo principantur, qui sunt cæteris meliores. Respondetur, quod si in aliqua communitate volente Aristocratice regi, inueniuntur aliqui pauci cæteris meliores, iustum est, quod illi nisi aliquid aliud impediat, cæteris principentur. Si autem non inueniuntur aliqui pauci, qui sunt cæteris meliores: sed sunt multi in sapientia & virtute æquales; & tot, quod non esset expediens omnes principari: tunc non potest fieri, heri, vt principantes aristocratice sint caeteris meliores: & tamen principatus aristocraticus est tori communitati expediens, si principatum regalem noluerit sustinere. Et vtilius tunc erit aliquos pauc'os de aequalibus ad principandum omnibus assumere, quam principatum politicum oligarchicum vel democraticum instituere. Ad illud, quod dicitur, Deum elegisse optimum de toto populo in primum regem Israel, scilicet Saulem: Respondetur, quod Saul non erat melior secundum virtutem & sapientiam omnibus aliis. Samuel enim erat multo melior illo: & forte complures alii ipsum virtute & sapientia excesserunt, propter tamen staturam proceram ipsius dicebatur, quod non erat ei similis in omni populo, ut habetur ibidem: altior fuit in omni populo ab humero & sursum. Ex isto colligunt multi, quod non est necesse vniversaliter absque omni exceptione Iemper eligere meliorem in regem, quia Samuel non fuit electus in regem: & tamen fuit multo melior Saule.
units.tr: Disciple. You have recited two ways of answering Aristotle; now recite another, as it occurs to you. Master. It is said otherwise that it is not just for some one man always to rule, unless he differs from his subjects only as much as gods and heroes differ from men; that is, if it is reasonably feared that equals, if they are not equally honoured, will bring about dangerous dissensions and seditions. Disciple. Now go through the authorities according to these points, which were alleged above in chapter 4. Master. This opinion grants the first authority of Aristotle, as it sounds. To the second it is said that when there are several equals in some perfect community, Aristotle wills that it is expedient for all to share in rule in turn, that is, sometimes to rule and sometimes to be ruled, when it is reasonably feared that otherwise dangerous seditions will arise, unless each man who is equally worthy should at some time rule. But if no fear of such sedition is entertained, it is expedient, if a suitable man is found, that one man should rule over all as king, even for his whole life; unless it is presumed that he would wish to turn royal rule into tyranny, or it is feared that something of that kind might happen through some malice. As for the other point taken from Aristotle, for what is equal is the same to like things, an answer was given before. To the other point, when it is taken from Aristotle that no one is regularly worthy to rule unless he surpasses all others in every good, it is answered that this is true if only the merit and dignity of the person who is to be king are considered, without regard to the common good. To the other point, when it is taken that the kingdom is instituted according to aristocracy, in which only those rule who are better than the rest, it is answered that if in some community which wishes to be governed aristocratically there are found a few men better than the rest, it is just that they should rule over the rest, unless something else hinders it. But if no few men are found who are better than the rest, but there are many equal in wisdom and virtue, and so many that it would not be expedient for all to rule, then it cannot come about that the aristocratic rulers are better than the rest; and yet aristocratic rule is expedient for the whole community, if it is unwilling to bear royal rule. And then it will be more useful to choose a few of the equals to rule over all, than to institute a political, oligarchic or democratic government. As for the point that God chose the best man from the whole people as the first king of Israel, namely Saul: it is answered that Saul was not better than all others in virtue and wisdom. For Samuel was much better than he, and perhaps several others surpassed him in virtue and wisdom; yet because of his lofty stature it was said of him that there was no one like him among all the people, as is recorded there: He was taller than any of the people from the shoulder upward. From this many conclude that it is not necessary, universally and without any exception, always to choose the better man as king, because Samuel was not chosen as king, and yet he was much better than Saul.

units.la: Discipulus. Die breviter applicando praedicta ad Papam: quomodo respondetur ad praescripta impossibilitatem probare videatur, quod nullus tanquam Papa praesse debet cunctis fidelibus, nisi omnes superet sapientia & virtute. Magister. Dicitur, quod si inveniretur aliquis catholicus, cuius excellentia talis esset nota: ille (nisi aliqua speciale impediret) deberet praeferri toti communitati fidelium. Ita quod si aliquis alius esset electus, vel etiam ante praesidens extitisset, minus perfectus amore communis boni et de necessitate salutis cedere teneretur: nisi cessaret huiusmodi aliqua specialis ratio impediret. Si autem non inveniretur aliquis, qui taliter excederet, de aequalibus esset aliquis assumendus. Quia quamvis non sit iustum naturale vel divinum, ut iste assumatur: tamen iustum naturale est, ut aliquis assumatur. Et ideo, quia non omnes aequales debent praesse: expedit ut si non possit rationabiliter aliter, quam per sortem: quod per sortem aliquis de aequalibus praeferatur. Quemadmodum Apostoli propter omnimodam aequalitatem, quam perpenderunt inter Matthiam & Ioseph, qui vocabatur Barsabas, dederunt eisdem sortem, & eum super quem sors cecidit ad Apostolatus officium assumpserunt. Si autem aliqui discernuntur in aliquibus inaequales, quamvis non in sapientia & virtute: tunc ad inaequalia potest respectus haberi pro temporis qualitate. Quia in uno tempore posset haberi iuste respectus ad unum: & in alio tempore ad contrarium, uno enim tempore posset iuste haberi respectus ad amicorum potentiam: & alio tempore ad carentiam amicorum: & sic de aliis a sapientia & virtute: putant quidam consimiliter esse dicendum.
units.tr: Disciple. Briefly, apply the foregoing to the Pope: how is the objection answered, which seems to prove the impossibility that no one should, as Pope, preside over all the faithful unless he surpasses all in wisdom and virtue? Master. It is said that if some Catholic were found whose excellence was so well known, he (unless some special reason stood in the way) ought to be preferred to the whole community of the faithful. So that if some other had been elected, or had even been presiding before, and was less perfect in love of the common good, he would be bound by necessity of salvation to give way, unless some special reason of this kind stood in the way and ceased. But if no one were found who excelled in this way, someone from among equals would have to be taken. For although it is neither natural nor divine law that this particular person be taken, it is natural law that someone be taken. And therefore, since not all equals ought to preside, it is expedient that, if it cannot reasonably be done otherwise than by lot, someone from among equals be preferred by lot. Just as the Apostles, because of the complete equality they perceived between Matthias and Joseph, who was called Barsabas, gave them a lot, and took him upon whom the lot fell into the office of the apostleship. But if some are distinguished as unequal in certain respects, though not in wisdom and virtue, then regard may be had to the inequalities according to the nature of the time. For in one time regard could justly be had to one thing, and in another time to the contrary; for at one time regard could justly be had to the power of friends, and at another time to the lack of friends; and so with other things besides wisdom and virtue: some think the same must be said.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: In quo notantur quinque vtilitates principatus monarchici & regalis, propter quas magis expedit regi ab vno, quam a pluribu- s.
units.tr: In which five advantages of monarchical and royal rule are noted, on account of which it is more expedient to be ruled by one than by many.

units.la: Discipulus. Audiui quomodo respondetur ad illa, quibus videbatur probatum, quod nullus deberet fieri summus Pontifex & caput cunctorum fidelium, nisi excelleret omnes alios sapientia & virtute. Nunc narra, quomodo respondetur ad illa, quibus supra cap. 2. huius secundi ostenditur, quod non expedit communitati fidelium subiici vni capiti & praelato, quia expedit sibi, quod regatur a pluribus. Ante omnia enim peto, ut dicas, propter quam vtilitatem secundum istos magis expedit communitati fidelium regi ab vno, quam a pluribus. Mag. Huius dicunt esse vtilitates plures. Quarum vna est, quod facilius haberur accessus ad vnum, quam ad plures. Propter hoc quod plures non semper reperiuntur in eodem loco, non modicum autem expedit subiectis, pro diversis necessitatibus facilem posse habere accessum ad principantem, propter quod principes tam saeculares, quam ecclesiastici sunt reprehensibiles reputandi, qui inaccessibiles exhibent se subiectis. Alia vtilitas est, quod vnus principans facilius potest regulariter (quando occurrit necessitas) facere iudicium & iustitiam, & pericula vitare, quam plures. Si enim vnus est principans, quandocunque oportet facere iudicium & iustitiam, & periculum aliquod vitare, non est necesse quod alium praestoletur. Si autem essent plures principantes, quamvis necesse esset celeriter talia expedire, nec sine periculo differri valeret, oportet vnum alium vel alios expectare. Tertia vtilitas est, quod facilius potest corrigi vnus, si exorbitauerit, quam plures, quia plures haberent plures defensores quam vnus. Quarta est, quod cum sine consilio multorum nulla possit bene regi magna communitas, iuxta illud Salomonis Proverbiorum 24. erit salus, vbi multa consilia. Vnde in laude dicitur Romanorum 1. Machabaeorum 8. quod quotidie consulebant trecenti viginti, consilium agentes semper de multitudine, ut quae digna sunt gerant: melius regetur eorundem communitas, si vnus aliis principetur, qui de tempore & loco consilii, & omnibus (puta de consiliariis admittendis, vel repellendis, & consimilibus) valeat ordinare: quam si principarentur plures, quorum vnus alium (etiam si machinaretur in malum rei publicae) non posset faciliter excludere a consilio, & caeteris quibusque agendis. Quinta vtilitas est, quia plura negocia & pluribus modis, & cum minori labore potest expedire vnus, quam plures: quia pluribus modis potest accidere impedimentum, ne plures simul de eisdem negociis diffiniant. Propter has & alias vtilitates plures dicunt isti, quod magis expedit communitati fidelium regi ab vno optimo viro, quam a pluribus optimis, & similiter magis expedit sibi regi ab vno & sapiente, qui de consilio velit agere sapientum, qui aliter non est bonus: quam a plurib. bonis & sapientibus. Hinc (vbi prius) dicitur ad laudem Romanor. quod committunt vno homini magistratum stratum suum super singulos annos dominari vniuersæ terræ, & omnes obediunt vni, & tamen, vt allegatum est, trecenti viginti erant consiliarii quotidie consiliantes, hinc Abimelech, vt habetur Iudicum 9. astute suasit per fratres matris suæ viris Sichen, vt acciperent eum in Dominum, prætendens id quod fuit eis vtilius, si iple fuisset bonus, dicens: loquimini ad omnes viros Sichen: quid vobis est melius, vt dominentur vestri septuaginta viri omnes filii Ieroboal, an vt dominetur vobis vnus vir.
units.tr: Disciple. I have heard how the arguments are answered by which it seemed proven that no one should be made the highest Pontiff and head of all the faithful unless he excels all others in wisdom and virtue. Now tell me how the arguments are answered by which, above in chapter 2 of this second book, it is shown that it is not expedient for the community of the faithful to be subject to one head and prelate, because it is more expedient for them to be ruled by many. Above all, I ask you to say on account of what advantage, according to those men, it is more expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many. Master. They say there are several advantages. The first is that access to one is easier than access to many. Since many are not always found in the same place, and it is of no small benefit to subjects to be able to have easy access to their ruler for their various needs, therefore princes, both secular and ecclesiastical, are to be considered blameworthy when they show themselves inaccessible to their subjects. The second advantage is that one ruler can more easily, as a rule, do justice and judgment and avoid dangers when need arises, than many can. For if there is one ruler, whenever it is necessary to do judgment and justice, and to avert some danger, there is no need to wait for another. But if there were several rulers, although such matters must be settled quickly and cannot be deferred without danger, one would have to wait for another or others. The third advantage is that one ruler, if he has gone astray, can more easily be corrected than many, because many would have more defenders than one. The fourth is that since a great community cannot be well governed without the counsel of many, according to the saying of Solomon in Proverbs 24: "there is safety where there are many counsels." Hence, in praise of the Romans, it is said in 1 Maccabees 8 that every day three hundred and twenty consulted, always deliberating about the multitude, so that they might do what is worthy. The community of those men would be better governed if one ruled over the others, who could arrange the time and place of counsel and all matters (for example, which counsellors to admit or reject, and the like), than if several ruled, one of whom could not easily exclude another (even if he plotted evil against the commonwealth) from the council and from all the other business. The fifth advantage is that one man can dispatch many affairs, and in many ways, and with less labour, than several can, because in many ways an obstacle can arise to prevent several from settling the same business together. On account of these and other advantages, those men say that it is more expedient for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one best man than by many best men, and likewise it is more expedient for them to be ruled by one wise man, who is willing to act on the counsel of wise men (for otherwise he is not good), than by many good and wise men. Hence (as stated before) it is said in praise of the Romans that they entrusted the magistracy to one man, to rule over the whole earth for one year at a time, and all obeyed one; and yet, as has been said, there were three hundred and twenty counsellors deliberating every day. Hence Abimelech, as is recorded in Judges 9, craftily persuaded through the brothers of his mother the men of Shechem to accept him as lord, putting forward what would have been more advantageous to them had he been good, saying: "Speak to all the men of Shechem: which is better for you, that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, should rule over you, or that one man should rule over you?"

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: In quo ponuntur responsiones ad rationes secundi capituli, probantes, quod non expedit magis communitati fidelium regi ab vno fideli, quam a pluribus. Et primo respondet ad tertiam, deinde ad sequentes. Ad primam & secundam allega- tiones, respondetur supra capitulo 15.
units.tr: In which answers are given to the arguments of the second chapter, which prove that it is not more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one faithful man than by many. First it answers the third argument, then the following ones. The first and second arguments are answered above in chapter 15.

units.la: Discipulus. Audiui vtilitates aliquas, propter quas isti dicunt, quod magis expedit communitati fidelium regi ab vno fideli, quam a pluribus, nunc narra, quomodo respondetur ad allegationes, quæ contrarium probare videntur, quæ supra capitulo 2. huius secundi sunt inductæ. Magister. Ad tertiam illarum, cum adducitur, quod per illum vel illos maxime expedit regi totam congregationem fidelium, cuius vel quorum iudicium est melius, vel certius in iudicando & discernendo, quæ sunt procuranda tanquam vtilia, & quæ tanquam inutilia & nociua sunt repellenda. Respondetur, quod hoc non est vniuersaliter verum, licet sit verum in casu. Constat enim, quod iudicium concilii generalis, in quo conuenire debent meliores & sapientiores de omnibus prouinciis & regionibus Christianorum, est certius & melius quam iudicium vnius vel paucorum, qui in aliquo vno loco valent continue commode commorari: Et tamen non expedit semper esse concilium generale pro communitate fidelium gubernanda, quamuis etiam pro quibusdam negociis specialibus, quæ per vnum vel paucos non possunt congrue expediri, sit expediens concilium generale conuocari, & sequi ipsius sententiam. Pro negociis autem, quæ per vnum vel pauciores possunt vtiliter expediri, non expedit congregari concilium generale, & ita regulariter magis expedit communitatem fidelium regi ab vno vel paucis, quam a concilio generali. Sic etiam expedit magis communitati fidelium regi ab vno sufficienter optimo vel bono vtente consilio, quam a pluribus simul principantibus: quia melius est, vt plures, absque quorum consilio non bene regeretur communitas fidelium, sint tantummodo consiliarii vnius optimi aut boni, qui possit eos, quando erit expediens, inuitare & omnes, aut quosdam vocare & diuersis diuersa committere, quam quod huiusmodi omnes sint principantes siue rectores. Quia necesse esset sæpe omnes conuenire pro negociis, quæ possent expediri per paucos. Aliæ etiam difficultates & incommoditates plures accideren t, quæ vitantur, si vnus bonus aut optimus, habens consiliarios sufficientes & æque bonos, sicut essent plures principantes, regit. Principatus enim neque sapientiam, neque bonitatem largitur. Ad Aristotelem autem, qui probare videtur in politicis, quod magis expedit communitatem regi a pluribus optimis, quam ab vno: quia turba melius iudicat, quam quisquam vnus. Respondetur, quod plures melius & certius sæpe iudicant quam vnus: & turba melius, quam vnus, & ideo bene requiritur disceptatio, consiliatio & iudicium plurium: non tamen tanquam principantium necessario, sed sæpe sufficit vt adsint tanquam consiliarii solummodo. Ita enim disceptat, consiliatur & iudicat discernendo inter bonum & malum, iustum & iniustum, ille qui solummodo est consiliarius habens intentionem bonam, sicut si esset principans & participans, sæpe etiam pro agendis sufficit deliberatio & iudicium vnius solius, & ideo magis expedit toti communitati fidelium, quod principetur vnus supremus principans, qui negocia, pro quibus ipse solus sufficit, expediat per seipsum, & alia pro quibus peritia ipsius solius non sufficit, expediat de consilio aliorum, quam quod principentur tales plures, quos pro omnibus negociis paruis & magnis facilibus & difficilibus oporteat conuenire.
units.tr: Disciple. I have heard some advantages, on account of which these men say that it is more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one faithful man than by many. Now tell me how one answers the arguments which seem to prove the contrary, which were introduced above in chapter 2 of this second book. Master. As to the third of those, when it is argued that it is especially advantageous for the whole congregation of the faithful to be ruled by that one man or those men whose judgment is better or more certain in judging and discerning what things are to be pursued as useful and what are to be rejected as useless and harmful. It is answered that this is not universally true, although it is true in a particular case. For it is clear that the judgment of a general council, in which the better and wiser men from all the provinces and regions of the Christians ought to meet, is more certain and better than the judgment of one or a few who are able to dwell continuously and conveniently in one place. And yet it is not always advantageous for a general council to govern the community of the faithful. Although for certain special matters, which cannot be properly settled by one or a few, it is advantageous to call a general council and to follow its opinion. But for matters which can be usefully settled by one or by fewer, it is not advantageous to convene a general council. And so, as a rule, it is more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one or a few than by a general council. So too it is more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one man who is sufficiently best or good and who uses good counsel, than by many ruling together. For it is better that the many, without whose counsel the community of the faithful would not be well governed, be merely counsellors of one best or good man, who can invite them when it is expedient, and either all of them or some of them, and commit different things to different people, than that all such men be rulers or governors. For it would often be necessary for all of them to meet for matters which could be settled by a few. Several other difficulties and inconveniences would also arise, which are avoided if one good or best man, having sufficient and equally good counsellors, rules, as he would if there were several ruling men. For rule does not bestow wisdom or goodness. As for Aristotle, who seems to prove in the Politics that it is more advantageous for a community to be ruled by many best men than by one, because the crowd judges better than any single man: it is answered that several men often judge better and more certainly than one, and the crowd better than one; and therefore the disputation, consultation and judgment of many is rightly required. Yet they are not necessarily required as ruling persons; often it is enough that they be present merely as counsellors. For he who is only a counsellor, having a good intention, debates, consults and judges, discerning between good and evil, just and unjust, just as he would if he were a ruler and participant. And often for acting, the deliberation and judgment of one alone suffices. Therefore it is more advantageous for the whole community of the faithful that one supreme ruler govern, who may settle by himself those matters for which he alone is sufficient, and settle with the counsel of others those for which his skill alone is not enough, than that many such men rule, whom it would be necessary to gather for all matters, small and great, easy and difficult.

units.la: Ad aliam auctoritatem Aristotelis, quæ videtur asserere, quod multi multis oculis, & multis auribus, plura percipiunt & melius, quam vnus duobus oculis & duabus auribus: & similiter multi plura possunt operari multis manibus & multis pedibus, quam vnus duabus manibus & duobus pedibus. Et ita magis expedit regimen plurium, quam vnius. Respondetur, quod si vnus bonus & sapiens regat communitatem fidelium non solum vtitur duobus oculis & duabus auribus, ac etiam duabus manibus & duobus pedibus, sed interdum vtitur multis modis huiusmodi organis, & magis expedit, quod interdum vtatur solummodo duobus oculis & duabus manibus, quam multis. Interdum vero magis expedit, quod vtatur multis quam solum duobus. Et ideo magis expedit toti communitati fidelium, quod regatur ab vno, qui aliquando, prout expedit, vtatur sua sufficientia propria, aliquando aliena, quam a pluribus qui absque necessitate ad omnia expedienda conueniant.
units.tr: To another authority of Aristotle, which seems to assert that many men with many eyes and many ears perceive more and better than one man with two eyes and two ears; and likewise that many men can accomplish more with many hands and many feet than one man with two hands and two feet. And so the rule of many is more advantageous than the rule of one. It is answered that if one good and wise man governs the community of the faithful, he not only uses two eyes and two ears, and likewise two hands and two feet, but sometimes uses many organs of this kind in various ways. And sometimes it is more advantageous that he use only two eyes and two hands than many; but at other times it is more advantageous that he use many rather than only two. And so it is more advantageous for the whole community of the faithful to be ruled by one man, who at times, as is expedient, uses his own ability and at other times the ability of others, than by many who gather without necessity to settle all matters.

units.la: Ad illud, quod ibidem accipitur Actuum decim. quint. conuenerunt Apostoli, & seniores videre de verbo hoc: quasi semper magis expediat negocia terminari & diffiniri per plures, quam per vnum. Respondetur, quod aliquando magis expedit negocia terminari per plures quam per vnum: & aliquando magis expedit, quæ tractentur per vnum. Et ideo expedit communitati fidelium, vt regatur ab vno optimo vel saltem bono, qui solus aliqua negotia & quaestiones tractet & diffiniat; aliqua vero tractet cum aliis pluribus vel paucioribus, secundum quod erit expediens, & diffiniat. Et ideo in casu, de quo fit mentio Actuum 15. erat expediens, ut de verbo illo, non unus solus, sed plures exquirerent. Et conuenerunt Apostoli & seniores, non quidem omnes principantes communitati fidelium, sed tanquam necessarii & utiles uni principanti, & capiti omnium pro fauore vel consilio. Quandoq; enim vocantur aliqui ad aliquos tractatus, in quibus sufficit sapientia unius magis pro fauore praestando contra resistentes vel inobedientes, quam pro consilio requirendo.
units.tr: As to what is taken from Acts 15: "The apostles and elders came together to consider this matter," as if it were always more advantageous for matters to be concluded and defined by many than by one. It is answered that sometimes it is more advantageous for matters to be concluded by many than by one, and sometimes it is more advantageous that they be handled by one.
