And so it is advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one best, or at least good, man, who alone handles and defines some matters and questions; but other matters he handles with several others or with fewer, according as it is expedient, and then defines them. And so in the case mentioned in Acts 15 it was expedient that, on that matter, not one alone but several should inquire. And the apostles and elders came together, not indeed all as rulers of the community of the faithful, but as necessary and useful to the one ruler, who is the head of all, for favour or counsel. For sometimes certain men are called to certain negotiations in which the wisdom of one alone suffices; they are needed more to grant support against those who resist or disobey than to seek counsel.

units.la: Ad Innocent. vero Papam, cum dixit, quod facilius inuenitur quod a pluribus senioribus quaeritur. Respondetur, quod hoc de multis dubiis continet veritatem: quando tamen ad alicuius inuentionem sufficit unus solus, qui tunc non indiget fauore vel auxilio; aut consilio plurium, melius est quod quaeratur & inueniatur ab uno quam a pluribus.
units.tr: As to Pope Innocent, when he said that "what is sought from several elders is more easily found." It is answered that this holds true for many doubts. When, however, one man alone suffices for discovering something, and so needs neither support nor help nor the counsel of several, it is better that it be sought and found by one than by several.

units.la: Ad aliam vero allegationem, quae fundatur in hoc, quod plures sunt minus peruertibiles & corruptibiles & malitiis & concupiscentiis & passionibus prauis quam unus. Et per consequens magis expedit communitati fidelium a pluribus regi quam ab uno, quia magis expedit sibi regi ab illo vel illis, cuius vel quorum voluntas minus est peruertibilis & corruptibilis a passionibus prauis. Respondetur, quod aliquo modo voluntas unius est minus peruertibilis & corruptibilis a passionibus prauis & affectionibus, quam plurium. Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur esse notandum, quod voluntatem plurium vel multitudinis esse peruertibilem dupliciter potest intelligi: vel quod sit peruertibilis secundum se totam accipiendo totam sincathegoreumatice vel secundum partem. Primo modo voluntas plurium est minus peruertibilis, quam voluntas unius. Secundo modo voluntas plurium est magis peruertibilis quam voluntas unius determinati: puta voluntas illius vel istius. Citius enim & facilius peruerti potest & corrumpi aliqua multitudo secundum partem, quam unus solus. Quia ad corruptionem cuiuslibet de illa multitudine corrumpitur illo modo & peruertitur ipsa multitudo. Quia quamuis non peruertantur singuli, tamen in multitudine ipsa aliqua peruersio reperitur. Et quia ad bonitatem & idoneitatem principantis requiritur, quod nec etiam secundum partem sit peruersus: ideo magis expedit communitati fidelium regi ab illo, qui etiam secundum partem est minus peruertibilis. Talis autem est unus, & non plures. Et ideo magis expedit communitatem fidelium regi ab uno quam a pluribus.
units.tr: As to the other argument, which is founded on the fact that several men are less easily perverted and corrupted by malice, lusts and wicked passions than one man. And consequently it is more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by many than by one, because it is more advantageous for it to be ruled by that one man or those men whose will is less perverted and corrupted by wicked passions. It is answered that in a certain way the will of one man is less perverted and corrupted by wicked passions and affections than the will of many. To make this clear, it should be noted that the will of several men, or of a multitude, can be understood to be perverted in two ways: either that it is perverted according to itself taken as a whole, taking "whole" in a syncategorematic sense, or that it is perverted according to a part. In the first way the will of several is less perverted than the will of one. In the second way the will of several is more perverted than the will of one particular man, say this man or that. For some multitude can be perverted and corrupted in part more quickly and easily than one man alone. For when any one of that multitude is corrupted, the multitude itself is corrupted and perverted in that way. For although the individuals are not each perverted, yet some perversion is found in the multitude itself. And since for the goodness and fitness of a ruler it is required that he not be perverse even in part, therefore it is more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by him who is less perverted even in part. Such a man is one, and not several. And therefore it is more advantageous for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many.

units.la: Ad auctoritatem Aristo. quae accipitur ex 3. politicorum ca. 8. respondetur, quod in casu, quando pauci non sufficiunt ad perfecte videndum, quid est agendum & quid omittendum, quamuis aliquo modo perpendant imperfecte: tunc expedit multitudinem conuenire, non quidem ad principandum, sed ad deliberandum & inueniendum, quid est toti communitati expediens; & ad consulendum quid facere principans teneatur. Quod si principans nollet sequi eorum consilium, & imminceat periculum notabile, haberent corrigere ipsum. Ideo autem in tali casu expedit multitudinem conuenire praedicto modo: quia omnes simul sunt aliquid melius, quam pauci: & tam circa mores quam circa intellectum possunt plura videre. Quando autem pauci sufficiunt ad videndum perfecte, quid est agendum & quid omittendum, non expedit multitudinem conuenire ad tractandum, sed melius est quod conueniant pauci sufficientes tamen. Et ideo quando unus sufficit, non oportet conuenire multos. Et si unus non sufficit ad inueniendum quid necesse est fieri, expedit vt quot sufficiant (multos vel paucos) valeat conuocare, & procedere de consilio eorundem, ita vt non principentur cum eo. Per praedicta patet, quomodo respondetur ad auctoritatem Aristotelis, cum innitur quod plures sunt magis imperuertibiles quam unus. Quia dicunt, quod uno modo sunt magis imperuertibiles, & alio modo sunt magis peruertibiles: non quidem vt omnes simul peruertantur facilius, quam aliquis vnus determinatus, sed quia facilius inuenitur peruersitas in eos, quam in uno determinato: quia quocunq; eorum peruerso, reperitur inter omnes peruersitas, quamuis non oporteat quod in aliquo vno determinato reperiatur peruersitas. Ad bonitatem autem & idoneitatem principantis requiritur, quod nulla in ipso sit peruersitas. Et ideo quando reperitur peruersitas in aliqua multitudine, etiam in vno solo illius multitudinis, eo ipso illa multitudo non est idonea ad principandum. iuxta Apostolum ad Gal. 5. modicum fermenti totam massam corrumpit. Quare magis expedit communitati fidelium vt regatur ab vno, quam a pluribus simul principantibus, & vicem vnius gerentibus. Quia non ita facile reperitur peruersitas in vno, sicut in quacunq; multitudine, cuius ille vnius sit pars & alius cum eo qui ita peruerti potest sicut ipse. Dices. Secundum ista sequitur, quod similiter nunquam essent vocandi plures, nec etiam multitudo ad consilium: cuius oppositum non solum Aristoteles & alii, sed etiam ista opinio tenet. Patet consequentia: quia facilius inuenitur peruersitas in multitudine, & inter quosq; plures quam in vno solo. Peruersitas autem summe fugienda est. Mag. Respondetur, quod quandocunq; vnus sufficit ita quod nec consilio nec fauore indiget aliorum, non sunt vocandi plures. Quia frustra fit per plures, quod atque bene potest fieri per vnum. Sed quando vnus non sufficit ad perfecte videndum vel agendum id quod agendum est: tunc expedit vocare plures, vel pro consilio, vel pro auxilio, vel pro fauore. Quia sicut inter plures & in multitudine potest inueniri peruersitas: ita inter plures & in multitudine maior scientia & prudentia & bonitas reperitur. Et ideo quando vnus non sufficit, conuenire debent plures: quamuis hoc possit esse indifferens ad bonum & ad malum. Plures enim conuenientes interdum bene, & interdum male procedunt. Et ideo quando propter bonitatem eorum, qui conuenire habent, probabiliter creditur, quod recte consulant & faciant, agendum est vt conueniant, si vnus non sufficit. Quando autem probabiliter inuenitur, quod à rectis itineribus deuiabunt, impediendi sunt ne conueniant. Quia melius est nihil agere quam malum facere. Unde si probabiliter creditur, quando aliq ad generale concilium conuocantur, qν nō rite concilium celebrabunt, impediendi sunt ne conueniant. Si autē probabiliter creditur, qν rite concilium celebrabunt, agendum est vt conueniant, nisi credatur quod minus vtilitatis faciant quàm sit incommoditas, quam incurrerent ex laboribus & expensis.
units.tr: I answer the authority of Aristotle, taken from Politics book 3, chapter 8, as follows. In a case where a few men are not sufficient to see perfectly what must be done and what must be left undone, even though they weigh it in some imperfect way, then it is useful for the multitude to assemble, not indeed to rule, but to deliberate and discover what is expedient for the whole community, and to advise what the ruler is bound to do. But if the ruler were unwilling to follow their counsel, and a notable danger threatened, they would have the power to correct him. The reason that in such a case it is useful for the multitude to assemble in the manner described is that all together are something better than a few, and they can see more both in matters of conduct and in matters of understanding. When, however, a few are sufficient to see perfectly what must be done and what left undone, it is not useful for the multitude to assemble for deliberation, but it is better that a few sufficient men assemble. And so when one man is sufficient, there is no need for many to assemble. And if one man is not sufficient to discover what must necessarily be done, it is useful that he be able to call together as many as are sufficient, whether many or few, and proceed by their counsel, so that they do not rule together with him. From what has been said it is clear how one answers the authority of Aristotle, when he insists that many are less corruptible than one. For they say that in one way they are less corruptible, and in another way they are more corruptible: not indeed that all together are more easily corrupted than some one determinate man, but because corruption is more easily found in them than in one determinate man. For when any one of them is corrupt, corruption is found among them all, although it need not be found in any one determinate person. But for the goodness and fitness of a ruler it is required that there be no corruption in him at all. And therefore, when corruption is found in some multitude, even in only one member of that multitude, by that very fact that multitude is not fit to rule, according to the Apostle to the Galatians 5: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump." Wherefore it is more useful for the community of the faithful to be ruled by one than by many ruling together and standing in the place of one. For corruption is not so easily found in one man as in any multitude of which he is a part, and another with him who can be corrupted just as he can. You will say: according to this it would follow that many should never be called, nor the multitude for counsel; yet not only Aristotle and others, but this opinion also, holds the opposite. The consequence is clear, because corruption is more easily found in a multitude, and among several, than in one alone. But corruption is to be shunned above all. The Master replies: whenever one man is sufficient, so that he needs neither counsel nor favour from others, many are not to be called. For what is done well enough by one is done in vain by many. But when one man is not sufficient to see perfectly, or to do what must be done, then it is useful to call many, either for counsel, or for help, or for favour. For just as corruption can be found among many and in a multitude, so among many and in a multitude greater knowledge, prudence and goodness are also found. And therefore, when one is not sufficient, those who ought to assemble must assemble, although this may be indifferent to good and to evil. For many assembling sometimes proceed well and sometimes badly. And so when, on account of the goodness of those who are to assemble, it is probably believed that they will counsel and act rightly, they are to be brought together if one is not sufficient. But when it is probably found that they will turn aside from the right paths, they are to be hindered from assembling. For it is better to do nothing than to do evil. Hence, if it is probably believed that, when some are called to a general council, they will not hold the council duly, they are to be hindered from assembling. But if it is probably believed that they will hold the council duly, they are to be brought together, unless it is believed that they would do less good than the inconvenience they would incur from their labours and expenses.

units.la: Discip. Nunc narra, quomodo respondetur ad verba Aristotelis, quibus videtur concludere, quod Aristocratia melior & eligibilior est, quam regnum. Mag. Respondetur, quod non intendit Aristoteles concludere, quod simpliciter & semper melior est & eligibilior Aristocratia quam regnum. Quando enim tota multitudo principantium in Aristocratia non est secundum se totam ita pervertibilis, sicut vnusquisque; qui esset de illa multitudine, & maior est prudentia & etiam virtus seu bonitas in tota multitudine, quam in vno, tunc potest accidere quod melius sit vt plures principentur Aristocratice, quam vnus. Quia ille, qui regaliter principaretur, potest peruerti aliis nō peruersis. Peius est autem quod aliquis peruertatur, quando solus principatur, quam quando principatur cum aliis. Si enim peruertatur, quando principatur cum aliis, minora & pauciora mala facere potest regulariter, quam si solus principans peruerteretur. Et ideo quandoq; melior est & eligibilior Aristocratia, quàm regnum. Sæpe tamen & communius, & ideo quodammodo simpliciter, melius est regnum quam Aristocratia propter vtilitates, quæ dictæ sunt prius c.18. & propter alias plures. Et hinc est quod antiqui rationabiliter aliquando Aristocratiam mutabant in regnum: aliquando regnum in Aristocratiam. Sicut de Romanis & aliis quam pluribus gentibus, possent poni exempla quam plura. Aliquando enim principabantur reges: & aliquando plures simul, & plures tam Romani quam aliæ gentes huiusmodi transmutationes fecerunt.
units.tr: Student: Now tell me how one answers the words of Aristotle, by which he seems to conclude that aristocracy is better and more eligible than kingship. Master: It is answered that Aristotle did not intend to conclude that aristocracy is absolutely and always better and more eligible than kingship. For when the whole multitude of rulers in an aristocracy is not in itself as corruptible as each single man who would belong to that multitude, and when there is greater prudence, and also virtue or goodness, in the whole multitude than in one man, then it can happen that it is better for many to rule aristocratically than one. For the one who would rule as a king can be corrupted by others who are not corrupt. But it is worse for someone to be corrupted when he rules alone than when he rules with others. For if he is corrupted while ruling with others, he can ordinarily do fewer and smaller evils than if he ruled alone and were corrupted. And so sometimes aristocracy is better and more eligible than kingship. Yet more often and more commonly, and therefore in some sense absolutely, kingship is better than aristocracy, on account of the advantages which were stated before in chapter 18, and on account of many others. And hence it is that the ancients reasonably sometimes changed aristocracy into kingship, and sometimes kingship into aristocracy. Examples of this could be given in very great number from the Romans and many other peoples. For at one time kings ruled, and at another time several together; and the Romans as well as other peoples made transformations of this kind.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: In quo specialiter quaeritur, vtrum expediat communitati fidelium habere potestatem transmutandi principatum Aristocraticum in principatum regalem, & econtra, quod sic. Prima opinio probatur decem rationibus, ad quas respondetur infra c. 27.
units.tr: In which it is specifically asked whether it is expedient for the community of the faithful to have the power of changing an aristocratic government into a royal one, and conversely. The first opinion holds that it is, and is supported by ten reasons, to which replies are given below in chapter 27.

units.la: Discipulus. Occasione eorum, quæ vltimo recitasti, interrogandum duxi, an scilicet secundum istam opinionem expediat communitati fidelium, vt habeant potestatem transmutandi principatum Aristocraticum, in principatum simile principatui regali, & econuerso: ita vt habeant potestatem constituendi vnum summum pontificem, qui omnibus aliis præsit, & habeant etiam potestatem constituendi seu eligendi simul plures summos pontifices, qui æqualem potestatem habentes simul Aristocratice regant, & præsint fidelibus aliis vniuersis. Vt vnum principatum in alium indifferenter (sicut videbitur expedire) valeat transmutare ad modum, quo gentes principatum Aristocraticum rationabiliter transmutarent in regalem: & econuerso. Magist. Circa hoc sunt diuersæ opiniones: & stante opinione, quæ ponit quod aliquibus aliquando melior est principatus Aristocraticus principatu regali: & aliquando eisdem præcellit principatus regalis: vna est quod expedit communitati fidelium, vt habeat talem potestatem transmutandi principatum Aristocraticum in principatum vnius summi sacerdotis, & econuerso, secundum quod necessitas & qualitas temporis vnum principatum vel alium exigit & requirit. Discip. Pro ipsa potest taliter allegari, sicut expedit, vt secundum varietatem temporum statuta varientur humana: extra, de consanguinitate, reprehensibilem: sic expedit, vt secundum varietatem temporum principatus varientur humani. Sed Ecclesia Christi habet potestatem principaliter super humanos principatus, quantum ad omnia quæ sibi expediunt. Ergo habet potestatem variandi huiusmodi principatus. Discip. Dici posset, quod principatus, quo summus sacerdos principatur cunctis fidelibus, non est humanus, sed diuinus. Quia à solo Deo institutus existit. Ergo non decet, & per consequens non expedit, vt etiam supra principatum Papalem habeat potestatem. Magist. Hæc responsio impugnatur. Quia licet principatus Papalis sit quo ad hoc diuinus, quod Christus ordinauit ipsum debere esse in Ecclesia, quantum ad multa tamen videtur esse humanus. Nā ad homines pertinet ordinare, quis assumi debeat ad ipsum, & qui debent eligere, & debent assumptum corrigere, si correctione indigeat, & consimilia. Ergo consimiliter quantum ad hoc erit humanus, quod per homines debeat ordinari, an vnus tantummodo vel plures quando expedierit ad talem assumi debeant principatum. Amplius, communitati fidelium quantū ad omnia quæ necessaria sunt pro his quæ sunt ppria Christianis, optime est prouisum: & non minus bene, quicunq; communitati vel genti, vt in omnibus talibus quantū ad omnia quæ expediunt & vt expediunt habeat potestatem. Sed si Ecclesia haberet potestatē transmutandi principatum, qui inciperet esse minus expediens, in alium principatum magis expedientem, melius est prouisum, quam si potestate huiusmodi non haberet. Ergo cum in talibus sit optime prouisum sibi, potestate habet transmutandi principatum vnius in principatu pluritm, si aduerterit ꝗ sit magis expediens, vt regatur à pluribus principatu Aristocratico, quam ab vno solo. Rursus, non minus expedit communitati fidelium, vt habeat potestatem tollendi principatus, qui incipiunt esse onerosi vel minus veiles, quam tollendi consuetudines onerosas, cum nihil possit plus nocere Ecclesiæ, quam principatus onerosus & inutilis, iuxta sententiam Augustī. qui, vt legitur dist. 81. nemo, ait: nemo quippe in Ecclesia amplius nocet, quam qui peruerse agens nomen vel ordinem sanctitatis & sacerdotis habet. Ex quo colligitur, quod nihil amplius nocet Ecclesiæ quam princeps peruersus, & principatus peruersus. Quare si Ecclesia animaduertat, quod Ecclesia peruerse vel minus utiliter regitur, ex hoc unus solus omnibus principetur, expedit ut habeat potestatem talem principatum in alium (qui pro tempore erit utilior) transmutare. Adhuc, non impedit Ecclesiae illi principatui alligari, qui potest in principatum pessimum transmutari. Sed principatus, quod principatur unus solus, potest in principatum pessimum transmutari. Quemadmodum principatus regalis, non obstante quod sit optimus: tamen quantum est ex natura principatus, potest in tyrannidem (qui est principatus pessimus) transmutari, secundum quod Aristo. in Ethicis asserit & probat aperte. Ergo non expedit Ecclesiae, ut principatui, quo principatur unus solus, taliter astringatur, quod non possit illum in principatum alium, scilicet Aristocraticum, utiliorem pro tempore transmutare. Praeterea, ut etiam lex ciuilis testatur: in rebus nouis constituendis euidens debet esse utilitas, ut recedatur ab eo iure, quod diu aequum visum est. Ex quo colligitur, quod propter euidentem utilitatem est nouitas facienda, ita etiam ut recedatur ab eo iure, quod diu aequum visum est. Sed non magis est recedendum a iure, quam a principatu. Quia in omni communitate nihil potest esse magis seruandum, quam ius. Quod enim iuri non congruit, nullo modo est seruandum. Ergo propter euidentem utilitatem est nouitas facienda, ut recedatur a principatu, qui diu rationabilis & aequus apparuit, quare si appareat euidenter Ecclesiae pro aliquo tempore, quod maior utilitas proueniat Ecclesiae ex principatu Aristocratico, quo plures simul regent communitatem fidelium, quam ex principatu unius, est talis nouitas facienda, ut a principatu unius, qui aequus visus est & utilis, recedatur. Item, quod in fauorem & utilitatem inductum est aliquorum, non debet in eorum damnum & dispendium retorqueri. Sed principatus, cui debeant subdi uniuersi fideles, inductus est in fauorem & utilitatem cunctorum fidelium. Ergo si aliqua species principatus incipit esse dispendiosa fidelibus vel minus utilis, expedit ut illa species principatus in aliam utiliorem pro tempore transmutetur. Quare Ecclesia habet potestatem constituendi Principatum Aristocraticum super cunctos fideles, si perpendunt, quod principatus unius incipit esse dispendiosus fidelibus. Amplius, secundum Leonem Papam, ut legitur dist. 45. c. licet enim: Quod prouisum sit ad concordiam, tendere non debet ad noxam. Ex quo concluditur, quod quicquid prouisum est ad concordiam, tollendum est, si tendit ad noxam. Sed principatus unius summi pontificis prouisus est ad concordiam cunctorum fidelium, scilicet ut unus praesset aliis, ne fieret schisma, secundum Gloss. ibidem. Igitur si principatus unius summi pontificis tendit ad noxam, id est, ad amorem damnandi seu tyrannice principandi vel etiam ad schisma periculosum inter Christianos: sicut si videlicet maior & potentior temporaliter, aut aequalis pars Christianorum nullo modo vult sustinere principatum unius summi pontificis, & tamen vult sustinere principatum Aristocraticum multorum simul regentium, quorum quilibet sit summus pontifex, quemadmodum aliquando fuerunt simul plures imperatores, & aliquando in eadem causa sunt plures iudices aequalem potestatem habentes: tollendus est saltem ad tempus principatus vnius regali principatui similis: & instituendus est saltem quousque praedicta mala seu pericula & consimilia cessent, Aristocraticus principatus. Rursus, cessante causa cessare debet effectus, extra, de appellationibus, cum cessante. Sed communis utilitas est causa, quare vnus summus pontifex debet praesse cunctis fidelibus. Ergo si ex principatu unius non proueniat communis utilitas, sed commune dispendium, talis principatus pro tunc cessare debet. Ergo communitas fidelium habet tunc potestatem instituendi alium principatum. Amplius, in cunctis Ecclesiis seruari debet, quod maior pars iudicat obseruandum, extra, de his que fiunt a maiori parte capituli. c. 1. & dist. 65. c. 1. & 2. & 3. extra, de electio. licet. Igitur si maior pars fidelium reputat instituendum principatum Aristocraticum super totam communitatem fidelium, habet tunc potestatem instituendi alium principatum. Et talis principatus instituendus est. Ex quo infertur, quod Ecclesia seu communitas fidelium habet potestatem instituendi huiusmodi principatum. Discip. Vt notat Glossa super allegatum capitulum, extra, de his que fiunt a maiori parte capituli. Non semper statur maiori parti, nec pluralitati, vt hic & 21. dist. Nicena, & supra de elect. Ecclesia vestra, & infra. Illud regale est, vt semper stetur maiori parti. Sed maior pars est illa, quae maiori pietate & ratione vi- titur 9. dist. sana quippe. & 60. dist. multi, in fine, 4. dist. 2. iurisiurandi. Hoc etiam Glossa dist. 60. super capitulum vltimum sentire videtur, dicens: non gradus elegantior, sed vita melioris actio comprobatur 23. q. 4. sicut. & 10. q. 1. sunt nulli. Est enim hoc argumentum, quod pars illa quae iustiori rationi innititur, maior dicitur, licet sit minor, dist. 31. Nicena 19. in canonicis. & 4. q. 3. & extra, de elect. in nostra. Ex his habetur aperte, quod non semper standum est maiori parti. Quare quamuis maior pars Christianorum iudicaret principatum vnius transmutandum esse in Aristocraticum principatum, non esset tamen hoc faciendum. Magist. Ista responsio impugnatur. Quia licet non semper sit standum est maiori parti, sed aliquando minori: tamen semper standum est maiori parti, nisi a minori parte probetur aperte, quod non est standum maiori parti. Hoc colligitur ex Gloss. super allegato c. supra De his que fiunt a maiori parte capituli, quae ait post praeallegata verba: praesumitur pro pluralitate. 61. dist. nullus: nisi in contrarium probetur, vt hic patet. & 23. dist. illud. & supra de elect. dudum. Et ibidem super vocabulo offensum, ait: non sufficit obiicere, nisi probetur. Cum ergo non possit probari, quod non est standum maiori parti, si pro vtilitate communi voluerit transmutari principatum vnius summi pontificis in Aristocraticum principatum: sequitur quod in hoc standum est maiori parti fidelium. Discip. Videtur quod rationabiliter possit ostendi, quod in hoc non est standum maiori parti Christianorum, si decreuerit instituere Aristocraticum principatum super cunctos fideles. Quia minor pars in contradicendo maiori iustiori niteretur ratione. Nam minor pars niteretur Diuinae ordinationi, quae omni praevaleat. ualet ordinationi humanæ. Magist. Nonnullis apparet, esto quod Christus ordinasset vnum summum pontificem debere cunctis fidelibus principari, quod pro vtilitate communi potest Ecclesia instituere alium principatum. Quod tali modo probatur, necessitas & vtilitas parificantur, vt Alexand. tertius insinuare videtur, extra, de aequalitate & aetate praeficienda, quaris. Sed pro necessitate licet facere contra praeceptum Diuinum etiam expressum in his, quæ non sunt de se mala: sed solum sunt mala, quia sunt prohibita. Ergo etiam pro vtilitate communi licet facere contra praeceptum Dei & ordinationem Christi. Ergo esto, quod Christus ordinasset vnum summum pontificem esse praeficiendum cunctis fidelibus: liceret fidelibus pro communi vtilitate alium instituere principatum, saltem ad tempus. Maior videtur manifeste probata: quæ etiam probatur ex hoc, quod necessitas & pietas parificantur, vt innuit Gregorius nonus extra, de feriis, c. vltimo. Pietas autem vtilitatem includit. Ergo necessitas & vtilitas parificantur, & per consequens quod si necessitas facit licitum, vtilitas etiam facit licitum. Minor multis modis ostenditur. Hoc enim Beda super Marcum, & habetur extra, de Regulis Iuris, cap. quod non est, patenter videtur afferere dicens: quod non est licitum in lege, necessitas licitum facit. Nam & Sabbatum custodiri praeceptum est: Machabei autem in Sabbato sine culpa pugnauerunt. Ex quibus verbis aperte videtur haberi, quod Machabei ex necessitate licite fecerunt contra expressum mandatum Diuinum. Hoc etiam Christus ipse Matth. 12. & Luc. 6. expresse docere videtur dicens, quod Dauid & qui cum eo erant, contra praeceptum Diuinum panes propositionis licite comederunt: eo quod explicite praecepit Deus, ne quis nisi sacerdos dictos panes comederet. Ex quibus aliisque quam pluribus colligitur, quod regula, scilicet Necessitas legem non habet, quæ penitur extra, de consuetudine, quanto: Et illa: Necessitas legi non subiacet, extra, de obseruantia ieiuniorum, c. 2. Et illa, Necessitas in legibus excipitur, extra de iureiurando, quaerelam: Et consimiles non tantum de legibus humanis positiuis, sed etiam de legibus diuinis positiuis, nisi in eisdem legibus diuinis contrarium caueatur, debet intelligi, vt necessitas legi Diuinæ positiuæ non subiaceat. Secus est de lege naturali & de lege Dei. Naturali, quia legi illi necessitas subiacet; nec potest aliqua necessitas excusare. Adhuc, quod non obstaret talis ordinatio Christi ordinationi, ostenditur. Nam non minorem potestatem super principatum sacerdotum mutandum habent Christiani in lege noua, quam habuerunt illi qui erant sub lege veteri constituti. Sed non obstante praecepto Dei de vno summo pontifice constituendo Exodi 29. prout etiam habetur in decretis, dist. 21. §. 1. postea Dauid constituit plures summos pontifices, vt colligitur ex 1. Paral. p. cap. 44. Vnde & Euangelista Luc. 2. testari videtur, quod tempore Christi erant simul plures principes sacerdotum. Ergo & Christiani habent potestatem constituendi plures summos pontifices, non obstante quod Christus ordinauerit aliquem vnum esse in summum pontificem sublimandum.
units.tr: Pupil. Prompted by what you recited last, I thought I should ask whether, on this opinion, it is expedient for the community of the faithful to have the power of changing aristocratic government into a government like royal government, and the reverse. That is, they would have the power to appoint one supreme pontiff who presides over all the others, and also the power to appoint or elect several supreme pontiffs at once, who, holding equal power, would rule aristocratically together and preside over all the other faithful. They would be able to change one government into the other as they think fit, in the same way that nations rightly changed aristocratic government into royal, and the reverse. Master. On this there are various opinions. One, which holds that for some peoples at some times aristocratic government is better than royal, and at other times royal government excels, holds that it is expedient for the community of the faithful to have such power to change aristocratic government into the government of one supreme priest, and the reverse, according as the necessity and character of the time demand and require one government or the other. Pupil. This can be argued for in this way: just as human statutes are varied according to the variety of times, extra, de consanguinitate, reprehensibilem: so it is expedient that human governments be varied according to the variety of times. But the Church of Christ has power, chiefly over human governments, in all matters that are expedient for it. Therefore it has the power to vary such governments. Pupil. It could be said that the government by which the supreme priest rules all the faithful is not human but divine, since it was instituted by God alone. Therefore it is not fitting, and consequently not expedient, that the Church should have power even over the papal government. Master. This reply is open to challenge. For although the papal government is divine in that Christ ordained that it should exist in the Church, in many respects it appears to be human. For it belongs to men to decide who ought to be raised to it, who ought to elect, who ought to correct the one raised up if he needs correction, and similar matters. Therefore, in these respects too, it will be human that it should be decided by men whether one or several should be raised to such government, when it is expedient. Further, the community of the faithful has been very well provided for in all matters necessary for things that belong to Christians, and no less well is it provided that whatever community or people has power in all such matters, as far as is expedient and as it is expedient. But if the Church had the power to change a government, which had begun to be less expedient, into another government more expedient, it would be better provided for than if it had no such power. Therefore, since it is very well provided for in such matters, it has the power to change government by one into government by several, if it judges that rule by several in aristocratic government is more expedient than rule by one alone. Again, it is no less expedient for the community of the faithful to have the power to remove governments which have become burdensome or less useful, than to remove burdensome customs, since nothing can harm the Church more than a burdensome and useless government, according to the saying of Augustine, which is read in dist. 81. nemo, where he says: nemo quippe in Ecclesia amplius nocet, quam qui peruerse agens nomen vel ordinem sanctitatis & sacerdotis habet. From this it is gathered that nothing harms the Church more than a perverse prince and a perverse government. Wherefore, if the Church perceives that it is being governed perversely or less usefully by one alone, it is expedient that it have the power to change such government into another, which will for the time be more useful. Moreover, it is not right that the Church be bound to that government which can be changed into a worst government. But a government in which one alone rules can be changed into a worst government. Just as royal government, although it is the best, nevertheless by its very nature can be changed into tyranny, which is the worst government, as Aristotle asserts and clearly proves in Ethicis. Therefore it is not expedient for the Church to be so bound to the government in which one alone rules that it cannot change it into another government, namely an aristocratic one, which is more useful for the time. Furthermore, as even the civil law attests: in rebus nouis constituendis euidens debet esse utilitas, ut recedatur ab eo iure, quod diu aequum visum est. From this it is gathered that, because of evident usefulness, innovation is to be made, so that one may depart from a law that has long seemed fair. But one must not depart from law any more than from government, since in every community nothing ought to be preserved more than law, for what does not agree with law must in no way be preserved. Therefore, because of evident usefulness, innovation is to be made so that one departs from a government which has long appeared reasonable and fair. Wherefore, if it evidently appears to the Church, for some time, that greater usefulness comes to the Church from aristocratic government, in which several rule the community of the faithful together, than from the rule of one, such an innovation is to be made, that one departs from the rule of one, which has seemed fair and useful. Likewise, what has been introduced for the favour and advantage of some should not be turned to their loss and harm. But the government to which all the faithful ought to be subject was introduced for the favour and advantage of all the faithful. Therefore, if some form of government begins to be harmful to the faithful or less useful, it is expedient that that form of government be changed into another which is more useful for the time. Wherefore the Church has the power to establish aristocratic government over all the faithful, if they judge that government by one has begun to be harmful to the faithful. Further, according to Pope Leo, as is read in dist. 45. c. licet enim: Quod prouisum sit ad concordiam, tendere non debet ad noxam. From this it is concluded that whatever has been provided for harmony must be removed if it tends to harm. But the government of one supreme pontiff was provided for the harmony of all the faithful, namely that one should preside over the others, lest there be a schism, according to the Gloss on the same passage. Therefore, if the government of one supreme pontiff tends to harm, that is, to the desire of oppressing or of ruling tyrannically, or even to a dangerous schism among Christians, as for example if the greater and more powerful part of the Christians, or an equal part, in no way wishes to tolerate the government of one supreme pontiff, and yet wishes to tolerate the aristocratic government of many ruling together, each of whom is a supreme pontiff, just as at some times several emperors have existed together, and at other times in the same cause there are several judges with equal power, then government like royal government must be removed, at least for a time, and aristocratic government must be instituted, at least until the aforesaid evils or dangers and similar ones cease. Again, when the cause ceases, the effect ought to cease as well, extra, de appellationibus, cum cessante. But common usefulness is the cause why one supreme pontiff should preside over all the faithful. Therefore, if from the government of one there does not arise common usefulness but common loss, such a government ought then to cease. Therefore the community of the faithful then has the power to institute another government. Furthermore, in all churches it must be observed that what the greater part judges to be observed is to be observed, extra, de his que fiunt a maiori parte capituli. c. 1. & dist. 65. c. 1. & 2. & 3. extra, de electio. licet. Therefore, if the greater part of the faithful judges that aristocratic government should be instituted over the whole community of the faithful, then it has the power to institute another government, and such a government is to be instituted. From this it follows that the Church or the community of the faithful has the power to institute this kind of government. Pupil. As the Gloss on the cited chapter notes, extra, de his que fiunt a maiori parte capituli. One does not always stand by the greater part or by the majority, as here, and in dist. 21 Nicena, and above in de elect. Ecclesia vestra, and below. That is a royal rule, that one should always stand by the greater part. But the greater part is that which is supported by the greater piety and reason, dist. 9 sana quippe, & 60 dist. multi, at the end, 4 dist. 2 iurisiurandi. The Gloss on dist. 60 also seems to hold this on the last chapter, saying: non gradus elegantior, sed vita melioris actio comprobatur, 23 q. 4 sicut, & 10 q. 1 sunt nulli. For this is the argument: that the part which rests on the more just reason is called the greater, although it is the lesser, dist. 31 Nicena, 19 in canonicis, & 4 q. 3, & extra, de elect. in nostra. From these things it is clearly had that one does not always have to stand by the greater part. Wherefore, even if the greater part of the Christians judged that the government of one should be changed into aristocratic government, this would nevertheless not have to be done. Master. This reply is open to challenge. For although one does not always have to stand by the greater part, but sometimes by the lesser, nevertheless one must always stand by the greater part unless it is clearly proved by the lesser part that one ought not to stand by the greater part. This is gathered from the Gloss on the cited chapter De his que fiunt a maiori parte capituli, which says, after the words quoted above: praesumitur pro pluralitate. 61 dist. nullus: nisi in contrarium probetur, vt hic patet. & 23 dist. illud. & supra de elect. dudum. And on the same passage, on the word offensum, it says: non sufficit obiicere, nisi probetur. Since therefore it cannot be proved that one ought not to stand by the greater part, if for the common good it should wish to change the government of one supreme pontiff into an aristocratic government, it follows that in this one must stand by the greater part of the faithful. Pupil. It seems that it could reasonably be shown that in this one need not stand by the greater part of the Christians, if they decide to institute an aristocratic government over all the faithful. For the lesser part, in opposing the greater, would rest on the more just reason. For the lesser part would rest on the divine ordinance, which is worth more than every human ordinance. Master. It appears to some, even granting that Christ had ordained that one supreme pontiff should rule over all the faithful, that for the common good the Church can institute another government. This is proved in this way: necessity and usefulness are made equal, as Pope Alexander III seems to hint, extra, de aequalitate & aetate praeficienda, quaris. But for the sake of necessity it is lawful to act against a divine command, even one expressly given, in matters which are not evil in themselves but are only evil because they are forbidden. Therefore, for the sake of common usefulness too, it is lawful to act against the command of God and the ordinance of Christ. Therefore, even granting that Christ had ordained that one supreme pontiff should be set over all the faithful, it would be lawful for the faithful, for the sake of common usefulness, to institute another government, at least for a time. The major premise seems clearly proved, and it is also proved by the fact that necessity and piety are made equal, as Pope Gregory IX suggests, extra, de feriis, c. vltimo. But piety includes usefulness. Therefore necessity and usefulness are made equal, and consequently, if necessity makes a thing lawful, usefulness also makes it lawful. The minor premise is shown in many ways. For Bede, on Mark, and it is found extra, de Regulis Iuris, cap. quod non est, seems plainly to assert, saying: quod non est licitum in lege, necessitas licitum facit. Nam & Sabbatum custodiri praeceptum est: Machabei autem in Sabbato sine culpa pugnauerunt. From these words it clearly seems to follow that the Maccabees, out of necessity, lawfully acted against an express divine command. Christ himself also seems expressly to teach this in Matth. 12 & Luc. 6, saying that David and those who were with him lawfully ate the showbread against the divine command, since God had explicitly commanded that no one but the priest should eat the said loaves. From these and many other things it is gathered that the rule, namely Necessitas legem non habet, which is cited extra, de consuetudine, quanto: and that rule Necessitas legi non subiacet, extra, de obseruantia ieiuniorum, c. 2. and that rule Necessitas in legibus excipitur, extra de iureiurando, quaerelam, and similar ones, must be understood not only of human positive laws but also of divine positive laws, unless the contrary is provided in those same divine laws, so that necessity is not subject to divine positive law. It is otherwise with natural law and the law of God. With natural law, because necessity is subject to that law, and no necessity can excuse. Further, that such an ordinance of Christ would not stand in the way of the ordinance is shown in this way. For Christians under the new law have no less power to change the government of priests than those who were established under the old law had. But, notwithstanding God's command Exodi 29 about the appointment of one supreme pontiff, which is also found in the Decretals, dist. 21 §. 1, David afterwards appointed several supreme pontiffs, as is gathered from 1 Paral. p. cap. 44. Whence the Evangelist also seems to bear witness, Luc. 2, that in Christ's time there were several chief priests at once. Therefore Christians also have the power to appoint several supreme pontiffs, notwithstanding that Christ ordained that one alone should be raised up as supreme pontiff.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Vbi arguitur in contrarium, scilicet quod Ecclesia non habet potestatem taliter transmutandi principatus. Et hoc 7. rationibus, ad quas respondetur, ad primam c. 22. ad secundam c. 25. ad tertiam & sequentes c. 26.
units.tr: Here the contrary is argued, namely that the Church does not have the power to change principalities in this way. This is argued by seven reasons, to which answer is given: to the first in chapter 22, to the second in chapter 25, and to the third and those following in chapter 26.

units.la: Discipulus. Puto te adduxisse fortiora motiua pro opinione praefata. Ideo pro opinione contraria nitaris allegare. Magist. Quod Ecclesia non habeat potestatem transmutandi summum pontificium in Aristocraticum principatum vel quemcunq; alium, videtur posse probari. Nam teste Christo, Matth. 10. non est discipulus supra magistrum suum: nec seruus supra dominum suum. Omnes autem Christiani discipuli sunt & serui Christi. Christus autem ordinauit & voluit quod vnus esset summus pontifex & caput omnium Christianorum. Quod in facto ostendit, cum ordinauit solum beatum Petrum in summum sacerdotem. Vnde Anacletus Papa, qui fuit tempore Apostolorum, hoc testatur, vt habetur di. 21. c. in noua, dicens: In noua testamento post Christum a Petro sacerdotalis incipit ordo, quia ipsi primo pontificatus in Ecclesia datus est, dicente Domino ad eum: tu es Petrus &c. Ergo omnes Christiani non habent potestatem tollendi summum sacerdotium, & instituendi quemcunq; alium principatum. Amplius, nulli Christiani, nec maior pars nec minor, habent potestatem tollendi vnitatem Ecclesiæ. Quia quicunq; scindit Ecclesiam, est schismaticus reputandus. Nulli autem multitudini Christianorum quantumcunq; magnæ licet in Ecclesiam schisma inducere. Vnitas autem Ecclesiæ in hoc videtur consistere, vt habeat caput, quod sub Christo omnibus principetur, teste beato Cypriano, qui, vt habetur 24. q. 1. c. loquitur, ait: loquitur Dominus ad Petrum, Ego dico tibi, quod tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Super vnum aedificat Ecclesiam. Et quamuis Apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam, parem potestatem tribuat & dicat: sicut misit me pater & ego mitto vos, accipite Spiritum sanctum, cum & vnitatem manifestaret vnitatis eiusdem originem ab vno incipientem sua auctoritate dispositu. Hoc erant vtiq; cateri Apostoli, quod Petrus fuit, pari consortio praediti & honoris & potestatis: sed ab vnitate exordium proficiscitur, vt Ecclesia Christi vna monstretur. Et infra: quam vnitatem tenere firmiter & vendicare debemus (maxime nos Episcopi qui in Ecclesia Dei praesidemus) vt Episcopatum quoq; ipsum vnum atq; indiuisum probemus. Nemo fraternitatem fallat. Nemo veritatem fidei praeuaricatione perfida corrumpat. Episcopatus vnus est singularis. In solidum pars tenetur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod vnitas Ecclesiæ, quæ firmiter est tenenda, ab vno procedit, & vnum Episcopatum requirit. Ergo nulli multitudini Christianorum licet Episcopatum vnum in principatum Aristocraticum vel aliud transmutare.
units.tr: Disciple. I think you have brought forward stronger arguments for the opinion stated above. So now strive to allege arguments for the contrary opinion. Master. That the Church does not have the power to change the supreme pontificate into an aristocratic principality, or into any other kind, seems capable of proof. For Christ bears witness, Matt. 10: the disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord. But all Christians are disciples and servants of Christ. Christ, moreover, ordained and willed that there be one supreme pontiff and head of all Christians. He showed this in fact, when he appointed the blessed Peter alone as chief priest. Hence Pope Anacletus, who lived in the time of the Apostles, testifies to this, as is found in dist. 21, c. in novo, saying: In the New Testament after Christ, the priestly order began with Peter, because the pontificate in the Church was first given to him, the Lord saying to him: you are Peter, etc. Therefore all Christians do not have the power to abolish the supreme priesthood and to institute any other principality whatever. Further, no Christians, neither the greater part nor the lesser, have the power to destroy the unity of the Church, because whoever splits the Church is to be regarded as a schismatic. But no multitude of Christians, however great, may induce schism into the Church. The unity of the Church seems to consist in this, that it has a head who rules all under Christ, as the blessed Cyprian testifies, who, as is found in 24, q. 1, c. loquitur, says: The Lord speaks to Peter: I tell you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. He builds the Church upon one. And although after his resurrection he gave equal power to all the Apostles and said: As the Father sent me, so I send you; receive the Holy Spirit, yet he also made clear the unity and the origin of that unity, beginning from one, by his own authority. The other Apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with equal partnership of honour and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one. And below: This unity we must hold firmly and assert (we bishops especially, who preside in the Church of God), so that we may also prove the episcopate itself to be one and undivided. Let no one deceive the brotherhood. Let no one corrupt the truth of the faith by perfidious betrayal. The episcopate is one and single; the part is held in solidum. From these words it is gathered that the unity of the Church, which must be held firmly, proceeds from one and requires one episcopate. Therefore no multitude of Christians is permitted to change the one episcopate into an aristocratic principality or any other.

units.la: Rursus: sicut nulla est vel potest esse Ecclesia, nisi Apostolica: sic nullus est in Ecclesia, nec esse potest verus, licitus & principatus primus, scilicet Episcopatus seu pontificatus, nisi Apostolicus. Quod Pelagius allegans beatum Augustinum clare testari videtur, dicens 24. q. 1. c. pudenda: nullam aliam (scilicet Ecclesiam) esse constat, nisi quae in Apostolica radice est fundata: a quibus (scilicet Apostolis) ipsam fidem universo orbe propagatam esse non potest dubitari. Quod ut nobis licet notissimum sit, beati Augustini testimonio approbemus. Audi quid in quodam opere suo dicat praeclarissimus doctor Ecclesiae. Ait enim: Quod si nullo modo recte dici possit Ecclesia, in qua schisma est, restat ut quoniam Ecclesia nulla esse non potest, quam ea quae fit in Sedis Apostolicae per successiones Episcoporum radice constituta, nullorum hominum malitia (etiam sit nota excludi non possit, sed pro temporum ratione toleranda iudicetur) ullo modo valeat extinguere. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod in Ecclesia nullus est verus principatus, nisi qui per successionem Episcoporum est continuatus in Apostolica Sede. Sed si institueretur principatus Aristocraticus vel quicunque alius, ille non esset Apostolicus, nec in Sede Apostolica per successiones constitutus. Ergo non esset licitus reputandus. Praeterea Papa in Ecclesia Dei habet plenitudinem potestatis. Quod ergo Papa non potest, multo fortius nec aliqua multitudo Christianorum. Sed Papa non posset ordinare seu constituere, quod post decessum eius vel eo consentiente & volente alius principatus quam pontificatus summus esset in Ecclesia Dei. Cum omnes Christianos regi ab uno summo pontifice spectat ad generalem statum Ecclesiae, contra quem Papa dispensare non potest, ut testari videtur Glossa 25. q. 1. super capitulum, quae ad perpetuam. Ergo nec aliqua multitudo potest instituere alium principatum.
units.tr: Again: just as there is, or can be, no Church except the Apostolic one, so there is in the Church, and can be, no true, lawful, first principality, namely the episcopate or pontificate, except the Apostolic one. Pelagius, citing the blessed Augustine, seems to testify this clearly, saying in 24, q. 1, c. pudenda: "It is established that there is no other Church (namely) than that which is founded on the Apostolic root; and it cannot be doubted that the faith itself has been spread throughout the whole world by the Apostles." Although this is very well known to us, let us confirm it by the testimony of the blessed Augustine. Hear what that most distinguished teacher of the Church says in a certain work of his: "For if the Church in which there is schism cannot be rightly called a Church, it remains that, since there is no Church which is not the one founded on the root of the Apostolic See through the succession of bishops, no malice of men (which is known to exist, but which must be tolerated according to the reason of the times) can in any way extinguish it." From these words it is gathered that in the Church there is no true principality except that which has been continued in the Apostolic See through the succession of bishops. But if an aristocratic principality or any other were instituted, it would not be Apostolic, nor established in the Apostolic See through succession. Therefore it would not be considered lawful. Moreover, the Pope has the fullness of power in the Church of God. What the Pope cannot do, much less can any multitude of Christians. But the Pope could not ordain or establish that after his death, or with his consent and will, any principality other than the supreme pontificate should be in the Church of God. Since it pertains to the general state of the Church that all Christians be ruled by one supreme pontiff, against which the Pope cannot dispense, as the Gloss on 25, q. 1, on the chapter quae ad perpetuam, seems to testify. Therefore neither can any multitude institute another principality.

units.la: Adhuc, illud non potest aliqua multitudo Christianorum, per quod haereticam incurreret pravitatem. Sed si quaecunque multitudo instituret alium principatum, cui subderentur omnes Christiani, ipso facto haereticam pravitatem incurreret: quia privilegium Romanae Ecclesiae conaretur auferre. Qui autem, ut testatur Nicolaus Papa 22. q. 1. Romanae Ecclesiae privilegium ab ipso summo Ecclesiarum omnium capite auferre conatur, hic procul dubio in haeresim labitur. Ergo nulla multitudo Christianorum potest instituere principatum alium primum quam principatum Romanae Ecclesiae, qui in hoc consistit, ut unus pontifex summus omnibus Christianis principetur. Praeterea in uno Episcopatu non possunt esse duo Episcopi: nec in uno Archidiaconatu duo Archidiaconi 7. q. 1. In apibus, & sunt verba Hieronymi. Igitur multo fortius in Ecclesia Dei non possunt esse duo aut plures summi pontifices. Constat autem quod Ecclesia Dei non debet carere omni summo pontifice. Ergo Ecclesia non habet potestatem instituendi alium principatum principalem, quam summum pontificem unius qui omnibus aliis principetur. Amplius, non licet quibuscunque Christianis facere conditionem Ecclesiae deteriorem, quo ad temporalia: quamvis sit licitum meliorare ipsam. Extra, de donationibus, fraternitatem. extra de restitutione in integrum. c. 1. Ergo multo magis non licet quibuscunque habere conditionem Ecclesiae deteriorem quo ad spiritualia. Unum autem summum pontificem Christianis omnibus principari ad spiritualia spectat. Quia principatus huiusmodi spiritualis est dist. 10. suscipiite. Ergo non licet quibuscunque Christianis principatum huiusmodi in deteriorem vel minus bonum quemlibet transmutare. Principatus autem Aristocraticus, & quilibet alius est minus bonus quam principatus, quo unus solus principatur: cum talis principatus sit regalis vel similis regali. Ergo non licet quibuscunque Christianis principatum Aristocraticum vel aliud loco principatus unius summi pontificis instituere quoquo modo.
units.tr: Again, no multitude of Christians can do that by which it would incur heretical depravity. But if any multitude whatever were to institute another principality, to which all Christians would be subject, it would by that very act incur heretical depravity, because it would try to take away the privilege of the Roman Church. And whoever, as Pope Nicholas testifies in 22, q. 1, tries to take away the privilege of the Roman Church from the very supreme head of all the churches, undoubtedly falls into heresy. Therefore no multitude of Christians can institute any principal principality other than the principality of the Roman Church, which consists in this, that one supreme pontiff rules over all Christians. Moreover, in one episcopate there cannot be two bishops, nor in one archdeaconry two archdeacons, 7, q. 1, In apibus, and these are the words of Jerome. Therefore, much more strongly, in the Church of God there cannot be two or more supreme pontiffs. But it is certain that the Church of God ought not to lack a supreme pontiff. Therefore the Church does not have the power to institute any principal principality other than one supreme pontiff who rules over all the others. Further, it is not lawful for any Christians to make the condition of the Church worse in temporal matters, although it is lawful to improve it. Extra, de donationibus, fraternitatem; extra, de restitutione in integrum, c. 1. Therefore much more is it not lawful for any Christians to make the condition of the Church worse in spiritual matters. But that one supreme pontiff should rule over all Christians pertains to spiritual matters, because such a principality is spiritual, dist. 10, suscipiite. Therefore it is not lawful for any Christians to change such a principality into one that is worse or less good in any way. But an aristocratic principality, or any other principality in place of the rule of one, is less good than the principality in which one alone rules, since such a principality is royal or similar to royal. Therefore it is not lawful for any Christians to institute an aristocratic principality, or anything else in place of the principality of one supreme pontiff, in any way whatever.

units.la: CAP. XXII. In quo ostenditur, quomodo ad praecedentes rationes secundae opinionis respondet prima opinio.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII. In which it is shown how the first opinion answers the preceding arguments of the second opinion.

units.la: Discipulus. Propter apparentiam magnam, quam allegationes pro opinione utraque inductae habere videntur, cupio eas magis discutere, & audire quomodo secundum diversas opiniones respondetur ad ipsas. Unde primo refer, quomodo opinio prima ad allegationes ultimo adductas niti tur respondere. Mag. Ad primam, quae fundatur in hoc, quod omnes Christiani non possunt contra ordinationem Christi: respondetur per ea, quae conata sunt probare. c. 21. quod videl. necessitas, & utilitas faciunt licitum aliquod, quod alias tanquam ordinationi Christi contrarium esset illicitum. Et non obstante, quod omnes Christiani sint discipuli & servi Christi, & non sint supra ipsum: tamen ex necessitate vel utilitate possunt aliquid contra ordinationem eius, hoc est, contra verba & facta eius secundum quod prima facie sonare videntur: Non tamen contra intentionem (quia ipse vult, quod in verbis eius urgens necessitas & evidens utilitas sint exceptae, ubi aliquid ordinat vel facit) cuius contrarium legi naturali minime adversatur: & ipse non explicat quod necessitas & utilitas nullatenus recipi deberent.
units.tr: Disciple. Because the arguments brought forward for each opinion seem to have great plausibility, I want to examine them more closely and hear how each opinion answers them. So first tell me how the first opinion tries to answer the arguments last adduced. Master. To the first, which rests on the point that all Christians cannot act against the ordinance of Christ, the answer is given through what was attempted to be proved in chapter 21: namely, that necessity and utility make lawful something which otherwise would be unlawful as contrary to the ordinance of Christ. And although all Christians are disciples and servants of Christ and not above him, yet from necessity or utility they may do something against his ordinance, that is, against his words and deeds as they seem to sound at first sight. Yet they do not act against his intention, since he wills that in his words urgent necessity and evident utility be excepted wherever he gives an ordinance or does something. The contrary of this is in no way opposed to natural law, and he himself does not state that necessity and utility should in no way be admitted.

units.la: Quod aliter quam prius probare conatur. Na Christus praecipit Apostolis, ut habetur Mat. 5. non resistere malo. Sed qui percusserit eos in unam maxillam, praebeant & alteram. Et tamen Apostolo Paulo percusso licuit dicere principi sacerdotum: percutiat te Deus paries dealbate. Ubi testatur Augustinus in sermone de puero centurionis, & ponitur 23. q. 1. c. paratus. Quemadmodum igitur secundum Augustinum ibidem, precepta illa de patientia magis sunt ad praeparationem cordis, quam ad opus, quod in aperto fit, ut teneatur in secreto animi patientia cum benevolentia. In manifesto autem id fiat, quod eis videatur prodesse, quibus bene velle debemus. Sic circa ordinationem Christi de uno summo pontifice constituendo servandum est id, quod magis prodest Ecclesiae suae pro cuius utilitate ordinavit unum summum pontificem constituendum, ut scilicet quando expedit Ecclesiae quod sint plures, fiant plures, qui Aristocratice regant Ecclesiam. Haec responsio videtur taliter posse confirmari. Quia silicet facere contra verba præcepti magis expressi, cōtra verba præcepti minus expressi licebit facere. Sed præceptū Christi de patientia data Apostolis Matth. 5. magis expressum fuit, quam præceptum de vno summo pontifice constituendo post Petrum. Quia expresse dixit absq; omni modificatione & exceptione siue determinatione: ego autem dico vobis non resistere malo &c. Nusquam autem inueniri potest, quod dixerit; dico vobis quod constituatis summum pontificem post Petrum, vel consimilia verba. Ergo si contra verba expressa Christi de patientia licet venire, non contra mentem. Quemadmodum & ipsemet Christus fecit, vt testatur August. vbi prius, vbi dicit: Liquido ostenditur, quod ipse Dominus exemplum singulare patientiæ, cum percuteretur in faciem, respondit, si male locutus sum, exprobra de malo. Si autem bene, quid me caedis? Nequaquam igitur præceptum suum, si verba sua intueamur, impleuit. Neque enim percutienti præbuit alteram partem, sed potius prohibuit ne faceret. Multo magis contra verba Christi non expressa de vno summo pontifice constituendo liceret facere Christianis, vt scilicet non constituant vnum, sed plures summos pontifices, quando hoc expedit Ecclesiæ Christi.
units.tr: This is attempted to be proved in another way as well. Christ commands the Apostles, as is found in Matthew 5, not to resist evil, but whoever strikes them on one cheek, let them offer the other also. Yet when Paul was struck, it was permitted to him to say to the high priest: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall." Augustine bears witness to this in his sermon on the centurion's boy, and it is cited in Causa 23, question 1, chapter "Paratus." Therefore, just as according to Augustine in the same place, those precepts about patience are more about preparing the heart than about outward action, so that patience with goodwill is kept in the secret of the mind, while what is manifestly done is what seems to benefit those to whom we ought to wish well. In the same way, concerning Christ's ordinance on constituting one supreme pontiff, what must be observed is what benefits his Church most, for whose utility he ordained that one supreme pontiff be set up; namely, that when it is expedient for the Church that there be several, several shall be made who govern the Church aristocratically. This answer seems to be confirmed in this way: it is lawful to act against the words of a more explicit precept, so it will be lawful to act against the words of a less explicit precept. But Christ's precept on patience given to the Apostles in Matthew 5 was more explicit than the precept on constituting one supreme pontiff after Peter. For he said plainly, without any qualification, exception or determination: "But I say to you, do not resist evil," etc. Yet nowhere can it be found that he said: "I tell you that you shall appoint a supreme pontiff after Peter," or words like that. Therefore if it is lawful to come against the express words of Christ on patience, it is not against his mind. Christ himself did just this, as Augustine witnesses in the passage cited above, where he says: "It is clear that the Lord himself, a singular example of patience, when he was struck in the face, answered: 'If I have spoken evil, bear witness to the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?'" Therefore by no means did he fulfil his precept, if we look at his words. For he did not offer the other side to the one who struck him, but rather forbade him to do so. Much more, then, against the words of Christ not expressed about constituting one supreme pontiff, it would be lawful for Christians to act, so that they do not appoint one but several supreme pontiffs, whenever this is expedient for the Church of Christ.

units.la: Christus expressis verbis nullum casum excipiendo, præcepit non iurare, dicens Matth. 5. Ego autem dico vobis, non iurare omnino: neque per cælum &c. Et post: Sit autem sermo vester est, est, non, non. Quod hoc amplius est, à malo est. Et tamen non obstante isto præcepto Christi expresso, licet in casu iurare, extra, de electi. significasti. Et extra de iureiurando. Et si Christus 22. q. 1. non est: vbi asserit August. quod iurare licet propter infirmitatem vel incredulitatem eorum, qui non aliter ad fidem mouentur. Ergo multo magis non obstante, quod Christus fecerit Beatum Petrum summum pontificem & caput omnium Christianorum, licet Christianis propter communem vtilitatem totius Ecclesiæ plures simul constituere summos pontifices, si hoc aliquando expediat.
units.tr: Christ, expressly excepting no case, commanded not to swear, saying in Matthew 5: "But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, etc. And afterwards: Let your speech be, Yea, yea; No, no. Whatever is more than this is of evil." Yet, notwithstanding this express precept of Christ, it is lawful to swear in some cases; see Extra, De electione, "Significasti," and Extra, De iureiurando, and "Si Christus," 22 q. 1, "non est": where Augustine asserts that it is lawful to swear on account of the weakness or unbelief of those who are not otherwise moved to faith. Therefore, much more, although Christ made blessed Peter the supreme pontiff and head of all Christians, it is lawful for Christians, for the common utility of the whole Church, to set up several supreme pontiffs at once, if this should ever be expedient.

units.la: Rursus, Christus præcepit Apostolis Matth. 10. ne possiderent aurum vel argentum, aut pecuniam, & ne haberent duas tunicas vel portarent calciamenta. Et tamen manifesta necessitate cogente, licebat eis contra ista venire, implendo, scilicet mentem Christi non verba. Quod ipse satis insinuare videtur dicens Apostolis Lucæ 22. Quando misi vos sine sacculo & pera & calciamentis, numquid aliquid defuit vobis? At illi dixerunt, nihil: dixit eis: sed nunc qui habet sacculum tollat: similiter & peram: & qui non habet, vendat tunicam suam, & emat gladium. Ex quibus verbis Beda elicit quandam regulam generalem, quod scilicet non obstante præcepto Christi alia est regula viuendi tempore pacis, alia tempore persecutionis. Ex qua regula Bedæ potest quædam alia generalior colligi: quod propter necessitatem & vtilitatem licet venire contra ordinationem Christi.
units.tr: Again, Christ commanded the Apostles in Matthew 10 not to possess gold or silver or money, nor to have two tunics or carry sandals. Yet under manifest pressing necessity, it was permitted them to act against these, fulfilling, that is, the mind of Christ rather than the words. This he seems to hint sufficiently when he says to the Apostles in Luke 22: "When I sent you without purse, bag and sandals, did you lack anything? And they said: Nothing. He said to them: But now let him who has a purse take it, likewise a bag; and let him who has none sell his tunic and buy a sword." From these words Bede draws a certain general rule: namely, that notwithstanding Christ's precept, one rule of living applies in time of peace and another in time of persecution. From this rule of Bede a somewhat more general one can be gathered: that on account of necessity and utility it is lawful to act against the ordinance of Christ.

units.la: Si enim non obstante præcepto Christi, alia est regula viuendi tempore pacis, alia tempore persecutionis: ratione consimili non obstante præcepto Christi, alia est regula viuendi in casu necessitatis & vtilitatis, alia extra casum necessitatis & vtilitatis. Cum non nisi propter necessitatem & vtilitatem sit alia regula viuendi tempore pacis, alia tempore persecutionis. Si enim nulla apparet necessitas nec vtilitas propter persecutiones regula viuendi præsertim nullatenus est imitanda. Propter necessitatem igitur & vtilitatem licet non implere verba Christi. Igitur non obstante quacunq; ordinatione Christi de vno summo pontifice constituendo, licebit, si euidens vtilitas hoc exposcit, plures constituere summos pontifices, qui Aristocratice gubernent totam vniuersitatem fidelium. Amplius, licet ex causa differre electionem summi pontificis. Igitur licet pro tempore constituere alios, qui gubernent communitatem fidelium.
units.tr: For if, notwithstanding Christ's precept, one rule of living applies in time of peace and another in time of persecution, then by a similar reasoning, notwithstanding Christ's precept, one rule of living applies in a case of necessity and utility and another outside a case of necessity and utility; since the rule of living in time of peace differs from that in time of persecution only on account of necessity and utility. For if no necessity or utility appears on account of persecutions, that rule of living is especially not to be imitated at all. Therefore, on account of necessity and utility, it is lawful not to fulfil the words of Christ. Therefore, notwithstanding whatever ordinance of Christ concerning the constitution of one supreme pontiff, it will be lawful, if evident utility demands it, to appoint several supreme pontiffs who govern the whole body of the faithful aristocratically. Furthermore, it is lawful to defer the election of a supreme pontiff for a cause. Therefore it is lawful to appoint others for the time being, who govern the community of the faithful.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: In quo arguitur & probatur, quod non licet facere neq; contra verba, neq; contra intentionem præcipientis, & præsertim præcepti Diuini, tribus rationibus. Ad quas respondetur capitulo immediate se- quenti.
units.tr: In which it is argued and proved, by three reasons, that it is not lawful to act either against the words or against the intention of the one commanding, and especially of a divine precept. Answers to these are given in the immediately following chapter.

units.la: Discipulus. Allegationes præscriptæ, & aliquæ aliæ prius adductæ fundantur in hoc, quod licet venire contra verba Diuini præcepti & Christi, licet non contra mentem seu intentionem præcipientis. Quæ aliquam apparentiam habere videntur. Ideo contra fundamentum eorum obiiciam, vt tam fundamentum quam dictas allegationes & consimiles melius intelligam & aduertere valeam, an quid contineant veritatis. Videtur igitur, quod nullo modo licet venire contra verba Diuini præcepti seu Christi, nec propter necessitatem nec propter vtilitatem. Nam de similibus simile est iudicium habendum. Igitur eodem modo censendum est de quocunque præcepto Diuino, & de omnibus. Sed præceptum de matrimonio inter virum & vxorem non soluendo sic obligat, quod in nullo casu excepto casu expresso à Christo, scilicet fornicationis, vel propter quamcunq; necessitatem vel vtilitatem licet vxorem dimittere, vt testatur ipsemet Christus Matth. 5. & 19. & Marc. 10. ergo omne præceptum Diuinum sic obligat, quod in nullo casu, qui non sit expressus à Deo vel à Christo, propter necessitatem & vtilitatem liceret venire contra præceptum Diuinum. Alias propter necessitatem & vtilitatem liceret non baptizare, vel aliter baptizare quam institutum est à Christo, puta in vino vel alio aliquo liquore, si aqua haberi non possit, & baptismus differri non possit. Liceret etiam conficere corpus Christi de alio pane quam triticeo, quando panis triticeus haberi non possit. Liceret etiam, quando vinum haberi non posset, conficere sanguinem Christi de aqua vel alio liquore. Et sic omnia sacramenta mutare liceret propter necessitatem & vtilitatem. Rursus, nulli licet venire contra verba alicuius praecepti, nisi qui habet potestatem dispensandi circa tale praeceptum, vel interpretandi idem praeceptum. Sed nullus potest dispensare contra praecepta diuina, nec interpretari eadem praecepta. Ergo nulli licet venire contra verba praecepti diuini. Ex his concluditur, quod si Christus ordinauit vnum summum pontificem esse praeficiendum cunctis fidelibus, nullo modo licet Christianis quibuscunque plures simul constituere summos pontifices. Ista sunt, quae mihi videntur efficacius improbare assertionem praedictam. Ideo narra, quomodo respondetur ad ipsa. Et incipias ab ultimo: quia forte aliquae responsiones ad alia dependent ab illo.
units.tr: Disciple. The allegations set out above, and certain others adduced earlier, rest on this: that it is lawful to go against the words of a divine precept and of Christ, but not against the mind or intention of the one commanding. These seem to have some plausibility. I will therefore object against their foundation, so that I may better understand both the foundation and the said allegations and similar ones, and be able to see whether they contain any truth. It seems, then, that in no way is it lawful to go against the words of a divine precept or of Christ, neither on account of necessity nor on account of usefulness. For concerning like things a like judgment must be held. Therefore the same must be judged of any divine precept whatever, and of all of them. But the precept about not dissolving marriage between man and wife binds in such a way that, in no case except the case expressly stated by Christ, namely fornication, is it lawful to put away a wife on account of any necessity or usefulness, as Christ himself testifies in Matth. 5 and 19 and Mark 10. Therefore every divine precept binds in such a way that, in no case not expressly stated by God or by Christ, would it be lawful, on account of necessity or usefulness, to go against a divine precept. Otherwise, on account of necessity and usefulness, it would be lawful not to baptize, or to baptize otherwise than Christ has instituted, for instance in wine or some other liquid, if water cannot be had and baptism cannot be deferred. It would also be lawful to make the body of Christ from bread other than wheaten, when wheaten bread cannot be had. It would also be lawful, when wine cannot be had, to consecrate the blood of Christ from water or some other liquid. And so it would be lawful to change all the sacraments on account of necessity and usefulness. Again, it is lawful for no one to go against the words of any precept, except one who has the power of dispensing with that precept or of interpreting the same precept. But no one can dispense against divine precepts, nor interpret those same precepts. Therefore it is lawful for no one to go against the words of a divine precept. From these things it is concluded that, if Christ ordained that one supreme pontiff be set over all the faithful, in no way is it lawful for any Christians whatever to appoint several supreme pontiffs at once. These are the points which seem to me to refute the aforesaid assertion more effectively. Therefore tell how answers are given to them. And begin with the last, because perhaps some answers to the others depend on it.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: In quo de potestate interpretandi & dispensandi de praeceptis quasi praeambulis aliquibus notatur. Deinde respondetur ad rationes capituli precedentis: & primo ad tertium.
units.tr: In which some preliminary remarks are made on the power of interpreting and dispensing the precepts. Then the arguments of the preceding chapter are answered, first the third.

units.la: Magist. Obiectio illa mentionem facit de duobus, scil. potestate dispensandi circa praeceptum Dei siue Christi: & de potestate interpretandi praeceptum Dei siue Christi. Quantum ad primum dicitur, quod Christiani quicunque non habent potestatem dispensandi contra praeceptum diuinum seu Christi, nisi dispensatio, interpretatio siue iuris declaratio appelletur. Qualiter Gloss. 25. q. 1. super c. sunt quidem, loqui videtur dicens, quod Papa dispensat in euangelio, interpretando ipsum. Cui concordare videtur assertio quorundam Iuristarum dicentium: dispensatio dicitur declaratio siue commutatio. Sic potest dispensare scil. Papa de voto & de his quae sunt de iure diuino & naturali: dummodo subsit necessitas vel vtilitas & compensabilitas. De potestate autem interpretandi praeceptum Dei siue Christi, & per consequens dispensandi praedicto modo quid dicendum sit secundum quandam opinionem ex prolixa nostra disputatione De potestate interpretandi dicta & statuta aliorum prima parte nostri Dialogi lib. 6. potest aduertere studiosus. De qua pauca recitabo, nonnulla addendo. Dicitur itaque, quod non est necessaria interpretatio alicuius dicti, praecepti, seu statuti diuini vel humani, nisi propter ignorantiam alicuius, cui necessaria est interpretatio: quia vbi verba non sunt ambigua, non est locus interpretationi, vt notat Glossa; extra de consuetudine super cap. cum dilectus. Ad illum igitur interpretatio pertinet, qui scit intellectum illius, quod interpretandum est, quando scil. aliquis alius dubitat de vero intellectu eius. Multi autem periti sciunt verum intellectum praeceptorum Dei & Christi. Et ideo praecepta illa possunt interpretari illis qui nesciunt: quia huiusmodi interpretatio non est nisi expositio vel declaratio, seu manifestatio veri intellectus praeceptorum Dei. Et ita Christiani habent potestatem interdum interpretandi praeceptum diuinum, quando scil. sciunt verum intellectum illius. Si autem nesciretur verus intellectus alicuius praecepti Dei, quia nesciretur intentio Dei in praecipiendo, nec per rationem nec per scripturas alias, sed solum modo per revelationem Dei posset sciri. Sicut secundum quosdam verus intellectus literalis multarum prophetiarum, quae ponuntur in libro Apocal. & aliis scripturis propheticis, non potest sciri, nisi per revelationem nouam: tunc interpretatio talis praecepti expectanda est a solo Deo. Sed intellectus praeceptorum siue ordinationum Dei de patientia conseruanda, iuramento non praestando, de non portando sacculo siue pera, & de summo pontifice constituendo, & multorum aliorum, & scitur a pluribus Christianis & sciri potest per rationem & scripturas. Ideo interpretari possunt Christiani periti talia praecepta, siue ordinationes, & secundum veram interpretationem ipsa seruare debent. Nec est semper inhaerendum verbis etiam Christi, sed menti, secundum Gloss. 43. q. 1. super c. paratum, quae ibidem specialiter loquitur de verbis Christi. Discip. Secundum ista non magis liceret Papae interpretari verba Dei & Christi, quam alteri sapienti & in sacris litteris erudito: nec plus esset credendum Papae in huiusmodi quam alteri sapienti. Magist. Respondetur, quod non aliter licet Papae interpretari verba Dei vel Christi quam alteri; nec magis est credendum sibi in huiusmodi quam alteri sapienti.
