Imo in huiusmodi sunt magis periti quam Papa, ipsi Papae praeferendi, vt habetur dist. 20. §. 1. Vbi habetur, quod diuinarum scripturarum tractatores in sacrarum scripturarum expositionibus summis pontificibus praeferuntur. Verumtamen si interpretatio seu expositio Papae fuerit catholica nullam habens errorem, est quodammodo magis authentica quam interpretatio alterius eruditi. Quia exinde nulli licebit publice contrarium opinari & tenere scienter. Quod non est verum de eadem interpretatione, si esset solummodo alterius eruditi. Quia si non esset de aliquo, quod quis teneretur explicite credere, liceret alii non obstante huiusmodi interpretatione publice opinando tenere contrarium, licet non pertinaciter. Si autem interpretatio Papae esset erronea & non consona veritati, liceret cuilibet scienti eam non esse consonam veritati manifeste & publice reprobare. Et quilibet hoc sciens pro loco & tempore de necessitate salutis ipsam impugnare deberet. Discip. Secundum ista Papa nullo modo posset dispensare contra Apostolum aut scripturam sacram. Cuius contrarium videtur Gloss. 25. quest. 1. super c. sunt quidem, dicens: Sustinuit potest quod Papa contra Apostolum dispensat: non tamen in his quae pertinent ad articulos fidei. Magist. Dicitur, quod Glossa accipit ibi dispensare pro interpretari, siue declarare intellectum Apostoli; quod Papa potest. Discip. Isto modo potest dispensare in his, quae pertinent ad articulos fidei: quod tamen negat Glossa. Potest enim declarare verum intellectum illorum, quae pertinent ad articulos fidei, sicut & aliorum. Magist. Respondetur, quod articulos fidei, qui ponuntur in Symbolo, de quibus loquitur Gloss. non potest aliter interpretari, quam interpretati sunt. Quia quoad sensum litteralem sufficienter interpretati sunt & declarati. Sed multorum aliorum articulos, qui inveniuntur in Scripturis sacris, potest Papa, si est peritus, nova interpretatione interpretari. Quia in speciali non inveniuntur taliter interpretati a prioribus, quin pro multis simplicibus, imo peritis, nova & explicita interpretatione indigeant, quam multi etiam literati ex omnibus scripturis summorum pontificum & tractatorum diuinarum scripturarum colligere nescirent. Nec est nec fuit aliquis summorum pontificum aut Doctorum ita peritus, quin potuit aut posset continue & semper in intelligentia scripturae diuinae proficere, etiam si viueret mille annis aut pluribus, inveniendo nouiter sensus catholicos literales, qui sunt aliorum sensuum fundamenta studendo in scripturis sacris. Et hoc propter difficultatem intelligendi scripturam sacram in diuersis locis. Discip. Satis dixisti de ista obiectione. Nunc narra, qualiter respondetur ad primam obiectionem, quam adduxisti in c. praecedenti. Magist. Ad illam allegationem dicitur, quod de similibus simile iudicium est habendum, quando non prohibetur nec explicite nec implicite simile haberi iudicium. Vbi autem prohibetur explicite vel implicite de similibus simile habere iudicium, ibi non est habendum simile iudicium de similibus. Abraham enim ex quo recepit mandatum de filio immolando, tenebatur parare se ad filium suum occidendum innocentem: & tamen ne occideret alios innocentes, de huit sibi cauere. Quia simpliciter erat sibi praeceptum, ut immolaret filium suum, & non alios. Et ideo alium intellectum non potuit elicere ex verbis praecepti, nisi quem primo sonabant. Et ita erant expressa omni ambiguitate carentia, quod non erat ibi locus interpretationi; nec aliquem alium intellectum potuit elicere. Ex quibus verbis Dei nec etiam per rationem potuit alium elicere intellectum, cum non ignoraverit Deum esse Dominum vitae & mortis. Quamuis ergo esset simile de praecepto Dei super matrimonio non soluendo, siue super vxore non dimittenda, & quocunq; alio praecepto Dei: tamen non est nec esset simile iudicium quo ad omnia habendum de praecepto praedicto & quocunq; alio praecepto Dei. Quia Christus excipiendo vnum casum specialem, in quo liceat dimittere vxorem, alios casus prohibuit. Quia quod de vno conceditur, de aliis negatur. dist. 25. c. qualis 15. q. 3. de crimine 45. dist. c. disciplina 1. q. 1. per Esaiam. Quae regulae tenent, vbi tenet argumentum a contrario aigumento, quod fortissimum est in iure, vt leges dicunt. In multis autem aliis praeceptis Dei & Christi speciales casus non excipiuntur explicite. Ideo in eis non plus est intelligendus vnus excipi quam alius. Quare ex aliis locis scripturae diuinae colligendum est, an aliquis casus debeat intelligi, licet non exprimatur: & an sit eadem ratio excipiendi talem casum in vno praecepto & in alio: & an praecepta sint consimilia quantum ad genus praeceptorum, puta an praecepta naturalia vel positiua, an aliquid naturale & aliquid positiuum. Si enim sint simpliciter praecepta iuris naturalis, nullus casus excipi debet, propter quamcunq; necessitatem vel vtilitatem, nisi Deus specialiter aliquem exciperet. Quemadmodum non obstante praecepto iuris meri naturalis de nullo innocente scienter interficiendo Deus praecipiendo Abrahae, vt immolaret filium suum, specialem exceptionem fecit. Si autem sint praecepta mere positiua, casus necessitatis & vtilitatis ita debet excipi in vno, sicut in alio, nisi ex scripturis specialiter colligi possit; quod in aliquo tali praecepto non est excipiendus casus necessitatis & vtilitatis. Et ita de praeceptis similibus simile potest haberi iudicium. Ad sequentem allegationem respondetur, quod non sequitur ex praedictis, quod liceat omnia sacramenta mutare. Quia aliud est praeceptum mutare, & aliud praeceptum omittere. Et similiter aliud est sacramenta mutare, & sacramenta omittere. Et ideo quamuis nonnunquam liceat aliqua sacramenta omittere, non licet tamen illa mutare. Propter quod nulli licet baptisare in vino vel in alio liquore, quam in aqua: nec licet conficere corpus Christi in pane triticeo & in vino. In casu tamen propter necessitatem vel vtilitatem licet omittere aliqua sacramenta.
units.tr: Master: That objection concerns two things, namely the power of dispensing with a precept of God or of Christ, and the power of interpreting a precept of God or of Christ. As to the first, I say that Christians in general do not have the power to dispense against a divine or Christ's precept, unless what is called dispensation is really interpretation or a declaration of law. The gloss on Gratian, Dist. 25, qu. 1, on the chapter Sunt quidem, seems to speak in this way, saying that the Pope dispenses in the gospel by interpreting it. The view of certain jurists agrees with this, who say: dispensation is called a declaration or a change. So the Pope can dispense concerning a vow, and concerning those things which are of divine and natural law, provided there is necessity or usefulness and the matter admits of compensation. As for the power of interpreting a precept of God or of Christ, and consequently of dispensing in the aforesaid way, what must be said about it according to a certain opinion, the diligent reader may learn from our lengthy discussion On the power of interpreting the sayings and statutes of others, in the first part of our Dialogue, book 6. I shall recite a few points from it here, adding some things. So I say that the interpretation of any saying, precept or statute, divine or human, is not necessary, except because of someone's ignorance, for whom interpretation is needed. For where the words are not ambiguous there is no room for interpretation, as the Gloss notes, Extra, On custom, on the chapter Cum dilectus. Interpretation therefore belongs to the one who knows the meaning of what is to be interpreted, namely when someone else doubts its true sense. Many learned people do know the true sense of the precepts of God and of Christ. And so those precepts can be interpreted for those who do not know them, because such interpretation is nothing but an explanation, declaration or manifestation of the true sense of God's precepts. Thus Christians sometimes have the power to interpret a divine precept, namely when they know its true sense. But if the true sense of some precept of God were unknown, because God's intention in commanding were unknown, and it could be known neither by reason nor by other Scriptures, but only by a revelation from God, then the interpretation of such a precept would have to be awaited from God alone. For example, according to some, the true literal sense of many prophecies found in the book of the Apocalypse and in other prophetic Scriptures cannot be known except by a new revelation; in that case the interpretation of such a precept must be awaited from God alone. But the sense of the precepts or ordinances of God concerning the preservation of patience, not swearing an oath, not carrying a purse or a bag, and the appointment of a supreme pontiff, and of many others, is known to many Christians and can be known by reason and Scripture. Therefore skilled Christians can interpret such precepts or ordinances, and they ought to observe them according to the true interpretation. Nor must one always cling to the words, even of Christ, but to the meaning, according to the Gloss on Gratian, Dist. 43, qu. 1, on the chapter Paratum, which speaks of the words of Christ in particular. Disciple: According to these views the Pope would have no greater right to interpret the words of God and of Christ than any other wise man learned in the sacred letters, nor would more credence be due to the Pope in such matters than to another wise man. Master: I answer that the Pope may interpret the words of God or of Christ no differently than anyone else, nor is he to be believed more than another wise man in such matters. Indeed, in such matters there are others more skilled than the Pope, who are to be preferred to him, as is found in Dist. 20, §1, where it is stated that the expounders of the divine Scriptures are to be preferred to the supreme pontiffs in the exposition of the sacred Scriptures. Nevertheless, if the interpretation or exposition of the Pope is Catholic and contains no error, it is in some sense more authoritative than the interpretation of another learned man. For thereafter no one will be allowed publicly to hold and knowingly to maintain the contrary opinion. This is not true of the same interpretation if it were only that of another learned man. For if it were not a matter that one is bound explicitly to believe, others would be allowed, notwithstanding such an interpretation, to hold publicly the contrary opinion, though not obstinately. But if the interpretation of the Pope were erroneous and not consonant with the truth, anyone who knew it not to be consonant with the truth would be permitted to reject it openly and publicly. And anyone who knew this ought, according to place and time, of necessity for salvation, to attack it. Disciple: According to these views the Pope could in no way dispense against the Apostle or against sacred Scripture. Yet the gloss on Gratian, Dist. 25, qu. 1, on the chapter Sunt quidem, seems to say the opposite, saying: It can be sustained that the Pope dispenses against the Apostle, but not in those things which pertain to the articles of faith. Master: It is said that the Gloss there takes to dispense to mean to interpret, or to declare the meaning of the Apostle, which the Pope can do. Disciple: In this way he could dispense in those things which pertain to the articles of faith, which nevertheless the Gloss denies. For he can declare the true meaning of those things which pertain to the articles of faith, just as of others. Master: I answer that the articles of faith which are set down in the Creed, of which the Gloss speaks, cannot be interpreted otherwise than they have been interpreted. For as to their literal sense they have been sufficiently interpreted and declared. But the articles of many others which are found in the sacred Scriptures, the Pope, if he is skilled, can interpret by a new interpretation. For these are not found to have been so interpreted by earlier writers in particular that many simple people, and indeed skilled ones, do not need a new and explicit interpretation, which many even of the learned could not gather from all the writings of the supreme pontiffs and the expounders of the divine Scriptures. Nor is or was there any supreme pontiff or teacher so skilled that he could not, or cannot, continually and always make progress in understanding the divine Scripture, even if he lived a thousand years or more, by discovering anew the catholic literal senses, which are the foundations of the other senses, by studying in the sacred Scriptures. And this is because of the difficulty of understanding the sacred Scripture in its various passages. Disciple: You have said enough about that objection. Now tell me how you answer the first objection, which you adduced in the preceding chapter. Master: To that argument it is said that like must be judged by like where it is not prohibited, either explicitly or implicitly, that like be judged alike. But where it is explicitly or implicitly prohibited that like be judged alike concerning like, there like must not be judged alike. For Abraham, once he had received the command concerning the sacrifice of his son, was bound to prepare himself to kill his innocent son; yet he took care not to kill other innocent people in this matter. For the command given to him was simply that he should sacrifice his son, and not others. And so he could not draw any other meaning from the words of the precept than the one they first sounded. And so they were expressed in such a way as to be free of all ambiguity, so that there was no room for interpretation, and he could draw no other meaning from them. Nor could he, from these words of God, draw any other meaning by reasoning, since he did not fail to know that God is the Lord of life and death. Therefore, although a precept of God concerning the non-dissolution of marriage, or concerning not dismissing one's wife, or any other precept of God, may be like, it is not and would not be a like judgment in every respect concerning the aforesaid precept and any other precept of God. For Christ, by excepting one special case in which it is permitted to dismiss a wife, prohibited the other cases. For what is granted of one is denied of the others. Dist. 25; c. Qualis; 15 qu. 3; De crimine; 45 dist., c. Disciplina; 1 qu. 1; per Isaiam. These rules hold where the argument from the contrary holds, which is the strongest in law, as the laws say. But in many other precepts of God and Christ no special cases are explicitly excepted. Therefore in them one exception is not to be understood any more than another. Hence from other passages of divine Scripture it must be gathered whether some case ought to be understood, although it is not expressed, and whether there is the same reason for excepting such a case in one precept as in another, and whether the precepts are alike as to their kind, for instance whether they are natural or positive precepts, or whether some are natural and some positive. For if they are simply precepts of natural law, no case ought to be excepted on account of any necessity or usefulness, unless God himself should specially except some case. Thus, notwithstanding the precept of purely natural law not knowingly to kill any innocent person, God, in commanding Abraham to sacrifice his son, made a special exception. But if the precepts are merely positive, a case of necessity or usefulness ought to be excepted in one just as in another, unless it can be specifically gathered from the Scriptures that in some such precept no case of necessity or usefulness is to be excepted. And so concerning like precepts one may form a like judgment. To the following argument I answer that it does not follow from what has been said that it is lawful to change all the sacraments. For it is one thing to change a precept, and another thing to omit it. Likewise it is one thing to change the sacraments, and another thing to omit the sacraments. And therefore, although it is sometimes lawful to omit some sacraments, it is not lawful to change them. For this reason it is lawful for no one to baptize in wine or in any liquid other than water, nor is it lawful to consecrate the body of Christ in wheaten bread and in wine. Yet in a case of necessity or usefulness it is lawful to omit some sacraments.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Vbi probatur, quod pluralitas summorum pontificum non scindit ecclesiae vnitatem, & hoc per responsionem ad secundam rationem c. 21. factam.
units.tr: Where it is proved that a plurality of supreme pontiffs does not break the unity of the Church, and this by answering the second argument made in chapter 21.

units.la: NVnc expone quomodo sustinetur, quod licet Christianis propter vtilitatem vel necessitatem constituere plures summos pontifices: non obstante quod non liceat eis scindere vnitatem ecclesiae, quae consistit in hoc quod vnum caput sub Christo omnibus principetur, in quo fundabatur secunda allegatio superius inducta cap. 21. Magist. Respondetur, quod nullis Christianis licet scindere vnitatem ecclesiae. Sed absq; vnitate summi pontificis potest vnitas ecclesiae perdurare. Vacante enim apostolica sede manet vnitas ecclesiae. Et ita non existente summo pontifice potest vnitas ecclesiae permanere. Nec scissa est ecclesia propter hoc, quod nullum habet summum pontificem. Alioquin saepe scinderetur ecclesia, cum saepe nullus sit summus pontifex. Et ita omni schismate caret ecclesia absque vno summo pontifice. Et per consequens ex hoc, quod essent plures res summi pontifices simul regentes ecclesiam non posset inferri, quod scissa esset ecclesia. Ad auctoritatem autem beati Cypriani respondetur, quod loquitur in casu, in quo plures discordes gerent se taliter pro summo pontifice, quod quilibet eorum diceret apud se solum esse pontificatum & ecclesiam. Quemadmodum accidit tempore beati Cypriani, de Cornelio & Novatiano: propter quorum discordiam dixit Cyprianus verba praescripta, sciens quod Cornelius erat verus summus pontifex & non Novatianus.
units.tr: Now explain how it is maintained that, although it is lawful for Christians, for the sake of usefulness or necessity, to appoint several supreme pontiffs, it is nonetheless not lawful for them to break the unity of the Church, which consists in this, that one head under Christ rules over all. On this the second argument introduced above was based, in chapter 21 of the Master. The answer is that it is lawful for no Christians to break the unity of the Church. But the unity of the Church can continue without a single supreme pontiff. For when the apostolic see is vacant, the unity of the Church remains. And so, when there is no supreme pontiff, the unity of the Church can remain. Nor is the Church split because it has no supreme pontiff. Otherwise the Church would often be split, since there is often no supreme pontiff. And so the Church is free of all schism without one supreme pontiff. Consequently, from the fact that several supreme pontiffs ruling the Church at the same time would be present, it cannot be inferred that the Church would be split. As for the authority of the blessed Cyprian, it is answered that he speaks in a case where several who disagree so conduct themselves as supreme pontiff that each of them would say to himself that he alone holds the pontificate and the Church. This happened in the time of blessed Cyprian, with Cornelius and Novatian. On account of their discord Cyprian spoke the words quoted above, knowing that Cornelius was the true supreme pontiff and not Novatian.

units.la: Si autem propter necessitatem vel utilitatem absque discordia de consensu fidelium plures simul haberentur in Apostolica sede & concorditer regerent ecclesiam Dei, ex pluralitate huiusmodi summorum pontificum nullum periculum schismatis sequeretur, quia nec inter ipsos summos pontifices, nec inter eis subiectos aliqua esset scissura. Quemadmodum si in eodem episcopatu essent plures episcopi se mutuo adiuvantes, nulla propter hoc in eodem episcopatu esset scissura. Et ex isto sumitur argumentum ad probandum, quod absque omni schismate & divisione unitatis ecclesiae possent propter necessitatem vel utilitatem esse simul plures summi pontifices. Nam idem iuris est in parte, quod in toto: & in paruis, quod in magnis. Sed in eodem episcopatu possunt simul esse duo episcopi 7. q. 1. c. non est autem & c. petisti & c. quia vero. Ergo consimiliter propter necessitatem vel utilitatem possent esse simul plures summi pontifices. Et quamvis nunquam fuit factum, tamen fieri posset. Quemadmodum licet ante tempora Augusti nec post legitur, quod episcopo existente incolumi, alius fuerit in eodem episcopatu episcopus ordinatus. Et tamen de beato Augustino hoc legitur factum. Nam 6. q. 1. c. non autem, sic habetur: Non autem hoc tantum scripsimus gratulandum, quod Augustinus episcopatum acceperit, sed quod Dei gratia hanc curam meruerit Africana ecclesia, ut verba caelestia Augustini oriri perciperet: qui ad maiorem dominici muneris gratiam novo more provectus & consecratus est, ut non succederet in cathedra episcopus, sed accedens ecclesiam incolumi Valeriano Iponensis ecclesiae episcopo coepiscopus Augustus factus est. Si igitur propter utilitatem ecclesiae Iponensis plures fuerunt simul in Iponensi ecclesia episcopi, multo magis propter utilitatem universalis ecclesiae plures esse possunt Apostolici simul.
units.tr: If, however, on account of necessity or usefulness, and without discord and with the consent of the faithful, several were held at once in the apostolic see and jointly ruled the Church of God, no danger of schism would follow from such a plurality of supreme pontiffs, because there would be no division either among the supreme pontiffs themselves or among those subject to them. Just as, if in the same bishopric there were several bishops helping one another, no division would arise in that bishopric on that account. From this an argument is drawn to prove that, without any schism or division of the unity of the Church, several supreme pontiffs could for the sake of necessity or usefulness be present at once. For the law of the part is the same as the law of the whole, and the law of small things the same as that of great things. But in the same bishopric two bishops can be present at once (7 q. 1 c. non est autem; c. petisti; c. quia vero). Therefore, similarly, for the sake of necessity or usefulness several supreme pontiffs could be present at once. And although it has never been done, it could nevertheless be done. Thus, although we do not read that before the time of Augustine, or after it, while one bishop was alive another was ordained in the same bishopric, it is read that this happened in the case of the blessed Augustine. For 6 q. 1 c. non autem reads thus: We have written not only that Augustine received the bishopric as a cause for rejoicing, but that by the grace of God the African Church merited this care, so that it would perceive the heavenly words of Augustine arising; he, advanced and consecrated in a new manner for the greater grace of the Lord's gift, did not succeed to the chair of a bishop, but, coming to the Church while Valerian, bishop of the Church of Hippo, was still living, was made co-bishop Augustine. If therefore, for the usefulness of the Church of Hippo, several bishops were at once in the Church of Hippo, much more, for the usefulness of the universal Church, several supreme pontiffs can be at once.

units.la: Discip. Contra hoc est Glossa super eodem c. non autem, quae dicit in haec verba: nunquid eodem modo possent esse plures Apostolici? argumentum quod non, supra c. factum dicens. Et Dominus tantum unum constituit 24. q. 1. loquitur & c. quicumque. Contra quod non potest dispensari 25. q. 1. sunt quidam. Praeterea, quia una sit catholica ecclesia & unum caput, tamen plures imperatores fuisse legimus, sed hic non est ita: quia offenderetur illa regula, scil. Unam sanctam ecclesiam. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod articulo fidei obviat, plures esse Apostolicos simul, illi videlicet articulo, Unam sanctam ecclesiam catholicam. Magist. Respondetur, quod Glossa ibi non loquitur assertive, sed solummodo allegando. Unde dicit, argumentum quod non. Et ideo non determinat partem illam, sed tantummodo argumentatur pro ipsa. Quae argumenta concludunt, quod non possunt esse duo Apostolici contrarii & discordes, quorum uterque vel alter dicat & affirmat se solum esse Apostolicum, & non alium, vel quorum alter non sit legitime Apostolicus constitutus. In quo casu legitur illud capitulum allegatum factum: quia loquitur de Cornelio & Novatiano, quorum Cornelius rite & legitime fuit electus, sicut idem capitulum asserit & testatur. Novatianus autem non propter necessitatem vel utilitatem ecclesiae, sed per ambitionem cum scandalo & divisione ecclesiae gradum Apostolicum usurpavit, testante sequenti c in quo sic habetur: Novatianus episcopus non est, qui Cornelio episcopo in ecclesia a 26. episcopi factus adulter & extraneus episcopus fieri a desertoribus per ambitum nititur. De quo in lib. 6. Ecclesiasticae historiae c. 35 sic habetur: Novatianus ecclesiae Romanae presbyter elatione quadam tumidus spem penitus eis salutis adimebat, etiam si digne poenituissent: ex quo & princeps haeresis extitit Novatianorum, qui ab ecclesia separati super bono nomine seipsos Cathaxos, id est mundos, appellabant. Oh quam rem concilium sacerdotale celeberrimum in urbe Romana congregatum est, episcoporum quidem 60. presbyterorum autem tot idem cum diaconis plurimis. Praeterea etiam per singulas quasque pronuncias de hac re magna deliberatione habita decretis signatur, quid facto opus sit, certamen initur. Igitur Novatum quidem cum hu qui eum mentis elatione tumidum sequerentur, quia ad humanam istam & nihil fraternae charitatis sententiam servantem declinarent, alienum etiam ab ecclesia. Et ita extat etiam & alia epistola Cornelii ad Fabianum Antiochiae episcopum scripta, edocens singula quaeque de Novato, quis qualisque fuerit vel vita vel moribus, & quomodo ab ecclesia declinaverit. In qua refert, quod episcopatus cupiditate, quam intra latenter gerebat, in haec omnia mala deciderit. Et infra: Sydonius & Cornelius qui valde clari in confessoribus habebantur, eo quod circa tormentorum genera superduerant. Sed isti, inquit, cum diligentius perspexissent agere eum (scilicet Novatum) cuncta fraudibus & dolo, mendaciis atque periuriis, & quia bonitatem adhuc solum simularet, ut deciperet ignorantes, relicto eo vel potius consecrato ad ecclesiam cum magna festinatione reuerti sunt, & praesentibus presbyteris & episcopis scilicet & laicis. Primo quidem errorem suum. tunc deinde & illius fraudis ac fallacias confitentur. Addidit praeterea & hoc in hac epistola: quod cum semper fratribus unitate solitus erat episcopatum se omnino non capere, subito & ex improviso velut novum plasma episcopus apparuit, scilicet qui disciplinam & instituta ecclesiastica vendicabat, episcopatum, quem non a Deo acceperat praesumebat. Tribus nanque episcopis simplicibus hominibus & omnium ignaris de remota Italiae parte adhibitis, imo potius subtili ab eo circumventione deceptis, imaginariam magis quam legitimam ab eis extorquere mutuas impositiones. Et infra: addidit autem & hoc, quod idem ipse Novatus in iuuentute spiritu immundo vexatus sit. Et cum tempus aliquantulum consumpsisset apud exorcistas, aegritudine incurreret grauem, it a vt desperaretur, & quod iacens in lecto pro necessitate confusus fit, nec aliqua in eo, quae baptismum sequi solent, solenniter adimpleta sint, nec signaculo crismatis consummatus sit. Vnde nec sp rtum sanctum vnquam potuit promereri. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Nouatus & summo episcopatu erat indignus, & non legitime sacerdotium vsurpauit, ac multis fraudibus & fallaciis vtebatur. Quare ecclesiam scindebat. Sed si dignus existens de consensu vnanimi catholicorum fuisset assumptus, non fuisset propter hoc scissa ecclesia, nec apostolicorum pluralitas concorditer gubernantium ecclesiam vnitati ecclesiae repugnat. Quemadmodum episcoporum pluralitas non obuiat vnitati episcopatus, nec pluralitas principantium aristocratice in ciuitate, ciuitas destruit vnitatem. Nec propter hoc offenderetur ille articulus fidei Vnam sanctam ecclesiam: quia propter pluralitatem apostolicorum propter necessitatem vel vtilitatem de vnanimi consensu fidelium assumptorum non fierent plures ecclesiae, sed remaneret vna propter vnitatem fidei & concordiam Apostolicorum eadem mente vnoq; consilio caeteris principantium orthodoxis. Cum igitur dicit Cyprian. vt allegatum est, quod ab vnitate exeunt proficiscitur, vt ecclesia Christi vna monstraretur. Respondetur, quod quando necessitas aut vtilitas non requirit pluralitatem apostolicorum, in quo casu loquebatur Cyprian. vnus debet esse apostolicus, vt ecclesia Christi non solum per vnitatem fidei, baptismi & caeterorum, quae enumerat Apostolus ad Ephes. 4. sed etiam per vnitatem apostoli, in quem vnanimiter consentiunt catholici, monstrantur vna. Quando autem necessitas vel vtilitas Apostolicos plures exposcit, sufficit quod ecclesia sit vna per vnitatem illorum, quae enumerat Apostolus ad Ephes. 4. per quorum vnitatem est vna, quando vacante Apostolica sede nec vni nec pluribus Apostolicis subditur ecclesia, inter quae vnum Apostolicum minime ponit cum de vnitate ecclesiae loquitur, dicens: Solliciti seruare vnitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis, vnum corpus & vnus spiritus, sicut vocati estis in vna spe vocationis vestrae: vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma, vnus Deus & pater omnium qui est super omnes & per omnia & in omnibus nobis. In quibus oportet, quod fideles vnitatem seruent, siue habeant aliquem Apostolicum siue nullum, siue etiam habeant vnum Apostolicum siue plures. Quandocunq; tamen expedit, vnum Apostolicum ecclesia debet habere: nec vnitas ecclesiae monstraretur, nisi (quando expediret & posset) ecclesia vni Apostolico subderetur. Et sic praedicta verba intelligit Cyprian. Quod ex verbis eiusdem sequentibus (quae etiam sunt superius allegata) ostenditur, cum dicit: Quomodo vnitatem tenere firmiter & vendicare debemus maxime nos episcopi, qui in ecclesia Dei praesidemus, vt episcopatum quoque ipsum vnum atq; indiuisum probemus. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod secundum beatum Cyprianum, non solum Apostolatus, sed episcopatus esse debet vnus atq; indiuisus: & tamen, sicut prius probatum est, in eodem episcopatu ex necessitate vel vtilitate simul plures possunt esse episcopi. Et per consequens in apostolatu possunt esse plures Apostolici. Aliter enim minus in necessariis esset prouisum Apostolatui, quam episcopatui. Sicut igitur in eodem episcopatu possunt esse plures episcopi: ita in apostolatu possunt esse plures Apostolici. Et tamen propter vnitatem voluntatum & caeterorum, quae enumerat Apostolus, & episcopatus & apostolatus vnus & indiuisus manebit. Quemadmodum propter vnitatem voluntatum plurium aristocratice principantium in eadem ciuitate remanet ciuitas vna, cuius vnitas vera interdum melius seruatur per plures, quam si vnus solus principaretur: licet si nihil singulare obsisteret, melius regeretur ab vno.
units.tr: Discip. Against this is the Gloss on the same chapter, "non autem," which says in these words: Could there not in the same way be several Apostolics? The argument says no, stating it above in chapter "factum." And the Lord appointed only one, 24. q. 1, speaks, and in chapter "quicumque." Nothing can be dispensed against this, 25. q. 1, "sunt quidam." Moreover, although the Catholic Church is one and has one head, we read that there were several emperors, but here it is not so, because that rule would be offended, namely, One holy Church. From these words it is inferred that it runs against an article of faith for there to be several Apostolics at once, namely that article, One holy catholic Church. Magister. The answer is that the Gloss does not speak here assertively but only by way of argument. Hence it says, the argument says no. And so it does not settle that side but only argues for it. These arguments conclude that there cannot be two Apostolics who are opposed and at odds, each of whom either says and affirms that he alone is the Apostolic and not the other, or of whom one is not lawfully constituted an Apostolic. In that case the cited chapter is read as made, because it speaks of Cornelius and Novatian, of whom Cornelius was duly and lawfully elected, as the same chapter asserts and attests. Novatian, however, did not seize the Apostolic rank out of any necessity or advantage of the Church, but through ambition, with scandal and division of the Church, as the following chapter attests, in which it is written thus: Novatian is not a bishop, who, an adulterer and outsider to the bishop Cornelius in the Church, which was made a bishop by 26 bishops, strives to be made a bishop by deserters through ambition. Concerning this, in book 6 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 35, it is written thus: Novatian, a presbyter of the Roman Church, puffed up with a certain pride, took away from the lapsed all hope of salvation, even if they had repented worthily. From this he also became the founder of the heresy of the Novatians, who, separated from the Church, called themselves Cathari, that is, the pure, out of love of a good name. On account of this matter a very famous priestly council was gathered in the city of Rome, of sixty bishops, and of many presbyters and likewise deacons. Moreover, after a great deliberation on this matter was held, by individual decrees it was determined what must be done, and the contest was begun. So Novatus, along with those who followed him, puffed up with pride of mind, because they turned aside to that human opinion which kept nothing of brotherly charity, was also judged alien to the Church. And there is also another letter of Cornelius, written to Fabianus, bishop of Antioch, teaching all the particulars about Novatus, what sort of man he was in life and morals, and how he departed from the Church. In it he reports that from the desire for the episcopate, which he secretly harboured within, he fell into all these evils. And further: Sidonius and Cornelius, who were held in high esteem among the confessors, because they had survived various kinds of torments. But these, he says, when they had more carefully observed that he (namely Novatus) did everything by frauds and guile, lies and perjuries, and that he only still pretended goodness so that he might deceive the unwary, left him, or rather, having been consecrated, returned to the Church with great haste, and in the presence of presbyters and bishops, namely also of laymen. First they confessed their own error, then afterwards also his deceit and trickery. He added moreover in this letter that, although he had always been unwilling to accept the episcopate, out of unity with the brethren, he suddenly and unexpectedly appeared as a bishop, like a new creature, one who claimed for himself the discipline and ecclesiastical institutions, and presumed to hold an episcopate which he had not received from God. For, having summoned three simple bishops, men ignorant of everything, from a remote part of Italy, or rather having deceived them by his subtle circumvention, he extorted from them, by mutual impositions of hands, an episcopate more imaginary than lawful. And further: He added also that this same Novatus, in his youth, was troubled by an unclean spirit. And when he had spent some time among the exorcists, he fell into a grave sickness, so that he was despaired of, and that while lying in bed, out of necessity, he was confused, and nothing that usually follows baptism was solemnly performed in him, nor was he completed with the seal of chrism. Hence he could never merit the Holy Spirit. From these words it is inferred that Novatus was unworthy even of the lowest episcopate, did not lawfully usurp the priesthood, and used many frauds and deceits. Therefore he tore the Church apart. But if he had been a worthy man and had been taken up by the unanimous consent of the Catholics, the Church would not on that account have been divided, nor does a plurality of Apostolics governing the Church in harmony conflict with the unity of the Church. Just as a plurality of bishops does not oppose the unity of the episcopate, nor does a plurality of rulers in an aristocratic city destroy the unity of the city. Nor would that article of faith, One holy Church, be offended by this: for on account of a plurality of Apostolics, taken up out of necessity or advantage by the unanimous consent of the faithful, there would not be several Churches, but one would remain, on account of the unity of faith and the concord of the Apostolics, who by the same mind and one counsel govern together with the other orthodox rulers. Therefore, when Cyprian says, as has been cited, that schismatics go out from unity, so that the one Church of Christ might be shown, the answer is that when necessity or advantage does not require a plurality of Apostolics, in which case Cyprian was speaking, there ought to be one Apostolic, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one not only by the unity of faith, baptism, and the other things which the Apostle enumerates to the Ephesians 4., but also by the unity of the Apostle, in whom the Catholics unanimously agree. But when necessity or advantage calls for several Apostolics, it is enough that the Church be one through the unity of those things which the Apostle enumerates to the Ephesians 4., through whose unity it is one, when, the Apostolic see being vacant, the Church is subject neither to one nor to several Apostolics. Among these things the Apostle by no means places one Apostolic when he speaks of the unity of the Church, saying: Being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, as you were called in one hope of your calling: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all of us. In these matters it is necessary that the faithful keep unity, whether they have some Apostolic or none, whether they have one Apostolic or several. Yet whenever it is expedient, the Church ought to have one Apostolic; nor would the unity of the Church be shown unless (when it was expedient and possible) the Church were subject to one Apostolic. And thus Cyprian understands the aforesaid words. This is shown from the words that follow in the same passage (which were also cited above), when he says: How we ought to hold unity firmly and to vindicate it, especially we bishops, who preside in the Church of God, so that we may also prove the episcopate itself to be one and undivided. From these words it is inferred that, according to the blessed Cyprian, not only the Apostolate but also the episcopate ought to be one and undivided; and yet, as was proved before, in the same episcopate several bishops can at once exist out of necessity or advantage. And consequently there can be several Apostolics in the Apostolate. For otherwise the Apostolate would be provided for less in what is necessary than the episcopate. Just as there can be several bishops in the same episcopate, so there can be several Apostolics in the Apostolate. And yet, on account of the unity of wills and the other things which the Apostle enumerates, both the episcopate and the Apostolate will remain one and undivided. Just as, on account of the unity of the wills of several rulers in an aristocracy in the same city, the city remains one, whose true unity is sometimes better preserved by several than if one alone ruled, although, if nothing singular stood in the way, it would be better governed by one.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: In qua ostenditur, quod pluralitas summorum pontificum non impedit, quin sint omnes Apostolici & successores Petri atque vicarii Christi. Et hoc inter respondendum ad tertiam, & continenter ad alias rationes supra cap. huius secundi adductas.
units.tr: In which it is shown that the plurality of supreme pontiffs does not prevent them all from being Apostolic and successors of Peter and vicars of Christ. This is answered here as the third objection, and continues the answers to the other arguments adduced above in chapter 2 of this book.

units.la: Discipulus. Verras te ad alias allegationes, quae supra cap. 21. sunt adductae: & narra breuiter, quomodo respondetur ad ipsas. Magist. Ad illam, quae fundatur in hoc, quod nullus est verus in ecclesia principatus, nisi Apostolicus: qualis non esset principatus plurium praesidentium orthodoxis. Respondetur, quod quamuis propter necessitatem vel vtilitatem esset plures principantes catholicis, tamen principatus eorum esset Apostolicus, & quilibet eorum esset vere successor beati Petri & vicarius Christi. Quemadmodum si essent plures Imperatores, quilibet eorum esset verus Imperator. Et ita quamuis simul essent plures Apostolici, tamen ecclesia esset vere in Apostolica radice fundata, esset principatus Apostolicus vere per successiones episcoporum absque omni schismate continuatus, si vnapinies pro vtilitati communi de concordi voluntate fidelium plures simul in Apostolica sede sederent. Quemadmodum Imperium Romanum fuit vnum & idem per successiones Imperatorum continuatum, quando fuerunt simul plures Imperatores, & quando fuit vnus solus. Sic etiam in diuersis regnis simul aliquando fuerunt plures reges, scilicet pater & filius: & tamen idem fuit regnum & per successiones regum continuatum. Discip. Si autem essent plures Apostolici, simul ipsi aristocratice regerent vniuersitatem fidelium, & principatus eorum esset aristocraticus reputandus. Sed principatus Apostolicus non est principatus aristocraticus, sed magis regalis, iuxta illud 1. Pet. 2. Vos estis genus electum, regale sacerdotium. Et in Apocal. dicit beatus Iohannes: Fecit Fundamentale: ergo si essent plures Apostolici, principatus regalis esset in Aristocraticum mutatus: ergo consequentia non esset Apostolicus. Magist. Respondetur, quod principatus Apostolicus non esset in aliud transmutatus: quia in principatu nulla esset varietas potestatis, sed esset solummodo pluralitas principantium non de necessitate principatus, sed propter utilitatem aliam vel necessitatem. Differt autem Aristocraticus principatus a principatu regali magis per diversam potestatem, quam per unitatem & pluralitatem principantis & principantium. Quia in hoc saltem principatus Aristocraticus differt a principatu regali, quod unus principantium Aristocratice absque speciali commissione alterius non potest exercere ea, quae ad Aristocraticum pertinent principatum. Quod non est in principatu regali, nec esset in principatu plurium Apostolicorum, si plures simul essent.
units.tr: Student. Return to the other allegations that were adduced above in chapter 21, and briefly tell me how they are answered. Teacher. To the one based on the claim that there is no true government in the Church except the Apostolic, which would not be the case with a government of several presiding bishops who are orthodox: the answer is that although, for necessity or advantage, there might be several rulers of the Catholics, their government would still be Apostolic, and each of them would truly be a successor of blessed Peter and a vicar of Christ. Just as, if there were several emperors, each of them would be a true emperor. So too, although several Apostolic men might at the same time be in the apostolate, the Church would still be truly founded on the Apostolic root, and the Apostolic government would be truly continued through the successions of bishops without any schism, if several sat together in the Apostolic see for the common good, by the unanimous consent of the faithful. Just as the Roman Empire was one and the same, continued through the successions of emperors, both when there were several emperors at once and when there was only one. So too in different kingdoms there have sometimes been several kings at once, namely father and son, and yet it was the same kingdom, continued through the successions of kings. Student. But if there were several Apostolic men, they would together rule the body of the faithful in an aristocratic way, and their government would have to be regarded as aristocratic. But the Apostolic government is not aristocratic but rather royal, according to 1 Peter 2: "You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood." And in the Apocalypse blessed John says: "the wall of the city had twelve foundations." Therefore, if there were several Apostolic men, the royal government would have been changed into an aristocratic one; therefore the consequence would not be Apostolic. Teacher. The answer is that the Apostolic government would not be changed into another kind, because in the government there would be no variety of power, but only a plurality of rulers, not by necessity of the government but for some other advantage or necessity. Now an aristocratic government differs from a royal one more by the kind of power than by the unity or plurality of the ruler and rulers. For in this respect at least an aristocratic government differs from a royal one: that one of the aristocratic rulers cannot exercise, without a special commission from the other, those things that belong to aristocratic government. This is not the case in royal government, nor would it be the case in a government of several Apostolic men, if there were several at once.

units.la: Discip. Dic quomodo ad sequentem allegationem respondetur. Magist. Multiplicitér respondetur. Vno modo, quod Papa non habet potestatem praeficiendi alium in summum pontificem: quia summus pontifex de fidelibus praeficii debet. Et ideo Papa non habet omnino plenitudinem potestatis. Aliter dicitur, quod Papa non habet regulariter, sed casualiter, potestatem praeficiendi alium in summum pontificem: quando videlicet videret imminere periculum fidelium seu fidei, nisi alius praeficeretur vel singularem utilitatem, si alius ordinaretur, & non posset facilis requirere consensum fidelium, & periculum esset in mora. Cum vero dicitur, quod Papa non potest dispensare contra statum generalem ecclesiae. Respondetur, quod Papa non potest regulariter dispensare contra illa, quae explicite vel implicite continentur in scripturis sacris: nec etiam contra ea, quae ad iura pertinent aliorum: tamen casualiter ex causa iusta & rationabili potest inducere novitates, quae fidei non repugnant. Et ideo ex causa rationabili posset alium constituere summum pontificem, qualiter secundum quosdam beatus Petrus alium fecit summum pontificem ipso vivente. Regulariter tamen hoc facere Papa non potest: & si fecerit minime tenet. Ad aliam allegationem dicitur, quod fideles ex causa instituendo plures summos pontifices, nequaquam incurrerent haereticam pravitatem. Quia privilegium ratione ecclesiae traditum sibi a Christo non auferetur ab ea. Quia remaneret eadem Romana ecclesia habens potestatem praeficiendi sibi & universitati fidelium unum summum pontificem: & etiam plures, quando expedierit. Ad aliam dicitur, quod in uno episcopatu possunt esse duo episcopi, sicut accidit tempore beati Hieron. de Augustino & Valerio, qui simul fuerunt episcopi Iponensis ecclesiae, sicut ostensum est supra. Discip. Glossa super illud capitulum 7. q. 1. non autem, videtur dicere, quod Valerius & Augustinus non regebant simul episcopatum eundem. Magist. Dicitur, quod talis Glossa, si esset, manifeste corrumperet textum. Quia textus dicit expresse, quod incolumi Valerio Iponensis ecclesiae episcopo coepiscopus Augustinus factus est. Sed si Valerius cessisset: Augustinus non fuisset factus coepiscopus. Ergo eodem tempore regebant eundem episcopatum. Nec Glossa asserit contrarium: sed dubitative loquitur dicens, forte Valerius cessit administrationi Augustini. Ad Hieronymum autem dicitur: quod ipse intendit, quod regulariter & absque aliqua causa non debent esse plures episcopi in eodem episcopatu: ex causa tamen possunt esse. Ad ultimam respondetur, quod fideles propter necessitatem vel utilitatem sufficienter movéntem & inducentem constituendo plures summos pontifices, non facerent conditionem ecclesiae deteriorem, quo ad spiritualia, sed meliorarent eam. Quia in tali casu magis expediret ecclesiae regi ab uno quam a pluribus. Cum autem dicitur, quod principatus Aristocraticus & quilibet alius est minus bonus, quam principatus regalis. Respondetur, quod quantum ad naturam principatur est minus bonus: interdum tamen melior est quodam modo, quia principatus est regalis. Quemadmodum multae medicinae in se deteriores sunt cibis, qui competunt sanis: & tamen nonnunquam meliores sunt quibusdam aegris. Et ideo licet quantum est de natura rei sit melius, quod principatus unus solus, quia, ut dicit Glossa super saepe allegatum capitulum 7. q. 1. nondum, facilius expeditur administratio per unum quam per plures ff. de administrat. tutor. l. 3. §. ultimo. Quod communiter habet veritatem, non tamen semper, quia in aliquo casu potest esse melius, quod principentur plures, & quandoque facilius expeditur administratio per plures, quam per unum.
units.tr: Student. Tell me how the next allegation is answered. Teacher. It is answered in many ways. In one way: the Pope does not have the power to appoint another as supreme pontiff, since the supreme pontiff ought to be appointed by the faithful. And therefore the Pope does not have fullness of power at all. Another way of putting it: the Pope does not have, as a rule, but only in exceptional cases, the power to appoint another as supreme pontiff; namely when he sees a danger threatening the faithful or the faith unless another is appointed, or a special advantage if another were ordained, and when it is not easy to seek the consent of the faithful and the danger would be in delay. As for the claim that the Pope cannot dispense against the general state of the Church, the answer is that the Pope cannot, as a rule, dispense against those things that are explicitly or implicitly contained in the holy Scriptures, nor against those things that pertain to the rights of others; yet in exceptional cases, for a just and reasonable cause, he can introduce novelties that do not conflict with the faith. And so, for a reasonable cause, he could appoint another as supreme pontiff, as according to some blessed Peter appointed another as supreme pontiff while he himself was still living. As a rule, however, the Pope cannot do this, and if he did, he would by no means be bound by it. To the other allegation it is said that the faithful, by reason of the cause, in instituting several supreme pontiffs, would by no means incur heretical perversity. For the privilege given by Christ to the Church is not taken away from her by this. The same Roman Church would remain, having the power to appoint for herself and for the whole body of the faithful one supreme pontiff, and also several when it was expedient. To the next it is said that in one bishopric there can be two bishops, as happened in the time of blessed Jerome with Augustine and Valerius, who were at the same time bishops of the church of Hippo, as was shown above. Student. The Gloss on the chapter "non autem" in 7 q. 1 seems to say that Valerius and Augustine did not govern the same bishopric together. Teacher. It is said that such a Gloss, if it said this, would plainly corrupt the text. For the text expressly says that Augustine was made co-bishop while Valerius, bishop of the church of Hippo, was still alive. But if Valerius had resigned, Augustine would not have been made co-bishop. Therefore at the same time they governed the same bishopric. Nor does the Gloss assert the contrary; it speaks doubtfully, saying "perhaps Valerius yielded the administration to Augustine." As for Jerome, it is said that he meant that as a rule, and without some cause, there ought not to be several bishops in the same bishopric, but for a cause there may be. To the last it is answered that the faithful, by constituting several supreme pontiffs for a necessity or advantage that sufficiently moves and induces them, would not make the condition of the Church worse as regards spiritual things, but would improve it. For in such a case it would be more expedient for the Church to be ruled by one than by several. As for the claim that aristocratic government, and any other kind, is less good than royal government, the answer is that as regards the nature of the government it is less good, yet at times it is in a certain way better, because the government is royal. Just as many medicines are in themselves worse than the foods suited to healthy people, and yet sometimes are better for certain sick people. And so, although in the nature of the thing it is better that the government be by one alone, because, as the Gloss on the often-cited chapter "nondum" in 7 q. 1 says, "administration is more easily carried out by one than by several" (ff. de administrat. tutor. l. 3, §. ultimo), this generally holds true, but not always, because in some case it can be better that several rule, and sometimes administration is more easily carried out by several than by one.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: In quo respondet ad rationes supra c. 20. factas, probantes, quod in casu possint eligi, siue constitui plures summi pontifices.
units.tr: In which he answers the arguments set out above in chapter 20, which prove that in the present case several supreme pontiffs could be elected or established.

units.la: Discipulus. Recitasti quomodo respondetur secundum unam opinionem ad allegationes ostendentes, quod fideles non possunt instituere plures Apostolicos simul: nunc secundum opinionem contrariam narra, quomodo respondetur ad allegationes contrarias adductas supr. c. 20. huius secundus: quibus ostenditur, quod non licet fidelibus plures constituere principantes communitati fidelium, siue quod possunt alium principatum, quam Apostolicum instituere; siue quod solum modo possint ad statum Apostolicum simul prouehere. Magist. Secundum tenentes, quod nullo modo possunt simul esse plures Apostolici: respondetur ad primam allegationem, quod statuta humana, quae divinis praeceptis non obviant, variari possunt. Sic etiam principatus, qui ordinationi divinae minime adversantur, variare licet: sed non illos, quorum aliquis repugnaret ordinationi divinae. Plures autem simul esse Apostolicos, obuiaret ordinationi Christi, qui vnum constituit. Et ideo non licet constituere simul plures Apostolicos. Ad secundam dicitur, quod in hoc communitati fidelium quantum ad omnia necessaria optime est prouisum, quod diligendo & obediendo Deo fidelibus omnia cooperantur in bonum secundum Apostolum. Et ideo licet quandoque esset melius & magis expediens, plures Apostolicos praesidere, quam vnum, si non esset contra ordinationem Christi: tamen melius est & magis Christianis expediens propter ordinationem Christi subesse & obedire vni Apostolico quam pluribus. Ad aliam respondetur, quod consuetudines, quae sunt consonae ordinationi Christi, quamuis inciperent esse onerosae, per Christianos tolli non possent. Quemadmodum leges diuinae datae populo Iudaico quamuis fuerint onerosae iuxta verba Petri, quae leguntur Actor. 15. tamen per eundem populum tolli non poterant: sic quamuis principatus vnius solius Apostolici inciperet esse onerosus, tamen tolli non posset, sed tolerandus esset, quemadmodum sunt tolerandi mali praelati.
units.tr: Disciple. You have recited how, according to one opinion, the arguments showing that the faithful cannot establish several Apostolic men at the same time are answered. Now tell me, according to the contrary opinion, how the contrary arguments are answered, those adduced above, chapter 20, of this second book: by which it is shown that it is not lawful for the faithful to set up several rulers over the community of the faithful, or that they could institute some other principate than the Apostolic one, or that they could only advance several men to the Apostolic state at the same time. Master. According to those who hold that several Apostolic men can in no way be together, the first argument is answered thus: human statutes, which do not oppose divine precepts, may be varied. So too principates which are in no way contrary to the divine ordinance may lawfully be varied; but not those of which any would oppose the divine ordinance. Now for several Apostolic men to be together would obstruct the ordinance of Christ, who established one. And therefore it is not lawful to set up several Apostolic men at once. To the second, it is said that in this the community of the faithful has been very well provided for as regards all things necessary, since to the faithful who love and obey God all things work together for good, according to the Apostle. And therefore, although it might sometimes be better and more expedient for several Apostolic men to preside rather than one, if it were not against the ordinance of Christ, nevertheless it is better and more expedient for Christians, on account of the ordinance of Christ, to be subject to and obey one Apostolic man rather than several. To the other argument it is answered that customs which agree with the ordinance of Christ, even if they begin to be burdensome, cannot be removed by Christians. Just as the divine laws given to the Jewish people, although they were burdensome according to the words of Peter, which are read in Acts 15, nevertheless could not be removed by that same people: so, although the principate of one Apostolic man alone should begin to be burdensome, it could not be removed, but would have to be endured, just as bad prelates must be endured.

units.la: Ad aliam respondetur, quod expedit ecclesiae propter bonum obedientiae si est voluntas Dei, illi principatui obligari, qui potest in pessimum transmutari. Quemadmodum propter bonum obedientiae expedit ecclesiae propter praeceptum Dei praelato pessimo obedire. Et ideo licet principatus vnius summi pontificis posset per malitiam eius transmutari in pessimum, quia potest effici tyrannus: tamen propter bonum obedientiae expedit ecclesiae sustinere eundem. Ad aliam rationem respondetur, quod propter euidentem utilitatem est nouitas facienda, ita vt recedatur ab eo iure humano, quod diu aequum visum est. Sed propter nullam utilitatem recedendum est a iure diuino, & diu aequum visum est. Sic etiam a principatu humanitus instituto propter utilitatem euidentem recedendum est: sed non a principatu a Christo instituto: quemadmodum a sacerdotio Leuitico propter nullam utilitatem licebat Iudaeis recedere. Principatus autem Apostolicus sic est diuinitus institutus, vt vnus solus debeat principari. Quare propter nullam utilitatem talis principatus in Aristocraticum vel alium transmutandus est: nec aliquo modo licebit fidelibus plures Apostolicos constituere. Ad aliam respondetur, quod principatus vnius summi pontificis non potest esse dispendiosus Christianis, nisi propter malitiam summi pontificis principantis vel propter malitiam subiectorum. Et ideo principatus ille non est transmutandus in alium: sed corrigendi sunt illi, propter quos tendit ad noxam, vel accidit dispendium Christianis. Per idem respondetur: quod quia interdum illud, quod prouisum est ad concordiam, propter malitiam aliquorum tendit ad noxam: non ideo ipsum est tollendum, sed corrigendi sunt illi, propter quos tendit ad noxam. Ad aliam dicitur, quod non semper cessante causa cessat affectus, sicut in multis casibus patet. Ad aliam respondetur, sicut responsum est: quod non semper est standum maiori parti, nec pluralitati. Et ideo licet maior pars Christianorum vellet constituere plures Apostolicos simul, non esset standum cum eis, quia maiori rationi minor niteretur, scil. ordinationi Christi, qui instituit vnum solum Apostolicum. Ad allegationes in contrarium dicitur, quod pro necessitate non licet facere contra praeceptum diuinum expressum: nisi quando potest colligi ex scripturis, quod necessitas est excepta in legibus diuinis. Non autem potest haberi ex scripturis, quod in ordinatione Christi de vno Apostolico constituendo aliqua necessitas sit excepta. Et ideo nec propter necessitatem nec propter utilitatem sunt plures Apostolici constituendi. Ad vltimam respondetur, quod Dauid ex inspiratione diuina fecit illam diuisionem sacerdotum. Et ideo si Deus ordinauerit, possent constitui plures Apostolici: sed absque praecepto diuino hoc legitime minime fieri posset.
units.tr: To another argument it is answered that, for the sake of the good of obedience, it is expedient for the Church, if it is the will of God, to be bound to that principate which can be changed into the worst kind. Just as, for the sake of the good of obedience, it is expedient for the Church, on account of God's precept, to obey even a most wicked prelate. And therefore, although the principate of one supreme pontiff could through his malice be changed into the worst kind, since he may become a tyrant, nevertheless, for the sake of the good of obedience, it is expedient for the Church to bear with him. To the other argument it is answered that for evident advantage innovation is to be made, so that one may depart from that human law which has long seemed fair. But for no advantage is one to depart from divine law, which has long seemed fair. Thus too one must depart, for evident advantage, from a principate instituted by man; but not from a principate instituted by Christ: just as the Jews were not permitted to depart from the Levitical priesthood for no advantage. Now the Apostolic principate has been so divinely instituted that one alone ought to rule. Therefore, for no advantage is such a principate to be changed into an aristocracy or any other form, nor will it in any way be lawful for the faithful to set up several Apostolic men. To another argument it is answered that the principate of one supreme pontiff cannot be harmful to Christians, except on account of the malice of the supreme pontiff who rules, or on account of the malice of the subjects. And therefore that principate is not to be changed into another; but those by whose fault it tends to harm, or by whom loss comes to Christians, are to be corrected. In the same way it is answered: that because sometimes what has been provided for concord tends to harm through the malice of some, it is not therefore to be removed, but those by whose fault it tends to harm are to be corrected. To another it is said that the effect does not always cease when the cause ceases, as is clear in many cases. To another it is answered, as has been answered: that one must not always stand with the greater part, nor with the majority. And therefore, although the greater part of Christians might wish to set up several Apostolic men at once, one should not stand with them, because the lesser side would rest upon the greater reason, namely the ordinance of Christ, who instituted one sole Apostolic man. To the arguments on the contrary it is said that, out of necessity, it is not lawful to act against an express divine precept, except when it can be gathered from Scripture that necessity is excepted in the divine laws. But it cannot be had from Scripture that any necessity is excepted in the ordinance of Christ concerning the establishment of one Apostolic man. And therefore neither on account of necessity nor on account of advantage are several Apostolic men to be set up. To the last it is answered that David made that division of the priests by divine inspiration. And therefore, if God should ordain it, several Apostolic men could be set up; but without a divine precept this could in no way be done lawfully.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: In quo narrantur aliqui casus, in quibus secundum opinionem tenentem plures simul posse esse Apostolicos, liceret illos eligere.
units.tr: In which some cases are described in which, according to the opinion holding that several Apostolic men may exist at the same time, it would be lawful to elect them.

units.la: Discipulus. Narrasti secundum opinionem vnam, quod quando expediret, liceret Christianis constituere plures Apostolicos. Nunc indica, an secundum eandem opinionem licet in aliquo casu plures constituere Patriarchas seu primates nullum superiorem habentes, quorum nullus pro Apostolico sit habendus. Magist. Secundum vnum modum ponendi opinionem praescriptam liceret (si communitati fidelium expediret) plures tales constituere Patriarchas seu primates. Quod ponit propter plures conditiones, quae adductae sunt supra 24. c. huius sectidi ad probandum, & liceret plures Apostolicos simul habere. Secundum alium modum ponendi hoc nullo modo liceret. Disc. Secundum primum modum habendi explica alios casus possibiles, in quibus liceret plures tales Patriarchas seu primates habere. Magist. Dicitur, quod vnus casus esset, si Papa & Cardinales efficerentur haeretici, & Romani facerent eisdem, aut nollent catholicum in summum pontificem eligere. Tunc enim liceret quibuscunque prouinciis & regionibus (quae hoc concorditer vellent) sibi vnum primatem eligere, qui in causis spiritualibus, omnibus aliis praesideret. Et ideo si aliquae prouinciae concordarent in vnum, & aliae in alium, possent plures tales primates non habentes superiorem, quorum nullus esset Apostolicus, praeesse Christianis, quousque de alio prouideretur vniuersitati fidelium. Alius casus esset, si propter haeresim Papae vel discordiam eligentium Apostolica sedes diu vacaret, ita vt negotia communia ecclesiae per ipsam expediri non possent, quemadmodum aliquando vacauit sex annis. Tunc enim liceret prouinciis, quae vellent sibi constituere primatem modo praedicto, qui negotia communia illarum prouinciarum expedire valeret. Alius casus esset, si catholici omnes praeter paucos, per bella intestina vel per infideles aut schismaticos, aut aliter taliter premerentur, quod ad Apostolicum verum non possent habere recursum. Et tunc diuersae prouinciae possent convenire ad praeficiendum sibi vnum caput. Tunc enim liceret quibuscunq; & quotcunq; prouinciis (quae possent & vellent) sibi constituere vnum primatem, qui super omnes potestatem haberet. Et ita possent aliquae prouinciae in vna parte mundi vnum, & aliae in alia parte mundi alium constituere sibi primatem. Quare possent licite fieri plures tales patriarchae seu primates. Disc. Aliquas allegationes adducas, qu in praedictis casibus vel aliis possent plures constitui huiusmodi primates seu patriarchae. Magist. Hoc videtur posse probari. Nam, vt habetur dist. 1. c. ius ciuile, vnaquaeq; ciuitas & populus potest sibi ius proprium diuina humanaq; causa constituere. Vbi dicit Glossa super vocabulo, ciuitas: Sic aliqua ecclesia ius sibi statuit, vt infra 11. dist. catholicam, & de consec. dist. 3. pronunciandum. Et super vocabulo humana, ait: prima contemplatione Dei & hominum in reuerentia Dei & utilitate hominum. Ex quibus colligitur, quod quaelibet ecclesia & quilibet populus Christianus potest sibi auctoritate propria ius proprium statuere pro utilitate sua. Ergo a simili vel multo fortius potest sibi pro reuerentia Dei & utilitate hominum constituere caput & praelatum: quia parum est ius esse in ciuitate, nisi sint qui iura regere possint & reddere. ff. de origine iuris l. 11. Amplius, cui licet cedere iuri suo, eidem licet super se superiorem recipere. Sed patriarchis & primatibus pro utilitate communi licet cedere iuri suo. Ergo multo magis licet eis super se superiorem recipere pro communi utilitate. Si autem licet episcopis, patriarchis, & primatibus: multo magis hoc licet inferioribus. Et per consequens possunt, si volunt super se constituere vnum caput, cui omnes subsint.
units.tr: Disciple. You have described, according to one opinion, that when it was expedient it would be lawful for Christians to appoint several Apostolic men. Now tell me whether, according to the same opinion, it is lawful in some case to appoint several Patriarchs or primates who have no superior, none of whom is to be regarded as Apostolic. Master. According to one way of stating the opinion set out above, it would be lawful (if it were expedient for the community of the faithful) to appoint several such Patriarchs or primates. This opinion rests on the several conditions adduced above in chapter 24 of this section, to prove that it would be lawful to have several Apostolic men at the same time. According to the other way of stating it, this would in no way be lawful. Disciple. Following the first way of holding the opinion, set out other possible cases in which it would be lawful to have several such primates or Patriarchs. Master. It is said that one case would be if the Pope and the Cardinals were made heretics, and the Romans either did the same or were unwilling to elect a Catholic as supreme pontiff. For then it would be lawful for whatever provinces and regions (which agreed in wishing this) to choose for themselves one primate, who would preside over all others in spiritual matters. And so, if some provinces agreed on one man and others on another, several such primates, having no superior, none of whom would be Apostolic, could preside over Christians until provision was made for the whole body of the faithful otherwise. Another case would be if, because of the heresy of the Pope or the discord of the electors, the Apostolic see remained vacant for a long time, so that the common affairs of the Church could not be dispatched through it, as once happened for six years. For then it would be lawful for those provinces which wished to set up a primate in the manner described, one who could manage the common affairs of those provinces. Another case would be if all Catholics, except a few, were so oppressed by civil wars, by infidels or schismatics, or otherwise, that they could not have recourse to a true Apostolic man. Then various provinces could come together to set over themselves one head. For then it would be lawful for whatever provinces, however many, which were able and willing, to set up for themselves one primate who would have power over all. And so some provinces in one part of the world and others in another part could set up a primate for themselves. Wherefore several such Patriarchs or primates could lawfully be made. Disciple. Bring forward some arguments by which several such primates or Patriarchs could be set up in the aforesaid cases or others. Master. This seems capable of proof. For, as is found in Distinction 1, the chapter "Ius ciuile", every city and people can establish for itself its own law, both by divine and by human reasoning. Where the Gloss says on the word "city": "So too a church establishes law for itself, as below in Distinction 11, 'Catholicam', and in De consecratione Distinction 3, 'Pronunciandum'." And on the word "human", it says: "in the first place with regard to God and men, in reverence for God and for the benefit of men." From which it is gathered that any church and any Christian people can, on its own authority, establish its own law for its own advantage. Therefore, by a similar and much stronger reasoning, it can for the reverence of God and the benefit of men set up for itself a head and a prelate, since it is of little use to have law in a city unless there are those who can govern and administer the laws. Digest, De origine iuris, law 11. Furthermore, whoever may lawfully surrender his right may also lawfully accept a superior over himself. But it is lawful for Patriarchs and primates, for the common benefit, to surrender their right. Therefore it is much more lawful for them to accept a superior over themselves for the common benefit. If it is lawful for bishops, Patriarchs and primates, much more is it lawful for inferiors. And consequently they can, if they wish, set up over themselves one head, to whom all are subject.

units.la: Disc. Isti opinioni sacri canones obuiare videntur, quibus statuitur & asseritur, quod noua dignitas non potest constitui sine licentia Papae. extr. de constitu. Cum accessissent, 22. dist. c. i. & extra de consuetudine, cum olim. Magist. Respondetur, quod quando potest haberi recursus ad Papam non est noua dignitas constituenda absq; licentia Papae: in quo casu loquuntur canones sacri. Sed quando non potest haberi recursus ad Papam catholicum, tunc pro utilitate communi licet aliquo modo nouam constituere dignitatem duraturam saltem vsque quo possit haberi ad Papam recursus. Sicut enim difficultas aliud admittit vel permittit, quod alias prohiberetur, sicut notat Glos. extra de ecclesiis aedificandis super c. ad audientiam: Ita etiam impossibilitas aliquid admittit vel permittit, quod alias prohiberetur. Quare propter impossibilitatem recursus habendi ad Papam, licet tales constituere patriarchas vel primates, quamuis hoc prohibeatur de sacris canonibus, qui intelligendi sunt loqui, quando potest haberi recursus ad Papam. Quemadmodum canones prohibentes quosdam excommunicatos absolui ab alio quam a Papa, intelligendi sunt, quando excommunicatus potest ad Papam recurrere, non quando ne recurrat ad summum pontificem impeditur, extra de sententia excommuni. Quamuis & in aliis pluribus sacris canonibus idem habetur. Sic etiam quando non potest recursus haberi ad Papam, vel non expedit, potest constitui nouus primas sine licentia Papae, si alicui nationi, aut regioni, vel regionibus, aut prouinciis fuerit expediens & necessarium, qui saltem auctoritatem & potestatem habebit, quousque per Papam fuerit aliter legitime & utiliter ordinatum.
units.tr: Disciple. The sacred canons seem to stand in the way of this opinion, by which it is laid down and asserted that a new dignity cannot be constituted without the Pope's licence. Extra, De constitutionibus, "Cum accessissent"; Distinction 22, chapter 1; and Extra, De consuetudine, "Cum olim." Master. The answer is that when recourse to the Pope can be had, a new dignity is not to be established without the Pope's licence: it is in this case that the sacred canons speak. But when recourse to the Catholic Pope cannot be had, then for the common benefit it is lawful in some way to constitute a new dignity, which will last at least until recourse to the Pope can be had. For just as difficulty admits or permits something which would otherwise be forbidden, as the Gloss notes on Extra, De ecclesiis aedificandis, on the chapter "Ad audientiam", so also impossibility admits or permits something which would otherwise be forbidden. Wherefore, because recourse to the Pope is impossible, it is lawful to constitute such Patriarchs or primates, although this is forbidden by the sacred canons, which are to be understood as speaking when recourse to the Pope can be had. Just as the canons forbidding certain excommunicated persons to be absolved by anyone other than the Pope are to be understood as applying when the excommunicated person can have recourse to the Pope, not when he is prevented from appealing to the supreme pontiff: Extra, De sententia excommunicationis. And the same is found in many other sacred canons. So too, when recourse to the Pope cannot be had, or is not expedient, a new primate may be set up without the Pope's licence, if it is advantageous and necessary for some nation, or region, or regions, or provinces; he will have authority and power at least until it has been otherwise lawfully and profitably ordained by the Pope.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXIX.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationem supra cap. 2. factam de diuitiis, quibus abundare debet, qui vult praeesse.
units.tr: In which is answered the argument, made above in chapter 2, concerning the riches with which he who wishes to preside ought to abound.

units.la: Discipulus. Ad plures allegationes supra c. 2. huius secundi inductas ad probandum, quod non expedit communitati fidelium vni capiti sub Christo subesse, responsiones recitasti, occasione quarum aliqua annexa tractauimus, circa quae quosdam opiniones & quosdam modos ponendi recitasti, quas & quos nolo ad praesens amplius pertractari. Ideo illis omissis ad aliud tempus, narra qualiter respondetur ad secundam allegationem supradicto c. 2. huius secundi adductam. Sed breuiter, quia alias de fundamento ipsius intendo tecum exquisite conferre. Magist. Illa allegatio in hoc fundari videtur, quod sine diuitiis, quibus carere debet caput fidelium, nemo potest efficaciter & utiliter subditis principari. Ad quam respondetur, quod potestas principandi Christianis in his, quae ad legem pertinent Christianam, sicut est instituta a solo Deo, quod per legem Christianam & solam ordinationem Christi a potestate & iurisdictione seculari Christiani minime sunt exempti. Vnde a tempore Apostolorum & multis post temporibus Christiani potestati & iurisdictioni etiam infidelium subiecti fuerunt in criminibus secularibus & aliis, quae specialiter ad legem Christianam nullatenus pertinebant. Propter quod caput Christianorum non habet regulariter potestatem puniendi seculares iniquitates poena capitis & aliis corporalibus poenis, propter quas taliter puniendas capitaliter potentia temporalis & diuitiae sunt necessariae. Sed talis punitio potestati seculari principaliter & regulariter est concessa. Poena igitur spirituali solummodo potest Papa regulariter coerigere delinquentes. Et ideo non est necessarium, quod temporali potentia praecellat vel temporalibus abundet diuitiis: sed sufficit, quod Christiani sibi prompte obediant.
units.tr: Disciple. You have recited the responses to the many objections brought forward above in chapter 2 of this second book, to prove that it is not expedient for the community of the faithful to be subject to one head under Christ. Occasioned by these, we treated some related matters, and you recited certain opinions and certain ways of positing things, which I do not wish to be discussed further at present. Therefore, setting those aside for another time, tell me how the second objection, brought forward in the same chapter 2 of this second book, is answered. But do so briefly, since I intend to examine its foundation with you more carefully on another occasion. Master. That objection seems to rest on this: that without the riches which the head of the faithful ought to lack, no one can govern subjects effectively and usefully. To this it is answered that the power of ruling Christians, in those matters which pertain to the Christian law, as it has been instituted by God alone, is by the Christian law and by Christ's ordinance alone in no way exempt from secular power and jurisdiction. Hence, from the time of the Apostles and for many ages afterwards, Christians were subject to the power and jurisdiction even of unbelievers in secular crimes and in other matters which in no way pertained specifically to the Christian law. For this reason the head of the Christians does not ordinarily have the power to punish secular wrongs with the penalty of death or other bodily penalties, for the punishing of which in this way temporal power and riches are necessary. Such punishment has been granted principally and ordinarily to the secular power. Therefore the Pope ordinarily can restrain offenders only with spiritual penalty. And so it is not necessary that he excel in temporal power or abound in temporal riches; it is enough that Christians obey him promptly.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CAP. XXX.

units.la: Soluit rationes capituli primi huius probantes, quod expediat communitati fidelium uni capiti sub Christo subesse.
units.tr: Answers the arguments of the first chapter of this book, which prove that it is expedient for the community of the faithful to be subject to one head under Christ.

units.la: DIscipulus.
