De hac materia tecum postea disputabo: ideo ipsam pertranseas, & qualiter secundum opinionem, quae tenet quod non expedit communitati fidelium vni capiti sub Christo subesse, respondeatur ad allegationes inductas superius primo c. huius secundi cura referre. Magist. Ad primam illarum respondetur, sicut tactum est ibidem, quod Christus est caput fidelium: ideo Christiani non subsunt vni capiti sub Christo. Ad rationem autem in contrarium respondetur, quod non est necesse, vt sub Christo sit vnus rector totius ecclesiae, sed sufficit quod sint plures diuersas regentes prouincias, quemadmodum sunt plures reges gubernantes plura regna. Ad aliam dicitur, quod expedit vni ouili, in quo oues simul morantur, regi & pasci ab vno pastore mortali. Vni autem ouili, in quo omnes oues non simul morantur, sufficit vt regantur a principe pastorum, scilicet Christo. Ad tertiam respondetur per idem, quod omni populo simul moranti expedit vni rectori mortali subesse, non autem vni populo comprehendenti plures populos in locis distantibus habitantes. Sed tali populo sufficit subesse Christo. Ad quartam respondetur, quod non omni communitati, quae non potest regi absq; multitudine iudicum, qui possunt circa causas & negotia contrarias habere sententias, expedit vni rectori supremo subesse. Quia communitas huiusmodi potest esse tanta, q; nullus vnus homo mortalis & in multis deficiens sufficit ad ferendum & determinandum omnia negotia, circa quae possunt alii iudices discordare. Et ideo cum communitas fidelium sic possit esse tanta, quod nemo mortalis possit omnia huiusmodi negotia sustinere, expedit communitati fidelium vt regatur a pluribus, non ab vno. Ad quintam consimiliter respondetur, quod quia vnus non sufficit ad cogendum vniuersos fideles ad seruandā vnitatem fidei ac ritauum & obseruantiarum, quos omnes Christiani seruare tenentur: ideo expedit communitati fidelium vt regatur a pluribus, qui ad huiusmodi vnitatem omnes compellant. Ad sextam respondetur, quod potentibus errare circa maiora negotia expedit habere vnum caput, quando vnus sufficit ad huiusmodi negotia omnia terminanda. Sed nemo sufficit ad huiusmodi negotia, quae possunt oriri inter Christicolas terminanda. Ideo non expedit sibi habere vnum caput sub Christo, sed plura. Ad septimam respondetur, quod non expedit communitati fidelium, vt multi inter ipsos & praecipue praelati, valeant delinquere insolenter, quando contra tale periculum potest remedium absque maiori periculo adhiberi. Sed maius periculum potest imminere communitati fidelium, si haberet vnum caput, quam habendo plura: quia cum facilius per malitiam inficiatur vnus quam plures, magis timendum est ne inficiatur per malitiam vnus principans vniuersis fidelibus quam plures principantes eisdem. Sed secundum sententiam sapientis Ecclesiastici 10. Secundum iudicem populi sic & ministei eius, & qualis rector est ciuitatis, tales & inhabitantes in ea. Cui concordat Anselmus, qui, vt habetur 6. q. 1. cap. ex merito air: capite languescente caetera corporis membra inficiuntur. Vbi dicit Gloss. Componitur orbis regis ad exemplum. Et per consequens corrupto capite quorumcunq; Christianorum de corruptione subditorum probabiliter est timendum. Ergo magis timendum est de generali vel fere de generali corruptione seu infectione Christianorum, si habuerint omnes vnum caput, quam si habuerint plura, licet magis esset timendum de aliqua particulari corruptione alterius partis Christianorum, si Christiani habeant plura capita. Ergo maius periculum imminet Christianis, si habeant omnes vnum caput, quod potest vniuersaliter, vel fere omnes Christianos inficere, quam si habeant plura, quorum nullum potest omnes vel fere omnes inficere, sed tantummodo sibi subiectos, quia non est tantum timendum, q; plura capita simul corrumpantur, sicut vnum solum. Discip. Quare addit ista opinio fere, cum dicit, quod magis est timendum de generali vel fere generali corruptione? Magist. Additur fere, propter promissionem Christi dicentis Matth. vltim. Vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi, propter quam nullatenus est timendum, quod vnquam propter malitiam vnius capitis erit generalis corruptio seu infectio omnium Christianorum. Quia talis corruptio Christianorum obuiaret promissioni Christi praescriptae. Sed fere generalis corruptio Christianorum promissioni illi nullatenus repugnaret: Staret enim eadem promissio Christi, si sub vno peruerso vel infecto capite omnium Christianorum inficerentur omnes praeter duos vel tres. Quare non esset aliqualiter metuendum, quod vnum caput omnium Christianorum inficeret omnes Christianos: sed credendum esset si inficeretur, quod inficeret fere omnes. Propter quod si Papa efficeretur haereticus, praesertim habens potentiam temporalem vel cui potentes temporaliter adhaerent, formidandum esset ne fere omnes Christianos inficeret haeretica prauitate. Sed si essent plura capita Christianorum, non ita faciliter omnia simul inficerentur. Sed vno infecto in moribus vel haeretica prauitate saepe aliud remaneret sanum in moribus & in fide cum sibi subiectis.
units.tr: Disciple. I shall dispute this matter with you later, so pass it over, but please set out how, according to the opinion that holds it is not expedient for the community of the faithful to be subject to one head under Christ, one should answer the arguments adduced above in the first chapter of this second book. Master. To the first of them, it is answered, as was touched on there, that Christ is the head of the faithful; therefore Christians are not subject to one head under Christ. To the argument on the other side, it is answered that it is not necessary that under Christ there be one ruler of the whole Church, but it is enough that there be several rulers governing different provinces, just as there are several kings governing several kingdoms. To the other argument it is said that it is expedient for one fold, in which the sheep dwell together, to be ruled and fed by one mortal shepherd. But for a fold in which all the sheep do not dwell together, it is enough that they be ruled by the chief of shepherds, namely Christ. To the third it is answered by the same reasoning: it is expedient for a people who dwell together to be subject to one mortal ruler, but not for one people that comprises several peoples living in distant places. For such a people it is enough to be subject to Christ. To the fourth it is answered that it is not expedient for every community, which cannot be governed without a multitude of judges, who may hold conflicting opinions about causes and affairs, to be subject to one supreme ruler. For a community of this kind may be so large that no single mortal man, weak and fallible, is sufficient to bear and decide all the affairs about which other judges may disagree. Therefore, since the community of the faithful may be so large that no mortal can sustain all such affairs, it is expedient for the community of the faithful to be governed by many, not by one. To the fifth likewise it is answered that since one man is not sufficient to compel all the faithful to keep the unity of the faith and of the rites and observances which all Christians are bound to keep, therefore it is expedient for the community of the faithful to be governed by many, who may compel all to such unity. To the sixth it is answered that for those who may err in greater matters it is expedient to have one head, when one man is sufficient to settle all such matters. But no one is sufficient to settle such matters as may arise among Christians. Therefore it is not expedient for them to have one head under Christ, but several. To the seventh it is answered that it is not expedient for the community of the faithful that many among them, and especially prelates, should be able to sin insolently, when a remedy against such danger can be applied without greater danger. But a greater danger may threaten the community of the faithful if it had one head than if it had several; for since one man is more easily infected by wickedness than many, there is more reason to fear that one man ruling all the faithful may be infected by wickedness than that many ruling them may be. But according to the saying of the wise man in Ecclesiasticus 10: Such as the judge of the people is, so are his ministers; and what sort the ruler of the city is, such also are its inhabitants. Anselm agrees with this, who, as is found in Dist. 6, q. 1, cap. ex merito, says: when the head languishes, the other members of the body are infected. Where the Gloss says: The world is shaped after the king's example. And consequently, when the head is corrupted, it is probable that the corruption of all Christians will follow from the corruption of their subjects. Therefore a general, or nearly general, corruption or infection of Christians is more to be feared if they all had one head than if they had several, although a particular corruption of some other part of Christians would be more to be feared if Christians had several heads. Therefore a greater danger threatens Christians if they all have one head, which can infect all Christians universally, or nearly all, than if they have several, none of which can infect all or nearly all, but only those subject to it, since it is not so much to be feared that several heads be corrupted together as that one alone be. Disciple. Why does this opinion add nearly, when it says that a general, or nearly general, corruption is more to be feared? Master. Nearly is added because of the promise of Christ saying in Matth. ult.: I am with you all days, even to the end of the world; on account of which promise there is by no means to be feared that a general corruption or infection of all Christians will ever come about through the wickedness of one head. For such a corruption of Christians would be contrary to the promise of Christ written above. But a nearly general corruption of Christians would by no means contradict that promise: for the same promise of Christ would stand if, under one perverse or infected head, all Christians were infected except two or three. Therefore there would be no reason to fear in any way that one head of all Christians would infect all Christians, but it should be believed that, if it were infected, it would infect nearly all. On this account, if the Pope were made a heretic, especially one having temporal power or to whom the powerful adhere in temporal matters, it would have to be feared lest he infect nearly all Christians with heretical depravity. But if there were several heads of Christians, not so easily would all be infected together. Rather, when one was infected in morals or heretical depravity, another would often remain sound in morals and in faith, with those subject to it.

units.la: Discip. Alias allegationes sequentes prosequere. Magist. Ad octauam respondetur, quod non semper idem est expediens toti & parti, magnis & paruis, nec vniuersaliter nec cum exceptione idem iuris est in toto & in parte, in magnis & in paruis. Licet hoc verum sit, quando est eadem ratio de toto & parte de magnis & paruis. Et ideo licet sit expediens, quod vno populo partiali fideli praesit vnus episcopus, non expedit tamen quod toto populo fideli praesit vnus solus.
units.tr: Disciple. Go on with the other arguments that follow. Master. To the eighth it is answered that what is expedient for the whole and for a part, for great and small things, is not always the same, and the law is not universally the same, nor with exception, for the whole and for the part, for great and for small things. Although this is true when the reason concerning the whole and the part, the great and the small, is the same. And so, although it is expedient that one bishop preside over one partial people of the faithful, it is not expedient that one alone preside over the whole faithful people.

units.la: Tum quia omnia negotia vnius populi partialis potest sustinere vnus solus: nullus autem vnus potest sustinere omnia negotia etiam maiora omnium Christianorum. Tum quia minus malum est, vt populus partialis & paruus inficiatur ab vno episcopo, quam vt totus vel fere totus populus Christianus inficiatur ab vno capite, quod omnibus praesit. Ad nonam dicitur, quod quamuis regnum sit optima politia in vna ciuitate secundum Aristotelem, qui solummodo loquitur de politiis, quae in ciuitatibus custodiuntur, vt in verbis eius quampluribus in lib. politicorum colligitur: tamen regnum non est optima politia in toto orbe, nec in omni parte orbis. Quia totus orbis & diuersa regna melius reguntur a pluribus, quorum nullus sit superior alio, quam ab vno solo, propter rationes tactas superius. Per hoc ad allegationem vltimam respondetur, quod non expedit vniuersitati mortalium, vt regatur ab vno monarcha totus orbis, sed regulariter expedit vt regatur a pluribus, quorum nullus sit superior alio, quamuis in aliquo casu, qui possit accidere, magis expediret quod totus orbis regeretur ab vno, quam a pluribus. Et haec de secundo libro.
units.tr: Because one bishop alone can sustain all the affairs of one partial people, but no one alone can sustain all the affairs, even the greater ones, of all Christians. And because it is a lesser evil that a partial and small people be infected by one bishop than that the whole or nearly the whole Christian people be infected by one head who presides over all. To the ninth it is said that although, according to Aristotle, kingship is the best polity in one city, since he speaks only of the polities which are maintained in cities, as may be gathered from his words in many places in the Politics, nevertheless kingship is not the best polity throughout the whole world, nor in every part of the world. For the whole world and the diverse kingdoms are governed better by several, none of whom is superior to another, than by one alone, for the reasons touched on above. By this, the last argument is answered: it is not expedient for the community of mortals that the whole world be ruled by one monarch, but it is ordinarily expedient that it be ruled by several, none of whom is superior to another, although in some case which may occur, it would be more expedient that the whole world be ruled by one than by several. And so much concerning the second book.

units.la: INCIPIT TERTIVS LIBER, IN QVO PERTRACTATVR, QVIBVS scripturis de necessitate salutis credere tenemur. Et ponuntur diuersae opiniones.
units.tr: BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK, IN WHICH IT IS TREATED WHICH SCRIPTURES WE ARE BOUND TO BELIEVE FOR NECESSITY OF SALVATION. AND DIVERSE OPINIONS ARE SET FORTH.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: In quo ponitur prima opinio, quae probat, quod tantummodo scripturis canonicis & generalium conciliorum est de necessitate salutis credendum. Et hoc quinq; allegationibus, ad quas respondetur infra cap. 8. n. 10. & 11.
units.tr: In which the first opinion is set out, holding that only the canonical Scriptures and the decrees of the general councils are to be believed for necessity of salvation. This is argued by five allegations, to which replies are given below, chap. 8, nn. 10 and 11.

units.la: Discipulus. Quamuis regulariter minime expediret totam vniuersitatem fidelium vni capiti subesse: tamen videtur, quod nullus catholicus debeat dubitare, quin propter necessitate temporis, vel propter excellentiam beati Petri, vel ex alia causa speciali nobis fortassis ignota, aut de potentia absoluta, Christus potuit constituere beatum Petrum caput, principem & praelatum aliorum Apostolorum & vniuersorum fidelium. Ideo specialiter nunc scrutemur, an de facto Christus tantam beato Petro contulit dignitatem. Verum quia istius inquisiti & aliorum complurium disputiendorum inferius, nec vna pars, nec alia aliter quam per scripturas vel auctoritates potest ostendi: circa scripturas autem recipiendas sunt diuersae opiniones & aduersae: quibusdam dicentibus quod solummodo scripturae canonicae & generalium conciliorum debent de necessitate salutis admitti; aliis aliter sentientibus. Ideo licet qualis fides scripturis aliis, quam canonicis, debeat adhiberi, in prima parte huius Dialogi (in qua quaesiuimus, quae assertio catholica, quae haeretica est censenda) disseruimus aliquantulum exquisite: sed tamen propter dicta quorundam, quae tunc non habuimus, non tædeat nos aliqualiter tangere de eodem. Circa hoc ergo diuersas opiniones cum motiuis earum non te pigeat recitare. Magist. Vna opinio tenens, quod nullam scripturam irrevocabiliter veram credere vel fateri tenemur de necessitate salutis æternæ, nisi eas quæ canonicæ appellantur, vel eas quæ ad has de necessitate sequuntur, aut scripturarum sanctarum sensum dubium habentium eas interpretationes seu determinationes, quæ per generale fidelium seu catholicorum concilium essent factæ, in his præsertim in quibus error damnationem æternam induceret, quales sunt articuli fidei Christianæ. Quod enim interpretationibus concilii generalis sit talis præstanda credulitas, patet. Quia pie tenendum est, quod tales interpretationes sunt nobis ab eodem spiritu revelatæ. Quod ex scriptura ostenditur. Nam veritas ipsa Matth. vltimo dicit: ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsque ad consummationem seculi. Vnde Rabanus ait: ex hoc intelligitur, quod vsque in finem seculi non sunt de futuri in mundo, qui diuina mansione & inhabitatione sunt digni: quibus scilicet ad fidei conseruationem Spiritum sanctum pie tenendum est semper adesse. Vnde Hieron. Quod igitur vsque ad consummationem seculi cum discipulu se esse promittit: & illos ostendit semper esse victuros, & se nunquam a credentibus recessurum. Idem aperte conuincitur Actuum 15. dicente Apostolorum & fidelium congregatione, post ambiguitatem illius & terminationem: visum est enim Spiritui sancto & nobis. Asseruerunt enim & asserit scriptura ipsorum determinationem in dubietate illa circa fidem factam esse a Spiritu sancto. Cum igitur fidelium congregatio seu concilium generale per successionem, vere representet congregationem Apostolorum & seniorum, ac reliquorum fidelium in determinandis scripturae dubiae sensibus in quibus maxime periculum æternæ damnationis induceret error: verisimile, quinimo certum est, deliberationi vniuersalis concilii Spiritus sancti dirigentis & reuelantis adesse virtutem. Hoc autem deductione infallibili (vt asserunt) ex scriptura vim sumente patere potest. Quoniam frustra dedisset Christus legem salutis æternæ, si eius verum intellectum, & quem credere fidelibus est necessarium ad salutem, non aperiret eisdem hunc quærentibus, & pro ipso inuocantibus simul, si circa ipsam pluralitatem fidelium errare sineret. Quinimo talis lex non solum seterad salutem inutilis, sed in hominum æternam perniciem tradita videretur. Et ideo pie tenendum est, determinationes conciliorum generalium in sensibus scripturæ dubiis a Spiritu sancto originem sumere.
units.tr: Disciple: Although it is generally not expedient for the whole body of the faithful to be subject to one head, yet it seems that no Catholic should doubt that Christ could, by reason of the needs of the time, or on account of the excellence of blessed Peter, or for some other special cause perhaps unknown to us, or by his absolute power, have appointed blessed Peter as head, prince and ruler of the other Apostles and of all the faithful. So let us now examine specifically whether Christ in fact conferred such dignity on blessed Peter. But since this inquiry, and several other matters to be disputed later, cannot be shown on either side except through the Scriptures or authorities, and since opinions about which Scriptures are to be received are various and conflicting, some saying that only the canonical Scriptures and the decrees of the general councils must be admitted for necessity of salvation, others thinking otherwise, therefore, although in the first part of this Dialogue (in which we asked which assertion is to be judged Catholic and which heretical) we discussed at some length what kind of faith is to be given to Scriptures other than the canonical ones, nevertheless, because of the arguments of certain people which we did not then have, I would not be wearied by touching on the same matter again in some way. So please do not hesitate to set out the various opinions on this, together with their grounds. Master. One opinion holds that we are bound to believe or confess as irrevocably true, for necessity of eternal salvation, no Scripture except those called canonical, or those which necessarily follow from these, or, where the sense of the holy Scriptures is doubtful, those interpretations or determinations which have been made by a general council of the faithful or of Catholics, especially in those matters in which error would bring eternal damnation, such as the articles of the Christian faith. That such belief is to be given to the interpretations of a general council is clear. For it is rightly held that such interpretations have been revealed to us by that same Spirit. This is shown from Scripture. For the Truth himself says in Matthew's last chapter: Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the end of the world. Hence Rabanus says: From this it is understood that until the end of the world there will be those in the world who are worthy of the divine dwelling and indwelling, to whom, namely, the Holy Spirit is rightly held to be always present for the preservation of the faith. Hence Jerome: Therefore, in promising that he will be with the disciples until the end of the world, he shows both that they will always live and that he will never withdraw from the believers. The same is plainly proved in Acts 15, where the assembly of the Apostles and the faithful, after that dispute and its settlement, says: For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. For that Scripture both asserts and affirms that their determination in that doubtful question about faith was made by the Holy Spirit. Since, therefore, the assembly of the faithful, or a general council, through succession truly represents the assembly of the Apostles and elders and the other faithful, in determining the doubtful senses of Scripture where error would most endanger eternal damnation, it is probable, indeed certain, that the power of the Holy Spirit, directing and revealing, is present in the deliberation of a universal council. This can be shown from Scripture by an infallible deduction (as they assert) which draws its force from Scripture. For Christ would have given the law of eternal salvation in vain if he did not disclose its true meaning, which it is necessary for the faithful to believe for salvation, to those who seek it and call upon him for it, and if he allowed them to err about this very plurality of the faithful. Indeed such a law would seem not only useless for salvation, but handed down to the eternal destruction of men. Therefore it is rightly held that the determinations of general councils, on doubtful senses of Scripture, take their origin from the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: In quo ponitur secunda opinio, quae tenet ultra primam, scilicet quod etiam decretis & decretalibus summorum pontificum & Apostolorum canonibus, qui in Biblia non habentur, & dictis Doctorum ab ecclesia approbatorum, est fides indubia adhibenda. Ad allegationes pro secunda tertia & quarta parte adductas respondetur infra c. 25.
units.tr: In which the second opinion is set out, which holds, going beyond the first, that besides the canonical Scriptures, the decrees and decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs and the canons of the Apostles, which are not found in the Bible, and the sayings of teachers approved by the Church, firm faith is also to be given. The arguments adduced for the second, third and fourth parts are answered below, in chapter 25.

units.la: Discipulus. Opinionem aliam recitare non differas. Magist. Alia est assertio, quod non solum scripturis canonicis & determinationibus seu interpretationibus conciliorum generalium est de necessitate salutis praestanda firma credulitas: sed etiam decretis & decretalibus epistolis summorum pontificum, nec non & Apostolorum canonibus, qui in Biblia non habentur, & dictis Doctorum ab ecclesia approbatorum, est fides absque dubitatione aliqua adhibenda. Quod enim Apostolorum canonibus supra dictis sit fides certissima adhibenda, videtur asserere Zephernius Papa. Qui, ut habetur distin. 16. c. sexaginta, ait: sexaginta sententias Apostoli perscripserunt, cum alii quamplurimi epistolae, & servandae rat esse censuerunt. Item Leo Papa, ut habetur in eadem distinct. cap. Clementis, ait: Clementis librum, id est Petri Apostoli itinerarium, & canones Apostolorum, numerant patres inter Apocrypha, excepti 150, quae decreuerunt orthodoxae fidei adiungenda. Item sexta synodus, ut legitur eadem distinct. cap. placuit, ait: placuit huic sanctae synodo, ut amodo confirmata & rata sint canones Apostolorum 85. cap. Hoc idem testatur Isidor. Qui, ut ibidem habetur, ait: propter eorum auctoritatem caeteris concilii praeponimus canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum: licet a quibusdam Apocryphi dicantur: quam plures eos receperunt, & sancti patres eorum sententias, synodali auctoritate roboraverunt, & inter canonicas posuerunt constitutiones. Ex his colligitur, quod saltem quibusdam canonibus Apostolorum est credulitas adhibenda indubia.
units.tr: Student. Do not delay in reciting the other opinion. Master. The other assertion is that not only the canonical Scriptures and the determinations or interpretations of the general councils must be given firm belief as necessary to salvation, but that also the decrees and decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs, as well as the canons of the Apostles, which are not found in the Bible, and the sayings of teachers approved by the Church, must be received with faith and without any doubt. That the most certain faith is to be given to the canons of the Apostles mentioned above seems to be asserted by Pope Zephyrinus, who, as is found in dist. 16, c. Sexaginta, says: "The Apostles set down sixty sayings, though many others thought they ought to be kept." Likewise Pope Leo, as is found in the same distinction, chapter Clementis, says: "The Fathers number among the Apocrypha the book of Clement, that is, the itinerary of the Apostle Peter, and the canons of the Apostles, except the 150, which they decreed should be added to the orthodox faith." Likewise the sixth synod, as read in the same distinction, chapter Placuit, says: "It has pleased this holy synod that from now on the canons of the Apostles, 85 in number, be confirmed and ratified." Isidore bears the same witness, who, as is found in the same place, says: "On account of their authority we place above the other councils the canons which are called the Apostles'; although some call them Apocryphal, very many have received them, and the holy Fathers have strengthened their sayings by synodal authority and have placed them among the canonical constitutions." From these things it is gathered that at least to some canons of the Apostles undoubted belief is to be given.

units.la: Quod vero decretis & decretalibus summorum pontificum credulitatem ac reuerentiam catholici debeant exhibere, testantur & Nicolaus Papa & Agatho Papa, quorum assertiones habentur distinct. 19. cap. si Romanorum & c. sic omnes. Ad quod etiam probandum aliae auctoritates sanctorum patrum possent adduci, quae abbreviationis causa non allegantur ad praesens.
units.tr: That Catholics ought to show belief and reverence to the decrees and decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs is attested both by Pope Nicholas and by Pope Agatho, whose assertions are found in dist. 19, c. Si Romanorum and c. Sic omnes. Other authorities of the holy Fathers could also be adduced to prove this, but for the sake of brevity they are not cited at present.

units.la: Quod vero dictis Doctorum ab ecclesia approbatorum oporteat credere distinct. 55. affirmari videtur, ubi diuersorum patrum recipienda enumerantur opuscula. Hoc etiam ratione probatur: Quia assertiones summorum pontificum non solum in diffinitione causarum & negociorum sunt recipiendae: sed etiam in expositione scripturarum sanctarum, quibus in expositione scripturae praeferuntur sancti patres tractatores diuinarum scripturarum, dist. 10. §. 1. Igitur expositiones huiusmodi tractatorum recipiendae sunt. Quod vero dicta summorum pontificum etiam in expositione seu interpretatione scripturae sint recipienda, Hormisda Papa videtur asserere; qui, ut habetur distinct. 15. cap. si ille, ait: nemo mihi, alia quaelibet contra auctoritatem sedis Apostolicae, vel contra 318. episcoporum & reliquorum canonum constituta obiiciat: quia quicquid contra illorum diffinitionem, in quibus Spiritum sanctum credimus locutum, dictum fuerit, recipere non solum temerarium, sed etiam periculosum esse non dubito. Huic consentire videtur Nicolaus Papa: qui ut legitur 25. quaest. 2. cap. si quis, ait: si quis dogmata, mandata, interdicta, sanctiones, vel decreta pro catholica fide, vel ecclesiastica disciplina, pro correctione imminentium vel futurorum malorum a sedis Apostolica praesule salubriter promulgata contempserit, anathema sit. Hoc idem per alios canones quamplurimos affirmari videtur.
units.tr: That one must believe the sayings of teachers approved by the Church seems to be affirmed in dist. 55, where the writings of various Fathers to be received are listed. This is also proved by reason: because the assertions of the supreme pontiffs are to be received not only in the definition of causes and business, but also in the exposition of the holy Scriptures, in which the holy Fathers, expounders of divine Scripture, are preferred in the exposition of Scripture, dist. 10, §. 1. Therefore the expositions of such expositors are to be received. That the sayings of the supreme pontiffs are to be received also in the exposition or interpretation of Scripture seems to be asserted by Pope Hormisdas, who, as is found in dist. 15, c. Si ille, says: "Let no one object to me other matters against the authority of the Apostolic See, or against the constitutions of the 318 bishops and the other canons; for I do not doubt that whatever is said against their definitions, in which we believe the Holy Spirit has spoken, is not only rash to receive but also dangerous." Pope Nicholas seems to agree with this, who, as is read in 25. quaest. 2, c. Si quis, says: "If anyone despises the dogmas, mandates, prohibitions, sanctions, or decrees wholesomely promulgated for the catholic faith or ecclesiastical discipline, for the correction of impending or future evils, by the prelate of the Apostolic See, let him be anathema." The same is seen to be affirmed by many other canons.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: In quo ponitur tertia opinio ultra precedentes, ponens quod etiam doctoribus ab ecclesia non approbatis est fides adhibenda, & hoc probat septem rationibus, ad quas respondetur capitulo 26.
units.tr: In which a third opinion is set forth beyond the preceding ones, holding that faith is to be given even to teachers not approved by the Church; and this it proves by seven reasons, to which answer is made in chapter 26.

units.la: Discipulus. Est ne alia opinio aliquid superaddens praedictae? Magist. Est quorundam opinio, quod non solum Christiani tenentur praedictis firmiter adhaerere: sed etiam doctoribus, qui non sunt ab ecclesia approbati, & qui se inuicem reprobant, etiam circa illa quae contingunt catholicam fidem, quantum ab ea in quibus omnes vel plures & praecipue magis famosi concordant, alii scil. Christiani credere constringuntur.
units.tr: Student. Is there another opinion that adds something to the one already mentioned? Master. There is an opinion of some people that Christians are bound not only to hold firmly to the aforesaid, but also to believe those teachers who have not been approved by the Church, and who condemn one another, even on matters that touch the Catholic faith, insofar as all or most of them, and especially the more famous, agree.

units.la: Discip. Scio plures, qui hoc sentire videntur, sed non sum memor quod audierim vel viderim quenquam eorum hoc auctoritate vel ratione probare. Ideo tu ad hoc allegationes aliquas nitaris inuenire. Magist. Quod hoc pluribus modis probari possit, apparet. Nam illis oportet adhibere fidem, quibus non credere est iniquum. Sed non credere doctoribus est iniquum, teste [illegible, ~12 letters] Leone Papa, qui, vt habetur 24. q. 3. c. quid autem, ait: quid autem iniquius est, quam impia sapere, & sapientibus doctoribus non credere? Ergo doctoribus est credendum, praesertim quantum ad illa in quibus omnes vel plures & magis famosi consentiunt. Amplius, in intelligendis scripturis divinis, illis credendum, a quibus scripturae sunt discendae, teste beato Clemente; qui, vt legitur distinct. 37. Verum, ait: oportet ab eo scientiam discere scripturarum, qui eam a maioribus secundum veritatem sibi traditam accepit. Igitur maioribus est credendum. Doctores autem sunt maiores. Ergo oportet doctoribus credere. Item praesumendum est pro multitudine & maxime sapientum distinct. 9. in canonicis. Et dis[?] nullus inuidi. Sed illis credendum est, pro quibus praesumitur. Igitur credendum est multitudini doctorum, cum inter sapientes debeant computari. Rursus, ille prudentiae suae innititur, quae ea quae sibi credenda seu tenenda videntur, doctorum assertionibus praesumit praeponere, vt colligitur ex verbis Hieron. quae ponuntur extra de constit. ne innitaris. Nemo autem prudentiae ... miti, Salomone hortante Proverb. 3. qui ait: ne innitaris prudentiae. Ergo assertionibus, quibus concordant doctores, nullus debet sententiam suam praeponere. Et per consequens omnes alii doctoribus in nullo modo credere constringuntur. Praeterea, fide dignorum testimonio est credendum. Doctores autem, qui fide digni sunt censendi, testes sunt assertionum suarum, quemadmodum Apostoli appellantur testes Christi, quia euangelicam auditi fuerunt, asserere veritatem. Ergo quando doctores concordant, praesertim famosi, alii credere tenentur eidem. Adhuc vnicuique experto & perito in aliqua scientia est credendum. Doctores autem Theologiae sunt experti & periti in theologica facultate. Ergo credendum est eisdem.
units.tr: Student. I know several who seem to hold this view, but I do not remember hearing or reading of anyone who proves it by authority or reason. So you should try to find some citations for it. Master. That this can be proved in several ways is clear. For we ought to give faith to those whom it would be wrong not to believe. But it is wrong not to believe the teachers, as witnessed by Pope [illegible] Leo, who says (as found in 24 q. 3, c. quid autem): "What is more wrong than to think impious things and not to believe wise teachers?" Therefore the teachers are to be believed, especially on those matters in which all or most of them, and the more famous, agree. Further, in understanding the divine Scriptures, one must believe those from whom the Scriptures are to be learned, as blessed Clement testifies; he says (as read in dist. 37, Verum): "One ought to learn the knowledge of the Scriptures from him who received it from his elders as truly handed down to him." Therefore one must believe the elders. Teachers are elders. Therefore one must believe the teachers. Likewise, what is presumed in favour of the multitude, and especially of the wise, is to be accepted (dist. 9, in canonicis). And, [illegible], no one is envious. But we must believe those in whose favour there is a presumption. Therefore the multitude of teachers is to be believed, since they must be counted among the wise. Again, a man who relies on his own prudence prefers his own opinion about what he thinks should be believed or held to the assertions of the teachers, as is gathered from the words of Jerome, which are cited outside under de constitutionibus, "Do not rely on your own" (ne innitaris). But no one [should rely on his own] prudence, Solomon exhorting in Proverbs 3, who says: "Do not rely on your own prudence." Therefore no one ought to prefer his own judgment to the assertions in which the teachers agree. And consequently all others are bound not to believe the teachers in any way. Moreover, one must believe the testimony of trustworthy men. Teachers who are judged trustworthy are witnesses of their own assertions, just as the Apostles are called witnesses of Christ, because they were heard to assert the gospel truth. Therefore, when teachers agree, especially the famous ones, others are bound to believe them. Furthermore, one must believe every man who is experienced and skilled in some science. But teachers of theology are experienced and skilled in the theological faculty. Therefore they are to be believed.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: In quo ponitur quarta opinio media inter alias (scilicet quod de necessitate salutis non tenentur fideles credere, nisi contentis in Biblia & scriptoribus eiusdem & universalis ecclesiae & Apostolis.
units.tr: In which is set out a fourth opinion, midway between the others (namely, that the faithful are not bound, for the necessity of salvation, to believe anything beyond what is contained in the Bible, in its writers, in the universal Church and in the Apostles).

units.la: Discipulus. Si est aliqua opinio, quae omnibus obviet supradictis, ipsam audire desidero, vt mihi detur occasio intelligendi profundius veritatem. Magist. Est quaedam opinio, quae viam eligens mediam praedictis omnibus in aliquo aducitatur: tenens quod scripturae divinae contentae in Biblia, & eiusdem sacrae scripturae scriptoribus, & universali ecclesiae, atque Apostolis, absque vlla dubitatione in omnibus est credendum. Nullis aliis, quantacunque doctrina vel sanctitate praepolleant, est in omnibus absque omni exceptione fides necessario adhibenda. Ita quod nec in concilio generali, si esset congregata vniuersalis ecclesia, nec decretis aut decretalibus, vel assertionibus summorum pontificum, nec doctorum dictis (siue fuerint ab ecclesia approbati, siue non fuerint approbati) est necessario credulitas in omni dicto & casu absque omni exceptione praestanda: licet in multis negari non debeant, & quo ad multa Christiani ipsis credere teneantur. Discip. Istam opinionem alias non audiui nec legi. Ideo vt cognoscam quod aliquid apparentiae vel veritatis contineat, ipsam intendo aliqualiter tecum discutere. Videtur primo, quod sibiipsi repugnet. Nam sicut qui in vno criminosus ostenditur, in nullo negocio admittendus est tanquam testis veritatis, sed suspectus est habendus. Ita qui in vno errat vel errare potest, in nullo sibi necessario est credendum; sed merito post est haberi suspectus: quod sicut erat in vno, ita errat in alio. Quod de intentione Augusti videtur esse aperte, secundum quam si in scripturis diuinis aliquod mendacium etiam minimum reperiretur, ei fides esset minime adhibenda. Unde dicit in prima epistola ad Hieron. vt habetur dist. 9. cap. si ad scripturas sanctas adm[?]ssa fuerint vel officiosa mendacia, quid eis remanebit auctoritatis? Quasi diceret, nihil. Si ergo concilio generali, summis pontificibus & quibuscunque doctoribus non est necesse in omnibus credere: sequitur, quod in nullo est eis fides necessario adhibenda. Cuius oppositum opinio praedicta tenere videtur. Videtur ergo quod sibimet repugnet. Tu vero narra, quomodo ad haec opinio eadem respondere conatur. Magist. Respondetur, quod secus est de criminoso, & de errante vel potente errare absque omni crimine & peccato. Criminoso enim in nullo credendum est: unde nec ad testimonium debet admitti. Ex quo enim damnabiliter a regula rationis recessit, non est firmiter praesumendum, quod rationem & veritatem velit in quocunque tenere: nisi forte in aliquo, quod ad concupiscentiam vel commodum eius absque omni contrario suae voluntati pertineat. Sed de errante aut potente errare absque omni crimine & peccato, nisi forte veniali, non est praesumendum, quod velit scienter aliquid asserere contrarium veritati. Unde & errantes in quibusdam, & opiniones falsas non scienter nec culpabiliter absque assertione, adhaesione vel defensione temeraria vel pertinaci aut damnabili tenentes, ad perhibendum testimonium veritati in iudicio, & extra debent admitti, & in multis debet adhiberi fides eisdem. Et ideo quamuis secundum istam opinionem non sit necessarium in omni dicto & casu absque omni exceptione credere concilio generali, Romanis pontificibus & doctoribus quibusque, tamen in multis est credendum eisdem: quemadmodum eorum testimonia sunt etiam in iudicio admittenda. Sed si generale concilium quodcunque vel Romanus pontifex, aut quicunque doctor scienter vel culpabiliter aliquod falsum asseret vel defenderet, vel quomodolibet adhaereret, nulli assertioni eius nisi aliter de eius veritate constaret, esset fides vel credulitas firmiter adhibenda. Discip. Contra ista auctoritas Augusti militare videtur. Ideo dic quomodo isti respondent ad istam. Magist. Respondetur, quod Augustus loquitur de scripturis, quaris quarum omnibus partibus est eadem ratio præstandi fidem. Et de omnibus talibus verum est: si vna sola pars inueniretur falsa, nulli parti talis scripturæ esset credendum, propter hoc quod ibi sic scribitur. Talis autem est scriptura diuina: quia cuilibet assertioni contentæ in ipsa, ideo fides præstanda est, quia instinctu Spiritus sancti ibidem est scripta & asserta. Sed quando est aliqua scriptura totalis, & non eadem ratio præbendi credulitatem cuilibet parti eius: quamuis vna pars admittatur, alia potest non admitti: quemadmodum libri Philosophorum & Poetarum & aliorum gentilium ac etiam secularium pro parte admittuntur & pro parte repelluntur. dist. 37. §. sed contra & c. turbat & c. si qui veri. Dicit Gloss. accipi argumentum, quod testes & instrumenta possunt in parte rata haberi, pro parte non. Sic etiam donatio pro parte est valida, pro parte non, argumentum 17. q. 4. quaest. Et vtor pro me, quo non vtor contra me, vt notat Gloss. dist. 9. c. 1. sic dicitur quod generali concilio & aliis in vno casu est credendum & in alio non: quia non est eadem ratio credendi in omnibus.
units.tr: Student. If there is some opinion that opposes all the things said above, I would like to hear it, so that I may have an opportunity to understand the truth more deeply. Master. There is a certain opinion which, taking a path midway between all the aforesaid views, departs from them in some respect. It holds that the divine Scriptures contained in the Bible, the writers of those holy Scriptures, the universal Church and the Apostles must be believed in all things without any doubt, while no others, however great their learning or holiness, are to be given necessary belief in everything without exception. Thus, neither in a general council, if the universal Church were gathered, nor in the decrees or decretals or assertions of the supreme pontiffs, nor in the sayings of teachers (whether or not they have been approved by the Church), is belief to be given necessarily, without any exception, in every saying and every case; although in many things they must not be denied, and Christians are bound to believe them in many matters. Student. I have not heard or read this opinion before. So that I may know whether it contains any appearance or truth, I intend to discuss it with you in some detail. It seems, first, that it contradicts itself. For just as a man who is shown to be criminal in one matter is not to be admitted as a witness to the truth in any affair, but is to be regarded as suspect, so one who errs, or can err, in one thing cannot necessarily be believed in anything; rather, he is rightly held suspect afterwards, since what he was in one thing he is in another. This seems to be clearly the intention of Augustine, according to whom, if even the smallest lie were found in the divine Scriptures, they would not be trusted at all. Hence he says in his first letter to Jerome, as found in Distinction 9, chapter "si ad scripturas sanctas": "If even officious lies are admitted into the holy Scriptures, what authority will remain to them?" As if to say: none. If, then, a general council, the supreme pontiffs and whatever teachers are not necessarily to be believed in everything, it follows that in nothing is belief to be given to them necessarily. Yet the aforesaid opinion seems to hold the opposite. It therefore seems to contradict itself. Now tell me how its supporters try to answer this. Master. It is answered that the case of a criminal is different from that of one who errs, or who can err, without any crime or sin. For a criminal is not to be believed in anything, and so he ought not to be admitted even as a witness. For since he has damnably departed from the rule of reason, it cannot be firmly presumed that he wishes to hold to reason and truth in anything, unless perhaps in something that concerns his lust or advantage and is wholly contrary to his will. But concerning one who errs, or can err, without any crime or sin (except perhaps a venial one), it is not to be presumed that he knowingly wishes to assert anything contrary to the truth. Hence those who err in certain matters, and who hold false opinions not knowingly nor culpably, without rash or obstinate or damnable assertion, adherence or defence, ought to be admitted to bear witness to the truth in court and outside it, and much trust should be placed in them. And so, although according to this opinion it is not necessary to believe a general council, the Roman pontiffs, or any teachers, in every saying and every case without exception, nevertheless they are to be believed in many matters, just as their testimony is also to be admitted in court. But if any general council, or the Roman pontiff, or any teacher, knowingly or culpably asserted or defended something false, or adhered to it in any way, then, unless it were otherwise established concerning its truth, no assertion of theirs would be to be firmly believed. Student. The authority of Augustine seems to militate against these views. So tell me how they answer this objection. Master. It is answered that Augustine is speaking of Scripture, all parts of which have the same reason for granting belief. And this is true of all such writings: if a single part were found to be false, no part of such a Scripture would be believed merely because it is written there. Such, however, is the divine Scripture, because belief is to be given to every assertion contained in it, since it was written and asserted there by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. But when a writing is a whole whose parts do not all have the same reason for giving credence, one part may be admitted while another may not be: just as the books of the philosophers, the poets and other Gentiles, and even of secular writers, are partly admitted and partly rejected. See Distinction 37, §. "sed contra", and the chapter "turbat", and the chapter "si qui veri". The Gloss says that the argument is taken that witnesses and instruments may be held valid in one part and not in another; so too a gift is valid in part and invalid in part (argument in 17, q. 4, quaest.). And I use it in my own favour, not against myself, as the Gloss notes on Distinction 9, chapter 1. Thus it is said that a general council and others are to be believed in one case and not in another, because there is not the same reason for believing in all things.

units.la: CAP. V. Assignat causam, quare non sit credendum in singulis concilio generali.
units.tr: CAP. V. The cause why one should not believe a general council in every case.

units.la: Discipulus. Quod recitasti de differentia inter criminosum errantem seu errare potentem absque peccato, quantum ad hoc quod non criminoso, sed alii est sæpe credendum, apparentiam videtur mihi habere: ex quo plura cogitandi est mihi data occasio. Nunc autem dic, quare tenet prædicta opinio, quod non est credendum in omnibus absq; omni exceptione generali concilio & aliis qui non fuerunt scriptores scripturæ diuinæ, qui nec soli ecclesiam vniuersalem constituunt. Magist. Hoc dicit propter hoc, quod concilium generale & omnes alii supradicti possunt errare etiam culpabiliter contra veritatem orthodoxam & aliam. Discip. Si concilium generale potest errare, multo fortius & Romanus pontifex, & quælibet alia congregatio partialis, ac quilibet doctor & scriptor, qui non fuit scriptor sacræ scripturæ, errare valebit. Et si non in omnibus absque omni exceptione est concilio generali credendum: multo magis aliis in omnibus absque omni exceptione minime est credendum. Quare sufficiat nobis ad præsens hoc de concilio generali tractare scil. opinionem præscriptam. Sane de his & aliis, quæ spectant ad ipsam primam partem nostri Dialogi lib. 5. c. 26. & 27. 28. & 29. aliquantulum diffuse tractauimus. Ideo circa hoc noli hoc diu morari, sed aliqua motiua breuiter tange absque deductione prolixa. Magist. Motiua ibi tractata fundantur principaliter in hoc, quod vna est sola ecclesia, scil. militans vniuersalis & tota (cuius concilium generale est solum modo pars) quæ non potest errare contra fidem. Et in hoc, quod illa congregatio, quæ valet ex voluntate humana dissolui & cessat (cuiusmodi est concilium generale) potest contra fidem errare. Et in hoc quod omnes illæ personæ, quæ existentes in diuersis locis possunt contra fidem errare, possunt etiam, si ad eundem locum conuenerunt. Et in hoc, quod nulla vocatio humana facta pluribus personis, præsertim paucis, potest eas confirmare in fide. Et in hoc, quod congregati in concilio generali non sunt dicendi non posse errare, neq; propter sapientiam eorundem, neq; propter sanctitatem, neq; propter auctoritatem vel potestatem, neq; propter promissionem factam a Christo, quæ saluari potest, si fides in aliis extra concilium generale remaneat. Quibus additur allegatio talis. Omnis congregatio illorum, qui pauci sunt respectu aliquorum catholicorum etiam prælatorum potest contra fidem errare: quia non est tenendum necessario, quod quidam pauci sint in fide confirmati, quantumcunque insimul congregentur. Quamuis enim sæpe legatur, quod præsumendum est pro multitudine, vt notat Gloss. dist. 19. in canonicis: non tamen ita legitur, quod præsumendum sit pro paucitate. Cum igitur non sit taliter pro multitudine præsumendum, quin liceat credere multitudinem posse errare, dicente Domino Exod. 23. Non sequeris turbam ad faciendum malum: multo minus præsumendum est pro paucitate. Et per consequens non est necesse credere quoscunque paucos, quorum nullus confirmatus est in fide, non posse errare. Sed pauci Christiani etiam respectu episcoporum possent sufficere ad celebrandum concilium generale, sicut sæpe respectu multitudinis prælatorum pauci ad generale concilium conuenerunt. Nam vt legitur in decretis dist. 18. c. sexta synodus, in generali concilio Anquiritario fuerunt solummodo 18. patres: in Antiocheno fuerunt patres 30. in Arelatensi fuerunt 19. in quodam alio Arelatensi fuerunt 11. patres. In alio Arelatensi fuerunt 18. in concilio Aurasiensi fuerunt 16. in Empanensi fuerunt 16. in Aurelianensi fuerunt 35. in Auernensi fuerunt 15. in Maticensi fuerunt 21. in Lugdunensi fuerunt 17. in alio Lugdunensi 20. Igitur concilium generale potest errare contra fidem. Amplius, illa congregatio potest errare contra fidem, quæ ad hoc, quod autentica sit censenda, indiget ab homine confirmari, qui valet contra fidem errare. Quia non magis confirmatur in fide indigens confirmatione, quam confirmans. Sed concilium generale, vt sit autenticum & vt eius assertio vel diffinitio sit reputanda autentica, & vt auctoritatem obtineat, indiget confirmari a Papa, qui potest contra fidem errare, teste Gelasio Papa, qui, vt habetur 23. q. c. 1. ait loquens de sede prima, per quam Papam intelligit, q vnamquamq; synodus sua auctoritate confirmauit & continuata moderatione custodis. Cui concordare videtur Pascasius Papa, qui vt habetur extr. de electi c. significasti, ait: cum omnia concilia per ecclesiæ Romanæ auctoritatem & facta sint & robur acceperunt. His consentit Iulius Papa, qui vt habetur distinct. 17. cap. regula, ait: nec vllum ratum est aut erit vnquam concilium, quod eius, (scil. Romanæ ecclesiæ) non fuerit sultum auctoritate. Hinc Gratianus 25. quaest. 1. §. his ita respondetur, loquens de sacris canonibus etiam generalium conciliorum ait: sacri quidē canones ita aliquid constituunt, vt sua interpretatione auctoritate sanctæ Romanæ ecclesiæ reserventur. Et hinc aliisq; quampluribus colligitur, quod concilium generale Papa confirmat, & ei auctoritatem præstat. Papa autem potest errare contra fidem. Igitur etiam concilium generale potest errare contra fidem. Et ita non est necessarium in omnibus absq; omni exceptione credere concilio generali: præsertim cum secundum quosdam aliquando erraverit, vt ex his apparet, & in prima parte isti{us} Dialogi li. 5. existit probatum.
units.tr: Disciple. What you recited about the difference between a wrongdoer who errs, or who can err, without sin, and the fact that he is not to be believed in the same way as another person, often seems to me to have some plausibility, and it has given me occasion for much reflection. Now tell me why the aforementioned opinion holds, namely that a general council and the others mentioned above are not to be believed in everything without any exception, even though they did not write Holy Scripture and do not alone constitute the universal Church. Master. It says this because a general council and all the others mentioned above can err, even culpably, against orthodox and other truth. Disciple. If a general council can err, then much more can the Roman pontiff, and any other partial assembly, and any teacher or writer who was not a writer of Sacred Scripture. And if a general council is not to be believed in everything without any exception, then much less is anyone else to be believed in everything without any exception. Therefore it will suffice for us, for the present, to treat only of the general council and the opinion stated above. Indeed, we have dealt somewhat at length with these and other matters that pertain to the first part of our Dialogue, in book 5, chapters 26, 27, 28 and 29. So do not linger long on this point, but touch briefly on some arguments without a lengthy argument. Master. The arguments treated there are based chiefly on this: there is only one Church, namely the whole universal Church militant (of which a general council is only a part), which cannot err against the faith. And on this: that an assembly which by human will can be dissolved and ceases to exist (such as a general council) can err against the faith. And on this: that all those persons who, living in different places, can err against the faith, can also do so if they have gathered in the same place. And on this: that no human summons made to many persons, especially to few, can confirm them in the faith. And on this: that those gathered in a general council are not to be said to be unable to err, neither on account of their wisdom, nor on account of their holiness, nor on account of their authority or power, nor on account of the promise made by Christ, which can be preserved even if faith remains in others outside the general council. To these is added the following argument. Every assembly of those who are few in comparison with some Catholics, even prelates, can err against the faith, because it is not necessarily to be held that a few who are not confirmed in the faith are kept in it, however many of them come together. For although it is often read that one must presume in favour of the majority, as the Gloss notes on dist. 19, in the canons, it is not so read that one must presume in favour of the minority. Since, then, one may not presume in favour of the majority in such a way that it is not permitted to believe that the majority can err, the Lord saying in Exodus 23, "Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil," much less must one presume in favour of the minority. And consequently it is not necessary to believe that any few persons, none of whom is confirmed in the faith, cannot err. Moreover, a few Christians, even in comparison with bishops, could suffice to celebrate a general council, just as often a few have come together to a general council in comparison with a multitude of prelates. For as we read in the Decretum, dist. 18, chapter "Sexta synodus": in the general council of Ancyra there were only 18 fathers; at Antioch there were 30 fathers; at Arles there were 19; at another Arles there were 11 fathers; at another Arles there were 18; at the council of Orange there were 16; at Epaon there were 16; at Orléans there were 35; at Clermont there were 15; at Mâcon there were 21; at Lyon there were 17; at another Lyon there were 20. Therefore a general council can err against the faith. Furthermore, that assembly can err against the faith which, in order to be considered authentic, needs to be confirmed by a man who is able to err against the faith. For a person who needs confirmation is no more confirmed in the faith than the one who confirms. But a general council, in order to be authentic, and so that its assertion or definition may be regarded as authentic, and so that it may obtain authority, needs to be confirmed by the Pope, who can err against the faith, as Pope Gelasius bears witness, who, as is found in 23 q. ch. 1, speaking of the first see, says that by this he understands the Pope, who confirmed each synod by his authority and preserved it by continual moderation. Pope Paschal seems to agree with him, who, as is found in Extra, "De electione," chapter "Significasti," says: since all councils both were made and received strength by the authority of the Roman Church. Pope Julius agrees with these, who, as is found in dist. 17, chapter "Regula," says: no council is or ever will be ratified which was not sanctioned by the authority of that (namely the Roman) Church. Hence Gratian, 25 q. 1, §. "His ita respondetur," speaking of the sacred canons, even those of the general councils, says: indeed the sacred canons so establish something that by their interpretation they are reserved to the authority of the holy Roman Church. And from this and from many other things it is gathered that the Pope confirms a general council and gives it authority. But the Pope can err against the faith. Therefore a general council can also err against the faith. And so it is not necessary to believe a general council in everything without any exception, especially since, according to some, it has sometimes erred, as appears from these things, and has been proved in the first part of this Dialogue, book 5.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Vbi ostenditur, in quibus credendum est concilio generali, & in quibus non.
units.tr: Where it is shown in what things one must believe the general council, and in what things not.

units.la: Discipulus. Sicut superius recitasti c. 4. quamvis secundum istam opinionem non sit simpliciter necessarium credere in omnibus (absq; omni exceptione) concilio generali: tamen secundum eandem in multis negari non debet, & quo ad multa Christiani tenentur eidem credulitatem præstare. Ideo ista duo ultima nunc secundum opinionem saepe dictam declara. Magist. Ad evidentiam istorum dicitur esse sciendum, quod eorum quæ asseruntur per concilium generale, quædam consistunt in facto, quia videlicet concilium generale narrat & asserit illa, quæ facta sunt: quemadmodum historia scripturæ Divinæ narrat rem gestam. Quædam autem non consistunt in facto, sed in ipsa natura rei, de qua loquitur. Sicut cum narrat & asserit ea, quæ spectant ad naturam Dei & creaturarum sive simplicium sive compositarum, vel etiam illarum quæ unitatem solummodo aggregationis vel ordinis habere noscuntur. Per istam distinctionem conatur ista opinio declarare præscripta dicens: quod si concilium generale erraret sive circa illa quæ consistunt in facto, sive circa alia, ille cui hoc constaret, ei credere non deberet, & eidem liceret in hoc contradicere, & negare concilium generale. Ille autem, cui hoc non constat, quantum ad illa quæ facti sunt deberet credere assertioni & testimonio concilii generalis, præsumendo quod concilium generale quantum ad illa quæ facti sunt, nihil assereret, nisi quæ essent sibi certa. Quemadmodum etiam iudex tenetur credere testibus, etiam quos non potest repellere, & reputare debet idoneos & veraces, licet in rei veritate deponant falsum. Nec iudex ignoranter credendo falsis testibus peccat: imo peccaret, si non crederet, ex quo nihil habet contra ipsos, unde suspicari possit quod falsum dicant. Sic fideles ignoranter credentes concilio generali erranti non peccant in huiusmodi: imo si nollent adhibere fidem, peccarent, ex quo nihil habent contra concilium generale. Si autem concilium generale erraret circa alia, quam circa ea quæ facti sunt (puta illa, quæ de Deo vel creaturis in sacris literis asseruntur) nulli Christiano, cui hoc non constaret, liceret assertionem concilii generalis negare, nec de ea publice disputare, nisi aliqui periti, & opinionis laudabilis impugnarent eandem. Et hoc propter scandalum evitandum, & ut concilio generali a quolibet, qui nescit ipsum errare circa huiusmodi, honor & reverentia debita deferatur. Debent q; singuli etiam qui assertionem contrariam antea tenuissent, non tamen fuissent certi explicite pro assertione concilii generalis præsumere, & quasi conditionaliter adhaerere, si scilicet non est contraria catholicæ veritati, ita ut publice non teneant opinionem contrariam etiam opinando, in mente tamen possunt opinari contrarium, & sollicite scrutando scripturas quærere veritatem. Si autem concilium generale non errat circa huiusmodi, quæ non consistunt in facto, nulli liceat maxime publica assertione ipsum negare, nec contrarium opinari, aut quomodolibet etiam dubitando publice defensare, etiam si prius opinatus fuisset contrarium. Cum de contrario, etiam ex quo est falsum, nemo possit esse certus, licet quis deceptus posset putare se esse certum. Si autem non errat circa ea, quæ in facto consistunt, ei omnes Christiani sine dubitatione credere debent, quia cum non errat, non possunt Christiani probabiliter suspicari, quod aliquo decipiatur errore in asserendo, vel narrando veritatem rei gestæ.
units.tr: Disciple. As you recited above in chapter 4, although according to that opinion it is not absolutely necessary to believe in everything (without any exception) the general council, nevertheless according to the same opinion it ought not to be denied in many things, and Christians are bound to give it belief in many matters. Therefore now declare these last two points according to the opinion often mentioned. Master. For the clarity of these matters it is said that one must know that among the things asserted by a general council, some consist in fact, namely, because the general council narrates and asserts those things which have been done, just as the history of Divine Scripture narrates an event that took place. Others, however, do not consist in fact but in the very nature of the thing of which it speaks, as when it narrates and asserts those things which pertain to the nature of God and of creatures, whether simple or compound, or even of those things which are known to have only the unity of aggregation or order. Through this distinction this opinion sets out to clarify what has been stated, saying: if a general council were to err either concerning those things which consist in fact, or concerning others, the one to whom this was evident ought not to believe it, and it would be lawful for him to contradict in this matter and to deny the general council. But the one to whom this is not evident ought, as far as those things that are matters of fact are concerned, to believe the assertion and testimony of the general council, presuming that the general council, as regards matters of fact, would assert nothing except what was certain to it. Just as also a judge is bound to believe witnesses, even those whom he cannot reject, and ought to regard them as competent and truthful, although in the truth of the matter they depose what is false. Nor does a judge sin by believing false witnesses in ignorance; indeed he would sin if he did not believe them, since he has nothing against them from which he could suspect that they are saying what is false. So the faithful, believing in ignorance a general council that is in error, do not sin in such a matter; indeed, if they were unwilling to give credence, they would sin, since they have nothing against the general council. If, however, a general council were to err about other things than those which are matters of fact (for example those things which are asserted in the sacred letters concerning God or creatures), it would not be lawful for any Christian to whom this was not evident to deny the assertion of the general council, nor to dispute about it publicly, unless some learned men of laudable opinion were to oppose it. And this is so that scandal may be avoided, and so that due honour and reverence may be shown to the general council by everyone who does not know that it errs in such matters. Likewise, each person who previously held the contrary assertion, but had not been certain explicitly, ought to presume in favour of the assertion of the general council and adhere to it conditionally, provided that it is not contrary to Catholic truth; so that they do not publicly hold the contrary opinion, even by opining it, yet in their mind they may opine the contrary and seek the truth by diligently searching the Scriptures. If, however, the general council does not err concerning such things as do not consist in fact, it is not lawful for anyone, especially by public assertion, to deny it, nor to opine the contrary, nor in any way, even by doubting, to defend publicly the contrary, even if he had previously held the contrary opinion. For no one can be certain about the contrary, since it is false, although someone who is deceived might think he is certain. If, however, it does not err concerning those things which consist in fact, all Christians ought without doubt to believe it, because since it does not err, Christians cannot reasonably suspect that it is deceived by any error in asserting or narrating the truth of the event that took place.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Exponendo praecedens capitulum 6. quaerit, quare aliter debent se habere Christiani adhaerendo in concilio generali in his quae sunt facti: & aliter in his, quae sunt scientia & iuris.
units.tr: Expounding the preceding chapter 6, he asks why Christians ought to hold themselves in one way when they adhere to a general council in matters of fact, and in another way in matters of knowledge and law.

units.la: Discipulus. Ista opinio multa tenet, quae magna discussione indigere videntur. De quibus forsan postea conferam tecum. Sed omissis ad praesens aliis, solummodo dicas, quare dicit aut innuit, quod aliter se possunt & debent habere Christiani in adhaerendo concilio generali, cum asserit aliquid circa ea quae facti sunt, & cum aliquid asserit circa alia, illa (scilicet quae scientiae sunt, & non facti. Magist. Ut hoc melius intelligas, scire debes, quod ea quae facti sunt in multiplici differentia sunt. Quaedam enim explicite in scripturis Divinis habentur, sicut quod Apostoli circumibant cum Christo, quod Paulus fuit Romae, & huiusmodi quae in libris historialibus Bibliae affirmantur. Quaedam vero non reperiuntur in Biblia, sed ab aliis quam a scriptoribus Bibliae, eorum accipitur certitudo, qui ipsa explicite in suis interuerunt historiis. Quaedam autem in huiusmodi solum habentur implicite, ita quod absq; subtili deductione ex illis minime elici possunt. Quaedam autem in libris huiusmodi non habentur, sed ipsis narrantibus per seipsos sunt nota. Et de istis principaliter intelligit opinio supra scripta. Rursus, non solum eorum quae facti sunt, sed etiam aliorum quaedam continentur in scripturis divinis explicite, & quaedam implicite, ita quod nisi a doctis cum magno labore, & studio ex illis quae in scripturis habentur, inferri non possunt. Et de illis etiam locuta est memorata opinio.
units.tr: Disciple. This opinion holds many things which seem to require long discussion. Perhaps I will confer with you about them later. But setting other matters aside for now, just tell me why he says, or hints, that Christians can and ought to hold themselves differently in adhering to a general council when it asserts something about matters of fact, and when it asserts something about those other things (namely those of knowledge, and not of fact). Teacher. To understand this better, you should know that matters of fact differ in many ways. Some are stated explicitly in the divine Scriptures, such as that the apostles went about with Christ, that Paul was at Rome, and such things as are affirmed in the historical books of the Bible. Others are not found in the Bible, but their certainty is received from others than the writers of the Bible, namely from those who explicitly took part in the events in their own histories. Still others are contained in such matters only implicitly, so that they cannot be drawn out from those texts without subtle deduction. Others again are not contained in such books, but are known to those who relate them through their own experience. And it is principally of these that the opinion written above speaks. Again, not only matters of fact but also other things are contained in the divine Scriptures, some explicitly and some implicitly, so that unless they are drawn out from what is in the Scriptures by learned men with great labour and study, they cannot be inferred. The aforesaid opinion also speaks of these.

units.la: Ex his dicitur, quod quia pauciores homines rarius decipiuntur, vel decipi possunt in factis & gestis, quæ per seipsos cognoscunt, quam in his, quæ solummodo ex aliis subtilis & multis incognita ratiocinatione eliciunt. Ideo magis creditur hominibus in his quæ asserunt se vidisse, vel audiuisse, aut aliquo sensu alio percepisse, quam in his quæ ex dictis aliorum, vel etiam ex sibi notis arguendo concludunt.
units.tr: From this it is said that, because fewer men are less often deceived, or can be deceived, in facts and deeds which they know through themselves, than in those things which they deduce only from others by subtle and many-stepped reasoning that is unknown to most, therefore men are more readily believed in what they assert they have seen, heard, or perceived by some other sense, than in what they conclude by arguing from the sayings of others, or even from things known to themselves.

units.la: Unde & sæpe Doctori Theologiæ de aliquo facto testimonium perhibenti, multi absque dubio credunt: qui tamen opinionibus eius, quantum ad ea quæ sunt scientiæ & iuris (quamuis firmissime, imo pertinaciter adhæreat eis) non credunt. Imo ipsum errare & falsa dicere, & asserere firmissime putant. Quia tenent quod scienter non diceret falsum, & arbitrantur, quod de illo quod est facti est certus, quem deceptum circa alia, scilicet scientiæ & iuris arbitrantur. Sic dicunt de concilio generali, quod cum asserit aliquid quod facti est, quod dicit per seipsum cognoscere, vel invenisse explicite in scripturis diuinis, vel in libris illorum, quibus quantum ad illa quæ asseruntur se cognoscere per seipsos, est credendum ab omnibus, qui de contrario non sunt, vel non possunt esse certi, semper est adhibenda fides concilio generali, nisi possit probari contrarium. Quo ad alia autem, quæ taliter minime cognoscuntur, sed solummodo arguendo ex aliis accipitur eorum notitia à petitis & scientibus argumenta sophistica à veris discernere, non est necessarium, tantam credulitatem præstare concilio generali. Eo quod notum est per certum plures literatos, & qui periti putantur, quantumcunq; sint in concilio generali, nescire in multis sophismata à veris argumentis discernere. Quia tamen plurimi fallaciarum naturam ignorantes: etiam qui memoriam literarum supra alios habere noscuntur, non solum in Theologia & Philosophia, sed etiam in scientiis legalibus paralogisantur, credentes demonstrationem & infallibile facere argumentum, quando (quamuis ignoranter) sophistice omnino procedat. Ideo quando in generali concilio congregati, præsertim si pauci sint, sicut aliquando fuerunt solummodo undecim, quemadmodum probatum est prius, & in scientia discernendi sophisticas rationes à veris sunt minime eruditi, vel non sunt notabiliter excellentes, non est tanta fides adhibenda eisdem, quando ratiocinando ex aliis quamuis indubiis, aliquam assertionem determinant, quanta adhibenda eis esset, si aliquid quod facti est, assertive proferrent, firmiter affirmando, hoc vel per seipsos evidenter cognoscere, vel per illos quibus omnino in huiusmodi est credendum.
units.tr: Hence also, when a teacher of theology bears witness to some fact, many believe him without doubt; yet they do not believe his opinions as regards matters of knowledge and law (although he cleaves to them most firmly, indeed stubbornly). Rather, they think he errs, says what is false, and asserts it with great firmness. For they hold that he would not knowingly say what is false, and they judge that he is certain about what is a fact, while they think he is deceived about the other things, namely matters of knowledge and law. So they say of a general council: when it asserts something that is a fact, which it says it knows through itself, or has found explicitly in the divine Scriptures, or in the books of those men whose testimony on those things it asserts they know through themselves, it must always be given faith by all who are not, or cannot be, certain to the contrary, unless the contrary can be proved. But as to other things, which are not known in this way but are only got by arguing from others, it is not necessary to show such great credulity to a general council, since it is known for certain that many learned men, and those thought skilled, however numerous they may be in a general council, do not know how to distinguish sophistical arguments from true ones in many matters. Yet many who are ignorant of the nature of fallacies, even those known to have a memory of letters above others, are led astray not only in theology and philosophy but also in legal sciences, believing that they make a demonstration and an infallible argument when it proceeds entirely sophistically, though through ignorance. Therefore, when a general council is gathered, especially if it is small, as at times there were only eleven, as has been proved before, and its members are hardly learned in the science of distinguishing sophistical reasons from true ones, or are not notably outstanding, then they do not deserve the same faith when they determine some assertion by reasoning from other matters, however undoubted, as they would deserve if they put forward something that is a fact, asserting it firmly, and affirming that they know it evidently through themselves, or through those whom in such matters they must wholly be believed.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Ad rationem primæ opinionis primo respondet quarta opinio, ostendendo quod concilium generale non innititur revelationi diuinæ, neq; Spiritui sancto, nisi secundum influentiam generalem: & hoc duabus rationibus.
units.tr: The fourth opinion first answers the argument of the first opinion, showing that a general council does not rest on divine revelation or on the Holy Spirit, except through general influence, and it does so on two grounds.

units.la: DIscipulus. Reor me aduertere intellectum opinionis prædictæ: quæ quo ad multa fundatur in hoc, quod concilium generale potest contra fidem errare: cuius contrarium tenet & probare conatur prima opinio superius r. c. recitata. Ad cuius allegationes narra qualiter ista opinio vltima nititur respondere. Magist. Ad primam cum inquit, quod pie tenendum est interpretationes concilii generalis esse nobis revelatas ab eodem spiritu, à quo revelatæ sunt Diuinæ scripturæ. Respondetur, quod non est necesse, nec semper oportet omnes Christianos hoc credere, quia concilium generale sæpe innititur vel inniti potest sapientiæ humanæ: quæ deviare potest à vero. Et ideo non oportet de necessitate salutis credere: quod quicquid concilium generale diffinit circa fidem tenendum, quod illud diffiniat tanquam sibi revelatum à Deo, & quod tunc spirituali revelationi innititur. Quod pluribus modis videtur probari. Nam vbi aliquid speratur reuelandum à Deo, non studio & meditationi humanæ, sed solummodo orationi vel aliis bonis operibus oportet insistere: vel saltem minus oportet insistere studio, quam aliis operibus bonis.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I think I understand the sense of the opinion just mentioned, which on many points rests on the claim that a general council can err against the faith. The first opinion, recited above in the chapter cited, holds the contrary and tries to prove it. Please tell me how this last opinion sets about answering its arguments. MASTER. To its first argument, that we are rightly to hold that the interpretations of a general council have been revealed to us by the same Spirit by whom the divine Scriptures were revealed, the answer is that it is not necessary, nor is it always required, that all Christians believe this. A general council often rests, or can rest, on human wisdom, which can depart from the truth. Therefore it is not necessary for salvation to believe that whatever a general council defines concerning faith must be held as if God had revealed it to that council, and that the council then rests on spiritual revelation. This seems to be proved in several ways. Where something is hoped to be revealed by God, one must devote oneself not to human study and meditation, but only to prayer or other good works; or at least one must devote oneself to study less than to other good works.

units.la: Hinc est quod cum Daniel speraret somnium Nabuchodonosor & interpretationem eius sibi revelandam à Deo, locios suos hortabatur, vt non per studium, quamuis essent docti, sed per orationem & supplicationem à Deo tantum quærerent sacramentum. Quod postea per orationem seafseruit Daniel consecutum, cum dicat ca. 2. Tibi Deus patrum nostrorum confiteor, teq; laudo, quia sapientiam & fortitudinem dedisti: & nunc ostendisti mihi, quæ rogauimus te: quia sermonem regis aperuisti nobis. Hinc etiam Christus, quia promisit Apostolis se revelaturum eisdem, quæ oporteret eos loqui, cum ducendi essent ante reges & præsides, ipsis inhibuit ne studio tunc vacarent, dicens eis, vt habetur Matth. 1. Cum autem tradent vos, nolite cogitare, quomodo, aut quid loquamini. Dabitur enim vobis in illa hora, quid loquamini. Non enim vos estis qui loquimini, sed Spiritus patris mei, qui loquitur in vobis. Quando igitur per revelationem aliquid solummodo est Iperandum, non est studio & meditationi humanæ, sed orationi vacandum. Sed cum in concilio generali est quæstio fidei terminanda, meditationi scripturarum insistitur. Ergo non per revelationem est necessaria quæstio fidei in concilio generali terminanda, sed per sapientiam, quæ habetur & haberi potest per studium & meditationem humanam, poterit eadem quæstio terminari, licet Deus de gratia speciali ipsam valeat revelare. Non est tamen tenendum certitudinaliter, quod per revelationem habeatur, nisi Deus hoc miraculose & aperte revelet. Amplius, quando certitudinaliter tenendum est aliquid per revelationem habendum, pro eodem adipiscendo non ad sapientiores, sed ad meliores, siue sint literati siue illiterati, siue clerici siue laici, siue sint viri siue fœminæ: vel ad Prophetas, est rationabiliter recurrendum.
