[illegible, ~40 letters] sed melioribus Deus communiter sua secreta revelat. Quod veritas ipsa testatur, dicit Matth. 11. Confiteor tibi Domine pater coeli & terre, quia abscondisti hoc a sapientibus & prudentibus, & revelasti ea parvulis. Hinc sanctus ille rex Iosias, ut habetur 3. Reg. 22. cum vellet per revelationem voluntatem Dei de verbis voluminis reperti in templo, misit ad Elchiam sacerdotem, & etiam ipsos sacerdotes & peritos legis Divinae: & ab ipsis sacerdotibus & peritis legis veritatem minime requisivit, licet Malachiae 2. dicantur: labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam & legem requirunt ex ore eius. Quia ex ore sacerdotis, qui scientiam & legem Dei explicite scire tenetur, requirenda est lex Dei, quantum ad illa quae per exercitationem & meditationem in lege habeti possunt. Quantum ad illa autem, quae per revelationem sunt habenda, ad habentes spiritum Prophetiae, si qui sint, & ad sanctiores, quorum orationes sunt Deo magis acceptae, est principaliter recurrendum. Nec quantum ad huiusmodi est necessario magis lex requirenda ex ore sacerdotis & summi pontificis, quam ex ore viduae vel laici literas nescientis. Sed pro quaestione fidei terminanda in concilio generali, ad sapientiores magis literatos, sive sint meliores sive non, etiam secundum communem opinionem hominum recurritur. Ergo non est tenendum necessario, quod semper per revelationem Divinam quaestio fidei terminetur. Ex his colligitur, quod non est necesse tenere semper quaestionem fidei per revelationem in generali concilio terminari: sed tenendum est (nisi contrarium reveletur miraculose a Deo) quod Deus permittit, ut congregati in concilio generali, in diffiniendo quaestionem fidei, & in aliis, secundum proprium sensum procedant, assistente sibi Divina influentia generali. Et ideo conceditur, quod non est impossibile, concilium generale errare.
units.tr: Hence it is that when Daniel hoped that the dream of Nebuchadnezzar and its interpretation would be revealed to him by God, he urged his companions not to seek the mystery by study, though they were learned, but by prayer and supplication to God alone. Daniel later testified that he obtained it through prayer, when he says in chapter 2: "I confess to you, God of our fathers, and I praise you, because you have given me wisdom and strength; and now you have shown me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king's word." Hence also Christ, since he promised the Apostles that he would reveal to them what they ought to say when they were to be brought before kings and governors, forbade them to be occupied with study at that time, saying to them, as is found in Matt. 1.: "But when they deliver you up, do not be anxious how or what you are to speak; for it will be given you in that hour what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you." Therefore, when something is to be hoped for only through revelation, one must give oneself not to human study and meditation, but to prayer. But when a question of faith is to be settled in a general council, the council devotes itself to meditation on the Scriptures. Therefore the question of faith in a general council is not settled by revelation, but by wisdom. That wisdom is had, and can be had, through human study and meditation, and by it the question can be settled, although God could reveal it by special grace. Yet it is not to be held with certainty that it is had by revelation, unless God reveals this miraculously and openly. Moreover, when something is to be held with certainty as had by revelation, one should reasonably turn, to obtain it, not to the wiser, but to the better, whether they are learned or unlearned, clergy or laity, men or women, or to the prophets. [illegible, ~40 letters] but God commonly reveals his secrets to the better. Truth itself bears witness to this, when it says in Matt. 11.: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little children." Hence that holy king Josiah, as is found in 3 Kings 22, when he wished to learn by revelation the will of God concerning the words of the book found in the temple, sent to Huldah the prophetess and to the priests and skilled men of the divine law. He did not ask the truth from the priests and skilled men of the law, although Malachi 2. says: "The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and men seek the law from his mouth." For the law of God is to be sought from the mouth of the priest, who is bound to know the law and knowledge of God explicitly, insofar as those things can be had by exercise and meditation in the law. But as to those things that are to be had by revelation, one must chiefly have recourse to those who have the spirit of prophecy, if there are any, and to the holier, whose prayers are more acceptable to God. In such matters it is not necessarily more right to seek the law from the mouth of the priest and high pontiff than from the mouth of a widow or a layman who cannot read. But for settling a question of faith in a general council, recourse is had, even by the common opinion of men, to the wiser and more learned, whether or not they are better. Therefore it is not necessary to hold that a question of faith is always settled by divine revelation. From these points it follows that it is not necessary to hold that a question of faith is always settled in a general council by revelation. Rather, we must hold (unless God reveals the contrary miraculously) that God permits those gathered in a general council to proceed, in defining the question of faith and in other matters, according to their own judgment, with the divine general influence assisting them. And so it is granted that it is not impossible for a general council to err.

units.la: Quod adhuc iuxta praedicta tali modo probatur. Existentes in concilio generali, tractantes, & deliberantes, ac diffinientes quaestionem fidei, aut innituntur praecise revelationi Divinae, aut innituntur sapientiae & virtuti humanae. Primum non potest dici: quia tunc iuxta praedicta pro quaestione fidei terminanda non oportet consulere in sacra scriptura peritos, nec volumina Divina nemente revoluere, nec opus esset cogitare quomodo esset quaestio fidei terminanda: sed totum esset committendum Deo, solummodo per orationem invocando ipsum, qui solus potest revelare quamlibet catholicam veritatem. Quod tamen non fit, quando quaestio fidei est in generali concilio. Quoniam de ipsa deliberant, & veritatem ex literis sacris niituntur elicere, ut iuxta scripturas Divinas de ipsa diffiniant. Quod concilia generalia de ipsa fecisse hactenus dignoscuntur: Quia per scripturas sacras diffinierunt suborias ex scripturis fidei quaestiones. Ergo existentes in concilio generali, volentes quaestionem fidei terminare, non committunt totum Deo, ab ipso per solam orationem diffiniones quaestionis fidei postulantes. Ergo innituntur sapientiae & virtuti humanae: quia peritiae innituntur, quam habent de scripturis, & quam per meditationem sollicitam habere possunt. Sed cum in omnibus, quae innituntur sapientiae & virtuti humanae, error poterit reperiri. Ergo existentes in concilio generali circa quaestionem fidei terminandam possunt errare. Nec est necesse tenere, quod congregati in concilio generali semper & in omnibus tractatibus suis, etiam quando tractatur de quaestione fidei terminanda, aliter dirigantur a Spiritu sancto, quam Papa, quando tractat negotia cum cardinalibus in consistorio suo: vel quam patriarchae seu primates aut Archiepiscopi vel metropolitani, quando celebrant concilia provincialia: aut aliter quam Episcopi & alii praelati, quando de Ecclesiasticis disponunt negociis. Licet aliquando accidit, & adhuc poterit accidere, quod ad concilium generale venientes, specialiter a Spiritu sancto dirigantur: & quod eis miraculose veritates aliquae revelantur: & quod Deus eos miraculose ab omni errore praeservet: ac diffinitionem eorum circa fidem, & alia ordinata per ipsos manifestis confirmet miraculis. Sed absque operatione miraculi non est necesse tenere, quod aliter aliquid reveletur a Spiritu sancto vocatis ad concilium generale, quam conciliis provincialibus, & aliis congregationibus Christianorum, de quibus constat, quod non sic dirigantur a Spiritu sancto, quin possint errare tam in moribus quam in fide. Ergo non est necesse asserere contrarium de omni concilio generali. Item, illa congregatio potest errare contra fidem, quae potest in negotiis male procedere, & malo exitu terminari. Sed haec de concilio generali possunt contingere. Nam, ut habetur 7. q. 1. c. principatus, difficile fit ut bono peragantur exitu, quae malo sunt inchoata principio. Ex quo patet, quod omnis congregatio, quae malo potest inchoari principio, potest non bono exitu terminari. Concilium autem generale potest inchoari malo principio. Concilium enim generale congregandum est per Papam, ut habetur dist. 17. per totum. Papa autem cum possit peccare & damnari, ac contra fidem errare mala intentione & corrupta: imo intentione aliquid diffiniendi contra catholicam veritatem, potest congregare generale concilium. Igitur concilium generale malo principio, & corrupta intentione congregatum, malo exitu peragi potest. Et per consequens poterit contra fidem errare.
units.tr: This is further proved in the following way, in line with what has been said. Those who are in a general council, discussing, deliberating, and defining a question of faith, either rest solely on divine revelation or rest on human wisdom and strength. The first cannot be said. For then, by what has been said, in settling a question of faith it would not be necessary to consult skilled men in Holy Scripture, nor to turn over the divine volumes diligently, nor would there be any need to think how the question of faith is to be settled. Everything would be committed to God alone, calling upon him only in prayer, since he alone can reveal any catholic truth. Yet this is not what happens when a question of faith is before a general council. For they deliberate about it and strive to draw the truth from the sacred letters, so that they may define it according to the divine Scriptures. This is known to have been done by general councils until now, for they have defined by the Scriptures the questions of faith that arose from the Scriptures. Therefore those in a general council who wish to settle a question of faith do not commit everything to God, asking him for the definition of the question through prayer alone. Therefore they rest on human wisdom and strength, because they rest on the skill they have in the Scriptures, which they can acquire through careful meditation. But error can be found in all things that rest on human wisdom and strength. Therefore those in a general council may err in settling a question of faith. Nor is it necessary to hold that those gathered in a general council are always and in all their deliberations, even when a question of faith is being settled, directed by the Holy Spirit in a different way than the Pope when he deals with business with his cardinals in consistory; or than patriarchs, primates, archbishops, or metropolitans when they celebrate provincial councils; or than bishops and other prelates when they settle ecclesiastical affairs. It has sometimes happened, and may still happen, that those coming to a general council are specially directed by the Holy Spirit, that some truths are revealed to them miraculously, that God preserves them miraculously from all error, and that he confirms their definition of faith and their other decisions by manifest miracles. But without the working of a miracle, it is not necessary to hold that anything is revealed by the Holy Spirit to those called to a general council differently from provincial councils and other assemblies of Christians, of which it is certain that they are not so directed by the Holy Spirit that they cannot err both in morals and in faith. Therefore it is not necessary to assert the contrary of every general council. Likewise, that assembly can err against the faith which can proceed badly in its affairs and end in a bad outcome. But such things can happen to a general council. For, as is found in 7 q. 1 c. Principatus: "It is hard for things begun with a bad beginning to be carried through to a good end." From this it is plain that every assembly that can be begun with a bad beginning can end without a good outcome. A general council, however, can be begun with a bad beginning. For a general council is convened by the Pope, as is found in dist. 17 throughout. But the Pope, since he can sin and be condemned, and err against the faith through an evil and corrupt intention, indeed with the intention of defining something against catholic truth, can convene a general council. Therefore a general council convened with a bad beginning and a corrupt intention can be carried through to a bad end. And consequently it can err against the faith.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad alias rationes prima opinionis.
units.tr: In which it is answered to the other arguments of the first opinion.

units.la: Discipulus. Indica quomodo antedicta opinio ad alias allegationes supra cap. 1. huius tertii adductas respondere conatur. Magist. Ad illam, quae in promissione Christi Matth. ultimo est fundata: respondetur, quod Christus futurus est cum Ecclesia universali usque ad consummationem seculi. Et ideo (vt dicit Rabanus, sicut allegatum est) vsq; in finem seculi non sunt defuturi in mundo, qui diuina mansione & inhabitatione sunt digni. Ex quibus verbis Rabani colligitur, quod dicta promissio Christi non debet intelligi de concilio generali. Tum, quia non dicit, non sunt defuturi in concilio generali: sed dicit, in mundo. Tum quia raro concilium generale est in mundo. Vniuersalis autem Ecclesia semper vsq; ad consummationem seculi erit in mundo. Ergo secundum Rabanum illa promissio Christi, non de concilio generali, sed de vniuersali Ecclesia debet intelligi, vt pie & absq; dubio est tenendum semper Spiritum sanctum adesse vniuersali Ecclesiæ. Sic etiam Hieronymus de vniuersali Ecclesia intelligit, cum dicit, Christum nunquam à credentibus recessurum, quia semper erunt vsque ad consummationem seculi aliqui Christo credentes, siue concilium generale sit, siue non sit. Ad illam allegationem, quæ in Actibus 15. est fundata, respondetur dupliciter. Vno modo quod determinatio facta per Apostolos, & seniores, de qua fit mentio Actuum 15. facta fuit per revelationem Spiritus sancti miraculosam, qualis adhuc fieri posset in concilio generali. Sed non est necesse quod fiat, nec semper fuit facta, nec forte semper fiet quandocunq; celebrabitur concilium generale. Nec est inconueniens dicere, aliquas revelationes factas Apostolis: tamen tales non posse fieri in omni concilio generali.
units.tr: Disciple. Show how the aforementioned opinion attempts to answer the other allegations brought forward above in chapter 1 of this third part. Master. To that argument founded on Christ's promise at the end of Matthew, the reply is that Christ will be with the universal Church until the end of the age. And so (as Rabanus says, as has been quoted) there will never be lacking in the world, until the end of the age, those who are worthy of the divine dwelling and indwelling. From these words of Rabanus it is gathered that the said promise of Christ ought not to be understood of a general council: first, because he does not say "they will not be lacking in a general council" but "in the world"; second, because a general council is rarely in the world, whereas the universal Church will always be in the world until the end of the age. Therefore, according to Rabanus, that promise of Christ is to be understood not of a general council but of the universal Church, so that we hold, piously and without doubt, that the Holy Spirit is always present with the universal Church. So also Jerome understands it of the universal Church, when he says that Christ will never withdraw from believers, because there will always be some who believe in Christ until the end of the age, whether there is a general council or not. To the allegation founded on Acts 15, the reply is twofold. In the first way: the decision made by the apostles and elders, mentioned in Acts 15, was made by a miraculous revelation of the Holy Spirit, such as could still happen in a general council. But it is not necessary that it happen, nor has it always happened, nor perhaps will it always happen whenever a general council is held. Nor is it unreasonable to say that some revelations were made to the apostles, yet such revelations cannot occur in every general council.

units.la: Aliter dicitur, quod Apostoli & seniores absq; revelatione Spiritus sancti tunc facta eis, ex verbis Christi quæ ab ore eius audierant, & ex factis eius quæ viderant, collegerunt determinationem illam. Viderunt enim ipsum non seruasse legalia multa, & ceremonialia, qui & docuerat eos, non esse necessarium seruare eadem. Quare absq; revelatione speciali poterant scire, quod credentes conuersi ex gentibus, ad huiusmodi seruanda minime tenebantur. Vnde & Apostolus Paulus ante congregationem illam hoc constanter asseruit. Quod non fecisset, nisi certus de hoc antea extitisset. Et quamuis si omnes alii contradixissent, ipse tamen à sua sententia minime recessisset, ipso attestante, cum ait ad Galatas 1. Licet nos aut angelus de cœlo &c. nec tamen pertinax extitisset, licet omnibus aliis resitisset. Et quia circa verum scienter assertum non potest pertinacia inueniri. Cum ergo dixerunt Apostoli, & seniores: visum est Spiritui sancto & nobis &c. sub tali intellectu dixerunt, sub quali dixit Apostolus 1. Corinth. 12. Nemo potest dicere Dominum Iesum, nisi in Spiritu sancto. Quia omnia bona sunt à Spiritu Sancto, quamuis Deus in omni tali sermone non faciat nouum miraculum. Et eodem modo respondetur ad auctoritates plurimas afferentes sententialiter, quod sancti patres in conciliis generalibus congregati, illa quæ diffinierunt, statuerunt, & egerunt, à Spiritu sancto inspirati fecerunt. Et per consequens interpretationes, quas fecerunt circa dubia fidei diffinienda, eis revelata fuerunt. Quia non ideo dicuntur à Spiritu sancto fuisse inspirati, quia ipsis tunc Spiritus sanctus vltra influentiam Spiritus sancti, quæ ad omne opus placens Deo requiritur, aliquod modo speciali, & non solito inspirauit: sed quia Spiritus sanctus ipsos monuit ad rectam diffinitionem fidei faciendam, sicut omnes monet ad quæcunq; opera meritoria exercenda. Propter quod iuxta sanctorum patrum sententiam, concilia generalia, quæ rite, iuste, sancte, & canonice celebrata fuerunt, sunt ab omnibus catholicis devotissime suscipienda, amplectenda & veneranda. Si tamen non fuissent catholice celebrata, quamuis omnes Episcopi orbis terræ præsentes affuissent, non essent à fidelibus recipienda, sed penitus respuenda. Et si quæratur, quis habet iudicare, an fuerint catholice celebrata? Respondetur, quod quia non diffinierunt aliquid, nisi quod potest elici ex scripturis diuinis: ideo periti in scripturis & habentes aliarum sufficientem intelligentiam scripturarum, habent iudicare per modum firmæ assertionis, quod diffinita ab eis sunt catholice diffinita. Summi autem pontifices si non fuerint præsentes, sed tantummodo auctoritate eorum, præsentibus legatis ipsorum, celebrata fuerunt autentice, iudicare habent quod catholice extiterint celebrata. Si autem summus pontifex præsens fuerit, sufficit quod autenticet ipsa. Discip. Nunquid secundum istam opinionem licet alicui, cui non constat concilium generale rite, & catholice celebratum fuisse, negare illud, quod est per idem concilium diffinitum vel saltem dubitare? Magist. Respondetur per distinctionem. Quia tua interrogatio est generalis, non specificans an concilium generale catholice diffiniat, vel erronee. Quia aut concilium generale catholice diffinit aliquid esse credendum, aut erronee. Si catholice: nulli licet publice negare, vel etiam publice dubitare taliter diffinitum. Nulli etiam licet pertinaciter occulte vel etiam mentaliter de tali etiam diffinito dubitare. Non tamen tenetur quis, etiam cui constat generale concilium catholice diffinisse, explicite & absolute absq; omni contradictione explicita & implicita, siue subintellecta credere taliter diffinitum: sed sufficit quod credat implicite. Si vero aliquid diffinitur erronee per generale concilium, siue per congregationem quæ à multitudine fidelium generale concilium æstimatur, ille quoniam scit generale concilium siue talem congregationem errare, præsumere debet pro tali concilio vel congregatione, non tamen præsumptione tam violenta, quin probatio sit in contrarium admittenda. Sicut præsumendum est pro sententia iudicis, quamuis in rei veritate iniusta fuerit & iniqua, donec probetur vel constet contrarium. Et ideo postquam per sacras scripturas constitit tale concilium errasse, (siue approbetur, siue reprobetur à Papa) tali generali concilio nullatenus est credendum; sed ab omnibus scientibus etiam publice pro loco & tempore reprobandum. Discip. Dic quomodo respondetur ad allegationem sequentem. Magist. Ad illam quæ consistit in hoc, quod congregatio fidelium, seu concilium generale per successionem vere repræsentat congregationem Apostolorum, seniorum, ac reliquorum fidelium. Respondetur, quod sola Ecclesia vniuersalis illam congregationem perfectissime repræsentat. Et illa sola sibi succedit proprie & primo. Et ideo illa sola errare non potest. Concilium autem generale nequa-
units.tr: Another answer is that the Apostles and elders reached that decision without any revelation of the Holy Spirit given to them at that time, from the words of Christ that they had heard from his mouth and from his deeds that they had seen. For they saw that he himself had not observed many of the legal and ceremonial precepts, and he had taught them that it was not necessary to observe them either. Therefore, without a special revelation, they could know that converts from the Gentiles were in no way bound to keep such things. Hence the Apostle Paul also asserted this firmly before that assembly. He would not have done so unless he had been certain of it beforehand. And although, if all the others had contradicted him, he would nevertheless not have departed from his opinion, he himself bears witness to this when he says to the Galatians in chapter 1: "Even if we or an angel from heaven..." He would not have been obstinate, even if he had resisted everyone else, because obstinacy cannot be found in one who knowingly asserts what is true. So when the Apostles and elders said, "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us," etc., they spoke in the sense in which the Apostle said in 1 Corinthians 12: "No one can say that Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit." For all good things are from the Holy Spirit, although God does not work a new miracle in every such utterance. In the same way, we reply to the many authorities that state in summary form that the holy Fathers, gathered in the general councils, did, decreed and settled what they defined, being inspired by the Holy Spirit. And consequently, the interpretations they made concerning doubtful matters of faith to be defined were revealed to them. For they are not said to have been inspired by the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit then breathed into them in some special and unusual way, beyond that influence of the Holy Spirit which is required for every work pleasing to God; rather, the Holy Spirit admonished them to make a correct definition of the faith, just as he admonishes all people to undertake every meritorious work. For this reason, according to the opinion of the holy Fathers, the general councils that were celebrated duly, justly, holily and canonically are to be received, embraced and venerated most devoutly by all Catholics. Yet if they had not been celebrated in a Catholic manner, even if all the bishops of the world had been present, they would not be to be received by the faithful but utterly rejected. And if it is asked who has the right to judge whether they were celebrated in a Catholic manner, the answer is this: since they defined nothing except what can be drawn from the divine Scriptures, therefore those who are skilled in the Scriptures and have sufficient understanding of the other Scriptures have the right to judge, by way of a firm assertion, that what was defined by them was defined in a Catholic manner. But if the supreme pontiffs were not present, yet the councils were celebrated authentically by their authority, with their legates present, they have the right to judge that they were celebrated in a Catholic manner. If, however, the supreme pontiff himself was present, it is enough that he authenticates them. Disciple: Then, according to this opinion, is it permitted for someone who is not certain that a general council was duly and catholically celebrated to deny what was defined by that same council, or at least to doubt it? Master: The answer is given by a distinction. For your question is general, not specifying whether the general council defines catholically or erroneously. For a general council either defines something to be believed catholically or erroneously. If catholically, it is permitted to no one to deny it publicly, or even publicly to doubt what has been so defined. Nor is it permitted to anyone to doubt, obstinately and in secret or even in the mind, such a definition. Yet a person, even one who knows that a general council has defined catholically, is not bound to believe explicitly and absolutely, without any explicit or implicit contradiction, or even tacit contrary understanding, that it has been so defined; it is enough that he believes implicitly. But if something is defined erroneously by a general council, or by an assembly which is taken by the multitude of the faithful to be a general council, the one who knows that the general council or such assembly has erred ought to presume in favour of that council or assembly, yet not with a presumption so violent that proof to the contrary is not to be admitted. Just as one must presume in favour of a judge's sentence, even if in the truth of the matter it was unjust and iniquitous, until the contrary is proved or established. And therefore, once it has been established from the holy Scriptures that such a council has erred, (whether it is approved or rejected by the Pope) it is by no means to be believed in such a general council; rather, it must be rejected by all who know it, even publicly, according to place and time. Disciple: Tell me how you reply to the following allegation. Master: To that which consists in this, that the congregation of the faithful, or a general council, through succession truly represents the congregation of the Apostles, the elders and the rest of the faithful. The answer is that the universal Church alone represents that congregation most perfectly. And that alone succeeds to it properly and first. And therefore that alone cannot err. But a general council does not by any means represent it most perfectly, nor does it succeed to it first.

units.la: Hieronymus; Rabanus; Actus 15. requaquam perfectissime repræsentat eam, nec ipsum illi primo succedit. Neq; successio illa, quam Christus promisit, cessset, ex quo sæpe cessat concilium generale. Illam tamen congregationem Apostolorum & aliorum repræsentat & quodammodo sibi succedit. Quemadmodum Papa cum collegio cardinalium aliquo modo repræsentat congregationem eandem, & aliquo modo succedunt: qui tamen tam in pertinentibus ad fidem, quam in moribus possunt errare. Et ita per repræsentationem & successionem huiusmodi probari non potest, quod concilium generale errare nequit.
units.tr: Hieronymus; Rabanus; Acts 15. A general council by no means represents that gathering most perfectly, nor does it succeed to it first. Nor has that succession which Christ promised ceased, since a general council often ceases to exist. Yet it does represent the congregation of the Apostles and the others, and in a certain way succeeds to it. In the same way, the Pope with the college of cardinals in some sense represents that same congregation and in some sense succeeds to it, yet they can err both in matters pertaining to faith and in morals. And so it cannot be proved, by such representation and succession, that a general council cannot err.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Vbi pro quinta allegatione prima opinionis in 1. c. duplicem distinctionem ponit, per quas etiam respondetur ad eandem.
units.tr: Where, in answer to the fifth allegation of the first opinion in the same place, he sets out a twofold distinction, by which the allegation is also answered.

units.la: Discipulus. Narra quomodo respondetur ad vltimam allegationem adductam ad probandum, quod concilium non potest errare, quæ consistit in hoc quod frustra dedisset Christus legem salutis æternæ, si eius verum intellectum quærentibus minime revelaret. Magist. Respondetur per duplicem distinctionem. Quarum prima est, quod eorum quæ in conciliis generalibus determinantur & determinari possunt, & similiter quæ possunt esse dubia circa fidem: quædam sunt quæ ex scripturis diuinis deductione infallibili possunt inferri, ita quod quamuis nec illud quod infertur, nec illud vel illa ex quo vel ex quibus infertur, possit vel possunt naturali ratione esse notum vel nota: tamen illatio potest naturaliter esse nota, cum etiam illatio falsi ex falso & falsis possit naturaliter & infallibiliter esse nota. Quædam sunt quæ ex scripturis diuinis infallibili deductione inferri non possunt: quemadmodum beatum Hieronymum & beatam virginem esse corporaliter in coelo ex scripturis certitudinaliter haberi non potest. Sicut etiam nec, quod illi de quibus dicitur Matth. 27. Multa corpora sanctorum surrexerunt cum eo &c. corporaliter ascenderint in coelum, nec quod corporaliter non ascenderunt, infallibiliter deduci non potest ex scripturis diuinis.
units.tr: Student. Tell me how the last allegation is answered, the one brought to prove that a council cannot err, which holds that Christ would have given the law of eternal salvation in vain if he did not reveal its true meaning to those who seek it. Master. It is answered by a twofold distinction. The first is this: among the things that are or can be determined in general councils, and likewise among the things that can be doubtful concerning the faith, some can be inferred from the divine Scriptures by infallible deduction, so that even though neither the conclusion itself nor the premise or premises from which it is drawn can be known by natural reason, the inference itself can be known naturally, since the inference of a falsehood from falsehoods can also be known naturally and infallibly. Other things cannot be inferred from the divine Scriptures by infallible deduction. Thus it cannot be held with certainty from Scripture that the blessed Jerome and the blessed Virgin are bodily in heaven. Likewise, from the divine Scriptures it cannot be inferred infallibly either that those of whom it is said in Matt. 27. Many bodies of the saints which slept arose and came out of the graves after his resurrection ascended bodily into heaven, or that they did not ascend bodily.

units.la: Secunda est, quod dubium circa fidem siue circa diuina, & ea quæ spectant ad salutem potest esse duplex. Quia aliquod est, cuius notitia explicita est necessaria ad salutem: & aliquod, cuius notitia explicita non est necessaria ad salutem. Per hoc respondetur ad allegationem prædictam, quia in concilio generali proponitur aliquod dubium terminandum, quod ex scripturis Diuinis deductione infallibili & naturaliter nota saltem sapientibus & peritis potest inferri: aut proponitur aliquid terminandum, quod ex scripturis Diuinis inferri non potest, sed per solam reuelationem Diuinam potest haberi. Rursus aut necessaria est fidelibus notitia illius, quod proponitur in generali concilio determinandum, aut non est necessaria fidelibus. Si illud quod proponitur in concilio generali potest infallibili deductione ex scripturis Diuinis inferri, & notitia eius est necessaria fidelibus, non exclusa oratione & aliis operibus bonis, debent sapientes in concilio generali congregati diligentissime scrutari scripturas sacras, exemplo illorum, de quibus dicitur Act. 17. Susceperunt verbum cum auiditate quotidie scrutantes. Si enim hæc itaque habeant, ne concilium generale & quilibet catholicus tentare Dominum videatur, cum aliquid sibi incumbit agendum, debet facere quicquid rationabiliter & prouide potest, exemplo Abrahæ, qui secundum August. in quæstionibus Genesis & habetur 23. q. 2. c. queritur, cum ingrederetur Ægyptum, timens propter pulchritudinem uxoris Ægyptios, quod potuit, fecit: quod non potuit Deo committit, in quem sperauit.
units.tr: The second distinction is that a doubt concerning the faith, or concerning divine matters and those things that pertain to salvation, can be of two kinds: one whose explicit knowledge is necessary to salvation, and one whose explicit knowledge is not necessary to salvation. By this the aforementioned allegation is answered: in a general council some doubt is proposed to be settled which can be inferred from the divine Scriptures by infallible deduction and is naturally known at least to the wise and learned; or something is proposed to be settled which cannot be inferred from the divine Scriptures but can be had only by divine revelation. Again, either the knowledge of what is proposed for determination in a general council is necessary for the faithful, or it is not necessary for them. If what is proposed in a general council can be inferred from the divine Scriptures by infallible deduction, and its knowledge is necessary for the faithful (prayer and other good works not being excluded), the wise men gathered in a general council ought most diligently to search the sacred Scriptures, after the example of those of whom it is said in Acts 17. They received the word with all readiness, and searched the Scriptures daily. For if these things are so, lest a general council or any Catholic seem to tempt the Lord, when something is incumbent upon them to do, they ought to do whatever they can do reasonably and prudently, after the example of Abraham, who, according to Augustine in his Questions on Genesis, and as is found in 23. q. 2. c. queritur, when he was about to enter Egypt and feared the Egyptians on account of his wife's beauty, did what he could, and committed to God, in whom he hoped, what he could not do.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Quoniam 10. c. quinta allegationi prima opinionis non ex toto, sed incomplete respondit: ideo nunc completam solutionem & ad formam repetit & soluit.
units.tr: Since in the tenth chapter he answered the first objection of the first opinion only in part and not fully, he now repeats the objection in its complete form and resolves it.

units.la: Discipulus. Per prædicta narra, quomodo respondetur ad allegationem contrarium opinantium. Magist. Respondetur, quod cum accipiunt, frustra dedisset Christus legem salutis æternæ, si eius verum intellectum & quem credere fidelibus est necessarium ad salutem, non aperiret eisdem hunc quærentibus, & pro ipso muocantibus simul, sed circa ipsum fidelium pluralitatem errare sineret; respondetur, quod si per pluralitatem fidelium, hoc est Christianorum recte credentium intelligant totam Ecclesiam seu congregationem fidelium, loquendo de vero intellectu cuiuscunq; contenti in lege Diuina, qui est necessarius ad salutem secundum quod verba eorum prætendunt: & de apertione talis intellectus per scripturas vel revelationem congregatis in concilio generali concedo antecedens. Nam & quando celebratur concilium generale & quando non celebratur multa necessaria ad salutem aperiuntur vel aperiri possunt tam per scripturas quam per revelationem miraculosam illis, qui non sunt in concilio generali, per quos ad existentes in concilio generali potuerunt peruenire, si digne exiterit celebratum vel fuerit necessarium Christiano populo ad salutem. Et ita ex hoc probari non potest, quod necesse sit credere determinationes conciliorum generalium in sensibus scripturæ dubiis a Spiritu sancto suæ veritatis originem habere illo modo, quo scripturæ Diuinæ eius sunt scriptoribus inspiratæ. Tum, quia intellectus legis necessarius ad salutem potest aliis aperiri vel per scripturas vel per miraculosam operationem. Quod non debet mirabile vel incredibile reputari, cum plures sæpe sapientiores & meliores non coniunctunt ad concilium generale, quam sint ibi congregati: possitq; generale concilium intentione corrupta vocari. Et etiam quamuis intentione recta fuerit congregatum, poterit tamen non rite postea celebrari, cum ibi congregati non sint nec in fide, nec in gratia, & bonis moribus confirmati: sed forte aliquando vel omnes vel plures fuerint aut esse potuerint peccatis grauibus inuoluti. Et ideo lex Christi non est inutilis, nec in hominũ tradita perniciem. Quia siue verus intellectus ipsius reueletur, vel aliter manifestetur existentibus in concilio generali, siue non venientibus ad idem concilium generale, vtilis poterit esse ad salutem aeternam, ipsam pie quaerentibus atq; recte. Multa enim quo ad intellectum legis Diuinæ, reuelauit Deus, & in modis aliis manifestauit peritis viris, & sanctis, & imperitis, qui ad generale concilium minime conuenerant: & non solum quia celebratur generale concilium, sed in tempore concilii generalis: & adhuc potens est Deus facere idem: tum quia intellectus legis ad multa potest aperiri per considerationem scripturarum, absq; hoc quod Spiritus sanctus modo speciali aperiat quibuscunq; intellectum ipsarum. Tum quia in concilio generali multa dubia circa fidem declarari possunt, quae non sunt necessaria ad salutem. Tum quia ostensum est prius, quod concilium generale, seu quod concilium generale a maiori parte Christianorum putatur, potest errare contra fidem. Si vero taliter opinantes per pluralitatem fidelium intelligant maiorem partem fidelium, siue Christianorum, & per intellectum legis intelligant absq; omni exceptione intellectum cuiuscunq; contenti in lege diuina: & intelligant loqui de quaerentibus intellectum ipsum: pro omni tempore nego antecedens. Item, si quaesierint huiusmodi intellectum & pro ipso inuocauerint, multipliciter errare possunt: nihilominus tamen antecedens non haberet veritatem, quod patet. Primo, quia non frustra esset lex salutis aeternae data Christo, quamuis maior pars fidelium, imo omnes praeter paucissimos, vel praeter vnum, errarent non solum damnabiliter, sed execrabiliter circa ipsum etiam circa intellectum, qui est necessarius ad salutem. Nec esset frustra data lex, licet omnes Christiani praeter paucos vel vnum damnabiliter errarent circa ipsum: quia tota fides Christiana absq; hoc, quod frustra esset data lex salutis aeternae in vno solo posset saluari. Quemadmodum in triduo tota fides in sola matre Redemptoris nostri permansit. Secundo, multa sunt contenta in scripturis diuinis, quorum verus intellectus primus & literalis non est omni tempore necessarius ad salutem: quamuis ab existentibus in concilio generali quaeratur solutio tam per meditationem vehementem in scripturis, quam per orationem, ita vt ipsum omnino diffinire proponant. Non est igitur necessarium credere, quod Deus aperiat ipsis per scripturas vel per reuelationem miraculosam huiusmodi. Quia quamuis Deus non deficiat Ecclesiæ suæ, scilicet congregationi fidelium in necessariis, tamen non semper praebet se ad illa, quæ non sunt necessaria ad salutem, sine quibus potest esse salus, quamuis ipsa nitantur precibus continuis impetrare.
units.tr: Student. Explain from what has been said how the objection of those who hold the contrary opinion is answered. Master. The answer is this: when they assert that "in vain would Christ have given the law of eternal salvation, if he did not disclose its true meaning, which the faithful must believe for salvation, to those who seek it and call upon him together, but allowed the faithful multitude to err about it," the answer is that if by "the multitude of the faithful" they understand, rightly, the whole Church or congregation of the faithful, that is, of Christians who believe rightly, speaking of the true meaning of whatever is contained in the divine law, which is necessary for salvation according to what their words intend, and of the disclosure of such meaning through the Scriptures or revelation to those gathered in a general council, then I grant the antecedent. For both when a general council is held and when it is not, many things necessary for salvation are, or can be, disclosed, both through the Scriptures and through miraculous revelation, to those who are not in a general council, and through them they could have reached those who are in a general council, if it has been worthily held or has been necessary for the Christian people for salvation. And so it cannot be proved from this that it is necessary to believe that the determinations of general councils, in doubtful senses of Scripture, have their origin of truth from the Holy Spirit in the same way in which the divine Scriptures were inspired in their writers. Further, because the true meaning of the law, necessary for salvation, can be disclosed to others either through the Scriptures or through a miraculous operation. This ought not to be thought wonderful or incredible, since often many wiser and better men do not assemble at a general council, more than those who are gathered there; and a general council can be called with a corrupt intention. And even if it has been gathered with a right intention, it may nevertheless afterwards be held improperly, since those gathered there are not confirmed in faith, in grace, and in good morals, but perhaps at some time either all or most of them have been, or could have been, entangled in grave sins. And therefore the law of Christ is not useless, nor was it handed down to the ruin of men. For whether its true meaning is revealed to those present at a general council, or is otherwise made manifest to them, or to those not coming to the same general council, it can be useful for eternal salvation to those who seek it piously and rightly. For God has revealed many things concerning the meaning of the divine law, and has manifested them in other ways, to skilled and holy men, and to the unlearned, who by no means assembled at a general council; and this not only because a general council is held, but at a time when a general council is held; and God is still able to do the same. Further, because the meaning of the law can be disclosed in many matters through the consideration of the Scriptures, without the Holy Spirit disclosing the meaning of them to whoever it may be in a special way. Further, because in a general council many doubtful matters concerning the faith can be declared which are not necessary for salvation. Further, because it has been shown before that a general council, or what is thought to be a general council by the greater part of Christians, can err against the faith. But if those holding such an opinion understand by "the multitude of the faithful" the greater part of the faithful or Christians, and by "the meaning of the law" understand, without any exception, the meaning of whatever is contained in the divine law, and understand that they speak of those seeking that very meaning, I deny the antecedent for every time. Likewise, if they have sought such a meaning and called upon it for help, they can err in many ways; nevertheless the antecedent would not be true, which is clear. First, because the law of eternal salvation would not have been given to Christ in vain, even though the greater part of the faithful, indeed all but very few, or all but one, erred not only damnably but execrably, even about that meaning which is necessary for salvation. Nor would the law have been given in vain, even if all Christians except a few or one erred damnably about it; for the whole Christian faith could be saved, apart from this, in one alone, so that the law of eternal salvation was not given in vain. In the same way, during the three days the whole faith remained in the mother of our Redeemer alone. Second, many things are contained in the divine Scriptures whose true and literal meaning is not at all times necessary for salvation, although a solution is sought from those present at a general council, both through vehement meditation on the Scriptures and through prayer, so that they propose to define it completely. It is therefore not necessary to believe that God discloses such things to them through the Scriptures or through miraculous revelation. For although God does not fail his Church, that is, the congregation of the faithful, in necessary matters, yet he does not always grant those things which are not necessary for salvation, without which salvation can be, even though they strive to obtain them by continual prayers.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: In quo contra duo praedicta obiicit & replicat in secunda parte solutionis: ad quae respondetur capitulo 13. & 14.
units.tr: In which he raises objections against the two points stated above, and argues back in the second part of the solution; to these answers are given in chapters 13 and 14.

units.la: Discipulus. Contra praedicta obiiciam aliqua: vt cum audiero responsiones ad ipsa, clarius intelligam, an praescripta aliquid contineant veritatis. Hoc itaq; videtur, quod nullo modo sit credendum, quod concilium generale possit diffinire contra catholicam veritatem. Nam sicut illi saepe accipiunt, qui opinantur praedicta, Deus nunquam deficiet in necessariis congregationi fidelium, quae est Ecclesia Dei. Sed concilium generale non diffinire aliquid contra fidem est necessarium Ecclesiæ suæ. Tum, quia totam Ecclesiam Dei non exponi periculo haeresis & errorum est necessarium Ecclesiæ Dei. Si autem concilium generale aliquid diffiniret contra fidem, tota Ecclesia Dei exponeretur periculo haeresis & erroris. Quia nemo tunc inueniretur, qui posset aut sciret defendere fidem contra concilium generale. Tum, quia non induci in tentationem est necessarium Ecclesiæ Dei. In oratione enim, quam Christus fideles docuit vniuersos, hoc petitur. Christus autem non docuit in Oratione Dominica petere nisi necessaria. Ergo non induci in tentationem est necessarium Ecclesiæ Dei. Tota autem Ecclesiæ Dei induceretur in tentationem grauissimam, si concilium generale aliquid diffiniret contra fidem. Ergo non diffinire aliquid contra fidem est necessarium Ecclesiæ Dei. Ex quo infertur, quod credendum est, concilium generale non posse errare contra fidem. Tum, quia illud concilium, quod est suscipiendum sicut sanctum Euangelium, non potest errare contra fidem. Concilium autem generale recipiendum est, sicut sanctum Euangelium, teste Greg. qui, vt habetur di. 15. sicut, ait: Sicut sancti Euangelis quatuor libros, sic quatuor concilia recipere & venerari me fateor. Igitur concilium generale errare contra fidem non potest. Tum quia vniuersalis Ecclesia errare non potest. Diffinitio autem & iudicium generalis concilii tanquam diffinitio vniuersalis Ecclesiæ debet haberi, quia vniuersali consensu constituta videtur, vt Gregorius vbi prius videtur asserere, dicens: Cunctos vero, quas prafata veneranda concilia personas respuunt, respuo, & quas venerantur completur: quia dum vniversali sunt constituta consensu, se & non illa destruet, quisquis praesumit absoluere, quos ligant, aut ligare quos absoluunt. Huic Gelasius Papa concordare videtur: qui, vt habetur 15. q. 1. 5. confidimus, ait: Confidimus quia nulla causa venerationis Christianus ignoret vnuscuiusq; synodi constitutum, quod vniuersalis Ecclesia probetur assensu, nullam exequi magis sedem pra ceteris oportere, quam primam. Ex quibus colligitur, quod id quod fecit concilium generale, ab vniuersali fit Ecclesia. Et per consequens concilium generale errare non potest. Secundo, contra prædicta specialiter, quo ad hoc quod dicit, quod non omnium contentorum in lege diuina verum intellectum esse omni tempore necessarium ad salutem, obiici potest. Nam si alicuius contenti in lege diuina verus intellectus & primus non esset omni tempore necessarius ad salutem, frustra illud fuisset positum in ipsa lege diuina, cum ipsa lex diuina non nisi propter salutem electorum fuit data. Sed posset dici de eo, vt quid membranas occupat? dist. 19. si Romanorum. vbi dicit Glossa: Ex hoc accipitur argumentum, quod nullum verbum positum in aliqua scriptura debet vacare, nec poni superflue. Verus ergo intellectus & primus omnium contentorum in ipsa lege diuina est necessarius ad salutem.
units.tr: Disciple. I will raise some objections against what has been stated, so that when I hear the replies I may understand more clearly whether the things set out above contain any truth. It seems, then, that it ought in no way to be believed that a general council can define anything against catholic truth. For, as those who hold the aforesaid often argue, God will never fail the congregation of the faithful, which is the Church of God, in necessary things. But it is necessary for the Church of God that a general council not define anything against the faith. Again, it is necessary for the Church of God that the whole Church of God not be exposed to the danger of heresy and error. But if a general council were to define anything against the faith, the whole Church of God would be exposed to the danger of heresy and error, for then no one would be found who could or would know how to defend the faith against a general council. Again, it is necessary for the Church of God not to be led into temptation. For this is what is asked in the prayer which Christ taught all the faithful. But Christ taught us in the Lord's Prayer to ask only for what is necessary. Therefore not being led into temptation is necessary for the Church of God. But the whole Church of God would be led into the gravest temptation if a general council were to define anything against the faith. Therefore not defining anything against the faith is necessary for the Church of God. From this it follows that it must be believed that a general council cannot err against the faith. Again, because that council which is to be received as the holy Gospel cannot err against the faith. But a general council is to be received as the holy Gospel, as Gregory attests, who says, as it is found in dist. 15, "Sicut": As I confess that I receive and venerate the four books of the holy Gospels, so I receive and venerate the four councils. Therefore a general council cannot err against the faith. Again, because the universal Church cannot err. But the definition and judgment of a general council must be held as the definition of the universal Church, because it seems to be established by universal consent, as Gregory seems to assert in the passage cited before, saying: Those persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, I reject; and those whom they venerate, I venerate. For since they have been established by universal consent, whoever presumes to absolve those they bind, or to bind those they absolve, destroys not them but himself. Pope Gelasius seems to agree with this, who, as is found in 15 q. 1, c. "Confidimus," says: We are confident, since no Christian ought to be ignorant of the ground of veneration for the decree of any synod, that it is approved by the assent of the universal Church, and that no see ought to claim precedence over the others, but only the first. From these things it is gathered that what a general council does is done by the universal Church, and consequently a general council cannot err. Secondly, against the aforesaid, specifically as to what he says, that a true understanding of all the contents of the divine law is not at all times necessary for salvation, an objection can be raised. For if the true and primary sense of some content of the divine law were not at all times necessary for salvation, it would have been placed in that divine law in vain, since the divine law was given only for the salvation of the elect. But one might ask of it, "why does it occupy parchment?" dist. 19, "si Romanorum," where the Gloss says: From this an argument is drawn, that no word placed in any Scripture ought to be idle, or placed to no purpose. Therefore the true and primary sense of all the contents of the divine law itself is necessary for salvation.

units.la: Amplius: verus intellectus eorum, quæ in noua lege traduntur, fuit necessarius ad salutem illis, qui fuerunt summi in veteri testamento. nam necesse fuit maiores in veteri testamento, trinitatis, & incarnationis mysterium explicite, & non solum implicite credere. ergo cuiuslibet expresse scripti in lege diuina, tam noua, quam veteri intellectus verus est necessarius ad salutem, vt saltem aliqui primum explicite credant, & non ignorent. Hæc sunt inter alia, quæ possunt obiici contra prædicta, ad quæ aliquas responsiones audire desidero.
units.tr: Further: the true sense of those things which are handed down in the New Law was necessary for salvation to the great men of the Old Testament. For it was necessary for the ancestors in the Old Testament to believe explicitly, and not only implicitly, the mystery of the Trinity and of the Incarnation. Therefore the true understanding of every expressly written passage in the divine law, both New and Old, is necessary for salvation, so that at least some first believe explicitly and do not remain ignorant. These are among the other things that can be objected against the aforesaid, and I desire to hear some replies to them.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Quod concilium generale possit errare, obiectiones respondendo defendit.
units.tr: That a general council can err; the objections are answered in its defence.

units.la: DISCIP. Ad primum respondetur per distinctionem de necessario, quia aliquid esse necessarium ecclesiæ Christi dupliciter potest intelligi: vel quia est vtile: vel quia sine illo non est necessarium: non est necessarium: vnquam erit salus.
units.tr: PUPIL. The first objection is answered by a distinction concerning the word "necessary," since to say that something is necessary to the Church of Christ can be understood in two ways: either because it is useful, or because without it there is never salvation.

units.la: Primo modo, accipiendo necessarium, concilium generale non diffinire aliquid contra catholicam veritatem est necessarium ecclesiæ Dei, sicut Papam non errare nec diffinire aliquid contra fidem est necessarium, id est vtile. sed quantum ad omnia talia necessaria, Christus non semper adest ecclesiæ: quinimo contraria permittit, vel potest permittere euenire. vnde & plures summi pontifices errauerunt pertinaciter contra fidem.
units.tr: In the first sense, taking "necessary" as "useful," it is necessary to the Church of God that a general council not define anything against catholic truth, just as it is necessary (that is, useful) that the Pope not err nor define anything against the faith. But as regards all such necessary things, Christ does not always stand by the Church; rather he permits contrary things, or can permit them to happen. Hence also several supreme pontiffs have stubbornly erred against the faith.

units.la: Secundo modo, accipiendo necessarium; concilium generale non errare contra fidem, non est necesse ecclesiæ: quia quamuis concilium generale erret, in multitudine fidelium, posset tamen per veram & catholicam fidem saluari. quinimo haberet scripturas sacras, quibus errorem concilii generalis posset conuincere manifeste, si diffiniret aliquid contra ipsas. si autem diffiniret aliquid esse tenendum, tanquam de necessitate fidei, quod tamen non esset necesse credere, poterant eisdem scripturas possent Christiani alii aperte ostendere, quod taliter diffinitum ad fidem minime pertineret.
units.tr: In the second sense, taking "necessary," it is not necessary to the Church that a general council not err against the faith, because although a general council might err, the multitude of the faithful could nevertheless be saved through true and catholic faith. Moreover, they would have the holy Scriptures, by which they could clearly refute the error of a general council if it defined anything against them. If, however, it defined something to be held as of necessity of faith, which it would not be necessary to believe, other Christians could plainly show from those same Scriptures that what was so defined did not pertain to faith at all.

units.la: Cum autem accipitur, si concilium generale diffiniret aliquid contra fidem, tota ecclesia Dei exponeretur periculo hæresis & erroris. Respondetur per distinctionem de periculo. est enim quoddam periculum tantummodo imminens seu circumstans: & est periculum inuoluens seu prosternens. Periculo imminenti seu circumstanti totam ecclesiam Dei exponi, negari non debet, sed concedi. hoc enim fatetur ecclesia ipsa, cum in quadam Collecta dicit: Deus qui nos in tantis periculis constituitos, &c. à quibus liberari deposcimus cum alibi dicit: à cunctis nos mentis & corporis defende periculis. talibus periculis expositus fuit apostolus Paulus, sicut ipse fatetur. 2. Corinth. 1. & à quolibet se liberatum fuisse dicit. 1. cum ait: de tantis periculis eripuit nos. In tali periculo etiam fuit aliquando tota ecclesia Dei, quæ erat sub veteri testamento, Deuteronomio 20. Dominus Deus vester in medio vestri est, pro vobis contra aduersarios dimicabit, & eruet vos de periculis. tali enim periculo se exponere ex causa rationabili est laudabile iudicandum. Vnde etiam in laudem prælantium contra infideles dixit Delbora, vt habetur Iudicum. 5. Ponte obtulistis de Israel animas vestras ad periculum. Inuoluens periculum seu prosternens est duplex: scilicet spirituale & corporale. sed neutri exponetur tota ecclesia Dei: licet corporaliter multi ex fidelibus inuoluantur non nunquam. Spirituale autem finaliter nullus electus incurreret, & de tali periculo videtur intelligere Sapiens, cum Ecclesiastici. 5. ait: Qui amat periculum, in illo peribit. Si itaque concilium generale diffiniret aliquid contra fidem, poterit tota ecclesia Dei exponi periculo hæresis & erroris. primo modo, accipiendo periculum, quemadmodum aliquando quia non potuit concilium generale conuocari, Christianitas quo ad multos fuit periculo hæresis conuoluta, & quo ad alios impugnata, teste Isidoro, qui, vt legitur di. 15. ait enim: In præcedentibus namque donu persecutione feruente, docendarum plebium minime dabatur facultas: inde Christianitas in diuersas hæreses scissa est. Posset tamen contingere, quod quamuis generale concilium diffiniret aliquid contra fidem, ecclesia Dei non exponeretur periculo: quia posset contingere, quod congregati in concilio generali essent pauci & viles tam in re quam in hominum reputatione, respectu illorum, qui ad illud concilium generale minime conuenissent. Et tunc illorum leuiter error extirpatur per multitudinem meliorum & sapientiorum & famosiorum illis, quibus etiam multitudo simplicium adhæreret, magis scilicet quam decem vel duodecim aut quindecim, per quos posset generale concilium celebrari. quemadmodum in concilio Arelatensi tantummodo vndecim patres fuerunt. dist. 16. sexta: quamuis tunc multiplicati fuerunt Christiani, & plures occupauerunt provincias, quam diebus nostris. Periculo autem inuoluenti seu etiam prosternenti nequaquam exponeretur tota ecclesia Dei, quamuis concilium generale diffinitret aliquid contra fidem: quia remanerent aliqui vel multi vel pauci, qui tali diffinitioni erroneae minime consentirent: sed pro loco & tempore contradicerent manifeste.
units.tr: But when it is taken that, if a general council defined something against the faith, the whole Church of God would be exposed to danger of heresy and error, the answer is given by a distinction concerning danger. There is a danger that merely threatens or surrounds, and there is a danger that involves or prostrates. That the whole Church of God is exposed to threatening or surrounding danger must not be denied but conceded. The Church itself confesses this when in a certain Collect it says: O God, who have placed us in such great dangers, etc., and elsewhere: Defend us from all dangers of mind and body. The apostle Paul was exposed to such dangers, as he himself confesses, 2 Cor. 1, and he says he was delivered from each of them, when he says: "He delivered us from so great dangers" [2 Cor. 1:10]. The whole Church of God was also at one time in such danger under the old covenant, Deuteronomy 20: "The Lord your God is in the midst of you; he will fight for you against your enemies and will deliver you from dangers." For to expose oneself to such danger for a reasonable cause is rightly judged praiseworthy. Hence also, in praise of those who fought against unbelievers, Deborah said, as is found in Judges 5: "You have offered your souls to danger from Israel." Danger that involves or prostrates is twofold, namely spiritual and bodily. But the whole Church of God will be exposed to neither, although many of the faithful are sometimes involved bodily. No elect person would finally fall into spiritual danger, and the Wise Man seems to mean this kind of danger when he says in Ecclesiasticus 5: "He who loves danger will perish in it." If therefore a general council defined something against the faith, the whole Church of God could be exposed to danger of heresy and error in the first sense of danger, just as sometimes, when a general council could not be convened, Christianity was for many entangled in danger of heresy, and for others was assailed, as Isidore testifies; as read in dist. 15, he says: "For in earlier times, while persecution raged, there was no opportunity to teach the peoples; hence Christianity was split into various heresies." It could nevertheless happen that, although a general council defined something against the faith, the Church of God would not be exposed to danger, because it could happen that those gathered in the general council were few and worthless, both in reality and in men's estimation, compared with those who had not come to that general council. Then their error is easily uprooted by the multitude of better, wiser and more famous men, to whom a multitude of simple folk would also cling, more, that is, than ten or twelve or fifteen, by whom a general council could be held. So it was at the council of Arles, where there were only eleven fathers (dist. 16). Sixth: although Christians were then more numerous and occupied more provinces than in our days. But the whole Church of God would by no means be exposed to danger of involvement or prostration, even if a general council defined something against the faith, because some, either many or few, would remain who would by no means consent to that erroneous definition, but would openly contradict it according to place and time.

units.la: DISCIP. Saltem multitudo Christianorum, maxime laicorum & simplicium, prosternenti exponeretur periculo, potissime si Papa esset praesens in tali concilio, atque errori huiusmodi consentiret: & Papa cum consentientibus sibi potentior esset aliis, quod tamen pro inconvenienti debet haberi.
units.tr: PUPIL. At least the multitude of Christians, especially laymen and simple folk, would be exposed to prostrating danger, most of all if the Pope were present at such a council and consented to such an error; and the Pope with those who agreed with him would be stronger than the others, which nevertheless must be regarded as an inconvenience.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur, quod in tali casu magis timendum est de periculo clericorum in sacris literis peritorum & aliorum, quam de multitudine laicorum, id est simplicium, praesertim quando multitudo clericorum per avaritiam, ambitionem, simoniam, & alias vias pravas ad ordines, dignitates, & beneficia ecclesiastica pervenisset, & aliis esset criminibus irretita, quia plura & maiora temporalia amitteret, quam simplices laici, si Papae temporaliter praevalenti persequerantur resisterent: & ab obtinendis dignitatibus & beneficiis ecclesiasticis clericos repelleret Papa, non laicos. Propter quod procliviores essent clerici ad assentiendum errori Papae & concilii generalis, quia ut testatur Iohannes Papa, prout legitur. 16. q. 2. c. 1. Humani mores est illum vereri, cuius iudicio & voluntate nunc erigitur, nunc deprimitur. clerici etiam propter sacrarum literarum maiorem noticiam, quam habent vel tenentur habere (& quia quaestio fidei licet spectet ad laicos, dist. 86. c. ubi nam, principalius tamen pertinet ad clericos) magis peccarent & gravius quam laici. & ideo magis verendum esset, ne Deus eos permitteret ruere in errorem. multitudo insuper Christianorum (dum tamen alii vel saltem unus fidelis remaneat) potest inuoluenti periculo haeresis & erroris (aliis exigentibus peccatis ipsorum) exponi. quibus in haereticam pravitatem labentibus valet ille qui de lapidibus potest suscitare filios Abrahae, vel de aliquibus ipsorum aut de aliis, quando voluerit numerum Christianorum augere.
units.tr: MASTER. The answer is that in such a case one must fear more for the danger from clerics skilled in Holy Letters and others than for the multitude of laymen, that is, simple folk, especially when the multitude of clerics had come to orders, dignities and ecclesiastical benefices through avarice, ambition, simony and other wicked ways, and were entangled in other crimes. For they would lose more and greater temporal goods than simple laymen if they resisted the Pope while he prevailed temporally, and the Pope would repel clerics, not laymen, from obtaining dignities and ecclesiastical benefices. For this reason clerics would be more inclined to assent to the error of the Pope and of the general council, as Pope John testifies, as read in 16 q. 2 c. 1: "It is human custom to revere him by whose judgment and will one is now raised up and now cast down." Clerics also, on account of their greater knowledge of Holy Letters, which they have or are bound to have (and although a question of faith concerns laymen, dist. 86 c. ubi nam, it pertains more principally to clerics), would sin more and more gravely than laymen. Therefore it would be all the more to be feared lest God allow them to fall into error. Moreover, the multitude of Christians (provided that another, or at least one faithful person, remains) can be exposed to the overwhelming danger of heresy and error, other sins of theirs requiring it. When they slip into heretical depravity, he who can raise up sons of Abraham from stones is able, from some of them or from others, whenever he wishes, to increase the number of Christians.

units.la: DISCIP. Indica breviter, qualiter respondetur ad allegationes sequentes, quibus probatur concilium generale non posse errare contra fidem.
units.tr: PUPIL. Briefly indicate how one answers the following allegations, by which it is proved that a general council cannot err against the faith.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad ista, quibus accipit, quod ecclesia Dei induceretur in temptationem gravissimam, si concilium generale aliquid contra fidem diffiniret. Respondetur, quod toram ecclesiam Dei induci in temptationem dupliciter intelligi potest. vel ut temptatio insurgat & ne hoc accidat, petitur in Oratione Dominica: & nunquam contingit, nec contingeret, quamuis concilium generale contra fidem erraret. vel ut temptatione impugnetur, quae graviter infestetur. & hoc poterit contingere, teste beato Iacobo, qui c. 1. suae canonicae ait: omne gaudium existimate fratres charissimi, cum in temptationibus variis inciderit is.
units.tr: MASTER. To those allegations by which it is argued that the Church of God would be led into the most grievous temptation if a general council defined anything against the faith: the answer is that the whole Church of God being led into temptation can be understood in two ways. Either as temptation arising, and that this should not happen is asked for in the Lord's Prayer; and this never happens, nor would it happen even if a general council erred against the faith. Or as the Church being assailed by a temptation which grievously harasses it. And this can happen, as the blessed James testifies, who says in chapter 1 of his Epistle: "Count it all joy, my dearest brethren, when you fall into various temptations."

units.la: Ad allegationem sequentem tenentem, quod generale concilium recipiendum est, sicut sanctum Euangelium secundum Gregorium. Respondetur, quod hoc intelligendum est de generali concilio rite, iuste & catholice celebrato. secundum quod dicitur, omnes apostolicae sedis sanctiones debere accipi. sicut si voce Petri essent firmatae secundum Gratianum dist. 19.
units.tr: To the following allegation, which holds that a general council is to be received as the holy Gospel, according to Gregory, the answer is that this must be understood of a general council rightly, justly and catholically celebrated; in accordance with this it is said that all the decrees of the apostolic see ought to be accepted, as if they had been confirmed by the voice of Peter, according to Gratian, dist. 19.

units.la: Hoc autem intelligi debet de illis sanctionibus vel decretalibus epistolis, in quibus nec praecedentium patrum decretis, nec euangelicis praeceptis aliquid contrarium inuenitur: ita tamen, quod hoc vocabulum, sicut omnimodam similitudinem nequaquam importet, sicut nec Math. 5. cum dicit Christus: estote perfecti sicut pater vester caelestis perfectus est: necillud c. 22. diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. hoc illud Iohannis 10. sicut misit me pater & ego mitto vos. quamuis enim generale concilium aliquid rite & catholice diffiniat & determinet: & ideo sicut sanctum euangelium suscipiendum. Sanctum tamen euangelium cum maiori reuerentia & devotione suscipiendum est quam concilium generale quodcunque.
units.tr: This, however, must be understood of those decrees or decretal letters in which nothing contrary is found either to the decisions of the earlier Fathers or to the precepts of the Gospel. Yet the word "as" (sicut) does not imply complete likeness in every respect, just as when Christ says in Matthew 5, "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect," or in the chapter quoted, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself," or as in John 10, "As the Father sent me, so I send you." For although a general council rightly and catholically defines and determines something, and therefore is to be received as the holy Gospel is received, the holy Gospel is still to be received with greater reverence and devotion than any general council whatsoever.

units.la: Ad aliam autem allegationem accipientem, quod diffinitio generalis concilii tanquam diffinitio universalis ecclesiae debet haberi. Respondetur, quod concilium generale non debet regulariter occulte seu secrete aut paucis scientibus celebrari: sed vulgandum est per universalem ecclesiam, hoc est per omnes regiones in provincia, in qua seu in quibus catholici commorantur, generale concilium convocari debere, quatinus omnes catholici tacite vel expresse consentiant, & quasi auctoritatem tribuant, ut ad concilium profecturi eorum nomine circa ordinanda & diffiniendam in generali concilio canonice & catholice atque rite procedant, ut merito quicquid catholice & licite statuerint vel diffinierint, universali statuatur & diffiniatur assensu. At vero si quid indigne aut illicite, & non canonice vel non catholice statuerint vel diffinierint, universalis ecclesiae nullatenus statutum vel diffinitum probetur assensu. Talis enim assensus ad nihil illicitum potest extendi: quia talis assensus ecclesiae universalis est secundum intentionem assentientium interpretandus, quemadmodum iuramentum secundum intentionem iurantis interpretari debet, ut notat Glossa extra de iureiurando. super c. quintavallii. Quando igitur concilium generale rite convocatur, & in omnibus catholice & sancte procedit, quicquid fecerit, ab vniuersali ecclesia fieri est putandum. & ideo de tali concilio generali loquitur Gregorius & Gelasius. Si autem aliquid fecerit illicite & non catholice, minime vniuersalis ecclesiæ probatur assensu. quia vniuersalis ecclesia, quamuis consenserit, quod conuocaretur concilium generale, non tamen putanda est nec expresse nec tacite aliquod illicitum consentire. Aliter respondetur, quod postquam acta generalis concilii per vniuersos catholicos populos fuerint promulgata, si nullus contradicens aut impugnans apparet, sunt putanda ab vniuersali ecclesia approbata. & de talibus conciliis loquuntur Gregorius & Gelasius. Si autem acta generalis concilii non fuerint apud omnes populos catholicos diligenter exposita, non est dicendum, quod tale concilium generale sit explicite ab vniuersali ecclesia approbatum, licet si sanctè & catholice fuerit celebratum, possit dici implicite ab vniuersali ecclesia approbatum.
units.tr: To another allegation, which holds that the definition of a general council must be regarded as the definition of the universal Church, the answer is this: a general council ought not, as a rule, to be convened secretly or privately or with only a few knowing of it, but it must be made known throughout the universal Church. That is, a general council ought to be summoned through all the regions of the province, or of the provinces, in which Catholics dwell, so that all Catholics may consent, tacitly or expressly, and in a sense grant their authority, so that those who set out for the council may proceed canonically, catholically and rightly in the matters to be ordered and defined in the general council in their name. Thus whatever is decided and defined catholically and lawfully may rightly be established and defined with the assent of the universal Church. But if anything is decided or defined unworthily, unlawfully, uncanonically or uncatholically, it cannot be shown to have been established or defined with the assent of the universal Church. For such assent cannot extend to anything unlawful, since the assent of the universal Church must be interpreted according to the intention of those who assent, just as an oath must be interpreted according to the intention of the one swearing, as the Gloss notes on Extra, de iureiurando, on the chapter Quintavallii. Therefore, when a general council is rightly convened and proceeds in all things catholically and holily, whatever it does is to be thought done by the universal Church; and it is of such a general council that Gregory and Gelasius speak. But if it does anything unlawfully and uncatholically, it is not shown to have the assent of the universal Church, since the universal Church, although it consented that a general council be convened, is not to be thought to have consented, either expressly or tacitly, to anything unlawful. There is another answer: once the acts of a general council have been published among all Catholic peoples, if no one appears contradicting or opposing them, they are to be thought approved by the universal Church; and it is of such councils that Gregory and Gelasius speak. But if the acts of a general council have not been carefully set out before all Catholic peoples, it cannot be said that such a general council has been explicitly approved by the universal Church, although, if it was held holily and catholically, it may be said to have been implicitly approved by the universal Church.

units.la: DISCIP. Istud est calumniabile, vt videtur. nam non minus ligat quicquid statuitur vel diffinitur per concilium generale, quam statutum apostolicæ sedis. sed illud vniuersalem ligat ecclesiam, ex de constitutionibus, omnium. nec oportet ad hoc, vt liget, quod omnium auribus inculcetur, extra de postulα. ad hoc. Igitur & quicquid statuitur vel diffinitur à concilio generali vniuersalem ligat ecclesiam: & per consequens pro approbato ab vniuersali ecclesia est habendum.
units.tr: STUDENT. This seems open to challenge. For whatever is decided or defined by a general council binds no less than a decision of the apostolic see. But the latter binds the universal Church, as in De constitutionibus, Omnium; and it is not necessary, in order to bind, that it be impressed on everyone's ears, as in Extra, De postulatione, Ad hoc. Therefore whatever is decided or defined by a general council also binds the universal Church, and consequently must be held as approved by the universal Church.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur, quod statutum apostolicæ sedis etiam post duos menses non ligat, nisi illos ad quos ipsius notitia poterat peruenire. quia ignorantes præsertim ignorantia inuincibili, minime ligat, extra de constitu. cognoscentes. Sic etiam q statuitur vel diffinitur in concilio generali, non ligat vniuersalem ecclesiam, nisi per vniuersalem ecclesiam fuerit legitime diuulgatum. & ideo non est censendum explicite approbatum ab vniuersali ecclesia, antequam taliter publicetur. non oportet autem taliter diffinitum singulorum auribus inculcare: sed sufficit taliter publicare, quod nullus se possit si in contrarium venerit per ignorantiam excusare.
units.tr: TEACHER. The answer is that a decision of the apostolic see does not bind, even after two months, except those to whom knowledge of it could come. For those who are ignorant, especially with invincible ignorance, are not bound, as in Extra, De constitutionibus, Cognoscentes. So too, what is decided or defined in a general council does not bind the universal Church unless it has been lawfully made known throughout the universal Church. Therefore it is not to be considered explicitly approved by the universal Church before it has been published in this way. It is not necessary, however, to impress such a definition on the ears of each individual; it is enough to publish it so that no one who acts against it can excuse himself by ignorance.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad illud, quod secundo & principaliter obiicitur, c. 12. Contra illud quod non omnium contentorum in lege diuina verus intellectus est omni tempore necessarius ad salutem.
units.tr: In which is answered the second and principal objection, ch. 12: against the claim that the true sense of not all the contents of the divine law is necessary for salvation at all times.

units.la: DISCIP. Nunc superest tractare ista, quæ secundo obiecta sunt contra dicta superius c. 12. quibus videtur ostensum; quod omnium contentorum in scripturis diuinis verus intellectus & primus omni tempore necessarius ad salutem. narra igitur quomodo opinantes illi respondent ad ipsa.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Now remains to treat those things which were objected a second time against what was said above in ch. 12, by which it seems to have been shown that the true and primary sense of all the contents of the divine Scriptures is necessary for salvation at all times. Tell me, then, how those holding that opinion reply to them.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad primum illorum, cum dicitur, quod frustra esset positum in scriptura illud, cuius verus intellectus non est omni tempore necessarius ad salutem. Respondetur, quod falsum assumitur. Quia ad hoc, quod aliquid non frustra ponatur in scriptura diuina, sufficit quod aliquando (licet non omni tempore) eius verus intellectus & primus sit necessarius ad salutem. Quemadmodum veritas ipsa multa dixit & protulit nequaquam frustra, quorum tamen intellectus verus non erat tunc necessarius ad salutem. mater enim sua sanctissima nunquam aliquo necessario ad salutem extitit destituta. & tamen quando Christus dixit sibi & patri putatiuo Lucæ 2.
