(quid est, quod me quærebatis? nesciebatis, quia in his quæ patris mei sunt oportet me esse?) ipsa verum intellectum & primum illorum verborum Christi non concepit, cum immediate subiungatur ibidem; & ipsi non intellexerunt verbum quod locutus est ad illos. quæ tamen sicut prius habetur, mater eius conseruabat in corde suo, verum intellectum ipsorum postea habitura. Christus etiam dixit apostolis, vt legitur Lucæ 16. Ecce ascendimus Hierosolymam & consummabuntur omnia quæ scripta sunt per prophetas de filio hominis. tradetur enim gentibus, & illudetur & flagellabitur, & conspuetur. & postquam flagellauerint, occident eum, & die tertia resurget. quorum verborum verum intellectum tunc minime habuerunt. Quia immediate subiungitur: & ipsi nihil horum intellexerunt. erat enim verbum istud absconditum ab eis, & non intelligebant quæ dicebantur. Eisdem etiam dixit Christus, vt habetur Ioha. 16. modicum & iam non videbitis me: & iterum modicum & videbitis me: quia vado ad patrem. quorum tamen verborum verum intellectum non habuerunt, quia de ipsis scribitur ibidem. dixerunt igitur ex discipulis eius adinuicem: quid est hoc quod dixit nobis, modicum & non videbitis me? & post: nescimus quid loquitur. Ex quibus aliisque quamplurimis colligitur manifeste, quod plura dixit Christus apostolis, quorum intellectum verum minime tunc habuerunt. Ex quo concluditur, quod verus intellectus illorum tunc non erat apostolis necessarius ad salutem. Cum igitur tunc essent in statu salutis, nihil defuit eis quod tunc erat eis necessarium ad salutem. Et tamen constat, quod tunc Christus non dixisset talia frustra. Ergo à simili poterunt in scripturis diuinis aliqua contineri, quamuis eorum intellectus verus & primus non sit omni tempore necessarius ad salutem.
units.tr: MASTER. To the first of them, namely that it would be in vain for something to be placed in Scripture whose true sense is not necessary for salvation at all times, the answer is that the assumption is false. For to show that something is not placed in divine Scripture in vain, it is enough that its true and primary sense be necessary for salvation at some time, though not at all times. Just so, Truth itself said and uttered many things, by no means in vain, whose true sense was not then necessary for salvation. For his most holy mother was never deprived of anything necessary for salvation. And yet when Christ said to her and to his putative father (Luke 2), "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father?", she did not grasp the true and primary sense of Christ's words, since it is immediately added in the same place that "they did not understand the word that he spoke to them." Yet, as was said before, his mother kept these things in her heart, to have their true sense later. Christ also said to the apostles, as we read in Luke 16, "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all the things written by the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, and will be mocked, and insulted, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again." They had by no means the true sense of these words at that time, since it is immediately added, "and they understood none of these things. For this saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was said." Christ also said to the same men, as found in John 16, "A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I go to the Father." Yet they did not have the true sense of these words either, as is written of them in the same place: "Some of his disciples therefore said to one another, 'What is this that he says to us, A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me?' … 'We do not know what he is saying.'" From these and many other passages it is clearly gathered that Christ said many things to the apostles whose true sense they did not then have. From this it is concluded that the true sense of those things was not then necessary for the apostles' salvation. Since, therefore, they were then in a state of salvation, nothing was lacking to them that was then necessary for salvation. And yet it is certain that Christ did not say such things in vain. Therefore, by parity of reasoning, some things may be contained in the divine Scriptures although their true and primary sense is not necessary for salvation at all times.

units.la: DISCIP. Forte dicerent ad ista, quod non est inconueniens aliqua in scripturis diuinis haberi, quorum verus intellectus non est omni tempore omnibus catholicis necessarius ad salutem; quemadmodum illa quæ dixit matri & apostolis, non erant eis necessaria ad salutem. verus tamen intellectus omnium, quae in scripturis diuinis habentur, semper est aliquibus (& si non omnibus) necessarius ad salutem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Perhaps they would reply to these arguments that it is not inconsistent for there to be things in the divine Scriptures whose true sense is not necessary for salvation to all Catholics at all times, just as those things which he said to his mother and the apostles were not necessary to them for salvation. Nevertheless, the true sense of everything contained in the divine Scriptures is always necessary for salvation to some, if not to all.

units.la: MAGIST. Vt videtur aliis, hoc non valet; quia qua ratione plurium intellectus, quae Christus dixit matri suae & apostolis, tunc nulli fidelium erat vllatenus necessarius ad salutem: ratione consimili non est inconueniens aliqua reperiri in scripturis diuinis, quorum verus intellectus nulli pro aliquo tempore est necessarius ad salutem. & tamen illa non sunt frustra posita in scripturis, nec frustra membranas occupant; quia verus intellectus ipsorum pro aliquo tempore erit aliquibus necessarius ad salutem, quo tempore idem intellectus aliquibus aperietur, vel per inuestigationem humanam ex scripturis, vel per reuelationem, si verus intellectus ipsorum humana intentione vel eruditione haberi non potest. propter quod etiam nullum verbum in scriptura diuina vacat, necaliquid est superflue positum. quia quamuis multa sunt in ea, quorum verus intellectus non est semper necessarius ad salutem, aliquibus tamen aliquando necessarius erit. Cum autem accipitur, quod verus intellectus eorum, quae in lege noua traduntur, fuit necessarius ad salutem illis qui fuerunt sub veteri testamento: respondetur, quod aliquorum, puta incarnationis & trinitatis, & non omnium erat verus intellectus literis explicitus necessarius ad salutem. quia multa continentur in lege noua, quorum verus intellectus literalis nulli in veteri testamento extitit reuelatus, quod veritas ipsa videtur asserere, cum dicit, vt habetur Math. 13. Multi prophetae & iusti cupierunt videre quae videtis, & non viderunt: & audire quae auditis, & non audierunt. & eadem sententia habetur Luc. 10.
units.tr: MASTER. As it seems to others, this does not hold. For by the same reasoning by which the meaning of many things Christ said to his mother and the apostles was at that time in no way necessary for salvation to any of the faithful, by a similar reasoning it is not inconsistent to find in the divine Scriptures some things whose true sense is at no time necessary for salvation to anyone. And yet those things are not placed in Scripture in vain, nor do they occupy the parchment for nothing; for their true sense will at some time be necessary for salvation to some, and at that time the same sense will be opened to some, either through human inquiry into the Scriptures or through revelation, if its true sense cannot be obtained by human effort or learning. For this reason also no word in divine Scripture is idle, and nothing is placed there superfluously. For although there are many things in it whose true sense is not always necessary for salvation, yet it will at some time be necessary for some. As for the objection that the true sense of those things which are handed down in the New Law was necessary for salvation to those who lived under the Old Testament, the answer is that the true sense expressed in the letter was necessary for salvation in the case of some things, for example the incarnation and the Trinity, but not of all things. For many things are contained in the New Law whose true literal sense was revealed to no one under the Old Testament, as Truth itself seems to assert when it says, as is found in Matt. 13: "Many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." The same sentence is found in Luke 10.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: Contra solutionem precedentis capituli 14, dicentis quod aliqua in lege diuina scribuntur non frustra aut superflue: & tamen quod eorum intellectus non per studium sed per solam reuelationem haberi possit; arguitur duabus rationibus, ad quas respondetur capitulo 18. infra cap. 19 & 20.
units.tr: Against the solution of the preceding chapter 14, which says that some things are written in the divine law not in vain or superfluously, and yet that their meaning can be obtained not by study but by revelation alone. It is argued on two grounds, to which an answer is given in chapter 18, and below in chapters 19 and 20.

units.la: DIS. Vnum in praemissis innuitur, f. c. 14. quod probabile omnino non videtur, q. fc. aliqua in factis literis habentur, quorum verus intellectus & primus solummodo per reuelationem diuinam haberi potest, quia quamuis posset alicui videri, quod aliqua in scripturis sacris non essent superflue posita, quorum verus intellectus per studium & meditationem in scripturis haberi non posset: sed quod per solam reuelationem diuinam haberi possit; tamen hoc non videtur probabile, quia ita posset Deus reuelare verum intellectum ipsorum, si non essent scripta, sicut, postquam sunt scripta. Cum igitur ex scripturis nulla capiatur vtilitas, nisi intelligantur: sequitur, quod illa, quorum intellectus per solam reuelationem valet haberi, prius inutiliter omnino scribuntur. Rursus non solum talia inutiliter, sed etiam periculose essent scripta. Quia ista scriptura, quae non potest intelligi, ad cuius tamen intellectum capiendum possunt niti legentes, & circa quam (si non intelligatur) periculose contingit errare, videtur esse periculosa legentibus. Sed ad capiendum intellectum quorumcunque, quae in scripturis diuinis habentur, possunt niti legentes; circa quae si erraverint, periculose errabunt. Quia, vt ait Hieronymus, & habetur 24. q. 3. c. haeresis, quicunque aliter scripturam intelligit, quam sensus Spiritus sancti flagitat, a quo scriptura est, licet ab ecclesia non receptus, tamen haereticus appellari potest. igitur periculose talia essent scripta. volentes enim ad verum intellectum ipsorum peruenire, & non valentes, laberentur faciliter in errorem. Haec inter alia sunt, quibus praedicta assertio posse improbari videtur. tu narra, quomodo respondetur ad ipsa, primo tamen nitaris pro opinione illa allegare.
units.tr: DIS. One point is hinted at in what was said above, in chapter 14, which seems altogether improbable: that some things are written in the sacred Scriptures whose true and primary meaning can be obtained only through divine revelation. For although it might seem to someone that some things in the sacred Scriptures are not set down superfluously, and that their true meaning cannot be obtained through study and meditation on the Scriptures, but only through divine revelation, this does not seem probable. God could reveal their true meaning just as well if they had not been written as after they have been written. Since, then, no benefit is drawn from the Scriptures unless they are understood, it follows that those things whose meaning can be obtained only through revelation were written to no purpose at all. Moreover, such things would not only have been written to no purpose but would also have been written dangerously. For a Scripture which cannot be understood, yet on whose meaning readers must rely, and in which (if it is not understood) it is easy to go wrong, seems dangerous to its readers. But readers must rely on the meaning of whatever is contained in the divine Scriptures, and if they go wrong about these things, they will go wrong dangerously. For, as Jerome says, and as is found in Decretum 24, q. 3, c. Haeresis: whoever understands Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit, by whom Scripture was written, demands, may be called a heretic, even if he is not received by the Church. Therefore such things would have been written dangerously, for those who wish to arrive at their true meaning and cannot will easily fall into error. These are among the other reasons by which the aforesaid assertion seems open to refutation. Tell me how they are answered; but first try to allege something in support of that opinion.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: In quo probatur rationibus, quod multa sunt in scripturis diuinis, quorum verus intellectus solum per reuelationum haberi potest.
units.tr: In which it is proved by arguments that many things are in the divine Scriptures whose true meaning can be had only through revelation.

units.la: MAGIST. Quod plura continentur in scripturis diuinis, quorum verus intellectus & primus virtute humani ingenii ex literis sacris colligi nequeat, sed per reuelationem diuinam solummodo possit haberi, videtur posse probari. Nam verus intellectus & primus proferentis orationem ambiguam habentem multos sensus haberi non potest, nisi proferens orationem eandem, quem intellectum habeat, aperte declaret. Si quis dixerit, Iohannes cantat missam, cum plures appellantur hoc nomine; audiens non sciet de quo loquens intelligit, nisi ipse sibi reuelet. Vnde & propter hoc videtur (vt nititur declarare quaedam opinio, quam tractauimus prima parte istius dialogi libro 7.) quod quando lex aliqua vel constitutio habet plures sensus, a conditore est interpretatio requirenda. Nemo .n. alius potest scire intellectum, quem habuit legis conditor in condendo. Plures autem orationes ambiguæ in scripturis diuinis habentur. nam secundum doctrinam sanctorum patrum, non solum voces, quæ in orationibus pronuntur, sunt signa: sed etiam res significatæ per voces sunt signa aliarum rerum. Unde & veritas ipsa (ut testatur Gregorius in Omelia super parabolam seminantis) insinuauit aperte, quod semen verbum, agen mundum, volucres dæmonia, spinæ diuitiæ signant. vna autem & eadem res plures alias res contrarias etiam in scripturis sacris significat. Leo etiam aliquando signat verbum, vt ibi, vicit Leo de tribu Iuda: aliquando diabolum, vt ibi: tanquam Leo rugiens, &c. aliquando virum fortem; aliquando crudelem. ergo orationum ambiguarum, quarum non parua inuenitur in sacris litteris multitudo, cum res significant, verus & primus intellectus non haberi potest, nisi ipse reuelet (scilicet Deus) qui huiusmodi orationes reuelauit. Hæc allegatio & conclusio principalis declaratur & confirmatur per aliam in exemplis fundatam apertis. Nam plura reuelata fuerunt Prophetis ac viris contemplatiuis in sapientia sublimissimis diuinorum, vel aliis, per quos ad Prophetas & viros illuminatos à Deo peruenerunt; ad quorum intellectum verum & primum ipsi Prophetæ antequam fuerit reuelatus eisdem, non poterant peruenire. ergo ratione consimili & multo maiori intellectus verus & primus illorum, qui solummodo ænigmatice & sub similitudinibus & figurationibus rerum in scripturis diuinis reuelata sunt à Deo, haberi non pōt, nisi Deus reuelet eundem. consequentia aperta videtur. Antecedens multis probatur exemplis. Iohannes enim euangelista singulariter illuminatus à Deo plura sibi in Apocal. reuelata minime intellexit, antequam intellectus eorum sibi reuelaretur à Deo. unde & expositione multorum indiguit. postquam enim vidit, vt legitur Apocalypsis 17. mulierem sedentem super bestiam ebriam de sanguine sanctorum, dixit ei angelus: quare miraris. ego dicam tibi sacramentum mulieris & bestiæ. Minime tamen intellexit, antequam angelus ei dixit. & ita ad verum intellectum & primum illius reuelationis ante aliam non peruenit. Sic etiam mysterium septem stellarum, & septem candelabrorum, de quo legitur c. 1. antequam Christus reuelauit sibi, ipse Iohannes minime intellexit. Unde & Christus dixit eidem post visionem prædictam: scribe igitur quæ vidisti & quæ sunt & quæ oportet fieri. post hæc: mysterium septem stellarum, quas vidisti in dextra mea, & septem candelabra aurea. septem stellæ angeli sunt septem ecclesiarum, & candelabra septem, septem ecclesiæ sunt. Idem etiam Iohannes, vt habetur 7. c. interrogauit ab vno de senioribus; hi qui amicti sunt stolis, qui sunt, & unde venerunt: respondit; domine mi tu scis. quasi diceret; quamuis ego viderim eos, tamen nescio qui sunt & unde venerunt: sed tu scis. & ita ad verum & primum intellectum visionis illius Iohannes, antequam sibi ille senior reuelauit, non peruenit. Ioseph etiam, de quo habetur Gen. 41. verum & primum intellectum somnii, quod sibi Pharao enarrauit, per reuelationem accepit. unde & Pharao dixit eidem. ostendit tibi Deus omnia quæ locutus es. sic etiam interpretationem veram somniorum pincernæ & pistoris Pharaonis per reuelationem accepit. nequaquam enim virtute humani ingenii poterat scire, quod tres propagines & tria canistra in somniis illis plus signabant tres dies, quam tres ebdomadas, vel tres menses, vel tres annos. Per reuelationem igitur solummodo post quam fuerunt sibi prædicta somnia, interpretationem veram agnouit. Unde & ipse, vt habetur 49. c. dixit: nunquid non Dei est interpretatio? quasi dicat; ille qui fecit vos somniare, & quid vera significarent somnia vobis minime indicauit, mihi interpretationem poterit reuelare. Item Daniel plurium visionum, quas viderat, verum & primum intellectum (antequam doceretur) non accepit. Capitulo enim 7. post visionem quatuor ventorum & quatuor bestiarum, subiungitur; horruit spiritus meus: ego Daniel territus sum in his, & visiones capitis mei conturbauerunt me. accessi ad unum de assistentibus, & veritatem quærebam ab eo de omnibus hiis: qui dixit mihi interpretationem sermonum, & docuit me. capit. etiam 9. post aliam visionem subiungitur. cum ego Daniel inquirerem intelligentiam: ecce stetit in conspectu meo quasi species viri: & audiui vocem viri inter Vlai & clamauit, & ait Daniel, fac intelligere istam visionem. Ex his aliisque quam pluribus euidenter colligitur (vt videtur) quod prophetis & illuminatissimis viris omnique sapientia diuina & humana peritis, plura reuelata fuerunt: quæ tamen antequam docerentur à reuelante, non intellexerunt. Unde & sæpe prophetis plures visiones fuerunt ostensæ, quarum postea interpretatio extitit reuelata: Sicut Ieremiæ 1. & 13. & Ezechiel. 17. & Esaiæ 5. & aliis locis quampluribus. Sicut etiam Christus parabolas, quas loquebatur turbis, apostolos docebat, vt legitur Matthei. 4. Si ergo prophetæ & viri illuminatissimi plurium, quæ viderunt, non poterant nisi per nouam reuelationem nouum & primum accipere intellectum: multomagis alii ænigmaticarum visionum non possent ad verum & primum intellectum pertingere nisi reueletur alicui, qui aliis manifestet eundem. Cum igitur in scripturis diuinis quamplures visiones & parabolæ ænigmaticæ & obscuræ, imo obscuriores quam sint quædam per reuelationem expositæ habeantur, sequitur quod plura in scripturis diuinis habentur, ad quorum verum & primum intellectum nemo valeat absque reuelatione pertingere. Amplius: sensus verus & primus orationis habentis sensus catholicos, quam ad quem libet illorum, poterit quilibet trahere sicut vult, haberi non poterit, nisi indicauerit ille, qui protulit eam. Quia ex quo trahi potest ad diuersos sensus, maxime vocis, non potest sciri, quem illorum intenderet proferens, nisi ipse exprimat. præsertim si non potest elici aliquis sensus nec ex verbis antecedentibus, nec consequentib. proferentis verba. Multa autem verba plurium visionum & parabolarum & ænigmaticarum locutionum in sacris literis conscriptarum habere possunt diversos sensus catholicos, ad quorum quemlibet potest quilibet, prout voluerit, trahere ea, unde & diversi sancti talia verba quam plura diversimode exponunt. Alii etiam absque omni periculo eadem verba aliter quam sancti ad diversos sensus traxerunt; & adhuc alii ad alios trahent. Quod etiam patet ex hoc, quod secundum beatum Clementem, ut habetur 27. di. c. relatum, multa verba sunt in scripturis divinis, quae possunt trahi ad eum sensum, quem sibi unusquisque elegerit. ergo multo magis possunt trahi ad diversos sensus catholicos. Ex quo concluditur, quod de ipsis verus & primus intellectus Dei revelantis absque nova revelatione sciri non potest. Amplius multa sunt in scripturis divinis, quae mystice solummodo debent intelligi, sicut docet Gregorius in Moralibus in diversis locis. imo secundum eundem plura si intelligerentur literaliter, generarent errorem. sensus autem mysticus, qui potest accipi ex verbis divinis virtute ingenii humani absque revelatione speciali, non est ita approbandus a catholicis, ut coaequetur illis, quae habentur in Biblia, vel recipiantur ad aliquid in fide catholica confirmandum, nisi alibi in scripturis divinis habeatur expresse. quod Augustinus etiam, Hieronymus & Gregorius sentire videntur. Nam secundum Augustinum, ut habetur dist. 9. in diversis capitulis, scriptura divina est literis & expositionibus omnium episcoporum & aliorum praponenda, ita ut soli scriptoribus Bibliae deferendus sit hic timor & honor, ut non credantur errare in aliquo. qualis honor & timor nulli deferendus est post ipsos. secundum Hieron. etiam in prologo in libris proverb & Gregorium in Moralibus liber Iudith, Tobiae, & Machabaeorum, ecclesiasticus atque liber Sapientiae non sunt recipiendi ad confirmandum aliquid in fide. Dicit enim Hieronymus, sicut Gregorius. Iudith & Tobia & Machabaeorum libros legit quidem eos ecclesia, sed inter canonicas scripturas non recipit. sic & hae duo volumina, scilicet Ecclesiastici & Sapientia legit ad aedificationem plebis, non ad auctoritatem ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam. Sed expositiones episcoporum & aliorum, qui fuerunt post scriptores canonicarum scripturarum, non sunt maioris auctoritatis, quam libri praedicti. igitur sensus quicunque, quem colligunt ex scripturis divinis, nisi alibi habeatur ex scripturis divinis, non est cum illa reverentia suscipiendus, ut debeat allegari ad confirmandum aliquid in catholica fide: sensus autem verus & primus cuiuscunque revelati a Deo in scripturis valet ad auctoritatem ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam. ergo multorum in scripturis divinis sensus verus & primus absque revelatione divina haberi non potest. Adhuc non magis virtute ingenii humani potest haberi sensus verus & primus aliquorum mysticorum divinorum, quam parabolarum humanarum. (sed multarum parabolarum & locutionum mysticarum, seu aenigmatarum humanarum primus sensus proferentis virtute ingenii humani saepe haberi non potest, nisi proferens manifestet. quomodo n. vxor Samsonis quamuis subtilissima extitisset, peruenisset ad sensum primum sui problematis, nisi forte a casu, quando dixit: de comedente exiuit cibus, & de forti egressa est dulcedo: nisi ipse reuelasset eidem? Ita enim potest per comedentem, & etiam fortem significari vrsus, vel elephas, aut draco, vel cete maris, aut alia bestia fortior leone, vel minus fortis sicut leo. Per cibum etiam & per dulcedinem non solum mel, sed etiam aliae res dulces comestibiles significari possunt. Alia etiam res per comedentem, & fortem: & rursus alia res per cibum, & alia per dulcedinem convenienter significari potest. Cum igitur, ut testatur apostolis 1. Corinth. 2. Nemo scit hominum quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est: nullo modo vxor Samsonis, virtute humani ingenii (quantumcunque fuisset instructa) sciuisset, quod Samson intelligebat per comedentem & fortem, leonem: & per cibum atque dulcedinem, mel: nisi ipse sibi dixisset. Ergo multo fortius verus & primus intellectus visionum, & revelationum divinarum haberi non potest virtute humani ingenii. quia sicut dicit apostolus 1. Cor. 2. quae Dei sunt, nemo cognovit, nisi spiritus Dei. Praeterea primus intellectus minus obscuri, non potest haberi virtute ingenii humani. Ergo multo fortius primus intellectus illorum, quae sunt magis obscura, virtute humani ingenii haberi non potest. Consequentia videtur probatione minime indigere. Antecedens videtur posse probari auctoritate beati Grego. secundum quem (ut videtur) primus intellectus, quem habuit Christus in parabola seminantis (quae est minus obscura, & minus aenigmatica, quam multae visiones & revelationes, quae non sunt expositae per revelationem in scripturis) virtute ingenii humani haberi non potuit. dicit enim super parabolam illam: Quis mihi unquam crederet, si spinas, divitias interpretari voluissem. quasi diceret, nullus. Etamen absque illa interpretatione, primus intellectus parabolae haberi non potuit: quia Christus exponendo praedictam parabolam sic interpretatus est. Ergo primus intellectus aliarum parabolarum, visionum, & revelationum, | quae per Deum revelantem non sunt expositae; virtute humani ingenii haberi non potest.
units.tr: MASTER. That many things are contained in the holy Scriptures whose true and primary meaning cannot be gathered from the sacred letters by the power of human wit, but can only be had through divine revelation, seems capable of proof. For the true and primary meaning of a speaker who utters an ambiguous statement with many senses cannot be had unless the speaker plainly declares which meaning he intends. If someone says, "John sings Mass," since many men bear that name, the hearer will not know whom the speaker means unless the speaker himself reveals it. Hence also it seems (as a certain opinion, which we discussed in the first part of this dialogue, book 7, attempts to show) that when some law or ordinance has several senses, its interpretation must be sought from its author. For no one else can know the meaning the lawgiver had in enacting it. Now there are many ambiguous statements in the divine Scriptures. For according to the teaching of the holy Fathers, not only the words that are uttered in speech are signs, but also the things signified by the words are signs of other things. Hence also the Truth itself (as Gregory testifies in his Homily on the parable of the sower) plainly showed that the seed signifies the word, the field the world, the birds the demons, and the thorns the riches. But one and the same thing also signifies several other, even contrary, things in the sacred Scriptures. The lion sometimes signifies Christ, as in "The Lion of the tribe of Judah has prevailed"; sometimes the devil, as in "as a roaring lion," etc.; sometimes a brave man; sometimes a cruel one. Therefore, of ambiguous statements, of which no small number is found in the sacred letters, since they signify things, the true and primary meaning cannot be had unless he himself reveals it (namely God), who revealed such statements. This argument and principal conclusion is declared and confirmed by another argument founded on plain examples. For many things were revealed to the prophets and to contemplative men most exalted in the wisdom of divine things, or to others through whom they came to the prophets and to men enlightened by God; the prophets themselves could not reach the true and primary meaning of these things before they were revealed to them. Therefore, by a similar and much greater reasoning, the true and primary meaning of those things which are revealed by God only in enigmatic form and under the likenesses and figures of things in the divine Scriptures cannot be had, unless God reveals the same. The consequence seems plain. The antecedent is proved by many examples. For the evangelist John, singularly enlightened by God, did not at all understand many things revealed to him in the Apocalypse until their meaning was revealed to him by God; hence he also needed the explanation of many things. For after he saw, as we read in Revelation 17, "a woman sitting upon a beast, drunk with the blood of the saints," the angel said to him: "Why do you wonder? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast." Yet he did not understand it before the angel spoke to him. And thus he did not reach the true and primary meaning of that revelation before another. So too the mystery of the seven stars and the seven lampstands, of which we read in chapter 1, John himself did not understand until Christ revealed it to him. Hence also Christ said to him after the aforesaid vision: "Write therefore what you have seen, and what is, and what must come to pass." Afterwards: "The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches." Likewise John himself, as we have it in chapter 7, asked one of the elders: "Who are these who are clothed in white robes, and whence have they come?" He answered: "My lord, you know." As if he said: although I have seen them, yet I do not know who they are or whence they came, but you know. And thus John did not reach the true and primary meaning of that vision before the elder revealed it to him. Joseph also, of whom we read in Genesis 41, received by revelation the true and primary meaning of the dream which Pharaoh related to him. Hence Pharaoh also said to him: "God has shown you all that you have spoken." So too he received by revelation the true interpretation of the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. For he could in no way know by the power of human wit that the three branches and the three baskets in those dreams signified three days rather than three weeks, or three months, or three years. Therefore he recognized the true interpretation only through revelation, after the dreams had been foretold to him. Hence he also said, as we have it in chapter 40: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" As if he said: He who caused you to dream, and did not show you what your dreams signified, can reveal the interpretation to me. Likewise Daniel did not receive the true and primary meaning of several visions which he had seen until he was taught. For in chapter 7, after the vision of the four winds and the four beasts, it is added: "My spirit was troubled: I, Daniel, was terrified at these things, and the visions of my head disturbed me. I approached one of those who stood by, and I asked him the truth about all these things. He told me the interpretation of the matters and taught me." In chapter 9 also, after another vision, it is added: "While I, Daniel, was seeking understanding, behold, there stood before me as it were the likeness of a man; and I heard the voice of a man between Ulai, and he called and said, 'Daniel, make this vision understood.'" From these and many others it is clearly gathered (as it seems) that many things were revealed to the prophets and most enlightened men, skilled in all divine and human wisdom; yet they did not understand them before they were taught by the one revealing them. Hence also many visions were often shown to the prophets, whose interpretation was afterwards revealed, as in Jeremiah 1 and 13, Ezekiel 17, Isaiah 5, and in very many other places. Likewise Christ taught the apostles the parables which he spoke to the crowds, as we read in Matthew 13. If therefore the prophets and most enlightened men could not receive a new and primary understanding of many things which they saw except through a new revelation, much more would others be unable to reach the true and primary meaning of enigmatic visions unless it were revealed to someone who would make it known to others. Since therefore many visions and parables, enigmatic and obscure, and indeed more obscure than some things expounded by revelation, are found in the divine Scriptures, it follows that there are many things in the divine Scriptures to whose true and primary meaning no one can attain without revelation. Furthermore: the true and primary sense of a statement having catholic senses cannot be had, since anyone may draw it to whichever of those senses he likes, unless the one who uttered it indicates it. For since it can be drawn to various senses, especially of a word, it cannot be known which of them the speaker intended, unless he himself states it; especially if no sense can be elicited either from the words preceding or following the speaker's words. Now the many words of several visions, parables, and enigmatic utterances recorded in the sacred letters can have various catholic senses, and anyone may draw them to whichever of these he pleases; hence various holy men have also expounded many such words in various ways. Others, too, without any danger, have drawn the same words to different senses than the saints did; and still others will draw them to other senses. This is also evident from the fact that, according to the blessed Clement, as we have it in Distinction 27, relatum: "There are many words in the divine Scriptures which can be drawn to whatever sense each one has chosen for himself." Therefore much more can they be drawn to various catholic senses. From this it is concluded that the true and primary meaning of these things, of God revealing them, cannot be known without a new revelation. Furthermore, many things in the divine Scriptures ought to be understood only mystically, as Gregory teaches in the Moralia in various places. Indeed, according to the same author, many of them, if they were understood literally, would generate error. But a mystical sense, which can be drawn from the divine words by the power of human wit without special revelation, is not so approved by Catholics as to be placed on a par with those things which are contained in the Bible, or received to confirm anything in the catholic faith, unless it is expressly found elsewhere in the divine Scriptures. Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory also seem to hold this. For according to Augustine, as we have it in Distinction 9, in diversis capitulis: "The divine Scripture is to be preferred to the writings and expositions of all bishops and others, so that only to the writers of the Bible is this fear and honor to be paid, that they are not believed to err in anything." Such honor and fear is to be paid to no one after them. According to Jerome also, in the prologue to the books of Proverbs, and Gregory in the Moralia, the books of Judith, Tobit, and the Maccabees, Ecclesiasticus, and the Book of Wisdom are not to be received to confirm anything in the faith. For Jerome says, as does Gregory: "The Church indeed reads the books of Judith, Tobit, and the Maccabees, but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures. So also these two volumes, namely Ecclesiasticus and Wisdom, she reads for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas." But the expositions of bishops and others who came after the writers of the canonical Scriptures are not of greater authority than the aforesaid books. Therefore whatever sense they gather from the divine Scriptures, unless it is found elsewhere in the divine Scriptures, is not to be received with such reverence that it ought to be alleged to confirm anything in the catholic faith; but the true and primary sense of anything revealed by God in the Scriptures is valid to confirm the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas. Therefore the true and primary sense of many things in the divine Scriptures cannot be had without divine revelation. Again, the true and primary sense of certain divine mysteries cannot be had by the power of human wit any more than that of human parables. (But the primary sense of many parables, mystical utterances, or human enigmas is often not to be had by the power of human wit, unless the speaker makes it plain. For however subtle the wife of Samson was, she would not have attained the primary sense of her riddle, except perhaps by chance when she said, "Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness," unless he had revealed it to her. For through "the eater" and also "the strong" a bear, or an elephant, or a dragon, or a whale, or some other beast stronger than a lion, or less strong like a lion, can be signified. Through "food" and "sweetness" not only honey but also other edible sweet things can be signified. Also, another thing can be signified suitably by "the eater" and "the strong," and again another thing by "food" and another by "sweetness." Since therefore, as the apostle testifies in 1 Corinthians 2, "No one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him," in no way could the wife of Samson, by the power of human wit, however well instructed she had been, have known that Samson meant by "the eater" and "the strong" a lion, and by "food" and "sweetness" honey, unless he had told her himself.) Therefore much more is the true and primary meaning of divine visions and revelations not attainable by the power of human wit, because, as the apostle says in 1 Corinthians 2, "No one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God." Moreover, the primary meaning of less obscure things cannot be had by the power of human wit. Therefore much more is the primary meaning of those things which are more obscure not attainable by the power of human wit. The consequence seems to need no proof. The antecedent seems capable of proof by the authority of the blessed Gregory, according to whom (as it seems) the primary meaning which Christ had in the parable of the sower (which is less obscure and less enigmatic than many visions and revelations not expounded by revelation in the Scriptures) could not be had by the power of human wit. For he says on that parable: "Who would ever believe me if I had wished to interpret the thorns as riches?" As if he said: no one. And yet, without that interpretation, the primary meaning of the parable could not have been had, since Christ, expounding the aforesaid parable, interpreted it in this way. Therefore the primary meaning of other parables, visions, and revelations which have not been expounded by God revealing them cannot be had by the power of human wit.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAP. XVII.

units.la: In quo idem probatur, scilicet quod multa sint in sacra scriptura, quorum verus intellectus per solam revelationem haberi potest, multis auctoritatibus.
units.tr: In which the same point is proved, namely that there are many things in Holy Scripture whose true meaning can be had only through revelation, by many authorities.

units.la: DISCIP. Deduxisti ratiocinationes fundatas in scripturis ad probandum conclusionem praedictam, nunc ipsam per auctoritates nitere confirmare. MAGIST. Nonnullis apparet, quod auctoritatibus tam scripturarum canonicarum, quam aliarum, poteris ostendi: de quib. adducam paucas. haec enim videtur Daniel dixisse c. 12. ubi sic legitur: Tu autem Daniel sermonem claude, et signa librum usque ad tempus statutum. Ex quibus verbis potest intelligi, ut videtur, quod quidam sermones revelati Danieli, ita sunt clausi, ut nemo possit absque revelatione ad primum eorum intellectum pertingere. Item, ut legitur Act. 8. Dixit Philippus Eunucho legenti Esaiam prophetam: putas ne intelligis quae legis? Qui ait: Quomodo possum, si non aliquis ostenderit mihi? quasi diceret, nullo modo. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod ex verbis scripturae, quae legit Eunuchus, non potest aliquis primum intellectum ipsorum colligere, nisi ab alio doceatur. Ergo ratione consimili aliorum quae aeque vel magis obscura sunt, non potest primum intellectus haberi, nisi revelatus appareat. Item psalmista ait: Da mihi intellectum &c. quasi diceret, ad primum intellectum multorum legis tuae scrutando penitere non potero, nisi tu revele. ideo da mihi intellectum primum eorum. Plura enim sunt in lege antiqua statuta, quorum nulla ratio potest per hominem assignari.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. You have drawn out arguments grounded in the Scriptures to prove the aforesaid conclusion; now try to confirm it by authorities. MASTER. It seems to some that it can be shown by authorities, both from the canonical Scriptures and from other writings. I will cite a few. Daniel seems to have said this in chapter 12, where it is read thus: "But thou, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book until the time appointed." From these words it can be understood, as it seems, that certain words revealed to Daniel are so closed that no one can reach their first meaning without revelation. Likewise, as is read in Acts 8, Philip said to the eunuch who was reading the prophet Isaiah: "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said: "How can I, unless someone shows me?" as if to say, by no means. From these words it is clear that from the words of Scripture which the eunuch was reading, no one can gather their first meaning unless he is taught by another. Therefore, by similar reasoning, the first meaning of other passages which are equally or even more obscure cannot be had unless it is revealed. Likewise the psalmist says: "Give me understanding," etc., as if to say: "I shall not be able to attain the first meaning of many things in your law by searching, unless you reveal it; therefore give me the first meaning of them." For there are many statutes in the old law for which no reason can be assigned by man.

units.la: quare praecepit illa Deus filius Israel. Sicut illa: non arabis in bove & asino, non indueris vestimento, quod ex lana linoq; contextum est &c. & per consequens primus intellectus talium contentorum in lege absq; revelatione haberi non potest. Hinc Hieronymus in prologo Bibliae ait ca. 7. quia enim digne exprimit tria & quatuor scelera Damasci, Gazae, & Tyri, & Idumeae &c. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod prophetia Amos prophetae digne explicari non potest, nisi per revelationem divinam.
units.tr: Wherefore God commanded those things to the children of Israel: such as "Thou shalt not plow with an ox and an ass together," "Thou shalt not wear a garment woven of wool and linen," etc. Consequently the first meaning of such matters contained in the law cannot be had without revelation. Hence Jerome, in the prologue to the Bible, chapter 7, says: "For he worthily expresses the three and four crimes of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom," etc. From these words it is gathered that the prophecy of the prophet Amos cannot be worthily explained except by divine revelation.

units.la: Hoc etiam beatus Gregorius super Ezechielem omelia 15. videtur asserere, dicens: scriptura sacra tota quidem propter vos scripta est, sed non tota intelligitur a vobis, multa quippe in illa ita aperte scripta sunt, ut pascant parvulos. Quaedam vero obscuriorib. sententiis, ut exerceant fortes, quatenus cum labore intellecta plus grata sint. nonnulla autem ita in ea clausa sunt, ut dum intelligimus agnoscentes infirma nostra caecitatis ad humilitatem magis quam intelligentiam profitiamur. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod aliqua sunt in scripturis sacris, quae intelligere non valemus. loquitur enim beatus Gregorius in persona omnium viatorum & fortium, qui obscuriores noluerunt elucidare sententias. Constat, quod per revelationem, quaeque scripta sunt, possunt intelligi, & eorum potest primum intellectus haberi. Idem etiam Gregorius pro se & pro omnibus aliis catholicis. 3. libro Moralium ca. 17. loquens de amicis Iob, ait: utrum continuis septem diebus & septem noctibus cum afflicto Iob sederint, an certe diebus septem & noctibus totidem instantia et crebra visitationis adhaerent, ignoramus. Sepe enim rem quamlibet, tot diebus agere dicimur, quamuis eisdem diebus ad eam continue non vacemus. Sepe vero scriptura sacra sic totum pro parte, sicut pro toto partem ponere consueuit. Ex quib. verbis colligitur, quod cum scriptor libri Iob determinate intendit loqui de septem diebus & septem noctibus continuis vel non continuis, quia de his vel de illis scriptura illa fuerit vera, & non de utrisque, sequitur quod nos ad primum intellectum verborum illorum determinate non possumus pervenire.
units.tr: Gregory also seems to assert this in his fifteenth homily on Ezekiel, saying: "Holy Scripture is indeed all written for your sake, but it is not all understood by you. For many things in it are written so plainly that they feed little ones; some things are in more obscure sayings, so that they exercise the strong, that what is understood with labour may be more pleasing; but some things are enclosed in it in such a way that, while we try to understand them, acknowledging the weakness of our blindness, we profess ourselves to humility rather than to understanding." From these words it is clear that there are some things in the holy Scriptures which we are not able to understand. For blessed Gregory speaks in the person of all wayfarers and the strong, who have not wished to clarify the more obscure sayings. It is agreed that through revelation whatever has been written can be understood, and the first meaning of it can be had. Gregory himself also, for himself and for all other Catholics, in the third book of the Morals, chapter 17, speaking of the friends of Job, says: "Whether they sat with afflicted Job for seven continuous days and seven nights, or whether they clung to a persistent and frequent visitation for seven days and as many nights, we do not know. For we often say that a man is occupied with some matter for so many days, although on those same days he is not continually free for it. Often, however, Holy Scripture is accustomed to put the whole for a part, as it puts a part for the whole." From these words it is gathered that, since the writer of the book of Job determinately intended to speak of seven days and seven nights, whether continuous or not, and since that Scripture is true of one or the other and not of both, it follows that we cannot arrive at the first meaning of those words determinately.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: In quo monstratur, quod multa sint in lege divina, quorum primus intellectus per solam revelationem possit haberi. nec defendit obiectionibus & replicis respondendo capitul. 15. supra adductis.
units.tr: In which it is shown that many things in the divine law can have their first meaning grasped only through revelation, and the objections and replies in chapter 15 above are answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Nolo plures allegationes audire pro assertione praescripta, sed cupio scire, quomodo respondetur ad allegationes in contrarium superius cap. 15. inductas. Ideo narra aliquas responsiones ad ipsas.
units.tr: STUDENT. I do not want more arguments in favour of the thesis set out, but I wish to know how the objections to the contrary, introduced above in chapter 15, are answered. So tell me some of the replies to them.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad primam, quae consistit in hoc, quod talia essent superflue posita in scripturis divinis, si primus intellectus ipsorum antequam essent impleta absque revelatione divina haberi non posset. Respondetur, quod non superflue posita sunt, quia scripta sunt ad exercitationem, quia in talibus verbis multiplices latent sensus praeter primum sensum revelantis, quos dum illi, qui in exponendis scripturis divinis allegorice, tropologice ex huiusmodi aenigmatice revelatis eliciunt, utiliter occupantur. Quemadmodum beatus Gregorius in Moralibus sibi profecit & aliis, verba beati Iob diversimode exponendo: & tamen ad illum intellectum, quem habuit Iob in pluribus verbis, absque revelatione (nisi forte a casu) non potuit pervenire. Verba enim plura Iob modis innumeris a beato Gregorio & aliis poterant exponi: quibus tamen modis beatus Gregorius ipsa nequaquam exposuit. Et ita verba Iob plures sensus possunt habere, praeter illum, quem habuit. Quis ergo scit, quod beatus Gregorius sensit, quod actualiter in mente Iob habuit in proferendo verba illa expresse? non videtur quod ipsemet Greg. hoc sciuit. Et ideo forte aliquando beatus Gregor. ad illum sensum, quem actualiter Iob intendebat, verba Iob exposuit, & tamen ipse hoc nesciuit. Sic etiam verba Iohannis in Apoc. & aliorum prophetarum, multos sensus possunt habere, teste Hieronym. qui in prologo Bibliae ita ait: In verbis singulis. (sc. Apoc.) multiplices latent intelligentiae. Sed quem intellectum habuit beatus Iohannes vel Christus revelans, hoc nullus exponens Apoc. certitudinaliter sciuit, nisi cui Deus revelauit.
units.tr: TEACHER. As to the first, which runs thus: such things would have been placed in the divine Scriptures to no purpose if their first meaning could not be grasped without divine revelation before they were fulfilled. The answer is that they were not placed there to no purpose, since they were written for exercise, because multiple senses lie hidden in such words besides the first sense of the revealer. Those who draw allegorical, tropological and enigmatic interpretations from such revealed matters in expounding the divine Scriptures are usefully occupied with these. Blessed Gregory profited himself and others in the Moralia by expounding the words of blessed Job in various ways, and yet he could not have reached the meaning Job had in many of the words without revelation (unless perhaps by chance). For the many words of Job could be expounded by blessed Gregory and others in countless ways, yet blessed Gregory by no means expounded them in all of these ways. So the words of Job can have several senses besides the one he had. Who, then, knows what blessed Gregory thought, or what Job actually had in mind when he expressly uttered those words? It does not seem that Gregory himself knew this. And so perhaps blessed Gregory sometimes expounded the words of Job to the very sense Job actually intended, and yet he himself did not know it. Likewise the words of John in the Apocalypse and of other prophets can have many senses, as Jerome testifies, who says in the preface to the Bible: "In the individual words (namely of the Apocalypse) many meanings lie hidden." But what meaning blessed John, or Christ who revealed it, had, no expounder of the Apocalypse knows with certainty, except one to whom God has revealed it.

units.la: DISCIP. Contra istud obiici potest: quia verba scripturae diuinae eodem spiritu (scilicet spiritu sancto) exposita sunt, quo sunt scripta. ergo eundem sensum, quem habuit reuelans, habuerunt & exponentes. quare exponentes verba diuinae scripturae, ad primum intellectum ipsorum peruenerunt. Amplius, omnes sensus catholici eorundem verborum, sunt aeque primi: quia non est ratio, quod unus sit primus magis, quam alius. scil. omnes sensus, secundum quos beatus Gregorius exposuit verba quaeque Iob, sunt catholici. ergo quilibet eorum est aeque primus. Et ita beatus Gregor. peruenit ad primum intellectum omnium verborum Iob. Et consimili ratione alii sancti exponentes Apoc. & alias prophetias, atque quaequo obscura scripturae diuinae ad primum intellectum peruenerunt.
units.tr: STUDENT. Against this it can be objected: the words of divine Scripture were expounded by the same Spirit (namely the Holy Spirit) by whom they were written. Therefore the expounders too have had the same sense that the revealer had, and so the expounders of the divine Scripture have reached its first meaning. Furthermore, all the catholic senses of the same words are equally first, since there is no reason why one should be first more than another. Namely, all the senses according to which blessed Gregory expounded each of the words of Job are catholic. Therefore each of them is equally first. And so blessed Gregory reached the first meaning of all the words of Job. And by a similar reasoning the other holy expounders of the Apocalypse and of other prophecies, and of whatever is obscure in divine Scripture, have reached the first meaning.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad primum istorum respondetur, quod quia omne verbum est a spiritu sancto: & omnis sapientia a domino Deo est (vt legitur Eccles. 1.) ideo scripturae diuinae, quando non erroneae exponuntur, quo sunt traditae. Sed quia traditae a solo Deo fuerunt, & nequaquam virtute ingenii humani inuentae sunt. Expositiones autem non erroneae, sanctorum saltem, saepe virtute ingenii humani assistente diuina influentia generali, ex scripturis & ratione infallibili fuerunt inuentae. Ideo non omnino eodem modo, verba scripturae diuinae, eodem spiritu sancto sunt scripta, & a viris sanctis exposita. Propter quod expositiones sanctorum non sunt tantae auctoritatis, quantae sunt illa, quae scripta sunt in scripturis canonicis. Si tamen expositiones huiusmodi per certitudinem exprimerent intellectum verborum scripturae diuinae, eiusdem essent auctoritatis. Non quia ab expositoribus sunt simpliciter expresse, sed quia in canone Bibliae reperiuntur. Sic etiam si plures (puta. 10. vel 20. magistri, lectores vel praedicatores verbi diuini aut alii, his temporibus sacras literas exponentes, eandem auctoritatem aenigmaticam & obscuram in Apoc. vel prophetia alia scriptam, secundum diuersum exponerent intellectum, non erroneum, sed verum & sanum, posset aliquo modo concedi, quod quilibet istorum, eodem spiritu, eandem auctoritatem exponerent. Quia omnis sensus verus & sanus est a spiritu sancto, a quo inspirati, locuti sunt scriptores literarum sanctarum: eodem modo esset quaelibet expositionum huiusmodi a spiritu sancto, quo modo ab ipso scripturae diuinae sunt traditae. Si etiam quilibet sensuum praedictorum inueniretur sententialiter in Biblia, quamuis vnus eorum in vno loco & alius in alio, quilibet eorum esset tantae auctoritatis, quantae sunt alia quae scripta sunt in Biblia. Non quia ab aliquo istorum exprimitur, sed quia sententialiter in Biblia reperitur. Et tamen non omnis, imo forte nullus talium sensuum esset primus intellectus & verus illius textus, quem tales exponentes exponerent. Si autem nullus istorum reperiretur sententialiter nec implicite nec explicite in canone Bibliae: tamen quilibet illorum esset verus & sanus: certum esset, quod nullus esset primus sensus auctoritatis expositae a quolibet istorum, vel saltem hoc non constaret: & tamen quilibet illorum esset aliquomodo a spiritu sancto. cum omnis doctrina sana & quae secundum pietatem est, sit aliquomodo a spiritu sancto.
units.tr: TEACHER. To the first of these objections the answer is this: since every word is from the Holy Spirit, and all wisdom is from the Lord God (as it is read in Ecclesiasticus 1), the divine Scriptures, when they are expounded without error, are expounded by the same Spirit by whom they were delivered. But they were delivered by God alone and were in no way discovered by the power of human genius. Non-erroneous expositions, however, at least those of the saints, were often discovered by the power of human genius, with the general divine influence assisting, from the Scriptures and from infallible reason. Therefore the words of divine Scripture were not written by the same Holy Spirit, and expounded by holy men, in exactly the same way. For this reason the expositions of the saints do not have the same authority as those things which are written in the canonical Scriptures. Yet if expositions of this kind expressed with certainty the meaning of the words of divine Scripture, they would have the same authority. This would be so not because they were expressly stated by the expounders, but because they are found in the canon of the Bible. So too, if several (say ten or twenty teachers, readers or preachers of the divine word, or others in these times expounding the holy letters) were to expound, each in a different way, the same enigmatic and obscure authority written in the Apocalypse or in some other prophecy, with an interpretation that is not erroneous but true and sound, it could in some sense be granted that each of them, by the same Spirit, expounds the same authority. For every true and sound sense is from the Holy Spirit, by whom the writers of the holy letters were inspired and spoke. In the same way each of such expositions would be from the Holy Spirit, just as the divine Scriptures themselves were delivered by him. Again, if any of the aforesaid senses were found in the Bible in substance, although one of them is in one place and another in another, each of them would have the same authority as the other things written in the Bible. Not because it is expressed by any of them, but because it is found in the Bible in substance. And yet not every one of these senses, indeed perhaps none of them, would be the first meaning and true sense of the text which such expounders expounded. But if none of them were found in the canon of the Bible, either in substance, implicitly or explicitly, still each of them would be true and sound. It would be certain that none of the senses expounded by any of them is the first sense, or at least this would not be established; and yet each of them would in some way be from the Holy Spirit, since every sound doctrine which is according to godliness is in some way from the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Ad secundum dicitur, quod primus intellectus verborum scripturae diuinae, quantum ad illa quae a solo Deo reuelata fuerunt, est ille propter quem fuerunt principaliter reuelata. sicut illorum verborum, quae angelus dixit Danieli vel beato Iohanni vel aliis prophetis, & quae etiam in prophetiis inspirata fuerunt, & quae Christus dixit discipulis suis: primus sensus est ille, propter quem inspirata vel prolata fuerunt. Vnde primus sensus parabolarum Christi est ille, quem Christus postea discipulis suis expressit, quia propter illum principaliter protulit eas: & tamen multos alios sensus possunt habere. Quantum autem ad illa verba scripturae diuinae, quae homines siue boni siue mali dixerunt, primus intellectus est ille, quem in mente habuit ille qui protulit. Sicut primus intellectus problematis Samsonis fuit ille, quem actualiter cogitauit, quod tamen problema sub eisdem verbis potuisset & adhuc posset alius proponere, & alium intellectum habere: qui intellectus esset primus intellectus eiusdem proferentis. & ita alius esset intellectus problematis Samsonis in quantum prolatum fuit ab ipso: & alius esset intellectus eorundem verborum, si alius eadem verba sub alio intellectu proferret. Quemadmodum istorum verborum non variatorū; Rex praecepit fures suspendi. Alius communiter est intellectus primus eorū, qui proferunt ea in Francia: & illorū, qui proferunt ea vel scribunt in Anglia: & illorū, qui proferunt ipsa in Castella, quia Franci communiter intelligerent ipsa de rege Franciae; Anglici de rege Angliae; & alii de rege Castellae, & audientes ipsa in diuersis regnis, diuersum ex eis capiunt intellectum. Si autem eadem verba proferuntur in ciuitate vel patria, quae secundum veritatem vel secundum opinionem hominum nulli regi est subiecta, audiens ipsa ex ipsis verbis praecise, ad primum intellectum proferentis peruenire non posset. Quia non posset scire, an intelligeret de rege Castellae vel alio; propter hoc, quod ista verba proferens poterit intelligere de vno rege vel de alio, secundum quod fuerit placitu voluntati; cuius voluntas ab alio sciri non potest, nisi Deus vel ipsemet sibi voluerit reuelare. Et si duo vel plures proferant verba praedicta, & de diversis regibus ipsa intelligant, almanach intellectus primus istorum verborum inquantum proferuntur ab uno, & inquantum proferuntur ab alio.
units.tr: To the second objection it is said that the first meaning of the words of divine Scripture, as far as those things are concerned which were revealed by God alone, is that for the sake of which they were principally revealed. Thus for the words which an angel spoke to Daniel, or to blessed John, or to other prophets, and which were also inspired in prophecies, and which Christ spoke to his disciples, the first sense is that for the sake of which they were inspired or uttered. Hence the first sense of Christ's parables is that which Christ afterwards expressed to his disciples, because he principally uttered them for its sake; and yet they can have many other senses. But as regards those words of divine Scripture which men, whether good or bad, spoke, the first meaning is that which the speaker actually had in mind. Thus the first meaning of Samson's riddle was the one he actually thought of, although another could have proposed the same riddle in the same words, and still can, and have another meaning; that meaning would be the first meaning of the one who proposed it. So the meaning of Samson's riddle, insofar as it was uttered by him, would be one thing, and the meaning of the same words would be another if someone else uttered the same words with another meaning. Consider these words, unchanged: "The king ordered thieves to be hanged." The first meaning of these words, as commonly understood, is one for those who utter them in France, another for those who utter or write them in England, and another for those who utter them in Castile. The French commonly understand them of the king of France, the English of the king of England, and the others of the king of Castile; and those who hear them in different kingdoms take from them different meanings. But if the same words are uttered in a city or country which, in truth or in men's opinion, is subject to no king, a hearer who has only the words themselves could not arrive at the first meaning of the speaker. For he could not know whether the speaker meant the king of Castile or some other king, since the speaker could understand them of one king or another, as he pleased; and his will cannot be known by another unless God or the speaker himself has chosen to reveal it. And if two or more people utter the aforesaid words and understand them of different kings, there will be a different first meaning of these words insofar as they are uttered by one and insofar as they are uttered by another.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Contra primam solutionem praecedentis capi. dupliciter arguit & soluit. Primo contra illud, scilicet quod beatus Gregorius non pervenit ad primum sensum beati Iob. Secundo contra illud, scilicet quod multa sunt scripta, quorum nullus sensus est authenticus.
units.tr: Against the first solution of the preceding chapter he argues and answers in two ways. First, against the claim that blessed Gregory did not arrive at the first sense of blessed Job. Second, against the claim that many writings exist of which no sense is authentic.

units.la: DISCIP. Adhuc dupliciter obiciam contra praedicta. Non enim videtur bene dictum, quod beatus Gregor. non pervenerit ad primum intellectum verborum beati Iob. Quia de multis verbis Iob, quae non debent ad literam sed mystice tantum intelligi, sicut de illis: per quae natus sum: & de multis aliis asserit manifeste, quod Iob ipsa intellexit, sicut ipse exponit. Quod non fecisset, nisi sciuisset illum fuisse primum intellectum Iob. Quia secundum praedicta ille est primus intellectus verborum alicuius, quem proferens actu habet in mente. Rursus secundum praedicta, multa essent verba in scriptura divina, quae quamvis legi possint & debeant ad aedificationem plebis, & convertendo ipsa in sensus morales & alios, qui absque eis ab ingeniosis hominibus accipi valent (quemadmodum fabulae poetarum & aliorum fingentium bruta fuisse locuta, & multa tractasse, atque aliae utiliter applicari possint ad mores informandos) tamen ad auctoritatem ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam, & ad roborandda illa, quae in contentionem veniunt, & ad firmandam fidem in re dubia, essent nullatenus allegranda. Cum primus intellectus ipsorum haberi non possit, & alii intellectus eorum authentici minime sint putandi: nisi per alias scripturas vel assertiones, quae refelli non debeant, valeant demonstrari. Cuius tamen contrarium sanctos patres fecisse cognoscimus. Augustinus enim ad Bon. ut habetur 23. q. 6. ca. schismatici, per vias & sepes schismaticos intelligit. de huiusmodi loquitur Christus Luc. 14. inter haereses & schismata volens per eadem verba probare, quod haeretici intrare ecclesiam sunt cogendi. Et tamen per vias & sepes ita possunt intelligi alia crimina, sicut haereses & schismata, unde & alii criminosi sunt per severitatem ecclesiasticam coercendi. nec habetur, quod Christus ibi per vias & sepes intellexerit haereses & schismata. Innocentius etiam tertius, ut habetur extra, de maiorit. & obedien. solita, & alii plures per illa verba dicta Hieremiae I. Ecce constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna, probant quod imperium sacerdotio est subiectum. & tamen quod illa verba Hieremiae I. de papa respectu imperii debeant intelligi, nequaquam revelatum est a Deo. MAGIST. Ad primum istorum respondent quidam dicentes, quod quemadmodum literatus quidam in libro, quem de praestigiis fortuna composuit, saepe tali expositione & modo loquendi visus est sententiam, id est contingere potuit: quandoque evenient, id est si quando evenire contigerit. Sic etiam beatus Gregor. cum saepe sententialiter dixit, Iob dixit, intellexit, vel dicere voluit, nihil aliud dicere intendebat, nisi quod Iob sic intelligere potuit. sed quod actualiter Iob sic intellexerit, non intendebat asserere. Et ad hoc designandum saepe tali modo loquendi utitur beatus Greg. aliter possunt verba Iob intelligi: per hoc insinuans, quod saepe non intendebat asserere, cum dixit, sic intellexit Iob, quod tunc Iob in mente talem habuit intellectum, sed quod talem habere poterat intellectum. Sic etiam multi praedicantes, & exponentes sacras scripturas, de diversis sanctis viris & feminis, vel alia determinata materia, tali modo loquendo utuntur: de hoc sancto prophetavit vel locutus est Esaias vel Hieremias, vel alius propheta, aut alius scriptor alicuius partis scripturae canonicae. Et tamen si recte sapiunt, non intendunt, quia tunc propheta, vel alius in mente de tali sancto vel materia loqui volebat, sed quod intelligere poterat, aut de tali materia talia verba possunt intelligi. Et ad hoc designandum intelligentes, frequenter talibus verbis utuntur: talia verba scripturae divinae de hoc vel de hoc possunt exponi. DISCIP. Possunt ne adduci aliqua exempla ex scripturis, p tali modo loquendi. MAGIST. Videtur quibusdam quod sic. Unde Exo. 8. dicitur de magis Pharaonis: fecerunt que similiter malefici incantationibus suis, ut educerent cinipes, idem facere conati fuerunt. In Iob etiam dicitur: Quis resistit Deo, id est, resistere voluit. & pacem habuit? Si enim resistit, ponitur pro resistere voluit: & fecerunt ponitur pro facere conati fuerunt, videtur q intellexit, potuit poni pro intelligere potuit. DISCIP. Dic quomodo respondetur ad secundam obiectionem, quam adduxi. MAG. Nonnulli concedunt, quod verba scripturae, de quorum primo intellectu per certitudinem non constat, adducit ad probandum illa sola, quae in contentionem veniunt aliorum, non debent. Ad manuducendum tamen & ad persuadendum vel aliquomodo declarandum aliquid, de quo est contentio, sub aliquo sensu sano, non erroneo, adduci possunt. Quemadmodum ad persuadendum aliquomodo articulos fidei, & etiam ea quae per solam revelationem possunt cognosci, rationes & argumenta a sanctis & aliis adducuntur: quae tamen ad probandum huiusmodi sufficienter allegari non debent. Et ideo quemadmodum sancti similitudines & naturales rationes assumunt ad declarandum, quomodo tres personae sunt unus Deus: & quomodo corpus Christi vere est in sacramento altaris, & similia: Sic etiam sanctus Augustinus, per verba Salvatoris de viis & sepibus voluit declarare, quod haeretici & schismatici intrare ecclesiam sunt cogendi. Si tamen de hoc esset apparens contentio, per illam solam auctoritatem Christi sufficientes probari non posset.
units.tr: STUDENT. I will press two further objections to what has been said. It does not seem rightly said that blessed Gregory did not arrive at the first meaning of the words of blessed Job. For of many words of Job, which ought not to be understood literally but only mystically, such as "the day on which I was born" (Job 3), and of many others, he plainly asserts that Job understood them in the way he expounds them. He would not have done so unless he knew that this was Job's first meaning. For according to what has been said, the first meaning of anyone's words is what the speaker actually has in mind. Again, according to what has been said, there would be many words in divine Scripture which, although they can and should be read for the edification of the people, and although by turning them into moral and other senses, which ingenious men can draw from them without these words (as with the fables of poets and others who feign that beasts spoke and did many things, and as those fables can be usefully applied to form morals), still could in no way be cited to confirm the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines, to strengthen those points which are brought into dispute, or to establish the faith in a doubtful matter. For their first meaning cannot be had, and their other meanings are by no means to be thought authentic, unless they can be shown by other passages of Scripture or by assertions that cannot be refuted. Yet we know that the holy Fathers did the opposite. For Augustine, in his letter to Boniface (cited in 23 q. 6, c. schismatici), understands by "the ways and hedges" schismatics, and Christ speaks of such in Luke 14, wishing by these same words to prove among heretics and schismatics that heretics are to be compelled to enter the Church. And yet other crimes may be understood by "ways and hedges" just as well as heresies and schisms, whence other criminals too are to be restrained by ecclesiastical severity; nor is it recorded that Christ there meant heresies and schisms by "ways and hedges." Likewise Innocent III, in the decretal Solita (de maioritate et obedientia), and many others, prove by those words spoken to Jeremiah (Jer. 1), "Behold, I have set you this day over the nations and over the kingdoms," that the empire is subject to the priesthood. And yet it has by no means been revealed by God that those words of Jeremiah 1 must be understood of the pope in respect of the empire. MASTER. Some answer the first of these objections by saying that just as a certain literary man, in a book he wrote on the tricks of fortune, often appeared to express a sentiment by such an exposition and manner of speaking, "it could happen" (contingere potuit), that is, "if it ever happens" (si quando evenire contigerit), so also blessed Gregory, when he often said in a general sense "Job said," "Job understood," or "meant to say," intended nothing other than that Job could understand it in this way. He did not intend to assert that Job actually understood it in this way. Blessed Gregory often uses this manner of speaking to mark this, and the words of Job can be understood otherwise; by this he hints that he often did not mean to assert, when he said "Job so understood it," that Job then had such an understanding in his mind, but that he could have had such an understanding. Likewise many preachers and expositors of the holy Scriptures use this manner of speaking about various holy men and women, or some other determinate matter: "Isaiah or Jeremiah, or another prophet, or another writer of some part of the canonical Scripture, prophesied or spoke about this holy man." And yet, if they think rightly, they do not mean that the prophet or other writer had in mind to speak about this holy man or matter, but that he could understand it, or that such words can be understood of such a matter. And to mark this, those who understand these things often use words like these: "such words of divine Scripture can be expounded of this or that." STUDENT. Can some examples from the Scriptures be adduced in this manner of speaking? MASTER. Some think so. Thus in Exodus 8 it is said of Pharaoh's magicians: "The magicians likewise did so with their enchantments, to bring forth gnats, and they tried to do the same" (they attempted it). In Job too it is said: "Who has resisted God and had peace?" that is, "who has wished to resist?" For if "resisted" stands for "wished to resist," and "did" stands for "tried to do," it seems that "understood" could stand for "could understand." STUDENT. Tell me how one answers the second objection I raised. MASTER. Some concede that words of Scripture, about whose first meaning there is no certainty, ought not to be brought forward to prove only those points which are in dispute between others. Yet they may be adduced to guide, to persuade, or in some way to clarify something about which there is contention, under some sound and non-erroneous sense. Just as reasons and arguments are brought forward by the saints and others to persuade in some way the articles of faith, and also those things which can be known only by revelation, though these must not be cited as sufficient proof of such things. And so, just as the saints take up similitudes and natural reasons to explain how three persons are one God, and how the body of Christ is truly in the sacrament of the altar, and similar things, so also St. Augustine, by the Saviour's words about the ways and hedges, wished to clarify that heretics and schismatics are to be compelled to enter the Church. If, however, there were an apparent contention about this, it could not be sufficiently proved by that authority of Christ alone.

units.la: Sic etiam per verba diuina dicta Hieremiæ (vt allegatum est supra) declarari potest, quod imperium est aliquo modo indignius sacerdotio & summo pontificatu, quod tamen per verba illa ostendi non posset, nisi aliunde constaret. Quemadmodum per quasdam similitudines & rationes naturales à sancto Augustino & aliis quibuscunq; adductas, sufficienter declarari non posset, quod tres personæ sunt vnus Deus, etiam apud Christianos, nisi per alium modum certitudinem ipsius accipérent. Propter quod, vt quidam putant, per illa verba Hieremiæ non potest ostendi, quod imperium est à papa, vel quod imperator, aut alius rex quicunq; est vasallus papæ: nec aliquid aliud, nisi quod p alias vias potest sufficienter ostendi. Sic generaliter aliqui arbitrantur, quod per nullum sensum mysticum cuiuscunq; auctoritatis scripturæ diuinæ potest aliquid sufficienter ostendi, nisi constet quod idem sensus mysticus est primus intellectus scribentis, aut reuelantis, vel docentis: vel nisi alibi in sacra scriptura tanq; sensus primus sententialiter habeatur: aut per alia viam manifestam irrefragabiliter possit ostendi. Ex quo videtur posse concludi, quod de stulta temeritate excusari non possit, qui per solos sensus mysticos scripturæ diuinæ (quos nec ex aliis locis scripturæ possunt argumento euidenti inferre, nec per rationem irrefragabilem possunt concludere, nec p certam ac specialem ac miraculosam revelationem certificati sunt de ipsis) aliqua futura contingentia audent prædicere, vel futura quando euenient (quæ absq; determinatione temporis in sacris litteris sunt prædicta) afferere non formidant: Vel quæq; alia non metuunt affirmare, quæp aliam viam indubiam & apertam manifestare non possunt. Cuilibet enim tali videtur Iohan. Apoc. vlt. comminari, cum dicit: Si quis apposuerit ad hæc, apponet Deus super illum plagas. cui Salomon videtur alludere, cum ait Prouer. 30. nec addas quicquam verbis illius, & arguaris inueniarisq; mendax. Tales enim temerarii, & prauitati hæreticæ propinqui, credentes se ad omnium contentorum in scripturis sacris primum posse pertingere intellectum, minime imitantur humilitatem beati Aug. qui quauis fuerit in scripturis supra alios eruditus, fatetur se non omnia intelligere, quæ in scripturis diligentissime legit. Vnde pertractans 10. de ciuitate Dei verba beati Pauli apostoli ad Thess. 2. vbi dicitur: Et nunc quid detineat scitis, vt reueletur in suo tempore, ait &c. Quid autem ait, & nunc quid detineat scitis, i.e. quid sit quæ causa sit dilationis eius, vt reueletur in suo tempore, scitis quoniam hoc scire illes dixit aperte, hoc dicere voluit. Et ideo nos, qui nescimus quod illi sciebant, peruenire cum labore ad id quod sensit apostolus tupimus, non valemus: præsertim quia & illa quæ addidit huic sensum faciunt obscuriorem. Nam quid est: iam enim mysterium iniquitatis operatur tantum, qui modo tenet, teneat donec de medio fiat, & tunc reuelabitur iniquus. Ego profiteor quid dixerit, me fateor ignorare. Quid in Epistola ad Rom. vt habetur dist. 9. ca. ego solus, insinuare videtur, dicens: Si alius, aut in eis (scil. scripturis canonicis) ostenderetur, quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud existimo quam mendosum esse codicem, vel non esse affectum interpretem quod dictum est, quod me minime intellexisse non ambigam.
units.tr: So too, by the divine words spoken to Jeremiah (as was cited above), it can be made clear that the empire is in some way less worthy than the priesthood and the supreme pontificate. Yet this could not be shown by those words unless it were established from elsewhere. Just as it could not be sufficiently made clear by certain similitudes and natural reasons adduced by St. Augustine and by others of any sort, that three persons are one God, even among Christians, unless they received certainty of it by another way. For this reason, as some think, it cannot be shown by those words of Jeremiah that the empire is from the pope, or that the emperor, or any other king whatsoever, is a vassal of the pope; nor can anything else be shown except what can be sufficiently shown by other ways. Thus in general some judge that nothing can be sufficiently shown by any mystical sense of any authority of divine Scripture, unless it is established that the same mystical sense is the first meaning of the writer, or of the one revealing or teaching; or unless it is found elsewhere in sacred Scripture as the primary sense, by assertion; or unless it can be irrefutably shown by some other clear way. From this it seems it can be concluded that he cannot be excused from foolish rashness who, relying only on the mystical senses of divine Scripture (which they cannot infer as evident argument from other passages of Scripture, nor conclude by irrefutable reason, nor are they certified of them by certain, special, and miraculous revelation), dares to predict any future contingent events, or does not fear to assert future events as to when they will happen (which in the sacred letters are foretold without determination of time), or does not shrink from affirming anything else which cannot be made manifest by some other certain and open way. For such a one seems to be threatened by John in the last chapter of the Apocalypse: "If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues." Solomon seems to allude to this when he says in Proverbs 30: "Add nothing to his words, lest you be reproved and found a liar." Such rash men, close to heretical perversity, who believe they can arrive at the first meaning of all the contents of the sacred Scriptures, by no means imitate the humility of blessed Augustine, who, though he was more learned in the Scriptures than others, confesses that he does not understand everything he reads most diligently in them. Hence, when treating in book 10 of The City of God the words of the apostle Paul to the Thessalonians (2 Thess. 2), where it is said, "And now you know what restrains, that he may be revealed in his time," he says etc. What he says, "and now you know what restrains," that is, what the cause of his delay is, "that he may be revealed in his time," you know, because he plainly said that they knew this, and this is what he wished to say. And therefore we, who do not know what they knew, cannot with labour arrive at what the apostle meant by the words we grope after.
