Especially because the words he added make the sense more obscure: "For the mystery of iniquity already works; only let him who now restrains, restrain until he is taken out of the way, and then the wicked one will be revealed." I profess that I do not know what he meant. In the Epistle to the Romans, as it stands in dist. 9, c. ego solus, he seems to hint, saying: "If it were shown in them (namely the canonical Scriptures) that something appears contrary to the truth, I think nothing else than that the codex is faulty, or that the translator has not understood what was said; and I do not doubt that I have by no means understood it."

units.la: DISCIP. Verba prædicta de apponentibus & addentibus aliqua contraria verbis scripturæ diuinæ debent intelligi non de apponentibus & addentibus, quæ ex aliis locis scripturæ nequeant extrahi euidenter. Aliter enim sancti patres complura verba scripturæ mystice exponendo grauiter deliquissent. Imo videtur, quod per verba saluatoris possit ostendi; quod verba huius scripturæ aliter, quam per reuelationem miraculosam possint intelligi, cum ait discipulis suis Matt. 24. Cum videritis abominationem desolationis, quæ dicta est à Daniele propheta stante in loco sancto qui legit intelligat. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Christus insinuauit aperte, intellectum primum prophetæ Danielis, de quo ibi fit mentio, aliter quam per reuelationem miraculosam posse haberi. M A G. Ad hoc respondetur, quod quadrupliciter potest aliquid addi scripturis diuinis. Quia potest addi aliquod falsum. Potest etiam eis apponi verum: non tanquam primus intellectus scripturæ. Potest etiam eis addi verum tanquam primus intellectus ipsarum possibilis haberi ex sola meditatione scripturarum suppositia influentia diuina. Potest etiam eis addi verum tanquam primus intellectus haberi possibilis per reuelationem vel alicuius facti noui exhibitionem apertam. Qui primo modo aliquid apponit vel addit scripturis diuinis, quandoq; pertinax hæreticus est censendus; quandoq; vero errans solummodo est putandus secundum diuersitatem falsi, quod additur, & etiam secundum varietatem adhæsionis addentis. Si vero apponatur eis aliquod verum, quod non est primus intellectus scripturæ, non tanq; primus intellectus, sed solummodo tanq; verum, nequaquam scripturæ contrarium; sed tanquam ædificans ad salutem, vel aliquomodo ad declarationem catholicæ veritatis, laudabiliter addi potest. & sic sancti veritates plurimas sacris literis addiderunt. Tertio modo potest addi aliquid scripturis, tanquam primus intellectus possibilis haberi ex meditatione scripturarum. Et si vere sic potest haberi, potest addi laudabiliter ad ea, quia sic addere non est aliud, q dicere explicite & aperte, quod scriptura dicit implicite & latenter. Si autem talis intellectus vere ex scripturis haberi non potest, (& tamen apponitur tanquam primus intellectus) falso apponitur. & aliquando apponens est tantummodo errans, aliquando hæreticus est censendus. afferere enim pertinaciter aliquid esse primum intellectum scripturæ diuinæ, quod non est, sapit hæresim manifestam; quia quamuis verum, quod apponitur, non fit falsum, nec contrarium catholicæ veritati, tamen assertio, qua dicitur esse primus intellectus scripturæ, est erronea atque falsa. Quarto modo potest aliquid addi scripturis, tanquam primus intellectus, dummodo habeatur per reuelationem vel per exhibitionem apertam noui facti, vt sancti apostoli per reuelationem nouam plurium parabolarum Christi, à Christo exponente ipsas acceperunt primum intellectum. Sic etiam discipuli videndo statuam Cæsaris poni in templo potetant accipere primum mùm intellectum prophetiae Danielis. Sic etiam discipuli, vt habetur Ioan. 2. videntes Christum resurrexisse à mortuis coeperunt intellectum illorum verborum Christi: Soluite templum hoc, & in tribus diebus excitabo illud. post haec enim verba ibidem subiungitur: ille autem dicebat de templo corporis sui. Dum ergo resurrexit à mortuis, recordati sunt discipuli eius, quia hoc dicebat, & crediderunt scripturae & sermoni, quem dixit Iesus.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. The words just cited, about those who add to or insert things contrary to the words of divine Scripture, must be understood not of those who add things that cannot clearly be drawn from other passages of Scripture. Otherwise the holy Fathers, in expounding many words of Scripture mystically, would have sinned grievously. Indeed, it seems that it can be shown from the words of the Saviour that the words of this Scripture can be understood otherwise than by miraculous revelation, when he said to his disciples in Matthew 24: "When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place, let him who reads understand." From these words it is gathered that Christ plainly indicated that the primary meaning of the prophet Daniel, of which mention is made there, can be had otherwise than by miraculous revelation. MAGISTER. To this it is answered that something can be added to the divine Scriptures in four ways. First, something false can be added. Second, something true can be attached to them, not as the primary meaning of Scripture. Third, something true can be added as the primary meaning of them, which can be had from the sole meditation on the Scriptures with the supporting influence of divine grace. Fourth, something true can be added as the primary meaning, which can be had through revelation or the open exhibition of some new fact. Whoever adds or appends something to the divine Scriptures in the first way is to be judged a stubborn heretic at times, but at other times is to be thought merely in error, according to the kind of falsehood that is added and also according to the nature of the adherence of the one who adds. But if something true is appended to them that is not the primary meaning of Scripture, not as the primary meaning but only as true, it is in no way contrary to Scripture, but, as edifying unto salvation or in some way serving to declare Catholic truth, it may be added laudably; and so the holy men added very many truths to the sacred letters. In the third way something may be added to Scripture as the primary meaning that can be had from the meditation on the Scriptures. And if it truly can be had in this way, it may be laudably added to them, since to add thus is nothing other than to say explicitly and openly what Scripture says implicitly and in a hidden way. But if such a meaning cannot truly be had from the Scriptures, and yet it is put forward as the primary meaning, it is falsely appended; and sometimes the one who appends it is only in error, sometimes he is to be judged a heretic. For to assert stubbornly that something is the primary meaning of divine Scripture when it is not, savours of manifest heresy; because, although the truth that is appended is not made false, nor contrary to Catholic truth, yet the assertion by which it is called the primary meaning of Scripture is erroneous and false. In the fourth way something may be added to Scripture as the primary meaning, provided it is had through revelation or through the open exhibition of a new fact, as the holy apostles received the primary meaning of many parables of Christ through a new revelation, Christ himself expounding them. So too the disciples, seeing the statue of Caesar set up in the temple, could receive the primary meaning of the prophecy of Daniel. So too the disciples, as is related in John 2, when they saw Christ risen from the dead, began to understand those words of Christ: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up"; for after these words it is added in the same place: "But he spoke of the temple of his body." Therefore, when he rose from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad secundam obiectionem capituli 15.
units.tr: In which the second objection of chapter 15 is answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Vt expediamus nos de ista materia, narra quomodo respondetur ad secundam obiectionem, quam cap. 15. induxi. MAGIST. Respondetur ad ipsam, quod sicut scriptura sacra & in locis planis & aliis obscurioribus, quorum tamen primus virtute ingenii humani poterit accipi intellectus, pie legentibus fructuosa existit, licet aliis occasio sit errandi (unde & communiter omnes haeretici haereses suas in scripturis divinis fundare conati sunt.) Sic etiam illa, quorum primus intellectus absque revelatione haberi non potest, salubria sunt, & utilia legentibus ea, non ad capiendum primum intellectum ipsorum. Sed ad humilitatem & alios sensus mysticos capiendos, licet periculosa & mortifera sunt superbis atque stultis, qui altiora se quaerunt & inuestigant, quae minime apprehendere valent.
units.tr: STUDENT. So that we may be done with this matter, tell me how the second objection, which I raised in chapter 15, is answered. TEACHER. It is answered thus: just as Holy Scripture is profitable to devout readers both in its plain passages and in its more obscure ones, the first sense of which can nevertheless be grasped by the power of human understanding, although it becomes an occasion of error for others (which is why all heretics have commonly tried to found their heresies on the divine Scriptures), so too those passages whose first sense cannot be had without revelation are wholesome and useful to those who read them, not for grasping their first sense, but for grasping humility and their other mystical senses; though they are dangerous and deadly to the proud and foolish, who seek and investigate higher things which they are by no means able to apprehend.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: Chapter 21.

units.la: Iterum probat opinionem capitulo primo recitatam, & hoc pluribus allegationibus, ad quas respondetur infra. 23. & 27. capitulis.
units.tr: Again he proves the opinion recited in the first chapter, and does so by several citations, which are answered below, in chapters 23 and 27.

units.la: DISCIP. Quia opinio supra primo cap. recitata quamuis concedat, quod scripturis canonicis & determinationibus generalium conciliorum sit certa credulitas adhibenda, tamen hoc generaliter negat de scripturis aliis quibuscunque. ideo videamus an illa sit consona veritati. primo autem pone opinionem cum motivis eiusdem. MAGIST. Opinio praedicta ponitur & probatur in haec verba. Quod autem scripturis aliis, quae scilicet humano spiritu revelante sunt traditae, nemo certam credulitatem aut veritatis confessionem praebere teneatur, apparet. Quoniam nulli scripturae falsum signari potenti tenetur quis firmiter credere aut ipsam tanquam veram simpliciter confiteri. hoc autem patiuntur scripturae innitentes humanae inventioni singularis personae, aut collegii partialis. Possunt enim a veritate deficere, vt experientia palam est. habetur etiam in Psal. ego autem dixi in excessu meo, omnis homo mendax. Scripturae vero canonicae non sic: quia non sunt ab humana inventione, sed immediate traditae Dei inspiratione, qui non potest falli, nec fallere vult. Hanc enim sententiam & differentiam humanarum & divinarum scripturarum aperte confirmat August. 13. epistolarum ad Iohannem, cum dixit: ego enim fateor charitati tuae omnino solum ex omnium scripturarum libris, quae iam canonica appellantur, didici hunc honorem timoremque deferre, vt nullum earum auctorem scribendo aliquid erraffe firmissime credam. ac si in eis offeratur literis, quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud quam vel mendosum esse codicem, vel interpretem non assecutum esse, quod dictum est: vel me minime intellexisse non ambigam. Alios autem ita lego, vt quantacunque sanctitate, doctrinaque praepolleant, non ideo verum putem, quia ita senserunt, sed quia mihi, vel per illos auctores canonicos, vel probabili ratione quod a vero non abhorrent, persuadere poterant. Sed hoc idem replicat & admonet in prologo libri de Trinitate, cum dixit: noli lector sic meis literis quasi scripturis canonicis inserviri, sed in illa & quod non credis cum inveneris, incunctanter crede: in ista autem (scil. meis) quod certum non habes, nisi certe intellexeris, noli firmiter tenere. Idem quoque dixit in epistola ad Fortunatianum, & aliis pluribus libris. Idem quoque videtur sensisse Hieronymus in expositione Catholica fidei, cum dixit: novum & vetus testamentum recipimus in eo librorum numero, quod sancta catholica ecclesia tradit auctoritas. Aug. ergo scripturas proprias a canonicis separavit: nec ipse, qui tantae fuit sanctitatis auctoritatis & scientiae, suas traditiones canonicas appellare praesumpsit. Hoc enim impium est, & sacrilegii modus quidam. quoniam circa humana traditione dicta vel scripta, error & falsum contingere potest: quod in canone secundum veritatem dicto, nullatenus evenire contingit. Propter quod etiam ex concilio Carthaginensi 3. prohibitum reperitur valde, ne sub nomine harum (canonicarum scilicet) alia quaevis scriptura legantur. unde legitur ibidem & in Isidori Codice continetur haec series: Item placuit, vt praeter scripturas canonicas nihil in ecclesia legatur sub nomine divinarum scripturarum. sunt autem canonica scripturae Genesis, & caeterae, quae de volumine Bibliae numerantur
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Since the opinion recited in the first chapter, although it grants that certain belief is to be given to the canonical Scriptures and to the decisions of the general councils, denies this in general of all other writings whatever, let us see whether it agrees with the truth. First, however, set out the opinion together with its grounds. MASTER. The aforesaid opinion is stated and proved in these words: "That no one is bound to give certain belief to, or to confess as true without qualification, other writings, namely those handed down under the revelation of the human spirit, is evident. For no one is bound to believe firmly, or to confess simply as true, any writing that can be shown to be false. Yet writings resting on the human invention of a single person or of a partial college do suffer this. For they can fall away from the truth, as experience plainly shows. It is also found in the Psalm: I said in my excess, every man is a liar. But canonical Scriptures are not so, because they are not from human invention but were handed down immediately by the inspiration of God, who cannot be deceived and does not wish to deceive." This very view, and the difference between human and divine writings, Augustine plainly confirms in his thirteenth letter to John, where he says: For I confess to your charity that I have learned to pay this honour and reverence to the books of Scripture alone, which are now called canonical, so that I firmly believe that none of their authors has erred in writing. And if in these writings something should be found that seems contrary to the truth, I do not doubt that either the copy is faulty, or the translator has not grasped what was said, or that I myself have not understood. But I read others in such a way that, however much they excel in holiness and learning, I do not therefore think a thing true because they held it, but because they were able to persuade me of it either by those canonical authors or by probable reasoning that it does not depart from the truth. He repeats and gives the same warning in the prologue to his book On the Trinity, where he says: Reader, do not so serve my writings as though they were canonical Scripture; but in the latter, whatever you do not believe, when you have found it, believe without hesitation; in the former (namely mine), whatever you do not hold as certain unless you have understood it with certainty, do not hold firmly. He also said the same in his letter to Fortunatianus, and in many other books. Jerome seems to have held the same view in his exposition of the Catholic faith, when he said: We receive the Old and New Testament in that number of books which the holy catholic Church hands down by authority. Augustine therefore separated his own writings from the canonical ones; nor did he himself, who was of such great holiness, authority and learning, presume to call his own traditions canonical. For this is impious and a kind of sacrilege, since error and falsehood can occur in whatever is said or written by human tradition, which cannot in any way happen in the canon, which is called true. For this reason also the Third Council of Carthage is found to have forbidden strictly that any other writing be read in church under the name of these (namely the canonical books). Hence the following sequence is read in the same place and is contained in the Codex of Isidore: Likewise it has been decided that, besides the canonical Scriptures, nothing shall be read in the church under the name of divine Scriptures. The canonical Scriptures are Genesis and the rest, which are counted in the volume of the Bible.

units.la: ibidem:
units.tr: Ibid.:

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXII.

units.la: Arguit in contrarium eorum, quae dicta sunt cap. primo & immediate praecedenti, & ex his quae possunt inferri ex eadem opinione & eius dictis.
units.tr: It argues against what was said in the first chapter and in the one immediately preceding it, and against what can be inferred from the same opinion and its statements.

units.la: DISCIP. Primo contra istam assertionem nitere allegare. MAGIST. Nonnullis apparet, quod ex ista possint plures absurditates inferri. Quarum prima est, quia ex quo scriptores scripturae canonicae de hoc seculo migrauerunt, nullorum mortalium scripturis credulitas est praebenda: & ita nulli mortales essent ad ferendum testimonium admittendi in quocunque casu. Quantae autem & quot absurditates ex ista sequuntur, nullus sanae mentis ignorat. Quod autem ista absurditas ex assertione praescripta sequatur, manifeste apparet. Nam quorum scripturis quibuscunque non est praestanda certa credulitas, ipsorum verbis minime est credendum, quia qui potest falsum asserere in scripto, in solo verbo falsum asserere potest. Secunda absurditas, quod nulli historiae, nulli Legendae cuiuscunque sancti, nullis gestis de summis pontificibus, aliis clericis, imperatoribus, regibus, & aliis hominibus fidelibus vel infidelibus, quae non in scripturis canonicis continentur, sed in aliis scripturis, est credendum. Ex quo vlterius concluderetur, quod dubitare licet, an praeter episcopos, imperatores & reges in quibuscunque partibus orbis terrarum, de quibus in scriptura diuina & conciliis generalibus fit mentio: & praeter illos, quos scimus nunc & vidimus praesidere, vnquam fuerint alii quemcunque fidelem vel infidelem populum gubernantes. Vel saltem dubitare de quolibet alio in speciali non erit illicitum, cum de aliquibus ipsorum validiori testimonio, quam per scripturam canonicam constare non possit. Sequeretur etiam, quod nulli esset illicitum credere, quod postquam scripta est scriptura diuina, Deus nullum fecit miraculum: quod ipse non vidit, vel non cognouerit per seipsum. Nec fortiori testimonio, quam per scripturas sanctorum patrum, quae tamen non sunt canonicae, sibi liquere potest. Ex quo concluditur, quod dubitare licet, an quicunque canonizati per Romanam ecclesiam sint legitime propter vitam & miracula cathalogo sanctorum asscripti, quia potissime de hoc liquet per Legendas ipsorum. Alia absurditas sequitur, quod videlicet libris antiquis, instrumentis productis ex archiuis publicis & scripturis quae factae sunt calumnhis, & aliis quibuscunque, quae non reperiuntur in Biblia, fides esset nullatenus adhibenda. Cuius contrarium in sacris legibus, & canonibus imperialibus reperitur expresse. Ex hac enim absurditate infertur aperte, quod per huiusmodi libros, instrumenta & scripturas nunquam esset ferenda sententia, quia per illas scripturas, quibus non est adhibenda fides, sententia ferri non debet. Sicut nec est ferenda sententia per testes, quibus credere non oportet.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. First, bring a charge against this assertion. MASTER. It appears to some that several absurdities can be drawn from it. The first is that, since the writers of canonical Scripture have passed from this age, the credibility of no mortal's writings is to be granted, and so no mortals would be admitted to give testimony in any case whatever. How great and how many absurdities follow from this, no one of sound mind is ignorant. That this absurdity follows from the assertion stated above is plainly evident. For whoever's writings are not to be given certain credence, their words are by no means to be believed, since one who can assert what is false in writing can assert what is false in speech alone. The second absurdity is that no history, no legend of any saint, no deeds of the supreme pontiffs, other clergy, emperors, kings, and other men, faithful or unfaithful, which are not contained in the canonical Scriptures but in other writings, is to be believed. From this it would further follow that one may doubt whether, besides the bishops, emperors and kings in whatever parts of the world are mentioned in divine Scripture and the general councils, and besides those whom we know and have seen presiding now, there have ever been others governing any faithful or unfaithful people; or at least it will not be unlawful to doubt about any other in particular, since about some of them no more reliable testimony can be had than through canonical Scripture. It would also follow that no one may be forbidden to believe that, since divine Scripture was written, God has performed no miracle that he himself did not see or know of through his own person; nor can it be clear to him by any stronger testimony than through the writings of the holy Fathers, which nevertheless are not canonical. From this it is concluded that one may doubt whether those canonized by the Roman Church have been legitimately enrolled in the catalogue of saints on account of their life and miracles, since this is chiefly made clear through their Legends. Another absurdity follows, namely that for old books, instruments produced from public archives, writings made in court proceedings, and any others that are not found in the Bible, faith is in no way to be given. The contrary is expressly found in the sacred laws and imperial canons. For from this absurdity it is plainly inferred that sentence could never be pronounced through such books, instruments and writings, since sentence ought not to be pronounced through those writings to which faith is not to be given, just as sentence is not to be pronounced through witnesses whom one ought not to believe.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad allegationes supra capitulo 21. adductas.
units.tr: In which the arguments adduced above in chapter 21 are answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Istae allegationes contra praescriptam assertionem ad praesens sufficiant: nunc dic, quomodo respondetur ad motiua eius. Ad primum cum dicitur, quod nulli scripturae salsum significari potenti tenetur quis firmiter credere, aut ipsam tanquam veram simpliciter confiteri. Respondetur, quod si ista propositio intelligeretur de scriptura vel de scriptore, posset concedi aliquomodo, quia scripturae falsae aliquomodo, praesertim postquam constiterit, quod ipsa est falsa, adhibere fidem non debet hoc sciens. Sed multae sunt scripturae non canonicae, quae hoc minime patiuntur, nec quod hoc minime patiatur per experientiam constare potest. Multae enim sunt scripturae non solum sanctorum patrum, sed infidelium philosophorum, & aliorum, imo & haereticorum, in quibus nullum falsum poterit reperiri. Quamuis enim haeretici in quibusdam scripturis errauerint, quidam tamen eorum in quibusdam aliis nullatenus errauerunt. Vnde & Origenes licet (vt fertur) turpissime erraverit, sicut recitat beatus Aug. 11. de ciuitate Dei, tamen in multis scripturis eius nullus error apparet. Et ideo multis scripturis infidelium licet adhibere fidem. Sed si intelligatur de scriptore (vt videlicet quamuis alicui scripturae alicuius, scilicet non scriptoris scripturae canonicae) adhibenda sit fides: (non quia a tali scriptore est scripta, sed quia per scripturas canonicas aut per rationem naturalem potest ostendi, quia nullam continet falsitatem.) Tamen ipsi scriptori potenti falsum asserere, seu significare, non tenetur quis firmiter credere. Et ideo scripturam eius non est necesse tanquam veram simpliciter confiteri, nisi possit aperte probari, quod est consona scripturis canonicis, vel rationi euidenti naturali, maiorem apparentiam habere videtur. Et tn sic intellecta a veritate aliena videtur. Ad cuius declarationem dicitur esse sciendum, quod sicut secundum iura canonica & alia, aliqua est praesumptio, in cuius contrarium est aliqua probatio admittenda & alia, in cuius contrarium nulla probatio est admittenda. Ita potest aliquis alii homini vel assertioni credere, & ipsam cofiteri tanquam veram dupliciter. Quia vel credulitate tam certa, vt nulla velit in contrarium probationem admittere vel audire, aut credulitate firma; non tamen tam certa, quin reputet quod sit probatio in contrarium audienda, si quis fide dignus offerat se contrarium probaturum. Primo modo, nulli scriptori cuiuscunq; scripturae nō canonicae in omnibus dictis aut scripturis eius est credendum. Alicui tamen assertioni eius taliter credere licet & oportet in quatuor casibus. Puta, si assertio eius patenter & aperte per scripturas canonicas, per assertionem vniuersalis ecclesiae, per rationem naturalem euidentem, praesertim consonam catholicae fidei, vel bonis moribus, aut per apertum miraculum possit ostendi. Secundo modo, pluribus aliis quam scriptoribus. Scripturae canonicae in multis aliis q; in praedictis quatuor casibus, est credendum, quia summis pontificibus, conciliis generalibus, & aliis sanctis episcopis, & doctoribus, atq; fide dignis viris, & ab ecclesia probatis, quantum ad ea quae facti sunt, quae videl. per seipsos, vel per alios fide dignos, quibus credere tenebantur, potuerunt cognoscere. Et peccat, qui eis non credit: quia reuerentiam, quam Deus tantis viris adhibuit, denegare praesumit. Quin n. eis & huiusmodi non crederet, dubitaret an scienter in huiusmodi mentirentur. Et ita sine causa ipsos non crederet esse veraces. In huiusmodi ergo credendum est eis, propter quod non solum per testes, sed etiam per libros antiquos, & instrumenta, quae de falsitate conuinci non possunt, & scripturas antiquorum, licite iudex fert sententiam, & peccaret si non ferret. Quantum autem ad illa, quae pure sunt scientiae & non facti, scripturis sanctorum patrum & auctorum ac consiliorum est reuerentia exhibenda. Quia doctrina eorum minime est spernenda, sed sollicite attendenda, & cum diligentia audienda, praesertim cum de aliquo pertinere ad fidem vel mores quaeritur veritas, de quo in scripturis suis tradiderunt, quod senserunt. & qui doctrinam eorum, cum posset, negligeret legere, si erraret, de temeritate plectibili esset merito arguedus. Quia contra praeceptum Salomonis, prudentiae seu peritiae propriae conuinceretur innixi. Doctrina insuper eorundem, si in aliqua sui parte videatur contraria veritati, pie & sane exponenda est, si potest, & ad verum intellectum trahenda. Et quamuis ad sanum intellectum trahi non possit, non sunt statim de haeretica prauitate notandi: licet errantes debeant reputari. Nonnullis tamen apparet, quod quantum ad decretales & constitutiones ac diffinitiones solennes summorum pontificum, & aliorum episcoporum ac generalium prouincialium & episcopalium conciliorum, & etiam capitulorum & collegiorum quorumcunq; intendentium alios ad suam assertionem firmiter defensandam cogere & artare: & quantum ad alias scripturas eorundem, & aliorum est discretio facienda. Quia si in primis scripturis inuenitur aliquid catholicae veritati contrarium, statim auctores eorum sunt haeretici reputandi: quia de pertinacia ex hoc ipso, quod cogunt alios suo errori pertinaciter adhaerere, possunt manifeste conuinci. Si in illis error aliquis reperitur, cuius contrarium tenens vel scribens, eundem errorem non tenetur explicite credere: non est statim auctor huiusmodi scripturae erroneae haereticus iudicandus, sed est de prauitate haeretica excusandus, nisi per alios modos (de quibus multa diximus in prima parte istius Dialogi lib. 4.) de pertinacia conuinci valeat apertissimis documentis. Porro licet viri huiusmodi venerabiles in aliquo aperte conuincantur errare, & ideo liceat eis, qui de hoc sunt certi, ipsos quantum ad hoc negare & improbare: in aliis tamen quibuscunque, de quibus non est certum ipsos errare, praesumendum est pro dictis eorum, ita ut absque temeritate culpari non possint neque in genere, neque in specie. & quanto plures virorum huiusmodi in aliqua sententia concordauerint, tanto magis praesumendum est pro eadem, non tamen sic, quin in contrarium valeat audiri probatio.
units.tr: DISCIP. Let these objections against the assertion set out above suffice for the present. Now tell me how its supporting arguments are answered. To the first, where it is said that no one is bound to believe firmly, or to confess as simply true, any writing that is known to signify something false, the answer is this: if the proposition were understood of the writing or of its author, it could be granted in some sense, because a writing that is false in some way, especially once it has been established that it is false, ought not to be trusted by one who knows this. But there are many non-canonical writings to which this does not apply at all, and this can be shown from experience. For there are many writings not only of the holy Fathers but also of unbelieving philosophers and others, and even of heretics, in which no falsehood can be found. For although heretics have erred in some writings, some of them have in other writings not erred at all. Hence Origen too, although (as is reported) he erred most shamefully, as the blessed Augustine recounts in book 11 of The City of God, nevertheless no error appears in many of his writings. Therefore it is lawful to give faith to many writings of unbelievers. But if it is understood of the author, namely that faith is to be given to some writing of a certain author, one who is not the author of a canonical writing (not because it was written by such an author, but because it can be shown from canonical Scripture or from natural reason that it contains no falsehood), nevertheless one is not bound to believe firmly an author who is known to assert or signify something false. And so it is not necessary to confess his writing as simply true, unless it can be clearly proved that it agrees with the canonical Scriptures or with evident natural reason, or else seems to have greater appearance of truth. And yet, so understood, it appears alien to the truth. In explaining this, it must be said that just as, according to the canon law and other laws, there is one presumption against which some proof is to be admitted, and another against which no proof is to be admitted, so one man may believe another man or an assertion, and confess it as true, in two ways. Either with a belief so certain that one is unwilling to admit or hear any proof to the contrary, or with a belief that is firm but not so certain that one does not think proof to the contrary should be heard, if some trustworthy person offers to prove the contrary. In the first way, one must not believe any author of any non-canonical writing in all that he says or writes. Yet it is lawful and right to believe one of his assertions in this way in four cases: namely, if the assertion can be plainly and openly shown by canonical Scripture, by the assertion of the universal Church, by evident natural reason, especially one agreeing with the Catholic faith or good morals, or by a manifest miracle. In the second way, more readily than in the case of other authors, one must believe the canonical Scriptures in many matters beyond the four cases just mentioned, because it is to be believed of the supreme pontiffs, general councils, other holy bishops and teachers, and men worthy of trust and approved by the Church, insofar as they concern matters of fact, which they could know either by themselves or through other trustworthy persons whom they were bound to believe. And he who does not believe them sins, because he presumes to deny the reverence which God has shown to such great men. Indeed, if he did not believe them in such matters, he would doubt whether they were knowingly lying in such things, and so he would be judging them without cause not to be truthful. Therefore in such matters they are to be believed; for this reason a judge lawfully pronounces sentence not only on the testimony of witnesses but also on old books and instruments which cannot be proved false, and on the writings of the ancients, and he would sin if he did not pronounce it. But as regards those things which are purely matters of knowledge and not of fact, reverence is to be shown to the writings of the holy Fathers, authors and councils. For their teaching is by no means to be despised, but carefully attended to and heard with diligence, especially when the truth is sought concerning something that pertains to faith or morals, about which they have handed down in their writings what they thought. And one who, when he could, neglected to read their teaching, and so erred, would rightly be charged with blameworthy rashness. For, against the precept of Solomon, he would be convicted of relying on his own prudence or skill. Moreover, if some part of their teaching appears contrary to the truth, it is to be explained piously and soundly, if possible, and brought to a true sense. And even if it cannot be brought to a sound sense, its authors are not at once to be marked with heretical perversity; although they must be regarded as erring. Yet it seems to some that, as regards the decretals, constitutions and solemn definitions of the supreme pontiffs and of other bishops, and of provincial and diocesan councils, and also of chapters and colleges of whatever kind which aim to compel others to defend their assertion firmly, a distinction must be made, and likewise as regards their other writings and those of others. For if something contrary to Catholic truth is found in the first kind of writings, their authors are at once to be reckoned heretics, because they can be plainly convicted of obstinacy from the very fact that they compel others to cling obstinately to their error. If some error is found in the others, the author of such an erroneous writing is not bound to believe explicitly the error whose contrary he holds or writes; he is not at once to be judged a heretic, but is to be excused from heretical perversity, unless by other means (of which we have said much in the first part of this Dialogue, book 4) he can be convicted of obstinacy by most manifest proofs. Furthermore, although men of this kind, venerable as they are, may be openly convicted of erring in some point, and so it is lawful for those who are certain of this to deny and disapprove them in that point, nevertheless in all other matters where it is not certain that they err, their statements are to be presumed correct, so that they cannot be blamed without rashness, either in general or in particular. And the more of such men agree in some opinion, the more that opinion is to be presumed correct; yet not so much that proof to the contrary may not be heard.

units.la: Et quamuis in his, quae pure sunt scientiae seu peritiae, praesumendum est pro huiusmodi scripturis ipsorum, tamen fortius praesumendum est pro scripturis eorundem quantum ad illa quae facti sunt: quia fortius praesumendum est ipsos nolle mentiri, quam per ratiocinationes non esse deceptos. Et ideo in his, quae facti sunt, praesertim de his quae per seipsos se insinuant cognoscere, tenetur quilibet credere ipsis, nisi per fide digniores de contrario certus existat.
units.tr: And although, in those matters which are purely of knowledge or skill, their writings are to be presumed correct, yet their writings are to be presumed correct much more strongly as regards matters of fact: because it is much more strongly to be presumed that they are unwilling to lie than that they have not been deceived by their reasonings. And so in matters of fact, especially those which they present themselves as knowing through their own experience, everyone is bound to believe them, unless he is certain from more trustworthy persons that they are wrong.

units.la: DISCIP. Contra praedicta obiici potest, quia non est necesse credere alicui testimonio, per quod infallibilis certitudo haberi non potest. Sed per humanum testimonium haberi no potest infallibilis certitudo, etiam cum de aliquo testimonium perhibet multitudo, teste Moyse, imo Deo per Moysen Exod. 21. qui ait: Non sequeris turbam ad faciendum malum, nec in iudicio plurimorum acquiescès sententiae vt a vero deuies. ergo non est necesse credere humano testimonio cuicunque. & per consequens non est necesse credere quibuscunque scripturis illorum, quorum testimonium est humanum tantummodo reputandum. cuiusmodi sunt scriptores omnes praeter illos, qui scripturas scripsere diuinas.
units.tr: DISCIP. Against what has been said it may be objected that one need not believe any testimony by which infallible certainty cannot be had. But infallible certainty cannot be had from human testimony, even when a multitude bears witness to something, as Moses bears witness, indeed God through Moses in Exodus 21, who says: "You shall not follow a crowd to do evil, nor in judgment shall you yield to the opinion of the many so as to turn aside from the truth." Therefore one need not believe human testimony of whatever kind; and consequently one need not believe the writings of those whose testimony is to be regarded as merely human. Such are all writers except those who wrote the divine Scriptures.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad hoc respondetur, quod saepe necesse est credere testimonio, quamuis per ipsum infallibilis certitudo haberi non possit, saltem credulitate illa, contra quam (non obstante quod dubitatione careat) debeat, aut possit admitti probatio. Alioquin in nullo negocio, quibuscunque testibus, qui non sunt confirmati in gratia, plusquam vniuersali ecclesiae esset credendum. Quare propter testimonium huiusmodi non esset a iudice contra aliquem ferenda sententia. Saepe igitur testimonio fide dignorum omni exceptione maiorum, qui reprobari aut conuinci de falsitate non possunt, est credendum: quamuis per ipsum certitudo infallibilis haberi non possit. In huiusmodi enim sufficit certitudo possibilis & sufficiens, quamuis non sit infallibilis. Cum autem accipitur, q; per testimonium humanum certitudo haberi non potest. Respondetur, q; quamuis per humanum testimonium praecise exclusoomni testimonio speciali diuino, infallibilis certitudo haberi non possit, tamen concurrente diuino testimonio certitudo infallibilis potest haberi, & nonnunquam per diuinum testimonium possumus esse certi, quod humanum testimonium debet infallibile reputari. Si enim humanum testimonium per diuinum miraculum approbetur, de infallibilitate eius debemus esse certi. de quo et infallibiliter possumus esse certi, si ab vniuersali ecclesia praesertim in his quae sunt necessaria ad salutem, fuerit approbatum. Propter premissionem Christi, ex qua colligitur, q; Christus nunquam deficiet ecclesiae in his, quae sunt necessaria ad salutem.
units.tr: MASTER. To this it is answered that it is often necessary to believe a witness, even though infallible certainty cannot be had from him. At least, that belief is not to be set aside, and no proof can be admitted against it, although it is free from doubt. Otherwise, in no matter whatever, with whatever witnesses who are not confirmed in grace, would more than the universal Church have to be believed. For that reason no judge could pronounce sentence against anyone on the strength of such testimony. Often, therefore, we must believe the testimony of trustworthy men, who are above every exception, who cannot be rebuked or convicted of falsehood, although infallible certainty cannot be had from it. For in such cases a possible and sufficient certainty is enough, even though it is not infallible. But when it is objected that certainty cannot be had from human testimony, the answer is this: although infallible certainty cannot be had from human testimony when all divine testimony is strictly excluded, yet when divine testimony concurs, infallible certainty can be had, and sometimes through divine testimony we can be certain that human testimony must be regarded as infallible. For if human testimony is approved by a divine miracle, we ought to be certain of its infallibility. And we can be infallibly certain of it if it has been approved by the universal Church, especially in those matters which are necessary to salvation, on account of the promise of Christ, from which it is gathered that Christ will never fail the Church in those things which are necessary to salvation.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: Vbi respondetur ad reliquas allegationes pro prima opinione factas capit. 21. scilicet ad Augustinum, Hieronymum, & concilium Carthaginense.
units.tr: Where a reply is made to the remaining allegations brought forward for the first opinion in chapter 21, namely to Augustine, Jerome and the Council of Carthage.

units.la: DISCIP. Sufficiant ista ad praesens, de allegatione praescripta. ideo dic, qualiter ad auctoritates sequentes, opinio memorata respondet. MAGIST. Quantum ad auctoritates Augustini & Hieronymi. Primo respondetur, quo ad hominem dicens, quod contrarium opinantes ipsos nequaquam allegare deberent, cum teneant quod non est necesse aliis credere scripturis quam canonicis, quae in Biblia continentur: quare vel frustra praedictas auctoritates allegant, vel opinionem propriam facto negant, cum allegando Augustinum & Hieronymum pro opinione sua firmanda, facto ostendant quod auctoritatibus Augustini, qui non fuerunt scriptores alicuius partis Bibliae, est credendum. Ad rem autem respondetur primo, ad auctoritatem Augustin. aut Hieronymi, quod intentio August. ibidem est, quod vniversaliter absque omni exceptione, solis scriptoribus Bibliae ille timor deferatur & honor, ut eo ipso, quod ibi aliquid inveniatur, credatur absque omni probatione in contrarium audienda, esse verum. Alii autem multi ita legendi sunt, ut quamvis in multis praecipue in his quae facti sunt, debeat eisdem credi tamen non in omnibus, quae facti sunt, vel scientiae seu peritiae eo ipso debeat aliquid reputari verum tam certitudinaliter, quod nulla probatio in contrarium possit admitti, quia ipsi ita senserunt, cum errare potuerunt, licet non semper erraverint, & aliqui eorum in nulla scriptura aliquod falsum protulerunt assertiones. Et ideo assertiones eorum in his quae sunt scientiae seu peritiae, nec sunt taliter necessario recipiendae a legentibus, nisi eaedem vel per scripturas sacras vel per irrefragabilem rationem vel approbationem vniversalis ecclesiae vel per operationem miraculi possint ostendere, quod sint consonae veritati. In his autem, quae facti sunt, quae asserunt vel per seipsos, vel fide dignorum relatione legitima cognouisse: ipsis tanquam fide dignis est credendum, nisi per alios credibiliores possit contrarium probari. Quia in huiusmodi non est inconveniens, quod plus credatur uni, quam alteri. Quemadmodum secundum quosdam in historiis & translationibus plus credendum est Hieronymo, quam Augustino. Veruntamen dicitur, sicut tactum est supra, quod pro assertionibus omnibus doctorum approbatorum ab ecclesia, praesumendum est, quousque de contrario constet. quemadmodum praesumitur pro assertione iudicis, & etiam multitudinis, tenentium contrarium. Notandum autem, quod Augustinus in auctoritate illa loquens de scriptoribus aliis, a scriptoribus canonum Bibliae, inter hos scriptores & illos non distinguit. Et ideo sive fuerint summi pontifices, sive alii: sive scripserint aliquid in concilio generali, sive extra: consimile de eis iudicium est habendum, ut in his quae scientiae sunt vel iuris, non ideo aliquid putetur certitudinaliter modo praedicto esse verum, quia ipsi ita scripserunt, nisi id aliquo praedictorum modorum, scilicet per scripturam divinam, vel rationes irrefragabiles, aut operationem miraculi, aut per approbationem vniversalis ecclesiae persuadere voluerint. Consimiliter ad auctoritatem aliam Augustini dicitur, quod scripturae suae non sunt tantae auctoritatis quantae sunt divinae. cum hoc tamen stat, quod in quibusdam sit ei credendum, & quod non est negandus, nisi ab illo, qui certus est ipsum a veritate recedere. Et eodem modo dicitur ad auctoritatem Hieronymi, quod solum novum & vetus testamentum recipi debent inter scripturas canonicas, & tamen pluribus scripturis aliis, quo ad multa, est credendum. Et in multis negari non debent. Et eodem modo respondetur ad concilium Carthaginense, quod ipsum solummodo prohibet praeter scripturas canonicas, quae sunt Genesis & caeterae, quae de Biblia numerantur, alias legi sub nomine divinarum scripturarum. cum quo stat, quod legendae sunt, & quod alicuius auctoritatis sunt, ita ut quo ad multa negari non debeant, & in multis sit credendum eisdem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Let these points suffice for the present concerning the allegation set out above. Therefore tell me how the opinion mentioned answers the following authorities. MASTER. As to the authorities of Augustine and Jerome: first, it is answered ad hominem, that those who hold the opposite view ought not to allege them at all, since they hold that it is not necessary to believe any writings other than the canonical ones contained in the Bible. Either, therefore, they allege the aforesaid authorities in vain, or by their deeds they deny their own opinion, since by citing Augustine and Jerome to confirm their view they show in fact that the authority of Augustine, who was not the writer of any part of the Bible, is to be believed. But as to the matter itself, it is answered, first, regarding the authority of Augustine or Jerome, that Augustine's intention there is that such fear and honour are owed universally, without any exception, to the writers of the Bible alone, so that by the very fact that something is found there, it is believed to be true without any proof to the contrary being heard. But many others must be read in such a way that, although they are to be believed in many things, especially in matters of fact, they are not to be believed in all things that are matters of fact; nor is anything to be regarded as true, by the very fact that they say it, in matters of knowledge or skill, so certainly that no proof to the contrary can be admitted. For they thought thus, and they could err, even though they did not always err; and some of them never put forward any falsehood in any writing. Therefore their assertions in matters of knowledge or skill are not to be received by readers as necessarily as that, unless the same assertions can be shown by the holy Scriptures, or by an irrefutable argument, or by the approval of the universal Church, or by the working of a miracle, to be consonant with the truth. But in matters of fact, which they assert either from their own knowledge or from the legitimate report of trustworthy persons, they are to be believed as trustworthy, unless the contrary can be proved by others who are more credible. For in such matters there is nothing wrong with giving more credit to one than to another, just as, according to some, more credit is to be given to Jerome than to Augustine in histories and translations. Nevertheless, as was touched upon above, it is said that for all the assertions of approved teachers accepted by the Church, a presumption holds until the contrary is established, just as a presumption holds for the assertion of a judge, and also of a multitude holding the contrary. It should be noted, however, that Augustine, in that authority, speaking of other writers as distinct from the writers of the canonical books of the Bible, makes no distinction between these writers and those. And therefore, whether they were supreme pontiffs or others, and whether they wrote something in a general council or outside one, the same judgement is to be made of them: in matters of knowledge or law, nothing is to be considered certainly true in the manner described above merely because they wrote it thus, unless they wish to persuade it by one of the aforesaid means, namely by divine Scripture, irrefutable arguments, the working of a miracle, or the approval of the universal Church. Likewise, to another authority of Augustine it is said that his writings are not of the same authority as the divine ones; yet this stands together with the fact that in some matters he is to be believed, and that he is not to be rejected except by one who is certain that he has departed from the truth. And in the same way it is said in reply to the authority of Jerome that only the New and Old Testaments are to be received among the canonical Scriptures, and yet in many matters, with respect to much, other writings are to be believed, and in many matters they ought not to be denied. And in the same way it is answered regarding the Council of Carthage that it forbids only that writings other than the canonical Scriptures, which are Genesis and the rest that are counted in the Bible, be read under the name of divine Scriptures; with which it stands that they are to be read, and that they are of some authority, so that in many matters they ought not to be denied, and in many matters they are to be believed.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: In quo ostenditur, in quibus quarta opinio cum secunda convenit, aut discordat, & qualiter. Et primo quod canonibus apostolorum in omnibus sit credendum. in quo quarta cum secunda & tertia conuenit. & ibidem ponuntur responsiones pro 2. & 3. dicto capit. 2.
units.tr: In which it is shown in what respects the fourth opinion agrees or disagrees with the second, and how. And first, that the canons of the apostles are to be believed in all things, in which the fourth agrees with the second and third. The replies to the second and third points of chapter 2 are also given there.

units.la: DISCIP. Nunc secundum praescriptam opinionem supra ca 4. recitatam, narra quomodo respondetur ad illa, quae supra. 2. cap. ostendunt, quod decretis & decretalibus summorum pontificum & canonibus apostolorum, qui in Biblia non habentur, & dictis doctorum ab ecclesia approbatorum est fides absq; dubitatione aliqua adhibenda.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Now, according to the opinion recited above in chapter 4, tell me how one answers those points which, in chapter 2 above, show that the decrees and decretals of the supreme pontiffs, the canons of the apostles (which are not found in the Bible), and the sayings of the teachers approved by the Church are to be accepted without any doubt.

units.la: MAGIST. Opinio illa concedit, quod canonibus apostolorum, quamvis non inferantur in Biblia, est adhibenda certa credulitas. quia quamvis non sint inscripti in scripturis canonicis, scriptores tamen scripturarum canonicarum fuerunt & auctores earum. Et ideo recipi debent cum reverentia & credulitate firma, ita ut non liceat credere, quod aliquid contentum in eis sit falsum aut peruersum.
units.tr: MASTER. That opinion grants that the canons of the apostles, although they are not included in the Bible, are to be received with firm belief. For although they are not written among the canonical Scriptures, their writers were nonetheless the writers and authors of the canonical Scriptures. They ought therefore to be received with reverence and firm trust, so that it is not lawful to believe that anything contained in them is false or perverse.

units.la: DISC. Licet teneamur credere, q nullus scriptorum Bibliae in scribendo quacunque parte Bibliae errare potuerit: sicut nec potuit errare praedicando vel verbis asserendo aliquid, quod tunc fuit scriptum, vel post fuit scribendum in quacunque parte Bibliae: tamen non artamur credere, quod nullus eorum potuerit errare in scripturis aliis a Biblia: sicut nec cogimur credere, nullum eorum potuisse errare alia asserendo, quae non erant scripta nec scribenda in Biblia. Cum ergo nequaquam credere astringamur, quod semper quilibet eorum in verbis & factis tenuerit veritatem (nam & beatus Petrus princeps aliorum apostolorum aliquando ad veritatem minime ambulavit) non tenemur ergo credere, quod in aliis scripturis a canone Bibliae nunquam dimiserit veritatem. MAGIST. Ad hoc respondetur duplicite. Uno modo, quod quamvis quilibet apostolorum per se a veritate deviare potuerit, sicut & Petrus: tamen collegium apostolorum errare non potuit. Unde & quando Petrus erravit, nequaquam erravit collegium apostolorum, sed unus eorum, scilicet Paulus, ipsum correxit. Unde videtur quod illa promissio Christi Matthaei ultimo, vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi, non tantum debeat intelligi de universali ecclesia, sed etiam de collegio apostolorum pro tempore eorundem, quia ipsis immediate fuit dicta promissio, & in ipsis fuit facta universali ecclesiae. Cum igitur Canones apostolorum dicuntur fuisse totius collegii apostolorum, videtur quod non sit dubitandum, quin quicquid continetur in eis, nullo modo sit falsum aut perversum. Aliter dicitur, quod Canones apostolorum per universalem ecclesiam, quae tunc parvi numeri fuit, approbati fuerunt. Ecclesia autem universalis errare non potest. Et ideo nihil erroneum aut iniquum continetur in eis.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. We are bound to believe that none of the writers of the Bible could err in writing any part of the Bible, just as he could not err in preaching or in asserting anything in words, whether it was then written or was afterwards to be written in any part of the Bible. Yet we are not obliged to believe that none of them could err in writings other than those of the Bible, just as we are not compelled to believe that none of them could have erred in asserting other things that were not and were not to be written in the Bible. Since, then, we are in no way bound to believe that each of them always kept to the truth in words and deeds (for blessed Peter, the prince of the other apostles, at times by no means walked uprightly toward the truth), we are not bound to believe that he never departed from the truth in other writings outside the canon of the Bible. MASTER. To this there is a twofold answer. In one way: although each of the apostles could stray from the truth on his own, as Peter did, yet the college of the apostles could not err. So when Peter erred, the college of the apostles did not err at all, but one of them, namely Paul, corrected him. Hence it seems that that promise of Christ at the end of Matthew, "I am with you always, even to the end of the age," ought to be understood not only of the universal Church but also of the college of the apostles for their time, since the promise was made to them immediately and in them was made to the universal Church. Since, therefore, the Canons of the Apostles are said to have come from the whole college of the apostles, it seems there is no reason to doubt that whatever is contained in them is in no way false or perverse. The other answer is that the Canons of the Apostles were approved by the universal Church, which at that time was small in number. But the universal Church cannot err, and therefore nothing erroneous or unjust is contained in them.

units.la: DISCIP. Quomodo respondetur ad allegationes, quibus ostenditur, quod decretis & decretalibus summorum pontificum adhibenda est fides. MAGIST. Ad illos datur responsio Graciani dist. 19, haec autem est, quod videlicet illis adhibenda est fides; in quibus nec praecedentium patrum decretis nec euangelicis praeceptis aliquid contrarium invenitur. Si autem aliquid illicite & non canonice scripserunt, repudiandum est ab illo, qui hoc cognoscit. De illis vero, quae sunt consona veritati, intelligunt Nicolaus papa & Agatho papa & alii sancti patres, qui de hoc loquuntur.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. How does one answer the arguments by which it is shown that faith is to be given to the decrees and decretals of the supreme pontiffs? MASTER. Gratian, dist. 19, gives the answer to those arguments: namely, that faith is to be given to those decrees in which nothing contrary is found either in the decrees of the earlier Fathers or in the evangelical precepts. But if they have written anything unlawfully and not canonically, it must be rejected by anyone who recognises it. Nicholas the pope, Agatho the pope, and the other holy Fathers who speak on this matter understand these decrees as those that agree with the truth.

units.la: DISCIP. Quid faciendum esset de decretalibus summorum pontificum, qui continerent aliquid erroneum aut perversum, si catholici hoc nescirent. MAGIST. Pro hac materia potes recurrere ad septimum librum primae partis istius Dialogi, ubi de hoc multa discussimus. DISCIP. Hoc non obstante, dic breviter, quid de hoc sentit opinio sup. cap. 2. recitata. MAGIST. Illa opinio tenet, quod si aliqua decretalis summi pontificis in rei veritate est contraria fidei aut bonis moribus, illi qui hoc ignorant praesumere debent pro ipsa: non tamen sic, quia possint & in casu tenentur probationem in contrarium admittere. Si vero aliqui, praecipue literati & scientiae excellentis vel etiam mediocris, se offerant probaturos decretalem summi pontificis esse contrariam fidei vel bonis moribus, aut non esse recipiendam inter scripturas authenticas: Alii eorum probationes audire tenentur, praesertim si periculum fidei aut morum aut etiam personarum imminet, quia in hoc casu quilibet Christianus salutem fidei, bonorum morum, & personarum catholicarum erroneae decretali summi pontificis & honori temporali ipsius praeferre tenentur. & quicunque commode potest audire rationes monstrantes, decretalem papae esse erroneam seu haereticalem, & noluerit, si ipsam defenderit, vel etiam pro ipsa praesumpserit, credens & fautor pravitatis haereticae est censendus. quia ignorantia talem non excusat, eo quod talis ignorantia est affectata vel crassa & supina, quae non excusat. DISCIP. Videtur quod probationes contra decretales summorum pontificum sunt minime audiendae: quia ratione consimili audiendae essent probationes contra sacram scripturam. Et ita doctor vel literatus alius, qui commode posset & non legeret libros haereticorum & philosophorum, contra scripturam sacram peccaret: quod tanquam inconveniens est habendum. MAGIST. Ad hoc respondetur, quod non est simile de sacra scriptura & de decretali summi pontificis. quia firmiter est tenendum, quod scriptura sacra errare non potest. Ideo nisi aliqua causa moveat specialis non oportet legere vel audire aliquam probationem contra ipsam, qualescunque & quotcunque affirmant se posse probare aliquid contra eam. Sed de papa firmiter catholici literati praecipue & intelligentes ac ratione vigente credere obligantur, quod potest errare: & per consequens quod contra quamcunque scripturam ipsius, praesertim in his, quae scientiae seu peritiae sunt, de qua in speciali non constat, quod est consona scripturae sacrae vel rationi evidenti vel auctoritati universalis ecclesiae: vel per divinum miraculum confirmata debet audiri probatio. Et ideo nolentes audire probationes contra decretales papae, cum possunt: si errant per ignorantiam, nihilominus excusantur. Sed de quolibet illorum verificaretur illud apostoli: ignorans ignorabitur. DISCIP. Qualiter respondetur ad allegationes, quibus ostenditur, quod dictis doctorum ab ecclesia approbatorum est credendum. MAGIST. Respondetur ad eas, quod dictis doctorum taliter est credendum & praesumendum pro ipsis, si non constet aperte, quod obuiant veritati. Et ideo opuscula eorum recipienda sunt cum reverentia, non tamen sic, quin liceat credere, quod aliquid poterat reperiri in eis contrarium veritati. Quia de facto unus contrariatur alteri & per consequens aliquis eorum errauit, quia contraria non possunt simul esse vera. Iste tamen honor deferendus est eis, ut nullus credatur fuisse pertinax in assertione falsae sententiae. Et ideo nullus eorum de pravitate haeretica est notandus. Sed praesumendum est de quolibet, quanta sollicitudine, quanta potuit, quaesierit veritatem, quamvis nos semper inveneriit. Ad illud, quod accipitur, quod assertionibus summorum pontificum & in expositione sanctarum scripturarum est credendum, quibus tamen praeferuntur expositiones doctorum. Respondetur, quod assertionibus huiusmodi summorum pontificum credendum est modo praepositio. Et ideo eodem modo credendum est dictis doctorum ab ecclesia approbatorum. Ad illud autem Hormisdae papae respondetur, quod intelligit de illis, quae a sede apostolica sunt catholicae constituta seu diffinita, pro quibus praesumendum est, nisi probatio evidens in contrarium afferatur. Et eodem modo dicitur ad canonem Nicolai papae.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. What ought to be done about the decretals of the supreme pontiffs if they contained something erroneous or perverse, and Catholics did not know this? MASTER. On this matter you may turn to the seventh book of the first part of this Dialogue, where we discussed it at length. DISCIPLE. Nevertheless, tell me briefly what the opinion recited above in chapter 2 thinks about this. MASTER. That opinion holds that if any decretal of a supreme pontiff is in truth contrary to the faith or to good morals, those who do not know this ought to presume in its favour; yet not in such a way that they may not, and in such a case are not bound to, admit proof to the contrary. But if certain people, especially the learned and those of excellent or even moderate learning, offer to prove that the decretal of the supreme pontiff is contrary to the faith or to good morals, or ought not to be received among the authentic Scriptures, the others are bound to hear their proofs, especially if danger threatens the faith, morals, or even persons. For in this case every Christian is bound to prefer the salvation of the faith, of good morals, and of Catholic persons to the erroneous decretal of the supreme pontiff and to his temporal honour. And whoever can conveniently hear the reasons showing that the pope's decretal is erroneous or heretical, and yet is unwilling to do so, and if he defends it or even presumes in its favour, is to be judged a believer in it and a supporter of heretical depravity. For ignorance does not excuse such a person, since such ignorance is deliberate or gross and supine, and does not excuse. DISCIPLE. It seems that proofs against the decretals of the supreme pontiffs ought by no means to be heard, because by similar reasoning proofs against Holy Scripture would have to be heard. And so a teacher or another learned man who could conveniently read the books of heretics and philosophers without doing so would sin against Holy Scripture, which must be regarded as an absurdity. MASTER. To this it is answered that the case of Holy Scripture and of a decretal of the supreme pontiff is not the same. For it must be firmly held that Holy Scripture cannot err. Therefore, unless some special cause moves us, there is no need to read or hear any proof against it, however many and whatever kind of proofs people claim they can offer against it. But concerning the pope, learned Catholics, especially those who understand and who hold firm to reason, are bound to believe that he can err, and consequently that a proof must be heard against any of his writings, especially in matters that belong to science or skill, concerning which it is not established in particular that it agrees with Holy Scripture, with evident reason, with the authority of the universal Church, or with divine miracle confirming it. And therefore, those who are unwilling to hear proofs against papal decretals, though they can, are nonetheless excused if they err through ignorance. But of each such person that saying of the Apostle applies: "The ignorant will be left in ignorance." DISCIPLE. How does one answer the arguments by which it is shown that the sayings of teachers approved by the Church are to be believed? MASTER. To these arguments the answer is that the sayings of teachers are to be believed and presumed in their favour in such a way, provided it is not clear that they oppose the truth. Therefore their little works are to be received with reverence, yet not so that one may not believe that something contrary to the truth could be found in them. For in fact one of them contradicts another, and consequently one of them has erred, since contrary things cannot both be true. Still, this honour is to be paid to them, that no one is believed to have been obstinate in asserting a false opinion. And so none of them is to be marked with heretical depravity. Rather, it must be presumed of each that he sought the truth with as much care as he could, although we have always found it. As for what is cited, that the assertions of the supreme pontiffs and their expositions of the holy Scriptures are to be believed, yet expositions of teachers are preferred to them, the answer is that such assertions of the supreme pontiffs are to be believed in the same way as before. And so in the same way the sayings of the teachers approved by the Church are to be believed. As for the passage of Pope Hormisdas, the answer is that he means those things which have been established or defined as Catholic by the Apostolic See, for which one must presume, unless clear proof to the contrary is brought forward. And the same is said in reply to the canon of Pope Nicholas.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationes cap. 3. huius adductas probantes quod etiam doctoribus ab ecclesia minime approbatis est fides indubia adhibenda.
units.tr: In which the arguments of chapter 3 above are answered, the arguments that undoubted faith is to be given even to teachers not at all approved by the Church.

units.la: DISCIP. Restat secundum opinionem saepe dictam, ut narres, quomodo respondetur ad allegationes inductas capit. 3. quibus quod etiam doctoribus ab ecclesia minime approbatis, quo ad ea in quibus omnes vel plures eorum & praecipue magis famosi concordant, alii fidem adhibere tenentur. MAGIST. Ad primam illarum allegationum, cum accipitur, quod teste Leone papa, non credere doctoribus est iniquum. Respondetur, quod intentio Leonis ibidem est, non credere doctoribus ab ecclesia approbatis, quo ad ea quae sunt consona pietati, est iniquum impia sapiendo. Et ideo praemittit ibidem, quid est iniquius quam impia sapere &c. Sed non credere doctoribus, qui se mutuo reprobant, non est iniquum.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. It remains, according to the opinion we have often mentioned, that you explain how one answers the arguments brought forward in chapter 3, by which it is held that even teachers not at all approved by the Church, in those matters where all or most of them, and especially the more famous ones, agree, must be given faith by others. MASTER. To the first of those arguments, where it is taken that, according to Pope Leo, not to believe the teachers is unjust, the answer is this: Leo's intention there is that not to believe teachers approved by the Church, in those things which accord with piety, is unjust for one who thinks impiously. That is why he says just before, what is more unjust than to think impiously, and so on. But not to believe teachers who reject one another is not unjust.

units.la: DISCIP. Secundum hoc non aliter credendum est doctoribus approbatis ab ecclesia, quam non approbatis: quia sicut iniquum est impia sapiendo non credere aliis doctoribus, qui sunt ab ecclesia minime approbati: Et ita non aliter credendum est illis, quam illis. MAGIST. Respondetur, quod impia sapere contingit dupliciter: scilicet impie seu pertinaciter, vel non impie & non pertinaciter. Quemadmodum etiam in his quae fidei sunt, contingit errare pertinaciter & non pertinaciter: & ita contingit errare impie & non impie. Nunquam autem vel raro discreditur doctoribus ab ecclesia approbatis, quando dicta eorum possunt haberi impia sapiendo, nisi impie: quia raro & eorum quidam in nullis penitus errauerunt. Sed saepe contingit impia sapiendo non impie tamen non credere doctoribus ab ecclesia minime approbatis: cum etiam sapiendo impia contingat in multis non credere eis, cum in multis errent. quod ex contrarietate inter ipsos perpenditur evidenter. Propter quam contrarietatem tam crebram & fantasticorum assertionem pro assertionibus eorum est minime praesumendum, Et ideo aliter credendum est doctoribus ab ecclesia approbatis, quam aliis. Propter sanctitatem enim & veritatem ac utilitatem doctrinae doctorum ab ecclesia approbatorum reverentia tanto merito debetur eisdem, ut nemo, qui non est certus eos vel eorum aliquem defecisse, debeat quodcunque dictum eorum vel alicuius ipsorum negare contrarium sapiendo aut aliquam assertionem alicuius eorum ad falsum aut perversum trahere intellectum, antequam mentem & motiva eorum vel alicuius eorum, si potest, viderit diligenter. Sed tantam reverentiam non tenemur doctoribus ab ecclesia minime approbatis necessario exhibere: praesertim cum studere in libris eorum propter diversas opiniones indociles & fantasticas ac vix opinabiles assertione vel opinatione insertas in eis impedimentum maximum praestet scientiae necessariae & utili ecclesiae Dei.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. According to this, teachers approved by the Church are not to be believed any differently from those not approved, because just as it is unjust, for one thinking impiously, not to believe other teachers who have not been approved by the Church, so one is not to believe the one sort differently from the other. MASTER. The answer is that thinking impiously happens in two ways: either impiously, that is, obstinately, or not impiously and not obstinately. Just as in matters of faith one may err obstinately or not obstinately, so one may err impiously or not impiously. Now, teachers approved by the Church are never, or hardly ever, discredited when their statements can be held to be impious thinking, except impiously, because hardly any of them have erred in anything at all. But it often happens, when one thinks impiously but not impiously, that one does not believe teachers not approved by the Church, since even when thinking impiously one may come to disbelieve them in many things, as they err in many. This is plainly weighed from their mutual contrariety. Because of this contrariety, so frequent, and because of the assertion of their fancies, one must by no means presume in favour of their assertions. And so teachers approved by the Church are to be believed differently from others. For on account of the holiness, truth and usefulness of the teaching of teachers approved by the Church, reverence is due to them on so great a merit that no one who is not certain that they, or any one of them, have failed, should deny what any of them has said, thinking otherwise, or twist any assertion of one of them into a false or perverse sense, before he has examined carefully, if he can, their mind and reasons, or those of one of them. But we are not bound to show such reverence to teachers not approved by the Church, especially since to study their books, with their various opinions that are unteachable and fanciful, and assertions or opinions scarcely credible, inserted into them, is a very great hindrance to the necessary knowledge and to the usefulness of the Church of God.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic qualiter respondetur ad allegationem sequentem. MAGIST. Respondetur, quod scripturae divinae principaliter docendae sunt a doctoribus ab ecclesia approbatis: & ab illis, qui sunt veritatis & non propriarum opinionum amatores: qui in docendo in divinis litteris & aliis authenticis scripturis ac rationibus irrefragabilibus solam veritatem, non inanem gloriam aut favorem cuiuscunque quaerentis se fundare nituntur, parati opiniones proprias revocare, si eas per se vel per alios doctores vel discipulos excellentes vel parum intelligentes cognoverint veritati quomodolibet adversari: non autem ab illis, qui opiniones vel assertiones proprias vel sui ordinis, collegii, nationis, amicorum vel adhaerentium aut fautentium vel cuiuscunque personae qualitercunque coniunctae, relictis aut spretis opinionibus seu assertionibus aliorum verioribus vel probabilioribus, tenent aut defendunt, vel tenere cupiunt aut defendi. DISCIP. Quid si aliquis superior vel praelatus voluerit cogere sibi subiectos approbare, & tenere opiniones seu doctrinam alicuius doctoris ab ecclesia minime approbati? MAGIST. Dicitur, quod talis praelatus peccaret mortaliter, & omnes consentientes sibi & fautentes. DISCIP. Nunquid secundum opinionem istamartantes sibi subiectos ad defendendum opiniones doctoris vel doctorum huiusmodi sunt haeretici computandi, si inter opiniones illas aliqua in rei veritate scripturae divinae repugnant, quamvis non patenter sed latenter? MAG. Respondetur, quod tales sunt haeretici reputandi, licet doctor tales opiniones inveniens posset a praevitate haeretica excusari: qua deceptus absque pertinacia, opinionem suam, quae est in rei veritate haeretica, quis hoc nesciat, poterit divulgare. Sed poenis, & flagellis, aut minis, vel terroribus, aut persecutionibus quibuscunque arcetes, seu cogetes sibi subiectos ad tenendam opinionem huiusmodi & tali artationi seu coactioni consentientes de pertinacia excusari non valent. Dicaliter n. artantib. seu consentientibus intelligi debet illud Vrbani, quod habetur 24. q. 3. c. Qui alioquin, cum ait: Qui aliorum errorem defendit, multo amplius est damnabilior illu qui errante, qui non solum ipse errat, sed etiam alios offendiculaerroris praeparat, & confirmat, quantum in eo est, cogendo alios per huiusmodi artationem seu obligationem, errori pertinaciter adhaerere. Unde quia magister erroris est, per compulsionem huiusmodi non tantum haereticus, sed etiam haeresiarcha dicendus est.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Tell me how one answers the following argument. MASTER. The answer is that the divine Scriptures are to be taught chiefly by teachers approved by the Church, and by those who love the truth and not their own opinions: who, in teaching, seek to ground only the truth, not empty glory or the favour of anyone seeking themselves, in the divine letters and other authentic writings and irrefutable reasons, and who are ready to retract their own opinions if they have recognised, through themselves or through other teachers or disciples, whether outstanding or of little understanding, that these in any way conflict with the truth. But those who hold or defend, or wish to hold or have defended, their own opinions or assertions, or those of their order, college, nation, friends, adherents, supporters, or of any person connected in any way, abandoning or despising the truer or more probable opinions or assertions of others, are not to be taught by them. DISCIPLE. What if some superior or prelate wishes to compel his subjects to approve and hold the opinions or doctrine of some teacher not approved by the Church? MASTER. It is said that such a prelate would sin mortally, and all who consent to him and favour him. DISCIPLE. According to this opinion, are those who compel their subjects to defend the opinions of such a teacher or teachers to be counted as heretics, if some of those opinions in truth conflict with the divine Scriptures, though not plainly but secretly? MASTER. The answer is that such men are to be regarded as heretics, although a teacher who finds such opinions may be excused from heretical depravity, since, deceived without obstinacy, he may publish his opinion, which is in truth heretical, though who does not know this? But those who restrain or compel their subjects to hold such an opinion by punishments and whippings, or by threats, terrors or persecutions of any kind, and those who consent to such constraint or compulsion, cannot be excused from obstinacy. For the words of Urban, found in 24 q. 3 c. Qui alioquin, must be understood of those who constrain or consent: He who defends the error of others is much more blameworthy than the one who errs, since he not only errs himself but also prepares and confirms stumbling-blocks of error for others, as far as he can, by compelling others through such constraint or obligation to cling obstinately to the error. Hence, because he is a master of error, he is to be called, through such compulsion, not only a heretic but a ringleader of heresy.

units.la: DISCIP. Alias allegationes prosequere. MAGIST. Ad aliam, quae accipit, quod pro multitudine & maxime sapientum praesumendum est. Respondetur, quod non est semper pro multitudine sapientum taliter praesumendum, vt in illis, quae scientiae sunt, aliquis multitudini sapientum, qui non sunt ab ecclesia approbati, credere teneatur, antequam inuenerit per scripturas sacras, aut rationem euidentem, vel operationem miraculi, aut per assertionem vniuersalis ecclesiae, quod eorum assertio sit consona veritati: licet pro eis taliter praesumere liceat, vt eorum assertio minime reprobetur aut negetur, nisi constiterit quod obuiat veritati.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Go on with the other arguments. MASTER. To the other argument, which holds that one must presume in favour of the multitude, and especially of the wise, the answer is that one must not always presume in favour of the multitude of the wise in such a way that, in matters which belong to knowledge, anyone is bound to believe a multitude of wise men who have not been approved by the Church, before he has found, through the holy Scriptures, or clear reason, or a working of a miracle, or through the assertion of the universal Church, that their assertion accords with the truth. Yet it is permitted to presume so far in their favour that their assertion is not rejected or denied, unless it is established that it stands in the way of the truth.

units.la: Ad aliam cum accipitur, quod ille prudentiae suae innititur, qui ea quae sibi tenenda vel credenda videntur doctorum assertionibus praesumit praeponere, secundum quod innuit Hieronymus extra, de constitutionibus, cap. ne innitaris. Respondetur, quod Hieronymus ibidem loquitur de decretis patrum, qui fuerunt scriptores scripturae diuinae, & de pluribus ab ecclesia approbatis: Non autem de aliis, qui se inuicem reprehendunt, & reprobant. Quia ad illos non oportet regulariter recurrere, licet in casu tenetur quis, quid senserint indagare.
units.tr: To the other argument, where it is taken that one relies on his own prudence who presumes to set what seems to him to be held or believed above the assertions of teachers, as Jerome hints in extra, de constitutionibus, cap. ne innitaris: the answer is that Jerome there speaks of the decrees of the Fathers, who were writers of divine Scripture and of many approved by the Church, and not of others who rebuke and reject one another. For one ought not to have recourse to those as a rule, although in a case one is bound to inquire what they thought.

units.la: Si enim dicant, se opiniones suas accepisse a scripturis diuinis, non sunt opiniones huiusmodi reprobandae, seu spernendae vel negandae ab eo, qui non est certus eas esse contrarias veritati, antequam motiua earum viderit diligenter. Si enim opiniones eorum fuerint catholicae, & in sacris fundatae scripturis, qui eas negauerint, praesertim assertores eorum persequendo, vel persequentibus in hoc fauendo, nolens notitiam eorum catholicam, quamuis commode possit, legere vel audire attendere, non potest de prauitate haeretica excusari. quia talis errans, qui non quaerit cauta sollicitudine veritatem, quando tenetur quaerere, est inter haereticos computandus, prout insinuat Augustus. vt habetur 24. quaest. 3. c. dixit apostolus.
