Et ita in casu non solum illi in insipientiam damnabilem cadunt, secundum Leonem papam, vt habetur 24. quaest. 3. cap. quid autem: Quid autem iniquius, quam qui ad cognoscendam veritatem aliquo impeditur obscuro, non ad propheticas voces, non ad apostolicas literas, non ad euangelicas auctoritates, sed ad semetipsos recurrunt? sed etiam illi, qui ad dicta aliorum, qui etiam non sunt ab ecclesia approbati, vel etiam sunt ab ecclesiasticis & clericis reprobati erronee & iniuste non recurrunt eorum motiua legere negligentes, suae prudentiae vel forsitan aliorum prudentiae erroneae innituntur. non autem illi qui scripturas sacras & doctrinam sanctorum patrum & aliorum opiniones scrutantur sollicite, cum eas possunt habere, suae prudentiae reprehensibiliter innituntur, licet inuentiones proprias validis munitas rationibus quorumcunque & quorcunque doctorum aliorum opinionibus, qui non sunt ab vniuersali ecclesia approbati, praeponant.
units.tr: For if they say that they have received their opinions from the divine Scriptures, such opinions are not to be rejected, or despised, or denied by one who is not certain that they are contrary to the truth, before he has carefully examined their reasons. For if their opinions were catholic and founded on the holy Scriptures, then those who deny them, especially by persecuting their authors, or by favouring the persecutors in this, and who unwillingly refuse to read or listen to their catholic notice, although they could easily do so, cannot be excused from heretical depravity. For such an erring person, who does not seek the truth with careful diligence when he is bound to seek it, is to be counted among the heretics, as Augustine suggests, as found in 24 q. 3 c. dixit apostolus. And so in such a case not only do those fall into a damnable folly, according to Pope Leo, as found in 24 q. 3 c. Quid autem: What is more unjust than that one who is hindered by some obscurity from recognising the truth should not have recourse to the prophetic voices, to the apostolic letters, to the evangelical authorities, but to himself? But also those who, through error and injustice, do not have recourse to the words of others, who are not approved by the Church, or who have even been rejected by the clergy and churchmen, neglecting to read their reasons, rely on their own prudence, or perhaps on the erroneous prudence of others. Not so those who diligently examine the holy Scriptures and the teaching of the holy Fathers and the opinions of others, when they can have them, and who do not rely blamelessly on their own prudence, although they set their own discoveries, fortified with strong reasons, above the opinions of whatever teachers, of whatever kind, who have not been approved by the universal Church.

units.la: Ad aliam allegationem, cum accipitur, quod fide dignorum testimonio est credendum. Respondetur, quod fide dignorum testimonio in his quae facti sunt omnes credere debent, nisi sint aliqui qui sciant eos a veritate declinare. sed in his quae scientiae sunt aut iuris aut peritiae, non est necesse omnes credere testimonio fide dignorum, etiam qui nesciunt eos errare, nec quo ad omnia in quibus non errant. & hoc quia notum est, quod vacantes scientiis etiam doctores, qui nullum falsum assererent, scienter errant in his quae scientiae sunt & artium, cum etiam peritissimi erraverint, & multa huiusmodi ignoraverint.
units.tr: To the other argument, when it is taken that one must believe the testimony of trustworthy men: the answer is that in matters of fact everyone ought to believe the testimony of trustworthy men, unless there are some who know that they stray from the truth. But in matters of science, law or skill, it is not necessary for everyone to believe the testimony of trustworthy men, even those who do not know that they err, nor in all points in which they do not err. And this is because it is well known that teachers who are devoted to the sciences, even though they assert nothing false, knowingly err in matters belonging to the sciences and the arts, since even the most skilled have erred and been ignorant of many such things.

units.la: Ad vltimam dicitur per praedicta, quod non omni experto in aliqua arte est credendum in omnibus, eo quod multorum non habet experientiam neque peritiam, quae tamen spectant ad artem. & ideo potest in multis errare & sophisticis rationibus decipi.
units.tr: To the last argument it is said, on the basis of what has been said above, that one must not believe every expert in some art in all things, because he does not have experience or skill in many matters which nevertheless belong to the art. And so he can err in many things and be deceived by sophistical arguments.

units.la: Explicit liber tertius.
units.tr: Here ends the third book.

units.la: INCIPIT LIBER QVARTVS, IN QVO VNA TANTVM QVÆSTIO PRINCIPALITER TRACTATVR: SCI- LICET VTRVM Christus constituerit Petrum principem aliorum apostolo- rum, vel non. & ponuntur diuersi modi dicendi.
units.tr: BOOK FOURTH, IN WHICH ONE QUESTION ONLY IS TREATED PRINCIPALLY: NAMELY WHETHER CHRIST APPOINTED PETER PRINCE OF THE OTHER APOSTLES OR NOT, AND VARIOUS WAYS OF SPEAKING ARE SET OUT.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: In quo ponitur prima opinio: scilicet quod Christus non constituit Petrum principem & prælatum aliorum apostolorum & vniuersorum fidelium, sed fuit æqualis ceteris apostolis. Probatur rationibus & auctoritatibus, ad quas respondetur infra c. 25.
units.tr: Here is set out the first opinion, namely that Christ did not appoint Peter prince and prelate of the other apostles and of all the faithful, but that he was equal to the other apostles. It is proved by arguments and authorities, to which replies are given below, chap. 25.

units.la: ISCIP. Postquam conferendo quæsiuimus, quæ scripturæ recipiendæ sunt ad ecclesiastica dogmata confirmanda, ad principale reuertamur intentum. an videlicet Christus de facto constituerit beatum Petrum principem & prælatum aliorum apostolorum & vniuersorum fidelium. circa quod diuersas opiniones studeas recitare: MAGIST. Vna opinio est, quod Christus de facto beatum Petrum non constituit principem & prælatum aliorum apostolorum, & vniuersorum fidelium, quod multis modis videtur posse probari. Et primo quidem ostenditur, quod nullus apostolus ex ordinatione Christi, cæteris apostolis nec quantum ad dignitatem sacerdotalem essentialem, nec quantum ad aliquam aliam potestatem, fuit superior. Quod videtur convinci ex Luce 22. c. nam tribuens Christus apostolis potestatem eucharistiæ consecrandæ, inquit ad eos: hoc est enim corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur. hoc facite in meam commemorationem: id est, hoc faciendi potestatem habete, proferendo tamen verba consimilia, quando actum hunc exercere debetis, videlicet, hoc est corpus meum. nec dixit hæc verba plus ad Petrum, quam ad alios. non enim dixit ei Christus: fac & aliis apostolis sic faciendi potestatem tribuas, sed dixit facite in plurali, & omnibus indifferenter.
units.tr: STUDENT. Having inquired by comparison which Scriptures are to be received for confirming ecclesiastical doctrines, let us return to the main purpose: namely, whether Christ in fact appointed the blessed Peter prince and prelate of the other apostles and of all the faithful. On this matter you wish me to recite the various opinions. MASTER. One opinion is that Christ in fact did not appoint the blessed Peter prince and prelate of the other apostles and of all the faithful. This can be proved in many ways. And first, it is shown that no apostle, by the ordinance of Christ, was superior to the other apostles, either in essential sacerdotal dignity or in any other power. This seems to be proved from Luke 22. For when Christ gave the apostles the power of consecrating the Eucharist, he said to them: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me." That is, you have the power of doing this, while, when you must perform this action, you utter similar words, namely "This is my body." Nor did he speak these words to Peter more than to the others. For Christ did not say to him, "Do this, and grant to the other apostles the power of doing so," but he said "Do" in the plural, and to all alike.

units.la: Item, idem quoque per omnia faciendum est de clauium potestate, siue his eisdem verbis trādite fuerint apostolis, siue aliis aut alio tempore. vt de his, quæ habentur Iohann. 20. postquam enim Christus dixit apostolis: sicut misit me pater & ego vos mitto. insufflauit & dixit eis: accipite spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, & quorum retinueritis retenta sunt. Dicit ergo Christus: mitto vos sicut me misit pater: nec dixit Petro, aut alteri apostolo singulariter: mitto te, sicut pater &c. & tu alios mitte. Nec rursum dicitur: Christus insufflauit ei: sed dixit eis, non vni per alterum. Nec dixit Christus ad Petrum; accipe spiritum sanctum, & aliis postmodum tribue. sed dixit, accipite in plurali, vt indifferenter omnibus loquens.
units.tr: Likewise, the same must be held in every respect of the power of the keys, whether these words were delivered to the apostles or other words, or at another time. Take what is found in John 20. For after Christ had said to the apostles, "As the Father sent me, so I send you," he breathed on them and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained." Christ therefore says, "I send you as the Father sent me," and he did not say to Peter, or to any other apostle singly, "I send you as the Father sent me, and you send the others." Nor is it said again that Christ breathed on him; he said it to them, not to one through another. Nor did Christ say to Peter, "Receive the Holy Spirit, and afterwards give it to the others"; but he said "Receive" in the plural, speaking alike to all.

units.la: Item apostolus ad hanc quæstionem diffiniendam, vt videlicet nemo credat aliquem apostolorum prærogatiuam habuisse seu auctoritatem super alios, ipsam expresse remouet à Petro: de quo fortasse videbatur hoc magis propter aliqua sibi à Christo singulariter dicta, & quia senior ceteris erat. Vnde 1. ad Gal. ait: Mihi enim qui videbantur esse aliquid, nihil contulerunt. sed e contra cum vidissent, quod creditum est mihi euangelium præputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis. qui enim operatus est Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est mihi inter gentes. & cum cognouissent gratiam quæ data est mihi, Iacobus & Cephas & Iohannes, qui videbantur columnæ esse, dederunt dexteras mihi & Barnabæ societatis &c. Qui igitur operatus fuit Petro in apostolatum, operatus fuit & Paulo. Hic autem fuit Christus. igitur huiusmodi officium non suscepit à Petro, & similiter nec apostoli reliqui. vbi in Glossa secundum August. hoc amplius exprimens inquit: Illi qui videbantur esse aliquid, scilicet Petrus & alii qui fuerunt cum domino, nihil contulerunt, id addiderunt mihi. In quo quod non illu inferior sum, quia à domino Deo persectus sum, vt nihil esset quod in collatione perfectioni addirent. Ecce quod Paulus non fuit inferior Petro, nec aliis. Consequenter ad hanc intentionem subiungit Gloss. Cum vidissent, quod euangelium præputii creditum est mihi, vt fideli, sicut Petro circumcisioni. Ecce quod æque principaliter missus fuit Paulus, quemadmodum & Petrus, & non à Petro aut apostolorum aliquo, sed à Christo immediate. Quod amplius exprimens apostolus eodem 1. cap. sic ait: Paulus apostolus non ab hominibus neque per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum & Deum patrem. vbi Gloss. secundum Amb. Paulus apostolus non electus neque missus ab hominibus, scilicet ab Ananía, vt quidam dicebant, vel ab aliis, vt quidam ab apostolis electus & missi fuerunt. denique parum infra subdit secundum August. Ceteri ei apostoli videbantur esse maiores, quia priores: ipse minimus, quia nouissimus. sed inde apparet dignior, quia priores constituti sunt per Christum adhuc ex parte hominum, id est mortalem: nouissimus vero per Christum iam totum Deum, id est ex omni parte immortalem, & vt Deum patrem, qui hoc fecit per filium. Atque vt aperiret cum dixerit: neque per hominem: subdit: qui suscitauit eum à mortuis. & ita dignius constituit me per immortalem Christum, quā alios per mortalem. Rursus confirmans hoc apostolus eodem c. ait: Notum enim vobis facio Euangelium, fratres, euangelizatum à me, quia non est per hominem docentem me vel mittentem. & vere non est ab homine, neque enim accepi illud ab homine, neque didici ab homine, vbi homo eligeret me ad euangelizandum vel mihi inungeret. non didici ab hominae docente me, sed per revelationem Iesu Christi. Ecce quod neque Petrus, neque alius, aut homo quisquam elegit, misit aut iniunxit Paulo mysterium euangelii. Idem quoque videndum est de apostolis reliquis. Nullam ergo potestatem, eoque minus coactiuam iurisdictionem habuit Petrus à Deo immediate super apostolos reliquos, neque instituendi eos in ossicio sacerdotali, neque segregandi eos seu mittendi ad officium praedicationis: nisi quod hoc sane concedi potest, ipsum fuisse priorem aliis aetate vel officio, fortasse secundum tempus aut in apostolorum electione, qui eum propterea reuerebantur merito. quamuis hanc electionem ex scriptura nemo conuincere possit.
units.tr: Likewise the apostle, in order to settle this question, so that no one should believe that any of the apostles had a prerogative or authority over the others, expressly removes it from Peter, concerning whom this might perhaps seem more likely, on account of certain things said to him by Christ alone, and because he was senior to the others. Hence he says in Gal. 1: "For those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me. But on the contrary, when they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, just as the gospel of the circumcision was to Peter (for he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also in me among the Gentiles), and when they had recognised the grace that was given to me, James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship," and so on. Therefore he who worked in Peter for the apostleship worked also in Paul. But this was Christ. Therefore Christ did not receive this office from Peter, and likewise neither did the other apostles. Here the Gloss, following Augustine, expressing this more fully, says: "Those who seemed to be something, namely Peter and the others who were with the Lord, contributed nothing; they added this to me. In this respect I am not inferior to them, because I was made perfect by the Lord God, so that there was nothing which they could add to my perfection in the conference." Behold, Paul was not inferior to Peter or to the others. Following this line of thought, the Gloss continues: "When they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me as to a faithful man, just as Peter was entrusted with the circumcision." Behold, Paul was sent with equal authority, just as Peter was, and not by Peter or by any one of the apostles, but immediately by Christ. The apostle, expressing this still more clearly, in the same first chapter, says: "Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father." Here the Gloss, following Ambrose: "Paul the apostle was neither chosen nor sent by men, namely by Ananias, as some said, or by others, as some said, who were chosen and sent by the apostles." Finally, a little further on, he adds, following Augustine: "The other apostles seemed to be greater to him because they were earlier; he was least because he was last. But he appears more worthy from this, that the earlier were appointed by Christ still in part as men, that is, mortal; but he last by Christ already wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect, and as God the Father, who did this through the Son. And so that he might make it clear when he said 'nor through man,' he adds: 'who raised him from the dead.' And so he appointed me more worthily through the immortal Christ than the others through the mortal." Again, confirming this, the apostle says in the same chapter: "For I make known to you, brethren, the gospel which was preached by me, that it is not according to man. For I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it by man, but it came through the revelation of Jesus Christ." Behold, neither Peter nor any other, nor any man at all, chose, sent, or enjoined on Paul the mystery of the gospel. The same must also be considered regarding the other apostles. Peter therefore had no power, and still less any coercive jurisdiction, immediately from God over the other apostles, neither to install them in the sacerdotal office, nor to separate them or send them to the office of preaching. It may certainly be conceded that he was prior to the others in age or office, perhaps in order of time, or in the choosing of the apostles, and that they rightly revered him on this account, although no one can prove this choice from Scripture.

units.la: Adhuc ergo per signum ostenditur, quia beatum Petrum nullam sibi assumpsisse singulariter auctoritatem supra reliquos apostolos inuenimus ex scriptura, sed magis cum ipsis aequalitatem seruasse. non enim sibi assumpsit auctoritatem determinandi, quae dubia erant euangelii praedicatione, quod pertinet ad doctrinam; sed quae dubia fuerunt in hoc ex communi deliberatione apostolorum & aliorum fidelium magis doctorum determinabant, non Petri aut alterius apostoli seorsum determinatione. Unde Actuum 15. Dissensione orta inter praedicatores euangelii, an oporteret circumcidere incircumcisos fideles ad salutem aeternam consequendam, quibusdam dicentibus oportere: Paulo vero & Barnaba reclamantibus contra hoc: conuenerunt apostoli & seniores videre de verbo hoc, super quod locuti sunt Petrus & Iacobus non oportere. quorum sententiae seniores & reliqui consenserunt apostoli. Unde subditur infra: tunc placuit apostolis & senioribus cum omni ecclesia eligere viros & mittere Antiochiam, &c. scribentes per manus eorum. & suit modus scribendi modo deliberandi conformis, & talis: apostoli & seniores fratres, his qui sunt Antiochiae & Syriae, & Ciliciae, fratribus ex gentibus, salutem, &c.
units.tr: Furthermore, it is shown by this sign that we find in Scripture that the blessed Peter did not assume to himself any singular authority over the other apostles, but rather kept equality with them. For he did not assume the authority of determining what was doubtful in the preaching of the gospel, which pertains to doctrine; but questions that were doubtful were determined by the common deliberation of the apostles and of the other more learned faithful, not by the separate determination of Peter or of any other apostle. Hence Acts 15: when a dissension had arisen between the preachers of the gospel, whether it was necessary to circumcise the uncircumcised faithful in order to obtain eternal salvation, some saying that it was necessary, while Paul and Barnabas protested against this, "the apostles and elders came together to consider this matter, about which Peter and James had spoken, that it was not necessary." The elders and the rest agreed with the opinion of the apostles. Hence it is added below: "Then it pleased the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to choose men and send them to Antioch, etc., writing by their hands." And the manner of writing was in accordance with this manner of deliberating, and was as follows: "The apostles and elders, brethren, to those who are at Antioch and in Syria and Cilicia, the brethren from the Gentiles, greeting, etc."

units.la: Similiter habetur hoc infra continuata sententia, cum dicitur: placuit ergo nobis collectis exnobis eligere viros & mittere ad vos. Et parum post infra: visum enim est, Spiritui sancto & nobis nihil ultra imponere, quam haec necessaria. non ergo determinauit Petrus supradicta dubia circa fidem de plenitudine potestatis. Deliberauit ergo dubium, elegit & scripsit fidelium doctorum congregatio. Hacetiam auctoritate validum fuit sic determinatum, atque mandatum. Congregatio enim apostolorum amplioris fuit auctoritatis, quam solus Petrus aut alter apostolus. Vnde ab ipsa Petrum legimus missum in Samariam, vt apparet Actuum 8. Cum igitur audissent apostoli, quia receperat Samaria verbum Dei, miserunt ad eos Petrum & Iohannem. Petrus igitur seruauit aequalitatem cum ceteris apostolis iuxta praeceptum Christi dicentis Matthaei 23. Nolite vocari rabbi. vnus est enim magister vester Christus. omnes autem fratres estis. Confirmatur haec sententia per apostolum ad Gal. 2. vbi ait; Ascendi autem secundum reuelationem, & contuli cum illis euangelium, quod praedico in gentibus. vbi Glo. secundum August. & non didici ab illis tanquam maioribus à Petro sciliicet, nec aliis principalioribus apostolorum, de quibus infra dicetur, sed contuli cum eis tanquam cum amicis.
units.tr: Likewise, it is held further on in the continuous sentence, where it is said: it has therefore seemed good to us, gathered together, to choose men and send them to you. And a little after: for it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose on you nothing further than these necessary things. Peter therefore did not settle the aforesaid doubts concerning faith by the fullness of power. The assembly of learned believers deliberated on the question, chose men, and wrote. This determination and command was also made valid by authority. For the assembly of the apostles had greater authority than Peter alone or any other apostle. Hence we read that Peter was sent by it into Samaria, as appears from Acts 8: When the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John. Peter therefore kept equality with the other apostles, in accordance with the precept of Christ in Matthew 23: Be not called rabbi, for one is your master, Christ, and you are all brethren. This view is confirmed by the apostle in Galatians 2, where he says: But I went up according to revelation, and conferred with them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, where the gloss, following Augustine, says: and I did not learn from them as from greater men, namely from Peter, nor from the other more principal apostles, of whom it will be said below, but I conferred with them as with friends.

units.la: Idem rursus infra eodem, cum dixit apostolus: cum autem venisset Cephas Antiochiam, in faciem ei restiti, quia reprehensibilis erat, &c. vbi Glossa secundum Hieronymum: ipsi nihil mihi contulerunt: sed ego contuli Petro. & subiungit consequenter: ego restiti ei tanquam pari: hoc enim non auderet facere, nisi sciret se non imparem fore.
units.tr: Again, further on in the same chapter, when the apostle said: But when Cephas had come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed, etc., the gloss, following Jerome, says: They added nothing to me, but I conferred with Peter. And it adds in consequence: I withstood him as an equal, for he would not have dared to do this unless he knew that I was not inferior to him.

units.la: Ecce ergo, quod Paulus fuit par officio & dignitate Petro, non inferior, licet Petrus fuerit aetate senior, & tempore prior pastor. Item Augustinus de quaestionibus noui & veteris testamenti. q. 44. ait: Eodem die, illa est Pentecostes, lex lata est, quo & Spiritus sanctus decidit in discipulos, vt auctoritatem caperent, & scirent euangelicum ius praedicare.
units.tr: Behold, then, that Paul was equal to Peter in office and dignity, not inferior to him, although Peter was older in age and earlier in time as minister. Likewise Augustine, in his Questions on the Old and New Testament, question 44, says: On the same day, which is the feast of Pentecost, the law was given, the day on which the Holy Spirit also descended upon the disciples, so that they might receive authority and know how to preach the gospel law.

units.la: Amplius, sicus Petrus Antiochae legitur electus in episcopum per multitudinem aliorum apostolorum confirmatione vel consecratione non indigens, sic & apostolorum reliqui praefuerunt in aliis prouinciis absque Petri scientia institutione vel consecratione aliqua. fuerunt enim per Christum consecrati sufficienter. propter quod similiter opinandum horum apostolorum successores non indiguisse aliqua confirmatione successorum Petri. quinimo multi successores aliorum apostolorum fuerint electi & instituti episcopi rite, ipsorumque prouinciae rite & sancte rexerunt absque institutione vel confirmatione de ipsis facta per successores Petri. & extitit hoc sic legitime obseruatum vsque ad tempora Constantini Imperatoris, qui quandam praeeminentiam & potestatem tribuit episcopis & ecclesiae Romanorum super ceteras mundi ecclesias. Item, aequalitatem Petri & apostolorum signauit apostolus ad Gal. 2. cum dixit: dexteras dederunt mihi, &c. Iacobus, Petrus atque Iohannes, vt nos in gentes, ipsi autem in circumcisionem. Dexteras societatis: igitur & aequalitatis. Ex Glossa secundum Augustin. latis ostensum est sup. quamuis hoc dictum apostoli sic sit apertum, vt Glossa non egeat. Quod etiam ex epistola Hiero. ad Euandrum patet, cum dicit, omnes episcopos siue Romae siue alibi eiusdem sacerdotii atq; meriti seu potestatis à Christo collatae immediate. Si autem B. Petrus à quibusdam sanctorum princeps apostolorum scribatur, dictum est large ac improprie sumendo vocabulum principis. & nisi sic, aperte contra Christi sententiam & oraculum est, vt Mat. 10. & Luc. 22. inquit: Principes gentium dominantur eorum, vos autem non sic. ideoque dicendum est sic sanctos loquutos, non propter potestatem aliquam a Christo super apostolos sibi datam immediate, sed fortiran quia aetate senior, aut quia Christum prius est confessus, fuisse verum Dei consubstantialem filium, vel quia forte fuit in fide feruentior atque constantior; aut quia cum Christo conversatus & frequentius vocatus in consiliis & secretis. unde apostolus ad Gal. 2. Iacobus & Cephas (id est, Petrus) & Iohannes videbantur columnae esse, vbi Glo. secundum Ambr. quia honoratiores erant in apostolis, quia semper in secretis cum domino fuerunt. Item quod Petrus super apostolos nullam a Christo habuerit potestatem, probatur auctoritate Christi potestatem huiusmodi interdicentis & dicentis Matth. 23. vos autem nolite vocari rabbi. vnus est enim magister vester: vos autem fratres estis omnes.
units.tr: Furthermore, just as Peter is read to have been chosen bishop of Antioch by the multitude of the other apostles, needing no confirmation or consecration, so too the remaining apostles presided over other provinces without any institution or consecration by Peter's knowledge. For they had been sufficiently consecrated by Christ. For this reason we should similarly suppose that the successors of these apostles did not need any confirmation from the successors of Peter. Indeed, many successors of the other apostles were lawfully elected and instituted bishops, and their provinces were ruled rightly and holily without any institution or confirmation made by the successors of Peter. And this remained lawfully observed until the time of the Emperor Constantine, who bestowed a certain pre-eminence and power upon the bishops and the Church of Rome over the other churches of the world. Likewise, the apostle marked the equality of Peter and the apostles in Galatians 2, when he said: They gave me the right hands, etc. James, Peter and John, that we should go to the Gentiles, but they to the circumcision. Right hands of fellowship, therefore also of equality. As has been shown above from the gloss, following Augustine, although this statement of the apostle is so plain that the gloss is not needed. This also appears from the letter of Jerome to Evangelus, where he says that all bishops, whether at Rome or elsewhere, are of the same priesthood and of the same merit and power, conferred immediately by Christ. But if the blessed Peter is called by some of the saints the prince of the apostles, the word prince is taken broadly and improperly. And if it were otherwise, it would be plainly against the sentence and oracle of Christ, who says in Matthew 10 and Luke 22: The princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you not so. Therefore it must be said that the saints spoke in this way not because of any power given to Peter by Christ immediately over the apostles, but perhaps because he was older in age, or because he had confessed before the others that Christ was the true consubstantial Son of God, or because he was perhaps more fervent and constant in faith, or because he had associated with Christ and was more often called into his counsels and secrets. Hence the apostle in Galatians 2: James and Cephas (that is, Peter) and John seemed to be pillars, where the gloss, following Ambrose, says: because they were more honoured among the apostles, since they were always with the Lord in his secrets. Likewise, that Peter had no power from Christ over the apostles is proved by the authority of Christ forbidding and saying such power in Matthew 23: But you, be not called rabbi, for one is your master, and you are all brethren.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod Petrus non erat caput & princeps aliorum apostolorum, per auctoritates doctorum.
units.tr: In which it is proved, from the authorities of the doctors, that Peter was not the head and prince of the other apostles.

units.la: DISCIP. Praeter praedictas allegationes, occurrunt aliae ad probandum, quod Petrus non erat caput, princeps & praelatus aliorum apostolorum, recta. MAGIST. Eusebius Caesariensis talem superioritatem videtur negare a Petro, & asserere quod fuerit inferior Iacobo fratre domini. Dicit enim in Ecclesiastica historia li. 2. ca 1. Iacobum, qui & iustus cognominatus est ab antiquis, virtutum merito, & insignis vita privilegio, primum historiae tradiderunt suscepisse ecclesiam, quae etiam Hierosolymis est. Sicut Clemens in sexto disputationum libro asserit dicens: Petrus enim & Iacobus, & Iohannes post assumptionem Saluatoris, quamuis ab ipso fuerint pene omnibus praelati, tamen non sibi vendicant primatus gloriam, sed Iacobum, qui dicebatur iustus, episcopum apostolorum statuerunt. Ex quibus verbis colliguntur duo. Primum est, quod Petrus non fuit Praelatus a Deo omnibus aliis apostolis, cum in verbis contineatur & scripturis, quod Petrus & Iacobus & Iohannes post assumptionem saluatoris praelati fuerunt a domino pene omnibus. igitur saltem Petrus non fuit praelatus Iacobo & Iohanni. Secundum est, quod Iacobus per electionem Petri & Iohannis fuit praelatus facultus aliorum apostolorum. & per consequens Iacobus fuit superior Petro, tanquam episcopus Petri, & aliorum apostolorum. Item in eadem Ecclesiastica historia lib. 3. c. 21. sic habetur: In urbe Romana Clemens quoque tertius post Paulum & Petrum pontificatum tenebat. Ex quibus verbis videtur haberi, quod non plus, erat pontifex Petrus in Roma quam Paulus. Idem videtur haberi lib. 4. cap. 5, vbi sic dicitur: Roma autem vicesimo primo anno memorati principatus sexto 21. annis ecclesiae gubernaculis functo Thelesforus septimus ab apostolis subrogatur. Et libro 4. capi. 11. sic habetur: Effloruit apud Alexandriam Clemens eodem vocabulo, quo & ille in urbe Roma apostolorum & successor & discipulus vocitatus. Clemens igitur successor fuit apostolorum. & per consequens vterque apostolus eodem fungebatur officio, quo & Clemens. ergo & Paulus fuit summus pontifex in urbe Roma. Item B. Anacletus hoc sentire videtur: qui, vt legitur dist. 21. c. in nouo, ait: Hic ergo (scilicet Petrus) ligandi soluendi primus potestatem accepit: ille a domino primum, ad fidem virtute sua praedicationis populum adduxit, verbo instituit: ceterique apostolici pari consortio honorem & potestatem acceperunt, ipsumque eorum principem esse voluerunt. Item B. Cyprianus, vt habetur 24. q. 1. capi. loquitur, ait: Hoc erant vtique caeteri apostoli, quod Petrus fuit, pari consortio praediti, & honoris & potestatis. Ex quibus verbis tam Anacleti quam Cypriani videtur, quod caeteri apostoli tam quantum ad honorem, quam quantum ad potestatem, pares fuerunt B. Petro. ergo non fuit princeps eorum, nec superior eis quoad officium & potestatem.
units.tr: STUDENT. Besides the arguments already cited, others present themselves to prove rightly that Peter was not the head, prince and prelate of the other apostles. TEACHER. Eusebius of Caesarea seems to deny Peter such superiority and to assert that he was inferior to James, the brother of the Lord. For he says in the Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 1: James, who was also called the Just by the ancients, on account of the merit of his virtues and the distinguished privilege of his life, they handed down in history as having first received the church which is also at Jerusalem. As Clement also asserts in the sixth book of the Disputations, saying: Peter, and James, and John, after the assumption of the Saviour, although they were preferred by him above nearly all, did not claim for themselves the glory of primacy, but appointed James, who was called the Just, bishop of the apostles. Two things are gathered from these words. The first is that Peter was not preferred by God above all the other apostles, since the words and Scriptures contain that Peter, James and John, after the assumption of the Saviour, were preferred by the Lord above nearly all. Therefore at least Peter was not preferred to James and John. The second is that James, by the election of Peter and John, was set over the other apostles as their bishop; and consequently James was superior to Peter, as the bishop both of Peter and of the other apostles. Likewise in the same Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 21, it is written thus: In the city of Rome, Clement, the third after Paul and Peter, held the pontificate. From these words it seems to follow that Peter was no more pontiff in Rome than Paul was. The same seems to appear in book 4, chapter 5, where it is said: At Rome, in the twenty-first year of the aforesaid reign, the sixth having discharged the government of the church for 21 years, Thelesphorus, the seventh from the apostles, is substituted. And in book 4, chapter 11, it is written thus: At Alexandria there flourished Clement, of the same name by which he who in the city of Rome was called both successor and disciple of the apostles. Clement, therefore, was the successor of the apostles, and consequently each apostle held the same office that Clement did. Therefore Paul too was the supreme pontiff in the city of Rome. Blessed Anacletus also seems to hold this view: he says, as is read in dist. 21, c. in novo: Peter, then, first received the power of binding and loosing; he first brought the people to faith by the power of his preaching and instructed them by word; and the other apostles, in equal partnership, received honour and power, and wished him to be their prince. Likewise Blessed Cyprian, as is found in 24 q. 1 c., says: Those other apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with equal partnership both of honour and of power. From these words of Anacletus and of Cyprian it seems that the other apostles were equal to Blessed Peter both in honour and in power. Therefore he was not their prince, nor superior to them in office and power.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: In quo ponitur secunda opinio de inaequalitate apostolorum, faciliter quod Christus beatum Petrum constituerit caput & principem aliorum apostolorum, quod probatur duabus auctoritatibus, quae soluuntur, & solutiones confutantur. c. 4. & 5. usque ad c. 10.
units.tr: In which the second opinion is set out, concerning the inequality of the apostles, namely that Christ appointed the blessed Peter head and prince of the other apostles. This is proved by two authorities, which are answered, and the answers are refuted. Chapters 4 and 5 through chapter 10.

units.la: DISCIP. Si alia est opinio circa istam materiam, ipsam cum suis motiuis non differas pertractare. MAGIST. Alia est opinio tenens, quod Christus constituerit beatum Petrum caput, principem & praelatum aliorum apostolorum: & quod Petrus fuit ipsis superior. quod multis modis ostenditur. Hoc enim ex verbis Christi, quae recitantur Ioh. vlt. videtur posse probari. ad Petrum enim Christus singulariter dixit: Pasce oues meas: pasce agnos meos. replicans eandem sententiam. & per consequens, cum Christus non distinxerit inter has oues & illas, primus & universalis pastor etiam apostolorum immediate a Christo beatus Petrus institutus fuisse videtur. quod ibidem Chrisostomus expresse videtur asserere, cum ait: Ex numero enim apostolorum erat Petrus, & os discipulorum, & vertex collegii. vnde & negatione debita mittit ei praelationem fratrum. DISCIP. Ex his, quae legitam in historiis authenticis, quam etiam in scripturis sanctorum patrum, quorum nonnullae sententiae in decretis habentur, mihi videtur, quod omnium Christianorum, praesertim obedientium Romanae ecclesiae fuerit communis sententia, beatum Petrum fuisse institutum a Christo caput & principem omnium fidelium. Quae tamen sententia his temporibus impugnatur. & ad motiua in quibus scriptura diuina fundari videtur, ex intentione lenius respondeatur.
units.tr: STUDENT. If there is another opinion on this matter, do not hesitate to discuss it with its arguments. MASTER. There is another opinion, holding that Christ appointed the blessed Peter head, prince and prelate of the other apostles, and that Peter was superior to them. This is shown in many ways. It seems that this can be proved from the words of Christ recited in Ioh. vlt. For Christ said to Peter alone: Feed my sheep, feed my lambs, repeating the same charge. Consequently, since Christ did not distinguish between these sheep and those, the blessed Peter seems to have been instituted immediately by Christ as the first and universal shepherd, even of the apostles. Chrysostom seems to assert this expressly in the same place, when he says: For Peter was of the number of the apostles, and the mouth of the disciples, and the head of the college. Whence also, by a fitting denial, he yielded to him the precedence over his brethren. STUDENT. From what I read in authentic histories, and also in the writings of the holy Fathers, some of whose sayings are found in the decrees, it seems to me that it was the common opinion of all Christians, especially those obedient to the Roman Church, that the blessed Peter was appointed by Christ head and prince of all the faithful. Yet this opinion is attacked in these times. Let the arguments on which divine Scripture seems to be founded be answered more gently, according to their intention.

units.la: {y} Iohannes ... intelligitur. sponderur. ideo vt mihi & aliis præbeatur occasio subtilius intuendi, an priores fuerint in hoc decepti, motiua præcedentium cum responsionibus modernorum ( quorum propono tecum discutere diligenter ) responsiones eorum non truncate, sed integre recitabo. & tunc recitabis, quomodo vere & realiter, aut apparenter seu sophistice valeat reprobari. MAGIST. Dicitur igitur ad motiuum præscriptum, quod sensus secundum Glossam præallegatorum verborum Christi, scilicet pasce oues meas, &c. est, quod oues pascere est credentes, ne deficiant, confirmare: terrena subsidia, si necesse est, subditis prouidere: exempla virtutum præbere: aduersariis obsistere, fide, scilicet: peccantes corrigere. Et subditur in Glo. & cum tertio audit à Petro sediligi, iubet pascere oues. terna negationi redditur trina confessio, ne minus amori lingua seruiat quam timori. Ex hoc autem non aliud conuincitur, nisi quod ipsum pastorem ouium Christus instituit: non tamen ex hoc sequitur, quod ipsum super reliquos apostolos prætulerit, quoad auctoritatem vel dignitatem priorem. nec rursum sequitur ex hoc, alios apostolos non fuisse institutos pastores. oppositum enim vtriusque consequentis iam dicti stat cum antecedente: videlicet cum sermone Christi prædicto.
units.tr: (Passage garbled in the scan.) So that I and others may have an occasion of examining more subtly whether the earlier writers were deceived in this, I will set out the arguments of the predecessors together with the replies of the moderns (whose replies I propose we examine carefully together), not cut short but in full. Then you will show how they may truly and really be refuted, or only apparently or sophistically. MASTER. To the argument stated above it is said that the sense of the words of Christ cited earlier, namely feed my sheep, etc., according to the Gloss, is this: to feed sheep is to strengthen believers lest they fail; to provide earthly help for subjects, if necessary; to offer examples of virtue; to resist adversaries by faith; and to correct sinners. And the Gloss adds: And when a third time he is charged by Peter, he bids him feed the sheep. The threefold denial is answered by a threefold confession, lest the tongue serve love less than fear. From this, however, nothing else is proved except that Christ appointed him the shepherd of the sheep. Yet it does not follow from this that he placed him above the other apostles in authority or dignity as their prior. Nor again does it follow from this that the other apostles were not appointed shepherds. For the opposite of each of these consequences stands with the antecedent, namely with the aforesaid words of Christ.

units.la: Testatur autem prædictis, quod ecclesia catholica cantat de omnibus apostolis indifferenter: vere dignum & iustum est, æquum & salutare, te domine supplicitèr exorare, vt gregem tuum pastor æterne non deseras, sed per beatos apostolos tuos continua protectione custodias, vt eisdem rectoribus gubernetur, quos operis tui vicarios eidem contulisti præsse pastores. Ecce apostolos in plurali rectores, vicarios & pastores per Christi collationem immediatam: non autem solum aliquem rectorem, vicarium atque pastorem constitutum per Christum. Interroganti vero, cur Christus hoc Petro singulariter dixerit? dicendum vtique est, quod Christus quandoque sermonem dirigebat in personam propriam, vt in remissione peccatorum, sanatione infirmorum, & suscitatione mortuorum. quandoque dirigebat sermonem ad alterum in personam omnium aut plurium, vt Ioh. 5. vade & amplius noli peccare, ne deterius tibi contingat. Unde idem officium Christus committendo Petro, ille loquebatur in persona omnium apostolorum, sicut ipsemet testatur hunc modum loquendi suum Matth. 13. cum dixit; quod vni ex vobis dico, omnibus dico. Specialiter tamen ad Petrum direxit sermonem, quia senior erat; vel quia charitate ardentior, vel vt significaret ecclesiæ futuræ quales debeant pastores institui.
units.tr: Moreover, the Catholic Church, as the above shows, sings of all the apostles indifferently: It is truly meet and just, right and salutary, that we humbly beseech you, Lord, eternal shepherd, not to forsake your flock, but to keep it under continual protection through your blessed apostles, that it may be governed by those same rulers whom you appointed as the vicars of your work to be its shepherds. Behold, the apostles are called rulers, vicars and shepherds in the plural, by the immediate appointment of Christ; not merely some one ruler, vicar and shepherd appointed through Christ. But to one who asks why Christ said this to Peter alone, it must certainly be answered that Christ sometimes directed his speech to a person in his own person, as in the remission of sins, the healing of the sick and the raising of the dead; and sometimes he directed his speech to one person in the name of all or several, as in John 5: Go, and sin no more, lest something worse befall you. Thus, in committing this office to Peter, he spoke in the person of all the apostles, just as he himself testifies to this manner of speaking of his in Matt. 13, when he said: What I say to one of you, I say to all. He addressed the speech specially to Peter, however, either because he was the elder, or because he was more ardent in charity, or to signify what kind of pastors ought to be appointed in the future Church.

units.la: Quoniam ætate maturi, ex qua signatur prudentia seu scientia. Et charitate pleni, ex qua significatur cura & diligentia, quas debent habere pastores. Aut fortasse ne videretur tanquam abiectior relinqui, quia Christum negauerat. Quod sapere videtur Glossa, cum dicit; trina negationi reddatur trina confessio, ne minus amori lingua seruiat, quàm timori. Hoc enim certissime constat quod omnibus Matth. vlt. dictum est indifferenter; Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, nec dixit Petro, vade & alios mitte. in quo signauit omnibus auctoritatis æqualitatem.
units.tr: Because he was mature in age, which signifies prudence or knowledge; and full of charity, which signifies the care and diligence that pastors ought to have. Or perhaps lest he seem to be left behind as more abject, because he had denied Christ. The Gloss seems to hint at this when it says: The threefold denial is answered by a threefold confession, lest the tongue serve love less than fear. For this is most certainly established: what was said to all indifferently in Matth. vlt., Go therefore and teach all nations, was not said to Peter as "go and send the others." In this he signified equality of authority among all.

units.la: Sicut etiam Matth. 13. ca. prædicto induximus, dum ad eos inquit Christus; nolite vocari rabbi, supple inuicem, aut vnus super reliquum vel reliquos. vnus enim est magister vester. vos autem omnes fratres estis.
units.tr: Just as we also cited above, in Matth. 13, when Christ said to them: "Do not be called rabbi" (supply: one to another), "or one over the other or over the rest. For one is your master. But you are all brethren."

units.la: Audiendum est valde probabiliter, atque secundum veritatem mihi videtur, quod pro tanto dixit Petro, pasce oues meas, vt sibi simpliciter, sicut & Moysi propter sui constantiam committeret populum Israel, qui duræ ceruicis populus fuit versus Deum, vt apparet Exod. 33. vt inducit apostolus per Esaiam Aduum vlti. Et quoniam propter hunc populum conuertendum & saluandum principaliter venerat. Unde Matth. 15. non sum missus nisi ad oues quæ perierant domus Israel. non sum missus, principaliter supple. ideo huiusmodi populi curam beato Petro specialiter commisisse videtur, cum dixit; pasce oues meas. Et videtur hic fuisse apostoli aperte sententia, cum ad Gal. 1. dixit; cum vidissent, quia creditum est mihi euangelium præputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis, &c. vbi secundum Aug. Cum vidissent quod euangelium præputii à Domino creditum est mihi vt fideli ita principaliter, sicut & Petro euangelium circumcisionis. Christus enim dedit Paulo, vt ministraret Iudæis.
units.tr: It is to be heard, very probably and, as it seems to me, according to the truth, that for this reason he said to Peter feed my sheep, so that he might commit to him simply, just as he committed the people of Israel to Moses on account of his constancy, that people which was stiff-necked toward God, as appears in Exod. 33, and as the apostle cites through Isaiah in Rom. 10. Since it was principally for the conversion and salvation of this people that he had come. Whence in Matt. 15: I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. "I was not sent," principally, is to be supplied. Therefore he seems to have specially committed the care of this people to the blessed Peter, when he said: feed my sheep. And this seems to have been the apostle's clear opinion when, in Gal. 1, he said: "when they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed to me, as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter, etc." Where, according to Augustine: "When they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed by the Lord to me as to a faithful man, and principally, just as also to Peter the gospel of the circumcision." For Christ gave Paul to minister to the Jews.

units.la: Ita tamen dispensatio distributa est illis: vt etiam Petrus gentibus prædicaret, si sic causam exegisset, & Paulus Iudæis. nec video, quod aliunde Paulus vel alter sanctus assumere poterit populum Iudaicum specialiter & principaliter fuisse Petro commissum, nisi ex eo quod Christus illi dixit; Pasce oues meas; cum dicat Paulus ad Gal. 2. sibi creditum euangelium præputii quemadmodum Petro circumcisionis. si namque creditum erat euangelium vniuersaliter Petro plus quam Paulo vel aliis apostolis, inconuenienter vtique dixisset Paulus verba prædicta: quinimo totus eius sermo prædictus fuisset inanis, & comparatio quam etiam fecit in eo.
units.tr: Yet the dispensation was so distributed between them that Peter also preached to the Gentiles, if the cause had so required, and Paul to the Jews. Nor do I see how Paul or any other saint could establish, from any other source, that the Jewish people was specially and principally committed to Peter, except from the fact that Christ said to him: "Feed my sheep." For Paul says in Gal. 2 that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed to him just as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter. For if the gospel had been committed universally to Peter more than to Paul or the other apostles, Paul would certainly have spoken the aforesaid words inappropriately. Indeed, his whole discourse above would have been empty, and so would the comparison he drew in it.

units.la: Ad Glossam autem ex Chrysostomo sumptam vna responsio datur, quæ generalis est ad illas & ad plures alias quæ idem sonant. Dicitur igitur, quod auctoritatem nullam essentialem, quam sacerdotalem isti vocant, neque auctoritatem aliquam pastoratus & excellentiam super reliquos apostolos Christus immediate Petro tradidit, sed ab illo & cæteris inuicem remouit. vt alibi conantur ostendere per scripturas & expositiones sanctorum doctorum. propter quod (vt dicunt Christum, & apostolum, & ipsorum quorundam & glossatorum alibi dicta sequentes) declinant sententiam, quam superinducta scripturae loca & alia quaeque similia dicere videntur de tali primatu seu principalitate aliter, quam alibi dicunt, scilicet 10. & 11. secunda editionis sui operis. quoniam talis sententia nec est canonica, nec canonicam sequitur; quinimo ipsorum aliqui oppositum dixerunt alibi exponendo scripturam ex propria sententia sequentes consuetudinem: & magis attendentes quaedam dicta famosa quam verba scripturae. Quis enim eorum esset maior inter se discipulis quaerentibus Christum respondisse semper inter ipsos aequalitatem esse debere, & prioritatem auctoritatis ab ipsorum quocunque negasse. Si intendebat beatum Petrum constituisse ipsis principaliorem & caput. denique Christus non dabat reliquis mandatum, ut Petro subessent in officio pastorali: ne tantum mysterium lateret eos & ipsorum successores, quando tunc erat caput ecclesiae. Nusquam enim legitur in scriptura tale mandatum fuisse datum apostolis. quomodo etiam dexteras dedit Petrus Paulo societatis: imo dare mandatum debuit tanquam superior. Quare materia haec huiusmodi sententiae oppositum clamat aperte.
units.tr: To the Gloss taken from Chrysostom, one general answer is given, which applies to that passage and to many others that say the same. It is said, therefore, that Christ did not immediately hand over to Peter any essential authority, which these men call sacerdotal, nor any authority of pastoral office and excellence over the other apostles, but removed it from him and from the others alike; as they elsewhere try to show from the Scriptures and the expositions of the holy doctors. On account of this (as they say, following Christ, the apostle, and certain of their own glossators' sayings elsewhere), they decline the opinion that the passages of Scripture cited, and any similar ones, seem to state about such a primacy or principality otherwise than they say elsewhere, namely in the tenth and eleventh chapters of the second edition of their work. For such an opinion is neither canonical nor follows the canon. Rather, some of them have said the opposite elsewhere, expounding Scripture according to their own opinion, following custom, and attending more to certain famous sayings than to the words of Scripture. For who among them, when the disciples were asking Christ which of them was greatest, answered that there ought always to be equality among them, and denied that any of them had priority of authority? If he had intended the blessed Peter to be appointed above them and their head, then Christ did not give the others a command to be subject to Peter in the pastoral office, lest so great a mystery be hidden from them and their successors, since he was then the head of the Church. For nowhere is it read in Scripture that such a command was given to the apostles. Just as Peter also gave Paul the right hands of fellowship, so he ought, as a superior, to have given a command. Wherefore this matter clearly cries out against an opinion of this kind.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Responsionem ad praedictam Christi auctoritatem impugnat. Quodque praedicta Christi verba Petro in persona propria & non aliorum dirigebantur, tribus rationibus multisque sanctorum auctoritatibus amplissime probat.
units.tr: He answers the aforesaid authority of Christ and, by three arguments and many authorities of the saints, proves at length that the words of Christ quoted above were addressed to Peter in his own person and not in the person of others.

units.la: DIS. In verbis praescriptis non solum habetur, quomodo ad praeddictam allegationem tenentes sententiam contrariam satagunt respondere; sed et plures allegationes pro sententia contraria continentur. Et ideo si vis nunc omnia discuti, oportet me non solum opponentis seu improbantis, sed etiam respondentis personam assumere. & tu vtrunque facias; sic forsitan magnam partem istius materiae disseremus. MAG. In verbis istorum duae responsiones principales habentur. Quarum prima in hoc principaliter videtur consistere, quod Christus illa verba, pasce oves meas, dirigebat ad Petrum in persona omnium apostolorum, licet aliqua alia quasi incidentaliter videtur adiungere. Ideo primo ante omnia aliquas allegationes adducam, quibus videtur posse probari, quod Christus verba praedicta dirigebat ad Petrum in persona propria, & non in persona omnium apostolorum. Quod ostenditur primo sic. Verba per quae aliquis promouetur ad aliquam dignitatem, vel officium, ad illum cui dicuntur in propria persona, non in persona aliorum diriguntur. Alioquin cum per verba aliqua aliquis instituitur in seculari vel ecclesiastica dignitate, omnes alii, praesertim eiusdem conditionis vel meriti, intelligerentur in eadem dignitate instituti. & ita si Imperator per literas vel ore proprio talibus verbis vel consimilibus, institutio, aut facio te iudicem, comitem, ducem, aut aduocatum talis vel talis regionis aut ciuitatis: omnes alii intelligerentur instituti in eadem dignitate. Et sic idem eadem ratione esset de institutione rectorum, plebanorum, & aliorum quorumcunque praelatorum ecclesiae sentiendum. Quod quam sit absurdum, nulli debet existere dubium, vt videtur. Sed per praedicta verba fuit in dignitate & officio & pastorali constitutus: sicut & praedicti opinantes concedunt, cum dicunt, quod ipsum pastorem omnium Christus instituit. Ergo illa verba dirigebantur ad beatum Petrum in persona propria: & non in persona quorumcunque aliorum.
units.tr: PUPIL. The passage above not only contains how those who hold the contrary opinion try to answer the aforesaid allegation, but also includes several further allegations for the contrary opinion. So if you want everything discussed now, I must take on not only the role of the objector or critic but also that of the respondent, and you should do both. In this way we may perhaps treat a large part of the matter. TEACHER. In the words quoted there are two main responses. The first seems to rest mainly on this: that Christ addressed the words feed my sheep to Peter in the person of all the apostles, although it adds some other points almost incidentally. So first of all I will adduce some arguments by which it seems possible to prove that Christ addressed the aforesaid words to Peter in his own person and not in the person of all the apostles. This is shown first as follows. Words by which someone is promoted to a dignity or office are addressed to the one to whom they are spoken in his own person, not in the person of others. Otherwise, whenever someone is installed in a secular or ecclesiastical dignity by some words, all others, especially those of the same condition or merit, would be understood to be installed in the same dignity. And so, if an emperor by letter or by his own voice used words such as these or similar, "I appoint you, or I make you, judge, count, leader, or advocate of such and such a region or city," all others would be understood to be installed in the same dignity. In the same way, the same reasoning would have to apply to the appointment of rectors, parish priests and any other prelates of the Church. How absurd that is, there should be no doubt, as it seems. But by the aforesaid words Peter was established in the dignity, office and pastoral charge, as the aforesaid objectors also concede when they say that Christ appointed him minister of all. Therefore those words were addressed to the blessed Peter in his own person, and not in the person of any others.

units.la: Amplius: Si verba praedicta dirigebantur ad beatum Petrum in persona aliorum. Aut ergo dirigebantur ad beatum Petrum in persona omnium aliorum Christianorum, aut in persona apostolorum & omnium presbyterorum, aut tantummodo apostolorum, aut omnium aliorum solummodo, qui erant praesentes cum Christo & beato Petro. Primum non potest dici; quia tunc quilibet fidelis fuisset constitutus pastor ecclesiae. Nec isti possunt dicere secundum, cum dicunt, quod ista verba dirigebantur ad beatum Petrum in persona omnium apostolorum, de aliis presbyteris nullam facientes ibidem penitus mentionem. Nec possunt dicere tertium, quod tunc fuisset data aliqua auctoritas beato Petro & ceteris apostolis super alios presbyteros, quod isti negant. Nec possunt dicere quartum, quia tunc non fuisset data eadem potestas siue auctoritas omnibus apostolis; cum non omnes fuerint tunc praesentes; Quia de apostolis solummodo erant praesentes Petrus & Thomas & duo filii Zebedei. tum quia tunc fuisset data maior potestas aliquibus aliis, quam quibusdam apostolis. quia tunc erant alii praesentes, scilicet Nathanael & duo alii ex discipulis Christi, vt patet Ioh. 21.
units.tr: Further: if the aforesaid words were addressed to the blessed Peter in the person of others, then they were addressed to him either in the person of all other Christians, or in the person of the apostles and all the elders, or only of the apostles, or only of all the others who were present with Christ and the blessed Peter. The first cannot be said, since then every believer would have been appointed pastor of the Church. Nor can they say the second, since they say that these words were addressed to the blessed Peter in the person of all the apostles, making no mention whatever there of the other elders. Nor can they say the third, since then some authority would have been given to the blessed Peter and the other apostles over the other elders, which they deny. Nor can they say the fourth, since then the same power or authority would not have been given to all the apostles, since not all of them were present at that time. For of the apostles only Peter, Thomas and the two sons of Zebedee were present; and moreover, a greater power would then have been given to some others than to certain apostles, since other persons were present, namely Nathanael and two other disciples of Christ, as is clear from John 21.

units.la: Rursus quod de vno conceditur, de alio negatur. di. 45. disciplina. 1. q. 1. c. per Esaiam. sicut quod de vno negatur, de aliis conceditur. di. 25. qualis 15. q. 3. decima. igitur consimiliter verba, quae dicuntur vni, ad alios minime diriguntur. Sed verba praemissa dixit Christus soli Petro: ergo ad alios minime diriguntur. & per consequens non dirigebantur ad Petrum in persona aliorum apostolorum. DISCIP. Ista allegatio efficax non apparet, quia non est vniuersaliter verum, quod illud, quod dicitur de vno, de aliis negatur. cum secundum assertiones sanctorum patrum, quod vni dicitur vel conceditur, ad omnes extenditur. di. 5. ad eius. di. 38. ignorantia. 16. q. 1. prædicatur, ergo illa verba memorata à Petro ad alios debent extendi. MAGISTER. Respondetur, quod verum est, regulas prædictas non esse vniuersaliter veras, quin aliquando fallant. tamen illa regula: quod de vno dicitur, de alio negatur, in casu isto de beato Petro non fallit, sed tenet.
units.tr: Again, what is granted of one is denied of another. dist. 45, Disciplina; 1 q. 1, c. Per Esaiam. Likewise, what is denied of one is granted of others. dist. 25, Qualis; 15 q. 3, Decima. Therefore, similarly, words spoken to one are in no way addressed to others. But Christ spoke the aforesaid words to Peter alone; therefore they are in no way addressed to others, and consequently they were not addressed to Peter in the person of the other apostles. PUPIL. This argument does not seem valid, because it is not universally true that what is said of one is denied of others, since according to the assertions of the holy Fathers what is said or granted to one extends to all. dist. 5, Ad eius; dist. 38, Ignorantia; 16 q. 1. It is proclaimed. Therefore those words recorded as spoken to Peter ought to extend to the others. TEACHER. The answer is that it is true that these rules are not universally valid, in that they sometimes fail. Yet that rule, that what is said of one is denied of another, does not fail in this case concerning the blessed Peter, but holds.

units.la: Cuius ratio assignatur. Quia sicut quando conceditur vnum, conceduntur omnia consimilia, vt innuit beatus Gregorius, prout habetur dist. 4. denique, & notat Glossa ibidem. Et consimiliter omnia conceduntur, quæ sunt eiusdem censuræ, extra, de exceptionibus, cum inter. tamen vno concesso, non conceduntur omnia dissimilia, nec illa quæ non sunt eiusdem censuræ. Sic quod vni dicitur, ad alios extenditur, qui sunt eiusdem conditionis. & est eadem ratio dicendi vni & aliis. & ita expedit, vt dicatur aliis, sicut vni. & vbi ad hoc; quod aliquid intelligatur aliquibus dici, non oportet vt illis explicite, & nominatim & æquipollenter dicantur. Sed in proposito non fuit expediens, vt in eadem dignitate constituerentur alii apostoli. ideo illa verba Christi dicta beato Petro non extendebantur ad alios.
units.tr: The reason for this is given. Just as when one thing is granted, all similar things are granted, as the blessed Gregory hints, as is found in dist. 4, Denique, and as the Gloss there notes; and likewise all things are granted which are of the same rank, Extra, De exceptionibus, Cum inter. Yet when one thing is granted, not all dissimilar things are granted, nor those which are not of the same rank. So what is said to one extends to others who are of the same condition, and the reason for speaking to one is the same as for speaking to the others; and so it is fitting that it be said to the others just as to the one. And where something is understood to be said to some, it is not necessary that it be said to them explicitly, by name and in equivalent terms. But in the present case it was not expedient that other apostles be established in the same dignity; therefore those words of Christ spoken to the blessed Peter were not extended to the others.

units.la: Rursus, nullus (sicut tactum est supra) promouetur per aliqua verba ad aliquam dignitatem, nisi de ipso per ea fiat mentio specialis, aut æquipollens speciali quo ad ipsum. Quemadmodum licet quod de iure communi conceditur vni, intelligatur alii eiusdem conditionis esse concessum: tamen quod ex priuilegio conceditur vni, non intelligitur alii, etiam eiusdem conditionis & meriti esse concessum, nisi explicite hoc dicatur, vel mentio etiam priuilegii fiat de ipso. 7. q. 1. petisti. & 6. q. 1. huic. Sed per verba illa Christi tanquam per priuilegium speciale fuit beatus Petrus ad dignitatem sublimatus. In ipsis autem nulla fit mentio de aliis apostolis. ergo ad alios apostolos minime debent extendi. Ista responsio colligi potest ex Glossa, dist. 5. super capi. ad eius vero concubitum. quæ ait in hæc verba super verbo vni: Ergo quod vni conceditur, per consequens aliis videtur esse concessum sicut supra ca. denique. Et hoc verum est: vbi de iure communi aliquid conceditur, secus est, si ex priuilegio. & 15. q. 1. huic. & 8. q. 1. c. petisti. Ex prædictis conuincitur, quod sancti tradentes verba Christi prædicta, & sententialiter, & verbaliter afferentes per eadem verba, speciali ter soli Petro commissam esse dominicarum ouium curam, rectum intellectum eorum & catholicum expresserunt. & quod alius intellectus ipsorum nisi patenter distorqueantur, non solum contra ipsa, sed etiam contra præcedentia & sequentia (si inspiciantur omnia diligenter) haberi non potest.
units.tr: Again, no one (as was touched on above) is promoted to any dignity by any words unless special mention of him is made in them, or something equivalent to special mention as far as he is concerned. Just as, although what is granted to one by the common law is understood to be granted to another of the same condition, yet what is granted to one by privilege is not understood to be granted to another, even of the same condition and merit, unless this is said explicitly or mention of the privilege is made concerning him. 7 q. 1, Petisti; 6 q. 1, Huic. But by those words of Christ the blessed Peter was raised to his dignity as by a special privilege. In those words, however, no mention is made of the other apostles; therefore they ought in no way to be extended to the other apostles. This answer can be gathered from the Gloss on dist. 5, on the chapter Ad eius vero concubitum, which says in these words on the word "one": Therefore what is granted to one is consequently seen to be granted to the others, as above in the chapter Denique. And this is true: where something is granted by the common law, it is otherwise if it is granted by privilege; see also 15 q. 1, Huic, and 8 q. 1, c. Petisti. From what has been said it is proved that the holy Fathers, in handing down the aforesaid words of Christ and in asserting both their sense and their wording by the same words, expressed the right and catholic understanding of them: namely that the care of the Lord's sheep was committed specially to Peter alone. And that another understanding of them cannot be had, unless they are openly distorted, not only against those very words but also against what precedes and follows them (if all is examined carefully).

units.la: Sed vt liquido pateat, quod nonnullis appareat, quod ista fuit sanctorum sententia, de multis paucas eorum autoritates adducam. Ait itaq; sanctus Maximus episcopus in sermone de Petro & Paulo, qui incipit, Gloriosissimos: Iam necessarium terminum reor, vt proprias eorum & apostolorum Petri & Pauli, speciales que virtutes (prout ariditas nostra lingua ingenii que tenuitas patitur, imo vt misericors Deus annuit) proloquamur. Et infra: Hic est Petrus, cui Christus ascensurus ad patrem pascendas ouiculas suas ouesque commendat, vt quos ille pietate misericordeque redemerat, hic fidei sua virtute seruatet & recte ei arbiter occultorum Dei filius, pascendas oues suas tuendasque commisit, cui nouerat in nutriendo grege dominico, nec studium deesse nec fidem. Ex quibus datur intelligi, quod cum sanctus ille primo dicat, se velle proloqui proprias speciales que virtutes apostolorum: & postea in speciali de beato Petro præscripta subiungat: ipse voluit, quod oues Christi generaliter soli Petro pascendæ essent commissæ per verba Christi prædicta. Item G. egorius super illud Ioh. 21. manifestauit se iterum Iesus ad mare Tiberiadis, ait: Iam credo quod charitas vestra aduertat, quid est, quod Petrus rete ad terram: ipsi quippe sancta ecclesia est commissa, ipsi specialiter dicitur: Simon Iohannis amas me? pasce oues meas. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Petro in propria persona, non aliorum, dixit Christus: pasce oues meas.
units.tr: But so that it may be clearly shown that this was the opinion of the saints, which is apparent to many, I will adduce a few of their authorities out of many. So saint Maximus, bishop, says in the sermon on Peter and Paul which begins, Gloriosissimos: "Now I think it necessary to set forth the particular and special virtues of them both, of Peter and of the apostle Paul (as far as the dryness of our tongue and the slenderness of our wit allow, or rather as merciful God grants)." And further on: "This is Peter, to whom Christ, about to ascend to the Father, entrusts his little sheep to be fed, so that he who had redeemed them with his love and mercy might keep them by the virtue of his faith; and the Son of God, the judge of hidden things, rightly committed to him his sheep to be fed and protected, knowing that in nourishing the Lord's flock there would be no lack of zeal or of faith in him." From these words it is clear that this saint, having first said that he wishes to set forth the proper and special virtues of the apostles, then adds in particular what was written above about the blessed Peter; he means that the sheep of Christ were committed, in general, to Peter alone to be fed, by the aforesaid words of Christ. Likewise Gregory, on that passage of John 21, "Jesus showed himself again at the Sea of Tiberias," says: "I believe that your charity now notices what it is that Peter drew the net to land. Indeed the holy Church has been committed to him; to him it is specially said, 'Simon son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep.'" From these words it is gathered that Christ said to Peter, in his own person and not in that of others, feed my sheep.

units.la: Item sanctus Leo Papa in quodam sermone de ascensione domini, qui incipit: Post beatam & gloriosam, ait: Petro apostolo supra cæteros post regni claues ouilis dominici cura mandatur intelligi: quod per illa verba, pasce oues meas, Petro erat commissa cura totius dominici gregis. Item Ambrosius in sermone, qui legitur in festo sancti Petri ad vincula, ait: Cum tertio interrogaretur à Domino: Simon amas me, respondit: Domine tu scis quia diligo te. & ait Dominus, pasce oues meas, & hoc tertio. Quod quidem (vt dictum est) ad operationem prioris profecit erroris. qui enim dominum tertio negauerat, tertio confitetur: & quotiens culpam delinquendo incurrerat, totiens gratiam diligendo conquirit. videte qualiter fletus profuit Petro. antequam fleret, lapsus est, postquam fleuit, electus est. & qui ante lachrymas prævaricator exstitit, post lachrymas assumptus est, aliis regendos accepit, qui prius seipsum non rexit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod illa verba, pasce oues meas, dirigebantur ad beatum Petrum in persona propria, non aliorum, cum per ipsa ad regimen ecclesiæ assumptus est, & rector aliorum effectus. nemo autem per verba, quæ dicuntur, eligitur, neque assumitur, neque rector aliorum efficitur. Pradictis beatus Grego. super illud Math. 16. Maria Magdalena, Maria Iacobi, &c. concordare videtur, pro vt habetur dist. 50. cap. considerandum, cum dicit: Considerandum nobis est, cur omnipotens Deus eum, quem cunctæ ecclesiæ præferre disposuerat, ancillæ vocem pertimescere & seipsum negare permisit, quod, mirum magna actum esse pietatis dispensatione cognoscimus, vt ii, qui futurus erat pastor ecclesiæ, in sua culpa disceret, qualiter aliis misereri debuisset. primum itaque præposuit eum sibi, & tunc præposuit cæteris. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Petrus post passionem domini cunctæ ecclesiæ præferebatur à Deo, cum constet Deum illud, quod de eo disposuerat, impleuisse. non autem legitur, quod Deus prætulerit eum cunctæ ecclesiæ, nisi cum dixit ei: pasce oues meas. igitur illa verba dirigebat ad eum Christus in propria persona, & non in persona aliorum apostolorum. Item hoc Ambrosius, vt habetur. di. 50. ca. fidelior, testari videtur, cum dixit: Fidelior factus est Petrus, postquam se fidem perdidisse defleuit. atque ideo maiorem gratiam reperit, quam prius amisit, tanquam bonum pastor tuendum gregem accepit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Petrus postquam perdidit fidem, pastor gregis dominici fuit effectus. Sed non nisi tunc, vel tunc potissime, quando dixit sibi Christus: Pasce oues meas. Ergo tunc factus fuit pastor. nemo autem fit pastor, aut praelatus per verba, quae in singulari dicuntur alteri. Ergo esto, quod Christus fecit alios apostolos pastores aequales Petro: saltem per verba, quae in singulari dixit Petro, dicens: Pasce oues meas; nullus alius apostolus fuit factus pastor ecclesiae, neque aequalis, neque inferior Petro. Ergo illa verba dirigebat Christus ad Petrum in propria persona non in persona aliorum. Hoc etiam Bernardus ad Eugenium Papam affirmat aperte, sicut postea patebit. Quod etiam idem sentire videtur in quodam sermone de septem panibus, dicens: Testis est Petrus, cui post trinam negationem totius ecclesiae pastoralis cura commissa est: sed nonnisi quando sibi dixit Christus: pasce oues meas. Ergo illa verba Christi dirigebantur ad eum in persona propria, non in persona aliorum. Quod ex canonibus Paschasii Papae extra, de electio. ca. significasti, & Innocentii, extra de maioritate & obedientia, ca. solita, patenter habetur.
units.tr: Likewise, Saint Leo the Pope, in a certain sermon on the Lord's Ascension beginning "Post beatam et gloriosam," says: "After the keys of the kingdom, the care of the Lord's flock is understood to be entrusted to the apostle Peter above the rest; for by those words, Feed my sheep, the care of the whole Lord's flock was committed to Peter." Likewise Ambrose, in a sermon read on the feast of Saint Peter ad Vincula, says: "When the Lord asked him a third time, Simon, do you love me?, he answered: 'Lord, you know that I love you.' And the Lord said, Feed my sheep, and this a third time. This, indeed (as has been said), served to undo his earlier error. For he who had denied the Lord three times confesses three times; and as often as he had fallen by sinning, so often he regains grace by loving. See how his weeping profited Peter. Before he wept, he fell; after he wept, he was chosen. He who was a transgressor before his tears was taken up after them, and received others to rule, though he had not ruled himself before." From these words it is gathered that the words Feed my sheep were addressed to the blessed Peter in his own person, and not in the person of others, when through them he was taken up to the government of the Church and made ruler of others; and no one is chosen or taken up, or made ruler of others, through words that are spoken to someone else. In agreement with the above, the blessed Gregory, on the words of Matthew 16, "Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, etc.," seems to agree, as is found in dist. 50, chapter considerandum, where he says: "We must consider why almighty God permitted him whom he had determined to set before the whole Church to fear the voice of a maidservant and to deny himself. We know that this was done by a wondrous dispensation of piety, so that he who was to be the pastor of the Church might learn from his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others. Thus he first set him before himself, and then before the rest." From these words it is gathered that after the Lord's passion Peter was set before the whole Church by God, since it is agreed that God fulfilled what he had determined concerning him. But it is not read that God set him before the whole Church, except when he said to him, Feed my sheep. Therefore Christ addressed those words to him in his own person, and not in the person of the other apostles. Likewise Ambrose, as is found in dist. 50, chapter fidelior, seems to bear witness to this, when he says: "Peter became more faithful after he mourned that he had lost faith. And therefore he found a greater grace than he had lost before, and as a good shepherd he received the flock to be cared for." From these words it is gathered that Peter, after he had lost faith, became the shepherd of the Lord's flock. But this was not so until, or especially when, Christ said to him: Feed my sheep. Therefore then he became the shepherd. But no one becomes a shepherd or is set over others through words that are spoken in the singular to another. Therefore, granted that Christ made the other apostles shepherds equal to Peter, yet by the words which he spoke to Peter in the singular, saying Feed my sheep, no other apostle was made shepherd of the Church, neither equal nor inferior to Peter. Therefore Christ addressed those words to Peter in his own person, and not in the person of others. Bernard also openly affirms this to Pope Eugenius, as will later be shown. He seems to hold the same view in a certain sermon de septem panibus, saying: "Peter is a witness: after his threefold denial the pastoral care of the whole Church was committed to him, but only when Christ said to him: Feed my sheep." Therefore those words of Christ were addressed to him in his own person, and not in the person of others. This is plainly found in the canons of Pope Paschal, extra, de electione, ca. significasti, and of Innocent, extra de maioritate et obedientia, ca. solita.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Vbi ad praedicta responsionis declarationem respondet magister, ostendens, quando verba Christi vni dicta ad alios diriguntur, & quando non.
units.tr: Where the teacher answers the declaration of the foregoing reply, showing when the words of Christ spoken to one are directed to others, and when they are not.

units.la: DISCIP. Allegasti contra illud: in quo prima responsio supra ca. 3 recitata fundari videtur. Ideo nunc tracta alia, quae opinantes illi videntur afferere respondendo, per quae argumentum adductum euacuare & suam responsionem declarare niituntur. Et primo incipias ab illo, quod dicitur, quod Christus tali modo loquendi visus est, quod scilicet aliquando aliqua verba dixit vni, & tamen dirigebat ipsa ad illum, cui loquebatur in persona aliorum. quod ipse solus testatur, cum dixit. Math. 13. quod vni dico, omnibus dico. MAGIST. Nonnullis apparet, quod per illa quae dicta sunt in praecedenti ca. intelligentibus patet aperte, quomodo illud ad propositum nihil facit; quia verum est quod Christus aliquando tali modo loquendi visus est; quia interdum loquendo vni dirigebat sermonem ad alios. sed hoc non fuit, nisi quando fuit eadem ratio docendi aliquid vnum & alios. Quod accidit, quando aliquis inducitur ad agendum vel non agendum aliquid, siue ad credendum vel non credendum aliquid, quod alii ita tenentur agere vel non agere, credere vel non credere. Sicut ille, cui dicitur in singulari & vniuersaliter, vbi ille cui aliquid dicitur & alii consimiliter se habent & habere debent, siue tenentur se habere ad illud quod dicitur. Quod veritatem habet in illo, de quo praecesserat termo Christi, cum postea dixit Math. 13. quod autem vni dico, omnibus dico: vigilate, ita indiguerunt, & indiget alii viatores vigilare, qui nesciunt, quando dominus veniet, sicut apostoli. Sed quia alii non consimiliter se habet vel non tenentur consimiliter se habere ad illud, de quo est sermo; tunc quod dicitur vni non propter hoc intelligitur aliis dictum. Non enim quando dominus dixit Petro: vade ad mare & mitte hamum, &c. omnes alii discipuli, & apostoli, qui hoc audierunt, currere cum Petro tenebantur ad mare. Sic quando Christus dixit Petro Ioh. vlti. sequere me; noluit vt Petrus intelligeret illud eodem modo esse dictum aliis, sicut sibi.
