Propter quod interroganti Petro de Iohanne: Domine hic autem quid? respondit ei Iesus: si eum volo manere donec veniam, quid ad te, tu me sequere. Sic dico, non semper quod dicitur vni intelligitur aliis esse dictum. Quod etiam non videtur veritatem habere, quando aliquid dicitur vni, vt praeficiatur alteri, sicut in proposito fuit. Per praedicta patet (vt videtur quibusdam) falsum esse, quod tamen post recitationem verborum Christi & Glossae dicunt opinantes praefati) quod ex hoc non aliud conuincitur, nisi quod ipsum pastorem Christus instituit; non tamen ex hoc sequitur, quod ipsum super reliquos apostolos ad auctoritatem vel dignitatem priorem praetulit. Nec rursum sequitur ex hoc, alios apostolos non fuisse institutos pastores. Errant enim aperte; quia etiam sequitur, quod Christus Petrum pastorem instituit, & quod constituit eum priorem auctoritate & dignitate apostolis aliis. Quia per verba illa Christus non constituit aliquem alium pastorem, quam Petrum, sicut aliquibus demonstratiue probatum videtur. & etiam non distinxit inter oues has Christi & illas. ergo etiam super alios apostolos, qui erant oues Christi, constitutus fuit per illa verba beatus Petrus.
units.tr: STUDENT. You have alleged against that point on which the first reply, recited above in chapter 3, seems to rest. So now take up the other things which those men seem to assert in answering, by which they strive to set aside the argument adduced and to clarify their reply. And first begin with what is said: that Christ seemed to speak in such a manner that sometimes he spoke certain words to one person, and yet directed them to the one he was addressing in the person of others. He himself alone bears witness to this, when he said in Matthew 13: What I say to one, I say to all. TEACHER. To some it appears, from what has been said in the preceding chapter, clearly enough, that this has nothing to do with the matter; for it is true that Christ sometimes seemed to speak in such a manner, since at times, in speaking to one, he directed his discourse to others. But this happened only when there was the same reason for teaching one and the others something. This occurs when someone is led to do or not to do something, or to believe or not to believe something, when others are likewise bound to act or not act, believe or not believe in the same way. Thus it is with the one to whom something is said in the singular and universally, where the one addressed and others are, and ought to be, similarly disposed, or bound to be disposed, to what is said. This holds true in the case of those about whom Christ's word had gone before, when he afterwards said in Matthew 13: What I say to you, I say to all: watch. So the apostles were in need, and the other wayfarers are in need, to watch, since they do not know when the Lord will come. But since others are not similarly disposed, or not bound to be similarly disposed, to that of which there is question, then what is said to one is not on that account understood as said to others. For when the Lord said to Peter: Go to the sea and cast a hook, etc., not all the other disciples and apostles who heard this were bound to run to the sea with Peter. Likewise, when Christ said to Peter in John 21: Follow me, he did not want Peter to understand that this was said to others in the same way as to him. Hence, when Peter asked about John: Lord, and what about this man? Jesus answered him: If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me. So I say that what is said to one is not always understood as said to others. Nor does it seem to hold true when something is said to one so that he may be set over another, as was the case in the matter at hand. From the foregoing it appears (as it seems to some) to be false, what the aforesaid men say after reciting the words of Christ and the Gloss: that from this nothing else is proved except that Christ appointed him a minister, but it does not follow from this that he set him above the other apostles in prior authority or dignity. Nor again does it follow from this that the other apostles were not appointed ministers. For they err plainly; because it would also follow that Christ appointed Peter a minister and constituted him prior in authority and dignity to the other apostles. For by those words Christ did not appoint any other minister than Peter, as has seemed demonstratively proved to some. And he did not distinguish between these sheep of Christ and those. Therefore the blessed Peter was also constituted over the other apostles, who were sheep of Christ, by those words.

units.la: Cum autem dicitur, nec rursum sequitur ex hoc alios apostolos non fuisse institutos pastores; non errant, si intelligantur verba, sicut prima facie sonant. quia non obstantibus illis verbis Christi, apostoli fuerunt constituti pastores per alia verba Christi. sed postea per illa verba dicta Petro singulariter: pasce oues meas, subiiciebantur Petro, retenta auctoritate & dignitate aliis apostolis, ante concessa a Christo.
units.tr: When it is said: nor again does it follow from this that the other apostles were not appointed ministers, they do not err, if the words are understood as they sound at first sight. For notwithstanding those words of Christ, the apostles were appointed ministers by other words of Christ. But afterwards, by those words spoken to Peter singly: Feed my sheep, they were made subject to Peter, while their authority and dignity previously granted by Christ to the other apostles was retained.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Ad reliquas tres allegationes pro declaratione praedicta responsionis tertio capitulo factas respondet.
units.tr: He answers the remaining three allegations, made in the third chapter of the reply, in support of the aforesaid explanation.

units.la: DISCIP. Narrasti quomodo improbatur responsio ante scripta: nunc narra, qualiter respondetur ad illa, quae in responsione eadem allegantur ad probandum aequalitatem aliorum apostolorum Petri. MAGIST. Ad evidentiam illarum allegationum, & multarum aliarum. Primo dicitur esse notandum, quod Christus non sic commisit etiam pastoralem Petro super apostolos omnes & cunctos fideles; ut ea, quae ipse fecerat revocandi potestatem absque causa iusta Petro concederet; nec sic ut ab omni regimine & cura apostolorum, & aliorum fidelium (etiam innotescente fidelibus) abstineret; quinimo voluit quod illa, quae fecerat, servarentur. & fidelibus saepe innotuit ipsum post ascensionem suam suum esse vicarium. Et postquam fecit Petrum vicarium suum plura fecisse miraculose, & potestative. Per hoc dicitur ad illud, quod allegatur de praefatione, quae de apostolis legitur & cantatur, quod Christus apostolos in plurali rectores vicarios & pastores constituit; non tamen per verba illa, pasce oves meas, sed per alia: omnes tamen subdidit rectori, vicario & pastori supremo, scilicet Petro: quamvis hoc non dicatur in praefatione illa, sed ex scriptura canonica, quae maioris auctoritatis habetur. Aliter dicitur, quod Deus multa dicitur facere, quae tamen facit mediantibus aliis & ideo cum in praefatione praescripta non dicatur, quod Christus nullo modo mediate constituerit apostolos operis sui vicarios; ex ipsa inferri non potest, quod non constituerit eos mediante Petro. Et per consequens multo minus potest ex ea concludi, quod non constituerit eos rectores vicarios, & pastores sub supremo pastore vicario & rectore, scilicet Petro.
units.tr: DISCIP. You have told how the foregoing reply is refuted; now tell how the arguments that the same reply adduces to prove the equality of the other apostles with Peter are answered. MAGIST. For the clarification of those allegations, and of many others: First, it is said that it must be noted that Christ did not so commit the pastoral office over all the apostles and all the faithful to Peter as to grant him the power of revoking what he himself had done, without just cause; nor so that he would withdraw from all government and care of the apostles and the other faithful (even when it was made known to the faithful); rather, he willed that what he had done should be preserved. And it was often made known to the faithful that he himself, after his ascension, was his vicar; and after he made Peter his vicar, he did many things miraculously and by authority. Hence it is said in reply to what is alleged from the preface, which is read and sung concerning the apostles, that Christ constituted the apostles, in the plural, as rulers, vicars and pastors; yet not by those words, feed my sheep, but by others; nevertheless he placed them all under the ruler, vicar and supreme pastor, namely Peter: although this is not said in that preface, but is drawn from canonical Scripture, which is held to be of greater authority. Otherwise it is said that God is said to do many things which yet he does through others; and therefore, since the aforesaid preface does not say that Christ in no way constituted the apostles as vicars of his work through a mediator, it cannot be inferred from it that he did not constitute them through Peter. And consequently it can much less be concluded from it that he did not constitute them rulers, vicars and pastors under the supreme pastor, vicar and ruler, namely Peter.

units.la: Ad aliam, cum dicitur, quod omnibus Matthaei ultimi indifferenter dictum est, euntes igitur docete omnes gentes: non dixit Petro, vade & alios mitte. Respondetur, quod auctoritas docendi data fuit omnibus apostolis immediate a Christo; nec alii apostoli eam habuerunt a Petro. sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod non fuerint inferiores Petro. Constat enim, quod in potestatibus saecularibus multi inferiores imperatore & rege dignitates obtinent seculares: quas tamen ab isto imperatore aut rege minime habuerunt, sed a praedecessore receperunt. quo tamen non obstante, isto imperatori, aut regi sunt inferiores, & eidem sunt subiecti. Sic etiam praelati inferiores nonnulli veras habent ecclesias & dignitates: & tamen non a superiori superstite, sed a praedecessore instituti fuerunt; nec alia institutione postea indiguerunt. Ergo multo fortius poterant apostoli alii auctoritatem docendi habere a Christo & non a Petro: & tamen esse inferiores beato Petro. Et ideo quamvis per illa verba, quae dixit Iesus apostolis; euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, &c. non possit probari, quod Petrus fuit superior aliis apostolis; tamen ex hoc non sequitur, quod Petrus non fuit superior, sed pau. Quia superioritas eius ex aliis ostenditur, sicut probatum est. quamvis ergo Christus non dixerit Petro vade, & alios mitte, sed quando dixit apostolis; euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, &c. tamen quando dixit sibi; pasce oves meas, implicite dixit, mitte saltem alios; quos non misit specialiter Christus. Quia concedendo siue imponendo sibi curam omnium generalem, iniunxit simul ea, sine quibus eadem cura salubriter geri non potest. Quemadmodum concesso principali, omnia accessoria conceduntur. extra de officio delegatorum, precedente. Non ergo, cum dixit Christus euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, significavit in omnibus auctoritatis aequalitatem, sed solummodo docendi iniunxit officium, quod aequalitatem auctoritatis inter doctores non requirit.
units.tr: As to the other allegation, that what Christ said in the last chapter of Matthew was said indifferently to all: going therefore, teach all nations; he did not say to Peter, go and send the others. The answer is that the authority of teaching was given to all the apostles immediately by Christ; and the other apostles did not receive it from Peter. But it does not follow from this that they were not inferior to Peter. For it is clear that in secular powers many who are inferior to the emperor or king hold secular dignities which they did not in the least receive from that emperor or king, but from a predecessor; yet, notwithstanding this, they are inferior to that emperor or king and are subject to him. So too some inferior prelates have true churches and dignities, and yet they were instituted not by a surviving superior but by a predecessor, and afterwards they needed no further institution. Therefore much more strongly could the other apostles have had the authority of teaching from Christ and not from Peter, and yet be inferior to the blessed Peter. And so, although by those words which Jesus spoke to the apostles, going therefore teach all nations, etc., it cannot be proved that Peter was superior to the other apostles, yet it does not follow from this that Peter was not superior; rather, his superiority is shown from other things, as has been proved. Although, therefore, Christ did not say to Peter, go, and send the others, but said to the apostles, going therefore teach all nations, etc., nevertheless when he said to him, feed my sheep, he implicitly said, at least send others, whom Christ did not send specifically. For in granting or imposing on him the general care of all, he at the same time enjoined those things without which that same care cannot be carried out beneficially. Just as, when the principal thing is granted, all accessory things are granted. Extra, de officio delegatorum, precedente. Therefore, when Christ said going therefore teach all nations, he did not signify equality of authority in all; he only enjoined the duty of teaching, which does not require equality of authority among teachers.

units.la: Ad aliam vero, cum dixit Christus apostolis; nolite vocari rabbi, &c. multipliciter respondetur. uno modo, quod hoc dixit apostolis & aliis antequam aliquem ex eis praeficeret aliis in praelatum. quia hoc dixit ante passionem suam, dum ipse & non alius erat praelatus fidelium. Aliter dicitur, quod Christus verba sua ibidem de supremo & primo rabbi & magistro volebat intelligi, ut scilicet praeter Deum seu Christum nullus primus seu supremus rabbi, pater, & magister fidelium putaretur. Neque enim Christus voluit, ut fidelium quilibet eum qui genuit, ipsum non haberet, pro patre vel ipsum recusaret vocare patrem, sed voluit ut Deum superiorem patre carpali pro patre superiori & principaliori haberet. sic proportionaliter de rabbi & magistro dicendum videtur. Ad cuius evidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod saepe moris est scripturae aliquod negare ab aliquo, cui primo & principalissime, seu anthonomatice non convenit; licet secundario & non principaliter anthonomatice de ipso dicatur. Sic enim dixit apostolis Mat.10. cum autem tradent vos, nolite cogitare, quomodo aut quid loquamini. & post; non enim vos estis, qui loquimini, sed spiritus Patris mei qui loquitur in vobis scilicet primo & principaliter. qui tamen secundario tanquam moti a principali erant qui loquebantur. Sic etiam dixit Christus, ut habetur Lucae 18. nemo bonus nisi solus Deus; scilicet essentialiter & primo: & tamen angeli boni, & beati in coelo atque iusti omnes sunt boni. Sic dicitur in proposito, quod Christus in verbis istis solummodo voluit, quod Deus & Christus principaliter & quasi anthonomatice haberetur pro patre, rabbi & magistro, & nullus alius.
units.tr: As to the other allegation, when Christ said to the apostles: do not be called rabbi, etc., the answer is given in several ways. In one way, that he said this to the apostles and the others before he set any of them over the rest as prelate, because he said it before his passion, while he himself, and no other, was the prelate of the faithful. Otherwise it is said that Christ in those words wished to be understood of the supreme and first rabbi and master, so that apart from God or Christ no one would be thought to be the first or supreme rabbi, father and teacher of the faithful. For Christ did not will that any of the faithful should not have him who begat him as a father, or refuse to call him father; but he willed that they should have God, superior to any carnal father, as the superior and more principal father. In the same way, it seems that the same should be said of rabbi and master. For the clarification of this, it must be known that it is often the custom of Scripture to deny something of someone to whom it does not belong first and most principally, or in the highest sense, although it is said of him secondarily and not principally in the highest sense. Thus he said to the apostles, Matt. 10: but when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what you shall speak; and after: for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you, namely first and principally. Yet those who spoke were secondarily, as moved by the principal. So too Christ said, as is found in Luke 18: no one is good but God alone; namely essentially and first; and yet the good angels, and the blessed in heaven, and all the just are good. So in the present case it is said that Christ in those words willed only that God and Christ should be regarded principally and, as it were, in the highest sense, as father, rabbi and master, and no one else.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: In quo auctoritates in tertia allegatione tertii capituli exponuntur.
units.tr: In which the authorities cited in the third allegation of the third chapter are explained.

units.la: DISCIP. Nunquid potest probari, quod verba illa Christi non debent intelligi, sicut ipsi prædicti opinantes intelligunt. MAG. Videtur quibusdam, quod sic dicunt enim, quod ista allegatio & consimiles sunt similes illi allegationi, in qua se fundant quidam hæretici dicentes, quod nulla ex causa licet iurare propter hoc quod Christus dixit Mat. 5. Ego autem dico vobis, non iurare omnino. Quia sicut illi dixerunt, quod nulli in quocunq; casu licet iurare propter prædictum præceptum Christi: sic isti videntur dicere, quod nullo modo est concedendum Christum instituisse aliquem apostolum superiorem aliis, propter prædicta verba, quibus eis videtur æqualitatem iniungere. Sed sicut non obstantibus Christi verbis præmissis de iuramento licet in casu iurare: ita non obstantibus verbis illis, quibus æqualitatem quandam fidelibus videtur imponere, licet vocari rabbi & magister & pater. Primo igitur ostenditur, quod intellectus, quem prædicti opinantes videntur habere de præfatis verbis Christi, non possit stare. Secundo explicabitur verus & catholicus intellectus illorum verborum, vt nonnullis apparet. Quod igitur Christus non intenderit illis, quibus loquebatur, per illa verba sic æqualitatem iniungere, vt ab eis præsertim pro futuris temporibus omnem superioritatem excluderet, multis apparet modis. Nam Christus dirigebat verba illa non solum ad apostolos, sed etiam ad omnes suos discipulos, imo etiam ad turbas. Sic enim ibidem promittitur: tunc locutus est Iesus ad turbas ad discipulos suos dicens: super cathedram, &c. sed non intendebat ab omnibus, saltem pro futuris temporibus, omnem inæqualitatem & superioritatem excludere. Tunc enim nunquam ex ordinatione Christi aliquis inter fideles fuisset superior aliis. & per consequens Petrus per ordinationem Christi nunquam fuisset superior quibuscunque constitutus à Christo: quod etiam opinantes prædicti negant. Et ita Christus æqualitatem omnimodam auctoritatis nec apostolis nec aliis tunc iniunxit. Amplius si Christus tunc apostolis æqualitatem auctoritatis iniunxit: ergo non licuit apostolis postea contra idem præceptum Christi, nec Petrum nec alium per se superiorem constituere. Quod tamen isti negant, dicentes quod apostoli elegerunt & constituerunt Petrum superiorem se. Imo sequitur, quod nec quibuscunque Christianis liceret aliquem super se eligere superiorem, cum Christus ibidem non ad solos apostolos, sed etiam ad alios discipulos præsentes, & futuros intenderit verba prædicta dirigere, & vtrosq; instruere. Tunc enim poterat Christus dicere illud quod dixit Matth. 13. quod vobis dico omnibus dico. DIS. Forte dicerent isti, quod licet Christus sic apostolis iniunxerit æqualitatem auctoritatis, non tamen interdixit eis, quin ex iusta causa possent postea aliquem super se constituere. MAGIST. Istud quibusdam non placet. nam si Christus non interdixit apostolis, & per consequens nec aliis, quin ex causa iusta posset postea aliquem super se constituere superiorem, multo magis sibi ipsi non imposuit legem, quin postea posset vnum apostolum præferre aliis. Ergo per illa verba, quæ dixit Matth. 13. non potest ostendi, quod postea Christus non prætulit aliis apostolis beatum Petrum: licet posset ostendi, quod per illa verba quæ recitat Matth. 13. non prætulerit eum aliis apostolis. quod conceditur à quibusdam. Rursus, apostoli verba illa Christi sicut prima facie sonant, non seruabant, quia sententialiter, & vocaliter se vocabant & reputauerunt se magistros, & patres & rabbi. Ait n. apostolus 1. Tim. 2. veritatem dico non mentior doctor gentium. Si autem doctor, & magister. Vnde. & 2. Tim. 1. ait: ego prædicator, & apostolus, & magister gentium. Et in eadem epistola vocat Timotheum dilectum filium. Si autem Timotheus fuerit filius, ipse reputauit se patrem. Et eidem scribitca. 5. seniorem ne increpaueris, sed obsecra vt patrem. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod licebat Timotheo vocare seniores, patres. & tamen Christus dixit: Patrem nolite vocare vobis super terram. Et beatus Iohannes. 1. epistola sua ca. 2. ait: scribo vobis filioli. & infra: Et nunc filioli manete in eo. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod licuit illis, quibus scribebat B. Iohannes, vocare eum patrem. Sententialiter ergo apostoli vocauerunt se magistros, & rabbi: quod nequaquam fecissent, si Christus interdixisset eis talibus vocabulis se vocare. quia non dubium est committere in legem, qui tam munterm quam verba legis transgreditur. Nequaquam igitur Christus omnimodam æqualitatem auctoritatis tunc apostolis pro temporibus futuris iniunxit. Oportet ergo alium quam prædictum promissorum verborum Christi quærere intellectum. Ad quorum euidentiam dicitur esse notandum, quod Christus omnia verba illa, nolite vocari rabbi; patrem nolite vobis vocare super terram, nec vocemini magistri, dixit propter Phariseos & Scribas, qui ambitiosi dignitatum erant, & Honorum & vehementes inanis glorie amatores: qui propter huiusmodi omnia opera sua fecerunt. de quibus Saluator dicit ibidem: omnia vero opera sua faciunt, vt videantur ab hominibus. vbi eos de inani gloria aperte notauit. quos etiam de ambitione notauit, cum dixit: Amant autem primos recubitus in cœnis, & primas cathedras in Synagogis, & salutationes in foro, & vocari ab omnibus rabbi. Dicitur igitur, quod cum Christus occasione vitiorum Phariseorum & Scribarum (scilicet inanis glorie, & ambitionis) post præmissa verba de Phariseis & scribis subiunxit: dicit discipulis suis omnibus: Vos autem nolite vocari rabbi, &c. Non æqualitatem auctoritatis discipulis suis iniunxit: neceriam tunc interdixit omnem superioritatem. Sed ipsos volens ad humilitatem inducere, ambitionem & inanem glotiam dissuasit, prohibendo, vel consulendo, ne extra casum necessitatis quæ tatis quæ etiam vtilitatem includit (vt notat Glossa. extra de iureiurando, Etsi Christus) magisterium: imo quamcunque prælationem, & superioritatem; aut maioritatem appeterent, vel etiam nominibus importantibus dignitatem aut superioritatem vocari gestirent. Quod non tantum per præcedentia in eadem serie, sed etiam per sequentia potest patentius declarari. Quia non magis interdixit cuilibet eorum omnem auctoritatem & superioritatem per illas negatiuas: nolite vocari rabbi, nec vocemini magistri: quā interdixerit eis subiectionem, quæ est respectu superiorum auctoritate per verba sequentia, cum dixit: Qui maior est vestrum, erit minister vester. Sed per illa verba noluit indicare, quod maior inter eos deberet esse subiectus aliis prælatis. Ergo per alia verba, scilicet per negatiua, noluit eis omnimodam æqualitatem auctoritatis iniungere: Sed ipsos ad humilitatem contra ambitionem & inanem gloriam incitare, propter quod post omnia verba præscripta subiunxit: Qui autem se exaltauerit humiliabitur.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Can it be proved that those words of Christ should not be understood as the aforesaid opponents understand them? TEACHER. It seems so to some, who say that this allegation and similar ones are like that allegation on which certain heretics rest, who say that it is lawful to swear on no ground at all, because Christ said in Matt. 5, But I say to you, do not swear at all. For just as they said that no one may swear in any case because of that precept of Christ, so these men seem to say that it must in no way be granted that Christ appointed one apostle superior to the others, because of the words cited, by which they seem to impose equality. But just as, notwithstanding Christ's words above about swearing, it is lawful to swear in a case, so, notwithstanding those words by which he seems to impose a certain equality on the faithful, it is lawful to be called rabbi, teacher and father. First, then, it is shown that the meaning which the aforesaid opponents seem to hold of those words of Christ cannot stand. Second, the true and catholic meaning of those words will be explained, as it appears to some. That Christ did not intend, by those words, to impose such equality on those to whom he was speaking, so that he would exclude from them, especially for future times, all superiority, appears in many ways. For Christ directed those words not only to the apostles but also to all his disciples, indeed even to the crowds. For it is promised there: Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, etc. But he did not intend to exclude from all, at least for future times, all inequality and superiority. For then, by Christ's ordinance, no one among the faithful would ever have been superior to others; and consequently Peter, by Christ's ordinance, would never have been superior to whomever was set over him by Christ, which the aforesaid opponents also deny. And so Christ did not then impose on the apostles, nor on others, an entire equality of authority. Moreover, if Christ then imposed on the apostles an equality of authority, then it was not lawful for the apostles afterwards, against the same precept of Christ, to appoint either Peter or anyone else as superior to themselves. Yet these men deny this, saying that the apostles chose and appointed Peter as superior to themselves. Indeed it follows that it would not be lawful for any Christians to choose any superior over themselves, since Christ there intended his words to be directed not only to the apostles but also to the other disciples present and future, and to instruct both. For then Christ could say what he said in Matt. 13, What I say to you, I say to all. DISCIPLE. Perhaps these men would say that although Christ thus imposed equality of authority on the apostles, he did not nevertheless forbid them to appoint someone over themselves afterwards for a just cause. TEACHER. That does not please some. For if Christ did not forbid the apostles, and consequently not others either, from afterwards appointing someone superior over themselves for a just cause, much more did he not impose on himself a law forbidding him to put one apostle before the others afterwards. Therefore by those words which he spoke in Matt. 13 it cannot be shown that Christ did not afterwards set the blessed Peter above the other apostles; although it could be shown that by the words Matt. 13 relates, he did not set him above the other apostles, which some concede. Again, the apostles did not observe those words of Christ as they sound at first sight, for in sentiment and in speech they called themselves and regarded themselves as teachers, fathers and rabbis. For the apostle says in 1 Tim. 2, I speak the truth, I do not lie, a teacher of the Gentiles. And if a teacher, then also a master. Hence in 2 Tim. 1 he says: I am a preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles. And in the same letter he calls Timothy my beloved son. If Timothy was a son, then he regarded himself as a father. And he writes to the same man in 1 Tim. 5, Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father. From these words it is gathered that Timothy was allowed to call elders fathers. And yet Christ said: Call no one your father on earth. And the blessed John, in chapter 2 of his first letter, says: I write to you, little children. And below: And now, little children, abide in him. From these words it is gathered that those to whom the blessed John wrote were allowed to call him father. Therefore the apostles, in sentiment, called themselves teachers and rabbis; which they would by no means have done if Christ had forbidden them to call themselves by such names, for there is no doubt that he who transgresses both the letter and the words of the law sins against the law. Therefore Christ by no means imposed on the apostles then an absolute equality of authority for future times. It is necessary, then, to seek a meaning other than the plain meaning of those promised words of Christ. For the clearer understanding of this it is said that we must note that Christ spoke all those words, Do not be called rabbi; call no one your father on earth; nor be called teachers, because of the Pharisees and scribes, who were ambitious for dignities, lovers of honours and vehement lovers of empty glory, and who for such reasons did all their works, of whom the Saviour says in the same place: But they do all their works to be seen by men. There he openly noted them for empty glory; and he also noted them for ambition when he said: And they love the best places at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplaces, and to be called rabbi by men. It is said, therefore, that when Christ, on account of the vices of the Pharisees and scribes (namely empty glory and ambition), after the words above concerning the Pharisees and scribes, added: he says to all his disciples: But you, do not be called rabbi, etc., he did not impose on his disciples equality of authority; nor did he then forbid every superiority. Rather, wishing to lead them to humility, he dissuaded them from ambition and empty glory, forbidding or advising them that, outside the case of necessity (which also includes usefulness, as the Gloss notes, extra de iureiurando, Etsi Christus), they should not desire the office of teacher, or indeed any precedence, superiority or greater rank, nor long to be called by names implying dignity or superiority. This can be made clearer not only from what precedes in the same series, but also from what follows. For by those negative words, do not be called rabbi, nor be called teachers, he did not forbid each of them all authority and superiority any more than he forbade them subjection to superiors, which he does by the words that follow, when he said: Whoever is greatest among you shall be your minister. But by those words he did not mean to indicate that the greatest among them ought to be subject to the other prelates. Therefore by the other words, namely the negative ones, he did not wish to impose on them an absolute equality of authority, but to urge them to humility against ambition and empty glory; on account of which, after all the words written above, he added: But whoever exalts himself will be humbled.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Vbi impugnatur secunda responsio tertio capitulo posita.
units.tr: Where the second answer, set out in the third chapter, is refuted.

units.la: DISCIP. Discute secundam responsionem, quam sæpe dicti afferunt opinantes. MAG. Illa responsio consistit in hoc quod per illa verba, pasce oues meas, specialiter beato Petro propter sui constantiam commissus fuit populus Israel, qui duræ ceruicis fuit versus Deum.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Examine the second answer, which the aforementioned writers put forward. TEACHER. That answer rests on this: that by the words Feed my sheep, the people of Israel was committed specially to the blessed Peter because of his steadfastness, the people who were stiff-necked toward God.

units.la: Sed nonnullis videtur, quod hæc responsio oppositum illius, quod tenet, patenter concludit. Nam si per illa verba, pasce oues meas: commissa fuit Petro cura populi Israel. Et Christus in illis verbis inter has oues & illas de populo Israel non distinxit: nec aliquas oues excepit: ergo omnium ouium Israel fuit cura commissa beato Petro. Inter oues autem Israel præcipue fuerunt apostoli: ergo per illa verba fuit commissa cura reliquorum apostolorum beato Petro.
units.tr: But some think this answer plainly contradicts the position it defends. For if by the words Feed my sheep the care of the people of Israel was committed to Peter, and Christ in those words did not distinguish these sheep from those of the people of Israel, nor except any sheep, then the care of all the sheep of Israel was committed to the blessed Peter. Now among the sheep of Israel the apostles were especially prominent. Therefore by those words the care of the remaining apostles was committed to Peter.

units.la: DIS. Forte responderent opinantes prædicti, quod licet Christus in illis verbis. pasce oues meas, non distinxerit inter has oues & illas, nec aliquas tunc exceperit: tamen alibi distinxit, & aliquas (scilicet apostolos) manifeste excepit. Tunc enim videtur apostolos excepisse, quando eos misit sicut Petrum, & eandem potestatem dedit eis, quam dedit Petro, cum dixit omnibus, vt habetur Matth. 18. Quæcunque alligaueritis super terram, &c. Et tamen dixit eis, vt habetur Io. 20. Sicut misit me pater, & ego mitto vos. Accipite spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, & quorum retinueritis retenta sunt. Et cum omnibus dixit Math. vlt. Euntes docete omnes gentes baptizantes eos, in nomine Patris, &c. Et cum omnibus dixit, vt legitur Mat. vlt. Euntes in mundum universum prædicate euangelium omni creaturæ, qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit, &c. In omnibus his videtur Christus apostolos ab aliis fidelibus omnibus distinxisse, & eos à potestate Petri penitus exemisse. Quia cum verba illa, pasce, &c. dicta a Petro fuerint generalia: & generale derogat speciali, extra de restitutis. 1. Sequitur quod illis verbis generalibus dictis Petro derogatum est specialiter quoad apostolos, quibus Christus dedit specialiter potestatem eandem, quam Petro, sicut per prædicta patet vt videtur. MAGIST. Hæc responsio impugnatur, quod licet Christus dederit apostolis aliquam potestatem specialem, nunquam tamen concessit eis potestatem generalem vel æqualem potestati Petri. verbo enim generaliori vsus est in præficiendo Petrum, scilicet verbo pascendi: quod communius est, quam verbum docendi, vel baptizandi, aut aliud tale. Quibus verbis vsus est in concedendo potestatem in aliis apostolis: Et ideo quamuis aliquando distinxerit Christus inter apostolos & alias oues suas; ac ipsos quoad aliquid exemerit aliquomodo à potestate Petri; tamen quando dixit Petro: pasce, &c. ipsum præficiendo omnibus non distinxit inter ipsos & alios. Et ideo ipsos non exemit nec manere exemptos voluit seu liberos à potestate Petri; nisi quantum ad illa, quæ expressit in concedendo eis potestatem specialem. Propterea non fuerunt exempti à potestate Petri, nisi quantum ad officium prædicationis, baptizandi, ligandi & soluendi à peccatis. Et si qua alia Christus expressit, quando eis contulit aliquam potestatem. Cum ergo dicis, quod mandatum speciale derogat generali; conceditur, quantum ad ista, quæ exprimuntur in speciali mandato, non quantum ad alia.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Perhaps the aforementioned writers would reply that although Christ, in the words Feed my sheep, did not distinguish these sheep from those, nor except any then, he did distinguish them elsewhere and expressly excepted some (namely the apostles). For he seems to have excepted the apostles when he sent them as he sent Peter, and gave them the same power he gave Peter, when he said to all of them, as is found in Matth. 18: Whatsoever you shall bind upon earth, etc. And yet he said to them, as is found in John 20: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them, and whose you retain, they are retained. And he said to all of them in Matth. last: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, etc. And he said to all of them, as is read in Matth. last: Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature; he who believes and is baptized shall be saved, etc. In all these passages Christ seems to have distinguished the apostles from all the other faithful and wholly exempted them from the power of Peter. For since the words feed, etc. spoken to Peter were general, and a general law derogates from a special one (extra de restitutis, 1), it follows that by those general words spoken to Peter, what Christ specially gave the apostles, the same power as to Peter, is derogated from specially, as is evident from what has been said. TEACHER. This answer is refuted: although Christ gave the apostles some special power, he never granted them a power general or equal to the power of Peter. For in setting Peter over the others he used a more general word, namely the verb "to feed," which is more common than the verb "to teach," or "to baptize," or any other such word. He used these words when granting power to the other apostles. And so, although Christ at times distinguished between the apostles and his other sheep, and in some respects exempted them in some way from the power of Peter, nevertheless when he said to Peter feed, etc., in setting him over all, he did not distinguish between him and the others. Therefore he did not exempt them, nor did he will them to remain exempt or free from the power of Peter, except as to those things which he expressed in granting them a special power. Accordingly they were not exempt from the power of Peter except as to the office of preaching, baptizing, binding and loosing from sins, and whatever else Christ expressed when he conferred some power on them. So when you say that a special command derogates from a general one, this is granted as to those things expressed in the special command, but not as to others.

units.la: Et ideo mandatum datum apostolis de baptizando, prædicando, docendo, soluendo & ligando derogabat mandato illi dato Petro: pasce oues meas, quantum ad illa solummodo, quæ Christus iniunxit apostolis. Et tamen non in casu omni. quia si huiusmodi excessissent, ratione delicti, etiam quoad illa fuissent subiecti Petro; quia exempti ratione delicti sortiuntur forum & priuilegium meretur amittere, qui permissa sibi abutitur potestate, extra de regularibus cap. licet. & 11. q. 3. priuilegium.
units.tr: And so the command given to the apostles about baptizing, preaching, teaching, loosing and binding derogated from the command given to Peter, Feed my sheep, only as to those things which Christ enjoined on the apostles. And even then not in every case: for if they had exceeded these powers by reason of fault, they would have been subject to Peter even in those matters, since those who abuse the power granted them, by reason of their offence, are exempt only so long as they hold the privilege, and they deserve to lose it (extra de regularibus, cap. licet; and 11 q. 3, priuilegium).

units.la: DISCIP. Ista impugnatio contra veritatem militare videtur; quia apostoli non solummodo fuerunt prædicatores & doctores habentes potestatem baptizandi, ligandi & soluendi; sed etiam fuerunt à Deo constituti pastores, teste apostolo ad Eph. 3. Vbi loquens de Christo ait; Et ipse dedit quosdam quidem apostolos, quosdam autem prophetas, alios autem euangelistas, & alios pastores & doctores. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Christus ita constituit alios apostolos pastores, sicut Petrum; & per consequens vocaliter seu sententialiter ita dixit cui iberi alii apostolo: Pasce oues meas, sicut Petro. Ex quo concluditur, quod omnem potestatem importatam per verbum pascenpascendi dedit aliis, sicut Petro, quia talem protestatem nullis magis dedit, quam apostolis: Ergo apostoli eandem auctoritatem habuerunt in omnibus cum Petro.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. This objection seems to run counter to the truth. For the apostles were not only preachers and teachers having the power of baptizing, binding and loosing; they were also appointed by God as ministers, as the apostle witnesses in Eph. 3, where, speaking of Christ, he says: And he gave some apostles, and some prophets, and others evangelists, and others ministers and teachers. From these words it is gathered that Christ appointed the other apostles as ministers just as he did Peter; and consequently he said to each of the other apostles, by word or sentence, Feed my sheep, just as to Peter. From this it follows that he gave the others all the power implied by the verb "to feed," just as to Peter, since he gave such power to no one more than to the apostles. Therefore the apostles had the same authority as Peter in all things.

units.la: MAGISTER. Huic obiectioni tuae respondetur, quod Christus, qui etiam nunc ecclesiam non desinit invisibiliter gubernare, secundum apostolum quosdam mediante Petro constituit pastores. Nec apostolus dicit, quod Christus dedit absque ministerio Petri quosdam pastores; sed quod dedit pastores, quia dedit eos mediante ministerio et auctoritate Petri. quod verum est.
units.tr: TEACHER. To this objection of yours the answer is that Christ, who even now does not cease to govern the Church invisibly, according to the apostle appointed some ministers through the mediation of Peter. Nor does the apostle say that Christ gave some ministers without the ministry of Peter; he says that he gave ministers because he gave them through the ministry and authority of Peter. That is true.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad auctoritates ex apostolo et Glossa adductas supra capitulo tertio huius.
units.tr: In which the authorities from the Apostle and the Gloss, cited above in the third chapter of this part, are answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic nunc breviter, quomodo respondetur ad auctoritatem apostoli et Glossae, quae adducuntur ad probandum aequalitatem specialiter beati Pauli ad Petrum.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Now briefly tell me how the authority of the Apostle and of the Gloss, which are cited to prove that blessed Paul was specially equal to Peter, is answered.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad omnes illas auctoritates respondetur per ea, quae dicta sunt prius; quia licet alii apostoli a beato Petro non fuerint constituti a Christo pastores universalis ecclesiae: nec super universalem ecclesiam habuerint potestatem eandem, quam habuit Petrus: tamen beatus Paulus officium praedicationis habuit immediate a Christo, quod officium, antequam vidisset ipsum, vel Petrus sciret ipsum fuisse conversum; exercuit: quia de ipso scribitur Act. 9. Surgens baptizatus est. Et cum accepisset cibum, confortatus est. Fuit autem cum discipulis, qui erant Damasci, per dies aliquot. Et quod continuo ingressus Paulus in synagogis praedicabat Iesum, quoniam hic est filius Dei; et quod tunc nullam auctoritatem habuerit praedicandi a Petro, videtur per illa, quae legquuntur; cum dicitur: Cum autem venisset in Hierusalem, temptabat iungere se discipulis. Et omnes timebant eum, non credentes quod esset discipulus. Barnabas autem apprehensum illum duxit ad apostolos, et narravit illis quomodo in via vidisset dominum. Et quia locutus est ei, et quomodo in Damasco fiducialiter egerit in nomine Iesu. Quod autem dixit apostolus, sibi creditum esse euangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis. Dicunt quidam, hoc non esse dictum ab apostolo, quia Paulus fuerit tantum doctor et praedicator gentium, Petrus solummodo Iudaeorum: cum hoc scripturae canonicae repugnare apertissime videatur.
units.tr: MASTER. All those authorities are answered by what has been said before. Although the other apostles were not appointed by Christ as shepherds of the universal Church by blessed Peter, and did not have the same power over the universal Church that Peter had, nevertheless blessed Paul received the office of preaching immediately from Christ, and he exercised that office before he had seen Peter, or Peter knew that he had been converted. For it is written of him in Acts 9: Rising, he was baptized. And when he had taken food, he was strengthened. And he was with the disciples who were at Damascus for some days. That Paul at once entered the synagogues and preached Jesus, that this is the Son of God, and that he then had no authority to preach from Peter, appears from what is read when it says: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples. And all feared him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took hold of him and led him to the apostles, and told them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had acted boldly in the name of Jesus. As for what the Apostle said, that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed to him, just as the gospel of the circumcision was to Peter, some say that this was not said by the Apostle, because Paul was only a teacher and preacher to the Gentiles, and Peter only to the Jews; yet this seems most plainly to contradict the canonical Scripture.

units.la: Verumque enim auctoritatem et potestatem habuit praedicandi tam praeputio quam circumcisioni: hoc est tam gentibus quam Iudaeis. Et aliquando utrumque praedicavit veritatemque. Et de Paulo quidem manifeste patet Act. 9. 7. 13. et 14. quod praedicavit Iudaeis. Quod autem fuerit etiam doctor gentium, ipse in epistolis suis asserit. quod etiam de ipso apostolica testatur historia. De Petro etiam patet idem, praedicavit enim Iudaeis, ut ex multis locis liquet; qui gentibus scilicet Cornelio et aliis, sicut patet Act. 10. praedicavit. Sed ideo dicit apostolus sibi creditum esse euangelium praeputii, et Petro circumcisionis; quia Paulus magis erat intentus conversioni gentium, et Petrus Iudaeorum. Ita ut saepe et in diversis provinciis praedicaverit duntaxat Iudaeis, teste Eusebio in Ecclesiastica historia, qui lib. 3. ca. 2. air: Petrus Pontum et Galatiam, Bithyniam, Cappadociam, catera, sed confines provincias, Iudaeis duntaxat praedicans, circumcisse deprehenditur. Et tamen biblicebat gentibus praedicare, quemadmodum Paulo fuit licitum praedicare Iudaeis. Quod Glossa, quam praedicti opinantes in responsione nunc tractata adducunt, asserit manifeste dicens: Ita tamen dispensatio distributa est illis, ut etiam Petrus gentibus praedicaret, si causa exegisset, et Paulus Iudaeis. Quod etiam ex Ecclesiastica historia asserente, quod Petrus et Paulus Romanam fundaverunt ecclesiam (sicut post dicetur) colligitur evidenter.
units.tr: Indeed, both Paul and Peter had authority and power to preach to the uncircumcision as well as to the circumcision, that is, to Gentiles as well as to Jews; and each at times preached both, and the truth of this is clear. Concerning Paul it is plainly evident from Acts 9, 7, 13 and 14 that he preached to the Jews. That he was also a teacher of the Gentiles he himself asserts in his letters, and apostolic history bears witness to this about him too. The same is evident concerning Peter, for he preached to the Jews, as is clear from many places; and he also preached to the Gentiles, such as Cornelius and others, as is shown in Acts 10. But the Apostle says that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed to him, and the gospel of the circumcision to Peter, because Paul was more intent on the conversion of the Gentiles, and Peter on that of the Jews; so that Peter often, and in various provinces, preached only to the Jews, as Eusebius witnesses in his Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 2, who says: Peter is found to have preached only to the Jews in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and the other neighbouring provinces. Yet it was lawful for him to preach to the Gentiles, just as it was lawful for Paul to preach to the Jews. The Gloss, which the aforementioned opponents cite in the answer now under discussion, states this plainly, saying: Yet the dispensation was so distributed to them that Peter also would preach to the Gentiles if the case required it, and Paul to the Jews. This is also evidently gathered from Ecclesiastical History, which asserts that Peter and Paul founded the Church of Rome (as will be said later).

units.la: Cum autem dicit Glossa illa, euangelium praeputii ita principaliter esse creditum Paulo, sicut euangelium circumcisionis Petro. Respondetur, quod hoc dicit Glossa propter hoc, quod Christus immediate tradidit Paulo officium praedicandi, et sine Petro; ita quod officium praedicandi non habuit a Petro, et tamen Paulus quodammodo erat subiectus Petro etiam quantum ad praedicationis officium; quia si in officio sibi a Christo commisso excessisset, fuisset corrigendus a Petro.
units.tr: As for what that Gloss says, that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed principally to Paul in the same way as the gospel of the circumcision was to Peter: it is answered that the Gloss says this because Christ gave Paul the office of preaching immediately, and without Peter; so that he did not have the office of preaching from Peter; and yet Paul was in some measure subject to Peter even as regards the office of preaching, because if he had exceeded the office committed to him by Christ, he would have been corrected by Peter.

units.la: Cum autem accipitur in ratione praefata, quod nec Paulus nec alter sanctus potuerit alias assumere, populum Iudaicum specialiter et principaliter fuisse Petro commissum; nisi ex eo, quod Christus illi dixit: pasce oves meas. Respondetur, quod Paulus plura dixit de Christo et apostolis, quae ex canonicis novi testamenti scripturis non accepit. Dixit enim 1. Cor. 15. deinde visus est (scilicet Christus) plusquam quingentis simul. Et ut legitur Act. 20. Beatus est magis dare quam accipere. Et tamen ista in scripturis novi testamenti prioribus non habentur. Sic etiam potuit dicere de beato Petro, tanquam ille qui gestorum Petri pro magna parte habebat notitiam, quod sibi erat creditum euangelium circumcisionis, quamvis nec ex illo verbo Pasce oves meas, nec ex aliquo alio, quod aliquis acceperit, antequam scripserit.
units.tr: As for what is adduced in the aforesaid argument, that neither Paul nor any other saint could have assumed otherwise that the Jewish people had been committed specially and principally to Peter, except from the fact that Christ said to him: Feed my sheep. It is answered that Paul said many things about Christ and the apostles which he did not receive from the canonical Scriptures of the New Testament. For he said in 1 Corinthians 15: Then he was seen (namely Christ) by more than five hundred at once. And as is read in Acts 20: It is more blessed to give than to receive. Yet these things are not found in the earlier Scriptures of the New Testament. So too he could say of blessed Peter, as one who had for the most part knowledge of Peter's deeds, that the gospel of the circumcision had been committed to him, although not from that word Feed my sheep, nor from anything else which anyone had received before he wrote.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Vbi iterum pertractantur verba Christi quae dixit ad Petrum, Pasce oves meas.
units.tr: Where the words of Christ spoken to Peter, "Feed my sheep," are again examined.

units.la: DISCIP. Quia, sicut antea dixi, multi vel omnes tenentes Christum constituisse beatum Petrum caput & principem aliorum apostolorum: per illa verba Christi, pasce oues meas, hoc principaliter probare conantur. Ideo illa verba volo adhuc amplius discuti, vt melius intelligam veritatem eorum. Videtur igitur primo, quod (sicut alii innuunt) per illa verba probari non potest, quod beatus Petrus fuerit constitutus princeps & praelatus quorumcunque. Quia verbis & exemplis & etiam subsidio corporali potest quis pascere alios, quamuis super eos nullam habeat auctoritatem omnino, ergo per hoc, quod dixit Christus Petro, Pasce, &c. nullam ei auctoritatem super alios pascendo commisit omnino.
units.tr: STUDENT. Since, as I said before, many, or indeed all, who hold that Christ made the blessed Peter the head and prince of the other apostles, try chiefly to prove this from those words of Christ, "Feed my sheep." So I want those words discussed still further, so that I may better understand their truth. It seems, then, first (as others also suggest) that it cannot be proved from these words that the blessed Peter was appointed prince and prelate over anyone at all. For a person can feed others by words, by examples, and even by bodily help, although he has no authority at all over them. Therefore, by Christ's saying to Peter, "Feed," and so on, He did not entrust him at all with any authority over others by the act of feeding.

units.la: MAGIST. Videtur quampluribus, quod ista responsio minime satisfacit. Nam sicut in concessione beneficii, priuilegii, concessio indefinite & simpliciter facta, intelligitur generaliter, extra, de priuil. Quia circa. Sic etiam commissio potestatis vel officii indefinite & simpliciter facta, debet intelligi vniuersaliter, vt scilicet omnia intelligantur esse concessa seu commissa, quae non sunt prohibita, & de quibus est eadem committendi vel concedendi ratio, & de quibus non est verisimile seu probabile, quod committens seu concedens ea in speciali commisisset minime seu concessisset. Quia qui nihil excipit, & potuit excipere, totum concessisse seu commisisse videtur, vt sacri canones protestantur.
units.tr: TEACHER. It seems to many that this answer by no means satisfies. For just as in the granting of a benefice or privilege, a grant made indefinitely and simply is understood generally (Extra, De privilegiis, Quia circa), so too a commission of power or office made indefinitely and simply ought to be understood universally: namely, that everything is understood to be granted or committed which is not forbidden, and concerning which there is the same reason for committing or granting, and concerning which it is not likely or probable that the one committing or granting would have committed or granted it specifically. For one who excepts nothing, when he could have excepted, is seen to have granted or committed the whole, as the sacred canons declare.

units.la: Sed Christus in verbis illis: Pasce oues meas: aliquid importatum per verbum pascendi commisit beato Petro, & iniunxit. Ista autem commissio seu iniunctio indefinite & simpliciter facta fuit. Ergo omnia intelliguntur esse commissa, quae non inueniuntur prohibita, & de quibus est eadem ratio committendi. de quibus non est verisimile seu probabile, quod ipsa committens in speciali minime commisisset.
units.tr: But Christ, in those words, "Feed my sheep," committed to the blessed Peter and enjoined something implied by the word "feeding." Now this commission or injunction was made indefinitely and simply. Therefore everything is understood to have been committed which is not found forbidden, and concerning which there is the same reason for committing, and concerning which it is not likely or probable that the one committing would have committed it specifically.

units.la: Sed per verbum pascendi non solum importatur pascere alios verbo & exemplo, ac subsidio corporali: sed etiam potestatiue & cum auctoritate, praesertim secundum quod verbum pascendi in scripturis sacris & expositionibus sanctorum patrum accipitur. Quod copiose posset ostendi, sed sufficiat pauca adducere. Ait itaque Ezechiel, imo Dominus per Ezechielem prophetam 34. ca. dicens: Ve pastoribus Israel, qui pascebant semetipsos. & post: quod infirmum fuit non consolidastis, & quod aegrum non sanastis, quod confractum non alligastis, & quod abiectum est non reduxistis, quod perierat non quaesistis. Errantes autem oues quaerere, & reportare inuentas, spectat ad potestatem habentem super oues.
units.tr: But by the word "feeding" is implied not only feeding others by word, example, and bodily help, but also feeding with power and authority, especially as the word "feeding" is taken in the sacred Scriptures and in the expositions of the holy Fathers. This could be shown at length, but it is enough to bring forward a few points. Ezekiel says, indeed the Lord through the prophet Ezekiel in chapter 34, saying: "Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who feed themselves... and after: The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the broken you have not bound up, the outcast you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought." But to seek the straying sheep and bring back those found belongs to one who has power over the sheep.

units.la: Et veritas ipsa, vt habetur Ioh. 10. ait: Qui autem intrat per hostium pastor est ouium. huic enim ostiarius aperit, & oues vocem eius audiunt, & proprias oues vocat nominatim & educit eas. & cum proprias oues emiserit, ante eas vadit, & oues illum sequuntur. Ex quibus verbis Christi aliis, quae sequuntur, colligitur, quod pastor fidelium Christi pastori suo impari, quantum ad officium, assimilatur. Sed ille ex officio aliquam habet superioritatem & potestatem super oues domini sui. Ergo etiam pastor ouium Christi, quasi fideles, ex officio potestatem & auctoritatem habet super eosdem.
units.tr: And the Truth itself, as is found in John 10, says: "But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. And when he has put forth his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him." From these words of Christ, and from what follows, it is gathered that the shepherd of Christ's faithful is likened, as to office, to his own shepherd, Christ. But that one, by his office, has some superiority and power over the sheep of his Lord. Therefore the shepherd of Christ's sheep, that is, of the faithful, also has power and authority over the same by his office.

units.la: Quod in expositionibus & assertionibus sanctorum patrum tam patenter & euidenter inuenitur, quod hoc probare per ipsos videtur omnino superfluum. Ergo Christus sibi per verba illa: pasce oues meas, aliquam potestatem super oues suas beato Petro commisit: praesertim cum non inueniatur prohibuisse sibi omnem penitus potestatem & auctoritatem. Fuit etiam eadem ratio concedendi sibi auctoritatem aliquam, & potestatem super omnes, & committendi sibi pascere oues Christi, bonis verbis & exemplis. Quia ita indigebant rectore & potestatem habente super ipsas, sicut indigebant pastore, qui aedificando bonis verbis & exemplis Christi oues pauisset. Et ideo non est verisimile, nec probabile, quod talem potestatem sibi in speciali minime concessisset. Ex quibus relinquitur, quod Christus aliquam potestatem concessit per illa verba, & commisit beato Petro.
units.tr: This is found so openly and evidently in the expositions and assertions of the holy Fathers that to prove it by them seems entirely superfluous. Therefore Christ, by those words, "Feed my sheep," committed to the blessed Peter some power over his sheep, especially since He is not found to have forbidden him altogether any power or authority. There was also the same reason for granting him some authority and power over all, and for entrusting him to feed the sheep of Christ with good words and examples. For they needed a ruler having power over them just as they needed a shepherd who would nourish them by building them up with the good words and examples of Christ. And so it is not likely or probable that He would not have granted him such power specifically. From which it follows that Christ granted some power by those words and committed it to the blessed Peter.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: In quo iterum pertractantur verba eadem in praecedenti capitulo improbata.
units.tr: In which the same words, rejected in the preceding chapter, are again examined.

units.la: DISCIP. Hic possem allegando ex dictis infirmare, quod Christus omnem etiam potestatem ac plenitudinem potestatis (talem, qualem Papae attribuit prima sententia primo huius 1. c. recitata, super oues suas) commisit Petro, ex quo illa commissio indefinite & simpliciter facta est: sed de hoc postea coferam tecum. Ideo ad aliam allegationem ad probandum, quod per illa verba: Pasce, &c. Christus non constituit Petrum superiorem aliis apostolis, me conuerto. Videtur itaque, quod saepe indefinita non aequipollet vniuersali, sed potest verificari etiam pro vno singulari. Cum ergo Christus indefinite dixerit, pasce, &c. hoc potest intelligi de aliquibus ouibus etiam absque hoc, quod intelligatur de omnibus. & per consequens absque hoc, quod intelligatur de apostolis. Non ergo per illa verba potest ostendi, quod B. Petrus fuit superior reliquis apostolis.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Here I could, by citing the sayings above, weaken the claim that Christ committed to Peter every power, even the fullness of power (such as the first opinion, cited at the beginning of the previous chapter, attributes to the Pope), over his sheep; but I will discuss this with you later. So I turn to another argument, to prove that by those words, "Feed," etc., Christ did not make Peter superior to the other apostles. It seems, then, that an indefinite statement is not equivalent to a universal one, but may be true even of a single individual. Since Christ therefore said indefinitely, "Feed," etc., this can be understood of some sheep without its being understood of all, and consequently without its being understood of the apostles. Therefore it cannot be shown by those words that Blessed Peter was superior to the other apostles.

units.la: MAG. Putant quidam, quod huic allegationi potest facilius respondere, nam licet tam in iudicatis quàm in aliis non semper verbum indefinite prolatum generaliter debet intelligi; tamen quando alicui committitur potestas super aliquos, verbum indefinite prolatum generaliter debet intelligi, ut nullus tunc intelligatur exceptus, nisi per alia possit probari exceptus. Cuius ratio assignatur. quia sicut iudices non debent esse incerti, quia de similibus simile iudicium est habendum. Ergo quando committitur potestas seu praelatio alicui super aliquos, prolatum tantum indefinite debet intelligi: quemadmodum nec procuratores nec tutores, nec arbitri, sicut testantur leges tam canonicae quàm civiles, & ratio hoc suadet: ita & praelati & subditi non debent esse incerti, imo omnes quibus idem est commune, debent intelligi: nisi aliunde possit ostendi, quod aliqui sint excipiendi. Aliter enim subditi in illo casu essent incerti. ergo per illa verba; pasce oues meas, omnes fideles Christi debent intelligi: ne oues pascendae a Petro sint incertae, nisi de aliquibus aliunde ostendatur, quod sint exceptae. Quod de apostolis ostendi non potest: sicut dicunt multi respondentes ad omnes allegationes, quibus ostenditur, quod apostoli erant a potestate Petri exempti.
units.tr: MASTER. Some think that this argument can be answered more easily. For although, both in judgments and in other matters, a word spoken indefinitely does not always have to be understood generally, nevertheless when power over certain people is committed to someone, a word spoken indefinitely must be understood generally, so that no one is then understood to be excepted unless it can be proved from other evidence that he is excepted. The reason for this is given: just as judges ought not to be uncertain, since like cases must be judged alike, so when power or pre-eminence is committed to someone over certain people, what is spoken only indefinitely must be understood universally, as is the case also with procurators, guardians and arbiters, as both canon and civil laws attest, and reason persuades: so too prelates and subjects ought not to be uncertain, but all to whom the same thing is common must be understood, unless it can be shown from elsewhere that some are to be excepted. Otherwise the subjects would in that case be uncertain. Therefore by the words "Feed my sheep" all the faithful of Christ must be understood, lest the sheep to be fed by Peter be uncertain, unless it is shown from elsewhere that some are excepted. This cannot be shown of the apostles, as many answering all the arguments, by which it is shown that the apostles were exempt from the power of Peter, rightly say.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Principatum Petri super alios probat per haec verba, tu es Petrus & super hanc &c. cuius contrarium arguitur auctoritatibus & rationibus, ad quas respondetur capitulo 18. 19. & 20.
units.tr: He proves Peter's primacy over the others from these words, "You are Peter, and upon this rock…" etc. The contrary is argued from authorities and reasons, to which replies are given in chapters 18, 19 and 20.

units.la: DISCIP. Allegationem, qua probatur, quod Petrus fuit superior ceteris apostolis per hoc quod Christus sibi dixit, pasce oves meas, diffuse tractauimus, ideo ad allegationem aliam pro assertione eadem te conuerte. MAGISTER. Hoc tali modo probatur. Christus singulariter dixit Petro: Ego dico tibi, quia tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam, & portae inferi non praevalebunt aduersus eam & tibi dabo claues regni caelorum, &c. Per quae verba Christus expresse videtur pronunciasse beatum Petrum futurum caput & fundamentum ecclesiae praesertim mortuo Christo. DISCIP. Quidam praecedens motivum nituntur repellere, etiam ad hoc tali modo respondent dicentes: caput & fundamentum ecclesiae unicum esse & fuisse ordinatione immediata Dei: & hoc Christum: apostolorum vero neminem etiam in absentia Christi. quemadmodum per scripturam indubie, ut dicunt, concurrunt, prout recitatum est supra primo huius ca. 3. Cum igitur dicitur, super hanc petram, &c. dicunt secundum Glo. & asserunt, super hanc petram, id est super Christum, in quem credis. vbi Glossa nihil addit. Tu es Petrus, id est a me petra, ita ut mihi retineam fundamenti dignitatem. Petrum autem vocauit Christus, id est constantem in fide. Quod isti non negant, qui & dicunt, quod esto quod aliis constantior fuerit, & merito perfectior: non propter hoc dignitate prior, nisi forte tempore. Quod confirmatur per Augustinum dicentem in libro Retractationum: dixi in quodam loco de apostolo Petro, quod in illo tanquam in petra aedificata sit ecclesia. Sed scio me postea saepissime sic exposuisse, quia a domino dictum est, tu es Petrus & super hanc Petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Et super hunc intelligeretur, quem confessus est Petrus dicens: tu es Christus filius Dei viui: ac sic Petrus ab hac petra appellatus, personam ecclesiae figuraret, quae super hanc petram aedificatur. non enim dictum est illi: tu es petra. sed tu es Petrus. Petra autem erat Christus, quem confessus est Simon. sicut enim Christo scilicet tota ecclesia confitetur, dictus est. Petrus Et potest de hoc ratio assignari secundum scripturas. quoniam Petrus, quamdiu viator existit, errare potuit & peccare per sui arbitrii libertatem: unde Christum negasse legitur, & quandoque ad veritatem euangelii ambulasse non recte. talis autem non poterat esse fundamentum ecclesiae. Sed ille solus fuit Christus, ut apparet. 1. Cor. 3. qui aberrare non potest eo quod ab instanti suae conceptionis etiam fuerit confirmatus. Unde apostolus vbi supra: Fundamentum autem aliud nemo ponere potest praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Et quod addebatur. tibi dabo claues regni caelorum: nullam Petro super reliquos apostolos auctoritatem tribuit. Quoniam hanc eandem iudiciariam potestatem ceteris apostolis tribuit secundum Hieronymum & Rabanum, quorum Glossas alibi inducunt. Amplius Christus potestatem clavium illi non videtur tradidisse per haec verba. inquit enim: tibi dabo, quod sonat futurum, non dixit do. Sed Ioh. 20. indifferenter omnibus dixit: Accipite Spiritum sanctum & quorum remiseritis peccata, &c. Esto tamen, quod Petrus his verbis potestatem hanc recepisset: non concluditur ex hoc, nisi quod tempore prius fuerit pastor institutus. Et ideo illi singulariter has tradidit Christus claues, significare voluit ecclesiae unitatem in fide, ad quam fideles inuitauit Christus per singulare clauium traditionem siue promissionem, ut Glossa dicit. Vel fortasse quia Christum Dei filium esse, primum constanter & manifeste confessus est: primum tempore dotatur clauibus & honoratur, aut honorari permittitur, ut sic etiam confitendi Christum palam & constanter per huiusmodi praemium vel promissum ceteris praeberetur exemplum. Non tamen propter hoc concluditur ipsum fuisse ceteris dignitate seu auctoritate priorem, quamuis hoc plures Glossatorum dicere videantur a se, non habentes hoc a scriptura. Significat autem infallibiliter (vt dicunt) eos verum dicere, quae habetur. Matth. 20. & Luc. 22. vbi Christus quaesitum hoc aperte diffiniens dixit, nullum esse ipsorum superiorem aliis. Facta enim erat contentio inter eos quis eorum esset maior, & idem habetur Mat. 23. ad quos sic inquit Christus, vos autem (inuicem supple) nolite vocari rabbi. vnus enim est magister vester. vos autem omnes fratres estis, id est aequales. non ergo excedit aliquem. Et est ridiculum, quod magis credere debeamus auctoritati Glossae, quam Christi, quicumque fuerit ille Glossator, etiam sanctus, & maxime cum hoc non dicat tanquam Glossator, sed proprio sensu. Series enim scripturæ tam manifesta est, quod Glossa non eget. Amplius, Glossatores ipsi oppositum dicunt exponentes apostolum ad Gal. 2. hæc est prior responsio, quam nitaris improbare; & qualiter ad motiva, quæ pro se adducit, valeat responderi secundum aliquorum opinionem studeas enarrare.
units.tr: STUDENT: I have discussed at length the argument by which it is proved that Peter was superior to the other apostles, because Christ said to him, feed my sheep. So turn now to another argument for the same assertion. TEACHER: It is proved in this way. Christ said to Peter alone: I say to you, that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc. By these words Christ seems to have expressly declared that blessed Peter would be the head and foundation of the church, especially after Christ's death. STUDENT: Some try to refute the preceding argument, and they answer this one too in this way, saying that the head and foundation of the church is and was one only, by the immediate ordination of God, and that this is Christ; but none of the apostles, not even in Christ's absence, is such. This, they say, is clearly agreed upon by Scripture, as was recited above in the first part of chapter 3. Therefore when it is said, upon this rock, etc., they say, following the Gloss, and assert that upon this rock means upon Christ, in whom you believe, where the Gloss adds nothing. You are Peter means: you are a rock from me, so that I keep for myself the dignity of the foundation. Christ called him Peter, that is, steadfast in faith. Those people do not deny this, and they also say that although Peter was more steadfast than others and rightly more perfect, he was not for that reason prior in dignity, except perhaps in time. This is confirmed by Augustine, who says in the Retractations: I said in one place about the apostle Peter that the church was built upon him as upon a rock. But I know that I have since very often explained it otherwise, because the Lord said, "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." And "upon this rock" would be understood as the one whom Peter confessed, saying, "You are Christ, the Son of the living God." Thus Peter, named from this rock, would represent the person of the church, which is built upon this rock. For it was not said to him, "You are the rock," but "You are Peter." The rock, however, was Christ, whom Simon confessed; for just as the whole church confesses Christ, so Peter was named. And a reason for this can be given from the Scriptures: Peter, as long as he was a wayfarer, could err and sin through the freedom of his will; hence we read that he denied Christ and at times walked not rightly in the truth of the gospel. But such a man could not be the foundation of the church. Rather, as appears from 1 Cor. 3., it was Christ alone, who cannot go astray, since he was confirmed from the very moment of his conception. Hence the apostle, in the place cited above: For no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. And as for what was added, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, it grants Peter no authority over the other apostles, since, according to Jerome and Rabanus, whose glosses they cite elsewhere, the same judicial power was given to the other apostles as well. Moreover, Christ does not seem to have handed over the power of the keys to him by these words, for he says I will give, which signifies the future, not I give. But in John 20. he said indiscriminately to all: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, etc. Yet even granting that Peter received this power by these words, it follows only that he was instituted as minister earlier in time. And so Christ gave the keys to him alone for this reason: as the Gloss says, he wished to signify the unity of the church in faith, to which Christ invited the faithful by the singular giving or promise of the keys. Or perhaps it is because he was the first to confess constantly and openly that Christ is the Son of God, that he was first endowed with the keys and honoured, or was permitted to be honoured, in time, so that by such a reward or promise an example might be given to the others of confessing Christ openly and steadfastly. Nevertheless, it does not follow from this that he was prior to the others in dignity or authority, although several of the Glossators seem to say this of their own accord, not having it from Scripture. Now they say that what is found in Matthew 20 and Luke 22 infallibly shows that they speak the truth, where Christ, clearly settling this question, said that none of them was superior to the others. For there arose a contention among them as to which of them should be greatest. The same is found in Matthew 23, where Christ says to them: But you (supply: one to another) do not be called rabbi; for one is your teacher, and you are all brethren, that is, equals. Therefore he does not exceed anyone. And it is ridiculous that we should believe the authority of the Gloss more than that of Christ, whoever that Glossator may have been, even if he was a saint, especially since he does not speak as a Glossator here but in the plain sense. For the sequence of Scripture is so manifest that the Gloss is not needed. Moreover, the Glossators themselves say the opposite, expounding the apostle at Gal. 2.; this is the first reply, which you strive to disprove. And as to how the arguments you bring forward on his behalf may be answered, according to the opinion of some, you should take pains to explain.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Assertores oppositi eius quod capitulo 12. in principio dictum est improbato.
units.tr: Refutation of the assertors of the opposite of what was said at the beginning of chapter 12.

units.la: MAGIST. Sunt quidam, qui prædicta opinantes, quo ad totam interpretationem seu expositionem præscriptorum verborum Christi, specialiter de temeritate & præsumptione nituntur arguere: quia esto (ut dicunt) quod præcise per illa verba: Tu es Petrus &c. nude intellecta non posset patenter contra proteruos ostendi, quod Petrus erat superior aliis apostolis. Tamen per ipsa & alia verba scripturæ canonicæ, & expositiones seu assertiones probatorum virorum, probari potest, quod illa verba Christi sic debent intelligi, ut credatur per ipsa tunc primatus super omnes fideles fuisse Petro promissus. Et esto, quod non esset necesse credere viris quantumcunque probatis post scriptores scripturæ canonicæ in his, quæ pure sunt scientiæ seu peritiæ: tamen omnino esset temerarium reputandum tam probatis viris (præsertim illis, qui discipuli apostolorum fuerunt, à quibus intellectum scripturæ canonicum audierunt vel vicini apostolorum operibus exiterunt) absque infallibili probatione contradicere, quoquomodo intellectum contrarium affirmando. Quia enim (ut leges civiles astruunt & Glo. 24. q. 1. super c. pudenda notat) nihil est ita indubitatum, quin sollicitam recipiat dubitationem, & etiam contradictionem. Et ideo contra multorum verborum scripturæ sacræ catholicum sensum multa possunt obiici & adduci etiam apparetur. Nam secundum beatum Clementem, ut recitatur di. 37. c. relatum: Sunt multa verba in scriptura divina, quæ possent trahi ad eum sensum, quem sibi unusquisque præsumpserit. Tamen hoc fieri minime debet: quia (ut dicit ibidem beatus Clemens) ex ipsis scripturis sensum capere veritatis oportet. Et ideo portet ab eo scientiam discere, qui eam à maioribus secundum veritatem sibi traditam servat, ut ipse possit eam, quam recte suscipit, competenter asserere, & intellectum verborum Christi, cum dixit: Tu es Petrus &c. qui accipi ex scripturis potest, ut eas intelligunt præcipue viri probati, qui eum à maioribus & præcipue ab apostolis didicerunt. Et esto (sicut tacitum est) quod non esset simpliciter necessarium credere eis, tamen horribilis & omnino stulta esset temeritas contradicere ipsis, maxime absque infallibili ratione, quæ etiam adversarios & viros intelligentes aperte convinceret.
units.tr: MAGISTER: There are some who, holding the aforementioned opinions, especially set about accusing us of rashness and presumption in regard to the whole interpretation or exposition of the words of Christ quoted above. For they say that, even if it could not be clearly shown against the obstinate by those words alone, "You are Peter" and so on, taken bare and by themselves, that Peter was superior to the other apostles, nevertheless it can be proved through these and other words of canonical Scripture, and through the expositions or assertions of approved men, that the words of Christ must be understood in such a way that we should believe that by them the primacy over all the faithful was then promised to Peter. And even if it were not necessary to believe men of whatever approval who came after the writers of canonical Scripture in matters that belong purely to knowledge or skill, it would nevertheless be altogether rash to contradict approved men (especially those who were disciples of the apostles, from whom they heard the canonical sense of Scripture, or who lived close to the apostles' works), by affirming in any way a contrary meaning, without infallible proof. For, as the civil laws assert, and the Gloss on Dist. 24, q. 1, on the chapter Pudenda, notes, nothing is so certain that it does not admit anxious doubt and even contradiction. And therefore many objections can be raised, and even appear to be brought, against the catholic sense of many words of holy Scripture. For according to blessed Clement, as cited in Dist. 37, chapter Relatum: "There are many words in divine Scripture which could be drawn to the sense that each one has presumed for himself." Yet this must by no means be done; for (as blessed Clement says in the same place) "it is necessary to take the sense of truth from the Scriptures themselves." And therefore one ought to learn the knowledge from him who keeps it as it was handed down truly from his elders, so that he himself may competently affirm what he rightly receives; and likewise the meaning of the words of Christ, when he said "You are Peter," and so on, which can be gathered from the Scriptures, as the approved men who learned it from their elders, and especially from the apostles, understand them.
