And even if (as has been said) it were not simply necessary to believe them, nevertheless it would be a horrible and utterly foolish rashness to contradict them, especially without an infallible reason which would also openly convince opponents and intelligent men.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: Pertractat intellectum verborum Christi: scilicet tu es Petrus &c. quomodo per ea Christus principatum super alios apostolos Petro tradiderit.
units.tr: Treats the meaning of Christ's words, namely "You are Peter, etc.", and how through them Christ handed over the primacy over the other apostles to Peter.

units.la: DISCIP. Circa responsionem prædictam, quam allegando esse temerariam ostendisti, nitaris nunc probare circa intellectum illorum verborum Christi: tu es petrus &c. quod credere tenemur aliis quam scriptoribus scripturæ canonicæ. MAGIST. Hoc (ut quibusdam apparet) tali modo probatur. fide dignis viris omni exceptione maioribus est credendum in his, quæ vocaliter seu sententialiter cognouisse se asserunt per ipsos vel per alios, quibus credere tenebantur seu quæ dicuntur tanquam à se cognita altero modorum illorum. Talia enim taliter cognita, quamvis ad ea, quæ scientiæ sunt valeant pertinere, tamen aliquomodo spectare possunt ad ea, quæ facti sunt, vel saltem cognitio, qua asseruntur cognosci inter ea quæ facti sunt, cóputari potest. In his autem quæ facti sunt fide dignis viris est credendum, ut probatum est. 3. huius. c. 21. Aliter enim pro veracibus & fide dignis minime haberentur, quod irreuerentia damnabili non careret. Sed fide digni viri omni exceptione maiores sententialiter asserunt, se non per ratiocinationem vel studium seu meditationis virtutem, sed per seipsos vel alios, quibus credere tenebantur, cognouisse prædicta verba Christi. tu es petrus &c. sic debere intelligi, ut per ea intelligatur primatus super apostolos & omnes alios fideles fuisse beato Petro datus vel commissus à Christo. Plures enim fide digni & probatissimi viri, qui fuerunt apostolorum discipuli vel per apostolorum discipulos in litteris sacris instructi, prædictum intellectum illorum verborum Christi asseruerunt expresse. omni autem probabilitate carere videtur, quod viri studiosi & literati sacrarum scripturarum indagatores solertissimi cum beato Petro & aliis apostolis & apostolorum discipulis fuerint conversati, & prædictorum verborum Christi verum ab ipsis non didicerunt intellectum, præsertim cum verus intellectus ipsorum ad sciendum, cui vel quibus tanquam prælato vel prælatis fideles obedire deberent: & cui tanquam prælato summo instituto à Christo parere minime tenerentur, fuerit necessarius toti ecclesiæ Christi. Non enim sunt omnes extra periculum ignorantes, quem tanquam verum pastorem debeant sequi. multo autem improbabilius videtur, quod huiusmodi viri apostolorum & discipulorum ipsorum discipuli sallsum circa prædicta verba Christi docuerint intellectum. & ita debent tenere fideles, quod ille est verus intellectus prædictorum verborum Christi, quem apostolorum discipuli & à discipulis apostolorum edocti firmifirmiter asserebant. quia illum intellectum non acceperunt solummodo per ratiocinationem ipsum ex verbis illis tantummodo concludendo: sed acceperunt eum ab apostolis, qui eos verum intellectum ipsorum sollicite docuerunt, tanquam necessarium toti ecclesiae Dei. & ideo didicerunt eum, non tanquam notum eis per viam scientiae seu ratiocinationis: sed tanquam expressum eis & dictum ab apostolis, quibus credere tenebantur: quia apostoli verum intellectum eorundem verborum certissime agnoscebant. propter quod dicere, viros fide dignos & probatos apostolorum discipulos vel a discipulis apostolorum edoctos falsum intellectum verborum dicere esse dicere ipsos non per ratiocinationem sophisticam deceptos: sed scienter fuisse mentitos. quia scienter dixissent intellectum contrarium illi, quem ab apostolis didicerunt. quod non est vacuum irreverentia & blasphemia detestanda.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Regarding the aforesaid response, which you showed by argument to be rash, you now try to prove, concerning the meaning of those words of Christ, you are Peter, etc., that we are bound to believe something other than the writers of canonical Scripture. MASTER. This, as it seems to some, is proved in the following way. Men worthy of trust, above all exception, are to be believed in those things which they state they have known, either vocally or in substance, through themselves or through others whom they were bound to believe, or which are said to be known by themselves in one of those ways. For such things, known in such ways, although they may pertain to matters of knowledge, can nevertheless in some respect relate to matters of fact, or at least the knowledge by which they are said to be known can be counted among matters of fact. Now men worthy of trust are to be believed in matters of fact, as was proved in book 3, chapter 21. Otherwise they would not be held true and trustworthy, which would not be free of damnable irreverence. But men worthy of trust, above all exception, state in substance that they did not know the aforesaid words of Christ, you are Peter, etc., to be understood in such a way that through them the primacy over the apostles and all other faithful was given or committed to blessed Peter by Christ, through reasoning or the power of study or meditation, but through themselves or through others whom they were bound to believe. For many trustworthy and most approved men, who were disciples of the apostles or were instructed in the sacred letters through the apostles' disciples, expressly asserted this sense of those words of Christ. Yet it seems entirely without probability that men who were zealous and learned, most diligent investigators of the sacred Scriptures, lived with blessed Peter, the other apostles and the apostles' disciples, and did not learn from them the true sense of the aforesaid words of Christ. This is especially so since the true sense of them was necessary for the whole Church of Christ, to know whom, or which persons, as prelate or prelates, the faithful ought to obey, and to whom, as the supreme prelate instituted by Christ, they were not bound to submit. For not all who are ignorant are free from danger as to whom they should follow as the true pastor. Much less probable is it that such men, disciples of the apostles and the disciples of those disciples, falsely taught a sense of those words of Christ. So the faithful must hold that this is the true sense of the aforesaid words of Christ, which the disciples of the apostles, and those taught by the apostles' disciples, firmly asserted. For they did not receive that sense merely by reasoning, concluding it from those words alone; they received it from the apostles, who diligently taught them the true sense of the words as necessary for the whole Church of God. So they learned it not as something known to them by way of knowledge or reasoning, but as something expressed and stated to them by the apostles, whom they were bound to believe, because the apostles most certainly recognised the true sense of those same words. Hence to say that trustworthy and approved men, disciples of the apostles or taught by the apostles' disciples, stated a false sense of the words, is to say that they were not deceived by sophistical reasoning, but knowingly lied. For they would have knowingly stated a sense contrary to the one they had learned from the apostles. This is not free of irreverence and detestable blasphemy.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Assumptum capitulo praecedenti probat: scilicet primatum Petri per expositionem Anacleti.
units.tr: He proves the point assumed in the preceding chapter, namely the primacy of Peter, by the exposition of Anacletus.

units.la: DISCIP. Aliquorum fide dignorum & probatorum testimonia, qui fuerint apostolorum discipuli, vel ab eorum discipulis saltem mediate instructi, asserentium saepe dicta verba Christi: tu es Petrus &c. praemissum debere intellectum habere, audire desidero. MAGIST. Hoc Anacletus papa, qui fuit apostolorum discipulus, & ab ipsis discipulis, imo a beato Petro in scripturis diuinis instructus, de quo improbabile omnino videtur, quod nesciret, an Petrus reputaret se super alios apostolos superioritatem habere: & qualiter Petrus intellexerit verba Christi praemissa: de quo nullatenus est credendum, quod falsum intellectum eorundem verborum scienter docuerit, & in scriptis reliquerit. eundem intellectum verborum illorum patenter astruit & expresse. qui, ut habetur in decretis dist. 22 c. Sacrosancta, ait: Sacrosancta Romana & apostolica ecclesia non ab apostolis, sed ab ipso Saluatore domino nostro primatum obtinuit, sicut beato Petro apostolo dixit, tu es Petrus, & reliqua usque, soluta sunt in coelo. Adhibita est societas in eadem Romana urbe beatissimi Pauli apostoli vasis electionis: qui uno die, unoque tempore, cum Petro gloriosa morte coronatus est. & ambae sanctam Romanam ecclesiam consecrauerunt, atque alii urbibus omnibus in uniuerso mundo tam sua praesentia quam venerando protulerunt triumpho. & infra: inter beatos mos apostolos quaedam fuit discretio potestatis. Et potest licet omnes essent apostoli, Petro tamen a Domino concessum est, & ipsi inter se voluerunt id ipsum, ut reliquis omnibus praeesset apostolus & Cephas i. caput & primatum teneret apostolatus. Ex quibus, ut videtur, patenter habetur, secundum Anacletum, qui fuit papa ante Clementem, ut testatur Ecclesiastica historia lib. 2. cap. 14. & qui fuit cum Petro apostolo conuersatus, Christus illis verbis: Tu es Petrus &c. promisit Petro vel dedit primatum. Et quod dederit sibi vel promiserit primatum, non solum super alios fideles, sed etiam super apostolos, patet, cum dicit, quod inter apostolos erat discretio potestatis, & quod praerat aliis apostolis, non solum de voluntate apostolorum, sed etiam de concessione seu ordinatione domini, cum dicat, licet omnes essent apostoli, Petro tamen a domino concessum est &c. Ex praescriptis etiam verbis Anacleti potest accipi alia ratio principalis ad probandum, quod Petrus deordinatione Christi praefuit aliis apostolis. Nam sub quo intellectu Christus dixerit Petro, ut habetur Iohann. 1. tu vocaberis Cephas. Anacletus hoc exprimit manifeste, cum asserit, Petrum fuisse Cephas, quia caput & primatum tenuit apostolatus. Cum itaque Anacletus vir fuerit eruditus & sanctus, & cum Petro conuersatus, verisimile non videtur, quod ignoraverit, quomodo Petrus illa verba intellexerit, quae dixit sibi Christus: tu vocaberis Cephas. nec est aliquomodo credendum, quod mentiretur scienter: & in hoc, quod per seipsum cognoverit, falsum astrueret: licet credetur, quod in his, quae pure sunt scientiae seu rationis, decipi potest. ergo Anacletus illorum verborum intellectum: tu vocaberis Cephas, quem habuit Petrus, expressit. Petrus autem illorum verborum verum habuit intellectum. Ergo Anacletus in verbis praescriptis illorum verborum verum protulit intellectum. Et per consequens Christus intendebat, quod Petrus vocandus erat Cephas, & caput, & princeps omnium aliorum apostolorum. Et per consequens tunc erat futurus pastor & praelatus eorum. Allegatio suprascripta taliter confirmatur. Moris erat apostolorum & discipulorum ipsorum mox, cum contra veritatem aliqui insurrexerunt, errores ipsos comprimere & publice confutare: ita ut cuicunque in hoc parcendum minime reputaret. Unde & beatus Paulus Petrum, cum non ambularet recte ad euangelii veritatem, reprehendit, ut legitur ad Gal. 2. Sed in nulla inuenitur historia vel Chronica, quae a catholicis habeatur, quod aliquis apostolus vel discipulus apostolorum super praedicta assertione reprehenderit Anacletum: quorum tamen tunc temporis plurimi erant haeresim & errorum orientium vigilantissimi correctores & correptores, quorum gesta & scripta ad nostra tempora peruenerunt. ergo omni veritatis similitudine caret, quod beatus Anacletus in hoc erraverit, & animas in errorem induxerit.
units.tr: STUDENT. I would like to hear the testimony of certain trustworthy and approved men, who were either disciples of the apostles or were at least indirectly taught by the apostles' disciples, asserting that the words of Christ, tu es Petrus &c., ought to be understood in the sense I have described. TEACHER. Anacletus, the pope, who was a disciple of the apostles and was instructed by the apostles' own disciples, or rather by the blessed Peter himself in the divine Scriptures, affirms this. It seems quite improbable that he did not know whether Peter regarded himself as having a superiority over the other apostles, and how Peter understood the words of Christ quoted above. It is in no way to be believed that he knowingly taught a false sense of those words and left it in his writings. He plainly and expressly asserts that same sense of those words. As is found in the Decretum, dist. 22, c. Sacrosancta, he says: The holy Roman and apostolic Church obtained its primacy not from the apostles but from our Saviour the Lord himself, as he said to the blessed apostle Peter, "You are Peter," and the rest, up to "shall be loosed in heaven." The blessed Paul, the chosen vessel, was joined with him in the same city of Rome. On one day and at one time both were crowned with a glorious death with Peter. Both of them consecrated the holy Roman Church, and by their presence and their venerable triumph they raised it above all the cities in the whole world. And below: Among the blessed apostles there was a certain distinction of power. Although all were apostles, it was granted to Peter by the Lord, and they themselves willed it among themselves, that the apostle Peter should preside over all the rest, and that Cephas, that is, the head, should hold the primacy of the apostleship. From these words it is plainly seen, as it appears, according to Anacletus, who was pope before Clement, as the Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 14, attests, and who lived with the apostle Peter, that Christ by those words, "You are Peter" &c., promised or gave the primacy to Peter. That he gave or promised him the primacy not only over the other faithful but also over the apostles is clear from his saying that there was a distinction of power among the apostles, and that he presided over the other apostles not only by the will of the apostles but also by the grant and ordinance of the Lord, when he says, although all were apostles, it was granted to Peter by the Lord &c. From the words of Anacletus quoted above another principal argument can also be drawn to prove that Peter, by the ordinance of Christ, presided over the other apostles. For he clearly expresses the sense in which Christ said to Peter, as we read in John 1, you shall be called Cephas: when he asserts that Peter was Cephas because he held the headship and primacy of the apostleship. Since Anacletus was a learned and holy man, and lived with Peter, it does not seem likely that he was ignorant of how Peter understood the words Christ spoke to him, you shall be called Cephas. Nor is it at all to be believed that he lied knowingly, or that he asserted something false about what he knew for himself; although it may be granted that a man can be mistaken in matters that are purely of knowledge or reason. Therefore Anacletus expressed the sense of those words, you shall be called Cephas, which Peter had. But Peter had the true sense of those words. Therefore Anacletus, in the words quoted above, gave the true sense of those words. And consequently Christ intended that Peter should be called Cephas, and the head, and prince of all the other apostles. And consequently he was then to be their pastor and prelate. The argument above is confirmed in this way. It was the custom of the apostles and their disciples, as soon as some rose up against the truth, to repress those errors at once and refute them publicly, so that they thought no one should be spared in this. Hence the blessed Paul also rebuked Peter when he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, as we read in Gal. 2. But no history or chronicle held by Catholics is found in which any apostle or disciple of the apostles rebuked Anacletus for the aforesaid assertion, although many of them at that time were the most vigilant correctors and reprovers of the heresies and errors that arose, and their deeds and writings have come down to our times. Therefore it has no semblance of truth that the blessed Anacletus erred in this and led souls into error.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: Hoc idem, scilicet primatum Petri, probat per expositionem Marcelli & Cypriani.
units.tr: Here too he proves the primacy of Peter by the exposition of Marcellus and Cyprian.

units.la: DISCIP. Orthodoxorum aliquorum aliorum, sed paucorum testimonia adducas ad probandum, quod praedictus fuerit intellectus illorum verborum Christi: tu es Petrus &c. MAG. Hoc sentit Marcellus papa & martyr, qui propter propinquitatem temporis apostolorum vel discipulorum ipsorum absque omni dubitationis scrupulo poterat scire, quomodo apostoli & ipsorum discipuli intellexerunt verba illa Christi. ait enim, ut habetur in decretis 24. q. 1. c. rogamus: Rogamus vos fratres dilectissimi, ut non aliud doceatis neque sentiatis quam quod a beato Petro apostolo & patribus accepistis. Ipse enim est caput totius ecclesiae, cui ait dominus tu es petrus & super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Idem etiam videtur sentire Cyprianus martyr: qui etiam propter similem propinquitatem ad tempora apostolorum non videtur ignorasse, quomodo apostoli intellexerunt verba illa Christi. ait enim, ut habetur 24. q. 1. c. loquitur. Loquitur dominus ad Petrum: ego dico tibi, quia tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Super unum aedificat ecclesiam: & quamuis apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam, parem potestatem tribuat & dicat, sicut misit me pater & ego mitto vos: accipite spiritum sanctum: tamen ut unitatem manifestaret ab uno suam auctoritatem disposuit. Ex his aliisque quam pluribus colligitur, probatissimi & literatissimi viri de vero intellectu scripturae sacrae, maximam curam habentes, qui per dicta aut scripta apostolorum aut discipulorum ipsorum verum intellectum praedictorum verborum Christi certitudinaliter accipere potuerunt, eadem verba Christi intellexerunt modo praedicto. Quare absque temeritate idem intellectus negari non potest, praesertim cum nullus inveniatur apostolorum discipulus, aut qui vicinus fuerit eorum temporibus, qui intellectum illum neget aut affirmet contrarium.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Would you bring forward the testimony of some orthodox writers, though few, to prove that this was the meaning of Christ's words you are Peter, etc.? MASTER. Pope and martyr Marcellus holds this view. Because he lived so close to the time of the apostles or their disciples, he could know without any shadow of doubt how the apostles and their disciples understood those words of Christ. As it is found in Decretum 24, q. 1, c. Rogamus, he says: We beg you, most beloved brothers, that you teach and think nothing other than what you have received from the blessed apostle Peter and the Fathers. For he is the head of the whole church, to whom the Lord said, You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church. Cyprian the martyr also seems to hold the same view. Because of a similar closeness to the times of the apostles, he does not seem to have been ignorant of how the apostles understood those words of Christ. As it is found in 24, q. 1, c. Loquitur, he says: The Lord speaks to Peter: I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church. He builds the church upon one man. And although after his resurrection he gave equal power to all the apostles and said, as the Father sent me, so I send you; receive the Holy Spirit, yet in order to show unity he arranged his authority so that it comes from one. From these and many other considerations it is gathered that these most approved and learned men, who took the greatest care over the true meaning of Holy Scripture, and who could receive the true meaning of Christ's words with certainty through the sayings or writings of the apostles or their disciples, understood the same words of Christ in the way described. Therefore this same understanding cannot be denied without rashness, especially since no disciple of the apostles, or anyone who lived close to their times, is found who denies that understanding or affirms the contrary.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Ostendit per qua verba Christus primatum promisit Petro.
units.tr: Shows by which words Christ promised the primacy to Peter.

units.la: DISCIP. Antequam procedas ulterius, dic secundum aliquam opinionem, per quae verba inter illa, quae dixit Christus Petro, cum dixit: tu es petrus &c. sibi primatum super apostolos & omnes fideles promisit.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Before you go further, tell me according to some opinion by which of the words Christ spoke to Peter, when he said you are Peter, etc., he promised him the primacy over the apostles and all the faithful.

units.la: MAGIST. Una est opinio dicens, quod Petrus, sicut & quilibet successorum, duplicem habuit potestatem. Unam scilicet ratione ordinis, & aliam ratione administrationis. Hanc duplicem potestatem ponit Glo. di. 21. super ca. in novo. Prima potestas promissa fuit Petro per illa verba: tibi dabo claves regni caelorum & quodcunque ligaveris &c. secunda promissa fuit sibi per illa verba, super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. primam autem recepit ante secundam, quia primam recepit simul cum aliis apostolis, quando Christus dixit sibi & aliis apostolis: accipite spiritum sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata &c. tunc enim omnes illi potestatem ligandi atque solvendi receperunt, quia potestas retinendi vel remittendi peccata est potestas ligandi & solvendi. Secunda autem potestatem recepit, quando Christus dixit sibi: pasce oves meas. & licet ista potestas pascendi fuerit data Petro post potestatem ligandi atque solvendi: tamen absque ipsa potest inveniri. Ista enim potestatem habet quilibet electus in summum pontificem, quamvis non sit sacerdos, qui solus habet potestatem ligandi & solvendi: & est tunc verus papa, quantum ad hanc potestatem. di. 23. in nomine. & per istam potestatem, quam ultimo percepit Petrus, factus fuit Petrus caeteris omnibus superior & praelatus. & ideo per illa verba, super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam, fuit primatus Petro promissus.
units.tr: MASTER. One opinion holds that Peter, like any of his successors, had a twofold power: one by reason of his order, and the other by reason of his administration. The Gloss sets out this twofold power Dist. 21, on the chapter "In novo". The first power was promised to Peter in these words: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind, etc. The second was promised to him in these words: upon this rock I will build my church. He received the first before the second, because he received the first together with the other apostles, when Christ said to him and the other apostles: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, etc. For then all of them received the power of binding and loosing, since the power of retaining or forgiving sins is the power of binding and loosing. He received the second power when Christ said to him: Feed my sheep. And although this power of feeding was given to Peter after the power of binding and loosing, it can nevertheless be found without it. For any elect person who becomes supreme pontiff has this power, even if he is not a priest, while only a priest has the power of binding and loosing; and he is then a true pope, so far as this power goes. Dist. 23, on the chapter "In nomine". And through this power, which Peter received last, Peter was made superior and preeminent over all the rest. Therefore the primacy was promised to Peter through the words upon this rock I will build my church.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XVIII.

units.la: Solvit rationem primam 12. cap. adducram: qua probatur, quod per illa verba, Tu es Petrus &c. non potest ostendi principatus Petri. Et solvendo probat multipliciter, quod non solum Christus, sed etiam Petrus dictus est fundamentum ecclesiae.
units.tr: He answers the first argument that I will adduce in chapter 12, by which it is proved that the primacy of Peter cannot be shown from the words "You are Peter," etc. In his answer he proves in several ways that not only Christ but also Peter is called the foundation of the Church.

units.la: DISCIP. Intellexi, quomodo improbatur responsio suprascripta, nunc indica, qualiter respondeatur ad mutua, quibus se munire conatur. MAG. Ad primum, cum accipiunt, ut dictum est supra c. 12. Caput & fundamentum ecclesiae unicum esse & fuisse ordinatione immediata Dei; & hoc Christum; apostolorum vero neminem &c. respondetur, quod hoc tam scripturae canonicae, quae expositoribus approbati scripturarum sanctarum aperte repugnat. Apoc. enim 21. sic habetur: murus civitatis habens fundamenta 12. nomina apostolorum. ex quib. verbis colligitur, quod apostoli fuerunt aut sunt fundamenta militantis ecclesiae vel triumphatis. Civitas enim illa, vel est ecclesia militans, vel triumphans, & si quidem est militans, habetur intentum. si quidem est triumphans, sequitur apostoli multo fortius fuerunt fundamenta ecclesiae militantis. quia non magis est solus Christus fundamentum ecclesiae militantis, quae triumphantis. Dicere ergo, nullo modo fuit aliquis apostolus fundamentum ecclesiae, apte sacrae scripturae repugnat. Hoc et assertionibus sanctorum patrum asserentium, beatum Petrum fuisse fundamentum ecclesiae & ecclesiam super ipsum fuisse fundatam, & aedificatam, obviat manifeste. Ait n. sanctus Aug. in sermone de cathedra sancti Petri: recte ergo ecclesia natalem sedis illius coluit, quem apostolus pro ecclesiarum salute suscepit, dicente domino: tu es tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Petrus itaque fundamentum ecclesiae nominatur. & ideo digne hoc fundamentum ecclesia colit, super quam ecclesiastici aedificii altitudo consurgit. unde convenienter Psalmus, qui hoc est, dicit: Exaltent eum in ecclesia plebis, & in cathedra seniorum laudent eum, dum eum dominus in ecclesia exaltari praecepit, quia dignum est, ut fundamentum hoc in ecclesia honoretur, per quod celum ascenditur. Vbi dicunt, notandum esse, quod tribus vicibus Augustinus nominat Petrum fundamentum ecclesiae. Item Hieron. super illud Matth. 18. venit Iesus in partes Caesarea Philippi. Quid est hoc, quod ait? & ego dico tibi? quia tu mihi dixisti, tu es Christus filius Dei vivi. & ego dico tibi, non sermone casso & nullo habente opus: sed dico tibi quia meum dixisse fecisse est: quia tu es Petrus & super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam, sicut ipse lumen apostolis donavit ut lumen mundi appellarentur & cetera, qua ex domino sortiti sunt vocabula: ita & Simoni, qui credebat in petram Christum, Petri largitus est nomen. ac secundum metaphoram recte dicitur ei: aedificabo ecclesiam meam super te. Ecce quod secundum Hieronymum Christus dixit Petro, aedificabo ecclesiam meam super te. ergo ecclesia Christi fuit aedificata super Petrum. Illa autem, super quem aedificatum erat aedificium ecclesiae, potest fundamentum ecclesiae appellari, quia fundamentum est illud, super quod erigitur aedificium. Item beatus Leo papa in sermone de festo apostolorum, qui incipit, Omnium quidem sanctorum, ait loquens de beato Petro: Iam Antiochenam ecclesiam, ubi primum Christiani nominis dignitas est exorta, fundaverat. Fuit igitur beatus Petrus fundamentum ecclesiae Anthiochenae; & eadem ratione Romanae. Item Beatus Maximus in sermone, qui incipit: Gloriosissimos, ait: Hic est Petrus, cui Christus dominus communionem sui nominis libenter indulsit. uti enim, sicut apostolus docuit, petra erat Christus: ita quod per Christum Petrus factus est petra, dicente ei domino: tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Nam sicut in deserto dominico sitiente populo aqua fluxit de petra: ita vniuerso mundo perfidia ariditate languenti de ore Petri fons salutifera confessionis emersit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod non solum Christus, sed etiam Petrus erat petra illa, super quam Christus suam erat fundaturus ecclesiam. Quare aliquo modo concedi debet, quod Petrus erat fundamentum ecclesiae. Item hoc dicit Gregor. qui, ut habetur di. 12. c. praeceptu, ait: cuius auctoritatis sanctionem omnes teneant sacerdotes, qui volunt ab apostolica petra (supra quam Christus vniuersaliter fundavit ecclesiam) soliditate diuelli. Super apostolicam ergo petram, id est super Petrum apostolum, fundata est vniuersalis ecclesia. Item Eusebius Caesariensis in Ecclesiastica historia libro 3. c. 4. asserit manifeste, apostolos fundasse ecclesias, dicens: si qui constantes in fide, & amulatores verbi reperti sunt, etiam qui regendas ecclesias, quas apostoli fundauerunt, susceperunt. Item Nicolaus papa, ut habetur extra de verborum significationibus ca. exiit, hoc idem asserit manifeste, cum dixit volens de apostolis facere mentionem: primi fundatores militantis ecclesiae prout ab ipso fonte (scilicet Christo) hauserant, in volentes perfecte viuere per doctrina ipsorum alueos deriuarunt. Fuerunt ergo apostoli, & non solum Petrus, fundamenta ecclesiae, & etiam fundatores.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I have understood how the above reply is refuted. Now show me how one answers the arguments with which they try to fortify themselves. MASTER. As for the first, they take it as stated above in chapter 12: that the head and foundation of the Church is and has been one only, by the immediate ordinance of God, and that this is Christ, while none of the apostles is. This is contradicted openly by the canonical Scripture, which the expositors of the holy Scriptures have approved. For Revelation 21 reads thus: the wall of the city had twelve foundations, bearing the names of the apostles. From these words it follows that the apostles were, or are, the foundations of the Church militant or of the Church triumphant. For that city is either the Church militant or the Church triumphant. If it is the militant Church, the point is established. If it is the triumphant Church, it follows that the apostles were much more the foundations of the Church militant, since Christ alone is no more the foundation of the militant Church than of the triumphant. To say, therefore, that no apostle was in any way a foundation of the Church plainly contradicts Holy Scripture. It also clearly opposes the assertions of the holy Fathers, who affirm that the blessed Peter was the foundation of the Church and that the Church was founded and built upon him. For St. Augustine says in his sermon on the Chair of St. Peter: Rightly, therefore, the Church has celebrated the birthday of that see, which the apostle undertook for the salvation of the churches, when the Lord said: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." Peter is therefore named the foundation of the Church, and so the Church rightly honours that foundation on which the height of the ecclesiastical building rises. Hence the Psalm, which is about this, fittingly says: "Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders" (Ps. 107:32), since the Lord commanded him to be exalted in the Church, because it is fitting that this foundation, by which one ascends to heaven, be honoured in the Church. Here they say that it must be noted that Augustine names Peter the foundation of the Church three times. Likewise Jerome, on the words of Matthew 18, "Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi": What does he mean by saying "And I say to you"? Because you have said to me, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." And I say to you, not with an empty word that does no work, but I say to you, because my speaking is doing: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." Just as he gave the apostles the light, so that they were called the light of the world, and so on, names which they received from the Lord, so he also gave to Simon, who believed in Christ the rock, the name Peter. And by metaphor it is rightly said to him: "I will build my church upon you." Behold, according to Jerome, Christ said to Peter, "I will build my church upon you." Therefore the Church of Christ was built upon Peter. But that upon which the building of the Church was erected can be called its foundation, because a foundation is that on which a building is raised. Likewise the blessed Pope Leo, in his sermon on the feast of the apostles, which begins "Of all the saints," speaking of the blessed Peter, says: "He had already founded the Church of Antioch, where first the dignity of the Christian name arose." Therefore the blessed Peter was the foundation of the Church of Antioch, and by the same reasoning of the Church of Rome. Likewise the blessed Maximus, in the sermon that begins "Most glorious," says: "This is Peter, to whom the Lord Christ gladly granted a share in his own name. For as, the apostle teaches, Christ was the rock, so through Christ Peter has become a rock, the Lord saying to him: 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.' For as in the Lord's desert, when the people thirsted, water flowed from the rock, so when the whole world languished in the dryness of unbelief, the saving fountain of confession welled up from the mouth of Peter." From these words it is gathered that not only Christ but also Peter was that rock upon which Christ was going to build his Church. Wherefore it must be conceded in some sense that Peter was the foundation of the Church. Likewise Gregory says this, as is found in Dist. 12, chapter "Praeceptu": "All priests who wish to be torn away from the firmness of the apostolic rock (upon which Christ founded the universal Church) should hold to the sanction of this authority." Therefore upon the apostolic rock, that is upon the apostle Peter, the universal Church was founded. Likewise Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 4, plainly asserts that the apostles founded churches, saying: "If there were found any who were steadfast in the faith and zealous for the word, even those who took up the governing of the churches which the apostles had founded." Likewise Pope Nicholas, as is found in Extra, On the Meaning of Words, chapter "Exiit," asserts the same plainly, when, wishing to make mention of the apostles, he said: "The first founders of the militant Church, as they had drawn from the fountain itself (namely Christ), so they led channels through their teaching to those who wished to live perfectly." Therefore the apostles, and not Peter alone, were the foundations of the Church, and also its founders.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Respondit ad aliqua motiva capitulo 12. adducta.
units.tr: He replies to some arguments adduced in chapter 12.

units.la: DISCIP. Qualiter respondetur ad motiva opinantium praedictorum, quibus probare nituntur, quod solus Christus erat fundamentum ecclesiae. MAGIST. Ad primum eorum, cum adducitur Glossa interlinearis, qua probatur, quod Christus sibi videtur retinuisse fundamenti dignitatem. Respondetur per distinctionem de fundamento, quia quoddam est fundamentum ecclesiae primatium & principale, absque quo nulla potest fundari ecclesia. & illud fundamentum est sol Deus sive Christus. Aliud est fundamentum ecclesiae secundarium, sine quo poterat fundari ecclesia, sine quo tamen non fuit fundata de facto, & tale fundamentum non est solus Deus nec solus Petrus: imo omnes apostoli fuerunt fundamenta ecclesiae, inter quos tamen quodammodo principalius & vniuersalius fundamentum fuit beatus Petrus. Glossa autem loquitur de fundamento primo modo dicto, & non de fundamento secundo modo dicto. Consimiliter dicitur ad auctoritatem Aug. sumptam ex libro Retractationum, quod Augustinus non reprobat dictum suum de apostolo Petro, quo asseruit, in illo tanquam in petra aedificata sit: sed dicit se aliter saepe exposuisse, ut per petram intelligatur Christus, tanquam petra principalis, super quam principaliter aedificata est ecclesia. Non enim in fundamento aedificii materialis ponitur semper vnica petra, sed saepe plures, & vna super alia: & ita per distinctionem tale petrae concordantur auctoritates sanctorum patrum, quae repugnare videntur. Nequaquam igitur Aug. dictum suum reprobat aut revocat vel corrigit, sed declarat & asserit, quod locus scripturae quem volebat exponere, alium potest habere sensum, qui priori sensui minime contradicit. Sed per distinctionem praedictam vnus est cum alio concordandus. Non enim Aug. semper reprobat aut corrigit quae retractat: sed aliqua dicitur retractare, quia iterum ipsa tractat declarando ipsa & cum aliis concordando. Ad rationem, qua saepe dicti opinantes probare nituntur, quod beatus Petrus non fuit fundamentum ecclesiae: quia fundamentum ecclesiae non potest errare nec peccare. Respondetur, quod principale fundamentum ecclesiae, sine quo totum aedificium rueret, imo sine quo nullo modo construi posset, nec peccare nec errare potest aut potuit. & illud fuit Christus, non Petrus. Sed secundarium fundamentum, sine quo poterat erigi totum aedificium ecclesiae, potuit errare & peccare, quamvis in quantum fuit fundamentum actualiter fundando non potuerit errare nec peccare. Quando n. Petrus negavit Christum, & quando postea ad veritatem euangelii non recte ambulavit, non actu fundavit ecclesiam: sed qui primo post Christum praedicando veritate apostolos ad veram fidem converterit, tunc novellam fundavit ecclesiam. Ad auctoritatem {a}storitatem autem apostoli Cor. 3. respondetur, quod apostolus ibi locutus est de principali fundamento ecclesiæ, non de secundario. & certe fundamentum principale nemo aliud ponere potest, præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Est autem sciendum secundum quosdam, sicut dictum est prius, ꝓ modus scripturæ sæpe est negare aliquid ab illis, quib. non competit principaliter, quamuis secundario competat. Sic enim dixit Christus Luc. 18. Nemo bonus nisi solus Deus. Sic etiam de Iohanne Baptista dicitur: non erat ille lux, Ioh. 1. Et tamen sicut apostoli erant lux, dicente eis Christo Matt. 5. Vos estis lux mundi. Sic & beatus Ioan. Bapt. fuit lux. Fuit enim lucerna ardens & lucens, Ioh. 5. Cum ergo dicitur, quod Christus potestatem clauium non videtur Petro tradidisse per hæc verba: Tu es petrus &c. Respondetur, quod tunc Christus non tradidit Petro potestatem clauium, sed promisit. nec etiam tunc præfecit eum reliquis apostolis, sed promisit. Et ideo qualiter & quibus præfecit eum, ex istis verbis: tu es petrus, ultimate nequaquam colligi potest, nisi referendo ad ipsa verba, quibus scil. postea præfecit eum, scilicet illa: Pasce oves meas. & tamen ex istis verbis, super hanc petram ædificabo ecclesiam meam, potest ostendi aliquo modo, quod promisit sibi primatum super omnes. ex quo indefinite dixit, ecclesiam meam, non distinguendo inter hanc ecclesiam particularem & illam. An autem Christus eandem potestatem clauium tribuerit aliis apostolis, postea poterit (si tibi placebit) inquirere. Cum autem dicitur, quod Christus potestatem clauium non tradidit per hæc verba: tu es petrus. sed Ioh. 20. quando indifferenter omnib. dixit: Accipite spiritum sanctum: & quorum remiseritis &c. Respondetur iuxta præmissa. sup. c. 17. quod potestate clauium, quæ competit ratione ordinis, accepit Petrus simul cum aliis apostolis per verba præscripta Ioh. 20. aliam tamen potestatem accepit super apostolos, cum Christus sibi dixit: pasce oves meas. Cum vero dicitur: Esto quod Petrus his verbis potestatem hanc accepisset, non concluditur ex hoc, nisi quod tempore prius fuerit pastor institutus. Respondetur, quod si Petrus illis verbis: tu es petrus &c. potestatem aliquam recepisset, illam potestatem recepisset super eos, qui erant de ecclesia Christi, quia (sicut tactum est prius) in collatione potestatis super aliquos certi debent esse, super quos conferetur potestas. quia sicut prælatus debet esse certus, ita subditi debet esse certi. Cum ergo nec per illa verba, nec per quæcunq; præcedentia vel subsequentia apparear, ꝓ Christus aliquos de ecclesia sua specialiter exceperit seu exemerit: si per illa Petrus recepisset super aliquos de ecclesia Christi, eandem recepisset super omnes potestatem. Et ideo Christus per illa verba non solum significare voluit ecclesiæ vnitatem in fide: sed etiam vnitatem capitis præferendi ecclesiæ vniuersæ. Nec tantummodo tempore prius dotatur clauibus: & honoratur aut honorari promittitur, vt isti dicunt sibimetipsis in hoc etiam contradicendo, quia secundum eos simul tempore omnib. apostolis Christus contulit clauium potestatem. Sed per illa verba: tu es petrus &c. vltra clauium potestatem communem sibi & aliis apostolis, quæ eis ratione ordinis competebant, alia fuit sibi promissa potestas super omnes. & ideo per illa verba: tu es petrus &c. intellecta, vt ea intellexerunt apostoli & eorum discipuli, aperte convincitur, Petrum fuisse cæteris dignitate siue auctoritate superiorem. Et ideo Glossatores dicentes, non acceperunt hoc à se, sed à scriptura intellecta, vt eam intellexerunt apostoli. qui intellectus ab ipsis apostolis vsq; ad ipsos serie tractatorum, & scriptorum catholicorum sibimet succedentium, & asserentium ipsum, perueniit.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. How do you reply to the arguments of the aforesaid opponents, by which they strive to prove that Christ alone was the foundation of the Church? MASTER. To their first argument, where the interlinear Gloss is cited to prove that Christ seems to have retained for himself the dignity of the foundation, the answer is made by distinguishing the word "foundation." There is a foundation of the Church that is primary and principal, without which no Church can be founded, and this foundation is God alone, or Christ. There is also a secondary foundation of the Church, without which the Church could have been founded, though it was not in fact founded without it, and this foundation is neither God alone nor Peter alone. Rather, all the apostles were foundations of the Church, among whom, however, the blessed Peter was in some sense the more principal and universal foundation. The Gloss, however, speaks of the foundation in the first sense, and not in the second. Likewise, to the authority of Augustine taken from the Book of Retractations, the answer is that Augustine does not retract his statement about the apostle Peter, in which he affirmed that the Church was built on him as on a rock. He says rather that he had often explained it otherwise, so that by the rock is understood Christ, as the principal rock upon which the Church is chiefly built. For in the foundation of a material building a single stone is not always placed, but often several, one above another. So by this distinction of rocks the authorities of the holy Fathers, which seem to conflict, are reconciled. Augustine, therefore, by no means rejects, revokes or corrects his statement, but clarifies and affirms that the passage of Scripture he wished to expound can have another sense, which in no way contradicts the former sense. But by the aforesaid distinction the one must be reconciled with the other. For Augustine does not always reject or correct what he retracts; rather, he is said to retract certain things because he treats them again, explaining them and reconciling them with others. To the argument, which the aforesaid opponents often strive to prove, that the blessed Peter was not the foundation of the Church because the foundation of the Church cannot err or sin, the answer is that the principal foundation of the Church, without which the whole building would fall, or rather without which it could in no way be constructed, can neither sin nor err, nor could it have done so; and that foundation was Christ, not Peter. But the secondary foundation, without which the whole building of the Church could have been erected, could err and sin, although, insofar as it was actually a foundation in laying the foundation, it could not err or sin. For when Peter denied Christ, and when afterwards he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, he did not actually found the Church; but he who first after Christ, by preaching the truth, converted the apostles to the true faith, then founded the new Church. To the authority of the apostle in 1 Cor. 3, the answer is that the apostle there spoke of the principal foundation of the Church, not the secondary. And indeed no one can lay any other principal foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. It must be noted, however, according to some, as was said before, that it is a common manner of Scripture to deny something of those to whom it does not belong principally, though it belongs to them secondarily. Thus Christ said in Luke 18, "No one is good but God alone." So too of John the Baptist it is said: "He was not that light," John 1. And yet, as the apostles were light, Christ saying to them in Matt. 5, "You are the light of the world," so also the blessed John the Baptist was light. For he was "a burning and shining lamp," John 5. Therefore, when it is said that Christ did not seem to have given Peter the power of the keys by these words, "You are Peter," etc., the answer is that Christ did not then give Peter the power of the keys, but promised it; nor did he then set him over the other apostles, but promised that too. And therefore how and over whom he set him cannot finally be gathered from these words, "You are Peter," unless by referring them to the words by which he afterwards set him over them, namely, "Feed my sheep." Yet from these words, "Upon this rock I will build my Church," it can be shown in some way that he promised him primacy over all, since he said indefinitely "my Church," without distinguishing between this particular Church and that. Whether Christ afterwards gave the same power of the keys to the other apostles, you may (if you wish) inquire later. And when it is said that Christ did not give the power of the keys by these words, "You are Peter," but by John 20, when he said indifferently to all, "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive," etc., the answer is in accordance with what was said above in chapter 17: Peter received the power of the keys, which belongs by reason of office, together with the other apostles, through the words cited in John 20; but he received another power over the apostles when Christ said to him, "Feed my sheep." When it is said: Suppose that Peter had received this power by these words, it does not follow from this except that he was instituted as shepherd earlier in time. The answer is that if Peter had received some power by those words, "You are Peter," etc., he would have received it over those who were of the Church of Christ, because (as was touched upon before) in conferring power over some, those over whom the power is conferred must be certain; for just as the prelate ought to be certain, so ought the subjects to be certain. Since, therefore, it does not appear, either by those words or by any preceding or following words, that Christ specially excepted or exempted any from his Church, if Peter had received power by those words over some of the Church of Christ, he would have received the same power over all. And therefore Christ by those words meant not only to signify the unity of the Church in faith, but also the unity of the head who is to be set before the whole Church. Nor was he merely endowed with the keys earlier in time, and honoured, or promised to be honoured, as these men say, thereby contradicting themselves, since according to them Christ conferred the power of the keys on all the apostles at the same time. But by those words, "You are Peter," etc., beyond the power of the keys common to him and the other apostles, which belonged to them by reason of office, another power over all was promised to him. Therefore by those words, "You are Peter," etc., understood as the apostles and their disciples understood them, it is clearly proved that Peter was superior to the others in dignity or authority. And therefore the Glossators, who say this, did not take it from themselves but from Scripture understood as the apostles understood it; and this understanding has come down from the apostles themselves to us, through the series of catholic writers and teachers who succeeded one another and asserted it.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: Soluit residua motiua ca. 12. adducta.
units.tr: Solves the remaining arguments of the motive adduced in chapter 12.

units.la: DISCIP. Narra, qualiter respondetur ad allegationem sequentem. MAGIST. Ad illam allegationem, cum accipitur; ꝓ series euangelii, quæ habetur Matth. 20. & Luc. 22. vbi Christus hanc quæstionem diffinit, cum contentio esset inter eos, quis eorum esset maior. Et Matt. 23. cum dixit Christus, nolite vocari rabbi: ostendit nullum fuisse superiorem aliis. Respondetur dupliciter. vno modo, ꝓ omnia illa verba Christi intelligeda sunt pro tepore illo, quo dicta fuerunt à Christo & pro tempore ante exaltationem Petri super reliquos apostolos. Tunc enim solus Christus fuit prælatus omnium. & nullus apostolus fuit tunc prælatus, sed solummodo apostolus. Aliter dicitur, ꝓ Christus no intendebat imponere eis æqualitatem excludente superioritate prelationis, saltem pro tempore futuro, sed ipsos ad humilitate exhortas imponebat eis omne æqualitate excludentem omne superioritate superbæ, iniustæ, asperæ, & tyrannicæ potestatis. quemadmodu Sapiens Eccl. 33. Rectori superioritatem concedit, & quandam æqualitatem iniungit, cum dicit: rectore te posuerunt: noli extolli. esto in illu quasi vnus ex ipsis. Sicut et 3. c. maiori non solu æqualitatem, sed et quandam inferioritatem inducit, dicens: quanto magnus es, humilia te in omnib. humilitas enim quandam infirmitate importat. Sic etiam Christus exemplo sui, qui maior existens se minore exhibuit; maioribus, non solum æqualitatem, sed etiam minoritatem quandam suasit, dicens Luc. 22. Qui maior est in vobis, fiat sicut minor. & qui præcessor est, sicut ministrator. Nam quis maior est, qui recubit, an qui ministrat? nonne qui recubit? ego autem in medio vestrum sum, sicut qui ministrat. Christus igitur nec Mat. 20. nec Luc. 22. nec Mat. 23. omne superioritate plationis apostolis interdixit: sed ipsos ad humilitate induces omne superioritate iniusta & illicita, ac modu regedi fatuosum & iniquum amouit. Nec mouere debet, ꝓ Christi dixit Mat. 23. vos autem vos fratres estis: quasi omne æqualitate inter eos esse tenenda insinuas. Nam nec et inter fratres est omnimoda æqualitas observanda, sed sepissime expedit, vt vnus aliis præferatur, quemadmodum sæpe à Deo & sanctis viris in scripturis diuinis legimus fuisse factum. Cum vero accipitur, ꝓ mirandum est, si magis credere debeamus auctoritati Glossa. ꝓ Christi. Respondetur, ꝓ nemo magis debet credere cuiquam Glossa vel sancto, quam Christo: tamen sepe p viros sanctos, q glosas vel scripta alia ediderunt, præcipue per illos, qui ab apostolis instructi fuerūt, quis sit catholicus intellectus verborū Christi addiscimus. & ideo quandocunq; verba Christi possunt esse ambigua, plectenda est temeritas ab assertionibus & expositionibus huiusmodi virorum recedere, & interpretationi seu expositioni propriæ adhærere. DISC. Forte dicerent isti, quod verba Christi, quæ adducunt, non possunt esse ambigua. vbi autem verba non sunt ambigua, non est locus interpretationi, vt notat Glo. extr. de consuetudine, cum dilectus. MAGIST. Multis apparet, quod istud sit irrationabiliter dictum. Nam multa verba Christi, quæ apertiora videntur, possunt esse ambigua. ergo & ista possunt esse ambigua. & de prædictis constat, quod possunt esse ambigua, cum prædicti opinantes aliter ipsa intelligant, quam multi alii literati viri & intelligentes & qui expositionem per similia & multos alios modos ostendunt. DISC. Quid dicitur ad hoc, quod isti dicunt, multos Glossatores dicere opposītum. MAG. Respondetur, quod Glossatores nusquam dicunt oppositum si intelligantur sane.
units.tr: STUDENT. Tell me how one answers the following allegation. TEACHER. As for that allegation, when it is taken: "Pro" — the sequence of the Gospel, which is found in Matthew 20 and Luke 22, where Christ settles this question when there was contention among them as to which of them was the greater; and in Matthew 23, when Christ said, "Do not be called rabbi," he showed that none of them was superior to the others. It is answered in two ways. In one way: all those words of Christ are to be understood for that time in which they were spoken by Christ, and for the time before Peter's elevation above the other apostles. For then Christ alone was set over all, and no apostle was then set over the rest, but only an apostle. Otherwise it is said: Christ did not intend to impose on them an equality that excludes every superiority of rank, at least for the time to come, but he urged them to humility, imposing on them an equality that excludes every superiority of proud, unjust, harsh and tyrannical power. Just as the Wise Man in Ecclesiasticus 33 grants a ruler a superiority and enjoins a certain equality, when he says: "They have made you a ruler; do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them." Likewise in chapter 3 he brings in to the greater not only equality but a certain inferiority, saying: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, for humility brings with it a certain weakness." So also Christ, by his own example, since he who was greater showed himself as less, persuaded the greater not only towards equality but also towards a certain lesser state, saying in Luke 22: "Let him who is greater among you become as the less, and he who is the leader as the servant. For who is greater, he who sits at table, or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at table? But I am among you as one who serves." Christ therefore, neither in Matthew 20, nor Luke 22, nor Matthew 23, forbade the apostles all superiority of rank; but he led them to humility and removed every unjust and unlawful superiority, and the foolish and iniquitous manner of ruling. Nor ought it to disturb us that Christ said in Matthew 23, "But you are all brethren," as if he were suggesting that complete equality among them must be maintained. For not even among brethren is complete equality to be observed, but very often it is expedient that one be preferred to the others, just as we often read in the divine Scriptures that this was done by God and by holy men. But when it is objected, "It is to be wondered at if we ought to believe the authority of the Gloss rather than that of Christ," it is answered that no one ought to believe any Gloss or saint more than Christ; yet, through holy men who have published glosses or other writings, especially through those who were instructed by the apostles, we learn what the catholic sense of the words of Christ is; and therefore, whenever the words of Christ can be ambiguous, one must take care to depart from the assertions and expositions of such men and to adhere to one's own interpretation or exposition. STUDENT. Perhaps they would say that the words of Christ which they adduce cannot be ambiguous. But where words are not ambiguous, there is no room for interpretation, as the Gloss notes on Extra, de consuetudine, "cum dilectus." TEACHER. It appears to many that this is said without reason. For many words of Christ which seem clearer may be ambiguous; therefore these also may be ambiguous. And it is evident from the aforesaid that they can be ambiguous, since the aforesaid authors understand them otherwise than many other learned men and men of understanding, who also show the exposition by parallels and by many other methods. STUDENT. What is said in reply to what they say, that many Glossators say the opposite? TEACHER. It is answered that the Glossators nowhere say the opposite, if they are understood soundly.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Petri principatum super alios probat per illa verba Christi: Ego autem rogaui pro te Petre, vt non &c.
units.tr: That Peter's primacy over the others is proved by those words of Christ: "But I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail," etc.

units.la: DISCIP. Aliam allegationem pro prælatione Petri adducas. MAGIST. Hoc ostenditur Luc. 22. cum ad ipsum specialiter dixit Christus: Ego autem rogaui pro te Petre, vt non deficiat fides tua: sed tu aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. apostolorum ergo & aliorum fidelium prima cura pastoralis & confirmatio beato Petro commissa fuit propter suæ fidei firmitatem. pro qua ne deficeret, specialiter Christus orasse videtur, ne deficeret in ipso, neque in ipsius aliquo successore. confirma, inquit, fratres tuos, cum te principem apostolorum constituerim. Hoc autem non solum intelligendum est de apostolis, qui tunc erant, vt roborarentur à petra: sed etiam de omnibus fidelibus. Et paulum infra subdit: Per pœnitentiam obtinuit Petrus, scilicet vt esset antistes mundi. DISCIP. Responsionem præcedentium opinantium ad istam allegationem recitabo. dicunt itaque, quod ex verbis Christi inferri non potest, quod Christus Petrum, reliquorum apostolorum prælatum fecerit. Quod probatur per scripturam. Quia Paulus contulit Petro in euangelio non econtra. hoc autem per Gloss. probatur ibidem, quæ ait: sicut ego te orando protexi, ne deficeres: sic tu infirmiores fratres confirma, ne de venia desperent. intelligens per fratres indifferenter fideles. Quod dicens Petro, voluit alios apostolos intelligere facturos. unde Mat. 13. quod uni dico: vel secundum aliam literam, sensum tamen eundem, quod vobis dico, omnibus dico. An forsitan illud Petro singulariter dixit. Etiam Gloss. hoc sentire videtur. quoniam præsciebat Christus Petrum le negaturum, unde tu aliquando conuersus, id est exemplo tuæ pœnitentiæ, eo quod verbo & sui exemplo, qui veniam meruerat, infirmos in fide singularius confortare seu confirmare valeat. Hæc est eorum responsio, de qua cupio scire, an omnibus opinantibus contrarium appareat non valere. MAGIST. Videtur quibusdam apparentia non carere, quia, vt videtur, per illa verba Christi præcise nō posset ostendi, quod Christus fecerit beatum Petrum prælatum & principem aliorum. Et ideo si inueniantur sancti exponere verba illa de primatu Petri, tenendum est quidem, quod sensus ille est verus: non tamen tanquam sensus literalis verborum illorum Christi, sed tanquam sensus mysticus. cuius veritas ex aliis verbis Christi literaliter intellectis potest sufficienter ostendi.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Bring forward another argument for Peter's pre-eminence. MASTER. It is shown in Luke 22, where Christ spoke to him in particular: But I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers. Therefore the first pastoral care and the task of confirming the other apostles and the faithful were entrusted to blessed Peter on account of the firmness of his faith. Christ seems to have prayed especially that this faith might not fail, that it might not fail in him, nor in any of his successors. "Strengthen," He says, "your brothers, since I have made you prince of the apostles." This, however, is to be understood not only of the apostles who were then living, that they might be strengthened by the rock, but also of all the faithful. And a little further on he adds: Peter obtained, through repentance, that he should be the leader of the world. DISCIPLE. I will recite the reply of the earlier objectors to this argument. They say, then, that it cannot be inferred from Christ's words that Christ made Peter the superior of the other apostles. This is proved from Scripture, because Paul ascribed [precedence] to Peter in the Gospel, and not the reverse. This is also proved by the Gloss on the same passage, which says: As I protected you by praying that you might not fail, so you strengthen the weaker brothers, that they may not despair of pardon, understanding by "brothers" the faithful in general. In saying this to Peter, He meant that the other apostles would do the same. Hence Matthew 13: What I say to one, I say to all; or, according to another reading, with the same sense, What I say to you, I say to all. Or perhaps He said that to Peter alone? The Gloss also seems to hold this, since Christ foreknew that Peter would deny Him; hence "when you have turned back," that is, by the example of your repentance, since by word and by his own example, he who had merited pardon might be better able to comfort or strengthen the weak in faith. This is their reply, and I want to know whether it appears to all the objectors to be of no force. MASTER. It seems to some that it is not without plausibility, because, as it appears, it could not be shown from those words of Christ alone that Christ made blessed Peter the superior and prince of the others. Therefore, if holy men are found to expound those words of the primacy of Peter, it must indeed be held that this sense is true, but not as the literal sense of those words of Christ, rather as a mystical sense. The truth of this can be sufficiently shown from other words of Christ understood literally.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Primatum Petri vnica ratione probat, quæ multis sanctorum auctoritatibus fulcitur.
units.tr: He proves the primacy of Peter by a single argument, which is supported by the authority of many saints.

units.la: DISCIP. Adhuc aliquas sed paucas allegationes adducas ad probandū superioritatem Petri respectu aliorum apostolorum. MAGIST. Hoc tali modo probatur. Quod à temporibus apostolorum vsque ad tempora nostra prælati & doctores ecclesiæ, sibi continua serie succedentes, & populi eius subiecti senserunt, ab omnibus catholicis est tenendum firmiter. Hæc, scilicet maior, auctoritate Augustin. in libro contra Manicheos, & habetur in decretis dist. 11. c. palam, videtur aperte posse probari, cum dicit: Palam est, quod in re dubia ad fidem valeat auctoritas catholicæ ecclesiæ, quæ ab ipsis fundatissimis sedibus apostolorum vsq; ad hodiernum diem, succedentium sibimet episcoporum serie, & tot populorum consensione confirmatur. Quæ nihilominus (quia quidam dicunt, vt patet supra auctoritates aliorum, quam scriptorum scripturæ canonicæ & generalium conciliorū non esse recipiendas) ratione probatur. Nam etiam secundum contrarios vniuersalis ecclesia errare non potest. quare quod sensit & sentit vniuersalis ecclesia, firmiter est tenendū. vniuersalis autem ecclesia solummodo comprehendit prælatos ecclesiæ & populos sibi subiectos. quare & prælati ecclesiæ sibi continua serie succedentes, & populi sibi subiecti à temporib. apostolorum vsq; ad tempora nostra senserunt, firmiter est credendum. Sed prælati ecclesiæ ab ipsis vsq; ad hæc tempora cum populis subiectis sibi tenuerunt & senserunt, Petrum fuisse superiorem aliis apostolis. Hoc tenuit Anacletus papa (vt allegatum est sup.) qui in hoc veritatem non potuit ignorare. Beatus etiam Clemens papa apostolorum discipulus idem sensit. qui, vt habetur di. 80. ca. in illis, ait: Nec inter ipsos apostolos par fuit institutio: sed vnus præfuit omnibus & non alius quam Petrus. Hoc etiam sentit Eusebius Cæsariensis: qui, quia in doctrinis, traditionibus: & scripturis illorum, qui fuerunt discipuli apostolorum & à discipulis eisdem edocti, fuit imbutus, quid præcedentes senserint, minime ignorauit, de quo nullo modo præsumendum est, quod falsum scienter docuerit, cui nullus prælatorum ecclesiæ aut doctorum postea contradixit: & per consequens omnes tacendo consenserunt eidem, ait itaque in Ecclesiastica historia, quam transtulit beatus Hieronymus, lib. 2. capitulo decimoquarto. Claudii temporibus clementia diuina prouidentia probatissimum omnium Apostolorum maximum fidei magnificentia & virtutum merito primorum principem Petrum ad urbem velut animaduersum humanigeneris communem pernitiem repugnaturum deducit quendam & magistrum militiæ suæ scientem diuina pra-lia gerere & virtutum castra ducere. Hoc sentit beatus Hieronymus, & Ambrosius, beatus Augustin. beatus Marcellus Papa, beatus Cyprianus, sicut per auctoritates ipsorum in locis diuersis superius allegatis patet expresse. Ab omni autem verisimilitudine alienum videtur, quod prædicti viri scripturarum canonicarum, historiarum, cronicarum, gestorum, consuetudinum, & traditionum vniuersalis ecclesiæ diligentissimi scrutatores nescierunt, quid circa rem tam necessariam toti ecclesiæ Christi senserint Apostoli & discipuli eorundem, de quibus etiam est nullatenus præsumendum, quod scienter falsum tenuerint, quare tenendum est, quod assertio supradicta ab ipsis Apostolis per cronicas & historias fide dignas, quarum nos fortassis aliquas non habemus, & per traditionem & consuetudinem vniuersalis ecclesiæ usque ad ipsos continuatam ad eosdem peruenit. Assertionem autem suprascriptam tenuerunt omnes alii prælati & doctores ecclesiæ a temporibus beati Syluestri usque ad tempora nostra, sicut multipliciter posset ostendi. Præmissis autem prælatis & doctoribus in eadem assertione catholici populi consenserunt: quia nullus inuentus est populus catholicus, qui contradiceret eis, ergo hæc assertio est vniuersali ecclesiæ tribuenda, & per consequens firmiter est tenenda.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Let me adduce some further, though few, allegations to prove Peter's superiority over the other apostles. MASTER. It is proved in this way. That what the prelates and teachers of the Church, succeeding one another in unbroken sequence from the times of the apostles until our own, and the peoples subject to them have held, must be firmly held by all Catholics. This major premise, on the authority of Augustine in his book Against the Manichaeans, and found in the Decretum, dist. 11, c. Palam, can clearly be proved, since he says: "It is plain that in a matter of doubt the authority of the Catholic Church bears weight for faith, which has been confirmed from the most firmly founded sees of the apostles down to the present day, by the succession of bishops following one another, and by the consent of so many peoples." Yet since some say, as appears above, that the authorities of others are not to be received as those of the writers of canonical Scripture and of the general councils, this is proved by reason. For even according to our opponents the universal Church cannot err. Therefore what the universal Church has thought and thinks must be firmly held. But the universal Church comprises only the prelates of the Church and the peoples subject to them. Therefore the prelates of the Church, succeeding one another in unbroken sequence, and the peoples subject to them, from the times of the apostles until our own, have thought this, and must be firmly believed to have done so. But the prelates of the Church, from the apostles down to these times, together with the peoples subject to them, have held and thought that Peter was superior to the other apostles. Pope Anacletus held this (as was alleged above), and he could not be ignorant of the truth in this matter. Likewise Pope Clement, a disciple of the apostles, thought the same, who, as is found in Dist. 80, c. In illis, says: "Among the apostles themselves the institution was not equal, but one presided over all, and no other than Peter." Eusebius of Caesarea also holds this. Since he was steeped in the doctrines, traditions and writings of those who were disciples of the apostles and taught by those same disciples, he was by no means ignorant of what the earlier writers thought; and it is in no way to be presumed that he knowingly taught something false. No prelate or teacher of the Church afterwards contradicted him, and consequently all, by keeping silent, agreed with him. So he says in his Ecclesiastical History, which blessed Jerome translated, book 2, chapter 14: "In the time of Claudius, by the merciful providence of God, Peter, the most approved of all the apostles, the greatest in the magnificence of his faith and the first in the merit of his virtues, was brought to the city, as one who would oppose the common ruin of the human race, like a champion, skilled to wage the divine battles and lead the camps of virtue." Blessed Jerome, Ambrose, blessed Augustine, blessed Pope Marcellus and blessed Cyprian also hold this, as is plainly shown by their authorities alleged in various places above. Moreover, it seems utterly unlikely that these men, most diligent investigators of the canonical Scriptures, histories, chronicles, deeds, customs and traditions of the universal Church, did not know what the apostles and their disciples thought, for the whole Church of Christ, on so necessary a matter. Nor is it in any way to be presumed that they knowingly held something false. Therefore it must be held that the aforesaid assertion has come down from the apostles themselves, through trustworthy chronicles and histories, some of which we perhaps do not have, and through the tradition and custom of the universal Church continued from them. Moreover, all the other prelates and teachers of the Church, from the time of blessed Sylvester to our own, held the aforesaid assertion, as could be shown in many ways. And the Catholic people, with the prelates and teachers, agreed in this same assertion, since no Catholic people has been found that contradicted them. Therefore this assertion is to be ascribed to the universal Church, and consequently must be firmly held.

units.la: Discipulus.
units.tr: Disciple.

units.la: Forte dicent aliqui, quod non omnes populi Christiani hoc sen-serunt, nam fertur, quod Græci, qui fuerunt Christiani & catholici, antequam Romani, hoc non tenent, & ita non omnes populi Christiani hoc usque ad tempora nostra crediderunt. Magister. Hæc responsio ab aliis impugnatur. Nam Græci, dum erant catholici, doctorum catholicorum sequentes doctrinam in hoc consenserunt. Non enim legitur & videtur probabile, quod populus Græcorum, antequam diuiderentur a Romana ecclesia, secutus non fuerit doctrinam catholicorum doctorum, doctores autem ipsorum assertionem prædictam publice docuerunt, & reliquerunt in scriptis. Eusebius enim Cæsariensis, qui Græcus fuit, & in scriptis omnium doctorum Græcorum peritus (vt ex Ecclesiastica historia, quam composuit, liquido patet) hoc docuit & scripsit, vt ex supradictis patet, ergo Græci, dum erant Catholici, prædictam sententiam tenuerunt. Errores autem ipsorum postquam se a Romana ecclesia diuiserunt, allegationem prædictam nullo modo impediunt, quare secundum Latinos tenendum est, quod Petrus omnibus aliis erat superior. Discipulus. Aliter forte aliqui responderent ad allegationem prædictam, dicentes quod quamuis omnes populi Christiani consenserint prælatis & doctoribus fidei in assertione præscripta, non tamen omnes de populo, ergo allegatio antescripta non procedit. Magister. Ista responsio per hoc refellitur, quia secundum Apostolum ad Roman. 8. Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem: quando scilicet periclitatur fides. Non sufficeret igitur aliquibus paucis de populo corde tenuisse assertionem contrariam, si esset catholica, nisi etiam ipsam ore publice contradicendo errantibus confessi suissent. Cum ergo non legatur, quod a temporibus Apostolorum vel discipulorum eorundem vsque ad tempora Patrum nostrorum, quicunque etiam pauci de populis Christianis assertioni publice contradixerunt memoratæ: tenendum est, quod eadem assertio vniuersali ecclesiæ debet ascribi, vniuersalis autem ecclesia nullo tempore, etiam paruo, errare potest contra fidem, & in his quæ iuris sunt pertinentia ad fidem vel bonos mores: licet secundum quosdam in his, quæ facti sunt, scilicet habendo aliquem pro Papa vel bono viro, licet non sit, & in consimilibus possit errare, ergo prædicta assertio firmiter est credenda.
units.tr: Perhaps some will say that not all Christian peoples thought this, for it is reported that the Greeks, who were Christians and Catholics before the Romans, did not hold it, and so not all Christian peoples have believed it down to our own times. MASTER. This reply is refuted by others. For while the Greeks were Catholics, they followed the doctrine of the Catholic teachers and agreed with them in this. For it is not read, and it seems probable, that the people of the Greeks, before they were separated from the Roman Church, did not follow the doctrine of the Catholic teachers; and their teachers publicly taught the aforesaid assertion and left it in their writings. For Eusebius of Caesarea, who was a Greek and well versed in the writings of all the Greek teachers (as is clear from the Ecclesiastical History that he composed), taught and wrote this, as appears from what was said above. Therefore the Greeks, while they were Catholics, held the aforesaid opinion. Their errors after they separated themselves from the Roman Church in no way hinder the allegation above; therefore, according to the Latins, it must be held that Peter was superior to all the other apostles. DISCIPLE. Perhaps some would answer the allegation differently, saying that although all Christian peoples agreed with the prelates and teachers of the faith in the aforesaid assertion, not all of the people did, and so the aforesaid allegation does not hold. MASTER. This reply is refuted by the fact that, according to the Apostle in Romans 8, "with the heart man believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation": namely, when the faith is in danger. It would not suffice that a few of the people held the contrary assertion in their hearts, if it were Catholic, unless they had also openly confessed it with their mouths by publicly contradicting those in error. Since, therefore, it is not read that from the times of the apostles, or of their disciples, down to the times of our fathers, any of the Christian peoples, even a few, publicly contradicted the aforesaid assertion, it must be held that this assertion ought to be ascribed to the universal Church. The universal Church, however, can at no time, not even a short one, err against the faith, or in those matters that pertain to law, to the faith or to good morals; although, according to some, it can err in matters of fact, such as holding someone to be the Pope or a good man when he is not, and in similar things. Therefore the aforesaid assertion is to be firmly believed.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Principatum Petri vnica ratione probat, quae est in his, quae sunt fidei & morum fun- data. Eamque vna confirmatione corroborat.
units.tr: He proves the primacy of Peter by a single reason, one founded on matters of faith and morals, and he strengthens it by one confirmation.

units.la: Discip. Adhuc pro ratione, fundata tamen in his quæ sunt fidei morum, conare probare, quod Petrus fuit cæteris Apostolis ex ordinatione Christi superior. Mag. Videtur quibusdam hoc tali modo posse probari. Christus ab Apostolis & ecclesia corporaliter recessurus instituit caput & rec-torem ecclesiæ vniuersalis: qui secundum optimum modum regiminis ecclesiam gubernaret. Christus n. qui ecclesiæ suæ in necessariis non deficit, ecclesiam suam acephalam non reliquit, nā habere caput est inter cætera maxime necessarium ecclesiæ, ergo Christus aliquod caput dedit ecclesiæ, non autem instituit caput ecclesiæ seu rectorem secundum debiliorem seu minus perfectum modum regiminis, ne facto videretur præcepisse ecclesiæ, q caput secundum optimum modum regiminis minime sustinerent, cum omnis Christi actio sit nostra instructio, optimus autem modus regiminis est regimen vnius, vt vnus oēs alios regat, quia talis modus regedi maxime principatui regali, qui est optimus secundum philosophos in hoc nō errantes: & principatui paterno, qui est naturalis, assimilatur, ergo Christus vnū caput dedit vniuersali ecclesiæ, & nō plura, non aut alium, q Petrum, quia nunq aliquis catholicus tenuit, q aliquis alius Apostolus, vel nō Apostolus, fuit caput & princeps aliorū Apostolorū. Hæc allegatio cōfirmatur, quia Christus fecit Apostolos capita, pastores & rectores aliorum fi-delium, delium, etiam secundum aduersarios, sicut per praefationem Apostolorum, q; allegant, aperte patet, aut ergo praefecit aliquod caput collegio Apostolorum: & habetur intentum, quia nullum alium praefecit illi q; Petrum, aut nullum caput praefecit Apostolorum collegio: q; absurdum videtur, quia ex hoc plures absurditates sequerentur. Quarum prima est, quod Christus collegium Apostolorum reliquisset acephalum. Secunda est, q; vniuersalem ecclesiam non secundum dispositionem optimam ordinassset: quia tunc solum o est aliqua societas seu communitas optime ordinata, qu̅ habet vnum caput, & regitur ab vno, & non a pluribus, eo quod simpliciter melius est regi ab vno, q; a plurib. etiam optimis, quemadmodum principatus regalis secundum Philosophum est principatui aristocratico praeferendus. Tertia est, quod Christus ex hoc ecclesiam docuisset, nec vni praelato, nec vni collegio debere subesse, quia Christus non praefecit Apostolos aliis fidelibus tanquam collegium, sed tanquam singulares personas, dispergendi enim erant Apostoli in vniuersum orbem ad regendum fideles minime congregandi, & ideo tanquam collegium non regebant. Cum enim aliqui aliquid faciunt, tanquam collegium, simul esse debent. Si ergo Christus Petrum non praefecit vniuersali ecclesiae, & multominus aliquem alium Apostolum: sed solummodo praefecit Apostolos tanquam singulares personas, exemplum dedit ecclesiae, vt nec vni praelato, nec vni collegio obedirer.
units.tr: Disciple. Still, for a reason that is founded on matters of faith and morals, try to prove that Peter was, by Christ's appointment, superior to the other Apostles. Master. To some people this seems provable in the following way. When Christ was about to leave the Apostles and the Church in bodily form, he appointed a head and ruler of the universal Church, who would govern the Church in the best possible way. For Christ, who does not fail his Church in necessary things, did not leave his Church without a head, since having a head is among the most necessary things for the Church. Therefore Christ gave the Church a head, and he did not appoint a head or ruler of the Church according to a weaker or less perfect mode of government. Otherwise it would seem that by his deed he had commanded the Church that it should not sustain a head governing in the best way. For every action of Christ is our instruction. The best mode of government, however, is the rule of one, so that one governs all the others. Such a mode of ruling is most like royal government, which the philosophers, who do not err on this point, consider the best, and like paternal government, which is natural. Therefore Christ gave the universal Church one head and not several, and not another than Peter, since no Catholic has ever held that any other Apostle, or any non-Apostle, was the head and prince of the other Apostles. This argument is confirmed because Christ made the Apostles heads, pastors and rulers of the other faithful, even according to our adversaries, as is clearly shown by the preface of the Apostles, which they allege. Therefore either he set some head over the college of Apostles, and the point is established, since he set no one over them other than Peter, or he set no head over the college of Apostles. This seems absurd, because several absurdities would follow from it. The first is that Christ would have left the college of Apostles without a head. The second is that he would not have arranged the universal Church in the best manner.
