For only that society or community is best ordered which has one head and is ruled by one and not by several, because it is simply better to be ruled by one than by many, even good ones, just as, according to the Philosopher, royal government is to be preferred to aristocratic government. The third is that Christ would thereby have taught the Church that it ought to be subject neither to one prelate nor to one college. For Christ did not set the Apostles over other believers as a college, but as individual persons, since the Apostles were to be scattered throughout the whole world to rule the faithful, and were not to be gathered together. Therefore they did not rule as a college. For when some people do something as a college, they ought to be together. If then Christ did not set Peter over the universal Church, and much less any other Apostle, but set the Apostles over it only as individual persons, he gave the Church an example that it should obey neither one prelate nor one college.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: Praecedentis capituli rationem duplici impugnat ratione, sed utrique rationi respondet.
units.tr: He refutes the reasoning of the preceding chapter in a twofold objection, but answers both arguments.

units.la: Dicta forte aliqui impugnarent. Primo: quia licet regimen vnius de se sit optimum, tamen aliquando per accidens & in casu non est optimum, quia quando sunt plures aequales, vel nullus omnes alios meritis & sapientia excedit, non expedit, vt vnus omnibus aliis praesit. Hoc (vt quibusdam videtur) ex multis quae allegata sunt secundo huius potest aperte probari, quod Petrus meritis & sapientia omes alios nullatenus praecellebat. Sapientia enim videtur minor fuisse Paulo. Meritis autem Iohanne videtur fuisse inferior. Ergo communitas fidelium non fuit optime ordinata, si Petrus fuisset a Christo caeterorum Apostolorum & omnium fidelium caput institutus. Amplius, Christus recedens corporaliter ab ecclesia, ipsam in optima conditione reliquit, quantum permittit haec vita, sed melius est, vt ecclesia habeat potestatem mutandi modum regendi quandocunq; expedit, qua quod alligetur determinato modo regendi, eo quod quilibet modus regendi in pluribus casibus potest esse nocius vel minus vtilis, quemadmodum principatus regalis, qui est vnius, quamuis de se sit optimus, tamen in multis casibus magis expedit, quod plures principentur aristocratice, quam vnus regaliter. Christus ergo non dedit vnum caput ecclesiae nec Petrum, nec alium; sed dedit ecclesiae potestatem instituendi sibi vnum caput vel plura, secundum quod ei expedire videtur. Mag. Ad primum istorum respondetur, q; licet regulariter non expedit, vt vnus principetur pro tota vita sua sibi aequalibus: nec principatus vnius ih tali casu sit regulariter optimus: tn casualiter potest principatus vnius esse optimus. In tali casu, sc. si inequales sint tales, quod de eis probabiliter presumatur, quod prompte ac sponte seu voluntarie in omnibus licitis & iustis, prout expedit, velint obedire vni: licet etiam sit meritis & sapientia minor. Causa enim secundum aliquos, quare non expedit, vt aliquis principetur sibi similibus & aequalibus, est: ne subiecti valeant dicere colorate, iniustum est aequalem eis dominari, & ipsos subesse, haec autem causa locum non habet, si aequales vel maiores ex humilitate vel obedientia aut amore rei publicae vel communis vtilitatis, prompte & sponte velint subesse. Apostoli autem scientes ordinationem Christi ex humilitate & obedientia, promptissimi erant obedire Petro pro toto tempore vitae suae. Et ideo licet Apostoli etiam omnes fuissent aequales vel maiores Petro: melius fuit, vt ipse praeesset aliis Apostolis & vniuersis fidelibus, quam vt praeessent plures. De aliis enim ab Apostolis, & maxime illis, qui proni erant ad dissensionem & inobedientiam, planum apparet, quod Petrus meritis & sapientia praecessit eos, & ideo debuerunt rationabiliter esse subiecti. Ad secundum respondetur, quod Christus instituendo Petrum, caput omnium fidelium ecclesiam suam in optima dispositione, quo ad genus regendi reliquit: quia eligendo & praeficiendo vnum cunctis fidelibus, facto docuit ecclesiam, quod optimum genus regendi, vt scil. sit vnum caput & rector omnium, debet omnino seruare, si potest absque detrimento boni communis. Plus autem profuit ecclesiae, quod Christus, qui sciuit certissime, quis esset magis idoneus ad regendum, praefecit Petrum: q; si ecclesia, quae non nisi per coniecturam scire potuit maiorem idoneitatem ipsius, elegisset eundem. Christus itaq; (secundum quosdam) praeficiendo vnum, alligauit ecclesiam suam optimo generi regiminis extra casum manifestae necessitatis & vtilitatis. Praeficiendo aut non quemcunq; vnum, sed Petrum, qui vel in ecclesia simpliciter optimus inter omnes, vel optimus & maxime idoneus est ad regendum: innuit facto, quod non totaliter ecclesiam suam optimo generi obligauit: quin in casu manifestae necessitatis vel vtilitatis posset illum modum regendi omittere vel mutare, nullum scilicet eligendo, vel eligendo plures, si id communitati fidelium manifeste expediret, vel aliquod illorum facere cogeretur. Sicut aliquando oportuit fideles dimittere per plures annos vacare Apostolicam sedem. Vnde sicut legitur in Legenda sancti Marcellini Papae & martyris, temporibus Diocletiani & Maximiniani Imperatorum, quod post mortem praedicti Marcellini Papae seueritate persecutionis per praefatos imperatores in Christianos agitante, vacauit sedes Apostolica annis septem mensibus sex, diebus viginti quinque. Cessante tamen necessitate, vel vtilitate, ad optimum modum regendi, (vt vnus sit caput vniuersalis & rector) redire tenentur, & ideo Christus praficiendo Petrum omnibus, ecclesiam suam, quo ad genus regiminis in optima dispositione reliquit.
units.tr: Perhaps some would object to what has been said. First: although the rule of one is in itself the best, yet at times, by accident and in particular circumstances, it is not the best. When there are several who are equal, or when no one surpasses all the others in merit and wisdom, it is not expedient that one should preside over all the rest. This (as some think) can be clearly proved from many things already alleged. For Peter was in no way superior to all the others in merit and wisdom. Paul seems to have been wiser than he, and John seems to have been inferior to him in merit. Therefore the community of the faithful would not have been best ordered if Peter had been appointed by Christ as head of the other Apostles and of all the faithful. Moreover, when Christ withdrew bodily from the Church, he left it in the best condition that this life allows. But it is better that the Church should have the power of changing the mode of governing whenever it is expedient, rather than being bound to a fixed mode of governing, because any mode of governing can be more harmful or less useful in many cases. Just as royal rule, which is the rule of one, though in itself the best, is in many cases more expedient when several govern aristocratically than when one governs as a king. Christ therefore did not give the Church one head, neither Peter nor anyone else, but gave the Church the power of establishing for itself one head or several, as it seems expedient to it. Master: To the first of these objections the answer is this. Although it is not usually expedient that one should rule for his whole life over those who are equal to him, and the rule of one is not usually the best in such a case, yet in a particular case the rule of one can be the best. Such a case is one in which the inferiors are such that it may reasonably be presumed of them that they will obey the one promptly and willingly in all things that are lawful and just, as expedient, even though he is less in merit and wisdom. For some hold that the reason why it is not expedient for someone to preside over those like and equal to himself is this: that the subjects might be able to say, with some pretext, that it is unjust for an equal to rule over them and for them to be subject. But this reason has no place if equals or greater men are willing, out of humility or obedience, or out of love for the commonwealth or for the common advantage, to submit promptly and willingly. Now the Apostles, knowing Christ's ordinance, were, out of humility and obedience, most ready to obey Peter for the whole of their lives. And therefore, even if all the Apostles had been equal to Peter or greater than him, it was better that he should preside over the other Apostles and all the faithful than that several should preside. For it is plain from the other Apostles, and especially from those who were prone to dissension and disobedience, that Peter surpassed them in merit and wisdom, and so they ought reasonably to have been subject to him. To the second objection the answer is that by appointing Peter as head of all the faithful, Christ left his Church in the best disposition as to the kind of government. For by choosing and setting one man over all the faithful, he taught the Church by deed that the best kind of government, namely that there be one head and ruler of all, ought to be wholly maintained, if this can be done without harm to the common good. Moreover, it was more to the advantage of the Church that Christ, who knew most certainly who was most fit to rule, appointed Peter, than if the Church, which could know his greater fitness only by conjecture, had chosen him. Therefore Christ (according to some) by setting one man over the Church bound his Church to the best kind of government, except in a case of manifest necessity and advantage. But by setting over it not just any one man, but Peter, who was either simply the best of all in the Church or the best and most fit to rule, he indicated by the deed that he had not bound his Church wholly to the best kind of government, so that in a case of manifest necessity or advantage it could omit or change that mode of governing, either by choosing no one or by choosing several, if this was manifestly expedient for the community of the faithful, or if it were forced to do one of these things. Thus it has sometimes been necessary for the faithful to allow the Apostolic see to be vacant for several years. As is read in the Legend of Saint Marcellinus, Pope and martyr, in the times of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, after the death of the aforesaid Pope Marcellinus, when the severity of the persecution stirred up against the Christians by the said emperors was raging, the Apostolic see was vacant for seven years, six months and twenty-five days. Yet when the necessity or advantage ceases, they are bound to return to the best mode of governing, namely that there be one head and ruler of the whole Church. And therefore, by setting Peter over all, Christ left his Church in the best disposition as to the kind of government.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Solutis rationes, quibus probatur capitulo primo, quod Christus non instituit Petrum super alios Apostolos.
units.tr: Answers to the arguments by which it is proved in chapter one that Christ did not set Peter above the other Apostles.

units.la: Discipulus. Puto, quod si praedicta, quibus ostenditur, quod Petrus fuisset superior aliis Apostolis, possent solui, omnia alia quae pro eodem allegari possunt, de facili refelli valerent, ideo causa breuitatis omissis aliis, qualiter illa assertio ad allegationes, quae supra prim. cap. huius quarti sunt inductae, respondeat, non differas indicare. Magister. Ad primam illarum, quae de potestate conficiendi corpus Christi procedit. Respondetur, quod potestas conficiendi corpus Christi omnibus Apostolis, quos Christus ante passionem suam elegit, data fuit immediate a Christo: quia ipse eos sacerdotes ordinauerat: & quantum ad hanc potestatem, omnes Apostoli erant pares. Quemadmodum nunc omnes sacerdotes in hoc sunt Apostolico pares: licet ex causa valeat Apostolicus sacerdotibus interdicere executionem huius potestatis. Ad aliam de potestate clauiū dicitur a quibusdam, quod Apostoli omnes ex speciali priuilegio Christi fuerunt pares B. Petro in quantum claues peccata specialiter in foro poenitentiali respiciunt: in aliis autem fuerunt inferiores eo. Christus ergo, quando dixit omnibus Apostolis: sicut misit me Pater, &c. tanquam praelatus & superior Petro, omnes etiam misit, & omnibus potestatem dedit super peccata, quos tamen postea B. Petro subiecit: absq; tamen reuocatione illorum, quae eis in speciali concesserat. Et ideo quamuis tunc non dixerit Petro: mitto te, & tu alios mitte: quia tunc non fecit eum praelatum aliorum, tamen postea cum dixit: pasce oues meas: dedit ei potestatem mittendi alios, qui non erant specialiter missi a Christo: quos tamen ex causa iusta & necessaria posset certis prouinciis deputare. Ad aliam allegationem sumptam ex verbis Pauli ad Gal. 2. respondetur, quod intentio Pauli, cum dicit; mihi enim qui videbantur aliquid esse, nihil contulerunt, &c. fuit, quod Paulus quantum ad doctrinam, non fuit inferior Petro, neq; reliquis Apostolis, nec fuit primo missus ad praedicandum a Petro, quia antea praedicauit tanquam immediate missus a Christo, cum quo tamen stat, quod in aliis fuit inferior Petro. Et ideo conceditur, q; officium praedicandi, siue Apostolatus, Paulus non suscepit a Petro, sed ex hoc non sequitur, quod Petrus non fuit praelatus eius. Sicut multi religiosi praedicatores verbi Dei tempore Clementis Papae V. vel Bonifacii VIII. non habuerunt officium praedicandi a Bonifacio Papa vel Clemente: & tamen Bonifacius Papa, aut Clemens fuit praelatus eorum, quia habuerunt officium praedicandi a praedecessore vel praedecessoribus. Si Paulus recepit officium praedicandi a praedecessore Petri, sc. Christo. Ad auctoritatem ibidem adductam secundum August. respondetur: quia secundum Augustin. Petrus & alii Apostoli, qui fuerunt cum Domino, nihil contulerunt, id est addiderunt Paulo, quantum ad doctrinam euangelicam. Et ideo in doctrina non fuit inferior Petro ac aliis Apostolis, quia a Domino fuit ita perfectus in doctrina, quod perfectioni suae doctrinae nihil addere potuerunt. Qui tamen, quo ad multa alia sibi addere valuerunt: sicut & de facto addiderunt, cum dederunt sibi & Barnabae dexteras societatis. Inferioritas ergo, quam negat Augustinus a Paulo, est solummodo inferioritas doctrinae euangelicae, de qua loquitur ibi Paulus. Et ideo conceditur illud, quod isti concludunt, quod quodammodo aeque principaliter missus fuit Paulus, quemadmodum & Petrus, sc. ad praedicandum, quia quando primo fuit missus ad praedicandum, non fuit missus neque a Petro, neque ab aliquo alio homine. Et hoc intendit Apostolus, cum dicit 1. cap. Paulus Apostolus non ab hominibus, neque per hominem, &c. Et sic dicitur intelligen da Glossa Ambrosii ibidem allegata, quia tunc Apostolus non fuit missus ab Ananía, neque ab aliquo alio puro homine. Ex qua Glossa notatur, quod Apostolus loquitur ibidem de sua prima missione, quando aliqui poterant putare eum missum fuisse ab Anania, a quo tunc extitit baptizatus. Et sic etiam de prima missione dicitur intelligenda Glossa, quae idem secundum Augustin. consequenter adducitur, quia Paulus tunc non fuit missus ab aliquo homine mortali, sicut caeteri Apostoli: sed a Christo, qui tunc extitit immortalis, & secundum hoc habuit quandam praerogatiuam supra alios: quorum tamen non erat praelatus. Et ideo ex verbis Augustini non potest ostendi, quod Paulus auctoritate fuit superior Petro, quamuis dicat, quod Paulus fuerit dignior, ita ex eodem non potest ostendi, quod non fuerit inferior auctoritate. Quare a simili licet inueniatur dictum a sanctis, q; Paulus fuerit par Petro: non potest tñ inueniri, quod Paulus fuerit par quantum ad praelationem. Quia sufficit, q; fuerit par, quantū ad aliqua alia: puta quantum ad doctrinā & auctoritatē praedicandi in hoc, q; non habuit primo auctoritate praedicandi a Petro, nec mediate, nec immediate, sed a Christo, & quo ad alia plura. Quia sicut nō omnes, qui dicūtur similes, in omnib. sunt similes, sic nec oēs qui dicuntur pares, sunt pares in omnibus. Et eodem modo respondetur ad auctoritatem aliā Apostoli, cum dicit: Notum vobis facio euangelium, &c. quia ex hoc sequitur, q; Paulus immediate missus fuit a Christo: quē nec Petrus, nec alius Apostolus tunc elegit, nam Christus tm misit aut iniunxit Paulo ministerii euangelii, sed ex hoc nō sequitur, q; non fuit subiectus Petro. Quemadmodū ex hoc, quod Deus immediate saepe misit Esaiā, & alios prophetas ad praedicandū, & increpādum idolatras & alios impios, inferri non pōt, quod nō fuerint auctoritate inferiores sūmo Pontifice, aut supremo rectore populi Israelitici. Qualem aūt potestatē, & in quib. habuerit Petrus super Paulum & alios Apostolos, postea valebis inquirere. Ad aliam allegationem, quae in hoc consistit, quod non inuenitur in scriptura Petrum sibi assumpsisse aliquale potestatem super ceteros Apostolos: sed magis cum ipsis aequalitatem seruasse. Respondetur, quod multa fecerunt Apostoli, quae non reperiuntur in Biblia: quorum tamen multa, licet non omnia, ad nos per scripturas discipulorum Apostolorum, & aliorum fidelium peruenerunt. Et ideo licet ex scripturis canonicis contra proteruos, efficaciter non posset conuinci, quod Petrus usus fuit auctoritate sibi concessa super Apostolos, sed magis de facto aequalitatem seruauit: non tamen propter hoc esset dicendum, ipsum non fuisse huiusmodi usum potestatis. Nec ex hoc, quod legitur aliquando ipsum seruasse aequalitate cum aliis, potest inferri, quod nunquam sua fuerit usus auctoritate seu potestate, quia sancti praelati saepe exemplo Christi, qui praelatus existens venit ministrare, suam potestatem nequaquam exercent: sed tanquam serui, vel etiam inferiores se exhibent sibi subiectis. An autem assumpserit sibi auctoritate determinandi illa, quae erant dubia circa euangelium, vel voluerit in hoc deferre Iacobo, aut toti collegio, cuius erat pars, postea poterimus inuestigare. Quod enim saltem toti collegio poterit fidelium in hoc deferre aut etiam tenebatur, multi tenentes praelatum fuisse vniuersorum concedunt: quia vt multi dicunt, in causa fidei summus praelatus fidelium est inferior vniuersali ecclesia, & etiam concilio generali.
units.tr: Student. I think that if the points by which it is shown that Peter was superior to the other Apostles can be answered, then all the other arguments that can be brought forward on the same question could easily be refuted. So, to keep things brief and leaving the rest aside, please do not delay in showing how that assertion answers the arguments introduced above in the first chapter of this fourth book. Master. Take first the argument based on the power of consecrating the body of Christ. The answer is that the power of consecrating the body of Christ was given immediately by Christ to all the Apostles whom he chose before his passion, because he had ordained them priests, and in respect of this power all the Apostles were equal. In the same way, all priests are now equal to the Apostolic priest in this respect, although the Apostolic priest may, for good reason, forbid priests to exercise this power. As for the argument about the power of the keys, some say that all the Apostles, by a special privilege of Christ, were equal to blessed Peter insofar as the keys concern sins especially in the forum of penance, but in other respects they were inferior to him. Therefore Christ, when he said to all the Apostles, "As the Father has sent me," etc., sent them all as one who was prelate and superior to Peter, and gave them all power over sins; yet he afterwards subjected them to blessed Peter, without revoking what he had specially granted to them. And so, although at that time he did not say to Peter, "I send you, and you send the others," because then he did not make him prelate of the others, nevertheless afterwards, when he said, "Feed my sheep," he gave him power to send others who had not been specially sent by Christ, though for a just and necessary cause he could assign them to certain provinces. As for the other argument, taken from the words of Paul in Galatians 2, the answer is that Paul's intention, when he says, "For those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me," etc., was that Paul, as to doctrine, was not inferior to Peter or to the other Apostles, nor was he first sent to preach by Peter, because earlier he had preached as one immediately sent by Christ; yet this agrees with the fact that in other respects he was inferior to Peter. Hence it is granted that Paul did not receive the office of preaching, or apostleship, from Peter; but it does not follow from this that Peter was not his prelate. Just as many religious preachers of the word of God in the time of Pope Clement V or Boniface VIII did not have the office of preaching from Pope Boniface or Clement, and yet Pope Boniface or Clement was their prelate, because they had the office of preaching from a predecessor or predecessors. If Paul received the office of preaching from a predecessor of Peter, namely Christ. As for the authority cited there according to Augustine, the answer is that, according to Augustine, Peter and the other Apostles who were with the Lord "contributed nothing," that is, they added nothing to Paul as regards evangelical doctrine. Therefore in doctrine he was not inferior to Peter and the other Apostles, because he had been made so perfect in doctrine by the Lord that they could add nothing to the perfection of his teaching. Yet they could add to him in many other respects, and in fact they did so, when they gave him and Barnabas "the right hands of fellowship." The inferiority, then, which Augustine denies of Paul is only the inferiority of evangelical doctrine, of which Paul speaks there. Hence it is granted what they conclude, that Paul was sent in a certain way equally principally, just as Peter was, namely to preach, because when he was first sent to preach he was sent neither by Peter nor by any other man. This is what the Apostle means when he says in the first chapter, "Paul, an apostle, not from men, nor through man," etc. And in this way the gloss of Ambrose cited there is to be understood, because at that time the Apostle was not sent by Ananias nor by any other mere man. From this gloss it is noted that the Apostle is speaking there of his first mission, when some could think he had been sent by Ananias, by whom he had then been baptized. And so the gloss that is cited next according to Augustine is to be understood in the same way about his first mission, because Paul was then not sent by any mortal man, as the other Apostles were, but by Christ, who was then immortal; and on this account he had a certain prerogative above the others, though he was not their prelate. Therefore from the words of Augustine it cannot be shown that Paul was superior to Peter in authority, although he says that Paul was more worthy; in the same way, from the same words it cannot be shown that he was not inferior in authority. Wherefore, although the saints have said somewhere that Paul was equal to Peter, it cannot nevertheless be found that Paul was equal in respect of pre-eminence. For it is enough that he was equal in certain other respects, for example in doctrine and in the authority of preaching, in that he did not receive the authority to preach first from Peter, neither mediately nor immediately, but from Christ, and in many other respects. For just as not all who are called similar are similar in all things, so not all who are called equal are equal in all things. And in the same way the other argument of the Apostle is answered, when he says, "I make known to you the gospel," etc., because from this it follows that Paul was sent immediately by Christ, whom neither Peter nor any other Apostle then chose; for Christ alone sent or enjoined on Paul the ministry of the gospel. But it does not follow from this that he was not subject to Peter. Just as, from the fact that God often sent Isaiah and other prophets immediately to preach, and to rebuke idolaters and other wicked men, it cannot be inferred that they were not inferior in authority to the supreme Pontiff or to the supreme ruler of the Israelite people. What kind of power Peter had over Paul and the other Apostles, and in what matters, you will be able to inquire later. As for the other argument, which consists in this, that it is not found in Scripture that Peter assumed for himself any kind of power over the other Apostles, but rather kept equality with them: the answer is that the Apostles did many things which are not found in the Bible; yet many of these, though not all, have come down to us through the writings of the disciples of the Apostles and of other faithful men. Therefore, although from the canonical Scriptures one could not effectively convince the stubborn that Peter used the authority granted to him over the Apostles, but rather in fact kept equality, yet it should not on that account be said that he did not use such a power. Nor can it be inferred from the fact that we read that at times he kept equality with the others, that he never used his authority or power, because holy prelates, following the example of Christ, who, though a prelate, came to minister, often do not exercise their power at all, but present themselves as servants, or even as inferiors, to those subject to them. Whether he assumed to himself the authority to determine those matters that were doubtful concerning the gospel, or wished in this to defer to James, or to the whole college of which he was a part, we may investigate later. For that he could at least defer in this to the whole college of the faithful, or even was bound to do so, many who hold that he was prelate of all concede; for, as many say, in matters of faith the supreme prelate of the faithful is inferior to the universal Church, and also to a general council.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: In quo probatur scriptura authentica, quod Petrus aliquando fuit usus potestate sua super alios.
units.tr: In which it is proved from authentic Scripture that Peter at one time exercised his authority over the others.

units.la: Dicitur ergo videatur aliquib. quod in aliquo authentico valeat reperiri, quod Petrus fuerit aliquando usus potestate sua super alios Apostolos. Mag. Nonnullis apparet, quod hoc ex verbis Clementis, qui gesta B. Petri minime ignorauit, colligitur euidenter, qui, vt habetur dist. 80. c. in illis, ait: In illis vero ciuitatibus, in quibus olim apud ethnicos primi flamines eorum atque primi legis doctores erant, episcoporum primates vel patriarchas B. Petrus poni praecepit, qui reliquorum episcoporum causas, & maiora negocia in fide agitarent. In illis autem, in quibus dudum apud predictos ethnicos erant eorum archiflamines, quos tamen minores tenebant, quam memoratos primates, archiepiscopos instituì praecepit, qui episcoporum tantum vocabula sortirentur. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod B. Petrus de facto disposuit non solum de episcopis & archiepiscopis, sed etiam de supremis primatibus & Patriarchis, qui erant in ecclesia Dei. Supremi autem & primi primates seu Patriarchae (quibus vocabulis idem importatur) vt eodem loco habetur, successores sunt Apostolorum. Nam, vt ait Lucius Papa, vt recitatur ead. dist. 80. c. vrbes: In ipsis vero vrbibus Apostoli, eorum successores Patriarchas & primates posuerunt. In quibus verbis Lucius Papa Patriarchas & primates Apostolorum successores appellat. Patet igitur ex supradictis, quod beatus Petrus aliquando fuit usus sua auctoritate in alios Apostolos.
units.tr: It is said, therefore, to some that it can be found in some authentic text that Peter at one time exercised his authority over the other Apostles. Master: To some it appears that this is clearly gathered from the words of Clement, who was by no means ignorant of the deeds of the blessed Peter, who, as is found in dist. 80, c. In illis, says: "In those cities in which formerly among the heathen the first flamens and first doctors of their law were, the blessed Peter commanded that primates or patriarchs of the bishops be appointed, who should deal with the causes of the remaining bishops and with greater matters of faith. In those cities, however, in which formerly among the aforesaid heathen there were their archflamens, whom nevertheless they held to be lesser than the aforementioned primates, he commanded that archbishops be instituted, who should receive only the title of bishops." From these words it is clear that the blessed Peter in fact arranged not only bishops and archbishops, but also the supreme primates and patriarchs who were in the Church of God. Moreover, the supreme and first primates or patriarchs (for both names signify the same thing), as is stated in the same place, are successors of the Apostles. For, as Pope Lucius says, as is recited in the same dist. 80, c. Urbes: "But in those very cities the Apostles appointed their successors as patriarchs and primates." In these words Pope Lucius calls the patriarchs and primates successors of the Apostles. It is therefore plain from what has been said above that the blessed Peter at one time exercised his authority over the other Apostles.

units.la: Explicit quartus liber primi tractatus tertiae partis.
units.tr: Here ends the fourth book of the first treatise of the third part.

units.la: TRACTATVS SECVNDVS, DE IVRIBVS ROMANI IMPERII, LIBER PRIMVS.
units.tr: TREATISE TWO, ON THE RIGHTS OF THE ROMAN EMPIRE, BOOK ONE.

units.la: INCIPIT LIBER PRIMVS SECVNDI TRACTATVS TERTIAE PARTIS, INQUIRENS VTRVM EXPEDIAT TOTI GENERI HUMANO VNUM IMPERATOREM VNIVERSO ORBI PRAESSE, & QUIBUS VIRTUTIBUS DEBEAT PRAEMINERE, & A QUO SIT ROMANORUM IMPERIUM, & SI POSSIT DESTRUI. PROLOGVS.
units.tr: HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE SECOND TREATISE OF THE THIRD PART, INQUIRING WHETHER IT IS EXPEDIENT FOR THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE THAT ONE EMPEROR RULE OVER THE WHOLE WORLD, WITH WHAT VIRTUES HE OUGHT TO EXCEL, FROM WHOM THE ROMAN EMPIRE IS, AND WHETHER IT CAN BE DESTROYED. PROLOGUE.

units.la: Disc. Scripturae diuinae Romanos p tempore, quo mundi imperium acquirere laborarunt, multis & magnis laudibus praeconiis noscuntur extollere, put in li. Macab. legimus manifeste. Proinde post tractatus de potestate Papae & cleri, tractatus de iuribus Romani Imperii, quem nonnulli literati ex sacris literis niituntur elicere subnectatur, praesertim cum occasione Romani Imperii quidam, quorum gesta, sicut & multorum maiorum, in tractatibus sequentibus (ad quos isti duo primi tertiae partis nostri dial. sunt praeparatorii & praeambuli) intendimus discutere, de fide altricari coeperint orthodoxa. Praesens autem tractatus tres libros continet, quorum primus inquirat an toti generi humano expediat vnum Imperatorem vniuerso orbi praesse, quib. excellentiis seu gratiis moribus & virtutibus Imperator mundi debeat praefulgere; a quo Romanum processit imperium; & an de iure seu destrui seu cassari, minui, diuidi valeat seu transferri. Secundus, quae iura habeat Imperator Roman. super temporalia, inuestigat, tertius perscrutat, an Imperator Roman. super spiritualia habeat potestatem aliquam, vel sit capax super spiritualia potestatis. Mag. Eorum perfecta cognitio, quae tractanda commemoras, ex libris sacrae Theologiae, vtriusque iuris, canonici videl. & ciuilis, philosophiae moralis, & ex historiis Romanorum, atque Imperatorum & summorum Pontificum & aliarum gentium esset patentius extrahenda & solidius munienda, de quib. solummodo Bibliis & Decretis cum quatuor libris Decretalium spem habeo obtinendi. Quare ne forsitan opus imperfectum, imo ridiculosum faciamus, videtur consultius desistendum. Disc. Quamuis his diebus opus perfectum facere nequeamus, cum de materia tam necessaria (vtpote quae totum tangit genus humanum) opus speciale, vt aestimo, est nullatenus ab alio attentatum; vtile erat penitus non silere, vt alios copiam librorum habentes ad faciendum perfecta opera prouocemus. Puto enim quod ex disputatione nostra futurae veritatis & iustitiae ac rei publicae zelatores aduertent aperte veritates quamplurimas circa praemissa in detrimentum communis boni latentes illos, qui alios regendo vel consulendo vel informando mando seu erudiendo gubernant, animabuntur periti, qui eorum, quæ iusta sunt & vtilia, fuerunt amatores, de præfatis operæ facere exquisita: falsa, quæ recitabimus, efficaciter improbando, & vera quæ narrabimus rationibus & auctoritatibus irrefragabilibus fulciendo, in hoc enim tractatu, sicut in toto isto dialogo, nihil nisi recitando dicemus propter quod circa quærendas sententias siue opiniones veras & falsas, stolidas, fanticasas recitabimus, quas fortius munire conabor. Non solum enim verorum assertio & declaratio, verum etiam pro fallis & fanta sticis sententiis allegationes apparentes (licet sophisticæ) ad manifestationem, diuulgationem & exaltationem sæpe occasionaliter conferunt veritati, quia per eas studiosorum excitantur ingenia, ex ipsarum irrationabilitate veritas contraria clarius elucescit, cum opposita iuxta se posita magis appareant, & veritas exagitata magis splendescat in lucem, & arguendo, opponendo, disputando, & ad allegationes contrarias respondedo veritas elucidetur. Quare nequaquam propter librorum penuriam est opus tam vtile dimittendum, præsertim cum in prænominatis libris, quos potes habere, plurima quæ tangunt discutienda valeas reperire, & plurima quæ legisti (vt opinor) à tua memoria non penitus exciderunt, vel verba vel sententiam recitando possis cum opportunitas fuerit allegare. Magister. Importunitate me vincis, vt totum tractatum aggrediar, qui vt dubito in præiudicium veritatis & iustitiæ nimias essem passurus calumnias malignorum, si in ipso quid circa inuestiganda sentiam explicare, ideoque vt tu vis de opinionibus recitandis, quid reputem approbandum, in hoc tractatu nullatenus indicabo, per hoc enim veritas non incurret periculum, sed vitabit, eo quod propter approbationem meam & arbitror nullus veritati firmius adhæreret, sed plures vt timeo ex odii inuidia & rancoris malitia ipsam verbis & factis acerbius nequius impugnarent, quod de aliis à quibusdam famulante inuidia fieri mihi non ignoro. Veruntamen si vnquam aduertero, quod quid teneam exprimendo veritas quærit exaltari, hoc expressis verbis non differam diuulgare, cum igitur velis omnino componi hunc tractatum, ipsum accelera exordiri.
units.tr: Disciple. Holy Scripture shows that the Romans, at the time when they laboured to acquire dominion of the world, are known to have been extolled with many great praises, as we clearly read in the books of the Maccabees. Therefore, after the treatise on the power of the Pope and the clergy, let there be appended a treatise on the rights of the Roman Empire, which some learned men strive to draw out of the sacred letters. This is especially so since, on the occasion of the Roman Empire, some men have begun to stray from the orthodox faith. We intend to examine their deeds, as well as those of many greater men, in the treatises that follow, for which these first two parts of the third section of our dialogue are preparatory and introductory. The present treatise contains three books. The first inquires whether it is expedient for the whole human race that one Emperor rule over the whole world, with what excellences, graces, morals and virtues the Emperor of the world ought to shine; from whom the Roman Empire proceeded; and whether it can by right be destroyed, cancelled, diminished, divided or transferred. The second investigates what rights the Roman Emperor has over temporal matters. The third examines whether the Roman Emperor has any power over spiritual matters, or is capable of such power. Master. A full knowledge of these matters, which you mention are to be treated, would have to be drawn more openly and fortified more soundly from the books of sacred theology, of both laws (canon and civil), of moral philosophy, and from the histories of the Romans, the Emperors, the supreme Pontiffs and the other nations. I have hope of obtaining it only from the Bibles and the Decrees, with the four books of the Decretals. Wherefore, lest we perhaps make an imperfect, nay ridiculous, work, it seems more prudent to desist. Disciple. Although we cannot make a perfect work in these days, since no one else, as I judge, has attempted a special work on so necessary a matter (as it touches the whole human race), it was useful not to be silent altogether, so that we may provoke others who have a supply of books to make complete works. For I think that from our disputation the zealots of future truth, justice and the commonwealth will notice very many truths about the matters above, which lie hidden to the detriment of the common good. Skilled men, who govern, advise, inform or teach others and who have loved what is just and useful, will be stirred to make exquisite works on these matters, by effectively refuting the falsehoods we will recite and by supporting the truths we narrate with irrefutable reasons and authorities. For in this treatise, as in the whole of this dialogue, we shall say nothing except by reciting. Therefore, in seeking true, false, foolish and fantastic opinions, we will recite them, and I will try to fortify the ones we recite more strongly. For not only the assertion and declaration of truths, but also apparent arguments (though sophistical) for false and fantastic opinions, often contribute on occasion to the manifestation, publication and exaltation of truth. By these the minds of students are stirred, and from their irrationality the contrary truth shines more clearly, since opposites placed side by side appear more distinctly, and truth, when agitated, shines more brightly into the light. By arguing, opposing, disputing, and answering contrary arguments, truth is made clear. Therefore, by no means should so useful a work be dropped on account of a shortage of books, especially since in the aforementioned books, which you can have, you may find very many things that touch on the matters to be discussed. Many things you have read (as I think) have not wholly fallen from your memory, so you may, when the opportunity arises, cite either the words or the sense by reciting them. Master. You overcome me by importunity, and I will tackle the whole treatise. Yet I doubt that, if in it I explained what I think about the matters to be investigated, I would have to suffer excessive calumnies from the malicious, to the prejudice of truth and justice. Therefore, since you wish me to recite opinions and to say what I judge should be approved, I will in no way indicate that in this treatise. For truth will not thereby incur danger; rather it will avoid it. I think that on account of my approval no one would cling more firmly to truth, but, as I fear, many would attack it more bitterly and wickedly with words and deeds, out of hatred, envy and the malice of rancour. I am not unaware that some do this to others at the instigation of envy. Nevertheless, if ever I notice that by expressing what I hold, truth seeks to be exalted, I will not delay to publish it in plain words. Since you wish this treatise to be fully put together, begin its exposition at once.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CAP. I.

units.la: In quo principaliter quaritur, vtrum expediat toti generi humano pro communi hominum salute & vtilitate vni Imperatori seu principi seculari subesse, & arguitur vnaecim rationibus quod sic, ad quas respondetur infra capitulo sexto, & tribus sequentibus.
units.tr: In which the main question is asked: whether it is expedient for the whole human race, for the common safety and advantage of mankind, to be subject in temporal matters to one Emperor or secular prince; and eleven reasons are given for saying that it is, to which replies are made below in the sixth chapter and the three that follow.

units.la: Discipulus. Romani iura imperii, non iura, sed iniuriæ & iniustitiæ ac crudeles tyrannides non indigne censeri deberent, si nullatenus expediret vnum Imperatorem seu principem cunctas mundi prouincias gubernare: Cum Romani super vniuersum orbem sibi vsurpauerunt principatum, quo circa de iuribus imperii Romani plurima quæsiturus, & ante omnia, an expediat esse vnum Imperatorem totius orbis interrogare decreui, aut ad totius generis humani commodum & vtilitatem pertineat totum orbem terrarum in temporalibus vni imperatori seu principi seculari subesse. Circa quod diuersas & aduersas sententias enarra. Magister. Circa hanc interrogationem, quam proponis, est vna opinio: quod per vnum principem secularem, qui non incongrue imperatoris nomine censetur, mundus, quo ad temporalia, optime regeretur. Nec sufficienter paci & quieti totius societatis humanæ potest per aliud regimen prouideri. Discipulus. Pro ista opinione allegare conare. Magist. Ista opinio videtur multipliciter posse probari. Nam illud regimen est maxime vniuerso expediens, per quod mali facilius, iustius & efficacius ac salubrius coercentur: & boni viuunt quietius inter malos. Ob hoc enim sunt rectores & principes maxime constituti, teste beato Petro, qui in canonica sua prima cap. 2. duces asserit missos à regibus ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum. Cui concordat beatus Paulus ad Rom. 13. dicens: Potestates seculares esse à Deo ad terrorem malorum & securitatem bonorum, vbi sic inquit: Vis autem non timere potestatem, bonum fac & habebis laudem ex illa, Dei enim minister est tibi in bonum, si autem malefeceris time, non enim sine causa gladium portat. Horum sanctorum Apostolorum sententiam secutus est beatus Augustinus, qui vt legitur 23. q. 5. cap. non frustra, ait: Reges, principes, iudices, potestas regis, iuris cognitoris, ungulæ carnificis, arma militis, disciplina damnantis, sed ut seueritas etiam boni principis. Habeant omnia ista modos suos, causas, rationes, & vtilitates. Hæc omnia cum timentur, & mali coercentur, & boni quieti inter malos quietius viuunt. Ab his ita minime discrepare videtur. Nam propter idem factæ sunt leges & institutii sunt principes seculares. Vnde principes ministri sunt legis, & imperator lex animata vocatur. Sed leges sunt factæ vt malorum audacia coerceatur, & boni tuto viuant, dist. 4. facta sunt leges, & ext. de hæreticis, in prologo, ibi scil. lex proditur. Igitur vt coerceantur mali & boni quiete viuant, est regimen principum institutum. Sed per regimen vnius principis secularis, qui super vniuersum orbem habeat potestatem, mali facilius, salubrius, efficacius, iustius ac seuerius coercentur: & boni quietius viuunt inter malos. Tum quia talis princeps mundi esset maioris potentiæ & securioris ad malos fortius comprimendos, & bonos potentius defendendos: sine qua, vt pluribus, nec mali coercentur, nec boni sunt tuti. Tum quia pauciores essent, vt oppressores bonorum & fautores malorum. Tum quia si non esset vnus princeps mundi, sed plures superiorem non habentes, quam plurimi essent promptiores & audaciores ad sustinendum guerras & bella, quâ si omnes principi obedirent. Vnde & videmus, vt sæpius periculosiores & crudeliores guerras inter reges & principes ac comites, qui vni principi obtemperare recusant: quam inter subditos, qui vni principi cipi seculari sunt parentes. Tempore autem guerrarum & bellorum insolescunt mali, & boni multipliciter turbantur. Igitur ꝑ unus sit rector & princeps mundi, qui super omnes mortales habet potestatem, orbi expedit vniuerso. Amplius, sicut spiritualia per sacerdotes, & viros ecclesiasticos ministrantur; & temporalia per principes seculares & laicos disponuntur, teste B. Petro, qui in ordinatione Clementis, vt habetur 11. qu. nc. Sicut enim, ait: sicut enim impietatis crimen est tibi, ô Clemens, neglectis verbi Dei studiis sollicitudines seculares suscipere: Ita vnicuique laicorum crimen est, nisi inuicem sibi etiam studiis, quae ad communem vsum vitae pertinent, operam fideliter dederint. Et idem eadem causa & q. c. te quidem, ait ad eundem Clementem: Neque enim iudicem, neque cognitorem secularium negociorum holie te ordinare vult Christus, ne praefocatus praesentibus hominum curis non possis verbo Dei vacare. Hac vero opera, quae tibi minus congruere diximus, exhibeant sibi inuicem vacantes laici. Quam doctrinam beati Petri, beatus Paulus confirmare videtur 1. ad Corinth. 6. Secularia igitur iudicia si habueritis, contemptibiles qui sunt in ecclesia, illos constituite ad iudicandum. Ex quibus verbis innuere videtur, quod per contemptibiles in ecclesia, qui laici vocantur, secularia negocia sunt tractanda: quemadmodum spiritualia sunt per clericos disponenda. Hanc doctrinam Apostolicam sancti Patres doctores in suis scriptis postmodum tenuerunt. Nicolaus etiam Papa, vt legitur in decretis dist. 96. cap. cum ad verum, ait: cum ad verum ventum est, vltra sibi nec Imperator iura Pontificatus accipiat, nec Pontifex nomen Imperatoris vsurpet. Quoniam idem mediator Dei & hominum Christus Iesus actibus propriis & distinctis officia potestatis vtriusque discreuit, vt & Christiani imperatores pro aeterna vita pontificibus indigerent: Et Pontifices pro successu temporalium rerum imperialibus legibus vterentur, quatenus spiritualis actio a temporalibus distaret incursibus, & Deo militans minime se negociis corporalibus implicaret: ac vicissim non ille rebus diuinis praesse videretur, qui esset negociis secularibus implicatus. Hanc eandem sententiam fere eisdem verbis ponit beatus Cyprianus, vt legitur distinctione 4. cap. quoniam idem. Praedicta etiam ponit Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur eadem distinctione. cap. Imperium, cum ait: Imperium vestrum suis publica rei quotidianis administrationibus debet esse contentum, non vsurpare quae sacerdotibus Domini solummodo conuenerunt. Ex quibus & aliis quasi innumeris sanctorum assertionibus & sacris canonibus, qui habentur in decretis distinctione decim. cap. certum, & cap. suscipi-tis, & distinctione 96. cap. denique, cap. duo sunt, & cap. si Imperator, & distinctione 88. cap. episcopus, & aliis locis quampluribus legitur & colligitur, quod sicut spiritualia per clericos, ita sunt temporalia per laicos disponenda. Sed quamuis totus mundus esset ad fidem conuersus vniuersitati fidelium expediret vni summo Pontifici in spiritualibus obedire non solum inquantum spiritualia concernunt clericos, sed etiam inquantum concernunt laicos. Igitur vniuerso orbi expedit vni imperatori in temporalibus subesse, non solum inquantum temporalia concernunt laicos: sed etiam inquantum concernunt clericos & summum Pontificem, vni principi seculari subesse. Rursus, simile iudicium tenendum est de toto & de parte, in magnis & in paruis, extra de appell. & 14. q. vlt. cap. vlt. & extr. de pra. cap. maioribus. Sed cuilibet regno partiali, quod est pars mundi, expedit quod vni principi seculari sit subiectum: alioquin omnia regna mundi iniqua vel inutilia aut nociua essent habenda. Igitur similiter expedit, vt totus mundus vni seculari principi sit subiectus. Adhuc, omnes qui communicationem in temporalibus habent adinuicem aut habere possunt, vt quilibet posset inuenire pariter & nocere, non optime gubernantur, nisi vni summo principi quo ad temporalia sint subiecti. Tum quia omnes tales vnum populum constituunt, sed secundum Salomonem Prouerbiorum 2. vbi non est gubernator, populus corruet, ergo si in omnibus communionem habentibus non est gubernator, aut praepositus, de eorum ruina & dispendio probabiliter est timendum. Dicens enim Salomon: vbi non est gubernator, non, vbi non sunt gubernatores, populus corruet, insinuare videtur, quod nullus populus vnus quantumcunque magnus poterit absque vno gubernatore consistere. Tum quia vt omnes communicationem adinuicem habentes vni ouili & vni gregi comparantur, vbi autem est vnum ouile & vnus grex, debet esse vnus pastor, ipsa etiam veritate testante, quae ait Iohan. decim. fiet vnum ouile & vnus pastor, eadem etiam veritate testante, quae ait Matthaei vigesimo sext. percutiam pastorem & dispergentur oues gregis, dicens autem, pastorem, & non pastores, videtur innuere, quod vnus grex seu ouile vnum pastorem principalem, non plus debent habere. Tum quia omnes, qui communicationem adinuicem habent, vel habere possunt, vnam ciuitatem, vnum collegium, vnam gentem, vnum regnum efficiunt vel efficere possunt, & nisi efficiunt vnum, sunt nullatenus ordinati, sed monstruosum est corpus & ciuitas & collegium, & gens atque regnum, quod nulla vel plura capita habet. Quare omnes, qui communionem habere possunt adinuicem in temporalibus, vni principi seculari debent esse subiecti, nec poterit aliter optime gubernari. Sed omnes mortales, quocunque spacio terrarum distantes adinuicem possunt habere communionem, ita vt vnum populum, vnum ouile, vnum gregem, vnum corpus, vnam ciuitatem, vnum collegium, vnam gentem, vnum regnum efficiant vel efficere valeant, nisi eos disiungat malitia. Hinc Apostolus ad Romanos duodecim, vnum corpus sumus in Christo, singuli autem alter alterius membra, manifeste insinuans, quod sicut omnes mortales non solum fideles, sed infideles, abrenunciando diabolo per fidem & amorem, debent Christo firmius adhaerere: ita omnes si bene fuerint ordinati, corpus vnum esse debent. Etiam Salomon Prouerbiorum decimo ait: fratet qui iniuriatur a fratre, quasi ciuitas firma, innuens, quod sicut omnes mundi mortales sunt fratres, ita nisi malitia obuiet, debet vnam efficere ciuitatem. Hinc Sapient. sexto. Sapiens increpans reges iniquos ait: Data est a Domino potestas vobis, & virtus ab altissimo, qui interrogabit opera vestra, & scrutabitur cogitationes: quoniam cum esset ministri regni illius, non recte iudicastis. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod quamuis
units.tr: Disciple. The rights of the Roman empire ought not to be called rights but wrongs and injustices and cruel tyrannies, if it were in no way expedient for one Emperor or prince to govern all the provinces of the world; for the Romans claimed for themselves dominion over the whole earth. Therefore, wishing to learn a great deal about the rights of the Roman empire, I have decided to ask, above all, whether it is expedient that there be one Emperor of the whole world, or whether it pertains to the common good and advantage of the human race that the whole earth be subject in temporal affairs to one emperor or secular prince. Set out the various and opposing opinions on this question. Master. On this question which you put, there is one opinion: that the world, as far as temporal affairs go, would be best governed by one secular prince, who may fittingly be called by the name of emperor. Nor can peace and quiet for the whole of human society be sufficiently provided for by any other form of government. Disciple. Try to argue for this opinion. Master. This opinion seems capable of being proved in many ways. For that government is most useful to the whole world by which the wicked are restrained more easily, more justly, more effectively and more beneficially, and by which the good live more quietly among the wicked. For rulers and princes have been appointed chiefly for this purpose, as blessed Peter witnesses, who in his first canonical epistle, chapter 2, says that governors are sent by kings for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Blessed Paul agrees with this in Romans 13, saying that secular powers are from God, for the terror of the wicked and the security of the good; where he says: But wilt thou not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same. For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, fear; for he beareth not the sword in vain. Blessed Augustine followed the opinion of these holy apostles, who, as we read in 23 q. 5, c. non frustra, says: Kings, princes, judges, the power of the king, of the judge of cases, the claws of the executioner, the arms of the soldier, the discipline of the one who condemns, but also the severity of a good prince. All these things have their own modes, causes, reasons and uses. When all these things are feared, and the wicked are restrained, the good live more quietly among the wicked. It does not seem that this differs at all from them. For secular princes were made and instituted for the same reason. Hence princes are ministers of the law, and the emperor is called a living law. But laws were made so that the audacity of the wicked might be restrained and the good might live safely, dist. 4, facta sunt leges, and ext. de haereticis, in prologo, where it says the law is put forth. Therefore, so that the wicked may be restrained and the good may live quietly, the government of princes has been instituted. But by the government of one secular prince, who has power over the whole world, the wicked are restrained more easily, more beneficially, more effectively, more justly and more severely, and the good live more quietly among the wicked. Both because such a prince of the world would be of greater power and more secure in restraining the wicked more forcefully and defending the good more powerfully, without which, for the most part, neither are the wicked restrained nor are the good safe. And because there would be fewer oppressors of the good and supporters of the wicked. And because, if there were not one prince of the world, but several having no superior, very many would be more ready and more bold to undertake wars and battles, which they would not be if all obeyed one prince. Hence we also see that wars and battles are more often more dangerous and more cruel between kings, princes and counts who refuse to obey one prince, than among subjects, who are the parents of one secular prince. In time of wars and battles the wicked grow insolent, and the good are troubled in many ways. Therefore, if there is one ruler and prince of the world, who has power over all mortals, this is expedient for the whole world. Moreover, just as spiritual things are administered through priests and churchmen, and temporal things are arranged by secular princes and laymen, as blessed Peter witnesses in the ordinance of Clement, as we find in 11 q. 1: For as, he says, it is a crime of impiety for you, O Clement, to neglect the study of the word of God and take up secular cares, so it is a crime for each of the laity unless they faithfully devote their effort to one another in those studies which pertain to the common use of life. And in the same cause and question, in the passage beginning te quidem, he says to the same Clement: For Christ does not wish you to be ordained as judge or arbiter of secular business, lest, choked by the present cares of men, you should be unable to devote yourself to the word of God. But let the laity, who are free, perform those works which we have said are less fitting for you. Blessed Paul seems to confirm this teaching of blessed Peter in 1 Corinthians 6: If then you have secular judgments, set those who are despised in the church to judge. From these words he seems to hint that secular business is to be handled through those called despised in the church, that is, the laity, just as spiritual matters are to be arranged through the clergy. The holy Fathers and teachers afterwards kept this apostolic doctrine in their writings. Pope Nicholas too, as we read in the decrees, dist. 96, c. cum ad verum, says: When it has come to the truth, neither may the Emperor further take to himself the rights of the Pontificate, nor may the Pontiff usurp the name of Emperor. For the same Mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, distinguished by his own and separate acts the offices of each power, so that Christian emperors might need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs might use imperial laws for the success of temporal affairs; so that the spiritual action might be kept apart from the intrusions of temporal things, and the one who fights for God might not entangle himself in bodily business; and conversely, that he who is entangled in secular business might not seem to preside over divine things. Blessed Cyprian sets down almost this same opinion in nearly the same words, as we read in distinction 4, c. quoniam idem. Pope Nicholas also sets down the things mentioned above, as is found in the same distinction, c. Imperium, where he says: Your empire ought to be content with the daily administration of public affairs, and not to usurp those things which belong to the priests of the Lord alone. From these and many other almost countless assertions of the saints and sacred canons, which are found in the decrees in distinction 10, c. certum and c. suscipitis, and in distinction 96, c. denique, c. duo sunt, and c. si Imperator, and in distinction 88, c. episcopus, and in very many other places, it is read and gathered that just as spiritual things are to be arranged by clergy, so temporal things are to be arranged by laymen. But although the whole world were converted to the faith, it would be expedient for the whole body of the faithful to obey one supreme Pontiff in spiritual matters, not only insofar as spiritual matters concern clergy, but also insofar as they concern laymen. Therefore it is expedient for the whole world to be subject in temporal matters to one emperor, not only insofar as temporal matters concern laymen, but also insofar as they concern clergy and the supreme Pontiff, to be subject to one secular prince. Again, the same judgment must be held concerning the whole and the part, in great things and in small: extra de appellationibus, 14 q. ult., c. ult., and extra de praebendis, c. maioribus. But it is expedient for every partial kingdom, which is a part of the world, to be subject to one secular prince; otherwise all the kingdoms of the world would have to be considered unjust, useless or harmful. Therefore it is likewise expedient that the whole world be subject to one secular prince. Further, all who have communication with one another in temporal matters, or are able to have it, so that anyone may find and harm one another equally, are not governed well unless they are subject in temporal matters to one supreme prince. Because all such people constitute one people; but according to Solomon, Proverbs 2, where there is no governor, the people falls; therefore if among all who have communion there is no governor or ruler, their ruin and loss are to be probably feared. For when Solomon says: where there is no governor, not where there are no governors, the people falls, he seems to imply that no people, however great, can stand as one without one governor. Again, because all who have communion with one another are compared to one fold and one flock; and where there is one fold and one flock there ought to be one shepherd, the truth itself bearing witness, which says in John 10: There shall be one fold and one shepherd; and the same truth bearing witness, which says in Matthew 26: I will smite the shepherd and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered. But when he says the shepherd, and not shepherds, he seems to suggest that one flock or fold ought to have only one principal shepherd, no more. Again, because all who have communion with one another, or are able to have it, make up one city, one college, one nation, one kingdom, or can make it, and unless they make one, they are not ordered at all; but a body, a city, a college, a nation or a kingdom that has no head or several heads is monstrous. Therefore all who are able to have communion with one another in temporal matters ought to be subject to one secular prince, and otherwise they cannot be governed well. But all mortals, however far apart they are in distance of lands, can have communion with one another, so that they may make, or be able to make, one people, one fold, one flock, one body, one city, one college, one nation, one kingdom, unless wickedness separates them. Hence the Apostle to the Romans, chapter 12: We are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another, plainly implying that just as all mortals, not only the faithful but also the unbelievers, who renounce the devil through faith and love, ought to cling more firmly to Christ, so all, if they are well ordered, ought to be one body. Solomon also says in Proverbs 18: A brother who is wronged by a brother is like a strong city, suggesting that just as all the mortals of the world are brothers, so, unless wickedness stands in the way, they ought to make one city. Hence in Wisdom 6, the Sage, rebuking wicked kings, says: Power has been given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will question your works and search out your thoughts; for although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly. From these words it is to be understood that although

units.la: uis nis propter peccata malorum multi sunt reges a Domino constituti. Qui etiam, vt habetur Iohan. tamen totus mundus vnum regnum est. Quare quo ad temporalia, vnum principem secularem debet habere. Item, illud regnum est optimum, per quod potissime & perfectissime, quantum est possibile pro praesenti vita, discordia ab vniuersitate fidelium remouetur, & tollitur, per quod concordia & iustitia praecipue conseruantur. Sed si vniuersitas fidelium vni principi seculari fuerit subiecta, efficacius tolletur inter mortales discordia, quam si plures fuerint principes vnum superiorem non habentes. Tum quia vbi pluralitas, ibi discordia. Tum quia sicut vnum regnum speciale per discordiam contra se diuisum desolabitur, teste veritate ipsa Luca 11. ita si vniuersitas mortalium habendo plures principes nequaquam vni subiectos fuerit per discordiam contra se diuisa, desolationem incurret, igitur expedit vniuersitati mortalium vni principi seculari obedire. Item, illud regimen est vniuersitati mortalium expediens, per quod iurgia & litigia (ad quae prona est natura mortalium) aequius & conuenientius deciduntur. Sed conuenientius iurgia & litigia inter litigantes, si vnum habuerint iudicem, vel dominum, aut principem, deciduntur, quam si habuerint plures qui vni minime sint subiecti. Si enim litigantes, quorum vnus alteri damnum vel nocumentum intulit, aut ius suum pluribus regibus vel principibus superiorem non habentibus sint subiecti, facilius poterit periclitari iustitia, nec apparet sub quo iudice tutum sit vtrique parti litigare, quia aut offensus litigabit sub Domino proprio, vel iudice per Dominum proprium constituto; aut litigabit sub rege proprio offendentis, vel iudice per illum deputato. Si offensus litigat coram Domino seu rege proprio vel iudice constituto per ipsum: ille merito poterit esse suspectus offendenti, extra de officio iudicis dele. c. tamen qua & insinuante. Periculosum est sub suspecto iudice litigare, vnde quodammodo naturale est suspectorum iudicium insidias declinare, 3. q. 5. quia suspecti. Igitur non est tutum vtrique parti litigare sub rege seu Domino offensi, seu iudice constituto per ipsum, nec est etiam tutum vtrique parti litigare sub rege vel Domino offendentis, vel iudice constituto per ipsum: quia ille poterit esse suspectus offenso per iura praedicta, & ita litigantes si habuerint plures Dominos superiorem non habentes, de facili poterit periclitari iustitia. Quare vniuersitati mortalium expedit vnum principem summum habere, ad quem tanquam ad communem iudicem possint quicunque litigantes recursum habere, in quo per dominium tam offenso quam offendenti suspitionem non irrationabiliter amouebit. Praeterea, illud regimen seu dominium est expediens vniuersitati mortalium, per quod non solum inferiores, sed etiam superiores si deliquerint, iuste poterunt castigari.
units.tr: Even though many kings are appointed by the Lord because of the sins of wicked men, nevertheless the whole world is one kingdom, as is said in John. So, as far as temporal matters go, it ought to have one secular prince. Likewise, that kingdom is best through which, most fully and most perfectly, as far as is possible in the present life, discord is removed and taken away from the whole body of the faithful, and through which concord and justice are chiefly preserved. But if the whole body of the faithful were subject to one secular prince, discord would be removed among mortals more effectively than if there were several princes with no superior over them. This is because where there is plurality, there is discord. It is also because, just as a particular kingdom divided against itself by discord will be laid waste, as the truth itself says in Luke 11., so if the community of mortals, having several princes not subject to one, were divided against itself by discord, it would incur desolation. Therefore it is expedient for the community of mortals to obey one secular prince. Likewise, that government is expedient for the community of mortals through which quarrels and lawsuits (to which the nature of mortals is prone) are decided more fairly and more suitably. But quarrels and lawsuits between litigants are decided more suitably if they have one judge, lord or prince, than if they have several who are not subject to one another. For if litigants, one of whom has inflicted loss or injury on the other, are subject to several kings or princes with no superior, justice can more easily be endangered, and it does not appear under which judge it would be safe for either party to litigate. For either the injured party will litigate under his own lord, or a judge appointed by his own lord; or he will litigate under the king of the offender, or a judge appointed by him. If the injured party litigates before his own lord or king, or a judge appointed by him, that lord may reasonably be suspected by the offender: extra de officio iudicis dele. c. tamen qua & insinuante. It is dangerous to litigate before a suspected judge. Hence it is in a way natural to avoid the snares of suspected judges, 3. q. 5. quia suspecti. Therefore it is not safe for either party to litigate under the king or lord of the injured party, or under a judge appointed by him, nor is it safe for either party to litigate under the king or lord of the offender, or under a judge appointed by him, because that judge may be suspected by the injured party on the grounds stated above. Thus, if litigants have several lords with no superior over them, justice can easily be endangered. Therefore it is expedient for the community of mortals to have one supreme prince, to whom any litigants may have recourse as to a common judge, and who by his lordship will not unreasonably remove suspicion from both the injured party and the offender. Moreover, that rule or lordship is expedient for the community of mortals by which not only inferiors, but also superiors, if they have done wrong, may justly be punished.

units.la: Aliter enim pax societatis humanae (quae tam dulcis est, vt propter ipsam etiam bella geantur, secundum Augustin. vt habetur 23. quaest. 1. c. noli) non poterit conseruari, nec iustitia (quam colere est summum bonum in rebus, secundum Gregor. vt habetur 12. q. 2. cap. cum deuotissimam) tenebitur, nisi quantum possibile est caueatur ne superiores delinquere valeant insolenter, vt ex verbis Innocentii 3. quae ponuntur extra de accusatione, qualiter & quando, potest colligi, vt videtur. Si enim fuerint multi reges seu principes in diuersis mundi partibus superiorem non habentes, libere & impune pacem & iura minorum perturbare valebunt. Sed si omnes reges fuerint imperatori subiecti, non solum inferiores, sed etiam superiores, si deliquerint, poterunt legitime castigari. Igitur toti mundo est expediens, vt vnus imperator regibus & principibus praelideat vniuersis, & super vniuersitatem mortalium iurisdictionem habeat coactiuam. Amplius, inter omnes mortales debet esse connexio, vt quilibet respectu alterius sit inferior vel superior, aut ambo inferiores respectu eiusdem, vt inter omnes vera fiat concordia, & quilibet cuilibet reverentiam vel dilectionem impendat, & hoc colligitur ex auctoritate Gregor. & Bonifacii papae, quae ponitur distinct. 89. cap. ad hoc, vbi sic loquitur: Ad hoc dispensationis prouisio gradus diuersos & ordines constituit esse distinctos, vt dum reuerentiam minores potioribus exhiberent, & potiores minoribus dilectionem impenderent, vera concordia fieret & ex diuersitate connexio, & recte officiorum gereretur administratio singulorum, neque enim vniuersitas alia poterat ratione subsistere, sed talis non est inter cunctos mortales connexio, nisi vnus praesideat omnibus aliis, igitur expedit vniuersitati mortalium, vt mundus per vnum principem gubernetur. Rursus, illud regimen, quod Deus inter mortales propter peccarum multitudinis non promittit, sed aufert, est melius illo, quod Deus propter peccata multitudinis punienda introducit. Sed quod supra vniuersitatem mortalium non dominetur vnus, sed multi, ordinat Deus propter peccata mortalium punienda, teste Salomone, qui Prouerbior. 28. Ait: propter peccata terra multi principes eius. Igitur similiter vniuersitati mortalium expediret, quod omnes essent subiecti vni. Item, si non expedit vniuersitatem mortalium vni imperatori subesse: Aut hoc est propter insufficientiam humanam, quia nullus poterit sufficiens reperiri pro orbe vniuerso regendo: aut propter nimiam potentiam temporalem vnius Domini totius, qua posset Secundum libitum in subiectos debacchare. Sed insufficientia no impedit: sicut insufficientia humana non impedit, quin vnus debeat etiam si vniuersitas mortalium conuersa esset ad fidem, toti mundo in spiritualibus praesidere. Nec nimia potentia impedit: ga proportionabiliter ita potest totus mundus resistere crudelitati vnius imperatoris totius orbis, sicut potest vnum regnum partiale resistere regi. Nec posset maiorem habere potestatem imperator totius mundi super totum mundum, quam vnus rex super vnum regnum partiale. Sed potentia regis non impedit, quin vnus rex debeat
units.tr: Otherwise the peace of human society (which is so sweet that wars are fought for its sake, according to Augustine, as is found in 23. quaest. 1. c. noli) cannot be preserved, nor will justice (which it is the highest good to cultivate in things, according to Gregory, as is found in 12. q. 2. cap. cum deuotissimam) be upheld, unless care is taken, as far as possible, that superiors cannot sin with impunity. This can be gathered, it seems, from the words of Innocent III, which are set down in extra de accusatione, qualiter & quando. For if there were many kings or princes in different parts of the world, having no superior, they would be able to disturb peace and the rights of their inferiors freely and with impunity. But if all kings were subject to the emperor, not only inferiors but also superiors, if they sinned, could be lawfully punished. Therefore it is expedient for the whole world that one emperor should preside over all kings and princes, and have coercive jurisdiction over the whole of mankind. Furthermore, there must be a connection among all mortals, so that each is either superior or inferior to another, or both are inferior to the same person, so that true concord arises among all, and each shows reverence or love to each. This is gathered from the authority of Gregory and Pope Boniface, which is set down in distinct. 89. cap. ad hoc, where he speaks thus: To this end the providence of the dispensation has established distinct degrees and orders, so that while the lesser show reverence to the greater, and the greater show love to the lesser, true concord may come about, and connection from diversity, and the office of each may be rightly administered; for the whole could not otherwise subsist. But there is no such connection among all mortals unless one presides over all the others. Therefore it is expedient for the human race that the world be governed by one prince. Again, that government which God does not grant among mortals on account of the multitude of sins, but takes away, is better than that which God introduces on account of the sins of the multitude to be punished. But that the whole human race should not be ruled by one but by many, God ordains on account of the sins of mortals to be punished, as Solomon witnesses in Proverbs 28, where he says: Because of the sins of the land, it has many princes. Therefore it would likewise be expedient for the human race that all should be subject to one. Likewise, if it is not expedient for the human race to be subject to one emperor, then this is either because of human insufficiency, since no one can be found sufficient to rule the whole world, or because of the excessive temporal power of one lord over the whole, by which he could rage against his subjects at will. But insufficiency is no obstacle: just as human insufficiency does not prevent one from having to preside over the whole world even in spiritual matters, were the human race converted to the faith. Nor is excessive power an obstacle, because the whole world can resist the cruelty of one emperor of the whole world in proportion, just as one partial kingdom can resist a king. Nor could the emperor of the whole world have greater power over the whole world than one king has over one partial kingdom. But the power of a king does not prevent one king from having to preside over one kingdom. Therefore neither should the power of the emperor prevent him from presiding over the whole world. Furthermore, if it is not expedient for the whole world to have one emperor presiding over it, it is not just that one should rule over all; and if it is neither just nor expedient, it is unjust for one to rule over all others. But it is not unjust, for it would have to be against right: either against natural right or against positive right. Not against natural right, for then it would always have been unjust, and so no one would ever have been a true emperor of the world, since empire usurped against natural right would not be true empire. Nor against positive right, for positive right, whatever it may be, could not be instituted so that someone should be emperor of the whole world, except by the whole human race. But the human race has never instituted this; rather the contrary. Therefore it is not unjust for one to hold empire over the whole world, and so it is to be judged expedient.

units.la: {y} Lessons on the reference marks: none printed on this page beyond the marginal citations shown above. præesse vni regno. Igitur nec potentia imperatoris impedire debet vniuerso orbi præesse. Praeterea, si non expediat vniuerso orbi vnum imperatorem præesse, non est iustum, vt vnus omnibus dominetur, si autem non est iustum nec expediens, est iniquum vnum omnibus aliis dominari, sed non est iniquum: quia esset contra ius, aut igitur contra ius naturale, aut contra ius positiuum, sed non contra ius naturale: quia tunc semper fuisset iniquum, & ita nunquam fuisset quis verus imperator mundi, quia imperium vsurpatum contra ius naturale non esset verum imperium. Nec etiam contra ius positiuum: quia ius positiuum, quocumque, ne aliquis sit imperator totius mundi, non posset institui, nisi ab vniuersitate mortalium. Sed vniuersitas mortalium hoc nunquam instituit, sed magis contrarium. Igitur non est iniquum, vnum super vniuersum orbem habere imperium, quare expediens est censendum.
units.tr: to preside over one kingdom. Therefore the power of the emperor ought not to prevent him from presiding over the whole world. Moreover, if it is not expedient for one emperor to preside over the whole world, it is not just for one man to rule over all; and if it is neither just nor expedient, it is unjust for one man to rule over all others. But it is not unjust, because that would be against law: either against natural law or against positive law. Not against natural law, for then it would always have been unjust, and so no one would ever have been a true emperor of the world, since an empire usurped against natural law would not be a true empire. Nor is it against positive law, because positive law of any kind, that someone should be emperor of the whole world, could not have been instituted except by the whole body of mortals. But the whole body of mortals never instituted this; rather the contrary. Therefore it is not unjust to have one empire over the whole world, and so it is to be judged expedient.

units.la: In quo ponitur secunda opinio contraria prima capitulo praecedenti recitata, & motiua eiusdem, quae sunt sex in numero, ad quae respondetur infra capit. II.
units.tr: In which the second opinion is set out, contrary to the first recited in the preceding chapter, together with its arguments, six in number, to which replies are given below in chap. II.

units.la: Discipul. Puto quod pro assertione praedicta fortiora recitasti motiua, quae copiam librorum habentes poterunt maiorum sententiis multipliciter communire, idcirco circa interrogationem meam, aliam opinionem enarra. Magist. Alia opinio est contraria, quod non expedit mundo, vt vniuersitas mortalium vni imperatori seu principi seculari sit subiecta. Discip. Istius opinionis motiua scire desidero. Magister. Pro ista opinione potest multipliciter allegari. Primo: nam illud, cuius contrarium est a Deo ordinatum, non est mundo expediens, omne enim contrarium ordinationi diuinae perniciosum est & malitiosum & non expediens est censendum. Sed diuisio regnorum ita vt diuersis regibus non habentibus superiorem subsint, non est a Deo vetitum, sed ordinatum, vt patet 3. Reg. 12. & 13. Dominus voluit filios Israel duos reges habere quorum neuter esset alteri subiectus, & qui superiorem regem non haberent. Igitur vnum principem secularem cunctis mortalibus dominari non est expediens iudicandum. Amplius, idem iuris est in magnis & in paruis, & in toto & in parte, sicut per plures sacros Canones superius est ostensum. Sed quemcumque regem seu principem secularem parti mortalium etiam illis, qui iustissimis vtuntur legibus, praesidere non est expediens, illud enim quod displicet Deo, non est expediens, sed solum Israeliticum, qui erat pars mortalium & iustissimis vtebatur legibus, quia Dominicis, esse subiectum regi vel principi seculari displicebat Deo, ita vt diceret ad Samuelem, vt habetur 1. Reg. 8. quando populus praedictus regem petebat: audi vocem populi in omnibus, quae loquuntur tibi, non enim te abiecerunt, sed me, ne regam super eos. Igitur multo magis vnum principem secularem regnare super vniuersum orbem (etiam si conuersus esset totus ad fidem) non est expediens. Adhuc, illud regimen est magis expediens vniuersitati mortalium in statu culpae, quod magis assimilatur regimini, quod fuisset, si homines in statu innocentiae permansissent (quia illud quod magis assimilatur meliori, est magis expediens.) Sed si homines in statu innocentiae permansissent, vnus non fuisset imperator omnium aliorum. Igitur in statu culpae non est expediens, vt vnus omnibus aliis dominetur.
units.tr: Disciple. I think that for the foregoing assertion you have recited the stronger arguments, and since you have a store of books, you will be able to fortify them in many ways with the opinions of the greater authorities. So, with regard to my question, set out the other opinion. Master. The other opinion is contrary: it is not expedient for the world that the whole body of mortals should be subject to one emperor or secular prince. Disciple. I want to know the arguments for this opinion. Master. This opinion can be supported in many ways. First, that which has a contrary that God has ordained is not expedient for the world, for every thing contrary to the divine ordinance is harmful and wicked, and must be judged inexpedient. But the division of kingdoms, so that kings who have no superior rule over different realms, is not forbidden by God but ordained, as is clear from 3 Kings 12 and 13, where the Lord willed that the sons of Israel should have two kings, neither subject to the other, and who had no superior king. Therefore it must be judged inexpedient that one secular prince should rule over all mortals.
