Furthermore, the same law holds for great things and small, for the whole and for the part, as has been shown above by many sacred canons. But it is not expedient for any king or secular prince to preside over a part of mortals, even over those who use the most just laws, for what displeases God is not expedient. Yet it was only the Israelite people, who were a part of mortals and used the most just laws, that displeased God by being subject to a king or secular prince, as is said to Samuel in 1 Kings 8, when the aforesaid people asked for a king: "Hear the voice of the people in all that they say to you; for they have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them." Therefore much more is it inexpedient for one secular prince to reign over the whole world (even if the whole of it were converted to the faith). Again, that government is more expedient for the body of mortals in the state of guilt which more closely resembles the government that would have existed had men remained in the state of innocence (because what more closely resembles the better is more expedient). But if men had remained in the state of innocence, one would not have been emperor over all the others. Therefore in the state of guilt it is not expedient that one should rule over all the others.

units.la: Rursus, quod iuri gentium obuiat & repugnat, non est expediens reputandum, cum ius gentium sequatur naturale, quia, vt habetur dist. 1. ius gentium est idem apud omnes gentes, qualo est solummodo ius naturale, cui nulla valet consuetudo aut multitudo vel ius positiuum quomodolibet derogare, extra de consuetud. cum tanto, sed vniuersitatem mortalium vni principi seu imperatori subesse iuri gentium obuiat & repugnat. Cum quia bella & captiuitates sunt iura gentium seu de iure gentium, dist. 1. ius gentium, quae cessarent, si vnus imperator vniuersitati mortalium imperaret. Tum quia de iure gentium connubia inter alienigenas prohibentur, eadem dist. & ca. quod non poterit intelligi de quibuscunque aliegenis, quia tunc essent connubia inter quoscunque diuersarum prouinciarum prohibita, igitur intelligitur de alienigenis, quae nullam communionem dicuntur habere adinuicem, quales non sunt quicunque, qui sunt vni imperatori vel Domino subiecti. Omnes enim qui vni Domino subiecti possunt & in multis casibus debent habere communionem adinuicem se mutuo adinuicem adiuuando & inuicem defendendo. Igitur non est expediens neque aequum, vniuersitatem mortalium vni imperatori seu principi obedire. Item, illi non debent vni principi vel imperatori obedire, qui nec vnum iugum ducere debent, nec inter se communionem habere tenentur, nec licite ad eundem iudicem pro iudicio etiam sustinendo recurrunt. Mortalium autem quidam sunt fideles, sed fideles cum infidelibus non debent idem iugum ducere, Apostolo prohibente 2. ad Corinth. 6. cum ait: nolite iugum ducere cum infidelibus, nec debent societatem cum eis vel communionem habere pacificam, Domino attestante, qui dicit Matthaei 10. Nolite arbitrari quod venerim mittere pacem in terram: non veni pacem mittere sed gladium &c. Deuteronomii 7. praecipitur expresse fidelibus, vt infideles percutiant vsque ad interemptionem, nec ineant cum eis foedus, nec miscceantur vxoribus eorum. Quod etiam docet Apostolus 2. Corinth. 6. dicens: Quae enim participatio iustitia cum iniquitate, aut quae societas lucis ad tenebras? quae autem concordia Christi ad Belial? aut quae pars fidelis cum infideli? Quibus concorditer dicit Sapiens Ecclesiastic. 13. Qua communicatio sancto bodo bominis ad vnum? nec etiam debent fideles ad iudicem infidelium pro iudicio recurrere, testante Apostolo, qui, vt habetur prima ad Corinth 6. fideles, qui coram infidelibus litigant, acriter reprehendit, dicens: Ad verecundiam vestram dico sic, non est inter vos sapiens quisquam, qui possit iudicare inter fratrem suum, sed frater cum fratre iudicio contendit, & hoc apud infideles. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod fideles ab infidelibus, quantum ad litigationem in iudicio, & quantum ad omnem pacificam communionem & participationem, debent penitus separari. Igitur vni imperatori seu principi seculari non debet vniuersitas mortalium esse subiecta. Praeterea: Ille non debet vniuersitati mortalium praesidere, qui eorum non potest debite gerere curam, sed nullus potest debite gerere curam vniuersitatis mortalium: cum quilibet sit insufficiens ex se vnius parui regni curam habere, testante Salomone, qui, vt legitur 2. Paralip. primo, loquens ad Deum ait: quis enim potest hunc populum tuum, qui tam grandis est, iudicare? quasi diceret, nullus, igitur multo fortius nemo potest digne vniuersitatem mortalium iudicare.
units.tr: Again, what opposes and conflicts with the law of nations must be reckoned inexpedient, since the law of nations follows the natural law; for, as it is said in dist. 1, the law of nations is the same among all nations, because it is only the natural law, which no custom or multitude, nor any positive law, can in any way override (extra, de consuetud., cum tanto). But for the whole body of mortals to be subject to one prince or emperor opposes and conflicts with the law of nations. First, because wars and captivities are rights of nations, or under the law of nations (dist. 1, ius gentium), and these would cease if one emperor ruled over the whole body of mortals. Second, because under the law of nations marriages between foreigners are forbidden (the same distinction and the chapter "quod non"). This cannot be understood of foreigners in general, for then marriages would be forbidden between any persons of different provinces; so it must be understood of foreigners who are said to have no fellowship with one another, and such are not all who are subject to one emperor or lord. For all who are subject to one lord can, and in many cases must, have fellowship with one another, by mutually helping and defending one another. Therefore it is neither expedient nor just for the whole body of mortals to obey one emperor or prince. Likewise, those ought not to obey one prince or emperor who ought not to draw one yoke, who are not bound to have fellowship with one another, and who may not lawfully appeal to the same judge even to sustain a judgment. Now some of mortals are believers, but believers ought not to draw the same yoke with unbelievers, the Apostle forbidding it in 2 Corinthians 6, where he says: "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers." Nor ought they to have peaceful fellowship or communion with them, the Lord bearing witness, who says in Matthew 10: "Do not think that I came to send peace on the earth; I came not to send peace but a sword," etc. Deuteronomy 7 expressly commands believers to strike unbelievers down to destruction, nor to make a covenant with them, nor to intermarry with them. The Apostle also teaches this in 2 Corinthians 6, saying: "For what fellowship has righteousness with lawlessness? What communion has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what does a believer share with an unbeliever?" To the same effect the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus 13: "What fellowship has the saint with the sinner?" Nor ought believers to appeal to the judge of unbelievers for a judgment, as the Apostle bears witness, who sharply rebukes in 1 Corinthians 6 the believers who litigate before unbelievers, saying: "I say this to your shame. Is there no one wise among you who can judge between his brothers? But brother goes to law with brother, and this before unbelievers." From these words it is gathered that believers must be wholly separated from unbelievers, both as regards litigation in court and as regards all peaceful communion and participation. Therefore the whole body of mortals ought not to be subject to one emperor or secular prince. Moreover: he ought not to preside over the whole body of mortals who cannot duly take care of them; but no one can duly take care of the whole body of mortals, since each is by himself insufficient to have care of even one small kingdom, Solomon bearing witness, who, as we read in 2 Chronicles 1, speaking to God, says: "For who can judge this your people, which is so great?" As if he said: no one; therefore much more surely no one can rightly judge the whole body of mortals.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Recitat opinionem tertiam circa quaesitum capitulo primo, & probatur vnica ratio- ne, ad quam respondetur capitulo 12. huius.
units.tr: He recites the third opinion concerning the question posed in chapter 1, and it is supported by one argument, which is answered in chapter 12 of this work.

units.la: Discip. Aliam recita opinionem circa interrogationem praedictam. Magister. Alia est opinio circa hanc: quod expediret vnum principem non secularem, sed ecclesiasticum vniversitati mortalium praesidere. Discipulus. Pro ista opinione possumus invenire multa in tractatu de potestate papae & cleri, ideo pauca pro eius confirmatione adducas. Mag. Pro ista opinione potest taliter allegari. Inter caeteras excellentias, quibus debet princeps, & qui in temporalibus praesidet, subditos superare, sapientia videtur esse praecipua. Unde & Salomon, qui sapientiam postulavit a Deo, vt digne posset regere populum Dei in temporalibus, a Deo legitur manifeste commendatus, cum dixit sibi Dominus 2. Paral. primo: quia hoc magis complacuit cordi tuo, & non postulasti divitias & substantiam & gloriam, neque animas eorum, qui te oderunt, sed nec dies vita plurimos, petisti autem scientiam & sapientiam, vt iudicare possis populum meum, super quem te constitui regem, sapientia & scientia data sunt, divitias autem & substantiam & gloriam dabo tibi. Et idem Salomon Proverbiorum primo dicit: intelligens possidebit gubernacula. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod principi praecipue est necessaria prudentia & sapientia, sed magis sapientia requiritur in viris ecclesiasticis, quam in secularibus, igitur non secularis princeps, sed ecclesiasticus dignus est toti mundo praeesse.
units.tr: Disciple. Recite another opinion regarding the aforementioned question. Master. There is another opinion on this: that it would be expedient for one prince, not a secular but an ecclesiastical one, to preside over the whole human race. Disciple. In support of this opinion we can find much in the treatise on the power of the Pope and the clergy, so please adduce a few points in its confirmation. Master. For this opinion one may argue as follows. Among the other excellences by which a prince, and one who presides over temporal affairs, ought to surpass his subjects, wisdom seems to be the chief. Hence Solomon, who asked God for wisdom so that he might be able to rule the people of God worthily in temporal matters, is plainly commended by God, when the Lord said to him in 2 Chronicles 1: Because this pleased your heart more, and you did not ask for riches, substance, or glory, nor for the lives of those who hate you, nor even for many days of life, but you asked for knowledge and wisdom, that you might be able to judge my people over whom I have made you king, wisdom and knowledge are given to you; riches and substance and glory I will give you. And the same Solomon says in Proverbs 1: The intelligent man shall possess the helms of government. From these words it is made clear that prudence and wisdom are especially necessary for a prince, but wisdom is required more in ecclesiastical men than in secular ones; therefore it is not a secular prince but an ecclesiastical one who is worthy to preside over the whole world.

units.la: Disc. Ista ratio non videtur mihi procedere: quia qui aliis praeest in temporalibus, debet alios praecedere in sapientia mundana & peritia negotiorum secularium: non autem sapientia alia. Sed seculares praecedunt in sapientia mundana: licet ecclesiastici praecellant in sapientia divina. Ergo qui praesidet in temporalibus, debet esse secularis, & non ecclesiasticus: laicus, & non clericus. Magister. Istam improbationem quidam niituntur improbare, quia ex scripturis divinis colligitur, quod qui praeest aliis in temporalibus, non solum in sapientia mundana, sed etiam in sapientia divina & lege Dei debet esse peritior: eo quod rex, qui in temporalibus praeest, debet in lege Dei assidue meditari, dicente Deo, qui loquens de rege Deut. 17. ait: Postquam autem sederit in solio regni sui, describat sibi Deuteronomium legis huius in volumine, accipiens exemplar a sacerdotibus Leuitica tribus, habebit secum, legetque illud omnibus diebus vitae suae. Iosue autem, qui in temporalibus praesidebat, praecepit Dominus dicens: non recedat volumen legis huius de ore tuo, sed meditare in eo diebus ac noctibus, vt custodias & facias omnia quae scripta sunt in eo. Ex quibus colligitur, quod in temporalibus praesidens non solum in sapientia mundana & secularium negotiorum peritia, sed etiam in sapientia divina debet alios superare.
units.tr: Disc. This argument does not seem to me to hold: for whoever presides over others in temporal affairs ought to excel others in worldly wisdom and skill in secular business, but not in any other wisdom. Yet secular men excel in worldly wisdom, although ecclesiastics excel in divine wisdom. Therefore whoever presides in temporal affairs ought to be a secular, and not an ecclesiastic: a layman, and not a cleric. Master. Some strive to refute this objection, because it is gathered from the divine Scriptures that whoever presides over others in temporal affairs must be more skilled not only in worldly wisdom but also in divine wisdom and the law of God, since the king, who presides in temporal affairs, ought to meditate assiduously on the law of God, God saying, speaking of the king in Deuteronomy 17: And when he has sat on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book, taking it from the priests of the tribe of Levi; he shall keep it with him and read it all the days of his life. And the Lord commanded Joshua, who presided over temporal affairs, saying: Let not this book of the law depart from your mouth, but meditate on it day and night, that you may observe and do all that is written in it. From these things it is gathered that one who presides in temporal affairs ought to surpass others not only in worldly wisdom and skill in secular business, but also in divine wisdom.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Ponit opinionem quartam, quam probat vnica ratione, ad quam respondetur infra capitulo tertiodecimo.
units.tr: It sets out a fourth opinion, which it supports by a single argument, to which an answer is given below in chapter thirteen.

units.la: Discipulus. Adhuc circa interrogationem meam, aliam opinionem audire desidero. Magister. Sunt quidam dicentes, quod non est expediens vnum principem secularem neque ecclesiasticum vniversitati mortalium praesidere: nec etiam est expediens, quod plures seculares vel ecclesiastici superiorem non habentes in diuersis prouinciis aut regnis diuersis mortalibus dominentur, sed mundus optime regeretur, si plures simul mundi dominium obtinerent, quemadmodum in pluribus ciuitatibus vel communitatibus non vnus solus, sed plures regere dignoscuntur. Discipul. Pro ista opinione motiva adducas. Magist. Ista opinio videtur posse taliter fulciri. Illud idem regnum vel dominium est mundo vniuerso expediens, in quo pauciores errores accidunt & peccata: quia per tale dominium vel regimen iustitia, pax & concordia omnium procuratur, & etiam conseruatur. Sed si plures sapientes & virtuosi dominarentur vniversitati mortalium, pauciores errores fierent, & peccata in regendo, quam si vnus solus omnes alios gubernaret: quia sicut veritas iustitiae, quae a multis quaeritur, facilius inuenitur 2. dist. de quibus, ita multi difficilius errant, quam vnus solus. Huic SaloSalomon Proverbiorum 13. & 14. assentit salutem esse, vbi multa sunt consilia. Hinc etiam primo Machabeorum 8. ca. post multas laudes Romanorum dicit, quod quicunque audiebant nomen eorum, timebant eos. Quibus vero vellent auxilio esse, vt regnarent, regnabant, quos autem vellent, regno deturbabant, exaltati sunt valde. Et in omnibus istis nemo portabat diadema, nec induebatur purpura, vt magnificaretur in ea. Et quia curiam fecerunt sibi, & quotidie consulebant trecentos viginti consilium agentes semper de multitudine, vt quae digna sunt gerant. Et committunt vni homini magistratum suum per singulos annos dominari vniuersae terrae: & omnes obediunt vni, & non est invidia neque zelus inter eos &c. Ex quibus verbis manifeste habetur, quod Romani in hoc laudabantur, quod nulli supra le regalem dignitatem nec diadema committebant: licet vnum per singulos annos ordinabant, qui auctoritate non propria, sed sibi a senatu commissa, vniuersae terrae Romanis subiectae dominabatur. Igitur magis expedit vniuersitati mortalium plures simul praesidere omnibus, quam vnum solum.
units.tr: Disciple. While we are still on my question, I should like to hear another opinion. Master. There are some who say that it is not expedient for one secular or ecclesiastical prince to preside over the whole community of mortals; nor is it expedient that several secular or ecclesiastical rulers, owing no superior, should hold dominion over mortals in different provinces or kingdoms. Rather, the world would be best governed if several men together held dominion over the world, just as in many cities or communities it is recognised that not one alone but several govern. Disciple. Offer arguments in support of this opinion. Master. This opinion seems to be capable of being supported in the following way. That kingdom or dominion is expedient for the whole world in which fewer errors and sins occur, because through such a dominion or government justice, peace and concord are both secured and preserved for all. But if several wise and virtuous men ruled the community of mortals, fewer errors and sins would occur in governing than if one alone governed all the others; for just as the truth of justice, which is sought by many, is more easily found (2. dist. de quibus), so many men err less readily than one alone. Solomon agrees with this in Proverbs 13 and 14, that there is safety where there are many counsels. Hence also 1 Maccabees 8, after many praises of the Romans, says that whoever heard their name feared them. Those whom they wished to help to reign, reigned; those whom they wished to depose, they deposed from the kingdom, and they were greatly exalted. Yet among all these no one wore a crown or put on purple to be magnified by it. And they made a council for themselves, and every day three hundred and twenty men consulted, always deliberating about the multitude, that they might do what is worthy. And they entrust their magistracy to one man each year to rule over the whole land; all obey one man, and there is no envy or jealousy among them, and so on. From these words it is plainly clear that the Romans were praised for this, that they never committed to anyone a royal dignity above themselves or a crown; although they appointed one man each year, who ruled over all the lands subject to the Romans, not by his own authority but by the authority committed to him by the senate. Therefore it is more expedient for the community of mortals that several should preside over all together than that one alone should.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Ponit quintam opinionem quodammodo mediam inter alias, quam probat tribus rationibus.
units.tr: He sets out a fifth opinion, which is in some sense intermediate between the others, and proves it by three arguments.

units.la: DIscipulus. Si est alia opinio circa interrogationem meam enarra. Magist. Alia opinio est, quod secundum diuersitatem qualitatem & necessitatem temporum expedit regimina & dominia mortalium variari: ita quod aliquando sit expediens vnum principem secularem vel ecclesiasticum praesse mortalibus vniuersis: interdum expedit plures simul seculares vel ecclesiasticos omnes alios gubernare. Nonnunquam vero sit vtile plures principes superiorem non habentes diuersis mundi partibus praesidere. Discipulus. Istam assertionem nitaris aliquibus allegationibus communire. Magist. Istam assertionem pluribus modis posse fulciri videtur. Nam sicut leges pro communi vtilitate debent institui, distinct. 4. erit autem: sic principes, rectores & Domini, tam seculares quam ecclesiastici, pro communi vtilitate prae caeteris sunt praeponendi, quam etiam ipsi magis, quam propriam procurare tenentur. Si enim vtilitati communi propriam praepoluerint, non rectores seu principes vel Domini, sed tanquam tyranni sunt censendi, vtilitas autem communis per vnum principem aliquando secularem vel ecclesiasticum, qui vniuersis dominaretur, videtur melius procurari, quam per plures non habentes superiorem, siue simul regentes, sive in diuersis provinciis residentes, eo quod interdum multitudo mortalium saepe minus sustineret dominium vnius principis secularis vel ecclesiastici, quia sapientia, iustitia & aliis virtutibus (quae requiruntur in principe) praefulgenti quam multorum, nonnunquam autem magna multitudo mortalium nullatenus sustineret dominium vnius, sed voluntarie se subderet dominio multorum, vel simul regentium vel diuersarum provinciarum curam gerentium, & per consequens tunc per plures melius procuraretur communis vtilitas, quam per vnum solum. Quare pro diuersitate & necessitate temporum expedit vnum vel plures mortalibus dominari. Amplius, illo modo regitur optime vniuersitas mortalium, qui magis assimilatur illo modo regendi, quo Deus disposuit populum Israeliticum regi sibi per veram fidem subiectum. Sed Deus disposuit populum Israeliticum sibi subiectum aliquando regi per vnum principem secularem, Dauid enim & Salomon super totum populum Dei regnauerunt. Interdum per vnum principem sacerdotem. Hely enim sacerdos totum populum Israeliticum iudicauit, nonnunquam per plures reges, quorum nullus esset alteri subiectus. Roboam enim & Ierobeam super populum Israeliticum in diuersis regionibus regnauerunt. Igitur secundum diuersitatem & necessitatem temporum est expediens, vt vniuersitas mortalium vni vel pluribus principibus siue rectoribus sit subiecta. Rursus, ille modus regendi vniuersitatem mortalium, qui aliquando fuit licitus & iustus, est expediens reputandus, quia omne iustum & licitum est iudicandum expediens. Sed aliquando mundus licite & iuste regimini vnius principis, interdum regimini plurium subdebatur. Igitur adhuc talis modus varius regendi vniuersitatem mortalium, secundum diuersitatem ac qualitatem & necessitatem temporum, est expediens aestimandus.
units.tr: Disciple. If there is another opinion on my question, explain it. Master. The other opinion is this: that, according to the diversity, quality and necessity of the times, the governments and dominions of mortals ought to vary, so that at one time it is expedient for one secular or ecclesiastical prince to rule over all mortals, while at other times it is expedient for several secular or ecclesiastical rulers to govern all others together. Sometimes, indeed, it is useful for several princes, who have no superior, to preside over different parts of the world. Disciple. Support this assertion with some arguments. Master. This assertion can apparently be supported in several ways. For just as laws ought to be instituted for the common good (Dist. 4, "Erit autem"), so princes, rulers and lords, both secular and ecclesiastical, are to be set above others for the common good, and they are bound to seek this even more than their own advantage. For if they put their own advantage before the common good, they are to be judged not rulers or princes or lords, but tyrants. Now the common good seems to be better promoted by one prince, secular or ecclesiastical, who rules over all, than by several who have no superior, whether ruling together or residing in different provinces. This is because at times a multitude of mortals would scarcely endure the dominion of one prince, secular or ecclesiastical, however much he shines with wisdom, justice and the other virtues required in a prince, whereas at other times a great multitude of mortals would by no means endure the dominion of one, but would willingly submit to the dominion of several, either ruling together or caring for different provinces. Consequently, at such times the common good would be better promoted by several than by one alone. Therefore, according to the diversity and necessity of the times, it is expedient for mortals to be ruled by one or by several. Furthermore, that mode of governing the whole multitude of mortals is best which more closely resembles the way in which God determined that the people of Israel, subject to Him through true faith, should be governed. But God determined that the people of Israel, subject to Him, should at one time be ruled by one secular prince: for David and Solomon reigned over the whole people of God. At another time by one priestly prince: for the priest Eli judged the whole Israelite people. Sometimes by several kings, none of whom was subject to another: for Rehoboam and Jeroboam reigned over the Israelite people in different regions. Therefore, according to the diversity and necessity of the times, it is expedient that the whole multitude of mortals be subject to one or to several princes or rulers. Again, that mode of governing the whole multitude of mortals which at one time was lawful and just must be reckoned expedient, because everything lawful and just is to be judged expedient. But at one time the world was subject lawfully and justly to the rule of one prince, and at another time to the rule of several. Therefore such a varied mode of governing the whole multitude of mortals, according to the diversity, quality and necessity of the times, must still be esteemed expedient.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad primam rationem capituli primi.
units.tr: In which an answer is given to the first argument of chapter one.

units.la: DIscipulus. Ista opinio cum aliis opinionibus contrariis, quantum ad aliqua, concordare dignoscitur, a quibusdam etiam in multis discrepare videtur, vel forte a prima secundum intellectum aliquorum in nullo discordat, licet quantum ad verba eius obuiare videatur, proinde sine omnino sit eadem cum prima opinione intellecta (vt quidam eam intelligunt) siue in aliquo repugnet: cupio scire, qualiter tenentes istam opinionem vltimam respondere nituntur ad allegationes adductas pro aliis opinionibus, in quantum sunt vel videntur contra istam. Primam itaque allegationem pro prima opinione, quae in hoc consistit, quod si vnus princeps secularis dominaretur cunctis prouinciis, & mali securius artarentur, & boni quietius viverent, pertractemus. Dic igitur quomodo respondetur ad eam. Magister. Respondetur, quod quamuis regulare sit & vt frequentius accidit, quod vno principe seculari dominante cunctis, & mali districtius coercentur, & boni quietius viuunt inter malos: hoc tamen in casibus specialibus fallit. Discipul. Explica igitur aliquos casus (paucos tamen) in quibus dicunt hoc fallere, quia forte explicatis paucis potero alios cogitare per memetipsum. Magister. Vnus casus est, in quo dicunt sub vno principe mundi nec malos strictius coerceri, nec bonos quietius viuere, & est, quando aliqua multitudo ex malitia recusantium obedire vni est tam magna & tam fortis, quod seditiones & guerras periculosas in notabile dispendium reipublicæ & bonorum contra mundi monarchiam concitare præsumerent, à quibus cessarent, si diversi principes seculares superiorem non habentes diversas mundi prouincias gubernarent.
units.tr: Disciple. This opinion is recognised as agreeing with other, contrary opinions in some respects, and it seems in many others to differ from them. Perhaps, on some people's understanding of the first opinion, it does not disagree with it at all, although its wording seems to oppose it. So either it is the same as the first opinion as some understand it (as some do), or it conflicts with it in some point. I want to know how those who hold this last opinion try to answer the arguments adduced for the other opinions, insofar as they are, or seem to be, against this one. Let us first consider the first argument for the first opinion, which consists in this: if one secular prince ruled all the provinces, the wicked would be more securely restrained and the good would live more quietly. Tell me, then, how it is answered. Master. It is answered that although it is the rule, and as happens more often, that when one secular prince rules over everyone, the wicked are more strictly restrained and the good live more quietly among the wicked, this fails in particular cases. Disciple. Then explain some cases (though few), in which they say this fails. Perhaps, once a few are explained, I shall be able to think of others for myself. Master. One case is this: they say that under one ruler of the world the wicked are not more strictly restrained, nor the good live more quietly. This happens when some multitude, from the malice of those refusing to obey one, is so large and so strong that they would dare to stir up seditions and dangerous wars against the monarchy of the world, to the notable loss of the commonwealth and of the good. These would cease if different secular princes, having no superior, governed different provinces of the world.

units.la: Discipulus. Vt expressius atque manifestius hunc casum intelligam: velim vt eius aliqua exempla inducas. Magist. Quamuis res manifesta probatione non egeat: tamen vt votis tuis satisfaciam, vnum exemplum ex gestis Romanorum adducam de Iulio Cæsare, qui quia Romanum imperium, quod prius in potestate Senatus & Consulum erat, solus occupare voluit, innumeræ consecutæ sunt seditiones, factiones, & strages. Nam tota vrbs Romana in bella intestina & ciuilia scissa est, itaque tot cædes exortæ sunt, quod vix superessent coloni, qui agros colerent, unde etiam plurimi quam optimi ciues & reipublicæ defensores crudeli morte interempti sunt: mali autem ad insolentiam & intolerabilem superbiam proiecti, unde necesse fuit Romanum imperium, quod multorum, utpote totius Senatus consilio & prouidentia in immensum excreuit, ad vnius dominium redactum paulatim decrescere. Item in aliis factionibus & bellis ciuilibus tam Romanis, quam aliis manifeste videtur, quomodo dum vnus multis potentibus prædominari vult, maximam sæpe concitat reipublicæ perturbationem, & bonorum exilia, aut occisionem. Quapropter in casu, quo multi nollent sufferre dominationem vnius, expediret reipublicæ plures diversis concorditer præesse. Discipul. Videor mihi nunc casum hunc intelligere. Nam sæpe id contigisse & quotidie contingere posse non ambigo, ideo paucis adhuc vnum casum mihi recita. Magister. Alius casus est: quando princeps totius mundi per potentiam temporalem crudelitate tyrannica sequiret contra bonos viros reipublicæ amatores & malos sibi in tyrannide sua fauentes & auxiliantes promoueret, veluti de multis tyrannis in historiis legere possumus, vt de Nerone Romanorum imperatore crudelissimo, qui parricidia in vxores, affines & necessarios suos complura commisit, tantaque mala perpetrauit, quod cætera regna ad rebellionem inuitauit, & tandem hostis à Senatu iudicatus in seipsum quoque manus conuertit, & suiipsius carnifex fuit. Similiter satis manifestum est, quantum perniciosus bonis viris Imperator extitit Domitianus: qui nisi solus imperium obtinuisset, tantam necem bonis ciuibus & optimis inter nobiles inferre non potuisset. Idem de aliis multis declarari posset. Sed hæc satis sint. In his duobus igitur casibus, sub vno principe mundi monarcha, insolescerent scilicet mali, & boni quamplurimum turbarentur, propter quod si mundus nec de iure nec de facto esset vni principi seculari subiectus: & ex assumptione alicuius ad monarchiam mundi, siue propter malitiam assumendi, probabiliter timeretur quod insolescerent mali, & boni turbarentur: non esset aliquis pro tempore illo ad totius mundi dominium assumendus. Discipul. Modum ponendi apud istos ex his, quæ nunc recitasti, magis aduerto, ex quibus etiam cognosco, quod omnes casus, in quibus isti dicunt malos insolescere posse & bonos turbari, sub vno totius mundi monarcha, ad duos prædictos modos, seu casus possunt reduci: quia secundum eos, vt æstimo, nunquam minus arcerentur mali, & boni minus quiete viuerent sub vno principe, quam sub pluribus, nisi propter periculosam rebellionem aut malitiam singularem alicuius multitudinis potentis & magnæ, volentis concitare periculosas guerras, vel propter malitiam vel ignorantiam, vel negligentiam principis, in quibus casibus secundum eos sic nunquam fuisset de iure aliquis princeps ad totius mundi dominium assumendus.
units.tr: Disciple. So that I may understand this case more clearly and plainly, I would like you to give some examples. Master. Although the matter is plain and needs no proof, still, to satisfy your wishes, I shall cite one example from Roman history, concerning Julius Caesar. Because he wished to seize alone the Roman empire, which had previously been under the power of the Senate and the consuls, countless seditions, factions and slaughters followed. For the whole city of Rome was torn apart by civil and internal wars, and so many murders arose that scarcely any farmers were left to till the fields. Many of the best citizens and defenders of the commonwealth were put to a cruel death, while the wicked were given over to insolence and intolerable pride. Hence it was necessary that the Roman empire, which had grown immensely under the counsel and foresight of many, namely of the whole Senate, was gradually reduced to the dominion of one and began to decline. Likewise, in other factions and civil wars, both Roman and others, it clearly appears how, while one man wishes to dominate many powerful men, he often stirs up the greatest disturbance of the commonwealth, and the exile or killing of good men. Therefore, in the case where many would be unwilling to bear the domination of one, it would be expedient for the commonwealth that several should preside in harmony over different parts. Disciple. I think I now understand this case. I do not doubt that it has often happened and can happen every day. So recount to me one more case, briefly. Master. The other case is this: when the prince of the whole world, by temporal power, with tyrannical cruelty, pursued good men who loved the commonwealth, and promoted wicked men who favoured and aided him in his tyranny. We can read of many such tyrants in histories, such as Nero, the most cruel emperor of the Romans, who committed many parricides against his wives, relatives and kinsmen, and perpetrated such evils that he invited the other kingdoms to rebellion. At last, judged a public enemy by the Senate, he turned his hand against himself and became his own executioner. It is similarly plain how harmful to good men the emperor Domitian was. Unless he had held the empire alone, he could not have inflicted such slaughter on good citizens and the best of the nobles. The same could be shown of many others, but these will suffice. In these two cases, then, under one monarch of the world, the wicked would certainly grow insolent and the good would be greatly disturbed. Therefore, if the world were subject to one secular prince neither by right nor in fact, and if by the elevation of someone to the monarchy of the world, whether because of the malice of the one elevated, it were probably to be feared that the wicked would grow insolent and the good be disturbed, then at that time no one should be elevated to the dominion of the whole world. Disciple. From what you have just recited, I now perceive better their way of positing the matter. From it I also recognise that all the cases in which they say the wicked can grow insolent and the good be disturbed under one monarch of the whole world can be reduced to the two said cases or kinds. For, as I reckon, according to them, the wicked would never be less restrained, nor the good live less quietly, under one prince than under several, except because of the dangerous rebellion or singular malice of some powerful and great multitude wishing to stir up dangerous wars, or because of the malice, ignorance or negligence of the prince. In these cases, according to them, no prince would ever be rightly elevated to the dominion of the whole world.

units.la: Quamobrem noli explicare plures casus, in quibus secundum eos minus arcerentur mali, & minus quiete boni viuerent sub vno Domino totius mundi, quam sub pluribus. Sed cupio bene scire, an secundum eos non obstante malitia cuiuscunque multitudinis nolentium obedire vni: & non obstante, quod probabiliter apparet, quod nullus esset de illis, qui posset assumi ad mundi imperium, & qui vellet & sciret vti iuste & legitime huiusmodi dignitate: esset aliquis assumendus ad imperatoriam dignitatem seu maiestatem, postquam de iure aliquis fuisset Dominus totius mundi, per electionem vel per successionem. Magister. Si volueris, postea habebis occasionem quærendi, cum inuestigabimus, an Romanum imperium possit destrui seu cessare. Discipulus. Hoc non obstante, dic breuiter, quid ad hoc isti responderent. Magister. Quidam eorum dicunt, quod in prædictis casibus esset assumptio cuiuscunque ad mundi imperium differenda: quia nihil, quod est in rei publicæ detrimentum, est agendum: præsertim si ex ordinatione humana & non ex diuina lege, nec ex lege naturæ processit, & ideo quamdiu assumptio alicuius ad mundi imperium esset in detrimentum reipublicæ, siue propter malitiam subditorum, siue propter insufficientiam assumendi, non esset talis assumptio attentanda: quia quod prouisum est ad concordiam, non debet tendere ad noxam,
units.tr: Therefore do not explain further cases in which, according to them, the wicked would be less restrained and the good would live less quietly under one lord of the whole world than under several. Rather, I want to know clearly this: according to them, notwithstanding the malice of any multitude unwilling to obey one, and notwithstanding that it is probable that none of those who could be elevated to the empire of the world, and who would wish and know how to use such dignity justly and lawfully, exists, would someone still have to be elevated to the imperial dignity or majesty, once someone had rightfully become lord of the whole world by election or by succession? Master. If you wish, you will have a later opportunity to ask this, when we inquire whether the Roman empire can be destroyed or cease. Disciple. Nevertheless, tell me briefly what they would answer to this. Master. Some of them say that in the cases mentioned, the elevation of anyone to the dominion of the world should be deferred, because nothing that is to the detriment of the commonwealth should be done, especially if it proceeds from human ordinance and not from divine law or the law of nature. Therefore, as long as the elevation of someone to the dominion of the world would be to the detriment of the commonwealth, whether because of the malice of the subjects or the insufficiency of the one to be elevated, such an elevation should not be attempted, because what has been provided for concord ought not to tend to harm.

units.la: distinct. 95. licet.
units.tr: distinct. 95. licet.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad tres probationes minoris prime rationis capituli primi.
units.tr: In which replies are given to the three proofs of the minor premise of the first argument of the first chapter.

units.la: Discipul. Intelligo, quomodo isti dicunt malos posse insolescere, & bonos turbari: & magis sub uno principe omnium, quam sub pluribus, ideo dic quomodo ad probationes, quae adducuntur in contrarium, respondetur. Mag. Ad primam, quae in hoc consistit, quod si unus esset princeps & Dominus vniuersitatis viuentium, ille esset potentior ad arcendum malos, & tenendum bonos. Respondetur, quod nonnunquam aliquis est Dominus totius mundi de iure, non de facto: quia multi sibi sunt rebelles; ideo potest accidere; quod Dominus & princeps totius mundi sit minoris potentiae ad coercendum malos & tuendum bonos, quam multi, quibus nulli vel non tot rebellare nituntur. Ad secundam probationem & tertiam, quae in hoc consistunt, quod si vniuersitas mortalium vni esset subiecta, pauciores essent oppressores bonorum, minusque essent homines proni ad guerras & ad bella: quam si essent plures superiorem non habentes in diuersis regionibus dominantes. Respondetur, quod haec possent contingere & accidere, si vnus sapiens & iustus potenter de facto omnibus principaretur, sed non est necesse, quod semper ex vnius dominio de iure minuatur multitudo opprimentium bonos, & refrenetur audacia concitandi guerras & bella: quia vno de iure omnibus dominante tam ex singulari malitia alicuius magnae multitudinis hominum iniquorum quaerentium bonum proprium & non commune, quam ex malitia, ignorantia & negligentia vnius omnibus imperantis potest augeri tam multitudo opprimentium bonos, quam audacia concitandi guerras & bella, & modi alii turbandi bonos: a quibus quandoq; etiam cessarent plures non habentes superiorem praesidentem, possibile est etiam, quod inter paucos molestę ferentes aliquid eis propositum plures populos prouocarent, vna cum eis vt superiori rebellent, & bonos opprimant, guerras & bella faciendo, etiam potest euenire, vt simul vno existente Domino totius mundi stulto vel desidè, aut contra bonos tyrannice saeuiente, mali sunt audaciores ad opprimendum bonos & concitandum guerras, quam si plures sapientes & iusti diuersis regionibus praesidentes essent. Quare contingere potest, quod magis insolescent mali, & minus quiete viuant boni, si vnus vniuersitati mortalium dominetur, quam si plures superiorem non habentes diuersas regerent regiones.
units.tr: Disciple. I understand how these men say that the wicked can grow arrogant and the good be disturbed, and that this happens more under one ruler of all than under several. So tell me how the proofs brought forward to the contrary are answered. Master. To the first, which consists in this, that if there were one prince and Lord of all the living, he would be more powerful in restraining the wicked and protecting the good: the reply is that sometimes someone is Lord of the whole world by right, but not in fact, because many are rebels against him. It can therefore happen that the Lord and prince of the whole world has less power to restrain the wicked and protect the good than many rulers, against whom none or not so many strive to rebel. To the second and third proofs, which consist in this, that if the whole multitude of mortals were subject to one, there would be fewer oppressors of the good, and men would be less prone to wars and battles, than if there were several rulers in different regions having no superior: the reply is that these things could happen and come about if one wise and just man were actually ruling over all with power. But it is not necessary that the number of those who oppress the good, and the boldness to stir up wars and battles, always be diminished by the rule of one by right. For when one man by right rules over all, the multitude of those who oppress the good can be increased, and the boldness to stir up wars and battles, and other ways of troubling the good, can be increased, both from the singular malice of some great multitude of wicked men seeking their own good and not the common good, and from the malice, ignorance and negligence of the one who commands all. From these things several rulers in different regions, having no superior over them, might sometimes cease; it is also possible that among a few who are displeased with something proposed to them, several peoples might be provoked to rebel together with them against a superior, and to oppress the good by making wars and battles. It can also happen that, while the Lord of the whole world is foolish or idle, or raging tyrannically against the good, the wicked become bolder in oppressing the good and stirring up wars, than if several wise and just men were presiding over different regions. Hence it can happen that the wicked grow more arrogant and the good live less quietly if one man rules over the whole multitude of mortals, than if several, having no superior, governed different regions.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad secundam rationem capituli primi.
units.tr: In which a reply is made to the second argument of the first chapter.

units.la: Discip. Dic quomodo secundum istos valeat sustineri, quod non semper expediat vniuersitati mortalium vnum secularem praeesse, non obstante quod sicut spiritualia per clericos, ita temporalia per laicos disponuntur, ex quo secunda allegatio supra c. 1. adducta nititur concludere, quod sicut vnus princeps ecclesiasticus praeest omnibus aliis in spiritualibus: ita expedit vnum principem secularem in temporalibus omnibus praesidere. Magister. Ad hoc dupliciter respondetur, vno modo, quod non est omnino simile de praesidente in spiritualibus, & de praesidente in temporalibus: quia quod in spiritualibus vnus praesideat vniuersis fidelibus (etiam si totus mundus esset conuersus ad fidem) est immediate ex speciali ordinatione diuina & non humana, vt ex sacris canonibus, qui ponuntur in decretis dist. 21. c. quamuis & dist. 22. c. omnes & c. sacrosancta, & in aliis locis quamplurimis colligi potest, & ideo nisi Deus aliter ordinaret, & hoc fidelibus reuelaret, omnes fideles etiam (si vniuersi mortales suscepissent fidem) deberent vno summo pontifici in spiritualibus obedire: quia non est in potestate hominum diuinam ordinationem aliqualiter immutare. Sed quod vnus princeps secularis in temporalibus toti mundo praesideat, est ex ordinatione humana, quae (quia non est de iure diuino, nec de iure naturae) potest licite per homines mutari, quia omnis res per quascunque causas nascitur, per easdem resoluitur, extra de regulis iuris, omnia. quamobrem antequam vnus princeps secularis cunctis mortalibus praesideret, poterant licite, qui volebant ex causa iusta & rationabili non consentire, quod aliquis assumeretur ad imperium totius mundi, quia quando libertati siue potestati siue iuri aliquorum detrahitur, omnium consensus est requirendus & habendus, dist. 54. c. 1. Ita similiter si ex causa aliqua vnum principem ad monarchiam mundi assumi esset in detrimentum notabile boni communis, non esset pro tunc ad imperium aliquis promouendus. Aliter poterit dici, quod quamuis Christus ordinauerit, quod omnes fideles debeant vni summo pontifici obedire: quia tamen ista ordinatio Christi fuit affirmatiua, & non negatiua, bene obligat ad semper, sed non pro semper, & sic non est necesse, quod omnes fideles omni tempore vni papae obediant, cum etiam hoc non sit possibile, eo quod necesse est sedem illam saepe vacare, & quamuis omnes fideles debeant esse semper parati pro loco & tempore & modo debito, summo pontifici obedire: electio tamen summi pontificis, quando sedes vacat, ex rationabili causa & manifesta potest deferri ad tempus, non solum paruum, sed etiam magnum: vt sic ex causa rationabili dilata huiusmodi electio per plures dies, aliquando per plures menses, nonnunquam vero per plures annos: (vnde aliquando sedes illa per sex annos vacabat) ita ex causa licita potest deferri ad centum annos vel ducentum vel plures, & consimiliter de assumendo ad mundi imperium potest dici. Discipul. Aduerto, quod ista vltima responsio, quantum ad aliqua, proportionabiliter dicit de assumendo ad summum mum sacerdotium, & summum imperium promouendo: quia ita ex causa potest deferri sublimatio vnius, sicut alterius. Sed vellem scire, an sicut fideles non possunt statuere, quod nunquam aliquis in summum pontificem eligatur, ita mortales non valeant ordinare, quod nunquam aliquis ad mundi imperium exaltetur. Magister. Respondetur, quod nec possunt, nec vnquam licite potuerunt mortales statuere, quod nunquam aliquis ad mundi imperium sublimaretur: quia nihil statui licite potest in perpetuum duraturum: quod aduersatur illi, quod est regulariter expediens bono communi, licet in casu posset bono communi nocere. Sed vnum principem cunctis mortalibus praesidere, est regulariter expediens bono communi cunctorum mortalium: licet posset in casu nocere. Igitur absolute (quod nunquam aliquis ad imperium promoveatur) statui minime potest, licet cum aliquibus modificationibus aut specificationibus seu conditionibus hoc licite posset ordinari, quod ad tempus nullus promoveretur ad huiusmodi dignitatem.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how, on their view, it can be maintained that it is not always expedient for the whole human race to be ruled by one secular prince, given that, just as spiritual matters are arranged through clerics, so temporal matters are arranged through laymen; on this basis the second argument adduced above in chapter 1 seeks to conclude that, just as one ecclesiastical prince presides over all others in spiritual matters, so it is expedient that one secular prince preside over all temporal affairs. Master. To this there is a twofold reply. In the first way: the presiding over spiritual matters and the presiding over temporal matters are not wholly alike. For that one man should preside over all the faithful in spiritual matters (even if the whole world were converted to the faith) comes immediately from a special divine ordinance and not a human one, as can be gathered from the sacred canons laid down in the Decretum, Dist. 21, c. Quamvis, and Dist. 22, c. Omnes and c. Sacrosancta, and from very many other places. Therefore, unless God had ordained otherwise and revealed this to the faithful, all the faithful (even if all mortals had received the faith) would have to obey one supreme pontiff in spiritual matters, because it is not in the power of men to alter the divine ordinance in any way. But that one secular prince should preside over the whole world in temporal matters is by human ordinance, which (since it is neither of divine right nor of natural right) can lawfully be changed by men, for every thing is dissolved by the same causes by which it came into being (Extra, De regulis iuris, Omnia). Hence, before one secular prince presided over all mortals, those who wished could lawfully, for a just and reasonable cause, refuse to consent that someone be raised to the empire of the whole world; for when the liberty, power or right of some is taken away, the consent of all must be sought and obtained (Dist. 54, c. 1). Likewise, if for some cause it were to the notable detriment of the common good to advance one prince to the monarchy of the world, then no one should be promoted to the empire at that time. In another way it may be said that although Christ ordained that all the faithful should obey one supreme pontiff, nevertheless, since that ordinance of Christ was affirmative and not negative, it binds always, but not for all times; and so it is not necessary that all the faithful obey the pope at every time, since this is not even possible, because that see must often be vacant. And although all the faithful ought always to be ready to obey the supreme pontiff at the proper place, time and manner, the election of the supreme pontiff, when the see is vacant, can for a reasonable and evident cause be deferred for a time, not only a short one but even a long one: so that for a reasonable cause such an election has sometimes been put off for several days, sometimes for several months, and sometimes for several years (whence that see was once vacant for six years); in the same way, for a lawful cause, it can be deferred for a hundred years, or two hundred, or more, and the same can be said of the assumption to the empire of the world. Disciple. I notice that this last reply, in some respects, applies proportionately to the assumption to the supreme priesthood and the promotion to the supreme empire, since for a cause the elevation of one may be deferred just as that of the other. But I would like to know whether, just as the faithful cannot decree that no one ever be elected supreme pontiff, so mortals cannot ordain that no one ever be exalted to the empire of the world. Master. The answer is that mortals neither can, nor ever could lawfully, decree that no one should ever be raised to the empire of the world; for nothing that is to last forever can lawfully be decreed, since it would run counter to what is ordinarily expedient for the common good, although in a particular case it could harm the common good. But that one prince should preside over all mortals is ordinarily expedient for the common good of all mortals, although it could harm in a particular case. Therefore it can by no means be decreed absolutely that no one should ever be promoted to the empire, although with some modifications, specifications or conditions it could lawfully be ordained that for a time no one should be promoted to such a dignity.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: Chapter IX.

units.la: Respondet tertia rationi primi capituli.
units.tr: It answers the third argument of the first chapter.

units.la: DIscip. Narra, quomodo regulariter, licet non in omni casu, sit expediens cunctos mortales vni principi seculari subesse, non obstante quod expediens sit cuilibet regno partiali habere vnum regem, cum idem sit habendum de toto & de parte iudicium, sicut idem iudicium est habendum in magnis & in paruis, super quibus ratio tertia fundatur supra pro prima opinione in primo capitulo recitata. Magister. Dupliciter respondetur, vno modo, quod non est semper consimile iudicium habendum de toto & de parte, sicut nec semper idem iuris est in magnis & in paruis: quia saepe quantitas rei diuersitatem iuris inducit, extr. de symonia, & si quaestiones, & 12. q. 2. c. bonarei & 1. q. 1. iudices. Deinde nonnunquam magna nocent, & non parua, nam & modicum quod nocet, non nocet, vt notatur in Glossa prologi decretalium, & extra de rubricis, si propositione, sed quando est eadem ratio de toto & de parte, & de magnis & de paruis, tunc simile iudicium de eis est habendum: & idem ius est in eis, quia vbi est eadem ratio, ibi debet esse idem ius, extra de constitutionibus, translato, nunc autem non est semper eadem ratio de toto mundo & de vno regno particulari: quia, sicut insinuatum est superius, potest contingere propter singularem & insolitam iniquitatem alicuius multitudinis praepotentis, vel insufficientiam assumendi, quod vnum praeficere omnibus erit in detrimentum boni communis: & vnum praeficere vni regno particulari erit ad vtilitatem incolarum eiusdem regni, & ideo in tali casu non est semper similiter iudicandum de toto mundo, & de vno regno partiali. Aliter dicitur, quod etiam saepe non expedit, quod vni regno vnus rex praeficiatur, imo sicut quandoque diuersi episcopatus sunt vniendi 16. q. 1. & temporis qualitas, sic expediret interdum reipublicae diuersa regna vniri, & vnum super plura regna regnare, & quando non esset vnus princeps mundi, quanto plura regna vnirentur, tanto vtilius regerentur, si aliquis iustus ipsa ad vtilitatem communem, non ad propriam gubernaret.
units.tr: The Disciple: Tell me how it is regularly (though not in every case) expedient for all mortals to be subject to one secular prince, even though it is expedient for each partial kingdom to have one king, since the same judgment must be made about the whole as about the part, just as the same judgment is made about great things and small things. On this the third argument, recited above for the first opinion in the first chapter, is founded. The Master: It can be answered in two ways. In one way: a judgment about the whole and about the part is not always alike, just as the law is not always the same for great things and small, because the quantity of a thing often brings a difference in law, extr. de symonia, & si quaestiones, & 12. q. 2. c. bonarei & 1. q. 1. iudices. In another way: sometimes great things do harm and small things do not, for even a small thing that does harm is not harmless, as is noted in the Gloss on prologi decretalium and extra de rubricis, si propositione. But when the reason is the same for the whole and the part, and for great and small, then a similar judgment is to be made about them, and the same law applies to them, because where the reason is the same, the law ought to be the same, extra de constitutionibus, translato. Now, however, the reason is not always the same for the whole world and for one particular kingdom. For, as has been suggested above, it can happen, on account of the singular and unusual wickedness of some powerful multitude, or the inability to find a suitable man, that setting one man over all will be to the detriment of the common good, whereas setting one man over one particular kingdom will be for the benefit of its inhabitants. And so in such a case it is not always to be judged alike concerning the whole world and one partial kingdom. In another way it is said that it is often not expedient for one king to be set over one kingdom. Indeed, just as sometimes different bishoprics are to be united, 16. q. 1. & temporis qualitas, so it would sometimes be expedient for the commonwealth that different kingdoms be united, and one ruler reign over several kingdoms. And when there is not one prince of the world, the more kingdoms are united, the more usefully they would be governed, if some just man governed them for the common benefit and not for his own.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: In quo datur responsio generalis ad omnes rationes residuas capituli primi, scilicet 4. vsque ad finem capituli, & hoc applicando solutionem singulis.
units.tr: In which a general answer is given to all the remaining arguments of the first chapter, from the fourth to the end of the chapter, and the solution is applied to each one separately.

units.la: DIscipulus. Prolixe tractare residuas rationes pro prima opinione supra 1. c. allegatas fastidium forte legentibus generaret, ideo si ad ipsas vna posset dari responsio, libenter audirem. Magist. Nonnullis apparet, quod ratione vnica dissoluuntur, eo quod omnes concludunt regulare esse, quod esset expediens totum mundum vni principi seculari subesse, quod tamen fallit in casibus, de quibus casibus istae rationes non concludunt. Discipulus. Ista responsio mihi nimis generalis esse videtur, ideo nullo modo rationalis apparebit, nisi ad rationes illas applicetur specialiter, illam igitur breuiter ad omnes alias nitere applicare. Magist. Quarta ratio supra c. 1. adducta, quae fundatur in hoc, quod cum omnes vniuersi mortales, qui possunt communionem in temporalibus habere adinuicem, non optime gubernabuntur, nisi vni principi seculari sint subiecti, & ideo expedit omnia vni imperio subiacere. Sed per hoc nequaquam concludi videtur, quod omnes volentes communionem adinuicem habere non optime gubernabuntur, nisi vni principi seculari sint subiecti, ideo in casu non expedit omnes vni imperio subiacere, quare in casu optimus modus gubernandi mortales propter iram impeditur, & ideo interdum propter singularem malitiam subditorum vel propinquitatis, aut insufficientiam ad imperium assumendi, vniuersitas mortalium optime gubernari non valet, ideo in aliquibus casibus melius est relicto optimo regimine, eo quod haberi non potest, diuersas prouincias diuersis principibus subiacere, quam in multorum perniciem vnum principem sibi mundi dominium vendicare, & eligentibus illis, qui si communitas mortalium esset bene disposita, & de iure & de facto dignum & idoneum ad mundi imperium promouere deberent. Quinta vero ratio, quae in hoc consistit, quod si vniuersitas mortalium vni fuerit principi seculari subiecta efficacius tolletur inter mortales discordia, quam si fuerint plures principes superiorem non habentes, ad hoc elicitur, quod quamuis regulare sit efficacius tolli discordias per principatum vnius, quam per plures, hoc tamen fallit in casibus, de quibus dictum est prius. Sexta ratio, quae ex hoc virtutem habere videtur, iurgia & litigia aequius deciduntur, si omnes mortales habeant vnum iudicem supremum, quam si fuerint riunt plures iudices supremum non habentes. Euacuatur per hoc, quod hoc habet regularem veritatem, quando omnes obedirent vni, & de iure & de facto, fallit tamen in casibus, de quibus saepe facta est mentio superius. Ad septimam rationem, quae fundatur in hoc, quod si vniuersitas mortalium esset vni subiecta, non solum inferiores, sed etiam superiores, etiam reges, si delinquerent, poterunt legitime castigari, quod non contingeret, si essent plures principes superiorem non habentes.
units.tr: Disciple. A lengthy treatment of the remaining arguments cited above in chapter 1 in support of the first opinion might perhaps weary the readers; so if a single answer could be given to them all, I would gladly hear it. Teacher. To some it seems that these arguments are dissolved by one answer, because they all conclude that it is generally right that it would be expedient for the whole world to be subject to one secular prince; yet this fails in cases, and in those cases these arguments do not conclude. Disciple. This answer seems to me far too general, and so it will not appear reasonable at all unless it is applied to those arguments specifically; please therefore set it out briefly and apply it to all the others. Teacher. The fourth argument, adduced above in chapter 1, is founded on this: since all mortals who can have fellowship with one another in temporal matters will not be governed well unless they are subject to one secular prince, it is expedient that all things be subject to one empire. But it does not seem to follow at all from this that all who wish to have fellowship with one another will not be governed well unless they are subject to one secular prince. Therefore in some cases it is not expedient for all to be subject to one empire. For in some cases the best way of governing mortals is hindered on account of wrath, and so sometimes, because of the singular wickedness of the subjects, or of their remoteness, or their unfitness to take up empire, the whole multitude of mortals cannot be governed well. Therefore in some cases it is better, since the best government cannot be had, that different provinces be subject to different princes, than that one prince claim lordship of the world to the ruin of many; and those who elect should, if the community of mortals were well disposed, promote to world empire the one who is worthy and fit both by right and in fact. The fifth argument, which consists in this, that if the whole multitude of mortals were subject to one secular prince, discord among mortals would be removed more effectively than if there were several princes with no superior, is drawn to this: although it is generally true that discords are removed more effectively by the rule of one than by many, yet this fails in the cases mentioned earlier. The sixth argument, which seems to have force from this, that disputes and lawsuits are more justly decided if all mortals have one supreme judge than if there are many supreme judges with none above them, is overturned by this: it holds as a general truth when all obey one, both by right and in fact, but it fails in the cases often mentioned above. To the seventh argument, which is founded on this, that if the whole multitude of mortals were subject to one, not only inferiors but also superiors, even kings, if they offended, could be lawfully punished, which would not happen if there were several princes with no superior: the answer is that it is generally true when no multitude rebels powerfully against the prince of the world who reigns powerfully and justly, but it fails when the Lord of the world does not reign thus by right.

units.la: Respondetur, quod regulariter verum est, quando nulla multitudo potenter rebellaret contra principem mundi, qui potenter & iuste regnaret, fallit tamen, quando Dominus mundi de iure taliter non regnat. Octaua ratio, quae fundatur in hoc, quod inter vniuersos mortales talis debet esse connexio, qualis esset respectu alterius, si sit superior vel inferior, vt colligitur ex auctoritate Gregor. & Bonifacii papae. Per hoc dissoluitur, quod absque tali connexione cunctorum mortalium vniuersitas non est optimo regimine gubernata, & ideo inter mortales talis debet esse connexio, & per consequens omnes mortales (si optime, quantum permittit conditio mortalium, essent dispositi) vni principi deberent esse subiecti, sed quia talis connexio per malitiam impeditur: ideo potest in casu contingere, quod etiam talis connexio cunctorum mortalium, etiam de iure non existat. Nona ratio, quae consistit in hoc, quod plures principes dominari mortalibus ordinauit Deus propter peccata hominum punienda, & per consequens tale dominium plurium principum non est optimum. Bene concludit, quod dominium vnius principis super totum mundum est melius plurium principum dominio superiorem non habentium: quod quandoque propter indignitatem hominum & iusto Dei iudicio tale dominium de facto haberi non potest, ideo in casu expediens est, quod etiam de iure & ad tempus cesset tale dominium, vt nullus de facto ad tale dominium subleuetur. Decima ratio, quae consistit in hoc, quod si non expedit vniuersitati mortalium vni imperatori subesse, aut hoc propter influentiam hominum, aut propter nimiam potentiam temporalem talis imperatoris ex insufficienti diuisione procedit: quia propter neutrum illorum accideret, vel propter insolitam & singularem malitiam subditorum, vel quia pro aliquo tempore determinato non constat, quod possit inueniri aliquis idoneus ad huiusmodi dignitatem. Ad vndecimam rationem, quae consistit in hoc, quod si non semper est expediens vnum imperatorem cunctis mortalibus dominari, hoc esset contra ius naturale, aut contra positiuum. Respondetur, quod cum ius naturale sit naturale praeceptum, sicut colligi potest ex Glossa quae ponitur distinct. 1. ius naturale: sicut naturalis praecepti est differentia duplex, ita iuris naturalis differentia duplex potest inueniri. Praeceptum autem naturale quoddam est absolutum absque omni conditione, modificatione seu determinatione, sicut: Non occides, Non moechaberis, & huiusmodi. Quoddam autem non est absolutum, sed cum aliqua conditione, modificatione vel specificatione seu declaratione, sicut vti alieno inuito Domino. Si fueris in extrema necessitate constitutus, abscinde vnum membrorum tuorum, pro sanitate corporis conseruanda, & consimilia. Sic est duplex ius naturale: quoddam absolutum, & quoddam cum aliqua modificatione vel specificatione, & huiusmodi. Contra ius naturale primo modo dictum, non oportet vnum imperatorem cunctis mortalibus praesidere: quia tunc in nullo casu vnquam posset imperator aliquis vniuersis mortalibus praesidere, sed vnum imperatorem cunctis mortalibus praesidere potest esse contra ius naturale secundo modo dictum, quia ratio naturalis dictat, quod non debet vnus imperator dominari cunctis mortalibus, quando huiusmodi dominium esset in detrimentum & perniciem reipublicae & boni communis. Ita etiam huiusmodi dominium regulariter esset iustum & expediens & consonum rationi & iuri naturali, sed in casu potest esse iniquum & iniustum secundo modo dicto contrarium.
units.tr: The eighth argument, which is founded on this, that among all mortals there ought to be such a connection as would exist between one thing and another if one were superior and the other inferior, as is gathered from the authority of Gregory and Pope Boniface, is dissolved by this: without such a connection the whole multitude of mortals is not governed by the best rule; and therefore among mortals there ought to be such a connection, and consequently all mortals (if they were disposed as well as the condition of mortals allows) ought to be subject to one prince. But because such a connection is hindered by wickedness, it can happen in a case that such a connection of all mortals does not exist even by right. The ninth argument, which consists in this, that God ordained several princes to rule over mortals in order to punish the sins of men, and consequently such a dominion of several princes is not the best, is answered thus: it rightly concludes that the dominion of one prince over the whole world is better than the dominion of several princes with no superior; yet because of the unworthiness of men and by the just judgment of God, such a dominion cannot in fact be had at some times, and therefore in such a case it is expedient that this dominion cease, even by right and for a time, so that no one is raised by fact to such a dominion. The tenth argument, which consists in this, that if it is not expedient for the whole multitude of mortals to be subject to one emperor, this comes either from the influence of men or from the excessive temporal power of such an emperor arising from insufficient division; for neither of these would happen, either because of the unusual and singular wickedness of the subjects, or because for some determined time it is not established that someone fit for such dignity can be found. To the eleventh argument, which consists in this, that if it is not always expedient for one emperor to rule over all mortals, this would be contrary to natural law or to positive law: the answer is that, since natural law is a natural precept, as can be gathered from the Gloss placed at Distinction 1, "ius naturale," just as there is a twofold difference of natural precept, so a twofold difference of natural law can be found. Now one natural precept is absolute, without any condition, modification or determination, such as "Thou shalt not kill," "Thou shalt not commit adultery," and the like. Another is not absolute, but has some condition, modification, specification or declaration, such as "to use another's property when the owner is unwilling," "If you are placed in extreme necessity, cut off one of your limbs to preserve the health of the body," and similar things. So natural law is twofold: one absolute, and another with some modification or specification, and so on. Against natural law in the first sense mentioned, it is not necessary for one emperor to preside over all mortals, for then in no case could any emperor ever preside over all mortals; but for one emperor to preside over all mortals can be contrary to natural law in the second sense mentioned, because natural reason dictates that one emperor ought not to dominate all mortals when such dominion would be to the detriment and ruin of the commonwealth and the common good. Thus also such dominion would generally be just, expedient, and consonant with reason and natural law; but in a case it can be unjust and unrighteous, contrary in the second sense described.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationes capituli secundi huius.
units.tr: In which replies are given to the arguments of the second chapter of this book.

units.la: Discipulus. Audiui, quomodo respondetur ad rationes, quibus videtur posse probari, quod semper & in omni casu sit expediens, vnum principem secularem cunctis mortalibus praesidere vel dominari, in temporalibus, nunc audire desidero, quomodo soluuntur rationes supra 2. c. adductae, quibus videtur posse probari seu ostendi, quod nunquam expediat vniuersitati mortalium in temporalibus vni principi seculari subesse. Magister. Ad primam rationem, quae in hoc consistit, quod diuisio regnorum a Deo, qui optime omnia regit & disponit &c. respondetur, quod Deus aliqua fecit propter peccata malorum plectenda, & illa expediunt, quando puniendi sunt mali, sed saepe quando non sunt puniendi mali, non expediunt, sed contraria, diuisio autem regnorum fuit a Deo in poenam peccati malorum, & ideo quando non essent sublimandi reges ad puniendum peccata, quae impii commiserunt, sed ad vtilitatem bonorum, & ad conseruandum & praeseruandum a malis committendis, esset expediens, quod omnia regna essent vni principi supremo subiecta. Ad secundam rationem, quae fundatur in hoc, quod Deo displicebat petitio populi Israelitici, qui iustissimis legibus vtebatur, quando petebat regem sibi dari, multipliciter respondetur. Vno modo, quod non ideo illa petitio displicebat Deo, quia petebant malum: sed quia mala voluntate, & mala intentione petebant, mala quidem intentione petebant: quia ideo petebant regem supra se, vt in hoc essent similes infidelibus. Vnde & dixerunt, vt habetur primi Reg. 8. Constitue nobis regem, vt iudicet nos, sicut & vniuersa habent nationes, & sequitur: Noluit autem populus audire vocem Samuelis, sed dixerunt, nequaquam: rex super nos erit, & erimus nos quoque sicut omnes gentes, mala etiam voluntate pete-
units.tr: Disciple. I have heard how replies are given to the arguments by which it seems possible to prove that it is always and in every case expedient for one secular prince to preside over or rule all mortals in temporal matters. Now I wish to hear how the arguments adduced in the second chapter above are answered, by which it seems possible to show that it is never expedient for the whole human race to be subject in temporal matters to one secular prince. Master. To the first argument, which consists in this, that the division of kingdoms was made by God, who governs and disposes all things best, the reply is that God made some arrangements on account of the sins of the wicked, to be punished, and these are expedient when the wicked are to be punished. But often, when the wicked are not to be punished, they are not expedient but the reverse. The division of kingdoms, however, was made by God as a punishment for the sins of the wicked. Therefore, when kings were not to be raised up to punish the sins that the impious had committed, but for the benefit of the good, and to preserve and protect them from the evils that others would commit, it would be expedient for all kingdoms to be subject to one supreme prince. To the second argument, which is based on the fact that the petition of the Israelite people, who were governed by most just laws, displeased God when they asked for a king to be given them, there are several answers. In one way: that petition did not displease God because they were asking for something evil, but because they asked with an evil will and an evil intention. Indeed they asked with an evil intention, because they asked for a king over themselves so that in this they would be like the unbelievers. Hence they also said, as we read in 1 Samuel 8: Appoint us a king to judge us, like all the nations have; and it follows: But the people refused to hear the voice of Samuel, but said, No; a king shall be over us, and we also shall be like all the nations. They also asked with an evil will

units.la: {y} Nomina et numeri marginales secundum ordinem paginae. petebant regem: quia tanquam ignari & stulti petierunt regem, vt hac occasione regimen Samuelis, qui eos iustissime rexerat, declinarent, quod Deus ipse, qui curam intuebatur eorum, restatus sui vt videmus, cum dixit Samuelj: iuxta omnia opera sua, quae fecerunt mihi, a die, qua eduxi eos de Aegypto usque ad diem hanc, sicut dereliquerunt me & seruierunt diis alienis, sic etiam faciunt tibi. Ex quibus verbis colligitur quod voluerunt iniquè declinare regimen Samuelis.
units.tr: {y} Names and marginal numbers according to the order of the page. They asked for a king, because, like ignorant and foolish people, they asked for a king so that on this occasion they might turn away from the rule of Samuel, who had governed them most justly. God himself, who looked after their welfare, showed this, as we see, when he said to Samuel: According to all their works, which they have done to me, from the day I brought them out of Egypt even to this day, as they have forsaken me and served other gods, so they also do to you. From these words it is gathered that they wished unjustly to turn away from the rule of Samuel.

units.la: Discipulus. Non videtur, quod ipsi desiderabant abiicere regimen Samuelis, sed filiorum suorum [?]iusti & impii fuerunt, & ideo merito fuerunt depelendi. Nam ibidem sic legitur: Factum est autem, cum senuisset Samuel, posuit filios suos iudices Israel, & post: & non ambulauerunt filii eius in vias eius, & declinauerunt post auaritiam, acceperunt munera, & peruerterunt iudicium. Congregati ergo vniuersi maiores natu Israel venerunt ad Samuelem in Ramatha, dixeruntque ei: Ecce tu senuisti, & filii tui non ambulant in vias tuas, constitue nobis iudicem seu regem, vt iudicet nos. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod contentabantur in regimine Samuelis: sed displicebat eis regimen filiorum suorum. Magister. Respondetur, quod quamuis noluerunt expressè dicere, sibi displicere regimen Samuelis, tamen innuebant verbis, cum dixerunt: tu senuisti, quasi dicerent, amodo non es aptus ad regendum, quod autem allegauerunt malitiam filiorum eius, non fuit nisi ad palliandum suam malam voluntatem: quia principaliter intendebant abiicere Samuelem, quod ex verbis Dei superius dictis datur intelligi. Discip. Ad istam rationem, vt quam responsionem audiui dari: nunc dicam aliam. Magister. Aliter respondetur, quod quamuis, vt saepe dictum est, plus regulariter expediat, vt rex in temporalibus dominetur: ta-men in ista non expedit, quando autem expedit, & quando non, licet saepe latet homines, & prae-cipue bonos & malos: hoc tamen Deum, cui nuda sunt & aperta omnia vera, nunquam latet, & ideo cum petiit illos petitores, quod non expediret eis regem habere, petitio eorum Deo displicuit, quia absque hoc, quod interrogarent eum, qui ordinauerat aliter regi quam per regem sciens, quod non expediret eis regem habere, indiscrete & imprudenter et importune petebant regem, non enim debebant petere mutationem modi regendi ordinati. Ideo, antequam Deum interrogassent: quamuis habere regem non sit regulariter malum, imo regulariter est bonum, & in casu malum. Tertia ratio, quae in hoc fundatur, quod illud regimen est melius, quod magis assimilatur regimini, quod fuisset si homines in statu innocentiae remansissent: quia vnum imperatorem omnium minime habuissent.
units.tr: Disciple. It does not seem that they desired to cast off the rule of Samuel, but his sons were just and wicked, and therefore they were rightly to be removed. For there it is read thus: And it came to pass, when Samuel was old, that he made his sons judges over Israel; and afterwards: And his sons did not walk in his ways, but turned aside after covetousness, took bribes, and perverted judgment. Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah, and said to him: Behold, you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways; now make us a judge or a king to judge us. From these words it is gathered that they were content with the rule of Samuel, but the rule of his sons displeased them. Master. The reply is that although they did not expressly say that the rule of Samuel displeased them, nevertheless they hinted at it in their words when they said: You are old, as if to say that henceforth he was not fit to rule. As for their pointing to the wickedness of his sons, this was only to cloak their evil will, because their chief aim was to cast off Samuel, as the words of God cited above make clear. Disciple. I have heard this reply given to that argument; now I will give another. Master. The answer is otherwise: although, as has often been said, it is usually more expedient for a king to rule in temporal matters, yet in this case it was not expedient. When it is expedient and when it is not, although it is often hidden from men, especially from good and bad men alike, yet it is never hidden from God, to whom all true things are naked and open. Therefore, when those petitioners asked for a king, knowing that it was not expedient for them to have a king, their petition displeased God.
