For without asking him, who had ordained that they should be ruled otherwise than by a king, they asked for a king indiscreetly, imprudently and importunately, knowing that it was not expedient for them to have one; for they ought not to have asked for a change in the ordained manner of government. Therefore, before they consulted God, although having a king is not in general evil, indeed in general it is good, yet in this case it was evil. The third argument, which is founded on this, that the kind of government which more closely resembles the government that would have existed if men had remained in the state of innocence is the better, since they would hardly have had one emperor over all.

units.la: Per hoc excluditur, quod propter diuersitatem inter statum innocentiae & naturae lapsae non semper illud regimen est melius in statu naturae lapsae, quod magis assimilatur illi regimini, quod fuisset in statu innocentiae, sicut nec regimen illud est melius in statu naturae lapsae, quod magis assimilatur regimini, quod est in statu naturae gloriae, quia tunc melius esset, quod quilibet regeret seipsum, & quod nullus regimen super alios seu praelationem haberet: quia regimen seu praelatio non erit in statu gloriae. Ad quartam, quae consistit in hoc, quod vnum imperatorem cunctis mortalibus dominari est contra ius gentium, quod est ius naturale: & per consequens numquam est expediens siue licitum, haec per illa, quae dicta sunt in praecedenti c. videtur posse repelli. Nam illud, quod est contra ius gentium, licet ipsum sit iniquum, non tamen semper est iniquum, imo quandoque est regulariter aequum & licitum, & in casu iniquum, pro eo quod ius gentium saltem quo ad multa non est ius naturale absolutum absque omni modificatione vel conditione, determinatione vel specificatione: sed est ius naturale conditionatum modificatum specificatum seu determinatum vel cum specificatione aliqua seu distinctione. Nam sicut habetur in decretis dist. 1. ius gentium, ad ius gentium spectant bella, captiuitates, seruitutes: quae tamen non sunt de iure naturali absolute absque omni modificatione: etiam quia tunc contraria nunquam essent licita, quia illa quae sunt contra ius naturale absolu-tum, numquam sunt licita, sed semper sunt illicita & indispensabilia, extra de consuetudine, c. causam, 9. quod licet ita quod vnum imperatorem omnibus dominari, bella, captiuitates atque iurgia domigenas sint interdum de iure gentium, & ideo valeant pertinere ad ius naturale condi-tiomodificatum, seu cum aliqua specificatione seu determinatione, non tamen sunt semper ius naturale, quia non spectant ad ius naturale absolutum, quod non variatur, sed inuariabile perseuerat, vt sup. licet & dist. 6. §. hic ita.
units.tr: By this it is excluded that, on account of the difference between the state of innocence and the fallen state of nature, that government is not always better in the fallen state of nature which more closely resembles the government that would have existed in the state of innocence; just as that government is not better in the fallen state of nature which more closely resembles the government that exists in the state of glory of nature, since then it would be better for each person to rule himself, and for no one to have rule or precedence over others, because rule or precedence will not exist in the state of glory. To the fourth argument, which consists in this, that for one emperor to rule over all mortals is contrary to the law of nations, which is natural law, and consequently is never expedient or lawful, this can be refuted by what has been said in the preceding chapter. For what is contrary to the law of nations, although it is itself unjust, is not always unjust. Indeed, sometimes it is generally fair and lawful, and in a particular case unjust; because the law of nations, at least in many respects, is not absolute natural law without any modification or condition, determination or specification, but is conditional natural law, modified, specified or determined, or with some specification or distinction. For as is stated in the decretals, dist. 1, ius gentium, wars, captivities and servitudes belong to the law of nations; yet these are not of natural law absolutely, without any modification. Otherwise contrary things would never be lawful, since what is contrary to absolute natural law is never lawful, but is always unlawful and non-dispensable, extra de consuetudine, c. causam, 9. Thus, although for one emperor to rule over all, and wars, captivities and domestic quarrels are sometimes by the law of nations, and so may belong to natural law conditioned, modified, or with some specification or determination, nevertheless they are not always natural law, because they do not belong to absolute natural law, which does not vary but remains unchangeable, as above, licet, and dist. 6, §. hic ita.

units.la: Secunda ratio fundata in hoc, quod mortalium quidam sunt fideles, quidam sunt infideles, qui non de-bent idem iugum ducere, nec adinuicem communionem seu pacificam societatem habere, nec ad eumdem iudicem pro iudicio suscipiendo recurrere: & per consequens non debent vni imperatori subesse, multipliciter videtur posse elidi. Primo, quia licet fideles non deberent ducere iugum infidelium cum infidelibus, nec debeant cum infidelibus communionem seu societatem pacificam habere, quando infideles impugnarent fideles, vel aliquid facerent in contumeliam imperatoris vel curatoris, aut nisi fideles trahere ad peccatum mortale: nec fideles deberent recurrere ad iudicium infidelis, pro iudicio sustinendo esset: tamen licitum esset fidelibus ducere iugum infidelium cum infidelibus, & cum eis communionem seu pacificam societatem habere, quando nihil mali molirentur, & cum eis ad iudicem fidelium pro iudicio sustinendo recurrere, & ideo licet non esset licitum fidelibus vni imperatori omnium mortalium infideli subesse: videtur tamen tam infidelibus, quam fidelibus licitum vni imperatori fideli subesse. Secundo quia fideles non debent idem iugum spirituale ducere cum infidelibus: possunt tamen licite cum eis ducere idem iugum temporale, unde & multi fuerunt fideles tam in nouo quam in veteri testamento, idem iugum temporale ducentes cum infidelibus principi infideli obedientes, fideles etiam licite communionem & pacificam societatem possunt habere cum infidelibus, sicut & multi sancti habuerunt, licet non in peccato, nec contra bono-
units.tr: The second argument, founded on this, that some mortals are faithful and some unfaithful, who ought not to bear the same yoke, nor have fellowship or peaceful society with one another, nor resort to the same judge to receive judgment, and consequently ought not to be subject to one emperor, can be refuted in several ways. First, although the faithful ought not to bear the yoke of unbelievers together with unbelievers, nor ought they to have fellowship or peaceful society with unbelievers when the unbelievers attack the faithful, or do something in insult to the emperor or governor, or unless they draw the faithful into mortal sin; and the faithful ought not to resort to the judgment of an unbeliever to receive judgment; nevertheless it would be lawful for the faithful to bear the yoke together with unbelievers, and to have fellowship and peaceful society with them, when they were plotting nothing evil, and to resort with them to a judge of the faithful to receive judgment. And so, although it would not be lawful for the faithful to be subject to one unbelieving emperor of all mortals, yet it seems lawful both for unbelievers and for the faithful to be subject to one faithful emperor. Second, because the faithful ought not to bear the same spiritual yoke with unbelievers, yet they may lawfully bear the same temporal yoke with them. Hence there were also many faithful, both in the New and in the Old Testament, who bore the same temporal yoke with unbelievers, obeying an unbelieving prince. The faithful can also lawfully have communion and peaceful society with unbelievers, as many saints have had, though not in sin, nor against the good-

units.la: Eeee 2 honorem Dei, licet etiam in casu fideles ad iudicem infidelem pro iudicio suscipiendo recurrere, exemplo multorum sanctorum, qui hoc fecerunt, & ita posset esse expediens in casu, quod etiam unus imperator infidelis cunctis mortalibus praesideret: tum quia accidit quod quidam sunt fideles, & quidam alii, alii autem mortales fuere fideles, & adhuc posset contingere. Sexta ratio in hoc consistens, quod nullus est sufficiens ad gerendum curam cunctorum mortalium: per hoc refellitur, quod licet nullus sit sufficiens ad gerendum curam cunctorum absque omni periculo, dispendio & incommodo omnium subditorum, multi tamen ad hoc habent sufficientiam, quam conditio naturae lapsae permittit, propter quam utilius est vniuersitati mortalium vni subesse quam pluribus: sicut etiam licet nullus sit sufficiens sine omni dispendio ad regendum vnum regnum parvum, utilius est tamen vni regno parciali, vni Domino quam pluribus subiacere. Unde & Salomon, licet aduerteret quod nullum populum Israeliticum posse t absque omni defectu in nullo deficiens iudicare, regimen tamen non renuit, sed sapientiam ad regendum perfectius & dignius postulauit.
units.tr: Eeee 2 honorem Dei: it is also permissible, even in a case, for the faithful to appeal to an unbelieving judge to receive judgment, following the example of many saints who did so; and so it could be expedient in some case that even a single unbelieving emperor should preside over all mortals. This is so because it happens that some are faithful and some are not, and others have been faithful, and it could still happen. The sixth reason rests on this: no one is sufficient to bear the care of all mortals. This is refuted as follows: although no one is sufficient to bear the care of all without any danger, loss and inconvenience to all subjects, many nevertheless have that sufficiency which the condition of fallen nature allows; for this reason it is more useful for the whole human race to be subject to one ruler than to many. Just as, although no one is sufficient, without any loss, to rule one small kingdom, it is nevertheless more useful for a partial kingdom to be subject to one lord than to many. Hence also Solomon, though he noticed that no one could judge the Israelite people without any defect, did not refuse government, but asked for wisdom to rule more perfectly and worthily.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: In qua respondetur ad rationem capitulo tertio, pro opinione tertia inductam.
units.tr: In which the argument put forward in chapter three for the third opinion is answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Ad motivum pro tertia opinione supra c. 3. recitata, an expediret mundo vnum praesidere, scilicet ecclesiasticum, non secularem, praesidere: alia adducas. MAG. Motivum illud consistit in hoc, quod sapientia, quae maxime est necessaria praesidenti sive in temporalibus sive spiritualibus, magis in ecclesiasticis quam in secularibus invenitur, ad quod respondisti, quod in ecclesiasticis inuenitur maior sapientia de diuinis, non de humanis. Quam responsionem aliqui improbare nituntur per hoc, quod secundum legem diuinam rex debet esse alius peritior in his, quae ad legem diuinam spectant, in qua debet continue meditari. Alii hanc obiectionem conantur excludere asserentes, quod quamuis ex praecepto, quod habetur Deuteron. 17. vt allegatum est, deberet rex legere legem Dei omnibus diebus vitae suae, congruis videlicet horis: magis tamen ad lectionem huiusmodi sacerdotes Dei praecepto tenebantur, & ideo quamuis rex non deberet totaliter sapientiae diuinae esse ignarus, non tamen tenebatur sacerdotes in sapientia diuina praecellere: praesertim cum sapientiam diuinam publice docere non deberet, quia nullus rex debet vsurpare sibi officium praedicationis: quod tamen officium ad sacerdotes spectat. DISCIPULUS. Ad hoc videtur ista responsio posse impediri, quoniam ille est magis idoneus in temporalibus praesidere, qui non solum in sapientia diuina, sed etiam in sapientia humana & peritia negotiorum secularium alios debet praecellere: teste Salomone. Prouerbior. 1. qui ait: intelligens gubernacula possidebit, qui etiam 17. c. ait: seruus sapiens dominabitur super fatuos. Sed praelati ecclesiastici non solum in sapientia diuina, sed etiam in sapientia humana & peritia negotiorum secularium alios debent praecellere, distinct. 39. §. vnus & c. 1. vbi Gregor. loquens de episcopo constituendo ait: Hoc tempore talis regiminis arte debet constitui, qui non solum de salute animarum, verumetiam de extrinseca vtilitate & cautela sciat esse sollicitus & 16 q. 1. c. nulli episcoporum, sic legitur: de episcopo, cum sit optimus prospecter, ita prospiciat, vt vniuersa sibi commissa omnes a se maxime alantur, atque in necessitatibus adiumentur. Ex quibus verbis sequitur, quod praelati ecclesiastici debent alios in peritia negotiorum secularium praecellere, quare non princeps secularis, sed ecclesiasticus debet non immerito propter maximam peritiam etiam in temporalibus, cunctis mortalibus praesidere. MAGISTER. Respondetur, quod quamuis propter malitiam aut negligentiam laicorum saepe fuerit opportunum, vt praelati ecclesiastici dispensationem quarundam temporalium rerum recipiant: & ideo tunc negotiorum secularium debent habere notitiam: non tamen excellentissimam huiusmodi negotiorum peritiam debent habere, sed eis sufficit mediocris, propter quod, vt lex testatur, & notatur in Glo. dist. 37. c. 1. opprobrium est praelatis ecclesiasticis, si relinquantur periti disciplinarum forensium, unde & leges ciuiles prohibentur audire, extra. ne cle. vel mo. super specula. cum enim nemo perfectissimam notitiam ciuilium legum & secularium negotiorum vna cum perfectissima scientia sacrarum litterarum possit acquirere: & ideo prohibentur monachi & clerici leges audire, vt plenius sacrae paginae insistant: restat, quod praelati ecclesiastici non debent in peritia negotiorum secularium alios superare, cum in notitia sacrarum litterarum praecellere debeant vniuersos. Quare regulariter praelatus ecclesiasticus non debet in temporalibus, mortalibus praeficiri vniuersis, ne, vt testatur beatus Petrus, secundum quod legitur in decretis 11. q. 1. c. quedam, praenotatis praesentibus hominum curis non possit verbo Dei vacare. Licet igitur in aliquo casu in temporalibus quando non inueniretur aliquis laicus idoneus, posset ad tempus aliquis ecclesiasticus curam omnium gerere: hoc tamen regulariter sustineri non debet: eo quod iuxta Apostolicam sententiam ecclesiastici tali curae & sollicitudini circa temporalia, nisi ex singulari causa, & in quantum minus possunt, se implicare non debent. Cui concordat beatus Petrus, qui, vt legitur in decretis ext. 1. 5. in ordine Clement. ait, te quidem oportet irreprehensibiliter viuere, & summo studio niti, ne omnes vitae huius occupationes abiicias, ne fidei iuffor existas, ne aduocatus litium fias, ne aliqua cautione occupatione immeniaris mundani negotii occasione perplexus.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. As to the argument for the third opinion, recited above in chapter 3, that it would benefit the world for one person to preside, namely an ecclesiastic rather than a secular ruler, please offer other arguments. MASTER. That argument rests on this: wisdom, which is especially necessary for one who presides in temporal or in spiritual matters, is found more in ecclesiastics than in secular men. To this you replied that greater wisdom in divine matters, not in human ones, is found among ecclesiastics. Some try to disprove this answer on the ground that, according to the divine law, the king ought to be more skilled than others in those things that pertain to the divine law, in which he ought to meditate continually. Others try to set this objection aside, asserting that although, by the precept found in Deuteronomy 17, as has been cited, the king ought to read the law of God all the days of his life, that is, at the proper hours, yet the priests of God were more bound by precept to such reading. Therefore, although the king ought not to be wholly ignorant of divine wisdom, he was not bound to surpass the priests in divine wisdom, especially since he ought not to teach divine wisdom publicly, because no king ought to usurp for himself the office of preaching, which office belongs to the priests. DISCIPLE. This answer seems open to objection, since the one who is better fitted to preside in temporal matters is the one who must surpass others not only in divine wisdom but also in human wisdom and skill in secular affairs. Solomon bears witness, Proverbs 1, who says: "The man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels" [intelligens gubernacula possidebit]; and in chapter 17 he says: "A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame" [seruus sapiens dominabitur super fatuos]. But ecclesiastical prelates must surpass others not only in divine wisdom but also in human wisdom and skill in secular affairs, as in distinction 39, §. "unus", and chapter 1, where Gregory, speaking of the appointment of a bishop, says: "At this time a man must be appointed by such an art of government that he knows to be anxious not only for the salvation of souls but also for their external welfare and caution." And 16 q. 1, chapter "nulli episcoporum", reads thus: "A bishop, since he is the best provider, should so provide that all committed to him are most nourished by him and helped in their needs." From these words it follows that ecclesiastical prelates ought to surpass others in skill in secular affairs; therefore it is not the secular prince but the ecclesiastic who, on account of his greatest skill even in temporal matters, deservedly ought to preside over all mortals. MASTER. The answer is that although, on account of the wickedness or negligence of laymen, it has often been expedient for ecclesiastical prelates to take on the management of certain temporal things, and therefore at such times they must have knowledge of secular affairs, yet they need not have the most excellent skill in such affairs; a moderate measure suffices for them. For this reason, as the law bears witness and the Gloss notes on distinction 37, chapter 1, it is a reproach to ecclesiastical prelates if they are left as experts in forensic disciplines; hence they are also forbidden to hear civil laws, extra. "ne cle. vel mo." super "specula". For since no one can acquire the most perfect knowledge of civil laws and secular affairs together with the most perfect knowledge of the sacred letters, monks and clerics are therefore forbidden to hear the laws, so that they may devote themselves more fully to the sacred page. It remains that ecclesiastical prelates ought not to surpass others in skill in secular affairs, since they ought to excel all in knowledge of the sacred letters. Therefore, as a general rule, an ecclesiastical prelate ought not to be set over all mortals in temporal affairs, lest, as blessed Peter testifies, as it is read in the decretals, 11 q. 1, chapter "quedam", with the cares of men at hand he be unable to devote himself to the word of God. Therefore, although in some case, when no suitable layman could be found, some ecclesiastic might for a time manage the care of all things temporal, this ought not to be sustained as a general rule, because according to the apostolic judgment ecclesiastics ought not to entangle themselves in such care and concern for temporal things, except for a special cause and only so far as they can do so with least harm. Blessed Peter agrees with this, who, as it is read in the decretals, ext. 1, 5, in the Clementine order, says: "You indeed ought to live blamelessly, and strive with the greatest zeal not to cast off all the occupations of this life, lest you become a non-performer of the faith, lest you become an advocate of lawsuits, lest you be found entangled in some worldly business by any caution or occupation."

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad rationem cap. 4. pro quarta opinione inductam.
units.tr: In which the argument of chapter 4, brought forward for the fourth opinion, is answered.

units.la: DIscipulus. De ista materia plura poterunt legentes in tractatu de potestate papae & cleri inuenire, ideo ad motiuum adductum supra cap. 4. pro quarta opinione te conuerte, & recita quomodo respondetur ad ipsam. Magister. Motiuum illud ad probandum, quod illud regimen mundi est optimum, quod est plurium sapientum, similiter, in hoc consistit, quod quando plures regunt simul, pauciores errores accidunt & peccata. Ad quod respondetur, quod illud motiuum videtur probabilitatem habere, si errores & peccata in regendo ex sola imperitia vel defectu consilii solum contingerent: Et si unus princeps secularis absque consilio sapientum sibi subditos gubernare deberet, sed quia errores & peccata in regendo non ex sola imperitia, sed etiam ex mala voluntate & negligentia eueniunt, & princeps sibi subditos debet regere de consilio sapientis, nec est aliquis promouendus ad principatum, nisi qui est melior & prudentior aliis, & de quo probabiliter aestimetur, quod quando oportet & expedit, velit requirere consilium sapientum, ideo regulariter principatus unius virtuosi & prudentis praeualet principatui plurium virtuosorum & sapientum. Quia enim tantum mortales proni sunt ad discordiam & ad quaerendum quae sua sunt nimis, & non quae sunt boni communis: ex quibus turbatio tranquillitatis & pacis corruptio & alia mala quasi infinita proueniunt, ab his maxime, qui super alios potestate habent. Quando autem essent plures rectores, quorum nullus altero esset superior, facilius accideret discordia, qui si unus esset superior aliis: eo quod nullus discordat a seipso, facilius etiam plures, qui a superiori refrenari non possent, quaererent propria utilitatem, qui si unus dominaretur aliis, ideo regulariter minus timendum esset deturbatio pacis & iustitiae & aliis malis, quae ex defectu boni regiminis punire noscantur, si unus esset rector, qui si plures essent simul rectores, quorum nullus esset superior alio: praesertim cum facilius sit populo, emendare unum rectorem (si taliter exorbitauerit) ut sit puniendus vel etiam amouendus, quam plures. Nec obstat, quod veritas iustitiae, quae a multis quaeritur, facilius inuenitur: & quod salus est, vbi multa consilia, quia, sicut dictum est, princeps virtuosus & sapiens, quando expedit, requirit consilia sapientum, & facit scilicet veritatem quaeri a pluribus, qui multo melius potest regere consiliarios quaerentes veritatem & modum debitum quaerendi pro loco & tempore, quod unicuique videtur eis imponere, quam possent ipsimet consulentes, si nullus haberet potestatem super alium: praesertim cum unus rector habens super omnes consiliarios potestatem de modo consulendi consiliarios possit vnumquemque eorum requirere: & cuius consilium videtur sanius, acceptare. Et ideo quantumcunque expediat veritatem in causis arduis quaeri a pluribus, utile est ut unus super omnes alios consulentes quaerendi veritatem habeat potestatem. Hinc est quod quamuis, ut allegatum est supra c. 4. Romani fecerunt sibi curiam, ut quotidie consulerent 322. consilium agentes de multitudine, ut habetur 1. Macchabeor. 8. tamen, ut ibidem legitur, commiserunt vni homini magistratum summum, & omnes obediebant vni regulariter, igitur melius est, quod unus virtuosus & prouidens habeat mundi imperium, quam plures.
units.tr: Disciple. Readers will find more on this matter in the treatise On the Power of the Pope and the Clergy. So turn to the argument advanced above in chapter 4 for the fourth opinion, and tell me how it is answered. Master. The argument for proving that the government of the world is best when it is in the hands of many wise men rests on this: when several rule together, fewer errors and sins occur. To this it is answered that the argument would seem to have some plausibility if errors and sins in governing arose only from inexperience or lack of counsel, and if a single secular prince had to govern his subjects without the counsel of the wise. But errors and sins in governing arise not only from inexperience but also from ill will and negligence. A prince ought to rule his subjects with the advice of the wise, and no one should be promoted to rule unless he is better and wiser than others, and unless it is reasonably judged that when it is fitting and expedient he will be willing to seek the counsel of the wise. For this reason, as a rule, the rule of one virtuous and prudent man is preferable to the rule of many virtuous and wise men. Mortals are so prone to discord and to seeking their own interests too eagerly, and not the good of the commonwealth, that from this come the disturbance of tranquillity, the corruption of peace, and almost endless other evils, and these arise chiefly from those who hold power over others. Moreover, if there were several rulers, none of whom was superior to the others, discord would arise more easily than if one of them were superior to the rest, since no one disagrees with himself. Likewise, several rulers who could not be restrained by a superior would more easily seek their own advantage than if one man ruled over the others. Therefore, as a rule, the overthrow of peace and justice and the other evils which are known to result from a lack of good government would be less to be feared if there were one ruler than if there were several rulers at once, none of whom was superior to another. This is especially so because it is easier for a people to correct one ruler, if he has gone astray in this way, so that he may be punished or even removed, than to correct several. Nor does it stand in the way that the truth of justice, which is sought from many, is more easily found, and that there is safety where there are many counsels. For, as has been said, a virtuous and wise prince, when it is expedient, seeks the counsel of the wise, and so causes the truth to be sought by many. He can govern his counsellors, who are seeking the truth, far better than they could govern themselves if no one had power over another, and he can prescribe for each of them the proper manner of seeking counsel, according to place and time. This is especially so because one ruler who has power over all the counsellors can question each of them about the way they give advice, and accept the counsel that seems soundest. Therefore, however expedient it is that the truth in difficult matters be sought from many, it is useful that one man, above all the other counsellors, have power to seek out the truth. Hence, although, as has been alleged above in chapter 4, the Romans formed for themselves a council, so that they might consult daily, taking counsel about the multitude, as is recorded in 1 Macc. 8, nevertheless, as is read in the same place, they committed the supreme magistracy to one man, and all regularly obeyed one man. Therefore it is better that one virtuous and provident man hold the rule of the world than many.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: Vbi incipit inuestigare, quibus virtutibus debeat pollere imperator: & primo de fide.
units.tr: Where he begins to inquire what virtues an emperor ought to excel in: and first, concerning faith.

units.la: DIscipulus. Hactenus inquisiuimus, an toti generi humano expediat vnum imperatorem seu principem secularem vniuerso orbi praeesse: & aliqualiter exquisite pertractauimus opinionem dicentem, quod regulariter est expediens, vt omnes mortales vni seculari principi in temporalibus sint subiecti, nunc autem intendo tecum inuestigare (quamuis breuiter) quibus excellentiis seu gratiis, virtutibus & moribus imperator mundi debeat praefulgere. Aestimo autem, quod fides, iustitia, veritas, peritia, potentia, diuitiae, liberalitas, & fortitudo in imperatore mundi maxime requiruntur, ideo de istis aliqua breuiter interrogare propono, primo an imperator mundi veram fidem & catholicam teneatur habere? Magist. Nonnullis apparet, quod interrogatio tua dubitationem non habet, cum quilibet etiam moralis adultus habens vsum rationis teneatur esse fidelis, praesertim si in fide potuerit informari, sed forsan quaerere intendebas, an aliquis posset esse verus imperator, qui non habeat veram & catholicam fidem, de quo sunt multae opiniones diuersae & aduersae.
units.tr: The Disciple. Hitherto we have inquired whether it is expedient for the whole human race that one emperor or secular prince should preside over the entire world, and we have treated with some care the opinion which holds that it is generally expedient for all mortals to be subject in temporal matters to one secular prince. Now I intend to inquire with you (though briefly) with what excellences, gifts, virtues and morals the emperor of the world ought to shine. I judge that faith, justice, truthfulness, skill, power, wealth, generosity and fortitude are especially required in the emperor of the world, and so I propose to ask briefly about these. First, I ask whether the emperor of the world is bound to hold the true and catholic faith? The Master. To some it appears that your question admits of no doubt, since every moral adult who has the use of reason is bound to be faithful, especially if he could have been instructed in the faith. But perhaps you intended to ask whether anyone could be a true emperor who does not hold the true and catholic faith, a question on which there are many diverse and opposing opinions.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Inquiris vtrum imperator debeat habere notitiam scripturarum, & respondet secundum diuersas opiniones.
units.tr: The author asks whether the emperor ought to have knowledge of the Scriptures, and answers according to the various opinions.

units.la: DIscipulus. De isto secundo inquiram aliqualiter postea exquisite, ideo transeo ad peritiam necessariam imperatori. Et primo cupio scire, an imperator mundi, si fuerit catholicus, teneatur habere peritiam scripturae diuinae? Magist. Circa hoc sunt diuersae opiniones. Vna, quod imperator mundi, si fuerit catholicus, peritiam legis diuinae & sacrarum litterarum debet habere. Quia non minoris perfectionis debet esse imperator catholicus in nouo testamento, quam fuerit rex in veteri testamento. Sed rex in veteri testamento debuit habere peritiam litterarum sacrarum, & in lege diui-
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I will inquire into this second point more carefully later, so I now pass on to the expertise needed by an emperor. And first I want to know whether the emperor of the world, if he is Catholic, must have expertise in divine Scripture? Master. On this question there are various opinions. One opinion holds that the emperor of the world, if he is Catholic, ought to have expertise in the divine law and the holy writings. For a Catholic emperor under the New Testament ought not to be of less perfection than a king was under the Old Testament. But a king under the Old Testament had to have knowledge of the holy writings and to meditate continually on the divine law. Therefore a Catholic emperor ought to have these things in a more perfect way. Likewise, it is the business of the Catholic emperor to defend the Christian faith, which is contained in the sacred letters, and to punish its assailants with due vengeance. But no one can defend what he does not know. Therefore the Catholic emperor more perfectly…

units.la: na conuina continue meditari. Igitur imperator catholicus perfectius debet ista habere. Item, ad imperatorem catholicum spectat fidem Christianam, quae in sacris literis continetur, defendere: & impugnatores ipsius vltione debita castigare, nullus autem defendere potest, quod ignorat; igitur imperator catholicus perfectius debet ista habere, scilicet literarum sacrarum peritiam. Alia est opinio: quod quamuis deceat imperatorem catholicum aliqualem literarum sacrarum habere peritiam, vt saltem sciat legem vel legendo intelligere literaliter scripturas sacras: non tamen est simpliciter sibi necessarium peritiam talem habere: pro eo quod absque tali peritia potest temporalia vtiliter & iuste disponere, quod solummodo ad imperatorem dignoscitur pertinere. Discip. Nunquid imperator tenetur notitiam legum ciuilium habere? Magist. Vna est opinio, quod sic, quia cum imperator sit summus iudex in temporalibus, non minorem peritiam legum, secundum quas est ferenda sententia, debet ipse habere, quam iudices inferiores. Sed iudices inferiores tenentur habere notitiam legum ciuilium, secundum quas iudicare tenentur. Igitur multo magis debet imperator legum ciuilium habere peritiam. Alia est opinio, quod non tenetur de necessitate legum ciuilium habere peritiam: licet valde conueniens sit & vtile, vt peritia talis non careat, multi enim suerunt imperatores & reges iusti, imo sancti, qui legum ciuilium peritiam minime habuerunt: qui tamen omnino didicissent leges, si de necessitate ad earum notitiam obligati fuissent, nec est simile de imperatore aut rege & aliis iudicibus inferioribus, quia enim imperator in imperio mundi, & rex in regno suo, solutus est legibus, nec tenetur de necessitate iudicare secundum leges, quemadmodum iudices inferiores secundum leges de necessitate iudicare tenentur: ideo non requiritur tanta notitia legum in imperatore aut rege, sicut in inferioribus iudicibus. Discip. Ex praedictis mihi probabile videtur, quod decet promouendum in imperatorem & regem tam sanctarum scripturarum quam legum profundam habere notitiam: & quod talis, si inueniretur, ante omnes alios (caeteris paribus) esset promouendus in imperatorem: & tunc in regem, quando per electionem non per successionem debet quis regni gubernacula suscipere. Sed nunquid si promotus in imperatorem vel regem non esset profundus in notitia sacrarum scripturarum & legum ciuilium, deceret eum desistere vel insistere studio pro huiusmodi excellenti notitia acquirenda: vel etiam si esset excellens in tali notitia debeat circa meditationem huiusmodi assidue occupari? Mag. Respondetur, quod laudabile esset imperatori aut regi vacare cum discretione huiusmodi studio, quantum posset, ita tamen, vt per tale studium non impediretur a sibi commissis. Negligere autem sibi subditos, & regni, imperii aut regnum alteri committere, vt tali studio insistat, in imperatore & rege est reprehensibile & damnabile reputandum: quia talis curam debitam subditis non impendit, & de ipso verificatur illud Apostoli: qui suorum & maxime domesticorum curam non habet, fidem negauit & est infideli deterior. Si enim praelatus ecclesiasticus propter vtilitatem subditorum vitam contemplatiuam debet nonnunquam praetermittere, & actiuae intendere, vt ex sacris canonibus colligitur S.q.i.ca.alia & c. inscriptis & c. quis episcopatum: multo fortius imperator aut rex debet omittere tale studium, vt regimen debitum non solum per alios, sed etiam per seipsum subditis impendat. Disc. Nunquid imperator debet habere excellentem notitiam secularium negotiorum? Mag. Respondetur, quod ille, qui caeteros ante cellit in peritia secularium negotiorum, & qui alios in sensu naturali & iudicio rationis excellit, caeteris paribus, debet ante alios in imperatorem aut regem, qui per electionem ad regni gubernacula assumitur, promoueri. Sensus enim naturalis & excellens rationis iudicium intelligit, quod in promouendo literatura, facundia, eloquentia, experientia, & memoria quilibet excellens videtur praeferri debere: cum in promouendo ad officium temporale etiam breui tempore duraturum excellenti iudicio rationis interdum tam litteratura quam experientia debeat anteferri. Postquam autem ad imperium aut ad mundi gubernacula fuerit quis assumptus, peritiae secularium negotiorum, & notitiae iuris naturalis, & praecipue illius circa quod contingit errare vel dubitare etiam eruditum, & cuius notitia ad suum spectat officium principaliter, debet insistere, & magis quam notitiae scripturarum sacrarum, vel secularium scientiarum, vel legum quarumcunque, nisi magis per eas quam per alium modum valeat peritiam secularium acquirere. Disc. Quare dicitur, quod insistendum est notitiae iuris naturalis, circa quod contigit errare aut dubitare etiam eruditum? videtur enim, quod nullum est tale ius naturale, omnis enim ignorantia iuris, circa quod contingit errare peritos, videtur excusare contra facientem, ideo enim ignorantia facti excusat, quia etiam peritos fallit, vt notat Glo. dist.38.c.1. Igitur si circa ius naturale contingit errare peritos, ignorantia talis iuris excusare valeret. Rursus, omnis ignorantia probabilis excusat, sed ignorantia, quae potest inueniri in peritis, potest esse probabilis, ideo aliqua ignorantia iuris naturalis excusaret, cuius contrarium notat Glo. dist.30.c.1. & Gratianus t.q.1. qui notandum dicit, quod omnis ignorantia iuris naturalis omnibus adultis damnabilis est. Ex quibus videtur colligi posse, quod nullum est ius naturale, circa quod contingit errare aut dubitare peritos. Mag. Respondetur, quod iura naturalia reperiuntur in duplici differentia. Quaedam enim sunt principia per se nota, vel ex talibus principiis immobilibus per se notis sequuntur & sumuntur, & circa talia iura nemo potest errare vel etiam dubitare: ipsa tamen ignorare potest, quia potest de ipsis nunquam cogitare, & talis ignorantia neminem excusat: qua talia iura naturalia, licet quis antea nunquam cogitauerit ea, statim cognoscit, quando secundum ea aliquis tenetur facere aliquid vel omittere, nisi absque omni deliberatione & regula rationis velit quid ad actum procedere, vel actum talem omittere: qua ignorantia talis iuris in tali casu ex damnabili negligentia vel contemptu procedit, & ideo non excusat. Si enim ex aliqua occasione nitetur occidere aliquem innocentem, qui nunquam nocuit, statim si deliberare velit, & breuiter, an debeat ipsum occidere, conconcludit, quod nō debet ipsum occidere. Et ideo si absq; omni deliberatione ipsum occiderit, talis ignorantia ipsum non excusat. Alia sunt iura naturalia, quæ ex primis principiis iuris patenter, & absque magna deliberatione seu consideratione eliciuntur, quemadmodum in scibilibus quædam conclusiones ex primis principiis patenter, & absque magna consideratione concluduntur etiam à minus eruditis, & talis ignorantia iuris naturalis non excusat: quia potest quilibet absq; magno studio statim illa iura naturalia scire, & de tali ignorantia iuris intelligitur dicta maior. Alia sunt iura naturalia, quæ à paucis etiam peritis, & cum magna attentione & studio, & per multa media colligantur ex primis iuribus naturalibus, circa quæ etiam periti interdum habent opiniones contrarias, quibusdam putantibus ea esse iusta, & quibusdam ea esse iniusta, & ignorantia talis iuris naturalis excusat præcipue in omittendo aliquid facere, quod tamen faciendum esset, si non ignoraret, nisi sit ignorantia crassa & affectata. Talium igitur iurium naturalium notitiæ acquirendæ debet imperator insistere diligenter: quia alia iura, scilicet primo modo & secundo modo dicta, leuiter, quando erit necesse, sibi ostendentur, nec huiusmodi iurium & secularium negociorum peritiam & persectam notitiam acquiri expedit, etiam vt plures consiliarios secum habeat sapientes, exemplo Romanorum, qui, vt est allegatum prius, constituerunt 32. qui quotidie consulebant & consilium agentes de multitudine, quia teste Salomone Proverbiorum decimo quinto. Dispensantur cogitationes, vbi non est consilium, vbi vero plures consiliarii sunt, confirmantur, & Proverbior. secund. ait, quod est salus, vbi multa sunt consilia. Discipulus. Doctrina sapientis obuiare videtur, imperatorem habere multos consiliarios. Quia Ecclesiastic. 6. sic legitur, multi pacifici sint tibi, & consiliarius tibi sit vnus de mille. Magister. Respondetur, quod consilium de diuersis & ex diuersis causis requiritur, aliquando enim requiritur consilium de secreto, quod periculosum est reuelare, nisi fidelibus & amicis ac discretis. Interdum requiritur consilium de publicis, vel de illis quæ absque periculo reuelari possunt infidelibus, inimicis & fatuis. Iterum, quandoque requiritur consilium aliorum, vt tot consiliorum habeatur consensus, quo habito illud, quod deliberatum est, efficiatur magis autenticum, etiam cum maiori ordinatione & amoris reuerentia vel timore ab aliis suscipitur. Quandoque autem requiritur consilium, vt quærens consilium illud, quod deliberatum est, per consiliarios exequatur. Nonnunquam requiritur aliquorum consilium, vt quærens consilium notitiam iuris vel facti, quod ignorat, per eorum responsionem acquirat: qua habita quid agere debeat, animaduertat, multotiens vero requiritur consilium aliquorum, vt quærens consilium probet & experiatur eorum consilia, & eorum discretionem, vel prudentiam, aut fidelitatem, vel affectionem, seu voluntatem, vel contra se vel erga alios. Quando igitur requiritur consilium de secretis, quod periculosum est reuelare, pauci debent esse consiliarii: quia solummodo probati fideles amici & discreti. Quando autem requiritur consilium, vt deliberatum per consiliarios executioni demandetur, requirendi sunt pauci: quia solummodo fideles sapientes & amici tantum, & in his duobus casibus intelligenda est auctoritas Ecclesiastici superius allegata. Quando autem requiritur consilium de publicis, vel de his quæ possunt sine periculo reuelari, requiritur consilium solummodo, vt habeatur consiliariorum consensus, quo habito illud, quod deliberatum fuerit efficiatur magis autenticum, vel vt quærens consilium per responsionem consiliariorum notitiam iuris vel facti, quod ignorat acquirat: vel vt ipsorum habeat experientiam, vt probet discretionem seu prudentiam vel fidelitatem aut affectionem vel voluntatem: multi debent esse consiliarii numero in tali casu. Quandoque etiam non est absurdum, consilium impiorum vel malevolorum requirere: quia quandoque sapiens ex eorum responsione etiam ipsis nocere volentibus & decipere intendentibus, quid sibi erit agendum, prospiciet. Quemadmodum non solum ex bonis operibus sapientum: sed etiam ex malis operibus stultorum sapiens accipit disciplinam, teste Salomone Proverbiorum vigesimo quarto, qui ait: per agrum hominis pigri transiui, & per vineam viri stulti: & ecce totum repleuerant vrtica operuerunt superficiem eius spina, & materia lapidum destructa erat: quod cum vidissem posui in corde meo & exemplo didici disciplinam.
units.tr: Discip. Is the emperor bound to have a knowledge of Holy Scripture if he is a Catholic? Magist. Opinions differ on this. One view is that a Catholic emperor of the world ought to have a knowledge of divine law and the holy writings, because a Catholic emperor under the New Testament should not be of lesser perfection than a king was under the Old Testament. But a king under the Old Testament was bound to have a knowledge of the holy writings and to meditate continually on the divine law. Therefore a Catholic emperor ought to possess these things more perfectly. Likewise, it belongs to the Catholic emperor to defend the Christian faith, which is contained in the holy letters, and to punish its assailants with due vengeance. But no one can defend what he does not know. Therefore a Catholic emperor ought to possess these things more perfectly, namely a knowledge of the holy writings. Another view is that, although it becomes a Catholic emperor to have some knowledge of the holy writings, so that at least he knows the law and can understand the Scriptures by reading them literally, nevertheless such knowledge is not absolutely necessary for him. This is because without it he can order temporal affairs usefully and justly, which is recognised as belonging to the emperor alone. Discip. Is the emperor bound to have a knowledge of the civil laws? Magist. One view is that he is, since the emperor is the supreme judge in temporal matters, and so he ought to have no less skill in those laws by which sentence is pronounced than the lower judges have. But the lower judges are bound to know the civil laws by which they are required to judge. Therefore the emperor ought much more to have skill in the civil laws. Another view is that he is not bound of necessity to have skill in the civil laws, although it is very fitting and useful that he should not lack such skill. For there have been many just kings and emperors, indeed holy ones, who had no skill at all in the civil laws, and yet they would have learned the laws thoroughly if they had been bound of necessity to know them. Nor is the case of the emperor or king similar to that of the other inferior judges. For the emperor in his empire, and the king in his kingdom, is released from the laws, and is not bound of necessity to judge according to the laws, as the inferior judges are bound of necessity to judge according to them. Therefore so great a knowledge of the laws is not required in an emperor or king as in the inferior judges. Discip. From what has been said, it seems probable to me that a profound knowledge both of the holy Scriptures and of the laws is fitting in one who is to be raised to emperor or king; and that such a man, if he were found, should be promoted to emperor before all others (other things being equal), and then to king when someone must take up the reins of the kingdom by election rather than by succession. But if one who has been promoted to emperor or king is not profound in his knowledge of the holy Scriptures and the civil laws, ought he to desist from, or to apply himself to, the study of acquiring such excellent knowledge? Or, even if he is excellent in such knowledge, ought he to be constantly occupied in meditating upon it? Mag. The answer is that it would be praiseworthy for an emperor or king to devote himself to such study with discretion, as much as he can, provided that through such study he is not hindered from the tasks entrusted to him. But to neglect his subjects, and to commit the empire or kingdom to another so that he may devote himself to such study, is to be regarded in an emperor or king as blameworthy and damnable. For such a man does not give his subjects the care that is due to them, and the saying of the Apostle applies to him: He who does not take care of his own, and especially of those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. For if an ecclesiastical prelate ought sometimes to set aside the contemplative life and attend to the active life for the benefit of his subjects, as is gathered from the sacred canons (S.q.i.ca.alia & c. inscriptis & c. quis episcopatum), much more ought an emperor or king to set aside such study, so that he may give due governance to his subjects not only through others but also through himself. Disc. Ought the emperor to have an excellent knowledge of secular affairs? Mag. The answer is that one who surpasses the others in skill in secular affairs, and who excels the others in natural sense and the judgement of reason, other things being equal, ought to be promoted before the others to emperor or king, who is raised by election to the government of the kingdom. For natural sense and an excellent judgement of reason understand that, in promoting someone, any man who excels in learning, eloquence, fluency, experience and memory seems to deserve to be preferred. But in promoting someone to a temporal office which will last even for a short time, an excellent judgement of reason may sometimes prefer experience as much as learning. Once someone has been raised to the empire or to the government of the world, he ought to devote himself to skill in secular affairs and to knowledge of natural law, especially that part of it about which even a learned man may happen to err or doubt, and whose knowledge belongs principally to his office. He ought to give himself to this more than to knowledge of the holy Scriptures, or of the secular sciences, or of any laws whatever, unless he can acquire skill in secular affairs more through these than in some other way. Disc. Why is it said that one must devote oneself to knowledge of that natural law about which even a learned man may happen to err or doubt? For it seems that there is no such natural law. For every ignorance of law, in matters about which even the skilled may err, seems to excuse the one who acts against it. For ignorance of fact excuses because it deceives even the skilled, as the Gloss notes on dist.38.c.1. Therefore if even the skilled may err about natural law, ignorance of such law would be able to excuse. Again, every probable ignorance excuses, but ignorance which can be found in the skilled can be probable. Therefore some ignorance of natural law would excuse, although the contrary is noted by the Gloss on dist.30.c.1. and by Gratian at t.q.1., who says it should be noted that every ignorance of natural law is damnable in all adults. From these things it seems that there is no natural law about which the skilled may err or doubt. Mag. The answer is that natural laws are found in a twofold difference. For some are principles known through themselves, or are drawn and derived from such immovable principles known through themselves; and no one can err or even doubt about such laws. Yet one can be ignorant of them, because one may never have thought about them at all; and such ignorance excuses no one. As soon as someone is bound by such natural laws to do or omit something, he at once recognises them, even if he had never thought of them before, unless he wishes to proceed to an act or omit such an act without any deliberation and rule of reason. Ignorance of such a law in such a case arises from damnable negligence or contempt, and so it does not excuse. For if on some occasion he strives to kill someone innocent who has never harmed him, then if he wishes to deliberate, even briefly, whether he ought to kill him, he at once concludes that he ought not to kill him. And so if he kills him without any deliberation, such ignorance does not excuse him. There are other natural laws which are drawn plainly from the first principles of law, without great deliberation or consideration, just as in matters of knowledge certain conclusions follow plainly from first principles, without great consideration, even for less learned men. Ignorance of such natural law does not excuse, because anyone can know those natural laws at once without great study, and the greater ignorance mentioned above refers to ignorance of this kind. There are other natural laws which are gathered by few even of the skilled, and with great attention and study, and through many means, from the first natural laws. About these even the skilled sometimes hold contrary opinions, some thinking them just and others thinking them unjust. Ignorance of such natural law excuses, especially in omitting to do something which would have to be done if one did not ignore it, unless the ignorance is gross and affected. Therefore the emperor must diligently devote himself to acquiring knowledge of such natural laws. For the other laws, of the first and second kinds mentioned, will be lightly shown to him when there is need; nor is it expedient that skill and complete knowledge of such laws and of secular affairs should be acquired, even so that he may have several wise counsellors with him, following the example of the Romans, who, as was said before, appointed thirty-two men who daily consulted and took counsel with the multitude. For, as Solomon witnesses in Proverbs 15, thoughts are disappointed where there is no counsel, but where there are many counsellors they are confirmed; and Proverbs 2 says that there is safety where there are many counsels. Discipulus. The teaching of the wise seems to stand in the way of the emperor having many counsellors. For Ecclesiasticus 6 reads thus: Let many be at peace with you, but let your counsellor be one in a thousand. Magister. The answer is that counsel is required for different matters and for different causes. For sometimes counsel is required about a secret which it is dangerous to reveal, except to the faithful, friends and discreet men. Sometimes counsel is required about public matters, or about those which can be revealed without danger even to unfaithful men, enemies and fools. Again, sometimes counsel of others is required, so that an agreement of many counsels may be obtained, and by obtaining it what has been deliberated becomes more authentic, and is received by others with greater order and with reverence or fear of love. But sometimes counsel is required so that the one seeking counsel may have what has been deliberated carried out by his counsellors. Sometimes the counsel of certain men is required, so that the one seeking counsel may acquire by their answer knowledge of law or of fact which he does not know, and having obtained it may consider what he ought to do. Very often the counsel of certain men is required so that the one seeking counsel may test and try their counsels, their discretion or prudence, or their fidelity, or their affection or will, whether towards him or towards others. Therefore when counsel is required about secrets which it is dangerous to reveal, the counsellors should be few, namely only proven faithful friends and discreet men. When counsel is required so that what has been deliberated may be committed to the counsellors for execution, those to be asked should be few, namely only faithful, wise and friendly men; and in these two cases the authority of Ecclesiasticus cited above is to be understood. But when counsel is required about public matters, or about things which can be revealed without danger, counsel is required only so that an agreement of the counsellors may be had, and by obtaining it what has been deliberated becomes more authentic; or so that the one seeking counsel may acquire, through the answer of the counsellors, knowledge of law or of fact which he does not know; or so that he may have experience of their discretion or prudence, or of their fidelity or affection or will. In such a case the counsellors should be many in number. Sometimes it is not absurd even to ask the counsel of the impious or ill-disposed, because sometimes the wise man, from their answer, will foresee even what he must do against those who wish to harm him and intend to deceive him. Just as the wise man learns discipline not only from the good works of the wise, but also from the evil works of fools, as Solomon witnesses in Proverbs 24, who says: I passed by the field of a lazy man, and by the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had covered the whole surface of it, and thorns had grown over it, and the stone wall was broken down. When I saw this, I set it in my heart, and by the example I learned discipline.

units.la: Inquirit de iustitia, quomodo in ipso Imperatore vigere debeat.
units.tr: Inquires how justice ought to flourish in the Emperor himself.

units.la: Discipulus. Licet de peritia vel prudentia necessaria imperatori possemus (vt arbitror) magnum volumen efficere: tamen ad præsens prædicta sufficiant, ideo ad iustitiam, quæ necessaria est imperatori, vt æstimo, me conuerto, cupio autem scire, an imperator debeat semper in omni casu rigorem iustitiæ exercere. Magister. Respondetur, quod imperator debet quandoque iustitiam totaliter prætermittere, vel differre ad tempus: interdum vero decet eum, imo de necessitate tenetur, rigorem iustitiæ temperare mansuetudine: quandoque autem de necessitate salutis tenetur rigorem iustitiæ exercere. Discipulus. Ista possunt, vt puto, innumeris rationibus & auctoritatibus demonstrari: sed abbreviationis causa omittamus, de vno tantummodo cupio ad præsens sententias diuersas audire: an videlicet apud imperatorem in exercendo iustitiam omnes pœnæ pro quocunque crimine sint arbitrariæ, vt liceat ei pecuniariam pœnam vel aliam pro quocunque crimine infligere? Magist. Circa hoc diuersæ reperiuntur sententiæ. Vna est, quod apud imperatorem omnes pœnæ sunt arbitrariæ, vt liceat ei pro quocunque casu & pro quocunque crimine quodcunque genus pœnarum infligere. Quae videtur hac ratione fulciri. Vbi poena non est taxata in iure, quae poena sit infligenda, arbitrio iudicis inferioris committitur: nec irrationabiliter: quia ex quo non est ius expressum secundum quod debeat punire, relinquitur quod secundum suum arbitrium puniri debeat. Sed Imperator est super omnia iura positiva. Igitur secundum nullum ius positivum tenetur punire crimen alicuius, & per consequens tenetur punire crimen alicuius pro suo arbitrio: & poterit quodcunque genus poenarum infligere. Alia est sententia, quod non semper Imperator exercendo iustitiam potest, quodcunque genus poenarum pro suo arbitrio pro omni crimine infligere. Poena enim pecuniaria non debet semper esse contentus, sed aliam debet infligere. Similiter etiam non semper debet sufficere sibi infligere poenam, scilicet verberum, vel deportationis, vel proscriptionis, vel exilii. Sed tenetur poenam mortis, vel mutilationis vel incarcerationis vel detentionis perpetuae imponere. Et saepe huiusmodi poenam nec ratione amicitiae, nec consanguinitatis, nec ratione voluntatis, aut aliqua alia occasione licet sibi remittere. Cuius ratio assignatur: quia sicut vbi certa poena non est statuta in iure, iudex inferior debet procedere aequitate servata, extra, de translationibus, cap. ultimo. Ita Imperator, quia est supra positiva iura, & non est super aequitatem naturalem, scilicet in exercendo iustitiam, non vult ex causa infligere poenam statutam in iure, tenetur de necessitate infligere poenam aequitate servata, secundum quod bonum commune & salutem subditorum viderit postulare, & maxime bonorum. Saepe autem absque dispendio communis boni & periculo obedientium bonorum poena & pecuniaria, vel deportationis, aut proscriptionis, vel exilii malefactorem minime castigaret, teste Ambrosio, qui in libro de officiis, & ponitur in decretis vigesimo tertio quaestione 4. cap. & est iniusta, ait: Si quis latronem filiis deprecantibus motus etiam lachrymis coniunctis eius inflexus absoluendum putat, ac adhuc latrocinandi aspiret effectum, nonne innocentes tradet exitio, qui liberat multorum exitia cogitantem? Hinc etiam Hieronymus, ut legitur distinctione quadragesima quinta, loquens de istis, qui parcunt malis, ait: Dum parcunt uni, universa ecclesia moliuntur interitum, quae ista bonitas est? quae ista misericordia est, uni parcere, & omnes in discrimen adducere? Ex quibus colligitur, quod si Imperator inferendo regi vel principi malefactori consanguineo vel alicui sibi coniuncto aut alieno appareret affectus turbandi imperium aut bonum commune vel innocentes solum modo poenam pecunialem vel aliam quamcunque, per quam a persecutione malae voluntatis minime perfectae reprimeretur, peccat mortaliter & damnabiliter transgreditur aequitatem, quam sequi tenetur. Igitur in huiusmodi casu, huiusmodi malefactor sive fuerit rex, sive princeps consanguineus, vel alienus poenam mortis corporalis aut incarcerationis perpetuae, aut aliquam aliam poenam, per quam a malis operibus & potentia mala faciendi penitus reprimatur, debet infligere.
units.tr: Student. Although we could (I think) write a large volume on the skill and prudence an emperor needs, let what has been said suffice for now. I turn instead to justice, which I judge necessary for an emperor, and I want to know whether an emperor should always exercise the strict rigour of justice in every case. Teacher. The answer is that an emperor must sometimes set justice aside altogether or postpone it, and at other times it is fitting, indeed necessary, that he temper the rigour of justice with mercy. Sometimes, however, the necessity of salvation requires him to exercise the strict rigour of justice. Student. These points, I think, could be proved by countless arguments and authorities, but for brevity let us pass them over. I wish to hear the differing opinions on one question only: whether, in exercising justice, every penalty before an emperor is at his discretion for any crime, so that he may impose a fine or any other penalty for any offence? Teacher. On this there are different opinions. One holds that before an emperor all penalties are at his discretion, so that in every case and for every crime he may impose any kind of penalty. This seems supported by the following reasoning. Where the law does not fix what penalty is to be inflicted, the choice is left to the judgment of the lower judge, and not unreasonably: since the law does not expressly state how he must punish, it follows that he must punish according to his own judgment. But the Emperor is above all positive laws. Therefore he is bound by no positive law to punish anyone's crime, and consequently he is bound to punish a person's crime at his own discretion, and may impose whatever kind of penalty he chooses. Another opinion holds that in exercising justice the Emperor cannot always impose, for every crime, whatever kind of penalty he pleases. A pecuniary penalty is not always enough, and he must impose some other. Likewise he should not always be content to inflict a penalty of flogging, or deportation, or banishment, or exile. Rather, he is bound to impose the penalty of death, or mutilation, or perpetual imprisonment or confinement. And he may not remit such a penalty for friendship, or kinship, or personal inclination, or any other reason. The reason given is this: just as, where no fixed penalty is laid down in law, the lower judge must proceed with equity preserved (extra, de translationibus, last chapter), so the Emperor, since he is above positive law but not above natural equity, when exercising justice and not wishing without cause to inflict the penalty laid down in law, is bound of necessity to inflict a penalty with equity preserved, as the common good and the welfare of the subjects, and above all of the good, may seem to require. Often, moreover, without loss to the common good and without danger to the good subjects, he would not punish the wrongdoer at all by a fine, or deportation, or outlawry, or exile. Ambrose testifies to this in his book On Duties, which is cited in the Decretum, Causa 23, question 4, chapter "Et est iniusta": "If someone, moved by the entreaties of sons and with their tears joined to his, thinks a robber should be acquitted, and the robber still aims to carry out his thieving, will he not deliver innocent people to destruction, when he frees one who plans the destruction of many?" Hence also Jerome, as read in Distinction 45, speaking of those who spare the wicked, says: "While they spare one, they plot the destruction of the whole Church. What goodness is this? What mercy is it to spare one and to bring everyone into peril?" From these things it follows that if the Emperor, in inflicting on a king or prince who is a wrongdoer, whether a kinsman, a relative, or a stranger, perceives an intention to disturb the empire or the common good, or to harm the innocent, and if he imposes only a fine or some other penalty by which the hostile will, not yet fully formed, would not be restrained from its pursuit, he sins mortally and damnably, transgressing the equity he is bound to follow. Therefore in such a case, whether the wrongdoer be a king, a prince, a kinsman or a stranger, he ought to inflict the penalty of bodily death, or perpetual imprisonment, or some other penalty by which he is wholly restrained from evil deeds and from the power of doing evil.

units.la: Discipulus. Videtur quod Imperator valeat licite tam gravem poenam etiam ei, qui incidit in crimen laesae maiestatis, vel aliud quodcunque flagitium commissum remittere: quia iudex in puniendo debet in humaniorem partem declinare, extr. de translationibus cap. ultim. & sententia, quae misericordiam vetat, fugienda est, dist. 50 pondere, potest igitur Imperator licite cuicunque flagitioso misericordiam facere ei poenam mortis vel quamcunque aliam remittendo. Magister. Hic respondetur, quod si Imperator quemcunque criminosum cognoverit perfecte emendatum, ita ut deseruerit omnem voluntatem malefaciendi; nec aliquis prosequitur contra eum iniuriam suam: potest ei Imperator omnem poenam remittere, si autem non fuerit emendatus perfecte, sed probabiliter timetur, quod habita facultate intendit iterare vias suas malas, & se consuetis itineribus vel aliis implicare: non licet Imperatori ei omnem poenam corporalem remittere, nec ei liceat talem misericordiam facere: quia talem minimam faciendo non declinaret in humaniorem partem, nec esset misericors, sed crudelissimus & inhumanissimus atque impius reputandus, teste Augustino, qui ad Lucanum, ut habetur 23. quaest. 5. cap. qui vitiis, ait: qui vitiis nutriendis parcet, & fauet ne contristet peccantem voluntatem, tam non est misericors, quam qui non vult accipere cultrum puero, ne audiat plorantem, cui etiam concordat Hieron. qui super Esa. & legitur eisdem, ca. & q. 1. c. non est, ait: non est crudelis, qui crudeles iugulat, talis igitur misericordia est iniusta misericordia, ut ait Ambro. imo est impissima misericordia, & deterior adulterio & rapinis, furto & aliis criminibus quam plurimis, quae apud Deum enormia reputantur. Disc. Ista sententia videtur aliqualiter habere apparentiam: recita quomodo ad motivum alterius sententiae respondetur, quod etiam non omni apparentia caret. Magister. Respondetur, quod iudices inferiores, vbi non est ius expressum, non possunt nec debent pro libito suo punire secundum arbitrium: sed in tali casu debent taliter arbitrari, ut aequitas servetur, ut scilicet iudex puniat tali poena, quae magis expedit rei publicae & conservationi iustitiae, & qua delinquens efficacius corrigatur, quia secundum Augustinum, ut dicitur in decretis 23. q. 5. prodest, & plectendo & ignoscendo hoc solum licite agitur, ut vita hominum bene corrigatur.
units.tr: Student. It seems that the Emperor may lawfully remit even so grave a penalty for one who has fallen into the crime of treason, or for any other shameful offence committed, since a judge in punishing ought to lean toward the more humane side (extr. de translationibus, last chapter), and "a sentence that forbids mercy is to be avoided" (Distinction 50, "Pondere"). Therefore the Emperor may lawfully show mercy to any shameful offender, remitting the penalty of death or any other. Teacher. Here the answer is this: if the Emperor has known any criminal to be perfectly reformed, so that he has abandoned every will to do evil, and no one pursues his wrong against him, the Emperor may remit the whole penalty. But if he has not been perfectly reformed, and there is a well-founded fear that, once he has the opportunity, he intends to resume his evil ways and entangle himself again in his former courses, then the Emperor may not remit all bodily punishment, nor may he grant such mercy. For in granting it he would not be leaning toward the more humane side, nor would he be merciful; he would be reckoned most cruel, inhuman and impious. Augustine testifies to this in his letter to Lucanus, as found in Causa 23, question 5, chapter "Qui vitiis": "He who spares and favours the nurturing of vices, so as not to grieve the sinning will, is no more merciful than one who refuses to take a knife from a child, lest he hear him crying." Jerome agrees with this, in his commentary on Isaiah, and it is read in the same place, Causa 6 (or 1), chapter "Non est": "He is not cruel who slays the cruel. Such mercy is unjust mercy, as Ambrose says; indeed it is the most impious mercy, and worse than adultery, robbery, theft, and very many other crimes that are regarded as monstrous before God." Student. This opinion seems to have some appearance of truth. Tell me how the argument for the other opinion is answered, since it too is not without some appearance. Teacher. The answer is that lower judges, where the law is not expressly stated, cannot and ought not to punish as they please at their own discretion. In such a case they must judge in such a way that equity is preserved: that is, the judge should impose the penalty that best serves the commonwealth and the preservation of justice, and by which the offender is most effectively corrected. For according to Augustine, as cited in the Decretum, Causa 23, question 5, "Prodest", it is right only to act by punishing and by forgiving so that the life of men may be well corrected.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAP. XVII.

units.la: In quo consequenter succincte quaerit de aliis virtutibus, se debeant inesse imperatori.
units.tr: In which he briefly inquires, in sequence, what other virtues ought to be present in the emperor.

units.la: Discipulus. Si de aliis virtutibus & moribus, quibus decet Imperatorem ornari, tractemus diffuse, opus nimis prolixum faceremus, ideo arbitror, quod ista duo scilicet peritia & discretio, sunt maxime necessaria Imperatori ad regendum utiliter sibi subiectos: imo quasi videntur sufficere ea, mea men ista ab aliis, quando erunt opportuna, separari non possunt, breuissime transeamus, vt ad latentiora & quae minus discussa sunt ab aliis, citius veniamus, praesertim cum in opere de optimo genere dicendi legaho, qui habuerint eos, potuerunt quamplurima de virtutibus necessariis Rectoribus inuenire: Primo itaque de veracitate, quandocunq; decet imperatorem, tenere breuiter videamus, dic igitur, an per aliquam sententiam imperator debeat veracitate fulgere, vt sicut non licet ei aliquod falsum asserere, vel aliquid dolose vel fraudulenter promittere, quod non intendit soluere: sic non liceat ei promissum aliqualiter reuocare, vel non complere, seu differre. Magister. Putant quidam, quamuis imperator nec male promissa soluere, nec illa quae promisit licite, & postea perpenderit esse nociua, teneatur soluere: sed teneatur rescindere, sicut & erubescere minime debet, si aliquid illorum melius, quae prius dixit, inuenerit, competentem correctionem eis impendere, nec debet expectare, vt ab aliis corrigatur. Tamen alia promissa non debet aliqualiter reuocare, nec absque causa manifesta differre. Cauere etiam debet, ne cito vel leuiter aliquid asserat vel promittat, nisi certus sit, quod sit asserendum vel promittendum.
units.tr: Student. If we were to treat at length of the other virtues and morals with which an emperor ought to be adorned, we would produce too long a work. So I think these two, namely skill and discretion, are the most necessary things for an emperor if he is to rule those subject to him profitably. Indeed they seem almost sufficient by themselves, since they cannot be separated from the others when the occasion calls for them. Let us pass over the rest briefly, so that we may come more quickly to the less obvious matters that others have not discussed in detail. This is especially so because those who have read De optimo genere dicendi could find very many things about the virtues necessary to rulers there. First, then, let us briefly consider whether an emperor ought to shine with truthfulness at all times. Tell me, then, whether by some rule an emperor ought to be distinguished by truthfulness, so that, just as he may not assert anything false or promise anything deceitfully or fraudulently that he does not intend to fulfil, so he may not retract, fail to keep, or delay a promise in any way. Master. Some think that although an emperor should neither keep rash promises nor those he has made lawfully but later judges to be harmful, he is nevertheless bound to annul them rather than to fulfil them. Nor ought he to be ashamed, if he finds something better than what he said before, to make a fitting correction, and he should not wait to be corrected by others. Yet he ought not to retract other promises in any way, nor to delay them without a clear cause. He must also take care not to assert or promise anything hastily or lightly, unless he is sure that it ought to be asserted or promised.

units.la: Discipulus. De potentia, diuitiis & liberalitate simul videamus, an sint imperatori opportunae. Videntur enim diuitiae repugnare liberalitati: quia ad liberalem spectat effundere diuitias, per quod diuitiae euacuantur. Magister. Nonnulli aestimant, quod sine istis non potest bene administrari imperiale officium: quia iurisdictio sine coercione nulla est censenda, extra, de officio delega. cap. pastoralis, & cap. ex literis, multomagis imperialis auctoritas absque coercione nulla est, coercio autem sine potentia exerceri non potest. Igitur potentia in imperatore requiritur, potentia autem maxime roborari videtur per diuitias, eo quod potentia absque amicis aut saltem obedientibus non videtur posse persistere, amici autem & obedientes diuitiis acquiruntur, teste Salomone, qui Prou. 19. ait: diuitiae addunt amicos plurimos, a paupere autem & ii quos habuit separantur, & 7. ca. ait: Multi colunt personam potentis: & amici sunt dona tribuentu, fratres hominis pauperis oderunt eum, insuper & amici procul recesserunt ab eo, & Eccl. 6. sic legitur: Vtilior est sapientia cum diuitiis, sicut enim protegit sapientia, sic protegit pecunia, & c. 10. dicit, quod pecunia obediunt omnia, diuitiae igitur sunt imperiali excellentiae optimae propter amicos & obedientes acquirendos, sed amici & obedientes nequaquam diuitiis acquiruntur & tenetur, nisi liberaliter effundantur; nec addunt amicos: & nisi per prodigalitatem consumantur, amici cito perduntur, igitur liberalitas pro amicis & obedientibus acquirendis & tenendis maiestati imperiali opportuna videtur. Discipul. Est ne fortitudo sic necessaria imperatori? Ma. Fortitudo, quae est virtus animae, debet in imperatore praecellere, sed fortitudo corporalis, quae est corporis robur, non est ita necessaria in imperatore, quamuis enim valde deceat imperatorem fortitudine corporali & arte praeliandi praecellere, non est tamen simpliciter necessaria, nec aliis excellentiis praeferenda, nec sapientiae, iustitiae & aliis virtutibus praeponenda, teste Sapiente, qui Sapient. 7. ait: Melior est sapientia quam vires: & vir prudens magis quam fortis. & Eccl. 9. ait Salomon: Dicebam ego, sapientiam esse meliorem fortitudine, & post eodem cap. Melior est sapientia quam arma bellica, & Prouerb. 19. ait: Melior est patiens sapiens viro forti, & qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore urbium.
units.tr: Student. Let us consider together whether power, riches and liberality are fitting for an emperor. For riches seem to be at odds with liberality, since it belongs to the liberal man to pour out his riches, and by this his riches are emptied. Master. Some judge that the imperial office cannot be well administered without these things, since jurisdiction without coercion is to be considered null (Extra, De officio delegati, cap. Pastoralis, and cap. Ex literis). Much more is imperial authority null without coercion, and coercion cannot be exercised without power. Therefore power is required in an emperor, and power seems to be especially strengthened by riches, because power does not seem able to persist without friends, or at least obedient subjects, and friends and obedient subjects are acquired by riches, as Solomon attests, who says in Proverbs 19: Riches add many friends, but the poor man is separated even from those he had. And in chapter 7 he says: Many court the person of the powerful, and friends are givers of gifts; the brothers of a poor man hate him; moreover his friends have withdrawn far from him. And Ecclesiastes 6 reads thus: Wisdom is more useful with riches, for as wisdom protects, so money protects, and chapter 10 says that all things obey money. Riches, therefore, are most excellent for the imperial dignity because they win friends and obedient subjects. But friends and obedient subjects are by no means acquired by riches, and they are kept only if riches are poured out liberally; nor do riches add friends, and unless they are used up through prodigality, friends are quickly lost. Therefore liberality seems fitting for the imperial majesty in order to acquire and keep friends and obedient subjects. Student. Is courage so necessary for an emperor? Master. Courage, which is a virtue of the soul, ought to excel in an emperor, but bodily strength, which is the robustness of the body, is not so necessary in an emperor. For although it greatly befits an emperor to excel in bodily strength and skill in fighting, it is not simply necessary, nor is it to be preferred to other excellences, nor placed before wisdom, justice and the other virtues, as the Book of Wisdom attests, which says in chapter 7: Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man is better than a strong one. And Solomon says in Ecclesiastes 9: I said that wisdom is better than strength, and after, in the same chapter: Wisdom is better than weapons of war. And Proverbs 16 says: A patient wise man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own spirit is better than the conqueror of cities.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Tractat quaestionem secundam huius libri, vtrum scilicet Romanum imperium fuerit a Deo, vel ab hominibus, & ponit tres opiniones, quarum tertiam prosequitur, & eam probat decem rationibus capitulis sequentibus, ad quas etiam respondetur, prima vero opinio probatur c. 26. huius & secunda 27.
units.tr: He takes up the second question of this book, namely whether the Roman empire was from God or from men. He sets out three opinions, pursues the third and proves it by ten reasons in the following chapters, to which replies are also given. The first opinion is proved in chapter 26 of this book, and the second in chapter 27.

units.la: Discipulus. Postquam disputatiue quaesiuimus, an expediret mundo vni imperatori subesse, & quibus virtutibus imperator mundi praecellere debet, ad Romanum imperium descendamus: inquirētes primo, a quo Romanum processit imperium, vtrum videl. fuerit ab hominibus, vel a Deo. Mag. Vna est opinio, quod imperium fuit a Deo constitutum, & non ab hominibus. Alia est quod fuit primo institutum a Deo, & tamen per homines, sc. per Romanos. Tertia opinio est, quod verum imperium Romanum fuit a Papa. Dicunt enim, quod Constantinus M. postquam fuit conuersus ad fidem catholicam, illam inordinatam potestatem, qua forte antea allegatiue utebatur, humiliter ecclesiae resignauit, sc. summo Pontifici, & recepit iterum a Christi vicario, successore sc. Petri ordinatam diuinitus potestatem imperii: qua deinceps ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum legitime vteretur, & qui prius vtebatur potestate permissa, deinde fungeretur auctoritate concessa, dicunt igitur isti, quod antequam Constantinus reciperet Romanum imperium a successore beati Petri, non verum imperium habuit, sed vsurpatum ab hominibus, & permissum a Deo, non concessum nec ordinatum. Disc. Quia constat mihi, quod ista ultima opinio fuit cuiusdam, qui erat de maioribus totius mundi praelatis: ideo ipsam volo tecum magis exquisite disputando discutere, allegando pro ipsa & contra ipsam ac etiam allegationibus respondendo, vt studiosi occasionem accipiant intelligendi catholicam veritatem, quae plurimos, qui literatissimi vocantur, forte latet, primo igitur pro ipsa studeas allegare. Magister. Ista opinio, quae videtur sententialiter in Glossis supra Decretum & Decretales saepius recitari, & etiam approbari, quamplurimis rationibus fundatis in dictis maiorum videtur posse probari. Unde & Glos. distinct. 96. cap. ad verum: Ab eo est imperium Romanum, qui potest Imperatorem deponere, sicut insinuat Glossa praedicta, Papa deponit Imperatorem 15. q. 6. cap. alius, & cap. iuratos, igitur verum imperium Romanum est a Papa. Discipul. Ista allegatio videtur aperte deficere, & Glossa allegata videtur male allegare capitula, quae adducit. Et ideo qualiter ad haec respondetur, manifesta. Magister. Dicitur, quod capitulum primum non loquitur de Imperatore Romano, sed de rege Francorum.
