Verba enim illius cap. sunt haec: Alius Romanus Pontifex (Zacharias scilicet) regem Francorum non tam pro suis iniquitatibus, quam pro eo, quod tanta potestate erat inutilis, a regno depositi, & Pipinum Caroli Imperatoris patrem in eius locum substituit, omnesque Francigenas a iuramento fidelitatis absolvit, in quibus verbis de Imperatore nulla sit mentio, igitur per illud cap. non potest probari, quod imperium Romanum sit a Papa, licet videatur probari, quod regnum Francorum sit a Papa. Discipulus. Si concederetur quod regnum Francorum sit a Papa, videtur posse concludi, quod Romanum imperium sit a Papa, quia non est maior ratio de regno Franciae, quam de Romano imperio. Magister. Ad istam obiectionem diversi diversimodeconantur respondere. Dicunt enim quidam, quod non est simile de Romano imperio, & de regno Franciae, quia magis, ut dicunt, potest subesse regnum Franciae Papae, quam Romanum imperium, nam, ut dicunt, regnum Franciae fuit antiquitus tam de iure quam de facto subiectum Romano imperio: & adhuc est de iure, teste Glossa, ext. qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem: ubi dicit Papa: Cum rex Franciae superiorem in temporalibus minime recognoscat de facto, tamen de iure subest Romano imperio, & Glossa, distinctio 2. ius Quiritum, ait: Imperator & princeps totius mundi. ff. ad L. Rhod. l. qui leuanda, dicitur: Qui igitur non vult esse sub Romano imperio, nec haereditatem habere potest ibidem, & Glossa, ext. de primis priuilegiis, cap. super specula, asserit manifeste, quod leges Romanorum Imperatorum debent de iure ab omnibus observari, licet de facto non ab omnibus observentur. Ex quibus aliisque quampluribus colligitur, quod regnum Franciae de iure est subiectum Romano imperio, quare Imperator Romanus (cui est subiectum) potest committere Papae, sicut & aliis, potestatem deponendi regem Franciae pro diversis iniquitatibus, in quibus non posset committere Papae potestatem deponendi Imperatorem, quare saltem ex commissione Imperatoris & Romanorum potest regnum Franciae esse magis subiectum Papae, quam Romanum imperium. Quod confirmatur quod Imperator Romanorum non est magis subiectus Papae, quam princeps, qui dicitur imperatori.
units.tr: Disciple. Having discussed in disputation whether it is expedient for the world to be subject to one emperor, and by what virtues the emperor of the world ought to excel, let us come to the Roman empire. Let us first inquire from whom the Roman empire proceeded, whether, that is, from men or from God. Master. There is one opinion, that the empire was established by God and not by men. Another is that it was first instituted by God, yet through men, namely the Romans. A third opinion is that the true Roman empire came from the Pope. For they say that Constantine the Great, after he was converted to the Catholic faith, humbly resigned to the Church, that is to the supreme Pontiff, that disordered power which he had perhaps previously used by mere permission. He then received back from Christ's vicar, the successor of Peter, the power of empire ordained by God, which he would thenceforth lawfully use to punish evildoers and praise the good. He who had previously used a permitted power then exercised an authority that had been granted. These men therefore say that before Constantine received the Roman empire from the successor of blessed Peter, he did not have true empire, but one usurped by men and permitted by God, not granted or ordained. Disciple. Since I am aware that this last opinion belonged to one of the greatest prelates in the whole world, I wish to examine it with you more carefully in disputation, adducing arguments for it and against it, and answering those arguments, so that students may have an occasion of understanding Catholic truth, which perhaps lies hidden from many who are called most learned. First, then, make your case for it. Master. This opinion, which is often seen to be recited, and even approved, in the Glosses on the Decretum and the Decretals, seems capable of being proved by very many reasons, founded on the sayings of the elders. Hence also the Gloss on distinct. 96, cap. Ad verum: The Roman empire is from him who can depose the Emperor, as the aforesaid Gloss hints. The Pope deposes the Emperor, 15. q. 6, cap. Alius, and cap. Iuratos. Therefore the true Roman empire is from the Pope. Disciple. This argument seems plainly to fail, and the Gloss cited seems to cite the chapters it adduces wrongly. How this is answered, therefore, should be stated plainly. Master. It is said that the first chapter does not speak of the Roman Emperor but of the king of the Franks. For the words of that chapter are these: Another Roman Pontiff (namely Zacharias) deposed the king of the Franks from his realm, not so much for his iniquities as because he was useless with so great a power, and put Pepin, father of the Emperor Charles, in his place, and absolved all the Franks from the oath of fidelity. In these words there is no mention of the Emperor. Therefore by that chapter it cannot be proved that the Roman empire is from the Pope, although it may seem to be proved that the kingdom of the Franks is from the Pope. Disciple. If it were conceded that the kingdom of the Franks is from the Pope, it seems one could conclude that the Roman empire is too, since there is no greater reason concerning the kingdom of France than concerning the Roman empire. Master. Various people try to answer this objection in various ways. Some say that the case of the Roman empire is not like that of the kingdom of France, since, as they say, the kingdom of France can be more subject to the Pope than the Roman empire can. For, as they say, the kingdom of France was anciently subject to the Roman empire both by law and in fact, and is still subject by law, as the Gloss testifies on ext. Qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem, where the Pope says: Although the king of France in fact recognizes no superior in temporal matters, nevertheless by law he is subject to the Roman empire. And the Gloss on distinctio 2, Ius Quiritum, says: Emperor and prince of the whole world. On ff. ad L. Rhod., l. Qui levanda, it is said: whoever does not wish to be under the Roman empire cannot have an inheritance there. And the Gloss on ext. De primis privilegiis, cap. Super specula, clearly asserts that the laws of the Roman emperors ought by law to be observed by all, although in fact they are not observed by all. From these and very many other sources it is gathered that the kingdom of France is by law subject to the Roman empire. Hence the Roman Emperor, to whom it is subject, can commit to the Pope, as to others, the power of deposing the king of France for various iniquities. He could not, however, commit to the Pope the power of deposing the Emperor. So at least by the commission of the Emperor and the Romans, the kingdom of France can be more subject to the Pope than the Roman empire. This is confirmed by the fact that the Roman Emperor is no more subject to the Pope than a prince who is called emperor.

units.la: Si igitur rex Franciae de iure subest imperatori: Imperator non est magis subiectus quam rex Franciae. Aliter dicunt quidam, quod Papa auctoritate Papali nec imperatorem nec regem Franciae potest deponere, nisi pro haeresi, tamen Papa auctoritate Romanorum posset pro quibusdam aliis causis deponere imperatorem, & auctoritate Francorum potest quibusdam aliis causis deponere regem Francorum, & haec Glossa super cap. allegato sentire videtur, quae super verbo deposuit, ait: dicitur depositisse, quia deponentibus consensit, recipiendo scilicet ab eis potestatem deponendi: ideo quasi una cum eis deposuit. Aliter dicitur, quod Zacharias Papa deponendo regem Francorum misit falcem suam in messem alienam, potestatem usurpando sibi ex officio nullatenus competentem, quod & alii summi Pontifices in praeiudicium laicorum facere dignoscuntur, teste Glossa quae extra de foro competent. cap. si quis clericus, ait: Papa siue sint negligentes (scilicet laici) in exhibendo iustitiam clericis, siue non, quotidie concedit literas clericis contra laicos super quacunque quaestione, & ita usurpat iurisdictionem aliorum, contra quod dicit cap. proximo super verbo nouit, vbi sic loquitur: Non putet aliquis, quod iurisdictionem istius illustris regis Francorum turbare minime intendamus: cum ipse iurisdictionem nostram nec velit, nec debeat impedire.
units.tr: So if the king of France is by law subject to the emperor, the emperor is no more subject than the king of France. Others say differently: that the Pope, by papal authority, can depose neither the emperor nor the king of France, except for heresy; yet by the authority of the Romans the Pope could depose the emperor for certain other causes, and by the authority of the Franks he could depose the king of the Franks for certain other causes. The Gloss on the aforesaid chapter seems to think this, for on the word deposuit it says: It is said he deposed, because he consented to those deposing, namely receiving from them the power of deposing; therefore he deposed together with them. Others say that Pope Zacharias, in deposing the king of the Franks, put his sickle into another's harvest, usurping a power in no way belonging to his office. Other supreme Pontiffs are also known to have done this to the prejudice of laymen, as the Gloss testifies on extra de foro competenti, cap. Si quis clericus, which says: The Pope, whether the laymen are negligent in rendering justice to clerics or not, daily grants letters to clerics against laymen on any question whatever, and so usurps the jurisdiction of others. Against this, the next chapter, on the word Novit, says, speaking thus: Let no one think that we intend in any way to disturb the jurisdiction of this illustrious king of France, since he neither wishes nor ought to hinder our jurisdiction.

units.la: Discipulus. Dixisti motiua aliquorum, quare male Glossa allegat cap. alius, nunc dic, quare eadem Glossa male allegat cap. iuratos. Magister. Hoc videtur quibusdam, quia illud capitulum nullam facit mentionem de imperatore: sed de quodam milite, qui vocabatur Hugo, cui iuraverant quidam alii milites, nec Papa ibi deposuit dictum Hugonem de dignitate vel potestate sua: sed tantum mandauit, ut praeciperetur militibus, ut non seruirent Hugoni praedicto, hoc autem non fuit deponere praedictum Hugonem: quia cum Dominus aliquis excommunicatus est, vasalli sui ei obedire vel communicare non debent, & tamen propter excommunicationem suam Dominus non deponitur a Domino suo: nec etiam tollitur obligatio, qua vasallus ei tenetur, teste Glossa, quae ii. q. 3. cap. Iulianus, ait: verum est, quod excommunicatio non tollit obligationem, qua vasallus est obligatus Domino suo: sed tantum effectum obligationis. Unde Domino absoluto ei obedire tenentur. Sed propter praedicta & nonnulla alia plura nonnullis apparet, quod per illud capitulum probari non potest, quod Papa deponere possit imperatorem: quoniam, ut videtur aliquibus, quod ad Papam non spectat de iure deponere imperatorem, quia no maiorem potestatem habet super imperatorem & Romanum imperium, quam super alios reges, & alia quaecunq; regna, quia si maiorem potestate haberet super imperatorem, q; super alios reges, aut haberet talem potestatem a iure diuino, aut a iure humano, no a iure diuino: quia in tota scriptura diuina non legitur, quod aliqua potestas sit tradita Papae super imperatorem Romanum, quae non sit sibi concessa super alios reges, nec habet potestate a iure humano: quia non videtur, q aliquis sibi dederit vel dare potuerit huiusmodi potestatem: quia si aliquis dedit vel dare potuit huiusmodi potestate, aut fuit imperator, aut inferior imperatore, no imperator: quia non potuit dare talem potestatem super imperatorem, & non super alios reges. Tum quia no potest imperator magis subiicere imperatorem Papae quam alios reges. Tum quia non habet imperium p imperatorem. Tum quia si imperator, qui dedit talem potestatem Papae super imperatorem, no fuit subiesubiectus Papæ, & imperator sequens fuit subiectus Papæ; imperator sequens non fuit verus successor: quia quando successor est magis subiectus, quam prædecessor, non est vera successio in ius alterius, ita imperator sequens non esset verus imperator, & per consequens imperator, qui taliter subiugasset Romanum imperium Papæ, fuisset destructor imperii quantum in se est, vel tuisset, & per consequens nihil egisset, quia nullus imperator valet destruere imperium, & quicquid egerit ad destructionem imperii, non teneret de iure: sed etiam per successorem suum de iure & de facto in irritum esset revocandum, nec aliquis inferior imperatore dedit vel dare potuit talem potestatem Papæ super imperatorem, ex quo imperator dare non potuit eam, propter hoc nonnullis apparet, quod ratio illa est invalida ad probandum, quod verum imperium Romanum est à Papa.
units.tr: Disciple. You have stated some people's reasons why the Gloss wrongly cites cap. Alius. Now say why the same Gloss wrongly cites cap. Iuratos. Master. To some it seems so, because that chapter makes no mention of the emperor, but of a certain knight called Hugo, to whom some other knights had sworn. Nor did the Pope there depose the said Hugo from his dignity or power, but only commanded that the knights be told not to serve the aforesaid Hugo. This, however, was not to depose Hugo, since when a lord is excommunicated his vassals ought not to obey him or communicate with him. Yet on account of his excommunication the lord is not deposed by his own lord, nor is the obligation by which the vassal is bound to him removed. The Gloss on II q. 3, cap. Iulianus, testifies to this, saying: It is true that excommunication does not remove the obligation by which a vassal is bound to his lord, but only its effect. Hence once the lord is absolved, they are bound to obey him. But on account of the aforesaid and many other reasons, it appears to some that it cannot be proved by that chapter that the Pope can depose the emperor. For, as it seems to some, it does not belong to the Pope by right to depose the emperor, since he has no greater power over the emperor and the Roman empire than over other kings and all other kingdoms. If he had greater power over the emperor than over other kings, he would have it either by divine right or by human right. Not by divine right, because nowhere in divine Scripture is it read that any power has been handed to the Pope over the Roman emperor which is not granted to him over other kings. Nor does he have it by human right, because it does not seem that anyone has given, or could have given, such power to him. For if anyone had given or could have given such power, he was either an emperor or inferior to the emperor. He was not an emperor, because he could not give such power over the emperor and not over other kings. Nor can an emperor subject the emperor to the Pope more than other kings. Nor does one have empire through the emperor. Again, if the emperor who gave such power to the Pope over the emperor was not subject to the Pope, and the following emperor was subject to the Pope, the following emperor was not a true successor. For when a successor is more subject than his predecessor, there is no true succession into another's right. So the following emperor would not be a true emperor, and consequently the emperor who had so subjected the Roman empire to the Pope would have been, so far as in him lay, a destroyer of the empire, or would have been one; and consequently he would have accomplished nothing, since no emperor is able to destroy the empire, and whatever he did toward its destruction would not hold by law. Indeed, it would also be revoked by his successor, by law and in fact, as void. Nor did anyone inferior to the emperor give, or could give, such power to the Pope over the emperor, since the emperor himself could not give it. For this reason it appears to some that the argument is invalid for proving that the true Roman empire is from the Pope.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Adducit aliam rationem probantem, quod imperialis potestas sit à Papa: ad quam etiam respondetur & obiicitur.
units.tr: He adduces another argument to prove that imperial power is from the Pope, and this too is answered and objected to.

units.la: DIscipulus. Aliam igitur rationem ad probandum idem adducas. Magister. Aliam rationem innuit Gloss. vbi prius, quæ potest sic formari. Ab illo enim est imperium, cui datæ sunt claues cœlestis & terreni imperii, sed beato Petro, & per consequens successoribus suis, datæ sunt claues cœlestis & terreni imperii. Vnde Nicolaus Papa, vt legitur 22. dist. ca. 1. sic dicit: Christus Romanam ecclesiam solus ipse constituit & fundauit, & supra Petram fidei mox nescientu erexit, qui beato Petro clauigero æterna vita simul terreni & cœlestis imperii iura commisit, ergo Romanum imperium est à Papa. Discipulus. Ista ratio fortis mihi videtur, & tamen si aliqui niterentur respondere ad ipsam, enarra. Mag. Nonnulli volunt eam repellere, quia dicunt, quod auctoritas Nicolai, in qua fundatur ratio ista, si intelligatur, sicut intelligunt eam illi, qui eam adducunt, plures absurditates, imo certi errores aperte sequuntur. Prima absurditas siue error est, quod omnia regna sunt à Papa: & quod nullus est verus rex, nisi qui regnum suum suscipit à Papa. Nam in tota sacra Scriptura vel quacunque scriptura autentica nullatenus inuenitur, quod Christus aliter plus commiserit beato Petro iura Romani imperii, quam iura aliorum regnorum. Si igitur per auctoritatem illam potest ostendi, quod Romanum imperium est à Papa, & quod non est verus imperator, nisi qui suscipit imperium à Papa; sicut tenet opinio, in cuius fulcimentum est adducta ista ratio: sequitur quod omnia alia regna sunt à Papa: & ita alii reges non sunt veri reges, nisi regna sua à Papa suscipiant, quare cum nulli vel pauci sua regna suscipiant à Papa, nulli vel pauci sunt veri reges. Discipulus. Satis videntur reges sua regna suscipere à Papa, ex quo parati sunt sibi obedire, qui etiam, si placeret Papæ, præparati essent resignare sua regna Papæ, & ipsa ab eo suscipere. Magister. Multi istud negarent. Vnde de rege Franciæ specialiter, vt notatur extra de elect. qui filii sunt legitimi, cap. per venerabilem, testimonium perhibet, quod superiorem in temporalibus non recognoscit: & tamen rex Franciæ est verus rex, nec vnquam fuit aliquis, qui putauit se in temporalibus superiorem habere.
units.tr: Disciple. Then you would offer another argument to prove the same thing. Master. The Gloss, in the passage cited above, hints at another argument, which can be formed as follows. Power belongs to the one to whom the keys of the heavenly and earthly kingdom were given. But the keys of the heavenly and earthly kingdom were given to the blessed Peter, and therefore to his successors. Hence Pope Nicholas, as is read in Distinction 22, chapter 1, says: Christ alone himself founded and established the Roman Church, and soon raised it upon the Rock of faith, he who committed to the blessed Peter, the key-bearer, the rights of eternal life together with those of the earthly and heavenly kingdom. Therefore the Roman empire is from the Pope. Disciple. This argument seems strong to me. Yet, if some people tried to answer it, explain how. Master. Some want to refute it, because they say that the authority of Nicholas, on which this argument rests, if it is understood as those who cite it understand it, leads to many absurdities, indeed to plain errors. The first absurdity or error is that all kingdoms are from the Pope, and that no one is a true king unless he receives his kingdom from the Pope. For in all of Holy Scripture, or in any authentic writing, it is nowhere found that Christ committed to the blessed Peter the rights of the Roman empire in any different way than the rights of other kingdoms. If, then, by that authority it can be shown that the Roman empire is from the Pope, and that no one is a true emperor unless he receives the empire from the Pope, as the opinion holds in whose support this argument is adduced, it follows that all other kingdoms are from the Pope. And so other kings are not true kings unless they receive their kingdoms from the Pope; hence, since none or few receive their kingdoms from the Pope, none or few are true kings. Disciple. Kings seem to receive their kingdoms from the Pope well enough, since they are ready to obey him; and even if it pleased the Pope, they would be prepared to resign their kingdoms to him and receive them back from him. Master. Many would deny that. Hence, concerning the king of France in particular, as is noted in the Extra, De electione, Qui filii sint legitimi, chapter Per venerabilem, testimony is given that he acknowledges no superior in temporal matters; and yet the king of France is a true king, and there has never been anyone who thought he had a superior in temporal matters.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunc videtur mihi, quod auctoritas Nicolai prius allegata potest in præiudicium regum, & specialiter regis Franciæ, intelligi. Sed quæso dic ibi, quid illi per auctoritatem prædictam Nicolai Papæ, & opinionem pro qua adducitur intelligunt, sicut & verba sonant, & quæ etiam arbitrantur, sicut iura omnium regnorum Christus commisit beato Petro, quod omnes reges tenentur recognoscere Papam superiorem, etiam in temporalibus, de rege Franciæ & de aliis regibus & principibus, qui etiam in temporalibus Papam minime recognoscunt superiorem, ansilicet eorum error sit talis, quod sit inter hæreses computandus? Magister. Dicunt nonnulli, quod si prædicta opinio vera est, error iste debet later hæreses computari: quia secundum opinionem illam ex sacra Scriptura colligitur, quod Christus sic omnia iura omnium regnorum comisit B. Petro, quod omnia regna legitima sunt à B. Petro summo Pontifice: & summus Pontifex etiam in temporalibus est superior omnibus regibus, sed omnis error, qui obuiat scripturæ diuinæ, est inter hæreses numerandus, asserere autem quod aliquis rex non debet recognoscere in temporalibus superiorem in terris, est contra scripturam diuinam, & per consequens hæreticum est censendum. Disc. Nunquid secundum istam opinionem rex Franciæ & alii tenentes istam assertionem, sunt inter hæreticos numerandi? Magister. Si ista assertio sit hæreticalis, & rex Franciæ vel alius non tenet eam pertinaciter: non est proprie hæreticus reputandus. Si autem sit hæreticalis, & rex Franciæ vel alius pertinaciter adhæret eidem hæreticus est censendus, qualiter autem debeat quis de pertinacia conuinci, in primo Sententiarum Dialogi libro quarto, est aliqualiter indagatum. Discipulus. Recitasti secundum opinionem quorundam, vnam absurditatem quamplures includentem, sequentes ex auctoritate Nicolai Papæ intellecta, vt ista opinio eam intelligit, nunc autem secundum alios dic, an aliqua alia absurditas hæc error sequatur ex eadem secundum intellectum eundem. Mag. Alia absurditas secundum quosdam sequitur ex ipsa: sci. quod regnum cœleste sit à Papa: quia ita asserit ista auctoritas, quod Christus commisit beato Petro iura cœlestis imperii, sicut terreni. Si igitur ex ista auctoritate potest concludi, quod terrenum imperium sit à Papa, eadem ratione concluditur ex ipsa, quod cœleste imperium sit à Papa: quod videtur absurdissimum. Tum quia ante Christum esset Papa supra cœleste imperium. Tum quia sine auctoritate Papæ multi recipiuntur in cœlesti imperio. Tum etiam quod quando sedes vacat, multi recipiuntur ad coeleste imperium. Discip. Audiui, quomodo aliqui moliuntur ex auctoritate Nicolai Papae intellecta, prout intelligit opinio in praecedenti cap. recitata, plures absurditates & errores concludere. Nunc dic, quomodo isti illam auctoritatem intelligunt: ex quo potero adducere, quomodo ad allegationem, quae fundatur super ipsam, respondere nituntur. Magister. Dicunt, quod sicut Nicolaus Papa per imperium coeleste non intelligit imperium, quod possidet ecclesia triumphans: quia illud regnum non datur a Papa, sed a Deo: licet Papa habeat claves illius, & sit clauiger, non dominus illius imperii, sic per terrenum imperium non intelligit imperium temporale, quod possidet imperator: sed per tale coeleste imperium supra bonos in ecclesia militante per terrenum imperium intelligit malos, super quos Papa noscitur potestatem habere. Aliter dicitur, quod Nicolaus Papa non dicit, quod commisit B. Petro dominium coelestis & terreni imperii, sed iura, & ideo terrenum imperium non est a Papa: & tamen Papa habet aliquod ius in terreno imperio, quando a Christiano gubernatur. Tum quia habet potestatem spiritualem super imperatorem. Tum quia habet ius participandi carnalia ab imperio, cui ministrat spiritualia. Ioxta illud Apostoli 1. ad Corinth. 9. Si nos vobis spiritualia seminamus: non est mirum, si carnalia vestra metamus.
units.tr: Disciple. Now it seems to me that the authority of Nicholas cited earlier can be understood to the prejudice of kings, and especially of the king of France. But I ask you to say there what those people mean by the aforesaid authority of Pope Nicholas and by the opinion for which it is cited, as the words sound, and what they also suppose: that Christ committed the rights of all kingdoms to the blessed Peter, so that all kings are bound to acknowledge the Pope as superior, even in temporal matters; and that the king of France and other kings and princes, who do not acknowledge the Pope as superior even in temporal matters, are in error of such a kind that it must be counted among heresies? Master. Some say that if the aforesaid opinion is true, that error must indeed be counted among heresies. For according to that opinion it is gathered from Holy Scripture that Christ so committed all the rights of all kingdoms to the blessed Peter that all lawful kingdoms are from the blessed Peter, the supreme Pontiff; and the supreme Pontiff is superior to all kings, even in temporal matters. But every error that opposes divine Scripture must be numbered among heresies. To assert, however, that some king ought not to acknowledge a superior on earth in temporal matters is contrary to divine Scripture, and therefore must be judged heretical. Disciple. Then according to that opinion, are the king of France and others who hold this assertion to be numbered among heretics? Master. If this assertion is heretical, and the king of France or another does not hold it stubbornly, he is not properly to be regarded as a heretic. But if it is heretical, and the king of France or another clings to it stubbornly, he is to be judged a heretic. How anyone ought to be convicted of stubbornness has been investigated to some extent in the fourth book of the first Dialogue of the Sentences. Disciple. You have recited, according to the opinion of some people, one absurdity that includes many, which follows from the authority of Pope Nicholas as that opinion understands it. Now tell me, according to others, whether some other absurdity or error follows from the same authority under the same interpretation. Master. According to some, another absurdity follows from it: namely, that the heavenly kingdom is from the Pope. For this authority asserts that Christ committed to the blessed Peter the rights of the heavenly empire just as of the earthly. If, then, from this authority it can be concluded that the earthly empire is from the Pope, by the same reasoning it is concluded from it that the heavenly empire is from the Pope, which seems most absurd. Both because before Christ there would have been a Pope over the heavenly empire, and because without the Pope's authority many are received into the heavenly empire, and also because when the see is vacant, many are received into the heavenly empire. Disciple. I have heard how some people, from the authority of Pope Nicholas as understood by the opinion recited in the preceding chapter, labour to draw out many absurdities and errors. Now tell me how they understand that authority, so that I can then learn how they try to answer the allegation that is founded upon it. Master. They say that just as Pope Nicholas does not by the heavenly empire mean the empire which the triumphant Church possesses, because that kingdom is given not by the Pope but by God, although the Pope has its keys and is its key-bearer, not its lord, so by the earthly empire he does not mean the temporal empire which the emperor possesses. Rather, by such a heavenly empire over the good in the militant Church, and by the earthly empire, he means the wicked, over whom the Pope is known to have power. Otherwise it is said that Pope Nicholas does not say that he committed to the blessed Peter lordship over the heavenly and earthly empire, but rights; and therefore the earthly empire is not from the Pope. Yet the Pope does have some right in the earthly empire when it is governed by a Christian: first, because he has spiritual power over the emperor; second, because he has a right to share in material things from the empire to which he ministers spiritual things, according to the saying of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 9: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Adducit tertiam rationem ad probandum tertiam opinionem capitulo 18. positam, ad quam respondetur & obiicitur.
units.tr: He adduces a third argument to prove the third opinion set out in chapter 18, and it is answered and objected to.

units.la: Discipulus. Aliam allegationem pro opinione praedicta adducas. Magister. Aliam rationem innuit Glossa, distinctione decim. capit. quoniam idem. Ex qua ratio talis potest sumi. Ab illo est Romanum imperium, qui transfert & transferre potest de una gente ad aliam. Sed Papa transtulit imperium de Graecis ad Germanos, extra de electione, venerabilem. Igitur imperium Romanum est a Papa. Discipulus. Ista ratio videtur insolubilis: & tamen cupio scire, an aliqui nitantur eam refellere. Magister. Putant aliqui, quod ex ratione intellecta, ut aliqui eam intelligunt, sequitur absurditas manifesta, quod videlicet Papa potest transferre quaecunque regna Christianorum & aliorum de domo in domum, & de gente in gentem, & ita potest transferre regnum Franciae in Anglicos & Theutonicos, aut Hispanos, vel alios, secundum quod transtulit Romanum imperium de Graecis in Germanos. Quod autem ista absurditas sequatur, probant per quoddam fundamentum, per quod multi nituntur probare quamplurima circa materiam istam. Est autem hoc fundamentum, quod etiam tactum est prius: scilicet quod nullam potestatem spiritualem dedit Christus beato Petro super Romanum imperium, quin illam dedit super regnum Franciae & alia regna quaecunque, quod duobus modis ostendere moliuntur.
units.tr: Disciple. You should adduce another argument for the aforesaid opinion. Master. The Gloss hints at another reason, distinctione decim. capit. quoniam idem. From it the following argument can be drawn. The Roman empire is from him who transfers it and can transfer it from one nation to another. But the Pope transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Germans, extra de electione, venerabilem. Therefore the Roman empire is from the Pope. Disciple. This argument seems insoluble, and yet I want to know whether anyone tries to refute it. Master. Some think that, from the argument as some understand it, a manifest absurdity follows, namely that the Pope can transfer any kingdoms of Christians and others from house to house and from nation to nation, and so could transfer the kingdom of France to the English, the Teutons, the Spaniards or others, just as he transferred the Roman empire from the Greeks to the Germans. That this absurdity follows they prove by a certain foundation, on which many rely to prove very many points about this matter. This foundation, which was also touched on before, is that Christ gave blessed Peter no spiritual power over the Roman empire that he did not also give over the kingdom of France and any other kingdoms whatever; and they attempt to show this in two ways.

units.la: Primo probatur sic. In tota Scriptura sacra, vbi fit mentio de potestate Papae collata sibi a Christo, nulla fit mentio specialis de Romano imperio: nec ab illa potestate aliquod regnum eximitur. Cum enim dixit Christus beato Petro: quodcunque ligaueris, &c. cum iterum dixit: pasce oues meas, non plus a tali potestate eximitur regnum Franciae vel aliquod aliud quam Romanum imperium, & idem in omnibus auctoritatibus, quibus probatur potestas specialis Papae. Cum enim dicitur Genesis primo: Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna, &c. per quae intelligit regnum & sacerdotium. Et cum dicitur Ieremiae primo: Ecce constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna. Et cum dicitur Lucae vigesimo secundo, ecce duo gladii hic, & in similibus, nulla fit mentio specialis de aliquo regno, nec intelligitur specialiter exemptum a potestate data Petro a Christo magis quam Romanum imperium, quod non acceperit super Franciam & alia regna. Quare si ex potestate data beato Petro a Christo, Papa potest transferre Romanum imperium de gente in gentem: poterit eadem potestate transferre regnum Franciae de gente in gentem.
units.tr: First, they prove it thus. In the whole of Holy Scripture, wherever mention is made of the power of the Pope given to him by Christ, no special mention is made of the Roman empire, and no kingdom is exempted from that power. For when Christ said to Blessed Peter, "Whatever you shall bind," etc., and again, "Feed my sheep," no more is the kingdom of France exempted from such power than the Roman empire, and the same holds for all the passages by which the special power of the Pope is proved. When it is said in Genesis 1, "God made two great lights," etc., by which he understands the kingdom and the priesthood. And when it is said in Jeremiah 1, "Behold, I have set you this day over the nations and over the kingdoms." And when it is said in Luke 22, "Behold, here are two swords," and in similar places, no special mention is made of any kingdom, and none is understood to be specially exempted from the power given by Christ to Peter any more than the Roman empire, which did not receive power over France and the other kingdoms. Therefore, if by the power given by Christ to Blessed Peter the Pope can transfer the Roman empire from nation to nation, by the same power he can transfer the kingdom of France from nation to nation.

units.la: Secundo probant idem sic, non fuit maior potestas beato Petro data super Romanum imperium, quam super partes Romani imperii, vel super regna quae erant subiecta Romano imperio, sed quando Christus dedit beato Petro potestatem Papalem, regnum Franciae, sicut & alia regna, fuit pars Romani imperii, vel subiectum Romano imperio, igitur non maiorem potestatem recepit beatus Petrus a Christo super Romanum imperium, quam super regnum Franciae. Disc. Forte dicerent aliqui, quod dominium regni Franciae erat subiectum Romano imperio, & omnem potestatem, quam habuit Papa super Romanum imperium, habuit etiam super regnum Franciae. Sed modo non habet eam, quia regnum Franciae non est subiectum Romano imperio. Mag. Ista responsio multis videtur absurda. Tum, quia per rebellionem regni Franciae vel exemptionem Papa non debuit aliqua potestate priuari. Tum, quia potestas, quam habet Papa ex ordinatione Christi, non potest mutari nec auferri ab eo per aliquem inferiorem Christo. Tum quia tunc Papa, qui fuit post rebellionem vel exceptionem regni Franciae, non fuisset aequalis potestatis cum Papa qui praecessit, & ita non fuit verus successor eius. Discipulus. Recitasti quomodo impugnatur: nunc narra quomodo respondeturad ipsam. Mag. Respondetur, quod per qualem potestatem & auctoritatem Papa Zacharias deposuit regem Franciae, & Pipinum instituit, vt allegatum est supra: per talem & consimilem transtulit Romanum imperium de Graecis in Germanos: regemque Franciae non deposuit auctoritate vel potestate sibi data a Christo, sed haec fecit auctoritate Fra- corum, eorum, qui sibi illa vice auctoritatem & potestatem dederunt talem. Vel secundum Glossam super illud ca. alium: Dicitur depositasse, quia dependentibus consensit. Sic Papa non auctoritate vel potestate sibi data à Christo, sed auctoritate Romanorum talem potestatem dederunt, illa vice transtulit Romanum Imperium de Græcis in Germanos. Vel potest dici transtulisse, quia transferentibus consensu. Discip. Ista responsio videtur fundari in illa opinione, quæ ponitur, quod Papa habet veram potestatem à Christo immediate, scil. potestatem in spiritualibus & ius percipiendi carnalia necessaria sibi pro sustentatione & exercendo officia sua habet aliquam à conciliis generalibus auctoritatem à congregatione fidelium, saltem per tacitum assensum ipsorum à diversis gentibus vel Imperatoribus vel principibus vel huiusmodi. De qua opinione poteris invenire quamplurima in tractatu De potestate Papæ & cleri. Ideo ad præsens quamplures impugnationes illius responsionis omittam, & vnam adducam, quæ talis est. Quando aliquid fieri dicitur à Sede Apostolica, non intelligitur fieri per aliquam potestatem concessam personæ Papæ solum, sed intelligitur fieri auctoritate officii concessi à Christo sibi & commissi. Decretalis autem illa venerabilem dicit, Sedem Apostolicam transtulisse Imperium de Græcis in Germanos, verba enim Decretalis sunt hæc. Istis principibus & ius & potestatem eligendi regem in Imperatorem postea promovendi cognoscimus, vt debemus, ad quos de iure & ant: quæ consuetudine noscitur pertinere, præsertim cum ad eos ius & potestas huiusmodi à Sede Apostolica prouenerit, quæ Romanum Imperium in personam Magni Caroli à Græcis transtulit in Germanos. Igitur Papa auctoritate ossicii commissi sibi à Christo transtulit Romanum Imperium. Magist. Respondetur ad impugnationem illam, quod sæpe Apostolica Sedes accipitur pro Papa, & sæpe illud quod fit à Papa inquantum Papa, dicitur fieri à Sede Apostolica. Et ideo quia Papa habens potestatem à Romanis transtulit Imperium, Sedes Apostolica dicitur transtulisse Imperium.
units.tr: Second, they prove the same thing thus. Blessed Peter was not given greater power over the Roman empire than over the parts of the Roman empire, or over the kingdoms that were subject to the Roman empire. But when Christ gave Blessed Peter papal power, the kingdom of France, like the other kingdoms, was part of the Roman empire or subject to it. Therefore Blessed Peter received from Christ no greater power over the Roman empire than over the kingdom of France. Pupil. Perhaps some would say that the dominion of the kingdom of France was subject to the Roman empire, and that whatever power the Pope had over the Roman empire he also had over the kingdom of France, but that now he does not have it, because the kingdom of France is no longer subject to the Roman empire. Master. That answer seems absurd to many. First, because a rebellion or exemption of the kingdom of France should not deprive the Pope of any power. Second, because the power that the Pope has by the ordinance of Christ cannot be changed or taken from him by any inferior to Christ. Third, because then the Pope who came after the rebellion or exemption of the kingdom of France would not have been equal in power to the Pope who came before, and so he would not have been a true successor to him. Pupil. You have recited how the answer is attacked; now tell me how it is answered. Master. It is answered that by the same kind of power and authority by which Pope Zachary deposed the king of France and installed Pepin, as was alleged above, he transferred the Roman empire from the Greeks to the Germans. He did not depose the king of France by authority or power given to him by Christ, but did this by the authority of the Franks, of those who on that occasion gave him such authority and power. Or, according to the Gloss on the words in the chapter "Alium," he is said to have deposed him because he consented to those who were dependent on him. So the Pope did not transfer the Roman empire from the Greeks to the Germans by authority or power given to him by Christ, but by the authority of the Romans, who on that occasion gave him such power. Or it can be said that he transferred it because he consented to those who were transferring it. Pupil. This answer seems to rest on that opinion which holds that the Pope has true power immediately from Christ, namely power over spiritual matters and the right to receive the material things necessary for his support and for the exercise of his office; and that he has some authority from the general councils, from the gathering of the faithful, or at least from their tacit assent, or from various peoples, emperors, princes, or the like. On this opinion you can find very many things in the treatise On the Power of the Pope and the Clergy. For the present, then, I will omit many objections to that answer and bring forward just one, which is this. When something is said to be done by the Apostolic See, it is not understood to be done by some power granted to the person of the Pope alone, but by the authority of the office committed to him by Christ. Now that Decretal, "Venerabilem," says that the Apostolic See transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Germans. For the words of the Decretal are these: "We recognize that these princes have the right and power to elect a king who is afterwards to be promoted to emperor, as they ought, and to whom it is known by right and by custom that this belongs; especially since this right and power has come to them from the Apostolic See, which transferred the Roman empire from the Greeks to the Germans in the person of Charles the Great." Therefore the Pope, by the authority of the office committed to him by Christ, transferred the Roman empire. Master. To that objection it is answered that the Apostolic See is often taken to mean the Pope, and that what is done by the Pope insofar as he is Pope is often said to be done by the Apostolic See. And therefore, because the Pope, having power from the Romans, transferred the empire, the Apostolic See is said to have transferred the empire.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXI.

units.la: Tertiam rationem adducit, ad probandum id, quod prius, quæ etiam impugnatur, & ad eam respondetur.
units.tr: He adduces a third reason to prove the point stated before; this too is challenged, and the challenge is answered.

units.la: Discipulus. Adhuc allegationes alias pro opinione prædicta discutiamus. Magist. Pro eadem opinione allegatur August. sic. Ab illo habet Imperator Romanum Imperium, à quo postquam electus est examinatur, confirmatur & inungitur, consecratur & coronatur, & cui iurat. Sed Imperator Romanus postquam est electus examinatur à Papa, confirmatur, inungitur, consecratur, & coronatur, & ei iurat. extra, de electione ca. venerabilem. & di. 63. tibi Domine. Ergo Imperator Imperium habet à Papa. Discip. Ista ratio videtur includere multas particulas. Dic ergo secundum aliquam sententiam, an per hoc, quod electus in Imperatorem examinatur à Papa, possit ostendi, quod Imperator Imperium recepit à Papa. Magist. Dicunt quidam, quod non. Nam & legati examinari debent ab illis, ad quos mittuntur dist. 97. nobilissimus, vbi dicitur Gloss. Legati sine periculo non recipiuntur. Vnde mi eis maior est facienda examinatio. Et tamen legationis officium non est ab ipsis. Ergo per examinationem probari non potest, quod examinatus non habet officium suum ab examinante. Tum quia licet examinare literas Papales. extra, de crimine falsi & falsariorum: & tamen examinatores huiusmodi non habent super literas examinatas aliquam potestatem. Ergo per hoc, quod electus in Imperatorem examinatur à Papa, inferri non potest; quod Imperator habet Imperium à Papa. Examinatur ergo electus in Imperatorem à Papa, non vt Papa conferat sibi Imperium, sed ne Papa & alii habeant, pro Imperatore vnum, qui non est electus legitime. Et per consequens, qui non est verus Imperator. Quemadmodum volentes vti literis Papalibus examinant eas, ne literas falsas pro veris recipiant. Discip. Video quare dicitur, quod per examinationem probari non potest, quod Imperium sit à Papa. Nunc refer, quid dicitur de confirmatione. Magist. Dicitur, quod in nulla scriptura authentica antiquia inuenitur, quod Imperator fuerit confirmatus à Papa. Vnde & in Decretali venerabilem, quæ magis sonare videtur, quod Imperium sit à Papa, de confirmatione non fit mentio. Vnde dicitur, quod Imperator antiquitus non confirmabatur à Papa. Si autem aliquis postea confirmatus fuerit à Papa, ex simplicitate vel humilitate Imperatoris processit: non tamen potuit legem Imperatori imponere. Discip. Nunquid per inunctionem, consecrationem, coronationem ostendi potest, quod Imperium sit à Papa? Magist. Dicitur quod non: quia alii reges inunguntur, consecrantur, & coronantur ab Archiepiscopis & Episcopis regnorum suorum, & tamen non habent ab ipsis sua regna. Discip. Nunquid per iuramentum potest ostendi, quod Imperium sit à Papa. Magist. Dicitur quod non: quia non potest probari, quod aliquis Imperator præstiterit aliquod iuramentum Papæ, quam illud quod fecit Otho Imperator Iohanni. Sed iuramentum Othonis non fuit iuramentum fidelitatis & subiectionis, quod præstat vasallus Domino suo pro feudo quod recepit ab ipso: ad quod probandum, tam iuramentum Othonis prædicti, quam iuramentum quod præstat vasallus Domino suo, adducuntur. Iuramentum autem Othonis habetur dist. 63. c. tibi Domino, tale fuit: tibi Domino Iohanni Papæ ego rex Otho promitto & iuramentum facio per Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, per hoc lignum vivificæ crucis, & per has reliquias sanctorum, quod si permittente Deo Romam venero, sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam & te tuetorem ipsius exaltabo secundum meum posse, & vitam aut membra necnon ipsum honorem, quem habes, mea voluntate aut meo consilio aut meo consensu aut exhortatione perdes. Et in Romana civitate nullum placitum aut ordinationem faciam de omnibus, quæ ad te aut Romanos pertinent, sine consilio tuo. Et quicquid de terra sancti Petri ad nostram potestatem peruenerit tibi reddam. Et cuicunque regnum Italicum commisero, iurare faciam illam, vt tui adiutor sit ad defendendum terram sancti Petri secundum meum vel suum posse. Forma autem, qua iurat vasallus Domino suo, est haec, vt dicit Hostiensis. Ego iuro super sancta Dei Euangelia, quod a modo in antea ero fidelis tibi, sicut debet esse vasallus Domino suo: nec illud, quod mihi sub nomine fidelitatis commiseris, pandam alii me sciente ad eius detrimentum. Aliam formam ponit idem Hostiensis, quae talis est: Ego Titius iuro ad sancta Dei Euangelia, quod ab hac hora in antea usque ultimum diem vitae meae ero fidelis tibi Otho Domino meo contra omnem hominem. De istis formis iurandi nonnullis apparet, quod iuramentum Othonis Imperatoris non fuit iuramentum fidelitatis. Tum quia in illo iuramento nulla fit mentio de fidelitate. Tum quia esto, quod per aliqua verba eiusdem iuramenti aliqua fidelitas debeat intelligi, per nulla verba tamen posita in illo iuramento intelligitur fidelitas illa, quam debet vasallus Domino. Non enim omnis fidelitas est fidelitas, quam debet vasallus Domino. Nam nonnunquam quis debet seruare fidelitatem hosti suo: quia fides hosti est seruanda 23. q. 1. noli. Et tamen fidelitas illa, quam debet vasallus Domino, non est hosti seruanda. Discip. Videtur, quod iuramentum Othonis fuit iuramentum fidelitatis ex hoc, quod iurauit sibi, quod nunquam vitam aut membra aut honorem perderet sua voluntate, consilio vel exhortatione. Hoc autem spectat ad iuramentum fidelitatis 22. q. vlt. ea de forma, vbi sic legitur: Qui Domino suo fidelitatem iurat, ista sexsemper in memoria habere debet, incolumem, tutum, honestum, utile, possibile, facile. Incolumem videlicet, ne fit in damnum Domino suo de corpore suo. Ex quibus verbis colligi potest, quod qui iurat alicui, ne sit ei in damnum de corpore suo, iurat sibi fidelitatem. Hoc autem continetur in praedicto iuramento Othonis. Ergo iurauit Papae fidelitatem. Magist. Dicitur, quod non omnis, qui iurat alicui, ne sit ei in damnum de corpore suo, iurat sibi fidelitatem, quam debet vasallus Domino suo. Nam sicut legitur 1. Reg. 30. Dauid iurauit puero Aegyptio, qui ducturus eum erat ad Amalechitas, qui percusserunt Sichelet, quod non occideret eum, & non traderet eum in manum Domini sui: & tamen Dauid non iurauit illi puero fidelitatem, quam vasallus debet Domino suo. Et per consequens ex hoc, quod Otho iurauit Papae, quod sua voluntate aut consilio non perderet vitam aut membra, non exhibuit sibi iuramentum fidelitatis: imo quavis iurasset sibi, quod nihil mali ei vnquam faceret, non posset concludi, quod iurasset ei fidelitatem, quam debet vasallus Domino suo: licet iuraverit ei, quod nihil noceret sibi. Abimelech similiter iurauit Isaac. Sic legitur enim Gen. 26. Ad quem locum cum venissent de Gerario Abimelech & Achosat ad amicos illius, & Phicol Dux exercitus, locutus est eis Isaac: quid venistis ad me hominem, quem odistis & expulistis a vobis? Qui responderunt: Vidimus Dominum esse tecum & idcirco nunc diximus: sit iuramentum inter nos & iuremus foedus, & non facias nobis quicquid mali. Et post surgentes mane iuraverunt sibi mutuo. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Isaac iurauit illi, cuius non erat vasallus: & econtrario, quod noceret ei. Et per consequens licet Otho iurasset Papae, quod non sibi in damnum nec de corpore suo nec secreto vel munitionibus neq; de iustitia sua, neq; possessionibus, neq; de quocunq; pertinente ad ipsum, non posset ex hoc concludi, quod iurasset sibi fidelitatem, quam debet vasallus Domino suo, quod non continetur in iuramento, quousq; ad vltimum diem vitae suae foret sibi fidelis contra omnem hominem, sicut vasallus Domino suo. Sed videtur, quod Otho Imperator poterat iurare fidelitatem, & subiectionem Papae absque hoc, quod iuraret sibi fidelitatem quam debet vasallus Domino suo. Nam sicut habetur extra, de iureiurando, ego Episcopus, Episcopi iurant illam fidelitatem Domino Papae: & tamen non iurant sibi illam fidelitatem, quam debet vasallus Domino: quia Episcopi non sunt vasalli Papae, sicut nec Papa est Dominus ipsorum, iuxta illud Beati Petri: Nec dominantes in clero. Magist. Respondetur, quod sermo est de iuramento, quod dicitur debere fieri ab Imperatore ratione Imperii Romani, quod dicitur esse a Papa: quia dicitur, quod nullus est verus Imperator Romanus, nisi percipiat Romanum Imperium a Papa. Ex quo concluditur, quod Imperator debet infeudari a Papa: & per consequens Imperator est vasallus Papae. Ex quo sequitur, quod si debet iuramentum praestare Papae pro Romano Imperio, debet sibi iurare fidelitatem, quam debet vasallus Domino suo. Discip. Videtur, quod Otho iurauit Papae Iohanni fidelitatem illam, quam debet vasallus Domino: quia vocat eum Dominum suum, cum dicit: tibi Domino Iohanni Papae. Magist. Respondetur, quod sicut ibi Otho vocat Papam Dominum: ita Papa vocat Imperatorem Dominum suum in q. 1. sacerdotibus. Igitur sicut ex tali modo loquendi non potest concludi, quod Papa est vasallus Imperatoris: ita ex modo tali loquendi Othonis non potest concludi, quod Imperator est vasallus Papae. Igitur quod Otho vocat Papam Dominum suum, non est quia Papa est eius Dominus temporalis: sed propter praerogatiuam officii & dignitatis: quemadmodum saepe Domini temporales vocant etiam Mendicantes Religiosos Dominos, propter praerogatiuam sanctitatis & religionis: non quia reputant se vasallos eorum. Qui & modus loquendi saepe legitur in scripturis Diuinis. Discip. Nunquid tenebatur Otho etiam non requisitus iurare Domino Papae? Magist. Respondetur, quod Otho spontanea voluntate iurauit Papae Iohanni. Ad tale autem iuramentum cogi non potuit. Quod tali ratione probatur. Nam non plus ex ordinatione Christi tenetur Imperator Papae pro Romano Imperio, quam rex Franciae & quicunq; alii pro regnis suis. Sed rex Franciae & multi alii reges non renentur iurare Papae, nisi voluerint. Ergo nec Imperator. Et ex hoc concluditur, quod Imperator non habet Imperium a Papa, nec est vasallus eius: quia vasallus tenetur iurare Domino suo potissime si fuerit requisitus.
units.tr: Disciple. Let us examine the other arguments put forward for the aforesaid opinion. Master. For the same opinion Augustine is cited as follows: "The Emperor holds the Roman Empire from him by whom, after his election, he is examined, confirmed, anointed, consecrated and crowned, and to whom he swears." But the Roman Emperor, after his election, is examined by the Pope, confirmed, anointed, consecrated and crowned, and swears to him (Extra, De electione, c. Venerabilem; and Dist. 63, c. Tibi Domino). Therefore the Emperor holds the Empire from the Pope. Disciple. This argument seems to contain several parts. Tell me, then, according to some opinion, whether it can be shown from the fact that the one elected Emperor is examined by the Pope that the Emperor received the Empire from the Pope. Master. Some say it cannot. For envoys too must be examined by those to whom they are sent (Dist. 97, Nobilissimus, where the Gloss says: "Envoys are not received without danger"). Hence a more careful examination must be made of them. Yet the office of envoy is not from those who examine them. Therefore it cannot be proved by examination that one who is examined does not have his office from the one examining him. Again, although papal letters are examined (Extra, De crimine falsi et falsariorum), those who examine such letters have no power over the letters they examine. Therefore it cannot be inferred from the fact that the one elected Emperor is examined by the Pope that the Emperor has the Empire from the Pope. The one elected Emperor is examined by the Pope, then, not so that the Pope may confer the Empire on him, but so that the Pope and others may not take as Emperor one who has not been legitimately elected, and consequently one who is not the true Emperor. It is like those who wish to use papal letters examining them, so as not to accept false letters as genuine. Disciple. I see why it is said that examination cannot prove that the Empire comes from the Pope. Now tell me what is said about confirmation. Master. It is said that no authentic writing of greater antiquity is found stating that the Emperor was confirmed by the Pope. Hence, too, in the Decretal Venerabilem, which seems to sound more like the Empire comes from the Pope, no mention is made of confirmation. So it is said that in ancient times the Emperor was not confirmed by the Pope. If anyone was afterwards confirmed by the Pope, this happened from the simplicity or humility of the Emperor; yet the Pope could not thereby impose a law on the Emperor. Disciple. Can it be shown by anointing, consecration and coronation that the Empire comes from the Pope? Master. It is said not: for other kings are anointed, consecrated and crowned by the archbishops and bishops of their own kingdoms, and yet they do not hold their kingdoms from them. Disciple. Can it be shown by the oath that the Empire comes from the Pope? Master. It is said not: because it cannot be proved that any Emperor gave the Pope any oath other than the one Otho the Emperor gave to John. But Otho's oath was not an oath of fealty and subjection, which a vassal gives his lord for a fief he has received from him. To prove this, both Otho's oath and the oath a vassal gives his lord are cited. Otho's oath is found in Dist. 63, c. Tibi Domino, and reads thus: "To you, Lord John, Pope, I, King Otho, promise and swear by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these relics of the saints, that if, God permitting, I come to Rome, I will exalt the holy Roman Church and you, its protector, to the best of my power; and that I will not cause you to lose life or limb, or that honour you hold, by my will, my counsel, my consent or my exhortation. And in the city of Rome I will make no decree or ordinance concerning all matters that pertain to you or the Romans without your counsel. And whatever of the land of St. Peter comes into my power I will restore to you. And to whomever I commit the Kingdom of Italy I will have him swear to be your helper in defending the land of St. Peter, to the best of my power and his." The form in which a vassal swears to his lord is, as Hostiensis says, this: "I swear upon the holy Gospels of God that from now on I will be faithful to you, as a vassal ought to be to his lord; and I will not disclose to another, to your detriment, anything you have entrusted to me under the name of fealty." Hostiensis gives another form, which is this: "I, Titius, swear upon the holy Gospels of God that from this hour onward, until the last day of my life, I will be faithful to you, Otho, my lord, against every man." From these forms of oath it appears in some measure that the oath of the Emperor Otho was not an oath of fealty. First, because in that oath no mention is made of fealty. Second, even if some fealty might be understood from some words of that oath, that fealty which a vassal owes his lord is not understood from any words set down in that oath. For not every fealty is the fealty a vassal owes his lord. Indeed, sometimes a man must keep faith with his enemy, since faith is to be kept with an enemy (C. 23, q. 1, Noli). Yet that fealty which a vassal owes his lord is not to be kept with an enemy. Disciple. It seems that Otho's oath was an oath of fealty, because he swore to him that he would never by his own will, counsel or exhortation cause him to lose life, limb or honour. Now this pertains to the oath of fealty (C. 22, q. ult., De forma, where it is read thus): "He who swears fealty to his lord ought always to keep these six things in memory: safe, secure, honourable, useful, possible, easy. Safe, namely, that there be no harm to his lord in his body." From these words it can be gathered that whoever swears to someone that there will be no harm to him in his body swears him fealty. But this is contained in the aforesaid oath of Otho. Therefore he swore fealty to the Pope. Master. It is said that not everyone who swears to another that there will be no harm to him in his body swears him the fealty a vassal owes his lord. For as we read in 1 Kings 30, David swore to the Egyptian boy who was to lead him to the Amalekites, who had raided Ziklag, that he would not kill him nor hand him over into the hands of his master; yet David did not swear to that boy the fealty a vassal owes his lord. Consequently, from the fact that Otho swore to the Pope that by his will or counsel he would not cause him to lose life or limb, it does not follow that he gave him the oath of fealty. Indeed, even if he had sworn to him that he would never do him any harm, it could not be concluded that he had sworn him the fealty a vassal owes his lord, just as Abimelech swore to Isaac. For so we read in Gen. 26: when Abimelech and Ahuzzath his friend and Phicol, the commander of his army, came from Gerar to Isaac, Isaac said to them: "Why have you come to me, a man whom you hate and have driven away from you?" They answered: "We have seen that the Lord is with you, and so we have said: let there be an oath between us, and let us make a covenant, that you will do us no harm." And they rose early in the morning and swore to one another. From these words it is gathered that Isaac swore to one whose vassal he was not, and conversely that he would do him no harm. Consequently, even if Otho had sworn to the Pope that he would not cause him harm in his body, nor in his secret places or fortifications, nor in his justice, nor in his possessions, nor in anything else pertaining to him, it could not be concluded from this that he had sworn him the fealty a vassal owes his lord, which is not contained in an oath that he would be faithful to him until the last day of his life against every man, as a vassal to his lord. But it seems that the Emperor Otho could swear fealty and subjection to the Pope without swearing him the fealty a vassal owes his lord. For, as is found in Extra, De iureiurando, "I, a bishop": bishops swear that fealty to the Lord Pope, and yet they do not swear him that fealty which a vassal owes his lord, because bishops are not vassals of the Pope, just as the Pope is not their lord, according to the saying of St. Peter: "Not lording it over the clergy." Master. The answer is that the discussion concerns the oath which is said to be owed by the Emperor by reason of the Roman Empire, which is said to come from the Pope. For it is said that no one is a true Roman Emperor unless he receives the Roman Empire from the Pope. From this it is concluded that the Emperor must be enfeoffed by the Pope, and consequently the Emperor is the Pope's vassal. From this it follows that if he must give an oath to the Pope for the Roman Empire, he must swear him the fealty a vassal owes his lord. Disciple. It seems that Otho swore to Pope John that fealty which a vassal owes his lord, because he calls him his lord, saying: "To you, Lord John, Pope. Master. The answer is that just as Otho there calls the Pope lord, so the Pope calls the Emperor his lord (Q. 1, Sacerdotibus). Therefore, just as it cannot be concluded from such a manner of speaking that the Pope is the Emperor's vassal, so from such a manner of speaking in Otho it cannot be concluded that the Emperor is the Pope's vassal. So when Otho calls the Pope his lord, this is not because the Pope is his temporal lord, but on account of the pre-eminence of his office and dignity; just as temporal lords often also call the mendicant religious "lords," on account of the pre-eminence of their holiness and religion, not because they consider themselves their vassals. This manner of speaking is also often read in the divine Scriptures. Disciple. Was Otho bound to swear to the Lord Pope even when not asked? Master. The answer is that Otho swore to Pope John of his own free will. But he could not be compelled to such an oath. This is proved by the following reason. The Emperor is not bound by the ordinance of Christ to the Pope for the Roman Empire any more than the King of France and all others are for their kingdoms. But the King of France and many other kings are not bound to swear to the Pope unless they wish to. Therefore neither is the Emperor. And from this it is concluded that the Emperor does not hold the Empire from the Pope, nor is he his vassal, since a vassal is bound to swear to his lord especially if he has been asked.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Ponit duas alias rationes idem probantes quod prius: ad quas etiam respondetur.
units.tr: He presents two other arguments proving the same point as before, and answers them.

units.la: Discipulus. Tange breuiter aliquas alias rationes pro sæpe dicta opinione. Magist. Alia ratio est: Papa supplet defectum Imperii, vacante Imperio, extra, de foro compet. cap. licet. Ergo imperium dependet à Papa. Discip. Dic breuiter quomodo respondetur ad illam rationem. Magist. Dicitur, quod sicut Papa ex auctoritate sibi data à Christo non intromittit se de temporalibus, vacantibus aliis regnis multis: nec etiam est tutor aliorum regnorum vel hæredum eorum infra ætatem legitimam: sic Papa auctoritate Papali sibi data à Christo non intromittit se de Imperio, vacante illo. Sed quod intromittat se, si rite faciat; intromittit se auctoritate Romanorum vel Electorum, ad quos spectat specialiter supplere defectum Imperii, Imperio vacante, qui potestatem suam transferre possent in Papam. Discip. Aliam rationem adducas. Magist. Alia ratio est. Papa habet utrumque gladium, materialem scilicet & spiritualem. Ergo Imperium est ab ipso. Discip. Dic quomodo respondetur ad istam. Magist. Dicitur, quod Papa non habet utrumque gladium, teste Nicolao, qui, ut legitur 30. q. 2. cap. inter hoc, loquens de Ecclesia, ait: Gladium non habet; nisi spiritualem: non occidit, sed vivificat. Discip. Glossa respondet ibidem, quod Ecclesia non habet gladium nisi spiritualem, quoad executionem: habet tamen gladium materialem quasi reconditum in vagina, cuius executionem Imperatori committit. In gremio enim fidelis Ecclesiæ ambo gladii sunt reconditi. Unde quisquis ibidem non fuerit, neutrum habet. Quod probatur per hoc; quod Dominus non dicit Petro: abiice gladium; sed <bl>conuerte</bl> <bl>gladium in vaginam</bl>, vt scilicet Petrus non per seipsum, sed per Imperatorem potestatem gladii communicet. Potestas enim gladii materialis apud Ecclesiam est implicita: sed per Imperatorem, qui eam recepit, explicatur. In cuius signum summus pontifex, quando coronat Cæsarem, exhibet sibi gladium in vagina contentum, quem acceptum princeps euaginat, & vibrando innuit se illius executionem accepisse. Magist. Ista ratio à nonnullis, qui eam hæreticalem reputant, multipliciter improbatur. Discip. Quia illa opinio, quam modo tractamus, hæreticalis æstimatur: ideo breuiter narra, quomodo illa ratio improbatur. Magist. Improbatur primo sic. Rex Franciæ & alii reges quam plures non recipiunt gladii potestatem à Papa: etiam quando regnare incipiunt; ipsum de nullo requiruntur, nec pro coronatione, nec pro alia potestate concedenda ipsis. Ergo nec Imperator recipit gladii potestatem à Papa. Secundo, quia extra Ecclesiam est gladii potestas. Aliter enim nullus paganus fuisset vere princeps. Tertio: quia quando Christus dixit Petro: Converte gladium tuum in vaginam, post resurrectionem factus fuit pastor, licet prius fuit Apostolus dist. 50. con fiderandum, & cap. fidelitér. Igitur per illa verba non potest ostendi, quod potestas gladii fuit data Papæ à Christo. Quarto: quia alii reges accipiunt coronam ab Episcopis vel Archiepiscopis regnorum suorum; per quam designatur auctoritas & etiam potestas temporalis: & tamen illi non habent ab Episcopis vel Archiepiscopis regnorum suorum Dominium. Omnem enim gladii potestatem & administrationem temporalem habent ante coronationem, quam habent post: & multo magis recipiunt in coronatione, quam clerici confirmati in consecratione; & tamen ante consecrationem consequuntur omnia, quæ sunt iurisdictionis; extra, de translatione Episcoporum c. 1. Quinto, quia electus in Imperatorem, ante coronatur in regem, quam in Imperatorem à Papa coronetur. Omnis autem rex habet potestatem gladii materialis. Ergo antequam Imperator recipiat à Papa gladium in vagina contentum, habet etiam quoad executionem gladium materialem.
units.tr: Student. Touch briefly on some other arguments for the opinion we have so often mentioned. Master. Another argument is this: the Pope supplies the lack of an empire when the empire is vacant (Extra, De foro competenti, cap. licet). Therefore the empire depends on the Pope. Student. Tell me briefly how that argument is answered. Master. It is said that just as the Pope, by the authority given him by Christ, does not interfere in temporal affairs when many other kingdoms are vacant, nor is he the guardian of other kingdoms or of their heirs below legal age, so the Pope, by papal authority given him by Christ, does not interfere in the empire when it is vacant. But if he does interfere, when he does so rightly, he interferes by the authority of the Romans or the Electors, to whom it belongs specially to supply the lack of an empire when it is vacant, and who could transfer their power to the Pope. Student. Bring forward another argument. Master. Another argument is this: the Pope has both swords, the material and the spiritual. Therefore the empire is from him. Student. Tell me how that argument is answered. Master. It is said that the Pope does not have both swords, as Nicholas testifies, who, as we read (30 q. 2, cap. inter haec), speaking of the Church, says: "She has no sword but the spiritual one; she does not kill, but gives life." Student. The Gloss answers in the same place that the Church has only the spiritual sword as far as its execution goes, yet it has the material sword as though it were kept hidden in its scabbard, and it entrusts the execution of that sword to the Emperor. For both swords are kept hidden in the bosom of the faithful Church. Hence whoever is not in that bosom has neither sword. This is proved by the fact that the Lord does not say to Peter, "Cast away the sword," but "Turn your sword back into its scabbard," so that Peter would not pass on the power of the sword through himself, but through the Emperor. For the power of the material sword is implicit in the Church, but it is made explicit through the Emperor, who has received it. As a sign of this, the supreme pontiff, when he crowns Caesar, hands him a sword contained in its scabbard, which the prince, having received it, draws out and, brandishing it, signals that he has received its execution. Master. This argument is refuted in many ways by some who consider it heretical. Student. Since the opinion we are now discussing is judged heretical, briefly tell me how that argument is refuted. Master. It is refuted first as follows. The King of France and many other kings do not receive the power of the sword from the Pope, even when they begin to reign; they are asked for nothing by him, neither for their coronation nor for any other power to be granted to them. Therefore neither does the Emperor receive the power of the sword from the Pope. Second, because the power of the sword exists outside the Church; otherwise no pagan would have been a true prince. Third, because when Christ said to Peter, "Turn your sword into its scabbard," after the resurrection he had become minister, though previously he had been an Apostle (dist. 50, Considerandum; and cap. fideliter). Therefore those words cannot show that the power of the sword was given by Christ to the Pope. Fourth, because other kings receive the crown from the bishops or archbishops of their kingdoms, by which authority and also temporal power is signified; yet they do not hold their dominion from the bishops or archbishops of their kingdoms. For they have all power of the sword and temporal administration before their coronation, which they have afterwards, and they receive far more in coronation than clerics confirmed in consecration receive; and yet before consecration they obtain all things that belong to jurisdiction (Extra, De translatione episcoporum, cap. 1). Fifth, because one elected as Emperor is crowned king before he is crowned Emperor by the Pope. Every king, however, has the power of the material sword. Therefore, before the Emperor receives from the Pope the sword contained in its scabbard, he also has the material sword as far as its execution goes.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Adducit sextam rationem ad idem: ubi etiam propter illam rationem determinatur, quod Papa non potest omnia sine omni exceptione.
units.tr: He adduces a sixth reason for the same point, in which, on account of that reason, it is also determined that the Pope cannot do all things without any exception.

units.la: Discipulus. Ista ratio apparenter refellitur: ad quam postea forte redibimus. Ideo tange aliam rationem ad eandem conclusionem. Magist. Alia ratio talis est. Ab ipso est potestas Romani Imperii, qui à Christo recepit potestatem ligandi omnia & soluendi. Sed talem potestatem dedit Christus beato Petro, qui, ut legitur Matth. 16. dicit ei: Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, et quodcumque ligaueris super terram, erit solutum & in coelis. Igitur Beatus Petrus omnia potuit. Et per consequens potuit dare Imperium Imperatori. Discip. Quamuis de fundamento illius rationis plura potestimus inuenire in tractatu De potestate Papæ & cleri: tamen dic breuiter hic, an omnes consentiunt, quod absque omni exceptione Papa omnia possit. Videtur enim quod sic: cum Innocentius tertius videtur hoc consentire, & dicere, sicut legitur extra, de maior. & obe. c. solet. ait: Nunc vix non illud tanquam notissimum omittamus, quod Deus dicit ad Petrum, & etiam Petrus dicit ad successores suos: quodcunque ligaueris &c. nihil excipiens, cum dicit: quodcunque ligaueris &c. Magist. Dicere quod Papa sine omni exceptione omnia possit, multi reputant hæresim, etiam loquendo de illis, quæ fieri possunt ab homine. Tum, quia nihil potest quod est contra ius diuinum vel ius naturale. Tu quia multa non potest, quæ nec sunt contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale, quorum multa ab aliis fieri possunt. Discip. Quod Papa non possit illa, quæ sunt contra ius diuinum vel ius naturale, non dubito. Ideo non ponas exemplum de illis: sed breuiter tange ali-
units.tr: Disciple. This argument is apparently refuted; perhaps we shall return to it later. So touch on another argument for the same conclusion. Master. Another argument runs as follows. The power of the Roman Empire comes from him who received from Christ the power of binding and loosing all things. But Christ gave such power to blessed Peter, of whom we read in Matthew 16 that he said to him: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be loosed also in heaven." Therefore blessed Peter could do all things, and consequently could give the Empire to the Emperor. Disciple. Although we could find much about the foundation of that argument in the treatise On the Power of the Pope and of the Clergy, nevertheless tell me briefly here whether all agree that the Pope can do all things without any exception. For it seems that they do, since Innocent III appears to concede this and says, as we read in Extra, On the Majority and Obedience, chapter "Solet": "Now let us omit almost as most well known that which God says to Peter, and which Peter also says to his successors: whatever you bind, etc., excepting nothing, since he says: whatever you bind, etc." Master. To say that the Pope can do all things without any exception is considered by many to be heresy, even when speaking of those things that can be done by a man. First, because he cannot do anything that is contrary to divine law or natural law. Second, because there are many things he cannot do which are neither contrary to divine law nor contrary to natural law, and many of which can be done by others. Disciple. I do not doubt that the Pope cannot do those things which are contrary to divine law or natural law. So do not give examples of those, but briefly touch on some examples which others adduce to prove that the Pope cannot do all things, which are neither contrary to...

units.la: {5} Discip. ... (marginal numbers 5, 10, 15 ... 40, 45, 50, 55, 60 mark line numbers of the text and are not notes.) aliqua exempla, quae alii adducunt ad probandum, quod Papa non potest omnia, quae nec sunt contra ius diuinum nec naturale. Mag. Primum exemplum est: quod Papa non potest sibi substituere successorem, qui post ipsum sit Papa 8. q. 1. c. hic omnibus. Secundum est: quia quod infideles suscipiunt fidem non est contra ius diuinum vel naturale, sed consonum. Et tamen Papa non potest cogere infideles suscipere fidem. dist. 35. de Iudaeis. & 13. q. 5. ad fidem. & c. quia nos. Tertium est: quod non potest {5}compellere aliquem abiq; culpa intrare religionem 20. q. 3. c. praesens. Quartum est: quod non potest alicui praecipere absq; culpa & causa patenti, quod quis seruet virginitatem, teste Ambrosio, qui ut legitur 32. q. c. integritas, ait: Sola autem est virginitas, quae suaderi potest, imperari non potest. Res magis est voti quam praecepti. Ex verbis istis sumitur quintum exemplum, quod scilicet nihil supererogatiuum potest praecipere alicui sine culpa & absq; causa: nec continentiam nec ieiunium, nisi ratione delicti, vel causa patenti posset alicui praecipere 74. dist. cap. gesta. vbi dicit Beatus Gregorius. Sicut iustum est, ut nemo credere compellatur inuitus: ita censendum puto, ne quisquam insons ab ordine sui ministerii deiiciatur iniuste. Ex quibus verbis sic arguitur. Papa de plenitudine potestatis non potest deiicere iniuste aliquem. Igitur nec de plenitudine potestatis potest aliquem inuitum compellere credere, nisi ratione delicti vel ex causa. Sextum est: quod Papa non potest dispensare cum Monacho, ut habeat proprium, vel contrahat matrimonium, extra, de statu Monachorum. ca cum ad monasterium. Vbi sic dicitur: Abdicatio proprietatis & custodia castitatis adeo est adiuncta regulae monachali, ut contra eam nec summus pontifex possit licentiam indulgere. Septimum est: quod Papa absque causa non potest in quocumque voto dispensare, teste Glossa extra, de voto & voto, redemptione, cap. non est voti. Quae ait super verbo adimplere: Non est secutum quo ad Deum, cum quo Papa dispensat, nisi subsit causa dispensandi. Sicut non dicitur absolutus, qui causam excommunicationis suppimit: habebit tamen exceptionem, quo ad Ecclesiam ille, cum quo fine causa dispensatum est, quo ad Deum sibi allegatio non valebit. Octauum est, quod Papa non potest alienare praedia & possessiones Ecclesiae, nisi ex causa & debito modo 12. q. 2. cap. non liceat. Vbi Symachus Papa ait: Non liceat Papa praedium Ecclesiae alienare quoquo modo: scilicet ad placitum suum: sed in casu & debito modo posset alienare. Nec Papa hic imponit legem successori suo, sed ostendit, quid de iure non potest, vt dicit Glossa dist. 60. cap. si Papa non potest. Nonum est, quod quondam non potuit cogere subdiaconos ad continentiam, secundum Beatum Gregor. vt legitur 27. quaest 2. c. multorum. & dist. 31. ante triennium, qui reprobat constitutionem antecessoris sui. Qui, vt dicit Glossa super cap. ante triennium, ordinauit, vt subdiaconi, qui non promiserunt continentiam, vel contentiessent vxoribus suis tantum, vel beneficiis priuarentur. Postea ibidem praedecessor Gregorii fecit constitutionem, in qua praecise prohibuit, vt subdiaconi nullo modo commisceri debent vxoribus suis. De qua constitutione scribit Beatus Gregorius dicens: Ante triennium olim omnium Ecclesiarum subdiaconi Siciliae prohibiti fuerant (scilicet a Pelagio Papa) vt more Romana Eccl. fiat suis vxoribus nullatenus misceantur. Quod mihi durum videtur atque incompetens, vt qui vsum incontinentiae non inuenit, neque constitutem promisit, compellatur a sua vxore separari, ac per hoc (quod absit) in deterius cadat. Vbi Glossa in assignando casum huius capituli loquens de illa constitutione Pelagii, dicit sic: Sed illa constitutio fuit iniqua. quod aliquis, qui non promiserit continentiam, cogeretur continere: retractatur hic a Gregor & constituitur hic, quod si qui diaconi non sunt, non cogantur continere, nisi voluerint. Si qui autem in futurum ordinandi, non admittantur, nisi promittat continentiam. Et Glossa super verbo durum, dicit: Sic statutum Pelagii fuit contra Euangelium, ex quo excipitur scilicet fornicatio. Et ideo reprobatum fuit. Discip. Si constat, quod illud, quod praecepit Pelagius Papa, fuit contra Euangelium, illud exemplum non probat, quod Papa non potest omnia, quae non sunt contra ius diuinum vel naturale. Magist. Respondetur, quod istud statutum Pelagii fuit tam contra Euangelium, quam contra libertatem siue ius illorum subdiaconorum & vxorum suarum. Quia cogere voluit subdiaconos continere, non obstante Euangelio & libertate siue iure tam subdiaconorum quam vxorum eorundem. In potestate enim subdiaconorum de consensu vxorum suarum fuit continere: nec hoc erat contra Euangelium. Sed illam potestatem subdiaconorum & vxorum suarum non potuit ab eis auferre Papa Pelagius, vt testatur Gregor. ergo non potuit omnia, quae sunt contra ius diuinum & contra ius naturale. Et ex ista sententia concludit Gregor. quod Papa nihil potest contra libertatem & ius vnius Christiani etiam in spiritualibus, nisi ratione delicti vel causa manifesta. Quoniam nullum potest priuare iure suo & libertate sua sine culpa & absque causa. Et ideo nisi ratione delicti vel ex causa non potest alicui praecipere continentiam, nec ieiunium, nec Eleemosynam, ad quod non tenetur sine consensu suo, nec aliquid simile. Discip.
