De hoc, & sicut de aliis, in tractatu De potestate Papae & cleri plura poterimus inuenire: ideo breuiter tange plura exempla. Magist. Decimum est: quod non potest cogere aliquem subdiaconum nolentem suscipere praelationem, vt notatur in Glossa 23. q. 4. c. displicet. Vndecimum est, quod non potest statuere, ne de haeresi accusetur, teste Glossa quae dist. 60. c. si Papa, quaerit: nunquid Papa possit statuere, ne de haeresi accusetur? Et respondens ait, non: quia per hoc periclitaretur tota Ecclesia. Et consimili ratione non posset statuere, ne possit qualitercunque accusari de illo crimine, pro quo potest deponi. Sed pro alio crimine quocunque potest in casu Papa deponi, teste Glossa ibidem, quae ait: Certe credo, quod si notorium est crimen eius quodunque & in scandalum Ecclesiae & incorrigibilis sit, quod inde possit accusari, & per consequens iudicari. Quia accusatio coram iudice fieri debet. Igitur non potest statuere, ne possit pro quocunque crimine accusari & iudicari. Duodecimum est: quod non potest compellere aliquem ad confitendum peccatum, quod alteri confessus est, qui absoluere potuit. Quia confessio sacramentalis cuidam diuino Imperio subiacent iacea est, non humano. Tertiodecimum est: quod Papa non potest compellere aliquem, vt contrahac matrimonium. Cuius rationem reddunt aliqui dicentes, quod secundum ea quae ad naturam corporis pertinent, homo homini obedire non tenetur, sed soli Deo. Omnes homines natura sunt pares: puta in his, quae pertinent ad corporis sustentationem & prolis generationem, sicut de matrimonio contrahendo, vel virginitate seruanda, vel aliquo huiusmodi. Quartumdecimum est: quod Papa in temporalibus legitimare non potest, vt notatur extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem. Quintumdecimum, quod includit quamplura; est quod Papa extra metas iurisdictionis suae temporali subiectas non potest illa, quae Dominus temporalis super seruos inquantum serui sunt. Discip. Istud exemplum habet vigorem ex hoc; quod non omnes homines sunt puri serui summi pontificis. Quia si Papa omnia posset, quae non sunt contra ius naturale, nec contra ius diuinum, ipse posset omnia in Imperatores & reges, principes, ac generaliter in omnes mortales, quae potest Dominus quicunque in quemcunque seruum suum: & ita nullus nisi Papa esset liber, sed omnes essent serui sui. Licet autem de isto, sicut de multis aliis, quae ad potestatem Papae & cleri spectant; possumus multa inuenire in tractatu primo huius tertiae partis nostri Dialogi: breuiter tamen hic allegare conabor, quod non omnes homines sunt puri serui Papae. Magist. Hoc multipliciter videtur posse probari. Primo sic: Reges & principes ac alii laici habent proprietatem rerum temporalium. Seruus autem non habet proprium. Igitur non omnes homines sunt puri serui Papae. Secundo: differentia est inter seruos Ecclesiae & aliorum. Igitur non omnes homines sunt serui summi pontificis. Tertio: non omnem eandem potestatem habet Papa in cunctis suae iurisdictioni subiectis, & in aliis suae iurisdictioni temporali non subiectis. Igitur non omnes sunt serui summi pontificis. Quarto sic: aliqui sunt Domini principales, qui non habent Dominos, extra de haereticis, excommunicamus. Igitur non omnes homines sunt serui Papae. Quinto: si omnes homines essent puri serui Papae: Papa posset ad libitum alienare quamlibet rem temporalem. Igitur posset ad libitum alienare praedia Ecclesiae, quod est contra illud 12. q. 2. non liceat Papae. Sexto sic: Papa non debet dominari super clerum, iuxta illud canonicae Petri, non dominantes in clero. Igitur clerici non sunt serui summi pontificis.
units.tr: Student. ... Let us hear some examples that others adduce to prove that the Pope cannot do everything that is neither contrary to divine nor to natural law. Master. The first example is that the Pope cannot appoint a successor to himself who would be Pope after him (8 q. 1 c. hic omnibus). The second is that it is not contrary to divine or natural law, but agrees with them, that unbelievers take up the faith; yet the Pope cannot compel unbelievers to accept the faith (dist. 35, de Iudaeis; 13 q. 5, ad fidem; and c. quia nos). The third is that he cannot compel anyone to enter religious life without fault (20 q. 3 c. praesens). The fourth is that he cannot order anyone, without fault and without a manifest cause, to keep virginity. Ambrose, as is read in 32 q. c. integritas, says: Virginity alone can be persuaded, but it cannot be commanded. It is a matter of vow rather than of precept. From these words a fifth example is drawn: namely, that nothing supererogatory can be commanded to anyone without fault and without cause. Nor can he command continence or fasting to anyone, except on account of a fault or for a manifest cause (74 dist. c. gesta), where Blessed Gregory says: Just as it is right that no one be compelled to believe against his will, so I think it must be judged that no innocent man be unjustly deprived of the order of his ministry. From these words the argument runs thus: the Pope, by virtue of the fullness of power, cannot unjustly depose anyone; therefore neither can he, by the fullness of power, compel anyone against his will to believe, unless on account of a fault or for some cause. The sixth is that the Pope cannot dispense a monk to have property or to contract marriage (extra, de statu monachorum, c. cum ad monasterium). There it is said: Renunciation of property and the keeping of chastity are so bound up with the monastic rule that not even the supreme pontiff can grant a licence against it. The seventh is that the Pope cannot, without cause, dispense from any vow, as the Gloss attests (extra, de voto et voti redemptione, c. non est voti). On the word adimplere it says: It does not follow, as regards God, that the one with whom the Pope dispenses is released, unless there is a cause for dispensing. Just as one is not called absolved who has suppressed the cause of excommunication, yet he will have an exception as regards the Church; but with respect to God, the plea of one whom he has dispensed without cause will not avail. The eighth is that the Pope cannot alienate the lands and possessions of the Church except for a cause and in the proper manner (12 q. 2 c. non liceat). There Pope Symmachus says: The Pope may not alienate the lands of the Church in any way at all, namely at his own pleasure; but in a case of need and in the proper manner he could alienate them. Nor does the Pope here impose a law on his successor, but shows what he may not do by right, as the Gloss says (dist. 60 c. si Papa non potest). The ninth is that Gregory once could not compel subdeacons to continence, according to Blessed Gregory, as is read (27 q. 2 c. multorum; and dist. 31, ante triennium), who rejected the constitution of his predecessor. This, as the Gloss says on the chapter ante triennium, had ordained that subdeacons who had not promised continence, or who were content with their wives alone, should be deprived of their benefices. Afterwards, in the same place, the predecessor of Gregory made a constitution in which he expressly prohibited subdeacons from having any intercourse with their wives. Blessed Gregory writes about this constitution, saying: Some time ago, three years since, the subdeacons of all the churches of Sicily had been forbidden (namely by Pope Pelagius) to have any intercourse with their wives, in the manner of the Roman Church. This seems to me harsh and improper, that a man who has not practised incontinence, nor promised a constitution of continence, should be compelled to be separated from his wife, and so (God forbid) should fall into a worse state. Here the Gloss, in setting out the case of this chapter, speaking of that constitution of Pelagius, says: But that constitution was unjust, that anyone who had not promised continence should be compelled to be continent. It is here retracted by Gregory, and it is established here that if there are deacons who are not to be ordained, they are not to be compelled to be continent unless they wish it. But if anyone is to be ordained in future, he is not to be admitted unless he promises continence. And the Gloss on the word durum says: Thus the statute of Pelagius was against the Gospel, from which fornication is excepted. And therefore it was rejected. Student. If it is established that what Pope Pelagius commanded was against the Gospel, that example does not prove that the Pope cannot do everything that is not contrary to divine or natural law. Master. It is answered that this statute of Pelagius was as much against the Gospel as against the liberty, or right, of those subdeacons and their wives. For he wished to compel the subdeacons to be continent, notwithstanding the Gospel and the liberty, or right, of the subdeacons and of their wives alike. For it was within the power of the subdeacons, with the consent of their wives, to be continent, and this was not against the Gospel. But Pope Pelagius could not take that power away from the subdeacons and their wives, as Gregory testifies; therefore he could not do everything that is contrary neither to divine nor to natural law. And from this opinion Gregory concludes that the Pope can do nothing against the liberty and right of any Christian, even in spiritual matters, unless on account of a fault or for a manifest cause. For no one can be deprived of his right and liberty without fault and without cause. And therefore, unless on account of a fault or for a cause, he cannot command anyone continence, nor fasting, nor almsgiving, to which he is not bound without his own consent, nor anything of the kind. Student. Concerning this, as concerning other matters, we may find more in the treatise On the Power of the Pope and of the Clergy; therefore let me touch briefly on several more examples. Master. The tenth is that he cannot compel a subdeacon who is unwilling to accept promotion (as is noted in the Gloss on 23 q. 4 c. displicet). The eleventh is that he cannot decree that he may not be accused of heresy, as the Gloss on dist. 60 c. si Papa attests, which asks: may the Pope decree that he shall not be accused of heresy? And it answers: no, because by this the whole Church would be put in danger. And by a similar reasoning he could not decree that he may not in any way be accused of that crime for which he can be deposed. But for any other crime whatsoever, the Pope can in a case be deposed, as the Gloss there attests, which says: Certainly I believe that if his crime, of whatever kind, is notorious, and to the scandal of the Church, and he is incorrigible, then he may be accused on that account and consequently judged. For accusation must be made before a judge. Therefore he cannot decree that he may not be accused and judged for any crime whatsoever. The twelfth is that he cannot compel anyone to confess a sin which he has confessed to another who was able to absolve him. For sacramental confession is subject to a divine command, not a human one. The thirteenth is that the Pope cannot compel anyone to contract marriage. Some who give the reason for this say that, according to what pertains to the nature of the body, man is not bound to obey man, but God alone. All men are by nature equal, in those things which pertain to the sustenance of the body and the generation of offspring, as in contracting marriage, or in keeping virginity, or in anything of the kind. The fourteenth is that the Pope cannot legitimate in temporal matters, as is noted (extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem). The fifteenth, which includes very many, is that the Pope, outside the bounds of his jurisdiction which are subject to temporal rule, cannot do those things which a temporal lord may do over his servants, insofar as they are servants. Student. This example has its force from this: that not all men are mere servants of the supreme pontiff. For if the Pope could do everything that is neither contrary to natural law nor to divine law, he could do over emperors and kings, princes, and generally over all mortals, whatever any lord may do over any servant of his; and thus no one but the Pope would be free, and all would be his servants. Although concerning this, as concerning many other things which pertain to the power of the Pope and of the clergy, we may find much in the first treatise of this third part of our Dialogue, I shall nevertheless try briefly to show here that not all men are mere servants of the Pope. Master. This seems to be provable in many ways. First, thus: kings and princes and other laymen have ownership of temporal goods. But a servant does not have property. Therefore not all men are mere servants of the Pope. Second: there is a difference between the servants of the Church and those of others. Therefore not all men are servants of the supreme pontiff. Third: the Pope does not have the same power over all those subject to his jurisdiction and over those not subject to his temporal jurisdiction. Therefore not all are servants of the supreme pontiff. Fourth, thus: some are principal lords who have no lords (extra de haereticis, excommunicamus). Therefore not all men are servants of the Pope. Fifth: if all men were mere servants of the Pope, the Pope could alienate any temporal thing at will. Therefore he could alienate at will the lands of the Church, which is contrary to that (12 q. 2, non liceat Papae). Sixth, thus: the Pope ought not to lord it over the clergy, according to that saying of Peter's epistle: not lording it over the clergy (1 Pet. 5). Therefore the clergy are not servants of the supreme pontiff.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: Adducit quatuor rationes probantes, quod Imperialis potestas sit a Papa: ad quas etiam respondetur.
units.tr: It adduces four arguments proving that imperial power comes from the Pope, and replies are also given to them.

units.la: Discipulus. De ista materia habeo postea occasionem loquendi. Ideo breuiter comple rationes pro opinione, quam nunc discussimus. Magist. Quod Imperium sit a Papa, tali ratione probatur. Imperium fuit a Christo. Quia ipse non solum fuit sacerdos, sed etiam fuit rex omnium temporalium, in cuius signum ipse aliqua fecit vt Imperator, & aliqua sicut sacerdos, vt not. Gloss. dist. 96. c. quoniam idem. Igitur Papa, qui est vicarius Christi in terris, est Dominus Imperii. Discip. Dic, quomodo respondetur ad rationem istam? Magist. Dupliciter respondetur. Vno modo, & haereticum est dicere, quod Christus inquantum homo mortalis fuit in temporalibus rex. Discip. De hoc latius habebimus in tractatu tertio tertiae partis huius Dialogi. Ideo dic, quomodo aliter respondetur. Magist. Aliter respondetur sic: quod non semper vicarius habet omnem potestatem, quam habet ille, cuius est vicarius. Et ideo licet Christus fuisset rex in temporalibus, & ab eo fuisset Imperium: ex hoc concludi non posset, quod Imperium esset a vicariis Christi. Discip. Aliam rationem allega. Magist. Alia ratio est: sacerdos veteris legis fuit super reges & regna, teste Deo, qui dixit Ieremiae Prophetae & sacerdoti: Ierem. 1. Ecce constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna. Igitur multo magis summus sacerdos nouae legis est super Imperium. Discip. Narra, quomodo respondetur ad hanc. Magist. Multipliciter respondetur. Vno modo sic: quod sacerdos veteris legis non fuit super reges, nisi in spiritualibus, & non in temporalibus. Et ideo summus sacerdos est super Imperatorem in spiritualibus, & non in temporalibus. Aliter dicitur, quod summus sacerdos nouae legis non assimilatur summo sacerdoti veteris legis. Et ideo esto, quod summus sacerdos veteris legis fuisset super regem: ex hoc inferri non posset, quod summus sacerdos nouae legis esset super Imperatorem. Aliter dicitur: quod licet Ieremias fuit sacerdos, non tamen fuit summus sacerdos. Et ideo per auctoritatem illam non potest probari, quod Imperium sit a summo sacerdote nouae legis; nisi etiam posset per eandem rationem probari, quod Imperium est a sacerdote inferiori summo pontifice: quod tamen non est verum. Discip. Adducas aliam rationem. Magist. Alia ratio talis est. Summum sacerdotium & Imperium intelliguntur per solem & lunam, de quibus dicitur Genes. 1. Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna &c. Ergo sicut luna recipit lumen a sole: ita Imperator recipit potestatem a Papa. Discip. Qualiter respondetur ad illam rationem? Magist. Respondetur, quod licet per solem & lunam intelligantur summum sacerdotium & Imperium: non tamen omnino eodem modo se habet Imperium ad summum sacerdotium, quo se habet luna ad solem. Hoc enim dato concludetur oppositum conclusionis rationis praefatae. Tum quia, sicut luna non est a sole; sed ambo sunt a Deo: ita Imperium non est a summo sacerdotio, sed ambo sunt vel essent ab alio. Tum, quia tunc sicut luna habet aliquam virtutem & aliquam potestatem, quam non habet a sole, scilicet supra aquas & humores: ita Imperator habet aliam potestatem, quam non habet a Papa. Ideo dicitur, quod quantum ad aliquid est simile de sole & luna, & de summo pontifice & Imperatore, & quantum ad aliquid non est simile. Quantum enim ad hoc, est simile: quia sicut sol est nobilior & dignior luna, sic summum sacerdotium est nobilius & dignius Imperio, quemadmodum spiritualia sunt digniora temporalibus. Item, sicut luna recipit lumen à sole, sic in multis Imperator debet recipere directionem à Papa, quando est catholicus bonus & sapiens, scilicet in causis divinis. Quantum autem ad multa alia, non est simile, ut dictum est. Discip. Adhuc aliam rationem adducas. Magist. Alia ratio talis est. Ecclesia est unum corpus: ergo habet unum caput. Sed Imperator non est caput. Ergo Papa est caput Ecclesiæ. A capite autem derivatur virtus in membra. Ergo Imperator est membrum Ecclesiæ, & non caput: & per consequens recipere debet virtutem à Papa, sicut à capite. Ergo Imperium est à Papa. Discip. Dic, quomodo respondetur ad hoc, Magist. Respondetur, quod Papa est caput Ecclesiæ, quæ est congregatio fidelium. Et ideo in spiritualibus subest Imperator Papæ. Ergo illam virtutem spiritualem & directionem recipere debet à Papa. Sed quia Papa non est caput in temporalibus: ideo Imperator in temporalibus non subest ei, nec Imperium recipere debet ab ipso.
units.tr: Discipulus. I shall have an occasion to speak about this matter later, so briefly complete the arguments for the opinion we have just discussed. Magist. That the empire comes from the Pope is proved by this argument. The empire came from Christ, for he was not only a priest but also king of all temporal things, and as a sign of this he did some things as emperor and some as priest, as the gloss notes at dist. 96, c. quoniam idem. Therefore the Pope, who is Christ's vicar on earth, is lord of the empire. Discip. Tell me, how is this argument answered? Magist. It is answered in two ways. In one way, and it is heretical to say so, that Christ as a mortal man was a king in temporal affairs. Discip. We shall treat this more fully in the third treatise of the third part of this Dialogue. So tell me how it is otherwise answered. Magist. Otherwise it is answered thus: a vicar does not always have all the power that the one whose vicar he is has. And so, although Christ was king in temporal affairs and the empire came from him, it cannot be concluded from this that the empire comes from the vicars of Christ. Discip. Give another argument. Magist. Another argument is this: the priest of the old law was over kings and kingdoms, God bearing witness, who said to the prophet and priest Jeremiah: Jer. 1. Behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms. Therefore much more the high priest of the new law is over the empire. Discip. Tell how this is answered. Magist. It is answered in many ways. In one way: the priest of the old law was over kings only in spiritual matters, and not in temporal ones. And so the high priest is over the emperor in spiritual matters, and not in temporal ones. Otherwise it is said that the high priest of the new law is not to be compared with the high priest of the old law. So even if the high priest of the old law had been over the king, it could not be inferred that the high priest of the new law is over the emperor. Otherwise it is said: although Jeremiah was a priest, he was not the high priest. So by that authority it cannot be proved that the empire comes from the high priest of the new law; unless it could also be proved by the same reasoning that the empire comes from a priest inferior to the supreme pontiff, which is not true. Discip. Bring another argument. Magist. Another argument is this. The supreme priesthood and the empire are understood by the sun and the moon, of which it is said in Gen. 1: God made two great lights, etc. Therefore just as the moon receives its light from the sun, so the emperor receives his power from the Pope. Discip. How is that argument answered? Magist. It is answered that although the supreme priesthood and the empire are understood by the sun and the moon, the empire does not stand to the supreme priesthood in exactly the same way as the moon stands to the sun. For if this were granted, the opposite of the conclusion of the aforesaid argument would follow. First, because just as the moon is not from the sun, but both are from God, so the empire is not from the supreme priesthood, but both are, or would be, from another. Second, because then, just as the moon has some virtue and power which it does not have from the sun, namely over waters and moisture, so the emperor has another power which he does not have from the Pope. So it is said that in some respects the sun and moon, and the supreme pontiff and the emperor, are alike, and in some respects not alike. For in this respect they are alike: just as the sun is nobler and worthier than the moon, so the supreme priesthood is nobler and worthier than the empire, as spiritual things are worthier than temporal ones. Likewise, just as the moon receives light from the sun, so in many matters the emperor ought to receive direction from the Pope, when he is a good and wise Catholic, namely in divine causes. In many other respects, however, they are not alike, as has been said. Discip. Bring yet another argument. Magist. Another argument is this. The Church is one body, therefore it has one head. But the emperor is not the head. Therefore the Pope is the head of the Church. Now virtue is derived from the head into the members. Therefore the emperor is a member of the Church, not its head, and consequently ought to receive virtue from the Pope as from the head. Therefore the empire is from the Pope. Discip. Tell how this is answered. Magist. It is answered that the Pope is the head of the Church, which is the congregation of the faithful. And so in spiritual matters the emperor is subject to the Pope, and ought to receive that spiritual virtue and direction from him. But because the Pope is not the head in temporal matters, the emperor is not subject to him in temporal matters, nor ought he to receive the empire from him.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: In quo improbatur opinio tertia, supra cap. 18. recitata, & iam in præcedentibus capitulis probata: ubi probatur illud dictum opinionis, scilicet quod nullum Imperium potest esse verum Imperium; nisi à Papa, esse hæreticum.
units.tr: In which the third opinion, recited above in chapter 18 and already refuted in the preceding chapters, is rejected: where it is shown that the statement of that opinion, namely that no empire can be a true empire unless it is from the Pope, is heretical.

units.la: Discipulus. Aliquantulum diffuse respondendo & arguendo tractavimus opinionem tertiam supra capitulo 18. recitatam. Nunc autem desidero scire, quomodo improbatur. Magist. Ista opinio duo dicit. Primum est, quod Imperium est à Papa. Secundum est, quod nullum potest esse verum Imperium, nisi à Papa. Primum quidam dicunt esse falsum. Secundum autem dicunt esse hæreticum.
units.tr: Student. We have discussed at some length, in answering and arguing, the third opinion recited above in chapter 18. Now, however, I want to know how it is refuted. Master. That opinion says two things. The first is that empire is from the Pope. The second is that no empire can be a true empire unless it is from the Pope. Some say the first is false; the second they say is heretical.

units.la: Discip. Trades primo secundum, & narra qualiter dicunt aliqui illud esse hæreticum. Magist. Quod sit hæreticum quidam niituntur sic ostendere. Quod repugnat scripturæ Divinæ est hæreticum reputandum. Sed non potest esse verum Imperium, nisi à Papa, repugnat Divinæ scripturæ. Nam per scripturam constat, ut dicunt, aperte quod plures pagani fuerunt veri Imperatores. Hoc etiam testatur Evangelista Lucas 2. Exiit edictum à Cæsare Augusto, ut describeretur universus orbis. Ex quibus colligitur, quod Octavianus, de quo ibidem fit sermo, fuit verus Imperator. Item, Matthæi vigesimo secundo dicit Christus Iudæis: Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari. Ex quibus verbis datur intelligi, quod ille fuit verus Cæsar: & tamen non habuit Imperium à Papa, imo fuit paganus & infidelis. Ergo verum Imperium, verum dominium temporale, vera iurisdictio temporalis, & vera potestas gladii materialis, fuit & esse potest apud infideles, & extra Ecclesiam catholicam. Licet infideles nonnunquam & forte ut plurimum tali potestate legitima abutantur: sed ex abusu inferri non potest, quod dignitas vel potestas sit minus vera, teste Augustino, qui, ut legitur in decretis dein. tert. quæst. quint. neque enim, ait: Nec tyrannica persecutionis perversitas est laudabilis, si regia clementia tyrannice subditos tractet: nec vituperatur ordo regia potestatis, si rex crudelitate tyrannica saviat. Aliud namque est iniusta potestate velle iuste uti: & aliud iusta potestate iniuste velle uti. Ex his verbis datur intelligi, quod vera potestate & vero dominio potest quis abuti, & ita ex abusu infidelium probari non potest, quod apud eos non sit verum dominium, nec vera potestas gladii materialis.
units.tr: Student. Tell me the second first, and explain how some say it is heretical. Master. Some try to show that it is heretical in this way. What contradicts Divine Scripture is to be held heretical. But that no empire can be true unless it is from the Pope contradicts Divine Scripture. For, they say, it is clear from Scripture that several pagans were true emperors. Evangelist Luke also bears witness to this in chapter 2: "A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled." From which it is gathered that Octavian, of whom the passage speaks, was a true emperor. Likewise Christ says to the Jews in Matthew 22: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's." From these words it is to be understood that he was a true Caesar, and yet he did not have his empire from the Pope; indeed he was a pagan and an unbeliever. Therefore true empire, true temporal lordship, true temporal jurisdiction and true power of the material sword were, and can be, among unbelievers and outside the Catholic Church. Although unbelievers sometimes, and perhaps for the most part, abuse such lawful power, it cannot be inferred from the abuse that the dignity or power is less true; as Augustine witnesses, who, as is read in the Decretals, dist. 3, qu. 5: "For neither is the perversity of tyrannical persecution praiseworthy, if a royal clemency treats its subjects tyrannically; nor is the order of royal power blamed, if a king rages with tyrannical cruelty. For it is one thing to wish to use an unjust power justly, and another to wish to use a just power unjustly." From these words it is to be understood that one can abuse a true power and true lordship, and so from the abuse of unbelievers it cannot be proved that among them there is no true lordship, nor true power of the material sword.

units.la: Discip. Quantum ad quidam impugnantes reputant opinionem prædictam hæreticam, ut puto, intelligo. Ideo solummodo auctoritates, quibus probare conantur, quod apud infideles sit verum dominium temporale, & vera potestas gladii materialis adducas. Magist. Ad hoc adducunt auctoritates tam Veteris quam Novi Testamenti, quam etiam auctoritates sanctorum patrum & maiorum. Abraham enim, ut habetur Genes. vigesimo tertio, noluit gratis recipere speluncam duplicem, ut sepeliret in ea uxorem suam, sed emit eam ab Effron infideli: quod tamen non fecisset, si Effron in ea verum ius nullatenus habuisset. Iacob etiam fidelis indicavit, quod Labam infidelis verum dominium aliquarum rerum temporalium habebat, cum dicit ei, ut legitur Gen. 31. Quicquid tuum apud me inveneris, aufer. Et post: quid invenisti de cunctis substantiis Domus tuæ? Et post: oves tuæ & tauri, pratuaster iles non fuerunt: arietes gregis tui non comedi. Item, Gen. 39. Benedixitque dominus domui Ægyptiï propter Ioseph, & multiplicavit tam in ædibus quam in agris tunc ea eius substantiam. Ergo iste infidelis habuit verum dominium rerum. Item, quadragesimo primo capitulo loquens de legitima potestate Pharaonis ait: Omne frumentum sub Pharaonis potestate condatur. Et quadragesimo quinto scribitur: Emit ergo Ioseph omnem terram Ægypti, vendentibus singulis possessiones suas pre magnitudine famis, subiecitque eam Pharaoni, & cunctos populos eius. Et sequitur: En ut cernitis & vos & terram vestram Pharao possidet. Item, Deut. 2. scribitur, quod Deus dedit quibusdam infidelibus verum dominium terrarum. Ubi sic legitur: transibitis terminos fratrum vestrorum filiorum Esau, qui habitant in Seir, & timebunt vos. Videte ergo diligenter, ne moveamini contra eos, neque enim dabo vobis de terra eorum quantum potest unius pedis calcare vestigium: quia in possessionem Esau dedi montem Seir. Cibos emetis ab eis pecunia & comedetis. Aliquam quam optam hauritis & bibetis. Et post: dixitque Dominus ad Moysen: Non pugnabis contra Moabitas, nec ineas adversus eos prælium, non enim dabo tibi quicquam de terra eorum, quia filiis Loth tradidi in possessionem. Et post: Locutus est Dominus ad Moysen dicens: Tu transibis hodie terminos Moab, urbem nomine Ar, & ascendes in vicinia filiorum Amon. Cave ne pugnes contra eos, nec movearis ad prælium. Non enim dabo tibi de terra filiorum Amon: quia filiis Loth dedi eam in possessionem.
units.tr: Student. As far as I understand, those who attack this opinion think it heretical; so, I suppose, you should now bring forward only the authorities by which they try to prove that among unbelievers there is true temporal lordship and true power of the material sword. Master. To this end they adduce authorities both of the Old and of the New Testament, and also the authorities of the holy Fathers and elders. For Abraham, as we read in Genesis 23, was unwilling to receive the double cave freely in order to bury his wife in it, but bought it from Ephron the unbeliever; which he would not have done if Ephron had had no true right in it at all. Jacob too, a believer, showed that Laban, an unbeliever, had true lordship over some temporal goods, when he says to him, as we read in Genesis 31: "Whatever you find that is yours among me, take it away." And afterwards: "What have you found of all the substance of your house?" And again: "Your sheep and oxen, which were not barren among you; the rams of your flock I have not eaten." Likewise Genesis 39: "The Lord blessed the house of the Egyptian for Joseph's sake, and multiplied his substance both in houses and in fields." Therefore this unbeliever had true lordship of things. Likewise, in chapter 41, speaking of the lawful power of Pharaoh, it says: "Let all the grain be gathered under the power of Pharaoh." And in chapter 45 it is written: "So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt, each man selling his possessions because of the greatness of the famine, and he made it subject to Pharaoh, and all his people." And it follows: "Behold, as you see, both you and your land Pharaoh possesses." Likewise, Deuteronomy 2 records that God gave true lordship of lands to certain unbelievers. There it is read: "You shall pass through the borders of your brethren the sons of Esau, who dwell in Seir, and they shall fear you. Take heed therefore diligently that you do not stir up war against them; for I will not give you of their land so much as the sole of a foot may tread upon, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau for a possession. You shall buy food of them for money, and you shall eat; you shall also buy water of them, and drink." And afterwards: "The Lord said to Moses: You shall not fight against the Moabites, nor engage them in battle; for I will not give you anything of their land, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession." And afterwards: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Today you shall pass over the border of Moab, the city called Ar, and you shall come near the sons of Ammon. Beware that you do not fight against them, nor be moved to battle. For I will not give you any of the land of the sons of Ammon, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession."

units.la: Item, vt legitur 3. Reg. 9. Salomon dedit Hiram regi Tyri, qui non est de filiis Israel, sponte 20. oppida in terra Galilææ: quæ tamen non dedisset ei sponte, si ille non fuisset capax alicuius dominii aliquarum temporalium rerum. Item 3. Regum. 9. Præcepit Dominus Heliæ Prophetæ, vt vngeret Azael in Regem super Syriam: qui tamen erat infidelis. Constat autem, quod regnum datum à Deo est verum regnum. Ergo infidelis fuit capax veri regni, & veri dominii, aut veræ potestatis temporalis. Item 2. Paral. c. vltimo. Et 1. Esdræ. cap. 1. sic legitur: Suscitauit Dominus spiritum Cyri regis, qui iussit prædicari in vniverso regno suo: Hoc dicit rex Cyrus Persarum, omnia regna terræ dedit mihi Dominus Deus cœli, & ipse præcepit mihi, vt ædificarem ei domum in Hierusalem. De quo etiam dicitur Esa. 45. Hæc dicit Dominus meus Domino meo Cyro, cuius apprehendi dexteram, subiiciam ante faciem eius gentes, & dorsa regum vertam.
units.tr: Likewise, as we read in 3 Kings 9, Solomon gave of his own accord twenty towns in the land of Galilee to Hiram, king of Tyre, who was not of the sons of Israel; yet he would not have given them of his own accord if Hiram had not been capable of some lordship over temporal things. Likewise 3 Kings 19: the Lord commanded the prophet Elijah to anoint Hazael as king over Syria, who nevertheless was an unbeliever. It is certain, however, that a kingdom given by God is a true kingdom. Therefore an unbeliever was capable of a true kingdom, and of true lordship, or of true temporal power. Likewise 2 Chronicles, last chapter, and 1 Esdras, chapter 1, read thus: "The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus the king, who commanded that it be proclaimed throughout all his kingdom: Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem." Of him also it is said in Isaiah 45: "Thus says the Lord to my Lord Cyrus, whose right hand I have held, I will subdue the nations before his face, and I will turn the loins of kings."

units.la: Item Thob. 2. legitur, quod cum Anna vxor Thobiæ, hædum caprarum detulisset domui eius, cum vocem balantis vir eius audisset, dixit: videte ne sit furtivum: sed reddite eum Domino suo: quia non licet nobis aut de furto aliquid edere aut contingere. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod infideles, inter quos habitabat Thobias, habebant verum dominium rerum. Item Dan. 2. dicit Daniel ad regem infidelem Nabuchodonosor: Tu rex regum es & Dominus cœli regnum, fortitudinem & Imperium & gloriam dedit tibi, & omnia in quibus habitant filii hominum, & bestias agri, volucres cœli dedit in manu tua, & vniversa sub ditione tua constituit. Item 5. cap. sic legitur: Dominus altissimus regnum et magnificentiam gloriam & honorem dedit Nabuchodonosor patri tuo. Ex quibus colligitur, quod Nabuchodonosor habuit verum regnum & Imperium. Non enim dat Deus falsum Imperium & regnum, sed verum. Item Herodes erat infidelis: & tamen erat verus rex Iudæ. Unde de eo dicitur Matth. 2. cap. Cum natus esset IESVS in Bethlehem Iudæ in diebus Herodis regis. Et Luc. 1. dicitur: Fuit in diebus Herodis regis sacerdos quidam nomine Zacharias.
units.tr: Likewise Tobit 2 reads that when Anna, the wife of Tobias, had brought a kid of goats to his house, and her husband heard it bleating, he said: "Take heed that it is not stolen; but give it back to its owner, for it is not lawful for us either to eat or to touch anything stolen." From these words it is gathered that the unbelievers among whom Tobias lived had true lordship of things. Likewise Daniel 2, Daniel says to the unbelieving king Nebuchadnezzar: "You, O king, are king of kings, and the God of heaven has given you a kingdom, strength, empire and glory; and wherever the sons of men dwell, the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven, he has given into your hand, and has set them all under your dominion." Likewise chapter 5: "The Most High God gave to Nebuchadnezzar your father kingdom, majesty, glory and honour." From these things it is gathered that Nebuchadnezzar had a true kingdom and empire. For God does not give a false empire and kingdom, but a true one. Likewise Herod was an unbeliever, and yet he was the true king of Judea. Hence it is said in Matthew 2: "When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of Herod the king," and Luke 1: "There was in the days of Herod the king a certain priest named Zacharias."

units.la: Item Matth. 17. legitur Christum interrogasse Petrum dicens: Quid tibi videtur Simon, reges terræ à quibus accipiunt tributum vel censum, à filiis suis an ab alienis? Et ille dicit, ab alienis. Et dicit illi IESVS, Ergo liberi sunt filii. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod alieni non sunt liberi à tributo, sed filii. Et per consequens alieni de iure debent tributum. Ex quo sequitur, quod reges etiam infideles sunt veri reges, quia de illis loquebatur Christus. Item Luc. 3. sic legitur: venerunt autem publicani, vt baptizarentur, & dixerunt illi, (scilicet Iohanni Baptistæ) Magister quid faciemus? at ille dicit, Nihil amplius, quam quod constitutum est vobis, faciatis. Publicani ergo licite poterant facere ea, quæ constituta erant eis: quæ tamen ab infidelibus fuerunt constituta. Item subiungit: interrogabant autem illum & milites dicentes: Quid faciemus & nos? & ait illis, Neminem concutiatis, neq; calumniam faciatis, & contenti estote stipendiis vestris. Si autem contenti debeant esse stipendiis, quæ à paganis principibus receperunt, ipsi principes verum Dominium illorum, quæ dabant militibus, habuerunt: quia non licet militibus recipere stipendia ab his, qui nihil habent, sed vsurpant solummodo tyrannice aliena.
units.tr: Likewise, in Matthew 17 we read that Christ asked Peter, saying: "What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth take toll or tribute: from their sons or from strangers?" And he said, "From strangers." Jesus said to him, "Then the sons are free." From these words it is gathered that strangers are not free from tribute, but sons are. And consequently strangers owe tribute by right. From this it follows that even unbelieving kings are true kings, since Christ was speaking of them. Likewise, Luke 3 reads thus: "Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him (namely to John the Baptist), 'Master, what shall we do?' He said to them, 'Collect no more than what has been appointed to you.'" Therefore tax collectors could lawfully do what had been appointed for them, and yet these things had been appointed by unbelievers. He goes on: "And soldiers also asked him, saying, 'What shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do violence to no one, and do not accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your wages.'" If soldiers ought to be content with the wages which they received from pagan princes, then the princes themselves had true ownership of the money which they gave to the soldiers, because soldiers may not receive wages from those who have nothing and merely seize other people's goods tyrannically.

units.la: Item Iohan. 19. dicit IESVS Pilato: Non haberes in me potestatem vllam, nisi data esset tibi desuper. Potestas autem, desuper data est legitima, & non vsurpata. Ergo Pilatus habet legitimam potestatem, licet non legitime vteretur ea. Item ad Roman. 13. ait Apostolus: Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit. Non est enim potestas nisi à Deo. Quæ autem sunt à Deo ordinata sunt. Vbi Apostolus de potestatibus infidelium loqui videtur, de illis videlicet, quibus Romani præstiterunt tributa. Dicebat enim Apostolus: Idem enim tributa præstatis. Et post: reddite ergo omnibus debita. Cui tributum, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal.
units.tr: Likewise in John 19 Jesus says to Pilate: "You would have no power over me at all, unless it had been given you from above." But the power given from above is lawful, and not usurped. Therefore Pilate has lawful power, although he did not use it lawfully. Likewise the Apostle says in Romans 13: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power but of God, and the powers that exist are ordained by God." Here the Apostle seems to be speaking of the powers of unbelievers, namely those to whom the Romans paid tribute. For the Apostle said: "For because of this you also pay tribute." And afterwards: "Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom."

units.la: Romani autem non reddebant tributa, nisi Cæsari & subditis eius, qui erant infideles. Ergo infideles etiam habuerunt potestatem ordinatam à Deo: & ita habuerunt veram potestatem temporalem. Item, 1. ad Corinth. 7. ait Apostolus: Unusquisque in qua vocatione vocatus est, in ea permaneat. Servus vocatus es: non sit tibi cura. Ante vocationem ergo ad fidem est aliquis servus: & per consequens aliquis est Dominus eius.
units.tr: The Romans, however, paid tributes only to Caesar and his subjects, who were unbelievers. Therefore unbelievers also held power ordained by God, and so they held true temporal power. Likewise, the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 7: "Let every man abide in the same calling in which he was called. Were you called as a servant? Do not let it trouble you." Therefore, before the call to faith, someone is a servant, and consequently someone is his lord.

units.la: Item ad Timoth. 6. Quicunque sunt sub iugo servi, Dominos suos omni honore dignos arbitrentur, ne nomen Domini & doctrina blasphemetur. Qui autem fideles habent Dominos, non contemnant, quia sunt fratres sed magis serviant quia fideles. Vbi Apostolus inter servos habentes Dominos infideles videtur distinguere, & Dominos fideles, & servos habentes Dominos infideles præcipit honorari. Quod minime facerent, nisi aliqui infideles essent vere Domini.
units.tr: Likewise, to Timothy in chapter 6: "Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, so that the name of the Lord and the doctrine may not be blasphemed. And those who have believing masters, let them not despise them, because they are brothers, but rather let them serve them all the more, because they are believers and beloved." Here the Apostle seems to distinguish between servants who have unbelieving masters and those who have believing masters, and he commands that those with unbelieving masters be honoured. He would not do this unless some unbelievers were truly masters.

units.la: Item Beatus Paulus asseruit se esse civem Romanum, sicut patet Actorum 16. & 22. non fuit autem ciuis Romanus, nisi auctoritate & concessione Romanorum: cum etiam tunc non fuisset Romæ. Ergo Romani habuerunt veræ potestatem, qua poterant aliis civilitatem Romanæ concedere. Ite vt legitur Actor. 24. Paulus dicit ad Lysiam paganum: Ex multis annis esse te iudicem genti huic sciens, bono animo pro me satis faciam. Vbi Paulus paganum verum iudicem recognouit. Item, vt legitur Actorum 25. Cæsarem verum iudicem reputauit, cum appellauit ad ipsam, dicens: Ad tribunal Cæsaris sto. Vbi oportet me iudicari. Et post: Cæsarem appello. Item beatus Petrus epistola 1. cap. 2. Subiecti estote omni creaturæ propter Deum, siue regi tanquam præcellenti, siue ducibus tanquam ab eo missis. Tunc autem nulli Christiani erant reges & Duces. Et ita beatus Petrus regibus & Ducibus infidelibus Christianos voluit esse subiectos. Item ibidem subdit: Serui subditi estote omni timore domino, non tantum bonis & modestis, sed etiam discolis. In quibus verbis innuit, quod etiam discoli possunt esse veri Domini, & quod est eis obediendum.
units.tr: Likewise, the blessed Paul asserted that he was a Roman citizen, as is clear from Acts 16 and 22. But he would not have been a Roman citizen except by the authority and grant of the Romans, although at that time he was not even in Rome. Therefore the Romans had true power by which they could grant Roman citizenship to others. Again, as is read in Acts 24, Paul says to Lysias the pagan: "Knowing that you have been a judge to this nation for many years, I will answer for myself with a good heart." Here Paul acknowledged a pagan as a true judge. Likewise, as is read in Acts 25, he regarded Caesar as a true judge when he appealed to him, saying: "I stand at Caesar's tribunal; there I ought to be judged." And afterwards: "I appeal to Caesar." Likewise the blessed Peter, 1 Peter chapter 2: "Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him." At that time there were no Christian kings or governors. Thus the blessed Peter wanted Christians to be subject to unbelieving kings and governors. Likewise he adds in the same place: "Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward." In these words he implies that even froward masters can be true masters, and that they are to be obeyed.

units.la: Hoc etiam quamplurimis sanctorum testimoniis, vt quibusdam apparet, posset ostendi: sed adducam pauca. Vnde Ambrosius ait, vt habetur in decretis 13. q. 1. c. Iulianus Imperator, quamuis esset apostata, habuit tamen sub se Christianos milites, quibus cum dicebat: producite aciem pro defensione rei publicæ obediebant ei. Et Augustinus de eisdem ait de eodem: Iulianus extitit infidelis Imperator, nonne extitit apostata & iniquus idolatra? vbi veniebatur ad causam Christi, non agnoscebant, nisi illum, qui in cœlo erat. Quando volebat, vt idola colerent, vt thurificarent, præponebant Deum. Quando autem dicebat: producite aciem, ite contra gentem illam: statim obtemperabant, Dominum æternum cum Domino temporali recognoscentes. Iulianus ergo quamuis Apostata fuerit, verus Dominus & verus Imperator erat. Discip. Istud videtur nimis absurdum, quod videlicet apostata hæreticus fuerit verus Imperator & verus Dominus in temporalibus: cum hæretici nullam rem temporalem de iure possideant, vt colligitur manifeste ex sacris canonibus, dist. 8. cap. iure & extra de hæreticis, excommunicamus & 23. q. 7. per totum. Iulianus ergo non fuit verus Imperator, nec verus Dominus rerum temporalium. Quod Glossa super prælegatum c. Ambrosii insinuare videtur, dicens. Adhuc Iulianus tolerabatur ab ecclesia, ne suscitaret scandalum aduersus Christianos. Ergo Iulianus, quamuis toleraretur aduersus Christianos ab ecclesia, non fuit verus Imperator: & quod plus est, nullam habuit dignitatem secularem. Magist. Respondetur; quod non est de iure diuino, quod hæretici nihil proprium habeant: sed de iure humano priuarentur dominio rerum temporalium, habebant verum dominium rerum temporalium. Et ideo quia tempore Iuliani, apostatæ & hæretici non fuerunt priuati temporalibus, Iulianus fuit verus Imperator & verus Dominus rerum temporalium. Postea autem per humana iura Imperatores & Papæ hæretici fuerunt priuati Dominio rerum temporalium. Et ideo extunc non fuerunt veri Domini temporalium rerum. Et pro illo tempore loquitur canon, non tamen pro tempore quo fuit Iulianus. Ad Glossam autem adducam dupliciter respondetur. Vno modo, quod Iulianus tolerabatur verus Imperator ab ecclesia, & non habens Imperium verum, sed solum vsurpatum. Aliter dicitur, quod Glossator ibi non habuit memoriam rerum gestarum tempore Iuliani. Quia Iulianus (vt legitur in diuersis scripturis autenticis) suscitauit scandalum, quod potuit aduersus Christianos: Sed ecclesia tolerauit eum, qui non potuit eum de facto priuare Imperio. Et si per sententiam priuasset, iam primo non profuisset, sed nocuisset ecclesiæ. Discip. Aliqua dicta maiorum pro eadem assertione adducas. Magist. Hoc ex legenda sancti Mauritii & sociorum eius colligitur; in qua leguntur sic dixisse milites: Summe Imperator, tui: sed tamen serui, quem libere confitemur, Dei. Tibi debemus militiam, sed illi innocentiam. Et ille Imperator, scil. Maximianus, extitit infidelis. Item Paulus & Iohannes, vt legitur in Legenda eorum, dixerunt Iuliano apostatæ: Non faciemus tibi hanc iniuriam, vt præponamus tibi qualemcunque personam (scil. secularem) Dominum tibi præponimus qui fecit cælum & terram. Ergo isti sancti Iulianum apostatam reputauerunt verum Imperatorem.
units.tr: This could also be shown, as it appears to some, by very many testimonies of the saints, but I will cite a few. Thus Ambrose says, as is found in Decretum 13 q. 1 c. "Julian the Emperor, although he was an apostate, nevertheless had Christian soldiers under him, and when he said to them, 'Lead forth the line for the defence of the commonwealth,' they obeyed him." And Augustine says of the same man: "Julian was an unbelieving emperor; was he not an apostate and a wicked idolater? When the cause of Christ was at stake, they acknowledged no one but him who was in heaven. When he wanted them to worship idols, to burn incense, they put God first. But when he said, 'Lead forth the line, go against that nation,' they at once obeyed, recognising the eternal Lord along with the temporal lord." Therefore Julian, although he was an apostate, was a true lord and a true emperor. Disciple. This seems quite absurd: that an apostate heretic should be a true emperor and a true lord in temporal affairs, since heretics by right possess no temporal property at all, as is clearly gathered from the sacred canons, dist. 8 cap. "Iure", and in the extra on heretics, "Excommunicamus", and 23 q. 7 throughout. Julian therefore was not a true emperor nor a true lord of temporal things. The Gloss on the aforementioned chapter of Ambrose seems to hint at this, saying: "Julian was still tolerated by the Church, lest he stir up scandal against the Christians." Therefore Julian, although he was tolerated by the Church against the Christians, was not a true emperor, and, what is more, he had no secular dignity at all. Master. The answer is this: it is not by divine right that heretics have nothing of their own; by human law they would be deprived of lordship over temporal things, but they had true lordship over temporal things. Therefore, because in Julian's time apostates and heretics had not been deprived of temporal goods, Julian was a true emperor and a true lord of temporal things. Later, however, by human laws, emperors and popes who were heretics were deprived of lordship over temporal things, and therefore from then on they were not true lords of temporal things. The canon speaks of that time, not of the time of Julian. As for the Gloss, it may be answered in two ways. In one way, Julian was tolerated by the Church as a true emperor, though he did not have true empire but only usurped it. In another way, it is said that the glossator there did not have in mind the events of Julian's time. For Julian (as is read in various authentic writings) stirred up what scandal he could against the Christians, but the Church tolerated him, since it could not deprive him of the empire in fact; and even if it had deprived him by sentence, that would have done no good at the outset but would have harmed the Church. Disciple. You should cite some sayings of the elders in support of this assertion. Master. This is gathered from the legend of St Maurice and his companions, in which the soldiers are read to have said: "Highest Emperor, we are yours; but we are servants of God, whom we freely confess. We owe military service to you, but innocence to him." And that emperor, namely Maximian, was an unbeliever. Likewise Paul and John, as is read in their legend, said to Julian the apostate: "We will not do you this wrong, to set before you any kind of secular person as your lord; we set before you the Lord who made heaven and earth." Therefore these saints regarded Julian the apostate as a true emperor.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: Vbi probatur opinio prima supr. cap. 18. recitata; scilicet quod Imperium Romanum est institutum à Deo.
units.tr: Where the first opinion, recited above in chapter 18, is proved: namely, that the Roman Empire was instituted by God.

units.la: Discipulus. Quamuis illa opinio, quæ ponit, quod Imperium est à Papa, esset amplius discutienda, & specialiter quo ad hoc, quod ponit, quod Imperium est à Papa: quia tamen de hoc, quod ponit, quod Imperium est à Papa: quia tamen de hoc & de aliis, quæ illa opinio includit, erit aliquando occasio loquendi, quando tractabimus alias opiniones. Ideo breuiter videamus de opinione illa, quæ ponit, quod Imperium Romanum est institutum ab hominibus: pro qua allegare conatur. Magist. Pro ista opinione adducitur auctoritas Iohannis Papæ, qui vt habetur in decretis distinct. 96. cap. si Imperator, ait: habet (scilicet Imperator) priuilegia potestatis sua, quæ pro administrandis legibus publicis diuinitus consecutus est. Vbi dicit Glossa super verbo diuinitus: non est igitur à Papa. Nam Imperium à solo Deo est. Vt 25. quæst. 4. quaesitum. Item eodem cap. Iohan. Papa loquens de Imperatore ait: Neque contra eum (scilicet Deum) tendat, à quo omnia constituta sunt, & contra illum beneficia pugnare videtur, à quo proprium consecutus est potestatem. Item beatus Cyprianus, vt habetur dist. 10. Quoniam idem, & Nicolaus Papa, vt legitur distinct. 96. cap. cum ad verum, eandem sub eisdem verbis sententiam dicentes: Idem mediator Dei & hominum homo actibus propriis & dignitate distinctis officia potestatis utrumque discrevit. Et dicit Glossa: imo videtur contra: quia non discrevit, sed confudit. [...] ipse vnius & idem vtrumque officium gessit per se, vt notaret, quod de eodem fonte processerant. Nam dicit lex, quod summa a Deo nobis dona data sunt, scilicet sacerdotium & Imperium, in autem. Quomodo oportet episcopos, in principio, colla. 1. Item Innoc. Papa, vt habetur 23. q. 4. 6. quaesitum, loquens de potestatibus secularibus ait: Meminerant enim (maiores scilicet) a Deo potestates has sibi concessas, & propter vindictam noxiorum gladium fuisse permissum, & Dei ministerio esse datum in huiusmodi vindices. Quomodo ergo reprehenditur factum, q auctore Domino videtur esse concessum. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod potestates seculares sunt a Deo. Ergo potestas secularis potissime est a Deo. Haec omnia confirmantur per Apostolum dicentem ad Corinth. 13. non est potestas nisi a Deo. Discip. Dic breviter, quomodo illa opinio improbatur. Magist. Improbatur per hoc, quod quia non legitur vbi Deus per ipsam vel per alium constituerit Imperatorem. Ideo ista opinio eadem facilitate contemnitur, sicut probatur. Disc. Quomodo respondetur ad motiva illius opinionis. Magist. Vnico verbo respondetur, quia cum dicitur, quod potestas Imperialis & vniuersaliter omnis potestas licita & legitima est a Deo, non tamen a solo Deo. Sed quaedam est a Deo per homines, & talis est potestas Imperialis, quae est a Deo, sed per homines.
units.tr: Disciple. Although that opinion, which holds that the Empire is from the Pope, ought to be examined more fully, especially on the point that the Empire is from the Pope, still, since this and the other things that opinion involves will sometimes give occasion for discussion when we treat other opinions, let us briefly consider that opinion which holds that the Roman Empire was instituted by men, and for which it tries to argue. Teacher. For this opinion appeal is made to the authority of Pope John, who, as found in the Decretum, distinction 96, chapter "si Imperator," says: "The Emperor has the privileges of his power, which he obtained from God for administering the public laws." Where the Gloss on the word "from God" says: "It is therefore not from the Pope, for the Empire is from God alone, as in 25 q. 4, quaesitum." Likewise in the same chapter Pope John, speaking of the Emperor, says: "Let him not strive against him (namely God) from whom all things have been established, and it seems to fight against those benefits from whom he obtained his own power." Likewise the blessed Cyprian, as found in distinction 10, "Quoniam idem," and Pope Nicholas, as read in distinction 96, chapter "cum ad verum," saying the same opinion in the same words: "The same mediator between God and men, a man, by his own actions and distinct dignity, separated the offices of power into two." And the Gloss says: "Indeed it seems to the contrary, because he did not separate but confused them." [...] He himself performed one and the same of each office by himself, to show that they had proceeded from the same fountain. For the law says that the highest gifts were given to us by God, namely the priesthood and the Empire, in the Authentic, "Quomodo oportet episcopos," in the beginning, collatio 1. Likewise Pope Innocent, as found in 23 q. 4, "quaesitum," speaking of secular powers, says: "For the elders (namely the ancestors) remembered that these powers were conceded to them by God, and that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of wrongdoers and given as a ministry of God to such avengers. Why, then, is the deed reproved which seems to have been granted with the Lord as its author?" From these words it is gathered that secular powers are from God. Therefore secular power is especially from God. All these things are confirmed by the Apostle saying, "ad Corinth. 13": "There is no power except from God." Disciple. Tell me briefly how that opinion is refuted. Teacher. It is refuted by the fact that nowhere is it read that God, either through the Empire itself or through another, appointed an Emperor. Therefore this opinion is set aside with the same ease with which it is proved. Disciple. How is the arguments for that opinion answered? Teacher. It is answered in one word: when it is said that imperial power, and universally every lawful and legitimate power, is from God, it is not from God alone. Rather, some power is from God through men, and such is imperial power, which is from God, but through men.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: In quo probatur secunda opinio supra cap. 18. recitata, & hoc rationibus & auctoritatibus sacrae scripturae.
units.tr: In which the second opinion, recited above in chapter 18, is proved by reasons and by the authority of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunc opinionem, scilicet tertiam, tactam supra cap. 18. tractemus. Magist. Illa opinio tenet, quod Romanum Imperium fuit primo institutum a Deo, & tamen per homines scilicet per Romanos. Et hoc restari videtur Glossa dist. 17. quae ait: Habet Romana ecclesia auctoritatem a Deo, sed Imperator a populo. Vtcunque legimus. Hinc etiam Glossa dist. 2. lex est constitutio populi, ait: Olim populus constituit leges, sed hodie transtulit hanc potestatem in Imperatorem. Ab illo autem est Imperium, qui Imperatori contulit potestatem condendi leges. Ergo a populo est Imperium. Item, ab illis fuit Imperium Romanum, qui caeteras nationes Romano Imperio subdiderunt & qui dominium gentium subiugatarum, cui volebant, commiserunt, & modum dominandi acregendi obedientes Romanis prout & quando eis visum fuit, incitaverunt. Sed hoc fecerunt Romani de gentibus subiugatis ab eis. Habetur enim 1. Macha. 8. vbi sic legitur: Et audivit Iudas nomen Romanorum, quia sunt potentes viribus. Et post. Et audierunt praelia eorum & virtutes bonas, quas faciunt in Galatia: quia obtinuerunt eos, & duxerunt sub tributum, & quanta fecerunt in regione Hispania. Quod autem dominium subiugatorum & obedientium eis, cum volebant, commiserunt, insinuatur ibidem, cum dicitur: in omnibus istis neque portabat diadema, nec induebatur purpura, vt magnificaretur in ea. Et post. Et committunt vni homini magistratum. Et infra: sinunt per singulos annos dominari vniversa terrae suae: & omnes obediunt vni, & non est invidia neque zelus inter eos. De mutatione autem modi dominandi & regendi obedientes habetur in scripturis fide dignis. Aliquando enim habuerunt reges, aliquando consules, aliquando vnum qui mutabatur singulis annis. Vltimo autem Imperatorem elegerunt, qui absque mutatione omnibus imperaret. Ergo a Romanis fuit Romanum Imperium institutum. Discip. Non videtur, quod a populo Romano fuerit Imperium verum, sed solummodo vsurpatum. Nam Romani alios oppresserunt. Magist. Ad hoc dupliciter respondetur. Primo, quod Romani cernebant, quod necessarium fuit pro vtilitate communi totius mundi vnum Imperatorem vniversis mortalibus dominari. Ideo qui contradixerunt vnitati Imperii, tanquam impedientes boni communis, potestas ordinandi de Imperio ad Romanos, & ad alios in hoc eis consentientes exitit devoluta. Et ex tunc poterant Romani licite contradicentes & rebelles suo Imperio subiugare. Aliter dicitur, licet Romani primo & per multa tempora post iniuste compulerunt alios sibi subesse: tamen postquam alii coeperunt consentire dominio Romanorum, Romani super ipsos verum Imperium acceperunt. Ideo postquam totus orbis sponte consensit in dominium & Imperium Romanorum, idem Imperium fuit verum Imperium, iustum & bonum.
units.tr: Student. Let us now take up the third opinion, touched on above in chapter 18. Master. That opinion holds that the Roman Empire was first instituted by God, yet through men, namely through the Romans. The Gloss on dist. 17 seems to support this, saying: "The Roman Church has its authority from God, but the Emperor has his from the people." However that may be, we read in the Gloss on dist. 2, "Law is the constitution of the people," the statement: "Formerly the people made laws, but today it has transferred this power to the Emperor." But the Empire comes from him who gave the Emperor the power of making laws. Therefore the Empire comes from the people. Again, the Roman Empire came from those who subjected the other nations to the Roman Empire, who entrusted the lordship over the conquered peoples to whomever they wished, and who prescribed the manner of ruling over the obedient Romans as and when it seemed good to them. But the Romans did this to the peoples they had subjected. For we have in 1 Macc. 8, where it is read as follows: "And Judas heard the name of the Romans, that they were mighty in strength." And afterwards: "And they heard of their battles and of the good valour which they showed in Galatia, because they had overcome them and brought them under tribute; and of what they did in the country of Spain." That they entrusted the lordship to whomever they wished among those subjected and obedient to them is indicated in the same place, where it says: "In all these matters he did not wear a diadem, nor was he clothed in purple, so as to be magnified by it." And after: "And they commit the magistracy to one man." And below: "They allow each one to rule the whole of their land for one year, and all obey one man, and there is neither envy nor rivalry among them." Concerning the change in the manner of ruling and governing the obedient, we have it in trustworthy writings: at one time they had kings, at another consuls, and at another a single man who was changed every year. Finally they chose an Emperor, who ruled over all without change. Therefore the Roman Empire was instituted by the Romans. Student. It does not seem that the Roman Empire was a true empire of the Roman people, but only usurped. For the Romans oppressed others. Master. To this there is a twofold answer. First, the Romans saw that it was necessary, for the common good of the whole world, that one Emperor should rule over all mortals. Therefore the power of ordering the Empire passed to the Romans, and to others who agreed with them in this, against those who opposed the unity of the Empire as hindering the common good. And from then on the Romans could lawfully subject to their Empire those who opposed and rebelled. The other answer is this: although the Romans at first, and for many ages afterwards, unjustly compelled others to be subject to them, nevertheless, after others began to consent to the lordship of the Romans, the Romans received a true Empire over them. Therefore, since the whole world freely consented to the lordship and Empire of the Romans, that same Empire was a true, just and good Empire.

units.la: Discip. Nunquid ad hoc, quod Imperium Romanum super totum mundum esset verum Imperium, oportuit quod totus mundus consentiret Imperio Romanorum? Magist. Respondetur, quod teste Glossa extra de constitutionibus, cum omnes, quoniam aliqui plures vnum sunt collegium, quantum ad illa quae sunt ex necessitate facienda, sufficit quod a maiori parte fiant. Omnes autem mortales sunt vnum corpus & vnum collegium: ita necesse fuit tempore, quo Romani coeperunt dominari cunctis mortalibus. Ergo tunc temporis maior pars mundi etiam aliis contradicentibus potuit Imperatorem praficere toti mundo, nec requirebatur consensus omnium. Etiam quando reges & principes praficiebantur, non fuit necesse, quod omnes consentirent: sicut etiam si aliqua patria esset invasa ab hostibus, posset maior pars etiam contradicentibus quibusdam facere sibi vnum caput pro patriae defensione.
units.tr: Student. Was it necessary, for the Roman Empire to be a true empire over the whole world, that the whole world should consent to the Empire of the Romans? Master. It is answered that, as the Gloss on the Extra, de constitutionibus, witnesses: "What all do, since some several persons make up one college, is sufficient to be done by the greater part, as far as those things are concerned which must be done of necessity." But all mortals are one body and one college. So it was necessary at the time when the Romans began to rule over all mortals. Therefore at that time the greater part of the world, even though others opposed it, could set an Emperor over the whole world, and the consent of all was not required. Likewise, when kings and princes were set over peoples, it was not necessary that all should consent; just as, if some country were invaded by enemies, the greater part, even against the wishes of some, could make for itself one head for the defence of the fatherland.

units.la: Discip. Videtur secundum ista, quod Romani iuste & absq; peccato subiugaverunt vniversum orbem, quod tamen non videtur: cum beatus Augustinus reprehendat in eis libidinem dominandi. Magist. Respondetur, quod si Romani ordinando de Imperio ex solo amore boni communis & rei publicae moti fuissent, & non ex libidine dominandi, aut vanam gloriam non intenti. intendissent, nec aliquam intentionem corruptam habuissent, in hoc absq; peccato fuissent, & forte aliqui eorum in acquirendo Imperium vel consentiendo acquisitioni Imperii minime peccauerunt. Si autem intendebant bonum proprium, vt dominarentur aliis, vel augerent diuitias, peccauerunt. Hæc beatus August. vt habetur in decretis 23. q. 1. cap. militare, ait: Militare non est delictum, sed propter predam militare est peccatum, nec rem publicam gerere criminosum est: sed ideo agere rempublicam, vt diuitias augeas, videtur esse damnabile. Ergo à simili laborare ad subiugandum vni principi, non est peccatum: sed hoc facere propter vanam gloriam, vel ad incutiendum timorem aliis, vel ex libidine dominandi, videtur damnabile reputandum. Discip. Numquid si Romani in acquirendo Romanum Imperium habuerunt intentionem corruptam, ita vt peccarent damnabiliter, fuit Imperium taliter acquisitum, vsurpatum, illicitum & non verum Ergo videtur, quod non erat verum Imperium, si fuit taliter acquisitum ex intentione corrupta: quia nulla res temporalis acquisita illicite & iniuste transit in verum dominium acquirentis. Quod August. videtur asserere, vt habetur 23. q. 7. 6. 1. vbi ait, quod iure diuino cuncta iustorum sunt, & nullo iure impii habent illa, qua sunt aliorum, scil. iustorum. Magist. Respondetur, quod non obstante corrupta intentione Romanorum Imperium acquisitum de consensu populorum fuit verum Imperium: quia corrupta intentio non impedit acquisitionem veri Dominii. Qui enim emit rem aliquam mala intentione, non propter hoc non acquirit verum Dominium rei emptæ. Et qui mala intentione recipit rem à donatore, qui eam donare potest, recipit etiam verum dominium rei donatæ & illa mala intentio nec in transferente rem aliquam temporalem, nec in recipiente translationem impedit acceptionem veri dominii. De auctoritate autem August. dicunt aliqui, quod quidam male intelligant eam. Non enim intendit August. quod in iure diuino cuncta sunt iustorum quo ad verum dominium: quia tunc nullus peccatorum haberet verum dominium alicuius rei temporalis. Et ideo quandocunq; aliquis rex vel aliquis Dominus princeps, vel alius Dominus peccaret mortaliter, verum dominium omnium rerum suarum transiret in iustos, & non remaneret penes aliquem peccatorem. Vult igitur August. quod iure diuino cuncta sunt iustorum quo ad dignitatem meriti. Hoc est, soli iusti sunt digni vero Dominio temporali, & nullus peccator est dignus quacunque re temporali. Unde indigne possidet. Discip. Adhuc videtur, quod Romanum Imperium, antequam illud resignaret Constantinus, non fuit verum Imperium: quia foris omnia ædificantes gehennam, dicente Apostolo ad Romanos 14. Omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est. Igitur extra ecclesiam nulla est à Deo ordinata potestas. Item, Constantinus non resignasset Imperium, nisi aduertisset, quod non habuit vetu Imperium. Igitur antea Romanum Imperium non fuit verum Imperium. Mag. Respondetur, quod non est vniuersaliter absq; omni exceptione verum, quod omnia quæ foris sunt ædificant ad gehennam. Non enim infideles peccant mortaliter in omni actu. Obstetrices enim, de quibus legitur Exod. 1. non peccauerunt mortaliter vel venialiter in mentiendo. Multi autem alii infideles in multis actibus suis non peccant mortaliter. Quod autem dicit Apostolus, quod non est ex fide &c. Dicitur Apostolum intelligere, quod illud, quod fit extra conscientiam, est peccatum, siue fiat à fidelibus siue ab infidelibus. Cum autem dicitur, quod Constantinus rex resignauit Imperium, dicunt in scripturis antiquis hoc minime inueniri. Sed quædam scripturæ insinuant, quod Constantinus dederit Apostolicæ sedi Imperialem honorem. Nam, vt legitur in decretis dist. 96. Constantinus, in gestis beati Siluestri sic loquitur: Constantinus Imperator quarta die sui baptismi priuilegium Romanæ ecclesiæ pontifici contulit, vt in toto orbe terrarum pontifices vel sacerdotes ita hunc habeant caput, sicut iudices regem. In quo priuilegio ita inter cætera legitur: vtile iudicantes vna cum omnibus satrapis nostris, & vniuerso senatu, optimatibus, & cuncto populo, Imperio Romanæ ecclesiæ subiacenti, vt sicut beatus Petrus in terris Vicarius Filii Dei videtur esse constitutus: ita & pontifices ipsius principis Apostolorum in terris principatum potestatem amplius quam terrenæ Imperialis nostræ serenitatis mansuetudo habere videtur, concessam à nobis nostroq; Imperio obtineant eligentes nobis ipsum principem Apostolorum vel eius vicarios firmos apud Deum esse patronos. Et sicut nostra est terrena Imperialis potentia, ita eius sanctam Romanam ecclesiam decreuimus & veneranter honorare & amplius quam nostrum Imperium terrenum thronum sedem sacrosanctissimam beati Petri gloriose exaltari, tribuentes ei potestatem & gloriam dignitatem & vigorem & honorificentiam Imperialem, atq; decernentes sancimus, vt principatum teneat tam supra quatuor sedes Alexandrinam, Antiochenam, Hierosolymitanam, Constantinopolitanam: quam etiam super omnes in vniuerso orbe terrarum ecclesias Dei. Et pontifex, qui per tempora sacrosanctæ Romanæ ecclesiæ exti- rit celsior, & princeps cunctis sacerdotibus & totius mundi existat: & eius iudicio, quæ ad cultum Dei vel fidem Christianorum vel stabilitatem procuranda fuerint, disponantur. Et infra: Ecclesiis beatorum Apostolorum Petri & Pauli pro continuatione luminarium possessionum prædia contulimus. Et infra: Ecce tam palatium nostrum, quam Romanam vrbem & omnes Italiæ siue Occidentalium regionum prouincias, loca, ciuitates, beatissimo pontifici & vniuersali Papa Siluestro concedimus atque relinquimus, & ab eo & successoribus eius per pragmaticam constitutum decreuimus disponenda, atq; iure sanctæ Romanæ ecclesiæ concedimus permanenda. Ex his verbis colligitur, quod Constantinus non assignauit Papæ Imperium, tanquam non habens potestatem legitimam recipiendi Imperium, & quod antea non habuisset verum Imperium, sed ex denotione & Imperiali munificentia concessit ei ea, de quibus in prædictis verbis & ab aliis ibidem, vt scil. de omnibus temporalibus, de quibus mentio fit, Papa Siluester nihil habuit, nisi ex dono Constantini, non ex resignatione alicuius prius iniuste detenti: nec vnquam Constantinus fatebatur, quod ante baptismum non habuerit verum Imperium.
units.tr: Student. According to this, it seems that the Romans subjected the whole world justly and without sin, which nevertheless does not seem so, since blessed Augustine rebukes in them the lust of ruling. Master. It is answered that if the Romans, in ordering the Empire, had been moved solely by love of the common good and of the commonwealth, and not by lust of ruling, nor aiming at empty glory, and had had no corrupt intention whatever, they would have been without sin in this; and perhaps some of them sinned not at all in acquiring the Empire or in consenting to its acquisition. But if they aimed at their own good, to rule over others or to increase their riches, they sinned. Blessed Augustine says this, as is found in Decretum 23, q. 1, cap. Militare: "Soldiering is not a crime, but to soldier for the sake of plunder is a sin; nor is it criminal to conduct public affairs, but to conduct public affairs in order to increase one's riches seems to be damnable." Therefore, by like reasoning, to labour to subject the world to one prince is not a sin; but to do this for empty glory, or to strike fear into others, or out of lust of ruling, seems to be reckoned damnable. Student. If the Romans, in acquiring the Roman Empire, had a corrupt intention, so that they sinned damnably, was the Empire so acquired usurped, unlawful and not true? Therefore it seems that it was not a true Empire, if it was acquired with a corrupt intention; for no temporal thing acquired unlawfully and unjustly passes into the true lordship of the acquirer. This Augustine seems to assert, as is found in 23, q. 7, c. 6, where he says that "by divine right all things belong to the just, and the wicked have by no right those things which belong to others," namely to the just. Master. It is answered that, notwithstanding the corrupt intention of the Romans, the Empire acquired with the consent of the peoples was a true Empire, because a corrupt intention does not prevent the acquisition of true lordship. For he who buys a thing with a bad intention does not for that reason fail to acquire true ownership of the thing bought; and he who receives a thing from a giver who can give it, with a bad intention, also receives true ownership of the thing given; and that bad intention, whether in the one transferring some temporal thing or in the one receiving the transfer, does not prevent the acceptance of true lordship. As for the authority of Augustine, some say that certain people misunderstand it. For Augustine did not mean that by divine right all things belong to the just as regards true lordship; for then no sinner would have true lordship over any temporal thing. And so whenever any king or lord, prince or other lord sinned mortally, the true lordship of all his things would pass to the just, and would not remain with any sinner. Augustine therefore means that by divine right all things belong to the just as regards the worthiness of merit; that is, only the just are worthy of true temporal lordship, and no sinner is worthy of any temporal thing; hence he possesses it unworthily. Student. It still seems that the Roman Empire, before Constantine resigned it, was not a true Empire, because all who build outside the Church build to hell, as the Apostle says to the Romans 14: "Whatever is not of faith is sin." Therefore outside the Church there is no power ordained by God. Likewise, Constantine would not have resigned the Empire unless he had perceived that he did not have a true Empire. Therefore the Roman Empire before that was not a true Empire. Master. It is answered that it is not universally and without any exception true that all who are outside build to hell. For unbelievers do not sin mortally in every act. The midwives, of whom we read in Exod. 1, did not sin mortally or venially in lying. Many other unbelievers, moreover, do not sin mortally in many of their acts. As for what the Apostle says, "whatever is not of faith," etc., it is said that the Apostle means that whatever is done outside conscience is sin, whether it is done by the faithful or by unbelievers. As for the statement that King Constantine resigned the Empire, they say this is not found at all in the ancient writings. But certain writings suggest that Constantine gave the Apostolic See imperial honour. For, as is read in Decretum dist. 96, Constantinus, in the Acts of blessed Silvester, the Emperor Constantine speaks thus: "On the fourth day after his baptism, the Emperor Constantine conferred a privilege on the Roman Church's pontiff, that the pontiffs or priests throughout the whole world should have him as their head, just as judges have the king." In this privilege, among other things, it is read as follows: "Judging it useful, together with all our satraps, the whole senate, the nobles and the entire people, that the Empire subject to the Roman Church, as blessed Peter has been set up as Vicar of the Son of God on earth, so also the pontiffs of that Prince of the Apostles should hold on earth a principality and power greater than the gentleness of our earthly imperial serenity seems to have, granted by us and by our Empire, choosing for ourselves the Prince of the Apostles, or his vicars, as firm patrons before God. And just as our earthly imperial power is, so we have decided to honour her holy Roman Church, and even more than our earthly Empire, to have the most holy throne and seat of blessed Peter gloriously exalted, granting to her power, glory, dignity, vigour and imperial honour; and we decree and sanction that she shall hold primacy over the four sees of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople, and also over all the churches of God in the whole world. And the pontiff who shall be higher through the times of the holy Roman Church, and shall be prince of all priests and of the whole world, shall have his judgment in matters which concern the worship of God, the faith of Christians, and the securing of stability. And below: To the churches of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul we have given estates for the upkeep of lights. And below: Behold, both our palace and the city of Rome and all the provinces, places and cities of Italy or the western regions we grant and leave to the most blessed pontiff and universal Pope Silvester, and we decree that they shall be disposed of by him and his successors by a pragmatic constitution, and we grant that they shall remain under the right of the holy Roman Church."
