From these words it is gathered that Constantine did not assign the Empire to the Pope as one lacking lawful power to receive the Empire, nor that he had not previously had a true Empire; rather, by devotion and imperial munificence he granted to him those things mentioned in the foregoing words and elsewhere in the same place. So that, as regards all the temporal things mentioned, Pope Silvester had nothing except by the gift of Constantine, not by the resignation of anyone previously held unjustly; nor did Constantine ever confess that before his baptism he had not had a true Empire.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII.

units.la: In quo probatur, quod Imperium non est à Papa.
units.tr: In which it is proved that the Empire is not from the Pope.

units.la: Discipulus. Cum ista opinio teneat, quod verum Imperium sit à populo Romano; & per consequens non fuit à Papa: nunc alias rationes speciales adducas ad probandum, quod Imperium non fuit à Papa. Magist. In Glossa super Decreta & Decretales aliquae rationes adhuc innuuntur. Dicit enim Glossa distinct. 4. c. quoniam idem, quod Imperium non habetur à Papa, & quod Papa non habet utrumq; gladium. Nam exercitus facit Imperatorem, ut dist. 93. legimus. Ex qua sic arguitur. Ab illo non est Imperium, qui non facit Imperatorem. Sed Imperator non fit à Papa, quia fit ab exercitu. Igitur Imperium non est à Papa. Discip. Per istam rationem Imperium non est à populo, sed ab exercitu. Magist. Respondetur, quod exercitus non facit Imperatorem, nisi auctoritate populi Romani. Hanc enim potestatem propter periculum, quod poterat imminere, ne moriente Imperatore in exercitu exercitus careret capite & Domino, populus Romanus commisit exercitui potestatem eius ad eligendum Imperatorem. Discip. Dic aliam rationem. Magist. Aliam rationem innuit Gloss. extra, qui filii sunt legitimi c. causam, dicens: Prius fuit Imperator quam coronam reciperet à Papa & gladium ab altari. 69. distinct. legimus quod ante fuit Imperator quam Apostolatus. Cum igitur prius non fuit Apostolatus, sequitur quod Imperium non est à Papa. Discip. Istae duae rationes videntur approbare, quod Imperium non fuit primitus à Papa, sed non probant quod modo Imperium non sit à Papa. Potestas enim ordinandi de Imperatore à Papa videtur nunc procedere, licet non fuit à principio penes ipsum: imo ante fuit Imperium, quam Papa. Magist. Dicunt quidam, quod per illas rationes probatur aperte, quod Imperium non est à Papa, inquantum Papa est vicarius Christi & successor beati Petri. Et hoc principaliter intendunt, qui tenent opinionem istam. Discip. Alias rationes adducas. Magist. Aliam rationem innuit Gloss. dist. 10. c. quoniam idem, si ab ipso Papa habetur Imperium, licite appellaretur ad ipsum in temporalibus: quod prohibet Alexander & dicit, quod illa non contingunt iurisdictionem suam extr. qui filii sunt legitimi cap. causam. Ab Imperatore autem contingit appellare ad illum, à quo est Imperium. Discip. Per istam rationem semper potuit fieri appellatio ab Imperatore: quia semper Imperator habuit Imperium ab aliquo. Magist. Concedo, quod in aliquibus casibus semper licuit appellare ab Imperatore: in quibus tamen casibus fuit licitum ab aliis iudicibus appellare. Leges igitur, quae dicunt, quod non est appellandum ab Imperatore, non sunt intelligendae de quibusdam causis singularibus, quae raro vel nunquam accidunt, sed de aliis. Quemadmodum canones sacri, qui dicunt, quod non est appellandum à Papa, nisi de causa haeresis: quia pro haeresi licet appellare à Papa. Discip. Aliam rationem adducas. Magist. Aliam rationem innuit Glossa ubi prius, dicens: Item ecclesia soluerunt tributum Imperatori ut 2. q 2. magnum. Ab illo non est Imperium, qui soluit tributum Imperatori. Ergo Imperium non est à Papa, si Papa soluit tributum Imperatori.
units.tr: Disciple. Since this opinion holds that true Empire is from the Roman people, and consequently was not from the Pope, now bring forward other special reasons for proving that the Empire was not from the Pope. Master. In the Gloss on the Decretum and the Decretals some further reasons are hinted at. For the Gloss says, Distinction 4, chapter "Quoniam idem", that the Empire is not held from the Pope, and that the Pope does not possess both swords. For the army makes the Emperor, as we read in Distinction 93. From this it is argued thus: from him from whom the Empire comes is not the one who makes the Emperor. But the Emperor is not made by the Pope, because he is made by the army. Therefore the Empire is not from the Pope. Disciple. By this reason the Empire is not from the people, but from the army. Master. It is answered that the army makes the Emperor only by the authority of the Roman people. For the Roman people, because of the danger that could threaten, lest on the death of the Emperor the army be left without a head and lord, committed to the army the power of choosing its Emperor. Disciple. Give another reason. Master. The Gloss hints at another reason, Extra, "Qui filii sunt legitimi", chapter "Causam", saying: "The Emperor existed before he received the crown from the Pope and the sword from the altar." In Distinction 69 we read that there was an Emperor before there was an Apostolate. Since therefore the Apostolate did not exist first, it follows that the Empire is not from the Pope. Disciple. These two reasons seem to show that the Empire did not originally come from the Pope, but they do not prove that the Empire is not now from the Pope. For the power of ordaining the Emperor by the Pope seems now to operate, although it was not in his hands at the beginning; indeed the Empire existed before the Pope. Master. Some say that by those reasons it is clearly proved that the Empire is not from the Pope, insofar as the Pope is the vicar of Christ and successor of blessed Peter. And this is chiefly what those who hold this opinion intend. Disciple. Bring forward other reasons. Master. The Gloss hints at another reason, Distinction 10, chapter "Quoniam idem": if the Empire were held from the Pope himself, an appeal could lawfully be made to him in temporal matters; which Alexander forbids, saying that those matters do not touch his jurisdiction, Extra, "Qui filii sunt legitimi", chapter "Causam". But an appeal from the Emperor is made to him from whom the Empire comes. Disciple. By this reason an appeal could always have been made from the Emperor, because the Emperor always had the Empire from someone. Master. I grant that in some cases an appeal from the Emperor was always allowed; yet in those cases it was lawful to appeal from other judges. Therefore the laws which say that one must not appeal from the Emperor are not to be understood of certain singular cases, which seldom or never occur, but of others. In the same way the sacred canons, which say that one must not appeal from the Pope except in a case of heresy, because for heresy it is lawful to appeal from the Pope. Disciple. Bring forward another reason. Master. The Gloss, in the place already cited, hints at another reason, saying: "Likewise the churches paid tribute to the Emperor, as in 2, q. 2, Magnum." From him who pays tribute to the Emperor the Empire does not come. Therefore the Empire is not from the Pope, if the Pope pays tribute to the Emperor.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: In quo inquiritur, utrum Romanum Imperium possit transferri: quod sic, probatur tribus exemplis. Et nota ibidem, quis & qualiter possit transferre.
units.tr: In which it is asked whether the Roman Empire can be transferred. That it can is proved by three examples. Note also who can transfer it, and how.

units.la: Discipulus. Adhuc circa originem Romani Imperii plura restarent tractanda, de quibus forte post hac occasio loquendi occurret. Ideo ad praesens illis omissis inuestigemus, an Romanum Imperium licite cassari, minui vel dividi valeat vel transferri. Inquiramus itaque primo, an Romanum Imperium possit transferri. Magist. Quod Romanum Imperium possit transferri, tribus exemplis probatur. Primum exemplum est, quod translatum fuit de Romanis in Graecos 69. dist. Constantinus. Secundum exemplum est, quod translatum fuit de Graecis in Romanos in personam Caroli magni extr. de electione venerabilem. Tertium exemplum est, quod fuit translatum de Francigenis in Teutonicos. Unde Glossa 63. distinct. ego Ludovicus, ait super verbo Francorum: nota, Imperium Francorum primum fuisse: sed postea Theutonici virtutibus Imperium promeruerunt. Discip. Dubitandum non videtur mihi, quin Romanum Imperium transferri possit de gente in gentem. Sed qualiter aliquis valeat transferre, videtur magnum dubium multis. Dic ergo secundum opinionem aliquorum, qualiter possit transferri Imperium. Mag. Imperium Romanum multipliciter potest intelligi. Uno modo, ut sic transferatur Imperium à Romanis, ut non sit plus Romanum Imperium, ac si Romani nullum ius habeant speciale in Imperio plusquam caeterae nationes. Alio modo potest transferri Imperium, ut tamen remaneat Romanum Imperium, & ut aliquam potestatem vel ius speciale habeant Romani in Imperio plusquam caeterae nationes. Et haec translatio adhuc multipliciter potest intelligi. Uno modo, quod detur Imperium alicui, cuius progenies iure successionis possideat Romanum Imperium. Alio modo, ut statuatur quod de certa natione vel gente Imperator eligatur, puta si ordinaretur quod nullus eligeretur in Imperatorem, nisi Theutonicus. Alio modo, ut alicui personae vel personis detur potestas & intelligendi Imperatorem de quacunq; natione.
units.tr: Disciple. There are still many matters concerning the origin of the Roman Empire to be discussed, and perhaps an occasion to speak of them will arise later. So, setting those aside for now, let us investigate whether the Roman Empire can lawfully be annulled, diminished, divided or transferred. Let us first ask whether the Roman Empire can be transferred. Master. That the Roman Empire can be transferred is proved by three examples. The first example is that it was transferred from the Romans to the Greeks, 69. dist. Constantinus. The second is that it was transferred from the Greeks to the Romans, in the person of Charlemagne, extr. de electione venerabilem. The third is that it was transferred from the Franks to the Teutons. Hence the Gloss, 63. distinct. ego Ludovicus, says on the word Francorum: note that the Empire was first of the Franks, but afterwards the Teutons earned the Empire by their virtues. Disciple. I do not think it can be doubted that the Roman Empire can be transferred from one nation to another. But how one may transfer it seems to many a great difficulty. So tell me, according to the opinion of some, how the Empire can be transferred. Mag. The Roman Empire can be understood in several ways. In one way, the Empire is transferred from the Romans so that it is no longer the Roman Empire, as if the Romans had no special right in the Empire beyond the other nations. In another way the Empire can be transferred while it remains the Roman Empire, and the Romans have some special power or right in the Empire beyond the other nations. And this transfer can again be understood in several ways. In one way, the Empire is given to someone whose descendants hold the Roman Empire by right of succession. In another way, it is established that the Emperor is to be elected from a certain nation or people, for instance if it were ordained that no one could be elected Emperor except a Teuton. In another way, the power of designating the Emperor from any nation is given to some person or persons.

units.la: Discip. Quis habet potestatem transferendi Imperium vno modo vel alio modo? Magist. Respondetur, quod potestas transferendi Imperium vno modo vel alio modo principalissime est apud vniuersitatem mortalium, sicut & apud ipsam principalissime constituendi Imperium. Quare si vniuersitas mortalium vellet, posset Romanum Imperium de quacunq; gente transferre in aliam. Discip. Nunquid posset vniuersitas mortalium (exceptis Romanis) transferre Imperium Romanum a Romanis? Magist. Respondetur, quod sine culpa Romanorum & absq; causa patenti totum residuum mundi non posset transferre ab eis contradicentibus Imperium: quia non debent priuari sine culpa & absq; causa iure suo: tamen pro culpa Romanorum & ex causa rationabili posset residuum mundi ab eis transferre Imperium. Quia, vt legitur distinct. 93. Orbis maior est urbe. Quod non solum est verum de orbe includente vrbem, eo quod totum maius est sua parte: sed continet veritatem de orbe includentem vrbem. Et ita ex causa vel per culpam Romanorum potestas transferendi est penes residuum orbis. Potestas autem transferendi Imperium a Romanis, est penes Romanos secundum vnam sententiam. Quia enim potest vnusquisque cedere iuri suo, & alii concedere, possunt enim Romani cedere iuri suo, quod habent super Imperium: & idem ius in alium vel in alios transferre. Quemadmodum populi Romani potestatem condendi leges & regendi Imperium, transtulerunt in Imperatorem. Verum tamen de modo transferendi Imperium per Romanos sunt diuersæ sententiæ. Vna est, quod Romani non potuerunt nec possunt a se transferre Imperium primo modo: ita videlicet quod nullum ius retineant speciale super Imperium plus quam cæteræ nationes. Sicut enim Imperator non habet legem imponere Imperatori, quia non habet Imperium par in parem: & ita non potest priuare successorem eo iure, quod habet: ita populus Romanus non potest imponere legem populo sequenti: nec potest ipsum priuare omni iure, quod habet super Imperium. Et ita populus Romanus non potest cedere omni iuri, quod habet super Imperium. Alia est sententia, quod populus Romanus potuit cedere omni iuri, quod habuit super Imperium: qui etiam omne ius potuit transferre in alios. Licet enim priuato pacto iuri publico minime derogetur, extra de foro compet. si diligenter tamen pacto consensu totius communitatis, quod tangat alios tanquam per ius publicum eidem iuri publico derogatur, dum modo illud ius publicum non sit ius diuinum, nec ius naturale, sed ius positiuum vel humanum. Quamuis n. clericus aliquis non possit renunciare priuilegio clericali, quod est concessum toti collegio clericorum: tamen collegium clericorum potest priuilegio renunciare. Cum igitur ius, quod habent Romani super Imperium, sit ius humanum positiuum, licet fuerit ius publicum concessum etiam communitati Romanorum, de consensu totius communitatis Romanorum poterit derogari eidem iuri. Et ita de consensu eorum potest idem ius totaliter transferri in alium vel alios.
units.tr: Disciple. Who has the power of transferring the Empire in one way or another? Master. The answer is that the power of transferring the Empire in one way or another lies chiefly with the whole body of mortals, just as the power of establishing the Empire itself lies chiefly with them. Therefore, if the whole body of mortals wished it, it could transfer the Roman Empire from one nation to another. Disciple. Could the whole body of mortals (apart from the Romans) transfer the Roman Empire away from the Romans? Master. The answer is that without fault on the part of the Romans and without a manifest cause, the rest of the world could not transfer the Empire from them against their will, since they ought not to be deprived of their right without fault and without cause. Yet for the fault of the Romans, and for a reasonable cause, the rest of the world could transfer the Empire from them. This is so because, as is read in Dist. 93, The world is greater than the city. This is true not only of the world including the city, because the whole is greater than its part, but it also contains truth about the world that includes the city. Thus, for a cause or through the fault of the Romans, the power of transfer rests with the rest of the world. The power to transfer the Empire from the Romans, according to one opinion, rests with the Romans themselves. For just as each person can give up his right and grant it to another, so the Romans can give up the right they have over the Empire and transfer the same right to another or to others. Just as the people of Rome transferred to the Emperor the power of making laws and governing the Empire. Yet there are differing opinions about the manner in which the Romans may transfer the Empire. One opinion is that the Romans neither could nor can transfer the Empire from themselves in the first way, namely so that they retain no special right over the Empire beyond the other nations. For just as an Emperor has no power to impose a law on an Emperor, since he has no authority equal over an equal, and so cannot deprive his successor of the right he holds, so the Roman people cannot impose a law on the following people, nor can it deprive them of every right it holds over the Empire. And so the Roman people cannot give up every right it holds over the Empire. Another opinion is that the Roman people could give up every right it had over the Empire, and could transfer every right to others. For although public right is in no way derogated by a private pact, extra de foro competenti, si diligenter, yet by a pact with the consent of the whole community, which touches others, the same public right is derogated as if by public law, provided that this public right is not divine law or natural law, but positive or human law. For although a certain cleric cannot renounce the clerical privilege, which is granted to the whole college of clerics, the college of clerics can renounce the privilege. Since, then, the right that the Romans have over the Empire is positive human law, even though it was a public right granted also to the community of the Romans, it can be derogated with the consent of the whole community of the Romans. And so, by their consent, the same right can be wholly transferred to another or to others.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CAP. XXX.

units.la: In quo investigatur, quomodo Romani potuerunt transferre ius Imperii ad Papam.
units.tr: In which it is investigated how the Romans were able to transfer the right of the Empire to the Pope.

units.la: Discipulus. Secundum istam sententiam Romani potuerunt totum ius suum, quod habebant, transferre in Papam super Imperium, & poterat esse Imperium a Papa. Magist. Secundum vnam sententiam Romani non solum potuerunt, sed etiam de facto transtulerunt ius in Papam. Et extunc Imperium fuit a Papa, & tunc Papa habuit vtrumq; gladium, non tamen quo ad executionem, sed quo ad hoc, quod poterat committere cui volebat materialis gladii potestatem. Et per hoc soluitur secundum sententiam illam multorum canonum & glossarum super Decreta & Decretales apparens contrarietas. Discip. Si Romani transtulerunt totum ius in Papam, vel transferre poterant in Papam: igitur transtulerunt vel transferre potuerunt in eum executionem gladii materialis vel gladium materialem quo ad executionem. Magist. Respondetur, quod Romani poterant transferre ius totum ad Papam & potestatem, quam habebat totalis multitudo Romanorum: non tamen transferre poterant totum ius, quod habebat aliqua persona vel alia particularis & specialis multitudo Romanorum. Nam non poterant sibi dare omne ius, quod habebat Imperator Romanus: nec omne ius, quod habebant senatores vel praefectus vrbis. Et ita iura partialia Romanorum, personarum vel congregationum seu collegiorum, aut communitatum particularium, non poterant transferre in papam. Executionem autem gladii non habebat totalis communitas Romanorum: sed habebat eam Imperator, vel aliqua persona alia sub eo, vel aliqua communitas particularis. Et ideo executionem gladii materialis non poterat communitas Romanorum transferre in Papam. Discip. Secundum istam opinionem Papa non habet in temporalibus vel in spiritualibus plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit. Magist. Ista opinio reputat haereticum dicere, quod Papa omnia possit: quia quod omnia possit, non habet a Deo, nec ab homine, nec ab hominibus. Quia a Deo immediate non habet gladium materialem, quo ad executionem; nec quo ad hoc quod possit committere executionem gladii materialis ab homine vel ab hominibus habere potest. Discip. Quod ius igitur transtulerunt Romani vel transferre poterant in Papam super Romanum Imperium? Magist. Respondetur, quod poterant sibi transferre & conferre potestatem ordinandi de promouendo in Imperatorem, vt scilicet ipse eligat Imperatorem, vel aliis committeret potestatem eligendi. Discip. Constat per dicta maiorum, quod Papa in multis se intromittit de Imperatore & Imperio. Et secundum opinionem istam Papa super Imperatorem vel Imperium non habet aliquam potestatem specialem à Deo plusquam super alios reges & regna quæcunque: sed solummodo à Romanis. Quid igitur de facto translulerunt Romani in Papam super Imperium? Magist. Respondetur, quod nemo potest hic dicere, nisi libere & diligenter vidisset Privilegia Papæ vel registra fide digna, vel scripturas autenticas de huiusmodi translatione vel collatione iuris super Imperium facta Papæ: eo quod Romani poterant conferre Papæ pinguius ius vel minus pingue super Imperium. Poterant etiam tale ius dare sedi Apostolicæ vel solummodo personæ Papæ. Poterant etiam dare Papæ pro una vice vel pro pluribus. Discip. Nunquid in hac vita est adhibenda fides soli personæ Papæ, dicentis in ipsum totum ius Romanorum super Imperium esse translatum, licet per scripturas autenticas vel alias probationes hoc nequaquam ostenderet? Magist. Quod assertioni unius quantacunq; fulgeat dignitate nunquam est credendum in præiudicium aliorum; patet 6. q. 2. per totum. Ideo assertioni solius Papæ in præiudicium Romanorum est in hac parte fides minime adhibenda, nisi probationes adhibeat competentes. Discip. Nunquid Papa potest sibi vendicare ius & potestatem disponendi de Imperio propter hoc, quod consuevit se intromittere de Imperio disponendo? Consuetudo autem legitima dat iurisdictionem, & per consequens ius & legitimam potestatem? Magist. Respondetur, quod in his quæ Papa præscripsit legitime contra Romanos, Papa habet ius & potestatem: & in aliis non.
units.tr: Student. According to this opinion, the Romans could have transferred all the right they had over the Empire to the Pope, and the Empire could have been from the Pope. Master. According to one opinion, the Romans not only could have done so but in fact did transfer the right to the Pope. And from then on the Empire was from the Pope, and the Pope then had both swords, not indeed as to the exercise, but in that he could commit the power of the material sword to whomever he wished. And by this, according to that opinion, the apparent contradiction among many canons and glosses on the Decrees and Decretals is resolved. Student. If the Romans transferred the whole right to the Pope, or could transfer it, then they transferred, or could have transferred, to him either the exercise of the material sword or the material sword as to its exercise. Master. The answer is that the Romans could transfer to the Pope the whole right and power which the entire multitude of Romans had; but they could not transfer the whole right which some individual person or other particular and special multitude of Romans had. For they could not give to him all the right which the Roman Emperor had, nor all the right which the senators or the prefect of the city had. Thus the partial rights of the Romans, of persons, of gatherings or colleges, or of particular communities, could not be transferred to the Pope. But the exercise of the sword was not held by the whole community of the Romans; it was held by the Emperor, or by some other person under him, or by some particular community. Therefore the community of the Romans could not transfer the exercise of the material sword to the Pope. Student. According to this opinion, then, the Pope does not have fullness of power in temporal or spiritual matters, so that he can do all things. Master. This opinion holds it heretical to say that the Pope can do all things, because he does not have the power to do all things from God, nor from man, nor from men. For he does not have the material sword as to its exercise immediately from God, nor can he have from man or from men the power to commit the exercise of the material sword.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXI.

units.la: Quæritur utrum Romanum Imperium posset cassari, aut dividi.
units.tr: Whether the Roman Empire could be annulled or divided.

units.la: Discipulus. Investigauimus breuiter, an Romanum Imperium possit transferri: nunc inquiramus, an diuidi, minui, destrui seu cassari possit. Primo igitur videamus, an Romanum Imperium destrui valeat vel cassari. Magist. Respondetur, quod Imperium Romanum pro eo quod est Imperium totius mundi, destrui vel cassari valeat, potest tripliciter intelligi. Uno modo sic, quod simpliciter destruatur ut Imperium quod nunc est Romanorum, nec apud Romanos, nec apud alios de iure remaneat. Alio modo sic, quod Imperium nec remaneat apud Romanos, nec vnquam ex quacunq; causa sit reuersurum ad ipsos. Tertio modo sic, quod Imperium non remaneat apud Romanos, potest ex causa reuerti ad ipsos. Isto modo & secundo magis proprium videtur dici, quod Imperium Romanum esset translatum, quam destructum vel cassatum. Primo modo diceretur proprie Romanum Imperium esse destructum seu cassatum. Discip. Nunquid primo modo posset ipsum Imperium Romanum destrui vel minui? Magist. Respondetur, sicut tactum est supr. cap. 8. quod de iure licite Romanum Imperium minui vel destrui potest: quia sicut antequam esset Romanum Imperium, statui non potuit etiam per vniuersitatem mortalium, quam nunquam aliquis ad totius mundi Imperium assumeretur: ita quod postquam omnes mortales vni Imperio sunt subiecti, etiam omnibus consentientibus statui vel ordinari minime potest; quod Imperium penitus destruatur: quia hoc esset in detrimentum boni communis.
units.tr: Disciple. We have briefly inquired whether the Roman Empire could be transferred; now let us inquire whether it can be divided, diminished, destroyed, or annulled. First, then, let us see whether the Roman Empire can be destroyed or annulled. Master. It may be answered that the Roman Empire, insofar as it is the empire of the whole world, can be destroyed or annulled in three ways. In one way, that it be simply destroyed, so that the empire which is now the Romans' does not remain by right either with the Romans or with others. In another way, that the empire neither remain with the Romans nor ever return to them from any cause. In a third way, that the empire not remain with the Romans but could return to them for some cause. In this third way, and in the second, it seems more properly said that the Roman Empire would have been transferred than destroyed or annulled. In the first way the Roman Empire would properly be said to have been destroyed or annulled. Disciple. Could the Roman Empire itself be destroyed or diminished in the first way? Master. It may be answered, as was touched upon above in chapter 8, that by right the Roman Empire can lawfully be diminished or destroyed. For just as, before there was a Roman Empire, it could not be established even by the whole multitude of mortals, since no one would ever be assumed to the empire of the whole world; so, after all mortals have been made subject to one empire, it cannot be established or ordained, even with everyone consenting, that the empire be utterly destroyed, because this would be to the detriment of the common good.

units.la: Discip. Nunquid potest Romanum Imperium destrui secundo modo? Magist. Una est sententia; quod illo modo destrui potest, ut scilicet ad Romanos nunquam conuertatur. Sed taliter ab eis auferri non potest absq; culpa manifesta Romanorum. Talis enim posset esse culpa eorum, quod possent totaliter priuari Imperio: quia sicut persona quæcunq; in se & in posteris suis, a culpa sua potest priuari omnibus bonis suis temporalibus ac honoribus iuribus & priuilegiis quibuscunq;: ita etiam quæcunq; vniuersitas seu communitas particularis propter culpam suam potest priuari in perpetuum quocunque honore & iure speciali. Alia sententia est, quod communitas Romanorum propter quamcunque culpam non potest in perpetuum priuari quodcunq; iure & honore speciali vel Imperio Romano: quia talis priuatio perpetua posset redundare in detrimentum totius vniuersitatis mortalium. Ergo non est licita reputanda. Discip. Ista ratio non concludit, quod sicut quemcunq; priuare omni iure suo possit redundare in detrimentum boni communis: non sequitur, quod omnis priuatio esset censenda illicita. Magist. Respondetur, quod quemcunque priuari omni iure suo, sic ut antequam sententia executioni mandetur, nullus posset eum reuocare propter quemcunque aduentum, neq; est licitum neq; iustum. Unde quamuis aliquis absolute propter quodcunque crimen damnaretur ad mortem: semper aliquæ conditiones generales subintelliguntur. Quemadmodum in omni iuramento, promisso, voto & pacto aliquæ conditiones generales debent subintelligi. Posset igitur communitas Romanorum absolute propter culpam priuari omni iure speciali & priuilegio, quod habet super Romanum Imperium: & tamen aliquæ conditiones generales debent intelligi. Et ideo quia communitas Romanorum penitus deleri non debet: igitur talis sententia nunquam contra Romanos sic debet ad executionem mandari: quoniam potest ex aliqua causa reuocari. Possunt autem Romani propter culpam vel ex causa sic priuari Imperio, ut nunquam absque noua collatione illius vel illorum, qui potest vel possunt eis conferre Imperium, iuste valeant Imperium adipisci, nisi omnes alii propter culpam iuste Imperium amitterent.
units.tr: Disciple. Could the Roman Empire be destroyed in the second way? Master. There is one opinion: that it can be destroyed in that way, namely so that it never returns to the Romans. But it cannot be taken from them in such a manner without a manifest fault of the Romans. For such a fault could be theirs, that they might be wholly deprived of the empire. For just as any person, in himself and in his posterity, can by his fault be deprived of all his temporal goods, honours, rights and privileges whatsoever, so too any particular community or corporate body, on account of its fault, can be deprived in perpetuity of any special honour and right. The other opinion is that the community of the Romans cannot, on account of any fault whatever, be deprived in perpetuity of any special right or honour or of the Roman Empire, because such perpetual deprivation could redound to the detriment of the whole multitude of mortals. Therefore it is not to be judged lawful. Disciple. That reasoning does not prove that, just as depriving anyone of all his right can redound to the detriment of the common good, it does not follow that every deprivation should be judged unlawful. Master. It may be answered that to deprive anyone of all his right in such a way that, before the sentence is carried out, no one could recall it on account of any later event, is neither lawful nor just. Hence, although someone may be condemned absolutely to death for some crime, certain general conditions are always understood. Just as in every oath, promise, vow and pact certain general conditions must be understood. The community of the Romans could therefore be absolutely deprived, on account of its fault, of every special right and privilege it has over the Roman Empire; and yet certain general conditions must be understood. And so, because the community of the Romans ought not to be utterly destroyed, such a sentence ought never to be carried into execution against the Romans in such a way that it cannot afterwards be recalled for some cause. The Romans, however, can on account of fault or for some cause be so deprived of the empire that they may never lawfully regain it without a new grant from that person or those persons who can confer the empire upon them, unless all others were also justly to lose the empire on account of fault.

units.la: Discip. Nunquid tertio modo potest Imperium cassari vel diminui, ut scilicet Romanum Imperium non remaneat apud Romanos: potest tamen ex causa reuerti ad ipsos? Magist. Respondetur, quod sic. Quia potest transferri de Romanis ad alias gentes. Discip. Potest ne Romanum Imperium diuidi vel diminui. Magist. Vna est opinio, quod absque consensu expresso vel tacito totius vniuer‐ sitatis mortalium Romanum Imperium non potest diuidi vel minui: quia si priuata persona vel communitas particularis seu partialis non debet priuari iure suo, multo fortius communitas vniuer‐ salis mortalium non debet priuari iure suo. Imperium autem Romanum principalissime spectat ad communitatem vniuersalem mortalium: quemadmodum dominium rerum temporalium ad eandem communitatem principalissime spectat. Unde pro tota communitate mortalium dicit Deus ad primos parentes: Replete terram, subiicite eam & dominamini piscibus maris. Igitur communitas mortalium non debet priuari iure suo super Imperium absque consensu. Si autem Imperium minueretur vel diuideretur, communitas mortalium aliquo iure, quod habet super Imperium, priuaretur. Quia postquam aliqua temporalia sunt diuisa inter partes alicuius communitatis non sunt totius communitatis. Igitur Romanum Imperium non potest minui vel diuidi, saltem absque consensu tacito vel expresso communitatis mortalium.
units.tr: Disciple. Could the empire be annulled or diminished in the third way, namely so that the Roman Empire does not remain with the Romans, but could return to them for some cause? Master. It may be answered that it can, because it can be transferred from the Romans to other nations. Disciple. Can the Roman Empire be divided or diminished? Master. There is one opinion: that without the express or tacit consent of the whole multitude of mortals the Roman Empire cannot be divided or diminished. For if a private person or a particular or partial community ought not to be deprived of its right, much more so ought the universal community of mortals not to be deprived of its right. Now the Roman Empire principally pertains to the universal community of mortals, just as the dominion of temporal things principally pertains to that same community. Hence God speaks to the first parents on behalf of the whole community of mortals: "Fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea." Therefore the community of mortals ought not to be deprived of its right over the empire without consent. If, however, the empire were diminished or divided, the community of mortals would be deprived of some right which it has over the empire. For once certain temporal goods have been divided among the parts of a community, they no longer belong to the whole community. Therefore the Roman Empire cannot be diminished or divided, at least not without the tacit or express consent of the community of mortals.

units.la: Discip. De potestate destructionis, diuisionis, minutionis aut translationis Romani Imperii essent tractanda quamplurima; sed quamplura eorum postea locum habebunt: ideo ad praesens ipsa inuestigare dimitto. Unum tamen interrogo: utrum scilicet aliqua pars communitatis mortalium absq; suo consensu expresso vel tacito valeat priuari iure suo. Magist. Respondetur, quod propter culpam quaelibet persona vel quaelibet communitas partialis potest priuari iure, quod habet in communi super Imperium: Ita ut totum ius illius ad alios deuoluatur: sicut nonnulli putant, quod totum ius Imperii deuolutum sit ad Christianos propter culpam haereticorum & Iudaeorum & aliorum infidelium: ut ita valeant libere Christiani disponere de toto Imperio, sicut vnquam potuit tota communitas mortalium.
units.tr: Disciple. Very many things would have to be treated concerning the power of destroying, dividing, diminishing or transferring the Roman Empire; but many of these will come up later, so I now set aside their investigation. I ask one thing, however: whether some part of the community of mortals can be deprived of its right without its express or tacit consent. Master. It may be answered that, on account of fault, any person or any partial community can be deprived of the right it has in common over the empire, so that the whole right of that person passes to others; as some think, that the whole right of the empire has passed to the Christians on account of the fault of heretics, Jews and other unbelievers, so that Christians may freely dispose of the whole empire, just as the whole community of mortals ever could.

units.la: Discip. Adhuc circa istam materiam quaero, an aliquis Christianus vel alius absque causa sponte & libere valeat renunciare omni iuri, quod in communi habet super Imperium. Magist. Circa hoc diuersae sunt opiniones. Vna est, quod licet omni tali iuri renunciare. Unde & Fratres Minores, ut dicitur, omni tali iuri licite renunciauerunt: quia omni iuri humano & positiuo licet renunciare. Alia opinio est, quod tali iuri renunciare non licet. Tale autem ius in communi est ius publicum. Et ideo ei renunciare non licet.
units.tr: Disciple. Still concerning this matter I ask whether any Christian or other person may, without cause, freely and willingly renounce every right which he has in common over the empire. Master. Opinions on this are divided. One is that it is lawful to renounce every such right. Hence the Friars Minor, as is said, lawfully renounced every such right, since it is lawful to renounce every human and positive right. Another opinion is that it is not lawful to renounce such a right. Such a right in common is a public right, and therefore it is not lawful to renounce it.

units.la: Explicit liber primus.
units.tr: Here ends the first book.

units.la: INCIPIT LIBER SECVNDVS, VBI INQVIRITVR, QVAE IVRA habeat Imperator super temporalia. CAP. I.
units.tr: BOOK TWO, WHERE IT IS INQUIRED WHAT RIGHTS the Emperor has over temporal matters. CHAPTER I.

units.la: In quo quaeritur, vtrum potestas Papae & Imperatoris sint potestates distinctae.
units.tr: In which it is asked whether the power of the Pope and that of the Emperor are distinct powers.

units.la: Discipulus. Sicut, canonibus sacris testantibus, ordo ecclesiasticus confundit‐ur, si sua iurisdictio vnicuique non conseruatur, extra de accu. sicut olim, in Gloss. & 11. q. 1. peruenit. Sic ordinem mortalium manifestum est confundi, si vnicuiq; praesidenti in temporalibus & maxime supremo sua iura non seruantur. Seruari autem non possunt, nisi cognoscantur. Et ideo post praedicta, quae sunt iura & potestas Romanorum Imperatorum censeo indagandum. Primo autem inquiram, quae iura & quam potestatem habet Imperator super temporalia. Vt tamen a fundamentis eorum incipiam, ante omnia quaero, an potestas Imperatoris & Papae potestas sint distinctae potestates, an vna sit ex alia aut non. Magist. Tenent multi, quod sunt potestates distinctae.
units.tr: Student. As the sacred canons testify, the ecclesiastical order is thrown into confusion if each person's jurisdiction is not preserved (Extra, De accusationibus, Sicut olim, with the Gloss; and C. 11, q. 1, Peruenit). In the same way, it is plainly clear that the order of mortals is thrown into confusion if the rights of each ruler in temporal matters, and especially of the supreme ruler, are not preserved. But they cannot be preserved unless they are known. Therefore, after the points just mentioned, I think the rights and power of the Roman Emperors must be investigated. First, however, I will inquire what rights and what power the Emperor has over temporal matters. Yet, to begin from their foundations, before all else I ask whether the power of the Emperor and the power of the Pope are distinct powers, or whether one is derived from the other. Master. Many hold that they are distinct powers.

units.la: Discip. Si aliqua decreta maiorum consonent assertioni, adducas. Forte enim ex illis melius intelligam omnia, quae circa hanc materiam recitabis. Magist. Multi canones sacri & plures Glossae super Decreta & Decretales videntur asserere, quod sunt potestates distinctae. Unde Nicolaus Papa, vt habetur 96. cap. cum ad verum, ait: Cum ad verum ventum est, vltra sibi nec Imperator iura pontificatus arripuit, nec pontifex nomen Imperatorium vsurpauit. Vbi dicit Glossa: Cum ista potestates sint diuisae, quod Imperator non habet gladium a Papa. Item habetur eadem distinctione cap. Duo sunt quippe, Imperator Auguste, quibus principaliter hic mundus regitur, auctoritas sacra pontificum & potestas regalis. Vbi Glossa super vocabulo principaliter, ait: Neuter pendet ex reliquo. Et ita est argumentum pro Imperatore. Item Glossa extra qui filii sunt legitimi cap. causam, super verbo quod ad regem, ait: sic patet quod iurisdictio temporalis a spirituali diuisa est & distincta. Item Glossa distinct. 10. cap. Imperium, super verbo administrationibus, ait: Distincta est enim potestas sua a potestate pontificali. Item Gregor. vt legitur de priuilegiis cap. sicut, ait: Sicut in iudiciis laicorum priuilegia turbare nolumus: ita cu praeiudicantibus nobis volumus moderata auctoritate resistere. Vbi dicit Glossa sic est argumentum, quod ecclesia non vult iura alterius sibi arrogare: quia iurisdictio distincta esse debet. Item Innocent. vt legitur, extra de iudiciis, ait: Aut non putet aliquis, quod iurisdictionem illustris regis Francorum perturbare aut minuere intendimus: cum ipse iurisdictionem nostram nec velit nec debet impedire. Discipulus. In his verbis non fit mentio de Imperatore, sed de rege Francorum. Magister. Ex his verbis habetur, quod potestas regis Francorum distincta est à potestate Papæ. Et p consequens à fortiori potestas Imperatoris. Tum quia maior est potestas Imperatoris, quam potestas regis Francorum. Tum quia (sicut tactum est supra) non videtur in scripturis, quod sit aliqua potestas tributa Papæ super Imperatorem, quam non habeat super regem Franciæ. Item Glossa super verbo Innocentii, quæ ait: Propter hoc quod hic dicitur, patet quod ecclesia vel Papa non habet utrumq; gladium. Et infra: non igitur de temporali iurisdictione debet se intromittere, nisi in subsidium, scil. cum iudex secularis est negligens. Item, sicut allegatum est supra, Cyprianus, ut legitur dist. 96. cap. cum ad verum: Actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis officia potestatis utriusq; discernitur, scilicet Christus. Vbi Glossa super verbo discernit: Cum ergo ista potestates sunt distincta: licet sit argumentum quod Imperium non habetur à Papa. Et ego credo potestates distinctas esse: licet Papa quandoq; utramq; potestatem sibi assumat. Ex his aliisque quampluribus colligitur, quod potestas Papæ & Imperatoris sunt distinctæ potestates.
units.tr: Student. If any decrees of the elders agree with this assertion, bring them forward. Perhaps from them I will understand better everything you are going to recite on this matter. Master. Many sacred canons and several Glosses on the Decretum and the Decretals seem to assert that they are distinct powers. Hence Pope Nicholas, as is found in D. 96, c. Cum ad verum, says: When it came to the true, neither did the Emperor seize for himself the rights of the pontificate, nor did the pontiff usurp the imperial title. Where the Gloss says: Since these powers are divided, the Emperor does not have the sword from the Pope. Likewise, in the same distinction, c. Duo sunt quippe: Emperor Augustus, there are two things by which this world is chiefly ruled: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal power. Where the Gloss, on the word principaliter, says: Neither depends on the other. And so this is an argument for the Emperor. Likewise, the Gloss on Extra, De filiis qui sunt legitimi, c. Causam, on the words quod ad regem, says: So it is clear that temporal jurisdiction is divided and distinct from spiritual. Likewise, the Gloss on D. 10, c. Imperium, on the word administrationibus, says: For its power is distinct from the pontifical power. Likewise Gregory, as is read in De privilegiis, c. Sicut, says: Just as we do not wish to disturb the privileges in the lay courts, so we wish to resist, with moderate authority, those who prejudice us. Where the Gloss says: This is an argument that the Church does not want to claim for itself the rights of another, because the jurisdiction ought to be distinct. Likewise Innocent, as is read in Extra, De iudiciis, says: Let no one think that we intend to disturb or diminish the jurisdiction of the illustrious King of the Franks, since he neither wishes nor ought to hinder our jurisdiction. Student. In these words there is no mention of the Emperor, but of the King of the Franks. Master. From these words it is clear that the power of the King of the Franks is distinct from the power of the Pope, and consequently, all the more, the power of the Emperor. Both because the power of the Emperor is greater than the power of the King of the Franks, and because (as was touched on above) it does not appear in the Scriptures that any power has been granted to the Pope over the Emperor which he does not have over the King of France. Likewise the Gloss on the words of Innocent, which says: From what is said here, it is clear that the Church or the Pope does not have both swords. And below: therefore he ought not to meddle in temporal jurisdiction, except as a help, namely when the secular judge is negligent. Likewise, as was cited above, Cyprian, as is read in D. 96, c. Cum ad verum: By their own acts and distinct dignities, the offices of each power are discerned, namely of Christ. Where the Gloss on the word discernit says: Since these powers are distinct, this is an argument that the Empire is not held from the Pope. And I believe the powers are distinct, although the Pope at times assumes both powers for himself. From these and many other things it is gathered that the power of the Pope and that of the Emperor are distinct powers.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Ostendit secundum quid distinguuntur hæ duæ potestates.
units.tr: Shows in what respect these two powers are distinguished.

units.la: Discip. Quod sunt distinctæ potestates, videtur q; non debet in dubiū reu ocari: sed qualiter distinguuntur ignoro. Ideo dic secundū aliquam sententiā, qualiter distinguuntur. Magist. Dicitur q; per hoc distinguuntur, q; Papa habet potestatem in spiritualibus & Imperator in temporalibus. Discip. Istam assertionem (si potes) auctoritatibus aliquibus fulcire nitaris. Magist. Ista assertio quamplurib-us auctoritatibus posset munirī. Ait enim Innocentius tertius, ut scribitur extra de maioritate & obedientia, cap. solite: Non negamus quin præcellat Imperator in temporalibus illos dumtaxat, qui ab eo recipiunt temporalia. Sed & pontifex in spiritualibus antecellit, quæ tanto sunt temporalibus digniora, quanto anima corpori præferitur. Item Cyprianus, ut habetur distinct. 10. cap. quoniam: Idem & Nicolaus Papa, ut legitur distinct. 96. cap. cum ad verum, dicunt officia istarum potestatum esse distincta à Christo, ut Christiani Imperatores pro æterna vita pontificibus indigerent: & pontifices pro cursu temporalium tantum Imperii legibus vterentur: quatenus spiritualis actio à corporalibus distaret in cursibus, & Deo militantes nimirum negotiis secularibus se implicarent, ac vicissim non illæ rebus diuinis deditus videretur, qui esset negotiis secularibus implicatus. Item idem Nicolaus eadem distinct. cap. denique sic ait: denique hi sunt, quibus tantum humanis rebus & non diuinis præesse permissum est, quomodo de his, per quos diuina ministrantur, iudicare præsumant, penitus ignoramus. Item Gregorius Nazianzenus scribens Imperatoribus Constantinis, ut habetur distinct. 10. cap. suscipitis, ait: Suscipitis ne libertatem verbi? liberè accipitis quod ex Christi sacerdotali vos subiicis potestati, atque istis tribunalibus subdidit. Dedit enim & nobis potestatem: dedit & principatum multo perfectiorem principatibus vestris. Nunquid aut iustum vobis videtur, si dicat spiritus sanctus tārbis: si à terrenis cœlestia separentur, si diuinis præferantur humana? Item Innocent. tertius, vbi prius, ait: Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna in firmamento cœli. Luminare maius, ut præesset diei, & luminare minus, ut præesset nocti. Vtrumq; magnum, & alterum maius. Et infra: Ad firmamentum ergo cœlestis est vniuersalis ecclesia, fecit Deus duo luminaria magna, id est duas instituit dignitates, quæ sunt pontificalis auctoritas, & regalis potestas. Sed illa quæ præest diebus, ea est spiritualibus, maior est: quæ vero carnalibus, minor. Vt quanta est inter lunam & solem diuersitas, tanta inter reges & pontifices esse cognoscatur. Ex his aliisq; auctoritatibus innumeris, (quarum aliquæ sunt adductæ supr. cap. 1.) colligitur, quod Imperator habet potestatem in temporalibus, & Papa in spiritualibus.
units.tr: Student: That these are distinct powers ought not to be called into doubt, but I do not know how they are distinguished. So tell me, according to some opinion, how they are distinguished. Teacher: It is said that they are distinguished by this: the Pope has power in spiritual matters, and the Emperor in temporal matters. Student: If you can, try to support that assertion with some authorities. Teacher: That assertion could be fortified by many authorities. Innocent III says, as it is written in Extra, On Majority and Obedience, chapter "Solite": We do not deny that the Emperor excels in temporal matters, but only over those who receive temporal things from him. But the pontiff also excels in spiritual matters, which are worth more than temporal things, as much as the soul is worth more than the body. Likewise Cyprian, as found in Distinction 10, chapter "Quoniam." Pope Nicholas too, as read in Distinction 96, chapter "Cum ad verum," says that the offices of these powers are distinct from Christ's, so that Christian emperors would need the pontiffs for eternal life, and the pontiffs would use the laws of the empire only for the course of temporal affairs. The reason is that spiritual action should be kept apart from bodily matters in their courses, so that those who fight for God would not entangle themselves in secular business, and conversely, that one who is entangled in secular business would not seem to be devoted to divine things. Likewise the same Nicholas, in the same distinction, in the chapter "Denique," says: Finally, these are the ones to whom it has been permitted to preside only over human, and not divine, affairs; we are utterly ignorant how they presume to judge those through whom divine things are ministered. Likewise Gregory of Nazianzus, writing to the Emperors Constantine, as found in Distinction 10, chapter "Suscipitis," says: Do you receive freedom of speech? You gladly accept that you are subject to the priestly power of Christ, and have submitted yourselves to those tribunals. For he has given us power, and he has given us a rule far more perfect than your rule. Does it seem right to you, then, if the Holy Spirit should say that heavenly things are separated from earthly things, and human things are set above divine things? Likewise Innocent III, in the place cited above, says: God made two great lights in the firmament of heaven: a greater light to rule the day, and a lesser light to rule the night, both great, and the one greater. And below: So the universal Church is the firmament of heaven; God made two great lights, that is, he instituted two dignities, which are the pontifical authority and the royal power. But that which rules the days, that is spiritual, is greater; and that which rules the carnal things is lesser. So let it be recognized that as great as the difference is between the moon and the sun, so great is the difference between kings and pontiffs. From these and countless other authorities (some of which were cited above in chapter 1), it is concluded that the Emperor has power in temporal matters, and the Pope in spiritual matters.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Vbi quæritur, quæ sint temporalia, & quæ spiritualia. Et respondetur sub variis distinctionibus.
units.tr: Where it is asked what things are temporal and what are spiritual, and it is answered under various distinctions.

units.la: Discipulus. Sufficienter videtur ostensum, quod potestas Imperatoris respicit temporalia, carnalia, seculFaria, & humana: & potestas papalis spiritualia. Sed quæ sunt temporalia & spiritualia, perfecte non intelligo. Ideo quę sunt temporalia & carnalia, secularia & humana, quæ respicit potestas Imperialis, inuestigare coneris. Magist. Quibusdam videtur, quod quæ sunt illa, in quibus consistit Imperialis potestas, ex diuersis distinctionibus, quę in diuersis scripturis habentur, colligitur. Discip. Libenter audiam distinctiones illas. Magist. Vna est, quod hominum quidam sunt carnales, & quidam spirituales. Et hæc distinctio habetur expresse ad Corinthios tap. 2. & 3. Vbi Apostolus ait manifeste: Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Et post: Spiritualis autem iudicat hæc omnia: & ipse à nemine iudicatur. Alia distinctio est, quod quædam sunt personæ ecclesiasticæ, & quædam seculares. Hæc distinctio colligitur ex verbis Hieronymi, quæ ponuntur 12. q. 1. cap. duo sunt, vbi ait: duo sunt genera Christianorum. Est autem vnum genus, quod mancipatum est diuino officio & deditum contemplationi & orationi, quibus ab omni strepitu temporalium rerum vacare conuenit, vt sunt clerici & Deo devoti, scilicet conuersi. Et infra: Aliud vero genus est Christianorum, vt sunt laici. Duo enim Græce est populus Latine. His licet temporalia possidere, sed non nisi ad vsum. Alia distinctio est, quod rerum quædam sunt ecclesiasticæ, & quædam temporales seu seculares. Hæc distinctio ex diuersis sa-cris
units.tr: Student. It seems sufficiently shown that the power of the Emperor concerns temporal, carnal, secular and human matters, and the papal power concerns spiritual ones. But I do not fully understand what things are temporal and spiritual. So please try to explain which things are temporal and carnal, secular and human, that the imperial power concerns. Master. Some think that the things in which imperial power consists are gathered from various distinctions found in various Scriptures. Student. I would gladly hear those distinctions. Master. One is that some men are carnal and some spiritual. This distinction is expressly stated in 1 Corinthians, chapters 2 and 3, where the Apostle plainly says: The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. And afterwards: But the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one. Another distinction is that some persons are ecclesiastical and some secular. This distinction is gathered from the words of Jerome, which are cited in 12 q. 1, chapter "Duo sunt", where he says: There are two kinds of Christians. One kind is devoted to the divine office and given over to contemplation and prayer, and should be free from all the noise of temporal affairs; these are the clergy and those devoted to God, namely the converted. And below: The other kind of Christians are the laity. For laos in Greek is populus in Latin. To these it is permitted to possess temporal goods, but only for use. Another distinction is that some things are ecclesiastical and some temporal or secular. This distinction is taken from various sacred canons, which call some things ecclesiastical and some secular. Hence, in the Council of Antioch, as it has: he has power over ecclesiastical things. Another division is: some are secular (12 q. 1, §1, in the Gloss). Another is that crimes are secular. This division is hinted at in the same place. Another is that penalties are one canonical, another secular or legal. This division is found under these words, and is hinted at by various teachers. Another is that causes are some ecclesiastical and some secular. This is gathered from many canons. Another is that some things are temporal and some spiritual. The Apostle hints at this division when he says: entangles himself in secular affairs. For when he says that no one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs, he implies that some things are spiritual, from which those serving God do not abstain. Another is that dignities are one ecclesiastical, another secular. This division is laid down in the Decretum, distinction 3, §1, where it is said: "All these kinds of secular laws are parts..." Another is that jurisdictions are one temporal, another spiritual. This division is gathered clearly from these things. Of constitutions, one is civil, another ecclesiastical, as I say.

Magist. licet temporalia, carnalia, spiritualia &c. in di- m quæritur, quam potestatem habent laici in onem restringuntur, vt per temporalia intelli- umani generis in solis naturalibus constituti qui nullam legem præter naturalem & positi- ffet impositä. units.tr: are found in the Scriptures. Therefore do not adduce them as a rule for understanding other matters, or for investigating what power the laity can have. Since, however, it follows from what has been said that the distinction between the ecclesiastical and the divine is still to be drawn, I will set out the opinion of some people. Master: Although "temporal, carnal, spiritual," and so on, are sometimes restricted to this sense, so that by "temporal" is understood the human race constituted in natural things alone, who have no law besides the natural law and such positive law as has been imposed on them, and by "spiritual" are understood those who are instructed by divine revelation. Disciple: They have undertaken to rule those subject to them. Master: This is granted. For all things that pertain to this, being neither among temporal nor spiritual things, are numbered...

Descending to temporal things, I first ask whether the Pope has this power over temporal things, and whether it is to be rejected. Master. On this point there are various opinions. Some hold that all kingdoms of the world are subject to the Pope in temporal matters.

units.la: quas Glossas super decreta & decretales hanc quas alias, si quæ sint, allega. Magist. Glossa ingulas prouincias, insinuare hoc videtur di- r. 72. quæst. 1. cap. amplius. Quod concedo: nisi Vnde & hic à capite suo dabunt tributum Impera- Si enim dicunt se non subesse Romano Imperio: Igitur st. 1. ius Quiritum. Fatemur igitur Imperatorem esse est maior ratio, quod Francia & Hispania sunt subiectæ subiecta Romano Imperio, quam alia regna. Igitur vniuersa regna fidelium & infidelium sunt subiecta Imperatori de iure, licet non de facto. Item Glossa extr. de elect. venerabilem, super verbo in Germanos, sic ait: Sicut Imperium mundi translatum est in Theutonicos. Nam ipsi habent regimen Romanae ecclesiae 9. distinct. 5. in diem. Et sic patet quod Imperium non est apud Graecos: licet largo modo appelletur Imperium, extra de maioritate & obedientia, cap. solite. Sicut & rex Francorum & Scotorum dicitur rex: quoniam extra ecclesiam non est Imperium, & 4. q. 1. §. sed illud. Sed est Imperator ille super Reges, 7. q. 1. c. in apibus. Et omnes nationes sub eo sunt 11. q. 1. hac si quis, ibi, volumus. Ipse enim est princeps mundi & Dominus ff. ad L. Rhodiam, qui le. Et hac deprecarie. Et etiam Iudei sub ipso sunt. supra de Iudaeis, Iudei: & omnes provinciae. Et 43. dist. Adrianum. Et omnia sunt in potestate Imperatoris, 8. dist. quo iure descendis & 23. q. 8. convenior. Item Glossa dist. 1. im Quiritum, quae pro parte allegata est prius, dicit, quod Iudei vtuntur iure Romano, & vocantur Romani: quia omnes vocantur Romani subiecti Romano Imperio, prout dicitur populus Romanorum habere filios in potestate, prout etiam sunt gentiles sub Romano Imperio. Nam Imperator est princeps totius mundi ff. ad L. Rhod. qui leuanda. Qui igitur non vult esse sub Romano Imperio, nec hereditatem habere potest, nec alia quae hic de iure humano enumerantur. Item Gloss. 23. q. 8. cap. convenior, super verbo omnia infert, ait: Igitur omnia sunt Imperatoris, vt supra distinct. 8. quo iure.
units.tr: ...the Glossa on the decretals, and others, if there are any, cite. Master. The Gloss seems to suggest this, saying that the Roman Emperor has jurisdiction over the individual provinces; see Dist. 72, q. 1, cap. Amplius. This I grant: unless they pay tribute to the Emperor from their own head. For if they say they are not subject to the Roman Empire, then they are not Roman citizens (ius Quiritum). We therefore admit that the Emperor is lord of the world, and that France and Spain are subject to the Roman Empire, as are other kingdoms. Therefore all kingdoms of believers and unbelievers are subject to the Emperor by right, though not in fact. Likewise the Gloss on Extra, De electione, Venerabilem, on the words "in Germanos," says: "Just as the Empire of the world was transferred to the Teutons, for they hold the rule of the Roman Church" (Dist. 9, c. 5, In diem). And so it is clear that the Empire is not held by the Greeks, although it is loosely called an Empire, as in Extra, De maioritate et obedientia, cap. Solite. Likewise the King of the Franks and the Scots is called a king, since there is no Empire outside the Church (C. 4, q. 1, §. Sed illud). But the Emperor is over kings (C. 7, q. 1, c. In apibus). All nations are under him (C. 11, q. 1, Hac si quis, where it says "we will"). For he is the prince of the world and lord, as in the Digest, ad L. Rhodiam, "qui leuanda" (and this is the prayer). The Jews too are under him (Extra, De Iudaeis, "Iudei"), and all provinces. And Dist. 43, Adrianum; and all things are in the power of the Emperor (Dist. 8, Quo iure, and C. 23, q. 8, Convenior). Likewise the Gloss on Dist. 1, "Quiritum," which was cited earlier in part, says that the Jews use Roman law and are called Romans, because all who are subject to the Roman Empire are called Romans, just as it is said that the Roman people have sons in their power; so too the Gentiles are under the Roman Empire. For the Emperor is prince of the whole world (Digest, ad L. Rhod., "qui levanda"). Therefore whoever does not wish to be under the Roman Empire can neither have an inheritance nor enjoy the other things that are listed here under human law. Likewise the Gloss on C. 23, q. 8, c. Convenior, on the word "omnia," draws the conclusion: "Therefore all things belong to the Emperor, as above, Dist. 8, Quo iure."

units.la: Discip. Satis apparet esse opinio aliquorum; Imperatorem Romanorum esse principem seu Dominium totius mundi. Pro qua opinione nitere allegare. Magist. Haec opinio in vno principio fundari videtur principaliter: quod tale est. Imperio Romano aliquando totus mundus fuit subiectus, & ipsum Romanum Imperium non est priuatum aliquo Dominio cuiuscunq; regni, quod sibi fuit subiectum: Igitur adhuc omnia regna Imperio Romano sunt subiecta. Discip. Quo modo probatur, quod totus mundus fuit subiectus Romano Imperio? Magist. Hoc testatur Euangelium, cum dicit: Exiit edictum a Caesare Augusto, vt describeretur vniuersus orbis. Hoc etiam testatur Constantinus; qui, vt allegatum est supra distinct. 96. Constantinus aut: Dis. ernente sanctissimo, vt principatum teneat (scilicet sedes Romana) tam super quatuor sedes, Alexandrinam, Antiochenam, Hierosolymitanam & Constantinopolitanam, quam super omnes in vniuerso orbe terrarum ecclesias Dei. Haec omnia vero, quae per hanc Imperialem maiestatem & sacra personalia diuinalia decreta statuimus & confirmamus, vsq; in finem mundi illibata & inconcussa manere decreuimus. Vnde coram Deo viuo qui nos regnare praecepit, & coram eius terribili iudicio obtestamur omnes nostros successores Imperatores & cunctos optimates & satrapas, etiam amplissimum senatum, & vniuersum populum in toto orbe terrarum hunc & in posterum, nulli eorum quoquo modo licere aut confringere aut in quoquam conuelli. In quibus quidem verbis Constantinus ostendit, vniuersum orbem terrarum sibi fuisse subiectum, non quidem de facto; quia tunc aliqui populi rebellauerunt. Igitur de iure &c. Discip. Quomodo probatur, quod Romanum Imperium non fuit priuatum iure & dominio, quod habuit super quodcunq; regnum vel prouinciam? Magist. Hoc sic probatur. Si Romanum Imperium fuit priuatum iure & dominio, quod habuit super quodcunque regnum vel prouinciam, aut fuit priuatum a iure, vel ab homine. Non a iure: quia de tali priuatione nullum ius habetur, quia nec diuinum nec humanum. Nec ab homine: quia nullus homo inferior Imperatore, qui erat Dominus mundi, poterat priuare Imperatorem tali iure aut Dominio. Videtur, quod illa ratio non procedit. Primo, quia Imperium Romanum potuit priuari tali iure & tali dominio per potentiam regnorum rebellantium. Quia, vt legitur extra de regulis iuris cap. omnis: Omnis res ex quibuscunque causis nascitur, per easdem dissoluitur. Romanorum autem Imperium acquisiuit ius & dominium super alia regna per potentiam gladii. Igitur per potentiam gladii potuit perdere idem ius & dominium. Secundo, quia Imperator Romanorum per negligentiam suam & culpam potuit perdere iurisdictionem suam quam habuit super multa regna. Nam sicut notatur in Gloss. 22. q. vlt. cap. de forma: eadem fide tenetur quis subdito suo, sicut subditus Domino. Et si non fecerit, priuatur Dominio, quod habuit in vasallo. Si igitur Imperator iniuste tractauit alios regnas vel non defendit ea in necessitate, iuste perdidit iurisdictionem, quam habuit super ipsa. Tertio: quia praescriptione iura tolluntur. Poterant igitur alia regna praescribere contra Imperium. Et sic Imperator potuit perdere ius & Dominium, quod habuit super quaedam regna. Magist. Nonnulli apparet, quod ista rationem praescriptam nequaquam impediunt. Primum non: quia, sicut tactum est prius, licet magna pars mundi fuit per potentiam gladii subiugata Imperio, omnes tamen sponte postea consenserunt subdi eidem Imperio. Et ideo extunc per potentiam gladii dissolui non poterat. Secundo, quod est de culpa Imperatoris vel Romanorum, quod etiam non impedit (vt videtur) quia nec in eo vel in eis apparet tanta culpa, quod Romanum Imperium priuari debuit iure & dominio, quod habuit super quaecunq; regna. Esto tamen, quod talis culpa commissa fuisset: non tamen debuit Imperium absq; sententia vniuersitatis mortalium aut alicuius vel aliquorum gentis vel gentium vicem eiusdem vniuersitatis tali iure priuari. Nulla autem talis sententia per vniuersitatem mortalium aut alicuius vel aliquorum gentis vel gentium vicem eiusdem vniuersitatis data fuit contra Romanum Imperium. Igitur Romanum Imperium tali iure vel dominio minime est priuatum. Nec tertium de praescriptione praescripta rationem impedire videtur. Tum quia non apparet, quod vnquam aliquis in hoc praescripserit contra Romanum Imperium: quia nullus potuit se bona fide alienare a Romano Imperio. Et ideo quicunq; se alienant se a Romano Imperio alienant se a sola potentia. Tum: quia sicut in spiritualibus & ecclesiasticis contra obedientiam & visitationem non praescribitur: sic contra Dominium Romani Imperii nullus potest praescribere. Quod patet ex hoc, quod praescriptio in temporalibus est ex iure Imperiali. Imperator autem hoc quam fecit legem vel statutum, quod aliquis posset praescribere taliter contra Romanum Imperium. Igitur nulla in hoc casu poterit allegari praescriptio.
units.tr: Disciple. It is sufficiently clear that some hold the opinion that the Roman Emperor is prince, or lord, of the whole world. Please give arguments in support of this opinion. Master. This opinion seems to be founded chiefly on one principle, which runs as follows: at one time the whole world was subject to the Roman Empire, and the Roman Empire has not been deprived of any lordship over any kingdom that was once subject to it; therefore all kingdoms are still subject to the Roman Empire. Disciple. How is it proved that the whole world was subject to the Roman Empire? Master. Scripture bears witness to this, when it says: "There went out a decree from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be taxed" (Luke 2). Constantine also bears witness to it, as was cited above in Dist. 96, Constantinus autem, where the most holy Constantine, to whom the Roman see holds the primacy over the four sees, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople, and over all the churches of God in the whole world, says: "All these things which we have decreed and confirmed by this Imperial majesty and sacred decrees we determine shall remain unimpaired and unshaken until the end of the world. Therefore we call upon God the living, who has commanded us to reign, and upon his dreadful judgment, to bear witness that all our successors as Emperors, all the nobles and satraps, the most august senate and the whole people throughout the whole world, now and in the future, are in no way permitted to break or overturn any of these things." In these words Constantine shows that the whole world was subject to him, not indeed in fact, since some peoples then rebelled, but by right, etc. Disciple. How is it proved that the Roman Empire has not been deprived of the right and lordship which it had over any kingdom or province? Master. It is proved thus. If the Roman Empire has been deprived of the right and lordship which it had over any kingdom or province, then it was deprived either by law or by a human being. Not by law, because there is no law, either divine or human, that provides for such a deprivation. Nor by a human being, because no man inferior to the Emperor, who was lord of the world, could deprive the Emperor of such right or lordship. It may be objected that this reasoning does not hold. First, because the Roman Empire could be deprived of such right and lordship by the power of rebellious kingdoms. For, as is read in Extra, De regulis iuris, cap. Omnis: "Every thing is dissolved by the same causes from which it arises." But the Roman Empire acquired right and lordship over other kingdoms by the power of the sword; therefore it could lose the same right and lordship by the power of the sword. Second, because the Roman Emperor, through his negligence and fault, could have lost the jurisdiction he had over many kingdoms. For as is noted in the Gloss on C. 22, q. ult., c. De forma: a man is bound to his subject by the same faith that a subject owes to his lord; and if he does not do so, he is deprived of the lordship he had over his vassal. Therefore if the Emperor treated other kingdoms unjustly, or did not defend them in time of need, he justly lost the jurisdiction he had over them. Third, because rights are abolished by prescription; therefore other kingdoms could have prescribed against the Empire, and so the Emperor could have lost the right and lordship he had over certain kingdoms. Master. It seems that these objections do not in any way prevent the argument. As to the first, they do not: for, as was said before, although a great part of the world was subdued to the Empire by the power of the sword, yet all afterwards willingly consented to be subject to the same Empire; and therefore from that time it could not be dissolved by the power of the sword. As to the second, which concerns the fault of the Emperor or of the Romans, this too does not stand in the way, since no fault so great appears in him or in them that the Roman Empire ought to have been deprived of the right and lordship it had over any kingdom. Yet even if such a fault had been committed, the Empire ought not to have been deprived of such right by the sentence of the whole body of mortals, or of some person or persons acting in place of that whole body, whether of one nation or of several. But no such sentence has been given against the Roman Empire by the whole body of mortals, or by any person or persons acting in place of that body, whether of one nation or of several. Therefore the Roman Empire has by no means been deprived of such right or lordship. Nor does the third objection, concerning prescription, seem to block the argument. For it does not appear that anyone has ever prescribed against the Roman Empire, since no one could in good faith alienate himself from the Roman Empire; and therefore whoever has alienated himself from the Roman Empire has done so only by force. Moreover, just as in spiritual and ecclesiastical matters no prescription runs against obedience and visitation, so no one can prescribe against the lordship of the Roman Empire. This is clear from the fact that prescription in temporal matters derives from Imperial law, and the Emperor himself made the law or statute by which anyone could prescribe in this way against the Roman Empire. Therefore in this case no prescription can be alleged.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: Adducit secundam opinionem, tenentem, quod Imperator nunc non est Dominus totius mundi: & hoc tribus rationibus, ad quas respondetur cap. 8. & 9.
units.tr: He adduces a second opinion, holding that the Emperor is not now lord of the whole world, and this by three arguments, which are answered in chapters 8 and 9.

units.la: Discipulus. Recita opinionem contrariam. Magist. Alia opinio est, quod licet aliquando Imperator Romanorum fuerit dominus totius mundi: nunc tamen non est Dominus omnium nationum. Discip. Pro ista opinione aliquas allegationes coneris adducere. Magist. Pro ista opinione allegatur primo sic. Quod Papa approbat, & nos approbare debemus, & pro veritate tenere debemus. distinct. 19. si Romanorum. Sed Papa videtur approbare assertionem Francorum & aliorum, qui asserunt se non esse Imperio subiectos. Si enim opinionem illorum minime approbaret, nihil deberet statuere propter assertionem ipsorum praeferentium, quod sonaret in approbationem assertionis eiusdem. Sed ut legitur extra, de privilegiis, super specula: Papa propter hoc, quod Franci & alii subtrahentes se ab Imperio Romano legibus Imperialibus non vtuntur, statuit quod ius civile Parisiis, vel in aliis civitatibus, seu aliis locis vicinis nullatenus doceatur vel audiatur, quod in assertionem vel approbationem dictae assertionis Francorum vel aliorum sonare videtur. Igitur eandem assertionem approbare & veram reputare debemus.
units.tr: Pupil. Recount the contrary opinion. Master. Another opinion holds that although the Emperor of the Romans was at one time lord of the whole world, he is not now lord of all nations. Pupil. Bring forward some arguments for this opinion. Master. For this opinion, the first argument runs as follows. The Pope approves, and we ought to approve and hold as true, what the Pope approves. Dist. 19, Si Romanorum. But the Pope seems to approve the assertion of the French and others, who claim that they are not subject to the Empire. For if he did not approve their opinion, he ought not to have enacted anything out of regard for their assertion that would seem to sound in approval of that same assertion. But as we read in Extra, De privilegiis, Super specula: the Pope, because the French and others who withdraw from the Roman Empire do not use imperial laws, decreed that civil law should in no way be taught or heard at Paris, or in other cities or neighbouring places, which seems to sound in support or approval of the French assertion, or of others. Therefore we ought to approve that same assertion and regard it as true.

units.la: Discip. Forte dicerent alii, quod Papa non fecit tale statutum, quia approbauerit dictam assertionem Francorum: sed quia voluit, quod litterati magis Theologiae insisterent, & quia frustra tale statutum dimisisset ad insinuandum se non approbare assertionem illam, quia propter hoc litterati & alii opinionem suam nullatenus reliquissent. Magist. Videtur multis, quod ista responsio non impediat praescriptam rationem: quia Papa, ad quem spectat omnia peccata & errores corrigere, insinuare debuit dictam assertionem, si est falsa, se nullatenus approbare. Discip. Aliam rationem adducas ad idem. Magist. Alia ratio talis est. Sancti canonizati ab ecclesia non sunt credendi existere in peccato mortali, aut in rebellione damnabili, vel alia iniuria decessisse. Sed plures fuerunt sancti reges & alii, qui Imperatorem minime recognouerunt superiorem in temporalibus, & in hoc finierunt dies suos. Exemplum de sancto Ludouico rege Francorum, & pluribus regibus Angliae. Igitur vere non fuerunt subditi Romano Imperio.
units.tr: Pupil. Perhaps others would reply that the Pope did not make such a decree because he approved the French assertion, but because he wanted the learned to devote themselves more to theology, and because he would have wasted such a decree if he meant to signal that he did not approve that assertion, since on that account the learned and others would by no means have given up their opinion. Master. It seems to many that this reply does not overturn the argument just stated, because the Pope, whose task it is to correct all sins and errors, ought to have signalled that he did not in any way approve the said assertion, if it is false. Pupil. Adduce another argument for the same point. Master. Another argument runs thus. Saints canonized by the Church are not to be believed to have been in mortal sin, or in damnable rebellion, or to have died in some other wrong. But there were many holy kings and others who in no way acknowledged the Emperor as their superior in temporal matters, and who ended their days in that state. Example: St Louis, king of the French, and several kings of England. Therefore they truly were not subjects of the Roman Empire.

units.la: Discip. Forte dicerent alii, quod isti sancti nesciuerunt se esse subiectos Romano Imperio: & si sciuissent, hoc facto & verbo recognouissent. Quare per ignorantiam iuris ciuilis poterant excusari. Magist. Apparet aliis, quod haec responsio non sufficit: quia reges & principes tenentur scire, an habeant superiorem vel non. Ignorantia autem iuris, quod quis tenetur scire, non excusat l. quaest. 4. sed notandum. Igitur reges & principes per talem ignorantiam nullatenus fuerunt excusati.
units.tr: Pupil. Perhaps others would say that these saints did not know they were subject to the Roman Empire, and that if they had known, they would have acknowledged it by deed and word. Therefore they could be excused on the ground of ignorance of civil law. Master. It seems to others that this reply is not sufficient, because kings and princes are bound to know whether or not they have a superior. But ignorance of law, which a person is bound to know, does not excuse: L. Quaest. 4, Sed notandum. Therefore kings and princes were in no way excused by such ignorance.

units.la: Discip. Forte dicerent aliqui, quod reges illi & principes non tenebantur habere tantam peritiam iurium ciuilium & historiarum, vt cognoscerent se subiectos Romano Imperio. Magist. Ad hoc dicitur, quod debuerunt ab aliis inquirere, si nesciuerunt per seipsos, teste Glossa quae dicit distinctione 36. cap. 1. ait: non excusatur quis per ignorantiam, qui potest habere peritorum copiam.
units.tr: Pupil. Perhaps some would say that those kings and princes were not bound to have such great skill in civil law and history that they would recognise that they were subject to the Roman Empire. Master. To this it is replied that, if they did not know it of themselves, they ought to have inquired of others, as the Gloss says on Distinctio 36, cap. 1, where it states: a person is not excused by ignorance when he could have access to experts.

units.la: Discip. Ad hoc respondetur, quod non inuenerunt peritos, qui in hoc eos instruerent: quia multi periti sunt, qui magis desiderant destructionem Romani Imperii quam exaltationem, & simplices tantum, quantum possunt, informant, quod non omnes mortales sunt subditi Romano Imperio. Non autem oportet, quod reges & principes ac alii laici sint nimis solliciti inquirendo, an sint subiecti Romano Imperio, teste Glossa, 72. quaest. 4. sed notandum. Ad hoc autem, quod quis probabiliter dicatur errare, non requiritur, quod sit nimis diligens, scrupulosus & curiosus in inquirendo: nec quod sit nimis negligens & dissolutus in inquirendo.
