Et ita adhuc reges & principes per ignorantiam poterunt excusari, licet non cognoscant se esse subiectos Romano Imperio. Magist. Contra hoc obiicitur: quia de bono communi debent maxime reges & principes summe esse solliciti, licet non debeant esse nimis diligentes, scrupulosi & curiosi. Sed ex Romano Imperio dependet bonum commune totius generis humani. Igitur circa hoc praecipue reges & principes summam diligentiam adhibere tenentur. Discip. Aliam rationem, si occurrat, allega. Magist. Adhuc pro opinione praedicta allegatur sic. Ad officium summi pontificis summe spectat instruere laicos & potissime reges & principes, ex quibus obedientia aliorum dependet in his, quae spectant ad fidem & iustitiam & bonos mores. Sed si de iure omnes mortales sunt Romano Imperio subditi, contra iustitiam agunt reges & principes, qui subiici Romano. Romano Imperio recusant. Igitur de hoc debent pontifices, Imperatores, reges & principes instituere diligenter. Hoc autem non fecerunt plures sancti summi pontifices: quod tamen fecissent, si hoc ad iustitiam pertineret. Aliter enim de bono communi & salute eorum, ex quibus rationem reddent Deo, non fuissent solliciti. Igitur non est probabile, quod omnes mortales sunt modo subiecti Romano Imperio, Discip. Videtur quod haec ratio dupliciter potest impediri. Uno modo dicendo, quod summi pontifices ignoraverunt omnes mortales debere subiici Romano Imperio. Hoc enim ad ius ciuile spectat. Ipsi autem iuris ciuilis non tenentur esse periti, nec in his quae spectant ad ius ciuile, tenentur fideles instruere. Aliter potest dici, quod summi pontifices aduerterunt reges & principes & alios laicos nullo modo velle acquiescere admonitioni, qua deberent esse Romano Imperio subditi. Et ideo tacuerunt, iuxta illud Salomonis Proverb. 23. in auribus insipientium ne loquatur. Despiciunt enim doctrinam eloquii tui. Magist. Nonnullis apparet, quod neutra istarum rationum impedit praescriptam rationem. Prima non: tum quia non est verisimile, quod summi pontifices ignoraverunt omnes esse subiectos Romano Imperio, si continet veritatem, praesertim cum hoc Glossatores canonum & decretorum, quae summus pontifex ignorare non debet, asserere manifeste videantur. Tum secundo, quia licet summus pontifex non teneatur habere peritiam excellentem iuris ciuilis, non tamen debet ignorare omnino omnia, quae sunt iuris ciuilis: imo illa quae tangunt totam universitatem mortalium, scire tenetur. Aliter enim de multis peccatis mortalibus, quae redundarent in periculum totius Ecclesiae, non posset corripere Christianos, quia de illis quae nescit esse peccata, non debet eos corrigere. Igitur cum omnes mortales esse subiectos Romano Imperio omnes tangat, ita ut quicunque scienter reculat subesse Romano Imperio, si est ei subiectus, peccat mortaliter. Hoc summus pontifex ignorare non debet, quia de illis, quae a pluribus & communiter fiunt, debet scire, an sint peccata mortalia vel non. Secunda responsio, ut videtur, non impedit rationem illam. Nam non constabat summis pontificibus, quod omnes laici, qui non subdebant se Imperio, erant ita obstinati, quod nullo modo vellent de veritate informari. Ergo saltem experiri debebant, an doctrinam veram in hac parte volebant recipere. Item constat, quod multi fuerunt sancti reges & alii laici quamplures, qui iustitiam dilexerunt & bonum commune, & odio habebant omnem iniustitiam. Aliter enim omnes reges & alii laici extitissent delectatores iniquitatis: & per consequens in statu damnationis fuissent. Igitur parati fuerunt de omni iustitia spectante ad ipsos informari. Et per consequens parati fuerunt erudiri, quod iure essent subiecti Romano Imperio, vel penitus a subiectione huiusmodi liberati. Amplius, aliqui sunt in veritate subiecti Romano Imperio de iure: & tamen nolunt de facto esse subiecti. Et tales nihil iuste possident: quia tales nihil possident iure Imperatoris, teste Beato Augustin. qui super Iohan. & ponitur in decretis dist. 8. quo iure, ait: Iure igitur humano dicitur: haec villa mea est, hic seruus meus est, haec domus mea est. Et infra: Noli ergo dicere, quid mihi & regi? quid tibi ergo & possessioni? per iura regum possidentur possessiones. Dixisti, quid mihi & regi? nolis dicere possessiones tuas: quia ipsa iura renunciasti humana, quibus possessiones possidentur. Et idem Augustin. ad Vincentium, ut legitur vigesim. quart. quasi. septim. cap. ait: Res quaecunque terrena nullo tempore possideri a quocunque potest, nisi iure Diuino, quo cuncta iustorum sunt: vel iure humano, quod in potestate regis terra est. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod nullus subiectus Imperatori vel regi aliquid iuste possidet, nisi iure Imperatorum vel regum. Et per consequens si omnes nationes de iure sunt subiectae Romano Imperio, nullus rex vel princeps aut alius laicus aliquid iuste possidet, qui renunciat iuri Imperatoris, & non vult esse subiectus Imperatori. Hinc Glossa dist. primi. ius Quiritum, ut allegatum est superius, ait: Qui non vult esse sub Romano Imperio, nec hereditatem habere potest nec alia quae hic de iure humano (scilicet Romanorum) enumerantur. Omnes igitur reges & principes ac laici, qui recusarent esse sub Romano Imperio, nihil iuste possiderent: sed de omnibus, quae iniuste possident, non possunt facere eleemosynam, nec aliquid alicui donare, nec oblationes publicas, nec holocausta siue sacrificia. Quia licet in casu de quibusdam illicite acquisitis possit eleemosyna fieri, vel oblatio aut sacrificium: tamen de iniuste possesso nullum praedictorum fieri potest. Peccant etiam omnes clerici & religiosi, qui extra tempus necessitatis & aperte recipiunt dona, eleemosynas, oblationes vel sacrificia de illis, quae possident de facto non de iure reges & principes ac alii laici, qui Romano Imperio subdi recusant.
units.tr: Pupil. To this it is answered that they did not find experts who might instruct them in this, because there are many experts who desire the destruction of the Roman Empire rather than its exaltation, and who inform the simple, as far as they can, that not all mortals are subject to the Roman Empire. Nor is it necessary that kings, princes and other laymen should be overly anxious in inquiring whether they are subject to the Roman Empire, as the Gloss says in Causa 72, quaest. 4, Sed notandum. Moreover, to say that someone is reasonably mistaken, it is not required that he be excessively diligent, scrupulous and curious in inquiring, nor that he be excessively negligent and careless in inquiring. And so kings and princes can still be excused by ignorance, even though they do not know that they are subject to the Roman Empire. Master. Against this it is objected: kings and princes ought above all to be most anxious about the common good, although they ought not to be excessively diligent, scrupulous and curious. But the common good of the whole human race depends on the Roman Empire. Therefore kings and princes are bound to apply the greatest diligence especially to this matter. Pupil. Bring forward another argument, if one occurs to you. Master. Further, for the aforesaid opinion the argument runs thus. It belongs above all to the office of the supreme pontiff to instruct laymen, and especially kings and princes, on whom the obedience of others depends in those matters which concern faith, justice and good morals. But if by right all mortals are subject to the Roman Empire, kings and princes who refuse to submit to the Roman Empire act against justice. Therefore popes, emperors, kings and princes ought to be diligently instructed about this. But many holy supreme pontiffs did not do this, which they would surely have done had it pertained to justice. For otherwise they would not have been concerned for the common good and the salvation of those for whom they will render account to God. Therefore it is not probable that all mortals are now subject to the Roman Empire. Pupil. It seems that this argument can be countered in two ways. In one way, by saying that the supreme pontiffs were unaware that all mortals ought to be subject to the Roman Empire. For this belongs to civil law, and popes are not bound to be experts in civil law, nor are they bound to instruct the faithful in those matters which concern civil law. In another way it can be said that the supreme pontiffs perceived that kings, princes and other laymen would in no way be willing to accept an admonition by which they ought to be subject to the Roman Empire. And so they kept silent, in accordance with that saying of Solomon, Prov. 23: Do not speak in the ears of fools, for they despise the teaching of your words. Master. To some it seems that neither of these replies counters the argument just stated. Not the first: because it is not likely that the supreme pontiffs were all ignorant that everyone is subject to the Roman Empire, if this is true, especially since the glossators of the canons and decretals, which a supreme pontiff ought not to be ignorant of, clearly seem to assert it. Second, because although a supreme pontiff is not bound to have excellent skill in civil law, nevertheless he ought not to be entirely ignorant of everything in civil law; indeed, he is bound to know those things which touch the whole community of mortals. Otherwise he could not rebuke Christians for many mortal sins which would bring danger to the whole Church, since he ought not to correct people for those things which he does not know to be sins. Therefore, since the fact that all mortals are subject to the Roman Empire touches everyone, so that whoever knowingly refuses to be subject to the Roman Empire, if he is subject to it, sins mortally, the supreme pontiff ought not to be ignorant of this, because about those things which are done by many and commonly he ought to know whether or not they are mortal sins. The second reply, as it seems, does not overturn that argument. For it was not certain to the supreme pontiffs that all laymen who did not submit themselves to the Empire were so obstinate that they would in no way be willing to be informed of the truth. Therefore at least they ought to have tried whether they were willing to receive true teaching on this point. Likewise it is evident that there were many holy kings and many other laymen who loved justice and the common good, and who hated all injustice. Otherwise all kings and other laymen would have been lovers of iniquity, and consequently would have been in a state of damnation. Therefore they were ready to be informed about all justice that concerns them. And consequently they were ready to be taught that they were by right subject to the Roman Empire, or else entirely freed from such subjection. Moreover, some are in truth subject by right to the Roman Empire, and yet are unwilling to be subject in fact. Such people possess nothing justly, because they possess nothing by the right of the Emperor, as blessed Augustine teaches in his commentary on John, which is also cited in the Decretum, Dist. 8, Quo iure, where he says: By human right it is said: this village is mine, this slave is mine, this house is mine. And below: Do not then say, what have I to do with the king? What then have you to do with a possession? Possessions are held by the laws of kings. You said, what have I to do with the king? You are unwilling to name your possessions, because you have renounced the human laws by which possessions are held. And the same Augustine, to Vincentius, as we read in Causa 24, Quaest. 7, cap., says: No earthly thing can at any time be possessed by anyone, except by divine right, by which all things belong to the just, or by human right, by which the land is in the power of the king. From these words it is gathered that no one subject to the Emperor or king possesses anything justly, except by the right of the Emperors or kings. And consequently, if all nations are by right subject to the Roman Empire, no king, prince or other layman possesses anything justly who renounces the right of the Emperor and is unwilling to be subject to the Emperor. Hence the Gloss on Dist. 1, Ius Quiritum, as cited above, says: He who is unwilling to be under the Roman Empire can have no inheritance, nor any of the other things which are enumerated here under human right (namely, of the Romans). Therefore all kings, princes and laymen who refuse to be under the Roman Empire would possess nothing justly; and of all the things they hold unjustly they cannot make alms, nor give anything to anyone, nor offer public oblations, burnt offerings or sacrifices. For although in some cases alms, an oblation or a sacrifice may be made from certain things acquired unlawfully, nevertheless none of the aforesaid can be made from what is unjustly possessed. All clergy and religious also sin who, outside a time of necessity and openly, receive gifts, alms, oblations or sacrifices from those things which kings, princes and other laymen who refuse to submit to the Roman Empire possess in fact but not by right.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Iterum probat, quod Imperator non sit Dominus omnium temporalium, & hoc unica ratione, ad quam etiam respondetur.
units.tr: Again he proves that the Emperor is not lord of all temporal things, and this by a single argument, to which an answer is also given.

units.la: Discipulus. Adhuc allega pro opinione praemissa. Magist. Pro ista opinione allegatur &c. Quod Imperator Romanorum non sit Dominus omnium temporalium, lacri canones asserere videntur, quod sunt plures, qui non habent superiorem: quod tamen non esset verum, si omnes seculares essent subiecti Romano Imperio. Innocentius namque tertius, ut legitur extra, de haereticis, excommunicamus, ait: Si vero Dominus temporalis requisitus & monitus ab Ecclesia suam terram purgare neglexerit ab haeretica foeditate &c. Et infra: eadem nihilominus lege seruata circa eos, qui non habent Dominos principales. Item, idem extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem, ait: Insuper cum rex Franciae superiorem in temporalibus non recognoscat, sine iuris alterius laesione in eo se iurisdictioni nostrae subdere potuit.
units.tr: Disciple. Now allege something further in support of the opinion put forward above. Master. The following is alleged for that opinion, etc. That the Emperor of the Romans is not lord of all temporal things, the sacred canons seem to assert, since there are several who have no superior. That would not be true, however, if all secular rulers were subject to the Roman Empire. For Innocent III, as read in extra, de haereticis, excommunicamus, says: But if the temporal lord, when requested and warned by the Church, neglects to cleanse his land from heretical filth, etc. And below: the same law being nevertheless observed concerning those who do not have principal lords. Likewise, the same Innocent in extra, qui filii sunt legitimi, per venerabilem, says: Moreover, since the king of France does not acknowledge a superior in temporal matters, he could, without injury to the right of another, submit himself to our jurisdiction.

units.la: Item, Glossa extra, de foro competenti, c. ex transmissa, loquens de ipsa ait: Licet concedat clerico contra laicum: dum tamen alium superiorem habet, non concedit laico contra clericum. Ex his colligitur, quod sunt plures laici, qui superiorem non habent: & per consequens non omnes sunt Imperatori subiecti. Disc. Licet ista allegatio appareat fortis: tamen secunda auctoritas de rege Francorum non videtur ad propositum pertinere. Tum quia Glossa ibidem, ut allegatum est primo huius cap. 18. asserit, quod rex Francorum de iure subest Romano Imperio. Tum, quia Innocentius non dicit, quod rex Franciae non habet superiorem in temporalibus, sed quod rex non cognoscit superiorem. Potest enim aliquis habere superiorem, licet non recognoscat. Magist. Non nullis apparet, quod neutrum istorum concludit, istam auctoritatem Innocentii non monstrare intentum: sed quod ex verbis Innocentii allegatis elicitur, quod idem Innocentius regem Franciae vere & iuste minime cognoscere superiorem in temporalibus, cum asserit; quia rex in temporalibus superiorem minime recognoscit, ideo sine laesione iuris alterius potuit se iurisdictioni Papae subiicere. Sed si rex false & iniuste recognosceret minime in temporalibus superiorem, non oportet propter hoc sine laesione alterius iuris se subiicere iurisdictioni Papae: quia falsa & iniusta abnegatio Dominii alterius non tribuit abnegato potestatem subiiciendi se iurisdictioni alterius absque laesione veri Domini sui. Innocentius igitur reputat, quod rex vere & iuste non recognoscit superiorem in temporalibus. Ex hoc concluditur, quod primum non valet. Etiam secunda Glossa videtur contrariari textui, cum Glossa dicit quod rex Franciae de iure subest Imperio. Et textus dicat, quod quia rex Franciae non recognoscit superiorem, potest se subiicere iurisdictioni Papae: quod tamen non esset, si de iure subiectus esset Imperio, quod esset in praeiudicium Imperatoris, si esset subiectus. Discipulus. Occasio est apparenter exclusa, ac per hoc praescripta allegatio videtur amplius confirmari: tamen narra, quomodo respondetur ad ipsam. Magister. Ad primam Decretalem respondetur, quod loquitur de his, qui de facto non habent Dominos principales: quia illi non minus tenentur obedire Papae circa haereticos expurgandos. Ad secundam dicitur, quod loquitur de rege Franciae, pro quo Imperator reputari videtur saltem de facto, quia scilicet rex Franciae non est subiectus, eo quod nec verbo nec facto sibi ostendit de iure dominari debere regi Franciae. In quo casu propter errorem vel negligentiam Imperatoris Papa non potestate data sibi a Christo, sed quia ex consuetudine obtinet talem iurisdictionem circa regem Franciae: si se subiiceret, nihilominus super ipsum iurisdictionem haberet Papa: non quia rex Franciae false & iniuste non recognoscit Dominium Imperatoris, sed quia Imperator negligit propria iura vel ignorat, quae iura habeat super regem Franciae & alios laicos universos. Sicut enim iudex Ecclesiasticus potest se immiscere seculari iurisdictioni, cum iudex secularis negligit facere iustitiam, extra de foro competenti, ex tenore. & c. licet, in Glossa, ita Papa potest in multis casibus supplere ignorantiam vel negligentiam Imperatoris circa subiectos eidem. Discip. Si Papa potest implere negligentiam vel ignorantiam Imperatoris exercendo iurisdictionem temporalem circa regem Franciae: igitur eadem ratione poterit priuare Imperatorem iure & dominio, quod habet Imperator super regem Franciae. Magist. Respondetur, quod Papa nulla potestate, quam habet vel a Christo vel a consuetudine licita, potest priuare Imperium a tali iure & dominio: quemadmodum non potest destruere imperium. Discip. Nunquid potest Imperator eximere regem Franciae vel alium, ne ullo modo subsit Imperio? Magist. Respondetur, quod licet Imperator possit multas libertates concedere regi Franciae & aliis: tamen nullo modo potest regnum Franciae vel aliud totaliter ab Imperio separare, ut nullo modo subsit Imperio. Quia hoc esset destruere Imperium, quod non potest Imperator. Discip. Dic quomodo respondetur ad Glossam superius allegatam. Magist. Respondetur, quod Glossa illa loquitur de laico, qui de facto non habet superiorem: habet tamen de iure omnino laicus fidelis & infidelis, quod subsit Imperatori.
units.tr: Likewise, the gloss on Extra, de foro competenti, chapter ex transmissa, speaking of this same matter, says: The Church grants a cleric a privilege against a layman, provided that the cleric has another superior; it does not grant a layman a privilege against a cleric. From this it follows that there are several laymen who have no superior, and consequently not all are subject to the Emperor. Student. Although this argument seems strong, the second authority, about the king of the Franks, does not appear to bear on the point. First, because the gloss there, as cited above in chap. 18, asserts that the king of the Franks is by right subject to the Roman Empire. Second, because Innocent does not say that the king of France has no superior in temporal matters, but that the king does not acknowledge one. For a man may have a superior even if he does not acknowledge him. Master. Some hold that neither of these points is conclusive, and that Innocent's authority does not show what is intended; rather, from the words of Innocent quoted, it is inferred that Innocent himself, when he asserts that the king of France truly and rightly does not acknowledge a superior in temporal matters, means that, because the king in temporal matters does not acknowledge a superior, he could therefore submit himself to the jurisdiction of the Pope without injury to another's right. But if the king falsely and unjustly failed to acknowledge a superior in temporal matters, he would not for that reason be able to submit himself to the Pope's jurisdiction without injury to another's right, because a false and unjust denial of another's lordship does not give the one denying it the power to submit himself to another's jurisdiction without injuring his true lord. Innocent therefore regards the king as truly and rightly not acknowledging a superior in temporal matters. From this it follows that the first point does not hold. Also, the second gloss seems to contradict the text, since the gloss says that the king of France is by right subject to the Empire, while the text says that because the king of France does not acknowledge a superior, he can submit himself to the Pope's jurisdiction; which would not be so if he were by right subject to the Empire, since that would be to the Emperor's prejudice, if he were subject. Student. The objection seems plainly excluded, and so the aforesaid argument seems to be strengthened further; yet tell me how it is answered. Master. To the first decretal it is answered that it speaks of those who in fact have no principal lords, for they are no less bound to obey the Pope in cleansing the land of heretics. To the second it is said that it speaks of the king of France, for whom the Emperor seems to be reckoned as lord, at least in fact, since the king of France is not subject, in that neither by word nor by deed has the Emperor shown that he ought by right to rule over the king of France. In such a case, because of the Emperor's error or negligence, the Pope holds such jurisdiction over the king of France not by the power given him by Christ, but because by custom he has obtained it; yet if the king submitted himself, the Pope would nonetheless have jurisdiction over him, not because the king of France falsely and unjustly fails to acknowledge the Emperor's lordship, but because the Emperor neglects or is ignorant of his own rights, which he has over the king of France and all other laymen. For just as an ecclesiastical judge may intervene in secular jurisdiction when a secular judge neglects to do justice, extra de foro competenti, ex tenore, and c. licet, in the Gloss, so the Pope may in many cases supply the Emperor's ignorance or negligence concerning those subject to him. Student. If the Pope can make up for the Emperor's negligence or ignorance by exercising temporal jurisdiction over the king of France, then by the same reasoning he could deprive the Emperor of the right and lordship which the Emperor has over the king of France. Master. It is answered that the Pope, by no power which he has either from Christ or from lawful custom, can deprive the Empire of such a right and lordship, just as he cannot destroy the Empire. Student. Can the Emperor exempt the king of France, or anyone else, so that he is in no way subject to the Empire? Master. It is answered that although the Emperor may grant many liberties to the king of France and others, nevertheless he cannot in any way wholly separate the kingdom of France, or any other, from the Empire so that it is in no way subject to the Empire; for this would be to destroy the Empire, which the Emperor cannot do. Student. Tell me how the gloss cited above is answered. Master. It is answered that this gloss speaks of a layman who in fact has no superior; yet every layman, faithful or unbelieving, is by right entirely subject to the Emperor.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Respondetur ad primam rationem, supra c. 6. adductam.
units.tr: It is answered to the first argument, adduced above in chapter 6.

units.la: Discipulus. Videtur, quod apparenter ad rationem adductam c. 7. respondisti. Ad rationes autem, quae allegatae sunt c. 6. ego responsiones aliquas recitavi: praeter quas audire cupio aliquas, si ad ipsas aliter respondetur. Magist. Ad primam illarum, quae in hoc consistit, quod illud, quod approbat Papa, nos approbare tenemur: Respondetur, quod hoc est verum, quando Papa auctoritate Papali aliquid diffiniendo & determinando approbat iuste & catholice. Si autem Papa non diffiniendo nec determinando aliquid approbat, & non iuste: illud propter hoc approbare non tenemur. Unde & Innocentius quartus, quamvis esset Papa, noluit opiniones suas autenticas reputari. Similiter nec opinio Innocentii quinti, quam etiam approbauit, postquam fuit Papa, non tenentur aliter approbare. Nunc autem non inuenitur, quod aliquis Papa diffiniendo & determinando approbauit, non omnes mundi provincias vel regnum Franciae non subiici Romano Imperio, & omnino hoc non approbare astringimur. Esto autem, quod aliquis Papa diffiniendo & determinando hoc approbasset: quia tamen hoc non iuste approbasset, non tenemur idem approbare. Disc. Contra istam responsionem duo occurrunt. Primum est, quod secundum istam responsionem non tenentur plus approbare, quod approbat Papa, quam quod alius Episcopus vel alius peritus in scripturis sacris nosciturapprobare. Quia quicquid Episcopus vel peritus in scripturis sacris iuste & catholice approbat, & nos approbare tenemur, eo quod omnem iustitiam & omne quod est catholicum approbare debemus. Secundum quod occurrit, est, quod si non tenemur approbare illud, quod Papa etiam determinando & diffiniendo approbat, sequitur quod possemus illud reprobare: quod videtur esse contra quandam constitutionem Papalem, quam dicitur fecisse in ordine Fratrum Minorum, qua cavetur, ut fertur, quod postquam quaecunq; conclusio fidei de ducta fuerit ad fidem Apostolicam, extunc antequam fuerit per Ecclesiam determinata, nullus frater audeat unam vel aliam partem approbare, eligere vel affirmare. Si enim postquam conclusio alia in curia fidei coeperit agitari, nullus debet nec unam partem nec aliam approbare: & per consequens neutram partem debet reprobare: multo fortius illud, quod Papa approbat, nullus aliqualiter debet reprobare. Magist. Ad primum istorum respondetur, quod plus debemus approbare illud, quod Papa approbat, quam illud quod approbat quicunque inferior ipso Papa: quia quando Papa approbat aliquid (nisi simus certi, quod errat contra fidem vel iustitiam) possumus & debemus in casu illo publice & occulte omnibus modis probare. Illud autem, quod inferior Papa vel alius approbat, licet non simus certi quod errat, possumus etiam coram aliis publice dubitare, vel opinionem negare, & contradicere assertioni eiusdem, licet si non errat, non debeamus asserere pertinaciter contrarium, cum nullum falsum pertinaciter debemus asserere. Ad secundum dicitur, quod si Papa etiam diffiniendo, determinando errat contra fidem, vel bonos mores, vel contra iustitiam, (& hoc constat nobis) possumus & debemus ipsum apertissime reprobare: sic etiam, si quaecunq; conclusio fidei inceperit in curia ventilari, quicunq; per scripturas sacras vel determinationes catholicas Ecclesiae est certus de veritate, potest & debet partem veram eligere, approbare & diffiterero, & partem falsam respuere & reprobare. Unde quod nonnulli putant, quod constitutio illa facta inter ordinem Fratrum Minorum a Papa, ut fertur, est haeretica, sapiens manifeste peiorem haeresim, quae unquam fuit inventa a quocunq; haeretico, ita quod peior haeresis non potest inveniri nec posset. Disc. In auribus meis recitas quoddam mirabile. Ideo volo de hoc tecum breviter conferre: licet in aliis operibus quorundam poterimus plura invenire: quia forte hoc opusculum ad manus aliquorum perveniet, qui opera alia non viderunt. Dicigitur breviter secundum praedictos opinantes, quae est illa haeresis pessima, quam sapit illa constitutio ante dicta, & quare est pessima, & quae absurditates secundum praefatos opinantes sequuntur ex ipsa. Magist. Haeresis pessima, ut dicunt isti, quam secundum eos sapit constitutio ante dicta, est quod Papa sic dominatur fidei Christianae, ut tota fides Christiana, quam Christiani credere astringuntur, sic pendet ex approbatione, diffinitione & determinatione cuiuslibet Papae, quod nullus Christianus debet firmiter credere aliquid spectans ad fidem, antequam sibi constet, quod Papa, qui pro tempore fuerit, hoc tenet & approbat. Dicunt enim, quod haec haeresis pessima est, quia secundum eam posset Papa mutare totam fidem, & omnes articulos fidei, & facere articulos contrarios articulis contentis in Symbolo Apostolorum. Et ita in tota fide Christiana nihil esset certum & immutabile: sed tota dependeret ex voluntate Papae. Et Evangelium & totam scripturam posset destruere, & facere novam scripturam contrariam, cui omnes Christiani, quamdiu Papa vellet, adhaerere deberent: quam tamen posset mutare successor suus. Et ita quilibet Papa posset dare Christianis novam legem, quam pro tempore suo, & quoniam reuocaretur per successorem, ipsam tenerentur accipere & approbare. Quo nihil peius posset dici contra fidem Christianam. Absurditates autem quamplures praeter illas concludunt per scripturas posse sequi ex constitutione praedicta. Dicunt plures inferri ex gestis temporis nostri; quarum una est, quod nullus Frater Minor quantumcunq; literatus & doctus debet amodo asserere nec approbare, quod mundus non fuit ab aeterno, nec etiam quod fuerit ab aeterno. Alia est, quod nullus Frater Minor deberet approbare amodo, quod in divinis sit aliqua distinctio in personis. Alia est, quod nullus eorum debet approbare, quod homo quantumcunq; iustus non convertitur in divinam essentiam, quemadmodum in sacramento altaris panis convertitur in corpus Christi. Alia est, quod nullus eorum debet asserere amodo, quod Beatus Petrus nec aliquis alius homo, qui non est Christus verus Deus & verus homo, non creavit stellas, nec quod sine tali homine Deus sciret quicquam facere. Alia est, quod nullus eorum amodo debet asserere, quod creaturae Dei non sunt purum nihil. Quod omnes illae absurditates, & quamplurimae aliae consimiles sequuntur ex constitutione praedicta, probant ex hoc, quod omnia praedicta & alia similia absurdissima opinabatur quidam Magister in Theologia de ordine Fratrum Praedicatorum nomine Aycardus Theutonicus, de quibus accusatus fuit primo vel denunciatus, & primo Archiepiscopo Coloniensi, in cuius curia datis auditoribus Aycardo praedicta, praescripta & alia consimilia ventilata fuerunt. Qui postea veniens in Avinionem, assignatis sibi auditoribus, se praedicta docuisse & praedicasse non negavit. Pro quibus non fuit damnatus, nec assertiones suae praescriptae, & aliae statim damnatae fuerunt: sed cardinalibus traditae fuerunt, ut deliberarent, an inter haereses essent computandae. Praeceptum etiam fuit quibusdam Magistris in Theologia, ut supra hac communem deliberationem haberent. Et ita notorium est, quod omnes assertiones praedictae & plures aliae consimiles Aycardi praedicti in curia agitatae fuerunt: nec postea Papa aliquis determinavit quaestiones seu conclusiones praedictas. Igitur de omnibus nec unam partem nec aliam debet aliquis Frater Minor eligere, nec approbare seu affirmare. Et consimiliter si in curia ventilarentur, an Christus fuit natus de virgine, vel an Beata Maria fuerit virgo, vel an resurrectio mortuorum sit futura, vel aliquod simile, non liceret asserere nec unam, partem nec aliam.
units.tr: Disciple. It seems that you have replied to the argument adduced in chapter 7 in a manner similar to the others. As for the arguments set out in chapter 6, I have recited some replies to them, and I wish to hear some others besides those, if they are answered differently. Master. To the first of those, which consists in this, that what the Pope approves we are bound to approve, the answer is this: it is true when the Pope, by papal authority, defining and determining something, approves it justly and catholically. But if the Pope approves something without defining or determining it, and not justly, we are not bound to approve it on that account. Hence Innocent IV, although he was Pope, did not wish his own opinions to be regarded as authentic. Likewise, we are not bound to approve otherwise the opinion of Innocent V, which he also approved after he became Pope. Now, however, it is not found that any Pope, defining and determining, approved that not all the provinces of the world, or the kingdom of France, are subject to the Roman Empire; and we are in no way bound to approve this. But suppose some Pope had approved this by defining and determining; since he would not have approved it justly, we are not bound to approve the same. Disciple. Two things occur against this answer. The first is that, according to this answer, we are not bound to approve more of what the Pope approves than of what another bishop or another expert in Holy Scripture is known to approve. For whatever a bishop or an expert in Holy Scripture approves justly and catholically, we too are bound to approve, since we ought to approve all justice and everything that is catholic. The second is that if we are not bound to approve what the Pope approves, even when defining and determining, it follows that we could reject it. This seems to be contrary to a certain papal constitution, which is said to have been made for the Order of Friars Minor, by which it is provided, as it is reported, that once any conclusion of faith has been referred to the Apostolic See, then, before it has been determined by the Church, no friar may dare to approve, choose or affirm one part or the other. For if, after another conclusion has begun to be debated in the court of faith, no one ought to approve either part, and consequently ought to reject neither part, then much more should no one in any way reject what the Pope approves. Master. To the first of these it is answered that we ought to approve what the Pope approves more than what anyone inferior to the Pope approves, because when the Pope approves something (unless we are certain that he errs against faith or justice) we can and ought, in that case, to approve it in every way, publicly and privately. But what an inferior to the Pope, or anyone else, approves, although we are not certain that he errs, we may also publicly doubt in the presence of others, or deny the opinion and contradict the assertion of the same; although, if he does not err, we ought not to assert the contrary stubbornly, since we ought never to assert anything false stubbornly. To the second it is said that if the Pope, even when defining and determining, errs against faith, or good morals, or justice (and this is clear to us), we can and ought to reject him most openly. So too, if any conclusion of faith has begun to be debated in the court, whoever is certain of the truth through the Holy Scriptures or the catholic determinations of the Church can and ought to choose and approve the true part and affirm it, and to spurn and reject the false part. Hence, the claim that some men make, that the constitution made by the Pope for the Order of Friars Minor, as it is reported, is heretical, savours manifestly of a worse heresy than any heretic has ever devised, so that a worse heresy cannot be found, or could not be. Disciple. You tell me something amazing. So I want to confer with you briefly about this, although in the other works of certain men we shall be able to find more, since perhaps this little work will come into the hands of some who have not seen those other works. Tell me briefly, according to the aforesaid holders of this opinion, what that most wicked heresy is which the aforesaid constitution savours of, why it is most wicked, and what absurdities follow from it according to the aforesaid holders of this opinion. Master. The most wicked heresy, as those men say, which according to them the aforesaid constitution savours of, is that the Pope so lords it over the Christian faith that the whole Christian faith, which Christians are bound to believe, depends in this way on the approval, definition and determination of whatever Pope there is: so that no Christian ought firmly to believe anything pertaining to faith until it is clear to him that the Pope who is in office at the time holds and approves it. For they say this is the most wicked heresy, because according to it the Pope could change the whole faith and all the articles of faith, and make articles contrary to those contained in the Apostles' Creed. And thus in the whole Christian faith nothing would be certain and unchangeable, but the whole would depend on the will of the Pope. He could even destroy the Gospel and the whole of Scripture and make a new, contrary Scripture, to which all Christians, as long as the Pope wished, ought to adhere, which nevertheless his successor could change. And so any Pope could give Christians a new law, which they would be bound to accept and approve for as long as it lasted, until it was revoked by a successor. Nothing worse could be said against the Christian faith. Moreover, they conclude from Scripture that many other absurdities besides these can follow from the aforesaid constitution. They say that several are inferred from the events of our own time. One of these is that no Friar Minor, however learned and erudite, ought from now on to assert or approve that the world was not from eternity, nor even that it was from eternity. Another is that no Friar Minor ought from now on to approve that there is some distinction in the persons of the Godhead. Another is that none of them ought to approve that a man, however just, is not converted into the divine essence, just as in the sacrament of the altar bread is converted into the body of Christ. Another is that none of them ought from now on to assert that blessed Peter, or any other man who is not Christ, the true God and true man, did not create the stars, nor that God without such a man would know how to do anything. Another is that none of them ought from now on to assert that the creatures of God are not pure nothing. They prove that all these absurdities, and very many other similar ones, follow from the aforesaid constitution, from this: that all the aforesaid and other most absurd similar things were held by a certain master in theology of the Order of Friars Preachers, named Aycardus the Teuton, for which he was first accused or denounced, and first to the Archbishop of Cologne, in whose court, with hearers assigned to Aycardus, the aforesaid and other similar things were debated. He afterwards came to Avignon, and with hearers assigned to him he did not deny that he had taught and preached the aforesaid things. For these he was not condemned, nor were his aforesaid assertions and others at once condemned; instead they were handed over to the cardinals, so that they might deliberate whether they should be counted among the heresies. An instruction was also given to certain masters in theology that they should have a common deliberation on the matter. And so it is notorious that all the aforesaid assertions and many others similar to those of Aycardus were debated in the court; nor did any Pope afterwards determine the aforesaid questions or conclusions. Therefore, about all of them no Friar Minor ought to choose, approve or affirm either part. And likewise, if it were debated in the court whether Christ was born of a virgin, or whether the Blessed Mary was a virgin, or whether there will be a resurrection of the dead, or anything similar, it would not be permitted to assert either part.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad secundam & tertiam rationes, supra cap. 6. adductas.
units.tr: In which an answer is given to the second and third arguments, adduced above in chapter 6.

units.la: Discipulus. De ista constitutione Papæ, vt formatur quæstio, potest variis modis excusari: & quomodo omnes excusationes viis quamplurimis impugnantur, & deterius, vt videtur, pluribus reprobantur, vt in quodam opere cuiusdam potero inuenire: ideo hic plura de ipso audire non cupio. Dic itaq;, quomodo ad secundam rationem 6. cap positam superius respondetur. Magist. Respondetur, quod Imperator non requisiuit reges & alios, vt recognoscerent eum suum superiorem: & ideo si illi parati fuissent recognoscere Imperatorem suum superiorem, si hoc eis patenter fuisset ostensum, per ignorantiam sufficienter de omni peccato excusandi fuissent. Cum autem dicitur, quod reges & principes de bono communi debent esse solliciti, & per consequens debuerunt summe esse solliciti quærere, an essent Romano Imperio (a quo dependet bonum commune) subiecti. Dicitur, quod licet summe debeant esse solliciti de bono communi: non tamen tenentur esse summe solliciti de omni eo, quod spectat ad bonum commune, & quod leuiter ab eis sciri non potest: præsertim cum non inueniuntur sapientes, qui eos ad hoc admoneant. Et ideo licet ex vniuersali Imperio dependeat bonum commune: quia tamen reges & principes plures & multi alii laici non poterant leuiter scire, se esse subiectos Imperatori: nec Imperator ad hoc requisiuit eos: nec sapientes eos monebant, vt de hoc essent solliciti, per ignorantiam excusantur. Sed contrarium asserebant multi, qui pro sapientibus habebantur. Ideo tenebantur de hoc non esse solliciti. Discip. Dic quomodo ad rationem tertiam respondetur. Magist. Respondetur, quod licet summi pontifices debebant instruere & docere reges & principes de his, quæ spectant ad fidem & iustitiam & bonos mores, non tenentur tamen de omnibus talibus eos instructe: quia non possent. Et nullus ad impossibile obligatur. Et ideo sufficit summis pontificibus in licitis & sanctis instruere illis de illos, quæ magis vtilia & necessaria erant pro temporibus suis: quia doctrina peritorum & prælatorum debet qualitati temporum contienire. Propterea enim quia temporibus plurimorum summorum pontificum erat magis vtile & necessarium reges & principes ac laicos alios aliis instrui, quam quod essent Romano Imperio subiecti, non tenebantur illis temporibus illos in hoc instruere: præsertim cum Imperatores non requisiuerunt alios inferiores, quod eos superiores suos recognoscerent. Et forte tunc expediebat illam veritatem tacere: quamuis nunquam expediuit asserere contrariam falsitatem. Ex his patet ad rationem, quod secundum istos multi reculabant subdi Romano Imperio: qui tamen in hoc mortaliter non peccabant, quia ignorantia probabilis excusauit eos. Et per hoc respondetur ad vltimum, quod tangitur in eodem ca. quia multi, qui de iure sunt subditi Romano Imperio, & tamen nolunt subdi eidem, iuste possident ea, quæ possident: quia sunt bonæ fidei possessores credentes se iuste & licite possidere, & dominium verum habere. Et ideo iuste & licite possunt ea dare, & de eis Eleemosynam & sacrificia facere. Clerici etiam, qui putant eos iustos possessores, si non laborant ignorantia crassa & supina, possunt ab eis Eleemosynas, sacrificia & oblationes accipere. Et cum dicitur, nihil tales possident iure Imperatorum. Respondetur, quod etiam iure Imperatoris quodammodo possident: quia huiusmodi bonæ fidei sunt possessores: quia propter hoc, quod sunt bonæ fidei possessores, auctoritate etiam iurium Imperialium possunt multa præscribere & vsurpare, & per continuationem temporum verum dominium acquirere.
units.tr: Disciple. This decree of the Pope, as the question is framed, can be excused in various ways, and all the excuses are attacked in very many ways and, as it seems, rejected by more persons still, as I may find in a certain work by someone. So I do not wish to hear more about it here. Tell me, then, how the second argument, set out above in chapter 6, is answered. Master. The answer is that the Emperor did not require kings and others to acknowledge him as their superior. So if they had been ready to acknowledge their Emperor as superior, had this been made plainly known to them, they would have been sufficiently excused of every sin through ignorance. But when it is said that kings and princes ought to be concerned for the common good, and consequently ought above all to have been anxious to inquire whether they were subject to the Roman Empire, on which the common good depends, the reply is this: although they ought above all to be concerned for the common good, they are not bound to be intensely concerned with everything that pertains to the common good, and which cannot easily be known by them, especially since no wise men are found to warn them of it. And so, although the common good depends on a universal Empire, nevertheless, because kings, princes and many other laymen could not easily know that they were subject to the Emperor, and because the Emperor did not require them to do so, and wise men did not warn them to be concerned about it, they are excused through ignorance. But many who were regarded as wise asserted the contrary, and so they were bound not to be concerned about it. Disciple. Tell me how the third argument is answered. Master. The answer is that although the supreme pontiffs ought to instruct and teach kings and princes in matters that pertain to faith, justice and good morals, they are not bound to instruct them in all such matters, because they could not do so. And no one is obliged to do the impossible. Therefore it suffices for the supreme pontiffs, in lawful and holy matters, to instruct them in those things which were more useful and necessary for their own times, because the teaching of the learned and of prelates ought to agree with the character of the times. For since in the times of most supreme pontiffs it was more useful and necessary for kings, princes and other laymen to be instructed in other matters than that they should be subject to the Roman Empire, they were not bound in those times to instruct them on this point, especially since the Emperors did not require the lower ranks to acknowledge them as their superiors. And perhaps at that time it was expedient to keep silent about that truth, although it was never expedient to assert the contrary falsehood. From these points it is plain, with regard to the argument, that according to these men many refused to be subject to the Roman Empire, yet they did not sin mortally in this, because a probable ignorance excused them. And by this the last point, touched on in the same chapter, is answered: that many who are by right subject to the Roman Empire, and yet are unwilling to be subject to it, justly possess what they possess, because they are possessors in good faith, believing that they possess justly and lawfully and hold true ownership. And so they can justly and lawfully give those things, and make alms and sacrifices from them. Clerics also, who think these possessors are just, may accept alms, sacrifices and offerings from them, provided they do not labour under gross and culpable ignorance. And when it is said that such people possess nothing by the right of the Emperors, the answer is that they do in a certain sense possess by the right of the Emperor, because they are possessors in good faith; for by reason of being possessors in good faith, they can, by the authority of the imperial laws too, prescribe and acquire many things, and by the lapse of time obtain true ownership.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: Inquiritur de potestate Imperatoris super malos: vtrum Imperator possit pro quocunque crimine punire. Et recitat tres opiniones. Secunda ponitur ca. 11. tertia ca. 13. & ad probationes minoris rationis in 8. ca. adducta respondetur infra capitulis 16. 17. & 18.
units.tr: The question is asked concerning the power of the Emperor over wicked men: whether the Emperor may punish them for any crime whatever. He sets out three opinions. The second is given in chapter 11, the third in chapter 13, and the arguments of the lesser premise adduced in chapter 8 are answered below in chapters 16, 17 and 18.

units.la: Discipulus. Hactenus inquisiuimus, an cunctæ mundi regiones Imperatori sint subiectæ. Intelligo de illis, quæ ad iurisdictionem temporalem seu patrimonium Ecclesiæ minime spectant. Nam de illis, quæ spectant ad Ecclesiæ patrimonium in tertio huius est sermo: de quibus in tractatu De potestate Papæ & cleri plura potuimus inuenire. Nunc autem ad personas, quæ non sunt de iurisdictione temporali Ecclesiæ, descendamus. Et primo videamus de malis, quam potestatem videlicet habet Imperator super malos, an videlicet Imperator pro omni crimine possit punire malos sibi subiectos. Et quia, sicut tactum est supra cap. 3. huius secundi, criminum quædam sunt Ecclesiastica, quædam secularia; inquiramus hic solum modo de criminibus secularibus: quia de criminibus Ecclesiasticis tractabimus in tertio huius secundi. Cupio itaq; inquirere, an Imperator valeat punire omnes subiectos pro quocunque crimine seculari, quod non est Ecclesiasticum. Magist. Circa hoc sunt diuersæ sententiæ. Vna est, quod pro omni crimine seculari potest Imperator punire omnes sibi subiectos. Quod tali ratione probatur. Idem pro eodem crimine non est a diuersis iudicibus puniendus: quorum vnus non est sub alio, vel qui non habent ab aliquo vno & eodem principe potestatem. Ex hoc enim (vt patet) posset periculosa contentio & seditio inter ipsos iudices oriri, dum vterq; vellet ad suum forum trahere criminosum: quod tamen nequaquam fieri posset. Sed ad iudicem Ecclesiasticum spectat punire criminosos pro diuersis criminibus secularibus. Ergo pro illis criminibus non debet Imperator punire eosdem. Maior huius rationis videtur de se patens. Minor per sacros canones videtur posse probari. Ex consilio enim Iohannis Papæ vt habetur extra, de officio iudicis ordinarii, perniciosa, sic legitur: habent enim Episcopi singularum vrbium in suis dioecesibus potestatem liberam adulteria inquirere, & scelera vlcisci, & iudicare. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnia crimina secularia sunt per Episcopos puniencia. Quia adulterium, quod etiam apud infideles & sola lege naturæ contentos putatur crimen. Tum quia indistincte dicit & scelera. Igitur omnia scelera intelligit. Item, Innocentius tertius, vt habetur extra, de iudiciis, nouit, ait: nullus, qui sit sanæ mentis, ignorat quoniam ad officium nostrum spectet de quocunq; peccato mortali corrigere quemcunque Christianum: & si correctionem contempserit, per districtionem Ecclesiasticam coercere. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod quilibet Christianus pro quolibet crimine est per iudicem Ecclesiasticum puniendus. Item, Calixtus Papa, vt habetur 24. quæst. 3. cap. si quis, ait: Si quis Romipetas & peregrinos & Apostolorum limina & aliorum sanctorum oratoria visitantes capere, seu rebus, quas ferunt, spoliare, & mercatores nouis Theloneorum & Pedagiorum exactionibus molestare tentauerit, donec satisfecerit, communione careat Christiana. Item, ex Concilio Agathensi vt legitur eisdem cap. & quæst. cap. itaque, sic habetur: Itaque censuimus homicidas & falsos testes à communione Ecclesiastica submouendos, nisi pœnitentia & satisfactione crimina diluerint admissa. Ex quibus etiam patet, quod capientes etiam laicos spoliatores, & qui Theloneis & Pedagiis molestant indebite mercatores, homicidæ & falsi testes per iudicem Ecclesiasticum puniuntur: & tamen constat, quod ipsa sunt secularia crimina. Item, iudex Ecclesiasticus punit incendiarios 23. quæst. vltim. cap. pessimam. Item, punit illos, qui filios occidunt extra, de illis quæ filios occiderunt, de infantibus. Et eos, qui exercent torneamenta, extra, de torneamentis, cap. felicis. & cap. ad audientiam. Et sagittarios, extra, de sagittariis cap. vno. Et stupra, extra, de adulteriis & stupris cap. 1. & cap. adulterium, per totum. Et raptores, extra, de raptoribus, cap. 1. & tamen ista sunt crimina secularia.
units.tr: Disciple. Hitherto we have inquired whether all the regions of the world are subject to the Emperor. I mean those which do not belong to the temporal jurisdiction or patrimony of the Church. For concerning those things which belong to the patrimony of the Church, the discussion is in the third part of this work, and in the treatise On the Power of the Pope and the Clergy we were able to find much on the subject. Now let us come down to persons who are not under the temporal jurisdiction of the Church. And first let us see concerning the wicked: what power, namely, the Emperor has over the wicked, that is, whether the Emperor may punish wicked men subject to him for every crime. And since, as was touched upon above in chapter 3 of this second part, some crimes are ecclesiastical and some secular, let us inquire here only concerning secular crimes, because we shall treat of ecclesiastical crimes in the third part of this second book. I wish, therefore, to inquire whether the Emperor is able to punish all his subjects for any secular crime which is not ecclesiastical. Teacher. On this there are various opinions. One is that the Emperor can punish all his subjects for every secular crime. This is proved by the following reasoning: the same person may not be punished for the same crime by different judges, of whom one is not under the other, or who do not hold their power from one and the same prince. For from this (as is plain) a dangerous contention and sedition could arise between the judges themselves, while each wished to draw the criminal to his own court; and yet this could in no way happen. But it belongs to the ecclesiastical judge to punish criminals for various secular crimes. Therefore the Emperor ought not to punish the same persons for those crimes. The major premise of this argument seems evident in itself. The minor can seemingly be proved from the sacred canons. For from the counsel of Pope John, as it is found in the Extra, On the Office of the Ordinary Judge, Perniciosa, it is read thus: "The bishops of the individual cities have in their dioceses free power to inquire into adulteries, to avenge crimes, and to judge." From these words it is gathered that all secular crimes are to be punished by the bishops, because adultery, which is thought to be a crime even among unbelievers and those content with the law of nature alone, [is included]. Also, because he says indistinctly "and crimes," he therefore means all crimes. Likewise, Innocent III, as found in the Extra, On Judgments, Novit, says: "No one of sound mind is ignorant that it pertains to our office to correct any Christian for any mortal sin, and if he has despised correction, to restrain him by ecclesiastical distraint." From these words it is gathered that any Christian whatever, for any crime whatever, is to be punished by the ecclesiastical judge. Also, Pope Callixtus, as found in 24 q. 3, c. Si quis, says: "If anyone has attempted to seize pilgrims visiting Rome and the thresholds of the Apostles and the oratories of other saints, or to despoil them of the goods they carry, and to harass merchants with new exactions of tolls and tributes, let him be deprived of Christian communion until he has made satisfaction." Also, from the Council of Agde, as read in the same canon and question, c. Itaque, it is held thus: "Therefore we have judged that murderers and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion, unless by repentance and satisfaction they have washed away the crimes committed." From these things it is also plain that those who seize even lay despoilers, and who harass merchants by unjust tolls and tributes, and murderers and false witnesses, are punished by the ecclesiastical judge; and yet it is certain that these are secular crimes. Also, the ecclesiastical judge punishes arsonists, 23 q. last, c. Pessimam. Also, he punishes those who kill their sons, Extra, On those who have killed their sons, concerning infants; and those who hold tournaments, Extra, On tournaments, c. Felicis and c. Ad audientiam; and archers, Extra, On archers, c. 1; and fornicators, Extra, On adulteries and fornications, c. 1 and c. Adulterium, throughout; and abductors, Extra, On abductors, c. 1; and yet these are secular crimes.

units.la: Igitur crimina secularia sunt per iudicem Ecclesiasticum puniencia. Quod etiam ex auctoritatibus Diuinæ scripturæ videtur posse probari. Ait enim veritas Matth. 18. Si peccauerit in te frater tuus &c. Ex quibus colligitur, quod ad Ecclesiam spectat etiam de peccatis, quæ committuntur in proximum, quæ constat esse secularia, quemlibet corrigere Christianum. Item, Apostolus 2. ad Corinth. 6. reprehendit Corinthios, qui litigabant apud iudices infideles, qui erant seculares: & quia non deferebant iudicium Ecclesiæ, quæ debuit iudicare inter fratrem, etiam de secularibus, dicens: Nescitis quoniam angelos iudicabimus: quanto magis secularia. Igitur de seculari pertinet ad iudicem Ecclesiasticum iudicare: & per consequens per iudicem Ecclesiasticum sunt criminosi & pro criminibus secularibus puniendi.
units.tr: Therefore secular crimes are to be punished by the ecclesiastical judge. This also seems capable of being proved from the authorities of Divine Scripture. For the truth says in Matthew 18: "If your brother sins against you, etc." From which it is gathered that it pertains to the Church to correct any Christian even concerning sins committed against a neighbour, which are plainly secular. Also, the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 6 rebukes the Corinthians who were going to law before unbelieving judges, who were secular; and because they did not refer the matter to the judgment of the Church, which ought to have judged between brother and brother, even concerning secular matters, he says: "Know you not that we shall judge angels? How much more things that pertain to this life?" Therefore it belongs to the ecclesiastical judge to judge concerning secular matters, and consequently criminals are to be punished by the ecclesiastical judge and for secular crimes.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: In quo ponitur secunda opinio contraria prima, scilicet quod ad secularem iudicem & non ad Ecclesiasticum spectat iudicare de criminibus secularibus.
units.tr: In which the second opinion, contrary to the first, is set out: namely, that it belongs to the secular judge and not to the ecclesiastical judge to try crimes of a secular kind.

units.la: Discipulus. Recita sententiam contrariam. Magist. Alia sententia est, quod ad Imperatorem & iudicem secularem solummodo spectat pro criminibus secularibus plectere criminosos, illos videlicet, qui criminibus secularibus sunt subiecti. Discip. Ista sententia duo asserit. Primum est, quod ad iudicem secularem spectat punire huiusmodi criminosos tantum. Secundum est, quod hoc non spectat ad Ecclesiasticum iudicem. Primo igitur allega pro primo. Magist. Quod ad iudicem secularem spectat punire huiusmodi criminosos, tam auctoritatibus sacræ scripturæ, quam sacris canonibus videtur posse probari. Apostolus enim loquens de potestatibus secularibus, ait ad Roman. 13, principes non sunt &c. Item, Beatus Petrus in canonica sua prima cap. 2. ait: Subiecti estote omni creaturæ humanæ propter Deum. Ex quibus auctoribus videtur posse probari, quod crimina, præcipue secularia, per seculares iudices sunt plectenda. Et etiam sacris canonibus videtur ostendi, vt habetur ex Concilio Teuronensi vt legitur 23. q. 5. cap. incestuosi, sic habetur: Incestuosi, parricidae, homicidae multi apud nos reperiuntur: sed aliqui ex illis nolunt sacerdotum admonitionibus aurem accommodare, volentes in pristinis perdurare criminibus, quos oportet per secularem potentiam disciplinam à tam praua consuetudine coerceri. Item, Cyprianus in nono genere Abusionum, habetur eisdem cap. & quæst. 6. rex. ait: Rex debet furta cohibere, adulteria punire, impios de terra perdere, parricidas & periuros non sinere viuere, filios suos non sinere impie agere. Ex quibus aliisq; quampluribus colligitur, quod huiusmodi crimina sunt à iudicibus secularibus punienda.
units.tr: Student. Recite the contrary opinion. Master. The other opinion is that it belongs only to the Emperor and the secular judge to punish criminals for secular crimes, namely those who are subject to secular crimes. Student. That opinion asserts two things. The first is that it belongs to the secular judge alone to punish such criminals. The second is that this does not belong to the ecclesiastical judge. So first cite proofs for the first point. Master. That it belongs to the secular judge to punish such criminals can seem to be proved both by the authorities of Holy Scripture and by the sacred canons. For the Apostle, speaking of the secular powers, says in Romans 13: "The rulers are not..." etc. Likewise, the blessed Peter in his first Catholic epistle, chapter 2, says: "Submit yourselves to every human creature for God's sake." From these authorities it seems that crimes, especially secular ones, are to be punished by secular judges. And it is also seen from the sacred canons, as is found in the Council of Toledo, as read in 23 q. 5, c. "Incestuosi", where it is said: "Many incestuous persons, parricides and murderers are found among us; but some of them are unwilling to lend an ear to the admonitions of the priests, wishing to persist in their former crimes, whom it is necessary to restrain from so depraved a custom by secular power." Likewise Cyprian, in the ninth kind of Abuses, which is found in the same chapter and question 6, "Rex": he says: "The king ought to restrain thefts, punish adulteries, destroy the impious from the earth, not allow parricides and perjurers to live, and not allow his sons to act impiously." From these and many other sources it is gathered that crimes of this kind are to be punished by secular judges.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Probat, quod non spectat ad iudicem Ecclesiasticum criminosos punire. Et hoc tribus rationibus: ad quas respondetur infra cap. 19. unica responsione.
units.tr: He proves that it does not belong to the ecclesiastical judge to punish criminals. And he does this by three reasons, to which an answer is given below in chapter 19 with a single reply.

units.la: Discipulus. Iam manifestum puto ad seculares iudices pertinere punire pro criminibus secularibus criminosos sibi subiectos. Ideo pro hoc non curo plures allegationes audire. Ideo nitere allegare pro secundo, quod ad iudices Ecclesiasticos non spectat punire huiusmodi criminosos. Magist. Hoc auctoritatibus sanctorum patrum videtur posse probari. Hoc enim Augustinus super Amos Prophetam, et ponitur 23. quaest. 25. sunt quedam, videtur asserere. Qui sic ait: Sunt quedam enormia flagitia, quae potius per mundi iudices, quam per antistites et rectores Ecclesiarum vindicantur. Sicut cum quis interficit pontificem Apostolicum, Presbyterum, Episcopum, sive Diaconum, huiusmodi reos reges et principes mundi damnant. Ergo non sine causa gladium portant, qui talia scelera vindicant. Sunt enim maxime constituti propter homicidas, raptores, ut etiam illos damnent, et alios suo timore compescant. Ex quibus verbis patet, quod raptores et homicidae non sunt per iudicem Ecclesiasticum puniendi. Et similiter omnia alia crimina secularia non debent per ipsum puniri.
units.tr: Student. I think it is now clear that secular judges are responsible for punishing, for secular crimes, the criminals subject to them. So I do not care to hear more arguments on this point. Instead, try to argue for the second point, that it does not belong to ecclesiastical judges to punish criminals of this kind. Teacher. This seems capable of being proved by the authority of the holy Fathers. For Augustine, in his commentary on the prophet Amos, seems to assert this, and it is cited in 23 quaest. 25, "There are some enormous crimes which are avenged by the judges of the world rather than by the bishops and rulers of the churches. For when someone kills the Apostolic pontiff, a presbyter, a bishop, or a deacon, the kings and princes of the world condemn the guilty. Therefore they do not bear the sword without reason, who avenge such crimes. For they are appointed chiefly on account of murderers and robbers, so that they may condemn even these, and restrain others by their fear." From these words it is plain that robbers and murderers are not to be punished by an ecclesiastical judge. And likewise all other secular crimes ought not to be punished by him.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Ponit medium viam inter duas iam dictas opiniones, per quam possunt concordari. Ubi etiam notatur, quod ad Ecclesiam spectat duplex punitio.
units.tr: He sets out a middle way between the two opinions already mentioned, by which they can be reconciled. Here it is also noted that the Church is concerned with a twofold punishment.

units.la: Discipulus. Auctoritates allegatae circa praemissa ita videntur esse contrariae, ut omnino alterae sint, nisi per sententiam seu assertionem, quae mediet inter opiniones praescriptas, valeant concordari. Ideo gestio scire, an sit aliqua sententia media inter sententias prius recitatas. Magist. Non nullis apparet, quod auctoritates praedictae possunt per unam sententiam mediam concordari.
units.tr: Disciple. The passages cited on the matter above seem so contrary to one another that they would be wholly opposed, unless they can be reconciled by some opinion or assertion lying between the opinions described above. I therefore wish to know whether there is any middle opinion between the views recited earlier. Master. It seems to some that the passages mentioned can be reconciled by one middle opinion.

units.la: Ad cuius euidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod ad ecclesiam spectat duplex punitio seu correctio, vna in foro poenitentiali: alia in foro contentioso, prima spectat ad iudicem ecclesiasticum respectu cuiuslibet Christiani pro quocunque peccato, & de illa multae auctoritates loquentes de illa materia debent intelligi, & istam nulla auctoritas allegata negat ab ecclesiastico iudice. Secunda correctio in criminibus secularibus in triplici casu spectat ad iudicem ecclesiasticum. Primus est, quando criminosi iurisdictioni temporalis iudicis ecclesiastici sunt subiecti. Secundus est, quando non est iudex secularis, vel quando iudex secularis est negligens facere iustitiam vel crimina punire. Tertius est, quando iudex secularis nullam potest delinquenti poenam inferre, cui tamen potest iudex ecclesiasticus poenam inferre, quod contingit, quando de iure est crimen manifestum: sed persona delinquens est ignota, quemadmodum fuit de illo, de quo legimus 5. q. 1. c. quidam maligno spiritu, qui scripsit libellum famosum contra Castorium notarium ac responsalem, quem Grego. poena excommunicationis astrinxit nesciens quis esset, quomodo iudex secularis, quamdiu ignorauit personam delinquentis, nulla potuit poena punire, & isto modo saepe iudices ecclesiastici excommunicationis sententiam proferunt in fures & alios delinquentes occultos, contra quos iudices seculares nullo modo possunt procedere.
units.tr: To make this plain, it should be understood that the Church has a twofold punishment or correction: one in the penitential forum, the other in the contentious forum. The first belongs to the ecclesiastical judge with respect to any Christian for any sin, and the many authorities speaking on that subject ought to be understood of it; no authority cited denies this to the ecclesiastical judge. The second correction, in secular crimes, belongs to the ecclesiastical judge in three cases. The first is when the offenders are subject to the temporal jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical judge. The second is when there is no secular judge, or when the secular judge is negligent in doing justice or punishing crimes. The third is when the secular judge can inflict no penalty on the offender, while the ecclesiastical judge can inflict one; this happens when by law the crime is manifest but the offending person is unknown. An example of this is the case we read of in 5 q. 1 c. Quidam, where a man of malicious spirit wrote a defamatory libel against Castorius, a notary and advocate, and Gregory bound him with the penalty of excommunication without knowing who he was. For as long as the secular judge does not know the person of the offender, he can impose no penalty; and in this way ecclesiastical judges often pronounce sentence of excommunication against thieves and other hidden offenders, against whom secular judges can in no way proceed.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: In quo obiiciendo ponuntur sex casus, in quibus causa secularis spectat ad iudicem ecclesiasticum.
units.tr: In which, by way of objection, six cases are set out in which a secular matter falls under an ecclesiastical judge.

units.la: Discipulus. De primo casu & tertio praedictorum nolo hic discutere, quia directe spectare videntur ad tractatum de potestate papae & cleri, sed secundum cupio aliqualiter tecum discutere. Primo autem cupio scire, an sit aliquis alius casus a praedictis, in quo iudex ecclesiasticus secundum praedictos opinantes inuito iudice seculari valeat plectere criminibus secularibus irretitos, qui iurisdictioni secularis ecclesiae minime sunt subiecti. Magister. Videtur eis, quod in nullo casu posset hoc iudex ecclesiasticus, nisi forte sit aliquis casus, qui valeat reduci ad aliquem praedictorum. Discipul. Contra hoc est Glo. expresse, ut videtur, extra de foro compe. c. licet, quae dicit in haec verba, super verbo vacante: Iste ergo est unus casus, in quo iudex ecclesiasticus potest se immiscere iurisdictioni seculari, scilicet cum superior non inveniatur. Alius est, cum iudex secularis negligit facere iustitiam, ut patet in c. proximo, arg. 23. q. 5. administratores. Tertius est, cum aliquid ambiguum fuerit & difficile & inter iudices variatur, extra qui filii sint legitimi, per venerabilem. Quartus casus est in omni crimine ecclesiastico, puta in usura & sacrilegio, & consimilibus, ut 5. q. 2. c. 1. & 12. q. 11. c. nulli liceat, & infra de usuris qui, qui metus causa. Quintus casus est cum per denunciationem criminis quis deseritur ad iudicem ecclesiasticum, ut supra 6. proximi novit. Item ratione connexitatis, quia potest iudex ecclesiasticus iudicare de dote, ex quo cognoscit de matrimonio, de dono dato inter virum & uxorem, de prudentia. Ex ista Glo. aperte patet, quod praeter omnes praedictos sunt tres casus, scilicet tertius, qui hic est enumeratus, & quintus & sextus, in quibus potest iudex ecclesiasticus immiscere se iurisdictioni seculari. Et per consequens in quibus potest punire criminibus secularibus irretitos: licet non sint iurisdictioni seculari ecclesiae subiecti, & licet ista videantur manifesta ex Glos. tamen dic quomodo respondetur ad ipsa. Magister. Respondetur, quod in quibusdam casibus potest iudex ecclesiasticus instruendo, monendo, & etiam praecipiendo immiscere se causis secularibus: in quibus tamen crimina secularia inuito iudice seculari (qui paratus est exhibere iustitiae complementum) punire non potest, nec etiam valet in eis diffinitiuam proferre sententiam: sed proserenda est sententia a iudice seculari, qui iustitiam facere est paratus, & si sic intelligit Glos. praedicta, est consona veritati, si autem aliter intelligit, sacris canonibus contradicit. Discip. Quibus canonibus contradicit? Magister. Dicitur, quod contradicit canoni Alexan. tertii, qui, ut legitur extra, de foro compe. 6. ex transmissa, ait: Ex transmissa nobis insinuatione Be. & VV. militum ecclesiae tuae intelleximus, quod cum R. de Casmiale eas super quadam possessione coram Trecen. episcopo traxisset in causam: nobilis vir de Capis eorum Dominus sub debito fidelitatis inhibuit ei, ne de seculari feudo in iudicio ecclesiastico responderet, & ita per Dominum feudi causam iubeas terminari: & si ipse maliciose distulerit, tu ei debitum finem imponas. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod iudex ecclesiasticus de causa spectante ad iudicem secularem, se intromittere non debet, imponendo per sententiam finem causae, si iudex secularis potest & vult iustitiam facere. Item dicunt, quod illud contradicit canoni Innocentii, qui, ut habetur ibidem c. ex tenore, ait: vos igitur attendentes, quod sic summus cum vidua iniustitiam debitores, quod aliis iniustitiam facere non debemus: mandamus quatenus, nisi sit talis causa, quae ad ecclesiasticum iudicem noscatur pertinere, ei supersedere curetis, dummodo per iudicem secularem suam possit iustitiam obtinere, alioquin non obstante contradictione ipsius, causam ipsam ratione praetia terminetis. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod iudex ecclesiasticus causae seculari supersedere debet, quandocunque iustitia potest per iudicem secularem obtineri.
units.tr: Disciple. I do not want to discuss here the first and third of the cases mentioned above, because they seem to belong directly to the treatise on the power of the Pope and the clergy. But I wish to discuss the second with you in some detail. First, though, I want to know whether there is any case other than those listed in which an ecclesiastical judge, according to the opinion of those I have mentioned, could punish with secular penalties people caught in secular crimes who are in no way subject to the secular jurisdiction of the Church, even without the consent of the secular judge. Master. It seems to them that an ecclesiastical judge could in no case do this, unless perhaps some case can be reduced to one of those listed. Disciple. Against this, the Gloss seems plainly to say, extra de foro compe. c. licet, where, on the word "vacante," it says in these words: Here is one case in which an ecclesiastical judge may interfere in secular jurisdiction, namely when no superior is to be found. Another is when a secular judge neglects to do justice, as appears in the next chapter, arg. 23. q. 5. administratores. A third is when something is doubtful and difficult and varies among judges, extra qui filii sint legitimi, per venerabilem. A fourth case is in every ecclesiastical crime, for example usury, sacrilege and the like, as in 5. q. 2. c. 1 and 12. q. 11. c. nulli liceat, and infra de usuris qui, qui metus causa. A fifth case is when someone is brought before an ecclesiastical judge by the denunciation of a crime, as above in 6. proximi novit. Likewise by reason of connection, since an ecclesiastical judge can decide about a dowry, since he takes cognisance of the marriage, about a gift given between husband and wife, and about prudence. From this Gloss it is clearly evident that, apart from all those mentioned, there are three cases, namely the third, which is listed here, and the fifth and sixth, in which an ecclesiastical judge can interfere in secular jurisdiction, and consequently in which he can punish people caught in secular crimes, even though they are not subject to the secular jurisdiction of the Church. And although these points seem plain from the Gloss, tell me how they are answered. Master. The answer is that in certain cases an ecclesiastical judge may, by instructing, admonishing and even commanding, interfere in secular causes; yet he cannot punish secular crimes in them against the will of the secular judge, who is ready to render full justice, nor can he pronounce a definitive sentence in them. The sentence must be pronounced by the secular judge, who is ready to do justice. If the Gloss is understood in this way, it agrees with the truth; but if it is understood otherwise, it contradicts the sacred canons. Disciple. Which canons does it contradict? Master. It is said to contradict the canon of Alexander III, who, as is read extra, de foro compe. 6. ex transmissa, says: From the report sent to us by Be. and VV., knights of your church, we learned that when R. de Casmiale had brought them to court before the bishop of Troyes concerning a certain possession, the noble lord de Capis, their lord, under the obligation of fealty, forbade them to answer in an ecclesiastical court concerning a secular fief; and so you are to have the case decided by the lord of the fief; and if he maliciously delays, you are to impose a due end upon him. From these words it is gathered that an ecclesiastical judge must not intrude into a matter belonging to the secular judge, by imposing an end to the case through a sentence, if the secular judge is able and willing to do justice. They also say that it contradicts the canon of Innocent, who, as is found in the same place, c. ex tenore, says: Therefore, considering that if we were to do injustice to the widow, the debtors would do injustice to others, we command that, unless it is such a case as is known to belong to an ecclesiastical judge, you take care to set aside the matter, provided that justice can be obtained through the secular judge; otherwise, notwithstanding his objection, you are to bring the case to an end on the basis of the (lawful) claim. From these words it is gathered that an ecclesiastical judge ought to set aside a secular cause whenever justice can be obtained through the secular judge.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad tertium casum, capitulo praecedenti in obiectione adductum.
units.tr: In which the third case, adduced in the objection in the preceding chapter, is answered.

units.la: Discipulus. Cum isti dicunt, quod nunquam ecclesiasticus iudex potest, vel debet punire clericos secularibus inuolutos, vel iudicialiter se intromittere de causa spectante ad iudicem secularem, diffinitiuam proferendo sententiam, quando iudex secularis potest & vult iustitiae plenitudinem adhibere, dic quomodo ad ista, quae Glo. praescripta allegat, in contrarium respondetur. Mag. Ad istud, quod adducitur de difficili & ambiguo in tertio casu, quem ponit: respondetur, quod saepe inter seculares iudices iudicium difficile & ambiguum prospicitur, cuius veritas absque auctoritate scripturarum sacrarum iudicari non potest: & in illo casu recurrendum est praecipue ad summum pontificem, ad quem spectat potissime in hoc casu iudicare iudicii veritatem: non quidem, in causa aliqua speciali, proferendo diffinitiuam sententiam, quando iudex secularis, cognita veritate, paratus est facere iustam sententiam, sed per auctoritatem scripturae diuinae debet indicare iudicii veritatem docendo, monendo & etiam praecipiendo, si oportet, ut quod iudex scilicet secularis, cuius interest iustitiae faciat complementum: quod si iudex secularis non voluerit, vel non potuerit, summus pontifex in pluribus casibus potest ferre iustam sententiam, & in quibusdam casibus, scilicet in causis sanguinis, debet hoc aliis committere. Discipul. Potest ne ista responsio aliqua ratione fulciri? Magist. Videtur, quod haec responsio tali ratione potest muniri, in auctoritate Domini Innocentii allegata immediate dicitur, quod si difficile & ambiguum apud te iudicium esse prospexeris inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, lepram & non lepram, & iudicium interportas videris variari, venies ad sacerdotem Leviticiae generis, & ad iudicem, qui illo tempore fuerit (per quos Innocentius intelligit summum pontificem & coadiutores) qui iudicabunt iudicii veritatem. Sed constat, quod circa causas sanguinis difficile & ambiguum potest apparere iudicium: potestque circa eos iudicium secularium variari. Igitur in casu pro causis sanguinis est ad summum pontificem recurrendum: non quod exercear iudicium in causis sanguinis, sed ut iudicet in genere, quale iudicium a secularibus iudicibus in talibus causis debeat exerceri.
