Igitur similiter in quibuscunque causis secularibus civilibus vel criminalibus, quandocunque inter iudices seculares difficile & ambiguum apparet iudicium, & inter eos iudicium variatur, recurrendum est potissime ad pontificem, ut indicet iudicii veritatem, non diffiniendo sed docendo & monendo, & si necesse fuerit praecipiendo, iuxta illud Malachiae 2. labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam & legem exquirent ex ore eius. Discipulus. Per istam rationem sufficeret, quod in tali casu iudices seculares recurrerent ad aliquem in sacris literis eruditum, qui eis per scripturas sacras sciret indicare iudicii veritatem. Magist. Respondetur, quod si iudices seculares parati essent (comperta veritate iudicii iustitiam perhibere) sufficeret, quod ad eruditum in sacris scripturis recurrerent: sed quia posset contingere, quod iudices seculares vel noluntaudire seu acceptare iudicii veritatem, vel nollent etiam facere iustitiam, etiam cognita veritate, ideo possent esse quam plures casus, in quibus necesse esset recurrere ad illum, qui habet praecipiendi auctoritatem principibus secularibus, ut iustitiam facerent, qui (etsi nollent) potest per se, vel per alios supplere negligentiam vel malitiam eorundem.
units.tr: Disciple. When these men say that an ecclesiastical judge can never, and ought never, punish clerics who are involved in secular matters, or judicially interfere in a case belonging to the secular judge by pronouncing a definitive sentence, when the secular judge is able and willing to apply the full measure of justice, tell me how they respond to the arguments the Gloss cites against this. Master. As to what is raised about the difficult and ambiguous matter in the third case which he poses: it is answered that secular judges often face a difficult and ambiguous judgment, whose truth cannot be decided without the authority of the sacred Scriptures. In that case recourse must be had above all to the supreme pontiff, to whom it belongs most of all in such a case to determine the truth of the judgment. Not indeed by pronouncing a definitive sentence in some particular cause, when the secular judge, having learned the truth, is ready to give a just sentence, but by the authority of divine Scripture he ought to indicate the truth of the judgment, by teaching, admonishing and, if need be, commanding, so that the secular judge, whose duty it is, may complete what is just. But if the secular judge is unwilling or unable, the supreme pontiff in many cases can pronounce a just sentence, and in certain cases, namely in causes of blood, he ought to commit this to others. Disciple. Can this answer be supported by any reason? Master. It seems that this answer can be fortified by the following reasoning. In the authority of Pope Innocent cited above, it is said directly: If you see that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and not leprosy, and you see the judgments within your gates varying, you shall come to the priest of the Levitical race, and to the judge who shall then be (by whom Innocent understands the supreme pontiff and his assistants), and they shall judge the truth of the judgment. But it is clear that a judgment can appear difficult and ambiguous in matters of blood, and that the judgments of secular judges can vary in such cases. Therefore, in the case of causes of blood, recourse must be had to the supreme pontiff, not so that he may exercise judgment in causes of blood, but so that he may decide in general what kind of judgment ought to be exercised by secular judges in such causes. Therefore, similarly, in whatever civil or criminal secular causes it ever appears that the judgment is difficult and ambiguous among secular judges, and their judgments vary, recourse must be had above all to the pontiff, so that he may indicate the truth of the judgment, not by defining but by teaching and admonishing, and, if necessary, by commanding, in accordance with Malachi 2: The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they seek the law at his mouth. Disciple. By this reasoning it would suffice that in such a case secular judges should have recourse to someone learned in the sacred letters, who could indicate to them from the sacred Scriptures the truth of the judgment. Master. It is answered that if the secular judges were prepared, once the truth of the judgment was known, to render justice, it would suffice for them to have recourse to one learned in the sacred Scriptures. But since it could happen that secular judges either would not wish to hear or accept the truth of the judgment, or would not wish to do justice even when the truth is known, there could be many cases in which it would be necessary to have recourse to the one who has the authority to command secular princes to do justice, and who (even if they were unwilling) can himself, or through others, make up for the negligence or malice of those men.

units.la: Discip. Unde habet solus pontifex hanc potestatem? Mag. Sicut invenire poteris in tractatu de potestate papae & cleri. Circa hoc sunt diversae ac contrariae opiniones. Una est, quod hoc habet ex Christi ordinatione expressa, alia est, quod hoc habet ex consuetudine rationabili & praescripta. Discipulus. Videtur, quod ista Innocentii textui aperte repugnat, nam Innocentius in decretali per venerabilem, non dicit, quod cum difficile & ambiguum prospicitur iudicium, ad summum pontificem spectat indicare iudicii veritatem solummodo docendo & praecipiendo, sed sic quod ad ipsum pertinet in hoc casu iurisdictionem temporalem exercere, dicit enim haec verba: Verum etiam in aliis regionibus, certis casibus inspectis temporalem iurisdictionem casualiter exercemus: non quia alieno iuri praeiudicare velimus, sed quia sicut in Deuteronomio continetur, si difficile & ambiguum &c. & infra: in quibus cum aliquid fuerit difficile & ambiguum, ad iudicium est sedis Apostolicae recurrendum, cuius sententiam si superbiens contempserit observare, mori praecipitur, id est per excommunicationis sententiam velut morbum a communione separari. Ex quibus verbis colligitur: quod papa in casu praedicto temporalem exercendo iustitiam fert sententiam. Magister. Respondetur, quod sicut quaedam verba Innocentii in eadem decretali videntur quasi violenter exponenda, ut ab haeretica pravitate salvantur: sic verba ista sane debent exponi, ne perperam & iniuste iniquis imperatoris & aliorum laicorum praeiudicare monstrentur.
units.tr: Disc. From where does the pontiff alone have this power? Mag. As you may find in the treatise on the power of the Pope and the clergy. Concerning this there are diverse and contrary opinions. One is that he has this from an express ordinance of Christ; the other is that he has it from reasonable and long-established custom. Disciple. It seems that this openly contradicts the text of Innocent, for Innocent, in the decretal Per venerabilem, does not say that when a judgment appears difficult and ambiguous it belongs to the supreme pontiff to indicate the truth of the judgment only by teaching and commanding, but in such a way that it belongs to him in this case to exercise temporal jurisdiction. For he uses these words: Moreover, in other regions too, in certain cases that have been examined, we exercise temporal jurisdiction by way of occasion: not because we wish to prejudice another's right, but because, as is contained in Deuteronomy, if a matter is difficult and ambiguous, etc.; and below: in which cases, when something is difficult and ambiguous, recourse must be had to the judgment of the Apostolic See, and whoever proudly scorns to observe its sentence is commanded to die, that is, to be separated from communion by the sentence of excommunication as by a disease. From these words it is gathered that the Pope, in the aforesaid case, pronounces a sentence while exercising temporal justice. Master. It is answered that just as certain words of Innocent in the same decretal seem to require forced interpretation, so that they may be saved from heretical depravity, so these words too must certainly be interpreted, lest they be shown to prejudice unjustly and wrongly the rights of the emperor and of other laymen.

units.la: Disc. Quae sunt illa verba Innocentii, quae sunt violenter exponenda, ut ab haeretica pravitate salvantur? Magister. Nonnullis apparet, quod ista verba Innocentii sunt: cum Deuteronomii lex secunda interpretatur ex vi vocabuli comprobatur: ut quod ibi decrevimus, in novo testamento debeat observari: nisi violenter exponantur, sapiunt haeresim manifestam: scilicet quod ceremonialia veteris legis in novo testamento debeant observari, eo quod ceremonialia, quae videntur, decernuntur, sicut patet fere per totum. Discipulus. Innocentius intelligit, quod illa quae decernuntur in Deuteronomio, spiritualiter observanda sunt in novo testamento, non ad literam, nec ad sensum literalem.
units.tr: Disc. What are those words of Innocent which must be forcibly interpreted so that they may be saved from heretical depravity? Master. To some it appears that these are the words of Innocent: Since the second law of Deuteronomy is interpreted by the force of the term, it is proved that what we have decreed there ought to be observed in the New Testament. Unless these words are forcibly interpreted, they savour of manifest heresy, namely that the ceremonial matters of the Old Law ought to be observed in the New Testament, because the ceremonial matters which are decreed are, as is almost everywhere evident. Disciple. Innocent means that those things which are decreed in Deuteronomy are to be observed spiritually in the New Testament, not according to the letter, nor according to the literal sense.

units.la: Magister. Magist. Videtur quod hoc non sufficit, nam illo modo omnia ceremonialia & quæcunque continentur in aliis libris Pentateucon & in aliis libris veteris testamenti sunt seruanda in nouo testamento, teste Gratiano, qui distinct. 6. dicit: sunt in lege quædam moralia, vt, non occides &c. quædam mystica, vt pote sacrificiorum præcepta, vt de agno, & bis similia, moralia mandata ad naturale ius spectant, atque nonnullam imitationem recepisse monstrantur, mystica vero quantum ad superficiem & à naturali iure probantur aliena, sed quantum ad moralem intellectionem inueniuntur sibi annexa, ac per hoc sunt & ad superficiem videntur esse imitata: tamen secundum moralem intelligentiam, imitabilitatem nescire probantur. Innocentius autem simpliciter dicit illa, quæ in Deuteronomio decernuntur, seruanda esse in nouo testamento, innuens quod illa, quæ decernuntur in aliis libris Pentateucon, non sunt seruanda in nouo testamento, aut ergo intellexit, quod illa quæ decernuntur in Deuteronomio, sunt seruanda in nouo testamento secundum sensum literalem, & hoc est hæreticum: aut secundum sensum moralem, & sic illa quæ decernuntur in aliis libris, sunt seruanda in nouo testamento. Discipul. Quomodo possunt exponi verba Innocentii superius scripta, quod nec vnum sapiant errorem, nec alium, quod scilicet ceremonialia, quæ Deutronomii decernuntur, sunt secundum su- perficiem literæ in nouo testamento seruanda, vel quod ceremonialia vel mystica, quæ in aliis libris decernuntur, non sunt seruanda secundum moralem intelligentiam in nouo testamento? Magist. Potest dici, quod Innocentius intelligit, quod non solum ex natura rei videtur haberi, quod illa quæ decernuntur in Deuteronomio secundum moralem intelligentiam seruanda sunt in nouo testamento: sed etiam quod hoc habetur ex vi vocabuli, eo quod Deuteronomium lex secunda interpretatur.
units.tr: Master. Master. It seems that this is not enough, for in that way all the ceremonial matters and whatever is contained in the other books of the Pentateuch and in the other books of the Old Testament would have to be observed in the New Testament, as Gratian attests, who in Distinction 6 says: There are in the law certain moral precepts, such as, Thou shalt not kill, etc.; certain mystical ones, such as the precepts concerning sacrifices, concerning the lamb, and the like. The moral commandments pertain to natural law, and are shown to have received some imitation; the mystical ones, as far as the surface goes, are proved to be foreign to natural law, but as far as their moral understanding goes, they are found to be joined to it, and thereby they are, and on the surface seem to be, imitated; yet according to their moral meaning they are proved not to be capable of imitation. But Innocent simply says that those things which are decreed in Deuteronomy are to be observed in the New Testament, implying that those things which are decreed in the other books of the Pentateuch are not to be observed in the New Testament. Either, then, he understood that the things decreed in Deuteronomy are to be observed in the New Testament according to the literal sense, and this is heretical; or according to the moral sense, and so the things decreed in the other books are to be observed in the New Testament. Disciple. How can the words of Innocent written above be explained so that they savour neither of one error nor of the other, namely that the ceremonial matters decreed in Deuteronomy are to be observed in the New Testament according to the surface of the letter, or that the ceremonial or mystical matters decreed in the other books are not to be observed according to moral understanding in the New Testament? Master. It can be said that Innocent means that it is held not only from the nature of the thing that those things decreed in Deuteronomy are to be observed in the New Testament according to moral understanding, but also that this is held from the force of the term, since Deuteronomium is interpreted as the second law.

units.la: Discipul. Nunc dic, quomodo exponuntur alia verba eiusdem Innocentii, ne iuribus imperatoris & aliorum laicorum præiudicare monstrentur. Magist. Dicitur, quod verba præscripta Innocentii intelligenda sunt, quando imperator & alii clerici non volunt secundum veritatem iudicii facere iustitiæ complementum, tunc enim potest papa casualiter iurisdictionem temporalem exercendo in causis spectantibus ad imperatorem & alios laicos, diffinitiuam ferre sententiam.
units.tr: Disciple. Now tell me how the other words of this same Innocent are to be explained, so that it is shown they do not prejudice the rights of the emperor and of other laymen. Master. It is said that the words of Innocent cited above are to be understood when the emperor and other clerics are unwilling to do justice according to the truth of judgment; for then the pope, exercising temporal jurisdiction by way of exception in causes that belong to the emperor and other laymen, may pass a final sentence.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad probationes minoris argumenti, supra capitulo 10. adducti.
units.tr: In which replies are given to the proofs of the lesser argument, adduced above in chapter 10.

units.la: Discipulus. Quia ista tertia sententia auctoritates, quæ videntur contrariæ, nititur concordare, & nullam vult negare: discurramus per eas, & videamus secundum istam sententiam, quomodo debent intelligi, per hoc enim melius ad veritatem istius forsan materiæ potero peruenire. Dic itaque primo, quomodo secundum opinionem istam decretalis illa debeat intelligi: scilicet extra de officio iudicis ordinarii, perniciosam. supra 10. c. allegata.
units.tr: Disciple. Since this third opinion seeks to reconcile the authorities that seem to conflict, and wishes to deny none of them, let us run through them and see how they must be understood according to this opinion; for by this means I may perhaps arrive more readily at the truth of this matter. Tell me first, then, how that decretal, Extra, De officio iudicis ordinarii, Perniciosam, cited above in chapter 10, is to be understood according to this opinion.

units.la: Magist. Vno modo respondetur, quod decretalis ista loquitur de potestate inquirendi, vlciscendi & iudicandi adulteria & alia scelera clericorum, & illorum, qui temporali iurisdictioni episcoporum sunt subiecti. Aliter dicitur, quod loquitur indistincte de omnibus, quando iudices seculares negligunt adulteria & alia scelera secularia debita animaduersione punire, sic enim in multis regionibus iudices ecclesiastici puniunt fornicationes & alia plura scelera, quia iudices seculares talia crimina non puniunt, vel fauent huiusmodi criminosis, & ideo si iudices seculares de fornicationibus, adulteriis & huiusmodi criminibus secularibus, debitam & sufficientem sumerent vltionem, iudices ecclesiastici de ipsis puniendis, inuitis iudicibus secularibus & prohibentibus, se intromittere non deberent.
units.tr: Master. It is answered in one way that this decretal speaks of the power of inquiring into, avenging and judging adultery and other crimes of clerics, and of those who are subject to the temporal jurisdiction of bishops. Otherwise it is said that it speaks indiscriminately of all persons, when secular judges neglect to punish adultery and other secular crimes with due censure. For in many regions ecclesiastical judges punish fornication and many other crimes because secular judges do not punish such crimes, or favour those guilty of them; and therefore, if secular judges were to exact due and sufficient vengeance for fornication, adultery and such secular crimes, ecclesiastical judges ought not to meddle in punishing them against the will and prohibition of the secular judges.

units.la: Discipulus. Hæc responsio, quantum ad crimen adulterii, veritati videtur contraria, cum adulterium, crimen ecclesiasticum sit censendum, & ad iudicem ecclesiasticum spectat, nam ad eundem iudicem spectat crimen adulterii, ad quem causæ matrimoniales pertinere noscuntur, sed causæ matrimoniales ad iudicem ecclesiasticum spectant, vt notat Glo. de foro compe. ex tenore, allegans c. extra de officio delegati causam quæ & c. extra de consan. & affini. ex literis. igitur & crimen adulterii spectat ad ecclesiasticum iudicem. Mag. Respondetur, quod tam crimen adulterii, quam causa matrimonialis, aliquo modo spectat ad iudicem ecclesiasticum, & aliquo modo ad iudicem secularem. Cuius ratio assignatur. Quia matrimonia non solum reperiuntur apud fideles lege ecclesiastica & diuina vtentes: verum etiam apud infideles & sola lege naturæ contentos, & ideo causa matrimonialis, in quantum matrimonium est à lege diuina, spectat ad ecclesiasticum iudicem, & in quantum est à lege naturæ, spectat ad iudicem secularem. Similiter crimen adulterii, in quantum est contra matrimonium, prout est à lege diuina, spectat ad iudicem ecclesiasticum. In quantum autem est contra matrimonium, prout est à lege naturæ, spectat ad iudicem secularem. Unde crimen adulterii, in quantum est contra prohibitionem diuinam vel ecclesiasticam, est puniendum per iudicem ecclesiasticum: sed adulterium, vt est contra matrimonium, vt à lege naturæ est, per secularem iudicem est puniendum. Et ideo si non est contra legem naturæ, quod vnus vir habeat plures mulieres, sed sit solum contra legem diuinam & ecclesiasticam, qui prius contraheret cum vna, & postea cum alia, quam cognosceret, pro adulterio non esset puniendus, per iudicem secularem, quia iudex secularis, post solam legem naturæ non iudicarent ipsum adulterum, sed puniendus esset per iudicem ecclesiasticum, qui per legem diuinam vel ecclesiasticam ipsum adulterum puniret. Discip. Dic qualiter respondetur ad decretalem Innocentii tertii, extra, de iudiciis, nouit. Magister. Dicitur, quod Innocentius signanter dicit, ad suum officium pertinere de quocunque peccato mortali quemlibet Christianum corrigere: non tamen semper spectat ad ipsum punire quemlibet Christianum de peccato mortali quocunque de foro contentioso, hoc enim esset totaliter absorbere potestatem puniendi crimina, quam habet imperator & alii iudices seculares. Quando tamen correctus de peccato mortali contemnit correctionem, & non est aliquis iudex secularis, qui contemnentem pro peccato commisso plectat: digne potest papa ipsum per districtionem ecclesiasticam coercere: in eo casu loquitur Innocentius: quem etiam (licet sit iudex secularis, qui sufficienter ipsum punit) pro primo crimine seculari potest punire pro contemptu, quo contemnit correctionem ecclesiæ, quia iste contemptus, quando est criminalis, debet inter crimina ecclesiastica computari. Discipul. Videtur, quod quando papa coercet quemlibet Christianum pro quocunque peccato mortali, non totaliter absorbetur potestas imperatoris, & aliorum laicorum, qui crimina secularia habent puniendi potestatem, quia alia est pœna canonica, & alia legalis, & ideo quamuis criminosus à iudice puniatur seculari, pœna legali, poterit nihilominus pro eodem crimine puniri à iudice ecclesiastico pœna canonica. Mag. Hoc videtur pluribus irrationabile, quia, sicut habetur extra de iudiciis, at si clerici, nullus debet duplici pœna puniri, quando vna sufficit. Et ideo qui per iudicem secularem pro aliquo crimine sufficienter punitur, per iudicem ecclesiasticum alia pœna puniri non debet, hoc consuetudo ecclesiæ conseruat, quia raptores & homicidæ & alii scelerati, quando coram iudice seculari conueniuntur & pœna condigna plectuntur, ecclesia eis nullam pœnam publicam imponit, nec extra forum pœnitentiæ pœnitentibus de eis se aliqualiter intromittit. Discipulus. Dic quomodo respondetur ad alios canones, qui in eodem 10. c. adducuntur. Mag. Respondetur, quod omnes debent intelligi, quando iudices seculares in puniendo huiusmodi scelera negligentes sunt: vel quando huiusmodi scelerati sunt occulti, ita quod in iudicio conuinci non possunt.
units.tr: Disciple. This answer, so far as the crime of adultery is concerned, seems contrary to the truth, since adultery is to be reckoned an ecclesiastical crime and belongs to the ecclesiastical judge. For the crime of adultery belongs to the same judge to whom matrimonial causes are known to pertain; but matrimonial causes belong to the ecclesiastical judge, as the gloss notes on De foro competenti, Ex tenore, citing Extra, De officio delegati, Causam quae, and Extra, De consanguinitate et affinitate, Ex literis. Therefore the crime of adultery also belongs to the ecclesiastical judge. Master. It is answered that both the crime of adultery and the matrimonial cause belong in some way to the ecclesiastical judge, and in some way to the secular judge. The reason for this is assigned: because marriages are found not only among the faithful, who use ecclesiastical and divine law, but also among unbelievers who are content with the law of nature alone. Therefore a matrimonial cause, in so far as marriage is from divine law, belongs to the ecclesiastical judge, and in so far as it is from the law of nature, belongs to the secular judge. Likewise the crime of adultery, in so far as it is against marriage as it is from divine law, belongs to the ecclesiastical judge; in so far as it is against marriage as it is from the law of nature, it belongs to the secular judge. Hence adultery, in so far as it is against a divine or ecclesiastical prohibition, is to be punished by the ecclesiastical judge; but adultery, as it is against marriage as it is from the law of nature, is to be punished by the secular judge. And therefore, if it is not against the law of nature for one man to have several wives, but is only against divine and ecclesiastical law, a man who first married one woman and afterwards another, whom he knew, would not be punished for adultery by the secular judge, because the secular judge would not judge that adulterer on the law of nature alone; rather he would be punished by the ecclesiastical judge, who would punish that adulterer by divine or ecclesiastical law. Disciple. Tell me how the decretal of Innocent III, Extra, De iudiciis, Novit, is answered. Master. It is said that Innocent pointedly states that it belongs to his office to correct every Christian for any mortal sin; yet it does not always belong to him to punish every Christian for any mortal sin of the contentious forum, for this would totally absorb the power of punishing crimes which the emperor and other secular judges possess. When, however, one corrected of a mortal sin scorns the correction, and there is no secular judge who may punish the contemnor for the sin committed, the pope may rightly restrain him by ecclesiastical censure. It is in that case that Innocent speaks; and him too (although there is a secular judge who sufficiently punishes him) he may punish for the first secular crime on account of the contempt by which he scorns the correction of the Church, because this contempt, when it is criminal, ought to be counted among ecclesiastical crimes. Disciple. It seems that when the pope restrains any Christian for any mortal sin, the power of the emperor and other laymen, who have the power of punishing secular crimes, is not totally absorbed; for the canonical penalty is one thing and the legal penalty another, and therefore, although the criminal is punished by a secular judge with a legal penalty, he may nevertheless be punished for the same crime by an ecclesiastical judge with a canonical penalty. Master. This seems to most people unreasonable, because, as is held in Extra, De iudiciis, At si clerici, no one ought to be punished with a double penalty when one is sufficient. And therefore one who is sufficiently punished by a secular judge for some crime ought not to be punished by an ecclesiastical judge with another penalty; the custom of the Church preserves this, because when robbers, murderers and other wicked men are brought before a secular judge and suffer a fitting penalty, the Church imposes no public penalty on them, nor in any way meddles with them outside the forum of penance for those who repent. Disciple. Tell me how the other canons, which are adduced in the same chapter 10, are answered. Master. It is answered that they must all be understood when secular judges are negligent in punishing such crimes, or when such wicked men are hidden, so that they cannot be convicted in judgement.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad auctoritates sacræ scripturæ capitulo 1o. adductas.
units.tr: In which the authorities of Holy Scripture cited in chapter 1 are answered.

units.la: Discipulus. Specialiter desidero scire, quomodo secundum eandem assertionem respondetur ad auctoritates, quæ de sacris literis adducuntur. Magist. Ad auctoritatem Saluatoris: si peccauerit in te frater tuus &c. multipliciter respondetur. Vno modo, quod intelligitur, quando iudex secularis negligens est in faciendo iustitiam. Aliter dicitur, quod per illa verba Saluatoris non tribuitur aliqua potestas iudicibus ecclesiasticis plus quam iudicibus secularibus, nam ibi non capitur ecclesia pro viris ecclesiasticis, qui clerici appellantur: sed pro congregatione fidelium vniuersali vel particulari, quæ clericos & laicos comprehendit, dicunt enim, quod in tota scriptura diuina non capitur hoc nomen ecclesia specialiter pro clericis: licet sic sæpe capiatur in canonibus sacris. Voluit igitur Saluator, quod peccatum delinquentis post secretam correctionem & adhibitionem testium, vltimo diceretur alicui congregationi fidelium laicorum, vel clericorum, vel simul vtrorumque, quod si non audiret, haberetur sicut Ethnicus & publicanus. Aliter dicitur, quod per illa verba ecclesiæ nulla datur potestas puniendi peccantes: sed solummodo attribuitur ei potestas corrigendi absque punitione aliqua. Nam per illa verba nihil plus attribuitur ecclesiæ, quam fratri, in quem peccatur, & testibus adhibitis, sicut enim dicitur: si te non audierit, adhibe tecum adhuc vnum vel duos testes. Et sicut dicitur si illos non audierit, dic ecclesiæ, ita dicitur, & si ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut Ethnicus & publicanus, per quæ verba innuitur, quod vltimo debet facere ecclesia illud, quod prius fecit frater, in quem spectabatur, & quod fecerunt testes adhibiti, quo facto ille, in quem peccatur, debet ipsum peccantem reputare Ethnicum & publicanum. Quia ibi dicitur, sit tibi sicut Ethnicus & publicanus, hoc est vita eorum sicut Ethnicum & publicanum amore iustitiæ & propter bonum commune. Vel, vt boni inter malos quiete viuant, trade eum iudici, qui de eo faciet complementum iustitiæ. Sed per prædicta verba Saluatoris non tribuitur Fratri, in quem peccatur, nec testibus adhibitis, potestas puniendi fratrem delinquentem, sed solummodo corrigendi. Igitur per eadem verba solummodo attribuitur ecclesiæ potestas delinquentem corrigendi. Quod tali ratione probatur, non magis licet fidelibus præiudicare imperatori & aliis laicis fidelibus, quam infidelibus: nec magis debent istis vel illis præiudicare vsurpando potestatem puniendi reos, qui puniendi sunt per illos: aut in negando eis censum, vel dignitatem temporalem in eorum præiudicium vsurpando. Sed Christus noluit, vt fideles præiudicarent imperatori infideli, negando ei censum, cum dixerit Matth. 12. reddite Cæsari quæ sunt Cæsaris: nec voluit, quod aliquis fidelium vsurparet sibi aliquam dignitatem temporalem in præiudicium imperatoris infidelis, in cuius signum noluit fieri rex temporalis super Iudæos, Ioh. 6. igitur etiam per prædicta verba noluit tribuere fidelibus potestatem puniendi reos, qui essent plectendi per alios.
units.tr: Student. I particularly want to know how, on the same assertion, the authorities drawn from the sacred letters are answered. Master. To the saying of the Saviour, "If your brother sins against you," and so on, there are several answers. In one way: it applies when the secular judge is negligent in doing justice. Another answer is that these words of the Saviour give no power to the church judges beyond that of the secular judges, for the word "church" is not there taken for churchmen, who are called clerics, but for the whole or a particular congregation of the faithful, which includes clerics and laymen alike. For they say that in the whole of divine Scripture this name "church" is not taken specifically for clerics, although it is often so taken in the sacred canons. The Saviour therefore willed that, after a private correction and the calling in of witnesses, the sin of the offender should at last be reported to some congregation of the faithful, whether of laymen, of clerics, or of both together; and that if he did not listen, he should be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. Another answer is that by these words no power of punishing sinners is given to the church, but only the power of correcting them without any punishment. For by these words nothing more is granted to the church than to the brother against whom the sin is committed, together with the witnesses called in, since it is said: "If he will not hear you, take with you one or two more witnesses." And just as it is said, "If he will not hear them, tell the church," so it is said, "And if he will not hear the church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector." By these words it is implied that the church must at last do what the brother against whom the sin was committed did before, and what the witnesses called in did; and when this is done, the one against whom the sin was committed ought to regard the sinner as a heathen and a tax collector. For it is said there, "let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector," that is, treat him as such in your way of life, out of love of justice and for the common good; or, so that the good may live quietly among the wicked, hand him over to the judge, who will carry out the full measure of justice on him. But by the aforementioned words of the Saviour, neither to the brother against whom the sin is committed nor to the witnesses called in is power given to punish the offending brother, but only to correct him. Therefore by the same words only the power of correcting the offender is given to the church. This is proved by the following reasoning: it is no more lawful for the faithful to prejudice the emperor and other lay believers than unbelievers; nor ought they to prejudice these or those by usurping the power of punishing the guilty, who are to be punished by them, or by withholding tribute from them, or by usurping temporal dignity to their prejudice. But Christ did not will that the faithful should prejudice an unbelieving emperor by withholding tribute from him, since he said (Matth. 12.): "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's"; nor did he will that any of the faithful should usurp to himself any temporal dignity to the prejudice of an unbelieving emperor, as a sign of which he refused to be made a temporal king over the Jews (John 6.). Therefore by the aforementioned words he likewise did not will to give the faithful the power of punishing the guilty, who were to be punished by others.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: In quo respondetur ad auctoritatem Apostoli supra cap. 10. ultimate inductam.
units.tr: In which an answer is given to the authority of the Apostle, cited last in chapter 10.

units.la: DIscipulus. Recita quomodo respondetur ad auctoritates Apostoli 1. Corinth. 6. cum dicit: Nescitis quoniam angelos iudicabitis: quanto magis saecularia? Magister. Respondent, quod Apostolus in illo c. non intendit prohibere Corinthiis in omni casu apud infideles iudicare: nec intendit asserere, quod soli fideles habeant saecularia iudicare, & ideo non reprehendit omnes illos, qui in quocunque casu requirebant iudicium infidelium: sic enim tam verbis quam factis sibimetipsi fuisset contrarius, sed reprehendit solummodo illos fideles, qui indiscrete aut malitiose aut scandalose apud infideles & iniquos iudicari volebant. Ad cuius intelligentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod sicut iudex, cum prospexerit aliquos velle litigare coram se, primum debet inducere partes, ut inter se componant antequam incipiant litigare, extra de transactionibus, ut extra de symonia, querelam 5. q. 2. si primates 90. dist. 6. studendum, ubi sic loquitur: studendum est episcopis, ut dissidentes fratres sive clericos sive laicos ad pacem magis quam ad iudicium coerceant, sic praelatus alicuius collegii specialis potest inducere subditos suos, ut si unus adversus alterum negotium habuerit, prius magis componant quam ad iudicium conveniant, & si inter se non potuerint amicabiliter componere, potest eos introducere, ut quando voluerint absque praeiudicio iudicis superioris, primo litigent coram iudice vel iudicibus constituto vel constitutis, aut electo vel electis per ipsos vel per collegium, antequam recurrant absque necessitate ad iudicem extra idem collegium. Sic possent monachi propter multa scandala & inconvenientia evitanda ordinare inter se, ut si monachus haberet causam adversus monachum, vel monasterium adversus monasterium, concordarent, si possent, antequam venirent ad iudicium episcopi, & si non possent absque iudicio concordare, quod antequam ad iudicium episcopi venirent, ipsam causam coram aliquibus monachis constitutis iudicibus vel electis a partibus vel a collegio agitarent: quo ordinato monachi, qui indiscrete vel malitiose aut scandalose relicto iudicio monachorum recurrerent ad iudicium episcoporum, essent merito arguendi: quamuis illi, qui necessitate compulsi, vel ex causa rationabili ad iudicium episcopi recurrerent, non essent reprehendendi, sed in casu laudandi. Ad propositum dicitur, quod Apostolus considerabat, quod aliqui Corinthii indiscrete vel malitiose aut etiam scandalose relictis iudicibus fidelibus, qui erant constituti vel constituendi pro causis fidelium terminandis, apud infideles iudicari volebant absque omni necessitate & utilitate, & hos reprehendit Apostolus: non illos (si qui fuerint) qui compulsi, vel per adversarios, vel ne auctoritati infidelium praeiudicarent, licite iudicari volebant apud eos, unde & ipsemet Paulus non refugit iudicium Caesaris, dicens (sicut legitur Actuum 25.) ad tribunal Caesaris sto: ubi me oportet iudicari. Iudaeis non nocui, sicut tu melius nosti, si enim nocui, aut dignum aliquid morte feci, non recuso mori, si vero nihil est eorum, quae accusant me, nemo potest me illis donare: Caesarem appello.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Recite how the authorities of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 6 are answered, where he says: "Do you not know that you shall judge angels? How much more things pertaining to this life?" MASTER. They answer that the Apostle in that chapter did not intend to forbid the Corinthians from bringing cases before unbelievers in every instance, nor did he intend to assert that only believers have the right to judge temporal matters. For this reason he did not rebuke all those who in any case sought the judgment of unbelievers; for in that case he would have contradicted himself both in word and deed. Rather, he rebuked only those believers who wanted to be judged before unbelievers and the unrighteous in a manner that was indiscreet, malicious, or scandalous. To understand this, it is said that one must observe that just as a judge, when he sees that some wish to litigate before him, should first induce the parties to reach agreement before they begin to litigate (see Extra, "De transactionibus," as in "De simonia," Querela 5, q. 2, "Si primates," and Dist. 90, c. 6, "Studendum"), where it is thus said: "Bishops must take care to restrain brothers who are at odds, whether clerics or laymen, rather toward peace than toward judgment." So too the prelate of a particular college may induce his subjects, so that if one has a dispute against another, they first seek to settle it rather than come before a court; and if they cannot settle it amicably among themselves, he may bring them to the point where, when they wish, without prejudice to a superior judge, they first litigate before the judge or judges appointed, or elected by the parties or by the college, before they needlessly have recourse to a judge outside that same college. Thus monks, in order to avoid many scandals and inconveniences, could arrange among themselves that if one monk had a case against another monk, or one monastery against another, they should come to terms, if they could, before coming to the bishop's court; and if they could not agree without judgment, that before going to the bishop's court they should argue the case before certain monks appointed as judges, chosen by the parties or by the college. Once this was arranged, monks who indiscreetly, maliciously, or scandalously, having set aside the judgment of the monks, had recourse to the judgment of the bishops would rightly be called to account; although those who, compelled by necessity or for a reasonable cause, had recourse to the bishop's judgment would not be blamed but in that case praised. To the point at hand: it is said that the Apostle considered that some Corinthians, indiscreetly, maliciously, or even scandalously, set aside the believing judges who were appointed or to be appointed to settle the cases of believers, and wanted to be judged before unbelievers without any necessity or advantage; and it is these the Apostle rebukes, not those (if there were any) who, compelled either by their adversaries or so as not to prejudice the authority of unbelievers, were willing to be lawfully judged before them. Hence Paul himself did not shun the judgment of Caesar, saying (as we read in Acts 25): "I stand at Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you very well know. For if I have done wrong, or committed anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die; but if none of those things are true of which these accuse me, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar."

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Respondetur rationibus supra capitulo 12. adductis.
units.tr: The reasons adduced above in chapter 12 are answered.

units.la: DIsc. Auctoritates adductae supra cap. 11. non videntur istii tertiae sententiae obviare. Ideo noli indicare, an aliqui respondere conentur ad ipsas, sed dic, quomodo respondetur ad auctoritates & rationes duodecimo capitul allegatas: quia illae videntur tertiae sententiae obviare. Mag. Uno modo respondetur ad ipsas, videlicet quod illae concludunt, quando seculares iudices non inveniuntur circa punitiones criminum saecularium negligentes, unde secundum istam opinionem, si laici circa illa temporalia dispensanda, & circa negotia saecularia & cutas seculares ac circa crimina saecularia punienda in nullo invenirentur defectuosi, seu negligentes vel desides, clerici & maxime episcopi de huiusmodi in nullo se intromittere deberent, sed deceret eos, omnia huiusmodi committere laicis, etiam res ecclesiasticas dispensandas, unde ad literam, sicut verba sonant, ea quae sacri canones (sicut allegatum est, supra c. 11.) circa hoc praecipiunt, adimplere deberent: & tantummodo verbo praedicationis ac lectioni & orationi vacare.
units.tr: Disciple. The authorities adduced above in chapter 11 do not seem to stand in the way of this third opinion. So do not ask whether some people try to answer those authorities; rather tell me how the authorities and reasons alleged in the twelfth chapter are answered, since they seem to stand in the way of the third opinion. Master. There is one way of answering them, namely that they conclude only when secular judges are not found to be negligent in punishing secular crimes. Accordingly, on this opinion, if laymen were found in no way defective or negligent or slack in managing those temporal matters, secular affairs and civil causes, and in punishing secular crimes, then clergy, and especially bishops, ought not to meddle at all in such matters, but it would befit them to commit all such things to laymen, even the management of ecclesiastical property. Thus, taken literally, as the words sound, they ought to fulfil what the sacred canons (as was alleged above, in chapter 11) prescribe on this point, and devote themselves only to the word of preaching, to reading and to prayer.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: Ubi inquiritur, quam potestatem habeat imperator super bonos, & primo utrum in omnibus licitis sibi sit magis obediendum.
units.tr: Where it is asked what power the emperor has over good subjects, and first whether he is to be obeyed in all lawful matters.

units.la: DIscipulus. Quaesivimus, quam potestatem habet imperator super malos: nunc investigemus, qualem potestatem obtineat super bonos sibi subiectos, utrum sibi omnes teneantur in omnibus obedire. Magister. Respondetur, quod in illicitis & iniustis nullus debet sibi obedire.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. We have asked what power the emperor has over the wicked; now let us examine what power he holds over the good who are subject to him, and whether all are bound to obey him in everything. Master. The answer is that no one ought to obey him in what is unlawful and unjust.

units.la: Discipul. Nunquid in omnibus licitis omnes sibi debent obedire, ita ut peccent, qui sibi recusaverint in licito quocunque obedire?
units.tr: Disciple. Must everyone obey him in all lawful matters, so that those who refuse him obedience in any lawful thing sin?

units.la: Hhhh 3 Magister. Magister. Respondetur, quod non ex hoc ipso, quod aliquis in aliquo licito sibi non obedierit, est iudicandus peccare, si enim alicui praecipiat ieiunare, vel non bibere vinum, vel aliquid tale, quod ad officium imperatoris non pertinet, sibi obedire minime tenetur, sed in his, quae spectant ad regimen populi temporalis: & hoc in temporalibus quilibet obedire sibi tenetur.
units.tr: Hhhh 3 Master. Master. The answer is that a person is not to be judged a sinner merely because he has not obeyed the emperor in some lawful matter. If the emperor ordered someone to fast, or not to drink wine, or something of that kind, which does not belong to the emperor's office, that person is by no means bound to obey him. He is bound to obey only in those matters which concern the government of the temporal people, and in temporal matters everyone is bound to obey him.

units.la: Discipul. Nunquid in huiusmodi quilibet tenetur magis obedire imperatori, quam cuilibet alteri: puta regi suo, aut Duci, aut Marchioni, aut alteri Domino suo immediato, videtur enim, quod quemadmodum episcopus est superior abbate, & tamen hoc non obstante in multis monachi magis tenetur obedire abbati quam episcopo: ita non obstante, quod imperator sit superior regibus, ducibus, & aliis Dominis temporalibus, tamen subditi aliorum dominorum magis tenentur obedire Dominis suis immediatis, quam imperatori? Magist. Respondetur, quod sicut secundum multos papa est immediatus praelatus omnium Christianorum in spiritualibus, ita ut omnes in omnibus huiusmodi magis debeant sibi obedire, quam cuicunque alteri praelato inferiori: ita imperator est Dominus in temporalibus omnium immediatus, ita ut in his quae spectant ad regnum mortalium magis sit obediendum imperatori, quam cuicunque Domino inferiori, quod beatus Augustinus super epistolam ad Romanos sentire videtur, qui super illud verbum, qui resistunt, sibi ipsis damnationem acquirunt, ait: Si quid ipse proconsul iubeat, & aliud imperator, nunquid dubitat illo contempto, illi esse seruiendum? Idem in lib. Confessionum 2. & ponitur dist. 8. c. quicunque, ait: In potestatibus societatis humanae maior potestas minori ad obediendum praeponitur. Est igitur semper magis obediendum imperatori, quam cuicunque alteri Domino inferiori. Discip. Ex istis videntur duo sequi inconvenientia. Primum est, quod omnes sunt serui imperatoris: & quod unus non est magis seruus quam alter, nec unus respectu imperatoris est magis liber, quam alius, quia qui aequaliter obedire tenentur, sunt aequaliter serui illius, vel aequaliter liberi. Igitur si omnes subditi imperatoris tenentur sibi, tanquam Domino immediato, in omnibus, quae spectant ad regimen populi, obedire, omnes aequaliter sunt serui illius vel aequaliter liberi. Secundum inconveniens, quod sequeretur, est: quod quicunque veniret ad bellum pro Domino suo contra imperatorem, committeret crimen laesae maiestatis, quia quicunque est immediate subditus imperatori, committit crimen laesae maiestatis, si cogitat de morte imperatoris: quod facit ille, qui venit ad bellum mortale contra imperatorem, quid autem dicitur de istis, enarra. Magist.
units.tr: Disciple. In such matters, is everyone bound to obey the emperor more than anyone else, for example his own king, or duke, or marquis, or other immediate lord? For just as a bishop is superior to an abbot, and yet in many matters a monk is more bound to obey the abbot than the bishop, so, although the emperor is superior to kings, dukes and other temporal lords, are the subjects of other lords nevertheless more bound to obey their immediate lords than the emperor? Master. The answer is that, just as according to many the pope is the immediate prelate of all Christians in spiritual matters, so that everyone ought in all such matters to obey him rather than any lower prelate, so the emperor is the immediate lord of all in temporal matters, so that in those matters which concern the kingdom of mortals the emperor is to be obeyed rather than any lower lord. Blessed Augustine seems to think this too, who, on that verse of the Epistle to the Romans, they who resist bring damnation upon themselves, says: If the proconsul himself commands one thing and the emperor another, does anyone doubt that, when the former is disregarded, the latter must be served? The same is found in Book 2 of the Confessions, and is cited in Dist. 8, c. quicunque: In the powers of human society, the greater power is placed before the lesser for obedience. Therefore the emperor is always to be obeyed rather than any other lower lord. Disciple. From these things two absurdities seem to follow. The first is that all are slaves of the emperor, and that one is not more a slave than another, nor is one more free with respect to the emperor than another, since those equally bound to obey are equally slaves or equally free. So if all subjects of the emperor are bound to obey him, as their immediate lord, in everything that concerns the government of the people, then all are equally slaves or equally free. The second absurdity that would follow is this: whoever went to war against the emperor for his own lord would commit the crime of treason, since whoever is immediately subject to the emperor commits treason if he plots the emperor's death. And he who goes to deadly war against the emperor does this. But what is to be said about these matters? Explain. Master.

units.la: Ad primum dicitur: quod non sequitur ex praedictis, quia, sicut dictum est prius, subditi imperatoris non in omnibus tenentur sibi obedire: sed in his tantum, quae spectant ad regimen populi: hoc est, in his, quae sunt necessaria ad regendam iuste & utiliter populum sibi subiectum, & ideo si praeciperet aliquid, quod est contra utilitatem populi sibi subiecti, non tenerentur sibi obedire: sed in his, quae sunt necessaria ad regendum iuste & utiliter populum sibi subiectum, & inde est, quod serui imperatoris & liberi non tenentur sibi aequaliter obedire: sed in multis tenentur sibi obedire serui, in quibus non tenentur liberi, nam serui ad solum praeceptum imperatoris omnia bona, quae tenentur sibi dimittere absque hoc, quod aliquam utilitatem communem praetendant, sed ad hoc liberi non tenentur, nec imperator potest eis hoc praecipere absque utilitate boni communis, imo etiam neque absque manifesta utilitate & necessitate. In multis etiam aliis tenentur serui imperatoris sibi obedire, in quib° liberi minime sunt adstricti. Dignitati enim humani generis derogaret, si omnes essent serui imperatoris, & ideo derogaretur eidem, si imperator in omnibus posset tractare liberos, sicut seruos, quare cum imperator teneatur procurare ea, quae spectant ad dignitatem & utilitatem totius humani generis, & nullo modo debet velle liberos tractare sicut seruos, quare etiam liberi non tenentur sibi obedire in omnibus, in quibus serui. Ad secundum dicitur, quod quicunque venit cuicunque Domino suo ad bellum iniustum contra imperatorem, incidit in crimen laesae maiestatis, & poena criminis etiam laesae maiestatis est puniendus & plectendus. Quod imperatores Honorius & Arcadius in 14. libro eodem ad Legem Iuliam & poena criminis laesae maiestatis testari videntur, & habetur 6. q. 1. si quis, ubi ait: si quis cum militibus vel privatis barbaris etiam scelestam iniuriam fecerit factionem, aut factionis ipsius susceperit sacramentum, & dederit de nece etiam illustrium virorum, qui consilia & consistoria nostra intersunt, Senatorum etiam (nam & ipsi pars corporis nostri sunt) vel cuiuscunque postremo, qui nobis militat, cogitauerit eadem enim seueritate voluntatem sceleris, quae effectum, puniri iura voluerunt, ipse quidem, utpote maiestatis reus, gladio feriatur, bonis eius omnibus fisco nostro addictis, filii vero eius, quibus vitam imperatoris speciali benignitate concedimus, paterno enim deberent perire supplicio, in quibus paterni (hoc est haereditarii) criminis exempla metuuntur, a materna & a successione omnium proximorum habeantur alieni.
units.tr: To the first it is said: this does not follow from what has been said, because, as was said before, the emperor's subjects are not bound to obey him in everything, but only in those matters which concern the government of the people, that is, in those which are necessary for governing justly and usefully the people subject to him. So if he commanded something contrary to the usefulness of the people subject to him, they would not be bound to obey him. Thus it is that the emperor's slaves and free men are not equally bound to obey him. In many things slaves are bound to obey him, in which free men are not bound. For slaves are bound to surrender all their goods at the mere command of the emperor, without having to allege any common benefit; but free men are not bound to this, nor can the emperor order it of them without the benefit of the common good, indeed not even without manifest benefit and necessity. In many other matters too the emperor's slaves are bound to obey him, while free men are in no way bound. For it would derogate from the dignity of the human race if all were slaves of the emperor, and so it would be derogated from if the emperor could treat free men in everything as he treats slaves. Therefore, since the emperor is bound to care for what concerns the dignity and welfare of the whole human race, and must in no way wish to treat free men as slaves, free men are not bound to obey him in everything in which slaves are. To the second it is said that whoever goes to an unjust war against the emperor, for whatever lord he fights, falls into the crime of treason, and he is to be punished and chastised with the penalty for the crime of treason. The emperors Honorius and Arcadius seem to attest this in Book 14 of the same title, on the Julian Law and the penalty for treason, and it is found in 6 q. 1, si quis, where it says: If anyone has committed a wicked wrong with soldiers or private barbarians, or has formed a faction, or has taken the oath of that faction, and has plotted the death even of illustrious men who attend our councils and consistories, or of senators (for they too are part of our body), or indeed of anyone who serves us as a soldier, the laws wish that the intention of the crime be punished with the same severity as its accomplishment. He himself, as one guilty of treason, is to be struck down with the sword, all his goods being adjudged to our treasury; but his sons, whose lives we grant by special kindness of the emperor, ought by paternal punishment to perish, since the examples of paternal (that is, hereditary) crime are to be feared, and they are to be regarded as strangers to their mother and to the succession of all their relatives.

units.la: Discipul. Hoc beato Augustino obuiare videtur, qui asserit, quod si quis vadat ad bellum etiam iniustum, dummodo non constet sibi esse iniustum, non peccat, aiet enim, ut legitur 23. q. 1. c. quid culpatur: Vir iustus, si forte etiam sub rege hodie sacrilego miliiter, recte potest (illo iubente) bellare, si vice pacis ordinem seruans, quod sibi iubetur, vel non esse contra praeceptum Dei certum est, vel verum sit, certum non est, ita ut fortasse reum faciat regem iniquitas imperandi, innocentem autem militem offendit ordo seruiendi. Ex quibus verbis colligi potest, quod si rex vel alius dux erit milites suos ad bellum etiam iniustum contra imperatorem, si non est certum militibus, quod bellum Domini sui est iniustum, licite contra imperatorem bellare possunt.
units.tr: Disciple. This seems to stand in the way of blessed Augustine, who asserts that if anyone goes to war, even an unjust one, provided it is not clear to him that it is unjust, he does not sin. For he says, as is read in 23 q. 1, c. quid culpatur: A just man, if perhaps he serves as a soldier even under a king who is today a sacrilegious man, may rightly (at that king's command) go to war, if, keeping the order of obedience in place of peace, he does what he is commanded, and it is certain that it is not against the command of God, or if it is true, it is not certain; so that perhaps the wickedness of the one who commands makes the king guilty, while the order of serving does no harm to the innocent soldier. From these words it can be gathered that if a king or other duke leads his soldiers to an even unjust war against the emperor, and it is not certain to the soldiers that their lord's war is unjust, they may lawfully fight against the emperor.

units.la: Magist. Respondetur ad hoc, quod si bellatores cum Domino suo pugnant contra alium, qui non est Dominus eorundem, excusantur a peccato, licet bellum sit iniustum; dummodo hoc ignorarent, & non laborarent ignorantia supina & crassa. Sed si vadunt ad bellum cum Domino suo inferiori contra dominum suum superiorem, & præcipue contra imperatorem (qui est dominus eorum immediatus) non excusantur à crimine lœsæ maiestatis, si bellum est iniustum, licet hoc ignorent, quia magis debent præsumere pro imperatore, quod habeat iustum bellum, quam pro domino eorum inferiori, ideo cum non sunt certi, quod dominus eorum inferior habeat bellum iustum contra imperatorem, non excusantur à crimine lœsæ maiestatis.
units.tr: Master. To this the answer is that if soldiers fight with their lord against another who is not their lord, they are excused from sin, even though the war be unjust, provided that they were ignorant of this and were not in gross and culpable ignorance. But if they go to war with their inferior lord against their superior lord, and especially against the emperor, who is their immediate lord, they are not excused from the crime of treason if the war is unjust, even though they are ignorant of it. For they ought rather to presume in favour of the emperor that he has a just war than in favour of their inferior lord. Therefore, since they are not certain that their inferior lord has a just war against the emperor, they are not excused from the crime of treason.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Vbi quaeritur, utrum potestatem habeat imperator super res temporales: & ponitur prima opinio responsalis, scilicet quod non, quae probatur septem rationibus: ad quas respondetur infra capitulo 24.
units.tr: Where it is asked whether the emperor has power over temporal things. The first opposing opinion is set out, namely that he does not. It is proved by seven arguments, to which replies are given below in chapter 24.

units.la: Discipul. Disputauimus, quamuis breuiter, de potestate imperatoris super personas: nunc videamus de potestate ipsius super res temporales, an videlicet ipse sit dominus omnium temporalium rerum, quae ad ecclesiam minime spectant. Mag. Circa hoc sunt diuersæ opiniones siue sententiæ, vna est, quod imperator omnium rerum huius mundi non est dominus. Discipu. Pro ista opinione aliquas allegationes adducas. Magister. Hæc assertio videtur multipliciter posse probari. Primo sic: Imperator non est dominus illarum rerum, quae nullius hominis sunt, & quae occupanti concedunter. Sed multæ sunt res, quæ nullius hominis sunt, & quæ occupanti conceduntur, distinctio prim. iuris naturale, dicitur in textu & in Glossa, igitur imperator non est dominus huiusmodi rerum. Amplius, qui est dominus quarumcunque rerum temporalium, eas, si vult vendere potest; i. quaest. i: cap. eos qui, vbi sic legitur: Omnis enim dominus quod habet, si vult, vendit, siue seruum, siue aliquod aliud eorum quae possidet, sed imperator non potest vendere, sicut nec alienare, multas res temporales, quia tunc posset vendere & alienare imperium: quod non est verum, igitur imperator non est dominus omnium temporalium rerum. Rursus, qui rem temporalem alteri donat, alienat à se dominium illius rei, sed imperatores multas res donauerunt non solum clericis, sed etiam laicis. Igitur illæ res à dominio imperatoris sunt alienatæ. Item, qui in distributione rerum temporalium habet portionem specialem, non est dominus aliarum partium, quæ aliis conceduntur. Sed imperator capiens prædia in bello iusto habet portionem specialem, distinct. i. ius militare, vbi sic legitur: ius militare est belli inferendi solennitas, & infra: Item præda decisio, & personarum quarumlibet pro laboribus iusta diuisio, ac principis portio, ergo imperator non est verus dominus aliarum partium. Item, res fisci propriæ sunt imperatoris, vt notat Glossa, extra de iudiciis, cap. cum venissent, sed res fisci à rebus aliis distinguuntur, quia quorundam & non omnium res confiscantur, 6. quaestion. i. §. verum, igitur imperator non est dominus omnium rerum temporalium. Item, si imperator est dominus omnium temporalium rerum, quæ ad ecclesiam minime spectant, aut omnes res sunt communes imperatori & aliis: aut sunt propriæ imperatoris. Sed non sunt communes imperatori & aliis, quia tunc nullæ res essent proprię: nec sunt propriæ imperatori, quia tunc nullus alius haberet dominium alicuius rei, nec aliquis alius posset dicere, mea est hæc res; cum imperator solus posset dicere, hæc res est mea, si est sua propria, eo quod, sicut dicit Glossa, distinctio prim. cap. ibidem, dicitur aliquid meum esse, & per consequens iudicatur tuum non esse, ff. de procreatione. pomp. in fine, igitur imperator non est dominus omnium temporalium rerum. Rursus, si imperator est dominus omnium rerum temporalium, aut est dominus omnium huiusmodi rerum iure diuino, naturali vel humano, non iure diuino, quia, vt dicit Augustin. super Ioh. & ponitur distinct. 8. quod iure diuino domini est terra & plenitudo eius; pauperes & diuites Deus de vno limo fecit: pauperes & diuites vna terra portat. Igitur imperator non est dominus omnium temporalium rerum, iure diuino præsertim, teste Augustin. ibidem per ius diuinum, quod in scripturis diuinis habemus. Nunquam autem legitur in scripturis diuinis, quod Deus dedit imperatori dominium omnium rerum temporalium. Nec imperator est dominus huiusmodi rerum iure naturæ: quia iure naturæ omnia sunt communia, nec iure humano: quia iura humana sunt secundum iura imperatorum, di. 8. quo iure. Imperator autem non potuit sibi appropriare dominium alienarum rerum, igitur iure imperatoris, quod est ius humanum, imperator non est dominus omnium rerum temporalium.
units.tr: Disciple. We have discussed, though briefly, the emperor's power over persons. Now let us consider his power over temporal things: whether he is lord of all temporal goods that do not belong to the Church. Master. On this there are different opinions or views. One is that the emperor is not lord of all the things of this world. Disciple. Please give some arguments for this opinion. Master. This claim seems capable of being proved in many ways. First, as follows. The emperor is not lord of those things which belong to no man and are granted to whoever takes possession of them. But many things belong to no man and are granted to whoever takes possession of them, as the first distinction, "Natural law," states in the text and in the Gloss. Therefore the emperor is not lord of such things. Again, whoever is lord of any temporal things can sell them if he wishes, as in i. quaest. i, cap. eos qui, where it is read: "For every lord sells what he has, if he wishes, whether a slave or anything else that he possesses." But the emperor cannot sell or alienate many temporal things, just as he cannot alienate them, for then he could sell and alienate the empire, which is not true. Therefore the emperor is not lord of all temporal things. Again, whoever gives a temporal thing to another alienates his ownership of that thing. But emperors have given many things not only to clerics but also to laymen. Therefore those things have been alienated from the emperor's ownership. Likewise, whoever has a special share in the distribution of temporal things is not lord of the other shares that are given to others. But the emperor, when he takes lands in a just war, has a special share, distinction 1, ius militare, where it is read: "military law is the solemnity of waging war," and below: "Likewise the division of booty, and the just apportionment of the labour of any persons, and the prince's share." Therefore the emperor is not the true lord of the other shares. Again, the property of the treasury belongs to the emperor, as the Gloss notes in extra de iudiciis, cap. cum venissent. But the goods of the treasury are distinguished from other goods, because the goods of some, and not of all, are confiscated, 6 quaest. 1 §. verum. Therefore the emperor is not lord of all temporal things. Again, if the emperor is lord of all temporal things that do not belong to the Church, then either all things are common to the emperor and to others, or they are the emperor's own. But they are not common to the emperor and others, for then no things would be private. Nor are they the emperor's own, for then no one else would have ownership of anything, and no one else could say "this thing is mine," since the emperor alone could say "this thing is mine," if it were his own. For, as the Gloss says in distinction 1, cap. ibidem, "a thing is said to be mine, and consequently it is judged not to be yours," ff. de procreatione, Pomponius, at the end. Therefore the emperor is not lord of all temporal things. Again, if the emperor is lord of all temporal things, then he is lord of all such things either by divine right, by natural right or by human right. Not by divine right, because, as Augustine says on John, and it is cited in distinction 8: "By divine right the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord; God made the poor and the rich from one clay; the earth bears the poor and the rich alike." Therefore the emperor is not lord of all temporal things, especially by divine right, as Augustine testifies in the same place, meaning by divine right what we have in the divine Scriptures. Yet it is never read in the divine Scriptures that God gave the emperor lordship over all temporal things. Nor is the emperor lord of such things by natural right, since by natural right all things are common. Nor by human right, since human laws are subject to the laws of emperors, distinction 8, quo iure. But the emperor could not appropriate to himself the ownership of other people's things. Therefore, by the emperor's right, which is human right, the emperor is not lord of all temporal things.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Ponit secundam opinionem praecedenti omnino contrariam, quae probatur 7. rationibus.
units.tr: It sets out a second opinion entirely contrary to the previous one, which is proved by seven arguments.

units.la: Discipulus. Pro opinione contraria libenter audiam aliquas rationes. Magister. Opinio contraria, quae ponit, quod imperator est dominus omnium rerum temporalium, videtur posse sulciri pluribus rationibus. Nam ille, qui est dominus totius mundi, est dominus omnium illorum, quae sunt in mundo, & per consequens est dominus omnium rerum temporalium. Sed imperator est dominus totius mundi, sicut probatum est supra capitulo 5. huius secundi. Igitur imperator est dominus omnium temporalium rerum. Item, si est dominus aliquarum personarum, est dominus rerum spectantium ad easdem personas. Sed imperator est dominus omnium, salte qui non sunt clerici, vel spectantes ad ipsos. Igitur saltem est Dominus omnium rerum pertinentium ad illos, qui sunt sibi subiecti. Item, ille in cuius potestate sunt omnia, est Dominus omnium temporalium rerum: quia res temporales potissime videntur esse in potestate Domini. Sed in potestate imperatoris sunt omnia, sicut testatur Glossa, extra de clement. venerabilem, quae allegata est supra quinto capitulo huius secundi, igitur imperator est dominus omnium rerum temporalium. Rursus, non minus est imperator dominus omnium rerum, quae sunt illorum, qui sunt in imperio suo, sive de regno suo, quam rex est dominus omnium rerum illorum, qui sunt de regno suo. Sed rex est dominus omnium rerum, quae sunt illorum, qui sunt in regno suo. Igitur Imperator est dominus omnium rerum, quae spectant ad illos, qui sunt de imperio. Maior videtur nota. Minor probatur per illud, quod legitur secund. Regum octau. ubi sic habetur: dixit itaque Samuel omnia verba Domini ad populum, & ait: Hoc erit ius regis, qui imperaturus est vobis; filios vestros tollet, & ponet in curribus suis, facietque equites & procursores quadrigarum suarum, & constituet sibi tribunos & centuriones & aratores agrorum suorum, & messores segetum, & fabros armorum & curruum suorum: filias quoque vestras faciet sibi unguentarias, & sutarias & pannificas: agros quoque vestros, & vineas & oliveta optima tollet & dabit servis suis: sed & segetes vestras & vinearum reditus addecimabit, ut det eunuchis & famulis suis: seruos etiam vestros & ancillas & iuvenes vestros & asinos auferet & ponet in opere suo: greges quoque vestros addecimabit, vosque eritis ei servi. Ex quibus colligitur, quod omnia, quae habebant, pertinebant ad ius regis: & per consequens ad dominium eius, praesertim cum sint servi eius, cum dicitur expresse, vosque eritis ei servi, quicquid enim servus habet, domini sui est, & quicquid servus acquirit, domino acquirit.
units.tr: Student. I would gladly hear some arguments for the opposing opinion. Teacher. The opposing opinion, which holds that the emperor is lord of all temporal things, seems to be supported by several arguments. For whoever is lord of the whole world is lord of all the things that are in the world, and consequently lord of all temporal things. But the emperor is lord of the whole world, as was proved above in chapter 5 of this second book. Therefore the emperor is lord of all temporal things. Likewise, if someone is lord of certain persons, he is lord of the things belonging to those persons. But the emperor is lord of everyone, at least everyone who is not a cleric or connected with clerics. Therefore he is at least lord of all the things belonging to those who are subject to him. Again, the one in whose power all things are is lord of all temporal things, because temporal things seem above all to be in the Lord's power. But all things are in the emperor's power, as the Gloss testifies on Extra, On Clemency, Venerabilem, which was cited above in chapter 5 of this second book. Therefore the emperor is lord of all temporal things. Further, the emperor is no less lord of all the things belonging to those who are in his empire, or in his kingdom, than a king is lord of all the things belonging to those who are in his kingdom. But a king is lord of all the things belonging to those who are in his kingdom. Therefore the emperor is lord of all the things that pertain to those who are of the empire. The major premise seems well known. The minor is proved by what is read in 2 Kings 8, where it is written thus: And Samuel told all the words of the Lord to the people, and said: This will be the right of the king who shall rule over you. He will take your sons and set them in his chariots, and make them his horsemen and runners before his chariots, and he will appoint for himself tribunes and centurions, and ploughmen of his fields, and reapers of his harvests, and makers of his weapons and of his chariots. He will also take your daughters to be his perfumers, cooks and bakers. He will take your best fields, vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants. He will also tithe your crops and the revenues of your vineyards, to give to his eunuchs and attendants. He will take your menservants and maidservants, your young men and your asses, and put them to his work. He will tithe your flocks, and you shall be his servants. From these words it is gathered that all the things they possessed belonged to the king's right, and consequently to his dominion, especially since they are his servants, when it is expressly said, and you shall be his servants. For whatever a servant has belongs to his master, and whatever a servant acquires he acquires for his master.

units.la: Amplius, non minus sunt omnia de imperio imperatoris, quam antiquitus illa, quae pertinebant ad regna regum infidelium, erant eorum. Sed illa, quae pertinebant ad regna regum infidelium, erant ipsorum. Igitur omnes res temporales, quae spectant ad imperium & ad illos, qui sunt de imperio, sunt imperatoris. Maior evidens est, ut videtur. Minor probatur per illud, quod legitur Genes. decimo quarto: Reduxitque (scilicet Abraham) omnem substantiam & Loth fratrem suum cum substantia illius, mulieres quoque & populum. Et post: dicit autem rex Sodomorum ad Abraham: da mihi animas, cetera tolle tibi, qui respondit: Levo manum meam ad Dominum Deum excelsum, possessorem coeli & terrae, quod a filo subtegiminis usque ad corrigiam caligae non accipiam ex omnibus quae tua sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, all things within the emperor's empire are no less his than those things which, in ancient times, belonged to the kingdoms of unbelieving kings were theirs. But those things which belonged to the kingdoms of unbelieving kings were theirs. Therefore all temporal things which pertain to the empire and to those who are of the empire are the emperor's. The major premise is evident, as it seems. The minor is proved by what is read in Genesis 14: He (namely Abraham) brought back all the goods, and his brother Lot with his goods, and the women also, and the people. And after: And the king of Sodom said to Abraham: Give me the persons, and take the rest for yourself. But he answered: I lift up my hand to the Lord God Most High, the possessor of heaven and earth, that I will not take anything of yours, from a thread to a sandal strap.

units.la: Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Abraham reputavit ista, quae reduxerat, fuisse regis Sodomorum, reduxerat autem multa, quae erant illorum, qui erant de regno illius regis, igitur Abraham reputavit, quod etiam illa, quae spectabant ad ipsos, qui erant de regno eius, erant ipsius regis. Et hoc confirmatur per aliqua in libro de Patriarchis, & habetur vigesim. tert. quaestion. quint. capitul. dicat, qui ait: dicat aliquis, cum ipse vicerit, quomodo dixerit ad regem Sodomorum, nihil sumam: cum praeda utique in potestate victorum fuerit, deceret militarem disciplinam, ut regi seruentur omnia. Ex quibus colligitur, quod praeda, quam capiunt militantes sub rege, est regis, & tamen praeda est victorum, & ista praeda militum victorum principaliter est regis, licet etiam aliquo modo sit ipsius militis. Igitur eadem ratione alia bona, quae sunt in regno, sunt principaliter ipsius regis.
units.tr: From these words it is gathered that Abraham considered the things he had brought back to belong to the king of Sodom. He had brought back many things that belonged to those who were in that king's realm, so Abraham considered that even the things that pertained to the people of his realm were the king's own. This is confirmed by some passages in the book On the Patriarchs, and it is found in twenty-third question, fifth, chapter Dicat, which says: Someone may ask, since he himself had conquered, how he could say to the king of Sodom, "I will take nothing." Although the spoil was surely in the power of the victors, military discipline would require that everything be kept for the king. From these words it is gathered that the spoil which soldiers take under a king belongs to the king, and yet it is the spoil of the victors; and that the spoil of the victorious soldiers belongs chiefly to the king, although in some way it also belongs to the soldier himself. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the other goods that are in the realm belong chiefly to the king himself.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Ponit tertiam opinionem mediam inter praedictas capitulis praecedentibus.
units.tr: He sets out a third opinion, midway between the ones mentioned in the preceding chapters.

units.la: DIscipulus. Si est aliqua opinio, quae mediet inter opiniones praedictas, non differas recitare. Magister. Est una opinio, quod imperator non est sic dominus omnium rerum temporalium, quae etiam minime spectant ad ecclesiam, ut ad libitum suum liceat sibi vel valeat de omnibus huiusmodi rebus, quod voluerit, ordinare, est tamen Dominus quodammodo omnium pro eo, quod omnibus huiusmodi rebus quocunque contradicente, potest uti & eas applicare ad utilitatem communem, quandocunque viderit communem utilitatem esse praeferendam utilitati priuatae. Ad cuius evidentiam est sciendum, quod rerum quaedam sunt mobiles & quaedam immobiles, & utrarumque quaedam spectant solummodo ad imperatorem, quarum nullus alius habet dominium vel dispensationem, nisi ex speciali commissione imperatoris, quae possunt vocari imperiales res & res fisci. Quaedam sunt, quae spectant ad alios, quae aliquo modo sunt dominorum earum rerum mobilium. Quae specialiter spectant ad imperatorem, imperator sic est dominus, quod potest de eis quicquid voluerit ordinare, absque hoc, quod ad restitutionem aliquam teneatur, aurum enim & argentum, & lapides pretiosos, vestes, arma, animalia & omnes alias res mobiles potest vendere, donare, legare, & alienare, prout voluerit, absque hoc quod ad restitutionem teneatur, licet enim peccaret illicite rex mala causa, res huiusmodi alienando, non tamen teneretur eas imperio vel aliis restituere. Quarundam etiam rerum immobilium ita est dominus, ut taliter dare vel alienare potest aliqua castra, vel aliquos agros, vineas & civitates, unde in talibus habet dominium & ius pinguissimum. Quarundam autem rerum immobilium non habet ius & dominium ita pingue, quia non potest eas vendere, donare vel legare vel alienare: sicut imperium & regna, quorum alienationes redundarent in notabile detrimentum imperii, & ideo alienare non potest: & si alienaret de facto, talis alienatio non teneret de iure, sed omnia essent ad ius imperii revocanda: & ipse si posset reddere teneretur, est tamen quodammodo Dominus talium, in quantum potest eas vendicare & defendere, & eis uti pro utilita-
units.tr: The pupil: If there is some opinion that lies between the opinions mentioned above, do not delay in reciting it. The master: There is one opinion that the emperor is not so much lord of all temporal goods, including those which do not even pertain to the Church, that he may dispose of all such goods as he pleases and wills; nevertheless he is in a certain way lord of all of them, in that, whatever anyone may say against it, he can use them and apply them to the common good whenever he sees that the common good is to be preferred to private advantage. To make this clear, it should be known that some goods are movable and some immovable, and of both kinds some pertain only to the emperor, and no one else has ownership or management of them except by special commission from the emperor; these may be called imperial goods and goods of the treasury. Some goods pertain to others, who in some way own those movable goods. Those which pertain specifically to the emperor, the emperor is so much their lord that he may dispose of them as he wishes, without being bound to make any restitution: for he may sell, give, bequeath and alienate gold, silver, precious stones, garments, arms, animals and all other movable goods as he pleases, without being bound to restitution. For although the king would sin unlawfully, with no good cause, by alienating such goods, nevertheless he would not be bound to restore them to the empire or to others. Of certain immovable goods too he is so much the owner that he may give or alienate in such a way some castles, or some fields, vineyards and cities; in such matters he has ownership and a very full right. Of other immovable goods, however, he does not have so full a right and ownership, because he cannot sell, give, bequeath or alienate them: such as the empire and kingdoms, whose alienation would redound to the notable detriment of the empire, and therefore he cannot alienate them; and if he were to alienate them in fact, such an alienation would not hold in law, but everything would have to be recalled to the right of the empire; and he himself, if he were able to restore them, would be bound to do so. Nevertheless he is in some way lord of such things, insofar as he can claim and defend them, and use them for the

units.la: vtilitate communi: nec aliquis alius ius in eis habere dignoscitur. Rerum etiam spectantium ad alios habet dominium inquantum ex causa & pro communi vtilitate populi, & propter delictum possidentium potest ab eis auferre, & sibi appropriare, vel aliis donare.
