Quia tamen hoc non potest pro suo arbitrio voluntatis, sed pro culpa possidentium, vel ex causa, sc. pro vtilitate communi: ideo non habet in eis dominium ita pingue, sicut in rebus primis, quas potuit, sicut placuerit, sibi alienare ad libitum, ita vt qualitercunque alienauerit (saltem conferendo obedientibus) alienatio tunc tenetur, nec sit per aliquem reuocanda.
units.tr: common utility: nor is anyone else recognised as having right in them. He also has ownership of goods pertaining to others, insofar as, for a cause and for the common utility of the people, and on account of the fault of the possessors, he can take them away from them and appropriate them to himself, or give them to others. Since, however, he cannot do this at his own arbitrary will, but only on account of the fault of the possessors, or for a cause, namely the common utility, he does not have ownership of them so full as of those primary goods which he could alienate to himself at his pleasure, as he liked, so that however he has alienated them (at least by conferring them on obedient subjects), the alienation is then binding and may not be recalled by anyone.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: Respondet ad rationes 21. capituli.
units.tr: He answers the arguments of chapter 21.

units.la: Disc. Secundum istam opinionem discurramus per allegationes pro opinionibus primis omnino contrariis sup. 21. & 22. ca. recitatis: & videamus quid ista opinio sentit de ipsis, dicitaq; primo, quid dicendum est de illis rebus, quae nullius hominis sunt? Mag. Ad hoc dicitur, quod illarum, quae nullius hominis sunt, dominium principale post dominium diuinum, est penes totum genus humanum, quia dominium temporalium rerum dedit Deus primis parentibus pro se & posteris suis, sicut ex Gen. 1. colligitur, imperator tamen nihilominus est dominus quodammodo omnium rerum huiusmodi inquantum pro vtilitate communi potest eas sibi taliter appropriare, vt occupanti non concedantur, nisi de beneplacito imperatoris, vt imperatori assignatur, si hoc vtilitati communi prospexerit expedire.
units.tr: Question. Let us now run through, according to this opinion, the arguments for the opposing views set out at chapters 21 and 22 above, and see what this opinion makes of them. First, what must be said about those things which belong to no man? Master. To this it is said that the principal dominion over things which belong to no man, after the divine dominion, rests with the whole human race, because God gave dominion over temporal things to our first parents, for themselves and their posterity, as is gathered from Genesis 1. Nevertheless the emperor is in a certain way lord of all such things, insofar as, for the common good, he can appropriate them to himself in such a way that they are not granted to an occupier except by the emperor's good pleasure, to be assigned as the emperor sees fit, if he judges this expedient for the common good.

units.la: Disc. Nunquid potest imperator iubere ad libitum suum, vt nullus inferior eo tales res sibi appropriaret? Ma. Respondetur quod non, ideo enim imperatori certa stipendia siue redditus, seu res temporales sunt determinatae & pro suis vsibus assignatae, vt res aliorum non recipiat, & res, quae nullius hominis sunt, occupati dimittat, nisi pro culpa vel ex causa, vel pro vtilitate communi viderit, quod eas debet appropriare sibi.
units.tr: Question. Can the emperor order, at his own will, that no inferior appropriate such goods to himself without his leave? Master. It is answered that he cannot. For the emperor has fixed stipends or revenues, or temporal goods, determined and assigned for his uses, so that he may not receive the goods of others, and so that he may leave to occupiers things which belong to no man, unless he judges, for fault or for some cause, or for the common good, that he ought to appropriate them to himself.

units.la: Disc. Dic, quomodo respondetur ad rationem secundam, quae in hoc consistit, quod dominus temporalis potest eas vendere, si vult: quod non potest imperator. Mag. Respondetur, quod dominus temporalium rerum, qui habet in eis diuinum & ius pinguissimum, potest eas vendere si vult, & de tali dominio loquitur decretum 1. q. 1. sed tale dominium non habet imperator respectu omnium temporalium rerum, sed solum respectu quorundam.
units.tr: Question. Tell me how the second argument is answered, which consists in this: that a temporal lord can sell such things if he wishes, which the emperor cannot do. Master. It is answered that a lord of temporal things, who has in them the divine and most ample right, can sell them if he wishes, and the decree at 1. q. 1 speaks of such a dominion; but the emperor does not have such a dominion over all temporal things, only over certain ones.

units.la: Disc. Quid dicitur de tertia ratione, quae fundatur in hoc, quod imperatores multas res donauerunt. Magist. Dicitur, quod saepe multi donant res plures, & tamen retinent sibi dominium principale earundem rerum, & ideo imperator potest alienare a se multas res: non tamen sic, quin in casibus multis ipsas valeat reuocare, & pro vtilitate communi eas sibi appropriare: & ideo semper remaneat aliquomodo dominus earundem.
units.tr: Question. What is said about the third argument, which is founded on the fact that emperors have given away many things? Master. It is said that often many men give away many things and yet retain for themselves the principal dominion over the same things; and so the emperor can alienate from himself many things, yet not so completely that in many cases he cannot recall them and appropriate them to himself for the common good; and therefore he always remains in some way their lord.

units.la: Disc. Dic, quomodo respondetur ad quartam, quae accipit, quod imperator de praeda capta in bello iusto habet portionem specialem. Mag. Dicitur, quod licet ius pinguius habeat portione speciali sibi assignata, est tamen dominus quodammodo omnium aliarum portionum, inquantum pro vtilitate communi potest eas sibi appropriare.
units.tr: Question. Tell me how the fourth argument is answered, which holds that the emperor has a special portion of the spoils taken in a just war. Master. It is said that although he has a fuller right to the special portion assigned to him, he is nevertheless in some way lord of all the other portions, insofar as for the common good he can appropriate them to himself.

units.la: Disc. Dic, qualiter respondetur ad quintam rationem de rebus fisci. Mag. Respondetur, quod quamuis imperator in rebus fisci habeat pinguius ius, quam in aliis, propter tamen rationes dictas, in omnibus etiam aliis habet aliquo modo dominium.
units.tr: Question. Tell me how the fifth argument, about the goods of the fisc, is answered. Master. It is answered that although the emperor has a fuller right in the goods of the fisc than in others, nevertheless, for the reasons given, he has in some way dominion over all the others too.

units.la: Disc. Quid dicitur de sexta, quae accipit, quod si imperator est dominus omnium, aut omnes res sunt communes, &c. Mag. Dicitur, quod quia imperator non est eodem modo dominus omnium rerum temporalium: sed vno modo est dominus suarum, & alio modo aliarum, ideo nec omnes res sunt communes, nec proprie: sed quaedam sunt propriae imperatoris, ita quod nullius alterius sunt, & nullus alius habet proprietatem in ipsis: quaedam vero appropriantur aliis, quarum tamen quodammodo est imperator dominus, inquantum potest ab illis tollere pro vtilitate communi.
units.tr: Question. What is said about the sixth argument, which holds that if the emperor is lord of all, either all things are common, etc.? Master. It is said that since the emperor is not lord of all temporal things in the same way, but is lord of his own in one way and of others in another, therefore neither are all things common, nor properly so; but some things are properly the emperor's, so that they belong to no other, and no one else has ownership of them; while others are appropriated to other men, over which nevertheless the emperor is in some way lord, insofar as he can take them away from those men for the common good.

units.la: Disc. Narra, qualiter dicitur ad rationem septimam, quae in hoc consistit, quod imperator non est dominus omnium nec iure diuino, nec humano, &c. Mag. Respondetur, quod imperator est dominus omnium modis praedictis iure humano: quia sicut imperium est ab hominibus, & a Deo mediantibus hominibus: ita dominium, quod habet imperator, est ab hominibus & per consequens iure humano habet dominium omnium huiusmodi rerum. Et cum dicitur, quod iura humana sunt iura imperatorum, dist. 8. quo iure. Respondetur, quod tempore Augustini, qui dicit illa verba, quae habentur dist. 8. c. quo iure, iura humana fuerunt iura imperatorum: quia tunc populus transtulit potestatem condendi leges in imperatorem, sed aliquando iura humana non fuerunt iura imperatoris: quia prius fuerunt humana iura, quam iura imperatorum, sed est quodammodo dominus omnium iure populi, qui populus transtulit in imperatorem tale dominium omnium rerum, quod dedit Dominus primis parentibus & posteris suis, & pro vtilitate communi possit eisdem & de eis disponere & ordinare, prout vtilitati communi viderit expedire.
units.tr: Question. Tell me how the seventh argument is answered, which consists in this: that the emperor is not lord of all, neither by divine right nor by human right, etc. Master. It is answered that the emperor is lord of all by the aforesaid means and by human right; for just as the empire is from men, and from God through men, so the dominion which the emperor has is from men, and consequently by human right he has dominion over all such things. And when it is said that human laws are the laws of emperors (dist. 8, quo iure), it is answered that in the time of Augustine, who speaks those words found in dist. 8, c. quo iure, human laws were the laws of emperors, because then the people had transferred the power of making laws to the emperor; but at other times human laws were not the laws of the emperor, because human laws existed before the laws of emperors. Yet he is in some way lord of all by the right of the people, which people transferred to the emperor such dominion over all things as the Lord gave to our first parents and their posterity, so that for the common good he may dispose and ordain over them as he judges expedient for the common good.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXV.

units.la: Respondet rationibus 22. capitulo adductis pro secunda opinione.
units.tr: He answers the arguments brought in chapter 22 for the second opinion.

units.la: Disc. Nunc breuiter narra, qualiter respondetur secundum opinionem tertia ad rationes adductas sup. c. 22. pro opinione secunda. Ma. Ad primam dicit, quod imperator non est sic dominus totius mundi, vt ad libitum bitum suum posset facere de omnibus hominibus mundi, quod sibi placeat: sed quia in his, quae spectant ad bonum commune, omnes sibi obedire tenentur, & ideo non est dominus omnium temporalium rerum, nisi modis praedictis supra cap. 23. Et ad secundam respondetur per idem, quod qui est dominus personarum, est quodammodo dominus rerum spectantium ad sibi subiectos vel ad personas easdem, & ideo imperator est dominus omnium rerum spectantium ad sibi subiectos: quia potest eis uti pro utilitate communi, non tamen ad libitum suum absque rationabili causa. Ad tertiam dicitur, quod omnia sunt in potestate imperatoris, quia omnia potest accipere sibi pro utilitate communi: non tamen ad libitum suum, & ideo est dominus isto modo, quo dictum est prius, non aliter. Ad quartam respondetur, quod rex est quodammodo dominus omnium, quae sunt in regno suo, non tamen sic, quod ad libitum possit de eis, quod voluerit ordinare: sed quia potest omnia tollere pro bono communi, & isto modo praedixit Deus, quod omnia, quae erant filiorum Israel, debebant spectare ad ius regis. Disc. Videtur quod non solum spectat ad illud ius regis accipere, quae erant subditorum suorum pro utilitate communi, sed pro utilitate propria, sc. regis. Cum in auctoritate allegata ibidem dicatur expresse; filios vestros tollet, & ponet in curribus suis: & constituet aratores agrorum, & messores segetum, & post: agros quoque vestros & vineas & oliveta optima tollet & dabit servis suis. Ex quib. aliisque omnibus, quae ponuntur in auctoritate allegata colligitur, quod ad ius regis spectabat omnia posse tollere seu accipere pro utilitate priuata regis. Mag. Respondetur, quod utilitas regis est communis utilitas, unde sicut qui peccat in regem, peccat quodam modo in omnes subiectos sibi: sic qui aliquid facit regi, hoc videtur quodammodo facere in omnes sibi subiectos, & ideo quando rex propria negotia non posset expedire per propprias res & proprios servos, posset tollere pro negociis propriis expediendis, & res & servos aliorum & filios subiectos sibi, ut in hoc subveniret utilitati communi, & isto modo Deus dicit, quod omnia illa pertinebant ad ius regis, quando autem non erat in tali necessitate, non poterat hoc facere, & ideo ut legimus 1. Regum 21. Naboth Israelita noluit dare, nec communicare, nec vendere vineam suam regi Achab: quia videbat, quod rex ex nulla necessitate quaerebat eam, nec propter bonum commune, sed solummodo ex avaritia, & cupiditate. Sic etiam omnis multitudo Israel, ut habetur 3. Regum 21. dicit ad Roboam filium Salomonis: Pater tuus durissimum iugum nobis imposuit, insinuando, quia contra iustitiam & legitimam potestatem regis oppresserat eos, quamvis igitur rex posset tollere res & servos per filios subditorum, & applicare utilitati suae quando propria non sufficiunt, & utilitas communis impediretur, nisi negocia regis propterea expedirentur: hoc tamen non potest, quando hoc in utilitatem communem minime redundare videtur. Discipulus. Hoc videtur valde urgere, quod Deus dicit: vosque eritis servi, servi enim nihil proprium habent. Magister. Respondetur, quod non ideo dicit eis, vosque eritis servi, quia futuri erant servilis conditionis, & non liberi: cum legitur 3. Regum 9. quod de filiis Israel non constituit Salomon servire quenquam: sed erant viri bellatorum & ministri omnium, & principes & duces eius, & praefecti curruum & equorum: sed erant futuri servi, large capiendo vocabulum servorum pro subditis; qui in certis casibus tanquam liberi sunt subiecti, cum Domino servire censentur.
units.tr: Disciple. Now briefly tell me how, according to the third opinion, the arguments adduced above in chapter 22 for the second opinion are answered. Master. To the first, it is said that the emperor is not lord of the whole world in such a way that he could do with all men in the world whatever he pleases at his own will; rather, since in those matters which concern the common good all are bound to obey him, he is not lord of all temporal things except in the ways stated above in chapter 23. To the second it is answered by the same reasoning: whoever is lord of persons is in some sense lord of the things belonging to his subjects or to those same persons; and so the emperor is lord of all things belonging to his subjects, because he can use them for the common good, yet not at his own pleasure and without a reasonable cause. To the third it is said that all things are in the power of the emperor, because he can take all things for himself for the common good, but not at his own pleasure; so he is lord in the way said before, and in no other way. To the fourth it is answered that the king is in some sense lord of all that is in his kingdom, yet not so that he may dispose of them as he wishes; rather, because he can take everything for the common good, and in this way God foretold that all that belonged to the sons of Israel would fall under the right of the king. Disciple. It seems that the right of the king extends not only to taking what belonged to his subjects for the common good, but for his own private advantage, namely the king's own. For in the authority cited there it is expressly said: "He will take your sons and set them in his chariots, and will appoint them ploughmen of his fields and reapers of his harvests," and afterwards: "He will also take your fields and vineyards and best olive groves and give them to his servants." From these and all the other things set out in the cited authority it is gathered that it belonged to the king's right to be able to take or seize everything for the king's private advantage. Master. It is answered that the king's advantage is the common advantage; hence, just as one who sins against the king in some way sins against all his subjects, so one who does something to the king seems in some way to do it to all subject to him. Therefore, when the king could not carry out his private affairs through his own property and his own servants, he could take the property and servants of others, and his subjects' sons, for the carrying out of his private affairs, so that in this way he would serve the common good; and in this way God says that all those things pertained to the right of the king. But when he was not in such necessity, he could not do this. Thus, as we read in 1 Kings 21, Naboth the Israelite was unwilling to give, grant or sell his vineyard to king Ahab, because he saw that the king sought it from no necessity and not for the common good, but only out of greed and covetousness. So too the whole multitude of Israel, as is found in 3 Kings 21, said to Rehoboam the son of Solomon: "Your father laid a very hard yoke upon us," hinting that he had oppressed them against justice and lawful power. Although, then, the king could take goods and servants through the sons of his subjects and apply them to his own advantage when his own resources were insufficient, and the common good would be hindered unless the king's affairs were thereby carried out, yet he cannot do this when it does not appear to tend in any way to the common good. Disciple. This seems to press hard, for God says: "And you shall be servants," and servants have nothing of their own. Master. It is answered that God does not say to them "and you shall be servants" because they were going to be of servile condition and not free; for we read in 3 Kings 9 that Solomon did not appoint any of the sons of Israel to serve, but they were men of war and ministers of all, and his princes and captains, and commanders of chariots and horses. But they were going to be servants, taking the word "servants" broadly for subjects, who in certain cases are subject as if free, and are reckoned to serve the Lord.

units.la: Discipulus. Dic, quomodo respondetur ad quintam rationem. Magister. Respondetur, sicut ad rationem praecedentem: quod omnia, quae sunt in regno, sunt regis quoad potestatem utendi eis pro bono communi, non quoad potestatem disponendi de eis ad libitum suum, absque utilitate communi, & sic praeda capta in bello iusto est regis, & est aliquo modo militum, scilicet quo ad potestatem dividendi eam, & distribuendi militibus, qui ceperunt eam iuste: tamen absque personarum acceptione, hoc dicit Glossa distinct. 2. ius militare, dicit, quod principis sunt omnia, quoad tuitionem: sed ipse tenetur omnia dividere secundum merita personarum, ut supra distinctione 2. ius militare, sic dantur episcopo decima, ut dividat eas 12. quaestione 2. cap. concessio, super verbo, omnia. hinc etiam dicit Glossa, 23. quaest. 5. cap. dicat, super verbo omnia: si sub aliquo militetur, tota praeda est domini: sed ipse tenetur aequaliter dividere secundum qualitatem personarum, ut supra distinctione 2. ius militare, sic decima dantur episcopo, ut dividat eas 12. quaestione 1. concessio. Quod igitur dicitur, quod iure gentium nostra fiunt, quae capimus in bello de adm. rerum do. naturale, §. ultimo, verum est, quod capientis est, sed tamen tenetur illud dare domino, ut dividat secundum merita hominum.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how the fifth argument is answered. Master. It is answered as to the preceding argument: all that is in the kingdom belongs to the king with respect to the power of using it for the common good, not with respect to the power of disposing of it at his own pleasure without common advantage. So booty taken in a just war belongs to the king, and in some sense to the soldiers, namely as to the power of dividing it and distributing it to the soldiers who took it justly; yet without respect of persons. The Gloss on Distinction 2, "ius militare," says that "all things belong to the prince as to protection, but he is bound to divide all things according to the merits of persons, as above in distinction 2, 'ius militare'; so tithes are given to the bishop that he may divide them, 12 q. 2 c. concessio, on the word 'omnia'." Hence the Gloss also says, on 23 q. 5 c. dicat, on the word "omnia": "if one serves under someone, the whole booty is the lord's, but he is bound to divide it equally according to the quality of persons, as above in distinction 2, 'ius militare'; so tithes are given to the bishop that he may divide them, 12 q. 1 concessio." Therefore, when it is said that by the law of nations what we take in war becomes ours (De adm. rerum do. naturale, §. ultimo), it is true that it belongs to the one who takes it, but nevertheless he is bound to give it to the lord, to divide according to the merits of men.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: Quaeris, utrum Imperator tantum in temporalibus habeat plenitudinem potestatis, quantam habet Papa in spiritualibus, & adducit unam opinionem, quae probatur 5. rationibus, ad quas respondetur infra capitulo 28.
units.tr: He asks whether the Emperor has as full a power in temporal matters as the Pope has in spiritual matters, and he sets out one opinion, which is supported by five reasons, to which he replies below in chapter 28.

units.la: Disc. Quaesiuimus de aliquibus in speciali, quam super ipsa imperator habeat potestatem, nunc quaero in generali, an in temporalibus imperator habeat plenitudinem potestatis: quemadmodum secundum multos Papa in spiritualibus potestatis plenitudinem habere dignoscitur. Magister. Circa hoc sunt assertiones diversae, una est, quod imperator in temporalibus sic habet plenitudinem potestatis, quod omnia potest, quae non sunt contra ius divinum, vel contra ius naturale, ita quod in omnibus huiusmodi tenentur sibi obedire omnes sui subiecti. Discipul. Pro ista opinione allegare nitere. Mag. Pro ista opinione potest multipliciter allegari, qui enim nulla lege humana astringitur, sed solummodo lege divina & lege naturali obligatur, omnia potest, quae non sunt contra aliquam legum prædictarū, sed imperator nulla lege humana astringitur, sed legibus diuinis & naturalibus: quia (sicut habetur ff. de legibus, & Glossa recitat extra de constitutionibus, canonum) imperator legibus solutus est, igitur in temporalibus sic habet plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit, quæ non sunt contra leges diuinas & naturales. Amplius, ille habet in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis, cuius voluntas in huiusmodi lege legis habet vigorem, sed quod principi (præcipue imperatori) placuit, legis habet vigorem, igitur imperator in huiusmodi habet plenitudinem potestatis. Rursus, ille habet plenitudinem potestatis in temporalibus, cuius etiam error ius facit in temporalibus, igitur in temporalibus habet plenitudinem potestatis. Item, si aliquis subiectus imperatori possit iuste resistere imperatoris præcepto in temporalibus, quod non est contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale, oportet quod aliquo iure possit sibi resistere, quia hoc recte possumus, quod iure possumus, aut igitur potest sibi resistere iure diuino aut naturali, aut humano, non iure diuino, aut naturali: quia, sicut dictum est, præceptum eius non est contra aliquod illorum iurium, nec iure humano; quia, sicut habetur distinctione octau. capitulo, quo iure, & allegatum est supra iura humana iuris imperatoris non sunt contraria, quia ipsa iura humana per imperatores & per reges seculi Deus distribuit generi humano, igitur iure impetatoris nullus potest eius præcepto resistere, quia imperator in omnibus huiusmodi omnia potest. Præterea illud, ad quod societas humana se obligat, eadem societas seruare tenetur, sed societas humana obligat se ad obediendum generaliter regibus: & per consequens multo magis imperatori. Ait enim Augustinus libro secundo Confessionum, vt habetur distinctione octau. qua contra: Generale quippe pactum est societatis humanæ, obtemperare regibus suis. Igitur in temporalibus generaliter obediendum est imperatori, vt omnia possit, quæ non sunt contra ius diuinum & naturale.
units.tr: Student. We have inquired about particular matters, what power the emperor has over them; now I ask in general whether the emperor has fullness of power in temporal matters, just as many hold that the Pope is recognised as having fullness of power in spiritual matters. Master. On this point there are differing assertions. One is that the emperor has such fullness of power in temporal matters that he can do everything which is not against divine law or natural law, so that all his subjects are bound to obey him in all such matters. Student. Try to adduce arguments for this opinion. Master. This opinion can be supported in many ways. For one who is bound by no human law, but only by divine and natural law, can do everything which is not against any of those laws. The emperor is bound by no human law, but only by divine and natural laws, because (as is found in On laws, in the Digest, and as the Gloss recites in Extra, On Constitutions, of canons) the emperor is released from the laws. Therefore he has such fullness of power in temporal matters that he can do everything which is not against divine and natural laws. Further, he who has fullness of power in temporal matters, whose will has the force of law in such matters, has it; but what has pleased the prince (especially the emperor) has the force of law; therefore the emperor has fullness of power in such matters. Again, he has fullness of power in temporal matters whose very error makes law in temporal matters; therefore he has fullness of power in temporal matters. Likewise, if a subject of the emperor could justly resist the emperor's command in temporal matters, which is not against divine law nor against natural law, it follows that he could resist him by some law, for we may rightly do what we may do by right. Either he could resist him by divine law, or by natural law, or by human law. Not by divine or natural law, since, as has been said, his command is not against any of those laws; nor by human law, since, as is found in distinction 8, chapter Quo iure, and as was alleged above, the human laws are not contrary to the emperor's right, because God distributes the human laws to the human race through the emperors and kings of the world. Therefore by the emperor's right no one can resist his command, because in all such matters the emperor can do everything. Moreover, that to which human society binds itself, that same society is bound to keep; but human society binds itself to obey kings in general, and consequently much more the emperor. For Augustine says in the second book of the Confessions, as is found in distinction 8, Qua contra: "It is the general compact of human society to obey its kings." Therefore in temporal matters the emperor is to be obeyed in general, so that he can do everything which is not against divine and natural law.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVII.

units.la: Ponit opinionem secundam precedenti contrariam.
units.tr: He sets out a second opinion, contrary to the preceding one.

units.la: Discipulus. Recta assertionem oppositam. Magister. Assertio contraria est, quod imperator non habet in temporalibus plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit, quæ non sunt contra ius diuinum, nec naturale: sed limitata est potestas, vt quo ad liberos sibi subiectos & res eorum solummodo illa potest, quæ prosunt ad communem utilitatem.
units.tr: Student: State the opposite assertion. Master: The contrary assertion is that the emperor does not have a fullness of power in temporal matters, so that he can do everything that is not contrary to divine or natural law. His power is limited, so that over free subjects and their goods he can do only those things that serve the common good.

units.la: Discipulus. Pro ista assertione aliquas allegationes adducas. Magister. Pro ista taliter allegatur, illenon habet plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit, cuius leges non pro priuato commodo, sed pro communi utilitate fieri debent, si enim haberet plenitudinem potestatis, posset condere leges non solum pro communi utilitate, sed etiam pro priuata & utilitate propria vel aliena, & etiam quacunque de causa, dummodo non esset contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale, sed leges imperiales & cæteræ fieri debent non pro priuato commodo, sed pro communi utilitate, teste Isidoro, qui, vt legitur dist. 4. c. erit autem, ait: Erit autem hæc lex honesta & iusta possibilis secundum naturam & secundum consuetudinem patriæ, loco, tempore, necessaria, vtilis, manifesta quoque, ne aliquem per obscuritatem in captione cotineat nullo priuato commodo, sed pro communi utilitate conscripta. Igitur imperator non habet talem potestatis plenitudinem, vt omnia possit, nisi quæ sunt pro communi utilitate. Amplius, si imperator in huiusmodi habet talem plenitudinem potestatis, omnes alii reges & principes, & alii laici sibi subiecti essent puri serui ipsius, nam dominus nō habet maiorem potestatem super seruos, quam quod omnia possit præcipere eis, quæ non sunt contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale: imo forte nec tantam potestatem habet super eos. Si igitur imperator nō solum possit ista, quæ sunt pro communi utilitate, sed etiā alia quæcunq; in temporalibus, quæ non sunt contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale, oēs alii sibi subiecti essent veri serui sui. Rursus, Papa non habet potestatem plenariā in spiritualibus, quia ea quę sunt supererogationis non potest alicui præcipere, sicut virginitatē, ieiunium in pane & aqua, intrare religionē, & huiusmodi. Igitur multomagis imperator in temporalib. non habet talem plenitudinē potestatis. Item, imperator non habet maiorem potestatem in temporalibus, quam habuit populus, cū imperator habeat potestatem suam à populo, vt allegatum est supra, quia populus plus iurisdictionis aut potestatis non potuit transferre in imperatorem, quam habuit. Sed populus nunquam habuit talem potestatis plenitudinem, vt posset præcipere cuilibet de populo omne illud, quod non est contra ius diuinum aut contra ius naturale: quia non poterat præcipere ista, quæ non erant de necessitate facienda, teste Glossa, extra de constitution. cum omnis, secundum quam in talibus, quæ de necessitate facienda nihil potest fieri nisi omnes consentiant. Ergo si populus præcipit aliquid alicui de populo, quod non est de necessitate faciendum, non tenetur illud facere, nisi velit, restat igitur, quod imperator non habet talem potestatis plenitudinem. Præterea salsare, alienare, vendere, dare, vel legare, non est contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale: & tamen imperator hoc non potest, igitur non habet plenitudinem potestatis. Rursus, imperator non habet periculosam potestatem bono communi, sed talis plenitudo potestatis esset periculosa bono communi, posset enim omnes subditos ad paupertatem redigere: quod esset contrarium bono communi. Item, potestas, quæ solummodo est constituta propter solam communem utilitatē, non se extendit, nisi ad illa, quæ ad communem utilitatem ordinantur, & per consequens non se extendit ad omnia, quæ sunt contra ius diuinum, aut contra ius naturale. Sed potestas imperialis est solummodo constituta ad vtilitatem communem, igitur non se extendit ad illa, quae ad communem vtilitatem non pertinent. Confirmatur hoc ratione, illud quod non ordinatur ad finem debitum, inordinatum videtur, quod autem est inordinatum, non est licitum iudicandum, sed finis institutionis imperatorum est communis vtilitas. Igitur quod imperator auctoritate imperiali facit, & non ordinat ad vtilitatem communem, est inordinatum: & per consequens illicitum. Ex quo infertur, quod imperator auctoritate imperiali non potest omnia, quae non sunt contra ius diuinum, nec contra ius naturale: sed solum illa, quae ad vtilitatem communem proficiunt.
units.tr: Student: Offer some arguments in support of this assertion. Master: In support of it the argument runs as follows. One who does not have a fullness of power, such that he can do everything, is one whose laws must be made not for private advantage but for the common good. For if he had a fullness of power, he could make laws not only for the common good but also for private advantage, whether his own or another's, and for any cause whatever, provided it was not contrary to divine or natural law. But imperial laws and the rest must be made not for private advantage but for the common good, as Isidore witnesses, who says (as is read in dist. 4, c. Erit autem): "Such a law shall be honourable and just, possible according to nature and the custom of the country, suited to place and time, necessary, useful, and also clear, lest through obscurity it entangle anyone in a snare; it is written for no private advantage but for the common good." Therefore the emperor does not have such a fullness of power that he can do everything, but only what is for the common good. Further, if the emperor had such a fullness of power in these matters, all other kings and princes and other laymen subject to him would be his mere slaves. For a lord has no greater power over his slaves than to be able to command them everything that is not contrary to divine or natural law; indeed perhaps he does not even have so great a power over them. If, then, the emperor could do not only those things that are for the common good but also everything else in temporal matters that is not contrary to divine or natural law, all his subjects would be his true slaves. Again, the Pope does not have full power in spiritual matters, because he cannot command anyone the things that are works of supererogation, such as virginity, fasting on bread and water, entering a religious order, and the like. Therefore, much more so, the emperor does not have such a fullness of power in temporal matters. Likewise, the emperor does not have greater power in temporal matters than the people had, since the emperor holds his power from the people, as was argued above. For the people could not transfer to the emperor more jurisdiction or power than it had. But the people never had such a fullness of power that it could command any one of its members everything that is not contrary to divine or natural law; for it could not command those things that were not of necessity to be done, as the Gloss witnesses (extra de constitutionibus, cum omnis), according to which in such matters as must of necessity be done nothing can be done unless all consent. Therefore, if the people commands one of its members something that is not of necessity to be done, that member is not bound to do it unless he wishes to. It remains, then, that the emperor does not have such a fullness of power. Moreover, to salt, alienate, sell, give, or bequeath is not contrary to divine or natural law, and yet the emperor cannot do this; therefore he does not have a fullness of power. Again, the emperor does not hold a power that is dangerous to the common good; but such a fullness of power would be dangerous to the common good, for it could reduce all subjects to poverty, which would be contrary to the common good. Likewise, a power that is constituted solely for the sake of the common good extends only to those things that are ordered to the common good, and consequently it does not extend to all things that are contrary to divine or natural law. But imperial power is constituted solely for the common good; therefore it does not extend to those things that do not pertain to the common good. This is confirmed by reason: what is not ordered to its due end seems disordered, and what is disordered is not to be judged lawful; but the end of the institution of emperors is the common good. Therefore whatever the emperor does by imperial authority and does not order to the common good is disordered, and consequently unlawful. From this it follows that the emperor by imperial authority cannot do all things that are not contrary to divine or natural law, but only those that advance the common good.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII.

units.la: Respondet rationibus supra capitulo vigesimo sexto adductis.
units.tr: It answers the arguments adduced above in chapter twenty-six.

units.la: Discipulus. Quia ista opinio secunda communitati mortalium & bono communi, pro qua quilibet zelare tenetur, sonare videtur, scire desidero, quomodo ad rationes pro opinione contraria respondetur. Dicitaque qualiter respondetur ad primam, cap. 26. addu-ctam. Magist. Respondetur ad ipsam distinguendo de lege humana, quarum quaedam sunt leges imperatorum & aliarum personarum & communitatum particularium imperatori subiectarum, quae ciuiles possunt appellari. Quaedam sunt quodammodo totius communitatis mortalium, quae ad ius gentium spectare videntur: quae quodammodo sunt naturales, & quodammodo humanae siue positiuae: sicut ex his, quae dicta sunt huius partis capit. 10. & 11. colligi potest. Imperator nequaquam astringitur de necessitate, licet deceat eum viuere secundum leges suas, seruatis legibus, quae spectant ad ius gentium, pro eo quod omnes gentes & potissime rationales & ratione viuentes tali iure vtuntur, prout imperator ad idem astringitur: nec licet sibi eas irregulariter transgredi, nisi in casu, in quo viderit eas derogare vtilitati communi. Vnde non liceret sibi generaliter prohibere occupationes sedium, bella, captiuitates, seruitutes, postliminia, legatorum non violandorum religionem, & alia quae ad ius gentium spectare videntur. Imperatorem autem non habere plenitudinem potestatis, vt omnia possit in temporalibus, quae non sunt contra ius diuinum & naturale absolutum, de quo dictum est huius capitulis 11. & 12. spectat ad ius gentium, sicut & aliquos esse liberos & non pure seruos ad ius gentium pertinere dignoscitur, & quod vnum sequitur ex alio, & ideo hac lege astringitur imperator, quamuis humana est, quia de consensu omnium mortalium contradicentes contrarium posset seruari pro lege. Discipulus. Dic quomodo respondetur ad rationem secundam. Magister. Ad illam dicitur, quod illud, quod placet principi, scilicet imperatori, rationabiliter & iuste propter bonum commune legis habet vigorem, quando hoc explicat manifeste, si autem aliquid placet non propter bonum commune, sed propter priuatum, non propter hoc legis habet vigorem, scilicet iuste, sed inique & iniuste. Discipulus. Ista ratio, sicut & opinio praecedens cap. praecedenti recitata veritati & auctoritati imperatorum derogare videtur, nam secundum praescripta imperator nullam posset condere legem, nisi generalem, quae respicit bonum commune. Ex quo sequitur, quod nullum posset priuilegium concedere cuicunque, quia priuilegia sunt priuatae scilicet legis, non communia seu generalia, dist. 8. secundum quod quidam, & c. priuilegia, sed imperatorem non posse priuilegium speciale concedere cuicunque tam veritati, quam auctoritati imperatoris derogare videtur. Mag. Ad hoc respondetur, quod quelibet priuata persona & quodlibet particulare collegium est pars totius communitatis, ideo bonum cuiuslibet priuatae personae & cuiuslibet particularis collegii, est bonum totius communitatis, & ideo illud ad bonum commune poterit redundare, & ordinari valebit, quare si imperator concedendo specialia priuilegia aliquibus personis vel collegiis particularibus, ratione non errante, contra bonum commune, priuilegia iusta sunt, & ad bonum commune spectantia, si autem non intendit modo praedicto bonum commune, sed concedit huiusmodi priuilegia ex amore priuato, vel alia causa minus iusta, priuilegia illa non sunt iusta, sed iniqua & iniusta: & concedens vitiosa acceptionis personarum incurrit, de quo minime excusatur. Disc. Dic qualiter respondetur ad rationem tertiam. Mag. Dicitur, quod error principis probabiliter ius facit, facit itaque, vt alii teneantur obedire, nisi appareat eis, quod error principis est contra ius diuinum, aut naturale, aut bonum commune, quia si sic, error principis non facit ius. Discipulus. Qualiter respondetur ad quartam rationem. Magister. Respondetur per ista, quae dicta sunt superius in responsione ad primam rationem, quia saepe praecepto imperatoris, quod nec est contra ius diuinum nec naturale, potest quis resistere iure humano, non quidem ciuili, sed iure gentium, sicut dictum est. Ad argumentum dicitur, quod loquitur de iuribus humanis ciuilibus, non de iure gentium, sed iura ciuilia sunt iura imperatorum & regum, sed ius gentium non est imperatorum, nec regum per institutionem ipsorum, licet posset per ipsorum approbationem & obseruantiam. Discipul. Dic, quid sentit ista opinio de vltima ratione. Magister. Hoc sentit, quod generale pactum est societatis humanae obtemperare regibus suis in his, quae spectant ad bonum commune, & ideo obligata est societas humana ad obediendum generaliter imperatori in his, quae ad vtilitatem communem proficiunt non in aliis, in quibus non dubitat, quod nequaquam bono communi proficiant.
units.tr: Student. Since this opinion seems to be harmful to the common good of mortals, for which everyone is bound to be zealous, I wish to know how the arguments for the opposing opinion are answered. Tell me, then, how the first argument, cited in chapter 26, is answered. Master. It is answered by distinguishing human laws. Some of these are the laws of emperors and of other persons and particular communities subject to the emperor, and these may be called civil. Others belong in a way to the whole community of mortals, and these seem to pertain to the law of nations. In a way they are natural, and in a way they are human or positive, as can be gathered from what was said in chapters 10 and 11 of this part. The emperor is by no means bound of necessity to live according to his own laws, though it befits him to do so, provided he observes those laws which pertain to the law of nations. All peoples, especially rational and reasonable ones, use this law, and the emperor is bound to it as well. Nor is he permitted to transgress it irregularly, unless in a case where he sees that it detracts from the common good. Hence it would not be permitted for him to forbid in general the occupation of seats, wars, captivities, servitudes, the right of return, the inviolability of ambassadors, and other things which seem to belong to the law of nations. That the emperor does not have the fullness of power to do everything in temporal matters that is not against the divine law and absolute natural law, which was discussed in chapters 11 and 12 of this work, belongs to the law of nations, just as it is recognised that some men are free and not purely slaves by the law of nations, and that one follows from the other. For this reason the emperor is bound by this law, although it is human, because by the consent of all mortals, a contrary practice could be kept as law. Student. Tell me how the second argument is answered. Master. To it is said that what pleases the prince, that is, the emperor, has the force of law rationally and justly for the sake of the common good, when he clearly explains it. But if something pleases him not for the common good but for a private interest, it does not have the force of law on that account; rather it is unjust and iniquitous. Student. This argument, like the preceding opinion recited in the previous chapter, seems to detract from truth and from the authority of emperors. For according to what has been prescribed, an emperor could enact no law except a general one, which regards the common good. From this it follows that he could grant no privilege to anyone, because privileges are private law, not common or general, dist. 8, "secundum quod quidam," etc., "privilegia," yet to deny that the emperor can grant a special privilege to anyone seems to detract both from truth and from the authority of the emperor. Master. To this it is answered that every private person and every particular college is a part of the whole community. Therefore the good of any private person and of any particular college is the good of the whole community, and so it can redound to the common good and be ordained to it. Accordingly, if the emperor, in granting special privileges to certain persons or particular colleges, does so with right reason and not contrary to the common good, those privileges are just and pertain to the common good. But if he does not intend the common good in the manner described, and grants such privileges out of private love or some other less just cause, those privileges are not just but iniquitous and unjust, and the one granting them, guilty of vicious partiality, incurs a fault from which he is by no means excused. Student. Tell me how the third argument is answered. Master. It is said that the error of a prince creates law in a probable way, and so it makes others bound to obey, unless it appears to them that the prince's error is against the divine law, or the natural law, or the common good. For if it is, the prince's error does not make law. Student. How is the fourth argument answered? Master. It is answered by what was said above in the reply to the first argument: often one may resist, by human law, a command of the emperor which is neither against the divine nor the natural law. This resistance is not by civil law but by the law of nations, as has been said. To the objection it is said that it speaks of civil human laws, not of the law of nations. But civil laws are the laws of emperors and kings, whereas the law of nations is not the emperors' or kings' by their own institution, although it may become theirs by their approval and observance. Student. Tell me what this opinion holds about the last argument. Master. It holds this: the general compact of human society is to obey its kings in those matters which pertain to the common good. Therefore human society is bound to obey the emperor in general in those things which advance the common good, and not in others, in which it doubts that they advance the common good in any way.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: Quæritur, si electus in imperatorem statim valeat se intromittere de regno in tempo- ralibus disponendo, & ponit tres opiniones.
units.tr: It is asked whether an elected man may at once take up the government and dispose of temporal affairs, and three opinions are set out.

units.la: Disc. Postremo discutiamus succincte, an electus in regem seu imperatorem eo ipso, quod est electus antequam electio præsentetur, vel etiam notificetur Papæ, de iure valcat & debeat se intromittere de regno in temporalibus disponendo. Mag. Ad hoc secundum diversas opiniones, quæ recitatæ sunt superius, diversimode respondetur. Nam secundum illos, qui dicunt, quod imperium est à Papa, electus nullam administrationem habet de iure, antequam confirmetur à Papa. Secundû illos qui dicunt, quod imperium non est à Papa plus, quam regnum Franciæ vel regnum aliud quodcunq; fidelium: & quod imperator non est plus subiectus Papæ in temporalib. quam rex Franciæ, ita quod quicunq; electus in regem seu imperatorem Romanor. eo ipso, quod est electus, absq; hoc q electio præsentetur vel notificetur Papæ, habet plenam administrationem in temporalibus, & potest & debet se intromittere de imperio seu regno Romano. Sed quia p Romanos vel illos, in quos Romani auctoritate suam iusq; & potestatem seu imperium transtulerunt, ex causa pro bono communi ordinaverunt, quod antequam electus se intromitteret de regno vel imperio, electio sua præsentetur, quemadmodum electio Papæ ante ordinationem suam præsentabatur imperatoribus, dist. 63. c. Agato. Disc. Omnino mihi videtur, quod si imperium est à Papa, & imperator debet præstare iuramentum fidelitatis Papæ, sicut vasallus domino suo, quod electus se intromittere non debet de regno, nisi electio Papæ præsentetur, & Papa declaraverit voluntatem, an velit quod electus intromittat se de regno. Nunc aliam opinionem prosequere, & pro ipsa nitere allegare. Ma. Quod electus statim debet administrare, videtur multipliciter posse probari. Nam consuetudo in talib. rationabilis maxime est spectanda & conservanda, sed consuetudo rationabilis fuit ab initio, quod electus statim se intromittat, antequam præsentetur electio Papæ, imperatores enim tam fideles, qui fuerunt imperatores veri, q infideles, nullam electionem præsentaverant Papæ, nec ipsum in aliquo requirebant. Quidâ etiam imperatores, qui coronati fuerunt à papa in imperatores, licet præsentaverunt & notificaverunt Papæ electionem suam, quando coronationem Romæ corona aurea susceperunt, prius tamen administraverunt & coronabantur alia vel aliis corona vel coronis, igitur ista consuetudo servanda est, ut statim electus administrare incipiat. Amplius, electus ad istam dignitatem secularem, pro qua nô est alteri subiectus, non tenetur alteri electionem suam præsentare, antequam administret, sed electus in imperatorem seu regem Romanorum, non est pro Romano regno subiectus Papæ; cum pro regno Romano nô sit vasallus Papæ, igitur administrare debet, licet non præsentaverit electionem suâ Papæ. Rursus, non magis est rex Romanorum subiectus Papæ, quam alii reges quicunque: quia neq; iure humano, &c. sed multi sunt reges fideles, qui etiam ministrat absq; hoc, quod notificent aliquid Papæ vel de seipsis, vel de morte prædecessorum suorum, sive suorum patrum, igitur & rex Romanorû statim debet administrare. Disc. Videtur quod iure humano Romanorum rex est magis subiectus Papæ, quam multi alii reges: quia eligitur au&ctoritate Papæ, qui instituit electores, qui eum debent eligere. Ma. Aliis videtur, quod illud non obstat; quia ius humanum aut est ius imperatorum, aut regum, aut ius canonicum, quod est summorum Pontificum, sed iure imperatoris non est rex Romanorum subiectus Papæ plus quam alii reges, nec iure canonico. Tum quia summus Pontifex non plus potuit sibi subiicere regem Romanorum, quam alios reges, & ita si potuit sibi subiicere regem Romanorû, posset per eundem modum sibi subiicere regem Franciæ & quoscunq; alios reges. Tum qui non potest tollere leges aliquas, non potest sibi subiicere conditorem aliarum legû, sed Papa non potest tollere leges imperiales, teste Glossa, quæ dist. 10. c. constitutiones, ait: nunquid igitur legibus semper derogatur per canones? absit: nisi quo ad causas spirituales, & infra: nec posset Papa leges tollere, nisi quo ad suum foru, igitur Papa per nullum canonem sive ius canonicum potuit sibi subiicere regem Romanorum, qui legum est conditor. Disc. Adhuc conare roborare opinionem præmissam. Mag. Rursus, quod rex Romanorum, eo quod est electus, administrare debeat, antequam electio præsentetur Papæ, probatur. Quia electus, qui non indiget ab aliquo confirmari, potest administrare, antequam sua electio præsentetur alteri, quia omne ius & potestatem administrandi, quam habet electus, aut habet per confirmationem, aut electionem. Unde etiam episcopi & alii, qui confirmantur & consecrantur, per ipsam consecrationem nullam administrationem acquirunt, sed quæ administrationis sunt, habent per confirmationem. Papa autem per electionem omnem administrationem habet, dist. 23. nomine, qui igitur non indiget confirmatione, eo ipso quod est electus, omne ius administrandi habet. Sed electus in regem Romanorum non indiget confirmari à Papa. Unde & Innocent. III. qui extr. de electione, venerabilem, magis explicare videtur, quid Papa facit in electione regis Romanorum, de confirmatione nullam facit mentionem, nec legitur, quod antiquitus aliquis electus in regem Romanorum, etiam fidelis, sic fuerit à Papa confirmatus, igitur electus in regem Romanorum, statim per ipsam electionem habet ius administrandi.
units.tr: Disc. Finally, let us briefly discuss whether a man elected king or emperor, by the very fact that he has been elected, before his election is presented or even notified to the Pope, may and ought by right to take up the government and dispose of temporal affairs. Mag. On this question, different answers are given according to the different opinions recited above. For according to those who say that the empire is from the Pope, the elected man has no right of administration before he is confirmed by the Pope. Secondly, according to those who say that the empire is not from the Pope any more than the kingdom of France or any other kingdom of the faithful, and that the emperor is no more subject to the Pope in temporal matters than the king of France, it follows that whoever is elected king or emperor of the Romans, by the very fact of being elected, even without his election being presented or notified to the Pope, has full administration in temporal matters, and can and ought to take up the empire or kingdom of the Romans. But because the Romans, or those to whom the Romans by their authority transferred their right, power and empire, ordained for the sake of the common good that, before the elected man takes up the kingdom or empire, his election must be presented, just as the election of the Pope used to be presented to the emperors before his ordination, dist. 63. c. Agato. Disc. It seems to me altogether that if the empire is from the Pope, and the emperor must render an oath of fidelity to the Pope as a vassal to his lord, then the elected man ought not to take up the kingdom unless the election is presented to the Pope and the Pope has declared his will as to whether he wishes the elected man to take up the kingdom. Now pursue the other opinion, and strive to allege arguments for it. Ma. That the elected man ought to administer at once can be proved in many ways. For reasonable custom is especially to be regarded and preserved in such matters, and it was a reasonable custom from the beginning that the elected man took up office at once, before the Pope's election was presented; for emperors, both the faithful who were true emperors and the unfaithful, presented no election to the Pope and did not ask him anything about it. Some emperors, too, who were crowned emperors by the Pope, although they presented and notified their election when they received the golden crown at Rome, nevertheless had already administered and were crowned with another crown or other crowns before that. Therefore this custom is to be kept, that the elected man begins to administer at once. Furthermore, one elected to a secular dignity to which he is subject to no one else is not bound to present his election to anyone before administering; but one elected emperor or king of the Romans is not subject to the Pope in respect of the Roman kingdom, since he is not the Pope's vassal in respect of the Roman kingdom; therefore he ought to administer although he has not presented his election to the Pope. Again, the king of the Romans is no more subject to the Pope than any other kings whatever, because neither by human law, etc. But there are many faithful kings who administer without notifying the Pope of anything, either concerning themselves or concerning the death of their predecessors or their fathers; therefore the king of the Romans too ought to administer at once. Disc. It seems that by human law the king of the Romans is more subject to the Pope than many other kings, because he is elected by the authority of the Pope, who instituted the electors who ought to elect him. Ma. To others it seems that this is no obstacle; for human law is either the law of emperors, or of kings, or canon law, which belongs to the supreme pontiffs; but by imperial law the king of the Romans is no more subject to the Pope than other kings, nor is he so by canon law. For the supreme pontiff could not subject the king of the Romans to himself any more than other kings; and so, if he could subject the king of the Romans, he could by the same method subject the king of France and all other kings. Again, one who cannot abolish certain laws cannot subject to himself the maker of other laws; but the Pope cannot abolish imperial laws, as the Gloss witnesses, which says on dist. 10. c. constitutiones: "Is law therefore always derogated by the canons? Far from it, except as to spiritual causes," and below: "nor could the Pope abolish laws except as to his own forum." Therefore the Pope could not, by any canon or canon law, subject to himself the king of the Romans, who is the maker of laws. Disc. Try still to strengthen the opinion put forward. Mag. Again, that the king of the Romans, because he is elected, ought to administer before his election is presented to the Pope, is proved thus. He who is elected and does not need to be confirmed by anyone can administer before his election is presented to another, because all the right and power of administering that the elected man has, he has either through confirmation or through election. Hence bishops and others who are confirmed and consecrated acquire no administration through consecration itself; what belongs to administration they have through confirmation. The Pope, however, has all administration through election, dist. 23. nomine. Therefore he who does not need confirmation has, by the very fact of being elected, every right of administering. But the elected king of the Romans does not need to be confirmed by the Pope. Hence also Innocent III, in extr. de electione, venerabilem, seems to explain more fully what the Pope does in the election of the king of the Romans, and makes no mention of confirmation; nor is it read that anciently any elected king of the Romans, even a faithful one, was so confirmed by the Pope. Therefore the elected king of the Romans has, by the election itself, the right to administer at once.

units.la: Explicit liber secundus.
units.tr: Here ends the second book.

units.la: INCIPIT LIBER TERTIVS TRACTATVS SECVNDI TERTIAE PARTIS DIALOGI, in quo inuestigatur, quam potestatem habeat Imperator super res ac personas ecclesiasticas. CAP. I.
units.tr: BOOK THREE OF THE SECOND TRACTATE OF THE THIRD PART OF THE DIALOGUE begins, in which it is investigated what power the Emperor has over ecclesiastical things and persons. CHAPTER I.

units.la: Quaerit quaestionem principalem, s. quam potestatem habeat imperator super personas spirituales. DISC. In scripturis diuinis non memini me legisse omnem potestatem in spiritualibus imperatori (si esset catholicus) denegari, ideo an imperator super spiritualia aliquam potestatem habeat, vel sit capax huiusmodi potestatis, hoc tertio libro inuestigare propono, porro non solum gratia, virtutes, dona Dei, sacramenta, iura ecclesiastica, & causae ecclesiasticae, ac res ad ecclesias pertinentes, & huiusmodi, quae specialiter ad clericos spectare dicuntur, sed & personae seu homines inter spiritualia computantur, ideo de potestate imperatoris super spiritualia quaesiturus, a personis spiritualib. inchoabo. In primis autem duxi quaerendum, an imperator super aliquas personas spirituales habeat potestatem. M. Nonnullis apparet, quod personae seu homines possunt dici spirituales dupliciter. Quidam n. dicuntur spirituales, quia secundum spiritum & legem Christianam (quae lex spiritualis est) virtuose viuunt, & de spiritualibus sic loquitur Apost. 1 ad Cor. 2. cum dicit: nos autem non spiritum huius mundi accepimus, sed spiritu qui ex Deo est, vt sciamus quae a Deo donata sunt nobis, quae & loquimur non in doctis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in doctrina spiritus, spiritualia spiritualib. cooperantes. Alii possunt vocari spirituales (licet non viuat secundum spiritum virtuose) quia sunt spiritualib. officiis spiritualiter deputati: sicut sunt clerici & religiosi, quorum multi non spiritualiter viuunt, nec vita virtuosam, sed carnalem & vitiosam ducere dignoscuntur: ita vt laici vitae cooperatione ipsos & episcopos, qui inter clericos sunt maiores, habeat iudicare, teste Hieron. qui, vt habetur 8 q. 1. c. verear, ait: plurimi in populis episcopos iudicent subtrahentes se ab ecclesiastico gradu, & ea quae episcopo conueniunt non exercentes. Super homines spirituales primo modo dictos, quamplures laici & sibi subiecti spirituales primo modo accipiendo vocabulum, sunt censendi. Quia non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum sunt viuentes. De hominibus spiritualibus secundo modo dictis sunt opiniones contrariae, quibusdam dicentibus imperatorem super eos nullam potestatem habere, aliis asserentibus contrarium.
units.tr: He raises the principal question, namely, what power the Emperor has over spiritual persons. DISCIPLE: I do not recall having read in the divine Scriptures that all power in spiritual matters is denied to the Emperor (if he is a Catholic). Therefore I propose to investigate in this third book whether the Emperor has any power over spiritual things, or is capable of such power. Moreover, not only grace, virtues, gifts of God, sacraments, ecclesiastical rights, ecclesiastical causes, and things pertaining to the churches, and the like, which are said to belong specially to the clergy, but also persons or men are counted among spiritual things. So, intending to inquire into the Emperor's power over spiritual things, I will begin with spiritual persons. First, however, I think we must ask whether the Emperor has power over any spiritual persons. MASTER: To some it appears that persons or men can be called spiritual in two ways. Some are called spiritual because they live virtuously according to the Spirit and the Christian law (which is a spiritual law). The Apostle speaks of such spiritual persons in 1 Cor. 2, when he says: "Now we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we may know the things that have been freely given to us by God. These things we also speak, not in the words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Spirit, combining spiritual things with spiritual". Others may be called spiritual (although they do not live virtuously according to the Spirit) because they are appointed to spiritual offices in a spiritual way, as clergy and religious are. Many of these are known not to live spiritually, nor to lead a virtuous life, but a carnal and vicious one. So the laity may, by reason of the conduct of such men, judge even the bishops, who are the greater among the clergy, as Jerome witnesses. He says, as found in Decretum 8, q. 1, c. Verear: "Very many among the peoples judge bishops, withdrawing themselves from the ecclesiastical rank and not performing what belongs to a bishop." Concerning spiritual men in the first sense, a great many laity and those subject to them must be counted as spiritual, taking the word in the first sense, because they live not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. Concerning spiritual men in the second sense, opinions differ: some say that the Emperor has no power over them at all, while others assert the contrary.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: Quaerit, an electio Papae spectet ad imperatorem, & recitat opiniones duas, secunda ponitur cap. sequenti, prima opinio probatur sex rationibus, ad quas respondetur cap. 4. huius.
units.tr: He asks whether the election of the Pope belongs to the emperor, and sets out two opinions. The second is put forward in the following chapter. The first opinion is proved by six reasons, to which replies are given in chapter 4 of this book.

units.la: DISC. De hominibus spiritualibus secundo modo dictis solum modo quaerere intendebam. Ideo prosequamur de ipsis a summo ipsorum, sc. a summo Pontifice inchoantes, inuestigantes primo, an imperator in electione summi Pontificis potestatem habeat, seu ius aliquod vel habere possit. Secundo an supra ipsum in summum Pontificem constitutum aliquam habeat vel habere valeat potestatem: primo autem cupio indagare, an electio summi Pontificis possit personae imperatoris competere. Mag. Circa hoc sunt assertiones contrariae, prima est, quod personae imperatoris non potest competere ratione, quamdiu manet imperator. Disc. Pro ista assertione aliquas allegationes adducas. Mag. Pro ipsa potest multipliciter allegari. Qui n. non est capax iurium spiritualium, non potest habere ius eligendi summum Pontificem, quia ius eligendi summum Pontificem videtur primum locum inter iura spiritualia obtinere. Sed imperator & alii laici non sunt capaces iurium spiritualium, teste Gl. ext. de iudiciis, quanto, quae ait: Laicus ius tale (sc. ius patronatus) potest possidere, cum non sit mere spirituale, sed ei annexum: sed alia iura spiritualia iure possidere non potest, igitur ius eligendi summum Pontificem non potest imperatori competere. Amplius, sicut Papa praest spiritualib. ita imperator in temporalibus, sed iura temporalia siue saecularia, maxime quae potissimum locum inter iura saecularia habere noscuntur, nullo modo possunt competere summo Pontifici & aliis clericis, vt iura causas sanguinis exercendi, quae praecipue iura, saecularia censenda videntur. Igitur iura praecipue spiritualia, inter quae ius eligendi summum Pontificem videtur primum, nullo modo potest competere imperatori & aliis. Rursus, ille qui solum modo actibus saecularib. debet esse contentus, non est capax potestatis, aut iuris eligendi summum Pontificem; quia eligere summum Pontificem inter actus spirituales est enumerandus. Sed imperator tm modo saecularibus debet esse contentus, teste Nicol. Papa, qui ait dist. 10. c. imperium: Imperium vestrum suis publica rei quotidianis administrationibus debet esse contentum, non vsurpare quae sacerdotib. Domini solum conueniunt, vbi dicit Gl. Distinctio est n. potestas sua a potestate Pontificali, vt infr. c. quoniam, & 86. di. cu ad verum. Alioquin si vsurpet eorum officia, lepra percutiatur, vt Azias 2. q. 7. c. §. iterum cum Baala, igitur imperator non est capax huius iuris eligendi summum Pontificem. Praeterea potestates distinctae habent actus distinctos, teste Nicol. Papa, qui, vt legitur dist. 86. c. ad verum, ait: idem mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus actib. propriis & dignitatibus distinctis officia potestatis vtriusque discreuit. Sed potestas saecularis & ecclesiastica, sunt potestates distinctae, igitur habent distinctos actus, constat autem, quod actus eligendi summum Pontificem conuenit potestati ecclesiae, igitur non competit potestati saeculari, & per consequens imperator tale actu exercere non potest. Ita, sicut in corpore humano diuersa membra habet diuersos actus, Iob. 22. ita in corpore ecclesiae diuersa membra diuersos actus habere debent. Unde Gregor. vt habetur dist. 89. singula: in ecclesia corpore multa membra sunt secundum veridicam sententiam Pauli in vno eadem, spiritualis corpore conferendum est officium hoc vni, alii committendum est illud, & infr. Sicut indecorum est vt in corpore humano, vt alterum membrum alterius fungatur officio, ita animarum nocium simul, turpissimum est, si singula rerum mysteria personis totidem non fuerint distributa. Sed clerici & laici sunt diuersa membra, igitur actus habent distinctos, eligere autem summum Pontificem spectat ad clericos, distinctione. 22. in nomine, ergo nullo modo poterit ad laicos pertinere. Item, imperator & alii laici non possunt eligere Patriarchas, archiepiscopos & episcopos & aliarū ecclesiarum collegiatarū prælatos, igitur multo fortius non possunt eligere summum Pontificē. Consequentia manifesta videtur. Antecedens per sacros canones videtur posse probari. Ait enim Adrianus Papa, vt habetur distinction. 63. capit. 1. Nullus laicorum principum vel potentum semel inserat electioni vel promotioni Patriarchæ, Metropolitanæ aut cuiuscunque, ne videlicet inordinata & incongrua fiat electio vel confusio vel contentio, præsertim cum nullam in talibus potestatem quenquam potestatiuorum vel caeterorum laicorum habere conueniat. Et Gregorius Nonus, vt habetur extra de electione, cap. sacrosancta, ait: Ius eligendi in collegiata ecclesia non cadit in laicum, & eo. ca. Massana, ait: Edicto perpetuo prohibemus ne per laicos electio Pontificu præsumatur: quod si forte præsumpta fuerit, nullam obtineat firmitatem, non obstante contraria consuetudine, quae dici debet potius corruptela, vbi dicit Glossa super vocabulo consuetudine, quod talis consuetudo, quia non est rationabilis, non potest præscribi. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod ex nulla consuetudine possunt laici habere ius eligendi prælatos, & per consequens non possunt habere ex iure humano: quia quicquid potest tribuere ius humanum, potest consuetudo tribuere, constat autem, quod laici non habent ius eligendi ex iure diuino: quia tunc eo priuari non possent, & per consequens nullomodo possunt habere ius eligendi ipsos & prælatos ecclesiarum collegiatarum: quod quamplurimi alii sacri canones, qui habentur distinction. cap. si per ordinationem, & cap. non est, & cap. omnis, & cap. non licet, & 79. cap. si quis pecunia, & 16. quæstion. 1. 7. cap. si quis deinceps, & 16. quæstion. 1. cap. quoniam, & capit. si quis episcopus, & quæstion. 2. cap. sane, & cap. si quis clericus, & cap. constitutum, & cap. nullus, & cap. per laicos, & cap. non placuit, & cap. laicis, & aliis locis quamplurimis videtur assentire manifeste.
units.tr: DISC. I had intended to ask only about the spiritual persons of the second kind. So let us go on with them, beginning from their head, namely the supreme Pontiff. First I will examine whether the emperor has, or can have, any power or right in the election of the supreme Pontiff. Second, whether he has, or can have, any power over the supreme Pontiff once he has been established. But first I want to inquire whether the election of the supreme Pontiff can belong to the person of the emperor. MAG. On this question there are opposing assertions. The first is that the office cannot belong to the person of the emperor by reason of his office, for as long as he remains emperor. DISC. Bring some arguments in support of this assertion. MAG. It can be argued for in many ways. He who is not capable of spiritual rights cannot have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff, since the right to elect the supreme Pontiff seems to hold the first place among spiritual rights. But the emperor and other laymen are not capable of spiritual rights, as the Gloss attests on Extra, de iudiciis, Quanto, which says: A layman can possess such a right (namely the right of patronage), since it is not purely spiritual but attached to something else; but he cannot possess other spiritual rights by right. Therefore the right to elect the supreme Pontiff cannot belong to the emperor. Again, just as the Pope presides over spiritual matters, so the emperor presides over temporal matters. But temporal or secular rights, especially those which are known to hold the chief place among secular rights, can in no way belong to the supreme Pontiff and other clergy, such as the right of exercising jurisdiction in cases of blood, which rights are especially to be considered secular. Therefore the chiefly spiritual rights, among which the right to elect the supreme Pontiff seems to be first, can in no way belong to the emperor and others. Moreover, one who ought to be content with secular acts only is not capable of the power or right to elect the supreme Pontiff, since to elect the supreme Pontiff must be counted among spiritual acts. But the emperor ought to be content only with secular acts, as Pope Nicholas attests, who says in Dist. 10, c. Imperium: Your empire, which is public, ought to be content with the daily administration of public affairs, and not to usurp those things which belong to the priests of the Lord alone. Where the Gloss says: The distinction is that his power is different from the pontifical power, as below, c. Quoniam, and 86 Dist., Cum ad verum. Otherwise, if he usurps their offices, let him be struck with leprosy, as Azariah was (2 q. 7, c. §. Iterum cum Baala). Therefore the emperor is not capable of this right to elect the supreme Pontiff. Furthermore, distinct powers have distinct acts, as Pope Nicholas attests, who says, as is read in Dist. 86, c. Ad verum: The same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, has separated the offices of each power by his own distinct acts and dignities. But secular and ecclesiastical power are distinct powers, therefore they have distinct acts. It is clear, however, that the act of electing the supreme Pontiff belongs to the power of the Church; therefore it does not belong to the secular power, and consequently the emperor cannot exercise such an act. Thus, just as in the human body diverse members have diverse acts (Job 22), so in the body of the Church diverse members ought to have diverse acts. Hence Gregory, as it is found in Dist. 89, Singula: In the Church, which is the body, there are many members, according to the true saying of Paul, in one body. The spiritual office is to be given to one, and that other office is to be committed to another. And below: Just as it is unseemly in the human body for one member to perform the office of another, so it is most shameful for the souls of the people, if the single mysteries of things have not been distributed to as many persons. But clergy and laymen are diverse members, therefore they have distinct acts; but to elect the supreme Pontiff belongs to the clergy, Dist. 22, In nomine; therefore it can in no way pertain to the laity. Likewise, the emperor and other laymen cannot elect the Patriarchs, archbishops and bishops, and the prelates of other collegiate churches; therefore much more surely they cannot elect the supreme Pontiff. The consequence seems plain. The antecedent can be proved from the sacred canons. For Pope Adrian says, as it is found in Dist. 63, cap. 1: No layman, prince or powerful man shall interfere in the election or promotion of a Patriarch, Metropolitan or anyone else, lest indeed the election be disorderly and unfitting, or there be confusion or contention, especially since it is not fitting that any of the powerful or other laymen should have any power in such matters. And Gregory IX, as it is found in Extra, de electione, cap. Sacrosancta, says: The right of electing in a collegiate church does not fall to a layman. And in the chapter Massana he says: By a perpetual edict we forbid that the election of Pontiffs be presumed by laymen. But if perhaps it has been presumed, let it obtain no firmness, notwithstanding any contrary custom, which ought rather to be called a corruption. Where the Gloss, on the word custom, says that such a custom, since it is not reasonable, cannot be prescribed. From these words it is gathered that laymen cannot have the right to elect prelates from any custom, and consequently they cannot have it from human law, since whatever human law can grant, custom can grant too. But it is clear that laymen do not have the right to elect from divine law, for then they could not be deprived of it, and consequently in no way can they have the right to elect them and the prelates of collegiate churches. Very many other sacred canons clearly agree with this, which are found in Dist. cap. Si per ordinationem, and cap. Non est, and cap. Omnis, and cap. Non licet, and 79 cap. Si quis pecunia, and 16 q. 1, cap. 7, Si quis deinceps, and 16 q. 1, cap. Quoniam, and cap. Si quis episcopus, and q. 2, cap. Sane, and cap. Si quis clericus, and cap. Constitutum, and cap. Nullus, and cap. Per laicos, and cap. Non placuit, and cap. Laicis, and in very many other places.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Recitat opinionem secundam contrariam primæ.
units.tr: He recites the second opinion, which is contrary to the first.

units.la: DIscipulus. Assertionem prædictæ contrariam libenter audirem. Magister. Assertio contraria prædictæ est, quod licet imperator specialiter ratione imperatoriæ dignitatis non habeat ius eligendi summum Pontificem, vel alios prælatos inferiores: in quantum tamen Christianus catholicus & fidelis, ius eligendi summum Pontificem potest sibi competere, ita quod imperialis sublimitas non reddit eum non capacem huiusmodi dignitatis, potestatis siue iuris: imo quodammodo reddit eum magis dignum huiusmodi potestatis vel iuris. Discipulus. Pro ista assertione aliqua motiua proferin medium. Magister. Pro ipsa multipliciter allegatur. Nam ipsa potestas vel ius potest imperatori competere, quam vel quod de facto alii reges habuerunt. Sed de facto aliqui reges habuerant potestatem, siue ius eligendi summum Pontificem. Igitur talis potestas siue ius potest imperatori competere. Maior videtur nullatenus probatione indigere, minor autem auctoritatibus videtur manifeste & aperte probari, nam ex historia Ecclesiastica, vt legitur distinction. sexagesim. tert. capitulo Adrianus, vbi sic habetur: Adrianus Papa Romam venire Carolum regem ad defendendas res ecclesiæ postulauit, & infra: deinde Romam reuersus (scilicet Carolus rex) ibi constituit synodum cum Adriano Papa in Patriarchia Lateranensi, in ecclesia sancti Saluatoris, quae synodus celebrata est à centum quinquaginta tribus episcopis & abbatibus & religiosis. Adrianus autem Papa cum vniuersa synodo tradidit Carolo ius & potestatem eligendi Pontificem, & ordinandi Apostolicam sedem, dignitatem quoque patriciatus ei concessit, insuper episcopos, archiepiscopos per singulas prouincias ab eo consecrationem accipere diffiniuit, vt nisi à rege laudetur & investiatur episcopus, à nemine consecretur, & quicunque contra hoc decretum ageret, anathematis vinculo eum innodauit: & nisi resipiscerent, bona eius publicari præcepit. Item Leo Papa, vt in eadem distinctione capitulo, in synodo, sic ait: In synodo congregata Roma in ecclesia sancti Saluatoris, & ad exemplum beati Adriani Apostolicae sedis antistitis, qui Domino Carolo victoriosissimo regi Francorum & Longobardorum, patriciatus dignitatem ac ordinationem Apostolicæ sedis & investituram episcoporum concessit: ego quoque Leo seruus seruorum Dei episcopus cum cunctò clero ac Romano populo constituimus, confirmamus & corroboramus & per nostram Apostolicam auctoritatem concedimus, atque largimur Domino Ottoni primo regi Theutonicorum, eiusque successoribus huius regni Italiæ in perpetuum sibi facultatem eligendi successorem, atque summæ sedis Apostolicæ Pontificem ordinandi: ac per hoc archiepiscopos seu episcopos, vt ipsi ab eo investituram accipiant & consecrationem, unde debent, exceptis his quos imperator Romano Pontifici & archiepiscopis concessit, & vt nemo deinceps cuiuscunque dignitatis vel religionis eligendi successorem vel patricium vel Pontificem summæ sedis Apostolicæ, aut quemcunque episcopum ordinandi habeat facultatem absque consensu ipsius imperatoris, & infra: si à clero & à populo quis eligatur episcopus, nisi à supradicto rege laudetur & investiatur, non consecretur. Ex his colligitur, quod aliqui reges in imperatores promouendi, potestatem & ius eligendi summum Pontificem habuerunt, igitur talis potestas vel ius potest imperatori competere.
units.tr: Student: I would gladly hear the assertion contrary to the one just stated. Teacher: The assertion contrary to that one is this: although the emperor, specifically by reason of his imperial dignity, does not have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff or the lesser prelates, nevertheless, insofar as he is a Christian, Catholic and faithful man, the right to elect the supreme Pontiff can belong to him, so that his imperial sublimity does not render him incapable of this dignity, power or right; rather, in some way it makes him more worthy of such power or right. Student: Put forward some arguments for this assertion. Teacher: It is argued for in many ways. For the power or right could belong to the emperor, which other kings have in fact held.
