But in fact some kings have held the power, or right, to elect the supreme Pontiff. Therefore such a power or right can belong to the emperor. The major premise seems to need no proof at all; the minor is manifestly and openly proved by authorities. For in ecclesiastical history, as is read in dist. 63, chapter Adrianus, it is written thus: "Pope Adrian asked King Charles to come to Rome to defend the property of the Church." And further: "Afterwards Charles the king, returning to Rome, there held a synod with Pope Adrian in the Lateran Patriarchate, in the church of the Holy Saviour. This synod was celebrated by one hundred and fifty-three bishops, abbots and religious. Pope Adrian, with the whole synod, handed over to Charles the right and power of electing the Pontiff and of ordaining the Apostolic See. He also granted him the dignity of patrician, and further decreed that bishops and archbishops throughout each province should receive consecration from him, so that no bishop should be consecrated unless he has been approved and invested by the king; and whoever acted against this decree he bound with the chain of anathema, and, unless they repented, he ordered their goods to be confiscated." Likewise Pope Leo, in the same distinction, chapter In synodo, says: "In a synod gathered at Rome in the church of the Holy Saviour, and following the example of the blessed Adrian, bishop of the Apostolic See, who granted to the lord Charles, most victorious king of the Franks and Lombards, the dignity of patrician, and the ordering of the Apostolic See and the investiture of bishops: I also, Leo, servant of the servants of God and bishop, together with the whole clergy and the Roman people, establish, confirm, strengthen, and by our Apostolic authority grant and bestow upon the lord Otto the First, king of the Teutons, and upon his successors in the kingdom of Italy, forever, the power of choosing a successor and of ordaining the Pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See; and so that archbishops or bishops should receive investiture and consecration from him, from whom they ought to receive it, except those whom the emperor has granted to the Roman Pontiff and the archbishops; and that no one, of whatever dignity or religious order, shall have the power to choose a successor, or a patrician, or a Pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See, or to ordain any bishop, without the consent of the emperor himself. And further: if a bishop is chosen by the clergy and the people, he shall not be consecrated unless he has been approved and invested by the aforesaid king." From these words it is gathered that some kings, once they had been promoted to emperors, had the power and right of electing the supreme Pontiff; therefore such a power or right can belong to the emperor.

units.la: Item ex concilio colligitur, vt habetur eadem distinction. 63. capitulo, cap. cum longe, sic: Cum longe late que diffuso tractatu terrarum commeantium impenditur celeritas nunciorum, quo aut nequeant regibus audientibus decedentis præsulis transitus notificari, aut de successore morituri episcopi libera principis electio expectari, & infra: unde placuit omnibus Pontificibus Hispaniæ atque Galliciæ, & salvo privilegio vniuscuiusque prouinciæ licitum maneat deinceps Tholetano Pontifici, quousque regalis potestas elegerit, & tam dicti episcopi Tholetani iudicium dignos esse probauerit, in quibuslibet prouinciis in præcedentium sedibus præficere præsules. Ex quibus verbis sequitur, quod aliquando reges habuerunt potestatem eligendi episcopos.
units.tr: Again, from the council it is gathered, as is found in the same distinction 63, chapter Cum longe, which says: "Since, because of the long and wide travel across lands, the speed of messengers is hindered, so that the death of a prelate cannot be announced to the hearing kings, nor can the free choice of the prince be awaited regarding the successor of a dying bishop..." And further: "Therefore it has pleased all the Pontiffs of Spain and Galicia that, saving the privilege of each province, it shall remain lawful henceforth for the Pontiff of Toledo, until the royal power has chosen, and has judged the said bishop of Toledo worthy, to place prelates in the sees of the preceding ones in any provinces." From these words it follows that at times kings have held the power of electing bishops.

units.la: Iiii
units.tr: Iiii

units.la: Amplius, imperator & laici possunt interesse electionibus episcoporum. Igitur imperatori poterit competere ius eligendi summum Pontificem, consequentia tenet: quia de uno & de alio videtur esse eadem ratio. Antecedens probatur per illud Synodi, quod ponitur dist. 63. c. Adrianus, ubi postquam synodus diffiniuit, ut nullus semet inserat electioni episcoporum, subiungit ibi haec verba: Si vero quisquam laicorum ad contractandum vel cooperandum inuitatur ab ecclesia: licet huiusmodi laico cum reverentia, si forte voluerit obtemperare sese assistentibus, vbi dicit Gloss. hic inuitantur laici ad electionem. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod laici saltem inuitati in electione episcoporum votum habere possunt, & ita potestatis huiusmodi sunt capaces.
units.tr: Furthermore, the emperor and laymen can take part in the elections of bishops. Therefore the right to elect the supreme Pontiff could belong to the emperor; the consequence holds, because the same reason seems to apply to the one and the other. The antecedent is proved by that decree of the synod which is found in dist. 63, c. Adrianus, where, after the synod has decreed that no one should insert himself into the election of bishops, it adds these words: "But if any of the laity is invited by the church to take part in or assist with this matter, he may, with reverence, obey, if perhaps he is willing, those attending." Where the Gloss says: "Here the laity are invited to the election." From these words it is gathered that laymen, at least when invited, can have a vote in the election of bishops, and so are capable of this kind of power.

units.la: Item, ut habetur dist. 63. c. Valentinianus, Episcopus Mediolanensis, quando fuit electus beatus Ambrosius, dicit sic: Nostis aperte eruditi diuinis eloquiis, qualem oportet esse Pontificem, & quia non decet eum verbo solo, sed etiam conuersatione gubernare subiectos, & totius populi semetipsum imitatorem virtutis ostendere, testemque doctrinae conuersationem bonam habere, talem itaque in Pontificali constituite sede, cui & nos, qui gubernamus imperium, sincere nostra capita submittamus, & eius monita, dum tanquam homines delinquemus, necessario veluti curantis medicamina suscipiamus, post quae verba immediate subiungitur: haec enim cum dixisset imperator, petiit synodus, ut magis ipse decerneret sapiens & pius existens. Ex quibus verbis, ut videtur, infertur aperte, quod secundum assertionem Synodi praedictae imperator poterat eligere episcopum Mediolanensem, quamuis noluerit, unde & ait Episcopis illis: super vos, inquit, est talis electio, ex quo enim imperator eligere recusauit, ad episcopos illos pertinebat electio.
units.tr: Again, as is found in dist. 63, c. Valentinianus, the bishop of Milan, when the blessed Ambrose was elected, speaks thus: "You know clearly, instructed in divine utterances, what kind of man a Pontiff ought to be, and that it is not fitting for him to govern subjects by word alone, but also by conduct, and to show himself as an imitator of virtue to the whole people, and to have good conduct as a witness of doctrine. Therefore, establish such a man in the Pontifical see, to whom we also, who govern the empire, may humbly submit our heads, and whose admonitions, since we as men sin, we should receive as necessary medicines from a physician." Immediately after these words it is added: "When the emperor had said these things, the synod asked that he himself, being wise and devout, should rather decide." From these words it seems to be clearly inferred that, according to the assertion of the aforesaid synod, the emperor could choose the bishop of Milan, although he was unwilling; hence he also says to those bishops: "The election is upon you," for since the emperor refused to choose, the election belonged to those bishops.

units.la: Rursus, non minus pertinebat imperatori ius vel potestas eligendi summum Pontificem, quam concedere episcopatus, pro suae voluntatis arbitrio ad preces summi Pontificis: quoniam minus esse videtur eligere summum Pontificem, quam summum Pontificem rogare debere imperatorem, ut ipse imperator concedat episcopatus personis idoneis ad preces summi Pontificis, unde Leo Papa, ut habetur dist. 63. c. Reatina, scribit Lotario & Ludouico Augusto, ait: Vestram mansuetudinem deprecamur, quatenus Colono humili diacono eandem ecclesiam ad regendum concedere dignemini, ut vestra licentia accepta ibidem Deo adiuuante consecrare valeamus episcopum, sin autem in praedicta ecclesia noluerit, ut praeficiatur episcopus, Tusculanam ecclesiam, quae viduata existit, illi vestra seueritas dignetur concedere, ut consecratus a nostro praesulatu Deo omnipotenti vestroque imperio grates peragere valeat. Ex quibus verbis habetur: quod imperator poterat concedere episcopatus personis idoneis, ergo & sibi potest competere ius eligendi summum Pontificem.
units.tr: Again, the right or power of electing the supreme Pontiff belonged to the emperor no less than the granting of bishoprics, at his own discretion, at the request of the supreme Pontiff; for it seems less to elect the supreme Pontiff than for the supreme Pontiff to have to ask the emperor that he himself should grant bishoprics to suitable persons at the request of the supreme Pontiff. Hence Pope Leo, as is found in dist. 63, c. Reatina, writes to the Augusti Lothar and Louis, and says: "We beg your gentleness that you deign to grant the same church to Colonus, a humble deacon, to govern, so that, with your permission received, we may be able to consecrate a bishop there, with God's help. But if he is unwilling in the aforesaid church, let your severity deign to grant the Tusculan church, which is left widowed, to him, so that, consecrated by our prelacy, he may be able to give thanks to almighty God and to your empire." From these words it is found that the emperor could grant bishoprics to suitable persons; therefore the right to elect the supreme Pontiff can also belong to him.

units.la: Item, illi potest competere ius eligendi summum Pontificem, cuius iussione potest fieri ordinatio summi Pontificis, sed iussione imperatoris potest fieri ordinatio summi Pontificis, quia ex gestis Romanorum Pontificum, ut legitur distinction. 63. ca. Agatho: Agatho Papa accepit ab illo (scilicet imperatore) diualem (id est regiam) epistolam, secundum suam postulationem, per quam leuata est quantitas, quae solita erat dari pro ordinatione summi Pontificis: sic tamen, ut si contingeret post eius transitum electionem fieri, non debeat ordinari, qui electus fuerit, nisi prius decretum generale introducatur in regiam urbem secundum antiquam consuetudinem, ut cum eorum conscientia & iussione debeat ordinatio prosperari, igitur imperatori poterit competere ins eligendi summum Pontificem. Discipulus. In verbis praescriptis quoddam insinuatur mirabile, quod scilicet electio summi Pontificis debuit praesentari imperatori, antequam ordinaretur in summum Pontificem. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod electus in summum Pontificem per imperatorem debuit confirmari: quia electio aliqua nulli debet praesentari, nisi ad quem etiam pertinet eandem confirmare. Si igitur electio summi Pontificis imperatori debuit praesentari, eadem electio debuit confirmari ab eodem. Magister. Videtur, quod non semper ad eundem pertinet confirmare aliquam electionem, cui debet praesentari, unde & nonnullis apparet, quod electio imperatoris debet nunc praesentari summo Pontifici, per quem tamen minime est confirmandus, praesentabatur etiam electio summi Pontificis imperatori, non ut imperator confirmaret eandem electionem, sed ut imperator examinaret eandem, qua examinata imperator consentiret eidem electioni, & mandaret ut omnes subiecti sibi haberent electum pro vero summo Pontifice, postquam esset ordinatus. Hoc Gratianus in supradicta distinction. 63. §. principibus, testari videtur, cum ait: principibus vero ac imperatoribus electiones Romanorum Pontificum atque aliorum episcoporum referendas visus atque constitutio tradidit pro schismaticorum atque haereticorum discussionibus, quibus nonnunquam ecclesia Dei concussa periclitabatur, contra quos legibus fidelissimorum imperatorum frequenter ecclesia Dei munita legitur. Repraesentabantur ergo electiones catholicorum principibus, ut eorum auctoritate roborata nullus haereticorum vel schismaticorum auderet contraire: & ut ipsi principes tanquam devotissimi filii in eum consentirent, quem sibi in patrem eligi viderent, ut ei in omnibus suffragatores existerent: sicut secundum quosdam modo repraesentatur electio imperatoris summo Pontifici, non ut Papa electionem confirmet, vel ut imperialem sibi conferat dignitatem, cum eoipso quod sit electus sit imperator verus: sed ut auctoritate Papae electio imperatoris sic roborata, nullus clericorum, vel adhaerentium Papae, qui imperii dissipationem affectant, quorum (ut creditur) est his temporibus maxima multitudo, audeat contraire, & ut ipse Papa tanquam zelator imperii & boni communis consentiat in eum, & eidem in omnibus, maxime in coercione malorum, coadiutor existat. Discipulus. Pro assertione vel opinione praedicta nitere adhuc allegare. Magister. Videtur, quod praedicta assertio possit tali ratione probari, si imperatori non possit competere ius eligendi summum Pontificem, hoc erit, quia hoc aliquo iure irrevocabili, vel indispensabili existit. tit prohibitum. Sed cum in nullo iure prohibeatur imperatori eligere summum Pontificem, ita posset eligere sicut quicunque alius, sed nullo iure irrevocabili siue indispensabili prohibetur imperatori eligere summum Pontificem, igitur ius eligendi summum Pontificem potest sibi competere. Maior videtur clara, & minor probatur: quia si imperatori prohiberetur eligere summum Pontificem, aut prohiberetur iure diuino, aut naturali, aut iure humano, sed non prohibetur iure diuino: quia ius diuinum in scripturis diuinis habemus distinction. octau. quo iure, sed nunquam legitur in scripturis diuinis, quod imperator electioni summi Pontificis non debeat interesse, igitur hoc iure diuino minime prohibetur. Discipulus. Videtur quod hoc sit prohibitum iure diuino, saltem implicite. Nam solis ecclesiasticis viris, qui sunt successores Apostolorum, a iure diuino potestas eligendi prælatos inferiores summo Pontifici conceditur, ergo multo fortius a iure diuino huiusmodi potestas eligendi summum Pontificem solis viris ecclesiasticis est concessa, & per consequens non potest imperatori competere. Antecedens probatur per hoc, quod solis Apostolis, qui erant ecclesiastici viri, concessa fuit potestas eligendi L x x i i. discipulos, quorum officium gerunt inferiores prælati distinction. 21. capit. in nouo, ait: videntes autem ipsi Apostoli messem esse multam, & operarios paucos, rogaverunt dominum messis, ut mitteret operarios in messem suam, unde ab eis electi sunt 72. discipuli, quorum typum gerunt presbyteri: atque in eorum loco sunt constituti in ecclesia. Si igitur soli Apostoli habebant potestatem eligendi successorem 72. discipulorum: soli successores Apostolorum habent potestatem eligendi successorem 72. discipulorum, quales sunt inferiores prælati, igitur ex iure diuino habetur, scilicet euangelico, quod soli viri ecclesiastici habent ius eligendi prælatos, & per consequens ex iure diuino concluditur, quod nec imperator, nec alius laicus potest habere ius eligendi summum Pontificem. Magister. Ad hoc respondetur: quod quamuis Christus voluerit, quod Apostoli rogarent ipsum, ut mitteret operarios scilicet 72. discipulos in messem suam, non tamen voluit ut soli successores Apostolorum in Apostolica dignitate haberent potestatem eligendi successores 72. discipulorum. Ex hoc enim sequerentur duae absurditates, vna est, quod canonici ecclesiarum cathedralium non possent habere ius eligendi episcopos, quia illi non sunt successores Apostolorum. Alia est, quod diaconi cardinales & presbyteri non possunt habere ius eligendi summum Pontificem, cum non fuerint successores Apostolorum: quia qui non potest habere ius eligendi episcopos inferiores, non potest habere ius eligendi summum Pontificem.
units.tr: Likewise, the right to elect the supreme Pontiff can belong to the one by whose command the ordination of the supreme Pontiff can be carried out. But the ordination of the supreme Pontiff can be carried out by the command of the emperor, because from the acts of the Roman Pontiffs, as we read in Distinction 63, chapter Agatho: "Pope Agatho received from that emperor a royal (that is, imperial) letter, granted at his request, by which the sum that used to be paid for the ordination of the supreme Pontiff was remitted. It was so provided, however, that if an election took place after his death, the man elected should not be ordained unless first a general decree had been brought into the imperial city, according to the ancient custom, so that the ordination might proceed with their knowledge and command." Therefore the right to elect the supreme Pontiff can belong to the emperor. Student. In the words quoted there is something remarkable: namely, that the election of the supreme Pontiff had to be presented to the emperor before he was ordained as supreme Pontiff. From this it seems to follow that the one elected supreme Pontiff had to be confirmed by the emperor, since any election must be presented only to the person to whom it also belongs to confirm it. If, then, the election of the supreme Pontiff had to be presented to the emperor, the same election had to be confirmed by him. Master. It seems that it does not always belong to the same person to confirm an election to which it must be presented. For this reason it also appears to some that the election of the emperor must now be presented to the supreme Pontiff, by whom, nevertheless, it is in no way to be confirmed. The election of the supreme Pontiff was also presented to the emperor, not so that the emperor might confirm the election, but so that he might examine it; once it had been examined, the emperor would agree to the election and order all his subjects to hold the one elected as the true supreme Pontiff once he had been ordained. Gratian seems to bear witness to this in the above-cited Distinction 63, §. principibus, when he says: "By the decree and ordinance, the elections of the Roman Pontiffs and of other bishops were to be referred to princes and emperors, to examine them against schismatics and heretics, by whom the Church of God was sometimes shaken and put in danger; against whom the Church of God is often read to have been protected by the laws of most faithful emperors." The elections of Catholics were therefore presented to princes, so that, once they were strengthened by their authority, none of the heretics or schismatics would dare to oppose them, and so that the princes themselves, as most devoted sons, might agree to the one they saw chosen as their father, and be his supporters in all things. Similarly, according to some, the election of the emperor is now presented to the supreme Pontiff, not so that the Pope may confirm the election or confer on him the imperial dignity (since by the very fact of his election he is the true emperor), but so that, with the authority of the Pope, the election of the emperor, thus strengthened, may not be opposed by any clergy or adherents of the Pope who aim at the dissolution of the empire (which, it is believed, are at this time a very great multitude), and so that the Pope himself, as a zealot for the empire and the common good, may agree with him and be his helper in all things, especially in restraining evildoers. Student. Bring forward further arguments in support of this assertion or opinion. Master. It seems that this assertion can be proved by the following reasoning: if the right to elect the supreme Pontiff could not belong to the emperor, this would be because it is forbidden by some irrevocable or indispensable law. But no law forbids the emperor to elect the supreme Pontiff; he could elect him just as anyone else could. But no irrevocable or indispensable law forbids the emperor to elect the supreme Pontiff. Therefore the right to elect the supreme Pontiff can belong to him. The major premise seems clear, and the minor is proved as follows: if the emperor were forbidden to elect the supreme Pontiff, he would be forbidden either by divine law, or by natural law, or by human law. But he is not forbidden by divine law, for we have the divine law in the Holy Scriptures (Distinction 8, Quo iure), and nowhere is it read in the Holy Scriptures that the emperor should not take part in the election of the supreme Pontiff. Therefore he is in no way forbidden by divine law. Student. It seems that this is forbidden by divine law, at least implicitly. For the power to elect the inferior prelates is granted by divine law to the supreme Pontiff only to the ecclesiastical men who are the successors of the Apostles. Therefore, much more strongly, this power to elect the supreme Pontiff has been granted by divine law to ecclesiastical men alone, and consequently it cannot belong to the emperor. The antecedent is proved by the fact that the power to elect the seventy-two disciples, whose office the inferior prelates perform, was granted to the Apostles alone, who were ecclesiastical men. The decree says (Distinction 21, chapter In novo): "Now the Apostles themselves, seeing that the harvest was great and the workers few, asked the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest; whence seventy-two disciples were chosen by them, whose type the presbyters bear, and in whose place they have been set up in the Church." If, then, the Apostles alone had the power to choose a successor to the seventy-two disciples, then the successors of the Apostles alone have the power to choose a successor to the seventy-two disciples, who are the inferior prelates. Therefore it follows from divine law, namely the Gospel, that ecclesiastical men alone have the right to elect prelates, and consequently it is concluded from divine law that neither the emperor nor any other layman can have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff. Master. To this it is answered that although Christ wished the Apostles to ask him to send workers, that is, the seventy-two disciples, into his harvest, he did not wish that the successors of the Apostles alone, in the Apostolic dignity, should have the power to elect successors to the seventy-two disciples. For two absurdities would follow from this. The first is that the canons of cathedral churches could not have the right to elect bishops, since they are not successors of the Apostles. The second is that the cardinal deacons and presbyters could not have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff, since they are not successors of the Apostles; for whoever cannot have the right to elect inferior bishops cannot have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Discipulus. Arguendo dixisti, quod iure diuino non prohibetur imperatori eligere summum Pontificem: nunc eandem argumentationem prosequaris. Magister. Iure etiam naturali videtur, quod imperator minime prohibeatur eligere summum Pontificem: quia hoc dictamini rationis naturalis minime videtur obuiare. Nec prohibetur iure humano irrevocabili siue indispensabili: quia omne ius humanum, quo prohibetur, est canonicum vel ciuile, sed vtrumque est revocabile seu dispensabile, ergo nullo iure humano irrevocabili, seu indispensabili, prohibetur, quare ergo ius eligendi summum Pontificem potest imperatori competere.
units.tr: Student. In your argument you said that the emperor is not forbidden by divine law to elect the supreme Pontiff. Now pursue the same line of argument. Master. It also seems, by natural law, that the emperor is in no way forbidden to elect the supreme Pontiff, since this does not seem to conflict with the dictate of natural reason. Nor is he forbidden by any irrevocable or indispensable human law. For every human law by which he is forbidden is either canonical or civil, but both kinds can be revoked or dispensed with. Therefore he is forbidden by no irrevocable or indispensable human law. Hence the right to elect the supreme Pontiff can belong to the emperor.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Respondet rationibus capitulo secundo pro prima opinione adductis.
units.tr: Replies to the arguments brought forward for the first opinion in chapter two.

units.la: Discipulus. Allegationes pro ista opinione secunda tam euidentes mihi videntur, vt non curem ad ipsas responsiones audire, & ideo dic, quomodo ad allegationes in contrarium respondetur. Magister. Ad primam earum dicitur: quod imperator & alii laici multorum iurium spiritualium sunt capaces.
units.tr: Disciple. The arguments for this second opinion seem to me so clear that I do not care to hear the replies to them. So tell me how the arguments to the contrary are answered. Master. To the first of them it is said that the emperor and other laymen are capable of many spiritual rights.

units.la: Quia sunt capaces omnium illorum iurium spiritualium, quae possunt alicui competere, non propter ordinationem quam habeat, nec propter aliquod diuinum officium cui mancipatus existat: sed propter communem vtilitatem ecclesiae, hoc est congregationis fidelium, & ideo cum ius eligendi summum Pontificem non competat alicui ratione ordinis, nec ratione officii, cui habens ius eligendi sit mancipatus, sed propter communem ecclesiae vtilitatem, vt scilicet ecclesia habeat caput, quod ipsam regat, ideo hoc ius potest cadere ad imperatorem & alios laicos. Quod enim plurium iurium spiritualium laici sunt capaces, vt etiam causas spirituales valeant terminare, hoc testatur Glossa extra de iudiciis, c. decernimus, dicens: Papa vero ciuiles, criminales & spirituales causas potest laico delegare, octauae. octau. distinct. Honoratus decim. qu. tert. illud dec. quart. distin. verum, & 63. distinction. in synodo, & Adrianus, & 4. quaestion. 6. illud. Igitur quod dicit Gloss. allegata ibidem, quod laici mere spiritualia possidere non possunt: si intelligat de iuribus mere spiritualibus, quae nulli competere possunt, nisi ratione ordinis, vel diuini officii est aliquis deputatus, sicut est ius consecrandi ecclesias, ordinandi clericos, & celebrandi missas, & quae huiusmodi sunt iura mere spiritualia, nec secundum iura diuina, nec secundum iura humana possunt laico competere, si autem intelligat, quod iuribus mere spiritualibus, quae ideo dicuntur iura mere spiritualia, quia solum ad ossicium spirituale non seculare tantummodo & principaliter ordinantur, sic secundum constitutiones & consuetudines humanas, quae iam ordinatae sunt & de facto obseruantur, seculares iura mere spiritualia possidere non possunt: quae tamen possiderent, si huiusmodi constitutiones & consuetudines humanae essent reuocatae, quae ex causa rationabili reuocari possent: quemadmodum aliquando constitutiones contrariae & consuetudines humanae rationabiliter consuetuabantur, & ideo huiusmodi iurium laici sunt capaces absolute, quauis non saluis constitutionibus & consuetudinib. humanis, quae nunc seruantur. Ad secundum dicitur, quod sicut aliqua secularia Papae convenire possunt, licet praesit in spiritualibus: sic aliqua iura spiritualia possunt competere imperatori, licet praesit in temporalibus siue in secularibus, & ideo sicut iura potissime spiritualia, non potest habere imperator: huiusmodi autem ius spirituale potissime, non est ius eligendi summum Pontificem: sed huiusmodi ius potissime spirituale est illud ius, quod ratione ordinis competit ecclesiasticis viris: quale ius cadere non potest in laicum. Ad tertium dicitur, quod imperator inquantum imperator secularibus debet esse contentus, & hoc intendit Nicolaus Papa distinctione decim. imperium. Sed tamen imperator inquantum Christianus, Catholicus & Romanus, potest intromittere se in spiritualibus. Et ita licet non ratione imperatoriae dignitatis, tamen inquantum Christianus & Romanus, potest imperator habere in eligendo summum Pontificem potestatem.
units.tr: They are capable of all those spiritual rights that can belong to anyone, not because of any ordination they hold or any divine office to which they are bound, but for the common benefit of the Church, that is, of the congregation of the faithful. Since the right to elect the supreme Pontiff belongs to no one by reason of order or of an office to which the one holding the right is bound, but for the common benefit of the Church, namely that the Church may have a head to govern it, this right can fall to the emperor and other laymen. That laymen are capable of many spiritual rights, so that they may even decide spiritual causes, is attested by the Gloss extra de iudiciis, c. decernimus, which says: The Pope may indeed delegate civil, criminal and spiritual causes to a layman, octau. octau. distinct. Honoratus decim. qu. tert. illud dec. quart. distin. verum, & 63. distinction. in synodo, & Adrianus, & 4. quaestion. 6. illud. Therefore, as for what the Gloss says in the passage cited there, that laymen cannot possess purely spiritual things: if it means purely spiritual rights, which can belong to no one except by reason of order, or because someone is assigned to a divine office, such as the right to consecrate churches, ordain clerics, and celebrate Masses, and other rights of this kind that are purely spiritual, these can belong to a layman neither by divine law nor by human law. But if it means that purely spiritual rights, so called because they are ordered solely and principally to a spiritual and not a secular office, cannot be possessed by secular persons according to the human constitutions and customs that are now established and in fact observed, then laymen would possess them if such human constitutions and customs were revoked, which could be revoked for a reasonable cause, just as contrary constitutions and human customs were at times reasonably introduced. And so laymen are absolutely capable of such rights, although not while the human constitutions and customs now observed remain in force. To the second it is said that just as some secular matters can belong to the Pope although he presides over spiritual things, so some spiritual rights can belong to the emperor although he presides over temporal or secular things. Just as the emperor cannot have the most eminently spiritual rights, so the right to elect the supreme Pontiff is not most eminently spiritual; the most eminently spiritual right is that which belongs by reason of order to ecclesiastical men, and such a right cannot fall to a layman. To the third it is said that the emperor, as emperor, must be content with secular matters, and Pope Nicholas means this in dist. 10, imperium. But the emperor, as a Christian, Catholic and Roman, can interfere in spiritual matters. And so, although not by reason of imperial dignity, yet as a Christian and a Roman the emperor can have power in electing the supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Ad quartum dicitur, quod quia potestas secularis & ecclesiastica, sunt potestates distinctae: ideo actus, qui competunt aliquibus ratione huiusmodi potestatum, sunt distincti, persona tamen habens potestatem, potest habere aliquem actum talem, qualem habet persona alia, habens aliam potestatem, alioquin Papa nec quicunque alius ecclesiasticus praelatus posset habere quemcunque actum iurisdictionis siue potestatis secularis, eligere aut summum Pontificem non competit laico ratione potestatis secularis, & ideo qui habet potestatem secularem, potest etiam habere actum & ius eligendi summum Pontificem.
units.tr: To the fourth it is said that since secular and ecclesiastical power are distinct powers, the acts that belong to persons by reason of these powers are distinct; yet a person holding one power can have an act of the kind that another person holding a different power has. Otherwise the Pope or any other ecclesiastical prelate could not have any act of jurisdiction or secular power. Electing the supreme Pontiff does not belong to a layman by reason of secular power; so whoever has secular power can also have the act and right of electing the supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Ad quintam respondetur dupliciter: uno modo, quod sicut membra diversa in corpore humano habent quaedam officia propria & quaedam communia, motum enim sentire possunt omnia membra humana, percutere & portare & plura alia potest homo diversis membris mediantibus. Alia autem sunt membrorum officia propria; sicut videre, audire, & huiusmodi, sicut in corpore ecclesiae sunt quaedam officia communia clericis & laicis: & quaedam propria clericis, quaedam propria laicis, eligere autem praelatum (nisi per consuetudinem & constitutionem humanam aliter ordinetur) ad utrumque, quia eius officium est commune clericis & laicis, spectat, & ideo licet eligere summum Pontificem competat clericis: nihilominus potest competere laicis. Aliter dicitur, quod non est omnino simile de membris in corpore humano, & de membris in corpore ecclesiae, licet enim simile sit quantum ad multa, officia enim propria membrorum in corpore humano ex natura sibi competunt, ita ut unum membrorum defectum alterius (ex necessitate quacunque) complere non possit, sed membra in corpore ecclesiae, quantum ad multa officia & quodammodo propria possunt mutuo defectus suos supplere, potest enim clericus supplere vicem & defectum secularium etiam quo ad illa, quae sunt quodammodo secularibus propria, sicut potest per multa, quae prius tacta sunt probari, sic etiam laici possunt in multis supplere defectum & negligentiam, ac etiam malitiam clericorum. Licet igitur quantumcunque corpus ecclesiae esset optime dispositum, quantum permittit status vitae praesentis, diversa officia diversis committi debent, quando tamen corpus ecclesiae diversos defectus in diversis membris patitur, non est inconveniens, imo necessarium, quod uni diversa committantur officia: & quod unum membrum alterius fungatur officio, & ideo est, quod eligere summum Pontificem esset quodammodo proprium clericis, non est inconveniens, quod in casu summum Pontificem vel eligat solus imperator, vel cum aliis. Ad sextam dicitur, quod modo imperatoi & alii laici non possunt eligere praelatos ecclesiarum collegiatarum, quia hoc est per constitutiones humanas prohibitum, & ideo quando non fuerit prohibitum per constitutiones humanas, tunc poterunt archiepiscopos, episcopos & aliarum ecclesiarum collegiatarum praelatos eligere, omnes igitur canones dicentes, laicos non debere interesse electionibus praelatorum, & ius eligendi non cadit in aliquem laicum, loquuntur pro tempore, pro quo laicis prohibitum est eligere praelatos per constitutiones humanas. Et cum dicitur, quod laici ex nulla consuetudine possunt habere ius eligendi praelatos, quia, sicut allegatum est, talis consuetudo non est rationabilis, nec potest praescribi. Respondetur, talem consuetudinem non esse rationabilem nec posse praescribi, non est ex natura rei, sed ex constitutione humana, multa enim sunt inpraescriptibilia per solam consuetudinem humanam, talis enim consuetudo non est modo rationabilis, quia est contra iura, & modo non potest praescribi, quia hoc ius (ne scilicet praescribatur) est ordinatum per iura humana, quae ex causa rationabili abrogari valerent, sic igitur licet de facto constitutum sit, ne imperator & alii laici non habeant ius eligendi summum Pontificem & alios praelatos: hoc tamen posset eis competere, si per constitutiones humanas irrevocabiles non esset prohibitum.
units.tr: To the fifth there are two replies. In one way: just as different members of the human body have some offices that are proper and some that are common (for all human limbs can feel motion, strike, carry, and a man can do many other things through various limbs, while other offices are proper to particular limbs, such as seeing and hearing), so in the body of the Church there are some offices common to clergy and laity, and some proper to clergy and some proper to laity. Electing a prelate (unless otherwise ordered by custom and human constitution) pertains to both, because its office is common to clergy and laity; so although the right to elect the supreme Pontiff belongs to clergy, it can nevertheless belong to laymen as well. The other way: the members of the human body and the members of the body of the Church are not wholly alike. Although they are similar in many respects, the proper offices of the members of the human body belong to them by nature, so that one member cannot supply another's defect (whatever the necessity). But the members of the body of the Church, in many offices and in a certain sense proper ones, can mutually supply each other's defects. For a cleric can take the place of and supply the defect of laymen even in those matters that are in a sense proper to laymen, as can be proved by many things touched on before; so too laymen can in many things supply the defect and negligence, and even the wickedness, of clergy. Therefore, however well ordered the body of the Church might be, as far as the state of this present life permits, diverse offices ought to be committed to diverse persons; yet when the body of the Church suffers diverse defects in diverse members, it is not inconvenient, indeed it is necessary, that diverse offices be committed to one person and that one member perform the office of another. And so, because electing the supreme Pontiff would in a sense be proper to clergy, it is not inconvenient that in a given case the supreme Pontiff be elected by the emperor alone, or by him together with others. To the sixth it is said that at present the emperor and other laymen cannot elect the prelates of collegiate churches, because this is forbidden by human constitutions; so when it is not forbidden by human constitutions, they will be able to elect archbishops, bishops and the prelates of other collegiate churches. Therefore all the canons saying that laymen ought not to take part in the elections of prelates, and that the right of electing does not fall to any layman, speak for the time during which laymen are forbidden by human constitutions to elect prelates. As for the objection that laymen cannot have the right of electing prelates by any custom, because, as has been alleged, such a custom is not reasonable and cannot be prescribed: the reply is that such a custom is not reasonable, nor can it be prescribed, not by the nature of the thing but by human constitution, for many things cannot be prescribed by human custom alone. Such a custom is not reasonable now, because it is against the laws, and it cannot now be prescribed, because this right is ordained by human laws (so that it may not be prescribed), and these laws could be abrogated for a reasonable cause. Thus, although it has in fact been established that the emperor and other laymen should not have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff and other prelates, this could nevertheless belong to them if it were not forbidden by irrevocable human constitutions.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Monet incidentaliter quaestionem circa dicta capitulo precedenti, scilicet unde huiusmodi habeat imperator potestatem, scilicet eligendi summum Pontificem, ad quam respondetur dupliciter secundum duplicem intellectum quaesiti, & pro ratione ad secundum intellectum quaesiti adducuntur tres rationes, ad quas respondetur infra capitulo 7.
units.tr: Incidentally, he raises the question concerning the things said in the preceding chapter, namely, from whom the emperor has such power, that is, the power of electing the supreme Pontiff. It is answered in two ways, according to the two senses of the question. For the second sense, three arguments are brought forward, to which an answer is given below in chapter 7.

units.la: Discipul. Si imperatori potest competere ius eligendi summum Pontificem: primo dic, quid sit secundum opinionem illam, unde hoc habet. Magister. Dupliciter potest tota dubitatio intelligi, uno modo, ut sit capax potestatis siue iuris, alio modo, ut sit sensus, unde habet hoc ius, scilicet eligendi. di summum pontificem. Si intelligitur primo modo, unde habet imperator, quod sit capax huius potestatis siue iuris. Respondetur, quod talem capacitatem habet ex hoc ipso, quod est Christianus catholicus & discretus & Romanus, si enim esset imperator, & non esset Christianus, non esset capax huius iuris, quia nullus praeterquam Christianus potest habere ius eligendi summum pontificem, illos enim, qui foris sunt, illa quae religionis Christianae sunt tractare non decet: hoc excepto, quod in casu necessitatis possit alius quam Christianus baptizare, si etiam esset imperator & Christianus: sed non catholicus, sed haereticus, quamdiu talis existeret, potestatem seu ius eligendi summum pontificem non haberet, quia nullus haereticus manens haereticus est capax huius iuris. Si enim esset imperator Christianus & catholicus, sed non discretus, hoc est non habens vsum rationis, sed in furorem versus, quam diu talis existeret, non esset capax huiusmodi iuris vel potestatis, saltem vt posset in actum exire, quamuis enim si prius haberet huiusmodi potestatem, siue ius, & in furorem postea verteretur, non ex eo ipso huiusmodi potestatem vel ius amitteret: tamen si primo esset alienatus a sensu, sibi non deberet huiusmodi potestas siue ius conferri, nec etiam posset sibi conferre, sic vt possit stante alienatione actum potestatis huiusmodi exercere. Si autem interrogatio tua intelligitur secundo modo, a quo scilicet imperator habet vel habere potest huiusmodi potestatem siue ius. Respondetur dupliciter, vno modo, quod imperator huiusmodi potestatem seu ius potest habere a summo pontifice: quia summus pontifex ius eligendi papam posset concedere clerico vel clericis, laico vel laicis, prout sibi placuerit. Quod probatur tripliciter. Primo sic: quia qui est caput in spiritualibus omnium Christianorum, habet disponere & constituere a quo sit caput eligendum: praesertim cum Christus ordinauit specialiter & explicite, a quo debeat eligi idem caput, sed papa est caput omnium Christianorum, igitur ad ipsum pertinet ordinare, quis debeat eligere summum pontificem, & per consequens a solo papa potest habere imperator ius eligendi papam vel summum pontificem. Secundo sic: Qui potest summum pontificem sibi successorem ordinare, potest cui vult summum pontificem & eius successorem eligendi committere, & eius successor cui vult potest concedere ius eligendi successorem. Sed beatus Petrus ordinauit summum pontificem sibi successorem, scilicet beatum Clementem, igitur & successor eius potest concedere cui vult potestatem eligendi summum pontificem. Tertio sic: per sacros canones, quorum plures allegati sunt c. 3. huius tertii, papa concessit aliquando regibus aut aliis ius eligendi, & non illicite, ergo nullus potest habere ius eligendi summum pontificem, nisi a papa. Aliter dicitur, quod imperator eo ipso, quod est Christianus catholicus discretus & Romanus, habet ius eligendi summum pontificem: nisi eidem iuri tacite vel expresse renunciet, vel electio summi pontificis, vel potestas & ius eligendi de consensu Romanorum alicui personae vel personis determinatae vel determinatis concessa exiterit, ita vt Romani non habeant a papa potestatem ius eligendi summum pontificem. Quod tali ratione probatur, Christus taliter ordinauit ecclesiam, vt ei in necessariis nequaquam non deficeret vel defecerit: vel vt nullus homo per suam negligentiam vel malitiam quocunque necessario priuare possit eandem. Sed inter alia necessaria ecclesiae, non est minimum, vt sint aliqui, qui decedente summo pontifice ius habeant eligendi summum pontificem successurum, in hoc ergo Christus non defecit ecclesiae: nec posuit in potestate cuiuslibet, vt possit per negligentiam suam aut malitiam hoc necessario ecclesiam Dei priuare, sed si nullus haberet ius eligendi summum pontificem, nisi a papa, posset papa per negligentiam suam vel malitiam priuare totam ecclesiam potestate vel iure eligendi summum pontificem, posset enim primo siue ex causa rationabili vel irrationabili priuare illos, qui non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem eodem iure, & antequam idem ius aliis concederet, posset praeueniri morte, vel per negligentiam vel per malitiam, collationem eiusdem iuris vsque ad finem vitae suae differre, & ita penes nullos remaneret ius eligendi summum pontificem, quare hoc necesse est ecclesiae, ne ipsa ecclesia per praeuentionem mortis papae, vel per negligentiam aut malitiam priuata maneret, ita quod absque miraculo speciali posset ecclesia nec vniuersalis nec particularis papam habere. Ex quo infertur, quod ius eligendi summum pontificem non est a papa, & ideo ius habent eligendi Romani non a papa, sed eo ipso quod sunt Christiani & catholici.
units.tr: Disciple. If the right of electing the supreme Pontiff can belong to the emperor, first tell me what that opinion holds, and whence he has it. Master. The whole doubt can be understood in two ways. In one way, it concerns whether he is capable of the power or right. In the other, it asks whence he has this right, namely, of electing the supreme Pontiff. If it is understood in the first way, whence does the emperor have his capacity for this power or right? It is answered that he has such capacity from the very fact that he is a Catholic, discerning Christian and a Roman. For if he were emperor and not a Christian, he would not be capable of this right, since no one except a Christian can have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff; for it is not fitting to deal with the affairs of the Christian religion with those who are outside it. The exception is that in a case of necessity someone other than a Christian may baptize. Likewise, if he were emperor and a Christian but not Catholic, that is, a heretic, then as long as he remained a heretic he would not have the power or right of electing the supreme Pontiff, since no heretic who remains a heretic is capable of this right. If he were an emperor, Christian and Catholic, but not discerning, that is, without the use of reason and turned to madness, then as long as he remained so he would not be capable of such right or power, at least so that he could put it into act. For although, if he had held such power or right before and afterwards turned to madness, he would not lose it on that account, yet if he were first alienated from his senses, such power or right ought not to be conferred on him, nor could he confer it on himself, so that while the alienation lasted he could exercise an act of such power. But if your question is understood in the second way, namely, from whom the emperor has or can have such power or right, it is answered in two ways. In one way, the emperor can have such power or right from the supreme Pontiff, because the supreme Pontiff could grant the right of electing the pope to a cleric or clerics, or to a layman or laymen, as he pleased. This is proved in three ways. First: he who is head in spiritual matters of all Christians has the power to arrange and determine by whom the head is to be elected, especially since Christ specially and explicitly ordained by whom that head ought to be elected. But the pope is head of all Christians; therefore it belongs to him to ordain who ought to elect the supreme Pontiff, and consequently the emperor can have the right of electing the pope or supreme Pontiff from the pope alone. Second: he who can appoint a supreme Pontiff as his successor can entrust the right of electing the supreme Pontiff and his successor to whomever he wishes, and his successor can likewise grant the right of electing a successor to whomever he wishes. But blessed Peter appointed as supreme Pontiff his successor, namely blessed Clement; therefore his successor too can grant to whomever he wishes the power of electing the supreme Pontiff. Third: by the sacred canons, several of which were cited in chapter 3 of this third part, the pope has at times granted the right of electing to kings or others, and not unlawfully; therefore no one can have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff except from the pope. Otherwise it is said that the emperor, by the very fact that he is a Catholic, discerning Christian and a Roman, has the right of electing the supreme Pontiff, unless he has renounced this right tacitly or expressly, or unless the election of the supreme Pontiff, or the power and right of electing, has been granted with the consent of the Romans to some determined person or persons. In that case the Romans do not have from the pope the power of electing the supreme Pontiff. This is proved by the following reasoning. Christ so ordained the Church that it never would fail, or did not fail, in necessary things; or that no man, through his negligence or malice, could deprive it of anything necessary. But among the other necessary things of the Church, not the least is that there should be some who, on the death of the supreme Pontiff, have the right of electing a successor. In this, therefore, Christ did not fail the Church, nor did he place it in anyone's power, through negligence or malice, to deprive the Church of God of this necessity. But if no one had the right of electing the supreme Pontiff except from the pope, the pope could, through negligence or malice, deprive the whole Church of the power or right of electing the supreme Pontiff. For he could first, whether for a reasonable or an unreasonable cause, deprive those who have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff of that same right; and before he conferred that right on others, he could be overtaken by death, or, through negligence or malice, could defer the conferring of that right until the end of his life. And so the right of electing the supreme Pontiff would remain with no one. Therefore it is necessary for the Church that the Church itself should not be left deprived, through the pope's untimely death, or through his negligence or malice, so that without a special miracle the Church could have neither a universal nor a particular pope. From this it follows that the right of electing the supreme Pontiff is not from the pope, and therefore the Romans have the right of electing not from the pope but by the very fact that they are Christians and Catholics.

units.la: Disc. Per rationem illam probatur, quod Romani non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, quia si sic, per negligentiam aut malitiam possent Romani priuare totam ecclesiam iure eligendi summum pontificem, possent enim renunciare eidem iuri, absque hoc, quod ius eligendi summum pontificem aliis quibuscunque concederet, igitur tunc remaneret ecclesia absque iure eligendi summum pontificem. Item, omnes Romani habentes ius eligendi summum pontificem, possent fieri haeretici vel se conuertere ad aliam sectam: quo facto ius eligendi papa amitterent, igitur tota ecclesia Dei remaneret sine iure & potestate eligendi summum pontificem. Amplius, si Romani non habentius eligendi summum pontifice a papa, quo iure habent ius eligendi summum pontificem? aut diuino: aut humano non diuino, quia non legitur in scripturis diuinis, Deus dederit eis tale ius, nec iure humano: quia ius humanum aut est ciuile aut canonicum, iura ciuilia sunt iura imperatorum & regum, & iura canonica sunt iura summorum pontificum, igitur Romani haberent ius eligendi ab imperatoribus vel regibus, vel a summis pontificibus, sed non habent huiusmodi ius eligendi ab imperatoribus, ergo a solis summis pontificibus habent huiusmodi ius eligendi. Et ita eligendi ius est a solo papa. Ista sunt propter quae apparet, quod opinio ista & allegata ratio pro ipsa probabilitatem habere non videntur: sed tamen narra quomodo respondetur ad ipsa.
units.tr: Disc. By that reasoning it is proved that the Romans do not have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff. For if they did, the Romans could, through negligence or malice, deprive the whole Church of the right of electing the supreme Pontiff, since they could renounce that right without its being granted to anyone else at all. Then the Church would remain without the right of electing the supreme Pontiff. Likewise, all Romans who have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff could become heretics or turn to another sect; by doing so they would lose the right of electing the pope, and so the whole Church of God would remain without the right and power of electing the supreme Pontiff. Furthermore, if the Romans do not have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff from the pope, by what right do they have it? Either by divine right or by human right. Not divine, since it is not read in the divine Scriptures that God gave them such a right. Nor by human right, since human right is either civil or canonical; civil rights belong to emperors and kings, and canonical rights to the supreme Pontiffs. Therefore the Romans would have the right of electing either from the emperors or kings, or from the supreme Pontiffs. But they do not have this right of electing from the emperors; therefore they have it from the supreme Pontiffs alone. And so the right of electing is from the pope alone. These are the reasons on account of which it appears that this opinion, and the argument alleged for it, do not seem to have any probability. Nevertheless, tell how these arguments are answered.

units.la: Magister. Ad primum istorum respondetur, quod opinio illa non dicit, quod soli Romani in omni casu habeant ius eligendi summum pontificem. Ad cuius evidentiam dicitur esse sciendum, quod summus pontifex non solum est praelatus & episcopus Romanorum, sed etiam aliorum, & ideo in casu electio summi pontificis potest spectare ad quoscunque catholicos, quorum est praelatus & episcopus. Cum igitur dicitur, quod si Romani haberent ius eligendi summum pontificem, possent per negligentiam aut malitiam privare totam ecclesiam Dei iure eligendi summum pontificem. Respondetur, quod haec ratio concluderet, si nulli alii a Romanis in casu nullo haberent ius eligendi summum pontificem, nunc autem licet Romani, eo quod sunt Christiani & catholici, habent ius eligendi summum pontificem: tamen si renunciarent iuri illi, vel efficerentur haeretici, eo ipso alii catholici, quorum etiam papa est episcopus, & etiam praelatus, possent eligere summum pontificem. Discipulus. Si alii catholici habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, eo quod summus pontifex est episcopus & praelatus omnium catholicorum, quare non eligunt semper cum Romanis summum pontificem: cum omnes illi debeant praelatum eligere, qui habent ius eligendi? & quare plus eligunt Romani, quam alii, si ita habent alii ius sicut Romani? Mag. Id quod quaeris, secundum istam opinionem aperit viam respondendi, ad secundum, quod quaeris, ideo secundum opinionem illam recitabo, qualiter respondetur ad secundum, ad quod dicitur, quod summus pontifex est quodammodo proprius episcopus Romanorum, in quantum videlicet Romani non habent alium in episcopum, & alii omnes praeter ipsos habent proprios episcopos, & ideo rationabiliter ad solos Romanos pertinet summi pontificis electio, quando sunt catholici, quia tamen eo ipso, quod quis est episcopus Romanorum, est episcopus omnium Christianorum: & ideo alii, licet pro casu aliquo habent ius eligendi, non tamen cum Romanis, quia licet semper habeant ius eligendi summum pontificem, non tamen ius eligendi habent, nisi pro casu, quando electio non spectaret ad Romanos.
units.tr: Magister. To the first of these it is answered that the opinion does not say that the Romans alone, in every case, have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff. To make this clear, it must be understood that the supreme Pontiff is not only prelate and bishop of the Romans but also of others; and therefore, in a given case, the election of the supreme Pontiff can pertain to any Catholics of whom he is prelate and bishop. When it is said that if the Romans had the right of electing the supreme Pontiff they could, through negligence or malice, deprive the whole Church of God of the right of electing the supreme Pontiff, it is answered that this argument would conclude only if no one other than the Romans had the right of electing the supreme Pontiff in any case. But now, although the Romans, because they are Christians and Catholics, have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff, yet if they renounced that right or became heretics, then by that very fact other Catholics, of whom the pope is also bishop and prelate, could elect the supreme Pontiff. Discipulus. If other Catholics have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff, because the supreme Pontiff is bishop and prelate of all Catholics, why do they not always elect the supreme Pontiff together with the Romans, since all who have the right of electing ought to elect the prelate? And why do the Romans elect more than the others, if the others have the right just as the Romans do? Mag. What you ask, according to that opinion, opens the way to an answer. For the second point you raise, I will set out, according to that opinion, how it is answered. It is said that the supreme Pontiff is in a certain way the proper bishop of the Romans, insofar as the Romans have no other bishop, whereas all others apart from them have their own bishops. Therefore it rightly belongs to the Romans alone to elect the supreme Pontiff, when they are Catholics. Yet because whoever is bishop of the Romans is bishop of all Christians, the others, although they have the right of electing in some cases, do not have it together with the Romans. For although they always have the right of electing the supreme Pontiff, they have that right only in the case when the election would not belong to the Romans.

units.la: Discip. Hoc videtur falsum: imo videtur ita facile ad alios pertinere, sicut ad Romanos: cum summus pontifex aeque bene sit praelatus immediatus aliorum, sicut Romanorum. Mag. Ad hoc respondetur, quod secundum rectam rationem electio praeficiendi semper debet concedi (si fieri potest) paucis, qui faciliter possunt convenire, ne si concederetur multis, qui non possent faciliter convenire propter difficultatem conveniendi, differretur electio in notabile detrimentum boni communis, & eorum quibus est rex praeficiendus. Quia igitur Romani respectu aliorum catholicorum sunt pauci: & summus pontifex nihilominus (sicut dictum est) est quodammodo proprius episcopus eorum, quia non habent alium episcopum, sicut alii catholici: ideo rationabiliter alii catholici non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, nisi quando electio non spectaret ad Romanos, quando Romani vel ex renunciatione iuris, vel apostasia, vel haeretica pravitate, carerent iure eligendi. Per hoc patet responsio ad id quod quaesisti, nam ideo catholici non eligunt semper cum Romanis, quia licet habeant ius eligendi, non tamen habent ius eligendi pro omni casu: sed solummodo pro casu, quando ius eligendi ad Romanos minime pertineret. Ex his concluditur, quod Romani si possint cedere iuri eligendi summum pontificem, sive omnes efficerentur haeretici, sive a fide apostatae, non possunt privare ecclesiam iure eligendi summum pontificem, quin in tali casu habeant alii catholici ius eligendi summum pontificem.
units.tr: Disciple. This seems false: indeed it seems that the election pertains as easily to others as to the Romans, since the supreme pontiff is equally an immediate prelate of others as of the Romans. Master. To this it is answered that, according to right reason, the election of one to be set over others ought always (if it can be done) to be granted to a few who can easily assemble; lest, if it were granted to many who could not easily assemble because of the difficulty of meeting, the election would be deferred to the notable detriment of the common good and of those over whom a ruler is to be set. Since, therefore, the Romans are few in comparison with the other Catholics, and the supreme pontiff nevertheless (as has been said) is in some sense the proper bishop of them, because they have no other bishop as the other Catholics do, it is reasonably the case that the other Catholics have no right to elect the supreme pontiff except when the election would not pertain to the Romans, namely when the Romans lack the right of electing, either through renunciation of the right, or through apostasy, or through heretical depravity. By this the answer to what you asked is made plain: the Catholics do not always elect together with the Romans because, although they have the right of electing, they do not have the right of electing in every case, but only in the case where the right of electing would in no way belong to the Romans. From these things it follows that if the Romans could cede the right of electing the supreme pontiff, or if they all became heretics or apostates from the faith, they could not deprive the Church of the right of electing the supreme pontiff, but in such a case the other Catholics would have the right of electing the supreme pontiff.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: Respondet tertia obiectioni capituli praecedentis, ubi etiam notatur, quod triplex est ius naturale, & quomodo omne ius naturale potest vocari divinum.
units.tr: It answers the third objection of the preceding chapter, where it is also noted that there is a threefold natural law, and how all natural law can be called divine.

units.la: Discipulus. Dic qualiter respondetur ad illud, quod accepi, quod Romani nec iure divino, nec iure humano habent ius eligendi summum pontificem.
units.tr: Disciple. Tell me how one answers what I have heard: that the Romans have the right to elect the supreme pontiff neither by divine right nor by human right.

units.la: Mag. Ad hoc respondetur, quod extendendo ius divinum ad omne ius naturale, Romani ex iure divino habent ius eligendi summum pontificem.
units.tr: Master. To this it is answered that, by extending divine right to all natural law, the Romans have the right to elect the supreme pontiff by divine right.

units.la: Disc. Ista responsio obscura mihi videtur, ideo secundum istam opinionem capio declarari, primo autem declara secundum eam, quare dicitur extendendo ius divinum ad omne ius naturale: secundo quare omne ius naturale potest vocari ius divinum.
units.tr: Disc. That answer seems obscure to me, so I would like it explained according to this opinion. First, explain according to it why it is said "by extending divine right to all natural law"; second, why all natural law can be called divine right.

units.la: Mag. Primum distinguitur propter tres modos iuris naturalis. Uno enim modo dicitur ius naturale illud, quod est conforme rationi naturali, quae in nullo casu fallit, sicut est, non machaberis, non mentieris; & huiusmodi. Aliter ius naturale est, quod seruandum est ab illis, qui sola aequitate naturali absque omni consuetudine vel constitutione humana vtuntur, quod ideo est naturale, quia est contrastatum naturae institutae, & si omnes homines viuerent secundum rationem naturalem aut legem diuinam, non esset faciendum nec seruandum, secundo modo, & non primo, ex iure naturali omnia sunt communia: quia in statu naturae institutae omnia fuissent communia, & si post lapsum omnes homines secundum rationem viuerent, omnia deberent esse communia, nihil proprium, proprietas enim propter iniquitatem inducta est 12. q. 1. cap. dilectissimis, isto modo loquitur Isidorus 5. libro Ethimolo. & ponitur in decretis, di. 1. ius naturale, cum dicit, quod secundum ius naturale est communis omnis omnium possessio & omnium vna libertas, non enim communis omnium possessio, & omnium vna libertas est de iure naturali primo modo dicto, tunc enim nullus posset licite sibi aliquid appropriare, nec aliquo iure gentium & ciuili posset aliquis fieri seruus, quia ius naturale est immutabile primo modo & inuariabile, ac indispensabile, dist.5.§.nunc autem, & dist.6.§.hic itaque respondetur. Contat itaque, quod aliqui iure gentium licite sunt serui, teste beato Gregorio, qui, vt inquit 12. q. & c. cum redemptor, ait: salubriter agitur si homines quos ab initio natura liberos protulit & iure gentium iugo subiici tuit seruitutis, vt in ea natura, in qua nati fuerant, manumittentis beneficio libertati reddantur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod iure naturali omnes homines sunt liberi, & tamen aliqui iure gentium sunt serui. Ex quo concluditur, quod ius naturale illo modo accepto vocabulo non est immutabile: Imo bene licet contra statuere, vt iuri fiat contrarium. Tertio modo dicitur ius naturale illud, quod ex iure gentium vel aliquo facto humano euidenti ratione colligitur, nisi de consensu illorum, quorum interest, statuatur contrarium, quod potest vocari ius naturale ex suppositione, sicut secundum Isidorum vbi supra. Ius naturale est de potestate rei, vt commodatae pecuniae restitutio, violentiae per vim repulsio. Ista enim non sunt iura naturalia primo modo, nec secundo: quia nec fuissent in statu naturae institutae, nec essent inter illos, qui secundum rationem viuentes sola aequitate naturali absque consuetudine, & constitutione humana essent contenti, quia inter illos nulla res esset deposita vel commodata, nec aliquis alteri vim inferret, igitur sunt iura naturalia ex suppositione, quia suppositio quod res & pecuniae sint appropriatae iure gentium, vel aliquo iure humano, euidenti ratione colligitur, quod res deposita & pecunia commodata debet restitui, nisi ex causa per illum vel per illos, cuius vel quorum interest, contrarium ordinaretur. Similiter suppositio, quod aliquis violentiam de facto iniuriose inferat alii, quod non est de iure naturali, sed contra ius naturale, euidenti ratione colligitur, quod licet per vim violentiam talem repellere. Propter istos itaque tres modos iuris naturalis, dicunt isti, quod Romani ex iure diuino habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, extendendo ius diuinum ad omne ius naturale, quasi solummodo extenderetur ad ius naturale primo modo dictum, qualiter accipitur ius naturale dist.5.§.1.& dist.6.§.hic itaque respondetur, quod ex solo iure diuino eligendi ius summum pontificem non habent.
units.tr: Mag. First, the distinction is made on account of three modes of natural law. In one way, natural law is that which accords with natural reason, which never fails in any case, such as you shall not commit murder, you shall not lie, and the like. In another way, natural law is what must be observed by those who use only natural equity, without any custom or human constitution. It is called natural because it is contrary to the state of nature as instituted; and if all men lived according to natural reason or divine law, it would not need to be done or observed. In this second mode, and not the first, all things are common by natural law: for in the state of nature as instituted all things would have been common, and if after the Fall all men lived according to reason, all things ought to be common and nothing proper, since property was introduced on account of iniquity, 12. q. 1. cap. dilectissimis. Isidore speaks in this way in the fifth book of the Etymologies, and it is put in the decretals, dist. 1, ius naturale, where he says that according to natural law there is common possession of all by all and one liberty for all. For common possession of all by all and one liberty for all is not of natural law in the first mode stated; for then no one could lawfully appropriate anything to himself, and by no right of nations or civil right could anyone become a slave, because natural law is immutable in the first mode, and invariable and indispensable, dist. 5 §. nunc autem, and dist. 6 §. hic itaque respondetur. It is clear, therefore, that some are lawfully slaves by the right of nations, as blessed Gregory bears witness, who, as he says in 12 q. and c. cum redemptor, says: It is a salutary act if men whom nature at the beginning brought forth free, and whom the right of nations has subjected to the yoke of servitude, are restored to liberty, in the nature in which they were born, by the benefit of a manumitter. From these words it is gathered that by natural law all men are free, and yet some are slaves by the right of nations. From this it follows that natural law, taken in this sense, is not immutable: indeed it is quite lawful to decree the contrary so that the contrary becomes law. In the third mode, that is called natural law which is gathered by clear reason from the right of nations or from some evident human act, unless the contrary is decided with the consent of those whom it concerns. This can be called natural law by supposition, as according to Isidore above. Natural law concerns the power over a thing, such as the restoration of a loaned sum, or the repelling of violence by force. For these are not natural laws in the first or second mode: they would not have existed in the state of nature as instituted, nor among those who, living according to reason and content with natural equity alone, without custom and human constitution, would be satisfied. For among such people nothing would be deposited or lent, and no one would inflict violence on another. Therefore they are natural laws by supposition, because, on the supposition that things and money have been appropriated by the right of nations or some human right, it is gathered by clear reason that a deposited thing and a lent sum must be restored, unless for some cause the contrary is ordained by him or those whose interest it is. Likewise, on the supposition that someone unjustly inflicts violence on another, which is not of natural law but against it, it is gathered by clear reason that it is lawful to repel such violence by force. Because of these three modes of natural law, these men say that the Romans have the right to elect the supreme pontiff by divine right, by extending divine right to all natural law, as if it were extended only to natural law in the first mode, the way natural law is taken in dist. 5 §. 1 & dist. 6 §. hic itaque respondetur, so that they do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff from divine law alone.

units.la: Discipul. Quia istam distinctionem iuris naturalis alias non audiui, volo obiicere contra eam, vt ex solutione obiectionum secundum opinionem istam magis intelligam, an contineat aliquid veritatis. Videtur itaque ista distinctio verbis Isidori in praeallegato capitulo ius naturale apertissime obuiare. Tum quia dicit Isidorus: ius naturale est commune omnium nationum, eo quod vbicunque, in statu naturae nō constituta aliqua habentur. Ista non possunt competere secundo membro huius praedictae distinctionis: quia illa quorum contraria possunt esse licita secundum ius gentium, non sunt communia omnium nationum, nec vbicunque habentur in statu naturae, quia non habentur ibi, vbi contraria secundum ius gentium obseruantur. Tum, quia ibidem dicit Isidorus: hoc autem si quid huic simile est, iniustum nunquam, sed naturale aequumque habetur, hoc neque de secundo membro, neque de tertio potest veritatem habere, omne enim illud, quod dicitur ius naturale secundo modo, potest esse iniustum, ex quo contrarium potest esse de iure gentium, quod enim iuri gentium est contrarium, censendum est iniustum. Illud etiam, quod dicitur naturale tertio modo, potest esse iniustum, ex quo contrarium potest esse de lege naturae secundo modo dicto, cum de iure naturali illo modo dicto sit, quod nulla pecunia commodetur, nulla res deponatur: quia secundum ius naturale sic accepto vocabulo, illa omnia sunt communia, & ita secundum illud ius nulla pecunia potest commodari, nec aliqua res deponi. Ista sunt, quae mouent me contra distinctionem praedictam: ideo dic qualiter respondetur ad ipsa.
units.tr: Disciple. Since I have not heard this distinction of natural law before, I want to object against it, so that from the solution of the objections I may better understand this opinion and see whether it contains anything true. This distinction seems most clearly to conflict with the words of Isidore in the aforesaid chapter ius naturale. For Isidore says: natural law is common to all nations, since wherever, in a state of nature, some things are held not established. These words cannot apply to the second member of the aforesaid distinction, because things whose opposites may be lawful by the right of nations are not common to all nations, nor are they found wherever there is a state of nature, since they are not found where the contraries are observed by the right of nations. Also, Isidore says in the same place: but if anything is similar to this, it is never unjust, but is held to be natural and equitable. This cannot be true of the second or third member. For everything called natural law in the second mode can be unjust, since the contrary may hold by the right of nations; for what is contrary to the right of nations is to be judged unjust. Also, what is called natural in the third mode can be unjust, since the contrary may hold by the law of nature in the second mode stated, since it is of natural law in that sense that no money is lent and no thing is deposited. For according to natural law so taken, all those things are common, and so by that law no money can be lent nor any thing deposited. These are the things that move me against the aforesaid distinction. So tell me how these points are answered.

units.la: Magist. Ad ista duo respondetur, vno modo quod quaedam verba in praedicto modo capiendi ius naturale intelligi debent solummodo de iure naturali primo modo dicto, & quaedam de aliis, ideo verba quae obiicis de iure naturali primo modo dicto debent intelligi, & sic contra praedicta non videntur concludere. Aliter dicitur, quod illa verba quae obiiciendo accipis de omni iure naturali intelliguntur: & sane debent intelligi. Cum igitur dicit Isidorus: Ius naturale est commune omnium nationum, cum omnes nationes indispensabiliter obligantur ad ipsum, & ideo in statu naturae hoc est ius rationis, quae nunquam fallit, habetur autem ius secundo modo dictum ius naturale, quod sic est commune omnium nationum, quod omnes nationes, nisi ex causa rationabili ordinetur contrarium, tenentur ad ipsum, & ideo est ex statu naturae, hoc est rationis naturalis, antequam contrarium statuatur per ordinationem humanam, ideo enim dicebatur, quod omnia sunt communia, antequam de consensu hominum appropriarentur. Ius vero naturale tertio modo dictum est commune omnium nationum ex suppositione, si scilicet omnes nationes statuerunt vel fecerunt illud, quo ius illo modo dictum euidenti ratione colligitur, & ideo in statu naturae, hoc est naturalis rationis, habetur, illo suppositio ex quo tali modo intelligitur. Consimiliter dicitur de illis verbis, quae secundo allegas: hoc autem & si quid simile &c. quod possunt de secundo membro intelligi naturale aequum, quia habetur, nisi contrarium aliquo iure humano ex causa rationabili constituatur. Ius etiam naturale tertio modo dictum aliquo modo nunquam est iniustum, sed semper vt naturale & aequum, vt habetur illo suppositio: ex quo euidenti ratione colligitur, nunquam iniustum sed semper naturale aequum est, quia habetur ibi per illum vel illos, cuius vel quorum interest ordinare contrarium.
units.tr: Magist. To these two points it is answered in one way: certain words, in the said mode of taking natural law, must be understood only of natural law in the first mode stated, and certain others of the other modes. So the words you object to, which concern natural law in the first mode, should be understood that way, and then they do not seem to conclude against what was said. Otherwise it is said that those words which you cite as objections are understood of all natural law, and indeed must be understood so. When Isidore says: Natural law is common to all nations, this is because all nations are indispensably bound by it, and therefore in the state of nature, that is of reason, which never fails, it is held. But natural law in the second mode is common to all nations in such a way that all nations are bound by it, unless for a reasonable cause the contrary is ordained; and therefore it belongs to the state of nature, that is of natural reason, before the contrary is established by human ordinance. For that is why it was said that all things are common before they were appropriated with the consent of men. But natural law in the third mode is common to all nations by supposition, namely if all nations have decided or done that which, by clear reason, is gathered from that third mode; and therefore it is held in the state of nature, that is of natural reason, on that supposition from which it is understood in this way. Similarly, it is said of the words you cite second, but if anything is similar, etc., that they can be understood of the second member as natural and equitable, because it holds unless the contrary is established by some human law for a reasonable cause. Natural law of the third mode is also, in a sense, never unjust, but always natural and equitable, as it is held by that supposition. From this it is gathered by clear reason that it is never unjust but always natural and equitable, because it is held there by him or those whose interest it is to ordain the contrary.

units.la: Discipulus. Videtur quod ista sint inconuenienter dicta, quia secundum ista illud verbum semel positum in verbis praemissis Isidori accipitur aequiuoce. Magister, Hoc non reputatur inconueniens, quia hoc notat Glossa distinctio. 63. c. nosse, dicens: nota verbum semel positum bis aequiuoce ponitur: Sic 28. dist. presbyterum. Discipulus. Declarasti secundum opinionem praescriptam: quare dicit Romanos habere ius eligendi summum pontificem ex iure diuino extendendo ius diuinum ad omne ius naturale: Nunc dicitur secundum eandem, quare dicit omne ius naturale vocari diuinum. Magist. Hoc ideo dicunt: quia omne ius, quod est a Deo, qui est conditor naturae, potest vocari ius diuinum, omne autem ius naturale est a Deo, qui est conditor naturae, igitur &c. Tum quia omne ius, quod explicite continetur in scripturis diuinis, potest vocari diuinum ius, quia diuinum ius in scripturis diuinis continetur, vt habetur dist. 8. c. quo iure, omne autem ius naturale in scripturis diuinis explicite vel implicite continetur, quia in scripturis diuinis sunt quaedam regulae generales, ex quibus solis vel cum aliis colligi potest, quod omne ius naturale primo modo, secundo modo, & tertio modo dictum, licet in eis non inueniatur explicite, sit ius diuinum.
units.tr: Discipulus. It seems that these things have been said inconsistently, because on this reading the word semel, used once in the preceding words of Isidore, is taken equivocally. Magister, This is not regarded as inconsistent, because the Gloss notes it in distinctio 63, c. nosse, saying: "Note that a word used once is used twice equivocally." So also 28 dist. presbyterum. Discipulus. You have explained the matter according to the opinion stated above. Now tell me, on the same opinion, why he says that the Romans have the right to elect the supreme pontiff by divine right, extending divine right to all natural right. Now tell me, on the same view, why he says that all natural right is called divine. Magist.
