They say this because every right that comes from God, who is the creator of nature, can be called divine right; but all natural right comes from God, who is the creator of nature; therefore, etc. Also, because every right that is explicitly contained in the divine Scriptures can be called divine right, since divine right is contained in the divine Scriptures, as is held in dist. 8, c. quo iure; but all natural right is contained in the divine Scriptures, either explicitly or implicitly, because the divine Scriptures contain certain general rules, from which, either alone or together with others, it can be inferred that all natural right, in the first, second and third senses, although it is not found in them explicitly, is divine right.

units.la: Discipul. Declarati secundum opinionem praescriptam duo quae videbantur obscura: nunc dicitur qualiter secundum eandem rationem ex iure diuino habent ius eligendi summum pontificem. Magist. Ad hoc dicitur, quod Romani ex iure naturali tertio modo dicto habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, supposito tamen, quod aliquibus fit aliquis praelatus vel princeps vel rector praficiendus, euidenti ratione colligitur, quod si per illum vel per illos cuius vel quorum interest, non ordinetur, illi quibus est praficiendus habent ius eligendi, & praeficiendi eis, unde nullus dari debet ipsis inuitis, hoc multis exemplis & rationibus poslet probari: sed adducam paucas. Et prima est ad hoc, quod vniuersitati mortalium nullus praeficidebet, nisi per electionem & consensum eorum. Amplius: quod omnes tangit, debet tractari per omnes, quod autem debeat aliquis praeficii aliis, omnes tangit, igitur per omnes tractari debet. Rursus, quorum est sibi facere iura, illorum est, si volucrint, eligere caput. Sed populus quicunque & ciuitas potest sibi proprium ius facere, quod ciuile vocatur, iustit. 1. in ciuile. Igitur & populus & ciuitas potest sibi proprium ius facere & caput eligere, & ita semper spectant ad illos, quibus est aliquis praeficiendus, praeficiendum eligere, nisi per illum vel illos, cuius vel quorum interest contrarium ordinetur. Quod ideo dicitur, quia illi possunt saltem in multis casibus cedere iuri suo, & transferre ius suum in alium vel alios, per quem modum licet populus ex iure naturali tertio modo dicto, vel secundo modo, habet ius condendi leges, illam tamen potestatem transtulit in imperatorem, & ita in potestate imperatoris fuit transferre in aliquem vel aliquos ius eligendi. Similiter illi, quibus est aliquis praeficiendus, sunt in huiusmodi subiecti alicui superiori, ille superior potest ordinare, quod illi non habent ius eligendi, licet habeant ius eligendi ex iure naturali secundo modo dicto, si scilicet nec per ipsos, nec per superiorem esset contrarium ordinatum, & ita videtur istis, quod propositio praeaccepta est euidens reputanda. Sed summus pontifex est specialiter quodammodo praeficiendus Romanis: quia non habent episcopum alium. Igitur ipsi ex iure naturali tertio modo dicto, id est ex iure naturali ex suppositione, ex hoc scilicet suppositio quod debent habere episcopum, habent ius eligendi ipsum, et ipsos Romanos vel alium superiorem Romanis, qui habeat in huiusmodi potestatem, statuitur contrarium vel ordinetur. Ipsi enim Romani potuerunt cedere iuri suo, vel transferre ius eligendi summum pontificem in alium vel alios, poterant etiam transferre ius constituendi electores summi pontificis. Superior etiam Romanis, qui in huiusmodi habuerit potestatem, potest concedere ius eligendi aliis quam Romanis, sed ille superior fuit Christus, & non papa. Et ideo Christus & non papa poterat priuare Romanos iure eligendi summum pontificem, sed Christus non priuauit Romanos iure eligendi summum pontificem, quando enim Christus praefecit beatum Petrum omnibus Christianis dans sibi potestatem, vt vbi vellet tedem eligere, ita vt ibi esset quodammodo proprius illorum episcopus, non priuauit eos iure illo, quod omnibus competit, quibus est aliqua praeficiendi potestas, siue saecularis, siue ecclesiastica, nisi per illos quibus est praeficienda potestas saecularis, vel ecclesiastica, vel per superiorem contrarium ordinetur, igitur cum beatus Petrus elegerit sedem Romae, sequitur quod Romani habent ius eligendi successorem beati Petri, qui eis praeficiendus est in spiritualibus, & ita Romani ex iure diuino extendendo ius diuinum ad quodcunque ius naturale, habent ius eligendi summum pontificem.
units.tr: Discipul. You have explained, according to the opinion stated above, the two points that seemed obscure. Now tell me how, on the same reasoning, the Romans have the right to elect the supreme pontiff by divine right. Magist. To this it is answered that the Romans have the right to elect the supreme pontiff by natural right in the third sense described, provided that someone is to be set over them as prelate, or prince, or ruler. It is clearly inferred from this that, if he is not appointed by him or by those whose interest it is, then those over whom he is to be set have the right to elect and to set him over themselves; hence no one ought to be given to them against their will. This could be proved by many examples and reasons, but I shall adduce a few. The first is this: no one ought to be set over the whole body of mortals except by their election and consent. Further: what touches all ought to be dealt with by all; but that someone should be set over others touches all; therefore it ought to be dealt with by all. Again: those who have the power to make laws for themselves have, if they wish, the power to choose their head. But any people or city can make its own proper law, which is called civil law, Institutes 1, in civile. Therefore both a people and a city can make their own law and choose their head; and so it always belongs to those over whom someone is to be set to choose the one to be set over them, unless the contrary is ordained by him or by those whose interest it is. This is said because they can, at least in many cases, yield their right and transfer their right to another or others. In this way, although the people have by natural right in the second or third sense the right to make laws, they nevertheless transferred that power to the emperor; and so it was in the emperor's power to transfer the right of election to one or more persons. Likewise, those over whom someone is to be set, if they are subject in such matters to some superior, that superior can ordain that they do not have the right of election, although they have that right by natural right in the second sense described, namely if the contrary has been ordained neither by them nor by a superior. And so it seems to these men that the proposition stated above is to be regarded as evident. But the supreme pontiff is, in a certain special way, to be set over the Romans, because they have no other bishop. Therefore they have the right to elect him by natural right in the third sense, that is, by natural right under a supposition, namely the supposition that they must have a bishop; and the contrary is not to be decreed or ordained by the Romans themselves, or by some other superior of the Romans who has such power. For the Romans themselves could yield their right, or transfer the right of electing the supreme pontiff to another or others; they could also transfer the right of appointing the electors of the supreme pontiff. A superior of the Romans who had such power could also grant the right of election to persons other than Romans; but that superior was Christ, and not the pope. And so Christ, and not the pope, could deprive the Romans of the right of electing the supreme pontiff; but Christ did not deprive the Romans of the right of electing the supreme pontiff. For when Christ set the blessed Peter over all Christians, giving him the power to choose a see wherever he wished, so that there would in a certain sense be a proper bishop for them, he did not deprive them of that right which belongs to all who have some power of setting someone over others, whether secular or ecclesiastical, unless the contrary is ordained by those over whom the secular or ecclesiastical power is to be exercised, or by a superior. Therefore, since the blessed Peter chose the see of Rome, it follows that the Romans have the right to elect the successor of the blessed Peter, who is to be set over them in spiritual matters; and so the Romans, by divine right extended to any natural right, have the right to elect the supreme pontiff.

units.la: Discipul. Videtur secundum istam opinionem, quod melius diceretur, quod ex iure gentium Romani habent ius eligendi suum episcopum, quia hoc est de iure gentium, quod omnes, quibus est aliquis praeficiendus, habeant ius eligendi praeficiendum, nisi cedant iuri suo, vel superior eis ordinet contrarium. Magist. Quamuis multa, quae pertinent ad ius gentium, sunt iura naturalia tertio modo dicto iure naturali, tamen secundum istam opinionem magis proprie dicitur, quod Romani habeant ius eligendi episcopum suum ex iure naturali tertio modo dicto, quam ex iure gentium: pro eo, quod ad ius gentium non spectat habere episcopum catholicum, sed hoc spectat ad ius diuinum praeficiendi & etiam eligendi ab illis, quibus est praeficiendus, licet ad ius gentium spectat: spectat nihilominus ad ius diuinum pro eo quod concludi potest ex illis, quae in scripturis sacris habentur vna cum aliis, & illa duo supposita, ex quibus colligitur, quod Romani habent ius eligendi episcopum suum, spectat ad ius diuinum, quamuis diuersimode, vnum autem solum spectat ad ius gentium, & propter hoc magis proprie dicitur, quod Romani habent ius eligendi episcopum suum a iure diuino, siue ex iure naturali tertio modo dicto, quam ex iure gentium. Isti tamen, qui de verbis non curant contendere, dicunt quod sufficit eis, quod Romani habeant ius eligendi episcopum suum ex hoc ipso, quod debent habere episcopum: & quod illi, quibus est praeficiendus aliquis, ab illis debet eligi, nisi cedant iuri suo, vel per superiorem contrarium ordinetur. netur. Verum tamen debeat dici proprie loquendo, quod Romani habent ius eligendi ex iure diuino, vel ex naturali tertio modo dicto, vel potius simul ex iure diuino, & iure gentium, magnam vim non faciunt. Apparet tamen non nullis, quod magis proprie dicitur, quod habeant ius eligendi simul ex iure diuino & ex iure gentium. Et ideo cum quaeritur an habeant ius eligendi ex iure diuino vel humano, dicunt, quod nec ex solo iure diuino, nec humano, sed utroque simul, extendendo ius humanum ad ius gentium, & non solum ciuile, siue canonicum.
units.tr: Discipul. According to this opinion, it would seem better to say that the Romans have the right to elect their bishop by the law of nations, because it is a rule of the law of nations that all those over whom someone is to be set have the right to elect the one to be set over them, unless they yield their right or a superior ordains the contrary. Magist. Although many things that pertain to the law of nations are natural rights in the third sense described, nevertheless, according to this opinion, it is more properly said that the Romans have the right to elect their bishop by natural right in the third sense described than by the law of nations. This is because it does not belong to the law of nations to have a catholic bishop; rather, this belongs to divine right, namely the right of setting someone over others, and also of electing him by those over whom he is to be set, although it also belongs to the law of nations. Nevertheless, it belongs to divine right because it can be concluded from those things which are contained in the sacred Scriptures, together with other things, and the two suppositions from which it is inferred that the Romans have the right to elect their bishop. One of these belongs to divine right, though in a different manner, while only one belongs to the law of nations. For this reason it is more properly said that the Romans have the right to elect their bishop by divine right, or by natural right in the third sense described, than by the law of nations. Those, however, who do not care to dispute about words say that it is enough for them that the Romans have the right to elect their bishop from the very fact that they ought to have a bishop, and that the one to be set over those people ought to be elected by them, unless they yield their right or the contrary is ordained by a superior. Whether it ought to be said, strictly speaking, that the Romans have the right of election by divine right, or by natural right in the third sense described, or rather by divine right and the law of nations together, they regard as of little importance. Some, however, think it more properly said that they have the right of election by divine right and the law of nations together. And so, when it is asked whether they have the right of election by divine or by human right, they say that it is neither by divine right alone nor by human right alone, but by both together, extending human right to the law of nations, and not only to civil or canon law.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Respondet tribus rationibus adductis pro responsione ad secundum intellectum quaesiti, data supra capitulo quinto.
units.tr: It answers the three arguments adduced in support of the response to the second sense of the question, given above in chapter five.

units.la: Discipulus. Ista opinione diffuse aliquantulum declarata videamus qualiter secundum eam ad allegationes in contrarium inductas superius s. ca. respondetur. Magister. Ad primum respondetur: quod quo ad ea, in quibus sufficienter & utiliter iure diuino & iure naturali catholicis est prouisum, non habet papa potestatem aliquam immutandi in praeiudicium quorumcunque catholicorum & in detrimentum, seu periculum boni communis, & ideo caput in spiritualibus omnium Christianorum non habet plenam potestatem ordinandi & statuendi, in quibus debet eligi caput, cum ius eligendi ex iure diuino & naturali competat Romanis, praesertim cum si haberent plenam potestatem, hoc posset redundare in detrimentum & periculum boni communis, sicut ostensum est prius.
units.tr: Student. Now that this opinion has been explained at some length, let us see how, according to it, the objections raised above in the contrary sense are answered. Master. To the first, the answer is this: in those matters in which the Catholics have been sufficiently and usefully provided for by divine and natural law, the pope has no power to change anything to the prejudice of any Catholics, or to the detriment or danger of the common good. So the head of all Christians does not have full power in spiritual matters to order and establish how the head is to be elected, since the right of election by divine and natural law belongs to the Romans. Especially so, since if they had full power, this could turn out to the detriment and danger of the common good, as has been shown before.

units.la: Discipulus. Quare dicunt isti, quod papa non habet in hoc plenam potestatem, cum secundum eos nullam habet potestatem in hoc, ex quo Romani habent ius eligendi ex iure diuino? Magister. Non dicunt, quod papa in nullo casu habeat potestatem quo ad hoc: imo volunt etiam, quod papa ex ordinatione Christi & ex potestate collata sibi a Christo, in aliquo casu habeat potestatem ordinandi illos, qui debeant eligere suum successorem. Ad cuius euidentiam dicunt esse sciendum, quod Christus sufficienter prouidit ecclesiae suae in omnibus necessariis, ideo committendo ecclesiam suam beato Petro, dedit beato Petro & successoribus eius plenitudinem potestatis in spiritualibus, quo ad omnia necessaria ecclesiae suae saluo iure aliorum, quando debite volunt & possunt uti iure suo: ita ut papa in omnibus necessariis spiritualibus possit supplere defectum illorum, qui nolunt vel non possunt uti iure suo, & ideo quia ex iure diuino Romani habent ius eligendi episcopum suum, papa non habet potestatem ordinandi de electione eadem in praeiudicium Romanorum, quando Romani vellent & possent ad bonum commune uti iure eodem. Similiter quia in casu catholici alii habent ius eligendi summum pontificem: ideo papa non habet potestatem ordinandi de eadem electione, quando in tali casu alii catholici vellent optime & opportune uti eodem iure, sed si Romani & alii catholici nollent aut non possent uti iure eodem, tunc papa non habet potestatem ordinandi de electione successoris sui.
units.tr: Student. Why do these men say that the pope does not have full power in this, when according to them he has no power in it at all, since the Romans have the right of election by divine law? Master. They do not say that the pope has no power in this in any case. Indeed, they want the pope, by the ordinance of Christ and by the power conferred on him by Christ, to have power in some cases to order those who are to elect his successor. To make this clear, they say it must be known that Christ sufficiently provided for his Church in all necessary matters. Therefore, in committing his Church to blessed Peter, he gave to blessed Peter and his successors the fullness of power in spiritual matters, with respect to all things necessary for his Church, saving the rights of others, when they rightly wish and are able to use their right. So the pope may, in all necessary spiritual matters, supply the deficiency of those who are unwilling or unable to use their right. And so, because by divine law the Romans have the right to elect their bishop, the pope has no power to order that same election to the prejudice of the Romans, when the Romans wish and are able to use that right for the common good. Likewise, because in some cases other Catholics have the right to elect the supreme pontiff, the pope has no power to order that same election when in such a case the other Catholics wish and are able to use that same right well and opportunely. But if the Romans and the other Catholics were unwilling or unable to use that same right, then the pope does have power to order the election of his successor.

units.la: Disc. Quare isti dicunt, quod papa habet in huiusmodi plenitudinem potestatis quo ad necessaria: & non dicunt absolute, quod habet plenitudinem potestatis in omnibus. Magist. Hoc dicunt, quia ipsi putant, quod Christus dedit legem tam perfectae libertatis, quod renocatis ceremonialibus veteris legis papa super Christianos nullam habet potestatem, nisi quo ad illa, quae praecepta sunt vel prohibita a Deo: & quo ad illa quae de necessitate sunt facienda, unde quod aliquis faciat aliquid, quod est supererogationis, nulli potest praecipere nisi in casu, quando esset de necessitate faciendum, & tunc non debet reputari supererogationis, sed necessarii: sicut propter culpam posset alicui praecipere ieiunare in pane & aqua, vel intrare monasterium, vel aliquid huiusmodi, sed in tali casu non esset illi supererogationis, sed necessarium, quia impletio debitae promissionis est inter necessaria computanda. Discipulus. Quid dicunt, ad quod accepi, quod Christus non ordinauit explicite, a quo debeat eligi caput Christianorum, igitur hoc relinquitur papae? Mag. Dicitur quod Christus de hoc nihil ordinauit specialiter & explicite, ideo voluit, quod quo ad hoc cuilibet conseruarentur iura sua, si ex iure gentium, quo scilicet gentes rationabiliter vtuntur, habent, & ideo quo ad hoc nullam potestatem communem papae in praeiudicium Romanorum.
units.tr: Student. Why do these men say that the pope has such fullness of power in necessary matters, and do not say absolutely that he has fullness of power in all things? Master. They say this because they hold that Christ gave a law of such perfect liberty that, with the ceremonial precepts of the old law abolished, the pope has no power over Christians except in those things that God has commanded or forbidden, and in those that must of necessity be done. So if someone does something that is supererogatory, no one can command it, except in a case where it would have to be done of necessity; and then it should not be reckoned supererogatory but necessary. For example, on account of some fault one might be ordered to fast on bread and water, or to enter a monastery, or something of the kind; but in such a case it would not be supererogatory for him but necessary, because fulfilling a due promise is to be counted among necessary things. Student. What do they say to what I have heard, that Christ did not explicitly order from whom the head of the Christians should be elected, and that therefore this is left to the pope? Master. It is said that Christ ordained nothing specifically and explicitly about this. Therefore he willed that in this matter each person's rights should be preserved, if they have them by the law of nations, which nations use reasonably. And so in this matter the pope has no common power to the prejudice of the Romans.

units.la: Disc. Dic qualiter respondetur ad secundam allegationem adductam superius eodem capitulo quinto. Mag. Respondetur, quod gesta sanctorum non semper ad communia sunt trahenda, & ideo saepe ex illis, quid debeat fieri de huiusmodi lege probari non potest: licet frequenter ex eis quid in casu valeat fieri posset ostendi. Ex hoc igitur, quod beatus Petrus sibi successorem instituit, quid papa valeat facere ex ordinatione speciali Christi probare nequit: ex hoc tamen elici posset, quid papa posset, qui esset talis in omnibus, qualis fuit beatus Petrus. Hoc autem dicit Gratianus, ut habetur dist. 8. q. 1. his omnibus. Illud autem beati Petri, quod scilicet dignitatem pontificalem tradidit beato Clementi, ab illis valet in argumentum assumi, quid tales sustinuerunt, qualem sibi beatus Petrus successorem quaesiuit. Disc. Si papa habet potestatem eandem, quam habuit beatus Petrus: quare non potest sibi substituere successorem, sicut beatus Petrus substituit? Mag. Ad hoc respondet Glo. dupliciter, uno modo, vbi prius, super verbo beatus, vbi quaerit: numquid papa adhuc posset facere sibi successorem? & respondet dicens, non: quia hoc esset immutare statum ecclesiae, ut patet 25. q. 1. quae ad perpetuam, & quia statum fecit in illud tempus, quo non est futurus iudex.
units.tr: Student. Tell me how the second argument adduced above in the same fifth chapter is answered. Master. It is answered that the deeds of the saints are not always to be drawn into general rules. So it often cannot be proved from them what ought to be done under such a law, although often from them one can show what may be done in a given case. From the fact, then, that blessed Peter appointed a successor for himself, one cannot prove what the pope may do by a special ordinance of Christ. Yet from this it could be inferred what the pope could do, if he were in all things such as blessed Peter was. Gratian says this, as is found in Dist. 8, q. 1, "his omnibus". But that blessed Peter handed the pontifical dignity to blessed Clement can rightly be taken as an argument for what such men maintained, namely, what sort of successor blessed Peter sought for himself. Student. If the pope has the same power that blessed Peter had, why can he not substitute a successor for himself, as blessed Peter did? Master. To this the Gloss responds in two ways. In one way, in the place cited above, at the word "blessed", where it asks whether the pope could still make a successor for himself, and answers no: because this would change the state of the Church, as appears in 25 q. 1, "quae ad perpetuam"; and because the arrangement was made for that time, in which the pope was not going to be judge.

units.la: Discipulus. Nunquid ista in nullo placent aliis? Magister. Dicitur quod non: scilicet quia neutra ratio responsionis valet, vt videtur eis, prima non: quia papa potest immutare statutum ecclesiæ, quo ad ea super quæ habet potestatem à Christo. Sicut enim rex potest iubere aliquid, quod neque ante ipsum quisquam, nec ipse vnquam iusserat, §. distinct. quæ contra: ita etiam papa aliquid noui potest iubere, & multa quæ consueuerunt fieri ex causa rationabili reuocare. Secunda etiam ratio non placet eis, quia per illam rationem probatur, quod nullus episcopus etiam de licentia papæ posset sibi eligere successorem, cuius contrarium habetur 7. q. 1. petisti. Discip. Dic aliam responsionem. Magister. Aliter respondetur: quod si beatus Petrus fecit sibi successorem ex speciali reuelatione vel inspiratione Christi, hoc fecit de voluntate & consensu Romanorum catholicorum, qui habebant ius eligendi. Discipulus. Vtrumque istorum ex quo non habetur per scripturas, ea facilitate contemnitur, quam probari nititur. Mag. Dicitur, quod alterum istorum fuisse, patenti ratione conuincitur, & ideo non vtrumque debet contemni. Discipulus. Dic quomodo respondetur ad tertiam allegationem capitulo quinto adductam. Mag. Ad hoc respondetur, quod quamuis ius eligendi Romanum episcopum habuerunt Romani ex iure naturali tertio modo dicto: istud tamen ius & potestatem instituendi electores poterant in alium, vel in alios multipliciter transferre: quemadmodum canonici omnes ecclesiarum cathedralium habent ius eligendi episcopum, & tamen possunt alteri id concedere, quia variis modis possunt concedere potestatem illam vni vel duobus, aut pluribus de scipsis: possunt etiam concedere potestatem eligendi extra de electione, causamque. Romani igitur potestatem instituendi electores poterant concedere summo pontifici: poterant etiam ius eligendi concedere aliquibus paucis de seipsis. Summus etiam pontifex, sicut dictum est prius, in casu habet potestatem ordinandi de electione successoris, ipse etiam papa quamuis vocem in electione papæ habere non possit, in quantum tamen Romanus est, potest simul cum aliis Romanis tractare & ordinare, quibus committi debeat ius eligendi: qui etiam in quantum catholicus in concilio generali, quod gerit vicem omnium Christianorum catholicorum, potest cum Romanis & aliis catholicis tractare & ordinare, quibus vel cui sit potestas eligendi summum pontificem: non obstante, quod ius eligendi pertinuerit ad Romanos. Concedendum est igitur, quod papa concessit aliquando quibusdam regibus ius eligendi summum pontificem, vel aliquando aliis: sed hoc non fecit, quod ipse solus semper habuit potestatem huiusmodi ius concedendi: sed quia Romani, vel in eum solum, vel in eum & alios simul, qui gesserunt vicem Romanorum, & aliiqui transtulerunt illud ius eligendi. Vnde etiam Adrianus papa, sicut habetur distinct. 63. c. Adrianum, non solus, sed ipse & Synodus celebrata Romæ, in qua plures fuere Romani, tradiderunt Carolo regi Francorum ius & potestatem eligendi summum pontificem, & ordinandi Apostolicam sedem. Leo etiam papa, vt habetur dist. 7. c. in Synodo, non solus, sed cum toto clero & populo Romano concessit Ottoni primo regi Theutonicorum summæ sedis Apostolicæ pontificem ordinandi, & ita Romani tali concessione concesserunt: quod facere potuerunt, sicut dictum est prius. Et ideo licet imperator ex eo, quod est catholicus & Romanus, habuit potestatem & ius eligendi cum Romanis aliis: tamen quod solus habuit ius eligendi absque aliis Romanis, hoc aliquando habuit à papa & aliis Romanis, quia etiam posset habere à solo papa, si Romani transtulerunt ius suum in papam, vel etiam si Romani in ordinando de electione summi pontificis inuenirentur in detrimentum ecclesiæ negligentes, & satis probabile est, quod Romani tale ius & potestatem transtulerunt in papam, & ideo ex tunc potuit papa solus concedere ius eligendi summum pontificem, vel imperatoribus, vel vicinis episcopis, vel Cardinalibus, vel Romano clero, vel Canonicis alicuius ecclesiæ Romanæ, vel aliis, prout vidisset vtilitati ecclesiæ conuenire. Discip. Si Romani ex iure diuino habent ius eligendi Romanum episcopum: quomodo possunt transferre ius in papam, cum nulli liceat venire contra ius diuinum? Mag. Respondetur, quod contra illud, quod est sic de iure diuino, quod explicite prohibetur vel præcipitur in iure diuino, vel ex solis contentis explicite in iure diuino colligitur, nulli liceret venire, sed contra illud quod est de iure diuino, quod colligitur ex aliquo contento in iure diuino implicite, & ex iure naturali secundo modo dicto, licet venire ex causa rationabili, sicut etiam ex causa rationabili licet venire contra ius naturale secundo modo dictum: quia quamuis testantibus sanctis patribus de iure naturæ omnia sunt communia, tamen licet res temporales appropriare. Isto modo Romani habent secundo modo ius eligendi Romanum episcopum, & non primo modo, ideo licet eis ex causa contra hoc ius venire.
units.tr: Student. Do these points not please others at all? Master. It is said that they do not. Neither reason for the answer is valid, as it seems to them. The first is not, because the pope can change the statute of the Church in matters over which he has power from Christ. For just as a king can order something which neither anyone before him nor he himself had ever ordered (§ distinct. "quae contra"), so too the pope can order something new and revoke many things that have customarily been done for a reasonable cause. The second reason also does not please them, because by that reasoning it would be proved that no bishop, even with the pope's permission, could choose a successor for himself; yet the contrary is held in 7 q. 1, "petisti". Student. Give another answer. Master. It is answered otherwise: if blessed Peter made a successor for himself by a special revelation or inspiration of Christ, he did this with the will and consent of the Catholic Romans, who had the right of election. Student. Since neither of these is found in the Scriptures, both are dismissed with the same ease with which they are attempted to be proved. Master. It is said that one of these two has been refuted by a clear argument, and so not both should be dismissed. Student. Tell me how the third argument adduced in chapter five is answered. Master. To this it is answered that although the Romans had the right to elect the Roman bishop by natural law in the third way mentioned, nevertheless they could transfer this right, and the power of appointing electors, to another or to others in many ways. Just as all the canons of cathedral churches have the right to elect the bishop, and yet can concede it to another, because they can in various ways concede that power to one, or two, or more of themselves; they can also concede the power of electing (see Extra, De electione, causamque). So the Romans could concede the power of appointing electors to the supreme pontiff; they could also concede the right of election to a few of themselves. The supreme pontiff too, as was said before, in a case has the power to order the election of a successor. The pope himself, although he cannot have a vote in the election of the pope, insofar as he is a Roman can, together with other Romans, deal with and ordain to whom the right of election should be committed. Insofar as he is Catholic, in a general council, which takes the place of all Catholic Christians, he can, with the Romans and other Catholics, deal with and ordain to whom, or to whom in particular, the power of electing the supreme pontiff should belong, notwithstanding that the right of election pertained to the Romans. It must therefore be conceded that the pope at times granted to certain kings the right of electing the supreme pontiff, or at other times to others. But he did not do this because he alone always had the power to grant such a right; rather, the Romans transferred that right of election either to him alone, or to him and others together who acted in the place of the Romans, and to others. Hence Pope Adrian too, as is found in Dist. 63, c. "Adrianum", did not act alone: he himself, together with a synod held at Rome, in which there were many Romans, handed to Charles, king of the Franks, the right and power of electing the supreme pontiff and of ordaining the Apostolic See. Pope Leo also, as is found in Dist. 7, c. "in Synodo", did not act alone but with the whole clergy and Roman people, and granted to Otto the First, king of the Germans, the power of ordaining the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See. And so the Romans, by such a grant, conceded what they were able to concede, as was said before. Therefore, although the emperor, because he is Catholic and Roman, had the power and right of electing together with the other Romans, nevertheless the right to elect alone, without the other Romans, he sometimes had from the pope and the other Romans. He could also have had it from the pope alone, if the Romans had transferred their right to the pope, or if the Romans were found negligent, to the detriment of the Church, in ordering the election of the supreme pontiff. And it is quite probable that the Romans transferred such right and power to the pope. Therefore from then on the pope alone could grant the right to elect the supreme pontiff, whether to emperors, or to neighbouring bishops, or to cardinals, or to the Roman clergy, or to canons of some Roman church, or to others, as he judged would suit the usefulness of the Church. Student. If the Romans have by divine law the right to elect the Roman bishop, how can they transfer that right to the pope, since it is permitted to no one to act against divine law? Master. It is answered that against what is of divine law in such a way that it is explicitly forbidden or commanded in divine law, or is gathered only from what is explicitly contained in divine law, it is permitted to no one to act. But against what is of divine law, which is gathered implicitly from something contained in divine law, and from natural law in the second way mentioned, it is permitted to act for a reasonable cause. Just as, for a reasonable cause, it is also permitted to act against natural law in the second way mentioned: because although, as the holy Fathers testify, by the law of nature all things are common, yet it is permitted to appropriate temporal goods. In this way the Romans have the right to elect the Roman bishop by the second way and not by the first; therefore it is permitted them, for a cause, to act against this right.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Quaeris, in quibus casibus potestas eligendi summum pontificem reuertatur ad Romanos, & respondetur tantummodo in vnico casu, quæ responsio probatur infra, c. 9. & hoc secundum vnam opinionem, aliæ opiniones ponen- tur infra c. 14.
units.tr: You ask in what cases the power of electing the supreme pontiff reverts to the Romans. It is answered that this happens in only one case. This answer is proved below, in chapter 9, and it is the answer of one opinion; other opinions are set out below, in chapter 14.

units.la: Discip. Quia res de facili ad naturam suam reuertuntur, interrogare decreui, si Romani potestatem ordinandi de electoribus Romani episcopi in summum pontificem transtulerunt, an in aliquo casu, & in quo ius eligendi & potestas ordinandi de electoribus papæ secundum istam opinionem reuertatur ad Romanos.
units.tr: Disciple. Since things readily return to their nature, I have decided to ask this: if the Romans transferred to the supreme pontiff the power of ordaining the electors of the Roman bishop, then in some case, and in which, do the right of electing and the power of ordaining the electors of the pope revert to the Romans according to this opinion?

units.la: Mag. Ad hoc diuersimode respondetur, vno modo dicitur, quod solum modo in vno casu ius eligendi & potestas ordinandi de electoribus reuertitur ad Romanos: puta si papa & electores ex eis infecti fuerint hæretica prauitate. vnde si Papa & omnes cardinales efficerentur hæretici, & Romani remanerent catholici, de fide & bono communi, inquantum spectaret ad ipsum, curam competentem habentes, eo ipso Romani haberent ius eligendi & etiam potestatem de electoribus ordinandi, si, quando imperator solus habuerit ius eligendi Papa & etiam imperator fuissent facti hæretici, Romani eo ipso recuperassent ius eligendi & potestatem de electorib. ordinandi. DIS. Istam opinionem volo quod aliquantulum tractemus diffuse. ideo antequam alleges pro ipsa, vt magis addiscam, an aliquid veritatis contineat, opto vt aliqua circa ipsam declares. primo igitur dic, quare innuit opinio ista, quod ius eligendi non reuertitur ad Romanos, nisi Papa efficeretur hæreticus. videtur, q si soli cardinales vel alii electores, si alii essent, efficerentur hæretici, reuerteretur ius eligendi ad Romanos, quia eo ipso, quod Cardinales, vel alii electores, efficeretur hæretici, essent priuati iure eligendi. Sed eo ipso, quod aliqui priuantur electione siue potestate eligendi, ius eligendi devoluitur ad alios; ad quos spectat de iure. ergo non oportet, quod Papa efficiatur hæreticus ad hoc, quod ius eligendi reuertatur ad Romanos. MAG. Ista opinio intelligit, quod Papa superstite ius eligendi non reuertitur ad Romanos, quamuis cardinales vel alii electores, si essent alii, sicut aliquado fuerunt alii, efficerentur hæretici, nisi etiam Papa efficeretur hæreticus, quia licet cardinales eo ipso, quod efficerentur hæretici, essent priuati iure eligendi: tamen Papa catholicus superstes non esset propter hoc priuandus potestate ordinandi de electoribus. Sed si Papa esset mortuus, eo ipso quod cardinales efficerentur hæretici, ius eligendi illa vice reuerteretur ad Romanos. DIS. Quare dicitur, quod ius eligendi illa vice reuertitur ad Romanos? MAG. Ideo dicitur, quia postquam post mortem Papæ vel etiam post infectionem Papæ hæretica prauitate, eligendus esset Papa catholicus, qui etiam haberet potestatem ordinandi de electoribus, sicut & alii prædecessores sui, posito quod Romani transtulerint ius & potestatem suam in Papam ratione officii & non ratione personæ.
units.tr: Master. There are various answers to this. One view holds that the right of electing and the power of ordaining the electors revert to the Romans in only one case: namely, if the pope and the electors have been infected with heretical depravity. So if the pope and all the cardinals became heretics while the Romans remained Catholic, keeping the faith and, so far as it concerns them, due care for the common good, the Romans would by that very fact have the right of electing and also the power of ordaining the electors. And if, when the emperor alone had the right of electing the pope, the pope and the emperor had both become heretics, the Romans would by that very fact have recovered the right of electing and the power of ordaining the electors. Disciple. I want us to discuss this opinion at some length. So, before you cite arguments for it, and so that I may learn whether it contains any truth, I ask you to explain some points about it. First, then, tell me why this opinion implies that the right of electing does not revert to the Romans unless the pope becomes a heretic. It seems that if only the cardinals or the other electors (if there are others) became heretics, the right of electing would revert to the Romans, because by the very fact that the cardinals or other electors became heretics, they would be deprived of the right of electing. But when some are deprived of the election or of the power of electing, the right of electing devolves on others, to whom it belongs by law. Therefore it is not necessary for the pope to become a heretic in order for the right of electing to revert to the Romans. Master. This opinion holds that while the pope survives, the right of electing does not revert to the Romans, even if the cardinals or other electors (if there are others, as there sometimes have been) became heretics, unless the pope also became a heretic. For although the cardinals, by the very fact that they became heretics, would be deprived of the right of electing, a surviving Catholic pope would not on that account be deprived of the power of ordaining the electors. But if the pope were dead, then by the very fact that the cardinals became heretics, the right of electing would revert to the Romans for that occasion. Disciple. Why is it said that the right of electing reverts to the Romans for that occasion? Master. Because after the pope's death, or even after the pope has been infected with heretical depravity, a Catholic pope must be elected, who would also have the power of ordaining the electors, as his predecessors did. This holds on the supposition that the Romans transferred their right and power to the pope by reason of his office and not by reason of his person.

units.la: DIS. Quare dicit ista opinio, quod in isto casu reuerteretur non solum ius eligendi, sed etiam potestas ordinandi de electoribus? MAGIST. Hoc dicitur, quia sæpe aliqua multitudo habet ius eligendi, & tamen non expedit, quod omnes eligant: quia multi mouerentur, malo zelo, & sæpe non possent in personam idoneam conuenire. aliquotiens etiam non possent in vnum locum congruum conuenire. & ideo expedit, quod ordinent, qui debeant eligere, committendo vni personæ vel personis paucis respectu totius multitudinis distinctis, & zelum fidei ac boni communis habentibus ius eligendi. propter hoc enim ab antiquo electiones prælatorum concessæ fuerunt clericis, quia licet omnes clerici & laici habuerunt ius eligendi: de consensu tamen laicorum propter hoc, quod clerici erant sapientiores & sanctiores laicis, ordinatum fuit, quod ipsi soli haberent ius eligendi. & ideo quando laici essent discretiores & meliores clericis, ius eligendi deberet auferri a clericis, & dari laicis, quia illa quæ spectant ad bonum commune, & non competunt aliquibus ratione ordinis aut officii diuini, cui mancipati existunt, per sapientiores & meliores & per quos potest bonum commune melius prosperari, sunt tractanda. & ista fuit causa, quare plures Romani pontifices, in quantum Romani, vna cum aliis Romanis, quibusdam imperatoribus, licet essent laici, dederunt ius eligendi summum pontificem. DISCIP. Quare dicit ista opinio, quod in casu prædicto ius eligendi reuerteretur ad Romanos, si Romani remanerent catholici. MAG. Hoc dicunt, quia si Romani cum Papa & electoribus efficerentur hæretici, vel de electione summi pontificis, ex qua pendet bonum commune Christianitatis, essent in detrimentum Christianæ religionis negligentes vel desides, ius eligendi non reuerteretur ad Romanos. DIS. Ad quos reuertetur vel devoluetur? MAG. Dicitur quod devoluetur ad alios Christianos catholicos debite de electione facienda sollicitos.
units.tr: Disciple. Why does this opinion say that in that case not only the right of electing but also the power of ordaining the electors would revert? Master. This is said because a multitude often has the right of electing, and yet it is not expedient for all of them to elect. Many would be moved by bad zeal, and often they could not agree on a suitable person; sometimes they could not even assemble in one fitting place. It is therefore expedient that they appoint who is to elect, committing the task to one person or to a few persons, set apart from the whole multitude, who have zeal for the faith and the common good and who hold the right of electing. For this reason, from ancient times, the elections of prelates were granted to the clergy. Although all clergy and laity had the right of electing, it was ordained with the consent of the laity that the clergy alone should have it, because the clergy were wiser and holier than the laity. So when the laity were more discerning and better than the clergy, the right of electing ought to be taken from the clergy and given to the laity. For matters that concern the common good, and do not belong to some people by reason of their order or of the divine office to which they are devoted, are to be handled by the wiser and better, and by those through whom the common good can be better promoted. This was the reason why several Roman pontiffs, as Romans together with other Romans, gave the right of electing the supreme pontiff to certain emperors, although these were laymen. Disciple. Why does this opinion say that in the aforesaid case the right of electing would revert to the Romans, provided they remained Catholic? Master. They say this because if the Romans, together with the pope and the electors, became heretics, or were negligent and idle in the election of the supreme pontiff, on which the common good of Christendom depends, to the detriment of the Christian religion, the right of electing would not revert to the Romans. Disciple. To whom will it revert or devolve? Master. It is said that it devolves on other Catholic Christians who are duly concerned about making the election.

units.la: DIS. Hoc videtur irrationabiliter dictum: quia alii catholici sunt in tanta multitudine, quod non possent in aliquem vnum locum conuenire ad tractandum de electione futuri pontificis. MAG. Respondetur, quod in tali casu provinciæ vel dioeceses aut multitudines & quæcunque personæ diligentiam, quam deberent, minime adhibentes ad eligendum summum pontificem, eo ipso essent iure eligendi & potestate de electione facienda ordinandi priuatæ, & ius eligendi devoluetur ad alios: ita quod si vnus solus clericus vel laicus remaneret, qui vt deberet esset sollicitus de electione facienda, ius eligendi devoluetur ad ipsum. DIS. Quid si nullus esset sollicitus, vt deberet? MAG. Respondetur, quod sicut nunquam usque ad finem mundi fides deficiet, ita semper aliquis erit in gratia & debito modo sollicitus de his, quæ sunt necessaria Dei ecclesiæ. Si autem nullus esset sollicitus, sed omnes essent negligentes circa electionem summi pontificis necessario faciendam, omnes essent extra gratiam & in peccato mortali, quod nunquam eueniet.
units.tr: Disciple. This seems unreasonably said, because the other Catholics are so numerous that they could not assemble in one place to deal with the election of the future pontiff. Master. It is answered that in such a case provinces or dioceses, or multitudes and whatever persons, who do not apply the diligence they ought to the election of the supreme pontiff, would by that very fact lose the right of electing and the power of ordaining the election to be made, and the right would devolve on others. So if only one clergyman or layman remained who, as he ought, was concerned about making the election, the right of electing would devolve on him. Disciple. What if no one were concerned as he ought? Master. It is answered that just as the faith will never fail until the end of the world, so there will always be someone in grace and duly concerned about what is necessary for the Church of God. But if no one were concerned, and all were negligent about the election of the supreme pontiff, which must necessarily be held, all would be outside grace and in mortal sin. This will never happen.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Rationibus probat responsionem datam ad quæsitum c. precedenti.
units.tr: It proves by reasons the answer given to the question in the preceding chapter.

units.la: DISCIP. Quantum volo, explicasti vel explicare curasti opinionem prædictam. Ideo nunc incipe allegare pro ipsa, aut primo conare respondere, quod electores quicunque, summi pontificis siue cardinales, siue imperator, siue aliqui quicunque clerici vel laici, si efficerentur hæretici, eo ipso essent priuati iure eligendi summum pontificem. MAG. Hoc videtur multipliciter pliciter posse, probari. primo sic: Illi qui non sunt de corpore ecclesiæ, nō possunt eligere caput ecclesiæ. quia caput ecclesiæ à membro vel membris ecclesiæ solummodo eligi debet. Sed hæretici quicunque siue cardinales siue alii nō sunt de corpore ecclesiæ, quia oēs hæretici per hæresim exeunt ecclesiam, teste beato Cypriano, qui vt legitur, 1.q.1.r.si quis, ait: Si quis de ecclesia hæretica præsumptione exierit, à semetipso damnatus est. ergo hæretici non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem. Amplius, illi cui catholici per præceptum iuris Dei communicari non debent, non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, quia electoribus summi pontificis communicare tenentur catholici, quomodo elegerunt audiendo. Sed hæreticis per præceptum iuris Dei catholici communicare non debent, teste B. Paulo, qui ad Titum tertio ait. hæreticum hominem post primam & secundam correctionem devita. Et B. Iohannes canonica sua ait: Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non affert, nolite recipere eum in domum, nec ave ei dixeritis. Qui enim dicit ei ave, communicat eius opinionib. malignis. super quib. verbis dicit Beda, vt legitur. 24.q.1.c. omnis: hoc Iohannes de hæreticis siue schismaticis cauendis, qua verbis docuit, etiam factis exhibuit. Narrat enim de illo auditor sanctissimus eius Polycarpus Smyrnæorum antistes: Quia tempore quodam, cum apud Ephesum balneis lauandi gratia fuisset ingressus, & vidisset ibi Cerinthum exire, continuo discessit non lotus: dicens, fugiamus hinc, ne & balnea ipsa nos corrumpant, in quibus Cerinthus lauatur inimicus veritatis. Ex quibus aliisque quam pluribus colligitur, quod hæreticis catholici communicare non debent. ergo hæretici cardinales vel alii ius eligendi summum pontificem habere non possunt. Rursus, qui habendus est sicut ethnicus & publicanus, ius eligendi summum pontificem habere non potest: quia infideles, scilicet ethnici, non sunt capaces talis iuris. sed hæreticus habendus est sicut ethnicus & publicanus, teste Hieronymo, qui vt legitur. 24.q.1.c. omnibus, ait: Hanc domum, (scilicet ecclesiam Dei) si quis corrigentem corripientemque contempserit, sit tibi, inquis, tanquam ethnicus & publicanus. ergo hæreticus iure eligendi summum pontificem, si habuerit, est priuatus. Præterea, qui nihil potestatis ac iuris habent, non habet ius eligendi summum pontificem, quod non minimum inter iura ecclesiastica est censendū. Sed hæretici nihil potestatis ac iuris habent, teste B. Cyp. qui, vt legitur, 24.q.1.c. didicimus, ait: didicimus omnino hæreticos & schismaticos nihil potestatis habere ac iuris. quod de iure ecclesiastico intelligit Cyp. quia iura secularia poterant aliquando habere hæretici. ergo hæretici ius eligendi summum pontificem habere non possunt.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. As far as I can see, you have explained, or taken care to explain, the opinion stated above. So now begin to argue in its favour, or first try to show that the electors, whoever they are, whether cardinals, or the emperor, or any clerics or laymen, would by that very fact be deprived of the right to elect the supreme pontiff if they became heretics. MASTER. This can be proved in many ways. First, thus. Those who are not of the body of the Church cannot elect the head of the Church, because the head of the Church ought to be chosen only by a member or members of the Church. But heretics, whether cardinals or others, are not of the body of the Church, because all heretics leave the Church by their heresy, as blessed Cyprian witnesses. As it is read in 1 q. 1 c. Si quis, he says: "If anyone has presumptuously gone out of the heretical church, he has condemned himself." Therefore heretics do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff. Further, those with whom Catholics must not communicate by the precept of divine law do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff, since Catholics are bound to communicate with the electors of the supreme pontiff, as they were chosen by hearing. But Catholics ought not to communicate with heretics by the precept of divine law, as blessed Paul witnesses, who says in Titus 3: "Avoid a heretical man after the first and second admonition." And blessed John in his canonical epistle says: "If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into the house, and do not say 'Hail' to him. For he who says 'Hail' to him communicates in his evil opinions." On these words Bede says, as is read in 24 q. 1 c. Omnis: "John taught by his words, and also showed by his deeds, that heretics or schismatics are to be avoided. For his most holy hearer, Polycarp, bishop of the Smyrnaeans, tells of him that once, when he had gone into the baths at Ephesus to wash, and saw Cerinthus coming out, he at once left unwashed, saying: 'Let us flee from here, lest the baths themselves destroy us, in which Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is washing.'" From these and many other passages it is gathered that Catholics ought not to communicate with heretics. Therefore heretical cardinals or others cannot have the right to elect the supreme pontiff. Again, one who must be held as a heathen and a publican cannot have the right to elect the supreme pontiff, since unbelievers, that is, heathens, are not capable of such a right. But a heretic must be held as a heathen and a publican, as Jerome witnesses, who, as is read in 24 q. 1 c. Omnibus, says: "If anyone scorns the one who corrects and admonishes him in this house (namely, the Church of God), let him be to you, you say, as a heathen and a publican." Therefore a heretic, if he has the right to elect the supreme pontiff, is deprived of it. Moreover, those who have no power or right whatever do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff, which must be counted no small matter among ecclesiastical rights. But heretics have no power or right whatever, as blessed Cyprian witnesses, who, as is read in 24 q. 1 c. Didicimus, says: "We have learned that heretics and schismatics have altogether no power or right." Cyprian understands this of ecclesiastical right, since heretics could sometimes hold secular rights. Therefore heretics cannot have the right to elect the supreme pontiff.

units.la: Item, inimici fidei Christianæ & omnium catholicorum non possunt habere ius eligendi caput omnium catholicorum, per quod pro fide Christiana etiam morti, si oportet, se debent exponere. Sed cardinales, si sunt hæretici, sunt inimici fidei Christianæ & omnium catholicorum. ergo cardinales, si sunt hæretici, non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem. Præterea, qui habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, in terra, vbi est electio celebranda, sunt tenendi per catholicos & fouendi. Sed cardinales vel alii, qui habuissent ius eligendi summum pontificem, si efficiantur hæretici, in nulla terra catholicorum sunt tenendi vel fouendi, perhibente concilio Lateranensi testimonium ex quo, vt legitur extra de hæreticis. c. sicut, sic habetur: sub anathemate prohibemus, ne quis eos (scilicet hæreticos) in domo vel in terra sua tenere vel fouere, negotiationem cum eis exercere præsumat. ergo cardinales si efficiantur hæretici, non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem.
units.tr: Likewise, enemies of the Christian faith and of all Catholics cannot have the right to elect the head of all Catholics, by which they ought to expose themselves, if need be, even to death for the Christian faith. But cardinals, if they are heretics, are enemies of the Christian faith and of all Catholics. Therefore cardinals, if they are heretics, do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff. Further, those who have the right to elect the supreme pontiff, in the land where the election is to be held, are to be held and cherished by Catholics. But cardinals or others who would have had the right to elect the supreme pontiff, if they became heretics, are to be held or cherished in no land of Catholics, as the Lateran Council bears witness, from which, as is read in Extra, De haereticis, c. Sicut, it is held: "Under anathema we forbid anyone to presume to keep or cherish them (namely heretics) in his house or land, or to carry on business with them." Therefore cardinals, if they become heretics, do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff.

units.la: CAP. X. Inuestigat, si habentes ius eligendi summum pontificem facti sint hæretici, & ab hæresi respiscant, vtrum ius eligendi recuperare possunt.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. It inquires whether, if those who have the right to elect the supreme pontiff become heretics, and return from heresy, they can recover the right to elect.

units.la: DISCIP. Ex quo secundum istam opinionem cardinales si efficiantur hæretici, non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, sed amittunt huiusmodi ius eligendi: nunquid ipsis reuertentibus ad catholicam fidem, recuperant idem ius? MAGIST. Respondetur, quod si cardinales efficiantur hæretici quantumcunq; occulti, non recuperant ius eligendi summum pontificem, quamuis reuertantur ad orthodoxam fidem, & culpam hæreticæ prauitatis per pœnitentiam diluant: nisi idem ius de nouo conferatur eisdem. & idem dicitur de quocunque cardinali, si aliquis eorum efficiatur hæreticus aliis remanentibus in catholica veritate. quia ex tunc non poterit eligere, nisi de nouo ius eligendi conferatur eidem. DIS. Pro ista assertione aliquas allegationes adducas. MAGIST. Hæc assertio taliter posse probari videtur. Nulla dignitas ecclesiastica per hæreticam prauitatem amissa retineri potest sine dispensatione. ergo similiter nullum ius ecclesiasticum siue spirituale per hæreticam prauitatem amissum poterit recuperari absq; noua collatione eiusdem iuris, nisi ex sola ordinatione Christi competat eis. & per consequens, si cardinales per hæreticam prauitatem amittant ius eligendi summum pontificem, idem ius recuperare non poterunt absque collatione noua eiusdem iuris: Cum cardinales immediate ex sola ordinatione Christi non habeant ius eligendi summum pontificem, sed mediante ordinatione humana.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Since, according to this opinion, cardinals who become heretics do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff, but lose such a right of election, do they regain the same right when they return to the Catholic faith? MASTER. It is answered that if cardinals become heretics, however secretly, they do not recover the right to elect the supreme pontiff, even if they return to the orthodox faith and wash away the guilt of heretical depravity by repentance, unless the same right is conferred on them anew. And the same is said of any cardinal, if one of them becomes a heretic while the others remain in Catholic truth, for from then on he will not be able to elect, unless the right of election is conferred on him anew. DISCIPLE. Bring some arguments in support of this assertion. MASTER. This assertion seems capable of being proved as follows. No ecclesiastical dignity lost through heretical depravity can be retained without dispensation. Therefore, similarly, no ecclesiastical or spiritual right lost through heretical depravity can be recovered without a new conferral of that same right, unless it belongs to them by the sole ordinance of Christ. And consequently, if cardinals lose the right to elect the supreme pontiff through heretical depravity, they will not be able to recover the same right without a new conferral of that same right, since cardinals do not have the right to elect the supreme pontiff immediately by the sole ordinance of Christ, but by human ordinance.

units.la: DIS. Hæc ratio non videtur concludere. Nam quod dignitates ecclesiæ per prauitatem hæreticam amittantur, non est ex natura rei, sed ex constitutione ecclesiæ. Ecclesia n. volens punire hæreticos statuit vt ecclesiasticas dignitates amitterent, quas possent, si non obuiaret constitutio ecclesiæ, retinere. quia potestates spirituales, quæ non sunt maiores dignitatibus ecclesiasticis, remanent in haereticis: sicut potestas conficiendi corpus Christi, si haereticus est sacerdos, & potestas conferendi ordines, si est episcopus. ergo etiamsi non obuiaret constitutio ecclesiae, dignitates ecclesiasticas retinerent. Ex quo infertur, quod haeretici retinent iura spiritualia, quae prius habuerant, nisi per constitutionem ecclesiae priuentur eisdem. Sed nulla inuenitur constitutio ecclesiae, per quam cardinales, si efficiantur haeretici, priuentur iure eligendi summum pontificem. ergo absque collatione noua recuperant idem ius, si ad veritatem redierint orthodoxam. MAGIST. Nonnullis apparet, quod ista responsio non sufficit. Nam, vt dicunt, haeretici non per solam constitutionem ecclesiae, sed eo ipso quod sunt haeretici (etiamsi nulla constitutio ecclesiae esset) amittunt ecclesiasticas dignitates, quantum ad omnia quae a viatoribus amitti possunt. quod sic probatur. Non est maior ratio de uno spirituali amissibili, quod amittatur, absque constitutione ecclesiastica per haereticam prauitatem, quam de alio: quia qua ratione diceretur, quod cum haeretica prauitate posse stare vnum spirituale amissibile, eadem facilitate diceretur hoc de quocunque alio spirituali amissibili. Sed aliquod est spirituale amissibile, quod ex natura rei non stat cum haeretica prauitate, quamuis nulla esset constitutio. ergo nullum etiam spirituale amissibile stat cum haeretica prauitate. maior videtur clara. Minor probatur. Nam papalis dignitas, quantum ad omnia amissibilia, quae sunt propria dignitati papali absque omni constitutione ecclesiae per haereticam prauitatem amittitur. quod sic ostenditur. Nullus potest ligari sententia canonis, nisi, quamuis non esset lata sententia canonis, sit minor & inferior conditore eiusdem canonis. Sed Papa, si efficiatur haereticus, ligatur sententia canonis conditi a praedecessore suo, teste Glossa, quae 24. q. 1. c. 1. ait: Hic est casus in quo Papa Papam ligare potest, in quo Papa in canonem lata sententia incidit. nec obuiat regula illa, quia par parem soluere & ligare non potest: quia si Papa haereticus est, in eo quod haereticus est, minor est quolibet catholico. quia lex factum notat sine sententia. ergo Papa effectus haereticus minor est conditore canonis, quo ligatur, etiamsi idem conditor nullam publicet sententiam. Ex quo infertur, quod dignitas papalis omni constitutione amittitur per haereticam prauitatem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. This argument does not seem to conclude. For that ecclesiastical dignities are lost through heretical depravity is not from the nature of the thing, but from the constitution of the Church. For the Church, wishing to punish heretics, decreed that they should lose the ecclesiastical dignities which they could otherwise retain, if the constitution of the Church did not stand in the way. For spiritual powers which are not greater than ecclesiastical dignities remain in heretics, such as the power of consecrating the body of Christ, if a heretic is a priest, and the power of conferring orders, if he is a bishop. Therefore, even if the constitution of the Church did not stand in the way, they would retain their ecclesiastical dignities. From this it follows that heretics retain the spiritual rights which they had before, unless they are deprived of them by a constitution of the Church. But no constitution of the Church is found by which cardinals, if they become heretics, are deprived of the right to elect the supreme pontiff. Therefore, without a new conferral, they recover the same right if they return to orthodox truth. MASTER. It seems to some that this answer is not sufficient. For, as they say, heretics lose ecclesiastical dignities not only by a constitution of the Church, but by the very fact that they are heretics (even if there were no constitution of the Church), as far as all those things are concerned which can be lost by wayfarers. This is proved as follows. There is no greater reason for one spiritual thing that can be lost to be lost through heretical depravity without a constitution of the Church than for another. For by whatever reasoning it would be said that one spiritual thing which can be lost can stand with heretical depravity, with the same ease it would be said of any other spiritual thing which can be lost. But there is some spiritual thing which can be lost and which, by its very nature, does not stand with heretical depravity, even if there were no constitution. Therefore no spiritual thing which can be lost stands with heretical depravity. The major premise seems clear. The minor is proved as follows. For the papal dignity, as far as all the losable things that belong to the papal dignity are concerned, is lost through heretical depravity without any constitution of the Church. This is shown thus. No one can be bound by the sentence of a canon unless, even though no sentence of the canon had been pronounced, he is lesser than and inferior to the author of that canon. But the Pope, if he becomes a heretic, is bound by the sentence of a canon enacted by his predecessor, as the Gloss witnesses, which says in 24 q. 1 c. 1: This is the case in which the Pope can bind a Pope, in which the Pope has incurred the sentence laid down in the canon. Nor does that rule stand in the way, that an equal cannot loosen or bind an equal, because if the Pope is a heretic, then in that he is a heretic he is lesser than any Catholic, since law marks the deed without a sentence. Therefore a Pope who has become a heretic is lesser than the author of the canon by which he is bound, even though that author has published no sentence. From this it follows that the papal dignity is lost through heretical depravity without any constitution.

units.la: DISCIP.
units.tr: DISCIPLE.

units.la: Non videtur verum, quod omne ius spirituale amissibile per haereticam prauitatem amittatur absque constitutione ecclesiae: & quod non possit recuperari absque noua collatione eiusdem iuris. Nam ius eligendi summum pontificem est ius spirituale, vt isti dicunt: & tamen si Romani efficerentur haeretici, non amitterent illud ius: quia tunc ipsis redeuntibus de haeresi non recuperarent ius eligendi, per rationem praedictam.
units.tr: It does not seem true that every spiritual right that can be lost through heretical depravity is lost without a constitution of the Church, and that it cannot be recovered without a new conferral of the same right. For the right to elect the supreme pontiff is a spiritual right, as they say, and yet if the Romans became heretics they would not lose that right, because then, when they returned from heresy, they would not recover the right to elect, for the reason given above.

units.la: Similiter si Romani & cardinales omnes, qui habent ius eligendi, efficerentur haeretici, ius eligendi illa vice deuolueretur ad alios catholicos. quo posito, ponatur iterum, quod omnes alii Christiani efficiantur haeretici, praeter decem. quo posito, omnes Christiani praeter illos decem amitterent ius eligendi summum pontificem. quo posito, de Christianis haereticis redeant ad fidem catholicam. 20. & illi 10. qui prius erant catholici labantur in haeresim: tunc quaeritur, an isti 10. reuersi de haeresi habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, aut non habeant. si habent ius eligendi: ergo absque noua collatione recuperauerunt ius spirituale, quod prius amiserant per haereticam prauitatem. si non habent ius eligendi: ergo tota ecclesia Dei esset priuata iure eligendi summum potificem: & per consequens Christus non in omnibus necessariis sufficienter prouidit ecclesiae.
units.tr: Similarly, if the Romans and all the cardinals who have the right to elect became heretics, the right to elect would for that time pass to other Catholics. Suppose next that all other Christians become heretics except ten. Suppose further that all Christians except those ten lose the right to elect the supreme pontiff. Suppose then that the heretical Christians return to the Catholic faith, and that those ten who had been Catholics fall into heresy. The question is then whether these ten, having returned from heresy, have the right to elect the supreme pontiff or do not have it. If they have the right to elect, then they have recovered without a new conferral a spiritual right which they had previously lost through heretical depravity. If they do not have the right to elect, then the whole Church of God would be deprived of the right to elect the supreme pontiff, and consequently Christ has not sufficiently provided for his Church in all necessary matters.

units.la: Item ius patronatus est ecclesiae & ius spirituale, & tamen quamuis amittatur per haereticam prauitatem, absque noua collatione poterit recuperari. nam si aliquis patronus fiat haereticus, amittit ius patronatus. sed si retineat tem, ratione cuius est patronus, & redierit ad fidei veritatem, recuperat ius patronatus, quod amiserat: quia ius patronatus transit cum vniuersitate, multo magis reuertitur ad illum, penes quem remanserat dominium rei, ratione cuius erat patronus. Item dignitates ecclesiae per haereticam prauitatem amissae recuperantur absque noua electione. ergo & iura spiritualia propter haereticam prauitatem amissa recuperari poterunt absque noua collatione eorundem iurium. Consequentia videtur aperta, quia eadem ratio videtur de uno & de alio. Antecedens auctoritatibus manifestis videtur posse probari. ait enim Augustinus, vt habetur. 23. q. 4. c. ipsa pietas, loquens de Donatistis haereticis. Habeant ergo de praeterito detestabili errore, sicut Petrus habuit de mendacii timore amarum dolorem: & veniant ad ecclesiam Christi veram, id est catholicam matrem. sint in illa clerici, sint in illa episcopi vtiliter, qui contra eam fuerunt hostiliter: non inuidemus, imo amplectimur, hortamur, optamus religiosissime.
units.tr: Likewise, the right of patronage belongs to the Church and is a spiritual right, and yet, although it is lost through heretical depravity, it can be recovered without a new conferral. For if some patron becomes a heretic, he loses the right of patronage. But if he retains the thing by reason of which he is patron, and returns to the truth of the faith, he recovers the right of patronage which he had lost, because the right of patronage passes with the whole estate; much more does it return to the one with whom the ownership of the thing remained, by reason of which he was patron. Likewise, the dignities of the Church lost through heretical depravity are recovered without a new election. Therefore spiritual rights lost on account of heretical depravity can also be recovered without a new conferral of those same rights. The consequence seems plain, since the same reason seems to hold for the one and the other. The antecedent seems capable of being proved by clear authorities. For Augustine says, as it is found in 23 q. 4, c. Ipsa pietas, speaking of the heretical Donatists: "Let them therefore have, for their past detestable error, the bitter sorrow that Peter had for fear of lying; let them come to the true Church of Christ, that is, the Catholic mother. Let there be in her clergy, let there be in her bishops who were hostile to her and now serve her profitably. We do not begrudge them; rather we embrace them, exhort them, and most earnestly desire it."

units.la: Item ex 6. Synodo, vt legitur 1. q. 7. c. conuenientibus, sic habetur: Religiosissimi monachi dixerunt, sicut receperunt vniversales sex synodi ab haeresi reuertentes, ita & nos recepimus. Sancta synodus dixit, placet omnibus nobis: & iussi sunt Basilius episcopus Anichirii & Theodorus episcopus Mireae ciuitatis, & Theodosius sedere in gradibus & sedibus suis. & infra: Constantinus episcopus Cypri dixit, sufficienter ostensum est quod ab haereticis venientes recipiendi sunt. Item Gregorius vt habetur dist. 12. c. nos consuetudinem, loquens de Donatistis episcopis reuertentibus ad fidem, ait; Sufficiat autem (illis episcopis Donatistis venientibus ad catholicam fidem) committere: sibi plebis curam gerere. propter ista videtur, quod praedicta sunt consona veritati. tu vero dic quomodo respondetur ad illa.
units.tr: Likewise from the Sixth Synod, as is read in 1 q. 7, c. Conuenientibus, it is recorded thus: "The most religious monks said: just as the six universal synods received those returning from heresy, so also we have received them. The holy synod said: it pleases all of us; and Basil, bishop of Anchialus, and Theodore, bishop of the city of Mira, and Theodosius were ordered to sit in their own ranks and seats." And further on: "Constantine, bishop of Cyprus, said: it has been sufficiently shown that those coming from heretics are to be received." Likewise Gregory, as is found in dist. 12, c. Nos consuetudinem, speaking of Donatist bishops returning to the faith, says: "Let it suffice (for those Donatist bishops coming to the Catholic faith) to entrust to them the care of the people." On account of these texts it seems that the things stated above agree with the truth. But you, tell me how these are answered.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad primum istorum dicitur, quod si Romani omnes efficerentur haeretici, ius eligendi summum pontificem amitterent, & secundum quorundam assertionem non recuperarent ius eligendi, licet ab haeresi reuerterentur ad fidem. Sed secundum aliam recuperarent idem ius, propter hoc, quod immediate ex ordinatione Christi & iure gentium habent ius eligendi.
units.tr: MASTER. To the first of these it is said that if all the Romans became heretics, they would lose the right to elect the supreme pontiff, and according to the assertion of some they would not recover the right to elect even if they returned from heresy to the faith. But according to another view they would recover the same right, because they have the right to elect immediately by the ordinance of Christ and by the law of nations.

units.la: DISCIP. Vbi ordinauit Christus, quod Romani haberent ius eligendi summum pontificem? MAGIST. Respondetur, quod tunc hoc ordinauit, quando fecit beatum Petrum caput & pontificem omnium Christianorum, dans ei potestatem eligendi sibi locum, vbi poneret sedem suam, & non priuauit illos, quorum eligeret esse episcopus quodammodo proprius, iure eligendi, & ibi praeficiendi, quod eis competit ex iure gentium, quamuis non sic, quia licite posset ordinare etiam fieri contrarium.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Where did Christ ordain that the Romans should have the right to elect the supreme pontiff? MASTER. It is answered that he ordained this when he made the blessed Peter the head and pontiff of all Christians, giving him the power to choose for himself the place where he would set his see; and he did not deprive those, of whom he chose that one should in some sense be the proper bishop, of the right to elect, by which they may set over themselves one there, which belongs to them by the law of nations, although not in this way, since he could lawfully have ordained even the contrary.

units.la: DIS. Dic quomodo respondetur ad secundam obiectionem, quam feci. MAG. Quibusdam apparet, quod ista obiectio sit fantastica, vt responsione censeatur indigna, ponit enim casum, qui nunquam euenit, necest probabile quod vnquam debeat euenire. DIS. Videtur aliis, quod illa obiectio non est ita fantastica, quod quamuis casus ille nunquam euenerit, posset tamen accidere, & temerarium est dicere, quod nunquam eueniet. ideo videtur utile ipsum discutere, quia ex discussione illorum, quae nunquam vel raro accidunt, profundius & subtilius intelliguntur ea quae saepe eueniunt. siue ergo illa obiectio fuerit fantastica, siue non: Dic qualiter respondetur ad ipsam, quia sicut scire mala saepe est utile, & discutere falsa frequenter ad cognitionem confert plurimum veritatis: ita discutere fantastica multotiens valet ad cognoscendum illa, quae vera & solida dinoscuntur. MAG. Respondetur ad ipsam, quod si omnes Christiani efficerentur haeretici, praeter 10. qui non essent Romani, illi immediate ex speciali ordinatione Christi haberent ius eligendi summum pontificem, & si postea 20. Romani redirent ad catholicam veritatem, & illi 10. efficerentur haeretici. 20. redeuntes ad fidem immediate ex speciali ordinatione Christi recuperarent ius eligendi summum pontificem, quod prius amiserant propter haereticam prauitatem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Tell me how the second objection I made is answered. MASTER. It appears to some that this objection is fanciful, so that it is judged unworthy of an answer, since it posits a case that never happens, and it is probable that it never ought to happen. DISCIPLE. It seems to others that this objection is not so fanciful that, although that case has never happened, it could nevertheless occur, and it is rash to say that it never will. Therefore it seems useful to discuss it, because by discussing those things that never or rarely happen, those that happen often are understood more deeply and subtly. So whether that objection was fanciful or not, tell me how it is answered, for just as it is often useful to know evils, and discussing falsehoods frequently contributes much to the knowledge of truth, so discussing fanciful matters often serves to know those things which are recognised as true and solid. MASTER. It is answered to it that if all Christians became heretics except ten who were not Romans, those ten would have the right to elect the supreme pontiff immediately by a special ordinance of Christ; and if afterwards twenty Romans returned to Catholic truth, and those ten became heretics, the twenty returning to the faith would immediately, by a special ordinance of Christ, recover the right to elect the supreme pontiff which they had previously lost on account of heretical depravity.

units.la: DIS. Vbi ordinauit Christus ista? MAG. Dicitur quod Christus specialiter ista ordinauit & prouidit ecclesiae, quando specialiter dixit Mat. vlt. Ecce ego sum omnibus diebus vsque ad consummationem seculi. tunc promisit, quod nusquam vsque ad consummationem seculi in necessarium deficeret ecclesiae suae. Et ideo quia habere potestatem eligendi summum pontificem est necessarium ecclesiae Dei: tunc insuper catholici vel omnes vel aliqui qualescunq; fuissent antequam haberent potestatem eligendi summum pontificem, ordinauit pariter. quare si essent solummodo 20. catholici & laici, & non Romani, qui ante fuissent haeretici: illi viginti catholici immediate ex speciali ordinatione & promissione Christi haberent ius eligendi summum pontificem: quia non esset maior ratio, quod vnus illorum 20. haberet ius eligendi quam alius: & ita omnes haberent ius.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Where did Christ ordain these things? MASTER. It is said that Christ specially ordained and provided these things for the Church when he said especially in Matthew's last chapter: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world." Then he promised that the Church should never, until the end of the world, be lacking in anything necessary. And therefore, since to have the power of electing the supreme pontiff is necessary for the Church of God, he likewise ordained this, then also for the Catholics, whether all or some of them, of whatever sort they were, before they had the power to elect the supreme pontiff. Wherefore if there were only twenty Catholics who were laymen and not Romans, who had previously been heretics, those twenty Catholics would have the right to elect the supreme pontiff immediately by the special ordinance and promise of Christ, because there would be no greater reason for one of those twenty to have the right to elect than another; and thus all would have the right.

units.la: DIS. Ista prioribus repugnare videntur: quia secundum ista cardinales effecti haeretici possent recuperare ius eligendi summum pontificem absque noua collatione eiusdem iuris. ponatur enim, quod cardinales primo efficiantur haeretici, & postea vel aliqui eorum redeant ad catholicam fidem, & omnes alii efficiantur haeretici. tunc quaeritur, an isti cardinales redeuntes de haeresi habet ius eligendi, aut non habent? Si habet, ergo recuperauerunt ius eligedi absq; noua collatione eiusdem iuris, eo ipso quod redierunt ad orthodoxam fidem. Si non habent ius eligendi, & non sunt alii catholici per casum illum: ergo tota ecclesia Dei caret iure eligendi summum pontificem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. These statements seem to contradict the earlier ones, because according to them cardinals who have become heretics could recover the right to elect the supreme pontiff without a new conferral of the same right. For suppose that the cardinals first become heretics, and afterwards some or all of them return to the Catholic faith, and all the others become heretics. Then the question is whether these cardinals returning from heresy have the right to elect or do not have it.
