If they have it, then they have recovered the right to elect without a new conferral of the same right, simply because they returned to the orthodox faith. If they do not have the right to elect, and there are no other Catholics in that case, then the whole Church of God lacks the right to elect the supreme pontiff.

units.la: MAG. Respondetur ad hoc, quod cardinales ius eligendi, quod habent ex ordinatione humana, puta ex concessione Papae vel Romanorum, in nullo casu recuperant eo ipso quod reuertuntur ad fidem absq; noua collatione eiusdem iuris. & sic intelliguntur illa, quae prius dicta sunt de hoc. Sed ius eligendi quod competit eis ex ordinatione Christi, possunt (saltem in casu, quando non essent alii catholici) recuperare eo ipso quod redirent ad veram fidem. DIS. Quare plus recuperarant ius eligendi, quod habent ex ordinatione Christi eo ipso quod redeunt ab haeresi ad catholicam fidem, quam ius quod non habent nisi ex ordinatione humana? MAG. Huiusmodi ratio assignatur: quia ab eodem est idem ius primo esse collatum, & post amissionem restitutum. & ideo quia Christus ordinauit & promisit, quod nullum vnquam necessarium deficeret ecclesiae suae: ideo ordinauit, quod haeretici in tali casu, quando non sunt alii catholici, eo ipso quod redeunt ad fidem, restituatur eis ius eligendi. sed per nullam ordinationem humanam habetur, quod si cardinales efficiantur haeretici eo ipso quod reuertantur ad fidem, recuperent ius eligendi. & ideo non habent tale ius absque noua collatione. posset tamen inueniri, quod eo ipso recuperarent ius eligendi catholici.
units.tr: MASTER. To this it is answered that cardinals, in no case, simply by returning to the faith, recover without a new conferral of the same right the right to elect which they have by human ordinance, for instance by the grant of the Pope or of the Romans. And so what was said before on this point is to be understood in that way. But the right to elect which belongs to them by the ordinance of Christ they can recover (at least in the case when there are no other Catholics) simply by returning to the true faith. DISCIPLE. Why do they recover more readily the right to elect which they have by the ordinance of Christ, simply by returning from heresy to the Catholic faith, than the right which they have only by human ordinance? MASTER. The reason assigned is of this kind: because the same right was first conferred by the same authority, and after being lost is restored. And because Christ ordained and promised that nothing necessary would ever be lacking to his Church, he therefore ordained that, in such a case, when there are no other Catholics, the heretics, simply by returning to the faith, have the right to elect restored to them. But no human ordinance provides that if cardinals become heretics, they recover the right to elect simply by returning to the faith. And therefore they do not have such a right without a new conferral. It could nevertheless be found that Catholics recover the right to elect simply by that means.

units.la: DIS. Dic quid dicitur de iure patronatus amisso propter haereticam prauitatem. MAG. Dupliciter dicitur: vno modo, quod recuperatur idem ius: quia hoc per ordinationem humanam concessum est: quia sicut ius patronatus transit cum vniuersitate, ita recuperatur recuperata re, ratione cuius habet aliquis ius patronatus. aliqui dicunt, quod ius patronatus non recuperatur, sed specialiter datur illi, qui rem recuperat. DIS. Dic quid dicitur de dignitatibus ecclesiasticis propter haereticam prauitatem amissis, quae dicuntur recuperari absque noua collatione vel electione. MAC. Dicitur, quod episcopatus & aliae ecclesiasticae dignitates, si propter haereticam prauitatem amittantur, non recuperantur absq; noua electione vel aliquo aequivalenti noua electioni, cuiusmodi est dispensatio, qua aliquando dispensabatur cum haereticis, vt reciperent dignitates, nec propter haereticam prauitatem amiserant. in illis n. dispensatio aequalet electioni, oes autem auctoritates inducta, intelligi debent ita, vt haeretici ad dignitates amissas recipiuntur & non aliter.
units.tr: DIS. Tell me what is said about the right of patronage lost on account of heretical depravity. MAG. It is said in two ways. In one way, the same right is recovered, because this has been granted by human ordinance: just as the right of patronage passes with the whole estate, so it is recovered when the property is recovered, and by reason of that a person has the right of patronage. Some say that the right of patronage is not recovered but is specially given to the one who recovers the property. DIS. Tell me what is said about ecclesiastical dignities lost on account of heretical depravity, which are said to be recovered without a new collation or election. MAG. It is said that bishoprics and other ecclesiastical dignities, if they are lost on account of heretical depravity, are not recovered without a new election or something equivalent to a new election, such as a dispensation. Sometimes dispensations were granted to heretics so that they might receive dignities which they had not lost on account of heretical depravity; in such cases the dispensation is equivalent to an election. All the authorities cited, however, must be understood to mean that heretics are received back into their lost dignities only in this way and not otherwise.

units.la: {y} Reference marks in the margin are not separately marked on this page. aliter, relicta Leone Papa, qui vt habetur 1.q.1.c. si quis haeretica, ait: si quis haeretica communionis contagione se maculauerit, hoc in magno beneficio habeat si adempta omni spe promotionis, in quo inuenitur, ordine perma-nere.
units.tr: Otherwise, Pope Leo, as is found in 1.q.1.c. si quis haeretica, says: "If anyone has defiled himself by contagion of heretical communion, let him count it a great kindness if, with every hope of promotion taken away, he is allowed to remain in the order in which he is found."

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Assertio opinionem tenentem, quod si cardinales omnes haereticarentur electio summi Pontificis ad Romanos devolueretur.
units.tr: That the opinion holding that, if all the cardinals were made heretics, the election of the supreme Pontiff would devolve upon the Romans, is asserted.

units.la: DISCIP. Assertio supra capitulo 8. recitata tenet, quod cardinales pro crimine haeresis potestate eligendi Papam priuantur; & non pro alio crimine, de quo nunc esset videndum. sed quia hoc ex sequentibus apparebit: ideo nunc excipe ostendere secundum assertionem illam, quod si cardinales omnes, qui soli nunc habent electionem, efficiantur haeretici an ius eligendi reuertitur ad Romanos. MAG. Hoc videtur diuersis rationibus posse probari: quia si Papa & omnes cardinales efficiantur haeretici, aut ius eligendi est penes alios catholicos, aut in tota ecclesia Dei nulli catholici habent ius eligendi summum pontificem, si penes alios est ius eligendi, & nulli alii quam Romani habent ius eligendi: quia minus videtur de aliis, quod ius eligendi denoluatur ad ipsos, quam de Romanis. ergo Romani habent in hoc casu ius eligendi summum pontificem. Si autem nulli catholici habent ius eligendi: ergo tota ecclesia Dei esse priuatur potestate eligendi summum pontificem, & ita non esset in necessariis sufficienter prouisum ecclesiae Dei.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. The assertion recited above in chapter 8 holds that the cardinals are deprived of the power of electing the Pope for the crime of heresy, and not for any other crime, which we should now consider. But since this will become clear from what follows, now please explain to me, according to that assertion, whether, if all the cardinals, who alone now have the election, become heretics, the right of electing reverts to the Romans. MAGISTER. This seems to be provable by several arguments. For if the Pope and all the cardinals become heretics, then either the right of electing belongs to other Catholics, or in the whole Church of God no Catholics have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff. If the right of electing belongs to others, then no one other than the Romans has the right to elect, since it seems less likely that the right should devolve upon others than upon the Romans. Therefore in this case the Romans have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff. But if no Catholics have the right to elect, then the whole Church of God is deprived of the power of electing the supreme Pontiff, and thus the Church of God would not be sufficiently provided for in essentials.

units.la: Amplius, non videtur aliquomodo credendum, quod minus per iura diuina vel humana sit prouisum ecclesiae Romanae, si electores & praelati ipsius priuentur potestate eligendi, quam aliis ecclesiis inferioribus, si electores ipsorum praelatorum ex aliquo casu priuentur potestate eligendi. sed huiusmodi inferioribus ecclesiis est prouisum, extra de elec. nec pro defectu credendum est, quod per iura diuina vel humana sit prouisum Romanae ecclesiae, quomodo praelatus eligi debeat, si sede vacante electores ipsius potestate eligendi priuentur. quod accideret, si omnes cardinales vna cum Papa mortuo, in haereticam prauitatem caderent. non autem aliter est prouisum nec per iura humana nec per iura diuina, nisi quod electio reuertitur ad Romanos. qui similiter ex iure diuino & iure gentium habuerunt ius eligendi. quia electio ad superiorem devolui non potest, sicut contigit per iura humana de aliis ecclesiis. igitur in hoc casu electio summi pontificis ad Romanos reuertitur.
units.tr: Furthermore, it does not seem in any way credible that less provision is made by divine or human law for the Roman Church, if its electors and prelates are deprived of the power of electing, than for the inferior churches, whose electors of prelates are deprived of the power of electing for some case. But provision is made for such inferior churches (Extra, de electione). Nor is it to be believed, for want of provision, that divine or human law has provided for the Roman Church how a prelate ought to be elected if, the see being vacant, its electors were deprived of the power of electing. This would happen if all the cardinals, together with the Pope now dead, fell into heretical depravity. Yet no other provision is made, neither by human nor by divine law, except that the election reverts to the Romans, who likewise have the right to elect by divine law and by the law of nations. For the election cannot devolve upon a superior, as has happened by human law in the case of other churches. Therefore in this case the election of the supreme Pontiff reverts to the Romans.

units.la: DIS. Ista ratio non videtur concludere. nam iura ad ea, quae frequentius eueniunt, aptantur: quia ex his, quae forte vno casu accidere possunt, iura non constituunt. quod ei semel aut bis contemnunt legislatores vt leges sacrae testantur. sed quod electores praelatorum aliarum ecclesiarum priuentur potestate eligendi, saepe contingit. quod autem electores summi pontificis potestate eligendi priuentur, nunquam accidit vel raro. ergo quantum per iura debeat prouideri, quem vel per quos sunt praefiendi praelati aliis ecclesiis, si illi, quibus concessa est electio, potestate eligendi priuentur, non tamen oportet quod iura prouideant, qualiter eligi debeat Romanus pontifex: licet illi, quibus concessa est electio potestate eligendi priuentur.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. This argument does not seem to conclude. For laws are adapted to what happens more frequently, since laws are not established on account of things that might happen perhaps once or twice; as the sacred laws testify, legislators disregard such cases once or twice. But that electors of prelates of other churches be deprived of the power of electing happens often. That electors of the supreme Pontiff be deprived of the power of electing never or rarely happens. Therefore, however much law ought to provide for whom or by whom prelates are to be set over other churches, if those to whom the election was granted are deprived of the power of electing, it is not necessary that the law provide how the Roman Pontiff ought to be elected, even though those to whom the election was granted are deprived of the power of electing.

units.la: MAG. Ista obiectio multos non mouet propter duo. primo: nam licet iura saepius aptentur ad ea, quae frequentius accidunt: tamen quandoque iura aptantur ad ea quae raro contingunt, & maxime vbi periculum spirituale totius communitatis fidelium vertitur, nisi ius subueniat sed si priuatur potestate eligendi illis, quib. data est electio summi pontificis, nullo iure neq; diuino neq; humano subueniatur ecclesiae, vt possit habere summum pontificem, spirituale periculum immineret toti ecclesiae. ergo si casus contingat, aliquo iure subuenitur ecclesiae. Cum igitur super hoc non inueni-tur ius humanum, recurrendum est ad ius diuinum, vt scilicet reuertatur electio ad Romanos. qui similiter ex iure diuino & iure gentium habent ius eligendi summum pontificem. Secundo quia sicut notat Glo. di. 28. c. de Syracusane, cautela debet adhiberi ex eo quod solet aliquis fieri, vt 93. c. Affros, & ex di. 23. c. in nomine potest colligi manifeste. Sed saepe accidit, quod electores summi pontificis propter haereticam prauitatem fuerunt potestate eligendi priuati. Igitur saltem tunc de iure humano debuit prouideri, qualiter esset eligendus summus pontifex. si hoc non fuit prouisum nisi iure diuino: quia tunc super hoc non fuit editum aliquod ius humanum. igitur ex iure diuino & ratione euidenti colligitur, qualiter sit eligendus summus pontifex, si electores priuentur potestate eligendi, & non sit Papa, qui valeat aliis electionem concedere. hic non videtur aliud probandum, nisi quod saepe accidit, quod electores summi pontificis propter haeresim fuerunt potestate eligendi priuati. quod probatur per hoc, quod saepe imperatores habuerunt potestatem eligendi summum pontificem, qui postea propter prauitatem haereticam fuerunt eadem potestate priuati, teste Gratiano, qui di. 63. c. quia qua verum, ait: frequenter etiam in haereticorum perfidiam prolapsi (scilicet imperatores) catholici matris ecclesia vnitatem impugnare conati sunt: ideo sanctorum statuta patrum aduersus eos prodiderunt, vt semet electioni non interserent.
units.tr: MAGISTER. This objection does not move many, for two reasons. First, although laws are more often adapted to what happens more frequently, yet sometimes laws are adapted to what rarely occurs, and especially where spiritual danger to the whole community of the faithful is at stake, unless law comes to its aid. But if those to whom the election of the supreme Pontiff was granted are deprived of the power of electing, and no law, neither divine nor human, comes to the aid of the Church so that it may have a supreme Pontiff, a spiritual danger would threaten the whole Church. Therefore, if such a case occurs, the Church is helped by some law. Since no human law is found on this point, recourse must be had to divine law, namely that the election revert to the Romans, who likewise have the right to elect the supreme Pontiff by divine law and by the law of nations. Second, because, as the Gloss notes on Dist. 28, c. de Syracusane, caution ought to be applied to what usually happens, as in Dist. 93, c. Affros, and as may clearly be gathered from Dist. 23, c. in nomine. But it often happens that the electors of the supreme Pontiff have been deprived of the power of electing on account of heretical depravity. Therefore at least in that case provision ought to have been made by human law as to how the supreme Pontiff is to be elected. If this was not provided except by divine law, then no human law was enacted on this matter. Therefore from divine law and from evident reason it is gathered how the supreme Pontiff is to be elected if the electors are deprived of the power of electing and there is no Pope who could grant the election to others. Here nothing else seems to need proving, except that it often happens that the electors of the supreme Pontiff have been deprived of the power of electing on account of heresy. This is proved by the fact that emperors often had the power of electing the supreme Pontiff, and afterwards, on account of heretical depravity, were deprived of that same power, as Gratian testifies, who in Dist. 63, c. quia qua verum, says: "Frequently also, having fallen into the perfidy of heretics, the emperors (namely) have tried to assail the unity of the Catholic mother Church; therefore the holy fathers issued statutes against them, that they should not interpose themselves in the election."

units.la: DIS. Videtur quod imperatores priuati non fuerunt potestate & iure eligendi summum pontificem, sed quod renunciauerunt huiusmodi iuri, quod dicit idem Gratianus eadem dist. sanctorum. quia ex his constitutionibus deprehenditur, imperatores renunciasse priuilegium, quod de electione summi pontificis Adrianus Papa Imperatori Carolo & ad imitationem eius Leo Papa Othoni primo regi Theutonicorum fecerat. MAG. Respondetur, quod plures imperatores, etiam de quibus non legitur in decretis, habuerunt ius eligendi summum pontificem, quorum aliqui perdiderunt idem ius propter haereticam prauitatem, aliqui renunciauerunt eidem iuri: & ita verum q; dictum Gratiani continet veritatem pro diuersis imperatoribus.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS. It seems that the emperors, once deprived, did not have the power and right of electing the supreme Pontiff, but that they renounced this right, as the same Gratian says in the same distinction, sanctorum. For from these constitutions it is apparent that the emperors had renounced the privilege which Pope Hadrian had granted to Emperor Charles concerning the election of the supreme Pontiff, and which, in imitation of him, Pope Leo granted to Otto the First, king of the Teutons. MAGISTER. It is answered that several emperors, including some not mentioned in the decretals, had the right of electing the supreme Pontiff; of these some lost the same right on account of heretical depravity, and some renounced that right. And so the saying of Gratian contains truth with respect to different emperors.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAP. XII.

units.la: Quærit ad quos Romanos devolvatur electio Papæ mortuo & cardinalibus prauitate hæresis infectis & respondetur sub opinionibus quatuor, ad primas tres & earum rationes respondetur capitulo sequenti.
units.tr: He asks to which Romans the election of the Pope passes when the Pope is dead and the cardinals are tainted by the depravity of heresy, and it is answered under four opinions; the first three and their reasons are answered in the following chapter.

units.la: DISCIP. Si ius eligendi Romanum episcopum reuertitur ad Romanos electoribus priuatis iure eligendi, & non existente Papa, qui de electione valeat ordinate, ad quos Romanos reuertitur, vtrum scilicet ad omnes vel ad aliquem & aliquos tantum.
units.tr: STUDENT. If the right of electing the Roman bishop reverts to the Romans, as private electors with the right of election, and there is no Pope who can properly ordain the election, to which Romans does it revert? Namely, to all of them, or to some one or a few only?

units.la: MAGIST. Circa hoc sunt diuersæ opiniones, vna est quæ reuertitur ad imperatorem Romanorum. Cuius ratio assignatur, quoniam quando aliqui electores priuantur iure eligendi, electio reuertitur ad illum, vel illos qui ante immediate habuerunt ius eligendi summum pontificem; sed antequam cardinales qui post imperatorem habuerunt ius eligendi immediate habuit imperator ius eligendi summum pontificem. Igitur si cardinales propter hæreticam prauitatem priuantur iure eligendi Romanum episcopum, ius eligendi reuertitur ad imperatorem.
units.tr: MASTER. On this there are different opinions. One holds that it reverts to the Emperor of the Romans. The reason given is this: when some electors are deprived of the right of election, the election reverts to the one or ones who immediately before had the right of electing the Supreme Pontiff. But before the cardinals, who had the right of election after the Emperor, the Emperor himself immediately had the right of electing the Supreme Pontiff. Therefore, if the cardinals are deprived of the right of electing the Roman bishop on account of heretical depravity, the right of election reverts to the Emperor.

units.la: Alia assertio est: quod si cardinales efficiantur hæretici & non sit Papa qui de electoribus valeat ordinare ius eligendi, reuertitur ad canonicos ecclesiæ vbi est sedes Papæ. Quia cessante priuilegio recurrendum est ad ius commune, sed cardinales non habent ius eligendi, nisi ex priuilegio speciali. Igitur si priuilegium illud propter prauitatem hæreticam perdiderint, recurrendum est ad ius commune. Est autem ius commune quod canonici ecclesiarum cathedralium habent ius eligendi episcopos, igitur in hoc casu ad canonicos ecclesiæ vbi est sedes Papæ reuertitur ius eligendi summum pontificem. Alia est assertio, quod in hoc casu electio summi pontificis devolvitur ad totum clerum Romanam. Quia quod soli clerici cathedralis ecclesiæ habent ius eligendi summum pontificem est ex priuilegio Papali, ius autem commune est, quod totus clerus habeat ius eligendi. Igitur ex quo ius eligendi summum pontificem non sit ex priuilegio Papali concesso ecclesiasticis ecclesiæ, vbi est sedes Papæ, vel si fuit eis concessum, postea fuit eis ablatum, quod fuit cardinalibus datum, & cessante priuilegio recurrendum est ad ius commune relinquitur, quod si cardinales efficerentur hæretici, electio ad totum clerum Romanum reuertitur. Quod autem sit ius commune, quod totus clerus habeat ius eligendi, videtur testari Gratianus, qui, vt legitur. dist. 63. §. ex his, ait: Sicut electio summi pontificis non à cardinalibus tantum, imo etiam ab aliis religiosis & ecclesiasticis auctoritate Nicolai Papa est facienda: ita ĭst & episcoporum electionem non à canonicis tantum, sed ab aliis religiosis clericis, sicut in generali synodo Innocentii, habita Roma constitutum est. Vnde idem Innocentius, c. obeuntibus sane episcopis, quando vltra tres menses vacare ecclesiam sacrotum patrum prohibent sanctionCS, sub anathematis vinculo interdicimus, ne canonici de sede episcopali ab electione episcoporum excludant religiosos viros, sed eorum consilio bonestam & idoneam personam in episcopum eligant. quod si exclusis religiosis viris electio facta fuerit, quod absque eorum consensu factum fuerit, irritum habeatur & vacuum. Ex quibus apparet, quod secundum ius commune ad totum clerum spectat electio. Alia est assertio, quod si cardinales efficiantur hæretici, electio reuertitur ad populum & clerum Romanum, ita quod ad omnes Romanos reuertitur, non quod omnes eligant, quia nisi essent valde pauci, hoc absque confusione, quæ est vitanda in huiusmodi, fieri non posset, sed vt de consensu omnium expresso vel tacito ordinatur, quod quis vel qui vicem omnium impleat vel implent episcopum suum eligendo possent Romani in hoc casu committere vices suas imperatori catholico, qui vice omnium eligeret Romanum episcopum. Pro hac assertione sic arguitur, si aliquis vel aliqui à Romanis posset vel possent iure diuino solo vel iure humano solo in casu sibi vendicare ius eligendi summum pontificem, aut hoc posset vel possent iure diuino solo aut iure humano solo, vel simul iure diuino & humano. non solo iure diuino: quia hoc ex scripturis sacris probari non potest. Nec solo iure humano: quia omnia iura humana de hoc propter canonica vel illud quod concessum fuit cardinalibus, quando fuit solum cardinalibus concessum ius eligendi abrogata fuerunt. nec iure gentium potest ab aliis vel ab aliquibus Romanis specialiter vendicare tale ius: quia secundum ius gentium ad omnes spectat eligere præsidem eis vel ordinare, quem eligere debeant. quia secundum ius gentium, quod omnes tangit, per omnes tractari debet. relinquitur ergo, quod ad omnes Romanos, tam clericos quam laicos ius eligendi reuertatur: vt si de consensu omnium tacito vel expresso ordinetur, qualiter summus pontifex eligi debeat. Amplius, quando potestas non habetur ex solo iure diuino, deficiente iure ciuili tam ecclesiastico quam seculari, recurrendum est ad ius gentium, quod est antiquius & communius, quam ius ciuile & ecclesiasticum siue seculare. Sed omnes Romani, non aliqui habuerunt ex iure diuino & iure gentium ius eligendi Romanum episcopum. ad quod probandum probationes sunt adductæ prius. ergo si circa electionem summi pontificis omnia iura ciuilia, canonica & seculnria defecerint, quod accideret, si omnes cardinales efficerentur hæretici, virtute iuris diuini & iuris gentium simul potestas eligendi Romanum episcopum reuertetur ad Romanos.
units.tr: Another assertion is this: if the cardinals become heretics and there is no Pope who can ordain the right of election among the electors, it reverts to the canons of the church where the Papal see is. For when a privilege ceases, recourse must be had to the common law, but the cardinals do not have the right of election except by a special privilege. Therefore, if they have lost that privilege on account of heretical depravity, recourse must be had to the common law. Now it is the common law that the canons of cathedral churches have the right of electing bishops; therefore in this case the right of electing the Supreme Pontiff reverts to the canons of the church where the Papal see is. Another view is that in this case the election of the Supreme Pontiff devolves on the whole clergy of Rome. For that only the clergy of the cathedral church have the right of electing the Supreme Pontiff comes from a Papal privilege, whereas the common law is that the whole clergy should have the right of election. Therefore, since the right of electing the Supreme Pontiff does not rest on a Papal privilege granted to the clergy of the church where the Papal see is, or, if it was granted to them, was afterwards taken from them and given to the cardinals, and since with the privilege ceasing recourse must be had to the common law, it follows that if the cardinals became heretics, the election reverts to the whole Roman clergy. That the common law is that the whole clergy should have the right of election seems to be attested by Gratian, who, as we read (dist. 63, §. ex his), says: Just as the election of the Supreme Pontiff is to be made not by the cardinals only, but also by other religious and ecclesiastical persons, by the authority of Pope Nicholas, so also the election of bishops is to be made not by the canons only, but by other religious clergy, as has been decreed at the general synod of Innocent held at Rome. Hence the same Innocent, in the chapter Obeuntibus: When bishops die, since the holy Fathers forbid the church to be vacant for more than three months, we interdict under the bond of anathema that the canons of the episcopal see exclude religious men from the election of bishops, but with their counsel elect an honest and suitable person as bishop. And if an election is made with religious men excluded, what is done without their consent is to be held invalid and void. From these things it appears that according to the common law the election belongs to the whole clergy. Another assertion is that if the cardinals become heretics, the election reverts to the people and clergy of Rome, so that it reverts to all Romans, not so that all should elect (for unless there were very few, this could not be done without confusion, which must be avoided in such matters), but so that, by the consent of all, expressed or tacit, one or some who act on behalf of all should elect their bishop. In this case the Romans could commit their powers to the Catholic Emperor, who would elect the Roman bishop on behalf of all. For this assertion the argument runs thus: if any one or more of the Romans could claim for themselves the right of electing the Supreme Pontiff in this case, either by divine right alone, or by human right alone, or by both together, then this cannot be by divine right alone, because that cannot be proved from the sacred Scriptures; nor by human right alone, because all human laws concerning this, whether canonical or civil, were abrogated when the right was granted to the cardinals alone. Nor can such a right be claimed specially by others or by some Romans under the law of nations, because under the law of nations it belongs to all to choose a head for themselves or to appoint one whom they ought to choose; for under the law of nations what touches all must be dealt with by all. It remains, then, that the right of election reverts to all Romans, clerics and laymen alike, so that the manner in which the Supreme Pontiff ought to be elected is settled by the tacit or express consent of all. Furthermore, when power is not held by divine right alone, and when civil law, both ecclesiastical and secular, fails, recourse must be had to the law of nations, which is older and more common than civil and ecclesiastical or secular law. But all Romans, not some only, held by divine right and the law of nations the right of electing the Roman bishop; the proofs for this have been adduced above. Therefore, if all civil, canonical and secular laws concerning the election of the Supreme Pontiff fail (as would happen if all the cardinals became heretics), then by virtue of divine right and the law of nations together, the power of electing the Roman bishop reverts to the Romans.

units.la: DIS. Videtur, quod ista ratio non procedit, nisi virtute iuris abrogati, quod nullo modo reuerti poterit, quod si ad aliquod ius abrogatur, perinde est, ac si nunquam fuisset, sed ius gentium, quo Romani aliquando potuerunt eligere Romanum episcopum, quoad eos abrogatum est. ergo virtute illius iuris potestas eligendi Romanum episcopum non reuertitur ad Romanos. MAG. Respondetur, quod virtute iuris penitus abrogati nulla potestas reuertitur. sed ius gentium cum iure diui no âmul quo Romani poterant eligere Romanum episcopum, non potest penitus abrogari, nisi pro tempore, quo secundum ius canonicum alii habent ius eligendi. & ideo cessante illo iure ciuili & ecclesiastico, statim ius gentium tale reuertitur, sicut quia de iure naturali est, quod omnia sunt communia. ideo cessante iure gentium & ciuili, quibus aliquid sit proprium, statim reuertitur ius naturale, vt omnia sint communia, sicut fuerunt ante omnem ordinationem humanam.
units.tr: STUDENT. It seems that this argument does not hold, except by virtue of a law that has been abrogated, which can in no way revert. If a law is abrogated, it is just as if it had never existed; but the law of nations, by which the Romans could at one time elect the Roman bishop, has been abrogated so far as they are concerned. Therefore by virtue of that law the power of electing the Roman bishop does not revert to the Romans. MASTER. The answer is that no power reverts by virtue of a law that has been utterly abrogated. But the law of nations, together with divine law, by which the Romans could elect the Roman bishop, cannot be utterly abrogated, but only for the time during which, according to canon law, others have the right of election. Therefore, when that civil and ecclesiastical law ceases, that law of nations immediately reverts, just as, because it is of natural law, all things are held in common; so, when the law of nations and civil law cease, by which something is held as property, the natural law immediately reverts, so that all things are common, as they were before any human ordinance.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Respondet ad rationes pro tribus primis opinionibus capitulo praecedenti adductas.
units.tr: He answers the arguments adduced in the preceding chapter for the three first opinions.

units.la: DISCIP. Quia ista assertio aliquam apparentiam habere videtur, dic qualiter secundum eam ad allegationes pro assertionibus contrariis respondetur. MAGIST. Ad allegationem pro prima assertione dicitur, quod non semper, quando electores priuantur iure eligendi, ius eligendi reuertitur ad eos, qui immediate ante habuerunt ius eligendi: quia saepe in tali casu ius eligendi ad superiores devoluitur, nonnunquam etiam reuertitur ad eos, qui ex antiquiori & communiori iure habuerunt ius eligendi. & ideo licet imperator immediate ante cardinales habuisset ius eligendi (si cardinales efficiantur haeretici) ius eligendi non reuertitur, nec revoluitur, ad imperatorem solum, sed reuertitur ad ipsum & alios Romanos simul, vt ipse cum aliis Romanis debeat ordinare, quomodo debeat eligi Romanus pontifex. in hoc tamen habet quandam praerogatiuam imperator super alios Romanos, quo ad electionem summi pontificis, vt sine eo (saltem si eius praesentia conuenienter haberi potest) Romani non debeant ad eius summi pontificis electionem procedere nec de electoribus ordinare.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Since this assertion seems to have some plausibility, tell me how, according to it, one answers the arguments for the contrary assertions. MASTER. To the argument for the first assertion it is said that the right of election does not always return, when the electors are deprived of the right of electing, to those who immediately before held the right of election: for often in such a case the right of election devolves upon superiors, and sometimes it also returns to those who held the right of election by an older and more general law. And so, although the emperor immediately before had the right of electing the cardinals (if the cardinals become heretics), the right of election does not return, nor revert, to the emperor alone, but returns to him and to the other Romans together, so that he, with the other Romans, may decide how the Roman pontiff ought to be elected. Yet in this matter the emperor has a certain prerogative over the other Romans, as regards the election of the supreme pontiff: so that without him (at least if his presence can conveniently be had) the Romans ought not to proceed to the election of the supreme pontiff nor make arrangements concerning the electors.

units.la: DISCIP. Quid si imperator vellet impedire electionem summi pontificis, quando cardinales effecti essent haeretici: vel si nollet etiam se intromittere, etiam requisitus per Romanos. MAGIST. Respondetur quod in hoc casu Romani possent, & deberent absque imperatore ad electionem procedere. quia sicut dictum est prius potestas eligendi summum pontificem non competit imperatori, inquantum imperator iure diuino vel iure gentium simul: sed competit sibi inquantum catholicus & Romanus in quibus secum conuenirent Romani alii. & ideo sicut alius Romanus non potest impedire Romanos quin in hoc casu debeant ad electionem procedere, quia sicut dictum est prius potestas eligendi summum pontificem &c. Ita nec imperator poterat eos impedire.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. What if the emperor wished to hinder the election of the supreme pontiff when the cardinals had become heretics, or if he were unwilling even to take part, even when requested by the Romans? MASTER. It is answered that in this case the Romans could, and ought, to proceed to the election without the emperor. For, as was said before, the power of electing the supreme pontiff does not belong to the emperor by divine law or by the law of nations as such, but belongs to him as a Catholic and a Roman, in which respects the other Romans agree with him. And so, just as another Roman cannot prevent the Romans from proceeding to the election in this case, since, as was said before, the power of electing the supreme pontiff etc., so neither could the emperor prevent them.

units.la: DISCIP. Si imperator non habet ius eligendi, virtute iuris diuini & iuris gentium nisi inquantum catholicus & Romanus igitur in hoc alii Romani pares sunt ei. ex quo infertur quod quo ad hoc non plus est vocandus vel requirendus aut expectandus imperator, quam alii Romani. MAGIST. Ad hoc respondetur, quod quamuis imperator & alii Romani sunt quodammodo pares (quo ad hoc quod qualem potestatem & quale ius habet imperator in electione summi pontificis, talem potestatem & tale ius habent alii Romani) tamen quando deberent eligere vel de electione, vel de electoribus tractare: alii Romani deberent in multis imperatori deferre, quemadmodum in aliis electionibus sapientioribus & potentioribus: melioribus & dignioribus est in multis ab aliis deferendum. & ideo sine imperatore quando zelat debito modo pro religione Christiana: alii Romani (si conuenienter potest haberi eius praesentia) non debent ad eius electionem procedere: imo in casu debent omnes alii sibi soli ius eligendi committere, quemadmodum sicut allegatum est prius quidam summi pontifices & alii Romani quibusdam imperatoribus totum ius eligendi dederunt. & tunc imperator vice omnium deberet eligere Romanum pontificem.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. If the emperor does not have the right of election by virtue of divine law and the law of nations, except insofar as he is a Catholic and a Roman, then in this respect he is equal to the other Romans. From this it follows that, in this respect, the emperor is not to be summoned, required or awaited any more than the other Romans. MASTER. To this it is answered that although the emperor and the other Romans are in a certain way equal (in that whatever power and right the emperor has in the election of the supreme pontiff, the other Romans have the same power and right), nevertheless, when they ought to elect, or to treat concerning the election or the electors, the other Romans ought in many things to defer to the emperor, just as in other elections the wiser and more powerful, the better and more worthy, ought in many things to be deferred to by others. And so, without the emperor, when he zealously cares for the Christian religion in the due manner, the other Romans (if his presence can conveniently be had) ought not to proceed to his election; indeed, in such a case all the others ought to commit the whole right of election to him alone, just as, as was said before, some supreme pontiffs and other Romans gave the whole right of election to certain emperors. And then the emperor, on behalf of all, ought to elect the Roman pontiff.

units.la: DISCIP. Dic qualiter respondetur ad allegationem pro secunda assertione adductam. MAGIST. Respondetur quod licet modo sit commune ius canonicum quod clerici cathedralis ecclesiae habent ius eligendi episcopum: tamen aliquando non fuit ius commune. sed ius commune fuit quod clerus & populus haberent ius eligendi. & illud ius est communissimum & antiquissimum; & ideo (cessante omni priuilegio & iure speciali) ad ius communissimum & antiquissimum est recurrendum. quamobrem si omnes cardinales efficerentur haeretici ad ius communius & antiquius est recurrendum, & non ad aliquod speciale ius aliarum ecclesiarum. hoc autem est ius diuinum & ius gentium virtute cuius vel quorum iurium Romanis, scil: clericis & laicis, competit ius eligendi summum pontificem. Et per hoc respondetur ad allegationes pro tertia assertione, quia licet aliquando fuerit ius commune, quod episcopi electio spectaret ad totum clerum, & non ad solos clericos cathedralis ecclesiae, sicut probant auctoritates inductae: non tamen semper fuit ius commune: nec fuit ius communissimum, sed per solam institutionem humanam ecclesiasticam fuit tantum ius commune. & ideo si cardinales efficiantur haeretici, & quod papa sit haereticus vel mortuus, deficiat omnia iura humana institute de electione Romani pontificis recurrendum est ad ius diuinum & ius gentium, virtute quorum electio ad plebem humanam, scilicet clerum & populum Romanum, reducitur.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Tell me how one answers the argument adduced for the second assertion. MASTER. It is answered that although it is now the common canon law that the clergy of a cathedral church have the right of electing the bishop, yet at some times this was not the common law; rather, the common law was that the clergy and the people had the right of electing. And that right is the most common and the most ancient; and so (when every privilege and special right has ceased) recourse must be had to the most common and most ancient law. Wherefore, if all the cardinals were to become heretics, recourse must be had to the more common and more ancient law, and not to some special right of other churches. This, however, is the divine law and the law of nations, by virtue of which laws, or of both, the right of electing the supreme pontiff belongs to the Romans, that is, to the clergy and the laity. And by this one answers the arguments for the third assertion: for although at some time it was the common law that the election of a bishop pertained to the whole clergy, and not only to the clergy of the cathedral church, as the cited authorities prove, yet it was not always the common law, nor was it the most common law, but by human ecclesiastical institution alone was it merely the common law. And so, if the cardinals become heretics, and the pope is a heretic or dead, and all human laws instituted concerning the election of the Roman pontiff fail, recourse must be had to the divine law and the law of nations, by virtue of which the election is brought back to the human people, namely the clergy and the Roman people.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XIV.

units.la: Ponit 4. opiniones responsiuas quaestionis supra capitulo octauo huius, quae probantur rationibus, ad quas respondetur capitulo sequenti immediate.
units.tr: It sets out four opinions answering the question raised in chapter eight above, which are supported by arguments; the replies to these follow immediately in the next chapter.

units.la: DISCIP. Supra capitulo octauo quaesiui, an in aliquo casu, & in quo ius eligendi Romanum episcopum reuertatur ad Romanos, & tu dixisti, quo ad hoc diuersimode respondetur. Recitasti autem vnum modum respondendi. nunc autem recita alium. MAGIST. Aliter respondetur, quod non solum pro haeretica prauitate, sed etiam pro fautoria haereticae prauitatis, si videlicet omnes cardinales sint fautores haereticae prauitatis, & papa sit mortuus, vel haereticus, ius eligendi summum pontificem reuertitur sicad Romanos. Pro hac opinione taliter allegatur. Qui fauet haereticae prauitati, videtur sic haereticam prauitatem defendere: non enim videtur, quod alius fauor, quam defensio, possit ei impendi. sed defendens haereticam prauitatem damnabilior est haeretico, teste Vrbano papa, qui, vt habetur 24. q. 3. c. qui aliorum, ait: qui aliorum errorem defendit, multo & amplius damnabilior est illi, qui errant: quia non solum ille errat, sed etiam alia offendicula erroris praeparat & confirmat. unde quia magister erroris est, non tantum haereticus, sed etiam haeresiarcha dicendus est. ergo defendens haereticam prauitatem dignus est omni poena, qua digni sunt haeretici. Item, qui fauet erroribus haereticorum: inter credentes eorum erroribus est merito numerandus. & per consequens haereticus est censendus, teste Greg. 11. qui, vt habetur, extra de haereticis. c. excommunicamus 2. ait: credentes eorum erroribus haereticos similiter iudicamus. ergo si omnes cardinales fauent haereticae prauitati, tanquam haeretici iure eligendi Romanum pontificem sunt priuati.
units.tr: DISCIPLE: In chapter eight above I asked whether, and in what case, the right of electing the Roman bishop reverts to the Romans, and you said that the answer to this varies. You recited one way of answering. Now recite another. MASTER: The answer is given differently: not only for heretical depravity but also for favouring heretical depravity, that is, if all the cardinals are favourers of heretical depravity and the pope is dead or a heretic, the right of electing the supreme pontiff reverts to the Romans. This opinion is supported as follows. Whoever favours heretical depravity seems to defend it, for it does not seem that any favour other than defence can be shown to it. But one who defends heretical depravity is more damnable than a heretic, as Pope Urban witnesses, who says, as it is found in 24 q. 3 c. qui aliorum: whoever defends the error of others is far more damnable than those who err, because he not only errs himself but also prepares and confirms other stumbling blocks of error; therefore, since he is the teacher of error, he should be called not merely a heretic but a heresiarch. Therefore one who defends heretical depravity deserves every punishment that heretics deserve. Likewise, one who favours the errors of heretics is rightly counted among those who believe their errors, and consequently is to be judged a heretic, as Gregory 11 witnesses, who, as it is found in Extra, de haereticis, c. excommunicamus 2, says: we likewise judge those who believe their errors to be heretics. Therefore, if all the cardinals favour heretical depravity, they are deprived of the right of electing the Roman pontiff as heretics.

units.la: Aliter respondetur, quod cardinales (non solum si faueant haereticae prauitati, sed etiam si sint fautores papae haeretici, viui vel mortui, vel aliorum haereticorum) iure eligendi priuantur, & electio ad Romanos reuertetur, etiam si papa est haereticus, vel mortuus, aut de iure depositus. Pro hac opinione taliter allegatur: pro quocunque crimine papa ipso facto seu iure a papatu dignitate deponitur, pro eodem crimine cardinales cardinalatu priuantur: & per consequens ius eligendi quod eis competit ratione cardinalatus amittunt. sed papa (si est fautor haereticorum) ipso facto seu iure a papatu deponitur. ergo & cardinales propter fauorem haereticorum iure eligendi priuantur. maior videtur probatione minime indigere. Minor exemplo probatur. nam Anastasius secundus propter fauorem haereticorum fuit depositus. non enim legitur de ipso, nisi quod fauerit Fotino & Achacio haereticis. nam in decretis. 19. di. c. Anastasius, sic habetur: Anastasius secundus natione Romanus, fuit temporibus Theodrici regis. eodem tempore multi clerici se a communione ipsius abegerunt, eo quod communicasset sine consilio episcoporum vel presbyterorum & clericorum cuncta ecclesia catholica diacone Thessalonicen. nomine Fotino, qui communicauerat Achatio: & quia voluit occultare vocare Achatium, & non potuit, nutu diuino percussus est. In quibus verbis non habetur, nisi quod Anastasius fauit Fotino & Achatio: & tamen fuit depositus. ergo propter fauorem haereticorum papa deponitur.
units.tr: Otherwise it is answered that the cardinals (not only if they favour heretical depravity, but also if they are favourers of a heretical pope, living or dead, or of other heretics) are deprived of the right of electing, and the election reverts to the Romans, even if the pope is a heretic, or dead, or has been lawfully deposed. This opinion is supported as follows: for whatever crime a pope is deposed from the papal dignity by the very fact or by law, for the same crime the cardinals are deprived of the cardinalate; and consequently they lose the right of electing which belongs to them by reason of the cardinalate. But the pope (if he is a favourer of heretics) is deposed from the papacy by the very fact or by law. Therefore the cardinals also, on account of favouring heretics, are deprived of the right of electing. The major premise seems to need no proof. The minor is proved by an example, for Anastasius II was deposed on account of favouring heretics. Nothing is read about him except that he favoured Photinus and Acacius, heretics. For in the Decretum, dist. 19, c. Anastasius, it is said: Anastasius II, a Roman by birth, lived in the time of King Theodoric. At that time many clerics withdrew from his communion, because he had communicated without the counsel of the bishops, presbyters and clergy; the whole Catholic Church (the deacon of Thessalonica, named Photinus, who had communicated with Acacius) ... and because he wished to conceal and to call Acacius back, and could not, he was struck by divine will. In these words nothing is found except that Anastasius favoured Photinus and Acacius; and yet he was deposed. Therefore the pope is deposed on account of favouring heretics.

units.la: Aliter respondetur: quod cardinales non solum propter haeresim & fauorem haereticae prauitatis, vel haereticorum, sed etiam propter schisma priuantur iure eligendi summum pontificem. Hoc talitet videtur posse probari. Quia qui nihil potestatis aut iuris habet, non habet potestatem eligendi summum pontificem neq; ius. Sed cardinales si efficiantur schismatici, nihil iuris aut potestatis habent, teste beato Cypriano, qui, vt habetur 24. q. 1. c. didicimus, sicut allegatum est prius, ait: didicimus omnino haereticos & schismaticos nihil potestatis habere & iuris. ergo cardinales schismatici non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem. Item, qui sunt extra ecclesiam, non habent ius eligendi summum pontificem. sed cardinales schismatici sunt extra ecclesiam, teste beato Cypriano, qui (vbi prius) ait: si autem foris cuncti schismatici, & haeretici non habent spiritum sanctum. & ideo apud nos manus eis imponitur, vt hic accipiatur, quod illic non est nec dari potest, manifestum est, nec remissionem peccatorum per eos dari posse, quos constat spiritum sanctum non habere. Ex quibus verbis euidenter videtur haberi, quod omnes schismatici sunt extra ecclesiam. Vnde & beatus Cyprianus Nouacianum extra ecclesiam & inter aduersarios & antichristos reputauit computandum, solummodo quia fuit schismaticus, dicens vbi prius: Nouacianus nec debet nec potest excipi, quominus ipse quoq; extra ecclesiam consistens & contra pacem ac dilectionem Christi faciens, inter aduersarios & antichristos computetur. ergo omnes schismatici sunt extra ecclesiam. ergo si ces cardinales efficerentur schismatici, tanq; extra ecclesiam existentes ius eligendi amittunt. Et p consequens in hoc casu ius eligendi reuertitur ad Romanos, sed cardinales (si efficiantur haeretici) iure eligendi priuantur. igitur etiam si sint fautores haereticae prauitatis, eodem iure priuantur.
units.tr: Otherwise it is answered that the cardinals are deprived of the right of electing the supreme pontiff not only on account of heresy and favouring heretical depravity or heretics, but also on account of schism. This can be proved in the following way. He who has no power or right has no power or right of electing the supreme pontiff. But cardinals, if they become schismatics, have no right or power, as the blessed Cyprian witnesses, who, as it is found in 24 q. 1 c. didicimus, as was cited earlier, says: We have learned that heretics and schismatics have no power or right at all. Therefore schismatic cardinals do not have the right of electing the supreme pontiff. Likewise, those who are outside the Church do not have the right of electing the supreme pontiff. But schismatic cardinals are outside the Church, as the blessed Cyprian witnesses, who (in the place cited above) says: If indeed all schismatics and heretics outside have not the Holy Spirit, and therefore among us hands are laid on them so that what is not there, and cannot be given there, may be received here, it is clear that remission of sins cannot be given by those who are known not to have the Holy Spirit. From these words it is clearly seen that all schismatics are outside the Church. Hence also the blessed Cyprian reckoned Novatian, merely because he was a schismatic, to be outside the Church and to be counted among adversaries and antichrists, saying in the place cited above: Novatian neither ought nor is able to be excused from being counted, while standing outside the Church and acting against the peace and love of Christ, among adversaries and antichrists. Therefore all schismatics are outside the Church. Therefore if the cardinals were to become schismatics, as those existing outside the Church they lose the right of electing. And consequently in this case the right of electing reverts to the Romans. But the cardinals, if they become heretics, are deprived of the right of electing. Therefore, even if they are only favourers of heretical depravity, they are deprived of that same right.

units.la: Aliter respondetur, & non solum propter pdicta crimina, sed etiam si papa existente haeretico vel mortuo, videl. cardinales, noluerint eligere, dicentes se non velle eligere, vel et per malitiam aut per damnabile negligentiam in notabile detrimentum & periculum Christianae religionis distulerint eligere summum pontificem, priuati sunt iure eligendi, & electio reuertitur ad Romanos. Pro hac opinione taliter allegatur. nō minus puisum est Romanae ecclesiae contra pericula, quae pericula ei accidere possunt, qua aliis fidelib. Si enim minus esset ei puisum quantū ad ea, quę ordinēda sunt per rectores ipsius, ipsi rectores essent de negligētia damnabili reprehensibiles iudicandi. quia vbi maius periculū vertitur, cautius & sollicitius est agendū. sed ecclesiis aliis sufficienter est puisum, selectores, qui debeant eligere, per malitiam, vel negligentiam distulerint eligere. quia si in fratres menec menses non elegerint, priuantur potestate eligendi ea vice, & potestas prouidendi ad superiorem devoluitur. igitur etiam Romanae ecclesiae est prouisum, qualiter papa eligi debeat, si cardinales per malitiam vel damnabilem negligentiam in notabile detrimentum & periculum religionis Christianae distulerint eligere. sed non est prouisum aliter, quam quod electio ad Romanos conuertatur. igitur saltem pro illa vice cardinales essent priuati potestate eligendi, & ius eligendi reuertetur ad Romanos.
units.tr: Otherwise it is answered that not only on account of the aforesaid crimes, but also if, while the pope is a heretic or dead, the cardinals refuse to elect, saying that they do not wish to elect, or through malice or damnable negligence delay the election of the supreme pontiff to the notable detriment and danger of the Christian religion, they are deprived of the right of electing, and the election reverts to the Romans. This opinion is supported as follows: provision has been made for the Roman Church against the dangers that can befall it no less than for other faithful churches. For if less provision were made for it as regards those matters that are to be ordered by its rulers, those rulers would have to be judged blameworthy for damnable negligence, because where the greater danger lies, caution and care must be the greater. But for other churches provision has been made sufficiently: if the electors who ought to elect delay electing through malice or negligence, for if they do not elect within the months [of the vacancy] they are deprived of the power of electing on that occasion, and the power of providing passes to the superior. Therefore provision has also been made for the Roman Church, as to how the pope ought to be elected, if the cardinals through malice or damnable negligence delay electing to the notable detriment and danger of the Christian religion. But no other provision has been made than that the election should revert to the Romans. Therefore at least on that occasion the cardinals would be deprived of the power of electing, and the right of electing would revert to the Romans.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: In quo respondetur rationibus pro opinionibus capituli praecedentis adductis.
units.tr: In which the reasons adduced for the opinions of the preceding chapter are answered.

units.la: DISCIP. Quomodo autem ad rationem istam vltimam poterit responderi, & qualiter responsio valeat improbari, poterit appetere ex his, quae tractata sunt superius 10. cap. ideo ad praesens nolo, quod de ista responsione & opinione, pro qua adducitur hic, amplius te intromittas. sed indica quomodo respondetur secundum opinionem, quae recitata est supra. c. 8. ad rationes pro opinionibus aliis recitatis capitulo praecedenti: & allegationes adducas. MAGIST. Ad allegationes pro secunda opinione adductas respondetur: quod pro omni fauore haereticae prauitatis (quae non est in fauente absque haeretica prauitate) essent cardinales priuati iure eligendi summum pontificem, & reuerteretur ius eligendi ad Romanos. Pro alio fauore non essent priuati, sed priuandi iure eligendi summum pontificem. an autem possit esse aliquis fauor haereticae prauitatis absque haeretica prauitate in fauente ex his quae dicta sunt libro 7. primae partis huius Dialogi aduertere poterit studiosus. Ad allegationem pro tertia opinione respondetur, quod licet papa (si efficiatur haereticus) sit ipso facto & ipso iure depositus, sicut in prima parte Dialogi huius libro sexto per quamplurimas rationes probatum existit. Et ideo licet pro fauore haereticae prauitatis (quae non est absq; haeresi in fauente) sit papa depositus ipso facto: tamen pro solo fauore haereticorum absque fauore errorum ipsorum non est papa ipso facto depositus: imo secundum aliquos nec etiam deponendus, nisi incorrigibilis appareat, & de eo scandalizetur ecclesia. Cum autem dicitur, quod Anastasius secundus non fuit depositus nisi pro fauore haereticorum. Respondetur, quod non est verum: imo fuit depositus pro haeresi & fautoria haereticae prauitatis, quod ex textu dist. 19. & glo. vt videtur, colligitur euidenter. ait enim Gratianus eadem dist. §. hoc autem: Anastasius enim secundum fauore Anastasii imperatoris, quos Achacius post sententiam in se prolatam sacerdotes & leuitas ordinauerat, acceptis officiis rite fungi debere decreuit, & erronee, supple.) unde in §. sequenti dicit Gratianus: quia ergo illicite & non canonice, sed contra decreta praedecessorum & successorum suorum haec rescripta dedit, vt probat Felix & Gelasius, qui Achacium ante excommunicauerunt, & Hormisda qui ab ipso Anastasio tertius eundem Achacium postea damnauit: ideo a Romana ecclesia repudiatur, & a Deo percussus fuisse legitur. Item Glo. super c. Anastasius, super verbo abegerunt, ait: Hi non recesserunt (scilicet clerici) ab Anastasio ante sententiam, quia inciderat in haeresim iam damnatam. Tunc super verbo communicauerat, dicit Glo. Hic communicauit (scilicet Anastasius) cum Achacio haeretico in malefi cio. unde potuit transfire (scilicet excommunicatio) ad tertiam personam. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Anastasius fuit haereticus & fautor haereticae prauitatis. & ideo fuit depositus ipso iure, & fuit excommunicationis sententia innodatus. Ad allegationem pro quarta opinione respondetur, quod non omnes schismatici sunt omni iure priuati. & de illis loquitur beatus Cyprianus. omnes enim schismatici, quamdiu sunt schismatici, non sunt capaces ecclesiasticarum dignitatum. & ideo Nouatianus secundum Cyprianum non potuit esse papa. schismatici autem non possunt habere executionem alicuius iuris ecclesiastici: licet aliqua iura ecclesiastica possunt habere, dummodo non sunt haeretici. & ideo cardinales propter solum schisma absque haeresi non perdunt ius eligendi summum pontificem, quamuis non debeant eligere, quamdiu in schismate perseuerant. Et per idem breuiter respondetur ad allegationem pro quarta opinione adductam. quamdiu enim in tali malitia & negligentia perstiterint, constat quod de facto sunt tali iure priuati. Si autem resipiscant, idem ius eis debetur.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. How that last reason can be answered, and how the answer can be shown to be weak, you may work out from what was treated above in chapter 10. So for now I do not want you to dwell further on that answer or on the opinion for which the reason is given here. Instead, tell me how the reasons for the other opinions set out in the preceding chapter are answered, according to the opinion recited above in chapter 8, and bring forward the authorities. MASTER. The authorities adduced for the second opinion are answered as follows. For every favour of heretical depravity (which cannot exist in the one favouring without heretical depravity), the cardinals would be deprived of the right to elect the supreme pontiff, and the right of electing would revert to the Romans. For any other favour, they would not be deprived, but liable to be deprived of the right to elect the supreme pontiff. Whether there can be any favour of heretical depravity without heretical depravity in the one favouring, the diligent reader can judge from what has been said in book 7 of the first part of this Dialogue. To the authority adduced for the third opinion, the answer is this: although a pope (if he becomes a heretic) is deposed by the very fact and by the law itself, as has been proved by very many arguments in the first part of this Dialogue, book 6, nevertheless, for favour of heretical depravity (which cannot exist without heresy in the one favouring), a pope is deposed by the very fact; but for favour of heretics alone, without favour of their errors, a pope is not deposed by the very fact. Indeed, according to some, he is not even to be deposed unless he appears incorrigible and the Church is scandalized by him. As for the claim that Anastasius II was deposed only for favouring heretics, the answer is that this is not true. On the contrary, he was deposed for heresy and for favouring heretical depravity, as is clearly gathered from the text of dist. 19 and the gloss, as it seems. For Gratian says in the same distinction, §. hoc autem: Anastasius, out of favour for the Emperor Anastasius, decreed that those whom Acacius had ordained priests and Levites after the sentence pronounced against him should be allowed to exercise their offices lawfully, and he did so wrongly. Hence in the following §. Gratian says: because he gave these rescripts illicitly and not canonically, but against the decrees of his predecessors and successors, as Felix and Gelasius, who had excommunicated Acacius before him, prove, and Hormisdas, who was the third from Anastasius himself to condemn the same Acacius afterwards, therefore he is repudiated by the Roman Church, and it is read that he was struck down by God. Likewise the gloss on c. Anastasius, on the word abegerunt, says: these (namely the clergy) did not withdraw from Anastasius before the sentence, because he had already fallen into a heresy already condemned. Then on the word communicauerat, the gloss says: he (namely Anastasius) communicated with the heretic Acacius in a wicked deed; hence the excommunication could pass to a third person. From these words it is gathered that Anastasius was a heretic and a favourer of heretical depravity, and therefore he was deposed by the law itself and was bound by the sentence of excommunication. To the authority adduced for the fourth opinion, the answer is that not all schismatics are deprived of every right. It is of those that blessed Cyprian speaks. For all schismatics, as long as they are schismatics, are not capable of ecclesiastical dignities, and therefore Novatian, according to Cyprian, could not be pope. Schismatics, however, cannot exercise any ecclesiastical right, although they may hold some ecclesiastical rights, provided they are not heretics. Hence cardinals, on account of schism alone without heresy, do not lose the right to elect the supreme pontiff, although they ought not to elect while they persist in schism. And by the same reasoning the authority adduced for the fourth opinion is briefly answered: as long as they persist in such wickedness and negligence, it is certain that they are in fact deprived of that right. If, however, they repent, the same right is owed to them.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Quaerit, vtrum imperator sit iudex ordinarius papae, & ponuntur diuersi modi di- cendi, & primus ponitur hic, qui tenet quod non.
units.tr: He asks whether the emperor is the ordinary judge of the pope. Various positions are set out, and the first, which holds that he is not, is put forward here.

units.la: DISCIP. Quamuis in prima parte nostri Dialogi li. 6. tractauerimus, an imperator sit iudex ordinarius summi pontificis. & cum ibidem circa hoc opiniones contrarias allegationibus pluribus conatus fueris confirmare: hic tamen de hac materia conferamus, vt excitemus alios tractatulum hunc visuros, qui primam partem huius operis forsitan non habebunt, ad solicite perscrutandum, an imperator supra papam in summo pontificio constitutum aliquam habeat vel habere valeat potestatem. Inuestigemus autem primo, an imperator ratione imperatoriae dignitatis sit in aliquo casu iudex ordinarius papae.
units.tr: DISCIP. Although we treated in the first part of our Dialogue, book 6, whether the emperor is the ordinary judge of the supreme pontiff, and although you tried there to confirm the opposing opinions with several arguments, let us nonetheless discuss this matter here. We do this so that we may move others, who perhaps will not have the first part of this work, to examine carefully whether the emperor has, or can have, any power over the pope, who is set in the supreme pontificate. Let us first inquire whether the emperor, by reason of the imperial dignity, is in any case the ordinary judge of the pope.

units.la: MAGIST. Circa hoc sunt diuersae assertiones & aduersae. vna est, quod imperator ratione imperatoriae dignitatis, non est iudex ordinarius in quocunq; casu summi pontificis. DISCIP. Pro ista assertione allega. MAGIST. Pro ista assertione poteit taliter allegari. si imperator, iuquaninquantum imperator, esset iudex ordinarius papæ, aut esset suus iudex in causa ecclesiastica, aut in causa seculari. non in ecclesiastica: quia solum ad iudicem ecclesiasticum spectat. ideo enim dicitur causa ecclesiastica, quia debet coram ecclesiastico iudice agitari. nec in causa seculari: quia nec in causa criminali nec ciuili, quod non in criminali causa seculari probatur. quia, sicut legitur di. 40. c. sipapa, ex gestis Bonifa. papæ martyris habetur: huiusmodi culpam ipsius idem redarguere nullus mortalium præsumit, quia cunctos ipse iudicaturus, à nemine est iudicandus, nisi deprehendatur à fide devians. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod papa pro sola deviatione à fide est ab aliquo iudicandus. deviatio autem non est culpa secularis. ergo pro nulla culpa seculari est papa ab imperatore vel ab alio iudicandus. Nec imperator est iudex ordinarius papæ in causa seculari ciuili: cum etiam in tali causa (sicut neque in causa criminali) sit iudex ordinarius cuiuscunque episcopi, teste Bonifacio, qui, ut habetur i. 1. q. 1. c. nullus, ait: nullus episcopus nec pro ciuili nec pro criminali causa apud iudicem quemlibet ciuilem, siue militarem producatur. relinquitur ergo ex prædictis, quod imperator in quantum imperator in nulla causa est iudex ordinarius papæ.
units.tr: MAGIST. On this there are opposing assertions. One is that the emperor, by reason of the imperial dignity, is not the ordinary judge of the supreme pontiff in any case whatever. DISCIP. Give arguments for this assertion. MAGIST. For this assertion the following argument can be made. If the emperor, as emperor, were the ordinary judge of the pope, he would be his judge either in an ecclesiastical cause or in a secular cause. Not in an ecclesiastical cause, since that belongs only to an ecclesiastical judge; for a cause is called ecclesiastical because it ought to be tried before an ecclesiastical judge. Nor in a secular cause, whether criminal or civil. That he is not judge in a criminal secular cause is shown as follows. As is read in Dist. 40, c. Si papa, taken from the acts of Boniface, pope and martyr: No mortal presumes to censure his fault, since he who is to judge all is to be judged by no one, unless he is found to have deviated from the faith. From these words it is gathered that the pope may be judged by someone only for deviation from the faith. Deviation from the faith is not a secular fault. Therefore for no secular fault is the pope to be judged by the emperor or by anyone else. Nor is the emperor the ordinary judge of the pope in a secular civil cause, since in such a cause (as also in a criminal one) he is the ordinary judge of every bishop, as Boniface attests, who, as is found in 1, q. 1, c. Nullus, says: No bishop, whether in a civil or a criminal cause, is to be brought before any civil judge, even a military one. It follows, then, from what has been said, that the emperor, as emperor, is in no cause the ordinary judge of the pope.

units.la: DISCIP. Vt mihi occasio sit intelligendi profundius istam materiam, pro ista assertione multas auctoritates adducas, etiam illas, quas in prima parte dialogi tetigisti. quia nolo, ut postea mihi referas exquisite, qualiter assertio contraria ad ipsas nitatur respondere. per hunc enim modum incitabimus alios ad veritatem acutius indagandam, & nobisipsis intellectus auctoritatem adducendarum clarius apparebit. MAGIST. Pro ista opinione auctoritates quamplurimæ adducuntur. Gelasius enim papa, ut habetur 9. q. 3. c. cuncta, ait: Cuncta per mundum novit ecclesia, quoniam quorumlibet sententiis ligata pontificum sedes beati Petri apostoli ius habeat resoluendi, utpote quæ de omni ecclesia fas habeat iudicandi. Item Melchiades, ut habetur 12. quæst. 1. c. futura, ait: Idem præfatus princeps (scilicet Constantinus) donaria immensa contulit & fabricam templi prima sedi beati Petri instituit, adeo ut sedem imperialem relinqueret, & beato Petro suisque successoribus profuturis concederet. Idem vero præsidens sancta synodo, quæ apud Nicenam congregata est, cum querelam quorundam coram se conspiceret deferendam, ait: vos à nemine iudicari potestis, quia Dei solius iudicio reseruamini. diuetenim vocati estis, & idcirco non potestis ab hominibus iudicari. Item Gelasius papa, ut habetur 9. quæst. 3. c. cuncta, ait: Cuncta per mundum novit ecclesia, quod sacrosancta Romana ecclesia fas habeat de omnibus iudicandi, neque cuiquam de eius liceat iudicare iudicio. Siquidem ad illam de qualibet mundi parte appellandum est, ab illa autem nemo est appellare permissus: sed nec illa prætermisit quod apostolica sedes sine vlla synodo præcedente & soluendi quod synodus iniquæ damnauerat: & damnandi nulla existente synodo actus quos oportuit habuit facultatem. Item Gelasius papa, ut habetur dist. 96. scribens Anastasio imperatori ait: Nosti itaque inter hæc ex illorum te pendere iudicio, non illos ad tuam posse regi voluntatem. Item Innocentius papa, ut legitur 9. quæst. 3. c. nemo, ait: Nemo iudicabit apostolicam sedem iusticiam temperare desiderantem. neque enim ab Augusto, neque ab omni clero, neque a regibus, neque a populo iudex iudicabitur. Item Iohannes papa, ut habetur di. 96. c. si imperator, ait: Si imperator catholicus est (quod salua pace ipsius dicimus) filius est non prasul ecclesiæ. Lex autem erubescit filios cateratores esse parentum. ergo nullo modo imperator poterit esse iudex papæ, qui pater est omnium. Item Symachus papa, ut habetur 9. quæst. 3. c. aliorum, ait: Aliorum hominum causas Deus voluit per homines terminare: sed sedis istius præsulem suo sine quæstione reseruauit arbitrio. voluit beati Petri apostoli successores cælo tantum debere innocentiam, & subtilissimi discussoris indagini inuiolatam habere conscientiam. nolite æstimare eas animas inquisitoris non habere formidinem, quas Deus præ cæteris suo reseruauit examini. & infra: Sanctorum voce pontificum dignitatem sedis eius factam toto orbe venerabilem esse, dum illi quicquid fidelium est vbique submittitur, dum totius corporis caput esse designatur. Item Nicolaus papa di. 21. c. nunc autem, ait: quoniam prima sedes non iudicabitur à quoquam. Item Antherius papa, ut habetur 9. q. 3. c. facta, ait: facta subditorum iudicantur à nobis: nostra vero à domino iudicantur. Item Sixtus papa, ut habetur 2. quæst. 5. c. mandastis, cum fuisset accusatus à quodam scriba, episcopis ait: facto consilio cum magna examinatione satisfacientes omnibus, licet euadere aliter satis potuissem, suspicionem tamen fugiens coram omnibus me purgauit: & me scilicet à suspicione & æmulatione liberans, sed non aliis, qui noluerint, aut sponte hoc non elegerint, faciendi formam dans. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod papa in nullo casu tenetur se purgare, si fuerit diffamatus. Ex quo infertur, quod nullius tenetur subire iudicium. vnde Gloss. ibidem super verbo potuissem, ait: papa autem nullo modo potest iudicari. Item Gelasius papa, ut habetur 9. q. 3. c. ipsi, ait loquens de sede Romana: ab ipsa vero nunquam prorsus appellare debere sanxerunt sancti canones: at per hoc illam de tota ecclesia iudicare, ipsam ad nullius commeare iudicium, nec de eius vnquam præceperunt iudicio iudicari, sententiamque eius constituerunt non oportere dissolui: cuius potius sequenda decreta mandauerunt. di. 27. §. hinc etiam, legitur: nec antedicta sedis (scilicet Romanæ) antistitem minorum subiacuisse iudicio. & infra: Episcopi vero in synodo residentes congregata auctoritate eiusdem Simachi dixerunt: Simachus papa sedis apostolicæ præsul ab huiusmodi opinionibus impeditus quantum ad homines respicit, sit immunis & liber, cuius causam totam Dei iudicio reseruamus. Item Nicolaus papa, ut habetur 9. quæst. 3. c. patet, ait: patet profecto sedis apostolica, cuius auctoritate maius non est, iudicium à nemine fore retractandum: neque cuiquam de eius liceat iudicare iudicio. iuxta quod Innocentius papa Rufo & cæteris episcopis per Thessaliam constitutis scribens ait: Nemo vnquam apostolicæ culmini, de cuius iudicio non licet retractari, manus obuias audacter intulit: nemo in hoc rebellis extitit, nisi qui de se voluit iudicari. Et beatus Gelasius papa: Nec de eius (id est Romanæ ecclesiæ) iudicio canones vnquam præceperunt iudicari iudicio, sententiamque illius constituerunt non oportere dissolui, cuius potius sequenda decreta mandauerunt. Ex prædictis omnibus videtur colligi, quod nec imperator, nec alius, iudex est iudex Romani pontificis.
units.tr: DISCIP. So that I may have the opportunity of understanding this matter more deeply, bring many authorities for this assertion, including those you touched on in the first part of the dialogue. For I do not want you afterwards to report to me in detail how the contrary assertion labours to answer them. In this way we shall spur others to search out the truth more keenly, and the force of the authorities to be adduced will become clearer to ourselves. MAGIST. Very many authorities are adduced for this opinion. Pope Gelasius, as is found in 9, q. 3, c. Cuncta, says: The Church knows throughout the world that the see of the blessed apostle Peter, bound by the judgments of no one among the pontiffs, has the right of annulling, since it has the lawful power of judging the whole Church. Likewise Melchiades, as is found in 12, q. 1, c. Futura, says: The same prince (namely Constantine) bestowed immense gifts and founded the building of the temple at the first see of the blessed Peter, so much so that he left the imperial seat and granted it to the blessed Peter and his successors who were to come. Moreover, when presiding over the holy synod gathered at Nicaea, he saw that a complaint of certain persons was to be laid before him, and said: You cannot be judged by anyone, since you are reserved to the judgment of God alone. For you are called gods, and therefore you cannot be judged by men. Likewise Pope Gelasius, as is found in 9, q. 3, c. Cuncta, says: The Church knows throughout the world that the most holy Roman Church has the lawful right of judging all things, and that no one is permitted to judge her judgment. For it is to her that appeal must be made from every part of the world, but from her no one is permitted to appeal. Nor has the apostolic see ever failed to have the power, without any preceding synod, to annul what an unjust synod has condemned, and to condemn, when no synod exists, the acts that it was right to condemn. Likewise Pope Gelasius, as is found in dist. 96, writing to the emperor Anastasius, says: You know therefore that in these matters you depend on their judgment, and that they cannot be made to submit to your will. Likewise Pope Innocent, as is read in 9, q. 3, c. Nemo, says: No one shall judge the apostolic see, which desires to temper justice. For she is to be judged neither by the Augustus, nor by the whole clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people. Likewise Pope John, as is found in dist. 96, c. Si imperator, says: If the emperor is Catholic (which we say with his peace), he is a son, not a prelate of the Church. The law blushes that sons should be the judges of their parents. Therefore the emperor can in no way be the judge of the pope, who is the father of all. Likewise Pope Symmachus, as is found in 9, q. 3, c. Aliorum, says: God willed that the causes of other men be decided by men, but he reserved the prelate of this see to his own judgment without question. He willed that the successors of the blessed apostle Peter should owe innocence to heaven alone, and keep their conscience inviolate to the scrutiny of the most subtle examiner. Do not suppose that those souls which God has reserved above others for his examination are without fear of the inquisitor. And below: By the voice of the holy pontiffs the dignity of his see is made venerable throughout the whole world, since whatever is faithful is everywhere submitted to it, since it is designated the head of the whole body. Likewise Pope Nicholas, dist. 21, c. Nunc autem, says: Since the first see is not to be judged by anyone. Likewise Pope Anterus, as is found in 9, q. 3, c. Facta, says: The deeds of subjects are judged by us; but our deeds are judged by the Lord. Likewise Pope Sixtus, as is found in 2, q. 5, c. Mandastis, when he had been accused by a certain scribe, said to the bishops: Having taken counsel with great scrutiny, satisfying everyone, although I could have easily escaped in another way, nevertheless, fleeing suspicion, I cleared myself before all; freeing myself, to be sure, from suspicion and rivalry, but not others, who were unwilling or did not of their own accord choose to do this, giving them a form to follow. From these words it is gathered that the pope is in no case bound to clear himself if he has been defamed. From this it follows that he is bound to submit to the judgment of no one. Hence the Gloss, on the same passage, at the word potuissem, says: But the pope can in no way be judged. Likewise Pope Gelasius, as is found in 9, q. 3, c. Ipsi, speaking of the Roman see, says: The holy canons have decreed that appeal must never at all be made from her; yet by this they did not mean that she should judge the whole Church, or that she should be subject to the judgment of anyone, nor did they ordain that her sentence should not be dissolved; rather they commanded that her decrees should be followed. In dist. 27, §. Hinc etiam, it is read: Nor was the aforesaid bishop of the see (namely Roman) subject to the judgment of lesser men. And below: The bishops sitting in synod, gathered by the authority of this same Symmachus, said: Pope Symmachus, the prelate of the apostolic see, is to be free and immune, as far as men are concerned, from such opinions; we reserve his whole cause to the judgment of God. Likewise Pope Nicholas, as is found in 9, q. 3, c. Patet, says: It is plainly evident that the judgment of the apostolic see, than whose authority there is none greater, is to be reopened by no one, and that no one is permitted to judge her judgment. Accordingly Pope Innocent, writing to Rufus and the other bishops established in Thessaly, says: No one has ever boldly laid hands on the apostolic summit, from whose judgment it is not permitted to dispute; no one has been rebellious in this, except one who wished himself to be judged. And the blessed Pope Gelasius: Nor did the canons ever command that her judgment (that is, of the Roman Church) be judged by any judgment, nor did they decree that her sentence should not be dissolved, whose decrees they rather commanded to be followed. From all the foregoing it seems to be gathered that neither the emperor nor anyone else is the judge of the Roman pontiff.

units.la: DISCIP.
units.tr: DISCIPULUS.
