units.la: DISCIP. Post auctoritates, aliquas rationes ad eandem assertionem probandam allegaMAGIST. Haec assertio ratione probatur. Nam minor non est iudex maioris, di. 21. c. inferior. c. denique. imperator & quilibet alius est minor Romano pontifice, teste Nicolao papa, qui hoc asserit, ut habetur di. 116. c. duo. ubi ad idem beatum Ambrosium allegat dicens: Qui (scilicet Ambrosius) in scriptis suis ostendit, quod aurum non tam preciosius est plumbo, quam regia potestate sit altior orde sacerdotalis. hoc modo circa principium sui Pastoralis scribens: Honor, fratres, & sublimitas episcopalis nulli poterit comparationibus adaequari. si regum fulgori compares & principum diademati, longe erit inferius, quam si plumbi metallum ad auri fulgorem conferas. quippe cum videas regum colla & principum submitti genibus sacerdotum: & osculata eorum dextera, orationibus eorum credant se excommunicari vel muniri. Hoc etiam testatur Innocentius tertius, qui (ut legi extra de maioritate & obedientia c. solita, loquens de pontificali dignitate, seu auctoritate & potestate regali) ait: Illa quae praesunt diebus, id est, spiritualibus, maior est, quam vero carnalibus, minor est: ut quanta est inter solem & lunam, tanta inter pontifices & reges differentia cognoscatur. Ex his aliisque quam pluribus colligitur, quod imperator est minor papa. ergo non est iudex eius. Amplius, nemo est iudex iudicis sui. sed papa est iudex imperatoris, cum ipsum valeat excommunicare, & imperator ei subsit: & sibi debeat obedire, teste beato Clemente, qui ut legitur 2. quaest. 3. c. Si autem nobis episcopi non obedierint omnes presbyteri, & reliqui clerici, omnesque principes tam maioris ordinis quam inferioris, atque reliqui populi, non tantum infames sed etiam extorres a regno Dei & consortio fidelium & a liminibus sanctae Dei ecclesiae alieni erunt. Hoc asserit Gelasius papa, ut habetur di. 96. c. duo, ait: Talibus igitur institutis, talibusque fultis auctoritatibus, plures namque pontificum alii reges, alii Imperatores excommunicaverunt. nam si speciale aliquid de persona principum requiritur exemplum: Beatus Innocentius papa Archadium imperatorem, quia consensit, ut sanctum Iohannes Chrysostomus a sua sede pelleretur, excommunicavit. ergo nunc imperator non est iudex papae: cum papa sit iudex ipsius. Quod etiam papa sit iudex imperatoris, ostenditur. Nam sicut se habet corpus ad animam humanam, sic princeps corporis ad principem animarum. sed corpus animae subest quantum ad regimen. ergo princeps corporum scilicet imperator, subest regimini principis animarum, scilicet papae. Rursus, imperator non est iudex illius, qui legibus imperialibus est solutus: & qui mundanis legibus nequaquam astringitur, teste beato Nicolao papa, qui, ut habetur 23. quaest. 2. c. inter haec, ait: Beata Dei ecclesia mundanis nunquam constringitur legibus. Et idem, ut habetur di. 10. c. lege, ait: Lege imperatoris non in ecclesiasticis omnibus controversiis vtendum est. Et infra: Imperiali iudicio non possunt iura ecclesiastica dissolui. Ex quibus patet, quod papa legibus imperialibus nequaquam astringitur. Quod & patet ex hoc, quod papa non astringitur canonibus papalibus, nec etiam canonibus generalium conciliorum. ergo nec astringitur legibus imperialibus, quae sunt sacris canonibus postponendae, teste Gratiano, qui 10. dist. §. 1. ait: Constitutiones vero principum ecclesiasticis constitutionibus non praeminent, sed obsequuntur. & eadem di. §. ecce, ait: Ecce constitutiones principum ecclesiasticis legibus postponenda sunt. Et idem, ut legitur 2. quaest. 3. §. hinc autem colligitur, dicit, quod seculi leges non dedignantur sacros canones imitari: ergo papa legibus imperialibus est solutus. & per consequens imperator non est iudex papae. Item, imperator non est iudex episcoporum inferiorum & clericorum; ut ex innumeris canonibus sacris colligitur. ergo non est iudex papae.
units.tr: DISCIP. After these authorities, bring forward some arguments to prove the same assertion. MAGIST. This assertion is proved by reason. For a lesser person is not the judge of a greater, di. 21. c. inferior. c. denique. The emperor, and any other man, is lesser than the Roman pontiff, as Pope Nicholas, who asserts this, testifies, as it is found in di. 116. c. duo. There he cites the blessed Ambrose on the same point, saying: He (namely Ambrose) showed in his writings that gold is not so much more precious than lead as the priestly order is higher than royal power. In the beginning of his Pastoral Care he writes in this way: Brethren, the honour and eminence of the bishop cannot be compared with anything. If you compare it with the splendour of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be far inferior, as if you were to compare a lump of lead with the lustre of gold. Indeed, you see the necks of kings and princes bowed before the knees of priests, and, kissing their right hand, they believe that by their prayers they are either excommunicated or protected. Innocent III also bears witness to this, who (as I have read outside de maioritate & obedientia c. solita, speaking of the pontifical dignity, or authority and power, compared with royal power) says: Those who preside over the days, that is, over spiritual matters, are greater, but those over carnal matters are lesser: so that, as great as the difference is between the sun and the moon, so great is the difference between pontiffs and kings. From these and many other sources it is gathered that the emperor is lesser than the pope. Therefore he is not his judge. Furthermore, no one is the judge of his own judge. But the pope is the judge of the emperor, since he is able to excommunicate him, and the emperor is subject to him and ought to obey him, as the blessed Clement testifies, who, as is read in 2 q. 3 c. If indeed all the bishops, presbyters and other clerics, and all princes, both of higher and lower rank, and the rest of the people, do not obey us, they will be not only infamous but also exiles from the kingdom of God, from fellowship with the faithful, and aliens from the threshold of the holy Church of God. Pope Gelasius asserts this, as is found in di. 96. c. duo, where he says: On the basis of such institutions, and supported by such authorities, many pontiffs have excommunicated kings and emperors. For if a special example is sought concerning the person of princes: Blessed Pope Innocent excommunicated the emperor Arcadius, because he consented that St John Chrysostom should be driven from his see. Therefore the emperor is now not the judge of the pope, since the pope is the judge of him. That the pope is also the judge of the emperor is shown thus. For just as the body stands to the human soul, so the prince of the body stands to the prince of souls. But the body is subject to the soul as regards governance. Therefore the prince of bodies, namely the emperor, is subject to the governance of the prince of souls, namely the pope. Again, the emperor is not the judge of one who is released from imperial laws, and who is by no means bound by worldly laws, as the blessed Pope Nicholas testifies, who, as is found in 23 q. 2 c. inter haec, says: The blessed Church of God is never bound by worldly laws. And the same, as is found in di. 10. c. lege, says: The emperor's law is not to be used in all ecclesiastical controversies. And below: Ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by an imperial judgement. From these it is plain that the pope is by no means bound by imperial laws. This is also clear from the fact that the pope is not bound by papal canons, nor even by the canons of general councils. Therefore neither is he bound by imperial laws, which must be placed after the sacred canons, as Gratian testifies, who in 10 dist. §1 says: Indeed the constitutions of princes do not take precedence over ecclesiastical constitutions, but yield to them. And in the same distinction, §ecce, he says: Behold, the constitutions of princes must be placed after ecclesiastical laws. And the same, as is read in 2 q. 3 §hinc autem colligitur, says that the laws of the world do not disdain to imitate the sacred canons. Therefore the pope is released from imperial laws, and consequently the emperor is not the judge of the pope. Likewise, the emperor is not the judge of lower bishops and clerics, as is gathered from countless sacred canons. Therefore he is not the judge of the pope.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Inquirit idem quod prius: & ponit sententiam omnino contrariam sententiae priori ca. praecedenti posita. ubi etiam ponuntur diversi modi dicendi circa unitatem iudicis inter fideles. & sunt quinque in numero. secundus impugnatur in hoc ca. tertius in ca. 19. quartus cap. 20. & quintus ca. 21.
units.tr: The same author inquires as before, and sets out an opinion wholly contrary to the opinion put forward in the preceding chapter. Here also are set out various ways of speaking about the unity of the judge among the faithful, and they are five in number. The second is attacked in this chapter, the third in chapter 19, the fourth in chapter 20, and the fifth in chapter 21.

units.la: DISCIP: Istae allegationes pro assertione praedicta sufficiant. ideo ad assertionem contrariam te converte. MAGIST. Circa assertionem contrariam varii sunt modi ponendi.
units.tr: DISCIP: Let these allegations for the aforesaid assertion suffice. So turn yourself to the contrary assertion. MAGIST. Concerning the contrary assertion there are various ways of stating it.

units.la: DISCIP. Recita illos modos varios. MAGIST. Unus modus ponendi est, quod imperator ratione imperatoriae maiestatis de omni crimine tam ecclesiastico quam seculari habet iudicare, & papam ipsum (si est probatum contra ipsum crimen dignum depositione) deponere.
units.tr: DISCIP. Recite those various ways. MAGIST. One way of stating it is that the emperor, by virtue of imperial majesty, has to judge every crime, both ecclesiastical and secular, and to depose the pope himself (if a crime deserving deposition has been proved against him).

units.la: DISCIP. Aliquas allegationes adducas ad probandum, quod imperator debet papam pro omni crimine iudicare. MAGIST. Ad hoc plures rationes sunt inductae prima parte huius dialogi libro 6. ca. 3. 4. & 5. quibus non facile erit invenire fortiores. ideo non videtur necesse, quod circa alias rationes adducendas me fatiges.
units.tr: DISCIP. Adduce some allegations to prove that the emperor ought to judge the pope for every crime. MAGIST. Several arguments for this have been advanced in the first part of this dialogue, book 6, chapters 3, 4 and 5, and it will not be easy to find stronger ones. Therefore it does not seem necessary that you should weary me with other arguments to be adduced.

units.la: DISCIP. Non est inutile, ut etiam rationes ibi factas aliter, quam ibi, tractemus: ideo alias tangas, & alias coneris inducere. MAGIST. Quod imperator possit & debeat papam pro omni crimine iudicare, quamplurimis viis ostenditur. quarum una (quae etiam est in prima parte tacta istius Dialogi) sumitur ex unitate summi iudicis, quam omnis communitas bene ordinata habere debet. Nam omne regnum, omnis civitas, omne collegium, & omnis communitas debet habere unum solum iudicem simpliciter supremum: vel plures summos idem officium habentes seu gerentes vicem unius, a quo vel à quibus omnes alii debent iudicari. ergo tota vniuersitas mortalium, si fuerit bene ordinata & gubernata, habet vnum simpliciter summum iudicem, vel plures habentes idem officium, à quo vel quibus omnes alii debent iudicari.religio autem Christiana non impedit aut destruit bonam dispositionem communitatis mortalium. ergo nihil inuenitur in ea repugnans optimæ dispositioni vniuersitatis mortalium. Ex quo concluditur, quod in nullo obuiat religioni Christianæ. quia quicquid inuenitur in ea est conueniens optimæ dispositioni mortalium: & per consequens vnum habere summum iudicem vel plures idem habentes officium tenentes locum vnius, à quo vel à quibus alii omnes pro omni crimine debeant iudicari, non repugnat religioni Christianæ. sed iste summus iudex non est papa: nec etiam papa habere potest tale officium. Ergo ipse papa debet ab illo summo iudicari. Ille autem summus iudex est imperator, qui de iure est princeps & dominus totius mundi. ergo imperator habet iudicare papam pro omni crimine.
units.tr: DISCIP. It is not useless that we also treat the arguments made there in a different way from how they were made there. So touch on others, and try to introduce others. MAGIST. That the emperor can and ought to judge the pope for every crime is shown by very many ways. One of them (which is also touched on in the first part of this Dialogue) is drawn from the unity of the supreme judge, which every well-ordered community ought to have. For every kingdom, every city, every college and every community ought to have one judge who is simply supreme, or several supreme judges holding the same office or acting in the place of one, by whom or by whom all others ought to be judged. Therefore the whole universe of mortals, if it is well ordered and governed, has one judge who is simply supreme, or several holding the same office, by whom or by whom all others ought to be judged. But the Christian religion does not hinder or destroy the good arrangement of the community of mortals. Therefore nothing is found in it that contradicts the best arrangement of the universe of mortals. From which it is concluded that it in no way opposes the Christian religion. Because whatever is found in it is agreeable to the best arrangement of mortals, and consequently to have one supreme judge, or several holding the same office and occupying the place of one, by whom or by whom all others ought to be judged for every crime, does not conflict with the Christian religion. But this supreme judge is not the pope, nor can the pope himself have such an office. Therefore the pope himself ought to be judged by that supreme judge. But that supreme judge is the emperor, who by right is the prince and lord of the whole world. Therefore the emperor has to judge the pope for every crime.

units.la: DISCIP. Ista ratio mihi aliqualiter est obscura. ideo antequam eam probes, vnum declara. pei hoc enim melius intelligam, an aliquid probabilitatis contineat. dic igitur, quid intelligis per vnum iudicem summum, vel plures idem officium habentes?
units.tr: DISCIP. This argument is somewhat obscure to me. So before you prove it, explain one thing: for by this I will better understand whether it contains any probability. Tell me, then, what do you mean by one supreme judge, or several holding the same office?

units.la: MAGIST. Hoc dicitur propter diuersum modum principandi, scilicet regalem, aristocraticum, & politicum: de quibus in morali Philosophia tractatur. nam in principatu regali vnus est solus iudex summus. in aliis autem sunt plures summi, à quorum nullo seorsum est aliqua referenda sententia: sed ex deliberatione communi & consensu ipsorum vel saltem valentioris partis secundum leges ipsorum & consuetudines approbatas est sententia proferenda. & ita tunc sunt iudices plures summi: idem tamen officium habentes, & eandem penitus potestatem, ita vt sepe in omnibus sunt æquales. & ideo gerunt vicem vnius & locum vnius tenent.
units.tr: MAGIST. This is said on account of the different modes of ruling, namely the royal, the aristocratic and the political, which are treated in moral philosophy. For in royal rule there is one sole supreme judge. In the others, however, there are several supreme judges, from none of whom alone is any sentence to be referred; rather, the sentence is to be pronounced by common deliberation and consent of them all, or at least of the stronger part, according to their laws and approved customs. And so then there are several supreme judges, yet holding the same office and altogether the same power, so that they are often equal in all respects. And therefore they act in the place of one and hold the place of one.

units.la: DISCIP. Rationem tacetam perficias. MAGIST. Circa eam non videtur aliquid probandum, nisi quod in nullo obuiat religioni Christianæ, vnitati mortalium vnum habere summum iudicem vel plures summos idem habentes officium: quod ex illis, quæ dicta sunt primo sep. huius videtur posse probari, quia vniuersitas mortalium nequaquam optime gubernatur, nisi vni principi, qui dominetur omnibus, sit subiecta ad quod probandum plures rationes sunt ibidem adducæ.
units.tr: STUDENT: Complete the tacit argument. TEACHER: On this point nothing seems to need proving, except that it in no way conflicts with the Christian religion for mankind to have one supreme judge, or several supreme judges holding the same office. This seems provable from what was said in the first part of this book, namely that the whole human race is by no means best governed unless it is subject to one prince who rules over all. Several arguments for this are set out in the same place.

units.la: DISCIP. Dimittamus ad præsens loqui de vniuersitate mortalium, quorum aliqui sunt fideles, & aliqui infideles: & ideo forte nullo modo concordarent in vnum iudicem, qui omnes alios de omni crimine iudicaret: & loquamur de tota communitate fidelium, quorum aliqui sunt laici. & videamus an ista communitas non possit esse optime ordinata, quantum permittit status vitæ præsentis, nisi tota habeat vnum iudicem solum & summum, à quo alii pro quocunque crimine debeant iudicari. MAGIST. Quia tota communitas fidelium non habet talem vnicum iudicem summum, potest poni pluribus modis. DISCIP. Explica modos illos, vt de aliquibus eorum, vel de singulis conferamus. MAGIST. Vnus modus ponendi potest esse, vt diuersa regna vel prouinciæ habeant diuersos iudices summos, qui vni superiori minime sint subiecti. Alius est, vt respectu eorundem sint diuersi iudices summi non habentes idem officium, secundum modum expositum, qui eosdem pro eisdem delictis habeant iudicare. Alius est, vt vna pars habeat vnum summum iudicem à quo etiam pro quocunque excessu debeat iudicari. & alia pars habeat alium summum iudicem à quo etiam pro quocunque crimine habeat iudicari. sicut secundum quosdam omnes clerici habent vnum summum iudicem talem, scilicet papam: & omnes laici imperatorem. Alius est, vt vna pars habeat vnum summum iudicem, à quo solo vel auctoritate ipsius pro quocunque delicto debeat iudicari, alia autem pars pro aliquibus delictis debeat iudicari ab vno summo iudice, & pro aliis ab alio: sicut secundum quosdam omnes clerici pro quocunque delicto debent iudicari à papa, & pro aliis à iudice seculari. Alius est, vt sit vnus summus, qui habeat facere iudicium de omnibus, vno vel paucis exceptis. sicut secundum vnam assertionem ex lege humana solus papa est exceptus à iurisdictione iudicis secularis. sed omnes alii clerici sola libertate eis concessa ab imperatoribus & regibus à iudicio secularium iudicum sunt exempti.
units.tr: STUDENT: Let us set aside for now the whole human race, some of whom are believers and some unbelievers, and who therefore perhaps could in no way agree on one judge to judge all others for every crime. Let us speak instead of the whole community of believers, some of whom are laypeople, and let us consider whether this community cannot be best ordered, so far as the present state of life allows, unless the whole of it has one sole and supreme judge by whom all others must be judged for any crime. TEACHER: Since the whole community of believers does not have such a single supreme judge, this can be laid out in several ways. STUDENT: Set out those ways, so that we may compare some of them, or each of them, in turn. TEACHER: One way of positing it could be that different kingdoms or provinces have different supreme judges, who are not subject to any higher power. (2) Another is that, with respect to the same persons, there are different supreme judges who do not hold the same office, in the manner already described, and who are to judge the same persons for the same offences. (3) Another is that one part has one supreme judge, by whom or by whose authority alone it must be judged for any excess, while another part has another supreme judge, by whom it must likewise be judged for any crime. So, according to some, all clergy have one such supreme judge, namely the pope, and all laypeople have the emperor. (4) Another is that one part has one supreme judge, by whom alone, or by whose authority, it must be judged for any offence, while the other part must be judged for some offences by one supreme judge and for others by another. So, according to some, all clergy must be judged by the pope for any offence, and for other matters by a secular judge. (5) Another is that there is one supreme judge who has the power to pass judgment on everyone, with one or a few exceptions. So, according to one assertion from human law, the pope alone is exempt from the jurisdiction of the secular judge, but all other clergy are exempt from the judgment of secular judges only by the freedom granted them by emperors and kings.

units.la: DISCIP. Si sint alii modi ponendi negatiuam prædicatarum assertionum ad improbandum istos: puto quod valeant reduci ad istos. ideo sufficit adducere motiua, quæ allegari possunt pro istis vel ad improbandum istos. Dic ergo quomodo improbatur prima. MAGIST. Quomodo possit ostendi & allegari, quod non sit expediens diuersa regna vel prouincias habere diuersos summos iudices, qui nulli superiori sint subiecti, ex his quæ allegata sunt primo huius cap. i. potest aduertere studiosus.
units.tr: STUDENT: If there are other ways of setting out the negative of the assertions just mentioned, for refuting these, I think they can be reduced to these. So it is enough to bring forward the reasons that can be alleged in favour of these positions or against them. Tell me, then, how the first is refuted. TEACHER: How it can be shown and argued that it is not expedient for different kingdoms or provinces to have different supreme judges who are subject to no higher power, a diligent student can notice from what was alleged in the first part of chapter 1 of this book.

units.la: DISCIP. Conuertte ad secundum, & indica quomodo potest improbari ille modus dicendi, qui tenet, quod non est contra dispositionem bonam communitatis fidelium, vt respectu eorundem sint diuersi iudices summi vel non habentes idem officium: sicut aliqui ponunt de papa & imperatore. quia vterque seorsum sine requisitione & consensu alterius potest eundem pro eodem delicto percellere. MAGIST. Hoc multis rationibus improbatur. Primo sic. Delinquentes non possunt debito modo puniri, nisi citentur vel capti ducantur ad iudicem, sed si sunt plures iudices, quorum quilibet seorsum absq; alio potest iudicare reum, poterit contingere vt nec citatus valeat comparere, nec captus aut capiendus valeat iudici præsentari. nam poterit contingere, q; vterq; iudex suam iurisdictionem cupiens exercere citet reum in eodem tempore, vel quod vterq; ad ipsum capiendum mittat familiam. Si autem vterq; citetur ab vtroq; aut comparebit coram vtroq; & hoc est sibi impossibile: aut comparebit coram uno solo, & tunc faciet alteri iniuriam, coram quo non comparet: cum non plus tenetur comparere coram isto, quam coram illo. & rursum, ab illo coram quo non compareret absque culpa illius de contumacia punietur: aut coram neutro comparebit: & tunc delictum eius erit impunitum. Si etiam vterq; illorum iudicum mittat familiam ad capiendum reum, aut altera illarum familiarum aut vtraq; erit inobediens domino suo. aut inter se pugnabunt, vt reus per potentiam perducatur ad iudicem, quibus pugnantibus euadet. & sic in populo seu communitate periculosa oritur seditio, & remanebunt crimina impunita. quare communitas, in qua talia ex potestate iudicum oriuntur, est pessime gubernata. Amplius, ex huiusmodi pluralitate iudicum omnis vtilitas publica & reorum impeditur punitio.
units.tr: STUDENT: Turn to the second, and explain how that way of speaking can be refuted, the one which holds that it is not contrary to the good ordering of the community of believers that, with respect to the same persons, there should be different supreme judges, or judges not holding the same office, as some maintain of the pope and the emperor, because each of them, separately and without the request and consent of the other, can condemn the same persons for the same offence. TEACHER: This is refuted by many arguments. First, as follows. Offenders cannot be punished in the proper way unless they are summoned or brought in custody before a judge. But if there are several judges, each of whom can try the accused separately and without the other, it may happen that the accused cannot appear when summoned, nor be presented to a judge when arrested or about to be arrested. For it may happen that each judge, wishing to exercise his own jurisdiction, summons the accused at the same time, or that each sends a retinue to seize him. If the accused is summoned by both, he will either appear before both, which is impossible for him, or appear before only one, and then he will wrong the other, before whom he does not appear, since he is no more bound to appear before the one than the other. And again, he will be punished for contumacy by the one before whom he did not appear, though it was not his fault; or he will appear before neither, and then his offence will go unpunished. Likewise, if each of the two judges sends a retinue to seize the accused, then either one of those retinues, or both, will be disobedient to its lord, or they will fight one another so that the accused may be brought to the judge by force, and by fighting they will let him escape. In this way sedition arises among the people or community, which is dangerous, and crimes remain unpunished. Therefore a community in which such things arise from the power of judges is very badly governed. Moreover, from this plurality of judges all public benefit and the punishment of offenders are hindered.

units.la: Quia poterit contingere, quod isti iudices voluerint subditos ad diversa loca pro eodem tempore pro criminosis plectendis vel pro tractandis negociis, quibus conuocare non possunt ad diversa loca aut eodem tempore conuenire. ergo & punitio malefactorum & communis vtilitas impeditur & de facili seditio oritur. quare talis communitas est pessime & periculosissime ordinata. Rursus, absque necessitate & vtilitate est pluralitas fugienda: quia frustra fit per plura, quod fieri potest per pauciora. sed pluralitas huiusmodi iudicum omni necessitate aut vtilitate caret: quia omnia melius disponerentur per vnum, quam per plures. dicitur ergo quod ex tali pluralitate faciliter oritur guerra & seditio ac discordia tam inter ipsos iudices sua potestate vti volentes, quam etiam inter ipsos subditos, quorum aliqui ex diversis causis, imo innumerabilibus possunt inclinari, vt vni obediant & non alteri. alii autem poterunt ad alium inclinari. ideo communitas, quae habet diversos iudices summos, quibus vel quorum vno seorsum absque alio valeat punire eosdem delinquentes, pessima & periculosissima est censenda. quod veritas etiam apertissime testari videtur, quae Matthaei 6. ait: Nemo potest duobus dominis seruire. aut enim vnum odio habebit, & alterum diliget, aut vnum sustinebit & alterum contemnetur. Ex quibus verbis habetur, quod nemo debet habere duos dominos vel duos iudices, quorum vnus non est sub alio. DISCIP. Ista auctoritas non videtur concludere opinioni: quia Christus loquitur de dominis contrariis, qui actu contraria iubent. MAGIST. Haec responsio ab aliis minime satisfacit: quia Deus loquitur non solum de dominis contrariis actu, hoc est qui actu contraria iubent: sed etiam de illis, qui proni sunt ad iubendum contraria, & de quibus est probabiliter formidandum quod inter se dissentientes iubebunt contraria. Cum ergo nostra natura humana sit prona ad dissentiendum: non immerito est timendum quod si eadem communitas habuerit duo capita, ipsa inter se erunt dissentientia: quia quot capita, tot sententiae & opiniones, dist. 19. dist. 10. sicut in sacramentis. quare timendum est, quod capita illa siue domini iubebunt contraria. Ex quo infertur, quod nullus subditus poterit eis seruire. & per consequens ista communitas, quae habet plura capita, est pessime ordinata. Ex quo concluditur, quod si communitas fidelium habet duos summos iudices, scil. imperatorem & papam: est periculosa societas reputanda. Et consimili ratione infertur, quod absque periculis manifestis non possunt in eodem regno vel provincia aut in ciuitate esse duo iudices supremi super eosdem, ecclesiasticus vel saecularis: praesertim in illo regno, provincia vel ciuitate, quod vel quae superiorem de facto in temporalibus non recognoscit. Ad haec roboranda adduci potest assertio veritatis, quae Matth. 12. ait: Omne regnum contra se diuisum desolabitur: & omnis domus vel ciuitas contra se diuisa non stabit. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod omnis communitas & congregatio propinqua diuisioni est propinqua desolationi & ruinae. Cum ergo communitas seu congregatio fidelium sit propinqua diuisioni, si habeat duos iudices supremos: quia capita diversa sunt prona ad dissentiendum: sequitur quod communitas seu congregatio fidelium est propinqua desolationi & ruinae. & per consequens contra bonum commune est, vt supra se duos habeat iudices supremos. Ad hoc etiam adducitur auctoritas Hieron. qui, vt legitur, 7. quaest. 1. c. in apibus, ad Rusticum monachum ait: In apibus princeps vnus est. grues vnam sequuntur ordine literato: imperator vnus: iudex vnus prouincia. Roma autem condita duos fratres simul reges habere non potuit, & fratricidio dedicatur in Rebecca vtero Esau & Iacob bella gesserunt: singuli ecclesiarum episcopi, singuli archiepiscopi, singuli archidiaconi, & omnis ordo ecclesiasticus suis rectoribus nititur. In quibus verbis Hieronymus probat aperte per plura exempla, quod in eadem ecclesia non debeant esse plures praelati, quorum vnus non est sub alio. per quem aeque aperte vel apertius poterit ostendi, quod in eadem communitate non debent esse plures iudices supremi. Quia si per vniuersitatem principis in apibus poterit ostendi vnitas episcopi in vna dioecesi, & vnitas archiepiscopi in vno archiepiscopatu: eadem ratione per vnitatem principis in apibus poterit ostendi vnitas iudicis supremi super vnam communitatem seu congregationem. Iterum, si ex hoc quod grues vnam sequuntur ordine, ostenditur vnitas episcopi & archiepiscopi in dioecesi: Consimili ratione ex hoc ostenditur vnitas iudicis supremi super vnam communitatem. Consimiliter si ex hoc, quod Roma condita duos fratres simul reges habere non potuit, sed fratricidio exti t dedicata, ostenditur vnitas episcopi & archiepiscopi & aliorum rectorum ecclesiae: multo fortius ex eodem poterit probari vnitas iudicis supremi super eandem communitatem, vt scilicet non sint duo: scilicet ecclesiasticus & saecularis. Quia non minus praesumendum videtur, quod iudex saecularis aduersabitur ecclesiastico vsque ad interitionem: quemadmodum vnus fratrum conditorum Romae alium interfecit, quam iudex ecclesiasticus alteri iudici ecclesiastico, vel vnus episcopus alteri episcopo. Si ergo per exemplum duorum fratrum, quorum vnus occidit alterum: probari poterit quod non debent esse duo episcopi in eodem episcopatu. multo fortius per idem exemplum poterit ostendi quod super communitatem fidelium non debent esse duo iudices: quorum unus sit secularis & alius ecclesiasticus. Et propter illud patet, quod si per exemplum de Esau & Iacob, qui in utero matris bella gesserunt, potest ostendi, quod non debent esse duo episcopi in una dioecesi: multo fortius probari potest per idem exemplum, quod super communitatem fidelium non debent esse duo iudices summi, sc. ecclesiasticus & secularis. Hoc etiam verba Hiero. sonare videntur: qui vult quod unius provinciae debet esse unus iudex, non autem dicit, quod unius provinciae debet esse unus iudex ecclesiasticus, vel unus iudex secularis, quasi vellet solummodo excludere pluralitatem iudicum ecclesiasticorum, & non pluralitatem iudicum secularium: sed dicit indistincte, quod unius provinciae est visus iudex, volens per hoc pluralitatem omnem iudicum summorum quorumcunque excludere. & ita super communitatem fidelium non expedit esse plures iudices qualescunque summos.
units.tr: Since it may happen that these judges want their subjects summoned to different places at the same time, either to punish criminals or to deal with business, and they cannot be summoned to different places or meet at the same time, both the punishment of wrongdoers and the common good are hindered, and sedition easily arises. So a community of this kind is badly and very dangerously ordered. Again, plurality is to be avoided where there is no need or advantage, because what can be done by fewer is done in vain by more. But a plurality of judges of this kind lacks all necessity and advantage, since everything would be better arranged by one than by many. It is said, therefore, that from such a plurality war, sedition and discord easily arise, both among the judges themselves, each wishing to use his own power, and among the subjects, some of whom can be inclined, for various causes, indeed countless ones, to obey one and not another, while others can be inclined to another. Therefore a community that has several supreme judges, by whom or one of whom apart from the others it may be possible to punish the same offenders, must be judged most wicked and most dangerous. The truth itself seems to bear witness to this very plainly, which says in Matthew 6: No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. From these words it is held that no one ought to have two masters or two judges, one of whom is not under the other. DISCIPLE: This authority does not seem to settle the opinion, because Christ speaks of contrary masters, who actually command contrary things. MASTER: This answer by no means satisfies others, because God speaks not only of masters who are actually contrary, that is, who actually command contrary things, but also of those who are inclined to command contrary things, and of whom it is reasonably to be feared that, disagreeing among themselves, they will command contrary things. Since, therefore, our human nature is prone to disagreement, it is not without reason to be feared that if the same community has two heads, they will disagree among themselves, for as many heads, so many opinions and views, dist. 19, dist. 10, as in the sacraments. Therefore it is to be feared that those heads, or masters, will command contrary things. From this it follows that no subject will be able to serve them, and consequently that this community, which has several heads, is badly ordered. From this it is concluded that if a community of the faithful has two supreme judges, namely the emperor and the pope, it must be reckoned a dangerous society. And by a similar reasoning it follows that, without manifest dangers, there cannot be two supreme judges over the same people in one kingdom, province or city, one ecclesiastical and one secular, especially in that kingdom, province or city which does not in fact recognise a superior in temporal matters. To strengthen these points, the assertion of truth may be adduced, which says in Matthew 12: Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every house or city divided against itself will not stand. From these words it is gathered that every community and congregation that is close to division is close to desolation and ruin. Since, therefore, a community or congregation of the faithful is close to division if it has two supreme judges, because diverse heads are prone to disagree, it follows that the community or congregation of the faithful is close to desolation and ruin. And consequently it is contrary to the common good that it should have two supreme judges over it. To this also is adduced the authority of Jerome, who, as we read in 7 quaest. 1, c. in apibus, says in his letter to the monk Rusticus: In bees there is one prince. Cranes follow one in orderly formation. One emperor; one judge for a province. But when Rome was founded, two brothers could not reign together as kings, and by fratricide Esau and Jacob, while still in Rebecca's womb, waged war. Each bishop of the churches, each archbishop, each archdeacon, and the whole ecclesiastical order rests on its own rulers. In these words Jerome plainly proves, by several examples, that in one church there ought not to be several prelates, one of whom is not under another. By the same argument it can be shown just as plainly, or more plainly, that in one community there ought not to be several supreme judges. For if from the unity of the prince among bees it can be shown that a bishop is one in one diocese, and that an archbishop is one in one archbishopric, by the same reasoning, from the unity of the prince among bees, the unity of a supreme judge over one community or congregation can be shown. Again, if from the fact that cranes follow one in order it is shown that there is unity of bishop and archbishop in a diocese, by a similar reasoning the unity of a supreme judge over one community is shown from this. Likewise, if from the fact that Rome, when founded, could not have two brothers reigning together as kings, but was dedicated through fratricide, the unity of bishop, archbishop and other rulers of the church is shown, then by the same reasoning the unity of a supreme judge over the same community can be proved much more strongly, so that there are not two, namely an ecclesiastical and a secular one. For it seems no less to be presumed that a secular judge will oppose an ecclesiastical one even to destruction, just as one of the founding brothers of Rome killed the other, than that one ecclesiastical judge will oppose another ecclesiastical judge, or one bishop another bishop. If, therefore, by the example of two brothers, one of whom killed the other, it can be proved that there ought not to be two bishops in one bishopric, much more strongly can it be proved by the same example that over the community of the faithful there ought not to be two supreme judges, namely an ecclesiastical and a secular one. And from this it is plain that if by the example of Esau and Jacob, who waged war in their mother's womb, it can be shown that there ought not to be two bishops in one diocese, then by the same example it can much more strongly be proved that over the community of the faithful there ought not to be two supreme judges, namely ecclesiastical and secular. The words of Jerome also seem to say this: he who wants there to be one judge for one province does not say that there ought to be one ecclesiastical judge or one secular judge for one province, as if he wished only to exclude a plurality of ecclesiastical judges and not a plurality of secular judges; but he says without distinction that for one province there is to be one judge, wishing by this to exclude every plurality of supreme judges of whatever kind. And so it is not expedient for there to be several supreme judges of any kind over the community of the faithful.

units.la: Praeterea, ista ordinatio communitatis non est bona, ex qua provenit, quod potentior eiusdem communitatis valentis magnam sequelam habere ad impatientiam & iracundiam provocetur contra alium potentiorem in eadem communitate: qui etiam poterit magnam habere sequelam, quia ex tali ordinatione sequuntur dissensiones, seditiones, & guerrae. Sed si in communitate fidelium ordinetur, quod sint duo iudices summi, sc. papa & alius: ex tali ordinatione sequitur facilter, quod unus contra alium ad impatientiam & iracundiam provocetur: quia sicut dicit poeta: Omnis potestas impatiens consortis est. cui satis videtur alludere Augustinus ut legitur 23. q. 7. c. qui a nobis, ait: Quis enim avarus quaerit compescere? quis dominandi cupiditate inflammatus, vel fastu dominationis elatus desiderat habere consortem? q. d. nullis talis. ergo ordinatio communitatis non est bona nec laudabilis, ubi sunt plures iudices summi nullum habentes superiorem. Ex quibus supra dictis concluditur, quod si in communitate fidelium fuerint plures iudices summi, sive plura capita simpliciter prima: qui vel quae eosdem pro eisdem criminibus habeant coercere, & eisdem de eisdem praecipere: Sequitur manifeste, quod eadem communitas fidelium semper erit dispositia discordiis, dissensionibus, seditionibus, pugnis, & guerris: tam inter capita ipsa contraria invicem, quam inter subditos, quorum aliqui adhaerebunt uni & alii alteri. & ideo pauci erunt vel nulli, quin unum odio habebunt & alterum diligent. & per consequens unum sustinebunt & alium si poterunt impugnabunt. ita semper erit timendum, quod non erit pax in communitate seu congregatione.
units.tr: Furthermore, that ordering of a community is not good from which it follows that a man who is more powerful in that community, and who has a large following, is provoked to impatience and anger against another, more powerful man in the same community, who also can have a large following; for from such an ordering dissensions, seditions and wars follow. But if it is ordained in the community of the faithful that there should be two supreme judges, namely the pope and another, from such an ordering it easily follows that one is provoked against the other to impatience and anger, because, as the poet says: Every power is impatient of a partner. Augustine seems to allude to this well enough, as we read in 23 q. 7, c. qui a nobis, where he says: For who that is greedy seeks to restrain himself? Who, inflamed by the desire to dominate, or puffed up by the arrogance of lordship, desires to have a partner? That is, no one of this kind. Therefore an ordering of a community is neither good nor praiseworthy where there are several supreme judges, none having a superior. From what has been said above it is concluded that if in a community of the faithful there are several supreme judges, or several heads, equal at the first, who may each coerce the same offenders for the same crimes and command the same persons in the same matters, it manifestly follows that this community of the faithful will always be prone to discords, dissensions, seditions, fights and wars, both among the heads themselves, who are opposed to one another, and among the subjects, some of whom will adhere to one and others to another. And therefore there will be few or none who will not hate the one and love the other, and consequently who will not uphold the one and, if they can, attack the other. Thus it will always have to be feared that there will be no peace in the community or congregation.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: In quo obiicitur contra ea, quae dicta sunt capitulo praecedenti.
units.tr: In which objections are raised against the things said in the preceding chapter.

units.la: DISCIP. Ut possim videre profundius, an ista aliquam verisimilitudinem habeant, contra ipsa obiiciam. Videtur enim per ista, quod omnis communitas, cui praesiderent plures & idem habentes officium, ita ut nullus sine consilio & consensu aliorum aut valentioris partis debet aliquid praecipere vel statuere seu ordinare aut aliquem coercere, non possent ex mente nec utiliter statuta observare. quia omnia inconvenientia, quae deducta sunt ex pluralitate iudicum summorum in communitate fidelium, eosdem ex pluralitate praesidentium idem habentium officium seu gerentium vicem unius, possunt inferri. Poterunt enim tales plures praesidentes reos ad diversa loca citare, vel mittere familias diversas, ut capiantur & ad diversa loca ducantur, sicut processit ratio prima. Poterit etiam subditos pro eis plectendis, vel quibusdam negociis pertractandis ad diversa loca vocare, sicut processit secunda. Frustra etiam regeretur quaecunque communitas per plures huiusmodi praesidentes, cum possit regi per unum secundum quod tertia ratio processit. Nemo etiam poterit taliter diversis dominis contraria iubere volentibus servire iuxta auctoritatem Salvatoris: Nemo potest duobus dominis servire. Talis etiam communitas propinqua erit desolationi & ruinae propter hoc, quod plures huiusmodi praesidentes proni sunt ad sibi dissentiendum iuxta auctoritate aliam Salvatoris: Omne regnum in se divisum desolabitur &c. Per exemplum etiam Hiero. quae ponit 7. q. 1. ca. in apibus, poterit ostendi quod non expedit esse plures huiusmodi praesidentes. Per hoc et, quod omnis potestas impatiens est consortis, probari potest, quod in nulla communitate debent plures tali modo praeesse, sicut nec in aliquo episcopatu debent esse plures episcopi quomodolibet praesidentes. semper enim videtur, quod si fuerint plures qualitercunque in eadem communitate praesidentes, timor erit de dissensionibus, contentionibus, seditionibus, rixis, pugnis, & guerris. Si praedicta concludit, quod non debet plures esse iudices summi in communitate fidelium, sc. ecclesiasticus & secularis, qui habet eosdem criminosos pro eisdem scelebris coercere. etiam & ista concludere videntur contra modum, qui nunc in ecclesia esse videtur. ¶ Amplius, multae communitates sunt bene ordinatae, in quibus tamen subest pluribus rectoribus. Ergo communitas fidelium poterit esse bene ordinata, licet in ipsa plures summi iudices praesint eisdem. Antecedens patet: quia videmus, quod idem est vasallus plurium dominorum & regum, quorum nullus est sub alio. Idem etiam clericus subest diversis episcopis pro diversis ecclesiis seu beneficiis, & in eadem causa eiusdem possunt esse plures iudices tam ordinarii quam delegati, & etiam arbitri, extra de sententia & remiss. in capitulo ultimo: & extra de rescriptis, cum contingat. ita videtur ostendi, quod allegationes praescriptae non concludunt intentum. tu autem indica, quomodo respondetur ad ipsas. MAGIST. Ad primam obiectionem respondetur, quod ubicunque in eadem communitate sunt plures præsidentes & idem habentes officium seu vicem gerentes vnius, non est optime disposita, sed est a b optima dispositione deficiens. quia optima dispositio communitatis est, quod sit vnicus præsidens summus in ipsa. ab ipsa tamen optima dispositione sæpe est necesse recedere propter diuersos casus. Quia aliquando subditi vnum nullatenus sustinerent: aliquando nullus posset inuenire qui sufficeret solus præesse. Vnde ex multis causis potest contingere, quod melius sit plures præesse quam vnum: licet melius esset disposita communitas, si vnus præsidens posset conuenienter haberi: ita vt quæcunque communitas præcipue notabiliter magna, quæ gubernatur à pluribus summis in eadem communitate nequaquam optimo regimine gubernatur: sicut tamen sæpe periclitantes in mari optimum modum nauigandi coguntur dimittere propter pericula euitanda, & nonnunquam viatores vias meliores compelluntur relinquere & longiorem ac deteriorem eligere: & frequenter multa bona ex causis necessariis omittuntur, & multotiens dispensatiue, quia alias essent indigni, multiplici ratione ad diuersa officia promouentur. sic nonnunquam ex causa rationabili necesse est optimum modum præficiendi relinquere, scilicet regimen vnius solius, & præsidentiam plurium acceptare.
units.tr: STUDENT. So that I may see more deeply whether these claims have any plausibility, I will raise objections against them. It seems from them that any community over which several men preside, holding the same office, so that no one may command, decree, ordain, or restrain anyone without the counsel and consent of the others or of the stronger part, cannot keep its statutes faithfully or usefully. For all the inconveniences deduced from the plurality of supreme judges in the community of the faithful can be inferred equally from a plurality of presiding officers who hold the same office or act as the vicar of one. Such several presiding officers could summon accused persons to different places, or send different households to arrest them and lead them to different places, as the first reason argued. They could also summon subjects to different places to punish them or to deal with certain business, as the second reason argued. Any community would also be governed in vain by several such presiding officers, since it could be governed by one, as the third reason showed. Nor could anyone serve diverse lords who command contrary things, according to the saying of the Saviour: No one can serve two masters. Such a community would also be close to desolation and ruin, because several such presiding officers are prone to disagree with one another, according to another saying of the Saviour: Every kingdom divided against itself shall be made desolate, etc. By the example of Jerome, which he gives in 7 q. 1 c. In apibus, it can be shown that it is not expedient to have several such presiding officers. From this also, and because all power is impatient of partnership, it can be proved that in no community should several men preside in this way, just as in no bishopric should several bishops preside in any manner. For it always seems that if several preside in the same community in whatever way, there will be fear of dissensions, contentions, seditions, brawls, fights and wars. If the foregoing concludes that there should not be several supreme judges in the community of the faithful, namely the ecclesiastical and the secular, who would both have to restrain the same criminals for the same crimes, then these arguments also seem to conclude against the arrangement which now appears to exist in the Church. ¶ Furthermore, many communities are well ordered in which, nevertheless, one man is subject to several rulers. Therefore the community of the faithful can be well ordered even though several supreme judges preside over it. The antecedent is plain: we see that the same man is the vassal of several lords and kings, none of whom is under another. Likewise the same cleric is subject to different bishops for different churches or benefices, and in the same cause there can be several judges, both ordinary and delegated, and also arbiters: extra de sententia et remissione, in capitulo ultimo; and extra de rescriptis, cum contingat. Thus it seems to be shown that the aforesaid allegations do not prove the intended point. Now you, indicate how these are answered. TEACHER. To the first objection it is answered that wherever in the same community there are several presiding officers who hold the same office or act as the vicar of one, the community is not best arranged, but falls short of the best arrangement. For the best arrangement of a community is that there be one supreme president in it. Yet it is often necessary to depart from this best arrangement because of various circumstances. For sometimes the subjects would by no means tolerate one man, and sometimes no one can be found who is sufficient to preside alone. Hence for many reasons it may happen that it is better for several to preside than for one, although the community would be better arranged if one presiding officer could suitably be had. So any community, especially one that is notably large and is governed by several supreme men, is by no means governed in the best way. Just as, however, those in peril at sea are often forced to abandon the best method of sailing to avoid dangers, and travellers are sometimes compelled to leave the better roads and take a longer and worse one, and often many goods are omitted for necessary reasons, and many people, by dispensation because otherwise they would be unworthy, are promoted to various offices for many reasons, so sometimes for a reasonable cause it is necessary to leave the best way of appointing, namely the rule of one alone, and to accept the presidency of several.

units.la: DISCIP. Per istam rationem responderi potest ad omnes rationes præcedentis capituli, inquantum probant, quod in communitate fidelium non debent esse plures iudices summi, scil. ecclesiasticus & secularis: quia solummodo probant, vt dicit ista responsio, quod si esset communitas fidelium optime disposita, vnum summum caput seu iudicem habere deberet. non autem est necessarium, quod communitas fidelium, quæ obnoxia est variis tribulationibus & aduersitatibus, semper sit optime disposita. poterit ergo plures iudices summos, scilicet ecclesiasticum & secularem habere, ita vt fideles omnes sint eisdem pro eisdem delictis subiecti.
units.tr: STUDENT. By this reasoning one can answer all the arguments of the preceding chapter insofar as they prove that there should not be several supreme judges in the community of the faithful, namely the ecclesiastical and the secular. For they only prove, as this answer says, that if the community of the faithful were optimally arranged, it ought to have one supreme head or judge. But it is not necessary that the community of the faithful, which is subject to various tribulations and adversities, should always be optimally arranged. It can therefore have several supreme judges, namely the ecclesiastical and the secular, so that all the faithful are subject to them for the same offences.

units.la: MAGIST. Ad hoc respondetur, quod propter tribulationes & aduersitates, quas sustinere posset communitas fidelium ex singulari malitia Christianorum posset contingere: quod pro aliquo tempore expediens esset, quod tota esset subiecta duobus supremis iudicibus: tunc tamen nimis periculosissime ab optima dispositione recederet. & ideo non debet tale regimen, nisi in casu singularissimo, sustineri. quare quantum potest conari tenetur, vt habeat solummodo vnum iudicem summum, qui omnes malefactores pro quibuscunq; criminibus per se vel per iudices inseriores ipso, à quibus ad ipsum licet rationabiliter appellare, habeat coercere. Iste autem iudex non potest nec debet esse papa. quia papa ex ordinatione Christi quantum potest, se debet à negociis secularibus sequestrare. ergo optime sit ordinata communitas fidelium, vnum iudicem secularem summum habebit, qui non debet esse alius quam imperator Romanus, quando est catholicus: sane vt intelligeres, quod allegationes præcedentis capituli concludunt: sed allegationes addunt vnum, quod nullus Christianus debet negare, vt eis videtur, quod scilicet nec per ordinationem Christi, nec per ordinationem apostolorum, nec per ordinationem summorum pontificum Christianæ fidei zelatorum, nec per ordinationem generalium conciliorum rite celebratorum, nec per ordinationem quorumcunque iustorum, optimus modus regendi fideles, quantum permittit status vitæ præsentis, qui & seruatus est inter multos fideles, & inter infideles laudatur secundum rationem viuere cupientes hoc esse vtile communitati fidelium: licet quandoq; tota communitas fidelium talem optimum modum regendi propter malitiam hominum non valeat adipisci. ergo ex isto inferunt, quod ex ordinatione Christi papa non habet iurisdictionem vniuersalem pro omni crimine super totum populum Christianum. Et per consequens ordinationi Christi non repugnat, quod aliquis alius super populum Christianum habeat potestatem. & hoc concludunt allegationes præscriptæ in c. precedenti, vel saltem videntur necessario concludere allegationes illæ quod tota communitas seu congregatio fidelium non optime regitur, si habeat plures iudices, qui eosdem pro eisdem criminibus habeant cohercere. & talis modus regendi per diuersos huiusmodi summos iudices non fuit ordinatus à Christo.
units.tr: TEACHER. To this it is answered that, because of the tribulations and adversities which the community of the faithful might have to endure through the singular malice of Christians, it could happen that for some time it would be expedient for the whole to be subject to two supreme judges. Yet it would then depart very dangerously from the optimal arrangement. Therefore such a government ought not to be tolerated except in a most singular case. Wherefore it is bound to strive as far as it can to have only one supreme judge, who may restrain all evildoers for whatever crimes, either himself or through inferior judges, from whom it is lawful to appeal to him reasonably. This judge, however, cannot and must not be the pope, because by Christ's ordinance the pope ought, as far as possible, to withdraw himself from secular affairs. Therefore, if the community of the faithful is optimally ordered, it will have one supreme secular judge, who ought to be none other than the Roman emperor, when he is Catholic. Indeed, so that you may understand that the allegations of the preceding chapter conclude, these allegations add one point which no Christian ought to deny, as it seems to them: namely that neither by the ordinance of Christ, nor by the ordinance of the apostles, nor by the ordinance of the supreme pontiffs zealous for the Christian faith, nor by the ordinance of lawfully celebrated general councils, nor by the ordinance of any just men, is the best way of governing the faithful, as far as the state of the present life allows, which has been observed among many faithful and is praised even by unbelievers as useful for the community of the faithful, for those who desire to live according to reason; although at times the whole community of the faithful cannot attain such an optimal way of governing because of the malice of men. Therefore they infer from this that by the ordinance of Christ the pope does not have universal jurisdiction over every crime over the whole Christian people. And consequently, it is not repugnant to the ordinance of Christ that someone else should have power over the Christian people. And the aforesaid allegations in the preceding chapter conclude this, or at least those allegations seem necessarily to conclude that the whole community or congregation of the faithful is not optimally governed if it has several judges who must restrain the same people for the same crimes. And such a mode of governing through various supreme judges of this kind was not ordained by Christ.

units.la: DISCIP. Indica quomodo ad secundam obiectionem respondetur. MAG. Conceditur quod multæ communitates sunt bene ordinatæ, in quibus idem subest pluribus rectoribus. sed istæ non sunt optime ordinatæ, in quibus idem subest pluribus rectoribus non habentibus superiorem. Licet igitur aliquis possit esse vasallus plurium dominorum, & in hoc aliquam habeat vtilitatem, quia plura feuda tenet: tamen maiorem vtilitate haberet, si pro omnibus feudis illis esset vasallus vnius solius: licet in casu vtilius sit sibi habere plures dominos quam vnum solum. sed hoc est propter malitiam domini vnius, vel aliquorum aliorum inquantum ab optima ordinatione mortalium aliquis vel aliqui recedunt, vel recedunt, qualia etiam damna patiantur sæpe illi, qui plures dominos habent magis quam qui soli domino sapienti & iusto sunt subiecti, experientia docere videtur. Cum secundo accipis pro exemplo, quod idem clericus est subiectus diuersis episcopis pro pluribus ecclesiis vel beneficiis. Respondetur, quod illud exemplum est ad oppositum: quia quod idem clericus sit subditus pluribus episcopis pro diuersis beneficiis est contra ius commune: & per dispensationem solummodo fieri potest. quare licet in casu ex aliqua speciali causa cum ordinatione bona clericorum stet, quod talis sit subditus pluribus episcopis: hoc tamen non stat cum optima ordinatione ipsorum. quia melius clerici regerentur, si posset semper seruari ius commune, vt nullus clericus haberet plura beneficia in pluribus episcopatibus. Cum autem pro tertio exemplo dicis, quod in eadem causa possunt esse plures iudices &c. Respondetur, quod iudices illi habent superiorem iudicem, & non sunt summi. ideo aliquando vtile est, quod sint plures non summi: praesertim cum illi iudices non sunt diuersi, ut unus pro libito possit absq; alio in casu procedere: imo vicem unius gerunt. & tamen quod sint plures, hoc accidit ex aliqua causa speciali, quae non haberet locum, quando litigantes essent optime dispositi, quantum permittit conditio litigantium. propter quod melius disponi videntur litigantes, quando concorditer eligunt siue compromittunt in unum, quam quando in unum discordant, & quia quando omnino diversos volunt habere. & sic est de omnibus litigantibus, quod illi minus a bona dispositione recedunt, qui nisi alia causa specialis impediat, sub uno iudice cupiunt litigare.
units.tr: STUDENT. Indicate how the second objection is answered. TEACHER. It is granted that many communities are well ordered in which one man is subject to several rulers. But those are not optimally ordered in which one man is subject to several rulers who have no superior. Therefore, although someone may be the vassal of several lords, and may have some advantage in this because he holds several fiefs, he would nevertheless have a greater advantage if he were the vassal of one alone for all those fiefs, although in a given case it may be more useful for him to have several lords than one. But this is because of the malice of one lord, or of others, insofar as one or more depart from the optimal ordering of mortals, or they depart in some other way; and experience seems to teach that those who have several lords often suffer such losses more than those who are subject to one wise and just lord alone. When you take as an example the second point, that the same cleric is subject to different bishops for several churches or benefices, the answer is that this example is to the contrary, because for the same cleric to be subject to several bishops for different benefices is against the common law and can be done only by dispensation. Wherefore, although in a given case, for some special reason, it may be consistent with a good ordering of clerics that such a man should be subject to several bishops, this is nonetheless not consistent with their optimal ordering. For clerics would be better governed if the common law could always be observed, so that no cleric held several benefices in several bishoprics. As for your third example, that in the same cause there can be several judges, etc., the answer is that those judges have a superior judge and are not supreme. Therefore it is sometimes useful that there be several who are not supreme; especially since those judges are not distinct, so that one may proceed in a case at his pleasure without the other, but they act in the place of one. And yet that there are several arises from some special cause, which would have no place if the litigants were optimally disposed, as far as the condition of litigants permits. For which reason the litigants seem better disposed when they concordantly elect or submit themselves to one judge, than when they disagree about one and wish to have entirely different ones. And so it is with all litigants: those depart less from good disposition who, unless some other special cause hinders, desire to litigate under one judge.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Tractat tertiam opinionem ca. 17. positam, & contra eam arguit ex rationibus contra secundam opinionem ca. praedicto adductis.
units.tr: Treats the third opinion, set out in chapter 17, and argues against it from the arguments adduced against the second opinion in the aforesaid chapter.

units.la: DISCIP. Visum est de secundo modo ponendi communitatem fidelium non habere vnum summum iudicem, qui ponitur supra ca. 17. nunc videamus de tertio, qui dictus est ibidem. MAG. Qualiter ille modus discuti valeat, ex illis quae tractata sunt primo huius ca. 1. usque ad ca. 13. patere poterit studioso. DISCIP. Hoc non obstante, de isto modo ponendi aliquid specialius videamus, an scilicet optimae ordinationi communitatis fidelium obuiet & repugnet, ut clerici omni crimine iudicentur a papa vel aliis iudicibus ecclesiasticis inferioribus: & etiam omnes laici a iudice seculari: quia contra istum modum ponendi totam communitatem fidelium non habere vnum iudicem summum rationes ca. 17. adductae non videntur concludere: quia secundum istum modum nec aliquis deberet citari aut vocari a diversis ad diversa loca: nec aliquis cogetur duobus dominis seruire: nec super eosdem plures potestatem habebunt: nec aliqua potestas consortis erit impatiens, secundum quas rationes istae processisse videntur. vel ergo declara secundam opinionem supra ca. 17. recitatam, quomodo allegationes istae concludunt contra tertium modum, de quo nunc quaero loqui: vel aliquas alias allegationes conaris adducere. MAGIST. Licet secundum opinionem supra ca. 17. recitatam modus regendi communitatem fidelium de quo cap. praecedenti & ca. 17. tractauimus, sit multo perniciosior isto modo, de quo nunc vis conferre. & ideo istae allegationes multo patentius concludunt contra illum modum, quam contra istum, cum eaedem allegationes vel aliquae illarum conuincunt, ut videtur, istum modum regendi communitatem fidelium ab optimo modo & puniendi reos deficere. primae autem duae allegationes contra istum modum inefficaces apparent. sed tertia contra ipsum aliquam apparentiam habere videtur: eo quod tota communitas fidelium posset regi per vnum. Frustra autem fit per plures, quod fieri potest per pauciores. ergo tales duo rectores, sc. ecclesiasticus & secularis illo modo frustra ponuntur. Quarta allegatio fundata in auctoritate Saluatoris Matth. 6. nequaquam videtur concludere contra istum modum: sed fundata in auctoritate Saluatoris Matth. 12. omne regnum contra se diuisum desolabitur &c. contra istum modum tali modo adducitur. non solum illa societas est propinqua desolationi & ruinae quae est contra se diuisa: sed etiam illa, quae ex modo regendi est dispositia diuisioni propinqua, iuxta auctoritatem Saluatoris. sed si communitas fidelium habeat duas partes, quarum vna habeat iudicem summum, & alia alium: communitas illa est dispositia ad diuisionem & diuisioni propinqua. quia propter assiduam mutuam communionem subditorum & summorum iudicum, qui sicut oes mortales sunt proni ad dissentiendum contra se faciliter diuiderentur. ergo si tali modo regatur communitas fidelium periculosa est cessenda. Alia autem allegatio fundata in auctoritate beati Hieronymi, videtur efficaciter concludere contra illum modum: quia per exempla, quae adducit Hieronymus, non solum probatur vnitas plati super vnum populum siue supra vnam multitudinem hominum: sed et probatur vnitas praelati super vnum locum, in quo subiecti morantur, vt in vna dioecesi, quae certam regionem comprehendit, sit tantum vnus episcopus: & in vna prouincia sit tantum vnus archiepiscopus. ergo per eadem exempla non tantum probatur vnitas iudicis summi super aliquem locum, in quo sibi subiecti morantur, vt in eodem loco nullus alius sit iudex summus quorumcunq; in illo loco morantium, sicut in dioecesi Parisiensi est vnus solus episcopus: & in prouincia Mediolan. est vnus solus archiepiscopus. Sequens allegatio etiam contra istum modum videtur concludere, quod potestas non solum est impatiens consortis super eosdem subditos: sed etiam impatiens est consortis in eodem loco. sicut enim iudex aliquis nollet, quod subditi sui essent alterius subditi, ita nollet, quod aliquis alius haberet potestatem in loco vbi subditi sui morantur. ergo non solum est periculosa societas fidelium, si sint plures iudices super eosdem populos vel subditos; sed etiam periculosa est societas fidelium, si in eodem loco etiam super diuersos subditos fideles fuerint plures summi iudices constituti. & ita non expedit, quod clerici habeant vnum summum iudicem ecclesiasticum, scilicet papam; & laici vnum summum iudicem, scilicet imperatorem; cum clerici & laici in eisdem locis simul commaneant.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. It has been considered the second way of holding that the community of the faithful does not have one supreme judge, which was set out above in chapter 17; now let us look at the third, which was described in the same place. MASTER. How that way may be examined can be clear to the diligent reader from what was treated at the beginning of this work, from chapter 1 to chapter 13. DISCIPLE. Nevertheless, let us look more particularly at this way of holding, namely whether it is opposed and contrary to the best ordering of the community of the faithful, so that clerics are judged in every crime by the Pope or other inferior ecclesiastical judges, and likewise all laymen by a secular judge. For the arguments adduced in chapter 17 against this way of holding that the whole community of the faithful has no one supreme judge do not seem to conclude; for according to this way no one would have to be summoned or called by different people to different places, nor would anyone be forced to serve two masters, nor would several have power over the same persons, nor would any power be intolerant of a partner, which are the arguments on which those earlier points seem to have proceeded. Either therefore explain the second opinion recited above in chapter 17, showing how those allegations conclude against the third way, about which I now ask to speak, or try to bring forward some other allegations. MASTER. Although the way of governing the community of the faithful set out in the second opinion recited above in chapter 17, which we treated in the preceding chapter and in chapter 17, is far more pernicious than this way which you now wish to compare with it, nevertheless these allegations conclude much more plainly against that way than against this one, since the same allegations, or some of them, seem to convict this way of governing the community of the faithful of falling short of the best way of governing and punishing offenders. The first two allegations, however, appear ineffective against this way. But the third seems to have some force against it, since the whole community of the faithful could be governed by one; and what can be done by fewer is done in vain by more. Therefore two such rulers, namely the ecclesiastical and the secular, are set up in that way to no purpose. The fourth allegation, founded on the authority of the Saviour in Matthew 6, does not seem to conclude against this way at all; but the one founded on the authority of the Saviour in Matthew 12, that every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and so on, is brought against this way in the following manner: not only is that society near to desolation and ruin which is divided against itself, but also that which, by its manner of governing, is disposed to division and near to it, according to the authority of the Saviour. But if the community of the faithful has two parts, one of which has a supreme judge and the other another, that community is disposed to division and near to it; for because of the constant mutual intercourse of subjects and supreme judges, who, like all mortals, are prone to disagree with one another, they would easily be divided. Therefore, if the community of the faithful is governed in such a way, it is to be avoided as dangerous. The other allegation, founded on the authority of the blessed Jerome, seems to conclude effectively against that way: for the examples which Jerome adduces prove not only the unity of a prelate over one people or one multitude of men, but also prove the unity of a prelate over one place in which the subjects dwell; as in one diocese, which comprises a certain region, there is only one bishop, and in one province there is only one archbishop. Therefore by the same examples it is proved that the unity of a supreme judge over some place in which his subjects dwell is required, so that in that same place no other supreme judge exists over all who dwell there, just as in the diocese of Paris there is only one bishop, and in the province of Milan there is only one archbishop. The following allegation also seems to conclude against this way that power is not only intolerant of a partner over the same subjects, but is also intolerant of a partner in the same place. For just as a judge would not want his subjects to be the subjects of another, so he would not want anyone else to have power in the place where his subjects dwell. Therefore the fellowship of the faithful is not only dangerous if there are several judges over the same peoples or subjects, but the fellowship of the faithful is also dangerous if several supreme judges are established in the same place even over different faithful subjects. And so it is not expedient that clerics have one supreme ecclesiastical judge, namely the Pope, and laymen one supreme judge, namely the Emperor, since clerics and laymen dwell together in the same places.

units.la: DISC. Video qualiter praescriptae allegationes adducuntur contra istum modum ponendi. ideo contra eundem modum ponendi coneris alias inuenire. MAG. Videtur quod contra eundem modum ponendi potest aliter allegari. Nam, vt allegatum est 1. huius c. 1. illud regimen est expediens vniuersitati mortalium: & eadem ratione toti congregationi fidelium, per quod iurgia & litigia, ad quæ prona est natura mortalium, æquius & conuenientius deciduntur. sed iurgia & litigia, quæ oriri possunt ex causis innumeris inter clericos & laicos, æquius & conuenientius deciduntur, si omnes tam clerici, quam laici habent vnum summum iudicem, sub quo omnes debent litigare, quam si habeant plures iudices tales, scilicet ecclesiasticum & secularem. nam si orta materia litis inter clericos & laicos coram ecclesiastico iudice, qui non sit summus iudex laicorum, debeant litigare, merito laici habebunt eum suspectum. Consimiliter si debeant litigare coram iudice seculari, qui non est iudex clericorum, non indigne clerici habebunt eum suspectum. ergo absque rationabili suspicione non dirimetur litigium aliquod inter clericos & laicos, si non est omnium vnus iudex summus. Amplius(vt communiter) maiores & plures occasiones discordiarum, contentionum, seditionum, præliorum & guerrarum ac rixarum emergunt inter morantes simul, quam inter distantes, si simul morantes non habent vnum iudicem summum, cuius metu ab huiusmodi refrenentur. Sed inter distantes valentes ad inuicem communicationem habere sæpe contingunt occasiones malorum huiusmodi. Ergo multo magis timendum est, ne talia inter morantes simul emergant, nisi habeant vnum summum iudicem, qui omnes impedientes tranquillitatem & pacem habeat coercere. Rursus, nulla communitas simul viuentium vita politica est optime ordinata, nisi sit ciuiliter vna. vnde fideles sicut sunt vnum corpus in Christo, ad Rom. 12. ita etiam debent esse vnum corpus seu collegium in vita ciuili. sed communitas illa, quæ habet diuersos summos iudices seu diuersa capita siue rectores, non est ciuiliter vna: sicut illi, qui non habent vnum regem, non sunt vnum regnum. Sed communitas seu congregatio fidelium vel est optime ordinata, vel laborare debet, vt sit optime ordinata & ciuiliter: quia vita ciuilis pro eo, quod includit diuersas partes & diuersos modos ponendi, competit religioni Christianæ & vitæ gratiæ non repugnat. ergo communitas fidelium, si non est vna, quia non habet vnum summum iudicem, qui malefactores omnes per seipsum vel per iudices constitutos ab ipso seu inferiores eo habeat castigare ad habendum vnum huiusmodi summum iudicem, vt sit optime ordinata ciuiliter: etiam ciuiliter vna debet efficaciter laborare. & ita non expedit, vt in communitate fidelium sint plures iudices summi, quorum vnus clericos, & alius laicos debeat castigare.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I see how the aforesaid allegations are brought against this way of holding. Therefore try to find other arguments against the same way of holding. MASTER. It seems that other allegations can be made against the same way of holding. For, as was alleged in the first chapter of this work, that government is advantageous to the whole of mankind, and by the same reasoning to the whole congregation of the faithful, by which quarrels and lawsuits, to which the nature of mortals is prone, are settled more fairly and more suitably. But quarrels and lawsuits which can arise from countless causes between clerics and laymen are settled more fairly and more suitably if all, both clerics and laymen, have one supreme judge, before whom all must litigate, than if they have several such judges, namely an ecclesiastical and a secular one. For if a matter of dispute arising between clerics and laymen has to be litigated before an ecclesiastical judge who is not the supreme judge of the laity, the laity will rightly regard him with suspicion. Similarly, if they have to litigate before a secular judge who is not the judge of the clergy, the clergy will not unreasonably regard him with suspicion. Therefore no dispute between clerics and laymen will be settled without reasonable suspicion, unless there is one supreme judge of all. Moreover, as is commonly observed, greater and more numerous occasions of discord, contention, sedition, battles, wars and quarrels arise among those who dwell together than among those who live apart, if those who dwell together do not have one supreme judge by whose fear they may be restrained from such things. But occasions of such evils often arise among those who live apart yet are able to have mutual dealings. Therefore it is much more to be feared that such things will arise among those who dwell together, unless they have one supreme judge who may have the power to restrain all who hinder tranquillity and peace. Again, no community of people living together has a well-ordered political life unless it is civilly one. Hence the faithful, as they are one body in Christ (Rom. 12), so also ought to be one body or one fellowship in civil life. But that community which has different supreme judges or different heads or rulers is not civilly one, just as those who do not have one king are not one kingdom. But the community or congregation of the faithful is either well ordered or must labour to be well ordered and civilly so; for civil life, since it includes different parts and different ways of holding, is fitting to the Christian religion and does not repugn the life of grace. Therefore the community of the faithful, if it is not one because it does not have one supreme judge who may have the power to punish all malefactors either himself or through judges appointed by him or subordinate to him, must strive effectively, in order to have such one supreme judge so that it may be well ordered civilly, to be civilly one. And so it is not expedient that in the community of the faithful there be several supreme judges, one of whom should punish clerics and another laymen.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAP. XX.

units.la: In quo impugnatur quartus modus dicendi supra ca. 17. huius assignatus.
units.tr: In which the fourth view stated above in chapter 17 of this work is attacked.

units.la: DISCIP. Nunc videamus qualiter impugnatur quartus modus ponendi, communitatem fidelium non habere vnum iudicem summum, sicut ca. 17. recitatur. MAGIST. Iste modus tenet, sicut dictum est ibi, quod vna pars fidelium, scilicet clericorum, habet vnum summum iudicem, a quo solo vel a iudicibus inferioribus eo debet iudicari: præsertim si circa iustitiam exhibendam non fuerit negligens aut remissus. pro quibusdam autem delictis iudicari debet, præsertim si circa iustitiam exhibenda non fuit negligens aut remissus, sicut & iudex summus a summo iudice alterius partis, scilicet a papa vel iudicibus ecclesiasticis inferioribus ipso.
