Sed quibusdam apparet, quod talis communitas non est optime dispositå ciuiliter: quia ista communitas non est optime ciuiliter ordinata, in qua quantum permittit status vitæ præsentis occasiones discordiarum & litium ac seditionum, rixarum, præliorum & guerrarum minime amputantur. sed in communitate fidelium, si prædicto modo fuerit ordinata, non amputantur quantum est possibile pro statu præsentis vitæ occasiones malorum huiusmodi. nam non minima occasio talium est, si diversi iudices simul & eodem tempore eundem reum, præsertim diuitem & potentem, ad diversa loca & iudicia trahere moliantur. poterit autem contingere, quod aliquis laicus potens & diues committat diuersa scelera: quorum aliqua ad iudicem secularem, & alia ad iudicem ecclesiasticum pertineant puniencla, quare poterit euenire, quod tam iudex secularis quam ecclesiasticus voluerit ipsum trahere ad suum forum, quod pro eodem tempore est impossibile. ergo ex hoc orietur contentio & seditio, rixa & guerra inter iudices ipsos: & per consequens inter subditos ipsorum. quare tali suppositâ pluralitate iudicum in communitate fidelium pax & tranquillitas subditorum & iudicum erunt leuiter dissipata. Contra istum etiam modum ponendi videntur concludere oes allegationes tam primo huius ca. 1. quàm in hoc tertio ca. 17. inductæ ad probandum, quod est expedicns, quod tota communitas mortalium habeat vnum principem, qui sit dominus omnium, & quod est expedicns vt tota communitas fidelium habeat vnum summum iudicem, qui oes alios fideles habeat, si deliquerint, coercere. quamuis n. plura inconuenientia sequuntur ad secundum modum ponendi & tertium superius. 18. & 19. ca. impugnatos, quad istum: tamen ad istum multa sequuntur, secundu quod per allegationes illas vel aliquas earum posset ostendi. DISC. Breuiter tange allegationes, per quas alios modos ponendi im pbasti. quia forte ex deductione earum, quam ibi fecisti, aduertetur, an aliquam apparentiâ habeant contra istum modum. MAG. Si laici sint subditi tam iudici ecclesiastico quam iudici seculari: quamuis pro diuersis casibus poterit contingere, quod vterq; istorum iudicum pro casu spectante ad ipsum & pro communibus negociis ad ipsum & laicos spectantibus pertractandis ipsos laicos eodem tempore ad diuersa loca vocare voluerint. cui ergo obedient laici? aut vtrique, quod est impossibile: aut neutri: & tunc talis communitas non est optime ordinata. quia illa communitas non est conuenienter dispolita, in qua lubditi superiori suo aut non debent aut non possunt obedire. si obediant vni & non alii: illi cui non obediunt, faciunt iniuriam & ipsum offendunt: à quo pro contumacia punientur. Amplius, per talem pluralitatem iudicii communis vtilitas laicorum impedietur: quia non poterunt obedire vtriq; iudici summo, si pro communib. negociis vocati fuerint eodem tempore ad loca diuersa. Rursus, nemo iuxta sententiã Saluatoris potest duob. dominis seruire. ergo laici iudici seculari & ecclesiastico, qui proni sunt ad dissentiendum, seruire non poterunt. Item, iudex secularis & ecclesiasticus ex causis innumeris poterunt diuidi contra se. quare tota communitas fidelium facilter desolabitur. Adhuc, sicut testatur Hiero. In una dicecesi debet esse vnus episcopus, & in vna prouincia vnus archiepiscopus, cuius vtilitatem per multa exempla probat. ergo super laicos debet esse tarum vnus iudexsummus, non tantum de eisdem criminibus, sed etiam pro omnibus, vt de omnib. criminibus ab vno solo iudice summo & aliis iudicibus inferioribus eo debeant iudicari. Rursus, omnis potestas est consortis impatiens, & praecipue super eosdem subditos, & pro causis diuersis. ergo iudex secularis erit impatiens, si iudex ecclesiasticus super laicos habeat potestatem. etiam eodem modo iudex ecclesiasticus habens super laicos aut clericos potestatem erit impatiens, si iudex secularis super eosdem habeat potestatem. quare cito ad iracundiam, & per consequens ad contentionem, rixam & bellum & guerram prouocabuntur. Concludi-tur ergo, quod communitas fidelium non erit optime gubernata ciuiliter, etiam quantum ad vitam politicam, nisi tota & omnis pars eius habeat vnum iudicem & rectorem supremum, de cuius iurisdictione immediata vel mediata in omni casu ab eo vel à iudicibus inferioribus eo omnis alius pro quocunq; delicto debeat iudicari.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Now let us see how the fourth view is attacked, the view that the community of the faithful has no single supreme judge, as recited in chapter 17. MASTER. This view holds, as was said there, that one part of the faithful, namely the clergy, has one supreme judge, by whom alone, or by judges inferior to him, they ought to be judged, especially if he is not negligent or remiss in administering justice. For certain offences, however, they ought to be judged, especially if he is not negligent or remiss in administering justice, just as the supreme judge himself is judged by the supreme judge of the other part, namely by the Pope or by ecclesiastical judges inferior to him. But it seems to some that such a community is not well ordered in civil terms, because a community is not well ordered civilly if, so far as the condition of this present life permits, the occasions of discord, lawsuits, sedition, quarrels, battles and wars are not largely removed. In a community of the faithful, however, if it is ordered in the aforesaid way, the occasions of such evils are not removed as far as is possible in this present life. For it is no small occasion of them if different judges, at the same time, try to drag the same defendant, especially a rich and powerful one, to different places and courts. It may happen that a rich and powerful layman commits various crimes, some of which belong to a secular judge to punish and others to an ecclesiastical judge; so it may come about that both the secular and the ecclesiastical judge wish to draw him to their own court, which at the same time is impossible. Therefore contention and sedition, quarrel and war will arise from this between the judges themselves, and consequently between their subjects. Hence, with such a plurality of judges in the community of the faithful, the peace and tranquillity of subjects and judges will easily be destroyed. Against this fourth view all the arguments brought in both the first chapter and in this third chapter 17 seem to conclude, to prove that it is expedient for the whole community of mortals to have one prince who is lord of all, and that it is expedient for the whole community of the faithful to have one supreme judge who may restrain all other faithful if they offend. For although many inconveniences follow from the second and third views attacked above in chapters 18 and 19, yet many follow from this one, as could be shown from those arguments or some of them. DISCIPLE. Briefly touch on the arguments by which you refuted the other views, for perhaps from their development, which you made there, it will be noticed whether they have any appearance against this view. MASTER. If laymen are subject both to an ecclesiastical judge and to a secular judge, then, although for different cases it may happen that each of these judges wishes to summon the laymen at the same time to different places, both for a case falling to himself and for common affairs pertaining to himself and laymen, to which of them will the laymen obey? Either to both, which is impossible, or to neither, and then such a community is not well ordered, because a community in which subjects either ought not or cannot obey their superior is not properly arranged. If they obey one and not the other, they do wrong to the one they do not obey and offend him, and they will be punished by him for contumacy. Further, by such a plurality of judicial authority the common benefit of the laity will be impeded, because they will not be able to obey both supreme judges if they are summoned at the same time to different places for common affairs. Again, according to the saying of the Saviour, no one can serve two masters. Therefore laymen will not be able to serve both a secular and an ecclesiastical judge, who are prone to disagree. Likewise, a secular and an ecclesiastical judge may be divided against each other for countless causes, so the whole community of the faithful will easily be laid waste. Moreover, as Jerome testifies, in one diocese there ought to be one bishop, and in one province one archbishop, whose usefulness he proves by many examples. Therefore over the laity there ought to be only one supreme judge, not only for the same crimes but for all, so that all crimes are to be judged by one sole supreme judge and by other judges inferior to him. Again, all power is impatient of a partner, especially over the same subjects and for different causes. Therefore the secular judge will be impatient if the ecclesiastical judge has power over the laity; likewise the ecclesiastical judge who has power over laymen or clergy will be impatient if the secular judge has power over the same persons. Thus they will be quickly provoked to anger, and consequently to contention, quarrel, battle and war. It is concluded, therefore, that the community of the faithful will not be well governed civilly, even as regards political life, unless the whole and every part of it has one supreme judge and ruler, from whose immediate or mediate jurisdiction, in every case, every other person is to be judged for any offence by him or by judges inferior to him.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXI.

units.la: In quo impugnatur quintus modus dicendi sup. c. 17. assignatus.
units.tr: In which the fifth mode of speaking, assigned above in chapter 17, is attacked.

units.la: DISCIP. Audiui qualiter secundus modus & tertius & quartus ponendi communitatem fidelium, non habere vnicum summum iudicem, sicut c. 17. recitati sunt, impugnantur: nunc audire desidero, quomodo impugnatur quintus. M A G. Quintus est quorundam, qui ponunt q imperator est iudex in omni casu omnium Christianorum, praeter quam papae. quia papa exceptus est totaliter à iurisdictione imperatoris & cuiuslibet mortalis. omnes autem alii clerici solummodo sunt excepti per priuilegia imperatorum & regum. Iste autem modus taliter impugnatur. Sicutnon absq; periculo dissipationis, tranquillitatis & pacis duae multitudines hominum simul in eodem loco morantur, si non habent vnum summum iudicem, qui malefactores coerceat: sic non absq; periculo dissipationis, tranquillitatis & pacis moratur aliquis non subiectus cum alio vel cũ aliis, qui potestatem & magnam sequelam potest habere. talis enim propter sequelam, quam po-test habere, est pro multis non immerito computandus: sed papa propter altitudinem officii, quofungitur, potest habere maximam sequelam Christianorũ. ergo si non est subiectus summo iudici Christianorũ, non morabitur cum ipso absq; periculo dissipationis, tranquillitatis & pacis.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. I have heard how the second, third and fourth ways of holding that the community of the faithful does not have a single supreme judge, as they were recited in chapter 17, are attacked; now I wish to hear how the fifth is attacked. MASTER. The fifth is that of certain people who hold that the emperor is the judge in every case of all Christians, except the pope, because the pope is wholly exempt from the emperor's jurisdiction and from that of any mortal. All other clerics, however, are exempt only by the privileges of emperors and kings. This view is attacked as follows. Just as two multitudes of men cannot dwell together in the same place without danger of dissolution, tranquillity and peace, if they do not have a single supreme judge to restrain the wrongdoers, so too someone who is not subject, and who can have great following, cannot dwell with another or with others without danger of dissolution, tranquillity and peace. For such a person, on account of the following he can have, is not undeservedly reckoned as a danger to many; but the pope, on account of the height of the office he holds, can have the greatest following of Christians. Therefore, if he is not subject to the supreme judge of Christians, he will not dwell with them without danger of dissolution, tranquillity and peace.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Positis fundamentis rationum omnium pro opinionibus adductarum: secundum funda- mentum magis probat, scilicet quod laici non sunt in omnibus subiecti summo pontifici.
units.tr: Having laid the foundations of all the reasons adduced for the opinions, he next proves the second foundation more fully, namely that laymen are not subject to the supreme pontiff in all things.

units.la: DISCIP. Certo quod ratio, quam à 17. ca. vsq; hic tractauimus, fundatur in duobus. Quorum primum est, quod nulla communitas seu congregatio mortalium, nec vniuersalis necparticularis est optime dispolita, nisi vnum caput seu rectorem summum habeat, cui omnes nullo excepto, quo ad omnia quae pro communi vtilitate sunt necessario facienda, sint subiecti, & quod multum apparentiae videtur habere. quia vbi non est vnitas, non est facile concordiam conseruare. non est autem vna congregatio seu multitudo neque vniuersalis neque particularis: quae non habeat vnum caput seu rectorem, quia, vt testatur beatus Cypria. prout legitur 24. q. 1. ca. loquiturvbi est vnitas, oportet quod eius origo ab vno incipiat: quia, vt dicit ibidem, ab vnitate exordium profiscitur. in quacunque communitate seu congregatione est vnitas: illa vnitas ab vno incipit. ille autem vnus non est nisi caput & rector communitatis. ergo nulla communitas est vere vna, nisi illa, cuius caput & rector est vnus, ita vt omnes alii sint membra ipsius. Item, vnitas communitatis seu congregatio non est nisi vnitas ordinis secundum superioritatem & inferioritatem, vt quilibet respectu alterius sit inferior siue superior: vel plures sint inferiores respectu vnius superioris: quia vbi essent plures superiores respectu vnius inferioris, non esset verissima vnitas, quae est optima dispositio communitatis. oportet igitur quod summus in communitate potissima sit vnicus: & ita videtur multum apparens, quod nulla communitas nec particularis nec vniuersalis est optime ordinata, nisi habeat vnum caput vel rectorem, cui omnes alii sunt subiecti. vnde & vna domus non est optime dispolita, nisi habeat vnum patremfamilias: nec vna villa, nec vna ciuitas, nec vnum regnum optime gubernatur, nisi ab vno summo regatur. Et ideo omnes volentes secundum rationem politice viuere, vnum caput summum constituerent super omnes. Secundum, in quo videtur fundari ista ratio, est quod imperator & alii laicinon non sunt in omnibus, quae spectant ad gubernationem ipsorum & correctionem, si deliquerint subditi summo pontifici. quod ut videtur non habet tantam apparentiam, sicut primum. ideo pro isto alias allegationes adducas. MAGIST. Pro ista poteris tu colligere allegationes quamplures ex primo huius ac pluribus ca. specialiter. c. 28. & ex secundo huius c. 1. & 12. & 14. & 15. DISCIP. Pro isto secundo fundamento praescriptae rationis alias speciales allegationes adducas: vel alias prius tactas magis exquisite pertracta. MAG. Primo huius c. 28. tacta est una allegatio, quae nonnullis apparet multum fortis, quae talis est. Ille non est inferior alio, quoad illa, in quibus ab ipso ad istum alium appellare non licet, quia in omnibus, in quibus unus iudex est inferior alio, licet appellare ad illum (superiorem vel saltem ad superiorem ipso. Sed in multis causis non licet appellare ab imperatore ad Papam, ergo ad multa imperator non est inferior Papa. quod per sacros canones probatur aperte. Fabianus Papa, ut habetur 2. q. 6. c. 1. ait: Licet appellatori vitiatam causam remedio appellationis subleuare. Idem eadem causa & q. c. liceat, ait: liceat etiam in criminalibus causis appellare, nec vox appellandi negatur eo quod in supplicio sententia destinauerit. Ex his colligitur, quod ubicunque habet iudex superiorem ad superiorem potest appellare. Minor, scilicet quod in multis causis non est appellandum ab imperatore ad Papam, multis modis probatur. hoc enim Glo. 2. q. 6. c. super verbo sacerdotum, videtur asserere dicens: ergo a seculari iudice ad Papam potest appellari: quod verum est vacante imperio, ut extra de foro compe. licet alias, & extra de appellationibus, sed duobus. Item Glo. eodem ca. super verbo in communi ait: primo publice, ut secularis iudex audiat seculares causas, ecclesiasticus ecclesiasticas audiat. & sic planum est, quod ducitur in textu. sed cum dicit Anacletus: coram patriarcha aut primate ecclesiastico & coram patricio secularia negotia iudicentur. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod in negotiis secularibus a iudice seculari: & per consequens ab imperatore non est appellandum ad Papam. DIS. Si secundum Glossam primam vacante imperio licet appellare ad Papam. ergo Papa habet disponere de imperio & per consequens imperator ratione imperii est inferior Papa. & ita etiam non vacante imperio licet appellare ab imperatore ad Papam etiam in secularibus causis. MAG. Respondetur tibi, quod Papa vacante imperio nihil habet disponere de imperio, nisi auctoritate imperatoris instituentis eum vicarium suum, vel auctoritate aliorum scilicet Romanorum vel principum, quibus concessa est potestas ordinandi quis debeat gerere vicem imperatoris vacante imperio. & ideo si vacante imperio contingit appellare ad Papam, hoc est, in quantum Papa gerit vicem imperatoris & locum imperatoris tenet. qui autem gerit vices alterius & locum eius tenet, est inferior eo in hoc. quia semper vicarius est inferior eo, cuius est vicarius, ergo Papa est in hoc inferior & minor imperatore: & per consequens ab ipso imperatore non licet appellare ad Papam. DISCIP. Licet ista instantia apparenter videatur exclusa, tamen adhuc videtur posse ostendi, quod pro negociis seu causis secularibus liceat a imperatore & aliis secularibus iudicibus appellare. Nam ad illum licet appellare, qui potest causam viciatam subleuare. sed si causa secularis in foro seculari vel coram iudice seculari fuerit viciata: quia imperator vel alius iudex secularis non vult facere iustitiae complementum: Papa potest causam taliter viciatam subleuare, & ad ipsum vel alium iudicem ecclesiasticum est recurrendum pro iustitia obtinenda, extra de foro competen. c. extransmissa. & c. verum. & c. licet, & c. ex tenore. ergo licet appellare ab imperatore & aliis iudicibus secularibus ad Papam. MAG. Respondetur, quod etiam in decretalibus, quae maiorem iurisdictionem & auctoritatem Papae & iudicibus ecclesiasticis tribuere videntur, nunquam invenitur, quod si imperator neglexerit facere iustitiam in causa seculari, eo ipso possit Papa auctoritate Papalis officii & ex ordinatione Christi in eadem causa facere iustitiae complementum, licet ex consuetudine inquantum imperator scit & approbat, vel saltem scit & non prohibet, sed coloráns hoc faciat, Papa & iudices ecclesiastici in quibusdam regionibus iudicant de aliquibus criminibus pure secularibus, irrequisito omni iudice seculari: quod tamen eis ex iure divino non competit. Et hinc est, quod ex consuetudine obtinent Papa & ecclesiastici iudices, quod quando iudex secularis negligit facere iustitiam, ad ipsos recurritur, quae quidem consuetudo si iudices seculares in illis regionibus fuerint notabiliter negligentes, potest ex causa rationabili praescribi; praesertim si imperator hoc sciens ipsam duxerit tolerandam. Cum ergo dicis, quod ad illum licet appellare, qui potest causam viciatam subleuare. Respondetur, quod hoc non est generaliter verum vocando causam viciatam, omnem quae iusta sententia minime terminatur; quia appellatio semper debet fieri ad maiorem & causam taliter viciatam, quae scilicet iuste minime terminatur: potest quandoque minor supplendo negligentiam maioris subleuare. sicut etiam in conferendo beneficio & aliis disponendis potest minor supplere negligentiam superioris. extra de elec. c. in cunctis. extra de concess. prebendarum. c. nulla. & c. quia diuersitatem. extra de institutionibus. grave. & 9. q. 3. cum simus. & 89. di. volumus. ubi dicit Glossa arg. quod si prelatus non vult vel negligit facere, quae debet, tunc ea debent supplere subditi. hoc etiam colligitur ex concilio Sardicen. quod ponitur dist. 65. c. ultimo, ubi dicit Glos. quod si subditi negligunt facere quod debent: debeat suppleri a maiori vel per se vel per alium, & econtra. Ex quibus aliisq; quamplurimis patet, quod inferiores possunt supplere negligentiam superioris; cum etiam saepe possunt superiores corrigere & coercere, teste Egino Papa, qui, ut legitur 9. q. c. saluo, ait: saluo in omnibus Romana ecclesia priuilegio nullus metropolitanus absque ceterorum comprouincialium episcoporum instantia aliquorum audiat causas, quia irrita erunt aliter, antequam in conspectu omnium eorum erunt. erunt ventilata: & ipsefi fecerit, contra patribus. cui concordare videtur Anitius Papa, quod dem causa 9. c. si autem. aut c. si autem aliquis metropolitanorum inflatus fuerit & sine omnium compromissium praesentia, vel consilio episcoporum vel causas eorum, vel eas tantum quae ad propriam suam pertinent parrochiam agere aut graviare eos voluerit, ab omnibus distincte corrigatur, ne talia deinceps praesumere audeat. Si vero incorrigibilis eisque inobediens apparuerit, ad hanc apostolicam sedem, cui episcoporum iudicia referri praecepta sunt, eius consummatio referatur, ut de eo vindicta fiat. Ex praedictis colligitur, quod minor potest supplere negligentiam maioris. & ideo non semper ille, qui potest causam vitiatam sublevare, est maior. & per consequens non potest semper appellari ad ipsum. quare licet Papa suppleat negligentiam iudicum secularium: & si supplere negligentiam imperatoris terminando causam, quam imperator terminare negligeret: non posset per hoc ostendi, quod ab imperatore liceat appellare ad Papam: nec quod imperator in talibus sit minor Papa. DIS. Quod minor valeat supplere negligentiam superioris, hoc non est nisi auctoritate canonis conditi a concilio, quod est superius illo inferiori, qui potest supplere negligentiam superioris, extra de concess. praben. quia diversitatem. sed Papa auctoritate talis canonis vel legis non supplet negligentiam iudicum secularium vel imperatorum: sed auctoritate propria. ergo ex officio maior est imperatore in talibus, & etiam omnibus aliis iudicibus secularibus.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. Certainly the argument that we have treated from chapter 17 onward rests on two foundations. The first is that no community or assembly of mortals, whether universal or particular, is best ordered unless it has one supreme head or ruler, to whom all, without exception, are subject in everything that must necessarily be done for the common good. This seems to have a good deal of plausibility, because where there is no unity, concord is not easily kept. Now no assembly or multitude, whether universal or particular, lacks one head or ruler. As the blessed Cyprian testifies, as read in 24 q. 1 c. Loquitur, where there is unity, its origin must begin from one, because, as he says in the same place, the beginning proceeds from unity. In whatever community or assembly there is unity, that unity begins from one. But that one is none other than the head and ruler of the community. Therefore no community is truly one unless it has one head and ruler, and all the others are its members. Likewise, the unity of a community or assembly is nothing other than unity of order according to superiority and inferiority, so that each member is either superior or inferior to another, or several are inferior to one superior. For where there would be several superiors to one inferior, there would not be the truest unity, which is the best arrangement of a community. It is necessary, therefore, that the chief in a community be one alone. Thus it seems very plausible that no community, particular or universal, is best ordered unless it has one head or ruler, to whom all others are subject. Hence a household is not best arranged unless it has one head of the family; nor is a village, a city, or a kingdom best governed unless it is ruled by one supreme ruler. And therefore all who wish to live politically according to reason would set one supreme head over all. The second foundation, on which this argument seems to rest, is that the emperor and other laymen are not, in all matters concerning their government and correction, subject to the supreme pontiff should they offend. This, it seems, does not have as much plausibility as the first. Therefore, adduce other allegations for this. MASTER. For this you may gather many allegations from the first book of this work and from many chapters, especially chapter 28, and from the second book, chapters 1, 12, 14 and 15. DISCIPLE. For this second foundation of the stated argument, adduce other special allegations, or treat more carefully those already touched on. MASTER. In the first book, chapter 28, one allegation was touched on which seems very strong to some, and it runs thus: he who is not inferior to another in those matters in which one may not appeal from him to that other is not inferior to him. For in all matters in which one judge is inferior to another, it is permitted to appeal to that one, to a superior, or at least to a superior of the first judge. But in many cases it is not permitted to appeal from the emperor to the Pope; therefore in many matters the emperor is not inferior to the Pope. This is plainly proved by the sacred canons. Pope Fabian, as found in 2 q. 6 c. 1, says: It is permitted to relieve a spoiled cause by the remedy of appeal. The same, in the same cause and question, c. liceat, says: It is permitted to appeal even in criminal causes, nor is the voice of appealing denied because sentence has been pronounced for punishment. From these it is gathered that wherever a judge has a superior, one may appeal to that superior. The minor premise, namely that in many cases one may not appeal from the emperor to the Pope, is proved in many ways. For the Gloss on 2 q. 6 c., on the word sacerdotum, seems to assert, saying: therefore one may appeal from a secular judge to the Pope; this is true when the empire is vacant, as in extra de foro competenti, licet alias, and extra de appellationibus, sed duobus. Likewise the Gloss in the same chapter, on the words in communi, says: first, publicly, let a secular judge hear secular causes and an ecclesiastical judge hear ecclesiastical ones. And thus it is plain that this is what is drawn from the text; but when Anicetus says: let secular business be judged before the patriarch or ecclesiastical primate and before the patrician. From these words it is gathered that in secular business one may not appeal from a secular judge, and consequently not from the emperor, to the Pope. DISCIPLE. If, according to the first Gloss, one may appeal to the Pope when the empire is vacant, then the Pope has to dispose of the empire, and consequently the emperor, by reason of his empire, is inferior to the Pope. And so, even when the empire is not vacant, it would be permitted to appeal from the emperor to the Pope even in secular causes. MASTER. It is answered that the Pope, when the empire is vacant, has nothing to dispose concerning the empire, except by the authority of the emperor who appointed him as his vicar, or by the authority of the others, namely the Romans or the princes, to whom power has been granted to order who should act in place of the emperor when the empire is vacant. Therefore, if while the empire is vacant it happens that one appeals to the Pope, this is so insofar as the Pope acts as the emperor's deputy and holds the emperor's place. But whoever acts in another's place and holds his position is inferior to him in that respect, because a vicar is always inferior to him whose vicar he is. Therefore the Pope is in this respect inferior to and less than the emperor, and consequently one may not appeal from the emperor himself to the Pope. DISCIPLE. Although this objection seems apparently to be answered, it still seems possible to show that, in business or causes that are secular, one may appeal from the emperor and other secular judges. For one may appeal to him who can relieve a spoiled cause. But if a secular cause has been spoiled in a secular court or before a secular judge, because the emperor or another secular judge does not wish to bring justice to completion, the Pope can relieve such a spoiled cause, and one must have recourse to him or to another ecclesiastical judge to obtain justice: extra de foro competenti, c. extransmissa, c. verum, c. licet, and c. ex tenore. Therefore one may appeal from the emperor and other secular judges to the Pope. MASTER. It is answered that even in the decretals, which seem to grant greater jurisdiction and authority to the Pope and to ecclesiastical judges, it is never found that if the emperor has neglected to do justice in a secular cause, the Pope may for that very reason, by the authority of the papal office and by the ordinance of Christ, bring justice to completion in the same cause. It is true that by custom, insofar as the emperor knows and approves, or at least knows and does not forbid it while pretending not to, the Pope and ecclesiastical judges in some regions judge certain purely secular crimes without any secular judge being consulted; yet this is not granted to them by divine right. Hence it is that by custom the Pope and ecclesiastical judges have it that when a secular judge neglects to do justice, recourse is had to them. And this custom, if secular judges in those regions have been notably negligent, may be prescribed for a reasonable cause, especially if the emperor, knowing of it, has thought it should be tolerated. When you say, therefore, that one may appeal to him who can relieve a spoiled cause, it is answered that this is not generally true, if by a spoiled cause we mean any cause not finally ended by a just sentence. For appeal must always be made to a greater authority, and a cause spoiled in such a way that it is not justly ended can sometimes be relieved by a lesser authority supplying the negligence of the greater. Just as also in conferring a benefice and in other dispositions a lesser may supply the negligence of a superior: extra de elect., c. in cunctis; extra de concess. prebend., c. nulla and c. quia diversitatem; extra de institutionibus, grave; and 9 q. 3, cum simus; and dist. 89, volumus, where the Gloss says, by argument, that if a prelate does not wish or neglects to do what he ought, then subjects ought to supply it. This is also gathered from the Council of Sardica, placed in dist. 65, c. ultimo, where the Gloss says that if subjects neglect to do what they ought, it ought to be supplied by a greater, either in person or by another, and conversely. From these and very many other passages it is evident that inferiors can supply the negligence of superiors; and also that superiors can often correct and restrain them. Pope Eginus bears witness to this, who, as read in 9 q. c. saluo, says: saving in all things the privilege of the Roman Church, no metropolitan may hear causes without the request of certain other comprovincial bishops, because otherwise they will be void before all of them have been examined in their presence. Pope Anicetus seems to agree, in 9 c. si autem: if any metropolitan has been puffed up and without the presence or counsel of all the bishops has wished to deal with their causes, or to burden them, or only those that pertain to his own parish, let him be corrected distinctly by all, lest he dare to presume such things henceforth. But if he appears incorrigible and disobedient, let his case be referred to this apostolic see, to which the judgments of bishops are ordered to be referred, so that vengeance may be taken on him. From what has been said it is gathered that a lesser can supply the negligence of a greater, and therefore he who can relieve a spoiled cause is not always the greater, and consequently one may not always appeal to him. Therefore, although the Pope supplies the negligence of secular judges, and if he supplies the emperor's negligence by ending a cause that the emperor would neglect to end, it cannot be shown by this that one may appeal from the emperor to the Pope, nor that the emperor is in such matters less than the Pope. DISCIPLE. That a lesser may supply the negligence of a superior is only by the authority of a canon established by a council, which is superior to that lesser who can supply the negligence of a superior: extra de concess. praebend., quia diversitatem. But the Pope, by the authority of such a canon or law, does not supply the negligence of secular judges or emperors, but by his own authority. Therefore, by his office, he is greater than the emperor in such matters, and also than all other secular judges.

units.la: MAGIST. Respondetur tibi, quod sicut inferiores auctoritate legis supplent negligentiam superioris: ita Papa virtute consuetudinis, quae aequipollet legi, supplet negligentiam iudicum secularium. Et ideo auctoritate officii sui non supplet negligentiam talem. & ideo non est maior in huiusmodi causis secularibus. DIS. cuius auctoritate vel consensu potest introduci talis consuetudo, quae tribuat Papae huiusmodi potestatem? MAGIST. Ad hoc tibi respondetur uno modo, quod potest introduci huiusmodi consuetudo auctoritate vel consensu tacito, vel expresso imperatoris & iudicum secularium, quibus potest placere, quod Papa negligentiam supplecat eorundem, aut possunt scienter tolerare, quod hoc faciat Papa. Aliter dicitur, quod potest introduci auctoritate populi, qui velint vel consentiat, Papa huiusmodi habeat potestatem. aliter dicitur, potest introduci auctoritate siue ratione naturalis rationis, quae dictat, ut iustitia est nullatenus negligenda, quin semper in communitate servetur. DIS. Numquid possent imperator & iudices seculares talem consuetudinem tollere? MAG. Respondetur, quod secundum istam assertionem, quae ponit, quod talis consuetudo potest introduci de consensu tacito vel expresso imperatoris & iudicum secularium imperator posset eam tollere; sed non alii iudices seculares. quia enim praescriptio est a iure imperiali, & non ab inferioribus iudicibus. ideo enim hoc non potest Papa praescribere contra imperatorem, si expresse & ex certa scientia tolerat huiusmodi consuetudinem. sed contra alios iudices seculares inferiores praescribere potest Papa. Si tamen imperator revocaret huiusmodi consuetudinem, aut aliquomodo negligeret facere iustitiam, vel etiam permitteret alios iudices inferiores negligere iustitiam, & nullatenus sustineret, quod Papa, vel alius suppleret tam perniciosam negligentiam, & omnibus verisimiliter huiusmodi confusio incorrigibilis appareret, esset tanquam destructor & peruersor iustitiae de dignitate imperiali deponendus.
units.tr: MAGIST. The answer to you is this: just as inferiors, by the authority of law, make up for the negligence of a superior, so the Pope, by the force of custom, which is equivalent to law, makes up for the negligence of secular judges. And therefore, by the authority of his office, he does not make up for such negligence, and so he is not greater than them in such secular causes. DIS. By whose authority or consent can such a custom be introduced, one that grants the Pope this power? MAGIST. To this there is one answer: such a custom can be introduced by the authority or tacit or express consent of the emperor and of the secular judges, who may be pleased that the Pope should make up for their negligence, or who may knowingly tolerate that the Pope does so. Another view is that it can be introduced by the authority of the people, if they wish or consent that the Pope should have such power. Another view is that it can be introduced by the authority or reason of natural reason, which dictates that justice must in no way be neglected, but must always be maintained in the community. DIS. Could the emperor and secular judges abolish such a custom? MAG. The answer is that, according to this assertion, which holds that such a custom can be introduced by the tacit or express consent of the emperor and the secular judges, the emperor could abolish it, but the other secular judges could not. For prescription derives from imperial law, and not from the inferior judges. Therefore the Pope cannot prescribe this against the emperor, if the emperor expressly and with certain knowledge tolerates such a custom. But the Pope can prescribe against the other, inferior secular judges. Yet if the emperor were to revoke such a custom, or in any way neglect to do justice, or even permit the other inferior judges to neglect justice, and would in no way suffer the Pope or anyone else to make up for such pernicious negligence, and such incorrigible confusion would probably appear to everyone, he would be deposed from his imperial dignity as a destroyer and perverter of justice.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIII.

units.la: Probat, quod Papa est inferior Imperatore iurisdictione coactiva.
units.tr: Proves that the Pope is inferior to the Emperor in coercive jurisdiction.

units.la: DISCIP. Diffuse tractata est ratio prima, quam incepi. c. 1. 17. ad probandum, quod imperator est iudex Papae, & quod Papa est inferior eo, quoad iurisdictionem coactiuam. Ideo nunc alias rationes adducas. MAG. Ista ratio comprehendit duas tractatas in prima parte ipsius Dlogi. li. 6 c. 4. & 5. talis est. Papa non est magis exemptus a iurisdictione coactiva imperatoris & aliorum secularium iudicum, quam fuerunt Christus & apostoli. sed Christus in quantum homo mortalis & apostoli, fuerunt ab imperatore, quantum ad iurisdictionem coactiuam, iudicati. ergo consimiliter & Papa. Maior est manifesta. Minor probatur, quantum ad utramque partem. quod enim Christus fuerit inferior imperatore & aliis iudicibus secularibus, quantum ad iurisdictionem coactiuam, probatur. quia qui potest accusari & contra quem possunt alii testificari, iudicari potest. sed Christus poterat accusari, quod ipsemet testatur, cum Ioh. 8. dicit: quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato? quibus verbis concessit Christus aliis potestatem accusandi ipsum. Quod etiam testatur Innocen. 3. extra de haereticis, cum ex inuncto, dicens: Nec quisquam sua praesumptione audacia illo defendat exemplo, quod ašina legitur reprehendisse prophetas, vel quod dominus ait: quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato? & infra: Rursus aliud est, quod praelatus sponte de sua confessus innocentia subditorum se accusationibus subponit, in quo casu pram sum domini verbum debet intelligi. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Christus poterat accusari. ergo & poterat iudicari ab illo coram quo poterat accusari. DIS. Istud non concludit intentum: imo contrarium ex ipso colligitur, quod Christus solummodo sponte, sicut innuunt praemissa verba, se supposuit accusationibus subditorum. & ita Christus non potuit iudicari, nisi quia voluit. & per consequens iudices non erant superiores Christo. Ex quo infertur, quod exemplo Christi non potest concludi de Papa, quod teneatur subire iudicium imperatoris. sed quod Papa sponte potest se subiicere accusationibus aliorum, ut plures sacri canones testantur. MAGIST. Videtur aliis, quod verba praemissa probant intentum: scilicet quod ChriChristus poterat accusari, ita quod iudices, qui accusatores audire debebant, non poterant repellere volentes accusare Christum, nisi ex causa: puta si non apparerent legitimi accusatores, vel aliomodo repellerentur ab accusatione secundum iura, ex quo Christus dedit iure volentibus accusare potestatem accusandi. & per consequens ex tali potestate data Christo erant iudices superiores Christo, in quantum erat homo mortalis: & Christus sic fuit est inferior, licet sponte fuit passibilis & mortalis.
units.tr: DISCIPLE. The first argument I began, at chapters 1 and 17, to prove that the Emperor is the judge of the Pope, and that the Pope is inferior to him in coercive jurisdiction, has been treated at length. So now bring forward other arguments. MASTER. This argument is developed in two treatises in the first part of the Dialogue itself, book 6, chapters 4 and 5, and runs as follows. The Pope is not more exempt from the coercive jurisdiction of the Emperor and of other secular judges than Christ and the apostles were. But Christ, as a mortal man, and the apostles were judged by the Emperor in respect of coercive jurisdiction. Therefore the Pope is likewise. The major premise is plain. The minor premise is proved on both counts. That Christ was inferior to the Emperor and to other secular judges in coercive jurisdiction is proved as follows. Whoever can be accused, and against whom others can bear witness, can be judged. But Christ could be accused, as he himself testifies when he says, "Which of you convicts me of sin?" (John 8). By these words Christ granted to others the power of accusing him. Innocent III also bears witness to this in the decretal On Heretics, where he says, in the words quoted: "Let no one presume, in his boldness, to defend himself by the example of what is read of the prophets being rebuked, or by the Lord's saying, 'Which of you convicts me of sin?'" And further on: "On the other hand, it is another matter when a prelate, confident of his own innocence, voluntarily submits himself to the accusations of his subjects; in that case the Lord's word ought to be understood as applying." From these words it is gathered that Christ could be accused, and therefore could also be judged by the one before whom he could be accused. DISCIPLE. This does not prove the point intended. Rather, the opposite is gathered from it: that Christ submitted himself to the accusations of his subjects only voluntarily, as the words just quoted suggest. So Christ could not be judged except because he willed it, and consequently the judges were not superior to Christ. From this it follows that by the example of Christ nothing can be concluded about the Pope, namely that he is bound to submit to the judgment of the Emperor; rather, that the Pope can voluntarily subject himself to the accusations of others, as several sacred canons attest. MASTER. It seems to others that the words quoted above do prove the point intended, namely that Christ could be accused, so that the judges, who ought to hear the accusers, could not reject those wishing to accuse Christ, except for a cause: for instance, if no lawful accusers appeared, or if they were otherwise barred from accusing by the laws. For Christ, by right, gave to those wishing to accuse him the power of accusing. And consequently, by such a power given to Christ, the judges were superior to Christ insofar as he was a mortal man; and so Christ was inferior, although he was willingly passible and mortal.

units.la: [Et haec de tertia parte Dialogorum pro nunc tibi sufficiant.]
units.tr: [And let these things from the third part of the Dialogues suffice for you for now.]

units.la: Haec postrema verba inclusa non videntur esse Auctoris Occami, sed editoris, qui hoc opus maligne truncavit, & sex totos tractatus, quos habes in Prologo huius tertiae partis enumeratos, abrupit, quibus speciatim & hypothetice vniuersam causam inter Ludovicum Bavarum Imperatorem & Iohannem ac Benedictum Papas controversam Auctor exposuisse dicit, liberius aliquantum in Papas inuehendo, & Imperatorem excusando, quam offensio primi editoris ferre poterat, ut videre est in praefatione Ascensii huic Dialogo praefixa.
units.tr: These final words enclosed in brackets do not seem to be the author Occam's, but the editor's, who maliciously truncated this work and broke off six whole treatises, which you find enumerated in the Prologue of this third part, in which the author says he had set out, specifically and hypothetically, the whole cause controverted between Ludwig the Bavarian, Emperor, and John and Benedict, the Popes, speaking somewhat more freely in attacking the Popes and excusing the Emperor than the offence of the first editor could bear, as can be seen in the preface of Ascensius prefixed to this Dialogue.

units.la: GVILHELMI DE OCKAM Compendium errorum Papae.
units.tr: William of Ockham's Compendium of the Errors of the Pope.

units.la: INCIPIT COMPENDIVM ERRORVM IOANNIS PAPAE XXII. EDITVM ET COMPILATVM A FRATRE GVILLERMO OCKAM DE ORDINE FRATRVM MINORVM.
units.tr: HERE BEGINS THE COMPENDIUM OF THE ERRORS OF POPE JOHN XXII, EDITED AND COMPILED BY BROTHER WILLIAM OCKHAM OF THE ORDER OF FRIARS MINOR.

units.la: Secundum Bokkyg super sacram scripturam, quatuor sunt sensus scripturae sacrae, videlicet hystoricus, allegoricus, tropologicus, & anagogicus. Unde sensus historicus secundum Isid. Ethi. li. 1. ca. ultimo. historia, inquit, est rei gestae narratio, per quam ea quae in praeterito tempore facta sunt demonstrantur. Allegoria est, quando per factum vnum figuratur factum aliud, pertinens ad instructionem fidei de Christo & ecclesia, sicut per Noe in arca Gen. 7. figuratur Christus in ecclesia. etiam per serpentem elevatum in palo, Num. 21. figuratum Christus elevatus in cruce & per Goliam victum a Dauid significatur diabolus victus a Christo. & sic de aliis. Vnde allegoria aliud sonat: & aliud significat. Tropologia est, quando per factum vnum intelligitur aliquid faciendum, quod pertinet ad morum informationem & honestatis conversationem. Vnde tropologia est moralis locutio ad instructionem morum & correctionem siue apertis siue figuratis sermonibus prolata. Anagogia est expositio, qua inuisibilia Dei per ea quae facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur, Rom. 1. Vnde dicitur ab ana quod est sursum, & goge quod est ductio, quia ducit nos sursum ad intelligentiam de supracoelestibus.
units.tr: According to Bokkyg on Holy Scripture, there are four senses of Holy Scripture, namely the historical, the allegorical, the tropological, and the anagogical. The historical sense, according to Isidore, Etymologies, Book 1, last chapter: "History is the narration of things done, by which those things that were done in past time are shown." Allegory is when one deed prefigures another deed, bearing on the instruction of faith concerning Christ and the Church. Thus, in Genesis 7, Christ is prefigured in the Church by Noah in the ark; and in Numbers 21, Christ lifted up on the cross is prefigured by the serpent lifted up on the pole; and by David's victory over Goliath is signified the devil overcome by Christ; and so on for the rest. Hence allegory says one thing and signifies another. Tropology is when, through one deed, something to be done is understood, which pertains to the forming of morals and the good conduct of honesty. Hence tropology is a moral discourse, delivered in plain or figurative words, for the instruction and correction of morals. Anagogy is an exposition by which the invisible things of God are seen, being understood through the things that have been made (Romans 1). It is called from ana, which means upward, and goge, which means leading, because it leads us upward to an understanding of the things above the heavens.

units.la: INCIPIT PROLOGVS.
units.tr: HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE.

units.la: Locuti sunt adversum me lingua dolosa, & sermonibus odii circumdederunt me, & expugnaverunt me gratis, qui se dicunt apostolos: sed inventi sunt mendaces & tyranni persequentes innoxios, promouentes perfidos, diffamantes catholicos, exaltantes schismaticos, odientes probos, veritatem opprimentes, & totis suis conatibus viisq; possibilibus haereticam extollentes intrepide prauitatem. Venit prohdolor tempus, de quo vaticinans B. apostolus Paulus. 2. Tim. 4. Erit enim tempus, cum sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt: sed ad sua desideria coacervabunt sibi magistros prurientes auribus: & a veritate quidem auditum auertentes, ad fabulas autem convertentur. quae revera prophetia diebus nostris (quod lamentando refero) est penitus adimpleta. Nam insurrexerunt in me & alios viros utique realiter Christianos, fideles, catholicos, & orthodoxos, testes iniqui, & mentita est iniquitas sibi. Qui, ut intentum suum horrendum ad finem possint optatum perducere, scripturas sacras subuertunt, dicta sanctorum denegant, sacros canones legesq; ciuiles reprobant. Defendentes veritatem molestant, persequuntur & captiuant, & vsque ad interemptionem absque misericordia cruciant. Et vt multa verbis paucis concludam: Regem etiam & legem diuinam, legemque humanam, fronte meretricia, ausuque execrabili subuerrere & satagunt & festinant. Sunt ne iuuenes & omnino illiterati talia nephanda etiam fabricantes? sed vt inferius luce clarius apparebit, sunt seniores populi, pontifices, scribae, & pharisaei, necnon legisdoctores, veluti fuerunt qui Christum crucifixerunt, vt signanter possimus dicere verbum Dan. 13. scriptum: Egressa est iniquitas de Babylone a senioribus iudicibus, qui videbantur regere populum. Per istos, i q iam, inductus sum cum aliis Christicolis, cum iniuria in Pathmos deportatus. Non tamen sumus extra spem auxilii vel praemii positi: quia manus Domini non est abbreuiata, & confidimus in altissimo, quod cum honore in Ephesum remeabimus, & iniurias Christi confessoribus, imo veraciter imprudenter illatas, pro loco & tempore his, qui nunc ignorant, aperte ostendemus. Quod si Deus noluerit, certus sum quod neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli, neque principatus, neque instantia, neque futura, neque fortitudo, neque altitudo, neque profundum, neque tribulationes, neque minae, neque promissa, neque alia creatura poterit nos separare a charitate Dei, sen defensione fidei Christianae, pro qua labores & erumnas didicimus cimus tolerare. Nec tamen inuite, quantum ex parte est veritatis catholicæ defendendæ, licet gementes doleamus, quod tot diebus nostris, qui videbantur esse columnæ in ecclesia Dei, & qui deberent fidem Christianam vsque ad sanguinem defendere, in hæresum foueam & errorum se præcipitant & labuntur: imo cum gaudio omnes iniurias, blasphemias & persecutiones pro Christi amore sustinemus. Scientes quod, vt scribit apostolus 2. ad Thim. 3. Omnes qui pie volunt viuere in Christo persecutionem patientur. Et quoniam, vt ait idem apostolus 1. ad Cor. 11. Oportet hæreses esse vt qui probati sunt manifesti fiant. posuimus facies nostras, vt petram durissimam; volentes & cupientes cum Dei adiutorio in negotio fidei multipliciter probari, vt probatiores possimus mundo manifestari: nec propter insidias hominum impiorum manum ad aratrum positam sauciati persecutionibus retrahemus. intelligentes voce veritatis Matth. 5. esse dictum: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam: quoniam ipsorum est regnum cælorum. & 1. Pet. 3. Si quid patimini propter iustitiam, beati. Et Psal. ait: Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum. Si quid autem scripsero in præsenti opusculo, quod scripturæ vel doctrinæ sanctorum seu sacrosanctæ ecclesiæ assertioni repugnet & aduersetur, correctioni præfatæ ecclesiæ catholicæ, non ecclesiæ malignantium, non hæreticorum, non schismaticorum, nec eorum fautoribus me, & dicta mea subiicio & expono.
units.tr: They have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue, and have surrounded me with words of hatred, and have attacked me without cause; they who call themselves apostles. But they are found to be liars and tyrants, persecuting the innocent, promoting the faithless, defaming the Catholics, exalting the schismatics, hating the upright, suppressing the truth, and with all their efforts and every possible means boldly extolling heretical wickedness. Alas, the time has come of which the blessed Apostle Paul prophesied (2 Timothy 4): "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts they will heap up for themselves teachers, having itching ears; and they will turn away their hearing from the truth, and will be turned unto fables." Indeed this prophecy, as I lamentingly report, has been completely fulfilled in our days. For "false witnesses have risen up against me, and against other men truly Christian, faithful, Catholic and orthodox, and iniquity has lied to itself." These men, so that they may bring their dreadful intention to the desired end, overthrow the holy Scriptures, deny the sayings of the saints, and reject the sacred canons and the civil laws. They harass, pursue and imprison those who defend the truth, and without mercy torment them even to death. And to conclude many things in few words: they both strive and hasten to overthrow with brazen face and execrable boldness both the divine king and law, and human law as well. Are they young men and wholly unlearned, who devise such abominable things? But, as will appear more clearly than light below, they are the elders of the people, bishops, scribes, Pharisees, and also lawyers, just as those were who crucified Christ; so that we may aptly say the word written in Daniel 13: "Iniquity has come out of Babylon from the elders and judges who seemed to rule the people." Through these men I, together with other Christians, have been led away unjustly and carried off to Patmos. Yet we are not placed beyond hope of help or reward, because the hand of the Lord is not shortened, and we trust in the Most High that we shall return with honour to Ephesus, and at the proper place and time we shall plainly show to those who now do not know the wrongs done to the confessors of Christ, indeed wrongs done unwisely in truth. But if God should be unwilling, I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor power, nor height, nor depth, nor tribulations, nor threats, nor promises, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, or from the defence of the Christian faith, for which we have learned to endure toils and hardships. Nor, however, do we grieve unwillingly, insofar as it lies in us to defend Catholic truth, though we lament with groaning that in our days those who seemed to be pillars in the Church of God, and who ought to defend the Christian faith even unto blood, are throwing themselves and sliding into the pit of heresies and errors. Indeed, we bear all wrongs, blasphemies and persecutions with joy for the love of Christ, knowing that, as the Apostle writes (2 Timothy 3), "all who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution." And since, as the same Apostle says (1 Corinthians 11), "there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest," we have set our faces like very hard stone, wishing and desiring, with God's help, to be tried in many ways in the matter of faith, so that we may be made more evidently approved before the world; nor shall we, because of the snares of wicked men, draw back wounded by persecutions from the hand we have put to the plough, understanding that the voice of truth has said (Matthew 5): "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," and (1 Peter 3): "If you suffer for righteousness' sake, blessed are you." And the Psalm says: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly." If, however, I should write anything in this present little work that contradicts or opposes Scripture, the teaching of the saints, or the assertion of the holy Church, I submit and expose myself and my words to the correction of the aforesaid Catholic Church, and not to the church of the malicious, nor of heretics, nor of schismatics, nor of their supporters.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: De erroribus Papæ.
units.tr: On the errors of the Pope.

units.la: Dives locutus est, & omnes tacuerunt, & verbum illius vsque ad nubes perducunt, pauper locutus est, & dicunt, quis est hic? & si offenderit, subuertent illum. verba ista Eccl. 13. (scripta possum ego & quidam alii Christiani pauperes non immerito ruminare, qui de necessitate salutis contra quosdam diuites mundi huius, qui confidunt in multitudine diuitiarum, pro iustitia certamus. Et quia in numero visibiliter sumus, licet in rei veritate plures sint nobiscum, quam cum illis: sumusque; rebus pauperes, ac Mammona iniquitatis omnino carentes: ab aliis, qui plus sapiunt quam oportet sapere ad sobrietatem, blasphemamur, diffamamur, & derisioni habemur, factaque; sumus opprobrium abundantibus, & despectio superbis. Et quia de facto inimici nostri sunt iudices, per quos falsidica & fraudulenta informatio, imo deformatio ad aures plurimorum fidelium tam principum quam inferiorum clericorum & laicorum de gestis nostris circa negotium fidei dinoscitur peruenisse: quod videlicet veritati resistimus, & errores ac hæreses pertinaciter defensamus: doxi Deo primo causam nostri certaminis, absque fermento mendacii, succincto sermone pandere, vt nescientes mortifera tormenta impudentium virorum, & veritatem rei gestæ, discant qualibus modis lestamur iniuriis, quibusque; excessibus fides catholica opprimitur, terrur, & calcatur.
units.tr: The rich man has spoken, and all have kept silence, and they extol his word to the clouds; the poor man has spoken, and they say, "Who is this?" And if he stumbles, they will overthrow him. These are the words of Ecclesiasticus 13. I and certain other poor Christians may not unreasonably take them up, for we contend for righteousness, which is necessary for salvation, against certain rich men of this world who trust in the multitude of their riches. We are visibly few in number, although in truth there are more with us than with them. We are poor in goods and wholly lack the mammon of unrighteousness. Yet we are reviled and defamed by others who are wiser than they ought to be for sober judgement, and we are held up to ridicule. We have become a reproach to the rich and a contempt to the proud. And because our enemies are our judges in fact, through whom a false and fraudulent account, or rather a distorted one, is known to have reached the ears of many faithful people, both princes and lesser clergy and laity, concerning our conduct in the matter of the faith, namely that we resist the truth and stubbornly defend errors and heresies, I first give God my cause of struggle, and I set it forth in a brief account, without the leaven of falsehood. This is so that those who do not know the deadly torments inflicted by shameless men, and the truth of what has been done, may learn by what kinds of injuries we are afflicted, and by what excesses the Catholic faith is oppressed, terrified and trampled.

units.la: Existens itaque; Ioh. vicesimus secundus in sede B. Petri (in cuius curia nonnunquam fui) dicens se esse sapientem, stultus factus est volens esse legilodoctor, non intelligens ea quæ loquebatur, neque de quibus affirmauit, quæque nunquam didicerat, temere docere præsumpsit, & qui prius non fuit discipulus veritatis, factus est magister hæresum. In arcum enim prauum conuersus, duo principaliter agere attemptauit; Romanum videlicet Imperium vel sibi subiugare vel penitus lacerare, & professionem pauperum fratrum Minorum erroneam esse & illicitam quibusdam documentis insanis declarare, vt istis peractis criminibus totum mundum subiiceret suæ ditioni. Et quia ad tam execrabile desiderium suum instinctu hostis generis humani adinuentum, si possibile fuisset, implendum, opus habuit mendaciis abundare, scripturas sacras vtriusque testamenti vna cum doctrinis sanctorum & sententiæ ministris ecclesiæ reprobare, leges criminales deserere, atque alumnos Christi affligere, persequi, & molestare, tres destitutiones scripsit, quas constitutiones vocaliter appellauit. Quarum prima, Ad conditorem canonum, Secunda cum inter nonnullos: Tertia, quia quorundam, incepit. in quibus sui conceptus pestiferi dementiam detexit cuidenter & monstrauit. Nam dictas destitutiones erroribus, hæresibus, mendaciis, & sophismatibus, fermentans, in fide & bonos mores damnabiliter impegit, & in præiudicium Christi & Christianitatis contra veritates catholicas intrepide scripsit, docuit, & affirmauit.
units.tr: Therefore John XXII, who sat in the see of St Peter (I was sometimes in his court), saying that he was wise, became a fool, wishing to be a doctor of law. Not understanding the things he said, nor the matters about which he affirmed, and having never learned them, he presumed to teach them rashly; and he who had not first been a disciple of the truth became a teacher of heresies. Turned to a crooked bow, he principally attempted two things: namely, either to subject the Roman Empire to himself or to tear it apart completely, and to declare by certain mad decrees that the profession of the poor Friars Minor was erroneous and unlawful, so that, these crimes accomplished, he might bring the whole world under his rule. And because, to fulfil this accursed desire, devised at the prompting of the enemy of the human race, he needed to abound in lies, he condemned the sacred Scriptures of both Testaments together with the doctrines of the saints and the teaching of the ministers of the Church. He deserted the criminal laws, afflicted, pursued and harassed the foster-children of Christ, and wrote three decrees, which he called constitutions by name. The first began Ad conditorem canonum, the second Cum inter nonnullos, the third Quia quorundam. In these he plainly disclosed and showed the madness of his pestilent conception. For, fermenting the said decrees with errors, heresies, lies and sophisms, he damnably assailed faith and good morals, and in prejudice to Christ and Christendom he boldly wrote, taught and affirmed things against the Catholic truths.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: IN prima quidem destitutione sua, videlicet Ad conditorem, Primus error suus est, quod reseruatio dominii rerum, quibus aliqui religiosi vtuntur, facta per summum pontificem ad statum perfectionis minime prodest. Quem errorem ponit sub his verbis: Ipsis quidem fratribus quantum ad statum perfectionis nequaquam profuit retentio dominii supradicta: Iste igitur error est idem cum quodam alio errore suo, quo affirmat, quod abdicatio proprietatis similium rerum tam in speciali quam in communi ad perfectionem non prodest. & ideo inferius, vbi ista verba ponit, similiter tractabatur.
units.tr: In his first constitution, Ad conditorem, his first error is that the reservation of ownership of goods, which some religious use, made by the supreme pontiff, does not in the least benefit the state of perfection. He states this error in these words: The aforesaid retention of ownership has by no means profited the brothers themselves as regards the state of perfection. This error is therefore the same as another of his errors, in which he asserts that the renunciation of ownership of such things, both individually and in common, does not contribute to perfection. For this reason, further on, where he sets out those words, the same point was treated as well.

units.la: Secundus error in eadem destitutione insertus est, quod via præcipue disponitur ad caritatem per amputationem solicitudinis, quam ipsa temporalia in acquirendo, conseruando & dispensando exigunt. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Cum enim perfectio vitæ Christianæ principaliter & essentialiter in charitate persistat, quæ ab apostolo vinculum perfectionis dicitur, & qua vnit seu iungit aliqualiter hominem suo fini, ad quem per oneremptum bonorum temporalium & ipsorum expropriationem via disponitur: per hoc præcipue, quod sollicitudo, quam ipsa temporalia in acquirendo, conseruando, & dispensando exigunt (quæ plerunque ab actu charitatis retrahit) amputantur. Hæc sunt verba eius, quæ veritati aperte contradicunt.
units.tr: The second error inserted in the same constitution is that the way to charity is chiefly prepared by cutting off the anxiety which temporal goods demand in acquiring, preserving and dispensing them. He states this error in these words: For since the perfection of the Christian life consists principally and essentially in charity, which the Apostle calls the bond of perfection, and by which man is in some way united and joined to his end, to which the way is prepared through the removal of the burden of temporal goods and their expropriation: this especially, that the anxiety which temporal things demand in acquiring, preserving and dispensing them (which for the most part withdraws a man from the act of charity) is cut off. These are his words, and they plainly contradict the truth.

units.la: Tum quia magis disponitur via ad charitatem per amputationem amoris inordinati ad temporalia, qui non potest esse effectus charitatis: quam per amputationem sollicitudinis, quam exigunt temporalia. Tum quia sollicitudo circa temporalia potest esse effectus charitatis & ex pura charitate proprocedere, sicut patet in illis, qui in charitate fundati propter eleemosynas faciendas, propter hospitalitatem sectandam, propter pauperes vestiendos, propter captiuos redimendos, propter peregrinos suscipiendos, & alia pietatis opera exercenda, die nocteque circa temporalia laudabiliter sollicitantur. Tum quia magis disponitur via ad charitatem per votum paupertatis, quam per amputationem sollicitudinis, quam exigunt temporalia: quia actus votendi paupertatem est difficilior atque perfectior, quam carentia sollicitudinis, quam exigunt temporalia. Quare iste error est merito reprobandus.
units.tr: Because the way to charity is prepared more by cutting off inordinate love of temporal things, which cannot be an effect of charity, than by cutting off the anxiety which temporal things demand. Also because anxiety about temporal things can be an effect of charity and can proceed from pure charity, as is evident in those who, grounded in charity, are laudably anxious about temporal things day and night, for the sake of giving alms, practising hospitality, clothing the poor, ransoming captives, receiving strangers, and performing other works of piety. Also because the way to charity is prepared more by the vow of poverty than by cutting off the anxiety which temporal things demand, since the act of vowing poverty is more difficult and more perfect than the freedom from the anxiety which temporal things demand. Wherefore this error deserves to be rightly rejected.

units.la: Tertius error in praedicta destitutione insertus est, quod expropriatio siue abdicatio bonorum temporalium per votum nihil potest conferre ad perfectionem, si eadem siue æqualis sollicitudo perseueret post expropriationem quæ inerat. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Restat quod si sollicitudo eadem post expropriationem huiusmodi, quae ante ipsam inerat, perseueret, ad perfectionem huiusmodi talis expropriatio valet nil conferre.
units.tr: The third error contained in the aforesaid deprivation is that the renunciation or abdication of temporal goods through a vow can contribute nothing to perfection if the same or equal care persists after the renunciation as was there before. He states this error in these words: It remains that if the same care persists after such an expropriation as existed before it, such an expropriation is worth nothing toward perfection.

units.la: Verba eius erronea & virulenta, in quib. veritati contradicit & perfectionem virorum religiosorum in officiis specialiter constitutorum dirimit & annullat. Nam constat, quod abbates, priores, & ceteri religiosorum prælati, nec non inferiores in officiis ordinis sui constituti maiore de communi lege habent sollicitudinem circa temporalia acquirenda, conseruanda & dispensanda post votum paupertatis & expropriationis propter officia assumpta vel eis iniuncta: quam in nouiciatu ante expropriationem talem habuerant. Nec propter hoc sequitur, quod expropriatio, quam voluerunt, nihil eis confert ad perfectionem. imo expresse sequitur contrarium, ut ait Anselmus qui in lib. suo de similitudinibus aperte dicit, quod opus bonum factum cum voto plus valet, quam factum sine voto. Quartus error est, quod carentia dominii Romanæ ecclesiæ reseruati, non reddit carentem pauperiorem, quam si res ipsas cum dominio obtinerent. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Adhuc nec utique potuit dictis fratribus ordinato supradicta, quantum ad hoc, quod propter carentiam talis dominii, se pauperiores dicere valeant: quam si ipsas cum illo, quo carere debent, dominio obtinerent. Qui error est contra determinationem ecclesiæ Romanæ, nam exita de ver. significatione. lib. 6. c. exiit qui seminat, expresse dicitur, quod per carentiam talis dominii abdicantes magis a temporalibus elongantur. Est etiam contra rationem, nam ille est pauperior quantum ad res temporales, qui non potest ipsas in iudicio repetere, nec pro eis in iudicio litigare, quam si talia posset pro temporalibus rebus exercere. Item qui habet tale dominium est ditior, cum possit res huiusmodi vendere & pro sua vtilitate alienare. Igitur carens tali dominio est pauperior, quam si huiusmodi dominium obtineret. Quintus error suus est, quod quantum ad res usu consumptibiles usus facti non potest a proprietate seu dominio separari. Et vocat res usu consumptibiles, ut postea apparebit, illa quæ in cibo & potu, pecunia & vestimentis constitunt. Vsum autem facti vocat actum vtendi, cuiusmodi est actus manducandi, bibendi, induendi, & huiusmodi. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Dicere siquidem quod in talibus rebus (sc. usu consumptibilibus) usus iuris vel facti separatus a proprietate rei seu dominio possit constitui, repugnat iuri & obuiat rationi. Hæc sunt verba eius, quæ sacræ scripturæ aperte contradicunt. Nam, ut habetur, Gen. 27. Iacob habuit simplicem facti vsum vestimentorum Esau fratris sui ab omni proprietate & dominio separatum. Vnde ibidem sic legitur: vestib. Esau valde bonis, quas apud se Rebecca domi habebat, induit eum. sc. Iacob. Sacerdotes etiam veteris testamenti habebant vsum facti panum propositionum, & cuiusdam determinatæ partis quorundam sacrificiorum: & tamen non habebant proprietatem & dominium illorum, quia non poterant illa vendere, nec donare, nec de illis aliquid ordinare, nisi solummodo manducare. Sacerdotes etiam novæ legis habent vsum paramentorum in altari ab omni proprietate & dominio separatum. Ista hæresis posset infinitis auctoritatibus scripturæ diuinæ & sanctorum auctoritatib. ac rationib. velridiculis & exemplis reprobari. Sextus error est, quod ius vtendi in rebus usu consumptibilib. separatè a proprietate seu dominio non potest constitui vel haberi. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: In rebus consumptibilibus vsus nec ius vtendi, nec vsus facti separatà rei proprietate seu dominio possunt constitui vel haberi. Iste error militat contra veritatem. Nam licentia vtendi etiam secundum istum, qui in quodam alio loco dicit sic: Si quis alicui licentiam concedat vtendi re sua visibili (ita quod licentiam tenat) constat quod habet ius vtendi re illa, cuius licentia est concessa. igitur secundum ipsum licentia est ius vtendi. Manifestum est autem, quod aliquis potest habere licentiam vtendi vestibus alterius sine omni proprietate & dominio. Ergo potest habere ius vtendi rebus usu consumptibilibus ab omni proprietate rei & dominio separatum. Septimus error est, quod vti re aliqua nihil aliud est proprie, quam fructus rei seu utilitatem in solidum vel pro parte recipere, quæ ex ea potest salua rei substantia prouenire. Istum errorem ponit sub his verbis: Cum enim vti re aliqua nihil aliud sit, proprie, quam fructus rei seu utilitatem aliquam in solidum vel pro partere capere, qui ex illa potest salua rei substantia prouenire. Hæc verba sua sunt erronea. ex quibus sequitur aperte, quod nullus possit vti cibo vel potu, quia ex illis non provenit communiter utilitas salua rei substantia. Quare dictum suum est erroneum reputandum. Quod & auctoritatibus similiter & rationibus posset euidenter & copiose probari. Octauus error est, quod illa re vti quis nequit, ex qua eius salua substantia, nulla pōt sibi puenire utilitas. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Restat quod re illa vti quis nequeat, ex qua eius salua substantia nulla sibi potest prouenire utilitas, qualei res usu consumptibiles esse constat. Hæc verba eius insana sacræ scripturæ & doctrinæ sanctorum ac etiam rationi aduerla sunt. Beatus enim Paulus. r. ad Tim. 5. scribit, vtere modico vino propter stomachum: tamen aliæ auctoritates innumeræ possent adduci edduci idem probantes demonstratiue. ratio indicat, quod contigit vti alimentis & rebus diuersis, quae ipso vsu consumuntur.
units.tr: His words are erroneous and virulent. In them he contradicts the truth and destroys and annuls the perfection of religious men who are specially placed in offices. For it is evident that abbots, priors, and the other superiors of religious orders, as well as the inferior officers of their order, ordinarily retain, by the common law, care for acquiring, preserving, and dispensing temporal goods even after the vow of poverty and expropriation, on account of the offices they have taken up or been assigned. They had this same care in the novitiate before expropriation. Nor does it follow from this that the expropriation which they embraced contributes nothing to their perfection. Rather the opposite clearly follows, as Anselm says in his book On Similitudes, where he plainly states that a good work done with a vow is worth more than the same work done without a vow. The fourth error is that the lack of the dominion reserved to the Roman Church does not make those who lack it poorer than if they held the things themselves together with the dominion. He states this error in these words: Nor indeed could it be said of the aforesaid order of brothers that, on account of their lack of such dominion, they can call themselves poorer than if they held those same things together with the dominion they ought to lack. This error is against the determination of the Roman Church, for in Exita, De verborum significatione, lib. 6, c. Exiit qui seminat, it is expressly said that those who renounce, through lack of such dominion, are farther removed from temporal goods. It is also against reason. For a person is poorer as regards temporal goods if he cannot recover them in court or litigate for them in court, than if he could exercise such rights over temporal goods. Likewise, one who holds such dominion is richer, since he can sell such things and alienate them for his own advantage. Therefore one who lacks such dominion is poorer than if he held that dominion. The fifth error of his is that, as regards things consumable by use, the use of the fact cannot be separated from ownership or dominion. He calls things consumable by use (as will appear later) those which consist in food and drink, money and clothing. He calls the use of the fact the act of using, such as the act of eating, drinking, dressing, and the like. He states this error in these words: To say that in such things (namely those consumable by use) a use of right or of fact separated from the ownership or dominion of the thing can be constituted is contrary to law and opposed to reason. These are his words, and they clearly contradict Holy Scripture. For, as we read in Gen. 27., Jacob had the simple use in fact of the garments of his brother Esau, separated from all ownership and dominion. Hence it is read there thus: Rebecca then clothed him, that is Jacob, in the very good garments of Esau her son, which she had at home with her. The priests of the Old Testament also had the use in fact of the showbread and of a certain determined portion of certain sacrifices, and yet they did not have the ownership and dominion of them, because they could not sell them, nor give them away, nor dispose of them in any way, except to eat them. The priests of the New Covenant likewise have the use of the vestments at the altar, separated from all ownership and dominion. This heresy could be refuted by countless authorities of divine Scripture and of the saints, by reasons and examples, and even by ridicule. The sixth error is that the right of using things consumable by use cannot be constituted or held separately from ownership or dominion. He states this error in these words: In things consumable, neither the use nor the right of using, nor the use of the fact, can be constituted or held separately from the ownership or dominion of the thing. This error militates against the truth. For according to him, who says elsewhere: If someone grants another a license to use his visible property (so that the license is held), it is clear that the one to whom the license is granted has the right to use that thing, therefore in his view a license is a right of use. It is plain, however, that someone can have a license to use another's clothes without any ownership or dominion. Therefore he can have the right to use things consumable by use, separated from all ownership of the thing and dominion. The seventh error is that to use any thing properly is nothing other than to receive, wholly or in part, the fruit or the advantage of the thing which can arise from it while its substance is preserved. He states this error in these words: For to use any thing properly is nothing other than to take, wholly or in part, the fruit or some advantage of the thing, which can arise from it while its substance is preserved. These words of his are erroneous, and from them it clearly follows that no one could use food or drink, since advantage does not commonly arise from them while their substance is preserved. Therefore his statement must be regarded as erroneous. This could also be shown clearly and abundantly both by authorities and by reasons. The eighth error is that a person cannot use a thing from which no advantage can come to him while its substance is preserved. He states this error in these words: It remains that a person cannot use a thing from which no advantage can come to him while its substance is preserved, such as things consumable by use are known to be. These words of his are insane, and contrary to Holy Scripture, to the doctrine of the saints, and even to reason. For blessed Paul writes, 1 Tim. 5.: Use a little wine for your stomach's sake; and countless other authorities could be adduced that prove the same thing demonstratively. Reason shows that it is possible to use foods and other things which are consumed by the very use.

units.la: Nonus error est, quod actus vtendi sine iure aliquo non potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel habere. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: nec actus ipse vt nisi sine iure aliquo potest in rebus vsu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi. Haec verba eius vesana, ex quibus sequitur, quod furans vestes alterius vel aliam rem quocunque vsu consumptibilem, statim cum vsu habetur vtendi ipsa. & per consequens non iniuste debet dici ipsa vti.
units.tr: The ninth error is that the act of using cannot be established or had in things consumable by use without some right. He puts this error in these words: "nor can the act of using itself, except without some right, be established or had in things consumable by use." These words of his are mad. From them it follows that a man who steals another's clothes, or any other thing consumable by use, has the act of using it immediately, and so it is not unjustly said that he uses it.

units.la: Decimus error est, quod rebus vsu consumptibilibus non contingit vti, sed abuti. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Licet in rebus vsu consumptibilibus nec in vtendi nec ipsum vti possit constitui vel haberi, ipsis tamen poterit quis abuti. Haec verba eius detestanda. Ex quo sequitur, quod Christus & apostoli, quotiens comederunt & biberunt & se induerunt, rebus vsu consumptibilibus abutebantur: quod est haereticum, & blasphemum. Similiter ex dicto errore sequitur, quod quicunque sacerdos vtitur speciebus in sacramento altaris, cum sint vsu consumptibiles, abutitur illis speciebus. quod est erroneum & iniquum. Abuti enim communiter & maxime in scriptura diuina sumitur pro male vti. Vndecimus error est, quod abuti exigit, cum actu superbia rei consumatur.
