And if Pope Melchiades seems to suppose that the believers never held those estates in common before selling them, since he says that the apostles by no means obtained them in Judea, we reply: Melchiades says this only in that sense, that the apostles did not obtain estates in Judea because they did not acquire them in such a way as to intend to keep them; and therefore they did not seem to have acquired them, since one who acquires a thing in such a way that he must immediately give it up is not properly said to have acquired it. From what has been said it is clear that the apostles were permitted to keep estates in Judea, if they had wished. Nor were they bound by a vow not to keep them; they did not keep them by their own choice, since they foresaw that they would not remain there but would pass on to the Gentiles. These words of his are heretical, opposing and contradicting the teaching of the saints and the decision of the Church.

units.la: Sextus error est, quod usus facti non potest competere communitati. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Usus facti communitati non conuenit: cum usus talis personam unam exigat. Haec verba eius, quae sacrae scripturae sunt contraria, cum dicatur Exo. 31. Sedit populus manducare & bibere. & 4. Regum. 4. Infunde turba vt comedant.
units.tr: The sixth error is that the use of a thing cannot belong to a community. He sets down this error in these words: The use of a thing does not befit a community, since such use requires one person. These words of his are contrary to Holy Scripture, since it is said in Exodus 31: The people sat down to eat and drink; and in 4 Kings 4: Pour out for the crowd, that they may eat.

units.la: Septimus error est, quod quilibet apostolorum habuit proprietatem & dominium non solum in communi, sed etiam in speciali post Spiritus sancti missionem. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Videtur etiam quod patenter possit dici, quod post distributionem bonorum usu consumptibilium, quae fiebat inter apostolos & credentes alios (ut dicit Actuum 2. & 4.) quilibet portionis sibi assignata proprietarius & dominus posset dici. Et infra: cum ergo dicat, quod nullus egens erat, pro eo quod vnicuique diuidebatur, prout opus erat, supponit aperte quod idem quod vnicuique dabatur diuisim cuilibet erat proprium. Haec verba eius haeretica, quae tam sacrae scripturae, quam allegat, quam dictis sanctorum & determinationi sanctae Romanae ecclesiae expresse contradicunt. Nam Actuum 2. sic legitur: Omnes etiam qui credebant pariter & habebant omnia communia. Et ca. 4. sic scribitur: Multitudinis autem credentium erat cor unum & anima una in Domino, nec quisquam eorum quae possidebat, aliquid suum esse dicebat, sed erant illis omnia communia. Constat autem quod apostoli fuerunt primi & praecipui inter credentes. Igitur ipsis apostolis post aduentum Spiritus sancti nihil fuit proprium, vt tenet error istius. Hoc etiam doctrina sanctorum & ecclesiae determinare docet euidenter.
units.tr: The seventh error is that each of the apostles, after the mission of the Holy Spirit, had property and ownership not only in common but also in particular. He sets down this error in these words: It also seems that it can plainly be said that, after the distribution of consumable goods, which was made among the apostles and the other believers (as Acts 2 and 4 says), each one could be called the owner and lord of the portion assigned to him. And further on: Since he therefore says that no one was in need, because distribution was made to each as there was need, he clearly supposes that what was given separately to each was his own. These words of his are heretical, contradicting as expressly both the Holy Scripture he cites and the sayings of the saints and the decision of the holy Roman Church. For Acts 2 reads thus: All who believed were together and had all things in common. And chapter 4 is written thus: The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul in the Lord, nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. Now it is certain that the apostles were the first and chief among the believers. Therefore, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, nothing was their own, as the error of this man holds. The teaching of the saints and the determination of the Church teach this plainly as well.

units.la: Octauus error est, quod bona temporalia usu consumptibilia (de quo fit mentio Actuum 2. & 4.) ante distributionem erant propria apostolorum. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Cum igitur daretur ab illis, qui dare poterant (scilicet apostolis) & illi qui recipere poterant, scilicet ea quae ad vitae humanae sustentationem pertinebant: videtur quod dominus quilibet fuerit portionis eius, quae sibi fuerit assignata. Et ita patet, quod habentibus temporalia est locutus, cum dixerit, quod det ei quia a se petit, quod non potest facere: cum dare sit accipientis facere dominium, quod non potest aliquis facere, nisi dominium etiam quoad temporalia obtineret. Haec verba eius: ex quibus manifeste colligitur, quod ipse intelligit, quod apostoli erant domini illarum rerum, quas credentib. dimiserunt. Et per consequens, quod illeres nunquam fuerunt communes: quia non ante distributionem, cum secundum ipsum tunc proprie fuerunt apostolorum. Nec post distributionem, cum quilibet fieret proprietarius portionis sibi assignatae. Qui error quantum ad vtranque sui partem est scripturae diuinae contrarius & etiam doctrinae sanctorum, sicut in operibus maiorum aperte est monstratum.
units.tr: The eighth error is that temporal goods consumed by use (of which mention is made in Acts 2 and 4) were the property of the apostles before the distribution. He sets down this error in these words: Since, then, things were given by those who could give (namely the apostles) and received by those who could receive, namely those things which pertained to the sustenance of human life, it seems that each became lord of the portion assigned to him. And so it is plain that he is speaking of those who hold temporal goods, when he says: let him give to him who asks of him, which he cannot do; for to give is for the one receiving to make ownership, which no one can do unless he also obtains ownership as regards temporal goods. These are his words, from which it is clearly gathered that he understands the apostles to have been the owners of the things they let go to the believers. And consequently those things were never common: not before the distribution, since according to him they then properly belonged to the apostles; nor after the distribution, since each became owner of the portion assigned to him. This error, in both of its parts, is contrary to the divine Scripture and also to the teaching of the saints, as has been clearly shown in the works of the greater writers.

units.la: Nonus error est, quod B. Petrus post missionem Spiritus sancti habebat proprietatem & dominium rerum temporalium in speciali. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Caliga & vestimenta assignata Petro proprie quoad dominium erant Petri. quare videtur quod pecunia, panis, vinum, & res aliae usu consumptibiles sibi diuisim pro vita sustentatione assignatae similiter eius essent. Haec verba eius scripturae sacrae, doctrinae sanctorum, & determinationi ecclesiae sunt aduersa, sicut prolixe in aliis operibus est ostensum. & hoc vnica auctoritate pandetur. Vnde Greg. super illud Mat. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, sic dicit: multum reliquit, qui nihil sibi retinet. multum reliquit, qui quantumlibet parum, totum deserit. multum igitur Petro dimisit, quoniam cum re possessa & concupiscentiis habendi renunciauit.
units.tr: The ninth error is that Blessed Peter, after the mission of the Holy Spirit, had property and ownership of temporal goods in particular. He sets down this error in these words: The sandals and garments assigned to Peter were, as regards ownership, properly Peter's. Wherefore it seems that the money, bread, wine, and other consumable things assigned to him separately for his sustenance were likewise his. These words of his are opposed to Holy Scripture, to the teaching of the saints, and to the decision of the Church, as has been set out at length in other works; and this is made clear by a single authority. Hence Gregory, on that passage of Matthew, Behold, we have left all things, says: He leaves much who keeps nothing for himself. He leaves much who, however little he has, gives up the whole. Peter therefore left much, since he renounced both his possessions and the desire to have them.

units.la: Decimus error est, quod votum viuendi sine proprio, non se extendit ad illa, quibus necessario eget vita humana. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Nec votum viuendi sine proprio videtur, quod sexfe extendit ad talia, quibus necessario eget vita humana. Hæc verba eius erronea, quæ expresse contradicunt sacris sanctionibus & doctrinæ sanctorum asserentium, q monachi & alii vouentes viuere sine proprio respectu naturalium rerum in vsu consumptibilium non debent habere proprietatem.
units.tr: The tenth error is that a vow of living without property does not extend to those things which human life necessarily requires. He states this error in these words: "Nor does a vow of living without property seem to extend to such things as human life necessarily needs." His words here are erroneous. They expressly contradict the sacred decrees and the teaching of the saints, who assert that monks and others who vow to live without property, with respect to natural things consumed in use, ought not to have ownership.

units.la: Vndecimus error est, q apostoli non reliquerunt temporalia p abdicationem dominii. Hunc errorem ponit sub verbis multiplicibus, & in fine sic concludit: Quare relinquitur, quia per illa verba relictu omnib. secuti sunt eum, non potest concludi apostolos à se dominiu omnium temporalium abdicasse. Hæc verba eius, quæ sacræ scripturæ, doctrinæ sanctorum, & determinationi ecclesiæ repugnat, sicut in diuersis operibus maiorum est diffuse probatum.
units.tr: The eleventh error is that the apostles did not leave temporal goods by renouncing lordship. He states this error in many words and concludes at the end: "Therefore it follows that, since by those words they 'left everything and followed him,' it cannot be concluded that the apostles renounced lordship over all temporal things." His words here are opposed to Scripture, to the teaching of the saints and to the determination of the Church, as has been proved at length in the works of the elders.

units.la: Duodecimus error est, quod si primi parentes non peccassent, omnia fuisset communia quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Ista scriptura (sc. decretum Clementini papæ positum 12. q. 1. c. Dilectissimus) supponit quod si primi parentes non peccassent, omnia communia fuissent quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Hæc verba eius, quæ sunt erronea, loquendo de dominio ciuili & mundano, p quo contingit in iudicio litigare & res vendicare, sed talis litigatio & rerum vendicatio in statu innocentiæ non fuisset. Igitur in statu innocentiæ non fuisset tale dominium seu proprietas: quis fuisset dominium accipiendo dominium pro potestate rem alienandi, sed de tali dominio non intelligit ille. Item in isto errore falsum imponit beato Clementi papæ. Nam Clemens papa tenet expresse contrarium illius, quod iste dicit. Vnde verba Clementis 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimus, posita sunt hæc: Communis vsus omnium, quæ sunt in hoc mundo, omnibus hominib. communis esse debet. sed per iniquitatem alius dixit hoc esse suum, & alius istud. & sic inter mortales facta est diuisio. Et sicut non potest diuidi aer nec splendor solis, ita nec reliqua quæ data sunt hominibus ad habendum deberent diuidi. Hæc verba Clementis, quæ non intentum istius habent, sed contrarium expresse concludunt.
units.tr: The twelfth error is that, had the first parents not sinned, all things would have been common as to lordship and ownership. He states this error in these words: "That Scripture (namely the decree of Pope Clement placed in 12 q. 1 c. Dilectissimus) supposes that, had the first parents not sinned, all things would have been common as to lordship and ownership." These words are erroneous when speaking of civil and worldly lordship, by which it happens that one goes to law in court and claims things. Such litigation and claiming of things would not have existed in the state of innocence. Therefore such lordship or property would not have existed in the state of innocence, if lordship is understood as the power of alienating a thing; but he does not mean such lordship. Likewise, in this error he falsely attributes something to the blessed Pope Clement, for Clement expressly holds the opposite of what he says. The words of Clement in 12 q. 1 c. Dilectissimus are these: "The common use of all things that are in this world ought to be common to all men. But through iniquity one man said this is his, and another that, and so division was made among mortals. And just as air cannot be divided, nor the splendour of the sun, so the remaining things given to men for having ought not to be divided." These are Clement's words, which do not have the meaning he intends for them but expressly conclude the contrary.

units.la: Tertiusdecimus error est, q apostoli non emiserunt votum paupertatis. Hunc errorem ponit sub multis verbis, de quibus pauca adducam. Vnde dicit sic: Item in eo, quod dicit beatum Augustinum dixisse apostolos vouisse rerum omnium abdicationem, dicit falsum. Hoc enim beatus August. non dixit. Et infra: dic mihi, quod est illud votum, quod vouerat? Certe dici non potest, quod votum illud esset abdicationis dominii seu proprietatis omnium rerum temporalium, cum de hoc in precedentib. seu sequentibus nullam fecerit mentionem, hæc verba eius. Beatus August. asserit omni rei veritati aperte contraria. Vnde dicit Aug. vt superius allegatum est; dixerant enim illi potentes: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia & secuti sumus te. hoc votum potentissime voauerant. Alii etiam sancti una cum beato Augusti. dicunt, quod in voto paupertatis religiosi tenent figuram apostolorum.
units.tr: The thirteenth error is that the apostles did not make a vow of poverty. He states this error in many words, of which I will cite a few. He says: "Likewise, in saying that blessed Augustine said the apostles vowed the renunciation of all things, he says what is false, for blessed Augustine did not say this." And below: "Tell me, what was the vow they had made? Certainly it cannot be said that the vow was the renunciation of lordship or ownership of all temporal things, since he has made no mention of this either before or after." These are his words. Blessed Augustine asserts a truth that is plainly contrary to all this. Hence Augustine says, as quoted above: "For those powerful men had said: Behold, we have left everything and followed you. They had vowed this most powerfully." Other saints too, together with blessed Augustine, say that religious who take the vow of poverty hold the figure of the apostles.

units.la: Decimusquartus error est, quod paupertas euangelica rerum vsu consumptibilium dominium & proprietatem non excludit. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Ad id autem, quod dicit, quod paupertas euangelica rerum vsu consumptibilium dominium & proprietatem excludit, dicimus, quod est falsum: imo illarum rerum supponit scriptura sacra ipsos (scil. apostolos) ad minus in communi habuisse proprietatem & dominium. Hæc verba eius erronea sacræ scripturæ falsum imponentia, & cum hoc sunt determinationi ecclesiæ & sanctorum doctrinæ contraria, sicut alibi est probatum.
units.tr: The fourteenth error is that evangelical poverty does not exclude lordship and ownership over things consumed in use. He states this error in these words: "As to what he says, that evangelical poverty excludes lordship and ownership over things consumed in use, we say this is false. Indeed, Scripture supposes that the apostles themselves had, at least in common, ownership and lordship over those things." His words here are erroneous, falsely attributing things to Scripture, and at the same time they are contrary to the determination of the Church and the teaching of the saints, as has been proved elsewhere.

units.la: Decimusquintus error est, q quotiescunq; sacra scriptura attribuit vsum rebus vsu consumptibilibus, sumit vsum pro consumptione rei. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Dicimus, quando sacra scriptura vsum in talibus rebus vsu consumptibilibus attribuit, pro rei consumptione ipsum sumit. hæc verba eius contraria scripturæ diuinæ, cum dicatur 2. Reg. 13. Filia regum virgines huiusmodi vestibus vtebantur. Quod etiam per aliquas auctoritates posset ostendi copiose.
units.tr: The fifteenth error is that whenever Scripture attributes use to things consumed in use, it takes use to mean the consumption of the thing. He states this error in these words: "We say that when Scripture attributes use to such things consumed in use, it takes that use to mean the consumption of the thing." His words are contrary to divine Scripture, since it is said in 2 Kings 13: "The virgin daughters of the king wore garments of this kind." This could also be shown copiously by many other authorities.

units.la: Decimusextus error est, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus nullus alius vsus, quam consumptio assignari potest. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Nec alius vsus valet, nisi sumptus in rebus vsu consumptibilibus, nec esse potest. Hæc verba eius, quæ sacræ scripturæ, & doctrinæ sanctorum (sicut sæpius est probatum) sunt expresse contraria.
units.tr: The sixteenth error is that, in things consumed in use, no use other than consumption can be assigned. He states this error in these words: "No other use is valid, nor can there be, except what is spent in things consumed in use." His words are expressly contrary to Scripture and to the teaching of the saints, as has often been proved.

units.la: Decimusseptimus error est, quod Christus non consuluit apostolis, quod omnia temporalia quo ad proprietatem & dominium relinquerent. Hunc errorem post multa alia verba ponit sic: Dicimus falsum esse quod hoc consuluerit (sc. Christ°) apostolis vel discipulis suis ad minus quod non haberent in communi. Hæc verba eius determinationi ecclesiæ in decretali, Exiit qui seminat, posita expresse sunt contraria, vbi dicitur, q Christus abdicatione omnium temporalium quantum ad dominium, tam in speciali q in communi, verbo docuit & exemplo firmauit. Necesse verisimile, q hoc non docuit apostolos & discipulos suos, cum alios hoc docuerit secundum euangelium, & secundum ecclesiæ Romanæ determinationem, ac et secundum doctrinam sanctorum. Decimusoctauus error est, q Christus inquantum homo mortalis fuit rex habens regni dominium temporale. Hunc errorem ponit in hæc verba: quæritur vtrum Christus aliquius rei temporalis dominium habuit & quale? Quod a. dominii temporalium rerum habuit, sacra scriptura tam in veteri testamento quam in nouo in multis locis testatur. multi quidem prophetæ eum regem futurum populi Israelitici prædixerunt, & per consequens habere regni dominium prophetauerunt. Hæc verba eius hæretica sacræ scripturæ & doctrinæ sanctorum ac determinationi ecclesiæ sunt aduersa. Nam Matth. 8: scribitur: Vulpes foueas habent, & volucres cœli nidos: filius autem hominis non habet vbi reclinet caput suum. Quæ verba Christus nequaquam dixisset, si rex in temporalibus extitisset. Item Aug. super illud Ioh. 18. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: dicit sic: Audite Iudei & gentes circumcisionem, audite prepucii, audite omnia regna terræ, quia Christus nō impedivit damnationē vestrā in hoc mundo. Quia dixit: regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Nolite metuere metu vanissimo, quo Herodes illemaior expauit, & tot infantes occidit. Regnum, inquit, meum non est de hoc mundo: quid vultis amplius? venite ad regnum, quod non est de hoc mundo: venite credendo. Et his verbis alludit Rabanus super epistolam Petri dicens: Manifeste ex hoc verbo regnum Christi non terrenum, sed caeleste ostendit esse.
units.tr: The seventeenth error is that Christ did not advise the apostles to leave all temporal things as to ownership and lordship. After many other words he states this error thus: "We say it is false that he (Christ) advised this to his apostles or disciples, or at least that they should not have things in common." His words are expressly contrary to the determination of the Church in the decretal Exiit qui seminat, where it is said that Christ taught by word and confirmed by example the renunciation of all temporal things as to lordship, both individually and in common. It is quite probable that he did not teach this to his apostles and disciples, since he taught it to others according to the Gospel, according to the determination of the Roman Church, and also according to the teaching of the saints. The eighteenth error is that Christ, insofar as he was a mortal man, was a king holding lordship over a temporal kingdom. He states this error in these words: "It is asked whether Christ had lordship over any temporal thing, and of what kind? As to the lordship over temporal things which he had, sacred Scripture, both in the Old Testament and the New, bears witness in many places. Indeed, many prophets foretold that he would be king of the Israelite people, and consequently prophesied that he would have lordship over the kingdom." His words are heretical and opposed to sacred Scripture, to the teaching of the saints and to the determination of the Church. For it is written in Matthew 8: "Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head." Christ would never have said these words had he been a king in temporal affairs. Likewise Augustine, on John 18, "My kingdom is not of this world," says: "Hear, Jews and Gentiles, hear, circumcision, hear, uncircumcision, hear, all kingdoms of the earth: because Christ did not hinder your condemnation in this world. For he said: my kingdom is not of this world. Do not fear with that most vain fear with which that greater Herod was terrified, and killed so many infants. My kingdom, he says, is not of this world: what more do you want? Come to the kingdom which is not of this world; come by believing." Rabanus also alludes to these words in his commentary on Peter's epistle, saying: "Clearly from this word he shows that the kingdom of Christ is not earthly but heavenly."

units.la: Decimusnonus error est, quod totus Psalmus, Eructauit cor meum &c. loquitur de rege temporali & sponsa eius ecclesia. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: unde totus ille loquitur Psalmus de rege isto & sponsa eius. Haec verba eius erronea, quibus scripturis sacris falsum imponit aperte. Nam dictus Psal. non loquitur de rege carnali seu temporali: sed solummodo de rege spirituali, sicut in aliis maiorum operibus est visum luculenter.
units.tr: The nineteenth error is that the whole Psalm, "Eructavit cor meum," etc., speaks of a temporal king and his bride, the Church. He states this error in these words: "Whence that whole Psalm speaks of this king and his bride." These words of his are erroneous, and by them he openly imputes falsehood to the sacred Scriptures. For the said Psalm does not speak of a carnal or temporal king, but only of a spiritual king, as has been clearly shown in other works of the elders.

units.la: Vicesimus error est, quod Christus inquantum homo viator habuit a tempore suae conceptionis vniuersale dominium rerum temporalium, sicut verus rex & dominus in temporalibus. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: praemissa autem (scilicet regnum & vniuersale dominium) habuit Iesus inquantum Deus ab aeterno, eo ipso, quod Deus pater genuit eum: & inquantum homo ex homine, scilicet a tempore suae conceptionis ex Dei datione. Haec verba eius haeretica catholicae ecclesiae Dei sunt inimica. Nam Christus docuit renunciationem dominii rerum temporalium ad perfectionem pertinere, cum Matth. 19. c. cuidam dixerit adolescenti: Si vis perfectus esse, vende omnia quae habes & da pauperibus & veni sequere me. Et per consequens renunciare temporalibus propter Deum ad magnam pertinet perfectionem. sed constat, quod nullus fuit Christo perfectior. Ergo Christus dominio temporalium renunciavit. Ex quo sequitur, quod non fuit temporalis rex, sicut iste haereticus dogmatizat. Quod etiam patet Mat. 8. & Luca 9. sicut superius est ostensum. vbi Christus fatetur se non habere dominium, necesse est referre. Vnde Ioan. Chrysostomus super dicta verba Christi, Vulpes foueas habent, dicit sic: aspice qualiter paupertatem, quam dominus docuerat, per opera monstrat. non erat ei mensa, non candelabrum, non domus, nec quicquam talium.
units.tr: The twentieth error is that Christ, as a man on his pilgrimage, had universal lordship over temporal things from the time of his conception, as a true king and lord in temporal matters. He states this error in these words: But the aforementioned things (namely the kingdom and universal lordship) Jesus had as God from eternity, by the very fact that God the Father begot him; and as man from man, namely from the time of his conception, by God's gift. These words of his are heretical and hostile to the catholic Church of God. For Christ taught that renunciation of lordship over temporal things belongs to perfection, since in Matt. 19 he said to a certain young man: If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me. Consequently, to renounce temporal things for God's sake belongs to great perfection. But it is certain that no one was more perfect than Christ. Therefore Christ renounced lordship over temporal things. From this it follows that he was not a temporal king, as this heretic teaches. This is also plain from Matt. 8 and Luke 9, as shown above, where Christ confesses that he has no lordship; this must be borne in mind. Hence John Chrysostom, on the words of Christ, Foxes have holes, says: Look how he shows by his deeds the poverty which the Lord had taught. He had no table, no lampstand, no house, nor anything of that kind.

units.la: Vicesimusprimus error est, quod Christus inquantum homo viator habuit dominium aliquarum rerum temporalium non a tempore suae conceptionis, sed postea successiue modis aliis. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Et nihilominus habuit dominium aliam rerum temporalium, non a tempore suae conceptionis, sed postea successiue modis aliis, vtpote ex collatione fidelium, vel emptione acquisitarum rerum. Haec verba eius tam haeretica, quam priori haeresi contraria. Quod autem haec sint prioribus dictis suis contraria, aperte patet. Nam in priori haeresi dicit, quod Christus habuit vniuersale dominium a tempore conceptionis suae. Hic autem dicit, quod dominium aliarum rerum habuit, non a tempore conceptionis suae, sed postea modis aliis. quae duo dicta expresse contradicunt. Quod etiam sit haeretica, patet tam per determinationem ecclesiae, quam per doctrinam sanctorum. Determinatio namq; ecclesiae, sicut superius est ostensum, dicit, quod abdicationem dominii, omnium temporalium tam in speciali quam etiam in communi Christus verbo docuit, & exemplo firmauit. Cui determinationi doctrina sanctorum consonat & alludit.
units.tr: The twenty-first error is that Christ, as a man on his pilgrimage, had lordship over some temporal things, not from the time of his conception, but afterwards, successively, by other means. He states this error in these words: And nevertheless he had lordship over other temporal things, not from the time of his conception, but afterwards, successively, by other means, namely by the gifts of the faithful or by the purchase of things acquired. These words of his are as heretical as they are contrary to the previous heresy. That they contradict his earlier statements is plain. For in the earlier heresy he says that Christ had universal lordship from the time of his conception. Here, however, he says that he had lordship over other things, not from the time of his conception but afterwards, by other means. These two statements expressly contradict each other. That this is also heretical is clear both from the determination of the Church and from the doctrine of the saints. For the determination of the Church, as shown above, says that Christ taught renunciation of lordship over all temporal things, both in particular and in general, by word, and confirmed it by example. The doctrine of the saints agrees with and echoes this determination.

units.la: Vicesimussecundus error est, quod Christus inquantum homo habuit temporale dominium vestimentorum & calciamentorum, loculorum, panis, & vini. Hunc errorem ponit sub multis verbis, de quibus pauca adducentur. vnde dicit sic: Certe narrant ipsum (scilicet apostoli & discipuli sui) habuisse aliqua, licet pauca habuit vestimenta. Et infra: Item beatus Iohannes Baptista videtur supponere, quod habuit calciamenta. Et infra: Item Iohannes supponit ipsum loculos habuisse. Et infra: & quod loculi essent Iesu, patet per Augustinum. Et infra: quod autem interdum habuerit, patet ad minus in coena illa, in qua eucharistia instituit sacramentum. Haec verba eius haeretica doctrinae sanctorum & determinationi ecclesiae aduersa sunt, sicut prolixe in maiorum operibus est declaratum. Et de calciamentis quidem dicit beatus Bernardus ea quae sequuntur: nec credas quod esset calciatus. quia nec ipse nec discipuli eius calciamentis vtebantur: Haec verba beati Bernard. in tractatu de 7. horis, hora tertia tradita & asserta.
units.tr: The twenty-second error is that Christ, as a man, had temporal lordship over clothes and shoes, a purse, bread and wine. He states this error in many words, of which a few will be cited. Thus he says: Certainly they relate that he (namely the apostles and his disciples) had some things, though he had few garments. And below: Likewise the blessed John the Baptist seems to suppose that he had shoes. And below: Likewise John supposes that he had a purse. And below: And that the purse belonged to Jesus is clear from Augustine. And below: But that he sometimes had these things is clear at least from that supper in which he instituted the sacrament of the Eucharist. These words of his are heretical and opposed to the doctrine of the saints and to the determination of the Church, as has been declared at length in the works of the elders. And concerning shoes, the blessed Bernard says what follows: Nor believe that he was shod, for neither he nor his disciples used shoes. These words of the blessed Bernard are handed down and affirmed in his tractate On the Seven Hours, the third hour.

units.la: Vicesimustertius error est, quod Christus non potuit renunciare regno & dominio temporali. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Euidenter apparet ipsum (scilicet Christum) regno & dominio non renunciasse praedictis. imo videtur quod nec potuerit renunciasse. & si fecisset, contra ordinationes patris fecisset. Haec verba eius insana, ex quibus sequitur haeresis, quam saepe asseruit, praedicauit & pertinaciter defensauit, quod videl. omnia de necessitate eueniunt, & quod Deum aliter vel aliud facere quam facit contradictionem includit. sed hoc est erroneum, iniquum & blasphemum. dominium etiam suum, quod videl. Christus non poterat renunciare regno & dominio temporali, est expresse contrarium doctrinae sanctorum & ecclesiae Romanae determinationi, prout in aliis operib. est ostensum.
units.tr: The twenty-third error is that Christ could not renounce the kingdom and temporal lordship. He states this error in these words: It is clearly evident that he (namely Christ) did not renounce the aforesaid kingdom and lordship. Indeed it seems that he could not even have renounced them; and if he had done so, he would have acted against the ordinances of the Father. These words of his are insane, and from them follows the heresy which he often asserted, preached and stubbornly defended: namely that all things happen of necessity, and that for God to act otherwise or differently than he does involves a contradiction. But this is erroneous, unjust and blasphemous. His claim that Christ could not renounce the kingdom and temporal lordship is also expressly contrary to the doctrine of the saints and to the determination of the Roman Church, as shown in other works.

units.la: Vicesimusquartus error est, quod regnum & dominium temporale non corrumpetur, sed sine fine durabit. Hunc errorem ponit isto modo. volens enim probare quod Christus non renunciauit dominio & regno temporali, & quod nec potuit renuntiare, adducit pro se Danielem prophetam dicentem in haec verba: Dicitur enim Dan. 2. vbi de eius regno fit mentio: Sic suscitabit Deus caeli regnum, quod in aeternum non dissipabitur: & regnum eius alteri non tradetur. Item Dan. 7. dicitur sic. Dedit ei potestatem & honorem & regnum, & omnes populi tribus & linguae seruient ei. Potestas eius potestas aeterna, quae non auferetur, & regnum eius quod non corrumpetur. hęc adductio eius; ex qua manifeste sequitur, quod regnum Christi, de quo ipse loquitur, in perpetuum durabit. & constat tam per praecedentia, quam per subsequentia, quod ipse intelligit de regno mundano & temporali. Igitur secundum ipsum regnum mundanum & temporale, quod non est aliud, quam mundus iste, in aeternum durabit. Ex quo sequitur, quod ista vita mortalis semper durabit. & per consequens quod nunquam erit resurrectio generalis mortuorum. quod est haereticum, & contra articulum fidei manifeste.
units.tr: The twenty-fourth error is that the kingdom and temporal lordship will not be corrupted but will last without end. He states this error as follows. Wishing to prove that Christ did not renounce temporal lordship and kingdom, and that he could not renounce it, he adduces in support the prophet Daniel, saying in these words: For it is said in Dan. 2, where mention is made of his kingdom: "So God of heaven will raise up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, and its kingdom will not be given to another." Likewise Dan. 7 says thus: "He gave him power and honour and kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues will serve him. His power is an eternal power, which will not be taken away, and his kingdom which will not be corrupted." From this citation of his it manifestly follows that the kingdom of Christ, of which he speaks, will endure for ever. And it is established both by what precedes and by what follows that he understands it of a worldly and temporal kingdom. Therefore, according to him, the worldly and temporal kingdom, which is nothing other than this world, will endure for ever. From this it follows that this mortal life will always endure, and consequently that there will never be a general resurrection of the dead. This is heretical and manifestly contrary to an article of faith.

units.la: Vicesimusquintus error est, quod carentia dominii rerum temporalium non facit Christum pauperem, sed carentia perceptionis fructus & obventionis rerum, quarum dominus erat. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Ad illud autem quod ... scriptura facta ipsum (scil. Christum) fuisse pauperem & egentem in plurib. locis testantur, dicendo quod ... Christus dominii sed cum pauperem & egenum, sed potius carentia perceptionis fructus & obventionis ... quarum dominum erat. Haec verba eius haeretica tam sacrae scripturae quam doctrinae sanctorum & determinationi ecclesiae expresse sunt contraria. Unde, sicut superius allegatum est, ipse Christus de seipso dicit Matt. 6. Et Lucae 9. Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput suum reclinet. Quod quantum ad facti simplicis usum non dicit, sed quantum ad dominium & proprietatem. Item Apost. 2. Cor. 6. ait: Scitis enim gratiam domini nostri Iesu Christi, propter nos egenus factus est, cum esset dives. nec Christus ulla terrena felicitate praefulgens, sed Christus crucifixus per totum orbem terrarum praedicatur.
units.tr: The twenty-fifth error is that the lack of lordship over temporal things does not make Christ poor, but rather the lack of receiving the fruit and income of the things of which he was lord. He states this error in these words: As for that which ... Scripture says, that Christ was poor and needy, testified in many places by saying that ... Christ (had) lordship, but not as poor and needy; rather, the lack of receiving the fruit and income ... of which he was lord. These words of his are heretical and expressly contrary to Holy Scripture, to the doctrine of the saints and to the determination of the Church. Hence, as was alleged above, Christ himself says of himself in Matt. 6 and Luke 9: The Son of man has nowhere to lay his head. He does not say this with respect to the mere use of the thing, but with respect to lordship and ownership. Likewise the Apostle in 2 Cor. 6 says: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor. Nor is Christ proclaimed throughout the whole world as one shining with any earthly happiness, but as crucified.

units.la: Vicesimussextus error est, quod temporale dominium a perceptione commodi in perpetuum separatum, dividem non facit habentem. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Nudum enim dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rei, habenti non facit divitem. Haec verba eius erronea & scripturae divinae adversa sunt. Nam ecclesiastes 6. capite habetur: Vir cui Deus dedit divitias & substantiam & honorem, & nihil deest animae suae ex omnibus quae desiderat, nec tribuit ei potestatem Deus ut comedat ex eo ... verabit illud. ubi expresse habetur, quod res faciunt possidentem divitem, quamvis non ... capiat commodum, quod etiam dicat rem. Nam non ex hoc solo dicitur homo ... aliter percipit commodum rei, cuius est dominus: sed etiam ex hoc, quod potest ... quando sibi placebit quamvis nunquam percipiat.
units.tr: The twenty-sixth error is that lordship over temporal things, separated for ever from the receipt of any advantage, does not make the one who has it rich. He states this error in these words: For bare lordship, separated for ever from every receipt of the advantage of a thing, does not make the one who has it rich. These words of his are erroneous and contrary to divine Scripture. For Ecclesiastes 6 says: A man to whom God has given riches and substance and honour, so that nothing is lacking to his soul of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to eat of it ... he will consume it. Here it is expressly stated that things make the possessor rich, even if he does not take the advantage of the thing, which the thing itself also ... For a man is called rich not only from this alone, that he receives the advantage of the thing of which he is lord, but also from this, that he can ... whenever it pleases him, even though he never receives it.

units.la: Vicesimusseptimus error est, quod dominium temporale separatum ab omni perceptione commodi rei est inutile reputandum. Hunc errorem ponit cum verbis in priori errore recitatis dicens: dominium separatum in perpetuum ab omni perceptione commodi rei habere non facit divitem, cum sit inutile reputandum. Haec verba erronea sua sunt & absurda. Nam dominium temporale, quamvis careat in perpetuum omni perceptione commodi rei temporalis, potest esse utilissimum propter commodum speciale secundum quod diffinit decretalis, Exiit qui seminat, ut superius est ostensum.
units.tr: The twenty-seventh error is that temporal lordship separated from every perception of the advantage of a thing is to be reckoned useless. He puts forward this error in the words recited under the previous error, saying: lordship separated forever from every perception of the advantage of a thing does not make a man rich, since it is to be reckoned useless. These words of his are false and absurd. For temporal lordship, although it lacks forever every perception of the temporal advantage of a thing, can be most useful on account of a special advantage, according to what the decretal Exiit qui seminat defines, as has been shown above.

units.la: Vicesimusoctavus error est, quod Christus in aliquibus gessit se pro rege & domino temporali.
units.tr: The twenty-eighth error is that Christ in some cases acted as a temporal king and lord.

units.la: Vicesimusnonus error est, quod Christus non fuit pauper propter carentiam dominii & regni temporalis: sed quia se eorum fructibus & proventibus non iuvabat. Hos duos errores simul hoc modo ponit: Christus rex regum & dominus dominantium quo ad perceptionem fructuum regni & rerum temporalium, nisi in valde paucis, pro rege vel domino se non gessit, propter quod merito pauper dici potuit voluntarie & egenus, non propter carentiam dominii sive regni sed propterea, quia se eorum fructibus & proventibus non iuvabat. Haec verba sua virulenta ex quibus duae haereses predictae colliguntur. cum dicit, quod Christus non gessit se pro rege vel domino temporali, nisi in valde paucis. Vbi aperte supponit & vult, quod in aliquibus se gessit pro rege & domino temporali, quod est haereticum. Nec in tota scriptura divina reperitur, quod se gessit pro rege vel domino temporali, sed contrarium, cum Christus expresse dixerit Ioan. 18. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Item Lucae 12. Christus ostendit se non esse regem & dominum in temporalibus, cum negaverit se esse iudicem & discussorem temporalium rerum, cuida sibi dicenti: Magister dic fratri meo ut dividat mecum hereditatem. Respondens Iesus ait: Quis me constituit iudicem aut divisorem super vos? quasi dicat, nullus hoc etiam plurib. auctoritatibus sanctorum posset aperte probari. Secundo haeresim quod videl. Christus non fuit pauper propter carentiam dominii & regni temporalis, non posset expressius ponere quam ponit. Quae haeresis est manifeste contra scripturam divinam, & doctrinam sanctorum, & determinationem ecclesiae, sicut est ostensum prius. Et adhuc una auctoritate ostenditur. Unde Zach. 9. dicitur: Iubila filia Hierusalem, ecce rex tuus venit tibi iustus & salvator, ipse pauper & ascendens super asinam &c.
units.tr: The twenty-ninth error is that Christ was not poor because he lacked lordship and a temporal kingdom, but because he did not profit from their fruits and revenues. He puts these two errors together in this way: Christ, king of kings and lord of lords, as regards the enjoyment of the fruits of a kingdom and of temporal things, except in very few cases, did not act as king or lord, and so he could rightly be called poor and needy by his own choice; this was not because he lacked lordship or a kingdom, but because he did not profit from their fruits and revenues. These are his virulent words, from which the two aforesaid heresies are gathered: when he says that Christ did not act as temporal king or lord, except in very few cases. Here he plainly assumes and asserts that Christ did act in some cases as temporal king and lord, which is heretical. Nor is it found anywhere in Holy Scripture that he acted as temporal king or lord; the contrary is true, since Christ expressly said, John 18: My kingdom is not of this world. Likewise, Luke 12: Christ showed that he was not king and lord in temporal affairs, when he refused to be judge and arbiter of temporal goods to the man who said to him: Master, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. Jesus answered: Who made me a judge or divider over you? as if to say that no one... This could also be clearly proved by many authorities of the saints. Secondly, the heresy that Christ was not poor because he lacked lordship and a temporal kingdom could not be stated more plainly than he states it. It is manifestly contrary to the divine Scripture, to the teaching of the saints, and to the determination of the Church, as has been shown before. And it is refuted by one further authority. Hence Zech. 9: Rejoice, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your king comes to you, just and a saviour, himself poor and riding on an ass, etc.

units.la: Tricesimus error est, quod Christus non dedit aliquam aliam legem viuendi apostolis, quam aliis discipulis. Et intelligit per discipulos quoscunque alios ad fidem conversos. Hanc haeresim ponit sub his verbis: Nec reperimus, quod Christus Iesus dominus noster aliam legem viuendi discipulis dederit, & aliam apostolis suis, imo beatus Clemens in quadam epistola sua, cuius pars recitatur 12. q. 1. c. dilectissimus, expresse supponit, quod eadem erat apostolorum & discipulorum vita dicens: Communis vita omnib. est necessaria, & maxime his qui vitam apostolorum & eorum discipulorum imitari volunt. Haec verba eius prophana, in quib. quod p discipulos intelligat oes ad Christum conversos, ex aliis suis verbis propriis colligitur manifeste. Unde parum ante dicit in haec verba: de discipulis aute constat, quod aliqui habuerunt multa a Ioseph ab Arimathia legitur Io. 19. & erat discipulus Iesu. Matth. autem 27. legitur, quod erat dives homo discipulus Iesu. Item constat, quod Symon leprosus erat discipulus Iesu, & tamen legitur Matth. 26. quod Iesus in Bethania erat in domo eius. Item Lazarus, Martha, & Maria Magdalena, qui erant eius discipuli, habebant multa bona. Unde legitur de eis Ioh. 11. quod castrum dictum Bethaniae erat Mariae Magdalene & Marthae, & quod in Bethania fecerunt ei cenam magnam, in qua Martha ministrabat, Lazarus autem erat unus ex discumbentibus cum eo. Maria vero accepta libra unguenti nardi pistici pretiosi unxit pedes Iesu, & extersit capillis suis. de Thabita quoque quae interpretatur Dorcas, quam Petrus suscitavit a mortuis, legitur Actuum 9. quod erat discipula & plena operibus bonis & eleemosynis, quas faciebat, & quod omnes viduae flentes ostendebant Petro tunicas & vestes, quas faciebat ei Dorcas. Ex quibus patet, quod ista, non obstante discipulatu, tempora alia habebat, de quibus faciebat eleemosynas praedictas. Hæc verba eius, ex quib᷃ expresse habetur, quod per discipulos intelligit omnes Christianos tunc ad Christum conuersos. Et quod Christus nullam aliam legem dedit apostolis plusquam omnibus aliis ad ipsum conuersis. Quod est manifeste heretica & scripturæ diuinæ contrarium. Vnde in istis verbis triplociter errat. Primo cum dicit, quod Christus nullam aliam legem viuendi dedit apostolis plusquam aliis Christianis, cum tres euangelistæ dicant oppositum. Vnde Matth. 10. legitur: Hos duodecim misit Iesus præcipiens & dicens: In viam gentium ne abieritis. Et infra: Nolite possidere aurum, neque argentum, neque pecuniam in zonis. Et Marci 6. sic habetur: vocauit duodecim & cœpit eos mittere binos. Et infra: Et præcepit eis ne quid tollerent in via, nisi virgam tantum, nec peram, non panem, neque in zonis aes. Et Lucæ 9. scribitur: Conuocatis autem duodecim discipulis, dedit illis virtutem & potestatem. Et infra: Nihil tuleritis in via, neque virgam, neque peram, neque pecuniam. Ista autem præcepta non fuerunt data omnibus aliis Christianis, quos iste hæreticus vocat discipulos. Igitur alia lex viuendi fuit data apostolis, quam aliis Christianis.
units.tr: The thirtieth error is that Christ did not give the apostles any other rule of living than he gave the other disciples. By "disciples" he means all others converted to the faith. He puts forward this heresy in these words: Nor do we find that Christ Jesus our Lord gave his disciples one rule of living and his apostles another; indeed, the blessed Clement, in a certain letter of his, part of which is quoted in 12 q. 1, c. dilectissimus, expressly assumes that the life of the apostles and of their disciples was the same, saying: a common life is necessary for all, and especially for those who wish to imitate the life of the apostles and of their disciples. That these words of his are profane, and that by "disciples" he means all who were converted to Christ, is clearly gathered from his other words. For shortly before he says this: Concerning the disciples, it is established that some had much wealth. We read in John 19 that Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple of Jesus; and Matthew 27 says he was a rich man and a disciple of Jesus. It is also established that Simon the leper was a disciple of Jesus, and yet Matthew 26 says that Jesus was in his house in Bethany. Likewise Lazarus, Martha and Mary Magdalene, who were his disciples, had many goods. For we read of them in John 11 that the village called Bethany belonged to Mary Magdalene and Martha, and that they made him a great supper in Bethany, at which Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him. Mary, taking a pound of precious spikenard ointment, anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped them with her hair. Of Tabitha also, who is called Dorcas, whom Peter raised from the dead, we read in Acts 9 that she was a disciple, full of good works and almsdeeds which she did, and that all the widows, weeping, showed Peter the tunics and garments which Dorcas had made for them. From which it is plain that these people, despite their discipleship, had other times, in which they gave the aforesaid alms. From these words it is expressly clear that by "disciples" he means all Christians then converted to Christ, and that Christ gave the apostles no rule of living different from that given to all others converted to him. This is manifestly heretical and contrary to the divine Scripture. In these words he errs in three ways. First, when he says that Christ gave the apostles no other rule of living than the other Christians, although the three evangelists say the opposite. Hence Matthew 10: Jesus sent forth these twelve, commanding them and saying: Go not into the way of the Gentiles. And below: Possess neither gold nor silver nor money in your purses. And Mark 6 says thus: He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two. And below: And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey but a staff only, no bag, no bread, no money in their belts. And Luke 9 is written: Then he called together the twelve disciples and gave them power and authority. And below: Take nothing for the journey, neither staff, nor bag, nor money. But these commands were not given to all the other Christians, whom this heretic calls disciples. Therefore a different rule of living was given to the apostles from that given to other Christians.

units.la: Secundo errat in verbis supradictis: quia secundum verba sua licuit apostolis, postquam ad apostolatum assumpti fuerunt, imo et post missionem spiritus sancti habere in speciali & sigillatim diuitias temporales, & dominia castrorum, & villarum, & bonorum temporalium quorumcumque. Nam secundum ipsum Christus non dedit aliam legem viuendi apostolis, quam cæteris Christianis, quos vocat discipulos, sed discipulos, quos ipse enumerat, & apostolis in lege viuendi æquiparat, habuerunt speciali sigillatim, postquam apostoli fuerunt ad apostolatum assumpti, bona temporalia quæ prius habuerant, ut patet de Ioseph ab Arimathia, quem nominat, & etiam de cæteris, quos ipse in cadem numerat & describit. Sed hæc dicere de apostolis, tam sacræ scripturæ, quam doctrinæ sanctorum, & determinationi ecclesiæ obuiat & repugnat. Et iste in hoc ordine pro tricesimo potest computari.
units.tr: Secondly, he errs in the words quoted above, because according to his words it was lawful for the apostles, after they were taken into the apostolate, and indeed even after the mission of the Holy Spirit, to have temporal riches in particular and individually, and the lordship of castles, villages and any temporal goods whatever. For according to him Christ gave the apostles no other rule of living than the other Christians, whom he calls disciples; but the disciples whom he enumerates, and whom he equates with the apostles in the rule of living, had, individually and particularly, after the apostles were taken into the apostolate, the temporal goods which they had previously possessed, as is plain of Joseph of Arimathea, whom he names, and also of the others whom he himself lists and describes in the same place. But to say these things about the apostles is contrary to and at odds with holy Scripture, the teaching of the saints, and the determination of the Church. And in this order he may be counted as the thirtieth.

units.la: Tricesimus primus error est, quod in verbis memoratis superius hæreticus errat: quia falsum beato Clementi summo pontifici impudenter imponit, sicut decretum eiusdem Clementis intuenti potest apertæ patere.
units.tr: The thirty-first error is that in the words quoted above the said heretic errs, because he shamelessly imputes falsehood to the blessed Clement, the supreme pontiff, as anyone who looks at the decree of the same Clement can plainly see.

units.la: Tricesimus secundus error est, quod præcepti Christi datum seu consilium Matth. 5. & Luc. 6. de non contendendo in iudicio, & de non repetendo sua in iudicio, fuit datum solummodo habentib. temporalia in proprio. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Constat a quod illa verba: Qui vult tecum in iudicio contendere, & tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & pallium, positum Matth. 5. & Luc. 6. intelliguntur de his, qui in proprio temporalia obtinebant. Loquitur enim illi domino, qui tunicam habebant & pallium. Cum dicit: Qui voluerit tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & pallium. Hæc verba eius, quæ veritati & doctrinæ sanctorum sunt aperte contraria, sicut diffuse in maioribus operibus est aperte monstratum. Sunt etiam contra doctrinam beati apostoli Pauli, veluti epistolam ipsius 1. ad Cor. 6. patet intueri.
units.tr: The thirty-second error is that the precept or counsel of Christ given in Matthew 5 and Luke 6, about not contending in judgment and not demanding back one's own in court, was given only to those who held temporal goods as their own. He puts forward this error in these words: It is agreed that those words: If anyone wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also, placed in Matthew 5 and Luke 6, are to be understood of those who held temporal goods as their own property. For he speaks to those who had a tunic and a cloak, saying: If anyone wishes to take your tunic, let him have your cloak also. These words of his, which are plainly contrary to the truth and to the teaching of the saints, as has been clearly shown at greater length in my larger works, are also contrary to the teaching of the blessed apostle Paul, as may be seen by looking at his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 6.

units.la: Hos 32 errores (cum plurib. aliis erroribus, hæresibus, falsitatibus, diffamationibus, vanis obiectionibus, excusationibus & responsionibus hic causa breuitatis omissis) præfatus hæreticus in dicta sua destitutione quia vir reprobus, in derogationem Christi & fidei Christianæ omnium q; fidelium Christianorum scribit, asserit, & dogmatizat. Declarat & demonstrat, ostendens seipsum esse pertinacem hæreticum, ex deliberatione & certa scientia hæc & alia flagitiosa documenta contra fidem & bonos mores impudenter fulminante. Prædicta vera destitutione (quia vir) cum erroribus & hæresibus in ipsa contentis ad notitiam Generalis Ministri sepedicti deducta, & diligenter inspecta & examinata, ipse Generalis cum sibi adhærentibus tam ab auctore quam ab hæretico pertinaci, quam ab ipsa destitutione tot & tantis hæresibus fermentata ad sanctam matrem ecclesiam, & ad concilium generale in loco tuto & rite & legitime congregandum & celebrandum, existens tunc temporis in Alemania superiori, ciuitate Mondensi, in loco Fratrum Minorum publice & solenniter appellauit. Appellationem q; suam tam in Auinion. quam ad alias mundi partes transmittens, qualis in ea fuit doctrina qualiaq; errorum commenta & hæresum p scripturas sacras, doctrinam sanctorum & sacros canones, necnon & per rationes irrefragabiles, quibus in prælegata destitutione, quia vir, asserta & dogmatisata obuiant & repugnant, luce clarius declarat.
units.tr: These 32 errors (together with many other errors, heresies, falsehoods, defamations, empty objections, excuses and replies, omitted here for the sake of brevity), the aforesaid heretic in his said deposition, Quia vir reprobus, writes, asserts and teaches in derogation of Christ, of the Christian faith and of all faithful Christians. He declares and demonstrates, showing himself to be an obstinate heretic who, from deliberate and certain knowledge, shamelessly hurls these and other scandalous teachings against the faith and good morals. The aforesaid deposition, with the errors and heresies contained in it, was brought to the notice of the General Minister mentioned above and was carefully inspected and examined. The General himself, with his adherents, then appealed publicly and solemnly, both against the author and against the obstinate heretic, and against the deposition itself, which was so leavened with so many and such great heresies, to the holy mother Church and to a general council, to be gathered and celebrated in a safe place, duly and lawfully. At that time he was in Upper Germany, in the city of Munich, in the house of the Friars Minor. He sent this appeal both to Avignon and to other parts of the world, and in it he makes clearer than light what kind of doctrine and what inventions of errors and heresies were in that deposition, Quia vir, and how they are asserted and taught, and how they clash and conflict with the holy Scriptures, the teaching of the saints, the sacred canons, and also with the irrefutable reasons by which they are opposed.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Svpradicti autem errores & hæreses cum aliis quamplurib. (vt pdicitur) hic causa breuitatis omissis, in prænominatis libellis siue destitutionibus dogmatisati non sufficerunt antedicto hæretico. Quinimo alias hæreses cuilibet fideli horrendas in sermonib. suis publice docuit, & pertinaciter defensauit & affirmauit. Quos sermones viri fide digni reportantes de verbo ad verbum scripserunt. Vnde anno domini M.ccc.xxxi. in festo Omnium Sanctorum publice fecit sermonem assumpto pro themate: Memento operum patrum vestrorum, in quo sermone dixit, docuit, & affirmauit, q animæ in cœlo beatæ non vident visione faciali, nec intuentur diuinam essentiam, nec ante diem iudicii generalis summam visuræ. Quam hæresim in diuersis aliis sermonib. suis approbando recitauit, & pertinaciter affirmauit. Pro qua etiam hæresi fulcienda unum magnum opus composuit, q vidi & legi. Necnon unum opus solenne a quodam magno viro factum in contrarium, pro veritate catholica defensanda, & prædicta hæresi confutanda, manu mea conscripsi. Vnde in prædicto sermone dicit in hæc verba: animæ iustorum vsq; ad diem iudicii erunt sub altari i.e. sub protectione & consolatione humanitatis Christi. Sed postquam Christus meruit ad iudicium, erunt supra altare, id est supra Christi humanitatem. Quia post diem iudicii videbunt sanctam trinitatem contemplabuntur, non solum Christi humanitatem, sed etiam eius diuinitatem, vt in se est. videbunt eam patrem & filium & spiritum sanctum. Anima igitur sanctæ ante diem. diem iudicii sunt sub altari i.e. sub protectione & consolatione humanitatis Christi, sed post diem iudicii ipse eleuabit eas, vt videant ipsam diuinitatem. Et infra: In gaudium non introibit anima sine eodem corpore. Haec sunt verba sua, quibus & multis aliis conatur ostendere, quod animae sanctorum ante diem iudicii generalis non videbunt essentialiter diuinam essentiam. Sed hoc est haereticum & contra scripturam sacram Apoc. 6. vbi dicitur: data sunt illis singulae stolae albae. Quam auctoritatem sancti exponunt de visione diuinae essentiae, qua nunc fruuntur animae separatae. Vnde Greg. 4. lib. Dialogorum dicit in persona Petri: nosse velim, si nunc ante resurrectionem corporum in caelo recipi valeant anima iustorum. Et respondet dicens: Hoc neque de omnibus iustis fateri possumus, neque necessario de omnibus negamus. Nam sunt quorundam iustorum animae, quae a caelesti regno quibusdam mansionibus adhuc differuntur, in quo dilationis damno, quid aliud innuitur, nisi quod de praedicta iustitia aliquid minus habuerunt. & tamen luce clarius constat, quod perfectorum animae iustorum, vt huiusmodi carnis claustra exiunt, in caelestibus sedibus recipiuntur. Et infra quaerit in persona Petri inquiens: Si igitur animae iustorum sunt in caelo: qui est, quod in die iudicii pro iustitia sua retributione recipient? & respondet dicens: hoc enim nimirum crescit in iudicio, quod nunc animarum sola, postmodum ac corporum beatitudine perfruuntur. Vnde in ipsa carne gaudebunt, in qua dolores pro Domino & cruciatus pertulerunt. Pro hac quippe geminata eorum gloria scriptum est. In terra sua duplicia possidebunt. hic ante resurrectionis diem de sanctorum animabus scriptum est: Data sunt illis singulae stolae albae. & dictum est ipsis, vt requiescant adhuc modicum tempus, donec impleatur numerus conseruorum & fratrum eorum, qui vtique nunc singulas acceperunt, binas in iudicio stolas habituri sint: quia modo animarum tantummodo, tunc autem & animarum & corporum simul in gloria laetabuntur. Et idem: fit in electis quoddam mirabilius: quia non solum eos cognoscunt, quos in hoc mundo noverant, sed velut visos ac cognitos recognoscunt beatos, quos nunquam viderunt. Nam cum aliquos patres in aeterna illa haereditate viderint eos incognitos per visionem non esse, quos in opere semper noverit: quia cum illis omnes communi claritate Deum conspiciunt. quid est, quod ibi nesciant, vbi scientem omnia sciunt? haec Gregorius.
units.tr: The aforesaid errors and heresies, together with many others (as has been said) omitted here for brevity, were not enough for the aforementioned heretic to teach in the said little books or depositions. Moreover, he publicly taught in his sermons other heresies, horrible to every faithful person, and obstinately defended and affirmed them. Trustworthy men who took them down wrote these sermons out word for word. Hence, in the year of the Lord 1331, on the feast of All Saints, he preached publicly a sermon on the theme: Remember the works of your fathers, in which sermon he said, taught and affirmed that the souls of the blessed in heaven do not see with the face-to-face vision, nor behold the divine essence, nor will they see it before the day of the general judgement. He recited this heresy, approving it, in various other sermons of his, and obstinately affirmed it. To support this heresy he also composed a great work, which I have seen and read. I also wrote out by my own hand a solemn work, made by a certain great man on the other side, to defend Catholic truth and refute the aforesaid heresy. In the aforesaid sermon he says these words: The souls of the righteous until the day of judgement will be under the altar, that is, under the protection and consolation of Christ's humanity. But after Christ has merited the judgement, they will be above the altar, that is, above Christ's humanity. For after the day of judgement they will see the holy Trinity and will contemplate not only Christ's humanity but also his divinity, as it is in itself. They will see it, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Therefore the souls of the saints before the day of judgement are under the altar, that is, under the protection and consolation of Christ's humanity, but after the day of judgement he himself will raise them up so that they may see the divinity itself. And further on: The soul does not enter into joy without the same body. These are his words, by which, and by many others, he tries to show that the souls of the saints before the day of the general judgement will not see the divine essence essentially. But this is heretical and contrary to the holy Scripture, Rev. 6., where it says: To them were given each one a white robe. The saints explain this text as referring to the vision of the divine essence, which the souls now separated enjoy. Hence Gregory, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, says in the person of Peter: I would like to know whether the souls of the righteous can now, before the resurrection of the bodies, be received into heaven. And he answers, saying: This we can affirm of neither all the righteous, nor do we necessarily deny it of all. For there are the souls of certain righteous who are still held back from the heavenly kingdom by certain dwellings; and what is hinted at by this loss of delay, except that they have something less of the aforesaid righteousness? And yet it is clearer than light that the souls of the perfect righteous, as soon as they leave the prison of such flesh, are received into the heavenly seats. And further on he asks, in the person of Peter, saying: If therefore the souls of the righteous are in heaven, why is it that they will receive their reward for righteousness on the day of judgement? And he answers, saying: For this indeed increases at the judgement, that now they enjoy the blessedness of the souls alone, and afterwards also of the bodies. Hence they will rejoice in the very flesh in which they endured pains and torments for the Lord. For it is written concerning this twofold glory of theirs: In their land they shall possess double things. Here, before the day of the resurrection, it is written of the souls of the saints: To them were given each one a white robe, and it was said to them that they should rest yet a little time, until the number of their fellow servants and brethren be complete, who have indeed now each received one robe, and will have two robes at the judgement; because now only the souls rejoice, but then both the souls and the bodies together in glory. And again: In the elect something more wonderful happens, for they recognise not only those whom they knew in this world, but they also acknowledge as seen and known the blessed whom they have never seen. For when they have seen certain fathers in that eternal inheritance, they will not be unknown to them through vision, those whom they always knew in deed, since all behold God in common brightness with them. What is it that they do not know there, where they know all things, knowing all? Thus Gregory.

units.la: Approbando autem praefatam haeresim, adiunxit secundam in sermone alio, qui incipit: Tolle puerum & matrem eius &c. Quae est, quod animae reproborum non punientur in inferno ante diem iudicii generalis. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Israel interpretatur videns Deum, vel visio Dei. De ista visione factum est dictum his diebus. Vbi etiam dixi, quod Deus non est magis promotus ad damnandum, quam ad retributendum seu praemiandum. Quia non prius damnabit malos, quam praemiabit bonos. Sed dictum est, quod beati ante diem iudicii non ibunt in vitam aeternam. Igitur nec mali ante diem iudicii ibunt in poenam aeternam in infernum, vbi erit fletus & stridor dentium. Haec verba sua haeretica tam sacrae scripturae quam doctrinae sanctorum aduersa. Vnde Iob. 21. scribitur: Ducunt in bonis dies suos, & in puncto ad inferna descendunt. Et Luc. 16. scribitur: Mortuus est autem dives, & sepultus est in inferno. Eleuans autem oculos suos cum esset in tormentis, vidit Abraham a longe & Lazarum in sinu eius: & ipse clamans dixit, pater Abraham miserere mei, & mitte Lazarum, vt intingat extremum digiti sui in aquam vt refrigeret linguam meam, quia crucior in hac flamma. Et infra: hic vero consolatur, tu autem cruciaris. Et infra: Tesletur illis ne & ipsi veniant in hunc locum tormentorum. Et Gregorius 4. libro Dialogorum 9. ait: Si esse sanctorum animas in caelo fari eloqui satis factione credidisti, oportet vt per omnia iniquorum animas esse credas in inferno. Nam sicut electos beatus do laetificat, ita credi necesse est, quod a die exitus sui igni reprobos exurat. Et infra: Colligere possumus ex dicto euangelii, quod incendium anima non solum videndo, sed etiam experiendo patiatur. Veritatis enim voce, quia dives mortuus in inferno dicitur sepultus. Cuius anima, quod in igne teneatur, insinuat vox diuitis, qua Abraham deprecatur dicens: Mitte Lazarum, vt intingat extremum digiti sui in aquam, vt refrigeret linguam meam, quia crucior in hac flamma. Cum igitur peccatorem damnatum diuitem ignibus perhiber, quisnam sapiens reproborum animas teneri ignibus neget?
units.tr: In approving the aforesaid heresy, he added a second one in another sermon, which begins: Take the boy and his mother, etc. This is that the souls of the reprobate will not be punished in hell before the day of the general judgement. He puts forward this error in these words: Israel is interpreted as seeing God, or the vision of God. Concerning this vision it has been said in these days. Where I also said that God is no more inclined to damn than to reward or recompense. For he will not damn the wicked before he rewards the good. But it has been said that the blessed will not go into eternal life before the day of judgement. Therefore neither will the wicked go into eternal punishment in hell before the day of judgement, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. These heretical words of his are opposed as much to holy Scripture as to the teaching of the saints. Hence it is written in Job 21.: They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they go down to hell. And it is written in Luke 16.: The rich man also died and was buried in hell. And lifting up his eyes, being in torments, he saw Abraham afar off and Lazarus in his bosom; and he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water to cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame. And further on: But now he is comforted, and you are tormented. And further on: Let him testify to them, lest they also come into this place of torment. And Gregory, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, chapter 9, says: If you have believed that the souls of the saints in heaven are enjoying themselves, it is fitting that you believe in every respect that the souls of the wicked are in hell. For just as the blessed rejoice the elect, so it must be believed that from the day of their departure the fire burns the reprobate. And further on: We can gather from the word of the gospel that the soul suffers the burning not only by seeing but also by experiencing it. For by the voice of truth, the rich man who died is said to be buried in hell. That his soul is held in fire is shown by the rich man's voice, in which he entreats Abraham, saying: Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, to cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame. Since therefore the Scripture presents the condemned sinner, the rich man, in the fires, what wise man would deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in fires?

units.la: Tertiam haeresim ponit in dicto sermone: Tolle puerum &c. quae est, quod Daemones non sunt necerunt in inferno ante diem iudicii generalis. Hunc errorem ponit sub his verbis: Non enim damnati (scilicet Daemones) possent nos temptare, si essent intrusi in infernum. & ideo non est dicendum, quod sint in inferno, sed quod sint in isto aere caliginoso, vnde patet eis via ad temptandum nos. ergo non videntur adhuc esse Daemones in inferno, sed supra infernum. Vltimum autem iudicium erit tunc, quando ipsi daemones includentur in inferno. Nescio quod magis clare possent dicere euangelicum, quod daemones non sint in inferno, quam quod dicit: venisti ante tempus torquere nos. Et infra: Paret suidenter, quod daemones non sunt in inferno, sed extra. & sunt supra nos & iuxta nos. Haec verba eius haeretica scripturae diuinae contraria & doctrinae sanctorum aduersa. Vnde in Apoc. 2.c. dicitur sic: Vidi angelum descendentem de caelo, habentem clavem abyssi & catenam in manu sua, & apprehendit draconem serpentem antiquum, qui est Diabolus & Sathanas, & ligauit eum per annos mille & misit eum in abyssum. & 2. Petri 2. scribitur, quod angelis peccantibus non pepercit, sed resputentibus in inferno cruciandos tradidit.
units.tr: The third heresy he sets out in the said sermon, "Tolle puerum", etc., is that the demons are not in hell before the day of the general judgment. He puts forward this error in these words: "For the damned (namely the demons) could not tempt us if they were shut up in hell. And so it is not to be said that they are in hell, but that they are in this misty air, whence there is a way open to them to tempt us. Therefore the demons do not yet seem to be in hell, but above hell. The final judgment will be then, when the demons themselves are shut up in hell." I do not know how more plainly they could say, in the words of the Gospel, that the demons are not in hell, than in what he says: "You have come before the time to torment us." And below: "It is evident that the demons are not in hell, but outside it, and they are above us and near us." These heretical words of his are contrary to divine Scripture and opposed to the doctrine of the saints. Hence Apoc. 20 says: "I saw an angel coming down from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a chain in his hand, and he seized the dragon, the old serpent, who is the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years and cast him into the abyss." And 2 Pet. 2 writes that God did not spare the angels who sinned, but delivered them into hell, to be tormented and kept for judgment.

units.la: Quartam haeresim ponit in praefato sermone: Tolle puerum. quae est, quod Christus non regnabit prius diem iudicii, nec vlterius habebit regnum. Hanc haeresim ponit sub his verbis: tunc (scilicet post iudicium generale) intrabunt omnes electi cum Christo in gloria, quando Christus dicet: Venite benedicti patris mei, possidete regnum vobis paratum ab origine mundi. & mali ibunt in supplicium aeternum quando dicetur eis. Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum, qui praeparatus est diabolo & angelis eius. tunc (secundum quod dicit apostolus) Christus tradet regnum Deo patri. & ipse Christus vltimo non regnabit in regno suo, i.e. in regno Dei. Non dico quod non sit rex, nec oportet: sed bene dico, quod est rex vsque ad diem iudicii. Quia modo habet illuminare, defensare & gubernare regnum suum, & ipsum custodire: sed tunc post iudicium tradet regnum Deo patri. sed quod dicit apostolus: tunc dico, quod non regnabit, nec illuminabit, nec reget, nec gubernabit. Haec verba eius haeretica & aduersa directe scripturae sacrae. Unde Luc. 1. de Christo & regno eius habetur sic: regnabit in domo Iacob in aeternum, & regni eius non erit finis. Et Dan. 2. sic scribitur: Suscitabit Deus caeli regnum, quod in aeternum non dissipabitur; & regnum eius alteri non tradetur. Et infra ca. 7. sic legitur: Potestas eius potestas aeterna, quae non auferetur: & regnum eius, quod non corrumpetur.
units.tr: The fourth heresy he sets out in the aforesaid sermon, "Tolle puerum", is that Christ will not reign before the day of judgment, nor will he have a kingdom any longer afterwards. He puts forward this heresy in these words: "Then (namely after the general judgment) all the elect will enter with Christ into glory, when Christ says: 'Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world'; and the wicked will go into eternal punishment, when it is said to them: 'Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels.' Then (as the Apostle says) Christ will deliver the kingdom to God the Father. And Christ himself will at last not reign in his kingdom, that is, in the kingdom of God. I do not say that he is not king, nor should he be; but I do say that he is king until the day of judgment. For now he has to illuminate, defend and govern his kingdom, and keep it; but then, after the judgment, he will deliver the kingdom to God the Father. But when the Apostle says 'then', I say that he will not reign, nor illuminate, nor rule, nor govern." These heretical words of his are directly adverse to holy Scripture. Hence Luke 1 says of Christ and his kingdom: "He shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." And Dan. 2 is written thus: "The God of heaven shall set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed; and his kingdom shall not be left to another." And below, in ch. 7, it is read thus: "His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away; and his kingdom, which shall not be corrupted."

units.la: Quintam haeresim ponit in sermone suo, qui incipit: Gaudete semper in domino. quae est, quod in diuinis nulla est distinctio. Hanc haeresim ponit sub his verbis: Beati in patria videbunt magnam multitudinem, sc. Deum trinum & unum. & est mirabilis vanitas, credere tres personas ad invicem non distinctas. Nam filius non distinguitur a patre, neq; spiritus sanctus a patre & filio, qui procedit ab eis: & tamen tres personae sunt; & hi tres unum sunt. Haec verba eius haeretica & fide catholicae inimica. Unde Athanasius in symbolo suo: Alia est persona patris, alia filii, alia spiritus sancti. Item extra, de summa trinitate & fide catholica, c. damnamus, sic habetur: nos sacro approbante concilio credimus & confitemur, quod distinctiones sunt in personis, & unitas in unitate.
units.tr: The fifth heresy he sets out in his sermon which begins "Rejoice always in the Lord" is that there is no distinction in the divine things. He puts forward this heresy in these words: "The blessed in the fatherland will see the great multitude, namely God, three and one. And it is a wonderful vanity to believe three persons not distinct from one another. For the Son is not distinguished from the Father, nor the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, from whom he proceeds; and yet they are three persons, and these three are one." These heretical words of his are hostile to the Catholic faith. Hence Athanasius in his creed: "Another is the person of the Father, another of the Son, another of the Holy Spirit." Likewise, in Extra, De summa Trinitate et fide catholica, c. Damnamus, it is held thus: "With the approval of the holy council we believe and confess that there are distinctions in the persons, and unity in the unity."

units.la: Sextam haeresim ponit in quodam alio sermone suo publice praedicante; qui sic incipit: Psallite domino, qui habitat in Syon. quae est, quod in diuinis filius est maior patre. Haec haeresim ponit sub his verbis: Quod autem ille, qui est incarnatus, sit maior, testatur Psalmista, cum dicit: Magnus & laudabilis nimis & magnitudinis eius non est finis. Verus enim filius Dei incarnatus est magnus, & salua reverentia patris & spiritus sancti maior utroque. Nam licet pater sit Deus, & spiritus sanctus sit Deus: tamen pater non est incarnatus, nec spiritus sanctus humanatus, sed solus filius. Et in hoc maior est patre & spiritu sancto. Haec verba eius haeretica tam sacrae scripturae quam doctrinae sanctorum aduersa. Unde Ioh. 14. sic habetur: pater maior me est. Et Athanasius in Symbolo suo sic scribit: Aequalis patri secundum diuinitatem; minor patre secundum humanitatem. Et Psalmista loquens de Christo secundum humanitatem dicit: Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis. Et apostolus ad Hebr. 2. dicit: Cum autem qui modicum ab angelis minoratus est, videmus Iesum propter passionem mortis gloria & honore coronatum.
units.tr: The sixth heresy he sets out in another sermon of his, preached publicly, which begins "Sing to the Lord, who dwells in Zion", is that in divine things the Son is greater than the Father. He puts forward this heresy in these words: "That he who was incarnate is greater, the Psalmist bears witness when he says: 'Great and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end.' For the true Son of God, made flesh, is great, and, saving reverence for the Father and the Holy Spirit, greater than both. For although the Father is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet the Father was not incarnate, nor the Holy Spirit made man, but the Son alone. And in this he is greater than the Father and the Spirit." These heretical words of his are opposed as much to holy Scripture as to the doctrine of the saints.
