Hence John 14 says: "My Father is greater than I." And Athanasius writes in his creed thus: "Equal to the Father as touching his Godhead; less than the Father as touching his manhood." And the Psalmist, speaking of Christ according to his manhood, says: "Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels." And the Apostle in Heb. 2 says: "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death."

units.la: Item septima haeresis est, quam ponit in quodam alio suo sermone publice praedicato, qui incipit: Iusti tulerunt spolia impiorum &c. Quae est, quod omnia de necessitate eueniunt, sic quod Deus non possit facere aliud vel aliter quam facit. Hanc haeresim ponit sub his verbis: Sicut impossibile est Deum esse mutabilem, ita quod tunc non esset Deus: ita impossibile est, quod illa, quae Deus de sua potentia ordinata facit, possit aliter facere quam facit. Et ideo impossibile est, quod saluaret hominem de absoluta potentia sine sacramento baptismi, & sine habitu caritatis. Quia sic est ordinatum ab aeterno de Dei potentia ordinata, quae idem est quod Deus, & mutari non potest. Et paulo post: Unde distinguunt quidam & dicunt, quod multa potest Deus in potestate absoluta, quae non potest de potentia ordinata, sed illud est falsum & erroneum: quia potentia Dei absoluta & ordinata idem sunt & non distinguuntur ab invicem. & infra: Impossibile est, quod Deus de potentia absoluta possit facere aliud quam faciat de potentia ordinata, quia idem sunt. Et post: cum ista potentia sint idem quod Deus: si Deus posset facere aliquid de potentia absoluta, quod non facit, vel non faciat de potentia ordinata: tunc esset mutabilis in seipso, & non esset Deus. Sicut igitur summum impossibile est Deum non esse Deum, ita summum impossibile est & erroneum dicere Deum posse aliquid facere de potentia absoluta aliter, quam facit vel faciat de potentia ordinata. Et infra: si igitur Deus de potentia absoluta posset aliquid facere, quod non facit de potentia ordinata, sequeretur, quod effectus potentia ordinata posset a Deo frustrari & mutari: & tunc non esset opus. Sequetur etiam, quod Deus in seipso non solum esset mutabilis, sed sibi ipsi & suae potentiae contrarius. & tunc non esset Deus. Et post: potest igitur quod erroneum & falsum est dicere, & etiam impossibile, quod Deus de potentia absoluta possit facere aliter siue alia, quam faciat de potentia ordinata. Haec verba eius haeretica omnipotentiam Dei limitantia, imo annihilantia aperte sunt. Quae quidem verba tam per scripturam sacram, quam per doctrinam sanctorum lucide confutantur. Unde Sap. 11. sic habetur: Quidam errantes colebant mutos, serpentes & bestias superuacuas immisisti illis multitudinem mutorum, aliquando in vindictam, ut scirent, quia per quae peccat quis, per hoc & torquetur. non enim impossibile erat, quod opus manus tua, qua creauit orbem terrarum ex materia inuisa, immitteret illis multitudinem vrsorum, aut audaces leones, aut nouos generis ira plenas, aut ignotas bestias, aut vaporem igneum spirantes, aut odorem fumi proferentes, aut horrendas ab oculis scintillas emittentes: quarum non solum lasura poterat illos exterminare, sed & aspectus per timorem occidere: imo & sine his vno spiritu occidi poterant. & per consequens Deus potuit fecisse aliter & aliud quam fecit. Quod etiam veritas ipsa Matth. 26. testatur, dicens: an putas, quia non possum rogare patrem meum ut exhibeat mihi plusquam 12. legiones angelorum? Ex qua auctoritate colligitur, quod filius potuit rogasse, quod non rogauit: & pater exhibere, quod non exhibuit. Et istam veritatem beatus Augustin. in multis locis affirmat. Unde in Enchiridion dicit sic: omnipotentis voluntas multa potest facere, quae non vult nec facit. potuit enim facere, ut 12. legiones pugnarent contra illos, qui Christum coeperunt.
units.tr: Likewise the seventh heresy is one he sets out in another sermon of his, publicly preached, which begins "The just have carried off the spoils of the wicked", etc. It is that all things happen of necessity, so that God cannot do otherwise or differently than he does. He puts forward this heresy in these words: "Just as it is impossible for God to be changeable, since then he would not be God, so it is impossible that those things which God does by his ordained power could be done otherwise than he does them. And therefore it is impossible that he should save a man by absolute power without the sacrament of baptism and without the habit of charity. For it has been so ordained from eternity by God's ordained power, which is the same as God, and cannot be changed." And a little later: "Hence some distinguish and say that God can do many things by absolute power which he cannot do by ordained power; but that is false and erroneous, because God's absolute and ordained power are the same and are not distinguished from one another." And below: "It is impossible that God, by absolute power, should be able to do otherwise than he does by ordained power, because they are the same." And after: "Since these powers are the same as God: if God could do by absolute power something which he does not do, or does not do by ordained power, then he would be changeable in himself, and would not be God. Just as it is the utmost impossibility that God should not be God, so it is the utmost impossibility, and erroneous, to say that God can do anything by absolute power otherwise than he does or would do by ordained power." And below: "If therefore God by absolute power could do something which he does not do by ordained power, it would follow that the effects of the ordained power could be frustrated and changed by God, and then there would be no work. It would also follow that God would be not only changeable in himself, but contrary to himself and to his power, and then he would not be God. And after: therefore it is both erroneous and false, and also impossible, to say that God by absolute power could do otherwise or something else than he does by ordained power." These heretical words of his, which limit, indeed annihilate, the omnipotence of God, are plainly evident. And these words are clearly refuted both by holy Scripture and by the doctrine of the saints. Hence Wisdom 11 says: "Those who erred worshipped dumb creatures, serpents and worthless beasts; you sent upon them a multitude of dumb creatures, as a punishment, that they might know that by what a man sins, by the same he is tormented. For it was not impossible that your hand, which created the world out of formless matter, should send upon them a multitude of bears, or bold lions, or new kinds of beasts full of rage, or unknown beasts, or beasts breathing fiery vapour, or giving out an odour of smoke, or sending out dreadful sparks from their eyes; of which not only the injury could destroy them, but also the sight could kill them through fear; and even without these they could be destroyed by one breath." And consequently God could have done otherwise and something else than he did. This the Truth itself also bears witness to in Matt. 26, saying: "Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?" From which authority it is gathered that the Son could have asked what he did not ask, and the Father could have given what he did not give. And blessed Augustine affirms this truth in many places. Hence in the Enchiridion he says thus: "The will of the Almighty can do many things which it neither wills nor does. For he could have made twelve legions fight against those who laid hands on Christ."

units.la: Et idem Augustin. in li. de natura & gratia, dicit sic: dominus Lazarum suscitauit a corpore. nunquid dicendum est, quod non potuit Iudam suscitare in mente. potuit quidem, sed noluit. Et super Gen. ait idem Augustinus: talem potuit Deus hominem fecisse, qui nec peccare posset nec vellet. Et 13. li. de trinit. sic ait: fuit & alius modus nostra liberationis possibilis Deo, quia omnia potest: sed nullus alius nostra miseria sanande fuit conuenientior. Ex quibus luce clarius patet, quod Deus multa posset alia & aliter facere quam faciat.
units.tr: And the same Augustine, in the book on nature and grace, says thus: "The Lord raised Lazarus from the body; shall it be said that he could not raise Judas in mind? He could indeed, but he would not." And on Genesis the same Augustine says: "God could have made a man who neither could nor would sin." And in the thirteenth book of the Trinity he says thus: "There was also another possible way of our deliverance for God, since he can do all things; but no other was more fitting for healing our misery." From these things it appears clearer than light that God could do many things otherwise and differently than he does.

units.la: Has septem haereses cunctorum auribus fidelium perhorrendas supradictus haereticus in suis sermonibus publice docuit, & pertinaciter affirmauit. Quos sermones fide digni praesentialiter in ipsis sermocinationibus suis existentes de verbo ad verbum (quantum fuit eis possibile) conscripserunt. Et ut venenum mortiferum in eisdem fulminatum absentibus innotesceret; & per scripturas authenticas lucidius reprobaretur, per diversa mundi climata celerius destinarunt.
units.tr: These seven heresies, dreadful to the ears of all the faithful, the aforesaid heretic taught publicly in his sermons and affirmed stubbornly. Faithful men, who were present in person at those discourses, wrote them down word for word (as far as it was possible for them), and, so that the deadly poison thundered forth in them might become known to those who were absent, and might be more clearly refuted by authentic writings, they sent them quickly through the various regions of the world.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Nota cavillationem derisoriam.
units.tr: Note the mocking objection.

units.la: VIsis pro parte haeresibus & erroribus per Iohannem 22. dogmatizatis: restat nunc quibusdam objectionibus cavillosis succinctè respondere. Et prima quidem objectio est, quod non potest Papa haereticari, nec contra fidem errare. Sed huic cavillationi leviter potest obviari. Primo quidem exemplo in sacra scriptura fundato. Unde Beatus Petrus, qui fuit Papa longe melior & sanctior Iohanne 22. erravit in fide. Quia contra veritatem Evangelii, ut Beatus Paulus aperte fatetur ad Gal. 2. sic inquiens: Cum autem venisset Cephas Antiochiam, in faciem ei restiti, quia reprehensibilis erat. Et infra: sed cum vidissem, quod non recte ambulaunt ad veritatem Evangelii, dixi Cephae coram omnibus, si tu (cum Iudaeus sis) gentiliter & non Iudaice vivis: quomodo gentes cogis Iudaizare? Et tibi expresse affirmat Apostolus quod Beatus Petrus non ambulavit ad veritatem Evangelii. Et per consequens contra fidem erravit. Quare sequitur, quod Papa potest contra fidem errare. Verumtamen Beatus Petrus non fuit haereticus, quia errori sui pertinaciter non adhaesit: imo correptionem Beati Pauli benigne suscipiens continuo se correxit. Et si suo errori pertinaciter adhaesisset, fuisset haereticus infallibiliter iudicandus. De isto etiam errore Petri habetur in decr. 2 quaest. 7. volo, ubi sic legitur: Petrus cogebat gentes Iudaizare, & a veritate Evangelii recedere: cum Iudaei gregem faciebant & a cibis gentilium latenter se subtrahebant. Par autem est in se & exorbitare, & alios verbo & exemplo a fide deiicere. Secundum exemplum habetur de Papa Marcellino contra fidem commisso, ut habetur in decretis 21. d. ubi sic legitur: Tempore Diocletiani & Maximiani Romanorum Augustorum, Marcellinus Episcopus urbis Romae, qui postea insignis martyr effectus est, adeo compulsus est a paganis, ut templum eorum ingressus, grana thuris super prunas imponeret. Cuius rei gratia collecto universorum Episcoporum concilio & inquisitione facta, hoc idem pontifex se egisse confessus est. Ex quibus verbis colligitur, quod Papa potest contra fidem errare: & per consequens haereticari. Verumtamen propter hunc errorem non fuit Marcellinus haereticus: quia non suit pertinax, sed metu mortis idolis thurificans de crimine per ipsum commisso poenituit, & sufficienter se correxit. Tertium exemplum habetur de Gaio Papa, qui compellente Diocletiano, de cuius genere erat, ut legitur in Chronicis, incensum idolis imposuit: sed postea poenituit coram centum & 80. Episcopis. Quartum exemplum est de Papa Liberio, qui tempore Constantii, Constantini Magni consensit haeresi Arrianae: quē Eusebius urbis Romae presbyter haereticū declarauit. De quo Liberio sic scribit Hieronym. tædio exilii victus Liberius & in haeretica pravitate subscribens, Romā quasi victus intravit. Et in lib. Pontificum de eodem Liberio sic habetur: Eusebius autem presbyter urbis Romae coepit ipsum Liberium declarare haereticum, multiq; per eius doctrinam communionem Liberii vitabant, populum congregatum in Domino confortabant. Tenetur a Constantio, ipso Liberio dicente: tu solus Christianus es in urbe Roma. Qui respondit: sic in Domino confidimus, quia fideles nos innominet Christus. Et infra: cui dixit Liberius nonne Iulii fungimur vicibus? ait illi Eusebius. Si perseverassis, inquit, in fide, quam in persecutione primo tenere visus eras, as ipsa res te docet & declarat. Quintum exemplum habetur de Anastasio Papa 2. De quo habetur in decret. dist. 19. ubi sic legitur: Anastasius 2. Episcopus fauore Anastasii Imperatoris, quos Achatius haereticus post sententiam in se prolatam sacerdotes vel Levitas ordinauerat, acceptis officiis rite fungi debere decreuit. Et post: Quod igitur illicite & non canonice, sed contra decreta praedecessorum & successorum suorum, haec rescripta probat & dedit, Felix & Gelasius, qui Achatium & Anastasium excommunicauerunt, & Hormisda, qui ab ipso Anastasio tertius eundem Achatium postea damnauit. Ideo a Romana Ecclesia repudiatur. Per praedicta exempla & plura alia hic causa breuitatis omissa euidenter ostenditur, quod Papa potest contra fidem errare; & per consequens haeretica prauitate maculari. Quod etiam per auctoritates quamplures posset probari; de quo pauca adducam. Unde in decret. dist. 40. sic legitur: huius (scilicet Papae) culpas redarguere praesumat nullus mortalium, quia cunctos ipse iudicaturus, a nemine iudicatur, nisi deprehendatur a fide deuius. Vbi aperte supponitur, quod Papa potest a fide deuiare: & per consequens haereticari: Quod aperte asserit Glossa. 2. 4. quaest. 1. cap. arrecta, quae dicit: Quaero de qua Ecclesia intelligas, quod dicitur, quod non possit errare. Non de ipso Papa, qui Ecclesia dicitur, ut 64. di. quicunque & 7. quaest. 1. Scire debes, quia certum est quod Papa potest errare, ut infra di. Anastasius. & 40. dist. si Papa. Praeterea qui potest cadere in sententiam latae sententiae, & fieri minor quocunque; catholico, potest errare contra fidem, & haeretica prauitate maculari. Sed Papa est huiusmodi 24. q. 1. Achatius: Quae sub verbis (quicunque in haeresim damnatam labitur, ipsa damnatione seipsum inuoluit) dicit sic: hic est casus in quo Papa Papam ligare potest, in quo Papa in canonem latae sententiae incidit. Nec obviat regula illa, quia par patrem soluere vel ligare non potest: quia si Papa est haereticus, in eo quod est haereticus, minor est quocunque; Episcopo catholico: quia factum notat Ecclesia sine sententia.
units.tr: Having dealt in part with the heresies and errors taught by John 22, it remains now to answer briefly certain captious objections. The first objection is that the Pope cannot be made a heretic, nor err against the faith. This quibble can easily be met. First, by an example grounded in holy Scripture. Blessed Peter, who was a far better and holier man than John 22, erred in the faith. For he acted contrary to the truth of the Gospel, as the blessed Paul openly confesses in Gal. 2, saying: But when Cephas had come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. And below: But when I saw that they did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, If you, being a Jew, live after the manner of the Gentiles and not as the Jews, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews? The Apostle expressly affirms that blessed Peter did not walk according to the truth of the Gospel, and consequently he erred against the faith. It follows that the Pope can err against the faith. Yet blessed Peter was not a heretic, because he did not cling obstinately to his error; rather, receiving Paul's correction kindly, he at once amended himself. And had he obstinately clung to his error, he would have been judged a heretic beyond doubt. This error of Peter is also found in Decr. 2, qu. 7, Volo, where it is read thus: Peter compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews and to withdraw from the truth of the Gospel, when the Jews made a party of their own and secretly held themselves aloof from Gentile food. Yet it is an extravagance in himself, and to cast others from the faith by word and example. A second example is of Pope Marcellinus, who sinned against the faith, as is found in the Decretum, dist. 21, where it is read thus: In the time of the Roman emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Marcellinus, Bishop of the city of Rome, who afterwards became a famous martyr, was so compelled by the pagans that he entered their temple and placed grains of incense upon the coals. For this reason a council of all the bishops was gathered and an inquiry made, and the same pontiff confessed that he had done this. From these words it is gathered that the Pope can err against the faith, and consequently be made a heretic. Yet Marcellinus was not a heretic on account of this error, because he was not obstinate; out of fear of death he offered incense to the idols, but he repented of the crime he had committed and sufficiently amended himself. A third example is of Pope Gaius, who, under compulsion from Diocletian, to whose family he belonged, as we read in the Chronicles, offered incense to the idols; but afterwards he repented before one hundred and eighty bishops. A fourth example is of Pope Liberius, who in the time of Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, consented to the Arian heresy; Eusebius, a presbyter of the city of Rome, declared him a heretic. Of this Liberius Jerome writes thus: Liberius, overcome by weariness of exile, and subscribing to heretical perversity, entered Rome as one defeated. And in the book of the Pontiffs, concerning the same Liberius, it is written thus: Eusebius, a presbyter of the city of Rome, began to declare Liberius himself a heretic, and many avoided communion with Liberius through his teaching, and they strengthened the people gathered in the Lord. He was summoned by Constantius, Liberius himself saying: you alone are a Christian in the city of Rome. He replied: we trust so in the Lord, since Christ calls us faithful. And below: Liberius said to him: do we not fill the place of Julius? Eusebius answered him: If you had persevered, he said, in the faith which you seemed at first to hold in the persecution, the very fact teaches and declares you. A fifth example is of Pope Anastasius II. Of him it is written in Decr. dist. 19, where it is read thus: Anastasius II, bishop, at the favour of the emperor Anastasius, decreed that those whom the heretic Achatius had ordained priests or Levites, after the sentence pronounced against him, should be allowed to perform their offices duly. And after: Therefore, since these rescripts prove and grant what was done unlawfully and not canonically, and against the decrees of his predecessors and successors, Felix and Gelasius, who excommunicated Achatius and Anastasius, and Hormisdas, who, third from Anastasius himself, afterwards condemned the same Achatius, he is therefore repudiated by the Roman Church. By these examples, and many others which are omitted here for brevity, it is plainly shown that the Pope can err against the faith and, consequently, be stained with heretical perversity. This could also be proved by very many authorities, of which I shall adduce a few. Thus in Decr. dist. 40 it is read: Let no mortal presume to censure his faults, since he himself is to judge all and is judged by no one, unless he is found to have strayed from the faith. Here it is plainly assumed that the Pope can stray from the faith and consequently be made a heretic. The Gloss plainly asserts this on 2, 4, qu. 1, cap. Arrecta, which says: I ask of what Church you understand what is said, that it cannot err. Not of the Pope himself, who is called the Church, as in 64 dist. Quicunque and 7 qu. 1. You must know that it is certain that the Pope can err, as below in dist. Anastasius, and in 40 dist. Si Papa. Moreover, whoever can fall under a sentence of latae sententiae and become less than any Catholic can err against the faith and be stained with heretical perversity. But the Pope is of this kind, 24 qu. 1, Achatius, which in the words (whoever slips into a condemned heresy involves himself in that very condemnation) says thus: here is a case in which a Pope can bind a Pope, in which a Pope falls under the canon of latae sententiae. Nor does that rule stand in the way, that an equal cannot loose or bind his equal; for if the Pope is a heretic, then in so far as he is a heretic he is less than any Catholic bishop, because the Church notes the fact without any sentence.

units.la: Secunda obiectio cavillosa est, quod Papa non habet superiorem in his. Et ideo de factis suis nullus debet se intromittere. Sed ista cavillatio non valet. Nam de factis illius, qui non habet superiorem in terris mortales non habent iudicare. Sed de factis Papae saltem in crimine haeresis habent mortales iudicare, sicut patet de Papa Anastasio 2. dist. 19. cap. Anastasius. Et de Marcellino Papa dist. 21. c. nunc autem. Et de Liberio Papa, quem Eusebius hæreticum declaratuit. Et de Symacho Papa, qui successit Anastasio, de quo habetur dist. 27. hic etiam, vbi dicitur in hæc verba: Symachus Papa in Romana Synodo, dignitate sua expoliatus, primus pristino statui reddi decernitur, vt tunc veniret ad caussam. Et si ita recte videretur accusantium propositionibus respondere dignanter visa est maximo numero sacerdotum atq; meretur effectum. Et cum postmodum ordinaretur, quomodo accusandus esset prefatus Papa, vt diceret ocewrreret: sed ab æmulis est impeditus. Ex quibus aliisq; quampluribus apparet, quod Papa potest accusari & iudicari. Et per consequens quod saltem in crimine hæresis habet superiorem in terris. Quod aperte testatur Glossa Ordinaria dist. 12. c. Anastasius, super verbo consilio, quæ dicit: videtur igitur quod Papa tenetur requirere consilium Episcoporum: quod verum est, vbi de fide agitur. Et tunc synodus maior est Papa 15. d. c. sicut sancti. Præterea qui potest de Papatu depoui, habet superiorem super quem deponitur. Sed Papa potest propter crimina sua deponi de Papatu. Vnde de Papa Iohanne 12. sic habetur in Chronicis: erat venator & totus lubricus, adeo quod publice fœminas tenebat. Propterea quidam cardinalium & Ro-manorum scripserunt occulte Ottoni principi Saxonum, vt scandalo compatiens Ecclesia sine mora Romam properaret. Hoc Papa percipiens Iohanni Diacono Cardinali, tanquam huius facti Consiliario, nasum & alteri Iohanni subdiacono, qui literas scripserat, manum amputari fecit. Hic cum frequenter per Imperatorem & clerum de sua correctione fuisset monitus, non correctus, præsidio Imperatoris de Papatu destitutus communi voto Leo Papa eligitur.
units.tr: The second captious objection is that the Pope has no superior in these matters, and therefore no one ought to meddle with his acts. But this quibble does not hold. For mortals have no right to judge the acts of one who has no superior on earth. But over the acts of the Pope, at least in the crime of heresy, mortals do have the right to judge, as is clear from Pope Anastasius II, dist. 19, cap. Anastasius. And from Pope Marcellinus, dist. 21, c. Nunc autem. And from Pope Liberius, whom Eusebius declared a heretic. And from Pope Symmachus, who succeeded Anastasius, of whom we read in dist. 27, Hic etiam, where these words are found: Pope Symmachus, stripped of his dignity in the Roman synod, was first decreed to be restored to his former state, so that he might then come to his cause. And if it seemed right, he deigned to answer the charges of the accusers, and was thought worthy of the effect by the greatest number of priests. And when he was afterwards ordained, the way in which the said Pope was to be accused was to be stated, so that he might say what had occurred; but he was prevented by his rivals. From these and very many others it appears that the Pope can be accused and judged, and consequently that, at least in the crime of heresy, he has a superior on earth. The Ordinary Gloss openly bears witness to this, dist. 12, c. Anastasius, on the word consilio, which says: It seems therefore that the Pope is bound to seek the counsel of the bishops; which is true where the matter concerns the faith. And then a greater synod is above the Pope, 15 dist. c. Sicut sancti. Furthermore, whoever can be deposed from the papacy has a superior by whom he is deposed. But the Pope can be deposed from the papacy on account of his crimes. Thus of Pope John XII we read in the Chronicles: He was a hunter and wholly lewd, so that he kept women openly. Therefore certain of the cardinals and Romans wrote secretly to Otto, prince of the Saxons, that the Church, moved with pity at the scandal, should hasten to Rome without delay. When the Pope learned of this, he had the nose of John the deacon, a cardinal, as adviser in this affair, cut off, and the hand of another John, a subdeacon, who had written the letters. Although he was often admonished by the emperor and the clergy about his correction, and was not corrected, he was deposed from the papacy by the emperor's protection, and by common vote Pope Leo was elected.

units.la: Tertia obiectio cauillosa est, quod à Papa non potest appellari. Sed ista cauillatio leuiter refellitur per prædictam. Nam ab illo, qui habet superiorem, potest appellari, sicut ostensum est in causa. Sed Papa habet superiorem, quia concilium generale. Cum etiam Papa hæreticus effectus minor sit quocunque catholico, vt ponit Glos. 24. quast. 1. cap. Achatius, vt superius allegatur. Igitur à Papa potest appellari. Præterea ab illo potest appellari, qui potest de hæresi accusari. Sed Papa potest de hæresi accusari, sicut patet de Symacho Papa, qui fuit accusatus de hæresi 2. quast. 7. Item, Balaam. Imo Papa non posset constituere, quod non posset accusari de hæresi, vt aperte dicit Glossa dist. 40. cap. si Papa, quæ loquens de Papa ait: hic specialiter fit mentio de hæresi. Ideo & si occulte statueret, quod non posset accusari de hæresi. Et respondet dicens: respondeo quod non, quia ex hoc periclitaretur tota Ecclesia. Ex quibus verbis aperte habetur, quod Papa potest de hæresi accusari. Et per consequens in illo casu ab eo poterit appellari. Item, ab excommunicato licet appellare. Sed Papa effectus hæreticus est ipso facto excommunicatus, vt notat Gloss. 29. q. 1. can. Achatius, quæ, vt sæpius est allegatum, dicit: hic casus in quo Papa incidit in canonem late sententia. Præterea effectus hæreticus nullam habet potestatem siue iurisdictionem, vt patet 24. q. 1. c. didicimus, vbi dicitur: Didicimus omnes omnino hæreticos & schismaticos nihil habere potestatis aut iuris, vbi de Papa hæretico nulla fit exceptio. Ergo ab ipso in hæresim lapso poterit appellari.
units.tr: The third captious objection is that the Pope cannot be appealed against. But this quibble is easily refuted by what was said above. From one who has a superior, an appeal can be made, as was shown in the case itself. The Pope has a superior, namely a general council. Moreover, a Pope who has become a heretic is less than any Catholic whatever, as the Gloss says at 24. quast. 1. cap. Achatius, cited above. Therefore an appeal can be made against the Pope. Furthermore, an appeal can be made against one who can be accused of heresy. The Pope can be accused of heresy, as is clear from Pope Symmachus, who was accused of heresy, 2. quast. 7. Item, Balaam. Indeed, the Pope could not decree that he could not be accused of heresy, as the Gloss plainly says at dist. 40. cap. si Papa, where, speaking of the Pope, it states: Mention is made here specifically of heresy. Therefore, even if he secretly decreed that he could not be accused of heresy. And it answers, saying: I answer that he cannot, because on that account the whole Church would be imperilled. From these words it is clearly held that the Pope can be accused of heresy, and consequently in that case an appeal may be made against him. Again, an appeal may be made against one who is excommunicated. But a Pope who has become a heretic is excommunicated by the very fact, as the Gloss notes at 29. q. 1. can. Achatius, which, as has often been cited, says: This is the case in which the Pope falls under the canon of sentence passed by law. Furthermore, a heretic has no power or jurisdiction, as is clear at 24. q. 1. c. didicimus, where it is said: We have learned that all heretics and schismatics have no power or right whatever, where no exception is made for a heretic Pope. Therefore an appeal may be made against him once he has lapsed into heresy.

units.la: Quarta obiectio cauillosa est: Ad Fratres Minores non pertinet de caussa fidei se intromittere, sed solummodo ad prælatos, cuiusmodi sunt Cardinales Archiepiscopi & Episcopi. Sed ista cauillatio faciliter expugnatur. Quia quæstio fidei ad omnes pertinet Christianos, & non solus ad prælatos: imo etiam ad laicos. Vnde etiam in decretis dist. 96. c. vbi nam, dicit Nicolaus Papa: vbi ham legistis Imperatores antecessores vestros synodalibus conuentibus interfuisse: nisi forsitan de quibusdam, vbi de fide tractandum est, quæ causa vniuersalis est, quæ omnium communis est; quæ non solum ad clericos, verum etiam ad laicos, & ad omnes omnino pertinet Christianos. Igitur ad minores pertinet de causa fidei se intromittere, cum sint de numero Christianorum reputandi. Quod etiam ratione patet. Nam quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus tractari debet. Sed fides Christiana omnes tangit Christianos. Igitur omnes Christiani de fide impugnanda habent se intromittere, & ipsam quantum possunt defensare. Præterea qui errori, cum potest, non resistit, ipsum errorem conuincitur approbare, vt patet per sacros canones quamplures. Vnde Innocent. Papa, vt habetur dist. 83. cap. error, dicit sic: Error, cui non resistitur approbatur; & veritas cum minime defensatur, opprimitur: nec caret scrupulo societatis occulta, qui ma-nisesto facinori definit obuiare. Et Leo Papa, vt habetur extra, de hereticis. cap. qui alios, ait: qui alios cum potest ab errore non reuocat, seipsum errare demonstrat. Et idco Papa, vt habetur dist. 86. c facientis, inquit: Facientis procul dubio culpam habet: qui quod potest corrigere, negligit emendare. Ex quibus aperte patet, quod si Fratres Minores nolunt fautores hæresum supradictorum reputari, debent & tenentur viis eius possibilibus eisdem resistere, & fortiter obuiare.
units.tr: The fourth captious objection is that it is not for the Friars Minor to meddle in matters of faith, but only for prelates, such as cardinals, archbishops and bishops. But this quibble is easily overthrown. For the question of faith belongs to all Christians, and not only to prelates; indeed it belongs even to laymen. Hence also in the decretals, dist. 96. c. vbi nam, Pope Nicholas says: Where have you read that your predecessor emperors took part in synodal assemblies, except perhaps in those where matters of faith are to be treated, which is a universal cause, common to all; which pertains not only to clerics but also to laymen, and to all Christians without exception. Therefore it belongs to the Minor friars to meddle in a cause of faith, since they are to be reckoned among the number of Christians. This is also clear from reason. For what touches all ought to be dealt with by all. But the Christian faith touches all Christians. Therefore all Christians have to take up the impugning of error concerning the faith, and to defend it as far as they can. Furthermore, one who does not resist an error when he can is shown to approve of that error itself, as is clear from very many sacred canons. Hence Pope Innocent, as is found in dist. 83. cap. error, says thus: An error which is not resisted is approved; and when the truth is not defended, it is oppressed; nor is he free from the stain of secret complicity who fails to oppose a manifest crime. And Pope Leo, as is found in extra, de hereticis, cap. qui alios, says: He who does not recall others from error when he can shows that he himself is in error. And therefore the Pope, as is found in dist. 86. c. facientis, declares: He undoubtedly has the guilt of the doer who neglects to correct what he is able to correct. From these passages it is clearly evident that if the Minor friars do not wish to be regarded as supporters of the aforesaid heresies, they must and are bound by every possible means to resist these errors and to oppose them vigorously.

units.la: Quinta obiectio cauillosa est, quod quamuis Iohannes 22. errores & hæreses dogmatizauerit quamplures, tamen de pertinacia non potest conuinci. Et ideo præsumendum est, quod talia dixit solummodo recitando. Sed ista cauillatio potest multipliciter confutari: eo quod multipliciter eum fuisse pertinacem potest demonstrari. Primo, quia sæpius & legitime admonitus erroribus resistentes hostiliter verbis & factis est persecutus, ipsos diffamando, excommunicando, quos potuit etiam capiendo, incarcerando. Et plures in diris sceleratos suis erroribus consentientes ad dignitates Ecclesiasticas promouit & exaltauit. Quarto quia nullum permisit magistrari Parisiis in Theologica facultate, nisi prius tactis sacrosanctis iuraret, quod constitutiones suas supradictas sanas & catholicas in perpetuum reputaret, & nunquam ipsas impugnaret. Quinto quod Parisiis prædictos in Theologia magistrandos ad statum ascendere magisterii non permisit, nisi prius veritastes catholicas suis destitutionibus contrarias tactis sacrosanctis tanquam hæreses abiurarent. Sexto quia cum appellantes ab eo & suos errores impugnantes ad generale concilium rite legitime congregandum & celebrandum appellauerit: & se ad veniendum ad ipsum concilium in loco tuto constituendum paratos obtulerunt, volentes mundo ostendere ipsorum innocentiam, ipse nefiere concilium similiter impediuit, nolens suas nequitias discuti & ventilari. Ex praedictis alisque quampluribus aperte claret, quod ipse Iohannes 22. fuit pertinacissimus haereticus iudicandus.
units.tr: The fifth captious objection is that although John XXII propagated many errors and heresies, nevertheless he cannot be convicted of obstinacy; and therefore it must be presumed that he said such things only by way of reporting them. But this quibble can be refuted in many ways, since it can be shown in many ways that he was obstinate. First, because, when he had been repeatedly and lawfully admonished, he persecuted with hostile words and deeds those who resisted his errors, defaming them, excommunicating them, and, where he could, seizing them and imprisoning them. And he promoted and exalted to ecclesiastical dignities many men who were notoriously wicked and who agreed with his errors. Fourth, because he allowed no one to take the degree of master in theology at Paris unless he first swore on the sacred oaths that he would regard his aforesaid constitutions as sound and Catholic for ever, and would never impugn them. Fifth, because he did not permit those who were to be made masters in theology at Paris to ascend to the status of mastership unless they first abjured, with their hands on the sacred oaths, the Catholic truths contrary to his decrees as heresies. Sixth, because, when those who appealed from him and impugned his errors had appealed to a general council to be lawfully and duly convened and held, and had offered themselves ready to come to that council, to be placed in a safe location, wishing to show the world their innocence, he likewise impeded the council, unwilling for his wickednesses to be examined and brought to light. From the aforesaid and from many other things it is clearly evident that John XXII himself was to be judged a most obstinate heretic.

units.la: Sexta obiectio cavillosa est, quod cum multitudo Christianorum praedictum Iohannem 22. usque ad mortem pro Papa habuerint, & absque impugnatione dictorum suorum eidem obedierint, Fratres Minores ipsius impugnatores, eo quod pauci fuerunt, debebant se multitudini per omnia conformasse. Sed huic cavillationi respondet ipse Deus, qui Exod. 33. c. praecipit dicens: non sequeris turbam ad faciendum malum: nec in iudicio plurimorum acquiesces sententiae, ut a vero devies. Quae auctoritas sufficit pro illa obiectione.
units.tr: The sixth captious objection is that since the multitude of Christians held the aforesaid John XXII as Pope until his death, and obeyed him without challenge to his sayings, the Minor friars, who were his opponents, ought, because they were few, to have conformed in every respect to the multitude. But God himself answers this quibble, who commands in Exod. 33. c., saying: You shall not follow a crowd to do evil; nor shall you yield to the judgement of the many so as to turn aside from the truth. This authority is sufficient against that objection.

units.la: Septima obiectio cavillosa est, quod non potest negari, quin ipsi Fratres Minores Iohanni 22. opponentes sunt excommunicati. Cum ipse Iohannes 22. saepe & saepius per se & per alios sententiam excommunicationis protulit contra eos. Sed ad istam cavillationem leviter potest responderi: eo quod canonicae sanctiones aperte testantur, nullum haereticum quicquam habere potestatis aut iuris. Unde Cyprianus, ut 14. q. 1. c. didicimus, ait: didicimus omnes omnino haereticos & schismaticos nihil habere potestatis aut iuris. Item, eadem ca. 1. quaest. si ergo, sic habetur: si ergo Episcopus in haeresim lapsus est, antiqua excommunicatione damnatus alios damnare non potest. Excommunicatus enim alios excommunicare non valet. Certum est autem, quod omnis haeresis est damnata & omnis haereticus est excommunicatus per concilium generale, ut habetur extra de haereticis c. excommunicamus & c. excommunicamus secundo. Igitur Iohannes 22. incidit in haereses damnatas: & ideo fuit excommunicatus. Et per consequens alios excommunicare non potuit. Item, c. & q. praedictis, si autem, sic habetur: Si autem ex corde suo novam haeresim confinxerit: ex quo talia praedicare coepit, neminem damnare potuit: quia non potest damnare quicquam iam prostratus. Et eodem c. & 9. Item cum Dominus, sic habetur: Liquido constat cum, qui ab integritate catholicae fidei recedit, maledicendi vel benedicendi potestatem minime habere dignoscitur. Catholicum namque, utpote se superiorem, maledicere non valet, in alienum a fide tanquam in sibi aequalem, sententiam dare non potest. Et eodem c. 2. q. hu auctoritatibus, dicitur sic: hu auctoritatibus perspicue monstratur, ex quo aliquis contra fidem tentat aliqua dicere, nec deiicere aliquem valet, nec damnare. Et quibus luculenter ostenditur, quod praedictus Iohannes 22. haeresi, ut probatum est, multipliciter maculatus Fratres Minores ab ipso appellantes & eius haereses improbantes excommunicare non potuit quoquomodo. Rursum esto sine praeiudicio, quod Iohannes 22. non fuisset haereticus (quod tamen est) adhuc sua excommunicationis sententia in praedictos fratres lata omnino fuisset nulla. Nam per appellationem rite interpositam eximitur appellans a potestate & iurisdictione illius, a quo appellavit, extra, de appell. c. propositum. Et appellatione pendente non potest nec debet in praeiudicium appellantis aliquid innovari, nec ei gravamen aliquod inferri 2. q. 7. c. appellatione. & ff. nihil innovari appellatione pendente. L. 1. & 16. Ad quem appellatum est habet de tali appellatione cognoscere, & non is, a quo appellatum est, extra, de ap. c. ut debitus. & c. cum speciali. Si autem ille, a quo appellatum est, posset de tali appellatione cognoscere, in causa propria ius sibi dicere posset. Sed nullus debet in causa propria ius sibi dicere, 23. quaest. 4. c. inter querelas. & q. 5. de occidendis. & q. 4. c. ne quis in causa propria iudicet vel ius sibi dicat, per totum. Sed Iohannes 22. prius & contra appellationem legitime interpositam, & non ante Fratres praefatos Minores de facto (licet de iure non posset) excommunicavit. Quare esto, quod idem Iohannes tunc temporis fuisset verus Papa: quod non est verum: sententia sua contra commemoratos Fratres lata, nulla fuit omnino reputanda.
units.tr: The seventh captious objection is that it cannot be denied that the Minor friars themselves, who opposed John XXII, are excommunicated, since John XXII himself often and repeatedly, both personally and through others, pronounced sentence of excommunication against them. But this quibble can be answered easily, since the canonical sanctions clearly attest that no heretic has any power or right whatever. Hence Cyprian, as at 14. q. 1. c. didicimus, says: We have learned that all heretics and schismatics have no power or right whatever. Likewise, in the same canon, q. 1, the passage si ergo reads thus: If therefore a bishop has lapsed into heresy, and is condemned by an ancient excommunication, he cannot condemn others. For one who is excommunicated is not able to excommunicate others. But it is certain that every heresy has been condemned and every heretic excommunicated by a general council, as is found in extra, de haereticis, c. excommunicamus and c. excommunicamus secundo. Therefore John XXII fell into condemned heresies, and so was excommunicated; and consequently he could not excommunicate others. Again, at the canon and question aforesaid, si autem, it reads thus: But if he has invented a new heresy from his own heart, then from the time he began to preach such things he could condemn no one, because one who has already been overthrown cannot condemn anything. And in the same canon, at 9: Item cum Dominus, it reads thus: It is plainly established that one who withdraws from the integrity of the Catholic faith is known to have no power to curse or to bless. For a Catholic, as being superior, cannot curse, and one who is alien to the faith cannot pass sentence on him as on an equal. And in the same canon, 2. q. 1, from these authorities it is said: From these authorities it is plainly shown that when someone attempts to say anything against the faith, he cannot cast out or condemn anyone. By which it is clearly shown that the aforesaid John XXII, having been, as has been proved, many times stained with heresy, could not in any way excommunicate the Minor friars who appealed from him and disapproved of his heresies. Moreover, even if we grant, without prejudice, that John XXII had not been a heretic (which in fact he was), his sentence of excommunication pronounced against the aforesaid friars would nevertheless have been wholly null. For by an appeal lawfully lodged the appellant is removed from the power and jurisdiction of the one from whom he appealed, extra, de appellationibus, c. propositum. And while an appeal is pending, nothing may or should be altered to the prejudice of the appellant, nor any burden inflicted on him, 2. q. 7. c. appellatione, and ff. nihil innovari appellatione pendente, L. 1 and 16. The matter appealed must be heard by the court to which the appeal is made, and not by the one from which the appeal is made, extra, de appellationibus, c. ut debitus, and c. cum speciali. But if the one from whom the appeal is made could judge such an appeal, he would be able to give judgement in his own cause. But no one ought to give judgement in his own cause, 23. quaest. 4. c. inter querelas, and q. 5. de occidendis, and q. 4. c. ne quis in causa propria iudicet vel ius sibi dicat, throughout. But John XXII, before the friars had appealed, and against a lawfully lodged appeal, excommunicated the aforesaid Minor friars de facto (though he could not do so de iure). Therefore, even if the same John had at that time been the true Pope (which is not the case), his sentence pronounced against the said friars must be regarded as wholly null.

units.la: Octava obiectio cavillosa est, quod quantumcunque Iohannes 22. erraverit, & pertinax haereticus fuerit: successor suus Dominus Benedictus 12. est catholicus & verus Papa. Et ideo supranominati Fratres, Iohanni 22. resistentes, in hoc quod Benedicto 12. non parent, imo, ut dicitur, ipsum realiter impugnant, damnabiliter delinquunt, & incidunt in poenas rebellibus Romanae Ecclesiae a iure taxatas. Sed huic cavillationi breviter verbis respondetur, quod solo nomine Benedictus duodecimus incidit in laqueum tortuosum, qui errores & haereses praedecessoris sui defendo, & approbando suos & suas facit esse. Ipse enim doctrinam pestiferam praedecessoris sui approbat, & potenter defendit, ostendens se cum praecessore suo praefato haereticum esse manifestum, ut signanter de eo posset dici verbum Eccles. 30. c. sic scriptum, ubi sic legitur: Mortuus est pater illius, & quasi non est mortuus. Similem enim sibi reliquit post se. Quare non debet dici Papa catholicus, sed fautor haereticorum & haereticae pravitatis. Imo haereticus & peior quam fuerit praedecessor suus, teste Urbano Papa, qui, ut habetur 24. quaest. 3. c. qui aliorum, dicit in haec verba: Qui aliorum errorem defendit, multo est damnabilior illis qui errant. Quia non solum ille errat, sed etiam aliis offendicula erroris praeparat & confirmat. Unde quia Magister erroris est, non tamen haereticus, sed etiam haeresiarcha dicendus est. Praeterea iste nomine non re Benedictus 12. ideo in sacra Pagina Magister, & ideo citius & virilius deberet haeresibus resistere, & fidem catholicam defendere, quam praedecessor suus, qui in Facultate Theologica omnino fuit ignarus. Ergo fauendo haeresibus & haereticae pravitati, nec non ipsis haereticis damnabilior est censendus, quam praedecessor suus. Et per consequens non summus pontifex, sed iimus pontifex est merito nominandus. Amplius, iste nomine non re Benedictus peior est haeresis auctor, quam fuerit praedecessor suus: quia simpliciter conatur totam fidem catholicam ponere in voluntate & dispositione sua & successorum suorum, sicut in quadam constitutione, imo verius destitutio-
units.tr: The eighth captious objection is that, however much John XXII may have erred and however stubborn a heretic he was, his successor, Lord Benedict XII, is a catholic and true Pope. Therefore the aforesaid Friars, who resisted John XXII, are said to disobey Benedict XII and, as they put it, to attack him in fact. They thereby sin damnably and incur the penalties that the law lays down for rebels against the Roman Church. But this quibble can be answered briefly. Benedict XII is a Pope in name only, and he falls into a twisted snare: by defending and approving the errors and heresies of his predecessor, he makes them his own. For he approves and powerfully defends the pestilent doctrine of his predecessor, showing himself to be manifestly a heretic together with that predecessor. So the word of Eccles. 30. could be applied to him, where it is written: "He is dead, that father of his, and it is as if he were not dead, for he has left behind him one like himself." Therefore he ought not to be called a catholic Pope, but a supporter of heretics and of heretical depravity. Indeed he is a heretic, and worse than his predecessor, as Pope Urban testifies, who says, as it is found in 24. quaest. 3. c. qui aliorum, in these words: "He who defends the error of others is far more damnable than those who err. For he not only errs himself, but also prepares and strengthens stumbling-blocks of error for others. Hence, since he is a master of error, though not himself a heretic, he is to be called not only a heretic but a heresiarch." Moreover, Benedict XII, a Master in sacred Scripture in name only and not in reality, ought for that very reason to have resisted heresies more quickly and manfully and to have defended the catholic faith more than his predecessor, who was entirely ignorant of the Faculty of Theology. Therefore, by favouring heresies and heretical depravity, and by favouring the heretics themselves, he is to be judged more damnable than his predecessor. And consequently he should rightly be named not the highest Pope but the lowest Pope. Furthermore, Benedict XII, a heresiarch in name only and not in reality, is a worse author of heresy than his predecessor was. For he simply tries to place the whole catholic faith in his own will and disposition and that of his successors, as he plainly shows in a certain constitution, or rather decree, which he is said to have imposed on the Order of Friars Minor to be observed.

units.la: Nnnn 2 tutione, quam ordini Fratrum Minorum, vt fertur, tenendam imposuit, indicat manifeste. Quæ quidem destitutio præfatam hæresim retro seculis inauditam continens talis est: Distringimus inhibentes, ne postquam super negotio fidei quæstio seu dubitatio aliqua, super qua sunt opiniones aduersæ vel diuersæ, deducta fuerit ad Apostolicæ Sedis examen, quisquam extunc alterutram partem declinare, eligere vel approbare præsumat, sed super ea Sedis eiusdem iudicium seu declaratio expectetur. Hæc verba eius veneno plena. Ex quibus expresse sequitur, quod nulli reuelato à Deo, si super eo moueatur quæstio seu dubitatio coram Papa, de quo etiam possunt esse opiniones diuersæ & aduersæ, debet aliquis Frater Minor, nec per consequens aliquis Christianus firmiter adhærere. Quia non debet secundum præfatam destitutionem suam alterutram partem eligere, determinare vel approbare: sed voluntatē Papæ in hoc expectare. Sed de omni reuelato à Deo potest quæstio mora deduci ad examen summi pontificis: & etiam possunt esse opiniones diuersæ & aduersæ. Ergo nulli tali reuelato à Deo debet Frater Minor, & per consequens nec Christianus ante sententiam summi pontificis firmiter adhærere, sed voluntatē summi pontificis totaliter expectare. Et idem potest dici de articulis fidei, & de omni contento in scriptura diuina. Quia super quolibet articulo fidei, & sub omni contento in scriptura diuina, potest moueri quæstio, & ad examen deduci summi pontificis: super quo possunt esse etiam opiniones diuersæ & aduersæ. Ergo secundum mandatum istius nomine non re Benedicti 12. nulli articulo fidei in scriptura sacra contento, si super ea moueatur quæstio, quę ducatur ad examen summi pontificis, & super eo possunt esse opiniones diuersæ & aduersæ, debet aliquis Frater Minor, nec per consequens Christianus quicunq; quamcunq; partem determinare, eligere vel approbare. Quod est erroneum, iniquum & blasphemum. Nam ex eo sequitur, igitur si talis quæstio: fuit Deus ab æterno vel non? vel, est Christiana fides vera vel non? & sic de aliis quibuscunq; quæstionibus moueatur coram summo pontifice, cum possunt de huiusmodi quæstione esse inter catholicos & hæreticos opiniones diuersæ & aduersæ: talis quæstionis nullus Frater Minor (& eadem ratione nullus Christianus) debet veritatem confiteri, donec summus pontifex suam declarauerit voluntatem. Quod non est aliud, quam fidem nostram totaliter in arbitrio hominis constituere, & quid credere debeamus ab eo expectare. Sed hoc sapit hæresim manifestam, cum dicat Beatus Paulus Apostolus 1. Cor. 2. Fides vestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in virtute Dei. Unde licet ille nomine non re Bened. 12. prædecessori suo, in doctrina hæretica nunquam participasset, nec hæresès ipsius tanquam propriam defendisset & approbasset: tamen propter istam solam hæresim, cuius est auctor, inventor & institutor, est inter hæreticos computandus, & ab omnibus catholicis facta ipsius scientibus merito detestandus. Cum dogmatisans contra fidem catholicam maxime scienter non solum à iure humano, sed etiam à scriptura sacra sit aperte excommunicatus. Etiam si esset possibile, quod angelus de cælo doceret contra fidem, dicente Beato Paulo ad Gal. 1. Si nos aut angelus de cœlo euangelisset vobis praeterquam euangelisauimus vobis, anathema sit. Et post: Si quis vobis euangelisauerit, praeter id quod accepistis, anathema sit. Veruntamen quia ista hæresis cum pertinentiis suis, aliisq; nomine non re Benedicti, 12. tangentibus est in quodam opere speciali maiori à me diffuse tractata, discussa & reprobata: Ideo de ipsa ad præsens non plus me intromitto. Sed ne prolixitas odiosa complurib[us] tædium generet, finem huic opusculo in hoc loco concedo.
units.tr: tutione, which he imposed on the Order of Friars Minor, as is reported, to be held, plainly shows this. The decree itself, which contains the aforesaid heresy unheard of for centuries, is as follows: "We command and forbid that, after any question or doubt concerning a matter of faith, on which there are differing or opposing opinions, has been brought before the examination of the Apostolic See, anyone presume thenceforth to lean towards, choose or approve either side, but that the judgment or declaration of that See be awaited concerning it." These words are full of poison. From them it follows expressly that no one, unless he has been revealed by God, ought to adhere firmly to any matter if a question or doubt about it arises before the Pope, on which there may also be differing and opposing opinions. A Friar Minor, and consequently no Christian, must not, according to that decree, choose, determine or approve either side, but must await the will of the Pope in the matter. Yet a question about any truth revealed by God can be brought by delay to the examination of the supreme Pontiff, and there can also be differing and opposing opinions about it. Therefore no Friar Minor, and consequently no Christian, ought to adhere firmly to any such truth revealed by God before the sentence of the supreme Pontiff, but must wholly await the will of the supreme Pontiff. The same can be said of the articles of faith and of everything contained in divine Scripture. For a question can be raised about any article of faith and about anything contained in divine Scripture, and brought to the examination of the supreme Pontiff, and about it too there can be differing and opposing opinions. Therefore, according to the command of this Benedict XII, who is Pope in name only, no Friar Minor, and consequently no Christian whatever, may determine, choose or approve either side on any article of faith contained in holy Scripture, if a question is raised about it, brought to the examination of the supreme Pontiff, and there are differing and opposing opinions about it. This is erroneous, unjust and blasphemous. For it follows from this that if such a question is raised before the supreme Pontiff, whether God was from eternity or not, or whether the Christian faith is true or not, and likewise about all other questions, since there can be differing and opposing opinions between catholics and heretics about such a question, then no Friar Minor (and for the same reason no Christian) may confess the truth about that question until the supreme Pontiff has declared his will. This is nothing other than to place our faith wholly at the discretion of man, and to expect from him what we ought to believe. But this savours of manifest heresy, since the blessed Apostle Paul says in 1. Cor. 2.: "Let your faith not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." Hence, although that Benedict XII, a Pope in name only, had never shared in his predecessor's heretical doctrine, nor defended and approved those heresies as his own, yet for this one heresy alone, of which he is the author, inventor and founder, he is to be counted among the heretics, and rightly detested by all catholics who know of his deeds. He is manifestly excommunicated not only by human law but by Holy Scripture itself, since he teaches against the catholic faith most knowingly. Even if it were possible for an angel from heaven to teach against the faith, the blessed Paul says in Gal. 1.: "If we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you otherwise than we have preached to you, let him be accursed." And afterwards: "If anyone preaches to you beyond what you have received, let him be accursed." Nevertheless, since this heresy, with its connections and with the other matters concerning Benedict XII in name only, has been treated, discussed and refuted at length in a certain larger special work of mine, I will not meddle further with it here. But so that tedious length may not breed weariness in many readers, I bring this little work to an end at this point.

units.la: IODOCI BADII ASCENSII, PROFESSORIS Regii Parisiensis SVMMARIA, SEV EPITOMATA CXXIV. CAPITVLORVM OPERIS XC. DIERVM M. GVILHELMI DE OCKAM, DILIGENTER COLLECTA.
units.tr: Summaries, or Epitomes, of the 124 Chapters of the Work of Ninety Days of Master William of Ockham, Diligently Collected by Josse Badius Ascensius, Professor at the Royal College of Paris.

units.la: SVMMARIA, SEV EPITOMATA OPERIS NONAGINTA DIERUM, M. Guilhelmi de Ockam.
units.tr: Summaries, or Epitomes, of the Work of Ninety Days, by Master William of Ockham.

units.la: Peris nonaginta dierum correspondentis sexto tractatui tertie partis Dialogi M. Guilhelmi de Ockam, quod à nonaginta diebus, quibus compilatum est, inscribitur, centum & viginti quatuor in eo contentorum capitulorum Epitomata seu summaria ad lectorum utilitatem colligimus. Sed primo compendiosam operis divisionem præponemus.
units.tr: Here we collect, for the benefit of readers, the summaries or epitomes of the one hundred and twenty-four chapters contained in the sixth treatise of the third part of the Dialogue of Master William of Ockham, which is entitled from the ninety days in which it was compiled, the Ninety Days. But first we set out a brief division of the work.

units.la: Operis nonaginta dierum divisio.
units.tr: Division of the Work of Ninety Days.

units.la: Dividit itaq; opus hoc in quatuor partes. Quarum prima continet prologum seu præfationem ipsius Ockam. Secunda proœmium constitutionis Quia vir reprobus. Tertia tres tractatus secundum tres constitutiones Iohannis 22. in ea discussas. Quarta vero & ultima conclusionem continet. Prima pars, quia præfationis loco ponitur, nullum habet capitulum. Secunda pars unum continet capitulum. Tertia 122. quia tres habet tractatus, quorum primus tractat de constitutione Ad conditorem canonum, incipit cap. secundo. Secundus tractat de constitutione Cum inter, & incipit cap. 82. Tertius tractat de constitutione Quia quorundam, & incipit cap. 120. Quarta pars unum duntaxat habet capitulum continens conclusionem, & incipit cap. ultim. hoc est 124. dicti operis.
units.tr: This work is therefore divided into four parts. The first contains the prologue, or preface, of Ockham himself. The second contains the proem of the constitution Quia vir reprobus. The third contains three treatises, according to the three constitutions of John XXII discussed in it. The fourth and last contains the conclusion. The first part, since it stands in place of a preface, has no chapter. The second part contains one chapter. The third, which has three treatises, runs to 122 chapters: the first treatise, on the constitution Ad conditorem canonum, begins at chapter 2; the second, on the constitution Cum inter, begins at chapter 82; the third, on the constitution Quia quorundam, begins at chapter 120. The fourth part has only one chapter, containing the conclusion, and begins at the last chapter, that is, the 124th of the said work.

units.la: In prologo praelibatur operis huius materia, de qua tractaturus est: Et eiusdem divisio.
units.tr: In the prologue the subject matter of this work, which he is about to treat, is previewed, together with its division.

units.la: Capitulum primum continet in prima sua parte exordium constitutionis Quia vir reprobus. In secunda autem eius parte ponitur dicti textus impugnatio. Nam in cæteris fere capitulis hic seruatur procedendi modus, ut prima capituli parte recitentur verba textus impugnati, hoc est Iohannis 22. In secunda eadem verba per Guilhelmum Ockam declarantur. In tertia autem quotiens aliquid contra appellantem, hoc est Fratrem Michaelem Cezena constitutum est, recitantur per dictum M. Guilhelmum Ockam dictæ constitutionis impugnationes. In vltima autem parte, quæ aliquando tertia est, aliquando quarta, semper notantur & exponuntur verba textus. In primo autem capitulo quia verba textus de se patent, non ponitur explanatio eorundem: sed quia appellantem taxant, impugnantur ab aduersariis in quatuor. Primo autem nituntur ostendere, quod depositio dicti Fratris Michaelis, de qua in litera fit mentio, de facto processit, & nullo modo de iure. Secundo quod propter missionem libellorum suorum non sit reprobandus. Tertio quod propter eandem non sit hæreticus iudicandus. Quarto quod impugnationes factæ contra tres dictas constitutiones Iohannis 22. sint validæ censendæ. Primum probatur duabus viis: in quarum prima probatur incidentaliter, Quod licet in causa hæresis à Papa appellare. Secundum probatur in secunda parte: tertium in tertia: & quartum infertur in quarta, vbi ad litteræ declarationem acceditur.
units.tr: The first chapter contains, in its first part, the opening of the constitution Quia vir reprobus. In its second part the said text is attacked. For in nearly all the other chapters this method of proceeding is observed: in the first part of the chapter the words of the attacked text, that is of John XXII, are recited; in the second, the same words are explained by William of Ockham; in the third, whenever something is laid down against the appellant, that is Brother Michael of Cesena, the objections to the said constitution are recited by the said Master William of Ockham; and in the last part, which is sometimes the third and sometimes the fourth, the words of the text are noted and expounded. In this first chapter, however, since the words of the text are plain in themselves, no explanation of them is given; but because they censure the appellant, his opponents attack them on four points. First, they try to show that the deposition of the said Brother Michael, mentioned in the letter, proceeded by fact and in no way by right. Second, that he is not to be condemned on account of the sending of his little books. Third, that for the same reason he is not to be judged a heretic. Fourth, that the objections raised against the three said constitutions of John XXII are to be considered valid. The first point is proved in two ways: in the first of these it is proved incidentally, that it is lawful to appeal from the Pope in a case of heresy. The second is proved in the second part, the third in the third part, and the fourth is inferred in the fourth part, where the letter is explained.

units.la: Prima constitutionis capitula.
units.tr: The chapters of the first constitution.

units.la: Capitulum secundum. In prima parte recitat principium impugnationis appellantis contra constitutionem Ad conditorem: & contra eam ab impugnato instatur. In secunda parte ponitur primæ partis explanatio, & modi procedendi impugnantium declaratio. In tertia parte recitantur eorundem impugnationes, quibus probant falsum esse, quod in rebus vsu consumptibilibus nec vsus iuris nec vsus facti potest à rei proprietate seu dominio separari. Pro cuius declaratione decem sunt. Primo ponitur quadruplex huius nominis vsus acceptio. Secundo quid vsus facti sit declaratur. Tertio quid vsus iuris, & quomodo diuiditur. Quarto quid ius utendi, & quomodo ab vsu iuris differt. Quinto qui sint simplices vsuarii. Sexto quæ sint tres vsu consumptibiles, & quomodo pecunia inter eas sit. Septimo quid dominium sit, & quomodo variè accipiantur hæc nomina, Dominium, Dominus, Dominator, Dominari & similia in diuersis scientiarum facultatibus. Octauo quid proprietas in scientiis legalibus significet. Nono quomodo varie accipiantur haec vocabula, meum, tuum, suum, ipsius, habere. Decimo inferuntur ex dictis Iohannis vigesim. secund. duo errores: quorum primus est, quod usus facti separatus a proprietate rei in rebus usu consumptibilibus haberi non potest. Secundus est, quod in talibus rebus ius utendi separatum a proprietate seu dominio rei habendi non potest, de quibus agitur cap. 3. parte tertia. In quinta parte capituli ponitur notatio literalis.
units.tr: Chapter 2. In its first part it recites the opening of the objection of the appellant against the constitution Ad conditorem, and against it the objector presses his case. In the second part the explanation of the first part is given, and the procedure of the objectors is set out. In the third part their objections are recited, by which they prove it false that in things consumed by use neither the use of right nor the use of fact can be separated from the ownership or dominion of the thing. For the explanation of this there are ten points. First, the fourfold meaning of the word use is given. Second, what the use of fact is, is explained. Third, what the use of right is, and how it is divided. Fourth, what the right of using is, and how it differs from the use of right. Fifth, who are the simple users. Sixth, what things are consumed by use, and what place money has among them. Seventh, what dominion is, and how the words dominion, lord, ruler, to rule and similar words are variously understood in different branches of learning. Eighth, what property signifies in the legal sciences. Ninth, how the words mine, yours, his, its, to have are variously understood. Tenth, two errors are drawn from the words of John XXII in the twenty-second [constitution]: the first is that the use of a thing, separated from the property of the thing, cannot be had in things consumed by use; the second is that in such things the right of using cannot be separated from the property or dominion of the thing to be had, which is treated in chapter 3 of the third part. In the fifth part of the chapter the letter is noted.

units.la: Cap. 3. In prima parte recitantur verba Iohannis 22, quibus circa ea, quae impugnantur, intentionem suam exprimit, ut declaratur in secunda parte. In tertia parte recitantur repugnationes adversariorum eius, quo ad quatuor dicta. Primum quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus ius utendi haberi non potest. Secundum, quod in eisdem rebus ius utendi a dominio non separetur. Tertium, quod in eisdem rebus actus utendi haberi non potest. Quartum quod huiusmodi rebus non contingit uti, sed abuti. Primum dictum impugnando ostendunt rationes impugnati ad intentum eius non facere. Circa quod plura de usura & de contractibus, qui fiunt in fraudem usurae. Item, de usurario, in quo secundum Chrysostomum differt a locante, & alia notatu digna adducuntur. Ostenditur etiam, ut in margine notatum est, quod iuri naturali renunciare non licet. In quarta parte notatur & explicatur littera: & nonnulla inseruntur notanda de materia usuratum.
units.tr: Chapter 3. In the first part the words of John XXII are recited, in which he expresses his intention concerning the matters attacked, as is explained in the second part. In the third part the objections of his adversaries are recited, on four assertions: first, that in things consumed by use the right of using cannot be had; second, that in the same things the right of using is not separated from dominion; third, that in the same things the act of using cannot be had; fourth, that such things cannot be used, but only abused. In attacking the first assertion, the objectors show that the arguments of the attacked party do not bear on his purpose. On this point many things are said concerning usury and the contracts made in fraud of usury. Likewise, concerning the usurer, in whom, according to Chrysostom, he differs from the one who lets out for hire; and other matters worth noting are adduced. It is also shown, as is noted in the margin, that it is not lawful to renounce natural law. In the fourth part the letter is noted and explained, and several things worth noting about the matter of usury are added.

units.la: Cap. 4. In prima parte impugnatus ad ea, quae impugnans propositit, nititur respondere, ut declaratur in secunda parte. In tertia parte pro impugnatione praedictorum assignantur ab impugnatoribus tria puncta, ut in principio recitatur. Habentur autem multa scitu digna, quae in marginibus indicantur. Inter quae sunt de iure utendi communissimo collato in primis parentibus toti generi humano. Item, de iure, quo res, quae in nullius est dominio, occupanti conceditur. De primis credentibus, quod non habebant liberum dominium disponendi ad libitum de rebus oblatis, sicut ante habuerunt. Item, quod sacra scriptura non semper seruat in narrando ordinem rei gestae. Item, quod ad concordandum scripturas tempora distinguenda sunt. Item, de bonis Ecclesiasticorum, quo iure ad eos spectent. Item, de modo arguendi peccante per fallaciam secundum quid ad simpliciter. Quorum plura notantur in quarta parte, quae literam exponit.
units.tr: Chapter 4. In the first part the party attacked tries to answer what the objector has proposed, as is explained in the second part. In the third part three points are assigned by the objectors in support of their objection, as is recited at the beginning. There are many things worth knowing, which are pointed out in the margins. Among them are: the right of use, most common, conferred on our first parents over the whole human race; likewise, the right by which a thing that belongs to no one is granted to the one who takes possession of it; concerning the first believers, that they did not have free dominion to dispose at will of the goods offered, as they had before; likewise, that Holy Scripture does not always keep to the order of events in its narration; likewise, that in reconciling the Scriptures the times must be distinguished; likewise, concerning the goods of ecclesiastics, and by what right they belong to them; likewise, concerning the manner of arguing from a fallacy of qualified to unqualified statement. Many of these are noted in the fourth part, which expounds the letter.

units.la: Cap. 5. In prima parte continuatur responsio impugnati, ut declaratur in secunda. In tertia parte recitantur impugnationes adversariorum, qui ex dictis quatuor errores colligunt. Quorum primus est, quod communitas primorum credentium habuit domos & agros quo ad dominium & proprietatem. Secundus, quod Apostoli habuerunt praedia in Iudea. Tertius, quod ideo in Iudea non retinuerunt praedia, quia transituri erant ad gentes. Quartus, quod Apostolis licuit praedia in Iudaea apud gentes possidere. Qui errores ibidem improbantur. Quartus autem praecipue auctoritate sancti Thomae de Aquino. In quarta parte explanantur verba textus: & notatur de causarum aliquibus rei multitudine & sufficientia, & de aliis quibusdam.
units.tr: Chapter 5. In the first part the answer of the attacked party is continued, as is explained in the second. In the third part the objections of the adversaries are recited, who draw four errors from the said points. The first of these is that the community of the first believers had houses and fields as to dominion and ownership. The second, that the Apostles had estates in Judea. The third, that they did not keep estates in Judea for this reason, that they were about to go to the Gentiles. The fourth, that it was lawful for the Apostles to possess estates in Judea among the Gentiles. These errors are refuted there, the fourth chiefly on the authority of St Thomas Aquinas. In the fourth part the words of the text are explained, and it is noted concerning the multitude and sufficiency of some causes of things, and concerning certain other matters.

units.la: Cap. 6. In prima parte prosequitur sequentem particulam, quae declaratur in secunda parte. In tertia autem impugnantur dicta Iohannis 22. Et declaratur incidentaliter, quomodo non omne ius dat civilem actionem, sed solummodo ius fori. Item, in quo licentia potest vocari ius, & in quo non. Item, de iure fori & de iure poli distinguitur, & communitate omnium fidelium, & aliqua speciali. Et de Apostolis & aliis credentibus. Ostenditur etiam multiplicitas huius nominis usus, & quae significationum eius sit propria censenda. Item, acerbius inuehitur in praefatum Iohannem 22. & iudicatur scientiarum sermocinalium ignarus; cum tamen logica secundum doctores sanctos, Augustinum, Anshelmum & Hieronymum sit necessaria ad Theologicas difficultates. Quin & alia cognitu iucunda ibidem reperies. In quarta parte exponitur textus literaliter.
units.tr: Chapter 6. In the first part the following clause is pursued, which is explained in the second part. In the third part the words of John XXII are attacked, and it is explained incidentally how not every right gives a civil action, but only the right of the forum. Likewise, in what sense licence may be called a right, and in what sense not. Likewise, the right of the forum is distinguished from the right of heaven, and the community of all the faithful from some special community; and concerning the Apostles and other believers. The manifold meaning of this word use is also shown, and which of its meanings is to be considered proper. Likewise, he inveighs rather bitterly against the said John XXII and judges him ignorant of the sciences of language, although logic, according to the holy doctors Augustine, Anselm and Jerome, is necessary for theological difficulties. Indeed you will find other pleasant things worth knowing in the same place. In the fourth part the text is expounded literally.

units.la: Cap. 7. In prima parte ponitur alia pars constitutionis dictae, quae in secunda parte declaratur. In tertia impugnatur, & in quarta literaliter exponitur.
units.tr: Chapter 7. The first part sets out another part of the said constitution, which is explained in the second part. The third part attacks it, and the fourth expounds the text literally.

units.la: Cap. 8. In prima parte recitat responsionem impugnati ad obiectionem appellantis, quae nititur ostendere, quod doctrina dicti impugnati omnem religionem habentem votum paupertatis destruat, ut dilucide declaratur in parte secunda. In tertia parte impugnatores contra responsionem impugnati quadrupliciter procedere recitantur. Primo, comprobando assertionem appellantis, videlicet quod impugnatus omnem huiusmodi religionem destruat. Secundo demonstrando, quod specialiter confundat regulam Beati Francisci. Tertio, ostendendo quomodo usus facti (ut saepe tactum est) a proprietate & dominio in rebus usu consumptibilibus possit separari. Quarto mentem appellantis specificando. In quarta parte explicando literam inseritur, quod propter modum loquendi Iuristarum non est modus loquendi Theologorum improprius reputandus. Infertur etiam conclusio principalis appellantis, scilicet quod Fratres Minores consumunt res, neque ut proprias, neque ut communes eis quantum ad dominium.
units.tr: Chapter 8. In the first part he recites the reply of the author under attack to the objection of the appellant, which seeks to show that the teaching of the said author destroys every religious order that has a vow of poverty, as is clearly explained in the second part. In the third part the opponents are described as proceeding against the author's reply in four ways. First, by proving the appellant's assertion, namely that the author under attack destroys every such order. Second, by showing that he especially confounds the rule of Blessed Francis. Third, by showing how the use of a thing (as has often been touched upon) can be separated from ownership and dominion over things that are consumed by use. Fourth, by specifying the appellant's meaning. In the fourth part, explaining the text, it is added that, because of the way of speaking of the lawyers, the way of speaking of the theologians is not to be regarded as improper. The principal conclusion of the appellant is also drawn, namely that the Friars Minor consume things, and hold them neither as their own nor as held in common as regards dominion.

units.la: Cap. 9. In prima parte recitat mentem impugnati. Qui (ut clarius habetur in secunda parte) asserit, quod post diuisionem rerum inter primos credentes quilibet tam Apostolus quam Dominus & proprietarius portionis sibi assignatae. In tertia parte recitantur improbationes impugnantium, qui tres errores & dictis impugnati colligunt & improbant. Et improbando primum errorem subtilissime concludunt Iohannem 22, qui determinationem Ecclesiae siue haereticam dicat siue non, eo quod eam improbet, haereticus sit censendus. Multis praeterea auctoritatibus sanctorum ostenduntur Apostoli omnium bonorum temporalium proprietatem abdicasse. Notantur etiam quatuor modi temporalia abdicandi. Item assignatur duplex paupertas actualis & habitualis. Ostenditur praeterea de clericis, de quibus rebus possent condere testamenta. Soluuntur deinde rationes impugnati. Pro quo primum ostenditur, quod verbum dare accipitur multipliciter. Plura sunt notanda passim in hoc capitulo, ut legenti patere potest. In quarta parte notatur & exponitur littera. In quo per exempla monstratur multiplicitas horum vocabulorum meum, tuum, suum, eius, ipsius, & similium possessivorum, & etiam huius verbi habere. Et inquiritur, cuius erant quaedam ad dominium caligae, quibus vtebatur beatus Petrus. Subduntur duae causae, propter quas primi credentes voluerunt omnia esse communia.
units.tr: Chapter 9. In the first part he recites the mind of the author under attack, who (as is more clearly set out in the second part) asserts that after the division of goods among the first believers, each one, the Apostle as well as the Lord and owner of the portion assigned to him. In the third part the refutations of the opponents are recited, who gather together and refute three errors from the statements of the author under attack. In refuting the first error, they very subtly conclude that John 22, whether he pronounces the decision of the Church heretical or not, is to be counted a heretic because he rejects it. Besides, by many authorities of the saints it is shown that the Apostles renounced ownership of all temporal goods. Four ways of renouncing temporal goods are also noted. Likewise a twofold poverty, actual and habitual, is assigned. Furthermore, it is shown concerning clergy what goods they could make wills about. The arguments of the author under attack are then resolved. In this connection it is first shown that the verb "to give" is taken in many senses. Many things are to be noted throughout this chapter, as the reader can see. In the fourth part the text is noted and explained, in which, by examples, the many meanings of the words meum, tuum, suum, eius, ipsius, and similar possessives, and also of the verb habere, are shown. And it is asked whose were certain things, such as the sandals under the dominion of which Blessed Peter used. Two causes are given why the first believers wanted all things to be held in common.

units.la: Cap. 10. In prima parte recitat textum impugnati, qui, vt patet in secunda parte, proponit aliam obiectionem appellantis ad eandem in sequenti capitulo responsurus. In tertia parte, quia verba appellantis sunt, approbando ea mentem eorum explanant. Quod idem in quarta parte iuxta consuetudinem idem faciendo ostenditur, quomodo monachi habentes proprietatem rerum in communi ab altissima paupertate Apostolorum & Minorum decidunt.
units.tr: Chapter 10. In the first part he recites the text of the author under attack, who, as appears in the second part, puts forward another objection of the appellant, to which he will reply in the following chapter. In the third part, since these are the appellant's words, they explain his meaning by approving them.
