The fourth part, following its usual practice, does the same and shows how monks who hold property in common fall away from the most high poverty of the Apostles and of the Friars Minor.

units.la: Cap. 11. In prima parte recitat responsionem impugnati ad obiectionem appellantis recitatam in capitulo praecedenti. In secunda declarat eandem. In tertia recitat impugnationes aduersariorum, qui primo improbant assertionem impugnati. Secundo respondent ad auctoritates per eum adductas. Et quantum ad primum praemittitur, qualiter sensus scripturae diuinae non ast nude accipiendus, sed respectiue ad accidentia & sequentia. Et subduntur duae conclusiones. Quarum prima est, quod Apostoli reliquerunt omnes possessiones, quo ad dominium tam speciale quam commune. Et hanc probant quadrupliciter. Secunda conclusio est, quod Apostoli omnium reliquerunt tam in speciali quam in communi, tam mobilium quam immobilium rerum proprietatem, quam probant determinationibus summorum pontificum, Nicolai tertii, Bonifacii octaui, & Clementis quinti. Ex verbis autem Nicolai tertii in decretali Exiit, quatuor conclusiones inferuntur de paupertate & abdicatione dominii. Distinguitur etiam triplex superfluum, & duplex sollicitudo circa temporalia: de quibus inuestigatur vtra sit necessitatis. Inquiritur etiam, an abdicatio proprietatis rerum in speciali & in communi exponat hominem periculo. In quarta parte notantur verba textus.
units.tr: Chapter 11. In the first part he recites the reply of the author under attack to the objection of the appellant recited in the preceding chapter. In the second part he explains the same. In the third part he recites the refutations of the adversaries, who first reject the assertion of the author under attack and secondly answer the authorities he has adduced. As to the first, it is premised how the sense of divine Scripture is not to be taken baldly, but with reference to circumstances and consequences. Two conclusions are then set down. The first is that the Apostles left all possessions, as regards dominion both special and common; and this they prove in four ways. The second conclusion is that the Apostles renounced, both in particular and in common, the ownership of movable and immovable goods alike; and this they prove by the decisions of the supreme pontiffs Nicholas III, Boniface VIII, and Clement V. From the words of Nicholas III in the decretal Exiit, four conclusions are drawn about poverty and the renunciation of dominion. A threefold superfluity is also distinguished, and a twofold care concerning temporal goods, and it is investigated which of these is necessary. It is also asked whether the renunciation of ownership of goods, whether in particular or in common, exposes a man to danger. In the fourth part the words of the text are noted.

units.la: Cap. 12. In prima parte, vt declaratu in secunda, recitat euasionem impugnati, nitentis verba beati Petri, Ecce nos reliquimus omnia &c. demonstrare intelligenda esse non de modo relinquendi quantum ad proprietatem, sed quantum ad affectionem & curam, maxime earum rerum, sine quibus haec vita transiri non potest. In tertia parte recitantur impugnationes vtriusque. Ostenditur enim, quomodo Apostoli omnia reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem, & non solum quo ad affectionem & curam. Et hoc sex rationibus. Item quod etiam illa reliquerunt quo ad dominium & proprietatem, sine quibus haec vita transiri non potest: & hoc tripliciter. In quarta parte notantur verba textus.
units.tr: Chapter 12. In the first part, as is made clear in the second, he recites the evasion of the author under attack, who strives to show from the words of Blessed Peter, "Behold, we have left all things," etc., that they are to be understood not of the manner of leaving as regards ownership, but as regards affection and care, especially for those things without which this life cannot be passed. In the third part the refutations of both sides are recited. For it is shown how the Apostles left all things as regards dominion and ownership, and not only as regards affection and care. And this by six arguments. Likewise, that they also left, as regards dominion and ownership, those things without which this life cannot be passed; and this in three ways. In the fourth part the words of the text are noted.

units.la: Cap. 13. In prima parte ponuntur verba Iohannis 22. In secunda declarantur eadem. In tertia probantur. In quarta litteraliter explicantur. Principaliter autem ostendunt impugnatores erroneum esse asserere, res quascunq; ab Apostolis post missionem Spiritus sancti, quo ad dominium & proprietatem possessas.
units.tr: Chapter 13. In the first part the words of John 22 are set down. In the second part the same are explained. In the third part they are proved. In the fourth they are expounded literally. Chiefly, the opponents show that it is erroneous to assert that all goods possessed by the Apostles after the mission of the Holy Spirit were possessed as regards dominion and ownership.

units.la: Cap. 14. In prima parte recitatur responsio impugnati ad obiectionem factam ab appellante per verba beati Clementis recitata 12. q. 1. cap. dilectissimus, vt latius patet in secunda parte. In tertia parte ponitur reprobatio dictae responsionis. Ostendendo, quod erroneum est, quod primi parentes, si non peccassent, habuissent tale dominium rerum in communi, quale nunc habent rerum possessores quo ad dominium. Notatur praeterea quale dominium habuissent primi parentes: & quomodo diuersarum rerum diuersi sunt modi vtendi. Et quomodo potestas vtendi angelis fuerit eis differenter, de aliis rebus concessa. In quarta parte exponendo literam, multa notatu dignissima inferuntur de statu primorum parentum. Ostenditur praeterea quasdam exemplis, quod non semper communia, dum diuiduntur, eodem modo fiunt propria, quod etiam communia, & conuerso. Distinguuntur etiam tria tempora primorum parentum, in quibus varie se habuerunt quo ad rerum dominia.
units.tr: Chapter 14. In the first part the reply of the author under attack is recited to the objection made by the appellant through the words of Blessed Clement, cited in 12 q. 1 c. dilectissimus, as is more fully set out in the second part. In the third part the rejection of that reply is given, showing that it is erroneous to hold that our first parents, had they not sinned, would have had over things in common such dominion as present possessors have over their goods as regards ownership. It is further noted what dominion our first parents would have had, and how the ways of using different things are different, and how the power of using things granted to them differed from that granted to the angels in respect of other things. In the fourth part, expounding the text, many things most worthy of note are drawn out concerning the state of our first parents. It is further shown by examples that things held in common do not always become private in the same way when they are divided, and that things which are common may also be the reverse. Three periods of our first parents are also distinguished, in which they stood in different relations as regards dominion over things.

units.la: Cap. 15. In prima parte recitat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua, vt declaratur in secunda parte, impugnatus per dictum capitulum Clement. conatur ostendere, quod Apostoli & eorum discipuli ante conuersionem Iudaeorum, de quibus in actibus fit mentio, aliqua possidebant. In tertia parte ponitur triuisdem impugnatio. In quarta litteralis explanatio.
units.tr: Chapter 15. In the first part he recites another part of the constitution, in which, as is explained in the second part, the author under attack, by the said chapter of Clement, tries to show that the Apostles and their disciples before the conversion of the Jews, of whom mention is made in the Acts, possessed some things. In the third part the refutation of this is given. In the fourth part, a literal explanation.

units.la: Cap. 16. In prima parte, vt declaratur in secunda, impugnatus nititur probare fassum esse, quod dixit appellans, Apostolos scilicet post verba Petri, Ecce nos reliquimus &c. vsos fuisse rebus consumptibilibus usu, cum in talibus usus reperiri, vt asserit, nequeat. Quae omnia improbantur in tertia parte. In quarta exponitur textus.
units.tr: Chapter 16. In the first part, as is explained in the second, the author under attack seeks to prove that the appellant was wrong in saying that the Apostles, namely after the words of Peter, "Behold, we have left all things," etc., used things consumed by use, since, as he asserts, use of such things cannot be found. All these points are refuted in the third part. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 17. In prima parte, vt declaratur in secunda, recitat responsionem impugnati, praetendentis Augustinum non voluisse dicere, quod Apostoli vouerunt abdicationem rerum in communi & in speciali: sed tantummodo Domini sequi. In tertia parte contra hanc responsionem impugnatores sex ostendunt. 1. quod Apostoli abdicationem rerum vouerunt in speciali. 2. quod in speciali & in communi. 3. quod Augustinus hoc sensit. 4. quod etiam illarum rerum, quas scriptura eos habuisse testatur, abdicatione vouerunt.
units.tr: Chapter 17. In the first part, as is explained in the second, he recites the reply of the author under attack, who pretends that Augustine did not wish to say that the Apostles vowed the renunciation of goods both in common and in particular, but only that they followed the Lord. In the third part the opponents set out six points against this reply. 1. That the Apostles vowed renunciation of goods in particular. 2. That they did so in particular and in common. 3. That Augustine thought so. 4. That they also vowed the renunciation of those goods which Scripture testifies they possessed.

units.la: Quintum quod vita Fratrum sancti Augustini & aliorum proprietatem in communi habentium ad summam altissimæ paupertatis Apostolorum perfectionem non attingat. Sextum quod medium, quo vitur impugnatus, est inualidum. In vltima parte declaratur textus.
units.tr: Fifth, that the life of the Friars of Saint Augustine and of others who hold property in common does not reach the highest perfection of the poverty of the Apostles. Sixth, that the means by which the author under attack proceeds is invalid. In the last part the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 18. In prima parte recitat, & in secunda explicat consequentem constitutionis particulam, in qua impugnatus respondet ad illud, quod in obiectione præmissa tangebat appellans de religiosis figuram Apostolorum tenentibus, dicens quod illud capitulum loquitur de monachis, qui possunt habere mobilia & immobilia in communi. Ergo & Apostoli. In tertia parte prædicta impugnantur propter tres errores. Ostenditur etiam quod duplex est perfectio: Et similiter duplex impedimentum perfectionis. Item quod habere possessiones ecclesiasticas diminuat vel impediat de perfectione. Ponitur item in quadam responsione triplex differentia possessionis propriorum & communium. Quarta pars declarat textum.
units.tr: Chapter 18. In the first part he recites, and in the second he explains, the next clause of the constitution, in which the impugned party answers the objection raised by the appellant, who had claimed that religious orders which hold the figure of the Apostles. He says that this chapter speaks of monks, who may have movable and immovable property in common. Therefore the Apostles may also have had it. In the third part the aforesaid points are refuted on account of three errors. It is also shown that perfection is twofold, and likewise that the impediment to perfection is twofold. Further, that to hold ecclesiastical possessions diminishes or hinders perfection. In a certain response a threefold difference between private and common possessions is also laid down. The fourth part explains the text.

units.la: Cap. 19. In prima parte recitat, & in secunda explicat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus recitat obiectionem appellantis. In tertia parte ostenditur impugnatum non recte recitasse verba appellantis, quæ ibidem subduntur. Et in quarta parte declarantur.
units.tr: Chapter 19. In the first part he recites, and in the second he explains, another part of the constitution, in which the impugned party recites the objection of the appellant. In the third part it is shown that the impugned party did not correctly recite the words of the appellant, which are set out there. In the fourth part they are explained.

units.la: Cap. 20. In prima parte recitat & in secunda declarat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus ad obiectionem, quam in capitulo præcedenti recitauerat, conatur respondere, dicens quod procedat ex falsis, cum assumit Leuitas habuisse vsum tantum Decimarum. Et deinde declarat causam, quare Dominus Leuitis dominium Decimarum dederit. In tertia parte prædicta impugnantur tria probando. Primum, quod impugnatus appellanti falsum imponit. Secundum quod auctoritates recitatæ non id prætendunt, quod impugnatus. Demonstraturq; quomodo sacerdotes & Leuitæ habeant dominium in oblationibus & Decimis. Tertium quod appellans intentum suum ex auctoribus bene concludat. In quarta parte declarando litteram ostenditur triplex differentia eorum, quæ diuinis vsibus applicantur. Item in quibus rebus ecclesiastici habent dominium.
units.tr: Chapter 20. In the first part he recites, and in the second he explains, another part of the constitution, in which the impugned party tries to answer the objection he had recited in the preceding chapter. He says that the objection proceeds from false premises, since it assumes that the Levites had only the use of tithes. Then he explains why the Lord gave the Levites ownership of the tithes. In the third part the aforesaid points are refuted by proving three things. First, that the impugned party falsely charges the appellant. Second, that the authorities cited do not support what the impugned party claims. It is also shown how priests and Levites have ownership of offerings and tithes. Third, that the appellant draws his conclusion from the authors correctly. In the fourth part, by explaining the letter of the text, a threefold difference is shown among the things that are applied to divine uses. Also, over which things ecclesiastical persons have ownership.

units.la: Cap. 21. In quatuor partibus, quibus recitat, declarat, improbat & exponit textum. Principaliter per impugnatores ostenditur appellantis verba truncate ab impugnato recitata.
units.tr: Chapter 21. It is set out in four parts, in which he recites, explains, refutes and expounds the text. Chiefly, through the refuters, it is shown that the words of the appellant were truncated by the impugned party when he recited them.

units.la: Cap. 22. In prima parte responsionem impugnati ad obiectionem præcedentis capituli recitat. In secunda eandem declarat, ostendendo quomodo impugnatus velit euadere, dicendo quod perfectissima paupertas plus consistat in animo quam in rebus, & in præparatione animi plus quam in effectu. Cuius contrarium asseritur in tertia parte. In quarta parte declaratur textus.
units.tr: Chapter 22. In the first part he recites the response of the impugned party to the objection of the preceding chapter. In the second he explains it, showing how the impugned party wishes to escape, by saying that the most perfect poverty consists more in the mind than in possessions, and more in the disposition of the mind than in the outward effect. The opposite of this is asserted in the third part. In the fourth part the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 23. In prima parte impugnatus respondendo asserit, quod paupertas euangelica non excludat proprietatem, cum constet Apostolos habuisse dominium rerum in communi. In secunda parte declaratur dictum impugnati. In tertia improbatur propter duos errores. Adducitur q; auctoritas beati Thomæ contra contrarium asserentes. In quarta parte expositionem litteralem solitam inuenies.
units.tr: Chapter 23. In the first part the impugned party, answering, asserts that evangelical poverty does not exclude ownership, since it is clear that the Apostles had ownership of goods in common. In the second part the statement of the impugned party is explained. In the third it is refuted on account of two errors. The authority of blessed Thomas is also adduced against those who assert the contrary. In the fourth part you will find the customary literal exposition.

units.la: Cap. 24. In prima parte, vt declaratur in secunda, impugnans nititur ostendere, quod abdicatio, quam Fratres Minores profitentur, non excludat sollicitudinem. In tertia parte impugnatur illud dictum. In quarta declaratur textus.
units.tr: Chapter 24. In the first part, as is explained in the second, the refuter strives to show that the renunciation which the Friars Minor profess does not exclude care. In the third part that statement is refuted. In the fourth the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 25. In prima parte, vt ostenditur in secunda, recitat responsionem impugnati ad obiectionem appellantis, quæ innititur auctoritati beati Remigii dicentis, quod Apostoli quantum ad abdicationem temporalium fuerunt ad dignitatem primi hominis reuocati, in qua fuisset vsus rerum sine proprietate. Hæc declarantur in secunda parte. In tertia declaratur intentio appellantis. In quarta verba eius.
units.tr: Chapter 25. In the first part, as is shown in the second, he recites the response of the impugned party to the objection of the appellant, which rests on the authority of blessed Remigius, who said that the Apostles, as regards the renunciation of temporal goods, were recalled to the dignity of the first man, in whom there would have been use of things without ownership. These points are explained in the second part. In the third the intention of the appellant is explained. In the fourth, his words.

units.la: Cap. 26. In prima & secunda partibus recitat & explicat aliam particulam constitutionis, in qua impugnatus ad obiectionem præmissam respondet quantum ad illud, quod ibi dicitur, primos parentes habuisse vsum absque dominio, dicens quod ipsi primi parentes saltem post illam benedictionem Crescite &c. habuerunt rerum dominium. In tertia parte impugnantur prædicta, eo quod ad mentem appellantis nihil faciant. Notantur præterea quædam de dominio communi & speciali, quod vocatur proprietas, quod non fuisset in statu innocentiæ. In quarta parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Chapter 26. In the first and second parts he recites and explains another clause of the constitution, in which the impugned party, answering the aforesaid objection, responds on the point that there it is said that our first parents had use without ownership, saying that our first parents, at least after that blessing, "Increase and multiply," etc., had ownership of things. In the third part the aforesaid points are refuted, because they have no bearing on the mind of the appellant. Certain matters are also noted concerning common and special ownership, which is called property, and which would not have existed in the state of innocence. In the fourth part the letter is explained.

units.la: Cap. 27. In duabus primis partibus recitat & explicat, quale secundum impugnatum fuit illud dominium in statu innocentiæ, scilicet an proprium an commune. Et determinat impugnatus, quod Adam primo habuit dominium proprium omnium rerum temporalium. Quod probat ratione & auctoritate. In tertia impugnantur prædicta propter duos errores. Primus est, quod illa benedictio Crescite &c. fuit data Adæ extra Paradisum ante formationem Euæ. Secundus q; Adam ante formationem Euæ habuit dominium proprium rerum temporalium. Vnde declaratur, quare aliquod dominium dicatur proprium. In quarta parte explanando litteram & soluendo quasdam instantias habentur quædam notatu dignissima de modo intelligendi & exponendi scripturas. Et quomodo in eis non seruatur semper ordo rei gestæ in narrando, vt probatur exemplariter.
units.tr: Chapter 27. In the first two parts he recites and explains what kind of ownership, according to the impugned party, existed in the state of innocence, namely whether it was private or common. The impugned party determines that Adam at first had private ownership of all temporal goods, which he proves by reason and authority. In the third part the aforesaid points are refuted on account of two errors. The first is that the blessing "Increase and multiply," etc., was given to Adam outside Paradise, before the formation of Eve. The second is that Adam, before the formation of Eve, had private ownership of temporal goods. Hence it is explained why some ownership is called private. In the fourth part, in explaining the letter and resolving certain objections, there are some matters most worthy of note concerning the manner of understanding and expounding the Scriptures, and how in them the order of the events narrated is not always kept, as is shown by examples.

units.la: Cap. 28. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad capitulum Clementis 12. q. 1. dilectissimis. In tertia improbatur responsio eius ostendendo, quod non procedat ad mentem appellantis, qui non negat primos parentes habuisse qualecunq; dominium temporalium: sed negat eos habuisse dominium, quod vocatur proprietas, qua aliquid est huius, quod non est illius. Quarta pars expositiua est litteræ.
units.tr: Chapter 28. In the first two parts he recites and explains the response of the impugned party to the chapter of Clement, 12, q. 1, "Dilectissimis." In the third his response is refuted, by showing that it does not proceed according to the mind of the appellant, who does not deny that our first parents had some kind of ownership of temporal goods, but denies that they had the ownership called property, by which a thing belongs to this person and not to that. The fourth part is an exposition of the letter.

units.la: Cap. 29. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat obiectionem appellantis, quæ est secundum dum euangelium: seruus potest uti pecunia domini sui absq; dominio & proprietate. In reliquis duobus ponuntur annotationes quædam super litteram.
units.tr: Chapter 29. In the first two parts he recites and explains the objection of the appellant, which is drawn from the second passage of the Gospel: a servant may use the money of his lord without ownership and property. In the remaining two parts certain notes are set out on the letter.

units.la: Cap. 30. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad dictam obiectionem dicentis, quod seruus nec utitur nec abutitur pecunia Domini sui mutuando, quia ipse non facit translationem Dominii, sed Dominus eius. In tertia parte impugnatur dicta responsio ostendendo, quod seruus ille euangelicus usus sit pecunia Domini sui. In quarta notantur verba impugnati.
units.tr: Chapter 30. In the first two parts he recites and explains the response of the impugned party to that objection, saying that the servant neither uses nor abuses the money of his lord by lending it, because he himself does not effect a transfer of ownership, but his lord does. In the third part that response is refuted, by showing that the servant in the Gospel did use the money of his lord. In the fourth the words of the impugned party are noted.

units.la: Cap. 31. In duabus primis recitat & explicat aliam obiectionem appellantis factam per decretalem Exiit. In tertia autem parte ostenditur, quomodo truncate recitatur obiectio appellantis ab impugnato. In quarta parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Chapter 31. In the first two parts he recites and explains another objection of the appellant, made from the decretal "Exiit." In the third part it is shown how the objection of the appellant was recited in truncated form by the impugned party. In the fourth part the letter is explained.

units.la: Cap. 32. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad dictam obiectionem, quæ prætendit, quod illa decretalis debeat intelligi de rebus quæ non consumuntur usu. Item quod dicta decretalis non fuit ab vniversali ecclesia in Viennensi concilio approbata, nec de consensu Fratrum promulgata. In tertia parte impugnantur prædicta quo ad octo puncta, in quibus dicunt impugnatum errasse. Primum quia dicit quod dicta decretalis non intelligitur de rebus usu consumptibilibus. Secundum quia dicit proprietatem tantum in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri, & non usum facti, nec ius utendi. Tertium quia dicit, quod in rebus usu consumptibilibus usus rei non potest penes unum & dominium penes alium remanere. Cuius contrarium ostenditur multis exemplis. Quartu quia dicit, quod in omnibus rebus consumptibilibus per usum siue per abusum usuarii, substantia rei definit esse. Quintum quia dicit diffinitionem Nicolai tertii non tenere in rebus usu consumptibilibus: quod improbant ex illa & aliis constitutionibus successorum eius. In quibus declaratur expropriationem Fratrum debere intelligi de omnibus rebus tam in speciali quam communi. Sextum est, quod decretalis Exiit quantum ad hoc non est per vniversalem ecclesiam approbata. Septimum quod dicit eam in concilio Viennensi non esse confirmatam. Octauum quia dicit eandem non esse de Fratrum consilio & consensu promulgatam. In quarta parte notatur & exponitur littera.
units.tr: Chapter 32. In the first two parts he recites and explains the response of the impugned party to the said objection, which contends that the decretal must be understood of things that are not consumed by use. Also, that the said decretal was not approved by the universal Church at the Council of Vienne, nor promulgated with the consent of the Friars. In the third part the aforesaid points are refuted with respect to eight points, in which they say the impugned party erred. The first, because he says that the said decretal is not understood of things consumed by use. The second, because he says that ownership is found only in things consumed by use, and not the use of a fact, nor the right of using. The third, because he says that in things consumed by use the use of a thing cannot remain with one person while the ownership remains with another. The opposite of this is shown by many examples. The fourth, because he says that in all things consumed by use, whether by use or by abuse of the user, the substance of the thing ceases to exist. The fifth, because he says that the definition of Nicholas III does not hold in things consumed by use; they refute this from that definition and other constitutions of his successors, in which it is declared that the expropriation of the Friars must be understood of all things, both in particular and in common. The sixth is that the decretal "Exiit" has not been approved by the universal Church in this respect. The seventh, that he says it was not confirmed at the Council of Vienne. The eighth, because he says it was not promulgated with the counsel and consent of the Friars. In the fourth part the letter is noted and explained.

units.la: Cap. 33. In prima parte recitat, & in secunda declarat partem constitutionis subsequentem: in qua impugnatus incipit respondere ad obiectiones appellantis contra secundam assertionem ab ipso appellante impugnatam. In tertia parte notatur littera.
units.tr: Chap. 33. In the first part he recites, and in the second part explains, the following part of the constitution, in which the impugned author begins to answer the objections of the appellant against the second assertion, which the appellant had attacked. In the third part the letter is annotated.

units.la: Cap. 34. In duabus primis partibus resumit dictam obiectionem per quoddam dictum Num. 21. In tertia parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Chap. 34. In the first two parts he resumes the said objection through a certain statement, Num. 21. In the third part the letter is explained.

units.la: Cap. 35. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus respondet ad obiectionem præmissam, dicens, quod Levitæ non habuerunt in dicimis tantum simplicem facti usum, sed & dominium. Nituntur; ostendere, quod aliud est dare alicui rem in usum, & dare ipsi usum facti: & q; ex Dei statuto non habetur usus in rebus usu consumptibilibus. In tertia parte tria impugnatur. Primo quia appellans non potuerat dictionem exclusiuam tantum in appellatione sua. Secundo quia dictam obiectionem impugnatus non soluit, sed concedit propositum appellantis. Tertio quod erroneum est dicere, quod ex Dei statuto usus in rebus usu consumptibilibus haberi non potest. Quia multæ res datæ sunt in usum ex Dei statuto, prout probatur auctoritatibus sacræ scripturæ. Soluitur igitur ratio impugnati. In quarta parte exponitur & notatur littera.
units.tr: Chap. 35. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the constitution, in which the impugned author answers the objection set out above, saying that the Levites did not have in the tithes merely a simple factual use, but also ownership. He strives to show that it is one thing to give someone a thing for use, and another to give him the factual use itself; and that, by God's ordinance, there is no use in things consumable by use. In the third part three things are attacked. First, because the appellant could not have used the exclusive term alone in his appeal. Second, because the impugned author does not solve the said objection but concedes the appellant's proposition. Third, because it is an error to say that by God's ordinance there cannot be use in things consumable by use, since many things have been given for use by God's ordinance, as is shown by the authorities of Holy Scripture. The impugned author's argument is therefore refuted. In the fourth part the letter is explained and annotated.

units.la: Cap. 36. Recitat quasdam auctoritates, quas appellans inducit ad ostendendum, quod usus reperiatur in multis rebus usu consumptibilibus. Tandem littera paucis declaratur.
units.tr: Chap. 36. He recites certain authorities which the appellant brings forward to show that use is found in many things consumable by use. Finally the letter is explained briefly.

units.la: Cap. 37. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad dictas auctoritates. In tertia parte impugnando responsionem eius multa declarantur scitu digna de variis propositionibus de huiusmodi materia loquentibus, virum concedi debeant. Concluditurq; quod prius Theologus & Philosophus debeat absolute concedere, quod contingit uti rebus usu consumptibilibus. Et idem videtur de Iuristis. In quarta parte notatur littera.
units.tr: Chap. 37. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned author's answer to these authorities. In the third part, in refuting his answer, many things worth knowing are explained about the various propositions speaking on this matter, which ones ought to be granted. It is concluded that first the theologian and the philosopher ought absolutely to grant that it is possible to use things consumable by use. And the same seems true of the jurists. In the fourth part the letter is annotated.

units.la: Cap. 38. Recitat & explicat quandam obiectionem de pecunia, qua contingit uti, & tamen interres usu consumptibiles numeratur. Deinde subditur improbatio, eo quod de hoc nulla facta fuerit mentio in obiectionibus contra assertionem prædictam.
units.tr: Chap. 38. He recites and explains an objection concerning money, which one can use and yet is counted among things consumable by use. Then a refutation is added, because no mention of this had been made in the objections against the aforesaid assertion.

units.la: Cap. 39. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus redit ad completionis respondendum auctoritatibus superius allegatis, dicens quod secundum leges neq; usufructus neq; ius utendi, quod est seruitus, neq; ius utendi quod non est seruitus, potest in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri. In tertia parte prædicta responsio impugnatur tanquam impertinens. In quarta parte notantur & exponuntur verba textus.
units.tr: Chap. 39. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the constitution, in which the impugned author returns to answering the authorities cited above, saying that according to the laws there can be found in things consumable by use neither usufruct, nor the right of using which is a servitude, nor the right of using which is not a servitude. In the third part the said answer is attacked as irrelevant. In the fourth part the words of the text are annotated and explained.

units.la: Cap. 40. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat consequentem dictæ constitutionis particulam, in qua impugnatus nititur ostendere, q; nemo potest uti rebus usu consumptibilibus: eo q; nullus potest habere fructu vel utilitate aliq; ex illis salua rerum substantia. Et q; inde est secundum Chrysostomum, q; non licet recipere mercedem pro pecunia mutuata. In tertia parte impugnantur prædicta propter quatuor errores. Quorum primus est, q; non contingit uti rebus usu consumptibilibus, capiendo vt proprie, q; fuit etiam impugnatus supra cap. 6. Secundus est, quod qui utitur proprie loquendo re aliqua, habere debet fructum vel utilitatem ex ea, salua rei substantia. Tertius est quod nullus ex re usu consumptibili potest habere fructum vel utilitatem salua rei substantia: cuius contrarium ostenditur in usu pecuniæ.
units.tr: Chap. 40. In the first two parts he recites and explains the following particle of the said constitution, in which the impugned author tries to show that no one can use things consumable by use, since no one can have any fruit or advantage from them while their substance remains intact; and that from this, according to Chrysostom, it is not lawful to receive a reward for money lent. In the third part the aforesaid is attacked on four errors. The first of these is that it is not possible to use things consumable by use, taking "use" properly; this was also attacked above in chap. 6. The second is that whoever properly speaking uses some thing must have fruit or advantage from it while the thing's substance remains intact. The third is that no one can have fruit or advantage from a thing consumable by use while its substance remains intact; the contrary of this is shown in the use of money.

units.la: Quintus Quartus quia dicit, quod secundum Chrysostomum ideo pro pecunia mutuata non licet mercedem recipere, quia non contingat ea uti salua rei substantia. Quod falsum esse probant ostendentes longe aliam esse rationem etiam secundum Chrysostomum, videl. quia per mutuum transfertur dominium pecuniae. Et ideo non licet recipere ultra valorem eius. De qua materia pulchra disseruntur. Similiter autem magis liceat locanti domum vel agrum recipere ultra valorem domus, quam mutuanti pecuniam. Notatur tamen casus, in quo etiam ex pecunia ad pompam concessa mercedem sine usura contingit exigi. In quarta parte exponitur & notatur littera.
units.tr: The fourth, because he says that according to Chrysostom it is not lawful to receive a reward for money lent, since one cannot use it while its substance remains intact. They show this to be false, demonstrating that according to Chrysostom too the reason is quite different, namely that ownership of money is transferred by a loan; and therefore it is not lawful to receive more than its value. Fine matters are discussed on this subject. Likewise it is more permissible for one who lets a house or a field to receive more than the value of the house than for one who lends money. Yet a case is noted in which a reward may be demanded without interest even for money granted for display. In the fourth part the letter is explained and annotated.

units.la: Cap. 41. In duabus primis partibus recitat & explicat particulam constitutionis, in qua impugnatus dicit, quod licet uti non posset reperiri in rebus usu consumptibilibus: tamen in eis consumptio & actus consumendi possunt reperiri. Nec tamen separantur a Dominio. In tertia parte impugnantur haec in tribus. Primo quia per haec dicta impugnatus ostendit se prius impertinenter locutum fuisse de usu & uti. Secundo quia erroneum est dicere quod actus consumendi in rebus huiusmodi non possit a dominio separari. Tertio quod ratio impugnati est erronea & inualida. Ostenduntur etiam multa notatu digna de multiplicitate utendi, & separandi. In quarta parte notatur & exponitur textus. Et pulchra inseruntur.
units.tr: Chap. 41. In the first two parts he recites and explains a particle of the constitution, in which the impugned author says that although use cannot be found in things consumable by use, yet consumption and the act of consuming can be found in them; nor are these separated from ownership. In the third part these points are attacked in three respects. First, because by these statements the impugned author shows that he had previously spoken irrelevantly about use and using. Second, because it is an error to say that the act of consuming in things of this kind cannot be separated from ownership. Third, because the impugned author's argument is erroneous and invalid. Many things worth noting are also shown about the manifold senses of using and separating. In the fourth part the text is annotated and explained, and fine points are inserted.

units.la: Cap. 42. Recitat & explicat partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus, quasi epilogando quaedam prius dicta, dicit, quod constitutio sua ad condendorem loquitur, sicut decretalis exiit, scilicet secundum leges, secundum quas usus & uti proprie sumendo non habent locum in rebus usu consumptibilibus. In tertia parte improbantur praedicta per quandam legem.
units.tr: Chap. 42. He recites and explains the part of the constitution in which the impugned author, as if summing up what was said before, says that his constitution speaks to the founder, as the decretal Exiit does, namely according to the laws, according to which use and using, properly taken, have no place in things consumable by use. In the third part the aforesaid is refuted by a certain law.

units.la: Cap. 43. In duabus primis partibus recitat & explicat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus expressius, quam ante, respondet ad auctoritates inductas supra Cap. 36. dicens, quod omnes illae auctoritates accipiunt usum & uti pro rei consumptione: & ita improprie. In tertia ponitur huiusmodi responsionis impugnatio. Ostenditurq; quod scientiae posteriores non possunt damnare modum loquendi scientiarum priorum. In quarta parte notatur littera.
units.tr: Chap. 43. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the constitution, in which the impugned author answers, more explicitly than before, the authorities introduced above in chap. 36, saying that all those authorities take use and using for the consumption of a thing, and so improperly. In the third part the refutation of this answer is set out. And it is shown that later sciences cannot condemn the manner of speaking of earlier sciences. In the fourth part the letter is annotated.

units.la: Cap. 44. Recitat & declarat aliam obiectionem: probatq; quod qui negat propositionem multiplicem, intelligitur negare omnem sensum eius, nisi sit consuetum talem propositionem accipi potius in uno sensu quam in alio. Notatur etiam littera.
units.tr: Chap. 44. He recites and explains another objection, and proves that whoever denies a multiple proposition is understood to deny every sense of it, unless it is customary to take such a proposition in one sense rather than another. The letter is also annotated.

units.la: Cap. 45. Recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati dicentis, quod appellans tanquam ignarus arguit legislatorem, arguendo constitutionem ad condutorem, quae loquitur de usu, sicut leges. In tertia parte impugnantur praedicta. In quarta declarando litteram notatur quomodo rubricae saepe sunt de rebus, quae contradictionem includunt, sicut in Physica de vacuo & infinito: & tamen auctores ita intitulantes non debent reprehendi, nisi postea in tractando dicant huiusmodi res esse.
units.tr: Chap. 45. He recites and explains the impugned author's answer, which says that the appellant, like one ignorant, argues against the lawgiver, by arguing against the constitution to the founder, which speaks of use, as the laws do. In the third part the aforesaid is attacked. In the fourth part, explaining the letter, it is noted how headings are often about things which include a contradiction, as in Physics about the void and the infinite; yet authors who so entitle them ought not to be reproached, unless afterwards, in treating the matter, they say that such things exist.

units.la: Cap. 46. recitat & declarat aliam obiectionem appellantis, probantis per verbum Augustini quod abusus est illicitus usus, & quod ideo Christus cibo & potu non abusus, sed usus fuerit. Declaratq; tandem litteram.
units.tr: Chap. 46. He recites and explains another objection of the appellant, proving by a saying of Augustine that abuse is an unlawful use, and that for this reason Christ did not abuse food and drink, but used them. And finally he explains the letter.

units.la: Cap. 47. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad dictam obiectionem, qui concedit conclusionem illatam ad sensum per se praeexpositum. In tertia parte ostenditur, quod sicut ipse impugnatus capit terminos ad placitum suum: sic etiam appellans tanquam Doctor Theologiae potuit uti isto termino abuti, ut capitur in sacra scriptura & Doctoribus sanctis. Deinde exponit litteram.
units.tr: Chap. 47. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned author's answer to the said objection, who concedes the conclusion drawn, in the sense previously set out by himself. In the third part it is shown that just as the impugned author takes terms at his own pleasure, so too the appellant, as a Doctor of Theology, could use this term "abuse" as it is taken in Holy Scripture and in the holy Doctors. Then he explains the letter.

units.la: Cap. 48. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam obiectionem appellantis, probantis quod non valeat dicere, quod abuti debeat sumi pro consumtione rei, eo quod abuti semper in mala significatione sumitur in sacra scriptura. In ultima exponitur littera.
units.tr: Chap. 48. In the first two parts he recites and explains another objection of the appellant, proving that it is not valid to say that "abuse" ought to be taken for the consumption of a thing, since "abuse" is always taken in a bad sense in Holy Scripture. In the last part the letter is explained.

units.la: Cap. 49. In duabus primis partibus recitat & exponit particulam constitutionis, in qua impugnatus respondet ad obiectionem immediate praemissam. Et quantum ad hoc, primo ostenditur, quod abuti potest sumi pro consumptione. Et quod abusus in bona significatione sumitur secundum leges, & etiam in sacra scriptura. Et ideo oportet, quod omnis abusus sit illicitus. In tertia parte improbatur ex tribus. Primo, quia non respondet ad mentem appellantis, quam ibi exponere declarat. Secundo quia falsum dicit asserendo, quod legislatores loquentes proprie de rebus, quae usu consumuntur, negant usum in omni sua significatione propria locum in rebus consumptibilibus habere. Tertio quia erroneum est, quod ille abusus, prout capitur ab impugnatis illicitus, cui non competit ius utendi & hoc deducendo ad inconveniens, videlicet quod status Fratrum Minorum sic esset illicitus, & ecclesia errasset ipsum approbando, & Franciscum canonizando. In quarta exponitur littera.
units.tr: Ch. 49. In the first two parts he recites and explains a clause of the constitution in which the impugned party answers the objection immediately before. On this point, it is first shown that abuti can be taken for consumption, and that abusus is taken in a good sense according to the laws and also in Holy Scripture; and therefore every abusus must be lawful. In the third part the answer is refuted on three grounds. First, because it does not meet the mind of the appellant, which he there sets out and declares. Second, because it speaks falsely in asserting that legislators, speaking properly of things consumed by use, deny that use in its every proper sense has a place among consumable things. Third, because it is wrong to hold that that abuse, as the impugned party takes it, is unlawful when the right of using does not belong to the one using; and this is pressed to an absurdity, namely that the state of the Friars Minor would then be unlawful, and the Church would have erred in approving it and canonizing Francis. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 50. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati, dicentis quod abusus pro consumptione rei sumitur, eo quod haec praepositio ab auget sensum dictionis, qui per compositionem praeponitur. In tertia parte dicta impugnantur. In quarta exponuntur litteraliter.
units.tr: Ch. 50. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned party's answer, which says that abusus is taken for the consumption of a thing, because the preposition ab intensifies the sense of the word to which it is prefixed by composition. In the third part these statements are refuted. In the fourth they are expounded word by word.

units.la: Cap. 51. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam constitutionis particulam, in qua impugnatus concludit, quod abusus in legibus Imperatorum in bona significatione accipitur, ratio responsio eius improbatur.
units.tr: Ch. 51. In the first two parts he recites and explains another clause of the constitution, in which the impugned party concludes that abusus in the laws of the Emperors is taken in a good sense; his reasoning and answer are refuted.

units.la: Cap. 52. In duabus primis partibus idem, quod in praecedenti capitulo ostenditur, per tatem Hieremiae cap. 18. In tertia parte improbatur. In quarta literaliter notatur.
units.tr: Ch. 52. In the first two parts the same point is shown as in the preceding chapter, by the parable of Jeremiah 18. In the third part it is refuted. In the fourth it is noted word for word.

units.la: Cap. 53. Recitat & declarat obiectionem appellantis, probantis quod diffinitio, quam dicta constitutio dat de uti, non sit vera diffinitio. Et ostendentis, quod sicut non est licitum cuiquam de novo imponere vocibus significationes, sic non est licitum cuicunq; diffinitiones novas dissonas diffinitionibus maiorum assignare.
units.tr: Ch. 53. He recites and explains the objection of the appellant, who proves that the definition which the said constitution gives of uti is not a true definition; and he shows that just as it is not lawful for anyone to newly impose meanings on words, so it is not lawful for anyone to assign new definitions at odds with the definitions of the elders.

units.la: Cap. 54. Recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad obiectionem praemissam, dicentis quod diffinitio sua est vera, prout ostendit per diffinitionem vsus, quae habetur consimilis. In tertia parte praemisso, quod hoc verbum uti non habet tot significationes, quot habet hoc nomen usus. Primo dicitur, quod licet usus in vera significatione sic diffiniatur: Usus est ius utendi rebus alienis salva rerum substantia: tamen uti sic diffiniri non potest: Uti nihil aliud est proprie, quam fructum rei seu utilitatem &c. Secundo dicitur, quod esto quod usus in una significatione diffineretur praedicto modo: ex hoc tamen non sequeretur, quod non possit aliter proprie diffinire, eo quod eiusdem vocabuli aequivoce sumpti possunt esse plures diffinitiones propriae. In quarta ponitur expositio & notatio litteralis.
units.tr: Ch. 54. He recites and explains the impugned party's answer to the foregoing objection, which says that his definition is true, as is shown by the definition of usus, which is found to be similar. In the third part it is premised that this verb uti does not have as many meanings as the noun usus has. First, it is said that although usus in its true sense is defined thus: Usus est ius utendi rebus alienis salva rerum substantia ("Use is the right of using another's things, the substance of the things being preserved"), yet uti cannot be defined thus: Uti nihil aliud est proprie, quam fructum rei seu utilitatem etc. ("To use is properly nothing other than to take the fruit or utility of a thing," etc.). Second, it is said that even if usus were defined in the aforesaid manner in one sense, it would not follow that it cannot be properly defined in another way, since a single word taken equivocally can have several proper definitions. In the fourth part the exposition and literal notes are given.

units.la: Cap. 55. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad hoc quod appellans dixerat suam diffinitionem non esse consonam diffinitionibus sanctorum, dicens quod hoc non est inconveniens. Quia aliter accipitur a sanctis, & aliter in decretali Exiit, & in constitutione Ad conditorem. In tertia parte impugnant praedictam responsionem. Primo quia non respondet ad mentem appellantis. Secundo quia sibiipsi contradicit. In quarta parte notantur verba textus.
units.tr: Ch. 55. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned party's answer to the appellant's charge that his definition does not agree with the definitions of the saints. He says this is no difficulty, because the saints take the term differently, and the decretal Exiit and the constitution Ad conditorem take it differently again. In the third part they refute that answer. First, because it does not meet the mind of the appellant. Second, because it contradicts itself. In the fourth part the words of the text are noted.

units.la: Cap. 56. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus reprehendit appellantem quantum ad modum loquendi in hoc, quod ponit simplicem vsum facti in rebus: cum tamen modus loquendi non sit vsitatus a sanctis Doctoribus. In reliquis duabus improbantur & notantur praedicta.
units.tr: Ch. 56. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the constitution, in which the impugned party rebukes the appellant for his manner of speaking, in that he posits a bare simplex usus facti in things, although that way of speaking is not used by the holy Doctors. In the remaining two parts the aforesaid points are refuted and noted.

units.la: Cap. 57. Recitat ultimam obiectionem appellantis &c.
units.tr: Ch. 57. He recites the appellant's last objection, etc.

units.la: Cap. 58. Recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati, quae per quatuor dicta procedit. Tertio improbat praedicta quatuor dicta tanquam falsa. Quorum primum est, quod Nicolaus tertius per verba sua in decretali Exiit, non concessit simplicem vsum facti. Secundum est quod quoad res vsu consumptibiles accepit vsum improprie. Tertium quod non concessit Minoribus vsum facti. Quartum quod si decretalis Exiit intellexerit de vsu facti proprie loquendo, non valeret, quia esset impossibilis. Haec, inquam, improbatur in tertia parte. Et soluitur vna instantia de vsu necessariae sustentationis. Et similiter ibi declaratur, quare dicitur simplex vsus facti. In quarta parte notatur verba textus.
units.tr: Ch. 58. He recites and explains the impugned party's answer, which proceeds through four statements. Thirdly, he refutes these four statements as false. The first is that Nicholas III, by his words in the decretal Exiit, did not grant a bare usus facti. The second is that, as regards things consumed by use, he took usus improperly. The third is that he did not grant to the Friars Minor the usus facti. The fourth is that if the decretal Exiit is understood of use of fact properly speaking, it would not hold, because it would be impossible. These, I say, are refuted in the third part. And one objection about the use of necessary sustenance is answered there, and there it is similarly explained why it is called a simplex usus facti. In the fourth part the words of the text are noted.

units.la: Cap. 59. Recitat & declarat tertiam assertionem impugnati, quam appellans reputauit erroneam. Quae est, quod nullus actus utendi potest esse licitus absq; iure utendi. In vltima parte exponitur litera.
units.tr: Ch. 59. He recites and explains the third assertion of the impugned party, which the appellant judged erroneous: that no act of using can be lawful without a right of using. In the last part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 60. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus resumit obiectionem appellantis contra dictam tertiam assertionem. Et stat obiectio in hoc; quod impugnatus loquitur de iure civili & mundano. Et tale ius nunquam habuerunt Apostoli in multis rebus, quarum tamen habuerunt vsum licitum. In tertia parte impugnando praedicta quinque facit, vt ibi patet. In primis autem scitu dignum est notabile de differentia inter vsum iustum & licitum. Et de triplici acceptione huius nominis iustitia. Et proportionabiliter, quomodo actus potest dici tripliciter iustus. In quarta parte exponuntur verba textus.
units.tr: Ch. 60. In the first two parts he recites and explains the part of the constitution in which the impugned party takes up again the appellant's objection to the said third assertion. The objection rests on this: the impugned party speaks of civil and worldly right, and the Apostles never had such a right in many things, although they had a lawful use of them. In the third part, refuting the foregoing, he does five things, as appears there. At the outset, however, it is worth noting the difference between a just and a lawful use, and the threefold sense of the word iustitia; and, by analogy, how an act can be called just in three ways. In the fourth part the words of the text are expounded.

units.la: Cap. 61. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem dictae constitutionis. In qua impugnatus respondet ad obiectiones appellantis, dicens quod appellans sibi falsum imponit. Quia constitutio sua Ad conditorem loquitur de vsu, pro quo competit ius utendi, quod est aliud a iure utendi. In tertia parte ponitur impugnatio praedictorum duo faciendo. Primo, declarando intentionem impugnati, & quomodo ponit ius utendi esse licentiam seu licitam potestatem utendi, & quod licentia utendi non est sine iure utendi. Secundo praedictam assertionem improbando. Et ibi primo distinguitur multiplex ius utendi. Quoddam enim est naturale, & quoddam positiuum. Et quomodo ius naturale semper, sed non pro semper sufficit ad utendum tempore necessitatis extremae. Et subditur & soluitur quaedam instantia, in qua notatur respectu cuius priuilegium est ius, & respectu cuius non est ius, sed gratia. Deinde ponitur licentia duplex: quarum altera ad placitum concedentis reuocari non potest, altera potest. Tertio reprobatur illa assertio, qua impugnatus dicit, quod aliquid potest habere ius utendi, quod est licentia utendi absque iure agendi. Et circa hoc ponuntur duae conclusiones. Prima est, quod non omnis licentia utendi est ius utendi. Quae probatur quadrupliciter. Soluitur etiam quaedam instantia concedendo, quod licet Fratres Minores non habeant ius positiuum in rebus, quibus vtuntur: habent tamen in eis aliquod ius utendi, scilicet naturale pro tempore necessitatis solum. Et sic cum habeant licentiam utendi rebus pro alio tempore, quam pro tempore necessitatis extremae, cum tamen non habeant ius utendi, nisi pro tempore necessitatis extremae, sequitur quod licentia utendi non est ius utendi. Secunda conclusio est, quod qui habet ius agendi positiuum re aliqua determinata, habet ius agendi seu repetendi iudicialiter, eo quod vnicuique licet repetere suum cum debitis circumstantiis. In quarta parte exponitur litera.
units.tr: Ch. 61. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the said constitution, in which the impugned party answers the appellant's objections by saying that the appellant falsely imputes something to him, since his constitution Ad conditorem speaks of a use for which there is a right of using, which is different from a right of using. In the third part the foregoing is refuted, in two steps. First, by declaring the intention of the impugned party, and how he holds that a right of using is a licence or lawful power of using, and that a licence of using is not without a right of using. Second, by refuting that assertion. Here, first, a manifold right of using is distinguished: for one is natural and another positive. And it is shown how the natural right is always, but not always, sufficient for using in a time of extreme necessity. Then an objection is added and answered, in which it is noted with respect to what a privilege is a right, and with respect to what it is not a right but a grace. Next, a twofold licence is laid down: of which one cannot be revoked at the pleasure of the grantor, and the other can. Thirdly, that assertion is rejected, by which the impugned party says that something may have a right of using which is a licence of using without a right of acting. And on this two conclusions are laid down. The first is that not every licence of using is a right of using. This is proved in four ways. An objection is also answered by conceding that, although the Friars Minor do not have a positive right in the things they use, they nevertheless have in them some right of using, namely a natural one, but only for a time of necessity. And so, since they have a licence of using things at other times than the time of extreme necessity, while they have no right of using except in the time of extreme necessity, it follows that a licence of using is not a right of using. The second conclusion is that whoever has a positive right of acting in some determinate thing has a right of acting or of recovering by legal process, since it is lawful for everyone to recover what is his, with due circumstances. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 62. Recitat & explicat in primis duabus partibus expositionem, per quam impugnatus ostendit, quod constitutio Quia quorundam, non loquitur de iure utendi, quod est proprium, quod tamen sibi imponit appellans: sed de iure utendi communi. In tertia parte hoc impugnatur propter tria. Primo quia illa constitutio loquitur de iure contentioso. Ergo de iure agendi. Et circa hoc soluitur quaedam instantia. Ibi etiam declaratur, quod saepe verbum indefinite prolatum nequaquam vniuersaliter debet intelligi. Et deinde ponuntur responsiones ad rationes contentas in constitutione, Quia quorundam, & specialiter per distinctionem de iustitia & iusto prius positam. Et sic soluitur illud argumentum, quo probatur impugnatus [?] quod exercens aliquem [?] qui nullum ius habeat exercendi ipsum, ini[?]nuincitur. [?]militer quod ille non est iu-stior, qui non habet ius vtendi, quam qui habet respectu rei, qua vtitur, & similia. Secundo ostendi-tur, quod constitutio quia quorundam, loquitur de iure vtendi proprio, non solum collegio, sed etiam personae. Tertio probatur, quod verba quae adducuntur ex constitutione quia quorundam plures errores includunt. Quorum primus est, quod Ordo Fratrum Minorum habet vsum iuris in rebus, quibus vtuntur. Secundus error est, quod Ordo Fratrum Minorum est persona repraesentata & imaginaria. Tertius est, quod quae facti sunt, Ordini nequeunt conuenire. Quartus est quod licet ordini non possint conuenire ea quae sunt facti: ei tamen possunt conuenire quae sunt iuris. Et vtrum quod improbatur. In quarta parte ponitur responsio litteralis.
units.tr: Cap. 62. First, in the two opening parts, he recites and explains the exposition by which the one under attack shows that the constitution Quia quorundam does not speak of the right of use that is proper (which the appellant nonetheless attributes to it), but of the common right of use. In the third part this is attacked on three grounds. First, because that constitution speaks of a contentious right, and therefore of the right of acting. On this point an objection is answered. There it is also declared that a word spoken indefinitely should by no means always be understood universally. Then replies are given to the arguments contained in the constitution Quia quorundam, especially through the distinction between justice and the just made earlier. In this way the argument by which the one under attack proves that one who exercises something he has no right to exercise is [?] is answered; similarly, that one is not more just who has no right of use than one who has a right in respect of the thing he uses, and similar points. Second, it is shown that the constitution quia quorundam speaks of a right of use proper not only to the college but also to the person. Third, it is proved that the words cited from the constitution quia quorundam include several errors. The first of these is that the Order of Friars Minor has a use of right in the things they use. The second error is that the Order of Friars Minor is a represented and imaginary person. The third is that things which are matters of fact cannot belong to the Order. The fourth is that although matters of fact cannot belong to the Order, matters of right can; and this is what is disproved. In the fourth part a literal reply is given.

units.la: Cap. 63. Resumit quandam responsionem appellantis ad rationem impugnati supra positam capitulo 59. Vbi arguitur, quod vsus concessus Fratribus non est sine iure vtendi, quia alias esset illicitus. Ad quod respondet appellans, quod sufficit licentia vtendi ad hoc quod non sit illicitus &c.
units.tr: Cap. 63. He takes up again a reply of the appellant to the argument of the one under attack, set out above in chapter 59. There it is argued that the use granted to the Friars is not without a right of use, because otherwise it would be unlawful. To this the appellant replies that a licence to use is sufficient for the use not to be unlawful, etc.

units.la: Cap. 64. Primo ponit & secundo exponit partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus praedictam responsionem appellantis reprobare conatur, dicens quod falsum est, quod aliquis possit habere licentiam sine iure. Probat de religioso, cui conceditur licentia consentiendi in electionem de se factam, qui etiam per hoc habet ius consentiendi. In tertia vero parte huius capituli reprobatur praedicta ratio, quia appellans non dicit vniuersaliter, scilicet quod omnis, qui habet licentiam, non habeat ius. Imo sicut dictum est capitulo 61. aliquando concessa licentia ius quoddam acquiritur, & aliquando non, prout hic & ibidem declaratur. In quarta vero parte ponitur responsio ad litteram.
units.tr: Cap. 64. First he sets out, and second he explains, the part of the constitution in which the one under attack tries to reject the aforementioned reply of the appellant, saying that it is false that anyone can have a licence without a right. He proves it with the case of a religious who is granted a licence to consent to an election made concerning himself, and who by this also has a right to consent. In the third part of this chapter the aforementioned argument is rejected, because the appellant does not say universally, namely that everyone who has a licence has no right. Indeed, as was said in chapter 61, sometimes a certain right is acquired by a licence granted, and sometimes not, as is declared here and there. In the fourth part a reply is given to the letter.

units.la: Cap. 65. In prima & secunda partibus recitat & explicat secundam rationem, quam adducit impugnatus ad probandum, quod qui habet licentiam vtendi re aliqua habet ius vtendi eadem. Et est ratio talis, qui vtitur re aliqua de licentia alterius sine iure; aut vtitur iuste, vel iniuste. Si iuste, ergo iure, extra de verborum significationibus cap. ius datur & 14. q. 4. quid dicam. Si iniuste, concordat cum constitutione Ad conditorem &c. In tertia vero parte ad reprobationem & solutionem dictae rationis proceditur quinque faciendo. Primo ponitur distinctio de iure: quia quandoque accipitur pro iure fori: quandoque vero pro iure poli. Ius fori vocatur iustum, quod ex pactione seu ordinatione humana vel diuina explicite constituitur. Et probatur ibidem, quomodo non debet ad placitum cuiuslibet violari, sicut nec mores, nec leges populi, respectu cuius sunt leges. Ius vero poli vocatur aequitas naturalis, quae absque omni ordinatione humana & etiam diuina pure positiva est consona rationi rectae pure naturali vel acceptae ex his quae diuinitus nobis reuelata sunt. Ideo est quod ius poli vocatur ius naturale; quandoque vero ius diuinum. Quoniam multa sunt consona rationi rectae iure naturali & diuino: sicut consonum est rationi rectae sumptae ex credibilibus, quod euangelium praedicantes in-de sustententur: quamuis tamen per solam rationem pure naturalem hoc probari sufficienter non possit: sicut nec quod illa quae praedicant, sint vera &c. Secundo in hoc capitulo ostenditur, quod quando in altercatione praesenti contenditur, an vsus rerum possit esse absque iure vtendi: tam appellans quam impugnatus loquuntur de iure fori, quo quis potest in iudicio litigare. Tertio distinguuntur quinque modi habendi ius ad res temporales. Primo ex meriti dignitate: & isto modo soli iusti digni sunt, & impius non est dignus pane, quo vescitur. Secundo modo ex debiti necessitate vel honestate: & isto modo superflua diuitum sunt pauperum: & similiter bona ecclesiae, quia debent elargiri pauperibus, qui ad talia habent ius diuinum. Quoniam per ius diuinum diuites & ecclesiastici tenentur talia indigentibus exhibere. Tertio modo dicuntur temporalia esse aliquorum iure poli: & simul quandoque iure fori & conscientia bona. Et sic res, quibus quis vtitur in articulo necessitatis extremae sunt illius, siue sint illius iure fori siue non. Quarto modo dicuntur res esse aliquorum sinceritate c[?]. Et sic temporalia sunt illorum, qui non ex auaritia vel mala intentione detinent, sed ratione [?]. Quinto modo aliqua sunt alicuius iure fori tantum modo, vel quo ad dominium & proprietatem, vel quo ad vsum fructum, vel ad vsum nudum: & sic de similibus. Quarto replicatur distinctio de iustitia & iusto supra posita. Quinto respondetur ad formam argumenti ante positi, concedendo, quod ille qui re vtitur ex licentia, vtitur iuste, capiendo iuste a iustitia tertio modo dicta: quia vtitur conformiter rectae rationi, & sic iure vel iuste vti est bene moraliter vti, non quidem iure fori, sed iure poli. Quia omne quod recte fit absque iure fori, fit iure poli. Et circa hoc soluitur vna instantia declarando; quod non solum in extremae necessitatis articulo licet vti rebus iure poli, sed etiam in aliis casibus. Et consequenter ibi declaratur, quomodo ius commune naturale, cui licet renunciari non possit, habeat tamen limitari & coartari, ne in multis casibus in actum exeat circa res temporales habendas & appropriandas. Licet non possit ex toto sic coartari, quin in necessitate omnia sint communia. Et extra talem necessitatem sufficit sola permissio vel licentia Domini ad hoc, quod quis re aliena vtatur iure poli, absque alio nouo iure, prout hic probatur. Et in quarta parte ponuntur notabilia super literam, vbi ostenditur qualiter omne quod bene & iuste possidetur, iure possidetur, & quomodo bonus vsus a iure vtendi non separatur loquendo de iure poli, quod est potestas conformis rectae rationi absque pactione. Ibi etiam ostenditur, quod ius fori non semper est ex pactione conformi rectae rationi, sed aliquando discordanti: quia multa possidentur iure fori, quae non bene possidentur, vt ait Augustinus. Male, inquit, possidet, qui qui male vtitur suis & qui aliena præsumit. Quod etiam multa bene possideantur, quæ iure fori minime possidentur, probat hic: quia qui legitime præscribit rem alienam ante præscriptionem completam bene possidet: & tamen ante illam nullo iure fori possidet, sed solum iure poli. Quare &c.
units.tr: Cap. 65. In the first and second parts he recites and explains the second argument, which the one under attack adduces to prove that whoever has a licence to use something has a right to use the same thing. The argument is this: whoever uses a thing by another's licence without a right either uses it justly or unjustly. If justly, then by right: extra de verborum significationibus cap. ius datur & 14. q. 4. quid dicam. If unjustly, it agrees with the constitution Ad conditorem, etc. In the third part, the rejection and solution of this argument proceed in five steps. First, a distinction is made concerning right: for it is sometimes taken as the right of the forum, and sometimes as the right of heaven. The right of the forum is called the just, which is explicitly established by human or divine agreement or ordinance. And it is proved there how it ought not to be violated at the pleasure of anyone, just as neither the customs nor the laws of a people may be, with respect to whom they are laws. The right of heaven, however, is called natural equity, which, apart from every human and even divine purely positive ordinance, accords with right reason, purely natural or drawn from those things which have been revealed to us by God. Hence the right of heaven is called natural right, and sometimes divine right. For many things accord with right reason in natural and divine right: as it accords with right reason drawn from things credible that those who preach the gospel be supported by it, although this cannot be sufficiently proved by reason purely natural alone, just as neither can it be proved that the things they preach are true, etc. Second, in this chapter it is shown that when in the present dispute it is contended whether the use of things can be without a right of use, both the appellant and the one under attack speak of the right of the forum, by which one may litigate in court. Third, five modes of having a right to temporal goods are distinguished. The first is from the dignity of merit; and in this way only the just are worthy, and the impious is not worthy of the bread he eats. The second mode is from the necessity or honesty of obligation; and in this way the superfluities of the rich belong to the poor, and likewise the goods of the Church, because they ought to be distributed to the poor, who have a divine right to such things. For by divine right the rich and the clergy are bound to provide such things to the needy. The third mode is that temporal goods are said to belong to some by the right of heaven, and at the same time sometimes by the right of the forum and good conscience. And so the things which a person uses in the case of extreme necessity are his, whether they are his by right of the forum or not. The fourth mode is that things are said to belong to some by sincerity [?]. And so temporal goods belong to those who hold them not out of avarice or evil intention, but by reason of [?]. The fifth mode is that some things belong to someone by the right of the forum only, either as to ownership and property, or as to usufruct, or as to bare use; and so on for similar cases. Fourth, the distinction between justice and the just set out above is repeated. Fifth, the form of the argument set out before is answered, conceding that one who uses a thing by licence uses it justly, taking justly from justice in the third sense stated: for he uses it in conformity with right reason, and so to use by right or justly is to use well in a moral sense, not indeed by the right of the forum, but by the right of heaven. For whatever is rightly done without the right of the forum is done by the right of heaven. And on this point one objection is answered by declaring that it is lawful to use things by the right of heaven not only in the case of extreme necessity, but also in other cases. And consequently it is declared there how the common natural right, which cannot be renounced, nevertheless has to be limited and restricted, so that in many cases it does not come into effect with respect to acquiring and appropriating temporal goods. Although it cannot be restricted in such a way entirely, so that in necessity all things are common. And outside such necessity, the mere permission or licence of the owner is enough for someone to use another's thing by the right of heaven, without any new right, as is proved here. In the fourth part notes are given on the text, where it is shown how everything that is held well and justly is held by right, and how good use is not separated from the right of use, speaking of the right of heaven, which is a power in conformity with right reason without agreement. There it is also shown that the right of the forum is not always based on agreement conformable to right reason, but sometimes discordant with it: for many things are held by the right of the forum which are not held well, as Augustine says: Male, he says, possidet, qui who uses his own badly and presumes upon what belongs to others. That many things are also held well which are least held by the right of the forum, he proves here: for one who prescribes lawfully concerning another's thing before the prescription is complete holds it well; and yet before that he holds it by no right of the forum, but only by the right of heaven. Wherefore, etc.

units.la: Cap. 66. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat obiectionem impugnati contra rationem suam præmissam dicens. Nec obstat, quod Isidorus inter iustum & iniustum ponit fas medium; cum dicit: Transire per agrum alienum, fas est, ius non est &c. Ad quam respondet, quod Isidorus non intendit ponere actum medium inter iustum & iniustum: sed quod aliquid est licitum de iure diuino, quod non est licitum de iure humano. In tertia parte reducuntur verba Isidori contra impugnatum, ut ibi patet. In quarta exponendo litteram declaratur exemplariter, quomodo inter iustum & iniustum per abnegationem ponitur medium: & quomodo refert dicere affirmatiue: Aliquid de iure diuino licet. Et dicere negatiue: Aliquid non est de iure diuino illicitum &c. Et alia multa huiusmodi.
units.tr: Ch. 66. In the first two parts he recites and explains the objection of the opponent against his premised reasoning, saying: "Nor does it stand in the way that Isidore places fas as a middle between just and unjust, when he says: 'It is fas to pass through another's field, but it is not ius,' etc." To which he replies that Isidore did not intend to place an act as a middle between the just and the unjust, but that something is lawful by divine law which is not lawful by human law. In the third part the words of Isidore are brought back against the opponent, as is clear there. In the fourth part, by expounding the text, it is shown by example how a middle is set between the just and the unjust by negation, and how one may speak affirmatively: "Something is permitted by divine law," and negatively: "Something is not unlawful by divine law," etc., and many other things of this kind.

units.la: Cap. 67. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat quartam assertionem impugnati. Videlicet, quod actus vtendi re vsu consumptibili separatus à iure vtendi haberi non potest: eo quod nullus actus vtendi potest esse in rerum natura. Quia nec ante actum, nec in actu, nec post actum. In tertia parte, dicta improbantur. Disseruntur præterea multa de successiuis, quomodo habeant esse. Et an ipsum esse solummodo rem perfectam significet. In quarta parte exponendo verba textus habentur multa subtilia ex physica de tempore, motu, mutatum esse, & similibus.
units.tr: Ch. 67. In the first two parts he recites and explains the fourth assertion of the opponent, namely that the act of using a thing consumed by use cannot be had separately from the right of using it, because no act of using can exist in the nature of things: neither before the act, nor in the act, nor after the act. In the third part these claims are refuted. Furthermore, many things are discussed about successive things, how they have being, and whether being itself signifies only a perfect thing. In the fourth part, by expounding the words of the text, many subtle points from physics are treated concerning time, motion, "having been changed," and similar matters.

units.la: Cap. 68. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat quandam obiectionem appellantis; inferentis, quod ex verbis impugnati superius recitatis destruerentur gesta Christi & Apostolorum eius. In tertia parte ostenditur quomodo dicta obiectio truncate ab impugnato recitatur: & quomodo contra eum ratio eius retorquetur. In quarta parte declaratur littera.
units.tr: Ch. 68. In the first two parts he recites and explains a certain objection of the appellant, inferring that from the words of the opponent recited above, the deeds of Christ and of His Apostles would be destroyed. In the third part it is shown how the said objection is recited by the opponent in a truncated form, and how his own reasoning is turned back against him. In the fourth part the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 69. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad dictam obiectionem appellantis. Quam quidem obiectionem impugnant in tertia parte, ostendendo quod non respondeat ad mentem appellantis: Et quod quinq; irrationabilia contineat, vt ibidem patet. In quarta parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Ch. 69. In the first two parts he recites and explains the opponent's reply to the said objection of the appellant. The opponent's objection is attacked in the third part, showing that it does not answer the appellant's meaning, and that it contains five irrational points, as is clear there. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 70. Recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad secundam obiectionem appellantis, quæ fuit, quod per rationem impugnati nullus posset habere vsum rerum consumptibilium non vsu. Ad quam respondet concedendo conclusionem, loquendo de vsu facti. In tertia ostenditur, quod conclusio ab impugnato concessa, est erronea & vana. In quarta parte exponitur & notatur littera.
units.tr: Ch. 70. He recites and explains the opponent's reply to the appellant's second objection, which was that by the opponent's reasoning no one could have the use of consumable things without using them. To this he replies by granting the conclusion, speaking of use in fact. In the third part it is shown that the conclusion granted by the opponent is erroneous and empty. In the fourth part the text is expounded and noted.

units.la: Cap. 71. In prima parte resumit & in secunda declarat quandam aliam assertionem positam ab impugnato, quam appellans impugnat, eo quod ponit, quod si vsus in rebus vsu consumptibilibus posset constitui, illetamen vsus non esset simplex, nec à dominio & proprietate separatus. Quia per talem actum & cum ipso actu & in ipso actu res huiusmodi consumitur. In tertia parte hæc impugnantur propter duo. Primum, quia erroneum est dicere, q; vsus simplex non potest esse à dominio separatus. Et ob hoc ponitur multiplex acceptio horum terminorum Simplex, Simplicitas, Simpliciter, secundum diuersos modos loquendi in diuersis scientiis. Ostenditur etiam, quomodo actus vtendi multipliciter potest dici simplex. Secundum, quia in ratione impugnati tres continentur errores, vt patet ibidem. In quarta parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Ch. 71. In the first part he resumes, and in the second part he explains, another assertion put forward by the opponent, which the appellant attacks, because he holds that if use could be established in consumable things, such use would still not be simple, nor separated from dominion and ownership, because by such an act, and with and in the act itself, the thing of this kind is consumed. In the third part these claims are attacked on two grounds.
