First, because it is erroneous to say that simple use cannot be separated from dominion; and on this account the several senses of the terms "simple," "simplicity," and "simply" are set out, according to the different modes of speaking in different sciences. It is also shown how the act of using can in many ways be called simple. Second, because the opponent's reasoning contains three errors, as is clear there. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 72. Recitat & explicat aliam obiectionem appellantis continentem duas instantias. Quarum prima est, quod nec vestis, nec panis semper consumitur in principio actus. Secunda est quod sicut quis habet dominium serui sui, ita habet dominium panis in ore serui existentis. Et tandem ponitur breuis expositio literalis.
units.tr: Ch. 72. He recites and explains another objection of the appellant containing two instances. The first is that neither clothing nor bread is always consumed at the beginning of the act. The second is that just as someone has dominion over his servant, so he has dominion over the bread which is in the mouth of the servant. Finally, a brief literal exposition is given.

units.la: Cap. 73. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad præmissam obiectionem, dicentis appellantem constituoni suæ falsum imponere, scilicet quod intelligat, quod per primum actum, qui est vsus imperfectus, res consumatur. Quia constitutio solum intellexit de actu perfecto, per quem res consumitur. In tertia parte ad impugnandum prædicta distinguitur primo triplex modus, quo actus potest dici perfectus. Secundo declaratur intentio appellantis, & quomodo ratio eius maneat insoluta. Deinde arguitur contra prædictam responsionem. In quarta parte exponendo litteram notatur duplex actus vtendi, scilicet perfectus & imperfectus. Et ponitur differentia inter consumi & consumptum est.
units.tr: Ch. 73. In the first two parts he recites and explains the opponent's reply to the foregoing objection, which says that the appellant falsely imputes to the Constitution the view that by the first act, which is an imperfect use, the thing is consumed; because the Constitution spoke only of a perfect act, by which the thing is consumed. In the third part, in order to attack these claims, a threefold mode in which an act can be called perfect is first distinguished; second, the intention of the appellant is declared, and it is shown how his reasoning remains unanswered; then an argument is advanced against the said reply. In the fourth part, in expounding the text, a twofold act of using is noted, namely perfect and imperfect, and the difference between "to be consumed" and "consumed" is set out.

units.la: Cap. 74. In duabus primis partibus recitat & explicat assertionem impugnati, quam appellans reputat erroneam. Et continet tres partes. Primo enim dicit, quod carentia dominii in rebus, quibus Fratres Minores vtuntur, non prodest eis quantum ad statum perfectionis, eo quod per eam non sint pauperiores. Secunda igitur est, quod carentia dominii omni temporali commodo denudat pauperiorem non efficit non habentem. Tertia est quod tale dominium est nudum verbale & ænigmaticum. De quibus inferius amplius differetur. In vltima parte ponitur notatio literalis.
units.tr: Ch. 74. In the first two parts he recites and explains the opponent's assertion, which the appellant considers erroneous. It contains three parts. First, he says that the lack of dominion over the things the Lesser Brothers use does not benefit them as regards the state of perfection, since through it they are not made poorer. Second, that the lack of dominion does not make the one who is stripped of all temporal advantage poorer, nor the one who does not have it. Third, that such dominion is bare, merely verbal and enigmatic; these matters will be treated more fully below. In the last part a literal note is given.

units.la: Cap. 65. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat obiectiones appellantis contra assertionem præfatam, quæ consistit in hoc, quod Christus abdicationem talis dominii cohsuluit, & Apostoli acceptauerunt, & religionum institutores imitati sunt. Vltima parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Ch. 65. In the first two parts he recites and explains the appellant's objections against the aforesaid assertion, which consists in this: that Christ counselled the renunciation of such dominion, that the Apostles accepted it, and that the founders of religious orders imitated it. The last part expounds the text.

units.la: Cap. 76. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad obiectiones appellantis contra assertionem præmissam. Et primo dicit, quod appellans truncate recitat verba constitutionis; quia omittit rationem, per quam probatur, quod retentio dominii facta per Papam non profuit Fratribus quantum ad statum perfectionis, eo quod Minores non minus solliciti inuenti sunt post huiusmodi retentionem dominiū à Nicolao tertio factam, quam ahtea. In tertia parte impugnantur dicta eius propter uses errores. Quorum primus est, quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium in speciali & in communi ad statum perfectionis non pertinet. Ad quam improbandum multa notatu digna ibidem habentur, ostendendo quomodo ex possessione temporalium amor eorum nascitur & nutritur, & impedimentum fit amoris diuini. Et contra quod abdicatio proprietatis omnium temporalium disponit ad perfectionem, eo quod removet diuitias, quarum vermis est superbia. Soluuntur etiam obiectiones de perfectis diuitibus, cuiusmodi fuerunt Abraham, Iacob & Iob. Ostenditur praeterea quomodo potest aliquid intelligi pertinere ad perfectionem quadrupliciter. Et quomodo aliquid multipliciter dicitur difficile. Et quis proprie sit status perfectionis. Et quod non est inconueniens, quod vnus status excedat alium in vno, & excedatur ab eodem in alio. Et in solutionibus declaratur, quomodo differenter diuitiarum possessio & earum abdicatio sint instrumentum virtutis & perfectionis. Consequenter discutitur, quomodo possessio diuitiarum ad statum perfectionis praelatorum spectet: & quod intelligendum est eam ad talem statum pertinere non per se, sed quodam modo per accidens. Et quod in casu magis expediret communitati fidelium bona communia ecclesiae committere laicis iustis, bonis & industriis dispensanda, quam ipsis praelatis, supplendo eorum negligentiam, aut vt ipsi praelati liberius diuinorum contemplationi vacent. Item in solutione ad instantiam, quae fit de bonis ecclesiarum ad ecclesiasticos spectantibus, declaratur primo, quomodo bona a fidelibus Deo oblata ad duo ordinantur. Secundo, quomodo bona ecclesiae dicantur communia. Et quomodo sint dispensanda ecclesiasticis non solum indigentibus, sed etiam habentibus aliunde viuere. Laicis autem non nisi in mera necessitate indigentiae plura consequenter de bonis ecclesiasticis pertractantur. Item quomodo punire poena corporali ad praelatos pertinet. Item quomodo ecclesiasticarum rerum dispensatio posset vtiliter laicis competere. Additur in solutionibus instantiarum quomodo non solum magnarum diuitiarum abdicatio ad statum perfectionis faciat, sed etiam paruarum. Secundus error principaliter ibidem improbatus est, quod praecipue via disponitur ad charitatem per amputationem sollicitudinis circa temporalia. Cuius contrarium ostenditur eo quod amputatio amoris inordinati magis ad eam dissonat. Non enim omnis sollicitudo circa temporalia mala est, sicut omnis inordinatus amor. Tertius error est, quod per abdicationem dominii huiusmodi non amputatur sollicitudo temporalium. Addunt his duo mendacia diffamatoria ab impugnato contra Minores commentata. Pro quorum impugnatione ostenditur, quomodo Minores nec per se nec per alium possunt pecuniam pertractare. In quarta parte ponuntur notabilia circa litteram.
units.tr: Ch. 76. In the first two parts he recites and explains the opponent's reply to the appellant's objections against the premised assertion. And first he says that the appellant recites the words of the Constitution in a truncated form, because he omits the reasoning by which it is proved that the retention of dominion made by the Pope did not benefit the Brothers as regards the state of perfection, since the Minor Brothers were found no less anxious after such retention of dominion by Nicholas III than before. In the third part his claims are attacked on several errors. The first is that renunciation of the ownership of all temporal goods, both specific and in common, does not pertain to the state of perfection. To refute this, many points worth noting are given there, showing how love of temporal goods arises and is nourished from their possession, and becomes a hindrance to the love of God; and that renunciation of the ownership of all temporal goods disposes one to perfection, since it removes riches, of which the worm is pride. The objections concerning perfect rich men, such as Abraham, Jacob and Job, are also answered. It is further shown in how many ways something may be understood to pertain to perfection, and in how many ways something is called difficult, and what properly is the state of perfection; and that it is not inconsistent for one state to surpass another in one respect and be surpassed by the same in another. In the solutions it is explained how the possession of riches and their renunciation are differently instruments of virtue and perfection. Next it is discussed how the possession of riches pertains to the state of perfection of prelates, and that it must be understood to pertain to such a state not in itself, but in some manner accidentally. And that in the case, it would be more expedient for the community of the faithful to entrust the common goods of the Church to just, good and industrious laymen to be dispensed, supplying their negligence, or so that the prelates themselves may more freely devote themselves to contemplation of divine things, than to the prelates themselves. Likewise, in the solution to the objection concerning the goods of the churches belonging to churchmen, it is first explained how goods offered to God by the faithful are ordained to two ends; second, how the goods of the Church are called common, and how they are to be dispensed to churchmen not only when they are in need, but also when they have other means of living; and to laymen only in pure necessity of want. Further matters concerning the goods of the Church are treated consequently. Likewise, how to punish with bodily penalty pertains to prelates. Likewise, how the dispensing of church property could usefully belong to laymen. In the solutions to the instances it is added how renunciation makes for the state of perfection not only of great riches but also of small ones. The second error is principally refuted there: that the way is chiefly prepared for charity by cutting off anxiety about temporal things. The contrary is shown, since the cutting off of disordered love is more fitting to it; for not every anxiety about temporal things is evil, just as not every disordered love is. The third error is that by renunciation of such dominion anxiety about temporal things is not cut off. To these are added two defamatory lies invented by the opponent against the Lesser Brothers. For the refutation of these it is shown how the Lesser Brothers can handle money neither themselves nor through another. In the fourth part notable points are set out concerning the text.

units.la: Cap. 77. In duabus primis partibus recitat & explicat subsequentem particulam constitutionis. In qua impugnatus rursum nititur probare, quod carentia dominii, quam volunt Minores, non reddat eos pauperiores. In tertia parte praedicta assertio & probationes eius impugnantur propter quatuor errores. Primus est quod dicit Minores propter carentiam dominii Romanae ecclesiae reseruati non effectos pauperiores. Quo improbato ad solutionem cuiusdam instantiae ostenditur, quomodo Papa per tale Dominium effectus sit ditior. Adduntur praeterea duae opiniones de potestate Papae super bona temporalia ecclesiarum. Quarum prima est, quod Papa in rebus ecclesiae non habet plenitudinem potestatis. Et quod ex intentione fidelium diversae res diversis ecclesiis & monasteriis sunt speciali titulo assignatae, a quibus sine culpa & causa rationabili auferri non debent, vt exemplariter probatur de bonis Templariorum. Alia est opinio contraria priori. Secundus error est, quod dominium rerum, quibus Fratres vtuntur, Romanae ecclesiae reseruatum, est nudum, verbale, aenigmaticum & simulatum. Tertius error est, quod dominium omni temporali & corporali commodo denudatum est inutile, verbale & aenigmaticum. Quartus est, quod carentia huiusmodi dominii non reddit carentem pauperiorem. In quarta parte notando litteram ostenditur, quomodo accidat stultui Fratrum Minorum, quod ecclesia Romana reseruauit sibi dominium rerum ipsis quo ad vsum concessarum. Ostenditur praeterea, quomodo res, quarum Fratres vsum habent, & res ecclesiasticae, non ita libere ad Papam pertinent, sicut res laicorum ad laicos. Et quomodo Papa peccaret mortaliter dictando parentes suos de huiusmodi bonis: & similiter retinentes huiusmodi bona, & alia quamplurima ibidem notantur.
units.tr: Chapter 77. In the first two parts he recites and explains the following clause of the constitution. Here the opponent again tries to prove that the lack of ownership which the Minorites desire does not make them poorer. In the third part this assertion and its proofs are attacked on four counts. The first error is that he says the Minorites, through lacking the ownership reserved to the Roman Church, have not been made poorer. Having refuted this, he shows how the Pope himself is made richer through such ownership, and a solution is given to a certain objection. Two opinions are also added about the Pope's power over the temporal goods of churches. The first is that the Pope does not have the fullness of power over church property, and that, by the intention of the faithful, different goods have been assigned with a special title to different churches and monasteries, and these may not be taken from them without fault and without a reasonable cause, as is shown by example in the case of the goods of the Templars. The other opinion is contrary to the first. The second error is that the ownership of the things the Friars use, reserved to the Roman Church, is bare, merely verbal, enigmatic and feigned. The third error is that ownership stripped of every temporal and bodily benefit is useless, verbal and enigmatic. The fourth is that the lack of such ownership does not make the one lacking it poorer. In the fourth part, by noting the wording, it is shown how it happens to the foolish Friars Minor that the Roman Church reserved to itself the ownership of things granted to them for use. It is further shown how the things the Friars use, and ecclesiastical goods, do not belong to the Pope as freely as the goods of laymen belong to laymen; how the Pope would sin mortally by giving his relatives such goods, and likewise by keeping such goods; and many other matters are noted there.

units.la: Cap. 78. In duabus primis partibus recitatur & explicatur responsio impugnati ad secundum, quod in praedicta obiectione tangit appellans, scilicet quod Christus tribuisset simulatam & fallacem doctrinam consulendo omnia relinquere volentibus ad perfectionem attingere. Unde dicit, quod Christus nec Apostolis nec discipulis consuluit, quod non haberent aliquam saltem in communi. In tertia parte improbatur dicta responsio duo ostendendo. In quarta notantur verba litterae.
units.tr: Chapter 78. In the first two parts is recited and explained the opponent's reply to the second point touched on by the appellant in the aforementioned objection, namely that Christ would have given a feigned and deceptive teaching by advising those who wish to attain perfection to leave everything. Hence he says that Christ advised neither the Apostles nor the disciples to have no property at least in common. In the third part the said reply is refuted by showing two things. In the fourth the words of the text are noted.

units.la: Cap. 79. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad tertium, quod tangit dictus appellans, dicens quod sancti religionum sacrarum institutores errassent huiusmodi paupertatem euangelicam instituendo & seruando. Ad quod dicit, quod falsum est, eos eam instituisse aut a Religiosis precipi a Minoribus obseruatam. In tertia parte improbatur dicta responsio, ostendo, quod ad medium in quo te appellans fundat, non respondeat impugnatus. In quarta exponitur littera.
units.tr: Chapter 79. In the first two parts he recites and sets forth the opponent's reply to the third point touched on by the said appellant, who says that the holy founders of the sacred orders had erred in instituting and maintaining this evangelical poverty. To this he says that it is false that they instituted it, or that it is observed by the Friars Minor as something commanded to the religious. In the third part the said reply is refuted, showing that the opponent does not answer the middle term on which the appellant founds his case. In the fourth the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 80. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam obiectionem appellantis, quam probauit de Leuitis, quod habuerunt vsum rerum, quarum Deus habuit dominium. In tertia ostenditur, quod obiectio appellatis ab impugnato truncate & peruerse recitetur. Unde repetitur in forma. Et multa inferuntur contra impugnantem ostendendo ipsum haeresim sapere. In quarta exponitur littera. Cap. 81 In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad dictam objectionem, dicentis quod Numeri 18. expresse habetur, quod Deus dederit Leuitis etiam dominium decimatum, & non tantum vsum. In tertia parte impugnatur huiusmodi responsio euasiua, ostendendo quod appellans non dixerit Leuitas in nullis rebus habere dominium: neq; id oportere dici ad concludendum intentum suum. Ad quod sufficeret probasse ipsos aliquarum rerum vsum habuisse, quarum non ipsi, sed Deus dominium habuerit. Ex hoc enim infertur, quod vsus posset a dominio separari. Ostenditur etiam, quomodo dominium Domini, quamuis esset omni temporali commodo denudatum, non erat nudum, verbale, aenigmaticum aut simulatum. In quarta parte exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 80. In the first two parts he recites and sets forth another objection of the appellant, which he proved from the Levites, that they had the use of things over which God had the ownership. In the third it is shown that the objection has been recited by the opponent in a truncated and perverse way. Hence it is repeated in full form, and many conclusions are drawn against the opponent, showing that he savours of heresy. In the fourth the text is explained. Chapter 81. In the first two parts he recites and sets forth the opponent's reply to the said objection, which says that it is expressly stated in Numbers 18. that God gave the Levites ownership even of the tithes, and not merely use. In the third part this evasive reply is attacked, showing that the appellant did not say that the Levites have ownership of no things at all, nor was it necessary to say so in order to conclude his point. For it would have been enough to have proved that they had the use of some things whose ownership belonged not to them but to God. For from this it follows that use can be separated from ownership. It is also shown how the Lord's ownership, although it was stripped of every temporal benefit, was not bare, verbal, enigmatic or feigned. In the fourth part the text is explained.

units.la: Secunda constitutionis capitula.
units.tr: The second chapters of the constitution.

units.la: Cap. 82. Aggreditur impugnationes constitutionis Cum inter. In prima enim parte recitantur duo dicta eiusdem constitutionis. In quorum primo declaratur haereticum esse affirmare, Deinceps Christum & Apostolos nihil habuisse in speciali nec in communi. In secundo declaratur haereticum esse affirmare, quod non habuerint ius utendi, vendendi, & donandi, aut commutandi illa, quae sacra scriptura asserit eos habuisse. In secunda parte haec declarantur. In vltima parte improbantur dicta, primo notando, quomodo male dicatur Deinceps &c. quia declaratio Papae non facit nouas haereses. Secundo, quomodo erroneum asseruit impugnatus.
units.tr: Chapter 82. He takes up the attacks on the constitution Cum inter. In the first part two statements of the same constitution are recited. In the first of these it is declared heretical to affirm: Hence Christ and the Apostles had nothing in particular nor in common. In the second it is declared heretical to affirm that they did not have the right to use, sell, give away or exchange those things which Holy Scripture states they had. In the second part these are explained. In the last part the statements are refuted, first by noting how it is wrongly said Hence etc., because the Pope's declaration does not make new heresies; second, by showing how the opponent has asserted something erroneous.

units.la: Cap. 83. In duabus primis partibus ostendit, qualiter impugnatus dicit appellatum verba praedictae constitutionis imperfecte recitasse. Unde melius recitantur, ut clarius in secunda parte declaratur. In tertia ostendunt verba omissa nihil facere pro impugnato, sed contra impugnatum. Et in quarta exponendo textum declarant quomodo Christus nullius rei habuerit dominium, nec se pro Domino gesserit, sicut nec Apostoli, qui pecuniae vsum in tempore extremae necessitatis, non dominium habuerunt.
units.tr: Chapter 83. In the first two parts he shows how the opponent says that the appellant recited the words of the aforesaid constitution imperfectly. Hence they are recited better, as is set out more clearly in the second part. In the third part they show that the words omitted do nothing for the opponent but tell against him. And in the fourth, by expounding the text, they explain how Christ had ownership of nothing and did not behave as its owner, nor did the Apostles, who had the use of money in a time of extreme necessity but not ownership.

units.la: Cap. 84. Recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus exprimit intellectum, quem appellans dictae constitutioni imponit, dicens quod secundum appellantem dicta constitutio loquitur de iure proprietatis, & dominii civilis & mundani. Et deinde in tertia parte improbatur dicta recitatio, tanquam truncata & imperfecta, ut patebit in sequenti capitulo.
units.tr: Chapter 84. He recites and sets forth how the opponent expresses the meaning which the appellant imposes on the said constitution, saying that according to the appellant the said constitution speaks of the right of property and of civil and worldly ownership. Then in the third part this recitation is refuted as truncated and imperfect, as will be clear in the following chapter.

units.la: Cap. 85. Recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus nititur ostendere appellantem imposuisse constitutioni suae, quod loquitur de iure proprietatis & dominii, de quo tamen non facit mentionem. In tertia parte ostendunt appellantem nihil falsi imposuisse. In quarta declaratur textus.
units.tr: Chapter 85. He recites and sets forth how the opponent tries to show that the appellant imposed on his constitution that it speaks of the right of property and ownership, though it makes no mention of these. In the third part they show that the appellant imposed nothing false. In the fourth the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 86. Recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus dat quandam responsionem generalem ad obiectiones appellantis, dicendo quod omnes vnico verbo repelluntur per hoc, quod constitutio de dominio mentionem non facit. In tertia parte ostendunt, quod licet de hoc ibi non fiat mentio vocalis, tamen ille est sensus, quem dictae obiectiones praetendunt, intelligendo scilicet de dominio humano.
units.tr: Chapter 86. He recites and sets forth how the opponent gives a certain general reply to the appellant's objections, saying that all of them are repelled by a single word, namely that the constitution makes no mention of ownership. In the third part they show that although no explicit mention of it is made there, nevertheless that is the sense which the said objections put forward, namely understood as referring to human ownership.

units.la: Cap. 87. Recitat & declarat principalem assertionem appellantis, videlicet quod Christus & Apostoli nullius rei temporalis proprietatem habuerunt, neque in communi, neque in speciali. Et consequenter ponitur declaratio litteralis, in qua ostenditur, quod dicta assertio appellantis non est certinax.
units.tr: Chapter 87. He recites and sets forth the appellant's principal assertion, namely that Christ and the Apostles had ownership of no temporal thing, neither in common nor in particular. And consequently a literal explanation is given, in which it is shown that the said assertion of the appellant is not obstinate.

units.la: Cap. 88. In duab' primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus primo ponit hanc conclusionem, quod dominium rerum temporalium non iure humano & mundano, sed diuino fuerit introductum. Et per consequens, quod iure diuino sunt dominia aliqua. Pro quo ostenditur, quod ius diuinum, & quo iure facta sit rerum diuisio, ut patet in textu & declarationem eius. In tertia parte procedit ad impugnationem textus, & ex eo illatorum, ponendo primo quinque conclusiones. Quarum prima est, quod in statu innocentiae nullum fuit dominium proprium. Secunda quod primum dominium proprium fuit post lapsum iure humano seu ordinatione humana introductum. Vbi multa pulchra in solutionibus obiectionum habentur de diuisione illa, & diuisorum dominio. Tertia conclusio est, quod iure humano absque legibus regum contra alios principatus & magistratus distinctorum multa rerum dominia introducta fuerunt. Quarta est, quod aliarum rerum temporalium diuersa & distincta dominia immediata ordinatione diuina introducta fuerunt. Quinta conclusio est, quod post promulgationem Euangelii nulla dominia a iure diuino, neque ex speciali collatione Dei fuerunt introducta. Vnde probatur, quod Christus illis, quos panibus & piscibus pauit, non dedit illorum dominium, sed vsum simplicem. Soluitur praeterea obiectio de clericis, qui videntur ordinatione Dei ex praedicatione viuere. Ostenditur etiam duplex ius diuinum, speciale & generale. Et alia multa, quae ibi clarissime habentur. Secundo ponuntur quatuor errores impugnati. Tertio in quarta parte discurrendo per litteram ostenditur, quid proprie iure diuino possideatur. Multa insuper notatu dignissima disseruntur de rerum dominio, quo iure, & a quibus habeatur.
units.tr: Chapter 88. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the constitution, in which the opponent first lays down this conclusion: that the ownership of temporal things was introduced not by human and worldly law but by divine law; and consequently that some ownerships exist by divine right. To support this it is shown that divine law, and by what divine law the division of things was made, as appears in the text and its explanation. In the third part he proceeds to attack the text and the conclusions drawn from it, first laying down five conclusions. The first is that in the state of innocence there was no private ownership. The second, that the first private ownership came after the fall, introduced by human law or human ordinance. Here many fine points are found in the solutions of objections concerning that division and the ownership of the divided things. The third conclusion is that by human law, without the laws of kings, many ownerships of things were introduced against other principalities and magistrates. The fourth is that ownerships of other temporal things, distinct and different, were introduced by immediate divine ordinance. The fifth conclusion is that after the promulgation of the Gospel no ownerships were introduced by divine law or by a special bestowal of God. Hence it is proved that Christ did not give to those whom he fed with loaves and fish the ownership of them, but only simple use. Moreover, the objection concerning clerics, who seem by God's ordinance to live from preaching, is answered. Two kinds of divine law, special and general, are also shown; and many other matters, which are very clearly set out there. Secondly, four errors of the opponent are laid down. Thirdly, in the fourth part, running through the text, it is shown what is properly possessed by divine right. Many things most worthy of notice are also discussed concerning the ownership of things, by what law it is held, and from whom it is held.

units.la: Cap. 89. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus nititur ostendere, quod dominium rerum temporalium nullo iure humano potuit dari hominibus, sed diuino tantum, eo quod Deus est Dominus omnium rerum, sine cuius voluntate dari non possunt. In tertia ostendiostenditur, quod hoc non est contra appellantem, qui non intendit negare, quod dominium temporale commune primo fuerit à Deo, à quo primum dominium datum fuit hominibus. Sed non sequitur, quod prima diuisio dominiorum non fuerit inducta à iure humano, quo alicui competit dominium proprium, sic quod potest illud in alterum transferre absq; reuelatione, quod hoc Deo placeat. Demum exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 89. In the first two parts, the one being refuted (the opponent) is recited and explained, showing how he seeks to prove that dominion over temporal things could not be given to human beings by any human right, but only by divine right, because God is the Lord of all things and they cannot be given without his will. In the third part it is shown that this is not against the appellant, who does not intend to deny that common temporal dominion was first from God, from whom the first dominion was given to human beings. But it does not follow that the first division of dominions was not introduced by human right, by which someone has his own dominion, so that he can transfer it to another without revelation that this pleases God. Finally, the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 90. Recitat & explicat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus ostendit, quid per ius humanum circa rerum dominium est inductum, dicens quot modi acquirendi dominium, & modi agendi pro temporalibus in iudicio. Deinde exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 90. It recites and explains another part of the constitution, in which the one being refuted shows what has been introduced by human right concerning dominion over things, stating how many modes of acquiring dominion there are, and the modes of pleading concerning temporal matters in court. Then the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 91. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad auctoritates pro contraria assertione allegatas. In tertia parte impugnando dictam responsionem reprehendit duos errores impugnati. Primus est, quod dicit, ius ciuile formulas duntaxat actionum induxise. Ad cuius euidentiam ponitur iuris ciuilis & iuris naturalis multiplex acceptio. Secundus est, quia dicit Augustinum non assertiue, sed disputatiue dixisse verba per appellantem adducta. In quarta parte notatur & declaratur littera.
units.tr: Chapter 91. In the first two parts, it recites and explains the response of the one being refuted to the authorities cited for the opposite assertion. In the third part, in refuting that response, it censures two errors of the one being refuted. The first is that he says civil law introduced only the forms of actions. To make this clear, the manifold meanings of civil law and natural law are set out. The second is that he says Augustine spoke the words cited by the appellant not assertively but disputatively. In the fourth part, the text is noted and explained.

units.la: Cap. 92. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionē impugnati ad secundam auctoritatem ab appellante adductam, dicens quod beatus Clemens per iniquitatem non intellexit ius gentium, sed peccatum primorum parentum. In tertia parte impugnatores retorquent responsionem in respondentem. In quarta exponendo litteram notatur primo, quod licet in statu innocentiæ communis vsus omnium fuisset, non tamen expediuit post peccatum propter pronitatem hominum ad dissentiendum & male agendum. Secundo multipliciter exponitur hoc verbum Per iniquitatem, quod habetur in cap. dilectissimis allegato. Exponitur etiam illud euangelicum: Facite vobis amicos de Mammona iniquitatis.
units.tr: Chapter 92. In the first two parts, it recites and explains the response of the one being refuted to the second authority cited by the appellant, saying that the blessed Clement did not understand by iniquity the law of nations, but the sin of the first parents. In the third part, the refuters turn the response back upon the respondent. In the fourth part, in explaining the text, it is first noted that although in the state of innocence the common use of all things was theirs, it was not expedient after the sin, on account of the proneness of human beings to dissent and to act badly. Second, the expression Through iniquity, which occurs in the cited chapter "Dilectissimis", is explained in many ways. That gospel saying is also explained: Make to yourselves friends by means of the mammon of unrighteousness.

units.la: Cap. 93. Accedit ad principalem quæstionem, in qua quæritur, vtrum Christus & Apostoli habuerunt alicuius rei temporalis dominium. In prima enim parte primo recitantur quindecim auctoritates, per quas impugnatus nititur ostendere, quod Christus fuit rex in temporalibus. Secundo octo, per quas conatur probare, quod Christus in quantum homo, fuit Dominus temporalium. Tertio determinat tempus, quando Christus habuit regnum & dominium. In secunda parte declarantur prædicta. In tertia parte improbantur, distinguendo de triplici regimine: & quomodo huiusmodi vocabula rex & Dominus varie accipiantur. Ostenditur deinde, quomodo Christus potuerit concedi rex & Dominus omnium. Et quomodo non regnauerit temporaliter, nec habuerit dominium vniuersale: & quomodo Cæsar fuerit Christo viuente verus Imperator, nec à Christo recognouerit dominium suum, nec Christus ab aliquo alio. Item pulchre ostenditur, quomodo vtile fuerit Christi fidelibus, quod Christus obtinuit summum sacerdotium, & etiam quod abdicauit rerum temporalium dominium. Et quomodo successor Christi, hoc est beatus Petrus, non obtinuerit per talem successionem alicuius rei temporalis dominium: & multa alia. In quarta parte discurrendo per litteram soluuntur omnes auctoritates perimpugnatum adductæ, multaq; scitu digna disseruntur, quæ ibidem facilíter inuenias.
units.tr: Chapter 93. It comes to the principal question, in which it is asked whether Christ and the Apostles had dominion over any temporal thing. In the first part, first fifteen authorities are recited, by which the one being refuted seeks to show that Christ was king in temporal matters. Second, eight, by which he tries to prove that Christ, insofar as he was a man, was Lord of temporal things. Third, he determines the time when Christ had kingdom and dominion. In the second part, the foregoing is explained. In the third part, they are refuted, distinguishing among three kinds of rule, and how such terms as king and Lord are variously understood. It is then shown how Christ could be granted to be king and Lord of all things, and how he did not reign temporally, nor have universal dominion; and how Caesar was the true emperor while Christ lived, and neither acknowledged his dominion from Christ, nor Christ from anyone else. Likewise, it is beautifully shown how it was useful for Christ's faithful that Christ obtained the supreme priesthood, and also that he renounced dominion over temporal things; and how the successor of Christ, that is blessed Peter, did not obtain, by such succession, any dominion over temporal things; and many other things. In the fourth part, going through the text, all the authorities adduced against the one being refuted are resolved, and many things worth knowing are discussed, which you may easily find there.

units.la: Cap. 94. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat quomodo impugnatus conatur probare, quod Christus præter vniuersale rerum dominium, quod ab initio habuit ex Dei datione, postea quarundam rerum temporalium dominium acquisiuit. Aliis modis, scilicet vel emptione vel collatione. Quod probat multis auctoritatibus & exemplis, vtpote de vestimentis eius, de calciamentis & de loculis, de pane & vino in cœna dicens, quod eorum habuit dominium. In tertia parte dicta improbantur ostendendo quatuor. Primo quod Christus nullius rei habuit dominium. Secundo quod non habuit calciamenta etiam quo ad vsum. Tertio specialiter quod non habuit proprietatem loculorum. Quarto concluditur quomodo aliquas res habuerit absque dominio & proprietate. In quarta parte declarando textum soluuntur auctoritates. Et soluitur etiam quæstio, qua quæritur: Cuius erant Christi vestimenta quo ad dominium? Item quomodo Christo consentiente Iudas, qui erat Apostolus, portabat loculos & pecuniam. Et quædam alia notatu digna ibidem inuenies.
units.tr: Chapter 94. In the first two parts, it recites and explains how the one being refuted tries to prove that Christ, besides the universal dominion over things which he had from the beginning by God's gift, afterwards acquired dominion over certain temporal things by other means, namely by purchase or by donation. He proves this by many authorities and examples, such as his garments, his shoes, and his purses, and the bread and wine at the supper, saying that he had dominion over them. In the third part, the said points are refuted by showing four things. First, that Christ had dominion over nothing. Second, that he did not have shoes even for use. Third, that he specifically did not have ownership of the purses. Fourth, it is concluded how he had some things without dominion and ownership. In the fourth part, by explaining the text, the authorities are resolved. It is also resolved the question: To whom did Christ's garments belong as to dominion? Likewise, how Judas, who was an Apostle, carried the purses and the money with Christ's consent. And you will find certain other things worth noting there.

units.la: Cap. 95. Primo recitat & secundo explicat partem subsequentem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus nititur probare, quod Christus regno & dominio non renunciauit: imo quod nec potuit illi renunciasse, quia fecisset contra ordinationem patris, qui regnum ipsius Christi in perpetuum durare ordinauerat. In tertia parte improbantur prædicta inferendo ex dictis impugnati duos errores. Quorum primus est, quod Christus non longe ante passionem habuit regnum temporale & dominium seu proprietatem temporalium. Secundus est quod ideo Christus nullo modo potuit renunciare regno & dominio, quia sic faciendo fecisset contra ordinationem patris sui. Pro cuius impugnatione ostenditur primo, quod ratio impugnati ad hoc probandum assumit, quod omnia de necessitate eueniunt. Contra quod quia hæreticum est, probant primo quod non omnia de necessitate eueniunt. Secunda quod nulla quantum ad diuinam potentiam de necessitate eueniunt. Tertio quod si Christus habuit huiusmodi regnum & dominium, ipse potuit eisdem renunciare. Quarto declaratur quomodo debeat intelligi, quod in Deo est duplex potentia, scilicet absoluta & ordinata, & quomodo Deus potest aliqua facere de potentia absoluta, quæ non facit de potentia ordinata. Et quinto ad rationes, quæ pro dicta hæresi adducuntur, respondetur. Et hoc faciendo exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 95. First it recites and secondly explains the following part of the constitution, in which the one being refuted seeks to prove that Christ did not renounce kingdom and dominion; indeed that he could not have renounced them, because he would have acted against the ordinance of the Father, who had ordained that Christ's own kingdom should endure forever. In the third part, the foregoing is refuted by drawing from the statements of the one being refuted two errors. The first of these is that Christ, not long before his passion, had a temporal kingdom and dominion, or ownership of temporal things. The second is that for this reason Christ could in no way renounce kingdom and dominion, because in doing so he would have acted against the ordinance of his Father. For the refutation of this, it is shown first that the one being refuted, in order to prove this, assumes that all things happen of necessity. Since this is heretical, they prove first that not all things happen of necessity. Second, that nothing happens of necessity with respect to divine power. Third, that if Christ had such a kingdom and dominion, he himself could renounce them. Fourth, it is explained how it must be understood that in God there is a twofold power, namely absolute and ordained, and how God can do some things by absolute power which he does not do by ordained power. And fifth, answers are given to the arguments adduced for the said heresy. In doing this the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 96. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat partem dictæ constitutionis, in qua impugnatus nititur ostendere, quod non obstante, quod Christus habuit regnum temporale & universale rerum dominium, ipse fuit pauper & egenus, non propter carentiam dominii, sed propter carentiam perceptionis fructuum. Quod probat rationibus, auctoritatibus & exemplis. In tertia parte impugnantur prædicta propter quatuor errores. Primus est, quia dicit, Christum non fuisse pauperem propter carentiam dominii, sed propter carentiam fructuum &c. Cuius primo contrarium probatur. Secundo quod congruebat ipsum suscipere huiusmodi defectum. Tertio quod nobis expediebat Christum huiusmodi dominium abdicasse. Unde in solutione cuiusdam objectionis declaratur, quomodo carentia proprietatis debeat reputari defectus in statu naturæ institutæ. Secundus error impugnati est, quod dicit, quod nudum dominium in perpetuum ab omni temporali commodo separatum habentem non faciat divitem. Tertius error est, quod omne dominium à perceptione temporalis commodi in perpetuum separatum, est inutile reputandum. Quartus est, quod Christus in quantum homo in quibusdam paucis pro rege vel Domino se gessit. In cuius improbatione ostenditur, quod Christus fugando de templo vendentes & ementes gessit officium ostiarii, & non Imperatoris. Et quod sententia Magistri Sententiarum est merito præferenda sententiæ Iuristarum: Qui cum se intromittunt de difficultatibus theologicis, ultra verba, quæ à Theologia receperunt, falcem mittunt in messem alienam. Quapropter quando de suo aliqua inserere præsumunt, facile in errorem incidunt. In quarta parte exponitur & notatur littera.
units.tr: Chapter 96. In the first two parts, it recites and explains the part of the said constitution in which the one being refuted seeks to show that, although Christ had a temporal kingdom and universal dominion over things, he was poor and needy, not because of lack of dominion, but because of lack of receiving the fruits. He proves this by reasons, authorities and examples. In the third part, the foregoing is refuted on account of four errors. The first is that he says Christ was not poor because of lack of dominion, but because of lack of fruits, etc. The contrary of this is proved first. Second, that it was fitting for him to undergo such a defect. Third, that it was expedient for us that Christ renounced such dominion. Hence, in the solution of a certain objection, it is explained how lack of ownership ought to be regarded as a defect in the state of instituted nature. The second error of the one being refuted is that he says that a man who has bare dominion, perpetually separated from every temporal advantage, is not made rich. The third error is that everything that is perpetually separated from the receiving of temporal advantage must be regarded as useless. The fourth is that Christ, as a man, acted as king or Lord in a few particular matters. In refuting this, it is shown that Christ, in driving the sellers and buyers out of the temple, performed the office of a doorkeeper, and not of an emperor. And that the opinion of the Master of the Sentences is rightly to be preferred to the opinion of the lawyers, who, when they meddle with theological difficulties beyond the words they have received from theology, put their sickle into another's harvest; so when they presume to insert something of their own, they easily fall into error. In the fourth part, the text is explained and noted.

units.la: Cap. 97. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus discutit utrum Apostoli habuerunt aliquarum rerum dominium in speciali vel in communi: & utrumcis licuerit pro temporalibus in iudicio litigare. Et præmittuntur distinctiones duæ. Primo de tempore, quo cum Christo fuerunt, & post. Secundo de tempore, antequam ad prædicationem mitterentur, vel postquam à prædicatione reuersi fuerant. Secundum quas distinctiones postea ad quæstionem respondebit. Nihil autem hic impugnatur: quia nihil disseritur, sed textus paucis explanatur.
units.tr: Cap. 97. In the first two parts he recites and explains the part of the constitution in which the impugned party examines whether the Apostles had ownership of any goods, individually or in common, and whether it was lawful for them to go to law over temporal matters. Two distinctions are first set out: first, concerning the time when they were with Christ and afterwards; second, concerning the time before they were sent out to preach, or after they had returned from preaching. The answer to the question will later be given according to these distinctions. Nothing is attacked here, because nothing is argued; the text is simply explained briefly.

units.la: Cap. 98. In duabus primis partibus recitat & explicat, quomodo iuxta membra præmissæ divisionis impugnatus determinat, quod Apostolis antequam ad prædicationem mitterentur, nulla temporalia interdicta fuerunt. Et hoc probat unica ratione. In tertia parte impugnantur prædicta. In quarta exponendo litteram soluuntur auctoritates per impugnatum adductæ. Et ostenditur quadruplex expositio illius, quod dicitur, quod Christus egrediens de Synagoga &c.
units.tr: Cap. 98. In the first two parts he recites and explains how, following the members of the divisions just stated, the impugned party determines that no temporal goods were forbidden to the Apostles before they were sent out to preach. He proves this by a single argument. In the third part the points just mentioned are attacked. In the fourth part, by expounding the text, the authorities cited by the impugned party are answered, and a fourfold interpretation of the statement that Christ, going out of the synagogue, etc., is shown.

units.la: Cap. 99. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat secundam rationem impugnati ad probandum, quod Apostolis, antequam ad prædicandum mitterentur, nulla temporalia interdicta fuerunt: eo quod dum eos ad prædicandum misit, tunc eis aliqua interdixit. In tertia parte ostenditur inefficacia prædictæ rationis: declarando primo, quomodo aliquo interdicto prius generaliter: postea non frustra illud idem interdicitur specialiter, quod exemplis declaratur. Et per ipsam inefficax ratio impugnati ostenditur. In quarta parte ponitur expositio litteralis.
units.tr: Cap. 99. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned party's second argument for proving that no temporal goods were forbidden to the Apostles before they were sent out to preach, namely because when he sent them to preach, he then forbade them certain things. In the third part the weakness of this argument is shown: first explaining how something may be forbidden in general beforehand and yet the same thing is afterwards forbidden specifically, not without reason; this is illustrated by examples. By this the impugned party's argument is shown to be ineffective. In the fourth part the literal sense is given.

units.la: Cap. 100. In duabus primis partibus recitat & explicat tertiam rationem impugnati ad probandum, quod Apostolis antequam ad prædicandum mitterentur, nulla temporalia fuerunt interdicta, per hoc quod Christus non dedit aliam legem viuendi Apostolis & aliis discipulis. Sed aliis discipulis non fuit interdictum temporalia habere, ut probat quatuor exemplis. Ergo nec discipulis. In tertia parte impugnantur prædicta: & ostenditur esse erroneum dicere, quod Christus non dederit aliam legem viuendi Apostolis & quibuscunq; discipulis. In quarta parte exponendo litteram ostenditur triplex fuisse discipulorum differentia.
units.tr: Cap. 100. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned party's third argument for proving that no temporal goods were forbidden to the Apostles before they were sent out to preach, from the fact that Christ gave the Apostles and the other disciples no other rule of life. But the other disciples were not forbidden to have temporal goods, as he proves by four examples; therefore neither were the Apostles. In the third part the points just mentioned are attacked, and it is shown to be erroneous to say that Christ did not give the Apostles and all the disciples another rule of life. In the fourth part, by expounding the text, a threefold difference among the disciples is shown.

units.la: Cap. 101. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat quartam rationem impugnati pro assertione prædicta, quæ potest sic formari. Christus non indixit Apostolis aliam viam, quando fecit eos Apostolos, quam prius habuerunt. Ergo cum antequam essent Apostoli, non dimiserunt omnia temporalia, sequitur quod nec postea. In tertia parte prædicta impugnantur. Primo quia ex scripturarum testimoniis minime probatur, quod cum Christus ex discipulis fecit Apostolos aliam viam non indixit. Secundo, quia insinuatur, quod tunc Christus eos Apostolos ordinauerit, quando misit eos ad prædicandum. Cuius contrarium ostenditur ex serie textus: & soluitur obiectio de Matthæi electione. In quarta parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Cap. 101. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned party's fourth argument in support of the above assertion, which may be put in this form: Christ did not appoint for the Apostles any other way when he made them Apostles than the one they had before. Therefore, since before they were Apostles they did not give up all temporal goods, it follows that neither did they afterwards. In the third part the above is attacked. First, because it is by no means proved from the testimonies of Scripture that when Christ made Apostles out of the disciples he did not appoint another way. Second, because it is suggested that Christ then ordained them Apostles when he sent them to preach. The contrary is shown from the sequence of the text, and the objection concerning the choice of Matthew is answered. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 102. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat responsionem impugnati ad quæstionem ab eo propositam iuxta secundum membrum suæ distinctionis, dicentis primo, quod Apostolis pro tempore quo ad prædicandum mittebantur, aliqua temporalia fuerunt interdicta. Quod tribus auctoritatibus probat. Et addit, quod illud præceptum fuit temporale, hoc est ad tempus datum. In tertia parte ostenditur prædictorum quadruplex error. Primo cum dicitur, quod huiusmodi præceptum fuerit temporale. Secundo cum imponit beato Augustino, quod dixisset, illud non fuisse præceptum, sed potestatem eis concessam. Ad cuius impugnationis euidentiam ostenditur, quod Christus mittens Apostolos ad prædicandum, aliqua eis præcepit, aliqua permisit, & aliqua interdixit. Tertio cum asserit præceptum datum 72. Discipulis, etiam temporale suisse, scil. tempore viæ tantum. Quarto cum dicit patere exdictis suis, quod quidam prædictorum 72. habuerunt largas possessiones, cum solum ostensum sit de Ioseph, Simone leproso, Dorca & aliis, qui non erant de 72. ad prædicandum missis. In quarta parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Cap. 102. In the first two parts he recites and explains the impugned party's answer to the question put by him, according to the second member of his distinction, which says first that during the time when the Apostles were sent out to preach, some temporal goods were forbidden to them. He proves this by three authorities. And he adds that this precept was temporary, that is, given for a time. In the third part a fourfold error of the above is shown. First, when he says that such a precept was temporary. Second, when he charges Saint Augustine with saying that it was not a precept but a permission granted to them. To make clear the refutation of this, it is shown that Christ, in sending the Apostles to preach, commanded some things, permitted some, and forbade some. Third, when he asserts that the precept given to the seventy-two disciples was also temporary, namely for the time of the journey only. Fourth, when he says it is clear from his own statements that some of the seventy-two had large estates, whereas it has been shown only of Joseph, Simon the leper, Dorcas and others, who were not among the seventy-two sent to preach. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 103. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem constitutionis, in qua impugnatus respondet ad propositam quaestionem iuxta tertium membrum distinctionis eiusdem. Unde specialiter probat, quod Apostolis, postquam fuerunt de praedicatione reuersi, licuerit habere omnia, quae eis pro tempore praedicationis praecedentis fuerant interdicta. Et ad hoc probandum adducit exempla. In tertia parte ostenditur ipsum errare in hoc, quod dicit Apostolos post reversionem a praedicatione habuisse panes, pisces, tunicas, pecuniam, & gladios quo ad dominium & proprietatem. In quarta parte exponendo litteram soluuntur auctoritates per impugnatum adductae & quaedam obiectiones curiosae & scitu dignae soluuntur.
units.tr: Cap. 103. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the constitution, in which the impugned party answers the question proposed, according to the third member of the same distinction. Hence he especially proves that it was lawful for the Apostles, after they had returned from preaching, to have all the things that had been forbidden to them during the time of the earlier preaching. To prove this he adduces examples. In the third part it is shown that he errs in saying that after returning from preaching the Apostles had bread, fish, tunics, money and swords as to ownership and property. In the fourth part, by expounding the text, the authorities cited by the impugned party are answered, and certain curious objections worth knowing are resolved.

units.la: Cap. 104. Prosequitur primum membrum secundae distinctionis dicens, quod pro illo tempore [?] quantum ad temporalia circa Apostolos immutatum. Et ibidem distinguit de tempore ante vel post missionem Spiritus sancti. Deinde in ultima parte ponitur duplex illius dicti intellectus.
units.tr: Cap. 104. He follows up the first member of the second distinction, saying that for that time [?] as regards temporal goods was changed for the Apostles. In the same place he distinguishes between the time before and after the mission of the Holy Spirit. Then in the last part a twofold meaning of that statement is given.

units.la: Cap. 105. In duabus primis partibus prosequitur secundum membrum dictae secundae distinctionis, ostendendo quod Apostoli & quidam alii post missionem Spiritus sancti habebant omnia communia quod ad dominium: licet non gentiles post eorum conversionem. Et ita distinguitur inter Iudaeos conversos & inter gentiles conversos. In ultima parte exponitur littera.
units.tr: Cap. 105. In the first two parts he follows up the second member of the said second distinction, showing that after the mission of the Holy Spirit the Apostles and certain others had all things in common as regards ownership, though not the Gentiles after their conversion. And so a distinction is drawn between converted Jews and converted Gentiles. In the last part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 106. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat aliam partem dictae constitutionis, in qua impugnatus pertractat assertionem contrariam assertioni appellantis, dicentis illa non erant Apostolis communia. Quod ipse impugnatus reprehendit ducendo ad hoc in consequens: quod sic dicendo Apostoli essent a numero fidelium excludendi, cum dictum sit, quod fidelibus omnia erant communia. In tertia parte impugnatores tria contra impugnatum asserunt. Primum, quod appellanti falsum imponit, dicentes eo quod non neget Apostolis omnimodo fuisse communia. Quomodo autem communia habuerint declarant. Secundum est, quod intentum suum impugnatus non probet sufficienter; eo quod arguendo a magis communi ad minus commune sine distributione committat fallaciam consequentis. Tertium quod non respondet ad quaestionem secundum debitum intellectum, quem declarando duo faciunt. Primo ostendunt quod communio, de qua mentionem fecit, non solum una die, sed multo tempore durauit. Secundo quod Apostoli toto tempore post missionem Spiritus sancti caruerunt proprietate & dominio temporalium, saltem quod esset alicui Apostolorum proprium, vel etiam speciali collegio ipsorum. Et ad hoc adducunt plures rationes soluendo quasdam obiectiones interpositas. In quarta declarantur & notantur verba textus.
units.tr: Cap. 106. In the first two parts he recites and explains another part of the said constitution, in which the impugned party treats an assertion contrary to that of the appellant, who said that those things were not common to the Apostles. The impugned party rebukes this by drawing a consequence from it: that if one spoke so, the Apostles would have to be excluded from the number of the faithful, since it has been said that all things were common to the faithful. In the third part the attackers make three assertions against the impugned party. The first is that he falsely charges the appellant, since they say the appellant did not deny that the Apostles had things in common in every way; and they explain how they did have things in common. The second is that the impugned party does not sufficiently prove his intended point, because in arguing from what is more common to what is less common, without distinction, he commits the fallacy of the consequent. The third is that he does not answer the question according to its proper sense, which they set out in two ways. First, they show that the community of which he spoke lasted not only for one day but for a long time. Second, that the Apostles, for the whole time after the mission of the Holy Spirit, lacked the property and ownership of temporal goods, at least such as might belong to any one of the Apostles as his own, or even to a special college of them. To this they adduce several arguments, resolving certain objections raised. In the fourth part the words of the text are explained and noted.

units.la: Cap. 107. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat quomodo impugnatus prosequitur aliud membrum dictae diuisionis positae capitulo 103. ostendens quod communicauerunt sua. Et ad hoc quatuor auctoritates adducit. In tertia parte improbant dictum eius, eo quod nihil ad propositam quaestionem faciat, neq; bene probetur. In quarta exponitur littera.
units.tr: Cap. 107. In the first two parts he recites and explains how the impugned party pursues another member of the said division given in chapter 103, showing that they shared their possessions. To this he adduces four authorities. In the third part they reject his statement, because it has no bearing on the question proposed and is not well proved. In the fourth part the text is expounded.

units.la: Cap. 108. Accedit ad tractandum hanc quaestionem: utrum licuerit Apostolis pro rebus temporalibus litigare. Unde in duabus primis partibus recitatur & declaratur, quomodo impugnatus improbat assertionem appellantis super hac re. Qui tenet, quod eis non licuerit in iudicio litigare, fundans se in tribus auctoritatibus sacrae scripturae, ostendensq; quomodo contendere in iudicio, licet stet cum perfectione essentiali, diminuit tamen perfectionem supererogationis & secundariam. Deinde exponuntur verba textus.
units.tr: Cap. 108. He now comes to treat this question: whether it was lawful for the Apostles to go to law over temporal goods. In the first two parts, therefore, it is recited and explained how the impugned party refutes the appellant's assertion on this matter. The appellant holds that they were not permitted to litigate in court, resting his case on three authorities of Holy Scripture, and showing how to contend in court, although it remains compatible with essential perfection, nevertheless diminishes the perfection of supererogation and that which is secondary. Then the words of the text are expounded.

units.la: Cap. 109 In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus reprobat assertionem appellantis, ostendendo q; auctoritates, in quibus se fundat, non probent intentu eius. In tertia parte oppositu ostenditur retorquendo in impugnatu varios errores: & ostendendo verba Christi de non contendendo in iudicio dicta esse ta perfectis, q; non perfectis: & tam habentib' ppria, q; non habentibus. Et quomodo aliud est esse perfectum, & esse in statu perfectionis. Et quomodo multiplex est perfectio: unde tres colliguntur perfectorum gradus. In quarta parte exponendo litteram declarant, quomodo dupliciter contingit transferre dominium donando. Et similiter quomodo mutuum dupliciter in scripturis sacris accipitur: & alia complura.
units.tr: Chapter 109. In the first two parts, he recites and explains how the impugned party rejects the appellant's assertion, showing also that the authorities on which the appellant relies do not prove his purpose. In the third part, in opposition, the impugner is refuted by turning back on him various errors. It is shown that the words of Christ about not contending in court were spoken to those who are perfect and to those who are not, to those who have property and to those who do not. It is also shown how it is one thing to be perfect and another to be in a state of perfection, and how perfection is manifold, so that three degrees of the perfect are gathered. In the fourth part, explaining the text, it is declared how the transfer of ownership by gift can happen in two ways, and similarly how a loan (mutuum) is taken in two ways in the holy Scriptures, and many other things.

units.la: Cap. 110. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat subsequentem particulam constitutionis, in qua impugnatus nititur ostendere, quod verba saepe dicta non erant Apostolis iniuncta: eo quod tunc cum ea verba Matth. 5. dicerentur, non essent adhuc Apostoli. In tertia parte declarando litteram & oppositum ostendendo multa subtiliter disseruntur de ordinatione Apostolorum, & de tempore ordinationis eorundem. Addituur notabile, q; saepe in scripturis prius gesta post narrantur: & econuerso.
units.tr: Chapter 110. In the first two parts, he recites and explains the following clause of the constitution, in which the impugned party seeks to show that the words often cited were not enjoined on the Apostles, because when the words of Matthew 5 were spoken they were not yet Apostles. In the third part, explaining the text and setting out the opposing view, many subtle points are discussed about the ordination of the Apostles and the time of their ordination. A notable point is added: that in Scripture things done earlier are often narrated later, and conversely.

units.la: Cap. 111. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus nititur probare, q; Apostolis licuit contra sibi iniuriantes & sua auferentes in iudicio contendere. In tertia parte improbat probationem eius, eo quod Apostolis nulla fuerunt ppria in communi vel speciali, p quib' cotendere possint. Ite declarant quomodo quis potest fratre suu fraternaliter corripere, & propter bonum commune denunciare ecclesiae extra iudicium. Et q; etiam Papa fraternaliter debeat corripi, maxime si in haeresim cadat. In quarta parte declarando verba constitutionis plura notanda inseruntur.
units.tr: Chapter 111. In the first two parts, he recites and explains how the impugned party seeks to prove that the Apostles were allowed to contend in court against those who wronged them and took away their goods. In the third part, he refutes this proof, because the Apostles had no property, either common or particular, by which they could contend. Also explained is how a man may rebuke his brother in a brotherly way and, for the common good, report him to the Church outside court; and that even the Pope should be rebuked in a brotherly way, especially if he falls into heresy. In the fourth part, explaining the words of the constitution, several points to be noted are introduced.

units.la: Cap. 112. Recitat & declarat probationem impugnati, qua nititur probare, quod praedicta verba Christi de non contendendo in iudicio fuerint omnibus dicta. Et hoc duabus auctoritatibus, Euangelii, scil. & Augustini. Quod impugnatores reprobant ex eo, quod contradicat dictis suis prioribus capitulo 109. Nouissime super litteram declaratur, quomodo dicta verba omnibus dicta fuerint, sed diuersimode: quia aliis sub praecepto, & aliis sub consilio &c.
units.tr: Chapter 112. He recites and explains the proof of the impugned party, by which he seeks to prove that the aforesaid words of Christ about not contending in court were spoken to all. He does this by two authorities, of the Gospel, namely, and of Augustine. The impugners reject this because it contradicts his earlier statements in chapter 109. Lastly, explaining the text, it is declared how the said words were spoken to all, but in different ways: to some under a precept, and to others under counsel, etc.

units.la: Cap. 113. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus probet appellantem male intellexisse verba Apostoli, 1. ad Cor. 6. Iam quidem delictum est in vobis, quia iudicia habetis, praedens illa verba esse dicta his, qui no abdicauerat rerum dominia. In tertia parte ostenditur impugnatores ea omnibus esse dicta, quauis Apostolus eam Epistolam ad Corinthios scribat. Quia qui virtute & bonos mores docent ad paucos scribentes, omnes docere volunt. Soluunt etiam rationes, quibus probatur, quod non semper sit peccatum litigare in iudicio. In quarta exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 113. In the first two parts, he recites and explains how the impugned party proves that the appellant misunderstood the words of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 6: Already there is indeed a fault among you, because you have lawsuits, holding that those words were spoken to those who had not renounced ownership of their goods. In the third part, it is shown that the impugners hold these words were spoken to all, although the Apostle wrote that Epistle to the Corinthians, because those who teach virtue and good morals to a few writers wish to teach everyone. They also resolve the arguments by which it is proved that it is not always a sin to go to law. In the fourth part, the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 114. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat mentem impugnati circa auctoritates praetactas, volentis quod verba Christi non semper seruanda sint in executione operis, sed in praeparatione animi. In tertia parte dicunt ipsum errare primum in hoc, quod dicit iudiftinctè illa praecepta Christi non esse seruanda in executione operis: Cum & praeceptorum & eorum quibus praecipiuntur magna sit differentia. Pro quo praemittunt octo notabilia. Primo quod habere diuitias & pro eis contendere potest esse sine peccato. Secundo quod eas abdicare propter Deum melius est & ad perfectionem spectat. Tertio quod eas non repetere litigando in iudicio melius & perfectius est quam repetere. Quarto quod huiusmodi repetitio raro fit sine peccato. Quinto quod in scripturis & praeceptis sanctorum etiam licita quandoq; prohibentur, vt magis bonum obtineatur. Sexto quod licitum est se astringere voto ad non faciendā, quę implicant ad peccatum. Et similiter ad non habenda, dum modo sine illis vita humana posset transfigi. Septimo, quod dicta Christi praecepta in monte diuersa sunt: quia alia affirmatiua, alia negatiua &c. Octauo quod ad perfectionem spectat aliquid velle fugere, eo quod ad peccatum implicat, quod in casu meritorum est suscipere, vt patet de prelaturis. Ex quibus concluditur, q praecepit Apostolis etiā in operis executione seruare pceptū de abdicatione dominii & no litigādo in iudicio: eo q ad peccatū implicant. Affirmatiua autē consilia nō semper in executione seruari debent, eo q non semper expediant. In quarta parte declarantur verba textus.
units.tr: Chapter 114. In the first two parts, he recites and explains the mind of the impugned party concerning the authorities mentioned above, holding that the words of Christ are not always to be kept in the execution of the work, but in the preparation of the mind. In the third part they say he errs first in this, that he says without distinction that those precepts of Christ are not to be kept in the execution of the work, since there is a great difference between precepts and those to whom they are addressed. For this they set out eight points to be noted. First, that to have riches and to contend for them can be without sin. Second, that to renounce them for God's sake is better and belongs to perfection. Third, that not to reclaim them by litigating in court is better and more perfect than to reclaim them. Fourth, that such reclaiming is rarely done without sin. Fifth, that in Scripture and in the precepts of the saints even things that are sometimes lawful are forbidden, so that a greater good may be obtained. Sixth, that it is lawful to bind oneself by vow not to do things that involve sin, and likewise not to have things, provided human life could be carried on without them. Seventh, that the sayings of Christ in the Sermon on the Mount are of different kinds, since some are affirmative and others negative, etc. Eighth, that it belongs to perfection to wish to flee something because it involves sin, which in the case of merits it is right to accept, as is clear in the case of prelacies. From these points it is concluded that Christ commanded the Apostles to keep, even in the execution of the work, the precept about renouncing ownership and not going to law in court, since these involve sin. But affirmative counsels ought not always to be kept in execution, since they are not always expedient. In the fourth part, the words of the text are explained.

units.la: Cap. 115. In duabus partibus recitat & declarat intellectum verborum Apostoli secundum impugnatum dicentem, quod non interdixerit Corinthiis simpliciter litigare & fugere quaecunq; litigia: sed duntaxat fraudulenta & iniuriosa, vel etiam iusta, sed coram infidelibus. In tertia parte impugnatores reprobant praedicta. Primo quia Apostolus interdixit eis omnes contentiones malas & iniquas, quae non semper fraudulentae aut iniuriosae sunt. Secundo quia etiam licita litigia Apostolus dissuasit. Unde multa vtilia in casu, eo quod ad peccatū implicant, passim in scriptura dissuadentur: similiter per quae maius bonum impeditur, vt matrimonium impediens virginitatem. In quarta parte declarando & notando verba textus, inquiruntur multa de peritia secularium rerum, quae ad Episcopum spectat.
units.tr: Chapter 115. In two parts, he recites and explains the meaning of the Apostle's words according to the impugned party, who says that the Apostle did not simply forbid the Corinthians to go to law and avoid all lawsuits, but only fraudulent and injurious ones, or even just ones, if they were brought before unbelievers. In the third part, the impugners reject these claims. First, because the Apostle forbade them all wicked and unjust contentions, which are not always fraudulent or injurious. Second, because the Apostle also dissuaded them from lawful lawsuits. Hence many things useful in a given case, since they involve sin, are everywhere dissuaded in Scripture; likewise those by which a greater good is hindered, as marriage hinders virginity. In the fourth part, explaining and noting the words of the text, many questions are examined about the skill in secular affairs that belongs to a bishop.

units.la: Cap. 116. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat repetitq; probationes impugnati, ad probandum verba Christi antedicta de praeparatione cordis non de executione operis esse intelligenda. In tertia parte inualidantur probationes eius, ostendendo quod solum de quibusdam consilijs affirmatiuis procedant. Ostenditur etiam, quomodo aliquid est licitū in vno & non in alio; Et quomodo multiplex est defensio. Et complura alia notatu digna. In quarta parte declaratur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 116. In the first two parts, he recites and explains, and repeats, the proofs of the impugned party, to prove that the aforesaid words of Christ are to be understood of the preparation of the heart and not of the execution of the work. In the third part, his proofs are invalidated, by showing that they hold only for certain affirmative counsels. It is also shown how something is lawful in one case and not in another, and how defence is manifold, and many other matters worth noting. In the fourth part, the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 117. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat sententiam propriam impugnati de praedicta materia dicentis, quod non habentibus propria non licuit pro aliquibus tanquam pro propriis litigare: sed qui habebant communia (quales iudicat Apostolos) licuit pro illis vt pro communibus litigare sine scandalo & fraude ex auctoritate curam habentis. In tertia parte contra praedicta duo probant. Primum est quod Apostolis non licuit pro rebus quibuscunq; tanquam pro suis litigare. Et ad hoc adducitur triplex ratio. Et soluitur instantia de Episcopis pro rebus suis sine peccato litigantibus. Secundum est quod Apostolis non licuit pro rebus temporalibus tanquam pro communibus litigare in iudicio. Ad quod probandum adducuntur quinq; rationes. Et soluitur obiectio de praelatis Ecclesiae &c. In quarta parte declarantur verba textus.
units.tr: Chapter 117. In the first two parts, he recites and explains the impugned party's own opinion on the aforesaid matter, saying that those who had no property of their own were not allowed to litigate on behalf of certain things as if they were their own; but those who had common goods (such as he judges the Apostles to have been) were allowed to litigate for those as common goods, without scandal or fraud, by the authority of the one who has care of them. In the third part, they prove two things against the aforesaid. The first is that the Apostles were not allowed to litigate for any things whatever as if they were their own. For this a threefold argument is brought forward. And the objection about bishops who litigate without sin for their own goods is resolved. The second is that the Apostles were not allowed to litigate in court for temporal goods as if they were common goods. To prove this, five arguments are adduced. And the objection about the prelates of the Church, etc., is resolved. In the fourth part, the words of the text are explained.

units.la: Cap. 118. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus conatur probare, quod pluribus religiosis licet pro communibus litigare. Imponit autem appellanti, quod asseruerit, quod nullis viris perfectis liceat vllo cunq; pro rebus communibus litigare. Ex quo sequeretur, omnes, qui bona cōmunia defendere tenentur, esse in statu damnationis. In tertia parte dicunt, quod impugnatus non procedat ad mentē appellantis. Qui nō dicit quibuscunq; perfectis prohibitum suis litigare: sed perfectissimis perfectione superogationis, quibus praeceptum est, omnium rerum abdicare dominium. Quales erant Apostoli, & non Minores. In quarta exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 118. In the first two parts, he recites and explains how the impugned party tries to prove that several religious may litigate for common goods. He charges the appellant with having asserted that no perfect men at all may litigate for common goods in any way. From this it would follow that all who are bound to defend common goods are in a state of damnation. In the third part, they say that the impugned party does not proceed according to the appellant's meaning. The appellant does not say that all the perfect are forbidden to litigate for their goods, but only the most perfect, by the perfection of supererogation, to whom it is commanded to renounce ownership of all things. Such were the Apostles, and not the lesser men. In the fourth part, the text is explained.

units.la: Cap. 119. In duabus primis partibus recitat & declarat, quomodo impugnatus probet per quinque auctoritates, quod Episcopis pro rebus Ecclesiarum suarum liceat litigare. In tertia concedunt impugnatores conclusionem, sed negant quod propterea Apostolis licuerit litigare in iudicio. Episcopi enim non tenent locum Apostolorum in omnibus, sed ab eorum summa perfectione deficiunt. Ideo licet Episcopis, vt minus perfectis, quae non licent Apostolis, vt patet de Episcopis Orientalibus vxore ducentibus, & de aliis quibuscunq; possessiones habetibus. In quarta exponitur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 119. In the first two parts he recites and declares how the one impugned proves, by five authorities, that it is lawful for bishops to go to law over the property of their churches. In the third part the impugners concede the conclusion, but deny that for this reason it was lawful for the Apostles to litigate in court. For bishops do not hold the place of the Apostles in all things, but fall short of their highest perfection. Therefore what the Apostles were not permitted, the bishops are allowed, as less perfect; as is evident concerning the Eastern bishops who take wives, and concerning all others who hold possessions. In the fourth part the letter is explained.

units.la: Tertia constitutionis capitula.
units.tr: The chapters of the third constitution.

units.la: Cap. 120. Accedit ad tertiam partem principalem. In cuius duabus primis partibus recitatur & declaratur, quomodo impugnatus conatur respondere ad obiectiones factas ab appellante contra constitutionem Quia quorundam. Unde primo dicit, quod appellans dictam constitutionem impugnare molitur: quia non ponit scientiam aliquo modo esse clauem Ecclesiae. In tertia parte dicunt impugnatores, quod obiectionem appellantis truncate recitet: nec pauca de huiusmodi clauie diseruntur, maxime ex declaratione Rabani. In quarta parte notatur litera.
units.tr: Chapter 120. He comes to the third principal part. In its first two parts it is recited and declared how the one impugned tries to answer the objections raised by the appellant against the constitution Quia quorundam. Hence first he says that the appellant sets out to attack that constitution, because he does not hold that knowledge is in any way the key of the Church. In the third part the impugners say that the appellant has recited the objection in truncated form, and much is discussed about this sort of key, especially from the explanation of Rabanus. In the fourth part a note is made on the letter.

units.la: Cap. 121.
